title: InfraTwin
pitch: InfraTwin lets engineers and WebMCP agents share one live network ChangePlan, using deterministic analysis and verified optimization to catch risky changes before production.
about_excerpt: InfraTwin lets engineers and WebMCP agents share one live network ChangePlan, using deterministic analysis and verified optimization to catch risky changes before production. Like Comment Story Updates Shared workspace: Engineer and WebMCP agent collaborate on the same live, browser-local ChangePlan before production. Remote failure: A planned outage plus 20% Payments growth exposes a remote Southeast–Central overload at 85% utilization. Human override: A human locks the proposed upgrade, invalidating the old mitigation and forcing the agent to replan. Verified design: 54 adaptive routing changes reduce modeled peak utilization from 85% to 67% with no new capacity or links. Scale validation: InfraTwin remains interactive on a 500-node, 1,200-link, 400-demand, 12-region network. Native WebMCP: document.modelContext exposes state-dependent WebMCP capabilities with provenance and optimizer diagnostics. Inspiration Network changes rarely fail in isolation. A maintenance outage in one region, expected traffic growth somewhere else, and a capacity restriction on another corridor can combine into a failure hundreds of miles away from the original change. That makes network change planning a coordination problem as much as a routing problem. Engineers have operational context that is difficult to encode completely in advance: a link may technically support an upgrade but be unavailable during a maintenance window, a corridor may be protected for business reasons, or an apparently cheap mitigation may conflict with another planned change. Traditional planning tools can model topology and run analyses, while AI assistants can explore ideas and explain results. The gap appears when the plan changes while the agent is reasoning. If the engineer selects a different resource, locks infrastructure, modifies traffic expectations, or invalidates an old proposal, the agent needs to operate on that exact new state rather than on a detached snapshot. InfraTwin started from a simple question: what if a network ChangePlan became a shared live artifact that an engineer and an agent could reason over together, while deterministic systems remained responsible for the engineering truth? The goal was not to build a chatbot attached to a topology viewer. It was to build an engineering workbench where human judgment, agent exploration, and machine-checkable computation each have a clear role. What InfraTwin does InfraTwin is a browser-native network change-planning, resilience, and optimization workbench. Engineers can model maintenance outages, restorations, traffic growth, individual demand changes, capacity upgrades, budgets, target utilization, and infrastructure that must not be modified, then analyze the consequences before those changes reach production. The underlying network remains separate from the editable ChangePlan . Proposed changes are therefore reversible and inspectable rather than silently modifying the canonical model. Analysis and optimization operate on the derived planned state while preserving provenance back to the original network and the human or agent action that created each change. The flagship workflow demonstrates one continuous human-agent decision loop. An engineer schedules a Northeast-to-Central backbone link for maintenance. A WebMCP agent sees that exact live plan and adds the expected 20% growth in Payments traffic. InfraTwin runs deterministic routing and capacity analysis and discovers that the combined change creates an overload on a different Southeast-to-Central corridor, reaching 85% utilization against an 80% target. The agent asks InfraTwin for the cheapest modeled mitigation and initially receives a capacity-oriented proposal. The engineer then supplies information the optimizer did not previously have: that corridor cannot be modified during this change window. The engineer locks it directly in the shared workspace. That edit immediately changes the valid design space. The old proposal becomes stale rather than remaining silently actionable, and the agent can no longer continue as if the earlier assumptions still held. The agent replans under the new human constraint. With adaptive routing enabled, InfraTwin finds a different design that changes 54 routing allocations, reduces modeled peak utilization from 85% to 67%, and requires no new capacity or new links. The proposal is not labeled safe or verified simply because an optimizer returned it. InfraTwin reconstructs the proposed design and checks its routing, demand conservation, capacity, utilization, restrictions, locks, budget, objective, scenario identity, and other declared constraints before it can receive a VERIFIED state. This division of responsibility is intentional: The human provides intent, operational knowledge, constraints, and approval. The agent explores the decision space and revises alternatives. InfraTwin supplies the deterministic evidence connecting them. Why WebMCP? WebMCP is central to InfraTwin rather than an alternate transport layer for backend APIs. The network and its unsaved ChangePlan exist inside the live browser workspace. Through native WebMCP capabilities, the agent can inspect the same current selection, plan state, human restrictions, analysis evidence, proposals, and verification freshness that the engineer is working with. That shared state matters because engineering intent changes continuously during planning. A conventional integration can give an agent a serialized representation of an application and expose operations over it, but synchronization becomes another problem to manage. The human may have selected a different link, edited a constraint, invalidated a proposal, or changed the current plan after the agent began reasoning. InfraTwin instead treats the browser workspace itself as the collaboration surface. When the engineer adds a lock, the agent sees the new restriction through the same application state. When a plan edit makes an earlier analysis obsolete, that evidence becomes stale. When the semantic state no longer supports a capability, InfraTwin can revoke that capability rather than leaving an invalid action available and hoping the model decides not to use it. That is one of the most important ideas behind the project: mathematical and product preconditions can become capability preconditions. For example, violation-specific tools only become useful when current analysis contains a violation. Proposal actions require a current proposal. Human edits can invalidate previously valid proposal actions. Long-running operations are also bound to the semantic revision they started from so that a result computed against an obsolete plan cannot later publish itself as authoritative. This creates a much stronger human-agent interaction than simply giving an agent buttons to press. The engineer can change the problem while the agent is working, and the agent continues inside the human's new decision boundary. What people and agents can do together InfraTwin is designed around complementary strengths rather than attempting to automate the engineer out of the loop. Humans are good at supplying context that may not exist in the mathematical model: which maintenance work is politically or operationally possible, which infrastructure must remain untouched, which services matter most, and whether a proposed tradeoff is acceptable. Agents are useful for exploring a large decision space, connecting evidence across views, requesting analyses, proposing mitigations, and quickly revisiting alternatives when assumptions change. The deterministic engine handles the part neither should improvise: routing, capacity calculations, resilience analysis, optimization, and verification. That means a workflow can evolve naturally: An engineer expresses intent. The agent explores the consequences. InfraTwin produces evidence. The engineer adds a constraint. The old answer becomes invalid. The agent replans. InfraTwin verifies the new proposal. The engineer retains final approval. Before WebMCP, implementing that interaction cleanly would typically require synchronizing human UI state with a separate agent-side representation or building a parallel backend state model. InfraTwin instead lets both participants operate through the same browser-local artifact. Evidence, not model guesses InfraTwin deliberately separates agent reasoning from engineering computation . The language model can inspect state, explain evidence, add or revise plan changes, request analysis, investigate violations, and explore mitigation alternatives. It does not calculate network feasibility by generating prose. InfraTwin's deterministic engine performs single-shortest-path and ECMP routing, utilization and capacity analysis, bottleneck and min-cut analysis, bounded N-1 contingency evaluation, and solver-backed optimization. Adaptive network design uses deterministic candidate paths and HiGHS LP/MILP optimization. Candidate routes are bounded and reproducibly gen

title: Interleave
pitch: Catch delayed agent actions before they overwrite a person's work.
about_excerpt: Catch delayed agent actions before they overwrite a person's work. Like Comment Story Updates The Plane workbench reproduces a stale agent write and shows the exact rule, expected value, and actual value. Inspiration WebMCP lets an agent take useful actions inside a website. But the person does not stop using the app while the agent works. That creates a quiet and dangerous race: an agent reads the current state and starts a slow task. The person makes a newer change. The delayed agent action then finishes with old information and overwrites the person's work. Every request can still report success, so normal logs may never explain what went wrong. We built Interleave to catch that moment, explain it clearly, and turn it into a test that prevents the same bug from returning. What it does Interleave records one shared session across the agent, the person, and the application. It captures the pending tool call, meaningful human edits, state revisions, and the final write on one ordered timeline. When a rule is broken, Interleave shows: the exact product rule that failed; what the final value should have been; what value was actually written; which state revision the agent started from; and which newer revision existed when the delayed work finished. The developer can then replay the same recording, compare the current behavior with a proposed fix, remove every unnecessary step, and export a deterministic regression test. Our flagship demo uses public issue makeplane/plane#9674. Plane queues a metadata crawler. A person saves a newer title while that crawler is waiting. The delayed worker later writes an older title over the human edit. Interleave witnesses the overwrite, reduces it to three required actions, and replays the same recording against a revision guard that preserves the person's work. The workbench also includes reservation and TodoMVC adapters to show that the recorder is reusable across different application models. Why WebMCP is essential Interleave is built around a real WebMCP interaction, not a chatbot wrapped around a dashboard. The Plane demo exposes nine native tools while idle. The agent can read the incident, start the delayed update, replay a recording, compare implementations, reduce a failure, and export proof. While the crawler is pending, the tool surface changes to five controls that match the application's live state: read, save newer metadata, hold, complete, or cancel. The slow tool returns a real pending promise. While that promise is unresolved, the person can keep using the visible application. That shared moment is the core experience: WebMCP gives the agent a clear semantic action, while Interleave observes how that action interleaves with human work. We use document.modelContext.registerTool directly. There is no WebMCP polyfill and no reconstructed agent transcript. Tools have clear names, input descriptions, state-aware availability, AbortSignal cleanup, and compact evidence receipts. Large recordings, tests, and patches stay behind explicit downloads instead of filling the agent's context. A better experience for people and agents Without Interleave, a person can watch a correct edit disappear and have no explanation. With Interleave, the app can show exactly which delayed action caused the loss, what should have happened, and whether a guard fixes it. This also changes what developers can do. A hard-to-reproduce session becomes a small, repeatable test. A person can continue working while an agent performs a slow task, and both can verify that the latest human intent survived. How we built it The application uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and native WebMCP. The reusable @interleave/recorder package has no runtime dependencies and no React dependency. Each integration supplies four things: a focused state reader, meaningful human actions, a correctness rule, and replay behavior. The recorder handles calls, results, errors, cancellation, timestamps, before-and-after state, immutable snapshots, redaction hooks, interruption, and bounded history. The Plane integration is pinned to public commit da1a7ab. We traced the issue from the API handler to the queued worker, built a deterministic local model, prepared a compare-and-set patch, and added focused worker and endpoint contract tests. The fixture never contacts a live Plane deployment or user data. Challenges we ran into Keeping the race real An animated log would look convincing but prove very little. We had to keep one actual tool promise pending while a real human edit changed the same state, then record the delayed completion at the correct checkpoint. Changing tools without cancelling the active call The available WebMCP tools need to change while work is pending. Re-registering too early can clean up and abort the call being recorded. Interleave waits for the active call to settle before replacing the tool surface. Recording meaning instead of noise Raw DOM mutation streams are large and fragile. Interleave records semantic actions such as edit_metadata and add_todo, so the person's intent survives in the evidence even when the stale write erases it from the screen. Reducing an asynchronous failure Reduction must rerun each candidate against fresh state. Interleave removes one command at a time and keeps it removed only when the same rule still fails. Accomplishments we are proud of A complete native WebMCP acceptance run in the browser: dispatch, real human click, delayed overwrite, replay, comparison, reduction, and export. A three-command minimal reproduction for a documented open-source bug. A proposed Plane patch with all 37 tests passing in the two affected upstream modules, including 13 new cases. A 50-test Interleave release gate covering the recorder, all three adapters, replay, reduction, exports, and the state-aware WebMCP surface. A dependency-free recorder package that another WebMCP application can install and adapt. What we learned WebMCP can be more than a way for agents to click fewer buttons. It gives web applications a structured boundary where agent intent, human intent, and application state can be observed together. We also learned that correctness rules must stay close to the product. Interleave provides the recording and proof system, while each application defines what must be preserved. What is next for Interleave Next we want to publish the recorder to npm, add adapters for editors and collaborative work tools, connect recordings to CI, and make browser-level regressions exportable to more test runners. We also want to take the Plane patch through upstream review and use that process to improve Interleave's contribution workflow. Built With concurrency css next.js node.js openai react sites tailwind testing typescript vercel vinext webmcp Try it out interleave-iota.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Built Interleave end to end: product design, native WebMCP tools, the reusable session recorder, three application adapters, Plane source analysis and patch, testing, deployment, and the demo film. title: Jig
pitch: A pattern that reads perfectly can still be impossible to knit. So Jig lets an agent size, chart and re-yarn a whole pattern with you, and refuses any number that will not knit.
about_excerpt: A pattern that reads perfectly can still be impossible to knit. So Jig lets an agent size, chart and re-yarn a whole pattern with you, and refuses any number that will not knit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration My family's business is yarn. I grew up around patterns covered in red pen, and around customers coming back into the shop a week after buying wool to say the numbers did not work. That is the part people outside the craft do not expect. A knitting pattern can read perfectly and still be impossible to knit. The numbers all have to agree with each other. A cast on has to be a multiple of the stitch repeat plus the edge stitches. A raglan yoke can only reach a target count in whole rounds of eight increases. Shaping has to land on whole rows. Every measurement has to grow as the sizes grow. Break one of those and the pattern still reads like English, prints fine, sells fine, and then fails on somebody's needles after they have paid for the yarn and knitted half a sleeve. Designers do this work in spreadsheets today. A spreadsheet will happily give you a cast on of 87 stitches, because 87 is a number like any other. That is why tech editing is a paid profession and why publishers keep permanent errata pages. So when I read the WebMCP spec, the thing that jumped out was not that an agent could fill in my form faster. It was that the page could say no, and say why. I built Jig for myself first, and I have been grading real patterns in it since. What it does Jig is a knitting design workbench that a person and an agent use at the same time, on the same live document. Ask it for a cast on of 87 stitches on a twelve stitch cable panel. It refuses, names the rule in knitter language, gives back the offending value, and gives back 86 and 98 as the nearest counts that actually fit. The agent reads that one sentence and corrects itself, without ever being told what the repeat was. On the human side those same numbers become one click fixes in the size table. Past that, the agent can do the whole job: read the pattern, read the chart as structured rows rather than a picture, set gauge, grade a full run of sizes while you keep typing into it, swap yarn against a second website and get the answer back in whole skeins, run a tech editing audit, and export. Every call, refusal and correction lands in a transcript in plain English, with whether a person or an agent did it. Why WebMCP fits this use case Three reasons, and all three are about the constraint living in the page instead of behind a server. The rules can refuse. A tool call here is a proposal, not a command. A wrong number comes back with the rule it broke and the nearest values that satisfy it, so the caller never has to work out the arithmetic. It reads one sentence and tries again. That loop is only cheap when the rules sit next to the caller. The rules cannot be bypassed. A person typing, an agent calling a tool, a declarative form submission and the page auditing itself all enter the same propose function. The committed document type carries a private symbol brand, so building one any other way is a compile error. The document is shared rather than handed over. The designer keeps editing while a grading run is in flight, and the run picks up the edit for every size it has not reached yet. There is no session to own and nothing to merge afterwards. What people and agents can do together here that was hard before Correct a refused instruction without ever being told the rule. Ask for 87 and say nothing else. The refusal carries the rule, the offending value, and 86 and 98. A correct second call can only have come from reading that refusal, because the prompt never mentioned the repeat. That is measured against a real browser, not asserted. Edit a number while an agent's grading run is still running. The run reads through a thunk rather than a snapshot, so every size it has not computed yet picks up your keystroke, and neither of you has to wait for the other. Swap yarn across two websites and get a whole skein answer. Change yarn and gauge changes, so yardage per square inch changes, while the new skein has its own length. Two variables at once, which is the classic way to get this wrong. To the agent it is one verb. Underneath it resolves tools on the other origin, invokes them, quarantines every string that crosses the boundary, revalidates through the same gate, and answers in whole skeins per size. Watch the whole negotiation in plain English. Every call, refusal, correction and human edit becomes a sentence in the transcript with its author, so the person is never guessing what the agent just did. How I built it Two real origins, both deployed on Cloudflare Pages. The workbench, and a separate yarn shop site that lends three read only tools to the workbench and to nobody else. The workbench also runs one Pages Function so the model key stays server side and a visitor never needs an API key. Fourteen tools, and deliberately every registration path the spec offers rather than the same one fourteen times: a React hook for the main verbs, raw registration with an AbortSignal for the two tools that only exist while a chart panel is selected, raw registration with exposedTo for the tool named to another origin, and one declarative HTML form that becomes a tool with no registration code at all. The rules live in a pure engine package that cannot import React, the DOM or WebMCP, enforced by a custom lint rule. Every write from every author goes through one propose function, and the committed document type carries a private symbol brand, so building one outside the engine is a compile error rather than a code review note. Sixteen formal correctness properties run over generated inputs with fast-check, including one that proves every repair offered is itself accepted and one that proves no valid value sits between the refused number and the repair. 1,641 tests across 108 files. It also works in a browser with no flag enabled, because a polyfill host stands in and reproduces the real behaviour, refusals included. Challenges I ran into The ones that mattered all came from driving a real browser instead of trusting a test double, and every one of them is now pinned by a test that fails if the fix comes out. An AbortSignal only withdraws a tool when it is the second argument to registerTool . Put it on the descriptor and Chrome accepts it and silently ignores it. executeTool will not take a tool name, it wants the tool object from getTools . Arguments have to be a JSON string, and an object gets rejected. And a refusal's first text part has to stand alone, because some hosts collapse the whole structured result down to content[0].text , so the rule and the repairs have to be in that first part or a model reading only that part gets nothing it can act on. All four of those live in one resolver now, and my fake host reproduces the browser exactly, so a finding cannot quietly regress. My favourite catch was the smallest one. A tool description named an example panel id that did not match the seeded document, which is invisible to every unit test in the suite and obvious the moment a real model follows the description. So now a test walks every panel name any schema mentions and checks it resolves against the real document. One small thing that made a large difference: the field parameter is a closed enum rather than a free string, because a model asked to change a cast on reaches for castOnCount first, which does not exist. Naming the options in the contract removed a whole class of failed first attempts. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The refusal is the product, and it holds up under a machine. npm run verify:browser launches a real browser against the live site, drives document.modelContext with no model and no API key, and proves the loop end to end: 87 refused, the repair parsed out of the first text part alone with zero knowledge of the document, sent back, accepted, and held. Eleven checks, eleven passed. The agent eval suite scores 4 of 4 with a real model choosing real tools. I am also proud that text arriving from the other origin is wrapped in a type with no string member, so interpolating a stranger's comment into a prompt is a compile error. The demo carries a real prompt injection in a community note. The scanner flags it, the broker declines it, and the declined instruction gets written into the transcript where a person can see somebody tried. What I learned That a tool result is a piece of writing. The difference between "rejected" and "here is the rule, here is your value, here are the two that fit" is the difference between an agent giving up and an agent finishing the job, and it is one sentence of prose in a JSON field. That a draft API has to be measured, not read. The four behaviours that shaped this build the most were ones the spec does not describe, and the only way to find them was to open a browser and watch. And that constraints belong in the page. Th

title: LASSO — Draw What Your Agent Can Touch
pitch: An AI-assisted dispatch console where a human draws what an agent may understand and change. WebMCP turns that visual scope into a live, typed capability contract.
about_excerpt: An AI-assisted dispatch console where a human draws what an agent may understand and change. WebMCP turns that visual scope into a live, typed capability contract. Like Comment Story Updates LASSO — Draw What Your Agent Can Touch | WebMCP Challenge 2026 Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of acting inside increasingly complex web applications. But there is still an awkward question: How does a human communicate exactly what the agent is allowed to understand and change? In visual applications such as dispatch maps, dashboards, CAD tools, scheduling boards, and other canvases, the relevant context is often obvious to a human. We can simply point at it. Explaining the same boundary to an agent usually means naming objects manually, writing long instructions, building application-specific permission systems, or trusting the agent to infer intent from the interface. LASSO explores a different interaction model: The human interface generates the agent interface. A dispatcher draws a boundary around the resources the agent may work with. WebMCP turns that transient visual selection into a live, typed capability contract for the visiting agent. The map is the prompt. The boundary is the permission. What it does LASSO is an AI-assisted dispatch console built around a seeded disruption scenario with six late deliveries. The dispatcher draws a freehand lasso around the deliveries and drivers the AI agent may reason about. That gesture does much more than highlight the map. LASSO compiles the selected UI state into revision-specific WebMCP tools whose JSON Schemas contain only the resources inside the human-defined boundary. The external agent then: Inspects the scoped operational state. Authors its own recovery plan. Submits the plan to LASSO for deterministic validation. Receives structured violations if the plan breaks capacity, vehicle, timing, overtime, or scope constraints. May request additional resources outside its current authority. Cannot grant that additional authority to itself. Repairs its plan after the human approves a scope expansion. Can modify live routes only after the human authorizes one exact verified plan. In the demo scenario, the agent discovers that delivery D15 requires refrigerated capacity that is unavailable inside its original scope. It asks for Mika, a suitable driver outside the boundary. The human chooses whether to include Mika. That single UI action invalidates the previous WebMCP contract and compiles a new revision in which Mika becomes available to the agent. The repaired plan reduces six late deliveries to one with three route changes and zero overtime. Only then can the dispatcher authorize execution. The resulting write capability is bound to the exact plan, current scope, workspace generation, and a single expiring use. Stale or replayed authority is rejected. Why WebMCP LASSO is not an optimizer with a tool wrapper. The agent authors the plan . LASSO provides the scoped world model, deterministic validation, authority negotiation, and execution boundary. The central WebMCP idea is that the tool surface itself changes as the human manipulates the live application. A visual gesture becomes structured machine-readable context. When the human changes the lasso, the agent's available resource IDs and capability contract change with it. Traditional browser automation can see a highlighted region, but it still has to infer what that highlight means and whether it represents authority. A conventional remote API or MCP server would require additional synchronization to know what the human just selected in the browser. With WebMCP, the page itself can expose that ephemeral application state directly to the visiting agent. How we built it LASSO is a lightweight, dependency-free web application built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG, JSON Schema, and the imperative WebMCP API. The architecture separates four responsibilities: Human UI — visual scope, operational constraints, authority decisions Scope compiler — converts UI state into revision-specific WebMCP contracts External agent — creates and repairs recovery plans Policy engine — validates and safely applies scoped state changes The application also includes deterministic browser, security, adversarial, package, and performance validation. The final local release campaign includes more than 150 correctness and security invariants plus a 5,000-case adversarial fuzz campaign. Challenges The hardest problem was not drawing a lasso. It was making the boundary meaningful. We had to ensure that: changing scope invalidates stale capabilities; an agent cannot expand its own authority; outside-scope assignments remain untouched; a delivery can never silently acquire multiple owners; application handlers validate authority independently of JSON Schema; partially registered WebMCP contracts fail closed; in-flight tool calls are not broken by contract recompilation; an authorized plan cannot be changed and replayed later. Several of these issues only appeared during adversarial testing and required changes to the underlying state-transition model rather than cosmetic fixes. What we learned WebMCP becomes especially interesting when tools are not static API endpoints. A web application's live human state can itself determine what capabilities an agent discovers. That creates a new interaction loop: human gesture → typed capability → agent reasoning → authority request → human decision → new capability The conversation between human and agent does not have to happen entirely in a chat box. The web interface itself can participate. What's next Dispatch is the demonstration, not the limit. The same interaction pattern could apply anywhere humans naturally identify context spatially: operations dashboards analytics CAD and design tools scheduling systems infrastructure maps logistics spreadsheets and visual workspaces The long-term idea is simple: Point at the context. Let the web turn that gesture into an agent contract. Built With actions apis chromium content css3 github html5 javascript json node.js schema security svg web webmcp Try it out smkzz.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I led the product direction, system design, acceptance criteria, testing strategy, and final release decisions. ChatGPT and Codex assisted heavily with implementation, debugging, security testing, documentation, and video production. I reviewed and challenged each iteration, performed the human parts of the native WebMCP workflow, and owned the final product and submission decisions. title: Threshold
pitch: One web page where several independent care organisations answer a person's AI assistant at the same time, and compose a single plan between them.
about_excerpt: One web page where several independent care organisations answer a person's AI assistant at the same time, and compose a single plan between them. Like Comment Story Updates Threshold Threshold is one web page where several independent care organisations answer a person's AI assistant at the same time, and compose a single plan between them. The person tells their story once, to the assistant they already trust, and no organisation receives anything identifying until the person presses Send. It is eleven at night. A carer has just been told she needs surgery on Thursday morning. Her mother has dementia and cannot be left alone. Arranging cover means three things at once: a respite bed, a wheelchair-accessible journey to it, and someone at the house until the transport arrives. Three organisations. Three phone calls that cannot be made at this hour, and each one depends on the answers to the other two. Her assistant asks Threshold once. Three organisations answer at the same moment. And the obvious combination comes back infeasible on exactly one link: arrival_before_admission required 06:40 offered 07:10 go back to: Northgate Accessible Transport The bed admits until 06:40. The earliest that van arrives is 07:10. Neither organisation can see the other, so neither can know. Threshold does. It names the failing link, names the one organisation to return to, a different van closes the plan, and the carer keeps a printable copy. That failing link is the whole product. The problem is fragmentation, and it is expensive £24.1 billion of income-related support goes unclaimed in Great Britain every year. 7.5 million people miss at least one benefit, an average of £3,203 each. (Policy in Practice, 2025/26.) Complexity and fragmentation are two of the named causes. "No Wrong Door" has been United States federal policy for two decades: whichever door a person knocks on first should get them to the right help, with agencies keeping their own services while sharing one way in. It has never been architecture, because it asks every agency to integrate with a central system, and they never do. WebMCP's exposedTo and allow="tools" make it architecture. The page is the way in. The agencies stay exactly where they are. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Threshold is several organisations, on separate origins, with separate databases, serving one person who never had to repeat themselves, with the person's private context staying inside their own assistant the entire time. The concept exists only because WebMCP exists. A browser-side broker that discovers and calls tools across origins is the one thing that turns three unconnected websites into one coordinated answer, with no shared backend and no data-sharing agreement between them. What people and their agents can do together that was impossible before Ask whether several offers, held at organisations that cannot see each other, satisfy each other. A federated search returns three independent answers, and one vendor with three product lines could serve that just as well. Composition is a different question. check_plan takes offers from three origins and asks whether the transport arrives before the bed stops admitting, whether there is a hoist at both ends of the journey, whether overnight cover lasts until collection. It returns the failing link and the organisation to renegotiate with. There is no non-federated way to build that, because the parts live at parties who will never share a database. Holding a scarce bed at machine speed When assistants act at machine speed against scarce humanitarian resources, two assistants will send two people to the same last bed. Threshold treats a hold as a first-class thing, with a timer and a release. It leases each part of a plan, one organisation at a time, scarcest first, and the organisation itself stays the authority on whether it holds. There is no shared transaction across these independent websites, so if any leg is refused, every lease already taken is released before the call returns. Nothing is ever left booked against a plan that cannot happen. Safety, by construction A malicious listing aimed at a person in crisis is a real risk. Threshold never carries provider-authored text into the assistant's context. Every field an organisation can return is an enum, a boolean, an integer, or a string under a pattern. An instruction to a model does not fit inside ^[A-Z]{1,3}[0-9]{1,4}$ , and it does not fit inside an enum. A test walks every provider contract and proves there is no free-text field for an instruction to hide in. Every capability claim is labelled by its source. A better experience for the person The person does one thing: she reads a plain-language panel and presses Send. The consent gate names the one organisation that will receive the referral, the exact four fields it will receive, and how long they may keep them. A host assistant can already ask for confirmation. What a page can do that a host dialog cannot is show the person the payload and let her change it , correcting the phone number before it leaves. make_referral returns a Promise that resolves on that press. Until then, nothing identifying has crossed an origin, and a boundary log on the page shows exactly what has, field names only. How I implemented WebMCP Each organisation publishes four tools with registerTool and exposedTo , scoped to Threshold's origin alone. Never a wildcard. The hub embeds each provider in an iframe that delegates the tools permission with allow="tools" , discovers their tools with getTools({ fromOrigins }) , and calls them with executeTool , passing arguments as a JSON string and treating a null return (a navigation) as a contract violation rather than an empty success. The hub exposes nine tools to the person's assistant, and the tool surface is a state machine. place_plan_holds does not exist until check_plan returns feasible, and make_referral does not exist until a lease does. An assistant cannot call a step out of order, because the step is not in its list. ontoolchange is how the hub learns a provider has withdrawn. Every provider result passes a typed firewall: parse, validate against a strict JSON Schema, project to the hub's own shape. A rejected payload never reaches a return value, a log line, or an error message. 176 unit and integration tests, 15 browser tests, real WebMCP federation verified in Chrome, and again as four containers on four origins. If a browser cannot do cross-origin WebMCP, the same providers on the same origins are reached over a typed postMessage protocol with the same schemas, the same firewall, the same leases and the same gate, and the page states in words which path it used. Threshold. Several organisations. One plan. One page. title: Vouchsafe
pitch: The letting agent gets an answer, not your life. Your facts stay in your browser; a WebMCP question comes back as one word. Withdraw it, and the tool stops existing on their side mid-conversation.
about_excerpt: The letting agent gets an answer, not your life. Your facts stay in your browser; a WebMCP question comes back as one word. Withdraw it, and the tool stops existing on their side mid-conversation. Like Comment Story Updates The problem To rent a flat in Britain you upload your payslips, your bank statements and your passport to six letting agents. Every one of them keeps a copy, forever. None of them wanted your salary. They wanted one answer: does your income cover three times the rent, yes or no. That gap between what is asked for and what is needed is the whole product. What Vouchsafe is Two origins. Your file lives on one; a letting agency lives on the other. Your facts never leave your browser. The agency asks a question through WebMCP and gets one word back. The interesting part is what happens when you change your mind. Withdraw a permission and the tool is not disabled on the agency's side, it is deregistered . Authority here is not a permission check. It is whether the tool exists. A withheld permission is not a guarded tool that refuses; there is no tool, so it cannot be called, guessed at, or talked into existence by anything written into a page or a prompt. How it is built Vanilla ES modules. No build step, no framework, no runtime dependencies, and zero third-party requests from either origin, which is enforced by a test rather than asserted in a README. The cross-origin round trip is the part we could not find anyone else doing in full: Your file registers each allowed question with exposedTo naming the agency's origin. The agency calls getTools({fromOrigins}) and discovers them. It re-registers each discovered tool as a local tool, so an agent sees one flat toolset and never has to know two websites were involved. On toolchange , it diffs and tears down proxies for anything that has stopped being offered. Step 3 and step 4 are what make revocation land mid-conversation. Things we found out about Chrome's implementation We wrote these down with reproduction steps because we could not find them documented anywhere. getTools() hands back inputSchema as a JSON string , but registerTool() demands an object . Re-registering a discovered tool fails silently until you parse it. getTools({fromOrigins}) also returns your own tools, so a naive proxy loop registers proxies for its own proxies. A cross-origin iframe's tools do not appear in the host's plain getTools() . You have to ask for them by origin. Federation is scoped to the frame tree, not the browser. toolchange fires once per registration, not once per batch, so a nine permission grant is nine events and the handler has to be idempotent. Revocation crosses the origin boundary with no channel of our own. The browser does it. The declarative form API derives the schema from the form's own inputs. We get sixteen parameters for free, and omitting toolautosubmit parks the call for a human, which is a consent gate written in HTML. The hard part, and the honest limit A yes-or-no predicate leaks more than one bit if the caller picks the threshold. Ask "is income at least 3x £2000", then £1500, then £1300, and five calls have bracketed a salary to a £3,600 window. Every individual answer is legitimate. The sequence is a salary disclosure wearing a predicate's clothes. So your file tracks the bracket each origin has established, prices what has been learned in bits, and stops answering once the remaining uncertainty falls below a floor. In the demo you watch five numbers get answered and the sixth refused. We are not claiming this is leak-proof. A patient caller spread across sessions, or several origins pooling answers, defeats a per-origin window. Adding noise would bound it properly and would also make an affordability check occasionally wrong, which is not a trade a letting decision can absorb. This is the cheap honest version, and it says so in the code. What we learned about testing this Playwright was the wrong tool and we can say exactly why: its launcher appends its own --enable-features flag after ours, so WebMCP is silently dropped and the API is simply absent. We drive Chrome and Brave over the DevTools Protocol directly instead, and the same suite runs against both. Two bugs worth confessing. Two new modules were written and never deployed, so a 404 killed the whole module graph and both live pages rendered blank while 108 tests passed, because every one of them ran against a local server where the files existed. And an announcer banner marked hidden painted on every page load anyway, because display: grid on the element beats the user agent's display: none for [hidden] . Both now have tests. 118 tests: 66 unit, 52 in a real browser. Verify it yourself Do not take any of this on trust. /proof.html reads the browser's own tool registry on both origins and redraws on toolchange . It registers nothing itself, which is what makes it a witness rather than a participant. Toggle a permission and watch a tool stop existing. Ask to flag them and the call suspends inside the page until she decides; decline and the agent gets declined_by_human , nothing written. Reclassify a field. The fingerprint no longer matches and the tool leaves getTools() — gone from the list, not refused when called — until a person re-approves it. The whole argument, in five numbers Entries in this challenge describing runtime tool creation, counted generously 116 of 868 …in which a non-developer doing their own job decides the tool's shape 3 Identifiers reaching a tool result, against 1552 with the policy layer deleted 0 An agent never told the tool exists reaches for it on the question it was made for 21 of 24 Assertions behind that, offline and against the deployed site 80 + 21 + 13 + 10 The first two say what is new here. Not runtime tool creation — between 19 (a narrow pattern), 62 (an outside reading) and 116 (widened until it hurts) other entries describe that, and webmcp-evaluator/field_position.py ships with all 868 pages so you can re-run the count and watch it get worse for us. What stays rare is who decides the shape . All 116 were read one at a time, without knowing which row was this project: in the great majority a developer decides the shape in code or config, and the rest divide between a model writing it, an imported OpenAPI or marketplace document, and a shape compiled out of the page's own DOM. In 3 the person doing their own job decides it. title: WebMCP Computer
pitch: An operating system that lives inside the browser, with WebMCP as its native control layer. A full computer built for agents as first-class citizens.
about_excerpt: An operating system that lives inside the browser, with WebMCP as its native control layer. A full computer built for agents as first-class citizens. Like 3 Comment Story Updates One machine, two users: WebMCP Computer Press any key—or call any tool—to wake the machine A real remote Browser, live Tool Monitor, Terminal, and agent-made app—one desktop A computer built for agents as first-class citizens. Instead of imitating humans with screenshots, mouse coordinates, and typing, agents control the machine directly through WebMCP - while the human watches and intervenes through the same desktop. Inspiration We wanted to see what a computer would look like if agents didn’t have to use it like humans. Instead of looking at screenshots, moving a mouse, and typing into interfaces, the agent gets direct access to the computer through WebMCP. Files, apps, windows, processes, settings, and the terminal are all tools it can call. The whole thing runs inside one browser tab. You see the same desktop as the agent, watch what it’s doing, and can take over at any point. Run agent-generated code without giving the agent access to your computer. Watch what it does and jump in whenever you want. The demo in 30 seconds Ask the agent to create a small website. Watch Files, Terminal, and Preview update in real time. The new page registers its own site_* tools. The agent calls those tools through the computer that created the page. That is WebMCP inside WebMCP : tools appear when an app opens or a page is served, then disappear cleanly when it closes. Why WebMCP WebMCP gives a page a structured way to describe what an agent can do: named tools, JSON schemas, descriptions, and safety annotations. WebMCP Computer treats that surface like a syscall table. Instead of exposing one form, it exposes the operating system— app_open , fs_write , term_exec , window_move , settings_set , ps , kill , and dozens more. For normal computer operations, the agent needs no screenshot and no coordinate. Every action is typed, bounded, and visible. What humans and agents can do together Build in a fresh machine. Edit files, run shell commands, serve a folder, and preview the result without touching the host computer. Share one live workspace. Human and agent use the same files, windows, processes, and terminal. See every action. An agent cursor moves to the affected window, activity toasts name the verb, terminal rows are tinted, and Tool Monitor records the call. Operate the real web. The Browser app drives a shared remote Chrome and can discover and call another site's WebMCP tools. Opt into real Linux. The cloud kernel adds a temporary container with Git, Node.js, and Python, streaming command output into the visible Terminal. Publish from the machine. An agent can publish a text-only site and hand the human a public URL and QR code. How we built it WebMCP layer: @nekuda/webmcp-sdk , with strict schemas and ask/act/transact annotations. Kernel: a pure-TypeScript Zustand store for processes, windows, settings, and the shared event stream. Local shell: just-bash with core utilities, awk , and jq ; network and language runtimes stay in the opt-in cloud container. Filesystem: ZenFS on OPFS with reload-safe session restore. Preview: a virtual in-tab server that runs pages in opaque sandboxed frames and bridges their dynamic tools to the host registry. Browser and cloud: capability-scoped Cloudflare Workers for remote Chrome, temporary Linux workspaces, and publishing. The UI is React 18, Vite, strict TypeScript, and hand-written CSS—no UI kit. The current build is covered by 339 unit tests and 27 native-Chrome end-to-end tests . title: webmcp-foundry
pitch: WebMCP Foundry turns web-app actions into minimized, tested, authority-governed agent tools—and automatically withdraws them when their evidence becomes stale.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Foundry turns web-app actions into minimized, tested, authority-governed agent tools—and automatically withdraws them when their evidence becomes stale. Like Comment Story Updates GIF Code changed → evidence stale → WebMCP tool withdrawn. Foundry keeps the browser’s live agent surface synchronized with verified state. WebMCP Foundry Agents propose. Evidence qualifies. Authority promotes. WebMCP makes it possible for websites to expose structured tools to AI agents. But exposing a function does not answer a harder question: Which actions have actually earned the right to become agent-callable tools? WebMCP Foundry is a capability compiler and verification workbench for the agent-native web. It takes actions that already exist in a human-facing web application and turns them into minimized, tested, effect-aware, evidence-backed, authority-governed WebMCP capabilities . Instead of treating registerTool() as the beginning of the process, Foundry treats native WebMCP registration as the output of an engineering lifecycle : human action → candidate → contract → minimized inputs → effects + authority → verification → evidence → promotion → LIVE WebMCP tool If the underlying implementation changes, its old evidence no longer silently remains valid. Foundry marks the affected capability STALE and withdraws it from the browser's native WebMCP registry until fresh evidence qualifies it again. What it does The demo uses Ledgerly , an ordinary human-facing financial web application. Foundry discovers actions such as transaction search, notes, balance adjustments, fund transfers, and account deletion. It then determines what part of each action should actually be agent-controlled. For example, an initially over-broad action with four controllable fields is reduced to only two agent-visible inputs, while trusted session and identity state remain application-controlled. Foundry then verifies proposed capabilities using explicit contracts, observed effects, negative tests, and deliberately incorrect must-kill mutants . A check only contributes evidence if it can reject its assigned known-bad implementation. The demo shows the complete lifecycle: Discover actions from the human application. Minimize an over-broad interface from 4 inputs to 2 agent-controlled inputs. Find a concrete counterexample in an incorrect implementation. Block promotion because the evidence is FAIL. Repair the implementation and obtain fresh evidence. Refuse an agent's attempt to self-promote a consequential financial capability. Allow an appropriately authorized human to promote it. Register it through native document.modelContext . Execute the capability through the browser's native WebMCP tool registry. Change the underlying source, causing LIVE → STALE and automatic native tool withdrawal. The browser registry and Foundry state are continuously reconciled: LIVE ⇔ present in document.modelContext.getTools() Everything else — CANDIDATE, VERIFIED-but-unpromoted, BLOCKED, STALE or WITHDRAWN — must remain absent. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, Foundry would only be a verifier describing which actions could be safe agent tools. WebMCP makes the final step real. A capability that passes Foundry's gates becomes an actual browser-native tool. When its evidence becomes stale, Foundry aborts its registration and the tool actually disappears from the agent's available interface. That closes the loop between software assurance and the browser's agent surface. How we built it Almost the entire authoritative system is implemented in dependency-free Julia using only the standard library . Julia owns: capability and effect models authority policy contract minimization verification mutation testing deterministic gates stale-dependency analysis the hash-chained evidence ledger HTTP serving JSON handling the demo application the Foundry UI native-host acceptance grading JavaScript is intentionally limited to the browser boundary where WebMCP exists. A small bridge projects Foundry's LIVE manifest onto document.modelContext , maintains one AbortController per tool, reconciles getTools() , and reports native browser observations back to the authoritative Julia system. The development polyfill is explicitly separated from native WebMCP and cannot satisfy Foundry's native acceptance gate . Challenges One of the biggest challenges was avoiding a verifier that simply agreed with itself. We addressed this with external observations, explicit non-PASS verdicts, counterexamples, and must-kill mutants. UNKNOWN, UNGRADABLE and BLOCKED cannot silently become PASS. Another challenge was the experimental nature of WebMCP itself. During native testing we found that our Edge build exposed the expected document.modelContext API but differed from the current WebIDL expectation for one executeTool() input form. Foundry records that disagreement rather than hiding it. Deployment was another practical challenge. The public entry point now monitors the live Foundry and Ledgerly services and redirects judges to their current HTTPS origins. Accomplishments we're proud of A working native WebMCP lifecycle rather than a simulated tool registry. LIVE → STALE → native withdrawal driven by real dependency changes. Agent self-ratification of consequential capabilities is refused. Trusted/session-bound fields cannot be forged through the agent contract. Verification checks must demonstrate that they can reject known-bad controls. A replayable, hash-chained evidence and promotion ledger. A dependency-free Julia authority kernel with only a minimal JavaScript WebMCP boundary. Native WebMCP acceptance tested against the deployed application. What we learned WebMCP makes exposing tools easy. The difficult engineering problem begins one level earlier: What should be exposed, under what contract, backed by what evidence, and for how long does that evidence remain valid? We found it useful to treat an application's agent interface as a derived software artifact rather than a static list of callable functions. What's next The next step is to generalize Foundry beyond the Ledgerly demonstration: richer application adapters, CI integration, additional capability-effect models, and standards-backed normative provenance. The longer-term idea is for WebMCP to be one compilation target of a protocol-independent capability IR. WebMCP lets websites expose tools to agents. WebMCP Foundry asks why each tool is allowed to exist. video_title: webmcp foundry challenge demo clean
video_transcript_excerpt: Web MCP can give an AI agent structured access to a website, but callable does not mean justified. Naively mirroring HTML forms exposes overbroad tools. Discovering search transactions produces four controls, exposing session and account IDs an agent could manipulate. Foundry refuses the unconstrained contract, minimizing it from four form fields to two agent parameters. Session state stays inside the app. Verified. The minimized tool registers live in Chrome. Anti-pattern two, green tests that prove nothing. A buggy adjustment tool passes unit tests, but adversarial probing debits foreign user A2. Counterexample found. Evidence fails and owner promotion is blocked. With ownership checks added in version two, fresh evidence qualifies the tool, clearing it for promotion. Anti-pattern three, self-ratification. An agent attempts to promote financial transfer funds. Foundry refuses, authority insufficient. Agents cannot self-ratify. A verified human owner promotes, registering the tool natively in Chrome. Anti-pattern four, overbroad in time. When repeated transfers exceed the hourly budget, Foundry refuses with structured retry guidance. The native Web MCP round trip succeeded. Foundry policy intentionally refused. In production, systems change underneath running agents. When a shared money helper changes, Foundry predicts the blast radius before the edit, withdrawing two of four live tools. The change lands. Dependent evidence turns stale. Via native abort controller, transfer funds and apply adjustment instantly vanish from Chrome's model context registry while independent tools survive. Evidence belongs to a specific version. When evidence expires, capabilities are revoked. No zombie tools allowed. Requalified with fresh evidence, the capabilities return to the ledger. Web MCP Foundry pairs a pure Julia capability ledger with native browser Web MCP on Google Cloud. Agents propose, evidence qualifies, authority promotes.

title: Gallery 402
pitch: A virtual museum where every door costs a cent or two over HTTP 402 — you look at the paintings; your agent reads the page's WebMCP tools, plans your own tour, and pays admission on-chain.
about_excerpt: A virtual museum where every door costs a cent or two over HTTP 402 — you look at the paintings; your agent reads the page's WebMCP tools, plans your own tour, and pays admission on-chain. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent asks before paying Tour stop 1 of 6 The x402 handshake One click, a real 402 The Great Wave at true size The live tool surface The keepsake receipt Live URL: https://gallery402.stacktr.ee/ · Video: https://youtu.be/TEGE-Sl1RXg · Repo: https://github.com/stevysmith/gallery-402 Sixty seconds, no wallet, no setup Open the live URL. The WebMCP pill turns green — the page has registered its tools with the browser. Click Buy on the Print Room ($0.01). Your wallet was staked 5¢ of test USDC on arrival, so it just works. Watch the ledger: quote → policy → EIP-3009 signature → settled on-chain → ticket issued . Your balance drops. The transaction hash links to Basescan. Click Enter . The full-resolution Hokusai is served only because you hold the ticket. Then, if you have ChatGPT desktop in Work mode, ask it "get me into the Van Gogh room" and watch it do the same thing through the page's tools. (Three host gates catch people out — Work mode, a Sol/Terra model, and an undocumented per-site permission prompt — all written up in CHATGPT-TESTING.md .) If the first load hangs for ~30 seconds, that's the box office waking up — it's on a free host that sleeps when idle. The page retries and narrates the wait; it isn't broken. Why this use case fits WebMCP Museums are visual: the whole point is to stand in front of the picture. Paying for admission is not. Today a paywall interrupts the thing you came for — a form, a card, a redirect, a login. Gallery 402 puts the human and the agent on the same page, literally: the visitor looks at Monet while an agent in their browser handles the box office through the page's own WebMCP tools. The agent doesn't scrape the page or drive the cursor; it calls gallery_buy_ticket and the page pays over HTTP 402 with a wallet the visitor controls, inside a spending limit the visitor set. That is the shape of a lot of the future web — content behind small, per-use prices, paid by agents on behalf of people — and WebMCP is the missing piece: a typed, page-provided surface so the agent can act with the site rather than on it. The real problem this solves The web's business model assumes a human who can be advertised to, tracked, or made to sign up. Agents break all three. A crawler that reads your archive shows nobody an ad; a subscription flow assumes someone to fill the form; a login assumes an account holder. So publishers reach for the only lever left — block the agent — and the open web gets smaller. That is happening right now: Cloudflare shipped pay-per-crawl because "block everything" was the only alternative on offer, and its Monetization Gateway — charge any caller for any resource over x402 — is currently waitlist-only. Gallery 402 is that product working end-to-end today, built from open parts: a Hono middleware, a public facilitator, a page that signs. Everything the gateway will do for a site, this repo shows a site doing for itself. Per-use pricing is the way out, and it has been technically possible since HTTP 402 was reserved in 1997. What was missing is not the payment rail — x402 settles a median $0.028 call today across roughly 165 million transactions — but a way for a page to tell an agent what it sells and let it buy without pretending to be a human . That is exactly what WebMCP adds: a typed, page-provided surface where "this costs two cents" and "here is your receipt" are first-class actions rather than a checkout page to be screen-driven. A museum is the demonstration, not the market. The same three pieces — a 402 at the door, a typed tool surface, a ticket bound to the payer — are what a news archive, a research corpus, a legal database, a stock-photo library or a metered API needs. We chose a gallery because it makes the paywall visible : you can see precisely what you bought, at the resolution you paid for, and the transaction hash under it. Swap the collection for a paywalled archive and nothing about the mechanism changes. The alternative being built instead is agents with saved card details and human-shaped checkout flows, which is worse for everyone: the merchant can't price per use, the user can't cap spend, and the agent has to impersonate a person to transact at all. How it improves the experience Nothing leaves the room. No checkout page, no redirect, no popup. The wall changes colour and the painting is there. The human sets policy; the agent operates inside it. "Auto-approve up to $0.05" or "ask me every time" — set in the wallet panel, honoured by buy_ticket , and deliberately not exposed as a tool. Every step is legible. The ledger narrates quote → policy → signature → settlement, and each settled payment prints a ticket stub with its transaction hash. Discovery is free; consumption is priced. The /wings manifest — works, artists, dates, real dimensions, teaser images — costs nothing and needs no ticket, so an agent can browse the catalog, compare rooms and quote prices before a cent moves. Only the full-resolution originals sit behind the 402. That split (open catalog → priced checkout) is the same shape agentic commerce is converging on, at museum scale. Same tools, two doors. The identical catalog is the ⌘K palette for humans and the WebMCP registration for agents. A visitor without an agent-capable browser gets the same actions by hand, or via the in-page agent. Why only WebMCP Each alternative fails at a different wall. Preprogrammed tours can't know the visitor — no curator wrote "boats, for a ten-year-old, in ten minutes," and the museum's own in-page agent knows only what you type at it. The visitor's agent can't know the museum — but through plan_tour the agent that knows the person composes an itinerary from the catalog, and the museum prices the doors: neither side could author that tour alone. Screen-driving can't be trusted with money — a "Buy" button is just pixels, but buy_ticket is a typed, discrete verb without readOnlyHint , which is exactly why ChatGPT paused to ask permission before paying in our end-to-end run; safe delegation of spending requires the page to declare the boundary, and tool registration is the only mechanism the web has for it. A server-side MCP could plan and even pay — but not stand in the room : here the agent's tour_step glides the same wall the human is looking at, and the human's click comes back as visitorPointing . A travel agent versus a docent beside you. One museum, four visitors, four different museums. We ran the same request — "ten minutes, my daughter loves boats and water, skip anything gloomy" — through four different agents, and got four different tours: a Claude harness composed four stops at $0.02; ChatGPT desktop composed five including the Great Wave; ChatGPT's cloud browser composed six and excluded the Wave as too fierce for a child, titling it "for a Young Explorer" and closing with a question to ask her ("Which boat would you choose?"); a second desktop run composed "Boats, bright water & blue skies." No curator wrote any of them. That variance isn't noise — it's the point: the agent brings everything it knows about this visitor (their kids, their taste, their ten minutes) to a page that knows only itself, and plan_tour is where they meet. Hyper-personalisation is what WebMCP unlocks that no preprogrammed tour, chatbot widget, or screen-scraper can: the page supplies the collection and the prices; the agent supplies the person. What humans and agents can do together that they couldn't before A visitor can say "give me a ten-minute tour about light" and watch the agent compose stops, pay two doors inside their limit, glide them in and spotlight the details — or "buy me a day pass and show me the Great Wave" and watch it happen on the page they are already looking at — the agent discovers the wings and prices, negotiates an HTTP 402, signs a gasless USDC authorization, receives a ticket bound to the visitor's wallet, walks into the room and stops at the right print — while the visitor keeps the only control that matters: how much the agent may spend without asking. Before WebMCP, an agent could only do this by screen-driving a checkout, with no way for the page to express prices, policy or confirmation as first-class actions. Implementation WebMCP: twelve tools in the lobby, thirteen once you hold a ticket, eighteen once you're inside a room, registered with document.modelContext.registerTool (falling back to navigator.modelContext ) via agentk's useWebMCPRegistration — prefixed gallery_ , with readOnlyHint annotations on the six read-only tools, title s, AbortSignal -based unregistration, and isError on failures so an agent can tell a rejected payment from a receipt. Tool errors are written as next-step instructions ("No ticket for the Van Gogh Room ($0.02). Call buy_ticket…") — the error channel

And it composed six stops for a daughter who loves boats, priced the cheapest set of doors and asked me before spending a real cent. Then it paid over HTTP 402 on chain and started walking. Gallery 402, a virtual museum where every door costs a cent or two and the box office is a tool service. Under every door, the same handshake. The box office answers 402 with a price.
