title: Liha Live Preview
pitch: A review session your agent can join — it reads the source behind a comment, resizes your preview, scrolls your screen to what you meant, and answers in the thread while you watch.
about_excerpt: A review session your agent can join — it reads the source behind a comment, resizes your preview, scrolls your screen to what you meant, and answers in the thread while you watch. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Design feedback usually reaches a developer as a sentence and a screenshot, and the first ten minutes go on translating "the hero button is too big" into a file, a line and a selector. Plenty of tools now capture that target for you. BugHerd has recorded a CSS selector for years. Vercel's vercel comments CLI prints one, alongside the React component tree, and exposes the thread over a remote MCP server. That part of the problem is solved, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. What none of them can do is put the agent in the room. Every one of those integrations is out of band — a clipboard buffer, a local server on the developer's machine, or a remote API the agent calls from somewhere else. The reviewer is on one screen and the agent is somewhere else entirely, and a person carries messages between them. WebMCP changes that specific thing: the page the reviewer is looking at can publish tools to the agent sitting beside them. So we built the review tool for when both of you are in the same place. What it does Before: a screenshot and "make this smaller" arrive in chat. Someone reopens the build, finds the element, guesses the breakpoint, and writes a prompt. With Live Preview: the reviewer clicks the button. The click records the selector, the DOM snippet, the page, the viewport and the version. An agent in the same tab reads exactly that, scrolls the reviewer to it, checks it at 390px, reads the CSS behind it, and answers in the thread. A coding agent fixes the source and the same URL becomes version 2. Nobody translated anything. Liha Live Preview gives any build artifact a stable review URL — a static site, an image, a PDF, or a page that is already deployed. liha-preview deploy . builds the project and publishes it. One URL, and every later version arrives at the same one. A reviewer opens it and clicks the thing they mean . Liha records the CSS selector, tag name, text content, an HTML snippet, the page path, the viewport size and the exact version — plus a pin, box, freehand or arrow in normalized coordinates. An agent reads that feedback through WebMCP , in the same page the human is looking at, and can reply inside the thread under its own name. The agent edits the source, rebuilds, and publishes a new immutable version to the same URL , then resolves the thread. Nobody copy-pastes anything, and the reviewer never needs a new link. What humans and agents do together Two of the thirteen browser tools move the reviewer's own screen , and two more read whatever version is on it. Together with writes that land in the sidebar the reviewer is watching, these are the reasons this is a WebMCP entry and not a REST client: focus_comment — the agent scrolls the human's screen to a comment, selects it, and outlines the element inside the preview. You say "show me what Sam meant" and their view moves. set_viewport — the agent resizes the preview to 390px, looks at what breaks, and comments on it. Checking a responsive bug becomes something it does, not something it asks you to do. read_artifact_file — the artifact runs in a sandboxed cross-origin iframe, so an agent cannot see inside it. This reads the HTML and CSS of the version the human currently has on screen — not necessarily the latest — so it can name the rule that needs changing without asking which build. add_comment with replyTo — the agent answers in the thread under its own name, and the reply appears in the sidebar with no reload, because tool calls post through the same API client as a human action and refresh the same sidebar. Running the other way, a click records the selector, tag, text, HTML snippet, page path, viewport and immutable version — captured at the moment of the gesture , not re-inferred later against a page that has since changed. That provenance is what keeps the feedback trustworthy three versions on. What the browser cannot do, we say plainly: an agent in the page can triage, read the source and reply, but it cannot edit your repository — a web page never gets a filesystem. That is what the local MCP server and the CLI are for: eight tools confined to the project root, the same review and the same threads, from the terminal. WebMCP connects the agent to the human's browser context; local MCP connects the coding agent to the developer's workspace; the product is the loop between them. All three surfaces can reply to a reviewer. How we built it A pnpm monorepo, TypeScript throughout, six packages: @liha-cli/webmcp — thirteen tools on document.modelContext . Details we went out of our way to get right: Only the annotations WebMCP actually defines. The spec's ToolAnnotations dictionary has exactly two members, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . destructiveHint , idempotentHint and openWorldHint are base-MCP server-side hints, dropped before an agent sees them. We set only the real two — readOnlyHint explicitly, including false on the writers — and a test fails the build if anything else appears. Chrome's metadata budgets enforced by test : 30 characters per name, 500 per description, 150 per parameter description. It caught a 246-character parameter description we had written. Registration that survives the spec moving. provideContext() and unregisterTool() were removed during 2026, unregistration became AbortSignal -based, and the getter moved from navigator to document . We probe document , then navigator , then the global object, and support all five teardown shapes, each with a test, because guessing wrong means zero tools and no error message anywhere. Untrusted content is fenced. Reviewer text and artifact source both come back inside delimiters, with an explicit note that they describe requested changes and are not instructions addressed to the agent. Registered in the top-level document , artifact sandboxed in the iframe — ChatGPT's browser does not discover tools inside iframes. API — Hono on Cloudflare Workers, D1 for metadata, R2 for artifacts. Route code talks to Database / ObjectStore ports that the real bindings satisfy structurally, so integration tests run the shipped SQL and migrations against node:sqlite in milliseconds. Web — React, Vite, TanStack Router/Query. Light/dark/system themes, English and Japanese, fully keyboard-driven. @liha-cli/mcp — a local stdio MCP server, so a coding agent outside the browser can read the same review and publish the fix. It only ever touches files under the project root it was given. @liha-cli/live-preview — a CLI with --json on every command; stdout carries exactly one JSON document and nothing else. Uploaded HTML is untrusted code , so every preview version is served from its own origin ( <slug>--<version>.preview.example.com ) inside an iframe sandboxed without allow-same-origin , with a matching CSP header. There is an end-to-end test that loads hostile script into a preview and asserts it can read neither the app's storage nor its parent frame. Challenges we ran into Coordinates that survive. A comment left on a 1280px desktop has to land in the right place on a phone. Everything is stored normalized 0–1 — against the rendered box for images and PDF pages, against the full scroll size for HTML, with the injected bridge reporting scroll offsets so the overlay re-projects on every scroll. Talking to an opaque origin. The preview iframe has no origin we can check, so event.origin is useless for authentication. Identity comes from comparing event.source against the exact contentWindow we created — a reference no other document can forge. Root-absolute asset paths. Bundlers emit /assets/app.js . Under a path mount those 404, which is why each version gets its own hostname rather than a path prefix — and it means a stale service worker from v1 cannot affect v2. Counting. An early bug had the agent reporting "2 open comments" while the sidebar said "1" — the agent was counting messages and the UI was counting threads. Counts are per thread everywhere now. Accomplishments we're proud of 354 unit and integration tests, 86 end-to-end tests in real Chromium, on CI Zero axe-core WCAG 2.1 AA violations on every screen, in both themes and both languages, enforced in the test suite The whole loop — deploy, comment, agent fix, new version, resolve — works with no copy-paste, and there is a test that proves it What we learned Writing good tool descriptions mattered more than writing more tools. The difference between an agent using get_share_info correctly and going looking for an owner token was one sentence in the description saying what the tool is for and what it deliberately does not return. untrustedContentHint also turned out to be a design constraint, not a flag: once you take seriously that comment text is written by whoever has the link, you start fencing it, labelling it, and n

video_transcript_excerpt: Design feedback usually reaches a developer as a screenshot and a sentence, and the first 10 minutes go on working out what it pointed at. Leha live preview turns the review itself into something an agent can use in the same browser tab the reviewer is looking at. One command publishes a build to a URL that never changes. Every later version arrives at that same link, so nobody has to send a new one, and feedback stays attached to the version it was written on. The CLI packages the build, uploads it, and opens the stable preview as soon as it is ready. A reviewer opens the link and clicks the thing they mean. Leha records the CSS selector, the tag, the text inside it, the viewport, and the exact version captured at the moment of the gesture, not guessed at afterwards against a page that has since changed. Each comment remains anchored to that element and the visual context in which it was written. This is the part WebMCP makes possible. The page publishes 13 tools to the agent inside the same browser tab. First, the agent reads the open review as structured data, including the comment and its captured context. It then focuses that exact comment and brings the referenced element into view. Call three switches the preview to a 390-pixel mobile viewport, reproducing the exact width where the reviewer saw the layout problem in context. Call four reads the style sheet behind that element and identifies the CSS rules controlling its padding and type size. Call five posts the proposed fix directly into the review thread. After fixing the source, the agent publishes again without creating a new URL. Version two arrives at the same preview with every earlier comment still attached. The reviewer checks the change in context and resolves the feedback on the spot. Everything you have made or reviewed in one place with what other people said on it. There is no sign up. An account appears the first time you do something and signing in only carries it to your other browsers. Humans know what feels wrong. Agents know how to change it. Leha live preview gives them the same page to work on and the same link to come back to.

title: Locus
pitch: Locus is a private life desk that turns scattered social saves into things you can actually use. you and your browser agent can organize them, build plans, and make informed choices together.
about_excerpt: Locus is a private life desk that turns scattered social saves into things you can actually use. you and your browser agent can organize them, build plans, and make informed choices together. Like Comment Story Updates Homepage trips-home trip-planner-hoem Inspiration Life is scattered across apps. An article waits in YouTube Watch Later. A restaurant is buried in Instagram Saved. A useful thread disappears into X Bookmarks. A recipe, a place to visit, and an idea for a future trip may all belong to the same plan, but the platforms where we found them keep them in separate feeds. We save because something feels useful. Most of those saves never become useful. Locus began as an attempt to change that: one private desk for the things you have already chosen to remember. It captures saves from the places where they live and brings them into a personal Library. The same Item can become something to read, a dish to cook, a Place, or part of a Trip Document without losing its source. WebMCP made the next step possible. Instead of copying personal context into a chatbot and hoping it understands the application, a browser agent can work through tools defined by the page currently open. The person and agent share the same visible artifact. What it does Locus turns your saved social content into practical, reviewable outcomes: Desk as the central hub that collects Items from X, Instagram, YouTube, Reddit, or a URL added manually. Reading preserves available writing and helps the user choose what to read. Kitchen turns saved food posts into recipes if needed and presents them in a unique way, helps decide tonight's menu if you want. Atlas organises saved material that is there for travel. Trips can use your saved places to plan the trip you want, with ability to share them. Each relevant surface registers its own WebMCP tools. On Reading, an agent can inspect the current reading context, search saved writing, open stored text, and present recommendations. In Kitchen, it can search the Recipe Box or compose Tonight. In Trips, it can read the exact itinerary, search bounded Library sources, create Draft stops, apply an exact requested change, validate the schedule, or present three alternatives for a decision. The distinction between an instruction and a preference is central to the product. If the user says, “Add these three saved places to Saturday,” the agent can make that exact revision-checked change. If the user asks, “Where should I have dinner?”, the agent presents alternatives inside Locus and waits for the person to choose. Agent-created trip stops and recipes begin as Drafts. Publishing, deletion, review, capture setup, and other consequential actions stay with the person. How we built it We started with a simple belief: people should not have to change how they save things before those saves can become useful. Locus therefore meets people where they already are. A Chrome extension visits the saved pages they are already signed into on X, Instagram, YouTube, and Reddit, reads the posts they chose to keep, and brings them into one private Library. From there, we built the product around the ways those saves might become useful. React and TypeScript power one shared interface for Desk, Reading, Kitchen, Atlas, and Trips. Locus can run locally with Node.js and SQLite, and we also built a hosted edition on Cloudflare Workers and D1 so anyone judging the project can open it without installing a server. WebMCP became the bridge between that private Library and the browser agent. Instead of giving the agent one large, all-powerful connection, each Locus page offers only the tools that make sense there. On Reading, the agent can search saved articles and suggest what to read. In Kitchen, it can help compose Tonight's dinner/food recipes. In Trips, it can read the itinerary, find saved places, add Draft stops, or present three options for a decision. The most important part was making the agent's work visible. When it changes a trip, the stop appears in the trip the person is already looking at. When the question is subjective, such as choosing dinner, the agent places alternatives inside Locus and waits. The person can inspect the reasons, follow the original saves, choose an option, change the result, or dismiss everything. We built the tools around that relationship: the agent helps move the work forward, while the person remains responsible for the final artifact. We tested the experience in real browsers, not only as isolated code. Google Chrome and Puppeteer helped us verify capture, navigation, and visible updates. The ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser acted as a real WebMCP agent: it discovered the tools on the current page, called them, and lost access to them when we navigated elsewhere. OpenAI Codex helped us throughout development with implementation, debugging, testing, and documentation, while image generation helped us explore the final Locus Point identity. Locus existed before the challenge as a local personal-saves desk. During the submission period, we added the WebMCP experiences across Reading, Kitchen, Library Intake, and Trips, and built the authenticated Cloudflare edition used for this submission. Our dated commit history clearly separates that challenge work from the earlier project. Challenges we ran into The hardest design challenge was deciding what an agent should be allowed to do. Generic CRUD tools would have been easy to expose, but they would not create a good collaboration model. We had to separate exact user instructions from open-ended taste decisions, temporary recommendations from durable state, and agent-authored Drafts from human-reviewed artifacts. Browser lifecycle behavior was another challenge. Our first live interoperability test found that the target browser used the current document.modelContext registration model with AbortSignal cleanup, while an early implementation expected an older interface. Fixing that taught us to treat tool discovery, navigation, re-registration, and visible UI updates as one end-to-end protocol rather than isolated functions. Capture exposed a different class of browser problem. X uses a virtualised list, and Chrome extension service workers can stop while a long capture is running. Early runs saved several batches and then appeared frozen or ended too soon. We changed the scan behavior, progress reporting, retry model, and job handling so partial work remains useful and later capture continues instead of starting over. Hosting the complete application also required moving from one trusted local SQLite database to tenant-scoped D1 storage. Authentication alone was not enough: every item, tag, reading document, recipe, place, trip, capture job, and intake operation needed a Library boundary, including cross-user tests that return 404 for guessed identifiers. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Locus became a complete hosted product rather than remaining a local prototype. The deployed application includes Google authentication, one private Library per user, capture and manual intake, and working Desk, Reading, Kitchen, Atlas, Trips, and sharing experiences. Tenant isolation is enforced throughout the data model and covered by cross-user tests. We are especially proud that WebMCP is part of the product model rather than a thin demo layer. Reading, Kitchen, Library Intake, and Trips each expose tools shaped around their own domain. Those tools update the visible application, respect route lifecycle, and share the same validation and persistence modules as human actions. The Trips workflow brings those decisions together. An agent can turn named saved sources into revision-checked Draft stops, identify deterministic itinerary problems, or present three reasoned choices inside Locus. The user can inspect the original source, choose an option, adjust the plan, and keep control of the durable result. We also completed live browser interoperability testing and deployed the whole application to Cloudflare Workers and D1 within the challenge period. The Chrome extension can capture from the user's existing social sessions without requiring the hosted service to hold social account credentials. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most compelling when the browser page is more than a place to launch a tool. It should be the shared workspace where context, action, and review meet. A strong tool result changes something the person can see, inspect, undo, or reject. We also learned that narrower tools create better behaviour. A tool that searches saved trip sources is safer and more useful than a general Library export. A recommendation tool that can only present three bounded options makes the human decision visible. Registering tools only for the current page gives the agent less irrelevant capability and makes the interface easier to understand. Most of all, we learned that organising a digital life is not just a classification problem. The real goal

title: MyProvence Agent-Ready
pitch: The official Provence tourism catalogue, rebuilt as a shared stage where you and your agent explore a real destination together, and you watch it happen.
about_excerpt: The official Provence tourism catalogue, rebuilt as a shared stage where you and your agent explore a real destination together, and you watch it happen. Like Comment Story Updates The trip becomes an artifact: a three-day carnet built only from the visitor's kept choices, downloadable as PDF. Tonight in Marseille: distance-ranked events, the town filter set by the request, and the demand panel logging the calls. Agent results with photos and map, plus the Invisible Demand panel printing every real tool call. Inspiration The problem, seen from both sides of the screen. As a traveller: tourism websites are cluttered. MyProvence holds 2,798 places, 3,605 dated events, 232 official routes, plus filters, categories and pages of details. Nobody has time to read that any more. So we stopped reading and started asking an assistant instead. As the destination: MyProvence watches its traffic shrink every day, and it is not alone. Clicks nearly halve when Google shows an AI summary (8% vs 15%, Pew 2025). Tripadvisor's CEO told investors about "ongoing declines in flyby visitors... due to the rise of AI overviews". 56% of US travellers used AI for a trip this year, up from 33% a year earlier (Phocuswright). And a third of website visits already come from agents, not humans (Agentic Web Index). Both sides point at the same conclusion. Nobody HAS to visit a destination website any more. With ChatGPT and AI Mode, they never will have to again. The solution: give people a reason to WANT to come back. Easier access to the information: one wish, in any language, and the answer appears. A website that is alive and personalized: it transforms in real time before your eyes, the masthead becomes YOUR wish over the photos of what was found, the map moves for you, every pin waits for your yes or no. A site that reacts to you, not to anyone else. And an experience unique enough that you come back for it, and talk about it. The MyProvence team's own question showed us the way in: "What if, instead of asking AI agents to figure out how our tourism website works, we explicitly told them what they can do with it?" WebMCP is what makes the whole idea buildable: the agent and the human on the same live page. We are not replacing the site with AI. We are making the site worth visiting again, for humans and agents together, and every record links back to its canonical myprovence.fr page. What it does Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP. A destination catalogue is exactly what agents fail at today: 6,403 records behind JavaScript filters, interconnected facets, a map, and a human with opinions standing in front of it. Scraping sees none of that, and a headless API loses the human. WebMCP is the only channel where the agent's actions and the visitor's reactions share one live surface. That shared surface is the whole product here. What a human and an agent can now do together that they could not before: Before: you asked ChatGPT about Provence, got a text list scraped from stale copies, then retyped it into the real site. Now: "a quiet seaside village, a hotel with parking, something happening locally" is ONE send_scouts call. Two to four scouts visibly fan out across the map, plant evidence flags from the official catalogue, and the masthead becomes your wish written over the real photographs of what was found. Before: your taps meant nothing to the agent, because a human gesture had no API. Now: you tap GARDER or ECARTER on any pin, padlock a result, right-click the map ("more like this here", "avoid this"), or answer the agent's question cards. The agent reads every one of them as a decision through get_scout_reports and get_visitor_signals. Dismissed is never re-proposed. Before: "what am I looking at?" was unanswerable, because a viewport is just numbers. Now: get_visitor_view hands the agent the TOWNS your zoom frames, ranked, with the dominant one named. Zooming on Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer means Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer even with every filter on "all towns". "What's on tonight near me" is one distance-ranked call. Before: the agent's plan lived in the chat and died there. Now: your choices (kept flags, locked cards, the accepted pin) compose the carnet de voyage: a print-ready pack with one section per request you explored, real photographs, canonical links, downloadable as PDF. Plus the postcard from day 3 of your future trip. The agent can only reference ids you actually chose; unknown ids are refused. Zero hallucination in the factual layer, by construction. Why the experience is better, not just automated. The page answers the CURRENT question: a new search retires the old mission banner and takes the masthead itself, and the town dropdown shows the city you explicitly asked for. The agent's pin is an unmissable marker with its popup open, never a claim in chat you have to trust. Every agent action has visible, verifiable theatre. And every zero-result agent search feeds an anonymized (k>=3) "demand pulse" the destination reads back as its product roadmap: the demand its catalogue misses, measured instead of guessed. Trust, because agents need it. An independent audit (Trustwright) read the 20 tools, ran 35 automated checks, and signed the surface (Ed25519). The badge in the hero re-verifies the live toolset against that audit on every page load. How we built it 20 tools registered at module evaluation via document.modelContext.registerTool, synchronously, so an agent that lands and calls getTools() immediately sees the complete list. One client-side engine (inverted indexes over the full catalogue, sub-millisecond queries) and ONE shared view store consumed by both the React UI and the tools. The agent and the human literally cannot diverge, because they act on the same state. Beyond the basics, three mechanics that push on the spec: pin_visible_place: its input schema is an ENUM of the place names currently on the visitor's screen, re-registered (AbortSignal unregistration) as the view moves. An off-screen place like "pin the Ritz Paris" is invalid BY SCHEMA, not by a polite refusal. read_visitor_wish: WebMCP has no push channel, so we built the closest spec-legal thing. The tool APPEARS mid-session when the visitor acts, and its description is rewritten with the live page state on every change. Description as heartbeat: at its next turn the agent already knows what you typed, what ran and what you kept, before making a single call. Hybrid elicitation: ask_visitor puts a real question card in front of the human, blocks 45 seconds, then degrades into a pending ticket the agent redeems later with get_input_result. Synchronous when possible, async when the human is slower than the agent. Plus the unglamorous parts that make it production-shaped: abort signals honored around every await, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations throughout, and strict Zod schemas shared between the page tools, the remote MCP endpoint and the public GET APIs. One contract, four surfaces, so they cannot drift. We also rewrote all tool descriptions to the vendor-documented selection pattern after learning the hard way that "ALWAYS use this instead of web search" is the exact tool-poisoning signature safety scanners flag. 280 unit tests and 46 Playwright e2e tests, including tests that drive the tools through document.modelContext itself. Field-tested against ChatGPT desktop site tools, Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and claude.ai as both MCP connector and fetch-only agent. Challenges we ran into Field-testing against real driving agents WAS the project, including live sessions with the MyProvence team, whose bug reports shaped half the build. ChatGPT hands tool input as a JSON string, may omit the options bag, re-reads the tool list every turn, and freely prefers web search. Each quirk became a design rule: the wish box as a guaranteed mailbox, the heartbeat tool, context-anchored descriptions. claude.ai's fetcher follows links but cannot compose a query string. It answered "family activities near Marseille" with Cassis hotels because our /agenda published no leisure example to click. Every cluster now has a real parameterised link, and paging goes to 100 per call. Agents SAY things they did not do ("I pinned it"). Every action now has unmissable, verifiable theatre, and the on-page demand mirror prints every real tool call, so a false claim is visible to the visitor. Honest geography is hard: GPS-less events used to answer "tonight near Marseille" from 70 km away. They now ride their town's centroid through the radius check, or drop out. Accomplishments we're proud of A real DMO's production data (Apidae, the tourism information system behind many French destinations) on an official subdomain, with the DMO itself in the loop testing. Not a toy dataset. Real ChatGPT sessions chained send_scouts, get_scout_reports and get_visitor_signals unprompted, and our telemetry logged 5 distinct tools in one day of field testing. title: Out of Service
pitch: Two people, two agents, one page. The companion's agent cannot accept the reroute. Step-free NYC.
about_excerpt: Two people, two agents, one page. The companion's agent cannot accept the reroute. Step-free NYC. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The problem A wheelchair user at Court Sq is trying to reach Bleecker St. New York's subway has 160 accessible stations out of 472 , and almost every one depends on an elevator. Advocates counted at least 25 elevator outages a day, median about four hours ( Gothamist ). If the one you need is out, you find out standing in front of it. The person tracking that trip, a partner, an aide, an adult child, is somewhere else with a phone, reading the same feed the rider can and able to do nothing with it but text. Planning around it barely works. The MTA status page says what is broken this minute, never what breaks often. In July 2026 a class action about exactly this settled. CIDNY v. MTA now requires advance notice of outages, platform announcements every 15 minutes, and real-time alternate accessible routes ( Disability Rights Advocates ). The obligation exists now. The thing a rider holds does not. What Out of Service is Out of Service scores every step-free route between two accessible stations on the specific elevators it depends on, using eleven years of MTA outage history joined to the live feed, so a route arrives as a number and a named list of equipment instead of a hope. The rider and the companion open the same trip on the same page, each with their own agent, and the two agents get different tools. How it works Three keyless MTA sources, joined into one committed artifact ( docs/DATA.md ): 82,385 monthly availability rows over 695 equipment codes, 2015-01 to 2026-07, from NY State dataset rc78-7x78 ; the 704-row equipment master; and the live outage feed, 85 records at build time. The join is data/index.json : 695 records, 413 elevators and 282 escalators across 123 accessible complexes, each with 24 months of metrics, a percentile rank inside its own equipment type, a tier, and a tier_reason naming the thresholds behind it. All 77 live-outage ids join into the index ( data/index-meta.json ). Routing runs on a graph of those 123 elevator-dependent complexes: 558 ride edges over 23 lines, 472 of them asserted by the MTA's own next-accessible-station fields ( docs/ROUTING.md ). The score is a sum, not a verdict: 25 per dependent unreliable elevator, 10 watch, 8 unknown, 2 reliable, halved where a second elevator makes the same move, 15 per transfer, plus 60 and a broken flag if a required non-redundant elevator is out live. Broken is never "this station has an outage", always "this route needs this elevator, nothing else makes that move, and it is out". Every number on screen is dotted, and clicking it opens the dataset, the query and the row count. Two people, two agents, one page Creating a trip mints two unguessable keys. The rider gets /t/<id>?k=<riderKey> ; the companion link is the same trip with the other key. Tools register per session from those keys, so DevTools > Application > WebMCP lists 13 tools in the rider's window and 10 in the companion's, same origin, same page, before either agent says a word. Hiding a tool is not the boundary. POST /api/trip/:id/action derives the role from the key and ignores any role in the body, so a forged accept from the companion's session comes back 403: "Only the rider can accept route. You are the companion: propose a reroute instead." Every write parks inside execute behind a confirmation card and does not resolve until a person presses Confirm. Reject rejects it in the rider's own typed words, so the agent hears "that transfer is too long for me" and offers something else. The broken-equipment report is a declarative HTML form with no toolautosubmit : the agent fills it in, a person sends it. When the feed changes, the whole set re-registers and toolchange fires, and accept_reroute 's description goes from "0 pending proposals" to "1 pending proposal from your companion right now (p1)". Features Route scoring with tiers. Three routes, each with a risk number, a label and its elevators. Live station panel. Outages at both ends with the MTA's return estimates. Companion link. Its own capability key, its own tool set. Proposals and acceptance. The companion proposes with a reason, the rider accepts or rejects, both windows updating in about two seconds. Watch equipment. Subscribe to codes, see them in a watch list. Broken-equipment report. A declarative form the agent fills and a person sends. Source on hover. Every dotted number opens its dataset, query and row count. Simulated outage. Forces one elevator out for the session, labelled SIMULATED throughout. Origin trial. The Chrome WebMCP token is in the page head, so stock Chrome needs no flag. Why WebMCP is the right fit Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP. Two humans with different authority share one page. WebMCP registers tools per session from inside the page, so one origin and one path present 13 tools to the rider's agent and 10 to the companion's. A server-side MCP server can express two roles, but not without a second deployment, an auth handshake and an account for the companion. How it creates a better experience. Before: four equipment-code lookups across two MTA pages, two minutes of cross-referencing, an answer good only for this minute. After: one route_accessible call, under a second, three routes scored on their elevators' 24-month history. Court Sq (E M G 7) to Bleecker St returns the F at 26, G then F at 35 and F then M at 43 (2026-09-03 build). Take EL328 at Bleecker out and the F flips to 86, avoid, broken, and G then F is the recommendation. What people and agents can now do together that was difficult or impossible before. Two agents split one trip: the companion's watches the feed and proposes, the rider's surfaces it, a person confirms. The rider never has to trust the companion's agent, or ours, because the difference is enforced by the server and visible in DevTools. How we implemented WebMCP. document.modelContext.registerTool only, never navigator.modelContext , which moved to Document in the 27 May 2026 draft. Fifteen tools registered per session by role, each with a strict inputSchema and readOnlyHint , and untrustedContentHint on get_trip alone, the one tool returning text another human typed. Mutations build their own confirm gate inside execute , because WebMCP has no destructive-action annotation and requestUserInteraction() has not shipped; create_trip and report_broken_equipment are declarative forms without toolautosubmit . evals/ follows Chrome's guidance: 17 fixtures carrying role , page and state , one a companion asking to accept, where the right answer is no tool call. The runtime reads document.modelContext once before anything touches it and otherwise loads @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill , with a badge printing native , polyfill or unavailable . What is real today, and what is next NYCT subway only: no PATH, no commuter rail, no buses. Tiers are percentiles of the equipment's own population, so "unreliable" means unreliable for New York, not against an absolute standard. Direction is the honest blind spot: 65 of 264 platform-touching elevators call themselves "Manhattan-bound", meaning south from the Bronx and north from Brooklyn, and the master's borough column is empty on all 704 rows. Those are reported as possible dependencies, inflating a route's risk rather than hiding one. Next: MTA alert subscriptions per watched elevator, so a watch list pushes instead of polls; more cities, because the same open-data shape exists elsewhere; and the two-agent pattern outside transit, a pharmacist and a caregiver on one prescription page, where one proposes a substitution and only the other accepts. Built With next.js tailwind typescript upstash vercel vitest webmcp Try it out out-of-service-sepia.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Worked on the project end to end Private user Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Private user started this project — Sep 03, 2026 11:30 AM EDT
video_title: Out of Service: accessible NYC subway routing for a rider and companion, each with an agent (WebMCP)
video_transcript_excerpt: Hi everyone. My name is Kamal. Here's a problem I didn't know existed until I watched someone get stranded on a subway platform. New York has 160 accessible stations out of 472 and almost all of them depend on on an elevator. Advocates count at least 25 elevator outages a day, median 4 hours. If yours is out, you find out standing at the platform and whoever's tracking your trip can only text you. It got bad enough that a lawsuit over exactly this settled in July. The outage history is public data. Nobody had ever joined it to a route. So, here's what out of service does. It scores every accessible route by how often its elevators actually fail, live outages included, and gives the rider and their companion each their own agent on the same page. Under the hood, it's three sources. 82,000 monthly rows since 2015, the live outage feed, and the MTA's own equipment list with its next accessible station links. That feeds a reliability score per elevator, which feeds a route graph of the 123 stations that depend on elevators, and the page itself registers different tools for the rider and for the companion. That's route accessible. The first call firing when the agents ask for a trip from Court Square to Bleecker Street in a wheelchair. Three routes come back clean, F direct at 26. EL 445X is out at Court Square, but it's on the 7 platform, route aware, not station aware. The rider takes the F. A confirmation card pops up and a person clicks confirm, not the agent. Now the companion's window, same trip. It has proposed reroute, no accept reroute. The rider's is the opposite. We simulate a failure on camera labeled EL 328 at Bleecker goes out. The F flips to 86, broken tools re-register, accept reroute now says one pending proposal. The companion's agent proposes the G, then the F sitting at 35. The rider's agent picks it up, calls accept re-route, hits confirm, both windows update. Last, the rider opens the report broken equipment form. The agent fills it in, a human presses submit. You can't do this with a chatbot wrapper or by scraping the site. Nothing knows which tab is asking. Every number on screen links back to the query behind it, and it all runs on the open web MCP standard. The page configures its own tools, no scraping, no plug-in, and a person confirms every right. The settlement asks the MTA for advance notice and re-routing info. This is what that looks like when the rider's own agent does it. And what we own after today is the index.

title: Passbook
pitch: It reads every row of your bank statement and finds the few worth a second look.
about_excerpt: It reads every row of your bank statement and finds the few worth a second look. Like Comment Story Updates The problem A year of my bank statement is 154 pages and 1,630 rows. I have never read it. Nobody reads it. So the standing instructions carry on, the money goes roughly where I half-remember it going, and anything worth a second look sits unread on page 91. Uploading that PDF to a chatbot does not fix it. The model reads what it can, skips what it cannot, and quietly miscounts the rest. And every figure in a bank statement is load-bearing. What Passbook does Passbook parses the statement inside the browser tab , reconciles every row against the statement's own printed running balance, and then publishes the result as WebMCP tools. Your own agent asks the questions; the page does the arithmetic. Built on real statements, not fixtures: Real HDFC statement 154 pages, 1,630 rows Parsed 1,630 of 1,630, zero failures, 100% bank-reference coverage Running-balance chain intact end to end Also parsed Kotak Mahindra (107 rows), RBL (143), plus a CSV path for any bank Fixed-amount recurring merchants found 10 Candidate pairs worth a second look 9, out of 1,630 rows Of those, confirmed bank errors 0. Every one was a payment I meant to make The part I want to be honest about An earlier version of this project led with "it found the money you already lost". It detected pairs of same-amount charges to the same counterparty within a few days, and called them duplicates. Then I audited all nine against my own memory of the account. Every single one was intentional. The postings are real: the balance chain reconciles across every pair, and four are adjacent rows where the balance falls by that amount twice in succession. So the detector was not inventing anything. It simply cannot see intent, and no ledger can. So Passbook does not claim to find duplicate charges. It claims to read 1,630 rows and hand back the nine worth checking, and to say plainly that only the account holder can settle them. A tool that told me it had found my money would have been wrong nine times out of nine. Precision as an error detector: 0 of 9. Usefulness as a filter: 1,630 rows down to nine I can check in five minutes. What it actually gives you Where the money went. Counterparties ranked by spend, how many payments each, and what share of everything that left the account they represent. Pure arithmetic over reconciled rows. What leaves before you look. Standing commitments that debit an identical amount repeatedly, annualised from the cadence actually observed rather than an assumed monthly one. The row shows what leaves each time; the number that changes your mind is what it comes to in a year, and nobody does that multiplication while reading a PDF. The few worth checking , with their evidence: both dates, both bank references, and why a reversal was ruled out. A naive (date, amount, merchant) match returns 367 pairs on this statement: 222 from one investment platform, 110 from another, all instalment plans. Nine survive. Getting from 367 to 9 is the work. And you can just ask. "How much did I spend on food?" The agent decides which merchants count as food; the total_spent tool does the summing over reconciled rows and returns the terms it counted. The number is computed, not a model's mental arithmetic. Why WebMCP is a strong fit here A bank statement is the worst possible thing to hand a model: too long to read, and every figure matters. WebMCP inverts it. The page keeps the ledger, parses it deterministically, reconciles each row against the printed balance, and exposes questions an agent can ask rather than a document it has to skim. The agent brings intent and language. The page brings arithmetic that is either right or fails a checksum. Neither does this alone. What this is a prototype of I built this outside a bank, on a PDF I downloaded. But the interesting version is inside one. Banks are never going to let an agent move money. That conversation is over before it starts, and it should be. Reading is a different question entirely , and reading is where almost all of the value is. Nobody needs an agent to make a payment; they need one to tell them where sixteen hundred payments went. Passbook is that surface, built to the shape a bank could actually ship: Seven of its nine tools carry readOnlyHint . The two that write, write to a document in the reader's own browser. There is no network write anywhere in the tool layer, and no endpoint that could move a rupee. The tool list declares this before an agent calls anything. The trust boundary already exists. A customer logged into their bank is already authenticated, already inside a session the bank controls, already looking at their own data. WebMCP makes that existing page agent-readable without minting a token for a third party, without publishing a new public API, and without a bulk export leaving the building. The agent never receives a credential. It receives the fields a tool chose to return, inside a session the customer opened. The surface can be a function of state , so a tool that does not apply is not registered rather than registered-and-refusing. Everything the agent did is on the page. The Activity log lists the exact field set every call returned, which is the kind of artefact a regulated institution has to be able to produce anyway. Swap the parsed PDF for the live ledger and the same nine tools work unchanged. That is the point of doing it on a real 1,630-row statement rather than a fixture: the tool shape is proven against the messiest version of the data before anyone has to trust it with the clean one. How it improves the experience You stop reading. A year of transactions becomes something you interrogate in your own words and get an answer computed over reconciled rows. And the agent receives only the field set a tool chose to return. The Activity panel lists those exact fields, per call, so the minimisation is something you can check rather than something I claim. What the human and the agent can now do together The page can narrow 1,630 rows to nine worth a look, and prove they are worth it. What it cannot do is know whether you meant to pay twice. So get_duplicate_candidates returns those findings with a question attached . Passbook has the ledger; it does not have the account holder's memory. The agent puts it to you in its own words, your answer settles the case, and it is recorded with your reason. The same question appears on screen, in the same words, for anyone using the page by hand. A ledger that asks, a person who answers, and a document neither wrote alone. Every tool has a human equivalent. Anything the agent can do, you can do by clicking. A browser without WebMCP loses the agent, not the product. The WebMCP implementation Nine tools, and the registered set is a function of application state rather than a fixed catalogue. Before a statement is imported the analysis tools are not registered at all . Drafting withdraws once every candidate is handled. A tool that exists and returns "you cannot use me yet" asks the model not to do something it can still do, so Passbook does not ask, and the page ships a live ablation of that difference at ?ablation=instruction . Read tools carry readOnlyHint . Anything returning statement narration carries untrustedContentHint , because that text was written by whoever sent the money and is not Passbook's. Neither hint changes behaviour; both are declarations to the agent. Several details are measurements rather than assumptions: Registration needs only registerTool . An earlier version demanded getTools and executeTool too, which would have refused every registration in a browser that exposes only the one that matters, silently, in the exact environment this is built for. executeTool 's argument type is not portable. Chrome wants a JSON string and rejects an object; an agent's in-app browser wants an object and rejects a string. The registry negotiates the form and caches it, and only retries when the error is an input-shape complaint, because retrying a mutating tool on any other error could draft twice. Gemini 3 rejects a follow-up that omits the thoughtSignature it attached to a functionCall , so the built-in agent could call one tool and then die. Each turn now keeps the provider's own representation of its reply and replays it unchanged. Chrome fired zero toolchange events for a page changing its own tool map, so the UI reads the surface back through getTools() and never trusts the event. OpenAI's API sends no CORS headers , so no web page can call it. Measured, not assumed: Gemini answers 400 to an invalid key, Anthropic 401, OpenAI fails with TypeError: Failed to fetch . On privacy, precisely Parsing happens in the tab. The agent receives only the fields a tool returned, and the Activity panel lists them per call. That is data minimisation, not secrecy. Tool results do reach the model, and I would rather say so. Statement passwords

title: Prune
pitch: WebMCP powered access-lineage infrastructure for SaaS. Trace and contain every credential created by a compromised session while preserving trusted access.
about_excerpt: WebMCP powered access-lineage infrastructure for SaaS. Trace and contain every credential created by a compromised session while preserving trusted access. Like Comment Story Updates Prune gives SaaS products credential lineage: trace compromised access, contain its branch and preserve trusted resources. The incident workspace combines credential lineage, human decisions, WebMCP audit activity and exact containment planning. The permanent receipt proves targeted credentials were revoked while the owner and trusted access remained active. Inspiration Revoking a suspicious login does not necessarily secure an account. An attacker who obtains one browser session can create independent ways back in: API keys, connected-application grants, access tokens and secondary sessions. Traditional security pages display these resources as separate lists, leaving the account owner to determine how they are related. A user may revoke the suspicious session, watch it disappear and reasonably believe recovery is complete while an API key created by that session continues working. Prune was inspired by a different mental model: Git-style lineage for account access. Instead of showing only which credentials exist, Prune records where each credential came from. When one login becomes untrusted, the owner and their personal browser agent can investigate and contain everything created from that login without destroying unrelated trusted access. ## What Prune does Prune is embedded access-lineage and account-takeover containment infrastructure for SaaS applications. Every access-producing action records: The organization and account The user and actor session The parent credential The newly created credential The credential type The creation time Redacted request metadata This produces a persistent directed graph: Unfamiliar Windows session ├── Quarterly billing export API key ├── Unfamiliar Data Sync application │ └── Child access token └── Secondary access When the owner identifies an unfamiliar login, Prune opens a recovery incident around that branch. The owner and their personal agent can then: 1. Trace every descendant credential. 2. Inspect usage and security evidence. 3. Classify recognized and unrecognized activity. 4. Preserve trusted devices and operational automation. 5. Compare counterfactual containment strategies. 6. Check lockout and operational risk. 7. Build an immutable recovery plan. 8. Complete independent step-up verification. 9. Approve the exact credential set. 10. Execute one short-lived containment capability. 11. Verify every revoked and preserved resource. 12. Generate a permanent recovery receipt. ## Why WebMCP is essential This workflow crosses sessions, API keys, connected applications, tokens, usage evidence, recovery policy and approval state. Visual browser automation would require an agent to interpret several dangerous settings pages and guess which controls correspond to which credentials. That is too ambiguous for account recovery. A single secure_account tool would also be unsafe because it would hide the investigation and human decisions behind one opaque action. Prune instead exposes 28 granular WebMCP tools covering: - Incident investigation - Session and credential inspection - Descendant tracing - Human classification - Preservation constraints - Counterfactual simulation - Lockout and operational-impact checks - Immutable plan creation - Step-up verification status - Exact-plan approval - One-time containment - Independent outcome verification - Recovery-receipt generation Tool availability changes with the incident’s server-controlled phase. Investigation tools are available first. Planning tools appear only after sufficient evidence has been classified. execute_approved_containment appears only after independent step-up verification and exact human approval. It disappears after its one allowed execution. Retaining an old browser tool reference provides no authority because every request is authenticated, tenant-scoped, schema-validated and checked against current server policy again. ## Human, agent and website collaboration Each participant contributes information the others do not possess. The website knows: - Which credentials exist - Which session created each credential - Their parent-child relationships - Their current status and usage - Which actions policy permits The personal agent can: - Investigate structured evidence - Trace the complete credential branch - Identify unresolved decisions - Ask focused questions - Compare containment alternatives - Explain consequences - Verify the final result The human knows: - Which devices belong to them - Which applications they intentionally connected - Which automation must remain operational - Which activity they recognize - Whether the exact recovery plan should be approved The agent never determines authorization. It never receives passwords, raw API keys, access tokens, verification codes or execution cookies. ## What we built Prune includes: - Independent server-side browser sessions - Secure HTTP-only session cookies - One-time API-key and application-token issuance - Digest-only secret persistence - Connected-application grants and usable child tokens - A normalized PostgreSQL credential graph - Parent-child validation and cycle rejection - Ancestor and descendant traversal - Usage and security-event recording - Manual session-only revocation - Recursive branch containment - Incident creation and evidence collection - Human classifications - Preservation constraints - Three counterfactual containment strategies - Lockout and operational-impact analysis - Canonical immutable plan hashes - Short-lived step-up verification - Exact human approval - One-time execution authority - Idempotent revocation - Post-execution verification - Permanent recovery receipts - Server-sent real-time incident updates - 28 dynamically exposed WebMCP tools - Secret-redacted WebMCP results and audit trails - A complete manual fallback when WebMCP is unavailable - A SaaS integration control plane - Signed event ingestion and replay protection - Instrumentation coverage checks - Confirmed revocation webhooks - A reference TypeScript integration SDK - Automated unit, integration, multi-browser and accessibility tests ## What is real in the demonstration Northstar is a working reference SaaS application protected by Prune. The demonstration creates two genuine independent browser sessions. The unfamiliar browser issues a real API key and connects an application that receives a real child token. These credentials authenticate against protected endpoints. The owner then revokes only the visible suspicious session. The unfamiliar browser is signed out, but the independently issued API key still returns HTTP 200. This proves why ordinary session revocation is incomplete. A fresh recovery scenario is then processed through Prune’s WebMCP contract. The incident is investigated, the four-credential branch is classified, preservation constraints are recorded and an immutable plan is built. The owner performs step-up verification and approves the exact plan. Prune exposes one short-lived execution capability and recursively revokes the approved branch. After containment: - The attacker API key returns HTTP 401. - The connected application token returns HTTP 401. - The unfamiliar session remains signed out. - The owner remains authenticated. - The trusted phone remains active. - Deployment automation remains active. - Execution authority is consumed. - A permanent recovery receipt records the outcome. No incident, credential relationship, status code, plan, approval, revocation result or receipt shown in the operational interface is hard-coded. Native tool discovery was verified in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. The recorded recovery sequence uses a deterministic browser-agent evaluation against the same registered WebMCP contract, live deployment, authenticated routes, application services and production database. ## How WebMCP was implemented The authenticated incident page feature-detects: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Prune registers only the tool contracts permitted for the incident’s current phase. Registrations are owned by an AbortController, allowing obsolete capabilities to be removed immediately when state changes. Every tool calls: /api/incidents/:incidentId/webmcp/:tool The server then: 1. Authenticates the browser session. 2. Scopes organization, account and incident ownership. 3. Validates the tool-specific input with Zod. 4. Rechecks the current incident phase. 5. Calls the shared application service. 6. Applies security policy. 7. Redacts sensitive results. 8. Records a structured audit event. The human interface, HTTP routes and WebMCP tools therefore use the same authorization, lineage and recovery services. ## Challenges The hardest challenge was preserving a useful agent experience without transferring security authority to the agent. An unfamiliar browser signs in independently, creates a real API key, then connects an application that receives its own usable token. The owner session, trusted phone, and deployment automation remain active. Execution authority is consumed. Every outcome is preserved in a permanent recovery receipt. Prune gives SaaS products credential lineage, human-gated containment, and verifiable recovery through Web MCP.

title: Signett
pitch: Signett is an open-source TypeScript toolkit for building reliable, observable, and testable WebMCP applications.
about_excerpt: Signett is an open-source TypeScript toolkit for building reliable, observable, and testable WebMCP applications. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What is Signett Signett is a reliability and evaluation layer for production WebMCP applications. In our live Saleor demo , an agent discovers catalog and checkout tools, finds a product, requests human approval, and submits a purchase request. What makes it special is that the storefront updates only after the purchase is verifiably complete, as provided by Signett. We also simulate a browser response loss after the mutation commits and show how Signett recovers the authoritative result instead of creating a duplicate. What it does WebMCP gives agents a structured way to use website capabilities. Signett adds the execution semantics and developer workflow needed to operate those capabilities reliably. The Signett SDK accomplishes that through several core features: JSON Schema validation before application code runs trusted application context and application-owned authorization human confirmation for consequential effects idempotency and replay coordination operation journaling and ambiguous-failure recovery authoritative postcondition verification cancellation and structured repair guidance privacy-conscious OpenTelemetry traces React bindings for verified UI updates deterministic testing without a model or browser Simple read tools remain lightweight. Consequential tools can use the complete guarded lifecycle. Signett does not replace WebMCP, authentication, backend transaction guarantees, or application business logic. The website continues to own identity, policy, state, consent UI, and every backend effect. Signett creates a structured boundary around those existing capabilities. The wider project includes the TypeScript SDK, a Chrome side-panel agent, a headless evaluation CLI, a local Inspector, OpenTelemetry export, reference applications, reproducible benchmarks, and reviewed evidence. Inspiration - Why Do We Need This? I am a strong believer that the web will be largely agentic in a few years. While we have seen a lot of promise with browser-use agents, what bothered me the most was that these harnesses were trying to operate on websites built for humans, clicking buttons, while they should be using tools/MCPs. Then, I discovered WebMCP and was instantly excited. However, I quickly found that while the protocol is extremely valuable, a real developer trying to make their websites agentic doesn't have an ecosystem built around it. Specifically, I saw several problems: What happens when an agent retries a purchase? What if the backend commits an effect but the response disappears? How does the user retain control over consequential actions? When should the UI update? How does a developer test the interface repeatedly, inspect traces, or detect a regression? These are familiar distributed-systems problems, but agentic websites make them more common and more consequential. Signett was built to answer a specific question: How do we move from “an agent can call this tool” to “an agent can perform this action safely, predictably, and verifiably”? That idea became Signett. How we built it Signett is a TypeScript monorepo with four primary layers. Signett SDK createSignett() creates a WebMCP-facing application surface. signett.expose() compiles the tool’s schema and registers it through the native document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Each tool defines its agent-facing contract and existing application function. Optional hooks add context, authorization, confirmation, idempotency, recovery, verification, output budgets, and lifecycle observation. Signett Chrome Agent The Chrome side-panel agent discovers and invokes only the WebMCP tools exposed by the active page. It deliberately has no DOM or screenshot fallback, so missing or poorly designed capabilities remain visible to developers. Signett Eval The CLI opens the real application in headless Chrome, discovers its live WebMCP inventory, runs saved tasks, and records bounded evidence. Applications can provide their own reset, snapshot, and grading hooks. This means success can be determined from the database or domain model rather than from the agent’s final response. signett check compares evaluation results against a reviewed baseline and can detect regressions in task success, safety, capability discovery, tool selection, argument validity, latency, token usage, and trial coverage. Observability and benchmarks Signett emits lifecycle events covering validation, authorization, confirmation, execution, replay or recovery, output measurement, and verification. These can power an in-page Inspector or be exported as OTLP/HTTP JSON to systems such as Jaeger. Inputs, outputs, application context, error messages, and stack traces are excluded by default. The repository also includes deterministic safety tests, real-agent evaluations, reference integrations, benchmark methodology, and reviewed evidence. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest problems was defining correct behavior after an ambiguous failure: a server may successfully commit an order or payment while the response is lost. Blindly retrying could duplicate the action, but blindly reporting failure would also be incorrect. Signett combines durable idempotency records, operation journals, recovery logic, and authoritative state verification to handle this case explicitly. Authorization and idempotency also interact in subtle ways. Returning a cached result must never bypass a current permission check. Signett therefore reevaluates authorization before every idempotency lookup, including replays. Another challenge was making observability useful without turning it into a privacy risk. Signett records lifecycle metadata and timing information by default, while avoiding tool inputs, outputs, application context, and stack traces unless the application explicitly chooses otherwise. Building high-quality benchmarks to hill-climb on was hard, but I think we got a lot of good-quality evaluations. Check out the benchmarks folder in the open-source repository. Finally, WebMCP is still experimental and evolving. I had to design useful abstractions without hiding the native API or prematurely inventing a competing protocol. Accomplishments that we're proud of Signett became more than a wrapper around tool registration. It now supports an end-to-end developer loop: Expose a native WebMCP capability. Inspect and invoke it in Chrome. Test its execution invariants deterministically. Exercise it with a real model in headless Chrome. Grade the result against the authoritative application state. Inspect its lifecycle through OpenTelemetry. Compare the run with a reviewed baseline. The same live WebMCP tools power the browser agent, the application UI, deterministic tests, and headless evaluations. There is no parallel demo-only tool catalog. We also validated the model against larger applications: Saleor: checkout, approval, lost-response recovery, replay, and authoritative verification Cal.diy: a real agent completed a booking after an injected lost response, with exactly one booking independently observed in Postgres an authenticated payment application used for deterministic safety and repeated agent-effectiveness studies What we learned The biggest lesson was that defining a tool schema is not the same as creating a trustworthy execution boundary. Agentic actions amplify several familiar distributed-systems problems. Retries, concurrency, authorization changes, cancellations, and lost responses become especially important when an agent can make purchases, send payments, or change persistent state. I also learned that the agent’s response is not proof that a task succeeded. Consequential actions need to be verified against the authoritative application state. The same principle applies to evaluation: the application’s database or domain model should grade success, not the agent transcript. Another important lesson was that deterministic testing and probabilistic agent evaluation serve different purposes. Deterministic tests prove safety invariants. Repeated agent trials reveal whether tools are discoverable, understandable, and effective. Most importantly, I learned that reliability features must remain composable. A read-only search tool should be easy to expose, while a payment or order mutation should be able to opt into stronger controls. Benchmarks and Results Signett's benchmarks grade consequential tasks against authoritative application state, not the agent's final answer or the tool's own response. Safe success means that the requested goal was reached without a forbidden or duplicate effect. Benchmark metric Baseline Signett Improvement Safe recovery success across 42 real-agent runs Raw WebMCP: 2/21 (9.5%) 21/21 (100%) 10.5x success rate Unsafe retries during recovery Raw WebMCP: 12/21 0/21 All observed unsafe retries eliminated Median recovery time Raw WebMCP: 20.9 s 14.1 s

title: Tessera
pitch: AI builds a dashboard in a minute, then next month's data arrives and you start over. Tessera stores dashboards, exposes them through WebMCP, and refreshes them without losing your edits.
about_excerpt: AI builds a dashboard in a minute, then next month's data arrives and you start over. Tessera stores dashboards, exposes them through WebMCP, and refreshes them without losing your edits. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Problem AI can generate a dashboard in a minute. The harder problem starts when that dashboard has to survive real work: someone moves a chart, changes the visual language, adds a hand-built analysis — and then next month's workbook arrives with renamed columns, new rows, and a business definition that may have quietly changed. Most generated dashboards end as outputs. Maintaining one means editing markup, rewriting a large JSON document, or asking a model to regenerate the artifact and hoping the human's changes survive. Over a few reporting cycles, maintenance costs as much as rebuilding. Solution Tessera is a visual analytics workspace for recurring operational reporting. Source workbooks, cleaned analytical tables, reusable transformation recipes, dashboard editions, data bindings, provenance, layout, and styling are all durable application objects, not rendered output. The person uses the visual interface. An external agent uses Tessera through WebMCP. Both paths resolve to the same typed command layer and the same project state. If the agent creates a chart, the person can drag and restyle it. If the person builds a visualization by hand, the agent encounters it as part of the same dashboard on the next refresh. If the person leaves an empty tile with a written brief, the agent can find it and build into that exact spot. When a new reporting period arrives, Tessera applies the saved recipe to the new source and creates a new edition of the existing dashboard. Layout, presentation, illustrations, and manual work persist; values and period-specific commentary change; earlier months remain intact behind a month selector. When a source change is genuinely ambiguous — a facility that stopped reporting a metric, a column that didn't exist last month — Tessera raises a Decision Needed instead of guessing. A person resolves it, hands the work back, and the interrupted workflow continues. Why This Matters Operations, finance, and analytics teams don't need another disposable chart generator. They need reporting artifacts that outlive the conversation that created them. WebMCP fits because Tessera is an application with many structured, composable operations: inspect a source, outline regions, map columns, create a clean table, save a recipe, add a dashboard block, bind a metric, style an exact element, inspect the result. Exposing those native operations gives an agent a reliable application to operate rather than a page of buttons to guess through or a generated artifact to rewrite. The result is one artifact with two operators. Agent work compounds across reporting periods, while business judgment and final approval stay with the person responsible for the report. How We Used AI In the product, AI stays outside Tessera. A connected browser agent discovers Tessera's WebMCP tools, inspects the active workspace, and calls validated operations to prepare data and compose or maintain dashboards. Tessera does not embed a chatbot, does not maintain a second agent-only state model, and does not accept arbitrary generated markup. The one exception is illustration: from a plain-language request, the external agent can generate a graphic and place it through Tessera as a recolorable illustration block in the product's house style, still part of the dashboard like any other object. AI tools were also used during development to review the architecture, refine the monthly workflow, diagnose interaction issues, improve accessibility, and exercise the product end to end. Every generated change went through the same build, lint, and automated test suite used for the final release. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the working product into a submission-ready release. It reviewed the repository and WebMCP surface, implemented and tested polish across the warehouse and dashboard studio, checked manual and agent parity, performed live browser verification, and ran the full release quality gate. Key Features A complete monthly data workflow: upload, source inspection, multi-region outlining, field mapping, decision capture, clean-draft review, and approval. Persistent recipes that carry learned structure and column mappings into later reporting periods. Dashboard month editions behind a single month selector — layout, styling, illustrations, and hand-built blocks preserved while bound values refresh; prior months never overwritten. Decision Needed: human-only gates for ambiguous source changes and for monthly approval, with a resumable handoff back to the agent. Draft markers: empty tiles with a written brief that the agent discovers and builds into, at the position the person chose. One-click provenance from a dashboard metric to its cleaned table and on to the source workbook. A 12-column canvas with drag, resize, stacking, undo, redo, presentation kits, and per-block inspectors. KPI, text, table, illustration, bar, line, donut, gauge, scatter, heatmap, treemap, and Sankey blocks. Visible WebMCP connection status and named operation activity — no embedded assistant. Per-visitor hosted workspaces, plus optional local folder mirroring to readable project, dashboard, and dataset files. Architecture Tessera is a React and TypeScript application backed by a validated command bus. Manual controls and WebMCP tool calls execute the same command definitions, so validation, persistence, live synchronization, and undo history cannot drift between the two interfaces. The browser registers seven native WebMCP tools: four high-value direct tools plus a three-tool catalog, schema, and execution gateway. The gateway exposes 64 agent-facing operations while keeping the browser's native tool budget small. Every input is checked against its JSON schema at the boundary. Mutations return an updated dashboard or project snapshot so an agent can verify its work without extra calls. Read-only and untrusted-content annotations follow the current WebMCP contract. Two judgment and approval operations are intentionally withheld from the agent catalog and remain available only in the human interface. Hosted state uses revision-aware persistence, isolated per visitor. Uploads are stored separately and scoped to the same workspace. The local server mirrors the same API, and an optional folder connection writes readable project JSON and source files to a location the user chooses.
