title: YOZZ: Zero-knowledge webmail
pitch: 🗿 Browser decrypt; server no key. WebMCP only way for 🤖. Server MCP cannot 🙅‍♀️.
about_excerpt: 🗿 Browser decrypt; server no key. WebMCP only way for 🤖. Server MCP cannot 🙅‍♀️. Like 1 Comment Story Updates YOZZ's three-pane inbox with multiple email addresses and a message open Inspiration YOZZ started with a personal problem. For years, I relied on Gmail’s “Send as” feature to send emails from my custom domains. When Google announced it was discontinuing the feature , I went looking for an alternative. After days of searching, I was unable to find anything that satisfied the privacy, aesthetics, and convenience that I was after. That is why I built YOZZ: a zero-knowledge, modern-looking webmail client that is private by design, clean to use, and accessible anywhere in the browser. Zero-knowledge password managers were the main inspiration for YOZZ: secrets are decrypted on the user’s device while the servers only handle data it cannot understand. What if I apply the same idea to webmail? Modern email interfaces and zero-knowledge cryptography were well-established and easy to learn from existing solutions. The real challenge lay in the networking: client-side JavaScript cannot open raw TCP sockets, so a direct connection to mail servers via IMAP/SMTP is impossible. Moving the connection to a backend server would defeat the whole zero-knowledge premise. The entire feasibility of YOZZ came down to whether I could solve that one fundamental constraint. Having previously built a zero-dependency ACME client in TypeScript, I knew low-level cryptographic handshakes were viable in pure JS. The missing link was the transport layer. The breakthrough was a Cloudflare Worker acting as a relay: tunneling WebSocket traffic from the browser into raw TCP connections to the mail servers, while ensuring TLS terminated exclusively between the JS in the browser and the mail servers. The worker sees only encrypted bytes. Once that proof-of-concept held up, I knew the architecture was sound. YOZZ has since become the daily driver for all my custom-domain email. The biggest capability YOZZ lacked was AI assistance. Moving my daily email workflow from Gmail to YOZZ made that clear: I had grown used to Gemini inside Gmail and to ChatGPT’s Gmail connector for more complex tasks spanning my other connected services. I first considered connecting YOZZ to ChatGPT through a conventional connector or server-side MCP. But YOZZ’s service has no readable access to mailbox credentials or mail, and giving it that access would break the product’s zero-knowledge premise. I also tested local models through Transformers.js, but the models I tried were either not reliable enough for work as sensitive as email or too slow and resource-hungry on my hardware. When this challenge introduced me to WebMCP, I realised that a capable external agent could instead work through the user’s active YOZZ client. What it does YOZZ is a zero-knowledge webmail client for supported IMAP and SMTP accounts you already own. Its server-side infrastructure receives no plaintext mailbox credentials or messages. Received mail remains with the existing provider and is cached only on the user’s device. Credentials, drafts and any sent-mail copies stored on the server are encrypted by the web app before reaching D1. YOZZ’s web app and the mail provider are the TLS endpoints. Since browser APIs cannot open the required TCP connections to mail servers, the relay simply forwards the ciphertext between them. It never receives the TLS session keys, mailbox passwords or plaintext messages, so YOZZ’s server-side infrastructure cannot decrypt the traffic it carries. This boundary is deliberately narrow. The existing mail provider retains its access, and an external agent can read mail returned through WebMCP. The user chooses which agent receives that mail; YOZZ’s servers gain no readable access in either case. YOZZ does retain limited operational metadata. “Zero-knowledge” here applies to stored vault contents and traffic crossing the relay. It does not make email end-to-end encrypted or protect against malicious client code delivered to the browser. After the user logs in, YOZZ registers six focused WebMCP tools: get_addresses : list the configured addresses. get_threads : search and read conversations without marking them as read. update_threads : mark conversations read or unread, star them, archive them or move them to Trash. save_draft : create a message, prepare a reply or update an existing draft. delete_draft : discard a draft, recoverable for 30 days. navigate : open a conversation or draft in the interface. Opening an unread conversation marks it read, just like the user’s own click. navigate is the only tool that changes what the user is currently looking at. The other tools work in the background without taking the user away from their current task. Before WebMCP, every multi-message task had to be completed manually inside YOZZ. Now the user and agent can divide the work: the agent can summarise unread mail across every configured address, find messages about a trip or purchase, clean up selected low-value threads and prepare a reply. The resulting draft can be opened inside YOZZ for review, but no WebMCP tool can send mail . Sending is a separate action in YOZZ's visible composer. A browser-capable agent may offer to perform that action, but only after surfacing the draft and requesting the user's confirmation. Why WebMCP belongs here For these workflows, a conventional server-side MCP integration would require moving readable mailbox access from the web app into server-side infrastructure, breaking YOZZ’s zero-knowledge premise. It would need mailbox credentials, an equivalent authorisation token or a server-terminated mail session. Any of those would give YOZZ’s infrastructure readable mailbox access it deliberately does not have. WebMCP instead uses the capabilities already present in the user’s logged-in web app, allowing an agent chosen by the user to work with mail without giving YOZZ’s servers new access. The immediate audience is people who already use custom-domain email or other IMAP and SMTP accounts and want webmail without entrusting another client operator with their credentials. YOZZ supports multiple inbound and send-only addresses, and Google’s upcoming change gives some of these users a concrete reason to seek another client. How I built it YOZZ is a deployed TypeScript application whose server-side infrastructure runs on Cloudflare Workers. Its web app implements TLS 1.3, X.509 certificate validation, IMAP, SMTP and MIME message handling. The API Worker handles three things: User authentication. Storing and updating ciphertext vault records in D1, including records for mailbox credentials, drafts and sent-mail copies. All are encrypted by the web app before reaching the Worker. The WebSocket-to-TCP relay. I initially considered making YOZZ accountless, with users connecting their IMAP and SMTP accounts directly in the web app. That would work on one device, but I wanted to access the same mailbox configuration across multiple devices. I therefore introduced authentication and an encrypted vault. The user’s password or a PRF-capable passkey provides the client-side material needed to unlock the vault. YOZZ’s server stores the wrapped data-encryption key and ciphertext vault records alongside the authentication and operational metadata described above. This provides multi-device access without giving the server the key needed to decrypt mailbox credentials, drafts or settings. The WebMCP tools call the same application services as the user interface. Tool actions immediately appear in the product and follow the same state rules as user actions. I started working on YOZZ on August 16, 2026. The challenge began on August 25, and the first WebMCP implementation was committed on August 26. Before the challenge, YOZZ was already a deployed mail client but had no agent tools. During the challenge, I added the six-tool WebMCP layer, defined the WebMCP no-send and untrusted-content boundaries, added behavioural tests and built the judge infrastructure. The existing TLS, X.509, IMAP, SMTP and MIME implementation is the foundation this extension works through, not challenge-period work. YOZZ lives alongside dozens of other projects in my private monorepo. That private repository contains YOZZ’s original development history and is the source of the dates above. Open-sourcing YOZZ was always part of the plan so others could inspect its implementation and evaluate its zero-knowledge claims. To do so without exposing unrelated private code, I built and published OpenRepo , a tool for cleanly exporting individual projects from a monorepo. I used OpenRepo to publish the standalone YOZZ repository . Its public history contains exported snapshots rather than the private monorepo’s original commits, so it documents the before-and-after contents rather than the original source chronology. v1.0.0 , exported on August 26 before the first WebMCP source commit, contains the existing mail cl
video_title: YOZZ: zero-knowledge webmail your AI agent can use (WebMCP demo)
video_transcript_excerpt: Hello, I'm Jason. I built a zero-knowledge webmail client called Yoz. Zero-knowledge roughly means the servers can't see your stuff. So, how is Yoz zero-knowledge? When you save sensitive data, your browser encrypts it right there on your machine before sending it off. Yoz's servers only ever store and return scrambled unreadable ciphertext. We don't hold the key and we can't see what's inside. For example, this API response contains my saved mail account, but the actual details are returned as ciphertext. Only the unlocked web app can turn that ciphertext back into something meaningful, in this case, the email address you see here. Mail traffic follows the same principle. The TLS connection runs between the Yoz web app in your browser and the mail server you use. Yoz's relay only transports encrypted traffic. The session keys exist at those two endpoints, so the relay cannot decrypt what passes through it. In short, Yoz's servers are blind. We cannot read your mail. So, how can Yoz connect with AI agents? A traditional server-side MCP is impossible because Yoz's servers are blind, cannot read mail. So, we need something that works purely on the client side that also connects to AI. Wait a second. Isn't this exactly what web MCP's for? Let's see this in action now. Here, I have Yoz open in ChatGPT desktop. Yoz registers six web MCP tools directly with the page. I give ChatGPT a simple request to summarize the inbox. ChatGPT gives me a clear summary of the mailbox. Notice how it also flags the suspicious confirm your mailbox email. Yoz marks tools that return mail as carrying untrusted content. This tells the agent to treat what it reads with caution. By design, every tool except one works in the background. So, you can use Yoz while the agent is working. The one exception is the navigate tool, which is used when the agent needs to show you something for review. Let's ask ChatGPT to reply to Sam about the lunch. It saves the reply as a draft, then uses the navigate tool to open the draft editor in Yoz. Now, I can review the message and press send myself. Together, these tools let your agents read, organize, and draft mail through the unlocked web app without giving Yoz's servers any new access. That is how Yoz brings capable AI to your mailbox without giving up its zero knowledge design.

title: AgentDesk
pitch: A capability-virtualization runtime that gives WebMCP agents the right tools at the right time—with human approval, receipts, and rollback for consequential actions.
about_excerpt: A capability-virtualization runtime that gives WebMCP agents the right tools at the right time—with human approval, receipts, and rollback for consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Desk Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a direct, typed way to work with agents. But a production application may contain dozens or hundreds of operations. Publishing all of them at once creates a flat, expensive tool surface, makes selection less reliable, and places dangerous actions beside harmless reads. AgentDesk started from a simple question: what if the WebMCP tool registry behaved like a task-aware interface instead of a static API dump? What it does AgentDesk is a capability-virtualization and governance runtime for WebMCP applications. The Meridian Ops demo contains 79 internal capabilities across customers, orders, inventory, shipping, billing, support, and reports. The agent initially sees only four bootstrap tools. When it describes a task, AgentDesk: ranks the catalog against the task and current application context; dynamically registers up to five relevant, typed WebMCP tools; retires stale tools while leaving structured tombstones for clients with cached tool lists; explains unavailable actions and suggests what can make them possible; separates reads, ordinary writes, and consequential actions; returns approval-required immediately for consequential work instead of leaving a tool call hanging; shows the human an exact before/after preview; executes only after human approval and re-checks state at commit time; returns durable receipts describing what actually changed; supports reviewable multi-step plans, idempotency, verification, rollback, and human reconciliation when an outcome cannot be proven. Guided execution keeps the agent and person in the same application: tool calls navigate to, reveal, and highlight the affected object while the structured result remains authoritative. A Baseline mode exposes the full catalog so judges can compare the two approaches using the same tasks and data. Why WebMCP is essential This experience depends on the page and the agent sharing one live application context. AgentDesk registers tools directly with document.modelContext ; the browser page owns capability state, approval UI, and the visible business data. A server-only MCP integration cannot provide the same shared attention, dynamic page-scoped registry, or approval card beside the exact value being changed. The result is a collaboration model that was difficult before: the agent can move quickly through structured operations while the human sees the affected state, governs consequential decisions, and receives proof afterward. How we built it The judged path is a TypeScript SDK, @agentdesk/webmcp , with no backend, database, model API, or external runtime service. A document-lifetime runtime owns the catalog, deterministic router, availability checks, policy engine, approvals, plans, audit events, receipts, and persistence. A single ToolSurfaceManager publishes capabilities through the WebMCP adapter; React only observes runtime state and renders the product experience. Dynamic retirement uses abort signals and tombstone tools. A stable invoke_capability gateway covers clients whose discovery lags behind registry changes. Evidence is detached and frozen at system boundaries. Idempotency claims occur before dispatch, and any post-dispatch uncertainty becomes an explicit indeterminate state rather than a fabricated success or safe retry. We also built a real-browser P0 harness that exercises native registration, same-turn dynamic tools, retirement, stale calls, re-registration, typed execution, approvals, and compatibility behavior. Challenges The hardest work was not registering a tool—it was making stateful tool lifecycles honest under retries, reloads, stale client snapshots, approval delays, partial failures, and interrupted rollback. We repeatedly tested the boundaries where a system is tempted to overclaim: whether a write actually landed, whether a rollback truly restored prior state, whether evidence can be mutated, whether a repeated call can execute twice, and whether a benchmark accidentally rewards AgentDesk by construction. Those failures now have explicit domain states and regression tests. Accomplishments A working, WebMCP-native SDK rather than a one-page integration A complete operations product spanning seven business domains Task-scoped dynamic tool registration over a 79-capability catalog Human approval with visual diffs and post-action receipts Governed multi-step plans exposed through WebMCP Guided execution that keeps human attention aligned with agent actions A reproducible Baseline-versus-AgentDesk benchmark Live validation in the Codex in-app browser and Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled An open-source MIT-licensed repository and static public deployment What we learned The registry itself can be an interaction surface. Registering, retiring, and rewriting capabilities based on task and state gives an agent clearer affordances than another layer of prompting. We also learned that governance needs more than a confirmation modal: it needs explicit acting identity, execution-time re-checks, idempotency, evidence, and a truthful representation of unknown outcomes. What's next AgentDesk can become an adoption layer for complex web applications: generated capabilities from existing application schemas, runtime-configurable routing, durable cross-session reconciliation, application adapters, and a browser extension that helps legacy sites expose governed WebMCP capabilities. The same model applies beyond operations software to editors, design tools, IDEs, and admin platforms. Built With playwright pnpm react typescript vite vitest webmcp Try it out webmcp.agentsdesk.dev webmcp.agentsdesk.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Amein Eskinder OSMAN AHMED Luc Mwansa Like Share this project: Updates Amein Eskinder started this project — Sep 03, 2026 12:45 PM EDT
video_title: Agentdesk
video_transcript_excerpt: AI agents can operate websites, but giving them every available tool creates confusion, risk, and unnecessary context. Agent desk turns web MCP capabilities into governed workflows. It reveals only the tools relevant to the current task while keeping consequential actions under human control. Here, a crew is stranded aboard Asteria. The agent discovers the mission state and prepares one rescue plan. Reserve oxygen, assign the drone, reroute power, and launch. These are real staged operations, not a description written by the agent. Agent desk derives the proposed changes from the application's own state. Nothing launches until a person authorizes the complete plan. After approval, every operation executes once, is verified, and produces evidence. The mission completes and the crew is recovered. The rescue interface is only one demonstration. The same agent desk runtime works inside an ordinary business application without changing its governance model. This application contains 79 capabilities. For Alice Johnson's shipping request, agent desk routes the task and exposes only five relevant tools. The agent finds Alice's unshipped order, confirms that she paid an $18 shipping fee, and proposes a refund. Because the refund changes customer and financial state, execution stops at a visible approval boundary. The human sees the exact impact before deciding. After approval, agent desk performs the refund once and verifies the result against live application state. The final evidence connects the operation to its consequences. Shipping is refunded, the customer receives an $18 credit, and the invoice becomes partially refunded. This governance also improves efficiency. The baseline exposes 79 tools and 28,894 bytes of schemas. Agent desk uses five tools and 3,776 bytes. 93.7% fewer tools and 86.9% less schema. Agent desk makes browser agents focused, observable, and safe enough to trust.

title: Alza
pitch: A floor plan is coordinates, not buttons. Alza publishes its geometry as 31 typed tools, so your agent draws the plan, checks its own work, buys from another origin, and raises it to walkable 3D.
about_excerpt: A floor plan is coordinates, not buttons. Alza publishes its geometry as 31 typed tools, so your agent draws the plan, checks its own work, buys from another origin, and raises it to walkable 3D. Like Comment Story Updates 3d-orbit-hero traced-over-the-drawing plan-2d tool-runner cross-origin-supplier supplier-product-placed constraint-engine agent-notes-on-ambiguity approval-gate approval-rejected-feed agent-authored-pieces catalogue-3d-previews 3d-top 3d-doors-open 3d-walk-eye-level Inspiration I had a floor plan as a photo and wanted to see it in 3D. That should be a solved problem, but every tool I found wanted me to redraw it by hand, wall by wall, in an editor built for a mouse. So I tried handing it to an AI agent instead. That was worse. An agent can read a screenshot and it can talk about a floor plan, but it cannot use one. There is no button that means "make this wall four point six metres" . There is no DOM worth scraping. A drawing is coordinates, joints and constraints, and none of that is reachable from the outside. WebMCP looked like the missing half. Not a way to describe the page to an agent — a way to hand it the actual geometry. What it does Alza is a floor-plan editor that publishes its own tools. You draw walls, rooms, doors, windows and furniture in a metric 2D canvas, then raise it to a 3D model you can walk through. An agent joins the same live page and works with the same tools you do. The demo is the honest test: I gave the agent a photo of a plan it had never seen. The drawing carries no scale, so it asked for one real dimension , set everything from that, and traced it — 12 walls, 14 openings, 10 rooms, 34 pieces of furniture . The drawing underneath is the source photo. The dark geometry on top is what the agent built from it. When the catalogue had no honest match for a symbol, it modelled the piece itself: an L-shaped sofa, a corner shower, a compact bath, a fitted L wardrobe, a washing machine Then it checked itself. The constraint engine reports in metres — this wardrobe crosses that wall, this basin blocks that door's swing — and the agent reads the complaint and fixes it. And where it could not be sure, it said so instead of guessing: it left a note that one symbol was ambiguous and explained how it had read it. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript, Three.js. No backend at all — it is a static site, and plans never leave the browser. The 31 tools are typed and registered on document.modelContext at load: document.modelContext.registerTool(descriptor, { signal, exposedTo }) There is a 32nd that only exists when it is relevant: select a wall in the UI and extend_selected_wall appears; deselect and it is gone, unregistered by aborting the AbortSignal its descriptor was registered with. The constraint engine is oriented-rectangle SAT: furniture against walls, door swing paths, whether an opening fits the wall it sits on, whether a room has a door at all. The part I am most pleased with is the partner. Nordika is a genuinely separate website on its own origin, deployed to a different host. It registers its own tools with exposedTo , and the studio discovers them with getTools({ fromOrigins }) and calls them with executeTool() . One instruction crosses that boundary and a real product lands in the plan at its real size — with no server anywhere in the path. Challenges I ran into The plan I first traced turned out to be copyrighted. I had pulled it off Google without thinking, and by the time I noticed, it was committed to a public repo — and the whole demo model was traced from it, so the layout was derived too, not just the image. Deleting the file did nothing: git keeps history. I deleted the repo, generated my own plan, and re-traced everything from scratch. That cost a full rebuild of the model, the film and the screenshots. The video fought me for a long time. The 3D looked juddery no matter what I did, and it took a while to find out why: the tool I was recording with caps at 25 fps and renders in software. Continuous camera motion at 25 fps with no motion blur reads as stepping, and no amount of conforming fixes it. I switched to real GPU screen capture at 60 fps and it went away. The worst bug was silent. The production build was shipping without its cross-origin headers, so the partner iframe was never allowed to publish its tools — the flagship feature, quietly dead on the live URL. The cause: Vite loads .env into import.meta.env but not into process.env , and the plugin that writes the headers was reading process.env . It failed by emitting a header that looked plausible. And building the demo found real bugs in my own app: the walk camera passed straight through walls and furniture, looking around orbited instead of turning your head, and the 2D auto-fit anchored the plan to a corner instead of centring it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The agent recovered from its own mistake without help. Running in Codex, it invented a wall id, the tool answered Wall "wall_10" not found , and its next call used the real one — then get_issues came back "0 issues — the plan is clean" . I did not script that. It is what happens when tool errors are sentences instead of failure codes. The constraint engine caught something about the drawing itself. It rejected the catalogue's standard 1.70 m bath — "Bathtub crosses wall" — because that alcove is 1.68 m wall to wall, 1.58 m clear. The drawing sizes its own bath shorter, at 1.53 m, so that is what got modelled instead. A geometry checker noticing that a drawing is tight is exactly the point. And the second origin is real . A different site on a different host, not a folder pretending to be one. What I learned That "the agent can see the page" and "the agent can use the page" are completely different problems, and only the second one matters. That an error message is an interface . Half of what makes the agent look competent is that when it gets something wrong, the tool tells it what is wrong in words it can act on. That degrading matters more than I expected. Cross-origin discovery is not in every runtime yet — ChatGPT and Codex register the page's own tools fine but fall back to postMessage for the partner. Because the same protocol runs over both, the feature gets quieter instead of disappearing. And that a build can fail silently and look fine . I now check the artefact, not the exit code. What's next for Alza Multi-floor plans, and stairs between them Export to IFC, so the model can leave for real CAD Cost and materials as tools, so an agent can answer "what does this room cost to finish" from the same geometry A shared session, so a person and an agent can work the same plan at the same time and see each other move Why this generalizes None of this is really about architecture. The pattern underneath is that a page already holds a rigorous model — geometry, a cart, a spreadsheet, a timeline, an audio track — and right now the only way an agent can reach it is by pretending to be a mouse. WebMCP lets the page hand over the model itself, with its validation still attached, so the agent works on meaning instead of pixels. I picked the hardest case I could think of to make that argument. A canvas has no DOM to scrape, and 5 cm of error is a wall through a sofa — which is exactly why the app can prove whether the agent got it right. If the pattern holds here, it holds for the easier ones. What building this taught me about the spec I ran into four of the explainer's open questions as actual problems, not as reading material. Here is what I did about each, in case any of it is useful to the people writing the standard. User prompting and elicitation ( #165 , #50 ). I needed this on day one. A tool that wipes someone's floor plan cannot just run because a model decided to call it. My answer lives entirely in the page: a tool marked destructive does not execute when it is called — it parks as a request bar in the UI, and the promise stays pending until a person presses Approve or Reject. Reject hands the agent an actionable failure ("the human declined; ask them what to do instead") rather than an error, so it recovers instead of retrying. The registration AbortSignal releases the request if the agent gives up first. It works, but every site has to build its own, and the confirmation UI is only as trustworthy as the page drawing it — which is the argument for the browser mediating it instead. One thing I hit there and want to flag: destructiveHint is in MCP's ToolAnnotations but not in WebMCP's, which right now defines only readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . I keep it on my own descriptors and enforce it page-side, so nothing depends on the browser passing it through. But if the browser is ever going to mediate confirmation itself, it needs some way to know which tools are destructive — so aligning the two sets looks worth doing. Multimodal input and output ( #41 , #86 , #81 ). This is the gap I felt hardest. Tracing a plan means the agent has to s

video_transcript_excerpt: This house was drawn, measured, furnished, and checked by an AI agent. It never touched a mouse. Agents can't drag a wall. A floor plan is coordinates, joints, and constraints. There is no button that means make this wall 4.6 m. And there is no DOM to scrape. Every trick an agent has has nothing to grab onto. So, Alza stops pretending the page is clickable and hands the geometry over directly. 31 typed tools published to the page that the agent calls the way you would use the editor. Nothing gets installed. Alza publishes its tools to the page, so any agent looking at the tab already sees them. You give it a photo of the plan and one sentence it asks for one real dimension and sets the scale from that. Give it a plan to reproduce and it draws. Walls, then the doors and windows that sit on them, then rooms, then the furniture. The same actions your mouse fires against one shared model. With every call logged on the page as it happens, and it checks its own work. A wardrobe placed through a wall, the constraint engine says so in meters, and the agent reads the complaint and fixes it. You never see the mistake. The furniture shop is a different website. Different company, different origin, publishing its own tools and sharing them with this page. One instruction crosses that boundary with no server in between and a real product lands in the plan at its real size, where the checker can tell you whether it fits before you buy it. And when the agent reaches for something destructive, it doesn't get it. It gets a request. The call waits on the page until a person decides, and if the answer is no, the agent is told so in words it can act on. Then the plan rises. Walls with real openings, doors on hinges that actually swing, and the whole house turning in front of you. Then step inside and walk it, room by room, at eye level before anyone has built a thing. Alza. 31 tools, one shared model, and a plan your agent can actually build. Open source. And live now.

title: BashMCP: Give agents a terminal for your website
pitch: Add one line of code to expose WebMCP actions as composable shell commands. Agents can inspect, filter, and chain them, saving hundreds of tool calls and up to 83% of token usage.
about_excerpt: Add one line of code to expose WebMCP actions as composable shell commands. Agents can inspect, filter, and chain them, saving hundreds of tool calls and up to 83% of token usage. Like Comment Story Updates 10/10 correct versus 2/10 natively, with 59–75% fewer tokens and 99–100% fewer calls and bytes. The same real agent and task: both carts correct, with 17 calls natively versus 3 with BashMCP. Live-store turn collapse: 517 host-visible calls become 2; 1.15 MB returned becomes 4.4 KB. One WebMCP tool named bash compiles site tools into /bin; tool save registers a new WebMCP tool. A saved pipeline becomes a WebMCP tool that the next agent finds and runs without being told. A browser-native computer: site and network files, typed commands with help, and persistent SQLite. BashMCP runs on any website, with or without existing tools; Shopify is the worked example. BashMCP: a command line inside any website. One script tag adds a site-side runtime above the WebMCP standard. WebMCP makes a website callable. BashMCP makes it a computer, and the computer gets better every visit. <script src="https://bashmcp.apptory.ai/bashmcp.js" data-bashmcp data-ui="drawer"></script> That is the whole install. BashMCP is a site-side WebMCP composition runtime that installs into an existing website and runs inside that page's live session—not a separate browser VM, a hosted sandbox, or a replacement for the site's tools. One tag boots a sandboxed Unix-like workspace inside the page's own origin. Every WebMCP tool the site already registers compiles into a typed shell command. The page's own network traffic becomes files. An origin-scoped SQLite database persists across tabs and visits. The primary composition entry point registers back into WebMCP as a tool named bash , whose input is { command } —the same string a person would type at a terminal. A separate read-only dom page reader is registered beside it. On the demo store, an agent composes Shopify's ten existing WebMCP tools with jq , grep , sort , and SQL in one auditable run instead of returning every intermediate result to model context. Measured with a blind GPT-5.6 Sol agent on a whole-catalog size audit, that turned 2 of 10 correct into 9 of 10 , while reducing a native median of 315 model-visible host calls to 2 . The person watching sees the same pipeline land in a shared terminal, can rerun or edit it, and can save it as a new WebMCP tool. Fresh agents found and reused such a saved tool unprompted in 14 of 15 measured warm sessions. Same-origin only. No host shell. Shopify is the worked example, not the boundary. The numbers first Same agent, same task, same store, and the same Shopify tools available in both conditions. The prompts never mention bash or prescribe a method. The design and primary metrics were declared before the first benchmark cell ran, exact verifiers read the resulting cart, and every failure is published. Task Site tools alone Same tools, bash beside them What it shows Whole-catalog size audit, clone, n=10 2/10 correct; median 315 calls 9/10 correct; 2 calls Local composition can finish work that serial model-visible calls often cannot Whole-catalog category census, clone, n=10 2/10 correct 10/10 correct The agent chose the shell unprompted in every whole-catalog run Three-step shopper session with a real cart mutation, live store, n=8 3/8 correct 8/8 correct; 41% fewer tokens [23–65%] Query, ranking, and mutation on the production store Single product lookup, control, n=10 10/10 correct 10/10 correct; 2% more tokens ; bash unused in 7/10 The shell adds no value where there is nothing to compose Saved tool reused by a fresh agent, n=15 — 14/15 found it; 15/15 correct; 67% fewer tokens The site's tool surface compounds 500-product catalog audit, n=4 0/4 completed; up to 1,545 calls 3/4 completed in 2–4 calls The benefit increases as the fan-out grows A host-visible call is a call the host makes on the model's behalf whose result enters model context. The site tools invoked inside a bash program still execute against the real application, and every nested call remains visible in the run receipt. BashMCP removes repeated model round trips; it does not hide or eliminate the underlying application work. We make no comparative wall-clock or cost claim. The shell is often slower on a single action, which is why the flat control remains in every results table. The complete methodology, intervals, provenance, and failure ledger are in docs/results.md . Why BashMCP is a strong fit for WebMCP In agent hosts today, broad tasks often become serial tool executions: each result returns to model context before the model decides what to call next. That is exactly right for one action— add this item to my cart or show me that variant . It becomes expensive and brittle when work spans an entire dataset. Auditing every product, ranking a catalog, or cross-referencing endpoints can require hundreds of model-visible round trips, each adding another payload the model must consume before continuing. The tools were not the problem. The turns were. The site's tools remain the correct, authoritative actions. BashMCP never reimplements them. It changes where their composition happens: search, filtering, ranking, joining, and mutation execute as one local program, while only the final answer returns to model context. A host could add batching or a code interpreter for its own users. A site-installed environment has three different advantages: It runs inside the visitor's live session. It can work with the current cart, prices, stock, locale, login state, and the person's own actions without exporting that state into a separate environment. Persistence belongs to the origin. Saved tools, history, and the database remain in the site's browser origin and are available on later visits. The tool surface ships with the site. Anything the site registers can help compatible agents from multiple hosts, and a developer can promote an agent-authored tool into the site's build for future visitors. So we asked: What is the most useful thing a site can register through WebMCP? Our answer was an environment rather than another verb. A better experience for the agent and the person For the agent , BashMCP provides a POSIX-shaped environment it already understands: a filesystem to explore, commands with familiar flags, pipes, exit codes, man pages, --help , jq , grep , sort , and SQL. It does not require a long instruction manual in the tool description. The description points the agent toward cat /README.md , tools , man <command> , and --help ; the environment teaches the rest. In every measured whole-catalog run, the agent selected bash without being told to use it while Shopify's ten original tools remained available. For the person , the developer installation mounts a shared terminal beside the page: One transcript. Two identities: you@host and agent@host . One command history. One filesystem. One SQLite database. You can watch the agent's pipeline land as it runs, press rerun to execute it yourself, arrow back through it, and change one flag. The Runs , Tools , and Events panels show every call, every byte returned, and a receipt for each run—including runs initiated by an agent host rather than the visible terminal. On the live store, ChatGPT's in-app browser sees twelve tools: Shopify's ten plus BashMCP's bash and dom . In a verified run, GPT-5.6 Sol discovered bash unprompted, completed a whole-catalog ranking task with one nested update_cart , and independently verified the resulting cart with a top-level get_cart . What people and agents can do together that was difficult before When a pipeline works, either the person or the agent can save it: tool save cheapest-in-size --description "Cheapest in-stock products in a size" \ --schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"size":{"type":"string"}},"required":["size"]}' < script The script is stored in the origin's SQLite database and registers as a real WebMCP tool immediately and on later visits. It appears: In tools . In man . As a command in /bin . In the agent host's own tool list. With the description, JSON Schema, and access level its author declared. Fresh agents found and reused the saved tool unprompted in 14 of 15 measured warm sessions, and all 15 executions produced the correct answer. tool export prints the production shipping format, so a developer can promote an emergent tool into the site's data-tools configuration. The loop is: A cold agent explores → builds a missing tool → the person inspects, edits, or saves it → a later agent starts with it → the developer ships it to everyone. A static tool surface cannot do this. BashMCP lets use itself reveal which higher-level tools the site should provide. The runtime carries no Shopify-specific knowledge. title: ClauseProof
pitch: Unit tests for contract language. A browser agent stages competing clause readings and repairs a fix through WebMCP tools; the page runs the tests; a person decides.
about_excerpt: Unit tests for contract language. A browser agent stages competing clause readings and repairs a fix through WebMCP tools; the page runs the tests; a person decides. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Contract clauses survive review because both sides read the same words with different pictures in their heads. The difference only shows up after a bad event, when it turns into termination rights, credits, or months of fees. Here is the clause family ClauseProof starts with. A SaaS agreement promises 99.5% monthly uptime, says service credits are the customer's "sole and exclusive remedy," and separately lets either party terminate for an uncured material breach. Now uptime is 98.7% in January and 98.9% in February, the fee is $10,000 a month, eight months remain, and the failure is not cured after notice. One reasonable reading: the customer gets $2,000 in credits and still owes $80,000. Another reasonable reading: the customer gets the same $2,000 and can walk. Nobody noticed at signing. What ClauseProof does ClauseProof runs the clause instead of arguing about it. On one page: A browser agent, working through WebMCP tools the page registers, reads the three clauses and stages two clause-cited readings with constrained semantics: vendor-favorable and customer-favorable. The page executes both readings against the same facts and shows the two commercial futures side by side. In the demo case they are $80,000 apart. Then a what-if: "what if March also missed?" The agent changes the facts through a tool and the page re-runs both readings on the new facts. Facts can change only before the lock. The person locks what the clause should mean: two misses within six months, written notice, a ten-day cure, termination without penalty, credits preserved. This step has no tool. It is person-only, and the agent's tool list changes when it happens. The agent proposes a structured rule. The page compiles the rule into exact clause wording, parses the wording back into a rule, checks that they agree, and runs six outcome examples plus eight altered-rule challenges (mutation tests for the clause boundary). If the candidate is wrong, the page says exactly why. In the walkthrough the agent first tries a three-miss rule: 5 of 6 outcome tests pass, 7 of 8 altered rules are caught, the failing test reports that termination was expected after two misses but the candidate gave none, and the surviving altered rule is "two misses instead of three." The agent repairs only that field and retests: 6 of 6, 8 of 8. The page marks the candidate eligible. The agent still cannot accept. The person accepts. The contract advances to revision 1 and the proof ledger keeps the failed candidate, the counterexample, the repair, the pass, and the acceptance, each attributed to who actually did it. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The agent has to act on live page state inside a governed workflow, not just talk about a document. WebMCP is what makes that safe and useful: Typed actions with live identifiers. Every tool call carries the page's current revision and the IDs returned by earlier steps. A stale revision, a wrong outcome-lock ID, an invented clause, or two readings that agree all fail with a stable error code and one recovery action. The agent cannot drift from what the page actually shows. Structured input, deterministic execution. The agent supplies semantics; the page calculates money, dates, rolling windows, and test results. Input schemas are strict Zod objects compiled to JSON Schema with plain-English descriptions, so a natural prompt like "stage a vendor-favorable and a customer-favorable reading" is enough. Phase-aware registration. The page registers only the tools that make sense in the current phase and revokes the others through the registration AbortSignal . The authority panel on the page renders the same phase-to-tool map the registry enforces, so you can watch the agent's powers change. Machine-readable failure. A failed verification returns the exact failing test and the surviving altered rule in the tool result. That is what turns "try again" into a real repair. Enforced human authority. Lock, accept, and reset are not tools. The WebMCP layer receives a frozen port with no such methods, actor identity is never accepted as input, and the audit trail cannot record an agent action as a person's. What people and agents can do together now Before: a person reads a clause, maybe asks a chatbot whether it "looks safe," and gets prose back. The disagreement stays hidden until the bad month. Now: the agent does the tedious, structured part (stage the competing readings, propose the rule, read the counterexample, repair) inside the page; the page does the part software should own (execute the readings, generate the wording, run the tests); and the person does the two things only a person should do (say what the clause is supposed to mean, and accept the wording that proved it). The whole exchange is recorded with provenance. How WebMCP is implemented Six tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool (with navigator.modelContext accepted for earlier Chrome previews): inspect_contract_case , stage_interpretations , run_contract_crash_test , set_scenario_facts , propose_clarifying_redline , verify_contract_tests . One AbortController per registration generation; a store subscription re-registers the phase's tool set on every state change. ?toolMode=static registers all six for agents that only read tools at load. Strict Zod schemas are the single source of truth. JSON Schema is generated from them with additionalProperties: false , min and max bounds, enums for semantic choices, and field descriptions. Tool results are small JSON objects: ok , data , and one next action when agent work remains. Failures carry a stable code, the current revision, and a recovery action. No stack traces. Annotations mark the read tool readOnlyHint: true and its contract text untrustedContentHint: true . The WebMCP layer imports only a restricted agent port. An architecture check fails the build if it ever imports a human-capable surface. Twelve Playwright tests drive the real registered tools through a fake document.modelContext , including the failed-candidate-to-repair path and the tool list revoking on reset. Built with TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Zod 4, Vitest, Playwright, GitHub Pages. No backend, no external AI API, no upload, no OCR. Limits ClauseProof supports one synthetic SaaS agreement, one adverse scenario, one constrained reading vocabulary, and one canonical clarification grammar. A passing run proves that the generated clause and the structured rule agree and that the rule satisfies the modeled examples and boundaries for this case. It is not formal verification, not arbitrary contract analysis, and not legal advice. The pattern generalizes to any clause with numbers in it (cure periods, notice windows, caps, renewal terms); this is the first instance. Hackathon-period work The repository's history begins August 28, 2026, after the August 25 start of the submission period. The domain engine, the governed workflow, the UI, the WebMCP layer, the release gates, and the adversarial hardening were all built during the challenge. docs/CHANGELOG_HACKATHON.md maps the work to dated commits. Try it (no login) Open https://by42ppcrps-dev.github.io/clauseproof/ in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser (a GPT-5.6 model that supports site tools) or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. The header pill reads WebMCP · dynamic tools live . Paste the prompt shown at the top of the page. The agent stages two readings and runs the crash test; confirm the $80,000 divergence. Click Lock this outcome yourself (2 misses, 6 months, 10-day cure). Watch the agent's tool list change. Paste the next on-page prompt: the agent stages a three-miss candidate, gets 5/6 and 7/8 with the exact counterexample, then repairs to two misses and reaches 6/6 and 8/8. Click Accept tested revision yourself. Revision 1, with the proof ledger. No agent available? Every panel has a manual fallback button that calls the same application service, and ?toolMode=static registers all six tools at once. Source: https://github.com/by42ppcrps-dev/clauseproof (MIT). Built With playwright react typescript vite webmcp zod Try it out by42ppcrps-dev.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Matt Brady Like Share this project: Updates Matt Brady started this project — Sep 02, 2026 04:47 PM EDT

title: Concord — an agent that cannot overpromise
pitch: WebMCP tells an agent what a site can do. Nothing tells it what a site can take back. Concord is that missing layer: it computes what it can honestly promise across sites before contacting any.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tells an agent what a site can do. Nothing tells it what a site can take back. Concord is that missing layer: it computes what it can honestly promise across sites before contacting any. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration An agent books your flight on one site and your hotel on another. Halfway through, the hotel fails. Ask what happens next and no part of the web can answer. inputSchema describes a tool's shape . readOnlyHint describes whether it has an effect . Nothing anywhere describes whether that effect can be reversed — which is the one fact an agent needs to plan across sites rather than to act and hope. So today that gap is filled by a marketplace: an intermediary both businesses have a contract with, which is why one sits between almost every pair of businesses an agent might transact with, taking 15–30% to stand there. The tax is not for the booking. It is for the guarantee. The failure mode of agentic commerce is not the booking going wrong. It is the agent telling you it went fine. What it does Concord is a convention over WebMCP by which any site declares its commitment surface — one of three rungs: Rung Meaning Example reservable hold it, release it, nothing happened an airline seat compensable undoable, but it leaves a mark a hotel charge and refund irreversible it cannot be taken back a government fee …and an in-browser coordinator that computes the strongest honest guarantee across several such sites before contacting any of them — then refuses when the honest answer is that atomicity is not available at any price. Three things to try on the live URL, in ninety seconds: Ask for a flight, a hotel and the visa fee. The agent reads back what it can promise, which step is the point of no return, and which charge becomes briefly real before being reversed. Only then does a Go ahead button exist. Ask for a flight, the visa fee and the entry permit — two things nobody can take back. It says it cannot do that as one commitment, and that nothing has been contacted. There is no button on that answer. Kill the coordinator mid-commitment. Reload. It asks every vendor what actually happened and puts back what can be put back. Why WebMCP, specifically This needs exactly the thing WebMCP uniquely provides and nothing else does: two mutually distrusting origins' authenticated, typed capabilities present in one execution context, under the user's authority, with consent enforced on both sides by the browser. That is not scraping and it is not an API partnership. A participant grants with registerTool 's exposedTo . The embedder grants with allow="tools" . The coordinator must ask by name with getTools({ fromOrigins }) . Three separate grants, none forgeable by any party, and none requiring the participants to have heard of each other. No server anywhere is in the commitment path. How WebMCP is implemented The permission model is registerTool itself. This is the idea the whole project rests on: concord_commit does not exist until a person accepts the exact guarantee they were shown. Not disabled. Not registered. Four read-only tools at boot. concord_explain_guarantee appears once something is proposed. Explaining is not consent, so the surface does not change when the agent reads the guarantee out. A human clicks Accept on the page — registerTool puts concord_commit on the surface. The commitment begins — an AbortController takes it away again, so a second call arriving mid-flight finds nothing to call. toolchange fires on every one of those transitions, and you can watch it in the tool inspector. There is no tool that grants that permission, and there will not be one. An agent has every door; none of them opens this one. The rest of the surface actually used: exposedTo — each participant exposes its tools only to the coordinator's origin, so cross-origin consent is explicit on the participant's side. allow="tools" + Permissions-Policy: tools=(self "…") — the embedder's half of the same consent, verified on every deployed origin. Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 — required for cross-document tool access; without it getTools() returns empty with no error . getTools({ fromOrigins }) — discovery, opt-in on both sides, asked one origin at a time. executeTool(tool, jsonString) — arguments as a JSON string, per Chrome's imperative API. annotations.readOnlyHint — used honestly: true on the two tools that perform nothing, and on nothing that acts. AbortSignal — a deadline on every call, enforced by the coordinator too, which does not assume a participant honours cancellation. modelContext.requestUserInteraction — feature-detected. Chrome 151 does not implement it, so we measure that and use it wherever it exists: a second door onto the same accept, deliberately not a lock. A test hands it a host that approves every request and requires the surface to stay exactly as it was. If asking for attention could produce consent, the central claim would be false. And it fills a gap in the standard rather than decorating it. SPEC §19 proposes the missing annotation upstream: annotations: { readOnlyHint: false, commitment: 'reservable' | 'compensable' | 'irreversible', reverses: 'release_seat', ttlSeconds: 900, } The receipt Every commitment produces an RFC 6962 Merkle receipt in which every statement is signed by the counterparty that made it , with per-vendor ECDSA P-256 keys resolved from each vendor's own origin over TLS — never from a map the coordinator writes. The outcome is derived from the statements, never read off the receipt , because that field is the one thing no vendor signs. Check one on an origin we do not run, or with npx concord-verify receipt.json , and nothing of ours executes. How we built it, and what broke Zero dependencies, on purpose. Node's own test runner, a ~100-line property-testing kit, and Chrome. An audit found the receipt was forgeable. Seven of fourteen forgeries verified clean: a coordinator could delete a charge, relabel the outcome "Committed", and the receipt passed, because verifyReceipt gated its strictness on a string nobody signed. Fixed by deriving the outcome from the entries and by provable silence — a vendor that did nothing signs that it did nothing, so an absence is distinguishable from a deletion. You can fire all fourteen at our own verifier from the live site. Running on the real API found two defects a polyfill can never surface. The coordinator was not delegating tools to the origins it embeds, so every participant registered and none was discoverable. And Chrome returns inputSchema as a JSON string where the polyfill returns an object. Both worked flawlessly under the shim — which is the argument for never trusting one. getTools({ fromOrigins }) rejects for the whole call when any one origin is unreachable. One dead site produced "0 of 6 answered" and a failure screen with five participants healthy. Discovery now asks one origin at a time. What we learned That a sampled mutation score is not a score. We reported 92%. It came from 60 mutants taken every-Nth from a list sorted by file and by operator — a stratified sample of a sorted population. Running all 116 gave 87% . Closing what that exposed took it to 97% (112/116) , and the four survivors are documented as equivalent with the reasoning attached, not hidden. That a property test which cannot fail passes loudest. Our first reference-model test registered the commit tool in 1% of the states it checked, and its unwind-ordering property was vacuous in 95% of runs because the fixture had one participant of each rung — so reversing and not reversing produced identical output. Mutation testing found it. Every property now asserts how much of the interesting space it reached and fails rather than going green faster. That the measuring instrument needs measuring too. Our mutation runner's timeout killed the npm wrapper but not the test process beneath it; two orphans took throughput from ten mutants a minute to ten every three — and a loaded machine turns survivors into false kills, silently inflating the score. Challenges Refusing well is harder than committing. Anyone can run a saga. The hard part is computing, from declarations alone and before contact, that no honest promise exists — and then having no button on that answer. Proving a negative in a browser. "The commit tool does not exist yet" is only worth something if you can watch it not exist. So the claim is checked through the same getTools() an agent calls, state by state, against the live deployment. Not overclaiming about our own proof. We ship a formal model — 855 reachable states, 9 safety invariants, breadth-first so a violation reports the shortest trace. spec/Concord.tla is generated from the same declaration the checker executes, so it cannot drift. But TLC has not been run against it, and the README says so in those words rather than letting a .tla file imply a proof nobody ran. What it can't do — said before you ask A vendor can lie about being compensable. One does, on purp

video_transcript_excerpt: Every website tells an agent what it can do. Nothing tells it what it can take back. This is Concord. Before it contacts anybody, it works out what it can honestly promise across sites that have never heard of each other. A flight that can be canceled, a hotel that can be refunded, and a visa fee that cannot be taken back. So that one goes last. Here is how that is enforced. Not a prompt and not a check inside a tool. This panel is the live output of get tools. Five read-only tools. The commit tool is not disabled. It is not registered. The agent has proposed and read the guarantee out, and it still has no way to commit because explaining is not consent. Now I accept and register tool puts the commit tool on the surface. No tool does that. A person clicked, and the moment the commitment starts, an abort controller takes it away again. Ask for two things nobody can undo and it refuses. Nothing was contacted, there is no button and no commit tool. A refused plan never produces one. Every statement in the receipt is signed by the counterparty, not by us. These are 14 real receipts, each edited the way a coordinator with a motive would. Seven of them verified clean until an audit found it. The outcome is derived from the statements now, and you can fire these yourself. And here is one on a different origin, which has no tools and no coordinator. It fetched each key from that vendor's own site. The coordinator that produced this receipt was never asked anything. A permission model made of register tool and abort controller, and an agent that cannot over promise because the words for it do not exist.

title: EgoLens: Teachable Driving-Data Viewer
pitch: Agents don't just use EgoLens, they extend it. Drop an unknown driving dataset: your agent writes the adapter, you judge the 3D render. Each does what it's best at, and the viewer keeps growing.
about_excerpt: Agents don't just use EgoLens, they extend it. Drop an unknown driving dataset: your agent writes the adapter, you judge the 3D render. Each does what it's best at, and the viewer keeps growing. Like Comment Story Updates Unknown dataset detected Teaching new dataset format New dataset learned! dataset rendered Inspiration Every perception team has sensor data in a shape no viewer understands: a research dataset, or their own model output stored next to one. Someone writes a loader, debugs why the point cloud renders sideways, and the loader dies with the notebook. EgoLens already renders Waymo, nuScenes, and Argoverse 2 in the browser, and every new format still meant a hand-written adapter. WebMCP changes who can add one: your agent teaches EgoLens through WebMCP, you approve the render, and the app's capabilities keep growing. What it does WebMCP tools usually let agents use the app. EgoLens flips it: agents extend the app. Together, a person and an agent can now add a dataset format to a viewer in minutes, in the browser, without touching the source code. Drop a folder EgoLens does not recognize and the page becomes a WebMCP tool provider. The agent inspects files within strict byte limits, reads the recipe schema and operator vocabulary, and submits adapter recipes as declarative JSON, never code. Every validated revision renders in the production 3D viewer, docked next to the review panel : orbit, scrub the timeline, toggle boxes and segmentation, switch camera POVs. You accept or reject each capability with a named issue and the verdict flows back to the agent. Finalize seals the recipe with content hashes; it can be exported, imported, and shared. Every taught format stays: drop that layout again and it renders in one click. The app's capabilities keep growing, and files never leave the browser. How we built it Five tools registered on document.modelContext : inspect , get_contract , apply_revision , get_state , finalize . Self-describing descriptions, normalized inputs, string results, so ChatGPT's browser, Chrome's native WebMCP, and the Codex app drive them with zero agent-specific code. Recipes are data, executed in an isolated graph runtime with resource limits. The person confirms the sensor layout before teaching starts; a recipe that does not bind exactly those sensors is rejected. React 19, TypeScript, three.js, Web Workers, IndexedDB, GitHub Pages. 1,100 unit tests and Playwright probes that drive Chrome's real WebMCP end to end. Challenges we ran into Agents stopping at the timeline. Fixed without shipping any dataset example, which would leak the answer: a sensor contract, coverage diagnostics, and a next-step hint in every state read. Bugs only eyes can catch. PandaSet stores cuboid yaw along the width axis. Every automated check passed and the boxes were rotated 90° on screen. That is why the full renderer is the review surface. Host budgets. Codex caps descriptor size and call latency; in-app browsers hang on the File System Access API. Each constraint pushed the tool surface toward the plainest contract. Accomplishments that we're proud of Three unknown datasets taught end to end by agents in one week: A2D2 (3 revisions, 6 cameras + 6 LiDARs fused), KITTI Raw (7 revisions), PandaSet (world-frame poses, pandas pickles). No example recipe is ever shown to the agent. The same five tools work unchanged across three hosts, and each dataset taught left EgoLens able to read more than before. What we learned The interesting question is not "what can an agent do in my app" but "what can an agent make my app able to do". Expose the extension points as tools and the agent's output becomes an artifact a person can inspect, reject, seal, and share. The person's rejections were the most valuable signal in the loop. What's next for EgoLens: Teachable Driving-Data Viewer A public recipe registry. A student or a researcher teaches EgoLens the dataset they need and publishes the recipe, so it renders for everyone after that. The goal: a visualization tool that can read any AV dataset, taught by the people who use it. title: gotothearchive
pitch: gotothearchive is a human-owned context and taste platform. By utilizing WebMCP it lets people control what agents access, trace what shaped their work, and decide what becomes Taste.
about_excerpt: gotothearchive is a human-owned context and taste platform. By utilizing WebMCP it lets people control what agents access, trace what shaped their work, and decide what becomes Taste. Like Comment Story Updates gotothearchive home inside the design folder lightbox preview of one design example the workbench the workbench expanded view stats taste view About gotothearchive Inspiration Context is probably the biggest problem with agents right now, and almost every product treats it as something the agent should quietly accumulate on its own. You end up with a per-agent memory store you cannot see into, cannot correct, and definitely cannot use to decide what a specific agent gets for a specific task. I think context is only the surface of the real problem anyway. Underneath it is taste, meaning the judgment behind what you save, what you throw out, and what you keep sending back for another pass, and an agent that is actually useful to you has to be working from that rather than from a summary of your last ten prompts. That is where gotothearchive started. You own the Archive, and the same interface where you organize it is the one that decides, task by task, what any agent is allowed to touch. What it does The Archive is a plain visual workspace for your images, links, documents, notes, and prior work, and it is genuinely useful on its own with no agent connected. When you do want help, you open Agent Access and pick, per folder/region, whether an agent can view, contribute to, or edit that part of the Archive for the current task. WebMCP takes those grants and compiles them straight into the agent's tool surface. Which tools appear on document.modelContext, and which regions are enumerable inside each tool's input schema, is exactly what you have granted at that moment. Narrow a grant and the tools re-register with tighter schemas. Revoke one and the affected tools are removed, not left as shells that fail on call, and the server rejects any request built against the schema the agent was still holding. The agent works from the context you allowed and returns its result to the Workbench as an immutable, versioned artifact. You see what it retrieved, which references actually shaped the output, who produced it, and what was denied along the way. You annotate a version, mark a region on it, approve it, request changes, or reject it. If the artifact is a component it runs live in the Workbench in an isolated iframe, so you can click through what the agent built rather than looking at a screenshot of it. From your feedback the agent can then propose a taste signal, tied to the exact annotations behind it, and nothing enters your profile until you confirm it. You edit the wording, rescope it from personal to a project, reject it, or accept it, and a confirmed signal starts steering retrieval on the next task. How I built it The build restarted more than once early on. Every time I laid out the full scope an agent would decide it was too ambitious and talk me into dropping something that turned out to be load-bearing, and I would end up rebuilding it a session later. The scope was fine. The restarts were the problem. Once I locked the surface to Archive, Workbench, and Taste and stopped reopening that decision, I finally started making progress. It runs on Cloudflare Workers with a single Durable Object holding the SQLite database for every Archive, region, task, grant, artifact, annotation, taste signal, provenance record, and audit event. One object is a real ceiling, but it also means that several people and their agents hitting the same Archive concurrently stay consistent by construction, with no coordination code, which is what makes the shared demo safe. R2 stores original media, and Workers AI produces the structured visual descriptions where they earn their keep. Since some of this incurs billed usage I calculated a quota for each user as well while we're in our "Beta" state. The core piece is a capability compiler, a pure function that turns the current application state, meaning your access, the agent's grant, the active task, the open artifact, and any expiry or revocation, into the exact set of WebMCP tools and region-constrained schemas that should be registered right now. Retrieval is deliberately not a managed search service. A hosted index hides the permission model in something I do not control and lags on write, and that lag breaks the entire premise of flipping a lock and having the next call fail immediately. So retrieval runs directly on the database. It resolves the authorized set first, then fuses full-text search, recency, and the context graph and multiplies through authority, curation, and confirmed-taste priors. Something you cannot see is absent from the candidate list, never present with a low score. Provenance is kept as three record types that never get collapsed into one. Influence means a reference shaped the result, access means it was retrieved for the task, and denial means it was unavailable, and only the first two show up in ordinary provenance. Taste corrections are bi-temporal. A materially changed signal is not overwritten. The old row is superseded and the new one points back at it, so the Taste page can show how a judgement moved over time. The part I got most wrong was taste itself. I built it server-side first, with a classifier that bucketed your annotations by dimension and a template that wrote the preference sentence from the most common words in the grouped notes. The output was things like "Leans away from the current typography on posters", which is vague and is exactly the kind of background inference this project exists to remove. So I deleted the whole path. A taste signal now exists only because an agent read your feedback and named the pattern with cited evidence through propose_taste_signal , or because you wrote it yourself, and the server's only remaining job there is to keep the evidence and confidence honest when you later edit a note. A bit less frequent, but it's high quality now, just takes longer to start curating. Partway through I ran the deployed site through an external WebMCP audit and fixed what it flagged, most of it around when tools register on first paint and where instruction-shaped text was leaking into tool descriptions instead of staying declarative. It tightened the surface noticeably. Challenges I ran into The hardest was making permission real in every layer at once. The interface, the compiled tool surface, retrieval, the context graph, and server authorization all had to agree, including in the second immediately after a revoke, and any one of them lagging would have made the whole claim a demo trick. Multimodal context was the next one. Images are how people actually communicate taste, but WebMCP is shaped around JSON-compatible inputs and outputs. I had to resolve media through short-lived signed URLs, keep the canonical original separate from every derived caption and palette, give the agent a structured representation it can reason over, and record the provenance of every derived field so a wrong value is visible rather than mysterious. Component artifacts added their own problem, since running agent-authored HTML meant an opaque-origin sandbox with a locked-down content security policy that still had to permit real fonts and the CDN scripts a component genuinely needs. And revocation had to go deeper than hiding items. A taste signal is a compressed version of the material behind it, so if a folder taught a preference, revoking that folder has to withdraw the preference from what the agent retrieves, not just the folder's contents. What I learned WebMCP can be much more than a cleaner way for an agent to operate a website. It can make the page itself the shared control surface between a person and an agent, where the action that organizes your work is the same action that sets the agent's boundary, and that framing changes what a web app is for in a multi-agent world. I also learned that a schema is good for communicating authority and useless for enforcing it, so every operation has to be re-checked at runtime, and that provenance matters as much as retrieval, because people need to know what shaped a result and not only what the agent opened. It also made me realize how much plumbing needs to go into the agentic web, something I've honestly been thinking about for a while, and WebMCP definitely has lots of room for improvement to accommodate multiple types of websites, I think right now its best suited for sequential work like e-commerce for example. Contributing back to WebMCP Building this made it clear that WebMCP has real gaps for anything visual or multimodal, and right now every developer is inventing their own conventions for representing images, files, previews, and instructions extracted from media, while every client is left guessing what it received.
