title: Hearth. Design a home with your agent.
pitch: A 3D interior-design studio humans and AI agents share. 40 WebMCP tools let your agent read rooms, place and resize furniture, import floor plans, shop a real Shopify catalog, and prep checkout.
about_excerpt: A 3D interior-design studio humans and AI agents share. 40 WebMCP tools let your agent read rooms, place and resize furniture, import floor plans, shop a real Shopify catalog, and prep checkout. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GIF Agent placing furniture, arranging, comparing layouts Living room at golden hour with catalog, inspector and activity log The Tools panel listing the WebMCP tools and schemas A home built from an uploaded floor plan, furnished The import sheet reading a floor-plan image Resized sofa and size-matched catalog results The import sheet reading a floor-plan image Resized sofa and size-matched catalog results Ghost preview of a Shopify product plus the cart Door-swing and clearance conflict diagrams with a fix Accessibility mode with turning circles and paths Exported design board Whole-home framing The seven floor-plan templates plus "Import your own plan" Orbit camera view Inspiration I was thinking of buying a home, and one question that kept coming was how will I furnish it. The hard question was not the price. It was: will the furniture fit, and will the door still open? Where should I place the furniture, will it look good as per my home layout, and what will be the total cost I might need. An AI agent should be able to help with this, but it can't. A chat model can't see the room. A screen-scraping agent can guess at pixels, but it can't measure a wall, and it certainly can't be trusted to drag a sofa. Room planners exist (IKEA Kreativ, Planner 5D); none of them let an agent in. Browser agents exist; none of them can measure a wall. When I read the WebMCP proposal the idea clicked: instead of making the agent reverse-engineer my page, I could hand it the same verbs I use. Interior design felt like the perfect test. It's spatial, iterative, visual, and it ends with a real purchase. So I built Hearth: a 3D home studio where a person and an agent work on the same rooms, and the agent gets forty real tools instead of a screenshot. What it does Hearth is a shared interior-design studio. You get a dollhouse-style 3D home you can drag furniture around in, with magnetic snapping and live dimension lines. Your agent gets the same home through tools registered on the page with document.modelContext.registerTool . It reads the space as data: rooms, walls and their free spans, door swings, every item in centimetres, and a conflict report (clearances, traffic paths, blocked doors) with a one-line fix for each. It designs with semantic anchors, so "put the sofa against the north wall facing the window" becomes move_furniture {anchor:{wall:"north", facing:"window:…"}} and no coordinates cross the conversation. It can arrange a room for a purpose, change the time of day, and turn on accessibility mode (90 cm paths, 150 cm turning circles) and then fix what that flags. It can also build the home. Pick one of seven floor plans, or drop a photo of your own and call import_floor_plan : a vision model reads room names, printed dimensions, doors and windows, and Hearth's layout engine turns that into a to-scale scene with shared walls snapped, doors paired across them, and starter furniture that arrives conflict-free. Every placed item has an exact size, resize_furniture changes it, and search_catalog ranks real Shopify products by closeness to that size and says whether each match is exact, close or off, with the centimetre delta. The shop is a live Shopify store with 71 products. The agent can filter by what fits a wall, ghost-preview a product in the room in a colourway, add it to the cart and hand you the checkout link. The purchase click stays yours, which is the only version of agent shopping I would actually use. A typical session: drop a photo of the flat and get a furnished home to scale; ask for a sofa that fits the north wall under $800 and watch it ghost into the room; confirm it, add it to the cart, take the checkout link. Nothing in that chain needs a coordinate or a product id from me. Everything is visible and reversible. Save layouts and compare two with a slider, undo anything, clear the home and restore it, export a design board. When the agent acts, an orb flies to the spot, a receipt lands in the activity log with the exact tool input and result, and an Undo chip appears. Destructive tools open a confirmation dialog in the page, and if I decline, the agent gets {error:"cancelled", detail:"The human declined…"} back, so it knows why, not just that it failed. How I built it I wrote the contracts before the code. TOOLS.md specifies every tool's name, description, parameters, result shape, group and gate; SCENE_SCHEMA.md pins the scene graph, units and coordinate frame. Everything else was judged against those two files. The stack is Next.js 16 and React 19 with React-Three-Fiber for the scene. A zustand store tags every mutation human or agent , and a pure TypeScript geometry engine (walls, clearances, traffic paths, floor-plan layout) has no React or three.js in it and is covered by a few hundred unit tests. The shop is the Shopify Storefront API; the floor-plan reader and the fallback assistant use the OpenAI Responses API through server-only route handlers. It runs in ChatGPT desktop's built-in browser, in Chrome with WebMCP enabled (the production origin ships an origin-trial token), and where a browser has no WebMCP yet, an in-page assistant drives the same tools through Chrome's polyfill. The WebMCP layer is one registry, src/tools/registry.ts . The surface I use: registerTool with an AbortSignal per group, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, the toolchange event and getTools() mirrored into a Tools panel so a judge can inspect the surface without an agent, executeTool through the polyfill for the fallback assistant, and Chrome's published budgets as CI assertions. Each tool is defined once with a zod schema and converted to JSON Schema. The registry asserts the budgets at definition time (names ≤ 30 chars, descriptions ≤ 500, parameter descriptions ≤ 150) and the test suite asserts every result stays under 1,500 characters across three scene fixtures. 29 tools register synchronously on load so DevTools and Lighthouse see them cold. 11 more live in four state-gated groups (build, preview, variants, checkout), each behind its own AbortController . When the scene changes the registry diffs the desired groups and registers or aborts, and any tool whose result changes the gate set ( set_mode , but also update_cart opening checkout or preview_in_room opening preview) waits for the registry to settle and returns tools_ready . Results are plain JSON envelopes. Success carries the room, the conflicts and a hint. Failure carries an error code, a detail and a suggestion; a blocked placement adds the free wall spans, an unknown id adds the three closest candidates, so the model can self-correct instead of retrying blindly. Every room , item or product parameter accepts an id or a name, item accepts selected , and room_id -style keys are rewritten to the documented ones before validation, because models send them anyway and a good call shouldn't die as invalid . A webmcp-evals suite of 32 prompts checks that the right tool is called with the right arguments in the right order. Challenges I ran into Chrome (before 153) cancels in-flight executions on abort. My first gating implementation aborted a group the moment the scene said it should go away, which killed the very tool call that had changed the scene. The fix was a deferral rule: never abort while a tool is executing, queue the sync, flush it on a macrotask afterwards, and have the tool that caused the change release its own executing count before waiting for the registry to settle. That one rule took longer to get right than most features. Describing a room to something with no eyes. Early tool descriptions were long and situational, and models made worse calls with them. What worked was static, short descriptions, all live context in get_scene_summary , semantic anchors instead of coordinates, and putting the "what to do next" hint inside the result rather than the description. Floor plans are messy. Vision models return bounding boxes drawn backwards, width and depth swapped depending on the image's aspect ratio, and room names in ALL CAPS. Getting from that to a scene where shared walls line up, doors are paired on both sides of a wall, every room is reachable and the starter furniture has zero conflicts took a per-axis scale from the printed dimensions, edge clustering, overlap resolution and a connectivity pass. I tested it on the three sample plans and a dozen more I pulled off the web; five recorded reader outputs now run as fixtures. Making agent actions legible without being noisy. Silent state changes feel like a haunted house. The orb, receipts, pulses and the eight-second Undo chip were as much design work as engineering, and stepper-driven resizes had to be coalesced so a human dragging a value didn't generate forty receipts. title: How I Choose
pitch: How I Choose is a local-first rehearsal workspace that checks whether a communication partner followed a person's self-authored protocol-never evaluating the person.
about_excerpt: How I Choose is a local-first rehearsal workspace that checks whether a communication partner followed a person's self-authored protocol-never evaluating the person. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Important conversations often become harder when speech, language, or processing gets difficult. Yet many communication tools still ask the person to perform better: answer faster, choose from someone else's categories, or fit a fixed conversational rhythm. We wanted to reverse that responsibility. How I Choose asks whether the communication partner adapted to the person—not whether the person performed correctly. The person defines what helps, what each signal means, how much time is needed, and what a partner must do next. The software turns those choices into a protocol that can be rehearsed and audited without inferring meaning from silence or delay. What it does How I Choose is a local-first communication rehearsal workspace for adults. A person authors their preferred channels, wording, pace, processing time, literal-language rules, semantic signals, and partner actions. They also choose exactly which fields an active browser agent may read. The workspace supports both human-only practice and an optional WebMCP agent rehearsal. Before any partner turn becomes visible, a deterministic engine checks it against the current protocol. It enforces one question at a time, word and option limits, channel rules, pending-signal acknowledgment, Pause, terminal Stop, revision freshness, conflicts, and idempotency. The person directly selects every semantic signal, including yes, no, not sure, more information, more time, rephrase, Pause, and Stop. Silence creates no event and never advances the rehearsal. Reports contain evidence about the partner's adherence and repairs ; they never score the person. The complete human-facing product includes: guided onboarding plus blank and clearly labeled synthetic profiles; profile, signal, and per-field agent-access editing; a large keyboard-accessible signal board; low-stakes rehearsal templates and partner-turn validation; partner-adherence audit and revision history; staged protocol suggestions with exact diffs and provenance; JSON import/export and a printable support guide; visible owner-only review and ratification; text-size, contrast, Quiet, and Plain language preferences. Why WebMCP This workflow needs an agent to operate inside the person's current, visible, revisioned protocol , not inside a detached chat containing copied instructions. WebMCP lets ChatGPT use the page's existing permissions, validator, state machine, and evidence while the person retains direct control of signals, rule changes, and approval. The workspace starts in Human-only mode. All eight Site tools fail closed until the person visibly enables Agent rehearsal. Once enabled, ChatGPT can read only allowlisted fields, audit readiness, start an already approved scenario, offer a validated partner turn, acknowledge the exact person-selected signal, inspect its own adherence, stage a draft improvement, and verify guide derivation. There is deliberately no tool for selecting a person's signal, answering for them, resuming, ratifying, publishing, sharing, exporting private data, deleting a profile, or assessing capacity, consent, diagnosis, comprehension, safety, or coercion. How we built it The app is a static Next.js and React application written in strict TypeScript. Dexie/IndexedDB is the durable local source of truth; Zustand holds hydrated read projections and transient preferences. Zod validates every persisted document, import, command, and Site-tool payload. Human controls and WebMCP handlers use the same application-service command path and pure domain logic. Compare-and-swap revisions, idempotency fingerprints, events, and state writes happen atomically in one IndexedDB transaction. Ratified profile snapshots are immutable and identified by canonical hashes. The top-level /demo/ page feature-detects WebMCP and imperatively registers a stable catalog through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_rehearsal_brief audit_rehearsal_readiness start_approved_rehearsal offer_partner_turn read_latest_signal get_rehearsal_report stage_protocol_patch verify_support_guide A singleton guard prevents duplicate registration under React Strict Mode. Every JSON Schema is bounded and closed with additionalProperties: false , then Zod validates again at the application boundary. Mutations require expected revisions and an idempotency key. Handlers resolve current IndexedDB state at invocation time instead of trusting stale UI state. The quality system combines Vitest, Testing Library, fast-check property tests, Playwright desktop and narrow-viewport suites, axe-core checks, dependency and secret audits, a static production build, and GitHub Actions. The release includes 76 unit, service, property, import/export, and agent-flow tests plus a complete 15-step browser judge path. Challenges we faced Treating discovery and authorization as separate problems. Registering a tool successfully does not mean it should be authorized in the current state. A real-browser test exposed an early version where Human-only was only presentation state. We fixed this by making owner-controlled agent access durable, revisioned session state and enforcing it inside every handler. Keeping agent authority physically narrow. Removing dangerous fields from a broad object was not enough. We created allowlisted agent DTOs and a separate AgentRehearsalService that cannot import owner-only ratification, signal selection, export, share, delete, or resume operations. Making concurrent changes recoverable. A person may change a rule while an agent is preparing a turn. Expected revisions cause the stale write to fail instead of overwriting the person's newer choice; the agent can reread the brief and adapt. Building safety without making clinical claims. The product is deliberately scoped to synthetic and low-stakes adult communication practice. It does not infer answers, assess a person, or present itself as a consent system, medical device, emergency plan, or legal instrument. Accomplishments that we're proud of One deterministic engine governs both human and agent partner turns. Human-only access fails closed, while owner-enabled agent access remains field-scoped and revisioned. Pause is immediately effective and Stop is terminal—no agent override exists. Stale revisions, duplicate requests, invalid turns, repair, signals, and provenance are visible and recoverable. Private notes are structurally absent from agent projections, and receipts contain metadata rather than authored conversation text. The full human product works without an account, backend, API key, remote database, analytics, or runtime external model call. The deployed production build was exercised in ChatGPT's real built-in browser: all eight tools were discovered and the guarded workflow, including Human-only denial and visible owner-enabled access, was verified. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it exposes an existing trustworthy application boundary rather than creating a second automation-only path. Tool discovery, state authorization, validation, persistence, and visible evidence all need independent treatment. We also learned that “local-first” needs precise disclosure. Profiles and rehearsals stay in local, unencrypted IndexedDB, but fields explicitly exposed through Site tools are processed by the active browser agent. The interface says that plainly. Most importantly, semantic safety becomes more reliable when it is structural: the agent cannot manufacture a person-authored signal, Stop cannot be reversed, silence cannot become an answer, and suggestions remain drafts until the person reviews them. What's next The next phase is compensated co-design with people who use diverse communication methods, followed by deeper accessibility research and independent review. We also want to explore portable protocol formats, more rehearsal templates, stronger assistive-technology testing, and longitudinal partner-adherence evidence without introducing person scoring or surveillance. How I Choose is an open alpha, not a clinically validated product. The challenge profiles and scenarios are synthetic. Its contribution is an executable pattern for accountable communication agents: the person remains the source of meaning, while adaptation becomes testable. Verification note Real ChatGPT built-in-browser verification is documented separately in the public repository. The submitted video is an editorial product walkthrough using the real deployed interface and synthetic data; it does not claim to be footage of the separate live Site-tool test. Human only blocks every site tool until the person enables agent rehearsal. Even then, the agent receives only exposed fields. It cannot answer, select a signal, resume, ratify, publish, share, or export. The guardrails do real work. A long two-question turn is rejected before it can appear. The result names both failures. Too many questions and a breached word limit. A repaired one-question turn passes the same engine used by human only practice. Only then does the question appear in the practice room. Maya herself selects a semantic signal. When she chooses amber, the system records exactly "Not sure." The partner must acknowledge it and rephrase without changing the choice's meaning. title: Kern
pitch: A kerning workbench that an AI agent operates through WebMCP. Load a font, give it one line of instruction, and it looks at every letter pair and fixes the spacing — then exports a real font file.
about_excerpt: A kerning workbench that an AI agent operates through WebMCP. Load a font, give it one line of instruction, and it looks at every letter pair and fixes the spacing — then exports a real font file. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Kerning is the space between two letters. AV needs less space. nn needs no change. There is no formula. The eye judges the shape of the white space, not the distance. A person must look at every pair. A typeface has hundreds of pairs. Thomas Phinney kerned one weight of one typeface. He made 632 adjustments. The work took about one week. Nobody can automate this with a formula. So the question was whether an agent could do it by looking instead — and whether it would know when a pair was already fine. What it does Kern is a kerning tool. It shows every pair in a font, and an agent fixes the spacing. Load any .ttf or .otf , give the agent one sentence, and it will: Survey every pair as a labelled contact sheet, up to 36 pairs in one image Compare candidate values side by side, one row per pair Apply the values it chooses, and mark the pairs it leaves alone Check the result in real words, shipped against kerned Export a .ttf with real GPOS and kern tables written into it Six of the eight tools return an image. The agent does not read a score and act on it. It looks at the render and decides. The person keeps control. Every value is visible on the page. Hover a pair to see the old value. Use the arrow keys to change any value. The agent and the person share one state, so nothing is locked. Why this fits WebMCP The agent must see the letters. It cannot decide from a number or a database row. The page already holds the font and the canvas. WebMCP lets the page draw the pair and give the picture to the agent. A tool can also answer a question that no interface asks. preview_pairs takes eight pairs and four candidate values, and returns one labelled image. No button on the page does this. Only an agent needs it. The tool list follows the page state. The tools register when you load a font. They unregister when you load a different font. This fires toolchange . An agent that arrives before a font is loaded finds no tools. What people and agents can do together Before, you kerned a font by hand, one pair at a time, or you shipped it unkerned. There was no middle option. Now the agent can also say that a pair is already correct: typeface shipped state reviewed changed left alone EB Garamond no kerning 51 46 5 Comic Relief no kerning 51 39 12 Roboto Condensed professionally kerned 51 10 41 The tools and the instruction were the same for all three fonts. The results are different. On Roboto the agent corrected only the L pairs and the punctuation. It kept the other 41 values. A tool that always finds a change has not looked. How we built it Vite, React 19, TypeScript, on Cloudflare Workers. opentype.js reads the font. Kern uses no MCP library. I removed the one I started with, so the specification call is visible in the source: document.modelContext.registerTool( { name, description, inputSchema, annotations, execute }, { signal: controller.signal }, ) Each registration holds an AbortController . The signal unregisters the tool. getTools() fills the tools panel in the app, so the page shows what is really registered. The annotations are the two that WebMCP defines: readOnlyHint on the four read tools, and untrustedContentHint on all eight. Every answer repeats the font family name, and that name comes from a file the user supplied. The export is real. opentype.js drops kerning when it writes a font. So Kern builds the GPOS and kern tables by hand and splices them into the original bytes. Every deploy runs a test that reads the exported font back. The build fails if the values are missing. Challenges we ran into The agent needed to know how to do the job. Look at every pair first. Compare a few values. Apply them together. Then check the result in real words. That is a short set of instructions, but WebMCP has nowhere to put it. You can describe each tool. You cannot describe the page. So there is no way to tell an agent how the work should go before it starts. I tried adding a help tool. That did not work. The agent that needs help is the agent that never calls it. What worked was attaching the instructions to the first answer the agent gets, whatever tool it happened to call first. A full run went from 4 minutes 17 seconds to 2 minutes 34 seconds . MCP, the protocol underneath, already has a field for this. WebMCP does not expose it yet. video_title: Kern - A kerning workbench a browser agent can actually operate.
video_transcript_excerpt: You know something's wrong. The letters are right. The spaces aren't. That's kerning. And one typeface can have hundreds of pairs. Type designers do this by hand, one pair at a time. Look, adjust, look again, then move to the next one. There are 632 pairs. It takes about a week. So, I built Kern. A kerning tool which shows every pair in a font, and an agent fixes the spacing. An agent drives it through Web MCP. Eight tools registered on the page itself. I gave it one instruction, nothing else. It looks at each pair the same way a person would. Then it decides. 16 tool calls, most of them answer with a picture, not a number. 51 pairs in 3 minutes. It changed 46. Five were already right. Hover any pair to see what it was before. Kern still works by hand. Pick any pair and change it yourself. The arrow keys move it. -55 to -95. Same words before and after. Then it checks its own work in real words. But fixing bad spacing is the easy test. What if the font is already good? Same tools, same instruction. This time on Roboto Condensed. This time it left 41 pairs untouched. It changed only 10. It looks first, that's the point. And the agent isn't controlling the page through clicks. The tools live on the page itself. That's Web MCP. When it's done, Kern gives you a font file you can drop straight into a design. Kern, try it on your own font.

title: Keycap Forge
pitch: **Design printable custom keycaps with ChatGPT, WebMCP, and browser-local 3D AI.**
about_excerpt: **Design printable custom keycaps with ChatGPT, WebMCP, and browser-local 3D AI.** Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Creating an artisan keycap usually requires several disconnected skills: generating a concept, modeling it in Blender or CAD, understanding keycap dimensions, building a switch-compatible mount, repairing the mesh, and preparing it for 3D printing. At the same time, most image-to-3D demonstrations stop after producing something visually interesting. They rarely answer the practical question: Can this model be edited, attached to a real keycap, validated, and printed? We also wanted to explore a better way for ChatGPT to interact with complex web applications. Traditional browser agents depend on coordinates and simulated clicks, which become fragile when layouts change. WebMCP offered a different approach: the website could expose meaningful tools such as find_parts , auto_place_part , and compose_keycap . That led to Keycap Forge: a browser-based workspace where a person and ChatGPT can collaboratively turn an image into a printable custom keycap. What it does Keycap Forge is a browser-local 3D keycap editor powered by WebMCP. A user can: Choose a standard key size, from 1U through 6.25U Space . Select an MX or Topre switch mount. Generate a standalone 3D statue from a PNG, JPEG, WebP, or SVG reference image. Create a lightweight 2.5D relief from a logo or silhouette. Import an existing watertight STL model. Select, move, rotate, and scale parts directly in the 3D viewport. Automatically center and fit a model on the keycap. Render the keycap and added model as one manufacturing solid. Inspect solid, section, and underside views. Validate manifold connectivity, volume, and dimensions. Return to the editable state without losing the original parts or transforms. Export an STL only after explicit user approval. Download a tolerance coupon before printing the complete keycap. The same project can also be controlled conversationally through ChatGPT. Keycap Forge exposes semantic WebMCP tools including: describe_project find_parts get_project_state transform_part auto_place_part compose_keycap repair_printability set_keycap_spec undo_last_action validate_printability export_project Instead of asking ChatGPT to locate a colored arrow on the screen, the user can say: Find the cat model, center it on the keycap, enlarge it slightly, and validate the result. ChatGPT can then operate on the actual project state while every change remains visible and reversible in the website. How we built it The editor is built with React, TypeScript, vinext, and Vite. Three.js and React Three Fiber power the interactive 3D viewport. The keycap itself is generated from deterministic manufacturing parameters rather than being a decorative cube. The geometry includes: A flat-top tapered shell Rounded corners An underside cavity MX cross or Topre mount geometry Stabilizer stems for supported wide MX keys Millimeter-based positioning and tolerances For photo-to-3D generation, we run a browser-compatible TripoSR ONNX pipeline using ONNX Runtime WebGPU. The uploaded image stays on the user’s device. The reconstruction pipeline: Removes a connected edge background and centers the subject. Converts the image into a 512 × 512 model tensor. Runs the TripoSR encoder, backbone, and decoder through WebGPU. Evaluates a (192^3) density field. Smooths the level set to reduce voxel noise. Extracts a surface using marching cubes. Welds duplicate vertices. Applies Taubin smoothing to improve print quality without excessive shrinkage. Corrects the generated model’s up axis and front-facing direction. Normalizes the statue to a practical keycap scale. The three model files total approximately 801 MiB. To make that viable on a static deployment, we implemented parallel byte-range downloading, retries, and resumable chunk storage using the Origin Private File System. A refresh can reuse chunks that have already been downloaded. Manufacturing composition uses Manifold WASM. During Render union , Keycap Forge applies the latest part transforms, removes geometry extending into the keycap cavity, preserves a small attachment overlap, and combines everything into one solid. WebMCP is integrated through a typed tool registry. Zod validates every tool input, and state-changing calls include an expectedRevision . If ChatGPT tries to modify an outdated revision, the operation is rejected instead of overwriting a newer human edit. Manual UI operations and WebMCP operations share the same command and history system. This keeps agent actions observable, undoable, and consistent with direct editing. Challenges we ran into Turning one image into a useful 3D object A single image does not contain information about hidden surfaces. Early approaches produced flat extrusions rather than statue-like objects. TripoSR provided genuine single-view reconstruction, but its raw output still required orientation correction, surface smoothing, normalization, and manufacturing checks. Running a large model on a static deployment The first browser model download is approximately 801 MiB. A normal Vite deployment could host the interface, but unreliable downloads made the main feature unusable. We addressed this by splitting model files into resumable ranges, downloading multiple chunks concurrently, retrying failed ranges, and storing completed chunks in OPFS. Correcting model orientation The reconstruction coordinate system did not match the editor’s coordinate system. Models initially arrived lying down, upside down, or facing away from the camera. We mapped the TripoSR axes into the editor’s right-handed millimeter coordinate system and added a front-facing correction before placement. Separating camera movement from model manipulation The 3D viewport needed to support both orbit controls and transform gizmos. Pointer events originally reached the camera while the user was dragging a model handle. We had to coordinate selection, transform controls, and camera controls so that dragging a gizmo manipulates the part while dragging empty space rotates the camera. Preserving edits during Boolean composition An early union path regenerated parts from their initial state, which discarded the user’s latest rotation or scale. We changed the manufacturing pipeline to operate on a snapshot of the current project revision and apply every stored transform before the Boolean operation. Protecting the keycap cavity A model could look correctly placed from above while extending through the roof and blocking the switch cavity. The manufacturing pipeline now prioritizes the keycap base and trims added geometry below the roof, while retaining a small overlap for reliable attachment. Designing safe agent tools WebMCP gives an agent real application capabilities, so tool boundaries matter. We separated read-only inspection, reversible editing, validation, and consequential export. ChatGPT may prepare an export, but only the user can approve the final download. Accomplishments that we're proud of Running a complete image-to-3D reconstruction pipeline inside the browser without a paid 3D generation API. Deploying the AI workflow as a static web experience backed by WebGPU, OPFS caching, and resumable model downloads. Producing a genuine statue-like mesh instead of simply extruding a 2D silhouette. Making generated and imported models directly editable through XYZ position, rotation, and scale controls. Exposing 11 semantic WebMCP tools that operate on the same live project shown in the viewport. Supporting atomic multi-step composition through compose_keycap . Keeping human and ChatGPT edits in one revisioned undo/redo history. Preserving editable source parts even after previewing the manufacturing union. Protecting the underside cavity by trimming overflowing model geometry. Requiring explicit human approval before exporting an STL. Building automated coverage across 52 test files and 156 tests. Verifying the complete workflow on the publicly deployed application. What we learned We learned that browser-local AI can be more than a privacy feature. It can become part of the product architecture: inference, post-processing, editing, validation, and export can all happen in one environment without transferring the user’s source image to an application server. We also learned that semantic agent tools are much more reliable than visual automation for complex editors. A tool such as auto_place_part carries domain knowledge about the keycap center, roof height, and safe dimensions. That is fundamentally different from asking an agent to drag an object toward an approximate screen coordinate. Another important lesson was to separate generative geometry from manufacturing geometry. AI can propose a useful shape, but deterministic systems should handle dimensions, coordinate conversion, trimming, Boolean composition, validation, and export. Finally, computationally valid does not automatically mean physically pr

We start with a ChatGPT generated reference designed for reconstruction, a full-body cat three-quarter view, connected toy-like volumes, and no fragile fur or whiskers. Export project opens an approval dialogue instead of downloading silently. Only the user releases the final STL. Keycap Forge turns browser-local 3D reconstruction and CAD-like editing into a visible, reversible collaboration between ChatGPT and a real web application without a paid 3D generation API.

title: Mastery Gate
pitch: Your own ChatGPT becomes a Socratic exam coach — but the site decides what it may know, say, and be. Answer keys structurally redacted; mastery gates that register new tools when you earn them.
about_excerpt: Your own ChatGPT becomes a Socratic exam coach — but the site decides what it may know, say, and be. Answer keys structurally redacted; mastery gates that register new tools when you earn them. Like Comment Story Updates Track hub: two PL-400 objectives, the four-dimension rubric, and the live Tool Roster your agent sees. Gate opens at 3 or above on all four. Mastery earned: advance_module and start_exam just materialized in the agent's tool list. Capability is the guardrail, not a prompt. Exam mode: every coaching tool revoked in the live registry, only get_exam_status and submit_exam remain. Train aided, test unaided. A micro-lesson: scenario first, commit before the reveal, governing rule, exam clue, and the aim your coach opens every session by asking. Every distractor maps to one of 17 named misconceptions. A miss returns the diagnosis and routes you to the paragraph that repairs it. Inspiration Every AI study tool has the same fatal flaw: ask it nicely and it gives you the answer. That's homework theater, and the research says it's worse than useless. Learning science is unambiguous: retrieval practice beats re-reading , feedback works when it names why you were wrong, and desirable difficulties (the friction) are where retention comes from. The AI-tutoring RCTs agree from the other direction: constrained Socratic tutors roughly double learning (Kestin et al. 2025), while unguarded chatbot access makes students worse once the aid is removed (Bastani et al. 2024). The guardrails are the active ingredient, and prompts are guardrails an AI can be talked out of. WebMCP made a different kind possible: architecture . The page owns the tools, so the site decides what the AI may know, say, and be. I had already built this pedagogy once without AI, with deterministic scoring, named misconceptions, and repair routes, for my daughter's engineering statics course. Mastery Gate is what that pattern becomes when you hand it to an agent. What it does Your own ChatGPT becomes a Socratic coach for Microsoft's PL-400 exam, and the site is the referee it cannot overrule. A deterministic TypeScript engine grades, counts attempts, diagnoses named misconceptions (a miss returns "policy-precedence-instinct", never the key), scores a four-dimension mastery rubric (Recall, Connections, Application, Transfer, every dimension at 3 or above, never an average), and gates progression. The agent coaches through the page's WebMCP tools: Socratic questioning, an earned hint ladder, remediation routed to the exact lesson paragraph. Ask it for the answer and it refuses, leading with the reason (the answer is in no tool it can call), then asks one smaller question instead. Capability is the guardrail. advance_module does not exist until the gate opens; it materializes in the agent's tool list when mastery is earned. Exam mode revokes the coaching toolset entirely: train aided, test unaided. On screen, the Tool Roster reads 13 tools with the gate closed, 15 when it opens, 2 during the exam . The site's decisions are visible to learner and agent alike. The rubric interview is the centerpiece. The engine's own routing hands the mic to the AI to judge free-form teach-back explanations, then validates its scores against verbatim lesson-text evidence and clamps them. The AI does what only AI can; the site does what AI must not. Zero AI infrastructure: static site, no backend, no API keys. The visitor brings the intelligence; the site brings the authority. Everything also works agent-less. The coach is an interface, not a dependency. How we built it A pure-TypeScript engine (MIT, packages/mastery-gate ) under a Next.js static export on Cloudflare Pages; the learner's state lives in localStorage and never leaves the browser. The lesson content is instrumented deeply: 34 questions across two PL-400 objectives, every distractor tagged to a 17-misconception taxonomy, remediation anchors into the exact authored sections. Two evidence-graded research briefs live in the repo mapping each mechanism to the learning-science literature. And every layer was adversarially cross-reviewed by a different model family than the one that wrote it. Challenges we ran into We probed the runtimes before trusting documentation , live at /spike . ChatGPT's runtime has no toolchange events; Chrome does. The registry feature-detects, and gate-crossing responses announce new tools. When the protocol gives you no push channel, the payload becomes the push channel. getTools() and registerTool() return Promises in real runtimes; our lenient mocks hid that until production crashed. Chrome also enforces executeTool(RegisteredTool, jsonString) strictly. The mocks now tell the truth, and each crash shape is a named regression test. The subtlest bug was pedagogical. Early on we redacted so hard the coach had no curriculum. It refused to leak answers, then taught from its own pretraining, probing about scenarios the learner had never seen. The fix became our design law: the agent gets exactly what a learner reading the page gets, no more and no less. Redaction is symmetry, not secrecy. The host moved under us (Aug 28 to Sep 2). The ChatGPT desktop app's plugin update broke its own browser bridge (a missing scripts/ dir in the cached skill), then native page-tool injection into conversations turned intermittent, and a long session tripped an undocumented 10-changes-per-page-load budget on the tool surface, read straight from the app's browser-service.mjs ( max_tools 100, max_total_descriptor_bytes 65,536, max_registration_changes 10). None of it was the page; Chrome 152's reference runtime returned every tool throughout. But a coach that stalls on a host quirk is a bad coach, so the kickoff self-heals all three: it falls back to the app's own WebMCP bridge (same registered tools, different transport), corrects the tools.call(name, input) convention, and refreshes the tab when the budget is spent, saying so in one line each time. We surveyed five agent surfaces and found only two can invoke page tools today (ChatGPT's desktop browser, Chrome 152 with the flag); three read but cannot call. The ecosystem gap is real. See What's next. Accomplishments that we're proud of The first live coached session: the agent read its tool descriptions and volunteered "I will not reveal or submit the answer", unprompted. The descriptions are its employment contract, and it signed. In the demo it refuses on camera. Cross-family adversarial review found and sealed, before any judge could: five independent exam-escape paths, a self-serviceable mastery gate (an agent quoting the question back as "evidence" to award itself 4/4/4/4), and an answer-cache side channel through coaching notes. The site reacts to its own state instead of asking the agent to. A miss scrolls the page to the repairing paragraph, a gate change updates the roster, and start_exam mounts the exam where the learner is standing. The page moves; the chat stays put. And when the interview isn't unlocked yet, the referee says why : request_next_action returns the per-dimension coverage ledger, so "not yet" always comes with "here's what's missing." A Tool Inspector on the page: schema-generated forms for every registered tool, so anyone in any browser can invoke the real surface, with the same guards and the same redaction, and no agent at all. A "Your model" panel showing the learner exactly what the agent sees (the misconception ledger with its evidence) next to a one-tap erase. Glass box, both directions. What we learned You cannot make a chatbot answer-proof with a prompt; the learner can always rewrite it. You can make it answer-proof with a tool surface. We learned that the hard way on our own machine: a tutoring skill installed in ChatGPT quietly announced a "direct-answer mode" and handed over an answer, outranking the pasted contract. Host-level instructions beat prompts every time. But even then the engine leaked nothing. The skill could only read what the page shows every learner. The kickoff now claims precedence over installed coach skills; the gate never needed to. And starving the agent is not governing it: the coach teaches best when it holds exactly the learner's page, nothing more. The future of the open web isn't agents driving websites. It's websites that stay authoritative while agents make them personal. What's next for Mastery Gate The bridge (in-repo companion, tested; live pairing is roadmap): an MV3 extension plus a local MCP server so any MCP-speaking client, CLI agents included, can invoke a page's WebMCP tools. Three of the five surfaces we surveyed need exactly this. The remaining designed lessons and more certification tracks; spaced-review scheduling keyed to the misconception ledger; concept-level deep links. The Mastery Debrief : an end-of-module film assembled from the learner's own ledger, directed by the agent, validated by the engine, narrated live by the coach (backend shipped; the film is roadmap). title: MicroDuck Lab
pitch: Teach a real robot RL in your browser. An AI agent drives the same controls, trains on your GPU, and brings the weights back. 53 WebMCP tools, real MuJoCo, real Microduck.
about_excerpt: Teach a real robot RL in your browser. An AI agent drives the same controls, trains on your GPU, and brings the weights back. 53 WebMCP tools, real MuJoCo, real Microduck. Like Comment Story Updates MicroDuck Lab Learn reinforcement learning by teaching robots. Live: microducklab.com · Repo: github.com/SynthReality-Labs/microduck-lab · Video: youtu.be/eZY9nkB0mYE · by SynthReality Labs Inspiration Ten thousand people just bought a reinforcement-learning robot. Microduck — the $399 open-source biped from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face — passed 10,000 units and $5M within days of launch , taking $2.6M in the first 24 hours. Demand was heavy enough that the Christmas delivery promise is gone; new orders now quote four to six months. So there are thousands of people who have paid for a robot whose entire premise is train in simulation → deploy → refine → retrain — and who will spend months waiting, many having never trained a policy in their lives. RL is taught badly because it is taught abstractly. The loop that actually produces understanding — change a thing, watch the robot fail differently, work out why — is buried under CUDA installs, YAML files and wandb dashboards. Newcomers read about reward hacking. They rarely watch it happen to something they configured. MicroDuck Lab is that loop, in a browser tab, with an AI agent beside you. The real robot model, the real published policies, real MuJoCo physics, and 53 WebMCP tools. No install, no GPU, no account. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Because a human and an agent are good at opposite halves of RL diagnosis , and until now there was no way to put them in the same room. You look at a rollout and know instantly that that gait is ugly , I don't like that fall , it should look more deliberate . That judgement is pre-verbal, immediate, and nearly impossible to write down as a metric. An agent can read thirty metrics, a reward decomposition, a curriculum state and a config diff at once, and cross-reference them against a documented catalogue of known failure modes. That is tedious and error-prone for a human. Neither does the other's half well. Without WebMCP, the agent is guessing at a screenshot and you are transcribing numbers into a chat box. With it, both of you act on the same live simulation — and the simulation is the kind of state a screenshot cannot carry: 61 observation values at 50 Hz, a reward decomposition per term, a selection that means this joint, this window, this rollout . Reward design is a search over a space no human can hold in their head. The run that produced base-walk logged 22 reward terms — velocity tracking, uprightness, foot clearance, foot slip, swing height, angular momentum, action rate, torque rate, self-collision, a fallen tax, and a dozen more — each with a weight, each interacting with the others across 4,000 iterations of 4,096 parallel environments. Change one weight and the policy does not get a little better or worse; it finds a different way to satisfy the objective, and the only way to know which way is to look. So every real experiment branches: this weight or that, this curriculum or that, and each branch produces its own curves, its own per-term breakdown, its own set of failures. Inspecting all of it — cross-referencing a suspicious reward curve against a config diff against a catalogue of known failure modes — is exactly the work a person finds tedious and gets wrong, and exactly the work an agent finds natural. What the agent cannot do is look at the duck and know the gait is ugly. MicroDuck Lab is built so that neither has to do the other's job: the human supplies the judgement and the intent, the agent supplies the reading and the bookkeeping, and WebMCP is what lets them do it on the same live state. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Your pointing gesture becomes the query. Drag a range on the rollout timeline. Click the duck that fell. Type five words: "What went wrong here?" The agent does not ask what "here" means. It calls get_selected_timeline_range and get_selected_joint , learns you mean episode roulade , 1.80s–3.12s, pulls the telemetry for exactly that window, and answers: Lost upright orientation in this window — the trunk went past horizontal. Trunk dropped to 0.049 m, well below the nominal 0.12 m stance. Large angular velocity peak (10.01 rad/s) — the trunk is being thrown, not steered. Action-rate spike at t=2.38 s — the policy is correcting hard. No transcription. No screenshots. No "at about two seconds in". And it points back: name a joint and it lights up on the robot you are already looking at. The agent arrives already knowing this robot. Not because the model was trained on it — it launched five weeks ago — but because the page hands over Pollen's own reward-design playbook through get_rl_playbook . Ask why a policy keeps falling and you get the maintainers' hard-won rules, not textbook RL. You can break a reward function on purpose. Reward is a function of a trajectory, so stored rollouts can be re-scored under any objective instantly — no retraining, no GPU. Give a penalty a negative weight and the ranking reorders: a forward roll overtakes a clean walk, 7.31 to 7.04. The breakdown shows why in one line: Angular-velocity penalty w=-3 mean=-1.538 contrib=+4.613 A penalty paying out. That is Pollen's own documented sign-convention bug — where butt-hopping and crash-sits come from — reproduced in a browser in one slider drag. check_reward_signs implements their "infallible check" (every penalty must contribute ≤ 0) so an agent can catch it before GPU time is spent. And the loop closes off the page. Training a 61→14 locomotion policy needs CUDA and hours, so the studio does not pretend to do it. Instead, compose_training_job emits a prompt — not just a command — that you paste to the assistant on your own GPU machine, or hand to Hugging Face Jobs. It clones microduck_rl , runs Pollen's 64×5 smoke test first, launches the real run, watches that every penalty stays ≤ 0, and exports to ONNX. Training continues the same conversation instead of becoming shell archaeology. Then you bring the weights back. import_policy validates the 61→14 contract on load — a wrong-shaped file fails there, not as a flailing robot — and the imported policy becomes first-class: in the list, drivable, and A/B-able. We did this for real: base-walk , trained overnight on an RTX 5080 ( velstand , 4096 envs, 4000 iterations), ships with the site. compare_policies runs it against the published alpha_walking over identical scenarios and seeds. It survives on ice where the baseline does not — 50% vs 0%, on 2 seeds × 5 s, which is a small sample and is stated as one. How it creates a better user experience Six guided lessons, each a real action with a real outcome, each ending by handing you a question worth asking the agent. The simulator is the lesson; the agent is the tutor that can read live state. The studio is built to be operated by either party. Everything the agent can do, you can do by hand — drop obstacles in the duck's path, make the floor slippery, shove it with the mouse, drag a reward slider — and everything you do, the agent sees. A policy trained elsewhere gets the same treatment as one that shipped. And when the duck goes down it says so, from a speech bubble anchored to its actual jaw. The bubbles are the studio's way of turning every moment into an invitation: a fall suggests a question to ask, an idle duck suggests something to try, a new obstacle suggests a comparison. One of the things it says is true and teaches something: "I have fallen and I cannot get up — there is genuinely no get-up policy." How we implemented WebMCP One command layer. No second path for the agent. Every state change goes through a single core module ( src/core/commands.ts ). The UI calls it; each WebMCP tool ( src/webmcp/registerTools.ts ) is a thin schema wrapper over the same function . So when the agent sets a velocity command, the slider physically moves . Human state and agent state cannot drift, because they are the same state. A parity test asserts it. 53 tools registered on document.modelContext (not navigator — deprecated in Chromium 150), grouped as knowledge, state, selection, attention, mutation, execution, analysis and escalation. Security annotations per Chrome's tool-security guidance: 25 tools marked readOnlyHint , 3 marked untrustedContentHint — get_rl_playbook returns third-party markdown verbatim, import_policy echoes a user-supplied URL. They are nested under annotations ; passed flat, Chrome silently drops them. Within the published budgets: names ≤30 chars (max 27), descriptions ≤500 (max 373), parameter descriptions ≤150. Errors are values — {ok:false, reason, suggestion} — and invalid input names the valid options, because an agent can recover from that. No enum freezes the policy list, so a policy you imported is as nameable as one we shipped. A dev panel lists eve

title: nema
pitch: A learning protocol for the web: any site adds one tag, readers keep signed proof of what they learned in a vault they own, and any agent connects the two.
about_excerpt: A learning protocol for the web: any site adds one tag, readers keep signed proof of what they learned in a vault they own, and any agent connects the two. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Time reduction with Nema Nema in action Inspiration Most of what we know we learned on the web, one page at a time: a blog post about browning meat, a chapter about syscalls, a course on pan sauces. None of those pages know each other, and none of them know us. Every site starts from zero, and nothing we did on one page survives on the next. WebMCP changes the shape of the problem. A page can declare what it can do as tools, and an agent in the browser can call them. So we asked: what if a page could declare what it teaches, ask a reader's own vault what they already know, and hand back a signed note of what they did? That is nema: your learning state, everywhere. What it does A vault you own. The vault is your own record of what you have learned: signed receipts of work you actually did, issued by the sites where you did it. From those receipts it derives your state: a band per concept and per ability (recognise, retrieve, explain, apply, transfer, discriminate), a memory schedule, and a list of what to learn next. It lives with you, in your browser or on your disk, not on any site, and there is no account. The demo vault is at https://nema-vault.migarci2.dev . A protocol a site installs in a minute. Two tags on any page. That page now exposes six WebMCP tools: it describes what it teaches, asks the vault about three prerequisites, adapts, and signs a receipt when the reader passes a check. No backend needed. A learner model with a source. The vault follows the principles of learning fast that Justin Skycak writes up at justinmath.com and that Kris Abdelmessih collects in "The Principles of Learning Fast" ( https://moontowermeta.com/the-principles-of-learning-fast/ ). Passing something advanced credits every prerequisite under it at a fraction and pushes its review date out, which Math Academy calls Fractional Implicit Repetition. The vault asks for a concept only when its prerequisites are held, and otherwise names the weakest prerequisite and the goal it is blocking. A session interleaves rather than drilling one concept, and keeps confusable concepts apart unless telling them apart is the point. Consent you can see. A site never reads the vault. It asks one question, and the vault shows a modal: what will be shared (three status bands), what will not (history, scores, other subjects), for which site, for how long. You approve. The answer is a signed token bound to that one site, valid thirty minutes. Two example cooking courses that look nothing like nema. Saucier School (pan sauces) asks your vault three things and turns 68 minutes of lessons into 21. Line Cook Lab (food safety on the pass) has never spoken to Saucier School, but recognises what you did there and unlocks its advanced lessons. Two real articles, with and without nema. We mirrored a CC BY-SA article on AES-GCM and an MIT chapter of "Putting the You in CPU", added retrieval questions inside the text, and put the original and the nema version side by side with the exact diff as the headline. Any agent. ChatGPT desktop and Chrome 149 call the tools on the page. Claude Code and Codex reach the same vault over MCP ( packages/nema-mcp , the same eleven tools, same schemas). The agent is a commodity; the vault is the infrastructure. nema in your browser. A Chrome extension puts the vault in the side panel and does the boring transport with no model: a bar appears on any site that works with nema, one click shares your bands, and receipts are collected automatically when you pass something. Sites that speak their own names. A site can use its own concept ids. An agent proposes what they mean, you confirm once, and the vault translates at its edges. Who translated a name never changes how much a receipt is worth; who signed it does. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS and ES modules. No framework, no bundler. Every page loads the Chrome Labs WebMCP polyfill and registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , exactly as Chrome documents it, so the same code runs natively in Chrome 149+ and ChatGPT desktop and degrades gracefully elsewhere. The protocol is six objects (LearningManifest, ReadinessRequest, ReadinessAssertion, EvidenceReceipt, LearningNeed, ConceptAlignment) carried as compact tokens: nema1.<payload>.<signature> , ECDSA P-256 over the exact payload bytes via the Web Crypto API, in browsers, Workers and Node alike. Trust has three tiers. Registered issuers (the courses, whose keys never leave a Cloudflare Worker), origin published keys ( /.well-known/nema-issuer.json ), and self certified receipts (a blog with no backend signs with a key it made in the reader's browser; the vault caps that evidence at self report weight). Learner state is never stored. It is derived from the ledger on every read with an explainable scoring model (grader weight, result, recency, a spacing schedule), so a better estimator later never invalidates evidence. Seven origins on Cloudflare Workers: the hub, the vault, two courses, a blog, two mirrored articles. A site talks to the vault through a popup handshake ( connect.html plus postMessage ), the way "Sign in with" works, because third party iframes do not share storage. packages/nema-mcp boots the browser vault inside Node with four shims (a file backed localStorage, an event sink, a repo backed fetch, module resolution hooks) and serves tools.js verbatim over MCP, with consent through MCP elicitation. packages/nema-extension is Manifest V3: the vault page as the side panel, a MAIN world bridge that is the only code touching document.modelContext , and a service worker that relays tool calls per tab. Verification: 237 unit tests, and native end to end scripts that drive Chrome for Testing 154 over the DevTools Protocol against the live origins: the golden path, the connect handshake, the extension, replay and tampering rejections, wrong audience, expired tokens. Challenges we ran into Native WebMCP differs from the polyfill in two ways that only show up in a real Chrome: executeTool wants a JSON string and returns one, and document.modelContext refuses to run on chrome-extension:// documents. We found both by testing on Chrome for Testing canary, not by reading docs. Tokens are long. Agents mangle thousand character strings. We moved every handoff off the agent's transcript: popups, postMessage , the extension's bridge, and hand delivery links, so an agent carries meaning, not bytes. Concept identity across sites. A closed registry is honest but limiting, so we let sites use local names and made alignment a first class, reviewable claim: proposed by the site or an agent, confirmed by the person. We built and then removed an in house chat agent. It contradicted the thesis (the agent is whichever you already use) and needed a model budget judges would exhaust. The extension does the transport with no model at all. Keeping the demo learner's numbers stable across three weeks of judging with a real spacing model meant designing the seed ledger against the formulas, not around them. Accomplishments that we're proud of The consent modal. A site asks for three things; the learner sees exactly those three, and what will never leave. Everything else in the project exists so that this moment is true. 68 minutes to 27 to 21, on a site that has no account, then a second site that recognises the first, with zero partnership between them. Two real articles from other authors, republished under their licences, gaining retrieval practice and portable evidence with about a hundred added lines, and the diff shown to prove it. The same eleven vault tools reachable from ChatGPT, Chrome, Claude Code, Codex and a Chrome extension, from one tools.js . Everything checkable: every claim in this text has a test that drives a real browser against the live URL. What we learned WebMCP works best when a tool changes something on screen. Judges and learners trust what they can watch happen, so every tool here moves the page. Evidence beats mastery. Storing what happened, signed, and deriving state from it is simpler and more honest than storing a score, and it makes the learner model recomputable. Human in the loop had to be built into the tool surface rather than promised in a description. Two things have no tool at all, on purpose: answering an activity and approving a disclosure. The pages got better every time we removed a panel, a pill or a number. What's next for nema A published nema-provider.js on a CDN, a well-known key helper, and a WordPress and Astro integration so the one tag install is one click. Alignment sharing between learners: once someone confirms that a site's "browning science" is Maillard, the next learner's agent can propose it with that provenance. The extension in the Chrome Web Store, with vault sync through a file the learner owns. Providers t

title: Relocates.io
pitch: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't.
about_excerpt: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We had one weekend of viewings, in a city none of us had lived in, and a spreadsheet. The question was simple and nothing could answer it: where can all four of us actually live? Property sites filter by price and bedroom count. But nobody is unhappy about a bedroom count. They're unhappy because the school run takes forty minutes, and because that got decided once, in a hurry, from three timezones away, and then paid for every morning for three years. So we guessed. Everybody guesses. It's a constraint satisfaction problem and it deserved a solver, so we wrote one. Every requirement becomes a comparison over a 250-metre grid of the real city: real schools from Google Places with their real ratings, real gyms, real parks, and real terrain, so a hill costs the minutes it actually costs. Where everyone's requirements overlap, a volume lights up over the photorealistic map. Then it goes to zero. Six honest requirements from four people usually don't fit in one city. Every tool we'd used treats that as a dead end. Empty list, try removing a filter. But "nowhere works" is genuinely useful information, as long as you also say which two requirements are fighting and how much one has to give. So the page tests dropping each requirement, then every pair, then sweeps the blocking thresholds to find the smallest concession that reopens the map. It draws both options at once, in the colours of the two people involved. That's the point where WebMCP stopped being a technology choice. The solver can tell you bending one limit reopens more ground than bending the other. It can't tell you that one of those limits is a bad knee and the other is a fourteen-year-old walking to school by herself. It can't know that the cheaper concession is the harder one to live with. Somebody has to say "hers is cheaper, but hers is the medical one" — and a slider is never going to say that. But it doesn't work from a server either. The agent offers two futures, the page draws both over the real city, and the person picks by looking at them. What's being compared is a shape on a map, not a number in a response. The state and the solver have to sit where the person's eyes already are. The loop runs both ways too, which is the part we didn't expect to matter as much as it does. People don't wait their turn. They drag a threshold while the agent is still talking, delete something, accept an option on their own. Those edits are real and they aren't the agent's. So the page logs who changed what and hands the agent everything a human did since its last turn. What it does Relocates.io finds the part of a city where everyone in a household gets what they need at the same time, draws it on a photorealistic 3D map, and when that region doesn't exist, tells you exactly which requirements collide and how far one has to move. You can describe your household to an agent or build it by hand. Both drive the same state. Pick a city. It builds a 250 m grid and loads the terrain. Add people, then their requirements. Not filters — requirements that belong to someone, each carrying their own reason in their own words. "She walks alone, it's her independence." "It's his knee, not a preference." That sentence matters later. Watch where they overlap. The intersection is contoured and extruded over the real buildings. The area in km² is the number on screen. When it hits zero, you get options, not an error. The page finds what's blocking, works out the smallest movement that reopens the map, and draws both candidate futures at once with the area each one buys. You choose. Click one and it resolves. Both numbers were already on screen — what the agent adds is which concession is cheaper, which is easier, and why those aren't the same. Then check a real listing. Paste an address, get pass or fail on every requirement with the margin, plus the nearest spots that would have worked. Or search homes restricted to inside the feasible region, so it can't return somewhere that fails one of your family. The 3D isn't decoration. If you can't fly out for a third viewing, the two things you most need to see are what a street looks like and how steep it is, and a flat map shows neither. Walking times run through Tobler's hiking function over real elevation, so a kilometre uphill costs about 40% more than a flat one. The hill you can see is the hill that makes the school walk eleven minutes instead of seven. Same dataset drives the picture and the arithmetic. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Google Maps Platform, WebMCP. About 4,600 lines. No server, no database, no API routes. Browser tab ├── Grid 250 m lattice over the search area ├── Layers one Float32Array per question — walk time, commute, grade ├── Solver masks · marching squares · diagnosis · relaxation sweep ├── Map3D photorealistic tiles + pooled extruded volumes ├── WebMCP 18 tools on document.modelContext └── Cache IndexedDB — a city is learned once Everything runs in the browser through the Maps JS SDK and caches locally. Nothing about the household leaves the page. That started as a constraint and turned out to be the reason the whole thing works: an agent can reach into live state and get an answer in the same tick. Places and Elevation are real. Commute times are modelled from distance and mode rather than routed, and we say so on screen. We skipped the Routes API on purpose. Real routed commutes meant thousands of billed matrix elements per origin and several seconds of latency on every threshold change, which would have killed the thing that makes the sweep feel like an instrument. Two functions carry the project. diagnose.ts answers why there's nowhere to live. With a dozen requirements over a few thousand cells there's no need to be clever, so it tests every leave-one-out combination, then every pair if none of those work. Exhaustive and exact. frontier.ts answers how far a requirement has to bend, sweeping its threshold across the grid for the smallest movement that opens any cell, then the area gained at every step after. It returns a curve, not a point, so the agent can describe what a concession costs. Both measure off the grid. Neither estimates. That's the whole technical claim, so it lives in the code rather than in a paragraph. The map uses Map3DElement with regions as extruded Polygon3DElement volumes and drawsOccludedSegments on, so buildings never hide the answer. Those are DOM nodes, not batched geometry, so they're pooled at startup and mutated in place. Three things about the tools mattered more than the rest. Descriptions say when to call something, not just what it does: "call this whenever the area is 0, before telling the user anything." Every requirement carries a required rationale field. And get_state returns humanChanges , so the agent finds out what a person did while it wasn't looking. Challenges we ran into deck.gl doesn't work over photorealistic tiles. The obvious stack was a dead end. Overlays float above the terrain instead of sitting on it. We dropped deck.gl for native Polygon3DElement , which Google renders against the same terrain as the tiles. Found it with a throwaway HTML file before writing any real code, which saved a day. Google has no ratings for schools. Gyms, parks and supermarkets all return them. Secondary schools returned zero out of eight. Our "4★ or better" filter emptied the pool, so every school requirement became permanently unsatisfiable and the map went permanently blank. Saying "nowhere qualifies" would have been a lie with a straight face, so the filter now drops itself, says so in a banner, and reports the caveat to the agent. Nobody agrees where WebMCP lives. Drafts disagree on navigator.modelContext versus document.modelContext . We built against navigator , and an agent looking at the live page told us exactly what that produces: "exposes WebMCP capability, but currently provides no WebMCP tools." It now checks document first, awaits each registration, and tears down with AbortSignal . Photorealistic tiles take no style array. No saturation: -100 , so the grey-out when there's no answer had to be a CSS filter on the container. It greys the regions too, but during a conflict there are no regions to keep coloured, so that worked out. The numbers sit in an unfiltered layer above. Cutting things. Routes API, air quality, saved sessions, multi-city. All had to go to keep one sequence working reliably: requirements, conflict, two futures, a choice. Accomplishments that we're proud of The empty state is the product. Treating "nowhere works" as the interesting case is the idea everything is built around, and it held up against real data from a real city. Every number is real. Every km² and every minute comes off the grid. The agent is told never to state a figure it didn't get from a tool, and the tools are shaped so it never nee
