title: Yange 2.0 — Bring This Look Home
pitch: The web can see the outfit. Only you can see the shirt on your chair. Yange lets the agent stop, ask, and continue.
about_excerpt: The web can see the outfit. Only you can see the shirt on your chair. Yange lets the agent stop, ask, and continue. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Online inspiration and the clothes we own live in separate worlds. I might find the perfect outfit on Pinterest, but recreating it means saving a screenshot, opening another app, remembering which similar pieces I own, checking what is clean, decoding care labels, accounting for weather, and rebuilding the plan by hand. A browser agent can understand the inspiration page, but it cannot know whether my trousers are actually available or whether an uncertain care label makes a wash plan unsafe. My wardrobe app knows my clothes, but before this rework it could not receive and complete an intention that began elsewhere on the web. That gap is personal. I built the original Yange alone in Kampala after repeatedly losing as much as 30 minutes to a wardrobe that had clothes but no memory. In Luganda, yange means mine . The promise is not another generic outfit generator; it is a system grounded in my clothes, my evidence, and my final say. Solution Yange 2.0 turns “bring this look home” into one visible collaboration between a person, a browser agent, and a physical wardrobe. While viewing a compatible public outfit page, the person asks the browser agent to bring the look home with Yange. import_current_outfit_inspiration carries the public image URL and source attribution into Yange. No screenshot is required for cooperative publishers or Pinterest image URLs. Yange first fetches without cookies or referrer. When Pinterest blocks browser CORS, a same-origin Vercel function accepts only i.pinimg.com , rejects private DNS and unsafe redirects, enforces a 12 MB limit, and validates both MIME type and actual file signature. Arbitrary hosts are rejected rather than turning Yange into an open proxy. Gemini extracts reviewable Look DNA: palette, silhouette, key pieces, layering, styling, and occasion cues. The agent opens a bounded mission and inspects a privacy-filtered projection of the Wardrobe Digital Twin—names, state, and evidence quality, never raw photos or the event ledger. Deterministic policy compares exactly three futures: wear now , wash first , and verified fallback . When the plan reaches something the internet cannot know, request_missing_evidence remains pending. Yange visibly asks the person to inspect the real garment or photograph its care label. The same tool execution resumes after confirmation or decline. The agent may prepare one feasible path, but approval is not a tool argument. The person approves the exact plan in Yange; only then can the agent commit it once. Yange returns the same evidence and operation receipt to both participants. The result is not “AI clicks my wardrobe app.” It is shared work divided by authority: the agent handles cross-page context and multi-step planning; the person supplies reality and consent; Yange’s deterministic domain protects truth. The journey begins with a look found elsewhere on the web. Yange turns it into reviewable palette, silhouette and styling cues—never imaginary wardrobe inventory. Why This Matters WebMCP makes Yange materially better. I did not add WebMCP simply to make an existing project eligible. Yange is close to my heart, so the integration had to remove a real piece of friction or it did not belong. It does: the idea now moves from the page where I discover it into the wardrobe that can act on it, without the screenshot → download → upload → explain-again ritual. More importantly, WebMCP lets the collaboration pause at the boundary between web knowledge and physical truth, ask me, and continue. That capability completes a product interaction I could not express honestly before. It removes the handoff tax. The intention begins where inspiration is found. A compatible outfit image—including a Pinterest image that blocks browser CORS—travels directly into Yange with attribution instead of forcing the person through screenshot, download, upload, and re-explanation. It gives the agent useful access without giving it everything. The agent can inspect a narrow wardrobe projection, discover missing evidence, simulate alternatives, and prepare a plan. It cannot read private image bytes, dump the event ledger, rewrite garment facts, purchase clothing, or bypass approval. It lets the web admit where it ends. Whether a garment is on the chair, in the basket, or already clean is a physical fact. Yange does not hide that boundary behind model confidence. It turns uncertainty into a visible request, keeps the tool call pending, and resumes from the person’s answer. This interaction was difficult before because neither side had the whole truth. WebMCP provides the semantic contract through which the browser agent and live Yange page cooperate while the person remains present. The Heart Of Yange: A Presence That Learns I wanted Yange to feel less like a static utility and more like a friend who notices the small things. Style Aura is that idea made visible: a living WebGL atmosphere behind the interface that gradually reflects the colours associated with confident, repeated wears. It does not snap to a new palette after one tap and pretend to know the person. Each accepted interaction can move the Aura only a small step—at most 8%—using exact colour feedback, recency and repeated confidence as evidence. Familiarity is earned over time. The Aura is deliberately human-facing rather than exposed as an agent tool: WebMCP carries the work, while Style Aura lets the person feel that Yange is becoming theirs. A wardrobe state change is immediate; learned familiarity is gradual. Style Aura makes that difference visible. What Existed Before And What I Added Yange is an existing project. I preserved the submitted foundation at commit bc3ae05 and built this WebMCP edition afterward in a separate repository and deployment. Existing Yange foundation Added during the WebMCP Challenge Event-sourced Wardrobe Digital Twin “Bring this look home” mission surface Garment, care-label, and inspiration capture Direct attributed public-image handoff Gemini Look DNA extraction Open-web input treated as untrusted evidence Deterministic outfit, laundry, and WearCast policy Eight imperative WebMCP tools Existing domain commands as mutation authority Phase-aware tool discovery and unregistration Human interface Real pending tool execution during physical evidence capture Replay-safe operations Prepare → visible approval → revision-bound commit → shared receipt The original Agentic Hackathon repository and deployment were left unchanged during judging. Yange 2.0 lives at github.com/NestroyMusoke/Yange-2.0 and web-jet-one-21.vercel.app . WebMCP Leverage Yange registers eight outcome-level tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() : import_current_outfit_inspiration open_wardrobe_mission inspect_mission_readiness request_missing_evidence simulate_plan_paths prepare_shared_plan commit_approved_plan get_mission_receipt This is intentionally not a tool for every button. Tool availability changes with mission phase. Obsolete actions are unregistered through AbortController ; reads declare readOnlyHint ; inspiration-derived output declares untrustedContentHint ; the open-web import declares openWorldHint ; schemas reject additional properties. The deepest WebMCP behavior is the pending human handoff. request_missing_evidence creates a Promise-backed interaction connected to the execution AbortSignal . The page visibly asks for one physical fact. Confirmation, decline, cancellation, and unmount each settle exactly once. After confirmation, the same native execution returns person-supplied evidence and the tool set advances to simulation. Approval cannot be smuggled in by an agent. commit_approved_plan accepts no approval argument. The UI stores human approval separately and binds it to the exact plan digest and wardrobe revision. If anything changes, commit returns STALE_PLAN and produces no mutation. Replaying a successful operation returns the original receipt instead of repeating effects. Architecture Public outfit page → browser agent carries source page + main image → import_current_outfit_inspiration → HTTPS / MIME / size / signature validation → private prepared copy + visible source attribution → human-reviewed Gemini Look DNA → privacy-filtered wardrobe inspection → missing physical fact? yes → pending WebMCP execution → person confirms/declines → same call resumes no → continue → deterministic wear-now / wash-first / fallback simulation → prepare against current revision + digest → visible human approval → existing Yange domain command commits once → shared evidence + operation receipt The WebMCP layer never writes directly to garment or outfit state. Existing Yange commands remain the sole mutation boundary. The physical handoff has a consequence: once care evidence is confirmed, deterministic rules block unsafe pairings and build explained wash groups
video_title: Yange ,The Agent That Learns You Like a Friend Would Built On Google ADK, Gemini, Cloud Run
video_transcript_excerpt: I haven't always had people around me who notice the small things, and I know what it feels like to go without that kind of attention. So, every morning, standing in front of clothes I'd forgotten I owned, wasting hours, I started wondering, what would it feel like to be made by something that actually paid attention? Not to fix me, not to judge me, just to notice. I'm also a chemist, right? And that question became what I built alone in Kampala, Yange. It doesn't just recommend outfits, it learns me. The way a friend would, slowly, on purpose. In Luganda, which is my local language, Yange means mine. My wardrobe, my evidence, my style. Yange starts simply. I take a photograph of my clothes, Gemini examines what is visible and proposes the garment type, color, and material cues. At the same time, a lightweight model removes the background in my browser, giving every item a clean, consistent place in my wardrobe, even when the original photograph looks different. Those jobs are deliberately kept separate. The cutout improves presentation, but it never becomes evidence and cannot change what Yange believes about a garment. Next, I photograph the care label. Symbols that people often ignore or struggle to understand become usable information. Gemini extracts the fabric composition, washing limits, bleaching rules, and drying instructions into a structured record I can inspect. Yange never silently turns an AI guess into truth. It shows me what it found, exposes the uncertainty, and waits for confirmation. AI proposes, I confirm, deterministic rules commit. Once saved, they're no longer two disconnected photographs, they become one evidence-backed garment in my wardrobe memory. What it is, what it looks like, and how it should be cared for. When I mark the trouser worn, Yange does more than change a badge. It updates the availability and carries the same confirmed care evidence into the next state. This recorded demo ends here, but the workflow continues. In laundry, Younger uses those saved instructions to block unsafe pairings, build compatible wash groups, and preserve the correct drying method. And certain garments are held for review instead of being placed in a risky load. That is the larger idea. Capture something once, verify it once, then let the memory keep working. One photograph becomes a clean digital garment. One caliber becomes trusted evidence. And one simple one action turns the evidence into help exactly when it matters. Because I wanted Younger to feel personal, since we all have different wardrobes and tastes, like a friend who takes time to learn you, I made the learning visible. Style aura is the cherry on top. With every confirmed wear and confidence check-in, its colors move gradually towards what makes you feel most like yourself. Not instantly, gradually, until Younger becomes, without any doubt, yours. Younger is running live on Google Cloud. Three Cloud Run services separate the public edge from authenticated workers, and the latest revision receives all production traffic. The live runtime deposits Gemini, transaction of Firestore, private Cloud Storage, Cloud Tasks, and Pub/Sub. Finally, Cloud Logging ties real edge and worker requests to exact revisions, service codes, latency, and trace IDs. This is the deployed system, basically. All of this exists because of one simple idea. This isn't only my story. Somewhere right now, someone else is standing in front of a closet needing to be understood, wasting precious time, not optimized. In an age where energetic AI promises to do everything, most of it forgets to start here. Younger didn't, because it wasn't built from a spreadsheet. It was built from a real story, mine.

title: Vouchsafe
pitch: Three agencies hold one household's record and may not pool it. Vouchsafe screens that household for six benefit programs anyway by putting yes-or-no questions to four origins and receiving no records
about_excerpt: Three agencies hold one household's record and may not pool it. Vouchsafe screens that household for six benefit programs anyway by putting yes-or-no questions to four origins and receiving no records Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration To find out whether a household qualifies for heating assistance, food assistance, or a childcare subsidy, a caseworker needs facts held by three separate agencies, and those agencies are forbidden to share them. The restriction is legal rather than technical, which is why the usual answer (put it all in one database) is not available. So the household becomes the courier: a portal and a login for every agency, documents printed and re-keyed into six forms that all ask the same questions. Benefits go unclaimed because the process is exhausting instead of people not being able to qualify. WebMCP is the first thing that fits the actual shape of that problem. It lets a site offer a capability without handing over the data behind it, and it expresses consent as something the browser already understands: an origin. A server-side MCP integration cannot do this, because the agencies would have to trust a central integrator with the records themselves, which is the exact thing the law forbids. What it does Vouchsafe is a benefits screening workbench for a caseworker. They ask one question in plain language, and six programs are determined across three agencies in seconds, with the reasoning shown requirement by requirement. Each agency keeps its record at its own origin and answers only predicates. attest_income_below(threshold, tax_year) returns {attested: true}, never 34200. The release of information a client signs is expressed as exposedTo: [' https://vouchsafe-app.vercel.app']: this site may ask, and no other site may. The office ends up safer than before, not merely faster. A disclosure ledger shows every question that crossed an origin boundary, which field stayed at the agency, and what came back. After a full screening, it reads eleven questions asked, zero record fields disclosed. A caseworker who never had the income figure cannot leak it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An assistant can compose a decision across mutually distrustful origins that will not share data, and none of them has to trust the assistant, the broker, or each other with a record. Three things follow: Determination without disclosure. Utility Arrears Relief comes back eligible having asked nobody anything, because it is categorically eligible via heating assistance. The determination is derived entirely from another determination. Consent that is revocable mid-session, from the UI. Withdraw a release at the agency and its AbortController fires, toolchange reaches the broker, and the tool stops existing. The assistant does not refuse the question; there is nothing left to call. An honest third answer. Programs that needed the departed agency turn indeterminate, never ineligible. Absence of proof is not proof of ineligibility, which matters when the output is somebody's benefits. How we built it Four separate origins. Plain ES modules, no build step, zero npm dependencies. The three agencies register attestation tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { exposedTo: [' https://vouchsafe-app.vercel.app' ], signal }), each returning a minimal-disclosure envelope of {attested, predicate, agency, ref, ts} and nothing else. Revenue also registers get_income_record without exposedTo, as a control case: the broker cannot see it, and a "Probe the boundary" button demonstrates that live. The broker is a composer, not a forwarder. It discovers agency tools with getTools({fromOrigins}), calls them with executeTool(), and re-syncs on toolchange. It then registers six tools of its own for the assistant, so the agent sees one coherent surface rather than a pile of forwarded predicates, and never sees an agency tool at all. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is young, and most of the real work was discovering how it actually behaves rather than how we assumed it would. Six findings are documented in smoke/RESULTS.md. The three that shaped the architecture: getTools({fromOrigins}) is additive, not exclusive. It returns the caller's own tools alongside those of the requested origins. Before we caught it, the broker's own facades landed in every agency's bucket, so agencies read as online while their tools were missing. The broker now partitions results by tool.origin. executeTool() takes a JSON string and returns a JSON string, not objects, so arguments and results both need serialising and the response needs parsing twice. Registering a tool that already exists throws InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name. Our toolchange handler was not awaiting its own callback, so two refreshes could overlap and the second collided with the first. Verification was its own problem: WebMCP does not exist in headless Chrome, so a normal headless test captures an empty, broken page. Every check drives a real headful Chrome over the DevTools Protocol instead, and cross-origin iframes are out-of-process, which needs Target.setAutoAttach with flatten: true to reach them at all. Accomplishments that we are proud of The central claim is measured rather than asserted. tools/verify-agent.js walks the entire agent path and scans every byte the assistant can see for the record values: leakedSecrets: [] across 9,940 bytes. tools/verify-revocation.js proves the revocation path against production, not a mock. ?selftest=1 runs seven assertions inside the live page, so a judge can check the claims without reading any code. Thirty-six unit tests cover the program graph and the envelope. The control case is the part we would point at first. A tool registered without exposedTo is not merely undocumented or unlisted; the broker genuinely cannot reach it, and the page lets you try. What we learned The important design decision was making the broker compose rather than forward. Proxying twelve agency predicates straight to the assistant would have been less code and a worse product: the agent would carry the burden of knowing which agency holds what, and every question would cross the boundary individually. Six facades that each consult several origins gave a better agent experience and a smaller disclosure surface at the same time. The second lesson was that a privacy claim is worth only as much as its instrumentation. "No records are disclosed" is easy to write and easy to break by accident, so the ledger counts real crossings and the verifier greps the agent's own view for the secret values. What is next for Vouchsafe The predicates here are hand-written per agency. The natural next step is a declarative attestation schema, so an agency can publish which predicates it answers without writing a tool by hand, and a signed attestation reference, so a determination can be re-verified later by a third party from the ref alone. Beyond benefits, the same shape fits anywhere a decision needs facts that are legally forbidden to pool: clinical eligibility, immigration casework, school enrolment, tenancy checks. The interesting property is not that the data stays put. It is that the consent to ask is a browser primitive an ordinary person can withdraw. Built With chrome css html javascript model-context-protocol node.js vercel webmcp Try it out vouchsafe-app.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Ismum Al-Araf Like Share this project: Updates Ismum Al-Araf started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:46 AM EDT
video_title: Vouchsafe Demo - OpenAI WebMCP Challenge
video_transcript_excerpt: Three government agencies each hold part of one household record. By law, they can't pull it. So, the household carries the paperwork between them. A conventional interrogation answers by handing back the record. Income, filing status, etc. Vouchsafe asks a yes or no question instead. The black block is where the value would be. It never leaves the agency it's holding. Four separate origins, not one page with three panels. They exchange tools through Web MCP, a proposed browser API that lets a site offer tools directly to an assistant. This is the Department of Revenue. It holds the income figure in the clear because it's the agency of record. It exposes one tool, a test income below a threshold, and one in deliberately doesn't expose the full record. The broker cannot see that one and that's the control case. Six tools face assistant, and each one may consult three separate origins. Six programs, three agencies, one question at a time. Four eligible, three ineligible, and one indeterminate. This is the whole surface. An assistant gets six tools, and this is what one returns. Three agencies were asked, and what came back is labels and pass or fail, not one record value. Every question that cross an origin boundary is here. What stayed at the agency on the left, what crossed on the right. 11 asked, 10 answered, and zero record fields disclosed. What the assistant received back was 10 booleans and an audit reference. No income, address, or household roster. And when the broker reaches for the tool that was never exposed to it, it does not get a refusal. It gets no origin at all. Consent is an origin named out loud. Withdraw it and the agency aborts its registrations, tool change fires, and the tool stop existing. The assistant doesn't refuse the question as there is nothing left to call. And the programs that needed it turn indeterminate, never illegible. The system says it cannot know, which is the honest answer. Four origins, six programs, and zero records. Thank you.

title: Focus Contract Studio
pitch: ChatGPT can read, propose, apply, and verify a live accessibility repair—but only the person can approve it.
about_excerpt: ChatGPT can read, propose, apply, and verify a live accessibility repair—but only the person can approve it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browser agents can inspect and act quickly, but important product decisions should not collapse into “the model suggested it, so the model changed it.” Accessibility and design-system teams need a shared surface where an agent can use the live page and prior decisions while an exact visible UI review remains the only source of application authority. Focus Contract Studio explores that future of the open web through one deliberately narrow, testable decision: which control should receive initial focus in a destructive Delete Account dialog. What it does Focus Contract Studio gives a reviewer and ChatGPT one shared, page-bound change-control loop. R13 makes that contract legible at first glance: a forensic editorial workspace shows the concrete Delete-versus-Cancel mismatch, then maps the Browser → Agent → Reviewer → Browser protocol before the first action. The browser renders implemented revision 1, where the dialog initially focuses Delete. The page retrieves synthetic, applicable precedent saying this exact destructive-dialog context should initially focus Cancel, and reports a bounded DECISION MISMATCH. ChatGPT reads the live review through WebMCP and stages an immutable Delete → Cancel proposal. The renderer stays on revision 1 and the proposal stays visibly NOT APPLIED. The reviewer inspects the exact diff, digest, and base revision. There is no approval tool: only the visible UI-mediated decision can authorize application. ChatGPT applies that exact approved payload. Guarded writes create revision 2 and a durable receipt. The person completes a keyboard rehearsal in the real dialog. ChatGPT reads the page again, receives the exact current committed browser rehearsal, and verifies six behaviors: initial focus, focus order, forward wrap, backward wrap, Escape, and returned focus. History, stale-state rejection, idempotent retries, reload recovery, revisioned undo, privacy limits, and a complete keyboard-accessible fallback remain visible on the same page. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Every operation depends on live page context: the rendered variant, implemented revision, browser observation, eligible precedent, immutable proposal, current review state, and committed rehearsal. A detached chatbot or generic API would lose the precise state boundary that makes each action useful and safe. The page registers exactly four typed top-level tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...): read_active_focus_review create_focus_contract_proposal apply_approved_focus_contract verify_focus_contract The WebMCP adapters and visible UI call the same protected application services. There is deliberately no approval, review, rehearsal-capture, reset, undo, URL, selector, or workspace-selection tool. Page text, retrieved precedent, tool output, and model language are untrusted evidence—not authority. How it creates a better experience The reviewer and agent work from the same live revision instead of exchanging screenshots and stale summaries. The agent can create a durable, inspectable proposal without silently changing the product. The exact visible UI review remains the only application authority. Application fails closed on stale revisions, changed digests, revoked or rejected decisions, foreign workspaces, and conflicting retries. Verification comes from fresh browser events, not from regenerating the expected answer from the configuration under test. The full visible workflow still works when WebMCP is unavailable. Before this, teams could combine chat, tickets, component previews, precedent documents, and browser testing, but the state and authority boundaries lived in separate tools. Focus Contract Studio turns them into one legible human-agent protocol on the open web. What people and agents can do together now ChatGPT can interpret bounded precedent, create a field-supported proposal, apply only the exact payload already authorized in the page, and return a durable verification receipt. The reviewer can inspect every transition, supply the only approval authority through the visible UI, replay receipts, recover from uncertain responses, and undo a committed revision without trusting hidden agent state. The current release retains the final page-bound handoff: after the browser rehearsal, read_active_focus_review returns a bounded verificationTarget for only the active workspace, variant, and revision. Foreign, stale, test-only, recording, uncommitted, and expired rehearsals are excluded. Judges no longer need a database console, copied cookie, workspace ID, or manually supplied rehearsal ID. How we built it Focus Contract Studio is a full-stack ChatGPT Site written in strict TypeScript with React and Next.js-compatible Vinext output. Sites-managed D1 stores isolated anonymous workspaces, focus revisions, synthetic precedent, immutable proposals, visible review decisions, allowlisted raw rehearsal events, and receipts. Zod defines strict route and WebMCP schemas. One indexed D1 query filters precedent by workspace, product, component, behavior, status, and valid time before deterministic TypeScript BM25, structured applicability, relationship ranking, and Reciprocal Rank Fusion combine the eligible lists. Proposal payloads use canonical SHA-256 digests. Apply uses expected revisions, scoped idempotency, repeated conditional guards, database constraints, and explicit zero-row handling. Verification consumes immutable finalized browser events rather than generating expected events from the configuration under test. The Site calls no model API: ChatGPT supplies reasoning through WebMCP, while deterministic code owns validation, persistence, authorization checks, application, and verification. Challenges we solved Preserving useful precedent without turning retrieved text into permission. Making proposed, reviewed, applied, and verified visibly and mechanically different states. Keeping retries, stale revisions, and concurrent applies from creating partial or duplicate mutation. Verifying the rendered dialog from raw events without recording optional reason-field text. Supporting an anonymous public judge flow with isolated, expiring, abuse-bounded workspaces. Making the final verifier target page-bound without introducing an unsafe implicit “latest rehearsal” mutation. Accomplishments verified for R13 The deployed R13 source, release/webmcp-challenge-2026-r13 branch, and annotated webmcp-challenge-2026-r13 tag resolve to commit 3a37d92cb22d39602acbb3bd323f40a8c96e70d8. ChatGPT Sites version 13 reports that exact source commit, and production deployment appgdep_6a9a6f2a52d081918f5b700cecc19f78 completed successfully on the public Site. The canonical clean-source release gate passed. Release integrity reported PACKAGE8_RELEASE_PASS with 724 packages and 16 checks; npm audit found zero vulnerabilities. The built-Worker browser, security, responsive, keyboard, and accessibility checks passed. A fresh R13 run in ChatGPT's in-app browser discovered exactly four tools and completed the full public flow: finalized revision-1 observation, proposal creation, visible human approval, guarded apply, revision-2 rehearsal, and all six verification checks. Successful agent mutations refresh the visible page without a manual reload. A fresh apply truthfully reports a revision change; retrying the same idempotency key recovers the same receipt while truthfully reporting no new revision change. R13 preserves the visible-only approval authority, guarded D1 state machine, native dialog, and independent raw-event verifier. R10 retains the historical Chrome trace for the same four-tool contract. Release and evidence: https://github.com/chvignesh07/focus-contract-studio/releases/tag/webmcp-challenge-2026-r13 What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a capability needs the precise state of the live page. Exposing a mutation-shaped function is easy; preserving ordinary authorization, exact review intent, revision safety, accessible fallback, and truthful recovery around that function is the real product work. We also learned to separate relevance from permission. Precedent can make an agent proposal better and determine whether it is admissible, but it cannot say whether this exact payload was approved. And a renderer cannot prove itself by producing its own expected events—verification needs an independent observation path. What's next This contest release proves one dialog family and two visual variants with synthetic precedent. The next evidence step is moderated testing with accessibility and design-system practitioners, measuring task time, correction count, unsupported-proposal rejection, and trust calibration before expanding to more components or organizational roles. Built with WebMCP, ChatGPT, ChatGPT Sites, TypeScript, React, Vinext, Cloudflare Workers, D1, Drizzle ORM, Zod, Web Crypto, Vi

title: GoSX 3D Studio
pitch: A 3D studio where browser agents stage exact scene edits and artists keep the only Apply.
about_excerpt: A 3D studio where browser agents stage exact scene edits and artists keep the only Apply. Like Comment Story Updates The problem 3D editors are dense and stateful. An artist can see which object matters; an agent needs stable identities, exact properties, and the current revision. Pixel automation guesses through controls, while a detached API pulls the work out of the artist's spatial context. That leaves a bad choice: manually repeat the agent's suggestions, or trust an invisible write. GoSX 3D Studio keeps person and agent aligned before anything becomes canonical. What it does The webpage itself is a shared collaboration surface. It registers exactly four focused tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...): scene_get_state reads canonical scene state and its revision. scene_find_objects searches stable IDs and names with typed filters. scene_focus_object brings the hierarchy and Inspector to the object under discussion without changing canonical state. scene_preview_actions validates and stages 1–12 reversible operations at an exact revision. A browser agent can inspect 150 entities, resolve Board to stable ID board, focus the visible Studio, and stage a rename plus material assignment. The artist sees the exact before/after diff in the live 3D viewport, can orbit the reversible result, and keeps the only Apply action. There is intentionally no WebMCP commit tool. The review retains affected IDs, actor, policy evidence, revision boundary, and result fingerprint. Apply sends only an opaque proposal ID; the server commits the exact stored transaction through the existing revision-safe engine. Stale work is rejected. Activity distinguishes agent://webmcp proposal authorship from human://webmcp-review approval. That makes WebMCP the product interaction model, not a badge or generic CRUD wrapper: the person and agent point at the same stable object, reason from the same revision, and create an auditable handoff from machine-prepared preview to human-approved canonical state. Why the experience is better Agents handle precise hierarchy search and proposal preparation without taking commit authority. Artists stay inside the spatial context of the real editor instead of translating detached advice. Focus, preview, approval, and discard reconcile in the same document without tearing down the Scene3D canvas. Every staged edit is bounded, policy-checked, attributable, and visibly reversible. A persistent viewport outcome makes the R → R+1 handoff obvious after approval. Implementation browser agent -> four WebMCP tools -> same-origin proposal service -> server checks -> Workspace.Execute(propose, revision R) -> visible non-applied review card -> human Apply UI -> exact stored transaction -> Workspace.Execute(direct, revision R) -> canonical R+1 Both human and agent paths reuse Workspace.Execute; WebMCP is an adapter over the same SceneDoc and typed SceneIR used by the Studio. Proposals are session-owned and one-use, expire, carry revision checks, and are committed through CSRF-protected UI actions. Server-side review checks fail closed and expose pass evidence for each staged operation. The demo uses GoSX server rendering, WebGPU-first Scene3D with WebGL fallback, Go, JavaScript, and Kubernetes deployment by immutable image digest. Challenge-period work GoSX 3D Studio existed before August 25, 2026. It already had its SceneDoc model, 3D workbench, stable IDs, fingerprints, undo/redo, revision conflicts, and a shared transaction path for human and agent commands. Those foundations are not claimed as Challenge work. During the submission period we added the WebMCP adapter; structured inspection, search, and focus; session-owned non-canonical proposals; server checks; the visible review and exact-commit boundary; typed-call evidence; shared-demo reset; focused tests; and deployment materials. We also added same-document Scene3D reconciliation, WebGPU-first rendering, a compact evidence dock, and a refined PBR sample scene. Final polish added the in-app native-tool disclosure, presentation-size reversible diff, sticky human-only approval, persistent revision outcome, race-safe reset, conflict-free hierarchy keyboard behavior, and a recorder that verifies the exact handoff. The pre-Challenge comparison point is commit a216194ebc0f415a011aa780386773c0750bccf9 from July 29, 2026. How we used AI A WebMCP-capable browser agent interprets the artist's goal, chooses page tools, finds relevant objects, and prepares a typed proposal with rationale. The Studio retains schema validation, revision checks, policy, fingerprints, authority, and canonical state; it does not hide a second chat backend or give the agent a privileged write path. OpenAI Codex helped trace the architecture, connect WebMCP to Workspace.Execute, implement and review boundaries, author tests, debug native-browser behavior, run checks, and prepare documentation and demo materials. Buckley generated and pushed the final structured commit, and Buckbot ran the pre-merge review. Verified public flow The current immutable deployment was built from main merge commit 1e68684cbe6d5a8a10257c1ea9b85e40c9046125 and pinned as sha256:facffa246e9377d49db38c5d0c008e4e6db1a593f10e1e5ebfaff8f2475e9b9c. On September 4, native Windows Chrome 152 completed the deployed flow at 1920×1080 using native document.modelContext and WebGPU: exactly four registered page tools and 145 rendered meshes; Inspect, Find, Focus, and Stage completed against stable ID board; the exact Board → Launch Board and Carved Wood → Brushed Steel proposal left canonical revision 3 unchanged; the visible Apply control advanced the scene exactly once to revision 4; PROPOSED and APPROVED activity shared the same plan token; Evidence remained 31/31 current; the same mounted WebGPU canvas survived with zero document reloads and three managed same-document transitions; the shared demo was then visibly reset to a clean canonical Board at revision 5 for judges. The repository's CI also passes the GoSX component contract, server checks contract, vet, unit/integration tests, WebMCP lifecycle tests, race detector, browser-free frame/ray smoke evidence, deterministic certification, production packaging, and unreleased-sibling drift check. Try it Open gosx3d.m31labs.dev in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. No credentials are required. Choose Reset clean demo if another visitor has edited the shared ephemeral scene, then wait for Agent tools ready · 4 tools. In an agent-enabled client, choose Copy demo prompt and send it unchanged. In Chrome alone, open DevTools → Application → WebMCP and invoke scene_get_state, scene_find_objects, scene_focus_object, and scene_preview_actions. Confirm Inspect → Find → Focus → Stage, stable ID board, the exact two-edit proposal, passed review checks, fingerprint, and canonical revision R unchanged. Orbit the live Brushed Steel preview, then click Apply 2 exact edits. Confirm Launch Board, Brushed Steel, revision R+1, and separate agent proposal/human approval activity. Links Live demo: https://gosx3d.m31labs.dev Public MIT source: https://github.com/M31-Labs/gosx3d-studio Known limitations The public demo is one shared, process-local, ephemeral workspace with revision-conflict safety, not a private account workspace or realtime CRDT room. WebMCP exposes only three reversible operation kinds, and every staged edit requires visible human approval. Broader editor capabilities remain honestly marked partial or planned; the submission claim is limited to the verified scene workflow. video_title: GoSX 3D Studio — Human-Gated 3D Editing with WebMCP
video_transcript_excerpt: 3D scenes contain many objects, materials, and revisions. Asking an AI to hunt through pixels is unreliable, but giving it invisible right access is worse. GoSX 3D Studio gives the browser precise scene access while keeping the final decision visible. This page exposes four web MCP tools: inspect, find, focus, and stage. Together, they let the browser understand and prepare work inside the real studio. There is deliberately no commit tool. First, Chrome inspects the current scene and revision. Then, it searches the structured scene data for board and resolves the stable object ID board. Notice that the coral piece is still selected. The search has not imitated a user click. Focus now brings board into the visible hierarchy and inspector. Stage checks two requested edits against the current revision and opens a reversible preview in the same workspace. The review shows the exact result. Board becomes launch board and carved wood becomes brushed steel. The live viewport renders that proposal, but the badge still says not committed and the canonical revision has not moved. The scene remains available for inspection before anyone decides. The browser has prepared the precise edit, but apply remains a normal human-facing studio control. It names the complete scope, two exact edits. So, the decision is clear before anything becomes permanent. One visible approval commits both edits together and advances the scene once. The persistent result and activity history distinguish who proposed the work from who approved it. That is GoSX 3D Studio, agent precision with human authorship. This narration was generated with OpenAI text-to-speech using the Cedar voice.

title: Agent Quote Desk — WebMCP Procurement for Shopify
pitch: Merchant-built WebMCP tools let buyers and agents spec-match 13,000 SKUs, compare supplier quotes line by line with live freight, and file a human-verified, pay-ready packaging quote.
about_excerpt: Merchant-built WebMCP tools let buyers and agents spec-match 13,000 SKUs, compare supplier quotes line by line with live freight, and file a human-verified, pay-ready packaging quote. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Quote Desk completes a live supplier comparison: $42.90 saved (12.1%). Instant product-page fit check using live WebMCP page context, with no network request. The buyer and agent share the same on-screen quote worksheet as tools add matched rows. A human-verified, pay-ready quote is filed only after explicit buyer consent. Chrome's native WebMCP API confirms Shopify's built-ins and Packrift tools coexist with zero collisions. Agent Quote Desk turns a live packaging storefront into an agent-native procurement workspace. Try it first Open https://packrift.com/pages/agent-desk?demo=1 and click ▶ Watch a demo agent work this desk . In about 60 seconds, the page runs the actual workflow in your tab: product matching, freight, comparison rows, and savings. No login or special browser flag is needed. If you are testing in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with its WebMCP testing flag enabled, skip ?demo=1 and ask: "Beat this supplier quote on this page." Why I built this At Packrift, customers do not buy packaging by keyword. They buy by dimensions, material strength, pack counts, and landed cost. Freight alone can be 30–100% of the product cost. A buyer may have a supplier quote with inconsistent product names and simply want to know: do these alternatives fit, and what will I actually save? Answering that usually means spreadsheets, product tabs, freight math, and email. I built Agent Quote Desk so the buyer and agent can do that work in one shared, visible workspace. What the agent can actually do Paste a competitor quote from Uline, Amazon, or another supplier in any format. The agent reads the worksheet, matches each line to Packrift's catalog, adds the comparison rows on screen, calculates live freight, and totals the savings. Ask a product-page question such as "Will an 11 × 8 × 3.5 inch stack fit in this box?" The check_fit_in_this_product tool answers from live page context with no network request. For parcel-size orders, use Shopify's built-in update_cart and proceed_to_checkout tools in the same tab. For freight-class orders, use file_pay_ready_quote_from_worksheet . It requires explicit buyer consent and sends the result to Packrift's human-verified quote workflow. Nothing is auto-charged. The buyer sees every tool call mirrored in the Agent Desk panel. The agent is not working behind a curtain. Why this is a WebMCP use case Shopify's built-in tools are useful, but they are the same on every store. They do not know Packrift's box specs, freight rules, quote workflow, or what makes one product a safe substitute for another. WebMCP lets the merchant give an agent that missing domain knowledge inside the page where the buyer is already working. The result is not just easier navigation. It is a procurement workflow that ordinary browser clicking cannot reliably complete. webmcp.json: the giveaway inside the giveaway I also built and deployed webmcp.json , a declarative manifest for agent tools. The idea is simple: what robots.txt did for crawlers, webmcp.json can do for agent capabilities. A merchant lists tools in one JSON file, including static answers, MCP bridges, or HTTPS APIs with page-level scoping. The kit compiles them into live WebMCP tools at page load and refuses unsafe endpoints at compile time. Packrift's get_agent_guide tool ships this way, so an arriving agent can learn the store's workflows before it acts. Anonymous aggregate telemetry records only the tool and page type, never PII, and is public at https://packrift-webmcp-telemetry.packrift-co.workers.dev/stats . How I built it webmcp-merchant-kit is an open-source, zero-dependency layer that registers merchant tools alongside platform tools. It waits for document.modelContext , detects name collisions, scopes tools to pages, validates required input, shapes outputs for agents, and emits register/call/result/error events for the visible UI. The project provides 15 merchant tools across three scopes: six global tools, two product-page tools, and six desk-page tools, plus one tool compiled from webmcp.json . The same production registry serves three transports: in-page WebMCP, remote MCP over Streamable HTTP at https://mcp.packrift.com , and Shopify UCP at https://packrift.com/.well-known/ucp . The live theme integration is about 40 lines of Liquid and one 17 KB script. A bundled polyfill harness makes the complete flow reproducible in any browser. The hard parts and what I learned The first challenge was coexistence. A merchant kit cannot break Shopify's built-in tools or quietly shadow their names, so registration fails safely on collisions and page-scoped tools unregister cleanly. The native API also exposed two details that changed the implementation. executeTool expects the RegisteredTool object rather than a name, and the browser does not enforce inputSchema for the tool. The kit now handles both correctly and validates required fields itself. The final challenge was trust. Maximum autonomy is not always the right goal. A small parcel can go to checkout, but a freight quote should pause for buyer consent and human verification. The workflow makes that boundary explicit. Built during the submission period Everything in the repository was built during the challenge window, beginning Aug. 25, 2026: the kit, all 14 coded tools, webmcp.json , the Agent Quote Desk page, the visible event panel, the test harness, and the theme integration. The existing Packrift store and its remote MCP and quote backend are pre-existing and outside the judging scope. Proof it works The one-click demo completes a real catalog and freight comparison and shows $42.90 saved, or 12.1% , on the sample quote. Native Chrome verification is reproducible with node scripts/verify-native.mjs . On the live desk page, 23 native tools coexist with zero collisions: Shopify's 10 built-ins plus 13 Packrift tools available in that scope. The repository includes 10 automated tests plus a browser demo verifier. Real stakes Packrift is a working packaging distributor with 13,000 SKUs, five US warehouses, live freight rates, and real customers. This is not a mock storefront. Agent Quote Desk writes into the same human-verified pipeline that produces pay-ready quotes today. The project is a working demonstration of a bigger idea: merchants should be able to teach agents how their business actually works, while buyers remain in control and can see every step. title: Cartwright — WebMCP-native storefronts
pitch: An open-source engine that scaffolds complete webshops where every page ships typed WebMCP tools — shown on a real coffee shop, with a test-enforced line: the purchase stays the human's.
about_excerpt: An open-source engine that scaffolds complete webshops where every page ships typed WebMCP tools — shown on a real coffee shop, with a test-enforced line: the purchase stays the human's. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What it is, and why WebMCP (the use case) In-browser AI agents act on websites by guessing at the DOM — brittle selectors, scraping, silent failures, no way to verify what happened. WebMCP fixes that at the platform level: the page declares tools, the agent calls them. But it only matters if sites actually implement it, and hand-wiring agent tools for every page of every site does not scale. Cartwright is an open-source (MIT) engine that scaffolds complete stores — design system, database, cart, checkout, admin, i18n — with one command. During the challenge window we made the engine WebMCP-native : webshop templates now scaffold with the surface ON ( npx create-cartwright my-shop --template coffee → a store whose every page registers typed, page-contextual tools via document.modelContext the moment an agent-capable browser opens it). Not one agent-ready site — a generator of them. Shopify has shown storefront-scale WebMCP for its hosted platform; this is the same idea for the self-hosted, open-source world: the whole engine is MIT, and every scaffold owns its stack. WebMCP leverage — the depth of the surface 13 tools on the demo shop, three registration styles, one shared core: Site-wide (imperative): search_products (reduced, bounded rows — no checkout endpoints or internal fields ever enter the browser surface), get_cart (verification-rich returns: line handles, stock ceilings, structured money), same-origin navigate . Contextual, per route — progressive disclosure (the shape proposed in the tool-collections discussion, webmcp#255): an agent only ever sees the collection that makes sense on the page it is on. The product page registers add_current_product_to_cart with the page's live variants as natural-language enum values ("Whole beans, 250 g" — not internal ids), prices and stock in the descriptor. The cart page registers update_cart_item_quantity / remove_cart_item (line ids enumerated in the schema) / go_to_checkout . The catalogue page registers list_visible_products (exactly what the human sees, zero network) and filter_products (schema server-derived from the live categories). Declarative forms: search, contact and newsletter carry toolname / tooldescription / toolparamdescription attributes — the form itself is the tool, answered via SubmitEvent.respondWith (preventDefault-first). toolautosubmit only on read-only search; the human confirms communication. Agent activity is visible : :tool-form-active styling highlights the form the agent is filling. Design-pack tools: the homepage brew calculator is also calculate_brew_ratio — the same math module serves the human's widget and the agent's tool, so the two can never disagree. Any design pack can ship tools ( DesignPack.webMcpToolBindings ); the safety tests aggregate them all. The engine also answers the frameworks meta-issue (webmcp#199) in shipped, test-pinned code: execute() reads state freshly at execution time (never captured props); effect dependencies are serialized props, so re-renders never thrash the registry; every mount owns an AbortSignal and cleanup runs before the next route's registrations (abort-then-register, the current-spec-safe order — our e2e fake rejects duplicate names, and a soft-navigation spec proves the swap inside one document); one rejecting registration cannot drop the tools after it. One governed tool registry, two transports: the same operations back the in-page WebMCP tools for browsing agents and a server-side MCP endpoint ( /api/mcp ) for headless agents — same session, same state in the browser; same scopes and audit trail on the server. Beneath the callable layer sits the readable and discoverable one: llms.txt with capability truth, JSON-LD on every citable page, content negotiation (the homepage serves markdown to agents that ask), an ARD catalog, OpenAPI — and on the payable side the engine carries protocol-pluralistic commerce rails (ACP endpoints and UCP identity-linking on the same engine), so the merchant doesn't have to bet. Readable, discoverable, callable, payable — one engine. Execution — a complete product, tested like one This is a production Next.js 16 App Router application deployed on Vercel: a real store with a live database, working cart and checkout, an admin, and i18n — not a mock. The WebMCP layer is held to the same bar: ~100 unit tests across the registrar, the per-route mounts, the declarative forms, the pack tool, and the safety moat (below). A Playwright e2e suite installs a faithful fake document.modelContext (current spec semantics: duplicate-name rejection, pre-aborted-signal rejection) and walks home → catalogue → product → cart → checkout, including one real add-to-cart round-trip against the database and a soft-navigation leg that proves route teardown inside one document. Evaluation-driven, with the Chrome team's own harness: we ran GoogleChromeLabs/webmcp-tools' webmcp-evals (smoke mode) against the live demo — 12/12 steps green across brew-ratio, cart reads, catalogue listing/filtering, search, a real add-to-cart and the checkout handoff (runner webmcp-evals@0.0.3 , repo commit d39eae4 , 2026-08-27). The run's three genuine findings (a prefetch loop on the empty-cart page, non-canonical URLs in two tool returns, Danish parameter names on an English store) were fixed the same day — the eval harness caught real bugs, which is the point of running it. Byte-identity discipline: with the flag off, no registrar mounts, no tool* attribute renders, the HTML is byte-identical — pinned by tests. The live surface is smoke-monitored : the store's deployment gate asserts /en/webmcp-check and the pack tool on every run. Potential impact — who this is for Every small store that will never hand-write agent tools. The economics only work at the engine level: implement WebMCP once, correctly, with tests — and every scaffolded site inherits it. The demo is a real storefront a judge can buy from (demo checkout), running the exact code a scaffold produces. And the scaffold proves it in a first minute: npx create-cartwright myshop --template coffee && cd myshop && npm run dev seeds the demo's own nine-product catalogue — images, stock, attributes, and real variants on one product (an agent must handle both shapes) — so the tools have something true to act on with no config and no API keys. The same engine runs a second live vertical (eyewear, different design pack, Danish locale) — the surface is engine-level, not bespoke to one demo. Creativity & ambition — the line we drew The collaboration model is explicit: the agent gets the errands, the human keeps the decisions. Every cart mutation returns the fresh cart, so the agent verifies instead of assumes; an ambiguous mid-request failure says so and routes the agent through get_cart before any retry. Communication forms never autosubmit — the agent fills, the human sees the copper glow on the form, the human confirms. The purchase is deliberately out of the agent's hands: a test-enforced safety moat holds the entire browser surface — across the layout, every per-route mount, and every registered design pack — to the cart/catalogue tool families. No order-placing tool exists in the browser. go_to_checkout opens the page; the checkout form is annotated for no one. Graceful handoff, in the commerce-protocol sense: the agent escorts the human to the door it cannot open. /en/webmcp-check documents the shop's own agent surface — generated from the same constants the moat test verifies, so the page structurally cannot lie — with an intent-first explorer ("I want to… → the tool + a copyable example") and the Chrome team's polyfill as fallback so it demonstrates in any browser. And the agent-experience layer is measured, not asserted: every change to the store's agent surface (WebMCP, MCP, llms.txt, discovery files) ships through tests + live smoke, and the store publishes machine-readable pricing, auth and capability truth alongside the tools. Prior work vs. this submission (per the rules) The engine — storefront, cart, checkout, admin, server-side MCP/REST APIs — pre-exists the challenge, as does a four-tool WebMCP experiment from June 2026 (v0.25.0: global search/add/get-cart/navigate behind a flag). The entire WebMCP surface submitted here was designed and built inside the submission window (Aug 27 – Sep 3, 2026): the shared registration core, contextual per-route tools, declarative form annotations, catalogue tools with server-derived schemas, design-pack tools with registry-aggregated safety tests, the moat, the e2e suite, the eval run, /webmcp-check , and the WebMCP-native scaffold default. title: CoDesign WebMCP
pitch: AI agents turn a shopper’s brief into a validated visual design inside an existing Shopify product configurator.
about_excerpt: AI agents turn a shopper’s brief into a validated visual design inside an existing Shopify product configurator. Like Comment Story Updates What We Built CoDesign WebMCP makes a Shopify product configurator agent-ready. It is an open-source integration layer for custom products that already have a visual designer, coupled choices and production rules. Shopify agents can discover products. Custom products are different. A request such as “make 100 branded totes in two versions” still requires someone to work through materials, handles, artwork, placement and manufacturing constraints. CoDesign lets the shopper describe the result in ordinary language while the merchant's existing configurator remains in control. The Studio Tote is the public, anonymous reference implementation. The protocol is the product. The tote makes it reproducible for judges and developers, while KORRHAUS proves the same core inside a real Shopify business. Try the Public Demo Open the public tote demo . No login is required. Paste this request without mentioning WebMCP or tool names: I need 100 premium branded studio totes for North Form. Give me a natural customer version and a darker staff version, show me both options, check whether they are ready to make, and do not save anything yet. The agent then: Reads the merchant's available choices. Creates two 50-unit designs in the live product renderer. Returns genuine previews from that renderer. Detects that the darker tote's upper-left branding is too large for the merchant's safe area. Applies the only repair the merchant allows, reducing the scale from 95% to 78%. Renders a fresh preview and confirms that both designs are ready to make. The natural version remains unchanged. The proposal stays temporary and reports persisted: false throughout. The customer can inspect the result and choose Keep or Revert on the page. Revert restores the original design without a write. Why WebMCP Fits The gap is not product discovery. It is the work inside a made-to-order configurator: dependent choices, artwork, visual layout, coordinated variants and production validation. CoDesign exposes exactly six narrow webpage capabilities: Read the current design. Read the merchant's available choices. Stage supplied artwork temporarily. Create or refine an atomic proposal. Return current renderer previews. Check configuration and production readiness. The agent chooses how to combine these capabilities for the shopper's request. The merchant defines the allowed values, renderer and manufacturing rules. The page also shows truthful activity from the actual calls, so the shopper can see what the agent is doing. A Reusable Shopify Layer CoDesign is not another tote designer and it is not a universal renderer. A merchant installs the TypeScript core, describes the public customizer surface in a manifest, and connects a small adapter to the store's existing state, renderer, previews and validation functions. The normal human interface keeps working when WebMCP is unavailable. The same public core is connected to KORRHAUS's pre-existing live Shopify Custom Sock Designer through a private adapter. The KORRHAUS designer existed before 25 August 2026. During the challenge, we created the reusable CoDesign core and integrated it with that existing designer. This separation lets us show a real business implementation without publishing customer data, pricing, suppliers or private application logic. See the live KORRHAUS Custom Sock Designer for the real Shopify integration. This pattern can support apparel, teamwear, packaging, uniforms, promotional products, furniture and other Shopify products that need more than a normal variant picker. Safety and Human Control Agent changes are temporary and do not use the customizer's normal autosave. Invalid atomic proposals leave no partial changes. A newer human edit makes an agent proposal stale instead of overwriting it. A current preview is required before Keep is available. There are no CoDesign tools for save, upload, quote acceptance, order, cart, checkout, payment, pricing, customer records or administration. How It Is Implemented The public package registers webpage tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Its proposal engine handles revision checks, idempotent retries, temporary assets, preview freshness and Revert. A guarded adapter rebuilds public results field by field so private merchant state does not reach the agent. The Apache-2.0 repository contains the source, public assets, clean-clone instructions, integration guide and tests. The verified release passes 28 test files and 235 tests, plus typecheck, production builds, browser checks and tote parity checks. Agent designs. Human approves. Shopify completes the sale. Here the agent changes the sock colors, chooses a pattern, and adds the studio name in the real customer renderer. It still stays temporary until a person approves it. title: Curbcut
pitch: Curbcut gives developers and ChatGPT a shared WebMCP workspace to inspect real axe findings, preview surgical fixes, preserve human judgment, and verify repairs together.
about_excerpt: Curbcut gives developers and ChatGPT a shared WebMCP workspace to inspect real axe findings, preview surgical fixes, preserve human judgment, and verify repairs together. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Scanned Workspace Mechanical Repair Preview Verified Mechanical Repair Blocked Agent Action Contextual Proposal Responsive Workspace Inspiration Accessibility scanners are good at finding problems, but finding them is only the beginning. A developer still has to find the correct source code, understand the evidence, choose the correct repair, preview its effect, and check the result. We built Curbcut around the question: What if the developer and an external browser agent could work together on the same live accessibility workspace? The agent could handle repetitive technical work, while the developer maintained authority over changes that require meaning, context, or design judgment. What it does Curbcut is a browser-native accessibility repair workbench for static HTML and CSS. The workspace keeps everything together: Editable source A securely isolated live preview Real axe-core accessibility findings Exact source mapping and rendered-element highlighting Proposed code diffs A rendered preview of each proposed repair Human approval for semantic changes Fresh verification scans Exact Undo and clean source export A shared timeline of human and agent actions axe-core scans the actual rendered preview, and the results aren't hard-coded. Selecting an issue focuses its exact source range and highlights the corresponding element in the preview. Every repair begins as a non-mutating proposal. Curbcut shows the exact source diff and proposed visual result before changing the working source. Technical repairs, such as removing a positive tabindex, can be applied and verified in the code directly. Contextual repairs, including form labels, image alternatives, button names, and document text, remain blocked until the developer reviews and approves the exact proposal. If the browser agent attempts to apply a contextual proposal early, Curbcut returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED, visibly records the blocked action, and leaves the source unchanged. Curbcut exposes ten focused WebMCP tools covering the real workflow: workspace inspection, scanning, listing and inspecting issues, previewing, applying, rejecting, undoing, summarizing, and exporting. These tools operate on the same React store and preview used by the visible interface. There is no arbitrary JavaScript tool, arbitrary DOM mutation, or whole-document AI rewrite. How we built it Curbcut is a browser-only React 19, TypeScript, and Vite application deployed as a static site on Vercel. It requires no account, backend, or database, and the developer’s source stays local to the browser. We use parse5 8.0.1 to parse canonical HTML with source locations and assign revision-bound internal node IDs. Mapping metadata is added only to generated preview markup, so it never contaminates the working or exported source. Repairs use validated raw-offset patches that preserve unrelated source text. Imported HTML is treated as untrusted. DOMPurify sanitizes it before it enters an iframe with sandbox="allow-scripts" and no same-origin permission. A nonce-based Content Security Policy blocks network requests, navigation, forms, embeds, and untrusted scripts. axe-core 4.13.0 runs inside that opaque preview realm. A validated postMessage bridge connects scanning and highlighting to the React workspace while checking the channel, request ID, message shape, and source revision. The top-level page registers exactly ten WebMCP tools through document.modelContext. Inputs are runtime-validated, imported source and accessibility snippets are marked as untrusted content, stale revisions are rejected, and read-only tools use the appropriate annotations. Most importantly, the agent cannot manufacture human approval. Contextual approval tokens are created only when the developer approves the exact visible proposal through the interface. Challenges we ran into The first major challenge was executing axe inside an opaque sandbox while safely returning useful results to the parent application. We needed enough communication for rendering, scanning, and highlighting without granting the preview same-origin access. The second was reliable source mapping. Existing HTML IDs were not sufficient because imported documents can have missing or duplicate IDs. We instead built parser-backed mappings using exact source ranges and preview-only internal metadata. The third was keeping proposals bound to the correct source revision. Rendering, scanning, agent calls, and human actions are asynchronous, so Curbcut rejects stale issue and proposal IDs and requires the exact proposed preview to report ready before Apply becomes valid. Finally, we had to make the human-agent boundary technically enforceable. A prompt asking the agent to wait was not enough. The application itself had to reject unauthorized contextual changes and preserve the proposal and source unchanged. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real end-to-end WebMCP workflow where external browser-agent actions visibly update the same workspace the developer is reviewing Real axe scans against an isolated live preview rather than stored or fixture-specific results Exact mapping from rendered axe nodes to editable source without relying on user-provided IDs Small deterministic patches instead of whole-document model rewrites A visible, enforceable human-approval boundary for semantic changes Fresh rescan verification, exact Undo, and clean export Five bounded repair families, with color contrast intentionally kept as evidence rather than guessed automatically An unrelated imported profile-form test proving that the scanner and mapping system are not hard-coded to the checkout demo 88 passing unit and integration tests and 30 passing browser tests A 72-trajectory WebMCP evaluation with 69 operationally correct workflows, zero approval-boundary violations, and zero infrastructure failures A production deployment exercised through browser-agent tooling with all ten tools discoverable and no WebMCP console errors Curbcut does not claim automated WCAG compliance. A cleared automated finding proves only that the targeted automated check disappeared after a fresh scan. Manual review, assistive-technology testing, and disabled-user expertise remain essential. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes meaningful product actions rather than generic browser control. The browser agent does not replace the application; it gains a structured way to participate in the application’s existing workflow. We also learned that accessibility repair is as much an authority problem as a code-generation problem. Some changes are mechanical. Others require someone to decide what an image, label, or control means. A useful agent should understand and respect that distinction. Finally, source mapping and safe execution boundaries were more challenging than generating the patches themselves. Making every action visible, reversible, revision-bound, and verifiable is what turned the idea into a coherent product. What's next for Curbcut Next, we would test Curbcut with more accessibility practitioners and frontend developers, improve the editing and diff experience, and carefully add more deterministic repair families where automation is defensible. Longer term, the same shared-workspace model could support reviewed accessibility contributions across larger projects. The principle would remain the same: let the agent handle mechanics while the human retains authority over meaning. title: Gildongmu
pitch: A Korean navigation app with no map, where screen reader users search places, plan trips and explore their surroundings in plain text, now declared to the browser agent as seven WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A Korean navigation app with no map, where screen reader users search places, plan trips and explore their surroundings in plain text, now declared to the browser agent as seven WebMCP tools. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Gildongmu means "traveling companion" in Korean. I started it in June 2026 to fix a small, stubborn problem of my own as a screen reader user: I wanted to look up an address and call a place as fast as possible. Map apps make both slow, because their answers live in an interface built around images. So Gildongmu has no map at all. Everything it knows, it says in words: places, routes, what is around you, and the accessibility details a screen reader user actually needs, such as station elevators, audio beacons, accessible restrooms, stairs-free walking routes and crosswalks with audible signals. Almost all of that comes from Korean public data. When I read about WebMCP, I realized that this had quietly prepared the app for agents. Every sentence a screen reader user hears is a sentence an agent can be handed. This entry is what happened when I handed them over. What it does Gildongmu is a free navigation app for South Korea with no account and no ads, on the web, on iOS, and as an npm command line tool and MCP server. It joins about thirty public and commercial APIs from nineteen organizations and turns them into plain text. As far as I know, it is the first navigation app in Korea where a screen reader user can search places, plan a trip and explore the surroundings with no barrier in between. For this challenge the web app declares seven WebMCP tools to the browser agent: describe_app: what this deployment can do and how the tools chain search_places: places, addresses and web results, with refs to pass on get_place_info: a place by ref; for stations the timetable, accessibility facilities, live arrivals and barrier-free facilities plan_directions: transit, walking and driving summaries for a destination get_transit_route_detail: one transit route in full, including the boarding door for a quick exit get_route_steps: walking or driving steps as a numbered page read_current_view: which screen the app is on and what it shows Ask the agent "Tell me the first train, the last train and the elevators at Gangdong Station (강동역)" and one tool call brings all of it back. Ask "Seoul Station (서울역) to Gangnam Station (강남역): which car and door should I board to get off next to the elevator?" and while the agent answers, the app in the browser tab has already moved to that route, so the user can turn on VoiceOver and check every line. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The answers were already text. Most navigation apps keep their answer in pixels, so an agent driving a browser has to guess at a canvas. Gildongmu had to write every answer as a sentence for VoiceOver users long before it ever met an agent. Those same sentences are what the tools return, and they come from the same code that draws the screen. The agent cannot be told something the screen does not say. Neither a plain browser agent nor a server MCP can do this alone. Behind one station answer are four public APIs, each with its own key, its own response format and, in Korea, its own coordinate system. An agent reading the page cannot rebuild that. A server MCP, on the other hand, cannot answer "where am I standing right now", because it has no browser tab. WebMCP sits exactly in between: the page keeps the keys and the location, and the agent asks in words. Location stays in the browser. A trip starts from the user's current position, which the page already knows. Tool output goes through a list of allowed fields that has no place for coordinates, so the agent's provider receives place names and sentences, never a coordinate pair. Gildongmu has promised since its first release that nothing personal is stored on its servers, and the tools keep that promise. How it creates a better user experience For a screen reader user the expensive part is not reaching a screen, it is exploring it. A transit plan on screen is dozens of items, one swipe at a time. As a tool result it is one spoken answer, and the app has still moved to that same screen, so the user can take over and verify anything. The size of an answer follows the same instinct. A full transit answer came out at 3,700 characters, far past the 1,500 the guidance recommends. Instead of cutting it off, I split it the way I would say it out loud: the recommended route in full, the other routes in one line each, and the details behind a second tool. Nothing got worse for people. The tools press the same functions a person clicks, and a person always wins. Type a new search or close a section while a tool is running and the tool call ends as superseded. If a dialog is open, the tool declines instead of closing it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before "Which car and door do I board so that I get off next to the elevator?" Gildongmu matches a public quick exit dataset to the live route, so get_transit_route_detail returns the boarding door for each leg. No map tells you this. Ask it in the chat, and the app is already sitting on that route. "Does Gangdong Station have an elevator, and when is the first train?" One call to get_place_info returns the timetable, the accessibility facilities, the real time arrivals and the barrier-free facilities. Without WebMCP the agent would open four sections one by one, and it could not call the four public APIs behind them at all. The handoff goes both ways. The agent and the user share one screen: the tools move the app, and read_current_view reads whatever the person did by hand. The agent can set up a trip that the user finishes by touch, or the user can search by hand and then ask the agent about what is on the screen. Before this, asking an assistant and using an app were two separate places that did not know about each other. Honest absence. Every tool tells apart "none", "not known" and "lookup failed", and says outOfCoverage outside Korea instead of inventing a result. A screen reader user cannot glance at a screen to catch a made up answer, so the tools never let the agent guess. The app has followed the same rule for people since version 1.0. How I implemented WebMCP I used the imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool with a name, a description, an input schema and an execute function. Here is how I understand what I built: One set of seven tools, registered once at the app root, because an agent reads the tool list once. A tool that is not configured on this deployment is still declared and answers notConfigured. A tool that needs another screen moves there itself. Each screen publishes a small bridge to a registry, and a tool reads it at the moment it runs. A tool that waits for a screen waits for a specific place id or sequence number, not for a screen name, so a call about place A cannot be satisfied by place B appearing first. Only one tool runs at a time, with a 30 second cap. A place handle is an opaque ref that remembers which search it came from, and a handle from a replaced search returns staleResult with the call that recovers it, rather than pointing at the wrong place. Every output leaves through one function. It keeps only the allowed fields, refuses coordinates, trims to the 1,500 character budget item by item, and pages a long answer with an offset. Calls to paid third party APIs are budgeted per provider. The human sentences come from the same modules the screen uses, so the screen and the tools cannot drift apart. It is covered by 19 test files and 104 tests. I checked the contracts by deliberately breaking the implementation and confirming that the tests caught each break, and I checked the deployed site with Chrome DevTools WebMCP inspection. Challenges I ran into How many tools to expose. My first design registered tools per screen, ten in all (nine on the directions screen, one on the home screen), and along the way I weighed going much further: four screen-specific sets adding up to 31 tools, or simply re-exposing the 24 tools my Gemini chat already had. Research pulled the other way. Real sites declare one to ten tools, and both OpenAI and Anthropic advise a small number of high-value tools. I settled on seven, always on, at the app root. Gildongmu is already screen reader friendly, so browser navigation and tool calls can share the work, and seven is a number an agent handles without strain. Whether to move the cursor. An early tool moved the screen reader cursor to the item the agent had found. I removed it. What a screen reader user wants from an agent is not help exploring the screen but the exact data, fast, without exploring at all. The tools now return answers, and the screen follows on its own.
