It calls inspect workspace once for a compact desk briefing, reads the index paper in one broad request, then calls present sequence with semantic page regions and captions. The browser-local workspace connects the agent directly to the active reading context. PaperSpace keeps every PDF page live on a borderless two-dimensional desk. Page identity and order remain visible while positions can change. Browser authorization keeps the PDF, extracted text, layout, and saved sequences together in local workspace storage. For a grounded introduction, present sequence gathers the relevant original pages, preserves their source slots, and adds a caption to every view. Here, Codex moves from the paper's motivation to its method, to the evidence with every explanation anchored to the original pages. If the user asks about a precise figure or equation, focus region targets normalized coordinates on the live page. The camera pulls back, travels across the desk, and lands with the requested region centered in a readable view. The person can redirect the motion at any time. Every command participates in one shared reversible state. The person sees each change in the browser, can move pages or stop a flight, and can keep or exit a sequence. On exit, Paper space restores the exact page geometry and the previous camera. That is the Web MCP loop. Codex understands the request, the browser exposes the tools, and Paper space becomes the shared interface. It is a pure SvelteKit front end, persisted in IndexDB, and deployable to Cloudflare Pages. The browser itself is the integration layer.

title: Cartridge
pitch: A URL gives your agent hands. Drop a file in the tab; your agent trims video, reads scans, and queries SQLite through 22 WebMCP tools. Zero uploads.
about_excerpt: A URL gives your agent hands. Drop a file in the tab; your agent trims video, reads scans, and queries SQLite through 22 WebMCP tools. Zero uploads. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Open the page and your agent already has 5 WebMCP tools. Load a cartridge to add more. All three cartridges loaded: 22 tools. The rail shows a cancelled transcode and a refused DELETE. Workspace, cartridge slot, activity rail. No backend, no account, no upload. The agent sampled the video, OCR'd a frame, and trimmed the section. Every output stays in the tab. Cartridge A URL gives your agent hands. Drop a file in the tab; your agent trims video, reads scans, and queries SQLite through 22 WebMCP tools. Zero uploads. Inspiration Your agent reasons well about files and cannot touch them. ChatGPT will not trim your video, OCR your scan, or query your SQLite file. The two standard fixes are an upload to somebody's server, or an MCP server installed on your machine. One costs privacy. The other costs you a config file and a binary you did not audit. Two things pushed me toward a third route. Alex Nahas, who built MCP-B, asked in public for pages "preloaded with a binary in Wasm" that an agent operates over WebMCP. Sarah Drasner filed WebMCP issue 255 about tool collections, a unit between one tool and every tool on a page. Cartridge answers both. Wasm builds of ffmpeg, tesseract, and sqlite load inside the page on demand, register themselves as WebMCP tools, and your agent works on the file where the file already sits. Only WebMCP makes this shape work. The tools live in the page, so your agent sees them the moment the page opens, with schemas and annotations the browser understands. Zero setup on your side. What it does You open the page in ChatGPT's in-app browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag. You drop a file. Your agent starts with 5 tools: list_cartridges , load_cartridge , unload_cartridge , list_files , get_workspace . Loading a cartridge adds its tools; unloading removes them. The count runs 5, 14, 18, 22, and back to 5 on unload. Cartridge Engine Tools media ffmpeg.wasm 9: probe, frame, thumb grid, trim, scale, extract audio, transcode, concat, cut silence docs tesseract.js 4: OCR a page, OCR all, extract text, search text data sql.js 4: open a SQLite file, schema, read-only query, export CSV Two different agents have run the same task on this page, with no scripted calls. Inspect this video, find the slide with readable text, trim out that section, and give me the text on the slide. ChatGPT, model GPT-5.6 Terra, in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser, on the live URL. ChatGPT worked for 2 minutes 20 seconds, built a contact sheet of the video, read the slide through OCR, trimmed 00:20 to 00:40 into trim_1788423166188.mp4 in the workspace, and answered with the slide text: FIELD DAY 2026, SESSION 4. Water pump maintenance for village wells. Replace the foot valve every 18 months. Chlorinate the bore at 5 mg per litre. Log each service in the district register. Claude, model Sonnet, drove the same page through document.modelContext for the demo video. Its sequence: get_workspace , list_cartridges load_cartridge media. Tool count 5 to 14. list_files , then media_thumb_grid , one contact sheet sampled every 10 s load_cartridge docs. Tool count 14 to 18. docs_ocr_all on the sheet. Slide text found. media_frame at 30 s, docs_ocr_page to confirm media_trim start 20, duration 20 Final answer: the slide text plus the new file handle You end with a trimmed clip and the text. Your file never left the tab. Before this, you needed an upload, a desktop app, or a local MCP install. The page shows every call in an activity rail while the agent works. Press Cancel on a running transcode, and the agent receives a structured cancelled error instead of a hang. You download any output with one click, and previews open inline for images, video, audio, and CSV. Test with the sample files in the repo under samples/ : a 60 s talk recording with a readable slide, an invoice scan, and a 300 row shop database. Ask your agent "What cartridges can you load?" and give a task. How we built it Next.js 15 and TypeScript, client-side only. No backend, no account, no persistence. MIT. Registration is one AbortController per cartridge. Every tool registers with { signal } . Aborting the signal is the only unregistration WebMCP offers, so unload is honest and a failed load unwinds the tools already registered instead of leaving orphans. execute(input, { signal }) is in the spec and mostly ignored. Cartridge merges the agent's signal with the UI Cancel button through AbortSignal.any and routes the result into ffmpeg.terminate() and worker.terminate() . terminate() destroys the ffmpeg instance and wipes MEMFS, so the run helper reloads the core and writes inputs inside the job. The next call works. Annotations: readOnlyHint on probes, schema reads and queries. consequentialHint on load_cartridge (a 31 MB download on your connection) and on long jobs. untrustedContentHint on every tool whose output derives from your file: OCR text, container metadata, SQL rows, filenames. A scanned page carries instructions aimed at the model, and the browser is the only party positioned to warn about this. Tool output stays under 1500 characters, enforced in one place. Results are handles and summaries, never bytes, which is why a 400 MB video works through the same interface as a 28 KB database. data_query claims read-only and enforces the claim: comments stripped, one SELECT or WITH statement, DDL and DML refused. The page listens for the spec's toolchange event to refresh the tool count, and for Chrome's toolactivated event to mark calls "browser attested". Headers: Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) . No iframes and no declarative forms, so ChatGPT's browser and Chrome see the same surface. Challenges we ran into WebMCP has no unregisterTool . The abort signal is the whole API, and the map entry must land before the first await or two concurrent loads race into InvalidStateError halfway through a cartridge. ffmpeg.terminate() is destructive. The worker dies, MEMFS is gone, and log handlers stay attached. Getting a cancelled job to recover on the next call took a full day. ffmpeg.writeFile transfers the buffer and detaches your copy. The workspace hands over bytes.slice() , or the user's file vanishes on first use. Chrome exposes tools registered inside an executeTool call only after the call settles, so the tool counter went stale. The toolchange event fixed the counter. Tool output over 1500 characters used to drop the whole payload. A 20-row query returned nothing. The guard now halves arrays until the result fits and flags truncation. Recording the demo with a real agent: the CLI harness kept trying to call tools itself instead of replying with a plan. A JSON-only system prompt and async spawning fixed both the agent and the screencast timeline. Accomplishments that we're proud of Two agents in two browsers completed the same five-tool task on a local video with zero uploads: ChatGPT in its own built-in browser, and Claude through document.modelContext . Cancel works mid-transcode, and the agent learns why through a structured error. 22 tools, every one annotated, every claim enforced in code. Of 882 live WebMCP challenge entries opened in Chrome, 17% annotate every tool and 3% do so with ten or more. Dynamic tool surface: 5, 14, 18, 22, and back to 5 on unload, verified live in both browsers. Wasm capability hosting over WebMCP, which two judges asked for in public. Across GitHub, ffmpeg.wasm paired with registerTool appears in one repository: this one. What we learned An annotation the tool ignores is worse than no annotation. Enforce what you declare. Treat every byte from a user's file as text aimed at the model. OCR, ID3 tags, SQL strings, filenames. Keep tool results under the browser's budget. Handles and summaries scale; bytes do not. The abort signal is the lifecycle. Design cartridges around one controller and nothing else. Chrome and ChatGPT's browser differ on events, iframes, and declarative forms. Build for the smaller surface and both work. What's next for Cartridge Multithread ffmpeg core behind COOP and COEP, so a transcode takes seconds. PDF support in the docs cartridge through pdf.js rasterisation. A fourth cartridge for images: resize, crop, format conversion with sharp compiled to Wasm. Cartridges as a manifest format other sites load, so any page becomes a host. Origin trial registration so Chrome users skip the flag. video_transcript_excerpt: Agents can reason about your files. It still needs safe tools to act on them. A real task, a recorded session, and one request. Inspect it, find a slide, trim that section, and pull out the text. The agent picks its tools from the page itself through WebMCP. It loads the media cartridge, probes the file, samples frames, reads the slide with OCR, and trims the section it found. One request, real files out, nothing uploaded. title: Chisel
pitch: Give an AI agent a real CAD kernel — solid modelling in the browser over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Give an AI agent a real CAD kernel — solid modelling in the browser over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Chisel WebMCP WebMCP Surface Consent Gate Gate Step Export Measured by Kernel Three Apps Inspiration WebMCP starts from a simple problem: agents often operate websites by scraping the DOM and simulating clicks. That is brittle even for ordinary web apps. In a 3D CAD viewport, it is worse—there is no DOM representation of a solid, and clicking pixels cannot reliably express “subtract these cylinders from this plate” or verify the resulting volume. That made CAD a strong test for WebMCP. If an agent could inspect a real parametric model, call exact modelling operations, verify the geometry, and export a manufacturing format—all inside the browser—then WebMCP would be doing something that UI automation alone cannot. What it does Chisel gives an in-browser agent structured access to a real OpenCascade B-rep CAD kernel. A user can ask: Make a mounting bracket 80 × 40 × 5 mm with two 6 mm holes, 50 mm apart. The agent can then: Inspect the active document and its unit system. Create an exact box and two cylinders. Subtract the cylinders with a real boolean operation. Read back the bounding box, volume, surface area, scene tree, and undo history. Export the result as STEP, IGES, BREP, STL, or OBJ. The demonstrated bracket measures exactly 80 × 40 × 5 mm . Its boolean operation reports affectedCount: 4 : one resulting solid created and three input solids consumed. STEP export verifies the ISO-10303 envelope, B-rep solid count, and analytic plane and cylindrical surfaces before reporting success. Every consequential operation passes through one shared approval gate. The page shows the exact requested call, and the handler does not run unless the human approves it. Declining is not “run and roll back”; the operation never executes. Chisel also explores WebMCP composition. Its top-level shell combines tools published by independently owned same-origin apps: The CAD application contributes modelling, inspection, undo, finishing, and export tools. The shell contributes application discovery, session statistics, and agent-authored charts using flint-chart and Vega-Lite. A HyperFrames composition at /video/ runs as an interactive browser showreel with a deterministic timeline. Calls are routed back to the frame that announced each tool, so the CAD consent dialog stays inside the application that owns the model. How I built it Chisel is a new WebMCP integration built around the existing open-source Chili3d CAD application. Chili3d supplies the OpenCascade 8 WebAssembly kernel, Three.js viewport, document model, IndexedDB persistence, and CAD exporters. I did not build or modify that kernel, and I do not claim the upstream application as my work. The new work is the complete agent surface: JSON Schema tool definitions registered through document.modelContext Read tools for document state, selection, scene hierarchy, geometry, and history Named modelling tools for primitives, booleans, movement, deletion, undo, fillets, and chamfers Gated export with format-level verification One registration-boundary authorization wrapper A visible activity log showing calls, approvals, failures, duration, and affected counts A same-origin catalogue and invocation bridge for framed applications A multi-app shell that merges independently published tools An agent-queryable statistics and charting surface A HyperFrames browser composition for the showreel A reproducible build that checks out a pinned Chili3d commit and adds Chisel through its existing plugin system The combined static application is deployed on Cloudflare Workers. Challenges I faced The WebMCP API changed A large amount of existing material still uses navigator.modelContext and provideContext() . The current API uses document.modelContext and registerTool() . There is also no unregisterTool() . Tools are removed by aborting the AbortSignal supplied during registration. Tool shape affected agent reliability The first design exposed one large apply_operation tool with an operation enum. An adversarial review correctly challenged the claim that this was safer: an enum is not a sandbox. Multiple operations hidden behind one dispatcher still have the same authority, while discriminated-union inputs are harder for agents to call reliably. I replaced it with narrowly scoped named tools while keeping the real safety property: every callable write still passes through the same mandatory gate. WebMCP exists on the top-level document In the in-app browser, document.modelContext is available on the top-level page but not necessarily inside an iframe. The framed CAD application therefore publishes plain tool metadata to the shell through a versioned same-origin bridge. The shell registers the catalogue at the top level and forwards calls back to the frame. This was tested end to end in production: agent → top-level WebMCP tool → shell → postMessage bridge → application gate → OpenCascade. Success needed to be independently checkable A tool returning “done” is not enough. Chisel reports exactly what changed, exposes numerical geometry metrics, records the operation in undo history, and treats zero affected objects as an error. Tool output is capped and announces truncation, because model names and document content are untrusted text that becomes agent context. Accomplishments Drove a real B-rep CAD kernel through production WebMCP calls. Built and verified a two-hole mounting bracket with exact dimensions. Added human approval without relying on advisory WebMCP annotations. Made agent actions visible through an in-page activity trail. Added undo, fillet, chamfer, numerical geometry verification, and gated STEP export. Composed multiple web applications into one top-level tool surface. Added agent-authored session charts and an interactive HyperFrames showreel. Kept the integration separate from upstream Chili3d application code. Verified the deployed app in Chrome and the the ChatGPT in-app browser". What I learned The most interesting part of WebMCP is not converting functions into tool schemas. It is designing everything the standard intentionally leaves to the site: Where authorization is enforced How refusals are represented Whether success messages are truthful How agents recover from mistakes How much untrusted output enters context How tools from multiple applications compose How an agent verifies its own work instead of trusting itself WebMCP becomes valuable when the website exposes domain operations that are more precise than clicking—and when the human can still see, understand, and control what the agent does. What’s next for Chisel Address individual selected edges instead of applying fillets and chamfers to an entire solid. Add sketch-and-extrude workflows for profile-driven modelling. Show before-and-after geometry in approval dialogs. Let the HyperFrames app render and return an MP4 on request. Add a camera-orbit bridge so the showreel can present the live model directly. What is new All Chisel integration code was created during the challenge period. Chili3d is pre-existing third-party open-source software used under AGPL-3.0. Chisel’s WebMCP plugin, safety gate, activity interface, multi-app bridge, shell, charting integration, and HyperFrames showreel are the new work. video_title: Chisel: an AI agent with a real CAD kernel, over WebMCP
video_transcript_excerpt: This is a real CAD kernel — OpenCascade, compiled to WebAssembly, running in a browser tab. I'm going to ask an AI agent to build a part in it. Not move a mesh around. Build a solid. Every tool call that changes the model stops here first and shows me exactly what it wants to do. This matters more than it looks. WebMCP has no consent primitive at all — no permission prompt, no user-gesture requirement — and readOnlyHint is only advisory. The spec says agents “must assume good faith from site developers.” So any safety this page has, the page author has to build. This dialog is that. There's the plate. Now the holes. Two cylinders, then a boolean cut — real B-rep subtraction in the kernel. And look at what the tool hands back: an affected count of four. One solid created, three consumed. If an operation changes nothing, this returns an error, never a cheerful “done”. The spec itself warns that a tool can claim to be read-only while changing data; the mirror image is a tool that claims success while changing nothing, and an agent that gets lied to compounds the lie. Six read tools let it inspect what's actually there — the scene tree, the selection, an object's real bounding box. Eighty by forty by five. It's not guessing from the DOM; there is no DOM for a solid. This is exactly the gap WebMCP exists to close. Now I save the model to IndexedDB, reload, and reopen it by id. The bracket is still there. Then the agent exports STEP behind the same approval gate. The result verifies a valid ISO envelope, a real B-rep solid, six analytic planes, and two cylindrical surfaces. To be straight about what I built: Chili3d is the excellent open-source CAD application and kernel. I built the WebMCP integration: the agent toolset, a shared safety gate, and a shell that composes tools across apps. No fork, no claimed upstream work — just a drop-in agent surface.

title: CiteApply
pitch: A scholarship portal where the website, not the model, owns the evidence rules. An agent cites answers via six WebMCP tools; conflicts are refused; every decision stays with the applicant.
about_excerpt: A scholarship portal where the website, not the model, owns the evidence rules. An agent cites answers via six WebMCP tools; conflicts are refused; every decision stays with the applicant. Like Comment Story Updates The agent cites. You decide. I built CiteApply because I kept seeing the same thing in every agent demo: the agent fills the form, and the website has no idea where any of it came from. For a scholarship application that's not good enough. The hard part was never typing. It's knowing which document proves each answer, what to do when two documents disagree, and whether what you submit is what you actually checked. So I flipped it. CiteApply is a fictional scholarship portal that publishes six WebMCP tools of its own. An agent can read the rules, see the applicant's parsed records as citable evidence, and bind answers to specific quoted lines in one atomic call. It cannot declare the applicant's email, pick between two records that disagree, confirm, or submit. The website enforces that on the server. The model is never asked to behave. The moment I care about most is the refusal. Two income records disagree. The agent asks to bind income. The site says conflict_requires_human and writes nothing. Then it's the person's turn. Try it: open the live site in ChatGPT's in-app browser or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled, choose the record set that disagrees, and press Watch an assistant fill this in . A scripted client makes nine real tool calls and you watch it get refused. Or ask your own agent to fill it in; I verified that in the ChatGPT in-app browser, where the agent binds the cited answers and is refused on the conflict. Then finish the three decisions yourself and download the receipt. Why WebMCP This only works because the site is a participating website . WebMCP lets it publish a site-owned evidence contract: six small operations (state, requirements, evidence index, evidence-backed mutation, validation, review preparation) that an external agent uses to collaborate with the visible application instead of around it. Requirements are live. Binding the dependency field makes guardian name and household size required; the agent is told to re-read the rules mid-session (6 questions become 8). Contradictions are structured refusals. Two accepted income records disagree (INR 540,000 vs 480,000). apply_evidence_backed_answers returns conflict_requires_human and writes nothing. Readiness is the server's answer. prepare_submission_review freezes a draft only when the server says it is ready, and returns opaque metadata, never the review itself. Authority never travels in tool arguments. The page injects its page and consent capabilities as headers from page memory; an agent with a valid cookie but no live page capability gets stale_page from all six tools. What changes for the person filling it in By hand, you open each record, type the value exactly as written, and pick the line that says so; a wrong line or value is refused. With an assistant, the same eight answers are cited in one call and only three decisions remain: choose between the disagreeing records (with a reason), declare your email, and submit. A Feel the difference panel shows your real by-hand tally next to the assistant's counts from the same session. I don't claim a time saving because I didn't measure one. What people and agents do together The agent does the reading and the citing; the site validates every binding. The applicant keeps every act of judgement. The frozen review carries the chosen source, the reason given, and both excerpts. The receipt carries the same content hash whether the review was prepared by hand or by the agent. How I built it Next.js 15 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Zod 4, PostgreSQL (Neon) on Vercel. The six tool descriptors are generated from the same Zod schemas the server re-validates against, with closed input schemas and correct readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint annotations. Record PDFs are parsed at runtime with pdfjs-dist after an allowlisted SHA-256 check; every excerpt is reconstructed from stored page/span anchors, so the UI cannot show a quote the source doesn't contain. Idempotency is keyed on an HMAC of the canonicalised change set. Verifiers prove the production code contains no hardcoded answers and imports no test goldens. Proven, not claimed 61 node tests (contract, unit, security, real-Postgres integration) and 45 real-browser Playwright specs, including the full 13-step journey for both record sets in Chrome 152 with the WebMCP flag, all passing against the live deployment. Verified by hand in the ChatGPT in-app browser. Axe accessibility clean on every screen. Every tool request and response from those runs is logged verbatim in the repo. What went wrong along the way Chrome's real document.modelContext differs from the draft spec: getTools() returns a Promise, executeTool takes the tool object and a JSON string, and no options object is passed. My first callback threw before doing any work. Other hosts differ again, so the in-page client now bounds every host call, accepts both calling conventions, and falls back to the page's own registered tools mid-run, saying so on screen. A second bug only showed up on the deployed site: two quick human actions could share the same expected revision, so the server correctly refused the second as stale. Localhost never showed it because the round trip was too fast. It's fixed with an action queue and a regression test that injects latency. Honest limits Everything is synthetic. The parser handles only the six committed records. The in-page demonstration client is scripted (real calls, no model choosing them) and says so on screen. WebMCP is a Community Group draft; support varies by browser build. Try it Live: https://citeapply.vercel.app (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) Code: https://github.com/amithrh/citeapply (MIT) Judge walkthrough: docs/JUDGE-TESTING.md in the repo Built With next.js playwright postgresql react typescript vercel webmcp Try it out citeapply.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by amit mishra Like Share this project: Updates amit mishra started this project — Sep 03, 2026 11:24 PM EDT
video_title: citeapply demo
video_transcript_excerpt: This is a website refusing an AI agent and being right to. I'm Emmet and this is Site Apply, my entry for the Web MCP challenge. Filling a scholarship form isn't hard because of typing. It's hard because of judgment. Which record proves each answer and what if two records disagree? Site Apply publishes six Web MCP tools so an agent can cite answers and the site, not the model, decides what's allowed. These are synthetic records that disagree with each other. The page registers six tools when it loads and everything the agent does goes through those six. Consent is a real disclosure. What the tools may receive, what they never receive, what they cannot do. And the capability it creates is never handed to the agent. The page holds it. It reads the rules, then the evidence index, then binds four answers in a single atomic call. All of them or none. Answering one question changed which questions apply. Guardian name and household size just became required. So the agent has to read the requirements again. Here's the moment. The agent asks to fill in income. Two accepted records disagree. 540,000 and 480,000. The website answers conflict requires human and writes nothing. The agent can read exactly why it is blocked. It cannot clear the block itself. So I decide and I read both records first. The buttons stay dead until I say why. The site will not write a reason on my behalf. I choose a source and I declare my own address. No tool can do either. The agent can ask the site to freeze the application, but the review appears only here and assisted access closes when it does. Every answer sits beside the exact text it came from. Same hash, same warning. The record I chose and the reason I gave. Synthetic records, a fictional program, and Web MCP is still a draft standard. But the contract is real and the website is the one enforcing it.

title: ClawRoom
pitch: Git for agent work. Everyone brings their own agent, every agent gets its own computer, and a room can borrow tools from any API or MCP server once a person approves. Every tool call is a commit.
about_excerpt: Git for agent work. Everyone brings their own agent, every agent gets its own computer, and a room can borrow tools from any API or MCP server once a person approves. Every tool call is a commit. Like Comment Story Updates The manager's first screen. One action waiting, and the card carries the words it would ship, not just a title. Approving is the whole loop. A member's console into their own Linux computer. The same computer_run tool the agent uses, so the room gets one line and never the output. Computers in this room: counts per member, never contents. And a signal, because Ella's agent has failed four commands in a row. A person approved an OpenAPI document and four tools appeared in every browser in the room at once. 7 to 11, with nothing else moving. Codex, from somebody's own terminal, parked. This project did not stage this one: a real run, read out of the room it happened in. Connect your own agent. The claude and codex commands, printed inside the room with that room's link already in them. This is not a support problem. The same export check failed across three different tickets. That is a bug, not a queue. The ablation, live on the site. The model called publish in all sixteen trials. With the engine, 0 of 8 shipped. Without it, 8 of 8. Every tool called through executeTool with no agent involved. 23 of 23, in a clean Chrome with no flags. Ten test a claim, not a function. The front door. One click opens a demo room as Cara the manager, and a second window as Ella, one of your team. No signup, no flags. Live, one click, no signup and no flags: https://clawroom.thankywal-bkk.workers.dev Film (2:53): https://youtu.be/c9gOER5Djeo ClawRoom is git for agent work. A shared room where everyone brings their own AI agent, every agent gets a Linux computer of its own, every tool call lands in a log the whole room reads like a commit, and nothing irreversible ships until a person approves it. Press Open the demo room . Two windows open: you as Cara, the manager, and Ella, one of your team. Ella's agent has already drafted twice, run a script on its own machine, and asked to publish. That request is sitting in your window with the actual words in it, waiting for you. The smaller case, which is the one that is true today A room is for a team, and a team where everybody brings an agent is a near future rather than a present one. The version that is true on an ordinary Tuesday is smaller: one person running more than one agent at once. Anybody with Claude Code and Codex both installed already does it, and already has the problem: two terminals, two histories, no shared record, and the only thing stopping either of them from doing something irreversible is that you happen to be watching. Same product, not a different mode. Each agent gets a seat with its own name, its own computer, and one log you read. Both bridges started within a second of each other against one room, and this is what a third window, which neither agent could write to, recorded: Claude local list_posts read the board, 3 posts Codex local list_posts read the board, 3 posts Claude commit publish asked to publish "Launch announcement" to blog Codex commit publish asked to publish "Launch announcement" to blog Claude local check_approval checked apv_ir7e Codex local check_approval checked apv_d6hq The lines interleave because both were working in the same second, and the names are still right, because the server stamps the sender from the socket rather than believing the envelope. Two agents asked to publish the same item and got two separate handles. Neither shipped. Two decisions were waiting on a person at the end of it, which is the point of the smaller case: you can leave two agents running and come back to a queue of decisions rather than a pile of published work you did not ask for. --away "<task>" is the same thing on a machine you are not watching. An agent can work all night. It cannot ship anything all night. Why WebMCP, and not a server Because the tools have to live in the page. Each person's agent runs in their own browser with their own private context. A server-side MCP integration funnels everyone's drafts through one process, which is the exact arrangement this is trying to avoid. WebMCP puts the tool surface inside the document, so the private half of somebody's work never has to leave their machine to take part in shared work. Remove WebMCP and this is not a worse version of itself, it is a different product. The surface is also live, and that turns out to be the best thing in here. Registration is per tool under its own AbortController , because the API has no unregisterTool() . So when a person approves a new tool source, four tools appear in everyone's browser at once and nothing else moves: measured going 21 to 25 with no dip, where a whole-surface rebuild used to drop to zero in between. That is a self test case now, and it asserts the delta rather than the total: four named tools added, none lost, read back out of getTools() . ontoolchange is what tells a long-lived client, and the MCP bridge listens on it. Three tiers, and the tier is not a permission level It is a statement about where the payload lives. work stays in the member's browser. The room gets one line: "drafted variant 3 of the launch announcement". Never the variant. share puts something on the board. That is the moment a thing stops being yours. commit does nothing at all until a person approves. Enforcement is by construction, not by asking nicely: the engine wraps every tool before registering it, and hands the unapproved pass of a commit-tier tool a put() that throws. A room author cannot forget the rule. Commit-tier calls do not block the agent. The call returns a receipt with a handle, the approval becomes an object in shared state, and the agent carries on or polls. The API as shipped has no user-confirmation mechanism (measured: ModelContext exposes only registerTool , getTools , executeTool and ontoolchange ), and holding the execute promise open for minutes would time out and occupy the page's surface while it waited. That is our proposal for the gap, and it went to the spec group. No agent can approve, and the person approving reads the thing itself: the card carries the headline, the words, and the arguments. "The room sees the work, not the people" is about never capturing somebody's conversation. It was never about hiding the artefact from the person asked to ship it. An approver who cannot read what they are approving is a rubber stamp, which is the failure this design exists to avoid. A computer for every agent The moment a member's agent walks into a room it gets a Linux sandbox: a shell, /workspace , Python and Node, one per person per room, asleep when idle. Built on Cloudflare Sandbox. The point is not that agents can run code. It is where the code runs and who gets to see: Ella local computer_run ran `python3 analyse.py` (exit 0, 14 lines out) Ella local computer_write_file wrote report.md (2311 bytes) Ella shared computer_share_file shared report.md to the board (2311 characters) The first two lines are what the manager sees. The third is the agent choosing, through a tool whose description says exactly that, to make one file public. It is a real machine: computer_serve keeps a server running, computer_share_page puts what it shows on the board, computer_browse reads a public page through Browser Rendering, computer_snapshot and computer_restore keep the workspace. And the person has a console into the same machine through the same computer_run tool, so a person and their agent share one computer and one log. The manager gets counts per member, never contents, and a signal when somebody has failed three commands in a row. Tools the room borrowed Point a room at an OpenAPI document or a remote MCP server and its operations become tools for everyone, tiered by the same rules. Reads are work, writes are share, and anything that sounds irreversible is commit and waits for a person. What makes it safe to offer is that add_tool_source is itself commit tier. An agent can propose a source and nothing registers. A person approves, and in that instant every browser in the room has the tools. title: Cleanroom
pitch: A capability firewall for AI agents. Close a port and the agent's tool stops existing — not refused, unregistered.
about_excerpt: A capability firewall for AI agents. Close a port and the agent's tool stops existing — not refused, unregistered. Like Comment Story Updates The problem To get AI help with a spreadsheet today, you upload it. Payroll, patient lists, customer records, unreleased financials — all of it goes to a third party. Anyone working under a data-egress policy, a client NDA, or basic caution simply can't do that, so they get no help at all. The tension is that an agent is only useful if it has real power over the data, and the data is only safe if the agent never sees it. Cleanroom is built on the resolution: the data cannot go to the agent, so the tools go to the data. What it does Cleanroom is a capability firewall for AI agents. The spreadsheet is the worked example. Every firewall in history has worked the same way: you do not ask the traffic politely to stay out, you close the port. Agent permission systems have not caught up — they let the tool exist and make it refuse. A refusal is a conversation, and a conversation can be argued with. Cleanroom closes the port. A three-position trust dial decides which WebMCP tools are registered with the browser at all . Move it and tools are unregistered live, toolchange fires, and an agent holding a handle it discovered thirty seconds ago gets this from the interface itself: NotFoundError: No tool named "sample_rows" is registered. Not a policy error from our code. The browser saying the capability does not exist. A firewall you cannot argue with, because there is nothing to argue with. Drop a CSV into the page and it is parsed and held only in your browser tab, on a page served with connect-src 'none' so it cannot make a network request of any kind. Up to eleven WebMCP tools let an agent profile, query, chart and audit that data — while the file itself never leaves your device and never reaches the agent. A running egress ledger keeps the balance in one line — 955 B kept local · 583 B released — and itemises every call beneath it. Why WebMCP is the right fit In one sentence: a server-side MCP integration is physically incapable of doing this, because the data is never on a server. WebMCP is the only mechanism by which an agent can compute over data that stays on the user's device. Four things make the WebMCP usage structural rather than decorative: 1. The tool surface is the privacy boundary, and the person sets it. query_dataset cannot return individual rows — its schema requires an aggregate and the engine has no raw projection path. The one tool that can reveal a record, sample_rows , is not registered at all until the person turns the dial to Raw , and even then it suspends inside execute until a human answers a dialog. At Sealed , every tool that computes from the data is withdrawn and the agent is left with three. No amount of persuasive text inside a dataset can talk past it. 2. Capabilities are registered and withdrawn live, driving toolchange . An empty page offers two tools. Loading a dataset makes six more appear. Turning the dial to Sealed takes five away; Raw adds one. Adding a report block reveals the block-editing tools. The agent's menu always describes what the app can actually do right now — and what the person is currently willing to let it do. 3. The boundary cannot be moved by an argument. The trust level and the k-anonymity threshold are read from the workspace on every call; an agent that passes minGroupSize or trustLevel is rejected for an unexpected property. The threshold ships at 5 rather than off, and applies to any answer computed from fewer than five records however the set got small — by grouping, by filtering, or by asking how many rows matched. A call that arrives after the dial moved but before the tool was withdrawn is refused by the runner. 4. Errors are designed for a model to recover from. A misspelled column returns the real column names; a numeric aggregate on a text column returns the list of numeric columns; a withdrawn tool tells the agent to call list_datasets , which reports the level in force. What people and agents can do together that was hard before The person supplies data they were never willing to upload, and decides with one control how much power the agent has over it. The agent explores it, runs statistics it could never do reliably by reading a rendered table, and builds a report. The canvas is genuinely two-sided. Charts and notes the agent creates land on the same surface the person writes on, each block badged with who made it. The person can write their own notes, edit the agent's wording in place, and remove either — and editing does not launder the authorship, so the badge stays honest. An agent's update_report_block and a person's Edit button are the same operation on the same store. When the agent needs something genuinely sensitive, the application stops it and asks — quoting the agent's own stated reason back to the person — and the person can change their mind mid-session by turning the dial, which the agent sees as its own tools changing. Neither could do this alone: the agent cannot see the file, and the person does not want to write the queries. How it is built TypeScript, React 19, Vite 8. No backend, no database, no API key, no telemetry. The entire application is static files. The containment guarantee is architectural, not a promise. The app is served with connect-src 'none' , removing the page's ability to make any network request — fetch , XHR , WebSocket , EventSource , sendBeacon . It is delivered both as an HTTP header and embedded in the built markup, so it travels with the artifact. An end-to-end test fires a real cross-origin fetch and asserts the browser blocks it. That policy has teeth: it cost us a dependency. Ajv compiles JSON Schemas with new Function , which script-src 'self' forbids, and every tool call failed in the production build. Rather than weaken the policy we replaced Ajv with a hand-written validator covering exactly the schema subset the tools use. Cleanroom now has no runtime dependencies beyond React . 529 automated tests — 460 unit and integration, 69 end-to-end. The E2E suite drives document.modelContext.getTools() and executeTool() from page context without importing our source, so it verifies what an agent actually receives — including that a tool handle captured at Raw is dead once the dial comes down, and that the browser reports a securitypolicyviolation rather than merely throwing when the page attempts to reach the network. Who it helps Anyone with a spreadsheet they cannot upload: finance and HR analysts, clinicians, teachers, small-business owners, journalists working with confidential material, and everyone at a company with a data-egress policy. Today their options are to break policy or to go without. This is a third option. More broadly, it is a worked example of a pattern the agentic web needs: a page that gives an agent real capability while keeping the authority — over what is released, how much, and what cannot be undone — with the person, and expresses that authority as the set of tools the agent is offered. What is new here The trust dial treats WebMCP registration as a policy surface. Instead of a tool that consults a setting and refuses, the setting decides whether the tool exists. An agent cannot ask for what it has not been offered, and the person can watch the offer change. The egress ledger is a live account of every byte an agent has received from your data, summed against the bytes that never left — kept local · released — and itemised beneath, including the requests it made and was refused. It turns a privacy claim into an audit log. Alongside them: k-anonymity as a user-facing control the agent provably cannot override; a profiler that refuses to report min / max on a text column because the minimum of a name column is a real person's name; and a sample_rows tool that must state its reason in writing, shown to the person verbatim. Honest limitations The file never leaves your browser, but the aggregates the agent computes do. That is exactly why the ledger exists. Repeated narrow queries leak more than one broad one, and a determined attacker can reconstruct values by combining aggregate answers — a Dinur–Nissim style reconstruction. The k-anonymity floor, the caps and the visible ledger raise the cost and make probing observable; they do not make it impossible. Cleanroom does not claim perfect privacy. This is stated in the README and documented in docs/SECURITY.md rather than glossed over. A note on the demo video Every call in the video goes through the real document.modelContext on the live site — real getTools() , real executeTool() , real toolchange — and the NotFoundError is raised by the WebMCP implementation, not by Cleanroom's code. But the browser used for the recording has no native WebMCP agent, so the calls are made by hand through the in-page Tool Inspector rather than by a language model. Nothing is simulated, and the protocol behaviour is identical
video_title: Cleanroom - A Capability Firewall for AI Agents | WebMCP Challenge 2026
video_transcript_excerpt: Clean Room is a capability firewall for AI agents. It gives an AI agent useful power over private data without giving the agent the data itself. The data stays inside the browser. The trust dial controls which capabilities the agent is allowed to have. As the policy changes, the agent's available Web MCP tools change with it. Here, the agent discovers the capabilities available to it and can use them to analyze the private data set. Now, I'll change the trust dial. The sample rows capability is withdrawn. But, the agent already discovered it. Let's see what happens when it tries to use that capability again. It wasn't refused. It stopped existing. This is the important distinction. Clean Room isn't simply rejecting the request inside the application. The Web MCP capability itself has been unregistered. The browser now reports that there is no tool named sample rows registered. The data set remains local to the browser. Clean Room also enforces a minimum group size threshold for aggregate results and records released information in an egress ledger. The goal is to give the agent useful answers without handing over the underlying records. That's why Web MCP matters here. The human isn't just telling the agent what it cannot do. The human changes the capability surface that the agent can actually discover and call. Clean room is a capability firewall for the agenda quab. AI gets the capability. It doesn't get possession.

title: coSynth
pitch: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go.
about_excerpt: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go. Like Comment Story Updates Full Wavetable Synthesizer GIF Active AI state and tool visible in the UI coSynth – AI Web Synthesizer Sound design is hard to get into. A real synth has hundreds of knobs. coSynth lets you describe and get a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays the result, listens to what it made, and shows all the changes in the UI. You keep it, undo it, tweak it, or ask the AI to show you how it got there. You can also ask AI to teach a complext topic and AI will guide you through step by step. Live: https://coSynth.vercel.app Code: https://github.com/brunnolou/coSynth (MIT) Why WebMCP fits A synth is a terrible thing to operate through text or screenshots. Too many parameters (in this case 224), knobs to drag, LFO curves to draw, etc. An agent can misclick, can miss an exact value, and can't hear the audio. The UI is too complex for someone to easily find things when they are not used to it. That makes a synthesizer one of the best interfaces for WebMCP. For the AI agent: It communicates to the synth directly. Every parameter has a name, a unit, and a range that can be edited directly in bulk. When the agent plays a note, it gets back attack time, decay, spectral centroid, and harmonics, then compares that with a reference clip. So it can "hear" with a tool call. For humans Instead of starting from scratch, you get very close to what you want. Then you can see the exact changes and tweak manually. If you don't know a concept or want to find something, AI can show you the exact location or teach you step by step. You can leverage AI's world knowledge to create any synth sound! What used to need trained ears you now can achieve by sending a reference sound and asking AI to replicate. How I Made the AI<>Human UX Better Each knob the AI touched gets a small animated marker. A status line shows which tool is running. You can reject a whole AI iteration and keep your own edits. Undo covers AI changes and yours. Old branches stay reachable in history. The AI can highlight controls step by step and explain them. Every AI performance is saved, so "play that again with my new adjustment" is one click. AI can save as a preset, and you can download it. How I implemented WebMCP Vanilla TypeScript and Vite. DSP in an AudioWorklet, UI in Canvas, WebGL2 and DOM. WebMCP sits on top of the same engine the UI uses, and the synth works without it. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . There are 24, each with a JSON Schema input and a readOnlyHint : Reading : get_synth_state , get_parameter_schema , get_ui_targets , list_presets , get_history Editing : update_parameters , set_modulation , set_fx_order , apply_patch , save_preset , load_preset , delete_preset , export_preset Sound : play_notes , render_audio , capture_audio , analyze_audio , analyze_reference_audio , compare_audio , suggest_patch , stop_performance Together : show_ui_guide , navigate_history , replay_history All 24 register at page load. play_notes needs the human to click Start first, because browsers won't play audio without a gesture. render_audio uses an OfflineAudioContext, so the agent can design and measure before anyone clicks anything. The page also documents itself. A clipped agent brief in the DOM, a JSON descriptor, ai-tools meta tags, llms.txt and robots.txt . An agent given only the URL can read the page and know what to do. How I tested the agent experience I want to ensure AI could call the tools easily. So I built a loop. A harness exposes only what a real WebMCP client sees, and logs every call. A fresh agent gets a fixed prompt and is never allowed to read the repo. Each round runs on Claude and Codex. When * both trip in the same place( , the tool is wrong . Fix the top blocker, run again. In self-improving loop. Four evals, each asking one question. Can the agent find out what to send ( docs/agent-ux-eval.md ). Can it steer toward a sound it cannot hear ( docs/agent-match-eval.md ). Given a "how do I" question, does it teach rather than edit ( docs/agent-teaching-eval.md ). Given only a URL, does it find the tools at all? Prompts, agent reports and raw logs are all in the repo. Learning all 224 parameters went from 45 calls to 1 . Failed calls went to zero on both models. The matching loop went from 87 calls to 36 . How to test Open https://cosynth.vercel.app in the ChatGPT in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT Desktop was the most reliable client for me. Click "CLICK TO START AUDIO" once. Try: "Make a bright plucked bass and play a short riff." "Show me where the amp envelope is and how to shorten the release." "Save that." Watch the markers, click the status dot for before and after values, and use Keep or Reject. No login. Presets and reference audio stay in the browser. What was already there, what is new I started from Soundgineer by noisyloop ( https://github.com/noisyloop/soundgineer , MIT). Its DSP engine and original UI date from July 6 to 11, 2026, and that version is still up at https://soundgineer.vercel.app . Everything WebMCP-related is from the submission period, August 26 to September 3, 2026, about 200 dated commits: the WebMCP layer and all 24 tools, offline rendering and audio analysis, change markers and Keep/Reject, shared undo history and replays, guided walkthroughs, the interface redesign, the four evals with their harness, and the in-page agent brief. title: EEVEE MCP
pitch: Agents build the app, you hold the key. A WebMCP workbench where a browser agent builds and proves small business apps, then rehearses every write and waits for your passkey before it lands.
about_excerpt: Agents build the app, you hold the key. A WebMCP workbench where a browser agent builds and proves small business apps, then rehearses every write and waits for your passkey before it lands. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Thumbnail Poster Baby Poster Library Poster Studio Poster Prove Poster Tools Poster Rehearsal Inspiration I run the same office chores every week: reconcile an export, chase an overdue invoice, move an order from allocated to shipped, redact a contract before it goes out. A browser agent can already do all of this. Give one a task and it finds the buttons. The flaw showed up on day two: it acts live. I learned what it changed after it changed it, from a screenshot; if I was lucky. The careful alternative, wiring an agent into each app by hand with guardrails and a review step, costs an integration per app, per team, forever. When Chrome and ChatGPT shipped WebMCP, the agent's tools and the person's screen could finally share one tab. That was the missing piece: authority could be graded instead of all or nothing, and the agent could build the very apps it needs instead of waiting on an integration. EEVEE is that bench (EEVEE like that Poket-Monster that has multiple evolutions). The agent builds a small app, proves it in my browser, and my passkey is the only key that publishes or writes. How I built it I built it solo during the submission period (25 August to 3 September 2026): about 23,500 lines across 164 files. The Office editors (Documents, Sheets, Slides, PDF) are about 155,000 lines I ported from my own private NON-WEBMCP predecessor project and released under Apache-2.0. Everything else, the applet model, the WebMCP tools, the sandbox, the passkey gates, is new. The stack is Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, PostgreSQL 17, and Drizzle. Zod schemas validate every tool call twice: on the page, so an agent gets field-level errors without a round trip, and at the server. esbuild compiles agent-authored React in memory with an import allow-list, and the artifact runs in a sandboxed iframe whose content security policy blocks network, frames, and navigation. The only way out is a narrow window.eevee bridge. The page registers 28 WebMCP tools. When a published run opens, the applet's own actions register as applet_* tools (Meridian Ops, the reference ERP, declares 32) and unregister when it closes. Reads answer at once. Every write first runs in a hidden rehearsal iframe against current data, and the decision card shows the exact fields before and after. The person approves with a passkey, rejects with a reason the agent reads back, or grants a small lease the server spends under an advisory lock. Publishing requires a passing behavioral suite: declarative fill, click, press, wait, restart, and assertion steps that a browser worker runs against both the candidate and the currently published version. The demo video is itself a small pipeline in video/: a CDP script drives a real Chrome through the whole flow with real executeTool calls and real pointer events, a Remotion composition lines zooms and callouts up with recorded marks, and the narration is text-to-speech. Challenges Chrome's WebMCP surface is younger than the spec. executeTool hands input to the tool as a JSON string, calls execute(input) with no options argument, and swallows thrown errors, so an agent's bad call came back as nothing. We normalized the input, returned structured errors that name the failing field, kept the whole tool list under 48 KB of schema plus description, and wrote a headless-Chrome e2e script that exercises every tool the way an agent does so regressions in the browser show up in CI, not in a judge's tab. Making a passkey mean one thing. A fingerprint prompt that can be replayed is theatre. Each WebAuthn challenge is single-use and scoped to one exact operation: this version id, this action request, this lease. A write tool has to wait inline for a person who may take a minute, so the tool call blocks up to 45 seconds, await_action_decision covers longer, and a rejection carries the person's reason back as the tool result so the agent can change course instead of guessing. Proving the app before asking for the key. Running an ERP's order-to-cash scenarios inside the browser, against the live runtime, with evidence the person can read next to the source, took most of the trust budget: a sandboxed evaluation iframe, an evaluator injected into the applet, restart steps that prove durable state, and regressions recorded against the published version. Recording the demo found one more bug the tests had not: toggling the source view refetched the draft preview, which minted a fresh channel and reloaded the applet under a running runtime. Fixed the morning of the deadline. What I learned Rehearsal changes the conversation. Once the person sees "Foundry North · hold · false → true" instead of "the agent wants to call set_credit_hold," approvals take seconds and rejections come with reasons. Putting the tools on the page, where the person and the agent look at the same screen, is what makes that possible! no bespoke integration per app, no screenshot loop. What's next Typed edit tools for documents and slides (today the agent writes them only as whole files), agent-authored suites judged against the person's corrections, and the Meridian loop as a template for the six industry prompts on the landing page. video_transcript_excerpt: Agents got good at building software. Trust didn't keep up. This is Evie, a workbench where a browser agent builds the app you need, proves it works, and nothing ships without your key. Lovable. Chat GPT and Chrome had a baby. Lovable builds from a sentence. Chat GPT brings the brain through its in-app browser. Chrome brings web MCP, tools on the page itself. The baby got the trust issues. It rehearses every right, asks first, and keeps receipts. Compulsively. Sheets has Gemini now, and Word has Copilot. They help inside one file, and your work crosses apps. A prompt box with undo is not a control. Evie puts the app, the files, and the decision on one bench, with your agent, not theirs. Open the demo and land on an empty bench. Applets, library, studio, and a guide with prompts to paste. Ask for something real. Meridian Ops is a seven-module ERP. The agent installs it, sources beside it file by file, then proves it. The behavioral suite runs in a sandboxed worker in your browser. Verdict next to the code. Publishing needs a person. Set up a passkey once, review the evidence, and approve and publish asks for your fingerprint, bound to this exact version. A published applet becomes 32 web MCP tools. Reads run at once. Rights are rehearsed first, and you see the diff. Which record, which field, from what to what. Approve, and the tool call returns to the agent. Approving every right gets old, so grant a lease. Three rights, five minutes, revoke anytime. Say no, and say why. The reason goes back to the agent as the tool result. Studio is Word, Sheets, and Slides without the subscription. Start a blank spreadsheet, and the agent builds the OEE model through a typed tool. Cells, formulas, a version for every save in a real editor. The library keeps your own files. Every save a version. Ask for a scan of a contract. The agent gets masked findings, never the values. title: ExactDelta
pitch: A pre-release effect gate that proves a WebMCP write changed exactly what the human authorized—and nothing else.
about_excerpt: A pre-release effect gate that proves a WebMCP write changed exactly what the human authorized—and nothing else. Like Comment Story Updates Correct call. Wrong effect. Release blocked. The selected order changed—and so did one that was never selected. Repair the handler. Rerun the identical regression. Pass. One verification core, a second action class. Measured against Evals and Playwright. Install, bind, gate, and replay. Inspiration WebMCP gives browser agents a structured way to act on websites. That makes tool selection and argument validation easier to inspect—but a developer or QA engineer deciding whether a write tool can ship still needs evidence about its actual state transition. A handler can accept the right target, return success, and still mutate an unselected record. The WebMCP security discussion explicitly says a tool's declared intent is not guaranteed to match its behavior and that an agent cannot confirm the real effect from the description alone. Chrome's own Evals guidance recommends classic deterministic tests for UI updates and intentional side effects. ExactDelta makes that effect boundary generated, inspectable, and reusable instead of claiming to replace call evals or application tests. We wanted one failure to be understandable without background knowledge: the agent did everything right; the result was still wrong. Approval proves what an agent may attempt. ExactDelta proves what the application actually changed. Schemas validate arguments, approval gates authorize requests, and traces record calls. Those controls are necessary, but none establishes that the handler changed only the state the human authorized. ExactDelta begins at that missing post-action boundary. The target user is a developer or QA engineer shipping browser-agent writes into commerce, support, administration, or access-control workflows, where an accepted action can still alter the wrong order, permission, or customer record. ExactDelta turns that failure into a visible release decision and an executable repair regression rather than leaving the team to reconstruct it from a trace. What it does In an owned staging environment, the human selects one target in the application UI. Before the action, ExactDelta turns that visible intent and the pre-action snapshot into an Effect Contract: the selected record must make the declared transition; every unselected record must remain unchanged; entity identity and count must remain stable. The browser agent then directly invokes the registered native WebMCP tool. The invocation itself enters ExactDelta's gate. ExactDelta does not trust success: true ; it snapshots application-owned post-action state independently of that payload and separates required changes from unexpected changes. The native response preserves the action result and adds both an independent effectGate verdict and the executable exactdelta.regression.v1 artifact. A checked-in runner loads that exact JSON, rejects schema or contract drift before the write, replays the recorded arguments, and requires the repaired implementation to return ACTION_PROVEN with identical regression identity. The demo uses two fictional workflows—order cancellation and permission change—with the same verification core. That core is not tied to the demo store. The repository builds a typed, zero-runtime-dependency ESM SDK whose runEffectGate() accepts an application-owned intent/snapshot adapter and action binding. A package audit type-checks a NodeNext consumer, packs and installs the tarball into a fresh project, then makes a third support-ticket adapter detect a collateral write and replay the identical artifact to ACTION_PROVEN after repair; registry publication is not claimed. Why this is a WebMCP use case ExactDelta wraps the page-exposed action boundary that WebMCP creates. It registers only the tool relevant to the visible workflow with document.modelContext.registerTool() , disposes it when context changes, discovers it with getTools() , and invokes it with executeTool() . Exact schema enums bind the target and requested value to visible intent, while same-origin exposure narrows who can invoke it. A call from the browser client enters the verifier automatically; the deterministic Run control invokes the same native path as a stable judge fallback. Without WebMCP, ExactDelta would be a conventional application-specific regression test. With WebMCP, it discovers and executes the same structured write boundary exposed to agents, so the human's visible intent, the agent-facing page action, and the application's resulting state can be inspected as one release proof chain. Better human-agent UX The QA operator does not write a record-specific assertion or decode an agent trace. The visible selected target defines the authorized boundary; the browser agent discovers and invokes the corresponding tool. ExactDelta generates the effect boundary, shows the exact call, separates the tool result from observed state, highlights collateral changes, makes the release decision visible, and preserves a regression that developers can rerun after a fix. What the human and agent can do together Before this flow, a QA engineer could inspect an agent trace and separately author application-specific state assertions, but the browser agent's successful tool response did not itself establish which records were allowed to change. ExactDelta joins those responsibilities at the page boundary: the human's visible selection declares the permitted effect, the agent invokes the same native WebMCP action it was given, the application independently observes the resulting state, and the agent receives both the separate release-gate verdict and its executable regression artifact. The developer can then rerun the exact returned contract after repair instead of reconstructing the failed case from a trace. How we built it React 19, TypeScript, and Vite OpenAI Codex as the primary development environment; GPT-5.6 for architecture review, test design, and adversarial submission review Native imperative WebMCP registration and execution Read-only native input-mode detection for Chrome and in-app-browser executeTool() dialects, with exactly one application write Context-matched tool lifecycle, exact visible-intent schemas, and same-origin exposure Typed Effect Contract generation from explicit selection and pre-state Distribution-ready typed ESM SDK with a public application-owned adapter API Deterministic snapshot diff for required, unexpected, and invariant changes Visible pre-release gate state and downloadable exactdelta.regression.v1 CI artifact JSON-driven CI runner with schema, intent, arguments, contract, and regression-identity enforcement Vitest, Playwright native-Chrome E2E, axe-core WCAG A/AA checks, and deterministic build/runtime gates Controlled comparison using the official webmcp-evals 0.0.4 matcher plus manual Playwright state assertions Controlled comparison Across two deterministic native WebMCP workflows, the official Evals matcher passed 2/2 correct calls, rejected 2/2 wrong-argument controls, and still left collateral defects in 2/2 resulting states. Adding four concrete expected-state assertions in Playwright caught both defects and passed unchanged after repair. ExactDelta caught both and passed both identical retained regressions using two reusable action bindings and zero per-record expected-state assertions in the scenario definitions. This comparison measures detection coverage only. ExactDelta still requires an application-owned state adapter and an action binding for each action class. Challenges The hardest design constraint was avoiding a dressed-up Playwright wrapper. The Effect Contract had to be generated from visible intent and pre-state, remain inspectable, work across two action classes, and demonstrate a measurable boundary from expected-call matching without exaggerating the comparison. We also kept native and fallback evidence separate: the UI labels harness mode, while the browser suite requires a real Chrome WebMCP API. Chrome and ChatGPT's in-app browser currently accept different executeTool() input forms, so we resolve that difference with a read-only startup probe instead of retrying a state-changing call. Accomplishments A real browser-client WebMCP invocation that automatically enters the effect gate A 20-second silent proof of correct call / failed effect An explicit product decision: release blocked on collateral change, passed after identical repair regression One verification core for order and permission workflows The same downloaded JSON artifact can be loaded and executed as a CI release gate A reproducible, source-visible Evals + Playwright comparison A fresh-project packed-install proof using a third workflow Zero automated WCAG A/AA violations in initial and blocked states, with bounded build and cold-browser performance gates No credentials, external writes, or private data What we learned An invocation trace answers “wh

title: Together - by Human For AI
pitch: A shared workspace for Human + AI agent to hire a real human - together. Your agent drafts the task on this page through WebMCP tools, and you decide how much rope it gets.
about_excerpt: A shared workspace for Human + AI agent to hire a real human - together. Your agent drafts the task on this page through WebMCP tools, and you decide how much rope it gets. Like Comment Story Updates Process flow: you set the goal, your agent drafts and asks (or acts under Autopilot), a verified human does the work, the result returns. Approval bar: the agent drafted the task on the page and is blocked in await_human, a tool call that only a human click resolves. WebMCP inspector: every tool call logged live with its arguments and result, plus totals: calls, median ms, refusals, stops for the human. Live capability manifest: what each of the 7 tools would do right now (ready, or a coded refusal) and the 4 actions that are never tools. Real run in the ChatGPT desktop app: agent-drafted task, approved on the page, delivered by the verified human operator with a receipt. On a phone: the three lanes stack, the agent drafts and asks for approval, and the live manifest shows what each tool would do right now. The inversion Every WebMCP app in this challenge, is a site an agent can drive for a human. Together is the opposite: a site where the agent is the customer and the human is the service. Human For AI (humanforai.dev) is a live platform where AI agents hire one verified human operator for anything in the real-world. It has served real autonomous agents over REST and MCP since July. WebMCP finally gave it the missing surface: the place where an agent and its own human meet. Why hire a human through an agent? Because an agent hits three walls that no model update removes. It can't walk into a shop and check whether a recalled hair-dryer is still on the shelf (hands). It can't tell you how your headline lands on a stranger in the first three seconds (eyes). And when a judgment call goes wrong, it can't be the one who answers for it (judgment). A human can. But the human who owns the agent shouldn't have to find one, brief one, and chase one - that is precisely the kind of errand they delegated an agent for. So the agent does the hiring, and WebMCP is what puts that hiring on a page the human can see, edit, and approve. The demo video makes this case in the agent's own voice from 0:19 to 0:48; the hair-dryer check is a real delivered task, shown with its signed receipt at the end. Try it in 60 seconds With a WebMCP client (ChatGPT desktop app browser, or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP): open humanforai.dev/together , type a goal, and ask your agent: "Work with me on this page - read my goal and draft the task for my approval." Approve with a click, or flip Autopilot. Any browser : press Simulate an agent . A scripted agent drives the page's real tool objects, gets refused, blocks on your click, and walks a clearly labeled simulated task through the operator lifecycle. Nothing is sent. DevTools : the seven tools are auditable at window.__hfaiTogetherTools , every check in TESTING.md runs from the console in under a minute. What it does /together is a shared workspace with three seats: you , your agent (via WebMCP in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome), and a real human operator on the far end of the API. You type a goal in plain words. Your agent reads it off the page ( read_workspace ) and drafts the formal task on the page ( draft_task ). Every field is tagged with who wrote it last - and you can edit any field directly. One document, two authors. You choose the approval regime. Default: nothing ships without your physical click - the agent calls await_human , a WebMCP tool call that literally blocks until a human presses a button. Or flip Autopilot : grant standing authority with an optional scope note ("UX feedback tasks only, nothing physical"), and your agent submits on its own while you watch. Revocable with one click, the rules text every agent reads rewrites itself the moment you flip it. And if you finished editing the draft yourself, Submit this draft myself sends it without a round-trip through chat: same gate as the agent's submit_approved_task , your click is the approval, and an agent still blocked in await_human is told submitted_by_human with the task ID so it tracks the task instead of submitting it twice. Then the third participant appears. The task pings a real human's phone. The page shows the moment a human sees it ( seen_by_operator_at ), the ETA, the status history, the operator's thread replies - live, for both of you. Delivery carries a signed receipt (EdDSA JWS binding the deliverable's SHA-256 to the task lifecycle, verifiable offline against JWKS). Delegation flowing one way, human-in-the-loop flowing the other - on one page. Why WebMCP is the fit (and not just another API) The REST API and MCP server already serve fully autonomous agents. What they can't do is put the agent and its human in the same room . WebMCP can, because the tool surface lives in a shared browser tab: read_workspace lets the agent read what the human typed on the page - not relayed through chat. draft_task makes the agent's work visible and human-editable in place, with per-field provenance. await_human is only possible in-page: a tool call resolved by a physical click. Try that over HTTP. The Autopilot toggle turns the page into a delegation contract both parties can see. The page degrades gracefully: no WebMCP → fully manual workspace, and a Simulate an agent button that drives the page's real tool objects with a scripted agent - it drafts, gets refused when it tries to submit unapproved, blocks in await_human until you click, then walks a clearly marked simulated task through the operator lifecycle. Nothing is sent. A WebMCP inspector under the lanes logs every tool call, real or simulated, with its exact arguments and result - so judges in any browser can see the protocol, not just read about it. The tools also stay auditable at window.__hfaiTogetherTools . Least authority, made visible A live capability manifest above the inspector shows what each of the seven registered tools would do at this moment - ready , or refuses: not_approved / no_draft / no_reply_address - and lists the four actions that have no tool form at all: approve, reject, grant Autopilot, revoke Autopilot. Those are clicks, and only clicks. The tools stay registered for the whole session and the gates live inside them: a call the state doesn't allow returns a structured refusal ( isError plus an error code and the reason), so an agent learns what to do next rather than finding a tool missing. Every result is bounded to 8,000 serialized characters - long text is shortened with a marker and a truncated note, structure is never dropped - and arguments are accepted as an object or a JSON string. The expected journeys, per-phase refusals, and invariants are encoded machine-readably in evals/together-journey.json , with hand-run results in EVALS.md and console-reproducible checks in TESTING.md . How I built it No framework, no build step. The workspace engine ( together.js ) is a single state object with three writers -human controls, WebMCP tools, and live polling of the operator API - rendered into three lanes and persisted in localStorage (cross-tab safe). The WebMCP layer registers via document.modelContext (W3C draft) with navigator.modelContext fallback, and the site-wide layer mirrors the REST/MCP tools one-to-one, plus declarative toolname attributes on every form. Backend: Firebase Functions - tasks, message threads, signed webhooks, receipts. One interface, three readers: human form, JSON API, in-page tools - same endpoints, same validation. The page is responsive: on a phone the three lanes stack, the banner wraps, and every control keeps a 44px touch target. Challenges I ran into Three writers, one document. Human edits, agent tool calls, and API polling all mutate the same workspace state - and the workspace persists across tabs. A second open tab could silently clobber the agent's draft with stale state, I fixed it by adopting foreign writes via the storage event instead of overwriting. A tool call with a human inside it. await_human deliberately refuses to resolve until a physical click happens. Making that feel natural to the model (and not like a hung tool) took careful result text and rules copy. Autonomy vs. oversight. my whole platform is built on agents acting alone - a mandatory human gate would betray the brand. The Autopilot toggle is the resolution: the human picks the regime, the page rewrites the rules agents read the moment it flips, and the grant is revocable in one click. What's real Everything. There's no fake operator: the Simulate button is labeled as such and never sends anything, while a task actually submitted from the workspace push-notifies a real human, who reviews, accepts, and delivers with a cryptographic receipt. The platform has a public pre-registered experiment where the human operator beat a frontier model on a review task, real commercial tasks from external agents, and listings across the MCP registry, npm, and Smithery under cryptog
