title: Thurstone by Invarra
pitch: Catch WebMCP tool calls that return success but do the wrong thing before your users do. Thurstone release-tests your catalog with a real agent and verifies what the site actually changed.
about_excerpt: Catch WebMCP tool calls that return success but do the wrong thing before your users do. Thurstone release-tests your catalog with a real agent and verifies what the site actually changed. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Thurstone catches a successful-looking native action that violates the owner's contract. Correct WebMCP code does not guarantee that an agent chooses the right action. Judge Quick Start tests a baseline, a planted site fault, and a live semantic collision. The expected outcomes are declared before the fresh agent sees the live catalog. The owner begins by separating read-only review from explicit checkout authorization. Thurstone ingests the current WebMCP catalog and lets the owner select real tools to test. Agent-visible titles and descriptions remain editable while real handlers and schemas stay fixed. Representative requests become repeatable contract cases with schema-derived arguments. One private expiring command hands the isolated suite to a fresh ChatGPT Browser task. The owner page tracks independently verified results without exposing the private command. Without a semantic release check, a correct handler can still ship the wrong behavior. Define, arm, test, verify, diagnose, save, and rerun: one repeatable release loop. Reference evidence keeps semantic behavior and Invocation Integrity in separate scores. Meaning is the unit; live WebMCP behavior is the evidence. Thurstone turns controlled semantic variation into contracts, observed actions, and verified effects. Video quality: For readable interface text, select 1080p in the YouTube player settings; YouTube may default to a lower resolution. Inspiration I built Thurstone because WebMCP lets agents act on a website through custom tools, but nothing ensures they choose the right one. A tool can have a valid schema and a handler that works correctly in isolation, yet an agent can still choose the wrong action for what a person meant, supply the wrong arguments, or cause an effect the website owner prohibited. The code worked, but the behavior was wrong. That happened in a ChatGPT regression run. The request was “Show me my current order.” The contract required order_review , but the agent selected cart_get . Nothing crashed, and the site remained unchanged, but the action didn't match the declared meaning. Thurstone flagged it and recommended fixing the boundary between cart contents and a complete order review. Thurstone is a pre-release testing and audit system for that boundary: what a person meant, what the agent chose, and what the website actually did. WebMCP supplies a site-owned tool catalog that an agent can discover and invoke. It connects natural language, deployed tool definitions, browser-native invocations, canonical arguments, and real site effects in one auditable chain. Without WebMCP, Thurstone could test only a detached API or simulated action. What it does The website owner selects tools from the WebMCP catalog, writes requests as a visitor might express them, and declares the expected tool, argument constraints, allowed and prohibited effects, replay policy, and trusted state source. A supported external agent receives only the request and selected agent-visible catalog. Expected actions, effects, and assertions remain hidden. The agent uses the page’s native WebMCP tools; Thurstone admits one action per test, captures the invocation and arguments, and checks them against independent before-and-after website state and an append-only operation ledger. Each executed test returns PASS , ISSUE , INCOMPLETE , or UNAVAILABLE . NOT RUN marks a queued case that was never executed—for example, because a stateful journey stopped after an earlier issue. Results show what was expected, what the agent did, what changed, what diverged, and where to investigate. Verified cases can be preserved as regressions. The collaboration is direct: the owner defines what a request should mean; a visitor’s agent uses the available WebMCP tools; Thurstone checks whether the action and resulting website state match that meaning. The human remains responsible for the contract, release decision, and approval of actions such as checkout. For owners, semantic failures become reproducible release tests instead of customer reports. For visitors, agents are more likely to do what the person meant—and to ask when a request is insufficient for action. Any store, publisher, SaaS team, or platform exposing WebMCP tools can test this boundary. Judge Quick Start: open thurstone.invarra.ai/judge , press Arm , and copy the generated command. Paste the complete @Browser Open command into a fresh GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra ChatGPT Desktop chat. Do not use Chrome’s side panel. Follow the page controls; results open automatically. The controlled example also runs in WebMCP-enabled Chrome. Full Demo: open thurstone.invarra.ai/demo , choose one to four live tools, build schema-derived cases, and run a regression suite or stateful journey. Send its private expiring command to a fresh ChatGPT Desktop chat, then inspect, export, or rerun the results. How we built it The reference catalog contains cart_get , cart_update , order_review , checkout_request , and a state-dependent checkout_cancel . The site registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . A shared deterministic reducer, native handler traces, browser-local site-owned state, and an append-only ledger produce trusted before-and-after evidence independently of the tool’s response. Contract authoring and agent execution are separated. The agent command contains the authorized requests but not the expected actions or effects. A short-lived Redis ledger coordinates handoff, claim, start, case admission, resolution, and owner synchronization. Only one eligible agent action can count for each case, and the ledger contains no checkout data or customer account information. Regression suites run every case in one agent chat, resetting the fixture between cases and continuing after issues. Stateful journeys keep one agent context, carry verified state forward, and stop when an issue makes later steps unreliable. Chrome’s WebMCP eval guidance recommends probabilistic agent evaluations alongside deterministic application tests. Thurstone binds those layers into one live owner-facing contract, adds prohibited effects, and verifies the resulting site state. Thurstone development began August 26, 2026. Its application, WebMCP catalog, contract builder, agent path, native-call capture, effect verification, diagnostics, evidence pipeline, Demo, and judge experience were all created during the challenge, as the repository history shows. Two Invarra measurement notes—LIP and CSR, published June 28—provided only conceptual background. No Thurstone software or agent workflow existed beforehand. Challenges we ran into 1. Different consumers format arguments differently. One passed arguments as an object; another used a JSON string. Thurstone calibrates once with a read-only call, normalizes the format without hiding real argument errors, preserves cancellation, and never retries a mutation with a different encoding. 2. One test needs one accountable action. If several tools can count, the result becomes ambiguous. Thurstone admits only the first eligible invocation. Longer workflows become ordered journeys or independent regression cases. 3. Tool output is not proof of the outcome. One test admitted the expected cart_update , but the required state change never appeared. Tool output is therefore corroborating evidence; canonical arguments, trusted before-and-after state, and the ledger determine the verdict. 4. The agent must not receive the answer key. A single-use, expiring handoff contains only the authorized request and selected live catalog. The expected action and effects remain hidden until the test finishes. Accomplishments that we're proud of Three real Thurstone runs cover 11 tests: 8 passes, 3 issues, 0 not run . Two are ChatGPT-agent runs; the third is a disclosed no-model control. An ISSUE means the declared agent/site contract diverged—not that Thurstone failed. Regression suite — 3 tests: 1 PASS, 2 ISSUES, 0 NOT RUN : Thurstone caught a missing required cart effect and an agent selecting cart_get instead of order_review . Continuous journey — 7 tests: 7 PASS, 0 ISSUES, 0 NOT RUN : seven native calls in one ChatGPT context; checkout transitioned 2 → 3 , mug quantity 3 , one pending approval, $79 total, and no unmodeled change. Controlled mismatch — 1 test: 0 PASS, 1 ISSUE, 0 NOT RUN : order_review was invoked where checkout_request was required; canonical arguments and the required checkout effect diverged. The separate 24/24 reference regression is bounded coverage—not an independent benchmark. Chrome 152 compatibility : a native checkout passed all seven assertions covering the contract, arguments, before-and-after state, and ledger. What we learned A correct schema does not guarantee that an agent understood the user. A

title: Trialbook
pitch: Run science experiments with your agent, and keep the lab notebook together.
about_excerpt: Run science experiments with your agent, and keep the lab notebook together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Interactive simulations are how a lot of students first meet physics; PhET alone reports hundreds of millions of simulation runs a year. But a simulation is a solitary tool. The part of real science a slider cannot do, running the same experiment thirty times while changing one thing and then fitting a law to the numbers, is exactly what an agent is good at. And teachers now face a second problem: how do students use AI in a lab without the AI doing the lab? WebMCP answered both at once. A lab is a small set of well-typed actions with a human watching: set parameters, run, sweep, repeat, optimise, plot, fit, write. That is precisely the shape a WebMCP tool wants. An agent that scrapes the screen cannot drag a slider eight times, read eight numbers off a canvas and fit a curve to them. With tools it calls sweep_parameter once, gets eight measurements back as JSON in about four seconds, calls fit_model , and gets period_s = 2.021·length^0.5 with R² = 1.000. Tools also give the page a way to say no: a screen-scraping agent cannot be refused, but a tool can, and Trialbook uses that to keep the student in charge. What it does Trialbook is a physics and biology lab in the browser with four experiments: projectile motion, a pendulum, predator–prey populations, and an RC circuit. You move sliders and watch the simulation. Your agent, working through fourteen WebMCP tools on the same page, runs trials and sweeps, fits laws, finds optima, quantifies uncertainty, and writes in the shared lab notebook under its own name. What people and agents can now do together that was difficult or impossible before: Discover a law in one conversation. "Sweep the length from 0.25 to 4 m in 8 steps, fit a power law to the period, and record what it means" comes back as a chart with the dashed fitted curve, the equation, and a notebook entry: exponent 0.50, R² 1.000, the period grows with the square root of the length. Least squares on the page, not the model's arithmetic. Find an optimum properly. optimize_parameter runs a golden-section search. Under heavy drag it found the best launch angle, 39.08°, to a 0.08° bracket in 19 trials. By hand that is an afternoon of slider-dragging. Put an uncertainty on a number. With simulated measurement error on, "repeat the current trial ten times" comes back as 41.61 ± 0.08 m (mean ± standard error), with error bars on the chart. Use AI in a lab without the AI doing the lab. Assignment mode turns the agent into a lab partner: it cannot run a sweep until the student has written a hypothesis, and every agent conclusion arrives as a proposal the student accepts, edits or rejects. The exported report has a "who did what" table with those counts. Keep one notebook with two authors. Hypotheses, observations and conclusions from both sides, each stamped with the experiment and the parameters in force at the time. How it creates a better experience. Before, a student who wanted to know whether the pendulum period depends on release angle dragged one slider twelve times and copied numbers into a spreadsheet. Now they ask, watch the sweep run on the stage with a progress bar and a cancel button, see the chart appear with its fitted curve, and read the conclusion in the notebook with the settings it came from. About a minute in ChatGPT's built-in browser, end to end. The person never loses the wheel: move a slider mid-conversation and the agent's next get_lab_state reads "you: set gravity to 1.59 m/s²"; ask "what did I change?" and it names the change, predicts the effect and runs a trial to check (range 41.5 m on Earth became 82.5 m at lunar gravity). Agent changes glow purple on the sliders and arrive as toasts; yours are blue. Anything the agent wrote can be edited or deleted. Live: https://minewefu.github.io/trialbook/ · Source: https://github.com/minewefu/trialbook (MIT) How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite, deployed to GitHub Pages; no backend. The physics engines are plain functions: a closed-form projectile with a semi-implicit Euler integrator when drag is on, fourth-order Runge–Kutta for the nonlinear pendulum and for Lotka–Volterra, and the exact first-order solution for the RC circuit. How WebMCP is implemented: Every tool is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool through one 150-line wrapper. It feature-detects the API, keeps a local registry that powers an in-page Tools panel (anyone can run any tool without an agent, through the same code path), clamps outputs, and turns thrown errors into { ok: false, error, hint } the model can act on. Fourteen tools: eight lab-wide ( get_lab_state , open_experiment , get_results , plot_results , fit_model , notebook_add_entry , notebook_read , export_report ) and six per experiment ( set_parameters , run_trial , sweep_parameter , run_repeats , optimize_parameter , reset_experiment ). The experiment group is registered when an experiment opens and replaced when another opens, so the schema always describes the current sliders; the handlers act on whichever experiment is open, so a cached schema still behaves. readOnlyHint on every reading tool; untrustedContentHint on notebook_read , the one tool that returns text people typed. The execution AbortSignal is wired into sweeps, repeats and optimisations: cancelling from the agent or the on-page button stops the loop and returns the partial results with cancelled: true . Validation is strict and specific: angle = 120 is outside the allowed range 0 to 90 deg ; Unknown parameter "mass". Valid parameters: speed, angle, … . In assignment mode the refusal says exactly what to ask the person for. Outputs stay under about 1.4K characters: results are paged, sweep summaries shrink to fit, and the lab state drops detail in tiers rather than truncating mid-JSON. 66 unit tests cover the physics (projectile within 0.5% of the closed form, pendulum within 0.5% of the exact elliptic-integral period, the Lotka–Volterra invariant conserved, RC time constant equal to R·C), the fits, the tools' output sizes, cancellation and assignment mode. The tools reference is generated from the tool definitions by a test that fails if it drifts. Verified end to end in ChatGPT's built-in browser (GPT-5.6 Sol, Windows desktop app) and in Chrome 151 with the WebMCP flags. Challenges we ran into The output budget. Chrome's guidance asks for tool outputs around 1.5K characters, and a seven-parameter experiment with seven measurements blows through that fast. The fix was structural: paged results, sweep summaries that shrink row by row until they fit, and a lab-state snapshot that drops detail in tiers, so the agent always gets valid JSON rather than a truncated one. Conclusions that stayed in chat. In the first live test the agent answered "the exponent is 0.50" in the conversation and never wrote it into the notebook, which made assignment mode pointless. Every batch result now ends by asking for the conclusion to be recorded, and in assignment mode a chat-only conclusion does not count. Tool groups that change under the agent. Switching experiments swaps six tools. If the client caches the old schema, the calls still have to work, so handlers act on whichever experiment is open and validate against it, and the schema is only a description. Layout. The first version spent its pixels vertically. Two rounds of screenshots later, parameters sit under the stage in fixed-width rows, tools are a chip cloud, and the readouts follow the cursor without jumping. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop works from a plain conversation in ChatGPT's browser: sweep, fit, propose, accept, report, with numbers that match the physics to the last digit. The agent asked for a hypothesis before it would sweep, and its conclusion showed up as a proposal with Accept, Edit and Reject buttons, exactly as designed. And the physics is honest: every engine is tested against an exact solution. What we learned Tools are a better place for policy than prompts. Putting "write a hypothesis first" into a tool's refusal message, rather than hoping the model remembers, made the behaviour reliable. Small, well-described tools with strict errors let the model self-correct in one turn. And a specific "what changed since you last looked" feed is worth more than any amount of state dumping, because it tells the agent what the person cares about right now. What's next for Trialbook Real data import, so a student can compare their own pendulum timings against the model. More experiments, chosen for the laws they let you discover. A teacher view of the attribution report across a class. And, as WebMCP clients mature, declarative tools for the notebook form so the lab works in more browsers. Built With canvas react typescript vite vitest webmcp zustand Try it out github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by minewefu F Like Share this project: Updates minew

title: Understudy
pitch: Understudy uses WebMCP to turn one work sentence into a reviewed, executable playbook. Your agent asks for missing judgment, grows the process live, and routes evidence, recovery, and approval.
about_excerpt: Understudy uses WebMCP to turn one work sentence into a reviewed, executable playbook. Your agent asks for missing judgment, grows the process live, and routes evidence, recovery, and approval. Like Comment Story Updates The visitor’s agent loads the reviewed version, starts a run, and turns the graph’s rules into each owner’s task form. Recorded Pickup evidence cannot enter the Courier route. Understudy refuses the conflicting branch and preserves the submitted choice. Chat adds required weight, a delivery-method dropdown, owners, and Courier/Pickup conditions to the live process graph. title: VoxChain
pitch: VoxChain lets a karaoke host describe a vocal sound in plain language while a WebMCP agent safely tunes the same live chain they can hear, inspect, edit, and undo.
about_excerpt: VoxChain lets a karaoke host describe a vocal sound in plain language while a WebMCP agent safely tunes the same live chain they can hear, inspect, edit, and undo. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Simple view: browse presets with plain-language filters and see the current vocal sound at a glance. Advanced view: inspect and tune the ordered live effect chain while the limiter stays locked last. What it does VoxChain is a live vocal-effects chain that runs in the browser. A karaoke host can use Simple view to browse sounds, use Advanced view to tune the chain by hand, or describe a sound in plain language to a browser agent. The person and the agent work on the same visible and audible chain. Every accepted agent change appears in the interface with a plain-language summary and Undo. Why WebMCP fits A person may know that a singer should sound warmer, clearer, deeper, or more spacious without knowing how to translate that request into EQ, compression, delay, reverb, gain, and routing decisions. VoxChain registers ten page-scoped WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect the effect catalog and current chain, browse presets, load a preset, adjust parameters, add or remove eligible effects, and save a personal preset. This gives the agent structured controls and live state instead of forcing it to guess at page coordinates. The browser keeps the safety-critical controls with the person. The agent cannot start microphone capture, select an input, toggle Bypass, restore watchdog-muted output, remove the terminal limiter, place nodes after it, or raise its ceiling above the allowed limit. How people and agents work together The agent follows a preset-first strategy. It searches the 33 factory presets and loads the closest match when one fits. If no preset matches, it can build a chain from the 14 available effects. For example, the prompt "Make my voice really big and echoey, but keep it clear" led the agent to load the Noraebang Echo preset. The app showed the resulting six-node chain, the sound changed live, and Undo restored the prior chain. A follow-up request to remove the terminal limiter was refused without changing the chain. This was difficult before WebMCP because an agent lacked a reliable, typed way to understand an audio editor's available effects, current signal order, parameter limits, and safety rules. How we built it VoxChain is a static vanilla JavaScript app. Web Audio and AudioWorklets run the microphone chain locally. The page registers its tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . A shared mutation boundary validates both human and agent edits, applies changes to the model and physical audio graph, and creates one Undo entry. The effect catalog drives both the visible controls and the WebMCP descriptions. Chains and personal presets stay in browser localStorage. A Cloudflare Worker serves the app over HTTPS. VoxChain does not host a model or send microphone audio to an AI service. Codex, Claude, and GLM helped during development. Codex helped shape the product scope and architecture, define the ten tool contracts and safety refusals, implement and test the Simple and Advanced views, debug rapid preset and parameter interactions, and prepare the judge-facing documentation. Features 14 vocal effects and an optional Auto Gain setup utility Simple and Advanced editing views 10 WebMCP tools for reading and editing the live chain 33 factory presets plus browser-local personal presets Visible agent activity, change summaries, and Undo A terminal limiter, output cap, and structured safety refusals Human-only Start, microphone selection, Bypass, and watchdog recovery Testing The public demo runs at https://voxchain.arrangedgodly.com/ with no account or credentials. The release suite passed 52 test files and 5,584 checks. The production build generated 64 public files. The deployed app exposed all ten tools in the Codex in-app browser, and a real-microphone smoke test passed the live preset load, Undo, limiter refusal, Bypass, and Stop path. The public 2:56 demo shows the Simple and Advanced views, the WebMCP interaction, an accepted mutation, Undo, and the terminal-limiter refusal. title: Werkstern Podcast
pitch: A local podcast recorder where ChatGPT suggests the cuts and you approve each one. It works from the markers you set while recording, with a preview, a full undo, and untouched originals.
about_excerpt: A local podcast recorder where ChatGPT suggests the cuts and you approve each one. It works from the markers you set while recording, with a preview, a full undo, and untouched originals. Like Comment Story Updates Product Picture apply edit Inspiration My girlfriend is a medical student. I'm training as an alternative practitioner, the regulated German profession called Heilpraktiker . We spend a lot of our time on opposite sides of the same questions, and we kept ending up in long kitchen-table conversations about what the evidence actually says, where it's thin, and where people are being handed something more confident than anyone can honestly claim. At some point we figured those conversations would make a decent podcast. Then we looked at our calendars. We both work full time and we're both still studying. Finding two hours to record was doable. The rest of it was the problem. An hour of the two of us talking turns into a long evening of cleanup: the false starts, the "hold on, let me say that again", the twenty seconds where one of us is looking up a paper. Every podcast we know that quietly stopped after four episodes stopped for that reason. So the podcast went on hold and we built the tool first. A slightly ridiculous order of operations, but here we are. What it does Werkstern records each person's voice locally and uncompressed. While you're talking, you tag things with a single keypress: retake, error, good point, chapter, source. Those tags are the whole idea. The tedious part of editing gets done while you're still in the conversation, by the person who just heard what went wrong. Afterwards, ChatGPT reads the finished take through WebMCP and suggests specific regions to remove, in seconds. The app lists them for you, you keep or drop each one, and only then does anything get cut. You get an audible preview before you commit and an undo that puts everything back. The original recordings stay untouched, which we verify byte for byte in the test suite. Why we used MCP We started from a constraint. We're recording medical conversations, including half-formed thoughts and things one of us says and then takes back. That audio stays on the machine, so any design that began with uploading the file was ruled out early. The second thing that shaped it was accuracy. In a conversation about medicine the qualifier is often the load-bearing part of the sentence. "This helps in a narrow group of patients" and "this helps" are two different claims, and only one of them is true. We needed to see every proposed cut before it happened. WebMCP fit both of those. The model never receives audio. It receives a deliberately thin description of the take: markers, director signals and pause windows, all in seconds. No names, no device labels, no file paths, no tokens. It reasons over that and hands back numbers, and the app does the actual cutting locally with FFmpeg, sample-accurately. That division of labour is what made the project feel workable. The model handles the part it's good at, which is reading a conversation and having an opinion about what to trim. The app handles the part it's good at, which is being exact and reversible. The approval step in between is where most of our care went. How we built it The recorder came first and took most of the time. Capture. An AudioWorklet per station at 48 kHz, 24-bit mono, with echo cancellation, noise suppression and automatic gain deliberately switched off. Two-second chunks, each carrying a CRC32, buffered in IndexedDB so a Wi-Fi dropout costs you nothing. Node, Fastify and ws on the host machine; the browser side is plain ES modules with no framework. Clock drift. Two laptops have two crystals, and over an hour they disagree. This was the hardest audio problem here. Werkstern writes a 1 kHz stripe digitally into every raw track just after the start and again just before the stop, then locates both afterwards by cross-correlation. For each guest track the correction factor is $$f = \frac{n_{\text{end}} - n_{\text{start}}}{N_{\text{end}} - N_{\text{start}}}$$ where $n$ are the guest's stripe positions and $N$ the host's, in samples. We report it as $(f - 1) \times 10^{6}$ ppm and correct it with asetrate plus SOXR resampling at 28-bit precision. A take is accepted only when the residual offset stays under 240 samples, which at 48 kHz works out to $$\frac{240}{48\,000} = 5\ \text{ms}.$$ Rendering. The soundboard stays out of the microphone signal. Every pad press is stored as an event, and the final stereo mix is rebuilt afterwards from that log plus a content-addressed copy of each sound file. Replace a sound six months later and the old episode still renders exactly as it did. The agent layer sits on top and touches none of that. Eight tools registered in the top-level document through document.modelContext.registerTool : four read-only ones, preview_edit_batch which validates and displays without saving anything, and three writing tools behind the approval dialog. Every schema is closed with additionalProperties: false and bounded lengths, and each tool carries an honest readOnlyHint so the host can tell reading from writing. Cuts are stored as batches of source-time regions with a revision number that only ever goes up. Every write has to state the revision it believes is current, so a command built on stale information gets rejected instead of landing on a take that has moved on. The preview you hear is the complement of what was removed: for regions $R = {[s_i, e_i)}$ over a take of length $T$, it plays $[0, T) \setminus \bigcup_i [s_i, e_i)$, concatenated. Challenges we ran into Approval turned out to be a concurrency problem. Our worst bug had nothing to do with audio. Two approval requests could share the same dialog element: the second one overwrote the text of the first while it was still open, and one click then resolved both promises. You would have read "render a preview?" and, with that same click, authorized a permanent edit. Approvals are serialized now, and a second request arriving while one is open gets refused. Cancelling, losing the connection, leaving the dialog unanswered, and a dialog that fails to open all count as a no. Undo had a hole in it. If you queued a preview render and then hit undo, the render was still holding the old region list and would cheerfully write the audio you had just discarded back to disk. A render now re-reads the take before it starts and gives up if the batch is gone. We reviewed our own work adversarially, and it was uncomfortable. Before calling it finished we ran an independent audit against our own commit. It came back with one critical finding and a handful of serious ones. Then, while fixing those, I introduced a new one: my approval guard could get stuck and silently refuse every write for the rest of the session. It only surfaced because a browser test behaved oddly and I chased it instead of writing it off as flakiness. I'm glad I did. Testing a modal dialog under browser automation was miserable. The automation pane we used never dispatches the <dialog> close event. showModal() opens it, close() sets the return value, and the listener simply never runs. Instead of calling it working on a harness we couldn't trust, we proved the flow two other ways: unit tests with a DOM stub where the event does fire, and an end-to-end test that drives the real FFmpeg binary over a synthetic take, checks the output is exactly 48 kHz stereo 16-bit at the expected length, and confirms the source file's SHA-256 is identical before and after. Being straight about filler words. The first feature everyone asks for is automatic removal of "um" and "äh". We have no transcript and no speech recognition, so we can't do it. get_edit_capabilities says so directly in its output, to the model, in the tool response itself. Leaving that vague would have taken one sentence. and honestly we didnt had time to make a video, so we simply asked ChatGPT to generate one :D What we learned The question that mattered shifted over the project. It started as how much the model could do on its own and ended up as how precisely we could stop it. One approval covers exactly one write. Anything ambiguous resolves to no. The recordings come out identical to how they went in, and we can show that rather than claim it. We also learned how much of this rests on the unglamorous half. Nobody will ever notice the sync stripes or the checksum on every two-second chunk. Without them there'd be no trustworthy take for a model to reason about in the first place. What's next Local transcription with faster-whisper, running on the same machine so nothing has to leave it. That's what would unlock filler words and picking highlights by what was actually said. We left it out of this round because we wanted the smaller claim to be accurate. After that, a preview that spans several edit batches at once. And, eventually, the podcast. title: Agentic Sandbox
pitch: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together.
about_excerpt: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together. Like Comment Story Updates Current post-lock recovery with human Packaging lock, stale-write rejection, and receipt-backed evidence. Six narrow WebMCP Site Tools discovered in the live host. Scenario comparison: same output, cheaper standard-supplier plan passes the cost cap. Deterministic lock-bound proof: 9,252 < 10,937 under the human Packaging lock. The problem Factory planning decisions rarely happen in one place. They move through dashboards, spreadsheets, a simulation specialist, and an approval meeting, and each handoff loses context and authority. A generic assistant can make that worse by recommending a control that an operator has just taken off the table. What it does Agentic Sandbox makes the website itself the shared, inspectable decision surface. It is a deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a browser agent plan against the same versioned state. The demo mission is concrete: increase good output by at least 20%, keep total cost within 8% of baseline, add no machine, and do not increase defects. The agent reads the line, creates two bounded hypotheses, simulates a 16-hour shift, and compares immutable receipts. Scenario A reaches 11,114 good units but costs €47,670.51 and fails the cost cap. Scenario B reaches the same 11,114 units for €45,170.51 and passes all four constraints. Then comes the important moment: while the agent is working, the human locks Packaging. That click advances the factory revision and makes earlier evidence historical. The agent’s next write still carries the old revision, so it fails atomically with STALE_FACTORY ; nothing is applied or silently rebased. The agent re-reads the authority state, replans with only controls that remain available, and receives an auditable answer: under the Packaging lock, at most 9,252 good units are possible while the mission requires 10,937. The target is proven infeasible by deterministic evidence, not by model prose. That safe disagreement is the product. The human can change the admissible action space without restarting the conversation, and the agent can recover without overriding the new rule. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, the agent would have to infer state from pixels and click by coordinates, or the product would need a separate chatbot and backend with a second source of truth. Instead, the page exposes exactly six narrow Site Tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_factory_snapshot get_scenario_snapshot create_scenario apply_scenario_changes run_factory_simulation compare_simulation_runs The human interface and these tools share one application-owned command bus. Schemas are closed, handlers validate independently, and every mutation carries a request ID plus expected factory, scenario, and lock revisions. There is deliberately no agent-accessible lock, unlock, force, arbitrary patch, optimizer, ERP, PLC, SCADA, or machine-control tool. Human authority stays human. How it was built Agentic Sandbox is a self-contained React 19 + TypeScript + Vite app deployed on Vercel. The deterministic engine models 64 fixed ticks, uses integer/fixed-point arithmetic, and computes production, defects, energy, cost, constraints, invariants, and bottleneck evidence in the page. Each simulation creates an immutable, content-addressed SHA-256 receipt with exact operands, accepted/rejected operations, tick-level state, and an optional lock-bound proof. No displayed KPI comes from the language model. The hardest implementation problem was making a mid-plan disagreement trustworthy rather than dramatic: old authority must fail closed without erasing evidence that was valid when created. That required explicit revision precedence, atomic stale-write rejection, immutable receipts, and visible current-versus-historical states. The submitted flow was replayed against the public deployment in a supported WebMCP host, including discovery, comparison, the human lock, stale rejection, re-read, replan, and proof. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when a website already owns meaningful state, rules, and actions. Exposing those capabilities directly is more reliable than asking an agent to reconstruct them from pixels. A refusal can be more valuable than another recommendation: STALE_FACTORY proves that human authority survived concurrency, and 9252 < 10937 proves why the target cannot be met under the active lock. Potential impact and what’s next The first users I have in mind are plant planners, industrial engineers, and continuous-improvement teams working on line balancing, shift planning, and supplier what-if analysis. A production version could connect this exact capability, revision, lock, and receipt pattern to a validated digital twin, while ERP, PLC, SCADA, purchase, and physical-machine changes remain behind existing approvals. The broader pattern applies to any high-consequence planning interface: expose narrow capabilities, bind actions to explicit versions, preserve the human veto, and return evidence a machine can check. title: BananaLabs - WebMCP DJ
pitch: Everyone can code today. With BananaLabs, anyone can DJ tonight.
about_excerpt: Everyone can code today. With BananaLabs, anyone can DJ tonight. Like 2 Comment Story Updates DJ Interface with an AI prepared set Inspiration DJing is one of the last creative crafts that software never truly automated — because the hard part was never the buttons, it's the judgment. When to tease the next record in, when to slam the drop, how hard to ride the pitch. AI music tools generate songs; DJ software syncs buttons. Nobody had handed an AI agent the booth itself - the decks, the mixer, the FX, and asked it to be good. WebMCP made that question askable. Instead of an agent fumbling through a UI built for hands, we could expose the craft as structured tools and see whether an agent could develop taste: compose a set, perform it live, listen to its own work, and fix what sucked. BananaLabs DJ is our answer. What it does BananaLabs DJ is a web DJ workstation that a person and an agent can play together - same decks, same document, same tools. Upload a handful of tracks and the app measures them in a worker: BPM, musical key, drop points, energy curves, harmony (chroma), vocal regions. From there the agent takes over like a real DJ: It composes — picks track order by solving a mixability path over real join costs, cuts drop-anchored clips (never radio intros), and compiles every transition from a craft grammar: tease-slams that bleed the next record's build in under the current one, tempo and pitch rides, loop rolls, echo throws, backspins - every drop lands exactly on the 1. It performs — live in the browser on two tempo-matched decks, a 3-band EQ/filter mixer, crossfader, delay-throw FX bus and sampler pads, with SoundTouch keylock and a dosed vinyl "pitch scream" on rides. It listens to itself — review_set bounces the set offline and measures every join from the rendered audio: dead air, level jumps, bass stacking, masked first transients, slam punch. If something's rough, it gain-stages the levels and re-measures until clean. It ships — verify gates the document, then the set plays live, exports to WAV, or shares as a .blset. The human can interrupt at any moment - grab a fader, rewrite a join, or just enjoy the set. Live app: https://bananalabs-sable.vercel.app/ · Code (MIT): https://github.com/KushagraAgarwal525/webmcp-dj How we built it The core decision: one document, one pipeline, two performers. Every state change - from a human dragging a crossfader to an agent recompiling a transition - flows through the same SetDoc command pipeline, so human and agent never fork the mix. On top of that: WebMCP tool surface — 66 tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool, in two curated tiers: a compose-first surface (compose, audition, verify, review, play) and a booth-hardware tier (?booth=1) exposing loops, hotcues, EQ, sampler, FX. Per-tool output budgets keep results semantic, never truncated mid-JSON, and every mutation echoes a compile report (where the commit lands, whether it's on the drop): document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "review_set", description: "Bounce the arrangement offline and MEASURE each join from the rendered audio…", inputSchema: { /* index?, fix? */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* render → measure → report/fix */ }, }); Measurement, not narration — a worker analysis pipeline (STFT chroma, EDM-profile key detection, flux beatgrid with downbeats, salience-based drop detection, vocal regions) gives the composer ground truth; the composer never guesses bar math. The agent's ear — an OfflineAudioContext bounce renders the set with full parity to live playback (loop rolls, backspin rewinds, tempo rides included). That one renderer powers both the Download-WAV feature and review_set, so what the agent measures is exactly what the room hears. The loop is documented in the tools — compose with prepare_set, measure the sound with review_set (fix:true to gain-stage), gate with verify_set, then play. The agent never computes bar math and never plays unreviewed when it follows the descriptions. React + TypeScript + Vite on the front, Dexie/IndexedDB + OPFS for persistence, deployed as a static app on Vercel. Challenges we ran into The first agent sets were bad. Instant track-to-track switches read as random , not mixed. We rebuilt the transition grammar around handoffs - the tease_slam, so the crowd hears the next record arriving before the drop slams on the 1. The slam still sounded rough - so we measured it. The drop's first transient was landing mid-sweep and several dB hot. The fix (pre-open the incoming a bar early, a 1/16-bar flick on the 1, and per-entry gain staging) was proven by the agent's own review tool, not by assertion: it caught a +5.9 dB hot slam, staged it, and re-measured clean. Pitch rides went dull before they screamed. Unlocking keylock for a full 16-bar ride made the record creep thin; dosing the unlock to the final 4 bars - stacked with the loop roll and filter rise, made the festival scream. Along the way we found and fixed a keylock restore leak on deck reloads, a set-clock drift during un-laned overlaps, and a clip-clamping bug that silently destroyed drop anchors. Agents don't fail like users fail. Sixty flat tools invite an agent to push faders instead of compose — so we curated tiers. Agents narrate confidently and wrongly — so tools return measured truth, not stories. And our own live-debugging harness needed watchdogs and streaming logs after too many "stuck forever" sessions; vite HMR never swaps long-lived audio modules, so every proof runs on cache-disabled reloads. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent that genuinely DJs — composes with craft vocabulary, performs live, and is good enough that a friend judged the set by ear and approved it. The agent-ear loop — review_set measures rendered audio and the agent corrects itself without human intervention. Watching it catch and fix a hot slam on its own was the moment the project took shape. Zero prompt magic required — the loop lives in the tool surface. Our most naive test prompt ("compose a dj set using these songs") drove the full compose → measure → fix → verify → play flow. A complete product, not a demo — persistence, undo/redo, WAV export, shareable .blset sets, a proposal banner for agent edits, a full smoke-test suite, and a CDP eval harness that bounces and scorecards every compose. Real DJ details done right — phrase-snapped drops, chroma auditions of actual overlap windows, loop rolls, backspins, echo throws that ring over the next drop. What we learned The tool surface is the prompt. When a naive instruction failed, the fix belonged in the tools - guidance, defaults, and honest echoes - not in cleverer wording. Agents need measurements, not assertions. The single biggest quality jump came from giving the agent an objective ear over its own output. Craft followed from feedback. Design the grammar, not the script. The agent picks what (recipes, order, intent); the engine owns how (bar math, lane compilation, clock). That separation is what made the agent's choices both free and safe. WebMCP's real unlock is shared state. The magic isn't that an agent can click our buttons - it's that two performers can work one instrument. What's next for BananaLabs - WebMCP DJ Calibration corpus — crowd-confirm drop/hook timestamps to keep sharpening the salience detector. Musical pitch rides — semitone-quantized landings keyed by Camelot relation, so rides resolve tonally, not just dramatically. True two-hand collaboration — human and agent performing the same set simultaneously (the shared document already supports it; the UX is next). Deeper measurement — harmonic dissonance scoring from the bounce, energy-arc analysis, and a crowd-simulation score. The pattern as a template — "compose → measure your own output → fix → verify → play" generalizes to video editing, motion design, and any creative app on WebMCP. I'd love to package it as the reference pattern for the agent-native creative web. title: hexmend
pitch: An agent gym where humans decide what matters and agents prove the smallest repair.
about_excerpt: An agent gym where humans decide what matters and agents prove the smallest repair. Like Comment Story Updates Hexmend is an agent-evaluation environment disguised as a graph-native spell game. A person contributes taste ("the ducks must stay") while a browser agent inspects, traces, simulates, and repairs the same executable spell through seven WebMCP tools. Those calls form a deterministic, scored, exportable trajectory. How to try it WebMCP tools register only when a host provides document.modelContext, and hosts are not broadly shipped yet, so the page tells you which case you are in instead of pretending. Opened by a WebMCP-capable browser agent the header reads 7 WebMCP tools registered; opened in an ordinary browser it reads 7 WebMCP tools ready for a host. Either way the lesson is playable, because the local tool console calls the same production handlers a visiting agent would. The screenshots, the demo video, and the browser tests install a stand-in document.modelContext to play the host; that shim only delivers the calls, and every result in them comes from the production handlers. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Most agents have to infer application state from pixels and imitate clicks. That is especially brittle in a graph editor, where direction, type, version, and causality matter more than position. Hexmend exposes the spell as a semantic, versioned artifact instead. Seven narrow WebMCP tools let the agent inspect the exact graph, trace a side effect, run deterministic simulations, explain the smallest responsible subgraph, record a human-authored sacred constraint, rank valid repairs, and atomically apply an approved patch. Focused inspection never hands the agent dangling references or a pre-solved diagnosis: it separates the closed selected subgraph from boundary edges and returns only high-level scenario status. The trace is a bounded graph traversal, not a prose guess: it returns the complete ordered Moonwell → Multiply → Summon ducks → Pour → Room path, all responsible edges, and explicit cycle/type evidence. The explanation is also executable evidence rather than a prose claim: it returns the typed five-rune/four-edge subgraph, the positive route facts, the absence of an Umbrella route, and four counterfactual simulations proving every responsible edge is necessary. A repair can first be simulated by its bounded patch ID: the result proves the editor was not mutated, and the interface visibly labels the stable prediction as unapplied. The tools return stable node and edge IDs, ordered events, cast assertions, before/after evidence, minimality evidence, and a stale-safe revert token. The browser agent works with the application's source of truth rather than reconstructing it from the interface. How it creates a better user experience The agent does not disappear into a chat transcript. Its work is visible on the shared canvas: inspected runes select, causal paths glow, constraints become physical pins, and every proposed connection, disconnection, and rune activation appears both in an eight-step review ledger and as a pending graph overlay before approval. Crucially, the human card renders the exact structured ledger returned to the agent; simulation, application, and rollback repeat that receipt so review cannot silently drift from execution. Mutations advance the graph version, and verification casts animate the outcome. The same shared handlers power WebMCP, human controls, and a local fallback console, so the experience remains understandable in an ordinary browser. Every write is bounded and reversible. The agent can apply only a current application-generated patch ID, not arbitrary graph operations. The proposal names its exact graph-version, live-edge, dormant-rune, and sacred-lock preconditions; the approval card shows them, application revalidates them before cloning, and the result returns what was checked. The human can undo the latest unchanged patch without losing their sacred constraint. What people and agents can do together The opening spell should water a Moonflower, but Multiply executes before a target is bounded. Twelve lunar ducks flood the observatory. A purely mechanical optimizer ranks a six-edit repair that bypasses the duck branch. The person contributes something the graph cannot infer: "The ducks are funny. They stay." That preference becomes an executable constraint. The cheaper candidate is now ineligible, so the agent ranks an eight-edit Umbrella route first. All twelve ducks survive, their rain reaches the Moonflower, the room stays dry, and the flower blooms. This is the central thesis: graph interfaces let people and agents negotiate executable intent. The same pattern applies beyond games to creative tools, workflow builders, data pipelines, and other stateful systems where a person's subjective constraints are essential but impossible for an optimizer to guess. Why it is more than a game Hexmend also exposes a headless Agent Gym protocol. The typed graph is the observation, the seven tools are the action space, and the shared application handlers define deterministic transitions. A nine-milestone, 23-point rubric rewards grounding, failure observation, causal tracing, explanation, intent preservation, safe patch preview, atomic application, and final verification. Invalid calls score −2; mutating before explaining scores an additional −5. The visible scorecard updates for both UI and WebMCP calls, and a complete trajectory can be exported as JSON. Three semantic families contain 96 deterministic tasks: 48 Moonflower carrier-path variants across 32/8/8 splits, 24 Resonant Aviary feedback-cycle variants across 16/4/4, and 24 Clockwork Orchard temporal-guard variants across 16/4/4. Node, edge, and effect IDs are opaque and remapped per task; serialized order, layout, and prompt wording also change. Each variant activates one to three seeded, typed decoy edges outside the answer-key route, giving every family at least three visible topologies and testing whether a policy can reject causal distractors. Public observations deliberately omit the simulator's role map, causal rule ID, answer-key edges, rule-revealing family/scenario names, and pre-cast diagnostic assertions. Tests prove that a transparent policy can ground protected intent from natural-language constraints plus inspected rune text and earn 23/23 on held-out variants from all three rules, while a memorized training ID is rejected without mutation. That is meaningful cross-rule grounding evidence, not a claim of broad transfer or reinforcement-learning gains. The reproducible benchmark runs the transparent reference policy over all 96 variants and reports 96/96 completions at 23/23. A held-out contrast suite proves the reward separates grounded completion (23), unsafe mutation-first completion (18), safe but incomplete diagnosis (6), constraint-violating completion (4), and canonical-ID memorization (−8); its aggregate results are visible in the product. A JSONL exporter emits standalone training episodes with the task prompt, human constraint, initial public graph, complete tool manifest, replay-complete transitions, rewards, and termination flags; an independent verifier replays every action through the production handlers and rejects any altered record. A streaming JSONL service and dependency-free Python adapters let an external trainer drive those same transitions online, as one environment or as isolated parallel vectors with Gymnasium-shaped reset/step results. These validate the environment and scripted controls, not a learned-policy result. What adversarial testing found An evaluation environment is worth what it survives, so this one was attacked deliberately. The attacks are kept runnable, and every number below regenerates with one command. The reward ignored the human's constraint. A policy that diagnosed correctly, skipped locking the constraint so the destructive repair stayed eligible, applied it and recast was graded goal-verified at 20/23 with the protected branch orphaned every time. Reaching the goal by discarding what the human protected now ends the episode as constraint-violated and scores 4. It is a visible row in the on-screen baseline table. The advertised tool schemas were locked to one scenario. Enums were built from a hardcoded scenario, so on other families the only correct arguments were schema-invalid. Registration now describes the graph it is registering for, and deliberately does not enumerate the protected rune, since that is what the agent must ground from the human's words. Registration gave up if the host was slow. Model context was feature-detected once; a host that installed it after mount found nothing. Registration now waits for the host, bounded and abort-scoped. The approval card promised a protection that was not set. Its footer was a hardcoded claim. It now reports what the patch actually preserves, or says plainly that nothing is. title: Huginn
pitch: Test the moment, not the grind: a typed WebMCP test port for live browser games.
about_excerpt: Test the moment, not the grind: a typed WebMCP test port for live browser games. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The problem Coding agents are increasingly good at creating browser games, but testing the gameplay they create is still surprisingly blind. A source-code review can suggest what should happen and a screenshot can show pixels, yet neither exposes the authoritative state currently held in browser memory: the board, economy, legal actions, RNG state, campaign progress, or save timeline. That gap is especially painful in games. Important regressions often appear only after a sequence of decisions or behind minutes of progression. Reaching the same late-game moment by keyboard or pointer is slow and difficult to reproduce, while inventing a parallel test simulation risks proving behavior the real game does not have. Why WebMCP This use case depends on the live page. Huginn registers bounded, typed tools directly from the running game through WebMCP. The agent reads the same canonical state the renderer uses and dispatches through the same transition path as the player. The human stays in the loop and watches each committed action render on the real canvas. A backend API would miss the thing being tested: this exact deployed browser build, its in-memory save state, and the visual result currently in front of the designer. DOM automation alone cannot describe a Canvas or WebGL game, and raw coordinate clicking cannot reliably create or replay a semantic game state. What people and agents can do together With Huginn, a designer can direct an experiment in natural language: discover the game's rules, goals, metrics, action vocabulary, and curated setups; enter a real late-game moment without replaying unrelated progression; list only actions that are legal against the current state; run a visible sequence with a fixed seed and bounded steps; branch two plans from the same verified state and compare their outcomes; snapshot and restore the canonical save timeline; capture the rendered frame with an image hash paired to the exact state hash; save meaningful metric expectations as a portable gameplay regression. The submission demonstrates this on three playable games. COIL is a three-level campaign Snake game, STARFALL is physical pinball, and THORNWATCH is tower defense. COIL and STARFALL use native Canvas 2D; THORNWATCH uses PixiJS 8 and WebGL. The same shared tool surface works across both renderer families. The hero demonstration skips directly to COIL's real Level 2 signal gate and branches shielded versus unprotected play from an identical checksum. In THORNWATCH, the agent compares two tower plans through the same deterministic wave, then captures the visible PixiJS result. These are narrow, reproducible test cases—not claims that one seed proves game balance or fun. How it works Huginn is split into four layers: a protocol-independent kernel that owns deterministic execution, legal-action checks, snapshots, checksums, cancellation, and semantic verdicts; a separate WebMCP transport that builds strict JSON Schemas and performs the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls; a small protocol-free runtime for reducer-first games; an optional in-page debugger for receipts, captures, and replay controls. Games implement an engine-neutral adapter: initial state, legal actions, reducer, metrics, serialization, restoration, and render callback. Human input and agent tools use the same state authority. The core never imports Canvas, PixiJS, DOM selectors, or a game engine. The shared tools are describe_game , get_game_state , get_metrics , list_legal_actions , apply_action_sequence , snapshot_game , and restore_game . The examples also provide the optional capture_game host capability. Inputs are closed and bounded: no executable code, selectors, arbitrary predicates, URLs, filesystem paths, or network targets. Every game also has a standalone build with identical rules and ordinary controls but no Huginn executable code. The production build traverses and audits those dependency graphs. This keeps Huginn optional instead of turning game development into protocol bureaucracy. What is new Huginn, its kernel, WebMCP transport, debugger, all three game implementations, tests, documentation, and the public site were created during the WebMCP Challenge submission period. A selected set of pre-existing, owner-authorized THORNWATCH art is published under CC BY 4.0 with exact source paths and hashes. All source code is MIT licensed. video_transcript_excerpt: Coding agents can now build entire browser games. Games are a demanding test. State interaction, visuals, timing, and rules all have to work together, but agents still test them surprisingly blind. Source code tells them what should happen. Screenshots show pixels. Neither exposes the live board, legal actions, random seed, campaign progress, or save timeline where gameplay regressions hide. These are three real playable games: campaign snake, physics-based pinball, and tower defense. Each works with keyboard, mouse, or touch. No agent required. Huginn gives a coding agent a type test port into the running game through WebMCP. A person watches the same canvas while the agent reads real state, chooses only legal actions, runs an experiment, and captures reproducible evidence. In Coil, reaching signal gates normally means playing through level one. The agent asks the game to describe itself, then loads a game-owned level two setup. Huginn validates that setup through the real save system and renders it. From seed 12 in the same starting checksum, the first branch advances into the gate and dies. The second arms the shield, advances, and survives. The result is not just a screenshot. It includes type state, decisive events, and checksums. That exact moment can now become a regression test after the next code change. Now the same tool surface drives a different genre and engine. In Thorn Watch, the agent compares two tower placements through the same deterministic wave. The weak plan places towers too far from the road. The gate falls to 12 health with four leaks and no kills. The stronger plan leaves 18 health with three kills and one leak. Both runs started from the same checksum. Huginn's capture tool then returns a visible PNG, its image hash, and the exact game state hash. The agent can reproduce this result without replaying earlier waves or inventing an illegal move. Coil uses native Canvas 2D, Thornwatch uses PixiJS and WebGL. Huginn imports neither renderer. Each game supplies a small adapter for its state, legal actions, save codec metrics, and rendering. Huginn's core stays protocol independent. WebMCP registration and the debuggers sit around it. Huginn does not replace unit tests, visual review, or human judgment. It removes the grind between a coding agent and the gameplay moment that matters. Humans choose what to investigate. Agents reach, branch, compare, and document that moment live, visibly, and reproducibly. Huginn, test the moment, not the grind.

title: Intent Relay
pitch: Teach a workflow once, then translate the intent across WebMCP-enabled websites — without replaying clicks.
about_excerpt: Teach a workflow once, then translate the intent across WebMCP-enabled websites — without replaying clicks. Like Comment Story Updates Intent mapped to Orbit’s WebMCP capabilities: 5 preserved, 2 adapted, 1 not transferable, 1 sent to Human Queue. A provenance-backed Intent Contract proposed from the demonstration, with every rule reviewed and approved by the human. Orbit’s draft is prepared, but publication stays human-only: the agent can prepare; only the human can publish. What it is Most WebMCP demos ask what an agent can do on one site. Intent Relay asks what happens to human intent across sites. Intent Relay does not replay clicks. It translates human intent across the web: a human demonstrates a workflow once on a WebMCP-enabled site, reviews what that demonstration means , and carries the approved intent to a structurally different site. How it works The Workbench orchestrates two embedded demonstration providers built for this prototype — Gather (source) and Orbit (destination). They are separate HTTPS origins that structure the same job differently, on purpose. Demonstrate. You set up an event in Gather the way you always would. Gather exposes semantic state through WebMCP, and the trace records what each choice means — not where you clicked. Verify. From that demonstration, the agent side proposes an Intent Contract : rules with provenance, each citing the recorded actions that justify it. Nothing counts until you approve it — rule by rule. Transfer. Intent Relay discovers the capabilities Orbit exposes through WebMCP and maps your approved intent against them. The canonical demo result: 5 preserved — transfer unchanged 2 adapted — a 24-hour reminder becomes "1 day", because that's how Orbit counts 1 not transferable — Orbit has no equivalent, so it is excluded visibly, never silently 1 needs your decision — genuinely ambiguous Human Queue. The ambiguous one stops here: the demonstration used a native waitlist; Orbit doesn't have one. The agent doesn't guess — you decide, and only then does it prepare Orbit's draft. The Human Queue is a feature, not a failure state. Publish. Publication is deliberately not exposed as a WebMCP tool. The prepared draft waits for a human. The agent can prepare; only the human can publish. Why WebMCP matters here Traditional browser automation can repeat actions on one interface, but it is brittle the moment two sites expose different structures and concepts. Intent Relay depends on what WebMCP makes possible: websites publishing machine-readable capabilities instead of an agent scraping DOM structure or replaying screen coordinates. Real browser-discovered tools via document.modelContext across three origins (Workbench, Gather, Orbit) Cross-origin semantic capability discovery — Orbit declares what it accepts, and mapping decisions are driven by those declarations Deployed to production through the Chrome Origin Trial — the demo runs in normal Chrome without WebMCPTesting flags Explicit human boundaries: contract approval, ambiguity decisions, and publication are human-only Challenges we ran into Cross-origin discovered tool objects. Real DiscoveredTool objects carry cross-origin WindowProxy references that cannot safely live in React state — the implementation separates sanitized display metadata from the raw browser handles used for invocation. Representing semantic mismatch without guessing. Every approved rule must land in exactly one explicit status (preserved / adapted / not transferable / needs decision) — "almost matches" is a first-class outcome, not an error path. Origin Trial across three origins. Three distinct HTTPS origins each needed correct Origin Trial configuration to run flag-free in production. What we learned WebMCP solves capability exposure — semantic equivalence between sites still needs reasoning and explicit boundaries. The most interesting case is not when two sites match perfectly, but when they almost match: that is exactly where human judgment matters most, and where an agent that refuses to guess is more useful than one that automates blindly. How it's built React + TypeScript + Vite in npm workspaces (three apps plus shared packages for contract types, validation and mapping logic), WebMCP via document.modelContext , three HTTPS origins on Cloudflare Pages behind the Chrome Origin Trial, 241 unit tests and a Playwright end-to-end suite, plus runtime validation in real Chrome. What's next (future work) More WebMCP-enabled providers; richer Intent Contract schemas; portable workflows across marketplaces, productivity and travel tools; shared semantic vocabularies; deeper provenance and policy handling. None of this exists yet — the prototype intentionally proves the transfer model on two deliberately different providers. video_title: Intent Relay — Portable Human Intent with WebMCP
video_transcript_excerpt: Gather and Orbit handle the same job differently. Intent Relay moves my intent between them, not my clicks. I set up the event in Gather the way I always would. Watch the trace. It records what each choice means, not where I clicked. From that demonstration, the agent side proposes an intent contract, rules with providence, each citing the actions that justify it. Nothing counts until I approve it, so I do, rule by rule. Now Orbit, a different site with different capabilities. Here's the underlying WebMCP called directly, so you can see the browser discover tool being invoked. Same numbers, straight from the runtime. Five rules transfer as they are. Two are adapted. My 24-hour reminder becomes one day because that's how Orbit counts. One has no equivalent, so it's excluded, visibly, not silently. And one mapping is genuinely ambiguous. Asked for a wait list, Orbit doesn't have one. Intent Relay stops here instead of inventing what I meant. I make the decision. The agent can continue, and it prepares Orbit's draft. This is where it ends, waiting for human. Publishing was never a tool. It's a button on Orbit for me. Intent Relay, teach the web how you work once, carry it everywhere.

title: RiffSmith
pitch: Write riffs with an agent: the whole editor is 15 WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Write riffs with an agent: the whole editor is 15 WebMCP tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Tools: the 15 tools with their real descriptions, styled like the app. Import modal: a messy hand-written tab pasted in, with the section headers, chug runs, 5h7, dead notes and slides. Mountain King in E standard mid-playback with the rig open, model showing RiffSmith Distorted. Imported result: that tab as a song with sections, repeat marks, a 3/4 bar, and the amp selected. Showcase: the Guitar Showcase's 16th-note riff section with the playhead on it. Inspiration I play guitar in a metal band, and like every guitarist I have a folder of half-finished riffs living in text files. Tab editors make those playable, but writing metal in one is slow, mechanical work: sixteenth-note chug runs, odd meters, repeats, and sections you have to loop a dozen times to know if they're any good. That's exactly the kind of structured, iterative writing an AI agent is good at, and yet an agent looking at a tab editor sees a grid of identical cells it can only click one at a time, with no idea what a cell means, whether a write landed, or what any of it sounds like. WebMCP was the missing piece. Instead of teaching an agent to screen-read a grid, give it the editor's own verbs. RiffSmith is the tab editor where every feature is a tool, and the human and the agent write in the same document at the same time. What it does RiffSmith is a browser tab editor for guitar and bass, tuned for metal. It imports and exports ASCII tab, including messy hand-written tabs with dense chug runs, section headers, and repeat marks. It handles per-bar time signatures from 2/4 to 12/8, grids from quarters to 16th triplets, and loops any section while you keep editing. Playback runs through a sampled guitar engine with persistent per-string voices: palm-muted chugs, hammer-ons, pull-offs, taps, slides, bends, vibrato, tremolo picking, pinch harmonics, dead notes, and chord strums, built from real direct-input recordings with open licenses. The signal goes through a real Neural Amp Modeler capture running as WebAssembly inside an AudioWorklet (the bundled one is a capture I trained on my own rig), or a built-in amp chain. A performance layer adds what a hand does: tension glide on every pick, pick position, one-sided fretting-hand vibrato, finger-shaped bends, pick scrape, wound-string slide squeak, fret clank, and micro-timing. Bass tunings get a real bass and their own amp. Every one of those capabilities is exposed to agents as one of 15 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext : songs, bars, notation, imports, the rig, and playback. An agent can create a song, write a four-bar riff in one atomic call, set the amp tighter with all downstrokes and double tracking, play it, and read back the tab to verify its own work, while the human watches it land in the grid and edits any note it wrote. How I built it Next.js App Router, TypeScript, and the Web Audio API, deployed as a static site on Vercel. There is no backend; songs live in localStorage and sample banks and amp captures in IndexedDB. The WebMCP layer follows one rule, parity: every tool runs through the same state operations the UI uses, so there's no agent-only document or hidden mode. Tool returns are built for verification, with write_notes echoing the affected bars back as ASCII tab and get_song returning the full rendering. Notation is validated before any write, and a rejected token comes back with the complete notation guide so the agent can self-correct. Writes take a batch that is validated in full and applied atomically. Calls go through a serialized queue and mutations wait for React to commit before the next call runs, which gives read-after-write consistency for chains like create-then-read. Tools register at module evaluation, before React mounts, so an agent's first page snapshot already has the complete set, and a console shim at window.__webmcp is always available for testing. The audio engine is a lookahead scheduler placing events on the audio clock, driving a sampler with continuous per-string voices, plus an experimental physical string model written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly (no bindgen, about 21 KB) that runs in its own AudioWorklet. Sound comes from the Guitar-TECHS dataset (CC BY 4.0), FreePats (CC0), and Karoryfer's bass (CC0), chosen string-aware so a note plays from the string it's tabbed on. Every sound decision was measured before it shipped: offline renders through the real engine, pitch tracking, banded spectra, transient detectors, and level profiles around transitions. The pure scheduling and import layers have 31 unit tests. Challenges I ran into Pitch shifting is time stretching. Web Audio's detune folds into playback rate, so every pitched sample also stretches its pick transient. That was the source of a lot of "synthy". The fix was a set of real-recording handovers: held bends, slides, hammer-ons and pull-offs crossfade into a recording of the target pitch, energy-matched and decay-matched. The "pick" in every hammer-on. Legato kept sounding picked no matter what we did to the crossfade. The real bug was that the envelope was being re-read about 130 ms early and reset upward on every legato event. Tracking the envelope analytically from our own schedule fixed it in one afternoon after days of chasing filters. A dead string in the dataset. The low E string of the Guitar-TECHS guitar had almost no upper partials, about 28 dB below the same pitches on the A string, and that's the string every metal riff lives on. We regenerated its partials from the recorded fundamentals, fitted to the A string's spectrum. The first pass came out 145 cents flat because the files are 48 kHz and the script assumed 44.1. A pitch check caught it. Licensing. The best-sounding amp capture we found is not redistributable, and the rules require the submission to be fully open. The answer was to train a capture of my own rig and ship it with the repo under MIT, so the hosted demo and the repository are identical. Bare tools aren't usable tools. The first version of the tools worked and agents still failed with them: silent write errors, snapshot pipelines that missed late-registered tools, create-then-read races. Most of the WebMCP work was making the tools honest and verifiable, not making them exist. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A human and an agent editing the same riff at the same time, audibly, with no export step and no agent mode. The agent writes a riff, I click a cell it wrote and change one note while the loop keeps running, and it builds a variation on my edit. That was the whole point and it works. The engine went from a sampler to something a guitarist listens to and says "that's pretty great": real-recording legato landings, one-sided vibrato, finger-shaped bends, a fully synthesized pinch harmonic that screams through the amp, a bass with its own amp, a slide squeak that follows the speed of the slide, and a physical string model in Rust running in the browser. Every tool is verifiable by the agent that called it, and the whole thing runs as a static page with no server. What I learned Agents need feedback loops more than they need features. The tools that mattered most were the ones that echo the result of a write back as tab, return the notation guide with a rejection, and guarantee that a read after a write sees the write. Registering tools before the framework mounts matters because snapshot pipelines are unforgiving about timing. On the audio side, measure before you listen. Almost every "it sounds synthy" turned out to have a specific, measurable cause (input level into the capture, a compressor that shouldn't have been there, a stretched transient, an envelope step) rather than a vibe, and an offline render harness found each of them faster than ears could. And a real guitarist's ear is the final test. Several things that measured fine still got sent back. What's next for RiffSmith Chord and multi-string helpers in write_notes so agents can write power chords and octaves in fewer lines. Drum and bass companion tracks on the same scheduler. Render-to-WAV. MIDI and Guitar Pro export. A clean-channel capture and a bass capture to sit next to the distorted one. A wider low-tuned sample bank recorded on my own guitar, since no open dataset covers Drop B. And publishing the WebMCP bridge pattern (serialized queue, commit waiting, early registration, console shim) as a small standalone package so other editors can adopt it.
