title: ClaimGate
pitch: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions.
about_excerpt: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP exposes privacy-safe candidate matching while private proof stays manual. Staff reviews aggregate eligibility and a redacted timeline, never evidence values. Atomic handoff completes the claim, returns the item, and resolves the report. ClaimGate — privacy-first lost-property claims with human release decisions. Problem Lost-property desks need enough public detail to find a likely item without publishing the details that prove ownership. Giving every field to an Agent would turn private proof into searchable material. ClaimGate separates public matching from private proof. The Agent handles structured preparation and safe reads. People publish, submit evidence, decide the claim, issue the pickup credential, and complete the release. Why WebMCP This workflow changes as the claim moves from draft to match, review, pickup, and collection. WebMCP lets the page expose the few actions that are valid now, with typed inputs and bounded results. The Agent does not have to infer controls from page layout, and sensitive actions can stay absent from the tool set. Better experience A Claimant can describe a loss once, let the Agent structure the public fields, and receive explainable candidates without copying data between screens. Staff gets a short queue and a redacted summary. Each person sees the next action in the same claim instead of reconstructing context after every role change. Before and after Before ClaimGate, the demo journey is a sequence of manual forms and page searches, with a risk of mixing public clues and ownership proof. With ClaimGate, the Agent prepares, searches, and summarizes through explicit tools while the UI reserves publication, proof, judgment, credential transfer, and handoff for visible human controls. What it does A Claimant starts a fresh two-hour instance with fictional Northbridge Campus inventory. The Agent can create or update a lost-report draft, list reports, find up to three candidates, and stage one candidate. Results contain broad fields, confidence bands, and public reasons, not internal inventory IDs. The Claimant publishes and submits masked evidence manually. Two correct slots are sufficient even if a third submitted slot is wrong. The browser receives only aggregate eligibility, insufficiency, or the third-attempt LOCKED state. Staff reads a bounded queue and redacted review summary, then decides manually. After approval, the Agent can read pickup instructions. The Claimant manually generates and copies a ten-minute, one-time credential, then Staff pastes it into the handoff form. One transaction marks the claim collected, item returned, and report resolved. The normal web flow also works without WebMCP. How implemented ClaimGate is one Next.js 16 application with separate report, matching, evidence, claim, authorization, audit, and WebMCP modules. SQLite scopes every record to a demo instance. Signed HttpOnly sessions and server routes enforce role, ownership, state, version, CSRF, origin, idempotency, and rate limits. The browser uses native document.modelContext.registerTool() . A page and state registry selects nine tools, and an AbortController removes the previous generation on navigation or state change. Tool visibility assists selection; the server remains authoritative. The tools are create_lost_report_draft , update_lost_report_draft , list_my_reports , find_candidate_matches , stage_claim_candidate , get_claim_status , get_pickup_instructions , list_pending_claims , and get_claim_review_summary . Publishing, evidence, decisions, pass issue or reissue, role switching, and handoff have no WebMCP tool. Matching uses fixed category, time, area, color, and tag rules. Runtime evidence comparison uses salted HMAC digests and a fixed three-slot shape. The public repository contains the readable fictional seed answers so judges can run the demo; the privacy boundary covers runtime clients, pages, APIs, WebMCP, logs, and stored raw evidence, not repository readers. Only a successful issue or reissue response returns the full pickup credential. The current Claimant page keeps it in memory and can reveal, mask, or copy it. Navigation or refresh clears it and cannot recover it. The server stores only a digest, and reissue invalidates the previous generation. Challenges we ran into State-aware tool lifecycle: Chrome 151 can briefly change membership while registrations are replaced. A serialized generation manager and server state checks make stale calls fail safely. Runtime privacy evidence: We separated public DTOs from private transports, signed opaque candidate handles, bounded outputs, and scanned tool results, HTML, logs, storage, history, and public build assets. Visible cross-role continuity: Claimant and Staff must resume the same authorized claim without hidden navigation. Contextual role switching and a 14-scenario visible Playwright suite cover that path. Accomplishments that we're proud of The complete report, match, proof, review, pickup, and handoff flow works in the normal UI and the WebMCP-assisted path. Nine tools appear only in valid page and state scopes; human-only actions stay absent. A clean production build completed three independent native Chrome 151 runs. Each used fresh SQLite state, exercised all nine tools, completed the manual transitions, and ended with Home tools [] . All 14 visible Playwright E2E scenarios passed after commit 04c618d added contextual cross-role claim navigation. The release path isolates its runtime, data, processes, ingress, and Nginx resources from unrelated services. These are implementation and test results, not claims of awards, adoption, users, or judging outcome. What we learned Tool discovery improves planning but is not authorization. Runtime privacy needs separate data paths, not hidden UI fields. Human control is clearest when a sensitive transition has no tool at all. Stateful WebMCP also needs navigation, stale-version, delayed-completion, and teardown tests, not only a happy path. What's next A production pilot would need institutional identity, enrolled Staff, accessibility and abuse review, retention policy, backup and recovery, and a database architecture for multiple application instances. Configurable matching and evidence policies should preserve the same public-match, private-proof, and human-release boundaries. The in-app browser discovers native web MCP tools for the current page. The agent turns my description into a structured private draft. The server still checks the sign session, owner, version, and rate limit. A bounded red confirms the saved report without exposing private proof. Publication has no web MCP tool. I make that decision in the page. Deterministic matching uses category, time, broad area, color, and public tags. The agent receives an opaque current candidate handle, not an internal inventory ID. The agent can explain the desk hours, readiness, and expiry, but it cannot issue the credential. Only this issue response returns the pass. It lives in this page memory. Leaving or refreshing cannot recover it. I transfer the one-time credential manually. It never enters a web MCP result. The handoff atomically marks the claim collected, the item returned, and the report resolved. The final status is read-only. Returning home removes every claim gate tool. Native acceptance records the resulting set as empty.

title: Fluent Notebook
pitch: A browser-based Python workspace powered by WebMCP, where AI agents act as active research partners to fetch datasets, fix bugs, and execute analysis code directly alongside you.
about_excerpt: A browser-based Python workspace powered by WebMCP, where AI agents act as active research partners to fetch datasets, fix bugs, and execute analysis code directly alongside you. Like 4 Comment Story Updates Product WebMCP Inspiration During my time working heavily in quantitative research and portfolio construction, I kept hitting the same friction: context switching. Jupyter is the industry standard for index research and data analytics, but jumping between the notebook to write boilerplate, browser tabs to hunt for dataset documentation, and terminal windows to manage environments breaks the analytical flow. I wanted an environment that respects deep work. By combining WebMCP with a strict, distraction-free UI, the goal was to turn the static notebook into an active research partner. What it does Fluent Notebook is a Jupyter-style Python notebook that runs entirely in the browser. Python executes in Pyodide (WebAssembly) with pandas, NumPy, matplotlib and %pip install via micropip, so there is no kernel server and no data leaves the machine. Around that kernel sits a Fluent UI workspace: a code editor with IntelliSense and Jupyter command mode, an Explorer with Python, Markdown, CSV and JSON files, a Problems panel fed by pyflakes, a Data Wrangler for DataFrames and CSVs, a Variables panel, interactive charts, and a Python terminal. The page registers 49 WebMCP tools , so a browser agent (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with the WebMCP flag) can read and edit cells and files, insert cells between cells, run cells and .py files, install packages, inspect kernel variables, find bugs, open a DataFrame in Data Wrangler, restyle and explain charts, write per-cell summaries, import notebooks from .ipynb JSON, rename, move and delete files, restart the kernel, and save or load the user's cloud workspace. Every tool returns real notebook state; nothing is mocked. Why WebMCP is a strong fit A notebook is not a page you can scrape. It is a live kernel, an editor, a file tree and a set of outputs. Screenshot-and-click agents cannot reliably "run cell 2" or "read the table under cell 3". WebMCP lets the notebook hand the agent the same levers a person has, each with a JSON schema, read-only and untrusted-content hints, and a structured result the agent can chain: add_python_cell → run_python_cell → get_cell_table . Because Python runs in the tab, the person and the agent share one kernel, one file tree and one problem list, with no server round trip. How it creates a better experience Ask "how expensive is the S&P 500 versus its own history?" and the agent writes the pandas cell, downloads Shiller's monthly data inside the kernel, drops the months with no valuation data, runs it, charts CAPE against its long-run average, and reports the answer, while you watch it happen in the notebook. That is the demo video, recorded live in the ChatGPT app. Ask "find bugs in analysis.py" and the agent runs static analysis, reads the Problems panel, edits the file with a find-and-replace, and re-checks. Ask "summarize each cell" and the agent pins its own two-line summaries under every cell and in the Outline. Every agent edit is badged with the tool that made it ( Agent · add_python_cell ) and keeps a one-click Revert until you edit the cell yourself. The WebMCP panel lists every call, linked to the cell it touched. What people and agents can do together now The person keeps the editor, the keyboard and the judgement; the agent gets the same kernel, files and problem list. Debugging, data cleaning and documentation become a shared loop inside one tab instead of a copy-paste relay between a chat window and a notebook. Cell and file tools resolve only once the change is on screen, so the agent can chain calls without racing the UI, and the person can step in at any moment: rerun, edit, revert, or keep going by hand. How I implemented WebMCP Each of the 49 tools is declared once and registered with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, annotations, execute }) . The page falls back to navigator.modelContext for Chrome's flag and keeps checking briefly for hosts that inject the context after load. execute calls the same functions the toolbar buttons use (insert cell, run cell, find bugs, rename, restart kernel), then awaits the React state flush, so results describe what is actually on screen. Results are structured JSON: cell ids, table summaries, chart specs, problems, file paths. Tools carry readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations and support abort signals. A tracking wrapper records every call for the status chip and the WebMCP panel, and tags cells the agent touched so the UI can show the badge and the Revert button. Tech stack React 19 in a Next.js-style app on Vite (vinext), Microsoft Fluent UI v9, Recharts for interactive charts, a custom code editor with Python IntelliSense; Pyodide with pandas, NumPy, matplotlib, micropip and pyflakes; static export hosted on Azure Static Web Apps (Free tier) with a managed Azure Functions API that stores each signed-in user's workspace in Azure Blob Storage behind optional GitHub or Microsoft sign-in. Challenges I ran into Running Python entirely in the browser brings sandboxing limits: no git clone , and CORS blocks many dataset hosts. I turned that into a showcase for tool use: the agent fetches what the page cannot and passes it in through import_notebook_from_json or create_project_file , or downloads inside the kernel with pyodide.http.open_url . The other hard part was timing: tool calls have to wait for React state to land, or a chained run_python_cell runs a cell that does not exist yet. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The human-agent loop feels fluid. Python IntelliSense sits alongside the agent's edits, so manual changes to a generated pandas DataFrame or chart script are smooth, and the agent can read a traceback from the Problems pane and inject the fix without the user leaving the keyboard. In the demo, ChatGPT completes a full market-valuation analysis with seven tool calls. What I learned Structured tool access beats open-ended prompting. Giving an agent specific, well-defined tools, such as converting a GitHub URL to raw .ipynb JSON and parsing the cells, produces faster and more deterministic help than letting it guess its way through a UI. What's next for Fluent Notebook Expanding the WebMCP tool set for data pipelines: tools for zero-copy business-intelligence queries, so the agent can explore large remote databases and stream aggregated results into the local browser session for visualization. title: Jobbbler
pitch: A job site any WebMCP agent can operate end to end - find, compare, keep watching, apply - with the person in control.
about_excerpt: A job site any WebMCP agent can operate end to end - find, compare, keep watching, apply - with the person in control. Like Comment Story Updates A job site that serves people through its pages and agents through its tools. The site announces 29 actions; any WebMCP client discovers them on every page, with nothing to install. One request becomes one typed call: search_jobs runs and the page follows with the filters the agent set. Quiet reads leave the page still; open_job_details moves it. Every call stays visible to the person. Three roles compared on the facts the site returns, in a single call. Saved once. The review waits for the person's decision; then the server keeps checking after the tab closes. An agent-prepared application: read-only while it works, with the exact review of what would be sent. The web is getting its agent interface Websites were built for people: a page to read, buttons to click, forms to fill. An agent can drive that interface too, the way a person would, but it is slow, brittle and blind to what the site actually offers. That is why agentic APIs appeared: MCP gave agents proper, typed tools. It came with a catch. Every service needed its own server, every person needed to install and configure it, and an agent only knew about the handful of services someone had wired up in advance. WebMCP closes that gap. The website itself publishes its tools, right on the page, and any WebMCP-capable client discovers them the moment it arrives: ChatGPT's built-in browser today, Chrome with WebMCP, external agent clients that speak the protocol. No setup, no separate server, no integration to maintain. An agent moving through the web meets, on every site that adopts it, an interface made for agents: typed actions with clear inputs and results, instead of a screen to interpret. That is a different web. Call it headless: the same site serves people through its pages and agents through its tools, from one place, with one set of rules. Three things follow: Agents get a native interface to the web. Actions, not pixels. Reliable enough to hand real work to. It scales like the web does. One protocol; every site that adopts it extends every agent at once, with nothing to install. Delegation becomes possible. A person states an outcome, the agent operates the site, and the site keeps the person in the loop exactly where it matters. Jobbbler is what that looks like on one concrete, everyday task. One sentence, a whole job search Looking for a Product Designer position, remote, $90k+. Compare options, pick the top 2, and apply. Schedule for daily updates (every morning). My CV is attached. Said to a person, that is a week of open tabs. Said to an assistant on Jobbbler, it becomes a sequence of site actions: Find. The assistant asks Jobbbler which filters it accepts, then runs one search: product designer, remote, $90k and up. The results page follows along: URL, filters and matches update in front of you. Compare. It opens the strongest roles and compares them on the facts the site returns: compensation, location, seniority, why each one matches. Apply, with control. It prepares two applications on its own: your request to apply is the authority to prepare. It proposes answers that stay marked as its own and requests one exact review of what would be sent. The page turns read-only while it works. Nothing leaves until you decide, in your client. Keep watching. It asks Jobbbler to monitor the search. The site states what it will check, how often, where the updates go and how to stop. You approve once. Then the tab can close: Jobbbler's server does the morning check, and the next time you ask, you hear only what changed. Every step is a real tool call, visible in the Agent activity panel on the page. That panel is for people watching (you, or a judge); the agent never needs it. Two kinds of tools, on purpose Some site actions should be silent, others should be seen. Jobbbler separates them: Quiet tools return structured facts and leave your page alone: search, read a role, compare, check what changed. The assistant can do most of the work without disturbing what you are looking at. Follow tools move the real page: open a role, show the results, open the comparison. Say "show me" and the site follows the agent, so you can watch instead of trusting. The assistant picks the tool. The person can always see what was done. Where control lives Discovery is automatic, but tool access is not authority. Two things always need the person: an email destination, and the final submission of the exact application to its recipient. Each is a request-bound decision: the site issues an expiring request, the client presents it, the person decides, and the server checks that the decision matches the exact request it issued. Consent can be withdrawn in one call. This is the part that makes delegation worth trusting, and it is the part most agent demos skip. Why this is bigger than jobs Nothing in this design is specific to job search. A shop, a clinic's booking page, a documentation site: any data-rich website can publish its actions the same way and become operable by the assistant a person already uses. Jobbbler is one worked example, end to end, of a web that works for people and their agents at the same time. Under the hood 29 WebMCP tools registered directly in the page, the same set on every route. Private or stage-specific tools answer with the next safe step instead of pretending to succeed. One command layer, two adapters: the visible interface and the tools share the same server commands, so the page and the agent never disagree. Honest continuation: WebMCP lives while the page is open; durable monitoring runs on Jobbbler's server with a leased worker. No second model behind the site: understanding and drafting stay with the person's client; Jobbbler supplies typed data, deterministic search, workflow state and enforced authority. TypeScript monorepo: Next.js, domain packages, SQLite for local runs and PostgreSQL (Supabase) in production, Resend-compatible email, a small design system. Production runs at jobbbler.com under the Chrome WebMCP origin trial and is verified with unit, contract and browser suites plus real tool runs in ChatGPT Desktop's browser. Try it Open jobbbler.com in a WebMCP-capable client, open Agent activity → Tools to see what the site offers, then say: Looking for a Product Designer position, remote, $90k+. Compare options, pick the top 2, and apply. Schedule for daily updates (every morning). My CV is attached. Or take it one step at a time: "Find remote senior platform roles in Europe, top three and why." "Show me the second one." "Keep watching this search, email me only what changes." "Prepare my application for the first role and show me exactly what would be sent." title: jobContext: The Memory Layer for Your Career, Agent-Ready
pitch: Career searches scatter context across tabs, docs, and tools. With WebMCP, jobContext gives you and your agent one shared memory for every role and next move, directly in your signed-in browser.
about_excerpt: Career searches scatter context across tabs, docs, and tools. With WebMCP, jobContext gives you and your agent one shared memory for every role and next move, directly in your signed-in browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The memory layer for your career, with a live Claude MCP call composing a cover letter. Every new AI chat starts from zero. jobContext is the persistent memory. 12 domain tools, 104 actions, one capability layer across desktop, cloud, and mobile. Readiness-aware: Oura sleep, HRV, and recovery on the dashboard to time your outreach. The dashboard is itself an agent surface: every tool is registered in-page over WebMCP. Private by design: same origin only, tenant isolated, open schema, no lock-in. The signed-in cloud dashboard: priorities, pipeline health, and readiness at a glance. Pipeline with AI fitment scoring: a role weighed against the candidate’s real materials. A generated résumé, versioned and linked to its application, previewed in the app. ChatGPT discovers all 12 jobContext tools in-page through document.modelContext, with no connector or second login. Assessment detail: fitment 8/10 with strengths, risks, and evidence weighed against the saved résumé. Provenance gate: every claim traces to source context, with a verifiable pass or fail. Long generations run as async work items, then return with their trust report. A cross-site call to /mcp is answered 401 Unauthorized, so a hostile page cannot ride your session. Inspiration I built jobContext after getting laid off and finding that AI job-search help came with its own tax: every new conversation began cold. I was repeatedly re-explaining my resume, what I had shipped, which companies were already in my pipeline, people I had met, my STAR stories, and the way I write. The context existed, but it was scattered across documents, tabs, and past chats. Copying it into every fresh session was exhausting when I needed that energy for the search itself. I started by building a few small tools to stop re-explaining myself. They grew into jobContext. What I built jobContext is a living career workspace: applications, job search, materials, interviews, people, STAR stories, and the context behind them stay structured and persistent across sessions. It works as a desktop app, hosted dashboard, mobile companion, CLI, and MCP capability layer. It is not another chat that gives advice and forgets the work. The person owns the workspace and stays in the loop; an agent can help move real work forward inside it. For this challenge, I made the signed-in browser workspace agent-ready through WebMCP. A person and an in-browser agent can work from the same live pipeline: understand the search, find or assess a role, create materials, log the work, and leave the result where the person can inspect and use it. No new connector, separate OAuth flow, or blank-slate conversation is required. How I built it jobContext is built with Python, FastMCP, FastAPI, SQLite with a JSON audit trail, and a React dashboard. After authentication, the dashboard asks the live FastMCP server for its tool list and registers the returned names, descriptions, and input schemas directly with document.modelContext. When an in-browser agent invokes a tool, the bridge sends a same-origin JSON-RPC request to the same stateless /mcp endpoint used by other clients. The browser surface is not a second, hand-maintained API. It reflects the running MCP surface, so browser tools cannot quietly drift from the tools the app actually offers. The current surface has 12 consolidated tools and 104 actions behind them. Challenges I ran into More context is not better context. While improving document generation, I discovered that the system had accumulated more context about my writing style than about what I had actually done. That drove a retrieval-first redesign: token budgets, diagnostics, context ceilings, selective retrieval, and a clear separation between stored knowledge and prompt assembly. The lesson was simple: better context beats more context. “No setup” still has to be safe. I wanted the browser agent to work with the signed-in dashboard, not make someone configure yet another connector. But a session cookie is not permission to trust every browser request. The server accepts that session only for same-origin requests to /mcp; a cross-site browser request cannot use it, while deliberate bearer-auth MCP clients still work. A browser tool call is shorter than real document work. In-browser clients can time out before resume or cover-letter generation finishes. I added durable submit-and-poll generation so an agent can start work, return promptly, then retrieve the finished result instead of pretending a long-running job completed. A generated file is not a finished workflow. If a draft lands untracked, it creates another loose end. Generated materials now automatically create or update the relevant pipeline entry. A read-only Generation Trust Report lets the person inspect the claims checked, verdict, correction passes, and durable audit record. Trust has to be architectural. An interview question exposed a gap in my own system: I could observe non-deterministic AI output, but I could not yet prove that a generated claim was grounded. That became a deterministic provenance gate that checks factual claims against the source material on every generation and records the outcome. Prompt instructions alone were not enough. What I learned The useful unit of AI collaboration is not a prettier chat response. It is a shared, current workspace where the human can see what happened and decide what comes next. WebMCP matters because it lets a page describe its live capabilities at runtime. That is fundamentally better than making a person configure a second integration or maintain a browser-only copy of an API. Reducing friction can create more value than adding features. One of the most satisfying product moments was sharing a job from a phone and having the relevant workflow already waiting at the desk. Good agent systems need grounded context, clear permission boundaries, durable work, and inspectable results. Those are product requirements, not cleanup work after the demo. What changed during this challenge The original jobContext project predates this challenge. The WebMCP agent surface and its supporting hardening below were built during the submission period. The core bridge dynamically reflects the live FastMCP tool surface into document.modelContext and calls the signed-in, same-origin MCP endpoint. Agent-driven testing exposed and fixed workspace-aware assessment, validation, and interview-prep round-trip issues. I added provenance reporting, durable submit-and-poll generation for short browser timeouts, workflow instructions for in-browser agents, and automatic pipeline tracking for generated materials. WebMCP implementation synopsis The WebMCP work began by turning the existing hosted dashboard into an agent surface without creating a second browser-only tool API. The React app probes for document.modelContext, with the older navigator.modelContext alias retained as a compatibility fallback. After the user is authenticated, the bridge calls the live FastMCP server's tools/list endpoint, takes the returned tool names, descriptions, and input schemas, and registers those definitions with modelContext.registerTool(). When the browser agent invokes a registered tool, the bridge forwards the call as JSON-RPC over the same-origin, stateless /mcp endpoint already used by other MCP clients. That architecture means the WebMCP surface is generated from the server's real capability layer. There is no separately maintained list of browser tools to drift out of date. At submission time, the live surface exposes 12 consolidated domain tools with 104 actions. New server-side actions can appear in WebMCP automatically through tools/list rather than requiring a second implementation. The bridge also preserves the signed-in experience without turning the session cookie into ambient authority for arbitrary websites. Same-origin browser calls to /mcp may use the existing jobContext session. Cross-site requests are denied session-cookie authority using Sec-Fetch-Site, with Origin and Host checks as a fallback. Bearer-authenticated MCP clients and non-browser clients remain supported. This was built specifically so WebMCP could feel like part of the signed-in application while still enforcing an origin boundary around side-effecting tools. Browser agents also exposed operational gaps that were easy to miss in ordinary chat or direct MCP use. Long-running resume and cover-letter generation can outlive a browser tool-call window, so jobContext gained a durable submit-and-poll control plane. The agent can submit generation work, receive a work-item identifier promptly, and later poll for completion rather than holding the browser call open. Remote LLM clients were then given finite request timeouts and stale-run reporting so

title: jsonloupe
pitch: The JSON surface humans and agents share: via WebMCP, an agent loads, queries, and points at the exact document you're looking at — one lossless viewer, two interfaces, no copy-paste loop.
about_excerpt: The JSON surface humans and agents share: via WebMCP, an agent loads, queries, and points at the exact document you're looking at — one lossless viewer, two interfaces, no copy-paste loop. Like Comment Story Updates GIF The whole loop, live: load_doc -> reveal_path flashes the failure -> highlight_matches lights the chip -> clear_highlights hands it back. reveal_path: the agent scrolled the tree to the failing delivery and flashed the row - pointing, not describing. highlight_matches: the tree filtered to the 9 FAILED deliveries via the toolbar's own filter chip - reversible by the user's button. load_doc: this document was opened by an agent, straight into the viewer the human is watching. No download, no paste. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP jsonloupe is local-first: the entire lossless JSON engine — worker-parsed, int64-exact, comfortable with five-million-element arrays — already runs inside the page. WebMCP tools execute in page context, so the bridge hands agents the real engine, not a proxy to a backend that doesn't exist. There is no server anywhere: the tools, the data, and the human's view live in the same tab. The tool vocabulary was already proven — jsonloupe ships a stdio MCP server with the same bounded verbs (schema → query → refine, capped responses, the document itself never leaves). WebMCP is the transport that puts those verbs where the human is actually looking, and it enables three tools no headless server could ever offer: pushing a document into the human's open viewer, scrolling their tree to a row and flashing it, and filtering their view through the toolbar's own state. How it creates a better user experience It kills the loop every AI-and-JSON workflow lives in: agent produces JSON → human downloads it → opens a separate viewer → finds the problem → pastes back → repeat. With WebMCP, agent output lands directly in the viewer the human already has open ( load_doc ), questions are answered against the on-screen document with exact int64/decimal arithmetic ( run_query , profile , sample , get_schema ), and instead of describing where something is, the agent points — reveal_path scrolls the tree and flashes the row; highlight_matches filters the view to the evidence. The agent's answers stay small and bounded (counts, groups, capped previews), so conversations stay fast and cheap — the document never round-trips through the model. And the human keeps authority over their own view: highlights use the toolbar's real filter state with the count visible in the chip, reversible by the human's own button at any moment. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Look at the same document at the same time. Before, "human + agent + JSON" meant two disconnected copies — one in the chat context, one in a viewer — synced by hand. Now the agent's load_doc , reveal_path , and highlight_matches operate on the very pixels the human is watching: the agent investigates and points, the human sees and steers, and every agent action is visible, bounded, and reversible in the human's own UI. It turns "the agent said the problem is in tasks[1847]" into the row flashing on screen. It also makes the collaboration safe to trust: every tool that returns document content is annotated untrustedContentHint , so the calling agent is told — at the protocol level — that a value like "IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS" inside the data is data. This carries forward jsonloupe's existing prompt-injection hardening work into the WebMCP era. How WebMCP was implemented A feature-detected, lazily-imported bridge ( src/webmcp/ , ~790 lines + 950 test lines) registers eight tools on document.modelContext : run_query , get_schema , profile , sample , load_doc , reveal_path , highlight_matches , clear_highlights . Tools dispatch over the same UI↔worker message protocol the human's own clicks use, so agent and human literally share one engine and one document. Responses are capped, staleness-checked against a document token (a doc swapped mid-tool aborts cleanly), and annotated with readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint . Query errors return a caret under the fault plus the grammar, so agents self-correct. Where the API is absent the bridge chunk is never fetched and the app is byte-for-byte unchanged (asserted by e2e). Verified by 70 unit tests plus a Playwright end-to-end suite that drives a real WebMCP-enabled Chromium through every tool, and live on jsonloupe.dev under the Chrome origin trial. Prior work vs. new work The viewer, engine, and stdio MCP server predate the submission window. Everything WebMCP — src/webmcp/ , its tests, the wiring, the e2e suite — is new work within the window; see WEBMCP.md and the timestamped commit history (PRs #50, #51). Built With github indexeddb mcp playwright typescript vite web-workers webmcp Try it out jsonloupe.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo project. I built jsonloupe itself over the past months — the lossless viewer, the worker engine, and its stdio MCP server. For this challenge I designed and shipped the WebMCP bridge: eight tools on document.modelContext that share one engine and one document with the human, including the three view-moving verbs (load_doc, reveal_path, highlight_matches) that are the heart of the idea. title: Offcut
pitch: A native WebMCP workbench where people and browser agents compare cutting plans, protect usable stock, and review an exact plan before approving its cut sheet.
about_excerpt: A native WebMCP workbench where people and browser agents compare cutting plans, protect usable stock, and review an exact plan before approving its cut sheet. Like Comment Story Updates fresh-human-review human-review planning-tradeoffs Cutting layout Inspiration A cutting plan is not just an answer—it is a decision about real material. For small workshops and makerspaces, planning starts with measured boards, usable offcuts, required parts, and the material lost to the saw blade. Copying that information into a chatbot creates a second version of the workshop: someone must reconcile the advice with the actual stock and translate it back into a usable cut sheet. Offcut explores a different workflow: let the person and the browser agent work from the same committed measurements, while keeping proposal and approval separate. Cutting-stock optimization is established work. Our contribution is the shared human–agent workflow around it: structured comparison, an exact review handoff, and approval that becomes invalid when its underlying measurements change. What it does Offcut is a shared cutting-stock workbench for straight crosscuts from stock of the same material and cross-section. People can: Enter stock lengths and required part quantities. Set blade kerf and the minimum length considered reusable. Protect stock needed for another job. Compare proportional cutting layouts. Review and approve an exact plan. Export its CSV cut list or print its cut sheet. Through native WebMCP tools, a browser agent can read the committed workshop, request checked alternatives, inspect their constraints, compare results, and stage one complete proposal for review. Three objectives make the trade-offs explicit: Use less stock Handle fewer boards Keep useful offcuts Sawdust, short scrap, reusable remnants, and unopened stock remain separate. A plan that produces less short scrap can still open more stock and require handling more boards; Offcut shows that trade-off instead of hiding it behind a single “waste” score. How we built it Offcut is a static React and TypeScript application built with Vite and published on GitHub Pages , with public MIT-licensed source. The interface and agent tools use the same workshop store and deterministic branch-and-bound planner. The language model chooses what to explore; the application checks part quantities, stock constraints, and material balance. Six JSON-schema-defined tools are registered through the browser’s native WebMCP API: get_workshop plan_cuts inspect_plan compare_plans stage_plan_for_review export_cut_list There is no WebMCP polyfill, embedded chatbot, application backend, or website API key. Manual planning also works without WebMCP. Connecting an agent depends on the browser host’s own model, permissions, and availability. The planner works in integer millimetres and has a bounded search. It reports optimality only when proved—not simply because it found a complete plan. Challenges we faced Keeping approval attached to the right decision Selecting another draft must not transfer approval. Reusing a checked solution must not transfer approval either. Approval belongs to one exact plan ID at one committed workshop revision. Acknowledgement and approval are separate interface actions; neither is a registered agent tool. Export checks the exact approved, fresh, complete plan. This is a tool-capability boundary, not authentication against an agent separately granted browser UI control. Distinguishing unfinished typing from changed measurements An unfinished measurement field is not a new workshop revision. Offcut distinguishes pending edits from saved measurements. Pending edits pause review and approval. Committing an actual change invalidates the previous approval and makes the old plan stale, so the agent must replan and return for a new review. Making native integration verifiable We tested real native tool registration, discovery, calls, disposal, and reinitialization across Chrome 149 and 152, including their differing API behavior. The demo uses a real model through an external recording harness. Its evidence rail summarizes retained native calls and UI events; it is not an embedded website chatbot or a ChatGPT screen recording. UI actions are automated for the recording, and waiting time is trimmed. Preserving correctness while improving performance We improved search pruning, reused checked solutions for identical committed requests, and reduced repeated UI work. Reuse still creates a new unapproved plan record and preserves the original computation’s proof status. What we learned Shared state matters more than conversational fluency. An agent becomes more useful when it can work with the same revision, identities, and constraints that the person sees. Approval is a state transition, not a reassuring message. Its meaning depends on the exact proposal, the measurements behind it, and what happens when those measurements change. Optimization needs explainable trade-offs. Less scrap, fewer boards, and less opened stock are different goals. The application should expose those differences rather than pretend one score answers every workshop’s priorities. Native tools should expose checked domain operations. The model can explore and explain alternatives without inventing measurements or bypassing the workbench’s release rules. What we accomplished Offcut 1.1.0 passed 884 source-contract tests and 72 browser cases : 18 contracts across local and hosted deployments in Chrome 149 and 152. We also verified the maximum 40-cut CSV export and visually checked all 12 rendered pages across two six-page print outputs. The 2:45 demo follows a complete workflow: compare alternatives, stage a proposal, acknowledge and approve it, export its cut list, then change kerf from 3 to 4 mm. The previous approval becomes invalid. The agent replans all 14 parts and ends at revision 2: staged, not approved . These are illustrative planning results—not measured workshop savings, machine instructions, or a safe-cutting guarantee. These illustrative measurements cover usable stock, parts, kerf, and the reusable remnant threshold. People own measurements and protection. Registered tools cannot change them. The right-hand panel is an external Mavo recording harness, not a chatbot inside the website. A real model chooses native WebM CP calls on the shared committed workbench. This is not a chat GPT recording. The model compares three complete alternatives, less stock, fewer boards, or useful offcuts. The deterministic branch-and-bound solver checks quantities, stock, and one kerf per part. A search limit is not proof of optimality. Less stock and fewer boards both open 7.2 m across three boards, 42 mm of sawdust plus 158 mm of short scrap. Keeping useful offcuts opens 10.08 m across six boards, 42 mm of sawdust, no short scrap, and 3.038 m reusable. Computed tradeoffs, not measured time or carbon savings. These UI controls are automated, not proof of human presence. Now, the controls check the acknowledgement. Then, they click approve cut sheet. The model inspects approval and exports the actual CSV. 14 parts, part identifiers, offsets, kerf, and the exact approved plan identifier. Another draft cannot inherit approval. Typing four leaves committed kerf at three. Pending at its block staging without moving focus or saving. Now commit. Revision two invalidates the old approval. The old plan is stale. The model replans 14 parts, 56 mm of sawdust. Revision two is staged, not approved. The acknowledgement stays unchecked. Offcut itself needs no account, model key or make end. The workbench and MIT licensed source are public. These are planning estimates, not machine instructions. Verify usable stock and safe cutting conditions at the bench.

title: RecipeBridge for CyberChef
pitch: Turn CyberChef into a shared live workspace for building, testing, and refining recipes through WebMCP, while raw data stays private
about_excerpt: Turn CyberChef into a shared live workspace for building, testing, and refining recipes through WebMCP, while raw data stays private Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration CyberChef provides security analysts, developers, and students with 503 browser-based Operations covering encoding, compression, cryptography, parsing, and data analysis. Even when users know the intended result, they may not know which Operations provide it, which arguments those Operations require, or how to arrange multiple Operations. The author of CyberChef issue #2691 reported working with unreadable data whose algorithms and processing order were unknown. Magic returned no useful Recipe, and manually testing dozens of likely algorithms in different orders did not recover the expected result. The author reported that a locally run AI model later identified the algorithms, arguments, and execution order. The issue discussion explained that sending processed data to an external AI service would conflict with CyberChef’s browser-local processing model. The issue was then closed as not planned. With CyberChef continuing to process the data in the browser, RecipeBridge focuses on two cases: locating and configuring relevant Operations among 503 choices when the intended result is known, and determining a possible Operation sequence when the processing chain is unknown. What it does The Agent can search CyberChef’s 503 Operations, inspect argument definitions, read a redacted view of the Recipe state, submit revision-checked Recipe changes, request a Bake, and use bounded Magic analysis to select subsequent actions. WebMCP provides the Agent with Operation metadata, Recipe structure, execution state, and limited analysis signals. Raw Input, raw Output, current Recipe argument values, Register captures, Magic previews, and candidate arguments remain inside the browser page and are excluded from WebMCP results. Every Agent change appears in the existing CyberChef interface. The user can inspect and edit the Recipe, stop WebMCP access, and restore the Recipe state that preceded the Agent’s latest change while that snapshot remains valid. The access audit classifies each Operation according to its behavior and side effects: direct (447): Operations that use CyberChef’s standard in-page processing flow. approval (51): Operations involving network access, signing and key generation, OTPs, rich-content presentation, nondeterministic results, Recipe flow control, or Input-derived arguments. These require one-use user approval. blocked (5): Magic uses a dedicated analysis flow. The other four still involve direct Input changes, remote resources, or SVG rendering risks. excluded (1): An internal validation Operation that is omitted from the product catalog. How I built it RecipeBridge registers six fixed workflow tools through WebMCP: search_operations get_operation_details get_recipe_state apply_recipe_patch bake_recipe inspect_output The fixed tool set controls the amount of context loaded during discovery. Search and detail tools provide CyberChef’s generated Operation metadata on demand, allowing the Agent to load only the names, options, defaults, and argument definitions required for the current task. Recipe arguments continue to use CyberChef’s existing metadata and validation rules. User and Agent changes pass through the same Recipe transaction. Each step has a stable ID, and each Recipe has a revision number. The Agent must provide the expected revision when submitting a change. CyberChef prepares and validates the complete change before updating the Recipe model and visible interface. A stale request fails and leaves the workspace unchanged. Each Bake records the Recipe revision, Input version, execution-options version, Output tab, and bakeId . These identifiers prevent delayed Web Worker or Magic results from replacing Output produced by a newer run. The page stores complete Magic candidate Recipes and their arguments in memory. inspect_output analyzes up to the first 1,000 bytes of the current Output and returns filtered analysis signals, candidate IDs, ranks, and Operation names. When the Agent applies a candidate ID, the page sends the stored Recipe through the standard access checks, validation, approval, and transaction flow. Magic ranking guides subsequent analysis, while the user verifies the result through the visible Output. Tool results are generated through a fixed field allowlist. Magic-derived results are also bound to the current Output tab and bakeId , preventing stale analysis results from being returned. The browser or Agent host can still observe the page and URL, so the project recommends disabling CyberChef’s URL updates before processing sensitive data. Challenges I ran into Exposing a large application through a small tool surface Registering a separate tool for each of hundreds of Operations would increase discovery context and make the interface harder to use. Six workflow tools provide a stable interface, while catalog search and pagination expose CyberChef Operations on demand. Coordinating a workspace shared by a user and an Agent CyberChef already supports manual editing, Auto Bake, multiple tabs, background Magic analysis, and Web Workers. Agent changes also require handling stale revisions, overlapping runs, and delayed results. Stable step IDs, atomic Recipe transactions, fixed Bake target information, and provenance checks give each state change clear ownership. Providing useful information while protecting user data The Agent needs feedback to refine a Recipe. Limited analysis signals and candidate references stored inside the page support further analysis while keeping raw data, key material, and decoded Output outside WebMCP results. Adapting to an evolving WebMCP implementation WebMCP remained a draft during the challenge, and available WebMCP hosts did not forward invocation cancellation signals consistently. RecipeBridge accesses the browser API through an isolated adapter with feature detection. Page lifecycle checks, session shutdown, timeouts, and stale-result checks protect Recipe and Output state when a host cannot cancel an active invocation. Reusing upstream behavior accurately An early design duplicated Operation rules through separate profiles, which could diverge as CyberChef changed. The revised design reads CyberChef’s defaults, argument structures, fixed options, and validation rules directly. A separate access audit handles only WebMCP permission classification. Accomplishments The deployed fork supports the complete visible workflow, including Operation discovery, Recipe editing, user approval, Bake execution, Output inspection, and Magic candidate application. Browsers without WebMCP support continue to load the existing CyberChef interface normally. The implementation reviews every generated Operation and defines explicit behavior for the direct , approval , blocked , and excluded classifications. It also handles stale Recipe revisions, rejected or expired approval requests, Operation runtime failures, interrupted or superseded runs, and page-scoped collaboration session shutdown. Current automated validation includes 507 passing Node API tests and 12 passing Chrome WebMCP browser scenarios. Independent testing of the deployed site covers 35 representative workflows across encoding, compression, cryptography, parsing, analysis, Recipe control, approvals, failure handling, and privacy checks. What I learned Shared-workspace development should begin by mapping each state owner, revision, authorization, and completion transition. This prevents user actions, Agent requests, and asynchronous Worker results from overwriting one another A large capability catalog should use a small, stable workflow API with on-demand metadata. This limits the Agent’s discovery context without maintaining hundreds of separate tool contracts. Accurate implementation begins with understanding the business meaning of each data value. That meaning must remain consistent across WebMCP tool descriptions, input arguments, result fields, validation, and tests. This reduces ambiguity when the Agent selects Operations, configures arguments, and interprets results. What’s next Future work will improve resource-intensive Intensive Magic analysis, expand interoperability checks as browser implementations evolve, and provide clearer candidate explanations while protecting candidate arguments and raw Output. User feedback can also guide adjustments to Operation access classifications and approval wording. RecipeBridge is currently an experimental fork. Manual review of the added and modified code remains limited, so further review and practical testing are required before using it in security-sensitive production environments. title: RetailAgentOS WebMCP Agent Storefront
pitch: RetailAgentOS uses WebMCP to let AI agents build valid carts and request quotes from a retailer’s real inventory, pricing, and policies—without guessing or taking control from shoppers.
about_excerpt: RetailAgentOS uses WebMCP to let AI agents build valid carts and request quotes from a retailer’s real inventory, pricing, and policies—without guessing or taking control from shoppers. Like Comment Story Updates Farm Eggs return STOCK_STALE, so cart preparation is withheld. The shopper — not the agent — approves the Cage-Free substitute Only after human approval does prepare_validated_cart register, returning a $15.99 cart. Checkout is never exposed Developer Evidence and Event Log Live Tool Registery - Fresh Corner Store WebMCP exposes only the next safe action. RetailAgentOS's deterministic engine decides what that action is Inspiration I did not start RetailAgentOS to build another shopping demo. I started it because the next interface to commerce will increasingly be an AI agent—and small retailers should not be left behind. My goal is to make agentic commerce accessible to every retailer, from a solo merchant to a global enterprise. Today, becoming "agent-ready" can require specialized engineers, custom integrations, and infrastructure that only large companies can afford. If that remains true, AI commerce will widen the gap between large platforms and the millions of independent retailers that make local commerce unique. I have a direct view of that asymmetry. By day, I lead engineering for one of the largest retail storefronts in the United States, where I have spent years working on the kinds of systems I am describing here: eligibility rules, inventory truth, fulfillment feasibility, promotion stacking, and the pricing context that determines what a given shopper may actually buy. At that scale, the reasoning layer exists—but it is distributed across backend services, much of it is enforced late in the journey, it is expensive to build, and it was designed for one company. Rebuilding another bespoke stack for another large retailer is not the interesting problem. Making these capabilities accessible to an independent merchant is. RetailAgentOS is my independent work. It is informed by my professional experience and general retail-engineering patterns, but it uses no proprietary employer code, data, architecture, or confidential information and does not imply employer sponsorship or endorsement. RetailAgentOS is my attempt to close that gap through an open-source platform. A retailer should be able to describe its products and selling rules once—inventory, pricing, eligibility, delivery, substitutions, customization, and quote policies—and let different AI agents interact with the business accurately and safely. I released RetailAgentOS under the Apache 2.0 license. Its specifications are published as versioned RFCs with their open questions left intact, and the specifications ship alongside a runnable reference implementation—so the rules a retailer reads are the rules the engine actually executes. That mission shaped the retailers I chose for this showcase. Fresh Corner Market represents the neighborhood grocery store: the kirana store found throughout India and South Asia, the neighborhood shop found across Europe, or the independent corner market serving communities in the United States. These stores operate with changing local inventory, narrow delivery windows, substitutions, and close customer relationships. Their commerce rules may look simple on a webpage, but they are highly contextual. An AI agent must know when inventory cannot be trusted, offer an acceptable substitute, and preserve the shopper's control. TheCustomHub represents another important small-retailer model: a specialized American business selling customized apparel. It is also the first real retailer working with me to explore how RetailAgentOS can support an operating business. Its transactions cannot always be reduced to "add item to cart." A request may include color, youth-size quantities, artwork, budget, and delivery requirements that a merchant must review before providing a price. The challenge demo uses an authorized controlled fixture—not a live production backend—but it reflects the real quote-first workflow RetailAgentOS is being designed to support. These two retailers were chosen deliberately. One needs an agent to recover a simple grocery cart when inventory is uncertain. The other needs an agent to preserve a complex custom order without fabricating a price. Together, they demonstrate why agentic commerce needs to support the diversity of real retail—not force every retailer into the operating model of a large marketplace. WebMCP made this vision tangible. It allows the retailer's own website to expose structured actions directly to an AI agent—no marketplace intermediary and no bespoke integration for every agent. RetailAgentOS determines what is valid; WebMCP exposes only the next action the retailer can safely honor; and the human shopper retains control over consequential decisions. The long-term vision is universal access: an open foundation that lets any retailer participate in agentic commerce without surrendering its policies, customer relationships, or independence. What it does RetailAgentOS is the merchant-controlled reasoning layer. WebMCP is the browser action surface. An agent can invoke only the next commerce capability the retailer can safely honor at that moment—and which tools exist changes as the engine evaluates inventory, price, fulfillment, policy, and shopper approval. The grocery mission. A shopper asks for a weekend breakfast cart under $30 from Fresh Corner Market, with Farm Eggs and Artisan Sourdough Bread. The eggs return STOCK_STALE , so cart preparation is not merely disabled in the interface—it is not registered as a tool at all . The engine proposes Cage-Free Eggs, explains the $0.50 difference and the equivalent local delivery, and stops. A human clicks Approve. Only then does prepare_validated_cart register, returning a $15.99 review cart. An optional revision to two loaves lands at $24.49, leaving $5.51 of the budget. Checkout is never registered anywhere in this showcase. The custom-order mission. Twenty-five black robotics-team shirts—six Youth Small, eleven Youth Medium, and eight Youth Large—with a one-color front logo, requested within fifteen days against a $500 ceiling. The plan reaches QUOTE_REQUIRED , which dynamically exposes request_quote . The structured request preserves every constraint the shopper stated and returns fixedPrice: null and deliveryPromise: null . The agent does not get to invent a price the merchant never set. No cart, order, payment, or checkout is created. That second mission matters most to me. Refusing to fabricate a price is not a limitation to apologize for—it is the feature that allows quote-first merchants to exist in an agentic world at all. How I built it The deterministic engine came first and predates this challenge. It runs a staged pipeline—visibility, then eligibility, then price, then fulfillment, then quote—through pure registered evaluators. The same inputs always produce byte-identical output; no model sits in the decision path; time is injected rather than read from the clock. That determinism is the entire basis for letting an agent act on a real store. The WebMCP layer was built during the challenge window on top of it: packages/webmcp is a framework-independent browser adapter owning one canonical catalog of seven Phase 1 descriptors: get_storefront_capabilities , search_catalog , evaluate_shopping_plan , find_valid_alternatives , apply_plan_repair , prepare_validated_cart , and request_quote . Three planning tools register at load; the others appear and disappear as the engine permits. revise_validated_cart is an optional post-cart extension. No state ever exposes every tool at once. Registration runs through document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , owned by an AbortSignal lifecycle so capabilities are revoked on reset, scenario switch, and unmount. Revocability is what makes "safe next action" an enforced guarantee rather than a convention. A controlled gateway validates input, injects time, calls the real engine, and maps its decision record into compact tool results. WebMCP never recalculates a decision—it can only surface one. Guided replay remains available as a clearly labelled fallback and walkthrough in every browser. It invokes the identical descriptors and handlers, with per-invocation telemetry marking native versus replay so the two paths cannot be confused. Challenges I ran into A registration race surfaced by cross-agent testing. A native run in Codex's in-app browser completed the post-approval journey, while a separate ChatGPT browser-agent run stopped after the shopper clicked Approve. The problem was not the approval itself: the SDK deferred the phase transition, allowing apply_plan_repair to resolve before prepare_validated_cart had necessarily finished registering. The second agent therefore received a valid repair result but did not continue automatically. I reproduced the timing window with a controllable fak
video_title: RetailAgentOS — a WebMCP storefront that exposes only the next safe action
video_transcript_excerpt: Retailers are about to have customers who are not people. They're agents. Today those agents shop by scraping pages and guessing at stock, prices, and delivery promises no merchant ever agreed to. Retail Agent OS answers a single question deterministically. What can this retailer actually promise right now? We already had the engine. What we lacked was a way to make an agent respect it. That is what Web MCP changes. Merchant can stop being a polite advice a model can ignore and becomes a hard capability boundary inside the browser. The agent does not decide what it is allowed to do. The store does. The storefront registers its tools with the browser through Web MCP. Three to start. Capabilities, catalog search, and plan evaluation. Not search and buy. Search and plan. Checkout isn't among them. It is simply never registered. An agent cannot call a tool that does not exist. The agent reads the storefront capabilities, searches the catalog, and submits a plan for evaluation. Retail Agent OS refuses it. The inventory on those eggs is stale. So, no card gets billed on a promise the retailer can't keep. It does not simply fail though. The engine returns a substitute that merchant has already approved and registers two repair capabilities that did not exist a moment earlier. The agent's option changed because the decision changed. Applying the substitution requires a person, a real approval. Never inferred, never granted by the agent on the shopper's behalf. Once approved, the repair tools are withdrawn and cart preparation is registered. The engine re-evaluates everything from scratch. Price, inventory, delivery mode, and the shopper's budget before a cart exists at all. And the missions ends at a cart for review. Checkout was never on the table. A second storefront shows the same engine drawing a very different boundary. Custom merchandise has no valid fixed price, so no cart tool is offered at all. Only a quote request routed to the merchant review filled with customization and size information. The agent can't invent a number the merchant never set. And all of it is auditable. The tools retail agent always track against the tool the browser actually observed, plus a full registration and invocation log. And that's the bit. Retail policy that agents can't route around expressed as a life capability surface. Every retailer decides what an agent may do in their store, and the browser enforces it.

title: Skulora Outfitter
pitch: Outfit any mission across every store: a shared board where you and your agent plan together.
about_excerpt: Outfit any mission across every store: a shared board where you and your agent plan together. Like Comment Story Updates thumbnail board kit replan checkout architecture board codriving Inspiration Real shopping rarely happens one store at a time. "Outfit me for a 3-day desert backpacking trip, under $600, I already own a stove" is one job, but today it is eight product searches across as many stores, a spreadsheet to keep the budget honest, and a lot of tabs. Agents can help, yet the ones we have shop a single site per page and treat you as a spectator: you type, they act, and if you disagree with a pick you start over in chat. WebMCP's brief asks what people and agents can do together that was hard before. Our answer is a planning board both of them work on. The agent does the tedious part, searching every Shopify merchant and building a kit that fits the budget; the person does the part only they can do, locking the sleeping bag they trust, rejecting the shoes they hate, and the agent re-plans around those decisions instead of over them. Shopify merchants already expose public Storefront MCP endpoints, and Shopify's Global Catalog MCP searches across all of them, so the missing piece was not the data. It was a page that exposes the mission itself as tools an agent can use. What it does Skulora Outfitter is a shared board for shopping missions . Open https://outfitter.skulora.com in ChatGPT's desktop browser or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled and tell the agent what you need. Then: The agent plans the mission . create_mission parses the goal, budget, constraints and what you already own; plan_kit turns it into slots (pack, sleeping bag, pad, water, sun protection…) each with a reason and a share of the budget. It searches every store . search_products runs per slot, in parallel, over Shopify's Global Catalog MCP plus curated merchants' Storefront MCP, dedupes and re-ranks candidates for fit, and choose_candidate picks with a stated reason. The board shows a live budget meter across merchants. You co-drive on the board . lock a pick the agent must keep, reject one it must never retry, choose a candidate yourself, or change the budget. Every edit is queued and delivered to the agent as mission_delta inside its next tool result, so it re-plans around you without being told. It explains itself . explain_tradeoffs writes a grounded "why this, versus the alternatives" under every slot, using only candidates that are actually on the board. It hands off, it does not buy . prepare_checkout creates one real cart per merchant through Storefront MCP and the board shows one checkout link each. You complete the purchase; nothing is bought on your behalf. In the reference run the agent planned 8 slots in about 6 seconds, filled them from 6 merchants at $553 of a $600 budget, and produced real checkout links. In ChatGPT's desktop browser it discovered the tools, found the Stage B tools that appeared after the mission was created, ran every search in parallel and finished with 8 merchants at $554.51 of $600. The demo video is one unedited run each: ChatGPT fills the board at $373.17 across 7 merchants; a lock and a reject lead to a re-plan that keeps the locked pack and swaps the rejected tent, ending at $446.96 across 8 merchants with real checkout links. The four things the rules ask every description to answer, in their order: Fit: why this use case belongs on WebMCP. A mission is structured state with a small, well-defined set of operations. Exposing it as typed tools lets any agent complete the job faster and more reliably than guessing through a UI, and lets the page shape what an agent may do (plan, search, choose, explain, prepare) while the human keeps the decisions that matter. Better experience: what changes for the person. One sentence, "outfit me for a 3-day desert trip, $600, I own a stove", becomes a 9-slot kit searched across every merchant and chosen with reasons in 27 seconds, instead of eight store searches, a spreadsheet for the budget and a dozen tabs. The person never leaves the board and never re-explains: the agent sees each lock and rejection as first-class input, the budget is enforced across stores instead of per cart, and the finale is one checkout link per merchant with the reasoning next to it rather than a wall of chat. Together: what people and agents can now do as a team. Plan a multi-store purchase as a team, in one place, with the agent doing the breadth (every merchant, every slot) and the person doing the judgment (this one, not that one, this much), and each sees the other's moves immediately. Lock a pack and reject a tent, say "re-plan", and the agent keeps the pack, replaces only the tent and says why, because the edits reached it as data. How: the WebMCP implementation. The page registers nine typed tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , disclosed in three stages as the mission advances ( toolchange tells the agent about each new stage), with readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations and results sized for an agent's context. Every result carries mission_delta (the person's edits since that agent's last call) and next_suggested_tools , and every rule (locks, rejections, budget, an incomplete kit) is enforced on the server with errors that name the valid ids and the next tool, so agents that call out of order or in parallel recover on the next turn. The built-in agent drives the same tools through document.modelContext.executeTool , so Chrome's DevTools logs it like any external agent. Details below. How we built it Tool surface. One tool table ( src/lib/webmcp/tools.ts ) defines nine tools with JSON Schema inputs and compact outputs sized for agent context: Stage A get_mission , create_mission , set_budget ; Stage B plan_kit , search_products , choose_candidate , explain_tradeoffs ; Stage C prepare_checkout , get_checkout_status . Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint ; tools that return merchant content carry untrustedContentHint . Every result ends with mission_delta (the person's edits since that agent's last call) and next_suggested_tools . Registration. src/components/WebMCPTools.tsx calls document.modelContext.registerTool(...) for the tools of the current stage, one AbortController per tool. When the mission advances it registers only the tools new to that stage, leaving existing registrations (and any call in flight) untouched, and agents learn about the additions through toolchange . Chrome's DevTools WebMCP pane shows the list, the per-tool call counters and the invocation log. Progressive disclosure. Stage A is registered on load; Stage B appears once a mission exists; Stage C once every required slot has a pick. Within a mission a stage only ever advances, so a tool is never pulled out from under a call in flight. The agent only ever sees tools that make sense right now. Shared state. Missions live server-side (Next.js route handlers on Vercel, Upstash Redis). Because agents call tools in parallel, writes are compare-and-set with retry, and anything slow (planning, merchant search, LLM re-ranking) runs outside the mutation. The board polls and the human's edits are stamped with a cursor the agent's mission_delta is computed from. Merchants. Cross-merchant discovery uses Shopify's public Global Catalog MCP (with a self-hosted agent profile) and per-store Storefront MCP for details and carts; no store setup, no credentials. A planner and re-ranker run on a small OpenAI model with strict JSON schemas. Same tools, any browser. A built-in agent panel drives the same tool table through the OpenAI Responses API. Where the browser provides WebMCP it runs each call through document.modelContext.executeTool , so Chrome's DevTools logs the built-in agent's calls exactly like an external agent's; elsewhere it calls the tool's execute directly. It makes the page work in browsers without WebMCP and gives us a deterministic harness ( pnpm harness ), probe ( pnpm probe ) and co-driving check ( pnpm g3 ) whose outputs are the only source of the numbers we quote. Abuse limits. Agent steps, mission mutations and mission creation are rate-limited per IP (Upstash), with a kill switch for the judging window; pnpm probe --burst exercises the limit. Guardrails for careless agents. Every mutation is validated on the server and every error names the valid ids and the tool to call next; create_mission on a board with picks needs replace: true ; a re-plan keeps what the person locked or chose; carts are cleared the moment a pick changes and prepare_checkout refuses while a required slot is empty; merchant_domain is allowlisted before the server contacts any host; tool stages only ever advance within a mission. pnpm misuse drives all of it out of order through document.modelContext.executeTool in headless Chrome (36 checks). Challenges we ran into Agents call tools in parallel. ChatGPT fired every search_products at once and a read-modify-write race dropped candidates. Fix: compare-and-set writes in Redi
