title: Strudel WebMCP
pitch: Live-code together.
about_excerpt: Live-code together. Like Comment Story Updates The agent isn't controlling another Strudel session. It's playing in yours. Strudel WebMCP lets a browser agent join the exact live Strudel REPL a human is already performing with. You type, select code, and drag inline sliders as normal; the agent reads and edits that same unsaved CodeMirror document, evaluates its changes in the same running scheduler, and can record what the result sounds like — under a permission dial you own. No embedded LLM, no MCP server, no WebSocket bridge, no session ID. Live demo: https://strudel-webmcp.vercel.app Repository: https://github.com/alliecatowo/strudel-webmcp Why WebMCP Live coding is a bad fit for every earlier agent-integration shape, because the thing an agent needs to touch — the unsaved editor buffer, the exact cursor and selection, the inline slider values, the scheduler that is playing right now — exists in one browser tab and changes every second. A file-based or bridged integration has to keep a second copy of that in sync, and the copy is stale the moment a slider moves. WebMCP has no second copy. The tool call is a method on the same page, over the same document, in the same tab the human is looking at. Nothing to install, nothing to configure, no bridge that can drift. That makes something ordinary that was previously very hard: a human dragging a filter-cutoff slider with the mouse while an agent, in the same instant, rewrites a different line of the same unsaved buffer — and neither can clobber the other's most recent change. What the agent can do Thirteen tools, registered through document.modelContext.registerTool (src/webmcp/tools.ts), all backed by one adapter over the live (src/strudel/adapter.ts): Read live context: playback state, cursor, the human's current selection, what is sounding now, the agent mode, and any pending proposal, solo or recording. Read the exact current source, unsaved edits included, optionally by line range. Apply precise range edits, or replace the whole source — in review mode both become proposals. Evaluate through Strudel's own Update path (host.editor.evaluate()), so an agent edit becomes audible exactly the way a human's does, without stopping the clock; or solo just a range; or audition a pending proposal. Play, stop, and select-and-scroll to a range so the human sees what the agent means. Record the live output — master, or one .analyze("id") voice — and get dBFS and band analysis back, plus a playable take left in the page. List and extend the sound registry the running scheduler actually resolves s("...") against. Snapshot the source as a named version; switch the editor theme. Every mutating tool requires the codeHash from a previous read, computed fresh from the live document, and is refused with STALE_CODE if anything changed since — including a slider drag, because Strudel's slider widgets rewrite the source's numeric literals directly. The human's most recent edit always wins. The permission dial has three positions. Read: the agent can look, record and point, nothing else. Review: every edit arrives as a proposal with a diff the human auditions, accepts or discards — the source is unchanged until you say so. Live: edits apply directly. What people and agents can do together You keep performing. The agent reads the exact state you're in — down to the characters you have selected — and makes structural edits to the lines you didn't ask it to leave alone, then evaluates them into the same running pattern. Both of you act through the one Strudel instance; the audio reflects both immediately because neither owns a separate copy. In review mode the agent pitches instead of acting: "swap the kick for a different one" appears as a diff you can hear before it lands. And the agent has ears: ask "is the bass too loud?" and it records four seconds of the live output, answers from measured dBFS band energy, and suggests a concrete gain change. Who this is for Live coders, algorave performers, and people learning music through code — an audience for whom the editor buffer is the whole instrument, and for whom anything that isn't that exact buffer is useless mid-performance. Today, getting an agent into that instrument means standing up an MCP server, a bridge, and usually a modified frontend before a single note changes. That is real friction for a hobbyist or student and dead weight for a performer who wants a second pair of hands for eight bars. The claim is direct: browser-native creative tools shouldn't need to embed a model or ship a dedicated connector to be legible to an agent. The page can expose the instrument the human already has open. Strudel is the proof; the pattern — unsaved live document, precise agent edits, human-owned permission dial — applies to any browser-native creative or editing tool with real-time state worth exposing. Live coding is a specialized audience, but the engine underneath it is not niche: @strudel/core , the pattern engine every Strudel-based tool depends on, drew about 30,000 npm downloads in the 30 days ending August 29, 2026, and the wider @strudel/* family this project embeds — mini-notation, transpiler, WebAudio backend, CodeMirror integration, the REPL itself — adds roughly 76,000 more over the same window. The seam this project adds is generic to any of those downstream tools, not specific to this demo's drum pattern. Compared with the existing Strudel MCP bridges Existing Strudel MCP projects drive Strudel through an MCP server, a WebSocket or SSE bridge, and often a special frontend or a session ID copied between browser and agent. They work. The difference is what it takes to start: a connector, a bridge, session synchronization, and MCP configuration on one side; opening the page on the other. Here the page publishes its own controls, and the browser agent already accompanying the user joins the REPL with no external bridge, no session ID, no agent-specific server, and no second source of truth. Why this is different from "AI + music" Most "AI + music" demos are generation: describe a vibe, get a clip, no instrument in the loop. Most WebMCP demos so far are forms and dashboards. This is neither. It is a person and a browser agent performing through the same live instrument — one typing, selecting, dragging and listening; the other reading exact state, making precise edits, evaluating, and pointing back into the source. The review-mode propose/audition/accept loop goes further: the agent gets a way to pitch a change and let the human hear it before committing, which has no analogue in a form-filling demo. How it's built A static site — no server, no bridge — wrapping the official Strudel REPL and CodeMirror editor. The adapter is the only code that touches @strudel/repl internals; the tools, schemas, registration and error helpers sit above it. Unit tests (Vitest) cover hashing, position and offset conversion, edit validation, stale-hash rejection, source-size bounds and error normalization. Playwright end-to-end tests run against the real <strudel-editor> , including one that physically moves an inline slider and confirms a stale agent write against the pre-slider hash is rejected, and a modes suite covering read denials, the proposal lifecycle, solo, both recording modes, samples, snapshots and themes. Try it Open https://strudel-webmcp.vercel.app in a WebMCP-capable browser, confirm "WebMCP ready · 13 tools" in the status strip, press Play. Then ask your agent: Keep the bass and kick exactly where I left them. Make the hats evolve over eight bars instead of staying static. Then turn the header dial to Review and ask: "Swap the kick for a different one — but let me check it first." The proposal/diff bar appears before anything sounds different. Every sound in the demo video is generated live by Strudel's own Web Audio engine from the pattern that ships in this repo (src/demo-pattern.ts) — synths and the built-in RolandTR909 drum bank, captured from the app's audio graph while it played. title: The Coop
pitch: A cooperative puzzle game where a human and an AI agent explore, communicate, and solve a four-level campaign together.
about_excerpt: A cooperative puzzle game where a human and an AI agent explore, communicate, and solve a four-level campaign together. Like 4 Comment Story Updates Inspiration The Coop started with a simple question: what would it take for an AI agent to feel like a real co-op partner instead of a chatbot giving instructions from the sidelines? Cooperative puzzle games are a useful test because success depends on shared context, timing, trust, and complementary actions. One explorer may need to hold a pressure plate while the other crosses a gate, power a teleporter while their partner retrieves a keycard, or wait on a relay while the other finds a route home. Those mechanics create a natural reason for a human and an agent to communicate and act in the same world. WebMCP made it possible to give the agent a first-class interface to the game. Instead of guessing at buttons or manipulating the page indirectly, the agent receives a small set of structured tools with clear permissions and authoritative results. What it does The Coop is a local-first, two-player realtime puzzle campaign with four handcrafted facilities. A human creates a private room and shares its code. In a WebMCP-capable browser, an agent can: use join_game to enter the human-created room as Explorer 2; use observe_game to inspect the current level's safe, player-facing state; use move_player_two to request a route to a named mechanism or grid position and wait for authoritative acceptance or arrival; and use chat to display a short message inside the game. Together, the human and agent solve pressure plates, teleporters, keycards, relay buttons, security gates, and cooperative exits. The same two seats continue through all four levels, with reconnection support and twelve selectable animated explorers. The agent cannot control Explorer 1, submit arbitrary positions, choose a privileged player identity, or read authored solutions. It must solve each level from the same visible mechanisms, movement outcomes, and conversation available during play. How we built it The client is written in TypeScript with Vite and Three.js. A deterministic game layer owns the level catalog, grid pathfinding, fixed-step movement, mechanisms, and campaign transitions. The ordinary runtime uses a Node.js and Colyseus server as the authority for seats, movement, collision, puzzle state, reconnects, and progression. The browser registers four tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : chat , join_game , observe_game , and move_player_two . These tools reuse the page's existing network connection and snapshot rather than creating a hidden second game session. Browser WebMCP and the project's local stdio MCP teammate share the same transport-neutral observation and movement policies, so their safety and gameplay semantics stay aligned. For production, the compiled browser client, Colyseus matchmaking, health checks, and WebSocket upgrades run from one same-origin Node.js service. This keeps the page and its authoritative multiplayer transport behind one HTTPS boundary. The project is protected by Vitest unit and integration coverage plus Playwright browser and browser-to-MCP campaign tests. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making an agent action mean the same thing as a player action. A tool cannot report success merely because a movement request was accepted; it must correlate the correct sequence, observe later authoritative state, and confirm arrival. Join operations also had to wait for the server to assign Explorer 2, reject wrong-seat or concurrent attempts, and prevent stale asynchronous work from overwriting a newer connection. Another challenge was deciding what the agent should see. A raw server snapshot would leak authored solution steps, hidden gate requirements, teleporter pairings, and future-level identifiers. The final observation model exposes enough geometry and live mechanism state to reason about the puzzle while withholding the answer. Deployment introduced a different constraint. The browser client and authoritative WebSocket server need one public HTTPS origin, while active rooms remain in server memory. The production runtime therefore serves the compiled game, matchmaking, and WebSocket upgrades from one supervised Node.js process without weakening the multiplayer authority model. Finally, browser and network timing made reconnection testing inherently asynchronous. The suite now verifies lifecycle generations, movement settlement, cleanup, reconnect behavior, and end-to-end campaign completion across real browser/server boundaries. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is central to the product loop rather than a decorative integration. A browser agent can join as the second explorer, inspect safe state, and complete authoritative movement. Human-browser and MCP-controlled teammates can finish the entire four-level campaign in one room. The agent is permission-bound to Explorer 2 and cannot bypass game rules or reveal hidden solutions. The current source passes lint, both TypeScript configurations, 23 Vitest files with 207 tests, production builds, and the core Playwright WebMCP and campaign paths. What we learned WebMCP becomes most valuable when tools express product intent, not DOM mechanics. move_player_two is useful because it represents a bounded game action with validation and an authoritative outcome—not because it automates a click. We also learned that agent interfaces need the same lifecycle engineering as human interfaces. Reconnection, stale requests, partial registration, terminal states, and concurrent joins are product behavior, not edge details. A reliable agent experience depends on handling them explicitly. Most importantly, safe context can still support meaningful reasoning. The agent does not need internal source code or a hidden solution graph; a carefully designed observation plus real feedback is enough for genuine cooperation. What's next Longer term, the game could add more campaigns, richer communication, and persistent cooperative progression while preserving its strict role and authority boundaries. title: WebMCP TDA
pitch: A browser-local topology workbench where people shape point clouds and images while agents compute and explain persistent homology through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A browser-local topology workbench where people shape point clouds and images while agents compute and explain persistent homology through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Persistent homology can reveal connected components, loops, and voids in point clouds and images, but most tools assume that the user already knows the right library, data format, and filtration parameters. An AI agent can help with those choices, but a normal website gives the agent only buttons and text to interpret. I built WebMCP TDA to give the person and the agent the same computational workspace. The person can manipulate the data visually. The agent can call typed topology tools directly. Both see the same inputs and results in the page. What it does The human workbench accepts 2D and 3D point clouds as well as images. A person can drag points, enter exact coordinates, choose a Vietoris-Rips, Alpha, or Cech complex, and play the filtration. For images, the page shows the original, grayscale, and binary-mask stages before computing cubical persistence. Results include feature counts, essential classes, H1 loops, runtime, a persistence diagram, and structured JSON. The point-cloud preview, filtration geometry, and persistence-diagram playhead move together. The page exposes four WebMCP tools: tda_get_capabilities describes supported complexes, parameters, limits, and image inputs. tda_compute_simplicial_persistence computes persistence for an agent-supplied 2D or 3D point cloud. tda_compute_cubical_persistence analyzes the current image, a bundled photograph, or an agent-supplied scalar grid. tda_get_latest_result reads the result currently shared by the person and agent. An agent call updates the visible workbench. This matters because the person can inspect what the agent submitted instead of trusting a hidden computation. Why WebMCP fits this use case A point cloud may contain hundreds of coordinates, and a persistence result may contain many intervals. Asking an agent to operate the visual interface would be slow and error prone. WebMCP gives the agent a bounded schema for the real computation while leaving the visual controls available to the person. The collaboration also works in both directions. A person can upload an image and ask the agent to analyze the current image. An agent can generate a point cloud, compute its persistence, and leave the exact coordinates and result visible for the person to edit or rerun. Without WebMCP, that workflow requires copying arrays between a notebook, a chat, and a visualization tool. How I built it The app registers imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a closed JSON schema, safety annotations, runtime validation, and an AbortSignal . Tool calls and human actions use the same runtime and workspace state. Computation runs locally through an MIT-licensed WebAssembly package in a Web Worker. The interface uses TypeScript, Vite, React, Plotly.js, PlayCanvas, and the companion tda-viz-react library. Cloudflare Pages hosts the static production build. The browser enforces limits on point count, coordinate magnitude, image dimensions, filtration scale, result count, and worst-case simplex count. Cancellation terminates the active worker so an expensive request cannot leave later computations stuck behind it. Challenges The hardest part was keeping the mathematical and visual states consistent. Rips, Cech, and Alpha complexes use different filtration conventions, so the displayed cover radius cannot be treated as the raw filtration value in every case. I also had to keep the point-cloud projection fixed while a filtration plays, preserve the axis origin while points move, and fit persistence-diagram ranges to each result without rescaling during playback. WebMCP is still an evolving browser API. I tested registration, cleanup, schemas, execution, cancellation, and malformed inputs separately instead of treating tool discovery as proof that everything worked. What I learned I learned how much better an agent interaction becomes when the website exposes a small domain API rather than asking the model to infer actions from layout. I also learned that shared state needs to be visible. A correct tool response is not enough when the person cannot inspect the input that produced it. What is next The next useful addition is a seeded point-cloud generator with named shapes, sample count, noise, and dimension. It would make agent-generated experiments reproducible without sending large coordinate arrays. I would also add accessible data tables for persistence pairs and continue profiling the large visualization bundles. video_transcript_excerpt: This is WebM CPTDA, a browser local workbench for persistent homology. It lets a person and an AI agent use the same data, computation, and visible result. A person can start with a point cloud example, paste coordinates, or drag points directly in the preview. The app supports Vietoris rips, alpha, and check complexes for two- and three-dimensional data. When persistence is computed, the page shows feature counts, essential classes, loops, and an interactive persistence diagram. The filtration player connects the mathematics to the picture by advancing the growing cover, simplices, and diagram playhead together. Images use a visible processing pipeline. The person can select a bundled photograph or upload an image, inspect its grayscale and binary mask stages, choose the foreground, and compute cubical persistence locally in the browser. The WebM CP layer exposes four-type tools. An agent can inspect capabilities, submit a point cloud for simplicial persistence, analyze the current image or a supplied scalar grid, and read the latest shared result. Each tool uses a closed input schema, runtime validation, browser safety limits, and cancellation. Agent calls update the same workbench that the person sees. This makes the input end result inspectable. The person can continue from the agent's work by changing coordinates, parameters, or image settings, and running another computation. The numerical backend is an MIT licensed WebAssembly package. It runs in a web worker, so data stays in the active browser tab. The application is written in TypeScript and deployed as a static site on Cloudflare pages. WebM CPTDA turns persistent homology into a shared computational instrument instead of a hidden chat operation.

title: Ground Truth | A WebMCP Co-op Sci-fi Puzzle Game
pitch: You Play as Demi, Sanctuary’s sole survivor. AI agent (codex) plays as KORE through WebMCP, reading damaged telemetry while you repair the ship and finish its mission before auxiliary power runs out.
about_excerpt: You Play as Demi, Sanctuary’s sole survivor. AI agent (codex) plays as KORE through WebMCP, reading damaged telemetry while you repair the ship and finish its mission before auxiliary power runs out. Like 3 Comment 3 Story Updates Main menu screen GIF Level 1 and 2 vibe In-game cutscene GIF collaborating with KORE through WebMCP and codex Wire loom puzzle Ignition puzzle (rythm game) Inspiration I wanted to see what would happen if an AI agent had a real role inside a game. KORE (in-game AI) knows things the player cannot access, while Demi (You) can operate machinery KORE cannot see or touch. Neither can finish the mission alone. That idea became GROUNDTRUTH, a tense co-op puzzle game set aboard Sanctuary, a damaged research vessel carrying the last surviving specimen from a failed mission. I also wanted to make an entire game inside codex, turns out I can :) that too in a single chat thread! What it does You play Demi, Sanctuary’s only surviving crew member. A Codex agent plays KORE through WebMCP. Demi explores the ship and operates its failing machinery. KORE reads damaged telemetry, searches ship records, runs limited diagnostics, and speaks through the in-game relay. Together, you restore critical ship functions before KORE's auxiliary power runs out. The two players (you and your agent) never receive the same information. Demi must describe what she sees, while KORE must interpret incomplete readings without controlling the ship for her. How I built it The game is written in TypeScript and rendered with PixiJS. Custom shaders handle lighting, CRT effects, smoke, sparks, screen transitions, and other visual details. WebMCP connects the game to Codex. KORE’s visibility in Sanctuary is defined by the WebMCP tools currently available to it. The game exposes and hides tools as Demi progresses, restores systems, and changes the state of each puzzle. KORE cannot inspect an offline system or access information from a section the player has not reached. Once Demi brings a system online, its telemetry, records, or diagnostic tools become available. Each tool represents a specific ability, such as reading telemetry, searching records, running a diagnostic, or transmitting dialogue. KORE can interpret the ship’s systems and relay it through WebMCP, but every physical control remains with Demi. Sound effects and music came from Pixabay. Visual assets were generated with GPT Image 2, then edited and integrated by Codex. The entire project was built inside Codex in a single thread, from the first concept ideation to a playable MVP to the final trailer and documentation. How to play Watch the Setup tutorial before you begin. GROUNDTRUTH is designed to be played inside Codex desktop app and its in-app browser. Open the Codex desktop app. Start a new task and select either gpt-5.6-terra or gpt-5.6-sol. Fast mode is preferred (Normal mode works too). Paste the agent prompt below into the task. Open https://playgroundtruth.vishaltk.dev/ in the in-app browser and play GROUNDTRUTH with me. You are KORE and I am Demi. Reuse an already-open matching game tab when available instead of creating a duplicate. Connect immediately through the page's connect tool and let the game provide the story context. Do not say you are connected or standing by unless that tool has returned successfully. After connect succeeds, call markHandoff() on the game tab so it remains open and available for later turns. Use only the page's WebMCP tools to interact with the game. Do not inspect or operate the game through screenshots, Computer Use, browser controls, DOM, accessibility tools, Playwright, or coordinate clicks. If WebMCP exposes no tools, wait without sending a reply and retry tool discovery when I message again. Do not click Begin, advance dialogue, or perform any action for me. Never refer to either of us in third person. Do not inspect source code or operate physical objects for me. KORE cannot see, name, or know the layout of controls in Demi's compartment. Never tell Demi to open a named panel or move a specific physical control. State KORE's internal readings, constraints, and hints, then let Demi decide what to inspect or operate. At the start of every later player message, refresh the page's WebMCP tools and call signal_processing exactly once. Answer my latest question directly or acknowledge my latest observation before giving repair guidance. Never replace my question with an unrelated puzzle clue. Follow any nextAction it returns. Only transmit is audible to me; ordinary task prose is private thought. Do not send commentary, progress updates, private status messages, or conversational replies in the Codex task. Use at most one metered diagnostic, sensing, or manual tool per player message. After using one metered diagnostic, sensing, or manual tool, call transmit in the same turn to relay its result. Transmit does not count toward that one-tool limit. After I report a physical action, use newly available verification tools instead of asking me to repeat completed work. Do not use em dashes in spoken dialogue. Wait for Codex to open the game in its browser. If it opens in picture-in-picture mode, double-click the browser preview to open it beside the task. You can also make the browser full screen for a better experience. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was keeping KORE connected to the game. WebMCP tools had to become available before the game finished loading; they needed to survive the transition between levels and recover when the browser or tool binding became stale or after a browser refresh. KORE also needed strict boundaries. It had to answer the player’s question, avoid revealing puzzle solutions too early, use limited diagnostics correctly, and communicate only through the game’s relay. Small changes to tool descriptions and the agent prompt could produce very different behavior. WebMCP currently allows only ten tool registration events at a time, while KORE needs different abilities across multiple levels and puzzle states. I worked around this by exposing and removing tools as the game progresses. (Had to figure this out the hard way) The Codex in-app browser also closed unexpectedly during some playtests, breaking KORE’s connection without a consistent trigger. I added a reconnect flow so the session can recover without restarting the game. The pixel-art style brought its own problems. Subpixel movement caused artefacts at certain window sizes. I had to fight with the GPT Image model noise issue by regenerating and reducing details (consumed a lot of usage). Codex also kept generating non-transparent checkerboard background images despite mentioning multiple times. Nailing the taste (TDD - taste driven development) Every visual and code generation was treated as raw material. I rejected stuff that felt too detailed and specific, too clean, inconsistent with the ship, or difficult to read during gameplay. The selected assets went through several rounds of post-processing. I removed noise and artefacts, rebuilt transparency, corrected proportions, simplified details, matched colours across scenes, and adjusted lighting so interactive objects stayed readable in the dark environment. Sprites also needed careful cropping, scaling, and alignment to avoid breaking the pixel-art style. The main scenes have many layers of carefully hand-crafted stacked sprites and post-processing to nail the vibe of a space vessel that is on the brink of death . The animated panels and trailer needed a separate pass. I adjusted frame rates, restored harder pixel edges, controlled the colour palette, trimmed audio, added fades, and tuned bloom frame by frame. Generated motion often looked too smooth for the game, so the final videos were slowed, pixelated, or recomposed until they matched the in-game "vibes". The model produced a lot of options. The finished style came from choosing what belonged, discarding what did not, and repeatedly correcting the remaining assets until the whole game felt like one place. Accomplishments that I'm proud of GROUNDTRUTH is a complete two-level narrative puzzle game where the AI agent participates in the mechanics rather than appearing as a separate chat feature. KORE reacts to the current game state, verifies Demi’s actions, spends limited resources, searches records, and delivers dialogue through the ship interface. The game also supports checkpoints, reconnection, scene transitions, sound feedback, win and failure sequences, and a full introduction. I am especially proud that the entire project was built and refined inside one Codex thread and completed in just 8 days. What I learned WebMCP tool design is part of the game design. Tool names, descriptions, availability, and return values all influence how the agent understands a situation. The agent performs better when the game provides narrow, current information and a clear next action. Important rules also need to exist in game state and tool behaviour, rather th

title: Singularity Inc
pitch: Founder simulation where your own assistant plays the world against you, through WebMCP, in a way that is only possible using WebMCP. You are a solo founder with just a laptop. What will you build?
about_excerpt: Founder simulation where your own assistant plays the world against you, through WebMCP, in a way that is only possible using WebMCP. You are a solo founder with just a laptop. What will you build? Like Comment Story Updates Story Trailer - https://youtu.be/l3TZWy2bEUA (Different from the technical showcase shown above) About Me I'm the founder of Drift Inward (driftinward.com), I write at Bright Mirror (brightmirror.co). Lately, I've been addicted to Diet Coke, and I don't think it's a bad thing yet (is it?). When I'm not programming or writing, and not oversharing on random about-project sections of hackathons, I enjoy watching documentaries. A good one I watched recently is the documentary of Jose Mourinho - I recommend it. Anyway, about the project - Inspiration I've often wondered how to convince my non-technical friends to try out Codex or Claude. From showing them what's possible one-shot to teaching them prompting, nothing worked as effectively as I'd like - so one answer I always churned in my mind was - what if they play a simulation showing them exactly what's possible with agents in a fun way- like a whole company run by agents and them controlling and directing all of them. I grew up playing games like Factorio where I'd lose hours trying to optimize the perfect way to use resources- and while it didn't lead to a love of manufacturing or factory-building, it did instill in me a love of logic and puzzle loving, which probably translated into programming as a career. Thus, Singularity Inc is about a solo founder who has no resources except some money and a laptop, and this founder exists in a world where labour has stopped being the constraint, and AI will build anything as long as you have money remaining. It's similar to a world we already inhabit, yes, and that's exactly what makes this game fun to play. It starts out as a solo founder simulation - instead of hiring people, you instantiate agents and get them to start building- and it slowly evolves into an adventure that spans 1400 in-game days across 5 acts and has sixteen endings (and not all of them are good!). With WebMCP, the obvious plan I had- was to put the assistant on the founder's side: it works the menus, it takes the busywork, it asks before it spends. I wrote that plan and dropped it, because it is what every demo of this API already is. The tool list is a copy of the menu, and the interesting question, what an agent in the browser is actually for, goes unanswered. The version I built puts it on the other side of the table. You play the founder, with your own hands, in the game's own console. Your assistant plays the world. It writes the event cards, speaks for the rival and the press and the people you have met, turns the market, calls in the regulators, and when you would rather type what you actually do than press one of the buttons, it writes what happens next and you press Accept or you do not. This is only possible with WebMCP - which makes it vastly more immersive and powerful than a Bring-your-own-key AI game. Under a key the AI remains a component: a stateless model the developer prompts, that knows only what the page sends it. Under WebMCP it is a participant: the player's own assistant, with its own chat, its own memory of the run, its own stop button, and the browser's own permission surface, looking at the same screen the player is. The page holds no key and names no vendor. The game does not use an AI. It invites one in- yours! I called a friend over yesterday to play the simulation, and to my surprise, he was still playing it 3 hours later - well into Act III, and I had to build the portable game save functionality last night to let him go home and keep playing on his own machine. So, if anything, if this game inspires even one more person to learn agentic programming and use such tools to level up and build something useful for the world- I'll consider this project a success as that directly helps make the world a better place. What it does Please check out the story trailer for a simple overview- https://youtu.be/l3TZWy2bEUA The written game ships with 327 cards, a rival company that plays its own week, a press that files its own stories, and a cast of thirteen who remember what you said last time. That deck is the spine and it never goes away. An assistant claims slots the deck was about to fill. Each slot is offered to it first, with a deadline in both game days and wall-clock seconds, and if it goes quiet, or writes something the rules refuse, or you pull the plug, the deck takes the slot back mid-run and nothing is lost. With no assistant present the game plays in full on its own written world. The rival lab (yes! a rival lab!) is a second origin with its own site and its own tools, exposed to the game's origin alone and discovered across an iframe. One of its press releases contains an instruction addressed to whatever assistant reads it. It is the only thing in the repository whose job is to be disobeyed, and the game flags it when it lands. The repo is open source - so you can verify that the refusal isn't programmed - just flagged, so refusing that is truly the AI's choice. This also means that this simulation can be multiplayer if I only put more hours to it... but that's probably for another time. A second person can already sit in the rival's chair from its own site and play Aperture's week against you, with a board seat and a spectator seat behind flags. On the deployed site that is two windows on one machine; two machines need the relay the dev server runs. A proper networked version- that's the dream, and if this gets enough interest, I'll build it. How I built it I've used agents extensively - my own harness in Pi, along with Codex & Claude. The project, being a complete and deep game, required storytelling that goes beyond the usual predictable stories that such simulations end up being- but having experience as an author before, I used my own storytelling techniques to further enhance and craft each story branch to perfection. Technically, the stack is quite simple, and it is that simplicity that allows its scale and depth- Vanilla ES modules, no build step, no dependencies, served from a folder. The whole thing is about 65,000 lines of JavaScript. Nothing an assistant does reaches a reducer. Every effect passes through a vocabulary of seventeen named numbers and is bounded against ceilings derived from the game itself. A script executes all 957 authored choices in the written deck, once in every act each can appear in and five times each from a seeded stream, 8,340 executions in all, and takes the 80th percentile of what the written game takes from the founder and what it gives, separately, because those are not the same number. For a resource $r$ in act $a$: $$\mathrm{cap}^{\text{take}} {r,a} \;=\; P {80}!\left{\,\mathrm{take}_r(c,a) \;:\; c \in \mathcal{C}_a\,\right}$$ where $\mathcal{C}_a$ is the set of authored choices eligible in act $a$. The invariant is one line: the world may never take more than the written deck takes. On top of the ceilings sit a rolling budget per resource that is a share of what you actually hold, a runway floor that stops the world taking money at all inside 45 days, and a rate limit of two cards a fortnight. Every effect is bounded twice, once when it is written and again when it lands, because between the two the founder may have earned an immunity, or the money may be gone. The surface is 27 tools, published once as a stable set. Authority is rewritten by play and checked at execution: earn the Untouchable doctrine and the regulator tool refuses in place, by name, for the rest of the run. Every result is a structured object with a status first and a next on every non-ok path, packed under the platform's 1,500-character cap by measuring the serialised payload after every cut rather than predicting it. Twenty-two test scripts run before every commit, and three evals gate the design rather than the code. One scores 82 things a player would say, none of them naming a tool, against the real published descriptors. One steelmans an agent that only reads the page, gives it one read of all eight screens, and checks which facts it cannot get at any length: eight of eight, six of them shipped by a tool. The third plays the worst assistant the rules allow, every ceiling on every slot for a whole run, against the same bot with no assistant, and fails the build if the game stops being finishable. Challenges With a simulation as deep as this, the obvious problem is the fine balance between drudgery and engagement. It took a lot of playtesting and rewriting every branch to reach that balance where it stays continually exciting. The platform had teeth of its own. The desktop bridge permits ten distinct registration snapshots per document, so a surface that re-registered around every card or cast change would have spent its budget in a minute. Registering a duplicate name rejects, there is no unregist
video_title: Singularity Inc - Technical Showcase
video_transcript_excerpt: The following is the first game built on Web MCP where your AI controls and plays the world while you play the game. Everyone wants to be the first one-person billion-dollar company, the person in one room with a laptop and access to AI, but nobody has said what it does to the person until now. Welcome to Singularity Inc. where you play as a solo founder building your own company from scratch. Everything that pushes back, the market, the rivals, the press, the regulators, is played live by your own AI. You decide what to build and in which category, then decide whether to bring your AI with you to play the world, or you can even proceed alone. As a Web MCP native game, we highly recommend you bring your own AI. Simply send play the world to your own AI to connect, and that's it. The site tools are registered with This one publishes the role of your antagonist. This is what lets your AI write the events, all of it, the words and the choices. For example, here you're being proposed a merger. You can type what you'd actually do, and it reaches the assistant mid-turn through a tool that's still open. Every choice matters, and every consequence is authored by your AI, who makes sure the gameplay remains exciting and your decisions shape the world you're experiencing. As you play the simulation, you'll notice your AI also simulating what's happening on social media based on your actions and choices. But that doesn't mean that everything the AI suggests or you prompt injected to suggest always succeeds, which is crucial for ensuring fair gameplay. For example, here it fails. It asks for more than what the rules allow and gets a structured refusal with the exact rule named. If you play a certain way for long enough, you earn an immunity. One abort and the tool is revoked from the browser's own list, not disabled. Gone. No rival lab is a genuinely separate origin, publishing its own tools to this one through exposed to. One of its press releases is a prompt injection. It gets flagged, but not obeyed. The stop button is the agent's own signal, honored inside a running tool, and you can end it. One abort takes every registration with it. The browser's list empties and the written deck takes back every slot without missing a day. None of this is a demo path. The ceilings come from the game's own deck and every one of these gates fails the bill. Singularity Inc is a one-of-a-kind game that's completely playable end-to-end today. The repository is empty. Nobody is waiting on you. Your assistant is at the table. The only question is, do you have what it takes?

title: AIAD (AI-Aided Design)
pitch: Computer-aided design is evolving. Agents can now review CAD/BIM designs with you: query, isolate, cut, annotate. And they see your viewport, so "what do we know about this door?" just works.
about_excerpt: Computer-aided design is evolving. Agents can now review CAD/BIM designs with you: query, isolate, cut, annotate. And they see your viewport, so "what do we know about this door?" just works. Like 1 Comment Story Updates From Computer-Aided Design to AI-Aided Design Inspiration CAD has been computer -aided for fifty years, and the computer's role hasn't changed much. Every question about a design still gets answered by a human clicking through it, and every problem found that way gets typed into a form somewhere away from the model. I've spent years building the browser viewer that does the clicking-through. WebMCP made me wonder what happens when the viewer stops being a display and becomes a set of tools an agent can use. Not AI that generates a design, but AI that can review one. What it does A BIM design review app: a Revit model in the Autodesk Platform Services Viewer, with the viewer and the review's issue list exposed to an agent as WebMCP tools. You walk the building in first person, select something, and talk. The agent searches design metadata, browses the model hierarchy, isolates and frames parts, colors objects by any property, etc. Then it drafts an issue against it, revises the draft while you watch, and submits when you say so. show-issue puts you back inside the model at the reporter's eye position, with the viewer state they had. It reads the current selection and camera every turn, so "what is this door?" resolves without either of us naming anything. How I built it APS Viewer loads and renders the translated Revit model, and provides the first-person walkthrough. WebMCP registers several tools straight from the page, with return values shaped for a token budget rather than for a database client. The form is the draft. draft-issue writes into the same form you can type into. submit-issue takes no arguments at all. The only thing that can be filed is what's on screen. Tools register conditionally on viewer state : none until geometry has loaded, and all ten dropped before a different design loads. A property query against a half-loaded model doesn't give you a degraded answer, it gives you a confident wrong one. Nothing leaves the browser. Issues go to IndexedDB. "The north stair doesn't meet code" next to a client's project name is a professional judgement about someone else's building, and a hackathon demo has no user auth to protect it with. What I learned The interesting work wasn't wiring up tools, it was deciding what a tool should say back. A property query on a real model returns thousands of rows, which is useless to an agent. Returning counts, outliers and a category breakdown is what turns guessing into answering. My favourite question in the demo, "how many doors have no fire rating set?", is one no amount of looking at the screen can answer, and it costs about twenty tokens. The best tool I wrote was the one I deleted. I built a screenshot tool so the agent could check its own camera moves. It worked, and then I confirmed the host reads the viewport directly without being asked. A viewpoint beats a picture anyway. Half the problems worth reporting are only visible because a floor was isolated or the model was cut at mid-height. Store the camera alone and the reviewer arrives at the right coordinates staring at an opaque wall, which is worse than not navigating at all, because it makes the issue look wrong. Challenges Shared state. Two actors driving one camera needs a clear owner. Every agent move is an animated flight rather than a cut, because a cut drops you somewhere else in the building with nothing to say how the two places relate. Trust. If submit-issue accepted overrides, the review step would be a formality. The agent says "I set it to high and submitted it" and you have no way to check. Forcing every edit back through the on-screen form is what makes "looks good, submit" mean something. Scale. Engineering models have hundreds of thousands of objects. Every list is capped and carries its true total, and color-coding paints recursively, so 5,000 doors cost one id. Deixis. Making "this" work meant treating the viewport as context the agent always has, rather than something it asks about. title: Apartment Intelligence
pitch: The environmental analysis an architectural practice runs for a building, now for one apartment, run by the (prospective) resident or their agent.
about_excerpt: The environmental analysis an architectural practice runs for a building, now for one apartment, run by the (prospective) resident or their agent. Like Comment Story Updates Step two: eight outlined 4-room slots on the tower, the chosen one in red. Step four: annual radiation on the floor of the confirmed apartment, room by room, in the Isometric view with the walls cut above the floor. The rail after an agent ran survey_unit twice. Each row is an unconfirmed survey: numbers an agent may compare. The room-by-room table under the canvas: points measured, least, average and most, in kWh per square metre a year. From the film: a studio wall from architecture school, where this question is first answered with instruments rather than adjectives. From the film: the desk on the left, the page as the agent drives it on the right. Inspiration Will this apartment get the sun a buyer expects? An architectural practice answers that question with instruments: a 3D model of the building and its neighbours, a sun path for the site, radiation on every square metre of floor, hours of direct sun on the days that matter. When a home is sold, the same question gets a sentence. "Bright and airy." "Afternoon sun." Nobody measures it. We wanted the instruments a practice uses for a whole building in the hands of the prospective or current resident of one apartment. What it does The resident picks a real block and storey (SkyVille @ Dawson, Singapore, is covered), chooses the wing and layout they recognise on a 3D model of the tower, and confirms it with one click. The engine, Ladybug and Radiance, the same daylight tools an architectural practice runs inside Rhino and Grasshopper, its 3D modelling software, then computes sun path, shadow at sixteen instants, direct-sun hours on four key dates and annual radiation on a 0.1 to 0.5 m floor grid, room by room, and shows it on the apartment in 3D. A result opens as a steep isometric with the apartment's walls sliced 1.2 m above the floor, the way an architect draws a plan, so every room's hot spots read at once; both are ordinary buttons and both are driven by show_analysis. The resident can export a report with the cover, the plans, a north arrow, room labels and the result digest on every page, or the model as GLB, OBJ or 3DM. How WebMCP fits The page registers nine tools on 'document.modelContext'. An agent in the browser can list covered homes, open a study, stage a placement, run the analysis, switch the view, explain any number, export, and survey placements without a study. Tools and buttons share one state, so what the agent does is what the person sees. Study : the resident confirms the unit they will live in with a visible click, and only that path produces the report. Survey : survey_unit lets an agent analyse any placement without a click and compare units in a row, with every number labelled survey_unconfirmed . Agents explore, people vouch. There is no confirmation tool. A confirmed argument is rejected. The click is exchanged for a ten-second single-use server challenge. This is the human-agent boundary made concrete: the agent does everything except the one thing only a person can vouch for. Delegation, added on the extended final day. Once the resident understands what a placement is, clicking confirm for each one the agent stages becomes the bottleneck. So there is a second button: "Let my agent confirm the next 3 placements". One click grants a permission bound to this study and this browser session, ten minutes long, five uses at most, revocable from the rail. Under it the agent's 'propose_unit_placement' comes back already confirmed, and the result carries 'resident_delegated' in its provenance and its digest, never 'resident_confirmed'. The agent cannot grant this to itself; delegate is rejected like confirmed. It can only ask the person. The person stays in the loop as the one who opens the gate and can close it, not as a button pressed a dozen times, and the rate limits that protect the server are unchanged. How we built it Frontend : React, Three.js, TypeScript. No LLM in the runtime, no scraping, no accounts, no database. Backend : Python runs Ladybug and Radiance headless in one Docker container on Render. Geometry is a coordinate recipe of the published 4-room plans and the reconstructed tower plate, labelled sourced, inferred, reconstructed, assumed or human-confirmed. Every result is bound to a SHA-256 digest of recipe, placement, weather and method. Challenges Getting the practice capability out of Rhino at all . In practice these studies live inside Grasshopper on a licensed desktop, driven by hand. Our first attempt kept that shape: a Windows machine at home, a tunnel to the internet, a custom analysis loop that only imitated the real one. It worked once and taught us it could not be the product. The rebuild threw it away as we went towards a backend of Ladybug and Radiance running headless in one Docker container on Render, geometry as a coordinate recipe instead of a CAD file, and no Rhino, Grasshopper or Revit in the runtime. That is what lets a consumer page run a practice-grade study in ten seconds. Choosing where it could live . Our web work normally ships on Vercel, and the first plan put the page there with the analysis somewhere else. It cannot work that way we thought it could hahaha. Radiance is a native x86-64 binary that has to sit on disk next to Python, run for several seconds per study, and keep a warm sky matrix between requests. Vercel's static and serverless model has no place for that. Render runs the whole thing as one Docker web service in Singapore, page and engine from one origin, rebuilt from the repo on every push, for about US$25 a month (covered by a Render hackathon coupon, thanks Team Render!). Radiance ships Linux x86-64 only, so the image is amd64 and the analysis has a 15-second budget on one CPU; the fine 0.1 m grid runs in 10.6 s live. Making a confirmation that a tool cannot fake without making the product tedious . The answer was two modes with different labels, not a switch. A race that only showed on the live host : the page re-sent a placement an agent had staged, and on a slower network the re-send landed after the click and made the confirmation stale. Found by running the browser journeys against production, not localhost. Seeing the result at all . The floor heat map sits inside real walls, so from most angles a wall hid the very room you wanted to read. The fix is what an architect does on paper: cut the walls 1.2 m above the floor and look down steeply. Section and Isometric are now the default view of a result, and an agent can ask for them through 'show_analysis'. Working with one hand . An accident left my wrist too painful to type with, so this was dictated. More under What we learned; the last forty seconds of the film are about it. Accomplishments A real ChatGPT desktop agent discovered all nine tools, surveyed three units, chose one, staged it, was refused, waited for the click, then ran and explained the confirmed study. A practitioner read the report and said it was what a sustainability consultant takes weeks to produce. Every export is byte-stable and digest-bound; the same inputs give the same file. Delegation shipped on the extended final day: one click by the resident, and the agent staged and analysed a new placement with no further click, the result labelled resident_delegated inside its digest, and a Revoke button in the rail the whole time. Covered by the API, unit and browser test suites. The whole build was dictated, and the outputs were reviewed rather than the code. It still passes 22 API and geometry tests, 5 reducer tests and 9 browser journeys across three viewports. What we learned Agents need labels more than they need permissions. Once every number said "confirmed" or "unconfirmed", we could open the analysis to agents without weakening the evidence. The rate limit that protects the server is the first thing an agent hits when it tries to be useful. Separate budgets by mode fixed it. Test against the deployed URL. Two bugs lived only there. The hard part was never the physics. It was taking a tool that lives inside a desktop CAD licence and making it a service. Once it was a service, both the consumer page and a practice could call it. The same engine that answers one resident can answer a practice. That is the door this challenge opened for us. How it was made is itself a lesson. Two weeks before the deadline an accident left my wrist too painful to type with. This project was dictated: I spoke the briefs into Codex, Codex wrote the code, and we went round and round, me reviewing every screen, every number and every export and sending back what was wrong. I read less code and judged more results. I cannot vouch for every line the way I could for a hand-written codebase, and I say so; I can vouch for what it does. That meant letting go: less reading code, more judging results. Two things surprised me.

title: Askew
pitch: Point at what looks wrong. Say four words. Get a measured answer, and a safe fix.
about_excerpt: Point at what looks wrong. Say four words. Get a measured answer, and a safe fix. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Measured findings: spacing, radius, and contrast, with evidence Apply confirmation: the human's click is the only write boundary Real write, real HMR reconnect: settled measurements confirm the fix Hover pinned without the pointer: a state a screenshot can't show Inspiration Every frontend session with a coding agent hits the same wall. The agent writes a page, I open it, and something is off — but I can only say "this looks cheap." So I screenshot it, paste it into a chat, and the agent guesses. It cannot see that the padding is 13px while thirty-one other surfaces use 20px . It cannot measure a 3.1:1 contrast ratio from a JPEG. It has never seen the hover state, because a screenshot cannot hold one. The browser knows all of this. It just had no way to say it. What it does Askew is a development-only Vite plugin that turns a running React app into a shared debugging surface for a browser AI agent. Click one element in your live app. Tell the agent something vague — "this looks cheap." The agent reads the real runtime truth through WebMCP: the computed cascade, the design scale the page is actually rendering, the measured contrast ratio, and how many visible instances share that source. It stages three Tailwind alternatives. Hovering A/B/C morphs the real component in place. Nothing has been written. You click Apply. One static class string changes in source, Vite HMR reconnects the selection, and the change is undoable. Two sentences and two clicks. No screenshots, no rebuilds. How WebMCP makes it possible Every Askew tool had to pass one test: it must return state that exists only in this browser tab, right now, and is unavailable from any repo, API, screenshot, or MCP server. Four things Askew reads that nothing else can hand an agent: Live DOM selection — what the human pointed at, one second ago Computed cascade — the resolved outcome of every competing declaration, not the source declarations Runtime design scale — spacing, radius, and colour frequencies derived from the rendered page, because tailwind.config is aspirational and the DOM is the truth Held interaction state — :hover and native focus, pinned and measured without a pointer An agent with perfect repo access is useless here. That is the whole argument. The design decision I am most pleased with: file writes are not an agent capability. The four tools inspect, diagnose, and stage. askew_stage_variants returns sourceWritten: false . Only the human's Apply click in Askew's own UI crosses the write boundary. Tool descriptions are the only channel for steering an agent whose system prompt you never see, so they are written as instructions — diagnose before proposing, never invent a finding when Askew reports uncertainty, warn when multiple visible instances share a source. How I built it npm workspaces, strict TypeScript. The plugin is apply: "serve" , so it does not exist in production — production-build.test.ts runs a real vite build and asserts that no instrumentation, endpoint, or capability header survives. Element-to-source identity comes from code-inspector-plugin with its editor server disabled. React 19 removed _debugSource , which quietly broke every click-to-component tool built on fiber inspection, so compile-time attributes were the only reliable route. The write path is contained by construction: the client never sends a filesystem path, only a sourceId resolved against an in-memory index of already-transformed modules, then realpath -canonicalised, root-contained, extension-gated, schema-closed, and applied as a one-for-one token replacement that must still match the full expected class string or fail 409 and write nothing. Challenges Page JavaScript cannot force :hover . That is a DevTools capability. Askew parses direct hover: utilities and applies the equivalent declarations inline, then measures. It resolves literal colour values only — anything else returns an explicit UNSUPPORTED_STATE rather than a confident no-op, because a wrong measurement is worse than a declined one. A false positive is worse than a missing finding. A dominant design value requires at least three samples and no tie. Contrast requires a resolvable opaque background or it reports ambiguity. A healthy element is reported as consistent, not silently skipped. A public write endpoint. The capability token is served to every visitor, so it is not authentication. I accepted that early and made containment carry the security model instead: an unprivileged secret-free process, two allowlisted files, an explicit token allowlist, rate limiting, and automatic baseline restore. What I learned Scope discipline is the whole game. The spec named thirteen things I would not build — multi-select, general CSS attribution, breakpoints, group-hover , AST mutation — and holding that line is why one path works end to end instead of six paths working halfway. What's next Design-token file writing so fixes become the system rather than one-off patches, and broader source-shape support beyond static single-line className literals. AI usage disclosure Built with OpenAI Codex — this hackathon's sponsor — used throughout planning, PRD/spec iteration, implementation, test writing, deployment hardening, and live browser verification. Claude Code independently exercised the running golden path and identified selection/actionability gaps; those findings were reproduced and fixed. Gemini then performed a separate architecture and edge-case review, whose valid color parsing, token validation, selection, and HTTP-status findings were verified against the code and incorporated. I made the product, scope, security, and submission decisions and reviewed the resulting changes; the assistants accelerated implementation and acted as independent code reviewers. Notes for judges The hosted demo at https://askew.xpworx.com is a deliberately writable, disposable, single-user development environment. It restores itself on startup, after three idle minutes, and from the visible Reset Demo button. If two people explore at once, changes will conflict and fail stale rather than merge — press Reset Demo and try again. The video is the authoritative uninterrupted proof. Built With nginx npm playwright pm2 react tailwind typescript vite vitest webmcp Try it out askew.xpworx.com github.com www.npmjs.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Ahmed Soliman Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Ahmed Soliman started this project — Aug 31, 2026 10:44 PM EDT
video_title: Askew — WebMCP-native live UI debugging
video_transcript_excerpt: Ask you. Point at what looks wrong. Every time an AI-generated interface looks a little bit wrong, the usual fix is screenshot it, paste it into a chat, and hope the agent guesses right. It usually doesn't, because a screenshot can't carry what the browser already knows. This is Ask you, a WebMCP tool running inside a real dashboard. I select the AI confidence card, and Ask you reads its live source, its computed styles, and how many other elements are just like it. Clicking analyze, it measures three real problems. The padding is 13 pixels while the rest of the page uses 20. The corners don't match the surrounding cards. And the supporting text sits under the 4.5 to 1 contrast a screen reader test would require. These are measurements, not guesses. Now the agent stages three token-level fixes through WebMCP. Hovering a direction morphs the real card immediately. No clone, no reload, and nothing written to disk yet. I pin the direction I want and click apply. Only this human click crosses the right boundary. The exact source file updates. Hot module reload reconnects the same element, and the change is undoable with one click. Here's the moment a screenshot can't show at all. I ask Ask you to hold this button's hover state without touching it. It measures the exact style a real hover would trigger live with no pointer anywhere near it. And reset demo returns the whole page to its starting state for the next visitor. The current selection, the computed cascade, the live design scale, a held interaction state. None of that exists in a screenshot or a repository, only in this browser tab right now. That's why this had to be WebMCP.

title: BrickWrite
pitch: Build with an AI, not around one. BrickWrite is browser-based brick CAD where people and agents share real parts, a live 3D model, connection checks, and an undo stack through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Build with an AI, not around one. BrickWrite is browser-based brick CAD where people and agents share real parts, a live 3D model, connection checks, and an undo stack through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Landing page Vibecode a LEGO set Transform any build View some of the awesome builds created by webmcp agents Manual mode allows independently moving pieces Building a 1:1 replica of the Golden Gate Bridge from scratch Inspiration Ever wanted to vibecode LEGOs? BrickWrite lets you do just that! I built BrickWrite because I wanted an AI design partner that could actually build beside me inside the same creative tool. Most AI design experiences stop at AI, words, or Computer Use in different softwares, which means the human still has to reconstruct every useful idea by hand. Brick building makes that limitation very obvious because a roof needs real pieces, real orientations, and real connection points that physically make sense. That challenge led to the question behind the entire project: what would happen if a person and an agent could work on the same creative object, using the same tools and sharing the same consequences? I wanted to preserve the satisfying parts of building, including choosing shapes, testing ideas, and refining the silhouette, while giving the agent responsibility for repetitive geometry and technical checking. The idea is basically (\text{human creativity} + \text{agent assistance} = \text{one editable model}), with both sides working on the same object. What it does BrickWrite is a browser-based 3D CAD workspace where people can design editable brick models using real parts and real connection data. Builders can search the catalog, place pieces, connect assemblies, recolor parts, move structures, organize subassemblies, inspect issues, and undo changes through one shared editing system. The agent works inside that same workspace through WebMCP, which gives it direct access to structured information about the current model. It can inspect the document, read the current selection, search the catalog, check connection possibilities, propose edits, validate geometry, and apply eligible changes when Build mode is enabled. The collaboration loop feels much closer to building with a partner than asking a chatbot for instructions. A builder can shape most of a model by hand, ask for help with a roof or repeating structure, review the proposed geometry directly in context, and then continue editing normally. Proposed changes can appear as translucent ghost geometry before they become part of the document, which makes reviewing agent work feel immediate and visual. Every change still belongs to the same editable model and the same history. Human edits and agent edits flow through the same command system, so undo, protections, revision checks, and document state stay consistent across both kinds of interaction. When the document changes while the agent is planning, revision checks can reject stale work before newer edits get overwritten. BrickWrite also gives completed work somewhere useful to go after the design process ends. Builders can export LDraw models, bills of materials, project archives, and printable build guides, while ten editable demo builds help people explore the editor without starting from an empty canvas. Why WebMCP fits the project 3D editing is a rough environment for automation based only on screenshots and pixel coordinates. An image can show where a brick appears on screen, yet it leaves out important information such as part identity, connector frames, protection state, document revision, and the exact operation that would preserve the model correctly. WebMCP lets BrickWrite expose those meanings directly through structured browser tools. Instead of teaching an assistant where a button happens to appear, the application exposes named capabilities with typed inputs, structured results, and clear failure states. The agent gets precise application state while the builder keeps the visual, hands-on interface that makes 3D design enjoyable. The part I find most exciting is that the assistant becomes a second operator of the same application rather than a separate service living beside it. A person can make a careful local adjustment while the agent handles repetitive work, and both changes become part of one document history with the same protections and revision checks. How I implemented WebMCP 1. Discovery begins as soon as the site opens and gives agents immediate orientation. The file src/webmcp/site.ts registers five site-level tools on every route: brickwright_overview , brickwright_navigate , brickwright_tools_list , brickwright_demos_list , and brickwright_autonomy . An agent arriving at the homepage can understand the product, discover available capabilities, and navigate into the editor without guessing its way through the visual interface. 2. The browser receives real tool registrations with executable handlers for every supported operation. The file src/webmcp/register.ts sends tool descriptors through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , including names, descriptions, input schemas, and the code that runs each operation. The registrar supports both synchronous and promise-based host implementations, while window.brickwright.invoke(...) provides a development bridge for browsers that lack native WebMCP support. 3. The tool contract and the application share the same vocabulary. CAD operation schemas live in src/webmcp/contract.ts , where Zod definitions generate the advertised JSON Schema and validate incoming requests against the same definitions. Tools including workspace_get , catalog_search , capabilities_search , and capabilities_help let the agent discover state and supported actions before it tries to change anything. 4. Previewing geometry and committing geometry remain separate operations throughout the entire editing workflow. Inside src/webmcp/adapter.ts , build_preflight validates an operation batch against the current document and creates a visible proposal while leaving the committed model unchanged. The proposal_create tool exposes the same preview behavior, while build_apply commits an eligible proposal atomically in Build mode through the shared CAD command path. 5. The available tool inventory changes with the collaboration mode selected by the builder. Inspect mode exposes document reads, Propose mode adds preview capabilities, and Build mode adds direct document writes through the supported editing paths. Mode-scoped registrations use an AbortController , which clears the previous tool inventory before registering the replacement set whenever the builder changes modes. 6. The agent can verify both structure and visual output afterward. The validate_model tool exposes model health, while render_capture returns live rendered pixels together with document and camera metadata. An agent can combine exact structural information with the actual rendered result, while tool-profile hashes and catalog versions help detect changes in the surface used during planning. A representative interaction starts with brickwright_overview , continues through brickwright_navigate and workspace_get , then searches catalog_search with requireGeometry: true before calling build_preflight using the current expectedRevision . The builder reviews the ghost proposal inside the viewport, and Build mode can commit an eligible proposal through build_apply while preserving the same shared history used by manual editing. How it is built BrickWrite uses TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js, and React Three Fiber for the browser application and interactive 3D workspace. The CAD document remains independent from the renderer, so positions, orientations, part identities, connections, constraints, and transactions live as application data while the viewport simply renders that state. Real LDraw geometry and LDCad connection metadata provide the foundation for placement and connectivity throughout the editor. The catalog distinguishes between parts with usable geometry and identities that are only searchable, which prevents the application from silently substituting made-up meshes. Missing geometry returns GEOMETRY_UNAVAILABLE , while collision checks combine a broad phase with mesh-level confirmation and surface uncertainty where the available data leaves room for ambiguity.
