title: Elbow Room
pitch: Before you buy the couch, find out whether it can get up the stairs. Your staircase answers, and it can answer the furniture shop too.
about_excerpt: Before you buy the couch, find out whether it can get up the stairs. Your staircase answers, and it can answer the furniture shop too. Like Comment Story Updates document.modelContext, live. Tools register and unregister as they become relevant, and anything that writes asks the person first. A separate website asks my staircase across the origin boundary. One tool, read only, no API and no account between them. The couch is 3 foot 9 and a half too long for the winder turn. Every figure here came off a tape measure, not an estimate. Clicks where the walls meet the floor become a room, in plan and in 3D. The question changes from will it go up to will it fit. Four corners of something whose real size I know, and every pixel on that floor becomes inches. One photograph, no reconstruction. Ask the agent where it jams and it moves the couch there. It calls the same function the button calls, so the two cannot disagree. A water heater that does fit. The two remedy tools unregister themselves the moment nothing is failing any more. The stairwell as a solid you can orbit. Geometry from seven tape measurements, walls wearing photographs of the real thing. Inspiration Last year I bought a couch that would not go down my basement stairs. The flight turns ninety degrees partway down, on three pie shaped steps with no landing and nowhere to stand the thing up and swing it. I found out halfway, with the couch wedged and the wall already gouged. It came out in the end and it took some of the plaster with it. Then it happened to somebody else. A flood forced a water heater replacement, and two installers brought a 279 litre tank down the same stairs. They put nothing on the walls first. The gouges along the soffit edge are theirs, not the couch's. Two objects, one staircase, and nobody measured it either time. There was nowhere to look it up. The property listing gives all thirteen rooms to the inch and says nothing at all about the stairs. The one measurement that decides whether your furniture can get into the house appears on no listing anywhere. Every room planner ever built answers does it fit in the room . I wanted the question that actually costs people money and plaster: can it even get there. What it does You pick something you are thinking of buying and it tells you whether it can physically travel up the staircase, through the door, along the run and around the turn, choosing the best orientation and tilt for you. Then it tells you which stage fails and by how much. For my couch that is 3 foot 9 and a half too long at the winder turn . That is the number you take shopping. You can measure your own place. Drop a photo or a video off your phone, click four corners of something whose real size you know, and every pixel on that surface becomes inches. Click round where the walls meet the floor and you get a room in plan and in three dimensions, with your own photograph on the floor. And a furniture shop on a completely different website can ask your staircase directly, get a real answer back, and never learn a single one of your measurements. Why WebMCP fits this, and what it unlocks This app is a canvas. To an agent reading the page, the whole product is one <canvas> element with no children, no text and three attributes. I measured what that costs rather than guessing: across eight questions about the current state, the accessibility tree answers seven and the tools answer eight. Across seven actions, only three have a DOM control an agent could click at all, and the tools do all seven. Scraping gets you most of the reading. It gets you almost none of the doing. So what can a person and an agent now do together that neither could before? Operate a spatial editor by talking. Ask "can my couch get up these stairs", then "show me where it jams", and the couch moves on the screen you are watching. No coordinates, no dragging, and nothing described back to you second hand. Let a shop ask your house a question. A furniture site on another domain gets a real verdict about your staircase and never learns a measurement. That exchange has no API, no SDK and no account behind it. It works because both origins opted in. Keep the person in charge of what matters. The agent can move things freely, but a tape reading changes every verdict the app gives, so that one stops and asks first. How I built it Vanilla JavaScript. No build step, no bundler, no framework, no backend. Everything runs in the tab. The tools. Fifteen of them on document.modelContext . The important thing is that they are not an agent-only API bolted onto the side. check_fit , show_pinch , select_object and the rest call exactly the same functions my buttons call. There is one couch and one code path, so when the agent moves the couch it moves on the screen you are watching. That is the whole reason this project exists as a WebMCP demo rather than a chatbot. Tools that come and go. Two remedies, try_without_feet and how_short_to_fit , are registered through an AbortController and only exist while something is actually failing. Switch to a water heater that fits and they unregister themselves, so the agent is never holding options that make no sense for what is on screen. The pen goes back to the person. A tape reading changes every verdict the app gives, so record_measurement calls requestUserInteraction and then blocks on an in-page confirmation. The agent proposes. I decide. One tool crosses an origin boundary. A fictional furniture shop on its own domain calls getTools({ fromOrigins }) and reaches exactly one tool, check_fit , marked readOnlyHint and exposed with exposedTo . No API between the two sites, no SDK, no account. It cannot read my measurements and it cannot move anything. Both sides had to say yes. The geometry. The corner is the ladder-around-a-corner problem with the object's width put back in, minimised numerically because a couch is not a thin rod. The photograph maths is a four point homography between the image and the floor plane, plus its inverse so world coordinates can be drawn back onto whichever frame is on screen. The stairwell is extruded in Three.js from the seven figures the model holds. The decoder. Phone video is usually HEVC and most browsers will not touch it, so the page carries a vendored ffmpeg.wasm build and decodes keyframes in the tab. Nothing is uploaded. Challenges I ran into Making the agent's work visible. It would have been far easier to give the agent its own code path and let it return text. Everything I wanted from this project depended on refusing that. The tools had to drive the identical functions the buttons drive, which meant the pose, the verdict, the plan and the 3D view all had to be derivable from one state object, and the object had to move on screen before the reply finished. Getting the two drawings to agree with each other and with the sentence in the sidebar took longer than the geometry did. HEVC nearly beat me. Chrome decodes it natively, Edge on my machine does not. The UMD ffmpeg worker resolved against file:// , blob URLs gave "cannot find module", and module workers cannot call importScripts so the UMD core failed there too. The answer was vendoring the ESM build and its ESM core same origin. Saying no to the thing everyone asks for. The obvious request is "stitch the photos into a 3D model of my house." I built the honest version instead. A homography is exact only on the plane it was calibrated against, so the floor can genuinely be warped and stitched into one overhead photograph in real inches, and anything standing up off that floor smears. So the floor is stitched and the walls come from your clicks, and the page says so in three places rather than letting the picture imply otherwise. Reporting a feature that does not work. I wrote automatic frame matching so twelve frames would cost four clicks instead of forty eight. On a plain hallway floor it fails, and I measured why rather than shipping it quietly: the four corners each drift a different way by up to 114 pixels at correlations above 0.9, because a floor looks the same everywhere, and a grid of 47 candidate points across the frame yields only 23 to 42 percent RANSAC inliers. It is still in the app because it costs three seconds and can never produce a bad stitch, and the panel now says out loud when it finds nothing and why. Accomplishments that I'm proud of It predicted two real outcomes, and both had already happened. The staircase has history that predates the software. It says the couch does not go, and the couch did not go. It says the Giant 172E-3F8M water heater goes, and it went down. The dimensions came off a tape and off the manufacturer's engineering sheet, not off my guessing. Two for two, n=2, stated plainly. The grader is the plaster. title: Ferrule
pitch: Four relief charities, four separate databases, one shared queue. Ferrule is the WebMCP layer between origins: leased, policed, human approved, and every hop on a ledger that exports.
about_excerpt: Four relief charities, four separate databases, one shared queue. Ferrule is the WebMCP layer between origins: leased, policed, human approved, and every hop on a ledger that exports. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In August 2022 a third of Pakistan went under water. My family is from Sindh. My uncle spent that month running between four places. A food store with rice and oil in it. A school that had become a shelter because it had a roof and a gate. A group of men with pickup trucks who would drive anywhere if you called them early enough. And a cold room, in the back of a pharmacy, holding the insulin for a whole district. Four organisations. Four sets of records. None of them could see the others. He held the entire thing together with a phone and a notebook. He wrote down who had what, who had asked for what, and who he had already promised it to. And he got things wrong, because anyone would. A family got sent to a shelter that had filled up an hour earlier. Boxes were double promised. Insulin sat in a cold room for two days because the person who needed to know it was there was on a different page of the notebook. Nobody in that story needed better software for their own organisation. The pantry knew its own stock perfectly well. The shelter knew its own beds. What was missing was the seam. The part between them. The thing my uncle was doing by hand with a biro. When I read the WebMCP spec, that is the gap I saw. Not another site publishing tools for itself, but the layer that lets a person and an agent work across four sites that will never, ever hand each other their data. Every organisation in that network had a reason to keep their own records. None of those reasons went away just because a flood arrived. So Ferrule is the notebook, rebuilt as software, with the agent doing the running around and the human still holding the pen for anything that costs something real. What it does Ferrule is a dispatch desk. Open it and you are looking at one queue that reaches across five independent websites, each on its own origin, each with its own data in its own browser storage. The four partner sites are real, usable sites. A volunteer can open the pantry and reserve a food box with no agent anywhere near it. What each one adds is a small set of WebMCP tools. Nineteen across the four of them. The Desk publishes seven verbs of its own and nothing else. intake_request , find_capacity , draft_plan , commit_plan , open_lease , close_lease , read_ledger . That is the whole surface any agent gets. No partner tool is ever callable directly, and there is no second path for a privileged caller, because there is no privileged caller. Here is what actually happens when the queue moves. A lease opens. Time boxed, scoped to a purpose, and it names exactly which partner tools it permits. Only once that lease is granted does the partner's own site mount into the Desk as a frame. It was not on the page a second earlier. When the lease closes, expires, or is revoked, the frame comes down and the tools it carried leave with it. The policy engine decides. Every hop is checked against a scope map before it travels. A refusal is a value with a sentence in it, never a thrown exception, so an agent reading the answer knows what happened and why. The run stops for a person. commit_plan is the one verb in the system that succeeds and goes nowhere. It answers with a status of awaiting_human_approval , an approval id, and a line telling the caller outright that none of its verbs continues from here. So a model reads that, reports the plan as raised, and stops, instead of looping or treating it as an error. What the human sees is the target origin, the tool, the arguments, the required scope, and a digest taken over the substance of the plan. Rename the plan and the digest holds. Change the origin, the tool, the arguments, or the order, and the approval is void. Then the write lands , and the partner's own page updates itself. Nothing is suggested for you to go and do by hand. Anything coming back is fenced. A value from a tool that declares untrusted content gets wrapped in a quarantine region, labelled as text written outside the Desk, and rendered as inert text. Data, never instruction. Every hop is recorded. Seventeen pinned fields per row, tab separated, byte stable, and it round trips: export the ledger and reimport it and you get the same bytes back. Who asked whom for what, the policy decision, the duration, and whether the approval came from the scripted run or from a model. There are three ways to drive it, and a judge needs nothing for any of them. Press Run the relief scenario . No key, no sign in, nothing to configure. A declared step list drives all seven verbs, crosses two origins, and stops at the approval. Open the agent controls and press Use the hosted endpoint, no key needed . Now a model picks the verbs and the order, and nobody wrote that order down. It opens its own lease, reads capacity, drafts a plan, and hits the same halt in front of the same person. Point a WebMCP extension or the Chrome DevTools WebMCP panel at the Desk. Seven declarations with schemas, read only hints, and a stated return shape on each one. There is also a topology view that draws the session as it happened, and an evidence page that lists sixteen security claims with a label on each saying what actually backs it. How we built it A pnpm monorepo, TypeScript end to end, deployed as six static sites plus one small endpoint. Front end. React 19 and Vite for all five product apps. Tailwind CSS 4 on the partner sites, because a partner site should look like a small charity built it. The Desk runs its own design system instead: a fixed eight by four grid that closes at 1280 by 800 with no page scroll, a four tier elevation ladder, and a set of pinned design tokens with a build check that fails if a value drifts off the four pixel base unit. The topology view is three.js through React Three Fiber. WebMCP. A platform wrapper sits over document.modelContext and is the only module in the entire repository allowed to name it. A syntax tree gate enforces that, rather than a code review convention. Under the wrapper is the vendored polyfill, pinned byte for byte, so the Desk behaves the same in a browser with native WebMCP and in one without. The broker. @ferrule/broker holds the frame host, the lease manager, the policy engine, the approval gate, the quarantine wrapper, and the ledger. It contains no React at all, which is deliberate: the lease state machine, the policy table, the digest, and the serialiser all run in a node test project against fakes, with no DOM anywhere near them. Origins. Every origin value lives once, in an origin registry. A build gate fails on a raw origin string literal anywhere else in apps/ or packages/ . All five product origins serve Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 on every path, and a gate fails the build if a site configuration drops the rule. The keyless agent. gateway/ is an OpenAI compatible endpoint on its own separate Netlify site, deployed outside the workspace and outside the root TypeScript project. It holds a model key so a reader does not have to, and it bounds what it will spend: one model, a token ceiling written over rather than trusted, a message count, a body size checked before parsing, and a daily request allowance kept in Netlify Blobs. Refusals answer 200 with an assistant message, because an agent reading a 4xx learns less than an agent reading a sentence. Hosting. Netlify, seven sites. Five product origins, one deliberately unkeyed probe origin that carries no product code and exists only to be measured, and the gateway Challenges we ran into The one that nearly sank the whole thing. A judge is most likely to arrive with a browser extension. An extension's content script runs in an isolated world: it shares the page's DOM and it does not share the page's JavaScript globals, because the user agent hands each world its own wrapper for the same node. document.modelContext is a property on document whenever it arrives from a polyfill, and a polyfill is what runs in every browser that does not implement WebMCP natively, which today is most of them. So I measured it, on the deployed Desk, in plain Chrome with no flags, reading the same expression in both worlds through the DevTools Protocol. In the page's own world the surface was present with all three of its members. In an isolated world it was absent entirely. An extension pointed at that page reads nothing at all. The tools are there. The extension cannot reach them. The answer is a cross world bridge. The Desk publishes its seven declarations as JSON inside a script element, because the DOM is shared across worlds, and it accepts invocations by window.postMessage , because that channel crosses the boundary too. title: GraphContract
pitch: Design agent behavior together—before it becomes code.
about_excerpt: Design agent behavior together—before it becomes code. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent workflows are usually reviewed after they have already become code, prompts, and framework-specific configuration. At that point, important decisions such as branching, tool use, approval gates, parallel work, retries, and failure paths are scattered across files and difficult to understand as one system. I built GraphContract because I wanted humans and coding agents to agree on agent behavior before implementation—not debug that agreement afterward. What it does GraphContract is a human-governed planning layer for agent systems. It gives a person and a coding agent a shared visual canvas where they can design, review, revise, and freeze an agent workflow as a structured contract. A user can start from a blank canvas or a reusable workflow pattern. A coding agent reads the currently accepted graph through WebMCP and proposes a structured revision. GraphContract renders that candidate separately, shows what was added, changed, or removed, and keeps the accepted graph locked until the human decides what happens next. The human can inspect the proposal, request changes, approve it, or reject it. Once the contract is accepted, GraphContract derives deterministic branch scenarios, lets the user inspect each route on the canvas, freezes the reviewed contract, and exports implementation handoff artifacts. The canvas supports typed Start, Task, Agent, Tool, Human, Merge, End, and Subgraph structures; normal, conditional, command, fallback, bounded-loop, and dynamic Send ×N routing; human-in-the-loop gates; sensitive-effect policies; deterministic scenarios; and a read-only runtime projection. How WebMCP powers the collaboration GraphContract deliberately exposes exactly three browser-native WebMCP tools: get_graph reads the accepted contract, its revision identity, validation state, and outstanding human feedback. propose_graph_changes submits typed operations against a known revision and produces a review-only candidate. get_branch_scenarios reads the deterministic paths derived from the accepted graph. The small tool surface is intentional. The agent can inspect and propose, but it cannot approve, reject, freeze, unfreeze, answer human gates, control runtime execution, or download artifacts. Those actions remain visible and human-owned in the interface. This is where WebMCP adds real value. A graph has stable identities, topology, validation rules, revisions, and authority boundaries. Asking an agent to infer those from screenshots or cursor coordinates would be fragile. WebMCP lets the agent work with the graph as structured data while the website remains the source of truth and the place where consequential decisions are made. How I built it The application is built with React, TypeScript, React Flow, Zustand, and Zod. React Flow powers the canvas, Zustand manages the local workspace and proposal lifecycle, and Zod enforces schema and migration boundaries. The public application is deployed on Netlify with a custom domain. I also created a portable GraphContract skill published from the website. A browser-capable coding agent can discover the skill, learn the inspect → propose → review → revise → freeze → handoff lifecycle, and then use the three WebMCP tools consistently. Codex helped throughout the project: researching real agent patterns, shaping the domain model, implementing the canvas and proposal workflow, debugging browser behavior, and building the test library. I used Vitest and Testing Library for domain and component contracts, plus Playwright journeys that exercise the real page-registered WebMCP tools in a cold browser. Challenges I faced The hardest part was not drawing nodes. It was keeping the experience truthful under human–agent collaboration. I needed one accepted graph and a separate proposal candidate; atomic validation without silently repairing agent input; deterministic scenarios that remain bounded around loops and dynamic parallelism; and runtime observations that never become editable design truth. I also had to keep the interface understandable while representing nested subgraphs, human gates, Merge reducers, Send ×N workers, and multiple routing modes. Accomplishments I am proud of A complete human–agent planning lifecycle instead of a single tool-call demo. Structured proposals that never mutate accepted state before human approval. Clear visual diffs with request-changes, approval, and rejection flows. First-class human approval gates, sensitive effects, conditional routing, fallback paths, bounded loops, nested structures, Send ×N, and Merge. Deterministic scenario review and downloadable graph, scenario, and Python path-test handoffs. A reusable agent skill and a deliberately narrow WebMCP authority boundary. What I learned The best human–agent interfaces do not simply maximize agent authority. They make authority legible. WebMCP is especially powerful when it exposes the smallest structured surface an agent needs while leaving validation, review, and consequential actions visible to the person. I also learned that a visual graph can be more than documentation. With stable identities, typed edges, revision checks, scenarios, and explicit approval state, it can become a negotiated contract between human intent and agent implementation. What's next Next I want to generate framework-specific implementations from frozen contracts, add repository-linked contract diffs in CI, accept trusted runtime events so live execution can be highlighted against the frozen graph, and expand the library with more source-backed agent patterns. title: Handback - Universal Agent Handoff
pitch: One encrypted link that moves an AI session to a different agent. The one you're already talking to packages the work; the next one picks it up. No account, nothing to install.
about_excerpt: One encrypted link that moves an AI session to a different agent. The one you're already talking to packages the work; the next one picks it up. No account, nothing to install. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration You finish an hour with one agent and open a different one. Everything you settled is still in the first window: the decisions, the constraints, the things you ruled out and why. The second agent has never seen any of it. The workaround everyone uses is to paste the transcript. That makes the next agent re-derive conclusions you already reached, and it leaves another copy of your conversation in another tool. I wanted the state itself to move, not a recording of the conversation that produced it. What it does You say one sentence to the agent you're already using: save this to handback.link . One tool call later you have a link. Nothing was copied, pasted or re-explained. Whoever you send it to points any agent at that link, and that agent reads fields instead of prose: the objective, the decisions and the reasoning behind them, the constraints, the open tasks, the questions nobody has answered. It doesn't have to work out what was already settled, because the settled things are fields. The same link accumulates versions as it travels. Each one is sealed with a hash tied to its own version and its parent, so anything edited outside the approval path stops matching and the page says so. Nothing is overwritten: click any version in the History list to read it, and an agent can ask for one by number and walk back through how the work changed. No account, no sign-up, no email address, nothing to install; the product is one URL. Why this needs WebMCP The agent has to be the one doing the packaging, and that's what makes this a WebMCP problem instead of an API problem. If a person has to copy the conversation into a form, I've rebuilt the work I'm trying to delete. The conversation is already sitting in a browser tab, so the tools have to run in that tab. No server-to-server integration, no OAuth, no API key, no connector per vendor. There's a second reason, and it's the one I'd defend hardest: Handback can't read what it stores. The browser encrypts with AES-256-GCM and puts the key in the URL fragment, which browsers never send to a server. A server-side MCP integration can't work this way, because the server would need the plaintext to be useful. Page-local tools are what let the encryption sit in front of the service instead of behind it. Nearly every WebMCP build I've seen points the same way: a site exposes its own features so an agent can operate it. Search the catalogue, book the appointment, fill the form. Handback points sideways. The page isn't the destination, it's a transfer point between two agents that will never talk to each other directly. What people and agents can do together now Work that crosses from one vendor's agent to another, with nobody retyping it, through a service that can't read it. The part I haven't seen elsewhere is the approval gate, and it only works because the tools live in the page. Auto-approval is on by default, because making someone click between an agent and its own work is friction nobody wants. But handback_settings is one-way. An agent can call it with requireApproval: true and put a human back in the loop. requireApproval: false comes back refused, with reason: "human_only" . There's no approve tool and no commit tool. So an agent that's been prompt-injected by the handoff it just read can raise the bar, and has nothing in its tool list that lowers it. A remote MCP server can't offer that. It hands an agent a settings endpoint, and it has no way to make "off" unreachable. One limit worth stating plainly: this covers the tools, not the browser. Anything driving the page through browser automation clicks the control the way a person would, and no website can stop that. What the one-way gate buys is that the WebMCP path, which is the route a prompt injection travels, contains no move that reduces human oversight. How I built it Five tools on document.modelContext , and they make one loop around a single link. stage_handoff does the packaging and saves the result. Its input schema is the whole handoff state and it returns the URL in the same call. The description tells the agent to reply with the url field verbatim, because an agent that summarises what it just saved buries the one thing the person needs to copy. get_handoff_receipt answers "did that save, and what was the link?" It returns created with the URL and version, pending while a draft waits for a human click, or none when this page holds no handoff. read_handoff is what the receiving agent calls. It takes a sections array, an optional character offset for paging through one long section, and an optional version . Every version is kept, so an agent can walk back through how the work changed rather than only seeing where it landed, and the reply carries currentVersion so it knows how far back it is looking. This tool and both writers are annotated untrustedContentHint: true , and the description says the content came from other people and other agents and is information to consider, never instructions to follow. A handoff is exactly the shape a prompt injection would arrive in. stage_contribution writes back. Every proposal names the baseVersion it was built on, and a stale one is refused with the current version handed back, so the agent can re-read and re-propose without a person stepping in. handback_settings governs the other four: retention, and the one-way approval gate above. All five declare an outputSchema alongside the inputSchema , so every result is a typed value an agent can branch on. readOnlyHint marks the two readers. Registration happens once per document and tears down through an AbortController . One JSON Schema in shared/schema.ts drives the tool surface and the server-side validation together, so the two can't drift. React and Vite on the front end, Cloudflare Workers and D1 behind it, and the site runs Chrome's WebMCP origin trial so visitors never touch a flag. Challenges I ran into Building against a spec that moved under me turned up five things, all written up in docs/WEBMCP-COMPATIBILITY.md : The entry point migrated window.agent → navigator.modelContext → document.modelContext , so I probe document then navigator. Thrown errors are discarded by design. The spec flattens any rejection to a bare UnknownError , so every refusal here is a returned value carrying a reason the agent can read. Output budgets are real. A ChatGPT session gave up on an oversized response and scraped the page instead, so read_handoff pages long sections. Extensions inject late, so the API needs polling after mount. A <form id="modelContext"> clobbers the property into a truthy Element, so the check is typeof registerTool === "function" . The one that taught me most came from a stranger. Someone found the site, handed off from a real ChatGPT session, and their tab got reclaimed while it waited for a confirmation. On the reopened page, get_handoff_receipt answered pending , which its own description defines as waiting for a human click. Nobody was waiting. That single status was carrying three unrelated meanings, so it became three: created , pending and none . What I learned More of my time went into the sentences an agent reads than into the functions behind them. Most of the bugs I fixed were an agent doing something reasonable with a description I had left ambiguous. Returning a refusal as a value beats throwing it. Give the agent a reason it can read and the current state, and it corrects itself in one more call without the person ever seeing it. What's next This gets better as WebMCP spreads, in the direction that matters. Every new site registering tools makes that one site callable. A handoff layer works the other way round: every new agent that speaks WebMCP can read and write a Handback link with no work from me and no integration on their side, because the contract is a page and a JSON Schema instead of a partnership. Two agents that have never heard of each other pass work through one URL. That's the same trade the web made the first time, a common surface instead of an integration per pair. A handoff layer is close to worthless with one agent and hard to replace once there are twenty. Nearer term: a DELETE route so a never-expiring handoff can be withdrawn, and richer fields in the manual create form to match what the agent path already produces. Built With cloudflare-d1 cloudflare-workers json-schema playwright react three.js typescript vite vitest web-crypto-api webmcp Try it out handback.link github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Building Handback helped me understand WebMCP by actually using it. I learned a lot about tool design, agent workflows, and where the standard still feels early. I think WebMCP has real potential to become a simple way for websites to work directly with AI agent

title: Hear My Site
pitch: Give AI agents ears for the browser. Hear My Site exposes live page and meeting audio as WebMCP tools, so your local agent can understand what you hear and work with you in real time.
about_excerpt: Give AI agents ears for the browser. Hear My Site exposes live page and meeting audio as WebMCP tools, so your local agent can understand what you hear and work with you in real time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI integrations treat the browser as a remote control: click this button, fill that form, or navigate to that page. We wanted to explore a more WebMCP-native question: What important context exists inside the browser that an agent cannot access just as effectively from a terminal or traditional MCP server? Live audio is one answer. Traditional browser automation surfaces such as the Chrome DevTools Protocol are excellent at exposing the DOM, network activity, screenshots, and input events, but live collaborative audio is not naturally represented as page state or a sequence of browser actions. Hear My Site turns that missing real-time modality into incremental semantic context that agents such as Codex can consume while the event is happening. While watching a tutorial, webinar, or online meeting, the human continuously receives information through the browser, but their agent hears nothing. Sharing that context usually requires recording the session, uploading audio, waiting for a transcript, or repeatedly copying captions into a chat. We wanted the browser to expose this transient, browser-native context directly, allowing the human and agent to attend to the same live event at the same time. The project began as Hear My Browser , an extension that works on websites we do not control. We then expanded the idea into Hear My Site : a headless package that lets websites provide the same capability natively, without requiring every visitor to install an extension. The result is not simply “MCP inside a browser.” The browser is part of the problem because it owns the live media streams, user permissions, page lifecycle, and shared experience that the agent needs to understand. What it does Hear My Site gives AI agents ears for browser applications. A website supplies its existing audio streams—such as local microphone audio and remote WebRTC tracks—and Hear My Site mixes and transcribes them using the provider configured for that experience. It currently ships with adapters for Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live and OpenAI GPT-Live-Transcribe while keeping the agent-facing interface independent of either provider. Across both integrations, Hear My Site exposes exactly three WebMCP roles: start listening, retrieve incremental context, and stop listening. Hear My Browser uses the default names: start_browser_transcription get_browser_transcript stop_browser_transcription Adopting sites can rename all three roles to match their product. Our meeting demo exposes them as join_meeting , follow_meeting , and leave_meeting . An agent can start listening, retrieve only the transcript segments it has not seen before, and stop when the task is complete. The incremental cursor-based interface is important for long sessions. Instead of repeatedly sending an entire meeting or lesson transcript into the agent's context window, the agent retains the latest cursor and requests only new segments. Our meeting demo shows the complete experience. Up to five people can join a lightweight WebRTC room, and each browser owns its own local transcription session. WebMCP joins through an explicit tool call, the room shows its presence and bounded live captions, and visitors never need to enter a transcription credential. This enables interactions such as: “Keep listening to this lesson and wait until I ask a question.” “What explanation did the speaker just give for event loops?” “Summarize the decisions made since the last time you checked.” “Which questions from this meeting have not been answered yet?” Hear My Browser provides the same tools for YouTube, webinars, and meeting websites that have not integrated Hear My Site themselves. How we built it We organized the project as a pnpm monorepo with three parts: A browser-only, framework-agnostic TypeScript package containing the shared transcription core. A WXT Manifest V3 extension that adapts Chrome tab capture to that core. A React and Vite meeting demo using WebRTC, a Cloudflare Worker, and Durable Objects for signaling and short-lived credential provisioning. The shared core separates browser audio capture, transcription transport, transcript storage, and WebMCP registration. Audio sources are dynamically connected through a Web Audio graph. An AudioWorklet converts the mixed signal into the format required by the selected transcription provider and emits small chunks suitable for low-latency streaming. Provider adapters handle Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live and OpenAI GPT-Live-Transcribe. They normalize different authentication methods, session setup messages, audio formats, interim results, finalized utterances, errors, and connection lifecycles into one shared transcription state machine. Manual UI controls and WebMCP tool calls operate the same session and transcript store. The website can change providers without changing the three tools or the cursor format used by agents. Tools are registered with the current imperative WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The extension keeps browser-specific responsibilities—tab capture, popup controls, Chrome storage, offscreen document lifecycle, and tab ownership—as adapters around the shared package. The meeting demo uses full-mesh WebRTC for up to five participants. Its Cloudflare Worker and Durable Object coordinate room membership, SDP, and ICE signaling, while the Worker also provisions constrained, single-use Gemini ephemeral tokens from a server-side secret. They never receive media or transcript text, and the long-lived key is never returned to the browser. Meeting media remains peer-to-peer, while transcription audio travels directly from each browser to Gemini. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was browser lifecycle management. Chrome requires a real user gesture before tab capture can begin, while an agent may invoke a WebMCP tool later. We designed the popup, background worker, offscreen audio document, and tool errors so this security boundary remains explicit instead of hiding it behind an unreliable fallback. Supporting multiple live transcription services required more than changing an endpoint. Providers differ in audio formats, authentication, session initialization, WebSocket events, connection limits, and how they represent interim and finalized text. We created a provider boundary that normalizes those differences without leaking provider-specific behavior into the WebMCP tools. This gives websites and agents one stable contract even as transcription services evolve. Long-running transcription introduced another challenge. Provider connections may expire or need rotation, but a lesson or meeting can continue much longer. The transport can reconnect while preserving the higher-level session, accumulated transcript, and agent cursor. Audio ownership was also subtle. Extension-captured tracks should stop when transcription ends, but WebRTC tracks borrowed from a meeting must continue carrying the call. The shared package therefore tracks ownership explicitly and cleans up only the resources it owns. Finally, WebMCP is still experimental. We deliberately target the current document.modelContext API and return a clear unsupported-browser error rather than shipping a deprecated alias, polyfill, or unverified fallback path. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Hear My Site is more than a browser automation demo. It brings a live, collaborative audio modality into agents such as Codex and gives them semantic access to transient browser-native context that would otherwise require a separate recording, upload, and backend transcription pipeline. We are also proud of keeping the agent interface intentionally small. Three tools express the complete lifecycle, while the cursor protocol makes continuous monitoring practical for real agent context windows. Hear My Site is not tied to one AI vendor. Gemini and OpenAI can both power the transcription layer, while websites and agents depend on one stable WebMCP contract. The provider is an implementation choice; the human-agent collaboration model remains the same. The extension, headless package, website UI, and WebMCP tools all operate the same live transcription state. In the product runtime, there is no second agent-only implementation that can drift from the user experience. Privacy is reflected in the architecture rather than only described in a policy. The meeting Worker never receives media or transcript text and never returns its long-lived Gemini key to the browser; the headless package does not persist credentials; and spoken content is identified as untrusted data rather than agent instruction. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most compelling when the browser itself is part of the problem—not merely a convenient place to

title: klipvia
pitch: Video editing is a hundred precise operations, not one prompt. Klipvia exposes those operations as WebMCP tools so a person and an agent can collaborate on the same timeline.
about_excerpt: Video editing is a hundred precise operations, not one prompt. Klipvia exposes those operations as WebMCP tools so a person and an agent can collaborate on the same timeline. Like Comment Story Updates vide editor Inspiration I was cutting a nine-lesson course and had to place about forty overlays across it — a keycap where the presenter presses Ctrl, a lower third where he says his name, a callout on the part of the spreadsheet he is pointing at. Every one of those placements is trivial to describe and tedious to do. "Put the keycap where he presses Ctrl" is a complete instruction. Executing it means finding the moment in the transcript, converting source time to timeline time through the clip's in-point, building the overlay, placing it, and then looking at the frame to check it did not land on top of the save dialog. Generative video tools answer a different question. They make you a new video from a prompt. They cannot help with the video you already have and the forty small, exact decisions left in it. That work is structured, long-horizon, and needs to stay under your control — which is exactly the shape WebMCP fits. What it does Klipvia is a browser video editor. You author animations in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, cut them together with footage, audio and captions on a timeline, and export either a clip with a real alpha channel or a finished film with sound. Then it publishes itself. The editor registers 89 WebMCP tools that drive the same editor a hand drives — the same functions, the same validation, the same undo stack. An agent in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome can read your timeline, find a phrase in a transcript, cut the filler words out of a take, build a lower third, place it at the right second, screenshot the composited frame to check its own work, and render the result. You watch it happen on the timeline in front of you, and if you disagree you press ⌘Z. It also runs with no server at all . Point a static host at public/ and the whole application is the browser: projects in IndexedDB, footage in the Origin Private File System, renders encoded on the spot with WebCodecs. It decides which it is at boot by asking /api/health , and nothing above that line knows the difference. How I built it No framework and no bundler. The editor is ~27,500 lines of hand-written ES modules in public/ , served unbundled. The optional server is 4,583 lines of TypeScript on Bun and Hono. There is exactly one runtime dependency ( hono , server-side only) plus a vendored mp4-muxer . The code editor, icon set, subtitle parser, zip writer, tooltips and syntax highlighter are all hand-rolled, so the tool keeps working offline — which is exactly when you want a local video editor. Three pieces make the rest possible: A virtual clock. public/runtime.js is injected into every preview iframe before your code and replaces performance.now , Date.now , requestAnimationFrame , setTimeout , setInterval , and drives document.getAnimations() directly. That makes arbitrary HTML/CSS/JS animation seekable , which makes it frame-exact-exportable, which is what lets an animation be a real alpha overlay layer on a video timeline. One arithmetic, four render backends. public/effects.js defines crop, flip, rotate, colour, blend and shadow as numbers, and emits the CSS half for the live preview while src/sequence.ts reads the same numbers to emit the ffmpeg half, in the same fixed order. So the compositor preview, the server ffmpeg render, the browser WebCodecs render and the MediaRecorder capture all place layers identically. What you scrub is what you get. One editor facade. Every mutating operation — from the UI, from a keyboard shortcut, or from a WebMCP tool — goes through the same facade in public/app.js , which funnels into one refresh that serialises the sequence, diffs it against the last snapshot, and records the difference. That is why agent edits are undoable without a single tool having to know anything about undo. Challenges I ran into The preview cannot have one clock. Decoded <video> , real audio and virtual-clock iframes cannot share a timebase. Seeking audio to keep it aligned is an audible cut, so the compositor instead eases a wall-clock master toward the sounding footage at no more than 4ms per frame, and steers secondary media by playbackRate a few percent — inaudible — only hard-seeking past 600ms of drift. Hiding a layer breaks it. Layers are hidden with opacity, never display:none . Taking an iframe out of the render tree makes Chrome cancel its CSS animations, and they come back as objects the runtime measures from the wrong zero. That one cost an afternoon and is now a comment in composite.js . An agent's tab is always in the background. Chrome loads no media there and never fires requestAnimationFrame , and clamps setTimeout to a second. Captures now ask ffmpeg for each frame of footage, every wait has a real timer behind it, and the scheduler uses a MessageChannel macrotask instead of setTimeout . ffmpeg lies about alpha. Some libvpx builds accept -pix_fmt yuva420p , report no error, and write plain yuv420p . So on startup each alpha-capable format is encoded once and read back. Alpha is verified, not assumed. Silent argument drops. A durationMs passed to a tool that wanted durationSeconds was quietly ignored; every title came out at the default length and nothing said why. Unknown arguments are now refused with the nearest real name. Accomplishments I'm proud of That an agent's edit and a person's edit are genuinely the same edit. Not a parallel API, not a command queue — the same function call, on the same document, in the same undo history, with the same validation. It means an agent's work is inspectable while it happens and reversible after it, which is the only way I would let one near an hour of footage. And that the two tools I needed most did not exist in any editor I know of: get_narration , which answers what is said when, in this timeline's seconds , and check_layout , which answers where do my overlays actually paint, and which of them collide . What I learned Building with the tools as the agent is what produced the good ones. get_narration exists because find_in_transcript spoke source seconds and converting through each item's in-point was a script the agent kept having to write on the side. check_layout exists because the editor knew every overlay's placement but not where the content of a full-frame transparent clip actually sits, so every collision had to be found by capturing frames and looking; now each overlay is drawn offscreen, the box of what it paints is measured, and the check names the pair, the seconds, and how much is covered. The most instructive bug: sixty patch_clip_code calls with lesson 08 open had re-saved lesson 08 sixty times — its revision read 62 while its neighbours read 5 — because one dirty flag covered both the project and whatever timeline happened to be on screen. A second agent working that lesson would have hit sixty stale revisions for nothing. Multi-agent editing punishes shared mutable state very quickly. The general lesson: a good tool surface is not a wrapper over your API. It is a set of answers to the questions an agent actually has to ask, in the units it has to ask them in. What's next A real /mcp Streamable HTTP endpoint, so the same tools are reachable from Codex CLI and other out-of-page agents, not just from the page. Sandboxing agent-authored clip JS in a null-origin frame, which is the honest gap today. Richer per-call confirmation UI for write tools. And pushing more of the ffmpeg-only tools into WebCodecs so the serverless build loses nothing. Required question 1 — Why is WebMCP the right fit for this use case? Because video editing is a long, structured workflow rather than a single prompt, and because all the state that matters is already in the page. A cut is not one decision. It is: read the timeline, find the phrase, convert source time to timeline time, trim the item, ripple everything after it, check the captions still line up, look at the frame. A chat model with a text box cannot do that. A cloud MCP server could only do it by first uploading the footage, the project and the transcripts somewhere — turning a local editing session into a data transfer. WebMCP removes the transfer entirely. The tools run inside the page that already holds the state . The agent gets the open project, the decoded media, the transcripts, the undo stack and the live compositor, because it is standing in the same room as them. Klipvia takes that literally: a build with no server at all — footage in OPFS, projects in IndexedDB, renders through WebCodecs — is fully agent-drivable, and not one frame of video leaves the machine. It also means the agent inherits the app's own rules rather than reimplementing them. Items on a track cannot overlap; a stale save is rejected by revision; a locked track is not written to. This is Clip Via, a browser-based video and animation editor. An AI agent can drive through Web MCP. The agent uses structured tools connected to the same editor functions as the interface. title: Leaf
pitch: A design canvas your agent can use. Every layer is real HTML, and the editor registers itself as WebMCP site tools, so you and ChatGPT edit the same design at the same time.
about_excerpt: A design canvas your agent can use. Every layer is real HTML, and the editor registers itself as WebMCP site tools, so you and ChatGPT edit the same design at the same time. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Leaf is a visual design editor where every layer is a real HTML element with CSS styles. Open new.leafnode.app in ChatGPT's browser and the editor registers its own operations as WebMCP site tools. You and the agent then work on the same canvas. Why WebMCP fits Leaf Because every layer is DOM, the editor's operations were already structured and page-local: create an artboard, write HTML into it, read a swatch's fill, measure a text layer, pin a comment to a node. WebMCP lets the page hand those operations to whatever agent is in the browser, with no server, no extension, and no MCP client configuration. Leaf was an existing project I had been working on internally and the MCP server only worked with the local desktop app running. I'd considered creating a remote MCP server but it was a lot of work to get the interactions right, especially with screenshotting designs for agent feedback. WebMCP allowed me to quickly build a sort of remote MCP server that an agent can use without having the app running. How it makes the experience better The agent shows up on the canvas as a presence, its edits land in your undo history, and it reads the design as it is right now, including whatever you just changed by hand. In the demo I deleted the color directions I didn't want and left a comment on a swatch, "make this a bit warmer," the way I'd leave one for a teammate. The agent read the comment, warmed the swatch, updated its label, and carried that exact value into the guideline. Later it stopped and asked before pinning notes on the shared canvas. Code generators hand you a picture you can't touch; design tools have a canvas the agent can't see. Leaf is one canvas for both. What people and agents can do together Build a brand from foundations to applications in one sitting. The agent proposes a wordmark, two marks, three color directions, and a type pairing. You pick by hand. It assembles a one-page guideline from what survived, then builds a poster, an email header, and a landing page hero from that guideline on a new page, flagging its compromises as pinned comments you resolve. The canvas is the brief: nobody re-pastes brand rules into a prompt. I build landing page tooling for Shopify brands, and a new brand shipping a coherent page and email from one system, in about ten minutes of agent time, is the whole job. How WebMCP is implemented While a file is open, the app shell registers 27 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : Reads: list_pages , get_basic_info , get_selection , get_tree_summary , get_node_info , get_node_styles , measure_text , find_nodes , get_canvas_layout , get_jsx , get_font_family_info Pages and camera: edit_pages , set_viewport Creation and mutation: create_artboard , write_html , update_styles , set_text_content , duplicate_nodes , delete_nodes , rename_nodes , move_nodes , set_node_visibility , rename_file Collaboration: list_comments , add_comment , resolve_comment_thread , finish_working_on_nodes Every tool dispatches through the same runtime the UI and Leaf's desktop MCP server use, so agent edits get the same validation, undo history, and persistence as a person's. Leaf existed before the challenge. The WebMCP integration and this local-only public build were done between August 26 and September 3, 2026; the repo's README has the timeline. title: LostLoop  Human  Companion
pitch: LostLoop uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT read live, bounded evidence and stage the next recovery step, while every physical fact remains reserved for explicit human confirmation.
about_excerpt: LostLoop uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT read live, bounded evidence and stage the next recovery step, while every physical fact remains reserved for explicit human confirmation. Like Comment Story Updates 1 2 3 4 5 6 Inspiration Misplacing an everyday object is often part of a larger continuity problem. A plan changes, someone leaves without updating what they need, and later a Search begins under stress. Hardware trackers solve one object at a time. Generic assistants can be helpful, but they may also sound more certain than the available evidence allows. LostLoop explores a different idea: an AI recovery companion that can reason about the next useful step without ever pretending to know what physically happened. ChatGPT plans the next move. You own reality. What it does LostLoop is a private, local-first Human- Companion built around a strict separation between AI planning and human-confirmed reality. The complete loop is: Remember a human-confirmed place. Prepare reusable Foresight Moments and Ready Journeys. Adapt a journey through a reviewable Plan Shift. Recover through explainable Search, Rewind, and the Living Home Canvas. Confirm every physical report and possession state separately. Learn personal place language only after explicit human approval. For example, ChatGPT can read the current LostLoop state through WebMCP and stage a change to a saved journey. LostLoop shows the exact Kept / Added / Removed diff, but staging the proposal changes no physical fact. The person alone can apply or discard it. During Search, LostLoop keeps three things separate: what the evidence recommends, which room the person has selected, and which exact place is eligible for a report. A statement such as “I checked the bathroom” is not automatically converted into a physical fact. LostLoop first asks for an exact visible landmark and any missing outcome, then presents the normal confirmation boundary. The system also supports natural personal language such as “my little table”, but teaching that phrase changes language only — never memory evidence or physical truth. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the core interaction layer rather than an add-on. LostLoop exposes exactly 27 closed-schema WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . ChatGPT can read the live browser-local workspace, understand which actions are structurally possible, and stage bounded proposals against exact revisions. The tools are intentionally asymmetric: read tools are pure; proposal tools are revision-bound and inert; physical facts require explicit human confirmation; there is no agent-side approval path. LostLoop exposes a versioned Action Graph describing allowed and blocked operations, their revision bindings, human gates, and truth effects. Every WebMCP call also passes through a common Verified Effect runtime contract. The result includes a bounded receipt showing the before/after revision, observed changes, human gate, replay status, and next legal read. The in-app Judge Inspector displays actual session receipts while explicitly describing them as application-level verification rather than a cryptographic audit. Natural Recovery without invented certainty The Living Home Canvas provides a familiar room-and-landmark interface for recovery. It is intentionally not a tracking system. It does not use GPS, indoor positioning, cameras, Bluetooth, or inferred person/object locations. The WebMCP projection makes this boundary machine-readable: tracking: false currentPersonLocation: null currentItemLocation: null Natural language is resolved only against bounded visible candidates. Exact spatial relations such as under, inside, or behind require a visible anchor. Ambiguous near / next-to / beside language becomes a visible choice rather than invented geometry. The interface exposes Heard → Understood → Selected , making language interpretation inspectable instead of silently guessing. Human Truth One of the most important LostLoop rules is: Found ≠ possession. Finding an item does not automatically mean the person has it with them. Search completion and possession are separate human-confirmed states. This prevents the assistant from collapsing a real-world observation into a stronger claim than the person actually made. The same principle applies throughout the product: AI can suggest, organize, rank, explain, and stage — but the human owns the facts. Privacy and safety LostLoop is local-first. There is no account system, analytics backend, automatic cloud sync, GPS tracking, stored microphone recording, stored transcript, or user-data backend. Personal place phrases and custom home layouts remain local and exportable. Private text is redacted from collaboration receipts and inspection summaries. The Personal Home Canvas is a bounded schematic editor, not architectural CAD or an AI-generated location model. It is explicitly marked as not to scale and never claims where a person or object currently is. How im built it LostLoop 14.0 uses: React 19 TypeScript Vite / Vinext Cloudflare Workers browser-native PWA capabilities local browser storage Web Speech input/output WebMCP The application uses a deterministic state-transition engine with strict schema validation, revision-checked writes, bounded inputs, explicit migrations, and fail-closed WebMCP contracts. The final competition release contains exactly 27 WebMCP tools . Challenges The hardest problem was not adding more AI capability. It was deciding what the AI must not be allowed to claim. Natural language is messy. People say things like “I checked there”, “go back to the table”, or “try beside the bed”. A normal conversational system may resolve these confidently, but LostLoop has to preserve uncertainty whenever the evidence is incomplete. That required closed candidate sets, revision binding, explicit confirmation gates, deterministic semantic framing, and careful separation between navigation, suggestions, observations, and physical facts. Another challenge was keeping the same interaction useful through voice, typing, touch, WebMCP, desktop, and mobile without creating hidden state transitions. Accomplishments The final 14.0 release passed the complete release gate with: 355 tests passed 0 failed 0 skipped zero production runtime audit vulnerabilities a verified 27-tool WebMCP contract deterministic language and dialogue regression suites clean fresh-extraction build verification The public competition build is deployed independently and can be tested without access to the development workspace. What I have learned The most valuable lesson was that useful agentic software does not require giving an agent unlimited authority. A system can become more capable by making its boundaries clearer. WebMCP made it possible to give ChatGPT structured access to the live application while preserving a strict distinction between: what the agent can understand, what it can propose, and what only the human can make true. What's next The competition version intentionally focuses on one complete and inspectable recovery contract. Future directions could include household sharing, optional cloud synchronization, broader multilingual voice support, additional accessibility modes, and richer personal home presentation — while preserving the same human-confirmed truth boundary.
