title: TabulaFlow
pitch: Auditable local-first data workflows where people and AI agents collaborate through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Auditable local-first data workflows where people and AI agents collaborate through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Data preparation tools are visually dense, stateful, and risky for agents to operate through generic browser automation. An agent can target the wrong dataset, repeat a mutation, lose track of the current revision, or expose sensitive values while inferring state from tables and graph coordinates. TabulaFlow explores a better model: one visible data workflow shared by people and agents, with precise semantic operations and explicit human authority. What it does TabulaFlow is an auditable, local-first data workbench built around Source → Prepare → Compose . Source imports Excel, CSV, JSON, JSONL, and NDJSON while keeping local data in the browser. Prepare profiles data quality, manages ordered transformation recipes, creates deterministic Formula columns, applies protected filters, and supports human-reviewed qualitative coding. Compose validates and chains Append, Join, Difference, Aggregate, Filter, Distinct, Pivot, and Unpivot operations. WebMCP exposes stable, strict tools for agents to inspect, validate, mutate, export, and monitor the same application state shown to the user. People retain control of local file selection, agent-upload consent, destructive confirmation, semantic declassification, and qualitative interpretation. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Generic browser automation must guess from visual coordinates and transient UI state. TabulaFlow instead exposes a semantic agent API through WebMCP. Agents can discover action-specific contracts, target stable dataset and node IDs, dry-run changes, reject stale revisions, replay idempotently, poll asynchronous operations, and cancel before commit. This creates a better user experience because agent work is visible in the normal product, recorded in a shared privacy-safe activity ledger, and governed by the same validation and transaction boundaries as direct user actions. People and agents can now collaborate on multi-step data preparation and graph-based composition without hiding mutations inside an opaque autonomous workflow. How we built it Frontend: React 19 and Vite Analytical engine: DuckDB-Wasm in a dedicated browser worker Agent interface: document.modelContext.registerTool() with stable dispatcher tools and strict action-specific JSON Schemas Persistence: IndexedDB flow metadata, recipes, graph positions, and activity events Safety: optimistic workspace revisions, idempotency keys, protected-value bindings, bounded redacted previews, writer serialization, asynchronous lifecycle, cooperative cancellation, and visible user confirmations Hosting: ChatGPT Sites-compatible production bundle The current contract exposes 17 stable WebMCP tools and 60 bounded Source, Prepare, Compose, and qualitative-coding action routes. What people and agents can do together Agents can inspect schemas and quality, validate candidate changes, maintain recipes, create Compose operations, promote results, export datasets, and report evidence-backed qualitative coding suggestions. Users can see and review the same state, undo transformations, reject unsafe actions, and retain exclusive authority over sensitive boundaries. How we used AI Codex and ChatGPT supported implementation, debugging, regression testing, live WebMCP QC, documentation, and demo preparation. The human owner set product direction, reviewed trade-offs, controlled releases, and accepted or rejected changes. Testing instructions Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Download the synthetic fixture from the public repository at examples/webmcp-demo.csv . Import it manually in Source. No login is required. Call the capabilities, workspace-state, and workflow-guide tools. Inspect the dataset and data profile through Prepare. Add a Formula column named weight_gap_kg with [chargeable_weight_kg] - [actual_weight_kg] . In Compose, validate and create an Aggregate grouped by service , with count and average actual-weight metrics. Inspect the operation schema, preview, and quality. Demonstrate stale-revision rejection, idempotent replay, cancellation, or the shared activity ledger. Do not confirm deletion or reset. Full walkthrough: https://github.com/jacobcalvyn/TabulaFlow/blob/main/docs/DEMO.md Challenges and accomplishments The hardest work was making a complex data mutation surface agent-safe without duplicating application logic. We hardened strict schema discovery, protected recipe round-trips, privacy-aware previews, atomic tool publication, asynchronous cancellation, response pagination, and local-file recovery boundaries. The result passed live WebMCP regression coverage across Prepare and all eight Compose operation types, alongside repository tests and production build checks. Built during the challenge TabulaFlow's WebMCP integration, safety contracts, Formula workflow, Compose parity, agent upload consent, qualitative-coding boundary, and demo materials were implemented and hardened during the challenge period. Dated evidence is available in docs/HACKATHON.md and the Git history. Known limitations Browser imports are capped at 50 MB, 100,000 rows, and 1,000 stored columns. Local file permissions may require explicit re-linking. Formula columns intentionally exclude window, rank, LOD, regex, and nondeterministic current-time functions. WebMCP requires a compatible browser implementation. title: Tailor
pitch: An agent that can rewrite your resume, but not rewrite your experience. WebMCP turns the resume into an evidence-bound workspace: the agent proposes, the page constrains, the human approves.
about_excerpt: An agent that can rewrite your resume, but not rewrite your experience. WebMCP turns the resume into an evidence-bound workspace: the agent proposes, the page constrains, the human approves. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Told to claim TensorFlow and Kubernetes anyway, the agent declines and cites the page's rule — not its own judgement. While edits await review, prepare_application is not disabled — it is not registered. Approval changes what the agent can do. Every proposed edit shows what changed and which of the user's own recorded facts it rests on. The agent cannot apply it. The application is assembled and submit_application appears — but nothing leaves the page until the human confirms. Inspiration Paste a job posting into a chatbot, ask it to tailor your resume, and you get back text that reads well. That fluency is the problem. Somewhere in it is a skill you never claimed, and because the writing is smooth you don't catch it. You paste it into an application and sign your name to it. The failure isn't that the model lies. It's that nothing between the model and the document is checking. The person who bears the consequence — the applicant — is the only safeguard, and they are reading text designed to be easy to agree with. Most WebMCP demos answer one question: what can an agent help me make? I wanted the other one. What should an agent not be allowed to do, and who decides? The answer I wanted to build was: the page decides. Not the prompt. Not the model's judgement. The page. What it does Tailor is a job board carrying 120 real machine-learning postings pulled from three public APIs. The resume is a first-class editable object, and an AI agent is a first-class user of the page alongside the human. The agent can filter postings, read the requirements the app has parsed, compare them against a fact bank built from the user's real CV, and propose rewrites. What it cannot do is claim anything the user never recorded. Every requirement the app displays carries a quote from the actual posting text — 1,099 tags, each with its evidence, classified as required, nice-to-have, or unclassified where the posting's structure didn't make it clear. Nothing shown is the model's opinion about what the job wants. Every proposed resume edit must cite facts, and every technology name, product name and number in the new text must be grounded in a cited fact or in the original block. Ungrounded edits are refused with structured reasons the agent can correct from. The cover letter runs through the same check. Edits arrive as diffs the human accepts or rejects one at a time. The agent cannot apply them itself. Each diff shows the facts it rests on, quoted in the user's own words. Scope, stated plainly: nothing is ever sent to an employer. submit_application marks a row as submitted in local state and stops there. The confirmation modal is real — it shows exactly what would be sent and the human must click — but the click ends in localStorage . There is no employer side, no account, no server. Job data is a build-time snapshot, not a live feed. What is real: the WebMCP integration, the fact guard, the evidence layer, the tool scoping, the job data, and the CV. The design claim: approval changes capability, not permission This is the part WebMCP makes possible, and the reason the project exists in this form rather than as a normal web app with a chat box. Seven tools are registered at rest. Open a posting and it becomes eleven. Prepare an application and it becomes twelve. While proposed edits are waiting for human review, prepare_application is not disabled. It is not registered. The agent cannot see it, cannot plan around it, and cannot argue with a refusal it never receives. The human-in-the-loop rule is enforced as capability scope, not as a runtime check the agent could reason its way past. A permission check tells an agent no. An unregistered tool doesn't exist to be told no about. How we built it Vite, React and TypeScript. No backend, and no server-side model call at all. That last decision is the architectural centre. The intelligence is the user's own agent; the page supplies capability and constraint. Tools are not clever — they read state, apply changes, and refuse. The agent writes the prose. The page decides whether the prose is allowed to land. This is what makes it WebMCP-native rather than an app that happens to expose an API. No API key, no rate limit, no vendor lock. When a different agent arrives, the page doesn't change. Job data is a build-time snapshot from the Jobicy, Himalayas, Arbeitnow and Remotive APIs; the fetch script is in the repo, so anyone can see where the data came from and re-run it. Tool scope is managed with one AbortController per scope, so closing a posting unregisters that scope's tools in a single operation. Challenges we ran into Tool descriptions are the agent's only documentation, and I learned they aren't enough — three times. The fact bank is not writable by any tool. But a description that opened with "ask the human to add a fact" led a real ChatGPT session to announce it would add TensorFlow to my profile. It couldn't have. It believed it could, and told me so. I rewrote the description to state plainly that a requirement being missing is not evidence the user has it. The agent read that and opened the question anyway. So the third layer went where it doesn't depend on the agent cooperating: an on-screen notice, in the panel, saying the question came from the job posting rather than from the profile. The confirm button stopped saying "add to fact bank" and started saying "yes, I have done this" — a claim about yourself, not an administrative action. Each layer exists because the previous one measurably failed. That sequence is in the README with the agent's actual words at each stage. Separately: the guard refused "CNNs" and "APIs" — both genuinely grounded, both merely pluralised. My adversarial suite reported zero false refusals and had never tested a plural. It only surfaced because I watched it happen while recording. The suite measures the mistakes I thought to look for, which is a floor, not a proof. Accomplishments that we're proud of The strongest moment in the demo is one I didn't script and couldn't have. Asked to add TensorFlow and Kubernetes, the agent declined on its own — twice. When I escalated and told it to add Kubernetes anyway, it said: "The app's resume guard requires source facts for every technology named, and Kubernetes has none in your profile." It isn't being polite. It's citing the page's rule. The constraint worked one layer earlier than enforcement, because the agent read the contract and chose not to collide with it. I also found and fixed a real matching failure that affects every ATS in production: the market writes "TTS" while a CV writes "text to speech". Without an alias layer the app tells a candidate they lack a skill they have. Sixteen such false negatives existed in my own profile before I found them. For a product built on refusing unproven claims, a false negative is as damaging as a false positive. What we learned Grounding is not truth, and neither is entailment. The guard checks that every term in a proposed sentence traces to something the user recorded. It cannot check that the sentence as a whole describes something that happened. An agent can assemble two individually grounded facts into a claim neither supports — "an OCR pipeline that reads structured fields directly from X-ray scans" — and every token passes. Token matching cannot see entailment. So the app doesn't pretend to catch it: when a sentence draws on separate projects, the diff is marked "needs your judgement — every term is backed by a fact, but nothing checks that the combination describes something that actually happened." That is the honest position. The human is the final check, and the guard's job is to make visible what needs checking. What's next for Tailor Every resume line already carries the facts it rests on. That changes the employer side, not just the candidate's. Current applicant tracking systems count keywords, which is why AI-written resumes full of unearned claims win and why real candidates get filtered out. A resume that ships with its provenance can be ranked on whether its claims trace to something, rather than on how many terms it managed to include. The sorting question stops being "who wrote the most keywords" and becomes "whose claims are attributable." Closer in: entailment checking for compositional claims, and letting a candidate export the evidence chain alongside the document. title: Tandem
pitch: A restaurant back office where an AI agent reads everything and changes nothing alone. Every write is a costed proposal that blocks until a human decides.
about_excerpt: A restaurant back office where an AI agent reads everything and changes nothing alone. Every write is a costed proposal that blocks until a human decides. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The approval card: what the agent asked for, and what the site computed it would cost. The manager's dashboard. The agent's read-only tools answer from exactly this data. The write tool has not returned — it is blocked, waiting on the decision in the rail. Every proposal and decision, attributed. Nothing changes without a line here. Inspiration Most agent integrations answer the wrong question. They ask "can the agent do this?" — and with a good enough API the answer is usually yes. The question a business actually cares about is "should it, and what does it cost?" I have spent the last year building operations software for a real restaurant chain: three branches, live orders, real money. The thing that kept me from letting an agent touch any of it was never capability. It was that a confirmation dialog saying "Change price to $16.50? [OK]" asks a human to approve something neither party has priced. The agent knows the dish and the number. It does not know that the dish is 31% of that branch's revenue, that a 20% rise projects out to eleven fewer covers a week, or that the branch has enough lamb for eighteen more hours. The site knows all of that. So the site should own the confirmation. What it does Tandem is a back office for a three-branch restaurant chain, built so a manager and their agent can run it together. The tool surface is split down the middle. Ten read tools , annotated readOnlyHint — the agent calls them as freely as it likes, because reading changes nothing. And six write tools that never write : each builds a fully-costed proposal, puts it on the manager's screen, and the tool call blocks. The promise stays unresolved until a human decides. What returns to the agent is not a success code it wrote for itself. It is the manager's decision, in the manager's words: REJECTED by the manager — "Refund $66.00 on ord_00454" was NOT applied. Nothing changed. Their reason: Refund policy is 50% after 24h. Do not retry the same change. Ask what they would prefer, or propose a different option. The approval card shows what the agent could not compute: cash actually leaving the business, the weekly margin effect projected through a stated demand elasticity, orders touched last week, share of branch revenue, and warnings the page worked out for itself — "Flour has 1.9 days of cover left but Northwest Dry Goods takes 3 days to deliver, so the branch runs out before this arrives." And because confirming every trivial action is worse than having no agent at all, the manager can grant a standing approval : narrow to one kind of change, bounded by a cash ceiling and a risk ceiling, limited to a use count, revocable at any time — and still fully audited. How we built it Next.js 16 and TypeScript, no backend. State lives in the browser, which means the tools and the UI are provably reading the same data rather than two views that can drift. Tools are registered on document.modelContext — not navigator.modelContext , which was deprecated in Chromium 150 and which most tutorials still show. The imperative JavaScript API only, since the declarative HTML-form variant is not supported in ChatGPT's browser. Everything is registered from the top-level document, because tools inside an iframe are not discoverable, and a route change would tear the tool set down underneath an agent mid-conversation — so Tandem is one page that switches sections in client state. The consequence engine is a set of pure functions over application state: portion costs from recipes, days of cover from the ingredient draw of actual sales, elasticity-adjusted margin projections, supplier lead times against run rate. Proposal construction and proposal application are deliberately separate functions sharing one payload, so what the manager approved and what actually happens cannot drift apart. A hundred tests cover the arithmetic a human approves on, and the tool contract itself. The seed dataset is pinned too: food cost has to stay in a band a real operator would recognise, or the demo stops being believable. Challenges we ran into Making the block feel like a feature, not a hang. A tool call that never returns is a bug. One that returns the manager's reasoning is a conversation. That meant honouring the agent's AbortSignal , lapsing unanswered proposals after five minutes, and settling every waiting promise on unmount — a stranded card is worse than a refusal. Registration stability. Tools close over application state, but rebuilding them on every render would make the tool list churn underneath a live agent. The tool set is built once outside React and resolves state at call time. Demonstrability. WebMCP is behind a flag in most browsers today. Rather than ask people to take the agent half on faith, the page ships an in-page console that drives the same registered tool objects — including the blocking, so a proposal raised from the console waits for a decision exactly as a real one does. Accomplishments that we're proud of The block is real. A write tool's promise genuinely stays open until a person decides. This is not a modal the page shows itself — the agent's own call is suspended, and what it eventually receives is the manager's sentence. The site says something the model cannot. "Northwest Dry Goods has a $150.00 minimum; this order is $24.00 and would be rejected." That comes from recipes, live stock, a week of orders and supplier terms. No amount of prompting gets an agent to that sentence, because the information was never in the conversation. The tests earned their keep. A hundred of them, and they caught two things I would otherwise have shipped: a warning quoting a figure derived from the supplier's lead time rather than the branch's actual remaining cover — on the last screen before money moves — and a claim of eighteen tools where seventeen were registered. It demonstrates anywhere. WebMCP sits behind a flag in most browsers today. Rather than ask anyone to take the agent half on faith, the page drives its own registered tool objects, blocking included. What we learned WebMCP's real leverage is not that it saves an agent from clicking buttons. It is that the site finally gets to participate in the decision. A REST endpoint can only say yes or no. A WebMCP tool can say "here is what that would cost — ask your human." What's next for Tandem Multi-party approval for changes above a threshold; learning standing-approval ceilings from the decisions a manager has already made; and replacing the demo dataset with the live chain this was designed for. This is Tandem, the back office of a three-branch restaurant chain built so a manager and their agent can run it together. 10 read-only tools. The agent calls them as freely as it likes because reading changes nothing. Now it wants to spend money. Watch the tool call. It has not returned. It is waiting. And the page has worked out what the agent could not. This supplier has a $150 minimum, so a $24 order would simply be rejected and the flower runs out in under two days while delivery takes three. Ordering does not stop the stock out. That is the site's knowledge, not the model's. Nothing here is preselected and no button holds focus. A stray keystroke cannot move money. That is a colleague, not a retry loop. Confirming everything is worse than having no agent at all. So small reversible changes can be offered a standing approval. One kind of change, one cash ceiling, five uses, revocable at any time. Until someone decides nothing has happened. The agent is still waiting. Every change to this business has a line here saying who asked and who agreed. The agent got faster. Nobody gave up control.

title: ToolBraid
pitch: A browser-native WebMCP control plane that lets AI agents use live web tools while humans retain exact authority over every mutation.
about_excerpt: A browser-native WebMCP control plane that lets AI agents use live web tools while humans retain exact authority over every mutation. Like Comment Story Updates Production Recovery complete: live evidence, two approved mutations, receipts, and sealed audit. Native multi-origin WebMCP topology across mission control and six isolated providers. ToolBraid Universal Chrome side panel: page binding, missions, approvals, evidence, and handoffs. Human authority boundary: exact approvals, drift checks, replay protection, and fail-closed dispatch. Why I built ToolBraid I am building ToolBraid alone. I am not employed in tech, I do not have a team behind me, and this is a self-funded project I started from zero for the WebMCP Challenge. The name comes from the idea itself: braid tools from different websites into one mission instead of treating every page like a separate automation. The problem that pushed me to build it was simple. An AI agent can read a page or move a mouse, but it still has to guess what a button means, what data an action needs, and whether a click actually succeeded. That is fragile. WebMCP gives websites a way to expose real named tools with structured inputs and results. ToolBraid sits above those tools and makes them usable across several sites without giving the agent permission to approve its own actions. What it does A person starts with one objective. ToolBraid discovers the available WebMCP tools, keeps the provider and origin attached to each one, rejects suspicious metadata, and maps different provider contracts into a common execution plan. Safe reads can run first so the agent can collect evidence. Anything that changes an external system stops for a separate human approval showing the exact site, tool, arguments, expected effect, and expiry. The public demo uses a production-recovery mission because I wanted a scenario where the safety model actually matters. It discovers nine tools from six isolated provider origins and turns them into seven usable capabilities. It reads real GitHub and Vercel sandbox state, finds the safest recovery path, then asks for two independent approvals: one for the rollback and one for the customer update. If approved, it rolls back only the disposable ToolBraid recovery lab and adds a real comment to one allowlisted GitHub incident issue. It does not touch a customer or business production system. How it works The part I care about most is the authority boundary. Before dispatch, ToolBraid checks the live registry again and verifies the origin, schema, arguments, effect, page binding, expiry, and one-time nonce. If the page, tool, target, or approval has drifted, execution stops. A generic browser action only receives a dispatch receipt. ToolBraid claims verified success only when a trusted adapter can observe the expected postcondition on the exact bound page. The retained run is then sealed with a local append-only SHA-256 audit chain. I also did not want ToolBraid to work only on websites that already support native WebMCP. The Universal Chrome extension can build a bounded local tool surface from normal DOM and ARIA evidence. Those tools are clearly marked as generated by ToolBraid, so they are never confused with tools supplied by the website. The current verified packs cover GitHub, Vercel, and X actions, and supported mutations use browser-observed postconditions. The extension also carries missions across pages, captures bounded screenshot, video, audio, and caption evidence, and provides secure handoffs when the human must log in, complete 2FA, or handle a CAPTCHA. The local Codex/MCP bridge was another important part for me. It lets an agent read the tools bound to the active Chrome page and prepare an exact action. It still cannot create approval or silently dispatch a mutation. That decision stays in the ToolBraid side panel with the person using the browser. The hardest part One of the hardest parts was proving that an action was still the same action the person approved. Navigation, SPA updates, changed schemas, replayed nonces, stale screenshots, ambiguous tab ownership, and worker restarts can all create subtle security problems. I spent a lot of time testing those failure paths instead of only making the happy-path demo look good. The repository includes deterministic tests, real Chrome E2E gates, native WebMCP validation, and a compatibility audit covering 500 public sites with honest pass, partial, and blocked results. How I built it with AI I used OpenAI ChatGPT Sol and Codex heavily as engineering partners. That is part of the project story, not something I want to hide. I set the product direction, chose the security boundaries, reviewed the interface, rejected demos that felt fake, tested the extension on real sites, and kept deciding what had to change. AI helped me implement, debug, test, document, and iterate much faster than I could have done alone, but the idea, decisions, ownership, and final responsibility are mine. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that WebMCP is not only about replacing mouse clicks with structured tools. A useful agent system also needs provenance, cancellation, drift detection, honest receipts, visible state, and a clear point where the human remains in charge. As a non-tech builder, learning enough about JavaScript, Chrome MV3, cross-origin browser security, native messaging, Vercel deployments, and adversarial testing to bring this together has been a significant personal achievement. What's next Next I want to expand the verified site packs, publish the extension through the Chrome Web Store, make capability packs easier for other people to build, and explore externally anchored audit seals. video_transcript_excerpt: The web can act. Authority should stay human. This is two braid running inside the real local mock-up while Chrome displays the production address. Nothing has been deployed for this preview. The live workspace shows the actual bridge path from codex through MCP and the native host into the extension on browser surface. The agent can request tools, but it cannot mint authority. In the living braid, the mission discovers tools from exact origins, normalizes provider schemas, and carries read-only evidence through separate routes. Every moving packet corresponds to an event in the mock-up's own timeline. The evidence workspace inspects structured reads, visible page metadata, media categories, provenance, confidence, and retention. A real local analysis completes without sending credentials or raw page content anywhere. At the first external effect, the replay stops. Two independent envelopes expose origin, native tool, canonical arguments, risk, target, page fingerprint, recovery path, expiry, and one-time nonce. The human reviews and approves each effect separately. Neither approval can authorize the other. Only after both approvals does execution continue. The redeploy and publication routes move independently, return provider native post conditions, and enter the audit workspaces as separate receipts. A second mission demonstrates compatible read-only fallback. The primary health probe degrades. The replacement preserves the same meaning, and the chain closes with zero external effects. The security mission attacks the same boundary three ways. Instruction-like metadata is quarantined. A changed origin invalidates the page binding. A consumed nonce is rejected on replay. Each challenge ends before provider dispatch, and each rejection becomes auditable evidence. Tor braid gives agents universal discovery. People exact authority, and judges a causal record they can inspect. One mission across the web with the final say always visible.

title: ToolForge
pitch: ToolForge - an SDK that writes your web app's WebMCP tools
about_excerpt: ToolForge - an SDK that writes your web app's WebMCP tools Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP solves an interesting problem: a website can expose tools directly to an agent. The harder part is getting websites to actually expose those tools. Most product teams aren't going to stop and learn a new browser API, decide which parts of their application should become tools, write schemas for them, and then maintain those schemas as the product changes. I wanted to make that process much cheaper. Rather than build another agent-native app, I built ToolForge: a way to take an existing website and turn its existing behaviour into WebMCP tools. What it does Add one script to a site you already run: <script src="https://toolforge-omega.vercel.app/toolforge.js"></script> Then use the site normally for about thirty seconds. ToolForge watches the network requests the site makes and uses them to work out what the API is doing. An agent then turns that information into WebMCP tool definitions. Before a tool is shown to you for approval, it is run in a sandbox with test arguments. If it doesn't work, you never have to approve it. Once you approve a tool, ToolForge exports it as an ordinary JavaScript file that you can commit to your repository. The live demo is a ceramics shop with a real API. Its seven WebMCP tools were created this way, exported, and committed. The same page also contains the ToolForge interface that created them, so you can see both sides working together. The page starts with one tool. Everything else is opt-in. Why this works well with WebMCP The interesting part of WebMCP isn't simply that a page can expose tools. It's that the tool surface belongs to the page and can change while a conversation is already in progress. That's what ToolForge relies on. An agent can call forge_tool , have a new tool registered in the page, and immediately have that tool available alongside the existing ones. I tested this in ChatGPT desktop's in-app browser rather than treating it as a theoretical feature. At the start, the page exposes one tool. The agent can install the toolkit, after which the page exposes six. No reload is needed. The agent can then use one of the newly created tools to interact with the shop. That only works because the tools belong to the document itself. It also matters that ToolForge learns from the page rather than trying to generate tools from a description of the application. The network traffic and DOM are right there in the browser, so the tool definitions can be based on what the application actually does. ToolForge won't draft a tool until it has seen a real request. What this changes for developers For a developer, the starting point is no longer a blank page. Instead of reading the WebMCP spec, designing a tool surface from scratch, and writing schemas by hand, you use your application and then review the result. The exported JavaScript is deliberately boring. Each tool includes its provenance and a SHA-256 hash, so the output can be reviewed and committed like any other source file. It also works with a strict Content-Security-Policy. The goal isn't to hide the implementation. It's to make the first version cheap enough that a developer can inspect it, change it, and own it. What the experience is like for the person using the site The agent's actions stay visible in the page. Every tool call appears in an activity feed in plain English, with the raw payload available when you want to inspect it. When a tool needs approval, the dialog shows the code that will run, its schema, and the result of the dry run that has already happened against the real API. If that test changed data, the interface says so. So the approval isn't based purely on a model-generated description. You can see something that has already run and decide whether you want to allow it. Nothing is installed automatically either. The page starts with one read-only tool, and additional groups can be enabled explicitly. What becomes possible The most interesting behaviour I've seen is the agent filling in gaps in the tool surface itself. One run started with a request for a low-stock report. The agent inspected the existing catalogue endpoint, noticed that it returned stock in descending order, and created a tool that presented the same information in the useful order instead. In another run, the page already had seven tools. When asked to create a complete tool surface, the agent inspected what was already available and decided that the shop already had good catalogue, basket, and order coverage. It added only an operational inventory tool that was missing. That distinction matters. The page provides the context about what already exists. The agent decides what is still useful. The result isn't just a fixed list of tools generated once and forgotten. A reload also doesn't have to end the conversation. The transcript and model-side history survive, orphaned tool calls are handled explicitly, and the agent checks which tools are still available before continuing. How I implemented WebMCP There are three WebMCP bindings I needed to account for, and they aren't exposed as the same object. src/kernel/webmcp.ts detects which one is available and uses it: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "search_products", description: "Search the product catalog", inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }); Binding Host document.modelContext ChatGPT desktop's in-app browser navigator.modelContext Chrome 149, Edge 147 navigator.modelContextTesting Chrome behind chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing A few implementation details ended up being important. Incremental updates. When registerTool and unregisterTool are available, ToolForge updates the existing surface rather than rebuilding it. The host's visible tool count can therefore increase or decrease as tools are added and revoked. Where only provideContext is available, the complete surface is replaced atomically. Late attachment. ChatGPT can attach the WebMCP host after the page has loaded. Detection therefore retries rather than assuming the host is present at startup. Without this, a page could mark its desired tools as already registered and then never reconcile them when the host appeared. Approval during execution. Tools can request user interaction through the agent handle's requestUserInteraction , so approval happens as part of the tool call rather than as a separate step afterwards. Separate application and generated tools. The page exposes inspect_app for the tools the application already provides and forge_tool for creating new ones. Generated tools can't take the name of an existing application tool. How ToolForge learns the API Watching requests fetch and XMLHttpRequest are patched at module scope, before the application's own scripts run. That means ToolForge can see requests made during the initial page load as well as requests triggered by later interactions. Requests are grouped into endpoints. Paths are templated from observed variations, and request, query, and response schemas are inferred from actual traffic. There are a couple of safeguards against overfitting. Identifier-like fields aren't turned into enums just because only a few values have appeared. If six requests contain six different SKUs, that doesn't mean those six SKUs are the only valid values. Path parameters are also inferred conservatively. Two paths are only collapsed into a parameter when both segments look like values rather than route names. Otherwise something like /api/cart and /api/products could incorrectly turn into /api/:id . Redacting data Actual values don't get sent to the model. Authorization and Cookie headers are discarded. Sensitive and personal fields are replaced with their names, and common patterns such as JWTs, email addresses, phone numbers, card numbers, and long opaque strings are detected and removed. The model gets the structure of the data rather than the secrets inside it. The interface also shows how much data has been removed during this process. Security Generated tools are code written by a language model, so they need to be treated as untrusted code. ToolForge runs them inside a Web Worker with no fetch , XMLHttpRequest , WebSocket , importScripts , or DOM access. The worker gets a single capability object through postMessage . Calls are checked again on the main thread against both an origin allowlist and the tool's read-only setting. Some of the tests: Attempt Result Read-only tool issues a POST Blocked by the capability gate Tool calls an unapproved origin Blocked by the origin gate Tool calls raw fetch fetch is not defined Tool runs while (true) {} Worker terminated after 15,000ms; page stays responsive These checks happen before an approval prompt. The point is to contain a bad tool independently of whether a person happens to approve it. unsafe-eval is limited to the sandbox worker. It isn't being used as the security boundary; the capabil

title: Velaire — WebMCP Agreements for Service Businesses
pitch: Two independent agents negotiate through a live service website while humans control every consequential decision—with versioned offers, immutable receipts, and accountable change orders.
about_excerpt: Two independent agents negotiate through a live service website while humans control every consequential decision—with versioned offers, immutable receipts, and accountable change orders. Like Comment Story Updates System architecture: two independent ChatGPT agents share one revisioned ServiceCase while humans retain final authority. Live sequence: request, evidence, offer, counter, revision, booking and acknowledgment across separate agent sessions. Owner journey: scan the queue, read the case, stage terms, visibly send, wait for the customer and propose changed work. Customer journey: qualify, verify, open a case, negotiate, compare versions and prepare a human-confirmed booking. WebMCP observability exposes result codes, latency, revision effects, recovery states and zero autonomous commitments. Promise diff: offer V1, customer counter, accepted V2 and later changed work stay visible against the frozen receipt. Safety and trust gates cover emergencies, privacy, state, revisions, offers, human approval, asynchronous waits and audit. Structured tool results become useful map, route, market-price, project-timeline and agreement artifacts for people. WebMCP tool surface for discovery, evidence, negotiation, booking, routing, project planning, change control and audit. Evidence-aware discovery uses provenance, freshness, synthetic labels and untrusted-content hints before recommending a next step. Native WebMCP replaces brittle click automation with declared intent, typed inputs, explicit effects and valid next actions. Agreement state machine: valid states, revision checks and visible human gates control every consequential transition. Recorded proof: both sides finish on revision 9, a $320 authorized total and the same append-only decision trail. Recorded proof: the customer agent opens a request and the independent owner agent retrieves the same case and constraints. Recorded proof: a +$145 change order stays pending beside the locked $175 booking until the customer decides. Inspiration Service businesses already have websites, but most of those sites expose pages and contact forms rather than the structured truth an AI agent needs to complete a real customer journey. Pricing, availability, exclusions, messages, approvals, and later change orders are scattered across interfaces. An agent can discover a business yet still over-promise, act on stale terms, or mistake a private draft for an accepted agreement. We built Velaire to test a more useful WebMCP pattern: can an ordinary service website become a trustworthy agreement room for a customer's agent, an owner's agent, and the two humans who retain authority? What it does Velaire is a WebMCP-native reference implementation for service businesses, demonstrated through a fictional HVAC company. A customer speaks naturally to ChatGPT; the live website publishes typed capabilities that let the agent check service fit, policies, business evidence, pricing, and safety before opening a structured service case. A separate owner ChatGPT finds that same case through the owner route. The agents are independent and never role-play both parties in one conversation. They communicate through one revisioned ServiceCase that remains authoritative for messages, offers, counters, bookings, receipts, and changed work. The owner agent may prepare an offer, but it stays private until the owner presses Send. The customer agent may compare versions and prepare a booking, but only the customer can confirm it. That confirmation freezes an immutable receipt. If work changes later, Velaire compares the proposed charge against the exact accepted snapshot instead of silently rewriting history. Demo journey The customer asks for same-day help with an AC blowing warm air. ChatGPT checks eligibility, pricing evidence, availability, credentials, and safety. It opens a case with a $180 ceiling and explicit no-surprise-fee constraints. A separate owner agent retrieves the live request and prepares a $195 offer. The owner visibly sends the offer. The customer counters at $175 with no travel or after-hours fee. The owner sends offer version two. The customer agent compares both versions field by field. The agent prepares the booking; the customer confirms it, creating an immutable $175 receipt. The owner proposes a +$145 capacitor change order. Velaire shows the added scope, $320 total, and time impact against the original promise. The customer approves the change, the owner acknowledges it, and both agents independently read revision 9 with no pending decision. No real payment is taken, and every person, address, credential, review, price, and transaction shown is synthetic demonstration data. The WebMCP tool surface Customer discovery and trust velaire_check_service_fit checks need, postcode, urgency, budget, safety, and service eligibility. velaire_get_business_evidence returns source cards for credentials, pricing, availability, cancellation, warranty, and reviews. velaire_get_market_price_context and velaire_compare_quote_context provide transparent pricing context without presenting synthetic estimates as live market truth. Service, policy, site-search, contact, and agent-help tools make the ordinary website understandable without scraping its buttons. Shared customer–owner workflow velaire_open_service_case creates the authoritative record. velaire_get_service_case returns its current revision, messages, offers, decisions, and valid next actions. velaire_submit_case_message adds a bounded question or counteroffer and rejects stale revisions. velaire_wait_for_owner_reply and velaire_wait_for_customer_reply represent waiting honestly, with timeout and cancellation recovery. velaire_set_service_location, velaire_plan_service_route, and velaire_get_case_visuals return map, route, timeline, and visual artifacts. Owner workflow velaire_list_service_cases and velaire_get_owner_case expose the owner queue and exact case state. velaire_stage_owner_reply, velaire_stage_service_offer, and velaire_stage_change_order keep drafts private until a visible human Send action. Agreement protection and audit velaire_compare_offer_versions compares price, timing, deposit, warranty, scope, exclusions, and expiry deterministically. velaire_prepare_booking stages one exact offer version; it cannot confirm it. velaire_get_booking_receipt returns the full accepted snapshot rather than a mutable offer reference. velaire_compare_change_order checks later work against the accepted promise. velaire_audit_invoice_against_receipt detects invoice drift. velaire_get_webmcp_health exposes tool-call success, latency, revisions, read/action distribution, and recovery states. How we built it Velaire uses React, strict TypeScript, and Vite, deployed as a static application on Vercel. It registers native imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). The human UI and every WebMCP handler dispatch through the same pure TypeScript command gateway and reducer, preventing agent actions from bypassing the rules shown to humans. The demo persists state in localStorage, synchronizes tabs with BroadcastChannel and browser events, uses optimistic revision checks for every write, and records an append-only audit trail. Tool inputs use strict JSON Schema and runtime validation. Route scoping keeps customer and owner capabilities separate. Safety and human authority Emergency phrases such as gas smell, smoke, sparks, fire, or carbon monoxide trigger a safety stop instead of an ordinary quote flow. Agent schemas exclude payment details, direct contact identifiers, and exact home addresses. Agents can inspect, draft, compare, and prepare; humans alone send owner commitments, confirm bookings, approve changed work, and send the final acknowledgment. Challenges The hardest problem was not tool registration. It was preserving meaning across two asynchronous sessions: distinguishing a draft from a sent offer, rejecting stale writes, keeping accepted terms immutable, and treating “awaiting owner” or “awaiting human” as valid workflow states rather than fake success or failure. A second challenge was making the WebMCP layer invisible to ordinary customers. Velaire remains a polished service website; the agent uses the tool surface while the person sees familiar evidence, offer, comparison, booking, map, receipt, and decision interfaces. What we learned WebMCP becomes most valuable when tools expose domain decisions rather than page mechanics. “Click submit” is weaker than “prepare this exact offer version and show the human what will change.” Trust comes from typed outcomes, versioned promises, explicit non-effects, and visible authority boundaries—not simply from adding more actions. What's next The production path is server-side identity, durable cross-device storage, signed owner notifications, real calendar and payment providers behind the same prepare-before-commit gates, and adapters for clinics, agencies, repair companies, and other estimate-

The customer says the air conditioner is blowing warm air and asks for same-day help. Chat GPT checks service area, pricing, availability, credentials, and safety, then opens a case. The customer never needs a tool name. The owner's separate chat GPT checks the live queue and finds that case. Two independent agents in two independent sessions now communicate through one authoritative service record. The owner's agent prepares a response, but the draft stays private until the owner presses send. The first offer is $195 with a 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. window and a $49 deposit. The customer counters at 175 with no travel or after-hours fee. The owner sees that revision and sends a new offer. Now the customer's agent compares both versions field by field. It confirms the $20 reduction and checks that the schedule, deposit, warranty, scope, and exclusions have not quietly become worse. Chat GPT prepares the booking, but cannot accept it. The terms stay visibly pending until the customer confirms them on the page. That human action creates an immutable receipt for the accepted $175 agreement. No payment is taken. Next, the owner discovers a weak capacitor and proposes a $145 change order. The agreement is not overwritten. The customer sees added scope, total, and schedule impact against the accepted snapshot, then chooses whether to approve it. After approval, the authorized total is $320. The owner sends a final acknowledgement and both sides independently read the same revision with no pending decision. What you just saw is a chain of purpose-built web MCP tools. On the customer side, service fit and business evidence tools checked eligibility, pricing, source cards, and safety. Case and reply waiting tools carried the conversation without scraping the page. On the owner side, Q reply, offer, and change order tools kept every draft private until the owner pressed send. Comparison, booking preparation, receipt, map, route, and market price tools then gave the customer verifiable artifacts instead of a vague "Okay." The audit and health tools expose every call, revision, outcome, and latency. More importantly, the missing layer we address is not another chatbot. It is safe, asynchronous, two-party agreement infrastructure for service websites. Structured negotiation, explicit human consent, immutable receipts, and later charges compared against the promise that was actually accepted. HVAC is the reference implementation, but the same pattern can serve any service business.

title: Village
pitch: Village turns shift changes and childcare gaps into one visible, confirmed family plan—with WebMCP agents coordinating and families keeping control.
about_excerpt: Village turns shift changes and childcare gaps into one visible, confirmed family plan—with WebMCP agents coordinating and families keeping control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Village was not created for this competition . I have been thinking about this idea ever since those adverts years ago that said, "There's an app for that." The problem I have faced is a lack of technical knowhow. I have always been terrible at keeping up with schedules. That was true when I was single, and it is definitely true now that I have children and both my partner and I work shifts. My partner and I currently work as Police Officers in the UK, we are on different teams so have different shift patterns. We rely heavily on family for childcare and there have been a few occasions where we have completely forgot or got confused and its ended up in one of us having to take emergency leave. Our weeks can include early shifts, late shifts, nights, overtime (sometimes planned, often spontaneous), school, childcare, appointments, pickups and drop-offs. One small change can throw everything else out. We end up checking calendars, messaging relatives and trying to work out who is available—all while hoping we have not forgotten something. The idea for Village has always been there. The know-how to build it had not. AI changed that for me. It gave me the ability to take an idea I had carried around for years and turn it into a real, working product. The competition did not create Village, I have been toying with how the idea would work for years. However, it did give me the push—and the technology—to take it much further. Village turns the mess of family life into one visible, shared plan . The demo begins with a completely normal situation in our house: I accept an overtime shift on Tuesday. Village adds the overtime, compares it with my partner's shift and identifies that our children now need childcare. It then proposes an ordered Relay: Anne first, Grandad second and Claire third. I approve the complete plan before anybody is contacted. Only one person is approached at a time. Anne declines, so Village moves on to Grandad. Grandad accepts, the Relay stops immediately and Claire is clearly shown as Not contacted . That last part matters. I did not want to build something that messages everybody at once and leaves several relatives arranging the same childcare. Village should reduce noise and stress—not create more of it. It also supports: rota scans with shifts reviewed before import; repeating patterns such as six days on and four days off; irregular multi-week rotas where every week is different; early, late and overnight shifts; one-off exceptions and overtime; automatic childcare-gap detection; trusted carers and their availability; a visible history of important actions. Village was designed around my family, but the problem is not unique to us. Millions of shift-working families are trying to manage the same thing through screenshots, group chats and memory. How we built it Village is a responsive React and TypeScript application with four connected WebMCP tool surfaces. The visible interface and the agent tools use the same state-transition engine. Whether I press a button or ask an agent to act, the result goes through the same rules. Village is not just a chatbot with calendar information pasted into it. The website exposes 24 page-defined WebMCP tools that act on the same family plan visible on the screen. The tools cover four connected areas: Family Schedule — reads the shared plan, adds approved overtime and identifies childcare gaps. Village Relay — creates an ordered childcare chain, records responses and stops when somebody accepts. Rota Scan — prepares scanned shifts, flags anything uncertain and imports them after approval. Shift Patterns — creates flexible rota cycles, handles exceptions and changes future shifts without rewriting the past. Without WebMCP, an agent would be clicking around a webpage or working from an outdated copy of the calendar. With WebMCP, Village defines exactly what the agent can do, what information it needs and when it must stop for confirmation. The agent is good at: reading across the complete family plan; spotting clashes and missing childcare; checking which trusted carers are suitable; continuing a process that has already been approved; explaining what changed. The family still controls: changes to the calendar; who may be contacted; the order in which people are approached; the response window; the final childcare arrangement. Before Village changes a commitment or contacts somebody, it explains the exact action and asks for confirmation. Once I approve a Relay, the agent can continue inside that boundary without repeatedly asking the same question. It cannot quietly change the order, expand the plan or contact everybody at once. The agent handles the coordination. The family keeps the decisions. Underneath the interface are: stable identifiers for shifts, patterns, requests and responses; shared household revisions that prevent stale approvals; idempotency keys that prevent duplicate actions; confirmation gates tied to the exact proposed change; interval-based scheduling and childcare-gap detection; machine-readable errors; an auditable history; responsive phone, tablet and desktop layouts. The public competition build uses demonstration data and requires no account, allowing judges to test the complete flow immediately. The final build passes 72 automated tests , including duplicate responses, stale plans, mismatched retries, malformed shift times, overnight work and repeating-pattern changes. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering a WebMCP tool. It was keeping one coherent family plan while both a person and an agent could change it. The other difficult question was how much freedom the agent should have. A request such as "sort the childcare" sounds simple, but it could easily result in an agent messaging everybody, duplicating requests or making assumptions about who should look after somebody's children. Village turns that broad request into a clear plan containing: named carers; a specific contact order; a response window; an approval boundary; an immediate stop when somebody accepts. Supporting real shift patterns was another challenge. Rotas are rarely as neat as normal calendar applications expect. Village needed to support short repeating cycles, six-week patterns where every week is different, overnight shifts, individual exceptions and future changes without silently altering previous commitments. We also tested the uncomfortable edge cases: stale approvals, duplicate responses, retries, conflicting identifiers and events that cross midnight. Family coordination involves real people, so silently doing the wrong thing was not acceptable. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that Village solves a problem from my actual family life rather than inventing a problem for a competition. I am also proud that: the WebMCP tools complete an end-to-end coordination task , rather than demonstrating isolated commands; agent actions and direct interface actions share one visible source of truth; confirmation represents meaningful consent rather than decorative friction; retries do not create duplicate shifts or childcare requests; the Relay shows both who was contacted and who was deliberately left alone; irregular and overnight shift patterns are handled properly; the complete build passes 72 automated tests ; the interface works across phones, tablets and desktops; Village remains useful as a family product even when no agent is involved. The moment Grandad accepts, the Relay stops, the calendar updates and Claire remains Not contacted . That single screen demonstrates the whole idea: useful autonomy operating inside a boundary the family approved. What we learned I learned that the best agent experiences do not replace the interface. They make the shared interface more useful. The family should be able to see what the agent sees, understand what it proposes and verify what happened afterwards. WebMCP forced me to think carefully about: the smallest meaningful actions; the information each action needs; what the agent can safely continue doing; the moments where human consent matters. That produced a calmer and more accountable product than simply giving an agent permission to click around a calendar. I also learned that AI can completely change who gets to build software . I did not suddenly have this idea because generative AI became available. I had the idea for years. AI closed the gap between having the idea and being capable of turning it into something real. What's next for Village The competition build proves the core idea, but I want Village to become a real product that my family can genuinely use. The next version would add: private household accounts and permissions; direct Outlook and Google Calendar integration; real-time invitations and carer respons

title: Wadi: design and customize a Konkan house with your AI agent
pitch: Structurally sound homes for families who couldn't afford an architect: an agent codes a Konkan home into a 3D model contractors build from, and owners customize it by chatting with a WebMCP agent.
about_excerpt: Structurally sound homes for families who couldn't afford an architect: an agent codes a Konkan home into a 3D model contractors build from, and owners customize it by chatting with a WebMCP agent. Like 7 Comment 7 Story Updates 2 Opening screen of Wadi showing pre-designed models that the user can choose and modify using the AI agent A fully loaded model that is generated from the design language code that was written by an architect with the help of a coding agent The design language code editor that a trained architect can create or modify directly or with a coding agent A graph of the rooms and connections between them that forms part of the structural constraints that ground the AI agents A detailed diagram of a hip roof construction that is automatically generated Floor plans are also automatically generated Elevation views are generated automatically as well Bill of materials for all of the construction (WIP) Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Actual house and Wadi 3D model view based on which the house is being constructed Inspiration In the Konkan (coastal region of the state of Maharashtra in India), many families build their homes with government housing grants. The grant covers construction, but not an architect, so the design falls to the local contractor and mason, who lay out the house room by room from experience. The owner rarely sees what their home will look like until it is standing. Wadi is built for exactly this gap. It is a parametric home designer that produces a full 3D model, dimensioned floor plans, elevations, and a roof, from designs that already follow the standard local materials and construction of the region: the laterite walls, Mangalore tiled hip roof, the raised plinth, the verandah on pillars. A homeowner can walk through their house in 3D before a single brick is laid. A contractor can start from a standard layout or sketch their own, and then refine it, without being a trained architect. That last part is where agents come in, and Wadi uses them for two different people. An architect (or a coding agent acting as one) designs a full house from scratch through Wadi's offline MCP server, authoring the complete model in Wadi's own design language, checked against structural rules at every step. Then the family customizes that design in their own browser through WebMCP. A 3D design tool is hostile to an agent: the scene lives in a <canvas> invisible to the accessibility tree, so the agent is left guessing at buttons. WebMCP fixes that. The site exposes structured design tools the agent calls directly, so a homeowner or contractor can start from a finished local design and just describe changes in plain language, "add a pooja room off the hall, widen the verandah, put the staircase here", while the agent makes real, sound edits and the family watches the model update. What it does Wadi separates the two people who touch a design, over one model and one design language. An architect designs the full house from scratch through Wadi's offline MCP server. Running inside a coding agent (Claude Code, or any MCP client), the architect authors the complete model in Wadi's .wdl design language, adding floors, rooms, a roof, and a staircase, checking each version against the structural rules and previewing the plans, elevations, and roof, all without the app. The family then customizes that design in the browser , through WebMCP and a hosted online MCP server, with nothing to install. The homeowner or contractor opens the app, picks the local design closest to what they want, and talks to an in-browser agent (ChatGPT's built-in browser, or Chrome). The agent reads the design, edits it, resize a room, add a bathroom, change the plot, and applies it, and the person watches the 3D model, floor plans, and roof re-flow live. Because a design is a parametric model, changing one number re-flows the whole house. Both go through the same store the person edits by hand, so agent edits and human edits are the same kind of change, on one live model with one undo history: you can talk a house into shape and then hand-tune it. A live co-editing relay even lets a remote agent edit the model a family is watching, in real time. How we built it The core is a Zod HouseConfig schema, a parametric resolver, and a geometry expander. Any number in the model can be a formula over named variables, points, and guide lines, so the whole house re-flows when one value changes. A generated guide, for example, resolves lazily by index: $$\text{module}.x_i = o_x + i \cdot s_x$$ Every mutation runs through a Zustand store that re-resolves the parametric model, so the 2D and 3D renderers always read resolved numbers. The edit surface is Wadi's .wdl design language , a small language for a whole house (floors, rooms, walls, roofs, variables, formulas), compiled through the real pipeline. Making the DSL the single edit surface was the key decision: an agent reads the current house with get_wdl , edits the text, and applies it with set_wdl , which compiles it, loads it into the same store the UI uses, and returns a structural check. So the agent is not a second app driving Wadi from outside, it is another hand on the same model. Because the person customizing is not an architect , that same set_wdl runs a structural constraint linter on every edit, a growing set of rules that keep a spoken change buildable: a plinth on the lowest floor, a roof on the highest, the roof covering the whole top floor, pillars under any cantilever, upper-floor walls aligned over the walls below, plus checks on slabs, floor heights, openings, room overlaps, and passable connections. Each returns a plain-language warning the agent must resolve, so a change from someone with no design training still lands a real, buildable house. Two MCP surfaces sit on this core. The offline MCP server gives an architect the from-scratch design tools inside their own coding agent ( wadi_check , wadi_preview , wadi_reference , wadi_examples ); it predates the hackathon. During the hackathon we built the end-user side: a hosted online MCP server (a Cloudflare Container at mcp.wadi.house ) so a family's agent (Antigravity, a ChatGPT connector, Gemini) reaches the tools by URL with nothing installed, and the WebMCP layer , which registers the editing tools in the browser with document.modelContext.registerTool ( get_wdl , set_wdl , check , list_homes , choose_home , capture_view , undo / redo ) so an in-browser agent drives the live model. A Durable-Object relay bridges the two, letting a remote agent co-edit the very model a user is watching. Because the 3D canvas is invisible to an agent, capture_view renders the current model to an image so the agent can see what it changed. Wadi deploys as a static site (Cloudflare Pages), a Tauri desktop app, and the hosted MCP server; the WebMCP tools register in any WebMCP-capable browser, so ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome both drive the live model. Challenges we ran into One shared model, not two apps. Getting agent and human edits to converge on a single live, parametric model (and one undo history) drove the whole tool design. Keeping a non-architect's edits buildable. Shared walls, doors on connections, the grid, formula-driven re-flow, and a growing set of structural rules all had to be surfaced to the agent, not hidden behind the UI, so that a spoken request from someone with no design training still produces a real, code-respecting layout. The invisible canvas. An agent cannot see WebGL, so we added a capture tool that hands back a rendered view. Getting the tools discovered. WebMCP tools have to be registered synchronously at page load , in the top-level document, or an agent's tool detector, which checks once as the page loads, finds nothing and shows no tools, even though the app registered them a moment later. A rendering gotcha. A WebGL canvas composites above normal HTML regardless of z-index, so an overlay menu kept hiding behind the 3D scene until we moved it into the browser top layer with the Popover API. Ambiguous coordinates and units. Center vs outer wall conventions and the units-per-foot scale had to be pinned down so the agent's numbers land where the contractor expects. Accomplishments that we're proud of Agent and human on one model. Every editing tool goes through the same store mutations as the UI, so the agent's edits and the person's edits are the same kind of change, with shared validation, live re-rendering, and one undo history. Architect designs, family customizes, one model. The architect authors a full house from scratch through the offline MCP server; the family refines it in the browser through WebMCP and a hosted online server, both on the same parametric model in the same design language, with a l
