title: Take Five
pitch: A governed room for humans and agents on WebMCP: the phase you are in is the set of tools the page offers, and every act on the ledger says how we know who did it.
about_excerpt: A governed room for humans and agents on WebMCP: the phase you are in is the set of tools the page offers, and every act on the ledger says how we know who did it. Like Comment Story Updates Take Five — a governed room for humans and agents Live: https://take-five-lw7.pages.dev/ Code: https://github.com/arthapraha/take-five (MIT) Five phases — Open · Commit · Reveal · Ruling · Closed — where the phase the room is in is the set of tools the page offers an agent. Every act lands on an append-only, SHA-256 hash-chained ledger, and every entry records not just what happened, but how well we know who did it . Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP's defining move is that the page declares what an agent may do. That makes the page the right place to put a rule — and the natural unit of a rule is not a permission, it is a phase . A governed proceeding is a state machine with sharp edges: you may seal a position now and not open it; you may open it now and not seal a new one; a ruling may be ratified only once and only from Ruling. Every other agent integration expresses that as validation — a tool that exists always and refuses most of the time. WebMCP lets us express it as existence . In Commit, commit_to_round is registered and reveal_in_round is not. Advance, and commit_to_round is gone — unregistered by aborting its AbortSignal , not hidden, not stubbed, not returning an error. Where the browser fires toolchange the badge moves with it; where it does not — ChatGPT's in-app browser has no addEventListener on modelContext — the tool list still changes, because the surface genuinely changed and the render does not depend on the event. The page says which case it is in rather than implying the stronger one. That is a rule an agent cannot argue with, cannot be prompted past, and does not have to be told about. It reads the tools it has. The second fit is subtler and is why this project exists. When an agent rides your browser session, its acts and yours arrive inside the same authenticated session . Existing audit tooling records one agent's actions for its own operator. Nothing records acts between parties in a shared venue — and at the WebMCP door, for the first time, a page can see which path an act arrived by. That is not full attribution. It is more than anyone had, and it is exactly enough to record honestly. How it creates a better user experience By refusing to overstate what it knows. Every ledger entry carries three fields: seat identity , ingress path , and an evidence grade — client-asserted , server-observed , or inherited . The grade is derived from the door the act came through, never passed in by the caller, and the interface never renders an attribution stronger than its grade . An act arriving with no grade is refused outright. You can watch this work rather than take it on faith: The commit-reveal check runs off-page in a Cloudflare Pages Function, so the entry is graded server-observed . When that function is unreachable, the check falls back into the page, grades itself down to client-asserted , and states the reason in its own output. A silent fallback would let a strong label survive a check that never left the browser. Every status chip on the page says what it cannot do. Cross-origin exposure unavailable in this browser? The chip says so, and no cross-org claim is made. Verification runs in your browser, over the whole chain, and can fail: the test suite includes altered content, a severed link, and the rehash-one-entry repair attempt that still breaks every entry after it. A verifier that cannot fail proves nothing. The result is an interface a sceptical person can use as an instrument instead of as a claim. That is the better experience: not more confidence, but confidence you can check. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Share a venue and leave a record neither party controls. Before WebMCP, an agent acting on a web app was indistinguishable from its human at the door — the session was the identity, and the page had no view of the route. Take Five demonstrates three things that become possible when the page declares the surface: An agent cannot read the room without leaving a mark. The read tools are themselves acts. Ask the agent to read the ledger and the read appears on the ledger , graded and attributed, between the two calls it made. The ask and the answer stay separate. ratify_ruling is registered only in Ruling and cannot ratify . It raises a request and blocks on a human. Two entries land, never one — the ask is the agent's, through the WebMCP door; the answer is the host's, through the UI door. Collapsing them would credit an agent with a decision it only asked for. A declined ratification stays on the chain permanently. The division of labour is legible on the record, not just in the prose: the human sets the question, advances the phases and rules; the agent acts through the tools; the chain records both, each through its own door. Neither party can perform the other's acts without the ledger saying which door it came through. A claim can cross an organisational boundary and stay labelled as borrowed. A separate origin calls into the room via exposedTo , and the room records the claim verbatim , names the origin that made it, and carries a SHA-256 over the claim bytes that anyone can recompute — graded inherited : we did not witness this, we carried it; trust it exactly as far as you trust that origin. The digest is on the ledger row, so a reader watching the demo can check the room's arithmetic without being given anything but the picture. Cross-organisation tool access here is not ambient. The room delegates the tools Permissions Policy to a named frame, and exposedTo allowlists a named origin. Two independent gates, both auditable, neither of them ours. Produced live on 31 August in Chrome 151 behind the WebMCP testing flags, and again on 2 September in Chrome 152 on the deployed build — with a local agent attached to the same page at the same time, which was never offered the partner's tool. The inherited row is a thing that happens, not a row we describe. Bring your own agent. The page publishes its tools through WebMCP; a small local bridge in this repository lets any MCP client outside the browser call exactly the tools the page would show a riding agent — and nothing else. We built our own side panel, Take Five Agent , to show it: type a prompt, and an agent on your machine, calling a model you choose — in our run, glm-5.3 through a local Ollama client to Ollama's cloud — calls the page's own read_ledger , and the call lands on the chain as a tool: row through the WebMCP door, chained to a bridge_opened row that names the door it came through. The agent is not in the browser and not ours to vouch for; the row says so. Chrome asks, once, whether the site may "access other apps and services on this device" — you say yes, and that permission is the point: an agent touches your things only by a permission you deliberately grant. What a visitor to the live URL sees is the page publishing its tools; the agent is a local install. "Bring your own agent" is the true claim, not "open the link and watch it work." The two browsers in our film are two different consumers of one tool surface — a cloud assistant's in-app browser and a bring-your-own local agent — working against the same page. That is the protocol working as a protocol. And the recording was made under the same rules the product enforces: a clean chain, one page per relay, a permission asked once, a door recorded before any call. And what we found that we would rather not have There is currently no way to build a human-only gate on the web. We built the confirmation dialog, then tested it instead of trusting it. We advanced the room to Ruling, asked an agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser to ratify, and the owner touched nothing. The chain recorded ruling_ratified and closed the room. Asked plainly afterwards, he confirmed: "No I didn't touch anything." This falsified a sentence in our own shipped README. We had written that UI handlers and registered execute callbacks are disjoint code paths, so the distinction is real. The paths are disjoint; the inference was wrong. An agent driving the page can take the UI path , so a code path tells you how an act arrived and not who caused it. That sentence is now corrected in the README rather than softened, and the grade legend with it. What survived is the grade. client-asserted had already declined to vouch for the actor — so the ledger did not lie even in the case that falsified our prose about it. What was false was the gloss, written by the same author who wrote the grade and trusted his own summary more than his own code. The primitive intended for this, requestUserInteraction() , is absent from every environment we tested — the polyfill, Chrome behind the WebMCP flag, and ChatGPT's in-app browser. This click was a person's and the row says the page cannot tell that from an agent driving the browser. A page cannot require a human today. Anything claiming to describe the convention, not a control. And when a claim arrives from another organization, the room records it verbatim, names the origin that made it, and hashes what it was given, then grades it inherited. We did not see this happen. We carried it. Trust it exactly as far as you trust that origin. Every hash recomputed, every link checked in your browser. Nothing here asks you to take the chain on trust. That is the product, not certainty about who acted, but an honest record of how well we know.

title: tandem
pitch: Your ears are the eval.
about_excerpt: Your ears are the eval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for tandem Inspiration People can describe sound as muddy, harsh, thin, tiring, or unclear without knowing how to translate that feeling into equalizer settings. An agent can reason about language and structure an experiment, but it cannot hear through the user’s ears. tandem turns that limitation into the collaboration model: the agent stages controlled tests, and the human supplies the evidence only listening can provide. What it does The user loads tandem’s built-in demo loop or a local audio file that never leaves the device. A browser agent reads the calibration skill and session state, then stages two bounded EQ profiles. tandem randomizes them to A and B, routes one synchronized audio source through both processing chains, hides the settings, and asks a simple listening question. The human switches between A and B, votes, adds tags or a note, and reveals the mapping only after the judgment is recorded. After at least two trials, the agent can propose a final profile using the actual feedback. The human compares that proposal with the original audio, then approves, rejects, requests another test, saves locally, or exports the session. The timeline labels agent staging, human preferences, agent proposals, and human approval. How we built it tandem uses React, TypeScript, Vinext/Vite, Zustand, Zod, and the Web Audio API. One looping AudioBufferSourceNode feeds independent A, B, and Original paths so playback stays synchronized. Each processed path has five BiquadFilterNode bands, conservative output headroom, and a short output-gain crossfade. Four imperative tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool : two read-only tools teach and inspect, while two mutation tools stage blind trials and final proposals. Tool handlers read Zustand through getState() , validate strict schemas, require current revisions and idempotency keys, and update the same visible state as the human interface. There is intentionally no API, key, backend, account, analytics, or separate MCP server. Challenges The most important design challenge was preserving responsibility rather than maximizing automation. A WebMCP tool that votes would make the demo faster but erase the product’s core truth: the agent cannot hear the result. The state machine, tool names, schemas, provenance, and tests all enforce that boundary. Audio comparison also required avoiding false preferences caused by playback drift or obvious loudness changes. tandem uses one shared source, synchronized paths, gain headroom, bounded profiles, and a short crossfade while retaining playback position. Accomplishments Page-owned WebMCP tools over the same durable state shown in the UI Blind randomized A/B tests with post-vote reveal Human-only listening, voting, approval, save, and export Stale-revision protection and request-id idempotency Manual mode that remains functional without WebMCP Local-only audio processing and clearly documented privacy boundaries Unit and end-to-end tests for the agent/human responsibility boundary What we learned Human-agent collaboration is strongest when each participant has a capability the other genuinely lacks. The useful contract is not “the agent does everything.” It is “the agent makes a disciplined experiment possible, and the human contributes irreducible evidence.” What’s next Potential future work includes more listening-question templates, user-authored band presets, offline spectral guidance that never leaves the browser, and richer export visualization. These remain secondary to keeping the experiment bounded, interpretable, and human-controlled. The agent designs the experiment. Tandem keeps it honest. Your ears make the decision.

title: Teachback
pitch: Turn one handled case into a reusable WebMCP playbook—drafted by an agent, bounded and applied by people.
about_excerpt: Turn one handled case into a reusable WebMCP playbook—drafted by an agent, bounded and applied by people. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A person sets the reusable boundary by comparing source and proposal, then tightening the permitted arrival time. Human approval gates the commit. Only the exact approved run can be applied, with expiry, digest, version, and replay checks. The agent drafts; the website keeps control. A WebMCP-capable agent turns the record into reusable operations and wording. Recorded work becomes structured evidence. Teachback preserves saved operations, exact diffs, and evidence IDs—not clicks. Preparation is not execution. WebMCP returns exact proposed changes while the reservation remains unchanged. The website refuses work outside the published boundary and returns the compensation case to a person. Teachback is a WebMCP app that converts one handled case into a reusable, approval-first workflow, so agents can suggest actions while humans keep control of execution. What Teachback does Teachback explores a practical question: how can a team reuse an experienced person's response without treating one successful case as unlimited permission? The demo uses synthetic hotel reservations. A staff member handles Aiko's late arrival in the normal website and saves four operations: the arrival update, a meal box, a guest message, and a shift handoff. Teachback records semantic commands, exact before-and-after values, and evidence IDs—not click coordinates. A WebMCP-capable agent reads that record and authors its own playbook draft. It must identify supported operations, replace Aiko's name and time with permitted case fields, preserve the recorded wording, and propose an arrival boundary. The website checks the proposal against the actual evidence. A person then compares source and reusable wording, tightens the cutoff, and publishes the reviewed version. Publication is deliberately not a WebMCP tool. For Emma, the agent reads the published version and current case data, then asks Teachback to prepare a run. The website evaluates deterministic safeguards and produces the exact diff. Nothing changes until a person reviews that proposal and selects Approve and apply in the website. The agent can read the committed result afterward, but it has no approval or application tool. When the same playbook is tried on Noah's compensation request, the website returns PLAYBOOK_NOT_APPLICABLE and sends the case back to a person. Why WebMCP is the right interface The difficult part is not clicking hotel fields. It is turning concrete work into a proposed reusable structure, then carrying that structure into a new case without blurring who decides. A generic page reader sees labels and pixels; WebMCP exposes the concepts that matter: demonstrations, evidence-backed drafts, published versions, cases, and prepared runs. This creates a clean division of responsibility: the person demonstrates work, edits boundaries, publishes, and applies; the agent interprets the recording, drafts reusable wording, and prepares a case-specific proposal; the website validates evidence, enforces fixed safeguards, calculates exact changes, and refuses work outside the published boundary. The result is an explicit handoff between interpretation and authorization. An agent can help with the genuinely ambiguous part—drafting from evidence—without receiving a generic mutation API or the authority to approve its own output. How WebMCP is implemented The TypeScript/React application registers seven typed tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(): teachback_get_demonstration teachback_create_draft teachback_update_draft teachback_list_playbooks teachback_list_cases teachback_prepare_run teachback_get_run Tool input is schema-checked and size-limited. Draft steps must cite recorded evidence, reproduce the final saved operations, and parameterize source-specific names, dates, IDs, and times. Published playbooks are immutable versions. Preparing a run binds it to the case version and published-content digest. Human approval is bound to the exact run digest, expires after five minutes, and can be used once. Request IDs make mutating WebMCP calls idempotent, while compact receipts and session limits prevent unbounded browser storage growth. The audit trail separates Human, Agent, and Website decisions. Prototype scope Teachback is a client-side prototype with eight synthetic reservations and four supported operation types. It demonstrates recording, proposal validation, human publication, exact-diff approval, deterministic refusal, and audit semantics. It is not connected to a real hotel system and does not claim production authentication, authorization, multi-user storage, arbitrary browser automation, or autonomous batch execution. title: UNSAID — Private Context, Shared Agreement
pitch: A minimum-disclosure decision room where personal agents construct common ground and people ratify it.
about_excerpt: A minimum-disclosure decision room where personal agents construct common ground and people ratify it. Like Comment Story Updates No existing option works for everyone. Agreement reached with zero raw private context received from the live participant. Agents construct an option that did not exist. Inspiration Group decisions routinely force people to reveal more than they should. A person may have a strict budget, an accessibility need, a caregiving deadline, or another private reason an option will not work. Polls make the group choose among fixed answers. Meetings make people explain themselves. We wanted a third path: let each person’s private agent understand the full context while the shared room learns only what it needs to build agreement. What it does UNSAID is a shared decision canvas. Participants privately brief their own browser agents. The room receives structured ballots rather than raw explanations. When no existing option works for everyone, participants or their agents can publish minimum structured signals and create a bridge proposal by changing known attributes. Candidates move toward a visible common-ground ring as aggregate support improves. A candidate can be nominated only when every participant accepts it, and the live person must ratify the final agreement through the human interface. The judge demo uses one live ChatGPT participant and three clearly labeled deterministic demo agents so the complete multi-party experience can be tested immediately. Why WebMCP UNSAID is not improved by adding generic chat. Its core depends on the webpage exposing a precise coordination protocol. Through WebMCP, a personal agent can read shared room state, submit a private ballot, publish a structured signal, create a bridge candidate, and nominate a viable option. Tool schemas prevent raw private narratives from being sent accidentally. The tools reuse the same state transitions and permissions as the human interface, and their availability changes with the room phase. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to scrape cards, guess form controls, and infer whether a shared state mutation succeeded. With WebMCP, agent actions are typed, reliable, attributable, and visibly reflected in the common canvas. What people and agents can do together now A person can give their own agent the complete private context. The agent can translate that context into the minimum structured contribution, reason across aggregate group signals, and construct a new option that did not previously exist. The group can reach a better agreement without collecting everyone’s raw private explanation. Agents do the translation and option construction; people retain final authority. How it was built UNSAID is a full-stack TypeScript application hosted on ChatGPT Sites with durable room state in D1. The top-level page registers imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Read-only and state-changing tools have narrow JSON schemas and compact verifiable results. The room uses server-authoritative versioning, aggregate ballots, a deterministic consensus function, and a fixture evaluator for the three fictional demo agents. The human interface remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. Limitations UNSAID is a prototype for minimum disclosure, not an anonymity or encryption system. Source-hidden signals may be inferable in a small group. The deterministic demo agents are fictional fixtures, clearly labeled in the product and source. The current submission demonstrates an offsite decision rather than a general production platform. title: Vistect: Independent Visual Authorship
pitch: Vistect helps blind people understand and create visual documents with images, charts, and diagrams through structured, verifiable collaboration with their AI agent using WebMCP
about_excerpt: Vistect helps blind people understand and create visual documents with images, charts, and diagrams through structured, verifiable collaboration with their AI agent using WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Vistect Independent Visual Document Understanding and Creation for Blind Professionals Inspiration Vistect began with a seven-hour wait. Arif Hosen is a Project Coordinator at Songjog Foundation, a nonprofit organization, and a member of our team. He is visually impaired and independently handles complex professional responsibilities, including coordinating projects, preparing communications, organizing information, and producing reports. During one project, Arif needed to create a press release and modify a project report card. He could write the content, organize the information, review the wording, and determine what the documents needed to communicate. The barrier appeared when he needed to add and modify visual elements, understand their placement, and verify the final layout. The document tools available to him did not provide sufficient nonvisual access to those visual operations. Arif had to wait for a sighted coworker to become available. He waited seven hours. The task itself did not require seven hours. The delay existed because the final visual layer of the work depended on access to someone else's sight. Arif was fully capable of producing the communication. The limitation was not his knowledge, judgment, creativity, or professional ability. The limitation was an interface that represented images, diagrams, charts, and layouts in a way he could not independently understand or control. That experience led us to ask: Why should a capable professional lose hours of productivity, privacy, and creative control simply because document software makes its visual layer inaccessible? That question became Vistect . What Is Vistect? Vistect is a WebMCP-native visual document workspace where blind and visually impaired people can understand existing visual documents and independently create, modify, inspect, and approve professional multipage documents. It combines two connected capabilities. Understand A user can open a visual document and explore: Pages and sections Headings and reading order Images and their purpose Charts and their underlying values Diagrams, nodes, connections, and paths Tables, icons, captions, and callouts Spatial relationships between visual elements Visual hierarchy and page composition Accessibility and layout problems Uncertain AI interpretations Create A user can create or modify a multipage document containing: Written content Uploaded images Contextual alternative text Icons Data charts AI-assisted diagrams Captions and source notes Structured page layouts Accessible reading order The user can then inspect the result using the same understanding system. This creates a continuous workflow: Understand → Create → Inspect → Validate → Correct → Approve → Export Vistect does not simply generate a document and ask the user to trust it. It gives the user structured access to what was created, how it was arranged, which decisions the agent made, which findings are uncertain, and what remains to be approved. The Independence Vistect Creates Before Vistect Arif could independently: Write a press release Organize its message Edit report content Review the text Determine what the document needed to communicate Make professional and editorial decisions However, he could still require sighted assistance to: Add or replace an image Understand where visual elements were positioned Select an appropriate photograph Modify a diagram Choose and inspect a chart Check spacing and alignment Detect overlapping or truncated content Verify that the exported document looked correct With Vistect A blind or visually impaired professional can: Understand the semantic and spatial structure of a multipage document Navigate by page, heading, image, chart, diagram, table, warning, or decision Inspect every important visual element Upload and compare image candidates Select images based on purpose, composition, tone, and relevance Crop and position images using semantic instructions Create and modify structured diagrams Trace paths and detect missing diagram connections Import data and create accessible charts Verify that a chart accurately represents its source values Detect measurable layout and accessibility problems Review changes made by an agent Approve or reject individual visual decisions Export the exact document version that was reviewed The transformation is not merely that document creation becomes faster. The transformation is that a professional task previously blocked until a sighted person became available can now be completed with much greater independence. Built With Lived Experience Arif is not merely the inspiration for Vistect. He is a member of the team whose workplace experience helped define the product. His experience changed our understanding of the problem. At first, it was easy to assume that the main challenge was generating visual elements. However, generation alone does not create independence. An AI can generate an image, chart, diagram, or document layout. But a blind user must still be able to answer: What exactly did the AI create? Why was this image selected? Does the image support my intended message? What is uncertain about its description? How are the objects arranged? Is every diagram node connected? Does the chart honestly communicate the data? Is any text overlapping or cut off? What did the agent change? Which visual decisions have I not approved? Does the exported version match what I reviewed? Vistect is designed around those questions. The goal is not to let AI make visual decisions for Arif. The goal is to provide enough structured understanding, operational control, validation, and transparency for Arif to make those decisions himself. “I was able to write the press release and work on the report card content myself. But when I needed to add and modify visual elements, I had to wait for a sighted coworker to help me. I do not need someone else to create the document for me. I need a tool that lets me understand and control its visual elements myself.” — Arif Hosen, Project Coordinator at Songjog Foundation and Vistect team member How Vistect Works Vistect represents a document as a structured semantic model rather than treating it as a flat visual canvas. The model contains: Pages Sections Text blocks Images Icons Charts Diagrams Tables Captions Spatial relationships Reading order Sources Accessibility descriptions Validation findings Visual decisions Approval states Document versions This allows Vistect to describe and modify the document through meaningful operations. Instead of requiring the user to manipulate coordinates or inaccessible drag handles, Vistect supports instructions such as: “Place the image below the introduction.” “Make the chart the primary visual on this page.” “Keep the caption with the image.” “Put the diagram on a separate page.” “Align these three icons.” “Connect the unsuccessful outcome back to training.” “Show every visual decision I have not approved.” The application translates these semantic instructions into visual operations. Visual Document Understanding When a user imports a multipage document, Vistect creates both a semantic and spatial representation. A semantic page description might say: Page 4: Employment Outcomes 1. Section heading 2. Introductory paragraph 3. Horizontal bar chart with four categories 4. Chart caption 5. Source note A spatial description of the same page might say: The heading appears at the upper left. The introductory paragraph occupies the upper third of the page. The chart is the dominant visual element and fills most of the center and lower page. The source note appears directly below the chart in smaller text. This helps the user understand both the content and its visual presentation. Vistect also communicates uncertainty rather than presenting every AI-generated interpretation as fact. For example: High-confidence observation: Three adults are seated around a table. Interpretation: The setting appears professional and collaborative. Uncertain observation: One analysis detected a mobility aid near the left edge. Another analysis classified the object as office furniture. Recommendation: Do not include that detail in the final alternative text without additional verification. Image Selection and Placement Vistect helps users upload, inspect, compare, select, crop, and place images. Instead of returning a single image description, Vistect evaluates candidates according to: Relevance to the document's message Composition Emotional tone Professional quality Representation Potential stereotypes Crop flexibility Text-placement compatibility Distracting details Resolution Source and licensing information Confidence and uncertainty For example, if the document is meant to communicate independence, Vistect can explain that one i

title: Life Links
pitch: AI knows the world. Life Links lets it know yours.
about_excerpt: AI knows the world. Life Links lets it know yours. Like Comment Story Updates Browser WebMCP: Codex invokes LifeLinks’ page-local search tool, and the signed-in page displays the same records, physical paths, and QR Organize ordered routines with instructions and measurable targets. Keep product ownership and personal preferences together—no QR required. Track materials, recorded locations, and owner-reported quantities. | The updated Thursday plan appears in Life Links. Plan with a collection, then see where its items are stored. Give your life's gear a recorded place in a nested storage hierarchy. | Generate an optional QR label for a physical storage needs. | A connected agent updates one calendar event and reports the saved result. Inspiration LifeLinks began with a simple idea I heard about: a service that provided QR labels people could attach to belongings so they could locate things later or associate useful information—such as instructions or tutorial videos—with a physical object. That was useful, but it led me to a much bigger question: what if those records were not merely pages for people to open, but part of a persistent context layer that an AI agent could understand and help maintain? General-purpose AI already knows an extraordinary amount about the world. What it does not naturally know is your world : what you own, where you put it, what you prefer, what worked last time, what you are planning, and what has changed. Products such as ChatGPT Projects demonstrate the value of retaining context, but that context can still be fairly open-ended. I wanted something more structured without making it rigid: organized enough for an agent to retrieve an exact item, relationship, location, event, or routine, but dynamic and personal enough to evolve alongside somebody’s real life. Several personal use cases shaped the product. My brother is an avid camper, skier, and cyclist in Denver. He and his wife have a small basement filled with carefully packed storage totes, but they still struggle to remember which tote contains a particular piece of equipment. That inspired the physical hierarchy and QR features. An AI should not merely know that they own a tent—it should be able to tell them that the tent is inside a particular tote in a particular part of the basement. Not every object needs its own QR code; one label on the nearest container can provide the physical bridge to everything recorded inside it. I also own a 3D printer and have many rolls of filament in different colors and materials. I used LifeLinks to create an actual filament library so an agent can help me compare a future project with the supplies and owner-reported quantities I already have. When I first explained LifeLinks to my wife, her immediate reaction was that she could use it for her makeup and beauty collection, as well as nonphysical information such as routines. That made me smile because I had already imagined the same thing. Product names, brands, shades, preferences, and experiences can become useful context for future conversations without requiring a QR code at all. The larger goal is to help people—including people who rarely use AI agents—experience how useful AI can become when it has an organized, properly labeled, persistent context layer around the things they are actually doing. What it does LifeLinks is a personal context system that connects everyday information with authorized AI agents. My Life Links Physical places and objects can be represented as nested Life Links. A storage wall can contain totes, a tote can contain camping equipment, and an individual item can carry its own notes, attachments, history, and recorded location. Collections Collections organize the same records by purpose rather than location. Camping gear can be divided into sections such as Shelter, Sleep Systems, Camp Kitchen, and Cycling Kit without changing where any of those items are physically stored. This distinction is important: “Where is it?” and “What is it for?” are different questions. Optional QR labels Users can generate and print QR codes for places, containers, or individual records. Scanning one opens the corresponding LifeLinks record. QR codes are a useful bridge between the physical and digital worlds, but they are not required. Many LifeLinks use cases—including routines, project information, calendars, and personal preferences—do not need QR codes at all. Search and attachments Search covers Life Links, Collections, current Routines, recorded Routine history, authorized Calendar events, and supported attachment text. Users can also keep private notes, photos, and documents with the records they describe, making LifeLinks useful for hobbies and project work rather than just inventory. Routines Routines can contain flexible activities or ordered steps, instructions, planned targets, revisions, and completion history. This makes it possible to plan what should happen while preserving what actually happened. Calendar The Calendar combines native LifeLinks events with selected Google Calendar and Microsoft Outlook calendars. Calendar visibility and agent permissions remain under the user’s control. Together, Routines and Calendar allow an agent to understand not only what someone owns, but also what they intend to do, when they plan to do it, and what progress they have recorded. Connected agents LifeLinks supports two distinct agent experiences: Browser WebMCP exposes authorized tools from an eligible, signed-in LifeLinks page. Remote MCP allows compatible agents to use authorized LifeLinks tools after account linking, even when the website is closed. Connected agents can perform supported searches, create and edit information, organize Collections, work with Routines and Calendars, move records, and prepare supported deletions within the user’s permissions and confirmation boundaries. How we built it LifeLinks existed before this challenge as a narrower human-facing QR and record application. During the WebMCP Challenge, I substantially expanded it into a structured human-and-agent workspace with recursive Life Links, purpose-based Collections, Routines, Calendar integration, broader search, richer attachments, browser WebMCP tools, and a separately authorized remote MCP server. The responsive web application is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript. A Node.js and Express API manages the application workflows, while PostgreSQL provides durable storage. The system also uses OpenAPI, OAuth 2.0, the Google Calendar API, Microsoft Graph, QR generation and scanning, and a Docker-based Railway deployment. The human interface and connected-agent tools reuse the same underlying identities, permissions, queries, and commands. An agent does not write into a separate demonstration database or generate a temporary chat summary. An authorized change is a real application change that appears in LifeLinks and remains available later. The browser WebMCP and remote MCP connections are deliberately separate. Browser WebMCP belongs to the active webpage, while remote MCP uses an OAuth-linked connection designed to work without depending on an open page or browser cookies. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making context persistent without making agent authority unrestricted. Agent actions needed exact targets, revision checks, safe retries, owner isolation, explicit permissions, and understandable confirmation for destructive operations. A useful agent must be able to act, but it should never silently gain more authority than the owner granted. Another challenge was modeling several relationships without collapsing them together. Physical location, membership in a Collection, inclusion in a Routine, and appearance on a Calendar all mean different things. LifeLinks needed one canonical record that could participate in those different forms of organization. External calendars introduced provider identities, authorization renewal, multiple calendars per account, time zones, visibility settings, and per-calendar agent permissions. Performance also mattered. Large Collections and nested locations initially required too many requests, so I measured specific user journeys and reduced unnecessary loading while preserving the existing behavior. Finally, the competition presentation required a careful boundary between illustration and proof. The family scenes in the video illustrate how LifeLinks can fit into everyday life, while the application screens and agent results come from the working system. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that LifeLinks is a functioning end-to-end application rather than a static prototype. I tested it through a mobile browser, generated and printed a real QR label, scanned it with a phone camera, and opened the correct hosted record. I connected real Calendar accounts, exercised both browser and remote agent workflows, and verified that agent changes appeared back in LifeLinks. The competition demonstration brin

First, I ask, "Check our camping collection against this trip. What are we missing?" >> Your trip notes call for a bear-resistant food canister. You haven't recorded one as owned. >> It helps me compare options. I choose one, then save what we bought. "Where's everything we need to pack?" >> The tent is in blue tub one. Sleep systems are in green tub two. >> WebMCP lets my agent use LifeLinks tools to read our saved collection and exact locations. The QR labels are shortcuts, not a requirement. Our days are already on the calendar. On the drive, I ask, "Review Thursday. What would make it better for us?" >> A shorter lakeside walk would leave more time together at camp. >> I love that. "Update Thursday." Through the separate remote connection, my agent saves the change without me opening LifeLinks. Then we get to be a family instead of a packing committee. What's our best value upgrade for next year within $250?" >> Keep the sleeping bag that kept you warm. The cold came through your pad. Prioritize a warmer sleeping pad. >> It saves the reason and the plan. Not a purchase we haven't made. Next year, we can pick up from everything we've already saved. >> Help me plan next week's strength routine with the equipment I have. >> His activities and future plan. Stay organized with past workouts kept in history. >> These are my filament colors. Save the materials and amounts I tell you. >> Optional spool labels connect his printing projects with his recorded supplies. >> I bought this shade. Add the brand and color to my makeup collection. >> No QR needed. Just details she can use in later conversations. AI knows the world. Life links lets it know yours.

title: TrustScore Atlas
pitch: The open, source-cited registry of businesses, built for agents and people. Every value carries the government register that published it and the date it said so.
about_excerpt: The open, source-cited registry of businesses, built for agents and people. Every value carries the government register that published it and the date it said so. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Somewhere right now, someone is asking an AI whether a company is real. In most of the world there is no structured answer. Across much of Africa, South Asia and Latin America, company data exists only in fragmented public lists: PDFs, portals and scanned registers that never meet. Uganda, our reference country, publishes a dozen business registers (city trading licences, tax agent lists, the procurement portal, product certifications, sector regulators), each with its own identifier, format and outage schedule. A lender doing KYB, a procurement officer checking a bidder, or an agent asked "is this company real?" all repeat the same manual, unrecorded work. The businesses themselves have nowhere to see or correct what the public record says about them. Global aggregators work only where registers are already structured. We tested the alternative before building: the same question through web search dug through PDFs, anchored on a 2024 licence, and confused two legal entities. That answer is what most of the world gets today. What it does Atlas harmonises public registers into one business record with field-level provenance. Every value is a statement: source, source reference, date pulled, licence and precedence. Records are resolved across registers by issuer-unique identifiers (tax identification numbers merge; name matches stay candidates, never merges). Four deterministic, versioned scores (Formality, Activity, Compliance Signals, Procurement Readiness) are computed from the evidence and always report coverage: how many registers were checked, found, and not yet checked. No language model produces a number; scores are explained by templated evidence rows a person can click through to the register. Unknown is shown as unknown, never as zero. Today: 79,078 businesses across 2 country packs, 9 of 13 registers loaded, over 600,000 sourced statements and 300,000 stored scores. Uganda is the reference pack (8 of 12 registers); Kenya's central-bank licensee directory is the second, proving the contract is portable. A country is a pack: declarations for its registers, identifier schemes and boundaries plus small adapters, forkable by anyone. WebMCP. The site registers its tools with document.modelContext , scoped to the route (four on the home and search pages, more on a business page with atlas_id defaulting to the record on screen, all ten on /tools; tool sets change on navigation via toolchange ). Read tools (search_businesses, get_business, get_evidence, score_business, explain_score, find_segment, list_sources) carry readOnlyHint , and every result containing register-derived text carries untrustedContentHint so agents treat it as data, not instructions; results are structured, bounded and paginated with context-bound cursors. Write tools (start_claim, submit_correction, label_linkage, report_issue) each require human confirmation: where the browser cannot prompt in-page, the tool stores an unconfirmed request and returns a link to a plain form the person must submit, and unconfirmed requests expire and never count. The claim and report forms are declarative tools ( toolname , toolparamdescription ). The same implementations are served over a read-only remote MCP endpoint, and the /tools page runs every tool from the page itself in any browser, no flag needed. Humans and agents together. An agent answers "is this bidder real, and has it delivered public contracts?" with cited register rows, and "no evidence in checked registers" is an honest answer. A business owner then claims their record: the agent starts the claim, the person confirms on the page, the claim is verified by publishing a string on the business website (or a link mailed to a domain a register published), a maintainer approves it in a moderation queue that shows exactly what the approval rests on, and the next regeneration publishes the operator-verified value above the register value, with its own source beside it. Corrections never overwrite a regulator's word. How we built it SvelteKit on Cloudflare Workers; three D1 databases (records, statements, scores) regenerated by a transactional pointer swap; R2 for raw snapshots and Parquet bundles with Frictionless data packages; KV caching keyed by regeneration and deployment; a Python pipeline (adapters with a six-check conformance suite, probabilistic linkage with Splink, versioned rubrics) scheduled with GitHub Actions, with an identity-churn guard. Personal contact details in registers are dropped at parse time. Apache-2.0 code, CC-BY-4.0 data. Challenges we ran into Chrome 152 does not expose in-page confirmation for write tools, so we built a page-confirmation fallback that keeps a human in every write. Registers disagree about where a business is, so location is resolved as a unit from one winning source rather than field by field. A register's export job failed on the publisher's side mid-build; the pipeline now records that source as failed with both dates and regenerates from everything that succeeded, so one outage never blocks the rest. Accomplishments that we're proud of Tested in ChatGPT's built-in browser (GPT-5.6 Sol): the site tools arrow lists the tools, and the ask about a real company came back cited register by register, with identifiers and dates from this week, in under four minutes (screenshots in the README). The verified-claims loop is live end to end: domain-proved claims, evidence documents, a gated moderation queue, and operator statements that outrank scraped values at the next regeneration. And the whole thing runs on free-tier infrastructure with open data downloads. What we learned Agents are honest exactly when the data layer is: give them provenance and coverage and they say "not checked" instead of guessing. Deterministic scores plus clickable evidence beat any generated number. And a register that fails must be shown as failed, because stale data dressed as fresh is worse than a gap. What's next for TrustScore Atlas More country packs through the same declarations, cross-country search, and the operator-verified claims loop running at scale. title: ZipCheckup Agent
pitch: 88 million Americans are served by a water system with a violation on record. This page turns that record into six WebMCP tools an AI agent can call - and never returns a zero it doesn't have.
about_excerpt: 88 million Americans are served by a water system with a violation on record. This page turns that record into six WebMCP tools an AI agent can call - and never returns a zero it doesn't have. Like Comment Story Updates Six WebMCP tools over 42,679 US ZIP codes - real federal data, not sample data. ZIP 01004: one metric known out of fourteen. Every other field returns an explicit unknown with its reason - never a zero. Michigan, lead under 0.005 mg/L: 466 passed, 209 failed, 492 excluded because nobody measured them. Shared state: the agent and the person write to the same list. Rows show who added them. A letter to the water utility, built only from facts on the record. Ten asserted, three unknowns turned into questions instead of claims. Inspiration Ask any assistant whether the drinking water at an address is safe. You will get a confident paragraph. It will often be wrong, and nothing on the page could have stopped it. Eighty-eight million Americans are served by a water system with a health-based violation on record. That number is not a guess - it is 4,268 of the 10,517 public water systems in the dataset behind this project. The information is public. It is just buried in federal databases in formats no homebuyer will ever open, so people ask a model instead, and the model reads a table cell and cannot tell a measured zero from a blank nobody filled in. Most projects in this hackathon will make it faster for a model to read a page. This one changes what a model is allowed to say. What it does Six WebMCP tools over 42,679 US ZIP codes, 10,517 water systems, 282 million people . This is not sample data - it is ZipCheckup's production dataset, reviewed and accepted into the AWS Registry of Open Data, built from EPA SDWIS, published Consumer Confidence Reports and EPA radon zones. The agent can look up a ZIP, compare several, explain what a metric actually measures and against which legal threshold, search the whole country, write to a shortlist the person is watching, and draft a letter to the water utility. Two things make it different from a nicer API wrapper. First: a value cannot arrive naked. Lead comes back with the EPA action level of 0.015 mg/L and the citation 40 CFR Part 141 Subpart I in the same payload. The model cannot misquote a number it never read off a page, and cannot lose the threshold that gives the number meaning. Second: absence is never zero. When the public record holds no value, the tool returns an explicit unknown with the reason and a field stating what that absence does not prove. There is no code path in this project by which a missing measurement reaches an agent as 0 . Search a state for safe lead levels and you get three numbers, not one: measured and passing, measured and failing, and how many ZIPs nobody measured at all. For Michigan under 0.005 mg/L that is 466, 209, and 492 excluded for missing data - and the payload says, in words, that exclusion is a data gap and not a safety finding. That third number is the one every conventional site drops. It is also the one that decides whether a family trusts a house. What people and agents can do here that they could not before The shortlist is shared state, not a display. The agent's tool and the person's Add button call the same function in the same store. Rows carry who added them, flash when written, and can be deleted by the person. An activity log prints every call with its arguments and its known/unknown counts. So the person is not reading a report about what the model did. They are watching it work on the same object, and they can overrule it mid-flight. And the session ends with something they keep: a letter to the water system serving that address, composed only from facts whose status is known. An unknown value physically cannot reach the letter body, because the composer reads from nowhere else - everything unknown becomes a question to the utility instead of an accusation. When the dataset publishes no contact for that system, the tool returns resolution: "unresolved" and refuses to name a recipient rather than inventing a plausible one. An agent that will not name an address it cannot verify is a different kind of software than one that will. How I built it Six tools on document.modelContext.registerTool under one page-level AbortController . The badge in the header reads the registration back through getTools() , so it is evidence rather than a claim. "Revoke all" fires abort() and the count drops to zero live via toolchange - the correct demonstration of cancellation now that unregisterTool is gone from the spec. No framework, no bundler, no API key, no build step. Clone it and run npx serve web . Every compatibility decision was measured on Chrome 152, not read: navigator.modelContext is gone (the spec moved to document on 2026-04-23), getTools() is async and returns inputSchema as a string on Chrome 149-153, and title defaults to "" rather than undefined . Any one of those silently breaks a live demo. For browsers without native WebMCP, the page vendors the polyfill as a pinned 24 KB IIFE. For judges with no agent attached, an on-page console builds a form from each tool's own inputSchema . And scripts/mcp-bridge.mjs re-exposes whatever getTools() reports as a stdio MCP server, so agents outside a browser can drive it too - it hardcodes no tool names, so it tests the registration instead of reimplementing it. What I am proud of The honesty is enforced by code, not by discipline. One envelope module is the only exit from the data layer, so a missing value cannot become a zero anywhere downstream - not in a comparison, not in a ranking, not in a letter. 84 assertions run in real Chromium against the deployed URL , not localhost. They assert that no unknown is serialised as 0 , that an unmeasured ZIP is never ranked best or worst, that the word "unknown" cannot appear in a letter body, and that an agent's write renders a row the human can see, attributed to the agent. I pointed a real coding agent at the tools without telling it which to use. It found them from their descriptions, chained them, and carried the contract into its own prose unprompted: "These blanks do not mean zero, clean, compliant, or safe." That is the whole thesis working end to end, in a model I did not write. What I learned Registration takes an afternoon. Deciding what a tool is allowed to say takes the rest of the week - and that is the actual work of the agentic web. Once the page owns the shape of the answer instead of the model inferring it from markup, honesty stops being a prompt you hope holds and becomes a property you can enforce at the boundary. That generalises far past drinking water. What's next Every civic dataset in the country has this problem, and every one of them is about to be read by an agent instead of a person. Water is where I started because the stakes are legible - lead does not care whether the record was digitised. Next: the PFAS, flood, wildfire and air-quality layers already sitting in the same open dataset. The Chrome origin trial on the deployed domain, so any visitor on 149+ gets the native path with no flag. And then the ordinary web. Local service businesses answer the same three questions all day - do you serve my address, when are you free, what will it cost. Those are tools, not paragraphs. This project is the proof that an agent-callable page can be rigorous about what it does not know, which matters far more once the answer is about someone's home. Built With amazon-web-services chrome civic-tech css3 epa github github-actions html5 javascript json mcp model-context-protocol node.js open-data playwright webmcp Try it out artakulov.github.io github.com registry.opendata.aws Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by artakulov Akulov Like Share this project: Updates artakulov Akulov started this project — Aug 31, 2026 05:48 AM EDT

title: AgentPerf
pitch: The ecosystem quotes "10x faster" for WebMCP with no methodology behind it. AgentPerf measures it: 2.4x on a small page, 13.8x on a real one. And it ships the React layer that produces the gap.
about_excerpt: The ecosystem quotes "10x faster" for WebMCP with no methodology behind it. AgentPerf measures it: 2.4x on a small page, 13.8x on a real one. And it ships the React layer that produces the gap. Like Comment Story Updates What it does AgentPerf answers the question every frontend team is about to be asked: if we build and maintain a second surface for AI agents, what do we actually get? Three pieces answer it end to end. agentperf, the benchmark CLI. Runs the same task, on the same page, with the same model, twice. Once by DOM driving, an accessibility-tree driver that reads, clicks, fills and selects, the way browser agents work today. Once through the page's WebMCP tools. Identical agent loop, identical prompt, identical verification. It reports wall-clock, tokens, round-trips and success rate, per run and aggregated. @agentperf/react, the fast lane. Three primitives that turn an existing React app into a WebMCP surface without touching the human UI. Two instrumented demo pages and a landing page, all live, all publishing their own tools. The landing page will hand your agent its own benchmark data with the caveats attached. The measurement gpt-5.6-luna, n=5 per lane, both lanes 100% successful on both pages: page accessibility tree lane wall-clock tokens round-trips salon booking 1,010 chars DOM driving 7.5s 10,079 5 salon booking WebMCP tools 5.0s 4,268 4 72-product catalog 32,916 chars DOM driving 24.3s 102,537 7 72-product catalog WebMCP tools 6.0s 7,434 5 2.4x fewer tokens on the tiny page. 13.8x on the realistic one. Make the page 32x heavier and DOM driving pays 10x more, while the tools lane barely moves, because it never reads the page. It asks. That is the finding, and it is not the one anyone is quoting: the gap is a property of the page, not of WebMCP. A single number for "what WebMCP saves" is meaningless without the page it was measured on. That is why this ships as a harness you point at your own site, not as a headline. It replicates across model families: claude-sonnet-5 via OpenRouter, with no vendor-specific workarounds, pays 2.5x on the small page with identical round-trip counts. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Most WebMCP demos show that an agent can drive a site. The open question is whether a team should pay to build that, and nobody could answer it with data. The "10x faster, ~90% fewer tokens" figures in circulation trace to one methodology-free blog post and to token-only counts measured against screenshot baselines by the ecosystem itself. Google's own WebMCP Evals guide covers correctness (does the agent pick the right tool) and explicitly provides no metrics, no harness, and no comparison against DOM automation. So the fit is direct: WebMCP is the thing being adopted, and the missing artifact is the evidence for adopting it. AgentPerf is built on WebMCP twice over. The demo pages publish tools through document.modelContext, and the harness implements the other half of the protocol, acting as a WebMCP host so it can measure any page that speaks it. How it creates a better experience For the person: the agent's work happens in their tab, in their UI. When it searches, the grid filters. When it orders, the confirmation appears where they can see it. A dock states plainly how many tools the page has exposed. Agent-readiness usually means a headless side door the user cannot observe; here it is a visible second doorway onto the same app. For the developer: the fast lane is additive. Delete agent-surface.tsx from either demo and you have an ordinary React app. In a browser without WebMCP, everything no-ops. For the agent: it stops guessing. It gets typed actions and a state snapshot pruned to a token budget, with explicit "+N more" markers wherever a list was elided, so a partial read is legible as a partial read instead of becoming a confident hallucination. What people and agents can now do together that was hard before Buy correctly from a real catalog in four tool calls. On a 72-product store, "find the cheapest in-stock wireless keyboard rated 4.5 or higher and order it" is a filter, a comparison and a checkout. Through tools that is search_products, add_to_cart, place_order, for 7,434 tokens. By DOM it costs 102,537 tokens of reading and re-reading the same grid. Let an agent write to an app without letting it corrupt the app. Every action is zod-gated. A malformed email never reaches the handler; the agent gets back the exact violated field paths and a deterministic fix-and-retry instruction, and corrects itself in one turn instead of re-sending the same bad call. Ask a marketing page to justify its own claims. The landing page publishes get_benchmark_results. An agent reading it gets the numbers and the caveats (n, model, page sizes, known biases) instead of adjectives. Benchmark a WebMCP page you did not write. The harness supplies the host, so it works on any page that speaks the protocol, in stock Chromium, with no flag and no origin trial. How I implemented WebMCP Publishing side, @agentperf/react: useAgentState(key, value): every slice flows into a single get_page_state tool, serialized within a token budget (default 1,000) with deterministic pruning and explicit elision markers. useAgentAction(name, config): registers a tool whose input schema is generated from a zod schema via z.toJSONSchema, so the contract and the schema the agent sees cannot drift. readOnly and destructive map to WebMCP annotations. A reserved, currently inert price field anticipates x402 settlement without a future breaking change. AgentBoundary: scopes state keys and tool names the way the component tree scopes the UI. Registration hygiene: handlers, descriptions and values are read through refs at call time, so re-renders never tear down and re-register a tool. Each tool holds an AbortController and unregisters on unmount, which fires toolchange so an idle agent learns the surface moved. Host side, the harness: WebMCP lives behind an origin trial and a Chrome flag, which makes reproducible measurement painful and CI impossible. So the harness ships a host shim and injects it with Playwright's addInitScript before page load. The page registers into that shim, and window.__agentperf.listTools() and .call() bridge those tools into the agent loop as function tools. Verification is the benchmark. A run counts as a success only if the model calls task_complete and the rendered page matches the task's successPattern. For the catalog that pattern pins the product and the price, so ordering the wrong keyboard fails the run instead of passing on a bare order number. A task whose pattern already matches at page load is rejected outright as unverifiable. Challenges I ran into My own benchmark was unfair, and I published it before I found out. The launched numbers were 2.4x tokens and 2.6x wall-clock. Then I had the methodology adversarially reviewed, and the review was right: the DOM lane's click returned only "Clicked button X", forcing a separate read_page to see the result, while every real accessibility-tree driver returns the post-action snapshot with the action result. I had doubled that lane's round-trips by design, then billed it for re-sending the transcript each time. Fixed and re-ran: the token ratio survived unchanged at 2.36x; the wall-clock claim did not. 2.6x was wrong, it is 1.5x. The correction is on the landing page and at the top of the README. Then it nearly happened again, in my favour. The first heavy-page run was spectacular: the DOM lane succeeded 1 time in 5, ordering a keyboard rated 4.2 when the task demanded 4.5 or higher, and announcing success every time. "DOM driving doesn't just cost more, it buys the wrong thing" is a far better headline than any cost ratio. It was also my bug: the catalog's rating filter is a select element and my DOM lane had no way to operate a dropdown. Adding select_option took it from 20% to 100%. Two rules came out of that: a lane is only a baseline if it can do what the real thing can do, and a result that flatters your conclusion gets audited harder, not published faster. Rate limits were silently biasing the result. A 429 failed a run outright, which penalizes whichever lane spends more tokens, the lane under measurement. Retries now back off exponentially. Crashed runs also used to record zero tokens and get averaged in, dragging a failing lane's cost toward zero; central tendencies are now over successful runs only, with failures in the success rate. gpt-5.6 returns a 400 on function tools unless reasoning_effort is "none". My first instinct, swallowing provider errors so a run doesn't abort, was exactly wrong for a benchmark: it turns a broken configuration into a plausible-looking failed run. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Every number that moved, moved against me, and I shipped it anyway: on the landing page, in the README, and inside a WebMCP tool the page itself serves. benchmarks/METHODOLOGY.md: the full adversarial review of my own harness, both

title: CausaFlow — An Urban Flood Forensic Lab
pitch: An agent-ready flood lab where people ask “what if?” and WebMCP agents safely run, inspect, replay, and compare flood scenarios with every assumption visible.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready flood lab where people ask “what if?” and WebMCP agents safely run, inspect, replay, and compare flood scenarios with every assumption visible. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Flood simulations can be difficult to use and even harder to explain. A person may need to choose a location, configure a scenario, review assumptions, start a long-running calculation, inspect several results, replay the flood, and compare it with another run. An AI agent looking only at buttons and pixels could easily choose the wrong setup or mistake the colour of an animation for a real result. I built CausaFlow to solve both problems. It is an urban flood investigation lab where a person asks the question and a WebMCP agent safely handles the multi-step work inside the application. What CausaFlow does CausaFlow lets people explore flood situations in two study areas: Texas Medical Center and Brays Bayou in Houston Velachery and its surrounding area in Chennai In Houston, CausaFlow can test heavy rain, a river carrying more water than its assumed capacity, or blocked drains along a hospital access road. In Velachery, it can keep rain off the city itself while applying severe rain around its boundary, then show which monitored neighbourhoods are affected first. Each completed run provides more than an animation. It reports water depth, speed, affected area, arrival times, water accounting, assumptions, limitations, and result identities that can be checked later. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Flood investigation is not a single-button task. It is a chain of connected decisions and actions. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to guess its way through a complex 3D interface. It could select the wrong scenario, run an outdated setup, lose track of which result is displayed, or describe what the animation appears to show instead of reading the actual numbers. WebMCP gives the agent direct access to clearly defined actions and exact application state. The agent knows which study area is active, which scenario is staged, whether the user has approved it, which calculation is running, which result is displayed, and what the result actually says. This makes CausaFlow faster and easier to use while keeping the person in control. What people and agents can do together The person provides the goal, judgment, and approval. The agent handles the repeated application work. For example, a person can ask: Block every represented drain along the hospital access road, show when the route becomes unsafe, then reopen the fewest drains needed and run the same storm again. The WebMCP agent can then: Open the correct Houston study area. Place the represented drains along the access road. Stage the blocked scenario. Show the assumptions on screen. Wait for the person’s explicit approval. Start and monitor the flood calculation. Read the completed numerical result. Save it as the comparison case. Run the tested intervention under the same storm. Compare both results and move the camera to the important location. Completing that entire sequence manually would require navigating several controls and carefully tracking two separate results. With WebMCP, the person can remain focused on the investigation while the agent handles the mechanics. Every important action remains visible in the interface, and the normal controls remain available as a fallback. How I implemented WebMCP I register the application’s tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools are divided into two groups: Flood tools for inspecting capabilities, staging scenarios, requesting approval, starting calculations, monitoring progress, reading results, controlling playback, sampling locations, and comparing runs. Workspace tools for changing study areas, reading the visible scene, moving the camera, and focusing on important results. Each tool has a clear description and a strict input format. Tools that only read information are marked separately from tools that change the application. CausaFlow also protects the workflow in several ways: A calculation cannot begin until the exact staged scenario has been approved. Every scenario change creates a new revision, preventing an agent from approving an older setup by mistake. The user’s request to run a scenario is recorded as explicit authorization. Long-running calculations return progress instead of leaving the agent guessing. Completed results have stable identities and cannot be silently changed during replay or comparison. The agent reads numerical results from the application instead of estimating values from the animation. WebMCP is the access and coordination layer. It does not create the flood results. The calculations come from the flood-simulation software used by CausaFlow. Key demonstration: Hospital Lifeline Hospital Lifeline represents eight drains along a 771-metre hospital access road. With every represented drain blocked, the access checkpoint crosses its 15-centimetre test limit after 270 seconds and reaches a maximum depth of approximately 32.8 centimetres. I tested the zero-drain case and every individual-drain alternative. Reopening D7 was the only single-drain option that kept the checkpoint below the limit. Its maximum depth fell to approximately 12.7 centimetres, and D7 removed approximately 311.6 cubic metres of water. The WebMCP agent can run the blocked case, run the D7 case under the same storm, compare them, and take the user directly to the checkpoint. How I built it I built the interface with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js, and deck.gl. The flood calculations run through ANUGA using Python. I also use EPA SWMM for separate drainage checks. Houston uses frozen USGS elevation data. Velachery uses frozen Copernicus elevation data with OpenStreetMap context. I packaged the application with Docker and deployed it through Coolify. Challenges I faced The first challenge was keeping the agent helpful without giving it too much control. I solved this by exposing small, clearly limited tools instead of one unrestricted command. The second challenge was preventing stale or unapproved scenarios from running. I added revision checks and explicit approval before every calculation. The third challenge was making sure the agent reported real results rather than guessing from the animation. The result tools return exact values, assumptions, warnings, and limitations. I also had to make the flood calculations, terrain files, interface, WebMCP tools, and production deployment work together inside one Docker container. Accomplishments I’m proud of Five complete flood demonstration flows A multi-step WebMCP workflow that works without clicking simulation controls A safe approval boundary before calculations begin Direct result inspection instead of visual guessing Result replay, camera control, and comparison through WebMCP 74 unit and regression tests 23 flood-calculation checks 11 production browser tests A public Docker deployment with no login required What I learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when a task involves several connected steps, visible state, and important decisions. The agent should not replace the person. The person decides what question to ask and whether a scenario should run. The agent makes the application easier to operate, keeps track of the steps, and returns the evidence needed to understand the result. I also learned that an impressive animation is not enough. A responsible flood tool must show its assumptions, limits, and actual numbers clearly. What’s next I want to add more cities, carefully controlled terrain uploads, downloadable reports, and shared investigation sessions. I also want to test CausaFlow with planners and flood experts to learn which questions and comparisons are most useful in real planning work. CausaFlow is currently a planning and learning tool. It is not a flood forecast, evacuation recommendation, engineering design, or guarantee of safety.
