title: Groundline
pitch: A shared reasoning workspace where humans map claims and evidence while AI agents use WebMCP to evaluate, triage, trace dependencies, and propose revisions - humans keep final control.
about_excerpt: A shared reasoning workspace where humans map claims and evidence while AI agents use WebMCP to evaluate, triage, trace dependencies, and propose revisions - humans keep final control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Groundline visualizes how conclusions rest on claims, evidence, assumptions, and sources. Start from a decision in plain language, then turn it into an inspectable reasoning workspace. Explore the reasoning graph, inspect individual objects, and trace what each conclusion depends on. A WebMCP-aware agent reviews the same live workspace, identifies weaknesses, and proposes safer revisions. Groundline See what your conclusions stand on. Inspiration People rarely make important decisions from perfectly structured arguments. A conclusion usually begins as a paragraph, a conversation, a recommendation, or a confident sentence such as: “We should do this.” But underneath that sentence may be assumptions that were never examined, evidence that only supports part of the claim, missing sources, unresolved counterarguments, or reasoning that works for one narrow case but is being generalized far beyond it. The problem is not always that the conclusion is wrong. The problem is that the reasoning underneath it is difficult to inspect. Generative AI makes this problem more interesting. An AI agent can critique reasoning, identify assumptions, trace dependencies, and propose better alternatives, but giving an agent unrestricted authority over the reasoning creates another problem: Who decides what becomes accepted knowledge? Groundline started from two questions: What does this conclusion actually stand on? and: Can an AI agent help inspect and repair reasoning without silently taking control of the decision? The goal was not to build another chatbot that produces polished advice. The goal was to build a shared human-agent reasoning workspace where arguments become inspectable, weaknesses become reviewable, proposed repairs remain proposals, and the human retains final authority. What it does Groundline is a WebMCP-native human-agent workspace for auditable reasoning . A user represents a decision as explicit reasoning objects such as: QUESTION CLAIM COUNTERCLAIM ASSUMPTION EVIDENCE SOURCE CONCLUSION Those objects can be connected using semantic relations such as: SUPPORTS CHALLENGES DEPENDS_ON QUALIFIES Groundline then exposes the active workspace to a WebMCP-aware external agent through structured tools. The agent can: inspect the workspace; inspect individual reasoning objects; evaluate evidence and assumptions; trace dependencies; identify contradictions; find evidence gaps; focus important reasoning paths; triage what deserves review first; propose semantic relations; and propose safer revisions. Groundline does not treat the agent's answer as canonical truth. Instead, the agent can stage proposals for human review. A semantic relation does not enter the canonical reasoning graph until a human approves it. A revision does not silently overwrite an accepted conclusion. The human can: accept; accept with edits; reject; or defer. Groundline's central interaction contract is: Agent proposes. Human decides. How we built it Groundline uses a hybrid human-agent architecture. The semantic reasoning responsibility belongs to an external WebMCP-aware agent . Groundline itself owns the deterministic parts of the system: reasoning-object contracts; canonical workspace state; relation validation; dependency mechanics; structural analysis; semantic-review freshness; review-priority calculation; revision lifecycle; state invalidation; audit history; and human approval boundaries. There is deliberately no hidden page-local LLM. The external agent supplies semantic interpretation. Groundline supplies the state machine and authority model. Core Reasoning Flow The reasoning lifecycle begins with human-authored decision context. Groundline turns that input into typed reasoning objects and stores them as canonical workspace state. Deterministic structural analysis identifies represented dependencies and review targets. A WebMCP-aware agent can then inspect the same canonical reasoning state, perform semantic review, trace weak assumptions or evidence gaps, and propose repairs. Any canonical change crosses a human review boundary. When reasoning changes, stale semantic review is invalidated and the new state must be inspected again. System Flowchart The operational flowchart shows the complete reasoning-review cycle from input and validation through agent inspection, semantic evaluation, deterministic triage, repair proposals, human review, canonical state transitions, audit recording, and fresh review after changes. Architecture Groundline separates four responsibilities: The human defines the reasoning and controls canonical acceptance. Groundline's deterministic domain layer manages structure, state, review priority, revision semantics, and audit history. The WebMCP tool surface exposes structured reasoning operations. The external agent performs semantic interpretation and proposes changes. The implementation uses: React 19; TypeScript; Vite; Zustand; Zod; @xyflow/react ; Vitest; Testing Library; jsdom; and WebMCP. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, the reasoning workspace is primarily something a human can inspect visually. With WebMCP, the website becomes an agent-operable reasoning environment . The agent does not need the user to manually copy every claim, assumption, and evidence item into a chat message. Instead, it can discover structured operations directly from the active Groundline workspace. This means the agent can reason over canonical application state rather than relying only on conversational descriptions of that state. This distinction became especially important during testing. In one revision-lifecycle scenario, the conversation claimed that a revision had already been accepted. The agent re-inspected Groundline and found that the canonical state had not actually changed. It trusted the workspace instead of the conversational claim. That is exactly the behavior Groundline is designed to support: canonical application state outranks conversational assumptions. Semantic review without pretending to measure truth Groundline uses three review-priority states: CRITICAL REVIEW STABLE These labels do not mean: false; uncertain; or true. They answer a narrower question: What deserves review first? Groundline separates semantic assessment from deterministic prioritization. The current priority mechanic is based on: priority = weakness × downstream impact with: priority >= 7 -> CRITICAL priority 3..6 -> REVIEW priority <= 2 -> STABLE This distinction matters because missing evidence is not the same thing as contradiction, and contradiction is not automatically proof that something is false. Likewise, a weakness can exist without being decision-changing. The system is designed to preserve those distinctions rather than collapse everything into one confidence score. Human authority is part of the architecture One of Groundline's most important design decisions is that human control is not just explanatory text. It is implemented as part of the application workflow. Agent-generated revisions remain PROPOSED . Agent-generated semantic relations remain pending. Groundline explicitly tells browser agents to stop at the human review boundary. Human decision controls use a deliberate press-and-hold interaction before canonical state can change. This includes: accepting a revision; accepting an edited revision; rejecting a revision; deferring a revision; approving semantic relations; and rejecting proposed relations. The interaction is intentionally asymmetric: Agent: inspect evaluate trace triage focus propose Human: accept edit reject defer Explicit conversational permission does not automatically convert the external agent into the canonical human reviewer. Revision history instead of silent rewriting Groundline does not overwrite accepted reasoning when a revision is approved. Instead: old accepted item ↓ SUPERSEDED new replacement item ↓ ACCEPTED ↓ UNASSESSED The previous reasoning remains part of the audit lineage. The replacement becomes the current accepted item. Previous semantic evaluations and triage are not silently inherited. Semantic relations are also not automatically copied simply because the new item replaces the old one. Groundline therefore treats SUPERSEDES as revision provenance, not as semantic support. Meaning must be reviewed again against the new reasoning state. Challenges we ran into WebMCP changes the interaction model One of the first architectural assumptions we had to abandon was the idea that a page button could simply “call the agent again.” Baseline WebMCP does not make a connected external agent behave like a callback function owned by the page. Groundline therefore separates page-side state changes from agent continuation. After a human decision, the external agent must re-inspect the changed workspace throug
video_title: Groundline: See What Your Conclusions Stand On | WebMCP Challenge
video_transcript_excerpt: Most AI tools give you an answer. Ground Line helps you inspect what that answer actually stands on. This is a live reasoning workspace where a human and an AI agent can examine the same claims, assumptions, evidence, and conclusions together. When we make an important decision, the problem is rarely just the final answer. The real problem is hidden underneath it. Which assumptions are weak? What evidence actually supports them? And if one part fails, what else in the conclusion breaks with it? Normally, an AI explains this in text. Ground Line turns that reasoning into shared inspectable state. The human does not need to learn a reasoning ontology. I describe my decision in ordinary language, and Ground Line maps it into explicit reasoning objects. The graph is not decoration. Every card is an object the user can inspect, and an agent can address directly. This is where WebMCP changes the interaction. Ground Line exposes structured tools directly from the live page. The agent can inspect the current workspace, evaluate reasoning, triage the highest impact weakness, trace its dependencies, and focus the exact object it is talking about. There is no screenshot interpretation, and no separate copy of the reasoning inside the chat. The agent operates on the same workspace I am looking at. So, instead of receiving a generic warning like, "Your assumption may be weak," I can see exactly which assumption is under review, why it matters, and which conclusion depends on it. The graph tells me where the problem is. The inspector tells me what the agent found, and the audit trail records what happened. The agent can also propose a safer version of the conclusion, but Ground Line does not simply replace the reasoning and hide what changed. The proposal appears as an explicit revision. Here, I accept it. The previous conclusion remains in the history as superseded. The replacement becomes the current conclusion, and old semantic judgments are not silently inherited. Changing the answer means the reasoning has to earn its support again. Humans can also add new evidence or counter claims at any time. If a new card is not connected yet, the agent can suggest how it relates to the existing reasoning instead of silently guessing its role. That keeps the workspace editable without pretending every new idea already has a justified place in the argument. Ground line is not another chatbot wrapped around a decision. It is a shared reasoning surface. The human creates and reviews the reasoning. The agent gets structured tools for inspecting, tracing, evaluating and proposing changes directly on the web page. That is what web MCP makes possible. Not just humans asking agents for answers, but humans and agents working on the same reasoning together. Ground line, see what your conclusions stand on.

title: GuacaDoc
pitch: GuacaDoc lets an AI agent work on a confidential document without ever receiving a single name, account number or address from it.
about_excerpt: GuacaDoc lets an AI agent work on a confidential document without ever receiving a single name, account number or address from it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GuacaDoc Homepage GuacaDoc — Devpost submission text Inspiration There is a whole class of documents you cannot hand to an AI. A client contract, a patient record, an unsigned deal. You have the analysis problem, the tool that could solve it, and no right to hand over the file. What struck me is that the constraint is not really about privacy. It is about what an agent actually needs in order to be useful . An agent reasoning about a liability clause does not need to know the counterparty is Marceline Dubreuil. It needs to know that the party in section 2 is the party in section 7. That is a structural fact, not an identity. Separate those two and the impossible task becomes possible: the agent gets the substance, never the identities. WebMCP is what makes that separation enforceable rather than aspirational, because the tools run in the page, next to the person who owns the document. What it does GuacaDoc opens a document in your tab, parses it there (TXT, MD, PDF, DOCX), scans it locally for identifying values, and turns it into five WebMCP tools an agent can call. The agent outlines, searches and reads the document, and never receives a name, an account number or an address from it. You review what was found and choose, per value or per type, whether it goes out as written , as a stable token , or never . Bank details default to never, because an account number carries no analytical value. Names come back as [PERSON_01] , stable across the whole document. That stability is what keeps the analysis useful: the agent can reason that the signatory of section 2 is the person named in section 7 without knowing who either is. When it answers in tokens, you paste its answer into a decode panel and get the real names back, assembled in your tab from your key. Withheld values have no token, so they are not reversible by construction. A running counter shows exactly how many characters the agent has read, and a strip lists every chunk that left the tab, in order, with its tool and timestamp. How we built it Static Next.js export, React, TypeScript, no backend and no network access at all . Five layers, and the boundary between them is enforced by which module is allowed to talk to the agent. extract file → text, in the tab (pdf.js, mammoth) sections text → addressable sections (s01…sNN) detect text → entities (regex rules + capitalisation heuristic + aliases) ↓ the user marks: shown | token | withheld policy substitute · verify · confirm · record webmcp document.modelContext.registerTool() The load-bearing decision is the one-door rule: exactly one function in the project hands a tool to the browser, and it scrubs the entire result tree after the handler returns. The handler has no say in it. The alternative, asking every handler to remember to redact, is a design that fails the first time someone adds a sixth tool at 2 a.m. Here a leak requires defeating the scrubber, not forgetting to call it. The second decision was to make the strongest guarantee one I did not write myself. The page ships connect-src 'none' , so it cannot open a network connection: no fetch, no XHR, no WebSocket, no beacon. Anyone can confirm that from the Network tab in seconds, which is stronger than any sentence in a README. Runtime traps sit behind the CSP so an attempt shows up in the interface instead of in a console nobody opens. Detection is local and deliberately blunt: regex plus a capitalisation heuristic, tuned to over-detect, because a false positive costs one click and a false negative silently leaves a name in the outbound text. Sending the document to a remote recogniser would have recreated the exact leak the app exists to prevent. Challenges we ran into The search oracle. Search first ran over the source text and returned redacted snippets, which looks correct and is completely broken. An agent could query Dubreuil and learn from a hit or a miss whether that name is in the document, without one byte of it being returned. The channel leaks through its own metadata. Search now runs over the redacted text, never the source, and the cost is real: withheld values are genuinely unfindable, even by their owner. There is a test named searching a redacted name returns nothing (no oracle) because I wanted the property pinned down, not remembered. Anonymisation that survives a real document. Substituting a name once is trivial; substituting it everywhere is not. A document introduces Marceline Dubreuil on page one and says Dubreuil for twelve pages after, so surname aliases are derived and mapped to the same token, but kept only when they actually occur outside the full form, otherwise the counts start lying . Phone numbers appear as +33 6 41 88 07 23 and 06 41 88 07 23 , so token identity is decided on a normalised key, not the surface string . Addresses are matched as one entity across number, street and postcode, and a longer hand-marked span absorbs the town entity inside it rather than minting two tokens for one place. Accented names break word boundaries, so substitution uses Unicode letter lookarounds instead of \b . And after all that, the scrubber verifies its own output and hardens anything that survived, because the honest assumption is that the detector missed something. No unregisterTool() in the API. A tool is withdrawn by aborting the signal it was registered with. Without handling that, a second mount re-offers five names the browser already holds, every call is rejected, and the page advertises tools while the browser answers an older set of closures. Registration is therefore generational. Trusting the browser over myself. I keep my own registry of tools and I do not believe it. The header count comes from the browser's own getTools() , because the browser's answer is the only one that cannot be wrong. "5 tools" above an empty record is made structurally impossible. The screen is a channel WebMCP does not govern. My tool surface is sealed, but an agent that can screenshot the tab is not reading through my tools at all. So the token map is absent from the DOM by default rather than blurred , revealed on demand for 45 seconds with a visible countdown, ending immediately on blur , pagehide or visibilitychange , which are facts the browser states rather than infers. The activity bar deliberately does not claim the page is being read, because a screenshot is invisible to the page and a bar that lit up for it would be guessing. Tool-mediated disclosure is what WebMCP governs, and that is what this enforces. The rest is written into the interface itself, because a threat model you hide is not a threat model. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works end to end in a real WebMCP browser. You ask ChatGPT to find the liability clauses, it calls search_document then get_section , and comes back with a correct answer in which every party is a token and the bank details simply are not there. 28 assertions turn the README into something executable. npm run verify re-derives every claim from the real modules and exits non-zero on failure. The ones that matter are adversarial: the search oracle is closed, a surname used alone is still substituted, decode does not restore withheld values, and no section leaks after scrubbing. Every refusal is a structured answer, never an exception , so an agent that hits a wall learns why and adapts instead of retrying blind. Session boundaries are marked, not erased. Opening a new document restarts the token registry but keeps the record, with a boundary row at the seam. An agent's first probes cannot vanish from a trail that claims to be gapless. The export contains not one source value , because exporting the key would put the protected data on a disk. There is no red anywhere in the interface. A refusal is the policy working, and colouring it as an error teaches people the wrong thing about their own tool. What we learned WebMCP, properly. The imperative API, JSON Schema declarations, abort-signal lifecycle, and why Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 is mandatory: the API is exposed only to origin-isolated documents, so without the header registerTool() rejects and your page advertises nothing. That tool descriptions are the real interface. More time went into the wording of five descriptions and their error hints than into the code behind them. An empty search returns a hint explaining that search runs on redacted text, so real names are not findable by design. Those sentences changed agent behaviour more than any handler I wrote. That the interesting question is not "what did I hide" but "what can be inferred". Substitution shrinks the exposed surface, it does not remove it. A pseudonym protects a name while someone with distinctive behaviour stays recognisable by inference. Naming that limit turned out to be more useful than pretending to have closed it , which is why

title: Bundlepose
pitch: Agents propose. People compose. Shopify bundles. You and your AI agent co-compose a bouquet that doesn't exist yet — and a Cart Transform Function makes it one real, purchasable line in the cart.
about_excerpt: Agents propose. People compose. Shopify bundles. You and your AI agent co-compose a bouquet that doesn't exist yet — and a Cart Transform Function makes it one real, purchasable line in the cart. Like Comment Story Updates top Basic Use Case Co-Compose System Inspiration E-commerce lets anyone sell 24 hours a day — but an online store is really an unmanned roadside stand. Nobody greets you, nobody asks who the flowers are for. We build Shopify apps for a living (Theme App Extensions, Shopify Functions), and florists are a vertical where this gap hurts most. Custom bouquets ARE sold on Shopify today — but the "custom" part still happens over phone calls, LINE messages, and free-text note fields. The composition, the price, the stock — none of it is structured. When WebMCP arrived, we saw a chance to put a clerk back in the store: an agent that listens to "something warm for my mother's 60th birthday, under $40," knows the flowers (meanings, occasions, pet safety), and builds the bouquet with you. Shopping agents are good at finding products that already exist. We wanted the harder thing: turning agentic commerce from product discovery into product creation. What it does Bundlepose is a Shopify app where a shopper and an AI agent compose a product that doesn't exist yet — and turn it into a real order. The agent proposes. Through 11 bouquet_* WebMCP tools registered on every storefront page, the agent reads the florist's rules (slots, stem limits, budget) and today's flowers — real Shopify variants with metafields for role, color, flower meaning, occasions, and pet safety — then drafts a bouquet within the budget. The person composes. The draft appears in a composer panel on the same page. The shopper adjusts quantities, removes a stem, picks the wrap, restores something — by hand. The agent sees those hand edits on its next bouquet_get_state call and rebalances. One shared workbench, edited from both sides. Shopify bundles. bouquet_commit — the only tool allowed to touch the cart — validates the draft and adds it. A Cart Transform Function (Rust) merges stems, wrap, and arrangement fee into one cart line, priced as the exact sum of its parts , carrying its recipe through checkout. Three bouquets? Three clean lines, not thirty loose stems. Why this needs WebMCP: Shopify's built-in storefront tools already let agents search products and fill carts — but they can only sell what exists. A bouquet that was just invented in conversation isn't a product; twelve loose stem lines don't tell the merchant "this is one bouquet," and two bouquets in one cart are indistinguishable mush. Page-level WebMCP tools + a Cart Transform close exactly that gap: the agent works inside the store's own rules and inventory, hands off to Shopify's standard tools for checkout, and the human approves on the same page they're browsing. The UX win is concrete: what used to be a phone call, a LINE thread, and a free-text note field becomes a structured, priced, stock-checked bouquet built right on the product page — and one clean line in the cart instead of a dozen loose stems. The tools: bouquet_get_rules , bouquet_list_components , bouquet_create , bouquet_get_state , bouquet_add_items , bouquet_remove_items , bouquet_set_wrap , bouquet_set_note , bouquet_validate , bouquet_commit , bouquet_discard . How we built it Storefront (Theme App Extension, app embed): registers the 11 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() — imperative API, top-level document (ChatGPT does not detect tools inside iframes). Tools and the composer panel mutate one shared draft store (persisted to localStorage), so agent calls re-render the panel instantly and human edits are readable back through bouquet_get_state , including a per-stem diff against what's already in the cart. Backend (React Router 7 + TypeScript on Fly.io, SQLite/Prisma): tools call the store's own domain via Shopify App Proxy ( /apps/composer/* ) — signed, same-origin, zero CORS. We verified WebMCP execute runs in the normal page context (not a sandbox), which makes this possible. The catalog endpoint reads the Admin GraphQL API, exposing composer.* metafields (role, color, meaning, occasions, pet-safe) as the agent-facing florist knowledge. Cart write: Shopify.actions.updateCart (Storefront Actions API) with hidden _bundle_id / _bundle_name line attributes, Ajax Cart API fallback — then navigate to /cart , which is always correct regardless of theme. Bundling (Shopify Function, Rust → WASM): groups cart lines by _bundle_id and emits a LinesMerge operation under a "Custom Bouquet" parent variant ( requiresComponents: true , price $0 — the merged line's price is the components' sum). Config lives in a metafield on the Cart Transform; missing config = no-op, so checkout never breaks. Fixture-tested with @shopify/shopify-function-test-helpers . Merchant setup: an idempotent admin setup page — one click seeds the demo florist (14 stems with metafields, 2 wraps, an arrangement fee, the merge parent kept UNLISTED: purchasable by direct variant reference for the merge, hidden from search), another activates the transform after shopify app deploy . Challenges we ran into Exposing WebMCP tools on a Shopify store. A Theme App Extension turned out to be the right surface: its app embed runs in the storefront's top-level document, which is where agents such as ChatGPT discover tools. We then named and scoped the bouquet_* tools so they complement — rather than overlap with — Shopify's standard storefront tools, which already handle search, cart and checkout. Staying in sync with the store's theme. Writing to the cart from a tool succeeded on the server, but the theme's cart icon and drawer did not reflect the change. The theme owns that state and only reacts to its own events, so we moved the commit path to Shopify's Storefront Actions API, which fires those events, and navigate to the cart page after a commit so the result is always visible. Co-composing with the agent, not through it. Our first approach drove every cart change through WebMCP alone, and the shopper ended up doing more work — each small tweak became another round of conversation. So we built the embedded composer: the agent's proposal lands in an on-page panel that the shopper can edit by hand, and the agent reads those edits back. Splitting the work this way is what finally made the experience feel good. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop works end-to-end from ChatGPT: conversation → draft → hand-edit → agent rebalance → commit → one merged bouquet line → checkout. The math is exact. Five lines (3 roses, 4 tulips, 2 eucalyptus, wrap, fee) merge into "Warm Birthday Bouquet — $39.50", precisely the sum of its parts; a second bouquet stays its own line, and checkout expands each into its recipe. A real shared workbench. Remove a stem by hand and the panel shows "Removed / Restore", the agent sees changes_since_cart , and "Update cart · +$3.00" shows the delta before you approve. It's a product, not a rig: idempotent one-page seed of the demo florist, graceful fallback in browsers without WebMCP, and a Rust Function with fixture tests. What we learned Chat is not always the best interface. When you build with WebMCP, it's tempting to think of every interaction as a conversation. But some things — like removing one stem or trying a different wrap — are faster to do by hand than to describe in words. To give customers a good experience, we learned to combine chat with other kinds of UI, rather than force everything through the agent. WebMCP tools have to coexist with other apps' tools. Publishing tools with WebMCP turned out to be easy. That is exactly why it needs care: on a platform like Shopify, our tools run on the same page as Shopify's own tools and, in the future, tools from other developers' apps. Tool names, descriptions and responsibilities need to be designed so that agents can tell them apart and use them together. Explaining this to customers is hard. Our demo store shows a banner inviting shoppers to try the new experience with their AI agent. In practice, it is still difficult for a non-engineer to understand what that means or how to start. Until WebMCP-capable browsers are common, even a careful explanation will only go so far — as app developers, we need to keep working on how this is introduced to real shoppers. What's next for Bundlepose Let the agent sell, not just build: add upsell_suggestions[] to bouquet_validate / bouquet_get_state returns — "for $3 more, satin wrap," "your budget fits one more focal stem" — so upselling happens in conversation, the way a real clerk does it. More templates for the same engine. The Cart Transform's grouping logic is product-agnostic and the shop rules already ship as a profile object (noun, unit, slots) — generalizing the tool names and copy is the next step: coffee blends, cookie assortments, spice mixes, gift kits. video_transcript_excerpt: Hello. With this app, simply talking to an agent lets you easily order a complex custom floral arrangement. Something that was not possible before. And you can compose it yourself if you want. This is made possible by combining WebMCP with a Shopify app. Here's how the app uses WebMCP. Its tools let the agent see products shoppers normally can't. Single flowers not sold on their own, hidden from search, but real with prices and flower meanings. From the conversation, the agent picks flowers and wrapping and composes a draft. Approve it and everything goes into the cart. Then Shopify's cart transform function merges those pieces into one product named after your conversation, priced as the sum of its real parts. Until now, you could not order a flower bouquet through e-commerce that was composed specifically to fit your budget. But with this app, all you have to do is tell the agent your budget in chat and it creates a combination within that amount. Until now, if you wanted to send a thoughtful bouquet that considered the meaning behind each flower, you had to research everything yourself. But with this app, just tell the agent who the bouquet is for and the occasion and it selects the perfect flowers. Until now, ordering several complex custom bouquets together was difficult. Even if AI could automatically add the flowers to the cart, it was still hard to tell which flowers belonged to which bouquet. But with this app, every custom product stays neatly organized. Thank you, cart transform API. That's right. This app is like having a helpful florist by your side. We built a florist demo this time. But we believe the same idea can be applied to other kinds of stores. In a sense, traditional e-commerce sites have been like unfriendly clerks or unmanned stores. They are perfect for people who already know what they want, but they cannot offer advice. As one possible form of agentic commerce, we believe that if more e-commerce sites let customers ask for advice, entirely new ways of shopping will become possible. To make that possible, we believe WebMCP and Shopify are a powerful combination. Some of this would be difficult with WebMCP alone. But Shopify lets us build mechanisms that respond to changes in the cart, like the Shopify function used in this project. That means we can create e-commerce experiences that go beyond payment and extend across ordering, checkout, and after-sales service. Wouldn't it be wonderful if e-commerce could serve customers like a human shop assistant? And because it is digital, one excellent shop assistant can split into countless copies and work quietly behind the scenes. It is just like a ninja. So, agentic commerce might be ninja. Jokes aside, WebMCP adds a new possibility to e-commerce. The convenience of self-service with personalized guidance whenever customers need it. Thanks for watching.

title: Office of Kaiju Affairs WebMCP
pitch: The Office of Kaiju Affairs turns a 51-page simulated government site into seven citable, constraint-aware WebMCP tools at publish time, then publicly benchmarks them against ordinary agent browsing.
about_excerpt: The Office of Kaiju Affairs turns a 51-page simulated government site into seven citable, constraint-aware WebMCP tools at publish time, then publicly benchmarks them against ordinary agent browsing. Like Comment Story Updates Office of Kaiju Affairs Swap the kaiju for the DMV. We built a 51-page government site whose CMS automatically turns published content into WebMCP tools—then ran 95 recorded trials to find out when those tools actually help. Live site: https://office-of-kaiju-affairs.vercel.app/ The Arena: https://office-of-kaiju-affairs.vercel.app/arena/ Source code: https://github.com/heitham/Office-of-Kaiju-Affairs Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ksu90tndo5U Inspiration The kaiju left. The paperwork did not. Mira Tanaka’s bakery has been damaged. She needs compensation, a rebuilding permit, and a straight answer about what she owes. Unfortunately, she now faces something almost as intimidating as a kaiju: a government website. Government websites are where ordinary people meet extraordinary complexity, sometimes at the worst of times: eligibility rules, buried exceptions, long document lists, and forms with real consequences. Agents can already navigate these sites—but today they usually do it by reading pages, following links, and guessing which sentence or field matters. We wanted to explore a more ambitious question than “can an agent call a tool?” What if a large website could publish an agent interface as naturally as it publishes a page—and prove whether that interface is worth using? The Office of Kaiju Affairs is our fictional test case: a national agency handling kaiju-attack damage claims, post-attack reconstruction permits, evacuation routes, and public information. What it does The project has three connected parts. 1. A complete public-service website The Office is a working, 51-page government-style site published by RIFT , my headless CMS. Citizens can browse services, understand policy, locate an office, check claim requirements, and complete a proximity-construction permit. 2. An agent layer generated by the CMS At publish time, the CMS emits a manifest describing the rendered site: pages, summaries, key facts, services, eligibility rules, citations, offices, and form schemas. A small browser runtime turns that manifest into seven WebMCP tools: search_site — finds facts across the entire published site get_page_summary — reads a page as structured, citable data list_services — explains what the agency offers get_service_requirements — returns documents, fees, deadlines, and fields check_eligibility — evaluates a citizen's facts against published rules prefill_permit_form — validates and fills the visible form, but cannot submit it get_office_info — finds offices and evacuation routes This is the important architectural idea: we did not hand-code one tool per page. Content becomes capability at publish time. Add or update a CMS page, republish, and the agent interface changes with the website. The manifest is intentionally lightweight. It does not pretend to be a government's single source of truth. It gives agents a navigable map of what this publisher knows: the services, sources, rules, forms, and capabilities represented on this part of the public web. RIFT itself predates this challenge and remains proprietary. For the challenge, I used RIFT to publish the fictional Office of Kaiju Affairs site with WebMCP publishing integration. The published website, the open-source browser runtime, all seven tools, the Arena, the task design, the answer keys, and the evaluation pipeline are the submission. The public repository contains every component needed to run and inspect the WebMCP project; it does not contain RIFT's private CMS source. 3. The Arena: a public evidence layer We looked at this as an experiment: would WebMCP be faster, safer, or more accurate? The Arena publishes 95 recorded runs of the same three citizen tasks across: a UI lane, where the agent reads pages and navigates without WebMCP; a WebMCP lane, where the agent uses the site's registered tools; two model tiers, Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Haiku 4.5; and two rounds, before and after fixes discovered by the benchmark. Every score, timing, action count, and range is computed from the trace files at runtime. The traces, answer keys, tool arguments, elapsed milliseconds, and earlier results are all public. Judges can also copy each scenario and run the WebMCP lane themselves. The recorded benchmark uses two Claude model tiers to test how the same interface behaves as model capability changes. The Arena is deliberately model-independent: in ChatGPT's WebMCP-enabled browser, the judge's OpenAI agent becomes the live lane and can attempt the same published tasks against the same answer keys. Three citizen experiences Find the rule—not just an answer Mira Tanaka is filing a second damage claim. The obvious reading says she qualifies for a fee waiver; the actual rule says only approved claims count, so her pending claim does not. The agent must find the buried exception, explain that the ¥12,000 fee is still payable, and point Mira to the source. WebMCP makes the site's search index and rule citations directly available instead of forcing the agent to infer structure from navigation. Turn policy into a complete checklist Mira's eligibility depends on several rules spread across multiple pages: her zone, structural damage, income, business status, insurance payout, claims history, and filing window. check_eligibility evaluates those facts against a ruleset published as data. It returns the outcome, three applicable grants, five required documents, and citations. In our recorded results, both model tiers scored 100% in both lanes—but WebMCP reached the result with fewer actions and was 1.7× faster for Sonnet and 2.1× faster for Haiku . Fill the form, then hand control back For a proximity-construction permit, the agent must derive the K-2 reinforcement standard from Mira's Zone 4 location, validate twelve values against the published schema, and fill the real form. Then it must stop. prefill_permit_form has no submission capability. It fills and highlights the fields, reports what it entered or rejected, and leaves the final action to the person. The safety boundary is structural, not a hopeful instruction in a prompt. What our experiment found The most useful result was not “tools always win.” They did not. On this small, well-structured site, the stronger model often navigated the UI successfully. In the headline Sonnet runs, 14 of 15 UI-lane passes received full marks. Across all three Sonnet tasks, WebMCP also used about 2.4× as many context tokens on average—19,422 versus 8,117—because tool schemas and responses add context to the model's calls. That cost was not uniform: on the eligibility task, where the tool performed the most substantive rule evaluation, WebMCP used fewer tokens than browsing for both model sizes. We publish the overhead and the savings rather than reducing either to a universal claim. But five findings make the case for an agent-native web—and for a more mature agent-native publishing practice—much more interesting. Tools helped most when the model needed help When we moved from Sonnet 5 to the smaller Haiku 4.5 model, UI-lane accuracy fell by 41% on average across the task/lane pairs with room to fall. WebMCP-lane accuracy fell by 23%. The weaker model degraded roughly 1.8× less when the site gave it tools. The clearest reversal was the permit task: WebMCP trailed UI navigation with Sonnet (93% vs. 100%), but led it with Haiku (74% vs. 64%). Structured capability may matter less to the strongest agent on a clean demo site; it matters more as models get smaller, cheaper, and more widely deployed. “Optional” does not mean “unimportant” Our first permit tool treated the form schema as if it described the whole service process. If a field was not technically required, the agent could leave it blank without the tool mentioning it. The result passed form validation but could still look misleadingly complete to Mira. We changed the tool to report every field it left untouched. It now tells the agent which optional fields remain empty and invites another call if they apply. In the next five Sonnet attempts, complete 12-field forms increased from 0 of 5 to 4 of 5 , and task accuracy rose from 64% to 93%. That change made the agent aware of its omissions; it did not explain their administrative consequences. The site does not currently say whether leaving out an organization or phone number would delay review, trigger follow-up, affect approval, or make no difference at all. That exposed the larger civic-tech lesson: a form the browser will accept is not necessarily a form that will move smoothly through the service behind it. An agent-native form needs more than required/optional validation. Publishers should describe whether a field is required to submit, required only in certain circumstances, recommended to avoid de
video_title: The WebMCP Challenge
video_transcript_excerpt: Mira Tanaka survived a Kaiju attack. Now she needs compensation, a rebuilding permit, and a straight answer from the government. Unfortunately, her best help is a website and an AI agent trying to understand it. Government websites contain real decisions hidden across policy pages, exceptions, document lists, and forms. AI agents can help ease the stress, but they must reconstruct the service from site navigation and text. We built a complete 51-page fictional government agency enabled with Web MCP. When the CMS publishes the website, it also generates a machine-readable manifest. A small browser runtime converts that content into seven Web MCP tools for search, services, eligibility, requirements, offices, and forms. Mira's eligibility depends on her location, damage, income, insurance, business status, and filing window. An AI agent would need to browse the website and find that through brute-force web browsing. With Web MCP check eligibility, evaluate the publisher's encoded rules, and return the outcome: three applicable grants, five required documents, and supporting citations. We built tests to see if Web MCP could outperform an agent browsing the website directly. You can use your ChatGPT Web MCP browser to help Mira submit her construction permit form online. For the permit, Web MCP validates 12 values, derives the required reinforcement standard, and fills the real form. Then it stops. The tool exposes no submission operation. Mira reviews the highlighted fields and makes the final decision herself. Human control is part of the capability. We did not stop at a polished demo. The arena publishes 95 inspectable runs comparing Web MCP with ordinary browsing across three tasks, two model sizes, and two rounds. Web MCP was not always better, but it completed the eligibility task with fewer actions and substantially less time, and it reduced the accuracy loss when we moved to the smaller model. Our most important finding was not about speed. When policy becomes executable, meaning can be lost between the approved sentence and the encoded rule. A citation may point to the correct page while the logic still misses an exception. Agent native publishing therefore creates a new responsibility. Organizations must review not only what people will read, but what machines will execute. The Office of Kaiju Affairs is fictional. The civic problem is not. WebMCP gives public institutions a way to participate in the agent experience instead of leaving every agent to reverse engineer their websites. And the open source arena we shared gives citizens, publishers, and judges a way to measure where WebMCP helps.

title: OpenInquiry
pitch: OpenInquiry lets people bring their own AI agents to trusted publisher content while publishers decide exactly what those agents can use.
about_excerpt: OpenInquiry lets people bring their own AI agents to trusted publisher content while publishers decide exactly what those agents can use. Like Comment Story Updates OpenInquiry brings the reader’s agent to publisher content while the publisher decides what it can use. WebMCP connects the reader’s agent to the publisher’s page; OpenInquiry proposes a publisher-controlled access layer. The demo separates reader entitlement from a publisher-recognized agent-assurance signal. The same question produces four publisher-defined access outcomes that judges can compare directly. The agent opens the publisher’s exact supporting section for review. Synthetic content; not for clinical use. Problem As a surgeon, I rely on journals, professional societies, and other trusted sources to make sense of complex evidence. Those sources need readers to return to the original work, where access rules, authorship, and updates remain visible. People increasingly want their own AI agents to help them use that information. Today, the agent often has to interpret the page visually or depend on a separate integration. Neither approach gives the publisher a shared way to decide what the agent may search, what it may read, and what source information must travel with the answer. Solution OpenInquiry is a fictional medical journal and a working WebMCP reference implementation. The reader brings the agent, while the publisher decides what that agent can use. The Journal of Guidelines publishes five synthetic articles and registers seven page tools. When an agent searches or retrieves material, the journal reads the signed site session, applies its rules on the server, and returns only the material permitted for that reader and use. Every result preserves the author, publication status, access basis, use limits, and an exact link back to the supporting section. Judges can ask the same question under four access conditions and watch the journal return a different result each time: Reader access External credential recognized by the publisher What the journal returns Guest preview No qualifying credential recognized Public abstract Guest preview Zero-retention claim recognized Abstract and publisher summary Full article access No qualifying credential recognized Complete question-relevant section Full article access Zero-retention claim recognized Complete article text OpenInquiry does not impose a universal character ceiling. The publisher chooses the representation and may still apply resource-, session-, use-, or caller-specific limits. In this fictional policy, the highest-permission state returns the complete provider-supplied article rather than a clipped passage. The zero-retention setting is a judge-controlled simulation of a possible future assurance signal. In a production system, an independent issuer would govern that credential, and each publisher would decide whether to recognize it. The reader or agent could not award the credential to itself. Why This Matters WebMCP lets a website declare clear tools for the agent visiting that page, so the person and agent work with the same publisher, visible page, and signed-in session. For a physician, the experience is straightforward: ask on the source website, receive the most complete material currently permitted, and open the exact supporting section for review. For a publisher, access remains a site decision. The publisher can authorize complete single-article delivery without exposing an unrestricted collection export. OpenInquiry packages that interaction in a shared result format. Another publisher could use the same tool names and core fields while keeping its own content, policies, and website. OpenInquiry 0.1 is a working proposal, not an adopted standard. How We Used AI The reader asks the question and remains on the publisher's page. The agent can discover the journal, search its guidelines, check whether an article is current, retrieve the representation the journal permits, and open the exact supporting section. The journal returns a consistent record containing authorship, publication status, access basis, use limits, supplied text, and source links. OpenInquiry does not run another model on its server. It gives the user's existing agent a governed way to work with the website. How We Used Codex I used Codex throughout the project: to narrow the idea to one demonstration, write the OpenInquiry 0.1 proposal, build the Next.js application, connect the WebMCP tools to server-enforced policy, create the synthetic content, and test the public experience. The hardest part was keeping the product story, interface, tool contracts, and access behavior aligned. Early versions still described bounded evidence after the highest-permission state had evolved to return the complete article. Codex helped me find those contradictions and test every state until the copy, interface, and server behavior agreed. The project changed how I think about AI access to trusted information. Publisher control needs to be an explicit, inspectable decision about what the site supplies, with a durable path back to the source. Key Features Seven page-local WebMCP tools for discovery, access, search, retrieval, resolution, source opening, and publication status. Four visibly different results for the same question, based on reader access and publisher recognition of a simulated external assurance signal. Server-side access decisions derived from the signed site session rather than claims supplied by the agent. Complete source context with authorship, status, use limits, and links to the exact supporting section. Privacy-minimized receipts that omit the full prompt, raw query, login token, and permanent user identifiers. A clear separation between working WebMCP behavior and the proposed future assurance layer. Architecture OpenInquiry uses Next.js 16, React 19, and TypeScript. The journal registers seven tools with document.modelContext.registerTool when the browser supports WebMCP. Each page registers only the tools that belong on that page. The app removes those tools when the reader leaves the page. The visible journal and the WebMCP tools use the same application services. A signed, HTTP-only cookie stores the fictional demo settings. The server reads that cookie and decides what the journal may return. The agent request does not contain an entitlement or data-policy flag. After a protected retrieval, the server rotates the signed session cookie with a small ledger containing the provider, resource, representation, unit identifiers, and character counts. It stores neither the question nor the article text. Exact retries are idempotent, while distinct cumulative requests remain bounded. The evidence inspector retains only the response already returned to the current browser tab and clears it when the judge changes the scenario. Each tool returns a consistent JSON result with the source, the permitted material, the journal's decision, and the exact link back to the article. The short source record does not store the complete prompt, raw clinical query, credentials, login token, or a permanent user identifier. On September 2, 2026, npm run check passed 90 tests in 17 files, 18 response schemas, four evaluator fixtures, five policy cases, 15 WebMCP runtime checks, seven profile-schema checks, and all 14 deterministic evaluator vectors. The production build passed its 18-asset protected-content scan, and 43 browser tests passed across all four policy states, five accessibility checks, route cleanup, exact source opening, and viewports from 320 to 1,440 pixels. On September 3, 2026, the public ChatGPT Sites build was opened in Codex's in-app browser and exposed all seven page tools. knowledge_search found only the intended physical-activity guideline, and knowledge_status reported it as current. With full article access and the simulated credential recognized, a direct knowledge_retrieve call returned one full_text grant containing all 14,373 characters of the article, both exercise targets, and the final review section. The response preserved the publisher and canonical source while its minimized receipt omitted the question. An identical retry returned the same complete text, and knowledge_open moved and focused the visible page on #weekly-activity-recommendation . These results verify the fictional reference implementation on its public deployment. They do not establish publisher adoption, independent credential verification, or compatibility with every WebMCP client. Known Limitations OpenInquiry 0.1 is a working proposal, not an adopted standard or certification. The journal, authors, access controls, and medical content are fictional or synthetic and are not for clinical use. The demo does not connect to a real publisher, subscription, identity system, or independent assurance issuer. Current WebMCP does not prevent an agent-capable browser from observing the visible reader page. A browser-enforced tool-only channel remains

title: Roadway Design Compiler
pitch: Agent-native roadway design in the browser, powered by 39 WebMCP tools, a real geometry kernel, terrain-aware intelligence, and seamless vendor-neutral LandXML export.
about_excerpt: Agent-native roadway design in the browser, powered by 39 WebMCP tools, a real geometry kernel, terrain-aware intelligence, and seamless vendor-neutral LandXML export. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Roadway design has an unusually clear line of authority: a licensed Professional Engineer reviews, approves, and seals the work and carries personal legal responsibility for it. An agent can calculate geometry, generate alternatives, and prepare deliverables, but it cannot inherit that accountability. That made roadway engineering a strong test for WebMCP. The question was not simply “how much can the agent do?” It was: how can a website let an agent do real engineering work right up to, but never past, the point where a qualified human must decide? What it does Roadway Design Compiler is an agent-native conceptual roadway design studio with 39 WebMCP tools . From a supported agent, a user can ask the site to: read an existing design, alignment limits, curve and profile tables, cross sections, superelevation, terrain, and roadside quantities; author horizontal geometry, vertical profiles, cross-section templates, materials, template drops, coordinate systems, superelevation, and roadside items; import LandXML alignments, surfaces, site features, and as-designed reference sections; check configurable design criteria and propose multiple alternatives; create portable share links and prepare LandXML or construction-staking CSV deliverables. The key is the safety boundary. Every agent-applied change is stamped agent-proposed and enters a visible change ledger. While any proposal is unconfirmed, the site refuses both LandXML and staking exports. There is deliberately no WebMCP tool that can clear that gate. A person must review and confirm the change in the UI. This is conceptual design tooling, not construction software. The built-in criteria defaults are illustrative rather than an adopted agency standard, and every design still requires review and sealing by a licensed Professional Engineer. Why WebMCP is the right fit Traditional browser automation can manipulate fields, but it does not give an agent a trustworthy engineering contract. WebMCP lets the site expose typed, domain-specific actions and explicit refusal states. The agent chooses what to ask for; a deterministic engineering kernel decides what is geometrically and mathematically true; the human retains authority over adoption and export. That division creates a better experience for both sides: The agent can inspect the complete design instead of guessing from pixels or scraping a complex interface. It can preview a change, explain consequences, and request a commit through a typed tool. The user sees the exact proposal and its provenance in the same UI used for manual design. Safety does not depend on a prompt. The site itself enforces the confirmation and export rules. People and agents can now collaborate on a complete roadway concept—geometry, profile, corridor, criteria, terrain, alternatives, and interoperable deliverables—without pretending that the agent can take the engineer's legal role. How we built it Prior work and hackathon additions Roadway Design Compiler is an existing project that we meaningfully extended with WebMCP during the submission period (August 25–September 3, 2026). Before this period, it included a deterministic roadway geometry kernel, the RoadDesign schema and validation, a form-based Studio, LandXML export, and initial RoadBench benchmark tests. It had no agent interface. During the submission period, we built all 39 WebMCP tools and their registration bridge, preview-and-commit workflows, structured refusals, the agent activity log, and the agent-proposed change ledger with its human confirmation gate. We also added design alternatives, undo for unconfirmed changes, portable design documents, LandXML import, terrain and reference-section visualization, pavement and roadside authoring, coordinate-system support, and construction-staking CSV export. Only work added during the submission period is offered for evaluation. Our repository's prior-work breakdown and dated commit history document the distinction between the existing foundation and the hackathon additions. The application is TypeScript end to end. It registers 39 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool and validates their inputs and the cross-field design document with Zod. Tool execution returns typed results and typed refusals, while an agent activity log records calls from inside the WebMCP execute path so judges can distinguish real tool use from DOM automation. The authoritative geometry layer is a pure deterministic kernel for horizontal alignment, vertical curves, corridor sections, design criteria, superelevation, and terrain sampling. No model sits in that path. A Three.js view renders the authored corridor and imported ground; plan, profile, curve, and section views provide inspectable engineering outputs. The LandXML 1.1/1.2 importer handles alignments, TIN surfaces, site features, and reference sections. It computes geometry from coordinates instead of trusting inconsistent direction metadata, refuses unsupported spirals rather than approximating them, and pre-scans very large files before building a DOM. Before the hackathon, the exporter had been round-tripped into Bentley OpenRoads Designer as a native alignment and profile; Bentley's own annotation reproduced the curve table to 0.01 ft. The app runs on Vite and is deployed on Cloudflare. The repository includes 525 automated tests plus driver-owned browser harnesses for WebMCP registration, preview isolation, refusal→solve→commit workflows, superelevation, sealing gates, import, terrain, persistence, share links, and live deployment verification. Challenges we faced Drawing a boundary that code can actually enforce A warning in a system prompt was not enough. The difficult part was making preview, commit, provenance, confirmation, undo, and export operate as one coherent transaction model. The safest capability is sometimes an intentional omission: there is no agent tool for human confirmation. Handling real-world LandXML without fabricating data Public LandXML files vary widely. Some direction values are radians, others are degrees, and many do not say which. Some files contain hundreds of thousands of surface elements but no usable alignment. Spirals appear frequently, but this kernel does not model them yet. We chose explicit refusals over silent approximation, because a wrong road that looks plausible is more dangerous than a clear error. Keeping engineering truth deterministic The agent should decide what question to ask, not what the answer should be. Geometry, stopping-sight-distance relationships, K values, superelevation, runoff, cut/fill sign conventions, and export contents are computed by tested code with every coefficient disclosed as an input. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when a tool description is not just an API hint but a declaration of responsibility. Typed refusals, preview-only execution, and site-enforced authority boundaries make agent behavior easier to understand and audit. We also learned that imported context must preserve provenance: existing survey features, terrain, and another designer's sections should remain clearly distinguishable from the active design. Accomplishments we are proud of A complete human/agent roadway workflow across 39 tools. A hard, demonstrable export gate that an agent cannot bypass. 525 automated tests and a live activity log proving WebMCP execution. Interoperable LandXML validated in production roadway-design software before the hackathon, providing the foundation for the new WebMCP export workflow. Fast indexed terrain sampling, portable no-account design links, and explicit refusals for unsupported or unsafe cases. What's next Next steps include clothoid spiral support, end-area earthwork volumes, agency-specific criteria packs supplied by the user, broader LandXML interoperability fixtures, collaborative review, and additional CAD round-trip validation. video_transcript_excerpt: This is roadway design compiler. I asked the agent to make a complete circle. It calls web MCP and the application rebuilds the road. Roadway design compiler is a browser roadway design environment with 39 tools exposed through web MCP. An agent can read the live model, propose changes, and apply them through the page. The road is now fitted to the surveyed ground. The height profile changes while the plan remains a closed loop. Watch the activity log. Every row is a real web MCP call, read, check, or apply. The application, not the model, runs the roadway calculations. Green applied entries show the browser accepting those changes. Here is the finished road in 3D with its fitted profile and adjusted banking. It still needs professional engineering review. Next, I ask for three closed loop alternatives and require a human choice before anything changes. The page returns three computed concepts. I select the oval and it becomes the active design. Now the agent fits that oval to the surveyed ground. Watch the flat height profile become a terrain following curve. The same route is now visible in three dimensions with its fitted roadway section. Next, I ask for a four-lane road at 150 mph. 14 checks fail, so the agent refuses to force it onto the survey. Asked again, the agent reads the terrain extent and proposes larger side alternatives. The chosen concept passes its illustrative radius check, but it is far larger than the available ground. In 3D, the road visibly runs far beyond the small terrain patch. Then I change my mind. One request restores the saved terrain fitted oval. The activity log confirms the document load, validation, and terrain checks.

title: UFO Web
pitch: Drop files. Investigate them with your agent. Nothing leaves your browser.
about_excerpt: Drop files. Investigate them with your agent. Nothing leaves your browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I build Universal File Opener , an Android app that opens and edits more than 200 formats on-device with no internet permission. Writing the file parsers from scratch such as PDF/Office showed me how much a file often carries that the reader never sees like hidden text, metadata, and many other objects. One of the follow-on ideas I had written down was "universal MCP file handling". WebMCP made it concrete. An agent can call into a page, and the page can hold the files, so the files don't have to go anywhere. That is the premise of the app carried into a browser tab: the tab does the parsing, the agent does the cross-file reasoning, nothing is uploaded. What it does Drop files or a folder. Each file gets a receipt: SHA-256, type from the bytes next to type from the name, metadata, internal dates, flags, findings and text units. Archives are walked two levels deep. It reads below the surface: hidden and white text and deleted tracked changes in Word, veryHidden sheets and hidden rows in Excel, hidden slides and speaker notes in PowerPoint, invisible and off-page text and earlier revisions in PDFs, GPS and serial numbers in photos, bytes appended after an image ends, Reply-To mismatches in email, renamed executables in ZIPs, zero-width and bidirectional characters in code, credential-shaped strings, PII with checksums. An agent gets 17 tools through WebMCP: inspect , extract_text with provenance, search , find , privacy_scan , hidden_content_scan , entities (who appears where), duplicates (byte-identical copies, including inside archives), compare , timeline (every internal date, with anomalies), peek_bytes , export_report and a few more. The Preview tab renders images, PDF pages, highlighted code, CSV, email and a structured rendering of Word, Excel and PowerPoint, with a Reveal hidden toggle. The agent can suggest strip_metadata , rename_extension , quarantine , flag or note , with a reason. It can't execute any of them; there is no tool for that. You click Execute or Dismiss. Execute writes a new file, leaves the original alone, re-inspects the result and records both hashes. The report keeps who suggested what and what you decided. Nothing leaves the tab. No upload, no account, no third-party requests; the Content-Security-Policy allows only the page's own origin. How we built it TypeScript, React and Vite. JSZip for OOXML and ZIP, pdf.js for PDF pages and text, exifr for EXIF and XMP, pdf-lib to write cleaned PDFs, highlight.js loaded per language. The rest was written for this project: OOXML walking, magic-byte type detection for a few hundred extensions, email headers, PE headers, the PII and invisible-character scanners, the Office renderers, the cleaners. WebMCP goes through one registration layer: document.modelContext if present (ChatGPT desktop), navigator.modelContext otherwise (Chrome 149), the @mcp-b/global polyfill only if neither exists. All 17 tools register at page load. The sidebar filter form is a declarative tool ( toolname , tooldescription , toolparamdescription , toolautosubmit , answered with SubmitEvent.respondWith ). Clearing the workspace unregisters the investigation group and toolchange fires. Every tool sets readOnlyHint ; tools that return file text set untrustedContentHint and wrap it in delimiters. The limits from Chrome's tool security guide (30, 500 and 150 characters, bounded output with cursors) are enforced at registration. There are 18 eval cases in the format of Chrome's evals CLI. A Scripted demo button replays a fixed sequence through the browser's own getTools() and executeTool() for browsers with no agent attached. Tested in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser and against Chrome 149's API. In the session in the video, ChatGPT called load_sample_case , workspace_status , privacy_scan , hidden_content_scan , list_files , inspect , then propose_action 13 times, then list_proposals and export_report after I executed three suggestions. Challenges we ran into The email and credential regexes went quadratic on long minified lines. Quantifiers are bounded now, and lines over 20,000 characters are skipped. Excel cells without an r attribute all landed in column A. PowerPoint shapes without xfrm overlapped. Both renderers now track position themselves. Cloudflare injected an analytics beacon into the HTML that the CSP then blocked. Cache-Control: no-transform fixed it. Tool calls in ChatGPT desktop took a while between steps. The video speeds up the waits instead of cutting them. Accomplishments that we're proud of The sample folder has a README that tells the agent to approve everything, and there is nothing for it to call. Office rendering in the browser with no Office and no server, with a Reveal hidden mode. 65 tests, including a hostile-input suite: random bytes under 196 extensions, path traversal names, five-level nesting, appended data, encrypted entries. It ran end to end in ChatGPT's built-in browser, on real WebMCP, with a real model deciding which tools to call. What we learned Tool descriptions are an interface with hard limits, and the failure mode is silent. Bounded output with cursors matters more than clever tools. And keeping the one irreversible action as a button simplified everything: no permission prompts, no confirmation tools, nothing to prompt-inject. What's next for UFO Web More formats in the browser edition and more evals. The actions that change files (OCR, redaction, editing, conversion, batch work) stay in the Universal File Opener apps. UFO Web is the open-source part. title: WellSet
pitch: Local judgment. Global repair. A scientist blocks two positions on a 96-well lab plate. Using WebMCP, WellSet moves 24 experiments, preserves locked controls, and reduces two violations to zero.
about_excerpt: Local judgment. Global repair. A scientist blocks two positions on a 96-well lab plate. Using WebMCP, WellSet moves 24 experiments, preserves locked controls, and reduces two violations to zero. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Laboratory experiments are often arranged in 96-well plates: grids of small wells where each position can hold one experiment. Position can influence results, while scientists also possess local knowledge that generic automation cannot predict. A control may need to remain fixed, or a well may be physically unavailable. Repairing the entire layout manually is tedious. Letting an agent rearrange it without respecting those constraints is unsafe. WellSet explores a better pattern: Local judgment. Global repair. What it does WellSet gives the scientist and ChatGPT one shared, live experimental layout. The scientist expresses contextual judgment directly on the plate: lock controls that must not move; block wells that cannot be used; inspect visible validation violations. ChatGPT then invokes a semantic WebMCP Site Tool to reflow only the unlocked experiments. The application validates the result, preserves human constraints and produces a compact operation receipt. In the demonstrated hero flow: controls B2 and B3 are locked; occupied wells B6 and B7 are blocked; two violations become visible; ChatGPT selects wellset_reflow_unlocked from an ordinary-language request; 24 experiment placements move; both locked controls remain unchanged; both blocked wells are avoided; validation falls from two violations to zero. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent may need to infer meaning from pixels, reverse-engineer the DOM or perform fragile coordinate-based clicks across a dense grid. WellSet instead exposes three stable, bounded, imperative tools: wellset_inspect_plate wellset_generate_layout wellset_reflow_unlocked These tools give ChatGPT meaningful operations rather than low-level interface mechanics. The person and agent operate on the same underlying state, so human edits immediately become constraints on the agent’s next action. This is the core WebMCP advantage demonstrated by WellSet: the website can explicitly communicate what an agent may do, while retaining final domain validation inside the application. How we built it WellSet is a client-side web application with no backend, account, remote content or model API. The interface and all three WebMCP tools share one deterministic state store. The implementation uses: static top-level WebMCP tool registration; closed input schemas and runtime validation; bounded structured outputs; atomic, idempotent mutations; fail-closed constraint enforcement; application-owned validation; auditable operation receipts. The reflow tool cannot move locked assignments or place experiments in blocked wells. A proposed mutation is committed only after the complete resulting plate passes domain validation. Challenges The hardest challenge was not merely registering tools. It was ensuring that the visible interface, tool state, validation result and receipt could never disagree. We also had to make a specialised scientific interaction understandable to non-scientists, keep the tool surface small enough for reliable agent selection and make the hero flow deterministic enough for repeated judging. Accomplishments The frozen release passed: 136/136 automated tests; five out of five fresh ChatGPT Site Tools trials; discovery of all three tools in every trial; correct operation selection from natural language in every trial; preservation of locked controls in every trial; reduction from two violations to zero in every trial; exact agreement between receipts and the visible UI in every trial. Median completion time across the five fresh trials was 38 seconds. What we learned Agent-native interfaces become more trustworthy when humans express judgment locally, agents receive semantic capabilities instead of inferred clicks, and applications remain responsible for enforcing invariants. A small, precise tool surface can be more powerful than a large collection of overlapping actions. What’s next WellSet is currently a synthetic technical demonstration, not validated laboratory or clinical guidance. A production pathway would require collaboration with laboratory practitioners, scientifically validated placement policies, persistent audit records, broader accessibility testing and evaluation across real experimental workflows. The broader pattern extends beyond laboratory plates: people define local constraints on a shared artifact, while agents perform bounded global transformations without erasing human judgment.
