title: WIDGENTIC
pitch: Widgets for agents. Your agent drafts into the designer you are looking at over WebMCP, you save, and ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot render it inline over MCP.
about_excerpt: Widgets for agents. Your agent drafts into the designer you are looking at over WebMCP, you save, and ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot render it inline over MCP. Like Comment Story Updates The loop Agent creates widgets using WebMCP tools Keys & Connect Agent uses the widgets Widgentic, widgets for agents - https://widgentic.dev/ Co-author with a browser agent - https://docs.widgentic.dev/develop/co-author-with-an-agent Widgets for agents, designed with one Inspiration widgentic started from a simple observation: agents are good at fetching data and bad at showing it. Every MCP tool result was a wall of JSON or a paragraph of prose. So we built widgets for agents : a payload contract { kind, data, hints?, meta? } , a built-in catalog (card, table and tree), a template DSL that is data rather than code, and an MCP server that renders any of it inline in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, VS Code Copilot Chat and ChatGPT. Then we noticed the two authors never met. An agent could read the authoring guide and draft a perfect widget definition, but it had no way to put it anywhere. A person had to copy the JSON, paste it into the designer, fix it, and save. We had made that separation a rule on purpose: there is no agent write path . API keys travel into prompt-injectable hosts, so they only read. People save. WebMCP lets us keep the rule and close the gap. A page registers tools; the agent in the person's own browser calls them, under the person's session, while the person watches. The designer the person is looking at becomes the agent's tool. The agent drafts, the person saves (or tells the agent to), and every agent with a key renders the result. What we built The product, before the challenge Three open-source npm packages under @widgentic : core (contract, adapters, mapper, catalog, theming, template DSL, actions, in-place reactive rendering), designer (embeddable widget, theme, schema and action designers, also as custom elements), mcp (the tool-output convention, server assembly, per-principal store, secrets). Zero runtime dependencies; MIT. Docs at docs.widgentic.dev , source at github.com/widgentic/widgentic . An MCP server with eight tools ( list_widgets , list_schemas , list_actions , list_themes , list_theme_tokens , get_authoring_guide , render_widget , execute_action ) whose widgets mount inline through MCP Apps and update in place as data changes. The host matrix records what each host does. widgentic.dev : sign in, design widgets, themes, shared data schemas, actions and secrets, mint read-only API keys, and see every save on the next tool call. Actions are declared as data: prompt proposes a message, http runs server-side behind an SSRF guard with secrets injected by name and never shown again. A self-host example : one container image, the authoring app plus the MCP endpoint over a single SQLite file. For the challenge @widgentic/webmcp (beta, published with provenance): the mounted designers as fourteen WebMCP tools. Read the draft, check a definition without touching it, load a definition, set example data, set the preview theme, load or merge a theme entry, load a schema or an action, read the authoring guide, list the theme tokens. One call after mounting; a reported no-op in a browser without a model context. Read tools carry readOnlyHint . No tool saves anything. After the first live round the tools gained the full authoring guide and a dry-run check, so an agent drafting through them follows the same rules as one reading the MCP guide. Co-author with a browser agent documents it. The loop on real hosts. demo.widgentic.dev is the unmodified self-host image running as a single Azure Container App, with /mcp forwarded so one origin serves both surfaces. widgentic.dev adopted the same package the same day. A Chrome origin-trial token on both origins, so a plain Chrome or Edge exposes the tools without a flag. ChatGPT Desktop's browser lists all fourteen under "Available site tools", and ChatGPT renders the saved widgets on web, mobile and desktop. How we built it Spec-first, with OpenSpec: every capability has requirements and scenarios, every scenario has a test that asserts rendered content rather than CSS class names, and each change is archived with its design decisions. The repository enforces its own rules in the test gate: dependency direction between packages, browser-safety of the browser packages, a snapshot of every public export so surface changes are reviewed diffs. Releases are Changesets with npm provenance. Our own hosts live in a private repository that consumes the published packages the way anyone else would. We built it with an AI coding agent as a pair, which is fitting for a project about agents and people co-authoring. The commits carry that attribution. Three decisions shaped the whole project, and the WebMCP layer inherited them: Templates are data, not code. No expressions; data selects and the author supplies every literal. That is what makes a template safe to store from an untrusted author and safe for an agent to draft. Refuse at the door, never lose a save. Invalid entries are rejected on write with a structured code and re-validated on read. The WebMCP tools relay the designer's own errors so the agent can fix its draft. The person saves. Keys read; sessions write. For WebMCP that meant getters resolved on every call (hosts remount designers on tab switches), results that are structured and never thrown, and no save tool at all. A host agent that can operate the page may still click Save when the person asks it to; our tools never do, and the draft is on screen first. What we learned MCP is becoming a UI protocol, not only a tool protocol. When we started, inline rendering was an experiment in one host. Within months the MCP Apps standard was shared by claude.ai, Claude Desktop, VS Code Copilot Chat and ChatGPT, and the vendor-specific way kept working only as an alias. Building on the open shape and treating each host's extensions as optional was the right bet. Same protocol, different manners. Hosts agree on the wire and disagree on everything around it: what they advertise, when they confirm, how they cache, how they treat a proposed message. A host matrix of verified behaviour became a product artifact in its own right, and "never guess a host, probe it" became a rule. Templates as data are what make agents welcome. No expressions means an untrusted author cannot execute anything, a validator can say exactly what is wrong, and an agent can draft a definition from the same rules a person edits by. Every guide and tool description is derived from the validators' own constants, so what the agent is told is what the code enforces. Trust has to be architectural. Agents read, people write. Keys that travel into prompt-injectable places must not be able to author; secrets are referenced by name and injected at execution. The boundary held under WebMCP without a new rule: the agent's tools act on the person's live session and never save; a host agent that can operate the page may click Save when the person asks, with the draft visible first. The browser is becoming an agent host, and the page is the interface. WebMCP turns the UI a person already uses into the agent's tool surface, so both see the same preview and the same diagnostics, and the copy-paste gap disappears. The standard is still moving — surfaces, argument shapes and permission models differ between browsers — so the layer has to feature-detect, stay thin, and put the collaboration boundary into the words the agent reads. Spec-first is what makes pair-building with an AI fast and safe. Requirements and scenarios written before code gave the agent a contract, gave us a review surface, and left a record of every decision. The challenge work landed in about two days because the shape of the system was already written down. Challenges Cold starts. Scale-from-zero on Container Apps measured 33 seconds end to end, long enough for MCP hosts to give up. One always-on replica and a readiness probe fixed it. Live data never migrates itself. A persisted-shape change once crash-looped a deploy against existing documents. Every shape change now ships with a normalization seam and an old-shape regression test before it deploys. Guarding server-side actions. Node's BlockList checks IPv4 addresses against mapped-IPv6 rules, so a naive rule blocked every IPv4; embedded addresses are re-checked instead. Redirects are refused, bodies are capped, and the frame never touches the network. First publish of a new package. Trusted publishing binds to an existing package, so @widgentic/webmcp needed a one-time bootstrap token, minted and deleted the same night. The designer's public surface. Its handle drops sample data on load, so the example-data tool writes the persisted dataExample instead, which turned out to be the better target. So, Wigentic turns data into customizable widgets that render inline in ChatGPT, Claude, and Copilot. Until now, a person designed those widgets alone. With WebMCP, the agent designs them with you. title: GamesLab
pitch: Let a browser agent turn an idea of a game variation such as "Tic-Tac-Toe, but the pieces are rock paper and scissors" into a safe, modular, online multiplayer board game with powerful bot!
about_excerpt: Let a browser agent turn an idea of a game variation such as "Tic-Tac-Toe, but the pieces are rock paper and scissors" into a safe, modular, online multiplayer board game with powerful bot! Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent building a game variation Ability for manual edits too! Inspiration For a couple weeks I've been hanging around online communities where people are trying to come up with new tile-based games. The same pattern kept happening: someone would suggest a variation, "what if bishops could jump," "what if pawns moved sideways," and there was no good way to tell whether the idea was actually fun or just novel. Trying it out meant having an AI build/update a website, republishing it, and only then finding out if the rule was any good. There was no shared framework, so every suggestion reinvented the wheel, and every small idea change cost a full deploy cycle before anyone could sit down and play it. AI agents already made the idea part faster: you could describe a rule change to a model and it understood you immediately. What was missing was a place for that understanding to land. Re-publishing a whole website for "what if the bishop jumps" is annoying at best. I wanted to create a board game website that was entirely modularly rule-defined such that telling an agent what you wanted and actually playing it online with a friend could be the same five minutes. The other half of this project is just personal: I've always liked breaking a game's rules apart and rebuilding them slightly different, trying to find the more-fun version than the original. And I know this isn't uncommon; if you look at the Wikipedia list of chess variants , you'll see hundreds of people who did exactly this. What I learned An important idea turned out to be that the game has to be entirely data and never code. If a rule can be an arbitrary function, you can't validate it, you can't hand it to an agent safely, and you can't run a search against it. A rule someone wrote has to be immediately safe to open and function in the same exact way as alternative rules. I also learned that giving an agent a tool is a design problem in its own right, not a wrapper around an API. The tool listing gets re-sent on every single turn of a conversation, so every tool that isn't earning its place is a tax paid forever. I ended up cutting the workbench's tool listing roughly in half by removing tools for things that the agent doesn't need to do: publishing, voting, starting a match, and keeping only what an agent is actually there for: reading a game, building one, checking it, and handing over a game of it. How I built it Everything centers on a single rule format; board, pieces, movement, capture, and win conditions are expressed as one finite JSON document. That document is read by three different engines that all have to agree: a TypeScript reader in the browser, a Go reader on the server (the authority), and a Rust core compiled to WebAssembly for speed (so bot engine can search millions of positions a second for better quality play). Keeping three implementations honest is done with a shared conformance corpus: a fixed set of recorded positions and legal moves that all three readers are tested against, so a format change that lands in one and not the others shows up as a failing test rather than a live bug. The Rust engine exists because an interpreted alpha-beta search over a general rule format is too slow to be useful. Compiling the document down to a program with names already resolved (offsets baked, kinds as indices) was worth roughly 40× the speed of just trying to make the interpreter faster. That speed is what makes it possible to validate a brand-new game variant by having a bot play hundreds of games against itself in well under a second, checking that one side doesn't always win and the game doesn't always draw. Alpha-beta pruning is what makes that search tractable at all: with good move ordering it cuts the size of the game tree explored from O(b^d) down to roughly O(b^{d/2}) for branching factor b and depth d. The difference between a bot that can check a variant in milliseconds and one that can't. The same rule format also generates the rulebook. Because moves, captures, and win conditions are structured data rather than arbitrary prose, the site can snapshot "interesting" positions from bot self-play and use them to show a stranger how a brand-new game is actually won, without anyone writing documentation/explanations by hand. On top of that sits a shared workbench: a person and an agent editing the same document, through the same functions, at the same time, with an activity ledger, pause, and a confirmation step before anything gets published. Challenges The hardest problem wasn't any single piece of code, it was scope discipline in the format itself. I really wanted to support every game, but if I add support for every possible game interaction or mechanic the rule-based game is actually worse than if it was just hard coded. If there's too many options, it's too hard to use and we don't get the benefit of the shared mechanics! Keeping three engines byte-for-byte consistent was a constant source of subtle bugs. Every format change had to be replicated in three places, so I planned ahead and leaned hard on automated equivalence tests between the interpreted and compiled paths rather than trusting careful reading. Measuring whether the bot was actually competent was tricky. Because there are many different possible games and I wanted a single bot that could learn any ruleset and play decently well, I had to weigh the eval parameters against known strategies for existing games, tying them to specific win conditions and piece values (when possible in the ruleset). This took a lot of trial and error in many different games, and it's not perfect, but it doesn't have to be! The point of the computation engine isn't to beat StockFish at chess, it's to be good enough to know when the game is bad . When the human is testing the game, it doesn't matter if they beat the bot 80% of the time, because just having an opponent is enough to validate if it would be a fun game and if they should invite their friends to play (with the built in challenge link). video_title: I told my browser's agent to break Tic-Tac-Toe. It did. | GamesLab (OpenAI WebMCP Challenge)
video_transcript_excerpt: Athell is a great game, so why not add fog of war? Checkers is a classic, but what if we'll play it on a hexagon? Chess is fun, but what if we take out the middle of the board? Tic-tac-toe is kind of lame. So, let's add rock, paper, and scissors to the game. Games Lab was designed to let us do exactly that. Just open the website in an agent powered browser and describe the game you want to see. In agent control, we can watch the game come to life. The agent plans out the new game and lets us interject at any point or pause its progress. All the games are strictly rule-based. At no point does the agent write or run code. This guarantees that no malicious code is being run. The game behaves exactly as expected and the agent only needs to modify a couple rules and not the whole game. After each rule is changed, we can see a live demo of two bots playing each other in the new game that is being created. The bot not only serves to show that the game visually looks and plays how it's expected, but because it was coded with a web assembly target of Rust and is so dang fast, it can play behind the scenes thousands of games a second. Once the agent is done, it can ask the website to use this bot to make sure the game is valid and doesn't have any gameplay issues. At any point, we can open the manual editor, look around, or change some rules. The website would automatically notify the agent of any conflicting changes, and instruct the agent to merge the two together. Once the agent finishes, it's our turn to try out the game. Right away, the bot is given the rule set and can immediately search millions of positions a second. And yeah, it it beats me a lot. We can tell the bot to make any changes we want. Why not try it so if you get three in a row, you lose? The agent does its thing, updates the plan, makes the changes, and then you can play again. The game's kind of fun, much better than normal tic-tac-toe. We can then publish the game and start paying other people. A rule book is automatically generated and shows exactly how to win and what pieces do what. Though, after playing a lot of games, something doesn't feel right. Let's ask the agent what's up with that. Well, would you look at that? The agent had the website run 400 games and found that blue almost always won. The times red one is almost certainly because of the random openings it's forced to do. In under 10 minutes, I was able to try out a new idea, try it against a pretty competent bot, play it in online multiplayer games, and scrap the idea in the end cuz it's unbalanced. That is the power of Games Lab. It allows rapid innovation of new games and I am so excited to see what people make. Please do let me know of any fun variations you come up with.

title: GatherLight
pitch: GatherLight uses WebMCP to channel spare human time and skills into peer-reviewed, verified contributions to the open web.
about_excerpt: GatherLight uses WebMCP to channel spare human time and skills into peer-reviewed, verified contributions to the open web. Like 2 Comment Story Updates GatherLight - Landing Page and Queries Quests and OSS Tools Integrated with - OpenStreetMap and Wikimedia Quest - Completion and Sign off on the Volunteer's name, Minimum Viable Information Screen to verify final submission details A Peer Selected Reviewer Views your contribution Let's Go! Star Lights up, And your community thanks your service! Architecture Diagram Detailing Deployment, Infra, Sites and Tools Inspiration Volunteering takes more time than most people expect. A person might have twenty free minutes and a genuine desire to help but the steps surrounding that desire often take much longer. They need to find a useful gap, learn an unfamiliar system, gather evidence, format it correctly, verify it and locate the right reviewer. And let's be real, most honestly helpful people drop off before they ever reach the step that only they can do. This led us to the enigma : what should an agent never do on behalf of a person? An agent cannot stand at a shop entrance and check whether it is step-free. It cannot make a phone call and take responsibility for what it heard. These actions require human presence, judgment and accountability. However an agent can remove nearly every obstacle surrounding those actions. GatherLight uses WebMCP capability to coordinate human-led civic work across the web. It finds real gaps in OpenStreetMap and Wikidata and guides a person through one useful task. It checks the result, carries it across sites, asks for explicit confirmation and routes it to another person for review. The agent handles the logistics and the human does the work. (A genuine win-win) What it does GatherLight takes one plain-language request and turns it into one verified civic contribution. "Find me something useful I can do near Koramangala in twenty minutes." (for people that don't know what Koramangala is, it is a place in an Indian city - Bangalore, known for parties,tech and ever upgrading infrastructure) The browser agent works through the below five WebMCP tools. find-quests finds gaps on OpenStreetMap or Wikidata that match the volunteer's location, available time and skills. open-quest opens the visible workspace and explains the parts of the work that must remain human such as calling a place, visiting an entrance or reading an independent source. check-contribution checks the form against source-specific rules and returns exact corrections instead of a generic error message. submit-contribution becomes available only after the check passes. It opens an HTML confirmation dialog showing the exact contribution, destination, visibility and licence. The tool waits for the person to click and then checks the contribution again before sending anything. approve-contribution is available only to a reviewer who has a submitted contribution. It rejects self-review, checks that the public source has not changed and records either an approval or a stale result. Some quests continue/handed off on another website. Well, that's the USP. We are not just building a Hackathon repository but something that expands on the very foundations of WebMCP. The handoff carries permission and provenance but it does not carry the volunteer's PII data, observation, credentials or source tokens . The person enters the evidence through the visible interface. After review, an approved OpenStreetMap contribution can be opened in an embedded iD editor. GatherLight reloads the live map element, compares its version and stages the exact change in iD's undoable state. Nothing is uploaded automatically. Approval also produces a visible collective result (Audit purposes when Crowd Sourced - obviously). A mark becomes fully lit only when the public source accepts the change. GatherLight does not treat "approved" and "published" as the same thing. How we built it (This gets fairly technical, fairly fast - bear with us - or if you wanna skip the text - Excalidraw Slides to Show what we did .) The main product is not the website. It is @gatherlight/quest-tools , a framework-neutral package that expresses the five verbs as a reusable WebMCP grammar. Quest is the React reference application and Survey is a separate partner site written in vanilla TypeScript. Both use the same package which is proof that the workflow is portable across sites, origins and frameworks. The package registers tools through document.modelContext . Each WebMCP tool is a thin wrapper over the same operation used by the visible interface so a button and an agent call run the same validation, confirmation, state transition and error handling. There is no hidden automation path that can bypass the human interface. A capability rack shows the tools available at the current moment. When the workflow state changes the package updates the registered tools. By design, The submit-contribution tool does not exist for the agent until the contribution passes its check. The package still validates availability inside every execution because dynamic registration improves tool discovery but it is not an authorization boundary. Every result uses a small quest/1 envelope with an explicit state. Human-readable guidance comes first and one stable machine-readable line comes last. Public place names, source titles, URLs and contribution text are treated as untrusted input. We cap and escape them and mark tool output with untrustedContentHint . Cross-origin state lives in one Cloudflare Durable Object that stores only two entities: contributions and handoffs. Handoffs include: hashed, origin-bound, action-bound, single-use and short-lived. Exchanging one creates a grant for one contribution without exposing the volunteer's session. The data used is real. Overpass finds OpenStreetMap places with missing opening hours or wheelchair information. SPARQL finds Wikidata statements that still lack a source. Nominatim and Photon resolve place names. opening_hours validates map syntax. iD stages reviewed OpenStreetMap changes. Offline snapshots of real source data keep the demo usable when a public endpoint is unavailable. Challenges we ran into Crossing the document boundary WebMCP tools belong to the document that registered them so a full navigation destroys that document and its registered tools, and this boundary is still under discussion in WebMCP issue #227 . We worked around this by having open-quest return the next URL along with an opaque handoff that the receiving site can exchange to register the next valid tools without needing a browser extension. Keeping the person in control A browser-owned elicitation mechanism does not yet exist (see issue #165 ) so our package uses a site-owned <dialog> that follows a fixed sequence of check, preview, wait for confirmation, check again and then submit. Nothing is sent if the form changes after confirmation or if the person declines at any point, though we acknowledge this is an application-level safeguard and not a browser security primitive. Working with live public data A correct contribution can become outdated while it waits for review so GatherLight captures the source revision when a quest opens and reloads it before any approval or iD staging step. If the source has changed the contribution is marked stale and nothing is overwritten silently. Accomplishments that we're proud of One agent coordinates a human-led workflow across two origins and three surfaces using a single shared package. Quest discovers the work, Survey receives the field contribution and iD stages the reviewed change and the same five-verb package works in both React and vanilla TypeScript without any framework-specific logic. The human contribution cannot be bypassed and submission cannot skip confirmation. The agent can open, check, route and submit but it cannot manufacture an observation, photograph or source judgment, and both the UI and agent paths go through the same check-confirm-check sequence. Every contribution is grounded in real public data with each stage of the lifecycle clearly labelled and the prototype produces concrete findings for the open WebMCP Skills proposal . What we learned In civic systems an agent is more useful when it removes the friction around work that still needs human presence and judgment rather than trying to do that work itself and WebMCP makes this possible because the agent acts inside the page's current session through capabilities the site owns while the visible interface stays in control. We also found that being honest about what a contribution has actually achieved is more valuable than overstating it because telling a user that their contribution is reviewed but not yet published builds more trust than an animation that implies more change than actually happened. What's next for GatherLight First we will contribute the implementation evidence back to WebMCP's active discussions. Cross-document

title: Heatline
pitch: A tenant and a legal-aid advocate each get an agent on one NYC building's own enforcement record.
about_excerpt: A tenant and a legal-aid advocate each get an agent on one NYC building's own enforcement record. Like Comment Story Updates 52 degrees at 7am, eleven mornings in a row That was the reading in a fourth-floor apartment on Barnes Avenue in the Bronx this winter. The landlord stopped answering in January. What the tenant did not know, and what I did not know until I pulled the data, is that the city already had a file on the building: 102 open class C violations. Class C is HPD's word for "immediately hazardous." The oldest has been open 601 days. All of that sits on NYC Open Data. No key, no login, one SODA query. It has never been in the same room as the tenant. What Heatline does with it Two people open one case page from two different links. The tenant gets 12 WebMCP tools; the legal-aid advocate helping them gets 9. Same origin, same deployment, different agents. I want to be precise about the difference because it is the whole product: Only the tenant's window has log_condition , file_packet , answer_evidence_request , share_case and the 311 form. Only the advocate's window has assemble_hp_action_packet and request_evidence . Open DevTools, Application, WebMCP in both windows and the lists are not the same. The role is a capability key in the URL. The server re-derives it on every write, so when the advocate's agent forges a file_packet call (I tried) it gets a 403 that reads: "Only the tenant can file packet. You are the advocate: this stays with the tenant's session." The hidden tool is a convenience. The server is the boundary. A tenant does not know what a BBL is The first version of building_violation_history required a 10-digit borough-block-lot number. The advocate's agent called it with {} and got "bbl is required." That is a tool written for a database, not for a person freezing in an apartment. It now reads the BBL off the open case and only takes one if you want a different building. Fixed the same hour, in the commit log. The same instinct runs through the rest. The tenant types "no heat again, 52 degrees at 7am." match_condition_to_code returns section 27-2029 with the rule in plain English: 68F from 6am to 10pm when it is under 55F outside, heat season October 1 to May 31. log_condition then stops inside a confirmation card until the tenant presses Confirm. The agent proposes; the person decides. Every number on the page carries the SODA URL that produced it. Paste the URL and you get the same 102. Four NYC Open Data feeds become one per-building index, the page registers a different tool set per link, and the server re-checks the role before any write lands. The loop the two agents run The advocate's agent asks for a photo of the thermostat at 7am tomorrow. That request lands in the tenant's window over a live stream, no reload. The tenant's agent answers. The advocate's agent then calls assemble_hp_action_packet , which writes five sections from the case plus the city record: parties (owner name and portfolio size from the HPD registration), conditions with code sections, the building record with a block comparison, a timeline, relief sought. It saves a draft. In the tenant's window, file_packet 's description now says "one draft packet waiting"; the agent calls it, a person presses Confirm, the packet is filed. The 311 complaint is a real <form toolname="draft_311_complaint"> with toolparamdescription on each field and deliberately no toolautosubmit . The agent fills it. Only a human can press Send. You cannot do this with a chatbot wrapper or by scraping the page. Nothing else knows which window is asking. The tenant's window and the advocate's window on the same case. The gate in the middle is the server, not the tool list. The parts that are not glamorous document.modelContext.registerTool , never navigator.modelContext . Native first, @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill as fallback, and a badge on the page says which one is live. Fourteen tools. untrustedContentHint on list_conditions and build_timeline , because those return text another person typed; that text is wrapped in <untrusted-user-text> on the tool path, the REST path and the SSE stream. Confirm gates are built inside each mutating tool's execute , since WebMCP has no destructive-action annotation. Seventeen eval fixtures. The negative ones assert the denied tool is absent from that session's toolsForRole , so "just file it for them" from the advocate expects zero calls. 125 tests. Read tools fetch through /api/building/* so the 1.3 MB index stays server-side; importing it into the client broke the production build on day one, and that fix is in the history too. The index covers 40 buildings in zip 10467, the Bronx zip with the most open class C heat violations, 6,077 rows. The build script and every query URL are in the repo. Everything here was written on 4 September 2026 with Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind 4, Upstash Redis, Vitest and NYC Open Data. The build script, every SODA query URL and the eval fixtures are in the repo. title: AutoWebMCP: Teach an Agent to Fish
pitch: Turn human workflows into agent-ready WebMCP tools. AutoWebMCP learns what a user means, not just where they click, and publishes verified, typed semantic capabilities with guardrails.
about_excerpt: Turn human workflows into agent-ready WebMCP tools. AutoWebMCP learns what a user means, not just where they click, and publishes verified, typed semantic capabilities with guardrails. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a semantic interface for agents. But what about the enormous number of applications that were never built to expose one? Most browser automation approaches teach agents where to click or how to reproduce a sequence of UI actions. That makes the agent depend on interface mechanics rather than application meaning. We asked a different question: What if a user could teach an application a capability simply by demonstrating how they already perform the task? AutoWebMCP turns those demonstrations into agent-ready WebMCP tools. Teach → Semanticize → Validate → Publish → Agent The key idea is simple: the demonstration is evidence, not the automation. What it does A user performs a normal workflow while the AutoWebMCP Teach Mode extension observes the interaction. AutoWebMCP analyzes that evidence and proposes a typed semantic capability representing what the user intended, rather than exposing individual clicks as agent actions. For example, a human editing several controls in Salesforce can become: update_opportunity_details(opportunity_id, stage, close_date, main_sponsor) The user reviews and confirms the semantic contract. AutoWebMCP then establishes an execution binding, validates it against the live application, and publishes the capability as a WebMCP tool. The resulting pipeline is: Human demonstration → Semantic capability → Execution binding → WebMCP tool → Agent We tested this with two very different applications. SignalBase is a cooperative application. AutoWebMCP can bind a learned capability to an action supplied by the application itself. Salesforce Lightning is the harder case. It was not built for AutoWebMCP, so learned capabilities execute against the application's existing interface through the AutoWebMCP runtime. To an agent, both appear as semantic WebMCP tools with names, descriptions, typed schemas, identity requirements, and safety semantics. In our demo, one natural-language instruction composes three independently taught capabilities: Find a VP-level contact in SignalBase. Search Salesforce for the relevant Opportunity and obtain its exact record identity. Update that Opportunity. The sequence is not hardcoded. The model chooses among the live WebMCP tools using their published descriptions, schemas, and results. How we built it AutoWebMCP has three main parts. Teach Mode is a Chrome extension that captures evidence while a user performs a workflow. It observes the interaction without treating the resulting event sequence as a replay script. Training Studio turns that evidence into a semantic capability. A model proposes the business intent, capability name, description, and typed inputs. The user reviews and confirms that contract before publication. The demonstration alone is not enough to safely execute the capability. AutoWebMCP combines observed evidence with platform, application, and tenant intelligence to help ground concepts such as business meaning, valid value domains, entity identity, tenant-specific vocabulary, execution semantics, and verification behavior. Critically, the semantic contract remains separate from the execution binding . An agent operates on concepts such as stage , close_date , and opportunity_id , while the runtime resolves how those concepts map to the application when the capability executes. We do not persist CSS selectors, XPath expressions, or screen coordinates as the semantic contract. Finally, WebMCP is the publication surface . Confirmed capabilities are compiled into tools with descriptions, typed input schemas, required fields, value domains where known, and supported annotations. For the cross-application demonstration, we also built a small page-side agent harness over the actual WebMCP API. On every step it: reads the current tools from document.modelContext.getTools() gives those descriptions and schemas to the model validates the selected tool and arguments against the live tool set invokes the tool through document.modelContext.executeTool() feeds the structured result back to the model for its next decision There is no separately hardcoded SignalBase-to-Salesforce workflow. The model has to infer the composition from the semantic tools it is given. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem turned out not to be recording browser interactions. It was deciding when an inferred capability is trustworthy enough for an agent to use. A demonstration contains incomplete and sometimes ambiguous evidence. A field label may be tenant-specific. A choice may have a constrained value domain. Two records can have similar names. A successful request does not necessarily mean the intended state was persisted. That pushed AutoWebMCP toward a stronger principle: Search may be fuzzy. Mutation must be exact. Writes therefore require an exact target identity, and execution verifies both the target and the requested outcome. If the runtime cannot establish what happened, it reports uncertainty instead of manufacturing success or blindly repeating a potentially committed mutation. Testing against a live Salesforce org exposed failure modes we would not have found in a controlled demo. Navigation can destroy the browser context waiting for an execution result. Browser extension service workers can disappear between captured events. A mutation can succeed even when its caller never receives the result. Those failures shaped the runtime's guardrails, retry semantics, target-identity checks, and distinction between requested state and verified state. Cross-application composition created another challenge. WebMCP tools belong to documents, while our demo combines a capability taught from SignalBase with capabilities backed by Salesforce. We therefore made publication location explicit and created a control surface where selected capabilities can coexist while still being invoked through the WebMCP API. Accomplishments that we're proud of The biggest accomplishment is that the original idea survived contact with a real enterprise application. We demonstrated the full loop: demonstrate → semanticize → human confirm → bind → live validate → publish → discover → compose → execute → verify The same learning pipeline supports two very different execution strategies: a cooperative application-provided binding in SignalBase and a learned browser execution binding against Salesforce Lightning. We are particularly proud that the agent-facing abstraction is semantic rather than mechanical. The agent sees: update_opportunity_details(...) not: click_button(...) → fill_input(...) → choose_option(...) → click_save(...) We also demonstrated model-driven composition across independently taught capabilities. From one business instruction, the agent selected a SignalBase contact capability, a Salesforce Opportunity search capability, and a Salesforce update capability based on the published WebMCP metadata and prior tool results. The safety behavior became an accomplishment of its own. AutoWebMCP can refuse to mutate an entity it cannot identify, distinguish an attempted change from a verified outcome, stop when a write may already have persisted, and preserve ambiguity rather than silently choosing among multiple candidate records. Those are not theoretical safeguards. Several were added after the corresponding failure happened during live testing. What we learned Our biggest learning is that turning a demonstration into an agent capability is fundamentally different from recording a macro . The interaction trace tells us what happened. It does not, by itself, tell us what the action means. The difficult work lies in extracting a durable semantic contract from imperfect evidence, grounding that contract in the application's concepts and environment, and then resolving it safely when an agent invokes the capability later. We also learned that semantic understanding and execution should remain separate. A stable concept such as close_date should not become synonymous with whatever DOM element happened to represent Close Date during the demonstration. And we learned that verification is part of the capability, not an afterthought. For autonomous systems, "I attempted the action" and "I established that the intended state now exists" are materially different outcomes. This changed how we think about AutoWebMCP. What began as an experiment in automatically generating WebMCP tools increasingly looks like a semantic capability compiler . What's next for AutoWebMCP: Teach an Agent to Fish WebMCP is the first publication target, but the learned semantic capability does not inherently belong to WebMCP. The same architecture could eventually publish a confirmed capability through WebMCP, an external MCP server, an API, or another agent runtime while preserving the semantic
video_transcript_excerpt: What if you could teach existing web applications to become agent ready without programming every tool by hand? For this demo, AutoWebMCP has learned three capabilities across two applications. Signal base can find right contact, Salesforce can search and update opportunity. These are published as typed WebMCP tools, so I can give an agent one business level instruction. With these WebMCPs in place, I can in natural language ask my agent to perform a series of tasks. It first finds the VP in Signal base. It then realizes Salesforce update requires an exact opportunity identity, so it searches for the opportunity before attempting the update. Notice the guardrails. If Salesforce is not in the required state, the tool changes context but reports nothing was updated. A mutation only proceeds against the exact requested record. Finally, the system verifies both the resulting values and the target identity. The agent is working with semantic capabilities, not browser clicks. So, where do these tools come from? A user teaches AutoWebMCP simply by doing the work they already know. I start teach mode and perform the workflow normally. But AutoWebMCP is not recording just a macro. The interaction trace is evidence, not the automation. The interesting part happens next, where all these traces are sent to the studio. AutoWebMCP takes the evidence and tries to understand user's intent. Instead of exposing individual clicks, it proposes one business capability with a semantic description and typed inputs. Application and tenant intelligence help ground that capability in what the application means, what values are valid, and how it can safely execute. The semantic contract remains separate from the execution binding. The user reviews what AutoWebMCP understood, confirms it, and tests the binding against a live application. Only after the save is confirmed is the capability published as a WebMCP tool that an agent can discover and compose with other tools, as you saw in the first act. The user teaches by doing. AutoWebMCP semanticizes the intent. WebMCP makes the resulting capability available to agents. AutoWebMCP, teach an agent to fish.

title: TripRescue
pitch: Human-controlled flight recovery with typed WebMCP tools, constrained search, exact-price preview, and verified booking changes.
about_excerpt: Human-controlled flight recovery with typed WebMCP tools, constrained search, exact-price preview, and verified booking changes. Like Comment Story Updates What it does An airline moves your flight. TripRescue lets a traveller—or a browser agent working with them—inspect the affected booking, state recovery constraints such as arrival time, maximum extra cost, and stops, compare ranked alternatives, preview the exact itinerary and price difference, approve the change in the page, and verify the updated booking. It runs against a real Duffel test-mode order. Duffel's sandbox generates the airline change, the booked airline supplies the change offers, and the app verifies the confirmed order change by refetching it. Why WebMCP fits Trip recovery is a high-stakes, multi-step, stateful task where guessing buttons from pixels is unsafe. The agent needs the current booking, must obey explicit limits, must never confirm without the traveller, and must prove the result. TripRescue registers five focused tools from the top-level page with the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool API: get_trip find_recovery_options preview_trip_change apply_trip_change get_change_status The tools use the page's signed session. Booking IDs, provider tokens, and passenger data never enter the prompt. Read, search, preview, apply, and verify remain separate operations with appropriate annotations and compact normalized outputs. A better human-agent experience Every tool call updates the visible page before resolving, so the traveller sees the same state the agent is reasoning about. An Agent Activity log records each call and its purpose. The consequential write is protected by a server-issued preview, order fingerprint, expiry, exact-price revalidation, and single-use idempotent confirmation. Calling apply_trip_change opens an in-page confirmation dialog. The traveller—not the agent—must review the itinerary and explicitly confirm it. This lets the traveller state intent once—“direct, arrive by 1 PM, no more than $150 extra”—while the agent converts it into a constrained search, ranks valid options, stages the best one, and hands control back exactly when the booking and test charge would change. Success is defined by the refetched provider booking, not merely an HTTP 200. How it was built TripRescue uses Next.js 16, TypeScript, Zod, Tailwind CSS v4, the WebMCP imperative API, and the Duffel Flights API in test mode. It is deployed behind nginx with pm2 on Hetzner. GitHub Actions runs lint, typechecking, tests, and a production build before deploying, then verifies the public URL. Testing Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Create a sandbox trip, simulate an airline change, and ask the browser agent to find a nonstop replacement arriving before 1 PM for no more than $150 extra. Preview the best option, apply it, approve the in-page confirmation, and verify the refetched booking. Honest limitations Duffel test mode only. Schedules and prices are synthetic, and the airline change is simulated by Duffel. No live bookings or real payments occur. The demo uses the LHR → LTN Duffel Airways scenario supported by Duffel's sandbox. Built With duffel-flights-api github-actions next.js nginx pm2 tailwind-css typescript vitest webmcp zod Try it out triprescue.slate-app.online github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by varun a Like Share this project: Updates varun a started this project — Sep 03, 2026 06:04 AM EDT
video_title: Triprescue
video_transcript_excerpt: Trip rescue turns a disrupted flight into a safe agent assisted recovery. The browser agent can search and prepare the fix, but it cannot make the irreversible change on its own. We start with a real sandbox booking, then simulate the disruption inside the page. Before the recovery can work, the page needs a signed in trip and a browser session that the tools can reuse. The agent can read the trip, search options, and stage a change, but the traveler still owns the final approval. The booking ID and provider token stay out of the prompt, so the model works inside a constrained boundary. The demo opens on a Duffel sandbox booking, and the page confirms that five web MCP site tools are registered. A browser agent reads the signed in trip, then the schedule change lands, and the itinerary shifts from the original departure to the disrupted one. The agent gets real state, not a mocked prompt. The agent reads the signed in trip, then searches for non-stop alternatives that arrive before 1:00 p.m. and cost no more than $150 extra. It ranks the results instead of grabbing the first match. That matters because constrained search turns a broad travel problem into a narrow auditable choice. Trip rescue previews the best option as an earlier Duffel Airways flight, but nothing changes yet. The important distinction is between a proposal and a booking. One is comparison, the other is an actual mutation. That separation keeps the agent useful without letting it silently commit the change. The preview shows the full $125 test charge before anything changes. Trip rescue stages the exact itinerary, the fare difference, and the penalty in one place, so the traveler sees the real cost up front. The agent is still asking to apply the change. When the agent asks to apply it, Trip Rescue opens an in-page confirmation dialogue. The traveler, not the agent, reviews the itinerary and explicitly approves the mutation. That is the irreversible step, and it happens under human control inside the browser. After Duffel accepts it, the agent calls get change status, re-fetches the order, and checks that the new itinerary is truly booked. The post-change read-back is just as important as the approval because it proves the mutation actually stuck. Without that verification step, the workflow would only be optimistic. The booking ID and provider token never enter the prompt because every tool reuses the page's signed session. The verified state shows the new itinerary booked and rechecked in the browser. That is WebMCP with real utility and human control at the irreversible step.

title: Incident Room
pitch: An agent fills the rollback plan on the page you are viewing. The WebMCP form leaves submission to you: narrow the scope, review the operation, press Submit.
about_excerpt: An agent fills the rollback plan on the page you are viewing. The WebMCP form leaves submission to you: narrow the scope, review the operation, press Submit. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT's Sources panel: the agent called inspect_current_incident twice and show_change_comparison once, all tools this page registered. The agent filled the Recovery Plan and stopped. The operator removed healthy payment from scope, so the plan is marked HUMAN EDITED. RECOVERED only after a real Cloudflare rollback returned the same fixed request to 200. Three permanent-fix paths follow, the human picks. PLAN_STALE: someone deployed while the plan was open, so the server refused and wrote no rollback. The plan is refreshed, not restarted. The problem Checkout starts returning 500 right after a deployment. An agent can inspect the incident and prepare a rollback plan, but a person still has to decide which production services get touched and when that plan becomes a real write. In the workflow I wanted to improve, that decision lived in a chat window. The agent described a plan, the person typed "yes", and production changed before the person had reviewed the operation on screen. The approval was real. The review was not. Incident Room puts that decision on the page. The agent fills one Recovery Plan, the person edits it, and the person presses Submit. What the model cannot do The WebMCP form has no toolautosubmit . The agent can fill the fields, but its tool call stays pending until a person submits the form. The Controller also checks the Worker name, target version, scope, and observedDeploymentId against a server-side allowlist. Those values are not open parameters, so the agent can't widen the operation. The page waits for server verification before showing RECOVERED. Why WebMCP fits The Recovery Plan is page state shared by the agent and the person looking at it. A remote MCP server may read the same incident data, but it does not automatically know what this tab currently contains, what the person just edited, or which deployment ID was visible when the plan was drafted. WebMCP lets both parties work on that object in place. I also checked the human gate directly: three seconds after the agent filled the form, the fields were populated and the tool promise had not settled. What changes for the operator The reviewer reads a form, not a paragraph. It shows the Worker, target version, included and excluded services, and the evidence required for success. In the demo, the agent initially includes checkout and payment. Payment is healthy, so the operator removes it with one click before submitting. That correction is visible on the same screen instead of being buried in a chat log. What people and agents can do together A plan can survive a refusal. If another deployment happens while the form is open, the Controller returns PLAN_STALE and performs zero writes. The agent reads the new page state and refreshes the existing plan instead of starting over. After recovery, the agent can call propose_remediation_options with a diagnosis and one of three paths: fix forward through a reviewed pull request, keep investigating on the rollback, or prepare an emergency hotfix. The person still chooses. How I implemented WebMCP Three imperative tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() inside a React effect. An AbortController removes them when the page goes away. inspect_current_incident reads live health and deployment IDs, then focuses the affected service. show_change_comparison opens a diff only for a change already listed in the incident. propose_remediation_options places a diagnosis and repair options on the recovered page. These tools update page state but do not write to an external system. They carry readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint , while the real authorization boundary remains in the Controller. The Recovery Plan is the declarative tool. It has toolname and tooldescription , but no toolautosubmit . Its submit handler uses SubmitEvent.respondWith() so the page and the agent receive the same result. What is real The lab uses three dedicated Cloudflare Workers, not mocks. A deployed checkout version returns 500. The Controller calls the Workers Deployments API to roll back, then replays the same cart request. RECOVERED appears only when that request returns 200. Cloudflare supplies the deployment IDs shown as evidence. I ran the full path in ChatGPT's built-in browser on GPT-5.6 Sol. I also ran it in Chrome 152 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , including the stale-plan case where the deployment list contained the competing deployment and no rollback. Boundaries There is no remote MCP server, generic connector, or multi-user platform. The public site shares one lab, so another rehearsal can make an open plan stale. Workers Logs are secondary evidence. The permanent-fix step produces a simulated issue draft and labels it as such. It does not call GitHub or claim that a pull request exists. title: Meant
pitch: A conversational creative editor where agents propose, people decide, and every change stays visible and reversible.
about_excerpt: A conversational creative editor where agents propose, people decide, and every change stays visible and reversible. Like Comment Story Updates A visible human Keep commits revision 2 and updates History. The agent requests Undo; the person confirms it visibly. Undo creates revision 3 while preserving the full History. WebMCP creates an Exploring direction without changing the kept revision. The agent proposes Keep; the person remains the decision-maker. Inspiration Creative direction begins as meaning: make the title quieter, give the page more room, or make the story feel more grounded. Conventional design software asks people to translate that intention into layers, coordinates, panels, and property names before they can even judge the result. An agent can remove some of that translation burden, but only if it understands more than pixels. It needs to know which semantic object is selected, what operations are valid, whether a direction is temporary, which revision is authoritative, and what exact change can be undone. We built Meant to make that relationship legible. The person directs the work in ordinary language. The agent inspects the composition and proposes a bounded change. The kept artifact changes only through an explicit, visible human decision. What it does Meant turns an ordinary-language brief into a structured deck, poster, or infographic that remains visible, selectable, and editable inside the application. The core loop is: Say it. Describe the outcome in ordinary language. See it. Meant renders a visible, inspectable direction. Shape it. Refine a selected title, frame, or visual object through text, direct controls, or a browser agent. Keep it. Accept the exact Exploring direction intentionally. Change your mind. Compare or undo with an inspectable recent revision trail. Every proposal begins as Exploring , leaving the kept document and durable revision unchanged. Compare names the kept and Exploring versions. Discard removes only the temporary direction. A visible human Keep creates the next durable revision. Undo restores the earlier artifact as a newer revert revision, preserving both events in History . Text and direct controls provide a complete working path. The code also contains an OpenAI Realtime WebRTC integration that maps voice conversation to the same bounded tools when an entitled session is configured. The submission does not present an unexercised live product-audio round trip as evidence. Why WebMCP is a strong fit The most important state in a creative workspace is not visible in a screenshot. It includes the document structure, active selection, allowed operations, design contract, current Exploring draft, authoritative revision, and exact change eligible for recovery. Meant exposes that state through seven WebMCP tools registered on the page: get_composition_context reads a compact, revision-aware summary of the active composition. create_composition_draft starts a deck, poster, or infographic as an Exploring proposal. preview_composition_turn interprets one ordinary-language direction through the bounded operation registry. preview_composition_change previews strictly validated semantic operations without committing history. keep_composition_draft requests that the person confirm the exact draft with the visible Keep control; it never commits by itself. discard_composition_draft requests visible human confirmation before removing the Exploring draft. undo_composition_change requests visible human confirmation for an exact, revision-bound revert; it never creates a revision by itself. That distinction is the point. WebMCP lets an agent collaborate through meaning and explicit authority instead of guessing through screenshots or receiving a private shortcut around the product’s rules. What people and agents can do together now Before WebMCP, an external browser agent could see approximate interface pixels and simulate clicks, but it could not reliably know whether a title was the selected semantic object, whether a preview was still temporary, whether another view had advanced the revision, or which historical change was safe to undo. With Meant’s WebMCP surface, the agent can inspect the current semantic context, create or refine an Exploring direction, and hand the exact consequential choice back to the person. The person can compare the proposal with the kept artifact, then Keep, Discard, or Undo through visible controls. The result is a single creative loop shared by language, touch, direct controls, and browser agents without collapsing authorship into automation. How we implemented WebMCP Meant stores each artifact as a composition document with stable frames, semantic nodes, layout modes, bounded style primitives, and an artifact-specific design contract. Decks, posters, and infographics use the same document model while retaining their own dimensions and visual grammar. The page registers seven tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Strict JSON schemas reject unknown fields and constrain text, geometry, style values, operation counts, and output size. Human-authored document content is treated as untrusted data. Inspect and preview receipts are compact enough for current browser guidance, while consequential tools return confirmation requests instead of silently changing durable state. Every edit is compiled into the same operation registry used by the visible product. Preview operations apply immutably to an Exploring branch. Keep rebinds the proposed operations to the authoritative server document, revalidates them sequentially, and commits the updated project plus History through a D1 compare-and-swap transaction. Stale drafts fail visibly. Undo targets one exact eligible commit and creates a newer revert revision rather than deleting history. The final browser verification used the native WebMCP capability against the running application and an isolated D1 database. Its seven sections passed 42 assertions and two actual races: the complete Exploring/Compare/Keep/reload/Discard/Undo/History loop, a two-page Keep race, a first-use bootstrap race, long public directions with bounded receipts, typed human Keep, a 390×844 mobile loop, and 768×844 touch-target verification. Complementary unit and contract coverage exercises malformed operations, stale authority, and interrupted-response reconciliation. The approved production build was then deployed to meant.protoperfect.io and verified over HTTPS with the expected security headers, session behavior, unavailable test-only routes, all seven WebMCP tools registered, correct rendered product state, and a clean browser console. Challenges we ran into The hardest engineering problem was preserving creative flow without weakening state guarantees. Conversation feels fluid; durable work must be exact. We solved that tension with a visible Exploring branch, deterministic operations, explicit human confirmation, revision-bound persistence, and undo-as-history. The second challenge was making agent authority honest. A tool named Keep can easily imply that an agent has committed work. In the final contract, agent-side Keep, Discard, and Undo are requests for visible human confirmation. Tool receipts report that boundary directly. The third challenge was concurrency and ambiguous network outcomes. Two views can act on the same draft, or the server can commit while the client loses the response. Meant uses compare-and-swap, conflict states, authoritative History reconciliation, and exact operation identities so it can recover without duplicating a change or claiming success prematurely. The fourth challenge was showing a coherent creative product rather than a technical proof. We kept the canvas central, preserved the client artifact’s own visual identity, gave desktop and mobile Compare explicit labels, and built the submission film from verified product captures instead of generated interface mockups. Accomplishments that we’re proud of Seven bounded WebMCP tools registered and exercised through a native browser-agent capability. A real structured artifact that changes inside the application rather than a screenshot-only demo. An explicit Exploring branch with legible Compare, Keep, and Discard states. Agent-side consequence requests that preserve the person’s final authority. Revision-bound D1 persistence with conflict protection and response-loss reconciliation. Undo that creates a newer revert revision and retains the original change in History. Desktop and mobile flows that keep the canvas, current revision, and draft status visible. A final evidence chain built from real product stills, real product clips, and a redacted machine-readable invocation receipt. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when a page exposes meaning and authority—not simply more buttons. The important primitive is not “let the agent click Keep.” It is “let the agent understand the exact document, propose a bounded change, and return the consequential decisio

title: RecallOps WebMCP
pitch: The website gives agents tools to investigate and prepare - then withdraws them where human authority begins.
about_excerpt: The website gives agents tools to investigate and prepare - then withdraws them where human authority begins. Like Comment Story Updates Capability Sculpting: WebMCP tools appear only when workflow state permits; human-only authority stays outside the visiting agent. Architecture: WebMCP browser tools meet FastAPI policy, CockroachDB governed memory, AWS hosting, and an authority receipt chain. Governed evidence: mem_47 scores 0.94 but is rejected for version mismatch and failed outcome; reviewed mem_12 remains eligible. Immutable postcheck: after human approval, the app records recovery measurements and an independent policy verdict before reuse. Independent review: a separate reviewer certifies pending memory before it becomes eligible for future governed recall. Gallery overview: five proof screens show capability sculpting, architecture, governed evidence, postcheck policy, and reviewed recall. Problem Operational agents often mistake semantic similarity for permission. The closest historical fix may target the wrong service version, have a known failed outcome, belong to another tenant, or contain unreviewed experience. Asking an agent to “be careful” does not create an authority boundary, and an agent that can approve its own proposal or promote its own memories can turn one unverified outcome into future operational authority. Solution RecallOps demonstrates Capability Sculpting: a WebMCP incident room whose server-authoritative workflow state continuously changes what the visiting agent can do as control moves between agent, operator, application, and reviewer. The agent can inspect an incident and at most three policy-evaluated candidate decisions, stage an exact mitigation proposal, assess a server-created postcheck, and recall compatible evidence only after certification. It cannot approve the proposal, apply the simulator action, activate memory, switch role, or override policy. Those protected transitions remain server-enforced UI actions for distinct operator and reviewer identities. When the agent stages a proposal, propose_mitigation is withdrawn. Only after exact human approval, an allowlisted simulation, and an immutable observation does record_postcheck_assessment appear. The agent submits an attributable assessment, while the backend independently computes the policy verdict. The new memory remains PENDING_REVIEW and retrieval-ineligible until an independent reviewer decides its disposition. Why WebMCP is essential This is not a chatbot with a static tool list. WebMCP lets the website and visiting agent collaborate over the same incident state while the website retains control of the capability surface. Native document.modelContext.registerTool registrations are lifecycle-bound with separate AbortController s, reconciled against server epochs, and withdrawn on state changes. Stale callbacks and guessed protected operations fail server-side even if a client retained old JavaScript state. The page makes protocol behavior judge-visible through a Capability Inspector and chronological Activity Rail. Judges can watch authority move without opening DevTools. What humans and agents can now do together The agent rapidly investigates bounded evidence and prepares a precise, digest-bound proposal. The operator owns authorization and attests only the isolated simulator action. The application owns measurement and policy evaluation. The agent interprets—but cannot invent—the observation. A different reviewer governs whether the experience may influence a future incident. The resulting Authority Receipt links evidence, proposal, approval, observation, assessment, policy verdict, and review in one independently verifiable chain. Four WebMCP tools inspect_incident — bounded, read-only incident, workflow, and at most three candidate decisions; similarity is separate from eligibility and rejection codes are machine-readable. In POSTCHECK_READY , it also returns the server-issued immutable observation and independent policy verdict required for assessment. propose_mitigation — proposal-only mutation bound to incident, evidence, idempotency key, and action hash; it cannot approve or execute. record_postcheck_assessment — appears only after server-created evidence; accepts an observation ID plus attributable opinion and can create only a pending-review memory. recall_reviewed_memory — read-only compatible recurrence; absent until certified evidence is admissible and withdrawn when governance no longer permits reuse. Human-only operations Approve/reject proposal, attest the simulator action, certify/quarantine/reject/revoke memory, role handoff, and policy override are never WebMCP tools. Separation of duties is enforced by authenticated subjects and database/API invariants, not by hiding buttons. The claim is deliberately scoped to WebMCP-mediated authority; RecallOps does not claim to prevent general browser automation or prove physical-person independence. Demonstrated impact The headline synthetic case uses one identical candidate set. Similarity-only retrieval selects mem_47 at 0.94 , even though it is version-incompatible and has a known failed outcome. RecallOps rejects it before ranking and selects reviewed compatible mem_12 at 0.81 . Across the committed 12-case governed benchmark, similarity-only retrieval makes 11 unsafe selections and leaks two pending memories; RecallOps makes zero unsafe selections, leaks zero pending memories, and produces all three expected abstentions. These are deterministic synthetic policy-regression results, not production incident-rate or universal-safety claims. Execution and proof The no-signup judge flow is isolated per run and deterministic. It covers successful recurrence, observation unavailability, stale tools, replay/idempotency, separate reviewer authority, refresh, reset, and constrained layout. Candidate-bound local assurance reports: 498 Python tests collected, with the base suite plus real CockroachDB integration exercised in the combined coverage run; 100.00% Python statement and branch coverage: 5,454/5,454 statements and 1,224/1,224 branches; 74.06% mutation score: 1,519/2,051 killed, with zero untested mutations or timeouts; 10/10 browser, 2/2 judge-journey, and 4/4 native Chromium WebMCP tests; 2/2 public browser tests and a distinct native Chromium 151 live lifecycle proof; 15/15 exact independent-verifier outcomes across one valid and 14 materially tampered bundles; zero known vulnerabilities in the production and development lock audits. The receipt signature proves integrity and policy consistency of the supplied authority chain. It does not prove external truth, physical presence, trusted time, or completeness against a compromised signer. The product states those limitations next to the proof. How Codex was used OpenAI Codex helped convert the frozen product requirements into transactional and protocol boundaries, implement the WebMCP lifecycle, red-team authority paths, expand tests, identify real TOCTOU and production-lock defects, verify coverage and mutations, and generate deterministic evidence. Claims were accepted only when backed by executable checks or explicit external proof; remaining final-release gates stay red rather than being inferred from older evidence.
