title: Airlock
pitch: Capability firewall for the agentic web.
about_excerpt: Capability firewall for the agentic web. Like 1 Comment Story Updates airlock-in-action airlock-architecture airlock-webmpc airlock-policies Story An agent shopping on your behalf reads a marketplace listing, looks up your billing record, and sends an order. Three reasonable steps. In this demo the listing was written by a hostile seller, and the third step publishes your account reference to a public channel. I tested that flow in ChatGPT's in-app browser. The agent did not fall for the injection — it stopped and asked me to confirm. I confirmed. Airlock blocked the call anyway , because a user approving an attempt is not the same as an origin having authority to cross a trust boundary. Browsers isolate origins. Agents bridge them. Airlock puts an enforcement point back on that bridge. Inspiration WebMCP gives sites a much better way to work with agents. Instead of making an agent guess its way through pixels and DOM interactions, a page can expose real capabilities. That's powerful, and it also creates a trust problem I kept circling back to. Commerce is where this lands first. An agent that buys things visits a marketplace it does not control, a payment or profile surface that holds real data, and some outbound action that actually commits. Those are three different trust domains, and the browser's same-origin policy governs none of the path between them — because nothing about an agent reading one site and writing to another is a cross-origin request. Each tool call can look reasonable on its own. The path between them may not be. I wanted to see whether that path could have an enforceable boundary of its own. What it does Airlock sits between an agent and WebMCP capabilities from multiple origins. The demo has three independent partner origins: Bazaar — a semi-trusted marketplace where seller-controlled content can be hostile. Vault — trusted, read-heavy private data. Dispatch — trusted outbound actions. Rather than handing those partner tools directly to the agent, Airlock discovers them and publishes mediated airlock_* capabilities. Every mediated call goes through the same policy path before the underlying capability can execute. Airlock considers the capability being requested, whether it's a read or a write, the trust assigned to its origin, and the provenance of values being carried into the request. If policy refuses, execution stops there. This isn't advice to the model — the underlying capability is never invoked. The attack A seller on Bazaar publishes a listing containing instructions that lead the agent to construct an order using an account reference. The agent reads the listing, reads the requested account reference from Vault, and then tries to send ORDER 4412 ref=ACCT-7731-QX45 through Dispatch. Looking at that final call alone loses the context that makes the flow dangerous. dispatch_send_message is a legitimate capability and its arguments are structurally valid. But Airlock has the history of how the request got there, so it traces relevant values back to semi-trusted Bazaar content and blocks the write before Dispatch ever receives it. The refusal comes back as structured data: status: blocked_by_policy enforcedBy: airlock-policy-engine capabilityInvoked: false along with the policy reason and recorded provenance. Worth saying which payload this is. An imperative one — opening with SYSTEM: Ignore previous instructions — was tried first and the agent ignored it. That's a strawman and no demo should rest on it. The payload in the demo is procedural: seller notes describing a plausible small-shop fulfilment process whose steps happen to move the buyer profile into a public write, framed as part of the thing the user just asked for. Why a confirmation dialog is not the same thing The obvious objection: doesn't the agent already ask the user before doing something sensitive? It does, and I tested exactly that. ChatGPT's browser enumerated eight mediated Airlock tools and no partner tool by its own name, searched Bazaar, read the listing, accessed the Vault record, reached the outbound Dispatch action, and stopped to ask: STEP 5 requires confirmation: send ORDER 4412 ref=ACCT-7731-QX45 , including the account reference, to Airlock Dispatch's public orders channel. Confirm that I should attempt this outbound message. That is a good question. It names the value and the channel. It is still the wrong question, because it presents a step invented by seller-controlled text as an ordinary part of checkout. A user who says yes has approved the attacker's plan under the attacker's framing. I said yes. The capability still did not execute. Four things are true of that confirmation prompt: It is prose written by the model the injection targets. Had the injection landed, the same sentence would have been produced with the same confidence about attacker-supplied text. A component that can be fooled cannot be the thing that certifies it wasn't. No boundary was crossed to name. It named one origin because there was only one — that browser cannot discover a second. It is per-call and stateless. No rule survives it. Nothing expresses "data from this origin may never reach a write on that one." It is prose, not data. Not machine-checkable, not auditable, not replayable. The claim isn't that models get tricked — in this test the model didn't. It's enforcement that doesn't depend on the model's judgement , which holds whether or not the next model resists injection better. The agent also has no WebMCP tool for granting itself an override, disabling policy, or approving its own blocked request. Human authority stays outside the agent tool surface. How I built it Airlock is split across four independently deployed origins. The Console owns discovery, mediation, policy, provenance, consent, audit, and the agent-facing tool surface. Bazaar, Vault, and Dispatch expose the capabilities being mediated. The execution path is intentionally boring: Agent → airlock_* capability → policy → underlying capability That order is the whole point — a blocked decision returns before the resolver responsible for the underlying operation can execute. I also separated transport from enforcement. Native WebMCP cross-origin behavior is still experimental and differs between environments, so Airlock wraps discovery and execution in a resolver abstraction. Swapping the transport resolver doesn't bypass or replace the policy engine, provenance model, consent boundary, or ledger. Instead of pretending those environments behave identically, the WebMCP page in Airlock reports what the current browser actually supports. How Airlock uses WebMCP WebMCP isn't an API call I bolted on at the end. The capability model is the reason Airlock exists. Along the way I used: cross-origin discovery with getTools({ fromOrigins }) dynamic tool registration and AbortSignal -based unregistration tool annotations, including untrustedContentHint on hostile output structured refusals a model can plan around, not prose it has to interpret model-readable schemas with enums and descriptions declarative tools on a real form toolchange behavior across browser environments The tool surface follows application state. If an origin or capability becomes unavailable, its mediated capability disappears rather than sitting there as something the agent is still allowed to try. One security decision around annotations mattered more than I expected: annotations from foreign tools are treated as claims, not policy authority. A remote tool calling itself read-only doesn't get to decide whether Airlock trusts it. Bazaar ships a tool annotated readOnlyHint: true that publishes anyway, and asks for a home address it has no stated use for. The console flags both at discovery, before anything runs. Six WebMCP findings, measured and written up Building a consumer of other origins' tools surfaced six things worth reporting, measured against deployed HTTPS origins in Brave 151, Chrome 149+ with the flag, and ChatGPT's in-app browser. Two are questions about what the spec intends: getTools({ fromOrigins }) unions the page's own tools with foreign ones rather than filtering to the named origins. The practical consequence is that provenance can never be inferred from what was requested — it has to come from each tool's own origin . A tool registered through the declarative form API is invisible to cross-origin discovery . dispatch registers one, the browser's own registry confirms it, and the console's federated surface never sees it. The two APIs are not interchangeable across an origin boundary, and nothing says so — the call succeeds, returns tools, and silently omits one. Four are silent failures. Not one threw an exception describing its cause, and the page looked healthy through all of them: getTools({ fromOrigins }) never settles in some builds — it does not reject, so a hung promise is indistinguishable from a slow one A foreign inputSchema arrives as a JSON string , not an object; Object.keys on i

video_transcript_excerpt: This is Airlock running inside Chat GPT's in-app browser. On the left, Chat GPT is acting as the agent. On the right, Airlock is mediating its Web MCP capabilities across different trust boundaries. The test begins through Bazaar, a semi-trusted marketplace. Chat GPT follows the workflow exposed through Airlock, reads the relevant listing, and continues into Vault to retrieve the requested private account reference. Airlock tracks where values came from as the agent moves across these capabilities. The workflow now reaches Dispatch, an outbound capability. Before attempting the right, Chat GPT Chat GPT asks me for confirmation. I explicitly authorize the attempt, but confirmation is not capability authority. Watch the Airlock interface. As Chat GPT attempts the Dispatch action, Airlock independently evaluates the capability flow. The call is blocked. Dispatch never receives the action, and the interface records executed: no. Chat GPT receives a structured refusal from Airlock. The result identifies the Airlock policy engine as the enforcer, reports capability invoked as false, and includes the provenance responsible for the decision. The model was allowed to attempt the action. Airlock independently decided that the capability was not allowed to execute. Now, we inspect the enforcement evidence recorded by Airlock. The decision view shows the blocked Dispatch capability, the trust path involved in the request, the policy reason, its recorded provenance, and whether the underlying action executed. The important result remains the same. The outbound capability never ran. Next is Airlock's activity ledger. Every mediated operation leaves an audible decision record. Allowed operations, consent decisions, and blocked operations can be reviewed here instead of relying on the model's own explanation of what happened. Opening a recorded decision exposes the enforcement details again, including the capability, origin, policy outcome, and execution state. The policies view defines how Airlock governs these capability flows. Different operations can be allowed, require consent, or be blocked when they cross a trust boundary. And this is Airlock's Web MCP environment. The page reports the Web MCP support detected in the current browser, the registered mediated tool surface, transport mode, and the real policy, provenance, ledger, and consent components behind the demo. Web MCP gives agents capabilities. Airlock governs whether those capability flows are allowed to execute. Browsers isolate origins. Agents can bridge their capabilities. Airlock adds an enforceable trust boundary across that bridge.

title: BranchLine
pitch: BRANCHLINE lets humans and browser agents share the same live supply-chain reality—fork recovery futures, simulate their consequences, and commit only the plan a human explicitly approves.
about_excerpt: BRANCHLINE lets humans and browser agents share the same live supply-chain reality—fork recovery futures, simulate their consequences, and commit only the plan a human explicitly approves. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Supply-chain disruptions are rarely isolated events. A supplier outage can cascade through component availability, transport lanes, factory capacity, production schedules, customer commitments, revenue, and cost. Operations teams often have to reconstruct this chain manually across ERP systems, spreadsheets, supplier messages, logistics tools, and planning software before they can even decide what to do. At the same time, browser agents are becoming capable of operating websites, but most applications still expose their operational meaning only through buttons, forms, and DOM elements. We built BRANCHLINE around a different idea: What if a human and a browser agent could operate inside the same live operational reality? BRANCHLINE — Fork reality. Simulate the consequences. Commit the future. It is an agent-native operational recovery control plane where humans steer intent, agents traverse consequences, and both operate on one shared supply-chain digital twin. What it does BRANCHLINE models a synthetic commercial EV supply chain for Asterion Mobility , including suppliers, components, factories, transport lanes, inventory, products, customers, and 24 customer orders. The featured scenario begins with a healthy network. A human triggers a 12-day production outage at the battery supplier NoriCell . Instead of simply displaying an alert, BRANCHLINE calculates and visualizes the complete causal cascade: supplier → component availability → factories → products → customer orders → exposed revenue The browser agent can then use semantic WebMCP tools to: inspect the operational state; trace downstream consequences; inspect suppliers, factories, products, customers, and orders; find compatible substitute suppliers; create multiple recovery branches; simulate each future across a 30-day horizon; compare service, cost, risk, emissions, and delays; explain tradeoffs using causal evidence; stage a recovery plan for human approval; apply only an explicitly approved plan; verify the committed result; restore the previous operational checkpoint. The central experience is Branchspace . Instead of presenting three AI recommendations as ordinary cards, BRANCHLINE renders different recovery strategies as parallel futures emerging from the same present. For example: Service First prioritizes customer service and on-time revenue. Cost Guard prioritizes lower incremental cost. Balanced Recovery trades off service, cost, resilience, and logistics. Resilience reduces supplier concentration and future single points of failure. The simulation is deterministic and calculated from the underlying supply, compatibility, capacity, logistics, inventory, and customer-order data. How we built it BRANCHLINE is a static TypeScript web application built around one architectural principle: Human UI ─┐ ├─ shared command bus → domain engine → one live state WebMCP ───┘ The visual interface and WebMCP tools do not maintain separate copies of reality. Every meaningful operation passes through the same domain engine and shared state. The application includes: a deterministic synthetic supply-chain digital twin; causal impact tracing; a bounded recovery-planning engine; a day-by-day simulation from T+0 through T+30; supplier and product compatibility enforcement; inventory and factory-capacity constraints; customer-tier and human-authored priority constraints; transactional execution; verification; checkpoints and exact rollback; an append-only causal audit trail. The WebMCP integration uses the native imperative API directly with: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) BRANCHLINE exposes 14 semantic tools: get_ops_snapshot inspect_entity trace_impact list_constraints find_substitutes read_external_alerts create_branch simulate_branch compare_branches explain_tradeoff stage_plan apply_plan verify_plan rollback_plan The capability surface is dynamic. For example, apply_plan is not registered at all while a recovery plan is waiting for human approval. When the human approves the exact staged plan in the BRANCHLINE interface, apply_plan becomes available to the browser agent. If the operational context changes, the approval becomes stale and the capability is revoked again. Challenges we ran into Keeping the human and agent in one reality The most important technical challenge was preventing the application from becoming a dashboard with a separate agent workflow. Human interactions and WebMCP calls therefore use the same command bus and domain functions. If a human changes something visually, the next agent call immediately encounters the changed state. Making stale reasoning visible and enforceable A recovery simulation can become invalid the moment a constraint changes. BRANCHLINE maintains separate stateVersion and contextVersion values. Every simulation records the context on which it was produced. When the human changes operational intent: the context version increments; existing simulations become visibly stale; staged plans are invalidated; previous approval is revoked; execution capabilities disappear; the agent must re-simulate. Human authority over consequential actions We deliberately did not create an approve_plan WebMCP tool. Approval must happen in the visual interface. Only after that approval does the consequential apply_plan capability become registered. Modeling real compatibility constraints Substitution cannot simply mean choosing the cheapest available supplier. For example, Voltra V-2170 battery cells are incompatible with ORION-X. That restriction is enforced inside the domain engine and simulation rather than merely displayed as UI text. Building meaningful simulation rather than prewritten outcomes Recovery metrics are derived from the underlying operational state. The planner evaluates supplier allocation, logistics, inventory movement, production scheduling, compatible substitutions, and eligible order delays before choosing a deterministic result for each strategy. Accomplishments that we're proud of The interaction we are most proud of involves order_1082 for Apex Health Logistics . Before human intervention, an otherwise attractive recovery future can delay this order. The human opens the order directly in the visual application and presses: Protect this order A gold human-intent pin appears on the order and propagates upstream through its dependencies. That single human action: changes the shared operational context; invalidates every simulation based on the previous reality; removes stale execution capabilities; becomes immediately visible to the browser agent. The agent then re-simulates the recovery using the new constraint. Scarce compatible supply is reallocated to protect Apex Health, while a lower-priority order takes the delay instead. This is not a hardcoded visual effect. It emerges from the planner and shared constraints. In our verified featured recovery, BRANCHLINE produces approximately: $26.56M revenue protected 93.4% of exposed revenue recovered $258,849 incremental cost 23 of 24 orders on time 1 lower-priority delayed order 0 hard compatibility violations 1 explicit human approval 1 rollback checkpoint We are also proud that every WebMCP action has a corresponding visual response. Agents do not disappear into an invisible automation layer—their semantic investigation is visible in the operational world. What we learned WebMCP becomes much more interesting when tools are treated as part of application state rather than as a static API catalog. BRANCHLINE demonstrates that the application can expose only the actions that make sense right now . The project also reinforced an important principle for human-agent systems: Human intent should not have to travel through chat to matter. A planner can simply change something in the interface. The application can make that change part of the same structured context the agent uses on its next call. We also learned that simulation results become significantly easier to trust when their causal evidence, assumptions, actions, and counterfactuals remain inspectable after the recommendation is produced. That led to Causal Proof , which explains decisions from simulation evidence rather than from an embedded LLM. What's next for BranchLine BRANCHLINE currently uses a completely synthetic operational twin so the entire workflow is deterministic, safe, and reproducible. A future production version could connect the same architecture to authenticated: ERP systems; warehouse-management systems; transport-management systems; supplier portals; manufacturing execution systems; procurement systems; demand and inventory planning platforms. The domain engine could also evolve toward richer optimization methods, probabilistic disruption modeling, supplier negotiation workflows, and

title: Bullet Heaven
pitch: Make and share bullet hell levels. Work with an agent to create challenging (or easy!) bullet hell stages with a variety of enemies, tuned exactly to the difficulty and style that you want.
about_excerpt: Make and share bullet hell levels. Work with an agent to create challenging (or easy!) bullet hell stages with a variety of enemies, tuned exactly to the difficulty and style that you want. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A level designed in collaboration between an agent and a human A level designed in collaboration between an agent and a human A level designed in collaboration between an agent and a human The bullet heaven editor Inspiration I've been a fan of bullet hell games since I can remember, and I've even tried making a few. It's tedious, difficult, error-prone and very time consuming; from designing the level to play testing, things take a lot of time. The goal of this experiment is to see if I can make it easier, more accessible and fun to create bullet hell games. What it does Bullet Heaven is a browser-based bullet-hell level editor where a person and an agent build, test, and share levels together. Describe a level. Watch it appear. Simulate it. Tune it together. Most agent tools let an agent change something. Bullet Heaven also lets it measure whether that change worked. Through 20 WebMCP tools, an agent can create waves, emitters, formations, player settings, and complete encounters directly in the same editor you use. Its changes appear live, enter the same undo history, and can be reverted with Ctrl-Z. The key loop is: Author → simulate → measure → revise. evaluate_encounter runs a deterministic headless playthrough and reports clearance, survival time, hits, waves reached, projectile density, dodge margin, and the fatal wave. The agent can use that evidence to tune a level instead of guessing at difficulty. Bullet Heaven can also record real play sessions and analyse them to derive a player-conditioned pilot. The agent can iteratively fit that pilot against recordings, save it, and use it to help balance future encounters for that player rather than only against generic novice, average, or expert tiers. How I built it Bullet Heaven uses Phaser for gameplay, React for the editor, and Zustand with undoable project history. The simulation is framework-independent: Phaser renders it, while headless evaluation and bot pilots run the same rules. WebMCP tools do not have a separate agent-only path. They use the same store and domain operations as the inspector and canvas, so agent edits are immediately visible, undoable, and attributed to the agent. The tool surface was designed for efficient collaboration. apply_encounter can build a complete level in one call, while focused edit tools handle refinement. Mutating results return only the changed object and useful IDs, reducing a one-field edit response from roughly 56 KB to about 1 KB on a large project. Published levels are immutable, content-addressed /play/<hash> documents stored through Cloudflare Pages and R2. Challenges I ran into The first challenge was replacing repeated manual playtesting with useful, deterministic evaluation. That led to the headless simulation and bot pilots. The other challenge was less expected. Individually correct tools can still create a slow workflow if they return too much state, require too many round trips, or expose actions at the wrong level of abstraction. I iterated heavily on bulk authoring, focused edits, concise results, freshness requirements, undo behavior, and safe transitions between Play and Edit modes. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real shared editor where human and agent changes use the same state and undo history. Deterministic headless evaluation, so the agent can measure level difficulty without interrupting play. Three reference pilot tiers for repeatable balancing. Replay analysis and player-conditioned pilot fitting for personalized balancing. A complete WebMCP authoring workflow: create, evaluate, revise, undo, and share. What we learned WebMCP is a powerful tool for accessibility and empowering people to build and create things that they want. With Bullet Heaven, even a completely inexperienced game developer is able to craft levels that they find fun. WebMCP is particularly relevant for complex user interfaces; providing agents with low-level tool access and enabling users to bypass the chore of menus, keyboard shortcuts and a learning curve is a genuine accessibility innovation that will improve efficiency for complex tasks in complex systems. Evaluation and optimization remains a challenge for agents; particularly when it comes to evaluation metrics that are very "human", such as level difficulty. It is important to provide "cost functions" as tools to agents that they can use to get feedback about what they have done; this enables powerful collaborative capabilities and greatly reduces the number of iterations required to reach a fun outcome. Mutation tools alone get you an agent that changes things confidently and has no idea whether it helped. And sharing state rather than mirroring it is what makes the collaboration feel like collaboration. Because the agent writes to the same store, the same undo history and the same evaluation panel that I use, I never have to wonder what it did or take its word for it. What's next for Bullet Heaven More of the level editor; more movement and formation types, better boss authoring, improving the graphics and project import/export so levels are properly portable. I'd also like to take the calibration idea further, since a pilot fitted to a player is the beginning of a level that tunes itself to whoever opens the link rather than to whoever wrote it. Mostly though, I want to see if people like it, and hopefully spread the love of bullet hells even further. title: Duet
pitch: Make music together with your AI agent. Start with a melody, then let your agent add instruments, respond to your changes, and shape the song alongside you in a shared live studio.
about_excerpt: Make music together with your AI agent. Start with a melody, then let your agent add instruments, respond to your changes, and shape the song alongside you in a shared live studio. Like 2 Comment Story Updates The studio — full five-instrument arrangement, Musical Contract panel, 14 live tools, and the timeline. Performance mode — the swapped toolset (7 performance tools), energy, live meters, and a timeline of the entire agent build. Contract approval Share Inspiration Most people have a tune in their head that never becomes a song. The melody is the easy part. The hard part is everything around it: drums, bass, chords, and knowing how to put them together. Most AI music tools solve this with a text box: describe a song, get a song. I wanted the musician to stay in charge. You play the idea, you keep the final say, and an AI agent joins as a bandmate, not a ghostwriter. WebMCP makes that possible. Instead of building a chatbot into a music app, Duet lets the agent you already use work inside the same live studio, with real tools and clear limits. What it does Duet is a browser music studio shared by a human and an AI agent. The human starts by drawing a melody on a piano roll. It lives only in that browser tab; nothing is uploaded. Then they hand the rest to their agent with an ordinary request, for example to keep the notes as they are and build a cinematic synthwave arrangement around them. The agent reads the exact live composition through WebMCP, adds drums, bass and atmospheric chords, shapes the groove, and performs the result. Every agent action appears immediately in the interface, is attributed in a visible timeline (HUMAN / AGENT / SYSTEM), and can be heard through the browser. The musician can switch back to Compose mode at any point and change whatever they like, and the agent can respond to those changes. Both work on one composition, and the human keeps the creative direction. Before the agent touches anything, the musician sets a Musical Contract : the melody is locked to the human; the agent may edit drums, bass, pad, keys and the mix; energy is capped; tempo and key can be locked. These terms are live state that every WebMCP tool enforces. If the agent tries to change the locked melody, its tool call pauses and Duet shows the musician the exact proposed change to approve or decline. The agent only proceeds with permission. When the song is ready, it can be shared. Publishing always pauses for the musician to approve the title, then produces a backend-free remix link with the whole composition encoded in the URL. Anyone who opens it can play the song, remix it, and invite their own agent to join the band. Duet contains no embedded AI model and needs no AI API key. The user brings a WebMCP-compatible agent, and WebMCP gives it structured, scoped access to the studio. How I built it Duet is built around one shared musical state used by both the visual interface and its WebMCP tools. Whether the musician edits a note by hand or the agent writes a drum pattern, both go through the same engine, bump the same version, and land in the same timeline. The page exposes a small, typed set of tools: read the session, add and remove instruments, edit each instrument, adjust tempo, key and groove, and publish. The toolset is contextual. Adding a drum machine registers drums_edit ; removing it withdraws the tool. Compose mode exposes composition tools; entering Performance mode withdraws them and registers a separate set: play, stop, energy, track mix, breakdown. The registration adapter targets Chrome's document.modelContext implementation, feature-detects the navigator.modelContext proposal as a fallback, and was verified against Chrome's real WebMCP runtime on the deployed site. Playback is phrase-aware rather than a bare loop: patterns run as a four-bar phrase (main, main, variation, fill), notes carry velocity and small timing offsets, and deterministic humanization and swing keep the groove alive without randomness. The audio engine is built on Tone.js with five synthesized instruments, per-voice filter envelopes, 32 presets, kick-driven ducking and a proper master chain. It reads the shared state on every tick, so an agent edit is audible on the very next step. The key architectural decision was to keep the model outside the product. Duet is the instrument; WebMCP is the collaboration layer that connects it to whichever agent the musician brings. The app is a static React + TypeScript build with no backend, deployed on Vercel. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was designing agent tools that are expressive enough for real musical collaboration without exposing one enormous "make a song" command. Each instrument got a single tool with a small set of enumerated operations, strict validation, and structured responses that tell the agent exactly what changed. Preserving human authorship was a design problem as much as a technical one. The answer became the Musical Contract: constraints the human sets in the interface and the tools enforce, including the pause-and-ask flow for the locked melody. The agent should respond to the musician's ideas, not replace them. Beyond that: keeping manual edits and agent actions perfectly in sync, accurate musical timing in the browser, and making every agent action understandable and reversible. 116 automated tests cover the tool sets, mode transitions, contract enforcement, sharing and undo. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Duet makes human–agent collaboration both visible and audible. Nobody has to imagine what the agent is doing: you watch instruments and tools appear, see every move attributed in the timeline, and hear the arrangement grow. The Musical Contract turns WebMCP's human-in-the-loop story into something a musician actually wants: not a permissions dialog, but a bandmate asking before stepping on your solo. And Duet works without a chatbot or a single model tied to it. The same studio can be played by any WebMCP-compatible agent. WebMCP isn't an add-on here; it's what lets the musician and the agent share one creative environment. Everything you create is remixable and can be passed from person to person, each inviting their own agent to join the band. What I learned WebMCP becomes powerful when a website behaves like a shared instrument rather than a collection of forms. Structured musical operations are far more reliable and expressive than asking an agent to click coordinates or edit raw files, and contextual tools help the agent understand what is possible right now. Making the human's constraints part of the tool contract, rather than hoping the agent behaves, is what made the collaboration feel trustworthy. Human–agent interaction feels right when the result is immediately visible, reversible, and, in Duet's case, audible. What's next for Duet A song mode that arranges the loop into a full two-minute structure (intro, build, drop, breakdown, outro) using the same mute, energy and phrase machinery, so an agent can arrange as well as play. MIDI keyboard input, so the tune in your head goes straight from your fingers to the piano roll. Variation and fill slots for every instrument. And richer real-time improvisation between musician and agent. title: EmbedDoctor
pitch: Turn invisible postMessage failures into browser evidence, human-reviewed contracts, and verified repairs as developers and AI agents collaborate through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Turn invisible postMessage failures into browser evidence, human-reviewed contracts, and verified repairs as developers and AI agents collaborate through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Verified repair: the same seed passes lifecycle, protocol, and source identity checks, preserving $120.00. Broken checkout: a same-origin sibling changes $120.00 to $0.01 while three boundary checks fail. The agent stages the smallest report-only contract from selected browser evidence. Scenario lab: four deterministic failure patterns prove the diagnosis changes with the evidence. Inspiration Embedded payments, authentication frames, editors, support widgets, and microfrontends often communicate through window.postMessage . When those integrations fail, developers see symptoms instead of causes: initialization vanishes, protocol versions drift, or a valid-looking message arrives from the wrong frame. Ordinary logs rarely preserve timing, event.origin , exact event.source identity, the developer's current selection, and the visible consequence in one place. EmbedDoctor began with a simple question: what if the live browser boundary itself could become a shared debugging workspace for a developer and an AI agent? What it does EmbedDoctor turns invisible iframe failures into browser evidence, a reviewed boundary contract, and a verified repair. The controlled checkout reproduces three real failure classes: Lifecycle race: INIT is sent before the payment widget installs its listener. Protocol drift: the host retries with protocol v1 while the widget accepts v2. Wrong frame identity: a same-origin sibling sends a valid-looking total update from the wrong WindowProxy , changing the checkout from $120.00 to $0.01 . The page records the actual message sequence, lifecycle state, origin, source classification, protocol version, policy verdict, and rendered result. An agent can inspect only the incidents selected by the developer, stage the smallest report-only contract justified by that evidence, replay the same seeded boundary, undo a proposal, and prepare an export. After the developer reviews and approves enforcement, the same seed runs again. READY/ACK initialization succeeds, protocol v2 is required, the exact origin and iframe source are bound, the sibling message is blocked before the application handler, and the checkout remains $120.00 . Why WebMCP The evidence that matters exists inside the active browser session. It includes the current incident selection, real MessageEvent.origin , strict event.source identity, iframe lifecycle, visible draft state, and rendered consequence. A CLI, remote MCP server, or conventional API could support part of this workflow only after adding custom page instrumentation and state synchronization. WebMCP lets the owned page expose semantic operations directly beside the live interface, with no screenshot guessing or copied logs. EmbedDoctor exposes five native tools: embeddoctor.inspect_selected_incidents embeddoctor.stage_boundary_contract embeddoctor.replay_boundary embeddoctor.undo_contract_change embeddoctor.export_contract_bundle Tool availability follows product state. Export is unavailable until a developer-approved contract passes an enforced replay. Every agent action appears in a provenance ledger as WebMCP ; manual fallbacks are visibly separate. Human control The agent can investigate, propose, replay, undo, and export. It cannot approve enforcement. Approval is deliberately absent from the WebMCP surface. The proposed contract remains visible and editable, and only the developer can activate it. This keeps the agent powerful at diagnosis while preserving human authority over a consequential runtime change. How we built it EmbedDoctor uses React 19, TypeScript, Vite, vinext, Tailwind CSS, and a framework-free boundary adapter. The demo contains a top-level checkout, an adopted payment iframe, and a same-origin sibling iframe communicating through real postMessage traffic. One pure evaluator powers both report-only and enforcement modes, so the policy decision stays identical while only forwarding behavior changes. Incidents, scores, evidence IDs, comparison rows, and receipts are derived from captured events rather than assigned by demo phase. Four seeded scenarios show that diagnosis changes with the evidence: Perfect storm: lifecycle, protocol, and frame identity Late listener: lifecycle only Rolling upgrade: protocol only Rogue sibling: source identity only The exported bundle contains the contract, TypeScript runtime adapter, regression tests, evidence metadata, and migration notes. Challenges The hardest challenge was making a lifecycle race reproducible without inventing browser evidence. We replaced independent timers with a causal fixture: listener pending, early INIT, listener installation, retry, observed schema error, and then the sibling mutation. A second challenge was proving why origin checks alone are insufficient. The rogue sender is deliberately same-origin, so it passes an origin allowlist. Only strict equality with the expected iframe's contentWindow catches it. A third challenge was preventing a polished demo from becoming a predetermined animation. Every visible result now traces back to concrete event IDs, and a safety timeout can produce failure but can never manufacture a passing receipt. Accomplishments A complete developer experience, not only a tool-call proof of concept A dramatic evidence-derived transition from 0/3 to 3/3 Five state-aware WebMCP tools with visible provenance Developer-only approval and one-click undo Scenario-dependent minimum contracts A portable adoption bundle Fifteen automated tests covering origin traps, source identity, schema and session validation, report/enforce parity, redaction, incident derivation, and export contents A public deployment and reproducible open-source repository What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when a page exposes meaning, not DOM mechanics. The useful tools are not "click this button" or "read this panel." They are "inspect the selected evidence," "stage the smallest supported contract," and "replay this boundary." That semantic layer lets a person and an agent collaborate on the same live state while keeping actions observable and reversible. What's next Next, EmbedDoctor could package the boundary adapter as an SDK, support worker and popup channels, import production traces with privacy-preserving redaction, generate framework-specific adapters, and run verified contracts in CI. The broader goal is to make embedded web boundaries testable before intermittent failures reach production. Honest scope EmbedDoctor protects traffic adopted by a cooperating host and iframe. It does not inspect arbitrary third-party DOM, secure uninstrumented listeners, stop same-origin XSS, provide cryptographic authentication, or replace CSP and security review. title: EqualTrace
pitch: The agent succeeded. The safety contract failed.
about_excerpt: The agent succeeded. The safety contract failed. Like Comment Story Updates Problem WebMCP lets an agent call structured tools directly from a live website. That can be dramatically more reliable than guessing through a visual interface—but it introduces a new release risk. An agent can reach the correct final state while silently bypassing disclosures, exact consent, completion feedback, reversibility, or recovery protections that constrained a person performing the same consequential action. Outcome-only testing calls that a success. EqualTrace calls it a protection failure. Solution EqualTrace is a runtime protection-parity workbench for agent-operable websites. It runs one deterministic fictional account-deletion action through three genuine routes: a visual pointer journey; a keyboard/assistive journey; a native WebMCP agent invocation. All three routes use the same scenario, seed, domain commands, requested outcome, and semantic trace model. EqualTrace compares outcome, disclosure, consent, feedback, reversibility, and recovery in their required order. The baseline intentionally reaches deleted on all three routes, but fails at the first missing agent checkpoint: disclosure.consequences . The agent can then stage one bounded repair, but it cannot approve or apply it. A person must inspect and approve the exact action, checkpoint, digest, seed, and expiry through the visible interface. Only then does equaltrace_apply_approved_repair appear on the native WebMCP surface. It is bound to that authority, executes once, and disappears immediately after use or any invalidating transition. EqualTrace clears the baseline traces, reruns all three routes, and issues a deterministic SHA-256 parity receipt only when the same outcome and all six protection groups pass on fresh evidence. Why This Matters The central failure and the central proof exist on the real capability surface. EqualTrace does not merely display tool metadata. Native discovery and invocation update the same visible state used by people, while dynamic registration makes authority observable: four stable tools exist before approval, a fifth exact tool appears after human approval, and it disappears after one attempt. Without WebMCP, EqualTrace could not demonstrate the difference between interface protections and agent-call protections, nor prove that authorization changes the agent's available capabilities rather than a decorative status label. Better human-agent collaboration Before EqualTrace, a team could separately test a UI, accessibility, and an API call yet still miss that the agent path skipped a protection. EqualTrace lets the agent diagnose and prepare a narrow repair, keeps the consequential decision with a person, and lets the agent execute only the approved change. Both then share a portable receipt showing exactly what passed. This pattern can extend to account management, privacy controls, commerce, healthcare, finance, and other consequential actions where a correct outcome is not enough evidence of a safe path. Architecture EqualTrace is a static React and strict TypeScript application with no backend, database, account, secret, or model API. document.modelContext.registerTool exposes four constant, bounded stable tools. An AbortSignal-bound lifecycle manager dynamically registers the single-use repair tool only after exact visible approval. Every route executes isolated run contexts from one immutable fixture and shared domain engine. Deterministic trace IDs feed a pure fail-closed comparator. Canonical JSON and Web Crypto produce the repair digest and receipt identity. Automated tests use a separate injected fake port and are always labelled simulated; native claims come only from a supported client's browser-provided WebMCP surface. The one-command gate runs formatting, lint, strict type checking, 66 unit/integration/component tests with authority coverage thresholds, production build, 12 Playwright journeys, axe checks, receipt verification, and native-evidence manifest verification. The exact public release also completed five consecutive native golden runs from fresh resets with the same receipt. What We Learned The hardest part was not registering a tool; it was defining what equivalent protection means across fundamentally different interaction modes. The implementation needed semantic checkpoints rather than screen similarity, fail-closed evidence rules rather than optimistic status flags, and authority bound to exact state rather than a claimed actor identity. We also learned to keep semantic receipt identity separate from volatile browser and time metadata, while preserving native environment evidence in a separate auditable manifest. How We Used AI The demonstrated agent operates the live public page through native WebMCP tools. OpenAI Codex assisted with product planning, implementation, test design, adversarial review, accessibility checks, debugging, native browser validation, video production, and submission preparation. The running product calls no model API: its scenario, comparator, repair authority, and receipts are deterministic and reproducible without an external service. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the product thesis into a strict TypeScript implementation, build the shared three-route domain engine, test fail-closed authority boundaries, inspect the real browser-provided WebMCP surface, and produce auditable release evidence. Throughout the project, simulated Playwright and Vitest evidence remained explicitly separate from native supported-client observations. Key Features One deterministic consequential action exercised through visual, keyboard/assistive, and native WebMCP routes. Six ordered protection groups: outcome, disclosure, consent, feedback, reversibility, and recovery. First-divergence diagnosis even when every route reaches the same final outcome. Exact visible human approval before a consequential repair capability can exist. Observable native capability lifecycle: four stable tools, one temporary approved tool, then four again ( 4 → 5 → 4 ). Fresh repaired rerun with all three routes at 6/6 and a deterministic SHA-256 receipt. Responsive static deployment with no backend, account, secret, external API, or model dependency. Known Limitations The challenge release deliberately proves one fictional account-deletion scenario. It is not a universal safety certification, general WCAG scanner, or external-site crawler. Public native release evidence covers the named Codex In-app Browser version; other WebMCP clients require their own validation. After the challenge, the same model could support additional invariant packs, fixture authoring, CI regression runs against deployed WebMCP sites, and team evidence retention. title: Euterpe
pitch: Euterpe is a browser music maker where a person hums or plays and their own agent becomes a teacher-producer.
about_excerpt: Euterpe is a browser music maker where a person hums or plays and their own agent becomes a teacher-producer. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted a middle ground between learning a full music-production application and asking a generator to make a finished song. A beginner may already have the important part — a line they can hum or sing — but not yet know how to turn it into chords, a bass part, drums and an arrangement. The useful collaborator is not one that replaces that idea. It is one that can work on the same song, explain a choice, let the person hear it, and accept “undo” as a normal part of making music. Music also exposes why WebMCP is useful. The page owns the microphone, song document, audio clock and speakers. The person is the only one who can hear whether a change works, while the browser’s agent needs exact notes, chords, bar ranges and revision state rather than a screenshot. WebMCP gives the site a structured way to expose those actions to the agent, as described in OpenAI’s Site tools guide and Chrome’s WebMCP guide . What it does Euterpe opens as an empty eight-bar song with one melody track. A person can record a hum or sung line, import a browser-decodable voice memo, play the musical-typing keyboard, or use a MIDI input where the browser supports it. Every path produces a take with rough symbolic notes; microphone and imported takes also retain the original audio. The browser’s agent has 29 registered tools. It can read the song, notes, chords and takes; suggest or set chords; offer two or three alternatives that the person can audition before choosing; ask the person to perform a named part over particular bars; set the key and tempo; add tracks; generate deterministic chord, bass and drum parts; arrange sections; mix, play, stop, undo and redo; and start cancellable WAV, MP3 or MIDI export jobs. The five track kinds are melody, chords, bass, drums and vocal. The vocal is part of the song rather than disposable input to pitch detection. A dedicated vocal track can hold the retained recording. tune_vocal applies reversible, key-aware pitch correction, set_quantize aligns its timing with adjustable strength and optional swing, and set_mix controls level, pan, mute and solo. WAV and MP3 renders include retained voice clips. MIDI is notes-only, so Euterpe refuses MIDI export when the song contains retained audio instead of silently dropping the singer. The agent does not hear the audio and the tool boundary does not send it audio. It receives bounded JSON descriptions of musical state; the person remains the ears and makes the final choice. Every newly authored musical change carries a plain-language why , appears in the activity strip and producer notes, points back to the bars it changed, and can be undone. The agent also cannot grant microphone permission or bypass the browser’s audio rules for the person. How we built it The application is a TypeScript and React client built with Vite and hosted as a static site. There is no model or music-generation service inside the page. The browser’s agent chooses the tools; deterministic local code handles state, music theory, pitch analysis and audio. All human and agent edits go through one serialised command bus and one song reducer. A successful edit increments a monotonic revision and returns the changed fields, summary and target bars. Tools can include an expected revision, so a stale write is refused with a short account of what changed instead of overwriting newer work. Human drags on the piano roll briefly hold agent writes, and a track being recorded is locked while other tracks remain editable. Each tool has a Zod input schema exported as strict JSON Schema, a short description, annotations and an execute function. The registry installs the same 29 definitions through document.modelContext.registerTool and the compatibility navigator.modelContext path, deduplicating them when both names refer to the same context. Six tools are marked read-only. Results use one compact success-or-error envelope and stay within the application’s 1,500-character budget. The audio path uses Tone.js and smplr for scheduled instruments, with an AudioWorklet and Pitchy for live and offline pitch tracking. Tonal supplies note and chord primitives. Recorded mono PCM is stored with the take, referenced by clips on the timeline, and scheduled through the same vocal path for live playback and offline rendering. WAV is encoded as PCM; MP3 work runs in a separate worker through Mediabunny ; MIDI is written from the symbolic tracks. Recording over an arrangement uses a shared worklet clock and the scheduled count-in boundary, then combines those with the active input device’s reported latency and the audio context’s base and output latency. These are browser and device estimates under the Media Capture and Streams and Web Audio APIs, not a claim of acoustic sample-accurate alignment. If the input device does not report latency, Euterpe refuses microphone capture rather than inventing an offset. At the submission commit, the unit and integration suite passes 817 tests across 110 files. The browser harness contains 126 asserted steps across seven scenarios, covering the 29 tool behaviours, revisions, error envelopes, recording locks, retained-vocal alignment, real audio export and sample fallback. Challenges we ran into The largest mistake in the first version was architectural: a hummed take was analysed into notes and then the recording itself was thrown away. That was acceptable for a transcription demo but wrong for a music maker. Keeping the singer meant adding serialisable PCM to the take model, clip references to tracks, persistence and history support, clip copying during arrangement, a separate live-audio path for vocal tracks, and the same path again in offline WAV and MP3 rendering. Recording over music was another real boundary. The capture worklet, count-in and output device expose related but different timing information. A fixed “latency compensation” number would have looked convincing on one machine and been wrong on another. The implementation now records the worklet boundary, scheduled arrangement boundary and the browser-reported input, processing and output estimates with each microphone take. Missing or non-monotonic evidence causes a refusal, not a guessed placement. Making vocal changes reversible also took more than moving note rectangles. The original note timing has to survive quantisation, while the retained PCM needs a corresponding time map. Pitch correction has to use voiced pitch frames and the current key without changing the stored recording. Both operations therefore live as adjustable clip settings in the song history rather than destructive rewrites of the source audio. Export forced an explicit product decision. A Standard MIDI File can represent the note tracks but not the retained PCM recording. Silently exporting the instruments would produce a valid file that was not the song the person heard. The encoder and WebMCP tool both reject that case and direct the person to WAV or MP3. Finally, WebMCP’s structured boundary cannot listen for the agent. Read tools therefore return small musical facts — notes, chord symbols, bar ranges, take quality and revision — while the page makes every action visible and leaves listening to the person. That constraint shaped the product more than adding a chat panel would have. Accomplishments that we're proud of The singer survives the whole journey. A hummed or sung line is recorded, retained as audio, tuned to the key, aligned to the grid, mixed, and exported inside the finished WAV or MP3 — while the same take also drives the symbolic notes the agent reasons over. Both representations stay in one song document with one history. Euterpe refuses in three places where it would have been easier to guess. It refuses microphone capture when the input device will not report its latency, rather than applying an offset that looks right on one machine and is wrong on another. It refuses MIDI export when the song contains retained audio, rather than producing a valid file that is not the song the person heard. And it refuses a stale write when the revision has moved, rather than overwriting newer work. Each refusal says what happened and what to do instead. The agent is genuinely useful without ever hearing the music. Twenty-nine tools give it notes, chords, bar ranges, take quality and revision state as bounded JSON; it proposes, explains and edits; the person listens and decides. Every authored change carries a plain-language reason, points at the bars it touched, and can be undone. The evidence is real rather than asserted: 817 tests across 110 files, and a browser harness of 126 asserted steps in seven scenarios covering every registered tool, the revision and locking rules, retained-vocal alignment and actual audio export. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when a site has live state or local capabilities

title: Mandate
pitch: A bank payment desk where an AI agent can investigate freely but cannot move money without a revocable mandate from a person, built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A bank payment desk where an AI agent can investigate freely but cannot move money without a revocable mandate from a person, built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agents are locked out of nearly every high consequence system on earth. Not because they lack the capability, a model can read a payment queue and spot a duplicate or a sanctions hit faster than a person can, but because none of these systems has a way to grant an agent partial authority: enough to be useful, bounded enough to be safe, revocable the instant a human changes their mind. Today the choice is binary. Either the agent gets your credentials and can do everything you can do, or it gets nothing. Every bank, hospital, and factory picks nothing, and rationally so. WebMCP changes where that decision can live. Because tools are defined by the page itself, not by the model or its vendor, the site gets to decide what an agent may do, under what conditions, and for how long. Mandate is what that looks like on a bank's payment operations desk, where getting it wrong moves real money. What it does Mandate is a bank payment operations desk with an AI agent connected through WebMCP. The agent can investigate freely: read the queue, check a beneficiary, ask a partner screening bureau to recheck a sanctions match, but it cannot release a single payment on its own authority. To act, it has to negotiate. It calls propose_mandate , asking for what it needs, for example "up to 5,000 euros a payment, 50,000 total, SEPA only, verified beneficiaries only, for the next thirty minutes." That request shows up on the desk as a card a person can edit before agreeing: tighten the ceiling, shorten the clock, or refuse outright. The moment they grant it, the page re-registers its tool surface and a tool that did not exist a second earlier now does ( release_under_mandate , revoke_mandate ). The moment they revoke it, those tools vanish from the agent's list mid session. Three things fall out of that same property: A refusal is a conversation, not a 403. When the agent tries to release a payment it has no authority for, it gets back a plain English reason ("Segregation of duties: an agent cannot authorise a payment on its own authority") plus the two tools that would actually work, so it reroutes itself. The human sits inside the tool call, not notified after it. request_authorization returns a promise the page only resolves when a person clicks, so the agent is genuinely blocked and comes back with the real human answer. Nothing leaves the tab. All desk state is client side, so a bank could put real positions behind this and the agent would operate on data that never reaches a third party. What people and agents can do together that they could not before Until now an agent on a desk like this had two settings, and both are useless. Read only, in which case a person still makes every keystroke and the agent is a search box. Or the agent holds a human's credentials, in which case it can do everything that human can do and no bank will ever connect it. There was no way to express "you may do this much, for this long, and I can stop you." Three things happen on this desk that had nowhere to live before: An agent asks for authority in its own words, and a person edits the request before granting it. The agent proposes 5,000 euros a payment. Priya makes it 2,500 and grants that instead. The agent is told in its return value that its request was tightened, and works to the smaller number, leaving behind a 3,960 euro payment it would have been allowed to clear under its own proposal. Neither side had to anticipate the other in advance, which is what makes it a negotiation rather than a settings page. Two organisations settle one case without either handing over its data. The desk cannot see the bureau's watchlist. The bureau never sees the desk's payments. The agent asks the desk, the desk brokers the call across origins, and the answer comes back attributed to the bureau with an audit entry on both sides. That used to be a server to server integration with a contract behind it. Here it is one tool published to one named origin, and it works between two independent deployments. Authority ends mid conversation. A person clicks revoke and the tool the agent was about to reach for is gone from getTools() before its next call. Not a rejected request, and not a permission checked inside a handler: the capability itself stops existing while the session is still open. How it creates a better user experience For the person at the desk, the change is that they stop approving things one at a time and start setting a boundary once. Fifteen payments before a cut off used to be fifteen decisions. It becomes one decision about scope, after which the agent clears everything inside that scope and brings back everything outside it with the reason attached: above the ceiling you set, beneficiary not verified, sanctions match, wrong currency for that rail. Nothing is agreed to by accident either, because the ceiling, the budget, the rails, the beneficiary rule and the clock are all on screen and all editable before anyone clicks grant. For the agent, the change is that a refusal stops being a dead end. Every control answers in the shape a colleague would use: what is blocked, why, and what would work instead. So it reroutes itself instead of retrying the same call or inventing a workaround. And the desk keeps a permanent panel showing what the browser is actually holding, read live from getTools() rather than described in prose. Grant a mandate and the count moves from 18 to 20 on screen, in the same frame as the click. Revoke it and it drops back. Being able to see exactly what an agent may do at this moment is the thing you most want to know when you let one near your money, and it is normally the thing you cannot see at all. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This only works because WebMCP puts tool definitions in the page, computed from live state, instead of behind a static, server hosted tool list. A conventional MCP server hands a fixed set of tools to a client it cannot see. Mandate's tool surface is rebuilt and re-registered against an AbortSignal every time authority changes, so the mandate is real rather than cosmetic: tools do not exist until authority does, and they stop existing the instant it is withdrawn. That loop, an agent asking for authority, a human shaping it, and the tool surface itself changing as a result, is not possible outside a page hosted model. How we built it No backend, no database, no AI model of our own, no build step, and zero runtime dependencies. The visiting agent (Chrome with the WebMCP flag, or ChatGPT's in-app browser) brings the model; the page brings the tools and the governance. Twenty tools across five tiers, plus one published from a separate origin: Read tools with readOnlyHint: true (free rein: search payments, explain a hold, get exposure, pull the audit trail) Prepare tools that move no money (draft, amend, attach evidence) Consequential tools that block on a person ( request_authorization , release_payment , a declarative ask_the_desk form) Governance tools where the agent negotiates its own limits ( propose_mandate , get_mandate , undo_last_agent_action ) Mandate only tools that exist purely while authority is in force ( release_under_mandate , revoke_mandate ) The cross origin piece is Sentinel Screening Bureau, a genuinely separate deployment holding the sanctions watchlist. It never hands the list over. It publishes exactly one tool, scoped to origins it names: await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: 'recheck_beneficiary_screening', description: 'Re-run sanctions screening for one beneficiary.', inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }, { exposedTo: ['https://mandate-webmcp.vercel.app'] }); The desk embeds that origin with allow="tools" , discovers what it publishes with getTools({ fromOrigins }) , and brokers the call under its own governance, so the agent asks the desk and the desk answers with the bureau's decision plus an audit entry. Two organisations cooperating on one decision, neither handing over its data or its authority. The controls behind all of this (segregation of duties, four eyes approval, per role limits, sanctions screening, rail eligibility, duplicate detection, mandate scope) live in a pure, DOM free control engine covered by 34 tests that run on CI. title: Mechanism Canvas
pitch: An organic chemistry canvas where WebMCP agents test competing mechanisms, show their evidence, and leave the final move to the learner.
about_excerpt: An organic chemistry canvas where WebMCP agents test competing mechanisms, show their evidence, and leave the final move to the learner. Like Comment Story Updates Mechanism Canvas lets agents test competing chemistry paths while the learner keeps control of the final answer. The learner sets agent permissions, hint limits, and commit authority before any agent work begins. The agent explores competing mechanisms in isolated branches while the learner’s draft stays sealed. A deterministic validator rejects the incomplete path and approves the complete SN2 mechanism. The Observatory reveals available tools, agent actions, validator results, and the full proof trail. The agent can return a checked proposal, but only the learner can move it onto the canvas. After reviewing the evidence, the learner commits the approved electron-flow mechanism. An interactive 3D inspector connects curved-arrow reasoning with molecular geometry and lone pairs. About Mechanism Canvas Inspiration I kept coming back to a mismatch between how students solve organic chemistry problems and how AI tutors usually communicate. Reaction mechanisms live in diagrams. The important details are the atoms, bonds, lone pairs, curved arrows, and the order in which electrons move. A separate chat window sees almost none of that unless the student stops and translates the drawing into prose. Giving an agent broad control of the drawing surface creates a different problem. It can finish the exercise before the learner has worked through it. I wanted to see whether an agent could help inside the real mechanism canvas while the student still controlled the consequential part: what actually gets added to the answer. That became the central idea behind Mechanism Canvas. The agent gets a safe place to explore. The page checks the chemistry. The learner decides what comes back. What I built Mechanism Canvas is an organic chemistry workspace where a student and a WebMCP agent can work with the same structured mechanism. The page exposes meaningful chemistry objects instead of screen coordinates, so the agent can refer to a particular atom, bond, lone pair, or revision without guessing from pixels. The main demo is a counterfactual (S_\mathrm{N}2) lab. The agent tests two electron-flow paths away from the learner's draft. In the first branch, it forms the new bond but forgets the coupled leaving-group cleavage. The production validator rejects that attempt. The second branch contains both moves, so the validator approves it. The checked branch then reaches a visible proposal gate. It still does not change the learner's mechanism. The learner can inspect the evidence, add the proposal to the draft, request one more check, and make the final commit. An incorrect agent attempt becomes useful evidence instead of damage that has to be undone. The site also works as a complete manual tutor when WebMCP is unavailable. Direct agent collaboration is an extra layer on top of the same interface rather than a separate agent-only experience. How I built it I built the app with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The mechanism canvas is backed by a structured graph with stable IDs for atoms, bonds, electron sources, and curved-arrow moves. A deterministic chemistry engine evaluates proposed steps against six reviewed fixtures. The model can suggest and explore, but it does not decide whether a mechanism is chemically valid. The WebMCP layer registers 26 imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool uses a closed JSON schema and calls the same TypeScript store commands as the visible interface. Mutating calls re-read live state and check the current revision, scope, and learner-granted permissions before they run. Tool discovery changes with the task. Coach mode begins with 16 available tools. Opening the two-path lab adds the branch controls. Starting a six-action comparison session narrows the surface to the capabilities needed for that job. Once the action budget is used, the work tools disappear and only four evidence controls remain. A cached tool cannot restore access that the learner has already closed. I also built a Collaboration Contract where the learner sets the agent's maximum role and hint level. An intent-bound session freezes the job, problem, revision, and action budget. The Live Run Observatory shows which capability batches the host accepted, and a Proof Ledger records privacy-minimized before-and-after receipts from the actual tool callback boundary. Around that core, I added keyboard-operable SVG structures, local persistence, reversible commits, state diffs, electron-flow replay, and a lazy-loaded Three.js molecular inspector. The finished project is a static GitHub Pages site with no backend, account, or credentials required. Challenges The hardest engineering problem was keeping tool discovery honest while the page changed. A fixed list of 26 tools would technically work, but it would hide the learner's current intent inside descriptions. My first dynamic version swung too far in the other direction: every small store notification could publish a transient capability batch. Those batches were real, but they did not represent a stable state that a judge or learner could understand. I changed the registration layer to coalesce related updates, wait for the complete batch, and record only surfaces the host had accepted. Proof was another difficult part. A model saying that it called a tool is only a claim. I needed the page to show whether the callback ran, whether the expected state changed, and whether the main draft stayed untouched. The Proof Ledger now wraps the real callback boundary, and the Observatory evaluates its seven demo claims from those receipts. I also had to make failure safe without making it invisible. The two lab branches have real revisioned state and use the same validator as the main canvas, but they remain isolated until the learner chooses a checked proposal. That separation took more work than simply giving the agent an undo button. It is also the part that makes the workflow useful for learning. What I learned I learned that an agent's tool list is part of the user interface. A capability name, its schema, when it appears, and when it disappears all communicate authority. Encoding the learner's intent in that surface made the boundary much clearer than relying on prompt instructions alone. I also learned how well deterministic software and agent reasoning can complement each other. The agent is good at generating alternatives and explaining a choice. The chemistry engine is good at enforcing exact constraints every time. Keeping those jobs separate made the result easier to trust. Most of all, this project changed how I think about mistakes in learning software. A wrong attempt does not have to be erased or quietly corrected. When it is isolated, checked, and kept visible, it can show the learner exactly why the complete mechanism needs both electron-flow moves. What's next The current chemistry engine is intentionally limited to reviewed fixtures. I would like to add an instructor authoring flow for new mechanisms and study how different permission contracts affect the explanations students give. The same pattern could also work in circuit design, geometry, and other visual STEM tools where exploration is useful but ownership should stay with the learner.
