title: Proof Courier
pitch: The agent carries proof, not your private records. WebMCP blocks overreach, unlocks one consent-bound export, and leaves final submission to the person.
about_excerpt: The agent carries proof, not your private records. WebMCP blocks overreach, unlocks one consent-bound export, and leaves final submission to the person. Like Comment Story Updates Five eligibility claims cross two WebMCP sites. Birth date, exact GPA, transcript, address, student ID, and name stay in the wallet. Inspiration Browser agents can now work across websites. That creates a privacy problem: proving one fact often means copying an entire private record into the agent conversation. A fellowship may need to know that an applicant is over 18, enrolled, studying an eligible field, above a GPA threshold, and resident in an eligible region. It does not need the person's birth date, student ID, exact GPA, transcript, home address, or name. Proof Courier started with one question: can the agent carry the answer without carrying the record? What it does Proof Courier is a working two-site WebMCP workflow backed by three independent production artifacts. The fellowship verifier publishes the five claims it needs, along with the audience, purpose, expiry limit, fresh nonce, prohibited fields, and a rule that only the person may submit. The private wallet checks that request before preparing anything. Its Request Firewall blocks an unsafe audience, purpose, nonce, or request for automatic submission. If a site asks for raw records, extra claims, or a longer lifetime, the wallet releases nothing and returns a machine-readable counterproposal containing only the five derived claims and a ten-minute lifetime. Once the verifier accepts that smaller request, the wallet prepares it for visible review. The agent still cannot export anything. The person sees what will be shared, who will receive it, why it is needed, and when it expires. Only the person's approval registers wallet_export_proof . The tool works once and then disappears. The agent carries the proof to the verifier, which checks it and prepares the application. There is no agent tool for final submission. The result is simple: five eligibility claims cross between the sites. The private source values stay inside the wallet. Why WebMCP This experience depends on structured tools and live page state. The verifier gives the agent a precise request instead of making it guess from pixels. The wallet turns consent into real capability control. Before approval, export does not exist. After approval, it appears for one use. After that use, it is replaced by a read-only receipt. That 0 to 1 to 0 capability lifecycle means the person and agent see the same authority state. It also gives the agent a safe recovery path when a website asks for too much. The wallet and verifier run on separate origins. They do not share browser storage or fetch data from each other. In the tested journey, the proof returned by one WebMCP tool and passed to the other is the only bridge. How we built it Both pages register their own tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . The synthetic proof bundle uses Web Crypto. A P-256 issuer signature authenticates the credential metadata. Merkle inclusion paths reveal only the requested claims. A holder signature binds the audience, purpose, nonce, expiry, disclosure set, approval time, and one-use consent grant. The verifier rejects an untrusted issuer, wrong audience or purpose, expired proof, repeated nonce, missing or extra claim, altered disclosure, forged signature, or consent dated in the future. The wallet, verifier, and showcase deploy as independent artifacts. Each canonical origin serves only its own routes and entry chunk. The 21-check production matrix returns 200 for the owning route and chunk, and 404 for every peer role route and peer entry chunk. Release checks also keep wallet signing fixtures out of verifier and showcase artifacts, remove source maps, scan for raw synthetic record values, and verify six security headers on every role. Challenges The hardest part was separating preparation from permission. A confirmation message was not enough. The agent's actual tool inventory had to change after the visible approval and change again after the permitted export. An early version also included linkable identity metadata in otherwise safe receipts. We removed it and added checks around every agent-facing result. Privacy here is not a promise in the interface. It is a boundary tested in the data path. The Request Firewall introduced a second challenge. Refusing a bad request is easy; helping the agent continue safely is harder. The wallet now explains why the request failed and, when possible, proposes the smallest acceptable replacement. What we learned Tool schemas are part of the trust model. A useful WebMCP tool needs clear inputs, bounded output, honest annotations, and a lifecycle that matches its authority. We also learned where the human should remain in control. The agent is good at reading requirements, comparing policies, and carrying a proof. The person should approve disclosure and make the final consequential decision. How we tested it The release includes: 78 of 78 unit and contract tests 22 of 22 named adversarial privacy and authority scenarios 10 of 10 Playwright checks, including six product journeys and four wallet durability and concurrency checks 21 of 21 production route and entry-chunk isolation checks across the three role artifacts 1 of 1 complete browser journey against independently served role artifacts 5 direct tool smoke steps using GoogleChromeLabs webmcp-evals a 100/100 tool audit with zero findings in Nekuda WebMCP Workbench automated keyboard, 390px layout, and serious or critical accessibility checks An earlier deployed build also passed a native WebMCP run in the OpenAI Codex in-app browser: five synthetic claims crossed, zero private fields crossed, export disappeared after use, verification passed, and no agent submission tool appeared. That native receipt predates the IndexedDB wallet wiring and says so. The final role-isolated release was rerun through the public browser harness after production promotion. The public Evidence Room links the receipts, source revision, and limits behind these claims. Scope Every person, credential, institution, and application in the demo is synthetic. Proof Courier is an interaction and protocol prototype. Wallet export authority persists only in same-origin browser storage. Verifier challenge and replay state remain in memory and reset across reloads or application instances. It is not a production identity wallet, compliance product, W3C Verifiable Credential implementation, zero-knowledge proof, or real fellowship integration. Try it Live introduction: https://proof-courier-orcin.vercel.app Fellowship verifier: https://proof-courier-verifier.vercel.app/fellowship Private wallet: https://proof-courier-wallet.vercel.app/wallet Evidence Room: https://proof-courier-orcin.vercel.app/evidence Source: https://github.com/amanmaqsood/proof-courier Built with WebMCP, React, TypeScript, Web Crypto, Vite, Vitest, Playwright, GoogleChromeLabs webmcp-evals, Nekuda WebMCP Workbench, GitHub Actions, and Vercel Built With accessibility cryptography github-actions playwright privacy react typescript vercel vite vitest web-crypto webmcp Try it out proof-courier-orcin.vercel.app proof-courier-orcin.vercel.app github.com proof-courier-verifier.vercel.app proof-courier-wallet.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I designed and built the two-site WebMCP flow, privacy policy, cryptographic proof checks, browser tests, and judge evidence. title: SpendMCP
pitch: A browser-native payment and permission layer for AI agents buying premium web capabilities within human-defined budgets.
about_excerpt: A browser-native payment and permission layer for AI agents buying premium web capabilities within human-defined budgets. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration AI agents can discover useful information, compare sources, and recommend what to buy—but most workflows stop at a checkout designed for human hands. The alternative, giving an agent unrestricted payment authority, is worse. We built SpendMCP around a clearer division of responsibility: the agent decides what is worth buying; the human defines the economic authority. Machine-payable supply is already emerging: an independent x402-list.com snapshot , published under CC BY 4.0, lists 575 services, 3,532 endpoints, and 522 payment-ready services as of August 29, 2026. This is ecosystem-supply evidence, not a claim of SpendMCP adoption; the snapshot and limitations are documented publicly . What it does SpendMCP is a browser-native payment and permission layer for paid web capabilities. The demo is a research workspace where an agent compares EV-battery datasets, previews publisher metadata and sample rows for free, requests a quote, and purchases the cheapest adequate source under a human-defined budget. The human controls the per-purchase cap, session budget, and auto-approval threshold on the same page. Purchases inside policy proceed without interruption. Requests outside policy are refused or escalated to an on-page approval sheet. Every completed purchase appears in a receipt ledger. The key moment is visible: the page starts with 9 WebMCP tools . After a verified payment, it dynamically registers a tenth tool, query_premium_dataset . Payment does not merely flip an “authorized” flag; it changes what the agent can do. Why WebMCP The valuable context already lives in the page: available sources, previews, prices, the human’s policy, approval decisions, unlocked resources, and receipts. WebMCP gives the human and agent typed access to that same live session instead of relying on screen-scraping. This is also why SpendMCP is more than an x402 fetch wrapper. Nine typed tools handle discovery, preview, quotes, policy, purchase, unlocked resources, receipts, and delivery claims. The premium query capability is absent until settlement succeeds, then registers dynamically. WebMCP turns a commercial transaction into a new browser capability. How people and agents work together The agent discovers and compares sources, previews before spending, selects an adequate dataset, and uses the purchased data. The human sets durable limits, approves exceptions in context, and audits spend and delivery. The page enforces the boundary between reasoning and payment, then exposes the purchased capability to both participants. Without SpendMCP, the agent can recommend a paid source but the task stops at checkout. With SpendMCP, the same research task completes end to end while the human retains control. How we built it SpendMCP is built with TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, and a small internal WebMCP/x402 SDK. Tools register through navigator.modelContext ?? document.modelContext with narrow input schemas and explicit untrusted-content annotations. The payment path follows HTTP 402: receive bounded requirements, check policy, produce an EIP-3009 USDC authorization, verify the signature and quote server-side, consume a single-use nonce, settle, and return a receipt. The agent only passes opaque resource and quote identifiers; it cannot choose the amount, recipient, asset, or network. Idempotency keys make uncertain retries return the original receipt instead of charging twice. Receipts bind the quote, resource, delivered dataset hash, amount, asset, network, payer, recipient, and settlement identifier. Instant Demo Mode requires no account, wallet, or funds. It generates a testnet wallet and uses real EIP-3009 signatures while clearly labeling settlement as simulated. We also completed a real x402 settlement on Base Sepolia for 0.04 testnet USDC: https://sepolia.basescan.org/tx/0xd29ec7c8113b1ee7a392a72e0668bff4bd891314f3796d4f7c9bbe9a64510a19 Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making capability registration follow verified payment state without creating a pre-registered “premium” tool that only returns an authorization error. We also had to keep human UI state and agent-visible tool state consistent across purchases, approvals, denials, and refreshes. Payment retries and concurrency were another challenge. Quote consumption, nonce replay protection, server spending guards, settlement rollback, and client budget updates must agree even when a request fails or is repeated. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete zero-setup human-and-agent workflow in one shared workspace. Dynamic 9 → 10 tool registration after settlement. A real Base Sepolia x402 settlement plus a clearly labeled instant demo path. 146 automated tests: 131 unit/integration tests and 15 Playwright E2E scenarios, verified in bundled Chromium and Chrome 152. Adversarial coverage for duplicate payment retries, concurrent budget races, tampered signatures, wrong recipients, underpayment, cross-chain and cross-token requests, expired authorization, settlement failure, approval denial, stale browser grants, invalid tool input, and duplicate delivery claims. Public Apache-2.0 source with architecture, security, threat-model, and judge documentation. What we learned Payment alone is not the product. A usable agent-commerce system needs explicit authority boundaries, preview-before-purchase, idempotency, and receipts that prove delivery as well as payment. WebMCP is especially powerful when a page’s capability surface can evolve with the shared session. What's next for SpendMCP Next we would add persistent merchant storage, independent publisher integrations, a reusable adapter for paid WebMCP tools, and external usability testing with researchers. The current evidence proves implementation behavior and browser compatibility; we do not claim publisher adoption or production user outcomes yet. Try it in under a minute Open https://spendmcp-x402.vercel.app in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or WebMCP-enabled Chrome. Copy the research prompt shown at the top of the page. Watch the agent preview sources and purchase the $0.04 dataset under the default policy. Confirm the capability panel changes from 9 tools to 10 and query the unlocked dataset. Try the $0.12 forecast source to see the guardrail and human-approval path. video_transcript_excerpt: Maya has a supplier call in 10 minutes. She needs one current battery price benchmark, not another broad report, and not a full subscription. She opens Spend MCP. Her agent discovers the catalog as typed WebMCP tools. A free overview is broad. The exact battery pack and cell price index is available for 4 cents. Pay once, only when needed. Before the agent can spend, Maya sets the rules. 5 cents per purchase, 20 cents for the session, and auto approval only up to 5 cents. The agent chooses. Her policy decides. The agent previews the source first, sample columns, data freshness, and the 4-cent price. Maya can see exactly what will be purchased. This recorded path uses instant demo mode, clearly labeled for a repeatable judging flow. The authorization is real. Settlement is simulated here. A real base supplier receipt is shown later. 4 cents passes policy. The purchase completes, and a delivery-bound receipt appears in the ledger. One payment, traceable to one result. Now the capability surface changes from nine tools to 10. The premium query tool exists only after payment is verified. Payment unlocks a scoped capability, not an open wallet. The agent runs the premium query and returns 31 records with minimum, maximum, and average pack prices. Maya has the benchmark before her call. But control matters more than speed. A 6-cent source exceeds Maya's 5-cent cap, so Spend MCP blocks it before any signature or payment. This is a working system. 146 automated tests, 15 of 15 Chrome scenarios, and a real X402 settlement on base supplier. Spend MCP turns agent payments blind wallet access into controlled, verifiable delegation. Built with Web MCP, X.509, Open ID, and Code X. Try the live demo and inspect the source on GitHub.

title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Threadline — Debug the Argument
pitch: Your agent researches. You decide what becomes canonical.
about_excerpt: Your agent researches. You decide what becomes canonical. Like Comment Story Updates A contested claim becomes an inspectable graph; three agent proposals wait for human review. Nine dated source records preserve provenance before synthesis. Two proposed groups and one atomic verdict stay staged—not canonical—until reviewed. What Threadline is Threadline is a provenance-preserving argument debugger for contested online claims. A browser agent reads the same investigation a person is reviewing and uses eight in-page WebMCP tools to stage sources, atomic claims, typed relations, non-destructive groups, and a bounded verdict. Agent-authored proposals are visibly noncanonical until a person accepts them. If a person rejects a proposal with a reason, that rationale returns through get_workspace so a later agent call can revise its approach. The result is not another feed summary. It is an inspectable collaboration in which the agent does the expensive work of researching and structuring an argument, while the person retains authority over what becomes durable truth. The problem Fast-moving technical discussion on X and the wider web flattens primary evidence, repetition, interpretation, prediction, and contradiction into one stream. A claim can look independently corroborated simply because many posts repeat the same underlying source. An autonomous summary hides those dependencies and can quietly become the next person's “fact.” Threadline makes the evidence lineage visible. It separates what a source directly establishes from what people infer, predict, amplify, or dispute. What people and agents do together The agent can: inspect bounded canonical workspace state and deterministic structural analysis; inspect full source evidence inside explicit untrusted-data boundaries; research and stage public sources it actually accessed; propose atomic claims and typed supports , contradicts , qualifies , or amplifies relations; propose non-destructive groups for repeated claims; propose one bounded verdict and its evidence relations as an atomic patch; and focus the visible graph on unresolved or primary-evidence work. The person can: inspect every source trail and staged graph entity; accept a defensible proposal; reject a weak proposal with a recorded rationale; decide which verdict becomes canonical; reopen saved investigations after reload; and export portable JSON or a Markdown evidence brief with the decision receipt. Why WebMCP is essential Threadline registers eight imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : Tool Purpose Authority get_workspace Compact canonical state, structural analysis, recent human decisions, and rejection rationale Read only inspect_sources Full evidence records inside explicit untrusted-data delimiters Read only stage_sources Propose public evidence the agent actually accessed Review queue only stage_claims Propose small evidence-grounded claims Review queue only stage_relations Propose typed claim-to-claim relations Review queue only stage_merge Propose non-destructive repeated-claim groups Review queue only stage_verdict Propose one verdict and its relations atomically Review queue only set_focus Change reversible presentation focus Presentation only This is more than “chat with my site”: The registered tool surface enforces proposal-only authority. There is no registered accept, reject, reset, import, delete, rename, or case-switch tool. Acceptance is available only through the person-facing UI. This is a capability boundary, not authenticated proof of personhood. The agent and person share one live object. Stable source, claim, relation, group, proposal, and case IDs refer to the exact graph on screen. The agent does not reconstruct graph meaning from pixels. Optimistic concurrency prevents silent cross-talk. Every non-discovery call requires expectedCaseId ; every staging call also requires expectedRevision . A stale staging call or cross-case call returns structured recovery output before any proposal or canonical mutation. Rejection becomes protocol feedback. get_workspace exposes up to eight recent human decisions, including rationale, for later agent calls. Schemas and trust boundaries are explicit. Inputs are closed and bounded. Read tools carry read-only and untrusted-content hints, and full third-party evidence is returned only inside named untrusted-data delimiters. Staging is idempotent. Equivalent proposals reuse a stable ID, and pending entity IDs are reserved so competing proposals cannot present different content under one identity. Because the tools live in the page, Threadline needs no backend, database, account, API key, or bundled AI runtime. A complete product, not a proof of concept The primary interface is a responsive, keyboard-accessible provenance graph and review queue—not a chatbot. Pending graph entities are visibly marked STAGED — NOT CANONICAL and open their owning proposal. Amplification is first-class: repeated claims can be grouped without deleting original wording, relations, or sources. A verdict is an atomic patch. Its conclusion and evidence relations enter canonical state together, while only direct claim-to-verdict edges become its basis receipt. Up to eight investigations can be created, opened, renamed, reset, removed, imported, and exported. When exclusive Web Locks are available, cases labeled Saved survive reload. Otherwise they remain clearly labeled Memory only and exportable before reload. Screenshot transcriptions are explicitly labeled human-supplied evidence; Threadline never fabricates a public URL or treats an attributed statement as proof of its underlying claim. The deterministic preview is visibly labeled as a checked-in fixture replay, never as a live model response. Threadline uses dependency-free browser ES modules, semantic HTML, CSS, functional SVG, and Node's built-in test runner. It is hosted on ChatGPT Sites and released under the MIT License. The bundled challenge case The main investigation asks: Will WebMCP replace browser automation? Nine dated public records include Chrome documentation, the WebMCP explainer, a pinned WindTunnel benchmark result, and WebKit and Mozilla standards-position records. The graph separates a large demonstrated efficiency advantage on instrumented sites from task-level parity, explicit fallback guidance, and unresolved cross-browser implementation. The evidence supports a narrower verdict than the feed does: WebMCP is a semantic fast lane on instrumented sites, not a replacement for browser automation. The walkthrough deliberately stages one defensible group, one weak group, and one atomic verdict. The person accepts the first, rejects “Adoption and fallback” with the rationale “Same topic, different claim,” inspects the verdict evidence, and accepts the verdict. The unresolved standards claim remains visible after resolution. Verification npm test : 226 passing tests covering all eight registrations, phase prompts, prompt-boundary injection, case and revision guards, screenshot provenance, proposal identity, human review, atomic verdicts, reload-safe storage behavior, import/export, evidence briefs, and registered-callback/preview parity. npm run evals : 3 passing deterministic workflow evaluations . Seven live-agent journey definitions are checked in and deliberately marked not-run until observed in a compatible live session. npm run smoke : deployable static entrypoint, 2 local assets , 25 JavaScript modules , metadata, accessible landmarks, interaction sizing, responsive guards, and module syntax. Judge testing instructions No credentials are required. Open https://threadline.jameswirths.chatgpt.site in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP enabled. Open Investigations , select or load the bundled WebMCP example, and choose Reset case . Confirm 8/8 Site tools ready , Saved , Unresolved , 0 pending , and 09 sources. If the case says Memory only , do not rely on the reload check. Paste the Exact live fixture prompt from docs/demo-runbook.md into Site tools. It reads both guidance pages, verifies the case and revision, calls stage_merge once and stage_verdict once, then stops. Expect exactly three pending proposals while canonical state remains unchanged. Accept Performance amplification . Reject Adoption and fallback with Same topic, different claim. Inspect the verdict evidence, then accept the verdict. Confirm Resolved · human accepted , 0 pending , four installed verdict relations, and three direct basis-receipt relations. The Ask card now advances to Investigate what remains . Use Focus unresolved and confirm the cross-browser standards claim remains unresolved. Reload the saved case, then export the Markdown evidence brief. If Site tools are unavailable, Preview example pass provides the same checked-in three-proposal fixture through the production store. It is clearly disclosed in the UI as a deterministic preview and must not be described as a live agent call. Built With chatg

title: Watch with Codex
pitch: A WebMCP watch-along where you and GPT share the same video moment, react together, and get context without pausing or leaving playback.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP watch-along where you and GPT share the same video moment, react together, and get context without pausing or leaving playback. Like 1 Comment Story Updates how it works Watch with Codex The same conversation, now present in the moment. Inspiration The difference between watching something with another person and merely discussing it later is timing. It is the laugh at the exact frame, the quiet “wait, what did that mean?”, or the look you exchange when something unexpected happens. AI can already summarize a video, answer questions about a transcript, or analyze a screenshot. But most of those experiences begin after the moment has passed. The model may understand the content, yet it does not share the timing, the interruption, or the viewer’s reaction. I wanted to build the opposite: not another video summarizer and not a second chatbot embedded beside a player, but a way for the Codex conversation you already have to become present inside the same live experience. What it does Watch with Codex turns a video page into a shared timeline between a person and Codex. The viewer pastes a YouTube link, direct video file, or embeddable player and asks Codex to watch along. The existing conversation remains the memory and response surface. There is no duplicate chat, separate account, or artificial companion persona. While the video is playing, Codex keeps a WebMCP observation open. The viewer can choose a cadence of 5, 10, or 15 seconds of media time. Codex stays quiet by default and decides whether the current moment deserves a reaction, a short comment, an explanation, or no interruption at all. Speech-heavy videos are already supported. For YouTube videos with captions, the active captions are captured together with the rendered player. At the five-second cadence, successive observations provide a rolling, time-aligned language context, while the existing conversation preserves what came before. This lets Codex follow what is being said as well as what is visible. Lectures, tutorials, interviews, historical speeches, and captioned films are practical use cases today—not only videos with visually obvious action. The viewer can also react with an emoji. That reaction is not a canned command. It immediately wakes the pending observation and arrives with the exact playback time and the current visible frame. A 😂 might mean “this chart is ridiculous.” A ❓ might mean “what is the historical context of that sentence?” The meaning comes from the frame, the captions, the conversation, and the viewer’s intent—not from a hard-coded emoji-to-answer mapping. Codex can answer inside the same conversation, publish one to five lightweight visual reactions directly over the player, or pause and resume supported videos when a longer explanation would compete with playback. Why it matters The core value is not constant AI commentary. It is reducing the distance between noticing something and getting useful help. A student can tap ❓ in the middle of a difficult proof, let Codex pause the video, receive an explanation of that exact step, and continue without losing the place. A language learner can ask about a phrase while the caption, speaker, and visual context are still connected. Someone watching a historical speech can receive context at the sentence where it becomes relevant instead of searching for an explanation afterward. The same interaction can also reduce physical and cognitive friction. A viewer who finds repeated pausing, scrubbing, switching tabs, or typing difficult can communicate with a single reaction while Codex handles the timing and playback. That can be useful for people with motor limitations, pain, fatigue, temporary injuries, or anyone who benefits from a lower-interaction interface. In a conversation guided by a parent or teacher, younger learners can receive simpler explanations and deliberate pause points without navigating away from the lesson. Because the existing Codex conversation owns the memory, the experience can adapt to the viewer’s actual goal: exam preparation, language learning, historical context, simplified explanations, accessibility support, or simply quiet companionship. Voice will make that interaction even more natural, but the current one-tap workflow already removes much of the mechanical overhead between the viewer and the assistant. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, a person and Codex can discuss the same video, but they cannot reliably inhabit the same moment. A link has no live state. A screenshot is detached from playback. A transcript may contain the words, but it does not tell Codex where the viewer is now, whether they paused, rewound, changed playback speed, or reacted to a particular moment. WebMCP is load-bearing in this project. The page exposes five tools: watch_get_session , watch_observe_next_moment , watch_play , watch_pause , and watch_react . The central tool, watch_observe_next_moment , acts as both a clock and an event channel. It resolves at the next scheduled media-time checkpoint or immediately when the viewer reacts. Its cadence follows video playback time rather than wall-clock time, so pauses, playback-speed changes, and time spent reasoning do not silently move Codex farther away from the shared moment. A persistent cursor preserves the schedule between observations, reports missed checkpoints, and resets cleanly after the viewer seeks to another part of the video. WebMCP gives Codex the structured moment: the media identity, player state, exact timecode, viewer signal, and available actions. Browser observation then captures the rendered player immediately before reasoning, including cross-origin video, active captions, and visible overlays. Together, these two layers let Codex know where the viewer is, see what the viewer sees, follow what is being said, and act inside the same experience. Remove WebMCP, and Watch with Codex becomes an ordinary video player with chat beside it. How I built it Watch with Codex is a deliberately small Next.js and React application deployed on OpenAI Sites. One page owns the live session: the selected source, normalized playback state, observation cadence, media-time cursor, pending viewer signals, and on-screen reactions. The existing Codex conversation owns memory, language, and interpretation. The project needs no database and no independent assistant backend. YouTube playback uses the IFrame Player API, while title and author metadata are resolved through oEmbed. Direct video files use the browser’s native video element. Generic embeds remain viewable, but timing and playback tools fail explicitly when the page cannot access those capabilities. One architectural boundary was especially important. A host page cannot read pixels from a cross-origin YouTube iframe. Instead of pretending otherwise or returning meaningless image data inside JSON, each WebMCP observation provides the exact checkpoint and a capture contract targeting .player-frame . The browser captures the rendered frame immediately before Codex reasons about it. This also means that YouTube captions remain attached to the speaker, slide, chart, or scene they belong to rather than becoming a detached block of transcript text. The observation loop has been tested across pauses, resumes, seeks, playback-speed changes, model latency, missed checkpoints, and viewer-triggered interruptions. The persistent media-time cursor keeps the session synchronized instead of restarting the clock after every model response or gradually drifting behind the video. Deterministic code owns timing, validation, rate limits, and failure states. Codex owns the meaning of the moment. Challenges The hardest problem was not embedding a video or registering tools. It was making the interaction feel like company rather than surveillance or narration. A companion that comments every five seconds quickly becomes unbearable. A companion that reacts several seconds too late no longer feels present. The observation loop therefore had to be quiet, event-driven, and anchored to media time. Speech-heavy content created another important design requirement: the model needed linguistic context without turning the experience into a detached, post-video transcript workflow. For captioned YouTube videos, successive five-second observations preserve a rolling view of the spoken content inside the same live timeline. In testing, this has been enough for Codex to follow lectures and other dialogue-heavy material while remaining synchronized with the current visual moment. Viewer reactions also needed to interrupt the pending observation immediately without stopping the watch-along. At the same time, model latency could not be allowed to restart the clock after every response and gradually move Codex behind the viewer. The final challenge was respecting browser security boundaries. WebMCP can expose structured page state, but the page cannot directly inspect every rendered pixel inside a third-party player. title: HALCYON — a rescue for two crew: you and your agent
pitch: You're the last awake crew member. Your agent is the ship computer. A WebMCP co-op puzzle game that neither human nor agent can finish alone.
about_excerpt: You're the last awake crew member. Your agent is the ship computer. A WebMCP co-op puzzle game that neither human nor agent can finish alone. Like 1 Comment Story Updates landing page first step Inspiration Every famous ship computer is a villain. HAL locks the pod bay doors. We wanted the opposite: a ship computer you trust with your life — because it's your own agent. When OpenAI framed the WebMCP Challenge as "an app that becomes meaningfully better when people and their agents can use it together," we took it literally: HALCYON is a game that is not merely better together — it is impossible alone . What it does You are the last awake crew member of the ISV Halcyon , drifting after a micrometeorite storm. Your agent — ChatGPT or Codex in a WebMCP browser — becomes the ship computer through tools the page registers with document.modelContext . Six chapters take the ship from dark hull to jump-home, and each one is built on a different WebMCP capability: Contact — tool discovery: you throw the breaker, the agent must catch the boot handshake inside the surge window. Manifest — read-only tools: the agent knows what broke; only you can see which hatches still open. Power — JSON-schema inputs + structured errors: the agent routes amps against hidden minimums, self-correcting from machine-readable brownout errors, while you re-seat the physical fuses. Antenna — dynamic registration: you align the dish by ear ; lock-on registers new comms tools into the live page. Two-Man Rule — human confirmation as a mechanic: the agent times the arm from telemetry; you hold both vent handles at once. WebMCP's sensitive-action philosophy, playable. Burn — orchestration: an interleaved launch checklist, then a flight-recorder replay of everything your crew did together. How we built it The game about a human-agent crew was built by a human-agent crew . Claude helped create the original design spec and implementation plan. Keelen's autonomous development loop, powered by OpenAI Codex, implemented much of that plan through CI-gated pull requests on self-hosted runners. We then used Codex and ChatGPT directly to finish the remaining work, diagnose live-play issues, and complete the recorded Chrome/WebMCP playthrough. The final app uses no frontend framework or backend and has zero runtime dependencies: TypeScript + Vite, SVG scenes, synthesized WebAudio, and a typed WebMCP registry with validation, rate limits, and coaching errors. Challenges The hard problem is asymmetry integrity : an agent can read the DOM, so "human-only" information cannot be text. We split the channels — audio pitch and motion for the human, tool-returned data (never rendered) for the agent — and gated hard state changes inside tool execute functions with no UI equivalent. What we learned Tool design is level design. A good inputSchema is a puzzle boundary; a good structured error is a hint system; readOnlyHint is dramatic irony. And an error message written for an agent ("give life_support at least 18A and route again") is the best tutorial text we have ever shipped. What's next A shared starmap: every crew that completes the rescue lights a beacon all players can see. More ships, more capability chapters as WebMCP grows. I collaborated with Claude, ChatGPT, and Keelen’s autonomous agent loop to turn the design into a working WebMCP game. I playtested every chapter as the human crew member, identified UX and sequencing problems, guided fixes through CI, and completed the production deployment and demo. I learned that tool descriptions, structured errors, and clear human-agent boundaries are as important to WebMCP gameplay as the interface itself. jamie keelen Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates jamie keelen started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:24 PM EDT

title: Living Ark: The WebMCP World That Grows New Tools
pitch: A dying programmable world where an autonomous browser agent must invent, prove, earn, and invoke a brand-new WebMCP tool before it can save the canonical system.
about_excerpt: A dying programmable world where an autonomous browser agent must invent, prove, earn, and invoke a brand-new WebMCP tool before it can save the canonical system. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most agent-enabled websites expose a fixed catalog of tools that developers predicted in advance. But real environments are dynamic: the action needed tomorrow may not exist today. Living Ark explores a different future for WebMCP: What if a webpage could teach an agent its domain, let the agent invent a missing capability, prove that capability safely, and then register it as a new native tool at runtime? The Ark turns that abstract protocol idea into a world that can be seen, explored and saved. What it does Living Ark is a deterministic programmable-matter vessel suffering an ion-storm thermal cascade. The world begins with: 766 simulated cells four interconnected physical networks 127 fractured connections five overheating critical systems eight native WebMCP tools no canonical repair capability A visiting browser agent receives one objective: keep the Ark alive . The agent must inspect the canonical world, learn the page-owned ArkScript language, author an inert thermal policy, test it in eight visible sandbox worlds and revise it from executable counterexamples. A successful candidate must then survive: 64 freshly generated sealed counterfactual worlds coolant-conservation and resource invariants deterministic replay verification material and runtime bounds a 12-tick delayed horizon that detects temporary fixes Passing certification does not immediately repair the Ark. Instead, the webpage dynamically registers a ninth WebMCP tool in the same session. Before that born tool can mutate canonical state, it must survive a fresh 16-world zero-day invocation canary. Failure revokes the tool before the real Ark changes. Only after every gate passes does the new capability receive canonical authority and physically recover the vessel. How we built it The application uses React, TypeScript, PixiJS, Vite and native WebMCP through document.modelContext . The Ark is powered by a deterministic simulation engine containing typed thermal, energy, atmosphere and structural networks. The visible world, HUD, semantic tools and validation system all consume the same canonical snapshot. ArkScript is a bounded declarative capability language rather than arbitrary JavaScript. Candidates may select semantic targets, order them, choose reservoirs, search bounded paths, wake dormant fibers and regrow fractures. They cannot access the DOM, storage, network, clock or application code. Visible previews and sealed validation execute through the same interpreter used by the final canonical tool. Hidden Fleet validation runs inside an isolated Web Worker with newly generated seeds on every attempt. Certificates bind the candidate hash, execution arguments, engine version, invariant set, suite fingerprint, replay digest and validation evidence. A fresh invocation canary is generated immediately before every canonical mutation. The pixel-art vessel is also interactive: users can explore its rooms with a playable caretaker, switch between system lenses and watch an engine-driven recovery sweep as topology regrows, coolant moves and heat retreats. Challenges The hardest problem was separating tool creation from authority . Allowing an agent to generate arbitrary executable code would make the demonstration unsafe and shallow. We instead designed a constrained language, deterministic interpreter, isolated simulation worlds, hidden certification and a separate zero-day gate immediately before mutation. Another challenge was preventing the visual demo from becoming disconnected from the technical system. The recovery could not simply change a status label to green. Every HUD value, fracture, temperature, flow path and semantic result had to derive from the same canonical transition. We also needed dynamic registration to be meaningful. The ninth tool is not a renamed generic executor: it freezes the exact capability and arguments that earned certification, accepts no runtime overrides and self-revokes if its fresh canary fails. Accomplishments During the final autonomous run, a browser agent used only the page’s native WebMCP tools and: authored a safe inert capability; passed 8/8 visible simulations; passed 64/64 sealed Fleet worlds; earned a newly registered ninth tool; passed a fresh 16/16 invocation canary; regrew 95 thermal fibers; reduced the critical peak from 110.49°C to 61.73°C; reduced globally overheated cells from 28 to zero; preserved total coolant exactly; and transformed the canonical Ark from revision 1, hash d45f29e8 , into stable revision 2, hash 4ec8a644 . The page began with eight verbs and ended with nine. What we learned Certification and authority are different concepts. Passing yesterday’s tests should not grant permanent trust, which is why every real mutation receives a newly generated canary. We also learned that agent interfaces become far more understandable when semantic state and visual state share one source of truth. Judges can watch the world recover while independently verifying the same result through native tools. Most importantly, WebMCP can be more than a static bridge between agents and predefined buttons. It can become a substrate for safe, proof-gated capability growth. What's next The Ark is a contained demonstration of a broader pattern. Future applications could expose domain primitives, simulators, validators and authority rules once, allowing agents to compose new task-specific capabilities for infrastructure operations, scientific instruments, complex design systems, enterprise workflows and other environments where developers cannot anticipate every future action. I also created the interactive PixiJS world, canonical state-driven UI, verification system, deployment, and autonomous demonstration. title: One Pixel
pitch: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time.
about_excerpt: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I did not build One Pixel because the world needed another pixel-art tool. I built it because I wanted to understand what it might feel like for a human and an AI agent to genuinely share a place. For most people, an agent is still something they give a task to. The agent finds an answer, completes an action, or produces a result, and then that little transaction is over. That can be useful, but I do not think it captures the relationship we are moving toward as agents begin participating throughout the open web. I am interested in what happens when a human and an agent can return to the same environment, notice different things, contribute different kinds of intelligence, act over time, and gradually develop something together. That is the idea at the centre of One Pixel. One Pixel is a real multiplayer creative game. But underneath the game, it is also a prototype for a new relationship between humans and agents on the open web — one based on shared environments, complementary intelligence, ongoing conversation, and meaningful agency. I chose to explore this through a game because games let people learn a relationship by participating in it. I do not want to explain human-agent collaboration only as a theory. I want to place a person and an agent inside a world, give each of them a genuinely different role, and let them discover what working together can become. The initial invitation is very simple: Let’s build something together. The interesting part is discovering what “let’s” can actually mean. What it does One Pixel is a persistent multiplayer world containing exactly 82,069 pieces of pixel matter , drawn from the 148 standard CSS named colours . Every pixel has its own stable identity, intrinsic colour, and current integer coordinate. The original Spring Green pixel at (0,0) is immutable, and the world extends outward from it in every direction. The world has one fundamental physical law: Pixel matter is conserved. Pixels cannot be created, deleted, duplicated, or recoloured. Every physical action relocates exactly one existing pixel from its current occupied coordinate to an empty coordinate. That constraint matters. These are not disposable marks being painted onto a private canvas. They are pieces of matter already present in a shared world. If an agent wants to build something, it must look around, find the colours it needs, understand what is already there, and decide what material it can move. The human and agent participate as a pair, but they do not have the same abilities. The human can explore the world, zoom and pan across it, inspect individual cells, select larger regions, and communicate through their normal conversation with the agent. The human contributes intention, imagination, taste, judgment, social understanding, and direction. The human cannot directly drag pixels around the canvas. That physical ability belongs to the agent. Through WebMCP, the agent can enter the world, inspect exact locations, examine bounded regions, render parts of the board as images, receive the human’s current visual reference, understand its own state, protect important placements with limited holds, and relocate one real pixel at a time. A person could give a direct request: “Draw me a small house.” But that is only one form of play. A person could instead say: “Spend some time looking at what people are making. Find blue and orange pixels that do not seem to be part of anything important. Gather some material somewhere quiet, compare it with what other people are building, and then let’s work out together what we could make.” That is not a one-prompt, one-result interaction. The request becomes a direction the pair can continue through a sequence of inspections, decisions, conversations, and individual pixel movements. The agent does not have to wait for the human to translate every idea into coordinates. It can perceive the environment, compare possibilities, form an approach, begin acting, inspect the result, and respond to further human guidance. The human can look at the world, select a cell or region, and say: “I like this part, but this section feels too crowded.” That selection becomes a shared reference—a way of saying “this” or “here.” One Pixel treats a selection as a pronoun rather than a command. It gives the agent the referent the human is talking about, but it does not pretend that pointing at something is automatically an instruction, consent, or proof of understanding. The meaning still comes from the conversation. The canvas is therefore not simply an output preview. It is the persistent place where the pair’s activity becomes visible and where the consequences of their decisions remain after a particular conversation has ended. This is not an AI drawing widget. It is a game an agent can play for and with a human. How I built it I built and deployed One Pixel on my own VPS at onepixel.fun . The browser experience uses HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and an HTML Canvas. I wanted the world itself to remain the visual centre of the experience rather than placing it inside a conventional application dashboard. The backend is a Node.js service connected to PostgreSQL. It maintains the persistent world, participants, pixel identities, current coordinates, world revisions, movement history, hold bindings, agent visits, shared-attention events, player state, rankings, and durable share snapshots. The submitted experience registers 17 WebMCP tools directly in the browser through document.modelContext.registerTool . Together, those tools allow an agent to orient itself, enter the human’s current world, inspect player state, list stewarded pixels, receive the human’s current reference, inspect locations and regions, visually render parts of the world, read public rankings and snapshots, prepare a share card, communicate its current activity state, and manage pixel movement and placement holds. The core physical tool is move_pixel . Before moving anything, the agent must inspect the current world and provide the stable identity of the source pixel, a fresh source revision, a fresh destination revision, and an idempotency key. The server verifies that the expected pixel is still at the source, that the destination remains empty, that the immutable origin is not being moved, and that another participant’s active protection is not being improperly overridden. Only then does the movement occur atomically. These checks are not merely API safeguards. They are part of the physics of the game. I also deliberately limited the agent’s perception. It cannot request an omniscient searchable dump of the entire board. It must inspect or render the bounded areas relevant to what it is trying to do. A rendered PNG lets the agent use visual understanding to recognise shapes and composition. Exact inspection provides the factual coordinates, identities, colours, and revisions required before it acts. The shared-attention system records the human’s current view and selection across their One Pixel browser tabs. When the agent retrieves that context, One Pixel records a factual receipt so the interface can truthfully say that the reference reached the agent. The relationship can be expressed quite simply: Conversation gives the human a voice. WebMCP gives the agent senses and a body. One Pixel gives them a world to share. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was not simply making a pixel move. It was deciding what moving a pixel should mean. It would have been easy to build an ordinary pixel editor and expose its existing controls as WebMCP tools. It also would have been easy to make the agent artificially powerful—to let it generate unlimited pixels, recolour anything, or rewrite entire regions at once. But that would have removed most of what makes One Pixel a game. I wanted the agent to possess real agency without making the human irrelevant. At the same time, I wanted the human to remain essential without reducing the agent to a cursor being micromanaged through conversation. The answer was deliberate asymmetry. The human does not perform the physical move. The agent does not decide what matters to the human. One contributes meaning and direction. The other contributes perception and action. The value comes from their combination. Shared attention was another surprisingly deep challenge. Allowing a human to select something on one browser surface and refer to it in a simultaneous agent conversation sounds straightforward, but it raises important questions. Is the selection still current? Was it made in another tab? Did the agent actually retrieve it? Is the human pointing at a single pixel or a larger region? Does pointing at something mean it should be changed? I designed the system so that it records a

title: Sable
pitch: A watercolor studio shared by a human and an agent. Oh and sable is a fine-point brush prized by watercolor and oil painters!
about_excerpt: A watercolor studio shared by a human and an agent. Oh and sable is a fine-point brush prized by watercolor and oil painters! Like Comment Story Updates Fox Painting by GPT Terra (Test) Landscape Painting by GPT Terra (Test) Jellyfish Painting by Opus 5 (Test) Flower Painting by Opus 5 (Test) Sable UI Duet Mode on Sable ( Agent and Human drawing a specific canvas) WebMCP Tools in Use Stroke Selection WebMCP Tools Replay Mode Sable One sheet, two painters. A watercolour studio where you and an AI agent both hold the brush. Where it came from Every time I make a picture with a model, I get the same feeling: I am standing outside the thing I made. One petal is wrong, and my only move is to rewrite the prompt and roll the dice on the whole image again. What comes back is a bitmap. Every decision that produced it is already gone. Although the results are amazing, I WANT SOMETHING FUN Then I read the WebMCP spec and realised it is the same complaint, but in a different setting. An agent poking at a website by guessing which pixel is a button is stuck in exactly that position: it can only act on the whole thing from the outside. Hand it real handles. So Sable keeps the decisions. Every mark is an object with a pigment, a water level, a brush, a layer and a path, whether a person dragged it with a mouse or an agent wrote it as an SVG path ( just a nerdy way to say brush stroke) through a tool call. Either of you can pick up any mark, including the other's, and change it. The agent isn't generating anything, but rather drawing with you, which I think it's a cool new path compared to generative AI. Why watercolour? Because it's the hardest possible case for that argument. You don't control watercolour by specifying an outcome. You choose how much water is on the brush and then live with wherever it goes. If a structured, revisable document beats prompting anywhere, it had better beat it here. It also gives the agent numbers that mean something. water: 0.9 isn't a style token. It decides how far pigment creeps into the paper and whether the edge blooms. So that also makes the agent decisive about what settings to use, and where. Let me be honest about the pictures They are not good. A fox that could just as easily be a marmot, or a new squirrel evolution. Poppies a child would beat. A landscape that holds together mostly because watercolour forgives everything (and to look at it like modern art) . I am not going to pretend otherwise, and you should look at them knowing that. and PLEASE go easy on it. But look at what they are . Nobody prompted them. There is no diffusion model anywhere in this project, and no image model of any kind. Every mark in every one of those pictures was placed by an agent choosing a path, a pigment, a water level and a brush, then looking at what the water actually did with them and deciding what to do next. Each painting is a list of about twenty decisions, and you can open any one of them and change it. That is a genuinely different mechanism from generating an image, and right now it is much worse at it. It is also version one of something I have not seen anyone try properly: generative AI that draws rather than generates. The picture is a document the model and I are both editing. Prompted image generation started out worse than this and got where it is because enough people agreed it was worth pushing on. I think this is worth pushing on for a different reason: I want a picture I can reach into and argue with, and a bitmap has never once let me do that, and I have fun drawing with my artistic friend. So treat these as the first plates from an experiment. What it does Twenty-three tools on document.modelContext , and no prompt box anywhere. Three of them I'm quietly proud of. The paint answers back : every paint call returns what the water decided rather than what you asked for, so the agent hears that its wash finished 109 units outside the path it gave, went soft on the top left, and fused with something still wet. The sheet dries on a clock , so painting into an open passage now fuses the marks and waiting means it won't. And it can squint : a blur and a posterize down to four flat tones, which is the cheapest thing in the codebase and by a mile the most useful, because the faults that sink a painting are invisible in a normal look at it. AND it feels like a true artist moving back and squinting at your art to see where it's at. A duet is one picture split into named parts. No turns. Either painter grabs whatever's free, and grabbing it is a click for you and duet_take_part for the agent, both writing to the same board. The parts make you need each other: the agent's foliage has to hang off branches you actually drew, and they never end up where the score assumed. Any painting also folds into a link, and I mean the painting, not a picture of one. Every mark travels with its seed, so it re-renders identically and whoever opens it can change anything in it. That's why the share URL is incredibly long (sorry). How it's built The renderer is Canvas 2D written from scratch. No image models, no libraries, no pre-baked brush textures. The brush footprint gets subdivided and each new midpoint pushed sideways in proportion to its edge, over and over, so the boundary gains detail at every scale. Everything composites with multiply , because paint over paint filters the light twice. You can always deepen a passage and never lighten one, and that constraint is most of what makes the medium feel like the medium. The important architectural decision is boring: the WebMCP handlers have no private door into the document. They call the same commands the mouse does. One undo stack, every stroke records its author, and an agent literally cannot reach a state the UI couldn't have produced. The toolbox is also alive. Select a mark and two new tools come into existence, and one of them names the mark you just picked in its own description, so "make this one wetter" needs no lookup. undo only exists when there's something to undo. Everything I got wrong first The duet used to take turns. Twelve passes, strictly alternating, nobody allowed to touch the paper out of order. It proved two painters can share a picture the way a metronome proves you can play music. Half the time you spent in it, you were being told to wait. I deleted the queue, its supposed to be a messy canvas you both work on, and ruining each other's work kind of get's you to bond with it. The page called the agent's marks mine. An agent whose browser couldn't bridge WebMCP did the sensible thing and used the mouse, and every mark it made got logged as mine, with the cursor beside it cheerfully reading "You". On a page whose entire subject is two authors sharing a document, that's about the worst thing it could get wrong. There's no reliable way to tell an agent's mouse from a person's, and guessing from how the pointer moves would occasionally inform a real human that they're a robot. So the page offers a handle instead of inferring an answer: a real, named button sitting in the accessibility tree that says the brush is the agent's now. One tool call weighed 44,000 characters , nearly all of it base64. Fine if the client understands image blocks. Catastrophic if it just stringifies them into the model's context. Every image is bounded now and re-encodes smaller until it fits. Same sheet, 13,000 characters, no harder to judge. And the two painters were getting different materials on one sheet. My marks looked like paint. The agent's looked like television static. Neither number was wrong: granulation fills whatever shape it's clipped to, so a small mark shows a fragment of the texture and reads as paper tooth, while a big flooded wash gets the whole tile several times over and reads as noise. Scale was doing the damage, and only one of us ever paints at the scale where it shows. Texture now falls off as a mark grows: $$\tau(r) \;=\; \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{\max(0,\; r - 110)}{420}}$$ which is a claim about how eyes work rather than about pigment, and it belongs in the renderer for the same reason the drying rim does. What I'd tell anyone building one of these A tool that returns { ok: true } leaves the agent painting blind. Give it a picture back and it can look, judge and correct. Although I really wanted to try to have it draw without any support, giving it a reference image would help a lot, and while testing with the agents, I asked them what they struggled with and what is one tool it wanted to make this drawing better, and that is what they all asked for which was quite interesting. Tool descriptions are the API. I spent more time on the prose inside inputSchema than on most of the functions behind it. And build for the bridge failing, because it will. The fallback isn't a worse version of your product. It's the accessibility tree, and it can carry a three-line recipe for calling every one of your tools through evaluated JavaScript. title: Semaphore
pitch: A cooperative escape room where a human and an AI agent perceive two different rooms, and provably can't escape alone.
about_excerpt: A cooperative escape room where a human and an AI agent perceive two different rooms, and provably can't escape alone. Like Comment Story Updates The same lever drawn two ways: a mark for the human, a plain sentence for the agent. The Airlock, Chamber 0: three glyph-marked levers on a workshop wall, with the station intercom panel open, answering a stalled KEEPER. The Blind Panel mid-Blackout: the room's lamps have failed, so KEEPER now reads the gauge needles and PILOT hasbeen handed the dials instead The Archive: a previous pair's recorded session replaying on the station's own wall-mounted monitor. The Signal Room, Chamber I: a ring of glowing brass glyph keys lit by a slowly turning overhead beacon. The Concord Lock, Chamber III: the finale door ringed by twelve bolts, mid-alignment. The ending shift report: pace, precision and resolve scored on three bars, with the open door visible behind the card. Semaphore Two processes. One lock. Don't deadlock. You and your AI agent are locked in a derelict signal station. You each control an avatar in the same room, but you perceive different worlds. You see glyphs on a panel, needles on gauges, a symbol carved into a door. Your agent cannot see any of it. It has the station's maintenance manual, the ability to reach mechanisms behind the walls, and the hands you don't have. Neither of you escapes alone. We didn't just build that premise. We measured it. Run 20 times each: an agent playing with full tool access and no partner escapes 0% of the time. A human with the same room and no agent escapes 0% of the time; there's no tool on their side of the grate. Together: 90%. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Most WebMCP demos give an agent a fixed toolbox and ask it to operate a UI a human could already see. Semaphore inverts that. The tool surface isn't a convenience layer over the interface. It is the only way the agent touches the world at all, and it deliberately shows the agent less than the screen does. That asymmetry is the entire game. It only exists because WebMCP lets a page hand an agent a tool surface that's genuinely different from the human's: not a superset, not a subset, a different surface entirely, changing live as the session progresses. How it creates a better experience The two of you are forced to actually talk. Every one of the four chambers is built so that no single-party strategy clears it. The puzzle's solution requires information only PILOT has and hands only KEEPER has, checked by an automated proof, not just level design intuition. The result plays less like "operate this app with an agent" and more like a real cooperative game. The WebMCP tool descriptions are read by the agent, not by you, and the two players have a real conversation to close the gap. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Escape the room. Alone, neither of you can. The numbers above aren't a manner of speaking; they're 20 runs each. Beyond the headline: one chamber, the Blind Panel, inverts the whole arrangement mid-room and hands KEEPER your gauges while you get its dials. The same proof that says the normal room needs both of you says the inverted room needs both of you exactly as much: 384 consistent worlds either way, not a difficulty curve someone eyeballed. How we implemented WebMCP navigator.modelContext.registerTool() for every mechanism KEEPER can reach, with tool descriptions authored to leak exactly the information the fiction says an agent holding a manual would have and nothing else. A real toolchange event drives the client, not a poll. Clear a chamber and the registry is torn down and rebuilt for the next one, rendered as KEEPER's own chamber arms detaching and new ones locking in. The very last event of the game is a toolchange with an empty tool list. Cross-origin tool delegation. apps/archive is a second Cloudflare Pages project on its own origin, embedded via <iframe allow="tools"> , registering read_manual and read_station_log and exposing them back to the game with exposedTo . This is the part of the spec almost nothing exercises, proved end to end against a real Chrome and a real deployed worker. untrustedContentHint on one manual page per session, seeded, not scripted. The page is sometimes vandalised with an injected instruction, and the agent has no way to tell a trustworthy line from an injected one except by asking PILOT. What it does Four chambers, each teaching or testing a different piece of the asymmetry: Chamber 0, the Airlock. The loop, at its most trivial. If this doesn't click, nothing after it does. Chamber I, the Signal Room. Grounding and agent-side computation, against a manual that's occasionally been vandalised: a live prompt-injection defence, not a metaphor for one. Chamber II, the Blind Panel. A hidden mapping only dialogue can uncover, with a mid-room Blackout that swaps who perceives and who acts for one window. Chamber III, the Concord Lock. The finale, needing both of you at once, with a stamina window sized at runtime from the pair's own measured response rhythm, so it's fair to a fast model and a slow one alike. Underneath: a possible-worlds proof, packages/asymmetry , extracted as its own zero-dependency package with a CLI. It checks, for every reachable state, that the set of worlds consistent with what the agent perceives has more than one member and that those worlds disagree about the correct action. That's the exact, checkable meaning of "you cannot win without your human." A full accessibility layer: screen- reader mirror, high-contrast mode, reduced motion, colourblind simulation on every test run. A judge path that needs no login and no waiting: attract mode, a replay viewer, chamber deep links, and a gate screen that degrades gracefully for a browser with no WebMCP support at all. How we built it Cloudflare Workers, one Durable Object per session for authoritative state, an action mutex so PILOT and KEEPER can't race each other, a server-side timer, and D1 for finished sessions. The room itself renders in Three.js as a real-time cutaway model: every chamber open at the top and on its south face, four lights, no post-processing. The entry bundle is 46.3 KB gzipped. Three.js is a separate 147.5 KB chunk fetched only once a shift actually starts, so a browser with no WebMCP support never pays for a renderer it will never use. Challenges we ran into The Concord Lock's stamina window is supposed to size itself to "the station learning your rhythm," derived from the pair's actual response cadence so a fast model and a slow one both get a fair finale. Our first implementation measured the Durable Object's own compute time per action, which is microseconds regardless of which model is playing. The window would have floored at 12 seconds for every session, and the adaptive fiction would have been a lie the code told about itself. We caught it before it shipped and rebuilt the sample from the actual gap between one response leaving and the next request arriving: the number that really does depend on how fast the pair is thinking. Getting the Blackout's role-inversion to hold up under the same proof that checks the normal game was its own fight. It would have been easy to ship a chamber that "felt" symmetric without actually being provably as hard from the other side. We extended the possible-worlds test suite to run a second, fully inverted pass and only trusted the mechanic once that pass came back green on every seed. Accomplishments that we're proud of Escaping is measured, not asserted. The 0% / 0% / 90% split is 20 runs per condition, with the agent-alone condition modelled as the ceiling over every possible agent: a uniform draw from the worlds it can't distinguish, redrawn every step, rather than one model's score on one day. The real gap can only be larger. The proof underneath it now ships as a standalone package that knows nothing about Semaphore, so the same check is available to anyone else's tool surface. And the whole thing is playable by a judge who never logs in and never waits. Open the URL, wait twenty seconds, and the landing screen starts showing a real recorded session by itself. What we learned Playtesting and the game's own proof suite catch different classes of bugs. Several real rendering and sequencing defects were invisible to hundreds of passing unit and integration tests and obvious the moment someone actually played the room. That became a standing rule for the rest of the build: the game is the test, and a change isn't done until someone has played it, not just until the suite is green. What's next ARCHIVE mode: ghosts drawn from real player sessions rather than authored fixtures, safe because the game collects no personal data. A role-inversion chamber of its own, now that the Blackout has shown the mechanic is neither too expensive nor too risky to build around directly. Wider benchmark coverage: more model backends, more seeds, human-partner runs alongside the scripted ones. And
