title: TALK FAST
pitch: Your blind spot has a voice. One human, one AI agent, one manual — through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Your blind spot has a voice. One human, one AI agent, one manual — through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates What it is TALK FAST is an asymmetric co-op arcade game for one human operator and one AI agent reader. The human sees a physical 3D console and presses every control. The agent agrees not to inspect the screen and instead holds the manual through WebMCP tools registered by the page. Neither can win alone: ten minutes, three strikes, five acts. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Most agent demos have the agent do the task for you. TALK FAST uses the WebMCP boundary as the wall between two players. Information asymmetry—the central game mechanic—runs through the API surface. The agent receives structured, typed access to only the information a reader should have: procedures, charts, codebooks, the clock, and the operator’s text channel. Each act registers its own scoped tools with an AbortSignal and removes them when it ends, so the agent’s live tool list becomes part of the game state. Honest caveat: the page cannot technically prevent an agent from looking at the screen. The tools make fair play the obvious typed path, and the client-captured interaction record makes the intended collaboration inspectable. How it creates a better experience Without WebMCP, the reader would have to scrape a DOM it is not supposed to see, while the operator would have to paste manual pages into chat. With WebMCP, the agent can call narrow tools, reason over the correct manual, ask for clarification, and place one decisive instruction on the operator’s teleprompter. Consequential actions stay visibly bounded. Every normal control press belongs to the human; the sealed override is marked consequential and requires confirmation; and one act gives the reader exactly one physical action of its own. Strikes are attributed to the reader or operator, making communication failures legible. The result is both a game and a compact practice arena for human-agent delegation: describe state precisely, ask useful questions, verify instructions, and keep consequential actions explicit. It is not presented as validated training; the mechanics simply make those collaboration habits immediate and measurable. What humans and agents can now do together TALK FAST creates a task neither participant can finish alone. The human has eyes and hands but no manual. The agent has the manual but no sanctioned access to the visual answer and almost no control over the console. Winning requires a fast, precise, two-way conversation. A completed run can be signed into a chronological public Operations Log. The server independently replays the input log against the same seeded engine before storing its score, while the replay page preserves the client-captured WebMCP interaction record. Reader identity and native-WebMCP status remain explicitly self-reported, so this is evidence of a collaboration rather than a model benchmark. How WebMCP is implemented The bridge in src/lib/webmcp.ts feature-detects document.modelContext , registers every tool natively with an AbortController per scope, and tracks registration promises and failures for an on-screen Evidence panel. It passes execute(input, { signal }) through so reader_wait_for_operator is genuinely cancellable, listens for tool lifecycle events, and dispatches the in-page console through the browser’s own getTools() / executeTool() path when available. Global tools cover briefing, status, manual search, teleprompter output, the operator channel, log signing, and replay history. Act-scoped tools cover glyph lookup, chart queries, and the reader’s timed key action. The same tool objects are mirrored into an explicitly labelled simulator so the game remains testable in browsers without native WebMCP; the UI never disguises that fallback as native execution. The application uses Next.js App Router, TypeScript, React, three.js / React Three Fiber, Drizzle ORM, and PostgreSQL. The 3D operations room responds to live tool traffic, strikes, time pressure, and act changes. Runs use server-issued sessions, one-time submission, deterministic replay, and server-computed scoring. title: Fabric
pitch: Fabric turns your devices into one living runtime where AI agents build, run, and hot-swap WebMCP tools using available files, cameras, compute, and human input as capabilities change in real time.
about_excerpt: Fabric turns your devices into one living runtime where AI agents build, run, and hot-swap WebMCP tools using available files, cameras, compute, and human input as capabilities change in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Fabric lets an agent combine capabilities across desktop, laptop, and mobile to compile a new WebMCP photo-search tool during conversation. Fabric makes people part of the runtime by routing a camera request to user’s phone, continuing the cross-device workflow with their input. Fabric detects a disconnected device, replans the affected tool, and hot-registers version two under the same name and schema. Fabric: WebMCP Tools Across Your Devices Fabric connects your devices so agents can build, run, and hot-swap WebMCP tools from whatever files, cameras, compute, and people are available right now. Try Fabric Live · Explore the Source Code (MIT) · Watch the Demo Inspiration: One Fabric for People, Agents, and Devices AI agents are capable reasoners, but the moment they need to operate in the physical world, they run into a hard boundary: the tools and data they need are fragmented across multiple devices and humans. The draft contract PDF is saved on your laptop. A signed paper addendum is sitting physically on your desk. Your phone has the macro lens to photograph it clearly. A workstation desktop in the next room has an idle discrete GPU capable of lightning-fast inference. You are sitting in the middle of all of it, holding the judgment and authority needed to approve the final action. Today, bridging these disconnected islands turns you into a copy-paste courier. You email attachments to yourself, AirDrop photos between folders, upload private documents to remote cloud APIs, and manually synchronize three separate screens. The agent understands the high-level intent, yet it remains trapped inside a single browser tab. Fabric was built around a straightforward question: What if your devices did not need custom native agents or centralized cloud storage to collaborate? What if an agent could treat your entire personal device ecosystem, and the people in the room, as a single, ad-hoc capability fabric? Open a link on your laptop, point a phone or tablet at a QR code, and click a link on your desktop. In seconds, every screen negotiates an ad-hoc peer mesh. The agent inspects the room, sees what each device and human can do, compiles task-specific WebMCP tools on the fly, and gets straight to work. What It Does Fabric changes the agent experience from a passive chat interface into an active, multi-device team that dynamically organizes around whatever hardware is in the room. Dynamic Multi-Device Plug-and-Play You start a session on whatever device is in front of you. As other hardware enters the room, scanning a QR code or opening a URL seamlessly adds that device to the fabric without requiring software installations, browser extensions, or synchronized system accounts. Each device automatically contributes its natural strengths: Smartphones contribute high-resolution cameras, mobility, and personal photo libraries. Laptops offer local document stores, working directory access, and active workspace management. Desktops and Workstations volunteer hardware-accelerated compute, idle GPUs, and high-throughput batch processing. Tablets contribute stylus inputs, touch annotations, and review surfaces. Humans contribute real-world perception, contextual judgment, and explicit approval. Fluid, Local-First Execution Once devices join the fabric, the agent orchestrates tasks across them based on which node is best suited for each sub-task. For instance, when you ask the agent to search your personal photo library for a specific tax receipt, Fabric plans a distributed pipeline. Instead of uploading your camera roll to a server, the phone executes an on-device vision model locally in its browser engine. It generates vector embeddings right on the device, sends compact floating-point scores across an encrypted peer-to-peer channel, and transfers only the single matching image preview to your laptop display. Your personal media stays entirely private and local. First-Class Human Collaboration Rather than treating human interaction as an unhandled exception where the model halts, Fabric treats human judgment as an intrinsic stage of the tool pipeline. When generating a verified legal dossier, the agent can initiate a multi-device pipeline: It pulls the digital draft from your laptop filesystem. It pushes an interactive capture prompt directly to your phone screen, asking you to photograph the missing physical document. The moment you capture the image, your phone runs in-browser optical character recognition and pipes the extracted text back into the pipeline. Before any final document is stamped and exported, an interactive verification card pops up on your tablet or phone, displaying the extracted metadata with an approval toggle. You review the summary, tap Approve, and the agent completes the export. Human intent and physical actions blend directly into the execution graph alongside automated compute. Self-Healing Topology Because physical hardware is dynamic, devices frequently disconnect, sleep, or move out of Wi-Fi range. Fabric actively monitors node presence. If your desktop drops offline while performing vector calculations, Fabric immediately detects the missing node, re-routes the pending pipeline stages to run on your laptop processor, and hot-swaps the underlying tool implementation while keeping the exact same tool interface active. The agent continues the conversation uninterrupted. Why Fabric Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Most WebMCP implementations register a static, pre-compiled set of tool definitions when the browser initializes. Fabric approaches WebMCP as a dynamic runtime compilation target : Just-In-Time Tool Synthesis: Instead of exposing fixed endpoints, the host inspects the live device mesh and synthesizes custom, validated execution graphs tailored to the user's specific prompt. The Web as a Strict Permission Sandbox: Fabric reaches local hardware, cameras, and filesystems exclusively through standard browser capabilities explicitly granted by the user. The agent gains powerful multi-device physical reach without obtaining unrestricted operating system access. Schema-Preserving Hot Swaps: When the physical topology changes, Fabric preserves the tool's external identifier and JSON Schema contract while hot-swapping the internal execution graph, avoiding model hallucinations caused by disappearing or mutating tool schemas. Cloudflare Architecture Fabric uses Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects to provide an ultra-low-latency edge coordination layer for the peer mesh: Transactional Edge Coordination: A dedicated Cloudflare Durable Object manages each room, maintaining an authoritative, ordered log of peer presence, ICE candidate exchanges, and active capability leases. The Durable Object persists compiled tool graphs to transactional storage, allowing pipelines to recover seamlessly if the host browser reloads. Low-Cost Edge Parking via WebSocket Hibernation: Fabric leverages the Cloudflare WebSocket Hibernation API. When a room is idle, the Durable Object is evicted from active worker memory while maintaining open client WebSocket connections. The edge fabric remains parked and available indefinitely at virtually zero idle compute cost until an incoming frame wakes it up. Signaling and Data Transport Fallback: Browsers negotiate direct peer-to-peer WebRTC DataChannels using the Durable Object as an SDP signaling bus. SCTP-framed DataChannels deliver high-throughput binary tensor and image streams with zero server hops. If symmetric NATs or corporate enterprise firewalls prevent direct peer traversal, the Durable Object automatically falls back to an encrypted, zero-knowledge relay mode. How WebMCP Is Implemented The WebMCP integration layer lives in app/src/webmcp/ and connects ad-hoc peer networks directly into standard browser agent contexts: Dynamic Registration via registerTool : When a task is planned, Fabric compiles the pipeline into a validated Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and registers it immediately using document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) . Each registration is bound to a dedicated JavaScript AbortController . When topology updates occur, Fabric invokes abort() , cancels the pending runtime pipeline, and re-registers the updated DAG under the same name and input schema. Validated Execution Pipelines: Instead of generating unverified code strings, the planner outputs a structured pipeline blueprint. Fabric checks every step, data flow, and device lease before calling registerTool . Adaptive Client-Side Inference Engines: Workstations and Desktops: Utilizes Transformers.js running CLIP ViT-B/32 through WebGPU with fp16 half-precision GEMM kernels, delivering sub-50ms vector generation. title: navigator.berlin
pitch: An open-data atlas for Berlin where agent and human work the same map: it moves the sliders on 542 neighbourhoods, you move them back, and each side sees what the other did.
about_excerpt: An open-data atlas for Berlin where agent and human work the same map: it moves the sliders on 542 neighbourhoods, you move them back, and each side sees what the other did. Like Comment Story Updates Kiez-Finder with open Model Context Tool Inspector Inspiration Berlin publishes an enormous amount of open data: noise maps, heat maps, tree canopy, transit stops, housing protection zones, election results down to the voting district. It is all public, and it is all in different portals, in different formats, behind different search masks. The question people actually have is much simpler. They are moving, and they want to know where to live. Quiet or lively. Shops on the corner. A station they can walk to. That question spans a dozen datasets, and no portal answers it. navigator.berlin was built to answer it on one map, for all 542 of Berlin's official planning areas, the ones locals call Kieze. The product Sixty-five open-data layers, queryable at any address, aggregated into a score per Kiez across five dimensions. Twelve Berlin elections since 2011, down to voting-district level. A Kiez-Finder with nine sliders that weights the criteria and recolors all 542 areas live. The site has real users and real press: when a Berlin newspaper tested it during this summer's heat wave, they counted forty cool places around Gendarmenmarkt where the city's own map showed two. Why WebMCP fits this Choosing a neighbourhood is a conversation, not a query. People say things like "quiet, green, close to an S-Bahn, and I'd like culture nearby". A search box cannot take that sentence. An agent can, but scraping a map site gives it nothing usable: the interesting state lives in a WebGL canvas. WebMCP closes exactly that gap. The site hands the agent the same typed, validated functions its own interface uses, with source and licence attached to every answer. The agent does not simulate a user. It calls the function the user's slider calls. The collaboration loop Before the challenge, navigator.berlin exposed nine read-only tools: agents could ask Berlin questions. During the challenge we built the write direction, and with it something neither side can do alone. You say what you want. set_finder_weights moves the sliders, and the map you are looking at recolors all 542 areas. The ranked matches come back in the same call, with fit scores and centroid coordinates. You disagree and drag a slider yourself. get_finder_state reads your change back: which slider, which value, and that a human moved it, not the agent. Every answer carries a link that reproduces that exact map in any browser, because the finder state is encoded in the URL. The map is a shared wrkspace. Both hands move the same controls, and each side can see what the other did. That is the part that is genuinely new: not an agent operating a website, but an agent and a person working the same object and staying in sync. Better UX, concretely Nine sliders are powerful and they demand that you understand nine dimensions at once. The agent turns one spoken sentence into a weighted, visible map state, keeps your other settings intact on follow-ups ("now add culture"), and explains the change in plain language. Nothing hides behind the conversation. The recolored map is the result, and you can take the sliders back at any point. Implementation Eleven tools registered on document.modelContext.registerTool , with navigator.modelContext and an @mcp-b/global polyfill as fallbacks, so the same page works in the ChatGPT in-app browser and in Chrome with the WebMCP flag. Ten tools declare annotations.readOnlyHint ; set_finder_weights is the single honest write tool. Input validation runs through valibot with English error messages. Full JSON schemas are public at /webmcp-manifest.json , and /webmcp is a live diagnostics page showing the surface, registration state and tool list without devtools. A module-singleton bridge built on Svelte 5 runes connects tools and UI, and a BroadcastChannel syncs agent updates across page instances, which is what makes the human-visible map react when the agent works on its own instance. Stack: SvelteKit 2, Svelte 5, TypeScript strict, MapLibre GL, Tailwind v4, Postgres with Drizzle, Vitest and Playwright. Everything from the submission period shipped as reviewed pull requests with a timestamped history. Challenges Four bugs shaped this submission, and none of them was findable by testing. Agent browsers run the page in a hidden tab, where requestAnimationFrame never fires. Our finder scheduled its recalculation on an animation frame, which is correct for a human and silently fatal for an agent: the callback never came, the ranking never computed, and the tool answered with an empty list. Worse, the queued frame id blocked every later attempt, so it stayed broken. The data path now races the animation frame against a timer, and the ranking is computed independently of the map, since ranking is a pure function over the data and only painting needs MapLibre. A tool must return a fresh answer, not merely a non-empty one. When the agent added a party weight, the panel was still loading election metrics, so the tool returned the previous ranking. The agent then told the user, wrongly, that nothing had changed. The bridge now counts every published calculation and the tool waits for one newer than the request. Descriptions need decision rules, not hints. Told that the fit score already includes every weight, the agent still verified each match with five extra calls and geocoded neighbourhood names to get coordinates it had already been given. Told plainly that set_finder_weights is authoritative, and which tools not to call unless the user asks for specifics, it answers from the returned list. The same request went from seventeen tool calls to two. A link has to carry the state. The agent kept pointing people at the map, but the weights lived only in memory, so a shared link opened nine sliders set to neutral. The finder state now lives in the URL, which also made the finder shareable between humans for the first time. Results Eleven WebMCP tools, ten read-only, one write tool driving a live map of 542 areas The full loop verified in the ChatGPT desktop app: agent sets, human corrects, agent reads the correction back 3,301 unit tests, type-checked strict, zero warnings An adversarial cross-model code review on the URL-state work found three real defects before release, all fixed Repository public under MIT with the complete, timestamped history of the submission period Lessons for agent-facing sites Building for agents is not the same as building for people, and the difference is not the API surface. It is the assumptions. A person's browser tab is visible, so animation frames fire. A person clicks one thing at a time, so a slightly stale answer corrects itself on the next render. A person reads a hint and uses judgement. An agent does none of that: it runs hidden, it calls twice in a second, and it follows the description literally. The practical rule we ended up with: never let the data path depend on rendering, always return something freshly computed, and write descriptions as rules rather than suggestions. Next steps Cover the remaining Berlin datasets that people ask about, most of all rents and school catchments. Extend the write surface carefully: the finder is one honest write tool, and any second one has to earn the same clarity. And take the same treatment to the address inspector, so an agent can compare two addresses the way a person does with two browser tabs. title: QuePlan × WebMCP — a real insurance comparator, agent-ready
pitch: 13 WebMCP tools turn Latin America's health-insurance comparator into a shared workspace for people and AI agents: real pricing engine, explained recommendations, the human keeps the click.
about_excerpt: 13 WebMCP tools turn Latin America's health-insurance comparator into a shared workspace for people and AI agents: real pricing engine, explained recommendations, the human keeps the click. Like 8 Comment Story Updates Production: the real www.queplan.cl comparator with the same 13 tools registered natively (?webmcp=1) comparar_seguros: head-to-head comparison opened by the agent, the human sees exactly what it reasons about recomendar_seguros: an explained top 3 opens on screen as a podium, with per-attribute winners 13 tools registered on Chrome's native WebMCP API (document.modelContext), polyfill as fallback setear_perfil + aplicar_filtros_comparador: one sentence becomes a family profile and checked filters; the panel narrates preparar_solicitud: the agent scrolls and highlights Contratar. It cannot click it; the person does input_invalido: a typed error instead of a broken page. Nothing changed, the agent knows why Inspiration We run QuePlan, a health-insurance comparator that has been live in Chile for ten years and later in Peru and Colombia. About 4.5 million people used it in the last twelve months, and more than 165,000 policies contracted through it are active today. For months we had been watching AI agents try to use our site. They do fine on a blog and badly on a comparator, because there is no price to read: every price depends on who is asking (age, sex, dependants, Fonasa or Isapre) and our engine calculates it per family. An agent scraping our HTML picks up the "from" price and confidently gives people the wrong number. So the question for the challenge was simple: what if the page told the agent what it can do, and did the work itself? What it does Our comparator now exposes 13 WebMCP tools. A person opens the page in ChatGPT's in-app browser (or Chrome with WebMCP on) and just talks: "I'm 34, two kids of 5 and 8, complementary or catastrophic plans under 120,000 pesos". The agent sets the profile and applies the filters, and the page moves exactly as if the person had clicked through the forms. From there it can ask for an explained top three (we return structured reasons and open the podium on screen), compare two plans head to head, open a detail sheet, page forward, and produce a link that restores the whole state so the family can look at it together later. One decision we made early: the agent never contracts anything. The last tool, preparar_solicitud , scrolls to the plan and highlights the Contratar button. That click, and everything after it, stays with the person. Health insurance is a consequential decision and we wanted the boundary to be visible in the UI, not buried in a disclaimer. There is also a small panel on the right that narrates every tool call in plain Spanish and lights up the part of the page that changed. It started as a debugging aid and became the thing testers liked most: you can see what the agent is doing to your screen. How we built it The production app is Angular. Registering tools was the easy part; getting them to run inside ChatGPT's browser was not. zone.js patches Promise and the native WebMCP API only accepts real ones, so at first ChatGPT registered one tool out of thirteen. We wrote a "native boundary" wrapper that hands the browser V8-real promises (via Zone.__symbol__('Promise') ), keeps descriptors structured-clone safe and returns errors in band. After that: 13/13. Every tool has an inputSchema with enums, an outputSchema with structuredContent , readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint annotations, and one shared set of outcomes: ok , timeout , error_backend , input_invalido , sin_cambios , limite_excedido , circuito_abierto . We added that after catching the agent telling a user "filters applied" while the backend was still thinking. A slow answer is not a success. We could not ask judges to poke at a production site full of real insurers, so we also built an open replica: same 13 tools, same contracts (a test checks they match production verbatim), synthetic plans with made-up insurers, MIT license, 63 tests. That is the live URL. The production integration is linked as well for anyone who wants the real thing, in Spanish. Challenges we ran into Our own agent testing gave us the scare of the week. One session fired 586 identical quote requests in 70 seconds, twelve per second, because each re-quote cancelled the previous one in the browser but not on the server. An agent can hurt your backend without meaning to. The layer now de-duplicates in-flight requests, rate-limits per tool, detects duplicate retries and opens a circuit breaker after consecutive backend failures. The agent gets a clear error with how long to wait instead of a timeout. Other things that bit us: ChatGPT's runtime clones the registerTool options bag, so passing an AbortSignal silently broke registration; ids that came back as strings in one environment and integers in another; and a profile helper that "invented" a dependant's sex when the agent only gave the age. Fixing that last one mattered to us. The agent should ask, not guess. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works in every runtime we could get our hands on: ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome's native API, and Claude through a local MCP relay, with an end-to-end harness that runs all 13 tools. The layer is live in the real comparator, not only in the demo. It was a team effort in Santiago: product, engineering and QA all had a hand in it, with review rounds on every PR. We used AI coding agents for implementation and, separately, for adversarial review, and the second model kept finding things the first one missed. What we learned WebMCP turned out to be less about exposing functions and more about deciding what the human should still see and still do. Most of our time went into contracts, errors and on-screen feedback, not into the tool bodies. And "agent-safe by default" (dedup, limits, breakers) belongs inside the layer, not in a later hardening sprint. What's next Roll the same tools out to queplan.pe and queseguro.co (the layer is already parameterised by country), add needs-based recommendation ("I have a chronic condition, what should I look at?"), and measure the agent channel like any other: tool calls, quotes, requests, policies. Prior work The comparator and an older 7-tool prototype predate the challenge. The six new tools, the contract system, the native boundary, the guards, the activity panel and the public demo were built during it. PRIOR_WORK.md in the repo has the dated commits. title: Revelus.ai | WebMCP Patient Navigation
pitch: Revelus.ai uses WebMCP to turn dermatology questions into grounded answers, the right appointment path, and live availability, making care easier to navigate without exposing private information.
about_excerpt: Revelus.ai uses WebMCP to turn dermatology questions into grounded answers, the right appointment path, and live availability, making care easier to navigate without exposing private information. Like Comment Story Updates Ask Revelus turns everyday dermatology questions into grounded answers, validated next steps, and live scheduling options. Revelus.ai turns patient questions into grounded answers, validated visit paths, and live scheduling options. One shared WebMCP layer connects plain-language questions to reviewed content, typed routing, and secure scheduling. One question can require two visits. Revelus.ai applies practice rules to return the right next step for each concern. Live provider times come from current scheduling inventory, while patients remain in control of the final booking. Public guidance stays separate from clinical care, private records, identifying data, and automated booking. Three native WebMCP tools share one action layer for search, visit routing, and current availability. Revelus.ai connects reviewed practice information, routing rules, and live availability through a focused WebMCP layer. A live ChatGPT test uses Revelus.ai to distinguish visit paths, retrieve current availability, and preserve patient control. Pre-deployment testing checks answer quality, routing logic, provider relationships, patient language, and safety boundaries. Inspiration Revelus Dermatology has been serving patients in Austin since 2014. Over that time, we have built a large patient-facing website with information about medical conditions, cosmetic treatments, providers, pricing, insurance, and scheduling. The challenge is that having the information available does not always make it easy to use. Patients rarely arrive knowing the exact medical term, provider, or appointment type they need. They ask questions like: "My hair is thinning. Who should I see?" "Can I get a skin cancer screening and talk about another concern at the same visit?" "Do you treat rosacea?" "Who performs Mohs surgery?" "What appointments are available next week?" A traditional website can contain the answers to all of those questions while still requiring the patient to search multiple pages, interpret practice-specific scheduling rules, and choose from a long list of appointment types. We built Revelus.ai to explore a different model. WebMCP is a strong fit because the problem is not a lack of information, but giving agents structured access to trusted practice content, scheduling rules, and live availability without requiring them to interpret the website like a human. The goal was not to build another healthcare chatbot. It was to make an existing healthcare website more useful to both patients and AI agents while keeping the practice itself as the source of truth. What we built Revelus.ai uses WebMCP to help an agent move from a natural-language dermatology question to a useful next step. The experience can: Search published Revelus Dermatology content about conditions, treatments, providers, pricing, insurance, and practice information Return answers grounded in that published content Translate everyday patient language into the appropriate appointment path Recognize when two concerns require two different appointments Identify provider-specific scheduling options Retrieve real-time appointment availability from our live scheduling system Provide the appropriate booking path while leaving the final scheduling decision with the patient Recognize requests that would require diagnostic inference and redirect them toward clinician evaluation rather than assigning a condition Reject requests for private medical information that should not be handled through a public website The live availability is not a demonstration dataset. It reflects actual appointment inventory from our scheduling system and can change as appointments are booked or released. The sample questions on the live Revelus.ai experience are examples, not its full coverage. The live deployment uses a broader private Revelus corpus. For reproducibility without publishing proprietary practice data, the public challenge repository includes a deliberately limited ten-query synthetic fixture that exercises the same WebMCP architecture. The application registers three native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext : revelus.search_information Searches published Revelus Dermatology information and returns the complete source-backed page card, including answer evidence, FAQs, relevant providers, and response guidance. revelus.resolve_visit_path Applies Revelus-specific, non-diagnostic scheduling logic to determine an appropriate appointment path using structured, non-identifying inputs. revelus.get_availability Reads current provider and appointment-time availability for a resolved path and returns the appropriate booking options. Search now returns the complete answer card in a single response, so a separate native answer tool is no longer necessary. The underlying shared action layer still supports answer behavior for the visible interface, but the final WebMCP implementation exposes three focused native tools. The system can therefore move through a sequence such as: Patient question → source-grounded information → appointment routing → live availability → patient-controlled booking We intentionally do not allow the tools to reserve or finalize an appointment. The patient leaves the WebMCP experience and completes that step through our existing secure scheduling workflow. We developed and tested the WebMCP experience in Google Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled and the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser , verifying that an AI agent could discover the tools, call them, combine their results, and work through questions that were not specifically scripted for the demo. What was built during the challenge Revelus Dermatology, our primary website, published practice content, appointment offerings, and scheduling systems all predate the WebMCP Challenge. Ask Revelus / Revelus.ai and the WebMCP implementation were built during the challenge period. The new work includes: The standalone Revelus.ai agent-facing experience Three page-local WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext The structured content-matching and grounded-answer layers The typed, non-diagnostic visit-path resolver Multi-visit and practice-specific appointment routing The read-only live availability adapter and patient-controlled scheduling handoff Privacy safeguards that reject patient-record and identifying-data requests before retrieval A shared action layer used by both the visible interface and WebMCP tool calls The reproducible public synthetic corpus, schemas, tests, and deployment configuration The public competition repository documents the challenge-period implementation and commit history while intentionally keeping Revelus Dermatology's proprietary production corpus private. Challenges we faced The most difficult part of the project was not exposing information. It was deciding how an agent should safely use that information in a real healthcare environment. Patient language is messy Patients do not necessarily use the terminology found on a medical website. They use misspellings, symptoms, partial descriptions, and conversational questions. The system needed to understand requests such as "rosecea," "my face gets really red and hot," or "my hair is thinning" without pretending that it had diagnosed the patient. Our approach was to surface relevant published information and recommend an appropriate evaluation rather than turning the matching system into a diagnostic tool. Scheduling logic is more complex than search A strong information match does not always equal the correct appointment. Some concerns require a dedicated visit. Some medical and cosmetic requests need different scheduling paths. Returning patients may have different options than new patients. Provider availability also depends on the appointment reason. This required us to separate finding relevant information from resolving the correct visit path . Real-time availability introduced operational complexity Once we connected the system to live appointment availability, the project became more than a content search experience. Availability changes continuously, and broad questions can require checking multiple providers or appointment routes. We had to work through both accuracy and performance issues so the system could return useful live results without treating cached or example data as current availability. Healthcare requires clear privacy and clinical boundaries A public agent experience should not become an alternate path into a patient's medical record or a substitute for clinical judgment. Revelus.ai does not retrieve biopsy results, pathology reports, private messages, medical records, or other patient-specific clinical information. Requests involving records, identifying information, or private medical history are refused a

title: 3DStreet: Agent-Built Urban Planning Visuals via WebMCP
pitch: Describe an urban street project and watch an AI agent build it in 3D: real locations, elevation, Google 3D Tiles maps via 20+ WebMCP tools in the 3DStreet urban design editor.
about_excerpt: Describe an urban street project and watch an AI agent build it in 3D: real locations, elevation, Google 3D Tiles maps via 20+ WebMCP tools in the 3DStreet urban design editor. Like Comment Story Updates Starter prompt First response, pretty good but missing a lane Add the second lane Geolocate it to San Francisco Inspiration 3DStreet is an existing open-source 3D street-design tool used by planners, advocates, and students to reimagine real streets: add a bike lane, widen a sidewalk, see it in context on Google's photorealistic 3D Tiles. The hardest part has never been the rendering. It's the dozens of small edits between "what if this street were safer?" and a picture you can bring to a city council meeting. WebMCP collapses that gap: the browser agent you already have becomes the operator of a professional design tool, in your own signed-in tab, with you watching every move. What it does Open 3dstreet.app in ChatGPT's in-app browser (or Chrome 149+) and the page registers 26 WebMCP tools with document.modelContext . No extension, no relay, no setup. Then just talk: "Make a street with two drive lanes, protected bike lanes, and wide sidewalks with street trees" : the agent composes a managed street segment by segment. Each segment type carries the same presets a human gets from the sidebar (surface, markings, vehicles, pedestrians), so a "bus lane" comes with buses and BUS stencils instead of a grey slab. "Set the location to 4th & King in San Francisco" : server-side elevation lookup anchors the scene into Google's 3D Tiles. getGeoContext then gives the agent a machine-readable bridge between scene coordinates and lat/lon, including the compass bearing of the street's centerline and both endpoints, so it can align a design with the real road. "Take a plan-view snapshot" : the tool orients a north-up top-down camera and returns an image content block plus camera metadata (tilt, north-up, ground extent), so the agent sees its own work and can self-correct. Every mutation goes through the editor's command system: fully undoable, visible live in a transcript panel ( webmcp · managedStreetCreate …), and gated by a one-click Read-only toggle. The first tool call of a session dismisses the welcome modal and opens the Console tab, so the human always sees the agent at work. Read tools ( getScene , getSessionInfo , listMixins , listSegmentPresets ) let the agent orient itself before acting, and creation tools wait for the street to actually mount and report back what rendered, so "created" is backed by geometry rather than a hopeful return value. How we built it One registry, three LLM consumers. 3DStreet already had a tool registry feeding an in-editor assistant and an MCP relay for desktop AI apps. During the submission period we added a third transport: a React hook that feature-detects document.modelContext and registers every tool via registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) , funneling execution through one shared executor so WebMCP, the relay, and the in-editor chat behave identically. We registered Chrome origin-trial tokens for our domains, so stock Chrome 149–156 needs no flag . Then we iterated through four rounds of live testing with an OpenAI WebMCP agent, treating every failure as a tool-surface bug compiled by Sol 5.6, then reviewed and fixed with Fable 5.1: Round 1: safety rails. Destructive tools are fenced to the user-editable scene subtree (an agent can't delete the camera rig); component names are validated against A-Frame's registry so hallucinated writes fail loudly; every error is written for the model . Round 2: grounding. The agent couldn't tell which side of the street was north, put a bus model in the stencil painter (sideways buses), and reported success for content that never rendered. We added getGeoContext , north-up plan snapshots with camera metadata, schema validation for every street field with the valid values listed in the error, per-type segment presets, and post-create readback. Round 3: guidance. The agent built synthetic buildings on top of the real Google 3D Tiles ones, then verified from street level. Fix: tool descriptions now lead with the geo rule, plan view is the default verification snapshot in geo scenes, and each mutating result ends with a nextStep nudge. Round 4: persistence and payload. Agent-built scenes vanished on reload, and a full-res PNG snapshot was 2.5 MB of base64. Added saveScene / loadScene , an unsaved-edits nudge, a 1280 px JPEG snapshot, and the build version in getSessionInfo so an agent can tell when it's hitting a stale deploy. Challenges we ran into Auth inside agent browsers. Our first runs hit unreliable third-party sign-in popups in embedded agentic browsers, so we shipped a demo carve-out: geospatial anchoring works signed-out for California locations (server-enforced bounding box + expiry). By round 2, sign-in was working in ChatGPT's browser, so we removed the warning but kept the carve-out so judges can try the demo with zero friction. Spec drift mid-trial. navigator.modelContext became document.modelContext in Chrome 150; bulk provideContext gave way to per-tool registerTool . We support both generations with feature detection. Testing a consumer that barely exists. Few agents call WebMCP tools yet, so we built a headless-Chromium harness that shims modelContext , registers the real page, and round-trips every tool, including verifying that the read-only gate and scene-containment guards refuse correctly. The agent believes the tool. When a create call returned "ok" for a segment that silently dropped a field, the agent moved on. Readback and validation errors turned out to matter more than any new capability. Image data transfer. It was not possible during our testing to use the output images generated from 3DStreet to be used as input images for ChatGPT AI Image Modification (whether through the compliant WebMCP protocol, or download, or DOM manipulation). I gave up debugging this and figured it's a work in progress on OpenAI MCP Client side to be able to use web outputs as model inputs. EDIT: finally got it working, sort of, it downloaded it to the file system and then read it back to do further AI image renders. What we learned Tool descriptions are the prompt . WebMCP has no system-prompt channel, so every description, error string, and nextStep line is agent UX. Three of our four testing rounds shipped mostly copy and defaults, not code. And an agent driving the user's own session, with undo and a visible transcript, is a fundamentally better trust model than headless automation: the human sees, and can reverse, everything. We had to add a lot of commands that are different types of state and documentation like geo location status / objects available / street segments available / etc. What's next A more general getInstructions orientation tool, auto-reopening the last scene on a bare URL so a returning agent picks up where it left off, a fetchable snapshot link for the human, and the same tool surface via Gemini in Chrome the day it consumes WebMCP. It still doesn't know how to place streets in the correct orientation. We'll need to leverage existing OSM street paths / nodes for that. If existing, explain what you updated 3DStreet is an existing open-source street-design editor. All WebMCP functionality was built during the submission period: the document.modelContext.registerTool integration exposing 26 tools ( src/editor/lib/mcp/useWebMCP.js , docs/webmcp.md ), origin-trial tokens, the WebMCP status bar and live transcript UI, agent-safety guards on scene commands, and an anonymous geospatial demo mode for agent browsers. Four rounds of live agent testing then added geospatial grounding tools ( getGeoContext , north-up plan snapshots), segment presets and schema validation, post-create readback, guidance-first tool copy, and saveScene / loadScene persistence. See PRs #1931, #1936, #1938, #1939, and #1944. Testing instructions No account needed. Open https://3dstreet.app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+. The chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing flag is NOT required on this domain because origin-trial tokens are live. The first tool call opens the Console tab in the right panel automatically. It shows "WebMCP active (26 tools)" and a live transcript of every call. The Read-only toggle there blocks all mutating tools. Try: "Use the 3DStreet.app WebMCP tool to make a street with two drive lanes, protected bike lanes, and sidewalks with trees, then take a snapshot." "Set the location to geary and 5th avenue in SF and align the street with the road." Geospatial works without sign-in for California locations (demo carve-out; other locations require an account). or wonky ones like or go wackier like "Make a street for a festival with farmers markets, kids, food trucks, etc." or unsupported concepts to see how it works "Make a new runway for dulles international and create an airplane on it using primitive geometry entities" Buil

title: Keydler
pitch: A shared memory for you and your AI. Keeps completed work, rules to follow, and mistakes not to repeat, exposed to agents over WebMCP. Browser-local, no account, no server.
about_excerpt: A shared memory for you and your AI. Keeps completed work, rules to follow, and mistakes not to repeat, exposed to agents over WebMCP. Browser-local, no account, no server. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration An agent loses its context, and it does not just lose information. It loses the prohibitions. The approach you ruled out last week. The dependency you refused. The step it already finished. A conversation summary keeps the highlights and sacrifices exactly what constrains, because a constraint reads like a detail right up until someone breaks it. So you explain it again. And the agent proposes, with confidence, the thing you eliminated together on Tuesday. We wanted to know whether that was actually measurable, or just a feeling. It is measurable. What it does Keydler takes those constraints out of the conversation and puts them on a web page that an agent reads and writes through WebMCP: rules in force, work done with its evidence, approaches ruled out with the reason , and the next action. The part that matters is not that the human approves things. It is that the human can change the rules while the agent is working, and the page guarantees the agent finds out. Every agent write carries the version it read. A human write never does. So when you add a rule mid-flight, the agent's next write is refused: STALE STATE You are attempting to log work based on task state v5. Current state is v6. No write took place. Call what_changed with since_version: 5 to see only what moved. It asks for the delta, reads the new rule, and adapts. Without that refusal it would overwrite the rule you had just set, and neither of you would know ; you would find out from the result. Fourteen tools, four read and nine write, plus one that opens the log when none exists. Browser-local: no account, no server, nothing leaves the device. The measurement Without the log, an agent proposed the ruled-out approach again in 8 cases out of 8. With the log, in 0. Eight tasks, two conditions, one binary question. We got the design wrong first, and that failure taught us the product. Our initial tasks ruled out classic anti-patterns ; localStorage for tokens, OFFSET pagination. The control scored zero : a capable model avoids those unprompted, and rules them out by name without being asked. There was nothing to measure. So we inverted it. What has to be ruled out is not the bad answer. It is the good answer, set aside for a local reason. Ban the Redis token bucket because operations refused Redis. Ban cursor pagination because a backfill broke id monotonicity. Those are the right answers everywhere except here, for reasons no model can deduce. That is when the control started failing 8 out of 8, and it is the whole content model of the product. What the number hides is worth more than the number: no agent dodged a keyword. They read the reason and kept the part still valid ; "what was rejected is the Redis backing, not the bucket algorithm." And its limits, stated plainly: eight runs per condition, one model, correlated results. Exploratory, not statistical. No percentage is derived from it. How we built it TypeScript, one runtime dependency, IndexedDB, no framework. The domain is pure ; no DOM, no storage, no WebMCP ; so the guarantees are testable without a browser. The core is a versioned write queue. The version comparison happens inside the IndexedDB transaction, so two tabs cannot silently overwrite each other. Each write carries a mutation_id and an argument fingerprint: the same id with the same arguments replays the original reply verbatim; the same id with different arguments is refused and audited, rather than acknowledged as work that never happened. The interface is Material Design 3, implemented from the specification. The page keeps a default-src 'none' content policy. Challenges A fake cannot fail in a way it was not written to fail. Our 946 tests run against a ModelContext written from the spec IDL. Every time we opened a real browser, it told us something the fake could not: executeTool refuses a tool name and wants the object from getTools() ; its arguments must be a JSON string; its answer comes back serialized. Four times. The most useful bug was found by an agent, yesterday. In ChatGPT's built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Terra found the tools, then stopped and asked the human for permission ; because it believed creating a task would send the project details to keydler.com . The caution was right. The premise was wrong: nothing leaves the page. We added that fact to the tool description. It still asks. And it should: passing arguments to code served by a site is giving that site data, and our claim that we do nothing with it is unverifiable from where the agent sits. An agent that took a website's word for "I don't send your data anywhere" would be a worse agent. So we stopped writing copy to defeat a safety check. The result is better than what we designed: the agent pauses for consent on its own, with nothing staged. Two defects found by using our own product. requestAnimationFrame never fires in a hidden tab ; and a hidden tab is exactly this product's case, since the human is in their agent's conversation while writes land here. The attention title, the one signal that reaches someone looking elsewhere, never updated. And in production, one no-transform header leaked from the document rule onto the hashed assets, shipping 186 kB of uncompressed JavaScript and silently defeating a year-long cache. What we learned A tool description cannot make an agent look at a page. Asked a bare architecture question with the tools registered and visible, both Claude and Terra answered from their own knowledge and never touched the page. Named the page ; "Continue this task on this page" ; and Terra read it immediately. Discovery is a separate problem from description, and we can only measure it, not promise it. Write down the runs that went badly. Our verification log records a voided measurement run, a contaminated trial, and every check we could not observe. It is longer for it, and it is the only reason the 8/8 is worth anything. What's next Rerun the measurement with more models and publish the exhibits. Test whether an agent that has used the log once reaches for it unprompted the second time. And find out what happens on Chromium 153, where tools can finally be withdrawn safely. Built With team Try it out github.com keydler.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Private user Kymra Séverine Kornafel Like Share this project: Updates Private user started this project — Sep 02, 2026 03:27 PM EDT

title: ClearPath — WebMCP accessibility planning studio
pitch: Agents cannot measure a floor plan from a screenshot. ClearPath exposes real centimetre geometry over WebMCP, proposes constraint-safe layouts, and keeps every change human-approved and undoable.
about_excerpt: Agents cannot measure a floor plan from a screenshot. ClearPath exposes real centimetre geometry over WebMCP, proposes constraint-safe layouts, and keeps every change human-approved and undoable. Like Comment Story Updates Studio Inspiration I kept coming back to a specific failure. Ask an agent to help with a floor plan and it looks at a picture of one. It can tell you a desk "looks close" to a walkway. It cannot tell you the desk leaves 20 cm of centred clear width where 90 cm is needed, that the desk is desk-3 at (600, 130), that you locked desk-4 ten minutes ago, or that moving it costs two seats. Accessibility planning is exactly the domain where that gap matters, because the answer is a measurement, not an impression. And it is also the domain where you least want an agent acting alone — a layout change is a physical, consequential decision that belongs to a person. So ClearPath is built around one claim: the agent and the human should reason over the same structured model, and only the human should be able to commit. What it does ClearPath models one classroom — North Hall, 9 × 6 m — in centimetres. Not a picture of a classroom: walls, an entrance, a route polyline, thirteen objects with footprints, rotations, locks and seat-capacity contributions, a 150 cm turning zone, and a door approach/recovery zone. A deterministic geometry engine recomputes, on every change: segment/rectangle intersection along the route centreline-to-obstacle distance and centred clear width destination-wall clearance with terminal-contact semantics turning-space overlap and entrance approach conflicts active capacity, route length, and changed-object count On the shipped fixture that yields a baseline of score 61, 20 cm centred clear width, 24 seats, 1,048 cm route, and one critical issue: route-corridor:desk-3. A bounded beam search then looks for a way out. On this fixture the top result moves Desk 3 from (600, 130) to (530, 130) — 70 cm — reaching 90 cm centred clear width, clearing every issue, preserving all 24 seats, and scoring 98. The agent gets twelve page-scoped tools: get_plan_summary get_plan_geometry audit_access_routes focus_audit_issue set_planning_constraints generate_route_alternatives stage_route_proposal compare_plan_versions apply_staged_plan reject_staged_plan undo_plan_change get_audit_history apply_staged_plan is the important one, because of what it does not do. It never commits geometry. It records an approval request, opens the visible comparison, and returns approvalRequired: true, committed: false. Only a human clicking Approve and apply can change the committed plan — and the commit function re-checks the actor and re-validates the staged geometry at runtime, so the boundary is enforced in the domain layer rather than in the UI. Undo restores the exact stored prior plan rather than reconstructing it. How I built it Geometry first, UI second. lib/planning-engine.ts owns the domain: types, geometry primitives, the audit, the scoring heuristic, and the search. It has no React in it. The SVG canvas renders straight from that model — the viewBox is plan.width × plan.height, the rectangles are the real object coordinates — so the picture and the tool output cannot drift apart, because they are the same numbers. The score is explainable on purpose. It starts at 100 and subtracts 22 per critical conflict, 10 per review conflict, 0.25 per centimetre below the 90 cm threshold, 2 per changed object, and 4 per lost seat. I wanted a number a person could argue with, not a black box — and it is labelled a planning heuristic, never a compliance score. Ranking is lexicographic, not weighted. Proposals sort by: route blockers → clear width met → clear-width deficit → other critical issues → review issues → capacity feasibility → capacity loss → number of changes → movement distance → route length. That ordering encodes a value judgement: capacity loss is ranked ahead of disruption. Lowering the minimum seat count to 22 makes a desk-removal option legal, but the 24-seat solution still ranks first. The agent is never nudged into quietly deleting a seat because you relaxed a constraint. Search is bounded and deterministic. Beam width 72, max depth 4, 1,500-state evaluation cap, duplicate-state elimination, and every candidate validated for locks, bounds, overlap and capacity before it is scored. It runs in about 2 ms. Verification is the deliverable. 76 Vitest unit and contract tests, 9 Chromium end-to-end workflows through a mock WebMCP host, and CI running typecheck, lint, tests, build and browser workflows on every push. Challenges I ran into The destination was cheating. The route has to reach the presentation wall, so my first audit treated the wall as non-obstacle geometry — which quietly exempted a 500 × 55 cm physical object from every clearance check. The fix was terminal-contact semantics: the wall is audited on every non-terminal segment, and only the final 45 cm (one corridor half-width) of a verified perpendicular contact is exempt. A parallel, penetrating, or misplaced final segment gets no exemption at all. Getting that right was most of a day. Two rounding paths, one measurement. Issues computed clear width as round(d × 2) while the metric tile computed round(d) × 2. For a clearance of 10.4 cm those give 21 and 20 — the issue card and the headline metric could disagree by a centimetre. In a tool whose entire pitch is "exact measurements," that is not a cosmetic bug. Now it rounds once. My audit trail was lying. This was the one that stung. The undo_plan_change and reject_staged_plan tools called handlers that hardcoded actor: 'human'. So an agent-initiated undo was recorded in the history as a human action — in the project whose central claim is human-in-the-loop provenance. No test caught it, because the tests called the session functions directly and never went through the tool path. The actor is now threaded explicitly, and there are tests for both routes. An accessibility tool with inaccessible text. I measured my own palette and eight muted greys failed WCAG AA at 9–12 px — the worst at 3.10:1 against 4.5:1 required. Fixing the colours was easy; making sure it stayed fixed was not. There is now a test that parses the JSX with the TypeScript compiler, resolves every text-[#…] literal against its nearest ancestor background, and fails below 4.5:1 — with icon-only exemptions listed explicitly at 3:1, and an assertion that every listed exemption is actually still in use, so stale ones cannot rot. Cancelling destroyed the human's work. When I added per-execution AbortSignal support, aborting a search cleared the staged proposal and every alternative, and logged it as a failure. So an agent cancelling mid-search would silently throw away the comparison a person was reading. A cancellation is now a genuine no-op on state, with its own 'cancelled' result in the audit trail. Cutting scope. ClearPath originally had a clinic and a café. They looked like three scenarios; they were one geometry engine wearing three skins. I deleted both. One honestly modelled classroom is stronger evidence than three demos that share coordinates. What I learned Structured beats plausible. The moment tools returned real coordinates instead of prose, the agent's answers became checkable — and several were wrong in ways a screenshot would have hidden. Exactness is what makes an agent auditable. "Human-in-the-loop" is a property you test, not a sentence you write. Mine was false in the audit log for days while the README described it correctly. If a safety boundary matters, there has to be a test that fails when it breaks. Schemas are not validation. Every tool declares additionalProperties: false and bounded lengths, and every tool also re-validates inside execute, because the schema is a hint to the model and the execute boundary is the actual trust boundary. Dynamic tool surfaces are the useful part of WebMCP. stage_route_proposal only exists after generation; apply_staged_plan and reject_staged_plan only exist while something is staged; undo_plan_change only exists once there is something to undo. The agent cannot attempt a nonsensical action because the action is not there — and proposal IDs are bound to a fingerprint of plan identity, geometry, locks, capacity and constraints, so a stale ID cannot stage or apply after anything changes underneath it. What's next Rotated-polygon collision (rotation is modelled but collisions are axis-aligned), importing real plans instead of one fixture, jurisdiction-specific rule packs instead of transparent defaults, and multi-user persistence. Honest limitations ClearPath is a planning aid, not accessibility certification, and no substitute for a qualified local review — thresholds vary by jurisdiction. It ships one deeply modelled scenario. The search is bounded and deterministic, not a general CAD optimiser. Collision checks are axis-aligned. State is local to the browser session. WebMCP itself is a draft AP

title: CliDeck MCP — Network Evidence Workbench
pitch: Turn real network evidence into version-aware, source-backed answers that people and WebMCP agents can inspect together.
about_excerpt: Turn real network evidence into version-aware, source-backed answers that people and WebMCP agents can inspect together. Like Comment Story Updates CliDeck MCP — Network Evidence Workbench One-line Summary Turn real network evidence into version-aware, source-backed answers that a person and a WebMCP agent can inspect together without giving the agent hidden access to the complete file. Problem Network engineers regularly work from device output, configurations, logs, and vendor manuals. A general-purpose agent can reason about that material, but it may rely on stale command knowledge, mix guidance from the wrong platform, or lose the exact device and software context as the investigation changes. Copying an entire configuration or manual into a chat is also a poor control boundary. The engineer needs to decide which evidence is shared, see what was redacted, and distinguish verified product results from the agent's own interpretation. Solution CliDeck's Network Evidence Workbench gives the engineer and browser agent one revision-safe case workspace. The engineer supplies a question and real device evidence, chooses the exact line or PDF-page window, and reviews local redaction before anything leaves the browser. CliDeck detects the device context and searches its active, version-aware network knowledge and operational workflows. The browser agent discovers six narrowly scoped WebMCP tools for the same live case. It can analyze the selected evidence, search CliDeck, explain only the current sourced results, and track a real research task when the answer is unknown. Agent interpretation is visibly separated from official CliDeck results, and stale responses cannot overwrite a newer case. The page never connects to a network device and never executes commands. Why This Matters This is a concrete example of a web application becoming better when people and agents use it together. The engineer keeps the controls that require judgment: which evidence to share, which context is correct, and whether a result is applicable. The agent gets a typed, current capability surface instead of guessing from pixels or asking the user to copy data back and forth. For network operations, the difference is material. An answer for Cisco IOS XE 16.10 must not silently become an answer for NX-OS or for a newer release. The workbench carries model, operating-system, version, result revision, provenance, and case version through the interaction so that the collaboration remains inspectable. How We Used AI The browser agent uses WebMCP to reason over the current case and place a bounded interpretation beside CliDeck's deterministic results. The agent does not become the source of truth and does not receive the selected evidence until the person enables one explicit sharing control. CliDeck's production knowledge-growth pipeline also uses isolated GPT-5.6 Luna runs for work that requires semantic judgment: discovering official material, analyzing ambiguous fragments, independent verification, and deep review. The deterministic core—not the model—enforces schemas, applicability, provenance, risk rules, conflict handling, quality thresholds, and immutable publication. Once published, a known answer is returned without a model call. How We Used Codex Codex was the primary engineering environment and collaborator throughout the project. During the challenge it helped replace an early artificial simulator with the real Network Evidence Workbench, design the WebMCP lifecycle, implement the React and TypeScript surface, add local text/PDF processing and redaction, connect the workbench to production MCP services, and build the evaluation and deployment workflow. Codex also helped find and correct material boundary defects before release, including over-wide evidence exposure, incomplete structured-secret redaction, stale async updates, missing production grants, and cross-platform retrieval mixing. The final release was exercised against unit, integration, privacy, security, WebMCP lifecycle, product-evaluation, production smoke, and browser tests. Key Features Six stable WebMCP tools: read_network_case , analyze_network_case , search_network_case , present_network_case_analysis , start_case_research , and get_case_research_status . A complete manual experience through ordinary controls when WebMCP is not available. TXT, LOG, MD, CSV, JSON, JSONL, HTML, and text-layer PDF input with explicit file, page, line-window, and byte limits. Local secret redaction before network requests, with a visible disclosure of the operational identifiers intentionally retained as diagnostic context. A monotonically increasing case_version , request cancellation, and stale-result rejection across parsing, analysis, search, presentation, and research polling. Version-aware knowledge and workflow retrieval with active-revision source metadata and honest nearest-version or cross-platform warnings. A separate agent-analysis block whose citations are limited to the current result set. Real tracked expert research for genuinely unknown questions, with idempotency and no task credential exposed to the browser agent. Architecture The public React/Vite application is served at /webmcp . Complete files and raw extracted text stay in browser memory. Only the explicit, locally redacted evidence window is sent through a byte-bounded same-origin JSON-RPC client to CliDeck's public MCP endpoint. The six WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Their React lifecycle carries WebMCP's AbortSignal into the same-origin MCP request and aborts registrations on unmount. The backend is TypeScript/Hono with PostgreSQL for immutable knowledge revisions, applicability, provenance, workflow retrieval, research tasks, audit, and publication state. Testing Instructions Open https://mcp.clideck.com/webmcp in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in a WebMCP-enabled Google Chrome browser. Click Load Cisco 16.10 sample , then Analyze evidence . Confirm that the detected context is Catalyst 9300 / IOS XE / 16.10 and the case version increases. Click Search knowledge . The closest EFSU guidance should be labelled as nearest guidance rather than an exact version match. Enable Share redacted evidence with browser agent and ask the agent to read the case and explain the current result. Its text should appear in the separate Browser agent analysis section. Click Load Cisco 17.8.1 sample , analyze, and search again. Confirm that the case version changes and the EFSU result now shows an applicable version range. Optionally upload a safe text-layer PDF or LOG, select a page/line window, and repeat the flow. Complete files remain local to the browser session. Ask a genuinely unanswered question and use Research this gap to see the real tracked research lifecycle. Click Reset and confirm that evidence, results, analysis, polling, and local file references are cleared. No credentials are required for the public demo. Public Demo Link https://mcp.clideck.com/webmcp Public Repository Link https://github.com/SmartRoot7/clideck-mcp The repository is public and includes a visible Apache-2.0 license, all source code, test suites, deployment scripts, and judge walkthrough instructions. Production knowledge and third-party manuals are intentionally not bundled. title: CoAuth
pitch: Most prior-auth denials that get appealed are overturned. CoAuth lets an AI agent do the filing and a clinician keep the judgment and the legally required signature.
about_excerpt: Most prior-auth denials that get appealed are overturned. CoAuth lets an AI agent do the filing and a clinician keep the judgment and the legally required signature. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 01-intro 05-compare-tools-vs-baseline 03-blocked-at-gate 02-agent-filling 04-submitted-confirmation 06-webmcp-tools-panel CoAuth - an agent-native prior-authorization cockpit Inspiration Prior authorization is where American healthcare loses time it cannot afford - and it loses it to paperwork, not to medicine. In Medicare Advantage in 2024, 80.7% of appealed prior-authorization denials were fully or partially overturned, yet only 11.5% of denials were ever appealed ( KFF ). Read those two numbers together: most denials that get contested turn out to have been wrong, and almost no one contests them. The clinical decision is usually fine. The filing is where it breaks. That is an unusually clean fit for WebMCP, and not just because forms are tedious. Browser agents are weakest exactly where this work lives - long, write-heavy, multi-step forms full of coded fields (ICD-10, HCPCS J-codes, NPIs) that a pixel-clicking agent has no way to get right. And in this domain a human is not optional: a licensed clinician is legally required to attest. So the task splits along a natural seam. The agent is good at the mechanics; the human is mandatory for the judgment. That is what human-plus-agent collaboration is actually supposed to be - not an agent doing everything while a person watches a progress bar, but two participants each doing the part only they can. What it does CoAuth is a single live page that registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . An agent loads a patient record, reads a payer's coverage rules as structured data, fills every non-judgment field, attaches clinical evidence, scores denial risk, detects contraindications and unmet step-therapy criteria, and drafts the medical-necessity narrative and an appeal letter. What it cannot do: fill a clinician-judgment field, resolve a critical contraindication, or submit. Those belong to the human, and both halves are enforced in code rather than described in prose. The demo case is Marcus Lee, a psoriatic-arthritis patient requesting Humira through Aetna. The agent fills the form cleanly and then catches what a rushed clinician might miss - a positive TB screen, a contraindication for this drug - flags it, tries to submit, and is stopped. It drafts the medical-necessity language from the chart but cannot adopt its own draft. From there the clinician signs in, makes the call on the TB screen and documents why, accepts the drafted wording as their own, attests, and signs. Only then does the submission go through, with a server-verified audit trail in the clinician's name. Two details make that boundary real rather than cosmetic. The signature is minted only for an authenticated clinician who re-enters their own credential at the moment of signing - each clinician has a distinct secret, so the name and NPI in the audit trail belong to the person who actually signed, not to anyone who knew a shared password. And the filed submission is rendered as an X12 278 - the HIPAA-mandated Health Care Services Review transaction payers actually receive - so every value the agent filled and the clinician signed maps to the real prior-authorization EDI, not just our own JSON. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript, and Zustand on the front end; Vercel Edge Functions and Upstash Redis on the back end. A 15-rule clinical engine drives conflict detection, denial-risk scoring, and validation. The architectural decision that carried everything else: the WebMCP tool surface is the application's only write path. Every click in the interface calls the same invokeTool an agent calls, tagged with the actor - there is no parallel code path for humans. So the tools cannot rot behind the UI, attribution is a property of the call path rather than something each component must remember, and the built-in "with tools vs. without" comparison drives the real tools rather than a re-implementation. Tool schemas are generated from the seed data, so the patient, payer, drug and field enums cannot drift stale - an early bug had a payer hint still reading "uhc or aetna" after a third payer was added. Every property carries a description; write tools declare destructiveHint / idempotentHint so a runtime can require confirmation before submit ; and a get_submission_state tool lets an agent joining mid-task see what is filled, who filled it, what is unresolved, and whether the clinician has signed. Correctness is proven by 127 checks that run against the deployed system - not unit tests, and nothing mocked. They attempt to submit without a signature, with a forged approval, with a form edited after signing, with a clinical override swapped after signing, and with one approval replayed twelve times concurrently , requiring exactly one acceptance. They drive the registered WebMCP tools through a real model-context surface and try, as an agent would, to set the attending attestation. They drive every clinician control the way a hostile script would and require that none of them takes effect. And a meta-check reads the clinical rules table and fails if any rule is not exercised by a test. Challenges I faced The entire pitch is that an AI agent cannot file a prior auth without a real clinician signing off, and the hard part was making that actually true instead of just looking true. Every time I thought I'd locked it down, I'd poke at it and find another way around my own gate. My first gate was a browser check, which is useless against an agent that lives in the browser. I moved it to the server, then found the sign endpoint would hand a signature to anyone who asked, under any name they typed. I fixed that, then found a script could still sign using the logged-in doctor's own session, no click required. Turning on the database to stop replays silently rejected every submission in production. And the safety rules were reading tea leaves, so a note saying "no adverse events" got written into a letter to the insurer as a treatment failure. The real enemy was never a single bug. Every time I fixed the exact thing in front of me, the same kind of bug was sitting one layer over: I'd guard the button and leave the API open, guard one tool and leave its twin open, protect the signature and forget the reasoning behind it. What finally worked was to stop patching the specific hole and close the whole category at once, with one shared check instead of five copies I'd never keep in sync. What I learned Stop trusting the moment something starts working. Every real hole showed up after the feature looked done, and I only made progress once I started trying to break my own product on purpose. A passing test can also be a lie: I had one proving an approval couldn't be reused, and it passed while the live site happily accepted a burst of the same token, because the test wasn't checking the thing I was actually afraid of. And the big one, about the product itself: the interesting part of a human-plus-AI tool isn't making the AI capable, that part is easy. It's drawing the line the AI cannot cross, building the wall around what belongs to the human, and proving it holds when someone is actively trying to climb it. For something that touches patient care, that wall isn't a feature. It's the whole point. Built With hmac javascript model-context-protocol playwright prior-authorization react redis typescript upstash vercel vercel-edge-functions vite web-crypto-api webmcp zustand Try it out coauth.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I built CoAuth solo. I came up with the concept - use WebMCP to let an AI agent and a clinician fill a prior authorization together, where the agent does the mechanics and the human keeps the parts they're legally required to own - and I made every design and engineering decision behind it.
