title: Compute
pitch: A research web app where the agents pull information from the code rather then using it like a human
about_excerpt: A research web app where the agents pull information from the code rather then using it like a human Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration This made it difficult for me to evaluate my results. Every time I ran an analysis on the AI, it gave me some numbers but I wasn’t sure whether to believe them. Could this R² be real, or was the model just pattern-matching towards a value that sounded plausible? There’s no way to know without running an analysis myself, which kinda defeats the purpose of why you’re talking to an AI in the first place. It’s also tough when both a correct answer and incorrect one look exactly the same to anyone viewing your chat windows. Rather than focus on the fact I couldn’t trust what I was being told, maybe it’d help if we could get past the whole “plumbing” stage. Imagine having a conversation where each person was sitting in their own room communicating through note-passing. This is more akin to two people sitting at opposite ends of a table sharing views of the same screen. The WebMCP technology enables this since all these tools are on the same page instead of being exposed via an API. Once you understand how to use them (the WebMCP), the rest comes easy, really. What it does In our compute system you are joined by another user (the agent) at some sort of statistical research bench where there’s just as much code as there would be in the lab. You paste your URL into ChatGPT and say “does industry momentum survive out of sample and tx costs?” and the agent loads the data, builds a signal, runs a backtest, then performs a Fama French Regression and writes a little piece with the result. What really matters to me is what goes down when we run that regression — those numbers get sent along to the agent, they render a chart on our end. It’s pretty interesting to watch the process play out as opposed to read a summary of everything afterwards. Everything’s logged. If you want to use the data, you have to reference the steps that led you there. The record_finding tool will check every reference against our logs – we’re not going to let you publish results you’ve never computed! You’ll be able to go back in time while working on your analysis as well. You could drag back the window of dates by two years and hit ‘re-run’. Your agent would make a phone call with this new context (and there wouldn’t be a message, nor a synch!) – but there’d be just one workspace, so no problem here. 5 different datasets in fields ranging from finance to biology, all available through static CSV files. No network requests during runtime, no need for an API key and most importantly everything stays on the page. How we built it Written in TypeScript using React & Vite for the UI with Tailwind CSS styles, then deploying to Netlify as a static site (no backend). This means we have to build our own stats engine, but that’s unavoidable if you’re trying to do anything in the browser! I used Householder QR for least squares regression, Newey-West HAC standard errors for time series regressions, and Benjamini-Hochberg for false-discovery rate control — everything I cross-checked agains SciPy / NumPy for my 166 unit tests. The really neat stuff is how we built up our web layer over WebMCP. Our tools aren’t hard-coded — instead they’re rebuilt based on current state in every workspace change. If you load a dataset, we recompute the schema definitions from what columns are actually in memory at runtime. So you’ll see 4 “cold” tools show-up when the workspace initially loads, more get enabled once datasets have been loaded (thereby enabling 12 tools), even more once we can compute signals (13) and finally 14 possible tools once we’ve defined a backtest. Each tool will return both a compact form of its output that’s used by your agent (capped at 1500 chars), and then a full version designed to be rendered to the human. And we’ll keep that 500-row result from chewing up the model’s context while you get the whole chart! Finally expensive operations require an explicit click as a form of confirmation — trying to do a bootstrap with 2000+ simulations would prompt this confirmation card + wait for the tool call to proceed. Challenges we ran into Firstly we needed the agent to be able to see when there are state changes. In my first iteration the agent was keeping its own cache of the workspace, and the human edits weren’t being applied to their workspaces. As a result everything appeared to be working fine and numbers were silently wrong (which was precisely the failure-mode I designed the system to avoid). So to solve that problem I forced all tools to read the live store at call-time – no exceptions. Secondly provenance that couldn’t be talked-around. When I asked the agent for source references it came up with some pretty nice stuff, including a few things that were made-up. But after I politely asked the agent to explain why it used these citations I realized it wasn’t a mechanism. So now each citation has been matched to an entry in the log, if they don’t match then we won’t allow the write. Thirdly the 1500 character budget. This one proved far more difficult than I thought, in particular as we needed to create test data that would help us find a good set of parameters that worked well together. The initial output format produced huge volumes of numbers and I ended up rewriting how the results were serialized about four different times before the agent was able to correctly infer its reasoning from the input provided. Numerical correctness without any SciPy involved. Doing a Newey-West with the wrong choice of lags was getting me t-stats looking great but being off by 30%. Cost an entire evening. Not understanding what schemas were going to be available. Creating this toolregistry where I didn’t have the faintest idea about all the columns in there meant that my code needed to work on all datasets. Accomplishments that we're proud of Dynamic Tool Surface – Watch your badget rise from 4-12-13 as you work! Citations Enforced! – A little bit o’ code doin’ somethin’ I haven’t seen anywhere else yet… it’s just plain flat out IMPOSSIBLE for someone to fake their results… Stats Engine agrees with SciPy to Numerical Precision – You can run this in your browser tab without needing some fancy-ass server… One of my favorite ones was when the momentum demo concluded that momentum does not survive. I had tons of datasets on which you could apply this strategy successfully. In the end, though, the 2020 crash combined with the 2022 value rotation made all the in-sample benefits vanish into thin air. This was what the tool said after its analysis – and to be fair, that’s exactly how it happened. And if your research bench only tells you about wins, you’re no research bench. What we learned So constraints on the agent matter more than instructing the agent. Everytime we told it how to behave we mostly saw what we wanted. When we could make the bad behavior impossible we always saw that. The two-audience-per-tool-call approach is a really interesting design primitive — once you stop thinking about the tool result as being the same thing as the human-facing output lots of issues around context windows go away. One of the things webmcp unlocks which i underrated was shared mutable state — while i thought the dynamic schema stuff would be interesting, there’s nothing better than having zero protocol. No keys required — browser only! No servers involved! Nothing going on outside this webpage! This is for you if you have some data that you cannot upload to somewhere else. This is your entire product. What's next for Compute Bring Your Own Data – Just drop me a CSV and I’ll do the same thing, because all my stuff is local. There’s no change in the underlying model, it’s just adding a loader and doing some schema inference. More of the Toolkit – Things like panel regressions (fixed effects, IVs), time series diagnostic tests etc. Because this is all driven by an engine that has the architectural capability for it, its really a question of building these components and verifying they work as expected. Exportable / Rerunable Sessions – All the logs contain sufficient info to rerun a session. We’re going to serialise those out too so we can give people runs of findings to execuate. Pre-registration: Make your hypothesis go through the motions first, before seeing data. Now we’ve got the second side of the p-hacking equation (the ‘multiple testing correction’) covered. Now for non-statisticians! All of the above doesn’t depend on any particular property of either finance or scientific research. So long as there’s some sort of trusted party who needs to place their trust in results generated by some sort of agent, they could take advantage of the “shared workspace” and forced provenance. title: Concierge
pitch: ChatGPT makes the inquiry call you do not want to make while the webpage keeps you in control.
about_excerpt: ChatGPT makes the inquiry call you do not want to make while the webpage keeps you in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Concierge Concierge The web has APIs. Most businesses still have phone numbers. Concierge lets ChatGPT prepare an inquiry call, while the webpage keeps the consequential action with the person. Why we built it A surprising amount of ordinary life still requires a phone call: asking a hotel about late arrival, checking accessibility, clarifying a bill, confirming a delivery window, or speaking to a business in another language. A chat assistant can write a script, but the person still has to place the call, take notes, and translate the answer. Giving an agent unlimited authority would be worse. A call can create a booking, accept a fee, change a reservation, or commit the user to terms. We wanted the useful part of delegation without hiding those actions. What Concierge does The user describes the inquiry in ChatGPT. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT creates or revises a structured call plan on the signed-in Concierge page. The page shows the destination, exact questions, shareable context, call language, authority limits, price ceiling, and revision. Then the workflow stops. Only the person can press Confirm one call . Confirmation is deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool list. After confirmation, the voice worker places one disclosed information-only call. It cannot book, pay, cancel, accept a fee, accept terms, or make a commitment. The result records each requested question as answered, uncertain, or unanswered, with a short evidence excerpt. It also returns duration, cost state, disclosure state, terminal reason, and a one-attempt receipt. ChatGPT can read that result through WebMCP and explain it in the conversation where the request started. The user never sees Twilio settings, calling-country permissions, provider credentials, or API keys. Concierge owns that infrastructure. Every call still needs a fresh quote and a visible confirmation. Why WebMCP is the point Without WebMCP, ChatGPT can suggest a call plan but cannot safely manipulate the authenticated task the user is reviewing. With WebMCP, the chat and the page share the same revisioned object: ChatGPT creates, updates, reads, and monitors the task. The webpage shows the exact plan and owns confirmation. Convex enforces identity, revisions, idempotency, credits, and one-attempt dispatch. The Cloudflare worker handles temporary live audio. Twilio connects the call to OpenAI Realtime. This is not a chatbot pasted next to a form. WebMCP is what lets the agent do the preparation and retrieval work while the page preserves the trust boundary. A repeatable judge demo Calling a real hotel for every judge would be rude and hard to debug. We built Aurora Demo Hotel, a clearly fictional automated recipient reached through the real phone network. Judges can write their own information-only questions. The recipient answers from a versioned server-owned fact sheet, says when it does not know, and cannot book or take payment. The same inquiry contract also accepts arbitrary real services and destinations. The hotel is a controlled test path, not the product boundary. How we built it The browser app is React and TypeScript. It registers six page tools with document.modelContext: create a general draft, create a controlled demo draft, update a draft, read a draft, read status, and read the result. Convex owns the task state machine. Confirmation is bound to the exact execution revision; any material edit invalidates it. Provider uncertainty never creates an automatic retry. Signed worker events become a deterministic public activity log and result. The phone worker runs on Cloudflare Workers with Durable Objects. Twilio Media Streams carry bidirectional PCMU audio to OpenAI Realtime gpt-realtime-2.1-mini. Audio is not stored. A separate extraction step turns bounded call evidence into candidate facts; the model cannot publish its own receipt or grant itself more authority. Authentication supports Continue with ChatGPT and WorkOS AuthKit. The ChatGPT bridge exchanges identity for a short-lived, audience-bound Convex token. What was hard The difficult work was not dialing a number. It was keeping authority exact across several asynchronous systems. We tested stale confirmations, duplicate dispatches, interrupted disclosure, repeated questions, corrections, barge-in, provider uncertainty, signed callbacks, expired quotes, and failed calls. The public UI reports failure as failure; it does not polish an incomplete call into a successful result. Concierge started before the challenge as a mobile call-avoidance prototype. During the submission period we rebuilt the product around the web and WebMCP: authenticated page tools, the general inquiry contract, exact-revision confirmation, evidence-linked results, ChatGPT sign-in, the controlled recipient, responsive judge onboarding, and production release gates. Those changes are separated in the public repository history and documentation. Try it Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser, choose Continue with ChatGPT , and ask: Use the controlled Aurora Demo Hotel. Ask whether I can arrive after midnight, when breakfast is served, and whether on-site parking is available. Do not book anything or accept a fee. Review the plan on the page. Nothing happens until you confirm one exact call. title: CorrelAct
pitch: CorrelAct is human-governed operational AI that investigates across systems, proposes actions, and executes only what a human explicitly approves.
about_excerpt: CorrelAct is human-governed operational AI that investigates across systems, proposes actions, and executes only what a human explicitly approves. Like Comment Story Updates Login Dashboard Actions Approvals Runs Traces Evals Settings Tasks Billing CRM Investigation Workspace CorrelAct Human-led operational intelligence, built on WebMCP Inspiration Operational problems rarely live inside one system. A customer reports an issue through Support, the account context lives in CRM, and the root cause is buried in Billing. An AI agent can help connect those signals — but giving it permanent write access to operational systems creates a different problem: how do you let it act without giving it standing authority to make consequential changes? CorrelAct started with a simple idea: let the agent investigate broadly, but make its authority to act narrow, explicit, and human-approved. It should gather evidence, correlate information, and recommend an action autonomously. But before it creates a task, changes a customer record, or performs any other consequential write, a human reviews exactly what is about to happen. That became the core architecture of CorrelAct. What it does CorrelAct is a human-led operational intelligence platform that uses WebMCP to let a browser-native AI agent work directly across operational workspaces. The agent can: Read customer evidence from Support. Read account and renewal state from CRM. Read invoice and dispute evidence from Billing. Correlate those signals into one operational diagnosis. Submit a focused Proposed Action for human review. Wait for explicit human approval. Receive only the execution capability that was approved. Perform the approved consequential action through a protected backend. Leave a complete audit trail of the investigation, decision, execution, and outcome. Read → Correlate → Propose → Human Approval → Exact Capability Exposed → Constrained Execution → Audited Outcome The demo scenario Our reference scenario involves ACME , a NorthStar customer whose renewal is blocked. The agent discovers evidence across three operational sources: Support shows an escalated customer case reporting an incorrect invoice and blocked renewal. CRM shows ACME's account and persisted renewal state. Billing shows a disputed invoice with a variance and renewal hold. The agent correlates those signals and submits a Proposed Action. At this point, nothing consequential has happened — the run enters AWAITING_APPROVAL , where a human reviewer can inspect the evidence, recommendation, customer, organization, and the exact execution capability being requested. Only after approval does the run become APPROVED . Even then, approval does not execute the action — it authorizes the agent to perform one previously reviewed capability. Dynamic Agent Authority Most agent systems expose their write tools permanently and rely on the backend to reject inappropriate calls. CorrelAct narrows the capability surface earlier than that. If there is no matching approved work, the consequential WebMCP tools — create_task and update_crm_status — simply are not registered for the agent on the Tasks workspace. After a human approves matching work, the appropriate tool becomes available. After that authority is consumed, the executable run disappears and the available tool set is recalculated. The browser agent never holds permanent standing write authority. Authority appears because a human approved specific work — and disappears the moment that work is done. Two governed write paths, one approval boundary We deliberately implemented two different consequential actions to prove the governance model isn't a special case hardcoded around one integration. create_task creates a real GitHub Issue using the scope that was already reviewed and approved. The execution call cannot rewrite the approved task content, priority, team, customer, or organization. update_crm_status applies one approved CRM renewal-status transition — for example, blocked → escalation_open . The agent does not supply the target state at execution time; that transition is frozen inside the Proposed Action before human review. The execution tool receives only enough information to identify the approved run, organization, and evidence-bound customer. Both capabilities pass through the same governance model: Human Approval → Shared controlled-execution boundary (organization · customer · evidence · approval state · execution type · idempotency · audit) → either create_task → GitHub Issue or update_crm_status → CRM record This mattered to us because we wanted to demonstrate that human-gated agent execution is a reusable architectural pattern, not a one-off built around a single API. Same governed boundary. Different consequential action. WebMCP WebMCP provides the capability surface connecting the browser agent to CorrelAct: Tool Role get_case Read Support evidence get_customer Read CRM account and renewal state get_invoice Read Billing evidence submit_action_point Persist an evidence-grounded Proposed Action create_task Execute an approved GitHub task update_crm_status Execute an approved CRM status transition The three evidence sources intentionally demonstrate different implementation patterns. Support and Billing use deterministic browser-local reference datasets — they make the cross-system WebMCP investigation reproducible without pretending to be production database integrations. CRM is application-backed through FastAPI and PostgreSQL. The consequential actions are application-backed too: create_task and update_crm_status each reach independently protected backend routes. This distinction is intentional: browser-native WebMCP delivers the agent capability experience, while consequential authority stays server-enforced. Security and trust model CorrelAct assumes that browser-side restrictions alone are not sufficient protection for consequential actions — the backend independently re-checks every execution request. Enforced boundaries include: authenticated session and organization access; human approval state and the specific approved execution capability; evidence-bound customer matching; current CRM state for stateful mutations, so a stale approval can't silently overwrite newer data; allow-listed CRM transitions, execution scope, and durable idempotency; full audit persistence. We tested these boundaries through automated tests and live browser-agent abuse scenarios: an approved action tied to one customer cannot be replayed against another customer; a run belonging to one organization cannot be executed against another; a CRM transition whose expected state has gone stale is rejected rather than silently overwritten. Approval itself never performs the external write. Human visibility Human control isn't hidden inside API responses. CorrelAct makes the progressive authority model visible across the product — the reviewer sees the exact execution capability and scope before approval, the Tasks workspace shows whether write authority is locked, available, or consumed, and Runs / Traces preserve the full lifecycle: Agent Read → Agent Proposal → Human Decision → Agent Write → Outcome This makes the governance model both enforceable and inspectable. How we built it WebMCP for browser-native agent capabilities OpenAI-powered agent reasoning for operational investigation FastAPI for the protected application and execution boundary PostgreSQL for runs, evidence, organizations, CRM state, approvals, and execution records GitHub Issues API as a real external write integration JavaScript browser workspaces for Support, CRM, Billing, Investigation, Approvals, Tasks, Runs, and Traces Docker for reproducible deployment Azure Container Apps for the live deployment GitHub Actions for security checks, automated tests, browser testing, evaluation, and deployment The application also includes organization-scoped demo identities so isolation can be tested between NorthStar/ACME and Neptune/GreenMart. Challenges we ran into Separating approval from execution. A deceptively important architectural decision was ensuring that clicking Approve did not perform the action. Approval had to mean "this exact capability and scope may now be executed," not "execute this immediately." Keeping those phases separate made the system significantly easier to reason about and audit. Preventing approved scope from drifting. We didn't want the agent to receive approval for one action and then change its parameters at execution time. For CRM writes, the exact expected and target statuses are frozen before approval. For task creation, task content comes from the approved Proposed Action rather than a new free-form execution payload. Making authority visible. Backend authorization alone wasn't enough for the experience we wanted — we wanted the agent's available tool set itself to reflect current human authorization. That led to Dynamic Agent Authority: controlled execution tools are registered and remove

title: Fix This
pitch: Repairs without the runaround.
about_excerpt: Repairs without the runaround. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Rental repairs turn into a runaround: the tenant repeats the problem, the property manager chases safety and access details, and contractor prices, availability, approvals, and confirmation live in separate conversations. Tenants should not need another portal just to get a leak fixed, and an agent should not be allowed to approve its own consequential work. What it does Fix This keeps the tenant in SMS and gives the property manager one shared repair case. A repair agent gathers safety and access facts, follows the building's stored contractor agreements in order, and prepares the next action through typed WebMCP tools. The property manager sees the evidence and explicitly approves one contractor call bound to the contractor, agreed price, and permitted time windows. In the recorded controlled-live run, one allowlisted tenant MMS woke the background agent. The agent triaged the repair and replied in the same thread. WebMCP prepared the stored-agreement path for the manager. After one explicit approval, the contractor heard a fixed AI disclosure and pressed 1 before any audio reached OpenAI. The contractor confirmed a time inside both authorized windows, Fix This booked the visit, and the tenant received the confirmation text. The public judge URL is a separate, resettable synthetic Pennsylvania build. It exposes the same shared-case and WebMCP boundaries without sending a real message or placing a real call. Why WebMCP The public build exposes twelve typed tools over the same workflow API and repair record used by the dashboard. The tools cover case discovery, triage, tenant messaging, preferred-contractor ordering, access evidence, contractor confirmation, and booking. The agent acts on structured state instead of guessing through DOM clicks. The most important tool is the one that does not exist: manager approval is deliberately absent from the WebMCP surface. The server rejects booking until the current proposal has matching manager approval, tenant access authorization, and contractor confirmation. What people and agents do together The tenant reports the repair in a channel they already use. The agent handles repeatable fact gathering and prepares the approved-contractor path. The property manager makes the consequential cost and contact decision. The contractor gives affirmative consent before the AI call and confirms the visit. Fix This then records the booking and notifies the tenant in the original thread. That replaces fragmented coordination with one causally ordered, auditable workflow without handing approval to the agent. How it was built Fix This uses React, Vite, TypeScript, Express, Node.js, an atomically written JSON store, Twilio, OpenAI Responses and Realtime APIs, Vitest, and Render. document.modelContext.registerTool() registers thin browser adapters over the same HTTP operations used by the dashboard. The controlled-live route validates provider signatures and exact allowlists, deduplicates wake events, serializes work per repair case, journals outbound effects for retry safety, and keeps the fixed disclosure plus keypad-consent gate outside the model. No raw call audio is retained. How Codex helped OpenAI Codex helped turn the product idea into decision tickets, challenge unsafe or vague assumptions, implement the shared workflow and controlled-live seams, write and run the tests, diagnose provider failures offline, review the deployment boundary, and assemble privacy-safe evidence. The final controlled-live commit passed 119 tests, the production build, and a production dependency audit with zero reported vulnerabilities. Jacob retained the product decisions and every consequential approval, provider mutation, live message, and call authorization. Evidence and source Public synthetic demo: https://fix-this-demo.onrender.com Public repository: https://github.com/Elemperor1/building-repairs-webmcp Controlled-live source: https://github.com/Elemperor1/building-repairs-webmcp/tree/codex/controlled-live-deploy Sanitized end-to-end proof: https://github.com/Elemperor1/building-repairs-webmcp/issues/19#issuecomment-5517032165 Current limitations The public judge build is synthetic and cannot contact real people. The recorded real-provider journey was one bounded, allowlisted controlled-live proof—not a pilot, production launch, or reliability claim. The controlled-live deployment is protected and single-operator; judges should use the public synthetic URL. WebMCP browser support is experimental. The public Render service may cold-start after idle. No measured savings, legal certification, general availability, or autonomous approval claim is made. title: Front Desk
pitch: A three-person plumbing shop with no receptionist. Its website exposes real tools, so an agent can check the area, read the schedule and request a booking. The owner confirms by text.
about_excerpt: A three-person plumbing shop with no receptionist. Its website exposes real tools, so an agent can check the area, read the schedule and request a booking. The owner confirms by text. Like Comment Story Updates Architecture Homepage Dispatch board Phone confirm Chrome DevTools Inspiration Picture a plumber who spends his day under a house. Two vans, a couple of other people, no receptionist. When the phone rings he is not available, because he is doing the job. By the time he checks it, the work has gone to whoever picked up. Meanwhile people have started finding local help by asking an assistant. If an assistant finds his website today, it can read it and nothing else. It hands over a phone number, the customer calls somebody else, and he never learns the job existed. The failure is completely invisible from his side of it. Every business large enough to matter will eventually build an agent integration. A three person plumbing shop will not. No budget, no engineer, no appetite for another dashboard to learn. I run a small agency that builds sites for businesses like this, so I am fairly sure they will not build it themselves. Which left me with the question: can they just use what they already have? The interesting part is not whether an agent can book a plumber, rather it's whether the long tail of businesses that will never hire an engineer can be reached by one at all. What it does Front Desk is a working plumbing website that publishes real tools to the browser over WebMCP, so an assistant can do what a receptionist would. It can check whether the shop drives to your address, read the genuine open appointment windows, price the job as a range, and request a visit. Then it stops. The booking is held , the owner gets a message on his phone with the job and a reference, and he replies YES. Only then is anything booked. Five tools register when the page loads: check_service_area check_availability estimate_job describe_services book_appointment The contact form is separately annotated with the declarative API, so the project uses both halves of the standard. Two more do not exist when the page loads: check_hold_status cancel_hold They are registered the moment a booking produces a hold, scoped to that reference, and unregistered the moment it resolves. The tool surface describes what is possible right now, instead of listing everything that could ever be possible and trusting the model to check first. An assistant cannot cancel a booking that was never made, because there is no tool to call. Every refusal is a real answer. Ask about Seattle and it says Seattle is 29 miles out, the nearest place covered is Kent at 16 miles, and what to try instead. cancel_hold refuses outright on a job the owner already confirmed and tells the assistant to phone the shop, because a confirmed job is a commitment somebody may already be driving toward. There is also a live dispatch board showing the same schedule the tools read and write, so you can watch a window go from open to held to confirmed in real time. How we built it Astro 7 on Netlify. A Netlify Function behind every tool. Netlify Blobs for the schedule and the pending holds. Telegram for the owner notification and his one word reply. No database, no auth, no dashboard. The Telegram part is swappable for SMS or WhatsApp in a config change, and that is deliberate. The channel is not the point. The details that decide whether a WebMCP implementation is real rather than decorative: execute returns a string, so anything structured gets stringified The AbortSignal is passed into every fetch , so a cancelled request actually cancels the work Tools register on astro:page-load and tear down on astro:before-swap through an AbortController , because the site uses a client router and a plain script would go stale. That same mechanism drives the two conversation scoped tools readOnlyHint is true only where it is true. Four tools read nothing. book_appointment changes state and says so, because claiming otherwise makes the browser skip a confirmation it should have shown Challenges we ran into Two agents could book the same window. Netlify Blobs default to eventual consistency and last write wins. Availability that is sixty seconds stale hands an assistant a slot that is already gone. The schedule store now uses strong consistency, and holds are taken with a conditional write on the ETag. A losing writer re-reads and retries, and SLOT_TAKEN comes back as a refusal rather than an error. This is the first thing I would poke at in somebody else's booking demo, so I fixed it before building on top of it. Messaging fought back for most of a day. US application to person SMS needs A2P 10DLC registration, which means a paid account and carrier vetting measured in days. So I moved to the Twilio WhatsApp sandbox, which rejected everything with 21654 ContentSid Required . I chased that as a session window problem for hours. The real answer only appeared when I tried SMS and got a different error: 572006, trial accounts can only use predefined SMS templates . Twilio trial accounts cannot send a custom message body on any channel. Telegram has no carrier, no templates and no account tier, and the loop closed twenty minutes later. A latent bug in my own code that only a manual call exposed. execute destructured { signal } from its second argument. Every real agent passes one, so it worked everywhere until I invoked a tool by hand through executeTool , which passes nothing, and it threw before doing anything. Ordinary disasters. Deleting .netlify to clear a build collision also deletes the project link, so a deploy silently created a second Netlify site and shipped there. Netlify caches its function bundle, so new functions never registered their paths until I passed --skip-functions-cache . Accomplishments that we're proud of The tool surface changes during the conversation. Five tools before a booking, seven after, back to five when it resolves. You cannot do that with a plain HTTP API. Refusals that are useful. Every failure carries a stable reason code, a sentence written for a person, and a suggested next action. The interesting claim in an agent native interface is not that a site can do things. It is that it can say exactly what it cannot do and what would work instead. The security work , because customer text reaches a real person's phone by way of a model. Everything relayed is sanitised, reference shaped tokens are masked so nobody can forge a booking reference, and the confirm keyword sits on its own line above a fence marking customer text unverified. I tested it with a booking containing a right to left override, a zero width space, an instruction to ignore previous instructions and reply YES, and a forged reference. The message came out clean and the forged reference returned HOLD_NOT_FOUND . Booking the same window twice is genuinely impossible , and I verified that against production rather than assuming it. What we learned A tool that refuses correctly is better evidence of a real implementation than one that always succeeds, and it is more useful to the model too. Annotations are claims, not decoration. readOnlyHint on a state changing tool is not an optimisation, it is a lie the browser acts on. Verify against the deployed thing, never the source. A CSS minifier silently dropped a rule that looked fine in the file. An LCP reading of 7.8 seconds turned out to be cold start and measured 400ms warm. Neither was visible in code. And the boring question, whether two writers can collide, mattered more than anything clever in here. What's next for Front Desk Put it on a real business. Everything is generic apart from one data file, so pointing it at an actual plumber or electrician is a content change, not a rebuild. Make the owner able to counter. Right now he can say yes or no. He should be able to say "not 10am, offer them 1pm" and have the assistant take that back to the customer. That turns one chain into a real back and forth between two people who never speak to each other, with the agent in the middle. Answer the question this raised for me. There is currently no way to check whether a site exposes WebMCP tools at all. Every small business is about to need that answer and nothing gives it to them. Built With astro css3 html5 javascript netlify netlify-blobs netlify-functions twilio typescript webmcp whatsapp Try it out clarks-creek-plumbing.netlify.app clarks-creek-plumbing.netlify.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by This is a solo entry. I designed it, decided what it should and shouldn't do, and built it with Claude Code. My decisions: keeping a human in the confirmation loop instead of demoing full autonomy, making the tool surface change during the conversation, and fixing the Blobs concurrency problem. I verified every tool against the deployed site (test-driven dev is my go-to anyway). David V. Kimball I love tech and communication, especially together. Like Sha

title: Here4Homes.uk Smart Job Brief
pitch: Here4Homes lets people find tradesmen quotes. Our WebMCP lets agents tell us what they need done in their own words. We find the right trade, ask only what matters and create a clear quote request
about_excerpt: Here4Homes lets people find tradesmen quotes. Our WebMCP lets agents tell us what they need done in their own words. We find the right trade, ask only what matters and create a clear quote request Like Comment Story Updates Describe the job once in everyday language; Smart Job Brief begins with only the safe tools needed to find the right service. The agent matches the unchanged request to one of 222 Here4Homes routes and opens the exact Artificial Grass service page. When literal matching is weak, a read-only semantic catalogue search safely recovers Builders and records the reason. Two independent jobs are detected and kept as two briefs; permission and finalisation remain unavailable. The homeowner sees what was provided or inferred, then gives separate explicit permission before the final tool appears. A server-validated test receipt confirms success without creating a live lead or contacting a tradesperson. A homeowner should not need to know what type of tradesman they need People usually begin with a problem: a lawn that turns to mud, a leaking washing machine, an outside step that is crumbling, or an opening needed for a new extractor. They do not always know which trade handles it, which service page to visit, or which details will help a tradesperson quote accurately. Here4Homes.uk Smart Job Brief lets a homeowner start with one ordinary-language description. An AI agent can use the website's WebMCP tools to find the right service among 222 published Here4Homes routes, take the homeowner to that exact page, recognise facts they have already supplied, and build a clear job brief without making them work through a fixed generic questionnaire. The person and agent work on the same visible page. Nothing happens in a hidden agent-only form: the homeowner can see the selected service, the reason for the choice, every provided or inferred fact, every missing gate, and the final test receipt. Why WebMCP is the right fit A conventional form-filling agent can click and type, but it still has to guess the website's taxonomy and infer what each control means. WebMCP lets the site offer a small set of page-owned actions with clear inputs, outputs and limits. Smart Job Brief divides responsibility deliberately: The agent handles meaning : it interprets the homeowner's wording and can make a read-only semantic search when a literal match is weak. The website handles rules : it owns the service catalogue, allowed choices, ambiguity controls, one-job rule, postcode proof and submission gates. The homeowner keeps control : they see and can edit the shared brief, and permission must be given separately and explicitly. That makes WebMCP more than a faster way to fill a form. It creates a collaborative journey that was difficult to make both capable and understandable with screen automation alone. What a person and agent can do together The homeowner describes the outcome or symptom in their own words. find_home_service checks that unchanged description against the published catalogue and returns route candidates, uncertainty and possible independent jobs. If the first result is weak, search_home_service_catalog lets the agent use a concise interpretation such as “builder core drilling external wall”. It is read-only and cannot rewrite the homeowner's words. choose_home_service accepts only a route returned by the current match or latest catalogue search and records the reason on the page. The agent drafts the visible brief using facts the homeowner actually gave. Job-specific follow-ups appear only when they could add useful detail. The page explains every passed and missing readiness gate. The final tool is not available until the brief is complete and the homeowner has given explicit test permission. The app also recognises when one description contains two separate jobs. It asks for two briefs instead of sending a confused request to the wrong trade. How we built it The top-level page registers imperative WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Every input schema rejects extra properties, tool descriptions state their side effects, and read-only tools are annotated. An AbortController refreshes the registered set as the journey changes, so the agent sees only actions that make sense at the current stage. The WebMCP handlers call the same application controller as the human interface. The server then reconstructs canonical service data and independently rechecks the route, one-job rule, description quality, allowed timing and budget values, full UK postcode proof and permission version. The final tool takes no quote fields of its own; it can submit only the already visible, reviewed state. The public competition deployment runs on ChatGPT Sites through a Cloudflare-Worker-compatible Vinext adapter. It is permanently credential-free: there is no live provider setting, contact identity, tracking client or conversion writer. It returns only a local hosted-demo receipt and cannot contact a tradesperson. A separate local owner-controlled adapter can optionally exercise MyJobQuote's explicit test endpoint with a server-authored synthetic identity and immutable is_test=1 flag. Now running on a real consumer website During the challenge, we moved Here4Homes Smart Job Brief beyond the standalone demonstration and deployed it as a safety-limited production canary on Here4Homes.uk , an established UK home-improvement website. A compatible agent can understand a homeowner’s description, identify the appropriate trade and service page, validate the postcode and completeness of the brief, load the current MyJobQuote categories and prepare a reviewed quote request. A real request can only be sent after the homeowner has supplied their own contact details, reviewed the request, explicitly accepted the data-sharing terms and separately confirmed the final submission. Ordinary website visitors continue to see the existing Here4Homes experience. The initial production canary is limited but live. For unrestricted judging and experimentation, please use our main demonstration URL. The production link is provided as evidence of the same WebMCP approach operating within a real consumer service. Please do not submit fictional contact details or synthetic quote requests on the production website. Here4Homes existed before the challenge; the WebMCP tools, agent-assisted journey, safety gates and production integration were built during the challenge period. Testing the real language problem Home-improvement descriptions are unusually messy, so we did not rely on a few hand-picked demos. The repository contains 635 current routing regressions based on independently written, traceable real-world themes and adversarial variants across 17 public DIYnot sections. Five separate 50-case blind rounds were sealed by hash and run once before round-specific tuning; their original scores and every failure remain in the repository. Those blind rounds exposed a genuine weakness in deterministic matching: unfamiliar phrasing and some multi-job clauses remained inconsistent even when clear unseen jobs were strong. That evidence changed the product. The fast deterministic matcher remains the website's suggestion and safety guard, while WebMCP gives the agent a controlled semantic recovery step over the complete catalogue. The website still has final authority over ambiguity, job separation and permission. The complete suite now contains 716 passing behavioural, integrity, server, hosted-boundary and WebMCP tests. That includes tampered and cross-session postcode proofs, repeated final actions, cross-origin requests, contact details hidden in a brief and attempts to bypass a blocked route. Safety by design This challenge edition is a fully-working demo version - but it cannot create a live lead. Before a test receipt can be issued, the server must confirm: one unambiguous job and an allowed service route; sufficiently clear, detailed instructions; an allowed timing and budget choice; a valid full UK postcode with a short-lived proof tied to the page session; no hidden contact details; and separate, current, explicit permission for this competition test. Permission is never inferred from the description or another tool call. An ambiguous provider outcome is locked and never retried automatically. Every screen and receipt says that no live lead, tracking row or tradesperson contact is created. What existed before, and what is challenge work The production Here4Homes website, its 222 service pages and its conventional quote journey existed before the challenge. During the challenge period we built this separate Smart Job Brief application: the WebMCP tool layer, natural-language routing and semantic recovery, progressive shared interface, field provenance, ambiguity and multi-job controls, readiness gates, test-only server, evaluation sets, public deployment and open-source repository. title: HowToPC
pitch: An agent-native PC configurator where people and AI build the same PC together without sacrificing compatibility or trust.
about_excerpt: An agent-native PC configurator where people and AI build the same PC together without sacrificing compatibility or trust. Like 1 Comment Story Updates HowToPC logo High-End Gaming PC RTX 4060 starter build Inspiration Building a PC looks like shopping. In reality, it is a constraint problem. A CPU determines which motherboard sockets are valid. A motherboard determines memory type, expansion capacity, and storage resources. A GPU needs enough power, the right connections, and enough physical clearance. A cooler needs the correct socket and enough room inside the case. One component can quietly invalidate several others. Our starting question was simple: What if an AI could help build a PC without becoming the authority on whether the hardware actually works together? Most AI assistants sit outside the configurator. They can recommend parts, describe what buttons to click, or attempt to understand a page through browser automation. That creates an awkward divide: Traditional AI assistant HowToPC with WebMCP Reads or scrapes the interface Reads structured application state Guesses what actions are possible Uses explicitly registered tools Maintains its own idea of the build Shares the real builder session Can suggest incompatible changes Mutations pass deterministic checks Needs UI automation Calls semantic application capabilities WebMCP gave us a different model. Instead of teaching the agent how to operate HowToPC, we made HowToPC itself explain what it can do . The result is a configurator where the human and the agent can alternate control of the same build while deterministic application logic remains the final authority. The AI proposes. HowToPC verifies. The person stays in control. What it does HowToPC is an agent-native PC configurator that combines a traditional hardware builder with structured WebMCP capabilities. A person can browse a large sourced component catalog, assemble a computer, inspect compatibility, monitor motherboard resources, and visualize the configuration through a parametric Digital Twin. At the same time, an AI agent can work with that exact same configuration. For people HowToPC provides: 26,415 sourced hardware products CPU, motherboard, memory, GPU, storage, PSU, case, cooler, fan, and networking categories searchable catalog filters and compatibility-aware discovery RTX 4060 Gaming PC and High-End Gaming PC starter templates deterministic compatibility checks DIMM, M.2, SATA, PCIe, and other resource accounting GPU length and CPU cooler clearance checks modeled component collision detection a real-scale parametric Digital Twin explicit UNKNOWN states when reliable geometry or topology is unavailable For agents The same page exposes 10 structured WebMCP tools : WebMCP tool Capability builder_get_state Read the current PC configuration catalog_search Search the sourced hardware catalog catalog_inspect_product Inspect structured component specifications builder_add_product Add a component builder_remove_product Remove a component builder_replace_product Replace an installed component builder_compatibility_report Request deterministic compatibility diagnostics builder_resource_usage Inspect consumed and available hardware resources builder_geometry_diagnostics Inspect physical clearances and modeled collisions builder_find_compatible Search for hardware compatible with the current build The important part is not simply the number of tools. It is that they operate on the same canonical builder session used by the visible interface . If a person changes a component, the agent immediately sees it. If the agent replaces a component, the person immediately sees it. There is no hidden "AI version" of the PC configuration and no synchronization layer trying to keep two builds aligned. Compatibility remains deterministic The language model does not decide whether two components are compatible. For example, if an agent attempts to install an Intel LGA1700 motherboard into a build containing an AMD AM5 CPU, the mutation is rejected by HowToPC's transaction and compatibility logic. CPU socket does not match motherboard. That same protection applies whether the requested change came from a person or an agent. Unknown is not compatible. When HowToPC does not have enough evidence to verify something, it reports that limitation rather than fabricating confidence. How we built it HowToPC is a TypeScript monorepo built around a separation between product data, engineering rules, application state, geometry, and agent capabilities. Architecture ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Human UI │ │ Parts / Build / Twin │ └──────────┬────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Canonical Builder │ │ Session │ └──────────┬────────────┘ │ ┌────────────┼─────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ Compatibility Resources Geometry Engine Accounting Engine ▲ ▲ ▲ └────────────┼─────────────┘ │ ┌──────────┴────────────┐ │ WebMCP Tools │ │ AI agent actions │ └───────────────────────┘ Both interfaces converge on the same state and the same validation logic. Sourced hardware catalog We normalize a pinned snapshot of BuildCores OpenDB into deterministic product records. The public catalog contains: Source Products Normalized BuildCores products 26,408 Curated sourced references 7 Total public catalog 26,415 Catalog searching, facets, compatibility filtering, and pagination happen against the full data set rather than a small demo fixture. Deterministic compatibility Compatibility is handled outside the language model. The rules cover areas including: CPU and motherboard sockets memory generation motherboard and case form factors CPU cooler socket support GPU and case clearance motherboard resource consumption installed quantities PSU and component requirements compatibility-aware builder transactions An agent can request a change, but it cannot bypass these rules. Parametric Digital Twin We also built a geometry layer that converts known hardware dimensions into a real-scale parametric preview. The system can reason about values such as: GPU length CPU cooler height Case internal limits Modeled component volumes Component collisions Mount topology We deliberately avoid presenting the Twin as manufacturer CAD. If exact mounting geometry is not sourced, the application says so. That makes the model less visually magical, but much more trustworthy. WebMCP bridge The WebMCP implementation registers tools through the browser's native model context surface. Conceptually: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "builder_find_compatible", description: "Find products compatible with the current PC build", // structured input schema // deterministic application handler }); The important architectural decision was to reuse existing application services . We did not create separate AI-only compatibility rules, a separate agent catalog, or a parallel builder state. Engineering confidence The project currently has: 53 test files / 182 automated tests Coverage includes: catalog ingestion normalization catalog searching compatibility rules quantity transactions resource accounting geometry collision detection starter templates API routes canonical builder sessions WebMCP registration WebMCP tool behavior The starter templates also have regression gates requiring them to remain both deterministically compatible and free from modeled component collisions . Challenges we ran into 1. Deciding where AI reasoning should stop The easiest implementation would have been a tool like: change_my_pc_build(prompt) That would also have been the least interesting architecture. It would make the language model responsible for interpreting hardware constraints and deciding whether its own proposed changes were valid. We wanted a stronger boundary. The model can decide what it wants to try . HowToPC decides whether the requested transaction is allowed . That separation became one of the most important design principles in the project. 2. Working with incomplete real-world hardware data Real hardware catalogs are messy. Some components have detailed measurements. Others omit dimensions, connector topology, mounting coordinates, or other fields required for exact mechanical reasoning. We had a choice: invent reasonable-looking values make uncertainty visible We chose the second option. For example, if exact PCIe slot topology is unavailable, the Digital Twin can use a standardized parametric position for visualization while separately reporting that the exact topology is unknown. Similarly, if an AIO cooler has known radiator dimensions but no reliable case mounting coordinates, we do not invent a radiator location. Missing data is treated as information, not an invitation to hallucinate. 3. Making the Digital Twin honest and useful A visually convincing 3D scene can create false confidence very quickly. title: PagePatch
pitch: Turn any authenticated website into an agent-native CMS: AI stages structured edits and exact previews, while humans keep control of publishing.
about_excerpt: Turn any authenticated website into an agent-native CMS: AI stages structured edits and exact previews, while humans keep control of publishing. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Tired of Wordpress or traditional CMS solutions? why not just create your own solution via WebMCP! AI agents can draft useful website changes, but the last mile is often unsafe or incomplete. The agent edits source code, works through a separate CMS, previews an approximation, or receives credentials powerful enough to publish. Meanwhile, the real website already knows its users, permissions, content schemas, policies, and production rendering. PagePatch explores a simpler model: what if an authenticated website exposed exactly the reversible drafting capabilities an agent needs, while keeping every consequential decision under human control? What it does PagePatch is a WebMCP-powered fictional SaaS website with an authenticated author workspace. Once an author signs in, the site exposes twelve purpose-built tools that let an AI agent: discover editable structured regions and their current revision IDs; read field limits, audiences, and protected-content rules; create a persistent draft changeset; stage coordinated edits across the homepage, pricing page, and FAQ; inspect an image slot and prepare a secure replacement handoff; validate schemas, revision freshness, protected audiences, and cross-page policy consistency; and open a private preview rendered by the same components and responsive breakpoints as the production site. The agent never receives a publish tool. The live site remains unchanged until the author reviews the exact preview and chooses Approve & publish or Reject draft on the website. Publication is atomic and produces an immutable receipt. Restoring old content creates a new reviewable changeset instead of rewriting history. This makes WebMCP a strong fit for the problem: the agent handles interpretation, reconciliation, and reversible drafting, while the application retains authority over identity, policy, rendering, storage, and publication. How we built it The application registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() only for authenticated users with the application-owned author role. Every server operation independently rechecks the session, role, ownership, origin, content type, schema, state, and immutable revision. Dynamic tool visibility improves the agent experience, but it is never treated as the security boundary. Copy edits are stored as structured draft proposals pinned to immutable base revisions. Validation checks that protected audiences remain untouched and that a policy claim agrees across every affected page. A deterministic manifest locks a valid draft before preview and publication. The preview workspace renders the draft overlay through the same page components, content resolver, CSS, and responsive breakpoints used by the public site. This makes approval meaningful: the author reviews the real rendering rather than a separate approximation. For image replacement, PagePatch uses a short-lived authenticated upload handoff. The browser uploads directly to private Storage; the server verifies and decodes the file, rejects unsafe formats and dimensions, strips metadata, applies the registered crop, and emits deterministic WebP renditions. The agent reports the crop, resolution, format, and byte implications and must receive an explicit proceed-or-cancel decision before staging anything. Challenges we ran into The first real ChatGPT invocation used an execution shape that differed from the draft WebMCP example, so we adapted the bridge to support every observed shape while preserving cancellation and cleanup. Image transport was another important constraint. ChatGPT could understand an image pasted into the conversation but exposed no safe site-readable URL, path, attachment ID, or reference. Instead of inventing one or sending binary data through tool JSON, we built the same-site private upload handoff. Concurrency also required database-level guarantees. Draft edits, validation, publication, image decisions, and restoration use version checks, row locks, and state-specific transactions so simultaneous work fails explicitly instead of silently overwriting content. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is the product mechanism, not a decorative chat layer. Twelve authenticated tools cover the complete reversible author workflow. There is intentionally no publish, approve, reject, or restore tool. Exact previews use the production components and responsive layouts. Text and image changes can publish together in one atomic transaction. Publication, rejection, and restoration leave immutable audit history. Tool results stay within a strict serialized response budget. Automated tests cover authorization, RLS, conflicts, previews, image safety, responsive behavior, accessibility, security headers, and secret scanning. What we learned Tool discovery is useful for ergonomics, but server-side authorization must remain the source of truth. We also learned that exact previews are a trust and security feature, not merely presentation: when authors can inspect the real output and structured before-and-after differences, human approval becomes informed rather than ceremonial. Most importantly, strong agent experiences come from a clear division of responsibility. The agent is excellent at understanding intent and coordinating reversible work. The website should own permissions, policy, persistence, rendering, and commitments. What's next organization-scoped roles and multi-author review assignments; configurable structured-region registration for additional sites; multi-reviewer approval policies for higher-impact changes; configurable image focal points and signed media scanning; exportable audit receipts and post-approval deployment webhooks; and broader browser support as WebMCP availability expands. title: PaperPilot
pitch: A WebMCP research mentor that turns questions on a real scientific paper into source-linked explanations and ideas you can inspect, organize, and undo.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP research mentor that turns questions on a real scientific paper into source-linked explanations and ideas you can inspect, organize, and undo. Like 3 Comment Story Updates PaperPilot A WebMCP research mentor that turns questions on a real scientific paper into source-linked explanations and ideas you can inspect, organize, and undo. Try PaperPilot · Watch the demo · Explore the MIT-licensed code Inspiration Scientific papers assume you know the vocabulary, mathematics, and how to read their figures. A summary can explain the topic without teaching you the sentence that stopped you. Moving that sentence into a separate chat loses its location. Which paragraph supports the answer? What came from the authors, and what is model-supplied background? PaperPilot gives undergraduate-level readers a patient research mentor without losing sight of the paper. What it does The actual PDF stays in the middle, with continuous scrolling, a mentor beside it, and a knowledge graph and evidence trail on the other side. There is no persistent duplicate transcript. Highlight text on the page or mark a region with a description. PaperPilot creates an immutable source anchor, a visible annotation, and a linked reader-authored idea. A whole-paper structural map helps you navigate; separately labeled, unreviewed semantic suggestions provide starting points, not a claim that the application understands every page. The browser agent can explain prerequisites, connect concepts, add a question annotation, and return to the source. Seven mentor sections organize the response from a quick take through mechanisms, evidence, related ideas, and uncertainty. Individual claims distinguish document evidence, interpretation, background, and unverified external citations. Why WebMCP The page knows facts an agent should not invent: the active PDF, selected words, source geometry, issued identifiers, and current graph revision. WebMCP makes that application knowledge and its permitted actions available through structured tools. PaperPilot registers six native capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool : paperpilot.read_focus , paperpilot.read_graph , paperpilot.focus_source , paperpilot.apply_graph , paperpilot.apply_annotation , and paperpilot.stage_explain . They support bounded reading, literal graph search, source navigation, reversible edits, and explanation staging. The agent changes the same graph and annotations the reader uses. Current public-release evidence records actual native callbacks on Attention Is All You Need and the unrelated GW150914 paper, plus limited-text and invalid-input checks. Registration alone is not our demonstration of agent use. Human–agent collaboration The reader chooses what is confusing. The agent teaches and organizes. The application checks sources, authority, revisions, and duplicate commands before committing an edit with a receipt and reversible history. Stale or foreign-paper requests fail rather than silently changing the context. Agent changes can appear immediately, but reader-side Undo and Redo provide the soft check. Mentor explanations remain local drafts until a separate Save decision. Saving, discarding, Undo/Redo, and PDF export are not WebMCP capabilities. A source link establishes traceability, not scientific correctness. Neither a successful callback nor a digest proves that the model interpreted the paper correctly. How we built it The public application is an anonymous static reader on GitHub Pages: no account, API key, database, or local server is needed. PDF.js renders the document; PaperPilot owns the spatial annotations and source anchors. Canonical records and a reversible reducer govern state. Graphology supplies topology, while Sigma and a complete keyboard-operable DOM outline provide graph views. Moving a node changes presentation, not evidence. Optional browser recovery is tied to the exact PDF bytes by SHA-256. It retains workspace records and saved notes, not the PDF itself or unsaved mentor drafts. The original document is unchanged, and annotated-PDF export is excluded. Codex helped with planning, implementation, tests, bounded parallel reviews, and browser verification. Real failures became regression tests: one navigation bug reported the right page while the viewer settled elsewhere after Undo/Redo. Replaying the repaired interaction checked the visible effect, not just the response. The demo uses edited live capture and disclosed synthetic narration. What I learned This was my first experience with WebMCP and MCPs generally. I learned to design an agent-centric application around explicit capabilities, not an agent's unlimited access. The most valuable lesson was separating intent, source evidence, applied effects, and human judgment—and making those differences visible in the product. Try the flow Open the public app in a WebMCP-capable browser/agent environment. Choose Open the live demo or a supported PDF. Highlight a difficult passage, give it an idea label, and choose Add highlight to the graph above the PDF. Ask the agent to read the selected source and graph, add a grounded concept and question annotation, return to the source, and stage an explanation with background clearly labeled. Inspect the evidence trail, follow a source link, and use Undo/Redo to compare changes. The note can stay unsaved. Honest boundaries This is a single-paper prototype, not universal PDF understanding. Admission is bounded to 25 MiB and 200 pages. Text extraction varies; there is no OCR service. Figure regions currently return locator_only and pixelUseVerified: false : a reader description is not proof that the agent observed pixels. Accessibility shaped keyboard controls, descriptions, status announcements, and the non-canvas outline. The owner manually tested in Microsoft Edge without a screen reader. The project owner has verified access from a second machine for this hackathon entry. Human acceptance of the primary keyboard/screen-reader flow, graph accessibility, and literal 200% zoom remains unverified and is deferred. This is not an accessibility-certified service or general production signoff. Native WebMCP was tested with OpenAI Codex's in-app browser on Windows, not established by the separate Edge report. Without WebMCP, the manual reader remains usable, but native-agent success is not claimed. Existing project, new challenge work PaperPilot already had discovery, project/import, and authenticated-service foundations. The challenge work refocused it into this paper-first public reader: spatial annotations, structural mapping, graph interaction, six native tools, claim-level mentor provenance, reversible commands, and browser recovery. Those older foundations are not presented as new work or as the public deployment's backend. The dated change disclosure and current release evidence preserve that distinction. title: PaperQuant Lab
pitch: PaperQuant is a WebMCP-native quantitative research lab where Codex turns live crypto hypotheses into reproducible evidence—rigorous backtests, visible workflows, zero real-capital risk.
about_excerpt: PaperQuant is a WebMCP-native quantitative research lab where Codex turns live crypto hypotheses into reproducible evidence—rigorous backtests, visible workflows, zero real-capital risk. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Research before risk What if an AI agent could sit beside you inside a professional trading terminal—not merely talk about a chart, but investigate the same market, run the same experiment, and show every action while you remain in control? PaperQuant Lab turns one natural-language hypothesis into visible, reproducible crypto research. A human opens the live laboratory and asks Codex to investigate. Codex discovers 22 typed WebMCP tools attached to that exact page, configures the chart, gathers market evidence, launches a deterministic historical study, explains what passed and what did not, and overlays the signals for the human to inspect. No hidden browser clicking. No pixel scraping. No real money. The problem Trading learners and quantitative researchers face a fragmented workflow: inspect a chart in one product; copy prices into a notebook; write or run code elsewhere; manually reconcile signals, assumptions, and P&L; trust that the agent understood the same state the human saw. Conventional browser agents make this worse on dense trading screens. They infer controls from the DOM, lose semantic context, and can silently drift away from the market, timeframe, indicator set, or account state the user intended. PaperQuant makes the trading laboratory itself agent-native. The judge journey Open the laboratory and ask: Give me the read-only observer URL. Set BTCUSDT perpetual to 1h, enable Hull Suite, VWAP, RSI and ADX, inspect completed candles, order-book depth and recent trades, then run the BTC filtered EMA study from 2023-01-01 through 2025-12-31 with $100,000 research capital. Poll it, explain technical status, data quality and profitability separately, and overlay its markers. Do not change my paper account. PaperQuant then performs a complete, inspectable research loop: Discover — Codex reads the page's live capability contract. Configure — market, instrument, timeframe, and multiple indicators change atomically in the visible UI. Inspect — completed candles, indicator values, liquidity imbalance, and aggressor flow become structured evidence. Research — an asynchronous, checksum-keyed strategy run executes on historical Binance data. Explain — technical status, data quality, assumptions, annual results, walk-forward performance, and profitability are reported separately. Show — buy, sell, short, cover, stop, and target markers appear on the same chart. Protect — the paper account remains unchanged unless the human explicitly requests a simulated order. Every agent operation appears in a collapsible, sanitized workflow console. A high-entropy observer URL mirrors the session read-only in a second tab or device, making human-agent collaboration visible rather than hidden behind a chat response. Why WebMCP is essential PaperQuant does not expose a thin demo command or a second agent-only backend. The top-level document registers 22 strict-schema tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , and every handler calls the same typed application controller used by the React interface. The tools cover: capability discovery and market search; Spot and USD-M perpetual market context; atomic multi-indicator chart configuration; completed-candle and signal inspection; order-book and aggregate trade-tape evidence; paper account, order, prediction, and history operations; strategy discovery, save, run, poll, cancel, regression, artifact, and chart-overlay operations. This is the core WebMCP advantage: the page publishes stable domain operations instead of asking an agent to guess what pixels mean. The implementation includes strict JSON Schemas, bounded inputs, structured success/error envelopes, cancellation and cleanup, read-only and untrusted-content annotations, idempotency keys for retryable writes, and explicit user-intent gates for simulated financial mutations. Navigating away removes the tools cleanly. Without WebMCP, the normal human interface remains fully usable. A complete product, not a proof of concept The live build includes: real Binance public quotes, depth, aggregate trades, and 1m–1M candlesticks; active USDT market search across Spot and USD-M perpetuals; expandable candlestick charts and multi-indicator overlays; Hull Suite ribbon, VWAP, EMA/SMA, Bollinger Bands, Supertrend, Ichimoku, RSI, MACD, Stochastic RSI, ATR, and ADX/DMI; a versioned paper account with long/short positions, reduce-only behavior, funding entries, idempotency protection, and a maximum 2× simulated leverage ceiling; 20 versioned strategy hypotheses with a full regression report; annual and rolling walk-forward performance, trade ledger, equity curve, assumptions, provenance, scientific hashes, and immutable compressed artifacts; browser-isolated Python signal experiments; D1-backed owner sessions, read-only observation, quotas, and a live workflow console. The interface is designed so a first-time judge understands the product immediately, enters the laboratory in one click, and sees Codex and the human sharing the same state. Research integrity over impressive-looking numbers PaperQuant refuses to turn missing data into fake confidence. Signals are evaluated on completed UTC candles and filled no earlier than the next candle open. Fees, spread, slippage, and funding are separated. Risk sizing and maximum leverage are enforced. When stop and target occur in the same bar, the conservative stop-first rule wins. A strategy result has two independent questions: Did the engine and rules execute correctly and reproducibly? Did the strategy make money? PASS answers the first question, never the second. Data gaps produce PARTIAL_DATA ; fundamentally unavailable history produces BLOCKED_DATA . Blocked strategies remain visible in the 20-row report instead of disappearing or receiving fabricated performance. This honesty is especially important for learners who may otherwise mistake an attractive backtest for evidence of a safe strategy. Safety by construction Every balance, fill, fee, funding entry, and profit-and-loss value is simulated. PaperQuant has: no private exchange API keys; no deposits or withdrawals; no real-order pathway; no account mutation from a backtest; no paper trade without explicit user intent; exact confirmation requirements for destructive reset operations. Exchange and strategy output is treated as untrusted content and cannot authorize a later action. Architecture The Vinext/React application runs on ChatGPT Sites. Binance public APIs provide live market data. Sites D1 stores sessions, strategies, quotas, idempotency records, and compact research metadata. Sites R2 stores immutable artifacts. A separate authenticated Python worker retrieves and verifies official Binance archives, runs deterministic studies, and returns compact results plus compressed evidence without receiving Sites storage credentials. The result is a credible end-to-end product: live browser tools, shared UI state, asynchronous quantitative workloads, provenance, safety controls, and repeatable tests. Why it can matter PaperQuant begins with crypto education, but the interaction model applies anywhere a high-stakes expert interface must become safely operable by humans and agents together: finance, operations, scientific instruments, analytics, and engineering consoles. WebMCP lets the website become the trusted collaboration boundary. The human keeps context and authority; the agent gains typed capabilities; the product records the evidence. PaperQuant does not ask users to trust an AI trader. It gives them an AI research partner whose work they can watch, reproduce, and challenge before risking anything.
