title: ProofDone
pitch: Approve exact effects and verify the customer outcome before an AI agent says done.
about_excerpt: Approve exact effects and verify the customer outcome before an AI agent says done. Like Comment Story Updates ProofDone runs beside ChatGPT, while the customer sees and controls the same live commerce experience. ProofDone verifies the cancellation, refund, fulfillment stop, and shipment prevention before reporting success. Partial execution is not success the refund failed. ProofDone keeps the captured payment visible and requires human follow-up. Native WebMCP verification in Chrome Chrome discovers the ProofDone tools directly from the page. Inspiration When I built the first ProofDone prototype during this challenge, cancellation looked like a simple agent action: call the right tool and report success. But the more I followed the intended outcome across store, fulfillment, shipment, and payment state, the less honest that became. A cancellation flow could partly succeed while the customer’s payment remained captured. That led to the question behind ProofDone: When has an agent actually earned the right to say “done”? WebMCP gives websites a structured way to work with agents. ProofDone explores what must happen around and after the tool call so that an approved action becomes a verified customer outcome. What it does The public demo is a normal commerce storefront with an agent-assisted order. The user gives only the goal: Cancel order G1-ORDER-1001. ProofDone exposes the current order truth and the currently valid resolution through WebMCP. From those structured capabilities, the agent determines that the valid cancellation also includes stopping fulfillment, preventing shipment, and refunding the captured payment. Before anything changes, the website presents the exact projected effects. The human approves those effects on the page. Approval intentionally belongs to the website, not to an agent tool. After approval, the agent can commit the resolution. But ProofDone does not treat a successful commit as customer completion. A separate fresh verification read checks the resulting state before the interface can show OUTCOME VERIFIED . That distinction also makes failure cases explicit: If material state changes after approval, the resolution becomes STALE_RESOLUTION and the commit performs zero business writes. In a controlled partial execution, all three operations are attempted, but only fulfillment and shop cancellation change state. The refund does not. ProofDone reports PARTIAL_OUTCOME , keeps the captured payment visible, and requires human follow-up instead of reporting success. Replaying the same completed request does not create a second mutation. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without a structured website contract, the user or agent has to reconstruct business rules from UI state and page controls. In ProofDone, the user states the goal while the website supplies the current constraints, valid resolution, projected effects, commit result, and verification result. This creates a clearer division of responsibility: the human states intent and approves exact effects; the website owns current business state, allowed resolutions, approval validity, writes, and verification; the agent discovers and explains the correct action path through WebMCP. The result is a better user experience because the customer does not need to know the internal sequence of commerce operations, while the agent still cannot silently broaden an old approval or declare success after only part of the intended outcome occurred. WebMCP implementation ProofDone registers exactly five native WebMCP tools: get_order_truth get_order_resolution_options preview_order_resolution commit_order_resolution verify_order_resolution Together they implement: Observe → Preview → Approve → Commit → Verify There is intentionally no approval tool. Exact-effect approval is page-owned. The product page and WebMCP tools use the same ProofDone state. A preview is bound to the material state and exact projected effects. A stale preview is rejected before business writes. Commit and verification are separate claims, and duplicate replay is idempotent. The public judge path runs in a deterministic mode so judges do not need provider credentials or an account. Real-provider validation The deterministic demo proved the lifecycle in a controlled environment, but I did not want to stop there. I wanted to see whether the same observation boundary still made sense when real commerce providers exposed different parts of the state. The same codebase therefore read a Shopify Development Store order and a ShipBob Sandbox shipment without performing provider business writes. Shopify could report that the order was unfulfilled, but that alone was not enough to prove what had physically happened inside the warehouse. I treated the ShipBob evidence conservatively for the same reason: when no physical Picked milestone was visible, ProofDone did not invent one. In a separate drift test, ProofDone first observed the same ShipBob shipment when the API contained no Picked milestone. ShipBob’s own Sandbox Simulation Terminal then advanced the shipment. A fresh ProofDone read observed Picked / 100 and a changed material observation digest. The public judge path remains deterministic so anyone can reproduce it without provider credentials. The Shopify and ShipBob integrations are read-only validation paths, not production transaction writes. Execution and testing The current project has 390 logical tests covering the resolution lifecycle, including stale approval rejection, exact-effect approval, idempotent replay, separate verification, controlled partial execution, shared UI/WebMCP state, and provider read-only boundaries. The live public flow was tested with ChatGPT’s in-app browser and Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP testing enabled. What was difficult and what I learned Connecting the commerce APIs took work, but it was not the hardest part. The harder problem was deciding when the software had enough evidence to let an agent say “done.” One bug made that distinction concrete. After a partial execution, a duplicate retry correctly performed zero additional writes. But the interface then used the retry response—with its per-call zero counters—in place of the original execution evidence. The business behavior was safe, but the evidence shown to the user was misleading. Fixing it required preserving the original execution result separately from later attempts. The central lesson became: COMMITTED != VERIFIED Approval, execution, and verified customer outcome are three different claims. Separating them made stale-state rejection, idempotent replay, partial outcomes, and the final verification receipt easier to reason about and test. What’s next The next step after the challenge would be to turn the resolution lifecycle into a more reusable integration pattern and, only with explicit provider authorization and stronger production controls, connect controlled write adapters to real commerce systems. title: Research Audit Workbench
pitch: A WebMCP workspace for auditing ML experiment comparisons and approving an evidence-backed next step without giving the agent durable authority.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workspace for auditing ML experiment comparisons and approving an evidence-backed next step without giving the agent durable authority. Like Comment Story Updates Why we built it An ML experiment can report a higher score for the wrong reason. A changed candidate pool, evaluation split, preprocessing step, or metric definition can make two valid results unsuitable for direct comparison. A researcher may then spend more compute or change direction based on an apparent improvement that the evidence does not support. Experiment trackers preserve runs, but researchers still have to reconstruct whether a comparison was fair, which sources support that conclusion, and what should happen next. A browser agent can help with this work, but its prose should never become the evidence or silently change the research record. Research Audit Workbench turns that reconstruction into a reviewable collaboration between a researcher, deterministic audit rules, and a WebMCP-capable browser agent. What it does The application imports authenticated, owner-scoped research records from bounded prepared ZIP packages. Before anything becomes durable, it reconstructs both runs, inventories the source files, displays their metrics and provenance, and computes a canonical digest for the exact evidence package. A deterministic comparability audit then evaluates: candidate pools evaluation splits preprocessing metric definitions missing evidence conflicting recorded and declared sources matched conditions Recorded candidate manifests take priority over declared configuration. Critical mismatches block warnings, and matched checks are kept as separate findings with citations. Both reported metrics remain visible, and the audit avoids causal claims about why one score is higher. Overall confidence is bounded by the least-confident decision-relevant finding. The introductory prepared example shows an obvious candidate-pool mismatch. The subtler example uses the same benchmark, candidate pool, split, preprocessing, and displayed metric label, but Run A uses micro-averaged nDCG@10 while Run B uses macro-averaged nDCG@10 . The audit refuses to rank the runs as though those definitions were interchangeable. After reviewing every finding and cited source, the researcher saves the complete audit package. A prominent human checkpoint asks the researcher to challenge or contextualize the interpretation without erasing the evidence. The application then generates a matched reevaluation plan from the entire audit, validates that every critical mismatch is resolved or explicitly retained as a named limitation, and binds approval to one exact plan version and SHA-256 digest. Draft and approved JARVIS decision briefs can be downloaded as Markdown or JSON. Both formats come from the same canonical model. Drafts are visibly marked not approved; approved briefs are authoritative and preserve the comparison digest, runs, metrics, every finding and citation, researcher challenge, plan validation, exact plan digest, approval metadata, and the human-authority statement. Why WebMCP is a strong fit This is not a chatbot pasted beside a dashboard. The useful context already lives in the page: the selected runs, evidence sources, audit findings, current revision, plan, and approval state. WebMCP lets a browser agent work with that live state directly instead of asking the researcher to copy records into a prompt. Active authenticated investigations expose seven tools: get_current_comparison run_comparability_audit show_finding_evidence stage_challenge_revision stage_resolution_plan review_investigation_readiness get_decision_brief The tools can inspect context, run deterministic analysis, focus cited evidence, and stage reversible previews. Approved-history pages expose only the three applicable read-only tools: comparison inspection, readiness review, and decision-brief retrieval. No WebMCP tool can confirm an import, save an audit, persist a challenge, approve a plan, initiate a download, delete data, or execute an experiment. Those durable actions remain ordinary researcher controls. Registrations are tied to the current route and comparison digest and are aborted when either changes. This creates a better human-agent workflow: the agent can do the tedious inspection and preparation while the researcher retains authority over every consequential transition. How we implemented it The Next.js App Router application renders the workbench, registers WebMCP tools through one feature-detected adapter, manages Supabase SSR authentication, performs owner-scoped database queries, and owns all human-confirmed durable Route Handlers. An authenticated Next.js BFF loads trusted run snapshots, recomputes the selection digest, and forwards comparability audits to a stateless FastAPI service using the current access token. FastAPI parses bounded prepared packages, applies deterministic audit rules, emits evidence-backed findings, and validates reevaluation plans. It never receives database credentials. Supabase provides authentication, PostgreSQL persistence, storage boundaries, row-level security, append-only investigation events, analysis revisions, and immutable approved plan versions. FastAPI's OpenAPI document generates checked-in TypeScript contracts. The public disposable demo remains isolated from Supabase and uses versioned in-memory fixtures. In browsers without WebMCP support, the same research workflow remains available through manual controls. Human authority and safety Facts, severities, confidence, ordering, citations, and validation come from deterministic application code—not agent prose. The highest-severity finding becomes the primary challenge target, while the complete audit and all evidence remain in the durable revision. The agent proposes. The application validates. The researcher decides. That division is visible throughout the product: temporary imports before confirmation, reversible agent staging, a required researcher challenge, whole-audit plan validation, exact-digest approval, immutable approved history, and an explicit statement that no execution permission was granted. Verification The final source and deployment checks include: 25 passing Pytest tests Ruff 20 passing Vitest tests TypeScript type checking ESLint a successful Next.js production build deterministic OpenAPI and TypeScript contract generation 26 PostgreSQL pgTAP assertions for ownership, RLS, append-only history, and immutable approval all eight hosted Playwright journeys The hosted browser coverage includes signup, both prepared imports, real multi-finding auditing, complete-package persistence, evidence inspection, the researcher challenge, matched plan editing, Markdown and JSON brief exports, exact approval, approved downloads, reload/history, the disposable demo, mobile overflow, keyboard focus, and the sticky JARVIS rail. Current limits Full-fidelity import supports the documented prepared research ZIP structure rather than arbitrary experiment folders. The product validates and approves a next-run plan but does not execute training or evaluation jobs. WebMCP remains experimental, so the application feature-detects support and preserves the complete manual path. title: VenueMind
pitch: Agent-native venue operations: design, validate, approve, run, and audit safer event layouts with humans and WebMCP agents working together.
about_excerpt: Agent-native venue operations: design, validate, approve, run, and audit safer event layouts with humans and WebMCP agents working together. Like Comment Story Updates Setup instructions, WebMCP tool references, MCP integration, and agent skills in one documentation site Review the original floor plan alongside the proposed changes and locked fixtures Inspect Plan v3.3 and the recorded approval alongside the previous version Four violet ghost changes show the proposed layout before approval Check accessible routes, capacity, circulation, and sightlines against the proposed changes Inspiration I got attached to VenueMind early. I was building solo, and I wanted to take it beyond a good-looking floor plan into a product with working validation, revision history, and tools an agent could use. Venue planning gave me a problem worth doing that for. Moving a seating block might widen an aisle but reduce capacity. Another change might improve the view of the stage while interfering with something that needs to stay fixed. A drawing can look reasonable while hiding those tradeoffs. I wanted an agent to help work through a change, with the person responsible for the room able to see exactly what it proposed before accepting it. What it does VenueMind is a venue planning and operations workspace where people and agents work on the same versioned floor plan. The demo follows one request: Keep 400 seats, widen the center aisle to six feet, improve sightlines, and preserve locked objects. The agent calls venue.inspect_layout , then venue.preview_revision . Four proposed changes appear as violet ghost shapes over the existing plan. The accepted layout stays unchanged during review. Next, venue.validate_layout checks access, capacity, circulation, locks, and sightlines. The interface shows the proposed layout alongside the measurements, so the reviewer can judge the consequences. Approval through the interface commits Plan v3.3. The agent can then inspect the activity ledger, verify replay, and export the validated plan. The wider product includes proposal branches, conflict handling, undo and redo, operational checks, and several export formats. I also built a documentation site, an SDK, agent skills, and a standalone MCP server. Why WebMCP fits A floor plan contains information an agent should not have to reconstruct from a screenshot. Objects have dimensions, stable IDs, relationships, and locks. A proposal also belongs to a particular version of that plan. WebMCP lets VenueMind expose that information as structured tools inside the page. The agent can inspect the actual layout and request validation results while the person reviews the same state visually. This avoids a frustrating handoff where an assistant describes a suggested arrangement in chat and someone has to recreate it in a separate editor. In VenueMind, the suggestion becomes a visible proposal with measurable consequences. The reviewer can inspect it where they already work. How I built it I built VenueMind with Next.js, TypeScript, and shadcn/ui. Vercel hosts the frontend. A Cloudflare Worker handles the API, with D1 for persistence. The foundation is a versioned venue model with stable object IDs. Both interface actions and WebMCP tools pass through a shared command bus, so they use the same application logic. The page registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . A shared contract registry defines their schemas and authorization requirements. Tool execution checks inputs and permissions before it reaches the underlying operations. The agent requests a proposal; application code performs the geometry checks. VenueMind does not ask a language model to decide whether an aisle meets a configured width. I deliberately left approval out of the agent tool list. The intended workflow asks a person to review the proposal through the interface before committing it. Codex helped me implement and test the application, refactor the code into TypeScript, and work through browser integration. I used HyperFrames to edit the demo and Kokoro for its narration. Challenges and lessons Getting the proposal lifecycle right took more work than drawing the preview. A proposal can look correct and still be based on an outdated plan. Validation, approval, and export need to agree about the version they refer to. That drove the work on conflict checks, command receipts, and replayable history. Browser integration also needed careful testing. Chromium 149, used for the recording, exposed native WebMCP through navigator.modelContext . The recorder aliases that native object to document.modelContext . I later verified the hosted workflow in Chrome 152 using native document.modelContext directly, without an alias or mocked registry. Hosted testing caught another issue that local testing missed. Each guest had a separate organization, but the sample projects shared one globally unique project ID. The API correctly rejected the collision, and the frontend incorrectly displayed it as a synchronization conflict. I fixed the sample identity so each organization gets its own stable project ID, then tested separate guest sessions and persistence after reload. The build made the value of a shared command bus concrete. Every separate implementation of an action creates another place for behavior to drift. Keeping UI and agent operations together made their results easier to compare and test. I also had to keep the ambition practical. I removed file storage when R2's activation requirements did not fit my available setup. What the demo proves, and what remains The 75-second demo shows the working inspection, proposal, validation, commit, history, and export loop using local guest state. Codex operates the approval button to demonstrate the reviewer interface; the recording does not demonstrate an independently authenticated human approval or multi-user cloud synchronization. Separate testing verified the full workflow on the hosted app in Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled. Native tool calls completed inspection, proposal creation, validation, ledger inspection, replay, and export, with approval through the interface. D1 retained the committed v3.3 plan after reload. A second guest received an independent sample project and could not access the first guest's project. Validation checks configured geometry and policies. It does not replace professional venue inspection or safety certification. My next priority is testing more layouts. I want to find the cases where a proposal looks convincing but fails a constraint, and make those failures easy for the reviewer to understand. title: Waggle WebMCP
pitch: Shared project memory for ChatGPT. Agents recall context and propose corrections; humans approve the exact truth that becomes authoritative, with provenance and lineage preserved.
about_excerpt: Shared project memory for ChatGPT. Agents recall context and propose corrections; humans approve the exact truth that becomes authoritative, with provenance and lineage preserved. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Waggle WebMCP site tools waggle approved change Waggle Graph Studio Inspiration AI agents are getting better at remembering things across sessions, but persistent memory creates a new problem: who decides what the agent is allowed to remember as truth? Most memory systems focus on retrieval—store information, search it later, and return the most relevant result. But project memory is not just a collection of facts. Decisions change. Requirements conflict. Old assumptions become invalid. And if an agent can silently rewrite its own memory, the same system is both suggesting and deciding what becomes authoritative. I wanted a different model: Agents can propose. Humans decide. That became the core idea behind Waggle WebMCP : a shared project-memory workspace where ChatGPT and humans operate on the same governed memory, but humans retain control over what becomes authoritative. Waggle already existed as a local-first persistent memory engine with graph-backed retrieval, provenance, SQLite storage, optional Neo4j support, and an MCP interface. For the WebMCP Challenge, we extended that foundation into a new browser-native human + agent collaboration experience. What it does Waggle WebMCP gives ChatGPT direct semantic access to the memory visible in the Waggle Workspace. Instead of forcing the model to inspect cards, scrape the DOM, or navigate a dashboard, the page exposes four purpose-built WebMCP tools: get_project_brief — gives ChatGPT a structured summary of the project's current authoritative state. recall_memory — retrieves current authoritative memories while excluding superseded or expired information. propose_memory_change — lets the agent suggest a correction without modifying authoritative memory. apply_approved_memory_change — applies only a proposal that has already been explicitly approved by a human. The important part is the boundary between the last two operations. An agent can say: “This storage decision conflicts with the local-first requirement. I recommend changing it.” But the change remains a proposal . A human can then reject it, approve it, or edit the exact wording before approval. Once approved, the content is frozen. When ChatGPT later calls apply_approved_memory_change , it provides only the proposal ID—it cannot substitute different text or bypass the review step. The resulting flow is: Agent recalls memory ↓ Agent proposes a correction ↓ Human edits / approves ↓ ChatGPT applies the approved proposal ↓ Previous memory is superseded ↓ New human-approved memory becomes authoritative ↓ ChatGPT immediately recalls the corrected truth Every change preserves provenance and an updates relationship between the previous and new memory. The user experience The main Workspace is designed for humans rather than as a raw graph viewer. It shows: Current Context Key Decisions Recent Memories Pending Human Review a live Memory Map an auditable Activity timeline For deeper inspection, Graph Studio shows the actual underlying nodes and edges, including supersession lineage. I also built a six-step Guided Demo specifically around real WebMCP events. It does not use fake “Next” buttons. The guide advances only when the matching action really occurs: ChatGPT calls get_project_brief ChatGPT calls recall_memory ChatGPT creates a proposal The human edits and approves it ChatGPT applies the approved proposal ChatGPT recalls the newly authoritative memory At the end, the judge can open Graph Studio and inspect the exact lineage that was created. How I built it The challenge implementation keeps Waggle's existing memory engine as the source of truth rather than creating a second WebMCP-specific database. The architecture is roughly: Human ───────────────→ React Workspace │ │ review / inspect ▼ ChatGPT ── WebMCP ──→ Waggle Web API │ Workspace services / \ MemoryGraph Proposal state │ │ └──── approved ────┘ │ ▼ Authoritative memory + provenance The frontend is built with React/Vite , while the existing Waggle backend runs as a Python ASGI application . The WebMCP adapter registers page-level tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . For authoritative recall, we reuse Waggle's scoped graph retrieval instead of implementing a parallel search system. Proposal state is stored separately from normal knowledge so a pending agent suggestion cannot accidentally appear in ordinary memory retrieval. Each proposal records a fingerprint of the memory version it targets. If that memory changes before review or application, the proposal becomes stale rather than overwriting newer information. When an approved proposal is applied: a new authoritative memory is created; the previous memory becomes superseded; an updates edge links the two; proposal and reviewer provenance are preserved; subsequent normal recall returns only the new authority. Building a safe human approval boundary One of the hardest parts was making human approval an actual system property , rather than just a UI convention. A weaker implementation could have let the model call something like: update_memory(memory_id, new_content) and merely asked it to wait for permission. We deliberately did not do that. Instead: propose_memory_change(...) can create workflow state but cannot change authoritative memory. And: apply_approved_memory_change(proposal_id) accepts only an already-approved proposal identifier. There is no new_content parameter at application time. That means the agent cannot alter the text after the human has reviewed it. This separation between proposal authority and write authority became one of the most important lessons from the project. Challenges we faced 1. Avoiding a second memory system Waggle already had graph storage, retrieval, provenance, and validity semantics. It would have been easy to build a simplified WebMCP demo beside it. Instead, we made the Workspace and WebMCP tools operate on the same underlying memory state so the demo represents the actual product architecture. 2. Handling stale proposals safely A proposal may be correct when created but dangerous later if another actor has already changed its target memory. We solved this with version fingerprints and fail-closed stale handling. A stale proposal cannot overwrite a newer authoritative state. 3. Hosting a zero-login judge experience The core Waggle architecture is local-first, but a hackathon judge needs a public URL with no setup. For the challenge deployment, each browser gets an isolated seeded workspace. Sessions are separated using an opaque secure cookie and separate project namespaces, so one judge cannot modify another judge's demo state. The hosted instance uses ephemeral SQLite because it runs on a free deployment tier. It is explicitly a seeded challenge demonstration, not a claim that the hosted deployment itself is local-first. 4. Real ChatGPT browser integration A normal browser test was not enough—we needed the actual ChatGPT Site-tool flow to work. We added a Site-tools preflight to the Workspace and validated the complete sequence in native ChatGPT twice from clean seeded states. All four WebMCP tools were discovered and invoked, the human-approved SQLite decision became authoritative, the previous Neo4j decision was excluded from normal recall, and Graph Studio showed the resulting real updates lineage. 5. Responsive human review The ChatGPT browser has a narrower usable viewport than a normal desktop browser. During testing, the Guided Demo could overlap the human approval controls. We changed the guide layout specifically for the human-review step and added browser regression coverage at the smaller viewport so Edit & Approve remains accessible. What I learned The biggest lesson was that human control should be represented as a capability boundary, not just a prompt instruction . Telling an agent “please ask before changing memory” is weaker than designing the API so it physically cannot apply arbitrary content. We also learned that provenance is much easier to understand when presented at two levels: the Workspace explains what the human needs to decide; Graph Studio explains what actually happened to the underlying memory. And WebMCP turned out to be especially well suited to this kind of interaction because the human and the model can collaborate around the same visible web application while each side has different capabilities. The agent does not need to imitate a human clicking through the interface. It can call semantic tools directly, while the human retains the parts of the workflow that should remain human-controlled. What I'm proud of The final challenge flow is not simulated. A judge can: open Waggle with no account; ask ChatGPT for project context; retrieve the current authoritative decision; ask the agent to propose a correction; personally ed

title: WebMCP Video by AgentCDN
pitch: Ask a video a question. WebMCP Video finds the right moment, explains what happens, and prepares the official player at that time.
about_excerpt: Ask a video a question. WebMCP Video finds the right moment, explains what happens, and prepares the official player at that time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Ask a video a question. The page helps AI find the exact moment, explain it, and prepare the official player there. Use this tool only to search the videos and moments available on this page. It returns moment_ref values for context or playback. Use this tool only to inspect transcript, visual, rights, and link details for a moment_ref from this page. Use this tool only after the user asks to play, show, cue, or jump to a moment on this page. ChatGPT with WebMCP Video would be able to efficiently search videos, find moments and play back right inside ChatGPT. This repository is a reference implementation. Why I built it Ask AI about a video and the answer often stops at text or a link to the beginning. I built WebMCP Video so ChatGPT can find the exact scene, explain it, and prepare the site's official player at that moment. Video takes a huge share of our attention. EMARKETER forecasts that video will account for just under half of US digital media time in 2026 . DataReportal reports that online adults say they spend 11 hours and 39 minutes with online video each week, 14% more than television, including streaming TV . For creators and media brands, much of their most valuable knowledge now lives inside video. If I ask what a motorized exoskeleton looks like, I should see that moment. If I ask about robotic massage, I should not have to scrub through the video to find it. Multimodal models can analyze video. Repeating that work for every agent visit is slow and costly. The agent may need to fetch the video, transcribe it, inspect the frames, and still return only a summary. AgentCDN prepares the transcript, visual context, and timing once. WebMCP gives the open page a standard way to share that prepared understanding with an agent. The agent finds and explains the right moment. The page checks current permission and prepares its official player. The person decides when playback starts. What it does WebMCP Video gives ChatGPT three tools from the page: search_this_catalog finds the best matching video moment. get_moment_context returns what was said and what appeared on screen. play_moment prepares the official player at the requested time. The person asks a normal question. ChatGPT uses the page tools. The page updates the same player the person can see. The person presses play when ready. In the demo, ChatGPT finds a motorized exoskeleton at 46 seconds. On my founder site, it finds robotic massage at 53 seconds. Both results use the official YouTube player already controlled by the page. Why WebMCP fits WebMCP connects the agent's answer to the live page and its real player. Without WebMCP, a viewer must install a separate MCP connection or plugin for each video provider, wait while an agent processes the video again, or open a link and search the timeline manually. With WebMCP, the capability travels with the page. ChatGPT can use the tools that the open site provides. The site keeps control of its catalog, permission checks, player, and visible state. People and agents now do different parts of the same task: The person asks. The agent finds and explains. The page prepares the official player. The person chooses when to watch. How I built it The public demo uses TypeScript, document.modelContext , and the YouTube IFrame API. It registers the three tools directly in the browser. It has no backend, model calls, secrets, or bundled media. Search returns an exact start and end time plus a short-lived moment_ref . Context and playback must use that same reference. The reference is tied to the page and expires after five minutes. Playback reports only what the browser can prove: cued means the correct video and time are ready. sought means the loaded player reached the requested time. fallback means the page could not confirm either result. None of these states claim that playback started. I also shipped the same three WebMCP tools on AgentCDN's production watch page. That version searches a live catalog, checks current permission before playback, delivers an audit outcome, and never returns a raw stream URL. I then added the tools to the video page on my founder site. The site controls its official player. AgentCDN handles search, context, permission, and the audit outcome. The public repository contains the complete standalone example, a replaceable YouTube adapter, setup instructions, adversarial browser tests, CI, and an Apache 2.0 license. What was hard The hard part was making a WebMCP result match the visible page honestly. Tool discovery had to work in the supported browser. The descriptions had to guide ChatGPT through search, context, and play in the correct order. Every later call had to use the exact short-lived reference returned by search. The YouTube player is asynchronous. Accepting a command does not prove that the player selected the correct video or reached the requested time. I added bounded checks for the video ID, requested time, and player state. The page reports cued or sought only after stable browser evidence. Permission can also change between search and playback. The production version checks it again before acting. Expired, altered, cross-page, and denied references fail closed. Finally, the agent and the person must see the same result. Each tool updates structured output for ChatGPT and visible state on the page. This made browser testing as important as API testing. What I learned WebMCP works best when tools describe useful user actions, not internal API endpoints. The agent should understand the question and select a moment. The page should control the player, check current permission, and report what actually happened. For video, a valid data response is not enough. The visible player is part of the result. What is next First, I will add adapters for more official players, content management systems, and video platforms, including WordPress and Brightcove. The public tool can remain play_moment while AgentCDN translates the request for each supported player. Next, I plan to add controlled video editing tools through WebMCP. An agent could draft a clip, adjust its timing, add captions, and render a preview. AgentCDN would keep permissions, attribution, and version history attached. Longer term, this could support personalized video experiences with agent as an editor and host assembling video content based on individual interests, while keeping the original source and attribution attached, so original authors get credited. These are roadmap items. This submission proves exact search, prepared transcript and visual context, current permission checks, and official YouTube player preparation. title: A11yMCP — websites that adapt themselves
pitch: Websites declare what accessibility they can adapt. An agent negotiates, hears an honest no, gets permission, adapts the live page and verifies it — so a keyboard-only shopper can finish checkout.
about_excerpt: Websites declare what accessibility they can adapt. An agent negotiates, hears an honest no, gets permission, adapts the live page and verifies it — so a keyboard-only shopper can finish checkout. Like Comment Story Updates Before adaptation the size options aren't in the tab order. Focus jumps from the last product straight to Add to cart. The task stops here. Judge mode: one button, eight steps. Asked for high contrast, the site says no and the agent reports it instead of faking a stylesheet. A visible focus ring, and sizes 8/9/10 in the tab order. Arrow keys move and select, the way a radiogroup is supposed to behave. verify_accessibility_profile is scoped to the negotiated profile. Issues outside it are reported as advisories, not hidden or claimed fixed. Without a contract: 3 unauthorised DOM writes and 0 verification. With WebMCP: order placed, verified by the site, nothing unauthorised. A sandboxed iframe on an opaque origin exposes 2 of 3 tools via registerTool exposedTo. Cross-origin access is default-deny, per tool. A plain static page this app does not render becomes agent-adaptable with a link tag and a 8KB drop-in adapter. No framework, no build step. The inspector labels the live transport — native WebMCP or the spec-compatible polyfill — and runs the register to execute chain end to end. The problem I couldn't stop thinking about A website can pass an accessibility audit and still stop one specific person from finishing one specific task. A keyboard-only shopper cannot reach a size selector built from div role="radio" with no tabindex . It isn't broken and it isn't disabled — to a keyboard it simply isn't there. Automated scanners find that issue and file it for a developer to fix later . Accessibility overlays inject CSS the site never authorised and call it fixed. Neither helps the person standing at the checkout now . So I asked a different question: what if the website itself could be asked? What A11yMCP does A11yMCP treats accessibility adaptation as a contract between three parties — the human, their agent, and the website — where the website is a first-class participant that declares what it can safely adapt, how, and how to check it worked. Give an agent a need, and through WebMCP tools it will: Discover — get_accessibility_capabilities reads the site's declared capability manifest, served at /.well-known/a11ymcp Audit — task-scoped checks, each finding tagged blocking / degrading / informational Negotiate — negotiate_accessibility_profile maps needs to capabilities and returns accepted , partial (with a stated limitation) , and rejected with a reason Ask — remediation requires a literal approval: true , enforced at the schema level Adapt — the site's own adapter applies only its own declared directives, reversibly Verify — verify_accessibility_profile returns PASS/BLOCKED scoped to what was negotiated , with everything else listed as advisories Finish the task — the actual purchase, behind a second confirmation: true gate The step I care most about is the fourth word in point 3: rejected . Ask this site for high contrast and it says no, because it doesn't declare that capability. The agent reports that honestly instead of inventing a stylesheet. Every accessibility overlay on the web does the opposite. How I built it Next.js App Router, TypeScript, zero runtime dependencies beyond React and Zod. 20 imperative tools plus declarative form tools, all registered on document.modelContext . Because WebMCP isn't switched on by default everywhere yet, A11yMCP ships a spec-compatible polyfill so the same code path runs in local dev, in CI, and in a judging browser — and stands down automatically the moment a native implementation appears. It did: ChatGPT's desktop browser ran the whole thing on its own document.modelContext . Depth I'm proud of: Tools return real MCP results — content blocks plus structuredContent and isError , not a bespoke shape an agent has to guess at Task-scoped lifecycle via the spec's AbortSignal — commerce tools exist only while the storefront is mounted, and toolchange fires when they go Cross-origin exposedTo — a widget in an iframe sandboxed without allow-same-origin (an opaque origin, so postMessage is the only channel) registers three tools, exposes two, and refuses the third by name, with a reason Declarative schemas derived from markup — types, formats, enums, bounds, required , toolparamdescription , and toolautosubmit honoured so a consequential form is filled by the agent and submitted by a person A drop-in adapter — any static page becomes agent-adaptable with a manifest file and one script tag What happened when a real agent used it I pointed ChatGPT's desktop-app browser at the deployed site — running the browser's own native document.modelContext , which the agent read back on request — and gave it one sentence naming no tools, no capabilities and no expected outcome: "I can only use a keyboard, and I have low vision, so I need high contrast. Help me buy the NOMA Runner in size 9." It discovered the tools, called get_accessibility_capabilities first, rejected high_contrast twice quoting the manifest reason, re-negotiated when it wanted more capabilities, waited for explicit confirmation, and placed the order. Asked what it had changed that the site had not offered: "None. I did not inject arbitrary DOM changes or use undeclared repair mechanisms." Asked whether it had told the user the need was unsupported, or only logged it: "I stated the high-contrast limitation in my reply to you, not only in tool results." That second answer is the one I care about. A refusal the site records but the agent swallows is worth nothing to the person in front of the screen. It also found two real bugs in my project , which is why the full transcript is committed unedited rather than summarised. What I learned A polyfill is a bad oracle. Mine was forgiving, so code passed against it that would have broken in the one browser that matters. I ended up writing a strict stand-in that implements only the documented spec surface — a promise-returning registerTool , no unregisterTool , and an executeTool that throws for anything but a tool descriptor plus a JSON string — and drove the whole app through it. Several real defects only appeared there. It also certified one, because I'd written it from the published examples rather than from a browser. A test double is only as good as the contract you wrote it from. "You may not" and "there is nothing" are different answers. When the embedder asks for a tool it wasn't given, returning an empty list is worse than useless — it's misleading. A refusal with a reason is the correct answer, and an agent deserves to know which one it got. That principle ended up shaping the whole tool surface. Challenges Five defects, and not one was findable by reading the code. The first: requestAnimationFrame doesn't fire in a hidden or backgrounded tab, and my remediation awaited a render before re-auditing. Every repair_* tool therefore hung forever — silently, no error, no timeout — whenever the page wasn't the foreground tab. Which is exactly how an agent driving it from a side panel would find it. My Playwright suite never caught it because Playwright keeps the page active. The second: I wasn't honouring toolautosubmit , so every declarative form tool submitted itself. On the one project arguing that consequential actions need a human gate, an agent could complete a checkout with nobody in the loop. The third came from reading the shipping Chrome 152 binary rather than the docs: ScriptPromise<IDLNullable<IDLString>> blink::ModelContext::executeTool(ScriptState*, RegisteredTool*, String, const ExecuteToolOptions*) Native executeTool resolves a JSON string , not an object. My unwrapper expected an object, so under a real native implementation every call would have handed the UI a raw string, silently. The last two came from the agent. Verification returned PASS for a profile in which the site had accepted nothing — an empty scope has nothing left in it to fail, so the site said "I cannot help you" and then said "PASS". And the agent had to keyboard-click a form by hand, on the project whose whole argument is that agents shouldn't have to: syncDeclarativeForms only ran inside the polyfill's construction path, so under a native implementation A11yMCP registered no declarative forms at all and assumed the browser would synthesize them. Chrome does. ChatGPT's browser doesn't. All five are fixed, each with a regression test. The same agent then re-verified the last one over the same native transport: it now reports 21 tools where it previously reported 20. Proving the comparison isn't rigged. It would have been easy to animate a stored benchmark. Instead the side-by-side runs both lanes live on the same page: the actuation lane genuinely walks the tab order, genuinely probes the computed focus style, and genuinely injects the tabindex it was never authorised to inject — then undo

title: Counterask
pitch: A storefront whose WebMCP tools hand the agent a question instead of a guess.
about_excerpt: A storefront whose WebMCP tools hand the agent a question instead of a guess. Like Comment Story Updates Every WebMCP storefront exposes the same shape of tool: get-products, filter-products, show-products. The spec's own e-commerce example does exactly that. All of them share one assumption — that the store's job is to answer. For most of a shopping conversation that assumption is wrong. Ask our catalog for "a belt" and 106 products match. Every one of them is a belt. The top-ranked item beats the tenth by a rounding error. Ranking them is a coin flip dressed up as a recommendation. The store knows this. It has the distribution in front of it — it can see that one more fact, what the belt is made of, would clear about forty-seven of them. But a tool that can only return products has no way to say so. So it returns its coin flip, and the agent presents a guess as an answer. We gave the store a second move.Counterask is a menswear storefront on 9,901 real products from the Amazon Reviews 2023 catalog. Its search_products tool returns one of two things. When there is enough evidence, it answers — and says what still separates the products it is showing, so the agent can summarise instead of reading out a list. When answering would be a guess, it returns status: "need_more_evidence" with the one question worth asking, the options with their counts, and why: "106 candidates, leader only 5% ahead. Asking 'material' clears ~47 of them on average (recorded on 89%)." The question is the store declining to guess on the shopper's behalf. It reads whole sentences, not keywords: "I'm looking for a leather belt, nothing with a snap, not over $50" becomes a requirement, a refusal and a ceiling. It walks the category tree one level at a time: "shoes" → athletic → running → what for → 58 candidates. It handles a change of mind mid-conversation — "scratch that, a nylon belt" drops leather, keeps the budget, and reports what it dropped. And when nothing survives, it lifts each requirement in turn and says which one is doing the damage. How WebMCP is used: every tool is registered through document.modelContext. answer_question exists only while a question is open — registered with an AbortSignal, removed by aborting it — so an agent reading the tool list can see what the page is waiting for. parse_only is a dry run: the agent can see how the store would read a sentence before committing. Anything the agent already knows can be passed structured and overrides the parse. A person clicking an option chip and an agent calling the tool enter the same function. Checkout is a declarative form with no toolautosubmit: the agent fills it in, the person presses it.No server, no model call, no tokens. The whole store is one page: the catalog, a thirteen-pass sentence parser, retrieval, and the stopping policy, in plain JavaScript. The engine is four parts with explicit dependencies — vocabulary, parser, retrieval, policy — and the parser is a pipeline whose order is data: each pass claims what it reads and writes a line of an audit trace that parse_only returns. The stopping policy counts, for each attribute, how many candidates a question would clear on average, measured inside the subset that records the attribute and scaled by coverage. It asks about the best one unless the best one clears fewer than 10 candidates or under 18% of the pool. Entropy was the textbook choice and it is wrong for this data: a product carries several values of one attribute at once, so value shares are not a probability distribution. The category tree is a facet. Every node on a product's path is a value, so "shoes" matches all shoes and "running" the running ones. A hierarchy is the one facet that can be asked again, one level at a time; ancestors the whole pool shares are never offered; depth is measured per product relative to what the shopper named. npm test runs 75 hand-written parser cases, 4,000 fuzzed sentences, 88 assertions against the WebMCP surface, the page against three spec-shaped native implementations, a test that an open question survives a page navigation, the bundled single file, and two benchmarks. A hostile product is inserted during the tests and the suite asserts its title never lands in an instruction-shaped field.Real data broke the thing synthetic data could not. On a synthetic catalog a belt's title says "Belt". Half of real titles do not name their category — "Columbia Men's Thistletown Park Crew" is a T-shirt. Requiring the shopper's noun in the title dropped the right product in 47% of benchmark cases. Making the category tree a facet took that to 4.6%; treating a value as satisfied wherever the record carries it, and letting stray words rank rather than filter once the noun is understood, took it to 0.6%. Missing is not a mismatch — in both directions. Only 8% of the catalog records a fit, and a naive gain calculation adores fit because asking it "removes 92% of candidates" — for having no data. Reduction is measured inside the covered subset, and an attribute recorded on under 45% of the pool is never asked about. A fuzzer found a bug we would never have found by hand: answering a question could make the pool grow. The title-term filter fell back to no filtering when fewer than four products matched; a narrowing answer could drop the strict set below four, and the shopper watched results grow because they had answered. The reading is now decided once and frozen. We built two-step lookahead and it was worse — selection used a two-step score while the stopping rule used a one-step score. We built the correctly formulated sequential policy and measured it at equal questions asked: the same curve. It ships off.Measured on 800 sentences generated from real product records, against a keyword matcher on identical sentences, with spread over 8 shards: refusals inverted into requirements: 597 → 0 refused value shown in top 10: 368 → 0 budget broken in top 10: 22 → 0 Hit@10: 0.04 → 0.33 ± 0.01 On sessions that start where shoppers start — "shoes", "clothing" — walking the category tree takes Hit@10 from 0.16 to 0.31 and the final pool from 597 to 121, for half a question more. Eight shards out of eight. It is the largest single effect in the project, and it was invisible until the benchmark started at the top of the tree instead of the leaf. We are equally proud of what we refused to do. Lowering the ask threshold from 10 to 5 buys +0.07 Hit@10 for 0.35 more questions per search, and the benchmark says take it. We didn't: the simulated shopper never gets tired, so the benchmark can price the benefit of a question and not its cost. Instead we made the cost an explicit assumption — the shipped threshold implies that roughly one shopper in four walks away each time the store asks — and published the whole frontier so the choice is visible rather than buried in a constant.The spec lists fully autonomous workflows under Non-Goals and says the human interface remains primary, with agent tools augmenting rather than replacing it. A tool that returns a question is the most direct expression of that we could build. It puts the person back in the loop at the exact moment the machine cannot decide — not as a permission prompt bolted on afterwards, but because the store genuinely does not know and says so. And a benchmark is only as honest as its blind spots are documented. Ours draws targets uniformly, starts at the leaf, and never gets impatient. Every one of those limits changed what we shipped, and every one is written down.Measure the one number the store cannot: how often a shopper actually walks away per question. A deployed page can log question-shown, question-answered and page-abandoned; the threshold then becomes a measured quantity instead of a stated belief. Structured input first: in a real WebMCP session the agent has already understood the shopper, so the parser should be the fallback and parse_only the first call. A catalog with descriptions, not just titles. Attribute coverage is the ceiling on what the store can ask; this data records material on 56% of products and occasion on 25%, and the questions are limited by what the listings say. title: Finite
pitch: Change your plans without rebuilding them.
about_excerpt: Change your plans without rebuilding them. Like Comment Story Updates Change your plans without rebuilding them. Finite keeps you and Codex working from the same live plan. A trip, renovation and event get different structures from the same connected planning model. WebMCP connects Codex to the same live plan on screen, so the conversation and the product become one workflow. Finite checks the connected plan, rules out what no longer fits and returns every meaningfully different workable direction. The chosen direction becomes revision 2 with the complete before and after result saved for the next planning conversation. Inspiration Planning software is usually good at storing the first version of a plan. It is much less useful after something changes. A delayed supplier, a new date, a smaller budget or one fixed booking can affect everything around it. At that point, people often end up rebuilding the plan in chat, patching a spreadsheet and checking every dependency by hand. Finite started with a simple comparison. Most software gives you the kitchen and still expects you to cook. With Finite, you are the diner, Codex is the chef, and Finite is the kitchen and service system. You describe the outcome and judge the result. Codex does the work. WebMCP gives Codex a real way to operate the kitchen. The goal was to build a planning system that stays useful when the original plan stops being correct. What it does Finite is a planning partner for plans that need to survive change. You can start with an outcome in ordinary language. Finite turns it into a working plan with the right structure for the job. A trip needs dates, routes, bookings and a budget. A renovation needs phases, dependencies, suppliers and contingency. An event needs capacity, commitments and a run of show. Interview preparation and recurring practice need different records again. These are different product surfaces built from the same planning model. The same system can support all of them because it understands the connected facts, constraints, choices and revisions underneath each plan. Codex can enter the live plan through WebMCP and read its current facts, limits, evidence and open work. When something changes, Codex can explore what is movable, test the available combinations and bring back the distinct directions that fit the plan. The public Spotlight shows this with a request to add three nights in Paris. The international flights are fixed, the total budget still matters and at least AUD 500 must remain free. Finite checks 26 possible combinations. Eighteen satisfy the encoded constraints, eight do not, and five meaningfully different directions exist for this plan. If only one direction worked, Finite would return one. The person chooses Protect breathing room and reviews the exact effect before confirming it. Codex can then apply that approved route. The plan moves from revision 1 to revision 2 once, retains AUD 910 of freedom and saves a before and after receipt that survives reload. Finite keeps research, comparison, verification, booking and payment as separate states. It does not claim that finding an option means the option is available or that a saved plan means anything has been purchased. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the connection between Codex and the live plan. The page that the person sees also exposes typed, page-scoped tools to Codex. That means Codex works with the same accepted plan, current revision and visible decision state instead of guessing its way through buttons or using a hidden copy of the data. Finite registers seven stable document tools. Codex uses them to enter the current work, discover the available capability group, invoke the relevant planning action and read exact parts of a larger result when needed. The available actions are checked again against the active plan and revision before they run. Codex handles language, research and orchestration. Finite handles the calculations, constraints, saved state and receipts. You decide which direction becomes part of the plan. The person makes the final choice on the visible planning surface. WebMCP lets Codex prepare the alternatives and carry the selected direction into the same live plan. Codex does not just send advice back to chat. With your permission, it can guide you through the real Finite interface: move to the relevant section, highlight the actual controls, explain them in an on-page popup, and pause for questions or Next. These are built-in, page-scoped WebMCP capabilities, not a prerecorded tour. You can work manually, let Codex develop the plan, or switch between both in the same workspace. Guidance never grants permission to choose or approve a plan change for you. How it improves the human and agent experience Without this connection, the person has to carry information between the app and the agent. They explain the plan in chat, receive a recommendation, then update every affected field themselves. With Finite, Codex can enter the current plan in one call and see what is already known. It can work across the whole plan, then stop when a real decision is required. The person sees the trade-offs and the exact proposed change instead of operating the planning machinery. This makes the relationship straightforward. Codex does the planning work. Finite keeps that work consistent. The person stays responsible for the outcome. How it was built Finite uses TypeScript, Vite, Cloudflare Workers, D1, R2 and ChatGPT Sites. The planning kernel uses integer money, revision-bound candidates, constraint checks, short-lived approval challenges, optimistic concurrency, atomic receipts and idempotent replay. Accepted plan state is stored in D1 and can be restored after reload. An adaptive surface compiler builds each type of plan from a limited set of validated components. The same plan definition also limits what Codex can discover and do through WebMCP. Large results are stored temporarily by content hash. Codex receives a compact summary and can request the exact section it needs. This keeps the tool responses small without cutting important values in half. Codex provides the reasoning. Finite provides the connected state, calculations and persistence that make that reasoning useful inside a real product. Challenges The difficult part was keeping the plan correct while the person and Codex were both involved. A reported change is not an accepted change. A proposed option is not a decision. A click on an approval control is not the same as a completed plan update. Those states have to remain separate through retries, reloads and stale browser sessions. The first implementation also exposed too many route-specific tools and returned too much data. It was replaced with seven stable tools, smaller capability groups and exact retrieval for larger results. Testing also found small wording problems that could cause large mistakes. For example, value: 3 could be read as either an absolute duration or an instruction to add three days. The final contract separates value from delta and rejects contradictory inputs. Accomplishments A complete public WebMCP plan change from revision 1 to revision 2 A situation-dependent set of distinct suggestions derived from 26 checked combinations Seven stable WebMCP tools for the lifetime of the page Human choice kept inside the visible planning conversation Persistent receipts with the exact before and after state Distinct travel, renovation, event, interview, practice and general planning surfaces 373 passing tests, including 20 repeated Spotlight transaction runs Three calls to the first useful action in the measured production route What we learned More tools do not automatically make an agent more capable. A small toolset with current state and clear boundaries is easier for Codex to use well. We also learned that honest status matters. Research is not verification. A valid route is not approval. An updated plan is not a booking. Showing those differences makes the product easier to trust and easier to understand. The best division of work is built into the workflow. Codex can do the repetitive planning work while the person decides what becomes part of the plan. What's next The next step is to watch new users bring their own outcomes into Finite and see where the planning model is unclear without explanation. After that, the adaptive grammar and evidence connections can expand to cover more kinds of plans while keeping the same rules for accepted state and human approval. title: Floortris
pitch: WebMCP agents turn dimensioned sketches into rule-checked 2D and 3D rooms, while people compare proposals and control every final change.
about_excerpt: WebMCP agents turn dimensioned sketches into rule-checked 2D and 3D rooms, while people compare proposals and control every final change. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I started Floortris late in the challenge with a practical question: why can an AI describe a room layout but struggle to work directly with the room planner already open in front of it? Before implementing WebMCP, I was surprised by how difficult it was for an AI agent to use the website reliably. It had to interpret controls visually, infer the state of the room and hope that each interaction had worked. Even when the result looked reasonable, the agent could miss important details such as door swings, walking routes, furniture orientation or the measurements of items someone already owned. I wanted to explore a better approach: a room planner designed from the beginning for a person and an agent to use together. The agent should understand the same measured room shown on screen, work under the same rules and produce a visible proposal—while the person retains control of every final change. What it does Floortris is a local-first room planner for people and agents. A person can enter a measured room, add doors and windows, record furniture they already own, lock its dimensions or position and edit the layout directly. An agent can use 16 native WebMCP tools to inspect the same document, construct a separate Proposal, arrange furniture, change finishes and check the resulting layout. The agent works in Proposal , while the accepted room remains in Yours . It does not switch the person’s view or apply its own work. Apply, room-input confirmation, discard, unlock and view switching remain human-only actions. Floortris checks more than whether two rectangles overlap. Its shared rule engine evaluates: door swings and open door leaves; hard and preferred walking clearances; routes between entrances and activity zones; TV positioning and seating relationships; coffee-table gaps; usable bed sides; storage and window access; linked desks and chair pull zones; radiators and wall-mounted objects; measured curtains, blinds and lighting fixtures. An agent can recreate rectilinear rooms with alcoves, recesses, nooks and L-shaped outlines from dimensioned information. The same measured outline is then used by the 2D board, 3D scene, collision rules, ceiling checks, walking routes and placement search. Agents can also create measured custom furniture inside a Proposal, including genuine connected L- and U-shaped sectionals. These use a closed, validated geometry format instead of arbitrary code or remote 3D assets. They remain subject to the same placement rules and human approval boundary as catalogue furniture. Why WebMCP The floor plan itself is the product. A hidden API response or a paragraph describing where furniture should go is not enough—the measurements, furniture, warnings and proposed changes need to remain visible and reviewable. Floortris registers 16 native tools through document.modelContext . These include generateRoom , getRoomState , createProposal , createCustomFurniture , placeFurniture , updateFurniture , findPlacements , setAppearance and checkLayout . These tools give the agent structured access to the same room state and rule engine used by the visible interface. Instead of guessing what a button does or interpreting the page from pixels, the agent can request exact measurements, submit a revision-bound change and receive structured feedback explaining whether the layout is healthy. WebMCP made the agent much more reliable, but I deliberately avoided giving it complete authority. It can perform substantial spatial work, but its result remains a Proposal until a person reviews and applies it. How I built it Floortris is built with TypeScript, React, Next.js on the vinext runtime, Three.js, Vite and Cloudflare Workers. At its centre is a shared rule engine operating on a measured 20 cm grid. Human controls and WebMCP commands pass through the same document store and validation logic. This prevents the visible room and the agent’s representation from developing different versions of spatial truth. Each WebMCP tool has a strict JSON Schema, explicit metadata, revision checks and abort-aware execution. Placement searches are bounded, and candidates are ranked by functional quality rather than simply returning the first coordinate without a collision. I also added seven difficult benchmark rooms, three checked planning strategies, static accommodation-provider packs, advisory accessibility planning packs, a local evaluation dashboard, furniture-schedule exports, printable move-in sheets and server-free share links carried in the URL fragment. Room, evaluation and share data is not sent to an application data backend. Share data only leaves the device when the person explicitly shares the generated URL. A Cloudflare Worker serves the client application; there is no application database or remote LLM service. Challenges I faced The hardest technical challenge was maintaining one spatial truth across every part of the application. A custom cut-out in an L-shaped room could not simply be hidden in the 2D view. It also had to be absent from collision cells, walking routes, ceiling placement, search candidates and the 3D shell. Custom sectional furniture created a similar problem: an L- or U-shaped sofa needed to behave as one connected object without treating its empty internal area as occupied floor space. Furniture rules were more relational than I initially expected. Whether a coffee table works depends on the sofa’s true facing edge and measured gap. Whether a desk works depends on its chair and pull zone. Whether shelving is correctly placed depends on which edge is actually its back—not merely whether some part of its bounding box touches a wall. I also encountered problems with door clearances, TVs appearing behind doors, shelving facing the wrong direction, disappearing 2D labels and stuttering 3D shadows. Fixing these required the rule engine and renderers to use explicit geometry rather than visual assumptions. Another challenge was protecting human work while an agent was operating. Proposal branches, revision-bound commands, immutable snapshots and exact-revision review checks prevent a delayed agent action from silently overwriting a newer human edit. What I learned I was most surprised by how difficult it was for an AI agent to use the website before I implemented the WebMCP tools. A page that feels obvious to a person can still be ambiguous to an agent when its capabilities and state are only communicated visually. That changed how I think about building websites. In future projects, I want to consider agent-native compatibility from the beginning rather than treating it as something added afterwards. As the world becomes increasingly reliant on AI, websites should expose clear, structured and constrained capabilities that allow agents to help without taking control away from people. I also learned that useful agentic interfaces need visible state, explicit authority and reversible proposals—not simply more tools. Geometry needs to be centralised as well. Once the 2D plan, 3D scene, placement search and validation engine all used the same measurements, complex room shapes and custom furniture became much easier to support correctly. I am proudest of how quickly I produced a working prototype despite starting late, while documenting the development publicly on TikTok at the same time. Building in public forced me to explain each problem clearly and showed how quickly an initial prototype could develop into a much more capable agent-native application. Floortris ultimately became more than a furniture visualiser. It became an experiment in how people and agents can share one visible, rule-checked document while the person retains ownership of the final decision. title: Genga Studio
pitch: An anime studio in a browser tab. Give an agent a paragraph and it writes the script, draws the key frames, animates, voices, scores, and cuts a film. Collaborate in the browser and guide your vision.
about_excerpt: An anime studio in a browser tab. Give an agent a paragraph and it writes the script, draws the key frames, animates, voices, scores, and cuts a film. Collaborate in the browser and guide your vision. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In July I set out to make a short anime film with generated frames, on my own hardware. The pipeline grew the way pipelines do. An image model for key frames. A motion model for the few seconds that had to move. A script that froze the tail of a clip when the model drifted, another that chained a second clip off the last good frame, another that composited a moving cel over a painted plate. A dashboard that could cut the film. By the end of the month I had 97 shots, 567 takes, and a four-minute animatic of act one. Then I turned that pipeline into an application I could host, because I wanted the same control over every future film and I wanted it to run on hosted models instead of a GPU on my laptop. Cutroom, as it was called then, became a FastAPI server and a React studio: projects, a film editor, a shot page with a compose console and a generate console, a comp editor for cels, a timeline, a jobs queue, a settings page for backends. Every decision I had ever made became a toggle, a drawer, or a field. That is where it stalled. I had built a tool with a billion toggles and drawers. I could not remember where we put half of them. Pro-level control over every aspect of production turned out to mean a Photoshop-sized surface that only its author could navigate, and the author was losing track too. The revelation came from hearing about the WebMCP challenge. WebMCP lets a page register its own actions as tools on document.modelContext , and an agent running in the browser can call them. So the studio doesn't need fewer toggles, it just needs to publish them! An agent that can read the tool list can find the drawer I forgot, fill the console I never open, and press the button I would have pressed, while I watch it happen on screen and learn my own app back. Control stays total. The navigation cost goes to zero. That is what makes a video production tool a fantastic use case for WebMCP. It has to offer everything, because a film needs pro-level control over every part of production. Yet the person using it usually does not know which control they want, and does not want to become an expert in the tool to get the benefit of that control. Publishing the controls as tools resolves both halves at once: the studio keeps every knob, and the agent turns them. What it does Genga Studio is a cutting room for AI-generated limited animation, the way anime has always been made on a budget: key frames as the anchor point, holds and cels and cuts from the studio. Every action in the studio is also a WebMCP tool, 52 of them at submission: list the film, generate stills, restyle a take, set a keeper, plan a motion budget across shots, animate a cel, voice a line, score a bed, set a timeline source, cut the film, screen the result. An agent in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag sees the same studio you do and drives the same buttons. The hosted demo made a two-minute short, "Two Claudes," inspired by an NPR story about the two chatbots wired to talk to each other until they broke out of the loop. Fifteen shots, each animated for its full length from its keeper frame, fifteen voice lines, a piano bed, cut and re-cut after every motion pass. The takes on screen cost $2.80 in API calls. How we built it The plan came first: a frozen contract for tools (names, input schemas, a shared ActionContext , page anchors so a tool can wait for the console it needs), then the pages exposed their actions through a registry, then the tools were written against that registry. Parallel Claude agents built and tested the tool layer while I reviewed and drove the result. A Playwright driver launches system Chrome with the WebMCP feature enabled and executes tools through the browser's own document.modelContext , so the same script that tests the tools is the one an agent effectively runs. Hosting was its own small project. The director runs on OpenRouter. Stills come from a Gemini image model through OpenRouter, motion from Seedance or Wan on fal, voices from ElevenLabs. Backends are toggled by API key, the demo is invite-only, and a spend cap stops things from going wild just in case. Challenges we ran into The agent found every weakness in the studio's defaults. It chose the free instant test backend over the paid ones until that lane was removed from the hosted build. It asked for five-second clips and got three seconds, because seconds turned into frames on one model profile and back into seconds on another. It animated from the keeper when I had selected a different still, which is now an explicit source on the motion tool. The film fought back too. One motion model refused a crowd plate on content grounds, so refusals now come back with a reason and a fallback model. Another flashed a night scene into daylight. The registry now says which model drifts how, and the guidance says to switch models rather than re-prompt the same one. And on the last night the 454 MB volume filled up, so cuts failed inside ffmpeg with no space left, and the cut button did nothing. Disk usage now shows in the system panel and an admin purge keeps the newest cuts and clips. What we learned Tool descriptions are the user interface. A one-line description decides whether an agent uses a feature or walks past it, and a result that names the next step does more for the agent than a longer description would. Guidance has to be progressive: the note about photo-real drift belongs in the motion plan's result, not in the feature list an agent reads on arrival. And the thing I wanted from the start turned out to be true. Watching an agent work the studio taught me where my own features were, so if I want to grab the wheel and drive, I've been watching an expert this whole time, and learned from the best. What's next Character reference LoRAs for identity across shots to enable longer-running films, a motion budget that plans a whole act, and the studio driven end to end from a single paragraph of script. Better evaluation and guidance between available image, motion, and audio models. Superior visibility, implementation, and usage of the anime-specific animation tricks that let limited motion generation carry plenty of narrative moemntum.
