title: BlockSmith
pitch: AI builds websites fast and generic. BlockSmith captures a design system from any site in seconds, hands the rules to the AI, checks its work, and tells it no when it breaks them.
about_excerpt: AI builds websites fast and generic. BlockSmith captures a design system from any site in seconds, hands the rules to the AI, checks its work, and tells it no when it breaks them. Like Comment Story Updates BlockSmith + Chatgpt generated the Moda design wiki in under a minute BlockSmith captured the Moda website to create a design wiki, then used it to generate this custom landing page Wiki is Interactive itself, you can visualize the design system within the wiki Snapshot of interactive wiki component playground generated within few minutes. Snapshot of a custom landing page built from the Moda design wiki Snapshot of a Chart Page built from the Different design wiki Blocksmith strict design governance Snapshot of a custom dashboard interface page built from the Different design wiki Snapshot of a custom landing page built from the Different design wiki Inspiration Anyone can ship a website now. You describe it, an AI writes it, it's live the same afternoon, and the web is filling up with work that is fast, competent, and completely interchangeable. The same gradient. The same drop shadow. The same rounded card. In short, website now are full of AI slops. It is tempting to call that a taste problem. It isn't. Nobody ever gave the agent a standard. Real companies usually have one: the exact colours, the exact spacing, the things you never do, but it lives in a Figma file, a Notion page, or Confluences. The agent is looking at a rendered web page, and none of it is in a web page. So it does the average thing, and the average of the whole internet is what we have all been looking at, which we all know is a disaster! Gradient borders, wrong spacing.... Halfway through building this, Vercel published how their agents build on-brand pages with a design.md , and it turned out to be the best argument for what I was making. They wrote the rules down, published them at a public URL, and measured the result: 57% fewer brand failures. And then the honest part: "every one of them, with or without the file, still had at least one failure serious enough to block shipping." A file is passive. The agent has to be told to fetch it, has to interpret it, their words: "every model reading it interpreted that description differently" , and has to not be working from a copy that went stale. Reading the rules and being told no are different things. WebMCP is what closes that gap. The page stops being a document the agent reads and becomes an authority it can ask. What does BlockSmith even do? Every big company has rules about how its product looks: the exact colours, the exact spacing, the things you never do. Almost nobody else does. If you are one developer shipping something this weekend, you have no design system, no time to write one, and no way to make an AI follow it. BlockSmith gives you one either way and makes it usable by people and by AI at the same time. If your team already has a design system, this is where it lives: point BlockSmith at your codebase or your Figma file and it becomes a documentation site anyone can read and edit. If you don't have one, point it at any website you admire (vercel, openai , any website you like) and you have one in about few seconds instead of months! From there it is the same product for both. It hands those rules to any AI working in your browser, checks what that AI builds, and tells it no quoting the rule a designer actually wrote, so the AI learns the rule instead of just deleting a line. When the AI wants to change a rule, it cannot: it has to ask you, and you approve or reject it. Every version is kept, so you can see what changed and undo it. And the same rules follow the work out of the browser into your code editor, into an installable package, and into a check that stops a commit before it breaks anything. Imagine you now have a jenkins pipeline for each ui component :v How do you get in? From How A live website Reads what a page actually paints: colours ranked by how much of the screen they cover, type and spacing scales, radii, and the repeated components it can find Your codebase Scans a local workspace or a GitHub repo: every React component, its props and variants, every CSS custom property Figma Imports variables and published components, and reconciles them against code: "Figma says X, shipped code says Y" , with renames and near-misses told apart from real drift A document Paste or upload the design system you already wrote with this, blockSmith turns your design system into a documentation site. You get pages for colours, typography, spacing, components, and usage rules. There is also a playground where you can test values and see which tokens the system allows. Everything can be edited from the page. Human edits and approved AI suggestions go through the same review process. If a component does not have a usage rule yet, BlockSmith can draft one for you to edit. You can also preview the whole documentation site using the colours and typography from the design system you captured. It gives the rules to AI BlockSmith turns the design system into tools AI can use: 16 tools on the design system page, 4 for any website through the bookmarklet or Chrome extension, and 16 for coding agents like Cursor and Claude Code. Agents can also discover all available tools through /.well-known/webmcp.json. It catches design system violations When AI creates something, BlockSmith checks it against the design system. If something breaks a rule, it tells the AI exactly what went wrong and can auto-fix simple issues, but if a real design decision is needed, it stops and asks instead of guessing. It keeps track of versions With a connected code repository, BlockSmith manages design system changes like software releases: changes can stay in draft until approved, and a lockfile keeps AI and CI on the same approved version. You can also roll back changes, view release history, and track approved exceptions. Systems that are only pasted, uploaded, or captured stay in preview mode until connected to a repository. The same rules work outside BlockSmith You can use the design system in other tools too. Export it as a file for a coding agent Connect it to Cursor or Claude Code Generate an npm package with tokens and components Add a pre-commit check that blocks code that breaks the rules It works for teams Teams can invite people by email, create API keys, see the history of changes to each component, and publish the design system to a public link. Why WebMCP Most agent tools help AI do more. BlockSmith does something different: it tells AI what it should not do . For example, a design system might use red on the page but still have a rule saying, "Don't use this red for buttons or interactive elements." An AI looking at the screenshot or DOM can see the color, but it can't see that rule. The same goes for components. BlockSmith can tell AI not to build things like a tooltip, carousel, modal, accordion, or hero banner, and tell it what to use instead. You can't scrape something that doesn't exist. BlockSmith gives AI those missing rules so it doesn't just guess or invent them. How it creates a better user experience The agent stops guessing, Before an agent writes a line it calls get_governance_rules and gets this system's palette, scales, motion timing and authored rules. When it is wrong, the verdict is specific enough to act on in the same turn: REJECTED: 4 violation(s) in Portfolio. - Line 1 `banned-shadow`: `shadow-lg`. Shadows are not allowed in this design system. Rule: "Do not add drop shadows to cards or buttons. Separation comes from the Rule (#e2e4ea) hairline and from space, not elevation." - Line 1 `off-token-utility`: `bg-blue-500` is a stock Tailwind color, not a design token. - Line 1 `off-scale-utility`: `p-5` resolves to 20px, not on the spacing scale. Use `p-4` (16px) instead. Then fix_violations repairs what is mechanical and hands back what isn't : Applied 5 fix(es): p-5 → p-4, rounded-lg → rounded-md, text-sm → text-[13px] … 5 need a decision from you: - `bg-blue-500`: no token matches this colour; pick one from the palette - `shadow-lg`: removing this changes the design, not just a value That is intentional. womp womp done by me. :v If AI is asked to use a color that is not allowed, BlockSmith should not quietly replace it with something else. Instead, it knows when to stop and ask. The goal is not just to make AI do more, but to make sure it does not make design decisions it was never allowed to make. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An agent can be told no by the product itself, and then be told what changed. The loop, in one conversation: You ask for a launch banner in #7c3aed . The agent calls propose_component . The system answers: "Nothing in Cohere is close to this color; the nearest is Accent (#4c6ee6), which is a different hue. Adding a new color is a design decision for the user, not a substitution to make silently." The agent cannot add the colour . I

title: CanvasMind
pitch: A floor plan an AI agent can actually read; audit for wheelchair and other access.
about_excerpt: A floor plan an AI agent can actually read; audit for wheelchair and other access. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A 13m × 8m banquet hall, audited: all 31 seats reachable on a 90cm > wheelchair route. Inspiration Generally, Canva is used for planning venue layouts, and most of time those designers are not accessibility auditors. Thus, one day someone in a wheelchair finds he cannot reach a table, let's say table six, or a fire exit – which perhaps is behind the buffet. The reason is nobody checks properly, because checking properly means measuring every gap and tracing every route from every door. That's tedious arithmetic by hand and genuinely impossible by eye , which is exactly the kind of work you'd want to hand to an AI. However, it’s not that simple. And before you think it's a matter of model quality, it’s not. Rather, the reason behind the inefficiency of AI here is poor structural understanding. What it does CanvasMind is a room planner that tells you whether a wheelchair user can reach every seat. You drag furniture, resize it by its corner handles, name the room. It checks four things continuously: furniture outside the room overlapping items the 150cm clear zone in front of every doorway whether every item can actually be reached from a door along a continuous 90cm-wide route That last one is the hard one, and it's what pairwise gap checks miss: furniture spaced perfectly but walled off, with no route to it. The verdict is stated in human terms — "8 of 31 seats unreachable" , not "8 rule violations" — and you can export the plan as an image with that verdict stamped on it, so the file is a record you can send a client. And you can ask an AI agent to do any of it. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript, the Canvas 2D API, and WebMCP. Zero dependencies, no build step, no framework — about 1,400 lines across three modules and one HTML file, deployed as static files. Deliberately no canvas library. SVG-based options (React Flow, D3-as-SVG, draw.io) render a readable element tree, which would defeat the entire premise. Canvas 2D emits pixels and nothing else. 18 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() , every one pointing at the same functions the mouse handlers call. One implementation, two callers — a person dragging furniture and an agent calling a tool run identical code, so they cannot drift apart. readOnlyHint splits the surface. The five audit tools ( get_layout , find_items , describe_selection , measure_gap , check_accessibility ) are marked read-only so an agent can investigate freely; the twelve that mutate the room aren't. A live tool list. fix_accessibility is registered with an AbortController passed as the registration signal ; aborting that signal unregisters it. The toolchange event drives the tool count in the UI: 17 → 18 → 17. AbortSignal honoured inside a running tool. auto_arrange animates a force simulation across many frames and stops on the frame when cancelled. Descriptions written for a model, not a human. Units stated ("all units are centimetres, (0,0) is the top-left"), preconditions stated, and guidance on when to call. That prose is the real interface, and most of the tuning went there. Provenance. Each item carries a dot showing whether a person placed it, the agent placed it, or the agent moved it. The geometry the model never has to do The agent decides to call check_accessibility . The page does the maths: rasterise the room at 10cm resolution mark cells occupied by furniture erode the free space by the 90cm wheelchair footprint flood-fill from each doorway, walking inward and stopping at the first obstruction — so a table parked in an opening makes that door unusable rather than being stepped over any item with no reachable cell touching it fails fix_accessibility repacks the room into rows with real aisles built in, so the result is compliant by construction rather than by luck, then relocates anything still boxed in. That split is the point: the model contributes intent, the page contributes domain expertise. Challenges we ran into Chrome and the spec disagree about inputSchema . Chrome's getTools() returns it as a JSON string while the W3C CG draft types it as an object . That double-encoded every schema in my UI until I normalised both. Chrome's executeTool() argument shape also diverges from the draft, so the built-in tool runner invokes registered functions directly rather than round-tripping through the consumer API. The agent path is unaffected — but the divergence cost real debugging time. Correct spacing does not imply reachability. My first repair implementation shoved furniture apart until every pairwise gap passed the 90cm standard. Every gap was legal and only 1 in 6 randomised layouts was actually accessible, because the packing left walled-off pockets. I replaced it with deterministic row packing that builds aisles in, so accessibility holds by construction. Now 6 of 6. Erosion arithmetic. Using ceil to size the erosion kernel demanded ~110cm of clearance to certify a 90cm route — so a corridor built exactly to standard failed its own check. One character, completely wrong answers. The flood fill stepped over blocked doorways. It seeded by searching outward from a door until it found any free floor, which meant it jumped straight over a table parked in the opening and declared the room reachable. Fixed by walking inward from the door and stopping at the first obstruction. Finding the right problem. The first version was a generic node-graph editor that proved the WebMCP point perfectly and helped nobody. The canvas argument was right; the domain was wrong. Reskinning it to accessibility auditing kept every line of the engine and gave it an actual audience. Accomplishments that we're proud of The reachability engine is genuinely correct, and I can prove it. It catches furniture that is perfectly spaced but walled off, and doorways that are technically clear but blocked in practice. 25 automated checks cover it, including a 20-layout randomised invariant that no repair ever pushes an item through a wall. The tool list is alive. Watching fix_accessibility appear when the room breaks and withdraw itself when it's repaired is the clearest demonstration I could build of something a static MCP server structurally cannot do. It degrades honestly. With no WebMCP at all — plain Chrome, Safari, Firefox — the planner still works by mouse or keyboard, and the built-in Tool runner panel invokes every tool directly. The whole project can be evaluated with zero setup. An accessibility tool that is itself accessible. Tab cycles items, arrow keys move the selection 10cm, Shift+arrow moves 1cm, R rotates, Delete removes, Esc deselects. It would have been embarrassing to ship an accessibility auditor that required a mouse. What we learned WebMCP's value isn't the plumbing — it's the app declaring what it means. An agent can guess your structure from your markup, and that guess is what browser actuation already is. What it can't do is derive intent. A registered tool is a contract the site author wrote; a scraped one is a guess an outsider made. Tool descriptions are the real interface. No validator checks them, and they determine whether the model picks the right tool. Stating units, preconditions, and when-to-call did more for reliability than any schema tightening. The model should contribute intent, not computation. Every time I was tempted to let the model reason about coordinates, the right answer was to give the page a better solver and let the model just ask. It's also why this beats a vision agent: the app already owned the spatial reasoning and only needed a way to be asked. Building on a moving spec means testing against the implementation, not the document. Two of my four real bugs came from trusting the CG draft over what Chrome actually ships. What's next for CanvasMind Import real floor plans — DXF or an image with a scale reference, so you audit an actual venue instead of a rectangle. Multi-room buildings with routes between them, including corridors and lifts. Reachability across a whole building is the same algorithm at a larger scale. Configurable thresholds per jurisdiction. The current figures follow the spirit of ADA / BS 8300 guidance; the numbers should be selectable, not baked in. A shareable audit link , so a venue and a client can look at the same plan and the same verdict. More than wheelchairs — turning circles, guide-dog space, step-free routes, seating sightlines. This is a demonstration project, not a certified compliance tool, and the roadmap is about earning that distinction. title: Companion
pitch: Turn human observations into confirmed, traceable memory that AI agents can query through WebMCP—preserving evidence, distinguishing hypotheses, and leaving missing information unknown.
about_excerpt: Turn human observations into confirmed, traceable memory that AI agents can query through WebMCP—preserving evidence, distinguishing hypotheses, and leaving missing information unknown. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable at reasoning, but I became interested in a different problem: What happens to the human context they need to reason well? People constantly produce valuable context through observations, measurements, decisions, hypotheses, conversations, and experience. Much of it remains unstructured: spoken aloud, written in notes, or trapped inside applications that were designed for humans rather than agents. My initial idea was simple: let a person describe something naturally, preserve what they actually said, and make that context reusable by an AI agent later. But that immediately raised a harder question: If AI helps structure that memory, how do we prevent the AI's interpretation from silently becoming part of the human evidence? That question became the foundation of Companion. Companion is a human-to-agent memory layer : Human context → Confirmed memory → WebMCP → Agent reasoning The application owns the evidence. The agent owns the reasoning. What Companion does Companion starts with unrestricted natural-language human input. A person can describe an observation without learning a schema or filling out a complex structured form. Companion proposes a subject, but the person reviews and can correct both the original text and the subject before confirming it. Once confirmed, the original evidence is preserved first. AI then helps construct a semantic representation of that evidence, but model output does not automatically become factual memory. Semantic construction happens in two stages: Semantic discovery finds candidate relations. Epistemic classification determines how each candidate is supported by the confirmed source. Relations are classified as: SOURCE_EXPLICIT SOURCE_STRONGLY_IMPLIED AGENT_INFERRED Only source-grounded relations are eligible for factual memory after deterministic validation. AGENT_INFERRED relations are kept outside that factual boundary and are never silently exposed as human-confirmed facts. This means AI can help build the memory without being allowed to redefine the evidence. Why WebMCP The next problem was retrieval. My first instinct was to make Companion intelligent enough to decide which stored information an agent needed. Experiments changed that design. If the external agent already understands the user's question and will ultimately reason over the answer, adding another AI inside Companion to predict what that agent needs duplicates intelligence and creates another place where interpretation can go wrong. Instead, Companion exposes two read-only WebMCP capabilities: get_companion_vocabulary Returns a deterministic, reusable vocabulary of factual semantic relations available for a subject. query_companion_memory Retrieves exactly the factual relations identified by the vocabulary IDs selected by the external agent. This creates an incremental protocol: Agent inspects vocabulary → selects evidence → retrieves it → evaluates sufficiency → requests more if necessary → reasons Companion does not interpret the question, rank evidence, decide sufficiency, or generate the final answer. WebMCP is a particularly good fit because it gives the application a discoverable and invocable capability without coupling Companion to one specific agent runtime. The same architecture could be implemented with custom APIs and agent-specific integrations. WebMCP changes the integration boundary: Companion can expose its memory capability directly from the application so compatible agents can discover what evidence exists, request only the evidence they need, and reason over it without Companion being coupled to a specific agent runtime. What becomes possible is a collaboration in which a human can capture context naturally once, while multiple compatible agents can later discover and retrieve that confirmed memory through a shared application-owned interface. How I built it Companion was built as a sequence of small architectural experiments rather than by implementing the first design that seemed plausible. The core pipeline became: Human natural-language context ↓ Human review and confirmation ↓ Persist confirmed raw evidence ↓ Stage A: semantic discovery ↓ Candidate semantic graph ↓ Stage B: epistemic classification ↓ Deterministic validation ↓ Factual memory / inference boundary ↓ Reusable factual vocabulary ↓ WebMCP deterministic lookup ↓ External-agent reasoning The AI-assisted part is deliberately bounded. Everything that can be checked mechanically—IDs, references, schema compliance, candidate correspondence, source excerpts, routing, lookup—is validated deterministically. One design principle emerged from this: Pay for intelligence once, then reuse the structured result deterministically. The confirmed rawText remains the authoritative primary source. Semantic memory stays traceable to it, and semantic-processing failure cannot erase the original evidence. Persistent semantic IDs are also owned by Companion rather than by the model, preventing temporary model-generated identifiers from becoming accidental persistent authority. Challenges I faced Semantic correctness is not factual correctness One of the biggest lessons came from deliberately trying to break the semantic builder. A model can identify a relationship that is completely reasonable and still not be justified by the source. For example, observations may strongly suggest a diagnosis. That does not mean the human actually reported that diagnosis. This forced me to separate semantic discovery from epistemic classification . A useful semantic candidate is not automatically a fact. Preventing silent information loss Another problem appeared when increasing epistemic strictness. A strict prompt could reduce unsupported inference but also cause legitimate semantic relations to disappear. The solution was a no-deletion architecture: Stage A discovers candidates first, and Stage B must classify every candidate exactly once. That makes three different failures observable: discovery failure, classification failure, inferred semantic content that should not become factual memory. Deciding where retrieval intelligence belongs I also experimented with retrieval strategies. The important realization was that Companion does not need to understand the user's question if the external agent already does. The external agent can inspect Companion's reusable vocabulary, choose the IDs it needs, retain previous context, and request additional evidence incrementally. That removed an unnecessary intelligent selector from Companion and produced a cleaner responsibility boundary. Keeping the demo honest The public challenge demo uses synthetic evidence and browser-session-local memory. It intentionally does not claim production readiness, universal semantic correctness, or objective truth. Human confirmation means that the representation corresponds to what the human confirmed. It does not mean the human statement itself is objectively true. That distinction became important enough to be part of the architecture rather than just a disclaimer. What I learned The most important thing I learned was that memory for agents is not just a storage problem . It is an authority problem. A useful agent-memory system needs to know where human evidence ends and machine interpretation begins. I also learned that adding more AI is not always the answer. Companion uses AI where semantic interpretation is useful, but deterministic software owns validation, persistence rules, identity, routing, and retrieval. And WebMCP helped reveal a particularly clean separation of responsibilities: The human provides the evidence. Companion preserves and structures it. WebMCP exposes it. The external agent decides what it needs and reasons over it. Validation I treated the hackathon prototype as an experiment that should be falsifiable rather than as a polished product claim. The final automated suite contains 52 passing tests , covering the semantic authority boundary, deterministic validation, factual/inferred routing, WebMCP vocabulary projection, exact-ID lookup, and incremental retrieval behavior. The final production walkthrough also verified: natural-language capture and human confirmation; real semantic construction; WebMCP tool discovery and invocation; reusable factual vocabulary; exact lookup of agent-selected IDs; incremental retrieval across multiple calls; resolvable source references; explicit handling of unknown IDs; zero evidence for an empty ID request; exclusion of AGENT_INFERRED relations from factual WebMCP results. The public demo starts empty and all challenge examples are synthetic. What's next Companion v0.1 deliberately leaves several problems open. The semantic metamodel is small. title: Constraint Canvas
pitch: Every rejection becomes a rule the agent cannot break again
about_excerpt: Every rejection becomes a rule the agent cannot break again Like Comment Story Updates Rejecting a table opens rule capture. The app turns that correction into a rule and applies it to future proposals. The agent replans around the new rule and finds 16 seats elsewhere. The layout reaches 144 seats with zero violations. Asked for 40 more seats, the agent proposes five tables through WebMCP. Nothing changes yet because proposals are previews until approved. Willowmere Hall on load. 96 seats, eight built-in rules, and three locked objects the agent cannot move. What it is ConstraintCanvas is a venue floor planner where a human and an agent work on the same canvas at the same time. You place the stage, lock anything that cannot move, and decide which sponsor gets the front booth. The agent handles the tedious parts, like fitting more seats without breaking egress, finding clearance violations, and explaining exactly which rule blocked a placement. The floor planner is only the demo. The real idea is what happens when the human says no. Inspiration Agent corrections are usually temporary. You tell the model not to do something, that instruction lives in context, and a few turns later you may have to repeat it. That felt like the wrong place to store human judgment. If I say seating must never block a door, that should not just be prompt context. It should become application state that is visible, editable, and enforced. In ConstraintCanvas, rejecting an agent proposal can create a named rule with provenance. That rule is added to a visible rulebook and enforced against every future proposal. The agent does not need to remember better. The application enforces the correction. Why this use case fits WebMCP The site owns the semantics. The application knows what counts as blocking an exit in metres. An agent using DOM automation would have to infer geometry from pixels. With WebMCP, the floor state and rules are exposed directly as structured data. State is shared. The human and agent both modify the same floor plan during the same session. Read, preview, and write are separated. Six of the nine tools use readOnlyHint . Tools that can affect the floor only generate previews, and the user approves changes before they are applied. That separation lives in the tool contract rather than in prompt instructions. Refusals are structured. A blocked proposal returns the rule ID, rule statement, offending item, and numeric shortfall. The agent can replan using actual constraint data instead of guessing why a call failed. What people and agents can do together The core use case is constrained spatial planning. The human defines the boundaries and important decisions. The agent optimises inside them. The application guarantees that those boundaries are respected. Without that enforcement, the human either does the optimisation manually or delegates it and rechecks every result. WebMCP enables a third model: delegate the arithmetic, keep the judgment, and turn corrections into persistent constraints. How WebMCP was implemented ConstraintCanvas registers nine tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , grouped into inspection, proposal, explanation, and constraint authoring. Two headers are required before document.modelContext is exposed: Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) Tools are defined as descriptors and registered through a shared bridge that wraps every execute call. This keeps logging and refusal handling at the tool boundary instead of duplicating it inside each implementation. Each tool has its own abort controller so the surface can be withdrawn and republished cleanly. Results are returned as JSON. The most interesting part is that the tool contract changes at runtime . When a user ratifies a new rule, the proposal tools are re-registered with the active constraints included in their description , then the surface emits toolchange . That means a correction changes what the agent is told it can do before the next call is created, not only what the application rejects afterwards. Validation runs in three passes: Check locks as hard boundaries. Compare rule violations before and after the proposal. Convert valid proposals into a preview for human approval. The differential check is important because an existing violation should not block a proposal that actually improves the layout. How I built it The app uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, SVG, and IBM Carbon design tokens. It is deployed on Vercel. There is no state library and no canvas library. The constraint engine is intentionally simple. Placement uses a greedy search with scoring rather than a general solver. The priority is not algorithmic complexity. It is producing layouts that remain valid and explainable. Eight built-in rules use the same evaluation engine as user-created rules. For egress, the app runs a flood fill outward from doors across the floor grid. Straight-line distance is not enough because an object can be physically close to an exit while still being blocked by surrounding furniture. Circulation also enforces a minimum free-area ratio: $$ \frac{A_{\text{floor}} - \sum_i w_i h_i}{A_{\text{floor}}} \ge 0.70 $$ This gives seat maximisation a hard upper bound. The app also includes a small agent panel that calls getTools and executeTool against the same surface, so the full interaction can be demonstrated without a separate agent browser. Challenges Different WebMCP implementations exposed different APIs. The spec describes ModelContext as an EventTarget , so I initially used addEventListener for toolchange . That worked in Chrome but failed in ChatGPT's implementation, causing React to unmount and render a blank page. Native calls are now feature detected against a minimum surface of registerTool , with regression tests for reduced implementations. Bad refusals waste agent turns. An early optimise_layout refusal only returned: Unknown objective. The agent had no way to discover valid inputs and spent several calls guessing. Refusals now require a next_step , and invalid values return the accepted alternatives. Thinking models preserve metadata across tool calls. Gemini 3 attaches a thought signature to function call parts. I initially rebuilt the response from extracted tool calls and dropped that metadata. The server route now forwards the original model turn unchanged. Valid layouts can still look wrong. Early plans passed every rule but broke the visual rhythm of existing seating. The optimiser now detects repeated furniture spacing and includes alignment in its scoring function. Model calls needed caching. One planning task could use five or six requests because the agent repeatedly inspected unchanged state. Inspection results are now cached per conversation and invalidated when a proposal changes the floor. What I learned A tool contract should be written as if it is the agent's only source of truth. A refusal should explain what failed and what the agent can do next. Otherwise it becomes a dead end that wastes tokens and tool calls. I also learned not to assume that one implementation of an emerging standard represents all of them. Most importantly, WebMCP is not only useful because a webpage can expose tools. The more interesting capability is that the tool surface itself can change at runtime. That allows a human correction to become part of the application's active contract, which is much stronger than asking the model to remember it. title: Data Airlock
pitch: Clean sensitive datasets with AI agents—without uploading raw data. WebMCP enables local analysis, human-approved cleaning, capability-gap detection, and safe tool evolution.
about_excerpt: Clean sensitive datasets with AI agents—without uploading raw data. WebMCP enables local analysis, human-approved cleaning, capability-gap detection, and safe tool evolution. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are extremely useful for understanding and cleaning data, but there is a fundamental problem with sensitive datasets: normally, the agent needs access to the data itself. Data Airlock explores a different model: An agent can work on a dataset it can never read. The raw file stays on the user's device and is processed locally in the browser. The agent receives only bounded, pseudonymized and aggregate evidence through WebMCP. What it does Data Airlock is a local-first environment for analyzing and cleaning JSONL and CSV datasets with an AI agent while keeping raw records outside the agent boundary. A user can ask ChatGPT to analyze a dataset in natural language. Data Airlock performs the actual work locally and exposes safe WebMCP tools that let the agent: inspect aggregate dataset profiles and quality findings; identify affected pseudonymous fields without revealing their original values; prepare cleaning actions; run a real local second-pass simulation; inspect aggregate simulation impact; detect structural patterns that are not covered by any active capability; create or evolve capabilities with Forge; evaluate candidates locally using aggregate coverage, specificity, overlap and stability metrics; retrieve the open-source source code of cleaning tools when needed; access an interactive Data Airlock guide. The included production demo is a real 500 MiB dataset processed by the same local engine used for user files. Human authority by design The agent can analyze, reason, propose and simulate, but it cannot approve a destructive operation on behalf of the user. The cleaning lifecycle is deliberately: PROPOSE → SIMULATE → HUMAN APPROVAL → EXECUTE Human approval happens independently in the Data Airlock UI. Changing an approved plan invalidates that approval and requires a new simulation and review. This separates two different security boundaries: data access and execution authority . Capability Gap Scan and Forge A fixed set of tools cannot anticipate every structure that may appear in real-world data. Data Airlock therefore includes a local Capability Gap Scanner . It recognizes broad structural families such as date/time formats, locale-dependent numbers, identifiers, encoded tokens, network formats, structured text, Unicode/script mixtures, length distributions and other patterns. If a field contains meaningful structure that no active capability explains, the agent can receive safe aggregate evidence about that gap without seeing the values that caused it. The agent can then use Forge to create a new capability or evolve a related existing one. Before adoption, candidates go through bounded validation and can be evaluated locally against the gap. The agent receives only aggregate metrics such as structural coverage, specificity, overlap and stability. The principle is: The agent can expand its capabilities, not its access to your data. Why WebMCP WebMCP is what makes the architecture possible. Instead of building a separate agent backend or uploading the dataset to an API, the website exposes a controlled set of capabilities directly to the agent. The browser owns the dataset and computation. WebMCP provides the agent with a narrow semantic interface containing only the information it actually needs. This means the agent can participate in a useful end-to-end workflow while the raw dataset remains local. Data Airlock currently exposes read-only analysis and guidance tools, controlled plan-management tools, Forge, and a dynamically gated execution capability that exists only after real human approval. Privacy boundary The agent never receives raw dataset records or original field values through the Data Airlock WebMCP tools. It can receive things such as: aggregate counts; finding categories; pseudonymous field IDs such as field_003 ; cleaning-plan metadata; aggregate simulation impact; aggregate capability-gap evidence; aggregate candidate-evaluation metrics; safe receipts and state; open-source tool source code. The application requires no backend, no account and no API key for local dataset processing. Building it Data Airlock is built in TypeScript and React and runs entirely in the browser. Large datasets are processed using automatic Web Workers. JSONL and CSV are streamed through the local processing pipeline, and output can be written using browser-local storage / file capabilities depending on the environment. The WebMCP layer is intentionally separated from the raw-data engine. Agent-visible results are projected through bounded privacy-safe representations before leaving the local runtime. The production deployment is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Challenges The hardest part was not detecting data-quality problems. It was preserving a meaningful agent experience while keeping a strict capability boundary. We had to make sure that: raw values never leaked through normal results, errors or edge cases; the agent could not manufacture human approval; stale approvals could not be replayed after a plan changed; WebMCP registrations remained safe across browser-host lifecycle changes; large files stayed practical without moving processing to a backend; Forge could evolve functionality without becoming an arbitrary-code escape hatch; capability discovery produced useful evidence without exposing examples from the dataset. We also built extensive deterministic, privacy, lifecycle and end-to-end tests around those boundaries. What we learned The most interesting lesson was that hiding raw data does not have to make an agent useless. If the local application exposes the right abstractions, an agent can still reason about counts, structural families, impact, coverage and state transitions. That led to the third principle behind Data Airlock: Airlock does not only hide data from the agent — it gives the agent enough safe evidence to know when it still does not know how to handle something. What's next The same architecture can extend beyond dataset cleaning. The broader idea is a capability-oriented interface where agents can work with sensitive local information through safe evidence and constrained actions rather than unrestricted access to the underlying data. Data Airlock is one demonstration of that model. title: DeskInTab
pitch: Give your AI agent a computer in your browser. Use the same apps to write, draw, analyze data, and work with files.
about_excerpt: Give your AI agent a computer in your browser. Use the same apps to write, draw, analyze data, and work with files. Like Comment Story Updates The Harbor release brief in Documents, with its exported PDF open in Preview. A Canvas diagram and project handoff with source files and a question for the user. Why I built it I wanted to give an AI agent its own personal computer. While exploring WebMCP, I started playing with the idea of a virtual operating system inside the browser. Each app could expose its own tools, letting the agent use a whole desktop to do different kinds of work. DeskInTab is that experiment. The agent gets a computer to work in, and you can use the same apps beside it. What it does DeskInTab brings everyday computer work into one browser desktop. You and your agent can: Take notes in Markdown or plain text, write formatted documents, read PDFs, and export reports. Analyze data in spreadsheets with formulas and charts. Sketch ideas and edit diagrams together in Canvas. Use Terminal to search files, extract document text, transform data, and run Bash pipelines. Browse and organize files, track tasks, and save project decisions and next steps. Turn JSON data into small apps with search, filters, and links to the original sources. The apps share one filesystem. A chart from Sheets can go into a document, and Terminal can process the files you see in Finder. You can open the agent's work, change it yourself, and continue together. Home saves preferences and reusable instructions. Projects keeps handoffs so an agent can leave a question for you and a later session can pick up your answer. Files persist after a browser reload. The video shows one example, planning a release for the fictional Harbor reading app. The agent works through interview notes, spreadsheet analysis, a release brief and PDF, tasks, and a Canvas roadmap. Why WebMCP fits The desktop exposes 89 WebMCP tools. Each tool calls the same application services as the human controls, so agent actions change the apps and files you have open. This lets the agent combine several apps in one task while you follow and edit the work. How it works Svelte 5 and TypeScript provide the interface. ZenFS stores the shared filesystem in IndexedDB. ZetaOffice handles documents and spreadsheets, Excalidraw handles drawings, and just-bash runs Terminal commands inside the browser without host or network access. What I learned Passing tool tests didn't guarantee that an agent could discover the full catalog. A client size limit blocked discovery until repeated schemas shared references. Tests now check the full payload and verify that every validation rule survives. Two desktop tabs can conflict over stored files. A Web Lock prevents that, and saved versions make edits recoverable. What's next Improve Office startup and workbook autosaving, and make project handoffs easier to find. The app currently keeps one workspace in your browser. Workspace packs let you back it up or move it. title: Ensemble
pitch: Your look does not come from one store. Ensemble composes a purchasable outfit across Shopify stores through the tools the stores themselves publish: try it on your photo, mix catalogs, and checkout
about_excerpt: Your look does not come from one store. Ensemble composes a purchasable outfit across Shopify stores through the tools the stores themselves publish: try it on your photo, mix catalogs, and checkout Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Shopify storefronts already register native WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . It is on by default on Liquid storefronts, no store opt-in: catalog search, product lookup, and cart updates, published by the page itself as a contract any agent may use. The contract is live. The agent side is what has been missing. Meanwhile the actual shopping problem has not moved. An outfit rarely comes from one store. Putting one together means tabs, screenshots, and re-finding everything at checkout, and the try-on tools that exist paste a product image onto a photo without knowing what the item is, what it costs, or whether your size is in stock. Ensemble puts the two together. Shopping across stores is the shape WebMCP was made for: the page itself declares what an agent may do here, search this catalog, add this variant, and the agent composes those grants across origins into one task. No scraping, no guessing at themes, just the surface the store maintains for itself. What it does Ensemble is a Chrome extension. Browse any Shopify store and its catalog loads into a side panel automatically; every store you visit becomes a chip, and one look spans all of them with a running total. Hover a product tile on the store's own grid and two buttons appear: Render on me shows that item on your photo without leaving the page, and Suggest matches proposes pieces from the store's live inventory that complete the outfit. On a product page, a compact pill offers the same controls and picks up the exact variant you selected, so US 2 on the page is US 2 in the cart. When the look is right, one click fills every store's cart with exactly those variants. Checkout stays native per store: Ensemble fills the carts, you finish each one in the store's own checkout, where trust and payment already live. Every item in a look is a specific, in-stock variant with a live price. A look in Ensemble is purchasable, not a moodboard. The division of labor is the point. The person makes the taste decisions: which jeans, which size, whether the jacket earns its place. The agent does the cross-store bookkeeping: searching the catalogs you have browsed, resolving each choice to an in-stock variant with a real price, filling carts on multiple origins in one action. And the storefront draws the boundary, because its registered tools define exactly what the agent may touch. None of that was reliably possible when acting on a store meant scraping its theme. How we built it The WebMCP layer is a MAIN-world content script injected at document_start . When the browser exposes the WebMCP API (Chrome with the WebMCP feature enabled), it wraps modelContext.registerTool and captures every tool object the storefront registers. On stock Chrome, where no native API exists yet, it plants a minimal modelContext shim first; Shopify's storefront script feature-detects it and registers its ten native tools into the shim unchanged. Either way the extension ends up holding the store's own tool objects and serves listTools and callTool to the extension's isolated world over a postMessage bridge. Product lookups and cart adds go through the store's registered tools first: get_product for variant data, update_cart with variant GIDs (Shopify's global IDs), get_cart to confirm what actually landed. Storefronts that register nothing fall back to the public /products.json and /cart/add.js endpoints, so the same flows work everywhere and the supported surface is preferred wherever it exists. The overlay UI lives in an open shadow root so store CSS cannot touch it, and finds product cards by climbing from the hover target to the smallest container holding exactly one product handle, which survives themes that cover their tiles with overlay layers. Try-on renders and style suggestions run on Gemini with the user's own key. There is no server: the photo and the key stay in local extension storage. Challenges we ran into The tool-call contract has sharp edges the examples do not show. executeTool at the API boundary takes a JSON string and rejects a tool name in place of the registered tool object, but a captured tool's execute callback takes parsed arguments, because the native layer parses before invoking. Passing the wrong shape does not error loudly; Shopify answers with a polite "No line_items provided" and your cart stays empty. We also learned that update_cart 's top-level id addresses existing cart lines only; adds must nest the variant GID under item . On a product page, the store's own get_product returns only the currently selected variant, a single-element array. To honor the size a shopper picked we resolve variants catalog-first and match requested IDs in both GID and numeric forms, verified live by watching a stored look flip from the default US 0 to the selected US 2. Repeat adds taught us that Shopify dedupes them, returning updated: false with no item count, so cart confirmation falls back to get_cart rather than trusting the add response. And real storefront themes fight overlays: one of the live demo storefronts covers its product tiles with layers that swallow hover targets, which is what forced the container-climbing card detection. Accomplishments we are proud of The full loop runs against live storefronts: catalog in, look built, render on the shopper's photo, and both stores' carts filled with the exact variants, a dress from one catalog and wool runners from another under one total. The native tool path works on stock Chrome today through the shim capture, so the WebMCP story does not wait for a browser flag. And variant fidelity is proven end to end, the size picked on the page to the line in the cart. What we learned WebMCP's design carries real weight in practice: because the page defines the tools, an agent can act on a store it has never seen without guessing at DOM structure, and the same contract that serves a chat agent serves a product UI like ours. The gap between a demo and a product is exactly the sharp edges above, and the supported surface made them tractable to debug. What's next Tighter checkout is the obvious V2, exploring how far per-store checkout can collapse toward one action. Beyond that, the look itself wants to become a page: a shareable board that registers its own WebMCP tools, so your agent can discuss, edit, and price a look you were sent. At that point Ensemble both consumes the open web's tools and contributes surface back to it. Try it Open https://ensemble-dhf.pages.dev and download ensemble.zip (or clone github.com/sneg55/ensemble). chrome://extensions, Developer mode, Load unpacked, pick the folder. Paste a free Gemini API key in the extension options (aistudio.google.com/apikey). Visit any Shopify store, click the toolbar icon or just hover a product tile. Optional, for the native API path: run Chrome with --enable-features=WebMCP. Without the flag the shim capture keeps every feature working. title: Galleon
pitch: Galleon lets Codex pay publishers for original content, delivering valuable answers while funding writers to produce more knowledge.
about_excerpt: Galleon lets Codex pay publishers for original content, delivering valuable answers while funding writers to produce more knowledge. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Publishers earn through subscriptions and advertising. Agents do not look at ads, and they often need one authoritative source rather than a full subscription. A publisher's work can become more useful to agents while generating less revenue for the people who created it. Galleon asks a simple question: what if a webpage could quote an exact price to an agent, let the person approve it, and return the licensed source with its canonical citation? What it does Galleon gives an AI agent an authenticated wallet with human-controlled spending limits. A participating publisher exposes two WebMCP tools. inspect_source returns free metadata, provenance, the exact price, access rights, and a signed offer. unlock_source redeems a short-lived entitlement and returns the full article as formatted Markdown with its canonical citation. Payment authority never enters the publisher page. After the person approves the exact source, price, and rights, the agent calls purchase_offer through the user's local Galleon wallet MCP. The wallet validates the offer, enforces spending policy, records the purchase, and returns an entitlement scoped to that source and publisher. The complete flow is intentionally small: const offer = await inspect_source({}); await human.approve({ source: offer.source.title, price: offer.offer.display_price, rights: offer.offer.rights, }); const purchase = await purchase_offer({ offer_token: offer.offer.offer_token, expected_amount_minor: offer.offer.amount_minor, expected_currency: offer.offer.currency, idempotency_key: crypto.randomUUID(), }); const article = await unlock_source({ entitlement_token: purchase.entitlement.token, }); return { markdown: article.source.markdown, citation: article.source.citation, }; The current prototype uses test credits. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the commercial terms travel with the source. The agent discovers the offer on the page instead of scraping a paywall or sending the user through a separate checkout. We pair WebMCP with a traditional MCP because they represent different trust boundaries. WebMCP belongs to the publisher page and exposes page-scoped source tools. The wallet MCP belongs to the user and holds identity, balance, policy, and purchase authority. Together, they let a person and an agent buy one authoritative source without exposing payment credentials or moving the article into an intermediary catalog. We believe the end-state of Galleon is one where the human browsing experience remains the same as it has historically been and ad-supported, while agents are metered for their consumption. How we built it We built and deployed Galleon on floo , which helped us ship a multi-service application with Codex and allocate necessary resources such as our postgres database. Codex was our primary agentic development tool. We used Codex to implement the TypeScript application, inspect the repository, test the real browser journey, exercise the WebMCP tools, review trust boundaries, diagnose deployment failures, and iterate on the product experience. The system has three parts: A consumer application for accounts, test-credit wallets, spending policies, and purchases. An authenticated wallet MCP that validates offers, records retry-safe ledger transactions in PostgreSQL, and issues short-lived entitlements. An independently hosted publisher that registers inspect_source and unlock_source through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Offers and entitlements are signed and bound to the content, publisher origin, and browser session. The publisher receives only the entitlement. It never receives the user's wallet credential. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was the economics of very small purchases. Traditional credit-card checkout is poorly suited to charging a few cents whenever an agent needs one source. We built a test-credit wallet and balanced ledger to prove the interaction before connecting production financial infrastructure. The second challenge was separating trust correctly. The publisher needs proof of purchase but must never receive the wallet credential. The wallet must pay the correct publisher but must never trust unsigned claims from page JavaScript. This led us to connect page-scoped WebMCP tools and the authenticated wallet MCP with signed, short-lived capabilities. Live testing also exposed a cross-service signing-key mismatch. Separate service containers generated separate keys, so the wallet correctly rejected the publisher's offer. We moved the key into shared secret-backed configuration and added tests for the multi-service boundary. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a coherent product experience, not only a tool demo. A user can create an account, fund a test wallet, connect Codex, inspect a paid source, approve the exact terms, purchase it, and unlock it on the publisher's own website. The publisher retains its content and canonical URL. The user retains payment authority. The agent receives the evidence and citation it needs. We think that this idea of building a consumer-grade wallet and payments infrastructure could really benefit publishers who need a way to transform their businesses for the AI era. What we learned WebMCP and MCP are complementary. WebMCP provides contextual tools controlled by the publisher. MCP provides durable authority controlled by the user. We also learned that agent payments are a capability and trust problem before they are a checkout problem. Origin binding, session binding, explicit approval, retry safety, and narrow entitlements make the experience understandable and safe. What's next for Galleon Our next step is focused: connect Galleon to real financial infrastructure and work directly with publishers to help them earn from agent demand. The prototype uses test credits today. The goal is real settlement that supports the people producing the knowledge agents depend on. title: Grounded - Collaborative AI Workspace for Construction
pitch: Agents excel at pulling evidence across a pile of docs. People excel at reading drawings. Grounded is built so each can stay in that lane instead of forcing one to do both.
about_excerpt: Agents excel at pulling evidence across a pile of docs. People excel at reading drawings. Grounded is built so each can stay in that lane instead of forcing one to do both. Like Comment Story Updates What I built I built Grounded because construction document review mixes work that agents handle well with judgments they should not make alone. An agent can search schedules and compare written requirements. Reading plan symbols, following linework, or counting openings on a drawing still needs a construction professional to do reliably. The tools are meant to work in a lot of review setups, but most people do not have contract drawings sitting around, so the demo ships with a fixed project. It includes an open-source Virginia Farmhouse drawing set and two example submittals. The door package is seeded with real issues for the agent to find. The window package is clean on purpose, so the review has a known pass case next to a known fail. What the agent actually gets is structured. It can search the evidence we already extracted from the PDFs, jump the workbench to a page, block, or region, and open an Assistance Request when it hits something it should not guess at. The human answers in the same workspace. The agent comes back later and finishes the disposition from that structured response. Why WebMCP fits These workflows are a mess of strengths and weak spots. Agents are good at finding textual evidence across a pile of sources and stitching it together. They still struggle at reading construction drawings the way the job requires. AEC-Bench is a useful look at how hard that still is. I treat drawings as close to a worst case for today's agents, and the cost of a miss is high. A denied submittal can add weeks. A bid off by 50% can be hundreds of thousands of dollars. So I stopped asking the model to do the part a construction professional already does well, and I stopped asking that professional to do the part the model does well: collecting and reconciling evidence across a pile of documents. WebMCP is what makes that split practical. Without it you usually get a painful loop. The agent asks for something, you open another app, mark up the drawing, export it, and paste answers back into chat. With WebMCP the agent discovers tools on the live page, works from immutable document versions, and creates a request tied to exact pages. The reviewer answers in place. After a reload the agent can recover the response without depending on conversation memory. I do not think this pattern is limited to construction. Anywhere an agent needs a durable human judgment tied to a specific artifact, the same shape applies. How I built it Grounded registers eight WebMCP tools in one all-or-nothing attempt and only reports "WebMCP ready" when the full set is up: get_grounded_help , get_project_workspace , list_project_documents , search_project_documents , inspect_document_evidence , navigate_document , create_assistance_request , get_assistance_request The document tools expose prepared artifacts. There is no runtime OCR and no external document-processing call in the demo path. Search can point at likely content, but a claim has to come from inspected evidence. Navigation moves the visible PDF workbench to a page, a semantic block, or a normalized region for visual inspection or to direct the user where they should be looking. Assistance Requests are the durable handoff. For a Point Set, the reviewer clicks locations on the PDF. Marks live in an overlay separate from the PDF.js display layer so they stay aligned through resize and zoom. Responses persist in IndexedDB under a tab-scoped Demo Session. Unfinished Zustand drafts intentionally die on reload. Committed responses do not. Contracts use TypeBox for TypeScript inference, browser registration, and runtime validation. A recording Model Context adapter exercises the same behavior under Vitest. Stack is React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Dexie, Zustand, a custom PDF.js display layer, and Cloudflare Workers with static assets via Wrangler. Challenges I ran into Getting the agent to stop inventing visual counts was the hard product problem. Early versions would "see" openings that were never marked. The fix was process, not prompting: search is a hint, inspect is required, and drawing interpretation goes to the human through a Point Set instead of a freeform chat answer. The other hard part was teaching the agent how to use the app without a skill. Normal MCP is starting to grow discoverable skills that come with the server. WebMCP has something drawn up for that, but it is early, and I did not want to hand judges a big skill install just to run the demo. So a lot of the work went into tool names, descriptions, and contracts that could carry the workflow on their own. That ended up working, but a skill would have made the same behavior clearer, and on a real project I would almost certainly put one on the agent so it knows how to work with our documents. I also wanted a much larger tool set than the eight that shipped. Context made that a bad idea. These reviews chew through a lot of the agent's window. A lot of it is cached across repeated tool calls, which can get better, but the structured evidence coming out of the document parser was still token-heavy and full of fields that did not help the decision. We had to thin that payload until the loop fit. It is in a decent spot now, but still could be better. What I learned The real benefit of WebMCP, for me, is collaboration. I went into this hoping an agent could own more of the review than it can. It cannot. Not yet. Drawing interpretation, accountable counts, and the judgment call behind a disposition still need a person who knows the work. That does not make the collaboration temporary. Even as the models get better at reading drawings, a shared workspace like this stays useful. The human still needs to stay current on what the agent found, what it skipped, and what it is asking for. WebMCP is a clean way to keep that loop in one place instead of exporting screenshots and pasting answers back into chat. I do not see WebMCP as a stopgap. Once you have a durable way for an agent and a professional to hand work back and forth against the same artifact, a lot of other workflows open up. Construction is just the one I built first. What's next Widen the Assistance response types past Point Sets, support real project imports beyond the bundled Virginia Farmhouse set, and harden the review trail so a disposition can cite every mark and every document version it used. Longer term I want this sitting inside an actual submittal workflow, not only a hackathon demo session. title: KumiDraw
pitch: KumiDraw is a system design tool. Type cache and the box becomes a Cache. Your AI reads that model, not a screenshot, so it finds the bottleneck and asks the right question.
about_excerpt: KumiDraw is a system design tool. Type cache and the box becomes a Cache. Your AI reads that model, not a screenshot, so it finds the bottleneck and asks the right question. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration We kept drawing the same architecture twice. Once on a whiteboard for the conversation, once in a document for the record, and the two disagreed by the afternoon. Then we watched an AI try to help with a diagram. It took a screenshot and guessed. It read a label wrong, missed an arrow that ran behind a box, and called a queue a database. That is not the model failing. We had handed it a picture of a system instead of the system. WebMCP is the fix for that. A page can hand an agent typed tools instead of pixels. It only helps if the page has something typed to hand over, and that is where our tool already was. What it does KumiDraw draws as fast as a whiteboard and stores a typed graph. Draw a box, and it is already a Service. Type cache and it becomes a Cache, with the right glyph. Type redis and it becomes Redis with cache kind, the same node refined rather than replaced. You are never asked to fill in a form. The notes are a projection of that graph, so the drawing and the write-up cannot disagree. Because the graph is typed, rules sit on top of it. KumiDraw lints an architecture the way a compiler lints code: a synchronous call crossing a trust boundary, a queue with no consumer, a store read by four services with nothing cached in front of it, the one node every path has to pass through. Your AI reads the graph, not the screen. Through WebMCP it calls read_design and gets nodes, boundaries and typed calls as text. No screenshot, and no guessing which arrow starts where. It knows an edge is async because the model says so, not because a dash pattern hinted at it. It sees the node that is scrolled off the canvas. It reads the same lint findings you see, so it spends its attention on the question a reviewer would ask next instead of on spotting the obvious. It also imports formats we never wrote a parser for. Paste a Terraform file and ask for it on the canvas. The agent already reads HCL, so it calls add_node and connect , and because kind is a closed list of thirteen words its mapping is constrained rather than invented. An aws_elasticache_cluster becomes a Cache with the Redis glyph. A VPC becomes a boundary. The same holds for CloudFormation, a Kubernetes manifest, a Pulumi program, or a page of meeting notes. We ship no parser for any of them, and we never will. How we built it using Nuxt 4 and Vue 3 and using codex, claude and gemini Four decisions made the WebMCP work small: Kinds are a closed vocabulary. The union that picks a node's glyph is the agent's JSON Schema enum. An agent cannot invent a type, and Other records the user's own word when the model has none. Every change is a named, invertible op. Undo, persistence and the command registry come out of one mechanism, so an agent's edit is an ordinary edit. One write surface. useDocument ends with a comment saying nothing outside its list may change the document. The tools are a projection of that list, not a second path into the store. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool and tear down with an AbortController. Work lives in IndexedDB. The build is static and ships to Cloudflare Pages. Challenges we ran into WebMCP brought churn of its own. The API moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext during the origin trial, and most of what ranks for "WebMCP" repeats itself and disagrees on dates, so we worked from the Chrome docs and the spec repo and treated the rest as rumour. The hardest call was paging. Chrome recommends 1.5K characters per tool result, and our first instinct was to page the node list. That is wrong. An agent handed page one reasons about a system whose datastore it never saw, and the failure is silent. We compress instead. One line per node, and the text that grows without limit moved to a tool an agent asks for on purpose. Then labels. Our @ links bind by label, because people type words. An agent cannot, because a label is allowed to be empty by design and two nodes can share one. Agents get ids, and every write returns the ids it created. Accomplishments that we're proud of The type earns its keep three times over. One closed union draws the right glyph, feeds the linter, and becomes the agent's input schema. We deleted a roadmap. Every import format we were going to write a parser for is now a conversation, and code we never write cannot rot. No confirmation dialogs on agent writes. The op log makes undo the answer to a wrong edit, which is a better answer than a modal. The privacy claim survives. Registering a tool transmits nothing, and no tool name, description or enum carries document content, so nothing leaves the machine until you ask a question. What we learned A screenshot is a lossy export of your own data. If a model has to look at your app to understand it, the app is hiding what it already knows. Decide what can be decided in code. We nearly shipped a critique tool, which would have been our rubric competing with a better one inside the model. Rules that are true or false run as lint, and the model does the judgement. Agents want intent shaped tools, not keystroke shaped ones. We nearly projected our command registry into forty tools. Commands are for hands. Tool metadata is read on page visit, before anyone has asked anything. An enum of live node ids would have leaked the document for free. Building for an agent made the app better for people. Every tool we wanted to expose turned out to be a gap in the write surface. title: lapse — what WebMCP tools actually accept
pitch: A WebMCP tool publishes an input schema. Nothing enforces it. lapse probes Google's own reference demos and finds 17 of 17 imperative tools accept input their own schema forbids. 225 of 289 probes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP tool publishes an input schema. Nothing enforces it. lapse probes Google's own reference demos and finds 17 of 17 imperative tools accept input their own schema forbids. 225 of 289 probes. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of## Inspiration A WebMCP tool publishes an input schema. That schema is a promise to the agent: these are the fields, this one is required, this one has to be one of three values. Nothing enforces it. Not the browser, not the API. That turns out to be deliberate, and the spec's own issue 92 has been debating whether it should change since February. I found it by accident while testing a tool I was writing. I sent it a quantity of "two" as a string where the schema declared a number, and it went straight through to my handler. Then I sent negative 999 cups against a declared minimum of 1. That went through too. The schema I had carefully written was decoration. So I stopped building what I was building and went to measure how far it goes. What it does lapse measures the gap between what a WebMCP tool promises and what it actually accepts. The targets are not toys written to fail. They are the official Chrome WebMCP reference demos from GoogleChromeLabs, vendored unmodified under Apache-2.0. The coffee shop, the pizza maker, the flight search, the ticket booking, the real estate map. The code Chrome ships to teach people how to build with WebMCP. lapse enumerates every tool through getTools, reads each declared schema, and generates input that schema forbids. Nulls where a string was declared. Booleans and arrays and objects where a scalar was declared. Values outside a declared enum. Numbers past a declared maximum. Required fields removed. A ten thousand character string. Control and bidirectional characters. Text written to sound like an instruction aimed at the agent. Then it calls the tool and records what happened. 299 probes across 23 tools on 8 sites. 225 violations. 17 of 17 imperative tools accept input their own published schema forbids, at 78 percent of every scored probe. The clearest single case: the pizza maker declares topping as a fixed list. Send it a value that is not on the list and it replies that it added one off-menu topping. The violations cluster identically across every site. That is what a platform property looks like, not seven separate authoring mistakes. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP It could not exist anywhere else. It runs inside the browser, against live tools, using the API's own enumeration and execution surface, and the thing it measures is a property of WebMCP itself that no existing tool reports. Chrome ships an evals CLI that tests whether a model picks the right tool. Nothing tests whether a tool honours what it published. How it makes for a better experience A developer who wants to know whether their tools are safe under an agent has one option today, which is to write eval cases by hand and read the output. lapse gives a verdict in under a minute, per tool, per constraint, with the failing input printed next to what the tool did with it. You do not have to guess which of your fields is unguarded. It tells you. What people and agents can do together here lapse registers four WebMCP tools of its own, so the audit is driven by conversation rather than by clicking. Ask which sites are loaded and what each one exposes. Ask it to run the audit. Ask for every violation on one site. Ask it to export the report for a bug filing. Auditing a site used to mean a person writing test cases one at a time and reading them one at a time. Here the agent generates and executes hundreds against live tools while the human watches the result form on a shared page. Neither side could do it alone at that speed. The agent has no way to reach into a page and call its tools without WebMCP, and the person has no patience for 299 hand-written cases. How I implemented WebMCP lapse uses the API in both directions. As a client it calls getTools to enumerate tools across a same-origin frame tree, executeTool to drive them with generated input, toolchange to track registration, AbortController to cancel calls that stop responding, and it reads annotations to check whether a tool that echoes agent-directed text sets untrustedContentHint. As a server it registers its own: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "run_audit", description: "Run the full contract audit across every vendored demo. Returns probe, violation and not-measured counts.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {} }, execute: async () => (await runAudit()) || "audit produced no findings", annotations: { readOnlyHint: false } }); Four tools in total: list_targets, run_audit, get_findings, export_report. Challenges, and the verdict that saved me twice Every probe lands as HONOURED, VIOLATED, or NOT MEASURED. A probe that could not be generated, could not be run, or never returned is recorded as unmeasured. It is never counted as a pass. That third verdict caught two false findings that would otherwise have shipped. The first version read inputSchema as an object. It actually arrives as a JSON string. Every schema-derived probe silently generated nothing while the tool confidently reported five violations as though that were the answer. The arithmetic gave it away: four tools, nine probes, exactly the two unconditional checks each. The second was worse because it flattered me. Declarative tools appeared to validate perfectly, which would have been a lovely headline. So I suppressed the form navigation that was cutting those tools short, reran, and the outcomes changed. The guard was altering the thing it was supposed to leave alone. I removed it and marked six declarative tools unmeasured rather than publish the better number. What I learned This is not a bug report. The working group already knows the schema is advisory. Issue 92 on the spec repo, "Who owns the validation layer?", has been open since February and argues that inputSchema is only a semantic hint, that validation falls to each tool author individually, and that the browser should probably own it instead. What that discussion has never had is a measurement. It has been argued from experience and intuition for six months. lapse gives it a number: across the reference demos Chrome itself ships to teach the API, 17 of 17 imperative tools have unguarded input paths, and 78 percent of probes that violate a declared constraint are accepted anyway. The separate question I could not settle is the declarative side. Calling a declarative tool submits its form and navigates the document, so it cannot be probed twice. I tried suppressing that navigation, watched it change the outcomes it was meant to leave alone, removed it, and marked those six tools unmeasured. Whether declarative validation is genuinely stronger remains an open question, and lapse says so rather than guessing. What's next More targets, including the demos that need a build step. Chrome publishes an eval JSON format for its CLI, and lapse should read and write it so the same cases can run in a browser against live tools instead of only in a terminal.
