title: Swarm | Spaces Where Humans and Agents Work Together
pitch: OS and Decision Graphs for model agnostic agentic AI work. Build complex systems using Swarm Spaces as building blocks, collaborate and fully manage with other Humans and Agents via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: OS and Decision Graphs for model agnostic agentic AI work. Build complex systems using Swarm Spaces as building blocks, collaborate and fully manage with other Humans and Agents via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP Tools (54 available) Initiating prompt pasted into demo showing Swarm UI in browser Human approval required before agent can execute task Separate agent from the ChatGPT hosted in Swarm Cloud begins executing the task ChatGPT uses WebMCP to return the results back into the thread and from here, collaborative work can continue Result is published in the Swarm UI as an artifact Inspiration For this challenge I wanted to explore a more consequential use of WebMCP: using a website as a secure gateway from one conversation into persistent work performed by other agents, without removing humans from important decisions. Real world work spans shared evidence, specialist agents, asynchronous execution, organizational permissions, and decisions that must remain accountable to a person. Swarm already organizes this work in persistent Spaces. The WebMCP Challenge gave me the perfect opportunity to make each Space directly understandable and operable by ChatGPT through a bounded, typed interface instead of DOM scraping/browser automation (or strictly API/regular MCP). What it does My demo takes place in a visually simple Supplier Launch Decision Space. The Space contains two supplier evidence Artifacts, a Decision Graph, an unresolved recycled material compliance claim, a connected Supplier Verification Agent (cloud hosted GPT5.6 Terra through Swarm), and a human approval policy. From one ChatGPT conversation, the user gives a single goal. ChatGPT then uses the tools exposed by the active Swarm page to: Read the Space metadata, Decision Graph, participants, and existing Artifacts. Identify the unresolved compliance claim and the exact evidence already available. Request a verification Run from Supplier Verification Agent. Post a durable status message containing the delegated agent and Run ID. Stop at a human approval gate before any agent execution begins. Observe the same Run transition into execution after the person approves it in Swarm. Read the completed Run, Markdown Artifact, action traces, evaluation state, evidence IDs, and approval timestamps. The connected cloud hosted agent verifies only what the existing Space evidence supports. In the recorded run, one supplier's recycled aluminum declaration is supported while the second supplier's evidence remains insufficient. The resulting Artifact preserves those distinctions and states that no supplier launch may be approved or promoted without a separate human decision. The Run and Artifact remain in the Space after the initiating ChatGPT conversation ends. Another authorized person or agent can inspect the same Space from anywhere in the world and pickup the work from there. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, a browser agent would have to inspect rendered text, infer which controls represent domain actions, and hope that UI changes do not break its workflow. It would also be difficult to communicate which actions the signed-in user is actually permitted to perform. With WebMCP, the page exposes a Space specific catalog of typed operations. ChatGPT works with concepts such as Runs, Artifacts, approval requests, evaluations, participants, and Decision Graph nodes rather than guessing at buttons or scraping layout. This produces a better experience in four ways: Less friction: one goal can initiate a structured multi-step workflow without repeatedly re-entering context. More reliability: calls target stable domain operations rather than visual coordinates or page structure. Durable collaboration: delegated work, provenance, and results survive outside the original conversation. Visible human control: the browser agent can request and observe an approval gate, but it cannot approve or deny on the person's behalf. This means WebMCP becomes the entry point through which one conversational agent can coordinate persistent execution by other agents inside a controllable workspace. Human authority is a system rule For the gated request, ChatGPT calls swarm_request_agent with: { "required_approval_actions": ["approve.launch"] } Swarm atomically creates the human message, blocked Run, and approval request. The Run is not claimable while the gate is pending. Approving queues that same Run for an authorized runtime; denying cancels it. Approval and denial are deliberately absent from the browser agent's WebMCP tool catalog, so prompt wording cannot bypass the policy. The final read only step compares the recorded approval and execution timestamps. It also distinguishes approval to perform verification from the separate authority to approve a supplier launch. A completed agent task is evidence for a decision, not the decision itself. How I built it The browser adapter is written in TypeScript and registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . The signed-in Swarm page obtains a bounded catalog filtered for the current user and Space. Tool inputs and outputs use explicit schemas, and mutations require stable idempotency keys. Each invocation returns through same origin Swarm API routes. The server remains authoritative for authentication, tenant isolation, Commands, Permits, approval policy, evidence access, response limits, and audit records. The browser receives neither provider credentials nor a general purpose HTTP or SQL tool. Long running work is reconciled through a bounded read only Space revision wait. When the revision changes, ChatGPT uses typed read tools to retrieve the exact Run, Artifact, approval request, trace, or evaluation that changed. This keeps asynchronous execution observable without granting additional authority. The broader Swarm application uses React and Next.js for the product interface, Go services, PostgreSQL, and Google Cloud Run. The public challenge repository contains the reviewed WebMCP browser adapter, public contracts, tests, build instructions, export provenance, and an Apache 2.0 license. It intentionally excludes credentials, provider implementation, and private deployment configuration. Challenges I faced The hardest part for me was preserving one coherent state across ChatGPT, the human facing thread, an approval record, a queued Run, a cloud runtime, and a durable Artifact. I had to make asynchronous state visually and semantically consistent. The approval card must remain linked to the exact Run; the same Run must transition live after approval; and every later read must select that Run rather than a similarly named historical result. I also had to separate observation from authority. A model needs enough context to identify a pending decision and explain it, but that does not mean it should receive the capability to resolve the decision. Enforcing that boundary in server side permissions, rather than relying on prompt instructions, was essential. Finally, I needed a public repository that demonstrates real production integration without exposing private infrastructure or secrets. So I created a reviewed, one way source snapshot with reproducible hashes and tests while keeping the hosted service as an explicit external dependency. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it describes domain intent and policy, not when it merely recreates clicks as tools. Stable IDs, typed contracts, idempotency, provenance, and explicit approval states make agent behaviour easier for both machines and people to understand. I also learned that human in the loop cannot be a sentence added to a prompt. It must be represented by durable state that prevents execution until the right person acts. Once that is true, the interface can clearly show what is waiting, what was approved, what executed, and what authority still remains with a human. What I added for the WebMCP Challenge Swarm existed before the challenge period, although it had no WebMCP capability. The challenge specific work is the WebMCP browser integration and the end to end experience around it: the document.modelContext.registerTool adapter, Permit filtered Space catalog, safe invocation contracts, approval aware agent requests, read only asynchronous reconciliation, public source export, tests, documentation, and the deterministic Supplier Launch Decision demo. What's next The demo uses one ChatGPT orchestrator and one cloud hosted verification agent so the flow is easy to follow. The same model can support larger Spaces in which people and multiple specialist agents contribute research, execution, review, and decisions over time. This means you can have Spaces with multiple humans, dozens of connected agents all working collaboratively. The even bigger scale comes from when you give agents permissions across multiple spaces, allowing for cross space connections and this turns Swarm into a global network layer for humans and agents. Built With chatgpt go google-cloud gpt5.6 javascript

title: Sweet Spot
pitch: SweetSpot helps people find the right area to live by combining their preferences, such as commute time, groceries, parks, schools, and healthcare and see it visually on the map
about_excerpt: SweetSpot helps people find the right area to live by combining their preferences, such as commute time, groceries, parks, schools, and healthcare and see it visually on the map Like Comment Story Updates application-page Inspiration We work for Apple Maps, so maps and geographic information systems are a big part of our daily work. For this hackathon, we wanted to explore the GIS domain from a different angle: helping people make complex location decisions with an AI agent. Choosing where to live often means balancing several needs at once. You may want a short commute, groceries within walking distance, a nearby park, and easy access to healthcare or nearby school for your child. Most map products can answer these questions separately, but finding the areas where all the requirements overlap takes a lot of manual work. That inspired us to build Sweet Spot. What it does Sweet Spot helps people find areas that match several travel and lifestyle needs. A user can ask: “Find an area within an 8-minute bike ride of San Francisco City Hall, a 5-minute walk of a supermarket, and a 4-minute walk of a park.” Using WebMCP, ChatGPT can work directly with the Sweet Spot map. It can search for real places, add travel limits, combine conditions, rank different areas, explain trade-offs, update the plan, undo changes, and create a shareable result. Some preferences are difficult to describe with words or forms. In those cases, the agent can pause and ask the user to draw an area directly on the map. The agent then continues its work using that boundary. Sweet Spot also records whether each action came from the user or the agent, keeping the process visible and reversible. How we built it We built Sweet Spot as a client-side web application using React, TypeScript, MapLibre, Web Workers, H3 spatial indexing, and WebMCP. The application uses real OpenStreetMap street and place data, along with official neighborhood data where available. Instead of drawing simple circles around a destination, Sweet Spot calculates reachable areas using the street network and different travel modes. The product exposes 18 WebMCP tools. These tools use the same application logic as the visible interface, so every agent action immediately appears on the shared map. The geographic calculations run on the user’s device. We use a Web Worker, spatial indexing, and reusable distance caches to keep the interface responsive. Challenges we ran into Our biggest challenge was running large geographic calculations inside the browser. Early versions were slow because they repeatedly searched the road network and recalculated the same distances. We improved this with H3-based lookups, bounded caches, and per-layer progress updates. Location search was also harder than expected. Users often enter partial names, different spellings, or small typos. We added normalized, word-aware, typo-tolerant search with an online fallback. We also learned that WebMCP tools need to support complete user goals, not merely copy individual button actions. We created an atomic planning tool for full requests while keeping smaller tools for later edits and conversation. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Sweet Spot is a complete product experience rather than a WebMCP demonstration added to a map. It was good to see that ChatGPT could build a real geographic plan, update the visible interface, explain the results, and hand control to the user when human judgment is needed. The agent can pause in the middle of its task, ask the user to draw a personal boundary, wait for the response, and then continue calculating. What we learned The agent is good at turning a natural-language request into several structured operations and comparing many results. The user is better at expressing personal preferences, judging the map visually, and making the final decision. WebMCP connects those strengths. The user no longer has to copy an AI recommendation into another product and rebuild the search manually. The agent can use the product’s real tools while the user watches, guides, and corrects the process. What's next for Sweet Spot Next, we want to support more cities and add public transit, live traffic, elevation, housing costs, accessibility needs, and other real-world factors. We also want to improve collaborative planning so families, friends, or teams can contribute their own destinations and preferences to the same workspace. Our larger goal is to make Sweet Spot useful for more than choosing where to live. The same approach could help people select an office, plan public services, compare business locations, or explore where community resources are most needed. Also, we feel that these sort of tools should be available in Google and Apple Maps. It will be very helpful for users in real life. title: Trafo
pitch: A grid dispatcher and an AI agent plan a day of field work on the same live map through WebMCP. The agent locates, computes and routes; the person decides. A morning of lookups becomes minutes.
about_excerpt: A grid dispatcher and an AI agent plan a day of field work on the same live map through WebMCP. The agent locates, computes and routes; the person decides. A morning of lookups becomes minutes. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every morning in an electricity distribution company a dispatcher opens two things: yesterday's work orders and a map of the grid. The orders say what customers reported and what maintenance is scheduled. The map says which transformer serves whom. Between the two sits the actual job: put every order where it belongs, understand who it affects, and turn the list into a route three crews can drive. In Lima that is hundreds of rows against 8,676 transformers, and it has always been done by hand, one lookup at a time. I am an industrial engineer with ten years in Peru's electricity sector, inside the body that regulates it. From that seat you see how the operations of a public service actually run: a spreadsheet, a map, and a dispatcher deciding who goes where with tools built for other purposes. The regulator publishes the whole grid as open data, nine million supply points and 139,000 substations, and for a long time I have thought about what happens when that data meets the work. Every situation described here is one I have dealt with in person. Now, as a developer, Trafo is the tool I built for those mornings. What it does Trafo puts the real published grid of Lima and the day's work orders on one map, and hands an AI agent the same map through 27 WebMCP tools. The dispatcher drops in the overnight intake as it arrived, a CSV or Excel with whatever each row carries. The agent places every row on the grid in one query, resolves each to its transformer, and lists the ones that still need a person. The dispatcher asks what each order touches. The agent returns customers behind the transformer, the service footprint, the schools and clinics inside it, and the interruption hours already on record against the regulatory tolerance, with no score attached. The dispatcher hands over the rows that are nothing but a sentence. The agent reads them, turns "the corner where the pharmacy is" into candidate points and the transformer under each, decides which fits the text, and writes back type, priority, scope and location. The order lands on the map while the dispatcher watches. The dispatcher says how many crews there are tomorrow. The agent groups the stops by transformer, orders them by distance, splits them into rounds and draws each round on the map, one colour per crew, stops numbered in visiting order. The dispatcher questions a proposal. The agent cross-checks orders sharing a substation across dates, shades the feeders carrying high-priority work on its own layer, and clears it when asked. The dispatcher closes orders, tags rows, asks for a cleanup. The agent applies status and priority in batches, previews a deletion, and only deletes once the preview has been seen. Every write can be undone. Why WebMCP is a strong fit for this use case A map is not a dataset. It is live state in a browser tab: a viewport, a selection, a transformer somebody clicked, a layer somebody turned on, thirty stops numbered in visiting order. Everything valuable about it is geometric, and everything geometric lives in the page. The page can resolve a supply number to a point, take the convex hull of 1,870 supplies, count the facilities inside it and order stops by distance, in milliseconds. What the page cannot do is read "twenty houses behind the market" and understand it as a fault near a landmark. A language model reads that easily. And neither of them should decide whether 900 customers outrank a school. That belongs to a person. WebMCP lets all three work on the same object. The page exposes its geometry as typed tools on document.modelContext , the agent calls them with what it read from the orders, and the dispatcher sees every result on the map in front of them, because the map the agent acts on and the map the person is looking at are the same one. A conventional API would have moved that exchange off the page: the agent would get JSON, the dispatcher would get a summary, and the two would be looking at different things. Keeping the tools in the tab is what makes the collaboration visible, checkable and fast. How it creates a better user experience The dispatcher works the way they already talk about the grid: three crews tomorrow, the hospital feeder first, leave the closed ones alone. The agent turns that into typed tool calls and the map updates in front of them. Orders land on their transformers, the ones that need reading get a location, the rounds draw themselves. Every proposal comes back with figures, so the dispatcher questions it, changes a constraint and asks again, in minutes. The planning that used to take a morning now takes a conversation. Against the 82 sample orders: 82 lookups become one call; 76 visits become 33 because 13 transformers carry 56 of the orders; 33 stops reorder from 51.2 km to 16.8 km and split across crews; the question "which orders sit on a transformer that also feeds a clinic", which used to be a day of cross-referencing, is three tool calls. And the page is complete without the agent, because in an operations room the agent may not be available and the work still has to happen. What people and agents can now do together Put a whole intake on the grid in one call, with the rows that need a person listed instead of lost. Until now it was one lookup per row in a billing system. Ask a spreadsheet which orders sit on a transformer that also feeds a school or a clinic, and get the facilities named. Until now that check waited for the day of the outage. Give the orders that arrived as a sentence a place on the grid. The agent reads, chooses, writes back; the dispatcher watches it land and can move it. Until now that reading stayed in someone's head. Turn 76 stops into 33 visits and a route two thirds shorter, drawn on the map per crew. Until now routing was experience and a paper map. Hand over a cleanup without handing over the keys. "Delete every closed order" gets a preview; the tool that deletes exists only after it, runs once, and everything can be undone. Real impact Measured against the 82 sample orders the app opens with, on the real grid of Lima: What the dispatcher needs Before With Trafo Planning time for the day's intake A morning of one-by-one lookups Minutes of conversation Locating every order on the grid 82 lookups 1 call Visits to cover 76 located orders 76 33, because 13 transformers carry 56 of the orders Driving for a 33-stop round 51.2 km 16.8 km, 67% less Orders that arrived as a sentence Unplaced until someone read them 6 of 6 read, placed and written back Orders on a transformer that also feeds a school or clinic A day of cross-referencing, rarely done 3 tool calls, facilities named Interruption hours against the NTCSE tolerance Checked after the fact Reported per substation while planning What that means on the ground: Prioritisation with facts. Every order carries its customers, its facilities and its accumulated hours before a crew is assigned, so the dispatcher decides what goes first with the consequence in view rather than from the row's text alone. Fewer kilometres and fewer trips per crew per day. Grouping by transformer and ordering the stops cuts the driving by two thirds on the sample day, and the same computation runs on any intake of any size. Outages on sensitive feeders caught at scheduling time. A planned outage on a substation that feeds a health post shows the facility when the order is placed, not on the morning of the work. Regulatory exposure visible while planning. Hours already accumulated against the tolerance are on the table before a new interruption is scheduled on the same customers. The rows nobody had time to read reach the map. Free-text claims get a place and a scope on the day they arrive. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet and SheetJS, plain files served over HTTP, no build step. 27 tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() , each with a JSON Schema inputSchema with bounded numbers and enums and an async execute returning plain JSON. Inputs are checked at runtime, not only in the schema: codes that reach the grid service are pattern-checked before a request leaves the browser, internal state fields are rebuilt on intake rather than accepted from the caller, and a filter-less bulk write needs all: true . confirm_deletion is registered dynamically by preview_deletion and unregisters itself after running. The page checks for the browser's own modelContext , names the cause in the header chip when it is absent, and falls back to a spec-compatible shim so every tool still runs from the built-in console. A 3×3 km bundle of central Lima ships with the app so the core flow runs with no network; the rest of Lima and beyond is queried live from the public service, and the status line names which tier answered. title: WordLift AI Audit
pitch: The machine reads the website. The human knows the business. ChatGPT compiles both into a governed service map for agents.
about_excerpt: The machine reads the website. The human knows the business. ChatGPT compiles both into a governed service map for agents. Like Comment Story Updates The machine reads the website. The human knows the business. ChatGPT compiles both into a governed service map. WordLift AI Audit turns a public website into an evidence-backed service map for AI agents. It reads representative pages, classifies the business, extracts domain entities and vocabulary, compiles the actions an agent should be able to perform, and verifies which machine interfaces actually work. But the machine output is deliberately a draft. Pages cannot prove every operating role, important entity, business term, or responsibility boundary. ChatGPT therefore interviews the human and compiles that judgment into a new immutable, human-refined service map. The problem Websites were designed as pages for people. Agents need explicit knowledge about the things a business offers, the functions they may call, the boundaries around those functions, and evidence that the interfaces really work. Most AI-readiness scanners stop at crawlability, metadata, or declarations. They cannot answer: Which action applies to which entity? Can people perform it today? Can an agent perform it? Who owns the action: the organization, a partner, or nobody? What evidence proves the conclusion? What governed contract would close the gap? What WordLift AI Audit does Analyzes up to four representative pages rather than only the homepage. Preserves the complete bounded WordLift foundation audit behind progressive disclosure. Classifies the site as commerce, publishing, travel, finance, SaaS, or a conservative fallback. Builds the Context Engine: domain graph — organizations, products, services, places, articles, offers, and provenance; lexical graph — categories, names, terminology, meanings, and aliases; action layer — expected actions, entity bindings, interfaces, boundaries, evidence, and contracts. Separates human-facing support from agent-facing declarations and successful invocation. Produces a machine-generated service-map draft with three priority gaps. Lets ChatGPT inspect that draft and interview the human about the business role, primary entities, terminology, and every expected action boundary. Compiles the human decisions into an immutable child report without altering the original evidence or allowing a human assertion to mark an action agent-ready. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is not an accessory to the interface; it is the collaboration protocol. The application exposes six generic tools: audit-website starts an audit of any safe public URL. get-audit-report follows a long-running audit through progress to completion. inspect-service-map gives ChatGPT the full machine review brief. explain-capability retrieves deeper evidence and the governed contract for one action. explain-foundation-audit returns the complete safe WordLift foundation audit. refine-service-map submits typed human judgments and returns the immutable refined report. The tool descriptions encode the intended protocol: audit → inspect → interview → explain where unclear → refine This creates a form of human–agent collaboration that was difficult before WebMCP. The machine contributes observation and inference. The human contributes business meaning and responsibility. ChatGPT mediates the conversation and turns both into structured symbolic commitments. Honest readiness A declaration earns zero readiness points. Structured data, OpenAPI, MCP, WebMCP, and other declarations remain unverified until the relevant interface is invoked successfully. Human decisions can change applicability, vocabulary, entity priority, and governance boundaries, but never evidence-based readiness. The report therefore keeps two scores separate: WordLift foundation readiness; verified agent action readiness. Example A tourism website may contain booking forms, accommodation pages, and hotel links. The machine can infer that availability matters, but it cannot safely conclude that the destination organization owns hotel inventory. The human can tell ChatGPT that the organization owns discovery and recommendations while availability is a partner handoff. The refined report then promotes the correct organization and destination entities, clarifies the terminology, changes the action boundary, updates the entity–action bindings and contract, records the rationale as human-provided provenance, and preserves the original machine draft for comparison. Implementation The application is a React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Express, and Node 22 service deployed on Google Cloud Run with immutable Firestore report revisions. It uses Zod contracts, a deterministic versioned action compiler, JSON-LD, Schema.org, Google Natural Language classification, and the WordLift AI Audit provider. Tools register on the top-level report document through the WebMCP imperative API on document.modelContext , with a compatibility alias for Chrome's current preview surface. Report-scoped tools register as soon as the route loads, before the report has finished rendering. Security controls include SSRF protection, DNS and redirect validation, response limits, sanitized evidence, rate limiting, bounded storage, server-only credentials, and truthful partial or failed states. New work created during the challenge The private WordLift AI Audit existed before August 25. The following public implementation was created during The WebMCP Challenge: a new open-source deployable application; the versioned six-archetype action compiler; multi-page context extraction and provenance; domain, lexical, interface, and entity–action schemas; verification-only readiness and safe invocation probes; six generic WebMCP tools; the inspect/interview/refine collaboration protocol; typed human assertions and immutable refined reports; the Context Engine and capability-map interface; deterministic fixtures, security boundaries, and the complete test suite. The challenge contribution is not a wrapper around the previous product. It is the new public context compiler and human-guided WebMCP experience. Testing The current release passed strict TypeScript checks, 323 unit/integration/component tests, the production build, and 12 Playwright browser scenarios. The browser suite includes the full Cyborg journey: audit, inspect, refine, open the immutable child, verify embodied human judgment, and confirm the original machine draft remains unchanged. No account is required. title: Woven
pitch: Seven site tools. One complete choice. Human-only confirmation.
about_excerpt: Seven site tools. One complete choice. Human-only confirmation. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Woven — one mission, two verified compatible carts. Woven - From model request to user-confirmed pickup receipt. One request, two complete carts. From one request to a pickup-ready order. Ask once. Review once. Confirm once. Why Woven is a strong fit for WebMCP Shopping agents can recommend individual products, but a real mission still requires quantities, compatibility, budget, current stock, pickup, and consent to work together. Woven turns that multi-step job into a structured collaboration between an agent and the person already using the page. On the fictional Woven Trail Market storefront, the agent does not guess at buttons or scrape the interface. Seven purpose-built site tools let it start or inspect a mission, rerank the visible cart comparison, select an offered cart, apply only a merchant-approved compatible alternative, refresh current price and stock, and verify an existing simulated receipt. How it creates a better user experience The canonical request asks for a rainy-weekend camping kit for two first-time campers that fits in one car boot and is pickup-ready today. Woven Trail Market shows the best two complete carts, each from one merchant and one pickup location, and explains how every quantity and component satisfies the brief. The lead proof is exact: 7 units, 5 categories, 89 L packed, and a 3,000 mm rainfly. Agent calls update the same React storefront the person can see. When the agent calls compare_carts , Woven reranks the visible inline kits rather than returning a disconnected text result. The person can review the same carts, prices, stock, compatibility proof, alternatives, and selected state. That removes repeated searching and cart reconstruction without hiding the decision from the person. What people and agents can do together now The agent can translate one outcome-oriented request into bounded, reversible preparation work across product choice, constraints, current catalog facts, and comparison. The person can inspect and steer that work in the same page, then retain sole control of the irreversible step. That boundary is intentional. Woven does not register identity verification, checkout preview, confirmation secrets, or purchase authorization as WebMCP tools. The agent may prepare and recommend; the person must complete the clearly labeled demo identity handoff, review exact expiring terms, and directly confirm or continue to a merchant. Inventory, identity, merchants, and payment authorization are simulated, Woven accepts no card credentials, and it cannot make a live charge. How WebMCP was implemented The dedicated top-level /webmcp storefront document registers seven imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : start_mission , get_mission , compare_carts , select_cart , swap_cart_item , refresh_carts , and verify_receipt . Each tool has a closed JSON schema. Read-only operations carry read-only annotations, content-bearing results are marked untrusted where appropriate, and every registration is attached to an AbortSignal so navigation removes the page's tool surface. The server sends Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) . Human submission, WebMCP, and the existing MCP App enter the same server-owned mission router, deterministic commerce verifier, SQLite state, and checkout controls. The agent cannot mark a cart checkout-eligible. Connected catalog facts may support a cart; cited web research remains research-only. Price, stock, compatibility, identity session, exact amount, nonce, expiry, and idempotency are revalidated at the human confirmation boundary. Inspiration Search gives links, but buying still takes work. A first-time camper has to size the shelter, duplicate sleep gear, check rain ratings, fit everything into one car, find one pickup location with stock, and rebuild the cart at checkout. Woven was built around a simple product promise: everything works together. What it does One natural-language mission becomes verified complete carts; the storefront shows the best two in solid comparison cards. The agent and person share a visible storefront state, current selection, merchant-approved alternatives, and refreshable catalog state. The agent can do reversible preparation through WebMCP while identity and exact transaction confirmation stay human-only. How we built it Woven is one Node.js and TypeScript service with a dedicated React storefront, seven top-level WebMCP site tools, HTTP and stdio MCP transports, deterministic cart verification, bounded LangGraph.js orchestration for non-camping missions, SQLite persistence, and a simulated payment adapter. Tests assert the exact tool surface, schemas, cleanup lifecycle, shared UI behavior, security headers, and absence of identity or purchase tools. Challenges The hardest design decision was deciding what not to expose. Treating a tool call as payment consent would erase the trust boundary. Woven exposes only reversible preparation work and keeps identity, exact terms, secrets, and final confirmation outside the agent's tool surface. The second challenge was preserving one source of truth across WebMCP, the MCP App, and the browser experience. All surfaces now share the same server routing, validation, persistence, cart rules, and confirmation boundary. Accomplishments Seven browser-discoverable WebMCP tools over a complete product workflow. Tool calls update the visible storefront instead of a parallel agent-only state. Two visible complete one-merchant kits with exact budget, volume, weather, quantity, stock, pickup, source, and verification proofs. One truthful glass activity surface; commerce cards and authorization controls remain solid, and total connector failure never fabricates a result. Merchant-approved substitutions, refreshable facts, signed simulated receipts, and deterministic failure behavior. Human-only identity and purchase confirmation enforced by the server and omitted from WebMCP. Automated tests plus desktop and mobile verification. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when the browser is not merely another API client. Its value is shared context: the agent can act through precise tools while the person sees and controls the same product state. Tool omission is also product design; the absence of a purchase tool makes Woven's consent model clearer and safer. Challenge-period provenance Woven was created during the challenge period. The challenge opened on 25 August 2026; the first public repository commit is dated 29 August 2026, and the dedicated WebMCP implementation is dated 31 August 2026. title: ForgeTwin
pitch: A WebMCP-powered AI engineering lab that turns plain-language goals into working 3D machines, simulates real physics, learns from failures, and redesigns until every constraint is met.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered AI engineering lab that turns plain-language goals into working 3D machines, simulates real physics, learns from failures, and redesigns until every constraint is met. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am both a mechanical engineer and a web developer , and this project came from combining these two parts of my experience. In mechanical engineering, having a good idea is only the beginning. The idea must become real geometry, materials, joints, forces, sensors, controls, and measurable results. In web development, I learned how a good interface and AI can make a complicated tool easier for more people to use. This made me ask one question: What if AI could do more than generate a picture or description of a machine? What if it could enter the same engineering workspace as the human, build the machine part by part, test it, see what failed, and improve it? This is why I built ForgeTwin. I wanted someone to describe a physical goal in normal language, without knowing every CAD command, and then watch an AI agent turn that goal into an editable, animated, and testable mechanical system. As an engineer, one principle was very important to me: A design should not be trusted only because it looks convincing. It should be tested with physics and evidence. Don’t generate it. Engineer it. What it does ForgeTwin is a browser-based AI engineering sandbox. The user describes a machine or mechanical goal, and ForgeTwin creates a versioned physical world from reusable parts. For example, a user can ask: “Build a conveyor that sorts red and blue boxes at 20 boxes per minute.” “Build an electric go-kart with four wheels, steering, accelerator and brake pedals.” “Build a brazing fixture that positions a heat exchanger and two copper pipes within 2 mm.” ForgeTwin then: Understands the requested machine, functions, and measurable requirements. Creates an engineering plan instead of returning only text. Breaks the design into assemblies and reusable low-level components. Gives every component dimensions, material, mass, position, and orientation. Adds physical connections, joints, motors, sensors, actuators, and control logic. Builds the machine in an interactive 3D workspace while the user watches. Runs a fixed-step 60 Hz Rapier simulation. Reads telemetry, collisions, movement, and requirement measurements. Finds the reason when a requirement fails. Changes the related geometry, physical property, actuator, motor, or controller and runs the test again. The app is not limited to conveyors. Its 39-part reusable vocabulary covers structures, power transmission, controls, road vehicles, motorcycles, aircraft, rotorcraft, tracked mobility, and articulated robots. It can compose cranes, lifts, bicycles, go-karts, motorcycles, cars, rovers, robotic arms, humanoid robots, gearboxes, suspension systems, airplanes, helicopters, solar trackers, bridges, warehouse systems, agriculture machines, recycling systems, HVAC fixtures, medical lifting mechanisms, and new systems made from smaller primitives. The current app includes 19 editable challenge briefs , but these are examples, not locked machine templates. The user can change the prompt, dimensions, load, speed, or target. If a special component is not already available, the planner can build it from lower-level parts such as beams, plates, tubes, shafts, wheels, pulleys, joints, sensors, and motors. The user can also: Use the built-in AI without entering credentials, or temporarily use their own OpenAI API key. Edit the existing design with natural-language chat instead of starting over. Select, move, resize, and rotate parts in X, Y, and Z. Orbit the full camera through 360 degrees with mouse or touch. Use a rotation gizmo, snapping, or numeric angle entry. Lock a manual change so the AI redesigns around it instead of moving it back. Animate the operating sequence of different machine families. Run physics and replay a failure in slow motion. Use X-Ray Mode to inspect joints, sensor paths, axes, collision boxes, actuator paths, and velocity information. Inspect requirement evidence and see what passed, failed, or was not evaluated. Undo changes, restore revisions, and compare a failed design with the improved design. Export the current world as PNG, JPG, PDF, STL exchange geometry, or complete ForgeTwin JSON data. How I built it ForgeTwin is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Rapier, and Zod . The main idea is that the machine is not saved as one opaque 3D model. It is stored as a shared engineering graph containing: Assemblies and individual bodies Dimensions, materials, mass, and rigid-body properties Position, rotation, and machine orientation Mechanical, power, and signal connections Fixed, revolute, prismatic, spherical, spring, rope, gear, and belt joints Motors, sensors, actuators, and control rules Simulation runs, telemetry, collisions, and failure evidence Human-owned edits and immutable revision history The 3D editor renders this graph procedurally. The same graph is used by the human interface, the built-in model agent, the physics simulator, the activity feed, exports, and an external WebMCP agent. The hosted AI uses GPT-5.6 Sol through the OpenAI Responses API . To keep generation faster and more reliable, the model creates a compact engineering intent: the object identity, architecture, motion, controls, primitive vocabulary, and requirements. ForgeTwin then expands that intent into the complete body-and-joint graph, validates it, repairs safe topology problems, and executes the design through guarded tools. The hosted key stays on the server, so judges can use the full AI experience without adding a key. A visitor can still connect their own key for the current browser tab. That key is kept only in memory and is not stored. If model access is unavailable, ForgeTwin also has a deterministic local engineering path for the main design, physics, optimization, and supported chat-edit operations. I also created one universal coordinate convention for every machine: +X is front, -X is rear, +Y is up, -Z is left, and +Z is right . This helped fix many problems with lights, wheels, propellers, steering, windshields, and joint axes. The design validator checks for missing supports, hubs, axles, joints, steering links, bad proportions, wrong orientations, floating components, incorrect joint axes, overlaps, blocked windshields, and unrequested systems. For example, a go-kart uses front wheel hubs, spindles, steering knuckles, separate kingpin axes, tie rods, a steering rack, column, and Ackermann-style steering instead of making the whole wheel rotate around one incorrect axis. Rapier runs the connected rigid-body world at a fixed 60 Hz and records replay frames and collision events. Some advanced engineering results, including aerodynamics, flexible cables, structural stress, detailed tire behavior, and some manufacturing processes, still use clearly labeled reduced-order checks. ForgeTwin is a concept-validation sandbox, not a replacement for certified CAD, FEA, CFD, medical approval, or safety analysis. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is what makes ForgeTwin an AI-operable engineering workspace instead of only a website with an AI button. ForgeTwin exposes 29 small, typed, state-aware WebMCP tools , including: inspect_workspace inspect_primitive_catalog set_design_goal create_assembly create_component set_dimensions , set_material , and set_mass move_component and rotate_component connect_components and create_joint add_motor , add_sensor , and add_actuator set_motor_speed , set_sensor_range , and set_actuator_timing set_control_logic and update_control_logic run_simulation inspect_telemetry , inspect_failure , and measure_constraint optimize_design remove_component and remove_joint compare_designs and restore_revision I did not create one giant generate_machine tool. The agent must inspect the current world, create parts, connect them, run the simulation, read the evidence, and make bounded changes. Every tool call is visible in the activity feed. This matters for human and AI collaboration. If I move a camera, sensor, or other component by hand, ForgeTwin creates a new revision and marks the transform as human-owned. The agent reads this new shared state and can redesign the rest of the machine without silently removing my decision. The built-in chat uses the same idea. It receives the current graph, selected component, latest measurements, human locks, and recent conversation. A request such as “move the right clamp 0.04 meters outward, preserve my camera position, and rerun the test” becomes a guarded change to the existing world, followed by a new simulation and revision. Without WebMCP, AI can give advice about the machine. With WebMCP, AI can work inside the engineering environment together with the human. title: Can an Agent Fly a Plane?
pitch: I built a flight simulator, then used WebMCP to see if an AI agent could fly the thing, handle an emergency it didn’t know was coming, and somehow land.
about_excerpt: I built a flight simulator, then used WebMCP to see if an AI agent could fly the thing, handle an emergency it didn’t know was coming, and somehow land. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I've been watching a lot of pilot content lately, and I've always been interested in planes. An agent-driven flight evaluation sounded cool, and using STL, where I'm from, felt obvious. What it does This project is a real-time WebMCP evaluation for model developers and evaluation researchers. Your agent has to take off from STL on a flight to MDW in Chicago, handle a sealed emergency, coordinate a diversion with simulated ATC (air traffic control), and land safely back in St. Louis. ATC defines the route and checkpoints, but the agent decides how to fly them. It chooses the flight targets, aircraft configuration, and activation conditions. The simulator applies those targets continuously using 60 Hz physics at a fixed 2x time scale. It never pauses or changes that rate while the agent thinks, and the emergency decision window and mission deadline still use real elapsed time. Completing the flight requires hitting the route checkpoints and configuring the aircraft correctly. The score deducts points for slow emergency decisions, exceeding the mission window, high G-force, abrupt motion, hard or off-center landings, and crashes. The page registers six WebMCP tools for reading the manual, starting the flight, programming commands, coordinating with ATC, and waiting for events. WebMCP gives the agent structured state and validated actions instead of making it guess at visual controls. A person can fly the same aircraft manually, or start an agent evaluation and watch it go. The exported trajectory records every WebMCP call, action, result, latency, before-and-after state, score change, and simulator event. How I built it I used Codex to build and test each version. My first Cesium.js scene used a real route from STL to Chicago, but it hurt performance and was very buggy. I switched to Three.js and built a simplified but representative wide-body twinjet flight envelope. The simulation runs outside React render state at 60 Hz. The WebMCP layer uses document.modelContext.registerTool to expose the six tools, but the simulator still works manually without WebMCP if you want to fly it yourself. I went through probably 15 to 20 iterations of the world itself, adding audio and the minimap along the way. The hard part was deciding what the agent should actually control. We revised the tools until the agent was calling the shots instead of taking credit for decisions buried in the simulator. Challenges I ran into The V1 version was kind of cool, but it was too easy. The agent was basically on autopilot. The deterministic simulator controlled pitch, bank, and power while the agent only decided whether to return or continue. I set a /goal challenging Codex to make a fresh subagent complete the flight using the actual flight model. The results were pretty interesting. After 13 hours and 73 attempts, it finally got three runs to land with scores around 90, but of course it cheated. Somewhere along the way it decided the easiest way to fly a plane was to stop time whenever it needed to think. That obviously defeated the entire point. That exposed the most interesting part. As soon as the agent has to think, time becomes part of the problem. Even Terra at low reasoning could take long enough that the aircraft crashed or flew too far away. The solution was to meet in the middle. Simulated ATC supplies the route, but the agent writes the flight program before takeoff and replaces it after the emergency. The simulator tracks its targets at 60 Hz without pausing or deciding what comes next. I tested that version with ten agents in cold threads, and all ten failed. I decided they needed a “manual” explaining the aircraft and command interface. I really didn't want to do this, but they needed enough context to land without moving the decisions back into the simulator. The manual publishes rotation speed, climb and landing configuration, approach speed, flare limits, and the go-around sequence. It does not reveal the emergency, choose the diversion, or provide a program. The agent still has to fly. The resulting architecture completed three fresh blind runs in a row without pausing, changing the fixed simulation rate, or revealing the emergency early. Every WebMCP interaction was captured in the browser-side trajectory export. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that I didn't stop at “this works because the agent said it does” (which happens every single time lmao). I grilled Codex on how the simulation worked and kept pushing until the agent, rather than a hidden policy, owned the decisions. Thinking still hurts performance here, but I believe that is useful signal rather than something to hide. Models should be able to judge when deeper reasoning is worth the time. What I learned I learned a lot about building with WebMCP and understanding the agent experience. It isn't as simple as “give the agent all the information and let it do the thing.” I had to run fresh agents repeatedly and fix ambiguous tools without taking decisions away from them. The manual is part of the interface, not an answer key. The same applies to human UX. If people and agents get stuck at the same point, the interface probably is not communicating clearly enough. What's next? This could become an evaluation environment for model developers and researchers testing decisions under time pressure. Most evaluations I've seen analyze time after the run. Here, time changes the environment. A longer response means the aircraft has traveled farther, burned more fuel, and moved closer to failure. The sealed scenario and exported trajectory make that measurable. The idea also does not have to stop at flying a plane. The same setup could test an agent acting as ATC, coordinating a ground crew, or handling another system where the world keeps moving while the model thinks. The bigger question is whether models can learn when to reason deeply and when they need to act now. title: InnerOS WebMCP Mission Control
pitch: A WebMCP coding control plane where a local AI proposes changes, InnerOS routes execution across real agent lanes, and every backend hop returns verifiable proof.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP coding control plane where a local AI proposes changes, InnerOS routes execution across real agent lanes, and every backend hop returns verifiable proof. Like Comment Story Updates Built for fastt operator workflows Trace every action from request to result Talk, coordinate, EXECUTE. Professional accesss for live presentations From prompt to physical action InnerOS WebMCP Mission Control Inspiration Most AI agents still interact with websites by looking at pixels, guessing what controls mean, and imitating human clicks. That is fragile for serious development, operations, and physical automation. We wanted a different model: the website itself should expose governed capabilities to the agent, while the human keeps a visible control room and every meaningful action remains verifiable. InnerOS already existed as our local-first multi-agent operating layer, coordinating local models, MCP/A2A agents, coding providers, infrastructure, evidence, and physical automation. For The WebMCP Challenge we built a WebMCP-native product layer that turns that infrastructure into one public, agent-operable development and operations cockpit. Live judge URL: https://webmcp.creatorcore.ai The core interaction rule Conversation is deliberation. Approval is the execution boundary. A user can talk to the local InnerOS Copilot for multiple turns, refine requirements, attach PDFs or source files, dictate a prompt by voice, change projects, and choose a different executor. None of that programs, registers, or physically executes anything. Only when the user is satisfied do they press Approve & Execute Plan . InnerOS then validates the selected project again and dispatches the latest refined plan through the selected lane. This gives Mission Control a clean universal workflow: Choose or create a project. Attach project context if useful. Converse with local Qwen and refine the plan. Choose AUTO / Local AMD / Codex / Cursor / AntiGravity. Press Approve & Execute Plan. Watch delivery, execution, verification, and evidence as different backend states. Delivery is not execution. Registration is not physical execution. A dispatch ID proves acceptance, not completion. A real browser development workspace The challenge build now goes beyond a one-shot demo console. Create Project Mission Control has an explicit Create Project action. Typing a new name into the Project field alone never creates anything. create_project_workspace creates a bounded local Git development workspace under the canonical InnerOS Projects root, initializes Git, and registers the project in Project Runtime. It deliberately does not create a GitHub or cloud repository behind the user's back. Before any coding dispatch, InnerOS verifies that the selected project exists and is a real Git workspace. PDF and source-code context Authenticated users can attach bounded PDFs and common source/text files. Attachments are stored privately per project and are passed to Qwen as read-only planning context . The Copilot now receives recent conversation history plus project-file context, so refinement is genuinely multi-turn rather than a chat UI that secretly sends only the latest message. Text PDFs are extracted locally; source/text files are decoded directly. If a PDF is image-only and no text can be extracted, the UI says so instead of pretending the model read it. A bounded portion of the same project context follows the execution brief after approval so the chosen executor can act on the relevant code/document information. Local voice dictation The voice button is local-first too. The browser records microphone audio using MediaRecorder, sends it to the authenticated WebMCP origin, and the server forwards it over loopback to our already-running local Whisper ASR service . The transcript comes back into the chat composer for review. Voice is dictation only. It never bypasses the approval gate. If local Whisper is unavailable, browser speech recognition is offered only as an explicit fallback rather than being mislabeled as local. Why WebMCP matters here WebMCP is not decorative in this project. It is the machine-facing interaction model. Instead of forcing an assistant to infer a human UI, the page publishes a compact set of semantic capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The current public surface has 13 WebMCP tools : ask_inneros_copilot list_agents get_project_status create_project_workspace inspect_blockers dispatch_agent_action resolve_project_blocker get_execution_trace get_evidence dmx_create_scene dmx_status dmx_set_scene dmx_blackout The browser sees only those governed actions. InnerOS can coordinate a much larger private MCP/A2A fabric without exposing raw internal tools, private infrastructure, filesystem roots, model endpoints, or credentials. Local-first AI and execution lanes The primary Copilot is Qwen3-Coder 30B , served locally through vLLM on our AMD node. The live provider fabric exposes four coding lanes plus AUTO: AUTO — after approval, InnerOS chooses the cheapest capable local-first route; a bounded native capability may be used directly when appropriate. Local AMD / Qwen3-Coder — local vLLM + durable A2A/local execution, preferred under local-first policy. Codex — headless-capable when the live provider fabric proves CLI/auth/process readiness. Cursor — remote IDE/inbox when headless execution is not proven; delivery is not execution. AntiGravity — remote IDE/inbox unless a real runnable session is proven; completion requires returned evidence. Explicit lane selection remains explicit. If the user chooses Codex, Cursor, AntiGravity, or Local AMD, AUTO does not silently hijack that choice. Physical execution with AG-59 DMX The same control plane reaches the physical world through AG-59, the InnerOS DMX Stage Orchestrator . A judge can describe a lighting behavior that does not exist, refine it in conversation, approve it, and then watch the local AI create the new governed capability. After approval: Local Qwen designs one bounded declarative scene. Common aliases such as purple , blue , or disco ball are normalized into the canonical trusted vocabulary. AG-59 validates scene name, targets, colors, brightness, step duration, loops, and total duration. AG-59 atomically registers the scene in the live registry. Mission Control automatically discovers and selects the scene. The physical lights are still idle. The user separately presses Apply scene . Only then does dmx_set_scene drive the real fixtures. Raw DMX channels, fixture addresses, private topology, and rapid full-stage strobe are never accepted from public/model input. That separation is important: proposal != registration != physical execution . Proof, not theater Global Live Trace is designed around one question: how do I know this actually happened? Browser intent and backend confirmation are visibly separate: BROWSER events represent client-side intent and are not presented as backend proof. BACKEND · CONFIRMED events come from real server responses. Project creation is confirmed only after Project Runtime reports a real Git workspace. A provider receiving a task is not shown as running until process/session evidence exists. A DMX scene-registry change is confirmed only after AG-59 reports the new catalog. Voice is labeled Local Whisper only after the loopback ASR service returns a transcript. Every WebMCP request receives proof metadata including request ID, tool name, bridge identity, backend, timestamp, latency, whether execution is being claimed, and durable dispatch ID when applicable. Safety and trust boundaries The public browser never receives raw access to the private MCP runtime, local Qwen endpoint, local Whisper endpoint, physical DMX node, server paths, or credentials. Key rules: only allowlisted WebMCP operations are accepted; direct MCP access remains loopback-only; project names and local workspaces are bounded and verified; attachment size/type/context are bounded and project-scoped; private topology, paths, sessions, tokens, and credentials are sanitized; the Copilot cannot claim execution; conversation never executes; delivery is not treated as running; completion requires backend evidence; higher-impact host/cloud changes remain behind audited approval gates; DMX creation is declarative, bounded, revalidated, and separate from physical execution; local-first routing is visible instead of silently escalating to paid external compute. What is new for The WebMCP Challenge InnerOS and its underlying local multi-agent infrastructure existed before the challenge. The challenge-period work is the WebMCP-native product layer that makes it directly usable from an agent-capable website. Challenge-period work includes: WebMCP registration with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ; the 13 public WebMCP contracts ; local Qwen3-Coder Copilot integration; real multi-turn conversation context; explicit approval-first execution semantics; local Git project creation from Missio

title: Agentic Stores (AMS) by 40rty
pitch: Agents arrive with intent, AMS builds the storefront to match. An ask arrives from an assistant, a feed, or a search - AMS serves the storefront to match it over webmcp.
about_excerpt: Agents arrive with intent, AMS builds the storefront to match. An ask arrives from an assistant, a feed, or a search - AMS serves the storefront to match it over webmcp. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every website ever built assumes a human is looking at it. That assumption is baked in so deep we stopped seeing it. Pages exist because humans need somewhere to land. A CMS exists because someone has to author those pages in advance, for every visitor, hoping one of them fits. Agents need none of it. An agent arrives with a specific intent already formed — "wide-fit running shoes under $140 that ship to Tel Aviv by Friday" — then does the absurd work of pulling apart a page built for nobody in particular to find the fraction that answers the question. A hero image it cannot use, a nav bar it will never click, a grid of 48 products to find the four that matter. Everyone is asking how agents should read websites better. The right question is why the website is still a fixed artifact at all. If the visitor states its intent up front, the site does not need to have been written in advance — it can be composed on arrival, from the merchant's catalog and brand system. One agent, one intent, one purpose-built storefront, then it is gone. WebMCP is what makes this possible, because for the first time the visitor tells the site what it came for before the site has to respond. What it does AMS is an agent that streams a storefront over WebMCP. An AI shopping agent arrives at a merchant's store and finds a declared tool surface on navigator.modelContext . It states what the shopper wants. AMS composes a branded storefront for exactly that intent — the right products, the right comparisons, the right attributes surfaced — and streams it back as RFC 6902 patches against a live layout tree. Not a page that was waiting for it. A store that did not exist until it asked. The next turn, the shopper narrows: "actually, only the ones with a wide toe box." The storefront recomposes. Different products, different comparison axis, different layout, same brand. The experience is a conversation, not a destination. The unit of the web stops being the page. It becomes the intent. There is no page to author, no page to maintain and no page to optimize — because there is no page until an agent asks for one. The merchant keeps their brand inside the agentic conversation. Today an agent shopping on a shopper's behalf strips the merchant to a title and a price in someone else's chat window. AMS streams a branded surface into that conversation instead. AMS declares 16 tools through navigator.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool's description and enabled state is overridable per merchant via webmcpConfig , served at session creation — a merchant can rename, re-describe or switch off any tool without a deploy. Tool What the agent gets send_message States an intent in natural language. Hands it to the composing agent and returns its prose. The storefront recomposes as a side effect. show_collection Asks for a named collection or category; the agent resolves it and composes a product layout. get_products Two shapes. Called bare, a compact survey of the canvas — title, price, availability, image. Called with productIds , the full record: description, option axes, and every variant with its exact option values and buyability. get_layout The raw layout tree — component types, props, children. Also the only way to read what was featured , since a look card carries its own product list. get_messages Full conversation history, role-tagged. get_status Session state: isRunning , hasLayout , error, live streaming prose, latest committed reply. get_visitor_context Standing preferences the shopper has stated — size, fit, colour, budget — under the brand's own key names. set_visitor_context States a standing preference. It survives every later recomposition. open_product Navigates the canvas to a product detail view. add_to_cart Adds by product plus {axis: value} selections. Same signal a human card click fires — stamped origin: 'webmcp' . get_cart Every line with its chosen option values, quantity, price, the totals, and whether checkout is available. update_cart_item Sets a line's quantity. Absolute, not a delta. remove_from_cart Removes a line; without selections, every line of that product. begin_checkout Hands off to Shopify's hosted checkout with the current cart. send_signal Escape hatch: a low-level typed interaction signal for anything the typed tools miss. clear_session Resets layout, conversation and session data. Three decisions there are worth naming. Agent-backed tools return the site's own voice, not a status. send_message and show_collection hand the request to the merchant's AI and resolve with its finished text. The operator contract, served to the calling agent at runtime through window.webmcp.instructions , tells it to relay that verbatim: "You operate the tools; the site AI is the voice." The merchant's brand voice survives the round trip instead of being paraphrased by somebody else's model. A turn that outruns the await window returns status: "running" — the caller polls get_status and reads latestResponse . The contract is that the site's voice reaches the agent, not that it arrives within a fixed budget. The cart is addressed by selections, never by variant id. get_products deliberately returns no variant id: those ids are unstable across the optimistic-write window, so an id an external agent held across a turn could aim a write at a line that has already been replaced. Cart verbs take a product plus {axis: value} selections and bind late, against live state — a stale reference can only miss , and fail loudly. This replaced a first version where add_to_cart fell back to "first in-stock variant", so a shopper who asked for size 8 got whatever was in stock first. add_to_cart books itself as a third actor — not the agent, not the visitor, but origin: 'webmcp' . Folding a WebMCP-driven add into either of the others would lie about which surface earned it, and that is the number a merchant asks about first. For agents that do not speak WebMCP natively, appending ?webmcp=1 installs a real host plus a window.webmcp client, so a JS-eval-capable browser agent can call the identical surface. It never overrides a real host — if Chrome or a bridge extension already provided navigator.modelContext , the sim is a no-op. That same flag also makes the URL a self-contained demo: it renders what the page is, and a prompt to paste into an agent. No repo to clone and nothing to send alongside the link. How we built it The storefront is composed, not served. A tool call arrives carrying an intent, and one fixed two-call flow runs: Reasoning — a multi-round tool loop bounded by step count and wall clock. The model fires tool calls as a parallel batch, sees the results and may fire another batch to refine. No prose, no layout. Compose — one streamText call with tools omitted entirely and the reasoning step's tool history flattened to plain text. It streams a jsonl-elements fence that parses line by line into RFC 6902 patch operations against the layout spec. The tool-free compose call is structural, not stylistic. A single tool-bearing call that also composes cannot guarantee output: the model emits a phantom functionCall , finishes with finishReason='tool-calls' and the visitor gets a blank canvas. Strip the tool registry and a phantom call has nothing to execute — the model is forced to compose. It is the most important architectural line in the system. The model split is not the one you would guess. Both calls run Gemini 3.6 Flash by default. The performance split is structural — two calls plus per-step reasoning budgets — not cheap-planner and expensive-composer. Reasoning runs at a minimal thinking floor because a fuller budget measured 13–24s per turn against ~4.6s warm: tried, measured, rejected. Claude Haiku 4.5 and any OpenRouter id are selectable per merchant. The catalog is Shopify's, through Shopify's own MCP. Product search hits the Global Catalog MCP, per-store reads hit the Storefront MCP over JSON-RPC 2.0. Live products, live inventory, live pricing. AMS composes the experience; Shopify stays the system of record, so nothing is mirrored and nothing goes stale. Serving is three planes. Vercel runs the Next.js app that mounts the storefront engine, Railway runs the Hono agent API and Supabase runs Postgres, with Redis holding session state. Streaming is a per-session WebSocket carrying typed events — tool_call , response_text_delta , layout_patch_op , layout_ready , done — so the agent acts on patches while the rest of the surface is still arriving. Entity-id hydration cuts the token bill by roughly 80%. The model never writes product data. It writes entity ids, the catalog declares which props are resolved() and the client resolves them through a HydratorMap . Tokens go to judgment, not to transcribing a product feed. Turns survive a dropped connect

title: DrawMCP
pitch: I rebuilt the public Excalidraw MCP as a WebMCP to showcase the power and utility of WebMCP with a measured almost 7x performance improvement by doing so.
about_excerpt: I rebuilt the public Excalidraw MCP as a WebMCP to showcase the power and utility of WebMCP with a measured almost 7x performance improvement by doing so. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 20 randomized production pairs: DrawMCP finished the measured task 6.58x faster at p50. Seven WebMCP tools let the browser agent read and update the same live Excalidraw canvas. DrawMCP: Excalidraw's public MCP rebuilt as a WebMCP Inspiration Excalidraw has a great MCP server. I used it and kept running into one awkward boundary: the agent generated a diagram in a remote widget while the canvas in front of me remained separate. I wanted the agent to work with me on the page I already had open. That is where WebMCP clicked. DrawMCP is my WebMCP take on the current Excalidraw MCP. You draw through the normal Excalidraw controls, and the agent works on that same canvas through WebMCP. What it does DrawMCP gives a browser agent seven tools over the Excalidraw canvas on screen: get_canvas_summary get_selection add_elements update_elements delete_elements fit_to_content organize_diagram A person can sketch an idea, select part of it, or move a shape by hand. The agent reads that exact state and can continue the drawing. Both edits use one revision history, so the normal Excalidraw Undo and Redo controls still work. There is no connector to configure for the WebMCP path, no export step, and no second canvas to reconcile. The site also places the official Excalidraw MCP and DrawMCP side by side. Both are useful. They solve the agent-to-canvas boundary in different places. How I built it The app uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and the published Excalidraw React SDK. The /canvas page registers seven closed-schema tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Read tools return bounded scene and selection summaries. Write tools validate their inputs again when they execute, serialize competing changes, support cancellation, and accept an optional expected_revision so a stale agent write cannot silently overwrite a newer human edit. Every agent mutation goes through one canvas service and Excalidraw's own element versioning. The tool returns after the editor has applied the change. Registrations are aborted when the page unmounts, and the ordinary editor still works when WebMCP is unavailable. I used Puppeteer for real-browser evaluation, Vitest for component and contract tests, AJV for runtime schema validation, and Vercel for the production deployment. The measured result I ran 20 randomized production pairs from the same machine. All 40 trials passed the same scene oracle. The DrawMCP lane called add_elements , called fit_to_content , and proved that the rendered Excalidraw pixels changed before its clock stopped. It measured 13.71 ms at p50. The official public MCP lane stopped when create_view returned its checkpoint, before the separate widget rendered, and measured 90.23 ms at p50. DrawMCP was 6.58 times faster for this measured task and 9.93 times faster at p90. Those clocks include different work, so I keep the boundary beside the result. This is a measured workflow result, not a claim that every WebMCP site beats every remote MCP server. Challenges I ran into Drawing rectangles was easy. Keeping Excalidraw normal after an agent write was the real work. Bound text, connectors, selection, revisions, stale writes, cancellation, local recovery, and native history all had to survive the tool boundary. The benchmark was the second hard part. The two implementations do not expose the same stopping point. I kept every failed trial in the denominator, randomized the lane order, throttled calls to the public service, checksummed the raw rows, and withheld p95 because each live lane had fewer than 40 successful samples. Accomplishments that I am proud of The final release passed 115 deterministic tests, 17 browser proof steps against both the development and production builds, 11 Chrome Labs smoke calls, 125 repeated local-model decisions, and nine desktop and mobile visual routes. The shared-canvas evaluation also proved a complete human edit, WebMCP read, agent write, rendered change, Undo, and Redo sequence. More importantly, the product still feels like Excalidraw. The person can use the normal keyboard shortcuts and pointer while the agent sees the same scene. Nothing has to leave the page for the two of them to continue working. What I learned WebMCP changes who owns the useful context. The page already knows the current selection, viewport, scene revision, and undo history. Exposing a small set of bounded tools lets the agent use that context without inventing another document model beside it. I also learned that tool design matters more than tool count. Seven narrow tools were enough because each one has a clear job, a closed input schema, bounded output, and visible consequences on the page. What's next for DrawMCP I want to prepare a narrow upstream proposal for the official Excalidraw MCP project after the challenge, so this can be officially integrated into the live Excalidraw platform For now, the live site shows the thing I wanted to test: a person and an agent can work on the same open Excalidraw canvas without passing a drawing back and forth. Built With ajv excalidraw node.js puppeteer react typescript vercel vite vitest webmcp Try it out drawmcp.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Designed and built DrawMCP end to end: the WebMCP tool surface, Excalidraw state boundary, tests and evals, benchmark methodology, visual system, documentation, and Vercel deployment. Abdul Moiz Shahzad AI engineer building agentic systems, MCP tooling, and full-stack products with Python, TypeScript, React, and PostgreSQL.
