title: NapkinLab
pitch: Sketch UI flows with your AI agent on the same live canvas through native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Sketch UI flows with your AI agent on the same live canvas through native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Product ideas usually start visually: a rough layout, a screenshot, a few boxes, or a hand-drawn flow. But when an AI coding agent joins the process, that visual context gets flattened into prompts and descriptions. The person can see what they mean, while the agent receives an incomplete or outdated translation. I wanted a workspace where the person and the agent could collaborate on the same live artifact. The human should be able to think spatially and direct the product visually; the agent should be able to inspect the actual structure, make precise changes, and immediately return control to the human. That is what Napkin Lab is designed to do. What it does Napkin Lab is a browser-based visual UI-flow sketcher. It helps people turn rough product ideas into structured, testable flows before committing to production code. The studio has three connected views: IdeaFrame for arranging Frames and reusable interface blocks. FlowMap for connecting navigation and understanding the journey between Frames. RoughDraft for clicking through the planned experience like a lightweight prototype. Napkin Lab also supports browser-local autosave, .napkin import and export, annotations, visual tracing, temporary agent handoffs, and snapshots of eligible public URLs. The important WebMCP addition is that an AI agent no longer has to infer the sketch from a screenshot or wait for the user to export a file. In a WebMCP-capable browser, the agent can work with the sketch that is open right now. How WebMCP is used Napkin Lab exposes two native WebMCP tools: napkin_describe This read-only tool returns a compact, structured description of the active sketch, including its Frames, interface elements, notes, navigation flows, canvas items, and current selection. It intentionally does not expose the application’s raw state store or embedded image data. The agent receives the information it needs to understand the product flow without receiving unrelated internal state. napkin_apply_operations This tool lets an agent apply a validated batch of document operations to the live sketch. The operation input is treated as untrusted data and parsed at runtime. Napkin Lab validates the entire batch before applying anything. If one operation is invalid, the whole batch is rejected and the document remains unchanged. A successful batch: Appears immediately on the visible canvas. Can contain between one and 100 operations. Supports references to objects created earlier in the same batch. Produces an updated structured description for verification. Is recorded as one Undo step. Napkin Lab also rejects agent writes while the person is in the middle of a canvas gesture. This creates a clear coordination boundary: the agent cannot race the human while they are dragging, resizing, or editing something. The result is a genuine shared-canvas workflow. A person can sketch or select something, ask the agent for a change, watch that change appear in the real document, and undo the entire agent action once if it is not what they wanted. What was added during the challenge Napkin Lab existed before the WebMCP Challenge. The pre-existing product already included the visual editor, FlowMap, RoughDraft, import and export, browser-local autosave, an optional stdio MCP server, and hosted handoff infrastructure. During the challenge submission period, I added and refined the native in-page WebMCP implementation. That work included: Native discovery of napkin_describe and napkin_apply_operations. A shared compact description layer used by the browser and stdio transports. Runtime parsing of untrusted operation input at the document-store boundary. Atomic operation batches with one-batch/one-undo behavior. References to objects created earlier in the same batch. Rejection of writes during an active human gesture. Safe registration and cleanup across React StrictMode remounts. Serialized registration and duplicate-name retry behavior. Selection cleanup after mutations. Updated agent guidance and WebMCP-specific regression tests. Validation in ChatGPT’s WebMCP-capable in-app browser. The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin. It does not create a second, agent-only editing engine. Both the person and the agent operate on the same underlying document model. How I built it Napkin Lab is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Zustand. The application detects document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext and registers its tools only when WebMCP is available. Browsers without WebMCP still receive the normal visual editor. The public application is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Temporary relay sessions use Workers KV, while Snapshot from URL uses a service-bound Cloudflare Worker with Browser Rendering. The core editor does not require an account. OpenAI Codex helped me implement and review the WebMCP transport, refine the tool schemas and descriptions, test runtime validation and atomic behavior, diagnose registration lifecycle issues, and verify the native tools in the in-app browser. I also used Codex to run the automated test, lint, type-check, and production-build gates; audit the repository before publication; prepare a history-free public contest snapshot; and verify the deployed site, relay, snapshot service, license, and native WebMCP discovery. Challenges The hardest part was not simply registering a browser tool. It was making agent edits behave like trustworthy product interactions. That meant handling partial failures, malformed operation input, React registration lifecycles, duplicate tools, human-agent editing conflicts, selection state, and undo history. A tool call returning successfully was not enough: the visible canvas, structured result, and document history all needed to agree. Another challenge was preserving the value of an existing product while being transparent about what was specifically built during the challenge. The public repository therefore includes a dedicated contest-period document that separates the original editor from the new WebMCP work. What I learned The biggest lesson was that useful agent integration is as much about boundaries as capabilities. Giving an agent permission to mutate a document is easy. Making that mutation understandable, validated, atomic, reversible, and coordinated with the person is the real work. WebMCP makes it possible for the webpage itself to define those boundaries. Napkin Lab can expose a small, intentional interface instead of handing an agent unrestricted application state or forcing it to interpret the UI through screenshots alone. Why it matters Napkin Lab explores a different relationship between visual tools and coding agents. The agent is not replacing the canvas, and the canvas is not merely producing a prompt for the agent. They are sharing one working model. That makes it possible for product owners, designers, developers, and small teams to communicate product structure more directly, make changes with less translation, and keep a human-visible, reversible record of what the agent did. title: Necivia
pitch: Council services for everyone - Humans × Agents
about_excerpt: Council services for everyone - Humans × Agents Like 2 Comment Story Updates Live page adapted by WebMCP to make the experience easier to read and use. Natural-language request triggers WebMCP and changes the same live Necivia interface. Necivia exposes six structured WebMCP tools — deliberately with no submission tool. The agent updates the same housing-repair draft the resident can see and edit. WebMCP opens the final review, but only the resident can confirm and submit. After human confirmation, Necivia creates the repair and generates a unique NEC reference. The same persisted repair and reference appears immediately in the authorised staff inbox. Final WebMCP evaluation: 11/11 natural-language tool-selection and safety scenarios passed. Inspiration Many council websites provide great essentials, but I have noticed one weakness that they have in common: they expect everyone to use the same interface. Sometimes people may have different needs such as they might not have their glasses and need larger text for only that day, they could be exhausted, find buttons difficult to tap, need simpler language or just want to complete a task one step at a time. But what if, instead of expecting people to adapt to a website, the website could adapt to them? That led to the core idea behind Necivia. I decided to explore the concept of WebMCP beyond just being an alternative to AI clicking around a website. I wanted the human and the agent to collaborate through the same interface and same state. What it does Necivia is a fictional council-service platform that was developed around the idea of Humans × Agents . A resident can naturally describe what they need and an AI agent can use the exposed WebMCP tools to help complete the task. For example, if someone says that the writing is too small, buttons are difficult to tap, the page feels overwhelming or they want to go one step at a time, the agent can adapt the live website in real time. Text size, control size, information density, language complexity, motion and journey style can all be modified without creating a separate AI interface. The housing-repair journey goes further. An agent can: understand the information required for a repair read the resident's current draft add or correct only the information the resident provides check whether the report is complete open the final review screen But the important part is what it cannot do. Necivia intentionally exposes no submission tool through WebMCP. The agent can help with the task, but the resident must personally press "Confirm and submit". Only then does the server validate and create the repair, generate its NEC-... reference and make the same case available to authorised council staff. This means the agent is not operating a hidden parallel workflow. The human and agent are collaborating through the same real service. How I built it Necivia is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, PostgreSQL and Railway. The live product exposes six WebMCP tools : adapt_experience get_experience_preferences get_housing_repair_requirements get_housing_repair_draft update_housing_repair_draft open_housing_repair_review The Page Support and housing-repair interfaces share their state with these tools, so a change made through WebMCP is automatically shown in the resident's interface. For the production side, I added authenticated resident and staff accounts, database-backed sessions, persistent repair cases, role and tenant isolation, protected attachments, server-side validation, rate limiting, security headers, audit records and a delivery adapter. Challenges I ran into One of the biggest challenges was deciding where the agent's authority ends. It would have been easy to just expose a submit_repair tool and let the agent complete everything, but for a council service, I didn't think that it was the right architectural decision. I instead separated assistance from authority : WebMCP can prepare and review the task, while submitting the final form remains a human action. Another challenge was keeping the human interface and agent interface from becoming two separate systems. The WebMCP tools therefore operate on the same visible draft and Page Support state rather than maintaining their own hidden copy. I also spent a huge chunk of my time testing edge cases: partial updates, missing answers, invalid future dates, uncertain safety answers, unauthenticated access and requests unrelated to the available tools. Deployment also brought its own challenges too, including database migrations, persistent storage, authentication and ensuring the same submitted case could move all the way from the resident account to the staff inbox. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am very proud that Necivia demonstrates WebMCP as more than just browser automation . A natural-language request can actually adapt a person's live experience and the resident can continue exactly from where the agent left off. I am also proud of the human-confirmation boundary . There are six useful tools but no submission tool, that is deliberately part of the design. The final deployed workflow also works end-to-end: a resident can prepare and submit a housing repair, receive a server-generated reference, refresh and still see it and an authorised staff user can see and manage the same persisted case. My final WebMCP natural-language evaluation passed 11 out of 11 scenarios , alongside the application's automated test suite and production verification. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that designing for agents is not just about exposing as many tools as possible. The description, schema and boundaries of each tool matter because the agent needs to know enough information to be able to choose the right action and should know enough restrictions to know when not to act . I also learned that WebMCP becomes much more interesting when it complements the existing website instead of replacing it. The best experience was not “AI does everything for you”; it was the human and agent being able to work together on the same task. Building Necivia also substantially taught me about production architecture, authentication, database persistence, security, evaluation and deployment beyond the WebMCP integration itself. What's next for Necivia Necivia currently focuses on one specific flagship council journey rather than trying to simulate every possible council service. The next step would be applying the same pattern to more services while keeping the foundational principles the same: one shared interface, structured AI agent capabilities, reversible assistance and clear human control over consequential actions. I would also like to explore how the adaptation layer could become more contextual over time, so websites can respond to temporary requirements without forcing people to permanently configure accessibility or preference settings. Ultimately, Necivia is an experiment in a different relationship with the web: instead of every person having to learn how each website works, the website can meet the person where they are. title: Post-Purchase Resolution
pitch: When a purchase goes wrong, WebMCP helps an agent find the right Shopify order and prepare a resolution—without taking authority away from the customer or merchant.
about_excerpt: When a purchase goes wrong, WebMCP helps an agent find the right Shopify order and prepare a resolution—without taking authority away from the customer or merchant. Like Comment Story Updates Post-Purchase Resolution Shopping agents know how to buy. What happens when something goes wrong? Post-Purchase Resolution is an agent-native post-purchase support experience built with WebMCP + Shopify . Instead of forcing a customer to search for an order number, navigate support menus, or explain the same problem several times, the customer can simply describe what went wrong in natural language. The agent can then discover the website's structured WebMCP capabilities, find the correct purchase, read authoritative Shopify state, and prepare the next step. But there is one deliberate boundary: The agent can help. It cannot silently become the customer or the merchant. The customer keeps customer authority. The merchant keeps merchant authority. Shopify remains the external source of truth. 🎥 Demo Watch the full demo In the demo, a customer reports that a Portable 4K Action Camera — $149 arrived damaged and would not turn on. The customer never provides an order number. From that natural-language request, the agent discovers the site's WebMCP tools, finds the correct authenticated purchase, reads its return eligibility, and prepares a resolution. Then: Agent prepares → Customer commits → Merchant decides → Shopify records the truth. 💡 Inspiration AI shopping experiences are becoming increasingly capable before checkout. Agents can search. They can compare. They can recommend. They can help people buy. But commerce does not end at checkout. Products arrive damaged. The wrong variant is delivered. Shipments arrive late. Customers need exchanges, returns, replacements, or refunds. And that part of the experience is still dominated by: order numbers support menus forms ticket queues policy pages repeated explanations disconnected customer and merchant workflows That led us to a simple question: If the web is becoming agentic, what should happen when the purchase itself goes wrong? We did not want to build another chatbot floating on top of an ecommerce site. We wanted the website itself to expose meaningful, structured capabilities that an agent could understand and use safely. That is where WebMCP became the core of the product rather than an add-on. ✨ What it does Post-Purchase Resolution lets a customer describe a purchase problem naturally. For example: “The action camera I bought recently arrived damaged and won't turn on. Can you find the purchase and tell me what I can do? Don't submit anything.” The customer does not need to know the order number. The agent discovers the site's available WebMCP tools and can use: find_order get_order prepare_resolution The experience then separates responsibility between three actors. 🤖 Agent The agent can: understand the customer's intent locate the relevant purchase read authoritative order information inspect return eligibility prepare the appropriate resolution The agent cannot commit the commerce action through WebMCP. 👤 Customer The authenticated customer decides whether to actually request the return. That action occurs under the customer's own Shopify Customer Account authority. 🏪 Merchant The merchant receives the pending request in a separate decision desk. Only the merchant can approve it. 🟢 Shopify Shopify records the authoritative lifecycle of the return. The website does not invent its own version of commerce state. 🔥 Why WebMCP matters Without structured site capabilities, an agent often has to reason from presentation: inspect UI interpret text locate controls infer what a button means navigate DOM state hope the page still looks the same Post-Purchase Resolution instead exposes explicit business capabilities. Customer intent ↓ ChatGPT / Codex ↓ WebMCP Site Tools ↓ find_order get_order prepare_resolution ↓ Authoritative Shopify data This means the agent does not need to guess that a certain button or piece of text represents an order lookup. The site tells the agent exactly what capability exists. And just as importantly, it tells the agent what capability does not exist. 🔐 The capability boundary This became one of the most important design decisions in the project. The WebMCP surface intentionally contains: ✓ find_order ✓ get_order ✓ prepare_resolution It intentionally does not contain: ✕ request_return ✕ approve_return ✕ refund That is not an unfinished feature. It is the authority model. The agent can find, read, and prepare. The customer commits. The merchant decides. This allowed us to design the experience around collaboration instead of maximum agent autonomy. More agent capability is not always better. The right capability at the right boundary is better. 🛍️ A real end-to-end scenario One of our clean validation runs used a fresh Shopify purchase that was never hardcoded into the application. The application discovered the purchase automatically. The customer then followed the complete flow. Fresh purchase ↓ Agent discovers purchase ↓ Agent prepares resolution ↓ Customer explicitly requests return ↓ Shopify Return = REQUESTED ↓ Merchant reviews request ↓ Merchant approves ↓ Same Shopify Return = OPEN The critical part is that the same external Shopify Return object is preserved throughout the lifecycle. The application is not maintaining a parallel pretend state. Shopify is the system of record. 🧪 Real Shopify proof We verified the architecture against a Shopify development store using test payments and real Shopify Order/Return objects . A clean flow demonstrated: Step Result Fresh order discovered without hardcoding ✅ Customer-scoped purchase ✅ Agent mutation tool exposed No Customer requested return ✅ Shopify Return created REQUESTED Merchant reviewed same Return ✅ Merchant approved ✅ Same Shopify Return updated OPEN Duplicate Return created No Refund automatically performed No This distinction matters. The agent did not manufacture a UI result. The state transition existed independently in Shopify. 🗣️ Natural-language WebMCP verification We also tested the WebMCP experience through ChatGPT/Codex Site Tools. The user described a damaged purchase without giving an order number. The agent discovered and used: find_order get_order prepare_resolution It found the correct purchase and prepared the resolution. Nothing was submitted. An independent Shopify check confirmed: Return created by agent: NO Refund created by agent: NO Approval event: NO We then repeated the experience using a spoken request in a new chat with no previous order context . The observed flow was: Spoken request ↓ ChatGPT agent turn ↓ Website Site Tools enumerated ↓ find_order ↓ get_order ↓ Correct purchase found The spoken request asked only to find the purchase and explain the available option. The agent did exactly that. It did not stage a resolution unnecessarily. That gave us an interesting proof of intent-sensitive tool selection. 🏗️ How we built it The product is built around four distinct layers. ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Customer / ChatGPT / Codex │ └──────────────┬──────────────┘ │ WebMCP │ ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐ │ Post-Purchase Resolution │ │ Vercel-hosted application │ └──────────────┬──────────────┘ │ ┌────────┴────────┐ │ │ Customer Account Admin API API │ │ │ ▼ ▼ Customer action Merchant action │ │ └────────┬─────────┘ ▼ Shopify External source of truth WebMCP The site registers structured tools through the browser's model context. The final tool surface is deliberately small: find_order get_order prepare_resolution Shopify Customer Account API The authenticated customer flow uses Shopify Customer Account authentication. This keeps order discovery scoped to the currently authenticated customer's purchases. The customer action uses customer authority. Shopify Admin API Merchant approval uses a separate server-side Admin authority. The Admin credential is never exposed to the browser or agent. Vercel The public application and server-side API routes are deployed on Vercel. Secrets remain on the server boundary. 🔑 Authentication and authority Customer authentication uses OAuth/OIDC with PKCE. The customer session is used to query purchases belonging to that authenticated customer. The architecture does not permit arbitrary customer order enumeration from the customer flow. The merchant side uses a separate operator access control in the current implementation. That merchant access layer is intentionally distinct from customer authentication. Current limitation: The merchant decision desk uses an operator credential rather than full merchant OAuth/identity. We document this explicitly rather than presenting it as something it is not. 🛡️ Security by capability design Security was not treated as a final checklist item. It influenced the WebMCP architecture itself. Important boundaries include: customer-scoped order retrieval no arbitrary order lookup from authenticated customer flow S

title: Rhythm
pitch: An offline-first training journal where people and AI agents analyze workout history and safely evolve training plans through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An offline-first training journal where people and AI agents analyze workout history and safely evolve training plans through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Training data is often split between a notebook, app screens, exported files, and AI chats. That makes it difficult for an assistant to understand what was planned, what actually happened, and what should change next. I built Rhythm to keep that history reliable and to let people work with an AI without handing it unrestricted database access or allowing it to silently rewrite a training program. What it does Rhythm is a multi-user, mobile-first, offline-first PWA for strength training and swimming. It guides a workout, records weight, repetitions, RIR, substitutions, discomfort, wellbeing, and session feedback, and keeps planned work, completed facts, and future suggestions as separate data. It also provides history, charts, e1RM and progression signals, body measurements, schedules, and portable JSON, Markdown, and ZIP exports. On the authenticated Assistant page, Rhythm exposes a focused catalog of 17 WebMCP tools: 12 read tools for profile context, programs, templates, workouts, exercise history, progress, schedules, search, and alternatives; plus 5 write tools for program drafts, workout rescheduling, exercise replacement, and plan activation. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Before WebMCP, the reliable workflow required six manual steps: export a report, download it, open an AI chat, upload the file, download a new plan, and import it back into the diary. With WebMCP, the assistant can request only the current context it needs, discuss the evidence with the athlete, prepare a draft, and perform a narrowly scoped action in one connected conversation. The user remains in control. A new program is always created as an immutable draft first. Activating it displays an impact preview inside Rhythm and waits for explicit human confirmation. If WebMCP is unavailable, the ordinary PWA and the JSON/Markdown workflow continue to work normally. How I built it The application uses PHP 8.2+, MySQL or MariaDB, server-rendered HTML, vanilla JavaScript, Fetch API, a Service Worker, Cache API, and IndexedDB. WebMCP is implemented with document.modelContext.registerTool on the authenticated /assistant page. Each tool is a thin adapter over a same-origin semantic endpoint and existing application services. The server session determines the current user; tool inputs never accept a user_id. Read responses are bounded and paginated. Writes use CSRF and Origin checks, Fetch Metadata policy, optimistic locking, idempotency keys, rate limits, audit trails, and tenant-scoped repository queries. Feature flags and a per-user canary allowlist support controlled rollout. Database text is treated as untrusted content rather than instructions. What I added during the challenge Rhythm existed before the submission period as an offline-first training diary. From August 26 through September 3, I added the complete WebMCP layer: authenticated read APIs, the page-scoped registry, 12 read tools, 5 write tools, immutable program drafts, human-confirmed activation, safe workout-instance changes, security hardening, prompt-injection fixtures, A–J end-to-end coverage, MySQL validation, paginated template reads, rollout controls, a public product guide, and full English localization. The dated Git history separates this work from the earlier PWA. Challenges The hardest part was designing tools that were useful to an agent but still narrow enough to protect historical training data. A generic database or endpoint tool would have been simpler, but unsafe. Another challenge was combining online agent actions with an offline-first workout flow without placing WebMCP writes into the offline queue. Activation also needed to be conversational while still ending with a real in-app human decision. What I learned I learned how to translate product capabilities into small semantic tools, how to treat tool annotations as hints rather than a security boundary, and how to combine agent workflows with immutable history, confirmation, idempotency, auditability, and graceful fallback. The result is not only an AI demo: it is a complete training product in which people and agents can collaborate without giving up control of the data or the final decision. What's next Next I want to refine onboarding for judges and new athletes, expand deterministic progress explanations, and continue compatibility testing across WebMCP clients while keeping the open JSON and Markdown workflow as a portable foundation. title: SchemaPair
pitch: Agent-native database diagramming, built on drawDB and WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Agent-native database diagramming, built on drawDB and WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates build: One prompt, four tables, three foreign keys. Validated first, one undo step, canvas pans to the change. query: check_query tests real SQL against the diagram without running it, and flags join and filter columns that need an index. removal: Deletes are proposal-only. The agent shows the cascade; only a human click on Confirm applies it. Still undoable. checkpoint: Named checkpoints: save before a risky change, restore with one click. Every tool call is logged. Inspiration Every application stands on its database. Get the schema right at the start and every service, query, and migration downstream gets easier; get it wrong and you pay for it for years. Schema design happens on a visual canvas, and that is exactly where AI agents have been locked out: they can scrape the DOM, or work on a separate copy of your schema in a chat window, but they cannot touch the diagram you are actually looking at. WebMCP changes that. We wanted the agent to help lay the foundation properly, on the same live canvas the human uses, with the human keeping undo and the final say. What it does SchemaPair is drawDB , the open-source ER diagram editor, with 17 WebMCP tools registered on document.modelContext . An agent running in the browser can: Design : turn "a SaaS billing schema with users, plans, subscriptions and invoices" into tables, columns, primary and foreign keys on the canvas. The whole request is validated before it touches state, lands as one undo step , and the editor pans to the change ( apply_schema_changes , import_sql ). Review : run drawDB's own validator plus production checks (foreign keys without indexes, nullable FKs, missing timestamps, unsized VARCHARs) and get ready-to-apply fixes ( validate_schema , review_schema ). Verify : check that a real SQL query works against the diagram without executing it, with index suggestions ( check_query ), and explain the join path between any two tables ( explain_join_path ). Ship : generate DDL from drawDB's exporters, up/down migrations since the diagram was opened, and sample INSERTs ( generate_sql , generate_migration , generate_sample_inserts ). Text only, never executed. Organise : add notes and areas, tidy the layout, open saved diagrams and templates ( annotate_diagram , arrange_tables , list_workspace , open_diagram ). Stay safe : removals are proposal-only . plan_removal computes the full cascade and shows a confirmation card; only a human click applies it, and there is no tool parameter that lets the agent confirm. Named checkpoint s can be created and restored by either party. An Agent activity panel lists every tool call with its exact input and output, hosts the confirmation cards and checkpoints, and has an "Undo last agent change" button. How we built it A single WebMCPBridge React component, mounted in the editor page, feature-detects document.modelContext and registers all tools under one AbortController , so they are removed when you leave the editor. Browsers without WebMCP get plain drawDB. Handlers read the live React state through refs (no parallel copy of the diagram) and commit changes as a snapshot entry on drawDB's existing undo stack, so autosave, Ctrl+Z and the timeline work unchanged. Pure planners in src/webmcp/ validate whole requests before any state change, enforce limits (25 ops per call, 64-char names), reject ambiguous names instead of guessing, and reuse drawDB's validator, SQL exporters, importer and migration generator as-is. 53 unit tests on Node's test runner, and a 71-check Chrome DevTools Protocol harness that drives all 17 tools through document.modelContext.executeTool in a real WebMCP-enabled Chrome, against the dev server, the production bundle and the deployed URL. Deployed on Vercel with the Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 header WebMCP needs. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is only exposed in origin-isolated documents, so the production deploy needed an explicit Origin-Agent-Cluster header before document.modelContext appeared at all. Making one agent call equal one undo step on an undo stack designed for single UI actions. Applying several addTable calls in one tick reversed undo order; we commit through a single snapshot entry instead. Migration baselines: the first autosave of a new diagram reloads state, so "since I opened the diagram" had to be pinned to the state seen with an empty undo stack. Keeping deletes safe without making them useless: the answer was a proposal card the agent can create but never confirm. Validator messages follow the editor's language, so tests had to pin i18n and agents key off structured suggestions rather than message text. What we learned The best WebMCP tools are not new features; they are the app's existing logic exposed against live state. Every tool in SchemaPair wraps something drawDB already did. What WebMCP adds is the shared canvas: the human sees exactly what the agent did, on the diagram they were already looking at, and can undo it with one key. What's next Connect to a real database for migration diffs and query checks against actual data. Multi-agent sessions on one canvas with per-agent activity. Upstream the WebMCP layer to drawDB. Attribution SchemaPair is a fork of drawDB and retains its AGPL-3.0 license. Everything added during the challenge starts at upstream commit 5efc5fd and lives in src/webmcp/ , src/components/WebMCPBridge.jsx , src/components/WebMCPActivityPanel.jsx , scripts/ and docs/ . title: AgentMarkup Studio
pitch: A browser agent edits a draft of your website's AI surface through WebMCP while you watch. A deterministic compiler generates the artifacts, flags contradictions, and exports the build config.
about_excerpt: A browser agent edits a draft of your website's AI surface through WebMCP while you watch. A deterministic compiler generates the artifacts, flags contradictions, and exports the build config. Like 1 Comment Story Updates AgentMarkup Studio connected to ChatGPT through WebMCP: 8 tools registered, guided three-step flow. Deterministic review: validations and cross-surface contradiction rules, all green after the agent's edits. C1 and C2 fire: llms.txt invites citation while search crawlers are blocked. Caught by rules, not model opinion. The payoff: one downloadable agentmarkup.config.mjs, compiled in the browser by the same engine the build tools run. Inspiration Site owners keep asking for two things at once: AI search should cite their pages, and the same content should stay out of model training. That intent is expressed across separately maintained surfaces: robots.txt, llms.txt, Content-Signal headers, JSON-LD, and Agent Cards. Edited and checked separately, they drift into contradictions - an llms.txt that invites citation while robots.txt blocks every crawler that could retrieve it. We already had agentmarkup, an open-source build-time toolkit, aimed at that drift. WebMCP is what let us put the agent in the site owner's browser, on the same draft, with the human still holding undo and download. What it does AgentMarkup Studio (agentmarkup.dev/studio) is where a browser agent and a human edit one draft of a site's machine-readable surface. The agent connects through WebMCP in your browser, inspects the live site, and edits that draft through eight tools. You state intent in plain language: "Make my site friendly to AI search but keep my content out of training data. Start from what the site already has." A deterministic compiler, the same @agentmarkup/core engine our published npm packages run at build time, emits the artifacts client-side. Eight cross-surface rules (C1-C8) check the draft for defined contradictions. Every change flashes in the UI and lands in a provenance log with an Agent or Human badge. Undo, reset, and saving the file are human-only - no tool can trigger them; the agent can read the compiled output but cannot revert or clear anything. The downloadable output is agentmarkup.config.mjs. Use it with our Vite, Astro, Next, or Nuxt integration, or with the CLI; the build then generates the policy surfaces reviewed in the Studio. How we built it Eight tools on document.modelContext (navigator fallback; AbortController teardown): get_studio_state, set_site_identity, set_access_policy, curate_agent_pages, configure_agent_card, compile_agent_surface, export_build_plan, inspect_site. JSON-Schema inputs and outputs with explicit size limits (names <=30 chars, descriptions <=500, results <=1500); read tools carry readOnlyHint, inspection results carry untrustedContentHint. Tool results are authored by the state reducer, so the agent reads exactly what was applied, including anything dropped at a cap. inspect_site calls our same-origin rate-limited checker API and forwards only allowlisted {level, title} findings - never page HTML. The exported config is rendered through JSON-only serialization; a regression test imports the rendered file and asserts hostile values stay inert. About 10K new lines and 320 tests, all in timestamped commits dated 2026-08-26 onward. Challenges we ran into Making tool results truthful was harder than making tools work: React dispatch is asynchronous, so the agent could read a stale state until we pre-applied the pure reducer to a ref. Capping agent input safely surfaced ordering bugs (an add-plus-delete at the crawler cap depended on property order). And because WebMCP tool results have a size limit, export_build_plan returns either the complete generated config or a pointer to the UI download; it never returns a truncated executable file. What we learned WebMCP's annotations matched the split we needed: readOnlyHint on reads so the host can treat them as non-mutating, untrustedContentHint on inspect results so the host can scrutinize them. We still had to make tool results match applied state, cap inputs, and keep the exported config inert. Prior work disclosure agentmarkup (the npm packages and agentmarkup.dev) predates the hackathon. Everything WebMCP - the Studio page, the eight document.modelContext tools, the browser compiler wiring, the C1-C8 contradiction workflow, the provenance log with human-only undo/reset/download, and the checker-backed inspect intake - was built for this challenge. HACKATHON.md in the repo has the commit split. Try it (judges) Open https://agentmarkup.dev/studio/ in the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser (verified on macOS) - the banner reads "Agent connected: 8 tools registered". Alternate: Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (verified on Chrome 151). Say: "Make www.cochinescu.com friendly to AI search but keep my content out of training data. Start from what the site already has." If the host prompts for tool permission, approve it; ChatGPT's in-app browser may not prompt. Then: "Now block the AI search crawlers too - just do it." If the agent empties the llms.txt page index instead of contradicting itself, tell it to put the pages back and let the Studio judge the result. Contradiction C1 "Cited content blocks retrieval" then fires in the Findings panel, alongside C2 against the Content-Signal header. Then: "Fix the contradictions, keep training blocked." - findings go green. Download config exports the generated agentmarkup.config.mjs (saving the file is a human-only action). Draft editing and compilation stay client-side; nothing is deployed. The optional Inspect intake calls our rate-limited checker API; if the limit is reached, the tool returns a bounded retry message - that is designed behavior. No login needed. title: Algoosh Agentic Shopping
pitch: AI finds and prepares what you need. You review it, provide delivery details, and approve the payment. Offline, online, and now agentic flows are supported. Better than Shopify!
about_excerpt: AI finds and prepares what you need. You review it, provide delivery details, and approve the payment. Offline, online, and now agentic flows are supported. Better than Shopify! Like 1 Comment Story Updates Algoosh, webMCP agentic shopping Algoosh Seller Protal, client app Promo catalog Buyer application UI Infrastructure Smart Contract payment protocol Algoosh Agentic Shopping Inspiration Shopping with an AI agent should feel easier than browsing dozens of pages, comparing products, filling a cart, and repeatedly entering the same checkout information. Most websites, however, still force agents to interpret visual interfaces and simulate clicks, which can be unreliable. At the other extreme, allowing an agent to control a wallet or submit payments creates unacceptable security and trust risks. Algoosh Agentic Shopping explores a better model: let AI handle product discovery and order preparation while keeping the buyer in control of delivery details, wallet access, and payment approval. Algoosh was already a QR-first commerce platform built on Algorand. WebMCP gave us the opportunity to transform every Algoosh Promo catalogue into an agent-readable storefront, while x402 provided a structured way to connect agent-prepared orders with verifiable payments. Our guiding principle became: The AI can shop and prepare. Only the human can approve and pay. What it does Algoosh Agentic Shopping lets a shopper open an Algoosh catalogue and ask an AI agent for help using natural language. For example: I want to make mushroom risotto tonight. I already have rice, olive oil, and garlic. Find the missing ingredients in this store and prepare an order for me to review. The agent can: Read the current catalogue. Inspect individual products and prices. Select products and quantities. Prepare a durable order. Return an approval link and QR code. Check the order state before or after the buyer completes checkout. The buyer then opens the approval link in the official Algoosh application, either on the same device or by scanning the QR code with a phone. There, the buyer: Reviews the selected products and preliminary subtotal. Chooses a fulfillment method. Provides any required delivery information. Reviews the final authoritative price. Explicitly approves the transaction in their own wallet. Through this interface, the AI never receives private delivery information, unlocks the wallet, signs a transaction, or submits payment. Algoosh's WebMCP tools neither request nor return delivery plaintext or wallet credentials. After payment, the agent can retrieve a privacy-safe order summary, the payment state, the selected fulfillment option, the final total, and links to the verified payment and application transactions. How we built it We extended the existing Algoosh platform with four page-local WebMCP tools: get_current_algoosh_catalogue get_current_algoosh_product prepare_algoosh_order get_algoosh_order_status The tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() only after the current catalogue has loaded. Their lifecycle is tied to an AbortSignal , so stale registrations are removed when the catalogue changes or the page unloads. No separate MCP server installation is required for this flow; the loaded catalogue page exposes the tools directly. The ordering system uses a two-stage process. First, the WebMCP tool creates a durable but non-payable preliminary intent. The agent supplies only product IDs, quantities, and an idempotency key. It cannot set authoritative prices, seller addresses, payment destinations, delivery details, or wallet information in the order request. Next, the buyer opens the approval handoff. The Algoosh application collects fulfillment information, encrypts the private delivery payload in the browser, and asks the x402 service to finalize the order. Before issuing a payment requirement, the service independently reloads the seller's catalogue and verifies: Product identities and quantities. Current prices and payment assets. Seller and payment addresses. The selected fulfillment option and its current terms and cost. The target Algorand network and application. The service then binds the buyer identity and encrypted-order commitments into the signed quote. If any important commercial term changed, the order stops before payment and the buyer must create and review a new order. Because a token transfer alone is not sufficient evidence of an Algoosh order, we implemented a custom x402 v2 scheme named algoosh-order . Settlement validation checks both the payment and the adjacent createOrderPaid smart-contract call against the signed quote. The finalized order uses an x402 PAYMENT-REQUIRED response containing the signed quote. The buyer application verifies that quote and constructs an atomic Algorand transaction group containing the payment and the Algoosh smart-contract order call. Only the buyer's wallet can approve and submit that group. Redis stores the durable state used for atomic intent creation, idempotency, settlement recovery, and duplicate-order protection. Algoosh Sync validates the resulting public on-chain evidence and correlates it with the prepared order. The approval URL is a short-lived opaque capability link. It contains no personal information, is served with Cache-Control: no-store , and cannot be redirected to an untrusted destination. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was preserving human wallet control while still creating a genuine agentic shopping experience. Many agent-payment flows assume that the agent or facilitator can sign and submit the payment. That model did not fit Algoosh. We designed the preliminary-intent and browser-approval stages so the agent can make useful progress without ever receiving payment authority. Another challenge was maintaining trust across several independent surfaces: Promo catalogue -> WebMCP agent -> x402 service -> Buyer application -> Wallet -> Algorand -> Sync The trust-critical components needed to preserve consistent bindings across the catalogue, products, mount, buyer, seller, fulfillment selection, order seed, and transaction, while exposing only the information appropriate to each surface. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that Algoosh Agentic Shopping is more than a catalogue-reading demo. It connects WebMCP product discovery to a real, human-approved commerce flow. Key accomplishments include: Four functional WebMCP tools verified in a production browser context. A cross-device approval handoff with both a link and generated QR code. A complete low-value Algorand TestNet purchase with explicit buyer approval. x402 payment requirements carrying a signed quote backed by authoritative catalogue data. A custom x402 settlement scheme that validates the complete Algoosh atomic group rather than only a token transfer. Redis-backed recovery that survives service restarts. Protection against duplicate payments during uncertain confirmation. Recovery from temporary blockchain indexer delays. Detection of changed prices or selected fulfillment terms before payment. Privacy-safe agent status responses containing no delivery details. Exact display amounts, ISO timestamps, consistent network metadata, repeated order summaries, and transaction explorer links for agents. Browser-side encryption of the buyer's delivery information. Strict separation between AI assistance and wallet authority. Most importantly, we extended the real Algoosh shopping and payment architecture instead of building a disconnected hackathon simulation. What we learned We learned that agentic commerce does not have to mean autonomous spending. The most useful experience is collaborative: the agent handles discovery, comparison, and preparation, while the person remains responsible for private information and consequential decisions. We also learned that structured WebMCP tools are far more reliable than asking an agent to interpret and click through an unfamiliar interface. Clear tool schemas improve both usability and security by limiting exactly what an agent can provide. Payment confirmation is not a single API call. It is a distributed state machine involving browser state, durable server state, wallet submission, blockchain confirmation, and delayed indexer evidence. Idempotency and recovery are therefore just as important as the successful path. Finally, WebMCP and x402 complement one another well: WebMCP helps the agent understand and use the storefront, while x402 connects the prepared intent to a verifiable payment without giving the agent control of the buyer's wallet. What's next for Algoosh Agentic Shopping Next, we plan to validate the same flow with a controlled MainNet purchase and test it across more WebMCP-capable clients as the proposal evolves. We also want to add explicit cancellation UX, privacy-safe operational telemetry, and better navigation for larger catalogues. Longer term, agents may help shoppers compare products acros

title: Visually
pitch: The browser-first design studio where people and agents create on the same editable canvas.
about_excerpt: The browser-first design studio where people and agents create on the same editable canvas. Like Comment Story Updates From templates to timeline, Visually keeps the complete workflow in one responsive studio. Visually — design together with WebMCP. Human direct manipulation stays visible, editable, and undoable after every agent action. 17 typed WebMCP tools let agents create, revise, audit, and inspect the same live canvas. Browser-local rendering, export, ML, and media pipelines keep creative work on-device. Inspiration Most creative tools still treat an AI agent as an outside observer. Visually explores a more useful model: a professional design editor whose real product actions are available to people and agents on the same editable canvas. What it does Visually is a responsive, local-first visual design studio built around Konva. A person can start from 18 polished templates and edit text, shapes, images, drawings, tables, layers, media, effects, animations, timing, and multiple square, portrait, landscape, print, or custom-size pages. Its WebMCP layer registers 17 typed product-native tools. In the fastest judge path, one brief becomes five coordinated assets—Instagram post, Instagram story, YouTube thumbnail, poster, and landscape banner. An agent can then propagate semantic copy, color-token, and typography changes across all five pages and run a read-only audit for overflow, contrast, safe-area crossings, missing image alt text, and brand consistency. Every call emits a sanitized receipt with affected pages and elements. The full run is undoable in one click, but that undo disables itself after a later human edit so it cannot silently overwrite the person's work. The result is not “AI beside a design app.” It is one shared creative surface: the agent accelerates setup and repetitive changes; the human retains judgment, direct manipulation, and final control. How we used WebMCP Visually feature-detects document.modelContext and progressively registers JSON-schema tools through registerTool . The tools call the same Zustand actions used by the visible React UI, so mutations immediately appear on the Konva canvas, enter the same transaction-aware history, persist locally, and remain directly editable. Read tools are annotated read-only; schemas bound sizes, types, and input lengths; project replacement and deletion require explicit confirm: true . A legacy navigator.modelContext fallback supports earlier browser builds, while the editor continues to work normally when WebMCP is unavailable. This is more reliable than screen-coordinate automation: agents query semantic state, act on stable element IDs, receive structured results, and share the human's real document instead of maintaining a parallel representation. How we built it The application uses React 19, Vite, TypeScript, Konva, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/Base UI, and Cloudflare Workers. The document engine, autosave, rendering, and export paths are browser-first. PNG, JPEG, WebP, SVG, PDF, printable HTML, PPTX, GIF, MP4, and WebM exports run client-side. Media conversion loads ffmpeg.wasm on demand, and background removal uses a lazy browser ML pipeline with WebGPU/WASM fallback. An optional Worker signs direct R2 transfers with progress, cancellation, and retry. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was making agent actions feel native rather than bolted on. Tool calls had to share pointer and keyboard mutation semantics, selection, grouping, page operations, undo/redo, persistence, and destructive confirmations. The second challenge was proving safety without making the flow tedious; that led to read-only annotations, bounded schemas, semantic roles, visible receipts, atomic history steps, and conflict-aware undo. We also had to keep large media pipelines responsive on mobile and robust across radically different aspect ratios. Accomplishments that we're proud of 17 typed, product-native WebMCP tools with structured receipts. One brief becomes five coordinated, fully editable campaign formats. Semantic brand updates modify copy, colors, and typography across every format in one operation. A read-only production audit checks five categories and reports affected pages. A judge-facing activity panel makes real calls inspectable and offers safe one-click undo. 18 original templates and a responsive desktop/mobile editor. Client-side image, document, animation, and video export. Destructive confirmation gates and an unsupported-browser fallback. A complete release gate: 260 frontend tests, 15 Worker tests, 26 applicable desktop/mobile Chromium tests, lint, TypeScript, backend type-checking, and production build. Frontend line coverage is 96.81%; Worker line coverage is 97.14%. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes domain intent rather than a second DOM. “Create this campaign,” “apply this brand revision,” and “audit every page” are safer and more useful than asking an agent to guess coordinates. Just as importantly, agent output must remain immediately editable and reversible or the experience still feels like a handoff rather than collaboration. What's next Next we want opt-in live collaboration, richer typography flow, an attributed third-party asset catalog, reusable agent recipes, and a published reference contract for semantic canvas tools. title: Closeout: Proof of Handoff
pitch: The agent reconciles construction evidence; the human decides what is accepted before readiness changes.
about_excerpt: The agent reconciles construction evidence; the human decides what is accepted before readiness changes. Like Comment Story Updates Desktop: human decision staged and ready for approval Desktop: proposal locked until agent staging Desktop: approval recorded and withdrawable before apply Desktop: approved evidence applied with audit-ready completion Mobile: staged human-decision controls Mobile: applied state and completion confirmation Who it is for For general contractors, owner representatives, closeout coordinators, and commissioning teams, Closeout catches stale, missing, or mislinked proof while keeping scope questions from becoming false completion. Judge in 60 seconds Open https://closeout-proof-of-handoff.vercel.app/ in a supported ChatGPT or Chrome WebMCP testing surface. An ordinary browser intentionally shows preview mode. Call closeout_read_state and closeout_identify_blockers : the clean seed is 9/14 with five explicit blockers. Stage fire-test with ev-fire-photo ; readiness must remain 9/14 . Use the visible Accept evidence control on the page. Apply the returned token once; readiness moves to 10/14 . Retry the same token and observe APPROVAL_CONSUMED . Preview the handoff: it remains not_ready_to_issue with four named exceptions. Use closeout_reset_demo afterward if you want to restore the clean seed in that browser context. Inspiration Construction closeout often fails at the last mile. The work may look finished while the proof needed for handoff is missing, stale, attached to the wrong revision, waiting on an owner decision, or mixed with a possible change order. A generic checklist hides those distinctions. Closeout turns them into one visible evidence-to-criterion workflow. What it does The demo opens one synthetic Unit 204 package at 9 of 14 requirements ready. Five exceptions represent different closeout failure modes: A current passing fire-damper test exists but is not linked. A kitchen warranty is one revision behind and expired. A ceiling repair may belong to a possible change order. The owner controls-training record is missing. Paint touch-up evidence still awaits owner acceptance. ChatGPT can use seven read Site Tools to inspect the structured state, criteria, revisions, evidence chain, blockers, recovery plan, pending decision, audit, and handoff result. It can use two bounded write tools to stage the one eligible FD-204 match or Paint Photo 12 owner-review record and apply it only after the same payload is approved through the visible human-only page control. A third destructive tool resets only the synthetic in-memory demo for judging. The successful path moves readiness from 9/14 to 10/14, records the exact actor/payload/decision/application chain, rejects replay of the consumed token, and keeps the handoff package at not_ready_to_issue with four explicit exceptions. Why WebMCP improves the experience Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer meaning from cards and click a UI that was designed for people. The page instead provides narrow domain contracts for requirements, evidence, revisions, scope lanes, approval state, and audit results. The agent and person operate the same live page and can both verify the visible outcome. This is not a button-replacement demo. The useful collaboration depends on the split between structured agent operations and human judgment: Structured blockers → digest-bound proposal → visible human decision → exact one-time application → replay rejection → truthful blocked handoff. The agent may inspect, reconcile, explain, and stage. A person alone may accept, reject with a reason, defer, or reopen. The agent may apply only the exact approved payload once. Neither side can silently convert unresolved exceptions into completion. How it was built Dependency-light HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with an evidence-centered responsive construction UI. Ten top-level imperative Site Tools registered sequentially with awaited document.modelContext.registerTool calls. Narrow JSON input schemas and accurate read/write/destructive annotations. SHA-256 project-state, payload, approval, decision, and result digests. Generation-bound one-time approval tokens with a random per-page nonce. Exact criterion, revision, evidence fingerprint, payload, approval, and expected-state checks before mutation. A visible actor audit and exception-aware handoff preview. Restrictive CSP, no network sinks, safe DOM construction, and entirely synthetic local data and imagery. A Playwright regression harness that captures the real registered handlers and exercises visible human controls. Challenges The first internal prototype discovered Site Tools but did not reliably invoke them because registration was not awaited and the test procedure reused stale session state. We isolated the problem with an official OpenAI control and a one-tool awaited local control, then registered the production tools sequentially and tested in a fresh supported ChatGPT session. The harder design problem was preventing “approval” from becoming a decorative button. The final workflow binds the exact criterion, revisions, evidence, state, payload, person-visible decision, token, and generation. Reset and replay paths fail closed, and the handoff package never claims that unresolved work is complete. Accomplishments Genuine production Site Tool discovery and invocation in ChatGPT desktop build 7303 with Recently Used/Sources evidence. A complete read → stage without mutation → preapproval block → visible human approval → exact apply once → replay rejection → audit → handoff flow. A second owner-acceptance flow for Paint Photo 12 that applies only after the visible decision and reopens back to the exact unresolved seed state. Ten consecutive complete automated production flows with zero unauthorized mutations, plus concurrent reset/apply, cross-generation replay, decision, keyboard, and untrusted-input coverage. A polished desktop/mobile evidence workspace that is separate from the frozen internal validation prototype. The final-fidelity main branch is deployed to the public Vercel origin with matching runtime assets, restrictive headers, excluded internal paths, and fresh desktop/mobile QA. Public-origin ChatGPT Terra/Sources returned the exact 9/14 seed and all five blockers, then passed the guarded stage → human approval → exact apply → replay rejection → audit → truthful handoff → reset → stale-generation sequence. That first public checkpoint finished at the clean generation-2 seed; the later same-generation demo capture reset cleanly to generation 3. Isolated Chrome native WebMCP independently passed read-only discovery and invocation. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when the page offers a domain contract instead of a second copy of its buttons. The agent needs structured operations and enough result data to verify the effect; the person needs the same state rendered clearly, with consequential judgment kept in the ordinary interface. What is next A production version would integrate authenticated project records and durable storage while keeping the same evidence, scope, approval, audit, and exception boundaries. This challenge entry intentionally avoids external systems and real project data so the judge path remains deterministic and safe. Built with WebMCP / OpenAI Site Tools, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Web Crypto, Playwright, and original synthetic evidence imagery. title: FlightSweeper
pitch: A browser agent buys a sandbox flight within exact, revocable limits set by the traveler.
about_excerpt: A browser agent buys a sandbox flight within exact, revocable limits set by the traveler. Like Comment Story Updates Untrusted supplier content cannot override the stored refundability and price rules. The issued sandbox ticket records policy evidence and resolves a duplicate request safely. Mission authority and the WebMCP-connected agent workflow. FlightSweeper lets a traveler delegate a complete sandbox flight purchase in one browser conversation—without letting the agent choose its own authority. The traveler sets the route, date, arrival deadline, cabin, connection limit, refundability rule, purchase cap, and execution mode. The agent searches, compares, and executes. FlightSweeper independently approves or denies the transaction and records why. The result is practical delegation with visible control: the traveler does not need to click through the booking flow, and the agent cannot silently expand the traveler’s limits. The proof in one transaction One supplier result contains an instruction telling the agent to ignore the traveler’s refundability rule. FlightSweeper marks the supplier output as untrusted and evaluates the exact quote against the stored mandate. The cheaper offer is denied. The agent then selects an eligible offer, refreshes the quote, requests policy evaluation, and issues one idempotent sandbox ticket. Repeating the purchase returns the original ticket instead of creating another transaction. The traveler can revoke future authority without erasing the evidence. This single flow demonstrates the core product idea: an agent can complete consequential work, but it cannot authorize itself. Why WebMCP Traditional browser agents infer controls from a visual interface. They can also carry stale or adversarial page content into a consequential action. WebMCP gives FlightSweeper a structured, page-scoped transaction surface with bounded inputs and explicit trust annotations. The human and agent share the same visible transaction state. All 10 tools remain discoverable so the agent can plan the complete workflow. Application-side checks expose the valid next actions and reject premature or prohibited calls. The responsibility split is explicit: The traveler owns purchasing authority. The agent owns search and execution. Suppliers own inventory. FlightSweeper owns policy enforcement and transaction evidence. A human can replace or expand the mandate. An agent can only narrow it. The traveler can revoke future authority at any time. What the traveler and agent do together The agent reads the mandate, searches sandbox inventory, compares visible offers, selects an exact quote, refreshes it, requests independent evaluation, purchases an eligible offer, and retrieves the receipt. The traveler watches the same mission, offer, authorization, and evidence states change on the page. This makes a multi-step booking executable through one agent conversation while preserving the limits that matter to the traveler. How we implemented WebMCP The page registers 10 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(), bounded input and result schemas, and accurate readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations. Every success returns data, mission status, and valid next actions. Every failure returns a typed error with the same state guidance. Human controls and WebMCP tools call the same application functions and persist state in versioned browser storage. Tool callers provide mission, offer, and idempotency identifiers—not price, passenger, payment, or authorization claims. Before every consequential decision, FlightSweeper reloads the stored mission and exact quote. Authorization, denial, and booking receipts record the policy and quote versions, stored limits, offered values, rule results, actor, timestamp, and resolution. We verified the complete lifecycle in ChatGPT desktop’s in-app browser and Chromium 151: adversarial denial, monotonic tightening, quote refresh, authorization, ticketing, replay, revocation, and receipt retrieval. What we built during the challenge Production FlightSweeper existed before the challenge. After the August 25, 2026 kickoff, we built this public, self-contained WebMCP Challenge Edition: sandbox inventory, the stable tool catalog, state-validated execution, the authority and policy engine, the adversarial fixture, durable evidence, repeat-safe ticketing, the browser interface, tests, documentation, and deployment. Production FlightSweeper remains private and unchanged. The challenge edition never charges a card or creates an airline order. It demonstrates authority, policy enforcement, quote binding, revocation, and idempotency controls. A live provider connection would require additional provider, payment, identity, operational, and regulatory controls. FinSync LLC operates FlightSweeper and is registered as a California Seller of Travel, CST 2172984-70. Registration as a seller of travel does not constitute approval by the State of California. I designed the human-controlled purchase mandate, agent authority limits, independent policy checks, revocation controls, repeat-safe execution, and durable decision records. I also built the interface, automated tests, security controls, documentation, and legal disclosures. title: GridTwin
pitch: A WebMCP civic microgrid sandbox where AI explores deterministic energy scenarios while humans retain final authority.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP civic microgrid sandbox where AI explores deterministic energy scenarios while humans retain final authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Planning context — synthetic baseline, approved criteria, and seven WebMCP tools ready. Visible exploration — genuine tool calls create and compare three deterministic scenarios. Outage proof — grid at 0 kW while the battery serves all eight critical hours. Human authority — the agent shortlists; only the planner approves. Decision brief — the approved plan becomes a transparent, print-ready recommendation. GridTwin One-line Summary GridTwin is a WebMCP civic microgrid sandbox where an AI agent visibly explores deterministic energy scenarios while the human retains authority over constraints, final plan selection, and export. Problem Climate and resilience officers at small councils and housing associations often need to choose one indicative solar-and-battery configuration before they can pursue a grant or commission a professional feasibility study. The decision spans budget, emissions, and outage resilience, but existing energy tools are usually designed for specialists and generic AI interfaces can hide what an agent changed or why it recommended an option. That is a poor fit for a consequential early-stage decision. A useful agent must make the decision space easier to navigate without obscuring assumptions, silently relaxing constraints, or taking final authority from the person accountable for the outcome. Solution GridTwin turns the fictional Riverside Estate into a shared, visible planning workspace. The human approves a £400,000 capital budget, a 40% emissions-reduction target, eight hours of critical-load coverage, and a resilience-first priority order. A real browser agent then uses seven page-defined WebMCP tools to read the baseline, run bounded solar-and-battery scenarios, compare transparent metrics, diagnose infeasibility, and shortlist a feasible candidate. Every scenario uses the same deterministic hourly dispatch model. Every tool action appears in the activity rail and visibly changes scenario cards, comparisons, or report state. Infeasible candidates show every violation in natural units. Agent advice remains reversible. Only the human can approve criteria, select the final plan, or open the browser print flow. The signature result is the fixed 18:00–02:00 outage: grid contribution falls to zero, the balanced 275 kWp solar / 500 kWh battery plan supplies critical load for all eight hours, and the final action belongs to the human approving the plan. Why This Matters GridTwin demonstrates a WebMCP pattern for consequential human-agent work—not just an energy calculator. Before WebMCP, a generic assistant could describe possible configurations, but it could not reliably operate the same visible, structured planning state as the human or leave an auditable trail of each action. With WebMCP, the agent can navigate a non-trivial decision space through narrow tools while the application remains the source of truth for calculations, feasibility, lifecycle state, and authority. The result is a better user experience because the human sees the work happen, can inspect assumptions and violations at the point of use, and retains explicit control over every consequential transition. The civic-energy example makes that collaboration concrete: abstract capacities become continued critical services during an outage. GridTwin does not claim to produce an engineering design. It helps a real target user make a transparent decision about what deserves professional evaluation next. How We Used AI GridTwin contains no embedded chatbot and calls no model API. AI enters through an external agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser, which discovers and invokes the page-defined WebMCP tools. The agent can: read the synthetic Riverside Estate baseline and fixed assumptions; stage constraint suggestions for human review without applying them; choose bounded solar and battery inputs and run real deterministic scenarios; compare two or three current scenarios without an opaque score; diagnose the nearest candidate when every option is infeasible; create a reversible shortlist for a feasible plan; and prepare an immutable decision-brief preview after human approval. The agent cannot approve constraints, approve or reconsider a plan, reset the comparison, print, download, or publish. Those actions have no WebMCP schema. After human approval, advisory mutations are frozen until the human explicitly reconsiders the decision. All authoritative metrics come from GridTwin's pure client-side model, not from model-generated arithmetic. WebMCP makes the agent's structured actions visible, testable, and subordinate to the application's lifecycle rules. How We Used Codex Codex was the primary development agent across the 30-hour solo build. It helped turn the initial idea into the scope, PRD, technical specification, and sequenced checklist; implemented the deterministic dispatch engine, reserve policy, lifecycle reducer, persistence, WebMCP adapter, civic interface, outage visual, and A4 report; added regression and browser tests; diagnosed integration failures; rehearsed the real in-app-browser workflow; deployed to Vercel; and prepared the handoff documentation. The builder actively directed the work rather than accepting a generated solution wholesale. Three mandatory review pauses produced concrete corrections, including refresh-safe activity identity, stricter restored-state validation, full post-approval agent freeze, HTTPS in-app-browser verification, and a settled chart capture. The builder also rejected an embedded-chat fallback, an opaque composite score, hidden constraint relaxation, and dramatic but dishonest tariff assumptions. That collaboration mirrors GridTwin itself: Codex explored and implemented within an explicit plan, while the human reviewed the consequential product, authority, credibility, and scope decisions. Key Features Exactly seven direct WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . One shared deterministic engine for every bounded solar/battery combination—no optimizer, randomness, precomputed scenario cards, or special-case balanced branch. Visible tool activity, a fixed 600 ms abortable pending interval, atomic scenario commits, and safe interruption handling. Versioned human-approved constraints with current/stale scenario lineage. Direct cost, emissions, reserve, resilience, feasibility, and natural-unit violation metrics with no composite score. Transparent all-infeasible diagnosis and staged—but never automatic—constraint suggestions. Distinct reversible agent shortlist and direct human-approved selection. Signature 18:00–02:00 outage view with grid at 0 kW and eight uninterrupted critical hours for the balanced plan. Immutable A4 decision-brief snapshot and human-controlled Print → Save as PDF flow. Session refresh recovery that restores committed work but never converts partial operations into completed results. Persistent synthetic-data, model-version, constraint-version, and indicative-planning caveats. Architecture GridTwin is a static React 19, TypeScript, and Vite application deployed on Vercel. Human UI or WebMCP callback ↓ shared validated command boundary ↓ pure deterministic domain calculation ↓ complete atomic reducer transition ↓ session snapshot and visible workspace/report src/domain/ : fixed synthetic inputs, validation, hourly dispatch, convergence, annualization, outage stress test, feasibility, and non-composite nearest ordering. It imports no React or browser code. src/state/ : context/reducer, versioned lifecycle, authority gates, interruption recovery, and sessionStorage compatibility. src/webmcp/ : seven JSON schemas, direct imperative registration, all-or-nothing discovery, cleanup, cancellation, readiness, and stable result envelopes. src/components/ : purpose-built civic planning interface, Recharts analysis, and a small fixed-node energy-flow SVG. Report path: an immutable snapshot of matching approved state; no recalculation, automatic download, or publication. The annual operating estimate and outage stress test share one dispatch function but remain separate calculation paths. Battery state converges across repeated representative days, a noon-to-outage reserve policy applies consistently, and the outage test clones the actual prepared 18:00 state. Confirm the header reads WebMCP ready · 7 agent tools available . Approve the default £400,000 / 40% / 8-hour criteria through the direct human button. Ask the browser agent: Inspect Riverside Estate and respect the approved budget, emissions, and eight-hour resilience criteria.
