title: Observatory
pitch: A local-first fantasy map builder where people and browser agents create together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A local-first fantasy map builder where people and browser agents create together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Fantasy maps help writers and game designers think, but creators often have to choose between complex graphics software and flattened AI images that are difficult to revise. Browser agents face a related problem: canvas interactions are hard to infer and fragile to automate visually. Observatory gives people and agents a shared, semantic mapmaking workspace. What it does Observatory is a local-first fantasy map builder where writers paint terrain, compose rooms, draw walls, place objects and labels, manage layers, undo changes, and export finished maps. Through WebMCP, a compatible browser agent can inspect and modify that same map using bounded, structured tools. A request such as “Build a map of a lone tower in a dense forest” becomes editable terrain strokes, structures, objects, and text—not a flattened image. Human and agent actions use the same state, persistence, revision, and undo paths. Destructive semantic changes require visible, single-use approval. How we built it Observatory uses Vue 3, Pinia, PixiJS/WebGL, IndexedDB, and Vite. Terrain remains editable vector data and is rendered through adaptive cached chunks. Structures, objects, labels, and layers retain stable semantic IDs. The WebMCP adapter registers library and project tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Strict JSON schemas, bounded responses, optimistic revision checks, idempotent operation IDs, abort handling, compact result envelopes, and approval tokens keep agent operations predictable and safe. IndexedDB is the durable boundary. Logical mutations increment a project revision and persist changed stores transactionally. Failed saves roll visible state and history back, while BroadcastChannel notifications prevent stale cross-tab writes. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping agent operations and human editing genuinely unified. Routing every action through the same application stores and transaction boundary required careful rollback and revision semantics. Terrain rendering also required balancing painterly materials, deterministic output, responsive previews, and large-map performance. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human map editor that remains useful without an agent. Structured WebMCP operations for discovery, inspection, terrain, geometry, objects, labels, layers, history, removal, and export. Agent changes that remain manually editable and undoable. Revision guards, idempotency, bounded payloads, and approval-gated removal. Local-first operation with no account, backend, telemetry, or runtime model API. Automated lint, type-check, locale, coverage, unit, browser, build, and dependency-security gates. What we learned WebMCP works best when it exposes the product's actual domain model instead of mirroring UI clicks. Stable IDs, revisions, and approvals make collaboration faster and more reliable while preserving human control. What's next for Observatory Future work could add restorable project archive import, richer templates, and optional collaboration while preserving the local-first core. Testing Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser, create a blank map, and ask: “Build a map of a lone tower in a dense forest.” Inspect and manually edit created elements, use undo and redo, request a refinement by element ID, test approval-gated removal, and export as PNG. No account or credentials are required. Maps remain in browser IndexedDB. title: OpenRoom
pitch: AI Room Planner & Furniture Shopping. WebMCP demo: furnish a real room photo with catalog products, by hand or through the AI app you already use.
about_excerpt: AI Room Planner & Furniture Shopping. WebMCP demo: furnish a real room photo with catalog products, by hand or through the AI app you already use. Like 1 Comment Story Updates AI room planning and furniture shopping through WebMCP. Securely connect Claude Code or another desktop MCP client. Review the room and approve its products before Shopify checkout. A Japandi redesign created with coordinated catalog products. The original room, ready for human or AI-assisted redesign. Browse and place true-scale catalog furniture directly in the room. Inspiration Planning a room is still a fragmented experience. Inspiration may begin in an AI conversation, but the room layout, product catalog, and checkout usually live in separate tools. The AI can suggest what to buy, yet it cannot see the current room, understand which object is selected, or safely make changes alongside the user. We built OpenRoom around a simple question: what if the room itself could become a shared workspace for people and AI? WebMCP made it possible to treat the web page as more than something an AI can describe. OpenRoom exposes a small set of safe, structured actions that let an AI inspect and edit the same room the user is viewing. Our goal was not to add another chatbot to a shopping site, but to create a human-and-AI design surface where every action remains visible, reversible, and under the user’s control. What it does OpenRoom is a photo-based room planner connected to a furniture shopping experience. The current demo begins with a calibrated room photograph and a set of mismatched furniture. A person can select, move, rotate, replace, undo, and reset individual pieces. An AI app can work on the same live scene through six focused tools: get_scene get_selection search_products replace_object move_object add_scene_to_cart The catalog contains 43 products across eight furniture categories. Products are placed using real-world dimensions, constrained to the room’s usable floor, and rendered with perspective-aware scale, depth ordering, alternate photographed views, and contact shadows. OpenRoom can also represent relationships such as a table lamp standing on a table. WebMCP-capable browsers can call the tools directly. Desktop AI clients can reach the same tools through OpenRoom’s local MCP companion, which pairs with the active browser tab and executes every command against the same live scene. When the room is ready, OpenRoom prepares a local approval sheet. A person can continue through a Shopify cart permalink, while an AI agent can receive mapped cart lines and the store’s UCP MCP endpoint. OpenRoom stores no Shopify credentials and never performs an external cart write on the user’s behalf. How we built it OpenRoom is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zustand, Immer, and Zod. At its center is one validated Scene model measured in real-world meters. Human interactions, native WebMCP calls, and local MCP calls all go through the same revision-aware command and history layer. This prevents the UI and the AI from developing separate versions of the room. Instead of relying on a 3D renderer or generating a new image after every edit, we built a deterministic photo compositor with ordinary DOM layers. A calibrated projection maps room coordinates onto the photograph’s floor plane. Product dimensions determine visual size, registered anchors keep cutouts grounded, and separate layers handle rugs, shadows, furniture, selection, and controls. Furniture images and alternate views are produced offline and checked into the project, so the application makes no runtime image-model calls. For agent access, we created a transport-neutral manifest for the six tools. Native WebMCP registers that manifest through document.modelContext. The local MCP companion exposes the same manifest over MCP stdio and forwards calls through a paired, loopback-only browser relay. The companion stores no copy of the room. Commerce follows the same minimal approach. OpenRoom uses a public Shopify store domain, static product-to-variant mappings, cart permalinks, and the store’s own UCP MCP endpoint. The application remains a static deployment on Cloudflare Pages, with no application backend or commerce token. Challenges we ran into The first major challenge was making a two-dimensional photograph behave like a spatial editor. The Scene needed to remain measured in meters while the image used perspective. We had to calibrate the visible floor, project rotated furniture footprints, keep every object on usable floor space, preserve realistic relative scale, and handle special cases such as rugs and furniture stacked on other furniture. The second challenge was safe co-editing. A person might change the selection or undo a command while an AI is preparing its next action. Every mutation therefore includes the expected scene revision and state version. Stale commands fail without changing the room, forcing the agent to read the latest state before continuing. Connecting desktop MCP clients to state held inside a browser tab was another difficult boundary. We built a local relay that listens only on 127.0.0.1, uses an expiring single-use pairing code, checks exact origins and manifest identity, and forwards only the six approved tools. We also explored a browser-side WebGPU image harmonizer. One candidate failed its licensing requirements, while another took a median of 86 seconds against an eight-second target and introduced visible artifacts without improving the composition. We decided not to ship it. That experiment led us back to a faster, more predictable photo compositor. Finally, commerce had to remain useful without quietly crossing the user’s trust boundary. We designed checkout so OpenRoom prepares the cart data and opens a visible approval step, while the person or their chosen AI client performs the final action. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that OpenRoom makes the same room genuinely co-editable by a person and an AI. There is no hidden agent-only state and no second implementation of the editing logic. We also built one consistent six-tool contract across native WebMCP and the local MCP companion. Both paths share the same schemas, validation, handlers, scene history, and approval flow. The finished experience combines true-scale photo placement, collision-aware movement, alternate furniture views, accessible pointer and keyboard controls, deterministic catalog search, and Shopify handoff without requiring an application backend, a commerce access token, or runtime image generation. Most importantly, OpenRoom remains useful without an AI connection. The human editor is the primary experience, and AI adds another way to operate it rather than replacing it. What we learned We learned that an agent-enabled interface is not simply a chatbot embedded in a web page. It is a stateful product with a small, explicit action surface, clear error recovery, and visible consequences. A single source of truth was essential. Once people and agents shared the same validated Scene and command history, actions became easier to test, explain, undo, and trust. We also learned that visual quality does not always require a generative model. Careful calibration, real dimensions, correct view selection, silhouettes, shadows, and layering produced a faster and more repeatable experience than the browser-side model we tested. Finally, approval is not just a security mechanism. In a shopping workflow, showing exactly what will happen before anything leaves the application is part of the product experience. What's next for OpenRoom The biggest next step is letting people bring their own room photographs. That will require room calibration, object and floor analysis, and a clear workflow for correcting uncertain measurements. We also have a deterministic natural-placement solver in the repository that is currently intentionally disconnected from the product. We want to reintroduce it through a transparent, reversible experience where users can preview an arrangement, understand what changed, and undo it in one step. Beyond that, we plan to expand room types and catalog coverage, add more photographed views, improve mobile editing, and deepen integration with Shopify and other stores that expose standard agent commerce tools. We also want to grow the evaluation suite around longer human-and-AI design journeys, especially interruptions, stale state, partial redesigns, and checkout handoffs. title: Relief Forge — From Prompt to Printable Wall Art
pitch: Turn an exact wall-art request into an inspected, printer-packed fabrication package through four visible WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Turn an exact wall-art request into an inspected, printer-packed fabrication package through four visible WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates One prompt creates an exact 48 × 48 inch Polar Bloom: 81 deterministic parts fitted across 62 plates. Four structured WebMCP tools create, constrain, inspect, and prepare the same visible project. Inspection returns exact measurements and confirms all 81 parts fit across 62 plates. The final tool prepares a 656,651-byte fabrication package while the reviewer controls the download. Inspiration Creative manufacturing software has powerful controls, but an agent usually has to imitate mouse clicks or stop at advice. Relief Forge explores a more useful interaction: structured tools that operate the same deterministic design engine and visible editor a person uses. The motivating request is concrete: Make me a four-foot-square Polar Bloom statement piece with a reproducible design and fixed palette. Fit every part to my printer, validate the exact plan, and prepare the fabrication files. That request combines units, aesthetic intent, fabrication constraints, inspection, and a deliverable. It is a stronger use of WebMCP than adding a chat panel to a design application. What it does Relief Forge registers four focused WebMCP tools: relief_forge_create_wall_art creates supported deterministic wall art at exact finished dimensions. relief_forge_set_printer_bed applies explicit bed dimensions, edge margins, spacing, rotation, and color-packing rules. relief_forge_inspect_fabrication_plan reports the current project identity, measurements, part and plate counts, and digital geometry and packing status. relief_forge_prepare_fabrication_package prepares an export only for the current validated project snapshot, while leaving the final download as a visible reviewer action. The agent and person share one visible, editable project. A first-run Judge Quick Start card shows tool readiness, explains the workflow, and copies the exact reproducible prompt. How to run the agent demo Relief Forge is the shared workspace, not the chat. On first visit, the Judge Quick Start card shows whether all four WebMCP tools are ready. After the card reports 4 AGENT TOOLS READY , select Copy prompt for AI chat , return to the Codex or ChatGPT conversation that opened Relief Forge, paste the prompt into that conversation's message box, press Send, and keep Relief Forge open. There is intentionally no prompt box inside Relief Forge. The agent's four tool calls update the same visible project the reviewer can inspect and edit. After dismissal, the instructions can be reopened with Run agent demo . If clipboard access is blocked, the complete prompt remains visible for manual copying. Why WebMCP improves the experience Before WebMCP, an agent could recommend settings or imitate fragile UI clicks. With WebMCP, it can translate the request into explicit units and constrained parameters, update the visible project, inspect the exact result the person sees, and prepare a snapshot-consistent package. The person remains in control and can inspect or edit the artifact after every step. Reproducible result The demo creates a 48 × 48 inch Polar Bloom using seed webmcp-polar-bloom-showcase-001 and a fixed warm architectural palette. The audited result is: 1219.2 × 1219.2 mm 2.4–30 mm actual depth range 81 deterministic parts 62 print plates 256 × 256 mm full bed 5 mm margins and 4 mm spacing No part exceeds 195.808 mm in either footprint dimension 195.808 × 190.805 mm largest actual placed footprint inside a 246 × 246 mm usable area Project wall-art-g6-238bfdaa Reference Chromium ZIP: 656,651 bytes Reference SHA-256: d86d4966242fd71542fcedab83bde3071447b9239e497fea2a9f59cc587462d0 Published-video clarification (1:27): The narration describes the largest part as just under 196 mm square. The exact largest placed footprint is 195.808 × 190.805 mm; the bed-fit conclusion is unchanged. The submitted Chromium reference ZIP contains 215 entries, including 81 part STLs, 62 packed-plate STLs, 63 3MF files, three assembly PDFs, a project recipe, and matching manifests. Its byte count and hash identify that audited browser artifact; exact ZIP bytes and equivalent near-tie packing choices are not claimed to match across JavaScript runtimes. Project identity, individual part geometry, dimensions, digital fit, inventory, and the 62-plate result matched across the audited runtimes. These are software checks, not claims of physical print, strength, or installation certification. How we built it Relief Forge is a React and TypeScript browser application. Geometry and stable identifiers remain deterministic local code. Printer packing, mesh checks, project state, and exports also run locally and repeat within the audited Chromium runtime; cross-runtime ZIP byte identity is not claimed. The challenge extension adds a narrow imperative WebMCP adapter around established editor actions. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool , use explicit schemas and physical bounds, update visible state before returning serializable results, read the current computed plan, and guard export preparation against stale project or printer configurations. Existing project and challenge extension Relief Forge existed before the challenge with deterministic geometry, exact-size controls, printer-bed packing, model and assembly previews, and STL, 3MF, PDF, manifest, recipe, and ZIP exports. During the challenge period, I added the four imperative WebMCP tools, lifecycle and schema validation, deterministic named WebMCP recipes including Polar Bloom, the visible agent-action status surface, stale-export protection, automated WebMCP coverage, Judge Quick Start, challenge documentation, and a separate sign-in-gated deployment. The public repository is a sanitized copy that excludes private tester records and private repository history. The pre-webmcp-public-snapshot tag records the copied pre-WebMCP application, and the comparison to main shows the challenge work: Baseline: https://github.com/ZivBY/relief-forge-webmcp/tree/pre-webmcp-public-snapshot Challenge diff: https://github.com/ZivBY/relief-forge-webmcp/compare/pre-webmcp-public-snapshot...main Challenges The hard part was defining a small, safe manufacturing contract: explicit units, deterministic style mappings, real printer dimensions, inspection of the same revision shown onscreen, and refusal to package stale or invalid state. Accomplishments Relief Forge lets a natural-language request drive a real creative-manufacturing workflow through structured tools rather than simulated clicks. Agent and manual interaction share one source of truth. Established geometry remains deterministic, and packing is repeatable within the audited Chromium runtime. What we learned Creative-software tools work best when designed like manufacturing commands: constrained inputs, explicit measurements, visible changes, reproducible results, revision-aware exports, and honest boundaries around digital validation. What's next Add more named deterministic recipes, verified printer profiles, optional slicer-supplied material and time estimates, and coverage for additional imperative WebMCP runtimes. title: VibeTide Live
pitch: VibeTide Live is a browser platformer and level maker where players and AI agents use WebMCP to build, validate, play, remix, and share levels instantly.
about_excerpt: VibeTide Live is a browser platformer and level maker where players and AI agents use WebMCP to build, validate, play, remix, and share levels instantly. Like Comment Story Updates Play the Level Instantly Paint Your Own Route WebMCP in Action Inspect. Build. Patch. Validate One URL. Ready to Remix. VibeTide Live Play VibeTide Live | View the source on GitHub What VibeTide Live does VibeTide Live is a browser platformer and level maker where a player and an agent can work on the same course. Build by hand, ask Codex for a first draft or a repair, press Play, and guide a headphone-wearing otter to the coral finish buoy. Players can: Paint platforms, hazards, enemies, and finish locations Resize the level from a short course to a larger vertical or horizontal stage Choose from ten ocean-themed backgrounds Generate a fresh course with Surprise Me Switch immediately between Build and Play modes Play with keyboard or mobile touch controls Undo manual or agent changes Share a complete level through a compact URL Open a shared level directly in Play mode, then remix it The site remains a complete game and editor when WebMCP is unavailable. WebMCP adds an optional creative partner, and every agent edit appears in the same level the player can see and play. Why WebMCP fits this use case A VibeTide level is live, structured browser state. It has dimensions, tiles, enemies, metadata, a background, a safe starting position derived from the tile layout, a finish, revision history, and playtest results. Giving an agent direct access to that level model avoids screenshots, guessed clicks, and descriptions copied into a separate chatbot. Each WebMCP tool expresses a game operation: create a platform, move the finish, resize the course, change the background, or check whether the goal is reachable under the game's safe-jump limits. The page handles the game rules and returns a clear result. The visual layout can change across screen sizes without changing what validate_level or apply_level_patch means. What people and agents can do together WebMCP lets the player and Codex work on the same level in the same browser tab. The demo shows the complete loop: Codex calls inspect_level to understand the course already open on the page. It uses create_level_from_blueprint and apply_level_patch to create Stormglass Skyclimb, a 64 × 32 vertical course with 12 ascending platforms and an elevated finish. It calls validate_level and gets 110 reachable cells with no issues. The player adjusts that same level by hand, presses Play, and completes the course. A compact share link opens the finished level directly in Play mode, ready for someone else to remix. The game can also report completion, deaths, timing, and recent playtest events, giving the agent concrete feedback for another repair pass. The headphone-wearing otter appears beside Codex as a custom animated Codex pet during the build. The agent handles large drafts, repetitive placement, structural checks, and precise repairs. The player supplies the idea, makes creative adjustments, and decides whether the course feels good. That division matters because reachability and fun are different questions. The validator checks a route against conservative safe-jump limits. A player still has to make the jump. Inspiration VibeTide is a project I come back to whenever I want to test a new way for people and agents to make games together. The core idea stays simple: turn an idea into a playable level as quickly as possible. Each version changed how the agent joins that loop. How VibeTide evolved Version 1: The chatbot The first version placed a chatbot beside the game. A player described a level, and custom code translated the request into level data and pushed it into the editor. Natural language worked well as a creative input, but the chatbot and game had separate views of the world. Extra code had to explain the current level to the chatbot, process its response, and send the changes back. Version 2: The MCP App When MCP Apps arrived, I returned to VibeTide and replaced free-form chatbot responses with structured game operations. The agent could inspect and change platforms, hazards, enemies, dimensions, backgrounds, and finish locations. That made the workflow more dependable: inspect the level, edit it, validate the result, and return useful feedback. The agent experience still felt attached to the game rather than native to the webpage where the level lived. Version 3: WebMCP For the WebMCP Challenge, I created a separate VibeTide Live repository and rebuilt the idea as a browser-first React, TypeScript, and Phaser game. The tools now live directly on the webpage. An agent can visit the same page as the player, inspect the open level, change it, validate it, start a playtest, and create a share link. The agent now works against the level already open on the page instead of a separate copy. How WebMCP was implemented VibeTide Live uses React, TypeScript, Phaser, and WebMCP. The public build is deployed with OpenAI Sites. The page registers 11 WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : inspect_level create_level_from_blueprint resize_level apply_level_patch set_level_metadata set_level_background validate_level start_playtest get_playtest_report undo_last_change create_share_link Every tool works against the same LevelStore used by the visual editor and Phaser game. There is no separate agent copy of the level. Human editor ─┐ ├── LevelStore ── Editor + Phaser game WebMCP tools ─┘ │ ├── Validation + undo ├── Playtest events └── Share URL Read-only tools declare that they do not change the level. Inputs use JSON Schemas plus runtime checks. Patch batches apply every requested change or none of them, so a failed edit cannot leave half a level behind. I wrote automated tests that discover and call the tools, reject bad inputs, and confirm that they clean up correctly. I also tested the deployed app with Codex in ChatGPT's built-in browser, covering discovery, creation, resizing, validation, playtesting, sharing, and reopening an encoded level. How WebMCP improves the experience The player never has to copy level data into a chat window, download JSON, edit source code, or wait for a new game build. Agent changes appear in the visual editor as they happen. Manual and agent edits share the same revision history. The player can immediately test the result, undo a change, or continue painting by hand. The current level is encoded into a versioned URL that preserves its dimensions, background, metadata, tiles, enemies, and finish. Opening the URL reconstructs the course and starts it in Play mode without uploading the level to a backend. Challenges Finding the right tool boundaries took several iterations. One large generation tool could make a complete course, but it would be difficult for an agent to correct. A separate call for every tile would make common requests slow and fragile. I settled on complete blueprints for large drafts and patch batches for focused repairs. Validation presented a different problem. A level can contain valid data and still be impossible to finish. The validator performs structural and reachability checks, returns concrete issues, and reports reachable cells. Human playtesting remains the final check for pacing and fun. Keeping every interface synchronized also required care. The visual editor, Phaser scene, WebMCP tools, undo history, local persistence, playtest events, and share links all operate on the same level snapshot. The final challenge was product design. The site needed to feel like a game someone would want to play while still giving an agent enough structured control to do meaningful work. Potential impact Level editors can be intimidating for players who have ideas but do not know the tool or want to place every tile manually. VibeTide lets those players begin with a plain-language description, receive a playable first draft, and refine it through play. Experienced creators can use the same workflow to test layouts, produce variations, resize courses, check reachability, and repair specific sections faster. The result is playable immediately. A player can describe an idea, try it, tell the agent what felt wrong, and play the repaired course without leaving the browser tab. What I learned Agents produce better results when they can inspect state before changing it and validate their work afterward. Tool responses also need to be concise and specific enough to guide the next action. WebMCP works best when the page exposes actions that mean something in the game rather than reproducing its buttons as tools. Move the finish is more useful than click at these coordinates . What's next I want to add richer interactive objects, more enemy behaviors, deeper playtest feedback, and community level discovery. I want shared courses to remain as easy to open as a link. title: Corsen Context
pitch: One owner-controlled WebMCP contract for the existing web: four read-only tools, governed extensions, deployed live across eleven stacks.
about_excerpt: One owner-controlled WebMCP contract for the existing web: four read-only tools, governed extensions, deployed live across eleven stacks. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Corsen Context gives an existing website an owner-controlled WebMCP read layer without replacing the human interface. The page registers explicit tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ; every call executes against a bounded, same-origin MCP endpoint (protocol 2025-11-25) and returns canonical public URLs and clean Markdown. Four read-only core tools are shared by every integration: search_site , get_page_content , list_content and get_sitemap . Live flagship: https://webmcp.corsen.ai (WordPress). Source: https://github.com/CorsenAI/corsen-context (MIT). Built by Corsen AI , France. Why WebMCP fits Browser agents currently parse interfaces built for people, guess which page is authoritative, and cannot tell what a site allows them to do. With Corsen Context the website itself exposes a small, typed, owner-selected capability layer. The capabilities live with the page instead of being reverse-engineered from the DOM, and the site owner decides what is exposed and can revoke it without touching the human pages. What people and agents can do together A person states a goal ("compare the editions, tell me what you may buy for me and what I must do myself"). The agent reads the owner's rules, calls the tools and returns grounded answers with sources. Governance is explicit and per product on the flagship store: the ten per-stack editions (9 EUR) carry agentPurchase: allowed : an agent acting for its user may complete the ordinary checkout; the production licence (29 EUR, slug corsen-context ) carries agentPurchase: forbidden with the owner's reason, so the agent hands that URL back to the human; the only write-shaped tool, request_expert_call , is annotated non-read-only and is refused server-side for every agent call ( human_only ) before anything is stored or emailed. The person keeps the decisions; the agent does the reading. How WebMCP is implemented A language-neutral tools.manifest.json declares tool names, JSON schemas and WebMCP annotations ( readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint ). The generated browser bridge registers each tool with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and forwards execute() to the same-origin MCP JSON-RPC endpoint; the browser never reimplements a tool and sends no cookies, credentials or API key. A TypeScript core (npm @corsenai/corsen-context 2.0.1 with Next.js and Astro adapters) and an independent PHP implementation (WordPress plugin 1.5.16 on WordPress.org) are checked against the manifest by parity tests. Eleven public deployments run the same four-tool core: the WordPress flagship, Express, Next.js, Astro, static HTML, Ghost, Strapi, Directus, Wagtail, MediaWiki and a Netlify template. A public verifier checks the ten stacks against one SHA-256 contract hash ( 3786c5d0d401cb9862291c9e3903ff0bd35925326b7dbc9be75f15ded2604ef4 ). The WordPress flagship adds five owner-toggled extensions ( get_product , get_sections , get_structured_data , check_agent_access , request_expert_call ), a Control Center, an audit log and a per-product agent policy published in llms.txt , on /for-agents/ and in every tools/list response. Shopify's own WebMCP, Storefront MCP and UCP surfaces are not reimplemented: a separate read-only verification kit checks them without installing an app. Integration shapes, stated honestly WordPress is a native plugin (one checkbox, no code). Next.js and Astro are published adapters with reference apps. Express and static HTML are reference servers. Ghost, Strapi, Directus, Wagtail and MediaWiki are deployable Node bridges over each CMS's public API, not native plugins. Every standalone repository ships install steps, a deployment guide, tests and CI. How to test it Open https://webmcp.corsen.ai in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Google Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and Chrome restarted. No account is needed. The page registers nine tools: the four core tools plus the five WordPress extensions ( request_expert_call is non-read-only and human-only). Ask: "Read this site's rules for agents, list the products with prices, and tell me which editions an agent may buy for me and which one it must hand back to me, with source URLs." Expected: eleven products; the ten 9 EUR editions are allowed ; the 29 EUR production licence is forbidden with the owner's reason; request_expert_call is not called. Optional: open any other live deployment listed on https://webmcp.corsen.ai/integrations/ and press Run live trace ; the four core tools answer from that site's own endpoint. Optional, repository: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm test && pnpm verify:live (expects VERIFIED: 10/10 ). Existing project and challenge delta Corsen Context existed before the challenge as an open-source MCP + llms.txt layer (baseline commit 73ecaee , 2026-08-06). Everything WebMCP was built during the submission period, starting at commit 8cedb8c (2026-08-30): the manifest-backed registration bridge, same-origin execution, WordPress owner controls and Control Center, per-product agent policy, the five WordPress extensions, framework handlers, parity and browser tests, the eleven public deployments, the twelve standalone repositories, the live verifier and the demo-store governance. Tested clients ChatGPT in-app browser (shared session: https://chatgpt.com/s/cx_6a99cd8a5ff48191ad323da4ca98a166): discovered the nine flagship tools, listed the eleven products, read the per-product policy and verified initialize , tools/list and the four-tool live trace on all eleven hosted deployments. That browser host exposed no document.modelContext , so the session proves endpoints and bridge definitions rather than native registration. Native WebMCP registration: verified in Chrome 152 with the WebMCP flags (nine tools registered on the flagship) and in the Codex desktop in-app browser. What we learned A governed contract beats a clever scraper: once a site publishes what an agent may read and may do, agents stop guessing, owners stop fearing, and the same four calls work on a WordPress store, a Django CMS and a static folder alike. title: JiuTuanZhuo 揪團桌
pitch: Group ordering, agent-native
about_excerpt: Group ordering, agent-native Like Comment Story Updates JiuTuanZhuo home — open a table in one tap. Share link generated after opening a table. Only people with the link can join. Ask Claude in Chrome to order combo vermicelli and sausage for Joe. The agent starts reading the page's WebMCP tools. The agent calls submit_order on the page. Joe's order appears instantly, tagged "Agent order," with no clicks on the UI. Host Elsa orders manually through the UI. The table now shows 2 people, 4 items, NT$220. Human and agent orders sit side by side. Host Elsa orders manually through the UI. The table now shows 2 people, 4 items, NT$220. Human and agent orders sit side by side. The host closes the table. Status flips to Closed and sent to the store; each share is locked. Inspiration Office group orders in Taiwan are rarely voluntary. Someone gets picked to ask everyone what they want, and that person has often never run a group order before. After a wall of "+1" messages in the LINE group, figuring out who ordered what, who changed their mind, and who hasn't paid lands entirely on them. JiuTuanZhuo was built for that person: open a table, drop the link, let the system handle the rest. What it does The official website of 油庫口蚵仔麵線 (Youkukou Oyster Vermicelli) now has a built-in "open a table" feature. The host gets a private link; only people with the link can order. Everyone orders from their own phone, every view syncs in realtime, and the host always sees the current combined order. Tables are fully isolated: three companies can each open a table at the same time without their orders mixing. Humans order through the UI; agents order through WebMCP tools declared on the same page. How we built it Lovable (React) + Supabase (anonymous auth, RLS, RPCs, realtime). The frontend is an interface, not a boundary: pricing, item validation, and permissions are all enforced in Postgres RPCs under RLS, so agents and humans go through the same rules. The page declares three WebMCP tools: get_table_status : marked readOnlyHint , returns structured JSON, with user-entered fields wrapped as user_content so they are treated as data, not instructions add_order : writes require an on-page human confirmation before execution close_table : registered only in the host's session; other participants' agents never see this tool All tools unregister when the table closes. Challenges we ran into The hardest part came first: breaking "+1 in a LINE group" into three actions (open, order, close) and deciding which rules belong in the database layer rather than the frontend. The second was environment setup: getting Chrome to actually call the WebMCP tools on the page took a fair amount of configuration and debugging. The third was pinning down where the latency actually lives. Measured on the page, tool execution is in the millisecond range: read tools return frontend state directly in 0.1–0.3 ms; write tools take 498 ms on the first call and settle at 66–72 ms after that. End to end, one order still takes about a minute. The gap sits entirely in the browser-side agent's tool discovery and reasoning; the page implementation itself is not the bottleneck. Accomplishments that we're proud of This is a 40-year-old street-food institution, and the second-generation owner built the system herself with AI vibe coding, so that customers' agents can place orders directly. Planning, architecture, and deployment were all done in-house, with no outside software vendor and no engineering team. The shop is the test bed: what gets built one day is in front of real customers the next. What we learned When the goal is clear enough, AI can build it. Writing code is not the barrier; knowing whose problem you are solving is. What's next for JiuTuanZhuo 揪團桌 First, reshape the flow around how people in Taiwan actually buy: separate pickup and delivery after an order comes in, and print tickets straight to an IoT kitchen printer. Then, service by service, connect Google Maps scooter-distance calculation, payment, the Lalamove delivery fleet, and e-invoicing, until every step from order to handoff is linked. JiuTuanZhuo is the entry point. From here we build inward, one piece at a time, into a full internal operating system for the shop that agents can run directly, ending with the POS itself. Ordering, ticketing, payment, fulfillment, and invoicing on one shared data layer is what a real closed loop looks like. title: AccessBridge
pitch: AccessBridge helps people and their agents confidently plan accessible outings using verified venue facts, compatible seating, and human-approved accommodations.
about_excerpt: AccessBridge helps people and their agents confidently plan accessible outings using verified venue facts, compatible seating, and human-approved accommodations. Like 2 Comment Story Updates AccessBridge combines a private access plan with verified venue facts and browser-agent coordination. Every requirement is evaluated separately, preserving matches, evidence, unknowns, and decisions. Compatible accessible and companion seats are filtered against the person’s active access plan. A reversible 10-minute hold protects the selected seats while the agent prepares the next step. The person reviews exactly what will and will not be shared before enabling submission. Only the approved disclosure is submitted; the full access plan and agent conversation remain private. The shared audit trail records human and agent actions without storing personal prompt text. Inspiration Planning an accessible outing should not require opening multiple venue pages, interpreting vague labels, calling a box office, and repeatedly explaining personal circumstances. Most event platforms answer a generic question: “Is this venue accessible?” People need an individual answer: “Will this specific event work for me, with my requirements, on this date?” The necessary information is often fragmented across venue descriptions, accessibility FAQs, seating inventory, and accommodation forms. Browser agents can help coordinate this work, but conventional UI automation introduces another risk: the agent may misinterpret ambiguous language, overlook an unknown fact, or disclose more personal information than necessary. AccessBridge was created to provide a reliable coordination layer between people, browser agents, venues, and ticketing workflows. What it does AccessBridge helps people and their agents confidently plan accessible outings using verified venue facts, compatible seating, and human-approved accommodations. A person creates a private access plan using functional requirements rather than diagnoses. For example: A step-free route A maximum walking distance Live captions Accessible and adjacent companion seating A lower-stimulation place for a break AccessBridge compares those requirements with a structured, venue-provided Access Contract. Instead of producing a generic accessibility score, it evaluates every requirement independently and preserves: Verified matches Conditions Blockers Unknown information Evidence sources and verification dates Venue-declared alternatives When a venue offers an alternative, AccessBridge does not decide whether it is acceptable. The person makes that decision, and the agent can record and coordinate the next steps. Once the plan is workable, the agent can find compatible seating, place a reversible hold, and prepare a minimum-disclosure accommodation request. Submission remains structurally unavailable until the person reviews and approves the exact version of the information that will be shared. Every human and agent action updates the same visible interface and appears in a shared activity record. AccessBridge is not a separate chatbot layered over a website—the website remains the source of truth, and WebMCP gives agents a reliable way to work with its live state. How we built it AccessBridge is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, and the browser-native WebMCP API. The application registers tools directly through: document.modelContext.registerTool() Its WebMCP surface is state-aware. Only search_events and assess_event_access are available initially. Additional tools appear only when their prerequisites are satisfied: accept_access_alternative find_compatible_seats hold_seats release_seat_hold draft_accommodation submit_accommodation Abort-signal lifecycle cleanup removes tools as soon as they are no longer valid. For example, assessment tools disappear during an active transaction, and the submission tool exists only while the currently displayed disclosure has exact human approval. Every tool has a strict JSON Schema and additional runtime validation. Human controls and WebMCP tools invoke the same application logic, so agent activity always changes the interface the person can see. The compatibility engine is deterministic and preserves unknowns rather than allowing an AI model to infer missing facts. Plans are versioned to reject stale operations, seat holds are reversible, and editing a request automatically invalidates prior approval. The public application is deployed on Vercel with restrictive security headers, responsive semantic UI, keyboard-accessible dialogs, ARIA live announcements, reduced-motion support, automated tests, and WCAG A/AA scanning. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was defining the boundary between coordination and authority. An agent should be able to perform repetitive work, but it should not silently relax a hard requirement, decide whether an alternative is acceptable, or submit personal information without informed approval. We addressed this by making consent part of the tool lifecycle rather than relying on prompt instructions alone. State synchronization was another major challenge. A WebMCP tool must always represent what is currently valid on the page. We introduced versioned plans, transaction guards, abortable tool registration, stale-state rejection, and exact-version approval to prevent outdated actions. We also had to design accessibility information without reducing people to a universal score. Access is individual and contextual, so the product preserves evidence, conditions, unknowns, and alternatives at the requirement level. Finally, an accessibility product must itself be accessible. We tested keyboard behavior, dialog focus, screen-reader announcements, color contrast, responsive layouts, and populated workflow states—not only the initial landing page. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete native WebMCP journey runs successfully in Chromium and ChatGPT-compatible browser contexts. Tools appear and disappear dynamically based on real workflow state. Missing venue facts remain unknown instead of becoming AI-generated assumptions. Hard blockers prevent incompatible seat and accommodation workflows. Seat holds are reversible and protected against stale plan versions. Personal disclosure cannot be submitted before exact human approval. Editing an approved request immediately revokes submission permission. Duplicate submission attempts are idempotent. Human and agent actions remain visible in one shared activity record. The production experience passes automated tests and WCAG A/AA scans with no violations. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it acts as progressive enhancement for a strong product—not as a replacement for the interface. A small, precise, state-aware tool surface is safer and more reliable than exposing every possible action at once. We also learned that important consent boundaries should be enforced structurally through application state and tool availability, not delegated to model behavior. For accessibility workflows, provenance matters as much as the fact itself. People need to know what was verified, when it was verified, what remains unknown, and whether an alternative is genuinely equivalent or simply another option. The strongest human-agent experiences give agents responsibility for coordination while preserving human authority over personal decisions. What's next for AccessBridge The next phase is turning the Access Contract into shared infrastructure for venues, event platforms, and accessibility communities. Planned work includes: Authenticated venue publishing and versioned Access Contracts Independent verification and community review workflows Integrations with real ticketing and seating inventory providers Secure, reusable personal access plans Signed consent and disclosure receipts Notifications when venue facts change after a plan is created Organization dashboards for identifying recurring information gaps Open adapters that let more event platforms expose compatible WebMCP tools The current public experience uses fictional venues, inventory, holds, and submissions so the complete workflow remains safe and repeatable. The product architecture is designed for real venue and ticketing integrations. title: Archive Evidence Room
pitch: Turn any webpage's history into cited evidence. A WebMCP agent finds comparable captures, inspects archived diffs, and pins findings with their sources to a caseboard shared with you.
about_excerpt: Turn any webpage's history into cited evidence. A WebMCP agent finds comparable captures, inspects archived diffs, and pins findings with their sources to a caseboard shared with you. Like Comment Story Updates The final finding stays beside its cited excerpt, ready for human review, source checking, and Markdown export. A scoped question becomes live coverage across public archives, with Arquivo.pt selected for comparison. The Evidence Room connects four WebMCP tools to one caseboard that the agent and the person can inspect together. One selected window becomes a bounded diff with both source captures and an explicit untrusted text warning. Index records produce six exact capture windows before any archived page body is downloaded. Why I built it Web archives contain real evidence, but working with them still feels like manual archaeology. Find snapshots, open a pile of tabs, compare dates, copy URLs, then try to remember which version actually proved the point. I wanted to ask a browser agent a sharper question: "How did this page change, and can you show me the exact captures that prove it?" This project also has some history. @agntn/archives started in April 2025 as one TypeScript interface over several web archives. It gradually gained caching, lazy provider loading, typed metadata and more sources. In 2026 it grew into a proper agent tool: first native OMP and Pi extensions, then an MCP server, archived body reads, pagination, capture diffs and finally a Nuxt explorer running on Cloudflare Workers. The WebMCP Challenge was a good reason to build the missing piece. Not another chat box, and not four aliases for buttons. I wanted the page itself to become a shared investigation room for a person and an agent. What it does Archive Evidence Room registers four native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext : scope_archive_case defines one historical question and checks which archives have evidence. find_change_windows finds consecutive captures without downloading archived bodies. inspect_archive_change reads one selected pair and returns a short cited diff. pin_archive_finding records whether that diff supports, contradicts or only adds context to the question. Every call updates the same visible caseboard. The agent can do the repetitive archive work, but the person still sees the dates, original URL, provider, underlying Memento archive, diff and final interpretation. No invisible research session and no uncited answer at the end. WebMCP is progressive enhancement here. Without the experimental browser API, the full workflow still works by hand. How I built it The UI is Nuxt 4, Vue and Docus. The server runs on Cloudflare Workers. I used the existing cached /api/coverage , /api/snapshots and /api/diff routes instead of creating a second archive backend for the hackathon. Those routes call the same @agntn/archives executors already used by MCP, OMP and Pi. Discovery is index first. The room requests between 3 and 12 capture records, groups them by exact URL and provider, keeps Memento captures inside the same underlying archive, then ranks useful windows. Archived bodies are fetched only after someone chooses a window to inspect. The result is much faster and much kinder to public archive infrastructure than reading everything up front. The caseboard keeps provenance all the way through. A diff can resolve to captures slightly different from the index rows, so the final citation comes from the diff result, not stale listing metadata. Findings store the interpretation beside the evidence instead of mixing both into one generated paragraph. What was hard Public web archives disagree about almost everything: timestamp formats, URL normalization, replay endpoints, metadata and failure behavior. Even www , default ports or letter case in a path can quietly produce the wrong pair. Memento adds another trap because one provider can return captures from several underlying archives. A plausible diff between unrelated records would be worse than no result, so I made the pairing rules deliberately strict. Cancellation was more subtle. Browser abort signals had to travel through $fetch , Nitro, cache misses and the archive executor. Sharing one cached promise also shared one caller's cancellation with another caller. That was wrong. Each cache miss now owns its request and one closed tab cannot kill another investigation. The other problem is trust. Archived HTML can contain instructions written specifically to manipulate an agent. Treating that as normal tool output would be ridiculous. The room exposes only a bounded text excerpt, marks it as untrusted, renders it as escaped text and keeps it separate from the finding written by the agent. What I learned The useful WebMCP abstraction is not "let the agent click my UI." It is a small protocol with state the user can inspect. caseId and changeId make the steps explicit, while the shared board makes mistakes visible. I also learned that archive research needs honest negative results. No capture in one bounded query does not mean a page never existed. A partial diff cannot prove text was absent outside the compared prefix. The product gets better when those limits stay visible instead of being polished into confidence. For the final smoke test I used sive.rs : seven captures became six safe windows, one exact archived diff and a finding pinned with both capture URLs. The public page does not preload this result because the caseboard belongs to the current browser session. Open the Evidence Room and ask the browser agent to investigate how sive.rs changed between 2020 and 2022 to reproduce the flow. title: Bankgraph
pitch: Bankgraph lets people and ChatGPT investigate a bank, the U.S. banking system, and the economy on the same live, editable research board.
about_excerpt: Bankgraph lets people and ChatGPT investigate a bank, the U.S. banking system, and the economy on the same live, editable research board. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Bankgraph turns a question about a bank, the banking system, or the economy into a live research board that ChatGPT can build with you. Compare the years before past failures with the reported paths of active banks today. Move from one bank to the banking system and the economy without rebuilding the data first. Start with the condition you care about, even when you do not know which bank to search for. Put bank behavior and economic context on the same working surface without flattening their different time bases. Trace what changed inside a bank, then see where it sits among comparable institutions. ChatGPT reads the exact data behind each view and continues from the board you change by hand. About the project A research surface for open data Bankgraph is my take on a Bloomberg-style research surface for public U.S. banking and economic data. Ask about an institution, the banking system, or the economy, and the work takes shape on a live board that you and ChatGPT can explore together. The data already exists. Every U.S. bank files a detailed quarterly record, while rates, credit, inflation, employment, and banking-system series are published by public agencies. Using that record is harder than finding it. A question such as “Is this bank an outlier?”, “Was deposit growth broad or concentrated?”, or “What tended to change before banks failed?” can still require regulator APIs, quarterly archives, matched institution histories, and series that run on different calendars. Bankgraph does that groundwork once. It brings FDIC institution records and financial filings together with official data from the U.S. Treasury, Bureau of Labor Statistics, and Federal Reserve Board. The reporting period, unit, definition, cohort, source, and coverage remain attached to the analysis. From one bank to the economy You can start with a familiar institution, compare it with a sensible peer group, and zoom out to the banking system. You can then place that behavior beside interest rates, credit, deposits, inflation, and employment. Or you can start without a bank name: describe a financial condition, screen the full population, and let the data determine which institutions belong on the board. The board combines histories, exact tables, peer distributions, reported component changes, metric relationships, headquarters maps, economic context, and written takeaways. Its views share the same banks, measures, periods, and cohort, so a change made in one place carries through the analysis. The same surface can help an analyst compare peers, a reporter test whether a headline trend is widespread, a researcher investigate the years before past bank failures, or someone simply understand what is happening at a familiar bank and in the economy around it. ChatGPT works with you on the screen Through WebMCP, ChatGPT operates Bankgraph directly. It can search institutions, define or revise a cohort, screen banks by financial measures, run multi-period and historical analyses, and arrange the results as charts, tables, maps, comparisons, and short takeaways on the site. The workflow can begin with named banks or with an open-ended question. ChatGPT can compare JPMorgan Chase with its peers, add more banks on request, switch the interface to dark mode, and read the figures behind the updated board. It can also start from a condition such as a high loan-to-deposit ratio, find the relevant banks first, and build the comparison from those results. The result remains a working Bankgraph board. You can change a bank, measure, period, chart treatment, or layout by hand, while ChatGPT reads and changes the same on-screen workspace. Each view provides structured data with reporting dates, definitions, units, cohort context, pagination, and source metadata, so ChatGPT can answer from the underlying values without interpreting a screenshot. How it works Bankgraph uses one workspace model for the visible interface and its WebMCP tools. Human and agent actions therefore operate on the same state and the same analytical vocabulary: institutions, measures, periods, cohorts, and views. The analytical results are deterministic. Change attribution uses reported components and explicit formulas, cohort analysis reports its usable population, and historical series preserve missing values. This keeps quick answers tied to inspectable data while still allowing the board to change freely. The application is built with SvelteKit, Svelte 5, TypeScript, and ECharts on Cloudflare Workers. D1, KV, and R2 support the application and its public-data pipeline. What was difficult, and what I learned The hardest part was making one workspace predictable while a person and an agent could both change it. Every analytical choice needed a visible meaning, every view needed a stable identity, and each agent action had to continue from the board as it stood. Time was the other challenge. A quarterly balance, a year-to-date income field, a reported ratio, and a weekly banking-system series are different kinds of observations. Bankgraph carries their time basis, units, transformations, coverage, and source definitions through ingestion, analysis, display, and export instead of flattening them into one misleading timeline. I also learned that useful WebMCP tools need to express analytical intent rather than mirror individual buttons. The tools can ask Bankgraph to construct a cohort, compare a set of institutions, or publish a result as an appropriate view. The visible interface still provides the controls needed to inspect and revise what the agent produced. What I built during the challenge Bankgraph’s public-data foundation predates the challenge. The product experience shown here—the shared Research board, its visual system, measure-led screens, multi-period and failure-pattern analyses, semantic board composition, structured reads behind every view, and the WebMCP system that connects them—was built during the submission period. Commit b852f9b records the pre-challenge baseline; the public history after it contains the complete extension. Testing instructions for judges Open bankgraph.app in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and keep the site visible beside the conversation. The live application needs no account, provider key, or local setup. Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled also works. Start with: “Compare JPMorgan Chase with Bank of America, Citi, and Wells Fargo.” Once the board appears, say: “Add Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and U.S. Bank. What’s the short version?” Then try a question that begins with the data rather than a bank name: “Start fresh. Which five active banks over $10 billion have the highest loan-to-deposit ratios? Build the comparison here.” Ask ChatGPT to add loan growth or problem loans, change one view by hand, and continue the analysis. The board should reflect both the changes you make and the changes ChatGPT makes through WebMCP. title: ClawDeals
pitch: Your agent negotiates. You stay in control.
about_excerpt: Your agent negotiates. You stay in control. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Your agent negotiates. You stay in control. Every sensitive action leaves a policy decision, confirmation state and redacted receipt. The agent ranks synthetic e-bikes while showing why each candidate fits or violates the owner's policy. Your agent negotiates. You stay in control. Why ClawDeals? Think of your agent as a mechanical claw: reaching into the chaotic second-hand market to seize a great deal, while you keep a firm, unyielding grip on budgets, identity, and the final word. ClawDeals is the trust layer for agentic commerce. Buyer and seller agents can search, evaluate, and negotiate real-world deals, while humans retain explicit control over budgets, approvals, and contact details. The agent negotiates. It searches, ranks, questions sellers, and prepares offers through page-scoped WebMCP tools. The server enforces human limits. Budgets, owner approvals, reservations, and bilateral consent are re-checked server-side. A confirmation modal is never the security boundary. Every protected action stays verifiable. It produces a redacted receipt containing a request ID, an input hash, and the resulting policy verdict. Inspiration Current shopping agents excel at searching catalogs and adding items to carts. But peer-to-peer commerce is a different challenge: two independent people, asynchronous back-and-forth negotiation, strict budget caps, and personal contact info that shouldn't be leaked to an unknown bot. WebMCP gave us the missing in-browser contract: the agent receives structured, page-scoped tools, while the human keeps the final say on the exact same UI. Who this is for Peer-to-peer marketplaces (used bikes, electronics, furniture, housing) where negotiation is asynchronous, and an unconstrained agent could easily overspend or leak private identity. What it does A buyer delegates a Deal Mission: target price, hard budget, search radius, and item requirements. The agent executes WebMCP tools to search and evaluate listings against a structured policy_fit (which the human sees mirrored live as badges on the cards). The agent can open threads, ask technical questions (e.g. battery health), and stage offers. When an offer exceeds the mission budget, the platform halts the autonomous flow with APPROVAL_REQUIRED . The human owner reviews the action on /my/approvals/:id , can edit the counteroffer (e.g., adjust to €1,290), and approves it. Once accepted, the listing flips to RESERVED atomically. Contact details remain masked until both buyer and seller explicitly consent. How we built it Built on Next.js (Pages Router), TypeScript, React, PostgreSQL, and Supabase. WebMCP Integration : Tools register via document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) and listen to toolchange . We scope tools contextually: 5 public read-only tools on the main marketplace, expanding to 11 authenticated tools inside the judge sandbox. Security Boundary : Client confirmations are editable, but all policy rules (budgets, consent, reservations) are strictly re-checked server-side. Testing & Evals : Vitest covers tool schemas and redaction. Playwright runs deterministic synthetic sandbox journeys (Paris e-bike scenario). Adversarial tests verify prompt injection resistance, over-budget halts, and zero contact leakage. What we built during the challenge ClawDeals existed before August 25, 2026, making this an Existing project . Only the WebMCP capabilities built during the hackathon window are submitted for judging: Official imperative WebMCP runtime ( registerTool , AbortSignal lifecycle). Contextual dual-mode tool registry (5 public tools / 11 authenticated tools). Deal Mission engine and visual policy_fit card badges. Mission-bound negotiation ( start_thread , send_message , make_offer ). Server-enforced hard budget stops ( APPROVAL_REQUIRED ) and editable owner approvals. Atomic listing reservation ( RESERVED ) and bilateral contact reveal. Verifiable Agent Activity drawer and redacted receipts ( get_action_receipt ). Isolated judge hub with synthetic fixtures and one-click reset ( /webmcp-challenge ). Challenges we ran into Registering tools was straightforward; preserving a bulletproof trust boundary was the real challenge. When an agent can trigger payments or commitments, an in-browser confirmation dialog is insufficient. Sensitive write operations are idempotent and re-checked server-side, and contact details require two independent, server-recorded consents. We also kept our evaluation honest: a mocked modelContext in tests proves wiring, not real browser execution. We carefully separated local unit mocks, headless Playwright sandbox runs, and native browser verification. Accomplishments that we are proud of Real in-browser WebMCP tool execution without relying on generic DOM scrapers. 11 focused contextual tools instead of a single dangerous omnipotent function. Server-enforced budget protection that safely intercepts out-of-bounds agent counteroffers. Redacted audit receipts that let agents inspect past decisions without leaking secrets. Full end-to-end mission demonstration with synthetic Paris e-bike fixtures. What we learned Practical agentic commerce requires three distinct layers: An in-browser tool contract for the agent (WebMCP). A server-side policy contract for the platform (budget and identity gates). A consent contract for the human (approvals and bilateral reveal). What's next The isolated authenticated sandbox is live at https://sandbox.clawdeals.com/webmcp-challenge . Chrome 149+ (or Chrome 151 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) exposes the native runtime and our full 11-tool registry once the private judge key (provided in Devpost judge instructions) is entered. Public read tools remain testable without any key. title: Cobweb - WebMCP enabled Micropython IDE
pitch: Cobweb is a zero-install browser IDE bringing WebMCP to physical hardware: AI agents can probe microcontrollers, edit device files, run MicroPython code live, and debug boards with human approval.
about_excerpt: Cobweb is a zero-install browser IDE bringing WebMCP to physical hardware: AI agents can probe microcontrollers, edit device files, run MicroPython code live, and debug boards with human approval. Like Comment Story Updates 💡 Inspiration Physical computing and IoT have always promised an exciting world of creativity—turning code into blinking LEDs, motor movements, robotics, and environmental sensors. Yet for beginners, educators, and even seasoned makers, the onboarding experience is plagued by toolchain friction: Hunting down and installing OS-specific USB-to-UART drivers (CH340, CP2102, FTDI). Configuring desktop IDEs like Thonny, Arduino IDE, or heavy VS Code toolchains. Juggling serial baud rates, COM port drops, and manual file transfer scripts. With modern browser capabilities like the Web Serial API and File System Access API , we realized that the entire embedded development lifecycle could run 100% inside the browser with zero installation . When WebMCP was introduced as an open standard for agentic web applications, we asked a fundamental question: Why should AI agents only interact with web forms, spreadsheets, and SaaS tools? What if an AI agent had physical hands on hardware? Cobweb was born to bridge this divide—creating a zero-install MicroPython IDE where humans and AI agents collaborate seamlessly to probe, code, execute, and debug physical microcontrollers. ⚡ What it Does Cobweb turns any Chromium browser into a full-featured MicroPython development environment that connects directly to microcontrollers (such as Raspberry Pi Pico, ESP32, or BBC micro:bit) over Web Serial at $115{,}200\text{ baud}$. Key capabilities include: Zero-Install Python IDE : Code editor powered by CodeMirror 6 with syntax highlighting, automatic indenting, and multi-file local storage. Interactive xterm.js REPL : Direct serial connection with live terminal streaming, ANSI color rendering, and raw-paste mode. Device Filesystem Management : Browse, read, write, edit, and delete files stored on the microcontroller's onboard flash memory. Deep WebMCP Integration : Exposes 15+ fine-grained, structured tools to external AI agents via document.modelContext.registerTool . Human-in-the-Loop Safety : Every mutating agent action (flashing files, modifying code, running hardware commands) triggers an interactive approval modal with live side-by-side diff previews before anything touches the physical board. Board Hardware Notes : Persistent scratchpad where the agent and user track pin mappings (e.g., $I^2C$ SDA/SCL pins, SPI buses, ADC channels, and sensor addresses). 🛠️ How We Built It Cobweb is built as a pure client-side Progressive Web App (PWA) with no backend servers or cloud dependencies: ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ External AI Agent │ │ (ChatGPT / Chrome with WebMCP) │ └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘ │ WebMCP JSON-RPC / Tools API ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Cobweb WebApp │ │ ┌───────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ WebMcpBridge.tsx │◄─────►│ Tool Registry │ │ │ │ (use-webmcp-tool) │ │ (15+ Structured Tools) │ │ │ └───────────┬───────────┘ └───────────┬────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ CobwebApproval Modal│ │ ReplInterface (TS) │ │ │ │ (Live Diffs) │ │ (Raw REPL State Mach.) │ │ │ └─────────────────────┘ └────────────┬───────────┘ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┘ │ Web Serial API ▼ ┌───────────────────────────┐ │ Physical Board (Pico) │ └───────────────────────────┘ 1. The WebMCP Bridge ( WebMcpBridge.tsx ) We utilized use-webmcp-tool to dynamically expose our tool registry to the browser's model context: useWebMCP({ name: def.name, description: def.description, inputSchema: def.parameters, async execute(args) { if (def.requiresApproval) { const approved = await requestApproval({ id, name: def.name, args }); if (!approved) throw new Error('Tool execution rejected by user.'); } return await tool.call(args, {}); } }); 2. High-Performance Serial Communication ( ReplInterface.ts ) MicroPython communication relies on a custom finite state machine implementing the raw-REPL protocol : Raw Mode Entry : The host sends \x01 ($\text{Ctrl-A}$) to enter raw REPL. Raw-Paste Windowing : To prevent buffer overrun on microcontrollers with constrained RAM ($\approx 264\text{ KB}$ on RP2040), we implement dynamic flow control: $$\text{Chunk Size} \le W_{\text{window}}, \quad \text{replenished by } \text{\textbackslash x01 bytes}$$ Execution & Stream Separation : Code is executed via \x04 ($\text{Ctrl-D}$), returning structured stdout and stderr delimited by end-of-transmission bytes: $$\text{Banner} \longrightarrow \text{OK} \longrightarrow \text{stdout} \longrightarrow \text{\textbackslash x04} \longrightarrow \text{stderr} \longrightarrow \text{\textbackslash x04}$$ Queue Serialisation : An AsyncBlockingQueue<Uint8Array> safely decouples serial reads from async execution promises while mirroring bytes to xterm.js . 🧗 Challenges We Ran Into 1. Single-Channel Serial Contention The Web Serial port is a single, non-multiplexed stream. If a user is typing in the REPL while an AI agent attempts to run get_board_info or read_device_file , raw bytes interleave and corrupt the state. Solution : We built a single-slot promise lock chain for all read/write/eval calls ( send , sendRaw , reset ), ensuring strict atomicity without blocking UI rendering or serial event dispatching. 🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 100% Client-Side Architecture : Zero backend servers, zero telemetry, zero credential relay. Everything runs directly between the user's browser and their USB port. True Agentic Physical Computing : An AI agent running in ChatGPT or Chrome can inspect the board identity ( os.uname().machine ), write sensor drivers, execute test snippets, and diagnose hardware errors in real time. Rich Human-Agent Co-Pilot Experience : Instead of replacing the human, WebMCP in Cobweb creates a fluid dialogue where the human handles breadboarding and hardware wiring, while the agent handles MicroPython syntax, pin registers, and driver debugging. 📚 What We Learned WebMCP is a Game Changer for Browser Capabilities : Traditional desktop agent tools require complex native MCP servers (stdio/SSE over localhost). WebMCP brings tool calling directly to the browser DOM and Web APIs, making cutting-edge capabilities like Web Serial, Web Bluetooth, and File System Access instantly accessible to AI agents. Structured Tools Beat Vision/DOM Scraping : Prior to WebMCP, agents navigating web IDEs had to guess button positions or scrape xterm canvases. With WebMCP, tool calls are typed, deterministic, and instant.
