title: Comake
pitch: Comake — one place for humans and agents to create and present together.
about_excerpt: Comake — one place for humans and agents to create and present together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I really like products such as ChatGPT Canva, Claude Design and the canvas-style experiences built into AI platforms. They show how powerful it can be when an AI can work directly on the same artifact as the user instead of only talking about it. But there is one thing that bothered me: these experiences are usually tied to one platform and one agent. If the presentation tool only works with its own built-in agent, another agent cannot really participate. When OpenAI highlighted WebMCP through the WebMCP Challenge, I thought it could be a really interesting bridge between humans and agents. Instead of building Comake around one model, one agent SDK, or one proprietary framework, the application itself exposes what an agent can do through WebMCP. Any compatible agent can understand the same tools. More importantly, WebMCP makes it possible for the agent to work inside the same context as the human. It can know which slide I am looking at, what I selected, and what I am currently focused on instead of trying to guess everything from screenshots or DOM elements. That became the idea behind Comake: a presentation workspace where humans and agents can actually work on the same thing together. What it does Comake is a shared presentation workspace for humans and agents. A user can start from a template, create a blank presentation manually, or ask an agent to create one through WebMCP. From there, both the human and the agent work on the same presentation. The human editor supports text, shapes, backgrounds, direct text editing, multi-selection, moving and resizing elements, alignment, z-order controls, keyboard shortcuts, and a command palette. For the agent, Comake exposes structured WebMCP tools for understanding the presentation. The agent can read the active slide, the user's current selection, the presentation outline, or a structured spatial map of the canvas. It can then create slides, rewrite text, move elements, change styles, add comments, or perform multiple edits as one atomic operation. Agent changes are also tracked in the Activity tab. If I don't like what the agent did, I can revert its ChangeSet and ask it to try something different. Comake also supports presentation mode. An agent can start the presentation, move forward or backward, jump to another slide, or exit presentation mode. This opens up an interesting use case for voice-capable agents: the human can speak while the agent helps control the pace of the presentation. Finally, presentations can be exported as real .pptx PowerPoint files. How we built it I built Comake with React, React Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Base UI, and Cloudflare. One of the most important decisions was to not build two separate editing systems: one for humans and another for agents. Instead, Comake has one canonical presentation model with stable IDs for slides and elements. Human actions and WebMCP agent actions eventually go through the same operation model and the same mutation kernel. This keeps the presentation consistent no matter who made the change. The browser keeps an interactive local view of the presentation and things such as the current selection and focus. The canonical document is persisted through a Cloudflare Worker into a WorkspaceRoom Durable Object backed by SQLite. For WebMCP, each page registers native tools through document.modelContext . The editor exposes structured read tools for context, selection, geometry, slides, and history, as well as write tools for editing the presentation. Tool registration also has its own lifecycle so tools from an old route cannot accidentally remain registered after navigation. I also added revision checking to agent writes. If the human changes the presentation while an agent is still thinking, an operation based on an old revision is rejected instead of silently overwriting newer work. For PowerPoint export, I ended up building the exporter directly. Comake converts its presentation model into the OOXML files used by PowerPoint and creates the .pptx ZIP archive in the browser. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not making an agent click buttons. The harder problem was figuring out what collaboration between a human and an agent should actually mean. For example, an agent needs more than the entire presentation document. It needs to know what the human is looking at right now and which elements the human selected. At the same time, that focus can change without the presentation itself changing. That led me to separate document revisions from focus revisions and expose the current human context directly through WebMCP. Another challenge was concurrent editing. An agent might read revision 10, spend some time planning an edit, and then submit its changes after the human has already created revision 11. I didn't want Comake to accept stale operations and accidentally destroy the user's work, so writes are revision-aware and atomic. Reversibility was another important problem. If an agent makes ten changes to improve a slide, undoing those changes one by one would be a bad experience. Comake groups accepted agent operations into attributed ChangeSets, which can be inspected and reverted as a unit. Building a usable slide editor itself also took a lot of work. Selection, multi-selection, resizing, element ordering, keyboard interaction, presentation mode, and translating the same visual model into a valid PowerPoint file all have a lot of small edge cases. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm especially proud that Comake is not just a presentation editor with an AI chat box added beside it. The agent is working with the actual application model. It can understand the user's current focus and exact selection, reason about the geometry of a slide using structured data, and make changes through the same canonical editing system used by the human. I'm also proud that Comake is not bound to one specific agent. There is no proprietary agent runtime required by the application. The integration boundary is WebMCP, so the presentation workspace itself becomes agent-capable. Another part I'm proud of is making agent actions attributable and reversible. I think being able to see what an agent changed — and undo that entire change if it was wrong — is important if humans and agents are going to work on the same artifact. And writing the PowerPoint exporter from the underlying format was probably one of the more unexpected parts of this project. Being able to create something together with an agent and then export it as a normal PowerPoint file makes Comake useful outside of the demo itself. What we learned The biggest thing I learned is that designing tools for an agent is also product design. It is not enough to expose every internal function as a tool. The agent needs a good starting point, compact ways to understand the current state, stable identifiers, clear schemas, and errors that tell it how to recover. I also learned how important human context is. Giving an agent the whole document is not the same as telling it, "this is what the human is working on right now." Selection and focus are a surprisingly powerful communication channel between a human and an agent. I also started thinking differently about undo and history. When an agent can perform many operations in one task, attribution and reversibility become much more important than they are in a normal single-user editor. Most importantly, WebMCP showed me that an application does not have to choose between being built for humans or being built for agents. The same web application can provide a visual interface for the human and a structured interface for the agent, with both working on the same underlying state. What's next for Comake The biggest missing piece right now is real authentication. The current demo uses an anonymous signed session, which is useful for the hackathon but is not enough for a real collaborative product. After adding accounts and sharing, I want to make Comake truly multiplayer. The backend is already centered around Cloudflare Durable Objects, with one WorkspaceRoom owning the canonical presentation state. I want to extend that architecture so multiple people can open the same presentation, see each other's presence and edits, and work together with agents in real time. I also want to add richer presentation content such as images and media, as well as PowerPoint import so existing presentations can become Comake projects instead of always starting from scratch. And I want to explore the presentation side further. If an agent can communicate through voice while also controlling presentation mode through WebMCP, the agent could become an actual presentation partner instead of only helping prepare the slides. The bigger goal is for Comake to become a place where it doesn't really matter whether an action came from a mouse, a keyboard

title: Consensus
pitch: Your agent can find what it cannot read. Drop confidential PDFs in — your agent searches without seeing the text, requesting human approval before reading a single page.
about_excerpt: Your agent can find what it cannot read. Drop confidential PDFs in — your agent searches without seeing the text, requesting human approval before reading a single page. Like Comment Story Updates Consensus The agent can find what it cannot read. A decision workspace for choices that run on confidential documents. You drop the PDFs in — they are parsed in your browser and never uploaded. Your ChatGPT agent can search them and tell you where the answers are, but it cannot read a single page without your explicit release. The problem I researched about & wanted to work on: So basically if u look at security evaluation, in most of the cases it looks like: multiple PDFs & SOC 2 Type II reports, vendor Data Processing Agreements (DPAs), pricing annexes, and a filled-in security questionnaire, and it leaves them in a frustrating spot: that is they want an AI to help for searching through documents with a lot of pages of legal text (or something else), but uploading those documents isn't actually allowed. When you ask why they aren't using an AI assistant like ChatGPT to help parse all those hundreds of pages, the answer in most cases is: the documents are under strict NDA. The core contradiction is provided below with two facts: It is exactly the work an AI should do . Reading lots of pages of legal annexes and compliance schedules to find whether a vendor has an unqualified SOC 2 report covering availability exceptions is mechanical retrieval. People are usually slow at it, and they miss buried facts in that. It is exactly the work you are contractually forbidden to give an AI . SOC 2 Type II reports and DPAs are distributed under strict non-disclosure terms that prohibit uploading or redistributing them to third-party cloud tools or SaaS platforms. So basically the core problem is: The documents that would make an AI genuinely useful for a high-stakes decision are precisely the documents you are contractually forbidden to upload. 1> Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP After clear evaluation of the constraints, the requirement I ended up with were: An agent that can tell you where the answer is in a document it is not permitted to read. *** Considered Architecture: Basically there were four ways with which we could approach this problem, but each of them fails for their specific reasons, which are specified below in detail. (For detailed analysis: docs/WHY-WEBMCP.md ) Approach Why it fails Server-side MCP Searching server-side requires uploading the PDF to a cloud server first, which immediately violates the NDA. A backend cannot search a document without reading the text. REST API There is no shared live interface. Approving a single page in real time requires both the user and the agent to be on the exact same open tab at the same moment. Browser automation Vision and screen-driving agents read text through screenshots. Sending screenshots of confidential contracts into the model leaks the exact data we need to protect. OS / extension agent Lacks a structured in-browser contract. There is no clean way to tell an OS-level agent: "you are allowed to know where this file matches, but you cannot open the text." Alternatives I considered and rejected: Searchable encryption : Still requires sending data over the network, which leaks search access patterns. Under a strict NDA, transmitting the file anywhere is forbidden. Localhost MCP server binary : Requires users to install a native binary on their machine. Documents would persist on disk instead of living safely inside an ephemeral browser tab that clears when closed. ** Why WebMCP was the only real solution:** WebMCP's execute() function runs directly inside the browser tab that is already holding the in-memory document . Because tool execution happens locally in JavaScript under a strict JSON Schema, we can cleanly separate searching for matches from reading actual text into two distinct tools. ** Where WebMCP would be the wrong choice:** To be transparent about its limits: WebMCP is not meant for backend cron jobs, background workers, or anything that needs persistent cross-session databases. It fits best where data is private and local, the browser tab is the security boundary, and a human is actively present to approve sensitive actions. What only WebMCP makes possible: WebMCP tool execution ( execute() ) runs directly inside the browser process that already holds the document text in memory . And because the execution happens locally in the tab, we can separate finding evidence from reading evidence into two independent tools with their own JSON schemas. Also here we have about WebMCP's limits: WebMCP is not the right choice for every use case: Anything genuinely server-side or long-running is much better served by a traditional server MCP. WebMCP tools are ephemeral and live only for the duration of the browser tab. Consensus embraces this exact constraint: the lifetime of the browser session is the security boundary. WebMCP is the ideal architecture when data is private, execution must stay local, and a human is actively in the loop. 2> How it creates a better user experience Dividing the work where it makes sense So instead of giving the agent full control or doing everything manually, the workload is divided cleanly: | What the agent handles | What the human controls | |---|---| | Searching across hundreds of pages in milliseconds | Setting criteria weights and importance | | Proposing score suggestions with exact citations | Approving or rejecting every proposal | | Flagging contradictions when a score looks unsupported | Releasing each page snippet individually | | | Changing any score on the matrix | This division is enforced in code, not system prompts . Write tools like set_score , set_weight , add_option , and finalize_decision are completely absent from the tool catalog. An automated test fails the build if any of those write tools ever appear. Keeping approvals rare so they actually get read So instead of spamming a lot of confirmation dialogs for every small action because that trains users to click "Confirm" without reading, consensus only prompts the user when requesting to open a specific page snippet. UX Design Choice Why it matters "Deny" is focused first Prevents users from accidentally approving a page by pressing space out of habit. Agent's reason shown verbatim Shows the agent's exact intent so you know why it needs the page. Permissions reset on reload Closing or reloading the tab immediately reseals all documents. Declined requests are logged The audit trail records every decision, including what was denied. Decisions you can actually audit later Citations attached to cells : Any score proposed by the agent links directly to the specific page and snippet it came from. Clear "no source" tags : If a score was entered manually without document backing, it is marked with a clear amber "no source" badge so nobody mistakes an unbacked guess for verified evidence. Full Markdown Export : Clicking "Export Brief" generates a complete report containing all scores, weights, citations, open challenges, and the disclosure audit log. 3> What people and agents can do together that was impossible before Before You had to choose between protecting your documents or using an AI. Now You and your agent reason together over documents the AI is never handed in bulk. The agent understands the overall shape of the evidence — where matches cluster, which sections look relevant, and which matrix cells lack evidence — and asks for access one page at a time. The novel capability: unreadRefs Most AI tools only let a model talk about what it has already read. When Consensus's flag_inconsistency tool runs, the agent can also point to pages it has located but is not yet permitted to read , displaying: "I have not read these pages yet. May I check them?" Clicking release on that card lets the human approve those specific references directly. An agent that is transparent about what it doesn't know yet — while still pointing you in the right direction — is far more useful and trustworthy than an AI that guesses or stays silent. This is only possible because searching and reading are two separate capabilities running locally in the browser. Walkthrough of an actual run (in ChatGPT's built-in browser) Step Tools Called Live Ranking Impact 1. Demo loaded — Vendor C (100%) · Vendor A (90%) · Vendor B (83%) 2. Entered unbacked score I score Vendor A 5/5 on Data Residency with no source Vendor C · Vendor A (93%) · Vendor B 3. Agent searches without reading Agent finds DPA p.13, Annex C p.21, questionnaire p.3 — reads zero text get_decision_state , locate_evidence 4. Challenge triggered Red challenge card appears; matrix cell pulses red with a ! badge request_disclosure , flag_inconsistency 5. Human releases Page 13 I click Approve on Page 13; agent extracts the US-only storage clause read_snippet 6. Score corrected I drop the score to 2 based on the citation Vendor C · Vendor B (83% ▲) ·

title: ConstraintLab
pitch: Describe the constraints. Let the solver prove the schedule.
about_excerpt: Describe the constraints. Let the solver prove the schedule. Like 1 Comment Story Updates logo main operating screen scheduling screen About the Project Inspiration Scheduling sounds simple until real-world constraints begin interacting: machines become unavailable, urgent jobs receive deadlines, tasks depend on one another, and operators override assignments. Traditional optimization software can solve these problems, but describing a model often requires specialized mathematical knowledge. AI assistants make natural-language interaction easier, but an LLM should not be trusted to invent a schedule and claim it is valid. ConstraintLab combines the strengths of both: Humans express goals and judge trade-offs. AI agents translate intent into structured actions. A deterministic solver computes and validates the schedule. We built ConstraintLab to explore what an agent-native optimization workspace could look like—one where the human interface, AI agent, solver, and audit history all operate on the same canonical application state. What It Does ConstraintLab is a browser-based job-shop scheduling workspace. Users can: View jobs, machines, dependencies, deadlines, and downtime windows. Inspect schedules through an interactive Gantt chart. Add or edit scheduling constraints manually. Ask a WebMCP-capable AI agent to inspect and modify the model. Run a real mixed-integer linear programming solver in the browser. Detect when a solved schedule becomes stale after the model changes. Receive deterministic explanations when a model is infeasible. Review every human, agent, and solver action in an audit timeline. A typical interaction looks like this: “Machine 2 will be unavailable between 1 PM and 3 PM, and Job 7 must finish before noon.” The agent discovers ConstraintLab’s site tools, adds typed constraints, and requests a solve. The HiGHS solver—not the language model—computes the resulting schedule. If another request creates a contradiction, ConstraintLab reports the genuine infeasible result and identifies the relevant constraints using deterministic conflict analysis. How We Built It ConstraintLab is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Zod, Web Workers, WebAssembly, HiGHS, WebMCP, Vitest, and Netlify. The most important architectural decision was to maintain one canonical application state. Human interface ──┐ ▼ Domain actions ▲ AI agent ─────────┘ │ Canonical Zustand store ├── Solver ├── Gantt chart └── Audit timeline The interface and WebMCP handlers call the exact same domain actions. There is no separate “agent state” or hidden model that can drift away from what the user sees. ConstraintLab exposes nine typed site tools: get_problem_state add_job update_job add_constraint remove_constraint set_objective solve_problem get_solution analyze_infeasibility Every tool input is validated with Zod, and write operations are validated again inside the domain layer. Agent arguments are treated as requests—not as trusted data. For optimization, we compile the scheduling problem into a CPLEX LP-format model and send it to HiGHS running inside a Web Worker. This prevents the WebAssembly solver from blocking the interface. The objective is to minimize makespan: $$ \min C_{\max} $$ For every job (j), completion must satisfy: $$ C_{\max} \geq S_j + p_j $$ where (S_j) is its start time and (p_j) is its duration. Precedence, deadlines, machine assignments, availability windows, and non-overlapping jobs are represented as linear constraints. Binary ordering variables handle jobs that may compete for the same machine. The resulting assignments are translated back into application objects and applied through a single solver-result domain action. We also track a modelVersion . Every structural edit increments this version, and every solution records which version it solved. If the two differ, the interface immediately displays: Model changed — re-solve required. Challenges We Ran Into One major challenge was correctly separating language understanding from mathematical correctness. The agent is useful for translating a human request into typed tool calls, but it must never become the scheduling engine. Keeping that boundary strict influenced the entire architecture. The solver integration was another challenge. HiGHS accepts LP-format text rather than a convenient JavaScript model object, so we built an explicit model compiler and solution translator. Variable names had to remain stable enough to map solver columns back to jobs and resources. Scheduling downtime is more complicated than adding a simple bound. A job must occur either before or after an unavailable window, which requires additional binary decisions and big-(M) constraints. Infeasibility explanations were also difficult. A solver can report that a model is infeasible without producing an explanation suitable for a user. Instead of asking an LLM to guess, we built typed, rule-based checkers that examine deadlines, precedence chains, locked starts, resource assignments, and machine availability. The generated summaries are based on computed scheduling facts. Finally, WebMCP is still an emerging browser capability. We needed feature detection, top-level tool registration, a fallback path, and a clear unavailable state so that the human scheduling interface remains functional even when WebMCP is not enabled. Accomplishments That We’re Proud Of We are especially proud that ConstraintLab demonstrates a complete agent-to-solver loop rather than a simulated AI demo. The AI agent modifies the same state that the human sees. The schedule is computed by a real deterministic MILP solver. Constraints have stable IDs and structured types. Invalid agent inputs are rejected safely. Solver work runs outside the main browser thread. Model edits automatically invalidate stale solutions. Infeasibility explanations come from deterministic analysis. Every human, agent, and solver action is auditable. The entire application works without an AI agent. The complete optimization stack runs inside the browser and can be deployed as a static application. Our headline demo intentionally creates a real contradiction involving Job 4, Machine 2, machine downtime, and a deadline. The solver returns an actual infeasible status, and ConstraintLab identifies the relevant conflict instead of showing a scripted response. What We Learned We learned that the most valuable role for an AI agent in optimization is not solving the mathematics itself. Its value is translating intent, operating tools, and helping users navigate the model. Typed tools are essential. Allowing an agent to submit arbitrary mathematical expressions would make validation, auditing, and explanations significantly less reliable. A deliberately small vocabulary of structured constraints creates a much safer system. We also learned that shared state is more important than chat history. The collaboration feels trustworthy because every agent action appears immediately in the visual workspace, and every human edit is visible to the agent during its next inspection. Finally, infeasibility is not merely an error state. In real optimization work, discovering why requirements conflict can be as valuable as finding an optimal schedule. What’s Next for ConstraintLab The current version deliberately focuses on one excellent scheduling loop. Future versions could expand that foundation with: Multiple optimization objectives, including lateness and utilization. Saved scenarios and side-by-side solution comparison. Checkpoints and reversible model changes. Transactional batches of agent-proposed changes. Interactive rescheduling and assignment locking. Richer deterministic conflict analysis. Larger industrial scheduling models. Import and export support for operational datasets. Additional optimization domains such as workforce, classroom, and logistics planning. Collaboration features for teams reviewing the same model. The longer-term vision is for ConstraintLab to become a general agent-native optimization workspace: natural enough for anyone to describe a problem, rigorous enough for experts to trust the answer, and transparent enough for humans to remain in control. title: CourseMCP
pitch: An agent can take your course, and edit it. 33 WebMCP tools scoped by route and permission.
about_excerpt: An agent can take your course, and edit it. 33 WebMCP tools scoped by route and permission. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent operating a live course GIF Authoring in motion One prompt, one new screen 33 total tools Reading live learner state Answering through the agent 33 tools on document.modelContext Tool surface follows the route The boundary: humanOnly Tools vary by route. Inspiration Online courses are built for one participant: the person clicking through them. An AI agent can read visible text or try to operate the page, but it does not reliably know what counts as a lesson, where the learner is, which choices belong to a question, or which edits the application actually permits. The same wall exists on the other side. Course authoring tools are dense forms. An agent asked to add a knowledge check has to find the right screen, open the right panel, fill a question prompt, create the right number of answer choices, mark exactly one correct, and write feedback for each, and a run that fails halfway leaves a broken question in a real course. On the learner side, a failed agent action wastes a turn. On an authoring side, it corrupts the course content. CourseMCP began with a question that applies to both: what if the course itself could explain its structure and capabilities to the agent working beside you? What it does CourseMCP turns a prompt or an uploaded TXT, Markdown, PDF, or DOCX file into a polished, shareable micro-course. A course can remain private, belong to an optional account, or be deliberately published to a public gallery. The human interface works in any modern browser. In a WebMCP-capable browser, the course also describes itself to an agent, but never the same way twice. CourseMCP defines 33 distinct tools. An agent is never offered all 33. Depending on the route and the signed-in user's permissions, it receives between 3 and 24: Route Purpose Tools /auth/callback Authentication callback 3 /gallery Public gallery 5 /account My Courses 5 /sign-in Passwordless sign-in 5 / and /#create Course builder 6 /c/:slug Learner course 17 /edit/difficult-conversations-demo Session-only demo editor 23 /edit/:slug Persistent course editor 24 Three tools are global, context, account status, and navigation. Everything else is earned by being somewhere specific. The learner route adds 14. Read the outline, get course info, inspect the current screen, read screen content, search real course text and receive stable screen IDs, list learning objectives, read progress, list questions, read notes, then navigate to a screen, submit an answer, reset the course, add a note, or bookmark content. Nothing on this surface can alter course content. The editor route adds 21. It begins with all 14 learner tools, because an author is also a reader: the agent can add a question, navigate to it, submit an answer, and confirm the feedback renders correctly. On top of that sit four authoring tools, add_screen , update_screen , add_question , update_question , and three management tools for sharing status, visibility, and opening the learner view. Four authoring tools cover the entire editing surface: lesson bodies, titles, image URLs, alternative text, image prompts, question prompts, answer choices from two to eight, the single correct answer, per-choice feedback, and summary takeaways. That is deliberate. Stable screen and answer IDs let a small number of well-typed tools compose, instead of exposing one tool per form field. Every agent action uses the same application state as the visible UI. When an agent moves to a lesson, the learner sees the player move. When it adds a knowledge check, the editor updates immediately. A visible activity trail records what happened. Why WebMCP Learning is semantic and stateful. A useful assistant needs stable screen identifiers, course structure, question models, progress, and clearly bounded actions, not DOM selectors. CourseMCP uses WebMCP as its capability contract. On the learner side, an agent can search the course, receive matching screen IDs, and pass one into the navigation tool. It can inspect assessment prompts without being told the correct answer. On the authoring side, the argument is stronger. Adding a knowledge check means a question prompt, between two and eight answer choices, exactly one correct answer, feedback for each choice, and a position in the outline. Through a DOM, that is a long sequence of interactions in which every intermediate state is a partially valid course. As a WebMCP tool it is one call against a strict schema: it either produces a complete, valid knowledge check or it produces nothing. The clearest expression of route and permission scoping is the difference between the two editors. The session-only demo editor exposes 23 tools. The real editor exposes 24. The difference is exactly one tool, set_course_visibility , because the demo is permanently public and must not be publishable or unpublishable by anyone. Not a guard clause inside a handler that refuses the call. The tool is never registered on that route, so an agent inspecting the demo editor cannot see that publishing is even a concept there. The same logic runs in the other direction. /auth/callback is a transient route, so its surface collapses to the three globals and nothing else. /sign-in offers get_sign_in_state and prepare_sign_in , an agent can fill the form, but there is no tool to send the magic-link email, because that decision belongs to the person. How I built it The frontend uses Vue 3, Pinia, Vue Router, and Tailwind CSS. WebMCP tools feature-detect the browser API and register against the top-level document. Route-scoped registration managers remove stale tools during navigation, and course tools do not appear until the exact requested course has finished loading. Every handler calls the same Pinia actions used by the human interface, there is no separate agent-only course engine. Inputs use strict JSON schemas, results are serializable and bounded, and stable IDs allow small tools to compose safely. The Node.js and Express server extracts supported documents and calls the OpenAI Responses API with a strict Zod course schema. Supabase provides passwordless accounts and PostgreSQL persistence for courses and redacted activity metadata. Row-level security is forced on the course tables, browser roles have no direct table access, and private editor credentials are stored only as SHA-256 digests. A single Render web service serves both the API and the built Vue app. Additional guardrails include pagination, explicit publication confirmation, permission-gated authoring tools, revision checks for visible drafts, and idempotent generation so retries do not create duplicate courses. Challenges I ran into The hardest problem was lifecycle correctness, and authoring is what made it hard. A tool set that belongs to one course must never survive navigation to another course, a loading screen, or an invalid route, and the consequence of a leaked authoring tool is an edit landing on the wrong course. I built isolated registration scopes with abort-based cleanup and tested rapid navigation explicitly. A second challenge was keeping human and agent state genuinely shared. Reimplementing actions inside tool handlers would have produced subtle drift between what an author saw and what an agent had done, so I routed both interfaces through the same stores and validation paths. Generation also needed production-grade failure handling. Document extraction, model latency, retries, and duplicate requests can all fail in different ways. I added bounded uploads, extraction limits, concurrency controls, timeouts, idempotency keys, and safe error messages. Finally, authentication and sharing required careful boundaries. Accounts remain optional, private courses stay private by default, and publication requires an explicit acknowledgement. Accomplishments that we're proud of A tool surface that ranges from 3 to 24 by route and permission, with the demo and real editors differing by exactly one deliberately withheld tool. 33 composable WebMCP tools where four authoring tools cover an entire editing surface, because the IDs are stable and the schemas are strict. An editor that is a superset of the learner surface, so an agent can verify its own authoring by reading the result back. A coherent creator, gallery, account, learner, and editor, not a disconnected tool demo. A no-login demo that lets judges inspect, navigate, annotate, bookmark, and edit a real course. Persistent signed-in courses with private-by-default sharing and an opt-in public gallery. 124 automated tests plus linting and a production build check. What I learned WebMCP is most powerful when tools expose application concepts rather than reproducing buttons. Small capabilities with stable identifiers compose better than one giant "do everything" tool, four authoring tools cover more editing surface than a per-field design would have, and they compose with th

title: DAG Studio: Agent-Ready Causal Modeling with WebMCP
pitch: DAG Studio lets researchers and AI build and analyze causal diagrams through WebMCP, with transparent assumptions and analysis-ready R or Python code.
about_excerpt: DAG Studio lets researchers and AI build and analyze causal diagrams through WebMCP, with transparent assumptions and analysis-ready R or Python code. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I'm a trained epidemiologist with about 10 years in pharma supporting drug development. When we approach the development of a study we begin with a directed acyclic graph (DAG). In a causal DAG, every node and arrow expresses a scientific assumption. Those assumptions determine which biases may be present, which variables should or should not be adjusted for, and whether a causal effect is identifiable. We created DAG Studio to give epidemiologists and other researchers an approachable, browser-based environment for constructing and examining those assumptions. However, an AI assistant interacting with a conventional web application still has to interpret what it 'sees' on the canvas. It cannot reliably distinguish a parts of a graph from a decorative line or know whether its internal description of the graph still matches what the researcher sees. WebMCP suggested a better model: give the agent structured access to the same scientific object the researcher is editing. That inspired DAG Studio WebMCP, a shared causal-modeling workspace for researchers. What it does DAG Studio WebMCP allows a researcher and an AI agent to collaborate on the same live causal DAG. The researcher sees and edits the visual canvas, while the agent uses nine structured WebMCP tools connected to the exact same client-side state: get_current_dag add_node remove_node add_edge remove_edge analyze_current_dag check_adjustment_set generate_analysis_code simulate_current_dag An agent can read the current graph, propose changes, inspect open backdoor paths, identify minimal sufficient adjustment sets, verify a researcher-proposed adjustment set, and generate R or Python analysis code. The simulation tool uses DAG Studio's existing linear Gaussian structural equation model to generate synthetic data from the live graph. For each node (X_j), the illustrative model follows [ X_j = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{pa}(j)} \beta_{ij}X_i + \epsilon_j. ] The tool returns bounded summaries, correlations, a small data preview, model-implied total effects, and crude and minimally adjusted ordinary least squares estimates. In our demo, a researcher can ask the agent to retain results from two different DAG hypotheses in the conversation and compare their implications using the same sample size, random seed, and coefficients. These simulations do not determine which DAG is scientifically correct. They reveal what follows from the assumptions encoded in each model. How we built it DAG Studio WebMCP extends the existing React and Vite DAG Studio application. We deliberately reused the established causal and simulation functions in dag-engine.js and its dag-engine.d.ts declarations rather than rewriting the algorithms for the Challenge. The WebMCP layer registers tools through the current document.modelContext API. It also includes a compatibility fallback for hosts implementing the earlier navigator.modelContext location. The WebMCP tools receive dependency-injected access to the same synchronous state references and React mutation functions used by the visual canvas. Therefore: an agent mutation immediately appears on the canvas; a human canvas mutation is immediately visible to the next tool call; agent and human graph edits share the same undo history; and analysis and simulation always operate on the graph currently visible to the researcher. Agent changes receive visible attribution. The simulation tool also opens DAG Studio's existing simulation interface, so the result is reflected in both the conversation and the application. Everything remains browser-side. The Challenge version is an isolated static HTTPS deployment on Cloudflare Pages, separate from the production DAG Studio website. The source is published under the MIT license, and GitHub Actions runs the original engine-parity suite together with the new WebMCP shared-state tests. Challenges we ran into The most important challenge was not tool registration, rather it was guaranteeing that the agent and researcher were truly modifying the same graph. React state updates are asynchronous, while a sequence of agent tool calls may need to observe each mutation immediately. We addressed this by wiring the tools to the canvas's synchronous references and existing mutation wrappers rather than creating a second “agent graph.” WebMCP is also an emerging standard, and browser implementations differed during development. The API appeared under different objects across environments, some Chrome testing calls required JSON-serialized arguments, and not every ChatGPT or Codex browser session exposed site tools. Clear connection diagnostics and compatibility support were essential. We also had to preserve the scientific boundary between assistance and authority. A variable being associated with an outcome does not automatically make it a confounder, and simulated data cannot validate a biological hypothesis. Tool descriptions, responses, and visible language therefore characterize graph changes as assumptions or proposals for researcher review. Finally, simulation results can become too large for a useful agent interaction. We bounded sample-size options, limited row previews, summarized variables and correlations, validated coefficient overrides, and made every run reproducible with a recorded random seed. Accomplishments that we're proud of Nine WebMCP tools operate on the exact graph visible in DAG Studio. Human and agent mutations remain synchronized and undoable. The original DAG Studio causal algorithms were reused rather than approximated by the language model. The agent can analyze competing hypotheses and retain reproducible simulation results for comparison. Simulation outputs explicitly separate model-implied effects from crude and adjusted estimates. The integration includes current and earlier WebMCP API compatibility and visible connection diagnostics. Thirteen automated tests cover engine parity, tool registration, shared state, mutations, cycle rejection, adjustment analysis, code generation, simulation reproducibility, input validation, bounded results, visible simulation state, and a two-hypothesis comparison. The project is available as an open-source repository and a static public HTTPS application. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes meaningful domain operations rather than reproducing every button in an interface. analyze_current_dag is more reliable and scientifically legible than asking an agent to visually inspect a set of arrows. simulate_current_dag is more useful than teaching an agent how to navigate a simulation panel one control at a time. We also learned that shared state changes the nature of human–AI interaction. The canvas is no longer just something the agent can see; it becomes a common scientific object that both participants can inspect and revise. The conversation can retain multiple hypotheses and their results even though the visual editor displays the current model. Most importantly, greater agent capability makes explicit epistemic boundaries more important. The engine can verify the graphical and statistical consequences of a DAG, but neither the engine nor the agent can decide whether its assumptions are scientifically true. What's next for DAG Studio: Agent-Ready Causal Modeling with WebMCP Next, we want to deepen hypothesis-centered workflows: named DAG versions, persistent side-by-side comparisons, researcher approval checkpoints, and exportable analysis reports that preserve the connection between assumptions, adjustment decisions, simulations, and generated code. We also see opportunities for collaborative provenance, where every proposed node or edge can carry a rationale, citation, reviewer comment, and acceptance status. Additional simulation families could support binary, count, survival, longitudinal, and nonlinear outcomes while preserving transparent assumptions about the data-generating process. The long-term goal is not an autonomous system that declares causal truth. It is an agent-ready scientific workspace that helps researchers articulate alternatives, expose disagreements, test implications, and document why a final model was chosen. Ideally this workspace can be called upon in a multi-agent orchestration that runs a research workflow from end to end. Live application: https://dag-studio-webmcp-sandbox.pages.dev/ Source code: https://github.com/Black-Swan-Causal-Labs/dag-studio-webmcp Original DAG Studio: https://dagstudio.blackswancausallabs.com/ Built With causal-inference chatgpt cloudflare data-simulation directed-acyclic-graphs javascript openai react vite webmcp Try it out dag-studio-webmcp-sandbox.pages.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by jdiazdecaro Diaz-Decaro Like Share this project: Updates jdiazdecaro Diaz-Decaro started this project — Sep 0

title: Dayflow
pitch: A real HR system that registers 31 WebMCP tools in the page. The agent reads receipts that were never uploaded, drafts the numbers, and the tools that move money accept no amounts at all.
about_excerpt: A real HR system that registers 31 WebMCP tools in the page. The agent reads receipts that were never uploaded, drafts the numbers, and the tools that move money accept no amounts at all. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Role-filtering Inspiration An agent can already read HR data and talk about it sensibly. It cannot finish the job. The last step of most HR work is a number being written down, a salary, a bonus, a reimbursement, and a figure that came out of a language model is not a figure you can pay somebody. So the reading gets automated, the deciding does not, and the gap between them is where the errors live. Dayflow is an Indian HRMS, denominated in rupees and lakh, applying Indian rules: provident fund, professional tax, CGST and SGST on a restaurant bill. So the case for it should be made with Indian numbers. Finding Source 48% of Indian companies have no way to detect travel and expense fraud , because claims are checked by hand. About 55% cannot retrieve past claims at all. Happay, via Economic Times Every ₹1 lost to fraud costs an Indian firm ₹4.00 , and 54% say fraud is rising. LexisNexis India, 2024 India has the worst payroll staffing shortage in Asia Pacific, at 75% of businesses , and employers named missing automation the top cause of payroll error. ADP India, May 2025 Over half of occupational fraud cases involve missing controls or an override of them , median loss $104,000, median 12 months undetected. ACFE, 2026 Then on 21 November 2025 India's labour codes came into force and changed what a salary structure is allowed to look like: wages must be at least half of total remuneration, and anything excluded beyond that gets added back, which moves PF and gratuity. Every CTC split in the country had to be re-checked. This is not the year for a tool that quietly rewrites pay structures. The model is also the wrong component to trust with the arithmetic. Frontier models score between 73.8% and 99.8% on plain numerical addition, then fall to 7.5% when the same problems are restated symbolically, which looks like retrieval rather than rule following ( arXiv 2504.05262 ), and multi digit multiplication is still an open failure case ( arXiv 2510.00184 ). So full autonomy makes this worse, not better. It removes the human control the fraud data says is load bearing, and hands the arithmetic to the part of the stack with the weakest claim on it. A better model does not fix that. A better place to put the human does. The insight came from the WebMCP explainer , in the line about tools running inside the page the human is already looking at. If the tool lives in the page, the proposal can live in the page too, so the agent never has to be the one holding the number. That is why the three tools that move money accept no amounts at all. Not validated amounts. None. There is no numeric parameter anywhere in their schemas, so a model that invented a total has nowhere to put it. Only a tool running inside the document that owns what is displayed can work that way. What it does Dayflow is a working HR management system that registers 31 WebMCP tools inside its own page , so a browser agent can work it beside whoever is signed in. One rule governs everything: the agent drafts, the human commits. human asks in plain language agent reads, and parses the local file the human dropped agent drafts a proposal into the page's own canvas store the proposal renders on screen, old and new values side by side human reads the actual figures and clicks approve the commit tool reads the canvas, not the model Every row below is a real registered tool. Intent Example ask What happens See what the human sees "What am I looking at?" get_page_context returns the live route, the current filter, the rows that survived it, who is selected, and whether a proposal is on screen Drive the interface "Open the roster and pull up Ankush" navigate_to , filter_directory and focus_employee move the human's actual UI Decide leave "Approve Ankush's paid leave" check_leave_coverage simulates the gap read only, then decide_leave stops on an approval dialog before writing Onboard from a CV "Add this candidate" (CV pasted) add_employee_from_description parses the text in the tab and labels every inferred value with how it got there Quote the employer, not the model "What is the meal cap? What are our PF rates?" get_policy and get_salary_model return the written rules, and say plainly when they have fallen back to statutory defaults Draft then commit a salary "Set up 12 LPA for EMP014", then "Save it" propose_salary_structure splits the CTC six ways and draws it on the Salary page. commit_salary_structure takes a reason and a name. No figures Score work, then pay a bonus "Who earned bonus this quarter? Split two lakh" read_contribution_import and get_contribution_scores , where only verified rows score, then propose_bonus_pool divides the human's stated budget on screen and record_bonus_decision commits it. No figures Audit and reimburse a claim "What is on this bill? Check it, then approve it" audit_expense_claim marks up the page with the rule behind every rupee removed. record_expense_decision takes a decision, a reason and a name. No figures, and the parsed claim is then discarded The tool set reflects the session. Anyone signed in gets 8 page context and UI tools plus 3 contribution tools.An admin adds 7 for roster and leave, 7 for bonuses, 3 for salary, 3 for expenses. An anonymous visitor gets nothing, because nothing registers before sign in. Sign out and you can watch the list fall from 31 to 11 live in Chrome's DevTools WebMCP panel, because teardown runs off the AbortSignal the spec provides for it. Drop the sample restaurant bill onto the Expenses page and audit_expense_claim walks the written policy over it line by line. A ₹6,133 claim comes back as ₹1,783 reimbursable, with the rule attached to every rupee removed: Line group Claimed Reimbursable Rule applied Eight food lines ₹2,910 ₹1,200 Spent down in order against the daily meal cap until the cap runs out Three drinks lines ₹2,400 ₹0 Alcohol is not reimbursable, even itemised inside a food bill Service charge ₹531 ₹291 Read as a tip, capped at ten per cent of that day's pre tax food CGST and SGST ₹292 ₹292 Tax passes through untouched Total ₹6,133 ₹1,783 ₹4,350 refused \( 1{,}200 + 291 + 292 = 1{,}783 \) reconciles against the printed total on the bill, so a judge can check the engine by hand instead of taking my word for it. Uncertainty is reported rather than resolved: conference spend is held for review, neither approved nor refused, unless an approved travel request covers those dates, and held amounts are totalled outside the reimbursable figure. What people and agents can do together here that was hard before. The agent can audit a private financialdocument that was never uploaded anywhere, quoting policy at individual lines while the file never leaves the tab. It can commit a financial decision without anyone trusting its arithmetic, because it has no field to put a numberin, so what reaches the database is what was rendered and checked. And it can take over the reading without taking the judgement: a twelve row work export is parsed and reported honestly, including the row that matches nobody, and imported rows arrive as claimed, so an import cannot quietly move the leaderboard that feeds bonus money. How I built it Why the browser was the right place. The explainer names three failures of backend tool integrations: they cut the site's own interface out of the loop, they make you copy the user's state and credentials onto another server, and they make you build a backend to expose what the client already does. HR and finance hit all three, then hit a fourth that no server side tool can solve: some of the data has no URL. A travel claim arrives as a photo of a bill or an export sitting on someone's laptop. Dayflow parses both in the browser, so nothing is uploaded and there is no OCR service in the middle, and the parsed claim lives only in page state, gone once the decision is recorded. Meanwhile get_page_context reports live in memory state no REST endpoint could expose, and the signed in Supabase session is already the credential, so there is no second copy of who the user is to get wrong. Oversight is the point rather than a constraint I designed around: WebMCP lists fully autonomous workflows as a non goal, and given what the fraud data says about control overrides, salaries are the last place you would want an unattended agent. The WebMCP layer. src/lib/webmcp/registry.ts looks for document.modelContext , falls back to the deprecated navigator.modelContext , then provideContext , then a bare array. It calls registerTool per tool with a JSON Schema inputSchema and an execute returning MCP content blocks. Because registerTool is async and rejects, the registry claims each name up front and keeps the promise rather than assuming success. Tools are composed from the session role in one expre

title: DentalSculptor WebMCP
pitch: An app that enables dental educators to generate 3D of tooth and share them, from library of images or web images by chatting inside ChatGPT
about_excerpt: An app that enables dental educators to generate 3D of tooth and share them, from library of images or web images by chatting inside ChatGPT Like 1 Comment Story Updates DentalSculptor — WebMCP Challenge project story Inspiration Dental educators often need custom 3D examples: a fractured cusp for one seminar, an occlusal lesion for another, or a preparation that matches a particular learning objective. Creating those assets usually means learning specialist modelling software, waiting for technical support, or settling for a generic model that does not fit the lesson. DentalSculptor began as doctoral research into educator agency and human–AI co-creation in dental education. The central question was not simply, “Can AI generate a tooth?” It was, “Can an educator remain the author while AI handles the technical complexity?” WebMCP made a new answer possible. Instead of asking an agent to guess its way through buttons, loading states, and a spatial 3D editor, DentalSculptor gives the agent a precise vocabulary for the real workflow. The agent can coordinate; the educator can keep ownership of anatomy, pedagogy, approval, and release. What it does DentalSculptor turns a dental image into an editable 3D teaching case in one visible browser workspace. An educator and an agent can work together to: inspect the current app, authentication, generation, and viewer state; choose a curated tooth image or attach an educator-provided image; start 3D generation and wait until the model is actually visible; continue into a guided clinical case or the Free Editor; synchronize the correct edit preset and mark the intended anatomy; generate a 2D review preview and a reversible 3D variant; accept or reject the revision; export for supported teaching/simulation targets or publish with explicit privacy approval. The result is not an agent-only back channel. Every tool acts on the same project, React state, 3D scene, revision history, and approval controls the educator sees. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer whether generation finished, whether a model is visible, which clinical preset is compatible, whether a mask exists, or whether the educator approved the result. Coordinate-based browser automation is especially fragile in a resizable 3D viewport. With WebMCP: tool schemas replace screen-coordinate guessing; live readiness state prevents premature actions; page-scoped discovery reveals only actions relevant to the current workspace; structured results tell the agent what happened and what remains; human approval boundaries are encoded into the workflow rather than left to prompting. This improves speed and reliability without making the clinical workflow less accountable. The human–agent partnership The agent is good at orchestration: inspecting state, explaining prerequisites, selecting a compatible workflow, keeping a multi-stage process on track, and preparing reuse. The educator is responsible for judgment: selecting source material, defining clinical intent, marking the exact anatomy, approving previews, accepting revisions, confirming privacy, and authorizing publication or download. That division is the project’s core contribution. WebMCP does not remove the person from the creative loop; it gives them a more capable collaborator. How we built it The production application uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Supabase Auth/PostgreSQL/Storage, Prisma, Modal GPU services, and Vercel. The WebMCP adapter is isolated in dentalsculptor-app/src/components/webmcp/ . Google Chrome Labs' lifecycle hook registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and unregisters them when their React surface disappears. The tools are organized by page: global app/authentication/navigation tools; image-to-3D generation tools; clinical case and editor tools; confirmed publishing tools in the visible share dialog; public community inspection and reuse tools. Every mutating tool has a constrained JSON Schema. Read-only tools advertise readOnlyHint . Model-dependent tools wait for the viewer—not merely a model URL—to report that geometry is visible. Publishing requires both explicit release approval and confirmation that the model contains no identifiable patient information. Challenges we faced Making 3D readiness truthful A generation API can return a URL before an embedded browser has downloaded, parsed, framed, and rendered the model. We added viewer-level readiness, bounded same-origin asset loading, actionable proxy errors, and a load watchdog. WebMCP reports modelReady only after the viewer confirms the model is visible. Keeping tools synchronized with a changing interface The landing page, editor, share dialog, and community page expose different capabilities. Page-scoped React registration lets the available tool set follow the visible UI and unregister cleanly during navigation. Preserving educator authority The fastest implementation would have let the agent mark anatomy, approve an edit, and publish in one opaque step. We deliberately separated those moments. The agent can prepare the next action, but spatial targeting, revision decisions, privacy confirmation, and release remain visible and reversible. Working with an emerging standard WebMCP is still evolving. We kept the browser adapter isolated, documented the imperative API, added a live diagnostics page, and retained a complete non-WebMCP interface as a fallback. Accomplishments 29 non-duplicated, page-scoped WebMCP tools spanning a real 3D authoring workflow. A model-readiness contract based on rendered geometry rather than optimistic API completion. Structured clinical case authoring with reversible human approval. Secure authentication handoff without exposing credentials, cookies, or tokens. Explicit confirmation gates for export, publishing, and patient privacy. A public diagnostic route that reads the browser’s real tool registry. What we learned The most valuable agent tools are not one-to-one copies of buttons. They expose the state transitions and safety boundaries that make a complex application understandable. We also learned that “human in the loop” is strongest when the loop is visible in the product architecture: the educator and agent should share one workspace and one source of truth. What is next We plan to evaluate how educators divide work with agents across different levels of experience, add richer model-semantic targeting, and contribute practical feedback from spatial authoring to the emerging WebMCP standard. Built With amazon-web-services and chrome glb modal next.js openai-chatgpt-in-app-browser postgresql posthog prisma python react react-three-fiber supabase tailwind-css three.js trellis typescript vercel webmcp webxr Try it out dentalsculptor.vercel.app github.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Job Oyebisi job oyebisi Deborah Ige Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Job Oyebisi started this project — Sep 04, 2026 02:06 AM EDT

title: Overturn
pitch: Analyze, recommend, and convert any website to WebMCP—in one shot.
about_excerpt: Analyze, recommend, and convert any website to WebMCP—in one shot. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web was built for people clicking. Some sites later gained APIs; many accumulated PDFs, hidden rules, multi-page forms, phone-only support, and offline handoffs. Browser agents can read those pages, but they still have to guess at the interface and often stall at the one consequential step that matters. WebMCP changes that by letting a website expose an explicit, typed contract for agents. The remaining adoption problem is substantial: a site owner still has to inspect an existing workflow, decide what should be a read, what should become an editable proposal, and what must wait for a human, then implement and verify the resulting tools. We built Overturn to make that retrofit process a product. For the end-to-end proof, we chose one of the hardest common workflows: appealing a health-plan prior-authorization denial. In Medicare Advantage in 2024, plans processed nearly 53 million prior-authorization requests. Only 11.5% of denied requests were appealed, even though 80.7% of appeals were partially or fully overturned ( KFF ). The fictional Larkspur Health Plan portal in our demo starts where many real workflows still start: a PDF letter, a six-page form, rules that are referenced but not exposed, and a fax or mailing address. What it does Overturn Retrofit takes a public URL and: Scans up to eight same-origin pages for forms, tables, detail pages, documents, offline submission instructions, cited policies, phone-only support, iframes, sign-in requirements, and WebMCP headers. Produces a 0–100 agent-readiness score and evidence-backed findings grouped as blockers, gaps, and notes. Recommends a typed WebMCP tool inventory. Reads are marked read-only, writes become on-page proposals, and consequential actions are explicitly human-gated. Generates a starter document.modelContext.registerTool() module and a Markdown implementation report. Exposes its own WebMCP meta-tools— analyze_site , get_readiness_report , list_recommended_tools , and get_generated_code —so a developer’s agent can drive the retrofit itself. The analyzer does not pretend it can infer and safely wire every site’s private business logic. It generates the tool layer and concrete fixes; a developer or coding agent connects app-specific handlers. To prove that the plan is actionable, we ran Retrofit against the fictional legacy portal, implemented its recommendations, and shipped the complete before-and-after experience on the same live site. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This project depends on WebMCP rather than merely adding it as a feature. On the Retrofit page, an agent can run the audit, inspect the findings, list the proposed tools, and retrieve the generated code through four page-native tools. On the rebuilt appeals portal, 14 tools expose the actual workflow: member context, denials, deadlines, policy criteria, drafting, evidence completeness, review type, submission, status, and external review. The tool surface is state-scoped. Drafting tools appear only in the appeal workspace; after filing, they disappear and status tools take their place. Every agent call is visible in the Activity panel, and every proposed write is rendered on the page for the person to inspect or edit. Without WebMCP, an automation agent must inspect the DOM, open PDFs, infer what fields mean, and eventually stops at the fax instruction. With WebMCP, the site itself tells the agent what it may read, what it may propose, and where the person must take over. How it creates a better user experience For a site owner, Overturn replaces a blank page with an actionable plan: what blocks agents today, which tools to expose, how to describe and scope them, which actions need confirmation, and the code to start from. For a person using the retrofitted site, the agent handles the repetitive work—reading the denial, matching records to five policy criteria, drafting one evidence-backed argument per criterion, checking completeness, and calculating deadlines. The person keeps the decisions that are actually theirs: choose records, edit the language, select standard or expedited review, and sign. The work never disappears into a chat window. Drafts are on the page, labelled and editable. Tool calls are logged. The person sees exactly what changed and remains in control. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Before: an agent can read a denial letter and locate the appeal form, but the workflow is unstructured and ends at a fax or mailing address. It cannot reliably know the plan’s five criteria, prove that the evidence is complete, or safely file the appeal. After: in one sitting and on one shared page, the agent reads the structured denial and criteria, opens the appeal, drafts five arguments tied to named records, and re-checks completeness as the member attaches evidence and edits the draft. The agent can request submission, but it cannot file. It returns pending_confirmation , the site renders a Sign & submit card, and only the member’s click creates a case number and starts the decision clock. That read → proposal → human commit pattern can extend beyond appeals to any claim-shaped dispute or regulated legacy workflow. How we built it Application: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, and Vercel. Analyzer: deterministic server-side heuristics using Cheerio. Crawling is SSRF-guarded: HTTP(S) only, private network ranges refused, and redirects, response size, page count, and time are capped. WebMCP layer: document.modelContext.registerTool() with a legacy navigator.modelContext fallback, one AbortController per tool, duplicate-safe registration, readOnlyHint annotations, concise descriptions, and bounded outputs. Safety: reads are free; writes render as proposals; submit_appeal and request_external_review return pending_confirmation . The server rejects submission without the human-click marker using 403 human_confirmation_required . State and judge access: each visitor receives an isolated localStorage sandbox. There is no login or database. A replay demonstrates the same flow for browsers without site-tools access. Verification: a comprehensive Puppeteer smoke suite exercises route scoping, the full appeal flow, generated code, analyzer guards, human-gated submission, and the post-filing tool transition. We also tested the deployed tools in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and WebMCP-enabled Chrome. Build workflow: we used Claude Code on an NVIDIA DGX Spark for research, implementation, debugging, testing, deployment, and the reproducible FFmpeg/edge-tts video pipeline. The submitted application does not depend on an LLM at runtime. Challenges we ran into Designing real human confirmation. WebMCP does not currently provide a tool-level confirmation primitive. We created an application protocol instead: an agent can propose a consequential action, the page renders a confirmation card, and a server-side gate accepts only the person’s click. Keeping tools synchronized with application state. The useful tool set changes as the member moves from denial to draft to filed case. We built one registry that derives tools from both the route and appeal status, unregisters stale tools, and remains stable under React Strict Mode and hot reloads. Analyzing arbitrary URLs safely. A URL analyzer can easily become an SSRF proxy or an unbounded crawler. We had to reject private addresses and tightly cap redirects, bytes, pages, and request time while still returning a useful partial report when some pages fail. Drawing an honest conversion boundary. Static HTML can reveal affordances, but it cannot reveal every private API or JavaScript-only state transition. Generated handlers therefore make app-specific wiring explicit instead of hiding it behind a false “one-click” claim. Accomplishments we are proud of Shipped the analyzer, legacy portal, agent-native portal, and readiness record as one coherent live product. Turned the legacy portal’s 40/100 audit—two blockers, two gaps, and nine recommended tools—into a working portal with 14 domain tools plus four Retrofit meta-tools. Made the agent’s work visible and editable while enforcing consequential consent on the server, not in a prompt. Built a complete, reproducible before-and-after demo and an automated verification suite during the hackathon window. What we learned Structured reads alone do not complete workflows. Agents also need typed proposals, deterministic validation, explicit commit paths, and post-action status. Human control works best as product architecture, not as a prompt instruction. Tool names, descriptions, scope, and lifecycle are part of the user experience. A generated scaffold is valuable only when it clearly shows what has been inferred and what a developer still needs to connect. title: DSTAR
pitch: Review agent-created documents in the document itself, with exact context, human decisions and portable history.
about_excerpt: Review agent-created documents in the document itself, with exact context, human decisions and portable history. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can already generate polished documents and artifacts in seconds. The collaboration layer has not caught up: review gets scattered across chat transcripts, copied excerpts, replacement files, and format-specific tools. Reviewers lose the exact sentence and version they meant, while agents lose the live state of the page. We built DSTAR so agents can create and revise, while people review, comment, and make the final decision in the document itself. DSTAR means document star : one HTML-based artifact model for anything an agent can create, with review built in. What it does DSTAR keeps one canonical artifact made of HTML, CSS, and local assets. The same Viewer renders conventional documents, rich interactive explainers, slides, and UI design specs. Reviewers can select exact text, open comment threads, and reply. An external agent can draft a comment or reply and can propose a complete new revision. Drafts remain editable, proposals remain pending, and only the Owner can explicitly accept or reject a revision. Comments and revision decisions stay separate: accepting a useful update does not silently resolve the discussion that motivated it. Every proposal is immutable and based on an exact accepted revision. Why WebMCP A conventional MCP server can expose a stored document, but it does not know what the person is reviewing in the browser right now. DSTAR registers narrow page tools with document.modelContext.registerTool so the external agent receives the exact displayed revision, selection, focused comment, current role, and pending proposals. That makes natural instructions such as “rewrite this” or “help me reply” possible without copying text, hashes, or comment IDs into chat. It also preserves the trust boundary: the agent can prepare an editable comment or reply draft and can submit a pending revision, but it has no tool to post, accept, reject, or resolve on the person's behalf. The public demo exposes five tools: get_review_context read_document draft_selection_comment draft_comment_reply propose_revision How we built it The top-level Viewer owns WebMCP registration and renders authored documents in a restricted frame. The persistent implementation crosses a limited JSON bridge into a filesystem-backed TypeScript Engine with immutable revisions, keyed mutations, role-bound sessions, reopenable history, and exact Origin and resource checks. The public static deployment applies the same exact-revision and human-decision model with browser-local sample state, so every judge gets a clean, credential-free workspace. We added one review model across four formats, a document library, comment threads, Owner and Reviewer capabilities, version review, slide thumbnails and keyboard navigation, scoped agent handoffs, and deployment tooling. The test suite covers unit, integration, security, conformance, real HTTP persistence, and process restarts. We also verified native WebMCP tool discovery and calls in the ChatGPT in-app browser without injecting a polyfill. Challenges The hardest part was keeping live page context useful without giving the agent invisible authority. Selections, focused comments, and revisions can all drift while an agent is working. We fail closed on those mismatches, bind proposals to an exact base revision, keep drafts explicit, and leave every consequential decision in the Viewer. A second challenge was unifying documents, rich HTML, slides, and UI design without forcing authors into a parallel source format. Treating HTML as the portable artifact and adding presentation behavior in the Viewer gave us both expressive rendering and one consistent review layer. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable where transient browser state matters. The benefit is not merely another way to call a backend; it is a precise bridge between what a person is looking at and what an external agent can safely prepare. The page can carry context while still reserving posting, acceptance, rejection, and resolution for people.
