title: DuckStudio
pitch: DuckStudio is a agent-native data app. Datasets stay on your machine. DuckDB-WASM runs queries in a Web Worker inside the browser tab.
about_excerpt: DuckStudio is a agent-native data app. Datasets stay on your machine. DuckDB-WASM runs queries in a Web Worker inside the browser tab. Like Comment Story Updates DuckStudio idle state prior to dataset selection, displaying upload controls on the left and an empty workspace placeholder. Default workspace screen showing no active tasks and prompting dataset activation from available presets or CSV upload. DuckStudio SQL & Lineage tab displaying the generated aggregation query, execution metadata (92.5 ms over 250k rows). DuckStudio displaying a DATASET_UNAVAILABLE error notification after attempting analysis without an activated dataset. DuckStudio Charts dashboard displaying summary KPI cards and an "accounts by tickets" distribution scatter plot completed in 92.5 ms. DuckStudio Charts view showing re-run or alternate query execution completed in 127.4 ms across 250,000 scanned records. Inspiration Analysts in healthcare and finance face strict data protection agreements (DPAs) and egress bans: data cannot leave the tab, but cloud LLMs cannot query browser memory. WebMCP bridges this actuation gap by giving an agent browser-level tools. However, browser agents can observe both tool outputs and the rendered DOM. Sanitizing tool payloads is ineffective if the UI renders raw sensitive rows where the model can inspect them. DuckStudio solves this through custody with controlled release : the agent steers the analysis and inspects safe aggregates, but raw records never cross into tool envelopes or the rendered canvas. What it does DuckStudio is a privacy-first, agent native analytical app where a human and an AI agent operate the same local DuckDB-WASM engine. Data remains in the client tab. WebMCP registers four imperative tools: duckdb_get_context — Returns capabilities, revision, schema digests, budgets, and permitted next actions. duckdb_activate_dataset — Switches datasets using optimistic concurrency through expectedRevision and idempotency keys. duckdb_execute_sql_to_canvas — Validates read-only SQL before execution, runs it locally, creates an immutable artifact with lineage, infers an aggregate KPI or chart specification, and pins it to the canvas. It returns an artifact handle and safe summary—never raw rows. duckdb_verify_zero_egress — Returns scoped evidence covering uploads, release decisions, network interceptors, and artifact lineage. Core Invariants: › Policy follows the dataset. : saas_churn (250,000 synthetic rows) runs under public_synthetic permitting bounded row display. healthcare_pii (100,000 rows with MRN and diagnosis) runs under sensitive_aggregate_only , suppressing raw grids entirely and rejecting cohorts smaller than 10 patients ($k \ge 10$). SQL is gated before execution : Permits only single, parameterized SELECT or WITH queries. Blocks DDL, DML, ATTACH , COPY , remote URLs, and extensions before DuckDB receives them. Deterministic state : Monotonic revisions and idempotency keys prevent race conditions, stale writes, and hallucinated retries. How we built it Stack : Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, lazy-loaded ECharts, and self-hosted @duckdb/duckdb-wasm in a dedicated Web Worker. Edge deployment & isolation : Deployed statically to Cloudflare Pages with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp . DuckDB-WASM binaries ( eh bundle) and fonts are self-hosted in /public to avoid third-party CDN failure under strict COEP. One command path : Human controls, prompt chips, the built-in simulator, and the 4 WebMCP tools all dispatch the exact same 6 domain commands through revisioned-workspace . Honest metrics : The initial workspace is empty—there are no pre-baked artifacts. SaaS metrics such as 14.2% churn and $182,400 impacted MRR are computed live by DuckDB from in- memory row generators and verified by CI contract tests Challenges we ran into DOM as an exfiltration surface : Because agents can scrape rendered elements, we implemented a single custody boundary across tool payloads and React rendering. If a requested view violates policy, it is rejected outright ("deny-over-strip") rather than partially rendered. Eradicating ambient state : Agents fail when tracking implicit context like "the last query." We eliminated ambient state entirely: every canvas view and query refinement references an immutable artifact ID containing a cryptographic SQL hash and parent lineage. Wasm limits & worker lifecycles : Single-threaded DuckDB-WASM ( eh bundle) runs under a browser wasm memory ceiling, clamped to a 5,000 ms execution budget and a 10,000-row cursor. Query cancellation requires terminating and respawning the Web Worker to prevent memory corruption without leaving orphaned partial artifacts. Evidence must be scoped honestly : The custody badge reads 0 Bytes of Dataset Uploaded . Interceptors audit fetch , XMLHttpRequest , sendBeacon , WebSocket , and WebTransport to separate analytical data from application bundle traffic, avoiding unsupported zero-knowledge claims. Accomplishments that we're proud of Sub-second analytical queries over 250,000 rows executed entirely in client wasm with 0 bytes of dataset egress. Agents receive compact envelopes containing KPIs, chart dimensions, and artifact handles instead of raw row dumps. Self-healing recovery: queries that fail validation or custody rules return structured error codes and actionable recovery steps, allowing models to self-correct autonomously. What we learned WebMCP is most reliable as an explicit, revisioned state machine. Providing schema digests and monotonic revisions prevents model hallucination far better than generic prompt engineering. Local execution is not sufficient for privacy. If an agent has DOM access, data custody must be enforced at the UI projection layer as strictly as the network layer. What's next for DuckStudio Interactive virtualized Data Grid : High-performance, keyboard-accessible table with range selection and clipboard support for public datasets. OPFS streaming export subsystem : Stream CSV/Parquet outputs directly to the Origin Private File System to bypass wasm memory ceilings during large exports. SQL editor deep links : URL-addressable analysis states to share reproducible artifact lineage graphs. * In-tab AI chat panel * : BYO-LLM and WebLLM support with explicit, user-gated PII consent boundaries. Multi-threaded execution : Transition to DuckDB-WASM's coi bundle once cross-browser WebAssembly threading ergonomics and worker isolation stabilize. title: Circuit Sim
pitch: One circuit, two native interfaces: people edit visually while agents inspect, author, highlight, and simulate the exact same design through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: One circuit, two native interfaces: people edit visually while agents inspect, author, highlight, and simulate the exact same design through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Electronic design is naturally visual, but agents are usually forced to guess their way through pixels or work in a separate text-only model. That creates two competing versions of the circuit. Circuit Sim explores a better model: one authoritative circuit that a person can see and edit while an agent can inspect, change, simulate, and explain through structured browser-native tools. What it does Circuit Sim is a collaborative schematic workbench for people and agents. A user works in the visual editor while an agent uses four WebMCP tools exposed directly by the live page: inspect_circuit discovers instructions, the component catalog, exact terminal keys, project state, ERC findings, and simulation freshness. author_circuit applies a validated complete circuit graph using an optimistic project hash. highlight_components focuses the same objects in the human-visible schematic for explanation and review. simulate_circuit runs the selected SPICE engine and returns measurements tied to the exact circuit snapshot. The demo shows Codex designing a beta-100 NPN bias stage from a natural-language target, creating the complete connected schematic, highlighting the bias network, running ngspice, and reporting node voltages and branch currents. It then changes the emitter resistor from 1 kΩ to 2 kΩ and simulates again to explain the stability-versus-headroom tradeoff using measured evidence. Why WebMCP is the right fit Without WebMCP, an agent would have to click through a dense CAD interface, infer component geometry, and scrape results from pixels. With WebMCP, the page advertises its capabilities and schemas directly. The agent can make precise, validated edits while every result remains visible to the user in the same workbench. This creates a workflow that was previously difficult: a person can describe design intent, watch an agent turn it into a real schematic, inspect exactly what changed, and challenge the design with another simulation—all without copying netlists between tools or maintaining a hidden agent-only circuit. How we built it The browser editor is React and TypeScript. Effect Schema defines and validates the canonical CircuitProject , edit operations, WebMCP inputs, and simulation responses. The page registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Agent edits cross the same domain validation used by the human interface. Connectivity and the SPICE netlist are derived from the saved project; the server runs ngspice in an isolated process and returns a validated simulation run associated with the project snapshot hash. IndexedDB persists validated projects and runs. The app is containerized and deployed on Render. The project is intentionally human-in-the-loop: hashes prevent stale agent writes, ERC findings stay visible, simulation evidence is inspectable, and component highlighting connects the agent’s explanation to the schematic. Challenges and learning The hardest part was keeping a visual editor, structured agent tools, connectivity extraction, and SPICE results consistent without creating a second source of truth. We learned that WebMCP is most valuable when tools expose domain operations and evidence—not a thin wrapper around UI clicks. Accomplishments Circuit Sim delivers a working deployed product rather than a mockup: four live WebMCP tools, validated authoring, shared human/agent state, ERC feedback, ngspice simulation, snapshot identity, undo/redo, persistence, and an end-to-end demonstration inside the Codex in-app browser. title: Enclave
pitch: The data stays in your browser. The agent gets tools, not rows — and anything it wants to change waits for you to approve it.
about_excerpt: The data stays in your browser. The agent gets tools, not rows — and anything it wants to change waits for you to approve it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Enclave keeps the store's data in the browser and hands the agent tools instead of rows. Anything it changes waits for a human. The landing page. The demo store is already loaded — no account, no upload, nothing to install. A write tool does not act. It proposes, shows its reasoning, and blocks until the operator approves or declines. Every tool call, with its cost in bytes. A full investigation of 59,615 rows: 6,851 bytes out, zero rows uploaded. Approved: four restock orders raised by the agent, and products below reorder level drop from seven to three. Asked why EMEA fell in March, the agent builds the board as it works: a chart, a table, a KPI, and a written finding. Inspiration Two things stop an AI agent being useful inside a real business, and they pull in opposite directions. It cannot see your data. Revenue, customers, orders — none of it can be pasted into a chat window, so the analysis that would actually help never happens. And it should not be clicking around your admin panel. An agent guessing its way through a UI is slow, brittle, and occasionally catastrophic. Nobody wants to find out it changed the wrong price because it inferred which button said "Save". WebMCP resolves both at once. The page declares exactly what an agent may do, so it never has to guess. And because the tools run inside the page, the data can stay in the browser: the agent asks questions of it without ever receiving it. What it does Enclave is the back-office of Northwind Trading Co., a fictional store. Its orders and catalogue load into the browser tab and stop there. Overview, Orders, Products and Analytics are all real views over that data — there is no server. An agent — ChatGPT over WebMCP, or a built-in panel using your own OpenAI key — operates the store through 22 registered tools . It investigates freely. When it wants to change something, it proposes and waits for you. The story the demo store carries The data has one real problem seeded in it, and the whole route to the fix is discoverable without the agent ever seeing a row. Asked "EMEA fell in March. Find the cause and fix it," GPT-5 walks it end to end: It notices. Revenue by region, month by month — EMEA falls 52% in March 2025 and no other region moves. It finds the cause. Broken down by supplier, one name is missing from March entirely: Aurora Supply sold nothing in EMEA that month. It checks the shelf. All four Aurora products are still at zero stock, below their reorder level. The revenue hole and the empty shelf are the same fact. You decide. It proposes restock orders with its reasoning, and stops. Sixteen tool rounds. No failed calls. About 7 KB left the browser. Zero rows uploaded. Nothing changes without you Reading is free. Anything that touches the business — a restock order, a price — is proposed : tool.execute() ├─ validate the product and the quantity ├─ await requestApproval({...}) ←── the call blocks here │ │ an approval card appears carrying the agent's own reason. │ "The agent is waiting. Nothing has changed yet." │ │ … the operator approves … │ ├─ raise the restock order └─ "Approved. RS-1042 raised for 900 × Nimbus Charging Dock." Decline it, or take too long, and the tool reports back honestly that nothing happened. That pause is the product. "The agent is supervised" is a policy; a tool call still blocked while a card says nothing has changed yet is a mechanism. How it works ┌─────────────── Enclave (browser tab) ───────────────┐ │ │ ChatGPT ───┼──→ document.modelContext ──┐ │ │ ├──→ TOOL REGISTRY │ Built-in ──┼──→ OpenAI Responses API ───┘ (22 tools, one │ panel │ (your own key) definition site) │ │ │ │ │ ┌──────────────┴───────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ approval gate DuckDB-WASM │ │ (writes only) store data │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ no server · data never leaves the tab One registry, two runtimes. Tools are defined once. One adapter registers them with document.modelContext ; another exposes the same list to the OpenAI Responses API. Identical capabilities and identical approval gates either way. The tool surface reads as well as it writes. Most only let an agent act. Enclave's lets it read the current state of the data, the analysis board and the catalogue — which is what lets it revise work it did not do itself. The global filter is a view swap. Analytics cards read from a view, not a table. set_global_filter runs one CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW and every card on the board re-renders against the filtered data. Every result is budgeted. Tool output passes through a single cap — 50 rows and 4 KB, adjustable in settings — before it can reach an agent. Raw row dumps are refused with a message steering the agent toward aggregation. The Activity Log counts the bytes on screen the whole time, so the privacy claim is metered rather than promised. How we built it Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand, DuckDB-WASM and ECharts. No backend — the only server-side artefact in the repository is a vercel.json that sets one header. 142 tests cover the data layer, the store, all 22 tools, the approval gate and both runtime adapters. Two scripts in the repo are receipts a judge can run: verify-native-webmcp.mjs proves a real WebMCP browser discovers and executes the tools on the deployed URL, and live-agent-check.mjs measures a full agent run against the real API. Challenges we ran into DuckDB-WASM versus WebMCP's headers. DuckDB's threaded coi bundle needs cross-origin isolation, which conflicted with how the page had to be served. It turned out selectBundle() only picks coi when the page is already cross-origin isolated — so by deliberately not setting COOP/COEP we get the eh bundle, which needs neither, alongside the Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 that WebMCP does require. Arrow's numbers are not numbers. DuckDB returns sum() over integers as DECIMAL(38,0) , which Arrow hands back as an object, and count() as a BigInt. Both had to be flattened before anything downstream could read them. An agent will happily spend its entire budget exploring. The first live run against GPT-5 used all ten tool rounds profiling columns and reached no conclusion. Raising the ceiling to thirty just moved the wall — it then made nine get_product calls, one product at a time, and still never proposed a fix. The fix was direction, not budget: tell the agent to group several dimensions in one query, to use list_low_stock instead of get_product per item, and to propose the fix as soon as the cause is established. The same investigation now finishes in 16 rounds with no failed calls. A race we only found in a screenshot. React StrictMode runs effects twice, and two concurrent bootstraps collided on the same DROP / CREATE . Bootstrap is now single-flight per engine, with a test that calls it three times at once. The native API is string-based. executeTool takes its arguments as a JSON string and returns the result envelope as one; passing a plain object fails with "Failed to parse input arguments" . inputSchema comes back as a string too. What we learned A good tool surface is mostly good error messages. Name a column that does not exist and the tool lists the ones that do. Give an ambiguous product name and it returns the candidates and asks for a product_id . Ask for a chart whose y column is missing from the query result and it names the columns the query actually returns. That did more for reliability than any prompt change — the agent recovers by itself instead of stalling. Context hygiene and privacy turned out to be the same mechanism. The 50-row / 4 KB cap started as a way to keep the agent's context small. It ended up being the thing that makes the privacy guarantee auditable. Accomplishments that we're proud of The approval gate, because it is a mechanism rather than a claim. And the byte counter, for the same reason: a figure a sceptical person can watch tick upward and check. What's next Multi-store tenancy; approval policies that let an operator pre-authorise low-risk actions while holding the rest; sharing a saved board as a link so another operator's copy re-runs it against their own data — the analysis travels, the data never does. title: Esbiko WebMCP Science Lab
pitch: Esbiko turns interactive science simulations into shared workspaces where people and AI agents configure, run, inspect, and compare real experiments through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Esbiko turns interactive science simulations into shared workspaces where people and AI agents configure, run, inspect, and compare real experiments through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Interactive science simulations are designed for people: learners move sliders, press buttons, watch animations, listen to sounds, and interpret measurements. For an AI agent, however, the same interface is ambiguous. It has to locate controls visually, infer their scientific meaning, approximate numerical values, determine whether an experiment actually ran, and scrape the result back from the page. I asked a different question: What if a human and an AI agent could operate the same scientific experiment together? Esbiko is an existing open-source science and mathematics learning platform with browser-based 2D and 3D simulations, classroom workflows, scientific visualisations, and media tools. For the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, I extended Esbiko with a semantic agent-facing layer that makes its Doppler Effect laboratory directly understandable and controllable through WebMCP. The goal is not to replace the learner or hide the experiment behind a chatbot. The human should still see, hear, inspect, and modify the experiment. WebMCP gives the agent a precise way to act on that same scientific environment. The result is a shared scientific workspace where human intent, agent actions, visible simulation state, physics calculations, audio, and recorded output all remain connected. What it does Esbiko WebMCP Science Lab turns a live Doppler Effect simulation into an agent-operable scientific instrument. The current implementation exposes 11 semantic WebMCP tools . Two site-level tools allow an agent to discover and open WebMCP-enabled science simulations: list_science_simulations open_science_simulation Nine Doppler tools allow the agent to read and control the experiment: get_doppler_state configure_doppler configure_doppler_scene set_doppler_playback reset_doppler create_doppler_video get_doppler_video_status stop_doppler_video download_doppler_video An agent can configure source motion, source speed, emitted frequency, observer state, direction, sound type, and multi-source scenes. It can also direct a complete scientific video. The final production demonstration creates a 30-second, 9:16 two-vehicle Doppler experiment at an emitted frequency of 440 Hz and a source speed of 60 m/s . A Real Car Engine travels from left to right. It approaches the stationary observer, passes at 7.5 seconds, and then recedes. An Ambulance Siren then approaches from the opposite direction, passes the observer at 22.5 seconds, and continues away. For a speed of sound of 343 m/s, Esbiko calculates approximately: 533.29 Hz while approaching and 374.49 Hz while receding. The pitch difference is clearly audible in the generated video. While the agent is recording, the user can also watch the same directed motion happening in the live browser. After recording, the agent can inspect structured recording status, confirm that real audio was captured, wait until the file is ready, and download the final WebM. How I built it Esbiko uses the WebMCP Imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The implementation is a progressive enhancement over the existing React application. Browsers without WebMCP continue to use Esbiko normally. Two persistent site-level tools provide discovery and navigation. Nine Doppler-specific tools are registered while the Doppler laboratory is active. A validated JSON-safe adapter connects WebMCP inputs to Esbiko's existing React state and scientific code. Semantic instructions such as approaching , receding , and explicit source directions are converted into validated physical parameters instead of arbitrary DOM interactions. Scientific results are never generated by an LLM. Esbiko's application code deterministically calculates values such as: Observed frequency Frequency ratio Percentage frequency shift Relative amplitude Sound level Motion classification The AI video workflow required an additional Doppler Director . The director creates an exact timeline from physical parameters using: distance = speed × time For the final 30-second story, each phase lasts 7.5 seconds and each vehicle travels 450 metres during each phase. The observer remains fixed at 500 metres. The recorder creates a deterministic 1080×1920 WebM and combines the rendered simulation with a real Web Audio track. Selected sound samples are preloaded before recording. Esbiko routes the Web Audio mix through an analyser and a MediaStreamDestination . Before accepting a recording, Esbiko checks that a measurable audio signal actually reaches the recording bus. A silent track is not treated as success. Most importantly, during AI-directed recording, the live browser motion, recorded motion, and Doppler audio are driven from the same deterministic director timeline . This keeps the audible pitch transition synchronized with the exact visual moment when each vehicle passes the observer. Challenges I ran into One of the hardest problems was not implementing the Doppler equation itself. It was keeping several real-time systems synchronized. Initially, the recorded video used a deterministic director clock while the sound was still driven by the ordinary browser simulation loop. Under the additional workload of rendering a 1080×1920 canvas and encoding WebM, browser frame timing could slow down. The vehicle in the video would reach the observer at the correct time, but the audio simulation could lag behind it. The Doppler shift was scientifically correct, but the audible pitch change did not always line up clearly with the visual crossing. I eventually removed that split-clock architecture. During AI recording, the audio source state is now derived directly from the same deterministic director timeline used by the live browser preview and recorded video. That made the higher-to-lower pitch transition clearly audible at the intended pass moments. Browser audio policy was another challenge. Modern browsers may prevent an AudioContext from starting without a human gesture. Esbiko preserves that browser security model and returns an explicit AUDIO_ACTIVATION_REQUIRED error when necessary. I also had to solve silent recording failures. Having an audio track attached to MediaRecorder does not guarantee that meaningful sound exists in it, so Esbiko performs a real analyser-based signal test before starting the recording. Finally, because Esbiko is an existing Progressive Web App, browser caching and Service Worker state had to be considered during production verification to ensure I was testing the current deployed revision. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I built an end-to-end WebMCP workflow inside a real existing educational application rather than creating an isolated WebMCP technical demo. The production system now demonstrates semantic discovery, navigation, scientific configuration, scene control, playback, physics-derived measurements, AI-directed recording, real audio verification, recording status, and downloadable scientific media. The final production test successfully demonstrated a 30-second two-vehicle scenario with a Real Car Engine and Ambulance Siren moving in opposite directions at 60 m/s. Both vehicles visibly move in the live browser while the recording is being created. The Real Car Engine passes the observer at approximately 7.5 seconds and the Ambulance passes from the opposite direction at approximately 22.5 seconds. In both cases, the transition from higher approaching pitch to lower receding pitch is clearly audible and synchronized with the visual observer crossing. Esbiko also supports a simpler 10-second single_pass mode where one continuous siren approaches for five seconds and recedes for five seconds, providing an especially clear A/B Doppler comparison. The implementation includes structured validation, bounded scientific inputs, explicit browser-audio errors, audio-signal verification, deterministic recording, shared human/agent state, and automated WebMCP contract and physics tests. The complete implementation, architecture, testing documentation, challenge evidence, deployment history, and MIT-licensed source code are public. What I learned I learned that the most useful WebMCP tools represent human intent , rather than mechanically exposing every UI control. A scientific user does not really want to say: "Move slider number three to pixel position 240." They want to say: "Show me a 440 Hz source approaching an observer at 60 metres per second." WebMCP provides a much better boundary for expressing that intent. I also learned that adding agent control makes the visible human interface more important, not less. The strongest workflow is not one where the AI operates invisibly in the background. It is one where the agent performs precise and repeatable operations while the learner can simultaneously see, hear, inspect, question,

title: Faultline
pitch: Design a cloud architecture with your AI agent on a shared canvas, then fail an availability zone or region and watch the blast radius spread. Price it, lint it, generate the Terraform, together
about_excerpt: Design a cloud architecture with your AI agent on a shared canvas, then fail an availability zone or region and watch the blast radius spread. Price it, lint it, generate the Terraform, together Like 1 Comment Story Updates Failing a zone: the agent runs the blast-radius analysis, nodes go red, resilience score drops to 61/100 with a DDIA-cited finding The agent swaps the database to Aurora and prices it: a before/after table showing +$49/month, beside the tool-call log "Explain the database node." The app panel and the agent both trace what depends on it and what fails if it dies The /learn route: all 13 WebMCP tools and their live schemas, as the agent sees them Per-resource monthly cost of a resilient three-tier stack, about $377 "Cheapest thing that runs." The agent reads the intent and lays down a single-AZ stack at $202/month Inspiration I work as a solutions architect. The job runs on a loop: sketch a topology, ask what breaks if an availability zone dies, argue the trade-off, write the Terraform, run a lint, repeat. A language model is good at that kind of reasoning, but only when it can work against the same diagram I'm looking at. An agent that takes screenshots and clicks can't read a canvas, and it can't run a blast-radius analysis over one. WebMCP fixes that. The page hands the agent the architecture graph and the analysis engine as typed tools, so it edits the same model I'm dragging around. What it does Faultline is an infinite canvas where you and your browser agent design cloud infrastructure together. You describe a system in a sentence and propose-architecture lays down a connected, configured, placed topology. The agent wires up dependencies, picks provider variants, explains any node or edge (its role, its blast radius, the principle behind it), and estimate-cost attaches a monthly-dollar figure to the design and to every change you make. Either of you can then run simulate-failure on one availability zone or a whole region, and the diagram turns red and amber as the outage spreads along the edges. Single points of failure get ringed. resilience-lint names the anti-patterns it finds and points each one at the chapter of Designing Data-Intensive Applications that explains why it matters. generate-iac writes the Terraform. Every tool also has a button in the UI, so the app works on its own; the agent is what makes the loop fast. How we built it A Rust compute core compiled to WASM. The graph model, the sentence-to-topology proposer, the blast-radius analysis for zone and region failures, the single-point-of-failure scan, the cost estimator, the resilience-lint rules, and the Terraform emitter all live in one pure library with #![forbid(unsafe_code)] , no async runtime, and about 90 tests. Both the UI and the WebMCP tools call into it, so they can't drift apart. A Svelte 5 and Vite shell. The canvas (pan, zoom, drag, orthogonal edges, status overlays) is hand-written SVG with no diagram library. 13 intent-level WebMCP tools in thin TypeScript against document.modelContext , one file each. They stay coarse rather than CRUD: propose-architecture turns a sentence into a topology, configure-resource sets variant, region, zone, and validation in a single call. Pure reads are marked readOnlyHint ; anything that echoes a label a human typed is marked untrustedContentHint . The /learn route lists every tool and its schema, live. Test-first, and the git history shows it. CI runs formatting, clippy, unit tests, headless-Chrome WASM tests, cargo-deny, Biome, the build, and a Playwright run of the full demo on every push. The site deploys statically to Cloudflare Pages under a strict CSP. Challenges we ran into In real Chrome, executeTool receives its input as a JSON string rather than an object, and the polyfill I developed against is more forgiving, so every tool's execute had to accept both. Keeping the tools intent-level took restraint: the quick version is set-node-property , the version worth having is configure-resource checking variant, region, and zone against a bundled provider profile before it commits. Everything crossing the WASM boundary is a string, so the Rust side has to keep its JSON readable by older documents as the schema grows. And because the agent never sees the rendered canvas, every visible cue (red nodes, failure rings, the outage banner) had to be computed from data the agent can read back just as easily. Accomplishments that we're proud of The resilience lint cites a specific book chapter for every finding rather than hand-waving, and the findings come from deterministic graph checks, so the agent can explain them instead of guessing. The failure simulator covers two failure domains, which lets it show you that a Multi-AZ database survives a zone outage but still goes down with its region. Because every tool runs through the same core the UI uses, the agent behaves like a design partner rather than a brittle UI script. Tool calls return in a few milliseconds. What we learned WebMCP works best when the page is a real domain model with an MCP interface on top, not a pile of buttons to press. Once the tools delegated to a tested core instead of carrying their own logic, the agent got noticeably more reliable. The Rust and WASM core turned out to be worth the setup cost: few other entries take that route, and the determinism it buys is what you want when an agent is going to read your results back to a user. What's next for Faultline GCP and Azure profiles over the same neutral core. The profile is already plain JSON, so another provider is a config file rather than a release. A staged accept-or-reject overlay so the agent's bigger edits preview before they land. Importing an existing Terraform state and linting that. Packaging Faultline as a standalone MCP server, so faultline check can run in CI and publish the resilience score as an artifact. I designed the concept and built all of it: the Rust/WASM compute core (graph model, blast-radius analysis, cost estimator, resilience lint, Terraform emitter), the Svelte canvas, all 13 WebMCP tools, the CI pipeline, and the Cloudflare deploy. title: FoodLoop
pitch: An agent-ready surplus-food rescue control room with explainable safety, role-scoped WebMCP, and human-approved handoffs.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready surplus-food rescue control room with explainable safety, role-scoped WebMCP, and human-approved handoffs. Like Comment Story Updates Completion view: four-stop route, 92 servings rescued, safety score, and verified handoff receipts. Proof view: the fresh-browser agent trace, role boundaries, and human dispatch checkpoint. Safety view: seven adversarial scenarios refused with evidence, safe alternatives, and no live-state mutation. FoodLoop FoodLoop is an agent-ready surplus-food rescue control room for moving good food before it expires. The problem Food rescue fails in the coordination gap. Donors know what is available, recipients know what they can safely use, and an operator must reconcile food category, dietary requirements, quantity, timing, vehicle capacity, pickup-before-delivery dependencies, and chain of custody. A generic chat box can suggest a match, but it should not silently dispatch a vehicle or claim a delivery happened. The solution FoodLoop gives browser agents a focused operations surface and gives the human operator one shared, inspectable control room. The agent can read current supply and community need, find compatible matches, reserve reviewable allocations, draft a dependency-safe route, independently audit timing and capacity, explain why a match won, model route delays, run sandboxed safety checks, request dispatch review, and stage delivery receipts. The operator must release the route and verify each final handoff. The guided Springfield simulation uses fictional data to demonstrate two compatible allocations, a four-stop route, 92 servings loaded, 100/100 safety, 22 minutes of minimum slack, a visible dispatch checkpoint, and two verified handoff receipts. Judge evidence The live app includes a dedicated proof surface: A 13-call fresh-browser walkthrough shows the Planner chain, independent Auditor checks, a forbidden Planner dispatch request, and a Dispatcher checkpoint. Seven adversarial safety cases refuse expired food, allergen mismatch, insufficient capacity, late delivery, duplicate handoff, malicious donor notes, and prompt-injected partner content. Each result shows refusal, evidence, a safe alternative, and sandbox-only state protection. Match counterfactuals show score components and the next-best safe alternative. Route counterfactuals show how a 15-minute departure delay changes deadline slack without mutating the plan. A role map makes capabilities explicit: Planner proposes, Auditor inspects, Dispatcher requests approval, Operator approves dispatch, and Recipient verifies the final handoff. The shared tool console, role trace, safety lab, decision queue, route map, impact ledger, and activity trail all reflect the same deterministic state. Published-data benchmark FoodLoop includes a reproducible adapter benchmark on the public FoodGo Test Dataset: 500 published food-rescue orders and 50 volunteer records from the U.S. Department of Transportation / Mobility21 at Carnegie Mellon University. Against a FIFO first-feasible baseline, the deadline-and-distance-aware adapter accepts 94 orders versus 91, reduces modeled route distance from 2,806.98 km to 2,277.92 km, and improves minimum modeled deadline slack from 4.0 to 40.1 minutes. It rejects 23,052 unsafe candidate plans before assignment. The coordination-time number is explicitly a scenario proxy, not a human study; the assumptions, source attribution, and reproduction command are in the public repository's benchmarks directory. Why WebMCP This is structured, stateful work shared between a person and an agent. Agents are good at scanning constraints and assembling a plan; operators are accountable for consequential actions and ambiguous real-world context. WebMCP makes that division legible in the product instead of hiding it behind an opaque assistant. app.js registers thirteen focused tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The portable contracts are separated into tool-contracts.js, with bounded JSON Schemas, compact outputs, readOnlyHint on read operations, and untrustedContentHint for partner-entered content. The consequential path is: observe → propose allocation → draft route → audit route → request review → HUMAN APPROVES DISPATCH → stage receipt → HUMAN VERIFIES HANDOFF The agent never impersonates either human approval. How we used AI FoodLoop itself is deterministic and self-contained for the competition. It does not call a hidden model, require an API key, or fabricate a logistics integration. OpenAI Codex/GPT-5 supported implementation, test design, browser replay, and product iteration. The refreshed demo narration uses the creator's private VoiceBank recordings; raw recordings remain private and are excluded from the repository. Testing The repository includes deterministic tests for matching, reservations, routing, audits, adversarial safety, counterfactual reasoning, role capabilities, approval boundaries, handoff validation, metrics, WebMCP contract annotations, and the external-data benchmark. npm test passes 25 tests. npm run verify passes the 13 tool contracts, JavaScript syntax checks, required judge artifacts, the benchmark result, and the compact orientation-response budget. The public GitHub Pages build, the refreshed 2:42 video, and the public video page were independently checked. Links Live app: https://moscraciunxxx.github.io/foodloop-webmcp/ Open-source repository: https://github.com/moscraciunxxx/foodloop-webmcp/ Judge walkthrough: https://github.com/moscraciunxxx/foodloop-webmcp/blob/main/docs/JUDGE_WALKTHROUGH.md Benchmark source record: https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/56260 Demo video: https://youtu.be/07p1pvKEuHI The prototype is self-contained and uses fictional Springfield simulation data for the product demo. It does not send messages, move food, call a fulfillment service, or require API keys. Production integrations would add identity, authorization, durable storage, observability, consent, and partner-specific retention controls while preserving both human approval gates. title: freenet.free
pitch: Turn your idea into simulation of actual network, watch requests flow and get billed, and let your agent build it with you through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Turn your idea into simulation of actual network, watch requests flow and get billed, and let your agent build it with you through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "can I build this for free?" conversation ends the same way: six pricing tabs open, a guess at request counts, and the real answer arriving on the first invoice. Teams draw architectures on whiteboards, then find out which box breaks the budget only after the code is written. We wanted the drawing itself to be the simulator. Lay out the network, watch honest traffic flow through it, and see which layer hits a quota and what the platform does about it, before a line of code exists. Then WebMCP made the second half obvious: if the studio exposes its actions as tools, the agent in your browser can ideate on the same canvas, under the same rules, and show its work. What it does freenet.free is a studio for choosing and validating a stack before you write code. Visualise the network. Products from Cloudflare and Vercel (and third-party services from OpenAI, Shopify and Netlify) sit as nodes on a canvas. Edges carry real request flow, coloured from source to target so you can read the topology at a glance. Simulate honest traffic. A daily mix of humans, search crawlers, AI crawlers, scrapers and botnets runs through the graph. Gates block, caches answer, stores meter reads and writes, compute meters CPU. Arrivals always equal served plus blocked plus dropped. See the free tier break. Quotas are enforced the way the platforms enforce them: past the cap, requests drop or the feature stops. The timeline plays a day, a month or a year with one track per layer as a percent of its allowance, so you see which meter breaks and on which day. Compare stacks. One key switches the same design between Cloudflare and Vercel. Names, prices and partner gaps update; the bill is computed from each provider's own pricing page, with a source URL on every meter. Ideate with an agent. 33 WebMCP tools cover everything a person can do: read and rewrite the design, set traffic, toggle protections, drive the timeline, read the bill and layers, analyse a product URL, propose an architecture, export config, save and remix designs. Chrome's agent and the in-page architect use the same tools, and every call lands in the conversation so you can watch the design take shape. The result is a plan you can trust: a diagram, a traffic model, a bill and a verdict, all from the same source of truth, before you commit to a stack. How we built it TanStack Start on Cloudflare Workers , with a Durable Object agent built on the Cloudflare Agents SDK, the AI SDK and Workers AI (gpt-oss-120b) as the in-page architect. One tool contract, three surfaces. Tools are defined once with zod. The derived JSON Schema is registered from an inline script in <head> so document.modelContext.getTools() is never empty, server-rendered as declarative <form toolname> elements for agents that only read markup, and registered imperatively after hydration for full coverage. The architect calls the same tools through executeTool , so WebMCP is the single execution path for both agents. A request-accounting simulator with linear per-class rates, node roles (source, gate, cache, compute, store, sink), a two-pass free-tier cap, and conservation tests. Pricing as data : 70 meters across Cloudflare and Vercel plus vendor meters for OpenAI, Shopify and Netlify, each with unit, allowance, overage behaviour and source URL. computeBill never invents a number. Challenges we ran into Tool discoverability before hydration. A browser agent listed tools while React was still loading and saw an empty bridge. Registering the surface from the server-rendered head, then handing execution to the app, closed the gap. Chrome's result envelope. executeTool returns a JSON string wrapping content[].text ; the architect had to unwrap it so both agents see identical results. Background tabs. Agents often drive a tab you are not looking at, where animation frames never fire. The clock, focus, and timeline all had to work without them. Honest pricing across five vendors. Per-day versus per-month quotas, 1k versus 1M units, credits versus dollars, and Marketplace partners had to be normalised without hiding the gaps. Accomplishments that we're proud of A design tool where the diagram, the simulation, the timeline and the bill are one model, so ideation and validation happen in the same place. A free-tier verdict that is concrete: the meter, the day it breaks, and what the platform does next. One tool contract serving Chrome's agent and our own architect, with a complete audit trail in the chat. Real products, real prices, real gaps: 40 Cloudflare meters, 30 Vercel meters, and 20 third-party services, every one sourced. What we learned Agents are very good at using a well-described tool surface and very bad at guessing a UI. Investing in describe_studio , precise tool descriptions and a few named workflows did more than any prompt. We also learned that "honest" is a feature: showing partner gaps and unverified prices made the tool more convincing, not less. What's next for freenet.free Partner pricing for Marketplace products such as Neon and Upstash. Shareable public designs with a read-only WebMCP surface, so an agent can review a plan without editing it. Export to infrastructure as code, so the validated plan becomes the first commit. A declarative-only mode that lets agents drive the studio with JavaScript disabled. title: Adaptive Web Experience
pitch: Instead of weeding through massive plant catalogs, just describe what your landscape goals are and have agent set all the ideal properties for what you should consider. Then the user can just browse.
about_excerpt: Instead of weeding through massive plant catalogs, just describe what your landscape goals are and have agent set all the ideal properties for what you should consider. Then the user can just browse. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Southern Horticulture is a garden center in St. Augustine, Florida, half a mile from salt spray. The staff spend most of the day answering one question in different clothes: "will this plant live in my yard?" The honest answer depends on light, salt exposure, irrigation, whether a deer eats the leaves, and how much the person actually wants to water. A website cannot ask all of that, so every plant catalog on the internet shows the same grid to everyone and lets the shopper guess. Agents changed what is possible. A shopper will happily tell an assistant about the dog and the sprinkler that broke last year, because it is a conversation rather than a form with nineteen fields. WebMCP was the missing half: a way for that conversation to reach into the page the shopper is looking at, instead of ending in a wall of text. What it does The Living Garden Center is a plant catalog that rebuilds itself around one specific yard or purpose. You tell your agent what the space is really like. It calls describe_garden, and the page next to you recomposes: a verified pet friendly section rises to the top because a dog shares the yard, salt-tolerant privacy plants group together, and other plants with no verified toxicity record move into a section that says plainly that a missing record is not evidence of safety. Every plant carries a verdict from a deterministic evaluator, from excellent down to insufficient data, and every verdict is explained. Tap a plant and you get why it landed there: the strengths, the compromises, and the care routine it actually asks for, on dials rather than in adjectives. Some plants get an honest no, with a "what would need to change" answer that names the single facet that would flip the verdict. The agent and the shopper share one live page and one context. Say the salt is worse than you first thought, and the sections reshuffle in front of you. Ask why bougainvillea is a compromise, and the agent answers from the same evaluation the page is showing. Add plants to a saved list, then take a link with you. The catalog never invents stock. Availability language comes from one recorded statement, and the tools say when we have no record rather than guessing. How we built it The core is a pure, deterministic evaluator. A GardenContext carries site conditions, household, and preferences, along with an assumption ledger that marks every value as known, derived, assumed, or unknown. Evaluating a plant against that context produces a fit with strengths, compromises, blockers, and unknowns. A rule table composes sections from those fits, and a page manifest renders through a fixed component registry. No language model writes copy at runtime, which is why the page recomposes instantly and says the same thing twice. WebMCP sits on top as a thin layer. Registration checks for the API and registers every tool once at load: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "describe_garden", description: "Interpret the shopper's words into structured garden conditions", inputSchema: { /* ... / }, execute: async (input) => { / ... */ } }); Eighteen tools in the public app, eleven read and seven write, each with explicit safety annotations so the browser can show which ones make changes and which three are destructive. Writes go through the same validation the human form uses. Context updates take a revision number and fail loudly on conflict, so the agent and the shopper cannot silently overwrite each other. Two details made it robust. The tools return a share URL that encodes the yard, so an agent working in a browser you cannot see can hand you a link that opens the same personalized page anywhere. And an agent activity panel logs every tool call beside the page, so a human can see exactly what the agent did and undo it. The app is Next.js 16 on Vercel. The repo ships a 60-plant sample catalog and reads a fuller catalog from an environment variable, so the demo is complete without publishing our whole inventory. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not the code. It was discovering where site tools actually run. Our first test failed because ChatGPT used its remote agent browser, so the tools executed in a browser we could not see and the visible tab never changed. Then Chrome reported no tools at all, which turned out to be the WebMCP flag being off. Then a regular ChatGPT chat said it could use the page and could not. Site tools live in the desktop app's built in browser under only a Local ChatGPT Work session, on GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra. Nothing on our page could fix any of that, so we made the page say it: a status chip that reads either "Site tools ready: 18 tools this agent can call" or a one line explanation of what to change. Chrome 151 has no way to unregister a tool, and registering a duplicate name is rejected. So tools register exactly once and read live state at execute time rather than closing over it. The subtler challenge was honesty. It is easy to build a recommender that sounds confident. We had to write an explicit contract: an unknown never becomes a negative, a missing toxicity record is never reported as safe, and no tool ever states a live stock count. That constraint produced the most distinctive part of the product. Accomplishments that we're proud of The page genuinely rebuilds itself around a conversation, and it does so from a deterministic evaluator rather than a generated layout, so it is fast, repeatable, and auditable. The honest no. Most catalogs cannot afford to say "we would skip this one for your yard." Ours does, with the reason and the condition that would change it. A garden center that tells you not to buy something is the one you come back to. The evidence gap. We surface the count of plants with no verified pet safety record and keep them visibly uncertain instead of quietly filtering them out or, worse, implying they are fine. Reaching parity between the human and the agent. Same page, same context object, same validation, revision checked so neither one clobbers the other, and a visible log of what the agent touched. And it works. In the ChatGPT desktop app under a local Work session, the arrow turns blue and the catalog reorganizes while you watch. What we learned Tools should carry judgment, not just data. A search_plants that returns rows makes the agent guess. A tool that returns a verdict plus the reasons behind it lets the agent explain, and the explanation matches what the human sees on screen. Annotations matter more than they look. Before we marked the write tools explicitly, the browser listed sixteen read and zero write tools, and a client has no good way to reason about a tool it cannot classify. Shared state needs concurrency control. Two actors editing one context is a distributed systems problem in miniature, and revision checking with an explicit conflict result solved it in about thirty lines. The failure mode nobody warns you about is invisibility. A page that offers tools looks identical to a page that does not when the browser lacks the API. Telling the user which one they are looking at was one of the highest value changes we made all day. What's next for Garden Center Web-MCP Real availability. We have a specification for inventory evidence flowing from the point of sale into a per variation availability state, which would let the agent answer "ten Podocarpus in seven gallon and two fifteen gallon Ligustrum, can you hold them" with a number instead of a hedge. The honesty contract already routes every availability sentence through one function, so this lands without touching a single tool. Filling the unknowns. Style and garden use tags are sparse, which is why some plants report facets we have not recorded. Backfilling them makes the fit explanations richer. Carrying the plan further. The share link already encodes the yard and the saved list. The next step is bringing it into the store on a phone, so staff see the same evaluation the agent produced and can walk someone to the right row. And the part we are most curious about: this pattern is not about plants. Any catalog where fit depends on the buyer's circumstances, and where the honest answer is sometimes no, can be built this way. title: Grapevine Care
pitch: WebMCP helps care coordinators investigate uncertainty, recover disrupted coverage, and preserve accountable context across an entire caregiver shift.
about_excerpt: WebMCP helps care coordinators investigate uncertainty, recover disrupted coverage, and preserve accountable context across an entire caregiver shift. Like Comment Story Updates Coverage Dashboard 5 Coverage Dashboard 4 Coverage Dashboard 1 Coverage Dashboard 3 Coverage Dashboard 2 Inspiration Care does not happen in one shift. A coordinator must reconcile schedules, caregiver readiness, resident-specific context, missing verification, visit records, and handoffs—often while plans change. Conventional dashboards scatter that context across screens and leave people to reconstruct what is known, what is still unknown, and who must decide next. We built Grapevine Care to explore how WebMCP can give an agent structured access to the same evolving, page-scoped state as a human coordinator without taking authority away from residents, caregivers, or clinical professionals. What it does Grapevine Care is a fictional, safety-first caregiver-continuity simulation. Its primary experience is one compressed Care Team Day across three residents: At 9:15 AM, Evelyn's visit lacks a verification record. The agent prepares a bounded inquiry; Luis answers in his own voice; the coordinator records the disposition. At 11:30 AM, Elena is available for Walter but lacks resident-specific readiness. The agent prepares an orientation packet and follow-up; Elena reports completion; the coordinator verifies it. At 2:15 PM, Maya calls out for Rose. The server evaluates four caregivers against eight named constraints, and the agent explains why only Jordan is eligible before a scheduler approves. At 5:00 PM and 7:35 PM, the coordinator requests and verifies Jordan's readiness and visit record instead of impersonating her. At 8:00 PM, Jordan approves the prepared handoff, Luis confirms receipt, and the coordinator verifies both sides. Time is the spine of the experience. The clock cannot advance until the current decision is resolved, escalated, deferred with a reason, or waiting on an identified person. Advancing time never reveals the answer to an open question. Why WebMCP WebMCP makes this workflow meaningfully better because an agent can traverse resident context, schedule constraints, readiness evidence, and handoff state through structured tools rather than scraping the interface or guessing through UI controls. People and agents work together through one visible state machine: observe → investigate → prepare → human decision → document → advance The agent does the connective work—finding context, comparing evidence, evaluating constraints, and preparing the next bounded action. People provide self-reports and retain authority over assignments, verification, and consequential decisions. How we built it The application exposes twenty purpose-built WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Only the subset valid for the current workflow state is registered. Read tools expose structured context, knowns, unknowns, provenance, versioned snapshots, and deterministic constraint results. Preparation tools stage bounded inquiries, orientation, coverage, or handoff records; they do not contact a person or change an assignment without a visible human decision. The server—not the model—enforces time gates, caregiver eligibility, snapshot freshness, idempotency, and legal workflow transitions. The agent cannot diagnose, make clinical or emergency determinations, change care plans, assign staff, answer for a caregiver or resident, or release medication. The stack includes React 19, TypeScript, Vite, a Cloudflare Worker API, D1 persistence, Zod runtime validation, generated JSON Schema inputs, OpenAI Sites packaging, and Vitest. Challenges The hardest problem was not maximizing what an agent could do; it was designing precisely where automation should stop. We separated preparation from execution, kept resident and caregiver responses on human-only surfaces, made unknowns explicit, and bound consequential proposals to fresh evidence and schedule snapshots. We also hardened the app for different WebMCP browser implementations, including implementations where registerTool returns synchronously rather than as a Promise. Accomplishments One coherent six-block Care Team Day across Rose, Walter, and Evelyn. Twenty state-dependent WebMCP tools with bounded schemas and explicit authority limits. Deterministic eight-constraint caregiver eligibility with no opaque suitability score. Versioned evidence and schedule snapshots with stale-state rejection. Idempotent preparation and conditional state transitions. Per-browser isolated demo runs and deterministic reset. Coordinator-led readiness, visit-record, and two-sided handoff loops. Responsive, keyboard-focusable, reduced-motion-aware interface. Thirty-one automated tests covering server invariants, WebMCP registration, safety boundaries, state transitions, and browser compatibility. What we learned Building for WebMCP shifted our thinking from exposing interface controls to exposing accountable jobs. A useful agent tool needs more than structured input: it needs provenance, explicit unknowns, freshness guarantees, idempotency, and a clear statement of who still owns the decision. We also learned that human-in-the-loop design is strongest when authority boundaries are enforced by the product and server state—not merely requested in a prompt. Project origin Grapevine Care was created during the submission period as a distinct healthcare adaptation of the MIT-licensed Project Grapevine foundation. The public repository contains a detailed origin record and timestamped commit history distinguishing the retained foundation from the healthcare-specific domain model, workflows, tools, interface, and judge scenario. Testing Open the live application in the latest ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser with Site Tools enabled. Reset Care Team Day and confirm that the opening block reads 9:15 AM · Morning verification . Ask: I am taking over the care coordinator desk. Tell me what needs attention now, investigate what is unknown, and prepare the next safe step for my review. Continue through Evelyn's inquiry, Walter's readiness loop, Rose's coverage recovery, Jordan's visit evidence, and the two-sided handoff. The clock remains blocked at every unresolved decision. Safety note This is a deterministic competition simulation, not production healthcare software. It has no protected health information, real messaging, electronic health record, pharmacy, workforce, medical-device, or emergency-service integration. All residents, caregivers, responses, and events are fictional. I designed the multi-resident Care Team Day, evidence and approval workflows, dynamic WebMCP tool contract, safety boundaries, and caregiver-facing interface. I also built and tested the React/TypeScript/Cloudflare application, deployed the live demo, and prepared the documentation, judge walkthrough, and submission video. title: Ground
pitch: Ground is a shared Markdown editor for people and agents. The owner decides who can edit, who can only propose, and who gets no access. The server applies those rules to every WebMCP action.
about_excerpt: Ground is a shared Markdown editor for people and agents. The owner decides who can edit, who can only propose, and who gets no access. The server applies those rules to every WebMCP action. Like Comment Story Updates 1. One shared Markdown document with Owner, Editor, and Reviewer sessions connected. 2. Pending participants cannot see document content until the Owner assigns a Role. 3. The Owner can assign, update, or revoke Roles from one access panel. 4. The Roles view shows which capabilities are allowed for each Role. 7. After one same-location Proposal is applied, the two remaining alternatives become explicit Conflicts. 9. Owner-only Activity shows the actor, Role, action, time, source, outcome, and target. Inspiration I once built an AI TTS editor at a company where I worked. That experience raised a question: Can people and AI work together inside the same editor? If so, what matters, and what needs to change? WebMCP lets a web page expose tools that an AI agent can use. That makes it possible for the agent to work inside an editor. But tools alone are not enough. The system also needs rules for who can read, propose changes, edit, and manage access. Without those boundaries, people and AI can simply write whatever they want, and the result is worthless slop. The real challenge is not putting AI inside an editor. It is designing a structure in which people and agents can work on the same document with different roles and responsibilities. That's why I built Ground. What it does Without structured tools like WebMCP, a browser agent has to infer meaning from buttons and input fields. This approach is especially likely to produce incorrect actions in complex web applications such as editors. Ground instead exposes explicit WebMCP tools for reading a document, replacing exact text, and proposing changes . For each page session, Ground registers only the tools allowed by the current participant's Role. Ground is a real-time collaborative editor for Markdown documents. The session that creates a document becomes its Owner . Anyone joining through the shared link remains Pending until the Owner assigns a Role. Create a document at / The session that creates the document becomes the Owner and receives an Owner recovery link Share the document using the Share button A new participant enters a display name and remains Pending The Owner assigns the Editor or Reviewer Role An Editor can edit directly, while a Reviewer creates Proposals The Owner reviews Proposals and resolves Conflicts After access is revoked, the participant can no longer access the document or WebMCP tools Owners and Editors can read documents, propose changes, and apply them through WebMCP. Reviewers can read documents and propose changes, but cannot edit directly. Pending and Revoked participants see only a status screen, and no document tools are exposed to them. Changes proposed by Reviewers enter the review list as Proposals based on the exact original text. The Owner can keep the current wording or apply the proposed wording. If a Proposal's target text has changed or can no longer be located at review time, it is marked as a Conflict . This keeps AI-assisted editing explicit and reviewable. Each Activity entry shows who acted, their Role at execution time, what they did, when it happened, the source, the target, and the outcome. How Ground was built Ground builds on CollabMD , an MIT-licensed open-source project. The following table shows the parts reused from the existing CollabMD and the parts extended by Ground for this challenge. Existing CollabMD and Ground additions Reused from CollabMD Added in Ground CodeMirror editor, Yjs synchronization, presence and cursors, Undo/Redo Owner/Editor/Reviewer Roles, Pending/Revoked Access states, Proposals/Conflicts, and Activity Text-based revision guard, reading the active document via WebMCP, and replacing text Role-based Tool discovery and execution-time server authorization - Document-specific URLs, Share, Owner recovery, Supabase persistence, Vercel deployment Features implemented in Ground Ground registers three WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : collabmd_read_active_document collabmd_apply_text_edits collabmd_propose_text_edit Another interesting Ground feature is that Roles can be defined declaratively in a file to suit different needs. { "roles": { "owner": [ "document.read", "document.suggest", "document.edit", "conflict.resolve", "grant.manage" ], "editor": [ "document.read", "document.suggest", "document.edit" ], "reviewer": [ "document.read", "document.suggest" ] } } When the Ground server starts, it reads and validates the project's collabmd.governance.json file, then passes the resulting Roles to the client. Non-Owner Roles can be added or changed by combining the five permission units (Capabilities) , while the Owner must have all five. Adding a new Capability requires corresponding code changes; the MVP uses only these five. The client uses these definitions to render the Roles and Manage Access screens and to expose the WebMCP tools currently allowed for the participant. Immediately before each WebMCP tool runs, the server checks the current Access state, Role, and Capability based on the user ID verified through the Supabase anonymous session. Markdown text, Proposal records, and Activity are stored as separate shared data within a single Y.Doc, while Conflict is represented as a Proposal state. The UndoManager tracks content-edit history. Proposal approval or rejection, Conflict resolution, Role changes, and Activity records are governance decisions and therefore remain outside document Undo/Redo. Challenges The first challenge was permission revocation . An agent may retain a reference to a WebMCP tool discovered before its Role changes. Removing the tool from later discovery results does not invalidate that existing reference, so authorization is checked again immediately before every execution. If the current Role no longer permits the tool, the call is rejected . The second challenge was stale Proposals . Just because Yjs can make concurrent document edits converge does not mean that an earlier Proposal can still be applied safely. If the exact target of a Proposal has changed, Ground treats it as a Conflict and asks the Owner to make a decision. Undo/Redo required another boundary. Both are forms of document edits. Role assignment, Proposal approval or rejection, and Conflict resolution are not text editing commands but governance decisions. Therefore, I kept them outside the editor's edit history. What I'm Most Proud Of I didn't just create a simple permissions panel. Within a single editor, Ground provides Role configuration, participant Access management, WebMCP tools based on Role scope, server-side authorization, a Proposal workflow, deterministic Conflict handling, and visible collaboration history . What I'm most proud of is that an Access change actually affects how the product behaves. When an Editor's access is revoked, that participant returns to a status-only screen. The editor and document tools disappear, and even if the participant attempts to use an editing tool discovered before revocation, the server denies the request. I am also proud of how I used the Role manifest to declaratively define Access control and the Roles shown in the interface. There is no longer a need to hardcode separate Roles in the client to add or modify Non-Owner Roles, and management has become easier as well. Lessons Learned Tool discovery and authorization have different lifecycles. Discovery determines what an agent should see at a given moment. Authorization determines whether a specific call is still permitted at the moment it is executed. For permission revocation to work as expected, this second determination must occur when the tool is executed. Convergence and consensus are also different problems. Even if Yjs synchronizes all participants to the same document state, the Proposal target may change and become invalid. Conflict preserves the intent of the change and allows it to be handled later. What's Next for Ground Ground's next step is to separate the Role and Capability configuration and the execution-time authorization layer into a reusable SDK so that it can be easily integrated into other WebMCP-based editors. I also aim to preserve the account-less sharing flow while moving toward a structure that can selectively support invitations, team-level document management, and application-specific Capabilities when needed.
