title: GWEN Zero-Credential Agent Authority
pitch: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials.
about_excerpt: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials. Like Comment Story Updates 01-GWEN-Devpost-Hero-WebMCP-Connected 02-GWEN-Zero-Credential-Browser-Verification 03-GWEN-One-Time-Email-Verification 04-GWEN-Agent-Requests-Address-Authority 05-GWEN-Human-Authorization-Grant 06-GWEN-Approved-Single-Use-Commit 07-GWEN-Authority-Consumed-Audit-Receipt 08-GWEN-Qwen-Returning-User-Email Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of doing much more than answering questions. They can interact with websites, update accounts, send messages, schedule appointments, change records, and perform other real actions for people. That created a question I kept coming back to: Why should an AI need my credentials just because I want it to perform one specific action? If I ask an agent to change a delivery address, I may want it to have permission to perform exactly that change. I do not necessarily want to give it my password, a reusable API key, an OAuth token, a broad authenticated browser session, or some other credential that authorizes much more than the task I requested. GWEN started from the idea that human authentication and agent authority should be separate things . The human should authenticate as the human. The AI should receive only the smallest amount of authority necessary for the action the human actually approved. That became the central model behind GWEN: Humans authenticate. Agents receive temporary authority. And the principle behind the project: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials. WebMCP was a natural fit for this idea because it allows a website to expose structured capabilities directly to an AI agent while the application still controls exactly what those capabilities mean and when they may be used. Instead of treating an AI as another fully logged-in user, GWEN treats the AI as an agent requesting narrowly scoped authority from a human-controlled security boundary. The delivery-address change in the demo is intentionally simple. The important part is not the address. The important part is the authority model behind it. What it does GWEN is a working WebMCP security prototype that separates human authentication from agent authority . A visitor begins by using their own email address to verify control of a browser session through a temporary, one-time sign-in link. The AI never receives that sign-in link, the browser session cookie, the Gmail App Password, or the visitor's credentials. Authentication establishes that there is a verified email-controlled human session. It does not automatically authorize an AI agent to make changes. Once the browser is verified, GWEN exposes structured WebMCP capabilities. The first capability is get_gwen_capabilities . This allows an agent to discover what GWEN supports and understand the authority model without receiving human credentials. The second capability is request_address_change_authority . This allows an agent to request permission for one exact delivery-address change and provide a reason for the request. Nothing changes when the request is made. Instead, GWEN displays the exact proposed value to the human in a visible authorization panel. The human can explicitly choose Authorize GWEN or Deny . Only after the human approves the exact request does GWEN dynamically expose another WebMCP capability: commit_approved_address_change This temporary commit capability does not accept another address. The value approved by the human has already been bound on the server. For example, if the human approves: 42 WebMCP Street the AI cannot substitute: 99 Something Else Street during final execution. There is no replacement-address parameter in the final commit tool. The agent receives authority to execute the exact action the human approved . The resulting GWEN Grant is: bound to the verified human session bound to one specific action bound to the exact approved value short-lived limited to one authorized use consumed after successful execution The current WebMCP grant has a maximum lifetime of 120 seconds. After successful execution, GWEN shows: 1 of 1 consumed and: Authority remaining: NONE The temporary authority disappears. GWEN then creates a persistent, human-bound audit receipt containing the action, previous value, approved new value, grant information, number of uses, remaining authority state, timestamp, and an internal identity hash associated with the verified session. The design principle is: Temporary authority should disappear. Evidence of what happened should remain. GWEN also includes Qwen , a local AI email conversation assistant running through Ollama. Qwen's conversation authority is deliberately separate from WebMCP action authority. A verified visitor can have a normal email conversation with Qwen without giving Qwen the human's Gmail password, magic-link token, or GWEN browser-session credential. The Qwen email capability has a hard 10-minute lifetime. Replies do not extend the original deadline. Per-message capabilities are single-use. Attachments are blocked. Oversized messages are rejected. URLs are not automatically fetched. Automated reply loops are guarded against, and restarting the Qwen worker revokes outstanding Qwen email capabilities. The visible email address remains normal. The short-lived capability is carried through email reply-chain metadata instead of forcing the user to communicate through a strange tokenized email address. GWEN can also maintain compact encrypted continuity for returning verified users without keeping their old authorization alive. That created another important design rule: Memory is not authority. How we built it GWEN's primary security and authority implementation is written in Rust using Axum . I built GWEN as a solo developer and deliberately kept the architecture small enough that I could trace the complete authority path myself. A simple rule emerged while I was building it: Browser shows state. Rust decides state. Redis authorizes state. SQLite records state. Rust and Axum Rust is the main policy and application layer. It handles: email-based browser verification temporary browser sessions server-side authorization WebMCP grant creation human approval exact-value binding one-use execution persistent audit receipt creation Qwen worker supervision application lifecycle and policy enforcement The security-critical authorization decisions are made on the server. Browser JavaScript presents the state and exposes WebMCP tools, but it is not trusted to decide whether an action is actually authorized. WebMCP GWEN registers structured WebMCP tools through the browser's model-context interface using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The initial capabilities are available for agent discovery. The final commit capability only appears after the human has approved the exact requested action. This means the available WebMCP tool surface itself reflects the current authorization state. Before approval, the agent has no commit authority. After approval, the temporary commit capability appears. After successful execution, the capability disappears. The final commit tool intentionally accepts no replacement address because the human-approved value is already bound on the server. Redis GWEN uses a dedicated Redis instance at: 127.0.0.1:6387 Redis stores temporary state including: one-time login capabilities browser sessions WebMCP grants remaining authorized uses temporary Qwen email capabilities worker ownership and lease state The host also has other software using Redis on port 6379 . GWEN deliberately does not use or modify that Redis instance. Redis is a good fit for GWEN because authorization should be temporary, expiring, and capable of being consumed atomically. SQLite SQLite stores information that should persist after temporary authority disappears. That includes: WebMCP audit receipts Qwen client accounting returning-user metadata encrypted compact Qwen continuity This creates a deliberate separation: Temporary authority belongs in Redis. Persistent records belong in SQLite. Human verification GWEN uses temporary one-time email verification. The sign-in link is short-lived and single-use. The resulting browser session also has a hard 10-minute lifetime. GWEN verifies control of the email-based session used by the demonstration. It does not claim to prove a person's legal identity. The correct description is therefore email-controlled session verified , rather than claiming biometric, legal, government, or cryptographic proof of personal identity. Qwen and Ollama Qwen runs locally through Ollama using qwen3-coder:30b . Qwen is the conversation assistant. Qwen is not the source of WebMCP authorization. The Qwen worker receives trusted GWEN project grounding separately from untrusted incoming email content. That means an incoming email cannot redefine GWEN's trusted security architecture simply by containing instructions that claim to change the system's rules. Qwen can also use encrypted compact continuity for returning

title: HenryKnows Special Agent
pitch: F-1 visa International students use their personal AI agent's to coordinate with a powerful tools for navigating fast changing visa rules, then produce practical guides to facilitate human advisement
about_excerpt: F-1 visa International students use their personal AI agent's to coordinate with a powerful tools for navigating fast changing visa rules, then produce practical guides to facilitate human advisement Like Comment Story Updates App with clickable WebMCP Problem International students must make decisions about study, employment, travel, and immigration compliance while complex rules around them are changing weekly. They also do a LOT of filling out forms and submitting their information to get things done. A personal AI assistant may know the student's goals and prior plans, but off-the-shelf AI does not have HenryKnows' specialized F-1 reference system or a deterministic implementation of brand new duration-of-status rules. HenryKnows has that regulatory capability, but starts each visit needing to essentially do an intake This can mean just another place already beleaguered students are having to reexplain themselves. Or they skip it altogether and arrive at advising appointments without a clear account of what matters or which questions remain unresolved -- and then having to reexplain themselves anyway. Solution HenryKnows now exposes a bounded set of WebMCP tools to an external browser agent. With the student's permission, the agent can propose relevant facts already present in their memory, ask only for consequential gaps or corrections, consult HenryKnows repeatedly throughout, and run the specialized Duration of Status Mapper once the calculation inputs are settled. The student confirms the situation before case-specific calculations. Deterministic code, not the language model, calculates the new-rule classification, dates, and timeline. The agent evaluates HenryKnows' student and professional answers against that evidence and authors two coordinated documents: a plain-language student preparation brief and a concise, source-linked DSO brief. Both can be downloaded as polished PDFs. Why This Matters The collaboration gives each participant the job it is suited for: The student owns the facts, choices, and final sharing decision. The personal agent contributes context, conducts the conversation, and handles the procedural work. HenryKnows supplies broad F-1 analysis grounded in primary authority. The mapper performs its narrower deterministic job: showing how the September 15, 2026 duration-of-status rules affect the confirmed timeline. The DSO receives a short case-specific briefing, not routine professional instruction or an AI demand for a decision. This is especially valuable where the sources do not resolve a new transition issue. The workflow preserves uncertainty, explains its practical significance, and directs human attention to the question that actually needs professional review. Why WebMCP This experience depends on capabilities that neither side has alone. A conventional website cannot access the context a student has already shared with their chosen agent. A personal agent cannot reliably reconstruct HenryKnows' curated regulatory retrieval or the mapper's deterministic rules. WebMCP allows the agent and student to work with the same live page and confirmed case while the website keeps specialized calculations, sources, validation, and visible state under its control. The agent can consult HenryKnows repeatedly, refine the student’s confirmed case, determine whether the new-rules timeline applies, compare one or two plans, and save both final briefs together. If an important fact changes, earlier results are marked outdated rather than reused. How We Used AI The external agent acts as an expeditor. It interprets the student's goal, reuses relevant conversational context with permission, asks focused follow-ups, decides when another HenryKnows consultation would resolve ambiguity, translates technical findings into practical choices, and writes the two audience-specific briefs. HenryKnows uses a model-backed answer engine over a curated index of primary F-1 sources. The model does not calculate legal deadlines or decide which duration-of-status branch applies. Those results come from the tested deterministic mapper and are supplied to the agent and HenryKnows as inspectable evidence. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the initial idea into the implemented WebMCP workflow: inspecting the existing HenryKnows and mapper codebases, defining the shared case and tool contracts, implementing the native site tools, connecting the existing answer and calculation systems, and building the retained two-audience document surface. The UX was developed through repeated real ChatGPT Work walkthroughs. Codex traced failures found during those sessions, including blank comparisons, repetitive confirmation loops, stale evidence, false completion claims, buried outputs, tool-language leakage, and Markdown downloads that opened in unrelated applications. Those failures became implementation changes and regression tests. The current suite contains 242 passing tests across 19 files, plus TypeScript and production-build verification. Additionally, the Duration Mapper tool was originally built with Codex for another OpenAI hackathon. Key Features Native WebMCP tools with visible shared-page state. Immediate connected status and restrained live activity pulse. Relevant conversational context proposed by the student's agent. Cumulative fact collection with one settled confirmation. Repeated HenryKnows consultation before or after clarification. Deterministic screening, plan calculation, timeline, and source references. Honest handling of unsupported or unresolved regulatory questions. Agent-authored student and professional briefs tied to the same case revision. Atomic document completion and stale-output protection. Polished student and adviser PDF exports with clickable professional sources. Server-controlled free judging access without changing the commercial HenryKnows product. Architecture Static HenryKnows interface hosted on Netlify. Eleven bounded site-tool contracts registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Versioned in-browser preparation case with confirmation and dependency invalidation. Existing TypeScript duration-of-status engine for deterministic rule calculations. HenryKnows retrieval and model-backed answer endpoint for broader F-1 guidance. Netlify Functions and Blobs for bounded continuation, long-running work, and short-lived transfer state. Client-side PDF generation loaded only when the user requests a download. Existing Project And New Work HenryKnows and the integrated Duration of Status Mapper existed before the challenge. The mapper was originally created for an earlier hackathon and was subsequently updated inside HenryKnows. They are not presented as new work for this challenge. Work added during the WebMCP Challenge includes the native site-tool layer, external-agent expeditor contract, versioned shared case, conversational confirmation boundary, cumulative connected interface, mapper/Henry orchestration, iterative consultations, revision and stale-work protection, atomic paired-document retention, audience-specific document validation, and client-generated PDF handoffs. The dated commit history and build log distinguish this extension from the prior products. title: kontier-ri
pitch: Ask ChatGPT why churn spiked. It reads the page's WebMCP tools, finds the cause, and proposes edits. A different human approves them. Attributed to the agent, undoable in one keystroke.
about_excerpt: Ask ChatGPT why churn spiked. It reads the page's WebMCP tools, finds the cause, and proposes edits. A different human approves them. Attributed to the agent, undoable in one keystroke. Like Comment Story Updates Kontier RI - a shared investigation workspace for humans and agents Inspiration Every agent demo ends the same way. Something impressive happens, and you have no idea whether to trust it. We kept hitting this inside our own product. Kontier is a billing platform, and the question customers ask most is some version of "why did churn spike last month?" An agent can answer that. What it cannot do is convince the person who has to act on the answer - the reasoning scrolls past in a chat window, the edits appear with no author, and no colleague can check the work before it becomes true. So we stopped asking how do we let an agent do more and started asking who reviews it, and how would they even see it. That question has a shape. It looks like code review: a proposal, a diff, a reason per change, a second pair of eyes, and a way back. WebMCP was the missing half - a page can declare what an agent may do, in the same tab a human is already looking at. The report becomes the shared surface instead of the transcript. What it does Several people and their agents work one live report. An agent reads the page's tools through WebMCP, investigates, and proposes. Nothing is applied. A human - often a different human, arriving on nothing but an invite link - reads the staged change set as a diff with a reason on every row, keeps what they agree with, drops what they do not, and approves. The result lands attributed to the agent that proposed it, not the human who clicked, as one entry and one undo step. In our demo, ChatGPT's own browser was asked in plain English why churn spiked in March. It listed the page's tools, read the work context, queried the data, and found the cause: one plan went from €99 to €149 that month, and 40 of the 44 cancellations came from it. Then it wrote two annotations onto the report and stopped, waiting for a human. How we built it A pnpm monorepo, TypeScript throughout, strict everywhere. packages/studio - the collaboration contract and the WebMCP layer. 40 static tools plus small bundles that mount and unmount with the state of the work. Chrome's own guide asks for exactly this: "register tools when they're useful in a certain page state, then unregister when the tool is no longer usable," with static registration as the default. One schema per tool. A zod v4 schema generates the protocol inputSchema via z.toJSONSchema() and re-validates the same shape inside execute, so the contract cannot drift from the implementation. packages/datasource - DuckDB-WASM. SQL runs in the tab, and registerRemoteParquet range-reads remote Parquet over HTTP, so 100 million rows are queryable without downloading them. packages/workspace - one WorkspaceStore interface, local and HTTP implementations, and a 23-test conformance suite run against both. apps/web - Next.js. Guest workspaces where the invite link is the credential, real OIDC through the platform's existing Keycloak, an ordered command log with server-assigned seq, presence, and cross-user approval. Deployed as a Node container at ri.kontier.eu, on the same infrastructure as the rest of the platform. What we learned WebMCP rewards being specific. Chrome publishes character budgets - 500 per description, 150 per parameter, 30 per name. Ours had one tool at 888 characters, repeating a grammar its own inputSchema already expressed. Nothing enforces those budgets, which is exactly why we wrote a test that does. Declaring nothing is worse than declaring false. Silence on a mutating tool is a missing signal, not a neutral one. All 46 tools now declare readOnlyHint explicitly - 13 reads true and untrusted-hinted, 33 writes false - pinned by a test that fails on any future tool that says nothing. Rejected calls are the ones you cannot see. A call the host rejects on schema validation leaves no trace anywhere — no document change, no activity entry. We had excluded those from our ledger, reasoning nothing ran. Wrong: an agent sending the wrong shape is one of Chrome's named failure modes, and the ledger is the only place it can surface. Chrome 152 wants a JSON string. executeTool(tool, {}) fails with "Failed to parse input arguments." It needs executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify(args)). We only found that by driving the real runtime. Challenges we ran into Two workers, one contract, five silent failures. We built the client store and server API in parallel against a written contract. Every piece passed its own tests. Then they met: /identity was never implemented, so nothing ever connected. The client PUT a shape the server rejected - and the conformance mock read the id from the body, so 79 tests passed against a server that did not exist. loadDashboard read a bare record where the server enveloped it, so documents arrived undefined and the report opened empty with no error. The workspace package re-exported its test suite, dragging vitest into the browser bundle. And peers tracked each other through the command stream alone, so a change producing no activity entry left a peer stale forever. The bug only production had. A reviewer opening an invite link erased the proposal they came to review - a freshly joined tab publishes an empty presence before its first read. It reproduced every time against the live site and never locally, because it is a race the fast path wins. The fix is one rule: read before write. We found it while recording the demo. Local edits that undid themselves. A poll could list dashboards before a save landed and finish after it, applying a stale document over edits made in between. A change that quietly reverts a second later is the worst thing an editor can do. Config describing a server nobody ran. Keycloak honours wildcards in the path, not the host - https:// .kontier.eu/ had always been a no-op that merely looked correct. And the realm file declared an organization scope the live server lacked, which fails the whole authorization request rather than being ignored. We put sign-in behind a wall to keep tests passing. It broke 41 of 42 end-to-end tests in one run - exactly what a first-time visitor would have experienced. The tests were right and we were wrong. What's next Entitlement-scoped tools. Our API keys already carry explicit permission scopes, so the toolbelt an agent sees can be derived from what the credential allows - an agent could not even see a tool it is not authorized to call, and the server would refuse it anyway. The machinery exists; it is scoped by workflow phase today and by permission tomorrow. title: LaunchMate
pitch: Policy-aware Google Play release studio built on WebMCP: a human and a browser agent co-edit screenshots and store copy, with verified facts, locks, revision guards, and human-confirmed publishing.
about_excerpt: Policy-aware Google Play release studio built on WebMCP: a human and a browser agent co-edit screenshots and store copy, with verified facts, locks, revision guards, and human-confirmed publishing. Like Comment Story Updates Note: LaunchMate is still in development. What you see works today, but a lot of it is a first version and I plan to keep improving it after the challenge. Live app: https://launchmate-policy-studio.kmagpie.chatgpt.site/ (no login needed for the editor and the WebMCP tools) Source (MIT): https://github.com/geonho1101/LaunchMate Demo video: https://youtu.be/24xXAtOLPvg Inspiration I make small Android apps as a solo developer under the name K-magpie. A few times, one of my apps quietly stopped showing up in Google Play search and I only found out later. The cause was a word in the listing that goes against Google Play's policy, the kind of promotional or ranking wording that is easy to write without thinking. Nothing crashes and nothing warns you, you just lose visibility and notice when installs drop. By the time I fixed it I had lost days or weeks. LaunchMate started as a way to catch that kind of mistake before I hit publish. I already had a small local tool that composed screenshots into store images, but it had no idea which claims were true, which text I had already decided on, or whether the listing was actually safe to ship. When I read about WebMCP, that was the missing piece: instead of an agent guessing from pixels, the page itself can tell the agent what is verified, what is locked, and what would break policy. So I built LaunchMate around that idea. What it does You name your app, add up to eight real screenshots (or pick frames that LaunchMate extracts locally from a screen recording), and then you and a WebMCP agent work on the same release pack in the browser. The page registers 12 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() (also listed at /.well-known/webmcp.json). With them the agent can: read the verified app facts and the full listing state (revision, copy, locks, theme, validation results) write or translate headlines and store copy, but only from facts I have marked as verified reorder slides and change the brand theme (it can never touch the screenshot pixels) run the Google Play policy check and get back structured errors and warnings open the release pack and the Google Play review dialog, which only a human can confirm Every tool that changes something needs an expectedRevision. If the state moved on since the agent last read it, the call fails with REVISION_CONFLICT instead of overwriting my edit. Locked fields and positions stay locked, every agent change is logged, and I can undo the last agent change with one click. If the agent tries to write "Korea's best free app" or "Download now", the policy guard rejects it before it ever reaches the design. The result is a reviewed release pack: the exact rendered screenshots, listing and alt text JSON, evidence mapping, a policy report and a SHA-256 manifest. You can export it as a ZIP, or, if you want, push it to Google Play through your own OAuth client after you confirm it yourself. How I built it One typed project state that both the human UI and the agent tools share 12 imperative WebMCP tools with strict input schemas and annotations Everything image related stays in the browser: uploads are object URLs, MP4/WebM frame extraction runs client side with size and duration limits, and nothing leaves the browser until you choose to publish Policy rules based on Google Play's official preview asset requirements, listing best practices and field limits Optional Google Play publishing with a per-user OAuth client. Credentials and refresh tokens live only in encrypted HTTP-only cookies, approvals are one-time and bound to the exact payload, and a D1 lock prevents duplicate commits Korean and English UI, bilingual docs, a unit test suite, lint and type checks, and no known dependency vulnerabilities at submission time I used OpenAI Codex heavily for the implementation, tests and the security review, and I did the product decisions, the verification and the final checks myself. Challenges I ran into Making agent edits safe. Revision conflicts, per-field and per-position locks, and evidence IDs were all needed before I trusted an agent to touch the listing. Keeping "human in the loop" honest for publishing. The agent can check readiness and open the review dialog, but the actual publish is tied to the exact copy and screenshot bytes I approved. Input friction. Uploading screenshots one by one was annoying, so I added batch import and local recording frame extraction. Security work right before going public: CSRF on the publish route, a path where unverified copy could slip through, dependency vulnerabilities and missing security headers. What I'm proud of WebMCP is doing real work here, not decoration. Policy validation, evidence-backed copy, lock preservation, localization and publish readiness all go through the tools. A judge can open the live app without logging in and run the whole flow. Publishing stops at a human confirmation step on purpose. What I learned Good WebMCP tools are not about how many tools you register. They are about exposing the things visual automation cannot see (is this claim verified, is this field locked, did the state change) and returning a clear refusal instead of quietly doing the wrong thing. What's next Title and metadata checks (special characters, emoji and all caps in the app name), importing existing listings and images from Google Play, a local device/ADB capture helper for brand new apps, stricter evidence rules for the short and full descriptions, and browser-level WebMCP evals for tool selection and multi-step calls. 한국어 소개 LaunchMate는 아직 개발 중인 프로젝트입니다. 저는 K-magpie라는 이름으로 혼자 작은 안드로이드 앱을 만들고 있습니다. 가끔 설명에 정책에 어긋나는 단어를 써서 구글 플레이 검색에 앱이 노출되지 않는 일이 있었습니다. 경고도 없이 조용히 안 보이게 되니 뒤늦게 알아채고 대응이 늦어져서 시간 손해를 본 적이 있어요. 그런 실수를 게시 전에 미리 잡는 도구를 만들고 싶었고, WebMCP를 이용해 사람과 에이전트가 같은 화면에서 등록정보를 함께 만들고 검사하는 LaunchMate를 만들었습니다. 실제 앱 스크린샷이나 화면 녹화에서 뽑은 프레임을 넣으면, 에이전트가 제가 검증한 기능만 근거로 한국어와 영어 문구를 쓰고, 과장 문구나 정책 위반 표현은 정책 검사에서 막히고, 제가 잠근 슬라이드와 리비전 충돌은 보호됩니다. 최종 게시는 항상 사람이 직접 확인합니다. title: Lectern
pitch: Lectern helps teachers share knowledge more efficiently with AI+web-MCP. Draft in UI → web-MCP fills gaps, sources, and builds tests → teacher reviews → publish. Students: read-only→ask AI (web-MCP).
about_excerpt: Lectern helps teachers share knowledge more efficiently with AI+web-MCP. Draft in UI → web-MCP fills gaps, sources, and builds tests → teacher reviews → publish. Students: read-only→ask AI (web-MCP). Like 2 Comment 1 Story Updates 6 Lectern landing page Lectern Studio Lesson crafted via user and agent using WebMCP Double-click on word to enter edit MD mode from that place Support formatting and math formulas with Markdown + LaTeX Provide list of Figure templates for the user and agent Quiz with generated media as an answer options Exported PDF that can be user as standalone material or uploaded back to lectern.click Landscape PDF export for LinkedIn and other Social Media Lectern WebMCP ToolBox Inspiration I build tools I will use myself, then share them. I have managed engineering and shipped products for years. I have also watched capable people fail at the last mile of teaching: they know the subject, and they still cannot put that knowledge into a shape others can take efficiently. Until now the rules were fixed, and they were bad for the person teaching. The AI writes in chat. You paste. You clean. You guess if it is ready. Learners get whatever survived the copy. Lectern is for anyone who is supposed to hand knowledge on — founder, researcher, practitioner. The world under that knowledge now changes every few months. Models, APIs, examples, even the words. A real lesson still needs materials and tests. Notes and last year’s deck are not that. That is the job I wanted to change. WebMCP changes the rules. The page is no longer a dumb canvas the model talks about . ChatGPT’s in-app browser (or Chrome with WebMCP) can use Lectern the way a colleague at your desk would: see what this screen can do, then do it, on the document you are looking at. Fill a gap. Add a figure. Write a check. You watch it. You edit it. You say no. The old game was: model generates, human pastes, lesson maybe. The new game is: human and agent share one lectern. That is why I built Lectern. What it does Lectern is a lesson studio. I work on the same page as the assistant. When the lesson is ready, a learner opens a locked copy, leaves marks, and asks questions answered from that lesson. Why WebMCP fits this problem. Authoring is not filling a form, and it is not a file you throw over the wall into chat. If the assistant cannot write into the live document, you are back to paste. If it can only guess at buttons, you do not trust it in front of a class. WebMCP is the missing rule: the studio exposes the work (gaps, sections, figures, checks, study mode), the agent does that work on screen, and the person who teaches stays responsible. What people and agents can do together now The person The assistant, on this page Author Sketch the idea. Keep your wording. Edit, reject, approve. Decide when it ships. Read the lesson, list what’s missing, write sections, add figures and quiz items, run the checklist. Learner Read. Mark “learned” or a question. Ask for a simpler explanation. Tutor from this text. It cannot rewrite what you published. You leave a PDF to print and hand out, or a .lectern file that keeps pictures and figures with the lesson so you can keep writing. Learners upload the PDF and start. The teacher tab reopens from a Lectern file only — restore-from-PDF leaves authoring. The same assistant still works on the student copy — still on the page, still inside your text. The studio is public, no account. The interface is in 17 languages, including Arabic. Generated images are labeled as AI. Try it Open https://lectern.click/studio in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. You should see a WebMCP banner. Ask: List what’s missing and fix every blocker. Watch the lesson fill in on screen. Open the student demo . Tap Copy reference on a section, paste it, and ask: Explain this section more simply. That sequence is the new rule in practice: you did not paste a lesson out of chat. The page and the agent did the work together. How I built it Lectern is a React 19 + TypeScript SPA. There is no agent backend and no account. The page is the MCP server: on load it registers typed tools on document.modelContext (older clients: navigator.modelContext ). Every handler mutates the same lesson store the Teacher and Student screens already use, so ChatGPT’s in-app browser writes into the document on screen — not into a transcript you paste later. Typed tools, not DOM scraping. Forty-two tools, JSON Schema inputs, descriptions written for the model. When you switch Teacher ↔ Student, the previous catalog unregisters and the new one registers. Teacher: 40 tools (meta, sections, SVG figures, illustrations, AMDP media, quiz, publish, Save & load / Your materials). Student: 12 (read, mark, ask, import). Authoring tools are gone on purpose — a learner’s agent cannot rewrite the lesson. The agent is pointed, not stuffed. Copy reference puts a short LECTERN_SECTION pointer on the clipboard, not the body. The model calls lectern_get_section . Completeness is a function ( analyzeGaps / isPublishable ): title, goals, materials, tests. lectern_publish_lesson returns an error while blockers remain. The lesson leaves the tab with its figures. Thirty SVG templates render in the page and attach to sections; generated rasters are labeled AI. Export writes a student PDF with a compressed LCT1 restore pack inside the file ( LECTERN_PDF/v1 system pages, pdf-lib / pdf.js) and a .lectern JSON so the teacher can keep writing. Students upload the PDF. Authoring reopens from the Lectern file only. Until then the draft stays in the browser ( localStorage , IndexedDB for large media). I treated WebMCP the way Chrome’s evals guide describes it. Isolation fixtures ( expectedCall ), full teacher and student schemas, deterministic tests for mutations and the publish gate, CI on every build. Probabilistic LLM evals stay opt-in. Production is static nginx on HTTPS at lectern.click — modelContext needs a secure context. The source is MIT. Challenges we ran into Putting the agent’s photos onto the page. Diagrams we already generate as SVG on the page. Photographs are different: the agent already has the bytes, and WebMCP executeTool is still a string. The path that worked — sixteen quiz JPEGs, one sitting — was begin / append / commit : 4k base64 slices through JSON and CDP evaluate . That is a +33% tax, dozens of round-trips, and it puts pixels where they do not belong (in the model’s context). Lectern has no upload server to PUT to. Native Blobs are not in the spec yet. So we pulled a small library out of the studio: AMDP — cite a SHA-256, fill a content-addressed store (Merkle slices, a generated body file input the page conceals and plane-puts on change , or json-chunk), bind purpose + alt onto the lesson. The model never has to hold the JPEG. Chunked JSON stays the fallback, not the protocol. Spec and diagrams in the repo. The lesson has to travel with its figures. A class already moves PDFs. A share URL that drops images — or a pretty printout you cannot reopen — is not a lesson. There is no packaging server: the tab has to emit the handout and the data in one sitting. First every path and URL figure is fetched in the browser and inlined as a data URL, so the pack does not depend on Lectern still hosting the file. Commit still writes that data URL onto the lesson so jsPDF can draw it and LCT1 can restore it. That document is JSON, deflated in-page ( LCT1. + base64url). Then two downloads from the same store: a .lectern file (embedded lesson, teacher project) and a PDF jsPDF draws — cover, sections, SVG rasterized to PNG at print DPI, prompt-only checks, an inverted answer-key page — after which pdf-lib attaches the LCT1 bytes inside that PDF. A student uploads the file; pdf.js pulls the attachment; Lectern inflates it into the live student document. Authoring reopens from the Lectern file only. Keeping control. I have watched enough “generate everything” demos to know teachers will not take that into the lesson. The hard product choice was slower on camera: the assistant writes into the document in front of you, change by change. You can stop it. That is the point of WebMCP here, and it was the constraint I refused to drop. Two roles on one lesson. A learner who can rewrite the text is a failed teacher experience. Authoring and studying had to be different sets of actions, not a cosmetic switch. Getting that boundary right took more care than adding another generate button. Knowing when it is actually done. After years in delivery I do not trust “looks ready.” Models make that worse: they add prose and skip the check. I put a checklist on the page — title, goals, materials, tests — that both of us can see. It does not ship while blockers remain. Accomplishments that we're proud of lectern.click is live. No account. The assistant writes on the same page you see. The rules actually changed. You do not paste a lesson out of chat. You watch it written into your document. Ready is on screen. title: Liminal Wiki
pitch: The wiki you update by asking—not editing. People decide. Agents maintain. The result lives in the wiki—not in another chat transcript.
about_excerpt: The wiki you update by asking—not editing. People decide. Agents maintain. The result lives in the wiki—not in another chat transcript. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Wikis rarely become stale because people cannot write. They become stale because maintenance is endless: finding the canonical page, preserving links, adding evidence, reconciling newer information, handling concurrent changes, and keeping history intact. This burden is especially costly for small research, product, policy, and engineering teams whose knowledge must remain sourced, connected, and auditable. Document chatbots can answer questions, but their result stays in a chat. AI features inside editors can draft prose, but people still have to maintain the source of truth. Visual browser agents can operate editing controls, but they must infer live state and may act outside the context a person intended. What Liminal Wiki does Liminal Wiki changes the primary interaction. The human-facing workspace is for reading and judgment, not direct page editing. A person opens the wiki, reads a page, and selects Request change. They describe what should be different instead of editing Markdown, moving files, repairing links, placing sources, or resolving a save conflict. The Site turns that intent into a structured handoff containing the exact wiki and target, current version, permalink, request type, user instructions, and authorized scope. It does not copy the page body or create a second request database. The agent reads the live wiki through the tools of the open page. The result lives in the wiki—not in another chat transcript. Applied changes appear in the same Documents and Explore topics views with stable page IDs, linked sources, claim-level evidence, immutable revisions, and an audit trail. Why WebMCP is essential The safe action depends on live product state: the active wiki, open page, signed-in role, current revision, evidence graph, and operational mode. Page-scoped WebMCP lets the Site expose precise, session-aware actions instead of making an agent scrape the DOM or use a separate automation identity. Before writing, the agent reads the workspace context and operating contract, searches for an existing canonical page, and inspects relevant pages, links, claims, sources, and topic insight. Grounded research is first captured in an immutable plan. Application requires the same plan hash, a current version, and a retry-safe operation ID. Every server API independently rechecks the wiki boundary and permission. What people and agents do together People remain responsible for intent, judgment, and scope. Agents handle the maintenance work required to turn that intent into durable knowledge: search before creating, reuse stable IDs, connect exact evidence, preserve uncertainty, avoid stale writes, and record revisions. The agent stops when the target is ambiguous, a warning expands the impact, the version changes, or the evidence does not support the requested conclusion. Complete product Each signed-in account receives an isolated private wiki with persistent storage. The product includes multilingual reading and request interfaces, folder and topic exploration, full-text search, connections, evidence-backed insights, revisions, recoverable page deletion, roles and sharing, portable and full backups, operational read-only mode, and a separate recovery Site. People directly manage membership, ownership, backups, operational settings, and wiki deletion. Authorized sessions may also expose wiki creation through WebMCP without granting membership or bypassing owner controls. What was built during the challenge The repository history begins during the challenge window. During that period we built the production Site and its page-scoped WebMCP integration, then redesigned the normal knowledge-change workflow around structured human requests. Challenge work includes session-aware tool registration, capability-based discovery, the Request change handoff, live context and policy inspection, search-before-create behavior, plan/apply workflows for grounded changes and topic insights, version and idempotency safeguards, provenance and revision verification, bounded observability, deployment, backup, and recovery. Third-party and adapted components are identified in the repository's provenance and notice files. title: Mandaneum
pitch: An infinite board you dump raw material onto — pasted notes, links, photos, sketches, half-thoughts. No folders, no markdown, no structure required. WebMCP lets the agent do the rest.
about_excerpt: An infinite board you dump raw material onto — pasted notes, links, photos, sketches, half-thoughts. No folders, no markdown, no structure required. WebMCP lets the agent do the rest. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Mundaneum is inspired by Paul Otlet’s original Mundaneum: an ambitious early attempt to collect, connect, and organize the world’s knowledge using millions of cross-referenced index cards. Modern knowledge tools are powerful, but capturing ideas often requires deciding on folders, filenames, and structure too early. We wanted a space where people could first think naturally—dropping in notes, links, files, drawings, equations, and unfinished ideas—and let organization emerge later. We also wanted AI collaboration to feel native to the interface. Instead of making an agent interpret every interaction from screenshots or manipulate the page through coordinates, Mundaneum uses WebMCP to expose the board’s actual content and permitted actions directly to the agent. What it does Mundaneum is an infinite visual research board designed for people and AI agents to work on together. People can add notes, links, images, documents, media, files, widgets, freehand drawings, YouTube videos, Spotify songs, PDFs, Excel, and expandable document canvases. Document canvases combine positioned text, handwriting, shapes, and equations into a single visual document that a multimodal model can inspect as an image. Users can select a card or Shift-click multiple cards to establish the current focus. WebMCP returns those selected items first, allowing ChatGPT to work on a specific group without scanning an entire large board. Selected drawings are provided as a cropped image, while cards retain their structured text and metadata. Users can also copy a card’s exact ID and reference it directly in a prompt. Through WebMCP, an agent can: Read the board and its current selection View a document canvas or the entire board as a PNG Add provisional cards Connect related cards Group and label information Annotate cards visually Identify and merge likely duplicates Request grid, masonry, cluster, tree, row, or column arrangements Create sketches without controlling their final position The central rule is that agents can contribute meaning, but they cannot provide coordinates. The page remains responsible for placement, collision detection, and layout. How we built it Mundaneum is a React and TypeScript application powered by Vite. Board state is stored locally in IndexedDB, while Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects support sharing, capture, and synchronization. The WebMCP layer registers imperative tools through document.modelContext . The same internal tool definitions are used by the visible application, ensuring that agent actions follow the same rules as human actions. The board performs its own organization work in the browser: Transformers.js generates semantic embeddings in a Web Worker. Pairwise similarity creates a graph of related cards. Louvain community detection identifies clusters. D3 Force calculates spatial arrangements. Collision detection and empty-space placement prevent cards and widgets from overlapping. An RBush spatial index supports efficient selection and region queries. Rich media uses a lightweight facade until the user activates it, preventing large boards from loading many expensive embeds simultaneously. Documents and spreadsheets are parsed through lazy-loaded libraries, while drawing and document canvases can be rasterized into PNG images for multimodal agents. Stylus input uses Pointer Events, pressure data, pointer capture, coalesced events, palm rejection behavior, and hardware-eraser handling to improve writing on tablets. ChatGPT, OpenAI Codex, and Anthropic Claude Code were used during development for research, implementation, debugging, testing, and documentation. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest problems was deciding how much information should be structured data and how much should remain visual. Text cards are easier for an agent to process structurally, but handwriting, equations, diagrams, and overlapping annotations lose meaning when converted into isolated text. Our solution was hybrid: preserve structured card data while supplying selected drawings and document canvases as images. Selection also required careful design. On a large board, returning everything equally can waste the model’s context and make focused requests unreliable. We made human selection an explicit attention signal, returning selected cards first and combining selected drawings into a single cropped image. Spatial layout created another challenge. Simple force-directed layouts often produced overlapping clusters, particularly in masonry, cluster, and tree arrangements. We separated semantic intent from geometry: agents request an arrangement, while the browser calculates positions, measures real card dimensions, and searches for available space. Tablet drawing introduced a different class of input problems. Pen input, touch gestures, palm contact, scrolling, erasing, and card dragging can all compete for the same pointer events. Supporting pressure-sensitive writing without breaking ordinary mouse and touch interaction required dedicated pointer handling and repeated device-oriented testing. Finally, converting the complete board into an agent-readable image was more complicated than returning its SVG representation. We added real PNG rasterization so multimodal models receive an actual screenshot-like image containing cards, links, drawings, and spatial relationships. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Mundaneum treats WebMCP as part of the product’s interaction model rather than as a thin demonstration layer. The agent operates on meaningful concepts—cards, selections, links, groups, drawings, and arrangements—without controlling screen coordinates. This creates a clear division of responsibility: the person directs attention, the agent contributes understanding, and the application protects the visual workspace. We are also proud of the document canvas. It allows typed text, handwriting, shapes, and equations to coexist in one movable and resizable document while remaining readable by a multimodal agent. Other accomplishments include: Selection-aware agent context Multi-card selection through Shift-click Image-based transfer of selected drawings Whole-board PNG capture Copyable card IDs Non-overlapping card placement Resizable document and widget cards Pressure-sensitive stylus support Multiple browser-computed arrangements A shared tool registry for the interface and WebMCP A public, MIT-licensed implementation What we learned We learned that good agent interfaces are less about exposing every possible action and more about defining strong boundaries. Preventing agents from setting coordinates initially appeared restrictive, but it simplified the tool surface and made agent contributions safer. The agent expresses intent, while deterministic browser code handles geometry. We also learned that visual and structured context should complement each other. Screenshots are excellent for handwriting, diagrams, and spatial meaning, while structured data is better for exact text, IDs, links, and targeted actions. Combining both creates a much stronger interface than relying exclusively on either representation. Human selection proved to be a powerful form of context engineering. A simple Shift-click can communicate scope more reliably than a long prompt explaining which objects matter. Finally, pen input demonstrated how much interaction design depends on hardware. A drawing system that works with a mouse is not automatically usable with a stylus and touchscreen. What's next for Mundaneum Our immediate focus is testing and refining the complete WebMCP workflow across more browsers, board sizes, and tablet devices. We also want to improve: Selection and movement of mixed groups containing cards and drawings Stylus responsiveness, palm rejection, and gesture handling Exporting and importing complete boards Collaborative editing and synchronization Accessibility and keyboard navigation Large-board performance More document-canvas editing tools Clearer review controls for agent contributions The repository also contains early experiments for optional in-page AI providers and dynamically extending the board’s tools. These ideas are not yet part of the fully tested experience. Future work will evaluate them carefully, including security, permissions, failure handling, and user review, before presenting them as supported features. Ultimately, we want Mundaneum to become a shared thinking surface where people can work visually and AI agents can contribute meaningfully—without taking control away from the person using the board. title: OpenCast
pitch: Edit video by editing words — you and your AI agent cut, clip, caption, swap backgrounds, and drop in visuals together, live in one editor, via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Edit video by editing words — you and your AI agent cut, clip, caption, swap backgrounds, and drop in visuals together, live in one editor, via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates OpenCast Inspiration Two ideas collided. The first: tools like Descript proved that the transcript is the best interface for editing talk-heavy video — you delete a sentence, the footage follows. The second: WebMCP proposes that a web page should hand agents typed, callable tools instead of making them guess at buttons. Put together, they describe the same product. If editing is already "operate on words," then an agent that speaks in words is a native editor, not a bolted-on chatbot. I wanted to build the version of that idea where the human and the agent aren't in separate worlds — they look at the same live page , pull the same levers , and every change lands in the same undo stack. Editing a podcast felt like the sharpest possible test: it's real work, it's language-shaped, and you can see whether the collaboration is real. What it does OpenCast is a transcript-first podcast/video editor. Upload a recording; the transcript becomes editable in about a minute; then you — or your agent, through 47 WebMCP tools — cut filler words and silences, fix mis-transcriptions, assemble named compositions (hooks, clips) from timeline ranges, turn on live captions, layer timed images over or under the footage, remove the background with in-browser ML, and export a finished MP4 with everything burned in — rendered entirely in the browser. How I built it The architecture is three layers, and it's the part I'd defend in any design review: Page state — a Zustand store holding words (with per-word timestamps), sources, compositions, overlays. One shared action hub — every edit is a narrow verb: cutWords , renameSpeaker , addToComposition , removeOverlay … Two front ends to the same hub — buttons for humans, and WebMCP tools ( document.modelContext.registerTool — a name, a JSON schema, a callback) for agents. Same verbs; nobody gets a special door. Tools return what changed , so the agent can verify itself, and destructive ones require explicit confirmation. Around that core: a Next.js app on Vercel; a Fly.io Docker worker that takes resumable 16 MiB upload chunks straight to a volume, extracts audio with ffmpeg, and runs a words-first pipeline — Whisper word timings through a bounded concurrent pool unlock the editor fast, while speaker diarization runs as a background enrichment that relabels the live transcript when it lands (and multi-track projects skip ML diarization entirely, because the track is the speaker). Exports use a canvas compositor: play the kept ranges once, draw background layer → footage (MediaPipe selfie segmentation for background removal) → B-roll layer → captions, and record it with the source audio via MediaRecorder to MP4. Challenges I ran into The silent five-minute ceiling. Long diarization calls kept dying with a cryptic Headers Timeout Error : Node's fetch (undici) aborts any request whose response headers take over 300s — and retried the doomed request forever. Diagnosing that, giving OpenAI calls a real deadline through an explicit dispatcher, and then restructuring to words-first (never let the slow model block the editable transcript) was the single biggest turn in the project. Embedded browsers are a different planet. ChatGPT Desktop's browser is narrow, blocks programmatic downloads without a user gesture, and can't be trusted with a GPU delegate. That forced real fixes: on-screen layers scoped to the footage's aspect ratio instead of the pane, a CPU fallback for segmentation, and layouts audited at 480px. Canvas taint. Recording a canvas fails if any drawn image isn't CORS-readable — one bad overlay URL could poison a whole render. Locally uploaded images are compressed into data URLs (always safe); non-CORS remote images are skipped rather than killing the export. Building on a moving spec. WebMCP is pre-standard; API names have already shifted. Keeping the tool layer thin over the action hub meant the churn only ever touches one file. What I learned Design tools as narrow verbs with clear side effects that report what changed — agents chain small verbs better than they wield big ones. Words-first beats complete-but-slow: shipping the editable thing early and enriching in the background changed how the product feels more than any feature. And the deepest one: the trust problem with agents isn't solved by logs or promises — it's solved by a shared screen , where every mutation happens in front of you and your undo key still works. What's next Program-cut-aware multicam rendering on the worker, cross-chunk speaker identity stitching, and a consent surface for tool calls that's worthy of the spec this is all betting on. title: Origami Gratis
pitch: I stopped asking how to make agents work with Office and started asking why Office still exists. Origami: deck, doc, sketch and chart as one HTML file, authored over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: I stopped asking how to make agents work with Office and started asking why Office still exists. Origami: deck, doc, sketch and chart as one HTML file, authored over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Have clean reports instantly Agents and humans can make together. No more need for MS Visio A Hub of MCP's that will keep growing Why cant my Spreadsheet be in my Presentation My document can be my spreadsheet And i can choose what in that sheet is shown in the presentation Validated working with GPT Cloud Browser Inspiration When a new technology arrives, we ask "how do I make it work with the old thing?" almost never do we ask "does the old thing deserve a future?" I hit this thought when making agents try to make the perfect PowerPoint at work. Why am I parsing zipped XML from two decades ago? Why is it three separate programs? Why can't my presentation have the document as a Slide? why cant i have a full spreadsheet in my report? What the hell is Visio? Surely we can combine Excel, PowerPoint and Word into one tool by now? Also, I find HTML presentations just look way more professional — anyone can scrape together a PowerPoint, but a slick HTML deck? Far less… until now. And that's why I built Origami Folio, my eyes set on a Chrome extension because it was the best way for agent and human to work together. That was until I randomly saw a post about this hackathon and WebMCP. What it does Origami Folio is a full next-generation Office suite built in HTML. Make presentations, word documents and spreadsheets from scratch. The word document doesn't link to the spreadsheet or paste a picture of it — it's in the document! And it all saves to a single file that opens in any browser around the world, ready to present and edit further. The Chrome extension version already allowed MCP control, but it required the extension. With this version, agents just need a website — they can make everything, save it, open files and resume where they left off. How we built it WebMCP is new enough that we measured most of it ourselves. The launch flag isn't documented — we found --enable-features=WebMCP by string-searching chrome.dll. Chrome silently drops destructiveHint , so every destructive warning had to move into the description itself. inputSchema arrives as a string. Halfway through, Chrome 152 removed navigator.modelContext under our feet. Challenges we ran into The hardest design work was honest saving: a page can't just write to your disk. So save_deck reports exactly which of three things happened: a real write through a file handle, a backstop copy in the browser's own storage, a started download. It never says "saved" when it can't verify bytes landed. Agents are also blind without native vision — not an issue for OpenAI models, but I want it supportable by all models. So inspect_render lays the deck out off-screen and reports the geometry — including the fold that validated perfectly and rendered as nothing. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent with no prior knowledge of Origami self-onboards from one origami_guide call and builds a complete deck. Venn diagrams, sketches, charts, flowcharts, Gantts — all unattended, through Chrome's own WebMCP surface. No mocks, no shim. The demo video is 54 native executeTool calls, and the file it produces plays on double-click, full screen, forever. This isn't a demo of a concept — it's something users can keep coming back to again and again as part of their tech stack. What we learned WebMCP inverts distribution. Instead of installing your tools into the agent, the page hands its tools to whatever agent shows up. Distribution becomes easy it's all self-contained. Once it's loaded, an agent can call the tools once or a million times and it costs me nothing either way. (Unless agents reload the page every time, which they don't need to — then I'd be thankful for Cloudflare Pages' generous scaling.) What's next for Origami Gratis Honestly, my mission statement has been the same from the start: I want to displace Microsoft Office. People, AI and the future of tech should not be beholden to the dead weight of a 25-year-old solution of zipped XML files masquerading as three different executables — and then paying extra for Visio. WebMCP is new, and because I saw this hackathon late I only had three days to port this — so I'll keep polishing the experience and adding features until it holds full parity with the extension. Anything your agent can make, you can edit; anything you make, the agent can pick up. Origami Gratis will be my hub: each petal added to the flower is a new WebMCP tool, until Origami Gratis is known as one of the go-to libraries of tooling for all agents. title: PageCTRL
pitch: Control what agents do next. The in-page trust and security layer for WebMCP, protecting both merchants and users.
about_excerpt: Control what agents do next. The in-page trust and security layer for WebMCP, protecting both merchants and users. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP lets an AI agent call real functions inside a web page. That is a big step forward, and it creates a new problem. Those calls never leave the browser tab. No firewall sees them. No API gateway sees them. No payment network sees them. Every security tool we have sits outside the page, and the agent is now inside it. So today a shopper has two options. Give the agent everything, or give it nothing. Most people pick nothing. The numbers say the same thing. About 77% of people already use AI to help them shop. About 75% will not let it complete the payment. People want the help. They do not want to hand over the card. That gap is the whole product. We did not want to build another agent. We wanted to build the thing that makes it safe to let one finish the job. What it does PageCTRL is one script tag. It wraps every WebMCP tool on a page and puts a human back in control. It patches document.modelContext.registerTool() at load. Every registered tool then runs inside a guarded pipeline: Validate the arguments against the tool's schema. Apply the policy: allow, ask a human, or deny. Check the rate limit for that tool. Check the quantity cap across the whole cart, not one call. Check the amount cap for a single action. Reserve the spend against the session budget, atomically. Ask the human, and wait. Run the tool under a timeout. Redact personal data from the result. Scan the result for injected instructions. Append the call to a SHA-256 hash-chained journey. The policy has two tiers. The merchant sets a floor in code, and it is locked. The shopper can only make it tighter. A user setting can never loosen a merchant rule. That matters, because the shopper and the merchant do not trust each other, and neither should have to. Payment is real. The shopper saves a card once through Stripe. After that the agent can pay inside the limits, and Stripe charges the card off-session. The page never sees the card number, so no agent tool can read it. The approval itself is signed. When a human clicks Allow, a separate service on a different origin issues an Ed25519 grant bound to that exact order: the amount, the quote, the session, and the origin. The shop server refuses to charge without it. That service runs on infrastructure the merchant does not control, so a rogue script inside the merchant's own page cannot approve its own payment. Two attacks are in the live demo, because both are real: A seller's reply comes back carrying hidden instructions. PageCTRL flags it and tells the agent to treat the text as data, not as commands. A third-party widget loads late and tries to replace the checkout tool. The guard refuses, because the tool surface was sealed when the page loaded. When a block happens, the agent can ask why. It gets the real rule and the real limit back, and the same answer appears on the shopper's screen. Blocking an agent is easy. Blocking it so it can still finish the job is the hard part. How we built it The storefront is Next.js 16 with the App Router, TypeScript, and Tailwind v4, deployed on Vercel. It registers 13 tools and guards 14. The SDK is public/pagecontrol.js . It is plain JavaScript with no dependencies, about 2,000 lines. It has to be, because a merchant should be able to add it to any page with one script tag, and because a build step is one more thing that can go wrong at the trust boundary. The signing service is a small Node server on Render. It holds the Ed25519 private key, publishes the public key as a JWK, checks a bearer token and an origin allowlist, and signs one grant per approval. The domain sits on Cloudflare. We split the deployment on purpose. The shop runs on Vercel with its own Stripe key. The signing key lives somewhere else. If both ran in the same place, the merchant could mint their own approvals, and the signature would prove nothing. Payments use Stripe twice. A hosted Checkout session in setup mode saves the card. A PaymentIntent with off_session: true charges it later, which is the pattern Stripe built for a payment the customer approved and then walked away from. We used Codex for most of the implementation and Claude to plan, review, and run the adversarial passes. Challenges we ran into Serverless has no memory. The first build kept approval state in a JavaScript Map . That works on one machine. On Vercel each request can land on a different instance, so the state vanished. We moved to signed cookies and signed quotes, and stopped assuming a server remembers anything. Two clocks never agree. Grants expire in 60 seconds. Render and Vercel drift apart by a few seconds, and our 5-second tolerance rejected valid approvals. We widened it to 60 seconds, which the short lifetime still bounds. A single space cost an hour. Every checkout failed with grant_mismatch . The signature was valid. The cause was a leading space in an environment variable pasted into a dashboard, so the issuer string never matched. We fixed it by trimming every environment read, and by logging which field mismatched and both values. The log found it in seconds once it existed. Stripe has field limits. Our signed quote ID runs to about 364 characters. Stripe caps an idempotency key at 255. Every charge was rejected before it reached the card. We keyed on the quote's UUID instead. Caps have to count the cart. Our first quantity cap limited one call to five items. The agent added five, then five again. The cap now counts what is already in the cart, so a limit of five means five. The cart kept emptying itself. Loading saved receipts overwrote the basket with an empty one, and that step ran again on every remount. Hydration now carries the live basket forward. Accomplishments that we're proud of Two adversarial security reviews found 16 defects. All 16 are fixed, and each one has a regression test. The guard is real, not a mock. 45 SDK tests and 6 service tests pass, covering native WebMCP, abort signals, approval binding, and call pairing. The payment is a real Stripe charge, not a simulation. The approval is cryptographically bound to one order, and a separate origin signs it. Remove the grant and the server returns 403. We check that. And it works with a real agent. In ChatGPT's browser the badge reads Native, so these are real WebMCP calls, not a simulation of them. What we learned Guardrails are easy to write and hard to place. Every check we first put in the page had to move to the server, because anything an agent can reach, an agent can skip. An error message is part of the product. Our first blocks just said no. The agent then retried the same thing. Explaining the rule and the limit turned a dead end into a next step. Two parties do not trust each other, and a design has to say so out loud. The merchant does not trust the shopper's agent. The shopper does not trust the merchant's page. The two-tier policy and the third-party signature both exist because of that, and neither would exist if we had assumed good faith. What's next for PageCTRL Publish the SDK on npm and a CDN, with Subresource Integrity. Add a <page-control-panel> custom element, so a merchant can place the UI. Ship a hosted merchant console with real keys, usage, and dispute evidence. Support the requestUserInteraction() approval hook when it lands in the WebMCP spec, and drop our own modal in favour of the browser's. Export the hash-chained journey as signed evidence for chargebacks. Extend past shopping. Booking, support actions, and account changes have the same problem and the same shape. title: PaperPup
pitch: A research library your AI can't wander out of — by design.
about_excerpt: A research library your AI can't wander out of — by design. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration PaperPup started as a personal itch, not a hackathon idea. It was needed to manage a real research library. There were real-world stakes in turning a recognized pattern of investigatory practices into a structured and AI-instrumented process. The frustration that actually drove the design: ask a general AI chatbot to help with research, and it happily answers from the whole internet, or from memory, or both — not from the specific papers you actually collected and have deemed useful. Drafts as well that needed controlled tests run against them against the literature that supported the research. Anyone who has followed a chatbot down a research rabbit hole and landed somewhere completely off-target knows the feeling. PaperPup was built to make that structurally impossible, not just less likely. WebMCP entered the picture partway through, and it fit almost too well. PaperPup already had a strict internal discipline — Library, Stack, and Room, each granting a narrower set of capabilities than the last with clear demarcation between them in the form of hand-off briefs. WebMCP was a way to expose any of that to an external agent with the demarcation points mapped to WebMCP site tools by context, and it was a natural fit. The hackathon became the deadline attached to work already in motion, not the reason the work started. What it does PaperPup is a personal, single-tenant research library. It is not a shared or social platform, and is organized around three deliberately narrowing contexts: Library — search, add, and organize the papers you've actually collected. Stack — pull a working set of papers together and investigate them with an AI, grounded only in that set. Room — promote a mature stack into a frozen, bounded investigation. The corpus locks at that point — nothing added, nothing removed, except through one specific human-approved channel. WebMCP added a twist to that because now the human had an AI agent on their side that, unlike the agents that PaperPup sandboxes and uses to pit literature against literature, this new agent was the user. Inside a Room is a bit more locked down for all because an investigating agent has constraints that make it genuinely useful. It can read the papers, follow a citation to a source that should be there but isn't yet, and propose adding it. What it can't do is add that source itself, or search outside the frozen set to find something else instead. There's no tool call that does either of those things registered in that context — not a rule the agent is trusting to follow, a door that structurally doesn't exist. WebMCP is what lets any AI agent someone already uses — ChatGPT, or any other WebMCP-capable client — work inside this system directly, live, in the same browser tab and session, rather than through a bespoke chat widget bolted onto the page. That enabled bring your own agent; PaperPup supplies the grounding. How we built it PaperPup is a Next.js app backed by PostgreSQL, with an adapter layer pulling papers from Zenodo, OpenAlex/Unpaywall, arXiv, bioRxiv, and CORE, plus citation resolution against PubMed and Crossref. The WebMCP layer lives entirely under one subfolder, src/webmcp/ : a declarative manifest.js listing every tool's name, schema, and which contexts register it; register.js , which walks that manifest and calls the real document.modelContext.registerTool() API, managing one AbortController per tool so the whole set can be cleanly unregistered and re-registered on every navigation; envelope.js , which maps the current context — library, stack, room, or nothing selected yet — to the tools that should be live; and one thin handler per tool. Every handler reaches application logic only over HTTPS, never a direct import of server-only code — a boundary now enforced by an automated test that walks the whole import graph and fails on any reach into the backend and database layer. Tools scoped to one specific stack or room don't take that stack or room id as a parameter - it is read directly from the page's own state since a tool visible only inside one specific room already proves which room that is. Asking the calling model to name it back would just be redundant. The user's agent translates both ways for the user to have flexibility in identifying resources in prompts and reading the responses after their agent has formatted the PaperPup response to present it however that agent knows their user likes to communicate. We tested against a real host end to end — ChatGPT's WebMCP-enabled models — and, for fast local iteration before and alongside that, against @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill , a real implementation of the same browser API with a dev-only testing shim for invoking tools directly with no AI client connected at all. Claude (architecture and design) and Claude Code (implementation and live verification) were genuine build partners throughout — a fitting way to build a project about grounding external-to-system AI agents in trustworthy work. Challenges we ran into A permission model that could actually be violated in code, even after we thought we'd designed it out. Early on, a Room-context tool for reading a paper's metadata took a global paper id. That meant there was nothing stopping an agent from simply naming a paper outside the room's frozen set and getting it back anyway. The interface didn't expose search, so it looked safe. The fix was structural, not a permission check: that tool now takes a position within the room's own paper list, not a global id. There's no way to even construct a request for something outside scope, because the parameter itself can't express it. This ended up being the single most important architectural decision in the whole submission — a stronger guarantee than any runtime check could offer. A crash that taught us to build a permanent test, not just fix the bug. One early handler reached for a server-only database module directly instead of going through an HTTP route, and it pulled pg straight into the browser bundle — crashing the app outright the moment that code path loaded. We fixed the immediate bug, then built an automated test that walks the entire import graph under the WebMCP layer and fails on any reach into server-only code, so the same mistake can't happen again silently. Getting genuine live verification, not just something that looked right in code. ChatGPT's WebMCP support turned out to depend on which underlying model was selected. One variant has it disabled entirely, which looks identical to a bug in your own tool descriptions if you don't know to check. The in-app browser also has no visible developer console by default, so confirming what was actually happening required either asking the model to report it back, or falling back to a real polyfill running locally for a tighter dev loop. Turns out, this was quite useful to see and gave us insights in how to structure the descriptions in our WebMCP site tool descriptions that allow the user's agent to learn the capabilities impressively well. Realizing a two-dimensional problem was actually a one-dimensional one. A room's frozen corpus can span multiple stacks, which made stack-plus-position addressing feel necessary at first. Checking it against an existing invariant — that a room's assigned stacks are frozen and can't change after assignment — showed a flat position across the room's whole corpus was just as safe and considerably simpler. The extra complexity wasn't buying anything. Accomplishments that we're proud of That the room-envelope guarantee is real, not asserted. An agent working inside a frozen investigation cannot search or read past its bounds. This can be confirmed by trying, not just by design intent, and it is immensely useful when running control tests whereby a standing agent must defend a corpus using only what is in that room. The only out is that the room's agent can propose a source, such as a citation reference that it wants the full text for, and the user must then intervene to approve whether that visibility will be allowed. Configurable of course, but that is a sizable document in itself to describe the capabilities envisioned and being built. That we built the discipline to actually verify claims rather than trust that code looked right: a manifest-invariants test that caught its own first-draft bug immediately; a boundary test proven with a deliberate red-then-green check rather than accepted on a single clean pass; a live investigation's output cross-checked word-by-word against the source papers to confirm it wasn't quietly blending in outside knowledge. That the two-way collaboration model — an agent can discover and propose, a human retains final authority, and neither side can silently override the other — came out of the architecture cleanly, rather than needing to be bolted on as an afterthought.
