title: PilotCircuits
pitch: Build it. See it. Understand it. An Arduino workbench for beginners, driven by an agent through the page's own WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Build it. See it. Understand it. An Arduino workbench for beginners, driven by an agent through the page's own WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does## Inspiration Everyone who opens an Arduino kit hits the same wall in the first hour. The LED doesn't light. The wire is one hole off, or the resistor is in the wrong row, and the PDF that came with the kit can't tell you which. You take a photo, paste it into a chat, and the answer is a guess about a blurry picture. I wanted the agent to stop guessing. If the page that draws the breadboard already knows where every lead is, the agent should read that , not the pixels. WebMCP is exactly the missing piece: the page hands the agent a small set of tools, in the page's own vocabulary, and the agent works on the same build you're looking at. What it does PilotCircuits is a guided Arduino workbench for beginners. Six chapters, each adding one idea: a breathing lamp, a traffic light, a motion night-light, a plant guardian, a touchless soap dispenser, and a pre-built parking barrier as the capstone. You wire each one by hand on a simulated bench, dragging real-looking parts off a kit shelf into breadboard holes and header pins. An agent connected through WebMCP sees the same bench. On the workbench it can: explain_project — say what the chapter is for and what each part does inspect_build — compare your wiring against the sketch and list what's off show_correction — pan the camera to the lead at fault point_at — frame any part, pin or hole you ask about, without touching anything attach_lead — the one tool that changes the build: seat a lead, or pull it loose verify_current_step , navigate_build_step , run_functional_test — walk the steps and run the chapter's own checks Two things on screen tell you what the agent is doing. A ring on the bench shows where it is working, and a small LED-shaped coach in the corner shows what : reading, thinking, pointing, testing, and a happy face when the test passes. What's new here is the division of labour. You build. The agent checks the build against the plan, shows you the mistake on the board itself, and if you say "fix it", it moves the lead through the same code path your own drag would take. You can undo its move. Neither side is watching a screenshot of the other. It works as a normal web app without a WebMCP host, and it's fully localised in English and Turkish, tool descriptions and refusal messages included. How I built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind. The breadboard, Uno and component artwork is ported from Wokwi Elements (MIT). Deployed on Vercel at https://pilotcircuits.com . The WebMCP layer lives in src/lib/agent/webmcp.ts and a React hook around it. Tools are registered with navigator.modelContext inside an effect, per route, and torn down when the route changes: the library registers the search and open tools, the workbench registers the nine above, and nothing is offered on a page that can't act on it. When the build or the language changes, every tool re-registers with the new descriptions. Thirteen tool names in total. Every tool call goes through the same queue as the buttons in the UI, so an agent's attach_lead and a person's drag are literally the same operation, with one activity log and one undo stack. Every handler validates its own input and returns refusals as data the model can act on ("no finding has that id, the ids come from inspect_build"), not as thrown errors. The AbortSignal the host passes is honoured, so a cancelled call doesn't keep moving the bench after the agent walked away. The "Connected via WebMCP" badge only lights up when registerTool actually resolved, not when the API merely exists. 971 unit tests across 28 files cover the circuit model, the tool handlers, the step verification and the copy. Challenges I ran into For most of the build, no browser shipped WebMCP. The whole layer was written against the spec and a fake host. The first time it ran in a real host (Chrome with the WebMCP flags, driven by Playwright) was one day before the deadline, and that run changed things. Chrome passed my MCP-style result envelope straight to the model as text: 6,618 characters for 2,425 characters of payload, with isError reaching nobody. I switched every tool to return bare JSON. Chrome also doesn't validate arguments against inputSchema , so the handlers had to. ChatGPT's in-app browser is a split pane. Below 1120 px the bench has no room for a canvas, so a narrow window registers only the five tools that make sense without one. I couldn't measure the pane itself, so the README says it out loud. The bench itself was the other half of the work: pointer capture on drags, the view panning under a lead mid-carry, a cable router that turned hairpins on every stub. And the first draft of the mascot looked too much like someone else's mascot. It went in the bin, and the lamp took its place. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Watching ChatGPT desktop, connected over WebMCP, take a jumper I'd plugged in wrong on purpose, find both bad ends, move the cable, then build the remaining 18 connections of the traffic light off the shelf and pass the functional test. That's the demo video, and none of it is scripted on the page's side. Also: tool descriptions that tell the truth. attach_lead 's description says what it costs, because that string is the only channel that reaches the model. What I learned Measure against the real host. My reading of the spec was reasonable and wrong in three places, and each one was visible within minutes of running Chrome with the flag. A face that mirrors a 300 ms tool call is invisible. The coach holds each mood for at least 1.2 seconds, because it's a presentation for the person, not a debugger for the agent. And the description field of a tool is documentation for a reader who can't open the source. Write it like that. What's next for PilotCircuits A real board beside the simulated one, so the last step of a chapter is flashing the sketch to the Uno on your desk. More chapters past the capstone. And a way for the agent to write a chapter: given a parts list, produce the steps, the sketch and the checks in the same format the six existing ones use. title: Protocol Mirror
pitch: Did the trial publish what it registered? Protocol Mirror gives an AI agent WebMCP tools to trace the record, quote the evidence, and stage a proposal. A human makes the final call.
about_excerpt: Did the trial publish what it registered? Protocol Mirror gives an AI agent WebMCP tools to trace the record, quote the evidence, and stage a proposal. A human makes the final call. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Protocol Mirror opens on a real ACTT-1 case with seven WebMCP tools ready for an agent-led, human-reviewed investigation. Original ClinicalTrials.gov outcomes sit beside PubMed evidence, with registry changes and exact source text visible. The responsive mobile view preserves the complete agent and reviewer workflow without horizontal scrolling. A 24-pair real-world stress test shows two local models making opposite errors from the same evidence. The session log separates every agent tool call from each human decision, creating a visible audit trail. An evidence-linked proposal remains in the review queue until a human accepts or rejects it. The evidence drawer places the agent’s reasoning beside exact quotations, source locators, and visible uncertainty. After a human decision, the eighth WebMCP tool appears and can export only the reviewed result. Inspiration I have a passionate affection for medicine. I also love using AI in my day-to-day life. I use it to learn new topics or subjects, research problems and examples, assist me in making cool apps such as my AI trading bot, and turn my brain dump of ideas into a working prototype. All of these use cases are reasons why I love AI. However, as I used AI more, one problem bothered me: AI, or an LLM, can give a fluent and confident answer even when the evidence behind it is incomplete or uncertain. In medicine and clinical research, we cannot afford to guess. Clinical trials are a good example of this. A trial registry records what researchers planned to measure, while a publication reports what readers eventually see. Comparing them requires searching through multiple registry pages and carefully matching the exact wording. This can be exhausting for a person and often takes a long time to complete. An AI agent could make the investigation faster and more efficient, but giving it the final judgment would create another problem. This problem inspired me to create Protocol Mirror: “Can an AI agent do the difficult, intensive investigative work while keeping the final decision in the hands of a human?” Protocol Mirror uses WebMCP to let an agent retrieve evidence, trace dated changes, quote exact source text, and propose a conclusion inside the webpage for the reviewer to see. The agent is useful, but it cannot approve or reject anything because that decision is left to the reviewer. What it does Protocol Mirror compares a clinical trial’s registered outcomes with what appears in its publication. The default example uses the real ACTT-1 trial, connecting its ClinicalTrials.gov record and registration history with its PubMed report. Using WebMCP, the agent can: Retrieve the live ClinicalTrials.gov record Retrieve the live PubMed abstract Examine the trial’s registration history Find the outcomes that were registered first Quote exact evidence with source locators Stage a matched, omitted, introduced, or uncertain proposal Request that a human review the proposal The page initially shows seven tools. None of them can accept or reject a proposal. That decision is made by the human reviewer after reviewing the information. Once the reviewer has made their decision, Protocol Mirror shows an eighth tool that lets the agent export a reviewed “receipt.” It includes only human-approved results, the evidence, source locations, and the audit history. If the reviewer undoes their decision, that tool is removed. A session log also records what the agent has called and what the reviewer has decided. If the reviewer rejects something, the application requires a reason and allows the reviewer to add notes, which are then returned to the agent. This lets the agent revise the proposal instead of allowing the review to be the end of the conversation. How I built it I used Codex as an AI engineering collaborator throughout the entire project. My first prompts involved introducing Codex to the hackathon, providing it with the official rules, judging criteria, and WebMCP documentation, connecting the Devpost plugin to Codex, and researching common hackathon project patterns. I first wanted to understand what WebMCP was and how it could change the structure of an experience instead of being used only as a decorative integration. After choosing clinical trials as the use case, I gave Codex a set of boundaries: Use real ClinicalTrials.gov and PubMed records. Preserve what the trial registered first. Connect every proposal to exact quotations and source locations. Treat external research text as untrusted. Give the agent no accept or reject tool. Make the human decision change the available tool surface. Test with real cases and record model failures. Keep benchmark results separate from clinical claims. One prompt did not create this entire project. It took a lot of planning, analysis, and development for it to become what it is today. Once Codex understood the challenge and had the necessary context, I used it to help create a plan, build the live-data adapters, model the evidence, implement the review workflow, improve the backend and frontend interface, examine security risks, and create the benchmarks. I reviewed each stage to find weaknesses before continuing. Near the end, I used Claude Code and followed the same process. I gave it the necessary context and background, then asked it to critique my project and identify what I should fix. I used Claude for two reasons. First, I wanted a fresh set of eyes to inspect my codebase. Second, Fable 5.1 had been released, and its enhanced thinking, reasoning, and coding capabilities helped find and fix bugs. I built the application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, GSAP, and WebMCP. Validated server routes retrieve public records from ClinicalTrials.gov and PubMed. The application converts them into stable outcomes and evidence spans with exact URLs and locators. The tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext . Pair-bound tools are registered again when the active trial changes. The receipt tool exists only while reviewed work exists. Each tool has a closed input schema, bounded values, runtime validation, and an AbortSignal for cleanup. Read tools identify their output as read-only and untrusted. The application also checks outcome and evidence identifiers against the active case, preventing a proposal from citing an identifier that the reviewer cannot inspect. I repeatedly asked Codex to reassess the project against the rubric at every stage, turning each weakness into the next engineering task to fix. The final checks covered WebMCP conformance, linting, TypeScript, the production build, 75 automated tests, and browser automation of the complete seven-to-eight-tool workflow. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was enforcing human decision-making authority in the code. A title that says “human decision” proves nothing if the agent still has an action that lets it approve or reject a proposal. I removed that function entirely. The reviewer decides through the application, and that decision changes which tool the browser registers. Getting dynamic registration, cleanup, undo behavior, and session restoration to work together took many revision sessions. PubMed presented another problem. When I called its API, it returned abstract sections rather than a clean list of publication outcomes. I kept those sections labeled as abstract evidence instead of presenting them as something the source does not provide. Testing also revealed browser-related behavior. WebMCP is new, and a local build has different origin requirements from the deployed application. I tested tool registration, live-source reads, proposals, reviewer feedback, receipt export, undo, reload, and case switching through the page’s actual WebMCP interface. Another challenge was reporting failures honestly. The two local models made opposite errors. I reported the run as evidence for keeping a human reviewer, not as a general measurement of hallucination or clinical accuracy. Only after a person reviews the evidence and makes a decision is the eighth tool revealed, allowing the agent to export the reviewed results. If the decision is undone, that tool is removed. title: s-m-r-t
pitch: Define a domain once, then give people and browser agents the same safe, structured application.
about_excerpt: Define a domain once, then give people and browser agents the same safe, structured application. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most web applications are built for people to click and for agents to guess. Agents scrape labels and infer controls from fragile DOMs. s-m-r-t asks a different question: what if an application's real domain model, permissions, workflows, and interface also defined a deliberate browser-native tool surface? Job hunting made that problem concrete. Finding opportunities, checking sources, triaging listings, recording notes, and preparing application packets are repetitive and stressful. They benefit from agent help, while final approval and employer submission should remain unmistakably human decisions. What it does s-m-r-t is the entry. It is a TypeScript framework for building operational applications around one typed domain model. Decorated business objects generate aligned persistence, REST, CLI, MCP, WebMCP, browser-data, and AI surfaces. WebMCP is not a separate demo API pasted onto an application: it is a governed browser projection of the same model and application contracts. For the challenge, s-m-r-t gained: canonical WebMCP definitions for deliberately API-exposed models; authenticated execution through the existing REST boundary; explicit exposure policies, effect classification, tool budgets, and namespaces; lifecycle-safe registration through document.modelContext ; mounted form-control and data-surface adapters, giving agents and people the same UI state; staged form edits requiring human review; bounded queries and durable actions with stable identity and confirmation boundaries; declarative view intents and layered playbooks that make the agent surface statically knowable; local, self-hosted, and managed-cloud runtime profiles preserving the same tools and policies. Iolaus is the demonstration application built with s-m-r-t. It is a local-first, single-user employment-search app using SQLite. A browser agent inspects source health, browses and investigates fictional job listings, records a triage decision and note, advances the queue, opens a shortlist, and inspects an application packet. Those actions update the same state the person sees. There is intentionally no WebMCP tool for final approval or employer submission. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, the agent needs brittle DOM automation or a separate privileged integration. With s-m-r-t, each page advertises bounded tools through document.modelContext . Those tools carry effect metadata, use authenticated application routes, respect field and exposure policies, and disappear with the page lifecycle. Mounted view tools change the same state the person sees, while background queries inspect data without disturbing the view. The collaboration is legible: the agent performs structured work, the person sees its results, and sensitive transitions remain behind explicit human review. The implementation is reusable across application domains instead of being tied to one job board or agent harness. How we built it s-m-r-t is a pnpm TypeScript monorepo. Its scanner reads @smrt() declarations and emits manifests, schemas, routes, clients, and canonical tool descriptors. @happyvertical/smrt-web validates and registers generated and bespoke browser tools. @happyvertical/smrt-svelte binds those contracts to mounted forms and data surfaces. Its application runtime composes SQLite/local, PostgreSQL/self-hosted, and managed-cloud profiles without changing domain objects or WebMCP policy. The execution path fails closed. The decorator controls model-operation exposure; authenticated REST remains the authorization boundary; undeclared effects are classified as destructive; sensitive fields are omitted; stale tools refuse execution; and staged edits cannot self-confirm. Integration fixtures exercise generated definitions, authentication failures, registration lifecycle, policy changes, mounted UI tools, and cross-profile parity. Iolaus consumes published s-m-r-t packages and provides an isolated demo profile. pnpm demo:prepare builds and migrates private SQLite state, seeds visibly fictional opportunities and crawl provenance, starts a loopback-only server, and opens a one-time owner handoff. pnpm demo:smoke runs an authenticated browser proof and verifies both the available capabilities and the absence of approval/submission tools. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was preserving one security and lifecycle model across generated model tools, page-mounted controls, custom component tools, and multiple runtime profiles. A capability policy is only useful if every registration path passes through it. We also had to separate discovery from authorization, exclude sensitive candidate fields, and prevent remounts or policy changes from leaving stale tools behind. The local-first install introduced another systems challenge: safe owner bootstrap, idempotent SQLite setup, private on-device state, deterministic fixtures, and recovery commands all had to work without weakening the deployed application model. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is a first-class generated framework surface, not a hand-built endpoint for one demo. The same declarations drive persistence, APIs, MCP, WebMCP, clients, and knowledge artifacts. Human-visible controls and agent commands converge on shared registries and state. Effect policy and human approval boundaries are explicit and testable. Iolaus installs locally and proves a useful workflow without transmitting an application. Cross-profile fixtures verify that infrastructure choices do not silently change the agent surface. What we learned WebMCP works best as an application architecture concern, not a thin automation layer. Browser tools should derive from the same source of truth as data and authorization. A strong human-agent experience also needs bounded inputs, visible shared state, effect metadata, lifecycle cleanup, deterministic testing, and carefully chosen places where the agent must stop. What's next for s-m-r-t We will continue hardening conformance across generated, mounted, and declared agent surfaces; improve route-aware capability discovery; and make the one-prompt local installation pattern reusable for other s-m-r-t applications. Iolaus will remain a real-world proving ground while preserving private local data and human control of external actions. Source and testing Framework source: https://github.com/happyvertical/smrt Demo application: https://github.com/willgriffin/iolaus Judge instructions: https://github.com/willgriffin/iolaus/blob/main/docs/judge-demo.md Related deployed application: https://willgriffin.dev Both repositories are MIT licensed. The deterministic demo uses Node.js 24.18+, pnpm 11.24.0, and a WebMCP-capable browser. Clone Iolaus, enable Corepack, run pnpm install --frozen-lockfile , then pnpm demo:prepare . Run pnpm demo:test and pnpm demo:smoke for the repeatable proof. The fixture is fictional, local, and never contacts an employer. title: Sigma Studio | AI driven Editor
pitch: Teaching materials meant TeX for math, Word for layout, PowerPoint for figures, and unusable AI. Sigma Studio puts it all on one page that's intuitive to edit, and AI edits it with you. Open source.
about_excerpt: Teaching materials meant TeX for math, Word for layout, PowerPoint for figures, and unusable AI. Sigma Studio puts it all on one page that's intuitive to edit, and AI edits it with you. Open source. Like Comment Story Updates math test template amde by this app rich 3d math editor rich 3d math editor Inspiration Making educational materials has long been a fight against fragmented tools. TeX for equations, Word or Notion for layout, PowerPoint for diagrams, and an AI trapped inside a chat window. On top of that, there are vested commercial interests baked into the software used in education. When a teacher makes a single worksheet, they type \( \int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \frac{1}{3} \) in TeX, draw a parabola in a different program and paste it in as a screenshot, and every time a single number changes, they have to redo everything from scratch. Generative AI was supposed to help, but all it does is turn into an endless cycle of copy-pasting from a chat UI. Teaching materials are not just text. They are publication-quality "page space" where paragraphs, TeX equations, geometric figures, and two-column problem layouts must line up without a millimeter of drift. Until the day the picture in someone's head can be beamed straight into an AI, there's no way for an AI to nail 100% of what a human is picturing on the first try. That's why we designed Sigma Studio around a simple, honest principle of collaboration: "Let AI handle the tedious 90% of the heavy lifting, and let the human quickly polish the crucial final 10% by hand, guided by intuition." What it does Sigma Studio is an open-source, agent-native document editor where an entire piece of teaching material lives on a single responsive page. Write like Word or Notion : paragraphs, headings, auto-numbered problems, and a two-column layout that reflows in real time as you type. Typeset beautifully at TeX quality : TeX-quality equations rendered via KaTeX, visually editable. We obsessed over baseline alignment, line spacing, and margins to achieve the precise typesetting that educational materials demand. Draw intuitively like PowerPoint (fully parametric) : shapes, guide lines, angle arcs, labels, and 2D/3D graphs sit on an overlay canvas directly above the text. Nothing is ever rasterized into an image — everything remains a vector you can re-edit at any time. Toggle "problems only" / "answers only" from a single source document : instantly switch one document between a "problems only" view/printout for class or exams and an "answers only" view/printout for self-grading and explanation. A "90% + 10%" collaborative workflow with AI : when a teacher says "draw the triangle formed by the intersection points of the parabola and the line in problem 3," the AI solves the equations and coordinates via WebMCP and instantly draws the graph and the three lines (that's the 90%). The teacher just reaches for the mouse and nudges a vertex label "A" that's overlapping something, to make it more legible (that's the 10%) — and it's done. Approval-gated proposals (human-in-the-loop) : the AI never overwrites the document on its own. Its changes are drawn on the canvas as a preview diff (a Draft), which a human can approve or discard with one click. Even after applying, it can be undone in a single step. Pixel-perfect vector PDF export : produces high-quality PDFs that match the editor screen down to the pixel. It is provided completely free of charge as MIT-licensed open source. How we built it Built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The body text uses Tiptap/ProseMirror, equations use MathLive and KaTeX, and diagrams are built on a custom overlay canvas plus Three.js for 3D. Exposing semantic document operations via WebMCP At the core of the architecture is exposing operations on the editor's own document model (SigmaDoc) to AI as first-class tools via WebMCP ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). Inside ChatGPT's in-app browser or on Chrome, the AI directly executes structured tools such as: insert_body_content , replace_block , move_blocks insert_shape , update_shape , align_shapes insert_graph , update_graph , insert_graph3d begin_visual_edit_session , inspect_visual_edit_session , propose_visual_edit_session Instead of fragile DOM scraping or guessing at screen coordinates, the AI reads a semantic document tree and injects parametric vector objects directly into the runtime. Challenges we ran into Shape anchors that follow the flow of text : the hardest engineering challenge was making diagrams follow the body text as it wraps and reflows. The instant a teacher hits Enter in the body text, a shape placed with absolute coordinates gets left behind. We built an anchor-binding mechanism that ties each shape to a specific body block ID with a relative offset, so shapes naturally follow along even as text grows, shrinks, or moves across columns. Two-column layouts and dynamic pagination : serious teaching materials require two-column layouts. We built a custom pagination engine from scratch that precisely measures actual rendered DOM heights so that paragraphs, equations, and anchored shapes break cleanly across page boundaries instead of being cut off mid-element. Relentless attention to precise typesetting : to reproduce genuine print-grade typesetting on the web DOM, we tuned equation baselines, Japanese line spacing, problem-number indentation, and line weights down to the millimeter to achieve layout quality comparable to a professionally published textbook. Resolving conflicts between simultaneous human and AI edits : while the AI is busy computing a complex geometric figure, the teacher keeps typing on the keyboard. We validate block IDs and version hashes so that a stale AI proposal for a spot the human has since touched is safely rejected and rebased, preventing accidental overwrites of what was just typed. A PDF pipeline with zero print drift : rather than maintaining a separate print engine, we unified everything around slicing the editor's actual rendered DOM page-by-page via Chromium and stitching the pages together with pdf-lib, achieving a 100% match between what's on screen and what comes out on paper. Accomplishments that we're proud of An intuitive feel for polishing that final 10% : we obsessed over drag handles, snapping, bounding boxes, and block-editor interactions so that refining an AI-generated first draft with the mouse feels as natural and effortless as sketching with a pencil and eraser on paper. Vector persistence (no images) : even when importing TeX or legacy materials, everything lives on as editable vector shapes and coordinate axes rather than static images. Keeping shapes editable in place is essential for teaching materials. A complete, self-contained OSS web app : because everything needed to create teaching materials lives in this one open-source web app, clients can freely modify and use the application with confidence — there is no vendor lock-in to worry about. What we learned Giving AI an "MCP" to manipulate a structured document alongside a human turned out to be a challenge on an entirely different level. Since AI cannot read a human's mind, expecting it to produce something perfect in a single shot is an illusion. We learned that true human-AI collaboration isn't about getting a complex prompt to deliver 100% — it's about providing instant undo, a visual preview, and extremely smooth direct manipulation , so that a human can intuitively carry the AI's 90%-finished foundation the rest of the way to the goal. What's next for Sigma Studio Extending to a learning workspace for students : beyond teachers authoring materials, evolving toward a learning environment where students can converse with AI and visually experiment with geometric proofs or calculus graphs through trial and error. Multi-agent collaborative authoring : building an environment where multiple specialized WebMCP agents — one for equation verification, one for geometric drawing, one for curriculum consistency, and more — can simultaneously propose changes on the same canvas. title: spec-commerce
pitch: Turn building and product specifications into bill-of-materials transactions online.
about_excerpt: Turn building and product specifications into bill-of-materials transactions online. Like 1 Comment Story Updates results from spec review 3-Second Version The easiest way for humans and agents to turn complex building and product specifications into purchasable bills of materials for large construction or infrastructure projects. Inspiration I co-founded and operate US Made Supply , a headless B2B e-commerce business built on Shopify. We domestically source compliance driven products including specialty fire extinguishers , cabinets and other code-driven building products. A lot of what we sell is tied to building specifications or codes, especially on complex projects like fab factories or data centers. The hard part is not just finding a product. It is figuring out which exact products and combinations of products match the specifications, drawings, engineering requirements and building codes. You also need to figure out the right quantities. I recently had to do this on a large project and it took many hours of tedious effort. The process today is still very manual. Someone has to read the specs, understand what is required and what the relevant building codes are, compare it against manufacturer product data, talk to manufacturer reps, review plan detail sheets, build the bill of materials and then turn that into a quote or order. AI agents can help read and reason through these documents but still have a hard time selecting and transacting on the right product combinations. Hallucinations are commonplace. That is the idea behind our spec-commerce prototype. We want to give agents the tools to turn building specifications into bill of materials transactions online. The global building and construction products market is over $2T USD today (just because this needs the usual mandatory ambitious market data!) What it does Helps agents turn complex building specifications and plans into bills of materials for construction projects. We are starting with fire life safety products. It is one script tag on a product page. The tag adds a small panel and registers six tools that an AI agent in the browser can use. The agent reads the customer's spec and passes the requirements to the page. The page checks them against product data, where every value has the cut sheet or product page it came from, and answers in plain words: this product meets the spec or it does not, here is why, and here is what on the site does. The agent can propose lines for a quote request. Only a person can approve them, on the page. There is no tool that can approve. The page never guesses. If a requirement cannot be checked from product data, it says so instead of rounding up. Why WebMCP A customer buying against a spec shows up with a stack of documents. The specification says what the product has to be. The schedule says how many go where. The plan detail sheets show how they mount. The building code sits behind all of it. Then there is the manufacturer's cut sheet, which is where the actual numbers live. An agent is good at reading that stack. It can pull the requirements out of section 2.3, find the quantities on schedule A-601 and keep the code citations straight. The three demo documents in the repo are exactly that stack: a spec excerpt, a schedule sheet and code citations. What the agent cannot do is the last step. Landing on a product page, it has to read the page like a person and guess. It cannot reliably tell whether the product in front of it meets the spec, or which other product does, and it makes things up when it is not sure. That is the wrong place to guess. A fire extinguisher rating is a fact on a cut sheet, and whether a cabinet fits is a matter of inches. WebMCP lets the merchant's own page answer those questions. The store already knows its products, the values on the cut sheets, and which cabinet fits which extinguisher. With WebMCP those facts become tools the agent can call on the page, in the browser the customer is already using. The agent reads the documents and brings the requirements to the page. The page checks them against product data and shows where each value came from. Quantities come from the schedule, never from the spec, and the page keeps that straight too. The agent does not scrape or guess. The store does not build an API or run a server. The customer sees every answer on the page they are looking at, with the source next to it. What people and agents do together Before this, a person read the spec, looked up the products, checked the numbers, built the bill of materials and wrote the quote. It took hours and it was easy to get wrong. An agent on its own could read the spec but could not be trusted with the rest. Now the work splits by who is good at it. The agent reads the spec and asks the page the questions. The page checks the facts and shows its sources. The person decides. The agent proposes lines, and the person approves each one, changes a quantity, or rejects it with a reason, right on the page. The agent reads those decisions back and carries on. Nothing is ordered without a click from a person, and there is no tool that can make that click. How I built it The whole thing is one script tag. The bundle reads the product from the page's JSON-LD, mounts a launcher and a panel in its own shadow DOM so nothing on the page moves and registers six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . This also allows us to add the functionality selectively to pages and also create a multi-tenant system into the future. The six tools: resolve_requirements takes a spec clause as written, or a list of requirements, and answers what in the catalog satisfies it. It understands a basis of design, numbered alternates and two-unit combinations. get_product returns this product's facts, each with its source. Read only. check_requirements checks this product against requirements, one row at a time, with the evidence. find_compatible finds cabinets that physically fit this extinguisher, or the reverse, with the clearance in inches. add_to_quote_request proposes lines and waits for the person to click Approve or Reject on the page. It returns their decisions, their reasons and their notes. get_quote_request returns the approved lines with indicative prices. Nothing is ever submitted from the page. Underneath, the code is in layers. The core is plain TypeScript with no browser in it: the requirement language, the comparators, the class rating math, the cabinet fit geometry, the catalog resolver, the spec reader and the quote request. One adapter per merchant holds the catalog snapshot, every value with its source. Every change to state goes through one set of commands, and the panel and the tools call the same commands, so the agent can never do anything the person could not do by hand. The tools are validated contracts over those commands, and a thin adapter turns them into WebMCP registrations. The panel is React in a shadow root. Matching is deterministic; there is no model in the compliance path. Unknown is a real answer and is never rounded up. An agent may propose; only a person may approve. Quantities never cite the specification as their source, because specs do not carry quantities. Right now we're keeping it pretty simple and there is no server, no database, no API key etc. The small catalog is a committed snapshot and state lives in the tab. It runs in the ChatGPT desktop app's browser in Work mode and in Chrome 149 or newer with the WebMCP flag on. Hosting is Cloudflare and our main site(s) also uses Cloudflare infra. The demo page mirrors our real product page and pins the exact bundle version. Actual demo can be seen in production at: https://usmadesupply.com/safety/fire-extinguishers/halotron/usms-marketplace/products/buckeye-11-lb-halotron-clean-agent-fire-extinguisher?spec-commerce What I learned Most of the surprises were about how agents hand things to a page. In ChatGPT, Chat mode reads pages but does not use site tools; Work mode does. A file attached to the chat stays in the chat and is not handed to a site's tools, but pasted text is. If "Approve for me" is on, the agent may decline on your behalf. What's next for spec-commerce We want to support more product categories and more of the construction workflow. Longer term this could plug into CAD, estimating, procurement and other software used by engineers, architects, contractors and distributors. Maybe over time, smaller models tuned specifically for this kind of work could also make sense. title: Steward
pitch: A WebMCP wallet copilot: any browser agent can audit approvals, vet tokens and stage revokes, transfers or swaps, but only your wallet can sign. Zero delegation. Injections quarantined.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP wallet copilot: any browser agent can audit approvals, vet tokens and stage revokes, transfers or swaps, but only your wallet can sign. Zero delegation. Injections quarantined. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP I built Steward because token approvals are how wallets get drained quietly. You approve a contract once, forget it, and years later it can still move your tokens. Auditing that is exactly the kind of tedious, high-stakes work people want to hand to an agent. But nobody should hand an agent their keys. That constraint is what makes this a WebMCP problem rather than an MCP problem. A server-side tool can read the same public chain data. It can never finish the job, because the signature has to happen where the wallet lives: in the browser, on the page. With WebMCP the agent can scan, explain, and stage a fix, and then the wallet's own signing popup takes over. Neither the page nor the agent can draw that popup, click it, or skip it. stage_revoke returns awaiting_user_confirmation , and everything between that string and the confirm button in your wallet is the product. Also I love the idea of the agent researching the market and assesing tokens with proposing "swap" transactions for the user, all the user has to do is "sign" or "approve" the transaction. How it creates a better user experience Today, checking your approvals means digging through explorer logs, decoding allowances, and guessing whether an unknown spender contract is safe. Most people never do it. With Steward, "is my wallet safe?" is a conversation. The agent calls scan_approvals on any address or ENS name, no wallet connected. It walks the worst results with explain_approval , where every point in the risk score is listed, so there is no black box. It can ask discover_tokens what is moving on Base, run assess_token on anything it finds (GoPlus contract checks, DexScreener liquidity, a Honeypot.is sell simulation, and it refuses to give a verdict on fewer than two sources), check check_gas , and then stage a revoke, a transfer, or a KyberSwap-quoted swap into one review queue. If the token it wants to buy is rated high-risk, the page refuses the swap until the agent has told you why and you have said yes. You see a plain-language summary and the exact calldata, and you sign only what you accept. If you have no wallet extension at all, you still get the full audit on any pasted address. That was a deliberate choice for judges opening this in a browser without MetaMask. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before An agent can now work on a live wallet, research a token's exit safety across three sources, and prepare real transactions, with zero delegated authority. The current industry answer to agents with money is delegation: session keys, agent wallets, spending caps. Those bound the damage, but a prompt-injected agent still complies within its budget, and the security literature treats that as an open problem. Steward gives the agent nothing to delegate. No keys, no session key, no policy to write, no server enclave. The agent does the reading across thousands of on-chain events. The page checks every claim with a live allowance() read, because Approval events can be forged by any contract. You spend your attention on one cryptographic yes or no. It also assumes the chain is hostile. Token names are attacker-controlled text, so every name and symbol is normalised, stripped of hidden characters, and wrapped in ⟦UNTRUSTED⟧ fences before an agent reads it. The demo wallet contains a token whose name is a prompt injection, with a zero-width space hiding the word "instructions" from keyword filters. Steward catches it, fences it, flags it, and scores the approval critical. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP Eight tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() through a small React hook I wrote, useStewardTool (GoogleChromeLabs' use-webmcp-tool was the prior art for its shape). The hook is where the rules live, so no tool can forget them: the standard MCP result envelope, a roughly 1.5K-character output budget measured across the whole envelope, and an automatic quarantine notice on every tool annotated untrustedContentHint . Read tools carry readOnlyHint . The three write tools ( stage_revoke , stage_transfer , stage_swap ) do not, and they can only stage into the review queue. Execution requires the user's wallet. Registration is AbortController-managed and survives React StrictMode. Browsers without WebMCP get a local fallback registry that says plainly that no agent is present. I verified against native Chrome ( --enable-features=WebMCPTesting , Chrome 151 and 152) with a CDP harness in the repo, scripts/verify-native-webmcp.ts , which checks that the real ModelContext holds all eight tools and can execute them. There are 51 tests around the quarantine, the swap gate, and the agent-facing formatting. Challenges I ran into Approval events are forgeable, so logs are only leads. Every candidate pair is checked with a live Multicall3 allowance() read, and only nonzero allowances survive. For vitalik.eth that is 2,293 candidate pairs from logs and 2,191 still live. Keyless data sources drift fast. Base's Blockscout went from usable to a ten-request budget during the week, so Base scanning moved to bounded eth_getLogs windows on the public RPC, and every failure shows as "live scan unavailable" instead of a blank page. I found a caching bug while staging the demo wallet: I set an allowance on-chain, confirmed it, and production kept serving the empty scan from before. Empty results were cached as long as full ones. They now expire in a minute. The first swap gate treated a missing risk verdict as clean. That is the wrong default for money. It now fails closed, and the gate is a pure function with its own tests. An adversarial review found two ways past the quarantine: fullwidth confusable characters that folded into a clean attack after normalisation, and keywords split by invisible characters. Detection now runs on the folded and stripped text as well as the raw bytes. What I learned Prompt injection through on-chain metadata is one token deploy away, not hypothetical. Setting untrustedContentHint is necessary but not enough; the page has to fence the bytes itself so the protection holds in an agent that ignores hints. And the safest consent design is the one with nothing to delegate: when the only signing surface is the user's own wallet popup, there is no policy for a steered agent to comply within. Honesty notes The demo address 0x1111…1111 is a fixture, hostile token included, and the UI labels it as demo data, so the headline demo survives any third-party outage. Every other address is scanned live. Claude Code helped me research, build, review, and write, and every commit it touched says so. The name, the thesis, the scope cuts, and every signature were mine. All code was written inside the submission period (first commit 2026-08-26). MIT licensed. title: StructSketch
pitch: Describe a structure by voice. StructSketch uses WebMCP to create, analyze, inspect, and safely improve the live 3D model with deterministic calculations and explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: Describe a structure by voice. StructSketch uses WebMCP to create, analyze, inspect, and safely improve the live 3D model with deterministic calculations and explicit human approval. Like Comment Story Updates A voice request turns spoken structural intent into WebMCP site tool calls. The existing S-Structures solver calculates the model; the agent never invents engineering results. The change is applied only after explicit human approval, then the analysis runs again. Agent Activity records tool calls, outcomes, UI changes, and analysis versions for an auditable review. Validated parameters generate deterministic geometry, supports, materials, and loads. WebMCP lets the agent inspect the live model, highlight critical members, and control the visible result view. A proposed section change is analyzed as a preview while the live model remains unchanged. StructSketch — Talk to Your Structure Open the tablet. Sketch the frame. Say what you need. See what needs attention. An agent-native workspace for fast, preliminary structural review in the field. Inspiration Picture a timber-framing crew in North America or a compact residential job in Japan. The question is often much smaller than a full building design: Is this light frame behaving as expected? Which member deserves attention? Would a larger section make a meaningful difference? Can we get a useful first answer before returning to the office? These decisions often begin with a hand sketch, a calculator, and practical experience. Full structural-analysis packages are powerful, but creating a model, entering loads, finding the governing result, and revising a member can be too much setup for a quick first look. I wanted that first pass to feel as natural as showing the structure to another person: draw or describe it, ask a question, and see the answer on the same screen. StructSketch does not replace professional design. It makes the preliminary check faster to start, easier to see, and possible to review later. What it does StructSketch is a browser-based 3D structural workspace designed for a tablet-sized field workflow. Sketch, open, or describe a simple structure. Let the agent translate the request into one of five bounded templates: timber warehouse, portal frame, canopy, roof truss, or multistory frame. Confirm the interpreted dimensions, supports, material, and loading before the current model is replaced. Run a deterministic preliminary check and see the model, deformation, warnings, and governing member in the same workspace. Preview a section or material change without modifying the model. Apply it only after explicit human approval. Export an auditable review record containing the model summary, assumptions, results, changes, and Agent Activity history. The key experience is simple: Spoken intent → live 3D model → deterministic analysis → visible result → human-approved change How to try it Open the live StructSketch demo in ChatGPT's in-app browser, then give the agent one of the prompts below. A single kickoff prompt schedules the complete workflow. The agent will pause only when human approval is required to replace the model or apply a proposed change. Timber warehouse — full workflow Use the StructSketch site tools on this page. I want a preliminary review of a timber warehouse: 12.2 m clear span, 4.9 m eave height, 4:12 roof pitch, two 4.8 m bays, cedar timber, pinned bases, collar tie and knee braces, 1.0 kN/m² snow load, and 0.3 kN/m² dead load. First, repeat the interpreted structure and parameters and ask me to approve replacing the current model. After I approve, create and analyze it, summarize the live model, run the deterministic quick check, show the overall deformation, find and focus the governing member, and explain the result in plain English. Then check whether the catalog contains a larger timber section for that governing member. If it does, preview it without changing the model, show the before-and-after result, and ask for my approval before applying it. If no larger timber section exists, do not invent or mix materials; explain the catalog limit and export the review report. Keep the Agent Activity panel visible if available. Steel canopy — full workflow Use the StructSketch site tools on this page. Review an 8 m steel canopy, 3.5 m high and 4 m deep, with fixed bases, a 1:20 roof pitch, and a 4 kN/m downward roof line load. Repeat the interpreted parameters and ask before replacing the current model. After approval, create the canopy, summarize it, run the deterministic quick check, show deformation, identify and focus the governing member, and explain what needs attention. Preview the H-400×200×8×13 catalog section (`h400`) for that member without modifying the model and ask before applying it. After approval, apply the change, rerun the analysis, compare the results, and export the review report. Keep the Agent Activity panel visible if available. Two-storey steel frame — full workflow Use the StructSketch site tools on this page. Create a preliminary model of a two-storey, two-bay steel frame with 8 m total frame width divided into two bays, 3.3 m per storey, 5 m frame depth, fixed bases, and a 4 kN/m downward beam load. Confirm your interpretation with me before replacing the model. After approval, create it and continue through the entire review: model summary, deterministic quick check, deformation view, governing-member search and focus, and a plain-English explanation. Preview the H-400×200×8×13 catalog section (`h400`) for the governing member without changing anything. Ask for approval, then apply it only if approved, rerun the check, compare before and after, and export the final review report with Agent Activity included. Reusable prompt template Use the StructSketch site tools to review [STRUCTURE TYPE] with [DIMENSIONS], [MATERIAL], [SUPPORTS], and [LOAD]. Confirm the interpreted parameters before replacing the model. After approval, create the model, summarize it, run the quick check, show deformation, find and focus the governing member, and explain the result. Preview a suitable improvement without changing the model, ask for approval, then apply it only if approved. Finally, rerun the analysis, compare before and after, and export the review report. Keep Agent Activity visible. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent has to guess what a technical page means from pixels, labels, menus, and click positions. That is fragile, especially when the important information is the live engineering state behind the interface. With WebMCP, StructSketch exposes meaningful actions directly: Summarize the structure currently open on the page. Run the preliminary analysis. Find and highlight the governing member. Show the deformation or check result. Preview a proposed change without touching the model. Apply the approved change and prepare a review report. The page is no longer just something an agent clicks. It becomes a shared workspace where the person and the agent see the same structure, the same result, and the same history. Clear responsibilities The person provides intent, checks the interpretation, and approves consequential changes. The agent translates natural language into structured actions and guides the workflow. StructSketch generates bounded geometry and performs the numerical analysis. The agent does not make up the engineering numbers. How we built it StructSketch is a static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript application deployed on GitHub Pages. It registers 11 site tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Those tools provide structured access to: the model currently visible on the page; the existing S-Structures linear-static solver; critical-member and result-view inspection; five validated structural templates; preview, approve, apply, and revert operations; and a structured review report. The five generators accept bounded parameters and create reproducible geometry, members, supports, sections, and loads. The existing S-Structures engine—not the language model—performs every calculation. Every tool call returns structured, JSON-safe results. The Agent Activity panel records its input, result, warnings, visible UI changes, and analysis version, so the interaction remains visible rather than hidden behind the conversation. Human control and safe editing Inspection and editing are deliberately separated. When someone asks whether a larger section would help, StructSketch first calculates a preview against the current analysis version. The model remains unchanged. Applying the proposal requires explicit confirmation. If the model has changed since the preview, the stale proposal is rejected. If an update fails, the mutation is rolled back. The person can see what was proposed, what was approved, and what changed. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was connecting an agent to a protected, pre-existing analysis core without rewriting it or duplicating its mathematics. title: Tangible Coding Studio: Mission Builder
pitch: A WebMCP-powered studio where primary teachers and AI agents co-create, adapt, validate and review screen-light tangible coding missions on one shared visual lesson canvas.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered studio where primary teachers and AI agents co-create, adapt, validate and review screen-light tangible coding missions on one shared visual lesson canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Teachers set the class context: stage, class size, lesson duration and computational-thinking focus. Available robots, tiles, mats and instruction packs determine grouping and rotation. The shared canvas turns accepted context into a structured mission across all four learning-cycle stages. Learner supports and extension challenges are reviewed separately from the core mission. WebMCP proposals stay pending until the teacher accepts, edits or rejects each operation. Deterministic validation reports 13 checks. Ready for teacher review is not approval. Accepted lesson content becomes a printable Teacher Guide preview. The printable Observation Checklist supports observation without inventing evidence. Inspiration Primary teachers who want to teach computational thinking through physical, screen-light activities face a complicated planning task. A usable lesson has to connect the curriculum goal, class size, lesson duration, available robots and tiles, learner differences, group participation and observable assessment evidence. A conventional AI chatbot can generate a lesson plan, but it normally works outside the teacher’s planning interface. It does not automatically share the application’s accepted class context, may rewrite too much when only one section needs changing, can overlook physical equipment limits, or present generated text without a clear human review boundary. We created Tangible Coding Studio: Mission Builder to explore a different relationship: a primary teacher and an AI agent working on the same structured lesson canvas through WebMCP. The agent can understand the available actions and propose precise changes, while the teacher remains the authority over every accepted lesson decision. What it does Mission Builder supports a seven-step teacher workflow covering: Class context Tangible resources and grouping Mission design Learner support and extension The tangible learning cycle Proposal review Deterministic validation The production application registers exactly five WebMCP tools: set_class_context select_tangible_resources build_tangible_mission adapt_for_learners validate_and_prepare_lesson The first four tools do not directly overwrite accepted lesson content. They create section-scoped pending proposals. The teacher can inspect each operation and then accept it, edit and accept it, or reject it. The fifth tool runs the same deterministic validator available in the visible interface. Validation can mark a lesson Ready for teacher review , but it cannot approve the lesson. Teacher approval and prepared-file generation are intentionally not implemented in this challenge prototype. The Preview workspace derives three browser views from currently accepted content only: Teacher Guide Pupil Mission Card Observation Checklist Pending and rejected proposal content is excluded. Native printing can print the currently selected browser preview, but no PDF-generation or prepared-output service is claimed. Why WebMCP fits this use case WebMCP changes the collaboration from “copy text out of a chatbot” into structured work on a live web application. The key shift is that the agent moves from outside the teacher’s workflow to operating through typed tools against the same structured lesson state. The browser exposes a small, purpose-built set of tools with typed schemas and meaningful descriptions. The agent can select the correct action, return a portable structured proposal and operate against the lesson’s current accepted context. The teacher can see exactly what is proposed inside the product before anything becomes authoritative. This makes several things possible together that are difficult in an ordinary chatbot workflow: The agent works with the application’s real class, equipment and lesson structure. Changes are section-scoped rather than uncontrolled full-document rewrites. Accepted content and proposed content remain separate. Context fingerprints detect stale downstream proposals. Every accepted contribution retains teacher/AI provenance. Validation checks the accepted lesson rather than the agent’s unreviewed draft. The manual workflow remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. WebMCP is therefore not an add-on chat box. It is the collaboration boundary between a browser agent and a teacher-controlled lesson state. Demonstration scenario For our public demonstration, we use The Lost Story Path, a fictional P4 literacy lesson designed for 24 pupils and a 45-minute session. The class has three robots, nine tile sets, three activity mats, three instruction-card packs and 24 role cards. Working in groups, pupils plan a route through a story, arrange the instructions in sequence and test their route using either a robot or a tile-only walkthrough. When they find the mixed-up instruction, they explain what went wrong and how their change repairs the story. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can suggest learner supports and extension activities using the lesson’s actual class context and resources. These suggestions never enter the lesson automatically: the teacher reviews each proposed change and decides whether to accept, edit or reject it. Once the accepted lesson is complete, it passes all 13 validation checks with no errors or warnings. Its status becomes Ready for teacher review, and the teacher can preview a Teacher Guide, Pupil Mission Card and Observation Checklist based only on accepted content. How we built it The application is a browser-local Vite, React and TypeScript prototype. Zod validates WebMCP inputs and portable proposal packages. The accepted lesson, proposal history, validation result and provenance are stored in browser localStorage for the exact origin. The proposal model supports operation-level review and atomic acceptance. Downstream proposal packages can bind to a SHA-256 fingerprint of copied accepted context so stale packages are rejected instead of silently applied to a changed lesson. The same domain validation logic is used by both the visible Validate workspace and the WebMCP validation tool. The Preview workspace reads accepted lesson state only and does not create a second output state. The public application is deployed on Vercel and the complete challenge source is available in a public MIT-licensed GitHub repository. Tangible Coding Ltd’s trademarks, commercial curriculum, hardware designs and other excluded commercial materials are outside the challenge repository’s licence scope. Challenges we faced Preserving human authority The hardest design decision was ensuring that a successful agent call never meant that lesson content had already been accepted. Tool execution may create pending proposal state, but only an explicit teacher action can move a proposed operation into accepted lesson content. Moving context safely between agent and teacher browsers Browser-local storage is intentionally origin- and profile-specific. We created portable proposal packages and accepted-context packages so the teacher controls what moves between contexts. Versioned packages, structural “before” values and context fingerprints protect against stale imports. Recovering a lesson without bypassing review During testing we restored a lesson from portable proposal evidence. The mission operations and learner adaptations were imported as pending changes and accepted individually. This demonstrated that recovery could preserve the teacher-review boundary instead of importing an authoritative lesson snapshot. Keeping readiness separate from approval The validator can determine that required planning information is present, durations match and resource/grouping conditions are feasible. It still reports Ready for teacher review rather than “approved.” This distinction is visible across Validate, Preview and the WebMCP result. Verified production result On 31 August 2026, we tested the complete workflow in production using a WebMCP-capable browser agent. The agent discovered and successfully used all five registered WebMCP tools. Across the session, the teacher reviewed and individually accepted 13 proposed changes. The completed lesson then passed all 13 validation checks with no errors or warnings, and all three accepted-content previews rendered correctly. We also refreshed the application to confirm that the lesson, resources, proposal history, authorship information and validation result were retained. The lesson remained Ready for teacher review, not approved. This is an important part of the design: the agent can help create and improve the lesson, but the teacher remains responsible for every accepted decision. What we learned The strongest lesson was that useful AI collaboration does not require giving an agent authority over the final state. A narrow tool catalogue, explicit proposal objects, visible rev

title: The Line List
pitch: An agent-native manufacturing copilot that turns a product idea into a manufacturer-ready plan, finds the right partners, and prepares outreach through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An agent-native manufacturing copilot that turns a product idea into a manufacturer-ready plan, finds the right partners, and prepares outreach through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Agent-Native Document Collaboration Package Design Comparing Manufactories Outreach Inspiration I started The Line List because my girlfriend sells banana bread, and we started asking a simple question: what would it actually take to get her product manufactured and into stores? The answer was way more confusing than it should be. Manufacturer websites are inconsistent, important details are hard to find, and new founders usually do not even know what questions they should be asking. I wanted to make that process feel less overwhelming. The Line List originally started as a public directory of food and beverage manufacturers. For the WebMCP Challenge, I built a new sourcing workspace that lets a founder and their AI agent work through the process together. What it does A founder can describe what they want to make in plain language. Their agent then creates a living product brief and helps them work through the decisions that actually matter, such as product format, production volume, shelf life, packaging, and where they want to sell. The founder can review everything visually in the browser, explore a packaging direction in 3D, and see which information was confirmed, suggested, or still unknown. Once the product is ready for research, the agent can find manufacturer possibilities and explain why each one appeared. The Line List does not pretend that missing information is a match. Supported details include sources and review dates, while unknowns and possible conflicts remain visible. The agent can also prepare manufacturer-specific introduction drafts, but it cannot contact anyone on its own. The founder selects the manufacturers, reviews the exact information being shared, approves the message, and separately confirms when they are ready to send it. How I built it I built the experience with Next.js, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Prisma, Three.js, and WebMCP. The website exposes structured tools that let the agent create and update the same product workspace the founder sees on the page. The tools cover workspace creation, product updates, packaging previews, manufacturer matching, PDF export, outreach preparation, and readiness checks. The important part was making WebMCP feel like part of the product instead of attaching a chatbot to the side of the website. The person handles visual decisions and final approvals, while the agent handles the repetitive research, organization, and drafting work. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was managing shared state between the person, the agent, and the website without letting them overwrite each other. I had to keep confirmed founder statements separate from agent suggestions, preserve unknown information, make mutations safe to retry, and ensure that manufacturer requirements could not be silently weakened just to produce more results. Packaging was another challenge. I wanted the agent to do more than recommend a package in text. It needed to open the actual 3D workbench so the founder could see the direction, make changes, and approve the exact version that would become part of the manufacturing brief. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am most proud of the broader-search approval flow. If no manufacturer publicly proves every required capability, the agent cannot quietly relax the search. The founder sees the exact before-and-after criteria, reviews what will change, and decides whether to continue. Even after broadening, unsupported details stay marked as unknown. I am also proud that the experience goes beyond a basic WebMCP demo. It creates a persistent workspace, connects agent actions to visible interface changes, includes a real packaging workbench, produces evidence-backed manufacturer possibilities, and keeps the founder in control of anything external. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when the website and agent each handle the parts they are best at. The agent is good at turning a messy idea into structured information, researching options, and preparing work. The browser is better for comparing results, reviewing visual changes, understanding what will be shared, and making final decisions. Building around that relationship made the experience feel much more useful than either a normal form or a standalone chatbot. What's next for The Line List Next, I want to improve the packaging models, expand the manufacturer data, and let founders manage multiple products and manufacturer conversations from one account. The larger goal is to make launching a physical product feel less like navigating an industry built for insiders. A founder should be able to start with an idea, understand what they need, find the right production partners, and move forward without guessing through every step. title: ToolMint
pitch: ToolMint lets non-technical site owners make their website agent-ready, by showing it how to do a job one time.
about_excerpt: ToolMint lets non-technical site owners make their website agent-ready, by showing it how to do a job one time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We provided small and medium businesses assistance with various no-code tools, such as site creators, form builders, and tools for automating processes over the years. What makes these tools work is simple: users don’t need to write detailed technical specifications. They show or explain the tool what they want, or build it visually(drag n drop editors), and the tool handles the technical work. That’s how a shop owner can create a booking form without needing to call a developer. When we explored WebMCP, we noticed a clear gap. Making a website agent-ready required writing tool definitions in code. But avoiding code is exactly why people choose no-code tools in the first place. This meant that many of the businesses that could benefit most from agents were also the least likely to adopt them. We started thinking about what a no-code approach to WebMCP might look like and built a workflow that feels familiar.A website owner records themselves performing an action on their site. ToolMint’s SDK converts that recording into a draft WebMCP action, along with a clear, human-readable description of what the tool does, what inputs it requires, and what action it performs - all in simple, non technical terms.The owner reviews and approves the draft. Once published, the action becomes available for visitors to use through their agents. What it does ToolMint lets a site owner perform a task once, like booking an appointment. It records the workflow and turns it into an approved WebMCP tool that agents can use. How we built it ToolMint runs as a single Node.js service on Render. It serves the demo website, SDK and a control-plane API , with SQLite storing approved tools and their versions. It has four main parts: Recorder (part of sdk) — Runs inside the website and observes the task performed by the owner. It captures meaningful form changes, actions, page outcomes and the structure of related same-origin network requests. Compiler — Converts the recording into a versioned capability. It identifies the successful workflow, determines possible agent inputs, builds a replay recipe, and creates success and failure checks from what actually happened on the page. SDK — Loads approved capabilities for the current website and user surface, then registers them as native WebMCP tools. Tools can be updated or revoked without changing the website’s application code. Runtime — Executes a tool inside the live authenticated page. It validates inputs, resolves the correct record, follows the recorded steps, respects confirmation policy, and verifies that the expected page state and network operation occurred. Individual tool calls do not pass through the ToolMint backend. OpenAI helps improve names, descriptions and input recommendations. It does not generate selectors, execution steps, permissions or success proofs. Those come from observed evidence, are reviewed by the owner, and are compiled deterministically before publishing. Challenges we ran into Knowing whether the task really worked was harder than replaying the clicks. A success message was not enough. Every write capability needs evidence that the page actually changed, together with the expected network response when available. If ToolMint cannot produce a reliable proof, it will not publish the capability. People make mistakes while recording. Our first version treated the entire recording as one script, so a typo followed by a retry became part of the generated tool. We had to split recordings into attempts, compile only the path through the final success, and preserve earlier failures as known failure conditions. Deciding what should become an agent input. Real pages contain many fields that have nothing to do with the task. ToolMint considers what the owner changed, what appeared during the workflow and what the success proof depends on. The owner makes the final decision, but cannot remove an input required to verify the result. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built the complete record-to-tool loop. A site owner can perform a real task, review the inferred inputs and policy, publish it, and see a new native WebMCP tool become available without writing a handler or building another API. The generated tools work across user sessions. A workflow recorded with one customer’s vehicles can be invoked with another customer’s vehicles because account-specific choices are rebuilt from the current authenticated page. The tools verify their own results. A write is not reported as successful just because the final button was clicked. ToolMint checks the observed page state and related network response before returning success. We kept AI assistance within clear boundaries. OpenAI can improve names, descriptions and recommendations, but it cannot invent selectors, execution steps, permissions or proofs. The final capability is compiled deterministically from recorded evidence and approved by the owner. What we learned A recorded workflow is evidence, not a finished tool. Raw clicks include mistakes, temporary state and values that only belong to the person recording. They need to be interpreted before they can become a reusable capability. Reliable agent tools need clear success conditions. Executing the final action is not enough. The tool must know what changed and whether it changed for the right record. What's next for ToolMint Tell the owner when a tool breaks. We already record every execution; right now that data stays in the browser. Sending it back gives us health status, drift detection at registration, and a reason to pause a capability automatically. Wider Capture - autocomplete widgets and shadow-DOM component libraries are all invisible to the recorder today.
