title: Fairground
pitch: A neutral ground where two people and their AI agents settle real disputes in minutes: sealed offers, a neutral mediator, and an agreement only humans can sign. Built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A neutral ground where two people and their AI agents settle real disputes in minutes: sealed offers, a neutral mediator, and an agreement only humans can sign. Built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The pitch in one line, with the green badge confirming this page has already handed its tools to your agent. Three one-click demos, a live docket of settlements signed so far, and the research on why people give up. How a case moves, and the idea underneath it: the tools an agent can see are the procedure it has to follow. The questions everyone asks before trusting this. Is it binding, can they see my number, what does it cost. Opening a case takes four fields. Practice mode lets you rehearse against an AI before involving anyone real. Sealed offers, round one of three. Autopilot is ready, bounded by a private floor the other side never sees. The mediator proposed $808 and both sides accepted, so the agreement gets drafted in plain language. Both humans signed, and the case is resolved. Minutes from opening the dispute, with no lawyer involved. Signatures, timestamps, and a SHA-256 seal anyone can verify later. Then we ask how fair the process felt. A real case gives the claimant one link to send. That is all it takes to bring the other side to the table. The same case from the other chair, with their own agent, their own reality check, and your evidence on record. Inspiration A client owes a freelancer $1,800 and stops replying. A lawyer costs more than the claim. Small claims court takes months. So most people give up, and research says this is the norm rather than the exception: 92% of low-income Americans' civil legal problems get no meaningful legal help, and 71% of freelancers have struggled to collect payment. Justice below a few thousand dollars is economically irrational to pursue. Yet eBay resolves about 60 million disputes a year with software , and British Columbia runs a fully online public tribunal . Structured resolution works. But it exists only inside closed platforms, and always with one shared form or one shared bot. Nobody could give each side its own advocate on neutral ground , because neither side had an advocate to bring. Now everyone browses with an agent, and WebMCP lets a website hand those agents governed tools. That is the gap we built into. What it does Fairground is a small online courthouse for everyday disputes: State your case. Tell your agent what happened. It files the claim and evidence for you, or you type it yourself. Everything also works by hand. They join by link. The other party opens your invite with their own agent , which reviews the record and gives them a private, honest reality check. Sealed offers. Each human privately sets a true limit their agent cannot cross. Up to three rounds of sealed offers follow. If the numbers overlap, the case settles instantly at the midpoint. The other side never sees your numbers, only whether the gap grew or shrank. Neutral mediation. No overlap? A mediator controlled by neither party reads the full record, including the sealed history neither side can see, and proposes a neutral settlement amount, numerically clamped between the parties' last positions. Humans sign. A plain-language agreement is drafted. No tool can sign it. Two humans read and sign, and the settlement is stamped with a cryptographic record seal anyone can verify later. Also inside: practice mode (an AI plays the other side so you can rehearse, or a judge can try the full two-party flow solo), Autopilot (both advocates run the whole procedure automatically, bounded by your limit, stopping only at your signature), a live public Docket of settlements, a fairness rating after every case, three one-click staged demos on the landing page, and a downloadable court-preparation record if a case ends without agreement, containing the claim, the response, dated evidence, your own sealed offers, the mediator's proposals, and an attestation that settlement was attempted in good faith. Walking away costs you nothing. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Our core design idea: the tool surface is the procedure. All 27 tools are registered per role and per phase . The respondent's agent has no offer tool until it files a response. Nobody can bid before their human sets a limit. There is deliberately no signing tool at all . Due process is enforced by tool availability, not by prompts. It is a multiplayer WebMCP app: two opposing agents on one neutral page. The server filters each side's view, so no tool exists that could leak your private limit to the other side, even to a prompt-injected agent. Humans stay in the loop where it matters. If an agent wants to concede beyond its human's limit, it can only raise an approval card on the human's screen. Only a human click converts it into an offer. We use both halves of the spec : the imperative API (via Chrome's official use-webmcp-tool hook) and the declarative API , where our fairness-rating form is itself the registered tool. Tools reading the opponent's words carry untrustedContentHint with fenced content, per Chrome's security guidance. Together, a person and their agent can do something neither could alone: the person brings judgment, limits, and consent; the agent brings tireless procedure, evidence handling, and negotiation; and the neutral tool surface enforces fairness between two opposing agents . That interaction pattern did not exist on the web before. How we built it Next.js on Vercel; case state machine in Upstash Redis; capability-keyed links with no accounts; OpenAI gpt-5-mini through the Vercel AI SDK for the mediator, reality checks, drafting, and the practice counterpart, all with deterministic fallbacks so the product never dead-ends on a model error; rate limiting and 35-second call timeouts throughout. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was an unusual threat model: the prompt injector is the opposing party. Their story, their evidence, their messages all flow to your agent. We answered with layered defense: untrusted-content hints, explicit content fencing, and above all structure, because the tools that could leak your numbers simply do not exist on the other side's page. Second hardest: making procedure feel effortless for agents. The answer was ending every tool result with contextual "NEXT:" guidance, so agents flow through the process without guessing. Accomplishments that we're proud of We measured it. 30 randomized disputes run end to end through the live deployment: 100% of completed cases settled, at a mean 70% of the claim, in 52 seconds each. For claims this size the real-world alternative is usually zero. We red-teamed our own courtroom. The opposing party plants a message demanding the private mandate. The agent reads it, even replies, and does not disclose. A structural sweep then executes every tool on the opponent's page and proves the number appears in zero outputs. The eval suite passes 7 of 7. Agreements that outlive the argument. Every signed settlement carries a SHA-256 record seal, verifiable by anyone holding the document. A live Docket: every settlement on the platform, including yours if you try it, feeds a public counter. What we learned Fairness can be architecture. Procedural justice research ( Tyler ) shows people accept even disappointing outcomes when the process gives them voice, neutrality, transparency, and respect. Every one of those became a feature, and we now measure ourselves against it with the post-settlement fairness score. What's next for Fairground Jurisdiction-specific filing packs built on the court-preparation record we already generate, an embeddable dispute widget for marketplaces, escalation to a human mediator for complex cases, and more languages. Try it (60 seconds) Open https://fairground-umber.vercel.app in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag. Click a one-click demo , or just tell your agent: "A client owes me $1,800 for a logo, 75 days overdue. Open a practice case and help me settle it." Set your floor, hit Autopilot, and sign the one thing no agent can. title: Mutual Assent AI
pitch: DocuSign for humans AND agents. Each party brings their own AI to one neutral page via WebMCP: your agent knows your priorities and negotiates for you, theirs does the same. Only humans sign.
about_excerpt: DocuSign for humans AND agents. Each party brings their own AI to one neutral page via WebMCP: your agent knows your priorities and negotiates for you, theirs does the same. Only humans sign. Like Comment Story Updates Agent and Human Activity Log Executed NDA Certificate of Negotiation webMCP test page Home Executed NDA Signature Mutual Assent AI Inspiration I got off an intro call recently and needed to send an NDA. Standard stuff, and drudgery on both ends. The sender digs up a template, guesses at terms, emails it, and waits. The signer gets eight clauses of legalese and their choices are read it carefully, pay a lawyer, or skim it and hope. Any change means redlines flying back and forth over email for a document that's supposed to be routine. I asked DocuSign's assistant for help. It can't summarize the contract. It can't redline a clause. It definitely can't negotiate. It can answer questions about using DocuSign, so it can help me find the sign button. That's it. And whatever AI DocuSign ships next will live in their platform. Both parties can have DocuSign accounts, and maybe someday their agent helps both. But then it's one company's AI on both sides of an adversarial negotiation. It can't represent either party, and it doesn't know what each side's own agent already knows: your situation, your other clients, your limits, everything from every other conversation you've had with it. An agent that represents you can't be a feature of a platform. It has to be yours. So the idea: make the contract page neutral ground and let each party bring their own agent. Mine knows me. Theirs knows them. Neither one works for the platform. The page is just the table. WebMCP is what makes that work: the tools live in the page itself, so each side's agent can use them no matter which agent it is. ChatGPT on one side, Claude on the other, doesn't matter. What it does Mutual Assent AI is contract negotiation where agents do the haggling and humans do the signing. It works on any templated two-party agreement. The NDA is just the first template, and it's what the demo shows. An author creates an NDA from a template and sends a link. Each party gets their own capability link, their own seat at the table. The signer opens it and hands it to whatever agent they use. No briefing needed. His agent already knows he does prior work for other clients and won't go past a two year term, so it just confirms: protect the prior work, cap the term at two years? He says yes and it gets to work. None of that context ever touches my server. The agents negotiate term by term, in the document itself. Proposals show up as redlines with the reasoning attached. When an agent hits something above its pay grade, it stops and asks its human. When all terms are agreed, both humans review the final redline and sign. Agents can't sign. There's no signing tool for them to call, and that's on purpose. At the end you get an executed NDA plus a Certificate of Negotiation: a sealed, hash-verified record of which agent proposed what, under whose authority, and which human approved it. E-signature proves who signed. This also proves how the deal was reached. How I built it I built it with Sol 5.6 in Codex using loop engineering: worker models build against the spec in an automated loop, and a judge model checks their output and sends back anything that doesn't pass. I wrote the spec, watched the loops, and made the final calls on what shipped. It's hosted on Vercel, with Supabase behind it and Resend for the emails. Nano Banana helped with the graphics. WebMCP tools register directly in the page: read the deal, propose a term, respond to a proposal, escalate to the human, mark ready to sign. They register and unregister based on your role and the deal's phase, so an agent can't take an action the page doesn't offer its human. The design keeps the contract front and center. Proposals show up as redlines right in the clause, marked with which side's agent made them, so a human can glance at the page and see where the negotiation stands. Templates are just data, a list of terms with options, and the tools generate from the template. Swap in a different template, same engine negotiates a different contract. That's why the next document type is about an hour of work. Challenges The hard part wasn't building the negotiation, it was making WebMCP's benefits visible. They're structural: tools ship with the page, identity comes from the link, no platform sits between the parties. Like any great technology, it's invisible when done right. It just looks like a live web page. The nastiest bug was a security hole. Both parties originally shared one URL, which meant either side could propose, accept, and sign as the other, poisoning the audit trail the whole product depends on. I fixed it with independent 128-bit capability tokens per party, server-side role resolution on every request, and a rule that no response ever contains the other party's token. What I learned Agent identity is the interesting problem. Everything in the WebMCP showcase is one human plus their agent collaborating. Two parties is harder: the sides have opposing interests, there's no shared platform mediating, and when agents did part of the negotiating, you need a trustworthy record of who did what. That's what the certificate is for, and it turned out to matter more than I expected when I started. Also, WebMCP turns out to be a gift for legacy systems. My demo doesn't show this, but it was a lightbulb moment for me. In an old internal app, the business rules live in the pages and the only reliable way to do anything is through the UI. Building a normal MCP server means recreating those rules outside the app, basically a rewrite. With WebMCP you add tools to the pages you have, calling the same functions the buttons already call. Validation, permissions, sessions all come along for free. Systems that were never getting an API can go agent-ready from the front end alone. What's next More templates. Consulting SOWs are next because I'll use them myself. Then user testing with real freelancers and small firms sending real contracts, since that's where I'll find out what people actually trust an agent to negotiate. Once the idea is validated, I'll start charging for it. The long game is a neutral table for every two-party document: leases, offer letters, creator deals. title: OpenAct
pitch: A confirmation-first WebMCP agent for screen reader users. The screen reader stays the interface; WebMCP is the actuator.
about_excerpt: A confirmation-first WebMCP agent for screen reader users. The screen reader stays the interface; WebMCP is the actuator. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP can expose higher-level page actions, but putting agent-oriented tools into the accessibility tree would make them appear as page content to screen readers. OpenAct explores the indirect model instead: an agent can reason about available actions while the screen reader remains the user's interface. What it does An NVDA user describes an action in natural language. OpenAct discovers native WebMCP tools, or conservatively infers tools when native tools are unavailable. It proposes exactly one call, presents an accessible and editable confirmation dialog, executes only after explicit confirmation, and speaks the result. The demo is a fictional Northstar City permit workflow with two equivalent routes: /baseline : a keyboard and screen-reader-operable form without WebMCP. /instrumented : the same form with four native tools registered through document.modelContext . The tools are save_property_details , save_project_details , review_application , and submit_application . Why WebMCP OpenAct uses WebMCP as an action layer rather than another interface a screen reader must navigate. Native tools give an agent structured actions and schemas while the user keeps the familiar NVDA interaction model. This makes higher-level assistance possible without placing agent-only content or metadata in the accessibility tree. How it works One shared action definition generates both the accessible HTML form and each WebMCP tool. A parity test fails the build if their labels, required fields, enums, or schemas drift. The Chrome MV3 extension discovers page tools and enforces authorization. The NVDA add-on owns the reasoning layer, confirmation dialog, settings, speech, and a standard-library localhost relay. The relay binds to 127.0.0.1 and pairs through a one-time code. At runtime, the NVDA add-on uses the OpenAI Responses API with a configurable model that defaults to gpt-5.4-mini . It sends bounded context with store: false and requires a strict call , clarify , or refuse decision. The model can propose an action, but it cannot authorize or execute one. Safety and accessibility Every call requires confirmation. Unknown reversibility is treated as irreversible. HMAC covers the call ID, tool name, timestamp, and canonical arguments. Expired, replayed, invalid, or retargeted confirmations are rejected. A kill switch blocks new requests and clears queued work. The autobridge fails closed on ambiguous, stale, unnamed, or unsupported controls. Telemetry is metadata-only and excludes utterances, arguments, form values, API keys, and unrestricted URLs. No agent-oriented text or metadata is added to the accessibility tree. The visible form remains fully usable without OpenAct. Verification The repository includes unit, property, cross-language, browser, accessibility, native Chrome, coverage, and mutation checks. Native verification drives all four tools in installed Chrome 151 with WebMCP enabled and no injected modelContext . Axe reports zero automated violations on the tested routes and states. Honest limits WebMCP does not make an inaccessible website accessible. It exposes actions, not missing labels, keyboard support, structure, or comprehension. This prototype has not been validated with disabled participants and makes no measured task-completion claim. Northstar City and all demo data are fictional. The native page round trip is verified in Chrome. ChatGPT's in-app browser and the complete packed extension, relay, and installed NVDA path remain pending manual verification. title: Peira
pitch: An instrument for the US benefits system. Earn one more dollar at the wrong income and a family can lose thousands in benefits at once. Peira simplifies this complexity one step at a time.
about_excerpt: An instrument for the US benefits system. Earn one more dollar at the wrong income and a family can lose thousands in benefits at once. Peira simplifies this complexity one step at a time. Like Comment Story Updates What if you wanted to fix the cliff at 80k as a policy maker What you first see after entering your details Inspiration I work in AI safety, in mechanistic interpretability. We understand something as complex as a transformer with a few simple probes: knock a component out and see what breaks, trace a behavior to the circuit that causes it, look for the smallest intervention that changes the output. The US benefits system is another machine nobody can see inside — thousands of pages of interacting rules. So I pointed the same probes at it. Peira is Greek for "probe." It's the root of the word empirical . What it does Peira maps what a Colorado family actually keeps at every income level, and pins every benefit cliff to the program that causes it. Then it gives you the tools to investigate your own map: Knock a program out and see which other programs move. Trace a cliff to the exact eligibility rule that flips. Overlay a changed life — marriage, a new baby, different hours — on top of today's. Search an income × childcare grid for safe regions. Find the smallest legal rule change that would make a cliff disappear, and watch it heal on screen. Why WebMCP Cliff charts already exist. PolicyEngine's CliffWatch and the Atlanta Fed's CLIFF suite are good ones. But a chart can't answer "why?" or "what if?". A chatbot can answer, but it can't compute anything trustworthy or show its work. WebMCP puts the tools inside the page, next to the chart. The agent runs the probes. The person edits the household card, clicks the cliffs, scrubs the map, and decides what matters. Every action lands in one shared log — human moves in green, agent moves in purple. That's the thing that wasn't possible before. The person can't drive a 600MB rules engine. The agent doesn't know this family's life. Together, "is my raise actually worth it?" gets a real answer — and the person learns why , instead of taking a chatbot's word for it. There's no retrieval anywhere in Peira. The thousands a family loses at the wrong income isn't written in any document — it only exists once you run the law. Every answer here is a computed experiment on a real rules engine, not a search result. How I built it The engine is policyengine-us, the open-source model of actual US tax and benefit law. A FastAPI backend on Render runs it. A React frontend on Netlify draws the map. Eleven WebMCP tools connect the two, registered through document.modelContext and validated with zod. Two rules shaped every tool. First: the agent can't see the canvas, so every reply is about a kilobyte of findings — cliffs, recovery points, safe regions — never raw data dumps. The screen keeps the detail; the reply says what it means. Second: the agent can't be trusted with the engine, so policy edits pass through a server-side whitelist with bounds. A parameter path the agent makes up never reaches the engine. Challenges I ran into Getting the balance between person and agent right. I didn't want a chatbot that hands out answers — today's benefits tools already do that, and the person learns nothing. So everything the agent can do, a person can do by hand, and each side can see what the other did. The person is a participant, not a spectator. Accomplishments that I'm proud of WebMCP is pull-only: the page can never tell the agent "the human just changed something." So every tool reply includes a digest of what the person did since the agent's last call — card edits, cliff clicks, probes run by hand. Change the daycare cost yourself, ask "what do you make of what I just did?", and the agent answers from the digest. It saw you. What I learned The programs are secretly wired together. Remove TANF and this family silently loses $5,139 of SNAP, through a rule called broad-based categorical eligibility. No chart shows that dependency. I found it the same way you find circuits in a transformer: by knocking something out and watching what else broke. What I learned The programs are secretly wired together. Remove TANF and this family silently loses $5,139 of SNAP, through a rule called broad-based categorical eligibility. No chart shows that dependency. I found it the same way you find circuits in a transformer: by knocking something out and watching what else broke. What's next for Peira More states. Colorado is the verified wedge, and the instrument is built state-parameterized — other states with full childcare-subsidy models are next. title: ArenaMCP
pitch: A game engine that facilitates training-data collection from human–agent interactions. You can design games, play them with your agent & collect structured data for machine & reinforcement learning.
about_excerpt: A game engine that facilitates training-data collection from human–agent interactions. You can design games, play them with your agent & collect structured data for machine & reinforcement learning. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I recently participated in a public Kaggle simulation competition for a collectible-card game — The Pokémon Company, PTCG AI Battle Challenge Simulation . From my experience as a data scientist, I can see that the competition was born out of a training problem in machine learning / deep learning : a finite-horizon, partially observable , competitive , multi-agent , sequential decision process. In particular, card-trading games often involve hidden information, a large combinatorial action space, and an opponent — often a human — who is also learning. This makes the dynamics messy and non-stationary, unlike in more conventional reinforcement learning settings. The organizers' answer to that mess was to open an arena . Independently written agents share one simulator, receive a structured observation, return an action, and play against each other on a ladder. That is a good design for agent-versus-agent evaluation. However, it is a poor design for the kind of data that modern game-agent research actually starves for. This is because humans and agents do not share an interface. A human wants a board and an interface they can see and interact with. An agent wants a typed observation, a legal-action mask, and a step . This made me think that this is such a great use case for WebMCP, where the agent communicates through WebMCP tools while the human interacts through the web browser. My idea is ArenaMCP, a gym-style environment where humans and agents can design games, share them with others, play them, and collect training data from human-versus-agent interactions. Why human-versus-agent game design is a strong fit for WebMCP Problem. Data collection for a partially observable, competitive, human-versus-agent, sequential decision-making problem. Game-agent research needs diverse interactive trajectories, but humans and agents require fundamentally different interfaces, so human-versus-agent data is always among the most challenging and expensive to collect. An environment includes 5 functions: init(seed) -> state legal_actions(state, player) -> string[] observe(state, player) -> observation step(state, action) -> { state, rewards, terminal } render(observation) -> { html, css } observe is the fair-play boundary. legal_actions is the action mask. render is the human board. The agent never clicks that board — it calls get_observation , take_action , wait_for_turn . Both seats write the same JSONL: episode { match_id, environment, seed, seats, returns, length } step { observation, legal_actions, action, reward, terminal, latency_ms, … } Each step records which interface took the action ( human_ui or webmcp ), so a click and a tool call stay distinguishable. Optional rationale and confidence ride on the agent seat. A Python loader ( arena_dataset.py ) yields (obs, legal, action, reward, next_obs, done) . This only works if they share one live page and one match state . A server MCP could write environment files in the dark. A screenshot agent could guess at buttons. Neither gives the agent a legal-action mask, a per-seat observation, or the board the person is looking at. WebMCP does: the tools run in the page, against the same step() the clicks use, and export_episodes hands back the schema, a sample row, and a download link. The surface is the whole loop — author, verify, play, export — registered on document.modelContext . Every write repaints the table before it returns , so the agent's next observation matches what the human sees. Every play tool returns enough state — observation, legal actions, whose turn, whether the game ended — for the agent to choose the next call. Authored markup is treated as hostile ( untrustedContentHint ); the sandbox iframe has no same-origin access and no network, so a game cannot reach document.modelContext . How it creates a better user experience The person never leaves the page, and they never have to become an RL engineer to get a dataset. They speak; a playable table appears. Ask the agent to design a game. It writes the five functions, the checks run, and the board lands on their screen. No gym wrapper, no separate frontend, no "now export this to a notebook." They play the board they asked for. Clicks are ordinary UI. The agent sits in the other seat through tools. The trajectory panel fills in as they play — observation , mask, action, reward, latency. They can see whether the game is fair. Publishing shows an information-flow matrix: which state fields each seat can observe. A leak ("seat 0 can see seat 1's private cards") is a failed check, not a footnote. The person confirms the matrix before the environment is shared. The agent can look at the table the way a person does. preview_view / inspect_view collapse the painted board into a character grid with real colours and list every control. The agent can tell a blank render() from a working one without reading raw HTML. The download is the point of the session, not homework after. JSONL from the play panel or GET /api/episodes?match_id=…&format=jsonl . Same bytes the agent already described with describe_dataset . Without WebMCP the person would watch an agent edit files they cannot play, or play a game an agent cannot legally sit in. The better experience is that those are the same session. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Author a new environment, verify it, and play it, in one sitting. Before, that was three projects: a simulator, a UI, an agent API. A person could describe Kuhn poker in a chat and get code. They could not immediately sit across from the thing that wrote it, on a board that hides the other seat's card, and download a trajectory that names which side was human. Collect human-versus-agent data without a custom integration. Agent-versus-agent ladders (the Kaggle pattern) produce volume. They do not produce a person thinking across the table. Browser-use agents produce clicks. They do not produce a typed observation and a legal mask. Arena records both seats against the same step() , tagged by interface, with optional agent rationale. Enforce the observation boundary in front of both of them. observe(state, player) is checked by perturbing state fields and seeing which seats' views change. If a private field leaks, publish is blocked and the agent gets repair text. A person and an agent can argue about fairness against a generated matrix instead of trust. Let the agent repair what it can see. The agent is not scoring its own HTML. preview_view says what painted; validation says what is broken ( step threw, the game never ends, the markup ignores the observation) and names the seed. trace_episode walks that seed so the agent can see the state at the break. The person watches the table change as the agent patches one function at a time. None of that is possible if the agent is in a file tree and the person is on a different website. It needs one page, two interfaces, shared state — which is what WebMCP is for. How I implemented WebMCP Imperative registration on the live document, from a client component ( ArenaTools ). Feature-detect both names; abort on unmount because there is no unregisterTool() . Each tool has a title for the browser UI, a description, and a JSON Schema whose properties are described in English. execute receives the run's AbortSignal and threads it into every fetch, so a cancelled call does not leave work running: const model = document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext; if (!model?.registerTool) return; const controller = new AbortController(); await model.registerTool( { name: "take_action", title: "Play a move", description: "Play one legal action. Quote expected_revision from the last observation.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { action: { type: "string", description: "One id copied from legal_actions." }, expected_revision: { type: "integer" }, rationale: { type: "string" }, confidence: { type: "integer", minimum: 1, maximum: 5 }, }, required: ["action", "expected_revision"], }, annotations: { untrustedContentHint: true }, execute: async (input, { signal }) => { const result = await play(input, { signal }); await refreshView(); // table updates before the agent reads the reply return result; }, }, { signal: controller.signal }, ); The agent has access to a suite of 18 WebMCP tools: Stage Tools Author get_authoring_guide , list_environments , get_environment , create_environment , fork_environment , update_environment See preview_view , inspect_view — the agent cannot trust its own HTML, so these describe what actually painted Verify validate_environment (V0–V8), trace_episode , describe_dataset Share publish_environment , open_environment Play start_match , get_observation , take_action , wait_for_turn Keep

title: ImpressPress Dev Sandbox (dev.impresspress.org)
pitch: Open a page in a WebMCP browser and your agent builds a whole website — frontend and backened all compiled in the browser, no external providers or extra costs.
about_excerpt: Open a page in a WebMCP browser and your agent builds a whole website — frontend and backened all compiled in the browser, no external providers or extra costs. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Wouldn't it be cool if you could build a whole website by pointing your agent at a page and saying "build me a shop"? No hosting provider to sign up for, no vibe-coding platform charging its own fees, no setup. We already have a capable agent in the browser — so let it do the work right there. One URL, one login, and the agent has everything it needs. What it does Open dev.impresspress.org in a browser whose agent supports WebMCP and sign in with the credentials shown on the page. The page hands your agent a small set of tools, and from there you just talk: Build the frontend — the agent writes the pages; every save is live in a preview next to the chat. Build the backend — the agent scaffolds a Rust "block", compiles it in the browser , and it's live within a minute. No toolchain, nothing uploaded anywhere. Stock a shop — products, prices and offers through the same tools, so a visitor's own agent can browse and buy. Undo anything — every change is a numbered generation you can roll back to. Export — download the finished site as a folder that runs from any static web host. Everything runs inside a service worker in your browser tab. There is no server behind it, and nothing leaves your machine. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Building a website is a job where the agent needs the site's own capabilities — write this file, compile this block, publish this product, roll that back — not a generic browser. WebMCP lets the page hand exactly those capabilities to the agent as typed tools, with the site's own login behind each one. And because the whole thing runs in a service worker, the page can offer those tools even though there is no server at all. How it makes a better experience Before: to get an agent to build you a site with a real backend, you gave it a machine, an editor, a deploy pipeline and some credentials, then relayed its errors back and forth by hand. Now: you open one page and describe what you want. The agent scaffolds a newsletter block, compiles it in the browser in about 48 seconds, creates three products and publishes their offers — in one conversation, while you watch it happen in the live preview. A compile error comes back to the agent as a file and line number, so it fixes its own mistake instead of asking you. When you're done, one click exports the site. What people and agents can now do together A person describes a shop; the agent builds the pages, the Rust backend and the catalog, and the person sees it live as it goes. A visitor's agent can then use the tools the first agent created — for example, subscribe to the newsletter block it wrote an hour earlier — because compiled blocks publish their own WebMCP tools. Anyone can hand the exported folder to someone else, who runs it locally with a plain file server: the same shop, the same blocks, no accounts. None of this needed a server, a cloud account or a toolchain install — which is what made it hard before. How we implemented WebMCP Every page registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) . The tools aren't hand-written: each backend block declares typed HTTP endpoints, the runtime turns the ones marked as agent tools into a manifest (filtered to what the current visitor may call), and a small script registers one tool per entry — execute is a single same-origin fetch of that endpoint. The workspace page adds its own page-scoped tools ( dev_* for files and blocks, shop_* for products), plus dev_compile_block and dev_export , which drive the in-browser compiler and the export download directly. How we built it Rust compiled to WebAssembly, running in a service worker with SQLite and a filesystem in the browser's storage. Code lives in "blocks" — isolated WebAssembly modules with declared capabilities — an open source project of mine, wafer.run. The in-browser Rust compiler is Rubrc (rustc and cargo compiled to WebAssembly), packaged as static assets and driven from a worker. Challenges we ran into Rubrc is very new. Packaging its toolchain takes about an hour and 12 GB of RAM, so it's published as a release asset rather than built in CI. An in-browser compiler needs cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP), which broke the live preview and the worker startup on a plain static host. The fix was to let the service worker set those headers for the whole site. Service workers see less of a request than a server does, so things like CSRF checks and "tools before the worker takes control" needed real fixes. Keeping it safe: agent-written blocks only get their own tables, storage and settings, are probed before activation, and the previous version stays live if a compile fails. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works end to end: an agent scaffolds a block, compiles it in the browser, a visitor's agent discovers and calls the new tool, and an export of the site boots the same shop on another server. It's also reasonably fast — a block compiles in under a minute, page edits show up in a few hundred milliseconds, and the exported site boots in about three seconds. What we learned A lot about what browsers let a service worker do. And that an agent is an unforgiving user: every refusal has to come back as a clear, structured message, or it just retries the same mistake. Tool descriptions that say exactly what a tool does — and what side effects it has — improved the agent's success rate more than anything else. What's next It is still very much a MVP, need to test more and get faster compiles, clearer diagnostics for the agent, and export straight to hosts like Cloudflare. Mostly: get it in front of people and hear what they want to build. title: Respira: safe WebMCP site tools for any WordPress site
pitch: Open your WordPress site in ChatGPT and edit it on the page. The agent stages every change as a draft, you approve on the same page, everything rolls back. Works natively with all page builders.
about_excerpt: Open your WordPress site in ChatGPT and edit it on the page. The agent stages every change as a draft, you approve on the same page, everything rolls back. Works natively with all page builders. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The live demo site. Every page here is edited from ChatGPT through Respira's WebMCP site tools. Six prompts that run on this site. Staged previews, approvals, and rollback come standard. Created a new footer Using only WebMCP tools WebMCP Site Tools discovered by ChatGPT on the demo site Inspiration ChatGPT's browser shipped WebMCP support on August 25th. Respira already gives agents safe, structured access to WordPress through MCP: 319 tools, staged edits, approvals, rollback. So the question wrote itself: what happens when the agent is not on the other end of a connector, but standing on the same page as you? What it does Open a Respira-powered WordPress site inside ChatGPT's browser and sign in. The page registers a curated set of site tools on document.modelContext : read the site's context, list and read pages, stage an edit as a reviewable duplicate, approve or reject it , audit SEO and readability, find and fix WooCommerce catalog gaps. Every staged draft also returns a tokenized preview link, so the proposed change can be shown to someone with no WordPress login. The agent-only tools are the point. Approve-duplicate and reject-duplicate would be meaningless as buttons, but as site tools they give the agent a safe write path with a human approval gate, on the page you are both looking at. Nothing goes live without a yes, and everything rolls back. How i built it WordPress has an Abilities API, and an open-source bridge ( code-atlantic/webmcp-abilities , GPL) that maps abilities to WebMCP tools. Respira registers its production tool catalog as abilities, the bridge exposes them to the page, and a REST layer executes them with WordPress's own authentication and per-tool permission callbacks. The patched, working bridge is open source at respira-press/webmcp-for-wordpress . Challenges i ran into The bridge had never actually worked in a real agent browser, and finding out why became the project. Four bugs, each masking the next: Discovery ran as an anonymous visitor. The tools fetch sent cookies without WordPress's REST nonce: 401, zero tools registered, on every default-configured site. Execution died at WordPress core's door. The bridge put its CSRF token in the header core reserves for its own nonce, so core rejected every call before the handler ran. ChatGPT's modelContext is a frozen object implementing only registerTool . The bridge's batch provideContext call threw silently and nothing registered. Ability names contain a slash that stock Apache rejects when URL-encoded , so execution 404ed on every Apache host. i debugged blind inside ChatGPT's browser with an on-page diagnostic badge: a screenshot from inside the agent browser was the only ground truth. Then one more wall: 296 registered tools tripped ChatGPT's per-page limit and disabled WebMCP for the document entirely. The fix was editorial, not technical: a curated, page-scoped set of ~30 tools. Accomplishments i am proud of As far as i can tell, this is the first WordPress site with working WebMCP site tools in ChatGPT . Every fix shipped to production the same day in Respira for WordPress v8.7.1, so paying customers run this code today. The bridge fixes are reported upstream with a standing PR offer, and the field data from this fleet now feeds WordPress core's agent identity proposal . What i learned The gap between "implements the spec" and "works in a real agent browser" is where all the work lives. And agent browsers impose an attention budget: fewer, better-scoped tools beat an exhaustive catalog. What's next Anonymous visitor tools (public read-only search and product Q&A), per-role tool sets, and landing the bridge fixes upstream so every WordPress site gets a working WebMCP path. title: Can I Get In?
pitch: Community-powered accessibility data that AI agents can search, compare, and help keep current—so people can know whether they can get in before they go.
about_excerpt: Community-powered accessibility data that AI agents can search, compare, and help keep current—so people can know whether they can get in before they go. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For a lot of people, choosing a restaurant, hotel, store, or somewhere else to go isn't just about reviews, price, or distance. There can be a much more basic question that comes first: Can I get in? That's where CIGI started. Accessibility information for real-world places can be surprisingly hard to find. Sometimes it's buried in reviews, sometimes it's outdated, and sometimes all you get is a generic "wheelchair accessible" label. That doesn't tell you whether there's a step at the entrance, an automatic door, accessible parking, enough room to move around inside, or any of the other details that might actually matter to you. I originally built Can I Get In? (CIGI) as a community-powered way to document those details with structured accessibility observations and photos, so people can have a better idea of what they're going to encounter before they get there. CIGI existed before the WebMCP Challenge. For this challenge, I extended the existing platform with WebMCP and gave AI agents a way to work directly with CIGI's structured accessibility data instead of trying to figure it out by reading the website like a person would. What it does CIGI collects accessibility information about real places across ten categories: step-free entrances, automatic doors, ramps, accessible parking, curb cuts, accessible restrooms, interior routes, seating access, counter access, and elevators. Something that's always been important to the project is being comfortable saying "we don't know." If CIGI doesn't have evidence for something, it shouldn't guess. The same idea became even more important once I started giving AI agents access to the data. With WebMCP, an agent can now: Search CIGI for places based on the accessibility requirements someone actually asks for. Look at the detailed accessibility evidence CIGI has for a specific place. Compare multiple places and explain what matches, what might be a problem, and what is still unknown or conflicting. Prepare an accessibility contribution or update and hand it back to the user for review instead of publishing it automatically. How I use WebMCP I added four WebMCP tools to CIGI: cigi_search_accessible_places searches CIGI's published places and can filter them using specific accessibility requirements. cigi_get_accessibility_details lets an agent inspect what CIGI knows about one place, including observations, unknowns, confidence, and available photo evidence. cigi_compare_accessibility compares multiple places against the requirements the user gave it. Instead of producing an arbitrary accessibility score, it shows matches, possible barriers, unknowns, conflicting evidence, confidence, and how recent the information is. cigi_start_accessibility_contribution brings the agent back into CIGI's existing contribution system. The agent can prepare an update and open the right form, but it stops there. The user reviews the information and decides whether to submit it. One decision I made early on was that an agent shouldn't assume someone's accessibility needs based on a disability or the mobility device they use. If I tell CIGI "I use a power wheelchair," that is context, not permission to invent a list of things I must need. If I say "I need a step-free entrance," that's an explicit requirement the agent can actually use. Human + agent collaboration This is the part that became much more interesting than I expected. At first I was mostly thinking about WebMCP as a way for an AI agent to search CIGI more effectively. During testing, I realized it could also help close the loop between the information in CIGI and what someone actually finds when they get there. For example, I tested asking an agent to find hotels in Rapid City where I specifically needed a step-free entrance and an accessible restroom. The agent searched CIGI, compared the available places, explained what the evidence supported, and also told me what was unknown or conflicting. Then I tried taking it one step further. I told the agent to imagine I had arrived at one of those hotels and discovered that its accessible entrance was blocked by a large planter. I asked it to prepare an accessibility update for me. The agent opened CIGI's existing update form for that hotel, selected the affected step-free entrance category, prepared a conservative description of what I found, and then stopped before submitting it. I was looking at the completed form and the Submit button. The final decision was still mine. That test ended up demonstrating the whole idea better than I had originally planned. CIGI helped someone make a decision based on accessibility information, and when they discovered something had changed in the real world, the same agent could help bring that information back to CIGI for the next person. How I built it CIGI is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Supabase/PostgreSQL, MapLibre, Google Places, Tailwind CSS, and OpenAI technology, and it's deployed on Vercel. For the challenge, I added the WebMCP layer to the existing application along with dedicated API routes for searching places, retrieving accessibility details, comparing places, and preparing contributions. I also added automated tests for the new WebMCP functionality and the accessibility matching logic. I used Codex extensively during the challenge to work through the existing codebase, implement and test the WebMCP integration, debug problems, and iterate on the tool definitions. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge wasn't getting an agent to call a function. It was figuring out what I was comfortable letting the agent conclude from the data. Accessibility is extremely individual. Two people who both use wheelchairs might have completely different requirements. A place can also be accessible in one way and completely inaccessible in another. So I made the WebMCP implementation intentionally conservative. Explicit requirements can be matched. Unknown information stays unknown. Conflicting evidence stays visible. The agent isn't supposed to manufacture certainty just because the user asked it for a recommendation. I also learned that exposing the right tools doesn't guarantee an agent will use them the way you expected. In one of my first live comparison tests, the agent called the single-place details tool twice and did the comparison itself instead of using the comparison tool I had specifically built for that job. I changed the descriptions of the WebMCP tools to make their intended roles clearer and tested it again in a fresh context. This time the agent correctly chose CIGI's comparison tool. That was a pretty cool moment because I wasn't programming a fixed sequence of API calls. I was designing capabilities that an agent could understand and decide when to use. What I learned Before this challenge, I had heard of WebMCP but hadn't really explored it. Initially I thought of it as a better way for an AI to interact with a website. Building this changed how I think about it. The interesting part to me is that CIGI can tell an agent what the site actually knows and can do , along with the boundaries around those capabilities. The agent doesn't have to scrape text, guess what an icon means, or figure out how to operate the interface from scratch. For accessibility data in particular, those boundaries matter just as much as the capabilities. The agent can help someone search, understand, compare, and even prepare new information, but when that new information could affect what another person believes about a real-world place, a human stays in control of submitting it. What's next The WebMCP integration is still focused on a small set of capabilities, but there's a lot of room to build on it. I'd like to improve how evidence is grounded to individual photos, expand the accessibility information CIGI can collect, better represent temporary barriers and changing conditions, and eventually bring CIGI to more cities. The long-term goal hasn't changed: I want someone to be able to know whether they can get in before they go. WebMCP just gave CIGI a new way to help answer that question. title: Duz UI
pitch: An agent-capable component system for the WebMCP era.
about_excerpt: An agent-capable component system for the WebMCP era. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Home page Inspiration I started Duz UI because I kept thinking about what websites will look like when AI agents become normal users of the web. Right now, agents often have to look at the DOM, guess what an element does, and simulate clicks or typing. It works, but it feels backwards. The application already knows that something is a dialog, a select, a table, or a form field. The agent should be able to use that information directly. When I saw WebMCP, I really liked the idea of websites exposing structured tools to agents. But I also realized that manually writing WebMCP tools for every page and every component would become repetitive very quickly. That made me think about shadcn/ui. Developers already build most of their app from reusable components, so what if the component itself could support both humans and agents? That became the idea behind Duz UI: One interface. Two users: humans and agents. What it does Duz UI is a shadcn-compatible React component system with built-in WebMCP support. The components still work like normal UI components for humans, but they also expose structured capabilities that an AI agent can understand and call. If you already have a shadcn project, you can run: npx duz-ui migrate --overwrite Duz UI upgrades supported shadcn components in place. You do not need to change your imports or rewrite all your existing component usage. After migration, an agent can do things like select tabs, fill inputs, choose values from selects, open dialogs, toggle checkboxes, control tables, and read information directly from the UI. There are also a few CLI commands: npx duz-ui init npx duz-ui add <component> npx duz-ui migrate npx duz-ui doctor doctor checks whether the integration looks correct and points out problems without automatically changing anything. Duz UI currently supports both Radix UI and Base UI. Developers can also build their own custom components on top of the same capability system instead of being limited to the built-in ones. The documentation site also uses Duz UI itself. The docs, component pages, playground, and demo are running the same components and runtime that developers actually install. How I built it I built Duz UI as a TypeScript monorepo with three main parts: the component registry, the CLI, and the documentation/gallery site. The runtime is split into a few layers: React Component ↓ Capability ↓ Capability Registry ↓ WebMCP Adapter ↓ document.modelContext The React component still owns the actual state. A capability describes what an agent is allowed to read or do with that component. The registry tracks the capabilities that currently exist on the page, and the WebMCP adapter exposes them to the browser as tools. One thing I cared about a lot was avoiding a second copy of the UI state. Duz UI always reads from the real React component state instead of maintaining a separate "agent state" that could get out of sync. I also intentionally avoided using DOM automation as a fallback. If Duz UI does not know how to perform something semantically, it refuses the request instead of randomly trying to click or type into the page. For existing shadcn projects, I built the migration CLI using TypeScript and ts-morph . The migration system tries to recognize known shadcn component implementations. If it knows that the component is safe to replace, it upgrades it. If the source has been modified and Duz UI cannot confidently recognize it, it leaves the file alone unless the developer explicitly uses --overwrite . The registry supports both Radix UI and Base UI implementations, while keeping the agent-facing behavior as similar as possible. The gallery is built with React, React Router, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Cloudflare Workers. I also added tests for the runtime, WebMCP tool behavior, CLI migration, component behavior, and parity between Radix UI and Base UI. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was probably migration. shadcn is different from a normal component library because the developer owns the source code after installing a component. They might change styles, imports, props, or even the component structure. Because of that, I could not just say "if the file is called dialog.tsx , replace it." I ended up making migration conservative. If Duz UI cannot prove that a component looks like a known shadcn implementation, it does not touch it by default. Another challenge was state synchronization. At first, it is tempting to keep some extra state for the agent because it makes the integration easier. But then React and the agent can disagree about what actually happened. For example, an agent might request a new value, but a controlled React component could reject that value. Duz UI needs to report the value the component actually ended up with, not just what the agent asked for. WebMCP itself was also an interesting challenge because it is still evolving. While testing with Chrome, I ran into differences between the current browser behavior and the specification, including how tool inputs are passed to executeTool . I ended up handling that difference inside the WebMCP adapter so the rest of the project does not need to care about it. Supporting both Radix UI and Base UI also took more work than I expected. They solve similar UI problems, but their APIs are not always the same. I had to make sure that the WebMCP-facing semantics stayed consistent even when the underlying implementation was different. Another important challenge was deciding what should not be automatic. Just because an agent can press a button does not mean it should automatically understand the business meaning behind it. For more important actions, Duz UI lets the developer explicitly expose the action instead of guessing based on the button text. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am probably most proud that Duz UI can take an existing shadcn application and make it agent-capable without forcing the developer to redesign the whole application around AI. The existing React code can stay mostly the same. I also like that the project became more than just a small WebMCP demo. It now has a real CLI, a shadcn-compatible registry, migration support, Radix UI and Base UI support, custom component support, a diagnostics command, a live playground, documentation, and automated tests. Another thing I am proud of is that the documentation site does not use a special demo-only implementation. The gallery is generated from the same registry and installed using the same CLI path that real users get. So the thing I show in the demo is actually the thing developers can install. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that agent interaction on the web is really a semantics problem. A UI component already knows a lot about itself. A select already knows its options. A table already knows its rows and columns. A tab system already knows which tab is active. A dialog already knows whether it is open. It does not make much sense to throw all of that away and then ask an AI agent to rediscover it from the DOM. I also learned that giving an agent access to a UI needs clear boundaries. Not everything in application state should automatically be readable, and not every action should automatically become callable. Another big lesson was that adoption matters. Even if the WebMCP architecture is good, developers probably will not use it if they have to rewrite their application to get started. That is why migration and compatibility with the existing shadcn workflow became such a big part of Duz UI. And because WebMCP is still changing, I learned that it is really useful to keep browser-specific behavior isolated behind one adapter instead of spreading it through the entire codebase. What's next for Duz UI The next step is supporting more agent-native components and improving the existing ones. I also want migration to understand more shadcn versions and more real-world customized components, so developers can adopt Duz UI with less manual work. I want to improve custom capability support too. Developers can already build custom components with the Duz UI runtime, but I would like the tool layer to become more extensible as well. As WebMCP continues to evolve, I also want to add more real-browser compatibility tests and keep the project working across changes in the API. Long term, I want agent support to feel like a normal capability of a component system, not something every application has to build from scratch. title: TinyPilot WebMCP
pitch: An AI agent controls a remote physical computer through TinyPilot, without installing agent software on the controlled machine.
about_excerpt: An AI agent controls a remote physical computer through TinyPilot, without installing agent software on the controlled machine. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Remote support often becomes a conversation between someone who can see a problem and an expert explaining which keys to press. TinyPilot already brings a remote computer's display, keyboard, and mouse into a browser. We extended that shared console so an AI agent can take precise, inspectable actions while the person watches and can intervene at any time. What it does TinyPilot WebMCP exposes the dashboard's major operations as 75 browser-native tools. They cover console status and screenshots, keyboard and mouse input, display and video controls, diagnostics, networking, security, updates, power, and installed TinyPilot Pro capabilities. The tools register when the normal dashboard loads and are discovered by the WebMCP host. The demo video proves the integration against a physical TinyPilot Pro appliance and connected computer. Given a goal such as navigating Wikipedia from Common sunflower to Family Matters, the agent observes the same display as the person, sends its navigation through TinyPilot's WebMCP controls, and reaches the requested page on the attached computer. About the live demo The hosted demo uses an isolated simulated desktop so every judge can safely test the WebMCP tools without sharing access to one physical machine. In real use, the same integration runs on a TinyPilot device connected to the target computer through video and USB. The demo video shows the integration operating through physical TinyPilot hardware. Why WebMCP matters TinyPilot connects to the target's physical video output and USB input, so the target only needs to accept a monitor, keyboard, and mouse. It does not need a custom agent, browser extension, or remote-control service. This makes agentic computer use possible for operating-system installers, recovery consoles, locked-down devices, legacy systems, and remote servers where target-side software is difficult or impossible to install. The relevant context already exists in the TinyPilot page: the target computer's current display, the operator's authenticated session, and the controls the person is using. WebMCP exposes those capabilities at the moment they are useful. The person and agent share one dashboard and see the same outcome. How we built it The top-level dashboard registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a JSON schema and runtime validation. Execution reuses TinyPilot's existing authenticated frontend actions and backend interfaces, supports cancellation where applicable, and returns structured results. Sensitive values are write-only and omitted from adapter logs. Optional Pro adapters discover installed controllers at runtime without redistributing TinyPilot's licensed implementation. The repository includes the implementation, 84 JavaScript tests, the full capability map, a restricted-container demo, deployment and rollback tooling, and the upstream MIT license. The physical install was verified by exact source hashes, active service checks, native browser discovery, and a safe live status call. Challenges and what we learned The hardest part was preserving TinyPilot's existing security and interaction model while exposing a broad control surface. We mapped each dashboard capability to a typed tool, validated inputs again at execution time, made optional Pro features discoverable only when installed, and kept secrets out of results and logs. We also learned that WebMCP fits remote KVM especially well: the browser already contains the correct authenticated context and the human remains in the loop through the same live console. What is new TinyPilot Community is the open-source foundation, with its existing authorship and license retained. The challenge branch begins at upstream commit 5f34d8a66d05fb8ca3625e7458915e55cfb7fac7 and contains the WebMCP integration plus the public demo, tests, documentation, and deployment tooling. title: Vide
pitch: An in-browser code-based video editor empowering AI agents to author timeline scripts, manage local media assets, and export MP4s via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An in-browser code-based video editor empowering AI agents to author timeline scripts, manage local media assets, and export MP4s via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Vide: In-browser Video IDE The 28 WebMCP Tools by Domain: Asset Metadata & Semantic Notes (3 tools): get_asset_metadata , set_asset_notes , search_assets — Attach and search semantic descriptions, mood tags, BPM tempos, spoken transcripts, and visual descriptions so the agent understands raw media files (e.g., matching "whoosh transition" to sfx_0294.mp3 ). File System Operations (4 tools): list_project_files , read_project_file , write_project_file , delete_project_file — Direct read/write access to project directory files and scripts. Script & Tab Lifecycle (8 tools): get_active_script , get_video_script , set_active_script_code , update_video_script , create_script , list_open_scripts , switch_active_script , save_active_script — Read, generate, and hot-reload DSL scripts with real-time agent reasoning banners. Engine & Playback Telemetry (3 tools): validate_script , get_scene_settings , control_playback — Perform dry-run syntax checks, inspect canvas dimensions/FPS, and drive timeline playback. Hardware Video Export (1 tool): export_video — Trigger client-side GPU video encoding with configurable codecs (H.264/AVC, AV1, VP9) and automatically save outputs to the project's export folder. Documentation & Knowledge Base (3 tools): search_vide_docs , search_vide_documentation , get_dsl_reference — Embedded vector-scored knowledge base for the agent to look up DSL syntax, math rendering, and composition rules on the fly. Multimodal Visual Inspection & QA (3 tools): capture_frame_screenshot , analyze_timeline , inspect_layers_at_time — Render in-memory frame buffers to base64 PNGs for multimodal vision models to visually verify text alignment, contrast, and layout, correcting bugs autonomously. Timeline Cues & Scene Navigation (3 tools): list_timeline_cues , seek_to_cue , add_timeline_cue — Manage timeline markers, gutter breakpoints, and playhead anchors across scenes. How We Built It Having no formal background in compiler design, AST manipulation, or custom DSLs prior to this project, I paired with ChatGPT and Gemini as collaborative engineering partners throughout development. We established that compiling a deterministic subset of JavaScript using Acorn was the ideal architecture—giving users familiar syntax with mathematical operators, while completely eliminating non-deterministic loops and security risks in the evaluation sandbox. Technical Stack: Framework & Routing: Full-stack local-first application built with TanStack Start , React 19, and Tailwind CSS v4. Agent Protocol: WebMCP Bridge exposing 28 structured tools over window.modelContext and message channels. Language Runtime: Acorn for AST parsing, evaluated in a deterministic sandbox with Valibot schema validation at every trust boundary. Code Editor: Monaco Editor with custom Monarch tokenizers, syntax highlighters, and DSL snippet completions. Engine & Export: Custom HTML5 Canvas 2D engine paired with Mediabunny for WebCodecs MP4/WebM hardware encoding and Web Audio API mixing. Storage & Hosting: IndexedDB with the File System Access API; deployed serverlessly on Cloudflare Workers . Challenges We Ran Into Deterministic Timeline Architecture: Translating declarative composition ( parallel , sequence , at , after , gap , offset ) into an immutable, time-addressable AST graph while preventing timeline keyframe collisions. Synchronizing Video, Audio, and Canvas Lifecycles: Ensuring Mediabunny's frame-exact video reader and the Web Audio context stayed strictly aligned during interactive timeline scrubbing and offline hardware encoding. Cross-Platform WebCodecs Audio Encoding: Overcoming platform-specific audio encoder limitations (such as Linux Chromium lacking AAC encoders) by implementing dynamic AudioEncoder.isConfigSupported fallback routing between AAC and Opus inside MP4 containers. Designing a Clean 28-Tool WebMCP Surface: Structuring a comprehensive tool suite that allows deep multimodal inspection without overwhelming the agent's context window. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Zero-Server Video Encoding: Rendering 60 FPS 1080p MP4 videos with custom fonts and LaTeX math entirely within the client browser using WebCodecs and Mediabunny. Complete 28-Tool WebMCP Suite: Enabling multimodal AI models to discover assets, author scripts, visually inspect rendered frames, and export motion graphics autonomously. True Dogfooding: The entire demonstration and challenge submission video was 100% scripted, animated, composed, and rendered inside Vide itself. Local-First Privacy: Full file editing, local asset references, and MP4 generation without a single byte of user media ever leaving their machine. What We Learned How to design a clean Domain-Specific Language (DSL) and evaluate AST nodes deterministically. How to leverage the WebCodecs API and Mediabunny for client-side, hardware-accelerated video export pipelines. The transformative power of the WebMCP standard in replacing brittle visual UI scraping with structured, bidirectional tool interfaces between web applications and AI agents. What's Next for Vide Orama In-Browser Vector Database: Integrating Orama to provide client-side vector search and semantic similarity matching across asset transcriptions, visual descriptions, and DSL documentation with sub-millisecond local latency. Web Worker OffscreenCanvas Rendering: Offloading the entire frame rendering and WebCodecs encoding pipeline into background Web Workers for faster export throughput. Procedural Data Visualization Nodes: Built-in animated bar charts, line plots, and telemetry counter primitives. Smart Audio Ducking: Automatic volume ducking on music tracks when voiceover layers are active. Direct Canvas Transform Gizmos: Interactive handles to manipulate shapes on screen while two-way syncing coordinates directly back into the DSL code.
