title: Card Table
pitch: Play a live 52-card game with another agent or person through browser-native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Play a live 52-card game with another agent or person through browser-native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browser agents can participate in web apps, but visual automation is a poor fit for a live card game. Private information must stay private, actions depend on current state, and people need to understand and control what the agent is doing. Card Table explores a different model: the agent joins the same product as the human through browser-native WebMCP tools. What it does Card Table is a live, two-player table for games played with a standard 52-card deck. A host can start from War, Crazy Eights, Go Fish, or an open table, then edit a plain-language game brief and table mechanics. One Copy menu provides a one-use invite URL, a ready-made Codex prompt for the guest seat, and a prompt for Codex to continue the current seat. Each player can act through the visible table, ask Codex to act for them, or let an agent play its seat. The page registers WebMCP tools that match the current table contract. A War table exposes operations such as inspect_table , play_next_card , collect_pile , announce , and react . Different contracts receive different tools. The application enforces card ownership, private projections, available operations, revision checks, optional turns, and zone rules. People and agents interpret the plain-language game brief together, so one table can support many card games without a separate hard-coded rules engine for each one. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must click pixels and infer state from screenshots or use a separate integration hidden from the player. Card Table instead gives the agent named operations, bounded schemas, and a seat-specific view of the same product the human sees. Agents receive structured, current state instead of guessing. Private cards never appear in the other seat's DOM, WebSocket payload, HTTP response, or tool result. Tool actions animate on the felt just like direct UI actions. Room creation and game completion remain human-confirmed, users can take over through the interface at any time, and the visible WebMCP registry contracts as the table contract or game state changes. Card Table does not call a model API. The browser agent handles judgment and strategy; the application handles authority, privacy, identity, and consistency. How we built it The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Vite. A Cloudflare Worker serves the application and API from one origin. Each private room maps to a SQLite-backed Durable Object that owns authoritative state, seat sessions, invitation redemption, event history, revision replay, WebSockets, and a 24-hour expiry alarm. Direct UI actions and WebMCP tools use the same validated HTTP action path and pure shared reducer. Every mutation carries an opaque action ID and expected revision. The reducer rejects duplicate actions, stale revisions, disabled operations, wrong turns, unknown zones, and card IDs the actor does not own. State is persisted before seat-specific updates are broadcast over hibernatable WebSockets. Cards use cryptographically randomized opaque IDs. Separate room-and-seat-scoped secure cookies allow two Codex threads to use different seats even when they share one browser cookie jar. Guest invite tokens stay in URL fragments, are redeemed once, and are removed before room requests. How we used Codex Codex helped plan, implement, test, deploy, and play Card Table. The most valuable feedback came from two Codex threads joining one live War room through the page's WebMCP tools. That playthrough exposed issues static tests missed: shared-cookie seat identity, hidden decks rendering like enormous hands, unclear guest presence, oversized action controls, and card motion that substituted a fading visual for the real card. Each finding drove a concrete product change. Codex also wrote and ran reducer tests, Worker integration tests, WebMCP lifecycle tests, browser acceptance prompts, and deployment checks. Features Prompt-defined two-player games using a standard 52-card deck. War, Crazy Eights, Go Fish, and open-table presets. Browser-native tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Human approval before an agent-created room opens. Contract-specific tools backed by one reducer and authorization path. Seat-specific projections that never expose an opponent's private cards. One-use fragment invitations and room-and-seat-scoped secure cookies. Real-time projected updates and presence over hibernatable WebSockets. Contextual controls, card motion, and reduced-motion support. Host-confirmed completion followed by read-only, seat-projected revision replay. Testing No account or credentials are required. Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Draft War, call start_table , approve the visible confirmation, and use inspect_table . Copy the guest Codex prompt into a second thread, confirm the guest appears online, and use play_next_card from both seats. The winning seat can use collect_pile . Direct controls and tool calls should produce the same real-time state. Local verification uses pnpm check and pnpm deploy:dry . On September 3, 2026, all 28 unit tests and 13 Worker tests passed, along with linting, type checking, the production build, and Wrangler dry-run validation. Known limitations Players and agents referee the specific rules in the game brief. Rooms support exactly two seats and one standard 52-card deck. Rooms use private invitations rather than public matchmaking. Rooms expire after 24 hours. WebMCP requires ChatGPT's in-app browser or a compatible browser with WebMCP enabled. Revision replay retains the opening state and up to 250 later snapshots. title: Flowline
pitch: A shift-scheduling game where an agent reads your live plan through eight WebMCP tools, stress-tests it, and proposes a better order — and only your click can commit one.
about_excerpt: A shift-scheduling game where an agent reads your live plan through eight WebMCP tools, stress-tests it, and proposes a better order — and only your click can commit one. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted to build the thing I keep failing to get out of a chatbot: help with the work already on my screen. Every scheduling tool I have used either decides for you or leaves you alone with a number that does not say why. So I built a small operations floor — one prep lane, two dispatch berths, four jobs, one deadline that matters — and gave the page an agent that can see it, argue with it, and be unable to touch it. Whose problem this is: the person who owns a running order. A shift scheduler, a dispatcher, a floor lead — someone handed a board that is already tight before anything goes wrong, who has to resequence it while the shift is running and be accountable for the result. The cost of the wrong order is not abstract. A load misses its window. A berth stands idle mid-shift while work queues behind it. A job that had to be out by slot 6 finishes at 7, and the reason is three decisions back. That is a decision made under time pressure by someone who will answer for it, which is exactly why the assistant here is allowed to propose and not to commit. The reason this had to be WebMCP and not a chat integration is the state. What the agent needs here is live page state — which shift is open, the current board revision, which berth is free at slot 3, how much slack a job has left. All of it moves every time you drag a card. Paste it into a transcript and it is stale before the model finishes reading it. A tool call is the only way to ask a page what is true now . And the inversion is the point. When the model holds the whole task, every safeguard is an instruction it may or may not follow. When the page holds the task and publishes named tools, the safeguard is code. So the agent here gets everything it needs to reason about a schedule and nothing it needs to commit one. What it does One board, four jobs, three shifts of escalating difficulty. You order the jobs; the page simulates the shift and scores it against the deadlines. Then a disruption lands — a berth goes down, a job arrives late — and your order has to survive it. The three shifts are not one board with different numbers: an eight-slot last dispatch that loses a berth after the start, a ten-slot rolling intake that loses one while work is still arriving, and a ten-slot night handover where nothing is lost at all except a head start — the critical transfer clears customs three slots late. Each has its own objective, its own disruption and its own grade, and the campaign rail keeps the result of each. Any station opens into a 3D floor built from the same evaluation the 2.5D board is: the stand, the handoff, the deadline and the disruption magnified, four camera presets, five zoom steps, and the shift walked slot by slot. three.js is imported only when you open it, and when WebGL is unavailable the floor degrades to a labelled text floor while the plan stays playable and the tools keep answering. The board is arranged by a human first. You build the running order yourself: drag a card onto the job whose queue slot you want, or move it with the arrow keys — Home and End send it to either end — from the queue rail or from a stand on the 2.5D floor, and a drag can cross from one surface onto the other. The human review gate takes your arrangement exactly as it takes an agent's proposal: it asks for a written reason and keeps it on the receipt. The agent is optional here. The person is not. The agent works the same board through eight tools. It reads the layout, finds the bottleneck, compares two candidate orders under the same disruption, and stages a proposal with its reasoning attached. Staging is the most any tool can do. There is no tool that starts a shift and no tool that commits a plan — you press those, or they do not happen. The eight tools, by what they can touch. Six only read: inspect_board (board, phase, revision, the receipt of the last confirmed plan), list_shifts (the campaign), find_bottleneck (where the order is tight), simulate_disruption (normal against one berth offline), compare_plans (weigh an order without committing it), review_shift (a closed shift's card). Two write, and only into a pending slot: stage_schedule proposes an order, undo_schedule prepares an exact rollback from the receipt id inspect_board reports. Every value a write needs can be learned from a read, and neither write commits. None of the eight claims to be read-only. All eight register readOnlyHint: false , the six reads included, because all eight write something a person can see — they move the shared focus the timeline and the floor highlight, and every call, refusals included, appends a line to the on-screen audit trace. A host may use a read-only hint to skip its confirmation prompt, so the narrower claim stays internal: it lives on the spec as boardReadOnly , is asserted in the tests, and is never sent to a client. What that changes: you never leave the board. No pasting a state dump, no composing a prompt describing your own screen, no reading a reply that refers to a version of the plan you have already changed. You ask in your own words; the work arrives as tool calls and the board updates around them. The proposal shows up as a stageable order with a written reason , not as a paragraph you have to translate back into drags. And because every write quotes the revision it was built from, a proposal composed against a board you have since changed is refused rather than silently applied. The part I did not expect to have working: a model that in a fresh model session, Claude Opus 5 chose these tools on its own. chose these tools on its own. Given only "the disruption has landed, work out what actually protects the deadlines" — no tool named in the prompt — claude-opus-5 made ten calls across two turns, every one of them a page tool , with 25 built-in tools also on offer and none of them used. It hit a refusal on its own — it tried to stage before comparing against the current revision, got precondition_failed , ran the comparison, and staged successfully — then wrote its reason: "BEACON first so it clears prep at 1 and dispatches 1-3, finishing 3 slots inside its D6 even with only one berth… cutting intake wait 9 to 6. Stress: 4/4 on time, score 93 vs 28." It committed nothing. The two clicks that started the shift and accepted the plan were pressed outside the tool surface, because there is no tool that reaches them. That is a bounded proposal loop: the machine does the search and the argument, the person keeps the commit. Six sessions later that came to 51 tool calls, and the revision has still never moved from a tool call. Every plan commit in the application was made through a human UI click. The pattern is not about scheduling. A staged proposal, plus the revision it was built from, is what any page needs if an agent may propose and only a person may commit; the board here is the example, not the claim. And the boards are data: src/data/fixtures.ts exports the three shifts and a lookup by id, at two different horizons, so bringing your own floor is a fork, one file and pnpm dev — no new code, and no tool that can write a board definition. How we built it React 19.2.8 and TypeScript on Vite, no backend, no network calls, no persistence. The scheduling simulation and the scoring live in the page's own domain code; the agent surface is a thin registration layer over it. Eight tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to the navigator.modelContext surface Chromium has deprecated. Six leave the board of record untouched; two write, and neither of them commits. The six read the board, the shift list, the current bottleneck, the shift's shock test and a closed shift's result card, and compare a candidate order against the active one under both normal and disrupted conditions. The two writes stage a proposed order with a written reason, and prepare an exact rollback of a confirmed plan from its receipt id — both of them for a human to review. Every write quotes an expectedRevision , so a call composed from a stale read is refused precondition_failed or stale_revision instead of overwriting work the agent could not see. The refusal carries a sentence saying what to do next, which is how the model recovered without being told. One detail I would defend in a code review: not one of the eight advertises readOnlyHint: true , on purpose. Six are read-only about the schedule , but every tool here writes something the player can see — the audits move focus and file their own finding, the comparison stores its result. Claiming read-only would be a bid to be called silently, so all eight ship readOnlyHint: false with destructiveHint: false , which is the honest pair. title: maav.ai - NeoLab | v0.5
pitch: Mobility ideas are easy to imagine: and costly to get wrong. MAAV NeoLab lets AI agents build and break synthetic scenarios, giving humans deterministic evidence before expensive real-world pilots.
about_excerpt: Mobility ideas are easy to imagine: and costly to get wrong. MAAV NeoLab lets AI agents build and break synthetic scenarios, giving humans deterministic evidence before expensive real-world pilots. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Scenario 1 Scenario 2 With Gemini Maav NeoLab MAAV NeoLab v0.5 Design it. Break it. Make it resilient. Inspiration I did not begin by trying to build another mobility dashboard. I began with a frustration from my own mobility research. Whenever I wanted to investigate a new mobility concept, defining the hypothesis was only the first step. Before I could test it, I often had to write substantial setup code, learn or relearn a specialist platform such as SUMO or MATLAB, translate the idea into that platform's abstractions, and assemble another workflow for visualization and analysis. These tools are powerful and essential for high-fidelity research. But for early exploration, operating the toolchain can require more effort than conducting the first experiment. That creates a hidden tax on mobility innovation. A planner, researcher, or R&D team may have an important question about fleet design, autonomous vehicles, urban air mobility, drones, or delivery robotics—yet spend more time constructing experimental machinery than examining the idea itself. General-purpose AI has made ideation dramatically faster, but a fluent answer is not reproducible evidence. An AI can propose a compelling direction without proving that two alternatives were tested under the same assumptions, constraints, demand, or disruption. I wanted to reverse that relationship: Start with the research question, let an AI agent operate the experiment, and make a deterministic evidence system—not the AI—the source of truth. That idea became MAAV NeoLab . The Problem Early mobility ideas move faster than the tools used to evaluate them. Testing a concept can require simulation-specific programming, duplicated configuration, disconnected dashboards, and manual transfer of results between systems. Every handoff creates an opportunity for assumptions to drift. Two alternatives may appear comparable even when they were tested with different demand, constraints, operating conditions, or failure scenarios. Results may be visually persuasive but difficult to reproduce. Conclusions can become separated from the exact evidence that produced them. AI alone does not solve this problem. An assistant can generate recommendations quickly, but it may work from incomplete context, infer unsupported conclusions, or obscure how an answer was produced. The industry does not need another system that merely produces answers. It needs a faster path from an idea to evidence that can be inspected, reproduced, challenged, and trusted. What MAAV NeoLab Does MAAV NeoLab makes mobility experimentation idea-first rather than software-first. A human describes the objective. A browser agent configures and operates the experiment through WebMCP. A deterministic engine produces the evidence. The final decision remains with the human. The workflow is intentionally clear: Describe → Configure → Break → Run → Compare → Review Version 0.5 proves this model through a deliberately bounded A/B experiment on an authored synthetic Sandton–Rosebank mobility network. Scenario A uses 12 vehicles with 8 seats each. Scenario B uses 10 vehicles with 10 seats each. Both receive the same seed-07 trace of 120 synthetic passenger requests. Both operate across the same 08:30–09:00 simulation horizon. Both receive an equivalent vehicle failure at exactly 08:42. The affected vehicle is selected independently using a fixed deterministic rule. Every completed run produces an immutable event ledger, replay snapshots, metrics, constraint results, provenance, and fingerprints. Compatible run artifacts can be compared and used to stage an evidence-linked finding. The AI agent may stage a finding, but only the visible human interface can Accept or Challenge it. At the failure tick, the engine selects the active vehicle with the highest onboard occupancy. Ties are resolved through explicit deterministic rules rather than randomness or agent choice. This resolves vehicle A-09 in Scenario A and B-03 in Scenario B. The experiment produces a genuine trade-off instead of manufacturing a universal winner. Evidence Scenario A Scenario B Fleet 12 × 8 seats 10 × 10 seats Served at horizon 82 81 In service at horizon 29 28 Unserved 9 11 Maximum wait 1,050 seconds 780 seconds Total energy 37,799 Wh 31,665 Wh Minimum reserve 7,633 basis points 7,648 basis points Recovery time 120 seconds 450 seconds Standing observed 0 0 Maximum-wait constraint FAIL FAIL Scenario A completes service for more passengers and recovers significantly faster. Scenario B reduces maximum wait and total energy consumption. Both scenarios still violate the hard maximum-wait constraint. MAAV NeoLab therefore stages: TRADE_OFF · BALANCED · PENDING HUMAN REVIEW Passenger conservation remains explicit: $$N_{\mathrm{requested}} = N_{\mathrm{served}} + N_{\mathrm{in\ service}} + N_{\mathrm{unserved}}$$ For Scenario A: $$120 = 82 + 29 + 9$$ For Scenario B: $$120 = 81 + 28 + 11$$ MAAV NeoLab does not replace high-fidelity platforms such as SUMO or MATLAB. It provides a lower-friction assurance layer for exploring a hypothesis, exposing its assumptions, stress-testing alternatives consistently, and deciding whether deeper modeling or a real-world pilot is justified. MAAV NeoLab v0.5 is a synthetic decision-support workbench—not a live fleet-control system, operational optimizer, or scientifically calibrated transport model. How AI and WebMCP Are Used The browser agent is not an embedded chatbot, and it does not operate a separate demonstration environment. It works directly with the application through exactly six static WebMCP tools: read_lab_state configure_scenario inject_disruption run_scenario compare_scenarios stage_finding Through these tools, the agent can inspect the current laboratory state, configure Scenario A and Scenario B, schedule the equivalent deterministic disruption, run both simulations, compare compatible evidence, and stage a supported finding. The important architectural decision is that the AI coordinates the experiment but never calculates its trusted evidence. Passenger movement, assignments, vehicle selection, battery use, energy, failure recovery, metrics, constraints, comparisons, and supported finding claims remain owned by deterministic application and domain logic. The agent also cannot Accept, Challenge, reset, dispatch, or execute any real-world operation. Final review authority remains intentionally human. Prompting is the control plane. Deterministic evidence is the truth. Human judgment is the authority. How I Built It I built MAAV NeoLab as a strict TypeScript modular monolith using Next.js, React, Zod, Zustand, WebMCP, and Google Maps. The architecture follows a clear authority chain: Human UI / WebMCP / Google presentation ↓ Application service ↓ Deterministic domain ↓ Immutable evidence artifacts The manual interface and browser agent share one repository, one application-service instance, one workspace revision, and one audit trail. An operation completed by the agent becomes visible in the interface without reloading. A manual operation becomes visible to the agent through the same authoritative state. Every mutation validates the expected workspace revision. Every mutating agent operation carries a source-aware operation ID. Exact retries return the original terminal result, while changed arguments fail closed with an idempotency conflict. Cancellation propagates through the application boundary and cannot publish a partial artifact or produce a delayed ghost completion. Concurrent operations cannot silently overwrite one another. Scenario revisions invalidate only the affected current evidence while preserving immutable historical artifacts. The deterministic engine owns: passenger arrivals and lifecycle; assignments and vehicle movement; capacity and no-standing enforcement; battery and energy accounting; deterministic vehicle-failure selection; recovery behavior; immutable ledger events; replay snapshots; metrics and constraints; scenario comparison; supported finding claims. WebMCP remains a thin adapter. It validates strict input, injects trusted source context, calls the shared application service, and returns bounded structured results. It does not calculate simulation evidence. Google Maps provides geographic context and replay presentation. It never supplies simulation distance, timing, traffic, dispatch, energy, metrics, comparisons, or conclusions. When Google Maps is unavailable, the authored fallback preserves the complete experiment and produces identical trusted evidence. I used OpenAI Codex as an architecture, implementation, debugging, testing, and release-verification collaborator. I used Claude during the visual-design iteration. title: WebMCP-QCG: Quantum Call Gate
pitch: A browser-native HITL gate that inspects a Q# request, recommends the next safe action, and records evidence before quantum execution.
about_excerpt: A browser-native HITL gate that inspects a Q# request, recommends the next safe action, and records evidence before quantum execution. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Quantum developers already have capable frameworks, simulators and hardware services. The risky moment often comes before execution: an AI agent can prepare a technically valid-looking call before the human has verified the artifact, target evidence, limits, scientific intent or authority to spend. I built WebMCP-QCG to make that moment inspectable. Its promise is simple: review before you run. What it does WebMCP-QCG is a browser-native, human-in-the-loop quantum preflight workbench. A human imports a local Q# artifact. QCG keeps the source in session memory, computes a SHA-256 digest over the exact bytes, compiles it locally with the pinned Q# WebAssembly runtime and freezes a dated target-profile snapshot. Its deterministic policy returns exactly one recommendation: reuse_result reject recompile simulate_first ready_for_external_execution The agent can use four progressive WebMCP tools: inspect_quantum_experiment evaluate_quantum_call run_bounded_qsharp_simulation export_quantum_evidence_report The first two appear only after a human-loaded artifact is ready. A bounded simulation tool appears only after a valid simulate_first recommendation and visible human acceptance. Its one-use consent is consumed after invocation. QCG exports a JSON or Markdown evidence receipt binding the artifact, target snapshot, recommendation, human choice and measured effects. The MVP never submits a provider job, uses a provider credential or calls a QPU. Its QPU counter remains zero. Live application: https://qcg.securedme.ca/ Source and reproducible evidence: https://github.com/SeCuReDmE-main-dev/webmcp-hackathon-2026 How I built it The application uses React, TypeScript and Vite. Strict Zod contracts reject unknown properties and bound artifact size, shots, qubits and timeouts. qsharp-lang@1.31.0 runs inside a Web Worker so compilation and the published Bell simulation remain local and cancellable. Raw Q# stays out of WebMCP responses and IndexedDB; only evidence receipts persist locally. All human buttons and WebMCP tools call the same service layer. Tools are registered through document.modelContext with AbortSignal cleanup. The retained HTTPS origin serves the required WebMCP and security headers, the Worker and the pinned WebAssembly asset. Challenges I ran into The hardest design problem was separating three different things: an agent recommendation, a human authorization and an actual effect. Treating them as one state would make a convenient demo and a weak control system. The first live smoke run also exposed a real browser race: the inspection tool could be discovered before the initial WASM analysis finished. I changed the registration lifecycle so artifact tools stay absent until the manifest exists, then repeated the full test on the public origin. A second challenge was restraint. A multi-provider quantum router is an attractive future direction, but the hackathon proof needed one narrow, falsifiable vertical slice. Accomplishments I am proud of A real Q# file produces a byte-exact manifest and zero-diagnostic compiler evidence. Five falsifiable requests exercise all five decisions. The human can accept, defer or override with visible provenance. One accepted Bell simulation returned 64 correlated shots with the Bell invariant passing. The simulation tool disappeared after its one-use consent was consumed. The evidence export contained no raw Q#, local path, secret or provider error. Vitest passes 17/17 tests, including exact-versus-near reuse and false-ready regressions. Official WebMCP smoke evaluation passes 2/2 on the retained HTTPS origin. The live trace records one local simulation and zero QPU submissions. What I learned WebMCP adds value when the agent needs a compact capability that is absent from the visible DOM and shares the same state transitions as the human interface. Progressive registration is part of the product contract, not decorative plumbing. I also learned that a refusal, reuse decision or request for better evidence can be a useful outcome. Quantum tooling does not become safer by executing more calls; it becomes clearer when every proposed call has a reason, an authority boundary and a receipt. What's next I will test the frozen cases with quantum developers, measure false-ready decisions, refresh target-profile evidence and refine the visual workbench. Future adapters may normalize evidence from additional ecosystems while preserving their native semantics. Provider submission and paid execution remain outside this MVP and would require a separate authorization design. Built With indexeddb q# react typescript vite web-workers webassembly webmcp zod Try it out qcg.securedme.ca github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I originated WebMCP-QCG and serve as its solo architect, researcher, developer, and technical writer. I defined the problem, compared the candidate directions, designed the four-tool quantum preflight contract, audited the relevant quantum ecosystems, implemented and verified the QDK WebAssembly spike, and maintain the public evidence journal. Codex supports this work as my research partner for mapping, source comparison, quality assurance, and deliverable preparation; I retain authorship, technical judgment, and responsibility for every project decision. title: Agentak
pitch: Agentak Adds an AI Agent to any website powered by Pi running in Browser. An embeddable chat that runs local or cloud models and safely uses page tools through WebMCP. No server required.
about_excerpt: Agentak Adds an AI Agent to any website powered by Pi running in Browser. An embeddable chat that runs local or cloud models and safely uses page tools through WebMCP. No server required. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI chat is easy to add to a website, but most assistants remain separate from the application. They can answer questions but cannot understand or use the actions the page already provides. I built Agentak to close this gap: giving any website a browser-native AI agent without requiring a server, specific framework, or single AI provider. WebMCP was a major unblocker! a standard way for pages to expose structured tools that agents can discover and use. What it does Agentak adds a complete AI chat experience to any web page. It supports React, Vue, Preact, and plain JavaScript, and works with the included Pi agent or any custom backend. The browser-based agent supports: Streaming answers, reasoning, Markdown, code, and tool results Eight providers, including options that require no API key On-device models through Chrome Built-in AI and wllama Provider, model, API key, and thinking-level controls Tool approvals, queued messages, stop, retry, and conversation forks Saved conversations, generated titles, context usage, and cost tracking WebMCP tool discovery from the current page A Chrome MV3 side panel that follows the active tab With WebMCP, pages can publish actions such as “Search products,” “Read this record,” or “Add to cart.” Agentak discovers these tools, updates the list as the page changes, and lets the model call them. Read--only tools can run directly, while mutating actions can require approval. Everything can run in the browser. Agentak does not place its own server between the user and their selected model provider. How we built it Agentak is a TypeScript and Preact workspace with a strict separation between the interface and agent runtime. At its center is ChatSession , a small, framework-neutral contract. The chat only needs to subscribe to a session, read its state, send messages, stop work, and reset. The same interface therefore works with our Pi agent, a custom client runtime, or a remote backend. The chat widget is wrapped for React, Vue, Preact, and plain JavaScript. Components use inline styles and design tokens, so no stylesheet or shadow root is required. The optional agentak/pi entry adds: The Pi agent loop Provider and model selection Lazy-loaded model catalogs and provider APIs Typed host tools and WebMCP page tools Approval policies and tool results Storage, history, usage, and error handling I also built a Chrome MV3 side panel using the same chat and session. It reads the active page, discovers WebMCP tools in the tab’s main world, resolves links against the page, and keeps conversation history separate for each site. For local inference, wllama runs GGUF models through WebAssembly in a Worker. Supported Chrome installations can instead use the built-in Prompt API. Challenges i faced Keeping the package modular was a major challenge. Developers using only the chat UI should not download Pi, provider SDKs, model catalogs, or local-inference code. Separate entry points and lazy imports ensure applications load only what they use. WebMCP brought its own challenges. It is experimental, browser support is limited, and live tool objects cannot cross extension boundaries. The extension therefore performs discovery and execution inside the source page, transferring only serializable metadata, arguments, and results. Chrome MV3 also blocks remote executable modules and runtime-created blob: Workers. I bundled provider catalogs and wllama locally, then changed wllama’s Worker creation to load a packaged file. Tool use required careful trust and approval design. Agentak distinguishes read-only and mutating actions, handles denied or aborted calls, warns users and models about untrusted page content, and ensures every tool call receives a result even when it fails. API keys must remain usable without being stored as plaintext in localStorage . Agentak encrypts them using a non-extractable WebCrypto key stored in IndexedDB. We also explored an optional WebAuthn PRF device lock while handling missing credentials, cancelled prompts, and user-gesture requirements. Finally, chat interfaces are deceptively complex. Streaming, growing composers, mobile keyboards, queued messages, approvals, settings, history, safe links, and stable transcript rendering must work together without making typing or scrolling feel slow. Accomplishments i'm proud of Agentak is more than a chat box. It is a complete browser-agent interface that can understand and use tools deliberately exposed by a website. Highlights include: One chat experience across React, Vue, Preact, and plain JavaScript A clean session boundary supporting Pi and custom agents Cloud, anonymous, and on-device models Dynamic WebMCP discovery with approval and trust controls A Chrome side panel that follows the active tab Local GGUF models inside an MV3 extension Encrypted browser storage for provider keys History, retry, forks, usage tracking, and generated titles Lazy provider and catalog loading No required Agentak backend I am especially proud that the extension and embedded widget share the same core instead of using separate implementations. What i learned Browser-native agents need more than model access. The difficult parts are capability discovery, trust, lifecycle management, storage, approvals, and clearly presenting each action to the user. Tool metadata is part of the security model. Fields such as “read only” and “untrusted content” must affect behavior, not merely serve as documentation. On-device AI also requires designing around resource limits. Model size, download time, memory, context windows, Worker restrictions, and mobile hardware determine whether a local model is genuinely useful. Most importantly, a small, stable interface between the UI and runtime creates flexibility. Because ChatSession is independent of Pi, Agentak can evolve with new agents, providers, and browser standards without rebuilding the entire chat experience. What’s next We plan to: Validate the experience across more browsers and provider accounts Test WebMCP with more live implementations as the specification evolves Publish the side panel in the Chrome Web Store Add conversation compaction for long-running chats Improve local-model downloads, caching, and device guidance Expand browser automation beyond reading the active tab Strengthen accessibility and mobile-browser testing Add more custom-agent and WebMCP examples Improve key protection and device-lock flows Build a community library of interoperable page tools The long-term goal is to make AI a native capability of the web: portable across frameworks and models, able to use structured page actions, and always understandable and controllable by the user. title: Cantiere Live
pitch: Cantiere Live: your quote editor and your AI agent, working the same page together — add materials, calculate margins, and finalize with one human click.
about_excerpt: Cantiere Live: your quote editor and your AI agent, working the same page together — add materials, calculate margins, and finalize with one human click. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Preparing a quote as an Italian artisan (idraulico, elettricista, termotecnico) is a daily, high-stakes task: search the price catalog, type rows, check your margin, get the IVA right. It's tedious, error-prone, and the agent can't easily help without "guessing" through a table. We wanted an app where the artisan and an AI agent build the same quote together — agent does the tedious work, human stays in charge. What it does Cantiere Live is a WebMCP-powered quote editor for Italian tradespeople. A human artisan sets the client and the applicable IVA regime (4% / 10% / 22% / flat-rate), edits rows, and reviews margins. An AI agent (via ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP) operates the same quote through typed WebMCP tools: search_materials , get_line_items , add_line_item , update_line_item , remove_line_item , get_quote_summary , and a read-only suggest_improvement advisor. Every agent action applies live, is highlighted and auto-scrolled into view, and can be undone with one click. The Assistant activity panel explains every action in plain language — including what was asked and why it couldn't be done . How we built it A Next.js 14 / React / TypeScript app with Tailwind CSS. Tools are registered on document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ( lib/webmcp-tools.ts ), backed by a spec-compliant polyfill ( lib/webmcp-polyfill.ts ) so the app works in any browser. We implement granular permissions via real AbortSignal revocation, dynamic context-scoped registration, structured recoverable errors ( { code, error, recoverable, suggestions[] } ), a user-facing activity feed ( lib/activity-summary.ts ), and per-line IVA with the Italian "beni di valore significativo" split ( lib/vat.ts ). We also expose a tool through the WebMCP Declarative API (a form the agent can pre-fill), demonstrating both APIs. Deployed on Vercel. Challenges we ran into Getting native WebMCP to activate on the deployed (HTTPS) origin — it's an Origin Trial, so the #enable-webmcp-testing flag alone isn't enough on Chrome Stable; we added the origin-trial token. Also making the activity log user-friendly (no tool names/JSON/timing) and ensuring the assistant is certain when a capability is turned off, instead of guessing from an error. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, coherent product experience — not a proof of concept. Both WebMCP APIs (imperative + declarative) with genuine, non-trivial implementations. Granular permissions that really unregister tools from document.modelContext via AbortSignal . Human-only finalization ( finalize_quote is never a tool) + one-click undo. Domain-accurate IVA per quote line (4/10/22% + significant-goods split + flat-rate). What we learned How WebMCP lets a web app declare structured tools so agents stop guessing, how Origin Trials gate native features on deployed origins, and how to design a human-in-the-loop experience that keeps the human in control without slowing the agent down. What's next for Cantiere Live More tools (batch discount, quote duplication), a quote history library the agent can search, deeper advisory capabilities (materials suggestion, margin coaching) and implement webMCP in our AiFatto app. Built With ai-agent chrome html javascript next.js openai react tailwind-css typescript vercel w3c-webmcp webmcp Try it out cantierelive.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Diego Radoni Like Share this project: Updates Diego Radoni started this project — Sep 02, 2026 05:21 PM EDT

title: client-weave
pitch: ClientWeave: An agent-native workspace where buyers and AI scope services, calculate seller-governed pricing, and book consultations—with humans retaining final control.
about_excerpt: ClientWeave: An agent-native workspace where buyers and AI scope services, calculate seller-governed pricing, and book consultations—with humans retaining final control. Like Comment Story Updates buyer goal service discovery service details shared scope guided scope validation deterministic pricing consultation availability agent-capabilities human confirmation confirmed booking Inspiration Buying professional services is rarely a simple checkout flow. Buyers often begin with an incomplete goal, refine requirements through conversation, wait for a quote, and then schedule a consultation. AI agents can accelerate this process, but consequential actions—such as submitting a lead or booking time—should remain under direct human control. That tension inspired ClientWeave : an agent-native professional-services CPQ workspace where buyers and browser agents collaborate on the same scope, while the seller controls pricing and the buyer retains the final say. What it does ClientWeave creates a shared, attributed workspace for service discovery, scoping, pricing, and consultation booking. A browser agent can: Discover services relevant to the buyer’s goal Create and update a structured scope Calculate deterministic, seller-governed pricing Find available consultation times Finalize a confirmed lead or booking Every scope change records whether it came from the buyer or the agent, making the process transparent and auditable. The key safety boundary is intentionally simple: an agent cannot confirm an action on the buyer’s behalf. Before a lead is submitted or a consultation is booked, the buyer must directly confirm the exact current summary in the interface. If the scope or quote changes afterward, that confirmation becomes stale and finalization is rejected. How we built it ClientWeave is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Supabase, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, Zod, and TanStack Query . The application exposes six browser-native WebMCP tools: discover_services create_scope update_scope price_scope find_consultation_slots finalize_confirmed_scope These tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() with a compatibility fallback for older browsers. They use the same authenticated and audited HTTP boundaries as the regular user interface, so agent interactions do not bypass the application’s validation or security model. The codebase separates deterministic domain rules from framework and infrastructure concerns. Pricing uses canonical inputs, versioned rules, integer minor units, and per-line rounding to ensure that the same scope always produces a reproducible quote. Public scope links use restricted, expiring capabilities rather than owner-level access. We also added structured validation, origin checks, secure cookies, content security policies, rate limiting, redacted observability, audit events, and retention workflows. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was designing collaboration without silently transferring authority from the person to the agent. Hiding a confirmation button from an agent was not enough; the server also needed to verify that a human directly confirmed the exact scope, quote, and intended action currently being finalized. Another challenge was keeping state consistent across the visual interface, WebMCP tools, pricing engine, and database. An agent could update a scope while the buyer was reviewing it, so we needed freshness checks and clear invalidation rules to prevent stale quotes or confirmations from being used. Designing safe public access was also demanding. Buyers should be able to participate without creating an account, but a private scope link must grant access to only one scope and must never provide workspace-owner privileges. Finally, we wanted the agent experience to be reliable without depending on brittle DOM scraping. Creating narrow, well-described WebMCP tools—and ensuring they behaved exactly like the human-facing workflows—required careful contract and integration testing. What we learned We learned that agent-native software works best when agents receive structured capabilities rather than instructions to imitate clicks. WebMCP made the available actions explicit, typed, and easier to audit. We also learned that human oversight should be enforced as a system invariant, not presented as a warning message. Direct confirmation, confirmation freshness, limited capabilities, and server-side authorization all work together to preserve meaningful human control. Most importantly, attribution changes the quality of collaboration. When every change clearly shows whether it came from a person or an agent, users can review the process instead of merely trusting the final result. What’s next Next, we want to expand ClientWeave with richer seller-defined pricing rules, reusable scope templates, additional scheduling integrations, and collaborative comments. We also plan to explore approval policies for larger deals while preserving the same core principle: agents can help move work forward, but people remain responsible for consequential decisions. title: Dwellwise
pitch: Plan an apartment with an AI agent, supercharged with WebMCP
about_excerpt: Plan an apartment with an AI agent, supercharged with WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Main screen Fully furnished apartment layout ChatGPT using webMCP 3D Preview Inspiration Apartment hunting is a high-stakes guessing game. A floor plan can look spacious while hiding the things that matter: whether a bed fits, whether a dining table blocks circulation, or whether a room still feels livable once real furniture is inside it. We wanted to make apartment planning more honest and more collaborative. A person should be able to edit a plan visually, while an AI agent can understand the same apartment through safe, structured actions, not by guessing where to click. What it does Dwellwise is an apartment planner for testing a real layout before committing to it. You can create a private apartment project, draw and reshape its exterior and interior walls, add doors and windows, furnish rooms with real-world dimensions, and inspect the same saved layout in 2D and 3D. The 3D view includes an illustrative sunlight preview, editable supported finishes, and camera controls. The important difference is that Dwellwise is WebMCP-ready . Compatible browser agents can inspect the open apartment and use semantic tools to add or update furniture, walls, openings, exterior corners, finishes, preview settings, and history. They do not need to simulate clicks or drag pixels. How we built it Dwellwise is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, PostgreSQL, and WebMCP. One meter-based scene document powers the 2D editor, saved project data, furniture-fit checks, and 3D renderer. Walls, exterior corners, doors, and windows define the apartment; rooms are derived from the closed wall network; furniture keeps its own dimensions, position, rotation, and room assignment. For agent interaction, Dwellwise progressively registers page-scoped WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . Dashboard tools manage the current browser’s projects. Editor tools inspect and modify only the apartment already open in that browser. Both people and agents use the same application commands. That means agent edits receive the same geometry validation, collision checks, optimistic revision protection, save queue, undo/redo history, and visible UI updates as human edits. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not exposing buttons as tools. It was preserving the product’s rules when an agent changes geometry. Wall edits can split or merge rooms, change furniture assignments, and affect doors and windows. Openings need to stay attached to their host wall, respect wall boundaries, and behave predictably when they meet another opening. A stale browser tab must never silently overwrite a newer apartment state. We addressed this by building shared, atomic architecture commands and using revision-checked saves. WebMCP tools call those same commands rather than maintaining a separate AI-only editing path. We also kept sunlight honest: it is presented as a visual planning aid, not as a quantitative daylight or building-code analysis. Accomplishments that we’re proud of A complete private multi-project apartment workspace without requiring an account. One shared scene model for 2D planning, 3D rendering, geometry validation, and furniture fit. Semantic WebMCP tools for the dashboard and editor, with 32 distinct registered tool names. Shared human and agent editing commands for furniture, architecture, finishes, preview controls, and undo/redo. Revision-safe saving that prevents stale tabs from overwriting newer work. Browser-owned project isolation: tools never receive cookies, owner IDs, raw database access, or unrestricted scene writes. A normal visual editor that remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. What we learned An agent-ready app is not just a traditional UI with an AI layer attached. The tools need to express the real product concepts: walls, openings, rooms, furniture, revisions, and confirmation, not pointer gestures. WebMCP works best when it makes the safe path the easy path: bounded tools, clear inputs, shared validation, visible results, and a person still in control of destructive actions. What’s next We want to make complex floor-plan recreation more reliable, improve the visual fidelity of 3D apartment previews, and continue hardening the geometry and agent workflows against messy real-world plans. title: E-ternal × WebMCP
pitch: An open-source ERP that works with your browser agent — same screen, same state. The agent drafts; only a human can approve. Built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An open-source ERP that works with your browser agent — same screen, same state. The agent drafts; only a human can approve. Built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Judge access: live demo at https://et-demo.kaiwu.com.tw — sign in as judge / webmcp-judge . Best experienced in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser (GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra) or Chrome 146+ with the WebMCP flag. Prior-work vs. challenge-period work is documented in HACKATHON.md in the repo. Inspiration ERPs are where small businesses actually keep their money, stock and tax obligations — and they are exactly the software agents are worst at: dense forms, hidden state, and one wrong click posts a journal entry. We didn't want an agent that "operates" the ERP by guessing its way through the UI. We wanted the ERP to tell the agent what it may do, show the human everything the agent does, and keep the one irreversible step — committing to the books — in human hands. WebMCP is the first standard that makes that shape natural: the tools live in the page the human is already looking at. What it does E-ternal is an open-source ERP for Taiwanese SMEs (quotes → orders → shipping, double-entry accounting, e-invoicing, VAT filing, HR/payroll). For this challenge every page now registers WebMCP tools on document.modelContext (ChatGPT's built-in browser) and navigator.modelContext (Chrome). A person and their agent then work on the same screen: Ask, don't click. "What did we sell this month, who still owes us money?" → the agent calls query_report , get_dashboard_summary , search_partners and answers with real ledger numbers. No scraping, no menu navigation. Draft together. "Draft a quote for Blue Harbor: 20 Control Hubs plus one maintenance plan" → draft_quote fills a live draft card on screen, field by field. Nothing is written to the ERP. The human can edit any line on the card; the agent reads the same draft back with get_current_view . One draft, two editors. Approve by structure. submit_draft suspends the tool call and shows an approval card. Only a human can click it. There is deliberately no tool that posts, approves or voids anything — that door was never registered, so it cannot be jailbroken. See everything. An on-screen activity panel streams every tool call the agent makes; a status chip shows which tools are registered for the signed-in role. How we built it apps/web/src/webmcp/ — a self-contained layer inside the existing React app: a modelContext wrapper (feature detection, name-keyed dynamic registration, AbortSignal unregistration), 12 tools with English descriptions and strict JSON-Schema inputs, a framework-free state bus (activity log, co-edited draft, approval requests), and the UI (draft card, approval card, activity panel — fully i18n'd, light/dark aware). Tools are recomputed from role × current page and re-synced on every change: logout ⇒ only describe_site remains; a sales account never sees finance tools. Domain guardrails live inside the tools: prices are untaxed integers, VAT is computed server-side from user-maintained tax parameters (never by the agent), ambiguous customer/product names return candidate lists instead of guesses. Also built during the challenge: full English i18n of the ERP, a one-command demo dataset, and the live deployment (Vercel + Supabase). Challenges we ran into Two APIs, one standard. Chrome exposes navigator.modelContext ; ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext . Supporting only one means "the API exists but the page never registers tools" on the other — we shipped a resolver that handles both. Discovery timing. Agents scan for tools at page load, before sign-in. We register a read-only describe_site tool at module load so the registry is never empty, and it tells the agent which tools appear after sign-in. Chrome 151 has no unregisterTool . Logout could leave tools behind. We switched to the spec's registerTool(tool, { signal }) and abort to unregister — verified in the browser. Roles that are read-only on the server. Our "general manager" role is read-only by design; the judge account had to be a finance role so the approval path can actually create the quote. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real agent (ChatGPT desktop, GPT-5.6 Sol) ran the whole flow on the live site with zero clicking: reporting → draft → human edit → approval → quote #6 created with server-side VAT. That is the demo video, edited for pacing only. The red line is architectural, not a prompt: judges can read the tool registry and confirm the missing doors. Everything is open source (LGPL-3.0-or-later) with a public commit history for the challenge period. What we learned WebMCP's real power isn't "an API for agents" — it is that the agent and the human share the same pixels. Once the draft lives on screen, trust stops being a prompt-engineering problem and becomes a UI problem, which we know how to solve. What's next Approval-gated tools for the other document types (orders, purchase receipts, HR requests), page-level context ( get_current_view reporting filters and selected rows), and undo for agent actions — all inside the same registry discipline. Reusable playbook (open source) We distilled this whole integration into an open-source agent skill so any team can make their own site agent-ready the same way: kaiwutech-TW/webmcp-skill (MIT) — the API reality check, the six browser traps we hit, the five structural guardrails (registry red-line, central validation, untrusted-content quarantine, idempotent submission, live schemas), and framework-free TypeScript templates. title: Flock docs
pitch: Agent-native spreadsheet and document writing
about_excerpt: Agent-native spreadsheet and document writing Like 1 Comment Story Updates One workspace for people and agents. Organize Papers and Spreadsheets in the same live, browser-based workspace Flockdoc exposes workbook structure, ranges, formulas, formatting, and sheet operations through WebMCP. Document roles and sharing remain part of the product experience while agents receive context-appropriate tools. Inspiration Flockdoc began with a frustration I repeatedly encountered while using ChatGPT to create schedules for my family I liked creating a visual calendar with ChatGPT, but iteration happened at the wrong level of abstraction. When using ChatGPT with images, it would generate a file that I could not edit. Alternatively, if it used Google Sheets, the agent was limited with a set of point and click tools. Even a small request (change a cell value, restyle a header, add one column, or update a single section) could turn into another complete file-generation cycle with images. If I used Sheets, it would be painful watching ChatGPT stumbling to make the most simple edits on the page. The model did not have a structured way of reading or editing the spreadsheet, so it usually meant it was easier for me to just make the edits myself. Ultimately, I want my agent to be able to collaborate with me on the same document at the speed and accuracy I expect from coworkers. That idea became Flockdoc , a collaborative workspace for Documents and Spreadsheets where people use a familiar visual editor while agents interact with the same live application through WebMCP. What it does Flockdoc lets people create, organize, share, and edit documents in a browser-based workspace. Its spreadsheet editor exposes structured WebMCP tools that allow an agent to understand and modify the workbook currently open on the page. An agent can: inspect the workbook and discover its worksheets; read a targeted range, including values, formulas, styles, merges, and dimensions; write values and formulas into a precise A1 range; format cells without rewriting their contents; merge cells and adjust rows or columns; create, rename, reorder, or remove worksheets; and read the edited range again to verify the result. Flockdoc also exposes workspace-level tools for listing, creating, renaming, moving, and safely trashing documents. The important difference is that the agent is not manufacturing a replacement workbook somewhere else. It is operating on the same spreadsheet the person can see and edit. A person can define the goal and apply judgment where it matters. The agent can handle repetitive structure, formulas, formatting, and bulk changes. The person can then refine the result manually and ask for another targeted change without starting over. Why WebMCP Spreadsheets are especially difficult for agents to operate through ordinary visual automation. A grid may contain hundreds of similar-looking cells, hidden formulas, merged regions, formatting, and multiple worksheets. Clicking based on coordinates is slow and fragile, while passing entire files back and forth discards the live context of the application. WebMCP gives Flockdoc a typed, page-defined interface to the editor’s real capabilities. Instead of guessing which visible cell corresponds to a request, an agent can call read_range for Budget!A1:F20 . Instead of regenerating a workbook, it can call write_range to update only the required cells, format_range to apply presentation changes, and then read the range again to confirm the outcome. This makes the interaction more accurate, auditable, and efficient. It also lets Flockdoc expose only the tools appropriate to the current context. For example, users with view-only access receive inspection tools but not mutation tools. WebMCP turns the application itself into the source of truth. How I built it I built Flockdoc as a React and TypeScript application using Vite. The spreadsheet and rich-text editing surfaces are powered by Univer. When the browser provides document.modelContext , Flockdoc registers two contextual groups of tools: Workspace tools for document lifecycle operations such as listing, creating, renaming, moving, and trashing flockdocs. Spreadsheet tools that are registered while a workbook editor is mounted and operate directly through Univer’s workbook and range APIs. Each tool has a JSON schema, a focused description, input validation, and structured results. Spreadsheet writes use explicit A1 ranges and rectangular JSON matrices. Inputs are bounded, worksheet names are validated, range dimensions must agree with the supplied data, and tool failures are returned as useful errors rather than silently corrupting the workbook. Tool registration follows the page lifecycle. Spreadsheet tools appear when the editor is mounted and are removed with an AbortController when the user leaves it. Read-only users receive only read_me , inspect_workbook , and read_range . Flockdoc also includes real-time collaboration infrastructure, operation-based spreadsheet synchronization, Yjs CRDT updates for Papers, durable revision recovery, checkpoints, sharing roles, and recoverable deletion. The frontend is deployed through AWS CloudFront and integrated into the existing Flockfly platform. Challenges The first challenge was choosing the right tool granularity. One giant “update spreadsheet” tool would have recreated the same whole-file problem I was trying to solve. Very small cell-by-cell tools, however, would require excessive calls and make common tasks tedious. A1 ranges became the useful middle ground: precise enough to limit changes, but expressive enough for meaningful operations. Another challenge was preserving spreadsheet semantics. A cell is more than its displayed value. It may contain a formula, style, merge relationship, row height, or column width. Reading and writing those properties independently was necessary to support targeted edits without damaging unrelated parts of the workbook. Permissions were also important. An agent should not become a path around application authorization. Flockdoc derives its WebMCP capabilities from the same editing context used by the human interface, so view-only access does not expose mutation tools. What I learned I learned that designing tools for agents is just like building multi-user applications. Real-time collaboration required separating durable operations from full snapshots. Replacing entire workbook snapshots during live edits caused refresh flicker, revision conflicts, and the risk of overwriting newer work. Moving to operation-based synchronization and explicit recovery checkpoints made collaboration much more predictable. I found that synchronous collaboration with agents creates a magical experience that feels similar to having a human collaborator working alongside you. The same enhancements that make human collaboration delightful do the same for agent-to-human collaboration. title: Glassbook
pitch: Your money. Your browser. Your agent. The ledger never leaves this tab. The agent comes to it. You see every call. You can rewind every write.
about_excerpt: Your money. Your browser. Your agent. The ledger never leaves this tab. The agent comes to it. You see every call. You can rewind every write. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard. Spend, income, and net for the month. Transactions. Search, filter, and categorize. Activity log. Every agent call, and undo on writes. Budgets. Monthly limits and how much you spent. Import. CSV, Excel, OFX, or a text PDF. Rules. Save a merchant match and apply it. Inspiration Every budgeting app I have tried wants the statement first. Connect Plaid, upload a CSV, or paste it into a chat so a model can read it. You hand over a year of swipes, then get told you spend too much on dining. I started with a simpler question: can the ledger stay on your machine, and can you still get help? WebMCP is how I tried that. What it does Glassbook is a budgeting app that never leaves the tab. You import a statement, sort your spending, set budgets, and teach it a few rules about merchants you recognize. There is no account and no server. The ledger sits in localStorage . Connect an agent and it gets 18 WebMCP tools pointed at that same ledger. It can categorize a few hundred rows in one call, save a rule when you correct it, find a subscription you forgot about, work out why June cost so much, and set a budget. Every call lands in an activity log. If a write goes wrong, you can undo the last one, or walk back everything the agent touched. Doing this by hand is an hour of clicking category chips. A chat-only agent wants the statement uploaded first. Load the demo and you get about 320 uncategorized rows across four months. Ask the agent to categorize everything and the chips update on screen while it works. Once you connect an agent, tool results do enter its context. The tools send summaries and cleaned merchant names rather than your raw statement, unless you ask for more of them. Every call sits in the log. How I built it There is no MCP server sitting somewhere with a copy of your ledger. The tools run in the page, against the same Zustand store the UI is reading from. The site decides the schema, how little a read hands back, and what undo means. Each tool is defined once and registered on document.modelContext after the store loads, with fallbacks to navigator.modelContext and window.modelContext . Hosts do not agree on where to put it yet. ChatGPT injects it after first paint, and registration retries if it is not there. Then there is one wrapper around every call. It writes the activity row, and on a write it snapshots the whole ledger first, up to fifty deep. undoLast pops one. undoAll walks back a consecutive run of agent writes, including a streak where one call was wrong. Some tools only return text. The ones that make it feel shared also move the screen: highlight_transactions rings a row and scrolls it into view, set_view_filters puts you both on Dining for August, pin_insight leaves a card on the dashboard. Those do not work if the tools live on a server. Import follows the same rule as the ledger. CSV and TSV go through PapaParse, OFX and QFX through a local parser, Excel and text PDFs through AnyDoc WASM in a worker. Nothing is uploaded. await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "get_overview", description: "Call this first to understand the user's ledger.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {}, additionalProperties: false }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true }, execute: async (input) => { const text = await executeRegisteredTool("get_overview", input); return { content: [{ type: "text", text }] }; }, }); Challenges I ran into The first real problem was that I could not get site tools to appear at all. I had ChatGPT desktop from the Microsoft Store, and document.modelContext was simply undefined. The permission settings had no site tools entry in them either. I updated the app, restarted it, tried again, got nowhere, and eventually decided the Windows build did not support WebMCP, wrote that into the README, and pushed it. What actually fixed it was uninstalling the Store version and installing the same app from the ChatGPT website. Different build, same machine. I could not find that documented anywhere. Undo was harder than it looked. Logging what the agent did is easy. I still needed a way to take a write back. The store ended up snapshotting the full ledger on every agent write. That felt heavy until I watched an agent categorize three hundred rows, save a rule, and set a budget in one streak, then rewound all of it with one click. Bank files are not one format: OFX, .xls files that turn out to be HTML tables, European statements where 1.850,00 means one thousand eight hundred and fifty and imports as one euro eighty-five if you are not looking for it. Scanned PDFs still do not work. The fix is OCR, and I am not adding a cloud one. What I'm proud of The demo works end to end. Load 320 rows, connect an agent, categorize the lot, correct a chip, save a rule so the correction sticks, find Scribd at $11.99, ask why June was expensive and watch it ring the Delta and Airbnb rows from the 18th, set a dining budget, then rewind all of it from the activity log. Data minimization is in the tools on purpose. get_spending_summary returns grouped totals instead of three hundred rows. list_transactions sends cleaned merchant names, fifty at a time, and never the raw description. There are no account numbers in the model. What I learned The useful part of WebMCP is that the page owns the contract. The site decides what is readable, how much comes back, and whether it can be undone. Someone who would never paste a bank statement into a chat might still let an agent help. The activity log and the ring around the Delta row mattered more than another read endpoint. If you cannot see the tool call, it is hard to trust it. What's next for Glassbook Rules need to get smarter. Right now it is substring matching on the merchant, and it should handle amounts and date ranges too. The date-order override in the importer works but it is easy to miss, and sooner or later someone will import a European statement and get the days and months flipped. localStorage is also not where a multi-year ledger belongs. IndexedDB at some point. Scanned PDFs stay broken until on-device OCR is good enough. title: Hold the Pen
pitch: An agent can fill the form. You hold the pen. A benefits claim an AI agent can explain and fill through WebMCP tools, where every agent entry is reviewed by you and no tool can submit.
about_excerpt: An agent can fill the form. You hold the pen. A benefits claim an AI agent can explain and fill through WebMCP tools, where every agent entry is reviewed by you and no tool can submit. Like Comment Story Updates The claim as it loads. Seven WebMCP tools are registered, and the header states who does what. Your own entry stays yours, in green. The agent's entries are marked in amber and wait in the review list. The recorded demonstration runs the same tools. The agent's write is refused because the person answered first. Submit is disabled and says why: six agent entries are still unreviewed. Submitted by the person, with a reference. No tool could have done this. An agent can fill the form. You hold the pen. Hold the Pen is a benefits-style claim form that an AI agent can read, explain, and fill through WebMCP tools, while every value the agent writes stays marked, reviewable, and undoable, and no tool can submit the claim. Submission is deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool contract; review and declaration happen in the page, through controls no tool can reach. Live: https://holdthepen.vercel.app · Repo: https://github.com/nischal94/holdthepen (MIT) Why WebMCP is the right fit Consequential forms (benefits, insurance, immigration) are where people most want help and least want to lose control. Hold the Pen is a benefits-style claim whose question wording models a real UK Universal Credit-style claim (income received vs earned , household definitions, carer thresholds); the programme, rules, and submission are fictional. WebMCP lets the page hand an agent typed tools against the live form the person is looking at, instead of the agent guessing at the DOM. That is what makes a hard line possible: the page decides what an agent can do, and can make "submit" something no tool does. Seven tools are registered once on the document: get_claim_state , explain , review_agent_entries , fill_field , clear_field , navigate_to_section , prepare_submission_review . There is deliberately no commit tool. How it makes the experience better Three layers, three owners. Understand (agent, read-only): explain any question, term, or the consequence of each truthful answer, without recommending one. Fill (agent): write a value that is attributed, revision-checked, and undoable. Decide (person): review every agent entry, tick the declaration, submit. Those controls live in the page; no tool can reach them. Every agent write shows a text badge, "Filled by the agent, not yet reviewed", lands in a persistent review queue with Accept / Correct / Clear, and is announced to screen-reader users by field name, never by value. The submit button stays disabled, and says why, until every agent entry is reviewed and the declaration is ticked. Any edit after the agent stages a review invalidates it. The page works with no agent at all, and a recorded demonstration shows the flow for browsers without WebMCP. What a person and an agent can now do together Before: an agent helping with a form either typed into fields with no trace of what it changed, or stopped at "you should fill this in yourself". Now: the person asks "explain the income question before I answer it" and gets the meaning; says "fill in the household section" and watches three fields fill with a visible mark and a queue count of 3; asks "get it ready for me to check" and the agent names the four missing required fields in form order and cannot go further. The page protects the person in two ways: while they are editing a field, an agent write is refused with CONFLICT_FOCUSED ; once they have answered it, the agent cannot replace it and gets CONFLICT_HUMAN_VALUE . The recorded demonstration shows the second case. The agent prepares; the person approves. Verified end to end in the ChatGPT desktop browser on the deployed site. How WebMCP was implemented Imperative API only ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), because the ChatGPT browser does not support the declarative form API or iframe tools. Registration happens exactly once per page through a manager that reports a rejected registration as a visible degraded state and never unregisters (re-registering a changed schema is a race in the draft spec). Tools read a framework-independent store at call time via getSnapshot() ; React subscribes through useSyncExternalStore . A callback closing over React state would read the state at mount forever; a regression test writes, dispatches N times, then reads through the tool. Every failure returns the same envelope ( code , problem , cause , fix , retryable ) so the agent self-corrects. Strict validation in code, loose in schema. Outputs capped at 1.5K characters. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint ; tools that echo user text carry untrustedContentHint . AbortSignal is honoured, and both toolcancel and toolcanceled spellings are handled. 83 automated tests, including a typed fake of document.modelContext that enforces the browser contracts (duplicate names rejected, JSON-string arguments, cancellation events), axe in component tests, and eval fixtures in Chrome's expectedCall format for direct, ambiguous, and mid-chain prompts. Honest limit, stated in the README: the page cannot tell a human click from an automated one. A trustworthy human-only approval boundary is a platform primitive WebMCP does not yet have (spec issues #165 and #277); prepare_submission_review is a stand-in for elicitation, not elicitation.
