title: Lastest: QA reports with WebMCP site tools
pitch: Lastest verifies web releases with real-browser runs and visual diffs. Every page now exposes typed WebMCP tools: agents read public QA reports without login, and run, review and approve in-app.
about_excerpt: Lastest verifies web releases with real-browser runs and visual diffs. Every page now exposes typed WebMCP tools: agents read public QA reports without login, and run, review and approve in-app. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Lastest: QA reports with WebMCP site tools Lastest: a QA platform that hands its own controls to the browser's agent Inspiration Lastest is a visual-regression / release-verification platform: it drives a real browser through your web app, captures every step, diffs screenshots, checks accessibility, and produces a verdict. Agents already talk to it over a remote MCP server (29 tools, OAuth 2.1). But the place where a human actually looks at a result is a web page: a run report, a build, a public /r/<slug> share. When ChatGPT's browser and Codex started consuming WebMCP "site tools" (2026-08-25), the missing piece became obvious: the page you are looking at should expose the same typed tools the remote server does, scoped to what is on screen, so the agent beside you never has to scrape a screenshot or guess a button. What it does Every Lastest page registers typed tools on document.modelContext (with a polyfill fallback for browsers that have not shipped it yet): Public report pages ( /r/<slug> , no login): lastest_report_summary , lastest_list_visual_changes , lastest_list_failing_steps . An agent visiting a shared QA report can read the verdict, the failing steps and the pixel diffs as structured data instead of pixels. Signed-in app (dashboard, Verify, tests): a curated 16-tool surface out of the 29 on the MCP server: list projects/builds, QA summary, coverage, failing tests, change map, run tests, review a build, approve/reject diffs, publish a share, heal a test. Route-scoped registration. The set narrows and re-binds as you navigate: the build page contributes its buildId , the test screen its testId , so the agent gets ids from the page, never from its own guesswork. Tools unregister on unmount. Consent on every mutation. Write tools ( run_tests , approve_diffs , heal_test , ...) call requestUserInteraction() where available and always go through Lastest's own consent dialog that names the exact action. A dismissed dialog is never consent. Same auth as the human. Tools call a cookie-authed, same-origin /api/mcp/session bridge (CSRF-guarded with a custom header), so the agent can only ever act with the signed-in user's permissions. Public share tools are slug-scoped and never consult a session. How we built it src/lib/webmcp/ : feature detection ( document.modelContext , falling back to the deprecated navigator.modelContext and to @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill ), registry/allowlist with readOnlyHint annotations, argument binding from route context, consent wrapper, result shaping. src/app/api/mcp/session/route.ts : JSON-RPC bridge that reuses the exact MCP server the remote endpoint uses ( createServer() over InMemoryTransport ), so the WebMCP surface can never drift from the MCP surface. A test fails if an allow-listed tool disappears from tools/list . src/app/api/webmcp/share/[slug]/route.ts : login-free read-only tools for public reports. React provider + route-context components mounted in the app layout and the share page. 30+ unit assertions plus a Playwright e2e suite that injects a recorder modelContext and checks registration, route narrowing, disposal and the consent gate. Prior work vs. new work Lastest existed before the challenge (visual regression, MCP server, share pages). All WebMCP work was created inside the submission window : design doc 2026-08-27, feat(webmcp) PR #119 and follow-up #123 merged 2026-08-31, e2e suite and polyfill/consent slices after that. The git history in las-team/lastest is the audit trail; docs/design/webmcp.md records the design and its dated status. Challenges Spec churn: navigator to document , unregisterTool to AbortSignal , provideContext removed. Everything API-facing is confined to one module with a feature-detect shim that handles both shapes. Prompt-injection safety: destructive/admin tools are on a never-register list enforced by a test; every mutation is gated by consent. Keeping one source of truth: the browser tools are descriptor-driven from the real MCP server rather than a second hand-written tool list. Try it Public report, no login: https://app.lastest.cloud/r/02PU3rqVfArPEW5maatXOw (3 read-only tools) Signed-in app: https://app.lastest.cloud (judge credentials in the testing instructions) Tools are visible in ChatGPT's in-app browser under "Available site tools", or in Chrome with the WebMCP extension. What's next Consume WebMCP tools on the pages Lastest tests (agents verifying an app through its own declared tools), and surface tool-call traces in the run report. title: LUMLON
pitch: Is the air safe today? LUMLON answers for a person and for an agent through the same six site tools — and tells the agent when its own hazard data has expired.
about_excerpt: Is the air safe today? LUMLON answers for a person and for an agent through the same six site tools — and tells the agent when its own hazard data has expired. Like Comment Story Updates The page reads three provinces on load and plots all 77. Every card carries its observation time and source — before any agent arrives. Six site tools, declared by the page itself — no plugin, no separate server. Watches live in this browser only, never on a server. Asked about official warnings, the agent reads the expiry itself and refuses to report an expired warning as current. Nobody told it to. Inspiration Every morning I check the same thing: what is the air like today, is it safe, and can I play tennis with my son this evening? I check because my son was admitted to the hospital for it: a severe asthma attack, his airways closing, after breathing PM2.5 over a stretch of days when readings in our area were many times the level the World Health Organization calls safe. That is why "is the air safe today?" is not a curiosity in my house. It is a decision, every morning, before anything else gets decided. So I started building LUMLON: a Thai app that reads air, weather, and hazard conditions in real time. It exists, and you can open it — https://lumlon-web-dev.vercel.app is our development build, mid-redesign and not launched yet. I would rather you looked than took my word for it. What it is for is simple — to tell a person, day by day, at a time they choose or the moment they ask, whether it is safe to be outside. Not so they can study a chart, but so a father and son can plan an ordinary evening without gambling on it. Air you can plan around is also cheaper than a hospital admission, and in my family, that is not a figure of speech. The data already exists. Checking it does not scale. Today that means jumping between several apps, government agencies, and websites — each with its own shape, its own gaps, and its own idea of what "no data" means. It takes time, and on a morning you are in a hurry, you skip it. Would it not be better to simply ask — or to be told at the moments that matter — without opening anything at all? That is the kind of problem WebMCP is actually for. The person asking does not want a dashboard; they want an answer, in their own words, about their own province, right now. And people have already moved. They reach for an AI tool first now, which makes an agent a practical way to get this kind of information to someone — not a novelty. LUMLON was always meant to reach people through whatever channel they already use, not only inside one app. What WebMCP adds is that the answer can come from us: specific readings, each carrying its source and the time it was taken, instead of whatever an agent can assemble on its own. An agent also does something a website cannot do for everyone at once — it turns a reading into an answer in the language and the words of whoever is asking. That is why one of these six tools does not return a number at all. It returns a judgment about a specific activity, together with the readings it used and the reason it reached that answer. A number tells you what the air is like. A person still has to decide whether to go outside. So we did not build a chatbot on top of a website. We made the website itself something an agent can read, and kept the human looking at the same screen the whole time. What it does LUMLON exposes six tools to any WebMCP-capable agent, for all 77 provinces of Thailand. Tool What it does Kind search_locations Turns a place name into a province code. Thai or English, loose spelling. read get_environment_snapshot Air quality, short forecast, and official hazard alerts — each alert carries its own expiry, because they come from a dated snapshot. read get_safety_briefing Decides whether an activity is advisable and explains why , quoting the readings. read create_watch Saves a rule that warns when a reading crosses a threshold. write list_watches Lists the rules saved in this browser. read delete_watch Removes one rule. destructive It is a working page before an agent arrives. Open it with no agent at all and it reads three provinces on load — live PM2.5 and AQI, plus the official hazard alerts from a dated snapshot, which every card says on its face — and plots them on a map of all 77 provinces drawn from our own registry. You can search a province in Thai or English and read it yourself, with one click, through the same data path a tool call takes. This matters for a reason beyond looks: an agent-ready site can only be judged on what the agent adds , and that needs a "before" to compare against. A blank page waiting for a tool call is not a product an agent improves — it is a log viewer. What people and agents do together, concretely. You ask "is the air safe for a morning run in Chiang Mai tomorrow?" The agent calls two tools and answers in a sentence. At the same moment, the page in front of you updates — the same reading, the same timestamp, the same source. The map moves to Chiang Mai on its own; the card that appears is labelled read by the agent , next to cards labelled read by this page , so you can always tell which of the two of you did what. You did not lose the screen by talking to an agent; you gained a second way to drive it. Then you say "watch this and warn me if it goes above 75," and a rule appears as a card you can see — and that you remove the same way you made it, by asking. The panel lists your watches; it does not hide them, and it does not let anything but a tool call change them. The map moves without a seventh tool. We deliberately did not add a set_map_view tool to let the agent pan the screen. The view follows the tools it already has: search a place, the camera frames it; read a place, the pin lights up. Tool descriptions are charged against the agent's context on every single turn, so a tool is a cost, not an achievement — and this one would have bought nothing that the existing events did not already carry. Three decisions that make this usable rather than merely present: Every block of data carries when it was observed and where it came from. A number without a timestamp is a number nobody can check — and the person hearing an agent read it aloud cannot see the screen to judge for themselves. Missing data is reported, never hidden. If a source cannot be read, the answer says so, in a gaps field the agent reads out. "Could not read" and "there are no alerts" are different facts, and collapsing them is the single most dangerous thing a safety tool can do. For the same reason, a briefing never says good while something it needed was unavailable: missing data can lower our confidence, but it never lowers a warning. Read tools and write tools fail in opposite directions, on purpose. A read tool with one number missing still answers the question that was actually asked, and names what it could not read. A write tool with anything unvalidated refuses the whole command. Both write tools are annotated as writes, and delete_watch is additionally marked destructive. In the session we recorded — with approvals set to allow everything — the agent still stopped and asked before it deleted a rule. How we built it The tools do not know where their data comes from. They only ever talk to a provider interface, and that interface is in this repository: src/webmcp/providers/types.ts . The implementation behind it here is the bundled one, which calls only public sources. Be precise about what you can and cannot check in this export. The second implementation — the one that reads the backend of the product we are building — is not in this repository. The export is generated by following what the shipped entry actually imports, and since this entry runs on the bundled provider, the other implementation is never reached and never copied. So what you can verify here is the seam, not both sides of it: one interface, one implementation, and six tool files that name neither. That seam is the reason this entry can be frozen for judging while the product keeps moving, and it is also the reason we are telling you the second half is missing instead of letting the sentence imply it is here. To be exact about what that does and does not mean: this WebMCP layer was built for this challenge, and the product ships with it switched off. The shared interface is what makes it portable — not a claim that agents are driving our production app today. The module is invisible when it is off. WebMCP registration lives behind a build flag and a dynamic import. With the flag off, a scan of our own build output finds no trace of the module — 2,838 files swept, zero hits, on the tree we build from. We check this rather than asserting it, because we found the opposite of what we assumed the first time we measured: an unset environment variable is not a constant, so the bundler could not prove the branch was dead, and it emitted the chunk anyway. The upstream sources are switchable without a cod

title: MarkDown Stripper
pitch: MarkDown Stripper uses WebMCP to help people and agents clean documents, detect sensitive data locally, and prepare AI-ready content—with human approval before anything is shared.
about_excerpt: MarkDown Stripper uses WebMCP to help people and agents clean documents, detect sensitive data locally, and prepare AI-ready content—with human approval before anything is shared. Like Comment Story Updates Description Input use cases Inspiration Sharing a document with an AI agent often begins with an unreliable manual process: remove formatting, repair broken structure, extract useful references, look for sensitive information, and decide what is safe to share. Traditional browser automation adds uncertainty because agents must guess which controls to use and how to interpret the page. We built MarkDown Stripper to create a safer, structured handoff between people and agents. WebMCP was a natural fit because it lets the application expose precise capabilities while keeping the person in control of the same visible workspace. What it does MarkDown Stripper is a local-first document preparation workspace. It imports Markdown, TXT, HTML, DOCX, PDF, and image files, then converts them into Plain, Readable, or AI-ready text. It extracts references, identifies unresolved references, performs OCR, and detects potentially sensitive information locally. Through WebMCP, an agent can inspect bounded document state, prepare an AI-ready handoff, run a privacy scan, check readiness, and redact findings that the person selected by ID. Sensitive content reads and export actions remain blocked until the person reviews the document and explicitly approves that exact version. If the document or relevant processing state changes, approval is automatically invalidated. Why this use case strongly fits WebMCP Document handoff is a multi-step, stateful workflow, not a single button click. An agent needs to understand the document’s current state, choose appropriate conversion settings, inspect risks, make controlled changes, and verify whether the result is ready. With conventional browser automation, the agent must infer all of this from labels, coordinates, and changing page layouts. WebMCP gives the agent narrow, typed operations that express the application’s real capabilities and return structured, verifiable results. It allows the agent to act reliably without creating a separate interface or bypassing the person. The result is a genuinely collaborative workflow in which the agent handles repetitive preparation while the human retains authority over sensitive content. How it improves the user experience The user no longer has to manually clean a document, hunt for references, run separate privacy checks, and repeatedly explain the page state to an agent. The agent can prepare the visible document, run local checks, and report exactly what still needs attention. Every mutation remains visible in the normal interface, privacy findings have stable IDs, long results are returned in bounded pages, and the readiness tool provides clear next steps without exposing document text. The approval gate makes the boundary understandable: preparation can be delegated, but content cannot be read, copied, or downloaded by the agent until the person approves the current version. What people and agents can now do together A person can import or paste a document and ask an agent to prepare it for a safe AI handoff. The agent can switch the output to AI-ready context, preserve useful references, open Insights, run the local privacy scan, and explain which findings require review. The person decides which finding IDs should be redacted and can see each resulting change in the editor. After a redaction, the agent can scan the new version and check readiness again. The person then reviews and approves that exact state. Only after approval can the agent retrieve a bounded text segment, list approved assets, copy the output, or initiate a local text download. This review-first collaboration would be fragile and difficult to verify through coordinate-based automation alone. How we implemented WebMCP The application uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with a Cloudflare Worker serving the production build. The top-level page registers 14 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools share the same live React state and actions as the human interface, so agent actions remain visible and verifiable. Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema plus runtime input validation. Content-bearing responses use bounded, cursor-based pagination and are marked as untrusted content. Successful calls return structured JSON, failures reject, and registration is cancelled through an AbortController when the page unmounts. Sensitive tools require an approval fingerprint tied to the exact document, conversion settings, privacy findings, scan status, warnings, and unresolved references. Any relevant change invalidates that approval. Conversion, OCR, privacy scanning, redaction, and document processing run locally in the browser. Aggregate telemetry contains only allowlisted dimensions and never includes document text. The repository includes automated tests for document processing, WebMCP tools, approval invalidation, pagination and output limits, atomic registration, and Worker behavior. Challenges we ran into One major challenge was giving agents useful access without exposing the entire document automatically. We solved this with bounded, cursor-based reads and a human approval checkpoint tied to the exact document state. We also had to keep agent operations synchronized with the visible interface. Instead of creating a separate automation layer, the WebMCP tools call the same actions used by the React application. Document imports created additional complexity because PDFs, scanned images, DOCX files, and Markdown preserve structure differently. OCR and privacy detection also needed to remain responsive while running entirely in the browser. Finally, changing or redacting a document had to invalidate previous approval reliably. We addressed this with an exact-state fingerprint covering the document, conversion settings, scan status, warnings, and findings. Accomplishments that we are proud of We created a non-trivial set of 14 WebMCP tools that supports a complete workflow rather than wrapping a single button. The application lets people and agents collaborate in one shared workspace while preserving a meaningful human privacy checkpoint. An agent can prepare and evaluate a handoff, but it cannot retrieve or export document content until the person approves the current version. We are also proud that document conversion, OCR, privacy analysis, and redaction happen locally. The project supports several document formats, provides multilingual OCR options, and remains fully usable as a human-facing editor when WebMCP is unavailable. What we learned We learned that agent-native applications need more than tool exposure. Tools need clear boundaries, verifiable state, careful handling of untrusted content, and mutations that remain understandable to the person using the page. We also learned that human approval should be attached to data state rather than represented by a permanent boolean. Approval must expire whenever the content or relevant processing state changes. Most importantly, WebMCP works best when agents and people operate on the same product state instead of using separate interfaces. What is next for MarkDown Stripper Next, we plan to add configurable privacy policies, more document formats, stronger multilingual detection, and clearer explanations for each privacy finding. We also want to introduce reusable handoff profiles for workflows such as research, customer support, legal review, and AI knowledge-base preparation. Longer term, MarkDown Stripper could provide a standard privacy-aware handoff layer for any web application that prepares user-controlled information for agents. title: Nightstand — a health diary you run by voice
pitch: A local-first health diary you run by voice. On WebMCP, every on-screen action is also an agent tool so people who can't type keep their records hands-free. Zero backend.
about_excerpt: A local-first health diary you run by voice. On WebMCP, every on-screen action is also an agent tool so people who can't type keep their records hands-free. Zero backend. Like Comment Story Updates The home screen — everything you do here, your agent can do by voice. 19 of 19. Entries it logs show "logged by your agent." Track medications by voice or on screen — the same tool either way. Schedules are versioned so past adherence stays truthful. Ask your agent to prepare a doctor summary — symptom trends, adherence, as-needed doses — downloadable as a real, selectable-text PDF. Inspiration The person I built this for has rheumatoid arthritis. Pain and stiffness in the hands make filling in a form miserable — and it's a disease that asks for a log every single day , for a consultation that happens once every three months, when nobody remembers the details. The people who most need to keep a health diary are often the ones who can least type one. So the diary shouldn't be typed. It should be spoken. WebMCP's own explainer names this exact motivation: it can "enable agents to assist users of accessibility technology." I wanted to take that literally — expose an entire app as agent tools, so someone who cannot comfortably type can run all of it hands-free by voice. What it does Nightstand is a local-first health diary you operate by talking to your AI agent. Speaking, hands-free, you can: Log naturally — "My knee hurts, about a seven, and I took my methotrexate" becomes two records from one sentence, with a single confirmation. Correct and undo by voice — "Actually, make it a five." "No, undo that." When you can't retype, the repair path is the product. Adjust the interface by voice — make the text bigger, jump to a section, raise contrast. Prepare a doctor's summary — "Prepare a summary for my doctor" reveals a printable report (symptom trend, medication adherence, as-needed doses), and one large 56 px button downloads it as a real, selectable-text PDF — generated in the browser, no backend. The whole flow is co-browsing : the person watches the screen while the agent acts, so every step is visible and reversible. How I built it WebMCP is the center of the project, not a wrapper around it. True parity, not a hand-typed number. Every capability is declared once — id, tool name, description, zod schema, handler — and from that one declaration come the on-screen control and the WebMCP tool, the published inputSchema , the runtime validation, and the TypeScript types. The "19 of 19" badge reads the registry, and a test compares the on-screen actions against the tools in both directions, so the number cannot drift. Three trust layers — 5 read-only answer tools, plus act and transact tools that change state. Because Nightstand is a co-browsing journey with a human present, it safely spans all three, with undo and explicit confirmations as the guardrails . An untrusted-input boundary. Tool arguments are produced by a language model, so every handler validates them with zod at the edge; past that point the data is typed and trusted, and invalid arguments return a readable error instead of writing a bad number into a medical record. One write path , so undo covers every write — spoken or tapped. You refer to things by name, never by id : the agent is never handed an identifier it can't hand back. Stack: Next.js (static output: 'export' ), React 19, TypeScript (strict), Tailwind 4, zod, idb over IndexedDB, pdf-lib (zero-dependency, lazy-loaded), Vitest. Zero backend — no API routes, server actions, or middleware — and zero outbound requests after load. The privacy promise holds because the repository has nowhere to hide anything. Challenges I ran into Printing is dead in the ChatGPT app's embedded browser. window.print() and Ctrl+P simply don't work there. I pivoted the doctor summary to a client-side PDF download that works both in a full browser and in the app. A page-initiated voice download loses user activation in that embedded browser and is stopped by the browser's policy — proven, not a bug I could fix. So the summary is a button : the agent prepares it by voice, and the person taps one large target. Timezone-correct clinical math. Adherence and local-day logic had to survive DST and non-UTC offsets, or a number handed to a doctor could be wrong. Pinned timezone test fixtures caught real bugs. Honest domain limits. The schedule model understands daily times, not weekly ones, so a weekly DMARD like methotrexate is logged as as-needed rather than scored — the app says so instead of reporting a wrong number. Which agents actually call the tools? I found that ChatGPT's Chrome extension drives the DOM instead of calling the WebMCP tools — while the judged surfaces (ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled) genuinely consume them. Verifying that shaped where the demo lives. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Capability parity that's real, not claimed — enforced by a test that gates every commit. Privacy by architecture — verified zero outbound requests three different ways. Accessibility as the reason the app exists — WCAG 2.2 AA, 56 px targets, a Lighthouse accessibility score of 100 . Independently validated by Google Chrome Labs' official webmcp-evals harness: 11/11 tool calls pass against the live deployment — real WebMCP calls, not DOM automation. What I learned WebMCP's value for accessibility isn't enabling voice — a DOM-driving agent can operate a site too. It's making agent operation reliable, safe, correct, and portable for something as sensitive as medical records: a typed contract with validation and undo, a smaller data footprint than screen-scraping, and one tool surface that works for any agent — in-browser or headless. And a design rule I'll keep: never hand the agent an identifier it cannot hand back. What's next Weekly and complex medication cadence, so DMARDs are scored for adherence. More entry types and languages. A caregiver mode: the same tool surface, operated by a headless agent someone sets up for a person who can't. title: Poll
pitch: Poll is a shared survey studio where people and AI agents build, launch, and analyze studies together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Poll is a shared survey studio where people and AI agents build, launch, and analyze studies together through WebMCP. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Home GIF WebMCP in action Results Inspiration The inspiration came from a routine observation of our friend, a PHD student. She rushed home to her laptop because she had to check in with her research participants and see how many had responded by a certain time. We remember thinking to ourselves what a tedious task, what if she could get a summary of her results and a summary of her participants feedback by asking an agent. That brought to mind the hours she spent in Qualtrics and Prolific and did the same tedious task: create a new page, pick a question type, click, type, repeat. She already knew her research questions. What if she could tell an agent to build the survey, and all she has to do is approve it. Later she can ask for a summary of results across her studies without needing to rush home. That is Poll: a survey studio where a researcher and their agent share one workspace, and a person still decides what goes out. What it does Poll is a survey research studio. A researcher works with an agent to build, share, and report results of the survey. The human has to give explicit approval for all participants facing tasks while the agent can help them get to the final draft quicker. In a WebMCP-capable browser, an authenticated user can use their favorite agent tool like Codex to interact with Poll to create a draft from a research goal, edit questions, preview, share, and summarize results or feedback. Tools call the same APIs as the buttons on the screen, allowing humans and agents to make edits the same way. Participant routes register no tools: people still consent and answer for themselves. How we built it We started by mapping out a researcher workflow and where an agent can help them. We wanted to see what the user workflow looks like end-to-end should a user choose to manually create a survey, edit the questions, and launch it. The majority of the tedious work came from survey building, so that became the focus of our first tool. We spent time in the documentation reading the example repos and WebMCP docs from Google, OpenAI's Site tools notes, and Cloudflare's WebMCP React starter. What we wanted was a survey studio that still works in a normal browser, and then researcher tools if WebMCP is there. Codex then did the majority of the implementation. We used Codex agents for most of the coding and also used automations to run long running PRs overnight that could be merged in parallel. We reviewed every open PR, no agent was allowed to merge their own work. We tested WebMCP with Codex's Chrome plugin, in-app browser and also the Chrome DevTools MCP. The gif on our landing page was entirely created by Codex and DevTools MCP . We used Cloudflare MCP directly as well to help with db configuration, setup and automated release pipelines. Stack : Our app uses React 19, React Router and TanStack Query with a Hono powering the api. We use D1 and Drizzle for the database. The UI, api and the WebMCP tools all share the same Zod contracts as well. Finally we are using Better Auth for authentication and Resend for email through a Cloudflare Worker cron. WebMCP implementation. Tools are registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool through a small React hook ( useWebMCPTool ). Registration is keyed on the public metadata (name, description, schema, annotations) while the handler is swapped in a ref, so navigating between Build, Share, and Responses does not tear the catalog down. Every tool carries annotations: readOnlyHint , idempotentHint , destructiveHint: false , and untrustedContentHint wherever participant-authored text appears. All of our tools are aware of the role of the logged in user as well to always allow authenticated access. edit_survey is a the core tools, it is a single transactional batch (add, update, move, replace, delete pages and questions, with same-call ref names for branching). Every write that the agent does returns the new revision, an outline, and a validation check, so the agent can see whether it broke anything without another tool call. The /demo route swaps the network transport for a browser local one behind the same tool code, so the entire app is usable without signup Stack. React 19, React Router, TanStack Query, Tailwind on the client; Hono on Cloudflare Workers; D1 with Drizzle; Better Auth; Resend for invitation email from a durable outbox drained after approval; Vitest with 250+ tests across jsdom and the Workers runtime. MIT licensed. Challenges we ran into The agent could not see the tools - In production Chrome refused the page: "WebMCP is disabled for this page because the site's WebMCP configuration exceeds supported limits." We could not find any published limit in the webmcp spec. Our first edit_survey schema, generated from Zod with every question type inlined wherever it appeared, and was close to 100 KB and about 30 levels deep. We rewrote it to define each question type and condition once and point to it with $ref , and hand-tuned the public shape. The same operations, same validation, now under 11 KB and 11 levels deep. The tools kept vanishing mid task - Poll is an SPA and moving from Build to Share rebuilds component state. Our hook treated every new tool object as a new catalog, unregistering everything. To the agent, the tools disappeared between calls. We split "what the tool is" (registered once) from "what it does right now" (a ref that always sees the current survey). Drawing the line between agent work and human approval - One of the hardest decisions to make while building this was what should an agent be unable to do even if asked? We debated this decision a lot because, as models are getting better, they are able to do much more work autonomously and correctly but on the other hand we thought from a researcher's POV and landed on prepare only approach. Anything that reaches other humans has to be explicity approved through the web interface. title: RigBuilder - the AI assisted PC Builder
pitch: RigBuilder is a PC part picker where your agent is the interface: the page solves compatibility, constraint and budget - ChatGPT or Chrome drives it through WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: RigBuilder is a PC part picker where your agent is the interface: the page solves compatibility, constraint and budget - ChatGPT or Chrome drives it through WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Andreas: For the past year I have been interested in one particular question - what does an application look like when its primary user is an agent? And how can humans and agents collaborate? Since the start of last year, I have explored the MCP spec at depth and how it can be used by agents, and chronicled my adventures at my blog ( https://nullpointer.se ). I've been especially interested in "agentic UI", and what the future of applications and UI will look like, as we enter the agentic era. I have spent a lot of time exploring protocols such as AG-UI, A2UI and MCP Apps to try to understand what lies in the future for agentic applications and user interfaces. I am a strong believer in the paradigm of "generative UI", and the agent dynamically presenting just the information and the functionality the user needs - when he or she needs it. My main realization from the last year of experimentation with MCP and adjacant tech is that agentic user interfaces are not only more efficient, they are also more fun to use. In July 2025 I read about MCP-B on Hacker News and the idea that web apps could expose MCP tools directly to an agent running in the browser. Since I was deep into MCP at that time, I was really excited by this and started exploring the spec. Being in the Microsoft space, I did experiments with MCP-B tools running inside a Power App , and when MCP-B was accompanied by the WebMCP proposal and Chrome shipped its first preview, I tried that too in various demos - for example here . When I heard about the WebMCP hackathon I got really stoked, since I had been wanting to try WebMCP more. I also already had a good demo scenario - at the conference AgentCon Stockholm earlier this year I gave a talk on agentic applications and used a PC part picker to demonstrate how to use AG-UI to share state between an agent and an app (still live here ). It was a good example of an agentic application, but the website had to ship the AI-assistant and foot the inference bill. WebMCP inverts that, which is an interesting idea. The user brings the agent, and the site hands it tools. So we (Andreas Adner and my friends Rafsan Huseynov (in the US) and David Lorenze (in Spain)) expanded upon this idea and built RigBuilder, a PC Builder where an agent can help you out, using WebMCP. What it does RigBuilder is an agent-native PC part picker. It is also a compatibility and constraint solver , making sure that all parts fit together and are within your budget. Your agent (ChatGPT's desktop browser, or Chrome 149+ with an agent) drives the build through 14 WebMCP tools and the agent gets access to validation and a gets a state revision back on every call. For example, ask for "a quiet, compact 1440p gaming PC under $1500" and the agent helps you assemble it. Swap the case by hand and say "fix whatever broke" and the agent reads your change from the shared state. Ask to get under $1400 and the page's optimizer computes the swap plan for the agent to present, and so on and so forth. Ask to see it, and render_build tool produces a brand-free impression of your parts using an OpenAI imagegen model (expect mixed results, it's AI after all ;-) There is a also a second user group - admins. An admin can curate the part catalogue in an WebMCP-enabled admin experience, where he for example can get help from his agent to research a newly launched part on the web and add it to the catalogue with the help of the agent. And RigBuilder is also a complete manual part picker, if you don't have an agent. :-) How we built it React/Vite/TypeScript with Zustand, and a single Cloudflare Worker: D1 for the catalog, R2 for renders and part cards, KV for share links, a Durable Object for the daily render quota, a Rate-Limiting binding for bursts, Turnstile for the render gate, Cloudflare Access to gate access to the admin side. The WebMCP surface was the priority, so it got the most design effort. Every tool returns the same envelope: validated build, conflicts, revision, so the agent never has to guess what changed. Shared state is versioned: a write based on stale knowledge is rejected even if the agent never learned about revisions, because the guard defaults to the revision the agent last saw. Tool descriptions carry untrustedContentHint where web-sourced text enters. The render_build tool sends only part ids and enums; the Worker rebuilds the prompt and cache hash itself and never trusts a client prompt or image. The catalog is 448 hand-authored parts, 82 verified against manufacturer spec pages with recorded sources; every tool result says which is which. Challenges The main challenge was deciding what the WebMCP tools should actually do. We did not want to expose a simple "remote-control" layer that simply mapped tools to normal user interactions - buttons and clicks. The tools needed to give the agent capabilities beyond what a user could accomplish: validating an entire build, identifying conflicts, optimizing against a budget, and returning a complete, structured view of the resulting state. Finding the right level of abstraction was a challenge. Each tool had to be powerful enough to add real value, but focused enough for an agent to understand when and how to use it. Shared state created another WebMCP-specific problem: both the human and the agent can modify the build. The agent might plan its next action from a state that the user has already changed manually. We solved this with versioned state and revision guards that reject stale writes, while still allowing agents to use the tools without explicitly managing revision numbers on every call. From my experiments with AG-UI I have realized that shared state between agent and app is a major unlock when it comes to agentic applications - and WebMCP is really good fit here. Finally, we had to treat the agent as capable but not inherently trusted. Tool inputs are validated by the application, web-sourced catalog text is marked as untrusted, and sensitive operations are reconstructed and checked on the server. WebMCP makes an application dramatically more accessible to agents, but it comes with some new and specific challenges when it comes to security. What we learned WebMCP changes who and what you design for. When the agent becomes the interface, tool descriptions form the foundation of the interaction model. Designing a good agent experience requires the same care as designing a visual one; that care simply moves into the tools, their contracts, and the state they share with the page. This is a pretty interesting shift. It's also an interesting challenge that we can't really make that many assumptions with regard to the agent that is consuming the WebMCP tools. We also learned that the entire “add an AI assistant” architecture can disappear/morph. RigBuilder has no embedded model, inference bill, or chat widget. The user brings the agent, while the application contributes its tools, domain knowledge, and interface. There is no assistant bolted onto the side anymore - also a major shift. What's next Lots of stuff to do. More verified parts, exact cards for the whole catalog, live pricing, and the part I care most about - bringing the same pattern back to the business applications I work with in my day job. title: Rundown - agentic dashboard builder
pitch: rundown allows you to create dashboards though WebMCP - while seeing the effects on the dashboard in realtime
about_excerpt: rundown allows you to create dashboards though WebMCP - while seeing the effects on the dashboard in realtime Like Comment Story Updates Screenshot of a marketing dashboard, created by rundown Inspiration I work as a product engineer at a digital advertising company, and dashboards are part of every working day. Giving clients and partner agencies real-time data takes work off both sides. Users do not have to open Excel files and build charts to understand how a campaign performs. Dashboard creators set a dashboard up once, and new data flows in every day without manual work. Tools like Looker Studio and Whatagraph let client and agency users work with those dashboards interactively. They filter for the data they need and look at visualizations built for their marketing goal. None of the tools I tried offer first-class agent support for creating dashboards. The dashboard creator knows the client's goals and therefore knows which data belongs on the dashboard and how. I think of this as the intent in the creator's head. I found no prebuilt way to get that intent into a dashboard without a lot of manual effort. WebMCP offers a unique angle on this. Dashboards are a visual interface. LLMs and agents are text interfaces. There are early formats like MCP Apps, but the gap is still open. So at the start of the hackathon I asked myself: Could WebMCP let me build dashboards with an agent while the dashboard, the visual artifact, still carries the intent of the person who made it? What it does As a tool, rundown covers most of what Looker Studio or Whatagraph do. You connect data sources, build dashboards out of widgets, add filters and controls, and share dashboards with other users. What makes rundown different is that every action in the dashboard editor is also a WebMCP tool. Open a dashboard in the ChatGPT desktop app and say "add a bar chart of spend per campaign for the last 30 days". The agent calls describeDatasource to learn the fields, then addWidget , and the chart shows up in the dashboard tab while the tool call runs. You drag it into place with the mouse, or ask the agent to call moveWidget . If a number looks off, explainWidget returns the compiled SQL. There are around twenty tools, filtered per page. The dashboard editor gets the full set, a datasource page gets the field and metric tools, and a share link only exposes read-only tools like queryWidget and getControlOptions , so an agent can answer questions about a dashboard it is not allowed to edit. The tools are deliberately generic: addWidget , updateWidget , updateLayout , upsertCalculatedField , shareDashboard , and so on, rather than one tool per chart type. Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP? A dashboard is a visual artifact. Its value is in how it looks, not in its JSON. A classic MCP server could expose the same tools, but the person would be editing something they cannot see. WebMCP puts the agent inside the page that already renders the result. The agent works in text, the human checks in pixels, and both look at the same state. The intent I described above survives because the creator sees every change the moment it happens and can correct it by hand or by prompt. The tools also get the page's context for free. The hook knows which dashboard is open, whether the user may edit it, and whether it is a share link. The agent does not need to be told any of that. How does it create a better user experience? Without WebMCP, the user has the tool in one window and the agent in another. The agent changes something through an API, and the user refreshes the tool to see what happened. The alternative is building a chat assistant into the tool, which locks the user out of their own agent setup: their skills, their AGENTS.md, their memory, their preferred model. With WebMCP the user keeps their agent and gets the live view. Rundown goes one step further. The first tool call switches the editor into agent mode, which hides the editor sidebars and gives the dashboard the whole screen. The user can switch back manually at any time. During an agent session the page turns into a preview of the result, not a form. How I built it What existed before About 1.5 years ago I drafted a data structure for a dashboard tool, at the time mostly inspired by what Looker Studio can do. It came closest to what agency users need. The draft and its iterations are in this folder . From that draft and a rough idea of the behavior, I wrote a plan for the first vertical slice together with GPT 5.6-Sol and Claude Fable 5. Architecture decisions like using DuckDB as the data layer were made at that point. After that the work was a loop of unattended implementation runs, GitHub review flows, and human-in-the-loop sessions to try different versions of a feature. Most of the code was written in T3 Code with GPT 5.6-Sol, with Opus 5 and Fable 5 pulled in for second opinions on specific tasks. Architecture How do I implement WebMCP? A React hook called useWebMcpTools() runs on every route. It receives the route's context (open dashboard, permissions, share token) and registers the matching set of tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The tools call the same API the GUI editor calls, so the agent and the mouse go through one code path and stay in sync. After a mutation the hook refreshes the page state, so the change is visible immediately. The first tool call also activates agent mode, which hides the editor chrome, unless the user has chosen a mode by hand. Challenges I ran into This was my first project on Cloudflare, and I had little experience with serverless functions. Early on I struggled to deploy DuckDB, the credentials, and the data in R2 in a way that worked together. Workers cap at 128 MB RAM and 10 MB of gzipped code, and DuckDB blows through both. In the end I moved the query engine into a Cloudflare Container, which has far higher limits and lets DuckDB read Parquet and CSV files straight from R2. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Every editor action has a tool equivalent. There is nothing the mouse can do that the agent cannot, and nothing the agent can do that the user cannot see. The architecture scales without code changes. DuckDB is a fast OLAP engine, and combined with R2 storage and Cloudflare's scaling it handles complex dashboards without special handling in the code. What I learned WebMCP sits in a different place than a classic MCP server. The standardized agent-tool interface is the same, but staying close to the UI lets the user inspect and act on the result. That makes it a good fit for GUI-heavy workflows, and a bad fit for things that are better done headless. Agents call tools faster than a page refreshes. Refreshing state after every mutation, and switching the UI into a preview mode on the first call, mattered more for the experience than any single tool. What's next for Rundown - agentic dashboard builder Blended data sources. Combining several sources into one is a niche but very valuable use case. Matching fields across sources is the hardest problem non-technical users face here, and an agent that can introspect both sources through WebMCP could do most of that matching. More data source types. Today rundown reads CSV and Parquet uploads stored in R2. For real use it needs SQL sources like PostgreSQL and BigQuery. Workspace metrics. A shared set of calculated fields per workspace is planned and partly built, but hidden from the UI until it is complete. Self-service registration. The tool is invite-only. Before opening it up I want a proper security audit and the GDPR work needed to run it in the EU. title: SafeShare
pitch: Redact sensitive PDFs and images locally with privacy-preserving WebMCP assistance.
about_excerpt: Redact sensitive PDFs and images locally with privacy-preserving WebMCP assistance. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Sharing a document often means choosing between speed and privacy. Existing redaction workflows are either manual, destructive, or built around uploading a sensitive file to another service. At the same time, giving an AI agent unrestricted access to document contents creates a new disclosure risk. SafeShare explores a narrower, more useful contract: the browser handles the private document locally, while WebMCP gives the agent structured access to the redaction workflow. The agent can help manage masks and verify readiness without tool responses containing the document text, file name, image, or detected private values. What it does SafeShare opens PDFs and images directly in the browser, detects likely sensitive information, and immediately draws editable masks. People can move, resize, delete, or draw masks directly on the page. Preview opacity can be adjusted without weakening the final redaction. When the review is finished, SafeShare creates a flattened PDF or PNG in which every visible mask is permanently fused into the pixels. The original file remains unchanged. A supported browser can also hand the finished copy to the operating system's native share sheet, but only after a human click. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Redaction is not a background automation task; it is a shared visual decision. The person and the agent need the same live page, the same selected mask, and the same reversible history. WebMCP makes that collaboration explicit. SafeShare exposes nine narrow tools. An agent can read a privacy-filtered editor summary, list safe mask metadata, focus a mask, explain generic detection signals, add or delete a visible mask, undo a change, run the export safety check, and prepare the final download. The agent cannot download or share the file. The final export remains a deliberate human action. This is substantially better than scraping buttons from the interface: tool inputs are constrained, side effects are described, results are verifiable in the page, and the application can enforce a clear privacy boundary around tool output. What people and agents can do together A person can ask the agent to inventory every mask, focus the least confident detection, explain why it was created, make a reversible correction, and verify the final export — while watching each change happen on the document. Before WebMCP, that required fragile visual automation or a separate integration disconnected from the live editing session. The human contributes contextual judgment and final consent. The agent contributes structured navigation, consistency checks, and reversible execution. Neither replaces the other. How we built it SafeShare is a React and TypeScript application built with Vite. PDF.js renders PDFs, Tesseract.js performs local French and English OCR, and deterministic pattern checks detect common personal data. Every detected region is converted to normalized page coordinates so the same geometry works for display, editing, WebMCP actions, and export. The application feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool() and registers nine imperative tools from the top-level page. The tools reuse the editor's existing state, validation, undo history, and safety report. Registrations share an AbortSignal for page-lifecycle cleanup. PDF-lib and Canvas produce the final rasterized document. The opacity slider affects only the editor preview; exported masks are always solid. The Web Share API is progressively enabled only when the browser confirms it can share the generated file. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was designing useful agent actions without turning WebMCP into a data-extraction channel. SafeShare's tool results intentionally return categories, IDs, pages, confidence levels and outcomes — not raw values, file names, images, document text, or mask coordinates. We also had to keep coordinates accurate across PDF text extraction, OCR output, responsive zoom, direct pointer editing and final raster export. A single normalized geometry model now drives all of those paths. Finally, native file sharing requires a direct human gesture. SafeShare prepares the current flattened file locally after edits so the operating system share sheet can open immediately from the user's click. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete redaction product rather than a WebMCP proof of concept. Nine working tools with visible, reversible effects and privacy-filtered results. A human-only final export boundary. Local PDF/image processing with no SafeShare application server. English and French interfaces selected from the browser language. Direct drawing, moving, resizing, deleting, undo/redo, preview opacity and zoom. Flattened PDF and PNG output plus progressive native sharing. Automated tests for privacy boundaries, geometry, detection, history, localization, file validation and sharing. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes the semantic operations of a live interface rather than recreating an application's backend API. The best tools are small, observable and honest about side effects. We also learned that privacy is not achieved by calling a tool “read-only”; it comes from deliberately limiting both inputs and outputs and preserving human control over consequential actions. What's next for SafeShare Next steps include more OCR languages, stronger local entity detection, reusable redaction presets, better keyboard editing, and an optional fully local model for document-specific suggestions. The core principle will remain unchanged: document processing belongs in the browser, agent actions should be inspectable, and export should stay under human control. title: Shopify Catalog Health Copilot
pitch: A WebMCP copilot that helps Shopify merchants and AI agents find, fix, and verify catalog issues together, turning product data into search - and agent-ready storefronts.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP copilot that helps Shopify merchants and AI agents find, fix, and verify catalog issues together, turning product data into search - and agent-ready storefronts. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard List of WebMCP Tools on Chrome Agent edit and Merchant's correction Architecture Inspiration WebMCP already lets shopping agents interact with storefronts (I noticed Shopify-powered stores have this). I wanted to explore the merchant side of that future: who makes sure the underlying product catalog is understandable enough for those agents to use? Based on my research, catalog hygiene was the first pain point in the Shopify Reddit Community's "most annoying manual task" thread. Product catalogs often contain missing identifiers, vague descriptions, incomplete image alt text, inconsistent variants, and weak taxonomy. These issues affect traditional search today and can make products harder for AI shopping agents to understand and recommend. Catalog Health Copilot turns catalog maintenance into a collaborative workflow between a Shopify merchant (human) and an AI agent via webMCP. What it does Catalog Health Copilot connects to a Shopify development store and audits its products across six areas: Identifiers Product content Media SEO Commercial data Agent readiness It converts those findings into a prioritized issue queue and health score. From the same live page or dashboard, a merchant and their agent can: Scan the catalog. Find the highest-impact issues. Open a specific issue and inspect its context. Generate an OpenAI-assisted fix for text. Review or edit the proposed field-level change. Apply approved changes to Shopify. Re-fetch the product and verify the live result. Preview how a shopping agent interprets the product before and after the fix. The web app remains usable as an ordinary web application when WebMCP is unavailable or when humans are using it. WebMCP adds a structured collaboration layer rather than replacing the interface. Catalog auditing involves large amounts of repetitive inspection, prioritization, drafting, and verification. An agent is well suited to that labor, while the merchant should retain judgment over brand voice and product accuracy. Instead of asking an agent to guess its way through buttons and page layouts, the application exposes ten WebMCP tools : scan_catalog , get_health_score , list_issues , show_issue , generate_fix , apply_fix , apply_approved , dismiss_issue , verify_fix , and preview_agent_view . This lets the agent work with structured product data while keeping its actions visible in the same interface the merchant is viewing. When the agent selects an issue, creates a draft, or applies a fix, the page updates too. The result is a governed scan → explain → draft → review → apply → verify workflow that would be fragile and difficult to coordinate through visual browser automation alone. How I built it The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. All WebMCP tools are registered in the top-level document using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The tools call the same catalog-controller functions used by the visible interface. This gives the human and the agent shared state, permissions, progress, and verification results. A Cloudflare Worker serves the application and its API routes. It connects server-side to: Shopify Admin GraphQL API for catalog reads and controlled product updates OpenAI API for context-aware fix drafts, with deterministic templates as a fallback Cloudflare rate limiting and observability for protecting sensitive endpoints and recording mutation outcomes Shopify and OpenAI credentials never reach the browser. Safe demo-store writes The public demo intentionally allows controlled writes so judges can experience the complete WebMCP workflow. I added several server-enforced safeguards: Only products carrying the catalog-health-seed tag can be modified. Variant and image IDs must belong to the selected seeded product. Only an explicit allowlist of product fields is writable. A request can contain no more than ten changes. Write and OpenAI endpoints have independent rate limits. ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES provides an emergency kill switch. Every attempted mutation is logged with its outcome. A guarded reset command restores the deterministic 30-product demo catalog. These restrictions let the demonstration remain interactive without exposing a production storefront. Challenges I faced One major challenge was designing for WebMCP as a genuine product capability rather than attaching tools to an existing interface. ChatGPT’s in-app browser requires tools to be registered imperatively in the top-level document, so the application could not be an iframe or embedded Shopify Admin app. Another challenge was keeping the visible interface synchronized with agent activity. I solved this by routing both UI controls and WebMCP tools through the same controller instead of creating separate automation logic. The most important challenge was safe write access. A public demonstration needs to be easy for you, the judges, to use, but unrestricted Shopify mutations would be inappropriate. The seed-tag policy, ownership validation, allowlist, limits, logging, kill switch, and reset workflow let me keep the full experience available. What I learned I learned that agent-native UX is not simply about giving an agent more autonomy. The best experience makes actions structured, visible, interruptible, editable, and verifiable. I also learned that verification deserves to be a first-class tool. A successful API response is not enoughthe application re-fetches Shopify data and returns evidence that the intended field actually changed. Most importantly, WebMCP makes it possible for a human and an agent to operate inside one coherent product experience: the agent handles scale and repetition, while the human keeps context and judgment. What’s next For a production store, I would add merchant authentication, Shopify OAuth, role-based approvals, persistent audit history, configurable catalog policies, and scheduled monitoring. I would also expand the checks using storefront analytics and order history to identify products that are technically available but consistently undiscoverable. title: ShowMeOnMap
pitch: Ask for a map. With WebMCP, the agent in your browser builds it, queries it and hands you the export — on the canvas you're watching.
about_excerpt: Ask for a map. With WebMCP, the agent in your browser builds it, queries it and hands you the export — on the canvas you're watching. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration ShowMeOnMap is a live product: you type a geographic question in plain language and get a professionally rendered map built from real, fetched data — never invented values — with a legend, a grounded caption and a shareable page. It already had a server-side MCP endpoint and a REST API for headless agents. What it did not have was any way for the agent in your browser to work with you on the page you are both looking at. That gap is sharper for a map than for almost any other kind of site. A WebGL canvas is the most illegible thing a browser agent can meet: pixels it cannot read, data it cannot touch, a camera it cannot move. Screen-reading it is hopeless; the DOM contains a <canvas> and a legend. WebMCP flips the problem: instead of the agent guessing what the page shows, the page tells the agent what it can do — and, crucially for us, what it currently shows. What it does showmeonmap.com registers 8 tools on document.modelContext . In an agent-capable browser (ChatGPT's built-in browser, or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP enabled) you can now say: "We just moved to Vancouver — show me the elementary schools in Kerrisdale and their catchment areas. How many are actually inside Kerrisdale? Zoom to them. Export a PNG." and watch it happen on the canvas: build_map → query_features → zoom_to_layer → export_image . Then "show me the secondary schools instead" ( mutate_map ) and "undo that" ( undo ). Tool What it does Cost build_map(query) natural-language query → fetched real data → rendered map 1 free daily map (anonymous) / 1 credit mutate_map(instruction) refine the current map's data or style 1 credit, auto-refunded on failure get_map_state() read-back: layers, exact feature counts, camera, filters, analysis headline free query_features(layerId, predicate) exact answers from the rendered data via a typed predicate grammar free set_camera(center?, zoom?) move the live MapLibre camera free zoom_to_layer(layerId) fit the camera to a layer's real extent free export_image(format?) render a legend-complete PNG/JPEG/PDF and hand the human the Save button free undo() rewind the last map change free Why WebMCP fits this use case. Half of these tools write to the page; the other half read from it. The read-back channel is the part a screenshot or a DOM scrape can never give an agent: query_features answers "how many schools are inside Kerrisdale?" with the exact count from the rendered layer, not a model's guess. The map stops being a picture the agent describes and becomes a grounded data source for the agent's next sentence. What people and agents can now do together. The person keeps the canvas, the legend, the undo history and the Save button. The agent gets typed verbs and honest read-back. Neither side has to trust the other's description of the map, because both are looking at the same post-apply state. "Agents propose, people click" is literal here: browsers block downloads that a human did not initiate, so export_image renders the full-size image and puts a real Save button on the page for the person. How we built it The integration is deliberately one thin boundary, three touch points: Mount. A WebMCPBridge component (renders nothing) runs registerWebMcpTools() once on the client. For the ~99% of visitors without an agent runtime that is a single property probe ( document.modelContext , with the legacy navigator.modelContext name as fallback — the entry point has been renamed twice already). Teardown aborts the registration's AbortController . The chat bridge seam. The chat panel owns sendMessage — the same submission pipeline behind the composer (mutate-first ladder, SSE streaming, store application, billing refresh). It registers that callable with the WebMCP layer, so build_map / mutate_map are processed exactly as if the human had typed: same quota, same 1-credit billing with auto-refund, same anonymous-visitor rules (anonymous sessions get a typed sign-in prompt from mutate_map , never a silent no-op). Store reads. The free tools read and write the app's existing map store directly — no server calls. Every result is summarized from post-apply state: layer and feature counts come from what actually landed, never from "the request was sent". If nothing rendered, the result says delivered: false — do not claim a map exists . Two safety pieces sit on top: every paid tool states its cost in its description (that is what runtimes use to classify a call as consequential — a silently-costed tool is the prompt-injection amplifier), and a gesture-reset budget refuses paid calls after 8 of them with no human interaction until the person touches the page. Tests: a unit suite pinning the budget semantics, the grounding rule and the cost-honest descriptions; a Playwright spec in the main app's CI where a stubbed agent runtime drives the real page; and, in the public repo, a live-site contract test that drives showmeonmap.com's registered tools through document.modelContext with no access to app internals — npm test , about 7 seconds, all 8 tools. Stack: TypeScript, React / Next.js on Cloudflare Workers (OpenNext), MapLibre GL + deck.gl, Zustand stores, Playwright. The tool schemas are plain JSON Schema. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. window.agent → navigator.modelContext → document.modelContext , and Chrome's docs show execute returning a string while ChatGPT's show an object. We probe both entry points and return JSON text, which both runtimes accept. A tool that says "ok" while the canvas didn't change is lying. Our first camera tool wrote to a legacy config channel the renderer ignores while a plan is active — it reported success and nothing moved. Caught in the first live ChatGPT-browser test, fixed by driving the live MapLibre instance and reading the camera back through get_map_state . Downloads. Agent-initiated tool calls carry no user activation, so export_image cannot save a file. It renders the image and hands the human a real Save button instead. Reading a map back honestly at neighbourhood scale. "Schools in Kerrisdale" means the area people call Kerrisdale, not the cadastral polygon; strict containment cut schools a block outside the line. Solid dots are inside, faded ones sit within 800 m outside, and the read-back says which is which. Cost. An agent in a loop can spend a person's credits. Cost in the description plus the gesture-reset budget is the answer we shipped; it is also why paid tools go through the same billing path as the composer, with auto-refund. title: ShrineKeep + WebMCP
pitch: A versatile collection manager for devoted collectors and hobbyists from any space, now with agent-automated onboarding and monetary analytics, making reasoned decisions even for niches.
about_excerpt: A versatile collection manager for devoted collectors and hobbyists from any space, now with agent-automated onboarding and monetary analytics, making reasoned decisions even for niches. Like Comment Story Updates Agent asked to set up data for a collection of the user's choice All edits are staged and require approval Staged edits that are not yet accepted are put in the review inbox Example output Activity of each tool use is recorded for technical users to debug Tool descriptions are also provided so technical users can be more productive and write more complex prompts Agent making decisions gives effective and reasonable automation of item valuation ShrineKeep + WebMCP project story Inspiration Collectors can end up hoarding rather than collecting, leaving them with questions. What do I already own? How much have I spent? What is all of this worth now? A lot of people have to manually make use of notes or spreadsheets, if they track them at all. That is the problem I made ShrineKeep to solve. It can organize collections in nested boxes and give you useful analytics, but there was an awkward catch: first, you had to manually add everything. Names, dates, purchase prices, current values, wishlist prices, and so on. The more useful I made the app, the more data it asked the user to enter. I've wanted to use agents for this for a while. An agent can research a niche product line, tell similar editions apart, find price references, and do in minutes what would be a very boring evening of data entry. But running those agents for every user would be expensive. Locking the feature behind a subscription would solve my problem by creating a new one for users. WebMCP and it solved my problems well! The user can bring an agent they already have, and ShrineKeep can give it the right context and a safe way to help. The agent does the research and reasoning; ShrineKeep knows what box is open, what the user owns, and what is actually allowed to change. I don't have to run an AI service or pass that cost on to the user. What it does On the dashboard or wishlist, a user can now talk to a compatible browser agent and ask it to work with the collection that is already in front of them. It can: research and initialize a new collection box; compare a complete set with the current box and stage only the missing items; estimate current values or likely acquisition prices for owned items; research expected prices for wishlist items; edit item names and descriptions through the same review flow; work only with the items explicitly selected in the interface; and optionally find a thumbnail for each newly approved item. The agent gets small, structured pieces of context instead of trying to scrape the screen. It can read the open box, include its child boxes when that is actually needed, look at the relevant wishlist, or ask for only the cards the user selected. There are seven tools on the dashboard and three on the wishlist page, each limited to what makes sense there. Tools are written in accordance to Chrome's WebMCP Best Practices The important part is that none of those tools silently changes the collection. Anything the agent wants to add or edit goes into a staging inbox. ShrineKeep shows the user the proposed names, prices, Owned/Wishlist choices, before-and-after values, reasons, sources, and possible duplicates. Every row can be edited, unchecked, approved, or thrown away. Only approved rows reach the real write APIs. I also built a new tutorial around these agent features. WebMCP will undoubtedly be unfamilar to most users, and I feel it is an essential UX requirement to introduce users to a newly adopted technology. It asks what the user collects, gives them a prompt to take to their agent, and walks them through confirming the researched set, reviewing the new cards, opening the created box, and trying a valuation. They learn the app by setting up something they already collect. They can skip individual steps, leave the tutorial, or use sample data instead. If WebMCP isn't available, ShrineKeep still works normally. How we built it ShrineKeep is built with Next.js 16, React, and TypeScript, with Supabase handling authentication, Postgres, row-level security, and image storage. The collection manager existed before the hackathon. During the submission period, I added the WebMCP tools, their staging and approval flow, and the new agent-based tutorial directly to the existing app. A reusable React hook checks for document.modelContext and registers the right tools for the page the user is on. Registrations are cleaned up with an AbortController when that scope changes. The same hook records calls as they happen, which let me show a status panel without pretending that “the browser accepted a registration” means “an agent is connected and understands everything.” The read tools use small authenticated routes that check ownership and return only the fields needed for the job, with pagination so a large collection doesn't become one giant prompt. Selection is even smaller: get_selected_items reads the current React selection state directly. I generalized the edit tools to accept just the fields being changed, so the same operation can fix a name, update a description, or suggest prices without a separate tool for each field. Shared tool copy lives in one module so those contracts stay consistent. Tools that can lead to a write only build typed suggestion batches. A shared client-side provider keeps those batches around while the user moves between the dashboard and wishlist. When the user finally applies one, the server authenticates them again, checks ownership and price fields, catches stale records through updated_at , and then reuses ShrineKeep's normal item and box operations. That also means value updates still appear in the existing value history. Optional thumbnail lookup reuses the regular image search and is allowed to fail without blocking the batch. The tutorial runs as a state machine inside the existing agent panel. It listens for the relevant tool calls, successful approvals, and box navigation. Tutorial progress is saved for the session, while completion or dismissal is saved to the account. The state also needs to handle someone skipping creation, opening a different box, or coming back after navigating away. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was deciding where the agent should stop. Niche product research is messy, and secondhand prices are even messier. I wanted the agent to save real time without letting a confident mistake rewrite someone's collection. The model I kept coming back to was a code review: let the agent prepare a useful diff, then let the person who owns the data decide what lands. The tutorial became a major challenge of its own. Exposing the tools didn't explain to a new user what to ask for, or why they were moving between an agent chat and ShrineKeep. I had to build a walkthrough that taught both sides of that interaction while helping them make a real collection. There also had to be a useful way through for someone without a compatible agent, or someone who just wanted to skip ahead. Another early mistake was treating “set up this collection” and “complete the collection in this box” as the same operation. They sound close, but one should create a new box and the other should reconcile against what is already there. Using the first flow for both produced duplicate cards and unnecessary child boxes. I split them into separate tools, and the completion flow now checks both owned and wishlist cards before proposing only what is missing. Choosing how many tools to expose was another balancing act. I didn't want a separate tool for every small task, with more schemas and descriptions for the agent to read. But making one tool do everything would bring back the scope confusion. I kept separate operations where the destination or approval flow really differs, and generalized edits within those boundaries. Furthermore, I directly acknowledge that destructive, relocation, and exploration actions should not be accessible to the agent, as these can destroy data, confuse users, and waste tokens, respectively. It was not worth it to implement this when users already have fast batch deletions and movement options. Pricing caused a different kind of ambiguity. Original retail, a current listing, a secondhand asking price, and a recent sold price are all valid approaches to price an item. I experimented with defaults, but collections from different spaces just aren't compatible with it and often lead to lots of time and tokens wasted looking at obviously wrong decisions. I ended up with just asking the agent to suggest a research approach for each requested field, wait for user approval on all of them, then research. The review still keeps the explanation and links next to the number. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that this became a complete bring-your-own-agent loop rather than a chat demo.
