title: SiteWorks-WebMCP
pitch: SiteWorks WebMCP makes a website builder's admin agent-native — ChatGPT builds your shop's catalogue from a photo of the menu, and only you can hit publish.
about_excerpt: SiteWorks WebMCP makes a website builder's admin agent-native — ChatGPT builds your shop's catalogue from a photo of the menu, and only you can hit publish. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In 2004 I built my own e-commerce platform, and I've run it and its successors ever since — over 30,000 stores at peak. In all that time, one thing never got easier: getting a real merchant's products into a store. The industry's answer is still "upload a correctly formatted CSV." The merchant's actual data is a flyer taped to the counter glass, a price list the printer was sent, a Word doc from 2019. I've watched merchants stall on that gap for two decades, thirty thousand ecom sites worth. When OpenAI shipped Site tools on August 25th, I saw the fix for the first time: don't build another bundled chatbot — make the admin page itself the tool surface, and let the merchant's own agent do the work. Storefront-side WebMCP already existed (Shopify ships it on every Liquid storefront; Chrome's official demos are shops). The admin — where the store gets made — had none. This is that half. What it does SiteWorks is a production site builder. During the Submission Period I added a WebMCP layer: the signed-in editor page registers 55 tools (19 read, 33 write, 3 skills) via document.modelContext.registerTool. The merchant's ChatGPT photographs the counter menu and drafts every item into the live store — reading the catalogue first, matching existing products instead of duplicating them, and flagging unpriced or ambiguous items for review instead of inventing numbers. The warnings live on the drafts, not in the chat. Then the same tools run outbound: export the catalogue and brand system, generate a printable flyer, inspect the result. Everything is draft-first with optimistic concurrency, an audit row per call, and one structural rule: nothing the agent can call publishes a page or a product. Publish isn't a guideline the model follows — it's a call that doesn't exist. The human holds the only commit button. How we built it On a real platform, which meant the hard part wasn't the tools — it was the boundary. One operations layer already served the human UI; WebMCP became a second caller of the same layer, and a server-side MCP endpoint a third. For the open-source release I extracted a standalone demo (SQLite, one container, a fictional bakery) that runs the identical layer, with prior work delineated in docs/PROVENANCE.md — the platform predates the contest; every WebMCP line postdates August 25th, and git grep at the cut-off commit proves it. Challenges we ran into Tools inside iframes aren't discovered. Our editor is a parent shell around a sandboxed preview — registration had to live on the parent, proxying into the preview. tools.call() can't return a file. Exports return a signed URL plus SHA-256 and expiry instead; the artefact rides the browser, the facts ride the tool result. Real defects, found by agent testing. A hero image/video conflict and a broken version-listing endpoint surfaced only when an agent actually drove the surface — both fixed, with the evidence baked into the tool contracts. Facts vs. decoration. Image models corrupt small text, so generated imagery decorates while names and prices bind from catalogue data. And the platform outage on deadline day, mid-render. Thanks for the extension. What we learned An agent doesn't need your platform to be smart — it needs it to be legible and governable. The intelligence is the user's; the structure is the site's. Twenty years of merchant onboarding pain turned out to be an interface problem: design the tool surface so the model's worst day is a review queue, not a live store, and everything else follows. What's next for SiteWorks WebMCP Shopper-side tools on the published storefronts (mirroring Shopify's vocabulary, so one platform carries both halves), deterministic flyer rendering so campaign artwork binds from the catalogue like everything else, and the same agent-native admin rolled out across the production estate — a thousand-plus small-business sites whose owners will never learn a page builder, but already know how to talk to ChatGPT. title: StreamBot | Agent Edition
pitch: A streamer dashboard with a built-in AI teammate: it proposes themed setups, teaches the UI with guided tours, and edits vertical clips you approve everything
about_excerpt: A streamer dashboard with a built-in AI teammate: it proposes themed setups, teaches the UI with guided tours, and edits vertical clips you approve everything Like Comment Story Updates Home Clipit Studio Custom Command Chat Alert Overlay Builder StreamBot — Agent Edition Project Story Inspiration Streamers run a one-person production studio. Before they ever go live, they may have to manage chat commands, alerts, timed promotions, overlays, clipping highlights for TikTok, and countless other pieces of production across a dozen different tabs. Meanwhile, AI agents are still largely stuck outside the product. They screen-scrape interfaces, guess which buttons to click, and operate without a real understanding of the application's state. We wanted to change that. StreamBot is a real streamer dashboard already in production use. The WebMCP Challenge gave us the missing piece: instead of bolting an AI chatbot onto the side of the product, we gave the agent a first-class seat inside the application . The agent uses the same tools as the streamer, operates against the same state, and leaves the same audit trail. That led to the question driving this project: What does setup feel like when a streamer and their AI agent share one workspace, while the human remains in control of anything that matters? What It Does Three experiences define StreamBot Agent Edition. 1. Propose, Don't Just Do The agent isn't simply given unrestricted control. A streamer can say: "Set up my horror night." Instead of immediately changing their dashboard, the agent creates a complete themed proposal: !scary and !brave commands 👻 Follow alerts Timed promotional messages A JUMPSCARE channel-point reward A follower goal bar Other relevant stream configuration The entire setup appears as a review card . The streamer can inspect the proposal, remove anything they don't want, and then hit Approve . Only after approval does the agent execute the changes. Proposal → Review → Approval → Execution It's collaboration with a veto, rather than blind automation. 2. Guides That Teach on the Live UI Agents shouldn't teach users from outdated screenshots or hallucinated interfaces. If a streamer asks: "How do chat alerts work?" The agent first uses discover_targets to inspect the actual DOM and identify the elements currently available on the page. It then uses compose_tour to build a spotlight walkthrough directly against those discovered elements. The result is a guide that operates on the real product, in its current state . No stale screenshots. No guessed buttons. No hallucinated UI. The agent discovers the interface first, then teaches from reality. 3. Skilled Hands, Not Chat The agent isn't limited to answering questions. Inside StreamBot's ClipIt editor, it can stage vertical social edits directly against the mounted editor state. That includes: Vertical layouts Facecam resizing Caption placement Real transcribed captions Designer-created caption presets Editor configuration The agent isn't pretending to edit a clip through text. It's operating the actual editor. How We Built It with WebMCP Route-Scoped Tool Suites Each StreamBot dashboard route registers the tools relevant to the feature currently being viewed. Examples include: Commands Alerts Timed Messages Rewards Canvas ClipIt This is implemented through src/webmcp/suites.ts . The agent only sees tools that are valid for the current context and available to its seat. The Agent Uses the Same API as the UI We didn't create a separate "AI version" of StreamBot's functionality. Every agent tool calls the same endpoints used by the human interface . That means the resulting state is identical regardless of who performed the action. For example: Agent creates !scary → the command immediately appears in the streamer's command list. There is no synchronization layer or second source of truth. Agent actions and human actions operate on the same application state. Tool executions are also written to the account's audit log, just like actions performed by other members of the team. A Bridge into Live Editors For ClipIt, we needed the agent to interact with a mounted editor rather than a traditional API. We built mountClipItEditorCommands , which connects the WebMCP suite directly to the ClipIt store. The bridge dispatches real reducer actions and waits for state convergence before reporting success. That distinction matters. We don't report success because an action was dispatched. We report success when the editor has actually reached the requested state. Human-in-the-Loop Primitives Human approval is built into the tool architecture itself. propose_stream_setup opens a PrepProposalCard and blocks execution until the streamer makes a decision. Our guide tools work similarly: they compose tours from curated block types that can only be placed on targets discovered from the current page. The agent therefore has useful autonomy without having unlimited authority. Permissions The agent is treated as a real seat within StreamBot. Its permissions are governed through: Settings → Your Team Tool suites are only registered in areas where the agent has permission to operate. Challenges 1. Timeouts That Lied Our first ClipIt bridge used pixel changes as proof that an operation had succeeded. That seemed reasonable until we encountered a simple case: A facecam was already in the requested position. The operation succeeded, but because the pixels didn't change, the bridge waited 12 seconds and eventually reported a timeout. We rewrote the system around state convergence instead. A no-op move is now considered a successful operation if the editor is already in the requested state. We also added fail-fast validation using valid-ID lists. 2. Making the Demo Deterministic Transcription and streaming are inherently live, variable, and slow. A two-minute demo can't wait around for production systems to finish processing. We built a simulated backend using: An in-browser API shim A simulated stream engine Deterministic application state This gives us a world that behaves like the real product without depending on unpredictable external timing. For captions, we went further. The demo pipeline uses real ASR transcripts generated with the same model and segmentation approach as production , then bakes those transcripts into the demo environment. The result is deterministic while still containing genuine transcribed speech , rather than lorem ipsum pretending to be captions. 3. Spotlight Honesty Our earliest tours referenced UI elements that didn't actually exist on the current page. That exposed a fundamental problem with agent-generated walkthroughs: The agent was assuming what the interface looked like. We turned the fix into a core design principle: Discover before you teach. Every walkthrough begins with discover_targets . The tour is then composed against what actually exists. What We Learned The biggest lesson was simple: Agents Don't Need More Autonomy. They Need Better Seats. Once the agent shared the human's: Tools Application state Permissions Audit trail Context the interaction fundamentally changed. It stopped feeling like: "Prompt and pray." And started feeling like genuine teamwork: Proposal → Review → Approval → Execution The guardrails aren't friction. Scoped tool suites, approval cards, permission boundaries, and discover-before-teach aren't there to make the agent weaker. They're what make the agent trustworthy enough to delegate to . That's the direction we believe the agent-native web should move toward: AI agents shouldn't sit outside applications, guessing how to use them. They should have a real seat inside the product with the right tools, the right context, and a human who stays in control. title: Talli
pitch: A conversational credit ledger that helps small businesses and their AI agents manage customer debt together, without taking financial control away from the human.
about_excerpt: A conversational credit ledger that helps small businesses and their AI agents manage customer debt together, without taking financial control away from the human. Like Comment Story Updates Talli helps small businesses and informal traders record and manage customer credit using ordinary speech, text, or Telegram. Instead of filling out accounting forms, a merchant can simply say, “Adele took goods worth $40 and will pay on Friday,” or “She paid $10 today.” Talli turns those conversations into structured customer balances and transaction histories. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can securely read the same live ledger, answer questions, identify overdue debts, and prepare proposed financial updates. However, the agent cannot finalize those changes. The merchant reviews and confirms every consequential update inside Talli’s visible interface. The Problem Millions of small businesses and informal traders sell goods on credit every day. A customer may take food, clothing, supplies, or other goods and promise to pay later. The business owner needs to remember: who took the goods how much they owe when they promised to pay whether they made a partial payment how much remains outstanding which customers are overdue Many business owners manage this information using paper notebooks, memory, calculator notes, chat messages, or a mixture of all four. This creates serious problems. Records can be lost, payments may not be reflected correctly, and business owners can struggle to explain how a customer’s balance was calculated. When several customers have similar names, it is also easy to update the wrong person’s record. Traditional accounting applications can help, but they are often designed around forms, tables, categories, and bookkeeping terminology. For someone who is busy serving customers and may not consider themselves an accountant, recording a simple credit transaction can feel like administrative work. The real challenge is not that these business owners do not understand their businesses. The challenge is that most financial software does not work the way they naturally communicate. The Solution Talli is a conversational credit ledger built around the way small businesses already talk about customer debt. Instead of completing a long form, a merchant can speak or type naturally: “Adele took goods worth $40 and will pay next Friday.” Talli converts that statement into a structured financial record containing the customer, amount, currency, transaction type, and relevant date. Later, the merchant can say: “Adele paid $10.” Talli records the partial payment, updates Adele’s outstanding balance, and preserves the history of how that balance changed. The merchant can also ask questions such as: “How much does Adele still owe?” “Who owes me money?” “Which payments are overdue?” “Show me Adele’s transaction history.” “How much have my customers paid?” “Mark this debt as settled.” Talli supports voice, typed conversations, a web interface, and Telegram. The same underlying ledger can therefore remain useful while the merchant moves between the channels they already use. Talli also understands that financial records require caution. If a request is unclear, Talli does not silently guess. It asks for clarification before allowing the wrong customer or obligation to be changed. The WebMCP Extension For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended Talli so that the live website can expose its financial capabilities directly to browser-based AI agents. Without WebMCP, an agent trying to assist a Talli user would have to inspect the page, interpret text on the screen, locate buttons, fill forms, and simulate clicks. That approach is fragile and can be especially dangerous when the website contains financial information. With WebMCP, Talli explicitly tells the agent what it can do, what information each operation requires, and which operations are read-only. The agent can discover structured tools for searching customers, checking balances, reviewing histories, finding overdue debts, and preparing ledger changes. It receives structured results from the same live ledger the person is viewing. This creates a shared workspace between the merchant, the browser agent, and Talli. A Typical Human-Agent Workflow Imagine that a merchant asks their browser agent: “Check Talli and tell me how much my customers owe me.” The agent calls Talli’s get_ledger_summary tool and receives a structured summary from the current ledger. The merchant then says: “Adele paid $10. Update her balance.” The agent calls prepare_ledger_mutation , but Talli discovers that several customers match the name “Adele.” Instead of choosing one, Talli returns clarification_required with a short list of matching customers and their balances. The ledger remains unchanged. The agent can then ask: “I found more than one Adele. Which customer made the payment?” After the merchant identifies the correct customer, the agent prepares the payment again. Talli validates the request and displays a visible review card containing the exact proposed change. The merchant reviews the amount and customer, then clicks Confirm inside Talli. Only at that point does the ledger change. This workflow demonstrates more than an agent operating a website. The agent helps with interpretation and preparation, Talli enforces financial safety, and the human retains final authority. Why Talli Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Talli is a strong WebMCP use case because customer credit management combines repetitive work with consequential financial decisions. An AI agent is well suited to: searching records summarizing balances finding overdue obligations reviewing transaction histories translating a natural-language request into a structured proposal However, an agent should not silently make an irreversible or incorrect financial change. WebMCP provides the structured boundary Talli needs. It allows the agent to interact with the application through clearly defined tools instead of guessing its way through the interface. Talli builds on that boundary with three important rules: Read operations can happen directly. Financial mutations must first become proposals. Only the human can confirm a proposal in Talli’s visible interface. The most important behavior is not simply that Talli knows how to act. It also knows when not to act. If two customers match a name, an obligation cannot be safely identified, or the ledger has changed since a proposal was prepared, Talli pauses the operation instead of guessing. This makes WebMCP part of the product’s safety model, not just another way to call backend functions. How Talli Creates a Better User Experience Talli reduces the amount of effort required to maintain accurate credit records. The merchant does not need to learn database fields, accounting terminology, or a complicated menu system. They can continue communicating naturally while Talli and their agent handle the structured work underneath. WebMCP improves this experience in several ways: The agent can access reliable structured data instead of trying to read values from the visual interface. The merchant can ask broader questions without manually searching through individual customer records. The agent can prepare a transaction while the merchant remains focused on running the business. Ambiguous requests produce clarification instead of silent errors. Proposed financial changes are shown in a visible, understandable review card. The merchant keeps control over the final decision. The agent and the person work from the same current ledger rather than separate or outdated copies of the data. Talli remains usable in browsers that do not support WebMCP. WebMCP is added as a progressive enhancement, so the normal voice, text, web, and Telegram experiences continue to work. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Difficult Before Before the WebMCP extension, Talli could already understand conversations and maintain the ledger. However, an external browser agent did not have a dependable, structured way to use those capabilities. Now a person and their agent can work together to: inspect the business’s total outstanding credit search for a customer without manually navigating the interface explain how a customer’s current balance was calculated identify overdue obligations prepare new credit, payment, or settlement entries detect ambiguous customer references ask the human to resolve uncertainty present the exact financial change for review prevent an agent from confirming its own proposal keep a record unchanged until the human explicitly approves it For example, the agent can do the time-consuming work of finding the correct records and preparing an update, while the business owner makes the final judgment. That division of responsibility was difficult to achieve reliably through ordinary browser automation. WebMCP makes it possible to define the collaboration explicitly. title: Tengu and Boykot web mcp the art of interact with agents
pitch: A real Santiago restaurant and a real art-supply store expose menu, catalog, live stock and forms as WebMCP tools. The agent does the tedious part and stops: you send, you pay.
about_excerpt: A real Santiago restaurant and a real art-supply store expose menu, catalog, live stock and forms as WebMCP tools. The agent does the tedious part and stops: you send, you pay. Like Comment Story Updates Tengu Swag Boykot Flow Restaurants and small shops are the most-attempted and worst-served agent task on the web. Every assistant can find a restaurant. Almost none can do anything with one. The menu lives in a PDF or a photo, the prices are stale, and the booking widget is a third-party iframe an agent cannot reason about. So the agent guesses — and it guesses wrong about the one thing the diner is paying for. We run two real businesses in Santiago, Chile, and we felt this from the other side. Agents were already describing our menu and our catalog to people, from blog posts written years ago. We had no way to be the author of what agents said about us. But the thing that actually kept us from opening the door was not the reading. It was the booking. Nobody wants an agent that reserves a table, or buys $80,000 CLP of paint, on their behalf while they are looking away. So we built for the opposite: the agent does the tedious part and stops. What it does Two businesses that have nothing in common expose the same pattern. Tengu — a kappo omakase restaurant, average table $300–400k CLP. Five tools on the page: get_carta (the live menu with real prices, by section), buscar_plato (search dishes, cocktails, wines and sake), get_guia (long-form guides the restaurant wrote about bluefin, sake and kappo cooking), get_info, and the one that matters — preparar_reserva. Boykot — an art and graffiti supply store, about 3.000 SKUs. Thirteen tools: catalog search, product detail, brand list, quotes, stock subscriptions, promotions, project planning, colour cards — plus agregar_al_carro, ver_mi_carro and guardar_en_lista. preparar_reserva fills the reservation form on the page with the party size, date, time and name the agent gathered in conversation — and then stops. It does not submit. The form is left visible, filled, scrolled into view, with the fields the agent touched marked, and a notice above it that says so and offers to discard. The human checks it and sends it. agregar_al_carro does the same on the store side. The cart gets built. Nobody pays. That is the division of labour we wanted. The agent parses "a table for four next Friday, somewhere quiet, my wife doesn't eat raw fish". The human keeps the part that costs money and social capital. The restaurant's host still sees a normal booking arrive. The read tools matter for a subtler reason: grounding. An agent asked "what's the sake situation at Tengu" now answers from the restaurant's own words and tonight's actual list, instead of from a 2023 blog post. For the first time, the business is the author of what agents say about it. How we built it Eighteen tools across the two sites — five on Tengu, thirteen on Boykot — registered on document.modelContext (with navigator.modelContext as the deprecated alias), feature-detected so each page degrades to an ordinary website when the API is absent: var mc = document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext; if (!mc || typeof mc.registerTool !== 'function') return; Both sites carry origin trial tokens, so the API is native — no ?webmcp flag, no polyfill, nothing for the judge to enable. Open the URL and the tools are there. The in-page tools are deliberately thin: they proxy to the same /api/mcp JSON-RPC server each business already runs for out-of-page agents. A browser agent and a server-side agent get the same answers from the same source. One truth, two transports. The exception is the write-side tools — preparar_reserva and agregar_al_carro only exist in the page, because their whole job is to touch the DOM in front of a human and leave it there. Tengu is static HTML and vanilla JS on Vercel with zero npm dependencies on the page — the smallest attack surface we could manage for something that hands tools to an autonomous caller. Reservations persist to Postgres through SECURITY DEFINER functions behind row-level security that denies all direct access; the page never holds a database credential. Boykot is Next.js, backed by the store's live inventory. Deliberately not exposed: anything that spends money or commits the business. No payment, no confirmation, no cancellation, no order modification. The reservation engine has its own caps underneath — 8 tables per slot, rate limit per name and phone — and the agent surface sits strictly inside them. A tool we don't register is a tool that can't be jailbroken. title: TuneQL
pitch: A PostgreSQL workbench where an AI agent can actually try out optimizations instead of just suggesting them.
about_excerpt: A PostgreSQL workbench where an AI agent can actually try out optimizations instead of just suggesting them. Like 1 Comment Story Updates PostgreSQL optimization workbench Verified optimization Create Workspace WebMCP agent actions Optimization constraints Execution plan Why I built it AI can suggest a SQL fix, but it can’t really prove that the fix actually made things better. I’d still have to open a database tool, check the execution plan, run some benchmarks, and manually make sure the result is still correct. So I built TuneQL to keep all of that in one place. What TuneQL does TuneQL is basically a PostgreSQL query optimization workbench that runs in the browser using PGlite. You can inspect the schema, run queries, check EXPLAIN ANALYZE , save a benchmark as a baseline, then change the query or indexes and compare the new version with the old one. It shows what changed, how much faster or slower it got, whether the constraints still pass, and if both queries return the same result. WebMCP The same workspace can also be used by an agent through WebMCP. TuneQL gives the agent tools to read schemas and indexes, explain and benchmark queries, create indexes, change SQL, save baselines, and compare the results. And whatever the agent does also shows up in the UI, so you can actually follow what it’s doing and continue from the same state yourself. How I built it TuneQL uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, PGlite, Zustand, and IndexedDB. PostgreSQL runs inside a browser worker, and the workspace data stays on your device. The UI and all 20 WebMCP tools go through the same command layer, so things like query validation, constraints, benchmarks, activity history, and revision checks behave the same in both places. Challenges and learning One of the harder parts was keeping the PGlite worker, saved workspace, UI, and agent actions all in sync. I also realised pretty quickly that you can’t judge an optimization from just one timing. So TuneQL does a few warm-up runs, runs the benchmark multiple times, and checks the full result instead of just comparing the few rows shown in the preview. title: Verb - Sight off. Voice on
pitch: Chat by intent, not by sight
about_excerpt: Chat by intent, not by sight Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Close your eyes and try to catch up on your messages. A screen reader gets you there, but it turns a ten-second task into a navigation exercise: find the unread thread, find the right control, react to the right message, figure out what's in the photo everyone is laughing about. Browser agents were supposed to help, but they still look at the screen and guess where to click — fragile, slow, and easily misled by page content. WebMCP flips that: the page names its own actions. And messaging is the perfect fit, because messaging is made of verbs — send, react, reply, summarize. Name the verbs, and nobody needs sight to use them. Nouns need eyes. Verbs need a voice. What it does Verb is a complete real-time messenger — 1:1 and group chats, reactions, stickers, image and file attachments, editing, unsend, drafts, search, typing and seen states — where every meaningful action is also a typed WebMCP tool: 22 in a signed-in session . So a blind or low-vision user can simply say what they want: "What did I miss?" → the agent lists, reads, and summarizes the conversation "Reply that Friday works." → draft_message saves it, the user reviews, send_message sends "What's in the photo?" → describe_image runs a vision model on the authorized file "Start a group with Maya and Tony." → people resolved, group created in one request The human chooses the goal, the agent composes tools, and the app stays the authority. Destructive actions (unsend, leave a group) require a second call with confirm: true . There's even a public sign_up tool that creates a passkey-only account : the agent collects a name and email, but the human completes the browser's own WebAuthn prompt. No password ever exists. How we implemented WebMCP Verb talks to the browser's document.modelContext API directly — no wrapper library. The lifecycle is session-aware. A connection provider owns registration end to end. Signed out, the page exposes just two public tools: get_connection_status and sign_up . The moment a Supabase session appears, it registers the 21-tool authenticated catalog; the moment the session changes or ends, an AbortController tears everything down — an agent can never call tools that belong to a previous user. const controller = new AbortController(); await document.modelContext.registerTool( { name: "get_connection_status", description: "Report whether the page is signed in and agent tools are connected.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {}, additionalProperties: false }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, untrustedContentHint: false }, execute: async () => ({ content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(connectionState) }], }), }, { signal: controller.signal } // sign-out → abort → tool gone ); Every call flows through the same pipeline: Human voice or text → agent chooses a registered tool → Verb validates the input in the page → the signed-in user's Supabase session executes it → Postgres row-level security authorizes the operation → a small structured result returns to the agent and the activity panel The catalog: 22 tools in an authenticated session , one file per tool, each with a focused description, a strict JSON schema ( additionalProperties: false ), and behavioral annotations so agents know what is safe to call: Discover — list_conversations , read_conversation , search_messages , search_people , get_my_profile Navigate — open_conversation , start_conversation Compose — draft_message , send_message , edit_message , delete_message , react_to_message , send_sticker Organize — create_group , delete_conversation Understand — summarize_conversation , describe_image , read_file , read_link Connection & account — get_connection_status , setup_passkey , sign_out (+ public sign_up , signed-out only) Rules enforced across the whole catalog: Reads are honest: read-only tools carry readOnlyHint: true , so agents can explore freely Writes are deliberate: composing and sending are separate tools; unsend and leave-group require a second call with confirm: true Other people's words are untrusted: message bodies are wrapped as labeled untrusted content before they reach the agent, so injected text stays data Results are bounded: a shared clamp keeps every tool response within a 1,500-character budget How we built it App: Next.js 15 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS WebMCP: document.modelContext directly. A connection provider registers two public tools while signed out, swaps in the 21-tool authenticated catalog on sign-in, and tears everything down with an AbortSignal when the session changes. One file per tool: focused description, JSON schema, behavioral annotations, execute . Authority: Supabase Postgres with row-level security. Tools run on the signed-in user's browser session — the database decides what's allowed, never the agent. Realtime: database-triggered broadcasts on conversation and per-user topics Files: private storage buckets with signed URLs AI: configurable Anthropic / Gemini / OpenAI provider for summaries and image descriptions Testing: Vitest unit tests and Playwright end-to-end accessibility specs Challenges we ran into Building on a brand-new spec. WebMCP lives behind a Chrome flag with thin documentation, so every design decision was tested against real agents, not just the docs. Tool lifecycle. Tools from a signed-out session must not survive. Abort-based cleanup on every session change took real care to get right. Prompt injection. Message bodies are written by other people — attacker-controlled by definition. We wrap them as labeled untrusted content and clamp every tool result to a 1,500-character budget so injected text stays data, not instructions. Safe without being annoying. Agents that confirm everything are useless; agents that confirm nothing are dangerous. The draft-then-send split and two-call confirmation pattern was our answer: composition is cheap, execution is deliberate. Passkeys are picky. Origin and RP ID must agree exactly, so we made the production build verify its own WebAuthn config and refuse to ship a broken one. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real messenger , not a demo — realtime, groups, files, reactions — fully drivable by voice through an agent Account creation where the agent never touches a secret : passkey-only sign-up completed by the human A trust model where the agent holds no keys: session-scoped tools, RLS as the enforcement layer, untrusted content labeled at the boundary Accessibility on both paths: the visual UI is keyboard- and screen-reader-conscious, and the agent path removes the need for sight entirely What we learned Tool descriptions are UX. Agents read schemas the way users read buttons — a vague description produces a wrong click, just invisibly. The page should be the authority. Once the app validates everything and the database enforces access, you can hand an agent real power without handing it trust. Separating composition from execution preserves human control — the draft-then-send pattern felt like a workaround and turned out to be the design. Accessibility and agent-readiness are the same work. Semantic actions help a screen-reader user and an AI agent for the same reason: both need meaning, not pixels. What's next for Verb - Sight off. Voice on More verbs: scheduled send, pinning, cross-conversation search, a "morning digest" tool that recaps every unread thread at once Voice-first onboarding so the very first session never needs a screen Adopting elicitation and richer annotations as the WebMCP spec evolves Extracting our lifecycle + safety patterns (abort-scoped registration, untrusted-content wrapping, confirm-twice writes) into a small open-source library, so any web app can add its verbs Built With chatgpt css liveperson-agent typescript webmcp Try it out github.com verb-webmcp.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Tony Nguyen Tony Nguyen A figuring-it-out person Hung Truong Like 2 2 people like this: Share this project: Updates Hung Truong started this project — Sep 03, 2026 10:47 PM EDT

title: webclerk
pitch: A WebMCP-powered trust layer for consequential forms that fills only evidence-backed fields, preserves uncertainty and conflicts, and keeps truthfulness and final submission under human authority.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered trust layer for consequential forms that fills only evidence-backed fields, preserves uncertainty and conflicts, and keeps truthfulness and final submission under human authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates webclerk uses WebMCP to prepare evidence-backed forms while preserving conflicts, uncertainty, and human control. webclerk exposes 9 semantic WebMCP tools over live browser state: 7 read & 2 write, with evidence-backed actions & no submit capability. Inspiration AI agents are getting very good at filling forms, navigating websites, and taking actions on behalf of users. But consequential forms create a harder problem: What happens when the agent sounds confident about something the evidence never actually proved? For scholarship applications, insurance claims, benefits, compliance workflows, and similar processes, a plausible answer is not necessarily a supported answer. That led to the core idea behind webclerk : Evidence > confidence. The agent prepares. The human commits. webclerk explores what happens when a website does not merely expose capabilities to an AI agent, but also defines the boundaries of the agent's authority. What it does webclerk is a WebMCP-powered trust layer for consequential forms . Instead of giving an agent unrestricted access to form fields, the website exposes semantic tools backed by deterministic trust rules. Every field can remain in one of several meaningful states: Verified — supported by current, accepted evidence Needs confirmation — plausible, but requires the applicant Conflict — the form and evidence disagree Human-only — the agent is not authorized to decide or attest it The agent can safely prepare the application while uncertainty stays visible. In the scholarship workflow, the agent can: inspect the current application state read supporting evidence find evidence-backed values explain why a field is unresolved check consistency run preflight checks request approval before making supported edits The site exposes 9 semantic WebMCP tools: 7 read tools and 2 write tools . There is deliberately no submission tool . Truthfulness declarations and final submission stay with the human. How WebMCP is used WebMCP is not an add-on to webclerk. It is the interaction model. The browser page exposes semantic capabilities such as: get_application_state fill_verified_fields_from_evidence inspect_field list_evidence suggest_field_value set_field_value find_missing_information check_consistency run_preflight These tools operate over the same live browser state the user sees . That means the agent does not need brittle DOM scraping or coordinate-based automation to understand the application. More importantly, the website itself controls what the agent is allowed to do. Writes pass through deterministic authorization rules before the visible form state can change. Live scholarship proof The scholarship demo begins at approximately 70% completion . When prompted: Fill everything you can verify from my documents. Don't guess anything. the agent identifies six evidence-backed fields and requests approval before writing. After approval: completion moves from 70% to 96% verified fields increase from 3 to 9 6 evidence-backed agent edits are made 0 unsupported guesses are made 0 consequential agent actions are performed Every agent mutation is visibly attributed to WebMCP. But the more important behavior is what webclerk refuses to do. For example, the enrollment certificate proves that the applicant is enrolled, but it does not establish whether the mode of study is full-time, part-time, or something else. webclerk leaves that field unresolved instead of inferring it. Conflicts stay conflicts The scholarship form intentionally contains an income conflict: application value: ₹3,50,000 supporting evidence: ₹3,20,000 webclerk does not silently choose one. The field remains blocked and preflight surfaces the conflict for human review. The system also detects stale evidence and preserves applicant-confirmation fields instead of promoting them into verified facts. The principle is simple: Blocked, not guessed. Human authority Some actions should not be delegated simply because an agent is technically capable of interacting with the page. webclerk therefore treats actions such as truthfulness declarations as human-only. If the agent attempts to perform a protected action, the trust layer rejects it. Final submission is even more explicit: there is no submit_application capability exposed through WebMCP. The absence of that capability is intentional. Proving the architecture generalizes I did not want webclerk to be a scholarship-specific automation script. So I built a second live workflow: a motor insurance claim . It uses the same trust engine and the same WebMCP tool factory, but with insurance-specific domain rules and evidence. The agent safely prepares: claimant name policy number vehicle registration incident date while preserving a deliberate repair-estimate conflict: form: ₹85,000 evidence: ₹78,500 Fault admission, incident narrative, and truthfulness remain under human authority. This demonstrates the underlying idea: Same engine. Same WebMCP layer. Different consequential workflow. How I built it webclerk is a browser-first TypeScript application with a reusable deterministic trust engine. The implementation separates: workflow data and evidence deterministic trust rules agent authority policy WebMCP semantic tools shared browser state human-facing provenance and preflight UI The WebMCP tool factory is reusable across both the scholarship and insurance workflows. The project also includes automated tests for: safe evidence-backed writes stale evidence conflicting evidence human-confirmation fields human-only actions tool metadata WebMCP read/write classification machine-readable authority rules adversarial agent behavior cross-domain generalization Challenges The hardest part was not getting an agent to fill a form. The hard part was defining when it must not fill one. That required treating uncertainty, stale evidence, conflict, provenance, and human authority as first-class states rather than edge cases. Another challenge was making those constraints useful without making the agent useless. The goal was not to block automation. The goal was to maximize safe preparation while preserving the decisions that genuinely belong to a person. What I learned WebMCP becomes especially interesting when websites expose more than actions. A semantic tool can communicate: what the agent can do what evidence supports an action whether approval is required why an action is blocked and what authority the agent does not possess That changes the relationship between websites and agents. Instead of an agent trying to infer what a page permits from its DOM, the website can participate directly in defining the collaboration model. What's next The current project demonstrates scholarship and motor-insurance workflows, but the trust model can extend to other consequential processes such as: financial aid government benefits visa applications compliance forms healthcare administration regulated onboarding The long-term idea is a reusable trust layer where AI agents can do substantial preparatory work while evidence, uncertainty, provenance, and human authority remain explicit. Autofill is easy. Authority is hard. webclerk is an experiment in making that authority programmable. title: 2030MCP LinkUp
pitch: LinkUp helps people recover after a flood, fire, or earthquake and more. Tell us what happened and agent turns it into a simple Situation Map for housing, power, documents
about_excerpt: LinkUp helps people recover after a flood, fire, or earthquake and more. Tell us what happened and agent turns it into a simple Situation Map for housing, power, documents Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration After a flood or fire, people often have to explain what happened over and over again—to the county, the utility company, housing programs, and different relief organizations. When your home is already damaged, even figuring out which form to start with can be overwhelming. The problem isn't always that nobody wants to help. It's that the help is spread across different websites, forms, and systems that don't really talk to each other. We started wondering: what if an agent could handle some of that coordination for you, without making decisions on your behalf? That is what made WebMCP interesting to us. A website can expose specific tools to an agent while still controlling exactly what the agent is allowed to do. The agent can take care of repetitive work, while the resident stays in control of what gets shared, approved, or submitted. What it does 2030MCP LinkUp is designed for the days after a flood, fire, earthquake, storm, or other disaster. Instead of entering the same information into multiple systems, you explain what happened once. LinkUp turns that into a simple Situation Map showing what it understood, what information is still missing, and which services may be relevant. For example, the system may identify that you need temporary housing, utility support, replacement documents, or disaster relief. The agent can then read provider requirements, organize the information you already provided, and prepare the next step for you. The important part is that it does not make the final decision. It cannot decide whether your story is true, approve your case, or submit something on your behalf without your review. You see what the agent plans to do first and choose whether to continue. How we built it We built LinkUp with Next.js App Router, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The WebMCP layer is built around document.modelContext.registerTool. Instead of registering every tool all the time, LinkUp rebuilds the available tool registry from the current signed case state. That means a tool only becomes available when the user has reached the right step and given the required consent. We also enforce the same boundaries on the server. Route handlers validate signed session data including the user's role, disaster scenario, and origin. We use strict Zod schemas, state version checks, idempotency keys, packet hashes, expiring grants, and rate limits to prevent replay, tampering, or unintended submissions. Every action that changes the case is also recorded in a server-side audit log. For the disaster flows, we created separate provider fixtures for floods, fires, earthquakes, and storms. The provider policy version is selected before evidence is collected, so changing the incident later cannot silently change the rules applied to the case. Testing was a major part of the project. We currently have 108 Vitest tests covering the WebMCP contract, dynamic tool registration and removal, replay prevention, tamper rejection, and session integrity. We also run strict TypeScript checks and GitHub Actions with pinned revisions. Most importantly, we tested the real WebMCP flow in a browser using the native document.modelContext interface. We verified that the send tool appears only after consent and disappears again after it has been used. For Chrome testing, the project also includes a Chrome 149+ path using chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. To keep the demo easy to run, the entire resident session survives serverless cold starts without requiring a database. Case state is stored in signed, Brotli-compressed cookie chunks with strict size limits. We also test the deployed version with npm run test:golden to make sure a fresh incognito session can complete the full flow from beginning to end. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making "the human is in control" something the system actually enforces. At first, it is tempting to put instructions in the tool description and say that the agent should ask before doing something important. But that still depends on the model following the instruction. We wanted the restriction to exist at the system level instead. So we moved permissions into the tool registry itself. A consequential tool does not exist until the user has explicitly given consent. After a one-time action is used, the tool removes itself from the registry. That gave us something we could actually test: not just whether the agent behaved correctly, but whether the tool was available at all. Another challenge was writing tool descriptions for an agent rather than for a person. We added clear authority boundaries such as CONSEQUENTIAL, ONE USE, explicit fields that prevent the agent from implying provider approval, and untrustedContentHint for information that comes from free-text user stories. Another challenge was keeping a complete resident session working across serverless instances without a database while still staying inside browser cookie limits. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that LinkUp actually works as a deployed product, rather than being just a mockup of an agent workflow. The WebMCP registry changes live as the resident moves through the process. A one-use send tool appears after consent, can be used once, and then disappears. We also built a read-only audit interface so another agent can inspect what happened without being able to change the case. And instead of using one generic disaster demo, we built separate provider contracts for floods, fires, earthquakes, and storms so the workflow behaves differently depending on the situation. What we learned If a tool should not be available yet, the safest option is not to register it at all. We also learned that tool descriptions matter much more than we expected. They are not just documentation for developers; they are part of the interface the model uses to understand its authority and responsibilities. Clear descriptions made the agent much more likely to ask for review instead of acting as if it had approval from a provider. WebMCP also showed us a different way to think about agent safety. Instead of putting every restriction inside a chat prompt, some of the rules can be enforced directly by the website and its tool lifecycle. What's next for 2030MCP LinkUp First, a server-issued human-presence challenge so consequential actions can verify that a real resident is still present. Second, an encrypted case database for longer-term recovery cases and larger documents. Third, real provider integrations for housing agencies, utilities, local government, and relief organizations. The WebMCP contracts are already structured so providers could publish their own requirement and submission tools. The county, housing, and utility portals in our demo are examples of how those provider-owned integrations could work. The long-term goal is simple: people should not have to rebuild the same disaster story for every organization they need help from. They should explain what happened once, review what gets shared, and stay in control of the process. title: ACKB Handshake
pitch: Design together. Approve with proof
about_excerpt: Design together. Approve with proof Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of suggesting and executing changes, but consequential design decisions still need clear human control. In kitchen and bath planning, even a seemingly simple suggestion—moving a fixture, changing an appliance, or adjusting a room layout—can affect cost, accessibility, clearances, utilities, and usability. We built Handshake to explore a better collaboration model: an AI agent can inspect a shared design, search for products, evaluate constraints, and propose improvements, but it cannot silently change the approved plan. Our guiding principle became our tagline: Design together. Approve with proof. What it does Handshake is a WebMCP-enabled kitchen and bath co-design workspace where a person and an in-browser AI agent collaborate on the same room plan. The agent can: Read the current room and design state Search a synthetic kitchen and bath product catalog Evaluate budget, geometry, clearances, openings, and planning guidelines Propose placing, moving, swapping, or removing products Propose changes to room dimensions and openings Explain warnings before a decision is made Generate a bill of materials from the approved design Retrieve evidence receipts for protected actions The agent cannot approve its own proposal or bypass the page’s consent controls. Every proposed change is versioned and shown to the person for review. Approval is bound to the exact proposal contents using a canonical hash, so an approved proposal cannot be silently replaced with something different. Consequential actions pass through an additional human-only confirmation step. Successful actions produce evidence receipts that record what was approved, which checks were shown, and what happened. How we built it Handshake is a TypeScript monorepo built with pnpm and deployed around a Cloudflare architecture. A Cloudflare Worker serves the application and API. Each synthetic design session is owned by a Durable Object, which maintains the authoritative room state, proposal versions, idempotency records, confirmations, and audit events. The browser exposes a governed WebMCP tool surface. Tools can read state, search the catalog, create proposals, apply an already-approved proposal, request protected actions, and retrieve receipts. Human approval and confirmation endpoints are deliberately excluded from the agent-callable tool surface. The policy layer is deterministic and side-effect free. It handles: Canonical proposal hashing Proposal expiry and state transitions Expected-version checks Idempotency and replay prevention Actor and authorization boundaries Budget and room-boundary evaluation Fixture overlap and approach clearance Door and appliance-opening conflicts Kitchen work-triangle guidance Work aisles, walkways, and landing areas Service-location warnings Accessibility-oriented turning-space checks Bill-of-materials calculation Rule thresholds are represented as named, reviewable constants with source information rather than unexplained numbers embedded in the implementation. The current project uses synthetic data and presents its checks as planning guidance—not as building-code certification. We use Vitest for unit and policy testing, Playwright for browser verification, GitHub Actions for continuous integration, and Wrangler for Cloudflare development and deployment workflows. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was preserving meaningful human control without making the agent collaboration feel artificial. It was not enough to place an “Approve” button beside an unrestricted mutation endpoint. We needed to prove that: The person reviewed the exact proposal that would be applied. The proposal was still valid for the current room version. The agent could not approve or confirm its own work. Replayed requests could not apply the same change twice. A protected action could not proceed without fresh, explicit confirmation. The resulting receipt accurately described the approved action. Another challenge was keeping the product claim aligned with the implementation. Handshake was described as a kitchen and bath workspace, but the earliest catalog and rules were primarily bathroom-oriented. Rather than hide that gap, we documented it and expanded the domain model to include kitchens, doors, windows, service anchors, appliance interactions, work-triangle evaluation, landing areas, and a bill of materials. We also had to distinguish authorization from design guidance. Authorization rules fail closed, but planning warnings should remain reviewable. A person may knowingly approve a design that carries a recommendation-level warning; Handshake’s job is to ensure that the warning was visible and recorded, not to pretend the agent owns the final decision. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Handshake treats consent as part of the architecture rather than a decorative UI step. The project now includes: A versioned proposal state machine Canonical hashes that bind approval to exact proposal contents Human-only approval and confirmation endpoints Replay-resistant and idempotent state transitions A shared, server-authoritative design session A governed WebMCP tool surface Protected-action evidence receipts Deterministic budget and geometry checks Kitchen and bathroom planning-rule support A derived bill of materials Negative-path tests for replay, self-approval, stale versions, expired consent, and altered proposals Continuous-integration validation for formatting, types, and tests We are especially proud that the system is explicit about its limits. It uses synthetic project data, does not claim code-compliance certification, and does not treat a green automated check as proof that deployment or final submission is complete. What we learned We learned that trustworthy agent experiences require more than permission prompts. The approval must be attached to the exact state transition, and the system must preserve enough evidence to explain the decision afterward. We also learned that deterministic policy code and generative agent behavior work best when they have separate responsibilities. The agent can help interpret goals and propose creative changes. The policy engine owns authorization, consistency, geometry, and repeatable checks. A third lesson was that missing information should not be invented. If a room has no modelled door, Handshake does not fabricate one and claim to have checked its swing. Evidence is only useful when it clearly distinguishes what was evaluated from what remains unknown. Finally, we learned that human control does not have to eliminate useful automation. The agent can still inspect, search, calculate, and prepare a complete proposal. The boundary is simple: the agent proposes; the person decides; the system records the proof.
