title: Action Check
pitch: Deterministic validation for WebMCP agent actions. Stop trusting AI agent replies. Action Check independently verifies WebMCP tool execution.
about_excerpt: Deterministic validation for WebMCP agent actions. Stop trusting AI agent replies. Action Check independently verifies WebMCP tool execution. Like Comment Story Updates Native WebMCP ready: three registered tools and the agent instruction (Chrome 152, 3 Sep) Human checkpoint: approve the exact payment, amount and request ID; the button is not a tool Checker validated: known-bad 2 calls -> 2 effects, protected 2 calls -> 1, read from the ledger Browser without WebMCP: the same four steps run by a labelled simulated agent Inspiration I started this hackathon building the same kind of thing most entries are: a site that exposes tools to an agent. The first commit in my working history, was an OAuth recovery workbench with six registered tools. A day into it I threw that out, because of something in Chrome's WebMCP evals guidance. In the troubleshooting table, for the case where a tool's output is wrong, it asks: was the UI state correctly updated, and did the agent receive the right information about the side effect? I went looking for anything that answered that question by actually calling a tool and then checking the site, and the readiness scanners I found only check whether a site exposes tools at all. When an agent calls issue_refund or add_to_cart , the reply is the only information it gets. If the reply says "done" when nothing happened, or when it happened twice, the agent cannot tell, and neither can the person who asked it. So I built the test. What it does Action Check calls a page's registered WebMCP tool the way an agent would, through document.modelContext.executeTool in real Chrome, and does not take the reply at face value. Before and after the call it runs an observe() function that reads the site's own state, whatever fits that site: a cart in localStorage, rendered rows, a read-only endpoint. The verdict comes from comparing what the tool claimed with what actually changed. observe() is never given the tool's result. It gets the live page, the phase (before or after), the tool name, the input and the page origin, and nothing else. I did it that way because the obvious shortcut, when you are writing an observer late at night, is to read the reply and return whatever it says, and I did not want that to be possible even for me. This is what WebMCP makes possible that scripted clicks did not. Before, checking a site's action from outside meant driving its UI, and what you ended up testing was the UI. Now the tool is an addressable thing with a name and a schema, so the check a developer runs from the command line is the same call the agent makes. The person's part gets smaller: approve the exact values once, on the page, and step back. The agent does the calls and the retries. The proof step reads a record neither of them wrote, so nobody has to take anybody's word for it. How I built it The live page registers three tools, stage_refund_comparison , issue_refund and prove_refund_comparison , and answers one question a payments team would ask before exposing a refund tool: can a retry refund twice? The state lives in a small Cloudflare Worker with a SQLite Durable Object per lane and run. /v1/invoke returns only a claim; /v1/observe returns the durable state, effect IDs and an evidence digest. Every trial starts with /v1/reset , which has to prove a zero-effect baseline, and the Worker caps each trial at two invocations per lane on its own, whatever the browser does. To make the retry path run, the harness commits the first refund and drops the provider's acknowledgement on purpose. The agent gets a bounded error and retries with the same request ID. On the known-bad lane that is two refunds from two calls; on the protected lane the request ID is honoured and there is one. The person approves the exact payment, amount, currency and request ID first, with a button that is an ordinary page control, so an agent cannot press it. The three tools register one after another under a single AbortController , with an abort check between each, and the page shows the count going up; it only says the tools are ready once all three are in. Taking the view down aborts that controller. The signal that execute receives is passed through to the fetch that posts to /v1/invoke , so cancelling a tool call cancels the request, and because a cancelled request is not proof of a cancelled refund the session treats it as uncertain and re-reads the ledger. Inputs are checked twice: each tool advertises a frozen JSON schema, and execute parses the same arguments again with a strict Zod schema before anything moves. A failed parse comes back as INPUT_MISMATCH naming the fields. Every error carries a code, a message and a nextAction , and the hints depend on state, so an agent that calls things in the wrong order is told what to do next. The tools carry readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . The CLI came on 2 September. It launches the installed Chrome with --enable-features=WebMCP (Playwright's bundled Chromium does not have WebMCP), reads the page's tools through document.modelContext.getTools() , and invokes the target once or twice with identical input. The target's own description, schema and annotations from that getTools() response go into the run's proof JSON, so each run records the contract it was checking in the site's words. Chrome 152 wants the input as JSON text, which the native test had already shown on 1 September, so the CLI sends text first and falls back to an object. On 3 September I added the external-target mode, so the same check can be pointed at a page I have nothing to do with. Challenges I ran into My own checker being wrong. Against Google's public WebMCP demos I recorded eighteen runs and set six aside because I could not stand behind the verdict. Three were on the observer side: a count-based observe() cannot see a retry that mints a second confirmation ID under the same banner, or a cart count hard-coded to 1. Three were my claim heuristic: it read a playful success reply ("You can't see me") as a refusal, and it had no answer for a tool that aborts its own registration mid-call. Those six are documented in the repository and not published. A fourth heuristic gap turned up on one of the published runs and I did fix that the same afternoon: a reply shaped {"status":"error"} now counts as a refusal, with two unit tests. A claim I had written in three places that turned out to be false. I had said the verdict "never comes from the tool's reply". In retry mode that is true, the verdict depends only on the observed delta. In once mode the verdict compares the reply's claim against the delta, which is how it tells a false success from an honest refusal. I corrected the page, the README and this text. What I can say accurately is that the observer never sees the reply. A page can only see tools registered on its own document.modelContext , not another origin's, so there is no way to build "paste a URL and check it" into the web page. The check has to drive a real Chrome from outside, which is why the CLI is the real product and the page is the front door to it. I added a builder to the page that takes a target URL, tool name, JSON input and mode, and writes out a starter observe() module and the exact command, so the first run is not a blank editor. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The results on pages I do not own. On 3 September, in Chrome 152, I ran twelve recorded checks against seven of Google's own WebMCP demos, and five found a bug. The ticket-booking demo's select_showtime replied "You can now proceed to checkout" while the checkout section stayed hidden, because the tool re-renders the page after opening it. The sports storefront's add_search_result_to_cart , retried once with identical input, put two of the same ball in the cart. Luxe Leather's add_to_cart doubled the quantity and the subtotal on retry while the header badge still said 1. Smart Home's rearrangeDOMComponents replied "Dashboard successfully updated with requested components" and rendered nothing. zaMaker's add_topping duplicated the topping on retry. The other seven runs passed and I published those too: three honest refusals, three that were idempotent, one positive control. The proof JSON for every run is in docs/evidence/ . The verdict names ended up more useful than I expected when I wrote them. Retry mode gives DUPLICATE_EFFECT , NO_EFFECT or IDEMPOTENT . Once mode gives FALSE_SUCCESS , SILENT_EFFECT , EFFECT_CONFIRMED or HONEST_REFUSAL . "Your tool claimed success and nothing appeared" is a bug report someone can act on. What I learned An agent cannot verify its own work by asking the tool, and no amount of prompting fixes that; the check has to sit outside. A verdict is only as good as what the observer reads, and I should say so. Chrome's implementation has quirks the docs do not cover yet (the JSON-text input, tools that navigate mid-call and leave nothing to observe), and a harness has to report those as harness errors, not dress them

title: AGENT CONTROL PLANE
pitch: The website-enforced authority layer for WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: The website-enforced authority layer for WebMCP agents. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Control Plane The website-enforced authority layer for WebMCP agents. Inspiration AI is moving from copilots that recommend actions to autonomous agents that execute them. These agents can issue refunds, contact customers and work with sensitive business data. As soon as AI begins taking consequential actions, prompt-level guardrails are no longer enough. The question is no longer only “What can this model do?” It is: “What is this agent authorized to do right now?” Prompt instructions such as “never refund more than €500” are not enough. Prompts can become stale, be misunderstood or be influenced by malicious content hidden inside invoices, emails and documents. We wanted to build a stronger model in which the website—not the agent’s prompt—enforces authority at execution time. That led to our core thesis: Capability is not authority. WebMCP exposes what an agent can do; Agent Control Plane governs what it is allowed to do. What it does Agent Control Plane is a website-enforced authority and security layer for WebMCP agents. We demonstrate it through a fictional Anthropic billing dispute involving a verified €1,200 overcharge. The agent uses real page-defined WebMCP tools to: Inspect two invoices Verify the signed contract Read its live delegated authority Propose an evidence-backed correction plan Attempt refunds Request an account credit Execute an exactly approved action Verify the final session state The agent initially has a cumulative €500 refund limit. When it attempts the full €1,200 refund, the website blocks the action and no money moves. The human operator then raises only that session’s authority to €800. The agent rereads the website’s live state and replans without being restarted: Execute an €800 refund inside delegated authority. Request human approval for the remaining €400 account credit. The approval is bound to the exact action, amount, customer, session, policy version and expiration. Approval does not execute the credit—the agent must make a separate matching WebMCP call that is revalidated at execution time. The app also demonstrates: Prompt-injection containment Cumulative-budget enforcement Replay and idempotency protection External-recipient blocking Human-reviewed customer messages Signed-record protection Emergency session revocation An automatic circuit breaker SHA-256-linked decision receipts All payments and deliveries are simulated inside the security lab. The WebMCP calls, enforcement decisions and state transitions are part of the working application. How we built it We built Agent Control Plane as a React and TypeScript application with 13 page-defined WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The React interface and WebMCP tools share the same observable store, pure domain actions and deterministic Authority Gate: React controls ──────┐ ├──> Shared store ──> Domain actions ──> Authority Gate WebMCP tools ────────┘ │ └──> Audit events and receipts This architecture ensures that a WebMCP tool cannot bypass the rules displayed by the interface. There is no separate demo-only execution path. Each consequential action receives one of four decisions: ALLOW ALLOW_WITH_LIMIT APPROVAL_REQUIRED DENY The WebMCP implementation includes tools for reading evidence, inspecting authority, proposing plans, moving money, requesting approval, sending customer messages, testing protected-record attacks and verifying the receipt chain. To make the enforcement visible, we created: A Control Center with live financial and authority state An Agent Plan Checkpoint A streaming Live Activity feed An Authorization Queue A WebMCP Recorder A detailed Audit Trail A live Security Posture board A guided Scenario Lab Every real WebMCP call creates a receipt containing its inputs, effective policy, decision, provenance findings and before/after state. Receipts are linked using SHA-256 hashes so the chain can be verified. Challenges we ran into Our biggest challenge was maintaining one trustworthy source of truth. The human interface and WebMCP tools had to call exactly the same domain actions. Otherwise, the interface could claim that an action was blocked while a tool silently bypassed the enforcement layer. We also had to carefully separate concepts that are often combined: Requesting approval is not executing an action. Human approval is not the same as execution. Pending funds are reserved but not completed. A policy change invalidates plans created under older authority. Evidence may inform reasoning but must never become authority. Discovering a tool does not imply permission to use it. Another major challenge was making invisible security understandable. When a security control succeeds, the dangerous side effect simply does not happen. We therefore designed strong blocked-action banners, inline explanations, live state changes and decision receipts that show exactly why an action was permitted, blocked or held for approval. We also had to prevent fragmented refunds, repeated requests and parameter-swapped approvals from bypassing controls that appeared safe when evaluating only one call at a time. Accomplishments that we’re proud of We are proud that Agent Control Plane is a coherent working product rather than a collection of disconnected security demonstrations. Our canonical workflow completes an entire agent journey: Objective → Evidence → Plan → Block → Live authority change → Replan → Autonomous execution → Human approval → Final execution → Verifiable proof We are especially proud of the live-authority interaction. The human can change a session’s authority while the agent is already operating. The agent then rereads the website state, recognizes the new policy version and changes its plan without being restarted. We are also proud of the WebMCP Recorder. It makes the underlying implementation visible by showing the real registered tools and the receipts produced by actual calls. Other accomplishments include: 13 working WebMCP tools Cumulative rather than per-call refund limits Replay protection using required idempotency keys Exact, expiring and state-bound approvals Recipient-domain enforcement before data release Immutable signed-record policies Emergency revocation of consequential actions Automatic circuit breaking after repeated denied writes SHA-256-linked decision receipts A complete suite of 25 domain and security tests Most importantly, even if an agent is manipulated by malicious evidence, the website’s authority boundary continues to hold. What we learned We learned that agent safety cannot live only inside the agent. The website owns the business data, consequential tools and current state. It is therefore the strongest place to enforce financial limits, approvals, recipient boundaries, leases and revocation. We also learned that useful human-agent collaboration does not mean asking the human to approve every step. A better model is: Autonomy inside the boundary. Human control at the boundary. The agent should work independently within clearly delegated authority and stop only when it reaches a meaningful limit or approval requirement. Finally, we learned that auditability should be created during execution, not reconstructed afterward. Recording the exact input, effective rule, decision and state transition gives operators stronger evidence than relying on an agent’s explanation of what it believes it did. What’s next for Agent Control Plane The current project is a focused security lab with simulated financial and communication actions. The next step is to turn the authority model into reusable infrastructure for websites exposing consequential WebMCP tools. As autonomous agents become a primary interface for using software, every website exposing consequential tools will need an execution-time authority layer. We want Agent Control Plane to become that layer for WebMCP. Future development could include: Authenticated human operators Passkey-backed approvals and authority changes Persistent, externally verifiable receipt storage Enterprise policy management Multi-tenant and customer-level isolation Reusable policy templates Real payment and customer-support integrations Approval notifications across devices Compliance exports and incident investigation A developer SDK for adding the Authority Gate to other WebMCP websites The billing scenario demonstrates the model, but the same architecture could govern agents working in customer support, commerce, finance, healthcare and enterprise administration. Our long-term vision is simple: WebMCP gives agents capabilities. Agent Control Plane gives humans control over how those capabilities are used. Built With agentic agents ai apis chatgpt css3 html5 human-in-the-loop javascript json openaisites react schema security sha-256 typescript vite vitest web webmcp Try it out agent-control-plane-anthropic.hicham-contact08.chatgpt.site github.

title: AI ACT SHIELD WEBMCP
pitch: AI Act Shield App masks the personal data in your contract without sending to any LLM. WebMCP tools run in your browser page using deterministic checksums. No sensible datas will leave the page.
about_excerpt: AI Act Shield App masks the personal data in your contract without sending to any LLM. WebMCP tools run in your browser page using deterministic checksums. No sensible datas will leave the page. Like Comment Story Updates The agent was never told which tool to use, and reports only the types it received. Left: what the human sees. Right: what leaves the page. external mask_document_in_page {} — the agent called the tool with no arguments, because the app never gives it the document Inspiration Law firms and accountants across the EU are stuck in a small, expensive trap. Generative AI would genuinely help them review a contract — but the contract is full of client data they are not allowed to paste into a cloud model. Under the AI Act and the GDPR that is not a formality; it is their licence to practise. The usual answer is a cloud "anonymization API", which moves the leak one hop away and calls it a solution. I wanted the masking to happen where the document already is: on the lawyer's own machine, in the browser tab, with nothing to trust but code you can read. What it does AI Act Shield detects personal data — tax codes, national IDs, VAT numbers, IBANs, payment cards, names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, company names — and replaces each with a placeholder, so the masked draft can safely go to any AI. When the answer comes back, it puts the real values back where they belong. Detection is deterministic: regular expressions plus real checksums (ISO 13616 for IBANs, Luhn for payment cards, the Spanish DNI/NIE and CIF control characters, the official Italian VAT algorithm). Never an LLM. A model would answer differently on the same document from one run to the next, and sending a document to a model to ask what to hide from that model defeats the purpose. Coverage is Italian, Spanish and English/international. The WebMCP part The app is built on one constraint: the text never leaves the browser. That constraint turns out to be exactly what makes a WebMCP tool trustworthy, because registerTool().execute() runs client-side, in the visitor's own tab. The page registers four tools. The one that carries the argument is mask_document_in_page , and what matters is what it doesn't take: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "mask_document_in_page", description: "Masks the personal data in the document the user has already loaded into this page, without the caller ever receiving the document.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { customTerms: { /* ... */ } } }, execute: async (input) => maskPageDocument(input), }); No text parameter. The person loads the confidential document into the page; the agent calls the tool passing nothing ; the page reads its own content and returns a masked draft plus the types of what it found. The document never enters the agent's context, so it cannot leak one even if it tried. Asked in plain language to mask a contract — without being told which tool to use — ChatGPT's agentic browser produced this row in the page's own log: 1:48:34 PM external mask_document_in_page {} external means the call came from outside the page rather than from its own buttons. {} means there was nothing to pass. That empty object is the whole project. This is also the case for "people and agents using an app together": the UI and the tools share one page-local state, so the person watching the tab sees the masking happen live and can step in — switch a detected entity off, add a custom term — while the agent works. How I built it Vanilla JavaScript. No framework, no dependencies, no build step — you can clone it and open it. 37 tests on node:test , which is built in, so that promise holds for the test suite too. Served as static files from my own nginx, not a platform: the page is the same folder that nginx serves. The detection engine is a port of the one shipping in iaCiao , my platform for local — edge — AI: 32 iApps across health, security and mobility, all built so the model runs on your device and the data stays there. AI Act Shield is the clearest expression of that idea, which is why I brought it here. An app whose entire value is that the sensitive part never leaves your machine turns out to be the natural shape for a WebMCP tool, because that is exactly where execute() runs. Challenges The ecosystem moved under me during the ten days. ChatGPT Atlas was deprecated days before the deadline. The Model Context Tool Inspector extension reports nothing for my page, because it looks for navigator.modelContext while the specification (26 August 2026) exposes ModelContext on document and never mentions navigator. I left that audit check failing rather than shim an API that does not exist — and left the declarative toolname / tooldescription / toolaction checks failing too, since the spec marks that API "entirely a TODO". ChatGPT's Chrome extension looks like it works and doesn't. Asked to mask the document, it produced a fluent, accurate answer — by reading the DOM, without calling a single tool. That is precisely the difference this project is about, and it would have been very easy to film it as a success. Chrome's origin trial has a quirk. It returns inputSchema as a JSON string and rejects a plain-object argument to executeTool() with "Failed to parse input arguments". Nothing in the spec asks for a pre-serialised input, so the code calls the spec-shaped way first and falls back only when that build refuses. My own buttons sabotaged two takes. The "Agent console" had a button labelled CALL MASK_SENSITIVE_DATA() . Asked to "use the page's tools", the agent clicked it — twice. Not a dim agent: the button had named itself after the API, so it was the closest match to the instruction. Renaming it to "Preview the masking response", and adding a line in llms.txt telling agents to call the tool instead, fixed what a better prompt could not. Cloudflare hid three deploys. Assets are served with a four-hour browser cache, so the page kept running the previous build and no hard refresh changed it. I lost two hours because I was verifying with curl --resolve ...:127.0.0.1 , which goes to the origin and bypasses the edge — always showing me the correct file. What I learned The one that mattered: a tool that takes the sensitive data as a parameter cannot protect it. My first version was mask_sensitive_data(text) . It returns only placeholders, never an original value, and I wrote in my notes that "the agent never saw the tax code". That was false, and I did not notice until, halfway through recording, I asked myself whether pasting the contract into the prompt defeated the point of the app. It did — and so, more quietly, did passing it as a tool argument. Whoever calls that tool must already hold the document. There is a real difference between "the response contains no secrets" and "the caller never receives them" , and only the second is a guarantee. mask_document_in_page exists because of that question. The second lesson: instrument your claims. I added a panel that logs every execute() the page receives and marks whether it came from the page's own buttons or from outside. It exists because you cannot otherwise see WebMCP working — the page looks identical either way. That panel is what caught the Chrome extension reading the DOM, and both takes where the agent clicked a button instead of calling a tool. Without it I would have shipped a video of something that wasn't happening. And a third, smaller one: tests find the bugs you just wrote. Four surfaced in a single session, three of them minutes old — including a legal form matching inside an ordinary word, which rewrote the heading "CONSULTANCY AGREEMENT" as "[COMPANY_NAME_1]REEMENT". Honest limits Detection covers Italian, Spanish and English/international formats. A document in another language will still have its IBANs, cards, emails and international phone numbers found, but not its names, addresses or company forms. No PDF or OCR import in this build. Ambiguous candidates — a capitalised pair that may or may not be a person, an amount that usually belongs in the draft — are proposed switched off , and whatever stays readable after masking is listed rather than hidden. An incomplete mask the user trusts is the real failure mode. restore_sensitive_data only works in the tab that masked the document, because the vault is page memory. That is a privacy property, not a missing feature. The guarantee is that the app never hands the document to the caller . It is not that an agent driving a browser is unable to look at the screen. What's next PDF and OCR import, pattern packs beyond the EU, and a tool that lets an agent request a masked excerpt rather than the whole document. Written with Claude (Claude Code), pair-programming style: the specification research, the port of the engine, the Spanish and English coverage and the test suite came out of that collaboration. title: AIMural
pitch: A self-hosted visual board where people and browser agents build ideas together through 24 WebMCP tools. No accounts, no cloud lock-in: every mural has a URL you can reopen and resume anytime.
about_excerpt: A self-hosted visual board where people and browser agents build ideas together through 24 WebMCP tools. No accounts, no cloud lock-in: every mural has a URL you can reopen and resume anytime. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Visual collaboration tools are blind to an agent. It has to guess pixel coordinates, click through menus, or hand back a wall of text that a human then rebuilds on the board by hand. We wanted the opposite: an agent that works with the board's real concepts (ideas, clusters, connections, decision matrices) while the person watches, edits and overrides every move on the same canvas. We also wanted the board to belong to you. No accounts, no cloud lock-in. Every mural has its own URL, it lives on your own server, and you can close the tab today and pick up the same session with the same agents next week. What it does AI Mural is a self-hosted visual board where people and browser agents build, cluster and argue together through 27 WebMCP tools. One live canvas for everyone. Ideas, questions, insights, actions, frames, connections and layers on an infinite canvas. UI clicks and agent tool calls go through the same action layer, so there is no hidden agent-only state. Humans can undo or redo anything an agent did. Come back anytime. Every mural has a UUID and a URL like /?mural=<uuid> . Boards are written to the browser first and synchronized to SQLite on your server, so a session survives reloads. Checkpoints and replay. The moderator saves editable timeline checkpoints at meaningful milestones. Anyone can step through the mural's history with Previous and Next controls without destroying the current state. Share from the app. Publish a local mural and create or rotate private collaborator links from the Share dialog, so a board that started offline can become a shared session in one step. Self-hosted in one command. A tiny Express + SQLite backend, a Dockerfile and a Compose file. No API keys, no external services, no analytics, no cookies. Multiple agents with visible identity. Agents join a mural with named roles such as Explorer, Critic and Synthesizer, each with its own color. The agent that opens a session becomes its moderator and can mute or reactivate others through a private capability, never through a visible ID. Focus leases so agents don't collide. Before editing, an agent claims a visible, expiring focus lease on the elements it is about to touch. Other agents and the human can see who is working where, and overlapping edits are prevented instead of merged after the fact. Capability links instead of logins. A GPT can create a hosted mural, return a separate URL for the human, and issue one private URL per invited agent. The mural UUID routes a request but is not a credential. Artifact Spec 1.0. Tables, cards, checklists and decision matrices are typed data with a published JSON Schema, not screenshots or opaque HTML. Agents read, create, update and reuse them across turns. Decision Trace. An optional recording of user messages, agent contributions, replies, board actions and the final board, exportable as JSON, Markdown or CSV. It never captures hidden chain-of-thought. The 27 WebMCP tools Group Tools Murals and access canvas_create_mural , canvas_rename_mural , canvas_join_session , canvas_invite_agents , canvas_redeem_agent_invite Board canvas_get_board , canvas_add_element , canvas_add_elements , canvas_update_element , canvas_remove_elements , canvas_connect_elements , canvas_arrange_board , canvas_create_cluster , canvas_focus_elements , canvas_set_element_layer Artifacts canvas_create_artifact , canvas_get_artifact_spec , canvas_update_artifact_records Collaboration canvas_set_focus , canvas_add_checkpoint , canvas_start_recording , canvas_record_contribution , canvas_comment_element , canvas_moderate_participant , canvas_watch_mural , canvas_get_recording , canvas_finalize_recording Try it with an agent Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser, then ask: We need to decide how to reduce food waste in our university cafeteria. Create a mural for it and invite three agents with different profiles: an Explorer that proposes at least 10 ideas, a Critic that challenges each one with risks and costs, and a Synthesizer that groups the survivors into Prevention, Redistribution and Composting and builds a decision matrix with the four strongest options. Save a checkpoint after each agent finishes. Send me the mural URL so I can follow along and add my own constraints. How we built it WebMCP: tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext for earlier browser builds. The app stays fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable and shows setup guidance in the Agent panel. Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite and React Flow for the canvas. Backend: Express 5, Drizzle ORM and better-sqlite3. The database initializes itself on first run. Persistence: localStorage first, SQLite sync when the backend is reachable, BroadcastChannel between tabs on the same mural. Security: capability tokens stored server-side only as SHA-256 hashes. Read and write tools are annotated so a client can tell them apart. Deploy: Docker Compose behind an nginx reverse proxy, one-command rsync deploy. npm install npm run dev Challenges we ran into Routing without authorizing. A public mural UUID has to be enough to open a board, but not enough to write to it or to take over a moderator role. Separating owner, user and per-agent capabilities solved it without adding accounts. Merging simultaneous edits. Two tabs and three agents can touch the same mural at once. Version stamps plus deletion tombstones were enough to merge changes instead of blindly replacing the board, without pulling in a full CRDT. Keeping 27 tools understandable for a model. Narrow JSON Schemas, batch limits (30 elements per call, 12 fields and 100 records per artifact), stable element IDs and structured results worked far better than one giant "do anything" tool. Agents talking over each other. Watch leases with a recommended polling interval, quiet periods and cooldowns keep agents from answering their own events. Expiring focus leases stop two agents from editing the same element at once. Syncing without stomping on the human. Hosted sync used to interrupt a person mid-edit when an agent wrote to the same board. Live editing is now preserved across sync cycles. Accomplishments that we're proud of A board where a human and several agents can genuinely work at the same time, and the human never loses control. A session you can leave and resume from any device by URL, with nothing but a SQLite file on your own server. Structured artifacts that an agent can reuse in a later turn instead of re-reading a screenshot. A replayable timeline: checkpoints let you scrub through how a decision was built, step by step. An agentic and free alternative to softwares as Mural or Miro What we learned WebMCP works best when tools expose product concepts, not UI mechanics. "Add 12 ideas and cluster them" beats "click at x, y". Read/write annotations and bounded inputs matter as much as the schema itself. Capability URLs are a surprisingly good fit for agent collaboration: each agent gets exactly one link and nothing else to configure. What's next for AI Mural Live cursors and presence for human collaborators. More artifact types and presentation options. Agent-to-agent handoff patterns built on the watch lease. A one-click self-host template. title: airlock relay
pitch: Airlock lets one Claude Code session use Anthropic, OpenAI, etc side by side. Airlock Relay is the control room on top of it, where a browser agent rescue a stuck session together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Airlock lets one Claude Code session use Anthropic, OpenAI, etc side by side. Airlock Relay is the control room on top of it, where a browser agent rescue a stuck session together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates AIrlock relay landing page happy path opus 5 w/o usage with usage 5.6 Sol limits path Opus 429'd -> handed off to Sol path Inspiration I maintain Airlock , an open-source launcher that lets one Claude Code session use Anthropic, OpenAI, Grok, and OpenRouter models side by side, with separate logins that never mix. Its local router records every rate limit, cooldown, and failover. So I had a runtime that already knew why a session stopped and what else was available. What I did not have was a way to act on that at 2 AM. When the active model's plan hits a rate limit mid-refactor, the session dies, and a person has to read router diagnostics, work out which route is free, whether it spends metered usage, whether the conversation even fits the next model's window, and how to resume without losing the checkpoint. A browser agent could do that reading for me, but only if it could understand the runtime instead of guessing from a dashboard, and nobody wants an agent switching their models on its own. WebMCP is exactly the missing piece: the page declares what a session, a route, and a handoff are , and both a person and an agent act on the same object. What it does Airlock Relay is a control room where a human and a browser agent supervise a stuck coding-agent session together. The agent sees the runtime through seven typed WebMCP tools: get_session , get_events , get_routes , prepare_handoff , get_handoff , execute_handoff , and get_replay . It inspects what broke, then proposes a handoff. The page refuses routes on cooldown, routes whose context window is smaller than the conversation, and metered routes it was not allowed, each refusal listing alternatives. The human sees the same state with ordinary controls: change the target, add a note, approve or reject. There is deliberately no approve tool . Approval issues a token bound to the exact proposal revision the human saw; any edit revokes it; execution is idempotent. The agent re-reads the proposal, sees what the human changed, and executes only with that token. The session resumes from its checkpoint and a replay shows who did what, in order. Two demo scenarios ship: a rate-limited Anthropic plan where only a metered Claude route or another provider can continue, and a context overflow where a 412k-token conversation needs a route with room. Every route carries its provider's plan headroom. It is built to be used, not only demoed. A small Python bridge runs the same console against a real Airlock session, plain Claude Code through hooks, or any agent through a documented ingest contract. It notifies you when the session blocks, records your approval itself with a one-shot nonce, persists the approved order with Airlock's own command, and offers a human-only button that relaunches the same conversation on the approved model. How I built it Page and tools : TypeScript with Vite, no framework. One store holds the shared state; the human UI and the WebMCP tools mutate it through attributed actions. Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , each with a JSON Schema, a use-case description, and annotations ( readOnlyHint on reads, untrustedContentHint on the event log). Results are bounded, every error is structured with a code, a message, and a hint, and every result starts with a one-sentence message so the agent reads the outcome before the fields. Demo data : the hosted demo is seeded from a real GET /diagnostics export of an Airlock router. Events copied verbatim are tagged airlock , seeded ones scenario , page-made ones relay . The session card's task and checkpoint are invented and say so. Bridge : a single standard-library Python file. It discovers the router and the Claude Code session id, serves the built page, feeds live facts, records approvals with one-shot nonces, runs airlock handoff set with the approved target first and the user's declared chain kept, and opens a terminal running airlock hybrid <route> --resume <id> (or claude --resume <id> --model <alias> for plain Claude Code). Airlock's launcher is a Bash script, so on Windows the bridge runs it through Git Bash. Verification : 22 Vitest tests on policy, approval, staleness, idempotency, and attribution; 25 bridge tests; a Chrome smoke test that drives the whole flow through the browser's own document.modelContext.executeTool against the deployed URL; a real hook run with the claude CLI; and a real resume run that launched Airlock with --resume on a scratch session and observed the Claude Code process. Console : dark-first with layered elevation, one accent, four actor tints, a live handoff pipeline, toasts, a Ctrl+K command palette, keyboard approval, inspectable tool calls with input and output, and a one-click Markdown incident report. Challenges I ran into Chrome serialises whatever a tool's execute returns into a JSON string. Returning MCP-style content arrays double-encoded everything; returning the plain result object gives agents one level of JSON. "The human decides" has to be enforceable, not a convention. That took a revision counter, a token bound to it, revocation on any edit, and idempotent execution so a retry cannot resume a session twice. In live mode the bridge keeps its own approval record, so a page script cannot reach the real command. A real orchestrator switch crosses a process boundary that only Airlock's launcher can drive. Rather than pretend, the bridge prepares the exact command, gates it behind a human-only button, and opens a terminal that runs it. Testing that for real on Windows exposed that the launcher is a Bash script Python cannot execute directly. A user's declared failover chain must survive a handoff. The bridge reads the current chain and moves the approved target to the front instead of replacing it. What I learned WebMCP changes the interaction model, not just the transport. Once the page declares semantics, the interesting design question stops being "how does the agent click this" and becomes "what may the agent do, what must the human do, and how does the page prove it". Tool descriptions are product copy: an agent that reads CONTEXT_EXCEEDS_ROUTE_WINDOW with a list of routes that fit makes a better next move than one that reads "error". What's next Ship the bridge as airlock relay inside Airlock itself, read live plan headroom from Claude Code's status line so live routes match the demo, and let the agent subscribe to events instead of polling. Airlock existed before the challenge; everything in the airlock-relay repository was written during it, documented in WEBMCP_CHALLENGE.md . title: AppStory
pitch: See how an app really works with a visual, evidence-backed flow built from its own source code.
about_excerpt: See how an app really works with a visual, evidence-backed flow built from its own source code. Like Comment Story Updates 1 About the project AppStory turns a public GitHub repository — or a local folder — into an evidence-backed visual story of an application. Built for the WebMCP Challenge . Live: appstory.ivanideas.com Inspiration Every team I have worked on hits the same wall. A product manager asks a simple question — "What can a user actually do in this app, and where could it break?" — and the only honest answer is "read the code." Routes, screens, validation, service calls, and tests each hold one piece of the journey. No single document holds all of it. The diagrams that try are stale within a sprint. Existing tools do not close this gap. Call graphs bury the product in every function. Hand-drawn flow charts read well, but they carry no proof, so nobody trusts them after the code moves on. The WebMCP Challenge gave me a reason to try a different shape: let an agent read the repository through a small, safe set of browser tools, propose a visual flow, and make a person approve that proposal before it becomes the shared picture. The agent does the reading. The human keeps the authority. What it does You connect a public GitHub repository or a local folder. AppStory builds a file index and shows what is approved to read and what is excluded. Connecting a repo is not the same as letting an agent read it. You grant a separate consent before any source text can leave the page. A WebMCP agent then searches the approved index, reads bounded source ranges, submits an analysis proposal, and marks it ready for review. You inspect every node — score, factors, cited lines — and every connection's score, then accept or discard the whole proposal. The accepted flow appears on one canvas and in a keyboard-accessible outline. Expand a screen to see its technical steps. Open the evidence. Review possible gaps. Every node and connection carries indexed evidence, evidence factors, and an AI confidence estimate. On GitHub, evidence links pin to the analyzed commit. Local folders use a content fingerprint instead of a blob URL. AppStory has no backend, never executes repository code, and never renders source as active HTML. How I built it Stack. Vite, React 19, and TypeScript for the single-page app. tldraw for the canvas. use-webmcp-tool to register tools on document.modelContext . oxlint and vitest for the quality gate. Cloudflare Workers for hosting, with a small worker that stamps security headers on every response. The canvas is a pure projection. This was the key architecture decision. The canvas holds nothing a reader can change. The source of truth is a plain data structure — the accepted analysis — and a single function, proposalToWorld , projects it into tldraw shapes. On every load the app throws away the old canvas and rebuilds it from that data: // App.tsx — onReady if (saved.acceptedAnalysis.nodes.length > 0) { applyWorld( ed, proposalToWorld(saved.acceptedAnalysis, saved.projectName, undefined, new Set()), ); window.setTimeout(() => ed.zoomToFit(), 0); } Persisting a tldraw snapshot instead would let a stale layout survive a code change. Rebuilding from data every time removed a whole class of bug. Six WebMCP tools, split by trust. Tool Purpose get_project_state Read repository, consent, proposal, and accepted-analysis state search_repository_index Search approved paths. No source text. read_repository_source Read one approved range and create a Read Record get_analysis_state Read a compact index of graph items submit_analysis_batch Add one validated transactional batch to the draft finalize_analysis_proposal Mark the draft ready for human review Read tools use readOnlyHint . Every tool that returns repository or graph text uses untrustedContentHint , because that text was written by a repository author or by the agent, not by me. Finalizing a proposal does not return that text, so it does not carry the hint. A batch cannot land until its evidence ranges were actually read in this session. That keeps the proposal tied to visible Read Records, not to paths the agent never opened. Confidence as a formula, not a vibe. Each fact carries evidence references and evidence factors. AppStory reduces them to one raw score. In words: source-code evidence is worth 30, a test is worth 10, documentation is worth 5, a screen capture is worth 10. Factors then add or subtract — a strong screen implementation is a big plus, a strong conflict is a big minus. The sum is rounded, then clipped to 0–100. $$ \text{score} = \operatorname{clip} {[0,100]}\left( \operatorname{round}\left( \sum {j \in \text{evidence}} e(\text{src} j) + \sum {i \in \text{factors}} w(k_i)\,m(s_i) \right) \right) $$ where $e(\cdot)$ weights an evidence reference by its source (source code $30$, test $10$, docs $5$, screen capture $10$), $w(k_i)$ weights the factor kind, and $m(s_i)$ scales by factor strength. Two rules then override the number. A fact with no traceable evidence is forced to $0$. A score that would look Confirmed is capped at $79$ if there is no direct source line, or if there is a strong conflict: $$ \text{score} \leftarrow 79 \quad \text{if } \text{score} \ge 80 \ \wedge \ \big(\lnot\text{direct source evidence} \ \vee \ \text{strong conflict}\big) $$ $$ \text{label} = \begin{cases} \textbf{Confirmed} & \text{score} \ge 80 \ \textbf{Inferred} & 40 \le \text{score} < 80 \ \textbf{Unknown} & \text{score} < 40 \ \text{or the fact is not traceable} \end{cases} $$ Confidence describes evidence quality, never business impact. Those two ideas stay on separate controls. Defense in depth for secrets. In local-folder mode a weak filter leaks a developer's real credentials, so exclusion runs in layers: Secret and dependency patterns are checked on every path segment, not just the filename. Segments are NFC-normalized and stripped of zero-width characters first. A content scan backs up the name filter. A file whose text matches a private-key block, a known token prefix, or a quoted credential assignment is blocked even when the name looked safe. Imported Project Files are re-validated for path traversal. The Markdown export degrades a bad evidence link to plain text instead of throwing. Every response carries Origin-Agent-Cluster , Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) , X-Content-Type-Options , Referrer-Policy , and X-Frame-Options — the same five headers in all four host configs (Cloudflare Workers, public/_headers , Netlify, and Vercel). Challenges I ran into Treating the agent's output as hostile. The natural instinct is to trust a tool result. Here I could not. A repository path, a source excerpt, and the agent's own proposed titles are all free text from outside my trust boundary. Every batch is validated as one transaction: an invalid evidence reference, node kind, endpoint, identity, or duplicate rejects the whole batch and changes nothing. Getting that all-or-nothing behavior right, with clear messages, took more test cases than the feature code. Keeping the proposal separate from the accepted graph. submit_analysis_batch and finalize_analysis_proposal never touch what is on the canvas. Finalization only marks a draft ready. Only a human click accepts it. Modeling two parallel analysis states — draft and accepted — and diffing them for the review screen (added, changed, possibly removed) was the hardest state-management work in the project. The progressive graph. A fully expanded graph hides the product journey in technical noise. Separate per-flow graphs hide the screens that flows share. The answer was one graph that starts as a flow overview and expands a screen into its technical steps in place, on request. Layout had to stay stable as nodes appeared and disappeared. WebMCP is still arriving. No shipping browser exposes document.modelContext without a flag or an origin-trial token. Unit tests cover indexing, consent gates, transactional batches, and the canvas projection. Native WebMCP still needs a person to flip a flag or register an origin trial. The status chip polls for fifteen seconds after mount, because a browser extension can inject the API after the page loads, and a one-shot check would leave the chip wrongly stuck on unavailable. Accessibility parity. The canvas cannot be the only way in. The keyboard outline renders from the same accepted analysis data: evidence factors, AI reasons, connections, read records, and the gap-review controls. On GitHub, those evidence links are pinned to the analyzed commit. What I learned Make the visual layer disposable. When the canvas is a pure projection of plain data, a redesign is a new projection function, and reload bugs disappear. Trust boundaries belong in the type system. Naming a value untrusted — in a hint, a type, a validator — changes how you write every function that touches it. A human-in-the-loop step is a feature, not a delay. The review screen is where a mixed team actually builds a shared understa

title: Arrastra Relay
pitch: AI agents are replaceable. Their work shouldn’t be. Arrastra Relay preserves every decision, proof, and handoff so teams can move faster without losing trust.
about_excerpt: AI agents are replaceable. Their work shouldn’t be. Arrastra Relay preserves every decision, proof, and handoff so teams can move faster without losing trust. Like Comment Story Updates The problem AI agents are replaceable. Their work shouldn’t be. Long-running agent work breaks at the handoff. When a task moves to a new conversation, model, provider, or person, the successor usually receives a summary. What it often loses is the authoritative state, supporting evidence, governing policy, and precise definition of done. That gap creates two expensive failure modes: silent drift and confident false completion. Arrastra Relay is a trust layer for agent workflows. Agents can investigate, hand off, and resume work, but the application—not the model—owns the state, the rules, and the authority to declare the job complete. What it does We built a synthetic checkout incident to demonstrate the complete trust chain, including the moment an agent tries to close the incident too early. A human establishes one non-negotiable closure rule: the checkout must be tested after rollback. An investigator agent calls read_incident to receive the authoritative state, current revision, evidence, and handoff contract. It calls submit_handoff with canonical structured data bound to the source-set hash and evidence identifiers. A successor context calls read_handoff and receives the retained artifact, remaining requirements, application receipt, and predecessor summary clearly labeled as untrusted. If the successor attempts to close the incident early, the application returns VERIFICATION_REQUIRED without advancing the revision. run_verification performs the application-owned synthetic checkout and issues a verification receipt. submit_resolution can then bind the handoff, verification receipt, evidence, and final artifact into a committed revision. The human can inspect or export the complete application-owned audit record. The arrastra visualization is not decorative animation. Seven visual beats are driven by real application events; the eighth occurs when the human opens the audit view. If the underlying workflow does not advance, neither does the mill. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP turns Arrastra Relay from a dashboard into an agent-native application. The page exposes exactly five semantic tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : read_incident submit_handoff read_handoff run_verification submit_resolution The human and the agent operate against the same authoritative application state, but they have different responsibilities. The human can inspect policy, evidence, status, receipts, and history. The agent receives structured tools for performing the workflow. The mutation sequence is intentionally not duplicated with manual buttons. A person cannot impersonate the agent path simply to make the demo advance. All five tools remain registered throughout the session because the refusal is part of the product. An early resolution attempt must reach the application so the application can reject it, preserve the failed attempt, and return the exact corrective action required. Agents also carry forward application-issued source, evidence, and receipt identifiers. They do not invent the hashes or decide whether the evidence is sufficient. Human-agent experience The human sets the rule and retains visibility into every consequential transition. The agent receives structured contracts, current-revision guidance, and actionable errors instead of guessing through a mouse-oriented interface. The application arbitrates between them. A rejected closure attempt becomes evidence that the gate worked. A successful resolution becomes a durable receipt tied to the evidence chain—not another unsupported statement that the task is “done.” Implementation The architecture is intentionally narrow enough to understand and audit: ChatGPT Sites serves the public Worker and static client. D1 stores an independent incident record for each visitor session while sharing that record across the visitor’s browser and conversation contexts. The same deterministic domain and service layer runs locally and in the hosted Worker. Revision checks provide compare-and-swap protection against stale writes. Submitted JSON is parsed, structurally validated, canonicalized, hashed, and retained with explicit evidence identifiers. Predecessor prose is labeled and handled as untrusted data. It never controls the completion gate. The UI, choreography, receipts, and audit table are all derived from application state. What makes it different Agent handoffs are usually treated as context transfer. Arrastra Relay treats them as continuity of authority. A successor receives more than the previous agent’s explanation. It inherits the current state, retained evidence, unresolved obligations, and application-issued receipts—without inheriting the predecessor’s right to be believed. Incident response is the first use case because the cost of a false “done” is easy to see. The same pattern can support other completion-sensitive workflows where teams want the speed of agents without allowing model confidence to become operational truth. Arrastra Relay is not another memory layer or a better summary. It is an application-level control layer for deciding when agent work has actually satisfied the rules. What we learned Trust does not come from a stronger model or a more persuasive handoff. It comes from placing authority at the correct layer. WebMCP callbacks do not establish trustworthy model identity. Hashes can bind an artifact to a record, but they cannot prove that an external-world claim is true. The prototype therefore makes narrow, testable claims: Revisions prevent stale writes. Canonicalization binds retained artifacts to stable hashes. Evidence identifiers preserve the application’s evidence chain. The verification receipt proves that the application ran its defined check. Only the application can advance the incident to resolved. Arrastra Relay does not claim that a hash makes an agent truthful. It demonstrates how an application can keep unsupported confidence from becoming committed state. How we used AI We used AI broadly, but not blindly. OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT, Anthropic Claude, selected NVIDIA-hosted and OpenRouter-hosted models contributed to concept exploration, adversarial threat modeling, test-oracle design, implementation review, and edge-case analysis. Meta AI produced the final entrant-directed interface image, and ElevenLabs provided the Adam narration voiceover. Every outside-model result was treated as a proposal. Claims, code, diffs, and tests were independently checked before adoption. How we used Codex Codex was the primary engineering and verification environment. It reconciled the challenge rules, maintained the project’s decision and assistance ledgers, implemented and reviewed the WebMCP and D1 application, ran the 16-test suite, exercised the complete reject-verify-resolve workflow in a WebMCP-capable browser, verified hosted state and logs, froze the rc3 release candidate, deployed the exact build, and published the matching source tree. Key features Five working WebMCP tools with strict input schemas and bounded outputs. Application-authoritative state shared across contexts within one visitor session. Evidence-linked, canonical structured handoffs. Revision checks and stale-write rejection. Visible rejection of premature completion. Application-owned verification receipts. Evidence-gated final commits. Untrusted predecessor-summary containment. Seven event-driven workflow beats, one human audit beat, and an exportable audit record. title: Ask, Don't Take
pitch: An agent can ask this page for a new capability. Only you can grant it. It can ask about your data, but the tool returns the answer, not the dataset. WebMCP with a human in the middle.
about_excerpt: An agent can ask this page for a new capability. Only you can grant it. It can ask about your data, but the tool returns the answer, not the dataset. WebMCP with a human in the middle. Like Comment Story Updates An agent can ask. Only the page owner can grant. One answer went to the agent. Twenty-eight rows stayed on the page - with a receipt saying so. The agent can propose a new data source. It cannot create one. The banner waits for the page owner. Rejected. No backend action occurred - no fetch, no compute, no cost. Approved. The source is being created - a few seconds, in the same conversation. A tool that did not exist a minute ago, now in the agent's toolbox. Created after human approval. Not a claim: the source, the records consulted, the model that computed the answer, and backend verification. ChatGPT calling ask_data_source in its in-app browser. The page shows every argument as it happens. Ask-only by default: the agent may ask questions, but the capability is not a directly callable tool. Switched to direct, the same sources become fetchable. The page owner decides, per source. The same registry, published as an A2A v1.0 Agent Card - discoverable by agents that never open a browser. scripts/acceptance.sh asserts the boundary against the live deployment, including that the dataset was not returned through WebMCP. Inspiration Agent protocols assume every company will build and host an agent. Most won't. When agents show up, most of the web will still be ordinary websites - full of things worth asking about, with no way to be asked and no way to say no. Why WebMCP fits this: a boundary between what an agent can ask and what it can take only exists when the page has an owner. Backend MCP is server-to-server with nobody watching, and its tool list is fixed config. WebMCP is different because a person is already there. What it does The agent asks. You grant. The agent can call propose_data_source(url, description) . It doesn't fetch anything. It puts an approval banner on the page and stops. You read it and click Approve. Konect4AI turns the URL into a structured API, the page refreshes its capability list, and the new tool shows up in the agent's toolbox - same conversation, no reload. Click Reject and nothing runs. The agent asks. It doesn't get the data. ask_data_source(jobId, question) is answered by my own model, using my own API key. The tool returns the answer. The rows behind it are shown to me, in the panel next to it, and stripped before the agent sees anything. The page shows this split: SENT TO AGENT - the question and one answer. NOT RETURNED THROUGH WEBMCP - the rows the answer came from, with a receipt: source, records consulted, which model computed it, backend verification. This is a boundary on what the tool returns. It is not browser-level isolation, and the page says so. I'd rather claim something smaller and have it be true. You decide per source what an agent can do. Every source has an access mode. ASK-ONLY (default) means the agent can ask questions but the capability isn't registered as a callable tool. DIRECT means it is. Flipping it re-registers the toolset right away. I added this after watching ChatGPT do the obvious thing: given both a bounded ask tool and an unbounded fetch tool, it used the fetch tool. People and agents use the same tools in the same place. There's an ask row under the two panels. It calls the same endpoint the agent calls and lands in the same history, labeled human instead of webmcp . And the same registry works for agents that never open a browser. A small A2A adapter publishes an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json , built live from the same registry. A site I connected ten minutes ago is discoverable by an external agent - without anyone building an agent for it. How we built it The tools aren't mocks. Each one runs on Konect4AI, a production system that turns a URL into a structured, scheduled, queryable API. POST /api/v1/scraping/requests - creates a capability, behind approval GET /api/v1/scraping/jobs - the tool-to-job mapping POST /api/byok/ask - the answer path that keeps the data server-side POST /mcp/{key} - existing MCP capabilities, turned into WebMCP tools GET /generated/{id} - the rows shown to me, never to the agent Registration handles the spec moving: document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext , a proper CallToolResult , and the spec's AbortSignal passed through to the backend fetch, so cancelling an agent actually cancels the work. scripts/acceptance.sh runs 18 checks against the live deployment, including the boundary itself: the page gets the rows, the receipt says rawRowsReturnedThroughWebMCP: false , an unknown jobId is rejected with a list of what's actually available, and no credential shows up in any public response. Challenges we ran into An agent takes the shortest path you leave open. Twice. First it called the unbounded fetch tool instead of the ask tool. Then, blocked, it read the source URL out of a tool description and went to fetch the data itself. I removed source URLs from agent-visible descriptions and made ask-only the default. Both. fixes came from watching a real agent, not from thinking about one. My own robots.txt check blocked one of my proposals. I approved a source and got back robots_disallowed . GitHub disallows /*/*/commits/ under User-agent: * , which covered three sources I was already using. I moved them to the public API. Consent isn't only about what an agent takes from a page. It's about what the page takes from the web. Creating a capability costs real compute. A public URL that lets any visitor trigger paid fetching is a liability. Instead of removing it, I put a human in front of it - which turned out to be the design. Accomplishments that we're proud of The boundary is checkable, not just claimed. A judge doesn't have to believe the description: the receipt is on the page, and the acceptance script tests it against the live deployment. I shipped against a moving spec and kept the claims small enough to survive it. WebMCP moved from navigator to document ; A2A moved from v0.2.5 to v1.0 with renamed methods. The app supports both WebMCP locations, and the README names the exact A2A subset implemented and lists what isn't. Every tool runs on a production system. The earthquake count is different every time, because the data is live. What we learned The interesting part of WebMCP isn't that a page can expose tools. It's that the page has an owner and the visiting agent doesn't. Most of the design questions come from that, and most of the answers are about holding back rather than adding capability. What's next for Ask, Don't Take The spec already lets a page expose tools to specific other origins ( exposedTo ) and discover theirs ( getTools({fromOrigins}) ), within one page tree and behind the tools Permissions Policy. That would make cooperating sites into each other's tools, with the human still holding the session. After that: per-tool consent scopes, an exportable approval log, and revoking a tool mid-conversation so the agent watches it disappear. Built With a2a byok codex hackathon json-rpc konect4ai model-context-protocol next.js node.js openai react typescript vercel webmcp Try it out konect4ai-webmcp.vercel.app github.com konect4ai-webmcp.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Sole author. Konect4AI, the backend this runs on, is my product. I designed, tested and shipped everything in this repository - the approval flow, the return boundary, the A2A adapter, and every data source. Both boundary fixes came from watching a real agent get around an earlier version. I used Codex for implementation and Claude for review, under my direction. title: Astrail: AI-native trip planner powered by WebMCP
pitch: Astrail turns the Instagram Reels you save into a routed trip on a live 3D map, and you build and edit the whole thing by talking to ChatGPT. The WebMCP tools run inside the page, not on a server.
about_excerpt: Astrail turns the Instagram Reels you save into a routed trip on a live 3D map, and you build and edit the whole thing by talking to ChatGPT. The WebMCP tools run inside the page, not on a server. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Four Reel links pasted into ChatGPT. One WebMCP tool saves them and starts extraction while the library fills in beside it. The run narrated stage by stage. Preferences recalled from memory, places verified, and a missing forecast reported rather than faked. Adding a stop by asking. The add_place call is visible in ChatGPT, and the new stop is labelled as yours, not borrowed from a Reel. Inspiration Instagram makes it easy to save a Reel about somewhere you want to go, then gives you nothing to do with it. Our own folders had about a hundred places across nine countries. When the dates finally got booked, the fastest route from that folder to a real itinerary was still twenty browser tabs, so we never opened it and planned off search results instead. So we built the conversion. Paste Reel links and a multi-agent pipeline on the OpenAI Agents SDK pulls the places out of the captions, verifies each one exists, checks weather and routes, and groups them into days by geography. Anything that will not verify gets dropped. It takes 60 to 180 seconds. Then we showed it to people and got this back: "It's unclear how to navigate the website, where to click, how to choose the reels, how to start generating a trip." We had spent a sprint treating that as a copy problem. It was not. The tool was not hard to understand, it was hard to operate, and we could either keep redesigning buttons or remove the need to find them. That is what took us to WebMCP. What it does Astrail turns saved Instagram Reels into a routed trip on a live 3D map, and you drive it by talking to ChatGPT. Say "save these reels" and paste some links; it saves them and starts pulling places out. Say "plan me two days in Osaka from those" and it shows an approval card with the cost, runs the pipeline, narrates each stage, and hands back a routed map. Say "add Tokyo Disneyland to day 2" and it asks you on the page, finds the place, adds it, and redraws the route. Ask why a stop is on your trip and you get one of three answers: the caption quote from the Reel it came from with a link to that Reel, Astrail's reasoning where it suggested the stop, or a note saying you asked for it. Where we cannot source a fact, like opening hours, the space stays empty. It also remembers how you travel. Tell it once and the next trip recalls it, names what it remembered on the card, and still asks before spending anything. None of that is the agent working alone. It plans, you approve. It offers what it remembered, you can override it. Before WebMCP those two halves could not meet: you could read the itinerary but not change it, and an agent could describe your trip but never touch it. How we built it Seventeen tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() , in two scopes. Fourteen in the signed-in app shell, three more only while a trip map is mounted, and six that work with no account on a public sample trail. The important part is where they run. A backend MCP server can describe a trip. Only WebMCP can move the map the person is looking at. Because execute() runs in the page, a tool already has the loaded trip, the session, and the same React state setters a click uses. Ask for day 2 and the page's own showDay runs, so the camera flies and the day chip lights up as if you had clicked. The agent inherits our security model instead of bringing its own. Reads run under the same row-level security a human gets, no access token crosses the tool boundary, and every edit to your trip stops for an approval card on the page rather than a question in chat. Tools address stops by pin number, so "move stop 7 to day 3" works and no UUID ever reaches the agent. Reel captions are text an attacker can write, so every tool whose output can carry one is annotated untrustedContentHint , and the extraction agents run behind input_guardrail tripwires. We also had a second model reviewing. Every plan and diff went to Codex before it landed, and it caught things we missed, including a bug inside a fix we thought was already correct. Stack: Next.js 15, React 19 and Mapbox GL on Vercel; FastAPI on Render; Supabase; the OpenAI Agents SDK; mem0; Apify. What we added during the submission period Astrail existed before 25 August, as a form. You pasted Reel links, waited, and got back an itinerary you could read but could not change. Everything in frontend/lib/webmcp/ was written on or after 26 August: the seventeen tools, the registry behind them, their contract tests, the on-page approval cards, the agent activity rail and the WebMCP status chip. So were the five owner-checked FastAPI edit endpoints they call, because until then the itinerary was immutable at every layer, with no endpoint, no frontend mutation and row-level security that was SELECT-only. Two other things were built in the window: the map was rebuilt so a stop that came from a Reel carries that Reel's own cover frame in its pin and links back to the Reel, and /app/trip/demo is new, a finished sample trail that opens signed out with six of the seventeen tools so the app can be judged without an account. The memory engine is older. It was built between 7 July and 2 August and we do not claim it as challenge work. What is new is that an agent can reach it, and the reason it could not is the first thing under Challenges below. The dated, commit-by-commit split is in docs/webmcp/WHATS-NEW.md . Challenges we ran into The worst one was a flaw in our own product that only showed up once an agent was driving. Astrail looks up what it remembers about you only when the preferences box arrives empty, on the logic that what you typed today beats what you said three trips ago. It saves a new memory only when that box arrives full. Those conditions never overlap. So an agent leaving the field blank could recall forever and never teach it anything, and the manual form, which pre-fills that box from your profile, was quietly switching recall off on the other path. Nobody had noticed because no path had exercised both halves. Three changes fixed it: the planning tool asks how you travel when it has nothing stored, the card names what it remembered before you approve, and a new tool reads the store back. Chrome's use-webmcp-tool hook cost us a day. It never catches the promise registerTool returns, and since aborting the signal is how a tool unregisters, every navigation threw an unhandled AbortError across the app. We could not patch it from outside, because registerTool is a non-writable property of a native interface, so we wrote our own. About 144 lines. Making an agent's action feel like your own took longer than expected. Early versions had a tool call an API and then hope the page noticed, which is a second rendering path, and those drift. Now a mutation will not resolve until the UI has caught up. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP fixed the thing users actually complained about, which was the whole point of trying it. Getting Reels in used to be copy, switch tab, paste, repeat, then find a separate button to start extraction. Now you paste four links in one message. A finished trip used to be frozen at every layer, with no endpoint and no frontend mutation. Now five tools edit it, each behind an approval card. Beyond that, nothing reaches the map unattributed, and a contract test fails if our own copy ever promises a caption quote for a stop that has none, because the false version of that sentence reads better than the true one. Our tests check the README's tool table against the registry too, so a stale claim goes red rather than shipping. What we learned None of us had used WebMCP before this. It was announced, we read the spec, and started. It is a DOM API, not a server. We spent the first evening looking for the deployment story before realising there is not one. Your tools ship with your JavaScript. Where you register matters as much as what you register. App shell versus trip page is the difference between a tool that always exists and one that appears only when there is something for it to act on. The description field does more work than the code behind it. It is the only place to teach an agent when to call something, and it is captured at registration, so it cannot say anything dynamic. We rewrote ours constantly. And the page cannot talk back. When someone clicks a pin, the agent has no idea. That asymmetry shaped more of the design than we expected. What's next for Astrail Group trips. Nobody plans a holiday alone and right now Astrail assumes you do. Several people on one trip, each with their own agent, editing the same map.
