title: Auricle
pitch: A climate dashboard that builds itself from your questions through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A climate dashboard that builds itself from your questions through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Data-rich websites make people do the mechanical work of understanding them: find the right chart, decode its visual grammar, hunt through tooltips, compare distant points, and repeat the process whenever the question changes. General-purpose agents can try to interpret screenshots, but pixels are an unreliable source for exact figures, units, and provenance. Exporting the data into another tool removes it from the page where its context and visual evidence live. This is especially costly for people who cannot rely on charts visually. A screen reader can traverse a table row by row, but a chart often collapses to “image.” The underlying problem is broader, though: conventional dashboards present answers chosen by their designers instead of letting each person interrogate the underlying evidence directly. Auricle opens with this gap in plain sight: 2,026 rows. Zero answers. Four real climate datasets are available as semantic tables, but no dashboard or on-page chatbot is present. Solution Auricle turns the webpage itself into an interviewable climate instrument. The page exposes WebMCP tools backed by its own data. A user asks through their browser agent; the agent calls the page's tools; Auricle computes an exact, source-attributed answer and mirrors the result into the shared page. Ask “Show me warming over time” and the page creates a NASA temperature chart. That action also registers the chart's five-tool family at runtime. Ask “When was the hottest year?” and Auricle answers +1.28 °C in 2024 while highlighting the point in gold. Ask “Play the century as sound” and it sonifies 146 years as a rising tone with a peak cue. Ask for warming stripes and the same data appears in a second, queryable form. The result is not a chatbot bolted onto a dashboard. The browser agent supplies the conversation; the site supplies authoritative tools, data, visual state, speech-ready answers, and sonification. Every chart on the screen exists because somebody asked for it. Why This Matters Auricle demonstrates a new interaction model for the agentic web: people and agents compose and interrogate a live dashboard together without exporting data or guessing at pixels. The page remains the source of truth, the human directs the inquiry, and everyone in the session shares one evolving surface. For blind and low-vision users, page-owned tools can replace pixel interpretation with exact, source-backed spoken answers and sonification. For everyone else, the same system makes complex evidence faster to explore and easier to verify. Accessibility is therefore a demanding proof case for a broadly useful product—not the boundary of Auricle's audience. The reusable contribution is an agent-accessibility grammar: Orient the agent before asking it to act. Make the tool surface follow the user's focus. Return narratable answers with figures, units, and provenance. Mirror every agent action into the visible and accessible page state. Treat non-visual encodings such as sound as first-class capabilities. This pattern can extend beyond climate data to finance, health, public policy, and any data-rich site where fixed dashboards or visual-only answers limit exploration. Key Features Dashboard by conversation: the initial publication has no charts; create_view commissions each requested view. Dynamic WebMCP surface: five global tools exist at boot, while dataset-specific families register, change with focus, and unregister when their final view is removed—21 tools across the complete experience. Exact page-owned answers: queries run against baked NASA, Our World in Data, and NOAA data, with figure, unit, and source in every narrated return. Shared visual evidence: tool calls create views, highlight points and ranges, and leave a provenance footnote on the page. Accessible HTML foundation: semantic landmarks, real data tables, chart labels, keyboard-operable controls, reduced-motion support, and a visually hidden aria-live answer log. Sonification: time series become a roughly three-second pitch sweep with a distinct peak cue. Nine visualization forms: line, area, warming stripes, vertical and horizontal bars, share bars, scatter, live, and stat views. Self-describing experience: describe_screen tells a newly arrived agent what is present, focused, available, and possible next. Architecture Auricle is a static Vite + React + TypeScript application deployed on Vercel with no backend. Source datasets are fetched by a keyless script and baked into JSON, so the production experience does not depend on runtime data APIs. A framework-agnostic registry wraps each internal tool definition into the WebMCP document.modelContext.registerTool shape. Five orientation and workspace tools register at page load. When create_view commissions a dataset, an AbortController-scoped family registers for that dataset; focus changes replace the active family, and removing the last view aborts it. The simulated live CO₂ view re-registers its family on each bounded tick so its tool description reflects current session state. Agent calls share one execution path: validate the input, run the page-owned handler, return speech-ready text, emit a mirror event to every relevant view, and append the answer to both the visible provenance trail and hidden aria-live region. Charts are hand-rolled SVG. Known Limitations Accessibility is an important beneficiary and proof case, not a claim that Auricle has completed user validation. The experience was built by sighted developers and has not yet been tested with blind or low-vision users. ChatGPT's built-in browser with Site Tools was the AI agent tested end to end: it discovered Auricle's five global tools, invoked create_view to draw the warming curve, observed five temperature tools register dynamically, and invoked temp-anomaly_describe_trend, whose exact answer Auricle mirrored visibly into the page. Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled and the Model Context Tool Inspector was used only as developer tooling for protocol-level inspection, not as another AI agent. The Mauna Loa “live” movement is a clearly labeled bounded simulation seeded from the latest baked NOAA weekly mean; it is not presented as a real-time NOAA stream. Sonification and warming stripes have established prior art. Auricle's contribution is combining them with exact, queryable WebMCP operations under a reusable agent-interaction and accessibility grammar. title: BenchPilot
pitch: Human evidence. Agent structure. Shared control for safer electronics troubleshooting.
about_excerpt: Human evidence. Agent structure. Shared control for safer electronics troubleshooting. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Hardware troubleshooting often becomes an unstructured stream of chat messages, photos, measurements, guesses, and repeated questions. The person can touch the physical system, but the agent can organize far more context than a person wants to track manually. BenchPilot gives both sides one inspectable workspace without letting the agent pretend it observed the hardware. What it does BenchPilot is a shared diagnostic canvas for safe low-voltage electronics. The human records symptoms and de-energized measurements. The app maps device topology, ranks evidence-linked hypotheses, maintains a safe test plan, preserves an append-only history, and produces a diagnostic report. In a WebMCP-capable browser, BenchPilot registers 12 typed tools over the same live case state. An agent can read the case and canvas, focus visible components, propose safe test steps, record only values explicitly supplied by the human, organize hypothesis updates, draft a cautious plan, and undo its own accepted changes. Every write is visible, attributed, reviewable, and reversible. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the product's collaboration layer, not a decorative integration. A troubleshooting agent needs structured topology, stable entity IDs, evidence provenance, unit and power-state validation, and a safe way to change the same workspace the person sees. Scraping page text cannot reliably provide those guarantees. BenchPilot's WebMCP tools use strict schemas and compact result envelopes. Human and agent actions share one command layer, so validation, revision checks, history, proposals, and undo behave identically from either interface. The site remains fully useful when WebMCP is unavailable. How we built it BenchPilot uses Vinext/Next.js App Router compatibility, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Zod, @xyflow/react, Drizzle migrations, and Cloudflare D1 on OpenAI Sites. A deterministic NEMA 17 seed and rule engine make the flagship journey repeatable without an external LLM or physical hardware. Safety is enforced at the domain boundary: allowlisted test templates, strict type/unit pairs, disconnected-power requirements for resistance, session/case isolation, optimistic revision checks, rate limits, proposal review, actor attribution, and targeted undo. The release gate includes unit tests, WebMCP contract tests, production builds, and desktop/mobile browser journeys. Challenges The hardest design problem was balancing useful agent autonomy with human ownership of physical truth. BenchPilot lets the agent organize and propose while preventing it from silently inventing measurements or replacing canonical wiring. We also kept tool results compact while still returning revision, changed IDs, and a visible verification target. Accomplishments that we're proud of Twelve discoverable WebMCP tools operating on live shared state. A production-verified read, focus, proposal, human accept, and targeted undo loop. Deterministic D1-backed guest sessions with no login or paid API dependency. Unsafe energized resistance writes rejected at the API/domain boundary. Responsive manual fallback, accessible canvas list, and shareable report. Public MIT-licensed source with automated release gates. What we learned The best human-agent interfaces make authority boundaries visible. Structured tools help, but collaboration becomes trustworthy only when users can see why the agent acted, review the exact change, and reverse it without damaging human evidence. WebMCP rewards strong internal state design: stable IDs, provenance, revisions, and narrow commands improve both the agent experience and the manual product. What's next for BenchPilot Next steps include team case sharing, richer but still allowlisted device templates, instrument imports that preserve provenance, image-assisted label capture, and organization-level diagnostic playbooks. The safety boundary will remain deliberately narrow until each new procedure has explicit validation and review behavior. title: Biomech Emcee — Shared 3D Movement Review with WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP-native biomechanics workspace where an agent can interpret, navigate, and annotate the same live movement evidence as the human reviewing it.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native biomechanics workspace where an agent can interpret, navigate, and annotate the same live movement evidence as the human reviewing it. Like Comment Story Updates Screen Capture at Subject 1 WebMCP at work on Subject 2 Elbow Flex Tracking Try the shared review Open the live application in ChatGPT’s in-app browser . Quick-start prompts appears directly below the header with one short example: “Show me the elbow angle when the front foot lands.” 2 more prompts opens a human foot-contact correction and a shared frame-linked note. Use either included session and keep the same chat. These are just examples; use your own words and explore other questions. The demo was recorded in ChatGPT’s in-app browser; native tools were also verified in Chrome for Testing 154. The guide adds no tools or measurements; the review capabilities shown in the video are unchanged. Problem Biomechanics review is visually and technically dense. Evidence is split across source video, a 3D reconstruction, event frames, measurements, definitions, confidence limits, comparisons, and notes. A non-expert may not know which anatomical term to search for; a coach may need to mark a precise moment; and an analyst may need to compare sessions without implying causation. A conventional AI chat has none of the page's live context. It can describe biomechanics in general, but it does not reliably know which session, frame, joint, camera view, overlay, or human correction is on screen. Solution Biomech Emcee turns an offline 3D reconstruction into a shared browser workspace and exposes that workspace through 13 WebMCP tools. Nine read tools give the agent structured access to the active session, phase events, measurements, definitions, confidence, references, and comparison limits. Four write tools let it seek the visible timeline, focus anatomy, change evidence overlays, and pin a note at the frame it describes. That creates a continuous interaction instead of a detached answer. A person can ask, “Show me what elbow flexion means at MER and leave a note.” The agent resolves the ordinary-language request, navigates the application to the evidence, focuses the throwing elbow, and leaves a persistent evidence-linked observation. The application draws the supported geometry; the agent does not invent a diagram. A coach can use the same workspace to review and annotate a precise frame, while a less experienced user can ask the connected GPT model for an explanation at the level they need. The product deliberately acts as a shared instrument rather than an autonomous coach. It refuses kinetic quantities that monocular video cannot establish and does not convert exploratory angles into clinical conclusions. Why This Matters — and Why WebMCP Is Essential Here This is not a generic “read the page and summarize it” integration. The useful state is transient and visual: what the human is inspecting now, which evidence layers are active, and which event the human has corrected. WebMCP gives an external agent a stable, typed interface to that state without forcing Biomech Emcee to embed its own assistant or forcing the agent to guess through screenshots and DOM clicks. The user can bring a compatible agent and model through the in-app browser; the specialist website contributes domain tools and evidence, while the agent contributes language, reasoning, and an explanation shaped to the user's question. The loop works in both directions. Agent writes visibly change the human's 3D workspace, and human event corrections immediately change subsequent agent reads because both use the same browser store. The result is shared evidence with shared control—not two parallel versions of the session. For the implemented pitching workflow, this reduces several kinds of friction: A casual question can become a precise event, joint, view, and supported visual explanation. A specialist can turn the same interaction into a persistent frame-linked review note. A comparison request can retrieve actual session differences while preserving capture and confidence caveats. An unsupported request can return a structured refusal plus the nearest observation the evidence can support, instead of producing a plausible-sounding biomechanical claim. How We Used AI Meta SAM 3D Body reconstructs 3D body landmarks from pitching footage in an offline GPU pipeline. The implemented pitching adapter derives deliberately bounded measurements, event signals, and a partial four-segment peak-order view from the reconstructed landmarks in the browser. WebMCP exposes structured capabilities to an agent. The agent can inspect evidence, explain limits, navigate the viewer, and leave review notes while the human remains the final interpreter. The tool surface contains structured refusals for unsupported quantities such as elbow valgus torque, ground-reaction force, pitch velocity, and injury risk. Demo production only: Kokoro v1.0 ( af_heart ) synthesized the published narration locally; Whisper small.en was used for transcription/caption checks. Neither is an application feature or runtime dependency. The recorded review actions are unchanged; only narration, captions and short title/closing cards were added. The optional Quick-start guide was added after the screen capture. How We Used Codex Codex was used as a critical product and engineering collaborator: auditing the repository and hackathon fit, tracing browser and analysis flows, challenging scientific claims, implementing and testing WebMCP handlers, tightening tool error contracts, adding the human event-correction loop, building reproducible Cloud Run deployment, and keeping the public documentation aligned with what the code actually proves. Each solid milestone was verified and committed separately. Key Features The following features work today in the baseball-pitching reference workflow. Other sports would need their own event taxonomy, measurements, references, and validation. Interactive 3D skeleton viewer with timeline, anatomical camera presets, motion trail, segment frames, axial dial, angle readouts, and landmark-grounded elbow/knee flexion arcs. Nine WebMCP read tools for session context, event and metric inspection, evidence definitions, cautious reference comparisons, and descriptive cross-session differences. Four WebMCP write tools that visibly seek the viewer, focus a joint, toggle an overlay, and pin an annotation in the shared workspace. Human-reviewed event correction: setting foot contact, maximum external rotation, or ball release recomputes dependent analysis and changes subsequent agent reads. Evidence contract shared by UI and tools, including confidence, citations, camera-frame caveats, timebase limitations, and structured refusals. Static public deployment with precomputed sessions; no GPU or backend is needed for judging. What Makes It Distinctive Biomech Emcee uses WebMCP as an interaction architecture, not as an export button or a chat wrapper. The read tools are paired with visible, domain-aware writes; the human can correct evidence that the agent then consumes; and the tool contract encodes what must be refused. The same natural-language surface therefore supports teaching, specialist review, evidence navigation, annotation, and cautious comparison without transferring scientific authority to the language model. Baseball pitching is the working example, not a claim that every sport is already supported. A new sport would require its own events, measurements, references, and validation. What generalizes is the WebMCP pattern: a complex specialist website can expose its live state and safe actions to the agent the user chooses. Architecture movement footage (pitching in the implemented workflow) → offline Python / SAM 3D Body reconstruction → frozen session.json contract → React + Three.js browser workspace ├─ browser-side biomechanics analysis ├─ Zustand live review state └─ 13 document.modelContext WebMCP tools ↕ human + agent share the same visible evidence surface The public build is a Vite application served by nginx on Google Cloud Run. Heavy model inference is offline; session review and WebMCP execution are browser-local. Known Limitations Both bundled sources have documented redistribution terms: Pexels License for delivery-02 and CC BY-SA 4.0 for the attributed, modified Wikimedia derivative in delivery-03 . Monocular reconstruction is camera-frame with an estimated focal length; distances are not metric. The 25 and 29.97 fps demo clips undersample fast arm motion, so event timing and rate-derived observations are bounded rather than treated as laboratory-grade. Only direct two-segment elbow and lead-knee flexion measurements are compared with published ranges. Other measurements are exploratory until their constructs and conventions are validated. The kinematic display is a partial four-segment order, not a complete published five-segment sequence. Event detection is heuristic. Humans can correct events, but a man

title: Classmate
pitch: Paste a lecture. Video, captions, notes, and the board share one page. ChatGPT sits in the sidebar and writes on that desk — seek, highlight, draw — instead of narrating a screenshot.
about_excerpt: Paste a lecture. Video, captions, notes, and the board share one page. ChatGPT sits in the sidebar and writes on that desk — seek, highlight, draw — instead of narrating a screenshot. Like Comment Story Updates Thumbnail We can ask as many doubts as we want through out the lecture and get all of them answered by a single click in our agent with timestamps. Flashcards could be generated. We can even upload our own material and go through the lecture accoring to it. Classmate Paste a YouTube lecture. Video, captions, notes, and the board sit on one page. ChatGPT sits in the sidebar and actually uses that page — seek, highlight, draw — instead of talking about a screenshot. Live: https://classmate-steel.vercel.app/ How to try it This only works if ChatGPT has the page open in its own browser , not Chrome. Open ChatGPT desktop . Use Sol or Terra . Luna has WebMCP off, so skip it. Open ChatGPT’s built-in browser (the in-app one it uses to visit websites). Go to https://classmate-steel.vercel.app/ Paste a YouTube lecture on the page. In the sidebar chat (not the Ask box on the right), type: Study with me. If the header shows a tool count, you’re good. ChatGPT talks in the sidebar. Stuff happens on the page. Chrome still plays the video. Tools just won’t attach. Lost / Got it stay hidden. That’s normal. Ask on the page is not a chat. It pins a question at this timestamp. Talk to ChatGPT in the sidebar. Lost / Got it mark this moment — they only show up when tools are live. What it is ChatGPT is the conversation. The page is the desk. There’s one clock ( LectureEngine ). Video, transcript, slides, notes, and the board all follow playback.t . ChatGPT doesn’t watch the YouTube iframe. It reads what’s happening now , waits a bit, then writes on the desk so you can see it. You paste a lecture, say study with me, and it already knows what to do. The tools carry the instructions. You shouldn’t have to explain the site. Ask / Lost / Got it stay on the page. Next time ChatGPT reads classmate_get_now , the open questions are sitting there. It answers oldest first, next to the question — not only in the sidebar. How I built it Next.js, React, a single LectureEngine , WebMCP tools on the page, YouTube IFrame API, pdf.js, JSZip. Optional Speechmatics, AIMLAPI embeddings, Whisper, image gen. I started from the clock and worked out: Everything on screen comes from engine.now() . No second timeline. Then the tools. Reads tell the model what to do next. If something’s missing (captions, image gen, player), the tool says so instead of making it up. Then loading stuff: YouTube captions, PDF/PPTX, notes, VTT, a timing[] JSON file. Then matching speech to slides/notes — word overlap first, embeddings if you have a key, and anchors when someone pins a slide at a time. Then the desk UI: flip cards, quizzes, chalkboard, diagrams. Dark and quiet on purpose. It waits on video time , not wall-clock time. No screenshot of the iframe. Architecture ChatGPT talks. The page holds state. Tools are the bridge. Bit Where What it does Conversation ChatGPT sidebar (Sol / Terra) Talk. Not the canvas. Tools document.modelContext on the page ChatGPT calls these. Engine LectureEngine in the tab One clock: video, cues, slides, notes, board. Server Next.js routes Captions, metadata, STT token, embeddings, diagrams, Whisper. Flow is simple: ChatGPT calls a tool → execute() hits the engine → it gets JSON back ( now() / snapshot() ), not a picture of YouTube. The page hits /api/youtube/captions and friends when it needs to. What’s in the engine: Store What playback status, t , duration, rate cues[] captions slides[] deck notes[] from files, live, or the agent anchors[] “at this time, this slide” asks[] questions waiting for a reply, oldest first signals[] Lost / Got it board diagrams, cards, quizzes, margin notes That becomes now() , which both the UI and classmate_get_now use. Tools live on the top-level page , not in an iframe. Chrome-only = player, no hands. Fine. The YouTube player reports t and honors seek/play through a nonce so it doesn’t fight the engine. Data structures type Cue = { id, start, end, text } type Slide = { id, index, title, text, html?, imageUrl?, embedding? } type NoteBlock = { id, index, heading, text, t?, origin: "file" | "live" | "agent", embedding? } type Anchor = { id, t, slideId, noteIds?, label? } type DeskAsk = { id, at, text, reply: string | null } type StudentSignal = { id, kind: "confused" | "got_it" | "question" | "bookmark", at, text? } type NowSlice = { sessionId, playback, timecode, transcriptWindow, windowText, activeSlide, slideReason: "anchor" | "text-match" | "semantic" | "none", noteHits: { block, score }[], recentHighlights, recentSignals } If auto-match is messy, pin a slide. That anchor wins later: last t <= playback.t . Asks aren’t a second bot. unansweredAsks is everything still open. classmate_reply needs an askId (or a replies[] batch) so it can’t just answer the last one and ignore the rest. Notes remember where they came from. Change the video, live junk goes away. File notes and agent notes stay. Seek/play are one-shot requests with a nonce so YouTube doesn’t get stuck looping the same command. How the agent is supposed to work The how-to isn’t a paragraph you paste. It’s the description on classmate_get_session , and every read sends back howToStudy + next . Open the URL in ChatGPT’s browser. Tools register. Say Study with me . It calls classmate_get_session . You paste YouTube. Captions go into cues[] . Loop: observe_next (wait ~12s of the video , or Lost / Got it / Ask) then get_now . New idea, they’re lost, or they asked → highlight, pin, draw, cards, reply. On the page. Otherwise stay quiet. observe_next watches playback.t , not setTimeout(12000) . Pause the video, it stops waking. Seek isn’t “12 seconds passed.” Lost / Got it cut in immediately. Cite like [title, slide N, 4:12] . Don’t invent the rest of the lecture. Don’t screenshot YouTube. Captions ChatGPT can’t hear the video. If captions never hit the page, get_now is empty and it starts guessing. YouTube from a Vercel IP is annoying. The watch page lists caption tracks, then the actual fetch comes back blank. This is the fallback order: Step Try If nothing 1 Watch-page timedtext next 2 InnerTube Android player + json3 next 3 iOS / TV player next 4 get-youtube-transcript in the function (PoToken) next 5 empty cues “Listen with the microphone” Android is what usually works in production. The old local script that minted a PoToken in a child process doesn’t ship on Vercel, so the library runs in-process now. Mic is opt-in. You can’t captureStream a YouTube iframe, so we don’t grab the mic on every paste. Matching slides and notes now() just asks: given this second of the lecture, what’s relevant? Take playback.t . Grab cues from about 18s behind to 4s ahead. If there’s an anchor at or before now, that’s the slide. Else overlap the spoken window with slide text. Else embeddings, if you have a key. Same idea for notes: words, nearby timestamps, embeddings. Word overlap is the default so it doesn’t invent a heading like “JavaScript Loops” from a video that never said that. Auto-generated notes were doing that, so I killed them. Empty notes beat wrong notes. Calls I stuck with The page is the desk. If ChatGPT only talks, this is a YouTube tab with extra steps. Writes have to show up on screen. Tools explain the site. classmate_get_session is the playbook. You say one sentence. If we don’t have it, say so. No captions → listen. No image gen → chalkboard SVG. No WebMCP → hide Lost / Got it. Ask isn’t chat. A second box posting to an LLM would hide state. Questions live on the desk until they’re answered, oldest first. Wait on the video, not the clock. Paused shouldn’t keep pinging. A seek isn’t progress. Cards are cards. classmate_make_cards is a flip packet. Quiz is a separate packet. Don’t dump a wall of quiz text. You can export / load a timing[] JSON plus YouTube, mp4, PDF, PPTX, VTT, notes. The engine doesn’t care which door the data came in. What was annoying Captions on Vercel. Worked on my laptop, empty in production. InnerTube Android first, then in-process transcript, then mic. Wanting to screenshot YouTube. Can’t. Cross-origin. Put speech on the page instead. Tools not existing on first paint. We poll document.modelContext until they stick, then show the count. Only the last Ask got answered. First version used .at(-1) . Now it drains the queue. Fake notes. Distill hallucinated titles. Stopped that. YouTube setSize on the docked 16:9 player. Had to tell the adapter, not just CSS. What I learned A better prompt about a website isn’t the fix. The website has to be a tool. If the model’s clock is the chat turn, it’s always in the wrong chapter. If it’s playback.t , highlights start to mean something. If you asked on the page and the answer only exists in the sidebar, that’s two products. Putting replies next to the question is when this started feeling like a desk. S

title: claustrum
pitch: Every WebMCP tool call that would change something is held as a proposal, priced against live routing, until a person releases it. A library plus two demos.
about_excerpt: Every WebMCP tool call that would change something is held as a proposal, priced against live routing, until a person releases it. A library plus two demos. Like Comment Story Updates claustrum InspirationWebMCP lets a page hand tools to an agent. A tool can say it only reads. It has no way to say it destroys. That is not something I found. It is in the spec. Section 6.3.2 admits there is no guarantee a tool's declared intent matches what it actually does, and the example they use is a checkout tool that says it finalises a cart and really buys. Only the site knows what an action will do, so the site has to be the one that says. claustrum is a small library. Register a tool with c.read and it runs. Register it with c.propose and it changes nothing at all. It returns held, plus an id, and the page shows the before and after next to what that action costs right now. In the video I ask an agent to cut my riskiest position in half. It reads the book, checks the price before committing, then proposes selling 90 billion BONK. Sounds sensible. Routing it returns 93,842 dollars on a position marked at 268,000. Two thirds gone to price impact. The same call on a deeper pair costs 0.08 percent. The agent cannot tell those two apart. Asking first can. Refuse it and you type a reason. Ask the agent afterwards what happened and it reads your reason back in your own words. ChatGPT's browser already asks before risky actions. That asks whether you want to proceed. It cannot tell you the number, because the number lives in the site. There is also a button that strips the write tools out mid session. It uses the abort signal from registerTool, which is the only way to remove a tool, since unregisterTool does not exist. Two apps run on the same library so it is not one clever page. A portfolio priced against live Jupiter routing, and a team access console with no money in it, where the cost is counted in what breaks instead of dollars. Chrome 151 differs from the spec in three places I could reproduce. executeTool wants a JSON string where the spec says object. execute never gets the abort signal the spec makes required. getTools hands back inputSchema as a string instead of parsed, so anything reading it sees a tool with no parameters. All three belong in crbug 2021259. Separately, inputSchema is not enforced at execution at all, so every tool here checks its own arguments and refuses in a way an agent can act on. 62 tests. One suite pulls the real functions back out of the shipped HTML and runs them, so the tests cannot drift from what ships. The page checks itself on load and prints what it verified rather than what it assumes. Prices only appear after a round trip, 100 dollars out and back, and anything that drifts more than 15 percent is marked not measured instead of guessed at. Registered for the WebMCP origin trial, so it works in Chrome 149 and up with no flag. I checked that in a clean Brave install with nothing turned on. title: codraw.app feat. humans & ai agents
pitch: Real-time collaborative rooms where humans and AI agents draw together.
about_excerpt: Real-time collaborative rooms where humans and AI agents draw together. Like Comment Story Updates codraw OG features features 2 demo room human dashboard Inspiration codraw.app is an interactive collaborative simple asset drawing app, where humans and agents can build on (humans via a browser, agentically: MCP, WebMCP, Skill+API, via the magic AI wand feature). What it does Open codraw.app with a WebMCP-enabled browser and your agent can: Draw with you, live. Shapes, batch pixels, flood fill, layers, undo — every stroke lands on the shared canvas in real time, next to yours and everyone else's. See before it paints. codraw_read_region returns the actual pixel colors of any area, so the agent works with what's there instead of over it. Move around the app. List rooms, create rooms, open a room, switch between a room's canvases, talk in the room chat. Tools register and unregister as you navigate — the page you're on defines what the agent can do. Play by the room's rules. Untrusted agents in moderated rooms get their work held in a pending queue, and the tool result says so. No special agent backdoor exists. The same tools also work outside the browser: a remote MCP server at codraw.app/mcp with OAuth 2.1 login (the agent acts as your account, with your per-room trust), and a plain HTTP API with a served skill file for curl and CI. One dispatcher handles all three, so the rules are identical everywhere. Every action is attributed. A room's history distinguishes humans, agents, and the in-app AI wand — "🤖 Claude Code acting as @joe", "✦ GLM 5.3 Flash prompted by @joe" — per stroke, per layer. And because every canvas has its own URL ( codraw.app/@you/game/sprites/hero/png exports it, PUT imports), what an agent paints, your build can pull. How we built it Go stdlib server (HTTP + WebSocket + SQLite), Vue 3 frontend. The WebMCP layer is one composable registering navigator.modelContext tools per view. The MCP server replays tool calls through the app's own router — no rule exists twice. OAuth 2.1 (discovery, dynamic client registration, PKCE, introspection) is stdlib-only on our auth service, D3BIT. Challenges we ran into Giving agents sight (the hex-grid read tool); scoping tools to SPA navigation; an OAuth discovery fallback that fetched /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server from the app origin and got HTML back — the app now mirrors the metadata; and keeping tool results honest about moderation instead of pretending success. Accomplishments that we're proud of A human and two kinds of agents; one in the browser via WebMCP, one headless via MCP with OAuth - drawing on the same canvas at the same time, under the same moderation, with every stroke attributed. We also deleted our API keys entirely: agent identity is user identity. What we learned Page-scoped tools beat a global toolbox: the current room is the context, and WebMCP lets the page say so. Honest tool results (moderation status, layer ids, coordinate conventions) matter more than tool count. Agents deserve real auth, not pasted secrets. What's next for codraw.app Sprite animation (layered cels, timeline, GIF export) with tools to build animations frame by frame; a graph view of who — human or agent — touched what; codraw Pro with AI credits. An open source codraw.app that can be run locally as well soon (MCP repo is open source). title: Conspiracy
pitch: A shared mystery corkboard where people and AI agents connect, inspect, and audit evidence together.
about_excerpt: A shared mystery corkboard where people and AI agents connect, inspect, and audit evidence together. Like Comment Story Updates A shared board for human and agent reasoning Visual reasoning spaces work well for people and poorly for agents. A person can glance at a corkboard and understand a suspicious cluster, a directional relationship, or a provisional theory. A browser agent usually sees pixels, coordinates, and brittle labels. Moving the investigation into a chatbot would make it legible to the model, but discard the spatial interface that makes the reasoning useful to the person. Conspiracy gives the person and the agent one living evidence board. People can pin, edit, drag, search, group, connect, discard, restore, and audit clues through a tactile noir interface. Compatible browser agents discover 22 typed WebMCP tools that operate on the same cases, cards, directional strings, semantic regions, trash, viewport, and undo boundary. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP makes the visual workspace understandable as a semantic tool surface instead of a screenshot. Stable evidence IDs, typed directional relationships, strict schemas, provenance, and proposal status let an agent act on what the board means without guessing at screen coordinates. People and agents can now collaborate on the same visible artifact: the person contributes spatial judgment and context, while the agent contributes structured inspection, search, synthesis, and traceable proposals. Every resulting change appears in the interface the person already understands. The mystery is a playful demonstration of a broader pattern that can support research synthesis, incident review, threat modeling, debugging, reporting, and risk analysis. Human judgment remains authoritative Agent-created deductions are deliberately provisional. A proposed string records its direction, relationship type, rationale, confidence, and provenance, then appears visibly on the corkboard for review. The person can inspect why it was suggested, accept it, reject it, or undo it. The resident WIRE detective can inspect, search, audit, and trace the case, then stage a proposed string or semantic group. It cannot edit source evidence, delete clues, accept its own deductions, or manage cases. If hosted inference is unavailable, a deterministic detective keeps the core experience usable. Implementation The React interface and WebMCP tools cross the same WebMCPActions boundary into one canonical local CaseLibrary. Cards, directional threads, semantic regions, freehand strokes, trash, and viewport state are persisted per case in browser local storage. Agent deductions always enter the model as proposed objects. src/webmcp/registerTools.ts defines the shared 22-tool catalog. A stable delegating action facade keeps registered browser tool handles current while React refreshes its handlers. Strict enums, stable IDs, coordinate bounds, color validation, additionalProperties: false, destructive annotations, and untrusted-content hints constrain the surface. WIRE executes seven allowlisted read/proposal operations through that catalog. Its same-origin server route adds request and output caps, rate limiting, timeouts, structured validation, store: false, and pseudonymous safety identifiers. Local attachment bytes, machine paths, and object URLs never enter model requests, exports, or WebMCP results. AI and Codex Codex was the primary build collaborator across implementation, debugging, regression tests, deployment hardening, QA, documentation, and demo editing. Agent-driven QA exposed stale tool handles, overlapping asynchronous registration, duplicate proposals, model prose getting ahead of successful tool calls, deployment-secret formatting, and mobile scrolling problems. Each issue was isolated, fixed, and preserved as a test or QA procedure. Conspiracy also uses the OpenAI Responses API for WIRE. Claude- and Qwen-shaped tool sequences generated from a sanitized public contract were replayed through the registered execution layer to test schema clarity and multi-step flows; these were contract replays, not claims of direct browser integration. The project produced significant learning. I have already begun applying WebMCP patterns to Android Hell and my Drabzin CAD editor, turning the experimental browser API into a professional skill I can bring to future products. Try it Open the live app and choose Open a Case . Confirm WEBMCP BRIDGE LIVE and open the 22-tool workbench. Inspect or search the board, then ask WIRE to propose a useful connection. Review its rationale and use Accept , Reject , or Undo . No account or credentials are required. The sample case and deterministic fallback provide the fastest judge path. title: Conversion Lab
pitch: Make products easier for buying agents to choose. Conversion Lab uses WebMCP to turn verified evidence into tested storefront copy, Shopify update previews and PAUSED OpenAI Ads projections.
about_excerpt: Make products easier for buying agents to choose. Conversion Lab uses WebMCP to turn verified evidence into tested storefront copy, Shopify update previews and PAUSED OpenAI Ads projections. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A product can be right for a shopper and still lose the recommendation. Most commerce pages are written for people, who can infer meaning from photography, brand language and scattered specifications. Buying agents need something more explicit: product facts they can discover, verify and connect to the shopper's actual constraints. That creates a new growth problem for merchants. Optimising the human-facing page is no longer enough. Merchants also need to understand whether an agent can identify the right product, explain why it fits and carry the same approved product truth into organic discovery and paid preparation. Conversion Lab explores that problem as a real merchant workflow. WebMCP supplies the missing interaction layer: the website can expose purpose-built tools to an agent while the merchant and agent work with the same visible page state. The result is more than a chatbot or a generic automation. It is an evidence-led conversion lab for agent-mediated commerce. What it does Conversion Lab begins with a fictional Shopify-style merchant, Fieldwork Supply, and a £159 modular commuter backpack. The generic listing contains too little explicit information for our frozen buyer-intent battery and scores 0/8 . Through ten page-scoped WebMCP tools, an agent can: inspect eight merchant-controlled product and policy facts; audit organic and paid-channel readiness; create an evidence-bound product representation; test it against eight deterministic buyer needs; move the result from 0/8 to 8/8 , with no unsupported claims; stage the exact variant at a visible review checkpoint; publish the approved representation to the demo storefront; prepare a Shopify Admin update preview; generate a locally validated OpenAI product-feed CSV and a PAUSED Ads projection with £0 spend ; export a content-addressed optimisation receipt linking the evidence, evaluation, approval and channel projections; answer a shopper need constraint by constraint and update a bounded shared cart. Approval and reset are deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. The public browser can record a digest-bound demo approval, but the app states clearly that this is not authenticated merchant authority. There is no live Shopify write, Ads upload, campaign activation, checkout or payment path in the public build. How we built it The reference application is built with React 19, TypeScript and Vite and deployed as a credential-free static application on Vercel. The interface contains a merchant growth studio and a shopper view backed by one shared workspace, so WebMCP actions and visible browser state remain consistent. The WebMCP layer registers ten narrowly scoped tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Inputs reject unexpected properties, read-only operations declare their intent, and every result reports what changed, what authority was used and the safest next action. Browsers without WebMCP still receive a useful human interface and an honest fallback message. Under the interface, versioned commerce contracts preserve product identity, evidence provenance, lifecycle state, evaluation results, approval and channel projections. A versioned SHA-256 digest binds the exact product target, commercial snapshot, representation and complete evidence content before publication or export. Inputs are captured as immutable canonical snapshots so caller mutation cannot change an output after verification. The Shopify spine includes a version-pinned Admin GraphQL read adapter, product identity checks and an exact productUpdate preview. The OpenAI Ads spine derives every exported field from the approved product snapshot, validates the product-feed row locally, serialises deterministic CSV and keeps the campaign projection paused. A portable optimisation receipt packages the mutually consistent workflow into content-addressed JSON. We supported the build with unit, contract, infrastructure, adversarial and Playwright browser tests, plus change-aware and complete GitHub Actions gates. Tests cover lifecycle legality, evidence provenance, contradictory shopper constraints, approval substitution, asynchronous mutation, feed-schema boundaries, tool-registration failure and the absence of prohibited external effects. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was preserving useful agent autonomy without quietly widening authority. An agent should be free to inspect, propose, test and explain. It should not be able to turn a readable product ID, a browser click or a provider credential into merchant approval or paid spend. That led us to separate representation approval from future external-effect authorization and to make the demo's current authority limitation visible rather than hiding it behind optimistic language. Product fit created another subtle problem. A keyword match is not a recommendation. A request for a waterproof bag for a 17-inch laptop must not pass because the product is waterproof when the evidence says it fits only a 16-inch device. We changed the shopper evaluator to classify each material constraint as supported, contradicted or unknown and to return an overall match only when every required constraint is supported. Cross-channel consistency was equally demanding. Copy, SKU, price, availability, URLs, brand and evidence all need to belong to the same approved product truth. We moved money to exact GBP minor-unit precision, bound every feed-bearing field to approval and independently recomputed validation results before producing receipts. Finally, WebMCP is not present in every browser environment. We kept the complete merchant workflow usable without it, then ran the deployed application in a WebMCP-enabled ChatGPT browser to verify native discovery of all ten tools and the end-to-end shared-state workflow. Accomplishments that we're proud of A live, repeatable WebMCP product experience rather than a collection of disconnected tool calls. A measurable 0/8 → 8/8 improvement using the same frozen buyer-intent battery and eight verified evidence records. Ten discoverable site tools spanning audit, drafting, evaluation, review, publication, paid preparation, portable proof, shopper fit and cart state. A visible authority boundary: the agent can stage an exact variant but has no approval tool. One digest-bound product truth reused across the demo storefront, Shopify preview, OpenAI Ads projection and optimisation receipt. A deterministic, downloadable CSV and JSON receipt without credentials, activation, spend, checkout or payment. A public Vercel deployment, native ChatGPT WebMCP acceptance run and a comprehensive automated quality gate. We are especially proud that the safety model is part of the product experience. The demo does not merely avoid external effects; it explains which effects are absent, which validations are local and what additional authority a production integration would require. What we learned Agent conversion optimisation is less about generating more persuasive copy and more about organising product truth. The strongest representation is the one whose claims can be traced to current, product-bound evidence and tested against concrete buyer needs. We also learned that WebMCP is most powerful as a collaborative surface. The agent is not operating in a hidden automation layer. It works inside the merchant's live page, over the same evidence, lifecycle and cart state the user can see. Approval, execution and observed outcomes are different claims. Approving a representation does not automatically authorize a Shopify write or an Ads operation. A production system must bind each external effect to the exact channel, destination, payload, limits, budget, expiry and replay policy. Later conversion observations must retain the representation and effect lineage that produced them. Most importantly, Conversion Lab is larger than this website. The website is the first reference host for a reusable optimisation capability. What's next for Conversion Lab The next bounded step is to extract a DOM-free Conversion Lab core and prove that the web application, a TypeScript SDK and a read-only CLI produce equivalent audit, evaluation and receipt-verification results from the same input. From there, we plan to add Shopify OAuth, multi-product ingestion, durable tenant workspaces, authenticated merchant approvals and controlled publication with rollback. OpenAI Ads delivery would follow the same governed model: explicit account authority, feed acceptance, a PAUSED default and separate authorization before activation or spend. The longer-term product is one core delivered through several surfaces: a standalone SaaS workspace, a Shopify embedded app, SDK/API and CLI integrations, MCP/WebMCP adapters and a module for larger age

title: Countersign
pitch: Agent-native invoice review. ChatGPT runs the three-way match, hunts duplicates, highlights the evidence on the scan, and asks. Only your click approves. 13 WebMCP tools, one audit log.
about_excerpt: Agent-native invoice review. ChatGPT runs the three-way match, hunts duplicates, highlights the evidence on the scan, and asks. Only your click approves. 13 WebMCP tools, one audit log. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent highlights the quantity cell on the scan after the match flags line 1: 120 invoiced, 100 received. Agent recommends HOLD. Approve stays disabled until the issue is resolved. The tool call waits for this click. Two-phase countersign: click, 25 s timeout, or abort. Timeout returns pending. Only the human click can approve. 4 queue tools always on, 9 invoice tools while an invoice is open, back to 4 on close. Blue reads, amber writes. Client-only: one registerTool path, Chrome budgets enforced, Zod schemas, clamped JSON, every call audited. One review, hop by hop: tool call → wrapper → domain → UI → request_countersign waits → human click → resolver → agent. One audit log for both sides: agent calls in blue, reviewer clicks in green, with arguments, result, duration. Tools tab: 13 tools, live state, call counts, last input and output, copyable example input for Chrome inspector. Agent comments pinned to a field; the reviewer replies; the agent reads the reply on its next tool call. LF-2026-0942: line 3 not on the PO and its text tells the agent to approve. Match catches it; click still rules. Ten synthetic invoices, one planted fact each, generated deterministically with draw-time bounding boxes. Chrome DevTools > Application > WebMCP: 13 tools registered by the page, 18 calls counted, 0 failed. Inspiration Accounts-payable teams review thousands of invoices a month. The work splits cleanly in two: matching numbers against a purchase order and a goods receipt, which an agent does perfectly and a human hates, and looking at the scanned page to see whether the number the agent read is really the number printed there, which a human does in two seconds and an agent cannot do at all. Today the two halves live in different tools, and an agent that approves a duplicate is a segregation-of-duties failure with a dollar sign on it. Every WebMCP showcase app I found was consumer or commerce: pizza, flights, greeting cards. None had money at stake, a mandatory human sign-off, or an audit trail. Countersign is the control: the agent proposes, the human countersigns, and both are on the record. What it does Countersign is an invoice-review workbench with thirteen WebMCP tools registered in the page. In the ChatGPT desktop browser (or Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag) you say "Work through my review queue" and the agent: lists the queue and opens an invoice on your screen; runs a three-way match against the PO and the goods receipt, line by line, with the vendor's price tolerance and tax arithmetic; searches every other invoice for duplicates ( INV-2291 and 2291 normalize to the same number); checks the vendor profile, including the bank account printed on the document against the one on file; draws a highlight on the scanned page for every number it cites, so you verify it where it is printed; flags typed, severity-rated issues; proposes GL codes for invoices with no PO; posts comments you can reply to; requests your countersign . A card slides in with its recommendation. The tool call waits up to 25 seconds for your click. Only your click can approve. Every tool call and every human click lands in one audit log. Ten synthetic invoices ship with the demo, each with one planted fact: a quantity overbill, a price above tolerance, a duplicate of an approved invoice, a changed bank account under a stamp, a missing PO, a two-cent tax rounding error, and one whose line description tries to instruct the agent to approve it. A scanned invoice table is the worst possible actuation target on the web: dense, tabular, low contrast, and often stamped over. Countersign exposes the extraction and the matching logic as typed tools with JSON Schemas, and it exposes them in the reviewer's page , where the same call that returns a value can also draw the evidence on screen. The tools are state-scoped. Four queue tools are registered for the life of the page. Nine invoice tools appear only while an invoice is open and are unregistered when the workbench returns to empty, so the agent works on the same document the human is looking at and cannot check invoice A while the reviewer looks at B. That is a WebMCP-native idea: the page's UI state is the agent's context. How it creates a better user experience The reviewer never re-types or re-computes. The agent never touches money without a click. Evidence appears where the reviewer is already looking: show_field_evidence draws the highlight on the page image and the Match tab fills in as the agent works. Activity toasts show every call as it happens. The countersign card shows how long the agent has been waiting for the click, highlights an issue's evidence when you hover it, and takes A / H / R / Esc. If the reviewer types a reply in the Comments tab, the agent reads it on its next call. A Tools tab inside the product shows all thirteen tools with live state, call counts, last input and output, and a ready-to-paste example input for anyone driving the tools by hand. With WebMCP the agent and the reviewer share one document, one state, and one audit log. The agent does the forty-line match; the human does the two-second visual check and the decision; the log shows who did what, with arguments and timing. How we built it Imperative WebMCP API only , registered from a client component in the top-level page. One document.modelContext.registerTool(definition, { signal }) call site in lib/webmcp/registry.ts , with a navigator.modelContext fallback for Chrome 149. Zod 4 schemas as the single source of truth : z.toJSONSchema produces the advertised schema, safeParse validates every call, and the wrapper turns errors into sentences that name the recovery step ("Call list_invoices to see valid ids."). Chrome's budgets enforced in code : defineTool throws in development if a name exceeds 30 characters, a description 500, or a parameter description 150; every output is clamped to 1,500 characters and stays valid JSON. Annotations carry readOnlyHint on reads and untrustedContentHint on anything that returns document text. Two-phase countersign : request_countersign creates a pending decision and races the reviewer's click, a 25-second timeout, and the AbortSignal. On timeout it returns pending and the agent polls get_decision . Repeat calls are idempotent. setStatus is typed so it cannot take 'approved' ; the only path that writes it is resolveDecision , and a test scans the source to prove that only the countersign card calls it. Client-only : Next.js 16, React 19, a zustand store persisted to localStorage , Tailwind 4. No server, no login, a Reset button. Deterministic documents : a Python generator (reportlab, PyMuPDF, Pillow) renders each invoice to PDF and PNG and records every field's bounding box at draw time, as page fractions, so highlights land on the ink. 86 vitest tests , including every tool against every invoice under the output budget, countersign idempotency and abort, and the human-only approval scan. Ten eval prompts in evals/scenarios.json with results from live runs in evals/RESULTS.md . Challenges we ran into The agent asked instead of acting. On the first live run GPT-5.6 Terra did the analysis correctly, then asked in chat whether it should flag the issue instead of calling flag_issue , so no card appeared. Descriptions with negative instructions are discouraged, so the fix was positive: the descriptions now say that flagging and requesting a countersign are the normal next step and pay nothing by themselves, and open_invoice returns a review_flow hint. The next whole-queue run was 8 for 8. 1,500 characters is small. Adding the tenth invoice silently pushed the queue listing past the budget and the clamp dropped rows. Queue rows lost three fields and a test now asserts the whole seed queue lists without truncation. Highlights that miss the text. Searching for bounding boxes after rendering was fragile; recording them while drawing, from the font metrics, made them exact. No agent in plain Chrome yet. Judges on the Chrome path drive tools by hand through the inspector's JSON textarea, so the Tools tab builds a valid example input for each tool from whatever is on screen. title: Cursus
pitch: A course planner whose tools refuse, say what a choice closes off two years before it bites, and hold a limit you set against the agent — including when you are the one asking.
about_excerpt: A course planner whose tools refuse, say what a choice closes off two years before it bites, and hold a limit you set against the agent — including when you are the one asking. Like Comment Story Updates Fourteen courses, put there by hand. Term 3 has six credits left, and the page has registered its thirteen tools with the browser. The student asks in their own words, naming no tool: what are my options, and what does each one cost? Both futures in one call. Either choice closes a specialisation — the slot is what costs, not the course. The student draws a line. Anything that would close Graphics is refused from now on, including if they ask for it themselves. A lock beside the track, and a line naming who it binds. Every other rule here belongs to the university. This one belongs to the student. The agent asks for NUM-201. The page refuses, citing the student's own instruction, and names both ways out. The refusal comes back as prose, so the agent reports it rather than retrying. Nothing instructed it to. Every call is an event and the plan is their reduction, so undo is replaying fewer of them. The protection unwinds with the rest. Each description says when to reach for it. That string is the only thing a model has to choose on, so the strings are the product. registerAll, on document.modelContext. No build step, no dependencies, no server: what is in the repository is what is served. The page counts calls by origin and states plainly that it cannot verify the second number. WebMCP gives the handler no caller identity. Apache-2.0, thirteen tools on document.modelContext, and no server behind any of it. Eleven files, no build step and no dependencies. Every import points downward, which is the whole reason the layering is worth drawing. Every tool call is an event, and the plan is their reduction. Refusing, undoing and auditing all fall out of that. Both environments named in the challenge rules, and both make real tool calls. The problem, and who has it A student picks four courses for their third term because those are the ones that fit. Two years later a specialisation they wanted is out of reach — not because anything refused them, but because the one course it needed runs in a single term, and that term filled up. No warning appeared. The cost landed twenty-one months after the decision, and by then it was not a decision any more. An adviser can work this out with the handbook open and twenty minutes. Most students never think to ask, and most advisers have more students than twenty-minute slots. So the calculation that decides which doors stay open is the one nobody performs — not because it is hard to explain, but because it has to be redone from scratch whenever anything changes. A timetable shows what you picked. That is all any timetable shows. What Cursus does Thirteen tools, registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , that do six things a rendered timetable cannot. They refuse. Ask an agent to enrol you in Advanced Calculus and the page says no — naming the missing prerequisites and, crucially, what would unblock them. That last clause changes the agent's behaviour: it stops reporting a failure and starts proposing a fix. In our first end-to-end test it went further and asked permission before applying it. Nothing instructed it to. They answer what the screen cannot. what_this_closes is forward reachability over the prerequisite graph under a credit budget. With terms 1–2 full and six credits left in term 3: Taking NUM-201 closes Graphics and Animation — GEOM-201 only ever runs in term 3, and the term is now full Taking GEOM-201 closes Data and Machine Learning — NUM-201 is required for ML-202 and everything after One slot, two futures, and either choice forecloses the other. They price the way out. Asked whether a specialisation is still possible, the page does not answer "no". It names the blocking course, the rule that stops it, and every way to make room — with what each one costs. In that fixture there are five ways, and every one of them closes another specialisation. They can be undone. Every tool call is an event and the plan is the reduction of those events, so rewinding is the same reducer with a smaller number rather than per-tool inverse logic. The timeline on the page is the log with a cursor. And they hold the student's own limits against the agent. This is the one that runs the other way. Every rule above belongs to the university — a prerequisite, a clash, a credit cap, the same for everyone. protect_track belongs to the person: say "whatever else happens, do not close Graphics" and from then on any course that would close it is refused, including when you ask for it yourself an hour later , and the refusal cites your own instruction rather than the handbook. The planner will not even propose a route through it. A tool surface that only exposes capability lets an agent do whatever the UI could do, faster. One that also carries the user's policy lets them say what they will not have done to their plan , and have it hold while they are not watching. It cost almost nothing to build, because a protection is an event like any other — so undo_to unwinds it with everything else, and no code was written to make that true. And this part is not really about courses. Anyone handing work to an agent has the same question: how do I let it act for me without it doing the one thing I would have vetoed? The usual answer is a prompt, and a prompt is a request. A page that carries the user's policy and enforces it structurally is a different answer — the limit lives with the state it protects, survives the conversation that set it, and applies to whoever asks next, including the same person in a hurry. Course planning is where we could demonstrate it. It is not where it stops. And they can be handed to someone else. share_plan returns a link, and there is no server behind it: the link carries the actions. What makes that more than a persistence trick is what happens when it is opened — every action is replayed through the same tools , so a link edited by hand cannot produce a plan the page would have refused to build, and anything the rules reject is named rather than quietly dropped. The rules are the gate on the way in as well as the way through, because there is no second path into the state. Why this fits WebMCP rather than an API Three reasons, and they are properties of the standard rather than of this domain. The tools act in the user's own session, on the page they are looking at , with no key to provision and no account to link. The plan is theirs, in their tab, and they watch it change. The tools are things the DOM cannot do . If an agent could get the same answer by reading the page and clicking, the tool surface adds nothing. Reachability under a budget is not on the screen. And the interface is prose . execute returns a string the model reads, so the strings are the product. That is why every mutation returns the resulting plan instead of ok — otherwise the agent's picture of the state silently drifts from the page's — and why every refusal carries a remedy. What people and agents can do together here that was hard before A student could always ask an adviser "what am I giving up if I take this?" and an adviser could always work it out, slowly, with the handbook open. What was not possible was asking the page , in the middle of choosing, and having it answer with a number instead of a shrug. And the direction that matters is the other one: the page can say no to the agent, in a way the agent can act on. A tool that refuses with a remedy turns an agent from something that either succeeds or fails into something that negotiates — it repairs the situation and, in our tests, asks before committing. That behaviour was not prompted. It came from the shape of the refusal. Where it was tested Both of the environments named in the challenge rules were tested, and both make real tool calls. Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag and the Inspector extension: an agent chose the tool on its own, was refused, and proposed the fix. That is the gate in docs/GATE.md , and it has no plan, mode or workspace conditions. ChatGPT's in-app browser : the page registers its tools and a model calls them — in Work mode . Outside it, four different phrasings produced no call at all, and confident answers read off our own README instead. Finding that out took an afternoon and is written up in docs/CHATGPT-WORK-MODE.md , including the part a judge most needs: site tools are not available in Enterprise or Edu workspaces , no setting changes it, and nothing on screen says so. On those, use Chrome. The video is recorded in ChatGPT's in-app browser , because that is the environment the rules name first and the one most judges will reach for. How it is built No build step, no dependencies, no server. Plain ES modules on GitHub Pages: what is in the repository is what is served. The rules allow any provider, and with nothing to compile

title: Cutlet
pitch: Small cuts, served fresh. A browser rough-cut editor where the agent reads the transcript, you judge the footage, and the WebMCP tools keep you editing the same visible clip.
about_excerpt: Small cuts, served fresh. A browser rough-cut editor where the agent reads the transcript, you judge the footage, and the WebMCP tools keep you editing the same visible clip. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration Every AI video clipper works the same way: upload, wait, receive highlights, then fix them somewhere else. The model does the judging and the editing, and you get whichever boundaries it computed. I wanted the opposite division of labour. An agent is good at reading a transcript and saying which stretches stand on their own. A human is good at watching the footage and feeling where a cut lands. WebMCP made it possible to put both in the same page, editing the same clip, with the browser keeping both honest about who changed what. A cutlet is a small cut. Small cuts, served fresh. What it does Cutlet is a rough-cut editor for spoken video. It is not a clip finder; no model scores your footage. The page holds the video, a transcript broken into sentences with stable ids, and a rail of clips. The agent reaches all of it through ten WebMCP tools registered on the top-level document. The core loop is anchor and expand : You click the sentence that must survive. The agent reads a window around it and proposes a clip as a range of sentence ids, s0009–s0013 , never floating timestamps. The player runs exactly that range and stops. You drop a line or move an edge. The clip's revision bumps. The agent's next write carries the revision it last saw. Yours is newer, so the write is refused with the real revision in the error. It calls get_editor_state and revises from your edit, not over it. cut_clip c2 keep s0008,s0010,s0011,s0013 → revision 2, 3 pieces, 37s ↓ human drops s0011 in the transcript → revision 5 cut_clip c2 expectedRevision 4 → REFUSED "it is now 5" get_editor_state → sees the real cut The active clip is coloured by who last touched it: blue while it is the agent's proposal, amber the moment you edit it, in the transcript, the timeline and the card. Beyond the loop: "find the best clips in this" makes the agent skim the whole transcript and create one clip per moment, each with a title and a reason. "Cut this to forty seconds" turns a clip into several pieces with gaps, and playback jumps the gaps. Every dropped sentence stays visible, struck through, with a control to put it back. When the recogniser missed a full stop, you select the words you want and make them their own sentence with their own id, so a boundary you can point at becomes a boundary the agent can name. The agent can split too. The agent gets every cut twice: the source transcript, and the sequence as it plays , with each gap marked by what was dropped and how long it ran. That is how it catches a dangling "its conquest" whose antecedent left with the cut. Export re-encodes each piece in the tab with ffmpeg.wasm, so boundaries are frame-accurate rather than keyframe-snapped, joins them, and writes an .srt rebased across the cut. Your video never leaves the tab. The transcript windows the tools return are shared with the agent; nothing else is. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript, CSS Modules. No backend, no UI library, no state library. 45 Node tests run directly against the TypeScript, covering parsing, sentence splitting, selection, reordering and tool registration. Transcript pipeline. Word-level JSON is primary; Whisper, Deepgram and ElevenLabs Scribe all parse, with SRT and VTT as coarse fallbacks. Sentence splitting handles abbreviations, initials, rhetorical pauses and a clause backoff at the length ceiling. Preview is the native <video> element, with the range boundary enforced on requestAnimationFrame , because timeupdate fires at about 4 Hz and visibly overshoots. Export is the single-thread @ffmpeg/core , lazy-loaded on first use. Single-thread means no SharedArrayBuffer , which means no COOP/COEP headers, which is why it deploys to plain static hosting. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool on the top-level document, with an AbortController for teardown. Read tools carry readOnlyHint . The page feature-detects the API and works fully without it; the header pill says whether tools are live, and clicking it lists them from the same table the registration reads, so the two cannot drift. Keyboard. The transcript is a listbox with one tab stop: arrows move the anchor, shift extends it, Enter plays, ⌘-click banks a range. Two recordings ship, both public domain and credited: Kennedy's "We choose to go to the Moon" at Rice, and the Apollo 11 crew interview. Transcripts were made locally; no keys ship in the client. Challenges I ran into WebMCP is one-directional. A page cannot call an agent. There is no "find clips" button because there cannot be one, so the empty state's job is to tell you what to ask. There used to be a lexical "rough pass" fallback for browsers without the API. I removed it: a heuristic dressed as judgement is worse than an empty rail that tells you what to ask. Ids stop being positional the moment you split. Renumbering after a split would silently repoint every later id at its neighbour, and a stale id that resolves to the wrong sentence is worse than one that fails to resolve. So the new half gets a fresh number and nothing after it moves. The agent kept overwriting the human's anchor. preview_clip used to set the selection, so an agent auditioning a range destroyed the very mark it was told to build around. Auditions now have their own state and render dashed, in the agent's blue, beside the anchor. Bugs only testing found. Number(undefined) is NaN , which is not nullish, so search_transcript returned empty context whenever the argument was omitted. A Whisper file's outer segments parsed as "words" and shadowed the real word timings. Deepgram's unpunctuated word beat punctuated_word and broke sentence splitting. Smooth scrollIntoView is silently ignored under reduced motion and in background tabs, so following the playhead just stopped; both now fall back to an instant jump. ffmpeg.wasm under a bundler. It has to be the ESM core, handed over as blob URLs. Otherwise the module worker cannot import it, and the dev server rewrites the path to a 404. What I learned The whole design fell out of one decision: every boundary is a sentence id , because an id means the same thing to both parties and a dragged pixel does not. That is why the sequence timeline is read-only, why sentence splitting exists, and why the revision check works at all. Optimistic concurrency turned out to be the right primitive for a human and an agent sharing one document. What's next More WebMCP hosts as they ship. Word-level trims inside a split. A library format other people can add recordings to without touching code.
