title: NexusCanvas
pitch: An architecture canvas ChatGPT draws on, audits and load-tests through WebMCP. Take a cache offline by hand and it reads the change, reruns the model, and tells you what broke.
about_excerpt: An architecture canvas ChatGPT draws on, audits and load-tests through WebMCP. Take a cache offline by hand and it reads the change, reruns the model, and tells you what broke. Like Comment Story Updates The host doesn't prompt, so the page does Open it in ChatGPT and just ask Every call, args, result, duration Tools appear when the human selects a component The canvas compiles to real YAML The WebMCP surface, listed live Poisson arrivals, bounded queues, true p50/p95/p99 The agent drew this in a single tool call The human broke it, the agent found it The page grades the design, the model can't argue with it The human edits the same state the agent reads Postgres at 110%, 3% errors, p95 1609 ms Inspiration Every time I asked an AI to design a system, I got a picture. It would produce a tidy Mermaid diagram, tell me the design "scales well," and move on. But the diagram was a dead artifact the moment it appeared. If I changed my mind, the conversation and the diagram drifted apart. And the model had no way to check its own claim, it asserted that the architecture held up, because asserting is all a language model can do about a system it cannot run. WebMCP changes what is possible, because the page stops being a canvas the model draws on and becomes a participant. The page can hold the state. The page can do arithmetic the model cannot fake. And critically, I can reach into that same state with a mouse while the agent is working. So I built the thing I actually wanted: a whiteboard that pushes back. The agent proposes an architecture, the browser computes whether it survives contact with load, and when I break something by hand, the agent has to notice. What it does NexusCanvas is a system-architecture canvas that ChatGPT operates directly through 14 base WebMCP tools plus 3 contextual ones. It runs entirely client-side, meaning no backend, no API keys, no account. The agent can build a whole system in one apply_blueprint call, audit it, model load against it, inject outages, and compile it to Docker Compose. But the point is not that the agent draws. The point is what the page does back: It computes what the model cannot fake. An audit engine finds single points of failure, missing caches, insecure protocols and orphaned queues, and returns a letter grade. Two independent load engines report utilisation, error rate and latency percentiles. A Compose generator emits real YAML from the graph. It reads my edits. I take Redis offline by hand in the Inspector. The agent calls get_architecture , sees the outage nobody told it about, reruns the same load, and reports that Postgres went from 36% to 125% utilisation as reads that were being absorbed by the cache fall through to the database. It asks before destroying anything. The host I tested never prompts on destructiveHint , so the page prompts instead, the tool call blocks on a real modal and the agent waits for my click. Clicking Cancel returns a declined result the agent reports honestly. The demo arc is a design review: the agent builds a 17-component e-commerce system, the audit grades it D (51) , we fix it together to A (94) , and then I break the cache to prove the improvement was real. How I built it Static React 18 + TypeScript, React Flow for the canvas, Zustand for shared state, Dagre for layout. Deterministic TypeScript engines for everything that produces a number. Deployed as static files. I wrote the specification before the code, a blueprint, numbered requirements with acceptance criteria, and a tool contract document fixing every tool's description, JSON Schema, annotations and example result. Tool descriptions were then copied into the implementation verbatim , because a tool description is a prompt: it is the only thing the model on the other side reads before deciding whether to call you. The closed-form capacity model walks the graph in topological order, excluding back-edges. For each component, $$C_i = \text{capacityRps}_i \times \text{replicas}_i \times s_i, \qquad s_i = \begin{cases} 0.5 & \text{degraded} \ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ $$u_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{C_i}, \qquad \text{served}_i = \min(\lambda_i, C_i), \qquad \text{dropped}_i = \lambda_i - \text{served}_i$$ Routers split their served traffic by normalised edge weight; services fan out $\text{served} i \times w {ij}$ per edge, so a weight of $0.2$ reads as a 20% cache-miss rate. Latency stretches as a component saturates, capped so the number stays finite: $$\ell_i(u) = \begin{cases} \ell_i & u < 0.5 \[4pt] \dfrac{\ell_i}{1 - \min(u,\,0.9)} & u \geq 0.5 \end{cases}$$ The discrete-event simulator exists because the closed-form model cannot show cascades. It runs a simulated clock over a binary min-heap event queue with Poisson arrivals, exponential interarrival times drawn as $\Delta t = -\ln(U)/\lambda$ , plus per-component concurrency limits, bounded queues, hop timeouts, bounded retries, and upstream workers held while awaiting downstream calls, so connection-pool exhaustion emerges instead of being asserted. It reports true $p_{50}$, $p_{95}$ and $p_{99}$ from completed-request samples. Randomness is seeded by an FNV-1a hash of the graph and scenario, driving a mulberry32 generator threaded explicitly through the run. Same graph, same seed, bit-identical output, which is what makes it testable, and what makes the agent's claims reproducible. 57 tests cover the engines, tool input validation, the WebMCP adapter against host stand-ins, and the demo sequence. Challenges we ran into I did not know what ChatGPT's browser actually did. So before writing a line of app code, I shipped a probe page registering seven deliberately awkward tools and ran it inside the ChatGPT desktop app. It answered questions no specification could: the host exposes document.modelContext but not navigator.modelContext , it accepts content-array results, it picks up tools registered seconds after load, and it waits on a pending promise. That one hour saved the project. The host has no unregisterTool . Calling it throws a TypeError . My whole contextual-tool design assumed tools could appear and disappear with UI state. Rather than pretend, the adapter keeps one stable dispatcher per registration and marks it dormant when its context is gone, excluded from active counts and from get_architecture , and returning a guarded {ok: false, error, hint} if the retained callback is invoked anyway. The Tools panel shows dormant rows honestly instead of claiming a removal that did not happen. My audit was confidently wrong. The first run graded the reference architecture F , flagging the load balancer, API gateway and message queue as single points of failure, all of which ran multiple replicas. A structural chokepoint is not a SPOF if it is replicated. Adding a replicas == 1 precondition took one line and turned an audit a judge would distrust into one that survives scrutiny. Killing the cache made the database less busy. The model routed reads catalog → redis → postgres at a 20% miss rate, so marking Redis down removed 80% of the database's load, the exact opposite of what a cache outage does. The fix is a rule the spec had never stated: a downed cache drops nothing and forwards 100% of its inbound traffic downstream. Postgres went from 110% to 217%, and the demo's most important beat became true. Accomplishments that we're proud of The page disagrees with the model, and the page is right. That is the whole thesis, and it holds: the agent cannot talk its way past an audit grade or a utilisation figure it did not compute. Two independent engines, a one-pass closed-form model and a seeded discrete-event simulator, reach compatible conclusions about the same graph from completely different mathematics. And the honesty of the submission itself. Where the host's behaviour is unverified, the documentation says so rather than rounding up. Where the engines are comparisons under stated assumptions rather than predictions of production, the UI says that too. What we learned A tool description is a prompt. Adding six words to add_component , noting that stateful types default to one replica, was the difference between the agent adding a redundant cache and adding a new single point of failure on camera. Tool granularity decides whether the demo is watchable. Fine-grained tools mean forty round-trips to draw one system. One coarse apply_blueprint call draws it in a single beat. Registration lifecycle is a product concern, not plumbing. Tools that linger after their UI is gone are tools the agent will call when they cannot work. Determinism is a feature, not an implementation detail. It is what lets a person re-run what the agent claimed and get the same answer. A cost estimator, and it is the feature I most want. Right now the page tells you whether a design survives load. It should also tell you what that design costs , because in practice the argument about an architecture is never purely about correctness. title: ONCE — Tell Your Story Once
pitch: One urgent story. Four coordinated services. Every disclosure visible. Every final action yours.
about_excerpt: One urgent story. Four coordinated services. Every disclosure visible. Every final action yours. Like Comment Story Updates The 15-second version One story in. Four services staged. Two schedule conflicts avoided. One unjustified Government ID request blocked. Zero applications sent before approval. ONCE is a working WebMCP demonstration of a better contract between a person, their chosen agent, and essential-service websites. The agent does the coordination; the person keeps the authority. Inspiration People facing one urgent life event often repeat the same painful story across disconnected forms. Each form asks for a slightly different set of personal data, appointments collide, and the person cannot see what an automated helper disclosed. We wanted to show a different web: tell one chosen agent once, let participating services expose precise capabilities, and keep one visible plan and final human authority. This is a documented service-design problem, not only a demo premise. The OECD reports that complex information and cumbersome application procedures contribute to non-take-up of social support. GOV.UK service guidance recommends avoiding repeated questions, collecting only necessary personal information, and explaining the purpose of every field. What it does The working demonstration lets a person tell an agent one urgent story: their home is unsafe, three children need temporary shelter, food and a health check, and the family needs accessible transport within 72 hours. The agent projects that story into reversible, non-sensitive local planning constraints, then coordinates four fictional provider simulations. It checks the simulations' published eligibility rules deterministically, avoids calendar conflicts, identifies the minimum purpose-bound fields for each service, blocks an unjustified Government ID request, and stages one coordinated plan. An outcome rail makes the result immediately inspectable: one story, four staged services, two avoided conflicts, one blocked overreach, and zero applications sent before approval. prepare_assistance_plan returns the same structured evidence to the agent. The agent can prepare and explain. It cannot approve. The person reviews every exact value beside its provider-declared purpose, then approves or rejects the proposal. An unjustified field is shown as withheld without revealing its value. Only after approval does WebMCP expose the consequential commit tool. Approval is fingerprint-bound, expires in five minutes, and can be used once. Synthetic receipts and an audit trail make the result visible. How we used WebMCP We use the Imperative API to register small, state-aware tools for updating planning constraints, reading intent, service discovery, deterministic eligibility, disclosure inspection, audit reading, plan preparation, visible review, and approved commit. Tools use the current standard read-only and untrusted-content annotations. Registrations are cancelled and rebuilt when page state changes, so the update capability disappears after staging and commit_approved_plan is literally absent until the person approves in the page. This is more than controlling buttons. WebMCP supplies a typed collaboration contract between the simulated service network, the agent, and the human. The agent receives concise structured results instead of scraping an interface, while every tool execution updates the human-visible state. The visible buttons remain as a progressive fallback and invoke the same application actions. The chosen agent receives approved planning constraints but never receives the synthetic Government ID or health notes. Provider simulations receive only purpose-approved fields after the person approves the exact proposal. What makes the experience new Today, agents often automate one website at a time and maximize data collection for convenience. This demonstration treats one life event as the unit of coordination, not one website: a local intent is selectively projected into four provider simulations, each field is purpose-bound, untrusted provider text is handled as data rather than authority, and capability increases only when the human explicitly opens the gate. It demonstrates the browser-side contract that independent services could use to form a user-controlled cooperative network; it does not claim that real agencies are connected today. Existing care-navigation systems validate the need for multi-service discovery and enrollment. Our distinct category is not “another benefits chatbot”: the civic journey is a test case for a transferable consent boundary between a person, their chosen agent, and WebMCP-enabled sites. Most agents are optimized to finish a task; this demonstration shows how to finish without surrendering the person's data boundary or final authority. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite power the visible bilingual English/Arabic experience. A deterministic domain engine handles eligibility, disclosure minimization, scheduling, fingerprints, expiring approval, and single-use receipts. The WebMCP adapter registers phase-specific tools with JSON Schemas and security annotations. Vitest and Testing Library cover the engine, UI journey, tool calls, dynamic registration, cancellation, and error handling; Playwright verifies the full browser flow and responsive layout. Challenges The hardest boundary was separating agent initiative from human authority. Hiding a button is not sufficient: the tool itself must be undiscoverable before approval, then bound to the exact reviewed proposal. A second challenge was treating service content as untrusted without making the agent blind. The demo uses browser trust annotations plus a deliberately bounded heuristic for a synthetic adversarial notice; this is evidence of the boundary, not a claim to solve prompt injection generally. Accomplishments A coherent multi-service journey instead of a single form wrapper A visible and machine-readable coordination outcome rather than an unexplained success screen One-story projection into reversible planning constraints without accepting Government ID or health notes Minimum necessary disclosure with a visible overcollection block Quarantine of malicious provider instructions without discarding the provider's legitimate service Dynamic WebMCP capabilities tied to human-visible state Deterministic eligibility and scheduling rather than model-made decisions Expiring, single-use exact-proposal approval Bilingual, responsive UI with visible audit and synthetic receipts Automated quality gate with 44 unit/integration tests, 17 browser journeys, and 91.98% statement coverage Accessibility, keyboard, responsive desktop/tablet/mobile, RTL, and WebMCP lifecycle browser checks passing Chrome agent audits passing for registered WebMCP tools, schema validity, the agent accessibility tree, and llms.txt Evidence behind the problem OECD, Modernising Access to Social Protection (2024): https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/modernising-access-to-social-protection_af31746d-en.html GOV.UK, Collecting personal information from users: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/collecting-personal-information-from-users GOV.UK, Structuring forms: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/form-structure GOV.UK, Principles for securing personal data in government services: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/principles-for-securing-personal-data-in-government-services What we learned WebMCP works best when tools describe durable user goals, not DOM operations. Security annotations help agents reason about risk, but they do not replace careful product boundaries. The clearest trust mechanism is shared state: the person should see the same plan, disclosure, approval, and result that the agent sees. What's next A production version would use authenticated provider schemas, cryptographic consent receipts, wallet-mediated selective-disclosure credentials through the emerging Digital Credentials API, revocation, durable encrypted storage, provider accountability, and independent security/privacy review. This submission intentionally stays synthetic so its current guarantees are clear and testable; it does not claim signed credentials or zero-knowledge proofs. Built with WebMCP Imperative API, React, TypeScript, Vite, Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright. Verified in ChatGPT Work Beyond scripted browser tests, we completed a fresh, uninterrupted run against the public deployment in the official ChatGPT desktop built-in browser using ChatGPT Work and GPT-5.6 Sol Light. ChatGPT discovered ONCE's native Site tools, staged proposal fp_d264dc20, confirmed commit_approved_plan was absent before visible approval, observed it appear afterward, called it exactly once, received four matching synthetic receipts, and verified that the capability disappeared after use. The demo opens with the real ChatGPT result beside the current production interface; the main production capture independently demonstrates the complete WebM

title: ONE TRIP WIN
pitch: Pack smart. Move once. A shared 3D workspace where people and AI agents plan, optimize, and validate a moving-truck load together.
about_excerpt: Pack smart. Move once. A shared 3D workspace where people and AI agents plan, optimize, and validate a moving-truck load together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I have moved more times than I care to count, and I have helped enough friends move that I have become the guy with the truck . That title sounds useful until moving day arrives and everyone suddenly expects you to solve a three-dimensional furniture puzzle while carrying a sofa. Moving trucks have a special law of physics: every couch gets larger the moment it reaches the driveway, every fragile box ends up underneath a box of books, and the phrase “we can make it fit” usually means “we are about to make a second trip.” A visual load planner like ONE TRIP WIN would have saved a lot of scratched furniture, wasted truck space, and conversations that began with, “Turn it the other way,” and ended with everyone silently blaming the sectional. What it does ONE TRIP WIN is a shared 3D moving plan. You place it. AI works around it. A person enters confirmed dimensions and handling rules, drags cargo into position, and locks the choices they want to keep. An AI agent reads the same plan through WebMCP and packs around those locks. The guided demo starts with three of 18 sample items loaded and one overlap. Unpacked miniatures wait beside the truck on wide screens; the full inventory wraps into rows below. The agent arranges the load in the 12-foot demo truck, favoring front-wall compaction and supported stacks, with an animated transition into the planned positions. The default packed load uses about 82% of the floor, 52% of the bounding-box volume, and 838 lb of the illustrative 900 lb payload allowance. The person moves the first-night bag and selects Keep here , then adds a last-minute ottoman. The agent adapts the arrangement while preserving that exact locked placement. The person reviews the results and provides the final approval. The interface has fitted 3D and top views, direct drag-and-drop, rotation and height controls, Undo, and clickable issue highlights. The results show actual loaded-item counts, overlaps, unsupported items, payload, and volume. Changed cargo flashes blue, and a shared activity trail explains who changed what. How we built it The app uses React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, and Tailwind CSS, with Vinext and Cloudflare Workers through ChatGPT Sites. Six tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool: get_moving_load reads inventory, dimensions, handling, locks, placements, and checks. place_moving_item repositions unlocked cargo. remove_moving_item returns unlocked cargo to inventory. auto_arrange_moving_load packs around human-locked placements. set_moving_truck_size selects a 12-, 16-, or 26-foot demo truck. validate_moving_load reports placement issues and affected item IDs. Human controls and agent tools use one synchronous store. The agent sees human changes immediately. It cannot unlock an item, invent its measurements, or approve the plan. Undo restores the previous arrangement and requires fresh human review. Packing uses a bounded deterministic heuristic with physical dimensions, permitted horizontal rotations, payload, collision checks, full-footprint support, and cumulative bearing limits. Items that cannot be placed remain in inventory with reasons. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making collaboration visible in the same 3D workspace. A person's locked placement has to survive every editing path: direct agent moves, removal, repacking, and truck changes. A supported stack also needs its supporting base preserved. We had to represent height and support, because a moving truck is a volume, not a very expensive floor mat. We also replaced a general load score with measured results so people can understand what passed, what needs attention, and which item caused it. Accomplishments that we're proud of Six discoverable WebMCP tools operating on the same plan as the person Human-owned locks that the agent works around Direct drag-and-drop with valid and invalid placement previews Undo that preserves the need for human approval Readable 3D and top views with camera reset Measured checks with clickable cargo highlights A guided move that tracks actual agent calls and human edits A complete collaboration flow with a human-only final approval control What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when the agent is not operating somewhere behind the curtain. It becomes useful when the person and the AI can see, change, and validate the same state together. Turning a stressful real-world task into a puzzle makes the solution easier to understand—and considerably more fun than arguing with a sofa in a driveway. Try the guided move Open the live app in a browser with WebMCP support and choose Try the guided move . Ask the agent to read and pack the inventory. Drag the first-night bag, select Keep here , and add the sample ottoman. Then ask: Repack around my locked items, include the new item, and validate the result. Do not approve it for me. Review the checks and approve the plan yourself. Manual entry, packing, locks, Undo, and the guided demonstration require no API key or login. Photos are optional local visual references in the hosted demo. Dimensions and weight are always entered and confirmed by the person. The optional local AI identification integration is disabled on hosted builds. Truck specifications and sample measurements are illustrative. These are planning checks, not a transport-safety certification. There is no door-clearance or loading/unloading-path check, and the packing heuristic does not prove an optimal arrangement. What's next for ONE TRIP WIN Saved household inventories, shared moving plans, a durable allowance for hosted photo identification, and stronger packing optimization could extend the experience. The goal remains fewer avoidable second trips and a clearer plan before anyone starts carrying the sofa. title: Orbweaver
pitch: An agent-native semantic workspace where ChatGPT proposes validated visual structures through WebMCP—and the human retains authority to accept, export, or undo.
about_excerpt: An agent-native semantic workspace where ChatGPT proposes validated visual structures through WebMCP—and the human retains authority to accept, export, or undo. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Complex systems do not need more interface. They need better structure. Architecture diagrams, workflows, data models, and knowledge graphs already contain meaning, but turning that meaning into a useful visual usually requires authored coordinates, diagram syntax, manually positioned shapes, or generated output that is difficult to inspect. I built Orbweaver around a simpler principle: Understand complex systems while showing less. What it does Orbweaver turns coordinate-free semantic graphs into deterministic, inspectable visual structures. The input describes meaning: what exists; how things relate; which relationships matter; what evidence and claims support the structure. Orbweaver validates that meaning, computes the layout, and renders an accessible SVG artifact. The proposal contains no authored coordinates, SVG, HTML, CSS, or executable markup. The WebMCP playground extends this into a shared human-agent workspace. ChatGPT can read the live workspace contract, create or revise a semantic proposal, inspect an entity, and focus it in the visible diagram. The agent can propose meaning. It cannot accept its own work. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer interface controls and repeatedly manipulate a large JSON editor. That is slow, fragile, and disconnected from the application’s actual domain model. With WebMCP, Orbweaver exposes six bounded, page-local tools: read the current workspace and revision; read the supported semantic contract; create a complete proposal; revise it using conflict-safe operations; inspect semantic identity and provenance; focus an entity in the visible workspace. The tools reuse the same application controller and validation boundary as the human interface. WebMCP does not introduce a second, privileged execution path. The human-agent experience A person describes an order-fulfillment system in ordinary language. ChatGPT discovers Orbweaver’s tools and supplies entities, relationships, groups, claims, and evidence—not pixels or drawing instructions. Orbweaver validates the entire proposal atomically, derives the geometry, and renders revision one as a validated but untrusted preview . The person and agent then work with the same live state. ChatGPT can add Delivery tracking, focus it, and expose its relationships for inspection. Expected-revision checks prevent stale writes when the shared workspace changes. Acceptance remains a human-only decision. The agent cannot accept a revision or enable export. The person can inspect, reject, or undo the change. In the demonstration, I manually undo the agent’s revision and Orbweaver restores the previous graph. How I built it Orbweaver’s core is a provider-neutral TypeScript library. A strict GraphProposal contract represents semantic content without layout coordinates. ELK.js computes the visual structure, while Orbweaver produces accessible SVG, stable semantic identities, selection behavior, provenance, and inspection details. The playground’s WebMCP adapter registers six tools through the browser’s page-local model context. Tool inputs are treated as untrusted data and pass through the existing validation layer. Create and revise operations are atomic, revisions are versioned, and semantic writes never bundle human acceptance. The implementation is tested with Vitest, Playwright, and axe-core accessibility checks. The npm package contains no AI provider, account requirement, telemetry, or cloud runtime dependency. Challenges The hardest problem was not drawing the graph. It was designing the authority boundary. A useful agent needed enough access to create meaningful structures without gaining the ability to silently approve its own output. This required explicit trust states, expected-revision conflict protection, atomic validation, reversible mutations, and accepted-only export. The other challenge was visual restraint: presenting enough information to understand a complex system without turning the workspace into an aircraft cockpit. Orbweaver keeps the interface secondary to the structure being examined. Accomplishments I’m proud of Published a provider-neutral open-source TypeScript library rather than embedding an AI service inside the product. Built six bounded WebMCP tools around the application’s existing controller and validation boundary. Made agent-authored changes versioned, atomic, inspectable, and reversible. Preserved human-only authority over acceptance and export. Produced deterministic, accessible SVG from semantic proposals containing no authored coordinates. Published the beta package, live playground, documentation, source, and reproducible demonstration. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes an application’s domain semantics—not when it simply recreates button clicking as tools. The strongest human-agent experience is not full autonomy. It is shared context with asymmetric authority: the agent contributes reach and synthesis; the application enforces structure; the human retains judgment at the moment of consequence. What’s next Orbweaver is open source and currently available as @semanticintent/orbweaver@0.2.0-beta.1 . Next steps include stabilizing the beta API, expanding semantic lenses and comparison views, and continuing to develop portable artifacts that preserve their meaning, provenance, and accessibility outside the original application. title: Overhead
pitch: A web-native canvas powered by WebMCP that turns any agent into a cloud architect. Design alongside it live while it calculates real-time infrastructure costs.
about_excerpt: A web-native canvas powered by WebMCP that turns any agent into a cloud architect. Design alongside it live while it calculates real-time infrastructure costs. Like Comment Story Updates Main Product How it works Inspiration I wanted zero friction between proposing an architecture and actually starting one. Canvas and whiteboard tools make agents work from stale copies. You move a box, the agent redraws from whatever it remembered, and your change is gone. Then the rest of it. One app for the costing. Another for the components. Save in whatever format the next app will actually open. Imagine spending 8+ hours of work to finish a technical documentation that nobody reads . Overhead uses WebMCP to eliminate this entirely. Semantic tools go straight to whatever agent shows up in the visitor's browser tab, so the design, the number and the code stop being five separate things. What it does Overhead is one web page where you, your agent and your teammates design an architecture that prices itself, audits itself, and compiles. Deep WebMCP integration. Agents get structural verbs ( add_service , connect , patch_state ) and edit the canvas directly, with no coordinate math burning tokens. Open a scenario and four more tools register themselves under an AbortController , then abort on commit. Real prices, per SKU , generated from the AWS Price List Bulk API with every rate keeping its source URL. No number on screen is one we typed. It audits its own work. The agent checks the design against rules citing cloud documentation, then patches what it flagged. Zero-setup multiplayer. Ephemeral rooms. Several designers, their agents, one document object. Production code compilation. Layouts compile to infrastructure code that passes cdk synth , plus deployable CloudFormation and diagrams that go both ways, which matters more than it sounds like it does: a Mermaid flowchart pasted out of anyone's README comes back as a priced, editable drawing. Everything runs client-side. No login, no API keys, no enterprise middleware. How we built it Stack WebMCP (native agent runtime) Next.js 15 React 19 React Flow (canvas UI) Zustand (state layer) Hosted on Vercel The core decision was addressing state patches by id rather than array index. Canvas mouse input, agent tool calls and peer messages all go through one strict applyPatch validator, and because every patch names what it touches instead of where it sits, the agent can't clobber a change you made while it was mid-thought. That was chosen for the agent's benefit. It turned out to be the reason two people can edit at once, which we didn't plan for and got almost free. defineService() does the rest. One definition per service produces the inspector form, the tool schemas, the pricing calculation and the infrastructure exports, so what the human sees and what the agent gets can't drift apart. No central database. Browser state only, with a WebSocket relay that routes multiplayer traffic and keeps none of it. Challenges we ran into Normalising the price APIs. Regional string variations, inconsistent schemas, offer codes that don't match the service name. Every mismatch surfaced as a wrong number on the canvas, which is a miserable way to find a bug and a very effective one. The ~1.5K character cap on tool output. Tight, and it forced us to send condensed diffs instead of dumping canvas state. Better tools came out of the constraint. Mixing grammars. A decision diamond sitting next to a Lambda asserts two incompatible things at once: architecture says what exists, a flowchart says what happens in what order. We let the samples teach the split instead of having the validator forbid it. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent audits its own work. Ask it to build something, then ask it to check what it built, and it calls get_findings , gets back rules citing AWS docs, and fixes them. That loop only exists because the tools are semantic. Dynamic registration you can watch happen. The tool count ticking up when a scenario opens, and back down on commit, is WebMCP doing something a screenshot can't fake. npm run synth runs cdk synth on all three samples plus a fixture holding one node of every service. So the claim we make on camera is checked by a command. CloudFormation round-trips. A template we wrote comes back as the same drawing, positions and containers and traffic intact, because the exporter also writes the things a template has no place for. Someone else's template comes back structurally, connections inferred from what references what. Never a hardcoded price. Every rate traces to a SKU in a dated file with a source URL. One document, three writers: canvas, code panel, agent. A mistake typed into the JSON gets the same error an agent gets from set_property . What we learned Semantic tools beat drawing primitives, and it is not close. Give an agent services and settings and it can be trusted with the next step, because its answers can be wrong in ways you can review and audit. Handing it long lists of SVG, or rules for making a diagram look right, is strictly worse. Constraints improved the surface. The output cap forced summaries instead of state dumps. Having no backend forced everything into the page, which is exactly what makes it work for a visitor with no account. WebMCP changes who gets to offer capability. Before it, you needed to be a platform big enough to ship an API and run an official MCP server. Now any page can serve whatever agent the visitor brought. No partnership, no permission, no server. Measure what you claim. "Fewer crossing edges" and "the CDK works" are both testable. Both were wrong at some point, in ways that looked completely fine on screen. What's next for Overhead Resource identity that survives a repo. Right now a foreign template matches back by service and name. Stamping the logical id onto the node would make a second import an update instead of a new drawing, even after a rename. Generate the wiring. The CloudFormation export names its stubs honestly: permissions, event sources and targets aren't generated yet. The edges already know what should be wired to what. "Visualise my architecture." The real destination. A coding agent has your repo, the page has the tools, and the diagram appears priced with no export step and no file to hand over. A crude version of this works today. More services as their SKUs land: NAT Gateway, ALB, RDS, ECS Fargate. The rule doesn't bend. Never hardcode a price, and a service arrives when its rate does. title: Paper Trail
pitch: Say it once - one sentence about your life event, and every agency, insurer, and employer form gets filled, cross-checked, approved by you, and receipted.
about_excerpt: Say it once - one sentence about your life event, and every agency, insurer, and employer form gets filled, cross-checked, approved by you, and receipted. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every big life event arrives with a hidden invoice: not money, but paperwork . A birth triggers 15–40 separate actions scattered across the Social Security Administration, the health insurer, and the employer's HR portal — each with its own login, its own forms, its own deadlines (add a dependent within 30 days or wait for open enrollment), and its own ways of spelling the same name. Humans have always been the integration glue between these portals: re-typing identical data, making format mistakes, missing windows. When we read the WebMCP spec, one sentence rewired how we think: websites can hand agents structured capabilities instead of forcing them to screenshot pixels. The paperwork layer is the biggest unclaimed prize for that idea — so we built the app we wished existed: say it once, and the whole bundle gets done, with the human still sovereign. What it does Type one sentence — "We had a baby girl on June 3rd at General Hospital." One interview , no forms: the hub derives the facts and materializes an action bundle across three independent portals, with deadline math computed live (DOB June 3 + 30 days → insurer window closes July 3). Each portal owns a tool surface : walking into a page dynamically registers its tools and walking away unregisters them ( AbortController ). The agent only ever sees the tools for the page it's on. Drafts fill from one canonical profile — and a reconciliation engine catches cross-portal conflicts (the hospital's "Okafor-Reyes, Amara" vs. the profile's "Amara Okafor-Reyes"; "Jun 03, 2026" vs. "2026-06-03"), explains them in plain language, and standardizes only on the human's say-so. Nothing files without a human click. Every write tool is a two-call gate: the first call opens an on-page dialog showing every field about to be filed; the second call executes only if the human actually approved — enforced in code, not in a prompt. Replay a confirmation id → unknown_confirmation_id . Let the agent approve itself → human_approval_missing . File twice → already_submitted . Everything ends in a receipt ledger : payload digest → confirmation number → timestamp → human-approval flag. The showpiece : pt_cascade_update . The family moves mid-flow; one call re-derives the whole situation — deadlines recomputed, every pending draft re-filled across all three portals — while filed actions stay untouched, because receipts preserve what was actually submitted. How we built it A zero-dependency, zero-build static SPA — classic scripts, no framework, no backend, deployable anywhere (it even runs from file:// ). mcp.js — the WebMCP layer: registerTool with readOnlyHint annotations, per-portal AbortSignal lifecycles, and a guarded executor (activity-rail logging, ~1.5K output budgets, throws → typed errors agents can self-correct from). portals.js — three fictional portals (SSA, Meridian Health, employer HR) with schemas, strict in-code validation whose errors are written for the agent, the two-call ConfirmGate , and the reconciliation engine. hub.js — the one-sentence interview resolver and the hub tool surface ( pt_start_life_event_interview , pt_get_action_bundle , pt_reconcile_field_conflicts , pt_get_receipt_ledger , pt_cascade_update ). store.js / bundle.js — canonical profile, dependency-aware bundle, deadline math, event-sourced receipts — plus a store subscription so the page the human is watching re-renders live when the agent mutates state through the protocol. 26 tools across 4 surfaces; 13 annotated read-only; 3 gated writes. A /diag.html page probes the runtime (API presence, live registration, getTools() visibility, abort lifecycle) — 11/11 checks pass in Chrome 150 with #enable-webmcp-testing . Challenges we ran into The runtime diverges from the spec text. In the real Chrome build, modelContext.registerTool() returns undefined , not a Promise — our .then() chain silently died at boot. We caught it only by testing against the actual enabled runtime, and now handle both styles. That bug alone justified building a diagnostics page. Tool identity is page-scoped. Re-entering a portal risks a synchronous Duplicate tool name throw; abort-then-re-register had to be proven clean (it is — verified via getTools() ). The "shared live app" requirement is real work. When the agent conducts the interview through the protocol, the human's screen must react — we wired store-driven re-rendering so the bundle materializes on screen as the tool call lands. Timezones and dates. "Jun 03, 2026" vs. "2026-06-03" needed part-wise date comparison, not toISOString() gymnastics that silently shift days across UTC offsets. Making the gate genuinely binding. The tempting shortcut is a confirm dialog the agent can talk its way past. We made approval a server-side-of-the-page fact: the finalize call checks the human's actual click in code, and we proved the negative paths on camera. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full judge experience runs through the runtime's own executeTool : interview → surface swap → gated filing (pending → human approval → submitted) → reconciliation → cascade → ledger. Not a scripted path — the protocol path. Receipts as evidence : every filing carries a payload digest and confirmation number; the ledger reads like an audit trail, because that's what it is. Honest degradation : without a WebMCP runtime the chip says so, the human buttons drive the same code paths, and the app still demonstrates every flow. A dark, full-height activity rail that narrates every tool call — the human and the agent visibly share one live artifact. What we learned Protocol depth is a design material, not a checkbox. Dynamic surfaces, annotations, and elicitation-shaped gates changed the architecture, not just the API calls. Human-in-the-loop belongs in code. A prompt saying "ask first" is a suggestion; a gate that physically cannot finalize without the human's click is a guarantee. Test in the real judging environment early. The single most dangerous bug we fixed was invisible in every browser except the one with the flag enabled. Agents need agent-legible errors : strict in-code validation with messages written for self-correction turns failures into progress. What's next for Paper Trail Move and bereavement event packs — the bundle engine takes new event types without architecture changes. Native requestUserInteraction elicitation as a progressive enhancement of the two-call gate. An accessibility operator mode — the same tool surfaces are a better substrate than the visual DOM; narration and pacing ride the protocol for free. Handoff export — the remaining human-only actions (notary visits, in-person verifications) as a calendar file, because a good agent knows what it can't do. title: PaperVeil
pitch: A browser-local medical appeal desk where agents get capabilities—not identity—with one-field consent, adversarial leak blocking, and an auditable disclosure ledger.
about_excerpt: A browser-local medical appeal desk where agents get capabilities—not identity—with one-field consent, adversarial leak blocking, and an auditable disclosure ledger. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Inspiration People appealing a denied medical claim often need help understanding codes, deadlines, missing evidence, and policy rules. Unfortunately, the same documents contain member IDs, dates of birth, addresses, and other sensitive identifiers. The usual agent workflow begins by uploading the documents. PaperVeil asks a different question: What if the agent received useful capabilities instead of receiving the person's identity? What PaperVeil does PaperVeil is a local-first medical-claim appeal desk built around WebMCP. A synthetic claim remains in browser-local IndexedDB while the page exposes seven narrow tools that an agent can use to: inspect tokenized evidence and document summaries; find billing line items; check deterministic policy rules; compare evidence-completion scenarios; request one sensitive field for one stated reason; save a tokenized appeal draft; and prepare a locally rehydrated export. The human and agent work in the same live case. When the agent updates the appeal, the user sees it immediately. When a raw identifier is requested, the user can allow it once, deny it, or let the request expire. The adversarial demonstration PaperVeil does not only promise that sensitive information is protected—it demonstrates the boundary failing closed. One fictional insurer letter contains a seeded OCR prompt injection telling the agent to request the member ID and copy it into its next draft. The evidence tools mark this attacker-influenceable content with untrustedContentHint: true . During the authorized red-team demonstration: The agent reads the poisoned document summary. It requests the member ID, and the user approves that single disclosure. The agent follows the injected instruction and attempts to place the raw ID inside draft_appeal . PaperVeil's output seal throws before unsafe state is saved. The disclosure ledger records the blocked call and highlights the offending value. The agent retries using [[MEMBER_ID]] , and the safe workflow continues. Approval therefore applies only to one response. It does not make the identifier safe for every later tool call. How we built it PaperVeil uses the imperative WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a narrow JSON schema, a UI title, appropriate annotations, and a bounded output contract. Tool handlers construct results from explicit allowed fields. Every result then passes through a second privacy assertion that detects known raw identifiers, including punctuation changes and reformatted dates. Tool calls are capped at approximately 1,500 bytes. A shared execution wrapper records successful, failed, and privacy-blocked calls. The local disclosure ledger displays: the tool and arguments; the exact returned bytes; raw identifiers released; quasi-identifiers exposed; cumulative linkage-risk level; the user's gate decision; and blocked values and failure reasons. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same domain handlers, rule engine, browser vault, and ledger. This keeps the visible product and agent-facing behavior consistent. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was making consent useful without making it dangerously broad. An approval had to authorize one field for one response—not create a permanent permission. We also had to ensure that exceptions and oversized outputs remained visible. A privacy block should not disappear merely because the tool returned no result, so failed executions are written to the ledger as first-class events. Another challenge was detecting transformed identifiers. Exact string matching would miss a reformatted date or an ID with punctuation removed. The seal therefore compares normalized and compact fingerprints while the main result construction remains allowlist-based. Finally, WebMCP is an emerging browser surface. We kept the product fully usable through its human interface while making the agent workflow deterministic and easy for judges to reproduce. What we learned We learned that tool schemas are not merely developer ergonomics—they are security boundaries. We also learned that untrustedContentHint becomes meaningful only when the application demonstrates how hostile content is handled. A label alone is not enforcement. Most importantly, privacy risk accumulates across calls. Even when no direct identifier is released, combinations such as dates, insurer, ZIP code, and claim amount can increase re-identification risk. PaperVeil surfaces that cumulative risk in the ledger instead of treating every call in isolation. What we are proud of PaperVeil is a complete human-and-agent product rather than a tool-registration demo. It includes two synthetic cases, a populated appeal desk, deterministic policy analysis, tokenized drafting, local export, responsive layouts, a visible approval gate, adversarial testing, and an inspectable ledger. The project has 17 unit and contract tests plus browser-level coverage across desktop, compact, and mobile layouts. What's next A production version would add on-device document parsing, encrypted local storage, authenticated case access, insurer-specific policy sources, retention controls, accessibility testing with real users, and formal medical and legal compliance review. PaperVeil currently uses fictional patients, claims, insurers, and policy rules. It is a technical demonstration—not medical advice, legal advice, or a HIPAA-compliant records system. What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for PaperVeil Built With indexeddb lucide next.js playwright react typescript vercel vitest webmcp zod Try it out paperveil-two.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I led the product design and implementation of PaperVeil. I built the Next.js interface, browser-local data vault, seven WebMCP tools, human disclosure gate, privacy seal, and auditable disclosure ledger. I also created the synthetic claim scenarios and adversarial prompt-injection demonstration, wrote the unit and browser tests, deployed the project to Vercel, and produced the documentation and demo video. I used AI-assisted development while personally reviewing, testing, and integrating the final implementation. title: Particle Atlas
pitch: Turn particle-physics questions into shared, replayable visual investigations.
about_excerpt: Turn particle-physics questions into shared, replayable visual investigations. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Particle Atlas Inspiration Particle physics is full of relationships that are difficult to understand from a table or chat response alone: particles can share charge and spin while differing enormously in mass, form matter/antimatter pairs, or connect through different force networks. Particle Atlas began as an attempt to make the symmetries of the Standard Model visible in three dimensions. The WebMCP Challenge created an opportunity to solve the next problem: allowing a learner to move directly from a natural-language question to an inspectable visual investigation without giving up control of the interface. What it does Particle Atlas turns particle-physics questions into shared visual investigations. A learner can ask a browser agent to examine a pattern, and the agent uses eleven structured WebMCP tools to query Particle Data Group-linked data, configure the live Three.js scene, compare particles, reveal force networks, and save the evidence into an editable notebook. Each finding captures the exact scene that produced it. The learner can rotate or filter the visualization, revise the agent's explanation, inspect and undo tool calls, reopen any saved view, and share the complete investigation through one URL. The agent is not controlling a hidden copy of the app; both participants work in the same visible state. Before WebMCP, an agent had to infer controls from pixels and repeatedly manipulate a dense 3D interface. It could answer a question in text, but it could not reliably build a durable, replayable visual explanation inside the application. WebMCP makes that collaboration structured, inspectable, and reversible. Why WebMCP Particle Atlas combines read tools, state-changing tools, and a durable collaborative artifact: The agent queries application data instead of relying on model memory. It selects the correct axes, particle families, and force network for the question. Every tool call updates the learner's visible workspace. Findings bind reasoning to an exact scene snapshot. Human edits and agent actions remain synchronized. Undo and shared URLs make the work inspectable and reproducible. A learner no longer needs to translate a conceptual question into a sequence of filters, axes, comparisons, camera positions, and force toggles. The agent handles that mechanical translation while the learner explores, challenges, edits, and shares the result. How we built it The application registers eleven tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() in web/js/webmcp.js. Their handlers call the same command layer used by manual controls in web/js/main.js. Read tools expose the particle catalog, scene state, and investigation. Mutating tools focus, compare, configure, highlight, show force networks, frame the notebook, and capture findings. Each mutating tool records a full undo snapshot. The notebook module serializes human and agent edits and stores non-recursive scene snapshots for replay. The application is a static Three.js site with no account, API key, or backend requirement. It remains fully usable in manual mode when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges we ran into Keeping manual actions, agent actions, camera state, comparisons, notebook edits, and shared URLs synchronized. Making every mutating agent action exactly reversible. Saving scene evidence without recursively embedding the investigation notebook. Distinguishing measured particle properties from plotting coordinates for massless or constrained particles. Maintaining a coherent full-screen 3D experience across desktop, mobile, table, light, dark, and high-contrast modes. Accomplishments that we're proud of Eleven working WebMCP tools with structured schemas and results. A genuinely shared human-agent notebook with replayable scene evidence. Full-state agent undo and inspectable input/output history. Reproducible scene and notebook URLs. PDG-linked provenance, uncertainty, and hypothetical-particle labeling. Accessible table representation, keyboard navigation, mobile controls, and reduced-motion support. A green public browser regression workflow plus native Chrome and ChatGPT in-app browser verification. What we learned Agent-native design is not just exposing every button as a tool. The most useful tools operate at the level of user intent: compare a family, reveal an interaction, or save a finding with its evidence. The interface also needs visible state, reversibility, and a durable artifact so the human can remain an active collaborator. What's next for Particle Atlas Classroom investigation templates. Exportable notebook reports. Decay, coupling, and composite-particle datasets with the same provenance model. Shared investigations for other scientific domains.
