title: UCE Evidence Lens
pitch: People and AI agents, alone or together, inspect the same public evidence - verifying integrity, chronology, assertions, and file matches with no work uploaded and creators keep control.
about_excerpt: People and AI agents, alone or together, inspect the same public evidence - verifying integrity, chronology, assertions, and file matches with no work uploaded and creators keep control. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Seven typed, read-only WebMCP tools discovered directly from the live production site. An agent invokes verify_uce_record and receives a structured, source-bound result—without DOM scraping. Browser checks verify schema, record identity, ES256 signature, and public transaction chronology. Chronology separates claimed dates, recorded system events, and independently retrieved public evidence. Authorship, identity, AI-use, and rights remain recorded assertions—not verified facts. A public UCE record binds the asset to its manifest hash, timestamps, source, and recorded authorship context. The verifier is itself evidenced: the production v1.0.0 site release has its own independently checkable UCE record. Overview A shared browser verifier where people and AI agents inspect the same cryptographic evidence, chronology, rights assertions, and local-file match. Problem Creators, agencies, reviewers, counsel, and journalists increasingly receive public evidence records that combine cryptographic facts with human claims. Understanding one record can require moving among a verification page, machine-readable JSON, a signature, an Arweave transaction, and the original local file. A person can miss a distinction; a general-purpose agent scraping the visible page can do worse by promoting a publisher statement or authorship claim into a verified fact. The difficult part is not merely retrieving data. It is preserving evidentiary boundaries: what this browser independently checked, what the publisher reported, what the claimant asserted, what is temporarily retryable, and what the public format does not yet support. Solution UCE Evidence Lens is a static, browser-first public record inspector. A person can load a CbyUCE verification URL, a direct Arweave manifest, pasted public JSON, or the bundled demonstration. The browser validates the record, checks its public ES256 signature, binds chronology to public Arweave block metadata, separates recorded assertions from verified results, and can compare a user-selected file by locally calculated SHA-256. The same page exposes seven read-only WebMCP tools. An agent can load, summarize, verify, inspect chronology, list assertions, inspect rights declarations, and report an already-selected local file comparison through structured operations rather than guessing from the interface. The human sees the same underlying state and wording. Why This Matters Evidence review is a strong fit for WebMCP because the workflow is structured, multi-step, and precision sensitive. Without page-defined tools, an agent has to infer controls and semantics from layout, possibly leaving out technical details or overstating a legal conclusion. With WebMCP, the site defines exactly which evidence operations are available and returns typed, source-bound results. For a reviewer, the experience changes from manually correlating several technical sources to asking one focused question while retaining a visible and easily understood inspectable record. For an agency or production team, the demonstration also shows a credible market path: a work can originate in the published Copyright by UCE Figma plugin ( the Figma plugin is now available for use), become a public UCE record, and then be inspected by both a person and an agent before delivery. This does not turn evidence into a legal verdict. It makes the evidence easier to inspect without erasing its limits. How We Used AI The product is agent-enabled without placing a model inside the trust boundary. Deterministic browser functions perform parsing, cryptography, chronology retrieval, and digest comparison. WebMCP lets an AI agent select and compose those operations, explain the structured results, and guide a person through the same evidence the interface displays. The key collaboration is intentional: the agent can inspect an already-selected digest but cannot open a file picker or access file bytes. The person controls the sensitive local input; the agent works with the resulting evidence state. How We Used Codex Codex helped scope the public/private boundary, scaffolded the TypeScript application, implemented and reviewed the seven WebMCP tools, debugged browser discovery and CORS, hardened trust and concurrency boundaries, built regression tests, ran security and dependency audits, tested responsive and live-browser behavior, prepared Cloudflare deployment, and helped me tighten the judge-facing language because I can get a bit wordy and go off on tangents...(see what I mean...). The development process repeatedly challenged optimistic claims. For example, canonical manifest recomputation remains explicitly unsupported because the public format does not define the exact hash construction. Publisher flags are recorded rather than substituted for browser checks. The result is a narrower but more defensible product. As the Copyright by UCE product grows, so will UCE Evidence Lens as an Open-Source resource helping creatives to secure their creativity. The Copyright by UCE Canva App plugin is in design review now having passed functional and technical review and the Pro Tools and Ableton plugin and extension respectively are being finalized over the next few weeks. The UCE Evidence Lens is poised to be a very useful tool for creatives and the agencies and organizations that serve them. Key Features Seven top-level, imperative WebMCP tools with strict JSON Schemas and readOnlyHint: true . Human/agent parity through shared controller operations and shared result wording. Public ES256 compact-JWS verification against a reviewed, application-owned P-256 key registry. Direct Arweave transaction, block, height, timestamp, and confirmation inspection. Consumer-oriented result states that distinguish verified, mismatch, retryable, reported, and unsupported outcomes. Recorded authorship, identity, originality, AI-use, and rights values clearly separated from verified facts. Local SHA-256 comparison without uploading the file or exposing its bytes to the agent. Bundled demo, direct Arweave, CbyUCE JSON, and pasted-JSON resilience paths. Static Cloudflare deployment with no account, backend, analytics, database, runtime secret, or production dependency. Architecture UCE Evidence Lens is a static Vite and TypeScript single-page application. Pure modules parse and verify records; a memory-only controller binds each result to its source and manifest hash; a semantic DOM renderer and the WebMCP adapter call the same controller operations. Browser Web Crypto provides SHA-256 and ECDSA P-256. WebMCP tools register before asynchronous demo loading and confirm same-origin discovery through document.modelContext.getTools() where available. Production headers opt the page into an origin-keyed agent cluster and allow same-origin tools. Remote access is restricted to validated HTTPS CbyUCE and Arweave routes, with byte, depth, and timeout limits. There are no production npm dependencies and no server function, Worker, proxy, database, or persistent application storage. Testing Instructions Open https://uceevidencelens.com/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and the browser restarted. Confirm the page reports: “7 read-only AI-agent tools registered and discoverable.” The bundled public UCE record loads automatically. Ask the agent to call verify_uce_record and summarize verified checks separately from recorded assertions. The result should begin with “No integrity problems found.” Ask the agent to call inspect_uce_chronology . Confirm it distinguishes the claimed creation date, system events, and the independently retrieved Arweave block. For the real Figma-origin example, load https://cbyuce.com/verify/cc7680c80721f69295dab10bb547065fd74c14de420d915df0da051ee5e0727a with load_uce_public_record , then repeat the verification and chronology calls. Optional local comparison: choose the matching public PNG in the normal interface. The browser displays its SHA-256 result; compare_local_file_to_uce_record can report that result but cannot access the file bytes or trigger selection. No login or credentials are required. If live retrieval is temporarily unavailable, reload the bundled demo or use the direct Arweave manifest URL shown in the public record. Known Limitations Independent canonical-manifest recomputation is unsupported until CbyUCE publishes a reproducible hash profile with test vectors. Direct chronology uses a public Arweave gateway rather than a trustless light client; pending or unreachable results are retryable, not mismatches. The trusted platform key registry requires a reviewed application release for rotation or revocation. Only UCE manifest schema 1.0.0, SHA-256 file digests, and ES256/P-256 compact JWS are s

title: Valence
pitch: Interactive chemical discovery.
about_excerpt: Interactive chemical discovery. Like Comment Story Updates Insipration Traditional online chemistry research can be a hassle, with multiple tabs and half an hour of searching just to look up a molecule. As an example, to find a non-toxic polymer precursor built from only period-2 elements, the typical routine is searching PubChem and noting down hazard classifications and cross-checking molecular weights, a tough ask if you want to do it in a single tab. What it does The interface is an interactive periodic table and chemistry bench. A user describes a research goal, and through WebMCP an agent runs the workflow. On the interface, there is a build panel that keeps the scientist(user or agent) in control; everything is audited(keystrokes, tool calls) and logged by the trace panel via a ghost cursor. Beginners/Non-experts can interactively play with the periodic table by combining elements. Full explanations for both successful molecules and rejected combinations. Across the app, 23 tools are registered on document.modelContext . Tools include Selection and bonding: for 2D/3D molecular visualization. ** PubChem lookup:** for data grounding via the public API. Molecular design and comparison: for similarity evaluation, comparative analysis, alternative search, hazard classification. All scored transparently. Constraint solving: Async routines for multivariable discovery jobs, status streaming, candidate ranking and task cancellation utilty and state: Full state serialisation. All numbers are sourced directly from PubChem live and PubChem cached. Honest degradation to an offline bundled set when the API is unreachable. How we built it Vite and TypeScript WebMCP. @mcp-b/global wraps a native document.modelContext when the browser has one; a small spec-shaped shim covers the rest. Tools register synchronously at module load, so an agent scanning on page load already sees them. The store is a tiny observable. Every UI handler and every tool mutates state through it. A built-in operator runs the same tool that an external agent calls, so the command bar and a real agent share one code path. That was also our test harness. Data comes from PubChem PUG REST and PUG View, called straight from the browser. Rendering. 3Dmol.js for the 3D viewer, lazy-loaded and smiles-drawer for 2D structures. Deployment: Vercel. Challenges we ran into PubChem rate-limiting Its public API throttles per client address and returns 503 under load, it was unreliable during quick iterations, so we bundled an offline compound set as fallback. Finding the right surface Our first version registered tools on navigator.modelContext . ChatGPT reported "no callable tools". Agents read document.modelContext . We moved there and added the shim. Async tool contracts The constraint solver could take fifteen seconds, and a timeout left half-built state on the canvas. We reworked it into a job that returns an id immediately, streams status, can be cancelled, and commits its result in a single step. The 3D viewer got stuck Two model loads racing in before the 3Dmol chunk finished each created their own viewer on the same element, and later updates landed on the orphan. We used a single-flight guard to resolve this. Trust in a science tool PubChem's aggregated GHS data includes minority-notifier misclassifications, so water in some examples was showing false hazards. We now read only the primary classification. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works in one turn. Ask for a molecule by constraints, get a ranked, hazard-checked answer with a 3D model on the canvas, then edit a constraint and re-run without re-prompting. The beauty of the shared canvas. The agent and the person operate one instrument exactly like we envisioned Every claim is checkable: source and fetch time on every number, evidence-based hazard language, per-candidate rejection reasons. Our bundled fallback held out when PubChem was unreachable. What we learned WebMCP's value is shared state on a live surface. A headless MCP server can answer questions. It cannot manipulate pixels or read back what you just did. Agent tools need async contracts. This is helpful for debugging. Test against the actual agent surface early. ChatGPT caught the registration bug in minutes. The built-in operator running the same tool path as an external agent was the best decision for development speed. What's next for Valence A richer chemistry surface with cross-references and deeper bioassay data. A shareable recipe-card permalink, so a build can be sent to someone. A multi-compound bench, so an agent can lay out a small reaction rather than one molecule at a time. A resilient data path for the PubChem rate limits, and more teach-mode content for beginners. title: VERROCCHIO
pitch: A WebMCP workshop that preserves missing proof, the next action, and human checkpoints for interrupted solo builders.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workshop that preserves missing proof, the next action, and human checkpoints for interrupted solo builders. Like Comment Story Updates What VERROCCHIO does VERROCCHIO is a WebMCP workshop for time-constrained solo builders whose projects are repeatedly interrupted. It keeps the next action, missing proof, active work, and human checkpoints together so an AI can help without turning an unverified claim into “done.” The browser exposes four bounded, state-aware WebMCP tools: inspect_workshop reads the live mission, missing proof (MANCA), active work, and the next bounded action. call_fermo stops when evidence, scope, safety, or intent is ambiguous. propose_workshop_draft validates and returns an unsigned plan that waits for human FIRMA. return_work_result records a structured CLAIMED result without marking its evidence verified. Human-only actions—FIRMA approval, evidence verification, resume, publication, and final submission—are deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. Why WebMCP is a strong fit A person and an agent must act on the same live project state. With ordinary DOM automation, an agent has to rediscover controls and infer whether visible text is a claim, approval, or proof. WebMCP gives the page an explicit contract and exposes only the transitions the agent is allowed to perform at that moment. The result is not simply fewer clicks. It is a clearer division of responsibility: the agent can inspect, draft, stop, and return bounded work; the human retains purpose, approval, evidence judgment, publication, and submission. Better experience for interrupted solo work A solo builder working around a full-time job carries coordination that a conventional team would normally distribute: rules, next actions, interruption recovery, evidence review, and stops before irreversible actions. VERROCCHIO makes that coordination visible and resumable. The core flow is: MANCA → unsigned plan → human FIRMA → bounded work → CLAIMED → human VERIFIED or CHANGES_REQUESTED After an interruption, the builder can reopen the workshop and see what is still missing, what is active, and exactly where human attention is required. What people and agents can now do together The agent works directly with structured browser state instead of guessing from screenshots or page text. It can propose the smallest valid next plan, detect ambiguity, and return a result with checks, evidence references, and remaining risk. The human can adopt or reject that plan and verify the claim without surrendering the decisions that matter. Implementation VERROCCHIO is a React and Vite application with browser-local persistence. Tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool ; their availability changes with workshop phase. Every mutation requires the state version returned by inspection and an idempotency key. Stale state is rejected, identical retries reuse the existing receipt, and conflicting reuse fails. The current ChatGPT or Codex host supplies reasoning, so the app does not require its own OpenAI API key. Evidence Public live app: https://verrocchio-workshop.honabochi.chatgpt.site/ Public source and MIT license: https://github.com/honabochi/verrocchio-public Frozen release: webmcp-submission-2026-09-03 at revision 439161e Automated test suite: 121 passing tests Hosted evaluation: seven fixed natural-language cases plus two DOM baselines Demo: a 70-second public YouTube video with audio The WebMCP-versus-DOM evaluation showed fewer actions for the tested stop and unsigned-plan paths (2 versus 3, and 2 versus 4). Recorded elapsed time was not faster, so no speed claim is made. Existing-project disclosure The July 19 baseline 91315a1 already contained the local workshop, MANCA proof gates, work packets, and human FIRMA/FERMO controls. Beginning with challenge-period commit 0176211 on August 27, the project added the four native WebMCP tools, state-aware availability, versioned and idempotent mutations, unsigned plans, CLAIMED results that cannot close proof, evaluation receipts, and the hosted judge path. Comparison: https://github.com/honabochi/verrocchio-public/compare/91315a120059cae3b9eb68566c81d5c8d87fd903...webmcp-submission-2026-09-03 Known limitations Persistence is browser-local rather than synchronized across devices. Human-only controls are a workflow boundary, not actor authentication. The keyless path depends on a WebMCP-capable host. title: VibeStudio
pitch: A shared creative workspace where creators and Codex turn inspiration and editable memory into consistent content through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared creative workspace where creators and Codex turn inspiration and editable memory into consistent content through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Problem General-purpose AI can generate copy and images, but creators repeatedly have to explain who they are, what their brand sounds like, what they like, and how each format should be produced. The context becomes scattered across chats, the agent cannot reliably act inside the creative workspace, and creators lose control over what the system remembers. Solution VibeStudio gives the creator and Codex one visible, shared workspace. The creator curates multimodal inspiration, records explicit taste signals, edits a persistent Template of brand and production rules, and works in Sessions that retain their source, context receipt, version history, and status. Through page-contextual WebMCP tools, Codex can read only the context needed for the current task, create or revise a carousel inside the workspace, and leave every material change visible and reversible. The challenge proof is one complete path: select an inspiration, state what is worth borrowing, retrieve a bounded creator context receipt, create an original seven-slide carousel, revise one slide, undo it, mark the piece Ready, and inspect the traceable learning that can shape the next piece. Why This Matters Content creation is not a single generation step. It is an ongoing collaboration among taste, brand memory, source material, format rules, iteration, and publishing state. VibeStudio makes that system durable and inspectable while letting creators keep the conversational agent they already trust. WebMCP is central to this experience because the agent and human work on the same live artifact. The agent does not have to infer the whole interface from pixels or receive an unrestricted export of the creator's memory. The page exposes a small typed tool set for the current view, while the creator sees the resulting session, version, status, and undo trail immediately. How We Used AI Codex transforms selected inspiration and a bounded creator-context receipt into an original seven-slide story. OpenAI image generation creates up to three text-free visual layers; VibeStudio's deterministic renderer owns typography, layout, and the final 1080 x 1350 slides. AI can propose focused revisions to a selected slide or Template slot without replacing the whole artifact. Accepted creator feedback can become source-linked learning, but one-off instructions do not silently become permanent rules. Existing optional Claude-backed routes remain in the broader local Studio, but the challenge's WebMCP collaboration path was tested with Codex. How We Used Codex Codex Desktop was the primary design, implementation, debugging, and testing partner. It helped research current WebMCP interaction patterns, turn the product thesis into a scoped PRD and technical specification, implement typed contextual tools, iterate on the UI with the creator, and run the end-to-end acceptance journey. For the product demo, Codex is also the user's agent. In ChatGPT's in-app browser it discovers VibeStudio's current page tools, reads the selected inspiration and bounded Template context, connects to the current Session, and creates or revises the artifact. This is not a simulated chat panel inside VibeStudio; it is the creator's existing agent operating the real workspace through WebMCP. Key Features Multimodal Inspire feed organized by YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, news, and websites. One-field source intake that accepts a link, free text, or both. Explicit likes, dislikes, notes, saves, and source following that curate the creator's taste. Editable Template containing identity, audience, voice, visual taste, goals, examples, and production rules. Session-based work with Draft, Ready, Scheduled, and Live states. Page-contextual WebMCP tools rather than one large global tool catalog. Shared Attention: the creator can point, draw, and place multiple UI targets in a visible Talking about tray for the agent. Versioned agent changes, attribution, review state, and undo. Reusable carousel skill with exactly seven validated slides and deterministic final rendering. Bounded context receipts that show which creator memories and rules shaped an artifact. Safety boundary: no publishing, scheduling, permanent deletion, arbitrary URL fetch, filesystem path, shell, or unrestricted creator-memory tool is exposed through WebMCP. Architecture VibeStudio is a Next.js 16, React 18, and TypeScript application. Its WebMCP adapter detects document.modelContext , registers typed tools for the current page, and unregisters stale tools when the view changes. The current challenge tool surface includes Session, Inspire, Template-context, carousel, status, review, and undo operations. Local records use append-friendly JSONL files for creators, inspiration, Template memory, context receipts, Sessions, and activity. Mutations use version checks and idempotency keys. External inspiration is marked as untrusted content, reads are annotated as read-only, responses are bounded, and the final carousel renderer deterministically composes text and generated image layers. The public judge build runs in a sanitized demo mode with generic seed data and an isolated writable root. It does not read the creator's adjacent private project data, reports local integrations as disconnected, and blocks server-side fetch, scraping, upload, publishing, metrics-sync, and embedded-assistant routes. title: Virtual Try-On + AI Stylist
pitch: Virtual try-on that runs entirely in your browser. Its catalog search, try-on, save and compare are WebMCP tools and an AI agent proposes outfits, you judge the fit. No server, no uploads.
about_excerpt: Virtual try-on that runs entirely in your browser. Its catalog search, try-on, save and compare are WebMCP tools and an AI agent proposes outfits, you judge the fit. No server, no uploads. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent applies the sangeet dress banner, composite, reaction chips The model, the 8-garment catalog, the "AI stylist tools live" indicator WebGPU backend, warm on-device timings (SEGMENT 34 ms / POSE 46 ms) The structured reaction ("❤️ Love it perfect for the sangeet"), first saved look A kurti on the model catalog range beyond dresses Agent applies the Blush Pink Lehenga Choli Two saved looks in the tray The side-by-side compare modal "Which one works?" Virtual Try-On + AI Stylist This is an existing project. The on-device try-on app existed before the hackathon; the last commit before it is dated July 29. Everything to do with WebMCP was built between Aug 29 and Sep 2: the five tools, the reaction bar, the saved-looks tray and compare view, the merchandised catalog, and the test suite for the tools. The git history dates all of it. Inspiration Virtual try-on is normally a server job. You upload your photo, a model runs somewhere, you pay per render, and you have to be fine with a picture of yourself sitting on someone's GPUs. We'd already built the opposite: a try-on that runs in the browser on WebGPU, so it's instant, free to serve, and the photo never leaves your machine. Then agents started shopping for people, and the thing they're worst at is the thing that matters: knowing whether an outfit actually looks good on you. WebMCP let us split it. The agent does the legwork; the person makes the call. And WebMCP is the right fit because the tools already exist. They're the buttons on the page. There's no API to build, no server, and the agent can only do what the page lets a person do. What it does You open the app with a photo or your webcam and it composites garments onto you on-device: segmentation, pose, and a garment warp, all in a Web Worker. The page registers five WebMCP tools on document.modelContext : Tool search_catalog filter by occasion, colour, category, budget (₹) apply_tryon run the pipeline and put a garment on the photo save_look snapshot the result into a tray compare_looks show saved looks side by side await_reaction get the verdict: love it, good, try another, not this Any WebMCP client picks them up: ChatGPT's browser, a Chrome agent, Claude through a bridge extension. So instead of setting filters, opening six product pages, and picturing each one on yourself, you say "a sangeet outfit under ₹8k". The agent runs search_catalog({ occasion: "sangeet", maxPrice: 8000 }) , gets the one match, and applies it. One turn. You say "love it" and it saves. You say "show me a lehenga too" and it applies a second one and puts the two side by side. You just react. Nothing behind the tools is new business logic, nothing scrapes the DOM, and no tool can spend money. How we built it The five tools are one file, src/webmcp/useStylistTools.ts . Each is a hook that registers on document.modelContext with a JSON-schema input and a handler that calls something the page already had: the garment-select function, the looks tray, the reaction bar. search_catalog is a keyword-scored filter with its own unit tests. apply_tryon loads a default photo if you haven't picked one, so the loop works cold. await_reaction is dual-mode: the agent passes the reaction it heard in chat and gets guidance back, or it leaves the argument out and the call blocks until you tap a chip. Either way the app shows what you said. @mcp-b/global installs document.modelContext where the browser doesn't have it and defers to the native one where it does, so the same code works in Chrome's native WebMCP and in ChatGPT's browser. The tool annotations pull weight too: search_catalog is read-only, the writes are idempotent, and apply_tryon 's response tells the agent to call await_reaction next. There's a Playwright test that runs every tool through getTools() / executeTool() and checks 19 things. Under it is the try-on pipeline: LiteRT.js on WebGPU with a Wasm fallback, MediaPipe segmentation, MoveNet pose, and a thin-plate-spline garment warp written from scratch and rendered as a triangle mesh. It's published as @practics/tryon-core ; the app is a thin React shell over it. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is days old. The spec renamed navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext mid-build, and no stable browser ships it yet. The main thing to check was that the polyfill actually steps aside for the native API when there is one. It does. The agent kept web-searching instead of using the tools. Half of that was our fault (we hadn't redeployed). The rest is that ChatGPT is careful about site tools: it needs "use sitetools:" in the prompt and a model that supports WebMCP. A console check confirmed the tools had reached ChatGPT's runtime, so the fix was on their side, not ours. await_reaction never fired in chat. You type "love it" and the agent just reads it off the transcript. That's why it's dual-mode now. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in a real agent against the live site, not a mock. Five tools, a reaction channel that works from a sentence or a tap, an end-to-end test, and no server or new business logic anywhere. And the human stays in charge: you see every move the agent makes, and you make the final call. What we learned WebMCP changes the design question from "what can the agent do" to "what should stay with the person". For a stylist that's fit and taste, and the tools are shaped to leave it alone. Tool wording matters more than we expected. The hint that apply_tryon drops about await_reaction changed the flow, and the agent started borrowing our chip labels ("Love it, Good, or try another?") into its own replies. And a blocking tool is wrong for a chat agent that already has the answer; meeting the person where they are, chip or sentence, worked better. What's next for Virtual Try-On + AI Stylist A paid HD tier as a render_hd tool: a server-side diffusion render, offered only after you've settled on a look. A checkout tool that runs only on an explicit confirmation from you, never the agent alone. A bigger catalog; the pipeline already handles pants and multi-piece outfits. And folding the tool layer into @practics/tryon-core , so any store widget built on the pipeline gets the agent surface for free. The on-device try-on pipeline underneath is my earlier work. title: VisaFlow: The Adaptive WebMCP Agent
pitch: VisaFlow turns a 55-field visa form into a guided voice conversation. It uses WebMCP to select the right path, derive answers, fill the live application, and flag only what needs review.
about_excerpt: VisaFlow turns a 55-field visa form into a guided voice conversation. It uses WebMCP to select the right path, derive answers, fill the live application, and flag only what needs review. Like Comment Story Updates Application completed Meet VisaFlow WebMCP in action One answer, many fields Inspiration Long forms force people to translate their life story into an unfamiliar sequence of fields. Conditional applications make this worse: users answer questions that may not apply, repeat information across sections, and often discover missing evidence only near the end. We wanted to explore a different future for the web—one where a person explains their situation naturally, an agent connects the details, and the website remains responsible for its own rules and safety constraints. What it does VisaFlow turns a deliberately long 55-field visitor-visa application into a guided voice or text conversation. A user can describe their trip naturally, speak their answers, type them, or attach supporting documents. The agent then: identifies whether the application is for tourism, business, or a family visit; selects the correct funding and prior-travel branches; removes questions that do not apply; extracts multiple supported facts from each answer; calculates transparent derived values such as trip duration; fills reasonable interpretations while clearly flagging them for review; asks one story-shaped follow-up covering several related gaps; shows every WebMCP action and live application progress; and consolidates uncertain and sensitive values into one editable final-review queue. After every applicable field and review item is resolved, the user can finish the fictional application and see a completion receipt. Why WebMCP An LLM alone could generate a possible JSON object, but it would need a hardcoded copy of the form schema, routing rules, and validation logic. Alternatively, it would have to manipulate fragile DOM selectors and click through every conditional page. WebMCP gives the agent a live semantic contract owned by the website. VisaFlow publishes 22 typed tools that let an agent inspect possible routes, select the applicable flow, discover missing requirements, apply structured answers, attach evidence references, calculate derived insights, resolve conflicts, and request human review. WebMCP is not decorative in this project: application changes go through website-owned tool handlers. Every write is validated for route applicability, field type, allowed choices, date ranges, confidence, provenance, and review requirements before it reaches shared application state. This enables something that was previously difficult: a person can tell one coherent story, an agent can connect that story across many conditional fields, and the website can safely accept only the values allowed by its current rules—without page-by-page navigation. Human-agent collaboration The human provides meaning and judgment. The agent extracts, connects, derives, and decides what to ask next. The website validates every action and keeps uncertainty visible. Explicit user statements, document facts, deterministic derivations, and AI proposals remain visibly separate. Sensitive or uncertain values are never silently treated as verified. The user reviews and corrects them once before completing the application. How we built it The application uses React, TypeScript, and Vite with a government-service-inspired interface. On page load, VisaFlow registers 22 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . A WebMCP-capable agent can discover these tools at runtime and execute them without knowing the DOM structure. A same-origin Worker endpoint uses the OpenAI Responses API with GPT-5.6 Terra and a strict structured-output schema. Each turn includes the current route, resolved answers, remaining applicable questions, recent conversation history, remembered partial facts, and pending review fields. The LLM returns a plan containing explicit facts, document facts, safe derivations, reviewable proposals, route decisions, and the next question. It never writes application state directly. The client converts the plan into WebMCP calls, and the website validates and applies them. Voice recognition, spoken questions, multilingual interfaces, document extraction, visible WebMCP activity, browser-local drafts, and the completion flow are integrated into one coherent experience. Challenges The hardest problems were preventing the conversation from forgetting previously stated facts, resolving phrases such as “this year,” extracting many useful facts from one answer, and avoiding repeated address questions. We also had to ensure route changes happened before field validation, preserve incomplete facts between turns, batch WebMCP writes safely, distinguish derived values from invented values, and keep document extraction useful without allowing documents to act as instructions. Accomplishments A working 55-field adaptive application rather than a single autofill demo 22 non-trivial WebMCP tools with typed schemas and validation Dynamic application routing with irrelevant-question removal Voice, text, document, and multilingual interaction Visible provenance, derived values, progress, and semantic actions A consolidated final-review experience A gated fictional completion receipt 32 automated tests across domain, WebMCP, and integrated UI behavior What we learned The most important lesson was that an agent should not own a website’s rules. The website should publish capabilities and remain authoritative, while the model focuses on understanding natural language and planning. WebMCP makes that separation possible. It allows an agent to be flexible without making application writes opaque or unsafe. We also learned that conversational form completion works best when the agent asks for coherent parts of a person’s story, rather than disguising several traditional form labels as a chatbot question. What's next Next, we would test VisaFlow with more external WebMCP agents, expand accessibility testing, support additional document formats and application domains, and add encrypted cross-device draft storage. The same architecture could support healthcare enrollment, insurance claims, benefits applications, university admissions, and other conditional workflows. title: Vivid
pitch: Vivid turns any dashboard into an agent editable surface - no MCP server, no vision model, just the browser tab exposing its own governed webmcp tools.
about_excerpt: Vivid turns any dashboard into an agent editable surface - no MCP server, no vision model, just the browser tab exposing its own governed webmcp tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept seeing the same demo of "agentic BI": a headless MCP server that spits out a chart, or a vision model squinting at a screenshot to figure out where to click. Neither one understands the chart it's looking at, and neither lets a person and an agent actually work on the same dashboard together. WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool offers a different answer — the page exposes its own tools, the tab itself becomes the tool surface, nothing in between. I built Vivid to see if that holds up on something real: a six-panel B2B SaaS revenue dashboard, not a toy chart. What it does Vivid is a live analytics workspace with two dashboards — a six-panel revenue report (Northbeam) and a product-usage report (Activity OS) — that an agent can read and edit right in the same tab a person is looking at. No MCP server behind it, no model reading screenshots. The agent can pull live report context, set filters (segment, region, plan tier, channel, contract type, account), and reshape specific charts. ARR bridge and NRR/churn retention take a validated patch to their underlying state — never a raw spec. ARR mix, top accounts, and net-new logos only let the agent swap between a couple of approved presentations, like donut vs. bar. A semantic layer — Cube Cloud over 7 real Postgres tables — grounds open-ended questions ("MRR by region") in real metric definitions instead of guessed column names. And it's genuinely shared: every edit, person or agent, goes through the same validation, persists to a room, syncs live to everyone on that room's link, can be undone, and lands in one activity log with both actors in it. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript. Two report surfaces, each with its own filter state and its own WebMCP tools, registered only while that tab is open. The two agent-editable charts (ARR bridge, retention) are Vega-Lite specs rendered via vega-embed, but the spec is derived from a small "knob" object, never written directly. Everything else is plain SVG/CSS. A lighter contract ( set_report_chart_contract ) later opened up three more panels — ARR mix, top accounts, net-new logos — to an allow-listed presentation swap, still no direct spec access. The tool layer is document.modelContext.registerTool calls made from the page: read-only ( get_report_context , list_report_options , find_field_values ) and mutating ( update_chart_spec , set_report_filters ), each validating input before touching state. Every call returns { ok: true, data } or { ok: false, reason, error } . Persistence is one JSON snapshot per room, mutated only through a Supabase Edge Function and a Postgres RPC that checks a capability digest, compare-and-swaps the version, and writes state plus an activity-log row in one transaction. RLS blocks direct table writes — no shortcut around validation. The semantic layer is Cube Cloud over those same 7 tables, reached only through an Edge Function proxy — the API token never touches the browser. Two more tools, get_business_definitions and query_business_metric , answer questions unrelated to either report's charts. Challenges I ran into document.modelContext is a draft API — I didn't have a browser that ships it. So I injected a minimal registerTool polyfill through devtools and added a re-entry point ( window.__vividRegisterTools() ) to still exercise the real execute functions end to end: discovery, validation, re-render, persistence, activity log. Not a live agent, but as close as I could get without one. Making "never dual-axis" actually true took longer than expected. Telling an agent not to do something is easy; making the schema incapable of expressing the bad state is harder. I kept finding invariants that were still just conventions until I pushed them into the validator. Adversarial input was its own problem once I accepted an agent writing state needs the same suspicion as a hostile user — oversized values, SQL-looking field names, injection attempts, spoofed capabilities, UUID reuse. A dedicated test suite covers all of it; the rule was every one has to fail cleanly, never a crash or a silent partial write. Keeping Revenue and Product Usage independent without duplicating everything was a constant judgment call — separate filters and tool sets, but one shared wire protocol and undo pattern underneath both. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A full WebMCP tool contract — discovery, reads, validated writes, real error reasons — running end to end with nothing mocked, verified without a shipping WebMCP browser in hand. Invariants that hold because the validator won't let them break, not because a tool description asked nicely. An adversarial security pass that throws real hostile input at every mutation path and degrades cleanly every time — no crashes, no silent writes. Multiplayer that isn't faked for the demo: agent and person edits share one path, one sync, one log. A semantic layer with zero shared imports back into the chart code — it'd survive being lifted into a different app. Something live at vividdata.pages.dev a judge can actually click through. What I learned Chart-as-data instead of chart-as-code is what makes this trustworthy. I could've let the agent send a raw Vega-Lite spec — I didn't. Every editable chart runs off a small typed object, and the spec is derived from it. That's the decision that made invariants real instead of aspirational. MCP and WebMCP aren't rivals — they're two stages of the same job. MCP gets you a fast first draft: a headless server hands an agent the data, it produces something in one shot. But getting a draft right after that is visual and iterative — "make the bars wider," "try it as a donut," "now filter to EMEA" — and a headless server has nothing on screen to see or touch for that. WebMCP picks up right there. A semantic layer changed what "grounded" meant in practice — real metric definitions instead of guessed column names made the gap between a correct answer and a confident wrong one a lot more visible. Multiplayer forced honesty about state. Once edits sync live into a shared log, you can't hand-wave version tracking — it's a real compare-and-swap, or two edits eventually stomp on each other. What's next for Vivid Right now this proves the idea on one dashboard. I want chart-as-data to stop being specific to Northbeam and become a pattern other people's dashboards use. That means pulling the governed-presentation contract and the knob-based chart state out of this codebase into something closer to a spec — small and documented enough that any team could implement it over their own charts without re-deriving these invariants from scratch. I also want Vivid to stop being a demo of one dashboard and become a place people actually work. Connect Data already proves the generic version — point at any Postgres table, get an agent-editable chart through a validated contract — I want that to be the default onboarding, not a hidden tab. The semantic layer should scale past one Cube deployment over 7 tables — the same shared-key discipline tying a chart's knobs to its metric definition could stretch across multiple warehouses. I like the idea of more than one agent in a room at once — a drafting agent proposing something, a review agent checking it against governed invariants, a person steering both — on the same activity log and undo stack that already treats a person and an agent as peers. Before any of that touches real data: real tenancy. The bearer-link model is deliberately bare-bones; authenticated rooms and real capability revocation are what turn this from a convincing prototype into something a company could point at its own numbers. And longer term — every BI vendor is racing to ship its own locked-in MCP server. My bet runs the other way: WebMCP means any agent, not just the vendor's own, can reach into a live chart. That only matters if more than one surface adopts the pattern, which is why I want to pull it out into something reusable instead of leaving it bolted to this one app. Built With cube-cloud deno mcp model-context-protocol oxlint postgresql react semantic-layer supabase supabase-edge-functions supabase-realtime typescript vega vega-embed vega-lite vite webmcp Try it out vividdata.pages.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Nitish Pamarty Like Share this project: Updates Nitish Pamarty started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:52 AM EDT

title: Voxel WebMCP
pitch: An agent-native voxel sandbox: AI Agent builds, and explores your 3D world by calling WebMCP tools directly — no clicking, no DOM guessing.
about_excerpt: An agent-native voxel sandbox: AI Agent builds, and explores your 3D world by calling WebMCP tools directly — no clicking, no DOM guessing. Like Comment Story Updates GIF Agent build house GIF Agent build pixelart GIF Agent build district GIF Building the beacon with the agent GIF Experimenting with dynamic seasons GIF The final seasonal loop around the beacon Inspiration The idea for Voxel Web MCP came from WorldEdit, a tool I used in voxel sandbox games as a kid. Back then, building anything large meant running around the world, selecting coordinates, and manually entering commands for every wall, region, replacement, or correction. When we first saw WebMCP, we wondered what would happen if an agent could use similar geometric operations directly inside a browser-based 3D world. Instead of telling it which exact blocks to place, could we simply describe the final intention in natural language? A voxel world felt like a particularly demanding test. It is not a form, a store, or a collection of buttons. It is a procedurally generated three-dimensional environment containing terrain, materials, structures, coordinates, and a moving player. If an agent could understand and meaningfully modify that through WebMCP, the same approach could potentially work across many other complex web applications. What it does Voxel Web MCP is a browser-based voxel sandbox where a human player and an AI agent can build together. The player can make requests such as: Build a seaside house with a pier. Inspect this small architectural model and transform it into a full-scale structure. Replace one material throughout a building. Recreate an attached image as voxel pixel art. Copy, move, rotate, mirror, or repeat an existing region. Inspect the terrain around the player before deciding what to build. The agent operates as a world editor around the player. It understands the player's position, viewing direction, targeted block, world boundaries, available materials, and selected regions of voxel geometry. We deliberately did not create semantic tools such as build_house . The application only exposes reusable geometric primitives. The agent must decide for itself what should become a wall, roof, window, tower, road, or complete building. This makes the experience open-ended: the tools are not tied to a collection of predefined demonstrations. How we built it We started with VoxelSrv, an open-source browser voxel game built on noa-engine and Babylon.js, and created our own WebMCP integration layer. The application registers eleven structured tools through the browser's document.modelContext API. They cover: operating guidance for the agent; world boundaries and the material catalog; player position and viewing direction; compact region scanning; batch block placement and replacement; copying, moving, mirroring, rotating, and stacking regions; WorldEdit-style undo. The game runs both its client and authoritative single-player server inside the browser. The server runs in a Web Worker, while WebMCP calls travel from the main page to that worker through correlated messages. World edits are applied by the authoritative server and sent back to the renderer as normal block updates. The world is stored locally in IndexedDB. Players can save, regenerate, export, and import worlds without requiring an external database or game server. We also added a Docker build that compiles the Vite application in a Node.js stage and serves the final static bundle through Nginx. The context problem Writing blocks was not the hardest part. The real challenge was giving the agent an affordable and reliable understanding of a three-dimensional space. The agent should not have to reconstruct the world from screenshots, and sending every voxel as raw JSON would consume an unreasonable amount of context. In one representative region, a raw dump required roughly 49,000 tokens. We therefore designed a progressive inspection system. The agent can begin with a cheap summary, request a heightmap when it needs terrain information, or inspect selected two-dimensional slices when it needs to understand floors, walls, roofs, and elevations. The application also provides an explicit coordinate basis: the player's forward, right, and up directions, along with the exact block being targeted. This allows the agent to interpret requests such as “behind me,” “in front of me,” or “continue to the right” without guessing camera geometry. Challenges we faced The upstream engine was built around an older JavaScript ecosystem. Making it work with a modern Vite build required pinning compatible versions of noa-engine, Babylon.js, the voxel protocol, and several legacy dependencies. The game also uses multiple browser execution contexts. The renderer runs on the main thread, while the authoritative world and terrain generation run in Web Workers. WebMCP edits therefore had to update the server's real world state and remain synchronized with the client's chunk cache and rendered meshes. Other challenges included: keeping world inspection compact enough for an agent's context; providing useful material descriptions without duplicating them across every tool; making large edits visible without flooding the renderer; supporting concurrent tool calls while preserving understandable undo behavior; restoring reliable mouse input after browser focus changes; adapting camera controls for agent browsers that cannot use relative mouse movement; preserving worlds locally and adding portable import and export. What we learned The most surprising result was how much an agent could accomplish with a relatively small set of general-purpose tools. It did not need a dedicated house generator or a library of predefined structures. Once it could inspect the terrain, understand the player, discover available materials, and perform geometric operations, it began producing coherent and often genuinely creative architecture. We also learned that agent context is part of the product's interface. Tool descriptions alone are not enough for spatial work. Coordinate systems, compact representations, world limits, material semantics, and clear operating guidance all directly affect the quality of the result. Most importantly, WebMCP allows the agent to stop being a chat window beside an application and become an active participant inside it. What's next The current version focuses on a single-player creative sandbox, but the same model can extend much further. An agent could work with a normal player's inventory and permissions, assist multiple players in a shared world, automate level-design workflows, manipulate other kinds of 3D editors, or interact with entirely different WebMCP-enabled applications. WebMCP creates a shared interface between agents and web applications. Compatible agents can change without requiring the application to be redesigned around each one, while the application can evolve without changing the basic way agents discover and use its capabilities. Today, that application is a voxel world. Tomorrow, it could be almost anything on the web. title: Waggle
pitch: My agent reads every word and can't send one. Proposals, not posts — my signed ✅ is the approval, from any device. The agent dances. Only I can fly.
about_excerpt: My agent reads every word and can't send one. Proposals, not posts — my signed ✅ is the approval, from any device. The agent dances. Only I can fly. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "agent in chat" design we have seen gives the agent an account: its own key, its own memberships, its own audit trail. That is right for an agent that works in the room as a peer. It is wrong for the agent at your elbow — the one reading over your shoulder that says "want me to answer that?" That agent should have no key at all . WebMCP is the first thing that makes that agent practical: the tools live in your tab, under your session, and they can see what you are looking at. No server, no OAuth, no bot account. What it does Waggle is a small NIP-29 group-chat client that publishes twelve WebMCP tools. Seven are reads — the current view (including the message you have selected), channels, a channel's messages, a thread, search, a member. Five are propose_* tools — message, reply, reaction, channel topic, join. A proposal is not a post: it is a card in the Waggles dock. You edit it, then Sign & send with a key the agent never touches, or reject it. The signed event carries ["proposed-by","webmcp","<n>"] , so anyone reading the relay can tell agent-drafted from hand-typed. How we built it src/tools/ is framework-free and talks only to a WaggleContext interface, so the same tools can be lifted into another client. Registration uses document.modelContext.registerTool with readOnlyHint annotations on reads. src/relay/ speaks NIP-29 + NIP-42 + NIP-50 over nostr-tools, with a mock relay for zero-network demos. Identity is NIP-07 if present, otherwise a key generated in the page. The demo relay is a real Buzz relay we deployed for this, open to throwaway keys so judges can post. scripts/e2e.mjs proves the loop through the browser's own API: getTools() → executeTool() → human click → event found on the relay by an unrelated key, provenance intact. Challenges Chrome passes execute() its arguments as a JSON string, and navigator.modelContext is deprecated in favour of document.modelContext — both learned by running the real browser, not the docs. The relay rejects events more than 15 minutes off server time, which shaped how we seed a believable conversation. And the hardest design question was the smallest one: the button says Sign & send , not Send, because the word sign is the whole point. What's next Carry the tools module into Buzz as a right-dock feature, and emit Buzz's reserved approval kinds (46010/46030) so a proposal, its ruling, and the resulting message are three linked events in one log — the correction log an agent can learn from. Testing instructions No login, no credentials: Waggle generates a throwaway Nostr key in your browser on first load, and the demo relay accepts it. Open https://app.waggle.thecrowbarcrew.cc in a WebMCP-capable browser: ChatGPT desktop app → Work → its built-in browser (Site tools on in Settings → Browser → Permissions), or Chrome 150+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled plus the Model Context Tool Inspector extension or DevTools → Application → WebMCP. The header chip should read WebMCP · 12 tools (green). In ChatGPT, "Site tools" in the address bar lists them. Try: "What did I miss in #general?" — then click any message and say "Reply to this saying thanks, I'll take a look." A proposal card appears in the right-hand dock; nothing is sent until you click Sign & send . The cross-site errand: "Check the shop for a leather bag under $200 and answer Marco" — the store's URL is findable in Marco's thread in #general. Zero-network mode for a quick look: append ?relay=mock . Manual tool bench: ?dev=1 . #try-waggle is the sandbox channel — post anything. title: WattWeave
pitch: Turn a peak-energy alert into a safe, visible load plan in seconds
about_excerpt: Turn a peak-energy alert into a safe, visible load plan in seconds Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When a building receives a demand-response event or sudden price spike, facilities operators must reduce peak load without disrupting critical equipment or violating occupant constraints. Existing energy dashboards show charts but leave operators to manually coordinate dozens of devices and schedules. The core problem is that reducing total energy is not the same as reducing the critical peak, and manual changes can create dangerous rebound peaks later. We were inspired by the need for a collaborative human-AI interface where operators define what cannot change (critical loads, departure targets, comfort bounds) while an agent discovers, simulates, and applies safe load-shifting plans—all with full visibility, cancellability, and reversibility. What it does WattWeave is an interactive building-energy sandbox where a human pins non-negotiable constraints and an agent discovers, simulates, stages, and applies a safe load-shifting plan inside the same visual interface. Core workflow: Operator locks critical loads directly on the timeline (server room, accessibility equipment) Agent reads the live demand event, locks, and flexible assets through WebMCP tools Cancellable simulation sweeps across the timeline, generating up to 3 candidate plans Operator compares candidates by peak, cost, comfort impact, and rebound risk Selected plan renders as a ghost preview on the load chart and energy-flow diagram Operator approves the exact schedule diff in a visible approval drawer Agent commits the plan; the live meter falls below the target line One-click rollback restores the exact prior schedule with full audit trail Key features: Deterministic 15-minute slot model with integer watt-hour precision Transparent heuristic constraint solver (not a black-box optimizer) Dynamic WebMCP tool registration based on UI state Safety model: critical loads never change, commit requires visible approval, stale plans rejected Animated "living grid" energy-flow visualization Offline deterministic sandbox mode (no API keys required) Optional Pro features: side-by-side candidate comparison, audit export, animated particle flow How we built it Tech stack: React 19.1.0 + TypeScript 5.9.2 + Vite 7.1.5 Zustand 5.0.8 for state management Zod 4.1.5 for schema validation and JSON Schema generation Web Workers for off-main-thread simulation with real cancellation Vitest 3.2.4 for unit tests and intent evals Playwright 1.55.0 for end-to-end browser journeys Remotion for polished demo video production Architecture: domain/ - Pure, framework-free core: types, time model, seed data, schedule logic, constraint solver sim/ - Web Worker bridge with AbortSignal support for clean cancellation webmcp/ - 10 semantic tools with dynamic state-scoped registration via navigator.modelContext state/ - Zustand store with pulse bus for tool-effect animations components/ - React UI: load timeline, flow view, asset panel, planner, approval drawer, inspector billing/ - Polar.sh integration with offline demo mode WebMCP integration: Tools are registered dynamically based on UI state— get_selected_asset only exists while an asset is selected, commit_load_plan is undiscoverable until the operator clicks approve. Every tool execution animates its effect on the UI so humans can see what the agent did. Testing: 36 unit tests covering solver logic, time model, and 15 intent evals 9 Playwright E2E journeys including external agent integration Intent evals drive real WebMCP tools headlessly, exactly as an agent would Challenges we ran into Cancellation semantics - Making AbortSignal work cleanly through Web Worker → solver → checkpoint without state mutation required careful architecture. We solved it with a structured CANCELED result and explicit checkpoint boundaries. Stale plan rejection - Ensuring operators can't accidentally approve plans based on outdated constraints. We implemented scenarioVersion bumping on every constraint change and rejection by name in simulate/preview/stage/commit. Exact rollback - Generating mathematically precise inverse schedules that restore the baseline array exactly. We solved this by negating every integer-Wh delta at staging time and storing the inverse alongside the staged plan. Untrusted content handling - The utility tariff feed in our scenario contains a literal prompt injection. We return it inside an untrusted envelope with warnings, keeping numeric data structured and separate. Dynamic tool registration - Making the tool list itself serve as the permission model. We implemented state-scoped registration where tools appear/disappear based on selection, staging, and approval state. Rebound peak detection - Naïve load-shifting can create worse peaks after the event window. We added explicit 60-minute post-event rebound analysis with guard thresholds. Accomplishments that we're proud of Semantic over scraping: WebMCP tools encode meaning (e.g., "pre-cool auditorium by 30 minutes within comfort bounds") rather than pixel coordinates, making agent actions reliable and interpretable. Safety-critical guarantees: Critical loads never change, commit requires visible human approval, cancellation is clean, rollback is exact, and untrusted content stays data. Transparent solver: We show the full scoring breakdown (peak 32 · rebound 25 · cost 20 · comfort 10) and explicitly state "best candidate found by the deterministic heuristic, not a claim of optimality." Real cancellation: AbortSignal propagates through Web Worker to solver checkpoints, returning structured CANCELED with zero state mutation—no hangs, no rejected promises. Deterministic demo: The entire hero scenario (212 kW → 168 kW, both EV targets met, 160 kW rebound) is reproducible without any external APIs or random data. Comprehensive testing: 15 intent evals prove the WebMCP contract, 36 unit tests cover domain logic, and 9 E2E journeys validate the full user and agent workflows. Beautiful "living grid" UI: Frosted translucent panels, animated particle flow tracking real dispatch numbers, springy motion, and full accessibility support. What we learned WebMCP is transformative for agent-human collaboration: Shared live state through a single Zustand store eliminates the drift that plagues chart-scraping approaches. The tool list itself becomes the permission model. Cancellation is a first-class feature: Real cancellation requires architectural commitment—checkpoint boundaries, structured results, and zero state mutation on abort. It's not an afterthought. Scoring transparency builds trust: Showing the full breakdown and explicitly disclaiming optimality is more honest than hiding the heuristic. Users appreciate understanding why a plan was recommended. The approval pattern is powerful: Making commit_load_plan undiscoverable until the human clicks approve creates a strong structural guarantee. The tool surface itself encodes the permission model. Integer arithmetic matters: Using 15-minute slots and integer watt-hours internally avoids floating-point surprises that could corrupt schedule calculations. Untrusted content needs structural boundaries: Returning prompt injections inside an untrusted envelope with warnings keeps the app safe while still displaying the information. E2E tests with external agents are invaluable: The Playwright journey that injects a real navigator.modelContext and drives the full lifecycle outside the app proves the WebMCP contract without spending model tokens. What's next for WattWeave Real control gateway integration: Complete the documented Home Assistant loopback adapter with organization authentication, transport security, command allowlists, and site-specific safety interlocks. Multi-building scenarios: Extend the deterministic seed data to support additional building types (office, retail, hospital) with different asset profiles and constraint patterns. Historical analysis: Add time-series exploration of past demand events, committed schedules, and their outcomes to support learning and refinement. Collaborative mode: Multi-operator support with role-based permissions, constraint proposal workflows, and team audit trails. Advanced solver strategies: Implement additional candidate generation strategies (thermal mass pre-conditioning, predictive battery dispatch, machine-learning-assisted feasibility analysis). Mobile optimization: Responsive design improvements for tablet and field-operator use cases. title: WebMCP Demo — a live map for thinking with your own agent
pitch: Put down what you want to think through. Your own ChatGPT grows the map with you — and it becomes a plan.
about_excerpt: Put down what you want to think through. Your own ChatGPT grows the map with you — and it becomes a plan. Like Comment Story Updates The live map: your own ChatGPT asks questions, clears "don't know" marks, and turns branches into checkable tasks — via 6 WebMCP tools. What it does Most WebMCP demos let an agent operate a site's transactional surface — fill a form, add to cart. This project inverts that: the page is a blank thinking canvas, and the tools it publishes are generative . You put down one thing you want to figure out ("I want to buy my first home"), and your own ChatGPT — with your context and memory — thinks with you on the map: It starts by asking questions as nodes , not by dumping a plan. You answer by growing branches yourself ; every edit you make on the canvas is delivered to the agent on its next tool call. Mark anything with "Don't know" and your confusion literally becomes the agenda — the agent clears those marks first, with concrete first steps. Steps become checkable task nodes , a Plan view folds the map into goal / premises / next tasks, and checking a task off in either place updates both. The page runs no AI of its own . It publishes six WebMCP tools; the visitor brings the intelligence. Thoughtful use of WebMCP The interesting problems turned out to be protocol-level, and we solved them in ways any WebMCP app can reuse: Read-before-write, enforced server-side. read_map returns a state token; every write requires it. A stale or missing token gets a 409 whose error text steers the agent back to read_map . The guard doubles as optimistic locking between the human and the agent. Human actions as first-class input. Everything the human does on the canvas (add, edit, move, delete, mark, check) is queued and delivered inside the next tool result — with a consuming read reserved for the agent and a non-consuming variant ( ?deliver=0 ) for the page's own refreshes, so the UI can never starve the agent of events. Granularity enforced by schema, not prose. add_nodes accepts at most 3 nodes per call (schema + server both), because a map that fills up in one shot stops feeling like a conversation. A capability split that matches the relationship. Agents can add, annotate, resolve, remove, and bulk-arrange — but the layout engine owns placement, and destructive actions on human-placed nodes are steered to require conversation first. Robust registration in the real world. Tools register before app mount, tolerate late injection of navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext (ChatGPT's browser and Chrome differ), and the footer shows live tool status for devtools-less in-app browsers. Why it matters "I know what I want, but not the way there" is a universal state — buying a home, relocating, incorporating, a first tax return. Chat alone answers and scrolls away; to-do apps assume you already know the steps. A shared, persistent map that your own agent can touch bridges the two: the conversation leaves a structure, and the structure becomes a plan you can execute and check off. Because the page hosts no model and pays no inference cost, this pattern is adoptable by any site: publish tools, let visitors bring their agents. How we built it Go + Postgres single-origin service (API, SSE live updates, static React/TypeScript SPA) on Render. The canvas is Miro-like: pan/zoom, drag, click-to-grow, right-click menu. A height-aware tidy-tree layout engine keeps the map clean after every structural change, verified against real DOM rects. WebMCP tool descriptions live in one file — they were the main behavior-tuning surface, iterated against the real ChatGPT desktop browser. What's next Multiple maps as a shelf, session-to-session continuity ("continue from where the fog cleared last week"), and the same canvas working with other WebMCP-capable agents out of the box. title: Labmate
pitch: An AI lab where your tutor watches the experiment, not the chat. The agent proposes evidence, the learner stays in control — bidirectional tutoring on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An AI lab where your tutor watches the experiment, not the chat. The agent proposes evidence, the learner stays in control — bidirectional tutoring on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When we entered the WebMCP Challenge, our honest goal was to check what we could do with it. The showcase examples were mostly agents filling shopping carts and forms — useful, but one-directional: the agent acts, the page obeys. Meanwhile, every AI tutor we knew worked beside an educational tool, never inside it. The learner plays with a simulation, then manually types what happened into a chat; the model reasons from a stale summary and, worst of all, happily does the thinking the student was supposed to do. That combination suggested a question: what if the tutor lived inside the lab page itself — reading the same live bench, proposing evidence, but structurally unable to take over the scientific method? A tutor that is bidirectional: the agent sees what the learner actually did, and the learner sees and approves everything the agent actually proposes. LabMate is our answer. What it does LabMate is a 15-minute high-school physics inquiry around one LED circuit, following the scientific method: Predict → Design → Evidence → Reflect . The learner states a prediction ("if resistance decreases, the LED gets brighter because current increases") and locks it. The hypothesis and the final conclusion are learner-owned : visible to the agent, writable by no tool. Through WebMCP, the agent sees the exact live bench — voltages, saved trials, the current stage, model limits, and the page's revision number. It proposes one fair experiment at a time. The proposal appears as a preview card and touches nothing until the learner approves, edits, or rejects it. The demo's climax is a confound challenge: the learner changes the voltage from 5 V to 9 V after the agent last looked. The agent's now-outdated proposal is rejected atomically ( stale_revision ), because it was written against a world it never observed. The agent re-inspects, spots the second variable, and proposes a revised trial that restores a valid controlled comparison. Once a controlled pair exists, the page compares trials and reports the valid pairs. The learner — not the agent — answers four reflection prompts (what changed, what stayed constant, what the measurements show, whether the prediction was supported) and locks the conclusion. Under the hood, the simulation is a conceptual teaching model: $I = V/R$, $P = V \times I$, LED brightness bands keyed to current, and six trial slots — of which the agent may fill at most four, so one slot is always reserved for the learner. Every accepted mutation increments a shared revision and records a Human/Agent receipt, so the collaboration is auditable. And when document.modelContext is unavailable, the status chip flips to LAB READY and the whole lab still works in a regular browser. How we built it The app is a static front end: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Tailwind CSS with shadcn-derived controls. No database, no login, no OpenAI API calls, and deliberately no custom chat surface. Everything — human clicks and agent tool calls — flows through one revision-safe command layer: gates → validation → revision + 1 → a single atomic state update → a receipt. The agent's three Site tools are thin views over those same commands: inspect_experiment() — the only read-only tool; returns the full experiment snapshot. propose_trial(...) — the approval gate; creates a visible preview card, not evidence. compare_trials(...) — surfaces controlled pairs. Two discipline points we refused to compromise on: every tool schema rejects extra fields ( additionalProperties: false ), and actor is never accepted from the model — the registration adapter pins it to agent . Failures are structured codes ( hypothesis_required , approval_required , student_slot_reserved , stale_revision , trial_limit_reached …), never prose, so the agent can actually replan from them. For quality: 26 Vitest unit/contract tests and 3 Playwright flows, including a document.modelContext shim that lets us test the full agent loop headlessly — plus a live run in ChatGPT's desktop browser. typecheck , test , test:e2e , build , and lint are all green. Challenges we ran into Trust by construction. The hardest question wasn't "how does the agent help" but "how do we guarantee it can't write the conclusion?" Our answer is structural: learner-owned fields exist in the page state but in no tool schema. There is nothing for the model to call. Two authors, one page. Human and agent mutate the same state concurrently. Optimistic concurrency ( expected_revision ) makes stale writes fail atomically — but making that rejection legible , so the agent understands "the world changed, look again," took real schema and prompt design. A deterministic demo with a probabilistic actor. Our centerpiece moment depends on the model doing the right thing on stage. We shaped the tools (one-proposal-at-a-time, structured errors) and the demo prompts so the inspect → propose → human-intervenes → stale-rejection → replan loop happens reliably. Testing without ChatGPT. CI can't drive the desktop app, so we mirrored document.modelContext in a Playwright shim and contract-tested the adapter against it. Honest scope. The simulation is a conceptual teaching model: overloaded is a teaching warning above 20 mA, not a real component rating, and forward voltage, tolerance, and temperature are intentionally omitted. The page always says so. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop runs live in ChatGPT's built-in browser: agent proposes → learner approves → human changes the world → stale proposal rejected → agent re-plans → learner concludes, with a receipt for every step. The agent is useful because it is constrained: one proposal at a time, a trial quota that always leaves the learner a slot, and zero silent writes. The lab never depends on the agent: in a plain browser, the pedagogy stays intact. The quality gate is green end-to-end: 26 unit/contract tests, 3 e2e flows, typecheck, build, lint. What we learned Treating the page as the source of truth turns tool design into contract design . Structured error codes beat chat prose for agent replanning. Human–agent experience is mostly a state machine: who may write what, when, and what happens when the world changes under the agent. Getting that machine right is the product. Strictness is what makes trust possible: additionalProperties: false and a pinned actor are the difference between learner control as an aspiration and as an invariant. "The agent may only propose" felt restrictive at first — it turned out to be the feature. It kept the experiments fair and kept the student thinking. What's next for LabMate More missions on the same Predict → Design → Evidence → Reflect skeleton — optics, kinematics, reaction rates — with teacher-authored content. A classroom view so teachers can see receipts, common confounds, and where students get stuck. Extracting the pattern : learner-owned fields, approval gates, revision-safe commands, and agent quotas generalize beyond this lab, and we want to package them for other "human-owned page, agent coach" sites built on WebMCP.
