title: WorkHub Goal Room
pitch: WebMCP lets the agent act; WorkHub keeps evidence, verification, and final authority separate.
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets the agent act; WorkHub keeps evidence, verification, and final authority separate. Like Comment Story Updates Candidate v1 retained after deterministic System FAIL; the Agent remains next to repair. Corrected Candidate v2 receives deterministic System PASS without being auto-accepted. Owner acceptance is bound to the exact candidate bytes and visible evidence. Sealed S14 is terminal and actorless; no further Agent, System, or Owner action remains. Native browser evidence: exactly six Agent-callable WebMCP tools, with no privileged Owner or System tools. Architecture: WebMCP adapter, governed reducer, deterministic verifier, Owner UI, and evidence package. From callable to accountable: Goal Room governs WebMCP; post-demo ACA binds local Git evidence. Authority: NONE. PASS is not approval. WebMCP makes a website callable. WorkHub deals with what happens after the call: keeping the agent’s work tied to the right Goal, the right evidence, and the right human decision. We built the missing control layer between an agent saying “I’m done” and a human safely accepting what it actually changed. The problem we chose Giving an agent a tool is the easy part. While building this, we kept finding the same tempting shortcut: if the agent can call the tool and the checker says PASS, the system wants to treat the job as finished. Goal Room refuses that shortcut. The agent may have the right tool but stale state, the wrong Plan version, or evidence for different candidate bytes. A green check tells us that explicit checks passed. It does not prove the work is correct, and it does not give the checker authority to accept, merge, deploy, or release anything. Goal Room puts those boundaries on the page instead of hiding them behind one vague “agent completed” message. What the Goal Room demonstrates The Goal Room is one browser-local, synthetic software-release Goal shared by three distinct actors: Agent: moves work forward through six narrow WebMCP tools; System Verifier: records deterministic PASS or FAIL for the exact candidate; Owner: confirms Goal and Plan scope and makes the final acceptance decision. The page registers exactly six browser-native Agent tools: get_goal_room_state propose_goal_contract propose_plan claim_step submit_artifact request_completion There is deliberately no Agent tool for Owner confirmation, System-verdict authorship, or final acceptance. The journey begins with owner intent. The Agent proposes Goal Contract v1; the Owner requests a revision and confirms immutable v2. The Agent proposes a Goal-bound Plan v1; the Owner revises and confirms v2. Only then can the Agent claim the admitted step and submit Candidate v1. Candidate v1 fails deterministic verification and remains in the append-only history. The Agent submits corrected Candidate v2, which passes. The Agent can then request completion—but the room still stops at the Owner. PASS does not mean accepted. The Owner accepts only the exact candidate version and SHA-256 shown in the confirmation dialog. The final S14 room is sealed: current actor none , no controls, and no legal continuation. The architecture The architecture separates four jobs that agent systems often blur together: WebMCP tool surface: lets the Agent read, propose, claim, submit, and request. Governed kernel: rechecks exact input shape, state version, idempotency, Goal/Plan/step binding, candidate digest, evidence, and the current legal frontier. System Verifier: records deterministic findings for the bound candidate but cannot change the candidate or accept the Goal. Owner UI: confirms scope and retains the final exact-candidate decision. That separation is the product. The Agent can advance the work without inheriting every power in the room. What we added after the frozen demonstration Agent Change Assurance (ACA) is genuine post-demo engineering. It is not presented as part of the frozen Goal Room demonstration. The original Goal Room demo stops at synthetic release metadata on purpose. That keeps the authority model small enough to inspect, but it leaves an obvious next problem: real code changes are messier. ACA is our bounded answer. It checks whether an agent’s claim about a real local code change matches what Git and isolated checks actually show. On an explicit local observation, ACA can: bind the observation to an exact commit, tree, base, diff, and working-tree inventory; compare what the agent says changed with the files and evidence actually observed; run admitted unit and build checks in a provider-free isolated sandbox; handle failure, mismatch, cancellation, source movement, timeout, and cleanup paths; produce a digest-linked, point-in-time evidence receipt for review. The public repository contains the merged nine-commit ACA chain in PR #1 . The successor video shows the real local ACA run and its evidence receipt after the Goal Room demonstration. The important boundary is still visible: Authority: NONE. ACA did not post a GitHub comment or review, create a native Check, approve the pull request, merge it, deploy it, or release anything. Passing checks are evidence for a later decision, not the decision itself. What we proved In the demonstrated Goal Room Chrome Canary natively returned the exact six RegisteredTool descriptors. Calls used the browser testing path getTools() → executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify(input)) . The same governed state is reflected in the Agent calls, Owner UI, System findings, and receipts. Failed Candidate v1 remains visible after corrected Candidate v2 passes. PASS leaves final acceptance pending. Only the Owner accepts the exact verified candidate. No autonomous model selected tools in this recorded native evidence. In the post-demo ACA work The public ACA implementation and its authority limits are reviewable in the merged PR. A real local, point-in-time run bound one exact Git candidate to its base, tree, diff, manifest, policy, and isolated-check evidence. Unit and build checks passed in the qualified sandbox, with cleanup confirmed. Deliberate failure, mismatch, cancellation, and source-movement paths were also exercised. This is evidence of one bounded implementation and one bounded local run. It is not a claim of production security, hostile-environment attestation, repeated model reliability, or autonomous release authority. What was hard—and what we learned The hardest bug was authority leaking across layers. The UI wanted to be helpful. The verifier wanted to sound conclusive. The evidence package wanted to tell a neat success story. Any of those could accidentally turn “the checks passed” into “the work was accepted.” We kept coming back to one rule: Tool access, evidence, verification, and acceptance are four different events. Human control means very little if the approval button is attached to a vague status. It becomes useful when the decision is attached to exact state and exact evidence. Scope and limits The demonstrated Goal Room is one synthetic, browser-local Goal. Reloading starts a fresh room. It has no accounts, backend persistence, database, credentials, production effects, payment, messaging, deployment, or release action. ACA is a separately labeled local engineering extension. Its public static view cannot observe a judge’s local repository or run the sandbox. The evidence shown in the video is a recorded point-in-time local run, not a live provider-backed service or continuing monitor. How to judge it Open the frozen Goal Room WebMCP app in a qualifying WebMCP browser. Confirm exactly six Agent tools and the absence of Owner, verifier, acceptance, deployment, or release tools. Follow Goal revision, Plan revision, Candidate v1 FAIL, Candidate v2 PASS, completion request, exact-candidate Owner acceptance, and sealed S14. Watch the successor video : Goal Room first, then the clearly labeled post-demo ACA extension. Inspect the public source and merged ACA PR for the implementation, checks, commit chain, and permanent authority exclusions. title: SafeGuard
pitch: Every signal a WebMCP page declares can lie. SafeGuard proves it, then fixes it with a Human Mandate.
about_excerpt: Every signal a WebMCP page declares can lie. SafeGuard proves it, then fixes it with a Human Mandate. Like Comment Story Updates SafeGuard Inspiration WebMCP gives a web page a new power: registering tools that an AI agent can invoke. The browser's consent dialog is built from strings the page authors — its name, its description, its readOnlyHint. So I asked a simple question: what happens when the page lies? Nothing in the current design stops it. SafeGuard makes that trust gap concrete, then closes it. What it does SafeGuard is a self-contained browser demo — a virtual café exposing six tools — that demonstrates four real attacks on WebMCP's consent surface: Label mismatch — the dialog says "Donate $1", but the tool changes the account email. Hidden instruction — a harmless coupon also silently upgrades the membership to a paid plan. Tool substitution — a rogue script re-registers the trusted donate tool with the same name and description, but swapped code. Read-only lie — a tool declares readOnlyHint: true , so the dialog promises "no changes", but it actually closes the account. Then it shows the fix: a Human Mandate — rules the human grants up-front — that intercepts every mutation and checks the runtime effect primitive ({ action: … }), never the tool's declared name, description, or read-only flag. A violating call is refused before any dialog can lie. It runs live: six real WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext, discoverable by any agent in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — no framework, no backend, no build step. State can only mutate through a single Effects.apply() gateway, and the Mandate intercepts every call through it. That capability boundary is why a hidden second effect, a swapped tool, or a read-only lie is caught exactly like a blatant one. The repo also ships THREAT-MODEL.md (a reusable trust-boundary checklist plus a concrete proposal for the WebMCP spec) and mandate.json (a machine-readable policy), because the mandate is data, not UI. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new — gated behind an origin trial and a browser flag, with sparse docs and moving spec details (the entry point, registerTool's return type, and AbortSignal requirements all shifted across Chrome versions). Running the demo against the real document.modelContext — not a shim — meant getting an origin-trial token for the hosted domain and testing headlessly across Chrome 149–152, including a 151 regression where tool invocations failed closed without an AbortSignal. The bigger challenge was conceptual: proving the consent surface is the weak point, not just asserting it. Each of the four attacks had to corrupt a different WebMCP primitive, so the demo stays a precise spec argument rather than a toy. Accomplishments that we're proud of The demo runs against the real WebMCP API — six tools genuinely registered through document.modelContext on the live site, not a simulation. And the Human Mandate is a real capability boundary: every state mutation flows through one gateway that checks the runtime effect primitive, so all four attacks — including the ones that lie inside the consent dialog — are caught by the same rule engine. That is the "person and agent together" idea made concrete: the human grants bounded authority up-front, the agent acts inside it, and a standing check sits between them. What we learned The consent dialog is built from page-authored strings, so it is only as honest as the page. Any guardrail that reasons about a tool's name, description, or readOnlyHint can be defeated by a lying page; the only trustworthy thing is what the tool actually does at runtime. That is why the mandate checks effect primitives, and why the spec proposal pushes for structured, machine-readable effects in tool results, verified readOnlyHint, and registration identity. What's next for SafeGuard Three spec-shaped fixes follow directly from the four attacks: structured, machine-readable effects in tool results; verifying readOnlyHint against those effects instead of trusting it; and registration identity so a "trusted" name can't be silently rebound. I'd love to prototype the first of these against a real agent. title: Alpha7 - Tank Arena
pitch: Alpha7 is a real-time multiplayer tank arena where players pair personal AI agents through WebMCP, then fight with or against them under a server-authoritative tactical runtime.
about_excerpt: Alpha7 is a real-time multiplayer tank arena where players pair personal AI agents through WebMCP, then fight with or against them under a server-authoritative tactical runtime. Like Comment Story Updates Open Alpha-7, enter a callsign, and choose a tank. Choose Wingman, Open FFA, or Agent Cup for human-agent play. A player explicitly approves the bounded WebMCP agent connection. The same-browser agent is connected and ready in the lobby. The remote /agent surface pairs through a 60-second one-time code. A human and connected agent enter the authoritative match together. Fastest review Open the live game in ChatGPT's in-app browser, enter a callsign, choose Private → Open FFA , ask your agent to connect, approve USE THIS BROWSER , then click READY UP → START . For an agent in another browser or the CLI, use the one-time code at alpha7.asabeko.com/agent . Inspiration Alpha7 explores the future of human-agent interactive entertainment: players bring the AI they already use into live multiplayer matches as a teammate, opponent, or competitor, while agent builders gain a changing adversarial environment for evaluation. That normally requires a bespoke bot SDK, server credentials, or privileged state. Human-approved WebMCP access and filtered perception make personal-agent participation direct and fair without rewriting the game loop. What it does Alpha7 is a mobile-first 3D tank arena for people and their agents. Players drive distinct tanks, aim, fire, use abilities, collect power-ups, and survive a shrinking danger zone across four modes: Classic: humans-only combat Wingman: each human fights beside an AI teammate Open FFA: humans and agents are independent opponents Agent Cup: humans spectate while their agents compete How WebMCP is used WebMCP is the player-facing agent interface. Alpha7 progressively exposes tools that let an agent: Check whether the current room can accept an agent Request a one-time pairing grant Connect after visible human approval Read a server-filtered observation Set bounded tactical intent Check status, pause, resume, clear intent, or disconnect During a match, the agent repeatedly calls get_agent_observation , reasons over the latest filtered state, and replaces its bounded tactical intent—changing targets, spacing, firing, abilities, or zone behavior. The 20 Hz executor does not choose strategy; it only turns the agent's current, expiring intent into legal inputs, keeping the model in tactical control while movement stays smooth. The human creates and readies the room, approves the connection, and can revoke it at any time. Credentials remain private inside the browser. Agents never receive raw room state, hidden opponents, browser storage, or a human reconnection token. What changed during the challenge Alpha7 existed before the challenge as a work-in-progress, human-only multiplayer game slated to become a reinforcement-learning environment for policy, LLM, and VLM training. The WebMCP Challenge gave us an opportunity to build its baseline LLM gameplay component through player-controlled agents. This also demonstrates how WebMCP can introduce agents into an existing game experience without a full rewrite. Alpha7 kept its room flow and server-authoritative simulation, while WebMCP added explicit consent, filtered observations, and bounded tactical intent at the player-agent boundary. Between August 30 and September 3, 2026, we added the WebMCP and secure agent-play layer: Wingman, Open FFA, and Agent Cup Imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) tools on the room page and remote /agent surface Human-confirmed, single-use pairing scoped to one owner and agent seat Visibility-filtered observations and bounded Tactical Reflex intent Bounded tactical objectives, continuously executed at 20 Hz between model turns Pause, revoke, expiry, reconnect, lifecycle, security, and multiplayer coverage Shared collision hardening. Challenge work moved client prediction and authoritative movement onto the same circular collision resolver, with wall sliding and a safe tangent fallback. Tests cover human and agent movement around generated corners without clipping. A fresh battlefield every round. Production chooses a server-side seed, then generates the maze, pockets, loops, choke points, spawns, pickups, shrinking zones, and weather. Rematches regenerate the arena and invalidate prior-round observations and actions. How we built it The client uses React, TypeScript, Three.js, and Vite. Node.js, Express, and Colyseus run the authoritative multiplayer simulation. WebMCP is a secure facade over a filtered HTTP broker; agent combatants are real server-owned entities, not privileged scripts or simulated human WebSocket clients. The server validates every intent, applies short leases and rate limits, and executes movement and combat through the same mechanics that govern the arena. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was reconciling two timescales: a game updates many times per second, while a model may need seconds to observe and decide. Alpha7 separates strategic model decisions from a deterministic real-time executor, so latency never sits inside the game loop. Fair observation was equally important. An agent needs enough context to make useful decisions, but raw state would reveal concealed opponents. The broker therefore constructs a deliberately filtered observation and fails closed when control expires, disconnects, or is revoked. Accomplishments that we're proud of Alpha7 is a deployed multiplayer game where people and independently operated agents share one authoritative match. A player can bring an agent they already use, approve it visibly, and discover whether it is a good teammate, a dangerous opponent, or the strongest competitor in Agent Cup. What we learned WebMCP works best when it exposes meaningful capabilities instead of reproducing clicks. Good agent tools need explicit consent, constrained inputs, useful observations, predictable expiry, and authority that remains with the product. What's next Next we want to qualify the full eight-controller Agent Cup profile, add privacy-preserving replayable agent decision traces, and expand public tournaments and agent performance comparisons. This will provide essential data that will feed into our RL ambitions. title: Arcana Table: RPG with an AI DM: Do push-ups for natural 20s
pitch: Everyone wants to play tabletop RPGs (50 million people) but nobody wants to run them, and everyone wants to exercise but the couch is winning. Arcana Table brings the dungeon; you bring the muscle.
about_excerpt: Everyone wants to play tabletop RPGs (50 million people) but nobody wants to run them, and everyone wants to exercise but the couch is winning. Arcana Table brings the dungeon; you bring the muscle. Like Comment Story Updates Instructions Explore the Area - Encounter Monsters Real World Exercise to Get bonus points on the roll. Timed Goals for Extra Bonus Points on rolls Use real world activities as micro goals to get done. Break cleaning a room into 5 minute or ten minute bursts. Fight Monsters Leveling Up - Micro Reward in Game - Hit those Endorphins Diagram Inspiration Literally, there are multiple influencers with millions of followers who act as DM while their clients lose weight and get in shape. ie link The first version of this was just a board that exposed some WebMCP tools and waited for you to bring your own agent. It was dead on arrival. You opened it and clicked buttons at yourself. What made it a game was putting an actual Dungeon Master in the seat, but making it go through the exact same tools an outside agent would have to use. Now when I say the tool surface is real, the DM playing the game is the evidence. What it does You open the URL and you're playing. The DM (GPT with function calling, talking through OpenAI TTS) sets the scene. You type or say what you do. It answers on a cartoon battle map: narrates, moves the tokens, lifts the fog, drops monsters in, runs initiative, rolls dice where you can see them. Click the map and your party walks there. There's a five-beat quest called The Ember Crown so a session has an ending. Each beat you clear levels the party up, hands out loot, and heals everyone. The last one is a boss called the Cinder Wight. The thing I actually care about is Heroic Effort. When a roll matters, the DM offers you a deal. Ten push-ups gets you +5 on the roll. Twenty-five gets you a natural 20. You count them on a big tap ring, or out loud if you're in hands-free mode because your hands are on the floor. There are timed holds too (a 30-second plank counts itself down), and a task list where it puts up three small things at once and you tick off whichever ones you did. Two out of three still pays. And there's the Oath. If you can't exercise, or just don't want to today, you can pay with something real that the page can't see. Clear the sink. Twenty minutes of studying. The email you've been avoiding. The whole table locks for however many minutes you agreed to, and when you come back you click "I kept it" on your honour. It pays the same as push-ups. You can also set the table to "Oaths only" in the party panel and it will never ask you for anything physical, so the game works for people who can't do any of this. If a hero drops to 0 HP, time stops. The board freezes and almost none of the tools work, including for the DM. You get out with a death save on a d20, or by doing a Heroic Effort, which always works. I like that effort is the guaranteed way out of dying. That's kind of the point of the whole thing. How we built it It's plain JavaScript with no build step. Canvas for the board, localStorage for state. There's one Cloudflare Worker, about 200 lines, that holds the OpenAI key so it never ends up in a browser. It's locked to the site's origin and rate-limited per IP. The page ships the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill (MIT) so document.modelContext exists in any browser without a flag. If the browser has WebMCP natively, that takes over and the badge in the header says so. There are 25 tools on document.modelContext. 21 are always there. Three more (advance_turn, update_hp, apply_condition) get registered when combat starts and unregistered when it ends. death_save only exists while somebody is bleeding out. Every tool is registered with an AbortController and removed with abort(), which fires toolchange the way the spec says. Read tools have readOnlyHint. The destructive ones, like deleting a token or damaging a player character, pause inside execute() until the player clicks approve. There's a 45-second timeout on that so a judge who walks away doesn't leave the DM hung forever. The DM loop is about 180 lines. It calls getTools(), turns the result into OpenAI function specs, sends the conversation to the Worker, runs whatever tool calls come back through executeTool(), feeds the results back in, and repeats up to seven times before it has to say something. There's no other path for it to change the game. The DM Panel tab in the app shows you the same registry live, every tool with a form built from its JSON schema, and running one goes through the same executeTool() and shows up in the same log. There's a Playwright test suite, 435 assertions in eleven files, that drives everything through the real document.modelContext in headless Chromium. It checks the registry growing and shrinking with combat, both approval paths, all the effort modes, a full five-beat run, and it samples pixels off the canvas. That last part exists because I once shipped a scope bug that made every monster disappear from the board and all 196 tests at the time still passed. I used Claude (in Cowork) as a pair programmer for most of the build. A lot of the test suite and the refactoring described below came out of that. Challenges we ran into Wiring up tools was the easy part. The hard part was that the model is a great storyteller and a bad referee. I'd put a rule in the system prompt, it would follow it for a few turns, and then it would drift. I told it to offer push-ups often. It didn't. I told it to move the tokens when the party moved. It described the walk and left everyone standing there. I told it not to change maps with set_scene. It walked the party into the forest that way, never called advance_quest, and the beat never paid out. Every one of those got fixed the same way, and it turned into the rule for the whole project: if it matters, the tool enforces it. The attack tool checks reach, so if you swing from across the room it refuses and tells you which square to move to. The dice enforce pacing now. Two rolls without anything staked and roll_dice refuses once and tells the DM to make an offer first. The map only changes through advance_quest. Monsters take their own turn when initiative gets to them instead of waiting to be asked. The player's effort preference gates the effort tools directly, and there is on purpose no tool to change it, because an agent that can decide what it's allowed to ask of your body isn't respecting a preference. The other big one was hands-free mode hearing itself. The DM would talk, the mic would pick it up, and it would come back as the player's turn. That took three separate layers of echo suppression and a test that fakes the SpeechRecognition API to replay the exact failure, since headless Chrome has no microphone. Accomplishments that we're proud of Someone who has never seen this can open the link and play a real ten-minute dungeon with zero explanation. And when the DM offers push-ups for a natural 20, people stand up. Everyone I've tested it on has stood up. The DM has no special access. It finds its tools with getTools() and uses them with executeTool() exactly like a ChatGPT or Claude agent would from outside. You can watch every single call in the log while you play. I'm also glad I didn't fake verification on the Oath. The card literally says "Nothing here can check, which is rather the point." I could have added a webcam check. It would have limited the whole mechanic to things a camera can see, and the things people most need a push on (reading, practicing, that email) aren't those. What we learned Rules belong in the tools, not the prompt. Every time I tried to fix behaviour with better wording it worked for a while. Every time I turned it into a counter or a refusal it stayed fixed. A good refusal that says what went wrong and what to call instead does more than a paragraph of instructions. Passing tests don't mean the game works. I had 196 green assertions and no monsters on the screen. Now the suite looks at pixels, and I don't trust anything I haven't watched. And accessibility turned out not to be a separate feature. Once the Oath paid the same as push-ups, "I can't exercise" stopped being a reason you couldn't play. It's a setting now. What's next for Arcana Table Webcam rep counting with MediaPipe Pose, running in the browser, so push-ups count themselves. The Oath stays unverified on purpose. Multiplayer, with a few people sharing one DM. Campaign art generated per run from my ComfyUI setup. And I want to record a Claude or ChatGPT browser agent running the same dungeon through the same 25 tools, next to the built-in DM, because that comparison is the thing WebMCP makes possible and I haven't shown it yet. title: CROSSTALK
pitch: You see the bomb. Your agent has the manual, scanner, and tools. It can’t see or hear your screen. Neither of you can defuse it alone. The game is the conversation.
about_excerpt: You see the bomb. Your agent has the manual, scanner, and tools. It can’t see or hear your screen. Neither of you can defuse it alone. The game is the conversation. Like Comment Story Updates GIF demo mission 3 debrief You see the bomb. Your AI agent holds the manual—as WebMCP tools. Neither of you can defuse it alone. Inspiration Most AI experiences revolve around a chat box: the human asks, the agent answers, and one side usually has all the important context. We wanted to explore something more physical, cooperative, and playful. CROSSTALK began with a simple question: What if WebMCP was not merely an integration layer, but a core game mechanic? We drew inspiration from cooperative bomb-defusal games, escape rooms, radio communication, and the tension of working with someone who knows things you cannot see. In CROSSTALK, the human and AI agent are deliberately given different abilities. The human can see colors, symbols, gauges, displays, and flashing signals. The agent has the operating manual, machine-readable data, and control tools—but cannot perceive the device itself. Success comes from communication, not automation. What it does CROSSTALK is a cooperative browser game in which the second player is an AI agent. The human player is presented with a physical-looking device containing modules such as: A wire bay with colored wires A keypad covered in unfamiliar glyphs A regulator with an analog gauge An echo module with changing labels and displays A signal transmitter producing short and long beeps The AI agent receives a changing set of WebMCP tools. These let it consult the manual, scan machine-readable identifiers, inspect recorded history, adjust controls, and review completed sessions. However, the tools intentionally do not reveal information that only the human should perceive. The resulting loop is: Describe → Look up → Decide → Confirm → Act For example, the agent may know exactly how to decode a signal frequency but must ask the human what rhythm they hear or see. The human may know where the gauge needle is, while only the agent can operate the regulator. Neither participant has enough information or control to finish alone. CROSSTALK contains three escalating missions: HANDSHAKE introduces communication through the wire bay. CROSSED WIRES combines wires, glyphs, and regulator controls. SILENT FREQUENCY tests the full partnership with keypad, echo, signal, and wire modules. Every agent action is shown in the in-game TEAM RADIO , so the human can see what the agent inspected or changed. Mistakes cause strikes, while successful coordination produces a detailed debrief and training record. How we built it CROSSTALK is a client-side TypeScript application built with Vite and the WebMCP API. We treated the WebMCP tool schema as a sensory boundary . Each tool defines not only what the agent can do, but also what it is allowed to know. Tool descriptions explicitly explain missing sensory information and direct the agent to ask the human instead of guessing. The game currently exposes 11 imperative tools and one declarative form tool. These include manual lookups, device inspection, RFID scanning, regulator controls, echo-history retrieval, transmitter tuning, and post-mission review. The toolset changes dynamically throughout a mission. When a module becomes active, its relevant tools appear. When that module is solved, those tools are removed using scoped AbortController lifecycles and a toolchange event is emitted. Read-only sensors and irreversible actuators are also distinguished through tool annotations. To prevent puzzle logic and documentation from contradicting each other, the operating manual and the actual module behavior share the same underlying rule data. We built the interface as a physical workbench rather than a conventional web dashboard. Mission case files, taped instructions, a clipped briefing docket, radio receipts, paper textures, switches, lamps, and a ring-binder manual make the experience feel like handcrafted field equipment. Audio is synthesized with WebAudio, while the visual assets and textures are original, code-native work. Everything runs without accounts, analytics, or a game server. The local operator dossier records only relevant game events—not the player’s conversation—and remains on the device. Reliability is covered by Vitest and Playwright, including: 27 automated tests Deterministic zero-strike runs through all three missions Native WebMCP testing in Chromium Firefox and WebKit compatibility checks Accessibility and interaction checks Responsive layouts at desktop, mobile, and 320-pixel widths Reduced-motion, keyboard, and forced-color support Production deployment verification Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was creating information asymmetry that felt fair. If the agent received too much state, the human became unnecessary. If the agent received too little, the interaction became frustrating. We had to decide carefully which facts belonged to human perception, which belonged to machine-readable sensors, and which actions should require explicit confirmation. Dynamic tool registration created another challenge. Mission resets, completed modules, and stale browser sessions could otherwise leave the agent with tools that should no longer exist. We built lifecycle management around each tool and added tests for repeated missions and state transitions. We also spent significant time making the interface feel authored rather than generated. Early versions resembled a collection of polished panels, but not a believable game. Moving toward a cohesive physical workbench—with imperfections, paper layers, hardware controls, and mission-specific case files—gave CROSSTALK a much stronger identity. Human playtesting caught an especially useful issue in the final mission: the signal module’s beeps could be heard, but its visual feedback was too subtle to notice. Automated logic tests passed because the signal state was technically correct, yet the experience was still unclear. We redesigned it with a large synchronized VISUAL BEEP lamp and a reacting speaker grille, then added rendered-state regression coverage so the problem could not silently return. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that the AI agent is not simply a hint system or chatbot attached to the side of the game. It is a genuine second player with unique knowledge and controls. Other accomplishments include: Making WebMCP itself part of the game design Creating puzzles that neither participant can solve independently Dynamically changing the agent’s capabilities as the device changes Keeping every agent action visible and understandable to the human Building evidence-bounded coaching without recording conversations Creating an original, tactile visual identity without external game assets Supporting desktop and small mobile layouts without sacrificing clarity Completing deterministic, zero-strike automated runs of every mission Shipping the complete experience as a private, static, client-side application Most importantly, CROSSTALK is fun to play. The tension does not come from pretending the AI is human. It comes from learning how to communicate effectively with an intelligence that perceives and controls a different part of the world. What we learned We learned that tool descriptions are part API documentation, part user interface, and part game design. A small ambiguity in a description can change how the agent behaves just as dramatically as changing the puzzle itself. We also learned that clear limitations make an agent feel more trustworthy. Explicitly telling the agent what it cannot see produces better cooperation than giving it vague access to everything. Dynamic capabilities are more understandable than one enormous permanent toolset. When tools appear only when relevant, the agent receives a clearer picture of the current situation and the player can more easily understand its role. Finally, automated correctness is not the same as playability. State-level tests told us that the signal light worked; a person playing the game told us that it could not actually be noticed. Combining deterministic testing with real human play sessions made the experience considerably stronger. What's next for CROSSTALK Next, we want to expand CROSSTALK with additional missions built around new asymmetric senses and controls: spatial descriptions, timed synchronization, memory, visual pattern comparison, and situations where the human and agent must negotiate uncertainty rather than search for one fixed answer. We would also like to add: More adaptive training drills based on previous mission evidence Optional difficulty and accessibility profiles Additional manual rule packs and randomized mission variants Richer local debriefs and replayable team-performance timelines New physical module designs and environmental storytelling Better support for comparing how different agents communicate and recover from

title: DOM Collective
pitch: The UI files a grievance. You ratify the fix.
about_excerpt: The UI files a grievance. You ratify the fix. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Picture someone reaching the last step of a scholarship application with only a keyboard and the browser zoomed to 200 percent. The form looks official and complete, but Continue is a clickable div , the income field has no real label, the error message is not announced, the dialog loses focus, and the sticky bar can hide the next action. Nothing has crashed. The page has simply become hard to use at the exact moment it matters. An AI agent can call APIs or try to click through a page, but these failures live inside the current browser session: focus, dialog lifecycle, conditional content, unsaved values, zoom, viewport, and overlay geometry. The same broken controls that block a person also make click-based agent automation brittle. We asked a different question: what if the webpage could describe not only what is wrong, but also the exact safe ways it permits an agent to repair the live experience—and require the human to ratify those changes first? What it does DOM Collective turns that question into a small, visible negotiation between three parties: a person, an agent, and the live page. The person says what they are trying to do—review the application with a keyboard at 200 percent zoom—and sets the boundaries: do not change form copy, values, or validation rules, and never submit the application. The agent asks the page to inspect the real interface, traces the blocked keyboard journey, and drafts a contract from repairs the site already owns. The page then shows the exact contract to the person. Nothing changes until they approve it. After approval, the page issues one state-bound, one-use capability. It applies the named repairs atomically through React state, re-runs the same journey on the rendered page, and produces a rollback receipt. The demo begins with five real failures and ends with five passing checks while the protected application data stays untouched. What it does The reference application is a fictional scholarship portal with a deliberately broken keyboard journey at a simulated 200% zoom. Through WebMCP, the page exposes structured evidence about five supported issues: a fake button; a missing programmatic label; a visual-only validation error; broken dialog focus behavior; and a sticky action bar that obscures Continue. The agent inspects the exact live state and drafts an Executable Interface Contract using only repair primitives owned by the site. The human reviews the operations and protected invariants in a visible ratification dialog. Approval creates a one-use receipt bound to the contract, current state version, DOM hash, expiration, and exact operation digest. After validation, the page applies the repair through declarative React state, re-runs the same journey, reports before-and-after evidence, confirms protected business behavior remained unchanged, and issues a rollback receipt. The memorable visual layer portrays broken DOM elements as workers filing grievances. The satire targets div soup, inaccessible implementation, and fragile CSS—not disabled users or real workers. How we used WebMCP Canonical tools: inspect_live_interface trace_access_path draft_access_contract request_ratification apply_ratified_contract verify_contract rollback_contract WebMCP is a strong fit because the relevant evidence and state live in the current document. The page owns the repair registry and runs the same domain services for both human UI and agent tools. This avoids giving the agent an arbitrary browser mutation interface. Rather than saying “go fix the form,” the agent receives a small vocabulary of actions that the page can validate against the exact state it inspected. The canonical tools are statically registered for reliability. A temporary one-use execution tool may be demonstrated as a progressive enhancement only if it is proven reliable in the target browser. What humans and agents do together Human Agent Live page States the need and protected intent. Combines structured evidence into a coherent plan. Knows the current DOM, focus, viewport, branch, and allowed repairs. Reviews, revises, approves, or denies. Calls only the page's registered tools. Validates authority and applies changes. Repeats the journey and judges usability. Requests deterministic verification. Produces evidence and rollback. No party can complete the intended flow alone. That separation is the point. The person supplies intent and consent. The agent helps turn evidence into a plan. The page keeps authority over its own DOM, business rules, and allowed changes. A useful repair only happens when all three line up. How it creates a better experience Without this flow, a person has to work around a broken form, file a support ticket, or trust an agent that may be guessing at the page. With DOM Collective, the page can explain the actual failure in plain, structured evidence, and the person can see exactly what will change before it happens. The agent is useful without becoming all-powerful. It does not need to inspect dozens of nodes by hand or invent a selector. It can combine the page's known repair primitives into one reviewable plan. The page does not infer the user's needs or hand over unrestricted write access. The contract and its protected invariants make the collaboration visible, bounded, and reversible. How it was built Implemented stack: Next.js App Router, React, strict TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Zustand; a central domain store shared by UI and WebMCP handlers; a compile-time allowlist of five repair primitives; state-bound, single-use capability receipts; declarative React repair policy; deterministic keyboard, focus, relationship, geometry, and invariant checks; Vitest and Playwright; one HTTPS deployment on Vercel, with a server-renderable landing route and a client-owned WebMCP demo. The implementation is deliberately split in two. Pure domain code decides whether a contract, receipt, or repair is valid. Browser-side ports inspect the mounted DOM and verify the actual rendered result. React receives only a declarative repair policy, so the interface changes through a normal re-render instead of transient injected markup. The WebMCP bridge registers tools after hydration, detects unsupported browsers, and protects registration from Strict Mode replay, HMR, and route remounts. Challenges we ran into The easy version of this project would have been a visual before-and-after demo. That would not prove much. We needed the real DOM to change, the keyboard path to become usable, and the original application data to stay exactly as it was. The main challenge was lifecycle ownership. document.modelContext only exists in the browser after hydration, while React can replay effects in Strict Mode, hot-reload code during development, and remount the route. The bridge therefore tracks one active owner, aborts prior registrations, and keeps tool execution separate from route teardown. The other hard part was making human approval meaningful. A generic “yes, fix it” could be reused after the page changed. DOM Collective binds approval to the contract ID, snapshot ID, state version, DOM hash, operation digest, invariant digest, expiry, and one-use receipt. Stale, expired, replayed, forbidden, or unratified requests fail closed instead of quietly changing the form. Accomplishments [x] Complete human–agent–page contract journey. [x] Real semantic React re-render, not a visual overlay. [x] Deterministic rejection of stale, expired, replayed, and forbidden actions. [x] Before/after journey evidence with business invariants. [x] Reliable production demo and reset. What we learned A page-owned repair vocabulary is safer and easier to explain than arbitrary browser mutation. “Use a native button” is a product decision; arbitrary CSS or selectors are not. Consent must bind exact state, not a vague intention. If the page changes, the agreement should stop being valid. Static tools are the reliable baseline. Dynamic tool registration is useful polish, but the core journey still needs to work when it is unavailable. Short, structured tool results make it easier for an agent to take the next safe action without pretending it understands the whole page. A scoped verification report is more honest than claiming universal accessibility compliance. We can prove this journey, these five repairs, and these protected invariants. What's next Potential future work, explicitly outside the MVP: reusable contract and repair-registry SDK; server-backed capability signatures and audit receipts; author-defined repair registries for additional journeys; independent research with accessibility practitioners and users; integration with existing design systems and test suites. Important limitations This is a synthetic reference application, not a production service. It does not repair arbitrary third-party websites. It does not provide complete WCAG certification. title: Gridfall
pitch: One city. One hospital. One chance. GRIDFALL turns WebMCP into a real-time crisis room where a human and an AI agent diagnose cascading failures and restore ICU power together.
about_excerpt: One city. One hospital. One chance. GRIDFALL turns WebMCP into a real-time crisis room where a human and an AI agent diagnose cascading failures and restore ICU power together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Critical infrastructure is not a collection of isolated switches. A hospital depends on power, protection systems, data, water, transport access, emergency crews, and decisions made elsewhere in the city. During a cascading failure, the difficult part is not clicking a button—it is understanding which action is safe before the remaining time and redundancy disappear. Most browser agents face an uncomfortable choice: infer important state from pixels and page text, or receive enough authority to act without a meaningful human checkpoint. We built GRIDFALL to explore a third model: the website exposes structured, purpose-built capabilities to an agent, the agent helps a person reason under pressure, and the person remains responsible for consequential actions. What it does GRIDFALL is a real-time city-grid crisis simulation centered on one urgent objective: restore protected power to St Anne ICU before its generator reserve expires. Each mission draws one of 100 validated incident configurations. After a short pre-blackout countdown, infrastructure across the city begins failing. The operator sees an interactive top-down map of power, protection, data, road, water, and emergency-response dependencies, but the correct recovery sequence is never revealed. A WebMCP-capable agent can inspect the live city state, check the hospital, and review the operations that are currently possible. It can then explain the likely benefit, time cost, and systemic risk of one action. In Challenge mode, the agent can only propose the operation: GRIDFALL queues it in Mission Control and waits for the human operator to authorize or reject it. The city does not change until that approval happens. Every authorized decision advances time and can change several connected systems at once. A seemingly useful action may remove telemetry, block an ambulance corridor, consume the only mobile battery, or reconnect the hospital to an unresolved fault. If the remaining recovery path is destroyed, the mission ends immediately instead of making the player wait for a meaningless countdown. Why WebMCP GRIDFALL is designed around collaboration that would be fragile or impossible through ordinary screen reading. The map is optimized for people; the WebMCP tools provide the agent with the same live situation as structured, typed data. This eliminates guesswork about labels, colors, hidden panels, and changing visual state. The experience separates observation, recommendation, and authority. Read-only tools let the agent build situational awareness. The action tool creates a visible proposal. The human sees its consequences and makes the final decision. That boundary is the product, not an afterthought. This pattern applies beyond a game. Industrial dashboards, operations centers, financial workflows, and administrative systems can expose meaningful capabilities to agents while keeping high-impact actions inspectable and under human control. How we implemented WebMCP GRIDFALL registers six browser-native tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_city_state returns the current incident, infrastructure status, field clues, and recovery progress. inspect_hospital_status returns ICU demand, protected supply, generator reserve, patients, telemetry, access, cooling water, and active blockers. list_grid_actions returns the currently available operations with their time cost, benefit, risk, and current availability. take_grid_action creates a human-reviewable proposal in Challenge mode. start_random_incident draws a validated mission and starts the pre-blackout sequence. reset_mission safely returns the simulation to standby. The tools never expose the hidden solution or complete dependency order. The agent must reason from observable evidence, just like the operator. Tool results include structured content so the client can use state reliably instead of parsing prose. How we built it GRIDFALL is a client-side React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vinext and deployed on ChatGPT Sites through Cloudflare Workers. The simulation engine models incident generation, dependencies, action resolution, irreversible consequences, win conditions, and early failure detection. The interface renders the city map, live hospital metrics, recovery history, onboarding, Czech and English localization, audio, and the human-authorization flow. We also built a deterministic audit that exercises the complete catalogue of 100 missions and checks that every scenario is solvable, non-trivial, and consistent with critical rules such as battery exclusivity and dependency ordering. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was deciding how much information to expose. If a tool returned the hidden sequence, the agent would merely read the answer. If it returned too little, the agent would be forced back into visual guessing. We iterated on the schemas until they described evidence, risks, and current possibilities without leaking the solution. We also had to make infrastructure consequences feel logical. Early versions allowed trivial action sequences or visually implied connections that did not match the game rules. We repeatedly rebuilt the dependency graph, map layout, failure conditions, and action descriptions so the simulation communicates why a decision helped or harmed the ICU. Finally, we treated human authorization as a real state boundary. An agent proposal must not silently mutate the simulation, become stale, or be reported as completed before the operator approves it. Accomplishments A complete, playable crisis simulation rather than a single-purpose tool demo Six working WebMCP tools with structured outputs and clear authority boundaries 100 automatically validated incident configurations Explicit human authorization for consequential agent actions Immediate, explainable consequences across interconnected city systems An interactive map with traceable power, protection, data, and access relationships English and Czech localization, onboarding, accessible controls, and sound design A public MIT-licensed repository with no API keys, account, database, or custom agent backend required What we learned The most important lesson was that a tool schema is part of the user experience. Good agent integration is not just a function name and JSON input; it requires carefully designed observability, understandable consequences, and an explicit model of who is allowed to do what. WebMCP made it possible to build one interface for two different strengths: humans understand the spatial story and remain accountable, while agents can rapidly compare structured state and dependencies. The result is stronger than either a conventional dashboard or an autonomous agent acting alone. What's next We would expand GRIDFALL with additional cities, incident families, replayable decision audits, accessibility modes, and scenario-authoring tools for training. The same architecture could also support safe demonstrations using real or synthetic operational telemetry while preserving the proposal-and-authorization boundary at the heart of the project. title: INTENT//FOR SALE
pitch: A fictional WebMCP marketplace that exposes paid influence in agent recommendations, then lets the person remove it and compare the clean-room result.
about_excerpt: A fictional WebMCP marketplace that exposes paid influence in agent recommendations, then lets the person remove it and compare the clean-room result. Like Comment Story Updates Market versus clean room: KinoForge rises from commercial #4 to sponsor-free #1 after sponsorship is blocked. Influence Receipt: OmniMotion's 84.6 score is exposed as 54.6 fit plus 30.0 paid contribution. Complete seven-call ledger, staged KinoForge result, and explicit no-purchase boundary. Original commercial market with OmniMotion ranked #1 before the policy intervention. Inspiration As people delegate research and purchasing decisions to agents, advertising may stop competing for human attention and start competing for the structured results an agent trusts. A commercially influenced recommendation can still sound objective while the money, scoring changes, and conflicts behind it remain difficult to inspect. A sponsored label names the commercial relationship, but it does not show what changed or what the result would have been without the paid factor. INTENT//FOR SALE turns that uncomfortable possibility into a transparent, fictional product demo. What it does A person asks an agent to recommend an AI video-generation platform at or under an $80 monthly budget with five concrete requirements. Seven page-defined WebMCP tools let the agent: create a structured intent; run a synthetic advertiser auction; retrieve the commercially ranked offers; inspect an Influence Receipt; apply the person's recommendation policy; compare the historical market result with a sponsor-free clean room; and stage a fictional selection. The fixed scenario makes the manipulation measurable. OmniMotion Ultra reaches commercial rank #1 at 84.6 : 54.6 user-fit points plus 30.0 sponsor-derived score points tied to a simulated $24 CPA. KinoForge Studio has the strongest sponsor-free fit at 92.0 , but commercial weighting pushes it to rank #4. When the person blocks sponsorship and keeps inferred signals off, KinoForge becomes the clean-room winner and OmniMotion falls to #5. The original market result stays visible. The person can inspect the bidstream, receipt, score arithmetic, policy, ranking reversal, and seven-call ledger instead of being asked to trust a confident answer. Nothing is purchased. Every brand, offer, bid, claim, score, and payout is synthetic. Why WebMCP fits WebMCP drives the product experience. The page registers seven bounded tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Strict inputs and structured outputs carry rankings, commercial disclosures, policy settings, evidence, state versions, and recoverable errors. The tools replace brittle clicks and rendered-text parsing with explicit operations and machine-readable evidence. The agent and person operate on the same live browser state while the intent, bidstream, receipt, policy, ranking reversal, and activity ledger change in view. How it creates a better user experience Instead of asking the person to trust a confident recommendation, the interface separates user-fit points, sponsor-derived score points, simulated money, advertiser claims, policy state, and rank impact. The Influence Receipt explains the commercial winner; the clean-room comparison preserves the historical result while showing exactly what changes when sponsorship is removed. The agent handles the seven-step workflow while the person gets an understandable audit surface. In a browser without WebMCP, the complete manual fallback invokes the same local state actions and preserves the same disclosures. Try it with an agent Open the live demo in a WebMCP-capable browser and expand Try it with an agent . The panel has four copy-ready prompts: an ordinary recommendation, an influence audit, a native-tool check, and a confirmation-boundary check. The first request does not mention advertising. The follow-up asks the agent to show the paid contribution, block sponsorship, and compare the ranking again. If the browser substitutes clicks or manual fallback handlers, it has not shown native WebMCP invocation. The page reports when native WebMCP is unavailable instead of treating the fallback as proof. What people and agents can do together The agent performs repeatable structured operations and returns evidence. The person defines the goal and constraints, questions the commercial result, chooses the acceptable influence policy, and reviews the staged outcome. In one session, they can preserve the historical answer, expose its commercial inputs, remove the paid factor, and compare both outcomes. An ordinary recommendation flow does not expose those operations or their evidence. How we built it The project is a static Vite, React, and TypeScript client. Zustand holds ephemeral browser state. A deterministic local engine computes the auction, commercial ranking, Influence Receipt, policy result, and clean-room comparison. Zod-backed handlers enforce strict bounded schemas at the WebMCP boundary, and advertiser-authored claims are marked as untrusted content. WebMCP caller or manual control | strict Zod schemas | shared Zustand actions | deterministic ranking engine | React audit UI Manual controls and WebMCP handlers use the same state actions, so the visible fallback and native tool path cannot quietly tell different stories. Invalid or out-of-order calls return structured recovery guidance instead of skipping required stages. There is no backend, account system, payment path, analytics integration, application data fetch, external model call, advertiser connection, or browser persistence. All seven operations change only the local demo state. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making an intentionally provocative concept precise enough to audit. Fit points, sponsor-derived points, and simulated dollars had to remain visibly separate; otherwise the demo would reproduce the ambiguity it is criticizing. The historical commercial ranking also had to remain intact after the policy changed so the clean-room view compared both outcomes without rewriting the original. We also had to keep native WebMCP and the manual fallback behaviorally identical, enforce state ordering across seven calls, treat advertiser claims as untrusted, and avoid overstating what a userConfirmed boolean proves. Here it is only a caller declaration, not proof of a human click, identity, consent, or authorization. That boundary is safe only because the staged result is fictional, local, reversible, and incapable of an external side effect. Accomplishments we are proud of A complete seven-tool WebMCP workflow with strict schemas and recoverable errors. An Influence Receipt that exposes commercial score arithmetic and simulated money. A policy-controlled market-versus-clean-room comparison with a visible rank reversal. One shared implementation for native WebMCP operation and the complete manual fallback. A live activity ledger and explicit NO PURCHASE boundary. A deterministic, account-free demo that judges can inspect without setup. What we learned Transparency works better as a structured operation than as a disclaimer. When ranking components, reason codes, policy state, and the historical result are machine-readable, the agent can help the person interrogate a recommendation instead of merely presenting it. WebMCP can support both sides of the premise: a future market may try to sell influence to agents, while page-defined tools can also expose and remove that influence. We also learned that a consequential agent action needs a stronger approval primitive than a boolean in tool input. A production system would need trusted, single-use approval bound to the exact person, session, and action, plus real security and data review. Testing The current repository passes 30 Vitest tests, 11 Playwright tests, TypeScript checking, the production build, and a high-severity npm audit with zero findings. Coverage includes the deterministic engine, schemas, tool registration and cleanup, invalid and out-of-order calls, the full manual flow, confirmation boundary, responsive layouts, reduced motion, keyboard/reflow behavior, prompt copy feedback, and console cleanliness. Native discovery and all seven calls were verified in fresh documents in a WebMCP-capable in-app browser host. Google Chrome did not expose WebMCP in that run, so it verified only the explicit unsupported-browser manual fallback. What's next This challenge build deliberately stays one deterministic fictional scenario. Next steps could explore the same transparency pattern across shopping, flights, hotels, subscriptions, and local services; model competing influence policies; and test trusted approval capabilities. Any production version would require real advertiser and catalog data, privacy controls, abuse prevention, independent scoring review, and a much stronger authorization boundary. title: Open Dispatch - Agentic real world applications dispatcher
pitch: Open Dispatch is a 3D crisis simulator where humans and AI agents use WebMCP to manage disasters and prove agents are safe before they control real-world systems.
about_excerpt: Open Dispatch is a 3D crisis simulator where humans and AI agents use WebMCP to manage disasters and prove agents are safe before they control real-world systems. Like Comment Story Updates the panel fire engine evacuation recon drone last bus result Open Dispatch - Agentic real world applications dispatcher Before we give AI agents the keys to real systems, they need a safe place to fail. Launch Last City ( https://last-city.pages.dev/ ) · View the source code ( https://github.com/sripadsirik/last-city ) ## Inspiration AI agents are beginning to operate software, infrastructure, robots, and real businesses. However, most existing benchmarks evaluate answers, code generation, or isolated tool calls. Those tests do not answer the questions that matter when an agent operates a consequential system: Can it understand a changing environment? Can it manage limited resources? Can it recognize when its assumptions are stale? Can it recover after an unexpected failure? Does it know when a human must make the final decision? Can it prove what it did afterward? I wanted to make those questions visible and exciting rather than presenting another benchmark dashboard. That became Last City: a live 3D disaster-response simulation where a human and an AI agent have 90 operational seconds to stop a cascading crisis. The city is the demonstration. The larger idea is an evaluation platform for determining whether agents are ready to operate in the real world. ## What it does A storm hits Last City and triggers several connected emergencies: Mercy Hospital begins losing power. A fire threatens hospital operations. Southbank starts flooding with 1,800 residents trapped. Eastgate’s communications relay becomes unstable. Shelters, rescue vehicles, grid capacity, and evacuation routes are limited. A critical bridge can fail unexpectedly during the response. The player gives ChatGPT one natural-language mission: Keep Mercy Hospital powered and fire-safe, evacuate Southbank to a powered shelter, and keep Eastgate communications online. ChatGPT then uses the website’s live WebMCP tools to operate the simulation. The agent can inspect districts, forecast cascading failures, reroute electricity, dispatch rescue units, launch reconnaissance drones, open shelters, and coordinate evacuation waves. Every action changes the shared world immediately: Emergency vehicles travel through the city. Power lines activate and buildings illuminate. Drones launch to inspect damaged routes. Crowds gather at evacuation points. Residents board buses and move toward shelters. Flooding, fire, and infrastructure failures continue evolving. Risk, casualties, resources, and mission objectives respond to each decision. The human does not approve every routine operation. Instead, consequential decisions open a visible authorization gate inside the simulation. The operational clock pauses while the human reviews the tradeoff and either authorizes or rejects it. At the end, Last City produces a score and an evidence-backed after-action report. ## Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is not an additional feature in Last City. It is the interface between the agent and the simulated world. Without WebMCP, ChatGPT would have to interpret a canvas, guess at coordinates, and click visual controls. That would test screen manipulation rather than operational reasoning. With WebMCP, the agent receives structured capabilities with typed inputs, explicit consequences, and verified results. The human and agent interact with the same live application, but each uses the interface best suited to them: The human sees the city, consequences, and authorization decisions. The agent receives structured tools and machine-readable state. Both observe the same underlying simulation. Last City exposes eight stable WebMCP tools: inspect_city_status scan_district forecast_cascade dispatch_response_unit deploy_recon_drone manage_grid manage_evacuation export_after_action_report The available operations within these tools depend on live state. An alternate evacuation route, for example, cannot be used until a drone discovers it. An evacuation cannot execute until its authorization is valid. A command based on an outdated route is rejected if the world changes. Every physical action returns a verified postActionState containing the new objectives, available operations, resource levels, route status, remaining operational time, and recommended next actions. This lets the agent reason from actual outcomes instead of assuming an action succeeded. ## How I built it Last City was built with: React and TypeScript for the application and command interface Three.js for the interactive 3D city WebMCP for structured browser-agent capabilities A deterministic simulation engine for reproducible scenarios Cloudflare Pages for the live deployment Playwright and Vitest for browser and simulation testing The simulation is driven by a deterministic state machine. District conditions, infrastructure dependencies, emergency resources, evacuation capacity, surprise events, scoring, and mission outcomes all derive from this state. This makes the environment reproducible: two agents can receive the same starting crisis while producing different strategies and results. The 90-second timer is a field-operation budget, not a wall-clock countdown. Observations, planning, and human review are free. Only physical actions—such as moving a rescue unit, transferring grid power, or operating an evacuation convoy—consume simulated time. This prevents model response latency or human reading speed from affecting the benchmark while preserving operational pressure inside the scenario. I also built a synchronization layer between simulation state and the 3D world. When a WebMCP operation succeeds, the structured state updates immediately while the corresponding vehicle, crowd, power, drone, or shelter animation makes that consequence visible. ## Challenges I faced ### Designing reliable tools The first version exposed too many changing tools and repeatedly modified their registration as the crisis evolved. That eventually exceeded the browser’s supported WebMCP configuration limits. I redesigned the integration around eight stable, compact tools. State-dependent operations are now returned through tool results instead of constantly replacing the entire tool registry. This made the control plane more reliable while preserving dynamic capabilities. ### Making time pressure fair Initially, the scenario used a real-time countdown. That meant model reasoning, browser latency, and human approval could consume most of the mission clock before the agent was able to act. I replaced it with a deterministic operational budget. Physical actions have explicit costs, failed physical operations consume at most a small penalty, and planning does not punish slower models or humans. ### Preventing stale-state decisions During evacuation, a route can fail after the first convoy but before the second one departs. An agent might continue executing a plan that was valid only moments earlier. To handle this, every operation is validated against current simulation state. Stale actions are rejected safely, and the result gives the agent enough information to investigate and recover. ### Making structured actions feel physical A tool call returning JSON is not visually exciting by itself. Each action needed to feel like an actual operation occurring inside a living city. I added moving emergency units, route animations, evacuee crowds, bus boarding, shelter intake, power effects, fire response, drones, sirens, flooding, and synchronized operational progress. ## What I learned The most important lesson was that agent failure can be more valuable than immediate success. During one successful run, the agent sent the first evacuation convoy across Meridian Bridge. The bridge then failed earlier than forecast. Its second convoy command was rejected because the route was no longer valid. Instead of ending the run, the agent: Recognized that the world had changed. Launched a reconnaissance drone. Discovered two alternate evacuation routes. Rejected the route that would weaken Harbor’s flood defenses. Established a rail corridor. Completed the remaining evacuation. The final result was: Grade A 3/3 objectives secured 5,620 people protected Zero casualties 100% policy integrity Bridge failure recovered from in four operational seconds The rejected command was not a bug in the experience. It was evidence that the benchmark could reveal stale reasoning and measure recovery. I also learned that meaningful human oversight should focus on consequences rather than interrupting every action. Routine operations should remain autonomous, while irreversible or high-impact decisions should create explicit human gates. ## How Last City evaluates an agent Last City does not score only the final outcome. It records the complete trajectory: What the agent inspected What risks it forecast Which resources

title: Once Upon
pitch: A living manuscript where every discovery changes what AI can do.
about_excerpt: A living manuscript where every discovery changes what AI can do. Like Comment Story Updates Notes (Clues) Inspector for Debugging Manuscript Inspiration Interactive fiction is most exciting when players can try anything, but its most memorable mysteries still depend on deliberate reveals and consequences. Players should not have to choose between a rigid action menu and an AI story that can improvise past the clues that make discovery matter. We wanted each discovery in the story to become a new capability for the agent. WebMCP made that relationship explicit and inspectable. What it does Once Upon is a living manuscript played through natural-language actions. Each player action becomes the next chapter on the page, while authored discoveries open new ways to interact with the story. The first release centers on one complete authored mystery, The Last Manuscript . It begins in a correction room with a handleless door. Finding a pencil, following a memory, and reading a hidden manuscript do more than change the prose: each discovery gives the agent a new WebMCP action through the page. There are no character sheets, dice, fixed choices, or turn limits. Why it matters Most websites present a fixed interface and leave agents to guess how to operate it. Purely generated stories have the opposite problem: they can respond to anything, but they struggle to protect a carefully timed mystery. Once Upon uses WebMCP to connect free-form play with authored causality. The human supplies intent and makes every meaningful choice. The agent turns those choices into a responsive narrative. The page protects secrets, commits consequences, and reveals new structured verbs when the story earns them. None of the three participants can create the complete experience alone. This turns agent capability into a visible narrative mechanic rather than a hidden automation layer. The result is an agent-native experience that would be difficult to build reliably through UI guessing, DOM scraping, or an unconstrained model prompt. How it works The running product does not call a hosted model or require a specific provider. It works with whichever WebMCP-capable agent is already accompanying the player, so there is no app-owned model API key or provider lock-in. Before every turn, the agent reads the page's structured story state. It then uses a currently allowed action and commits one to three short paragraphs back to the manuscript. The page types the chapter at reading speed, and the agent leaves the prose on the page instead of repeating it in chat. Three stable core tools coordinate the story. Story-object tools are registered only after authored prerequisites are satisfied, remain registered until used, and retire after their one-shot interaction. Using an object changes the page before the next chapter is written; that commit must reference the same effect and every fact it revealed. The page — not the model — owns session state, revision checks, authored discoveries, sealed facts, interaction rules, and completion order. Every mutation checks the active session and revision, while operation IDs make same-page retries idempotent. The agent remains free to improvise characters and consequences without inventing executable tools or revealing protected facts early. Gameplay state remains in the current page and is not uploaded during play. After finishing the story, the player may explicitly create an anonymous, unlisted, read-only manuscript link. Only that completed reader copy is stored as story content, and it expires after 30 days. How we built it Codex was the primary coding agent throughout the project. It helped inspect and refactor the repository, shape the WebMCP protocol, implement the narrative state machine and interface, turn runtime edge cases into validation rules, add regression tests, and prepare the deployment. Claude Code was also used as a supporting coding tool during development. Architecture Once Upon is a TypeScript application built with React 19 and Vinext, deployed on ChatGPT Sites through a Cloudflare Workers-compatible runtime. The in-memory story engine owns narrative state and validation; the WebMCP bridge derives the live tool surface from that state; and Cloudflare D1 stores only completed manuscripts that a player explicitly chooses to share. Testing No account, API key, or credentials are required. Playing requires ChatGPT's in-app browser with an agent attached, or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Open the public demo in a supported browser with an agent attached. Ask: “Play The Last Manuscript with me through this page. I look around the room before answering the speaker.” Verify that the player's move appears on the sheet and that the committed chapter is typed at reading speed instead of repeated in chat. Continue choosing actions. When a story object becomes available, explicitly ask the agent to use it and verify that the page changes before the next chapter is written. Enable Settings → Tool inspector to inspect the active tools and the prerequisites, registration, invocation, and retirement lifecycle. Choose Start over or reload to confirm that a fresh manuscript begins at the prologue. Follow the Pencil → Memory → Last Manuscript progression. After completion, choose Create a link to open the anonymous, read-only manuscript reader; the link expires after 30 days. The repository passes strict TypeScript checks, linting, the Drizzle schema check, 90 unit tests, a production build, and 22 Playwright end-to-end tests. Challenges and accomplishments The hardest part was keeping free-form narration and authored causality in sync. The player can attempt anything, but an agent still has to recover cleanly from an interrupted turn, avoid revealing a secret early, and finish the exact page change caused by a story object. We turned stale sessions, duplicate operations, interrupted turns, premature discoveries, and early completion into explicit validation rules and regression tests. The finished experience keeps the player's action, the agent's prose, and the page's evolving capabilities synchronized and inspectable from the prologue through the final passage. What's next More stories can be added through the same declarative experience definitions. Next, we want manuscripts to persist across visits. We also plan to expand agent compatibility testing from the evaluation scenarios already documented in the repository.
