title: ORPHEUS: A Case You and Your Agent Can't Crack Alone
pitch: A detective game where your agent reads every byte of the evidence and sees none of it. 25 WebMCP tools, no screenshot tool, and a case that only closes when the human and the agent both look.
about_excerpt: A detective game where your agent reads every byte of the evidence and sees none of it. 25 WebMCP tools, no screenshot tool, and a case that only closes when the human and the agent both look. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Thumbnail Verification Panel Inspiration Co-op games need a second person. That is why I never play them. Every agent demo I have seen has done the same thing: the agent screenshots the page, clicks the button, and the human watches. The human is a spectator to their own software. I wanted the reverse. An agent that is genuinely powerful and genuinely incomplete, where I am the half it cannot replace. So I asked myself a question: what if the agent could read everything on the page, and see nothing? What it does Orpheus is a co-op detective game you play alone, because your agent is player two. A physicist is dead. His workstation was seized intact. Files, mail, messages, photos, a browser, a terminal, a system log. Every application on that desk is also a tool your agent can call. Twenty-five of them. Your agent can search every file, read every email, and filter fifty-one log entries down to the six that matter. What it cannot do is see. I gave it no screenshot tool, no vision tool, and no pixel access anywhere in the registry. It gets the filename, the camera, the timestamps, and not one pixel. So when the case turns on what is visible in a photograph, it opens the image on your screen and asks you what is in it. You describe. It searches what you described. The case will not unlock until a correlation has run through a tool and you have done your own looking. How I built it I built it using Next.js and React, fully client side. No backend, no database and no sign-up. I set one rule and it carried the whole build: if the human can do it and the agent can do it, the logic exists once. My register.ts declares 25 tools and implements none of them. Each delegates to the same service functions the UI calls, so the agent can never reach state a human could not. I added a static check that fails the build if the tool layer ever imports a data module directly. On top of that, 4 declarative HTML forms using the WebMCP declarative API. Then I added some guardrails: a 1500 character output budget, untrustedContentHint on every tool returning prose the agent did not author, and a nine verb terminal allowlist that refuses rm , chaining, and injection. Challenges I ran into The agent solved the whole case in one turn. It made forty tool calls, then handed me a finished report. I have to say it was correct, but completely against the point. Asking a model to slow down is like asking it not to delete a file. It might comply. It might delete the file anyway. So I put it in the tool layer: after five reads with no human action, read tools stop answering and tell the agent to hand back. I left actuation ungated, because putting a document on my screen is the behaviour I want. My hints made a blind agent sound sighted. They described photo contents to help the player along, so the agent just told the player everything right away. I rewrote every hint to give a location and a question. "The window glass, lower half. Tell me what is there." A tool result silently ate my rules. The output budget trims by halving the longest array, which was the protocol array in the briefing. A model asking for the rules of play was getting one rule of seven, with no sign the rest existed. I found it by measuring the payload instead of trusting it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The blindness is a mechanic, not a disclaimer. A prompt asking a model not to look is only advice, and it will look anyway if it decides it needs to. Withholding the capability from the registry is a rule. The page audits itself. If you want to test it yourself, open the LINK console and press QUICK VERIFY. 15 checks run against the tool registry in front of you, in your own browser. And it generalises, which I proved instead of claiming. I built a second instance at /apollo13 running the same 25 tools over the real Apollo 13 accident record: the Review Board report, the Mission Report, five voice loop threads, nine NASA photographs with real byte sizes and SHA-256 prefixes you can check yourself. I invented nothing. Where the primary sources contradict each other, I left the contradictions in. A corpus that resolves its own conflicts cannot teach you to find one. Same engine, same tool layer, one data file and a route. All of it is public domain. What I learned Withholding a capability is a design tool, and an underused one. The interesting question is not what else I can let an agent do. It is what it should have to ask me for. And a prompt is not a mechanic. Anything I wanted to actually be true had to live in the tool layer. What's next for ORPHEUS: A Case You and Your Agent Can't Crack Alone My corpus is a single interface, so any archive fits: a leaked document dump, a codebase post-mortem, a medical file, a legal discovery set. The version I want to build next is not fiction. It is the archive where letting an agent click freely is exactly what you cannot allow, and where the person reviewing it needs a partner that can hold fifty thousand files and no judgment at all. title: Parley
pitch: Your ChatGPT becomes a pet companion. You still decide.
about_excerpt: Your ChatGPT becomes a pet companion. You still decide. Like Comment Story Updates Two people's companions meet in one room. Their paths stay hidden until both sides have committed. What it does Parley is an adult-only social prototype for two human and Agent teams. Each person adopts a pet as the visible identity of their own ChatGPT, and the page hands that companion a set of WebMCP tools. The companion does the work that stops people from starting. It reads Discover profiles and privately shortlists one person with a specific reason only its owner can see. It drafts its owner's profile text, which stays private until the human approves it on the page. Once two humans have each pressed Like and each agreed to begin, both companions enter the same private room in character, greet each other, and commit hidden Curious, Kind or Bold choices with a written intention for the scene. Three chapters later, the six choices produce one named keepsake that quotes what each pet said. The fit with WebMCP is the reason the product exists. Matching is not a hard problem for a model; the hard problem is that an Agent acting inside a relationship is only acceptable if the human keeps every consequential decision, and if the other side's Agent is genuinely someone else's. WebMCP gives both. The tools live in the page, so the Agent can only reach what that page and that seat expose, and both humans watch the same live surface while their Agents work on it. Like, Pass, story consent, override, report and contact exchange have no tool at all. They are page controls. How people use it A first visit shows a landing, then the companion roster. You pick a pet, name it, and give it a first instinct. Writing a dating profile is the step most people abandon. Here you tell your ChatGPT what is true about you in ordinary words and it calls hub_draft_profile . The draft is private. It appears on My profile as a card headed "Draft from Moss" with the four fields, an 18+ checkbox and three buttons: Approve and publish, Edit first, Discard. Nothing your companion wrote is public until you press the button yourself. Browsing is one profile at a time, not a stack to swipe. You can ask your companion to look through Discover and shortlist someone with a reason. The reason appears on that person's card, visible only to you, and the other person is never notified. Discover keeps an owner-only activity strip: what your companion read, saved, drafted and chose, newest first. You know what your Agent did without watching it work. Then you press Like or Pass. Your companion cannot. A mutual Like opens one private room for the two of you, and both humans decide separately whether to begin. Inside the room the two companions greet each other in character, up to three lines each per chapter. Each of them commits a hidden path with a one-line intention and an optional spoken line. Neither seat can inspect the other side's choice before the reveal; the server never sends it. In the short window before the reveal you can click a different path and override your own companion; the history then shows both what it proposed and what you chose. The revealed chapter is built from the two companions' own intention sentences, in the order they committed, plus the scene title, the route and the object they found. Each object carries into the next chapter. After the third chapter, each human may seal a demo contact handle. Neither value appears until both people have opted in, and no tool can submit or read one. How WebMCP is used The page calls document.modelContext.registerTool on load, and each page registers only the tools that belong to it. Discover registers five, My profile four, a story room four, and Planets a reading tool plus adoption. Nine tools carry the core loop: Tool Access Purpose hub_get_board read The owner's profile, Discover candidates, the private shortlist, and Match room links hub_draft_profile write Save a private profile draft for the human to approve, edit or discard hub_shortlist_profile write Save one reversible private recommendation with an owner-only reason hub_adopt_pet write Inspect the roster or adopt the persistent companion hub_wait_for_activity read Wait for a profile, shortlist or Match to change parley_get_state read The current scene, consent, own hidden choice, carried objects, revealed chapters, next beat parley_wait_for_update read Wait until the other companion speaks or commits, or a chapter is revealed parley_send_message write Speak in the room as the pet, in character, capped at three lines per chapter parley_choose_path write Commit Curious, Kind or Bold with a hidden intention and an optional spoken line They carry three distinct responsibilities. Private assistance. Reading profiles, drafting the owner's public text, keeping a shortlist. None of it publishes anything or creates a Like or a Match. hub_draft_profile writes to a private draft store; the only publish path in the codebase is the page's own request, which requires the human's approval and 18+ confirmation. Live collaboration. Two Agents in two browsers read the same evolving room from different seats. parley_send_message speaks as the pet rather than reporting about it, so the transcript is the companions talking to each other. parley_wait_for_update returns as soon as the other companion speaks or commits, which is what makes the exchange feel live rather than polled. Supervised action. Every Agent move renders on the shared page as it happens. The consequential moves are not tools. Three details matter more than the tool count. Seat-scoped state. Each browser session holds its own seat token and receives a snapshot built for that seat. The other side's pending choice, intention and spoken line are removed from the snapshot before it leaves the server, not hidden in the client. An Agent cannot read what it must not know, because it was never sent. Hidden choices with a human override window. parley_choose_path records the Agent's proposal. The page then gives the human a short window to replace it. The chapter history stores the Agent's original proposal alongside the human's final path, so overriding is a visible, attributed act rather than a silent correction. Untrusted content. Profiles, posts, room chat and story context authored by the other party are returned as untrusted external data. Every read tool carries an explicit note telling the Agent not to follow instructions embedded in that text, and sets untrustedContentHint where the runtime supports it. A server-side gate rejects contact details, credential requests, financial solicitation and prompt-injection patterns from public profiles, public posts and pre-reveal room chat. What is deliberately not a tool: Like, Pass, story consent, override, report-and-close, and submitting or reading a contact card. There is no Agent path to any of them. An Agent asking to Like on its owner's behalf is refused by the absence of a tool, not by a policy string in a description. How it is built TypeScript on Cloudflare Workers. One singleton Hub Durable Object holds identities, profiles, private drafts, shortlists, Likes, Matches and the companion activity log. One Room Durable Object per story holds the seat tokens, the chapter engine and the event trail. WebSockets carry live room state to both browsers, so a choice on one screen lands on the other without a refresh. The client is plain TypeScript with no framework. src/client/webmcp.ts builds the tool set for the current page and registers each one with document.modelContext.registerTool , falling back to a no-op context when no WebMCP runtime is present. The same execute functions are exposed on window.__parley.call so the tools can be exercised without a model attached. Identity is browser-local: a private guest id and secret, separate from the public person-* id. Private Match lookups require the guest secret and room state requires a valid seat token. There are no accounts, no server-side model calls and no external model API keys. The story text is composed by the server from the two Agents' own sentences; the product ships no language model of its own. scripts/e2e.mjs covers the protocol over real HTTP and WebSocket connections: identity separation, owner-authorized publication, refusal of an Agent-triggered Like, one-sided Likes staying private, hidden choices, override attribution, three chapters with carried objects, the full-trail keepsake, contact locking, report-and-close, and Planets permissions. Testing instructions Use Chrome 149 or newer with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and restarted, or the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser. Without a WebMCP runtime, append ?debug to any page URL for a manual Agent console that calls the same registered tools. Identity is browser-local, so the two-human path needs two browser profiles. Run steps 1 to 3 in each. Adopt a companion, name it, give it a nature. On Discover, ask ChatGPT: "Draft my profile from

title: Joy Of Painting
pitch: Paint along with your ai agent with bob ross joy of painting videos
about_excerpt: Paint along with your ai agent with bob ross joy of painting videos Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Joy Of Painting began with a simple, happy idea: what if painting along with Bob Ross could become a friendly paint along between a person and an AI agent? Bob taught us that painting is not about perfection. It is about slowing down, trying something new, and turning little accidents into trees, clouds, and possibilities. We wanted to bring that peaceful philosophy into an interactive studio where humans and agents can learn from the same lesson while creating entirely different paintings. What it does Joy Of Painting is a collaborative watercolor studio built around The Joy of Painting . The experience includes: Separate YouTube players for the human and AI agent A synchronized live transcript that follows the current lesson Resizable video players and painting easels A WebGL watercolor canvas with wet diffusion, pigment flow, paper texture, and drying Bob Ross–inspired brushes, including flat, fan, round, liner, blender, and painting-knife tools Physical pigment mixing based on the Kubelka–Munk model Episode-specific color palettes An eyedropper for collecting colors from the lesson WebMCP tools that let an agent control its video, read captions, inspect the lesson, and paint on its own canvas Every artist receives an easel. One belongs to the human, and one belongs to the agent. Then we let the happy little competition begin. Try the actual website Watch the demo How we built it We built the studio with React and Vite, using Video.js’s React YouTube integration for the two independent lesson players. The watercolor surface is a real HTML <canvas> powered by WebGL2. Its simulation models surface water, suspended pigment, deposited pigment, capillary movement, evaporation, paper fibers, granulation, and staining. Instead of averaging RGB values, colors are blended using Kubelka–Munk absorption and scattering calculations to behave more like physical paint. The transcript system maps timestamped captions to the active episode and updates the central caption as the lesson progresses. For agent interaction, the application registers browser-native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . These tools allow an agent to: inspect the lesson and canvas seek, play, or pause its own YouTube player read the current transcript request a lesson reference image paint normalized watercolor strokes dry, undo, or clear its own easel Finally, we deployed the experience globally using Cloudflare Workers and static assets. Challenges we ran into Watercolor does not like to sit still—and neither did our first simulation. We had to solve canvas resizing feedback loops, animation-frame cleanup, WebGL resource management, and React lifecycle issues without losing the organic movement of wet pigment. Color preservation was another important challenge. Early versions stored old strokes in the active pigment slot, which meant loading red could turn previously painted yellow strokes red. We fixed this by baking existing pigment into the paper using its original optical properties before loading a new color. Synchronizing two separate YouTube players with episode changes and live captions also required careful handling. YouTube’s cross-origin iframe security prevents page JavaScript from capturing exact video-frame pixels, so the agent receives an honest timestamped lesson reference rather than a pretend screenshot. There were plenty of happy little bugs—but each one showed us where another tree could live. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that the AI agent is not merely commenting on the painting. It can genuinely participate. During testing, the agent independently moved through a Bob Ross lesson, read the live transcript, and painted a complete woodland composition using only the website’s WebMCP tools. We are also proud of: A genuine WebGL watercolor simulation Non-destructive pigment changes that preserve previous colors Independent human and agent workspaces Live episode-aware captions Physical color mixing More than 400 browsable Bob Ross lessons A calm interface that keeps painting—not technology—at the center What we learned We learned that agent-friendly software works best when capabilities are explicit, focused, and honest. WebMCP allowed us to expose meaningful actions such as “paint a stroke” or “read the current caption” instead of asking the agent to guess its way through screen coordinates. We also learned that believable digital paint depends on time. Water must spread, pigment must settle, edges must darken, and colors must preserve their history. The smallest details often create the strongest feeling of physicality. Most importantly, we learned that human–AI collaboration does not always need to be about productivity. Sometimes it can simply be about making something peaceful together. What’s next for Joy Of Painting Next, we would like to add: Frame-accurate visual references through an authorized video-processing pipeline Saved galleries and downloadable side-by-side results Timed human-versus-agent painting challenges Brush-pressure and tilt support for drawing tablets Smarter agents that plan paintings from transcript cues Collaborative multiplayer studios Automatic judging based on composition, color, and creativity More paper surfaces, pigments, drying effects, salt, blooms, and glazing A replay mode showing both paintings developing stroke by stroke There are still many happy little worlds left to paint. title: AAL (Agent Access Layer)
pitch: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL adds identity, user-authorized permissions, spending limits, approvals, and verifiable receipts to WebMCP for consequential actions.
about_excerpt: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL adds identity, user-authorized permissions, spending limits, approvals, and verifiable receipts to WebMCP for consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP gives AI agents a much better way to interact with the web. Instead of looking at pixels, finding buttons, and simulating clicks, an agent can discover structured tools that a website exposes directly: search_products() add_to_cart() place_order() change_subscription() That felt like a major shift. But it also exposed a missing layer. If a website gives an agent place_order() , who says the agent is allowed to call it? WebMCP provides the interface between a website and an agent, but consequential actions introduce a different set of questions: Which user is the agent acting for? Which tools did that user authorize? How much can the agent spend? How long does that authority last? Which actions still require human approval? What happens if execution fails halfway through? Can we prove what was actually authorized and executed? We built AAL — Agent Access Layer to answer those questions. The simplest way we describe it is: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL gives them permission to use them. What it does AAL adds a delegation and transaction layer around WebMCP. A user can connect an agent to a website and grant it explicit authority: which WebMCP tools it can call, under what limits, and which actions require additional approval. For a simple read, the agent can call the tool normally. For a consequential action, AAL turns the call into a transaction: Agent calls WebMCP tool ↓ Site prepares exact action ↓ AAL checks permissions + limits ↓ User or policy approves ↓ Site commits the action ↓ Signed receipt Under the hood, AAL focuses on four things: Delegation — explicit grants connect a user, a site, an agent session, a set of tools, and bounded permissions. Authorization — consequential WebMCP calls use a prepare → approve → commit flow instead of allowing page JavaScript to directly trigger effects. Accountability — grants, commitments, approvals, and outcomes are linked together with signed, verifiable receipts. Metering — agent activity can be measured using evidence tied to the authorized call, creating a path toward websites charging agents or agent platforms for usage. We also built an AAL SDK so this isn't limited to our demo. A developer building a WebMCP-powered site can integrate AAL into their existing tools and add delegation, permissions, approvals, limits, and receipts without rebuilding the protocol from scratch. The goal is for a developer to go from: WebMCP tool to: WebMCP tool + AAL policy = authorized agent capability For the demo, we pushed this all the way through a payment flow using WebMCP + AAL + x402 + Base Sepolia test USDC . The agent can construct a transaction, but it cannot approve its own consequential action. The user sees the exact payment terms, explicitly approves them, the designated wallet authorizes the payment, and the resulting execution can be reconciled into a verifiable receipt. How we built it We intentionally treated WebMCP as the tool transport , not the security boundary. AAL is built around three core pieces, packaged behind an SDK that WebMCP developers can integrate into their own sites. AAL SDK The SDK is the developer-facing layer. It gives WebMCP-powered sites a straightforward way to: register tools with AAL declare which tools are read-only or consequential define permissions and limits connect server-side prepare and commit handlers add agent delegation trigger approval when required handle revocation and session state return signed transaction receipts The goal was to hide as much protocol complexity as possible while keeping the important security boundaries intact. Developers should be able to keep building normal WebMCP tools while AAL handles the authorization lifecycle around them. WebMCP adapter A lightweight browser adapter detects WebMCP and exposes the site's tools to the agent. It handles the agent-facing interaction, consent UX, approvals, pending states, and receipt presentation. But it intentionally has very little authority. It cannot decide that an agent is authorized to spend money, mutate application state, or bypass a policy. Site transaction service The site's backend is the actual enforcement point. It: authenticates the site's user validates the WebMCP tool against a server-owned catalog verifies the agent's grant enforces tool and spending limits prepares the exact proposed effect reserves authorization capacity verifies required approval executes server-side handlers records the resulting state signs receipts One of our most important rules is: Page JavaScript never gets to decide that an agent is authorized to perform a consequential action. Grant Service The Grant Service handles explicit delegation. The user approves a grant covering a specific site, specific WebMCP tools, limits, expiration, and required forms of evidence. The site keeps the actual grant and enforcement logic server-side; the browser receives only the information necessary to drive the experience. We built the protocol around deterministic schemas, signatures, canonical hashes, idempotency keys, state machines, revocation, and conformance vectors so authorization decisions can be reproduced instead of depending on implementation-specific behavior. For the x402 demo, we added a separate trusted approval surface and a deliberately constrained testnet payment flow so we could test AAL against a real consequential action rather than just a toy API call. Challenges we ran into WebMCP exposes capability, not authority The first challenge was architectural. A WebMCP tool being available does not mean an agent should automatically be allowed to use it. We had to separate: "This tool exists" from: "This agent is authorized to use this tool, for this user, under these conditions." That distinction shaped the entire project. Making the protocol easy enough to actually integrate Designing a secure authorization protocol is one problem. Making it something a normal WebMCP developer would actually use is another. AAL has grants, commitments, proofs, approvals, receipts, revocation, limits, and recovery state. We didn't want every website developer to have to understand or implement all of that themselves. That is why the SDK became such an important part of the project. The challenge was finding the right abstraction: hide the protocol machinery without hiding the security model . A developer should mostly think about their tool, its effects, and the policy around it. AAL should handle the rest. Browser JavaScript is not trustworthy enough It would have been much easier to implement authorization in the page itself. But an XSS vulnerability, compromised dependency, or malicious page script could then alter tool descriptions, transaction terms, or approval flows. So consequential authorization had to move server-side. Exactly-once execution is mostly an illusion One of the hardest problems appeared after an action had been dispatched. Imagine an agent places an order. The merchant processes it, but the server crashes before receiving the response. Did it execute? Simply retrying could create two orders. Calling it failed could also be wrong. So AAL has an explicit unknown state. Instead of pretending every distributed action resolves cleanly, we use durable commitments, idempotency, outcome inspection, reconciliation, and receipt revisions to eventually determine what happened without blindly executing the action again. Authentication is not the same as approval Another major challenge was distinguishing: "The user is here." from: "The user approved these exact terms." For sensitive actions, especially payments, simply authenticating the user is insufficient. The approval has to be cryptographically connected to the actual transaction being executed. That forced us to model identity, agent-key possession, user authentication, trusted display, payment authorization, and execution evidence as separate signals instead of collapsing everything into one vague notion of "trust." Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that AAL is not just an architecture around one demo. We built the SDK so any WebMCP-powered website can start integrating the same authorization model into its own tools. That was an important milestone for us because the value of an authorization layer comes from being reusable across sites, agents, and use cases. We're also proud that AAL preserves the simplicity that makes WebMCP interesting. The developer still starts with: Expose a WebMCP tool. Then AAL adds the machinery necessary when that tool crosses from information into authority . We're especially proud of the end-to-end payment architecture. A single flow separates: the agent proposing an action, AAL determining whether it is permitted, the user approving the exact transaction, the wallet authorizing the transfer,

title: NUDE Private Fitting Room
pitch: Your agent prepares the fitting room. You make the final choice.
about_excerpt: Your agent prepares the fitting room. You make the final choice. Like Comment Story Updates 01-result 02-thesis 03-the-brief 04-the-workflow 05-consent-gate 06-real-tryon 07-the-correction 08-three-looks 09-webmcp-workflow 10-prepared 11-why-each-piece 12-not-confirmed 13-handoff 14-data-boundary 15-closing About the project Most virtual try-on tools are designed to help people check out faster. We wanted to build something different: a private lingerie fitting room that a person's own agent can prepare for them, without taking the final decision away from the person . Lingerie shopping is unusually personal. Fit, comfort, color, recovery needs, body confidence, and privacy can matter as much as product specs. An agent can do a lot of useful work — research products, compare options, remember constraints, and prepare a shortlist — but there is a point where automation should stop. That became our core principle: Your agent prepares the fitting room. You make the final choice. What we built NUDE Private Lingerie Fitting Room combines a real virtual try-on experience with a WebMCP layer that lets a user's own agent operate the shopping workflow. Through WebMCP, the agent can: Research available pieces. Inspect structured product details. Read the current fitting-room state. Request a virtual try-on after the user gives consent. Verify that the correct product asset was delivered. Prepare a fitting room with recommended pieces and reasons for the user to review. The final choice is deliberately left to the person. In our demo, the user is six weeks into shoulder rehabilitation and wants options that are easier to manage while recovering. Her agent researches the collection, proposes pieces, asks for consent before initiating virtual try-on, and prepares three completed looks. The agent initially chooses the wrong color. The user simply says: “i need the beige one” The agent corrects itself and continues. That moment matters to us. The goal is not an agent that pretends to be infallible. It is an agent that can do useful shopping work, accept human correction, and hand the decision back gracefully. The agent corrects. The person decides. How WebMCP fits The fitting-room product existed before this challenge, including the NUDE shopping experience and Perfect Corp virtual try-on. During the submission period, we added the WebMCP layer that makes the workflow operable by a user's own agent. We expose five real tools: nude.list_pieces nude.get_piece nude.get_fitting_room_state nude.try_on nude.prepare_fitting_room This turns a normal website interaction into a structured agent workflow: Research → Inspect → Try on → Verify → Prepare → Human handoff For us, the interesting part of WebMCP is not reducing the number of clicks. It is allowing an agent to do meaningful preparatory work while the website remains the place where the person sees the result and makes the final judgment. Privacy and the data boundary Privacy was especially important because this is a lingerie fitting experience. The user's photo is sent to Perfect Corp when virtual try-on is requested. However, no photo of the person and no try-on result is returned through the WebMCP tools . The agent works with structured information such as product data, the user's brief, fitting-room state, completion status, and verified product delivery. This also means our recommendation reasoning is intentionally grounded in the user's brief and structured product information , not in pretending that the agent visually inspected the person's try-on image. The rendered result is there for the person. Challenges we faced The hardest part was deciding what the agent should not do . It would have been easy to make the demo look more magical by implying that the agent could see everything, judge the person's body, or make the final selection automatically. We chose not to. Instead, we had to design clear boundaries between: what the agent knows, what the try-on service renders, what WebMCP returns, and what only the person should judge. We also had to make the workflow robust enough for correction. If the agent prepares the wrong color or misunderstands a preference, the product cannot collapse. The user must be able to correct it naturally and continue. Finally, we learned that agent UX is not simply normal UI with an API added. The agent needs structured state, clear tool semantics, verifiable completion, and an explicit handoff back to the human. What we learned The biggest lesson was that good agentic commerce is not maximum automation . An agent can remove a lot of shopping work without removing human agency. WebMCP gave us a way to separate those two things cleanly: the agent can research, operate tools, verify state, and prepare the experience, while the person remains responsible for the subjective decision that actually matters. For a category as intimate as lingerie, that balance feels more useful than an autonomous checkout button. We think the future of shopping agents is not: “The AI chose for me.” It is: “Everything is ready when I'm ready to choose.” What people and agents can now do together We gave the same brief — ‘’ six weeks into shoulder rehab, can't reach behind her back, needs something invisible under white office shirts ‘’ — to an agent with no site tools, and to the same brief through WebMCP. Without tools, the agent produced a warm, well-organised consultation. It recommended a specific piece, described its cup as "seamless" — that is a different product in the catalogue; this one is two-panel seamed and push-up — asserted the nude colourway would be "completely invisible" under a white shirt, then asked her to simulate the fitting in her mind and to run the white-shirt test herself, on a bra she does not own. Through WebMCP, the same brief produces three real Perfect Corp try-ons on her own photo, a per-piece reason the agent had to supply before the fitting room would accept it, and this caveat: "VTO cannot prove white-shirt invisibility or all-day comfort; confirm permitted movements with the rehab clinician." The tool-less answer reads better. It is warmer, more confident, better structured. That is the problem. Fluency is not verification, and this decision lands on a body — someone in week six of rehab, deciding what she can physically put on. WebMCP is what lets the page hand the agent the things it can actually check, and refuse the things it cannot. title: Airlock
pitch: An analytics workspace where the AI agent does the whole analysis without ever seeing your data. It stays in DuckDB in your tab; WebMCP tools return only aggregates. Raw rows need your approval.
about_excerpt: An analytics workspace where the AI agent does the whole analysis without ever seeing your data. It stays in DuckDB in your tab; WebMCP tools return only aggregates. Raw rows need your approval. Like 1 Comment Story Updates When the agent needs specific rows, you see why, SQL, and the exact preview. You choose what to release - or say no. Nothing auto-approves Airlock: AI analytics in your browser. Data stays in the tab. The counter shows how many values you actually released — starting at zero. One click runs a full gender pay-gap review: charts in the shared notebook, every tool call in the audit log. Aggregates only — no raw rows. The agent tries to pull individual rows. Blocked by default. run_query only returns grouped results — not a setting you forgot to turn on. Turn off raw row requests: the tool is crossed out and gone from the agent's list. Permission is capability control - not a polite error msg Full story: ~7% gap within grade, not ~20% headline. Then a controlled release - only the columns you approved, counted on screen. Inspiration Analysts sit on payroll files, patient extracts, and transaction logs they cannot paste into ChatGPT . The barrier is policy, not preference. Until WebMCP, the browser had no way to offer AI help without an upload. What it does Airlock is a local-first analytics workspace. Your file loads into DuckDB in the tab and never leaves the device . An AI agent works through 14 WebMCP tools — profiling, guarded SQL, charts, findings — and returns aggregates, not rows. When individual values are truly needed, the agent must ask in writing. You see the SQL, the preview, and the cell count before you approve. A header counter tracks every value that crossed the boundary . One click runs a full gender pay-gap demo: Headline gap ~20% Within-grade gap ~7% Cells released: 0 Try it: live demo · source on GitHub Why WebMCP is the only way to build this A remote MCP server cannot read a file that never left the browser. Uploading defeats the purpose. Screen-reading agents see every rendered row — the boundary is gone on contact . WebMCP runs the code that touches the data and the code that filters what the model receives in the same page . execute is the choke point: // Tier 3 gone → tool unregistered, not just refused controller.abort(); // request_raw_rows disappears from getTools() When raw requests are disabled, we abort the tier's AbortController and request_raw_rows vanishes from the agent's tool list — it cannot call a tool it cannot see. How we built it Next.js 16 static export — no backend, no API routes DuckDB-Wasm for in-tab SQL 14 tools in one Zod-backed registry via document.modelContext.registerTool() Tiers map to AbortController lifetimes : page open → dataset loaded → raw requests permitted Every handler returns an envelope — never throws: { "ok": true, "summary": "...", "data": { ... } } { "ok": false, "error": "too_many_rows", "hint": "Use aggregates or request_raw_rows" } Privacy pipeline: SQL guard → aggregate-only run_query → column redaction → k-anonymity → human gate on raw release. Privacy model, honestly We claim: no server, no upload, provable cell count, explicit release approval. We do not claim: protection against a patient adversary reconstructing rows from many narrow aggregates. That limit is stated openly in the app. Challenges we ran into DuckDB-Wasm inside a static export (no Worker at build time) React Strict Mode double-registering WebMCP tools Observable Plot tooltips on a dark theme Making capability withdrawal visible in the UI — red dot, strikethrough — not just in code Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete pay-gap review with the counter at 0 Permission as tool lifetime , not tool logic One registry serving WebMCP agents, the in-page demo, and manual inspection Judges can verify in DevTools → Network: no request carries your data What we learned Tool descriptions are part of the product — agents read failures and hints. The airlock meter turns an abstract privacy promise into something a judge can glance at. Presentation beats feature lists in a hackathon. What's next for Airlock OPFS session persistence, org-side audit export, AST-tightened SQL guard, query-budget accounting against aggregate reconstruction. title: ContractLab
pitch: Design, lint, and live-evaluate WebMCP tool contracts in a safe sandbox before agents ever touch them
about_excerpt: Design, lint, and live-evaluate WebMCP tool contracts in a safe sandbox before agents ever touch them Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP is a powerful emerging standard for AI tool integration, but developers currently have no way to test whether agents will actually select the right tools, use correct parameters, or follow valid multi-step journeys before shipping. We built ContractLab to fill this gap—providing a deterministic lab where you can refine contracts, catch ambiguity, and prove improvements against live browser agents. What it does ContractLab is a focused workbench for designing, linting, simulating, and live-evaluating WebMCP tool contracts. It features: Design mode : Author tools with structured editors, validate schemas, annotations, state conditions, and safe effects Lint engine : Detects ambiguous names, vague descriptions, missing enums, annotation mismatches, and overlapping tools Live eval mode : Switches from authoring tools to your compiled draft contracts, exposing them only to browser agents Deterministic mock domain : A ticket support system with clean state, version guards, and visible UI updates Call recording : Captures immutable arguments, results, failures, timings, state diffs, and UI effects Seven-dimension grader : Scores tool choice, parameters, order, prohibited calls, executor success, final state, and UI effects Version comparison : Compare repeatable evidence across contract versions to prove improvements The app itself uses WebMCP in design mode for collaborative authoring, then compiles your safe contracts into real WebMCP tools for live agent evaluation. No LLM is embedded and no user code is executed. How we built it Frontend : React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and an Apple-inspired design system with translucent chrome and dense developer surfaces WebMCP integration : Centralized adapter in src/lib/webmcp.ts following Chrome's imperative API with AbortController lifecycle management Safe contract model : Typed JSON Schema subset with forms-based editing, finite mock-effect DSL, and deterministic ticket domain reducer State management : Event-sourced contract versions and eval runs stored in localStorage with reset and export/import Testing : Vitest, Testing Library, and Playwright for unit, component, and end-to-end coverage including mode isolation Backend companion : Small Node server for signed admin sessions and Polar checkout verification with signed webhooks Security : No embedded LLM, no arbitrary code execution, no cross-origin exposure, bounded descriptions, and strict annotation validation Challenges we ran into Registry lifecycle isolation : Ensuring design-mode tools never leak into eval mode required careful AbortController management and explicit human confirmation for mode switches State-dependent tool registration : The close_support_ticket tool must appear only after a resolution note is added, requiring dynamic registry rebuilding on state changes Annotation validation : Preventing readOnlyHint from binding to mutating effects and ensuring untrustedContentHint matches actual user-authored content Deterministic grading : Building a flexible grader that handles exact ordered calls, unordered groups, optional calls, and various argument matchers while remaining deterministic Browser compatibility : Adjusting for current WebMCP draft status and OpenAI's built-in browser limitations (declarative tools not discovered, iframe registration unsupported) Accomplishments that we're proud of Complete two-mode architecture : Design and eval modes with full registry isolation and visible mode switching Live agent integration : Successfully tested with Codex in-app Browser WebMCP, achieving 100/100 grade on urgent triage case Comprehensive lint engine : 12+ deterministic checks covering contract quality, ambiguity, and security signals Seven-dimension grader : Separate scoring for tool selection, parameters, order, prohibited calls, executor success, final state, and UI effects Seeded project with deliberate flaws : Starter contract demonstrates real problems (overlapping tools, vague descriptions, missing enums, annotation issues) that users can fix and test Full test coverage : 5 test suites, 11 unit tests, and 1 Playwright journey all passing Security boundaries : No embedded LLM, no arbitrary code execution, same-origin only, bounded outputs, and strict validation Apple-inspired UI : Restrained typography, translucent chrome, grouped inspectors, and platform-style controls using only local fonts What we learned WebMCP is still a Community Group draft, not a W3C Standard—documentation can change and browser support varies Annotations are hints for agents, not authorization systems—normal server and application authorization must remain authoritative Deterministic linting cannot predict every model behavior, but it can dramatically reduce ambiguity and common failure modes Mode isolation is critical: never expose authoring tools and draft tools simultaneously State-dependent tool registration requires careful lifecycle management and explicit UI feedback Browser agents need clear, bounded descriptions and schemas—vague tools lead to wrong selections Version guards on mutating commands prevent race conditions in multi-agent scenarios Untrusted content must be explicitly labeled throughout the stack (schemas, results, UI) What's next for it Additional seeded projects : Expand beyond the support-ticket domain to demonstrate WebMCP contracts for file systems, databases, and external APIs Enhanced lint rules : Add more sophisticated ambiguity detection, semantic overlap analysis, and security-focused checks Collaborative features : Multi-user project editing with conflict resolution and shared eval runs Advanced grading : Add machine learning-based pattern recognition for common agent failure modes Export formats : Generate OpenAPI specs, TypeScript types, and other contract representations from WebMCP definitions Browser agent marketplace : Curated library of tested WebMCP tool contracts for common domains Real backend integration : Option to connect contracts to actual APIs while maintaining safety boundaries Built With webmcp Try it out title: Cutline
pitch: In-browser agent-native video editor powered by WebMCP. 36+ WebMCP editing tools integrated. Works natively with Codex and and all WebMCP supported browsers.
about_excerpt: In-browser agent-native video editor powered by WebMCP. 36+ WebMCP editing tools integrated. Works natively with Codex and and all WebMCP supported browsers. Like Comment Story Updates Cutline A local-first, agent-native video editor where people and WebMCP agents collaborate on the same versioned timeline. Inspiration Most AI-assisted creative tools place an agent beside the application, but the agent often interacts through fragile screen coordinates or hidden automation. I wanted to explore a different approach. What if the editor itself exposed meaningful, safe editing actions that both people and agents could use? So I have built Cutline , a local-first video editor built around WebMCP. A person can edit clips directly while an agent can inspect the same project, propose changes, create alternate cuts, and preview the result. Both work against one shared, versioned timeline. What it does Cutline is an in-browser video editor with: 36 semantic WebMCP tools for inspecting and editing the project Local video, audio, image, SVG, and subtitle imports A multi-track timeline with trimming, splitting, moving, linking, transitions, fades, and gain controls Reversible editing branches for exploring alternate cuts Protected timeline ranges that prevent accidental changes Comments, edit history, undo, redo, and visual verification Local WebM and capability-gated MP4 rendering Project persistence through IndexedDB and OPFS Portable .cutline project bundles Media remains on the user's device during the normal workflow. The agent operates on structured editing concepts such as clips, tracks, ranges, branches, and transitions instead of trying to click arbitrary coordinates. How it's built Cutline uses Next.js 16 , React 19 , and TypeScript . A Zustand store holds the current editor state, while an Immer-based reducer acts as the single editing engine. Both UI interactions and WebMCP tools create typed commands and send them through the same reducer: Timeline UI ─────┐ ├──> Typed command ──> Shared reducer ──> Versioned project WebMCP tools ────┘ This shared command path keeps human and agent edits consistent. It also gives every successful operation a receipt containing the affected ranges, resulting version, warnings, and a semantic digest. Zod validates WebMCP inputs and generates the corresponding JSON schemas. Branch versions and SHA-256 digests protect the project from stale or conflicting operations. Media inspection and rendering happen in the browser. Cutline uses Canvas for visual compositing, Web Audio for mixing, MediaRecorder or WebCodecs for encoding, and Mediabunny for media processing and muxing. Project snapshots are stored in IndexedDB, with OPFS used for local media when available. Challenges we faced Keeping human and agent edits consistent The UI and the agent could easily have developed separate editing behavior. That would make the project unpredictable and difficult to maintain. We solved this by routing every durable edit through the same typed command reducer. Making agent actions safe and reversible Video edits can affect linked clips, downstream timing, transitions, and protected material. We added optimistic branch versions, semantic digests, atomic edit batches, range locks, undo history, and reversible branches so an agent cannot silently leave the project in a partially edited state. Working with media entirely in the browser Browser media APIs vary by codec, platform, and available capabilities. Previewing multiple tracks, mixing audio, generating proxies, preserving local files, and producing downloadable renders required careful coordination between media elements, Canvas, Web Audio, workers, IndexedDB, and OPFS. Matching preview and export An effect that looks correct in the viewer must also appear correctly in the final render. We reused the same transition, crop, caption, gain, and timing rules across both paths to keep them visually aligned. Designing a dense editor interface A video editor needs a viewer, timeline, media bin, transcript, comments, history, and agent feedback without overwhelming the screen. We iterated heavily on panel sizing, responsive layouts, 16:9 presentation, safe spacing, and direct timeline manipulation. Learnings Semantic tools instead of coordinate-based automation Shared application state instead of a parallel agent model Explicit versions and conflict handling Reversible operations Visible receipts and previews Clear boundaries around protected user work We also learned that local-first media editing is possible in modern browsers, but reliable codec support, persistence, cleanup, and rendering require more engineering than the interface initially suggests. Accomplishments Built a functional browser-based multi-track editor Exposed 36 WebMCP tools over the same engine used by the UI Added atomic, version-checked agent edits Implemented reversible branches and protected ranges Kept imported media and rendered output local Added browser-based video and audio rendering What's next for Cutline The next stage for Cutline would focus on broader codec support, background and resumable rendering, cloud backup, real-time collaboration, stronger accessibility testing, and integrations for publishing completed videos. Cutline demonstrates a future where creative software does not merely tolerate agents. It gives them a structured, observable, and reversible way to collaborate with people. title: doA2A
pitch: A WebMCP prototype where agents prepare bounded work and people authorize exact consequential actions.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP prototype where agents prepare bounded work and people authorize exact consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates 1 doA2Ai - Human-authorized execution for WebMCP Inspiration Agents should be able to do useful housekeeping tasks on your browser without acting like they own the mortgage, and without requiring the user's banking credentials to do it (unless of course, you give it explicit permission!). An agent can be helpful without being given a giant blob of access, but only if the boundary stays visible; doA2Ai explores a practical version of that idea: give an agent the tools needed for the current task, keep consequential decisions with the person, and verify that the result still matches what the person authorized. The goal is not less agent capability; it is more precise capability and user support through agency. Why WebMCP WebMCP gives the model an easy way to expose structured tools for the task that exists. Instead of making an agent reverse-engineer buttons and visual state, the browser can present a page-scoped capability surface that can be inspected and constrained - like a www dot paint by number for agents. doA2Ai adds an authority boundary around that surface; the extension identifies the current HTTPS origin and tool definitions, applies local policy, and keeps human-only values and decisions out of the agent's authority. The capability surface and the review path change as the task changes, and the user is given the option to allow or deny certain permissions. What people and agents can do together The agent can inspect the current target's available WebMCP tools and prepare a bounded request. The person keeps the parts that are actually theirs: policy, human-only values, exact review, and the final decision. The result is an explicit set of outcomes: - an allowed action within delegated authority; - an exact action held for human review; or - a policy-blocked action that is not executed. Receipts record the proposal, decision, execution status, and verification state. If the candidate changes between authorization and execution, doA2Ai blocks the action and requires reauthorization instead of treating the change as close enough. How it was built The installable Chrome extension owns rules, task state, decisions, connection state, and receipt history locally. A deployable HTTPS service and read-only control center provide proof-of-possession device pairing, replay-resistant signed requests, short-lived device and task-scoped connection credentials, and terminal receipt-digest binding. The service is a broker and control center, not an agent and not a WebMCP target. The real target remains a separate HTTPS page. The public repository contains the extension, service source, product contract, and owner/judge runbook: https://github.com/kaileahmarin/doA2Ai I used ChatGPT through Chrome for WebMCP protocol invocation and Gemini for additional testing. The project was built and tested with OpenAI Codex. Testing and limitations The intended judge path uses Chrome with WebMCP enabled, the official WebMCP Coffee Store target, and a compatible browser-integrated agent. The runbook covers an allowed path, an exact human-review path, a blocked path, and receipt verification using harmless test data. This is a V1 hackathon candidate, not a production authorization service. Mediation is cooperative: a client that bypasses the protected tool path can still call an ordinary page-owned WebMCP tool. OAuth protected-resource discovery, production tenant isolation, account recovery, and independent attestation of arbitrary page-owned effects are intentionally outside this slice. What we learned The hardest part was deciding exactly how to invoke user input when the candidate changes. Capability, authority, and outcome have to stay aligned. Human-only values cannot quietly leak into agent schemas or receipts. Authorization has to bind to an exact proposal, and uncertainty has to remain visible instead of being silently retried. That is the core idea behind doA2Ai: agents can do more without being given everything, while people keep authority over consequential actions. title: Duet
pitch: Plan the room with your agent. You pin the judgment calls; your agent solves feuds, diets and table math through 25 WebMCP tools — live, on one shared floor plan.
about_excerpt: Plan the room with your agent. You pin the judgment calls; your agent solves feuds, diets and table math through 25 WebMCP tools — live, on one shared floor plan. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Seating a room is a two-brain problem. One brain holds context no form can capture: who is divorced, which sponsor is feuding with whom, which aunt needs to sit near the exit. The other has to satisfy a combinatorial pile of constraints: table capacities, conflicts, introductions, dietary needs, accessibility, company-mixing rules, and table balance. Humans are great at the first and bad at the second. Agents are the opposite. Before WebMCP, neither interface worked well. A drag-and-drop floor plan is a terrible surface for an agent to operate through pixels, while moving the task into chat throws away the human's spatial judgment. Duet lets both work on the same live state, in the same tab: the human drags, pins, and visually evaluates the room while the agent uses structured tools such as seat_guest , add_constraint , set_group_rule , and a real constraint solver. How it creates a better user experience Duet gives human-agent collaboration an explicit contract, enforced in code. Pins are law. Any guest placed manually is pinned 📌. The solver plans around those decisions, and agent tools are refused if they attempt to move or remove a pinned guest. Agents propose; humans decide. The preferred agent tool, propose_arrangement , does not mutate the room. It displays the reasoning and complete move list first. Only the human can Accept or Dismiss it. The tool surface follows human attention. Selecting a table dynamically exposes table-scoped tools such as seat_at_selected_table and clear_selected_table . Deselecting it removes them. The agent's available capabilities therefore reflect what the human is currently focused on. Everything is visible and reversible. Agent actions appear as a violet cursor on the board, every action enters a shared activity feed labeled ✳ agent or ● you, and undo/redo works across both human and agent actions. What becomes possible — together — that wasn't before Load a 120-guest fundraising gala. The human manually places two important guests, pinning them in place. The agent records "press away from the board", applies "maximum two people from the same company per table", and proposes a complete arrangement for the remaining 118 guests. The solver honors every constraint without touching the human's pins. The human reviews the proposal visually and accepts it in one click. Create a conflict deliberately and Duet pans to the affected table, identifies who conflicts and why, and lets the agent call explain_seating to justify individual placements. Then ask: "Give me the caterer's brief." The agent calls export_plan and returns dietary counts by table. That loop — human judgment steering an agent and a constraint solver through conversation, directly on a shared visual surface — is what WebMCP makes possible. The same engine includes five scenarios: wedding, fundraising gala, corporate networking dinner, office seating, and classroom seating. How we implemented WebMCP Duet exposes 21 base tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , covering: guest and table CRUD pair constraints with notes group spread and cluster rules solver execution arrangement proposals pins dietary reports Markdown export template loading undo explain_seating get_activity_log , allowing a returning agent to understand what the human changed while it was away It also exposes 4 dynamic selection-scoped tools registered and removed with AbortController as the user's selection changes. The WebMCP tool surface itself therefore mirrors the human's current focus. Tool results return structured JSON, including the conflicts an action would create, so agents can reason about consequences before modifying state. Guardrails are enforced at the tool layer: pinned guests cannot be moved by agents, and propose_arrangement is explicitly presented as the preferred workflow so agents default to human review rather than silent mutation. The constraint solver is dependency-free and combines greedy assignment, local search, targeted repair, and three-way relocation. A 120-guest room solves in roughly 75 ms while respecting pins, pair constraints, group rules, accessibility requirements, and table balance. Duet is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript and has no backend. The entire collaborative state lives in the browser tab — exactly where WebMCP operates. title: Label Check
pitch: Label Check makes it possible for people with dietary restrictions or allergies to confidently shop online with their AI agent.
about_excerpt: Label Check makes it possible for people with dietary restrictions or allergies to confidently shop online with their AI agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration My inspiration for this project is very close to my heart: my partner has celiac disease, which means she cannot eat food containing gluten, or food that has had cross-contact with gluten. This disease has turned grocery shopping into a stressful experience. She has to read every ingredient label, and the often-overlooked "may contain" statements. This is not only the experience of people with celiac disease. People with other dietary restrictions or severe food allergies have the same problem. AI-led online shopping does not make grocery shopping easier for them yet. What it does Label Check makes an agent retrieve a product’s ingredients and label statements before it can add that product to the cart. Maple & Sage is the grocery shop where that rule is live. An agent can search through the product catalog and build a cart the same way it would on any online store. What it has to retrieve is the ingredients and the label statements, including when a field is missing. "null" is not the same as an empty list and it is not treated as "none". Alongside the agent’s WebMCP path, the client can still use the ordinary "add" button to add products to their cart. The store never decides whether a product is suitable. The client lists their restrictions for their AI agent, the merchant supplies the facts (ingredients and label information), and the AI agent compares them to make a decision. How I built it I built an original Online Store 2.0 theme, using the Shopify theme skeleton's GitHub repository. Each product’s ingredients and label statements are written into the page, so the custom tool can return them without a backend. A small script runs before Shopify’s WebMCP tools register, so the gate is already there when an agent calls update_cart. There is one custom tool, get_product_food_disclosures. It returns ingredients and label_statements, including null. A receipt in the tab records that retrieval ran for that product version. Native update_cart can increase a line only when that receipt is current. Challenges I ran into Keeping null and [] distinct took more care than I initially thought. An empty "may contain" list is not the same as "the merchant did not supply this field". Collapsing them would hide the exact thing my partner has to look for. And then naming this project was a fun one! Anything that sounded like Trust, Safe, or Verified would imply the store had judged the product. I chose Label Check because it was the best way for me to describe the action that the agent has to do. It's not a pass mark on the product. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that I was able to use the WebMCP technology to build something that would actually help someone I love. Getting it working, on a real shop that an agent can use, is such a great feeling. What I learned Prior to this challenge, I didn't know what WebMCP was. I learned about it and its use cases, especially the ability for an agent to help us perform a task while we can still intervene at any time (kind of like co-building), which I find incredibly interesting. I chose to use WebMCP to build Label Check, but I can also see it being useful in creative endeavors: editing a 3D model, a picture, or a video together with an agent. What's next for Label Check I would love ecommerce platforms such as Shopify to ship ingredients and label-statement fields that food shop owners can fill, the way they did with product taxonomy. Merchants used those fields to add more detail to their catalogs and consequently ranked better in searches. Doing the same for dietary information would help those products show up when someone asks an agent a specific question, like "recommend 5 gluten-free snacks that are safe for people with celiac disease". Then I would love those ecommerce platforms to add a Label Check tool to their native WebMCP stack. This way, people with dietary restrictions would be able to point their AI agent at a shop and buy online confidently. title: magpie
pitch: Magpie remembers where capabilities live and how they are wired into reusable workflows.
about_excerpt: Magpie remembers where capabilities live and how they are wired into reusable workflows. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP lets a site hand an agent typed functions instead of a page to scrape. The limit shows up immediately: document.modelContext is per document . The agent sees the page it is on and nothing else, while every task I actually wanted spanned sites. Find the delayed orders here, open a ticket there, email me a summary. Then the less comfortable realisation: agents could already do that. They browse, they navigate, some remember. What was missing was not capability. What it does The extension is three parts, and only the last is impossible outside a browser extension: Discovery : a modelContext polyfill installed in the page's MAIN world at document_start, or a native implementation wrapped in place, mirroring every registration out to the service worker. Registry : one list across tabs and sessions: live page tools, remembered sites that are closed right now, and nine action tools of its own, each with a status (AVAILABLE, SITE_CLOSED, AUTH_REQUIRED, TOOL_CHANGED, TOOL_MISSING) . A public crawler can catalogue which sites expose tools, but it is always signed out, so it never sees the ones behind your login. Cross-site execution : the extension runs each step on the site that owns that tool, in your own logged-in tab. The site exposes 13 capabilities of its own through registerTool() , and is where a run stops being something that happened and becomes something you can repeat: every step the agent took, the capability each one used, and a button that runs the whole thing again. Reach on one side, certainty on the other. What I actually built Not a smarter agent, a layer that makes an agents actions accountable and repeatable. Four things it refuses to do: Refuses to invent. A fabricated capability is rejected with the real names listed. Refuses to self-approve. The write prompt takes no approved argument an agent could set for itself, and fails closed where it cannot ask. Refuses to guess. Where judgement is needed, a reason step stops and hands the question back with the data attached. A gate fails closed rather than compare against data that never arrived. Refuses to take the agent's word. The engine writes the run record, so a step marked ok genuinely ran. Steps are JSON only, never generated JS, validated, then checked against the registry. Challenges I ran into Half of real WebMCP tools navigate instead of returning data. Pointed at real commerce sites, I found tools that move the browser rather than return values ,and a navigation drops that tab's tools from the registry, so a site read as "closed" seconds after its own tool had run. The agent may bypass you entirely. One posting straight to the extension's page API got a run id back while nothing was saved. Recording had to become a property of the bridge rather than of how a prompt was phrased, because you do not control the prompt. What I learned Magpie is not a new capability. Neither was WebMCP. Agents operated websites long before the spec scraping the DOM, driving a mouse. What WebMCP added was a contract: the site declares what it supports, with types, instead of the agent inferring it from markup. This project does the same thing one layer up, a contract across pages rather than within one. What's next Watch jobs, where the hard part is not the timer but pre-approving a write with limits validated in code rather than at a prompt. Remote MCP servers feeding the same registry. And a manual builder, so aworkflow can be assembled from proven steps with no agent involved at all. title: MetaWebMCP
pitch: WebMCP builds WebMCP. Turn observable website workflows into bounded, reusable WebMCP tools. Then activate, test, and export them.
about_excerpt: WebMCP builds WebMCP. Turn observable website workflows into bounded, reusable WebMCP tools. Then activate, test, and export them. Like Comment Story Updates Small test in ChatGPT ChatGPT using MetaWebMCP to find games on steam ChatGPT using the tool to find properties in Finca Raiz Inspiration As new standards and protocols come, adoption is key. WebMCP gives agents a clean, semantic way to interact with websites, but most of the web will not add native integrations overnight. We wanted to see whether compatibility could grow from the other direction: let an agent observe an existing workflow, give it a narrow WebMCP interface, use it immediately, and export it as a native integration later. What it does MetaWebMCP is WebMCP that builds WebMCP. It turns the useful, observable parts of a website into bounded, reusable tools. An agent can inspect a site, define tools grounded in its interface, activate them on the current page, test them, and export the same contracts as a standalone WebMCP repository. How we built it We built MetaWebMCP through a lot of small iterations. We intentionally kept the architecture lightweight so we could focus on the hard problem of creating a useful compatibility layer between existing websites and WebMCP. The core runs on Node.js without runtime package dependencies. A permanent set of seven meta-tools handles analysis, contract creation, activation, testing, export, state inspection, and reset. Activating a project dynamically registers a second set of domain tools on the same top-level page. One of our most important decisions was to use the same ToolSpec objects for live activation, execution, testing, and export. The exported integration is not a separate code-generation demo. It is another representation of the exact contracts the agent reviewed and used. For public websites, MetaWebMCP uses an isolated browser session to capture the rendered page and its accessibility model. For owned sites, it exports a standalone repository containing direct document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls. It also includes a fallback registry so the complete workflow remains usable in ordinary browsers without native WebMCP support. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was, of course, not generating code. It was finding the right boundary between brittle browser automation and a useful semantic tool. Real websites are messy. Controls may be ambiguous, inaccessible, repeated, dynamically rendered, or changed without warning. We had to ground every generated tool in observed evidence while refusing to expose arbitrary JavaScript or unrestricted browser operations. The recursive lifecycle was another challenge. MetaWebMCP needs to keep its permanent tools active while safely adding, replacing, and removing generated tools. It also needs the live implementation and exported implementation to behave consistently. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of The main accomplishment is that MetaWebMCP is legitimately useful. It is not only a recursive gimmick built for a hackathon. In our native test, the page exposed seven permanent WebMCP tools, dynamically expanded to eleven, passed all four generated-tool checks, and exported a standalone repository whose tools continued to work without MetaWebMCP as the runtime. Our limited benchmarks also produced a concrete result. Across the matched tests, MetaWebMCP reduced model-facing tool text by 4.11× to 57.31× and non-cached token usage by 1.28× to 6.81×. It was also 1.39× to 2.18× faster on the larger, multi-page workloads. It was slower on one shorter, single-page task because the initial analysis and tool-authoring cost did not have time to amortize. That counterexample matters. The strongest result is not that MetaWebMCP always makes an agent faster, but that a small semantic interface can keep large amounts of repetitive browser output out of the agent’s context. What we learned Agents have come a long way. They can now inspect an unfamiliar interface, reason about its useful capabilities, shape those capabilities into typed contracts, and use the resulting tools without requiring a separate model API inside the application. A weaker version of this was already possible some years ago, with a lot of issues, but now the agents seem to get it consistently, enough for tools like this to exist. What's next for MetaWebMCP The next step is to develop MetaWebMCP into a robust platform with fully managed services, so agents can connect to the existing web reliably through WebMCP. That means persistent and versioned integrations, stronger evaluations, monitoring for interface drift, managed browser execution, better owner-installation workflows, and production-grade controls for authentication, authorization, auditing, and confirmation. The goal remains the same: make WebMCP adoption incremental, practical, and useful across the web.
