title: Persona
pitch: We give doctors, landlords, employers, and government agencies the same information again and again. What if they requested what they needed from ONE profile, and we chose exactly what each received?
about_excerpt: We give doctors, landlords, employers, and government agencies the same information again and again. What if they requested what they needed from ONE profile, and we chose exactly what each received? Like Comment Story Updates Persona Intro Persona. The Universal Form Across our lifetime, we fill out hundreds of forms. We put in the same names, the same health history, we name our parents, where we went to school, we put in our address, and we do it all over again and again: at the doctor, when renting a home, when applying for government services or a job, at the bank... What if we only had to maintain one form instead, one that those institutions could request access to? A place where we know exactly who is asking for our information, and we keep track of what has been shared throughout our lifetime. What it does Persona keeps one profile of the facts you normally retype: legal name, date of birth, address, contact details, insurance, employer and income, health history, etc. You fill out that profile once, and maintain only when you have a life update. When an institution needs your information, it sends a request that names who is asking, why, and which fields it wants. You open that request through your agent or directly through the website, choose what to release, and approve it. Persona then sends only the approved fields to that one institution and shows you a transfer record: how many fields went out, and whether the destination confirmed it received them. Institutions never see your full profile, only the necessary fields. When an active permission still matches the institution, purpose, and requested information, Persona can complete the request without asking you to approve the same disclosure again. Anything new, sensitive, or out of date waits for you. Persona tracks when you last confirmed each fact and flags anything that may be out of date before you send it. Why WebMCP fits Completing forms includes repeatable steps and decisions that only a person should make. WebMCP lets the agent find requests, read what each institution needs, open a request, check its status, start an approved transfer, and confirm what the destination received. The person still controls corrections, temporary answers, outdated information, and consent. WebMCP tools receive metadata such as field names and request status. The approved personal information moves directly from Persona to the intended destination through a separate browser channel. How I built it Persona is a Next.js and React app written in TypeScript. Locally, one server process serves two web addresses, for the demo, I used: localhost for Persona and 127.0.0.1 for the destination page. Browsers treat those as separate origins, which is what lets the demo show information crossing between these servers. The agent talks to Persona through WebMCP. The top Persona page registers seven tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool returns metadata only: field names, counts, request state, transfer state, and destination confirmation state. No tool takes in or hands back a raw profile value. Approved values move on a separate path. After you approve a request, Persona creates a one-use authorization bound to your browser session, the request version, the recipient, the destination origin, the frame instance, the exact field list, and an expiration time. Persona checks every one of those before it sends the approved values to the destination iframe with postMessage . The destination counts the fields it accepted and reports that count back on its own. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was keeping the real person's information away from the AI agent. The agent can read a lot of what the page produces: status messages, error text, the web address, the text a screen reader would read out. A real value like a date of birth could slip into any of those by accident. I built one checked path for all of those places that shows field names and counts instead of values, and I wrote tests that fail if a real value ever shows up where the agent can see it. Another challenge was deciding which jobs the agent is allowed to do. Give it too little and the person still approves every field by hand. Give it too much and it can send something the person wanted to hold back or edit first. I set clear boundaries for the agent and kept the review step in Persona short, so the person sees what would be shared and can change it before anything moves. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm a self-taught builder. Thanks to the tools I have access to now, an idea I have carried for so many years can finally be real. A tool like Persona could have an incredible impact on everyone's life. What I learned Simple ideas with clear boundaries beat a fancy UI. This first version is not the prettiest, but it shows the core product and the idea behind it. What's next for Persona Holding a person's personally identifiable information comes with great power and responsibility. I want to put my effort into making Persona a secure platform, with thoughtful guardrails in place, so that information is not leaked or accessed by bad actors or future AI agents. This next version of Persona will need to meet the rules institutions already follow, like HIPAA, and others. This means that in the future, for Persona to work, it also has to meet the rules institutions already follow, like HIPAA, the U.S. law that governs how health information is stored and shared. title: ShowMe
pitch: Where did they hide that setting? Your agent lights up where to click next, on your own screen. No help article, no guessing, no handing over your account. Next time you won't need to ask.
about_excerpt: Where did they hide that setting? Your agent lights up where to click next, on your own screen. No help article, no guessing, no handing over your account. Next time you won't need to ask. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I'm bad at finding things in apps. Not proud of it, but it's true. Some real ones: Auth0. I needed to change one setting for a login flow and spent way too long clicking around the dashboard before I found it. The docs said "go to Settings". There are a lot of places called Settings. Jira. New team, new board, and a few days in I'm running standup from it in front of everyone, trying to find where you change an issue type or add a column while people wait. Datadog. When I was learning it I couldn't find where to filter logs properly, and later I struggled to find where the RUM integrations live. And that's me, with a technical background. I can only imagine how the websites regular people use every day make people from other backgrounds struggle. These all have the same problem. The answer exists, someone wrote it down, and it still doesn't help, because it's not on your screen. The AI answer to this is "let the agent do it for you". Agents are great, I use them all day. But that answer has two problems. You didn't learn anything, so next month you'll ask again. And the site now has to trust a robot with your login settings or your money. And sometimes you just can't hand it off. You're presenting. You're running standup. You're the one who's supposed to know where it is. Nobody wants to say "hold on, let me ask the agent" in front of the room. So I didn't want an agent that does it for me. I wanted one that points at my screen and says "there", waits for me to click, and next time I don't need it. That's ShowMe. What it does You open a site in a browser that has WebMCP, and you ask your agent something like "how do I turn on international transfers?" Then this happens: The site gives the agent a map of its own interface. Every screen, every menu, every button, with a sentence about each one. The agent works out the path and hands the whole thing to the page in one call. The page lights up the first thing you need to click, with a short message. You click it. The next one lights up. And so on. You don't wait for the model between steps. It's not involved between steps. Click the wrong thing and the page tells the agent, which re-plans. Say "just do it for me" and the site decides. Opening a menu, fine. Pressing Confirm on a transfer, no. The agent tells you why. When you're done, the agent tells you the path in one line so you remember it. I made two sites to show it. Neither has any guide code in it, just the attributes. PeruBank is a fake bank. The switch for international transfers is four levels deep, and the final Confirm is a button I never want an agent pressing. Meridian is a fake team tracker. Board settings behind one three-dots menu, project settings behind another, a type icon nobody realises is a button. Basically the board I struggled with. Who it's for: anyone in an app with hundreds of settings, like developer dashboards and admin consoles. People who should never hand an agent their account, like my parents and their bank. And anyone learning a tool in front of other people. Why WebMCP To show someone where something is, you need three things, and only the page has them: A map of the interface that's actually true right now. A way to wait for a real click and know it happened. A say in what the agent is allowed to do. A screen-reading agent guesses at all three. You could maybe get the map from an accessibility tree. You can't get the other two. WebMCP gives the site one standard way to hand all three to whatever agent the person is using. That's why this works now and didn't before. How I built it One JavaScript file, one stylesheet, no build step. Both sites use the same two files. The site marks its elements: data-guide is the id. data-guide-desc is a sentence about it, written like you'd explain it to a new colleague. data-guide-delegable means an agent may do this step for you. Leave it off and it's yours. data-guide-danger means it can't be undone. Never delegated. data-screen , data-panel , data-dialog , data-menu group things so the agent knows what has to be open first. The map is rebuilt from the live page every time it's asked for, so anything rendered later is in it too. Whether something is open is read from what's actually visible on screen. Five tools, all registered through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_ui_map and get_current_view . Read-only. Flagged untrustedContentHint because they echo text people typed. run_walkthrough . The long one. Takes the whole path, paces you through it on the page, listens for the AbortSignal , and comes back with what you did and where you are now. If it's taking a while it returns in_progress after 40 seconds and the agent calls again. do_step_for_person . Reads the policy from the markup. Refuses anything not marked delegable. end_walkthrough . Only exists while a guide is running. Registered with an AbortController , so when the guide ends the tool disappears and toolchange fires. A Playwright test drives both sites through getTools and executeTool , with Google's polyfill injected so it runs on plain Chrome. Each site also has an Agent activity panel. It shows which bits of the API have actually been used this session, plus a transcript of every call and every click. I added it because the agent's own call log is just two lines, and everything interesting happens inside one of them. Challenges I ran into The first version did one spotlight per tool call. In ChatGPT's browser every round trip was 10 to 20 seconds, so you'd click and then sit there. Handing the whole path to the page in one call fixed that. Then I hit tool timeouts, which is where in_progress came from. Knowing what the person actually did. Clicks are easy. Text fields need Enter or a pause. Checkboxes fire change, not click, if you hit the label. "Clicked somewhere else" needed a listener on the whole document that ignores the overlay, the label around a checkbox, and the panel button. Things that aren't visible yet. If the agent asks for something inside a closed menu, the page has to say what to open first, in a sentence the agent can act on. Annotations. Not every browser accepts every one, so registration retries without the rejected one and the panel says which. The map is big. About 20K characters on the bank, 40K on the tracker. It works, but it's most of the minute the first answer takes. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The first time it worked end to end in ChatGPT's browser. I asked how to turn on international transfers, the profile menu lit up, I clicked, Settings lit up, I clicked, and it kept going all the way to Confirm without me waiting once. Seven steps, planned once. The version before that had a spinner between every click, so that was the moment I knew the design was right. The bank saying no. I asked the agent to press Confirm for me, and instead of doing it, it came back with PeruBank's own words: this is irreversible and an agent never does it. The agent didn't decide that. I didn't put it in a prompt. It's one attribute on one button, and the tool reads it. That's the part I'd show a bank. Getting the wrong click right. I clicked somewhere else on purpose, and instead of the guide silently breaking, the agent got back exactly what I'd clicked, said so, and re-planned from where I actually was. It took a while to teach the page the difference between "clicked the thing", "clicked the label around the thing", "clicked the panel", and "wandered off". A tool that appears and disappears. end_walkthrough only exists while a guide is running. Open Site tools mid-guide and it's there. Finish, and it's gone. Small, but it means the agent's own tool list tells it what state the page is in, and the browser fires toolchange to say so. The whole thing is one file and one stylesheet, and both demo sites run the exact same two. Nothing in PeruBank or Meridian knows about the guide except the attributes. And the one I actually care about. After the guide, I turned the setting back off myself. No agent, no help article. Profile menu, Settings, Transfer limits, Advanced. Four clicks. That's what it was for. What I learned The biggest one: keep the model out of the loop between steps. My first version asked the agent after every click, and every answer took 10 to 20 seconds. Once the agent planned once and the page did the pacing, the whole thing went from painful to instant. The agent is good at reading a map and planning. The page is good at waiting for a click. Let each do its job. Writing the sentence for each element is the real work. It's the same work as writing a help article, one line per button, written for a colleague. The difference is these lines show up on the person's screen at the moment they need them, instead of in a doc nobody finds. U

title: Spacio
pitch: Warehouse managers and an AI agent plan slotting on the same 3D model through WebMCP. The agent reconciles reports and proposes moves; the person decides and approves.
about_excerpt: Warehouse managers and an AI agent plan slotting on the same 3D model through WebMCP. The agent reconciles reports and proposes moves; the person decides and approves. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Managing a warehouse is a stream of decisions with real consequences: where a new product line goes, which items move closer to dispatch before the season peak, whether the cold area can absorb next month's intake, where twenty incoming pallets will live. Each decision draws on reports from several areas, in several formats, each telling part of the story. Logistics keeps the article master, commercial sends the sales export, purchasing announces intake, quality flags holds. Units vary, SKU codes follow different conventions and the operational constraints live in a notes field. The manager reconciles all of it with experience, applies rules learned on the floor and takes responsibility for the outcome. I have done that job in several sectors, among them automotive parts and food distribution, and Spacio is the tool I wanted on those days: a model that knows the rules, an assistant that does the reconciliation and the arithmetic, and a clear line around the decisions that stay with the person in charge. Who we are Spacio is a two-person project. I bring the warehouse side: years managing operations in automotive, food and other sectors, the reports that arrive every month, the rules learned on the floor and the decisions that come with them. My husband, a software developer, brings the engineering: the 3D model, the WebMCP tool catalog, the validation rules and the traceability log. Every tool in Spacio started as a situation from my work and became code through his. What it does Spacio is a browser app where that work happens. The manager keeps a 3D model of the facility (perimeter, racks, aisles, docks), the inventory that lives in it and the slotting plans under consideration. An AI agent works on that same model through 32 WebMCP tools: The manager hands over the reports as they arrive. The agent normalises units, spellings and codes, maps notes such as "keep upright" to constraints, validates every container against rack geometry and storage type, loads what fits and explains each rejection with a reason code such as STORAGE_TYPE or CONTAINER_TOO_LARGE . The manager states the operating rules in plain language: heavy items on the two lower levels, cold chain in cold storage, keep the batteries where they are. The agent pins heavy items low, locks bins and works around them. The manager hands over a month of order lines. The agent aggregates them into picks per SKU, assigns each product its ABC class, reloads the inventory with it, generates deterministic slotting strategies and compares them by route metres, time, number of moves, free reserve and weight rules, then explains every relocation. The manager questions a proposal. The agent traces the pick route of the top seller to packing and dispatch, focuses the camera on a rack and reads back the move list. When the data calls for it, the agent adjusts the building: more pallet racks, a dispatch dock at the front, a wider aisle, with the layout validated for clearance and reachability. The manager approves the facility revision and approves the plan. Those are page buttons, the tools report approvedByHuman truthfully, and the approved plan freezes its move list. Every call, human or agent, lands in a traceability log with parameters, results and durations. Why WebMCP is a strong fit for this use case Three kinds of reasoning meet in every slotting decision. The reports are unstructured and full of context that a language model reads well. The building is a geometric model that the page reasons about precisely: rack dimensions, aisle clearances, weight per level, distances to dispatch. The decision belongs to a person who carries the responsibility. WebMCP lets those three work on the same model: the page exposes its domain functions as typed tools, the agent calls them with what it read from the reports, and the manager sees every result in the same 3D scene they use to decide. The value is in the combination. The agent's reading of a workbook becomes useful the moment it can be validated against real geometry, and the page's validation becomes useful the moment someone can feed it 200 rows in one call. Each tool returns exact numbers, so the agent reasons on the same figures the manager sees, and the manager can check every claim the agent makes. How it creates a better user experience The manager works the way they already talk about the warehouse. They hand over the reports and describe the rules in their own words. The agent turns that into typed tool calls and the model updates in front of them: racks take their category, products appear in their bins, the route of the top seller draws itself to the dock. Every proposal comes back with figures and reasons, so the manager questions it, adjusts a constraint and asks again, in minutes. The buttons that carry liability stay in the interface, and the whole exchange can be reviewed afterwards in the log. What people and agents can now do together Go from two departmental exports to a validated inventory in the 3D model in one conversation, with every rejected container explained. Until now this meant days of spreadsheet reconciliation followed by manual entry. Turn a month of order lines into an ABC classification and a set of slotting strategies compared on route metres, moves, free reserve and weight rules, then choose one with the numbers in view. Until now reslotting was a project that waited for a quiet week. Apply the operating rules across hundreds of SKUs on every load and every plan, so a rule the manager states once is enforced every time. Adjust the building from the data: when 20 pallet SKUs are short of locations, the agent proposes more pallet racks, the manager accepts, and the layout is validated before anything is built. Keep a decision trail: the approved plan freezes its move list with the reasoning attached, and the log answers "who decided this and why" for auditors, insurers and the next shift. Impact on the operation Time. Reconciling the departmental reports and loading a validated inventory takes one conversation. The same work done by hand, cleaning the article master, matching it against the sales export and typing the result into a planning sheet, takes days, which is why reslotting is usually postponed. With the reconciliation and the arithmetic handled by the agent, reslotting can follow the season and a new intake can be planned the day the purchasing report arrives. Accuracy. Every container is checked against real rack geometry and storage type, and every rule the manager states is applied to the whole catalog, on every load and on every plan. A 25 kg container on an upper level, a refrigerated item in an ambient rack or a pallet in shelving is caught before the move, with a reason code, rather than found on the floor. The manager still decides, but with the exceptions listed instead of hunted. Picking productivity. Slotting strategies are compared on route metres and picking time before a single box moves, so the manager chooses the plan knowing what it saves. In the sample scenario the compact strategy shortens the picking route by roughly a quarter while keeping every heavy item on an allowed level. Safety and losses. Weight-per-level rules and storage segregation are enforced by the tools, which means fewer injuries from heavy boxes stored high and fewer write-offs from mixed storage. Free reserve is reported on every plan, so peaks are absorbed in the building already paid for. Accountability. The approved plan freezes its move list with the reasoning attached, and the log records every call, human or agent, with parameters, results and durations. The answer to "who decided this and why" is available to auditors, insurers and the next shift without reconstructing it from spreadsheet versions. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript and Three.js, with state in localStorage and plain files served over HTTP. 32 tools registered imperatively with navigator.modelContext.registerTool() (with a document.modelContext fallback), each with a JSON Schema inputSchema , annotations.readOnlyHint and an async execute returning plain JSON. A shared validator checks every input against its schema and rejects unknown parameters. The Design mode runs in an iframe, so the main page registers proxy tools for it, because agents only see tools on the top-level document. A logging wrapper traces every call into the Log panel. Mutating tools record undo snapshots. Layout and plan approval are page buttons only. Challenges Keeping approval honest across reloads (the facility signature depends on geometry only), making validation identical for humans and agents, and describing 32 tools so an LLM picks the right one and fills a 300-row product payload in a single call. What's next Import real floor plans, connect a W

title: TaskDrop
pitch: A WebMCP-powered human-agent handoff workspace for refining and moving working context across AI clients.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered human-agent handoff workspace for refining and moving working context across AI clients. Like Comment Story Updates Hero Image workspace page landing page Inspiration Before WebMCP, TaskDrop was a handoff layer. With WebMCP, it became a workspace. TaskDrop started as a way to move working context between AI clients. Different AI tools are good at different things, but their context is usually trapped inside individual conversations and applications. TaskDrop originally addressed this with temporary, versioned Markdown Handoffs that AI clients could read and update through MCP. That worked for AI-to-AI transfer, but it exposed a bigger limitation: the human was still mostly outside the shared working state. A Handoff could move from one AI to another, but there was no first-class place where a human could inspect what was being transferred, correct stale assumptions, refine missing details, or collaborate with a browser agent before the next AI continued. TaskDrop started as a way to move working context between AI clients. WebMCP transformed it into a shared human-agent workspace where that context can be inspected, refined, corrected, and safely committed before the next AI continues. What WebMCP changed WebMCP changed TaskDrop from a handoff transport into a shared human-agent workspace. Before WebMCP, TaskDrop could move committed context between AI clients. With WebMCP, that Handoff becomes a visible workspace where the human and browser agent can inspect and refine the same Working Draft . When the agent updates the Working Draft, the change appears immediately in the editor the human is already looking at. The human can continue editing, correct the agent, or discard the Draft. Human + WebMCP agent ↓ Working Draft ↓ explicit Commit ↓ Immutable Revision ↓ Remote MCP clients The Working Draft creates a clear boundary between work in progress and shared state . Human and agent edits remain local until an explicit Commit creates the next immutable Revision. Once committed, another MCP client can immediately continue from that state. WebMCP also makes TaskDrop's shared memory more transparent. The workspace exposes Revision history and records whether a committed Revision came from mcp , human , or webmcp . And when another client commits a newer Revision while the browser is still editing, TaskDrop preserves the local Draft and lets the human decide how to proceed instead of silently overwriting either state. Before WebMCP, TaskDrop moved context. With WebMCP, humans and agents can work on that context together. How we built it We kept TaskDrop's immutable Handoff model and added a lightweight, browser-owned collaboration layer on top of it. The core architectural rule is simple: Browser owns unfinished collaborative work. Server owns committed immutable Handoff state. The Working Draft therefore lives in browser-session storage. Human edits and WebMCP edits modify the same local Draft, while the server continues to store only immutable, append-only Revisions. Remote MCP and the browser workspace use different interaction surfaces, but both ultimately operate on the same Handoff application logic: Remote MCP ──────┐ ▼ Handoff Application ▲ Browser API ─────┘ ▲ Web UI + WebMCP We also designed the WebMCP tools as page-scoped capabilities . The browser agent operates on the Handoff already open in the workspace instead of receiving the user's underlying Space Key as a normal tool parameter. That gave us another principle we want to preserve: The agent should receive capability, not credentials. These choices let us add meaningful human-agent collaboration without turning TaskDrop into a full collaborative document platform. Challenges and what we learned The biggest challenge was not exposing TaskDrop through WebMCP. It was deciding what should become collaborative, and where that collaboration should live . TaskDrop originally assumed that committed Handoff state moved between AI clients through MCP. Once a human and a browser agent could both participate, that model was no longer enough. We needed a place where both sides could safely inspect and refine the same state without turning every intermediate edit into a server Revision. That challenge led directly to the Working Draft model. The same principle also helped us handle concurrency. If another MCP client updates the Handoff while the browser is editing, TaskDrop preserves the local Draft and asks the human how to proceed instead of silently overwriting either version. Credential handling taught us a similar lesson. An agent should operate within the application context the human has already opened, rather than being handed the credentials that created that context. Together, these challenges changed how we think about WebMCP itself. With Remote MCP alone, TaskDrop was good at moving state between AI clients , but there was no natural shared surface where a human and an agent could work on that state together. WebMCP fills that missing layer. Remote MCP AI Client A ↓ Handoff ↓ Human + WebMCP agent Working Draft ↓ Commit ↓ Handoff ↓ Remote MCP AI Client B It allows the agent to participate directly in the application state the human is already seeing. MCP helps agents connect to services. WebMCP helps agents enter the human's application workflow. For TaskDrop, that difference turned an AI-to-AI handoff layer into a place where humans and agents can inspect, correct, refine, and commit shared working context together. title: Product Tutor
pitch: A `Get Started` that teaches you how to use the product, step by step, to accomplish what you actually came for.
about_excerpt: A `Get Started` that teaches you how to use the product, step by step, to accomplish what you actually came for. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For years, I thought I was the only one who skipped quickstarts. Turns out, most poeple do the same thing. Quickstarts have never really worked for me, and when I thought about why, the answer was simple: they don't know what I'm trying to accomplish. They follow a predefined path, walking me through features that might be useful, but aren't necessarily the ones I came to try. Built-in AI agents do a much better job. I can ask for the thing I actually came for, in the order I want it. But I have to explain my setup first, and there's a harder limit. If I need to run something locally, connect an integration, or touch anything on my machine, they simply can't. So why not use a server-side MCP server? Because a quickstart is often the first time I'm seeing a product. I'm not just checking whether it works; I'm deciding whether I want to use it. If my agent does everything through an API and hands me the result. I'm still left in an unfamiliar console with little idea of what happened or where things live. Why WebMCP is a strong fit for quickstarts WebMCP brings those missing pieces together. With WebMCP, I don't need to repeat my requirements because my agent already knows what I'm trying to accomplish. And it doesn't stop there. It can work with my repo, my stack, my integrations, and my machine, while also working through the product console. That's particularly important for a quickstart. I don't know the product yet, so seeing the interface matters almost as much as reaching the result. With WebMcp, I can watch how the task is actually done, where it navigates, what it clicks, and what values it enters, step by step. What we built ThunderID is an open-source identity platform under the OpenWallet Foundation. We introduced WebMCP-powered quickstarts to bring human-like guidance into the Get Started experience. The ThunderID console registers a set of WebMCP tools, and importantly, the write tools don't call the management API directly. Instead, they open the real wizard, fill in the values, and click the same buttons a user would. Because the agent works through the actual UI, I can follow along, see where things live, and understand the product as the task gets done. And because it's my own agent, the experience doesn't have to stop at the product boundary. If accomplishing my goal requires an integration or some local setup, the same agent can help with that too. For example, I can give it one instruction: create an application in ThunderID, connect it to a sample app, and run it locally. It creates the application, sets the redirect URIs and requested attributes, and configures the login journey through the console I'm already signed into. I see every change happening on the screen where that setting actually lives. Then the same agent moves to my local environment, clones the sample, installs the dependencies, configures it, and runs it. Instead of following a generic tutorial, I'm learning ThunderID by doing exactly what I came to try. Where WebMCP changes the experience A traditional quickstart shows me the product, but doesn't know what I want to accomplish. A built-in assistant can tailor the journey, but can't leave the product. An external agent can work with my machine, but if it does everything through APIs, it doesn't really show me the product. WebMCP brings those worlds together. One agent can understand what I'm trying to accomplish, work with my repo, stack, integrations, and local environment, while operating the product through the console in front of me. The journey follows what I actually came to find out. title: HomeWheel
pitch: HomeWheel lets wheelchair users negotiate room layouts with a browser agent using live geometry, explicit transfer zones, and consent-based proposals.
about_excerpt: HomeWheel lets wheelchair users negotiate room layouts with a browser agent using live geometry, explicit transfer zones, and consent-based proposals. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Room-layout advice often sounds simple: move a dresser, rotate a table, clear a path. For someone who uses a wheelchair, however, a few centimeters can decide whether a bed, desk, or storage area is usable. The technically shortest route is not automatically the right answer. Daily routines, transfer sides, outlets, light, reach, and personal preference matter too. We wanted to build an agent experience where those lived constraints are not treated as edge cases. They are the decision-making authority. Evidence-grounded user stories The prototype includes composite user stories derived from public evidence, not invented customer testimonials: A wheelchair user needs the bed-transfer side and furniture stability preserved, even if another arrangement produces a clear route. A person needs the simulation to use their actual chair and transfer technique because access needs are not one-size-fits-all. A person adapting their home needs authority over trade-offs involving independence, safety, reach, light, storage, and daily routines. Those stories became testable requirements. HomeWheel now validates an explicit approach zone at each transfer, work, or reach destination; calculates it from the person’s movement profile; refuses to move stability-critical furniture; and shares the person’s priorities with the agent before any proposal is created. Research basis: United Spinal’s accessible studio account , wheelchair transfer focus groups , and a qualitative study of home usability . What it does HomeWheel gives a person and a browser agent the same editable floor plan. The person sets a personal movement profile, marks required destinations and their transfer, work, or reach zones, chooses what proposals should prioritize, and protects furniture positions that matter. The agent can: read the complete room and personal constraints; simulate all required and optional routes; identify movable barriers; create an exact, collision-checked proposal; compare the proposal with the live layout; and restore a baseline or previous state. Every proposal appears as a purple overlay with route evidence, exact moves, and trade-offs. Nothing moves until the person clicks Accept. If the proposal misses a lived detail, the person can reject it and explain why. The next agent sees that feedback in the workspace state and can produce a targeted revision. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the bridge between agent reasoning and the application’s actual state. HomeWheel registers eight tools directly from the page: get_workspace_state , set_mobility_profile , simulate_routes , find_barriers , create_layout_proposal , set_object_constraint , compare_layouts , and restore_layout . The key design choice is that the agent has a proposal tool, not an “automatically rearrange my room” tool. WebMCP gives the agent precise capabilities while the interface preserves human consent and makes every change inspectable. How we built it HomeWheel is a static Next.js and TypeScript application. It uses browser-side A* pathfinding over an obstacle grid, personal clearance envelopes, purpose-specific approach zones, collision-checked furniture geometry, multi-destination metrics, and turning-space detection. State is shared between direct manipulation and WebMCP tools, stored locally, and exportable as JSON. Challenges The most important challenge was not pathfinding; it was deciding where agent authority should stop. Direct mutation made the demo faster but weakened the product. We redesigned the workflow around preview, explicit acceptance, structured rejection, and feedback-aware revision. We also had to make geometric evidence understandable without pretending it was professional certification. HomeWheel clearly separates personal simulation from building-code or medical claims. Accomplishments The agent and person operate on the same live room state. Locked human constraints are enforced at the tool-validation layer. Stability-critical furniture cannot be moved by the person or the agent without first releasing that protection. Transfer, work, and reach zones are visible and validated separately from the route leading to them. Personal priorities are part of live WebMCP state rather than hidden prompt context. A proposal cannot silently mutate the room. Rejection feedback persists and is available to the next agent turn. The prototype supports authored scenarios and fully editable rooms. Public evidence is visible inside the product without being presented as fabricated user validation. The complete experience works without a backend or user account. What we learned Human-in-the-loop design becomes much more meaningful when feedback is part of the tool state, not just a chat message. The agent can optimize geometry, but the person defines what “better” means. What is next A production version could add measured floor-plan import, richer door and wall geometry, collaboration with occupational therapists, uncertainty ranges, and optional checks against local accessibility guidance. Those features would remain advisory and would continue to require real-world validation. title: Web MCP Consent
pitch: adding human authentiation to agent workflows
about_excerpt: adding human authentiation to agent workflows Like Comment Story Updates What it does A Chrome extension that holds every WebMCP write until a human approves it. Reads run freely, around 5ms, no prompt. Works on any WebMCP site, including sites that never adopted anything and don't know it exists. No SDK, no code change, nothing for the site to install. The approval card shows the tool name, the real arguments, and the site. Not a yes/no on an opaque tool name Catches sites that lie. A tool that declares readOnlyHint: true and then fires a POST while running is held at the network layer. "Always allow" is per site + tool, listed in the popup, and revocable there. A cache you can't see or undo isn't consent. A declined call tells the agent plainly that a human declined it and not to retry, instead of a generic error it would just try again. How we built it A document_start content script in the MAIN world replaces registerTool before any page script runs. The site registers its tools the normal way and is calling our wrapper. It never finds out. MAIN world is what makes this possible. The default isolated world hands the script a private copy of the context, and you'd patch something the page never reads. MAIN-world scripts can't touch chrome.* , so decisions cross a private MessagePort → an isolated-world bridge → chrome.runtime → an MV3 service worker that owns the queue, the allow list and the badge. Classification is one line: def.annotations?.readOnlyHint !== true . No annotation means gated. It never reads the tool's name or description to guess intent — that's attacker-authored text, and putting it in charge of a security decision is the problem we're solving. window.fetch is patched too, with a call stack tracking which tool is executing, so a "read-only" tool that POSTs gets caught. Pending proposals live in chrome.storage.session so they survive service-worker eviction. The allow list is in chrome.storage.local , keyed origin::toolName . Zero dependencies, no build step, ~15 KB. ## Challenges we ran into We found a vulnerability in our own approval channel. Approvals were relayed over window.postMessage , which page scripts share with the interceptor. A page could watch for its own proposal, read thepproval — approving its own writes with no human involved.Fixed with a private MessagePort handed over at document_start , before any page script exists. Re-ran the exploit: the page can't even see a proposal now. We were silently destroying tool results. On approval the code did typeof result === 'string' ? result : 'Approved.' . On the network path, commit resolves with a Response — so an approved request hring "Approved." Our own demo never caught it because itdiscards its response. Only showed up testing against a site we didn't write. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works on sites we didn't build. On Cloudflare's WebMCP coheld with the cart at 0 , and only after approval did itbecome 2 × Guji Shakiso, $44.00 . The network-layer catch is confirmed two independent ways: wire on decline, **exactly one * on approve — verified byResource Timing inside the browser and by the server's own access log outside it. We found and fixed our own self-approval vulnerability beforather than quietly patching it. We removed two features that didn't earn their place. Shipping less than we built was the right call both times. Zero dependencies, no build step, 15 KB. Download, unzip, lo What we learned Real sites don't annotate. Chrome Labs' own hotel demo hying readOnlyHint . That's exactly why gate-by-default isright, and exactly why one-click "always allow" has to exist. Testing against sites you didn't write finds things your own worst bugs surfaced that way. The WebMCP runtime replaces a thrown error with generic text, so a rejection reaches the agent looking like a bug — and an agent that thinks a tool is buggy retries it. A declined call has to resolve with a clea API details that cost us time: getTools() returns a Promise , and inputSchema arrives as a JSON string , not an object. Reading navigator.modelContext logs a deprecation warning nt.modelContext` first. The honest summary: this raises the cost of an injection from "the agent was convinced" to "the agent was convinced and a human approved a card describing the action." That's a big gap. It isn't a proof. What's next for WebMCP Consent Advisory-only LLM triage. A model offers a plain-Englishith the raw metadata beside it — but a human still clicks towhitelist. Advisory on purpose: a model that auto -approves based on a tool's own description reopens the exact vulnerability we're defending against. Support destructiveHint and idempotentHint , the other stextensions of the same model. Patch XMLHttpRequest and sendBeacon to close the non- fetch gap. Community-curated allow lists, ad-blocker style. Credible wirt problem today. For browsers that don't accept extensions, a local proxy injecting the same patch. Platform-agnostic, but it asks the user to trust a local root CA. title: Web2MCP
pitch: Web2MCP watches the requests a site makes as you browse, learns their shape, and injects them into the page as native WebMCP tools an in-browser AI agent can call.
about_excerpt: Web2MCP watches the requests a site makes as you browse, learns their shape, and injects them into the page as native WebMCP tools an in-browser AI agent can call. Like Comment Story Updates chrome extension agent use case Inspiration WebMCP is a beautiful idea — websites exposing their functionality to AI agents as callable tools. But it has a chicken-and-egg problem: it only works if the website adds it. Almost no site has, and most never will. Meanwhile, every one of those sites is already making perfectly good API calls in your browser, right now, as you use it. So we asked: what if the agent didn't need the site's cooperation at all? What if you could just browse a site normally, and have its APIs turn into agent-callable tools automatically — learned from the traffic the site already produces? What it does Web2MCP is a browser extension that records the API calls a website makes while you browse and injects them as native WebMCP tools an in-browser AI agent can call. Records every JSON API a page calls — its own backend and third-party APIs — while filtering out static assets and trackers. Aggregates requests into endpoint templates (/users/123 → /users/{id}), inferring JSON Schemas and required fields from what it observes. Injects each endpoint as a WebMCP tool via document.modelContext. Calls replay from the page's own context, so cookies and captured auth headers just work. Pools by website, so subdomains and pages share one tool set; shows a live tool count on the toolbar badge; lists tools in a popup (including the site's own first-party WebMCP tools); and lets you disable injection per site. No config, no schemas to write, no per-endpoint wiring. How we built it WXT + TypeScript + React for a Manifest V3 extension. A MAIN-world content script patches window.fetch and XMLHttpRequest to observe traffic and to register/replay tools; an ISOLATED-world bridge relays messages to a background service worker that does all aggregation, schema inference, and local storage. Injection uses the browser's native WebMCP registerTool API; replay uses the saved native fetch so tool calls never re-trigger recording. The "brain" — URL templating, schema inference, tool naming, aggregation, filtering — is pure, dependency-free modules covered by vitest (60+ tests). A landing page and privacy policy shipped on Cloudflare Pages. Challenges we ran into We tested on real sites, and the real world fought back — which turned out to be the most valuable part. Anti-automation is everywhere. We hit three distinct walls: Linear injects auth in a service worker below the page's fetch (invisible to us → 401); X and GitHub use one-time nonces (x-client-transaction-id, x-fetch-nonce) that expire after a single use (→ 422); Xiaohongshu signs the request body client-side (x-s), so changing any argument breaks the signature (→ 406). We had to map — and honestly document — exactly where record-and-replay can and can't work. Agents under-supply parameters. An LLM calling a search tool would omit sortBy or invent a sessionId, getting empty results. The fix: surface the real recorded request body as an example and merge the agent's fields over it, filling in what it left out. The little things: a signal destructuring crash that broke every tool call, extension-context invalidation after reloads, JSON responses truncated mid-object, and getting WebMCP itself enabled in a custom Chromium browser (via a Finch/variations study). Accomplishments that we're proud of It's genuinely zero-config. Browse a site and its tools appear — with a badge counting them and a popup listing them. It works end-to-end on real sites. We watched an agent successfully call a live government job-search API and read GitHub data through tools Web2MCP recorded — cross-domain, authenticated, no keys. It's honest. We built the "Works great / Can't replay" boundary into the product and the site instead of overselling. It's smart about the data it already has — auto-filling session tokens and merging partial request bodies from real recordings so agents stop failing on missing fields. Users stay in control — per-site disable, one-click clear, everything stored locally and nothing leaves the device. What we learned The real boundary of record-and-replay: it works whenever the request's content isn't itself part of authentication — cookie-authed apps, static tokens, read endpoints, your own products. It can't beat mechanisms designed to stop exactly this (SW-injected auth, one-time tokens, body signatures). Knowing that boundary precisely is more useful than pretending it doesn't exist. Agents need examples, not just schemas. A JSON Schema tells a model the shape; a real recorded request tells it what actually works. Honesty is a feature. Being upfront about limits made the product more trustworthy, not less. What's next for Web2MCP Chrome Web Store release and broader reach as WebMCP ships in stable browsers. Smarter body handling — deep merge, and richer per-parameter examples. First-party passthrough — surface and manage a site's own WebMCP tools alongside recorded ones. An adapter path for hardened sites — optionally invoke the site's own signing/request code (or fall back to driving the real UI) for signature- and nonce-protected APIs. Sharing & sync — export a site's recorded tool set so a team can reuse it. title: WebMCP Guard
pitch: WebMCP Guard is a security control plane between your app's WebMCP tools and the agent, providing data protection and other security policies for agents accessing data through your WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Guard is a security control plane between your app's WebMCP tools and the agent, providing data protection and other security policies for agents accessing data through your WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Organizations often run their own internal apps that have access to sensitive data. They often have tools to enforce data protection and security policies on these apps, but an improperly implemented WebMCP tool may circumvent them. I wanted to create something that would allow them to have these same kind of policies for their WebMCP tools without forcing them to code it themselves. But it needed to do more than block data for the agent. I wanted it to control data access in a way that preserved the agent's ability to reason about the data. What it does WebMCP Guard is an SDK that wraps WebMCP functions written with the Imperative API and injects controls. It has a corresponding management console that allows the organization to define policies. It has the following types of policies Data Protection This gives the company control over what data the agent can see. It classifies sensitive data, including names, SSN, credit cards, and more, and transforms them before the agent sees it. It can replace this data with a unique token. If the same piece of data appears across multiple records, it will use the same token identifier, which allows the agent to reason about the data without actually knowing what it is. In some cases, it can contextualize the data while removing the specificity. For example, it can replace a DOB from a patient health record with an age range. Human confirmation To prevent errant destructive actions polices can be created that require the user to approve (via an on-page modal) an action before it can be completed. This is most often used before an agent takes an irreversible action, such as deleting a record. Posture Assessment It can restrict what types of agents can access the tools. For example, you can block unidentified agents or restrict it to agents from one provider, such as OpenAI. Justification Policies can require the agent to provide a written justification before a sensitive action runs — bulk export, for example. The requirement is injected directly into the tool's input schema, so the agent learns about it from the tool definition rather than from a refusal. The agent is instructed to stop and ask its user for the reason and relay it verbatim, and the justification is evaluated and stored on the audit record as the human's stated reason. How we built it TypeScript end to end, in a pnpm monorepo. The SDK splits into a browser half and a server half: the client package wraps document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback) and runs every call through a gate → execute → transform pipeline, while everything secret — the policy engine, the data classifier, the deterministic tokenizer, the encrypted token vault, and the audit writer — lives in a Node package the host app mounts as ordinary API routes. Tokens are deterministic by construction: HMAC-SHA256 over a canonicalized value under an org secret, so the same SSN or name yields the same token in every tool, every turn, even inside the free text of a clinical note. The vault encrypts originals with AES-256-GCM, using the token itself as authenticated data so a tampered row fails closed instead of decrypting to the wrong person. Storage is a small adapter interface (SQLite for the demo, in-memory for tests, both run against one shared conformance suite) so an organization brings its own database. This way the organization isn't reliant on SaaS infrastructure to protect their audit logs, etc. We also built an example medical app for the demo. It existing in the same repo. We used AI coding assistance for this project. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new, and building against it seriously means finding the edges. Three real ones: tools' execute is invoked with no second options argument despite the typings declaring one (every tool crashed on its first real call); registering a live tool name again silently keeps the old tool, so policy-driven schema changes must abort-then-re-register; and feature detection has to cover both document.modelContext and the older navigator.modelContext surface. Tokenizing a structured name field is easy. A clinical note that says "Reached Tricia by phone" is not, and an agent can de-anonymize the token if information like that leaks. We fixed this by resolving bare name fragments to the same token as the full name (never hashed independently, which would split one person into two tokens), replaced only when the fragment maps unambiguously to one known person. Early on, the justification refusal told the agent what a justification should contain, so agents composed plausible ones themselves, defeating the control. The message now instructs the agent to stop, ask its human for the reason, and relay it verbatim. The denial text turned out to be as much a part of the security design as the policy engine. In the future, we will probably replace it with a modal like the approval workflow. Accomplishments that we're proud of The tokenization loop working end to end was a big win. An agent searches, gets tokens instead of names, reasons about them, passes one back into another tool, and the real value is swapped in server-side. The agent is actually able to reason about the data without access to the cleartext value. Getting the justification flow to work correctly was also a big win. Like I said earlier, a lot of agents just wrote the justification themselves, which isn't exactly what is intended. It's not foolproof, but this tool isn't supposed to be silver bullet for security; it is meant to complement other security measures for organizations that want to implement WebMCP. What we learned We'll still need some kind of control surface for the DOM. Agents that cannot accomplish their task via the WebMCP tool may fall back to DOM inspection. Currently, this requires a separate security tool to address, like an enterprise browser. But I think we could come up with some kind of native solution. Alternatively, this tool might be better as a browser extension, and then the SDK would merely enforce the use of the extension before serving the page. This would give us more control over what the agent can access, but it is also a bigger deployment than the current state. But when it comes to security, perfect can't be the enemy of good. Easily deploying controls on a WebMCP tool still greatly improves security and compliance, especially if it eliminates it as a path to circumventing other security controls. What's next for WebMCP Guard Smarter classification: NER-based name detection beyond the host-supplied dictionary, and free-text detectors for addresses and insurance ids. Structured export rows so bulk export gets the full transform treatment instead of leaning on the justification gate. Richer policy: combined confirmation-plus-justification actions, per-class control over inbound detokenization, and the pluggable LLM justification evaluator the interface already supports. Real identity: SSO/OIDC session resolution in place of the demo's mock personas. This allows the user to attach policies to specific people or user groups. LLM-as-a-judge: For justifications, I want the admin to be able to define what an acceptable justification is and use an LLM to determine if the justification given is adequate. Better agent posture controls: I want to determine a better way to identify agents so our posture controls are more reliable. End user notifications: Alert end users during WebMCP activity to prevent adversarial attempts to hijack the users session while hiding their activity. An optional browser extension: A stretch goal is to use a browser extension to better lock down the DOM so agents can't circumvent controls through DOM inspection. This will have to be optional since it significantly increases the deployment complexity, but it will close a major gap. Demo The live demo has two sites: Example EHR app: https://webmcp-guard-portal.onrender.com/patients Admin console: https://webmcp-guard-console.vercel.app/login?token=Nit52TvyXZWpgzot1UIqMV4ktAB3oCdFbrk5M5AFSYg%3D Built With chatgpt claude codex nextjs render sqlite vercel Try it out github.com webmcp-guard-portal.onrender.com webmcp-guard-console.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Andrew Akers Like Share this project: Updates Andrew Akers started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:49 PM EDT

title: AgentRep
pitch: WebMCP makes websites agent-ready. AgentRep helps AI agents discover and compose those capabilities across the web to accomplish a user's goal.
about_excerpt: WebMCP makes websites agent-ready. AgentRep helps AI agents discover and compose those capabilities across the web to accomplish a user's goal. Like Comment Story Updates Capacity Discovery Problem New Capability Adaptability Outcome Inspiration WebMCP makes individual websites agent-ready by letting them expose structured tools directly to AI agents. But that creates another problem: if thousands of websites expose capabilities, how does an agent know which websites can actually help accomplish a user's goal? We built AgentRep — a capability discovery layer for the agentic web. WebMCP makes websites agent-ready. AgentRep makes their capabilities discoverable and composable. What it does A user gives ChatGPT a goal rather than a sequence of websites to visit. AgentRep helps discover the WebMCP capabilities needed for that goal. ChatGPT reasons over those capabilities, composes a plan, invokes provider tools, adapts when requirements change, and asks for human approval before irreversible actions. Our birthday-planning demo is deliberately a proof of this broader model. The demo begins with three independent WebMCP providers: PartyHub — venues FoodHub — catering CakeHub — cakes ChatGPT uses AgentRep to discover and compose these capabilities into one plan. Then the requirements change. The cake preference changes. The guest count increases from 20 to 25, making the existing cake invalid. Instead of restarting a fixed workflow, the agent preserves what still works and recomposes the invalid parts. Then something more important happens: A fourth WebMCP provider becomes available while the task is already underway. PokémonPartyHub exposes a new entertainment capability. The user simply asks to add Pokémon entertainment — without naming the provider. AgentRep discovers the newly available capability, and ChatGPT incorporates it into the existing plan. The final composition spans four independent websites and remains within the updated ₹20,000 budget. Before booking, AgentRep creates a single human approval checkpoint for the exact plan and total. Only after approval does ChatGPT invoke the transactional WebMCP tools. The demo ends with four real booking confirmations across four independent providers from one user goal. How we built it AgentRep and each provider are independent web origins exposing tools through WebMCP. The implementation uses document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and @agentrep/webmcp to register structured tools with descriptions, JSON schemas, and execution handlers. Provider origins expose domain-specific capabilities for search, details, availability, pricing and transactional actions. AgentRep provides capability discovery, shared plan state and the human-approval boundary, while ChatGPT remains responsible for reasoning and composition . Cross-origin provider tools are exposed in one agent-visible workspace using WebMCP tool permissions. For irreversible actions, approval is bound to the exact plan using plan hashes, state versions and single-use approval tokens, preventing stale approvals from executing changed plans. The dynamic discovery proof For the demo, provider indexing is intentionally simulated so the discovery transition is deterministic and easy to reproduce. The important distinction is that PokémonPartyHub and its WebMCP tools are real . Before indexing, its entertainment capability is unavailable to AgentRep. After indexing, the same running task can discover and use that new capability without the user providing the website URL. This demonstrates the larger direction for AgentRep: an open capability registry where WebMCP-enabled websites publish machine-readable capabilities and agents discover providers based on what they need to accomplish. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem wasn't making another AI planner. It was maintaining a clean boundary between discovery, reasoning and execution . AgentRep should not secretly become the reasoning agent. ChatGPT reasons and composes; AgentRep discovers capabilities and maintains shared state; independent websites own and execute their WebMCP tools. We also had to solve cross-origin tool exposure, changing constraints without restarting the workflow, dynamic capability arrival, and safe human approval for transactional actions. What we learned WebMCP becomes especially interesting when you stop thinking about one agent using one website. If many independent websites expose capabilities, agents need a way to discover and compose those capabilities around user intent. Our birthday example is only the proof. The birthday is not the product. Capability discovery is. What's next Today, AgentRep demonstrates discovery across registered WebMCP providers, including a new provider becoming discoverable during an active task. The larger vision is an open capability registry for the agentic web — where websites publish what they can do and agents discover capabilities based on goals instead of starting with URLs. Discover → Compose → Execute. title: Sushi Daw
pitch: A code-native browser DAW where producers, live coders, and AI agents compose together through one synchronized Strudel workspace.
about_excerpt: A code-native browser DAW where producers, live coders, and AI agents compose together through one synchronized Strudel workspace. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Sushi: A DAW Built in Code, Controlled Through WebMCP Inspiration Sushi began with a compatibility problem disguised as a music problem. My collaborator Avery and I both love making music, and we share a lot of the same taste, but we approach the process from almost opposite directions. Avery is comfortable in traditional DAWs. He uses Logic Pro, has experience with FL Studio and BandLab, and understands music through tracks, effects, timelines, and familiar production controls. I have used those tools, but they have never been the way I naturally want to make music. I am much more interested in Strudel and TidalCycles: writing patterns as code, changing them live, and treating a composition as something programmable. That left us without a good place to meet. When Avery sent me a Logic project, I could not simply open it on Linux. Even if we were using DAWs on the same platform, proprietary project formats and different software would still make collaboration awkward. In the other direction, I could send him a Strudel composition as a few lines of text, but unless he learned the syntax, there was not much he could do with it. We wanted a workspace where neither of us had to abandon the way we preferred to work. Avery should be able to interact with music through a visual interface. I should be able to work directly in Strudel. An agent should be able to participate without pretending to be a person clicking through a DAW. That shared workspace became Sushi. What it does Sushi is a browser-based, code-native DAW powered by Strudel and its TidalCycles-inspired pattern language. Underneath the interface, the composition is still code. That makes a Sushi project lightweight, inspectable, programmable, and easy to share. On top of that code, Sushi provides a more familiar music-production interface for arranging tracks, selecting sounds, adjusting effects, and shaping a composition without requiring the user to understand Strudel syntax. The important part is that these are not two separate modes. When someone changes a supported property in the interface, the Strudel source changes with it. When someone edits the source, Sushi reflects that change back into the interface. A traditional producer, a live coder, and an agent can therefore manipulate the same underlying composition instead of passing increasingly lossy translations between different tools. WebMCP adds the third side of that collaboration. An agent can inspect the composition and its current playback state directly in the page, modify or write music, validate the result, and observe the updated source and interface without requiring the user to copy code back and forth between a chat window and the editor. When an edit fails Strudel validation, the agent receives diagnostics from the running environment and can correct its work. This feedback loop makes a major difference. The agent is not writing music blindly and returning a plausible-looking block of code. It is working inside the actual instrument. Because the composition itself is programmable, the musical program becomes a high-leverage control surface for both humans and agents. The DAW is built in code, and WebMCP gives the agent access to that code in its real context. How we built it Sushi started as a relatively simple Astro application written in TypeScript. Astro was a pragmatic choice because it is the framework I already enjoy using, but it also gives the project room to grow without splitting everything into separate repositories or deployments. The application, documentation, and other supporting pages can coexist in the same project while the interactive workspace remains focused and lightweight. Inside that scaffold, we integrated Strudel as the musical runtime and built Sushi’s interface around its source representation. We deliberately avoided treating the interface as a separate DAW model that merely exports Strudel later. Instead, every feature has to respect the same contract: Anything that happens in the interface must be represented in the code, and anything represented in the supported code must remain visible and editable through the interface. That constraint shaped nearly every architectural decision in the project. A track cannot exist only as hidden application state. An effect cannot be added through a UI-only shortcut that the source does not understand. The interface must work with the musical program rather than bypassing it. We then connected the workspace to WebMCP so an agent could participate through that same underlying model. Rather than automating coordinates or simulating mouse clicks, the agent can work with the composition structurally and receive feedback from the running application. Sushi registers a typed WebMCP surface against the browser’s native model context. Agents can inspect a structured snapshot of the project, read or patch the canonical Strudel source, validate candidate source against the running Strudel engine, control playback, edit tracks and timeline state, and load or inspect composition templates. Mutating operations carry a base revision and transaction ID, so stale or duplicated actions are rejected instead of silently overwriting human changes. Successful source edits pass through the same validation and source-to-interface synchronization path as human edits, returning structured state, diffs, and diagnostics to the agent. The result is a shared artifact with three possible collaborators: one person working visually, another working in code, and an agent working through WebMCP. Challenges we ran into Performance became a challenge almost immediately. Strudel is already a mature and highly interactive environment, so Sushi could not merely produce the same output eventually. Editing and playback had to feel responsive enough to function as an instrument. As we introduced interface state and synchronization, we repeatedly found places where our application was doing substantially more work than Strudel itself. We had to become much more careful about when the composition was evaluated, what caused components to update, and how changes moved through the application. Music software makes performance problems unusually obvious: latency and interruption are not just technical metrics. They directly affect whether the creative process feels usable. The larger challenge was maintaining synchronization between code and interface. Almost every feature sounds straightforward until it has to work in both directions. Adding an effect button is easy if it only changes hidden state. It becomes much harder when that action must create valid Strudel, preserve the rest of the user’s source, remain editable as text, and still be understood by the interface after the code changes again. It was tempting at several points to introduce shortcuts: parallel state, special internal representations, or UI features that only resembled Strudel behavior. Those approaches might have made an individual feature easier to ship, but they would have broken the central promise of the project. WebMCP introduced another form of synchronization problem: an agent may act on a project while a human is still editing it. We addressed that by requiring mutating operations to carry a base revision and transaction ID. Stale or duplicated actions return a structured conflict instead of silently overwriting newer work. Over time, we established more reliable patterns for preserving these contracts. Once those patterns became part of the architecture, development became noticeably smoother. I could describe a feature to my coding agent and expect it to extend the existing model rather than inventing another path around Strudel. Accomplishments that we’re proud of The accomplishment we care about most is that Sushi stopped being merely a hackathon idea and became something we actually wanted to use. A large part of building it was the impatient feeling that we needed to finish the next feature so we could stop developing for a moment and start making music with it. Avery and I have already been able to play with the workspace from our different perspectives, which is the original problem Sushi was meant to solve. We are also proud that the visual editor and code editor are not competing sources of truth. They are two views into the same instrument. That gives Sushi the accessibility of a DAW without giving up the expressive power and portability of Strudel. The WebMCP integration demonstrates something we find especially exciting: an agent interface does not always need to be a giant catalog of tiny actions mirroring every control in an application. By exposing a coherent, programmable representation, a bounded set of high-level operations can give an agent meaningful control over an entire creative system. The agent is not clicking blindly th

title: FormCoach — an AI coach that sees numbers, not your video
pitch: A workout coach that sees numbers, never frames: MediaPipe Pose tracks reps and form in-browser, and WebMCP tools let any AI agent coach you live — your camera stream never leaves the tab.
about_excerpt: A workout coach that sees numbers, never frames: MediaPipe Pose tracks reps and form in-browser, and WebMCP tools let any AI agent coach you live — your camera stream never leaves the tab. Like Comment Story Updates cover 04_approval_modal 02_agent_creates_plan 05_rest_gesture 03_live_rep_tracking 06_session_summary Inspiration Home workouts get people hurt because nobody is watching their form — and every existing AI fitness coach wants your video. We wanted a coach that knows how you're moving without ever seeing you . WebMCP made that possible: the camera can stay inside the browser tab, and the agent gets numbers instead of frames. What it does FormCoach turns your webcam into a privacy-preserving workout sensor. MediaPipe Pose runs on-device in the tab, measuring reps, joint angles, tempo, and form faults (like knee valgus) in real time. Those measurements — and the workout controls — are exposed as WebMCP tools, so any WebMCP-aware browser agent becomes your coach: Ask it to build a plan ("3x12 squats, 90s rest, my left knee is sensitive") It watches your live metrics and flags form breakdowns mid-set It can propose program changes — swap the exercise, cut reps, extend rest You confirm proposals with body gestures (raise both hands to accept, cross your arms to decline), because mid-set your hands are busy and sweaty During rest, show an open palm for one second to skip the timer How we built it Seven imperative tools plus one declarative form , registered on document.modelContext : Read tools ( getWorkoutPlan , getLiveMetrics , getSetHistory ) are annotated readOnlyHint so agents can poll freely. Write tools ( startSet , setRest , adjustProgram , endSession ) are gated by the human — adjustProgram returns a pending promise that only resolves after a gesture or a 20s timeout. The tool set follows the workout phase (idle → countdown → set → rest → done): registrations are scoped to AbortController s and swapped on every transition, so the agent only ever sees actions that make sense right now. createPlan is a declarative <form toolname> ; the handler reads SubmitEvent.agentInvoked to credit the plan to the agent or the human. The pipeline: webcam → MediaPipe Pose (33 landmarks/frame, on-device) → pose engine (rep FSM, form rules, gesture dwell) → session state machine → WebMCP tools. No backend, no accounts, no uploads — video frames never leave the <video> element. Challenges we ran into Detecting knee valgus in 2D: a naive angle threshold broke on front-view footage. We redefined it sign-based — the knee drifting past the ankle toward the midline — which survives both mirrored and non-mirrored coordinates. Background-tab timer throttling: browsers throttle timers in hidden tabs, which froze our replay engine mid-test. We rewrote replay as elapsed-time catch-up instead of tick-based stepping. Testing an API the test browser doesn't have: WebMCP isn't in stock Chromium, so we built an adapter layer with an internal tool registry, a window.__formcoach debug bridge that hits the same execute path a real agent does, recorded pose fixtures for camera-free replay — and a Playwright suite that mocks document.modelContext to verify the real API path (registration mirroring, {content:[...]} wrapping, AbortSignal cleanup). Confirming actions when hands are busy: buttons don't work mid-squat. Gesture confirmation ran through the same pose model, with on-screen buttons as a fallback. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human–agent loop with zero video leaving the tab, phase-scoped tool registration that keeps the agent honest, gesture-based consent for agent write actions, and a fully camera-free test story: 40 unit tests + Playwright end-to-end sessions, all green. What we learned WebMCP changes where capability lives. A server-side MCP with this job would need the video uploaded; in-tab, the agent gets a live numeric contract instead. We also learned that agent UX is mostly trust UX: an on-screen agent log of every tool call, explicit attribution badges via agentInvoked , and human confirmation for anything that changes the program. What's next Moving the "eyes" into a browser extension so any workout or rehab site can publish its own exercise spec and be coached by the same agent — and rehab verticals, where physiotherapy ranges-of-motion become first-class tool schemas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does## Overview Glyph Motion Studio is a visual GSAP editor where users direct vector composition and animation in natural language through their own WebMCP-compatible browser agents.
