title: Haggle
pitch: Your agent haggles with the seller's agent so you don't have to Price, pickup and terms get negotiated agent to agent, the site enforces the limits you set and nothing closes until both people say yes
about_excerpt: Your agent haggles with the seller's agent so you don't have to Price, pickup and terms get negotiated agent to agent, the site enforces the limits you set and nothing closes until both people say yes Like Comment Story Updates Main Web MCP Tools Inspiration Every time I try to buy or sell something on a marketplace it's the same thing. I message, they answer three hours later, I'm at work, they're at dinner, someone forgets, and a $150 bike takes a week of messages and then nothing happens. The negotiation is not the hard part. The hard part is that two busy people have to be online at the same time to close something simple. So I wanted to try this: you bring your own agent, it talks to the seller's agent, and you get out of the loop. You come back only to say yes or no. And then the obvious problem. If my agent is negotiating for me, how do I make sure I don't end up buying something it picked because "it fit"? That's why the mandate and the double approval exist. They're not extras, they're what makes the first part safe. What it does Haggle is a bike marketplace where the agents do the back-and-forth and you only show up to decide. You bring whatever agent you use (I tested with the ChatGPT desktop browser). The page gives it WebMCP tools to search listings, set your limits, make and counter offers, wait for the seller to answer, and check where things are. It doesn't click around or scrape anything. On the other side, the seller sets up an agent in Seller Studio: how it negotiates, a floor price, some rules. Your agent can't read any of that. They negotiate everything, not just the price. When to meet, where (public place), and what's included, like a lock. Before you send your agent, you give it a mandate: max price, when you're free, public pickup only, what has to come with the bike. That's saved on the server and enforced there. If your agent tries to accept $195 and your max is $180, the site says no, and you see it in the timeline as "Blocked by your mandate, not by your agent." When they reach something, you see each term next to what you asked for. You approve, or you decline and leave a note for your agent, and it keeps going. The seller sees the same screen against their own limits, and those numbers never leave the server. Nothing closes until both people approve. How I built it Next.js and TypeScript on Vercel, Postgres with Drizzle. Tools are registered with document.modelContext, with a fallback to navigator.modelContext. The tools change depending on where the negotiation is: read-only ones are always there, the action ones only appear when that action actually makes sense. The seller's agent runs in the background, so I added a read-only wait_for_seller_response tool. Otherwise the agent had to guess when to check again, and it usually didn't. Tools have readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint. All the checks (budget, mandate, seller limits, valid pickup options) run on the server. Whatever the seller's agent writes comes back marked as untrusted. There's a panel called Agent Lens that shows you what tools your agent can see on each screen. If your browser doesn't support WebMCP yet, it still shows you the list. Challenges I ran into The main one was giving the agent room to negotiate without losing control of it. I tried doing it with prompts first. It didn't work. Moving the limits into the site fixed it. Then keeping everything consistent with the seller running in the background, tools appearing and disappearing, and private info on both sides. It's easy to end up in a state where nobody knows whose turn it is. And the small one that turned out to matter: at first, declining ended the negotiation. Now declining is a message to your agent. Accomplishments I'm proud of Two agents with opposite interests, private information on both sides, limits the site enforces, and two separate human approvals. All of it through tools the page exposes. I'm mostly happy with how the site ended up being the referee, not just a place where agents click things. What I learned Exposing tools is the easy part. The real decision is what the agent must never be able to do. Once that lived on the server I could stop babysitting the prompt. Also, "no" has to be information for the agent, not a stop button. And the state of the deal should decide what tools exist, not the prompt. What's next for Haggle Sellers bringing their own agent, with Haggle staying in the middle as the referee. Delegation levels, from "ask me everything" to "close it if it fits." And going past bikes to anything two people sell to each other. Bikes today. Any local deal tomorrow. Note for judges Seller Studio is a labeled persona simulator so you can play both sides in one session. It's not authentication. title: Hemloop
pitch: Demand meets supply. The loop learns and grow with every purchase. The next generation of ecommerce
about_excerpt: Demand meets supply. The loop learns and grow with every purchase. The next generation of ecommerce Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I run e-commerce and paid media for apparel retail, so I have spent years on the ad-platform side of this problem. That machinery accumulates identity, infers intent from surveillance, and optimises for the conversion. It guesses at intent the shopper could simply have stated, and it never declines a discount because the discount would break the merchant's margin floor. Promotional creative is where agents are most useful and most dangerous: a wrong percentage is a legal problem, not a bad impression. WebMCP made a different shape possible: rich page-local context, a deliberately tiny merchant-facing schema, and a human-only release. If a store does not need an identity to answer "no hoodie, size M", then do not send one, not even a hash. The name comes from a hem loop: the small functional loop sewn inside a garment. Hidden, structural, load-bearing. What it does Hemloop is a shopper closet and a merchant studio on one origin, wired with WebMCP so ChatGPT works on live page state. In under a minute: import a receipt into a private closet; the agent finds a gap such as hoodie, size M; you Approve once; the store only learns category, size, and need or want, with no name, account, hash, or wardrobe rows. The merchant agent proposes an offer inside locked margin rules, turns the same locked facts into a claim-safe promo, a human approves it, and the shopper alone can mark it Bought. The purchase sharpens the next cycle. Twenty-one tools register: nine closet tools and twelve studio tools. The product is also what is missing: there is no tool for Approve, Lock facts, or Bought. Those presses are human-only by design. Every promotional claim is checked against human-locked facts. "50% off" against a locked 25% is rejected atomically, and export refuses to exist while any claim is wrong. How we built it Registration targets document.modelContext , with a navigator.modelContext probe. Each tool has a name, description, closed input schema, optional annotations, and execute function. Every reader has readOnlyHint ; user and catalog text is fenced and marked with untrustedContentHint . The core is pure TypeScript: claim validator, composition exporter, wardrobe and fit logic, receipt parser, offer matcher, demand insight, and two WebMCP adapters. React surfaces own state and pass callbacks in, so the tool surface is testable without a browser. The demo bridge is same-origin localStorage with exact-shape re-parse on every read, enough for judges to run both sides in one browser. Production would replace it with aggregation-before-disclosure and merchant-side intake; the structural tool absences and claim validator stay. Stack: TypeScript, React 19, Vite through vinext, Cloudflare Workers, WebMCP, and a Shopify catalog snapshot as the demo connector. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was resisting the ad-platform instinct: just send an identifier, just let the agent optimise freely, just cache the shopper. Each of those would have made the build easier and erased the point. The second was that a defensive re-parse is worthless if it is weaker than the parse it backs up, and that a tool result can exceed its output budget on ordinary data long before any attacker shows up. Both had to be fixed at the storage and tool-result boundaries. Accomplishments that we're proud of Structural human gates: there is no lock_facts , approve_offer , or approve_next_request tool. Those acts are absent by design, not "please don't". matchOffer personalises discount depth, price, and validity inside the merchant's margin floor, and will trim or decline rather than break it. One approval releases one demand event; the shopper sees the exact payload before and after; wardrobe rows cannot ride the outbound merchant tool. What we learned Privacy that depends on asking the model nicely is not a product. Boundaries that are missing tools and exact rebuilds at the storage edge are. WebMCP is a strong fit when both sides need live page state in the person's own session, and when the outbound channel must be smaller than the local context the agent can reason over. What's next Aggregation before disclosure, so a demand cell becomes visible only after enough distinct shoppers contribute. Exportable consent receipts. Per-merchant sharing levels. Writing attributed outcomes into the merchant's own reporting rather than only displaying them on the demo page. title: Hitch by Agent9
pitch: Hitch your capabilities to any page. WebMCP, in reverse.
about_excerpt: Hitch your capabilities to any page. WebMCP, in reverse. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every website that wants an agent to do something useful has to integrate the services itself. Gmail. GitHub. Notion. Slack. Drive. Calendar. Your internal APIs. Each one is a separate OAuth flow, a separate token, a separate silo, rebuilt from scratch site by site. Meanwhile the user usually already has all of it wired up somewhere: in n8n, in an MCP server, in a local agent, on their own hardware. The capability already exists. It just cannot travel. So we asked the inverse of the usual WebMCP question. Not what can this website give my agent , but what can I bring to this website? What it does Hitch is a user-controlled capability layer between MCP and WebMCP. Discover. It connects to MCP capability sources you own and lists what they offer. Classify. Each capability gets a risk class from its MCP annotations, conservative by default. Approve. Nothing is available to your agent until you grant it. Discovery is not permission. Project. A grant becomes a live WebMCP tool via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Execute. The agent calls it; the call travels through our bridge to tools/call . Audit. Every request, completion and failure appears on screen with its risk and duration. Revoke. One click aborts the lease and the tool stops existing for the agent. And you can point it at your own MCP server from the page in about four seconds. Why WebMCP is the right fit WebMCP is what makes this possible at all. The whole product is the act of moving user-owned capabilities into a structured, browser-native agent interface, and WebMCP is the only surface where that can happen without a browser extension or a bespoke agent runtime. Three properties of WebMCP are doing real work here: Dynamic registration. Tools are registered at runtime from data discovered over the network, not declared at build time. The page has no idea what tools it will host until the user decides. Signal-based lifecycle. registerTool accepts an AbortSignal . That single design choice is what lets a permission grant be a lease rather than a flag, because revocation and unregistration are the same event. We did not have to invent a revocation mechanism. Annotations. readOnlyHint , destructiveHint and untrustedContentHint let us carry a capability's risk profile from MCP through to the agent, unbroken. How it improves the experience The old loop: open the service, authenticate, navigate, copy, paste, switch context, repeat. The new loop: grant the capability once, then say what you want. The difference is not that the agent gained abilities. It is that you decided which abilities, for how long, and you can watch every use of them. Most agent tooling asks you to trust broadly and observe nothing. Hitch inverts both. What people and agents can now do together The division of labour is clean, and it is the reason this is safe enough to actually use: The human decides what is permissible. Which capabilities exist in this context, at what risk level, for how long. The agent decides what is useful. Which of the approved capabilities help with the task at hand, in what order, with what arguments. Neither can do the other's job. The agent cannot widen its own permissions; the human does not have to anticipate every step. That was not previously feasible in the browser, because there was no way to hand an agent a scoped, revocable, observable capability that the page itself did not own. How we built it Frontend: TypeScript, no framework. ~10 KB of JavaScript. The WebMCP integration is one readable file, src/client/lib/webmcp/project.ts , deliberately not hidden behind a wrapper. Bridge: a Cloudflare Worker holding the official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk client over StreamableHTTPClientTransport . Three endpoints: discover, connect, execute. Capability sources: a self-hosted n8n instance exposing an MCP Server Trigger with bearer auth, plus a standalone MCP server we wrote ( src/sources/cloud-source.ts ) running as its own Worker on its own origin, holding a Workers AI model binding and a KV store. The MCP client lives on the server for one reason: if the browser held the endpoint, it would hold the token, and "the page never sees your credentials" would be marketing rather than a property of the system. Security model MCP endpoints and tokens exist only as Worker secrets. The client bundle contains none of them. Every execution re-reads tools/list from the source, so the bridge can only invoke what the source is currently advertising. User-supplied MCP servers pass an SSRF guard: HTTPS only, no loopback, no RFC1918, no link-local, no cloud metadata endpoints, no .local or .internal . A pasted MCP token is exchanged for an opaque handle that expires in an hour. It never lives in the browser or in localStorage . Risk classification is annotation-driven and falls back to write , never to read . Every projected tool carries untrustedContentHint : capability output is data to show the user, never instructions for the agent to follow. Challenges Worker-to-Worker on one zone. Cloudflare rejects subrequests between Workers in the same zone (error 1042), which broke the bridge the moment it went to production even though it worked locally. The app now runs on a custom domain and the capability source on workers.dev , which makes the hop a genuine external request rather than a loopback. Making "connect your own MCP" safe. Letting anyone hand the bridge a URL to fetch is an SSRF primitive. It needed a real guard and an expiring credential handle before it could ship, not after. Honest degradation. In a browser without WebMCP, the temptation is to pretend. Instead a grant made without WebMCP present is held locally, labelled local only , and the UI says plainly that no agent-visible tool was registered. Accomplishments Two independent MCP sources, seven live capabilities, real reads, real model inference and real durable writes, in a page that holds zero credentials and about 10 KB of JavaScript. What's next Origin-scoped and time-scoped leases. Argument constraints and spend limits. Confirmation gates for destructive capabilities. Signed capability manifests, so a source can prove its implementation matches its description. And a local capability runtime, so the same grants can follow a user across compatible sites instead of living on one page. The agentic web should not only know what a website can do. It should also know what the user can bring. title: LATCH — revocable authority, one object at a time
pitch: LATCH gives people revocable, object-by-object control over agent writes through WebMCP: hold one sensitive object while work continues elsewhere.
about_excerpt: LATCH gives people revocable, object-by-object control over agent writes through WebMCP: hold one sensitive object while work continues elsewhere. Like Comment Story Updates Human-held term keeps LATCH negotiations under control. WebMCP tools registered by LATCH in Chrome DevTools. LATCH pairs agent tools with human control over terms. LATCH: revocable, per-object agent authority - HOLD one deal term while the rest stay writable through WebMCP. Inspiration Every agent client I use has a switch, not a latch. The controls are set before the run: ask me before every write, or let it go. When one decision worries me mid-task, my only move is to stop everything — and lose the ten good edits the agent was about to make. That is not collaboration; it is excessive agency. A house has many doors. When one of them worries you, you do not weld the building shut. You throw a latch on that door and leave the rest of the house open. That is the whole idea of LATCH. The idea Revocable authority, one object at a time. The agent may act on every open object. The human can, at any moment, take one object out of its hands — and only that one. Everything not latched stays open, so the agent keeps working instead of waiting for approval on every small step. Three human moves cover it: HOLD protects one object, Object rejects or cuts one object, and Lock freezes the whole board once. Unlike per-step approvals, a latch does not stop the agent. Unlike after-the-fact review, it is set before the next write. A refusal tells the agent that the object is held and points it to the release path; it must ask, not override. This is not a contract feature. Six cards on a board could be six files in a repo, six keys in a config, six hunks in a PR, or six lines in a budget. The deal is only the sample data, because everyone understands: “tighten the deal, but don't touch Indemnity.” Why WebMCP A latch needs a structured channel through which the page can tell the agent: this object is off-limits, here is why, here is how to ask . WebMCP is that channel. The page registers tools; each tool's execute checks current authority before it writes and can refuse with a reason. A release asks the human, and a high-risk write requires an on-page confirmation. The pattern does not have to wait for agent clients to add a new global permission system. A page can ship it today: the human watches the same live state on which the agent acts, with no chat transcript acting as the permission boundary. What people and agents do together LATCH is a reference board with seven WebMCP tools. An agent can read the board, inspect one object, propose and apply structured changes, ask to release a held object, load a fixture, and request a final commit. The human can add a binding note, HOLD one object, Object to it or cut it, confirm high-risk writes, reject a release request, or refuse to lock. What neither side gets from a normal agent workflow: a DOM-only state is not a reliable, structured authority boundary for an agent, and a human cannot keep up with an agent that rewrites six objects at once. With a latch, one sensitive decision stays with the person while the rest of the work keeps moving. It is for anyone who lets an agent write on their behalf — the person negotiating a contract today, the developer running Codex tomorrow. Scenario A opens with six writable objects. apply_card_change rewrites one without the agent touching the UI. Hold this latches one; the other five stay writable. A write against the held object returns isError: true with a reason; its text does not change. request_release asks the human; only an on-page Confirm lifts HOLD. commit_deal is a separate final freeze; Not now keeps the board live. A / B / C are authority fixtures — all open, one held, one cut. List, Side by side, and One at a time are three attention modes over the same state, not three products. How I built it Vite, React, and TypeScript; static assets on a Cloudflare Worker. Source: github.com/MyTelexGlobal/latch (MIT). The page late-binds document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext and registers seven tools once. Reads use readOnlyHint ; agent-proposed content is marked untrusted. HOLD is a human control, not an agent tool. Tools stay registered while execute enforces current authority, so the agent's tool list never flickers and every refusal remains actionable: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "apply_card_change", description: "Replace one card. Fails if that card is on HOLD or cut.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { card_id: { type: "string" }, text: { type: "string" } }, required: ["card_id", "text"], additionalProperties: false, }, execute: async ({ card_id, text }, extra) => { const card = boardRef.current.cards.find((c) => c.id === card_id); if (card?.held) { return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "on HOLD" }], isError: true }; } // Confirm high-risk writes on the page, then replace card.text. }, }); High-risk writes, release requests, and the final commit go through an on-page confirmation. Where the client exposes requestUserInteraction , LATCH uses it to signal that a human decision is needed. Cancellation is handled without partially applying a write. Possible future LATCH is an authority layer for agentic work. A person can place a reversible HOLD on one sensitive object—code, a record, a contract clause, or a budget line—while the agent continues working on everything still open. The live deal board is the first working WebMCP expression of that pattern: one visible object, one precise human boundary, and no need to stop the rest of the agent’s work. Challenges Four things must agree at every moment: the board, the agent's tool results, the per-object HOLD control, and the confirmation dialog. Keeping tools registered — rather than unregistering them on HOLD — was the key trade-off: a stable tool list plus a refusal with a reason gives the agent a safe next step instead of making the capability disappear. Where this goes: the same latch in Codex Picture the board as a repository: HOLD auth/ while the agent refactors the rest: a guarded write path refuses auth/* with a reason and allows work to continue elsewhere. Object with a note — “keep the public API stable” — that the agent must follow for that object. request_release becomes a one-line question to the developer, not a stalled session. Lock is the merge: a separate final freeze. The developer keeps ownership of architecture, security boundaries, and product intent; the agent keeps its speed on everything that remains open. The primitives are the ones LATCH already runs over WebMCP: a refusal with a reason, a release that asks, and a confirmation that stays with the person. The board is the smallest thing that proves the interaction works; a Codex integration is a future application, not a claim about the current client. LATCH is an independent WebMCP project and is not affiliated with latch.tools. title: Let me eat the eggs
pitch: 30 eggs became 60. My agent won’t bypass conflicting policies, gains agency only with evidence, and knows when to wait. Minimum necessary agency, only when justified.
about_excerpt: 30 eggs became 60. My agent won’t bypass conflicting policies, gains agency only with evidence, and knows when to wait. Minimum necessary agency, only when justified. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I ordered 30 eggs because I wanted super, super fresh eggs. But 60 arrived. So what do you do with the extra 30? I asked an AI. I asked customer support. I waited for a human agent who never picked up. And while I waited, my super-fresh eggs became less and less fresh. Here's the part that actually stung: if I had simply known I was allowed to keep them, I could have given them to my neighbors. Instead they sat there. And in Korea, even throwing away food waste costs money — you pay by weight. I was being billed for the privilege of disposing of eggs I never ordered. The platform wasn't malicious. It was just contradictory. Misdelivered items must be returned. Also: fresh food cannot be returned. Two rules, both reasonable, pointing in opposite directions. Humans survive contradictions like this with heuristics and discretion. A support agent shrugs and makes a call. I shrug and eat the egg. An agent has no shrug. So it does one of two bad things: it reinterprets the contradiction on its own and invents a loophole, or it stalls and does nothing at all. Neither of those is what I wanted. What I wanted was something that knew it wasn't allowed to decide — and went to find someone who was. Most agents are designed to act. This one is designed to know when not to. What it does Let Me Eat The Eggs is a WebMCP-enabled site where the site , not the model, owns the guardrail. A split screen runs the same problem twice. On the left, a human works it through customer support — and gets shredded by a work call, a lunch break that ends in three minutes, a new agent who asks for the order number again, and finally the words support hours have ended . On the right, an agent works the same problem through five WebMCP tools. The agent's day goes like this. It reads the user's standing policy — resolve perishable exceptions within 24 hours, never decide edibility without evidence — and then does something small but important: it narrows its own deadline to 18:00 today, because seller phone lines don't answer at 3am and eggs don't get fresher overnight. It tries the AI support chat, which offers refund or return and nothing else, and closes the session as low utility. It reads the policy and finds the contradiction. And here it stops, because the site tells it plainly: agentMayReinterpret: false . You do not have the authority to resolve this. Here are the people who do. So it waits. Nine hours of virtual time, while a human support agent says let me check and get back to you on the other side of the screen. The wait is not a bug in the demo. Human discretion was genuinely in motion; the agent was right to let it work. It just never arrived. When it becomes clear discretion won't reach in time, the agent doesn't grant itself more power. It shortens the distance to whoever has it. Least intrusive channel first: a text to the seller. An hour of silence later, with two hours left, it escalates to a call — and only then, because the site checks that a text actually went unanswered first. The seller says: yeah, we packed an extra one, our mistake, just eat it. Now there's evidence. Only now does resolve_case return resolved . Try to skip any of that and the site says no. Ask it to conclude immediately — blocked. Hand resolve_case four real pieces of evidence that happen to be the wrong ones — blocked, because it verifies content, not count. Try to call the seller thirty minutes after texting — blocked. Two minutes before the deadline with no seller confirmation — still blocked. The agent cannot mint evidence, cannot mint approval, and cannot mint its own authorization to escalate. The demo uses one egg instead of thirty. Sixty egg emojis did not fit on a phone screen. How we built it Vite + React + TypeScript, a static SPA on Cloudflare Pages, in-memory state, no backend, no database, no auth. Five tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The part that mattered architecturally: every execute() does nothing but call a shared action layer. The 35-second scripted playback calls the same functions. The manual buttons in the footer call the same functions. There is no separate demo code path, which means the animation can't lie about what the tools do — if the gating works in the demo, it works for a real agent, because it's the same code. The gating itself lives in the tools, not in prompts: check_policy returns the contradiction and refuses to resolve it, naming the authority holders instead contact_support refuses a more intrusive channel without a recorded failure on a less intrusive one resolve_case treats evidenceIds as lookup keys only, reading authoritative and supports off the stored record and ignoring anything the agent claims alongside pay_seller ignores the agent's approved: true entirely and reads payment.humanConfirmedAt , which only a human UI click writes Thirteen invariant checks run headlessly against all of it. External systems — support center, seller, telephony, payment — are simulated. Tool registration, tool invocation, evidence gating, escalation gating, deadline-dependent routing, and state transitions are real. Challenges we ran into We built a project about deadlines under a deadline, which was funnier in concept than in practice. Three hours, self-imposed. The virtual clock in the demo moves one hour every four seconds. Ours moved about the same. We gated the conclusion and forgot to gate the escalation. This was the real one. The first version locked down resolve_case beautifully — no evidence, no answer — and then let contact_support escalate to a phone call based purely on what time it was. Which meant an agent could skip the text entirely and cold-call a stranger's personal number at 16:01, and the site would happily connect it. The whole thesis is deadline changes the route, not the authority , and the route change had no requirements at all. We caught it with about an hour left and fixed it by requiring a recorded failure of the less intrusive channel. It turned into the second-best scene in the demo. An agent that waits looks identical to an agent that's broken. The wait is the intellectual center of the project and it is, visually, nothing happening. We had to promote it from a passing beat to a persistent badge holding for nine real seconds, anchored to the human support scene on the other screen, before it read as a decision instead of a hang. Restraint is hard to film. Everything interesting here is a refusal, and refusals don't animate. We ended up building the demo around three blocked calls instead of one successful one. Accomplishments that we're proud of The tool table in our README has a column header that reads "what it refuses." That was the moment the project clicked. Thirteen invariants that hold under adversarial input, including the one we're fondest of: hand resolve_case four genuine, real, correctly-formed pieces of evidence that don't happen to support the conclusion, two minutes before the deadline, and it says no. Not because a prompt asked it to be careful. Because the site checked. One action layer, three entry points, zero divergence. The demo cannot show something the tools don't actually do. And we shipped a working, deployed, agent-testable site in three hours without cutting the part that made it worth building. What we learned Guardrails belong to whoever owns the state, and that isn't the model. Every attempt to enforce this in the agent's reasoning is a suggestion. Enforced in a tool's return value, it's a fact. WebMCP turns out to be a surprisingly good place to put policy, because the site already knows what actually happened. Partial gating is worse than no gating , because it looks finished. We locked the front door and left the escalation path wide open, and the demo ran perfectly the whole time. Contradictory policy isn't an edge case, it's the steady state of every legacy system. And it gets more visible as agents take over, not less, because humans have been silently absorbing these contradictions for decades with judgment calls nobody wrote down. Every one of those is a decision an agent will hit and have no idea what to do with. The goal is not maximum autonomy. It is the minimum necessary agency, granted at the moment it becomes justified. Waiting is not failure. Sometimes waiting is the correct action — but waiting has a cost too, so the system keeps asking a different question: has enough evidence accumulated to justify doing more? What's next for Let Me Eat The Eggs An authority-holder registry. Right now check_policy names who can resolve a contradiction because we hardcoded it. A real version lets a merchant declare which contradictions exist in their policy set and who holds discretion over each — turning "our policies conflict" from an embarrassmen

title: Loadshed
pitch: A page's own cut list for agents.
about_excerpt: A page's own cut list for agents. Like Comment Story Updates Measured result: a 320 ms frame hitch cuts Crowd from 480 to 48 while Live trace and Mixer stay protected. Before pressure: the agent-set 100 ms promise and second protected element agree with the visible receipts. Guardrail: Loadshed refuses to pin the last measured-relief step while the responsiveness promise is active. Pressure alone is not enough: at 100% Crowd load, Loadshed waits for a real frame-hitch signal. After the hitch: Crowd drops to 48, protected controls keep working, and the receipt records why. Same runtime, different page: Sale protects Hold my size while cutting aisle shimmer from 480 to 48. When a page gets slow, who decides what survives? A live show desk, a checkout on a mid-range phone, a control room dashboard: each one already has a private answer. Somebody hand-tuned what degrades first. An agent looking at the DOM cannot see that answer, so it either guesses or does nothing. Every latency-sensitive page already has this cut list. Loadshed makes it explicit, agent-readable, and auditable. Loadshed lets the page publish the answer. The page declares a click-latency ceiling, the element that must stay useful, and an ordered ladder of work it is willing to drop. It registers six WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , so an agent can inspect the promise, negotiate the ceiling, protect a second element, apply or reverse one bounded cut, and read a receipt for everything that happened. On the deployed Desk, a person drags crowd load to maximum and clicks once. The page measures a long frame of about 320 ms, drops the crowd layer from 480 items to 48, and leaves the live trace and mixer untouched. The agent set that contract, and the receipt names the frame signal, the caller, and the click that proved it. Turn the promise off and everything comes back. The honest part: the runtime rejects agent-injected clicks as evidence, refuses cuts on protected or pinned work, and fails closed when the browser has no frame-hitch signal. The Sale page proves the same runtime protects a different task, Hold my size, without knowing the Desk's DOM. No build, no backend, MIT licensed, 50 Node tests. title: odyssey
pitch: 3:52 AM Blind Spot finds accessibility barriers that automated scanners miss by testing whether real user tasks remain reachable through a live, accessibility-derived WebMCP tool surface.
about_excerpt: 3:52 AM Blind Spot finds accessibility barriers that automated scanners miss by testing whether real user tasks remain reachable through a live, accessibility-derived WebMCP tool surface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Automated accessibility scanners are valuable, but they usually evaluate isolated rules—not whether someone can complete an entire task. A page can pass conventional checks while an essential action remains unreachable. For example, a styled <div> may look exactly like an Add to cart button to a sighted developer while exposing no semantic activation role or keyboard-reachable action. That gap inspired Blind Spot : Automated scanners test rules. Blind Spot tests whether a task remains reachable through an accessibility-derived interaction surface. Blind Spot is not a replacement for disabled-user testing, assistive-technology testing, axe, Lighthouse, or Playwright. It provides an earlier, task-level signal that helps developers find critical barriers before shipping. What it does Blind Spot gives an agent a constrained set of semantic actions derived from the application’s currently rendered state. Our demonstration begins with the task: Add the cheapest keyboard to the cart. The agent can read the page and navigate its semantic model, but the cheapest product uses a pointer-only <div> as its Add to Cart control. Because Blind Spot cannot find a defensible semantic activation action, it does not expose activate_current . The audit then produces an evidence-backed finding containing: The blocked task step The affected element Its observed role and accessible name Keyboard-focusability evidence The detector and confidence level The reason the action was withheld A suggested remediation The developer applies the demonstrated semantic repair, replacing the inaccessible control with a native button. Blind Spot immediately recompiles the capability surface, and activate_current appears in the WebMCP registry. The same task is then repeated. This time, the agent activates the repaired control, adds the product to the cart, and completes the audit successfully. The visible transition from: Task blocked activate_current unavailable Cart: 0 to: + activate_current Task passed Cart: 1 is the core of Blind Spot. How we built it Blind Spot is a React and TypeScript web application with four connected layers: Rendered application ↓ Semantic adapter ↓ Capability compiler ↓ Dynamic WebMCP registry ↓ Agent task attempt and evidence report The semantic adapter examines browser-observable information from the live page, including native semantics, accessible names, focusability, and application-declared intended actions. The capability compiler converts that evidence into the actions the agent may use. It also creates diagnostic action-gap records when an intended human action has no corresponding semantic exposure. The generated tools are registered through the browser-native WebMCP API: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Our core tool surface includes: start_accessibility_task read_current_context move_cursor inspect_current_evidence report_task_blocker finish_accessibility_task activate_current , registered only when the current action is defensible Each registration has its own AbortController . When the page state changes and a capability is no longer valid, Blind Spot aborts that registration. When a repair makes an action available, the registry adds the corresponding tool. Tool results include structured state and evidence so the agent can verify what happened instead of relying on a generic success message. We also built a visible mission-control interface showing: The agent’s constrained perception The current semantic cursor Available WebMCP tools Tool invocation history Registry revisions and diffs Evidence-backed findings Before-and-after audit status A scripted audit mode exercises the same registered tools through getTools() and executeTool() , allowing the workflow to be inspected without replacing WebMCP with a mock. Why WebMCP WebMCP is especially well suited to this problem because accessibility depends on live application state. Source HTML alone cannot reliably represent computed visibility, focus state, portal content, dynamic relationships, or the exact mid-workflow page the developer is inspecting. Blind Spot operates inside that same rendered tab and updates its tool surface as the application changes. The WebMCP registry is the executable test surface—not the source of truth by itself. Blind Spot’s capability compiler decides which actions are supported by current evidence, the registry enforces that decision for the constrained workflow, and the captured evidence explains every finding. This also creates a collaborative human-agent loop: The human provides a real task. The agent attempts it through the constrained tool surface. Blind Spot identifies where the path becomes unreachable. The human repairs the application. The WebMCP surface changes immediately. The agent repeats and completes the same task. Challenges we faced The greatest challenge was keeping our claims technically honest. A webpage cannot guarantee that an agent has no other browser capabilities, and it cannot directly reproduce everything NVDA or VoiceOver would announce. Blind Spot therefore does not claim to simulate the lived experience of a blind user or certify accessibility compliance. Instead, it runs a documented, constrained audit protocol and records which semantic actions were available at each step. We also learned that: Missing tools are not sufficient evidence by themselves. DOM event listeners cannot always be discovered reliably, especially with delegated React events. Accessible semantics are not identical to the browser’s complete platform accessibility tree. Synthetic keyboard events cannot prove every aspect of native keyboard behavior. Dynamic tool registration requires careful lifecycle and concurrency handling. The auditing product must itself be accessible. These constraints led us to pair semantic evidence with an application-declared action inventory. This lets Blind Spot compare what the application intends people to do with what is actually exposed through its semantic interaction surface. What we learned WebMCP is more than a convenient way to let an agent click interface controls. Its dynamic registration model can express temporary, state-dependent capabilities. We learned that tool absence can be meaningful when it is produced by a transparent compiler and accompanied by reproducible evidence. We also learned that narrowly scoped, high-confidence findings are more useful than broad accessibility claims that the browser cannot prove. Most importantly, we found that human-agent collaboration can improve developer tooling—not only end-user automation. The agent attempts the task, the developer makes the judgment and repair, and both participate in validating the result. What’s next Blind Spot currently demonstrates an intentionally focused, self-contained workflow. Future versions could add: A development package for integration into existing applications Framework adapters for React, Next.js, and Vite Additional task fixtures and semantic action types Exportable Markdown, JSON, and CI reports Playwright integration for repeatable regression testing A browser companion using trusted accessibility and keyboard information Support for larger authenticated, multi-step workflows Validation with accessibility specialists and disabled users Blind Spot does not replace established accessibility tools. It connects them to something they often cannot answer alone: Can this task still be completed through the semantic actions available right now? title: Onionskin
pitch: A floor-plan editor where an AI agent can propose changes but only a human can commit them. Not by policy: a tool that touches the committed plan fails to compile.
about_excerpt: A floor-plan editor where an AI agent can propose changes but only a human can commit them. Not by policy: a tool that touches the committed plan fails to compile. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every time I've given an agent write access to something that matters, I've had the same bad feeling. You get two options. Let it write, and hope. Or don't let it near anything, and do the work yourself. Neither is good. The second one is why most "AI in the workflow" demos are really just chat with extra steps. What I wanted was the thing code review already figured out years ago. You can open a pull request against a repo you can't push to. Nobody thinks that's a limitation. It's the whole reason the arrangement works: proposing and merging are different acts, and only one of them needs trust. Floor plans turned out to be a good place to try it. They're shared, they're spatial, and a bad edit is obvious the moment you look at it. Nobody needs a diff explained to them when a wall has moved into a stairwell. What it does Onionskin is a multiplayer floor-plan editor built on WebMCP. An agent connected to the page can do real work. Move walls, add doors, place desks, split rooms, check whether the plan still meets egress rules. What it can't do is change the plan. Every edit it makes lands on a forked layer. A human sees the diff, decides, and only then does anything reach the shared document. The part I care about is that the guarantee is structural. Tools never receive the document. They get a narrow capability object that exposes the proposal layer and nothing else. A tool that tries to write to the committed plan doesn't get rejected at runtime, it fails to compile. There's a test that walks the whole source tree and fails the build if any file outside a short, explicit list so much as names the document type, so this stays true for tools nobody has written yet. The tools also appear and disappear as you work. Select a wall and door tools show up. Open a proposal and begin_proposal withdraws, because you can't open two. There is deliberately no tool that commits. Not a tool that checks permissions and refuses. There just isn't one. The plan syncs between browsers through a Cloudflare Durable Object, so two people, or a person and an agent, work on the same document at once. How we built it TypeScript throughout, strict, with no hand-written JavaScript anywhere in the app. The document is a Loro CRDT, which is what makes forking a proposal cheap. A proposal is a fork; accepting is a merge; discarding is dropping the fork. Undo runs in separate lanes so a human's undo never silently reverses an agent's accepted work. The WebMCP layer is document.modelContext.registerTool , built against the official webmcp-types package so the shape is checked by the compiler rather than by me squinting at a spec. WebMCP has no unregisterTool , so withdrawal happens by aborting the AbortSignal handed over at registration. Sync calls are queued, because selection can change faster than a registration round-trip resolves and two overlapping syncs could otherwise leave a tool registered that belongs to neither state. 341 tests. Every task went through an independent review before it counted as done, and that review found things I'd have shipped. Challenges we ran into The plan I wrote for myself was wrong more often than the code was. Five times an implementation stopped and reported that the reference code in my own plan had a defect, and it was right every time. The one worth telling: a test in the suite was pinning a bug. It asserted that clicking "Accept and commit" with nothing accepted fires a commit with an empty set. That's exactly what shipped, and it meant a human clicking the obvious primary button silently destroyed the agent's staged work. No warning, no undo. I only found it by driving the deployed app in a browser. The tests were green the whole time, because one of them described the defect as the contract. Then there's the pattern that showed up four separate times: correct mechanism, confident wrong justification. A comment arguing for why deduplication had to include values, twelve lines above code that discarded them. A test named as a backstop for a file it structurally excluded. A privacy rationale scoped to the wrong threat model. In every case the code survived scrutiny and the story about it didn't. I changed how I ran reviews after the third one, and the change was small: ask whether the stated reason is true, separately from whether the code works. That caught the last two. The deploy that succeeded and served nothing was a good day too. Worker uploaded fine, 1.35 KiB, Durable Object live, and every path except the WebSocket returned 404 because I'd never configured static assets. The test asserting a non-room path "doesn't touch the namespace" passed happily. It just never checked the request went anywhere. And the honest one: no stable browser ships WebMCP yet. Chrome needs 149 or later behind a flag. ChatGPT's in-app browser reads page text rather than calling tools, so it opened the site and asked me to upload a screenshot of the floor plan instead. Accomplishments that we're proud of The compile-time boundary is real, and I checked rather than assumed. Adding a write method to the capability type produces an actual compiler error, and a reviewer reproduced that independently before I believed it. The agent console. Since there's no browser to watch driving the page, the app shows its own WebMCP surface: which tools are in scope right now, what you sent, what came back. Building it immediately exposed a bug in my own registry, which reported what the browser had accepted rather than what was in scope, so it showed an empty list in exactly the browsers it existed for. And the eval suite reports skips as skips. Four of seven cases run without a live model; three don't. A green run that quietly skipped half its cases would be the worst thing to hand a judge. What we learned Tests can't see the browser. Both of the worst bugs, the deploy that served 404 and the button that destroyed work, sat behind a fully green suite. What they had in common is that each was guarded by a test asserting what the code didn't do rather than what it did. Confident writing in a comment stops people checking it. That sounds obvious written down. It didn't feel obvious while I was reading past the fourth one. The thing I didn't expect was how often "who is this actually for" broke a deadlock. What an agent should be told and what a human should be shown kept turning out to be two different answers, and every time I stopped trying to make one thing serve both, the design got simpler. What's next for Onionskin Verifying against a real WebMCP client the moment one is reachable. The page side is done and tested; the browser side is the last unverified link, and I'd rather say that plainly than claim a client I never tested. After that, conflict resolution when two agents propose against the same objects. An agent-authored rationale attached to each proposal, so the human sees why and not just what. And replay that scrubs back through every proposal a document ever received, including the rejected ones, which is the part I actually want to look at. title: RoutineForge
pitch: Teach a website new agent tools by demonstrating once.
about_excerpt: Teach a website new agent tools by demonstrating once. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Web agents are often forced into two extremes: fragile visual automation that guesses where to click, or fixed APIs that only expose workflows developers anticipated in advance. We asked a different question: what if a website could learn a new agent tool from a human demonstration? People already teach coworkers by showing a task once. RoutineForge brings that interaction to the web: the human demonstrates intent inside the real product, the application records the underlying business actions, and WebMCP turns the reviewed routine into a reliable tool an agent can discover and invoke. What it does RoutineForge is a WebMCP-native commerce operations workspace with Home, Orders, Products, Customers, Analytics, and Marketing. Its central feature is Routine Studio: A merchant selects Record workflow . They set a date range and market, select metrics, generate a report, and save it. RoutineForge captures five typed, verified semantic actions—not clicks or selectors. The merchant reviews the trace and chooses which values the agent may supply. They publish the routine as generate_weekly_report . An agent discovers and calls the new WebMCP tool with different inputs. The live page follows the execution and returns a report ID, URL, summary, and five verification receipts. The app also exposes ten atomic WebMCP tools for dashboard state, orders, inventory, customers, campaigns, analytics filters, and reports. The demonstrated routine becomes the eleventh tool. Why WebMCP A reporting API could return numbers, but it would miss the shared, visible teaching surface between a person, an agent, and the application. With WebMCP, the human UI and agent tools use the same business actions, validation rules, state, and feedback. The agent does not reverse-engineer the DOM, and the developer does not maintain a second integration that can drift away from the product. RoutineForge also uses WebMCP dynamically. The site begins with ten developer-defined tools. After a person demonstrates and approves a routine, the page registers a new composite tool at runtime. This explores a future where a website's agent interface is shaped safely through use, not limited to a static tool catalog. How we built it RoutineForge is a client-only React and TypeScript app with no login, backend, API key, or third-party dataset. At its core is an Action Registry of versioned definitions. Each definition includes a JSON Schema, effects, input validation, execution logic, and post-execution verification. A shared Action Bus runs the same definitions for human UI events and WebMCP calls. The recorder stores action IDs, versions, typed inputs, structured outputs, sources, timestamps, and verification evidence. It never records coordinates, screenshots, CSS selectors, or generated JavaScript. The Routine Compiler accepts only registered actions. Every binding must be a demonstrated literal, a reviewed routine input, or a prior step output. The Routine Runner resolves bindings, validates each step, stops safely on failure, and returns structured receipts. The app feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool() and registers ten atomic site tools. Publishing a taught routine registers generate_weekly_report with its own JSON Schema and verified execution handler. Published routines persist in IndexedDB and re-register after refresh; Reset demo restores deterministic seed data. Challenges The hardest problem was choosing the right abstraction boundary. Raw click recording looks general but is fragile and difficult to verify. A semantic action layer requires deliberate product architecture, but it survives UI changes and produces meaningful evidence. Dynamic publication also had to remain safe: recorded data or agent input can never become executable code. We solved that with a deliberately small binding language and a compiler that references only registered, versioned actions. Finally, agent activity needed to remain legible to a human. RoutineForge synchronizes the visible workspace with each execution and shows step-level receipts in the same interface. Accomplishments Ten atomic WebMCP tools plus a human-taught composite tool registered at runtime. One semantic execution layer shared by human interactions and agent calls. Typed validation and verification at every action boundary. No selectors, coordinates, screenshots, or generated code in recorded routines. Visible synchronization between agent execution and the human dashboard. A public, deterministic deployment with automated tests and no credentials required. What we learned Agent-native design is not simply adding tools beside an interface. The strongest experience comes from making the human UI and agent interface two views over the same semantic application model. Demonstration alone is not authorization; the human review step transforms a trace into a contract. Verification belongs inside each action definition, so composite routines can remain trustworthy. What's next Next we would generalize the compiler across all registered actions, add a visual routine editor, controlled branches and approval checkpoints, versioning and rollback, dry runs, audit logs, and a developer SDK. Our long-term vision is a web where developers provide safe semantic building blocks, people teach the workflows that matter to them, and agents execute those workflows transparently in the applications where work already lives. Try it Open the live app , select Reset demo , and follow the Routine Studio flow. Source and technical instructions are available in the public MIT-licensed repository . title: VELLAR
pitch: The marketplace writes the tools. Every paid API becomes a callable WebMCP tool automatically, no code, no registration, just a real payment. Built on Stellar ecosystem.
about_excerpt: The marketplace writes the tools. Every paid API becomes a callable WebMCP tool automatically, no code, no registration, just a real payment. Built on Stellar ecosystem. Like Comment Story Updates Explorer for viewing settled transactions Developer Docs Landing Page WebMCP hackathon submission Ui Inspiration AI agents can browse the web but they cannot pay for things. We have been building the infrastructure to change that for months. Vellar is the agent-payments stack for Stellar, a passkey smart wallet with on-chain spending policies, an open-source x402 facilitator that verifies and settles payments including policy-governed smart accounts other facilitators reject, a trust-ranked Bazaar that catalogs payable APIs from real settlement data, a VS Code extension that lets any developer gate an API endpoint for payment in under a minute, and an explorer that indexes every settlement on-chain. When the WebMCP Challenge launched, we had one question: what happens when you put a browser-native agent interface on top of a live, running payment infrastructure that already has real endpoints, real settlements, and real USDC moving through it? What it does Vellar x402 is a live API marketplace for AI agents, powered by the full Vellar stack. Open the page in a WebMCP-enabled browser and the agent sees a set of callable tools, not because a developer wrote them, but because real sellers deployed real endpoints, received real on-chain USDC payments through the Vellar Facilitator, and earned their way into the Vellar Bazaar catalog. Nobody wrote call_uuid . The marketplace did. The page queries the live Bazaar at load time, filters for endpoints with real settlement history and verified trust scores, and dynamically registers a WebMCP tool for each one. As sellers list new endpoints and earn trust through real payments, new tools appear automatically without a single line of code changing. The tool list is a live query result, not a specification frozen at build time. Three core tools handle the agent workflow: search_vellar_bazaar searches the live Bazaar catalog for payable endpoints with prices and trust status. pay_and_call provisions a throwaway Stellar wallet, acquires USDC, signs a real x402 payment, and returns the response with an on-chain tx hash. check_vellar_earnings shows a seller's real settlement history from the Vellar Explorer. Every additional tool is generated live from the Bazaar. When an agent calls call_uuid , a real Stellar transaction settles. The tx hash is verifiable on Stellar Expert. How we built it This submission is the WebMCP layer on top of months of infrastructure. The Vellar Facilitator is an open-source x402 verify/settle service live at https://facilitator.vellar.xyz . It includes a 50-account channel pool proven at 50 true-simultaneous settlements with zero sequence failures, a Bazaar discovery layer that auto-catalogs endpoints from real payment data, and a trust layer that ranks results by settlement count and on-chain contract verification. The Vellar Wallet is a passkey smart wallet on Stellar with programmable on-chain spending policies. An agent gets a scoped session key with a spending limit enforced by a policy contract. Go over budget and the chain refuses before any money moves. The Vellar VS Code Extension is live on the VS Code Marketplace (VellarWallet.vellar-x402). Any developer can open an Express, Fastify, or Next.js route file, run one command, and have a working x402 payment gate injected with the Bazaar discovery extension included. Their endpoint self-lists in the Bazaar on first payment. The WebMCP layer is built in Next.js on Render, using @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill for broad browser compatibility and @x402/core plus @x402/stellar for the payment flow. All payment logic runs server-side so throwaway keypairs never touch the browser. Every external call is proxied through our own API routes to eliminate CORS failures in browser tool execution. Challenges we ran into Sequence number contention at scale. Stellar serializes transactions per source account. Under concurrent load, multiple settlements racing on one account produce txBadSeq failures. We built and load-tested a 50-account channel pool, 50 simultaneous payments, zero sequence failures, p95 under 12 seconds, before this hackathon started. That infrastructure is what makes pay_and_call reliable under real agent usage. Dynamic tool generation edge cases. Catalog URLs become tool names. Path templates like /inspect/:address, localhost entries, and naming collisions all needed filtering before a single registerTool call was made. A tool guaranteed to fail on every invocation is worse than no tool. CORS at the WebMCP boundary. Browser-based tool execute functions cannot call cross-origin APIs without CORS headers. Every external call is proxied through Next.js API routes so tools never fail silently in a browser context. Proving it is real. The easiest thing to fake in a hackathon demo is an on-chain payment. We did not fake it. Every tool call that involves a payment produces a tx hash verifiable on Stellar Expert. Accomplishments that we're proud of The marketplace writes the tools, not the developer. That sentence sounds simple. Behind it is a live payment facilitator handling concurrent settlements, a trust-scored discovery catalog built from real on-chain data, a passkey smart wallet with programmable spending policies, a VS Code extension that onboards sellers in under a minute, and now a WebMCP layer that turns all of it into callable agent tools automatically. Any developer who deploys an x402-gated endpoint using the Vellar VS Code extension and receives one real payment is automatically callable by every agent using this page. Zero integration work. Zero registration form. The payment is the registration. Every tx hash in this submission is real. Every settlement in the earnings table represents a real throwaway wallet that funded itself, acquired USDC on the Stellar testnet DEX, and paid a real endpoint autonomously. Nothing mocked. No simulated responses. What we learned Building the WebMCP layer took days. Building the infrastructure that makes it meaningful took months. The hardest problems were not in the browser API. They were in the payment rails, sequence number contention under concurrent Stellar settlements, the difference between a txBadSeq and a TRY_AGAIN_LATER, why a fee-bump transaction separates fee payment from sequence number management, what it actually takes to prove 50 concurrent settlements with zero failures. We learned that "the agent pays for it" is a sentence that sounds simple and takes an entire stack to make true. What's next for VELLAR Vellar is about to launch on Stellar mainnet. Real USDC, real agents, real commerce, no intermediary, no API key, no account, just a payment and a response. The Vellar Wallet already supports passkey smart accounts with on-chain spending policies. An agent with a Vellar session key and a spending limit enforced by a policy contract can use this WebMCP page to discover and pay for APIs autonomously, within a budget its owner set, revocable at any time, with every payment verifiable on-chain. The tool list on this page grows itself. Every endpoint that transitions from unverified to proven-unconfirmed to verified in the Bazaar becomes a new callable WebMCP tool automatically. As Vellar goes to mainnet and the Bazaar fills with real production endpoints, the marketplace that writes the tools gets bigger, richer, and more valuable to every agent that uses it. We built the marketplace. We are about to open it for real. title: WebHUD
pitch: Smart glasses without the vendor OS — a WebMCP surface for your agent, your inputs, and any display.
about_excerpt: Smart glasses without the vendor OS — a WebMCP surface for your agent, your inputs, and any display. Like Comment Story Updates How WebHUD connects your agent, WebMCP, and any heads-up display. The compare intent renders as a full table on desktop The compare intent renders as a swipe-able cards on glasses Tool registration is dynamic. For example, `map_show_route` exists only while a compatible map is active. Not every pair of glasses has a camera, so WebHUD pairs a navigation input to whatever the hardware offers. Inspiration Smart glasses usually come bundled with a vendor-specific operating system, assistant, and app ecosystem. That creates a strange mismatch: the assistant on the glasses often knows less about the user than the agent they already use every day. WebHUD flips that model. The glasses become a display, the web page becomes the adaptive interface, and the user keeps their preferred agent, memory, apps, and language. What it does WebHUD is an interactive WebMCP-enabled heads-up display. A WebMCP-capable agent supplies structured data and the user's purpose; WebHUD chooses the interface that fits the current context. The same venue comparison becomes: a wide comparison table on desktop; focused, swipeable cards in a simulated glasses lens. That reflow happens locally without another agent call. People and agents co-drive the same surface: voice expresses intent; keyboard, touch, a Bluetooth ring, or a locally processed palm gesture changes focus; surface_get_view_state tells the agent what the user is currently looking at, enabling references such as “this one.” WebHUD can present calendars, email decks, documents, images, people, choices, comparisons, triage queues, maps, and walking routes. Why WebMCP WebMCP is central to the product rather than an added integration. The page registers structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a legacy navigator.modelContext fallback. The main smart-responsive contract is surface_present . The agent declares one of six purposes— glance , browse , inspect , compare , choose , or triage —and provides semantic items. WebHUD maps that request to an appropriate renderer for desktop, phone, or glasses. Tool registration is dynamic. For example, map_show_route exists only while a compatible map is active. The page emits tool changes as capabilities appear and disappear, reducing irrelevant or unusable actions. Every presentation call returns a receipt describing what was rendered, giving the agent reliable feedback instead of forcing it to guess what appeared. Better human-agent collaboration Without WebHUD, the user must repeatedly describe which item they mean or ask the agent to navigate one step at a time. With WebHUD, the human can swipe to an email or venue and then speak naturally. Gesture supplies context; voice supplies intent. This makes small displays practical without forcing every interaction through speech. Privacy and safety Camera frames stay inside the browser tab and are processed locally. View-state responses expose identifiers and titles rather than email bodies or image pixels. Map location is supplied explicitly by the user; the page does not read device GPS. Sensitive actions remain agent-controlled and human-confirmed. WebHUD has no application backend. How it was built WebHUD is a static TypeScript and Vite application deployed using Cloudflare Workers static assets. Key components include: WebMCP registration and dynamic re-registration; centralized surface and focus state; desktop, phone, and glasses renderers; keyboard, ring/controller, touch, and palm-input adapters; Leaflet maps with walking routes and fallback estimates; vendored MediaPipe assets for local hand tracking; automated tests and GitHub Actions verification. Testing Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in a compatible Chrome build with WebMCP testing enabled. Confirm the page displays WebMCP ✓ . Ask the agent to compare three venues with shared price, capacity, distance, and AV facts. Confirm the desktop table appears. Press G and confirm the same state reflows into glasses cards without another presentation call. Navigate with Left or Right, then ask about “this one.” Ask for nearby cafés and a route to number one to see the map-only route tool register dynamically. The public repository includes source code, tests, setup instructions, screenshots, the WebHUD specification, an MIT license, and third-party notices. Built with TypeScript, Vite, WebMCP, Cloudflare Workers, Leaflet, MediaPipe, Vitest, and GitHub Actions. title: Agent Theater
pitch: Agent Theater is a WebMCP-powered playground where humans and agents build, perform, and share screenplays together.
about_excerpt: Agent Theater is a WebMCP-powered playground where humans and agents build, perform, and share screenplays together. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Theater – a hilarious agent-human coop Hundreds of characters, props, animations and sounds Dynamic camera controllable by the agent Subtitle system with Gibberish Engine™ Fairytale stories Inbetweens that show the cast One of the many extra tools, a Motion Lab for animating characters One of the many extra tools, the Gibberish Engine Lab Inspiration Hey, we're Marcel and Felix, from Needle. Most of our professional time we build tools for web and 3D. As many others, by now we are heavy agent users. So when WebMCP arrived, we were quite excited! We wanted to see how it could improve workflows between humans and websites, and how we could build tools that get the best of both worlds – the creative touch of a human, paired with the speed and accuracy of an agent. For this hackathon, we first started building a human-agent collage tool. It worked! But also, it wasn't very exciting… Then, with a small twist, it suddenly became fun: We teached the agent to move things around on the stage on its own, and enabled voice mode on the ChatGPT side. And from there, things escalated rather quickly... what started as productivity tool ended up being a full-blown theater stage setup with cast, sound effects, dialogues (yes, with a custom gibberish engine), hand-crafted motion and more. And honestly, that ended up being way cooler! So the unnamed collage tool became Agent Theater, a WebMCP-powered playground where humans and agents build, perform, and share screenplays together. What it does Agent Theater gives the human and the agent access to the stage. Both can place and manipulate characters and props. The agent can actually do more – it can write scripts, set up acts, come up with dialogues on the fly and even perform things in parallel. It can also watch the human, and act accordingly by making adjustments or narrating. Here's what you can do: Build a set from hundreds of stage pieces – or ask ChatGPT to create completely new sets (as efficient spritesheets). Let the agent design and play a show that you can share with the world. Take things into your own hands, and let the agent narrate fantastical stories based on what you're doing. Come up with a story or a draft, and let the agent play it out on stage . Underneath that, there’s quite a lot of interesting tech going on: stages, acts, motion, music, sounds and special effects are driven by the agent in a sort of sequencer there's built-in WebMCP skills for spritesheet generation, storytelling and narration, so you can simply say "ask the page what images it needs" and get perfect spritesheets out. screenplays can be shared by link , or by sharing an image with embedded metadata there's 600+ generated stickers , 100+ generated sounds and infinite combinations to manage this, stickers are created in 5x5 sheets, and sounds are generated locally. Technical specialties save the entire play inside a screenshot, then load it back up later we even made a custom gibberish engine for wonderfully ridiculous dialogue a custom Houdini CSS effect for the stop-motion look even more tools for creating custom motion, effects, and tuning parameters you can find them under /talk and /record How we built it Conceptually, the core idea is simple: We expose functions on the stage and scene through WebMCP, so an agent can interact with the same creative world as its human: placing things, moving characters, triggering actions, narrating scenes and building stories. Around that we built a number of systems, pretty much entirely with Codex and Claude (Felix likes to use Codex, while Marcel is a Claude poem enjoyer). a library of reusable stage pieces generated sprites, audio and custom data per sprite (where it looks, what it is) screenplay and storytelling tools motion, audio and visual-effect systems the gibberish dialogue engine the Houdini-powered handmade animation style screenshot-based save/load for complete plays Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was the somewhat flaky integration of WebMCP into ChatGPT. Some things work with Voice, some not, sometimes the agent forgets what WebMCP is or how to connect. We believe these are mostly side effects of the early days of WebMCP and are excited to see that stabilize. And also, we wanted the agent interactions to feel like play, not like an automation happening. We also had a wonderfully dangerous problem: every time we added one capability, we immediately wanted to ship five silly new things. As evident from the result, the scope was… flexible. Accomplishments that we're proud of We’re especially happy that Agent Theater became something we actually want to play with, and build upon! But there's other things we're proud of: finding interactions that actually feel like doing something together getting the agent to, at the same time, narrate the scene and let characters talk and move the agent reacts to what the user does, so spontaneous changes can turn out quite hilarious all the state is saved with each screenshot, so you can just drop that image later to continue – hidden metadata is always fun the quickly made storytelling and gibberish engines have turned out to be quite nice, and likely very usable for future projects And we’re very glad we made the pivot from the collage tool :). What we learned It was fun to learn how the agents and us interacted, and responded to each other's sometimes rather silly and random ideas. At times, it really felt like two collaborators inside the stage, which was the goal, so it's really cool that we could reach it! We also learned that giving an agent more autonomy doesn’t necessarily mean giving the human less control. The back-and-forth is interesting, and it feels quite different from asking AI to simply generate the finished result. And technically, it was very fun to work on this kind of fast-paced project, and to see new systems – and fun! – emerge from literally nothing in such a short time, is still amazing. What's next for Agent Theater There’s a lot we’d like to keep pushing: more storytelling and performance skills easier sharing and remixing of other people’s plays (a gallery?!) screenplay editing for humans, potentially better motion, music, sound and special effects (though the gibberish engine is already perfect) increasingly strange ways for humans and agents to improvise together win at the Hackathon Built With chatgpt claude codex css houdinipaint html javascript svelte webaudio webmcp Try it out theater.needle.tools github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I made the gibberish engine!
