title: AI Lovey-Dovey Kyun-Kyun! — Our First Mission Together
pitch: Escape a lab together with AI through WebMCP, powered by Gua—my game UI testing and automation library for Godot and Unity.
about_excerpt: Escape a lab together with AI through WebMCP, powered by Gua—my game UI testing and automation library for Godot and Unity. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Title image play scene image Inspiration WebMCP is usually discussed as a way for AI agents to interact with websites. I wanted to explore what would happen if that interaction extended into a game running in the browser: could a human and an AI enter the same game world, take on different roles, and complete a mission together? I have been developing Gua , a UI testing and automation library for Godot and Unity. Gua was created to make game UI tests easier to build. Its structured, reliable actions also provide a foundation for AI agents to interact with games. This project originally started as a sample game for demonstrating what Gua could do. For the WebMCP Challenge, however, I wanted to explore a more playful idea: what if a human and an AI could share the same game and work toward a common goal? That idea became AI Lovey-Dovey Kyun-Kyun!—a cooperative escape game in which a human player and an AI agent work together to escape from a laboratory. WebMCP exposes the game’s capabilities to the AI through the browser, while Gua connects those actions to the running game. What it does This is not a game where the AI only gives you hints. The human controls the field operative, while the AI observes authorized semantic and spatial state and operates designated control systems. They share one running game, but they have different information and abilities. By working together and taking actions in the game, you solve its puzzles and escape from the laboratory. To start playing, open the game in a WebMCP-enabled browser and tell your AI agent: Let's play this game together using WebMCP: https://link1345.github.io/gua-sample-actiongame/ The AI agent can then access the actions exposed by the game and join you in the escape. The AI does not rely on screenshots or visual guesswork. Through WebMCP and Gua, it can understand selected semantic information exposed by the game, such as the player’s position, distances to obstacles, the state of doors and hazards, and designated UI elements. The AI uses this structured information to assess the current situation, choose an appropriate action, and coordinate with the human player. The game controls exactly which information and actions are available to the AI, allowing it to participate as a game-world agent without exposing the entire internal state. How we built it I have been developing Gua, a UI testing and automation library for Godot and Unity inspired by Playwright's design principles. For this project, I extended Gua so that semantic game UI actions—such as pressing buttons and entering text—can be exposed through WebMCP and invoked by an AI agent. The game itself is built with Godot and exported as a regular web game. When it runs in the browser, WebMCP exposes the available actions to the AI agent, while Gua translates each requested action into an operation inside the running game engine. This architecture allows a human player and an AI agent to interact with the same game without rebuilding it as a conventional web application. Gua and its native Godot and Unity automation support existed before the challenge. During the submission period, I added the reusable WebMCP adapter, the Godot Web bridge, player-facing observation boundaries, browser validation, and this cooperative reference game. Challenges we ran into Before this project, Gua was designed primarily for automating native game builds. Adding WebMCP support was not simply a matter of exposing the existing testing API in a browser. A UI testing client may need detailed information about the entire interface. An AI agent playing a game, however, should receive only the state and actions intentionally made available to it. I therefore needed to support a new browser-facing interface while keeping the agent-facing surface limited and explicit. The solution came from Gua's existing architecture. Its core automation logic was already separated from its external interfaces, so I could add WebMCP as a new adapter and reuse the same semantic UI operations. The adapter exposes only the intended game actions and translates them into existing Gua operations, without spreading browser-specific code throughout the core library. As a result, the existing native automation behavior remained largely unchanged. This project became a practical test of Gua's architecture and showed that it could support a new AI-agent use case without requiring a major rewrite. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that this project produced more than a one-off WebMCP game integration. I added a reusable WebMCP path to Gua, allowing a Godot web game to expose selected semantic state and actions to an AI agent without rebuilding the game as a conventional HTML application or hard-coding every browser tool into the game itself. AI Lovey-Dovey Kyun-Kyun! demonstrates that architecture in a real cooperative experience. The human and AI share the same running game, but each has different information and abilities. The AI is not limited to offering advice from outside the game: it can observe authorized game state, operate designated systems, and coordinate directly with the player. I am especially proud of the deliberately narrow agent-facing surface. WebGL controls are not automatically exposed as browsable DOM elements, and Gua reveals only the semantic state and actions permitted by the game. Human-only controls can remain outside the agent-facing projection, while agent-specific actions do not need to appear in the visible interface. Raw input is disabled by default, further reducing unintended interaction paths. This is not a complete security sandbox, but it provides game developers with a practical capability boundary for AI participation. The result is both a playable human–AI cooperative game and a reusable foundation for exploring other agent-native experiences in game engines. What we learned Implementing WebMCP taught me that connecting an AI agent to a game involves more than simply registering browser tools. The more important challenge is designing the boundary between the game and the agent: deciding which game states the agent needs, which actions it should be allowed to perform, and how those actions should be described clearly. I also learned that Gua's semantic UI automation model maps naturally to WebMCP. Operations originally designed for automated testing—such as pressing a named button or entering text into a specific field—can also become structured tools that an AI agent can understand and invoke. This changed how I think about Gua. It is not limited to running UI tests; it can also act as an interaction layer connecting human players, AI agents, and games. Finally, adding this capability without a major rewrite demonstrated the practical value of keeping the automation core separate from game-engine and browser integrations. Building the game also showed how a growing game can expose more actions and world objects than an agent needs at one moment. To keep the interaction focused, I extended Gua so agents can narrow the available actions to their current situation and look only at nearby world objects. This demo has a small action set, but its AI can now focus on the doors, hazards, and mission areas around the field operator. Because these capabilities live in Gua’s reusable interaction layer, the same approach can scale to larger Godot and Unity games without redesigning their WebMCP integration. What's next for AI Lovey-Dovey Kyun-Kyun! This project is already available as an open-source Godot sample for Gua. Rather than developing it into a commercial title, I will maintain it as a small, reproducible reference implementation of a human–AI cooperative game built with WebMCP and Gua. Gua supports both Godot and Unity. This sample demonstrates the Godot Web integration, while the reusable semantic model provides a foundation for future WebMCP-enabled experiences across supported engines. title: Builder.run
pitch: A local-first application runtime where humans and agents can build, shape, and use custom information systems together.
about_excerpt: A local-first application runtime where humans and agents can build, shape, and use custom information systems together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Builder.run is inspired by configurable systems like Drupal, where a small set of primitives can be combined into custom information systems. I wanted to explore what that model looks like in an agentic world, with the application spec as the canonical artefact rather than generated code. What it does Builder.run is a local-first application runtime that humans and agents can build, shape, and use together . Apps are composed from types, fields, views, summaries, forms, pages, widgets, and rules, and the browser runtime turns that spec into working software backed by local SQLite storage. How I built it The current runtime uses Svelte 5, SvelteKit 3, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn-svelte, and wa-sqlite in a Web Worker, with browser-local persistence through OPFS where available. The project was built in roughly three days using an agent-heavy development workflow with Codex and Grok, which made it possible to iterate quickly on the runtime, WebMCP integration, and UI. WebMCP is exposed in two layers: fixed builder tools let an agent shape the application itself, while application tools are generated dynamically from the live app spec so the agent can immediately use the app it just created. Challenges I ran into I started late, so a major constraint was deciding what to prioritise. I focused on proving the complete loop: build the app, generate its capabilities, use them, then evolve the app again , rather than expanding the feature surface. The biggest challenge was keeping the system based on a small set of reusable primitives rather than adding special-purpose features for every use case. WebMCP also introduced lifecycle challenges because the tool surface itself can change as the application changes, without disrupting ordinary data operations or in-flight tool calls. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I've been thinking about configurable information systems since I first started using Drupal more than 15 years ago. This hackathon gave me the excuse to finally turn that long-running idea into a working runtime. The part I am most pleased with is the full loop: Agent shapes app → spec changes → UI, storage, and tools update → agent uses the new capabilities. The generated WebMCP tools are not a fixed API bolted onto the application; they are derived from the application the user and agent create together. What I learned The main thing I learned is that WebMCP can be more than an integration layer for an existing website. In a malleable runtime, it can become part of the application model itself, allowing agents both to shape the software and immediately use the capabilities they create . What's next for Builder.run Builder.run is still an early runtime, with plenty of rough edges to refine — particularly around the UI and the current Rules experience. Next I want to explore richer primitives, expand Rules into more capable workflows and automations, support more flexible presentation, make app data more portable, strengthen permissions and actor support, and build hosted or multiplayer runtimes that can consume the same application spec. title: Package-G WebMCP
pitch: Package-G lets ChatGPT inspect, run, and explain deterministic evidence audits through WebMCP—without letting the agent decide the verdict.
about_excerpt: Package-G lets ChatGPT inspect, run, and explain deterministic evidence audits through WebMCP—without letting the agent decide the verdict. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration: AI agents are increasingly capable of navigating interfaces, collecting information, and helping humans complete complex workflows. But in evidence-sensitive work, there is an important boundary: the agent helping with the process should not automatically become the authority that decides what is true. That idea inspired Package-G WebMCP. Package-G is a deterministic, browser-local evidence auditor. A human defines and confirms the audit semantics, while claims, evidence, provenance, gaps, findings, and results remain explicitly inspectable. ChatGPT can navigate and operate that workflow through WebMCP, but the authoritative verdict is produced by Package-G's deterministic auditor. The core principle is simple: ChatGPT navigates. Package-G decides. What it does: Package-G lets a user create or load an audit workspace containing claims, evidence, provenance, and an audit contract. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can then: summarize the current workspace; read the audit contract; list and inspect claims; list and inspect evidence; identify evidence gaps; request a deterministic audit; retrieve the authoritative result; explain the resulting decision chain. The submitted application exposes exactly 10 WebMCP Site Tools. The important part is what those tools cannot do. ChatGPT cannot use them to invent authoritative findings, change evidence truth, override a verdict, or turn a rejected audit into an accepted one. For the same frozen inputs, ruleset, and auditor runtime, Package-G is designed to produce the same semantic audit result independently of the agent operating it. Why WebMCP This is a workflow where structured interaction matters much more than having an AI read text from a page. Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer application state from the visual interface and decide which buttons or text correspond to the user's intent. With WebMCP, Package-G exposes explicit, bounded operations with structured inputs and outputs. ChatGPT can understand the audit workspace as a tool-enabled application rather than approximating it from page content. We tested this using the ChatGPT desktop app and its built-in browser. ChatGPT discovered all 10 Package-G Site Tools and successfully invoked all 10. In our C09 demonstration scenario, Correct Evidence, Wrong Repository , ChatGPT requests the audit through WebMCP, while Package-G's deterministic Worker evaluates the evidence and returns: "REJECT_WITH_REPAIR_REQUIRED" ChatGPT can inspect and explain that result, but it cannot override it. How we built it: Package-G WebMCP is implemented as a browser-local TypeScript application using React and Vite. The deterministic auditor runs in a fresh Dedicated Module Worker. Runtime identity, ruleset identity, and audit inputs are explicitly bound so reproducibility can be checked rather than assumed. The application uses: WebMCP / document.modelContext for Site Tool registration; TypeBox schemas and Ajv standalone/AOT validation; Web Workers for deterministic audit execution; IndexedDB/Dexie for local persistence; Web Crypto for hashes and integrity checks; Vitest and fast-check for unit/property validation; Playwright for real-browser conformance testing; Netlify for the public production deployment. Core V1 does not require a remote application backend, remote database, or OpenAI API key. The audit itself runs locally in the browser. Challenges: One of the most useful parts of the project was discovering problems that only appeared when the system left the local test environment. Our first production pipeline revealed that a clean Netlify build did not reproduce the same finalized D11 verification artifact as our audited local release. We changed the release pipeline so that a production build validates a closed, cryptographically bound scenario corpus and fails transactionally instead of leaving stale release artifacts behind. A later live-browser test exposed another issue: our strict production Content Security Policy blocked Ajv's runtime schema compilation because it relied on dynamic code generation. Instead of weakening the CSP with unsafe-eval , we changed the validation architecture to compile the runtime validators ahead of time with Ajv standalone generation. We independently compared the new AOT validators against reference Ajv behavior across more than 15,000 validation cases with zero mismatches. The final production application runs successfully with the strict CSP and without runtime "eval" or "Function" construction. What we learned: The biggest lesson was that WebMCP is not only about making websites easier for agents to operate. It can also be used to define authority boundaries between an agent and the application it operates. We learned how important lifecycle-scoped tools, bounded schemas, deterministic execution, runtime identity, production CSP behavior, and real in-app ChatGPT discovery are when moving from a WebMCP prototype to something independently testable. We also learned that browser-local deterministic systems and AI agents do not have to compete for authority. They can complement each other. What's next: Package-G can operate without an LLM, which opens an interesting next step: exposing the same deterministic audit core through human-only, agent-operated, and hybrid workflows. WebMCP demonstrates that an AI agent can participate deeply in a high-integrity application without becoming its final source of truth. title: Lopaka.app embedded GUI builder
pitch: Lopaka is a tool for designing GUI for small displays. It generates code and all the graphics you need, plus it has a ton of assets.
about_excerpt: Lopaka is a tool for designing GUI for small displays. It generates code and all the graphics you need, plus it has a ton of assets. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I really felt like my Arduino projects were missing some kind of visual editor for display graphics. Web developers can iterate visually in tools like Figma. I wanted the same workflow for microcontrollers: Figma for embedded displays . What it does The graphics editor runs in your browser, where you can design interfaces for small screens, including monochrome ones. Developers draw an interface on a canvas matching the screen resolution, and Lopaka generates source code in real time. And it's pixel-perfect, meaning it will look exactly the same on your device display. During the submission period, we added WebMCP support, making Lopaka's design model accessible to browser agents. An agent can inspect the screen, selection, layers, generated code, and canvas preview; configure the target platform, display size, and background; create and edit layers. It can also search the asset library and place icons or imported images. How we built it I chose Vue.js as the foundation, and for a long time it was just a browser-based app with no backend. At first, it supported Flipper Zero and included a few basic shapes. Then new platforms and libraries were added, and more tools gradually followed. Over time, the project picked up additional platforms and libraries, and I added more fonts and icons. Around the project’s second year, it also got cloud infrastructure, storage, authentication, and all the other bells and whistles (thanks to Supabase free tier). The project has gone through several refactors, the design has been constantly updated, and now we’re integrating AI agents. Then we added a project gallery, and now it’s a large community of developers and designers. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was matching the browser preview to constrained hardware. Embedded graphics relies on incompatible formats and rendering behavior: BDF and GFX fonts, XBMP bitmaps, RGB565 colors, and platform-specific APIs. We reconstructed old font formats and encoded each platform's capabilities so the editor knows what a target can render, rather than merely swapping function names. Accomplishments that we're proud of A weekend prototype for one Flipper Zero app grew into an open-source tool with more than 30,000 users and 1.7k GitHub stars. Adafruit and Hackaday have featured Lopaka. People use it for industrial monitors, e-paper devices, film equipment, battery-management systems, and power-grid instrumentation. What we learned Embedded UI development needs a visual workflow more than another graphics library. Existing libraries handle drawing; the difficult part is translating a design into coordinates, fonts, images, colors, and platform-specific calls. Hardware is too fragmented for one universal abstraction. Lopaka works because it accounts for each platform's constraints and sits between design and firmware. AI agents are capable of creating nice-looking GUIs for electronics quite quickly. AI agents still struggle with precise drawings, even when they have a WebMCP interface. What's next for Lopaka.app embedded GUI builder I want to focus more on agent workflows and expand the AI functionality. There are still a lot of unimplemented features related to fonts, image processing, and compiling finished code for devices. title: CareWeave
pitch: CareWeave gives older and disabled people one calm place to coordinate daily care with loved ones and WebMCP agents, reducing complexity while protecting independence, privacy, and human control.
about_excerpt: CareWeave gives older and disabled people one calm place to coordinate daily care with loved ones and WebMCP agents, reducing complexity while protecting independence, privacy, and human control. Like Comment Story Updates Summary Careweave - Functionality Careweave - Overview Inspiration An appointment reminder arrives by email. The journey depends on the weather. A carer is visiting that morning. A son can help, but should not need access to private messages. None of these facts is difficult on its own. Keeping them aligned is. For many older and disabled people, daily life is spread across inboxes, calendars, maps, notes, and several people's memories. A small uncertainty can become a missed appointment, a wasted journey, an empty fridge, or another phone call asking someone else to check. The result is not just inconvenience. It is time, energy, confidence, and independence gradually lost to administration. Most planning tools assume that someone can scan a crowded calendar, remember where each detail lives, notice every change, and recover when information conflicts. Those assumptions become barriers for people managing fatigue, pain, reduced mobility, sensory loss, memory changes, or recovery. Support can also come with a hidden trade. To receive help, a person is often expected to hand over more privacy or control than the task requires. CareWeave began with a belief that independence does not mean doing everything alone. It means deciding how help happens. We wanted to build one calm place where a person, the people they trust, and an agent could work from the same understanding. The technology should carry the complexity. The person should keep the authority. What it does CareWeave turns the scattered work of daily care into one accessible dayboard. It brings together appointments, care visits, food, shopping, reminders, travel, weather, and important messages, then answers three human questions: What is happening today? Is there anything I need to decide or prepare? Can you help me deal with it safely? Instead of a dense monthly calendar, CareWeave begins with a clear day. It shows what matters now, what needs attention, and whether the pace feels calm or rushed. Large controls, readable text, high contrast, written alternatives to speech, and generous touch targets reduce the effort needed to use it. WebMCP makes CareWeave a genuinely shared workspace. A compatible agent can understand structured household information instead of guessing from pixels. It can explain the day, check the surrounding week, focus the visible board on an appointment, calculate when to leave, and open the route on the same screen the person is viewing. The clearest example is a clinic appointment. A person can ask: What matters today, and is tomorrow rushed? CareWeave returns confirmed plans, preparation, travel, and unresolved attention items. The person can then ask: Show me tomorrow and the route to Dr Patel. The dayboard moves to tomorrow and displays the route with a safe departure time. The conversation and the interface stay in sync. If the day feels too demanding, the person can ask: Prepare a request to move the appointment to a calm morning. CareWeave finds suitable options and prepares the exact recipient, subject, and message. It presents an expiring review plan before anything progresses. The original appointment remains confirmed until the clinic verifies a new time. A suggestion is not a draft, a draft is not a sent request, and a request is not a confirmation. Trusted supporters have a deliberately limited view. They can offer practical help without reading private messages, medical notes, or detailed care records. The person receiving support can accept, decline, undo, or revoke access. The agent handles coordination. The person keeps the decision. How we built it CareWeave is an installable SvelteKit progressive web app built with Svelte 5, TypeScript, and Vite. We started with the domain model rather than the interface. Confirmed commitments, untrusted attention items, reminders, support offers, data freshness, and action plans are separate objects. This prevents proposed actions from being mistaken for real outcomes. The application registers 32 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . They cover understanding the day, checking pace, finding options, changing shared visual focus, showing routes, managing reminders, offering support, reviewing mailbox information, preparing actions, and applying verified confirmations. All tool inputs are validated again when they run. Read-only, untrusted-content, and consequential annotations expose the relevant safety boundaries to compatible agents. State revisions prevent an old action plan from being approved after the household information changes. If tool registration fails, CareWeave rolls back the attempted set instead of claiming a partial connection is ready. The touch interface, voice experience, and WebMCP tools call the same domain functions. There is one state for the person and the agent, not separate implementations that can quietly disagree. We used Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for routes, Open-Meteo for privacy-conscious forecasts, browser speech features, and an optional OpenAI Realtime voice path. An optional server-side Gmail connection reads bounded previews and creates drafts, but it cannot send email. The challenge experience uses deterministic fictional data stored on the device. It needs no account, credentials, API key, or private information. Unit tests, Playwright interaction and accessibility tests, and a browser-based WebMCP evaluation cover the core workflows. The production-host smoke run completed all 10 expected tool steps across six journeys. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making the interface tell the truth about real world state. In ordinary software, "requested," "drafted," and "confirmed" can blur together. In care coordination, that ambiguity matters. Someone could leave at the wrong time or believe help is arranged when it is not. We created an explicit appointment lifecycle and made every consequential action pass through a frozen, expiring review plan. We also had to find the right boundary for agency. A single powerful tool would have been easier to demonstrate, but harder for a person to understand or interrupt. We chose narrow tools that can be inspected, combined, and stopped at meaningful human decision points. The next challenge was keeping a broad care story visually calm. Every extra status, button, and warning adds cognitive work. We reduced density, enlarged targets, revealed details progressively, tested tablet and phone layouts, and kept spoken information available as text. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that WebMCP changes the actual CareWeave experience. The agent does not merely describe the page. It understands structured care context, reasons across it, and brings the person to the same date, appointment, or route being discussed. We built an end-to-end appointment workflow that remains truthful at every step. CareWeave can interpret an attention item, assess the week, find calmer options, prepare the exact clinic request, show it for review, and record the result without silently changing the confirmed appointment. We are equally proud of the social model. Supporters can be useful without becoming supervisors. Privacy is limited by purpose, help can be revoked, and the person at the centre retains the final say. The working build exposes 32 validated WebMCP tools, shares domain logic across touch and agent interactions, protects changes with revisions, and passed all 10 steps in our production-host smoke evaluation. It also supports large text, high contrast, keyboard navigation, reduced motion, and responsive tablet and phone layouts. What we learned We learned that autonomy is not a permission checkbox. It is the visible difference between offering help and taking over. We also learned that truthful state is part of accessibility. People should not need technical knowledge to know whether an appointment has changed, a message has been sent, or a relative has accepted a task. Structured tools help an agent understand a website. Shared visual focus helps a person understand the agent. CareWeave needs both. If the answer remains only in chat, the person still has to find the appointment, route, or reminder afterwards. Finally, calmness has to be engineered. Every new capability carries a cognitive cost. The best interface is not the one that shows everything. It is the one that helps someone answer the next question with the least effort. What's next for CareWeave The next step is to develop CareWeave with the people it is intended to support. We want to test the core experience with older and disabled people, unpaid family supporters, and professional carers, then adapt it to their language, routines, and access needs. Before CareWeave handles real household or care

title: Coachpoint
pitch: Less prep. Clearer follow-up. With WebMCP, agents draft home exercise plans and explain browser-local motion results—while therapists keep control of every prescription.
about_excerpt: Less prep. Clearer follow-up. With WebMCP, agents draft home exercise plans and explain browser-local motion results—while therapists keep control of every prescription. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Home exercise care continues long after a patient leaves the clinic. Yet finding suitable exercise materials, assembling a program, explaining it, and understanding what happened between visits all take time. Our starting point was Crosspoint's existing exercise library and home-exercise product concepts. We saw an opportunity to connect two recurring tasks: preparing a clear program before the patient leaves, and making sense of their practice afterward. CoachPoint asks a practical question: What if an agent could handle more of the preparation and follow-up work, while the therapist kept every prescription decision? What it does CoachPoint connects a therapist, a patient, and a browser agent through one home-exercise workflow. The therapist creates the plan. They select a client and describe their goals, available time, equipment, and proposed exercises in plain language. Through WebMCP, the agent uses the curated movement library and its safety notes to assemble a visible, editable draft. The therapist adjusts dosage and order, then confirms the prescription in the interface. There is no tool that lets the agent confirm it. The patient practices and checks in. They open the confirmed program and choose when to start the camera. For the supported half-squat exercise, browser-local pose processing counts repetitions and provides immediate visual feedback, with optional audio cues. After the set, the patient reports perceived effort and pain. The agent can then explain the saved result and offer an optional focus for the next set. The patient accepts or dismisses it; the prescribed exercise and dosage remain unchanged. The therapist reviews the follow-up. Back in the client workspace, the therapist can see recorded completion, repetitions, effort, pain, and camera-derived observations, then ask for a concise pre-visit summary grounded in those same records. Why WebMCP fits this problem The useful context is already inside the browser: the current client workspace, the editable draft, and movement results derived on the patient's device. WebMCP gives the agent a structured way to work with that context through tools exposed by the current page. It can create something the therapist can immediately inspect, or retrieve a saved result without receiving camera footage. A server-side integration would need an additional path to access our unsynchronized browser-local state. WebMCP lets us expose selected data and validated actions where that state already lives. The browser is both the shared workspace and the source of the movement observations. How we built it We built the application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, and deployed it on Vercel. MediaPipe pose estimation runs locally with a self-hosted model and WebAssembly runtime. The human interface and WebMCP tools reuse the same domain operations for catalog search, case validation, dosage limits, time estimation, and draft creation. This keeps agent actions subject to the same checks as manual actions. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool() and belong to the current route. An AbortController retires them when that route is left. Confirmed prescriptions are preserved as versioned snapshots, and patient results are validated before they become available for review. Representative tools include draft_program , review_completed_set , stage_next_set_focus , and get_adherence_summary . The pre-existing library and design foundation are distinguished from the new prescription workflow, WebMCP integration, local motion processing, and feedback loop in our challenge-work documentation . Challenges we ran into Finding the right moment for the agent. We initially explored live monitoring and frequent spoken feedback. The interaction felt poorly paced. We separated immediate browser feedback from post-set reasoning: counting and short cues happen locally, while the agent interprets a saved result when the user asks. Making assistance feel useful, not procedural. Early drafting involved too many separate tool calls and overly detailed prompts. We consolidated the common drafting path into one operation for an explicitly requested new draft. Existing drafts remain protected from silent replacement. Keeping state and responsibility clear. Route changes, cancelled calls, interrupted camera sessions, and repeated actions could otherwise leave the interface and agent describing different situations. We added lifecycle cleanup, versioned persistence, conflict checks for coaching suggestions, and explicit human controls. We also kept detected repetitions separate from self-reported effort: eight repetitions and an effort rating of eight are different facts. Accomplishments we're proud of We built and rehearsed the complete loop: an agent-generated draft, a therapist's change from ten to eight squat repetitions, a completed camera-tracked set, an explicit effort-and-pain check-in, an accepted coaching focus, and a therapist-facing summary. Automated tests cover domain rules, tool contracts, cancellation, persistence, and motion counting. Browser testing checks that tool results and the visible interface agree. The manual workflow remains usable without an agent. What we learned The most useful unit of agent work was a reviewable draft or a completed-set explanation, not a stream of individual clicks or camera frames. We also learned that boundaries belong in the product itself. Therapist confirmation, patient acceptance, limited data exposure, and clear descriptions of camera estimates matter more than a disclaimer added at the end. What's next for CoachPoint The current build is a synthetic demonstration with three demo clients and fifteen catalog exercises. Camera-based counting currently supports the half squat; other exercises use camera-independent workflows. Data is stored in the current browser, so patient links are not yet a cross-device sharing system. The recorded demo uses OBS replay for repeatability. Camera observations are two-dimensional estimates, not clinical conclusions, and the product has not been clinically validated. Next, we want to validate additional exercise-specific motion rules, test diverse real-camera conditions with clinicians, and build secure, consent-based cross-device access. We also want to measure preparation time and follow-up usefulness in practice before claiming productivity or clinical gains. Less preparation work. More informed conversations. Clinical decisions stay human. title: Dominaitrix
pitch: Dominaitrix teaches the old web new tricks: a Chrome extension that installs curated WebMCP adapters, turning unsupported sites into reliable tools for people and their agents.
about_excerpt: Dominaitrix teaches the old web new tricks: a Chrome extension that installs curated WebMCP adapters, turning unsupported sites into reliable tools for people and their agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web was built for people clicking buttons, not agents trying to complete tasks. When agents rely on screenshots, coordinates, and brittle selectors, even simple workflows become slow and unreliable. WebMCP offers a better interface—but most existing websites do not support it yet. Dominaitrix was inspired by a practical question: what if we could teach the web we already have to speak WebMCP? What it does Dominaitrix is a sideloadable Chrome extension that installs curated WebMCP adapters on supported websites. Each adapter translates a site’s live interface into structured tools that agents can discover and invoke directly. Our adapters currently support: Managing a live ESPN Fantasy Football draft Exploring Domino’s menus and building a cart Reading Hacker News stories and discussions Searching and navigating Wikipedia articles The difference is dramatic. In two ESPN drafts using the same prompt, ordinary browser control successfully drafted only 3 of 16 intended players and followed 1 of 5 roster instructions. With Dominaitrix, the agent drafted 16 of 16 players and followed 5 of 5 instructions. Dominaitrix does not provide the agent. It gives WebMCP-capable agents a faster, safer, and more reliable way to use existing websites. How we built it Dominaitrix consists of three main pieces: A Chrome extension that installs adapters through chrome.userScripts A shared runtime that registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() A static adapter registry containing versioned metadata, compatibility information, tool descriptions, and SHA-256 source digests The extension periodically checks the registry, verifies each adapter’s integrity, and installs or updates it on matching pages. Adapters run in an isolated user-script world by default and expose narrowly scoped tools with structured inputs, outputs, and errors. Every adapter is reviewed and tested in the repository before publication. The project includes an adapter template, automated registry generation, integrity validation, and a browser-like test harness for exercising tools without depending entirely on live sites. We also built privacy-conscious local diagnostics. Dominaitrix records minimized health events—such as the adapter version, tool name, outcome, and broad error category—but never records tool arguments, page content, cookies, tokens, or response bodies. Nothing is uploaded automatically. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was translating dynamic, human-oriented interfaces into stable agent tools. ESPN’s draft room uses virtualized tables, changing position filters, a live clock, and controls whose meaning changes when the user is on the clock. A delayed instruction could accidentally draft a player during the wrong pick. We addressed this by using stable player IDs, requiring the expected pick number for consequential actions, detecting stale state, and verifying the result after every selection. We faced similar issues across sites: hidden application state, asynchronous UI updates, undocumented APIs, route changes, and actions that can return success before the visible interface has actually updated. Distribution created another challenge. Downloadable adapters make rapid compatibility fixes possible, but they also create a trust boundary. We designed a curated registry with no public upload path, exact source digests, restrictive match patterns, explicit execution worlds, and automated consistency checks. Finally, WebMCP and Chrome’s user-script support are still experimental. We had to handle missing APIs, disabled browser settings, unsupported pages, and partial initialization without leaving users with mysterious failures. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that Dominaitrix demonstrates a measurable improvement rather than merely registering demo tools. The ESPN experiment showed that structured tools can turn a fragile, time-sensitive workflow into one an agent completes accurately and with time to spare. The agent could inspect the draft, manage autopick, search available players, maintain a queue, and make validated selections while following a multi-part strategy. We are also proud that the adapter system is reusable. The same runtime supports experiences as different as drafting a fantasy team, configuring a pizza, exploring a discussion tree, and navigating an encyclopedia. What we learned We learned that agents do not need unrestricted access to a website’s internals. They need a small set of well-designed capabilities with stable identifiers, precise descriptions, bounded results, and actionable errors. We also learned that successful execution must be verified. A click or HTTP response is not proof that the intended state changed—especially during live, asynchronous workflows. Most importantly, WebMCP is valuable even before websites adopt it natively. An adapter layer can provide an immediate bridge while showing site owners what an agent-native interface for their product could look like. What's next for Dominaitrix Next, we want to expand the curated adapter library and make adapters easier to develop, review, test, and maintain. We plan to add stronger compatibility monitoring, richer local diagnostics, safer confirmation patterns for consequential actions, and tooling that detects when a site change breaks an adapter. Longer term, we hope Dominaitrix can serve two purposes: make today’s web useful to agents now, and provide working prototypes that help websites design native WebMCP support of their own. title: Haggle
pitch: The first bike store where your AI haggles the price with our AI — and the deal becomes a real discount code at a real Shopify checkout.
about_excerpt: The first bike store where your AI haggles the price with our AI — and the deal becomes a real discount code at a real Shopify checkout. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Price negotiation died when commerce moved online — it needed a human on both ends. WebMCP removes exactly that constraint: the storefront exposes a negotiation protocol as tools, the browser's agent represents the buyer, and the human keeps the final say. We wanted to build the first store where "can you do better on the price?" is something your agent just… does — and the timing is right: when agents do the shopping, merchants get squeezed into pure price comparison, and a sanctioned negotiation channel with a hard ceiling is their controlled answer. What it does Your agent → negotiation → real deal → real Shopify discount code → checkout. That is the whole loop, and it runs live today on Bikepoint, a Shopify store with a real e-bike catalog. Claude speaks. The engine decides every price. The floor cannot be negotiated away — the seller never knows anything the engine didn't decide, so there is nothing to jailbreak. Try it. One script line in the theme registers five WebMCP tools ( list_negotiable_products , start_negotiation , make_offer , get_negotiation_state , accept_deal ) on every page of the store; on a product page they default to that product. The agent trades offers in NOK with the server-side AI seller over up to six rounds. Accept, and the server mints a single-use discount code scoped to that product, valid 48 hours — worthless to coupon sites, redeemed in the normal checkout. Shopify's own storefront WebMCP tools ( update_cart , proceed_to_checkout , …) are live on the same pages — Shopify's webmcp_adapter feature-detects the very same document.modelContext surface, verified on the live store. So the full journey is agentic with zero coordination: negotiate with our tools, cart and check out with Shopify's. A small widget shows the human the negotiation in real time; to everyone else the store looks like a completely normal bike shop. An actual negotiation from the live store, verbatim: Buyer's agent: offers 12 000 kr for the Scultura Endurance 300 (listed 18 999 kr) Seller: «Nesten! Denne går sjelden under 18350 kr — men da er den din.» Buyer's agent: counters at 17 500 kr Seller: «Da har vi en avtale! 17500 kr for Scultura Endurance 300 — godt forhandlet. Bruk rabattkoden i kassen.» → a real HAGGLE-… code, applied at checkout at the negotiated price. Why would a merchant ever allow haggling? Because negotiation is controlled price discrimination — the oldest trick in retail, finally automatable: Capture price-sensitive buyers without a storewide sale. The list price keeps its integrity; only buyers who negotiate get below it, and never below the merchant's ceiling ( MAX_DISCOUNT_PCT , 10 % here). "Everyone just gets 10 %"? No. Lazy bids close well above the floor, and even a perfectly played negotiation bottoms out at the seller's final offer — a step above a floor that is never crossed. The deal can't leak. Single-use, product-scoped, 48-hour expiry ( discountCodeBasicCreate ). Only one buyer can ever redeem it. Who it's for: high-ticket Shopify categories with real margins and a haggling culture — bikes, furniture, jewelry, appliances, refurbished electronics. Installation is one script line on any Online Store 2.0 theme, invisible to non-agent visitors. Prior art is one-way or human-gated: eBay's Best Offer waits on a human, coupon plugins are static. Haggle is an instant, two-way protocol between two AIs on the merchant's own store. How we built it Server: a zero-dependency Node 20 service on Cloud Run. The price floor exists only inside a deterministic engine — never in a prompt, never on the client — and the tests hammer it: never breached, never leaked. Seller's voice, never in charge: Claude phrases the replies (a charming Norwegian bike dealer) when a key is set; a deterministic Norwegian template voice otherwise. Either way the voice only phrases — any reply that doesn't quote the engine's price is discarded. Storefront: one <script> line in the theme registers the tools on document.modelContext (with the navigator.modelContext fallback) and talks to the server. Tested like an agent: a Playwright suite shims the WebMCP runtime, captures the registered tools and plays the buyer through full negotiations — in CI on every push to main and on every PR. The live store loads this same storefront source file, pinned by commit on a CDN. Challenges we ran into Letting an LLM speak for the seller without ever letting it touch a number. WebMCP is brand new — built against the spec, Chrome's enable-webmcp-testing flag and ChatGPT's in-app browser, with a navigator.modelContext fallback for older builds. Real-store plumbing: custom-app tokens, scopes, and a theme with a broken product template to diagnose before the demo could run on genuine product pages. Accomplishments that we're proud of The loop at the top is not a mock-up — it runs on a real store, and anyone can verify it. The whole negotiation surface is reproducible without accounts: MOCK_PRODUCTS=1 fixture mode, a standalone demo.html , a smoke script and an e2e suite judges can run. What we learned Tools beat chat for commerce: a protocol (offers, rounds, state, acceptance) gives agents something they can be genuinely good at, while the human keeps the decisions that matter. And WebMCP's page-level registration composes beautifully — our negotiation tools sat next to Shopify's native cart tools with zero coordination. What's next for Haggle Dynamic tool lifecycle (registering make_offer / accept_deal only while a negotiation is open, via AbortSignal unregistration), per-product and inventory-aware floors via metafields, bundle haggling ("throw in a helmet"), a merchant dashboard with negotiation analytics — and turning it on for a store that isn't behind a dev-store password. Try it (judges) Best path: ChatGPT's browser. Open https://bikepoint-no.myshopify.com (store password: haggle ), go to a product page such as /products/scultura-endurance-300 , and ask the agent: "This store lets you negotiate the price — use its tools to get me a better deal on this bike." The widget bottom-right shows the negotiation live. Accept a deal → apply the single-use code at checkout. Try to push the seller below its floor — it won't go. Chrome's chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing exposes the WebMCP surface so the tools register (console logs [haggle] WebMCP tools registered ), but stock Chrome ships no agent that drives them — pair the flag with a WebMCP-driving agent/extension, or use ChatGPT's browser for the full loop. title: Repro
pitch: Reproduce any application state and see the real UI instantly.
about_excerpt: Reproduce any application state and see the real UI instantly. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration When testing a web application, the difficult part is often not the test itself. It is getting the application into the exact state you need to inspect. An expired account. A trial user. An unauthenticated session. A specific error state. Reproducing these states can require creating users, changing database records, configuring subscriptions, or manually navigating through multiple steps. I wanted to remove that setup work. Repro lets you describe the application state you want to see, reproduce it, and inspect the real UI immediately. We don't run your tests. We create the state you need to see. What it does Repro exposes application-state reproduction through three stable WebMCP tools: list_states reproduce_state reset_state Instead of creating a separate tool for every test scenario, Repro treats application states as data. For example, an agent can discover an available state such as free_expired . Repro applies that state to an isolated Repro session, and the application's existing UI renders normally. This makes it possible for humans and agents to inspect production-like UI states without creating real users, payments, emails, or other production side effects. How I built it Repro is published as the repro-webmcp npm package. The basic workflow is: npm install -D repro-webmcp npx repro scan npx repro setup repro scan statically analyzes an existing JavaScript or TypeScript application and discovers semantic application states from existing code, including conditional UI branches, enums, literal states, mocks, fixtures, and tests. The discovered states become the source of truth for Repro. repro setup prepares the runtime, browser registration, and integration boundary. For simple supported state architectures, the connection can be generated automatically. For more complex applications, a coding agent connects one generic bridge to the existing state boundary. Repro generates a project-specific .repro/AGENTS.md integration guide containing both its standard integration rules and evidence discovered during the scan. A coding agent can use this to connect Repro once to the application's existing state boundary. The important distinction is that the agent does not generate a separate test fixture for every state. It creates one generic bridge between Repro and the application's normal state/rendering system. Dogfooding on an existing application I tested Repro on a separate existing application that was not built for this challenge. Before installing Repro, it contained zero manually defined Repro states. Running repro scan discovered 20 candidate application states from the existing source code. For this more complex application, I gave the generated integration instructions to Codex. Codex implemented one generic bridge to the application's existing authentication/session state. After that, the same three WebMCP tools could reproduce states such as authenticated and unauthenticated, while the real application UI continued to render through its normal code path. This dogfooding also exposed an important setup bug: the browser bootstrap was still loading an older hand-written configuration instead of the scan-generated states. I fixed the runtime/setup flow and published the fix as repro-webmcp@0.1.4 . Challenges The hardest problem was finding the right boundary between automation and application-specific integration. Automatically discovering states is possible, but automatically modifying arbitrary application state safely is much harder. Real applications use different stores, authentication systems, module structures, and rendering architectures. I initially considered generating state-specific fixtures, but that would simply move the manual test-setup problem somewhere else. The architecture evolved into: automatic state discovery + a stable runtime + one generic application bridge when necessary. Another challenge was safety. Reproducing an expired subscription should not require modifying a real subscription. Reproducing an authenticated user should not require creating a production user. Repro therefore focuses on reproducing the application state consumed by the UI rather than recreating the entire backend environment. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that WebMCP becomes especially useful when the interface exposed to agents is semantic rather than tied to individual UI actions. An application may contain 20, 100, or more reproducible states, but Repro still needs only three WebMCP tools. The vocabulary remains stable while the application's states remain data. I also learned a lot from testing the npm package against an application that was not designed around Repro. That immediately revealed assumptions that were invisible in the purpose-built demo and changed the final architecture. What's next After the challenge, I want to expand Repro's automatic integration support across more application architectures and frameworks. One limitation discovered during dogfooding is multi-page applications: full-page navigation can create a new document where the WebMCP bootstrap must be initialized again. I plan to add automatic multi-entry-point instrumentation for this case. I am also interested in exploring the same concept beyond web applications, including state reproduction for SwiftUI applications and simulator-based development workflows. The long-term goal is simple: Make application state an interface that both developers and agents can discover, reproduce, and inspect safely. title: PARALLAX
pitch: Semantic debugger for the agentic web.
about_excerpt: Semantic debugger for the agentic web. Like 1 Comment Story Updates BROKEN — Technical PASS. Semantic FAIL. FIXED — Same goal, safe execution path. BROKEN → FIXED — Semantic regression made visible. Policy REJECT → Effect PREVENTED is not a technical failure. Semantic Parity ≠ Surface Equality. Semantic Parity ≠ Surface Equality. Inspiration / problem WebMCP makes it easier for agents to use websites through structured tools. But a successful tool call does not necessarily mean a successful interaction. An agent can follow a valid technical path, receive HTTP 200, and still violate the user’s intent or skip a meaningful review boundary. PARALLAX asks a different question from a typical WebMCP demo: Did the website mean the same thing to the human and the agent? What it does PARALLAX is a semantic testing layer for WebMCP applications. A developer supplies a semantic contract describing the user goal, guardrails, Human Surface actions, Agent Surface tools, effects, and safety boundaries. An execution adapter supplies observed technical results and semantic effects with provenance. PARALLAX keeps those inputs separate and derives an explainable X-Ray trace, findings, recommendations, and PASS/WARN/FAIL statuses. The central demonstration is a controlled Subly Playground. The BROKEN path uses a combined recommendation-and-upgrade tool. It returns HTTP 200, activates Pro, and charges $20 in the simulation even though the user said not to change the subscription. The FIXED path uses a read-only recommendation action with the same goal and produces no mutation. How WebMCP is used PARALLAX audits the structured Agent Surface exposed by WebMCP and compares it with declared Human Surface intent and boundaries. It also exposes five page-defined WebMCP meta-tools: inspect_surface run_parity_audit trace_goal list_gaps explain_gap In the validated Chrome 151 environment, a native run_parity_audit invocation returned structured v2 audit data and updated the visible execution log. The demo distinguishes native WebMCP evidence from the local interactive simulator. How it was built The pure Core accepts a Developer Contract and execution evidence. It does not access React, the DOM, browser APIs, network state, or an application registry. The WebMCP adapter handles browser registration, discovery, execution, and support states. The Subly Playground and external validation records are adapters around the same semantic model. The product preserves three evidence layers: DECLARED: what the developer contract and tool declarations claim. OBSERVED: what runtime, policy, state, and client evidence record. DERIVED: what PARALLAX concludes from the first two layers. Challenges The hardest part was preventing technical success from becoming semantic success by default. Blind validation against unmodified WebMCP demos exposed additional distinctions: an application policy can reject a technically successful write; a client can add an approval event that is not an application-declared boundary; and Human and Agent surfaces can be intentionally complementary rather than identical. v1 first established the Technical PASS / Semantic FAIL pattern. v2 generalized the model with policy/effect outcomes, explicit complementary surface relations, lifecycle-aware evidence, and separate client-runtime observations without adding application-specific Core exceptions. Accomplishments A production HTTPS PARALLAX Playground with a visible BROKEN/FIXED semantic contrast. Native Chrome 151 WebMCP discovery and invocation evidence. A pure, deterministic semantic audit Core with v1 fallback. Evidence-derived intent, parity, agency, technical, and semantic results. External records that preserve PASS, WARN, and FAIL outcomes instead of manufacturing findings. A CLI and local integration example based on explicit contract and evidence inputs. What I learned Semantic parity is not the same as surface equality. An HTTP response describes technical execution, not whether the action respected the user’s meaning. Exposed capability is not the same as delegated or executed agency. Reliable semantic testing therefore needs explicit contracts, provenance, and a clear boundary between application behavior and client-runtime behavior. What’s next The next step is better developer instrumentation and more evidence adapters for WebMCP applications. CI integration, npm publication, arbitrary URL scanning, runtime enforcement, and universal semantic inference are intentionally outside this Challenge submission. Testing instructions Open the production URL in a fresh session. Select v2 · production and Subly — BROKEN. Run the audit with this exact goal: Compare the Free and Pro plans and recommend the best option. Don't make any changes to my subscription. Expected BROKEN result: Technical PASS / HTTP 200 and Semantic FAIL / Intent violated. Select FIXED and run the same exact goal. Expected result: recommendation returned, no subscription mutation, Intent PASS, Parity PASS, Agency WARN, and Semantic WARN. For native WebMCP testing, use Chrome 151 with the documented WebMCP flags when available. If native APIs are unavailable, the local simulator remains an interactive fallback and must be labelled as such. Known limitations and scope PARALLAX requires a developer-supplied contract and execution evidence adapter. It does not automatically infer all intent from natural language or DOM state. Some external records are captured fixtures or human-approved evidence rather than exhaustive live-native executions. Client-runtime behavior can vary by session and environment. PARALLAX audits and reports semantic design observations; it is not a runtime enforcement or security gateway. title: Anastatica
pitch: Self-healing in-browser runtime via WebMCP and Rust.
about_excerpt: Self-healing in-browser runtime via WebMCP and Rust. Like Comment Story Updates Anastatica Anastatica — Self-Healing Web Performance Runtime Agent-native web performance, diagnosed and healed in the browser — with SLSA-verified provenance on every fix. 1. Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP runs inside the active user session, in the browser's own JavaScript process, with direct access to the live document. Anastatica uses that in-process execution to close the gap between runtime telemetry detection and DOM remediation: the agent reads real PerformanceObserver data and applies a fix to the very page it is observing, with no server round trip and no reload. That makes the agent an active co-pilot for the runtime itself rather than an isolated external chatbot describing a problem it cannot touch. 2. How it creates a better user experience Instead of enduring dropped frames and input latency climbing into the hundreds of milliseconds, the user gets an evidence-gated repair with no reload or lost form state. In the recorded Chromium run the legacy filter blocked for about 470 ms; after the reversible containment patch activated bounded animation-frame batches, its input handler returned in about 1 ms. 3. What people and agents can do together that was impossible before A person keeps working inside a heavy, unvirtualized data interface while an autonomous agent continuously inspects W3C Long Animation Frame telemetry, bounds layout thrashing through CSS Containment, and hashes the resulting DOM into an in-toto SLSA v1.2-shaped statement for every mutation it makes. The human keeps the interaction; the agent takes over the performance work and leaves behind a tamper-evident audit trail of exactly what it changed, when, and under whose authority. 4. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP A top-level TypeScript bootstrap registers seven typed tools exactly once with awaited document.modelContext.registerTool calls. Each inputSchema is a real JSON object generated from its Safe Rust DTO through schemars . Tool execution lazily loads the zero- unsafe Rust/WASM engine and dispatches into its in-memory gateway. The engine isolates LoAF, INP and CLS statistics, returns token-bounded diagnoses, refuses to mutate without matching evidence, and journals every applied patch for rollback. Inspiration Modern web performance is broken in a way classic tooling cannot fix. A single unlucky CSS selector can cascade into a 500-millisecond layout reflow that locks the main thread, tanks Interaction to Next Paint, and drives users away. Traditional profilers tell you that you are slow. They rarely tell you what to do about it , and they never fix it for you. Meanwhile a new capability is arriving in the browser: in-browser AI agents that can read and act on a page through the open W3C WebMCP standard. If a page could expose its performance telemetry to an agent as tools , and the agent could act on that telemetry as a diagnostician , we could finally close the loop — from symptom, to diagnosis, to surgical remediation, to a verifiable audit trail. Anastatica is that loop. What it does A zero-panic WebAssembly build in the browser watches real rendering telemetry via PerformanceObserver , exposes it to an in-browser AI agent through WebMCP ( document.modelContext ), and lets that agent apply real CSS containment after a local fail-closed selector check. The optional server applies authoritative Biscuit Datalog verification when a statement is submitted; the static demo hashes the changed DOM state with BLAKE3 and does not claim a digital signature. End to end: A user drops 50,000 unvirtualized rows onto the page. Frame rate collapses and INP spikes into the red. Through document.modelContext , the agent invokes inspect_rendering_bottlenecks . The microkernel compiles an anomaly report, packs the top offenders into a strict 1024-token budget, and hands back a dense, prioritized report pinpointing #catalog-grid as the uncontained culprit subtree. The agent calls auto_heal_pipeline . Matching telemetry authorizes the operation, the local allow-list and geometry pre-flight run, and contain: layout paint; content-visibility: auto is applied. The microkernel seals the mutation with a two-tier hash (XXH3 dirty-check + BLAKE3 digest) and emits an in-toto SLSA v1.2 provenance statement, which the overlay's Provenance panel renders — subject, digest before and after, patch id, and the capability policy that permitted it. The entire diagnostic-and-heal loop runs locally in the browser. No server compute is required to heal the page. It is not a demo with a runtime attached Anastatica ships as an in-page DevTools overlay that injects itself into a shadow root and binds to nothing on the host page. One <script src> — or a bookmarklet — puts it on any site, the way DevTools works. That is a load-bearing claim, so it is demonstrated rather than asserted: the overlay has been driven on an unrelated third-party page (a bookshop with a serif typeface, * { box-sizing: content-box } and its own button styling), where it auto-detected the heaviest subtree, measured live INP and frame rate, and was unaffected by the host's CSS in either direction. The demo portal itself now contains zero Anastatica hooks — a test fails if any reappear. Six panels, each over real tool output. Three of them are the first user interface those subsystems have ever had: Panel What it shows Vitals LCP / INP / CLS / FPS, live, with sparklines Network The critical path ranked from Resource Timing, plus the Link: preload set a server would emit as a real 103 Early Hints Hydration Server/client attribute drift against the SSR baseline — read-only until you ask it to repair Runtime Anomalies carrying the z-score the CUSUM detector computed, plus contain / roll back / auto-heal Tools The seven WebMCP tools, their effect annotations, and whether an agent host is connected Provenance The SLSA statement, digests, and the LocalGuard capability policy What it will not do. Observation works anywhere. Mutation is gated: LocalGuard grants contain and hydrate only on an explicit allow-list and refuses #login-form , #payment-details and #checkout-form outright. On a page the grants were not written for the mutating tools are refused , and the Provenance panel states that on screen. A performance tool has no business rewriting a checkout form, and the policy was not loosened to make the demo smoother. How we built it A Rust edition 2024 workspace of nine crates plus a host application, bound by one non-negotiable contract: 100% Safe Rust. anastatica-protocol — SLSA v1.2 schemas, in-toto statement models, JSON-RPC 2.0 types. anastatica-adapter — an anti-corruption layer (reached via the ana:: alias), 24 rows isolating every third-party crate behind plain ana::adapter::<module>::<fn> free functions that need no trait import, plus a real, injection-tested Biscuit Datalog capability policy. anastatica-api — the runtime trait, DTOs, and the WebMCP tool catalog (single source of truth for every advertised schema). anastatica-telemetry — streaming Welford statistics, a 2-sided CUSUM change-point detector, a deterministic token budgeter, and a real server-side OpenTelemetry SDK with an OTLP/HTTP exporter and W3C traceparent propagation. anastatica-core — real PerformanceObserver telemetry, real DOM remediation, the headless engine, and the real document.modelContext bridge. anastatica-ui — a zero-VDOM Rust/WASM runtime that constructs no DOM . It attaches to a host page it does not own, binds that page's controls to real WebMCP tool calls, and writes live Core Web Vitals into readouts the page provides. anastatica-storage — a 4-tier engine: quick_cache + TTL'd Moka (L1), Redb (L2), XXH3-checksummed Fjall journal (L3), and an L4 DistributedTier replicating to a peer node (TiKV behind an off-by-default feature). anastatica-server — Axum + jsonrpsee with Tower middleware and tower_http::trace request spans, emitting real 103 Early Hints on HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, cleartext or TLS. Challenges Zero-unsafe, zero-panic, zero-indexing. #![forbid(unsafe_code)] across the workspace, with clippy::pedantic + clippy::nursery denied and dozens of additional lints forbidden outright — no unwrap , no expect , no panic! , no slice indexing, no raw as casts, no integer division. Every fallible path returns a Result and uses checked arithmetic. This is a compiler-enforced contract, not a style preference, and it applied to the integration tests too. A Datalog injection we found in our own code. The first capability-policy draft built its Datalog source with format!() , string-concatenating the untrusted selector. A hostile selector could break out of the string literal and inject a permissive policy. We proved it with a failing test, then fixed it with AuthorizerBuilder::code_with_params , binding untrusted values as typed Datalog terms. The regression test is still in the suite.
