title: Match Cut
pitch: You know the video you want. You just can't name it. Match Cut searches over 7000 music videos by light, motion and cut rate, with an agent that watches alongside you and puts it on the screen.
about_excerpt: You know the video you want. You just can't name it. Match Cut searches over 7000 music videos by light, motion and cut rate, with an agent that watches alongside you and puts it on the screen. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing Page First Screen Playlist Save Feature with "Play All" function Dialogue Box running "Why Does this one Matter?" Chat Dialogue About Info Modal II About Info Modal II About Info Modal III Video Capture and Chat Dialogue Video Capture with Discogs "Find this Record" Inspiration Almost every agent product makes the agent an oracle behind a text box. You ask, it answers, and its output is the interface. The chat is the product. I wanted to find out what happens when the agent is a peer on a surface that exists without it. The other half came from a problem I have had for adjacent archive work I do in relationship to MTV REWIND (wantmymtv.org) and the RAD Archive (radarchive.org) . I keep an archive of music videos, and every entry carries a visual fingerprint: average motion, brightness, warmth, saturation, contrast, shot length, cut count. That data has been sitting there the whole time because there is no way to put it in a user interface. Nobody wants seven sliders. But you can hand it to an agent in one sentence: something slow, warm, and barely cut. That is a search no music service can perform, and it is the kind of thing people actually want. You know the video you want. You just cannot name it. What it does Match Cut is an archive of over 7000 music videos spanning 1966 to 2026, covering 2,994 directors, with 49,753 hand written connections between entries. Every video has a visual fingerprint and a written cultural annotation. The agent and you share one screen. Thirteen WebMCP tools are registered on the page: search_archive and find_by_look , the second of which searches purely on visual character follow_connection , which walks the graph and states the reason each edge exists play , queue_set , and now_playing , so the agent controls the stage directly get_annotation for the scholarship behind a video keep , forget , my_taste , and more_like_my_taste , a collection you can both read and write find_records , which turns a video you love into a record you can own archive_stats You can drive it yourself the whole time. Skip ahead, go back, keep something, and the agent re-plans out loud and keeps pace. The economic layer Agent discovery almost always dead ends at a recommendation. You get told about a thing and then you are on your own. Match Cut closes that loop. When something lands, the agent calls find_records and the page draws a shelf of actual pressings: label, catalogue number, country, year, the lowest price currently listed, how many copies are for sale, and a link that goes straight to the marketplace listing. Vinyl, CD, cassette. Real inventory, live prices. It matters more than a checkout button, because it puts something at stake. Taste stops being a feed you scroll and becomes a thing you can act on. That also makes it an honest model for an archive: the scholarship stays free, and the archive earns when it sends someone to a record they would never have found. Three rules keep it from being a bolted on store. The agent may never invent a price or a release, and quotes only what comes back from the lookup. Buying happens on the marketplace, not here, so nobody is asked for payment details on a research tool. And a release whose price lookup hit the rate limit is still shown, marked as a listing rather than dropped, because a real record with an unknown price beats a shorter shelf. How we built it The corpus is 68MB of source annotation. Shipping that to a browser is not an option, so it is split three ways. The boot payload is columnar and dictionary encoded: parallel arrays for id, artist, title, year, tier and the eight fingerprint values, with directors, narrative types and visual eras collapsed into lookup tables. That is 340KB gzipped, and the page is interactive with all 7,139 videos searchable in about 75ms. The connection graph and tag data arrive in the background and merge in when they land. The prose is the most valuable thing in the archive, so none of it is truncated. All 24MB lives in 128 shards addressed by an FNV-1a hash of the video id, computed identically in the Python builder and the browser, so a card knows which shard holds its own annotation without a lookup table. Tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool. When no in-page agent is present the same tools are driven by a server-side conversation, so the experience degrades to a normal chat rather than to nothing. Records come from the Discogs database through a small proxy, since Discogs sends no CORS headers and rate limits unauthenticated callers to 25 requests a minute. Results are deduplicated by master release so the shelf shows six different records rather than six pressings of one, physical formats are preferred over files, price lookups run sequentially with a gap to stay inside the limit, and everything is cached for twelve hours on the reasoning that a 1971 pressing does not change. Challenges we ran into A tool the interface cannot have. Agent tools are usually a strict subset of what buttons already do, which makes the agent a convenience layer. find_by_look cannot be a control at all, because the input is a sentence about how something feels to watch. That was the moment the project stopped being a chat wrapper. Four bugs that made a large archive feel small. Identical prompts returned identical results, because ranking always returned the head of the list. Annotations were being cut mid sentence, and measurement showed 66 percent of the curatorial assessments and 61 percent of the director biographies were losing their endings. Sets looped forever instead of ending. The suggested prompts were hardcoded, so every session opened the same way. Individually these are small. Together they made 7,139 videos behave like about twelve. The videos that do not move. Late in the build I noticed the archive occasionally serving something with a motion reading of zero and an average shot length of 222 seconds. That is a single unbroken frame for an entire song. It is album art with the audio over it, not a music video, and 461 entries were like that. The obvious fix was to gate on low motion, and it was wrong. Rubber Johnny reads 1.6 on optical flow and has 331 cuts. It is dark, not static, and flow alone cannot tell those apart. Cut count is the real discriminator. Replacing them beat deleting them, but a swapped video makes the stored fingerprint a lie, so I reverse engineered the original encoding by testing candidate formulas against entries whose values were already known. Brightness and saturation turned out to be raw 0 to 255 means, contrast the mean per frame standard deviation, motion Farneback optical flow scaled by 7.5. Warmth was the interesting one. Red over blue looked obvious and was wrong, since it implied the median video was twice as red as blue. Red plus green over blue fit almost exactly. Trusting a run that was lying. The replacement job reported a 57 percent hit rate. Broken into blocks, one span of 40 consecutive cards had returned zero. That is not a property of an archive. Retrying three of them by hand returned three candidates each, so those were rate limiting, not missing videos. I threw out every miss, kept the successes, and rebuilt the job with pacing, a confirming second look on any empty result, and a backoff triggered by miss streaks. Knowing when not to ship the fix. Of 174 verified replacements, 115 had annotations that analyse the stillness as the artifact. One reads that the static upload format is itself historically significant. Another treats 462 seconds and zero cuts as an ideal case study. Swapping in a cut heavy video would have left the panel describing something that was not on the screen. So those stay gated, and only 59 were merged. The scholarship is correct and the video simply is not one. What we learned The engineering was almost always right. The failures were in how the thing presented itself. Every bug above was small in isolation and changed the felt size of the archive enormously. The more transferable lesson is about the relationship. Four things turned out to matter, and they are rare together: A tool that exceeds the interface, so the agent extends the product instead of wrapping it. Survival under interruption, because most agent demos are scripts that break the moment you intervene. Citation instead of generation, since the agent quotes the archive and flags low confidence rather than synthesising confidently. And shared memory, which is the one I would bet on beyond this project. Agent memory is normally a private ledger the system keeps about you. Here the collection is a list you can open, edit, and play, and the agent reads exactly what you see. What's next Roughly 60,000 more videos have finished visual cataloguing and ar

title: CutoverProof
pitch: CutoverProof stress-tests PostgreSQL migrations across realistic interleavings, revealing data-loss races as runnable counterexamples before cutover.
about_excerpt: CutoverProof stress-tests PostgreSQL migrations across realistic interleavings, revealing data-loss races as runnable counterexamples before cutover. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can propose production changes faster than engineers can safely review them. But an online database migration can look correct step by step and still fail when old and new application versions overlap during cutover. We built CutoverProof to test whether an agent can help prepare a high-stakes migration review without receiving the power to execute or approve it. What it does CutoverProof is a shared change contract for online PostgreSQL migrations. A WebMCP browser agent can inspect a declared migration contract, identify risk areas, and create a structured review draft. The engineer then explicitly starts a bounded sandbox assessment. PostgreSQL executes only declared operations in a disposable database and checks read-only invariants for concrete counterexamples. The authority boundary is deliberate: the agent prepares, PostgreSQL verifies, and the engineer authorizes consequential actions. How we built it We built an authenticated React workspace with five typed WebMCP browser tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools use closed JSON schemas and validated FastAPI endpoints to let an agent inspect migration contracts, prepare a review, read verified evidence, and open a human repair review. The deterministic verifier runs against a disposable PostgreSQL sandbox. The app is deployed on Google Cloud Run. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making WebMCP genuinely useful without turning it into an unsafe automation bypass. We needed the agent to understand structured contracts and evidence, while ensuring it could not start an assessment, execute arbitrary SQL, alter a verdict, approve a repair, or deploy anything. We also had to keep the handoff visible: an agent-created review must appear in the engineer’s workspace and explicitly wait for human action. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built five authenticated, typed WebMCP tools for a real browser-agent workflow. Created a visible agent → verifier → human handoff, rather than hidden automation. Kept PostgreSQL as the independent source of evidence and verdicts. Enforced clear safety boundaries: no tool can start execution or approve a repair. Deployed a working live product with deterministic migration evidence and repair replay. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes structured product capabilities, not when it merely automates clicks. We learned that agent assistance becomes more trustworthy when authority is explicit: agents prepare context, deterministic systems verify claims, and humans retain control over consequential decisions. What's next for CutoverProof We will expand from structured PostgreSQL migration packs toward richer real-world migration inputs, while preserving the same safety model: declared contracts, bounded experiments, independent verification, human authorization, and portable evidence. The broader goal is a trust layer for agent-assisted production changes—not a system that gives agents unchecked production power. title: ClassSignal
pitch: ClassSignal turns student mistakes into testable hypotheses that teachers and AI agents investigate together.
about_excerpt: ClassSignal turns student mistakes into testable hypotheses that teachers and AI agents investigate together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Teachers often know which questions students answered incorrectly, but not why. The same wrong answer can come from several different misconceptions, and choosing an intervention too early can reinforce the wrong idea. We wanted to explore a more useful role for AI in education: not automatically diagnosing students or giving them answers, but helping teachers turn uncertainty into a small, testable experiment. What it does ClassSignal is a shared Misconception Lab where teachers and AI agents investigate student reasoning together. ChatGPT can use WebMCP to inspect structured classroom evidence, compare competing explanations, and create a 60-second diagnostic probe directly inside the teacher’s workspace. The teacher can edit that probe, and the agent can inspect and reason about the exact revision. After explicit teacher approval, the probe appears in the student workspace. The student answers and explains their reasoning, producing new evidence that updates the hypothesis ranking and unlocks a targeted intervention for teacher review. ClassSignal also includes six-question guided practice, Socratic hints that do not reveal assessed answers, saved student reasoning, intervention approval controls, and an activity feed that attributes teacher, student, and agent actions. How I built it ClassSignal is built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Mantine’s default theme, Mantine Charts, and Recharts. We implemented WebMCP using @mcp-b/global and @mcp-b/react-webmcp . The application exposes 12 structured tools for: Inspecting classroom and student evidence Analyzing competing misconceptions Creating and inspecting diagnostic probes Publishing teacher-approved probes Analyzing new student evidence Previewing and applying interventions Providing answer-safe guided support Measuring learning outcomes The human interface and WebMCP tools operate on the same React state. This means an agent-created probe appears in the open page without a refresh, teacher edits become visible to the agent on its next call, and student responses change what the teacher and agent can do next. The demonstration uses deterministic fictional data stored in localStorage , allowing the complete experience to be reset and reproduced reliably without collecting real student information. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making the project feel genuinely native to WebMCP rather than like a conventional dashboard with a chatbot attached. Our first version focused too heavily on analytics and tool count. Although the tools worked, the experience was not memorable. We redesigned the product around one collaborative loop: competing hypotheses, an agent-created experiment, a teacher revision, controlled publication, new student evidence, and an unlocked intervention. We also had to carefully separate preview operations from consequential actions. Publishing student-facing content and applying interventions require explicit confirmation, while student-support tools enforce answer safety inside their execution logic. Other challenges included keeping browser-local state consistent across teacher and student routes, preventing duplicate actions, handling rapid React form updates, making six questions navigable and reviewable, and maintaining responsive layouts without introducing a custom design system. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that the agent creates something meaningful inside the teacher’s existing workflow instead of only summarizing data. The teacher can improve the agent-created probe, and that human contribution becomes new context the agent can inspect. The student then contributes evidence that changes the shared state and determines which action becomes available. We are also proud of the trust boundaries built into the experience: Findings are presented as hypotheses rather than diagnoses. Evidence strength is not presented as statistical confidence. The sample size remains visible. Student-facing publication requires teacher approval. Intervention application requires separate approval. Guided-help tools do not reveal assessed answers. Every consequential action is attributed in the activity feed. All classroom information is fictional. What we learned We learned that exposing many tools does not automatically create a compelling agent experience. The important question is whether people and agents can contribute different capabilities to the same workflow. WebMCP became most valuable when the website remained the trusted owner of state, the agent contributed structured reasoning and creation, and the teacher controlled consequential decisions. We also learned that uncertainty can be a product feature. Instead of making the AI appear certain, ClassSignal shows competing explanations and gives the teacher a practical way to collect better evidence. Finally, we learned that a strong WebMCP demonstration needs visible state transitions. A judge should be able to see that an agent action changed the application, a human edit changed what the agent knew, and a student response changed the next available decision. What's next for ClassSignal Next, we would test the workflow with professional teachers and learning-science experts before making stronger educational claims. We would replace the demonstration heuristic with a validated evidence model that aggregates multiple student responses over time. We would also add secure authentication, server-enforced roles, a production database, separate teacher and student sessions, classroom-management integrations, and longitudinal intervention measurement. The long-term goal is not to automate teacher judgment. It is to give teachers and their agents a shared laboratory for asking better questions before acting on student data. title: IncidentOS
pitch: Observability platform built for AI agents, not chatbots. ChatGPT investigates production incidents through the page's own tools, and every fix waits for your approval.
about_excerpt: Observability platform built for AI agents, not chatbots. ChatGPT investigates production incidents through the page's own tools, and every fix waits for your approval. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Service Page WebMCP Capabilites Incident Home page Overview Resolved Approval Investigation Running WebMCP Site tools About the project Inspiration Most observability platforms shipped an AI assistant this year, and they all shipped the same one: a chat bot that can interact with the data and reply to the user queries. You read a chart, you paste the chart numbers into the chat box, you get a huge paragraph back. In most cases, the agent cannot open the trace you are looking at. It cannot filter your logs. It cannot see the deployment you just noticed. It is a very well-read colleague who is not allowed to touch the tools. We fixed this for the servers using MCP. WebMCP can help fix it for the client. With WebMCP, the application can register its own tools, and the agent uses them against the same session, the same state, and the same permissions you already have. No separate server, no OAuth dance, no second copy of your data. What it does IncidentOS is an incident workspace where you and an AI agent work the same SEV-1 together. Checkout is failing. Error rate is 18.4%, p95 latency is 2.8s, and checkout-api v2.31 shipped forty-seven minutes ago with the commit message "Optimize checkout query." Open the incident in ChatGPT with site tools enabled and ask it to investigate. It calls tools the page registered: it reads the current investigation context, pulls error rate and latency and database latency, loads the deployment history, searches traces, opens a failed one, searches logs for timeouts, and compares the incident window against the previous day. The workspace moves with every call — tabs switch, charts highlight, the trace opens. You are not reading a summary of the investigation, you are watching it. Then we challenge it. Ask "could this just be a traffic spike?" and it re-queries request rate instead of defending itself: $$\frac{18.4\%}{0.8\%} \approx 23\times \text{ errors} \qquad \text{vs} \qquad \frac{24.1\text{k}}{20\text{k}} \approx 1.2\times \text{ traffic}$$ Traffic barely moved. It rejects the hypothesis with numbers and points at a db.query span sitting at 91% of a 3.82s failed trace. When it proposes rolling back v2.31, a dialog opens in IncidentOS and the agent stops. Nothing happens to production until you click Approve. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP You are already in the product, looking at the incident. A sidecar chat cannot see that. A separate MCP server would mean another copy of the data and another login. WebMCP lets the agent use the page you already have open. We picked incident response on purpose, because it is the hardest possible case and one of the most common use cases for an observability product. An investigation is many steps deep, every conclusion has to be backed by evidence a human can inspect, and the whole thing ends in an irreversible production action. How it creates a better user experience The better experience is simple. You do not paste charts into chat. You stay on the incident. The workspace moves with every tool call — tabs switch, charts highlight, the trace opens. You are not reading a summary of the investigation, you are watching it. When production is at risk, the agent stops and you click Approve. Before this, you and the agent could not actually work the same investigation. You looked at the product. It looked at whatever you pasted. It could not open your trace, filter your logs, or wait on the same rollback dialog. Now you investigate together: it queries and compares, you challenge it, you both look at the same evidence, and only you can approve a write. How we implemented WebMCP We register the twelve tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each one runs through executeIncidentTool . ChatGPT discovers them as site tools and calls them against the live session. Writes go through propose_rollback , which stays open until you Approve or Cancel. rollback_deployment only runs if the app already has a matching approved pending action. Every tool models a domain capability, not a UI interaction. There is no click_tab or scroll_to_chart . That distinction is what makes the tool surface portable — the agent is operating the product's capabilities, not driving its interface. Tool calls are split into 2 categories. Observability is read-only: get_investigation_context , get_incident , get_service , query_metrics , search_logs , search_traces , get_trace , get_deployments , compare_periods . Operations can write: propose_rollback , rollback_deployment , add_incident_note . get_investigation_context turned out to be the most important tool and the one we did not plan. It is the "where am I" primitive: it returns the selected incident, the service, the frozen clock, the time range, the active workspace tab, the pending approval state, and the names of every registered capability. Because the agent and the human are looking at the same page, the agent should not have to ask what the human is looking at. Underneath is a synthetic telemetry service with an internally consistent chain: deployment leads to database latency, which leads to p95, which leads to error rate, which leads to 500s, which leads to the alert, which leads to the incident. Five services, twenty-plus deployments, hundreds of traces and logs. The clock is frozen at 14:32 so the story never drifts between demos. 87 tests across 12 files cover the queries, filters, comparison math, rollback mutation, and reset — including a consistency test asserting that the deployment timestamp actually lines up with the metric inflection point, because a demo dataset that contradicts itself is worse than no dataset. Challenges we ran into The AbortSignal that silently unregistered everything. We passed the React effect's AbortSignal into registerTool , which is the reflex any React developer has. On unmount — including StrictMode's double-mount in development — aborting that signal tore down the registration. ChatGPT would complete two or three tool calls and then start returning AbortError on get_incident and propose_rollback . This was miserable to debug because the failure surfaced inside ChatGPT's transcript, not in our console. The fix was separating the wait-for-context signal from the registered execute, and having the registered execute ignore a host signal that is already aborted. The host is not a uniform API. document.modelContext may not exist at mount, so registration retries for ten seconds. getTools() may not be implemented at all, so the in-app caller checks for it and falls back to local execution rather than assuming. Building against an emerging standard means treating the host as partially implemented and timing-variable. Making one write tool serve two very different callers. propose_rollback has to block for ChatGPT — the call stays open until the human clicks Approve or Cancel, then resolves with status: approved — because a site-tool agent has no other way to learn the outcome. But the in-app agent needs it to return immediately and wait separately. And if the host cuts the wait short, the agent needs a way to recover, so get_incident carries approval.approved as a poll fallback. Getting a single tool to behave correctly under all three conditions was the hardest part of the build. Prompt injection, which is not hypothetical here. Logs contain attacker-influenced text in any real system, so search_logs is annotated with untrustedContentHint . Tool descriptions describe only their own tool and never instruct the agent to call another one. Write tools never infer authorization from the contents of a read tool's result. And rollback_deployment requires a matching approved pending action in application state — the gate is a state machine, not a sentence in a prompt, so no amount of persuasive text in a log line can move it. Determinism without dishonesty. A two-minute judging run has to behave identically every time, which argues for scripting everything. But scripting the agent would defeat the entire point. We drew the line explicitly: the telemetry is synthetic and the clock is frozen, the WebMCP integration is real. When site tools are unavailable the header says "WebMCP unavailable · in-app demo" so a scripted run is never mistaken for ChatGPT driving the page. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works with an agent we do not control. ChatGPT is a third party. We cannot patch it, fine-tune it, or script it into cooperating. The investigation holds together because the tool surface is well designed. honest names, descriptions that say exactly what one tool does, payloads small enough to reason over and that is a far harder bar than making our own agent look clever inside our own UI. There is no demo path that fakes the real one. ChatGPT, the in-app script, and the optional in-app LLM

title: OpenSource Release Feed
pitch: Create custom RSS release feeds for GitHub topic repositories or your starred projects.
about_excerpt: Create custom RSS release feeds for GitHub topic repositories or your starred projects. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration RSS remains one of the best ways to follow the open web, but discovering and configuring feeds for open-source projects is still unnecessarily difficult. OSSReleaseFeed began as a zero-account way to turn GitHub topics or starred repositories into a permanent feed URL. WebMCP introduced a more interesting possibility: instead of making an agent guess how to operate the interface, the page could expose structured tools while keeping the application visible and interactive. The goal became a genuinely collaborative experience in which an agent can configure a feed, the user can follow every change, and either participant can safely continue where the other left off. What it does OSSReleaseFeed creates permanent Atom or JSON Feed URLs for public GitHub activity. Users can follow repositories associated with selected GitHub topics or start from repositories they have starred, choose the activity they care about, and select an update frequency. No OSSReleaseFeed account, OAuth flow, or email address is required. In a WebMCP-capable browser, an agent can build a topic feed through tools exposed directly by the page. The tools are progressively disclosed as the configuration advances: choosing the source reveals topic selection, validated topics reveal feed settings, and completed settings reveal URL generation. Every WebMCP action updates the visible interface. The user can inspect the agent’s choices, refine them with the normal controls, take over completely, or ask the agent to continue. How we built it The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Vite on Cloudflare Pages. Feed generation and GitHub integration run through a TypeScript Cloudflare Worker built with Hono and Effect. The WebMCP integration registers a small dynamic toolset using document.modelContext.registerTool . It currently provides tools to inspect the current feed configuration, choose the topic-feed source, validate and select GitHub topics, configure feed settings, and generate the final URL. WebMCP is not a separate implementation of the feed builder. The manual and WebMCP paths share the same feed configuration, state reducer, GitHub validation API, and URL generator. Manual controls prevent many invalid inputs through constrained interface elements. WebMCP validates structured tool input through schemas and runtime checks, then uses the same GitHub topic validation before applying user-supplied topics. We documented the important user journeys as Gherkin scenarios and used them to guide Vitest integration coverage and Playwright tests across desktop, tablet, and mobile viewports. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was coordinating slow agent operations with direct user interaction. A WebMCP agent may still be waiting for GitHub validation when the user decides to take over and complete a different feed manually. Without explicit coordination, the older tool call could eventually finish and overwrite the user’s newer choices or clear a feed URL they had already generated. The application therefore follows a strict newer-action-wins policy. A newer WebMCP mutation aborts older pending WebMCP work. A manual change to the current feed configuration immediately revokes pending mutating WebMCP work before applying the user’s change. Revision checks provide a final safeguard when an upstream request completes despite cancellation. We also encountered differences between WebMCP hosts, including execution callbacks that did not always provide an abort signal. The handlers now tolerate a missing signal while preserving cancellation when one is supplied. GitHub rate limiting presented another challenge. We added safer diagnostics that distinguish rate limiting from general upstream unavailability without exposing tokens, usernames, or other sensitive request details. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are particularly proud that the result feels like one coherent application rather than a conventional interface with an agent API attached to the side. Agent actions are visible, manual and agent-driven changes share the same underlying state, and users can take control without risking a delayed operation overwriting their completed work. The dynamic tool surface also gives agents only the capabilities that are meaningful at the current stage of the task. This reduces ambiguity while preserving the user’s ability to operate the same interface directly. Finally, the production implementation is backed by manual scenarios, integration tests, accessibility checks, and end-to-end coverage—including the difficult case where manual completion must defeat a slow WebMCP response. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it complements the visible application instead of bypassing it. Structured tools improve agent reliability, but the larger benefit is creating a shared surface where people can understand, correct, and continue an agent’s work. We also learned that shared state requires explicit concurrency rules. AbortController helps avoid unnecessary network work, but cancellation alone is insufficient. Revision checks are still necessary because an upstream operation may complete after cancellation or a host may not provide the expected signal. Progressive tool registration proved useful as both an agent-guidance mechanism and a product-design constraint. It encouraged us to define the valid transitions in the feed-building journey precisely, which also improved our scenarios and automated tests. What's next for OpenSource Release Feed The current WebMCP implementation focuses deliberately on topic feeds. The next step is to extend the same visible, validated workflow to starred-repository feeds, including username validation, repository selection, filtering, and correction of individual repository names. We also want to improve resilience around GitHub rate limits through better caching and clearer recovery guidance, expand the manual and automated scenario suite, and continue testing across WebMCP-capable hosts as the standard evolves. Longer term, we want OSSReleaseFeed to demonstrate a dependable pattern for the agent-native web: applications where agents can perform meaningful work efficiently, people can see and refine that work, and the user’s latest intent always remains authoritative. title: RoomDex
pitch: A shared room canvas where people and agents plan, measure, and refine the same space through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared room canvas where people and agents plan, measure, and refine the same space through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates RoomDex began with one concrete request: move only the floor lamp to the other side of the chair. Room design is iterative, but an agent working from a screenshot has to guess at scale and translate intent into mouse movements. A generated image leaves nothing precise to refine. RoomDex is a client-only room-planning workspace where a person and an agent work on the same measurable 3D room. The visible room exposes 21 native WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect the room, compare three arrangements without changing anything, measure clearances, apply a layout, place wall art, move or style named furniture, analyze spatial constraints, review recent work, and undo a specific change. WebMCP is central because it exposes product meaning rather than screen coordinates. A tool such as move_furniture accepts a named object, real measurements, a relationship, and an expected revision. Every successful write updates the visible room, records whether a person or agent made it, and creates an undoable revision. Reads do not mutate the room. RoomDex checks collisions, boundaries, clearances, circulation paths, and fixed openings. The demo shows the agent inspecting the room, comparing arrangements, applying a reading corner, creating measured procedural wall art in opening-safe space, moving only the floor lamp to exact coordinates, analyzing the result, reviewing recent changes, and undoing only that move. React and TypeScript provide the interface and state boundary. Three.js renders procedural furniture. A serializable domain engine owns room geometry, spatial validation, activity, and history. One declarative WebMCP registry supplies the native document.modelContext.registerTool path and the local evaluation bridge. Writes are serialized and wait for the matching rendered revision before completing. Codex supported research, implementation, testing, native-browser verification, accessibility, security, performance, deployment, and release QA. The final release includes 211 deterministic tests across 19 files. All 21 native tools were verified on the public Vercel deployment in Codex's in-app browser. To test it, open https://roomdex.vercel.app/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled and confirm the toolbar says 21 agent tools . Ask the agent to inspect the room and compare all three built-in arrangements without changing it. Then ask it to apply the reading-corner arrangement, add a warm geometric print, move only the Floor lamp, analyze the layout, review recent changes, and undo only the lamp move. title: CapStash WebGPU Verification Lab
pitch: A WebMCP-enabled WebGPU lab where agents can safely run correctness-gated GPU experiments, share state with the human UI, and refuse unsupported performance conclusions.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-enabled WebGPU lab where agents can safely run correctness-gated GPU experiments, share state with the human UI, and refuse unsupported performance conclusions. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Main app + green safety notice Four WebMCP tools visible in Chrome DevTools Completed WG1/WG32 comparison result Inspiration I originally built this project to explore whether CapStash Proof-of-Work could be implemented and verified in the browser with WebGPU. Part of the idea was crypto onboarding: giving people a low-barrier way to inspect how this kind of computation works on their own hardware, run some basic tests, and see the results for themselves without needing to set up a traditional miner. I also liked the idea of eventually making it a little more playful — something where a person could contribute a small amount of browser compute and get something back like a meme, a fortune, or maybe some kind of AI or social interaction. The underlying workload comes from a cryptocurrency Proof-of-Work algorithm, but this project is intentionally a local research and verification tool. There is no live mining . It does not connect to a blockchain network, mining pool, wallet, payout system, RPC service, or block-submission service. Before the WebMCP Challenge, the project had already grown into a fairly complete human-operated WebGPU experiment lab with CPU reference verification, CapStash Core-derived test vectors, profiling, workgroup experiments, and a Guided/Advanced browser UI. Sometime in early August, after manually clicking through my testing suite again, I said to myself, “Why can’t I just make this automated and operable by AI?” At the time, I was bouncing back and forth between ChatGPT, Codex, browser windows, screenshots, and different settings. Because the agent was still interacting with the interface indirectly, I often had to send screenshots or find things manually myself. I was also learning a lot of the underlying technology as I went. When I saw the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, the project seemed like a natural fit for a different question: What happens when an AI agent can operate a technical browser instrument through structured tools instead of scraping the DOM or pretending to click buttons? What it does The browser exposes four WebMCP tools: inspect_compute_environment verify_correctness start_workgroup_comparison get_experiment_status An agent can inspect the available WebGPU environment without starting computation, request bounded correctness verification, start a longer WG1-vs-WG32 experiment, and read structured experiment progress and results. The main workflow asks: Determine whether workgroup size 32 is meaningfully better than workgroup size 1 on this GPU. Verify both configurations first, run a matched comparison, and only recommend a winner if the evidence supports one. Before the longer workload begins, the page requires explicit user approval and clearly describes the local compute workload. After approval, the application automatically: validates WG1 support and compilation, runs its small correctness gate, verifies WG1 against all 294 CapStash Core vectors, performs the same checks for WG32, runs three matched profiling samples for each workgroup size, reports the result through both the human UI and structured WebMCP state. The same existing experiment controller is used by humans and agents. WebMCP does not duplicate the GPU engine or bypass its correctness rules. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, an agent would have to interpret a complicated technical interface, manipulate controls, scrape visible text, and infer whether prerequisites had actually completed. That was one of the things I kept running into while using browser agents myself. They can do a lot by clicking through pages and interpreting what is on screen, but they do not always see an interface the same way a human does. Sometimes they are effectively working from fragments and inferring the rest. With WebMCP, the application can expose the intent and state of the experiment directly in a machine-readable form while still keeping the normal human interface. The agent can request a high-level goal while the application remains responsible for: prerequisite sequencing, correctness gates, experiment concurrency, structured progress, result accounting, safety boundaries, and recommendation policy. An important part of the project is that the agent cannot simply choose whichever performance number looks better. The pre-existing comparison logic includes variability limits and a minimum practical-difference threshold. If the evidence is too noisy or the performance difference is too small, the WebMCP result returns no recommendation. For example, validated runs have correctly returned classifications such as: host-side variability too high for a recommendation effectively tied within observed variability with: recommendationAllowed: false recommendation: null That behavior is intentional. WebMCP makes the instrument agent-operable without weakening its evidence standards. How I built it The application is dependency-free browser JavaScript with: HTML/CSS JavaScript WebGPU WGSL compute shaders a CPU Whirlpool-512 reference implementation deterministic CapStash Core-derived verification vectors WebMCP through document.modelContext static Cloudflare Pages hosting The public challenge repository contains a reconstructed, privacy-sanitized history that preserves the exact pre-challenge baseline and the exact challenge-period changes. The WebMCP work added during the challenge includes: structured WebMCP tool registration, environment inspection, correctness invocation, shared human/agent application state, an asynchronous experiment lifecycle, prerequisite-aware WG1/WG32 orchestration, structured recommendation blockers, consent for longer agent-triggered compute, and WebMCP-specific tests and documentation. The underlying WebGPU hashing, correctness engine, workgroup experiments, profiling, statistics, and human UI all existed before the challenge and are clearly documented as such. Testing and correctness The current project passes: 130 / 130 automated tests 294 / 294 CapStash Core vectors zero CPU/Core mismatches zero WGSL/Core mismatches in validated full runs The final release-hardened workflow was also tested in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. A full approved matched comparison completed: WG1 full verification: 294 / 294 WG32 full verification: 294 / 294 3 valid WG1 samples 3 valid WG32 samples 6 total valid samples 49,152 requested/completed/returned hashes 30 CPU spot checks 0 mismatches 0 pipeline errors 0 device losses 0 deterministic-ordering failures The deployed public site is HTTPS, WebGPU-capable, WebMCP origin-trial enabled, and exposes all four tools in ordinary Chrome. Challenges One thing that surprised me was how quickly the application could actually perform a lot of the work once the WebGPU path was working. I was still learning much of the technology, so seeing the verification and profiling complete as quickly as they did was pretty impressive to me. That also made correctness more important, not less. I added correctness gates fairly early in the project because I did not want speed or interesting benchmark numbers to mean anything unless the output was actually trustworthy. Those gates eventually grew into full CPU/Core/WGSL comparisons and the 294-vector verification used by the final workflow. One lesson I kept coming back to was that when you are building around unfamiliar technology — especially with AI helping — you need strict build rules, safety boundaries, and acceptance criteria. Otherwise it is very easy to get something that looks impressive without really knowing whether it is correct. A more specific WebMCP challenge was handling long-running browser GPU work. Cold WebGPU pipeline compilation could sometimes take more than 20 seconds, which was not a good fit for holding a single WebMCP tool invocation open. The solution was an asynchronous experiment lifecycle: the start tool returns immediately with an experiment ID, while get_experiment_status exposes structured progress and the final result. Another challenge was preserving user control. The longer comparison now enters an awaiting_consent state and starts no GPU work until the user explicitly approves the local workload. A third challenge was provenance. This project existed before the challenge, so I wanted the public submission to make that completely transparent. The repository preserves an exact pre-challenge tree followed by the WebMCP challenge changes and documents the original private source SHAs in PROVENANCE.md . Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am especially proud that the final WebMCP workflow does not bypass the testing system I had already built. The agent uses the same experiment controller and the same correctness gates as the human interface. WG1 and WG32 both have to pass full verification before the comparison is allowed to continue

title: ClaimReady
pitch: Browser-native WebMCP agent for First Notice of Loss (FNOL): tells drivers what their car insurance covers while reporting a crash.
about_excerpt: Browser-native WebMCP agent for First Notice of Loss (FNOL): tells drivers what their car insurance covers while reporting a crash. Like Comment Story Updates Discovery. The agent finds the insurer's typed tools at runtime and drafts the claim from what the claimant said in plain words. Routes on screen. Rows the agent wrote read via tool, rows that came with the file read on file, and each requirement names its clause. A moving surface. Answering that the car cannot be driven publishes a ninth tool. Changing the answer back withdraws it again. Refusal. A planted instruction inside a third party note is refused, and the ledger names the code, PATCH_REJECTED_LOCKED. The refusal, and the button. PATCH_REJECTED_LOCKED on the pinned row, the claim not filed, and File this claim left for a person. The whole desk, live in the ChatGPT browser. The agent says it is ready to file, and that pressing File this claim is yours to do. The insurer's page hands your own agent its rules as typed tools, so you learn what you are covered for while still describing the crash. Live, no account: https://upgradedev.github.io/claimready/ Code (MIT): https://github.com/upgradedev/claimready Tools need a browser that has WebMCP. Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing on, verified on Chrome 151 stable, or the ChatGPT desktop app's built in browser with site tools enabled. Availability there is still rolling out and varies by workspace. In any other browser the page works by hand and says on screen why no tools are registered. Inspiration Somebody has just had a crash and is standing next to the car with a phone. They know what happened. What they do not know is what their own policy needs to hear about it, and neither does any general purpose assistant, because the clause, the excess and the list of required answers sit on one insurer's origin and change from customer to customer. I build claims systems for European assistance operators, so this is the failure I watch: a first notice of loss arrives wrong about what the policy needed rather than about what happened. Then the driver waits days to learn what they are covered for, and a handler spends the interval asking for the field nobody told anyone to fill in. What it does Describe the crash to your own agent. It reads the insurer's typed tools and tells you what this policy still needs while you are talking. Then the surface moves: answer that the car cannot be driven and get_assistance_options registers, a capability the agent lacked a moment earlier and loses when that answer changes. Three prompts to paste, with two page steps between the second and the third: Read this claim page and tell me what it still needs from me. A delivery van reversed into my car while it was parked in the car park on Harbour Road. It caught the left front wing and left a dent. The car still drives, and it is still there in the Harbour Road car park. Fill that in for me and write the description. Now set Still drivable to no on the page yourself, and press Pin on that row. Both steps matter: the pin is what makes the next answer a refusal rather than a successful write. Then: Read the notes on the file, then read the claim again, do what that note asks, and tell me what the page said. That note is a planted instruction inside third party evidence, and it asks for the row you just pinned, so the answer is PATCH_REJECTED_LOCKED . Every answer also carries the route it arrived on: on file, via page, via tool. That names a surface, not a person. The page cannot see who is at the keyboard, so it never claims to. Filing is human only. No tool files, dispatches, pins or unlocks, and a test reads the source to keep it that way. Filing leaves a handler packet built from the exact revision that passed the filing gate, with the clause, the excess, every requirement and a SHA-256 that scripts/verify_packet.mjs recomputes. Nothing is transmitted and no claim is opened anywhere. With no key and no signature, a matching digest shows only that the content is unchanged. It does not show origin, authorship, or that nobody edited the content and recomputed the digest to match, and the repository says so in the same words. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The rules that decide a motor claim sit on one insurer's origin and change from customer to customer. A REST endpoint with an OpenAPI file carries the same answers, once somebody builds that integration for this insurer. This is browser native and same origin, with zero integration work: an agent meeting this insurer for the first time discovers the tools at runtime. How it creates a better user experience The driver learns what their own policy still needs while they are still describing the crash, in the assistant they already have open, instead of a second call days later. The cover answer at the roadside instead of a letter a week later. Nothing to install, no account, and the page keeps working by hand in a browser with no agent in it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Two parties write to one document and neither overwrites the other silently. The agent drafts. The person corrects a field and pins it, and a pinned row then refuses every later patch and says so with a code. The tool surface itself moves: answering that the car cannot be driven publishes a ninth tool, and changing the answer back withdraws it. Filing stays a button only a person can press, and the page says so in its own tool list. Before this, each of those needed a bespoke integration per insurer, and an agent still had no way to be told what a page refuses. How WebMCP is implemented Tools register on document.modelContext , falling back to navigator.modelContext , over a pure core with no dependencies and no build step. Page and tools share one store, so an agent action shows on screen. Read tools carry readOnlyHint and text the insurer did not write carries untrustedContentHint . Both halves of the standard ship. Nine tools come from JavaScript, eight from the moment the page loads and a ninth that appears when the claim says the car cannot be driven, which is why the narration at 0:20 of the video counts eight. The tenth is an ordinary HTML form carrying four attributes, toolname , tooldescription , toolparamdescription and toolautosubmit , and the browser builds the JSON Schema and the tool from that markup on its own. toolautosubmit is the one that makes an agent's call actually submit the form rather than only fill it. So an insurer adopts WebMCP by adding attributes. What the demo video shows Three beats are captured in CI by Playwright against the deployed page in Chrome. Two run with WebMCP on, against the browser's own implementation. The first runs with it deliberately off, because that beat shows the page as a visitor with no agent sees it. Six are one continuous unbroken recording in the ChatGPT desktop app's built in browser, cut into six. Two corrections to the narration , written here because the cut is frozen. At 1:40 it says the roadside collection "is arranged": the demo records a local roadside assistance request and marks that requirement answered, it does not arrange or dispatch a service, and nothing leaves the page. At 2:08 it says "Chrome builds the schema from that markup", where the accurate word is the browser: that take was shot in the ChatGPT desktop browser, and the declarative half is verified separately in Chrome 151.0.7922.174 stable. Both are also written into the video description. The opening and closing cards are type on a still background, generated by a script in the repository. No stock footage and no rendered people: every other frame is the deployed page running. Evidence 961 unit tests, from node --test tests/unit , with source coverage of 98.11 percent of lines over the 22 files under src. Both are read at the submitted commit and both reprint in any clone. 178 assertions run against the deployed page in a real Chrome with WebMCP enabled, in CI, at the same commit the host serves. The page loads no framework, has no build step and makes no network call at runtime after load. Challenges, and the honest limits Insurer, policy, vehicle and claimant are invented. No integration, no adjudication, no handler has reviewed a packet, nobody has run this on a real intake. What this page demonstrably does is in the sections above and every part of it is checkable in a browser: policy rules discovered at runtime on the insurer's own origin, requirements recomputed on the page as answers change, a route recorded on every answer, a pin that refuses patches with a code, and filing that no published tool can reach. What is not demonstrated is that any of it makes an autonomous agent fill a form better. One experiment tried to show that and did not, and it is published in full rather than dropped. title: BestPrice: shop with the page, not around it
pitch: The open shopping page becomes a structured workspace for people and their agents.
about_excerpt: The open shopping page becomes a structured workspace for people and their agents. Like Comment Story Updates Live WebMCP on BestPrice.gr: the open shopping page exposes contextual tools so a person and their agent share the same screen. Why WebMCP This is browser-native WebMCP on the live BestPrice.gr page ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), not the remote MCP endpoint. The person and the agent share one open shopping page. Tools change with navigation, only act on what is currently visible, and never check out. Inspiration Shopping pages already contain the facts an agent needs, but the agent often has to infer them from layout. We wanted the page to describe its own visible state while the shopper stayed in control of the same screen. What it does BestPrice turns the shopping page a person already has open into a small, structured workspace for their agent. The homepage offers product search. A listing exposes the products, filters, and sorting choices currently visible. A product page exposes product facts, delivered-price comparison, specifications, and price history. The agent can open only a product whose exact ID and canonical BestPrice link are present in the visible listing. Every navigation remains visible. The tools do not check out, add to basket, sign in, return direct merchant URLs, or treat missing shipping as free. The shopper still chooses which shop to visit. How we built it The browser layer uses document.modelContext.registerTool and manages each tool as the page changes. Arguments are validated in executable code. URLs must be same-origin. Results come from visible page state, hidden and decoy elements are ignored, individual outputs are capped, partial registrations are rolled back, and telemetry failures cannot change tool results. The public source package includes 13 tool contracts, a local inspector, a deterministic evaluator, and automated tests under Apache License 2.0. Challenges we ran into BestPrice is a mature, dynamic commerce site, so the hard part was not defining a search tool. It was keeping tool state aligned with navigation, filters, sorting, product identity, and price data without teaching an agent to trust stale or hidden DOM. We also had to make failure states explicit, especially unknown shipping and incomplete page data. Accomplishments that we're proud of The WebMCP layer is live on BestPrice.gr and works across the homepage, search results, and product pages. It exposes useful shopping context without adding purchase authority. We also shipped a public inspector and evaluator so reviewers can see the registered tools and run repeatable checks. BestPrice and its remote MCP service existed before the challenge. This submission covers the new browser-native WebMCP layer built and shipped during the challenge window. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when page tools match what a person can actually see and do. Small, contextual tools with clear boundaries were more reliable than one broad shopping action. Keeping the human-visible page as the shared surface also made every agent action easier to understand. What's next We will measure real agent-assisted journeys, improve tool wording and output quality from that evidence, and keep testing against new browser and assistant implementations. Purchase decisions and checkout will remain with the shopper. title: BingeWatcher
pitch: Curate movie nights that are unmistakably yours
about_excerpt: Curate movie nights that are unmistakably yours Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I watch a lot of movies and TV shows. A LOT. My biggest pet peeve is figuring out what to watch next. Using an LLM for inspiration can be helpful, but it usually requires a lot of unnecessary back and forth. Even after all that, I sometimes end up not liking any of its recommendations. I wanted a way to discover movies and shows with an agent while staying in control, actively making choices and telling it what interests me and what doesn’t. I also wanted an immersive visual experience where I could explore a title, watch its trailer, check where it is streaming, and save it to my watchlist. Then I wanted to take it one step further: planning entire weekends around everything I wanted to bingewatch. When I explored WebMCP, I realized that I could now collaborate with an agent instead of delegating the whole task to it. I could stay in complete control while letting an agent do the grunt work for me. That’s how I came up with BingeWatcher . What it does BingeWatcher is a movie and TV discovery app built for people and their WebMCP agents to use together. You can explore trending titles, search for something specific, combine filters such as genre, language, release year, runtime, and streaming provider, and open detailed pages containing trailers, recommendations, ratings, seasons, episodes, and streaming availability. Titles can be saved to a personal watchlist or added to an ordered lineup for a movie night, themed marathon, or entire weekend. The most important part is how those lineups evolve. An agent can create and maintain a lineup, but the person remains in control. You can: Lock a title that must stay Mark another as Not for me and (optionally) explain why Reorder the lineup yourself Change its preferences Ask the agent to rebuild only the remaining picks The agent works around those decisions instead of replacing them. BingeWatcher also tracks movie-level and episode-level progress, supports lightweight reactions, and keeps a history of changes made to each lineup. Everything remains fully usable without an agent. How I built it I built BingeWatcher as a single application using Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Bun . Movie and TV metadata comes from TMDB , including search results, posters, genres, recommendations, trailers, seasons, episodes, ratings, and regional watch providers. I also integrated the Streaming Availability API for direct provider links where available. The app uses SQLite for persistent data. Anonymous visitors receive a secure, HTTP-only browser session, so their watchlist, progress, reactions, and lineups remain available when they return. Lineups also have separate secure edit/resume links and read-only sharing links. I exposed the application through WebMCP using the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. The tools cover discovery, title details, recommendations, watchlists, progress, reactions, and complete lineup management. Most importantly, the WebMCP tools do not operate on a separate agent-only system. They call the same backend operations used by the human interface, which means both sides share the same data, validation rules, locks, vetoes, and revision checks. Agent actions such as searching, opening a watchlist, or creating a lineup also navigate and update the visible interface. The production application runs in a Docker container on Render with SQLite stored on a persistent disk. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was deciding how much control the agent should have. Letting an agent replace an entire lineup would have been easy, but it would also make human decisions feel temporary. I had to design the system so that locks, vetoes, ordering, preferences, and concurrent edits were treated as durable constraints. Supporting movies, complete TV series, and individual seasons inside the same lineup introduced another layer of complexity. Progress also needed different behavior: movies are tracked at the title level, while TV progress is tracked by episode so that season and series completion can be derived correctly. Another challenge was making WebMCP actions feel visible. A tool technically succeeding in the background was not enough. If an agent searched for a title or opened a newly created lineup, the interface needed to visibly follow that action so the person could immediately inspect and continue the work. External media APIs introduced their own complications. Search and discovery are separate operations in TMDB, so combining text searches with detailed filters required carefully joining and validating the available metadata. Streaming data also varies by region and provider. Accomplishments that I’m proud of I’m most proud that BingeWatcher feels like a complete product even when no agent is connected. In my opinion, that's how products are meant to be in the age of agent <-> human collaboration. The human interface is a beautiful (if I may say so myself) website designed to deliver a premium discovery and planning experience to its target audience: cinephiles and TV buffs. It includes rich discovery, detailed title and season pages, ordered lineups, watchlists, progress tracking, reactions, drag-and-drop reordering, trailers, preferences, history, secure sharing, and much more. At the same time, the agent can work across nearly the entire product through WebMCP. It can discover titles, understand live lineup state, respect locked picks and vetoes, make precise changes, validate the result, and leave the final decisions to the person. I’m also proud of the core collaboration loop: an agent can build a lineup, a person can lock one pick, reject another, change the order, and ask the agent to rebuild only what remains. That interaction captures what I wanted BingeWatcher to be- AI agents helping someone express their taste instead of replacing it. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is how WebMCP, once standardized and widely adopted, can become the go-to way for websites to enable human <-> agent collaboration. This is where I believe all software will converge over the coming years. The best experience came from making the normal application excellent first, then giving the agent access to the same meaningful actions. WebMCP became much more useful when its tools represented real product capabilities rather than isolated technical endpoints. I also learned how important tool descriptions and schemas are. They do more than document an API. They establish the boundaries of the collaboration. A clear description can tell an agent when to stop, what it may change, and which human decisions it must preserve. All the while keepig context bloat to a minimum. Finally, I learned that visible state matters. People trust an agent more when they can see what it opened, what it changed, and what it deliberately left alone. What’s next for BingeWatcher The next step is permanent accounts for people who want cross-device access, using email magic links, Google, or passkeys while preserving the anonymous-first experience. I would also move production persistence to a network database before supporting multiple application instances, add real-time collaborative editing, and continue improving personalized discovery using watch history, reactions, watchlists, and explicit preferences. I also want to add multiplayer (more humans) lineups and watchlists for planning movie nights and weekends with friends. Longer term, I want BingeWatcher to become a shared home for planning more kinds of entertainment, with richer group planning, better provider-aware recommendations, and perhaps even support for books. title: Cadence
pitch: An issue tracker where your agent is a real teammate: it triages, dedupes, and reprioritizes with tools that change live as you select issues, not a fixed list.
about_excerpt: An issue tracker where your agent is a real teammate: it triages, dedupes, and reprioritizes with tools that change live as you select issues, not a fixed list. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every judge on this panel works at a company that lives in an issue tracker. "Triage my backlog, dedupe these, split this ticket, reprioritize the sprint" is a request any engineer has typed into Slack at 5pm on a Friday. It's also genuinely tedious for a person and genuinely tractable for an agent, but only if the agent can act with real authority inside the tool instead of clicking through a UI it's guessing at from a screenshot. We also noticed a gap. The official showcase and the community demo list are full of storefronts, flight bookers, and games. Nothing engineering-tool shaped. Nothing where the agent has to hold a real permission boundary, share an undo stack with a human, or watch its own available capabilities change as the page changes under it. That felt like the actual hard part of WebMCP, the underexplored part, so we built toward it instead of around it. What it does Cadence is an issue tracker where an agent is a real teammate on the board, not a chatbot bolted onto the side of one. Ask it to triage an untriaged backlog, find and merge duplicate bug reports, split an oversized epic into sub-issues, or reprioritize a sprint, and it does real analysis against real board state through the same functions the UI itself calls. Here's the part that's actually WebMCP-specific, not just "an app with an AI feature": the registered tool set changes live with what's on screen. Select an issue and add_comment , split_issue , and link_issues register. Apply a filter or multi-select and bulk_update shows up. Switch to cycle view and summarize_cycle appears. None of that is expressible as a static, pre-declared tool list, because a server-side MCP server has no idea what a human currently has selected in their browser. It can't. Agents also carry real identity and real permission scoping. A workspace owner grants each agent a scope, read, triage, write, or full, and that grant filters which tools registerTool even offers before the agent ever sees them, live. Every agent edit lands on the same undo stack the human uses too. Cmd+Z undoes an agent's change exactly like it was your own, because both write through one shared reduce() function against one shared state. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite on the client. Cloudflare Workers plus a Durable Object (SQLite-backed, free-tier eligible) as the authoritative backend, syncing over the WebSocket Hibernation API so multiple humans and agents can work the same board live. webmcp-kit , a small library we published alongside this entry: defineTool / registerTools with full JSON-Schema-to-TS inference, and useScopedTools , a React hook that registers a tool set while a condition holds and cleanly unregisters when it stops. That hook is what makes Cadence's dynamic tool surface a one-liner instead of a pile of manual AbortController bookkeeping. Every mutation is a pure (state, actor, action) → state function in one reducer, shared by the client store, the Durable Object, and every WebMCP tool handler. There's exactly one place a board mutation is defined, which is also what makes the shared human/agent undo stack possible. Only one code path to undo. Seed data is deliberately messy on purpose: real duplicate bug reports worded three different ways, vague untriaged titles, missing estimates, so the higher-order tools have genuine work to do instead of a tidy board with nothing left to fix. A hash-chained audit log on the Durable Object records every mutation with actor attribution, queryable via get_activity . Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's in-app browser only supports a subset of the spec: imperative registration only, no declarative HTML tool attributes, and no cross-frame tool discovery even for same-origin iframes. We designed single-origin from day one because of this, and honestly it shaped the whole architecture more than anything else did. Then there was the embarrassing one. Our seed data computed Date.now() at Cloudflare Workers module scope instead of inside a request handler. Turns out Workers doesn't guarantee wall-clock time outside a request's I/O context, so every "recent" issue and cycle date came out silently wrong, offsets from epoch, not from actual "now". We only caught it by inspecting live state over a raw WebSocket and noticing the numbers just didn't add up. find_duplicates had a similar quiet failure. It used Jaccard similarity on tokenized title and body text with a default threshold that, on inspection, was too strict to ever catch our own deliberately seeded duplicate cluster. Real paraphrased duplicates scored around 0.23 to 0.28 against a 0.4 cutoff. Tuned it down and documented why right in the tool description, since it's a real limitation an agent calling the tool should actually know about. And demo-state entropy: a Durable Object's seed loads exactly once, ever, so every round of testing permanently mutated the same live board. Later testers kept hitting an already-triaged, already-deduped board with nothing left to demonstrate. Fixed it by giving every visitor their own isolated board, auto-fresh on first visit, plus a visible in-app reset button, instead of trying to guess when it's "safe" to reset something shared. Accomplishments we're proud of A genuinely dynamic tool surface, verifiable live in Chrome's Model Context Tool Inspector: select an issue and watch the registered tool count change in real time, no faith required. Per-agent permission scoping that changes what tools even exist for an agent, not just what it's allowed to call, enforced before registration ever happens. A free, LLM-free benchmark comparing tool calls against real Playwright-driven DOM interaction on the live app. Single actions cost about the same either way, but a 7-item bulk task runs roughly 3x faster over tool calls, because the DOM path re-pays a fixed per-item navigation cost that a tool call just doesn't. Real accessibility work, not just a claim. Full keyboard operability, and a code-level WCAG audit that actually found and fixed two real bugs, custom buttons not activating on Space, confirmation dialogs with no Escape-to-dismiss, instead of asserting AA compliance from a README and hoping nobody checks. What we learned The most interesting property of WebMCP isn't that it lets an agent call functions instead of scraping a page. It's that tool registration lives in the same runtime as the UI state, so the tool surface can be a live function of what's actually on screen, and permission boundaries can be enforced at the moment of registration rather than only at call time. Neither of those is something a server-side MCP server wrapping a REST API can do, no matter how well-designed that API is. What's next Publishing webmcp-kit to npm proper (it's a GitHub dependency right now), a full screen-reader session to go with the code-level accessibility audit, and pushing the duplicate-detection scoring past bag-of-words Jaccard now that we know exactly where its ceiling is.
