title: Careers WebMCP
pitch: The careers page is the connector.
about_excerpt: The careers page is the connector. Like Comment Story Updates The argument. Every way an agent can help you on a website today requires taking your authority and handing it to the agent. A scraper gets your whole session and guesses meaning from markup. An MCP connector gets a token you pasted and acts on your behalf forever, out of sight of the page. In both cases the agent's power is a copy of yours, and the site has no say in what it can do. WebMCP inverts that: the publisher defines the capabilities, so the publisher defines the limits. That is the whole reason this project exists. A careers site can expose "fill in my application" while making "submit it" structurally impossible for an agent — not guarded, not confirmed, impossible — because the site owns both the tool surface and the code behind it. Live demo: https://careers-webmcp.vercel.app/careers/open-positions Repository: https://github.com/alliecatowo/careers-webmcp The problem Job seekers do an enormous amount of unpaid data entry, and candidate funnels leak in three predictable places: search that can't answer the question you actually have ("staff or above, SF or remote, at least $220k" is not a keyword); the account wall standing between a person and a role they have already decided to apply for; and retyping the same nine fields at every employer. All three are data entry. None of them is a decision. The audience is candidates browsing employer career sites — and the employers who lose them. Why WebMCP specifically A careers site is a destination you visit occasionally and would never configure as a permanent integration. Nobody installs an MCP connector for one employer's job board, uses it for ninety minutes, and maintains it. WebMCP covers exactly that long tail: the capability arrives with the page, runs on the session the human already has, and leaves when the visit ends. What it is A working careers portal for a fictional employer, fully usable with no agent present. When WebMCP is available it registers eighteen candidate-facing tools on document.modelContext: page context, semantic job search, job detail, navigation to any page on the site by name, control of the site's own search view, the employer's own careers content as structured data, saved jobs, application drafts with revision-safe patching, field focus, account sign-up, submission hand-off, and handle-based CSV export. Try it Open https://careers-webmcp.vercel.app/careers/open-positions and ask your agent to find staff-level-or-above engineering roles in San Francisco or remote, paying at least $220k base. Watch the site's own search box type that query and the job list narrow live — that's the real page reacting, not a summary in a side panel. Ask it to start an application on one of those roles and fill in what's missing; the draft's revision counter moves on every write, whether the write came from the agent or from you. Then try to get it to submit that application. It can't. grep -cE "submitApplication\(|completeSignUp\(" src/webmcp/tools.ts returns 0 — submitApplication and completeSignUp were never registered as tools, so there is nothing for an agent to call. The last click is always yours. How this makes the UX better Today, "better UX with an agent" almost always means a chat panel bolted onto the side of a page, describing back to you what it thinks you see. Here the agent's output is the page: a compound filter query becomes the site's own search box typing itself and the visible list narrowing; "find that job" becomes the real job page opening in your real tab; "fill in my application" becomes the real form filling in front of you, field by field, while you can still click into any of it and correct it by hand. A visitor with no agent sees zero extra UI and loses nothing; a visitor with an agent gets the same site, faster, with the boring parts done for them. What people and agents can do together that was hard before You ask one compound question the board has no filter UI for, and the agent answers it and applies it to the page you are looking at — typing into the site's own search box, character by character, while the visible list narrows. You click Save with your own hand and the agent sees it, because it reads the same store the button writes to, not a copy. You and the agent co-edit one application draft: it fills the empty fields, you write your own cover note, and every agent write carries the revision it last read, so a stale write is rejected with STALE_APPLICATION and your text always wins. And the agent can reason over the entire catalog without pulling twenty job descriptions into its context, because the site hands it a CSV handle it pages through. Where the agent stops, and why you can verify it Two tools deliberately never complete. careers_create_account fills the real sign-up form and returns; careers_submit_application runs the same validation the human Submit button runs, opens the draft and rings the button. Both return status: "awaiting_human_confirmation". There is no confirm: true escape hatch because there is no second code path: src/webmcp/tools.ts never imports the function that submits an application or the function that creates a session, and each of those has exactly one caller in the entire codebase, both inside a human-clicked button. One grep proves it. The agent does the typing; the person stays the person, and sends the thing. How WebMCP was implemented A client provider feature-detects document.modelContext and registers eighteen tools once per page load, unregistering via an AbortSignal, guarded by a WeakSet against React StrictMode double-mounts; registration failure is swallowed so it can never break the site. Nothing reads or drives the DOM. The human UI and the tools import the same module-level functions from src/domain — search runs the identical deterministic scorer behind the visible job list, so the page and the agent cannot disagree about what matched; mutations run the same validators as the form; navigation uses the app router, so the user's real tab moves. Context isn't scraped or parsed: the pages publish it. Tools carry JSON Schema inputs, WebMCP annotations, AbortSignal support, a structured recoverable error model, and central output bounds with a truncated flag. A presence layer wraps each tool's execute at registration and pushes to a store the site's normal components subscribe to, so the agent's work appears in the real UI, and it builds its captions from counts and enums only, never from site text, so a prompt injection in a job description has nowhere to land. No LLM, no AI SDK, no chat panel, no MCP server, no recommendation model, no DOM automation. The site is the integration. The bigger picture Imagine every Greenhouse board, Workday portal, university portal, marketplace and support site exposing its own semantics this way. Nobody installs hundreds of connectors; the open web becomes its own integration registry. This is one employer's site, built the way the rest could be. Built on the MIT-licensed Baalvion Jobs Portal, pinned at a specific upstream commit. The careers UI and admin dashboards are upstream; the WebMCP layer, presence layer, context bridge, semantic search, candidate session, saved jobs, revision-protected application drafts, sign-up hand-off, exports, tests and docs are the challenge-period contribution — 192 files changed, over 14,000 lines added, on top of that pinned commit. How we built it Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Zustand for client state, on top of the MIT-licensed Baalvion Jobs Portal template. The WebMCP layer is additive: a client provider registers tools once per page load and every tool calls straight into the same domain functions the visible UI already uses, so there is exactly one implementation of "what jobs match this search" or "is this application valid," not two that can quietly drift apart. Challenges we ran into The hardest part wasn't registering tools — it was making sure two specific ones structurally could not finish without a human. That meant auditing the whole call graph so that careers_create_account and careers_submit_application have no path to the functions that actually create a session or submit an application, rather than relying on an if-check that a future edit could accidentally remove. Getting revision-safe co-editing right for the application draft was its own puzzle: a human typing a cover note and an agent filling other fields at the same time needed a merge rule where the human's text always wins, not just whoever saved last. Accomplishments that we're proud of Every mutation an agent can trigger runs through the exact same validators and store as a human click — there is no shadow code path for the agent, which is also what makes the "the agent can literally never press Submit" claim independently verifiable with a single grep rather than something you have to trust. title: Compass
pitch: Your personal context. Your rules. Your agent.
about_excerpt: Your personal context. Your rules. Your agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Personal agents become far more useful when they understand our current projects, open tasks, references, and decisions. But the obvious shortcut—handing an agent an entire personal workspace—creates an uncomfortable privacy and control tradeoff. We wanted a product where the user can see and change the boundary, not merely trust a broad authorization screen. Compass turns that boundary into a first-class object: a Context Pack. It is a temporary, understandable bundle of Spaces and selected items, further constrained by item type and live read/write switches. What it does Compass stores notes, tasks, bookmarks, and snippets locally in IndexedDB. Users can create Spaces, build Context Packs, search deterministically, link related items, complete tasks, and import or export a validated JSON backup. When WebMCP is available, Compass registers ten typed tools for reading the active context, listing Spaces, searching and retrieving items, reviewing recent activity, creating and updating items, completing tasks, linking records, and creating a new inactive Pack. Permission changes rebuild the registry immediately. Every handler repeats the permission and Pack checks, and agent writes appear live in the UI with readable audit entries and Undo. The included fictional Project Atlas workspace gives judges a safe, useful flow immediately: ask the agent to find launch blockers, create a high-priority task for the most urgent one, disable writes, confirm the write surface disappears, then undo an agent change. How we built it React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Vinext for the responsive interface Dexie over IndexedDB for local-first persistence and reactive updates Zod and closed JSON Schemas for import and tool-input validation The WebMCP imperative API with AbortController-managed registration Shared repository and permission modules for both UI and agent operations Vitest and fake-indexeddb for deterministic permission, validation, undo, registration, and end-to-end tool tests Cloudflare/OpenAI Sites deployment configuration Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making permissions a real runtime boundary rather than decorative switches. Tools must disappear when a capability is disabled, but a stale or in-flight handler also needs to reject the operation. We solved this with both dynamic registration and repeated handler-level gates. Undo also required careful design. We record the exact before-state inside the same repository layer used by agent writes, then associate the audit event with a bounded undo record. That keeps the feature explainable and avoids pretending the app has unlimited version history. Finally, strict import validation needed more than parsing JSON. Compass checks size, schema version, unexpected properties, safe URLs, unique identifiers, and references between Spaces, items, Packs, relations, settings, activity, and undo records before any replacement occurs. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete local-first product that remains useful without WebMCP support Ten real, typed tools backed by persistent application state Immediate permission-driven registration plus defense-in-depth handler checks Live UI refresh, transparent denial logging, and reversible agent writes A judge-ready fictional demo with no account, API key, or onboarding dependency Deterministic automated tests for the highest-risk trust boundaries What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when the website exposes meaningful domain operations rather than reproducing button clicks. A compact tool like search_personal_context can return ranked, permission-scoped records with stable IDs and clear provenance; the agent does not need to infer state from pixels. We also learned that tool metadata is part of the safety design. Concise descriptions, read-only hints, untrusted-content hints, closed schemas, and small structured responses give the client and model better information for deciding how to use a tool. What's next for Compass Optional end-to-end encrypted sync between a user's devices Pack expiration, scheduled deactivation, and per-tool rate limits Richer relation editing without exposing additional context Import adapters for common note and bookmark formats Signed export manifests and stronger local backup history Broader browser interoperability as the WebMCP specification evolves Built With cloudflare dexie indexeddb openai react typescript vite vitest webmcp zod Try it out compass-control-plane.alx21.chatgpt.site github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Alexander Ammann Like Share this project: Updates Alexander Ammann started this project — Aug 30, 2026 01:15 AM EDT

title: Cutoff
pitch: A restaurant operations desk where managers and browser agents replan orders, stock, labor, and handoffs before the supplier cutoff via WebMCP
about_excerpt: A restaurant operations desk where managers and browser agents replan orders, stock, labor, and handoffs before the supplier cutoff via WebMCP Like 2 Comment Story Updates Rosa’s absence triggers two releases and Nadia’s proposed 4-hour prep cover. Cancelled derby and private booking produce a 910-cover order preview before adoption. The agent records chicken at 30 kg on hand with 6 kg expiring. Manager actions and agent tool calls appear in one filterable service-day record. One desk connects Order, Stock, Labor, and Shift log through shared browser state. Inspiration Restaurant orders often lock at a supplier cutoff. The forecast may have been correct yesterday, but the shift changes in real time. A nearby event gets cancelled, a private booking arrives, a shelf count changes, or a staff member calls out. Those facts affect the order and roster together, yet they often live in separate notes or in the manager's head. I built Cutoff so a manager can state a change once and work through its effects with a browser agent on the same page. What it does Cutoff is a shift operations desk for a fictional restaurant. Order, Stock, Labor, and Shift log share one revisioned state inside the browser. The Saturday scenario starts with 1,140 covers, 95 required labor hours, and a 3,629-unit supplier order. An 80-person booking and a cancelled derby produce a preview of 910 covers, 76 hours, and a 2,767-unit order. Every changed line explains its reason before the manager adopts anything. Once the manager adopts the order, Labor reads the approved 910-cover plan. The agent can record an absence and propose releases or on-call cover without changing the roster until the manager approves it. A corrected stock count feeds the same state. Recording chicken at 30 kg on hand with 6 kg expiring changes the recommendation from 15 to 16 cases and raises the proposed order cost to 2,835 units. The agent can also save a bounded handoff for the next manager. Shift log joins the manager's actions and the agent's tool calls into one filterable record that can be downloaded as JSON. Why WebMCP The state that matters is not fully visible in the page. It includes local signals, shelf counts, quantity pins, roster absences, preview identifiers, and the current shared revision. An agent cannot recover that state reliably by reading pixels. Cutoff exposes this information through WebMCP. The manager gives the agent the task in plain language. The agent discovers the tools available on the current page, reads the latest revision, and uses the tools it needs. The manager never has to name a tool or copy values between systems. The result appears in the same interface the manager is already using. Proposed changes stay visible and reversible, while final approval remains with the manager. How I built it Cutoff is a static React and TypeScript application with no backend, account system, or application keys. It registers 16 hand-built tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each page exposes only the tools relevant to that section. Order has 6 tools at rest and 7 while a preview can be adopted. Labor follows the same pattern with 4 and 5 tools. Stock exposes 4 tools, and Shift log exposes 3. The two adoption tools exist only while their preview is current. Route changes replace the previous page's tools before navigation finishes. Every write requires expectedRevision . If another action has changed the state, the tool returns a structured stale-write error with the current revision instead of overwriting newer work. Human-entered text is marked as untrusted when it appears in tool results. Small deterministic engines calculate order quantities, labor demand, waste, and roster proposals. The visible controls and WebMCP tools call the same store methods, so the manager and agent cannot drift into separate versions of the plan. Challenges The hardest part was keeping previews, adoption, invalidation, undo, navigation, and tool registration consistent under one revision. A stock count must make an old order preview stale without invalidating an unrelated labor preview. Adopting an order must update labor demand. Changing pages must remove the previous tools before the agent continues. Undo must restore the saved plan without printing a breakdown that no longer matches it. The interface also had to remain readable as the product expanded from one order page into a four-section desk. I tested the final layouts on laptop and mobile widths and added direct links from agent-change notifications to the affected row or receipt. What I learned WebMCP works best when the page and its tools share the same product model. The tools should expose state and calculations that an agent cannot obtain reliably from the rendered interface. The page should still show every result and keep consequential decisions under human control. Tool availability can also communicate state. An adoption tool appearing only when a valid preview exists is clearer and safer than exposing an action that may fail or apply to an old proposal. Accomplishments 16 contextual WebMCP tools across 4 decision pages Dynamic preview and adoption tool lifecycles One shared revision with structured stale-write recovery Reversible local order and labor adoption Agent-driven navigation between sections Local handoff and Shift-log JSON exports 111 deterministic tests and a clean production build Direct production testing in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled Nothing sends an order, updates a rota, contacts a supplier, or writes restaurant data to a server. All names, events, inventory, quantities, and costs are fictional. title: HOUSELIGHTS
pitch: HOUSELIGHTS turns seat maps into 14 WebMCP tools, letting AI find and hold the best seats while people see every action and retain final purchase authority.
about_excerpt: HOUSELIGHTS turns seat maps into 14 WebMCP tools, letting AI find and hold the best seats while people see every action and retain final purchase authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Buying theater tickets should be a perfect job for an AI assistant: compare hundreds of seats, balance price against view quality, and keep adjacent seats together. In practice, agents see most seat maps as pixels. They must guess where to click, and the person cannot easily understand or correct what the agent is doing. HOUSELIGHTS asks: what if the box office exposed its real structure to the agent while the person stayed in control? What it does HOUSELIGHTS is a shared live-theater box office for a person and an AI agent. Through 14 WebMCP tools, an agent can search performances, inspect every seat's availability and price, compare sightline, acoustic, and value scores, recommend adjacent seats, and place time-limited holds. Those actions immediately appear on the same seat map the person is viewing. Agent-held seats pulse amber with a visible countdown. The person can inspect, veto, release, or move them into the cart before completing checkout. The agent provides machine-speed comparison across the whole house. The person keeps taste, context, and final purchase authority. How we built it HOUSELIGHTS uses vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS with one shared in-memory AppStore . Human interactions and agent tools mutate the same store, preventing the UI and agent from developing separate versions of the box office. The top-level page registers 14 imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Every tool has a JSON Schema contract and returns structured data rather than forcing the agent to scrape the DOM. Core tools include: get_seat_map for structured availability, pricing, and seat-quality data recommend_seats for budget-aware adjacent-seat ranking hold_seats for visible, expiring reservations get_board_state for shared human-agent context announce_to_user for visual and screen-reader announcements undo_last_action for reversing agent-authored changes checkout for requesting—but not completing—human confirmation The checkout form is deliberately not exposed as an agent tool. Its confirmation token is bound to the exact cart snapshot, and only a trusted human submission can create the order. The app is deployed on Cloudflare Pages and includes a fallback registry so the same tool handlers can be tested in browsers without WebMCP enabled. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was making collaboration visible rather than merely functional. A successful tool call is not enough if the person cannot see what changed. We connected every hold, cart update, announcement, and expiration to the live seat map and activity feed. The second challenge was defining the purchase boundary. The agent needs enough authority to be useful, but it must not silently complete a transaction. We therefore separated requesting checkout from confirming checkout and bound confirmation to the reviewed cart. We also had to handle expiring holds, conflicting seat requests, stale confirmations, undo ownership, performance switching, and accessibility without letting human and agent state diverge. What we learned WebMCP works best when it exposes an application's real domain model—not when it recreates screen clicking with different syntax. We also learned that accessibility and agent usability reinforce each other. HOUSELIGHTS uses a real ARIA grid, keyboard navigation, live-region announcements, reduced-motion support, and state indicators that do not rely on color alone. The same explicit structure that helps assistive technology also gives agents a safer and more understandable interface. What's next HOUSELIGHTS is currently a client-side interactive simulation. A production version would connect the tool surface to authoritative inventory, atomic server-side seat locks, persistent sessions, idempotent checkout, and a real payment provider. The larger idea extends beyond ticketing: agents should handle structured comparison and reversible preparation while people retain informed authority over consequential actions. The project taught me how to design agent tools around a real domain model while keeping consequential actions visible, reversible, and under human control. title: ihateaudio
pitch: 49 free browser audio tools, now agent-operable via WebMCP. One sentence; your agent does the work; audio never leaves your tab.
about_excerpt: 49 free browser audio tools, now agent-operable via WebMCP. One sentence; your agent does the work; audio never leaves your tab. Like Comment Story Updates Say it once — your agent trims, cleans, levels and exports across 49 browser tools, and the audio never leaves your tab. From the homepage, the agent calls list_tools and open_tool to route itself to the right tool. The agent drives the real waveform and controls while you watch — and nothing is uploaded. ihateaudio is 49 free audio tools that run entirely in your browser — trim, convert, clean, split, master — with no upload, no account, and no file‑size limit. For the WebMCP Challenge, we made every one of them operable by an AI agent, and wired them together so a single request runs as a complete, cross‑tool workflow. The problem Ask any AI agent to fix a recording and it hits a wall. It can't hear, it can't run a DSP chain, and its only real option is "upload it to some server." That's exactly what people with a private voice note, an unreleased track, or a confidential interview won't do. Audio has been a blind spot for agents. What it does Open ihateaudio.com in an agent browser and say: "I have a voice note — make it podcast‑ready." The agent: Calls list_tools , reads the site's catalog, and open_tool to open the trimmer. You choose the file — once. (A web page can't read your disk; that's the privacy guarantee, not a limitation.) set_trim keeps the part that matters, then send_to_tool hands the result to the silence remover — already loaded, no re‑upload. set_silence_removal tightens the pauses; every candidate cut is highlighted on the waveform. send_to_tool → normalizer, set_loudness_target({ platform: "podcast" }) . render_preview , then export_download when you say so. One sentence. Four tools. One click from you. The agent ran the pipeline; you kept the judgment. Why WebMCP is the right fit The agent stands on the same page as the person and uses tools the page itself defines. It gets back numbers — a duration, a list of quiet gaps, a slider value — never the audio. The samples never leave the tab. Generic pixel‑guessing automation can't drive a waveform with drag handles, or a threshold slider whose effect is a re‑scan of every sample. set_silence_removal({ threshold: -45, minimumGapSec: 0.5 }) does it exactly, and you watch it happen. What people and agents can do together that was impossible before A whole job, hands‑free after one click — trim, clean, level, export, across four tools, from one sentence. Human judgment stays human. Which pause matters, whether the voice still sounds natural — you decide, on the waveform. The agent measures and sets. Zero‑upload agent audio. Loudness, true peak, and quiet‑gap timing are computed in the tab and returned as numbers. An agent reasons about a recording it will never hold. One toolkit, learned once. Five base tools on every page plus one named action per tool. Learn the trimmer, you already know the equalizer. How we built it The site's 49 pages share one runtime, so the WebMCP layer lives in one place and every page inherits it: Host boundary detects document.modelContext (ChatGPT) and navigator.modelContext (Chrome), registers on every host found, and degrades to an ordinary editor when neither exists. Site tools on every page: list_tools (a catalog built at deploy time from each page's own manifest, so names can't drift) and open_tool (replies before navigating, so the host never loses a result). Base tools on every tool page: inspect, set format, render_preview , send_to_tool (a lossless hand‑off via IndexedDB), load_audio_from_url , and export_download . 33 named actions — set_trim , set_silence_removal , set_equalizer (8 bands), set_stems (4 stems), and more — each a real JSON schema. Agent values are clamped to the control's range and applied by firing the same events a human drag does, so live drawings and previews respond. 40 browser tests shim a WebMCP host on both document and navigator , call every action on every page, and assert the visible controls, reports, and the tool‑to‑tool hand‑off. Built with Astro + TypeScript, the Web Audio API, a WASM ffmpeg/AI tier, and IndexedDB, deployed on Cloudflare Workers. New for the Challenge (prior work vs. new work) ihateaudio existed before as a browser audio‑tool site. Everything agent‑related is new , all dated in the public commit history from 2026‑08‑26 onward: src/lib/webmcp.ts , src/lib/agent.ts , src/lib/site-tools.ts , the agent layer in src/lib/tool.ts , 33 page manifests, and the tests. The split is documented in docs/WEBMCP.md in the repo. Try it yourself ChatGPT desktop app — Work chat, ⌘⇧B for the built‑in browser, Settings › Browser › Permissions › Enable site tools → open https://ihateaudio.com → "make this voice note podcast‑ready." Chrome 149+ — enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , open any tool page, and drive the tools from DevTools › Application › WebMCP. Free, for everyone, forever. Any agent that can open a web page now has a complete audio studio — and the audio never leaves the tab. title: Inference Chip Index
pitch: A source-linked MLPerf leaderboard that lets people and AI agents compare inference hardware safely in the same visible workspace.
about_excerpt: A source-linked MLPerf leaderboard that lets people and AI agents compare inference hardware safely in the same visible workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Inference-hardware comparisons are easy to get wrong. A leaderboard can silently mix workloads, scenarios, accuracy targets, units, or system-level and per-accelerator numbers. Traditional browser automation makes that worse because an agent has to infer meaning from controls and tables. I wanted a safer collaboration model: the website should expose the exact research operations it supports, the agent should act on the same visible interface as the human, and every answer should remain traceable to immutable benchmark evidence. What it does Inference Chip Index turns official MLPerf Inference v6.0 results into workload-specific, source-linked comparisons. Its leaderboard now exposes four imperative WebMCP tools: list_inference_slices discovers valid exact comparison boundaries. configure_inference_leaderboard changes the filters visible to the human. compare_inference_accelerators compares 2–8 accelerator families inside one exact slice and renders the result on the page. clear_inference_comparison removes the shared comparison without resetting the leaderboard. The central safety rule is simple: a tool cannot claim that one chip is universally fastest. Every comparison is constrained to the same release, Closed division, workload, scenario, accuracy target, metric, and unit. Results include immutable GitHub source URLs and SHA-256 hashes. If evidence is missing, the tool returns an explicit missing-evidence reason instead of inventing a number. How I built it The application uses Next.js App Router, TypeScript, React, and Cloudflare Workers through OpenNext. The normalized data is generated deterministically from the pinned MLPerf Inference v6.0 commit 4d3916ac9cf474b679cdfcf492d43a0559418ad1 . During the WebMCP Challenge submission period I added the browser-native collaboration layer with the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Pure validation and comparison logic lives in src/webmcp/leaderboard-tools.ts ; registration and visible state updates live in the leaderboard React component. An AbortController unregisters the tools cleanly when the component unmounts. The WebMCP layer reuses the same checked-in dataset and exact-slice invariants as the site. It does not introduce a parallel ranking implementation, fetch untrusted runtime data, invoke paid endpoints, or expose secrets. Tool input schemas reject unknown fields and validate all slice IDs, vendors, submitters, grouping modes, metric views, and accelerator slugs. Challenge-period work The reproducible data index and Lucid API existed before the event. The WebMCP extension was built specifically during the challenge window. Public commits 7b89ee5 through fd9f65f add the imperative tools, shared-state UI, tests, documentation, security header, MIT license, and production URL documentation. The public deployment includes that extension. Challenges I ran into Converting a dense technical leaderboard into a small, predictable tool surface without duplicating ranking logic. Keeping agent actions visible to the human while preserving manual control of the same React state. Preventing incompatible benchmark dimensions from being compared even when an agent supplies plausible-looking inputs. Explaining absent results as evidence gaps rather than treating them as zero. Preserving immutable provenance in every structured response without overwhelming the visual interface. Accomplishments that I am proud of One agent call can build a three-vendor comparison that immediately appears in the human's browser. Every returned row stays inside an exact benchmark slice and links back to immutable source evidence. The tool surface is read-only with respect to servers and payments, while still making useful visible changes locally. The app contains 145 verified results, 50 submitted systems, 13 normalized accelerators, and 9 exact slices. The implementation passes type checking, 21 automated tests, and a production build. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes domain invariants, not when it merely turns every button into a tool. A good tool contract can make an unsafe action impossible, keep agent and human context synchronized, and communicate uncertainty as structured data. I also learned that browser-native tools can be a better accessibility and audit surface than invisible automation: the human sees the filters change, sees the comparison render, and can verify the same immutable sources the agent used. What's next Add WebMCP tools for methodology explanations and dataset-diff inspection. Let a human pin a baseline row and ask an agent for compatible deltas. Extend the importer to later MLPerf releases while preserving immutable snapshots and tombstones. Add signed dataset manifests so agents can verify provenance independently. Study how WebMCP tool descriptions affect agent selection and user trust in data-heavy workflows. Repeatable demo Open the live leaderboard in a WebMCP-capable browser. Ask: “List the available exact inference comparison slices.” Ask: “For the GPT-OSS 120B Offline slice, compare AMD MI355X, NVIDIA B200, and Intel Arc Pro B60 using official system results.” Observe the comparison appear in the shared page with values, source links, and missing-evidence handling. Ask the agent to clear the comparison or configure another visible slice. Verification npm ci npm run type-check npm test npm run build Verified locally: TypeScript passed, 21 tests passed, and the production build passed. The deployed leaderboard registered all four WebMCP tools, and a live three-vendor comparison returned exact-slice values with immutable sources. title: Ingram Sheets
pitch: A spreadsheet whose engine runs in your browser and publishes twelve tools to whichever agent is driving the tab. Spreadsheets for models, not models for spreadsheets.
about_excerpt: A spreadsheet whose engine runs in your browser and publishes twelve tools to whichever agent is driving the tab. Spreadsheets for models, not models for spreadsheets. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Ingram Sheets is a spreadsheet whose calculation engine runs in the browser. It publishes its operations to whichever agent is driving the tab: read a range, write a block, extend a pattern, format, restructure, undo, point at a cell. ChatGPT supplies the model; we supply the sheet and hold no inference key. Why it needs WebMCP The engine is IronCalc compiled to WebAssembly, holding the live workbook in memory. There is no server-side copy of the sheet you are looking at: nothing that could recalculate it remotely, no endpoint that knows where your cursor is. An agent outside the tab has nothing to call. Spreadsheets for models, not models for spreadsheets The engine keeps every intermediate result at a stable address, so the model writes D17 instead of recopying a value it can transcribe wrong. It owns the dependency graph, so the model declares one local relation at a time and the engine keeps the global result consistent. And every write returns the cells whose computed values changed, recalculation ripple included. That return value is the tool contract: the model is corrected at each edit rather than at the end of a script, and it can skip the read that would otherwise confirm what it just did. Working alongside it Person and agent are in the same document at the same time. The agent's writes recalculate on screen, its focus moves across the grid in its own colour, and it can highlight a range and attach a note. Edit a cell while it works and your change is attached to its next tool result, so it re-plans against the current sheet. A code interpreter cannot do this. Its state ends with the session and its output is not editable. In a workbook every intermediate value sits next to the formula that produced it, and whoever knows the discount rate is wrong fixes the cell. How it is built Twelve tools, generated from the Zod schemas that also drive the built-in chat agent, so the two surfaces cannot drift. Every write goes through one controller, so an outside agent gets the same cursor and highlight behaviour as the built-in one, and its edits ride the same compare-and-swap save as a keystroke. Reads are marked readOnlyHint so the host can run them unattended. The two that return cell contents are marked untrustedContentHint : a cell can hold any text, including text shaped like an instruction, and the agent is told up front that what comes back is data. Results are returned as plain text rather than MCP content blocks, because the host serializes whatever a tool returns and the wrapper reaches the model as JSON noise around the grid. Prior work and hackathon work Ingram Sheets is a pre-existing project. WEBMCP.md in the repository separates what shipped before the submission period from what was built during it, with the commit history. Trying it Open https://sheets.ingram.tech/try in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser, on GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra. No sign-in. The panel on the right logs every tool call with its result. title: LoadGuard 3D
pitch: Agent-native 3D truck load planning where WebMCP agents can inspect, plan, validate, and stage proposals while humans retain control over operational execution.
about_excerpt: Agent-native 3D truck load planning where WebMCP agents can inspect, plan, validate, and stage proposals while humans retain control over operational execution. Like Comment Story Updates Main Page Implementation Stack Workflow Data Flow Main page of WebMCP Info about WebMCP Problem live data Live Activity Github page Project Workflow Inspiration As AI agents become capable of doing more inside real applications, I kept coming back to one question: How do we make an agent genuinely useful without allowing it to give itself permission to perform consequential actions? Logistics gave me a practical way to explore that problem. Truck loading involves real constraints: available space, weight limits, fragile cargo, delivery order, package dimensions, and operational state. An agent can be very useful here because it can inspect the current situation, coordinate planning, validate a proposal, and prepare the next action. But there is an important boundary. If an AI can both create an operational plan and authorize that same plan , then human oversight becomes mostly cosmetic. That idea became the foundation of LoadGuard 3D . The agent reasons. The operator authorizes. The website defines and enforces the contract. LoadGuard 3D explores how WebMCP can give agents structured access to meaningful website capabilities while keeping consequential execution under explicit human control. What it does LoadGuard 3D is a WebMCP-native 3D truck load-planning workspace. The application starts with a real operational state. In the main demo scenario, truck TRK-042 already contains eight loaded packages while an urgent, fragile package, MED-901 , is still inbound. The system can create a candidate loading plan that incorporates the new package while respecting the current truck state and package constraints. The workflow is intentionally separated into stages: Inspect the current truck state Retrieve package constraints Create a candidate load plan Validate the candidate Stage the valid proposal Attempt operational execution Require human authorization Execute the exact approved proposal Protect against duplicate execution The operator sees the candidate directly in a 3D truck visualization before deciding whether to approve it. For the demonstration scenario, the candidate reaches: 9 / 9 packages placed 1011 kg total weight 78.4% utilization 0 hard validation violations 2 fragile-cargo review warnings The important part is what happens next. If commit_load_plan is called before a human has approved the proposal, LoadGuard returns: APPROVAL_REQUIRED The active truck does not change. The human then reviews the exact staged proposal in the LoadGuard interface and chooses whether to approve or reject it. Human approval is intentionally not exposed as a WebMCP tool. After approval, the same operational commit can succeed because the application and database can verify that the exact proposal being executed is the one the operator authorized. A successful execution returns: EXECUTED and advances the truck state revision. If the same commit is accidentally retried, LoadGuard returns: ALREADY_EXECUTED instead of applying the operation twice. This makes human authorization, execution, and replay protection part of the real operational contract rather than just UI conventions. How we built it LoadGuard is built as several cooperating layers rather than one large autonomous-agent function. WebMCP interface LoadGuard registers structured capabilities through document.modelContext . The website exposes exactly seven WebMCP tools: get_load_state get_package_constraints create_load_plan validate_load_plan stage_load_plan commit_load_plan get_action_ledger I deliberately kept the tools narrow. Reading truck state is different from creating a candidate. Creating a candidate is different from staging it. Staging is different from operational execution. Most importantly, there is no approve_load_plan WebMCP capability available to the agent. The agent can request execution, but it cannot manufacture its own authority. Deterministic planning The language model does not generate the package coordinates. The model or agent orchestrates the workflow, while LoadGuard's deterministic planner computes the spatial candidate. This was an important design decision because physical placement should not depend on an LLM inventing geometry. Independent validation The candidate is validated before it can become a staged proposal. The validator checks constraints including: truck boundaries collisions between packages weight limits fragility delivery ordering malformed placements unplaced packages complete target-package coverage A candidate can therefore be rejected independently of the reasoning that requested it. 3D operator workspace The frontend is built with React and TypeScript, with Three.js / React Three Fiber providing the 3D truck visualization. The operator can compare the current load with the candidate plan and review: package count weight utilization validation status warnings manifest state candidate geometry approval controls activity history This gives the human meaningful information before authorization. Database-enforced authority Supabase PostgreSQL is used as the authority and persistence layer. The database stores trucks, packages, load plans, plan items, and an action ledger. Protected functions enforce the transition from staged proposal to approved proposal to executed state. The authorization model includes concepts such as: exact proposal hashing approved hash verification state revisions proposal expiry session isolation immutable approved plan items complete target-package coverage idempotent execution This means the safety boundary is not based on trusting the model to behave correctly. Even if an agent asks to commit a plan before approval, the operational layer can refuse it. Technology The main stack includes: WebMCP React TypeScript TanStack Start / Router Vite Tailwind CSS Three.js React Three Fiber Supabase PostgreSQL Zod Vitest Cloudflare Workers The project also includes dedicated pages for the live workspace, WebMCP contract, system architecture, and verification evidence so judges and developers can inspect the project at different levels. Challenges we ran into Designing the authority boundary The hardest challenge was not the truck visualization itself. It was deciding exactly where agent capability should end and human authority should begin. An early temptation in an agentic workflow is to expose every action as a tool. But if approval were also exposed as a WebMCP tool, the same agent could potentially plan, approve, and execute its own operation. That would defeat the purpose of human review. The solution was to make approval a separate human-controlled application state that cannot be produced through the agent capability surface. Separating candidate state from active state A proposed load plan needs to be useful before it is executed. That meant the candidate had to exist independently of the active truck state. LoadGuard therefore treats the staged plan as a proposal that can be visualized, validated, approved, rejected, or expire without immediately changing the truck. Making approval refer to the exact plan A vague approval such as "yes, load the truck" is not sufficient for an operational system. I wanted the authorization to refer to the exact candidate the operator reviewed. That led to canonical plan hashing, approved-hash verification, revision checks, proposal expiry, and immutable approved plan items. If the plan changes after approval, or if the underlying truck state becomes stale, the old authorization should not silently apply to a different operation. Handling retries safely Agents and distributed systems can repeat requests. An operational commit therefore cannot assume it will only ever be called once. LoadGuard makes execution idempotent. Once a proposal has executed, another commit attempt returns ALREADY_EXECUTED instead of mutating state again. Making a technical system understandable LoadGuard combines WebMCP, deterministic planning, validation, 3D visualization, human authorization, database enforcement, and an audit ledger. A major challenge was presenting all of that without making the interface feel like a developer console. The final workspace keeps the 3D truck and decision rail central while exposing deeper WebMCP and architecture details through dedicated views. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part I am most proud of is that human approval is not just a visual confirmation dialog. It is part of the system's actual authority model. A pre-approval operational commit is rejected. A human can then authorize the exact staged proposal. Execution succeeds only after that authorization exists. A repeated execution is safely rejected as already completed. I am also proud that the project uses WebMCP for a non-trivial operational workflow rather than exposing a single broad "do everything" function. Lo

title: Nirnay
pitch: Agents can't read a canvas. Nirnay gives them the exact overshoot, settling time and stability margins behind its plots, so human and agent tune the same controller together, live.
about_excerpt: Agents can't read a canvas. Nirnay gives them the exact overshoot, settling time and stability margins behind its plots, so human and agent tune the same controller together, live. Like 1 Comment Story Updates These are the Parameters 1 a These are the Parameters 2 a These are the test results got by setting the parameters as in the Image Nirnay-Parameters 1 b and 1 a These are the Parameters 1 b These are the test results got by setting the parameters as in the Image Nirnay-Parameters 2 b and 2 a These are the Parameters 2 b This is image that depicts how Nirnay works. These are the Graphs got by setting the parameters as in the Image Nirnay-Parameters 1 b and 1 a These are the Graphs got by setting the parameters as in the Image Nirnay-Parameters 2 b and 2 a Home page After changing some parameters (Random parameters part B) Home page After changing some parameters (Random parameters part A) These are the test results that shows all passed 46/46 Inspiration We spend a lot of time in control systems coursework, and tuning a controller is a strange kind of work: it is entirely about numbers, but you do all of it by staring at pictures. You drag a gain, you squint at a step response, you decide the wobble looks a bit better, you drag again. When we started reading the WebMCP spec, the first thing we wanted to know was what an agent could actually do on a page like that. The answer turned out to be almost nothing, and the reason was specific enough to be interesting. A step response, a Bode plot and a root locus are drawn on an HTML <canvas> . A canvas is coloured pixels. There is no text under it, no DOM, nothing to scrape. Hand a vision model a screenshot of a step response and ask for the overshoot and you get "roughly 25%" — a guess read off pixel positions. You cannot tune a controller on "roughly". The entire task is hitting a number like "under 10%", and 12% and 18% call for opposite corrections. So this was not a case of an agent being clumsy with a UI. The information the agent needed did not exist anywhere it could reach. It only existed as floating point numbers inside the running program. That felt like the sharpest possible answer to "why WebMCP?", so we built the page around it. What it does Nirnay is a control-system design bench. You pick a plant, drag sliders for the three PID gains, and three plots redraw instantly — step response, Bode, and a root locus / pole-zero map. On the right there is a scoreboard: every performance metric with a green PASS or red FAIL chip against design targets you set yourself. The page exposes eight WebMCP tools, so an AI agent in the same page can read the exact simulation numbers and tune alongside you. The important part is that there is one shared state behind everything. The sliders and the agent's tools write to the same place. When the agent changes a gain, the sliders physically move, the plots redraw and the scoreboard updates while you watch. You can grab a slider back mid-conversation and the agent's next reading reflects it. Neither side is driving a copy of the other's world. There is also an agent activity log on the page that prints a line every time a tool is called, so a human watching the screen can see exactly what just happened and why. The page opens in a deliberately failing state — 50.6% overshoot against a 10% target, three of four specs red. That is on purpose. It gives the agent something real to fix instead of a victory lap. The eight tools Five read, three write. Read: get_system (full current setup), run_step_response (exact overshoot, rise time, settling time, steady-state error), get_frequency_response (gain and phase margins, crossover frequencies), get_pole_zero_map (closed-loop poles, damping, and how far the gain can be pushed before instability), evaluate_design (score against targets, and what is still failing and by how much). Write: set_controller_gains , set_plant , set_design_spec . Three design decisions shaped how well this actually works: Every write tool returns the full measured result. set_controller_gains does not reply "done". It replies with the new overshoot, settling time, margins, pole positions and a pass/fail verdict. The obvious design is write-then-read, two calls per attempt. Returning the measurement with the write halves the round trips, but the real reason is that it keeps the agent anchored to a measurement instead of to its own prediction of what those gains would do. Agents are good at confidently predicting the wrong outcome. No tool ever returns a bare OK. Every response carries numbers the agent can check itself against. That is what lets it notice a change made things worse and back it out, rather than marching in the wrong direction. Bad input gets a sentence, not a stack trace. Pass a string where a number belongs and you get Error: Kp must be a finite number, got a string. A crashed tool call teaches an agent nothing. A sentence naming the mistake lets it retry. Read tools are marked with readOnlyHint so the browser does not interrupt with a confirmation prompt on every measurement, which matters a lot once the agent starts iterating. How we built it Everything runs in the browser. No server, no backend, no libraries, no build step — plain JavaScript files the browser loads directly. That was a deliberate choice: one deployable artifact, one failure point, and nothing between the plot and the tool that could make them disagree. The numerics, roughly in layers: Polynomial arithmetic as the base, since transfer functions are ratios of polynomials. Durand–Kerner for root finding, which chases all roots simultaneously. Roots sitting exactly at zero stall it, so those get peeled off first. RK4 integration for the step response, running twenty times finer than it records so the stored curve is smooth and trustworthy. Bisection to locate the gain and phase crossover frequencies exactly, rather than reporting the closest point on a sampled grid. Root locus by sweeping gain and matching each root to its nearest previous position, so drawn branches follow one root smoothly instead of jumping where two roots pass close together. Tool registration sits behind a feature check, so in a browser without WebMCP the page is simply a complete engineering tool with no agent. Nothing breaks and nothing looks broken. Who built what Nirnay was built by two of us. Challenges we ran into The bug that the cross-check caught. The gain at which a system goes unstable can be computed two entirely different ways: from the root locus, tracking roots in one mathematical space, and from the frequency response, tracking phase in a completely different one. They share no code. We wrote a test asserting they agree. They did not. The root locus said 6, the frequency path said 6.0577. The root locus was right. The bug was a rare edge case in the frequency path: the search grid happened to land exactly on the answer, which broke an assumption the refinement step depended on. We would never have found that by looking at a graph. Both curves looked fine. It is exactly the kind of quiet wrongness that makes a tool useless to an agent, because the agent has no way to sanity-check what it is handed — it will act on 6.0577 with total confidence. Testing before implementing. The test suites were written independently of the implementation and check against answers known from theory, not from our own code: closed-form textbook formulas for second-order overshoot and peak time, matched to within 0.5%, and classic worked examples whose margins can be derived by hand. 46/46 numerics tests and 111/111 browser tests pass from a fresh clone. Testing the browser half. Node cannot test browser behaviour, so there is a second suite that loads the real page markup, fakes the WebMCP connection, and checks the things that only exist in a browser: that all eight tools register, that each describes its inputs properly, that read tools are correctly marked read-only, that bad input produces a readable error, and that when a tool changes a gain, the sliders on the page actually move. That last assertion is the entire human-and-agent premise in one line. Learning the platform. A few things cost us time and are not obvious from the spec alone: it is document.modelContext , not navigator.modelContext , which many older examples still use. Tools registered inside iframes are not discovered, even same-origin, so everything has to live on the top-level page. The declarative HTML form API is not supported yet, so registration is JavaScript only. And WebMCP is a secure-context feature, so opening the file over file:// silently gives you no tools at all. Writing descriptions the agent actually reads. Our first pass had terse tool descriptions and the agent kept reaching for generic browser control before listing site tools. Tightening the input schemas — real descriptions on every property, additionalProperties: false — was what made it go straight to the right tool. What we learned Th

title: Open Application Desk
pitch: A WebMCP application workspace that audits live drafts, requests applicant-owned facts, stages visible fixes and submits only the exact hash-bound revision the applicant authorizes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP application workspace that audits live drafts, requests applicant-owned facts, stages visible fixes and submits only the exact hash-bound revision the applicant authorizes. Like Comment Story Updates A human-led application workspace where the page publishes five live WebMCP tools. A deterministic audit finds seven blockers - without changing the live draft. The agent stages a visible 3/10 → 7/10 improvement; only the applicant can apply it. The completed revision passes all ten checks but remains unapproved and unsubmitted. Human authorization is bound to one exact draft hash and expires after five minutes. A single-use receipt records seven blockers caught, 10/10 readiness, and the reviewed hash. Five typed WebMCP tools expose the page’s live state through closed input schemas. Inspiration Near a real submission deadline, I was reconciling official rules, deployment links, repository evidence, test results, and draft claims across several tabs. One stale claim nearly survived into the final submission. That experience exposed a deeper problem: application portals are built for clicking, not collaboration. An AI agent must scrape text and imitate UI actions, even when one invented fact or accidental submission could cost someone an opportunity. I built Open Application Desk around a safer idea: the agent prepares, the applicant supplies the facts, and only the applicant authorizes the exact submission. What it does Open Application Desk lets an applicant and an AI agent work on the same live application. The agent can inspect the requirements, find blockers and propose corrections, but it cannot apply changes, invent applicant facts, approve the application or even submit an unapproved draft. The page publishes five typed WebMCP tools that let an agent: Read the program requirements and exact live draft. Run a deterministic readiness audit without editing anything. Stage a bounded patch as a visible before-and-after diff. Prepare a passing revision for exact review. Submit only a review already authorized by the applicant. The reference journey begins at 3/10 ready with seven blockers . The agent proposes three bounded corrections and the page previews the result as 3/10 → 7/10 , but nothing changes until the applicant clicks Apply proposed changes . When an applicant-owned fact is missing, a contextual tool temporarily appears. Instead of allowing the agent to invent an answer, the page asks the applicant directly. After the applicant shares the answer, that tool disappears. When all 10 checks pass, the page creates a five-minute approval tied to a digital fingerprint of that exact draft. Any later edit cancels the approval. The applicant approves that version and only then can the agent submit it and receive one receipt. The OpenAI API supplies the reasoning; WebMCP lets the page publish its live tools, state and boundaries. How we built it I built the application with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Zod, WebMCP, Vitest, Playwright, and OpenAI Sites. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same workspace controller and domain rules. There is no separate agent-only state. Tool inputs use closed JSON Schemas and runtime Zod validation. The deterministic audit checks the live revision and performs bounded verification of public GitHub repository metadata and license availability. Proposed edits are evaluated against an in-memory candidate before the page shows their projected readiness, without mutating the real draft. prepare_submission re-audits the expected revision and creates a short-lived review bound to its SHA-256 draft hash. Any later edit invalidates that review. Submission also uses a browser-provided exclusive lock so repeated calls for the same approved review reconcile to one receipt. For the Chrome demonstration, I built an optional open-source developer inspector. It discovers the page’s registered WebMCP tools, maps their schemas to OpenAI Responses API functions, and returns structured tool results to the model. The API key remains in the local Chrome session. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was separating assistance from authority. It was easy to build an agent that could change fields; it was much harder to prove that it could not apply its own proposal, invent applicant facts, attest, or authorize submission. The contextual human handoff also required careful design. A WebMCP call should not remain open indefinitely while waiting for a person. The tool therefore returns an immediate awaiting_human result, the page collects the answer, and the agent re-reads the updated live state. WebMCP is still an emerging browser capability, so I also had to distinguish between ordinary browsers, ChatGPT’s supported in-app browser, and Chrome with WebMCP enabled. The developer inspector made discovery and every tool call visible during testing and recording. Accomplishments that we're proud of A deterministic audit that changes zero application fields. A visible readiness projection before any proposed edit is applied. A contextual tool that appears only when a specific human-owned fact is missing. An agent that asks instead of inventing. A five-minute review bound to the exact draft revision and SHA-256 hash. Native human authorization before submission becomes possible. A single receipt recording seven blockers caught, 10/10 readiness, and the reviewed hash. One shared controller for both the human interface and WebMCP tools. Automated domain, component, WebMCP-registration, and browser-journey testing. The project was created during the submission period, beginning August 26, 2026. Its public commit history documents the implementation through the final challenge build. What we learned The most important lesson was that WebMCP is not the reasoning engine. Its value is allowing a webpage to publish a precise contract for what an agent can see and do. Structured tools are also not enough by themselves. Meaningful safety comes from combining typed capabilities with deterministic validation, state-dependent availability, visible human controls, revision checks, expiration, and exact-artifact authorization. I also learned that a tool disappearing can be as meaningful as a tool appearing. Once the applicant supplies the missing fact, the agent no longer needs permission to request it. What's next for Open Application Desk The current challenge sample intentionally stores its state in the visitor’s browser and uses a fictional reference program, making it easy for judges to reset and reproduce without an account. The next step is to replace that persistence layer with authenticated server storage while preserving the controller, five WebMCP contracts, deterministic gate, visible patch review, and human authorization boundary. Foundations, accelerators, admissions offices, fellowship programs, and procurement teams could publish their own requirement sets while applicants and agents work safely against the same authoritative state. Future versions could also support additional evidence providers, organization-defined policies, durable receipts, and accessible multi-user review. title: Ops Co-pilot
pitch: An AI-friendly infra dashboard where agents check real service health and act but every risky action needs a human's explicit approval before it runs.
about_excerpt: An AI-friendly infra dashboard where agents check real service health and act but every risky action needs a human's explicit approval before it runs. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP lets websites expose structured tools directly to AI agents but most demos of "agent + web app" either lock the agent out of anything meaningful, or hand over full control and hope for the best. Neither felt like the real future. The real question was: what does it look like when an agent can genuinely operate something consequential real infrastructure without a person having to babysit every click, but also without blindly trusting the agent's judgment on anything that could break production? That tension is where Ops Co-pilot came from. What it does Ops Co-pilot is a dashboard that exposes real infrastructure service health, alerts, and operational actions as WebMCP tools an AI agent can call directly. Read-only and low-risk tools (checking health, listing alerts, acknowledging them, adding incident notes) execute immediately. High-risk actions (restarting or scaling a service) never execute on the agent's say-so alone: the backend halts the action, shows a human a clear on-screen confirmation dialog describing exactly what's about to happen and why, and only proceeds via a real Render API call against a real deployed service after explicit human approval, using a single-use, cryptographically bound confirmation token. How we built it Go backend (service registry, alert engine, guardrail/token system, audit log) with a React/TypeScript frontend that registers all 7 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool. Instead of monitoring simulated services, we wired it to a real, separately-deployed production app (a Social Publishing MCP server), adding real /readyz, /metrics, and /version observability endpoints to that app so Ops Co-pilot has genuinely live data real uptime, real DB/Redis connection status, real error counts to work with. High-risk actions call Render's actual restart API, gated behind a token that's single-use, expiring, and bound to the exact service and action it was issued for. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge wasn't writing the tools it was making sure "it works" actually meant it works. Early on, a self-reported "all tests passed" summary turned out to gloss over real gaps: commit history had been silently rewritten to look like proper development discipline, and a rate-limiting test's own summary numbers didn't match its own raw logs. We caught both by re-deriving the numbers by hand instead of trusting the summary. Later, live end-to-end testing (calling our own WebMCP tools directly through Chrome's navigator.modelContextTesting API) surfaced a genuinely serious bug: restart_service was returning "success" without the real Render API call actually succeeding confirmed by checking Render's own Events log and finding no matching restart event. We also found a live production issue this way: our own observability endpoints revealed Redis was actually unreachable on the real monitored service, which we fixed before it affected real users. Accomplishments that we're proud of Every claim in this project is backed by something we personally verified against a live system not a unit test result taken at face value. We caught a false-success bug in the exact action that matters most (the one with real infrastructure consequences) before it ever reached a demo, by insisting on checking Render's own event log instead of trusting our own backend's response. The confirmation-guardrail flow token generation, single-use enforcement, replay rejection, cross-service scope binding held up under adversarial testing (forged tokens, expired tokens, replay attempts, concurrent race conditions) with real HTTP evidence for every case. What we learned An agent (or an AI coding assistant) reporting success is not the same as success. The most valuable thing in this build wasn't a feature it was the habit of independently re-verifying claims against ground truth (Render's own dashboard, raw HTTP responses, actual git history) instead of accepting a summary. That same discipline is exactly what Ops Co-pilot enforces structurally for AI agents operating on real infrastructure: a claim of "done" isn't enough, a human checks before anything consequential actually happens. What's next for Ops Co-pilot Move authentication from a single shared API-key gate to real per-user sessions with role-based permissions, support monitoring multiple real services instead of one, and add richer remediation tools (log inspection, rollback to a previous deploy) all still behind the same human-confirmation guardrail for anything irreversible. title: OwnerOps
pitch: AI Store Manager where humans edit agent plans, WebMCP re-evaluates them, and only reviewed changes are applied.
about_excerpt: AI Store Manager where humans edit agent plans, WebMCP re-evaluates them, and only reviewed changes are applied. Like Comment Story Updates One live operating state across people, sales, stock and costs. The agent materializes a reviewable plan — not just a chat answer. The owner can directly change the agent's proposal. WebMCP re-reads the exact human-edited candidate before commitment. One operating model, adapted across markets and languages. Inspiration OwnerOps started from a problem that feels very practical to me. In Korea, I see many people worrying about stable employment or considering small businesses as another path. But running a small store is difficult in ways that are easy to underestimate. Labor costs keep increasing. Employee schedules are difficult to manage. Ingredient prices change. Rent is expensive. And even understanding how much money is actually left after all of those costs can be surprisingly difficult. Large companies have separate people for finance, purchasing, HR, and operations. A small business owner often has to do all of that alone. My background is not traditional web product development, so I did not start this project because I wanted to build an impressive AI demo. I started with a much simpler question: Could AI actually make running a small business a little easier? To me, this feels like one of the positive ways AI can be used — not replacing the owner, but helping them understand the business, organize information, compare options, and make better decisions. That idea became OwnerOps , an AI Store Manager built with WebMCP. What it does I tried to build OwnerOps around the kinds of questions I think a real store owner might ask: Am I spending too much on labor? Can I change this schedule without hurting service? Which inventory items are becoming risky? Are ingredient costs getting too high? How much money is the store actually keeping? What happens if operating costs increase? OwnerOps brings staffing, schedules, sales, inventory, waste, purchase costs, operating costs, and profitability into one working store state. The owner uses a normal visual application. The AI agent uses nine structured WebMCP Site Tools. Both work with the same StoreState. For example, the owner can ask: Improve this week's operating profitability without creating a service coverage gap. The agent can read the relevant store information and create a StorePlan Preview. But I did not want the AI to simply make the change by itself. The owner can modify the proposed worker or shift time directly in the UI. When that happens, the previous review becomes invalid. The agent must then read the exact human-edited candidate again using evaluate_current_plan . Only after that version becomes REVIEWED can the owner apply it. The core flow is: Agent proposes → Human edits → Agent re-evaluates the exact edit → Human applies That became the most important interaction in OwnerOps. Why WebMCP I did not want the AI to understand the store by looking at screenshots and moving a mouse around a website. The application already knows its schedules, sales, inventory, costs, and current plan. WebMCP lets the agent work with those capabilities directly. The OwnerOps UI is for the human. The WebMCP tools are for the agent. But both operate on the same state. I deliberately kept the WebMCP surface to nine intent-level tools instead of exposing every internal function. The tools represent things the agent actually needs to do — read the store, create and preview plans, record events, evaluate the current candidate, and apply reviewed changes. Direct interaction with the rendered UI is left to the human for things such as editing the proposal and approving Apply. How I built it OwnerOps is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL/Supabase, and WebMCP through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Because web product development is not my main professional background, I used AI tools heavily throughout the project. I used them to learn unfamiliar technologies, implement and review code, debug problems, generate tests, and repeatedly verify whether the product actually behaved the way I intended. I still tried to make decisions from the problem first rather than adding AI features simply because they were possible. The current prototype covers connected operating areas including staffing, sales, inventory, waste, purchasing, operating costs, and profitability. I also experimented with different markets including Seoul, New York, Tokyo, Madrid, and Shanghai to see how the same operating model could adapt to different currencies and local contexts. Challenges The hardest part was not getting the AI to generate a recommendation. It was making sure the human and the agent did not silently end up working with different versions of the same plan. If the agent proposes a schedule change and the owner manually changes it, the AI cannot continue reasoning about its original proposal. The human-edited version has to become the current truth. That is why OwnerOps invalidates the previous review after a human edit and requires the agent to evaluate the current candidate again before Apply. Testing the real WebMCP flow was also harder than I expected. There were cases where ChatGPT could see the OwnerOps Site Tools, but that did not always mean it would actually stay on the structured tool path. I had to test the real ChatGPT desktop workflow repeatedly and make the Site-Tools-only boundary clearer. Several proof attempts failed before the complete flow worked reliably. That taught me an important difference: A tool being registered is not the same as a real agent successfully using it end to end. I also tried to be careful about data. It would have been easy to make every number in the demo look like live external data, but I did not want to do that. OwnerOps distinguishes store data, deterministic demo data, cached or seeded references, and external observations. During final video production, the schedule-history data source returned no usable history rows. Instead of fabricating the missing states just to make the demo look better, I left that sequence out. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that useful AI for real operations is not only about generating a good answer. The state behind the answer matters. The person using the system needs to understand what the AI is proposing, be able to change it, and remain in control of consequential actions. I also learned how much AI development tools can lower the barrier between understanding a problem and being able to build software around it. For me, going from a small-business problem to a working WebMCP application was one of the most valuable parts of the challenge. What's next There are several areas where I think OwnerOps could become much more useful. One is public data. Ingredient prices, wages, consumer prices, rent, weather, and local economic information could be connected to public APIs and open datasets. That would allow a store owner to compare their real operating costs with broader market conditions instead of relying only on stored reference data. I am also interested in the openness of POS and store data. Today, a lot of small-business operating data is tied to specific POS vendors, credit-card companies, delivery platforms, or other closed systems. I would like to see a future where store owners can control and use their own sales, inventory, cost, and operating data more freely. With more open standards and open-source software, tools like OwnerOps would not need to belong to one POS vendor or one platform. Different developers and AI agents could build useful tools around the same open store data. That is much bigger than this prototype, but it is the direction I would like to explore. I hope AI can make capabilities that were once practical mainly for larger companies more accessible to small business owners — while keeping their decisions and their data under their own control.
