title: Furrow
pitch: A garden plan you draw. Your agent comments in the margin, proposes in pencil, and never plants without you. Built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A garden plan you draw. Your agent comments in the margin, proposes in pencil, and never plants without you. Built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates svg What it is Furrow is a garden plan you draw and your agent reviews in the margin. You lay out raised beds by season and put crops on wooden plant stakes in your own hand. Your agent reads the live plan through WebMCP, leaves comments anchored to the exact bed and strip, and proposes plantings in pencil. It never plants. Only you can. Live: https://anusree-j.github.io/furrow/ Code: https://github.com/Anusree-J/furrow (MIT) Why this is a WebMCP use case Planning a vegetable garden is a shared-document problem wearing wellies. The plan is a structured artifact that one person authors from what only they know: which bed floods, what the kids will eat, how many hours they really have. A good adviser adds what they do not know: rotation, sowing windows, succession, effort. The natural shape is the one everyone recognises from a shared document: the author writes, the reviewer comments in the margin anchored to the exact spot, the author resolves. That shape needs the page. The agent has to read the live plot, not a description of it, and its comments have to land on the bed and season they are about. Its proposals have to be visible next to the person's own choices without becoming the plan. A chat cannot hold a plot; a remote server cannot see the page the person is editing. How it improves the experience You never describe your garden twice. get_garden gives the agent beds, sun, last year's families, this year's plantings, the household profile, and the page's own agronomy flags in one call. The page computes the facts (rotation, sowing season, sun, antagonists) deterministically and tells the agent not to restate them, so the agent spends its turn on judgement: what this household should grow, where, and why. Agent proposals appear as pencil stakes with reasons. Tick one, plant them all, or skip. A comment with a suggested alternative is applied in one click. Every change from either side is attributed in one log and undoable. What becomes possible together The division of labour is enforced by the tool surface. Planting, moving, removing, accepting, and resolving are page controls with no tool behind them. The agent cannot propose anything until you have told it about your climate and frost dates: propose_planting and propose_plan are not registered until the profile is set, so the agent's first move is to ask. withdraw_comment exists only while the agent has open comments. You keep authorship; the agent keeps the margin. How I built it Vanilla ES modules, no build step. Nine imperative tools on document.modelContext with JSON Schemas and readOnlyHint annotations, registered with AbortSignal so availability follows plan state and fires toolchange . Every mutating tool returns the changed object plus phase, current page flags, and suggested next actions. A single store with snapshot undo persists to localStorage. A 25-crop catalog and a deterministic rules module drive page flags. All illustrations are an inline SVG sprite. A built-in Tool inspector invokes the registered tools through the agent's code path for anyone without an agent host. Verified on Chrome with the WebMCP testing flag: tools register natively, getTools reflects availability changes, and executeTool drives the full loop. What I learned An approval gate is only meaningful when the agent could act without you. Here the agent can only propose, so the honest design is pencil versus ink, not a confirmation dialog. And state-gated tool availability is a better way to make an agent ask first than any instruction in a prompt. What's next for Furrow Month-level sowing windows, a multi-year rotation memory per bed, and a climate-aware catalog so the same page works in Kerala as well as Kent. Impact Home and allotment growers plan a season every year and most get rotation and timing wrong, which is the main reason beds underperform and beginners give up. Furrow makes the plan itself the shared object, so advice arrives where the decision is made and the person stays in charge of their own ground. title: Gather
pitch: Human priorities. Agent exploration. Deterministic group decisions.
about_excerpt: Human priorities. Agent exploration. Deterministic group decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Company retreat planning forces people-ops leads and executive assistants to reconcile attendee origins, travel burden, dates, budget, venue fit, activities, and stakeholder preferences. When a human edits the plan in one surface while an AI reasons in a separate chat, state drifts and recommendations become difficult to trust. Gather makes the website itself the shared operating surface. What it does Gather is a mobile-first group decision room organized around Align → Explore → Decide. Stakeholders propose priorities and constraints, but only a human can accept or decline them. A compatible WebMCP agent then reads that exact live plan, explores thousands of venue × routing × activity × meal × schedule combinations, and returns three trade-off finalists plus a versioned Decision Receipt. Every meaningful human and agent action is visibly attributed in the same workspace. Agent changes highlight the affected UI, remain reversible with one-click undo, and never bypass the human-only proposal approval and PDF download boundary. Why WebMCP WebMCP is essential because the agent needs structured access to the same changing decision state the human sees—not a copied prompt or brittle UI automation. Eleven narrow semantic tools expose the live, versioned decision model. This lets people and agents collaborate in one visual workspace while Gather deterministically verifies the result. The experience is better than chat alone: people see every consequential agent effect immediately, can inspect fairness by origin, review honored constraints and metric deltas, and undo a change without translating a recommendation back into the plan. How we built it Gather uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, Zustand, Zod, and jsPDF. Native imperative tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool and share the same typed Zustand/domain actions as the human UI—there is no duplicate agent implementation. Every agent write requires the current state version. Compound operations also require an idempotency key. Registration uses an AbortController lifecycle. Stale or impossible requests return structured, non-throwing business errors without mutation. Gather verifies canonical state after every successful write, and proposal preparation is bound to an exact version and snapshot hash so stale proposals cannot be approved. The deterministic optimizer evaluates more than 2,000 combinations, applies hard constraints, computes attendee-level travel fairness, and selects three Pareto-style finalists. Challenges The hardest parts were keeping compound constraint changes atomic, preventing stale writes, making fairness inspectable rather than hidden inside a score, and preserving human authority structurally while still giving an agent useful planning power. Accomplishments and verification The public build includes 11 native WebMCP tools, visible provenance, atomic constraint handling, one-click undo, stale-write protection, canonical verification, a Decision Receipt, and a human-only approval gate. The release passes lint, TypeScript, 90 automated tests, and a production build. It is deployed publicly with no login or API key required. Synthetic prototype disclosure All venues, routes, prices, scores, and availability are original synthetic demo data. Gather does not book travel, use live inventory, or connect to production Offsite systems. This is a synthetic WebMCP Challenge prototype. title: House Design Tool
pitch: A 3D home designer that allows humans and agents to collaborate on a proejct. WebMCP gives agents 21 tools on the live house design, while a shared rulebook keeps every wall and walkway legal.
about_excerpt: A 3D home designer that allows humans and agents to collaborate on a proejct. WebMCP gives agents 21 tools on the live house design, while a shared rulebook keeps every wall and walkway legal. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every AI design tool today works like a vending machine: you describe what you want in a chat box, and a finished result drops out. That's backwards for spatial work. Nobody designs a home by describing it. They nudge a wall, stand in the kitchen, drag the sofa two feet, and look . We wanted the agent in the room with you, not on the other side of a chat log. WebMCP made that possible: if the page itself exposes its live state as tools, the human and the agent can finally work on the same object at the same time. What it does WebMCP Home Design is a 3D floorplan editor that registers 21 tools on document.modelContext . A human picks a shell (floors, then a template per floor), reshapes rooms, and furnishes by dragging, rotating, and resizing, while an agent in the browser reads the same live design and edits it through tools: placing furniture, moving walls, cutting doors, batching twenty edits in one call, even proposing three alternative layouts that ghost over the plan for the human to compare and apply. A simplified residential constraint engine (13 rules: door widths, bedroom egress, kitchen aisles, toilet clearances, furniture facing walls) referees both parties identically: every edit returns what changed and what it broke. Designs autosave locally, export as JSON, and travel as share links with the whole compressed design in the URL fragment. No server, no accounts. How we built it TypeScript end to end. The domain layer models rooms, shared walls, openings, and furniture in plan inches, with pure operations (clone in, result out) that both the UI and the agent tools call: one rulebook, two doors in. React Three Fiber renders the scene: procedural canvas-painted textures with bump and roughness maps, parametric furniture built from primitives (a resized sofa grows a third cushion), dollhouse-cut walls overhead and full walls in a street-view-style walkthrough. Zustand holds per-floor state with undo history; Zod schemas define tool inputs and compile to the JSON Schemas agents see. Everything is generated in code, with no model files and no fetched assets, so the app works fully offline. Challenges we ran into The hardest problems were about shared control. Coincident walls desynchronized until we rebuilt the model around one wall per partition. Agent calls serialize at roughly a second each in the browser, which pushed us to design apply_edits for single-round-trip furnishing. Grid snapping silently moved agent placements until every operation learned to echo where things actually landed. And a long tail of 3D truths: coplanar surfaces z-fight into flicker, room polygons run along wall centerlines so furniture sank 3 inches into walls, and an agent with no orientation guidance will happily face a wardrobe into a wall, which became both a smarter placement default and a new validation rule. Accomplishments that we're proud of The loop genuinely works both ways. An agent can validate a plan, fix a too-narrow door, furnish a bedroom, and then walk the human through the result with the camera; a human can drag a sofa and the agent's next get_layout reflects it. We're proud that refusals are as useful as successes (every rejected edit explains what would break and suggests a fix the grid can actually produce) and that 267 tests pin the whole thing down, from constraint rules to camera math to the persistence format. What we learned Tools-on-the-page is a different discipline from tools-on-a-server. The agent needs what a colleague needs: honest echoes of what actually happened, actionable refusals, bounds included in summaries so it doesn't ask twice, and documentation precise enough to reason about (our rotation docs went from "0 faces the bottom" to a full compass after watching agents guess wrong). We also learned that the referee matters more than either player: the constraint engine is what turns two editors sharing one document from chaos into collaboration. What's next for House Design Tool Furniture variants: extending propose_variants beyond wall moves so an agent can ghost three complete room arrangements, pre-validated, for the human to pick from. Stacked multi-floor 3D with stairs and alignment rules. Real collaboration transport (two humans plus an agent on one design). And a richer catalog with materials, lighting fixtures, and cost estimates, so the conversation can become "make it nicer for under $3,000." title: InkWitness : a shared agent-human workspace
pitch: A human-sealed WebMCP reading desk that lets agents investigate uncertain handwriting without silently overwriting human evidence basically a shared desk where humans and agents work together
about_excerpt: A human-sealed WebMCP reading desk that lets agents investigate uncertain handwriting without silently overwriting human evidence basically a shared desk where humans and agents work together Like Comment Story Updates Overview: Eight WebMCP tools help agents inspect handwriting while final decisions stay human-controlled. Stale protection: An outdated proposal is rejected, preventing old AI work from overwriting new human evidence. Human-sealed result: The final export records decisions, evidence revisions, and a SHA-256 integrity hash. Why I made InkWitness Old handwritten documents are often difficult to read. Some letters are faded, damaged or missing. AI can help, but it may also guess a word with too much confidence. In historical records, one wrong name or place can create a lasting mistake. That problem gave me the idea for InkWitness: let the AI help with the investigation, while keeping the final decision with a person. How it works InkWitness uses a synthetic historical ledger with three unclear words. The agent can examine each word, compare it with other letters written by the same hand, check possible answers and suggest a reading. The evidence it uses appears on the page, so the person can understand why that suggestion was made. A suggestion is not automatically accepted. Only the person using InkWitness can accept it, reject it or decide that the word should remain illegible. Why WebMCP matters The person and the agent work on the same visible desk. They are not working with separate copies of the information. The desk also keeps track of revisions. For example, if a person adds a new clue after the agent reads the page, the agent’s old proposal is no longer safe. InkWitness rejects it with STALE_REVISION. The agent must read the latest version and reconsider the evidence. This prevents old AI work from replacing newer human work. How I built it I built the project with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It has eight native WebMCP tools that allow the agent to read the desk, inspect unclear words, compare handwriting, check possible readings and prepare proposals. The WebMCP tools and the buttons on the page use the same state and functions. I also included manual testing controls so the workflow can still be demonstrated in a normal browser. No real historical documents or personal data are used in the demonstration. The difficult part The hardest part was deciding exactly what the agent should and should not be allowed to do. The agent can investigate and make suggestions, but its tools do not include accepting a reading, declaring a word illegible or sealing the final record. Those actions belong only to the person reviewing the document. I also had to make sure an outdated agent action could not overwrite a newer change. That is why every proposal must include the desk revision that the agent previously read. What I learned This project taught me that making AI safer does not always mean making it less useful. The agent can still do the repetitive work of comparing letters and organizing evidence, while the person handles decisions that require judgment. I also learned how WebMCP can connect an agent directly to the information and controls inside a webpage. Final record After every word has been reviewed, the agent can prepare a provenance packet. The person then chooses whether to seal and export it. The exported receipt includes the evidence, revisions, proposals and human decisions. Its SHA-256 hash helps detect later changes, but it does not prove identity or document authenticity. What I would add next I would like to support real archival collections with permission, multiple human reviewers and export formats used by libraries and researchers. links :- Live application: https://inkwitness.webscales3.chatgpt.site Source code: https://github.com/Yuviiix/inkwitness Demo video: https://youtu.be/YzMe_8w1qAM?si=Uql4lAva6F7Y6JJl Built With chatgpt-sites codex css html javascript sha-256 web-crypto-api webmcp Try it out inkwitness.webscales3.chatgpt.site github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I worked independently on the idea, planning, design, testing, presentation and final submission. title: Kenny
pitch: Preserve the good work. Recover the broken part.
about_excerpt: Preserve the good work. Recover the broken part. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can complete multi-step actions on the web, but partial failure creates a difficult problem. If four actions succeed and the fifth fails, restarting may repeat valid side effects, while rolling everything back can destroy work that was already correct. Kenny explores a safer recovery model for WebMCP applications. What it does Kenny gives WebMCP tools a recovery contract. In the demo, an AI agent is onboarding a new employee. It successfully: creates the employee account creates the workspace account assigns the software licence orders the laptop Then the orientation booking fails because Monday is full. Instead of restarting the whole workflow, Kenny tells the agent what should be: PRESERVED RECOVERED BLOCKED The agent can inspect the workflow, inspect the recovery plan, search alternative orientation slots and propose Tuesday. The irreversible welcome email remains blocked until a human approves the recovery in the webpage. There is deliberately no WebMCP approval tool. After approval, the agent resumes from the failed step without replaying the successful work. Result: 4 valid actions preserved · 1 failed action recovered · 0 completed actions repeated How we built it Kenny uses a protocol-independent recovery core with: append-only workflow journaling idempotency application-declared recovery semantics human approval selective resume The demo exposes six WebMCP tools: get_onboarding_state start_onboarding get_recovery_plan search_orientation_slots propose_recovery resume_onboarding The interface is built with React, Vite and TypeScript. Workflow and recovery state persist locally with IndexedDB. The demo uses deterministic simulated services so judges can reliably reproduce the partial failure and verify the recovery behavior. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the recovery contract be exposed directly to an external agent operating the application. The agent does not only learn which actions exist. It can learn what already succeeded, what remains valid, what failed, what can be recovered, where execution should resume and where human authority is required. The human and agent therefore have different capabilities: Agent: inspect, search, propose and resume after authorization. Human: approve recovery. Challenges The hardest part was making selective recovery safe rather than simply adding a retry button. Kenny has to preserve completed work, reject stale approvals, avoid duplicate execution and maintain the human approval boundary while still allowing the agent to continue the workflow. What we learned Recovery semantics such as idempotency and saga-style compensation already exist in software systems. Kenny's experiment is about where those semantics live and how an application can expose them through WebMCP so an external agent can recover safely from partial execution. What's next Kenny is currently a deterministic reference implementation. The next step would be applying the same recovery contract to real multi-step workflows such as account provisioning, commerce, support operations and other applications where agents create consequential side effects. Preserve the good work. Recover the broken part. Continue safely. title: NextPlay
pitch: Call the play. Lock your vision. Let AI replan the rest.
about_excerpt: Call the play. Lock your vision. Let AI replan the rest. Like 1 Comment Story Updates NextPlay Call the play. Lock your vision. Let AI replan the rest. Inspiration Basketball play design is collaborative by nature: a coach sketches an idea, tests the timing, changes a screen or route, and keeps refining until the sequence works. But most AI tools break that workflow. They generate a diagram, description, or recommendation somewhere outside the actual product. Once the coach edits the board, the AI no longer understands the current state—or which decisions are intentional and must not be overwritten. We built NextPlay around a simple question: What would a basketball tactics board look like if the coach and an AI agent could work on the same live play? WebMCP made that possible. Instead of relying on screenshots or a hidden copy of the play, the page exposes structured tools that let the agent read and modify the exact state the coach is viewing. What It Does NextPlay is a browser-native basketball tactics board for human–AI collaboration. A coach can ask an agent to create a sideline out-of-bounds play for a right-corner three. The agent: Reads the current formation, clock, actions, locks, and revision. Adds six structured basketball actions. Validates the play against deterministic execution constraints. Animates the result directly on the court. Then the coach can intervene through the normal interface. In our core demo, the coach: Moves A3’s screen to the right_elbow . Locks A3. Locks O2’s route in A4. Shortens the clock from 4.2 seconds to 2.0 seconds. That creates a clock-overflow error because A6 finishes too late. The agent then rereads the live page, sees the coach’s edits and locks, and retimes only the unlocked pass and shot in A5 and A6. A3 and A4 remain unchanged, the repaired play passes all seven validation checks, and the final animation completes within the new two-second clock. That second turn is the heart of NextPlay: the AI does not start over or overwrite the coach. It adapts around the coach’s decisions. Why WebMCP Matters The important state in NextPlay is live and page-local: Current player positions The action timeline The shortened clock The selected action Coach-made edits Locked actions Validation results The current play revision A generic assistant would have to infer that state from pixels, manipulate small controls, or work from an outdated description. NextPlay instead exposes exactly five semantic WebMCP tools: get_play_state add_play_actions validate_play animate_play update_play_action There is deliberately no agent tool for locking or unlocking actions. Locks are a coach-only authority boundary. This means the coach remains in control while the agent handles structured construction and replanning. How We Built It NextPlay is built with React, TypeScript, Zustand, Zod, Vite, and Vercel . We designed the application around one architectural rule: Every persistent mutation—whether initiated by the coach or the agent—must pass through the same command and transaction layer. The WebMCP tools do not maintain a separate copy of the play. Their handlers call the same application commands used by the visible coach interface. As a result, agent changes immediately appear on the: Court Timeline Action inspector Validation panel Activity rail Each successful content mutation increments the play revision exactly once. Write tools can include an expected revision, allowing NextPlay to reject stale updates when the page has changed since the agent last read it. We also implemented atomic action batches. When the agent creates the initial play, all six actions are accepted together or none are committed. The validation engine checks deterministic structural properties such as: Whether all actions fit within the clock Whether one player has incompatible overlapping actions Whether referenced players and actions are valid Whether possession order is consistent Whether the play contains the required inbound pass and shot Whether locked coach actions were preserved NextPlay does not claim that a play is tactically optimal, likely to score, or physically realistic. It validates the structure and timing of an animated tactical diagram. Challenges We Faced Preserving Human Authority The hardest product question was not how to let the agent edit the play—it was how to stop the agent from erasing intentional human decisions. We solved this with coach-only action locks. Before every agent mutation, NextPlay snapshots locked actions and verifies that they remain unchanged. Attempts to modify a locked action return an ACTION_LOCKED error without changing the play revision. Keeping the Agent and Interface Synchronized It would have been easy to build a demo where the agent edits hidden JSON while the UI displays something similar. Instead, we made the visible application state the source of truth. Tool success is returned only after the updated state has been committed through the same data model used by the coach interface. Handling Stale Agent State A coach may change the play after the agent reads it. Without concurrency protection, the next agent write could accidentally overwrite a newer version. Revision-aware writes let the application detect that situation and ask the agent to reread the play before continuing. Making Validation Honest We wanted the validator to be useful without making exaggerated basketball claims. That required carefully separating deterministic facts like timing, possession order, references, and lock preservation from subjective questions like whether the play would fool a real defense. Building a Reliable Live Demo A hackathon project has to work repeatedly, not just once. We reduced the scope to one polished sideline out-of-bounds scenario, kept the WebMCP surface to five tools, added strict runtime schemas, tested fresh-context production flows, and included an honest manual fallback for browsers that do not support WebMCP. What We Learned The biggest lesson was that giving an agent more autonomy is not always the same as making it more useful. In collaborative software, an agent needs three things: Semantic access to the real application state. Clear authority boundaries defining what it may change. Observable, revision-aware actions that both the user and the system can verify. WebMCP turns the page from a visual interface the agent must guess at into a structured collaboration environment. We also learned that the most compelling agent experiences are not single-prompt generation demos. They are iterative workflows where a human changes the constraints and the agent successfully adapts without losing prior intent. What We Are Proud Of NextPlay demonstrates a complete human–agent loop: Intent → structured construction → validation → animation → human intervention → constraint violation → agent repair The coach remains the decision-maker. The agent accelerates execution. That is the interaction model we believe will matter far beyond basketball: humans defining intent and protecting critical decisions while agents operate directly inside live, structured applications. title: NotASprint
pitch: NotASprint uses WebMCP to let humans and AI co-design the same live racing circuit: humans edit and lock visually; agents read, analyze, simulate and refine that exact shared state.
about_excerpt: NotASprint uses WebMCP to let humans and AI co-design the same live racing circuit: humans edit and lock visually; agents read, analyze, simulate and refine that exact shared state. Like Comment Story Updates NotASprint Thumbnail NotASprint — a WebMCP-native circuit design lab. Live canvas, telemetry panel, Formula 1 reference loaded. Design for Formula 1, Formula E or MotoGP: three references per discipline plus Create Custom. Human edits visually, agent works semantically: a real reshape_sector call through WebMCP, receipted in Activity (High-speed 77 → 94). Deterministic analysis: Flow · Technical · Overtaking · High-speed, sector character, overtaking zones, speed trace. Presentation mode, Mugello. The human designs visually. The agent works semantically. Both work on the same live circuit. Reference Library → Formula E → Create Custom: a seeded, discipline-aware concept, reproducible by the agent. GIF Drag Turn 7, press L to lock, ask the agent for a technical Sector 2 — it adds and reshapes corners around the lock, never through it. GIF Save snapshots, compare on the canvas, export in Technical / Presentation / Minimal / Analysis styles. GIF Race-flow simulation: 12 cars, 5 laps, findings ranked in the panel — design turned into testable signals. Inspiration Circuit design is visual, iterative, and full of tradeoffs. A designer might move a corner because it feels better, inspect how that affects speed or overtaking, lock the decision they care about, and keep refining everything around it. That made circuit design a natural fit for WebMCP. We did not want to bolt a chatbot onto the side of a design tool or make an agent operate the UI by clicking buttons. We wanted the webpage itself to become the shared workspace . The human should be able to design visually. The agent should be able to understand and modify that exact same live circuit semantically. That became NotASprint . What it does NotASprint is a WebMCP-native motorsport circuit design workspace where a human and an AI agent design the same racing circuit in the same live browser state. The human can directly: reshape turns on the circuit inspect sectors and telemetry lock design decisions define measurable design constraints switch between Formula 1, Formula E, and MotoGP start from reference-inspired layouts or generate custom circuits run race-flow simulations save design snapshots compare iterations undo and redo changes export technical, presentation, minimal, and analysis views At the same time, ChatGPT can use NotASprint's WebMCP tools to: read the exact live circuit analyze flow, technicality, high-speed characteristics, and overtaking identify braking-zone opportunities reshape entire sectors by design intent make precise turn edits apply design inspirations generate new circuits run simulations and inspect their findings work within a design brief respect turns locked by the human compare iterations export the final design The important part is that there is no separate agent copy of the circuit . Both the human interface and the WebMCP tools operate on the same live artifact. A human can manually change Turn 7 and lock it without telling the agent its new coordinates. The agent can then re-read the live circuit through WebMCP, understand that Turn 7 changed, preserve the locked decision, and redesign the rest of the sector around it. The human designs visually. The agent works semantically. Both work on the same live circuit. How we built it NotASprint is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Lucide, and SVG , and is deployed on Vercel . The application owns the deterministic parts of the product: circuit geometry motorsport-specific design heuristics circuit analysis design constraints simulation locks history snapshots references exports WebMCP is registered directly in the browser using the page's model context. NotASprint exposes 14 semantic WebMCP tools covering: live circuit reading deterministic circuit analysis turn-level design moves sector reshaping design inspiration precise turn editing human-controlled locks reference circuit loading custom circuit generation undo simulation design briefs design snapshots export These tools describe domain intent , not mouse clicks. For example, the agent can request a faster Sector 2 or create a stronger overtaking zone rather than receiving instructions for which UI control to press. The human UI and WebMCP tools route into the same underlying application state and design operations. When either side changes the circuit, the other side immediately sees the new state. NotASprint does not require its own embedded LLM, backend, database, or separate agent service. The browser application provides the structured design environment and semantic tools; ChatGPT provides the agent. We also built three motorsport contexts: Formula 1 — emphasis on braking zones, long straights, overtaking, and top speed Formula E — compact technical sequences and stop-start braking MotoGP — flowing corner sequences, sustained direction changes, and wider arcs Each discipline includes three reference-inspired starting layouts plus custom seeded circuit generation. The circuit intelligence is deterministic and explainable. A point-mass speed profile and geometry analysis produce metrics for lap length, estimated lap time, braking zones, sectors, overtaking, flow, technicality, and high-speed running. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering WebMCP tools. It was making the human-agent collaboration genuinely shared and reliable . We had to ensure that: manual human edits were immediately readable by WebMCP agent actions updated the same circuit visible on screen locked turns remained exact human decisions semantic redesigns could work around those locks invalid geometry was prevented or surfaced clearly analysis updated deterministically after every change simulation results became stale when the circuit changed undo and redo worked across both human and agent actions references and custom generation correctly changed motorsport context WebMCP activity was visible enough to understand what the agent actually did We also found that generated circuits or aggressive semantic edits could occasionally create distracting geometry warnings. Instead of hiding those warnings, we improved the generation and geometry-safety paths and added regression tests around the exact demo flows. Another challenge was distinguishing WebMCP from computer use . The goal of NotASprint is not to teach an agent where to click. The value comes from exposing circuit-design semantics directly while still keeping the same rich visual workspace available to the human. Accomplishments that we're proud of The interaction we are most proud of is simple: The agent reads and improves the live circuit. The human manually reshapes Turn 7. The human locks Turn 7. The agent is not told the new coordinates . The agent re-reads the circuit through WebMCP. It preserves Turn 7 exactly and redesigns the surrounding sector. That is the clearest demonstration of why WebMCP belongs in this product. We are also proud that NotASprint now includes: 14 tested semantic WebMCP tools Formula 1, Formula E, and MotoGP design contexts nine reference-inspired circuit starting points reproducible custom circuit generation deterministic design analysis human-controlled locking measurable design briefs race-flow simulation simulation-driven redesign loops shared undo/redo history saved design snapshots and comparison multiple export formats and presentation styles visible activity receipts for WebMCP and human actions Before submission, we ran an end-to-end WebMCP audit against the real application and exercised every exposed tool, including the human-edit → lock → agent-adapts workflow repeatedly. What we learned The biggest thing we learned is that WebMCP becomes much more interesting when the webpage itself is part of the work . NotASprint is not fundamentally about making an agent faster at pressing buttons. The human and agent have different strengths. The human is good at visual judgment: "I like this corner here. Keep it." The agent is good at semantic goals: "Make Sector 2 faster, preserve three overtaking opportunities, and stay within the design brief." WebMCP gives both sides a common language without forcing either one into the other's interaction model. The application remains responsible for deterministic geometry, validation, simulation, history, and permissions. The human remains responsible for judgment and final decisions. The agent remains responsible for understanding intent, analyzing structured state, and choosing useful semantic operations. We also learned that visible trust mechanisms matter. Locks, undo, activity receipts, deterministic analysis, and before/after metrics make agent actions easier for a human to understand and control. What's next for NotASprint The next step is to expand NotASprint from conceptual circuit design

title: OpenScene Studio
pitch: A trainer asks ChatGPT to add a missing exchange to the video lesson already open. OpenScene waits for the learner before releasing the recorded answer.
about_excerpt: A trainer asks ChatGPT to add a missing exchange to the video lesson already open. OpenScene waits for the learner before releasing the recorded answer. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A video lesson about changing trains in Germany includes an announcement that the current train ends here and the connecting train leaves from railway platform two. It never teaches a passenger who cannot use stairs how to ask a station employee for the lift. The learner does not know the German words. The trainer can create a separate exercise or re-edit the recording. A separate exercise removes the practice from the original scene. Re-editing repeats the production work. OpenScene Studio lets the trainer add that missing exchange to the lesson already open in the browser. What it does The trainer tells ChatGPT what the learner needs. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT reads the current OpenScene project and adds a practice path using the response clip, route board, and timing already approved in that project. OpenScene pauses the lesson before the recorded station employee's answer. The learner chooses Wo ist der Aufzug zu Gleis zwei? Only then does the page release the response clip and show the LIFT → PLATFORM 2 board. The trainer can keep the path or undo it. This gives each person a clear role: The trainer defines the learner need and approves the lesson change. ChatGPT maps the request to the open project's branch fields. OpenScene supplies the approved German line, recorded response, board, timing, and revision history. The learner performs the missing turn before seeing the answer. Why WebMCP An ordinary chat can suggest the German sentence, but it cannot edit the OpenScene lesson already open in the browser because it cannot access that lesson's cue, trainer-approved response clip, pause point, or revision. Through WebMCP, OpenScene exposes those controls as narrow page-owned tools. OpenScene registers six narrow tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : openscene_inspect_project openscene_configure_project openscene_propose_branch openscene_update_branch openscene_preview_branch openscene_undo_last_edit ChatGPT can describe the learner need, supply the learner-facing line, and select a page-approved response pack. It cannot inject response words, board text, media paths, or answer timing. Those remain page-owned. The demonstrated writes carry the expected page revision, so a stale request fails without changing the project. That shared state lets one plain-language request coordinate the lesson cue, learner line, pause, recorded response, preview, and undoable project revision on the page the trainer is already using. How we built it OpenScene Studio is a React and TypeScript application built with Vinext and hosted on ChatGPT Sites. A revisioned StudioBus owns the project state and validates every WebMCP read and write. Playwright covers the visible browser flow, while deterministic tests cover schemas, stale-revision handling, unknown-field rejection, learner gating, trainer approval, media decoding, accessibility, and the production build. The public release passes 137 deterministic tests, 45 browser checks in development, and the same 45 checks against the production server. The local release package also passes five private evidence checks that are intentionally excluded from the public source archive. The demo displays the trainer's request on a labeled editorial card. The next split view shows the authentic privacy-cropped ChatGPT and OpenScene browser capture. Four jump cuts enlarge the recorded tool names, inputs, results, and page revisions while removing model waiting time. The learner click and the six-tool implementation proof appear on separate, clearly labeled frames. Challenges and lessons The main design decision was what the agent could change. Letting it write the station answer or choose arbitrary media would weaken the trainer's authority. We kept those elements in approved response packs and exposed only the learner-specific edit through WebMCP. The second challenge was proving the human turn. The response cannot start as soon as ChatGPT edits the project. The page must pause, wait for the learner's German line, then release the answer. That sequence turned the idea from an editor automation into a real practice exchange. WebMCP works here because ChatGPT interprets the trainer's request while OpenScene controls the lesson content, project state, and the decisions left to the learner and trainer. Potential impact For the learner, this turns a passive scene into the exact exchange they need to practise before a trip. For the trainer, it adds that exchange inside the original lesson instead of creating a separate exercise or editing the whole video again. The same page-owned pattern could support other approved practice paths, including a caption-first explanation, a slower language turn, or a shorter sequence. This prototype proves one mobility-and-language path. It does not yet measure learning or accessibility outcomes. Scope The demonstrated station lesson is fictional and intended for at-home language practice. It provides no live travel data, wayfinding, speech recognition, character perception, or measured learning outcome. The scene-partner imagery is synthetic and the authored response clips are silent. title: OutcomeMesh
pitch: Ask once, approve once: dinner and a ride booked via WebMCP
about_excerpt: Ask once, approve once: dinner and a ride booked via WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates The booking runs a second origin's WebMCP tool, called only after the human pressed Confirm. Six WebMCP tools become eight live, no reload: the page lists every tool call with its origin. One combined receipt: exact prices, cancellation windows, and only the ride was retried. Inspiration Jordan uses a wheelchair. Booking dinner and a ride tonight means two websites, and the restaurant's site gives an AI assistant nothing to call. Agents can navigate many websites, but navigation is not a safe, inspectable action contract. Cross-site tasks still break when a capability is missing, a route violates a human constraint, consent is vague, or one provider fails after another action already succeeded. OutcomeMesh explores a different layer: a neutral control plane between web capabilities and human outcomes. The open web needs both a way to create missing agent-native supply and a way to route that supply under visible human control. What it does Deterministic, fixture-driven demo: two bundled sample connector packages stand in for community submissions; all providers are synthetic. The demo begins with one synthetic intent: dinner tonight at 7 for two people, wheelchair accessible, with a ride included and a total budget under $80. The page registers six WebMCP tools when it loads; the header shows the live count ( 6 WebMCP tools live for your AI assistant ). Restaurant booking is not one of them, so the outcome cannot complete. Community Foundry reviews a sample restaurant connector package, submitted the way a community package would be. The risky version is rejected; the safe version passes an executable 18-check validator and is published with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The header count changes from 6 to 8 without a reload, and the Step 2 screen lists every WebMCP call as it runs: publish_connector twice, plan_outcome , then the brand-new restaurant_search_accessible_slots . Router rejects a cheaper restaurant because its entrance has three steps, and shows the exact plan: $44 restaurant + $26 ride = $70 , who receives what data, and the cancellation boundary. Nothing is booked until the person presses Confirm on the page. An agent that calls execute_outcome earlier receives a structured consent_required result, and the page shows that call as Needs your OK . After Confirm, Step 4 lists the booking calls: execute_outcome , restaurant_hold_slot , and then stepway_book_accessible_ride , which runs on a second origin ( https://outcomemesh-provider.pages.dev ). The first ride fails deterministically, the table stays held, and only the ride is retried. Done shows one confirmation, RCPT-OM-0007 , with exact prices and cancellation windows. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP is the lifecycle being demonstrated, not an add-on. The restaurant tools genuinely do not exist at startup. Community Foundry publishes them with the imperative API; a WebMCP-aware browser then discovers and calls them as structured, page-origin tools. Chrome DevTools' Application → WebMCP pane shows the same eight tools plus the provider tool, with live invocation status. If WebMCP is unavailable, the demo blocks instead of pretending that a badge or browser macro created native tool supply. The provider ride is a real cross-origin WebMCP call: the synthetic Stepway page registers stepway_book_accessible_ride with exposedTo limited to the OutcomeMesh origin, and OutcomeMesh discovers it with getTools({ fromOrigins }) and runs it with executeTool only after the page-owned consent grant. How it creates a better user experience The human and agent share one visible state. The agent receives structured tool schemas instead of guessing at page controls. The human sees why one route was rejected, exactly what data will be shared, who receives it, what will change, what costs $70, and which boundary is irreversible before anything consequential executes. Every tool call is visible on the page as it happens, with its origin, so trust does not depend on a hidden log. Accessibility needs change which tools are called: the route with three entrance steps is rejected even though it is cheaper. This is a fixture-driven demonstration, not validated accessibility evidence. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An agent can inspect the page's current capabilities, publish the missing sample connector package, create the route, and attempt execution. The page stops it at a human-only approval boundary, then exposes the approved state so the agent can resume and retrieve the same receipt the person sees. Together they complete a multi-provider task while preserving provenance, constraints, consent, failure, recovery, and outcome evidence across the full loop. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite, using WebMCP's imperative API. Six platform tools register when the page initializes: inspect_capabilities publish_connector plan_outcome approve_outcome execute_outcome get_outcome_receipt Foundry publication dynamically registers two domain tools: restaurant_search_accessible_slots restaurant_hold_slot A second static origin hosts the synthetic Stepway provider page, which registers stepway_book_accessible_ride for the OutcomeMesh origin only. Every registered tool is wrapped so each call (from the page or from a browser agent's executeTool ) is recorded with its origin and result and rendered on the Find and Book screens. Tool callbacks, Router, the consent checkpoint, execution, recovery, event ledger, and receipt all read and mutate one deterministic runtime store. A Playwright verifier uses native getTools() and executeTool() to prove the 6 → 8 lifecycle, the cross-origin provider call, receipt integrity, and recovery. Hosting is two static Cloudflare Pages projects; there is no backend, login, or API key. Challenges we ran into Keeping one system instead of two: a visual workflow plus a nominal WebMCP layer would have been easy and dishonest. Every visible phase and every tool callback share one state machine. Modeling failure honestly: a pre-consent stop resets to a safe six-tool state because nothing mutated; after a consequential mutation the UI starts a fresh proof and does not claim provider rollback. Browser differences: Chrome's WebMCP testing surface parses executeTool input as a JSON string, so the runtime tries the object form first and falls back to a string. Accomplishments we are proud of The page-origin registry really changes from six to eight tools without a reload, and the page shows the count live. A second website's WebMCP tool is discovered and executed cross-origin, only after visible human consent, and the call is shown with its origin. Exact rejection, least-privilege consent, deterministic failure recovery, and one combined receipt stay synchronized. Zero-key, deterministic, responsive, keyboard-operable, runnable without accounts or services. What we learned The strongest WebMCP experience is not "an agent can click less." It is that a website can expose a precise capability contract while the human stays inside the same visible state and consent boundary. Dynamic availability matters as much as schema quality, and a receipt is credible only when it is derived from the same actions the tool callbacks actually performed. What's next Validate one agent builder who wants the Action Contract／connector workflow and one website owner who wants to provide it. The prototype does not claim that demand, adoption, payment, or production integration evidence exists. title: FORGE — Human-Agent World Laboratory
pitch: A human-governed WebMCP control plane where agents inspect, repair, test, and safely reverse changes to a shared game world.
about_excerpt: A human-governed WebMCP control plane where agents inspect, repair, test, and safely reverse changes to a shared game world. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Game teams use disconnected tools to inspect world state, reproduce progression failures, rebalance encounters, approve risky changes, validate fixes, and recover from regressions. General-purpose browser agents add friction when they must infer domain meaning from pixels or manipulate fragile UI controls. FORGE explores a better model: one shared, typed control plane where humans and browser agents can understand and safely operate on the same interactive world. What it does FORGE is a human-governed live-operations and QA laboratory demonstrated through Ashen Reach, a playable medieval RPG world. A WebMCP agent can: Inspect locations, characters, quests, gates, items, encounters, and player state Analyze the real quest graph and discover progression blockers Run deterministic, seeded combat and reachability simulations Propose narrowly scoped world repairs Execute approved changes through the same service layer as the human interface Validate the result, inspect provenance, and roll back to a prior checkpoint The primary demonstration contains a real circular dependency: the key required to open the Ashen Sanctum is spawned inside that locked sanctum. The agent finds the defect from structured world state, proposes relocating the key, and waits for a person to approve it. A regression run then proves the repaired quest route is reachable. Rollback restores the original checkpoint and makes the defect reproducible again. Why WebMCP is essential FORGE exposes 30 browser-native capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(). These tools span world inspection, player actions, quests, encounters, seeded simulation, QA, repair, and governance. WebMCP gives the agent typed domain capabilities instead of forcing it to guess from pixels or button labels. Closed schemas validate nested input, stable identifiers are checked against the current world, and mutation tools clearly advertise their approval boundaries. The human interface and every WebMCP tool call the same typed application service. That shared boundary performs validation, permission checks, proposal routing, checkpoint creation, execution, audit recording, and activity publication. WebMCP is the product interface—not a chatbot placed on top of the product. A better human-agent experience FORGE deliberately separates capability from authority: OBSERVE: agents may inspect and simulate, but cannot mutate the world PROPOSE: agents may prepare consequential changes, but a person must approve them AUTONOMOUS: bounded changes may execute immediately only after a human explicitly opts in Every reversible mutation creates a checkpoint. Activity and audit views distinguish native WebMCP agents, human actions, approvals, validation runs, demo helpers, and registry examples. A person can inspect parameters, modify them, reject a proposal, approve it, or restore a previous world state without erasing governance history. This creates a workflow that was previously fragmented across debug tools, scripts, dashboards, and manual playtests: Structured inspection → bounded proposal → human approval → measured execution → deterministic validation → audit and rollback How we built it FORGE uses React and TypeScript with a client-first, deterministic world model. The WebMCP registry and human UI share a single executeForgeTool application service. The QA layer performs reference validation, quest-graph validation, progression reachability analysis, and seeded combat simulation. The project includes: 30 registered WebMCP tools with schemas and lifecycle cleanup Recursive runtime validation for nested tool input Human approval, rejection, parameter editing, checkpoints, audit, rollback, and deterministic reset Seeded combat simulation and measured difficulty calibration Responsive desktop and narrow ChatGPT-style layouts 19 service-level tests and a Playwright end-to-end matrix Public-origin verification through ChatGPT’s in-app browser Security headers, open-source licensing, CI, and zero known production dependency vulnerabilities How we used AI and Codex Codex helped evolve the concept into a production-ready implementation. It reviewed the shared-service architecture, traced authorization and persistence edge cases, strengthened nested validation, replaced misleading metrics with measured methodology, designed difficulty calibration, improved the accessible judge flow, added automated testing and CI, diagnosed rollback and hydration issues, and verified the public deployment. Human judgment remained responsible for product positioning, public access, approval boundaries, evidence review, and final release decisions. Try it Open the live app in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Open the WebMCP inspector and confirm all 30 capabilities. Ask the agent to find the most serious progression blocker and propose the narrowest reversible repair without applying it. Review and approve the proposal as the human. Run the regression and confirm the deadlock disappears. Inspect the audit trail, roll back, and retest to reproduce the original defect. No credentials are required. Links Live app: https://forge-human-agent-world-laboratory.themfpretty.chatgpt.site Source: https://github.com/jpretty01/forge-webmcp Demo video: https://youtu.be/wIQB_eFURDI Known limitations WebMCP is an evolving Chromium preview API and is not available in every browser. World state is currently isolated in browser storage rather than a shared multi-user backend. Combat simulation is deterministic and abstract rather than a frame-by-frame game-engine replay. title: Ruleloom
pitch: A human-governed game design workspace where WebMCP agents inspect, propose, validate, and playtest while creators keep final authority.
about_excerpt: A human-governed game design workspace where WebMCP agents inspect, propose, validate, and playtest while creators keep final authority. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Designing a tabletop game means coordinating rules, card costs, timing, win conditions, play length, and balance. An agent that relies on pixels has to guess how those parts relate, while unrestricted mutation can remove the designer from the decision that matters most. Ruleloom explores a better agentic-web pattern: the page exposes semantic operations, and the person keeps authorship and final approval. What it does Ruleloom is a visual game-design studio where a person and a WebMCP agent work on the same versioned specification. An agent can inspect, validate, run deterministic seeded playtests, and stage a bounded patch. Staging is inert: Ruleloom shows every operation, path, and value while the game remains unchanged. Only a direct human click creates a short-lived, proposal-bound, version-bound, one-use approval. That action dynamically registers apply_approved_patch . The agent can apply once; Ruleloom advances the version, consumes approval, removes the tool, and shows post-change evidence in the same workspace. In the captured public flow, Lunar Orchard advanced from v1 to v2. Replay was unavailable because the dynamic tool disappeared. Validation returned 0 errors, 0 warnings, and 1 informational finding. A 200-game deterministic run with seed 42017 produced 78 Player 1 wins, 89 Player 2 wins, and 33 draws, averaging 15.835 turns. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the product architecture, not an add-on. Five stable native tools expose inspection, draft creation, proposal staging, validation, and seeded playtesting. A sixth tool exists only while a current direct human approval is valid. The React UI and every WebMCP call share one versioned store. Tool mutations update the visual workspace, and human actions change which tools exist. Human authority and replay protection Approve, Reject, Reset, and Undo are UI-only. The approval value stays in a private store closure and never appears in tool input, output, persistence, or the activity trace. Approval expires and is tied to one proposal and base version. Stale or mismatched work is rejected without partial mutation; one successful apply consumes and unregisters the capability. How we built it Ruleloom is a static React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Zod app on Vercel. src/domain contains the strict schema, versioned store, allowlisted patch engine, validator, and seeded simulator. src/webmcp owns native document.modelContext registration, JSON Schemas, validation, bounded results, and registration lifetimes. src/App.tsx renders the human workspace from the same store. There is no login, server, remote database, production API, private package, or required secret. The complete MIT-licensed source, tests, threat model, evaluation definition, judge guide, and reproducible video materials are public. OpenAI Codex helped scope, implement, test, verify, and prepare this new standalone project. The runtime does not call an LLM API. Challenges The hardest problem was useful agent mutation without a reusable bearer token. We solved it with a private approval closure and a dynamic tool bound to proposal, version, expiry, and one successful use. Native WebMCP support also varies by client, so Ruleloom feature-detects support and names only tested clients. Seeded simulation stays reproducible through strict schemas, workload limits, recorded seeds, and versioned reports. Accomplishments Five stable WebMCP tools plus one state-dependent tool Direct human approval without agent-visible approval material Observed one-use apply and replay prevention 45 passing unit tests and 6 passing browser tests Public no-login deployment and MIT repository 2:44 public narrated demo with authored English captions Honest live-agent subset reporting without a fabricated full-suite rate What we learned Dynamic tool registration can express authority directly: if the person has not approved, the mutation capability does not exist. Strong human-agent interfaces need clear state, constrained mutations, version binding, and visible evidence. What's next We want to support more bounded tabletop systems, richer simulation distributions, side-by-side scenarios, opt-in collaboration, and the full frozen 27-task evaluation across more WebMCP clients. Testing Open https://ruleloom-nu.vercel.app in the Codex in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Confirm five tools, use the Judge Quickstart prompt, review the staged proposal, click Approve for agent , ask the agent to apply, then validate and run 200 playtests with seed 42017. Confirm v2 and that the apply tool disappears. No credentials are required. title: Semantic City — Shared-World WebMCP Simulator
pitch: A playable city-management sandbox where humans and agents share one live city. WebMCP exposes traffic, budgets, and utilities so every agent action is visible, validated, and reversible.
about_excerpt: A playable city-management sandbox where humans and agents share one live city. WebMCP exposes traffic, budgets, and utilities so every agent action is visible, validated, and reversible. Like 2 Comment 1 Story Updates One visible city; a semantic surface agents can use. An agent asks for congestion; the exact returned roads light up. The agent previews affected city state before changing anything. A visible improvement is not enough—58% traffic forces a fresh inspection. The shared world verifies the goal: 5/5 constraints satisfied. The idea Most websites expose pixels, buttons, and forms for people. When an AI agent needs to help, it often has to infer meaning from that visual surface or operate through a separate API the person cannot see. Semantic City asks a different question: What if a website exposed the meaning of its live interface directly to agents? A city simulator is an ideal proving ground. A person sees roads, congestion, utilities, budgets, and tradeoffs. An agent needs those same concepts as structured objects, metrics, constraints, and legal actions. Both should work on one world. What I built Semantic City is a playable, deterministic city-management sandbox on a 24 × 18 grid. A human can build and upgrade roads; place residential, commercial, industrial, park, and power buildings; manage taxes and a city budget; advance simulation ticks; demolish; undo; and save or load locally. The simulation tracks population, jobs, happiness, traffic, pollution, power coverage, cash flow, construction spend, and challenge constraints. Its rules are deliberately understandable and deterministic, so interventions have reproducible causes and results. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is the product interface, not an automation wrapper. The page registers 14 domain tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...), including city and metric reads, area, traffic, and budget inspections, building and road mutations, tax changes, deterministic simulation, undo, challenge evaluation, and non-committing intervention previews. Every tool is connected to the same authoritative, revisioned CityStore used by the React interface. There is no hidden "agent city" or scripted winning state. Human clicks and WebMCP calls dispatch the same validated commands. Mutations require the latest observed revision and return affected objects and cells, direct cost, metric deltas, constraint results, world ID, state hash, and rules version. This makes agent actions safe, deterministic, and verifiable. Making agent behavior visible Semantic View reveals what the page exposes semantically: stable object IDs, road connectivity, traffic and capacity, neighborhood boundaries, building effects, utility coverage, pollution, happiness, costs, and placement constraints. When an inspection tool returns roads, buildings, or cells, those exact entities light up on the visible map. Before a mutation, affected cells are hatched as a preview without advancing the city revision. After a commit, the map, metrics, constraints, revision, hash, undo history, and activity timeline update together. The timeline records the selected tool, arguments, affected objects, cost, metric changes, execution time, and before-and-after proof. The human can see exactly what the agent inspected, intended, and changed. The Rivergate challenge The featured goal is: Reduce traffic below 50%, maintain happiness above 70%, and spend no more than $400,000, without raising taxes or demolishing homes. Rivergate starts at 83.80% traffic . The agent first inspects the authoritative city, traffic hotspots, and budget, then previews and commits a seven-cell avenue upgrade. Traffic falls to 58.44% - better, but still failing. Instead of assuming success, the agent inspects revision one, finds the remaining bottleneck, previews and commits a second five-cell upgrade, advances one deterministic tick, and verifies the new world. The final state reaches 48.06% traffic with $204,000 spent, happiness above 70%, no tax increase, no demolished homes, and 5/5 constraints passed . The first intervention is deliberately insufficient, forcing an inspect - act - observe - iterate loop rather than a one-shot macro. How it was built Semantic City uses React, TypeScript, and Vite . A pure domain engine owns CityWorld; derived systems recompute connectivity, traffic, power, pollution, jobs, happiness, cash flow, and constraints. Commands validate complete building footprints and road paths atomically, reject stale revisions, enforce available cash and hard scenario rules, and return structured success or error envelopes. Canonical serialization produces a deterministic state hash. The WebMCP adapter translates strict snake_case tool inputs into the same commands used by human controls. Unit and Playwright tests cover the engine, shared store, revisions, undo, tool registration, semantic highlighting, previews, the two-step Rivergate solution, activity evidence, and responsive UI. I also rehearsed the complete flow against the public deployment using a native WebMCP-enabled browser. Challenges and lessons The hardest problem was guaranteeing that there is only one world. A tool mutation must become visible immediately, while a human action must be readable by the next agent inspection. One store, one dispatcher, revision checks, and hashes make that guarantee explicit. Traffic also needed to create meaningful tradeoffs without becoming a research-scale simulation. Deterministic weighted paths, fixed capacities, aggregate commuter and freight loads, and stable tie-breaking create explainable congestion. The larger lesson is that agent transparency can be a product feature. Domain tools, exact inspection highlights, previews, and audit trails let a person collaborate with an agent instead of trusting opaque UI automation. Accomplishments Built a real playable simulator rather than a WebMCP mockup Exposed 14 meaningful tools over one authoritative live world Added deterministic metrics, stale-revision protection, and world proofs Added exact inspection highlighting and non-committing previews Added placement validation, hard constraints, demolition, undo, and local persistence Created a two-step scenario that visibly requires iteration Made every agent action legible through a semantic overlay and activity timeline What’s next The same shared-semantic-world pattern can extend to operational dashboards, logistics networks, infrastructure simulations, planning canvases, and digital twins, any interface where people need to inspect, preview, and audit agent changes to live state. Future versions could add scenario authoring, richer utility networks, shareable saves, more challenge prompts, and additional semantic layers without changing the one-store architecture. I developed the simulation, Semantic View, activity timeline, testing, deployment, and demo. title: Signal Timing Workbench
pitch: A San Francisco intersection that a human and an AI agent retime together. The simulation lives only in the tab, eight WebMCP tools let an agent search hundreds of signal timings while you supervise.
about_excerpt: A San Francisco intersection that a human and an AI agent retime together. The simulation lives only in the tab, eight WebMCP tools let an agent search hundreds of signal timings while you supervise. Like Comment Story Updates Interface What it is A four-arm signalised junction that a human and an agent operate together. The traffic simulation runs entirely in the tab — no backend, no API, nothing meaningful to scrape off a canvas. The state exists only in the page. That is the point. A conventional browser agent could screenshot this and learn nothing: it cannot read mean_wait_s out of pixels, and evaluating a candidate timing would cost it a slider drag, a button click and a screenshot round trip. It would manage perhaps five experiments while an agent with site tools runs two hundred. Not faster — categorically different. The junction exposes seven WebMCP tools. An agent arrives cold, reads the model specification, searches the timing space off the main thread while the traffic keeps flowing on screen, and hands back a scrubbable explanation of what it found. The operator watches, locks parameters mid-search, and decides. The design argument The interesting part is not the simulation. It is the shape of the tool surface, and three decisions in particular. run_batch reports physics. apply_config enforces policy. run_batch evaluates any timing, including ones that are illegal to deploy, and reports honestly what would happen. It checks nothing. apply_config is the only tool that can commit a timing to the junction, and the only one that enforces the constraints. Keeping those separate means the agent can discover that the fastest timing is inadmissible rather than being silently steered away from it. Under school-run demand the best-scoring timing is a permissive-left plan at 27.4 s mean wait; it is prohibited, because opposing volume × left-turn volume exceeds the phasing threshold. The best legal timing costs 45.8 s. An agent that only ever saw filtered results would never understand what admissibility cost. The refusal says so explicitly: a refusal is a fact about what may be deployed, not a scoring signal — a refused timing may well be the fastest one. Constraints ship with their derivations, and it changed agent behaviour describe_model publishes every constraint with the arithmetic behind it. Yellow and all-red are not tuning parameters; they are safety intervals derived from the ITE change-interval formulae: approach speed v = 15 m/s (54 km/h) yellow y = t + v/(2a) → 3.50 s → floor 4 s all-red r = (W + L)/v → 1.33 s → floor 2 s Two measured effects on a real agent run: Unprompted, it used 5 seeds and 60-minute runs. run_batch's description warns about ±2 s of simulation noise and recommends averaging at least 3 seeds; the agent went further on its own. It never hit the phasing refusal. Its 50-config refine batch was entirely left_protected: true — it read the cross-product rule, worked out that school-run demand mandates protected phasing, and pre-filtered its search space. Publishing constraints in full meant a careful agent self-checked instead of learning by rejection. Locks are a permission boundary with no unlock tool The operator can pin any parameter. read_state reports which are locked; apply_config refuses to change one and says so. There is deliberately no tool that unlocks a parameter. The agent can read the lock, reason about it, and re-optimise around it — only a human clicking the button releases it. A permission model expressed through the shape of the surface rather than a confirmation dialog. Tools Tool Kind Purpose describe_model read Parameters, metrics, constraints with derivations, scenarios read_state read Committed timing, phase, per-arm queues, locks, live metrics run_batch read Evaluate ≤50 timings in a Web Worker apply_config write Commit; enforces constraints and locks set_scenario write Switch demand profile; re-checks the committed plan pin_result write Surface a candidate to the operator with a rationale play_sequence write Narrated, scrubbable explanation Other choices worth naming: Tool results are budgeted. run_batch returns full per-arm detail for the top 3 rows and summary metrics for the rest, and does not duplicate the payload into structuredContent. Measured on a 36-config batch: 53,558 → 11,284 characters, a 79% reduction. Context bloat is what degrades an agent over a long session. run_batch runs in a Web Worker. A 50-config batch is ~500 ms; on the main thread that freezes the junction every time the agent thinks, and the premise is that the human watches a live workspace while the agent works. apply_config restarts the live run and says so, along with the ~4 simulated minutes before metrics settle. Otherwise the agent commits, re-reads two seconds later, and reasons about a transient. set_scenario re-checks the committed timing. Switching demand can make the deployed plan illegal. It reports that and leaves the plan committed — the agent asked to change the demand, not to redeploy the signal plan. pin_result re-measures over 3 seeds regardless of what produced the original figure, so two pins are always comparable. The agent's search is drawn in the domain's own notation. Evaluated candidates appear as miniature ring-and-barrier phase diagrams — the diagram a traffic engineer actually reads — with bar width encoding cycle length. A scatter plot would show convergence more precisely and say nothing about what was tried. Verification npm run agentsim mocks document.modelContext, registers the real tool surface, and drives the exact sequence a competent agent follows: cold discovery, coarse sweep, the constraint refusal, recovery inside the legal region, a lock refusal, malformed input, two pins, a scenario round-trip, a narrated replay, and AbortSignal cleanup. It runs in about four seconds and caught several schema bugs before any browser was involved. The simulation itself was validated before any UI existed: metric spread of 162 s against 1.6 s of seed noise, an interior optimum in cycle length that moves with demand (57 s under morning rush, 87 s under event egress), and four scenarios with four distinct optima. Notes on the model A stochastic cellular automaton (Nagel–Schreckenberg). Arrival rates are representative of a mid-size German town, not measured. Two modelling details matter for the decisions the agent faces: Opposing traffic is platooned. Gap acceptance uses the opposing flow concentrated into its green window, not the hourly average — the platoon is released by the same green in which a permissive left-turner is trying to cross. Without this, permissive lefts are far too easy and left_protected becomes a parameter with one always-correct answer. The left-turn bay is 60 m. When it fills, left-turners spill back and block the through lane behind them. That is why protected phasing is ever worth its cycle time, and why sizing the protected phase wrong is worse than not having one: at school-run demand, protected at 8 s scores 214 s against permissive's 74 s, while protected at 16 s is the best timing available. Running it bash npm install npm run agentsim # headless tool-surface harness npm run dev # then open in a WebMCP-capable browser Node 22+. WebMCP is secure-context only; localhost qualifies. Try: "Optimise this junction for mean wait under the school run scenario, then pin the two options you think I should choose between."
