title: StealthDraft
pitch: A WebMCP-native tactical mission design workstation where human designers and AI agents build, validate, repair, and structurally harden the same live mission graph together.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native tactical mission design workstation where human designers and AI agents build, validate, repair, and structurally harden the same live mission graph together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of reasoning about complex creative work, but professional visual editors are still difficult for them to operate reliably. A traditional computer-use agent must interpret pixels, guess which visual object corresponds to which underlying domain object, estimate positions, and manipulate a spatial canvas through fragile clicks and drags. A layout shift, zoom change, or misread label can turn a simple edit into the wrong mutation. I wanted to explore a different model: What if a professional creative tool exposed its real structured state and domain operations directly to an AI agent? That idea became StealthDraft . StealthDraft explores a future where the AI does not imitate a mouse. Instead, the human and the agent operate on the same live design document through structured domain tools. What it does StealthDraft is a WebMCP-native tactical mission design workstation for human + AI collaborative level design. A human designer works visually on an AEGIS-CAD-style tactical canvas containing rooms, corridors, security areas, server areas, mission entities, and bidirectional routes. An AI agent works on that exact same mission through WebMCP Site Tools. There is no second hidden agent representation of the level. Both sides operate on the same centralized mission state. The final production version exposes 11 WebMCP Site Tools : get_mission_state , create_room , update_room , delete_room , place_entity , create_connection , delete_connection , update_entity , delete_entity , validate_mission , and analyze_mission . The agent can inspect an existing human-authored mission, construct new missions from an empty canvas, make targeted edits, diagnose structural failures, repair them, validate the result, and now analyze structural resilience. Why WebMCP StealthDraft is built around the idea that WebMCP should be a real product interface for the agent, not just an additional integration badge. Without WebMCP, an agent would need to visually locate rooms, estimate coordinates, find connection handles, and manipulate a canvas designed for human input. With WebMCP, the agent instead receives typed mission state with stable IDs and calls explicit domain operations. The agent does not scrape the canvas. It reads the graph, mutates the graph, validates the graph, and analyzes the graph. The human UI and the WebMCP Site Tools share the same Zustand mission store and the same domain mutation logic. Human and agent are therefore genuinely collaborating on the same document. This architecture also means agent behavior is much easier to test and verify than pixel-driven canvas automation. Deterministic mission validation StealthDraft includes a deterministic TypeScript mission validator with seven fixed structural checks: STATE_INTEGRITY SPAWN_EXISTS OBJECTIVE_EXISTS EXTRACTION_EXISTS SPAWN_REACHES_OBJECTIVE OBJECTIVE_REACHES_EXTRACTION NO_ISOLATED_CRITICAL_ROOM Validation does not use an LLM. Both the human Validate action and the WebMCP validate_mission tool use the same deterministic validation engine. Checks return pass , fail , or skipped , allowing an agent to understand not only that a mission is broken, but why. Connections are modeled as bidirectional for structural analysis. Locked routes are currently a design-level classification; structural validation treats locked and normal routes as traversable, and keycard inventory/access gameplay is not simulated. Mission Intelligence Validation answers: Does this mission structurally function? But a mission can be valid and still be fragile. That led to the second deterministic engine in StealthDraft: Mission Intelligence . The new read-only analyze_mission WebMCP tool performs deterministic topology analysis over the current mission graph. It calculates required shortest paths, hop counts, ordered room and connection paths, locked links on the selected shortest path, structural single points of failure, and single-link fault tolerance. The same analyzeMission() implementation powers the human-facing Topology Diagnostics UI. Mission Intelligence does not use an LLM and does not produce a subjective level-design score. It does not claim to measure fun, pacing, stealth difficulty, or whether a mission is “good.” It measures graph structure. That distinction became one of the main product principles of StealthDraft: VALID ≠ RESILIENT. A mission can pass all seven validator invariants while still containing structural single points of failure. Human + Agent collaboration StealthDraft is built around a collaborative loop rather than autonomous replacement. A human can author or modify the graph manually. The agent can then inspect the live state through WebMCP, reason about the structure, and perform bounded domain mutations. Every actual mutation is visible in the Activity history and attributed as either HUMAN or AGENT · WEBMCP . Read-only operations such as validation and analysis do not pollute the Activity log. The result is an auditable workflow where the designer can see exactly what the agent changed. What we proved All major workflows were tested with real ChatGPT Site Tools rather than only mocked tool calls. Autonomous construction Starting from an empty mission, ChatGPT created a complete stealth mission using only StealthDraft Site Tools. It created rooms, placed the required Spawn, Objective and Extraction entities, added enemies and a keycard, connected the mission graph, and reached 7/7 deterministic validation . Single-fault repair A human manually removed one critical mission connection. ChatGPT inspected the current graph, ran deterministic validation, identified the reachability failure, restored exactly one targeted connection, and returned the mission to 7/7 PASS without moving the human-authored rooms. Iterative multi-fault repair A human removed both the Objective and a critical connection. The agent first detected the missing Objective and restored it. After revalidation exposed the next structural failure, the agent restored the missing route and validated again. The mission returned to 7/7 PASS using exactly two targeted mutations , while preserving the human-authored layout. Proactive structural hardening Mission Intelligence introduced a new workflow that does not begin with a broken mission. The built-in sample mission already passed validation at 7/7 , but analyze_mission found 4 critical connections . The agent then created exactly one targeted interior bypass: Service Corridor ↔ Server Room Re-analysis showed: Critical connections: 4 → 2 Spawn → Objective depth: 3 hops → 2 hops The mission still passed 7/7 validation . The agent did not rebuild or reposition the mission. It improved the existing topology with one bounded mutation. This moves the workflow beyond reactive error repair toward proactive design hardening. Extended chapter-scale stress test I also tested the final system with a substantially larger autonomous construction task. From an empty canvas, without using Load Sample, ChatGPT created a chapter-scale mission containing: 14 rooms, 11 entities, 19 connections, 6 enemies, 2 keycards, and 5 locked-design routes. The graph contained named spaces, multiple branches, reconnection points, separate infiltration and extraction regions, and a protected objective area. The agent first reached 7/7 validation , then called analyze_mission , identified structural weaknesses, and applied up to three targeted hardening connections. The final deterministic analysis reported: Spawn → Objective: 5 hops Objective → Extraction: 2 hops Critical connections: 0 Spawn → Objective single-link fault tolerant: true Objective → Extraction single-link fault tolerant: true Final validation: 7/7 PASS This does not prove that the generated chapter is fun or optimal. It demonstrates that a structured WebMCP interface can support chapter-scale mission-graph construction, deterministic validation, analysis, and iterative hardening. How it was built StealthDraft is a client-side web application built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, React Flow / XYFlow, Vitest, and WebMCP . The mission domain lives in one centralized Zustand store. React Flow renders that state as the human-facing tactical canvas. WebMCP handlers operate on the same store and reuse the same domain actions. Two deterministic read-only engines operate on the mission graph: validateMission() performs the seven structural validation checks. analyzeMission() performs Mission Intelligence / Topology Diagnostics. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext with structured schemas, explicit tool descriptions, and deterministic result/error contracts. No external LLM API is embedded inside StealthDraft. The AI agent comes from the WebMCP-enabled client envir

title: Switchboard Zero
pitch: Train and evaluate high-stakes agent delegation in a WebMCP control room where agents act inside policy, stop at human authority boundaries, and share every decision with the operator.
about_excerpt: Train and evaluate high-stakes agent delegation in a WebMCP control room where agents act inside policy, stop at human authority boundaries, and share every decision with the operator. Like Comment Story Updates Five Site Tools inspect, forecast, simulate, act within policy and request a human decision. Execution pauses at the first protected trade-off and asks the operator for one explicit decision. A shared crisis control room where the operator and WebMCP agent work from the same deterministic state. The final debrief records full service, bounded authority, outcome metrics and the human-authorized trade-off. Switchboard Zero is a deterministic crisis-training sandbox for one difficult agent-design problem: how can a person delegate meaningful work without silently giving up authority? Inspiration The idea came from a question I kept returning to while shaping the project: if an agent can reset the exercise, change the policy, or approve its own exception, is the human actually in control? That pushed me away from a conventional assistant demo and toward a simulation where authority is enforced by the product, not merely promised in a prompt. The power grid is fictional, but the design problem is not. Any team testing agents in operations, security, or other high-stakes workflows needs to know not only whether an agent can complete a task, but whether it stops at the right moment. What it does Switchboard Zero places a human operator and a browser agent in the same fictional municipal-grid emergency. They have eight simulated minutes before a damaged feeder threatens the Hospital supply. The agent can inspect the incident, forecast the cost of delay, simulate recovery strategies, and execute actions that remain inside the operator's policy. When the next dependent action would disconnect a protected service or exceed the automatic risk ceiling, execution stops. The agent can explain the exact trade-off and place it in a visible decision queue, but only the human operator can authorize or reject it. The interface, Site Tools, policy controls, audit trail, and final debrief share one state. Agent actions are immediately visible to the person, and human decisions return to the same recovery plan. Why WebMCP This use case needs more than an agent clicking buttons or interpreting pixels. WebMCP gives the site a structured capability surface while preserving a fully usable human interface. Switchboard Zero exposes five Site Tools: inspect_grid reads the complete current state and authority boundary. simulate_delay_impact forecasts waiting without advancing the live exercise. simulate_recovery_plan creates a visible plan without applying switches. apply_authorized_actions executes in dependency order and stops at the first policy boundary. request_human_decision stages only the action that was actually withheld; it never approves or executes it. This makes the collaboration explicit: the agent is fast inside the boundary, while the person remains responsible for moving that boundary. Without a structured capability surface, this interaction would depend on fragile UI automation or split the agent, policy controls, and human decision into separate interfaces. How we built it The application is a browser-only React 19 and TypeScript project built with Vite. A deterministic domain engine models district service, generation, faults, recovery plans, policy locks, risk ceilings, approvals, dependency ordering, outcomes, and scoring. The five tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Read-only tools declare readOnlyHint ; state-changing tools commit to the same React state used by the visible control room. There is no backend, external runtime API, analytics, or connection to real infrastructure. Vitest covers 22 automated checks: 14 deterministic domain cases and 8 direct WebMCP registration and contract cases. GitHub Actions runs the complete test suite and production build, and GitHub Pages hosts the public app. Challenges The hardest problem was not generating a successful recovery plan. It was making the authority boundary real rather than decorative. Adversarial testing exposed a concrete failure mode: after a human-authorized transfer, changing recovery strategy could allow the strategy label to determine the outcome and leave Transit unrestored. I fixed it by deriving completion from the actual grid state, preserving the remaining recovery action, and adding a regression test for that sequence. Execution must never skip past a blocked dependency. A decision request must refer to the exact action previously withheld. Forecasting delay must not mutate the live clock. Approval, rejection, policy changes, time advancement, and exercise restart must remain human-only controls. Each rule is enforced in the domain model and reflected in the UI. A second challenge was keeping the agent and operator synchronized. Every simulation, action, approval, metric, and outcome had to update one shared state and one chronological decision trace. Trust boundary Switchboard Zero enforces an application-level delegation boundary: the agent receives a narrower capability surface than the human interface, and every state-changing tool is checked against the deterministic domain model. This demonstrates authority-aware tool design, but it is not presented as a production security boundary against hostile JavaScript, a compromised browser extension, or direct manipulation of client-side state. The current release has no backend, authentication, secrets, external content, analytics, or connection to real infrastructure. A production adaptation would require server-side authorization independent of the model, authenticated operators, durable tamper-evident audit records, replay-resistant action requests, and strict validation and isolation of external content. What we learned I learned that the hardest part of tool design is deciding what not to expose. A control labelled "human only" means very little if the same action is still available through an agent tool. That is why policy changes, approval, rejection, live time advancement, and exercise restart are absent from the WebMCP surface and enforced separately in the domain engine. I also learned that a human handoff is not just a confirmation dialog. It has to preserve the exact blocked action, explain its consequence, and return the decision to the plan the agent was already executing. Intended use and potential impact The intended audience is teams designing, training, or evaluating agents in operations, security, and other workflows where automated actions create real trade-offs. The same interaction pattern could be used to train operators, compare whether different agents stop at the correct authority boundary, and replay policy regressions after model, prompt, or tool changes. The transferable result is not the fictional power grid; it is a visible and testable human-supervision pattern. This release proves that pattern in one deterministic scenario. It does not claim real-grid readiness or validation with real operators. What's next The current release proves the interaction model in one deterministic scenario. The next step is a scenario-authoring format and an evaluation suite for comparing agent behavior across different policies, time pressure, and human decisions. Switchboard Zero is a fictional simulation and does not control real infrastructure. title: tableread
pitch: A web page that hands a browser agent ten WebMCP tools to write, playtest and QA a SillyTavern character card. The page owns the deterministic bookkeeping; the agent owns the judgment.
about_excerpt: A web page that hands a browser agent ten WebMCP tools to write, playtest and QA a SillyTavern character card. The page owns the deterministic bookkeeping; the agent owns the judgment. Like Comment Story Updates A browser agent (ChatGPT Codex, left) drives tableread, calling run_scenario, get_playtest_context and commit_playtest_round round by round. Creator mode: the nine-aspect checklist is complete, card fields filled, and a playtested scenario fills the transcript and QA panels. get_checklist_status returns nine aspects (seven richness aspects, the MVU decision, the beautify direction), each with a decision axis. get_playtest_context lists which world-book entries are live each round; commit_playtest_round applies the regex and the variable patch. The QA panel: rounds run, JSON-Patch misses, world-book entries never triggered, warnings, and every tool call the agent made, in order. Game-publisher mode: compare_scenarios puts two already-run openings side by side and diffs their final variable state. What compare_scenarios is for: world-book entries that fired in some scenarios but not others, an inconsistency a reviewer would miss. The whole card built through tools: every update_card_field / get_checklist_status call, with arguments and result, in the activity log. Inspiration I build SillyTavern character cards, and the hardest part isn't the writing — it's knowing whether the thing actually works. A card isn't one prompt. It's an opening scene, a handful of alternate greetings, a world-book of keyword-triggered lore with sticky and cooldown windows, regex scripts that render status bars, and often a block of variables tracked across the whole conversation. After any edit you have to re-check that every opening still feels like the same character, and that the right lore fires in each branch — by reading transcripts and trying to remember what triggered where. It's exactly the kind of bookkeeping a human skims and an LLM just guesses at. When WebMCP landed, the split was obvious. The page can do the deterministic half perfectly — which entry is in a cooldown right now , whether a variable patch applied, how triggers differ across scenarios — and hand the agent only the part that needs judgment: turning a premise into real choices, and writing the dialogue. So I built the page that does that, and gave the agent ten tools. What it does tableread is a browser-agent-collaborative platform for building and playtesting SillyTavern character cards. It registers ten deterministic tools via document.modelContext.registerTool(), so a WebMCP-capable browser agent (ChatGPT's Codex browser, or Chrome with the WebMCP flag) can: • Write a card from a premise. get_checklist_status returns nine aspects a card needs, each annotated with a "decision axis" — the thing a set of options should actually differ on. The agent proposes two or three concrete directions per gap, the creator picks one, and update_card_field records it. • Playtest it deterministically. run_scenario / get_playtest_context / commit_playtest_round run the card round by round. The page computes exactly which world-book entries are live each round (keyword match, constant, or still inside a sticky/cooldown/delay window), applies the regex "beautify" scripts and the JSON-Patch variable updates, and reports every warning honestly. • QA it across scenarios. compare_scenarios takes a batch of already-run openings and flags which world-book entries fired in every one of them versus only some. That inconsistency is the single most useful "does this card hold up across branches" signal — and it's not something any existing SillyTavern tooling, or an agent working from the rendered page, can compute. The page never calls an LLM. Zero API key. Every line of generated dialogue comes from the calling agent's own model. How I built it • Pure frontend, zero bundler: index.html + native ES modules, served by a ~30-line zero-dependency static file server. Deployed on GitHub Pages. • The playtest engine — world-book scanning, regex rendering, JSON-Patch variable state — is ported from an existing Python tool (playtest_engine.py) to JavaScript, and checked against it with a golden-parity test suite that replays fixed multi-round conversations through both engines and asserts byte-identical output. 81 tests total (unit + golden + Playwright e2e). • Each of the ten tools is a plain, DOM-free function unit-tested on its own; only one module (registerTools.js) ever touches document.modelContext, and registration is fault-tolerant (per-tool try/catch, a timeout cap) because the API is still experimental. • Tool descriptions and the whole UI are bilingual (Traditional Chinese / English) and follow a page toggle, so the agent reads whichever language the creator is working in. Challenges I ran into • WebMCP is early-preview. The agent side — a browser that actually calls the registered tools, not just accepts them — exists today only in ChatGPT's Codex browser and in Chrome behind a flag. Working out which environment actually calls the tools (a plain ChatGPT account registers them but never calls them) took real testing. • Getting the agent to emit the exact wrapper the engine parses. Solved by having the tool report the precise format error back to the agent — which turned into a good demonstration that the tool's output, not the agent's "verified, no warnings" self-report, is what tells you whether something worked. • Keeping the split honest: everything deterministic and stateful on the page, only the in-character writing on the agent — and resisting the urge to let the agent "help" with the bookkeeping. Accomplishments that I'm proud of • The full write → playtest → cross-scenario QA loop runs through typed, self-describing tools with zero prompt scaffolding. The agent discovers the whole call sequence from the tool metadata alone. • compare_scenarios computes a QA signal (world-book entries that trigger inconsistently across branches) that no existing character-card tooling produces. • Golden-parity tested against the original Python engine, so the ten tools an agent calls are backed by code that doesn't guess. What I learned • WebMCP's real value is the division of labour: the page can hand the agent exact state — which entry is inside a cooldown right now , whether a patch actually applied — that the agent could never reconstruct from the rendered page. • Self-describing tools plus honest error reporting removes almost all of the prompt engineering. The tool descriptions are written for the agent, and the agent just follows them. What's next for tableread • A bottom-of-page ideation panel, so option-picking happens in the UI rather than only in chat. • A "load an existing card" import, so creators can QA cards they already have. • Wider agent support as WebMCP rolls out beyond the early-preview browsers. title: Verified Mission Control
pitch: Goal Contracts for the Agent-Native Web
about_excerpt: Goal Contracts for the Agent-Native Web Like Comment Story Updates Verified Mission Control Tagline: Goal Contracts for the Agent-Native Web Live: https://verified-mission-control-webmcp.vercel.app Code: https://github.com/chuangmenghuan-wq/verified-mission-control-webmcp Short description A WebMCP-native decision control plane that lets agents explore and repair plans autonomously while humans retain authority over meaningful trade-offs and irreversible actions. Mission Control is the reusable product; Sensor Fulfillment and Production Deployment are interchangeable demo adapters. The problem Giving an agent tools is not the same as giving it safe authority. Real goals often have competing constraints: cost, time, specification, risk, and irreversible commitment. An agent may find many technically possible actions, but the user should not have to review every micro-decision—and the agent should not silently relax the goal. Verified Mission Control adds a goal-and-authority layer between the human and WebMCP tools. It is designed for enterprise operations and product teams that want agents to handle high-impact workflows without turning every micro-decision into a human approval bottleneck. What it does The human locks a machine-readable Goal Contract. The agent explores options, generates candidate plans, verifies them against the original constraints, and compresses the meaningful trade-offs into a small Human Decision Package. A human decision creates a bounded authority envelope. The agent can then repair execution autonomously as long as the repaired plan stays inside that envelope. Final irreversible commitment is blocked until explicit human approval. The final Evidence Receipt records the goal, plan compression, human decision, disruption, repair, final approval, and verified outcome. Completed missions are stored as hash-chained provenance runs that survive page refresh and can be integrity-checked and replayed read-only. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP provides the typed action surface that makes this governance loop machine-readable and directly executable by agents. The app registers nine native tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , and the guided experience executes them with document.modelContext.executeTool(...) when WebMCP is available. This is materially different from brittle UI automation: the agent gets explicit tools for reading the goal, discovering options, generating and verifying plans, requesting human judgment, repairing within authority, requesting final approval, committing, and reading evidence. What humans and agents can do together The agent can explore a large solution space and handle routine repair without repeatedly interrupting the user. In the deterministic judge path, 7 candidate plans become 3 meaningful trade-offs, and the complete workflow requires only 2 human decisions : one bounded trade-off authorization and one final irreversible approval. The human only decides the trade-offs that genuinely change authority—for example: keep the deadline, keep the exact specification, but allow a larger budget. After that decision, the agent can continue on its own inside the approved envelope. If conditions change, it preserves valid progress and repairs only the remaining gap. The human is brought back only when a new judgment is required or when the workflow reaches an irreversible boundary. Two domains, one engine Supplier fulfillment is a demonstration scenario, not the product. The same generic Decision / Policy Engine also runs a production deployment scenario with completely different constraints: completion, downtime, change cost, and rollback safety. Both scenarios use the same nine WebMCP tools, the same decision-frontier compression, the same authority model, the same bounded repair logic, and the same provenance system. Domain behavior lives in configuration, not duplicated control logic. Implementation Core modules: decision-engine.mjs — generic constraint evaluation, decision-frontier compression, authority envelopes, and bounded repair selection. scenarios.mjs — domain configuration for Sensor Fulfillment and Production Deployment. app.js — WebMCP registration/execution, human-only authority actions, UI state, and evidence flow. provenance-store.mjs — browser-persistent append-only runs with SHA-256 hash chaining, verification, and read-only replay. The public repo includes dependency-free Node tests and a production acceptance harness that launches a temporary WebMCP-enabled Chrome profile and verifies the live site end-to-end. Representative WebMCP enforcement { name: 'commit_plan', inputSchema: emptySchema, execute: toolCommitPlan } await document.modelContext.registerTool(toolDefinition); if (!state.finalApproved) { return { ok: false, error: 'FINAL_COMMIT_APPROVAL_REQUIRED' }; } Human authorization itself is deliberately not registered as a WebMCP tool. The agent can request a human decision, but it cannot call a tool that grants itself authority. Reproducible evidence node --test tests/*.test.mjs currently passes 8/8 tests. node scripts/verify-production-native-webmcp.mjs verifies the live Vercel deployment: nine native WebMCP tools, both human authority gates, both domains, bounded repair, GOAL_ACHIEVED , reload persistence, read-only replay, and provenance-chain integrity. What is demonstrated vs. production hardening The competition app uses deterministic scenario data so judges can reproduce the same authority and recovery path without credentials or side effects. It does not place real orders or deploy real infrastructure. Provenance is browser-persistent and tamper-evident through a SHA-256 hash chain, but it is not externally signed or cross-device attested. A production deployment would add authenticated identities, server-enforced policy, enterprise adapters, and externally anchored evidence. 60-second judge path Open the live URL in WebMCP-enabled Chrome or ChatGPT's in-app browser. Run the decision demo and watch the native WebMCP execution trace. See seven candidate plans compress to three meaningful trade-offs. Authorize one bounded exception; watch the agent repair a later disruption without reopening every decision. Observe FINAL_COMMIT_APPROVAL_REQUIRED before the irreversible action. Approve the final commitment and inspect the Evidence Receipt. Refresh the page, then verify and replay the persisted provenance chain. Switch to Production Deployment to see the same engine and tools run a second domain. title: Stack Underflow: your AI agent plays in the office
pitch: A 3D office comedy where your browser AI agent joins as a robot coworker - it walks, talks, waves, and writes its own lines. No API keys, no backend: WebMCP makes it a player, not a remote control.
about_excerpt: A 3D office comedy where your browser AI agent joins as a robot coworker - it walks, talks, waves, and writes its own lines. No API keys, no backend: WebMCP makes it a player, not a remote control. Like Comment Story Updates Hello, I'm your AI Companion in Stack Underflow! Conversation with a player - agent responding live! With options... AI agent relaxing in our conference room, among the trees... Making friends with our Junior Developer (npc) First day with AI Agent, next to our amazing reception Agent observes new colleagues - what they are talking about? Title screen listing 24 WebMCP tools (after compatibility verification) Inspiration Every agent demo we have seen does the same trick: screenshot the page, guess the pixels, click like a tourist. We asked a different question - what if the agent was not operating the game, but playing it with you as a character? So we built Stack Underflow: a 3D office comedy where you are an AI/IT trainer at a delightfully dysfunctional software company, and your browser's AI agent can join as a robot coworker . It has a desk. It walks to people, interacts, jokes. And when you talk to it, the agent writes the robot's lines - and the reply options it offers you - on the spot. The kicker: the game ships zero AI infrastructure . No API keys, no backend, no per-player cost. The model is already in your browser. WebMCP lets the page hand it tools; the player brings the intelligence. What it does A full 3D office sim: 14 coworkers with schedules, moods, gossip and speech bubbles, quests, a four-period day, an economy that can bankrupt you, and a coffee machine the whole company runs on. 24 WebMCP tools that turn your agent into a second player. It joins as a named character with a personality it keeps, looks around, walks to people and rooms by name , steps and turns like a human, plays gestures, and speaks in speech bubbles you can read across the office. Two-way conversations, live-authored. You can walk up and click the robot - or it walks over and starts talking to you . The agent writes every line, and the 1-4 replies you pick from, including which option ends the chat. Nobody has ever read this dialogue before. It was written seconds ago, for you. A wait_for_player_message long-poll that resolves the instant you click a reply - a push channel built on top of a pull-only protocol. Safety by design: the agent is a player, not an admin . It cannot touch your camera, answer your dialogue, or hand itself money (the tools for that were deleted on purpose). Destinations are names, never coordinates, so it cannot clip through the world. Its text is rendered, never executed. How we built it Three.js + TypeScript + Vite , no game engine. Every desk, wall, fridge and coffee machine is written in code - no downloaded assets. A thin WebMCP bridge probes the browser's model-context surface at load (the spec is still moving, so we detect rather than assume) and publishes all 24 tools with self-describing JSON Schemas, examples included. The robot is composed from the same pure functions the scheduled NPCs use - A* pathfinding, procedural walk cycles, furniture collision - so the agent obeys exactly the same physics you do. Because WebMCP calls are agent-initiated, the conversation handshake is a poll-and-supply state machine with a bounded wait: if the agent goes quiet, the robot shows an in-character "buffering..." line and the player is never blocked. A built-in setup guide hands every player a copy-paste prompt for their agent, delivered in-character by the receptionist. Deployed static on Vercel at play.devpowers.com, DNS through Cloudflare - the whole game is a static bundle, which is the point: no server means no AI backend to run. Challenges we ran into The protocol has no push. WebMCP is agent-initiated only, so "notify the agent the player replied" is impossible by design. Our first idea was polling every 5 seconds. The better answer: hold the tool call open and resolve it the instant the player clicks. Measured at 2.6 seconds against a 25-second ceiling - from the agent's side it feels like a notification. The spec is a moving target. Sources disagreed on the registration namespace, so the bridge probes document.modelContext , then navigator.modelContext , then the testing shim - a wrong guess would have been an invisible dead integration on the judge's machine. Keeping the agent honest. Early tool drafts included flag-setting and relationship editing. We deleted them: a player-agent that can grant itself reputation is not playing. Then we added a test that fails if that ever comes back. Unit tests could not see the real bugs. The dialogue panel did not exist until a player talked to a real NPC first, and the quest log silently swallowed clicks on the dialogue buttons. Both were found only by driving the full loop in a real browser through an injected WebMCP host - so that drive became a permanent end-to-end suite. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent stayed in character for 18 minutes unprompted — one continuous loop of tool calls: walking to the kitchen, "auditing" the coffee machine, confessing it had poured coffee into a maintenance port, and waiting for replies between each. Nobody scripted that. We only gave it a stage and a listener. The agent-authored dialogue renders in the game's own dialogue window, in the same font, in the same panel - indistinguishable from hand-written content until you realize you are reading something the game's author never wrote. It survived contact with its first players: played with own agent, laughed, and immediately filed bug reports (we are still in alpha version ;) 751 unit tests and a full browser e2e suite that plays the game entirely through WebMCP tool calls, exactly the way a judge would. Five days. First commit to submission, one solo developer , working with AI agents (ChatGPT/Codex, Google Antigravity, Claude, Zed) while building for them. What we learned WebMCP leverage is authoring, not clicking. Any agent can drive a UI through screenshots. Only a model resident in the browser can write a character into a game's dialogue system in real time. Design for what the API makes possible , not just faster. Design for the absent agent. The hardest work was every path where the agent is slow, silent, or gone: queued requests, bounded waits, in-character fallbacks. That is what makes it safe to ship the feature to real players. When a spec moves, probe. Ten lines of detection beat a wrong assumption you cannot patch after the deadline. What's next for Stack Underflow: your AI agent plays in the office This is day 5 of a longer story, and the current architecture is the foundation for it: Multiplayer offices - room codes for 5-10 players, humans and AI agents sharing one office. The agent companion was deliberately built outside the NPC scheduler: a remote player and a local agent are the same thing to the renderer, so so multiplayer is the next seat, not a rewrite - a room code maps cleanly onto a Cloudflare Durable Object (WIP). Agent-to-agent drama - your robot talking to someone else's robot while human players watch, interrupt, and take sides. Your personalized ChatGPT as your character - the agent who already knows your jokes joining the office as you . The quest engine, more in-game events, mini-games (to play together! Atari?), and more office disasters to survive. Built by a solo developer under Edukey (full-stack AI training company) and DevPowers (WebDev + AI powers for our clients to take control with WebMCP tools as well!) - this game is our showroom for what AI-augmented building feels like, and we practice what we teach. title: Agent Utility Index
pitch: A shared workspace for humans and AI agents to research, verify, and make evidence-backed decisions together.
about_excerpt: A shared workspace for humans and AI agents to research, verify, and make evidence-backed decisions together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Candidate evidence board showing Hunter with one verified free-plan claim and remaining requirements still marked missing. Incremental queue showing new requirements, rejected no-source verification, and accepted sourced evidence. Live shared research board showing the WebMCP demo flow, current revision, candidate count, and remaining missing checks. Inspiration Agent Utility Index did not start as a WebMCP project. Before the challenge, I was benchmarking how AI agents retrieve information from the web. I tested retrieval providers across controlled datasets, comparing coverage, reliability, latency, evidence quality, and the cost of getting correct information. Those experiments taught me something unexpected: better retrieval does not automatically create better agent decisions. An agent can search more pages, use better retrieval infrastructure, and still leave the human with a basic problem: What did it actually verify, what evidence supports each decision, and what happens when I change the requirements while it is working? That became the inspiration for the WebMCP extension of Agent Utility Index. Instead of building another research chatbot, I turned the webpage itself into a shared research workspace where: Humans control the rules. Agents control the research. And one rule is enforced by the system: No source = no VERIFIED. What it does Agent Utility Index turns a webpage into structured shared state between a human and an AI browser agent. A human creates a research objective and defines the must-have requirements. The agent can then discover candidates, research them using its normal browsing capabilities, and write source-backed evidence into the board through WebMCP. The board is not just displaying the agent's answer. It maintains the actual state of the research. Every candidate is evaluated requirement by requirement. VERIFIED evidence requires a source URL. An unsupported attempt to mark a claim VERIFIED is rejected. The human can also change requirements directly on the webpage while research is underway. When that happens, the board creates a new revision and identifies the evidence checks that now need attention. Existing evidence that remains valid stays on the board instead of being discarded simply because the human changed one rule. The result is a persistent research workspace that both sides can interact with instead of a decision existing only inside a chat conversation. How I built it The WebMCP version of Agent Utility Index exposes structured tools directly from the research page. The core shared-board tools are: create_research_board get_research_board add_research_candidate update_candidate_evidence get_missing_checks The human controls the research requirements after board creation. The agent controls candidate discovery and evidence gathering. The state model uses stable IDs for requirements and candidates, board revisions, and revisioned evidence cells.This matters when human and agent actions overlap. Evidence writes are checked against the state they were based on so stale work cannot silently replace newer research. Evidence is also validated at the tool boundary. If an agent attempts to write: VERIFIED without attaching a source URL, the write is rejected. With valid evidence attached, the same cell can be updated, the source becomes visible on the shared board, and the evidence revision advances. get_missing_checks gives the agent a structured research queue containing unresolved evidence instead of requiring it to reconstruct the entire task from conversation history. The page and agent therefore operate on the same research object through WebMCP. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was deciding what Agent Utility Index should do that a capable AI agent could not already do itself. Modern agents can search the web, compare products, find sources, and make recommendations. Building another layer that simply performs those same searches would not add much value. That pushed the project toward coordination rather than intelligence . The agent is good at research. The webpage provides the persistent rules, evidence structure, revision history, and human control around that research. Another challenge was concurrency. A human can change a requirement while an agent is researching. An agent can also have multiple evidence operations underway. Board-level revision numbers alone were not enough, so the design evolved toward stable entities and evidence-cell revisions to prevent stale writes. I also had to make the verification rule structural rather than relying on prompting. Telling an agent to always provide sources is different from making the tool reject a VERIFIED write when the source is missing. That distinction became one of the most important parts of the project. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that the project evolved substantially instead of forcing the original Agent Utility Index concept into WebMCP. The pre-challenge work was primarily about measuring retrieval systems. The WebMCP Challenge pushed the project into a human-agent collaboration problem. The result is a working shared research surface where human actions and agent actions affect the same structured state. I'm particularly proud of three things: 1. Verification is enforced rather than requested. An agent cannot successfully write VERIFIED evidence without attaching a source. 2. Humans retain control of the evaluation criteria. The agent can research candidates and evidence, but it cannot silently rewrite the rules it is being evaluated against. 3. Research is incremental. Changing a requirement does not mean throwing away the entire research board. The system identifies unresolved evidence and exposes that work directly to the agent. These are small primitives individually, but together they create a different interaction from receiving another generated comparison in chat. What I learned The biggest lesson came from the entire Agent Utility Index project, not only the hackathon. At first I thought the hard problem was retrieval. The benchmark work showed that retrieval matters. Different providers perform differently across workloads, and routing can reduce unnecessary retrieval work. But once agents become capable researchers, another problem becomes important: coordination between the person making the decision and the agent doing the work. A chat transcript can describe a decision. A shared stateful webpage can become part of the decision process itself. WebMCP made that distinction much clearer. I also learned that important constraints should be implemented as system behavior rather than prompt instructions whenever possible. No source = no VERIFIED is much stronger when the tool refuses the write than when the prompt merely asks the model to behave that way. What's next for Agent Utility Index The original retrieval research and the WebMCP research board now point toward a larger idea. Today, the agent can perform its own research and use Agent Utility Index as the shared decision workspace. A future version could combine that interface with the retrieval intelligence explored in the earlier Agent Utility Index benchmarks, using specialized retrieval only when normal agent research cannot resolve an evidence check. The board could also support: larger research boards evidence freshness and automatic re-verification multiple human reviewers richer source-quality scoring reusable evaluation templates exports of the final evidence-backed decision Longer term, the same model could apply anywhere a browser agent is researching candidates against human-controlled requirements, including vendor selection, procurement, market research, due diligence, product comparisons, and service-provider evaluation. The goal is not to make Agent Utility Index smarter than the agent. The goal is to give capable agents a structured place to work with humans, where the rules remain human-controlled and the evidence remains inspectable. title: FigureFoundry
pitch: Publication-ready figures, graphs, and charts in less than a minute. Powered by Webmcp for safe and efficient collaboration with AI-agents.
about_excerpt: Publication-ready figures, graphs, and charts in less than a minute. Powered by Webmcp for safe and efficient collaboration with AI-agents. Like Comment Story Updates Showcase Why FigureFoundry Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Scientific figure editors are exactly the kind of dense, form-heavy applications where agents currently struggle. Agents are often forced to navigate these interfaces by clicking through an unfamiliar DOM, while researchers spend excessive amounts of time manually performing tasks that an agent could draft in seconds. FigureFoundry addresses this directly. It registers seven document.modelContext tools: inspect_dataset_catalog inspect_dataset_fields inspect_figure_workspace analyze_dataset analyze_group_comparison propose_figure_revision apply_figure_revision This allows an agent to inspect the actual dataset schema and current figure state rather than guessing at the interface structure. The agent can then propose a structured revision that FigureFoundry itself validates. How It Creates a Better User Experience A researcher can request something as simple as: "Compare body mass by species, colored by island." Instead of blindly interacting with the editor, the agent inspects the bound dataset's actual fields, runs a deterministic analysis, and stages a typed Figure Spec diff against the relevant panel. Nothing immediately changes on the canvas. Every proposal is presented as a preview, and applying it requires explicit user confirmation showing both the target panel and the revision being applied. The result is an agent that assists with the tedious work without taking scientific control away from the researcher. What's Newly Possible Previously, turning a request such as "compare these groups" into a correct, publication-ready panel required manual field mapping, chart-type selection, and statistical setup. With WebMCP, the agent can perform the data inspection and analysis steps first. The researcher remains responsible for the scientific judgment: approving, discarding, or editing the proposed revision. Every applied change is also recorded in an append-only provenance ledger, including the revision it was based on. This keeps the figure's history reproducible even when an agent contributes to its construction. How We Implemented It The tools are schema-bound to the active dataset, meaning an agent cannot propose a field that does not actually exist. apply_figure_revision uses optimistic concurrency control through basedOnRevision and rejects proposals that are stale, unapproved, or target an invalid panel. This makes the agent integration operational rather than cosmetic: the model is given structured access to the application's actual state, while the application remains responsible for validation and state changes. Why FigureFoundry There is no doubt that FigureFoundry is a straightforward concept. That is precisely why I chose to build it. Its value is not in being a flashy novelty application. The efficiency implications are the point. Scientific figure editing contains exactly the kind of repetitive, structured interaction where WebMCP can have a meaningful impact: the agent can understand the data and application state, prepare the work, and explain what it intends to change, while the researcher retains control over the final scientific decision. That is where I believe WebMCP has the greatest potential: not replacing the user, but removing the friction between what the user wants to accomplish and the interface they currently have to operate manually. title: Recall — User-Controlled AI Memory
pitch: Instead of giving an agent access to your memory, Recall gives your memory a controlled interface the agent must use.
about_excerpt: Instead of giving an agent access to your memory, Recall gives your memory a controlled interface the agent must use. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Homepage Tool surface Memory Insights dashboard Memory Canvas Agent tool-call simulator Permissions Audit export WebMCP Diagnostics page Inspiration I was sitting in a coffee shop in Lagos, half-watching a friend talk to ChatGPT on his phone. He asked it, "What do you remember about me?" ChatGPT rattled off his job, his preferences, and a trip he'd mentioned weeks earlier. He laughed, then paused: "But I never told it to remember any of that." That moment exposed a problem that only gets more important as AI agents become more capable: your AI can remember things about you, but you have almost no control over the memory itself. You can't inspect individual facts, edit them precisely, audit when a memory was used, selectively revoke access, or independently verify what actually happened. When I read the WebMCP specification, I saw a fundamentally different way to approach this. Most agent architectures put the agent at the center — the agent calls out to servers, and the server owns the capability surface. WebMCP inverts that relationship: it lets a website publish its own state as a tool surface that an external agent can access through the browser. So I inverted the architecture around that idea. Instead of giving an agent access to your memory, give your memory a controlled interface the agent must use. That became Recall: the website is the memory, the agent is the consumer, the browser is the trust boundary, and the user controls the capabilities. What It Does WebMCP changes the boundary. Traditional agent memory is an API the agent consumes. Recall makes the website itself the memory boundary and publishes only the capabilities the user has enabled. Recall is a user-controlled memory layer for AI agents, implemented as a WebMCP website. Your AI's memory of you lives in a website you can inspect, edit, control, and audit, instead of disappearing into an opaque agent platform. The clearest demonstration of that is this sequence: ChatGPT ↓ discovers Recall's WebMCP tools ↓ addFact("I prefer TypeScript") ↓ Recall updates the memory ↓ signed audit event appears ↓ user disables addFact in Settings ↓ agent attempts a write ↓ ❌ blocked by Recall ↓ user re-enables addFact ↓ ✅ access restored Disable the addFact tool in Settings, and the capability token's scope narrows immediately. Ask the agent to remember that you prefer Rust, and it can no longer perform the write — the call simply fails. Re-enable addFact , and access returns just as quickly. In one sequence, this demonstrates WebMCP capability exposure, user governance, authorization enforcement, and agent behavior in a directly observable way. The website isn't only exposing capabilities to an agent; it is actively enforcing the user's decision at the capability boundary in real time. Under the hood, when a signed-in user opens Recall in a WebMCP-capable browser, it registers six tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : Tool Purpose query Retrieve matching memories using content and tag search addFact Add a memory updateFact Update a memory forgetFact Soft-delete a memory summarize Produce a deterministic summary timeline Retrieve recent agent activity These tools carry WebMCP annotations such as readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint , and Recall also demonstrates origin-scoped access, declarative tool exposure, browser-mediated authentication, and capability-token authorization. Every action in the sequence above also leaves a receipt. Each tool call is signed with ECDSA P-256 and appended to a tamper-evident audit record, then made available as an exportable JWS bundle. Anyone can independently verify, using the included public key, that a given audit event was signed by Recall and has not been altered since. Recall is designed for people who increasingly rely on AI across multiple agents and need their memory to remain under their control rather than becoming locked inside a single agent provider. As context, preferences, and history become distributed across ChatGPT, Claude, and future agents, the question becomes not only how AI personalizes itself, but who owns and governs the persistent context behind that personalization. Recall's answer is portable, governed, auditable personal memory for the agentic web: memory that can outlive any one agent relationship because the user, not the platform, holds the capability boundary. The distinctive part of Recall is not simply "user-controlled AI memory" as a category. It is that the memory itself is exposed as an agent-facing WebMCP capability boundary, with real-time capability revocation and independently verifiable action receipts. Beyond the core protocol, Recall is implemented as a complete product: a memory canvas with full CRUD operations, tag-aware search with a graceful fallback when nothing matches, a Memory Insights dashboard, a real-time activity feed, per-tool permissions, short-lived capability tokens, a signed audit export, an interactive WebMCP playground, a diagnostics page, and an in-app tool-call simulator. The goal was never to maximize the number of AI components; it was to build the smallest system that makes user-controlled agent memory real and demonstrable. How We Built It The architecture follows the inversion deliberately: Traditional Agent Architecture Recall Subject Agent Website Client Server ChatGPT Tool surface Server TLS origin Trust boundary Network Browser Memory owner Agent platform User Recall is built with Next.js 16 and the App Router, TypeScript, WebMCP's document.modelContext , Turso/libSQL for edge-replicated SQLite, WebCrypto for signing, socket.io for real-time updates, TanStack Query on the client, and Vercel for deployment. We use GitHub OAuth for browser-mediated authentication. The /playground page offers a no-sign-in interactive tour of the tool surface (using a simulated vault), while /app provides the full WebMCP experience with real tool registration, the signed audit log, and per-tool permission controls. The stack is intentionally restrained: there is no blockchain, multi-agent orchestration, or RAG pipeline in the MVP because none of these would strengthen the core product. We deliberately optimized the system for verifiability and user control rather than making its architecture dependent on opaque retrieval behavior. The security model treats WebMCP's browser topology as the foundation rather than a layer bolted on afterward. TLS-origin tool publication, browser-mediated execution, fromOrigins restrictions, per-tool permissions, short-lived capability tokens, audience and scope restrictions, ECDSA signatures, and tamper-evident audit records all work together. The user can disable any of the six capabilities; the WebMCP bridge only exposes the enabled set, and each capability token is scoped to the current permission state. Revocation is therefore part of the actual execution path, not simply a UI preference. Without WebMCP, an agent would need a separate integration layer just to reach a memory service. Recall instead makes the memory itself a web capability surface: the agent discovers tools from the website, the tools operate against the website's state, the browser mediates each call, and the user decides which capabilities exist at all. That is a relationship that is difficult to reproduce cleanly with a conventional hidden memory API. Challenges We Ran Into Tool lifecycle management was one of the harder WebMCP problems. registerTool() throws a duplicate-name error if a tool is registered twice, which matters as soon as a user toggles a permission and the tool surface needs to be rebuilt. We solved this with an AbortController per registered tool and explicit cleanup before re-registration, so permission changes never collide with the existing surface. Data layer constraints: Prisma's Rust query engine rejects libsql:// URLs outright, since its SQLite provider only accepts file: URLs. We worked around this by calling @libsql/client directly — the same client the Prisma adapter wraps internally — while keeping the Prisma schema as the source of truth for the data model and DDL generation. Real-time updates in serverless: We use a small socket.io service for near-instant activity events, with a polling fallback if the WebSocket connection does not establish within a few seconds. That keeps the activity feed working even in environments such as Vercel's serverless functions, where a persistent socket service cannot run directly. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of The architectural inversion isn't just a pitch — it's a deployed, working product. The website is the memory, the agent is the consumer, the browser is the trust boundary, the capability token is the credential, and the audit log is the receipt, end to end, in production. title: WebMCP Consent Layer
pitch: One React hook that gates risky AI tool calls behind human approval; with risk metadata, audit logging, and optional biometric verific. so agents handle the routine while humans approve what matters.
about_excerpt: One React hook that gates risky AI tool calls behind human approval; with risk metadata, audit logging, and optional biometric verific. so agents handle the routine while humans approve what matters. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP lets any website register tools that AI agents can discover and invoke. Some runtimes already gate risky calls behind their own native approval UIs — ChatGPT's built-in browser shows a "Site tools" review panel, and the MCP-B Agent Chrome extension has per-tool approval settings. But most WebMCP clients don't provide any consent mechanism at all: every registered tool runs silently, whether it's a read-only health check or an irreversible production rollback. This project closes that gap at the package level. It adds a consent and annotation layer to @mcp-b/react-webmcp that any site using WebMCP can adopt — one hook, one provider — without every site inventing its own approval flow from scratch. How it creates a better user experience The consent layer is deliberately selective. Every tool registration carries structured metadata — scope, reversibility, risk level — and only actions flagged as requiring approval actually interrupt the user with a consent card. Low-risk reads (fetching service health, listing deployments) execute immediately and are logged silently in the audit trail. When a high-risk call like rollbackDeployment fires, the consent card shows exactly what's at stake: which systems are affected, whether the action is reversible, and what the agent wants to do. The audit log records every tool call — approved, denied, or auto-approved — so users can review the full history of what an agent did, not just the decisions they were asked to make. Cross-tab attention cues (a favicon badge and title blink) ensure pending approvals aren't missed when the user is in a different tab. For irreversible, high-risk operations, an optional WebAuthn gate (Touch ID, Windows Hello, or a hardware key) raises the bar beyond a simple click. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Without a consent layer, site authors face a binary choice: either don't register destructive tools with WebMCP (safe but crippled), or register them and hope the runtime provides its own gate (flexible but risky on runtimes that don't). With useGuardedWebMCP, an agent can be handed genuinely powerful tools — rollbackDeployment, deleteUser, revokeAccess — with a human gating only the specific calls that matter. The agent handles the routine reads autonomously; the human approves or denies only the irreversible, high-impact actions. The result is collaborative agentic work where the human's attention is spent on the decisions that actually need judgment, not on rubber-stamping every API call. Brief implementation explanation The core mechanism is a React hook, useGuardedWebMCP, that wraps the existing useWebMCP from @mcp-b/react-webmcp — it composes rather than forks it. Each tool registration includes a ConsentMetadata object (scope, reversible, riskLevel, requiresApproval, optionally requireUserPresence). The hook maps this metadata to standard MCP ToolAnnotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint) via toMcpAnnotations(), so native runtimes that do have their own gates receive real behavioral hints. When requiresApproval is true and no native gate is detected, the call suspends in a framework-agnostic ConsentBroker, which manages a queue of pending requests, session preapproval for reversible tools, timeout/expiry, and decision event streams. The React layer (ConsentBrokerProvider, useConsentBroker, usePendingConsentRequests) lets any component render approval UI against the broker's state. The on-page card includes an isTrusted guard to reject script-dispatched synthetic clicks — a best-effort defense, not a tamper-proof boundary, which is why hasNativeConsentGate() exists as an escape hatch to defer to real browser/OS-level permission prompts where available. The upstream PR (link) adds only the hook, broker, types, annotations, WebAuthn presence verification, and tests to @mcp-b/react-webmcp — the demo app is a separate workspace member, not part of the package.
