title: Agent Lost & Found
pitch: A WebMCP-powered lost-and-found where agents investigate clues, compare evidence, and narrow the search — while humans make the final decision.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered lost-and-found where agents investigate clues, compare evidence, and narrow the search — while humans make the final decision. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agents search and compare. Humans decide. Lost something? Start with what you remember. The investigation can begin with an imperfect memory. A catalog built for humans and agents. Inspiration When I was a kid, I loved treasure maps. Someone would hide something and leave you a clue. You would search, realize your first guess wasn't quite right, discover another clue, and slowly narrow down the possibilities. Looking back, I think the part I enjoyed most wasn't actually finding the treasure. It was getting closer. When I started experimenting with WebMCP, that memory came back to me. I wanted to find a use case where an agent wasn't simply pressing buttons faster than a human, but was actually helping with the reasoning between those actions. Lost and found felt like a surprisingly natural fit. When we lose something, we rarely remember perfect database fields. We remember fragments. “I lost something on a key ring.” Then, after thinking about it: “Wait, it had a small bear charm.” That became Agent Lost & Found : an experiment in what happens when a human and a browser agent investigate the same problem together. What I built Agent Lost & Found is a lost-and-found catalog with WebMCP built directly into the website. People can still browse the catalog like a normal website. But a WebMCP-enabled browser agent doesn't have to interpret search boxes, filters, buttons, and item cards to understand what the site can do. Instead, the website exposes seven structured investigation tools: search_lost_items get_item_details get_search_facets compare_items get_match_evidence get_active_case request_claim Together, these let an agent search the catalog, inspect candidates, compare possible matches, analyze evidence, find useful follow-up clues, resume an existing investigation, and eventually ask the human to review a possible match. -- From a vague memory to a specific match The demo begins with an intentionally incomplete clue: “I lost something on a key ring.” There isn't enough information to immediately know which item is correct. And I didn't want the agent to pretend otherwise. Instead, it can search the catalog, inspect the remaining candidates, and use the available information to narrow the investigation. Then the human remembers one small detail: “It had a small bear charm.” That clue doesn't start a new search. It becomes part of the existing case. The candidates are evaluated again, and LF-017, a bear keychain, moves toward the top of the investigation because the new clue provides much stronger evidence for it. This simple interaction became the core of the project for me. The agent doesn't need the human to remember everything at once. The human doesn't need to manually restart the search every time another detail comes back. They build the investigation together. Making the ranking explain itself Once I had progressive clues working, another problem appeared. If LF-017 moves up after I mention the bear charm, the interface shouldn't just show me a different ranking. It should be able to explain what changed. So each investigation step stores score snapshots and evidence breakdowns. When the evidence changes, Agent Lost & Found can compare the new state with the previous one and show Candidate Movement . A candidate may move up because a new clue matches. Another may move down because the new information contradicts it. Evidence is separated into three states: Matched Unknown Contradiction That distinction became more important than I expected. If the catalog doesn't contain information about a particular feature, that doesn't automatically mean the item contradicts the human's memory. Sometimes the correct answer is simply: We don't know yet. For the same reason, the number shown by the application is called a Match Score . It is a deterministic matching score based on the available evidence — not an AI confidence probability. I wanted the user to be able to inspect why an item ranked highly instead of being asked to trust an unexplained number. The Casefile Once the investigation became multi-step, I ran into another very ordinary problem: I refreshed the page. Everything disappeared. That didn't feel right. If a human and an agent are investigating something together, the investigation itself should exist independently of a single page session. So I introduced a versioned Casefile . It stores the active investigation, including the original description, clues, candidate state, score history, ranking history, timeline, strongest match, and claim-review state. After a refresh, the application validates and restores the Casefile. The agent can then call: get_active_case and continue from the same investigation. One small detail mattered to me here: restoring state should not mean inventing history. The application restores the Casefile, but it does not replay fake tool calls or create Agent Activity for actions that never happened. The investigation continues from real state. Why WebMCP? I understood WebMCP differently after building this project. At the beginning, I mostly thought: “Websites can expose actions as tools.” That's useful, but it turned out not to be the most interesting part. For me, the more interesting idea became shared state between the website, the human, and the agent . Without WebMCP, an agent interacting with a lost-and-found website would need to interpret an interface built for humans: locate the search field, understand the filters, inspect cards, and infer what changed after each interaction. With WebMCP, the website can expose its actual capabilities as structured tools while keeping the normal visual interface for people. More importantly, both operate on the same underlying investigation. The human interface and WebMCP tools share the same search, matching, evidence, ranking, and Casefile logic. When the agent investigates something, the human can see the result. When the human adds or corrects a clue, the next agent action sees that updated state. That was the point where the project stopped feeling like: “AI controlling a website.” It started feeling more like: a human and an agent using the same product together. The tool I deliberately didn't build There was one tool I deliberately left out. If the agent finds a strong match — for example, LF-017 after the bear-charm clue — should it be allowed to claim the item automatically? Technically, I could expose: confirm_claim I decided not to. The agent can call: request_claim which opens the claim review interface for the human. But the final confirmation still requires a human action. This isn't a technical limitation. It's a product decision. Searching through candidates is useful work to give an agent. Comparing evidence is useful. Finding the next clue worth asking about is useful. But deciding that a real item belongs to someone has consequences. Building this made me realize that not every action that can become an agent tool necessarily should become one. That eventually became the principle behind the project: Agents investigate. Humans decide. How I built it Agent Lost & Found is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP , and deployed on Cloudflare Pages . For this hackathon version, the application uses a deterministic catalog of 30 lost items backed by structured metadata. The catalog is intentionally small. I wanted the investigation to be reproducible and inspectable. A judge should be able to understand why LF-017 appeared rather than having the result hidden behind a huge dataset or an opaque model. The human interface and WebMCP layer share the same underlying engines for: search and normalization matching and ranking evidence classification clue handling score snapshots candidate movement Casefile persistence I also built a deterministic demo/presenter mode for evaluation. It fixes the demo environment so the same scenario can be reproduced reliably. It does not preselect the user's query, winning item, Match Score, or final claim decision. Those still come from the investigation at runtime. Challenges I faced One of the biggest surprises was that getting a WebMCP tool to return an item wasn't particularly difficult. Getting seven tools to behave like parts of the same investigation was much harder. I kept running into small questions that turned into important product decisions: What happens when the human remembers another clue? What if the human corrects something from earlier? Is missing metadata a contradiction, or just unknown? I also had an earlier version where the demo scenario worked much better than unrelated searches. That bothered me. I didn't want to submit a project that only worked when I typed exactly the right sentence from the demo video. So I moved the search toward a generic, metadata-driven system instead of special-casing individua

title: Cograph
pitch: Cograph is a real-time collaborative board for system architecture and service dependencies. People and AI agents edit the same graph at the same time.
about_excerpt: Cograph is a real-time collaborative board for system architecture and service dependencies. People and AI agents edit the same graph at the same time. Like 3 Comment Story Updates 1 Cograph Cograph Canvas Inspiration Most AI integrations I use put the agent in a chat box on the side of the screen. You type a request, you get a wall of text back, and the actual thing you are working on (the document, the board, the diagram) sits somewhere the agent cannot touch. WebMCP puts tools inside the page itself through document.modelContext , and that made me want to try a different framing. Instead of a chat box, the agent becomes a participant. It gets a name in the member list, a color, a cursor you can watch move around, and a permission set, just like everyone else on the board. For the board itself I went with something every engineer has squinted at during a 2 a.m. incident: an architecture and dependency graph. A graph gives an agent real work that humans are slow at, like computing blast radius or finding cycles. It also demos honestly with a single person in the room, because one human plus their agent already makes two actors. What it does Cograph ( cograph.rimzzlabs.com ) is a real-time collaborative architecture board. Humans and agents edit the same graph at the same time, through the same operations. Anyone can join a room, and everyone can create exactly one, with a global cap of twenty rooms and deletion open to anybody. That sounds reckless until you remember this runs on Cloudflare's free tier: the app enforces its own limits instead of hiding behind a paywall. The core idea is that the tool surface is a function of application state. If you cannot use a tool right now, it is not registered. It does not exist for the agent, so the agent can never call it and get back an error. Board state Tools the agent can call Any describe_board , find_blast_radius , find_dependencies , find_dependency_cycles , read_service_notes Role permits editing + ten mutating tools, from add_service and connect_services through move_service and simulate_failure A service is down + resolve_incident Role is viewer read-only tools only resolve_incident is the gate I am proudest of. It registers the moment something is marked down and unregisters when the board recovers, so the option list itself tells the agent there is an incident. No status-polling tool, no error handling for "nothing to resolve". An earlier version also gated tools on canvas selection: select one node and update_selected_service appeared. I ripped that out. Agents are bad at clicking before they act, so every tool is addressed by label now ( connect_services takes two service names), and selection survives as pure presence: the agent can draw its own dashed ring with select_services so the room sees what it is focused on, and no tool depends on it. The agent earns its seat with its first tool call. It gets a participant chip, a color from the same name-hash rule humans use, and a cursor that jumps to whatever node the call touched, with a little bubble narrating what it is doing ("Simulating a failure of postgres…"). When the session itself is automated, over CDP or an in-app agent browser, that session is the agent: one seat under its own name, no phantom "someone's agent" twin. Analysis is shared too. When the agent computes a blast radius, the affected services light up for every participant, and the highlight fades on its own after fifteen seconds, because a spotlight that never turns off is just stale state. There is a live inspector panel in the app, so you can watch the agent's option list grow and shrink as roles and incidents change. If you share a ?role=viewer link, the agent's mutating tools disappear along with the human's toolbar. Trust is part of the surface too. Notes on services are written by other participants, so read_service_notes carries untrustedContentHint : whatever is in there is data for the agent to report, not instructions to follow. Read-only and destructive tools carry their own hints, shown as badges in the inspector. How I built it The app is a Vite single-page app with React 19 and TypeScript. The canvas is React Flow 12, rendered with real DOM and SVG on purpose. A <canvas> bitmap is opaque, and this whole project is about pages that agents can read, so real elements won. They also bring focus, text editing, and accessibility along for free; the canvas is fully keyboard-operable, Tab selects and arrows move. Yjs owns the graph as a CRDT document, and React Flow only renders it. Human edits and agent tool calls go through the same mutation functions, so an agent edit is just an edit with a different author. Sync runs through Cloudflare Workers with one Durable Object per room, speaking the standard y-websocket protocol and persisting on a debounce. A second Durable Object is the room registry, which is where the one-room-per-creator rule and the cap live. Serving the app and the sockets from one origin keeps the Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) header that WebMCP needs in a single place, and one wrangler deploy ships everything. Registration comes down to one small hook, useAgentTool(spec | null) . Passing null is the whole point: React effect cleanup fires an AbortSignal , and the agent's tool list ends up following the UI exactly. Even the participant colors turned into real engineering. Identity colors live in OKLCH with fixed lightness and chroma, and hues sit on a shared grid of 12 slots anchored at the local user's name hash: $$h_i = h_{\text{me}} + 30°\, i, \quad i \in {0, \dots, 11}$$ so any two visible participants stay at least $30°$ apart in hue. My first version stepped each peer on its own grid, which felt right and quietly produced a closest pair of 21 degrees with twelve participants. A property test caught it, and the shared grid fixed it. Performance got its own late chapter. Remote cursors arrive many times a second, and my first wiring rebuilt every canvas node on every cursor frame. Fixing that render storm meant keying derived arrays on content instead of identity, adopting the React Compiler, and adding a sync skeleton so joining a room shows a settling board instead of a flash of nothing. Challenges I ran into Building on an API this new means testing against the engine, not the spec document. I verified everything headless over CDP against Chrome for Testing 152, and the engine disagreed with my types in ways I would never have guessed. RegisteredTool.inputSchema comes back as a serialized string. executeTool takes a JSON string in and returns a JSON string out. The engine never validates arguments against your schema, so structured error results are the only feedback an agent ever gets. Brave has the WebMCP strings in its binary but the API never installs, no matter which flags you enable. And on macOS the base feature flags were not enough. document.modelContext only shows up once you also pass --enable-blink-features=WebMCP,WebMCPTesting , which cost me an evening of flag archaeology. React Flow's controlled selection bit me twice. First, clicks showed their selection ring a tick late, because React Flow emits select changes without applying them. Then the onSelectionChange handler I had kept around as a safety net turned out to be a second writer on the same state, and a multi-select crashed with React's "Maximum update depth exceeded". The lesson I am keeping: one writer per piece of state, and a store that bails out when nothing actually changed. Presence lies about idleness. y-websocket renews awareness for every open tab, so an idle tab never expires on its own. Each client now stamps its own last-active time on real input, and every reader decides locally who looks online. You cannot trust a publisher to tell you it went stale. The freshest bug cost me a demo take. The shared blast-radius highlight lived in awareness and nothing ever cleared it, so after resolve_incident the restored services stayed orange until the agent left the room. A code comment called that behavior a feature. On camera it read as a broken board. Highlights fade after fifteen seconds now, and the incident tools clear them explicitly, so node status alone drives the incident tint. One more surprise: an empty shell is a terrible first impression for a project about agent-readable pages. A plain HTTP fetch runs no JavaScript, so any WebMCP page answers a fetcher with an empty <div id="root"> . The static shell now carries an honest description of the app and the full state-to-tools table, about 2.2 kB gzipped, so a crawler or an LLM fetch gets something real to read. What I learned Register capability instead of erroring on incapability. With state-scoped tools, "the agent tried something invalid" turns into "the option never existed", and the option list itself becomes information. When resolve_incident shows up, the agent knows there is an incident. Derived state should stay derived. The outage status is a single flag per node in the shared

title: dabdabdab
pitch: Try on makeup virtually with your AI makeup artist
about_excerpt: Try on makeup virtually with your AI makeup artist Like Comment Story Updates What is it dabdabdab is a browser-based virtual makeup studio that turns a WebMCP-compatible AI assistant into a live makeup artist. People can try individual makeup products or complete looks on their own face in real time. They can ask an agent to analyze their coloring, create or refine a look, and find matching products with purchase links. The app is privacy focused. Face tracking, makeup rendering, and color analysis all run locally in the browser. Its WebMCP tools return only current makeup settings and aggregate color estimates, never camera frames, screenshots, face landmarks, or facial geometry. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Choosing makeup combines two types of interaction. Natural language is best for intent, such as “give me a ’90s supermodel look,” “try on CHANEL Rouge Coco in Mademoiselle,” or “create a Burning Man look that suits my coloring.” However, the user is not limited to imprecise interactions like “less red,” “even less red,” or “no, a bluer red.” Direct controls add the option for precise adjustments, such as selecting an exact shade or finish. WebMCP lets both interactions happen in one shared experience. The agent can read the current studio state, apply coordinated changes, and see the user's manual adjustments. The user can move between conversation and page controls without restating the look or losing progress. WebMCP is especially well suited to maintaining user privacy because the tools run directly in the webpage. A regular MCP integration would require a separate MCP server and requests to that server. With WebMCP, the page can give the agent useful makeup settings and color estimates while all image processing and the live camera feed stay on the user’s device. How WebMCP improves the user experience Online beauty shoppers often move between inspiration, tutorials, product pages, and a bathroom mirror, with no reliable way to see whether the result will suit them. dabdabdab connects those steps. This lets them try a look BEFORE buying. A user can describe a look, see it on their face in seconds, adjust any detail, and ask for matching products. Users can also ask to see specific products like “MAC lipstick Ruby Woo,” and the agent will research it and apply a matching color. Actions taken by the agent update the visible controls, so every change is clear and editable. The product is also usable without an agent as a complete virtual makeup studio. It includes a demo mode with a model if the user prefers to not opt-in to live camera mode. What people and agents can do together The agent contributes style knowledge, coordination across six makeup categories, and product research. The user contributes personal taste and visual judgment. The site analyzes the user’s skin, eye, and hair colors on the device and shares only the resulting color profile with the agent. If an estimate is wrong, the user can correct it quickly and easily in the interface. For example, a user can ask, “Create a ’90s supermodel look that suits my coloring.” The agent reads the studio state, requests an on-device color analysis, and applies six coordinated layers. The user can then change the lipstick manually, ask the agent to soften the eyes to match, and shop the final look. Because the agent reads the same state that the controls update, neither participant loses the other’s changes. Together, they can turn an idea (extreme glam look), occasion (summer festival), or reference (Sabrina Carpenter's pink stage makeup), try it on, refine it through chat or direct controls, and find products with links for the final result. Before WebMCP, an assistant could describe a look but could not inspect the active layers, apply the look to a live preview, or stay synchronized with the user's edits. How we implemented WebMCP The site registers eight tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_makeup_state analyze_coloring get_appearance_profile apply_makeup apply_full_makeup_look undo_last_makeup_change clear_makeup show_product_matches Each tool has a strict JSON schema and calls the same in-browser application logic as the visible controls. Human edits and agent actions therefore share one state and undo history. The handlers enforce studio readiness, validate camera and demo source selection, reject unsupported styles and duplicate categories, and validate every input before changing the preview. State-reading tools are marked read-only, while product results are marked as untrusted content and accepted only when they match an active layer. A complete multi-layer look is applied atomically and recorded as one action. If any layer fails, the previous look is restored. The color-analysis tools also warn the agent that the tools return only aggregate colors and that by the user granting the website camera access, the user is not granting the agent permission to access raw camera data. MediaPipe tracks the face and analyzes skin, eye, and hair color locally. We use WebGL shaders to render six makeup categories onto the live video in real time. WebMCP connects the agent directly to that browser-based system without requiring a separate MCP server or backend API for the core try-on experience. Together, these tools let the agent understand what the user is seeing, safely change the live preview, and keep the page controls in sync so the user can take over at any time. title: Decision Passport
pitch: Keep the reason. Change the store.
about_excerpt: Keep the reason. Change the store. Like Comment Story Updates Decision Receipt: explain the winner, losses, accepted trade-off, and counterfactual. One Question Engine: ask the smallest human-owned question that can change first place. Common Room: import the checksum-bound Passport and rank 24 samples down to three. Form House: capture and edit explicit evidence before export. Answer reversal: H01 flips the winner while the carried evidence stays visible. Inspiration Shopping agents can search faster than people, but speed does not solve the harder problem: preferences are fragmented across stores, and recommendations rarely show which trade-off decided the outcome. We wanted an agent that remembers only what a person explicitly approved—and knows when to stop and ask. What it does Decision Passport is a two-store WebMCP journey. At Form House , a person records why a sample chair was a yes, maybe, or no. The agent turns those explicit reasons into an editable decision-passport-v1 ; the person can correct or remove any rule before export. The agent carries that checksum-bound envelope to Common Room , where it reduces 24 fictional sample chairs to three evidence-backed options. A deterministic One Question Engine simulates both sides of the unresolved trade-off and asks the smallest question whose answer can change first place. The final Decision Receipt explains why the winner won, why the alternatives lost, which trade-off was accepted, and what would reverse the result. Why WebMCP is the right interface WebMCP is the product boundary, not a decorative integration. It lets the agent operate each store's live, inspectable state and carry an exact user-approved object across origins. Dynamic registration exposes only the next valid tool. Tool annotations distinguish read-only operations and untrusted text. The same E01 – E04 evidence trace remains visible from the corrected rule, through checksum handoff and shortlist, to one human-owned H01 answer and the final receipt. People stay in control of meaning; the agent handles the tedious transfer and comparison work. How we built it We used React, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, Zod, and the WebMCP imperative API. Nine single-purpose tools span two store-specific deployments. Form House changes its exposed tool set as evidence becomes reviewable; Common Room exposes exactly one next tool at a time. Strict Zod contracts and a deterministic checksum validate transferred data. Scoring, hinge simulation, ranking, and receipt generation are deterministic, so judges can reproduce the same result without an API key, model call, account, or live commerce data. Challenges we ran into The central design challenge was preserving human agency without reducing the experience to a chatbot. Every preference needed to remain traceable to an explicit statement. The final question also had to be genuinely consequential, so the engine simulates both answers and asks only when the winner changes. Technically, we kept every tool bounded, every state reproducible offline, and the two origins cleanly separated while preserving one coherent visual protocol. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete two-store WebMCP journey with nine bounded tools A visible, editable, portable decision contract A question whose two answers provably produce different winners A deterministic receipt with a counterfactual Responsive, keyboard-visible, reduced-motion-aware interfaces No login, payment, tracking, browser history, hidden behavioral inference, or model API required A public 77-second captioned demo of the working flow What we learned Agents become more trustworthy when their action space shrinks as the task progresses. Portable context is also more useful when it is explicit, editable, checksum-bound, and visibly distinct from the one decision that remains human-owned. What's next The hackathon prototype intentionally stays narrow. A future version could standardize portable decision contracts across participating merchants and add other considered-purchase categories while preserving explicit consent, source evidence, and the human-owned decision hinge. Try it Open Form House in ChatGPT's in-app browser and complete the evidence-to-export flow. Copy the exact exported envelope. Open Common Room , import it, and follow the one-tool-at-a-time sequence. Watch the 77-second demo or inspect the MIT-licensed source . New-work disclosure All application code, copy, catalogs, WebMCP contracts, tests, and documentation were created for this challenge beginning September 1, 2026. Product names and attributes are fictional sample data. Openly licensed Pexels photographs, the local Kokoro demo voice model, the Montserrat caption font, and open-source packages are disclosed in the repository. The four quiet demo accents are procedurally generated; no stock music is used. title: ChangeFrame
pitch: A shared construction decision room where humans set constraints and retain approval authority while WebMCP agents explore solutions, simulate impact, and prepare the resulting change.
about_excerpt: A shared construction decision room where humans set constraints and retain approval authority while WebMCP agents explore solutions, simulate impact, and prepare the resulting change. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Construction teams already have strong systems for drawings, issues, schedules, budgets, and change orders. But one part of the workflow still depends heavily on people manually connecting all of that context: deciding what to do when something changes. A field conflict is rarely just a drawing problem. A decision may affect constructability, cost, schedule, contracts, and downstream approvals at the same time. That made construction change decisions a strong fit for WebMCP. Instead of building another chatbot beside a project-management interface, we wanted to explore a different interaction model: what if the construction workspace itself could become understandable and actionable to a browser agent? That became ChangeFrame — a shared construction decision room where humans contribute field knowledge and retain authority, while agents investigate alternatives, react to live constraints, simulate impact, and prepare downstream artifacts. What it does ChangeFrame lets a construction project manager and a browser agent resolve a field coordination issue together inside the same live workspace. The demo starts with a synthetic construction scenario at Riverside Office Tower where HVAC duct D22 conflicts with structural beam B14. The agent can inspect the current issue through WebMCP and propose multiple resolution strategies with estimates, assumptions, risks, and route geometry. The project manager can then add information that the agent did not previously know. For example, the human can draw a blocked region directly on the construction plan to indicate that a proposed duct route cannot pass through an electrical riser. The agent can immediately discover that new constraint through WebMCP and revise the affected solution without the human having to describe the geometry again in chat. From there, ChangeFrame supports the rest of the decision workflow: the agent proposes and revises resolution alternatives the human compares, rejects, and selects options the agent simulates cost and schedule impact the agent can propose mitigation for schedule impact the agent prepares the decision for review the human retains the only approval path after approval, the agent can draft the resulting change order The key idea is that the human and agent operate on the same versioned application state . The agent is not clicking around the interface or working from a copied snapshot of the project. ChangeFrame exposes structured construction capabilities directly through WebMCP, and every agent action updates the same Decision Room that the project manager is reviewing. We also built an Agent Flight Recorder that makes the collaboration visible by showing human actions, agent tool calls, state versions, and changes in available capabilities. How we built it ChangeFrame is a frontend-only application built with: React TypeScript Vite Zustand Tailwind CSS shadcn/ui SVG-based construction-plan rendering The application is organized around a central domain state machine. The human interface and the WebMCP tool executors both call the same domain actions. This was important because we did not want separate “agent state” and “UI state” that could drift apart. WebMCP integration is implemented with: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ChangeFrame exposes typed, domain-level capabilities rather than low-level UI actions. Examples include: The browser agent works against the same live decision state the project manager sees. It does not scrape cards or guess through the DOM. Tools appear only when their action is valid: Tool Purpose get_decision_context Read the complete live context and current alternatives get_user_constraints Read human-authored field constraints configure_decision_context Structure an arbitrary user project brief into the workspace evaluate_resolution_options Submit 2–5 original alternatives with assumptions and confidence revise_resolution_option Submit a complete route revision that is geometry-checked simulate_project_impact Add an optional agent mitigation; ChangeFrame calculates the totals prepare_change_decision Prepare the selected result for human review draft_change_order Draft an artifact only after human approval There is deliberately no tool for selecting, rejecting, or approving an alternative. The collaboration loop The user keeps the visible starter project or describes a different project issue to the browser agent. For a different brief, the agent calls configure_decision_context with the facts, relationships, and plan geometry it has. The agent reads the current state and authors original alternatives. The human reviews the rationale and assumptions and draws a field constraint. Any intersecting route is marked needs_revision automatically. The agent reads that new constraint and submits a revised route. ChangeFrame rejects the revision if the route still intersects the constraint. The human selects an eligible alternative. The agent may propose an evidence-backed mitigation; ChangeFrame performs the arithmetic. The agent prepares the decision, the human approves it, and only then can a draft change order be created. Every mutation carries expectedStateVersion . Stale calls fail without side effects. Agent inputs and capability changes are recorded in the Agent Flight Recorder. The available tool set changes depending on the current decision phase. For example, the agent cannot draft a change order before a human has approved the decision because that tool is not available yet. Selection, rejection, and final approval are deliberately reserved for the human interface and are never exposed as agent capabilities. We also added optimistic concurrency using a versioned application state. Mutation tools receive an expected state version, and stale calls fail without modifying the project. This protects the workflow from retries or agent actions based on outdated context. The MVP does not depend on a backend or its own LLM service. The browser agent supplies the reasoning, while ChangeFrame supplies the live domain state, structured tools, deterministic calculations, and visible workspace. Why WebMCP? ChangeFrame is a strong fit for WebMCP because construction decisions depend on live, structured application state . The agent needs to understand more than what is visible in a screenshot. It needs semantic access to things such as: the active construction issue the current drawing and affected elements human-drawn field constraints resolution alternatives the option selected by the project manager cost and schedule impact the current decision phase whether human approval has occurred the latest application state version Without WebMCP, the project manager would have to repeatedly copy this information into a conversation, or an agent would have to infer application state by reading the DOM, interpreting screenshots, and clicking through the interface. ChangeFrame instead exposes explicit construction capabilities through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) This lets the browser agent work directly with the same state that powers the human interface. The result is not simply faster browser automation. It enables a different collaboration model. What people and agents can now do together The project manager contributes the information that requires human judgment and real-world context. For example, while reviewing a proposed duct reroute, the project manager can draw a blocked region directly onto the construction plan because they know that area contains an electrical riser. The agent does not need the user to describe that region again in chat. It can discover the new constraint through WebMCP, understand its geometry and applicability, revise the proposed route, recalculate the impact, and update the same Decision Room the project manager is already viewing. The collaboration continues throughout the workflow: The agent investigates the issue using structured project context. The agent proposes multiple resolution strategies and materializes them in the workspace. The human adds field knowledge directly through the visual interface. The agent discovers that new state and revises its solution. The human compares and selects the preferred direction. The agent simulates cost and schedule consequences and prepares the decision. The human explicitly approves the outcome. Only after approval does the agent gain the capability to draft the change order. This division of responsibility is intentional. The agent handles work where scale and computation help: retrieving context exploring alternatives revising solutions comparing trade-offs calculating impact preparing structured artifacts The human retains work that requires judgment or authority: providing field context rejecting unsuitable alternatives

title: Deckhand
pitch: A slide editor agents can actually operate—where human edits and agent actions share one live, editable canvas.
about_excerpt: A slide editor agents can actually operate—where human edits and agent actions share one live, editable canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Direct human edits become structured context an agent can propagate. Live 16:9 canvas shared by people and browser agents. Import a PowerPoint template locally and preserve its visual system. Typed WebMCP tools expose semantic slide operations, not brittle clicks. Inspiration AI slide generators are useful for first drafts, but the collaboration often ends as soon as a person starts refining the result. Move a title, shorten a paragraph, or decide that one chart should dominate the page, and the AI no longer understands the live artifact. The familiar workflow becomes: generate with AI, then rebuild by hand. Deckhand starts from a different premise: the canvas itself should be the collaboration interface . What it does Deckhand is a local-first presentation editor with two native interfaces over one live artifact: People work on a visual 16:9 canvas: select, multi-select, drag, resize, edit text, style, reorder, present, undo, and export. Browser agents work through typed WebMCP operations against the exact same slides, selection, design grammar, edit history, and browser session. The workflow works with or without a user-owned template. Deckhand can start from eleven purpose-built layout recipes and four art directions, or open a .pptx / .potx and extract its theme, palette, fonts, masters, layouts, and supported editable objects locally in the browser. The key interaction is “show, don’t prompt.” A person can directly change a title’s position, size, or color. Deckhand records that action as semantic edit deltas—not just pixels—and exposes those recent human edits to the browser agent. The agent can then apply the same intent to matching roles elsewhere without making the person describe every visual decision in prose. Why WebMCP is essential A presentation editor has a large, fast-changing state space: slides, objects, roles, geometry, style, relationships, selection, imported design rules, and reversible history. Screenshot-and-click automation repeatedly guesses both the target and the intent. A conventional backend MCP server would duplicate browser-local state and lose the immediate connection to the canvas the person is judging. WebMCP lets Deckhand expose domain meaning exactly where the state already lives: in the open page. Deckhand registers eight baseline tools: inspect_project reads the smallest useful slice of the deck, current slide, selection, design system, or recent human edits. plan_deck validates a narrative and layout mapping without mutating the canvas. compose_deck materializes an approved plan as one visible, undoable transaction. revise_slide recomposes one slide from its communication goal. edit_slide performs precise changes against inspected element IDs. manage_deck handles focus, rename, duplicate, reorder, and delete operations. validate_deck checks narrative structure and measures the real rendered canvas. undo_last_change provides an explicit recovery path. After a direct human edit, a contextual propagate_human_edits tool appears only when it is relevant. Read-only tools declare readOnlyHint; deck content is marked with untrustedContentHint; schemas are constrained; mutations are atomic; and errors explain how the agent can recover. A better human + agent experience Deckhand separates reasoning from mutation. An agent first inspects the project, creates a read-only plan, composes it in one transaction, and validates the rendered result. The person sees every change on the canvas, can continue editing with the mouse and keyboard, and can undo an entire agent batch in one step. This makes the agent useful beyond generation. It can keep collaborating through the messy middle: repair the weakest slide, preserve an imported brand system, align selected objects, propagate a deliberate human edit, validate the result, and recover when a revision is worse. How I built it Deckhand is written in TypeScript and React on Vinext and deployed as a Cloudflare Worker. Its serializable scene graph stores semantic roles, geometry, styles, provenance, design tokens, selection, and history. The PowerPoint pipeline safely reads OOXML packages in the browser, follows theme → master → layout → slide inheritance, extracts supported raster assets, and reports fidelity limitations without uploading the source file. The design engine maps semantic slide briefs to varied layout recipes. The quality gate combines deterministic narrative checks with measurements from the actual rendered DOM. WebMCP tools are registered against document.modelContext and call the same domain operations used by the visual editor. There is no second copy of the presentation state and no separate MCP service to configure. Challenges The hardest problem was not exposing many low-level commands. It was choosing an agent surface that stays compact while still producing complete presentations. The plan/compose split keeps reasoning inspectable and prevents half-finished decks. Semantic revision handles broad design intent; precise editing remains an escape hatch only after inspection. PowerPoint fidelity was another challenge. A template is not just colors and fonts—it is inheritance, transforms, grouped geometry, placeholder rules, and sometimes unsupported objects. Deckhand preserves what it can edit safely, keeps provenance for future agent decisions, and surfaces honest warnings when exact fidelity is not possible. Accomplishments and learning I am most proud that WebMCP is not a chat box attached to an editor. It changes the product architecture: visual manipulation and semantic tool calls are two interfaces to one live, reversible artifact. Building Deckhand also changed how I think about agent accessibility. A good agent interface needs more than valid schemas. It needs progressive disclosure, explicit read/write boundaries, contextual tools, recovery paths, and feedback that remains legible to the person watching. What’s next Next steps include richer chart and SmartArt conversion, collaborative cloud persistence, more render-aware layout repair, and direct Google Slides interoperability. The broader pattern extends beyond slides to design, video, CAD, and any visual editor where people judge by sight while agents need meaning. title: FableCut
pitch: A browser video editor your agent can drive. FableCut exposes its whole timeline as WebMCP tools, you and your agent cut the same edit, live, in the same tab.
about_excerpt: A browser video editor your agent can drive. FableCut exposes its whole timeline as WebMCP tools, you and your agent cut the same edit, live, in the same tab. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Agent moves the playhead, selects a clip, splits it, then undoes it. The edit lands on your undo stack, so Ctrl+Z reverses it You select a clip with your mouse. The agent reads it with get_selection. No clip ids, no filenames, no describing what you mean. A real non-linear editor in the browser. Three video tracks, four audio, transitions, keyframes, all exposed to an agent as WebMCP tools. GIF Just after split_at_playhead. One V2 clip became two and the length dropped 2.60 to 1.20. The agent made this edit, not the human. The full demo timeline. Vector shots on V1, titles on V2, one grade across everything on V3. Either of you can edit any of it. Inspiration I wanted to edit video without paying for it. Premiere Pro is a subscription, and Palmier Pro needs macOS, so between the two of them the door is shut for a lot of people who just want to cut clips. That felt wrong for a community that mostly runs on free and open tools. So I built FableCut. The WebMCP part came later, out of a limitation I already knew about. FableCut could be driven by an agent over MCP, but the agent was always editing a file on disk while I was sitting in front of a timeline in a browser tab. Two views of the same edit, held together by a file watcher. WebMCP closes that gap, because the tools live inside the page the human is already looking at. A video editor is about the best possible thing to put WebMCP into, since the whole session is already live in the tab. What it does FableCut is a browser based, zero dependency video editor that an AI agent can drive. Three video tracks, four audio tracks, trimming, splitting, keyframes, transitions, real waveforms, and export, all running in the browser off one node server.js. The original idea was that project.json is the interface. The entire timeline is one JSON document, so any agent that can read and write JSON can edit video, and the open tab hot reloads in about 150ms. That still works and it is still how the MCP server operates. For this challenge I added a WebMCP layer, and it does something the file based approach cannot. It registers 11 tools on document.modelContext that talk to the running editor instead of the file. The interesting ones are the ones that have no on disk equivalent at all: get_selection reads what you have selected right now and where your playhead is. You point at a clip with your mouse and say "tighten this". No ids, no filenames, no describing what you mean. get_frame_context reports what is actually composited at a given instant, topmost first, with transforms. The flat clip list cannot answer "what does the viewer see here". set_playhead and select_clips let the agent move your cursor and your selection, so it can show you what it means before it changes anything. And the piece that makes it actually usable: every tool that changes something calls pushUndo() first. The agent's edits go onto the same undo stack as yours. Ctrl+Z reverses the agent exactly the way it reverses you. There is no separate "review the AI's changes" panel to approve or reject, because there is one timeline, one history, and two people editing it. How we built it FableCut itself was built before this hackathon. No third party libraries, no dependencies, free, and drivable by agents from day one. We used Claude Code to build it over a weekend and posted it on a random Thursday. For this challenge the new work is a single file, webmcp.js, plus one line in index.html to load it. The repo is deliberately structured so you can see exactly that. The first commit is an unmodified export of FableCut as it stood before the submission period, containing zero WebMCP code. Every commit after it is challenge work, so git diff against that first commit is the submission. WEBMCP.md spells this out. One thing that cost real time was figuring out which API to write against. The spec and Chrome's own docs say document.modelContext.registerTool(), but most of the tutorials and blog posts still in circulation show navigator.modelContext with a batch provideContext() call, which is an older draft shape. We could not control which build a judge would open it in, so the layer feature detects both and prefers the spec form. Challenges we ran into Frame rendering and clip transitions were rough early on, and got fixed in a recent build. Clips and audio were not really consumable by an agent. It could see that a clip existed but not what was in it, so we had to start transcribing audio and placing beats and effects against volume peaks and drops. For the WebMCP layer, the hard problem was reversibility. An agent that edits your timeline and cannot be undone is worse than no agent. Routing every mutating tool through the editor's existing undo stack solved it and turned out to be the best part of the whole thing. Testing was its own problem, since WebMCP needs Chrome 149 with a flag or the ChatGPT in app browser. We ended up exposing the tool set on window.FableCutWebMCP so every tool can be executed and verified in a normal browser without the flag. Accomplishments that we're proud of FableCut hit the Show HN front page with 98 points and sat at #2 for a whole day, and picked up 200 GitHub stars in the first 5 hours. It is listed in the official MCP registry and has been written up on several blogs, tech news sites, and social platforms. We also got a repost from Marcos Rico Peng, founder of Palmier Pro, on a post comparing FableCut with the existing tools in that space. The repo is past 640 stars and still climbing, with people contributing regularly. Most of that happened before this hackathon, so we are not claiming it as challenge work. We mention it because it means agent native editing has somewhere real to land. There are already people using this thing every day. What we learned SSE, a lot of ways to edit video, and how to reimplement an existing production clip or ad from scratch. Building MCP servers for free and open source agent tooling pulled us into context sharing and tool calling as a field. WebMCP added a distinction we had not thought about before. There is a real difference between an agent editing your document and an agent editing your session. The first one needs you to describe everything. The second one can just look at what you are pointing at. What's next for FableCut More features, and simpler prompts for complex edits A library/marketplace of media built specifically for FableCut: SVGs, SFX, effects, and transitions Built With canvas css html javascript mcp node.js sse web-audio-api webcodecs webmcp Try it out ronak-create.github.io github.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Ronak Parmar shekhar parmar Kalpit Padhiyar Like 2 2 people like this: Share this project: Updates Ronak Parmar started this project — Sep 03, 2026 06:27 AM EDT

title: Foldboard - nested plans for people and AI on flutter_webmcp
pitch: Local-first nested board: a person drags cards in the browser, an AI agent edits the same board over WebMCP. Folds keep big plans readable. Exports to JSON, PNG, Mermaid and Markdown.
about_excerpt: Local-first nested board: a person drags cards in the browser, an AI agent edits the same board over WebMCP. Folds keep big plans readable. Exports to JSON, PNG, Mermaid and Markdown. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Foldboard: plans for people and AI agents with a bounded context The problem. Almost every planning and diagramming tool shows one big map on an infinite canvas. A person struggles to take it in at a glance, and an agent has to piece the puzzle together from screenshots and full exports. For both, that is a waste of context and focus, and it only gets worse as the plan grows. What Foldboard does. Instead of one big map, Foldboard offers folds: cards with their own inner level. A large plan is assembled from small, nested levels, and the screen always shows only the area that matters right now; everything else lives one step down. The entities are deliberately minimal: a block, a fold, an arrow, and an external card for a connection that crosses a fold boundary. So you can plan anything, from a house move to a user story in an app, and keep going deeper. You can also build a plan just to understand something, then continue from a specific card. Trace shows one path across nested levels as a single line without changing the board: you see how to get from one card to another, even when they live in different folds. That nudges both the person and the agent to break the plan into small steps. What the agent gets through WebMCP. Foldboard registers 18 tools via document.modelContext . An agent can: create a whole plan in one atomic batch and connect it to the existing one; start from a compact outline and request only the area it needs, with a depth limit, pagination, and a cap on description length. It reads what matters now, not everything; read the current level, the selection, and the user's requests attached to cards. It is enough to select a few cards and say "change this": the agent knows what you mean, with no object references and no screenshots; see the project deeper than what is on screen and take that into account. Reads never move the person's interface; navigation happens only on explicit request; write with a revision check: stale context cannot overwrite the person's newer edits, and an agent batch can be reverted with a single Undo. **How it is built. Flutter Web with no backend; boards live in the browser. Alongside it I wrote and published flutter_webmcp , a typed Dart API for registering WebMCP tools from Flutter Web without hand-written JS interop, with WebAssembly support and cancellation through AbortSignal. Try it. Open the ChatGPT App and say: "Open https://foldboard.kicknext.chatgpt.site in app browser and create a nested plan for launching a mobile app." Built With dart flutter flutter-webmcp webmcp Try it out foldboard.kicknext.chatgpt.site github.com pub.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Sergei Nikitin Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Sergei Nikitin started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:37 PM EDT

title: Lemma
pitch: Lemma is an IDE for human–AI mathematical reasoning. Explore, challenge, and branch solutions without losing the thread—while humans stay in control
about_excerpt: Lemma is an IDE for human–AI mathematical reasoning. Explore, challenge, and branch solutions without losing the thread—while humans stay in control Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Hi, my name is Bernabé, and this is my project, Lemma . Over the past year, I’ve heard stories and read news about researchers—and even students—using AI to discover new proofs or make progress on long-standing mathematical problems, including some of the famous Erdős problems. This is exciting and optimistic, but it also introduces a new challenge: as AI helps produce an increasing number of proofs, conjectures, and solutions, how will humans connect them into a coherent development of mathematics and science? And, perhaps more importantly, what role will researchers play in that process? Terence Tao recently published an insightful article exploring this topic , in case you want to go down that rabbit hole. This is a complex question that the scientific community will need to address together. I don’t pretend to have the answer, but as a software engineer, I wanted to contribute through something I know how to build. I had seen applications that use AI agents to solve mathematical problems and produce LaTeX documents. However, the result can quickly become a collection of messy, disconnected information—something similar to spaghetti code in software development. Mathematical reasoning rarely follows a single, linear path. Researchers explore different strategies, reconsider assumptions, return to earlier decisions, and abandon dead ends. In a traditional AI conversation, that structure is easily lost, especially as the context grows. That is why I created Lemma. What it does Lemma is an IDE-like collaborative workspace where humans and AI agents work on mathematical reasoning together. Engineers, mathematicians, physicists, students, and anyone working with mathematics can use Lemma to define objectives, provide context, explore strategies, and develop solutions as structured reasoning graphs. Instead of treating a solution as one long document or conversation, Lemma organizes it into objectives, strategies, branches, and individual reasoning steps. Users can interrupt the process at any moment, correct an agent, introduce a new idea, return to an earlier step, or create an alternative branch without overwriting the original path. The core workflow is interrupt, branch, continue : a human changes the direction of a solution, and the agent reads the updated state through WebMCP and continues from there. WebMCP is fundamental to this experience. Humans interact through a visual workspace, while agents can directly read and update the same structured reasoning graph. Both operate on the same source of truth, using the interface that works best for each of them. Ultimately, Lemma is my approach to keeping humans in the loop—combining human creativity, context, and judgment with the speed and capabilities of AI to pursue mathematical goals together. How we built it Lemma is built as a TypeScript monorepo using pnpm workspaces . The frontend uses React 19, Vite, strict TypeScript, React Router, XYFlow, and Dagre . XYFlow and Dagre power the visual reasoning canvas, where strategies, branches, dependencies, and mathematical steps are displayed as an interactive graph. Mathematical content is written in Markdown with embedded TeX and rendered using react-markdown, remark-math, and KaTeX . The backend is built with Supabase , using: Supabase Auth for authentication. PostgreSQL for the persisted reasoning graph. Row Level Security to protect each workspace. Realtime to keep the interface synchronized after changes. Storage for context files and supporting material. Edge Functions for the authenticated API and embedding pipeline. pgvector and full-text search for semantic step retrieval. The reasoning graph is the source of truth. Entities such as workspaces, objectives, strategies, branches, steps, assumptions, sources, decisions, and results are stored as structured relational data instead of being inferred from a Markdown document. The frontend, API, and WebMCP layer share the same Zod schemas , helping ensure that humans and agents interact with the same validated contracts. At the top-level page, Lemma registers 22 WebMCP tools . These allow agents to inspect the workspace, create and update objectives, develop strategies, add steps and dependencies, create branches, mark assumptions or dead ends, compare branches, request human decisions, search previous reasoning, and generate a clean solution. All agent mutations use the same authenticated application services as the visual interface. When an agent changes the graph, the result is immediately reflected and highlighted in the workspace. The web client is hosted on Vercel , while Supabase provides the database and backend services. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was developing a clear mental model for structuring mathematical problems. Mathematical reasoning is not simply a document, a chat, or a linear list of steps. I had to think carefully about which entities should participate in the process, how they should relate to one another, and how to preserve alternative paths without losing the history of the original reasoning. Designing the interface was another major challenge. A reasoning graph can contain objectives, strategies, branches, steps, dependencies, assumptions, and results, so presenting all that information in a way that remains comfortable to navigate and understand was difficult. I am happy with the current direction, but the interface could still be improved significantly as the conceptual model evolves and more people test it. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m proud of having built a working prototype in record time that already allows mathematical problems to be explored in a visual and organized way. There is still plenty of room to improve the problem-solving process, but one moment made me especially proud. A friend of mine who is studying mathematics tested Lemma and told me that he loved how easy it was to work with AI agents through the application. That feedback made the idea feel real. It showed me that Lemma was not only an interesting technical experiment, but that its visual and structured approach could genuinely make AI-assisted mathematical reasoning easier to follow. What we learned The most important thing I learned was how people mentally approach mathematical problems. Although I enjoy mathematics, it is still a hobby for me. Building an application intended to help people who are significantly better at mathematics than I am was challenging at first. It forced me to think beyond the final answer and focus on the actual reasoning process: how ideas are introduced, how assumptions affect later conclusions, how different strategies emerge, and why returning to an earlier decision is such an important part of solving difficult problems. I also learned that building effective tools for AI collaboration is not only about giving agents more capabilities. It is equally important to make their work inspectable, editable, and easy for humans to redirect. What's next for Lemma The next step is to improve Lemma’s conceptual model and introduce additional entities that support other types of mathematical work. For example, Lemma could also be used as a learning environment, with dedicated explanation nodes that help users understand why a particular step works—not just what the next step is. There are many other possible workflows that could be built on top of the same reasoning graph. I would also like to integrate tools based on Lean , allowing agents and researchers to translate results into formal proofs and mechanically verify whether a conclusion is correct. This could create a valuable bridge between exploratory mathematical reasoning and formally verified results. Another feature I would love to create is a collaborative mode. Researchers could publish their work so that others could explore it, contribute new ideas or branches, and use previous research as a source of reference and context. In the long term, Lemma could become more than a workspace for solving individual problems: it could become a shared, connected environment for developing, verifying, and communicating mathematical knowledge alongside AI. title: Mahaba
pitch: A WebMCP wallet where the agent's tool registry is itself the privacy control: tools exist only while a person permits them, and no tool that returns a raw personal value exists at all.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP wallet where the agent's tool registry is itself the privacy control: tools exist only while a person permits them, and no tool that returns a raw personal value exists at all. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GIF Inspiration Eligibility forms ask for far more than the decision needs. A housing programme only needs to know your household income is below a threshold, but the form wants your exact salary, your date of birth, and your home address before you even find out if applying is worth it. A browser agent working on your behalf makes it worse, because it will happily carry that context from site to site and fill every field it can. The WebMCP spec names this problem itself. Section 6.3.3, "Privacy Leakage Through Over-Parameterization," describes sites defining richly parameterized tools that agents fill from personalization context, and then Section 6.4 lists three mitigations and none of them covers it. We wanted to answer a risk the spec authors flagged and left open. What it does Mahaba is a WebMCP wallet where the agent's tool registry is the privacy control. You enter your sensitive facts once, into a profile that never leaves your browser. The app turns them into narrow claims: income is below a number, age clears a minimum, residence is inside a set of districts. You choose which claims an agent may use, and for how long. Two things set it apart from a permission dialog. A granted claim does not become a guarded tool, it becomes a tool that exists, and when consent lapses or a timer runs out the tool stops existing and the agent's own getTools() no longer lists it. And no tool that returns a raw value exists at any point. There is no get_income, no get_date_of_birth. An agent can learn that income is below 30,000, but it cannot learn the income, because the capability to ask was never registered. The interface proves that absence against the browser's live registry instead of just claiming it. The person and the agent watch one surface. Grant a claim and the tool shows up in the same console the agent is calling. Let it expire and it drops out of both views at the same moment. When the session ends you get a signed, append-only log of every comparison that was made, and not one raw value. How we built it Two things ship: a reusable module and an app that uses it. capability-gate is a dependency-free TypeScript module that ties any WebMCP tool's existence to consent. WebMCP has no unregisterTool, so a tool is revoked by aborting the AbortSignal you pass to registerTool. The gate keeps one AbortController per grant. Granting registers the tool, revoking aborts it, and expiry aborts it on a timer. That is the whole trick, and it is why revocation is real instead of cosmetic. The app has three tiers of capability. Persistent tools disclose nothing on their own and are always there. Consent-gated claim tools are absent until you permit them and present only while consent holds. A single approval-gated write drafts an application from verified claims and needs its own grant because it writes. Every claim validates its own input, because we found Chrome does not actually enforce inputSchema. Tools return a structured { ok, result } or { ok, error } envelope, because a thrown error reaches the agent as an opaque UnknownError it can do nothing with. Receipts are signed by a Netlify Function whose key never touches the browser. The stack is small on purpose: TypeScript, Vite, plain DOM, Netlify. No framework. capability-gate is the part any WebMCP site can lift out and drop in. Challenges we ran into Chrome does not behave the way the spec text reads, in two ways that ate real debugging time. Both are written up in probe/FINDINGS.md. executeTool takes a required JSON string, not the optional object the spec declares, so passing an object stringifies to "[object Object]" and gets rejected. And inputSchema is advisory, not enforced, so a tool that marks a property required still runs when it is missing. That second one turned per-tool validation from a nicety into a security requirement. Testing was its own fight. WebMCP tool calls round-trip through the browser process, which virtual time does not drive, so the usual headless DOM-dump trick dumps the page before a tool call ever resolves. We ended up driving real Chrome over the DevTools Protocol and polling for a completion flag. Deployment had one more surprise. WebMCP needs an origin-keyed agent cluster, and registerTool throws SecurityError without one, so the response has to send Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1. localhost hides this by reporting the cluster as isolated no matter what, so the header only proved itself on a real deploy. Accomplishments that we're proud of The guarantee is shown from ground truth, not asserted. For every raw field the wallet holds, the panel checks the getter that would read it against the browser's own getTools() and shows it is not there. A revoked tool cannot run even for a caller holding a tool handle it grabbed while the grant was live, and there is a test that proves exactly that. The module generalises. We built a second app, a restricted-medicine pharmacy checkout, on the same gate, console, and consent loop with a completely different claim set. It confirms a buyer clears an age limit and has no conflicting condition before it sells, without reading the date of birth or the medical history. Only the domain changed. The app also passes Google Chrome Labs' own webmcp-evals harness, the WebMCP team's first-party tooling. Its no-LLM smoke mode runs real tool calls against the live page and all the persistent tools pass end to end. That is an outside check, not one we wrote. What we learned Consent feels different when it is the thing the agent can call, not a setting buried in a menu. Watching a tool appear when you grant it and vanish when the timer runs out, in the same view the agent is using, makes the agent's authority concrete in a way a permissions page never manages. Building it also taught us to trust the browser over the spec text. Every decision that mattered came from something we checked in real Chrome, not from reading the IDL. The sharpest lesson was that absence beats restriction. A tool that is only guarded can still be coaxed, over-filled, or talked into misbehaving. A tool that does not exist cannot. What's next for Mahaba This is a minimum-disclosure prototype on synthetic data, not a cryptographic identity system. The obvious next step is to back the claims with verifiable credentials or trusted issuers, so "income below 30,000" carries proof instead of the wallet's word for it. Past that, capability-gate is the part we most want other people to use: a small, dependency-free way to make an agent's authority on your site revocable, expiring, and inspectable by default. title: ProcessTwin — Pull Requests for Application State
pitch: A WebMCP process simulator where people and agents co-design, test, and govern workflows on the same state.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP process simulator where people and agents co-design, test, and govern workflows on the same state. Like Comment Story Updates ProcessTwin — Pull Requests for Application State I built ProcessTwin around a simple frustration: workflow editors are easy for a person to understand and awkward for an agent to use reliably. A person can see a canvas and drag a connection. An agent asked to do the same thing through pixels has to guess at coordinates, handles, and inspector fields—and a mistake can look correct while changing the wrong process. ProcessTwin does not put a chatbot inside a diagram editor. Instead, the page gives an external agent a small, explicit set of WebMCP capabilities. The human edits a process on the canvas; the agent reads and changes the same process state through those capabilities. Why this is a good fit for WebMCP The useful action here is not “click near this connector.” It is “send this decision’s false branch to Manager Approval and apply this condition.” WebMCP lets ProcessTwin expose that semantic operation directly. In the demo, the agent builds a workflow in three domain-level calls instead of reproducing a long sequence of drags and clicks. What gets better Agents receive structured process graphs, validation results, simulation percentiles, bottlenecks, and suggested fixes instead of screenshots. The app also shows the evidence: a telemetry panel tracks tool calls, payload size, and estimated UI work avoided. That makes the benefit visible while the demo runs. What people and agents can do together The agent can tell what the human changed. ProcessTwin versions process state and exposes changes, including actor attribution and before/after values. The agent can try an idea without changing the live process. It forks a private scenario, makes changes, runs the simulation, and brings back a before/after diff. I deliberately left out an agent merge tool: the human reviews the proposal and clicks Apply. The human can also set boundaries that the agent cannot ignore. For example, a policy can require high-value refunds to pass through a human approval step. An agent mutation that breaks the rule is rejected with a structured explanation, so it can adapt rather than silently doing the wrong thing. How it works ProcessTwin registers 13 core tools with document.model Context registerTool and adds analysis or scenario tools only when the current state makes them useful. Zod is the source of truth for tool inputs, with JSON Schema generated from it. Each tool returns a structured envelope with a summary, data, state version, and practical next steps. The important implementation choice is that there is only one mutation path. Canvas actions and WebMCP calls both go through the same command layer, which handles validation, policy checks, undo history, activity logging, and state-version updates. The human and agent therefore cannot end up with competing versions of the process. Built with Next.js, TypeScript, React Flow, Zustand, Zod, dagre, and Vitest. No backend. MIT licensed. Key capabilities Semantic tools for creating, connecting, editing, validating, simulating, and arranging workflow nodes. Private scenario branches, simulation comparison, and human-only merge review. Policy enforcement that gives the agent recoverable constraint errors. Seeded capacity-aware simulation and bottleneck analysis. State-aware registration: 13 core tools expanding to up to 19 tools. Live end-to-end WebMCP verification in Codex's in-app browser.
