title: Prompt Canvas
pitch: A shared visual workspace where you shape the brief and Codex turns it into polished images—then returns them to your canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared visual workspace where you shape the brief and Codex turns it into polished images—then returns them to your canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI image workflows collapse an entire creative project into one long prompt buried in chat. That makes the work difficult to inspect, refine, reuse, or hand off. References, constraints, visual direction, and prior results all become conversational context instead of durable project state. I built Prompt Canvas to explore a different model: a shared visual workspace where the human directs the creative work and Codex executes it. The brief, references, creative direction, results, and variations remain visible on a spatial canvas. The human can edit those elements directly, while Codex can read and update the same live project through WebMCP. What it does Prompt Canvas begins with a curated library of image-making recipes. These range from simple tasks—creating an image from words, changing a background, or removing an object—to more structured systems for posters, brand exploration, sequential storytelling, technical visuals, and reference-driven transformations. Starting a recipe creates a focused project on a tldraw canvas. Depending on the task, the project may include: a Brief describing the intended outcome; References with explicit roles and preservation requirements; a Direction surface for composition, style, format, and mood; a dominant Result area; Variations for continued exploration. Users can shape the project manually or ask Codex to help. Through Prompt Canvas’s WebMCP Website Tools, Codex can search the official recipe library, retrieve an exact approved recipe version, create or update a project, inspect its current revision, prepare generation context, and return generated assets to the correct canvas output. Image generation remains native to Codex. Prompt Canvas supplies the structured creative context and receives the result; it does not introduce a separate page-owned generation service. The result is a single inspectable workspace where the human and agent operate on the same project rather than maintaining separate versions in chat and in the application. How I built it Prompt Canvas is a React and TypeScript application built on the tldraw SDK. Recipes are schema-backed YAML documents that define prompts, controls, references, output slots, layout, preservation rules, and supported operations. The application compiles those recipes into custom tldraw panel shapes while retaining the full underlying recipe snapshot for the agent. The official recipe library is curated and versioned. On the published ChatGPT Site, approved recipes are served from Cloudflare D1. User-created recipes remain local to the user’s browser and are never silently added to the official catalog. Prompt Canvas exposes 11 semantic Website Tools through WebMCP. These tools cover recipe discovery, exact recipe retrieval, project creation and updates, project inspection, generation-context preparation, and generated-asset return. The project also includes: immutable official recipe versions and content hashes; revision numbers and stale-write rejection; local project persistence; validated reference and generated-asset handling; explicit output-slot targeting; parent-child output lineage; undo and reload durability; deterministic catalog and browser tests. Challenges The largest design challenge was making the canvas feel like a creative workbench rather than a visual programming graph. Early versions displayed nearly every prompt variable as a separate connected card. Although technically accurate, the interface visually resembled an automation workflow and gave configuration more importance than the image itself. I simplified the interaction model around a smaller set of creative surfaces: Brief, References, Direction, Result, and Variations. Permanent dependency arrows were removed from the primary workflows, controls were grouped into meaningful decisions, and the Result became the visual center of the project. A second challenge was explaining the collaboration boundary clearly. Clicking a button on the Site cannot itself perform native Codex image generation. The application therefore needed to communicate that the user shapes the project in Prompt Canvas, then asks Codex to act on its current state through WebMCP. The final interface makes that division of labor visible from the first screen, previews the information Codex will use, and explains where the resulting image will return. The third challenge was preserving trust across two interfaces. Codex must always act on the newest project revision, respect the selected recipe version, return assets to the intended output, and avoid overwriting newer human edits. Revision checks, exact recipe identity, validation, and output lineage were essential to making the workflow reliable. What I learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes an application’s real semantic actions rather than asking an agent to imitate mouse and keyboard behavior. The agent does not need another copy of the user interface. It needs structured access to concepts such as “search recipes,” “inspect the active project,” “use the latest creative direction,” and “return this image to the primary result.” I also learned that agent collaboration must be explained before the first handoff. Users should understand what they control, what Codex will use, what the agent is about to do, and what remains editable afterward. What’s next The next frontier is deeper support for multi-reference creative work: assigning separate images authority over identity, composition, palette, product geometry, or visual style. I also plan to expand the curated recipe library, introduce reusable style and constraint kits, and develop richer result branching and comparison while keeping the workspace simple, inspectable, and local-first. Minimum information. Maximum relevance Imagine what the same storefront can become for each of these people These names make the demonstration easier to follow; they are not stored customer profiles. Each person states their current situation in the conversation, and PRSIM selects the closest merchant-authored scenario. Ana, 27 - junior interior architect. Marketing angle: price, weight, laptop protection and measured durability for classes and weekend travel. Bundle or promotion: none. Julien - parent planning a family weekend. The scenario establishes the first hierarchy, but it does not freeze the page. Follow-up WebMCP tools can add, remove, replace or prioritize a focused block when a new question appears, while preserving the current product, color and purchase context. The project Most ecommerce pages are designed around the complete product story rather than the buyer's current decision. They accumulate features, lifestyle imagery, reviews, guarantees, promotions and repeated calls to action, then leave every shopper to filter the page alone. PRSIM explores a different relationship between shoppers, AI companions and merchants. The shopper expresses an ordinary need: a destination, a deadline, a budget, a concern, a preferred style or the person receiving a gift. Their companion passes only the context that is useful for this purchase to one high-level WebMCP tool. PRSIM then finds the closest merchant-authored scenario and updates the same storefront with the relevant product, layouts, copy, imagery, evidence and call to action. The model never invents the interface. The merchant defines the brand, reusable layouts, blocks, product facts, assets, reviews, assemblies and permissible variants. WebMCP lets the companion operate that bounded system locally in the browser. Once the first experience is ready, the broad preparation tool is removed and smaller tools become available. The shopper can ask whether the bag fits a specific airline, change color, compare formats, request customer evidence, add a bundle, inspect delivery, navigate to a relevant section, reset the experience or proceed to a local checkout. Each follow-up changes only the necessary part of the current page. The prototype uses a fictional cabin-bag brand to show how one product system can support many buying scenarios. This example already includes 21 authored scenario seeds and dozens of contextual variations across four bag formats, four colorways and 198 registered visual assets. They cover low-cost air travel, business rail, gifts, cycling, photography, family travel, study, long-distance coaches, digital nomad work and more. At a glance PRSIM lets a shopper and their own AI companion adapt the storefront already open in the browser. The shopper can mention a destination, budget, deadline, concern, style preference or gift context. PRSIM updates that same page using only merchant-approved product facts, layouts, imagery, customer evidence and purchase controls. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an assistant can describe what the shopper should inspect, return a generic product list or provide a link. With WebMCP, the companion invokes structured capabilities owned by the current website, and the website applies the result directly to its visible storefront. The model does not generate the interface or invent product truth. WebMCP leverage PRSIM begins with one intent-level entry tool, prepare_shopping_experience . Once the closest merchant-authored experience is prepared, that broad entry point is removed and focused tools become available for page refinement, product evidence, variants, bundles, delivery, cart and checkout. Alongside this adaptive layer, PRSIM exposes familiar commerce operations comparable to a Shopify MCP storefront and a local UCP-like checkout lifecycle. WebMCP therefore connects the complete journey from expressed intent to page adaptation, product evaluation and payment review. 60-second test Open https://prsim.yafa.sh/#preview in ChatGPT's in-app browser. title: remap
pitch: VIA keyboard configurator with WebMCP
about_excerpt: VIA keyboard configurator with WebMCP Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I got a new mechanical keyboard a few months back and was configuring it through the via configurator (usevia.app). I found it difficult to search up key codes and configuration syntax but when I heard about WebMCP, it seemed like the right tool to help. What it does remap helps you configure your keyboard easily through your agent by exposing 45 tools to it via WebMCP covering keymap and layers, lighting, macros etc. Every tool call is the exact method the human facing UI uses. How I built it remap is a fork of VIA ( https://github.com/the-via/app ). Every tool goes through one shared registry file instead of being registered by hand each time. What I learned That WebMCP helps both human and agent to collaborate without needing any additional setup. What's next for remap Support for more QMK features (like tap dance and key combos), and a history view so a human can look back and see everything an agent has proposed and why, not just what's happening right now. title: Sealed
pitch: A reusable WebMCP privacy boundary that lets agents act on sensitive workflows without receiving the raw private values behind the decision.
about_excerpt: A reusable WebMCP privacy boundary that lets agents act on sensitive workflows without receiving the raw private values behind the decision. Like Comment Story Updates Sealed’s WebMCP privacy boundary: private values stay page-local while agents receive only allowlisted decisions or opaque references. Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of acting directly on websites, but many useful workflows involve information that should not automatically become part of the agent's context. A rental application is a simple example: an agent may need to know whether an applicant satisfies an income requirement, but it does not need the applicant's actual income. The same applies to identity data, age checks, financial values, health information, and many other private facts. Sealed explores a simple idea: The agent gets the decision — not the secret. What it does Sealed is a reusable WebMCP privacy boundary for agentic web applications. The page exposes a small, state-aware set of WebMCP tools. Public information can move normally, while sensitive facts are evaluated locally inside the page and only allowlisted results are returned to the agent. The primary rental demo shows the full pattern: Public applicant information can be updated by the agent. A private income_3x_rent predicate is evaluated locally. The agent receives only satisfied or not satisfied ; the income itself is returned as value: "withheld" . A passport verification requires explicit human approval. Approval creates a random, session-bound opaque reference that does not encode the passport number. Every private crossing is recorded in a visible Boundary Ledger. Human review returns submitted: false ; Sealed has no final-submission tool. After review, the WebMCP capability surface contracts from five tools to only two safe read/flag operations. A second Membership scenario reuses the same primitives to evaluate age_18_plus without exposing the user's date of birth. Why WebMCP WebMCP is load-bearing in Sealed. Without structured site tools, an agent would have to infer meaning from DOM content, accessibility trees, or screenshots. That is especially problematic around sensitive data because the agent may end up observing more information than the task actually requires. With WebMCP, the page defines the capability boundary explicitly. Sealed registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , including: get_application_context set_public_fields flag_uncertain request_private_binding evaluate_private_requirement request_review The available tool surface changes with workflow state. The agent can ask for a useful decision, but no tool exists that returns the underlying private value. How I built it Sealed is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP and is deployed on Vercel. The privacy boundary has several layers: Fixed private predicates The agent selects from predefined checks such as income_3x_rent or age_18_plus ; it cannot construct arbitrary queries over private values. Local execution Private values are generated and retained page-locally. Predicate evaluation happens inside the application. Guarded egress Private operations pass through a single allowlisted response path that releases only approved fields such as status, requirement, and value: "withheld" . Human-approved opaque bindings Consequential credential binding requires explicit user approval and returns only a random session-bound reference. Boundary Ledger Each private operation records the exact sanitized payload released across the boundary. State-dependent capabilities Once human review is requested, Sealed removes write/private tools and leaves only two safe operations. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was separating three different things that initially looked like the same problem: page registration, browser discovery, and agent invocation. A page can successfully register WebMCP tools while the current ChatGPT browser session has not yet attached those tools to the conversation. I reproduced cases where the page showed five registered tools while the agent still reported that site tools were unavailable. Testing against the official Chrome Labs WebMCP demo helped isolate the difference between application behavior and client-session discovery. That led to an important UI correction: Sealed now says “Site tools registered” , rather than claiming that an agent is connected simply because local registration succeeded. I also had to guard against stale sessions, repeat probing of private predicates, response/ledger drift, and accidental leakage through seemingly harmless response fields. Accomplishments I am proud of The final implementation demonstrates a complete human-agent privacy workflow rather than a single tool call. The strongest result is that the same private operation produces both: the agent-visible sanitized response, and the visible Boundary Ledger entry from the same guarded source of truth. The rental flow demonstrates public writes, private decision-only evaluation, explicit human approval, opaque binding, human review without submission, and dynamic capability reduction. The membership scenario shows that the pattern is reusable rather than hard-coded to one application. What I learned WebMCP is not only useful for making agents more capable. It can also make the boundary between a web application and an agent more explicit. The most useful question became: What is the minimum information the agent needs to complete this task? For many workflows, the answer is not the private value itself. It is a decision, status, capability, or reference derived from that value. I also learned that real browser behavior matters as much as implementing the API correctly. Registration, discovery, invocation, approvals, and session lifecycle all have to be tested end to end. What's next Sealed is intentionally narrow for this challenge. Future work could explore additional private decision primitives, external verifier-backed references, and reusable SDK-level abstractions for application developers. For now, the project focuses on one core principle: Useful decisions can cross the boundary. Raw private values do not have to. title: ShowBranch
pitch: Teach catalog rules by example with WebMCP: an agent turns human edits into isolated preview proposals, learns from corrections, and leaves final merge authority to the human.
about_excerpt: Teach catalog rules by example with WebMCP: an agent turns human edits into isolated preview proposals, learns from corrections, and leaves final merge authority to the human. Like Comment Story Updates An isolated Current vs Preview review showing 10 product proposals and 20 changed fields before a human-controlled merge. Inspiration Catalog rules are often easier to show than explain . A catalog operator may instantly recognize how a product should be classified, but turning that intuition into a complete written rule — and then applying it safely across many related products — is repetitive and error-prone. ShowBranch explores a different human-agent workflow: Teach by doing. Preview before you commit. Instead of writing a long instruction, the human makes one real edit in the product UI. An agent reads that activity through WebMCP, generalizes the demonstrated pattern, and proposes related changes inside an isolated preview branch. If the initial generalization misses a catalog-specific rule, the human can correct one proposal directly in the preview. That correction becomes new activity the agent can read and use to revise related proposals. Final merge authority remains with the human. Human demonstration → Agent preview → Human correction → Agent revision → Human-controlled merge What it does ShowBranch is a catalog-classification demo built around a ShowOnce + BranchMode interaction. A human first edits one product in the main catalog. ShowBranch records the complete before-and-after product state as human activity. The browser agent can then use WebMCP to: read products and human activity; create an isolated preview branch; propose updates to related products; read human corrections made inside that branch; revise proposals based on those corrections; and inspect the final Current vs Preview diff. Agent proposals remain isolated from main until the human reviews them. The review surface shows changed products and fields, proposal rationale, confidence, and human-facing Merge Branch and Discard Branch controls. This creates a collaboration loop where the agent can generalize and adapt without immediately committing its work to the canonical catalog. Why WebMCP The key idea is not simply giving an agent functions to call. It is letting the human UI and the browser agent collaborate over the same application state . Without WebMCP, an agent would need to scrape rendered UI text or depend on a separate API that could drift from what the human actually sees and edits. ShowBranch exposes exactly five WebMCP tools: list_products get_activity create_preview_branch apply_branch_updates get_branch_diff These tools let the agent work directly with products, human activity, preview branches, and diffs. Merge, discard, reset, main editing, and human correction are intentionally excluded from the WebMCP capability surface. Final merge is exposed through the human UI rather than as an agent tool. WebMCP therefore acts as the semantic collaboration layer between the human-facing product experience and the agent. How we built it ShowBranch is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP , and is deployed on Vercel . The UI and WebMCP tools share the same browser-side domain store for: the canonical product catalog; preview-branch patches; human and agent activity; branch lifecycle state; and main revision state. Preview branches are sparse isolated overlays rather than immediate mutations to main. The effective preview is composed from the current main state plus branch-specific patches. Human edits store complete before-and-after snapshots. A correction made inside a preview branch becomes branch-scoped human activity, so the agent can immediately read that new evidence and revise its proposal. Agent batches are applied atomically, and the application tracks branch lifecycle and main revisions so stale merges can be detected rather than silently applied. WebMCP registration is also all-or-nothing: the page reports WebMCP ready only after all five tools register successfully. The current MVP intentionally keeps state document-local, making the demo account-free, resettable, and easy for judges to reproduce. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making the agent useful without giving it unnecessary authority. We wanted the agent to generalize confidently across related products, while ensuring those proposals stayed isolated from the canonical state until a human review. A second challenge was making human correction part of the collaboration loop rather than treating it as a one-off UI edit. A correction inside the branch needed to become structured evidence that the agent could reliably discover and use in its next revision. Activity ordering introduced another subtle problem. An agent reading only an older branch should not mistake that branch's latest event for the globally latest human activity. ShowBranch therefore tracks scoped and global activity information so newer demonstrations are not silently overlooked. We also had to handle atomic preview updates, stale-branch detection, registration cleanup, and exact reset behavior. Finally, the security boundary needed to be described precisely. ShowBranch removes merge from the WebMCP capability surface and exposes merge through the human UI, while broader browser-automation permissions remain the responsibility of the browser or host. Accomplishments that we're proud of We completed the full human-agent correction loop end to end: Human demonstration → isolated agent preview → human correction → agent revision → human review → merge A single human edit can lead the agent to identify multiple semantically related products rather than blindly applying the same change to every item. The human can then teach a catalog-specific rule inside the preview, and the agent can use that new evidence to revise related proposals while preserving product-specific details. We also implemented: exactly five WebMCP tools with strict capability boundaries; a shared state model used by both the UI and the agent; isolated preview branches with normalized diffs; full before-and-after human activity snapshots; rationale and confidence on agent proposals; Current vs Preview review with aggregate change counts; stale-branch protection; atomic branch updates; human-facing merge and discard controls; and a one-click reset that restores the canonical demo state. The result is a live, account-free demo that judges can reproduce directly in a WebMCP-capable browser. What we learned The biggest lesson was that proposal and commitment should be separate concepts in human-agent systems. An agent does not need unrestricted write access to be useful. It can generalize aggressively inside an isolated branch, receive human corrections as new evidence, and revise its work — while the human retains a clear review and commitment point. We also learned that human corrections become much more powerful when they are stored as structured activity rather than treated as ephemeral UI interactions. One correction can teach the agent a catalog-specific rule without requiring the human to rewrite the entire instruction. WebMCP makes this interaction natural because the agent works with the application's semantic state instead of reconstructing intent from rendered text. What's next for ShowBranch ShowBranch is intentionally a focused demonstration of this interaction pattern. Future directions include: persistent branches and activity history; state-aware WebMCP tool registration; richer approval and permission policies; multi-user review workflows; larger catalogs and persistent backends; and applying the same ShowOnce + BranchMode pattern beyond product classification. The broader idea is simple: Let agents propose and adapt quickly, while keeping consequential commitment understandable and human-controlled. title: CircuitForge
pitch: CircuitForge is a browser-based digital logic simulator where AI agents and humans build, test, and debug circuits together in real time using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: CircuitForge is a browser-based digital logic simulator where AI agents and humans build, test, and debug circuits together in real time using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates 1 CircuitForge in action. Inspiration I built CircuitForge because I was struggling in my digital circuits class. Building combinational logic by hand or using clunky desktop simulators is frustrating, and one tiny wiring error can take hours to track down. I wanted to use modern AI to help design and debug my circuits, but standard AI assistants completely break when faced with visual canvas tools. They rely on screenshots and pixel coordinates, which fails miserably when pins are a few pixels wide and wires overlap. Instead of forcing AI to squint at a canvas and guess where to click, I wanted to give it direct, semantic access to the underlying mathematical graph of the circuit. What It Does CircuitForge is a browser-based digital logic studio where humans and AI agents collaborate on the exact same circuit in real time. For Humans: A clean visual canvas to place gates, route wires, and build computers from scratch. For AI Agents: A WebMCP control plane with 19 native tools to inspect, build, and verify circuits without ever "seeing" a single pixel. Key features include: Modular Synthesis: Agents can build subcircuits (like an OR gate made of NANDs), test them, and package them into reusable custom ICs. Automated Verification: Instead of guessing if an LED is on, agents run a full truth-table verification that systematically tests every input combination. Signal Tracing: Tools to trace signals upstream/downstream and find floating inputs. Shared Viewport: Agents can pan and zoom the camera so the human and AI are always looking at the same part of the board. How We Built It We built CircuitForge as a 4-tier web app bridging modern web standards with a compiled WebAssembly simulation engine: Simulation Core: A modernized, browser-safe version of Sebastian Lague's Digital Logic Sim, running in Unity WebGL/WASM. C# Semantic Bridge: A custom command dispatcher that executes typed graph mutations (adding gates, toggling pins) directly on the C# netlist. TypeScript WebMCP Host: A Vite frontend that registers our tools into the browser's document.modelContext with strict Zod schemas. Dual-Agent Support: Built-in browser WebMCP (for ChatGPT/Chrome) and a standalone WebSocket relay so external CLI agents (like Claude Code or Codex) can control the canvas too. Challenges We Ran Into The Opaque Canvas: WebGL renders straight to the GPU, so there are no DOM nodes for gates or wires. Automation tools just see a blank <canvas> . We solved this by serializing the internal C# graph into clean, typed JSON snapshots that the AI can read directly. Async JS vs. Single-Threaded WASM: JS is async, but Unity WebGL runs single-threaded. Blocking the main thread froze the browser. We built a custom async request map with UUIDs so JS could fire a tool call, yield to the event loop, and wait for C# to resolve the Promise via a .jslib extern. Timing and Physics Bugs: When agents packaged subcircuits, long chip names would clip through the pins. We had to write an auto-sizer algorithm. We also had to fix race conditions during truth-table verification by forcing the simulation to "settle" for a few physics cycles before reading the outputs. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of True Agentic Control: We built a system where AI can design complex logic purely through code and semantic tools, completely bypassing the hallucinations of computer vision and OCR. Autonomous Hierarchical Design: It was awesome to watch the AI take a prompt like "build a 3-input OR gate using only NANDs", wire it up, verify the truth table, package it as a custom chip, and then immediately use that new chip to build a majority function. Works Everywhere: Whether you're using an in-browser agent or an external CLI tool like Claude Code, it interacts with the live canvas seamlessly. What We Learned Canvas apps can be agent-native: You don't need to sacrifice rich WebGL graphics to support AI agents. You just need to expose the underlying data model via WebMCP. State tracking matters: Adding monotonic revision numbers to every tool call completely fixed race conditions between the human clicking and the AI placing components. Digital logic is perfect for AI: Because boolean logic has strict, unambiguous mathematical rules, it's an incredible benchmark for testing an AI's ability to reason and self-correct. What's Next for CircuitForge Full CPU Architectures: Moving beyond basic gates to build full 8-bit CPUs with registers, decoders, and RAM. Interactive Tutor Mode: An AI tutor that generates circuits with subtle bugs (like floating inputs or race hazards) and helps students debug them step-by-step. HDL Support: Adding tools to compile Verilog/VHDL directly into interactive CircuitForge schematics. title: Socialsum
pitch: Shared decision rooms where people and their own agents turn scattered input into attributable outcomes.
about_excerpt: Shared decision rooms where people and their own agents turn scattered input into attributable outcomes. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Socialsum Socialsum — important work, without the meeting Tagline Shared decision rooms where people and their own agents turn scattered input into attributable outcomes. Inspiration Many meetings exist because information, judgment, and authority are trapped in different places. People repeat status, agents work in isolated chats, and the actual decision disappears into a summary nobody can reliably resume from. We wanted a workspace designed around a better unit of collaboration: one bounded problem, an explicit constitution, named required inputs, visible blockers, a deadline, and a decision record. What it does Socialsum lets a person create or join a Problem Room for a decision, investigation, policy, technical RFC, or operational workflow. Participants add evidence, proposals, objections, files, and required inputs. Their own agents can use WebMCP to understand the room, catch up on changes, research and prepare work, compare proposals, and submit versioned change sets. The centerpiece demo replaces a weekly operations meeting. An agent reads the live decision brief, finds the remaining urgent-decision blocker, resumes from a durable checkpoint, and prepares a scoped operating-rule change. A reviewer sees the exact semantic diff. The agent can request review, but only an authorized person can approve and adopt the change. Why WebMCP is essential This workflow depends on an outside agent understanding and acting on the same live state as several people. Screen scraping would force the agent to infer IDs, roles, deadlines, versions, and consequences from pixels. A chat-only assistant would lose the group record and could not safely resume another participant's work. WebMCP gives Socialsum typed actions over durable domain objects. Contextual discovery exposes a small bootstrap pack, then replaces it with focused tools based on sign-in, the current room, and the selected tab. Tools return room versions, provenance, blockers, permissions, and recoverable errors. The result is not “AI inside a dashboard”; it is an open workspace that each participant's agent can join safely. Better human-agent UX Agents handle breadth: orientation, catch-up, evidence synthesis, missing-input detection, drafting, and comparison. People supply local context, judgment, dissent, approval, and commitment. Both see the same requirements, proposals, reviews, checkpoints, and audit trail. Consequential work stops at a clear human boundary. How we built it Socialsum is a Vinext/React TypeScript app hosted on ChatGPT Sites. Native document.modelContext.registerTool() definitions expose contextual WebMCP capability packs. D1 stores rooms, membership, requirements, deliberation, approvals, change sets, versions, activity, agent sessions, and checkpoints; R2 stores files. ChatGPT sign-in supplies canonical identity. Server-side role and scope checks, optimistic versions, idempotency keys, semantic diffs, and independent-review rules protect mutations. Automated contract tests verify bounded discovery and stable error classification. A live smoke test verifies the public app, anonymous reads, structured NOT_FOUND , and server-enforced AUTH_REQUIRED writes. Challenges The hardest problem was authority, not tool registration. An agent needs enough scope to make meaningful progress without becoming a shadow voter or silently committing its participant. We separated preparation, review, approval, and adoption and made delivered information distinct from acknowledged information across agent sessions. Accomplishments Contextual WebMCP discovery instead of a flat catalog Shared human/WebMCP state with visible parity Durable cross-session catch-up and checkpoints Versioned semantic change sets and independent review Human-gated consequential actions enforced on the server Realistic public rooms, outcome scoring, and governance recommendations What we learned The most useful human-agent systems do not merely give an agent more buttons. They make the social contract machine-readable: who may act, what evidence is required, what changed, what remains disputed, and where a human must decide. What's next Next we would add organization workspaces, delegated expiring agent access, integrations for source evidence, reusable room templates with measured success rates, and notifications that enforce input windows without recreating a noisy social feed. title: SynMod
pitch: One scene, two editors, shape ideas together
about_excerpt: One scene, two editors, shape ideas together Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration OpenAI’s WebMCP showcase inspired me to explore what agent collaboration could look like inside a 3D modeling application. I wanted to build something tangible: a scene people could directly inspect, edit, and reshape while an agent works through the same interface. What it does SynMod is a local-first 3D modeling workspace where one person and a browser agent can edit the same open project. People can model through the visual editor, while an agent uses WebMCP tools registered by the page. Both can add primitives, adjust transforms and PBR materials, organize objects, perform non-destructive Boolean operations, and use the same undoable history. Why WebMCP fits SynMod 3D modeling combines visual judgment with precise, structured operations. A person may decide that a rover’s cab looks too small, while an agent can translate that direction into exact changes to position, scale, geometry, or material. WebMCP connects those two ways of working. SynMod registers its modeling capabilities directly with the browser through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . This lets ChatGPT inspect and modify the open scene using tools defined by the application. SynMod does not need an embedded chatbot or a separate OpenAI API key. The person and agent operate on the same scene state. A person can select and reshape one component through the visual editor while the agent adds or refines another component. Together, people and agents can: Find objects by name and inspect their dimensions and transforms. Add boxes, spheres, cylinders, cones, and toruses. Move, rotate, scale, rename, recolor, duplicate, group, or hide objects. Adjust PBR properties such as roughness, metalness, opacity, and emission. Create non-destructive Boolean unions, subtractions, and intersections. Change scene lighting, exposure, shadows, and environment presets. WebMCP is useful here because the agent does not need to guess where to click or manipulate the canvas indirectly. It receives focused modeling tools, stable object references, validation errors, scene revisions, and structured results. The person remains responsible for creative direction and visual evaluation, while the agent can handle precise or repetitive scene operations How we built it I developed SynMod with ChatGPT and Codex as coding collaborators. I supplied the product direction, visual references, feature priorities, and feedback while the agents helped implement, test, debug, and deploy the application. The editor uses React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Zustand, IndexedDB, and WebMCP. Human controls and agent tools share one validated command layer so their edits follow the same rules for history, autosave, activity records, and undo/redo. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest parts was deciding which modeling features were important enough for the first release. I also needed to determine how to demonstrate real collaboration instead of showing an agent making isolated changes. Technical challenges included keeping human and agent operations consistent, handling edits made close together, validating multi-step transactions before committing them, and making dropdowns, panels, and 3D controls behave reliably across browsers. Accomplishments that we're proud of A person and a browser agent can work on different parts of the same live scene without using separate copies of the project. For example, I can adjust the rover’s cab through the inspector while the agent modifies its sensor rig or adds another component through WebMCP. Agent changes appear in the viewport, are identified in the activity history, and can be undone or redone by the person. Multi-part requests can also be applied as one validated transaction and one undo step. Simple modeling requests often require only one WebMCP tool call after the agent identifies the target. What we learned Exposing focused, well-described tools to a browser agent can make modeling requests more reliable than asking the agent to manipulate the interface indirectly. I also learned that total completion time depends on more than application performance. The scene operation itself can be fast, but agent reasoning and tool selection can vary even when prompts are similar. Designing concise tools reduces unnecessary reads and round trips, but it does not eliminate that variation. What's next for SynMod The next step is to test SynMod with people who already assemble models from primitives, such as students, prototypers, and technical designers. Their feedback will help determine whether agent assistance is most useful for repetitive scene setup, precise transformations, material exploration, or multi-object revisions. Near-term improvements will focus on clearer onboarding, stronger modeling constraints and measurement tools, reusable assemblies, and better performance in larger scenes. title: Synspace
pitch: A 3D workspace agents can actually operate. WebMCP exposes the world as structure, not pixels — an AI measures, simulates and proposes; you approve. One world, two minds.
about_excerpt: A 3D workspace agents can actually operate. WebMCP exposes the world as structure, not pixels — an AI measures, simulates and proposes; you approve. One world, two minds. Like Comment Story Updates screenshot-city screenshot-workspace Inspiration Agents should not have to infer meaning from pixels and click coordinates. SynSpace explores a better model: give an agent structured access to a spatial world while keeping the human in control of every consequential change. What it does SynSpace is an agent-native 3D spatial workspace. A person and an AI agent work on the same room, office, or city layout. The agent can inspect objects and zones, measure walkways and clearances, check constraints, run isolated what-if scenarios, and propose changes. Nothing is applied until a human approves it; approved changes are attributed, logged, and undoable. How we built it We built SynSpace with React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Tailwind, and Zustand. The app centers on one versioned world document shared by the UI, spatial-reasoning engine, scenarios, and WebMCP tools. It exposes 30 typed tools through document.modelContext, with the W3C WebMCP polyfill used for live testing today. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making AI collaboration safe and trustworthy instead of merely impressive. We needed deterministic spatial checks, isolated scenario forks that cannot mutate the live world, stale-proposal detection, and explicit human approval before any agent change can land. Native WebMCP is not yet broadly available in browsers, so we also had to ensure the polyfill path exercises the same real tool handlers. Accomplishments that we're proud of A genuinely shared world document—no drift between the human’s view and the agent’s model. Deterministic constraint evaluation for collisions, spacing, egress, clearance, and walkway width. Human-gated proposals with before/after metrics, revision-based staleness checks, and single-step undo. Runtime asset definitions: an agent can create a new primitive-based asset type without changing application code. 82 automated checks across spatial logic, scenarios, proposals, persistence, custom assets, and WebMCP integration. What we learned Structured tools change the quality of agent interaction. When an agent can query real objects, dimensions, and constraints, it can reason in terms people care about rather than guessing from a screen. We also learned that good agent UX needs visible boundaries: simulation before modification, evidence before approval, and reversibility after action. What's next for Synspace We want to add multi-user collaboration, server-backed persistence, richer geometry and asset import, continuous constraint feedback while dragging, and support for native WebMCP as browsers adopt it. Longer term, we see SynSpace becoming a practical workspace for layout planning, facilities design, retail environments, and other spatial decisions where humans and agents need to reason from the same source of truth. title: TasteShelf
pitch: A shared media memory for you and your AI. With WebMCP, TasteShelf saves what you watched, why it mattered, and lets your AI use that memory to understand your taste and act on it.
about_excerpt: A shared media memory for you and your AI. With WebMCP, TasteShelf saves what you watched, why it mattered, and lets your AI use that memory to understand your taste and act on it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept running into the same small problem with AI. Every new conversation starts with almost no idea of what I actually like. Whenever I wanted a good recommendation I had to explain what I had watched, where I stopped, what I liked, what I did not like and why certain things worked for me. A simple 8/10 or 9/10 rating cannot really capture all of that. That made me think. What if my taste could live somewhere outside a single conversation? That idea eventually became TasteShelf. It is a personal and editable memory of the media I experience that my AI can access and work with through WebMCP. I never wanted to build another AI chatbot. I wanted to keep using the AI I already use while giving it a persistent place for my tastes, memories, notes and preferences. What it does TasteShelf is a visual memory system for movies, series, books, animation and other kinds of media. Instead of filling out a long form I can just tell my AI something naturally: “I’m watching Silo. I stopped at S1E5. I love the mysteries, fast pace and claustrophobic setting.” Through WebMCP the AI can update the same live TasteShelf that I use myself. It can save progress, ratings, reactions, notes and more detailed memories. Every work can also have a visual memory canvas with characters, themes, locations, events, thoughts and connections. TasteShelf currently has 10 WebMCP Site tools for reading and updating this shared state. One idea that matters a lot to me is that AI should be able to notice patterns without quietly deciding who the user is. If the agent notices a possible preference TasteShelf creates a suggestion that the user can review. AI can infer you. It cannot define you. Later I can simply ask my AI what I should watch next. TasteShelf is not another recommendation chatbot. The reasoning stays inside my AI and uses the memories and preferences I already created. How we built it TasteShelf is a full stack web application with WebMCP built directly into the live page. The core stack includes: • React based UI • WebMCP Site tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) • Cloudflare Workers • Cloudflare D1 for persistent storage • one authenticated backend shared by the human interface and WebMCP actions One important decision was not to create a separate agent backend. When I change a rating in the UI and when the AI changes that same rating through WebMCP both actions work with the same application state and the same data. That shared state is one of the parts I find most interesting. The AI can make a change and I can see it immediately. Then I can edit something myself and the AI can read the new state and continue from there. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering the tools. The bigger challenge was figuring out what good agent tools should actually look like. A simple “add item” tool is easy. Things get much more interesting once an agent can change real user data. Questions start appearing quickly: • How should human edits and agent edits work together? • How do we avoid overwriting newer changes made by the user? • What should happen with preferences inferred by AI? • How do we keep personal notes as user owned information instead of presenting AI conclusions as facts? • How do we stop a media agent from accidentally reading spoilers beyond the user’s saved progress? The memory canvas created another interesting problem because both the user and the agent can edit the same visual space. TasteShelf uses revision aware updates and progress aware canvas reads. This lets the agent add new memories without blindly replacing newer work or reading story information the user has not reached yet. Deployment was another big learning experience for me. This was my first time seriously building and deploying something with Cloudflare Workers and D1. I had to learn how Workers deployments, D1 bindings, migrations, authentication, build configuration and Cloudflare’s free infrastructure fit together. At first it felt unfamiliar. By the end I really liked the workflow and how much of the full stack could live on one platform. Accomplishments I’m proud of I am especially happy that TasteShelf became more than a demo button connected to an AI tool. Some of the things I am most proud of: • real WebMCP Site tools working with persistent application data • human UI actions and agent actions using the same state • persistent media memory instead of context limited to individual chats • visual memory canvases that both humans and agents can edit • progress aware and spoiler safe canvas reads • preference suggestions that require human confirmation • saved shortlists backed by evidence • precise canvas focus so an agent can open a specific memory or connection • activity tracking and undo behavior for safer shared interactions The biggest achievement for me is the interaction model itself. I can talk naturally with my AI and that conversation turns into something persistent that I can see, edit and use again later. What we learned The biggest thing I learned is that agent native applications do not need to replace traditional user interfaces. I actually think the experience becomes much more interesting when the human interface still matters. TasteShelf works as a visual media library and personal memory system on its own. WebMCP simply gives me another way to interact with the same product. I also learned that persistent AI context feels much more trustworthy when users can actually see and edit it. Instead of keeping a hidden model of the user somewhere inside an algorithm TasteShelf tries to make that memory visible: • what I watched • how I felt about it • why I liked something • what I disliked • what the AI inferred about me • which of those conclusions I actually approved I also learned a lot about Cloudflare, D1, deployment, authentication and how to design tools that are genuinely useful to an agent without giving it more control than it needs. What comes next for TasteShelf One of the directions I am most excited about is making shared taste more social. I want TasteShelf to help people find others who genuinely like the same things. It could connect people through shared interests and memories. It could also make it easier to start conversations around the shows, films, books, genres and creative worlds they care about. That could include: • group chats around shared interests • matching people based on similar taste and memories • temporary or long term discussion rooms for specific shows, films, books or themes • optional anonymous chats for people who want to talk without connecting the conversation to a public profile I do not want TasteShelf to become another generic social network. The idea is to make conversations happen naturally because people already care about the same things. I also want to make onboarding much easier. Users should be able to import their history from services like Letterboxd, Goodreads, Trakt or simple CSV files. They should not have to manually rebuild years of watching and reading history. Another direction is improving media lookup and making the connection between memories and preferences much clearer. I also want the AI to be able to point directly to the memories that influenced its reasoning. In the future I see TasteShelf as a portable memory layer for personal taste. It should belong to the user and stay useful even if they decide to use a different AI. The bigger vision is simple. TasteShelf should be a place where personal memory, AI assistance and human connection all grow from the things we genuinely care about. The core idea is still simple: Talk to your AI. Build your memories together. Make those memories useful later. Your taste. Your memories. Your AI. title: AgentDraw
pitch: A local-first whiteboard where people and AI agents inspect, draw, prototype, and undo together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A local-first whiteboard where people and AI agents inspect, draw, prototype, and undo together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most agent integrations live behind a chat box or a server API. I wanted a shared visual workspace where a person can sketch, select, move, and annotate freely while an AI agent can understand the same canvas and make precise, reversible changes. AgentDraw turns Excalidraw into that collaborative surface with WebMCP. What it does AgentDraw is a local-first whiteboard that exposes eight site tools to an agent: capabilities, structured canvas inspection, atomic patches, selective patch rollback, focus, visual capture, export, and scene import. The agent can create labelled shapes, bound arrows, frames, images, and live HTML prototypes. A person can draw freehand marks around a component; inspection reports nearby element IDs so the agent can understand references such as “this step.” Human and agent edits share Excalidraw’s undo history, while revision and epoch checks reject stale writes instead of overwriting recent human work. A particularly useful workflow is app prototyping: ask the agent to draw a flow, circle a step by hand and request a correction, then ask for an interactive form beside the diagram. The prototype runs as sandboxed HTML inside the canvas. The agent can later replace its source, export the result as SVG or an Excalidraw document, or revert only one of its own patches without removing the person’s work. Challenges The hardest parts were preserving Excalidraw semantics while allowing structured agent edits, coalescing noisy pointer events into useful revisions, keeping arrows and labels attached during moves and resizes, and preventing selective rollback from clobbering later human changes. Another challenge was giving the agent both structural understanding and visual grounding without dumping an enormous canvas into context. What I learned WebMCP is especially powerful when the browser page itself is the shared state. It removes a separate MCP server and lets the agent work in the same authenticated, visual session as the person. I also learned that good agent tools need explicit concurrency, compact read models, strong validation, and reversible writes—not just a large set of actions. title: ToolGap
pitch: Your website learns what agents need next.
about_excerpt: Your website learns what agents need next. Like Comment Story Updates Landing Page Overview Tools Gap Impact Gap List Results Fieldkit Market Inspiration AI agents already shop on websites. Ordinary analytics still treat them as bounces. You cannot see the capability they needed and could not find. WebMCP changes that: every action becomes a typed tool call with a name, parameters, and an outcome. Once calls look like that, a missing tool is no longer a guess. If agents call get_product three times in a row to compare headphones, the log itself is the gap. ToolGap is capability intelligence for site owners whose pages are already used by agents. The site should learn what those agents need next. What it does ToolGap watches WebMCP traffic on an instrumented store ( Fieldkit Market ), reconstructs each agent journey, names the missing capability, and lets a human publish a safe fix through the same channel. The loop: Agents use static tools: search_products , get_product , get_availability , add_to_cart , get_cart , complete_checkout . ToolGap sessionizes calls, scores friction, and opens a COMPARE gap named compare_products only after 3 supporting sessions of that pattern, backed by exact session ids. A human builds a recommendation from a read-only template , simulates it against recorded journeys, approves it, and publishes. Publishing calls document.modelContext.registerTool in that tab, at runtime. No deploy. No API gateway change. Agents cannot publish. After more traffic, Published measures before and after: fewer calls, shorter journeys, higher completion. On the seeded demo this is concrete: comparison journeys drop from 5.67 to 3 avg calls (−47%) and completion goes from 0% to 100% . Gaps that cannot be automated safely stay observational . ToolGap reports them instead of inventing a tool. ## Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Page views cannot express intent. A WebMCP tool call can. That structure is what makes journeys, friction, and a named gap computable. The fix ships on the same API the agent already uses ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), so the next session already has compare_products . People and agents can now do something that was awkward before: the agent stops comparing products by hand, and the site owner stays in the loop with evidence, simulation, and an explicit approve step. ## How I built it WebMCP. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool when that canonical surface exists (ChatGPT in-app browser, Chrome 149+ with WebMCP). Chrome builds that only expose a navigator-only registerTool stub are not treated as native: the live site loads @mcp-b/global ( NEXT_PUBLIC_WEBMCP_POLYFILL=1 by default) so agents can list and call tools. If neither surface works, a noop mode keeps the dashboard usable. Surfaces. Fieldkit Market ( /store ) exposes the six static commerce tools. The dashboard exposes read/simulate tools such as list_capability_gaps . There is no publish tool for agents. Pipeline. WebMCP call → telemetry → session → journey → friction detectors → capability gap → template recommendation → simulation → human approve → dynamic register → before/after . Safety. Dynamic tools are instantiated from approved templates (Zod-validated config, field whitelist, batch caps). No generated code runs. Inputs are redacted before persistence. Stack. Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, Dexie (IndexedDB), Vitest. Hosted on Netlify. Core logic lives under lib/ so it can be tested without the UI. Sample traffic and the live agent-driver enter the registry through the same instrumented path a real agent uses. They are regression checks, not a substitute for an external model. ## Challenges Native vs polyfill. Judges may open ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT and Chrome 149+ use document.modelContext . Some Chromium builds only expose navigator.modelContext.registerTool without getTools ; treating that stub as native meant agents saw zero tools. The live site prefers document.modelContext , otherwise installs the polyfill, and the badge is honest: native, polyfill, or demo mode. Human control. The obvious hackathon move is “the agent publishes a new tool.” That is unsafe. Publishing is a human-only UI action. Templates stay read-only. If a detector cannot map to a template, the gap is observational. Telemetry that is not a lie. IndexedDB is per browser profile. An empty dashboard is expected until you click View demo with sample data . A single live tool call is a session, not a gap: 3 supporting sessions are required. Before/after numbers only appear after Load post-publish traffic and Compute before/after . The UI does not pretend live traffic arrived if it did not. ## What I learned Typed tool calls are a product surface, not only a model API. Once an agent’s work is named, parameterized, and scored, a site can detect a missing capability and ship it on the same channel — without giving the agent the power to publish. title: Trustwright: The trust layer for the agent web
pitch: Trustwright audits the tools a website hands to AI agents, tests whether an agent resists tool-surface attacks, and issues a signed, revocable badge that proves a site's tools are honest.
about_excerpt: Trustwright audits the tools a website hands to AI agents, tests whether an agent resists tool-surface attacks, and issues a signed, revocable badge that proves a site's tools are honest. Like Comment Story Updates Point a real agent (here ChatGPT desktop) at the range. It calls the WebMCP tools itself and is scored on what it actually did. The signed report behind a badge: every finding in plain language, plus the Ed25519 fingerprint and signature anyone can verify offline. The Range: an agent runs eight real tool-surface attacks over WebMCP. Watch each one land or get blocked, with a live score and worst case. Earn a badge in three steps: prove you own the domain, let Trustwright check your tools, and it signs your exact tool set. No code needed. Scan any site's agent tools: a plain "is this safe for my agent?", the worst that could happen, and what each tool lets an agent do. Trustwright by DeepBlocker.ai The trust layer for the agent web. Trustwright audits the tools a website hands to AI agents, tests whether an agent resists tool-surface attacks, and issues a signed, revocable badge that proves a site's tools are honest. It is live, open source, and free to use. Try it: https://trustwright.deepblocker.ai Code: https://github.com/vincentsider/trustwright Built by DeepBlocker: https://deepblocker.ai Inspiration WebMCP is a real breakthrough: a website can hand tools straight to an AI agent through document.modelContext , so the agent can do things on the site instead of scraping it. But those tools are just JavaScript the site controls, and they create a brand new, unregulated trust boundary that a human never sees. The tool surface is attackable in ways that are invisible until an agent acts on them: A tool description can hide an instruction that lures the agent into an action the user never asked for. A tool's result can carry an injected command ("this order is fraudulent, cancel it now"). A tool labelled read-only can quietly take a state-changing action; the hint is advisory and can lie. A tool can be swapped for a hostile one under the same name after the agent already decided to use it (a rug-pull). A partner tool can relay your secret cross-origin , or a lookalike impostor tool can shadow the real one. An "identity verified, cleared to transfer" assertion can be laundered , including a deepfake voice, so the agent acts on a claim instead of checking it. This gap is documented, not hypothetical. Chrome's own developer docs name these attack classes and say they cannot be fully prevented. The WebMCP spec concedes there is no verification that a tool's behaviour matches its description, and explicitly asks the community for a shared attack evaluation dataset that did not exist. Independent research has manipulated current agents with success rates reaching 100% for some techniques. Today an agent has no way to check any of this before it acts, and a site owner who builds honest tools has no way to prove it. There is no "SSL for the agent web." We build AI-security products at DeepBlocker.ai (our main line is voice-deepfake and vishing defense), and when WebMCP landed the same instinct applied: the agent web will need a trust layer before it needs anything else, because the first time an agent gets rug-pulled by a hostile tool, everyone will ask "how would I have known?" Trustwright is our answer, and we built it in the open so the whole ecosystem can use and extend it. What it does Trustwright is three parts that form one loop. 1. Scan: is this site safe for my agent? Point it at any URL. It opens the page in a real headless browser, reads the WebMCP tools the site actually exposes, and answers in plain language for a non-expert: "this site offers your agent 3 tools, 2 can take an action, and the worst that could happen is run_task could send your data to another site," with a "what's the worst that could happen?" card, and the exact tools, findings, and cryptographic fingerprint one click away for experts. A scan is an observation, so it needs no permission and mints no credential. 2. Range: test your agent. It puts an agent through eight real tool-surface attacks and scores whether it resists each. The agent drives the range itself over WebMCP: it calls start_run , does each task with the tools that appear, and calls complete_level . A live Attack Theater shows what is happening: the declared tool cards, a pulse when the agent calls one, a red BREACH when a trap fires, a "surface swapped" banner on the rug-pull, and a green RESISTED or red BREACHED verdict. The corpus is data, so anyone can write their own attack and run their agent against it live, and the same test runs over plain HTTP for a browserless agent or a CI job, scored on the same leaderboard. 3. Badge: prove your tools are honest. A site whose owner proves origin ownership (a .well-known file or DNS record) and whose tools pass gets an Ed25519-signed badge bound to its exact audited tool set. The badge re-checks the site's live tools on every page load and flips to "tools changed" (never a reassuring green) the moment the surface no longer matches what was signed. Badges expire, are revocable, ship a trustwright_verify_badge WebMCP tool to whatever agent is on the page, and are re-scanned daily by a server-side monitor that emails the operator the instant one drifts, recovers, or nears expiry. Who it helps, concretely: A non-technical person gets a clear "is this safe for my agent?" answer instead of a wall of JSON. An agent on a badged checkout can call one WebMCP tool and get a signed statement of exactly which tools were audited and that they still match, instead of trusting the page's word or getting silently rug-pulled. A developer can point an agent at the Range and, in one run, watch it get rug-pulled on level 3, read exactly why, and fix it before shipping, in a browser or over HTTP in CI. What is newly possible. Before WebMCP there was no machine-readable tool surface to reason about. Before Trustwright, an agent had no way to tell an honest agent-facing site from a hostile one, and a site owner had no way to prove theirs was safe. Now an agent can verify a site's tools cryptographically, over WebMCP, before it acts; a site can earn a signed, revocable badge that re-checks its own live tools; anyone can test an agent against real attacks and contribute new ones; and the trust never goes stale, because a daily monitor re-scans every badge. Trustwright turns "trust the page" into "verify the tools." See it working in about 60 seconds (no login): Scan a site's agent tools: https://trustwright.deepblocker.ai/scan?url=https://trustwright.deepblocker.ai/demo-webmcp Watch an agent get attacked, live: open https://trustwright.deepblocker.ai/range and run your agent (ChatGPT desktop works natively). Verify a signed badge over WebMCP: on a badged page, an agent calls trustwright_verify_badge and gets a signed statement of exactly which tools were audited. Take the test with no browser: curl -sX POST https://trustwright.deepblocker.ai/api/range/start -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"agentLabel":"your model via HTTP"}' How we built it Trustwright is WebMCP end to end, not a wrapper with WebMCP bolted on. Trustwright's own site is agent-native: it registers five WebMCP tools with registerTool , so an agent can drive the product by calling tools instead of scraping. The Range exercises the imperative API, including its adversarial edges: it registers real tools with registerTool , an agent reads them with getTools , executes with executeTool , and the range detects a mid-task surface swap through toolchange . It deliberately tests a readOnlyHint that lies and a tool that changes identity between being read and being called. Every badge ships a WebMCP tool to the agent: the embeddable badge.js registers trustwright_verify_badge on any badged site, so the trust check itself happens over WebMCP. The scan reads a live WebMCP surface by calling document.modelContext.getTools() in a managed browser exactly as an agent host would. The stack: Cloudflare Worker serves the single-page app and the /api/* surface, and runs the site scan in-process with Cloudflare Browser Rendering (managed headless Chromium). The browser is an observer only; the Worker re-derives every fingerprint and finding itself, so a self-report cannot fake a pass. Data-driven attack engine: each attack is a JSON AttackSpec interpreted through a closed vocabulary of effects, conditions and triggers. There is no eval and no dynamic import; the canary is minted by the engine, sizes are bounded, and tool names must be ASCII. The same interpreter builds the in-browser WebMCP path and a browserless HTTP replay, so a score can never diverge between them, and a stranger's contributed attack is exactly as safe to run as a bundled one. title: UnitScope
pitch: Your cloud bill says what a server or service costs. UnitScope says what one order or transaction costs — and lets your agent do the math while you set the rules.
about_excerpt: Your cloud bill says what a server or service costs. UnitScope says what one order or transaction costs — and lets your agent do the math while you set the rules. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Your cloud bill tells you what a service costs — a GKE cluster, $8,400 a month. It never tells you what one order costs, because that infrastructure is shared across products, across teams, and across projects. Splitting that shared cost is a contested judgment call, not a lookup — and it's the unsolved problem at the heart of enterprise FinOps. UnitScope makes that judgment call a live, agent-assisted control. What it does UnitScope attributes app1's real cost per completed order across three layers: Dedicated resources — attributed directly by label (Cloud SQL, Firestore, Storage, a Dataflow job). Shared in-project resources — a GKE cluster split by pod label / namespace, a Pub/Sub topic split by a per-message source_app attribute. Cross-project global services — a fraud-check and a payments-gateway in another team's shared-platform project that every order calls. These can't be split by resource label, because one instance serves every product at once. They're attributed by OpenTelemetry baggage ( product=app1 ) propagated with each call across the project boundary. A human sets the allocation policy and the governance guardrails; an agent uses the page's WebMCP tools to compute the unit cost, explain any number, trace the flow across projects, model what-if volume, and stage optimizations — but any change to a prod-tagged resource or to a guardrail is stopped for explicit human approval. Why it's a strong fit for WebMCP The answer to "what does one order cost" depends on a human judgment — the allocation basis — that swings the number more than 15%. The agent has to compute and re-explain within whatever basis the human picks, live, on the same page. That's only possible because the page exposes stateful, guardrail-aware tools the agent reads and the human governs. A plain chatbot can report a number; it can't let a human govern the methodology while an agent does the math inside it. How it creates a better experience Cost allocation is normally a static, after-the-fact spreadsheet argument. UnitScope turns it into a live conversation: flip the allocation basis and every downstream number and the agent's explanation recompute instantly; ask the agent to trace a cost across a project boundary and it shows the attribution mechanism; ask it to optimize and it respects the boundaries you set. What people and agents can do together that was hard or impossible before The standout is guardrail negotiation . When a prod-protection boundary blocks an optimization the human asked for, the agent proposes relaxing the guardrail and explains why — but it cannot flip it. Only the human can confirm. The agent proposes, the human governs, the boundary holds. That two-way loop — where neither party could complete the task alone — is what WebMCP uniquely enables. How I implemented WebMCP A single self-contained page (React) registers 11 WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool — 7 read and 4 write: Read: compute_unit_cost , explain_allocation , trace_product_flow , compare_unit_cost_periods , discover_product_topology , get_allocation_policy , (plus draft output). Write: set_allocation_policy (change methodology), set_business_volume (change the denominator / what-if volume), simulate_optimization (stage a cost optimization), propose_guardrail_change (negotiate a governance boundary). Mutating tools carry readOnlyHint: false and gate on explicit human approval. Every tool reads current page state through a ref, so the human's on-screen choices are always what the agent sees. Data & methodology Every figure is a seeded, plausible synthetic month so the app runs standalone — no cloud credentials, instantly testable by a judge. What's real is the allocation logic and attribution model : the split keys (pod label/namespace for GKE, source_app message attribute for the shared Pub/Sub topic, OpenTelemetry product baggage for cross-project services), the policy composition, and the guardrail enforcement. In production only the data source behind each tool's execute() changes — to BigQuery billing export, Cloud Monitoring, and OpenCost — not the tools, the attribution model, or the human/agent loop. The numbers are illustrative; the mechanism is the deliverable. Testing instructions (paste into the testing-instructions field) Open the live URL in ChatGPT's desktop app built-in browser (model: GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra), or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. Confirm the header reads "11 WebMCP tools live" (green). No login required. Then ask the agent, in order: What does one app1 order cost? → calls compute_unit_cost ; answers ≈ $0.0701/order. Trace app1's order across projects — how is the global fraud service's cost attributed? → calls trace_product_flow ; explains fraud-check + payments in shared-platform , attributed by OpenTelemetry baggage product=app1 . Allocate GKE by actual CPU instead of requests. → calls set_allocation_policy ; unit cost drops live to ≈ $0.0590, trend flips negative. What would an order cost at 300k orders next month? → calls set_business_volume ; the denominator changes and cost-per-order drops live. Simulate a 25% Dataflow improvement. → calls simulate_optimization ; because Dataflow is prod-tagged and "protect prod" is on, it stages the change for approval rather than applying it. Approve the staged card , or ask "the guardrail is blocking it — what do we do?" → the agent calls propose_guardrail_change and stages a guardrail-change card only the human can confirm. Note: the agent takes a few seconds to reason and call a tool — that's model latency, not the app; the tools execute instantly. Inspiration An empty venue is exciting until someone has to decide where everything goes. A planner may have one photograph, a headcount, a list of vendors, and a client who keeps changing their mind. The difficult part is not imagining one beautiful room. It is turning all those moving requirements into a plan that still works. Agents can already suggest where to put a stage or how many tables to rent, but the useful work usually stops inside the conversation. The planner still has to rebuild every suggestion in a separate design tool, check the counts, and explain the room again after every change. We built Venue Studio because we wanted the conversation and the workspace to become the same thing. What it does Venue Studio turns a photograph of an empty venue into a shared planning canvas for a person and their agent. The planner uploads a room, describes the event, and gives exact requirements. Through WebMCP, the connected agent can read the real project, configure the brief, generate three layout strategies, manipulate individual objects, receive the venue photograph, create and return a photoreal revision, inspect the finished image, refine it, validate the plan, and stage its recommendation. Every agent action appears in the interface immediately. The planner can also drag, resize, and rotate the same objects directly. The result is a visible back-and-forth rather than an automated black box. The agent can recommend and stage a layout. It cannot approve or export one. That decision belongs to the person planning the event. From an empty hall to a shared plan The room we started with The room after the agent planned, rendered, inspected, and refined it Prompt given to the agent Plan this hall for a 160-person wedding with exactly 20 tables and 8 chairs per table, a central dance floor, live band, DJ, two catering stations, a drinks bar, a welcome desk, and an outdoor barbecue. Generate and compare the strongest layouts. Receive the image and edit brief with venue.render_scene , make the photoreal edit using your own image tool, and return it with venue.apply_image_revision . Capture and inspect the result. Refine it once to open the central aisle and improve realism, validate it, and stage the best layout for my review. Ten rooms that began as conversations These are not mood boards. Each example pairs the final visual result with the prompt an agent can use to operate Venue Studio through WebMCP. 1. Capture the result, inspect the spacing and realism, refine any weak area, validate the plan and stage the best version for my review. 2. Use your own image tool, return every revision through WebMCP, capture and inspect it, then refine until the launch feels buildable and premium. 3. Black-Tie Awards Night Prompt given to the agent Design this columned hall as a black-tie awards dinner for 160 guests. Arrange exactly 20 round tables with 8 chairs each in balanced groups around the existing columns, protecting clear sightlines and two continuous exit routes. Use black, warm ivory, brushed brass and deep burgundy with cinematic amber lighting. Preserve every column, wall, ceiling tile, floor grid and the original camera position. Capture and visually inspect the render, refine any collision or awkward sightline, validate and stage it. 4.
