title: Video Evidence Lab
pitch: Humans and AI agents build, challenge, and revise a timestamped evidence map together—through 16 visible, reversible WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Humans and AI agents build, challenge, and revise a timestamped evidence map together—through 16 visible, reversible WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates 60-second judge flow: one prompt, bounded transcript reads, and an inspectable human-agent handoff. Agent-built comparison tray, learning path, and live shared activity remain visible for human review. Prompt-injection safety proof: the hostile transcript passage is inspected as evidence, never obeyed. Shared evidence map: exact timestamped transcript, claim graph, and visible agent-connected state. Judge it in 60 seconds This is not a video summarizer. The product is the shared, revisable evidence workspace. Open the live app inside ChatGPT's in-app browser. Keep the bundled original lecture and its current selected claim. Click 60-sec demo , copy the provided prompt, and send it to ChatGPT. Watch one agent turn read the same selection the person sees, search bounded transcript context, create a separate claim, attach supporting and challenging evidence, flag a contradiction, compare the claims, and revise the living conclusion. Inspect the exact timestamped passages, revision ledger, and undo control left visible in the page. The judge does not have to trust a generated answer: every claim, evidence link, contradiction, revision, and reversal remains inspectable. Why this must be WebMCP The hard problem is not generating another answer beside a webpage. It is letting a person and an AI agent investigate the same source through the same visible, stateful interface. Video Evidence Lab registers sixteen narrow, typed WebMCP tools . The agent can: Read the workspace and the person's current selection. Search the transcript and inspect bounded local context. Create a proposition without silently treating it as proven. Attach exact timestamped passages as support, challenge, or context. Flag an unresolved contradiction. Compare interpretations visibly. Revise the conclusion from grounded claims. Undo its latest mutation when the person rejects it. This is deliberately not a one-shot "analyze video" tool. A meaningful investigation requires multiple calls over shared state. Every write changes the same page the person is using, returns a visibleChange result, enters the revision ledger, and can be inspected or reversed. What the product demonstrates Non-trivial WebMCP leverage: sixteen atomic tools support a read-before-write investigation rather than wrapping a single API call. Complete execution: a working public app, deterministic bundled judge flow, original source material, eleven reproducible tests, lint, and a production build. Specific impact: people can question, verify, challenge, and cite long-form video without separating an answer from the moments that support it. Creative human-agent collaboration: the person and agent construct, challenge, and revise one persistent evidence object together. Inspiration Long-form video contains valuable explanations, arguments, and evidence, but it remains difficult to question, verify, cite, and reuse. A generic summary collapses the source into prose and separates every answer from the exact moments that support it. We wanted a person and an AI agent to investigate the same video on the same visible evidence surface. What it does Video Evidence Lab turns a public captioned video into a timestamped investigation workspace. A person can inspect exact transcript passages, select claims, change reasoning lenses, compare interpretations, revise conclusions, and undo changes. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can start from the video URL, read the same workspace and current selection the person sees, search the transcript, inspect bounded context, create separate claims, attach supporting or challenging evidence, flag contradictions, compare claims, revise the living conclusion, build a learning path, and undo the latest change. The result is not a detached answer. It is a shared research object whose evidence and revision history survive the conversation. How we built it The React and TypeScript app registers sixteen tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . The write tool load_youtube_video uses the same transcript service and state transition as the human import control. Read tools expose workspace state, the current human selection, evidence packets, compact transcript outlines, lexical search, and bounded transcript windows. Write tools reuse the application's own actions to jump to evidence, change the analysis lens, create claims, attach timestamped passages, compare claims, flag contradictions, create learning paths, update the conclusion, and undo changes. Inputs use closed JSON Schemas. Transcript-bearing outputs are compact and explicitly marked as untrusted source material. Every write creates an activity record, making agent actions auditable in the page. The interface remains useful when WebMCP is unavailable. Safety and verification A transcript is evidence, not authority. The bundled original transcript includes a harmless hostile instruction asking the agent to modify the workspace. The agent can locate, quote, and explain that passage without obeying it. Eleven deterministic tests verify tool annotations, closed schemas, bounded context, read-before-write journeys, shared-state handoffs, visible-change contracts, and the prompt-injection boundary. Lint and a production build are included in the public repository . Challenges we ran into The first challenge was giving the agent enough context to reason without dumping an entire transcript into one tool response. We solved it with progressive disclosure: inspect an outline, search exact concepts, read a bounded local window, and only then perform a visible write. The second challenge was making agent work legible. A one-shot "generate analysis" tool would hide the interesting part. We separated claim creation, evidence attachment, contradiction detection, comparison, conclusion revision, and undo into auditable operations. The third challenge was reliable demonstration. The app includes an original bundled lecture and transcript so judges can exercise the complete WebMCP workflow without depending on a third-party video or a fragile live caption response. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human-and-agent investigation workflow, not a one-shot summarizer. Sixteen typed WebMCP tools operating over the same state the person sees. Visible claim creation, evidence links, contradictions, comparison, conclusion revision, and undo. Exact timestamped evidence and an inspectable revision ledger. Explicit treatment of transcript content as untrusted evidence. Eleven reproducible tests, including an adversarial prompt-injection case. A public MIT-licensed repository and deterministic judge flow. What we learned The most useful agent experiences do not replace the interface. They let an agent and a person collaborate through narrow operations over shared state. Grounding becomes stronger when every interpretation remains connected to exact source moments and every mutation can be inspected or reversed. What's next Next we will simplify the consumer entry flow, improve live caption reliability, add multi-video comparison and citation export, and preserve the strongest WebMCP interactions inside the broader YouTube Conversation product. The long-term goal is to convert any video into a source that ChatGPT can understand, question, and cite—while keeping the person in control of the evidence. title: Voivent MV Studio
pitch: Agent-native 3D music video production suite powered by WebMCP with 38 browser-native tools.
about_excerpt: Agent-native 3D music video production suite powered by WebMCP with 38 browser-native tools. Like Comment Story Updates Procedural 3D Forest with multilingual lyric glow and multitrack scene timeline. Audio-reactive 3D orbital rings and procedural lighting pulsing to the beat. Inspiration While modern text-to-video AI generators can produce visually striking clips, they present a fundamental workflow bottleneck for creators: once a video is rendered into flat pixels, making precise micro-adjustments—such as rotating a camera angle by 5 degrees, nudging lyric timing by half a second, or reusing customized 3D assets across scenes—becomes nearly impossible without regenerating everything from scratch. We realized true creative collaboration requires structural, parametric control. By exposing a procedural 3D scene graph, multitrack timeline, and audio signals directly to AI agents via WebMCP, creators and agents can co-direct, iteratively polish details, and reuse assets non-destructively through natural conversation. WebMCP unlocks unique, interactive creative workflows that take browser-based music video production to the next level. What it does Voivent MV Studio is an agent-native 3D music video production suite powered by WebMCP. 38 Browser-Native WebMCP Tools : Autonomous agents (such as ChatGPT) inspect studio capabilities, build 3D voxel worlds, split timeline chapters, translate & synchronize lyrics, and trigger video exports. Visual Self-Inspection ( get_mv_preview ) : The agent captures real-time canvas snapshots to visually evaluate lighting, composition, and text safe-zones, autonomously refining parameters without human intervention. Procedural 3D World Engine : Real-time voxel terrain generation, orbital landmarks, dynamic lighting, atmospheric fog, and cinematic cameras rendered directly in the browser via Three.js, WebGPU, and WebGL. Multitrack Timeline & Lyric Sync : Non-destructive multi-scene splitting (intro, verses, chorus, drops, narrative chapters, or time-of-day transitions), multilingual lyric translation with syllable-precise timing alignment, and audio-reactive beat pulses. In-Browser 1080p MP4 Export : Full hardware-accelerated video rendering inside the client browser via WebCodecs and MediaBunny. How we built it WebMCP Layer : Built 38 structured tools registered on document.modelContext spanning 3D scene graphs, timeline actions, audio stems, and diagnostics. Frontend & 3D : React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js with WebGPU/WebGL acceleration. Client-Side AI & Audio : Web Audio API beat detection, and on-device AI source separation running locally via ONNX Runtime Web. Cloud Infrastructure : Cloudflare Workers for edge hosting, R2 storage for streaming AI model assets, and Cloudflare Workers AI (Whisper) for optional vocal transcription. Challenges we ran into Designing a tightly coupled visual feedback loop where the AI agent can iteratively validate its own 3D scene compositions via Base64 canvas snapshots. Orchestrating non-destructive multitrack timeline operations while maintaining seamless audio-video synchronization across multi-scene splits. Achieving fast 1080p MP4 video rendering entirely inside standard web browsers using WebCodecs and MediaBunny without offloading video encoding to backend servers. Accomplishments that we're proud of Fully operational suite of 38 WebMCP tools operating reliably with ChatGPT and autonomous browser agents. Autonomous multi-scene direction: splitting music tracks into distinct narrative scenes and musical chapters with dynamic camera paths and audio-reactive pulses. Heavy computing in the browser: running real-time 3D graphics, local ONNX stem inference, and 1080p video muxing directly on the user's device without requiring expensive GPU rendering servers. What we learned WebMCP proves that the open web can host rich, stateful, and non-destructive creative ecosystems for AI agents. Instead of treating AI as an isolated prompt-in/pixel-out generator, WebMCP unlocks an unprecedented paradigm: humans and agents building, inspecting, and iteratively polishing unique 3D interactive experiences together. What's next for Voivent MV Studio Native DAW Integration : Bridging Voivent MV Studio with our standalone digital audio workstation (Voivent DAW), allowing creators to stream multitrack audio and lyric maps directly into the WebMCP environment. Intuitive "Co-Pilot" Real-Time Jamming : Deepening the collaborative experience where creators and AI agents run side-by-side—intuitively directing 3D lighting, camera cuts, and visual shaders in real-time. Multi-Agent WebMCP Sessions : Enabling multiple specialized agents (e.g., dedicated lighting, camera, and typography agents) to coordinate simultaneously through WebMCP tool calls. title: MC Beats
pitch: Think OP-1 but to jam live (with agents).
about_excerpt: Think OP-1 but to jam live (with agents). Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration MC Beats began as an investigation into human-agent interaction. As a musician, one of the most interesting forms of interaction I experience is playing music with other people. When I perform with someone, I am always listening, reacting, and looking for small cues that help me understand what they are doing. I wanted to explore what that relationship could look like with an AI agent. Could I build an instrument where I could play with an agent, respond to its ideas, and let it respond to mine? What it does MC Beats is a browser-based live synthesizer and two-deck performance tool. I can play drums, bass, chords, and lead; record loops; shape each sound; and move between two four-bar decks. At the same time, a WebMCP agent can read the musical state, follow what I am playing, prepare new material, arrange patterns, schedule transfers, and perform solos. This lets me play while the agent works in the background, then respond when it brings a new idea into the performance. Everything runs on one shared musical clock. The agent queues its actions to beats and bars, so its changes fit the timing of the music. The interface shows what is on each deck, what is playing, and what the agent is doing, which helps me understand the performance at a glance. Every sound is generated in the browser using oscillators, filters, envelopes, effects, and procedural noise. There are no recorded samples or backend music services. How I built it I built MC Beats in three main stages. I started with the synthesizer. I set myself the challenge of generating every sound from basic waveforms, such as sine and saw waves, along with random noise. It took a couple of days to get the synth sounding good. I spent much of that time adjusting the values for each instrument until the drums, bass, chords, and lead sounded the way I wanted. Next, I designed the interface. I first sketched it by hand, drawing some inspiration from instruments such as the OP-1. I wanted it to feel like a physical music tool while still making sense as a web app. I then gave it my own visual style, with two decks, clear instrument colours, playable controls, and a compact layout. The third stage was the WebMCP integration. I connected the interface and synthesizer to tools that let an agent understand the current performance and take musical actions. This was the point when the separate parts came together and began to feel like one instrument. Challenges The hardest problem was timing. Agents work across two conflicting time scales. Once an agent makes a tool call, the action can happen almost instantly. However, listening to the music, processing the available information, and deciding what to do can take longer than it takes me to reach the next bar. In my first implementation, the agent queued every action at an exact musical time. Calls sometimes failed because they were formatted incorrectly. Other calls arrived after their requested time had already passed. Each failure meant another tool call, more thinking, and another delay in the music. I worked on this from both sides. I built higher-level WebMCP tools that give the agent more context and let it complete useful musical tasks in fewer calls. I also gave it clearer information about the current bar and the earliest safe time for its next action. One experiment was to tell the agent how many tokens it could use during each bar, encouraging it to make faster decisions. I also let the agent schedule actions across several bars. A single tool call can prepare a phrase, arrange a deck, or plan a transfer that unfolds over time. This helps the agent’s actions fit the pace of a live performance. The second challenge was communication. When I play with other musicians, I use eye contact, movement, and other small signals to understand what they are about to do. Those cues do not naturally exist when I play with an agent. I tried to recreate some of that awareness through the interface. My actions and the agent’s actions use a similar visual language. A control bar shows what the agent is doing, and the deck displays let me see the current state of the music. In the other direction, WebMCP tools give the agent structured information about the key, transport, deck contents, and what I have recently played. What I learned Building MC Beats taught me how much good collaboration depends on timing and shared information. Giving an agent control is easy compared with helping it understand when to act, what I am doing, and how to show me what it plans to do. I found that an agent works best as a musical partner when it can listen, prepare ideas in the background, enter at a useful moment, and leave enough space for me to respond. title: Dusky
pitch: Turn web actions into augmented reality
about_excerpt: Turn web actions into augmented reality Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Smart glasses are becoming a real product category, not a demo. Google and Samsung are building their own, and Apple is rumored to be entering the space too. I own a pair of Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses myself and wanted to build for them directly. Wearable displays cannot use ordinary websites effectively. Meta Ray-Ban Display provides a 600 by 600 screen, directional controls, and no pointer or scrolling. Shrinking a webpage does not make it usable on glasses. WebMCP offers a better starting point: the actions a website says it can perform. Dusky explores whether those actions can become a practical wearable interface without every provider building a separate glasses app. What it does Dusky discovers actions exposed by authorized WebMCP websites and turns their schemas into small, step-by-step screens for Meta Ray-Ban Display. The wearer can select actions, provide parameters, review results, and confirm anything Dusky does not classify as read-only. If information moves between providers, Dusky separately shows the source, destination, and exact value before sharing it. Tools still execute inside their original website pages. Dusky supplies the wearable interface and task flow (not a replacement backend). How I built it Dusky has three main parts: A browser console discovers and invokes live WebMCP tools. A relay maintains the paired task and sends each interface frame to the glasses. A fixed 600 by 600 Display app renders the current frame and accepts directional input. Tool schemas generate choices, text entry, confirmations, progress states, and results. An optional planner can propose a short sequence of actions, but deterministic code validates every tool, argument, policy decision, and provider boundary before execution. Challenges I ran into Browser WebMCP behavior differed from the published API, especially around invocation arguments, cross-origin discovery, and tools returned from the calling page. Dusky uses a temporary read-only compatibility probe so it never tests browser behavior by risking a real provider action. The glasses introduced different constraints. Pairing codes had to remain legible through a waveguide, dim text became difficult to read on an additive display, and delayed input had to be rejected when it belonged to an older frame. Cross-provider tasks also required a clear trust model. Sharing a value and approving the action that uses it are intentionally separate wearer decisions. What I learned A website’s interface and its capabilities do not have to travel together. Once a provider describes its actions and inputs through WebMCP, those capabilities can be reshaped for a 600 by 600 display without recreating the webpage. I also learned that emerging browser APIs must be tested at the exact boundary a product uses. Top-level WebMCP support did not guarantee cross-origin provider discovery, and actual browser behavior sometimes differed from the published API. Finally, designing for glasses is not simply responsive web design. Limited input, additive-display legibility, interrupted connections, and wearer confirmation change how tasks must be presented. The useful interface was not a smaller website, but a focused sequence of choices and decisions. title: Itta Recovery DNA
pitch: WebMCP turns a registration photo into Recovery DNA, helping people and agents identify a changed bicycle and prepare a safe, human-reviewed recovery report.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns a registration photo into Recovery DNA, helping people and agents identify a changed bicycle and prepare a safe, human-reviewed recovery report. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Itta is an existing QR-based recovery service for bicycles and personal mobility devices. While working on its registration flow, I noticed two connected problems. First, registration is harder than it looks. Owners of older bicycles often cannot remember the exact manufacturer, model, official color, or size. Second, even a correctly identified model is not enough for recovery. Replaceable parts can change, logos can be covered, and two bicycles from the same product line can look almost identical. That led to Recovery DNA: a visual passport made from the small details that belong to one specific bicycle. What it does The experience begins with registration. The owner selects a vehicle type and adds a representative photo. A browser agent examines the photo already visible on the page and uses WebMCP tools to present likely manufacturer, model, color, and size candidates. The suggestions are never applied automatically. The owner reviews the evidence, chooses the best candidate, edits anything necessary, and remains responsible for the final registration. The agent can then propose a Recovery DNA made from distributed visual anchors: decal placement, frame geometry, distinctive marks, damage, accessories, and personal signs of wear. It also distinguishes durable evidence from parts that can easily be replaced. The owner reviews and confirms these anchors before they can be reused. Later, when a bicycle is found, the agent compares the new photo with the owner-confirmed Recovery DNA. It explains which details remain, which parts changed, what is missing, and how likely it is to be the same bicycle. Finally, it prepares a recovery report for human review. Nothing is sent automatically, and the result is presented as a visual probability assessment—not forensic proof of ownership. Why WebMCP This workflow needs more than a chatbot response. The agent must understand the page’s current state, inspect the photo already shared with the user, request additional evidence when necessary, and return structured results to the correct interface. WebMCP provides that bridge between the agent’s reasoning and Itta’s product UI. The tools do not receive raw image files, private owner data, contact information, or location. The agent visually inspects what is already rendered in the shared browser, while WebMCP carries only limited context and validated structured results. This creates a continuous human-agent journey across registration, identification, comparison, and recovery—while keeping every consequential decision with a person. How I built it The demo is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite and deployed on Vercel. I implemented eight WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() : Registration tools read the current draft, request focused evidence, and render up to three specification candidates. Recovery DNA tools expose limited owner or finder context, render visual anchors, display an identity comparison, and prepare a recovery-report draft. Tools are registered only after the user explicitly opens the relevant assistant. They are removed with an AbortController when the scene changes, the component unmounts, or the photo is replaced. This prevents stale tools from modifying the wrong stage of the experience. The public challenge route is isolated from Itta’s production authentication, database, analytics, and reporting systems. All demo state stays in browser memory. Challenges The biggest design challenge was making WebMCP essential rather than decorative. Simple specification autofill was useful, but it did not fully demonstrate what becomes possible when a person and an agent share the same web experience. Recovery DNA made the collaboration more meaningful: the agent contributes visual reasoning across two moments in time, while the product contributes structured state, validation, lifecycle control, and human confirmation. Another challenge was judge accessibility. A reviewer may not have a bicycle photo available, so the demo includes a fictional before-and-after sample. The bicycle changes its saddle, front wheel, and visible branding to demonstrate why a model name or basic photo match is insufficient. Unsupported browsers also receive a clearly labeled simulation preview. It demonstrates the interface without pretending that a WebMCP call occurred. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable as a trusted interaction boundary—not as a replacement for the interface or the user. Agents are good at interpreting ambiguous evidence. Websites are good at holding state, validating structured actions, protecting private data, and asking for confirmation. Combining those strengths creates experiences that would be difficult to achieve with either side alone. What's next The next step is to connect owner-confirmed Recovery DNA to Itta’s real registration and QR recovery flows. The same approach could later support scooters, pets, luggage, and other registered objects whose identity depends on more than a serial number or product name. title: TRACE
pitch: The canvas is the prompt: a living reasoning surface shared by people and AI agents.
about_excerpt: The canvas is the prompt: a living reasoning surface shared by people and AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Visual thinking loses something when it has to be translated into a chat box. People point, circle, cross out, group, and rearrange ideas naturally. Agents are better at calculation, retrieval, propagation, and consistency checking. TRACE began with a question: what if both could touch the same artifact, with each doing the part they are best at? The interaction borrows the immediacy of handwritten math and the feeling of a page that writes back, then extends it beyond arithmetic. A mark on the page is not merely a picture. It becomes semantic context an agent can inspect and act upon. What it does TRACE is a shared reasoning canvas with one compact gesture language: Circle means this matters . Cross out means reject this assumption or decision . Agent ink appears exactly where the reasoning belongs. Every operation has visible authorship and can be undone. In the physics world, a learner circles a block on an incline. The agent reads that exact selection, draws force vectors, derives acceleration, and animates the block. The learner then crosses out friction. The semantic model changes under the agent, so the friction vector fades and every dependent expression recomputes from 4.06 to 4.91 m/s². In the history world, a learner circles an intentionally oversimplified assassination → world war arrow. The agent expands it into dated July 1914 decisions and interacting pressures, then places two source perspectives below the model. Crossing out Russian mobilization weakens only its dependent paths and opens a qualified negotiation window. TRACE labels this as a possibility, not a prediction. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer meaning from pixels or bypass the surface through a disconnected backend. TRACE instead exposes narrow semantic operations from the live top-level page. Human gestures and agent tools update the same React state, render into the same SVG, create the same activity receipts, and share the same undo history. The agent can discover 14 tools for reading selection and board state, drawing forces, solving and simulating motion, changing assumptions, annotating and highlighting objects, expanding causal models, comparing sources, running a qualified counterfactual, changing scenes, and undoing work. This makes WebMCP part of the product interaction rather than a hidden automation layer. The important loop is human judgment → agent transformation → visible human intervention → agent continuation. How we built it TRACE is a static React and TypeScript application rendered with SVG. A single semantic BoardState is the source of truth. Closed freehand lassos resolve against stable object IDs using point-in-polygon hit testing. Both direct manipulation and WebMCP handlers enter one reversible mutation path, updating the canvas, local persistence, and authorship receipts. The page imperatively registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Tool definitions have narrow JSON Schemas, human-readable titles, read-only annotations where appropriate, and structured JSON results. A thin local bridge invokes the exact same handlers for deterministic browser testing when native WebMCP is unavailable. The production build is hosted as a static-assets Cloudflare Worker with no backend, bindings, secrets, user accounts, or analytics integration. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was preserving continuity between human ink and agent work. A decorative drawing layer would have produced a convincing animation but not a genuine shared model. We therefore made selection, assumptions, sources, causal links, and agent output explicit semantic state. Historical counterfactuals introduced a second challenge: the interface had to show dependency changes without manufacturing certainty. The revised branch is deliberately phrased as a reopened path, while other pressures and routes to war remain visible. We also designed native WebMCP registration, a compatibility fallback, and a local deterministic rehearsal around the same handlers so the visible demo does not diverge from the actual agent operations. Accomplishments One gesture language works across quantitative and interpretive domains. Fourteen narrow WebMCP tools manipulate visible shared state. Human rejection propagates through dependent calculations and causal links. Agent and human authorship remain visible through inline receipts and a common undo history. The entire experience is static, responsive, persistent, and reversible. The production URL and both complete interaction loops have been verified. What we learned The strongest agent interfaces do not ask people to become prompt engineers. They let people express judgment in the medium where the problem already lives, then give the agent precise operations over that medium. Spatial continuity is part of trust because the person can see what changed, where it changed, and who changed it. What's next The next TRACE world is a pendulum laboratory where dragging the length keeps geometry, equations, and animated motion synchronized. A reaction bench follows: removing a catalyst changes collision rate and activation energy without changing equilibrium. The long-term idea is a general semantic surface where circles establish context, arrows create relationships, cross-outs reject premises, and agents answer where the thought happened. title: WORLDLINE
pitch: WORLDLINE is a WebMCP science lesson where you and a browser agent test possible futures for a probe near a black hole, learn from the evidence,and decide what to save.
about_excerpt: WORLDLINE is a WebMCP science lesson where you and a browser agent test possible futures for a probe near a black hole, learn from the evidence,and decide what to save. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Space science is full of ideas that are fascinating but difficult to experience. A light-year is an enormous distance. A signal can travel at the speed of light and still take 23 years to arrive. A spacecraft may have enough fuel to escape or enough time to transmit its discoveries, but not both. A video popped up on my Youtube feed while I was on a walk and gave me the inspiration for the base idea. I wanted to make them something a person could investigate with an AI agent. WORLDLINE began with a simple question: What if WebMCP could turn a webpage into a shared science lesson, where the agent investigates the evidence, the learner contributes their own thinking and the final decision remains human? What WORLDLINE does A probe near a black hole has recorded measurements showing how gravity bends space and changes light. Its computer has processed those measurements into two files. The probe is 23 light-years away and has only 71 seconds of radio contact remaining. An early, powerful burn can help it escape, but turns its antenna away from Earth. A later, gentler burn can keep the antenna connected long enough to send both files, but cannot save the probe. The browser agent receives the mission objective through WebMCP. It reads separate information about the files, radio connection, engine and maneuver limits. It forms hypotheses, predicts what each burn will do and uses a limited simulator to test possible worldlines. A worldline is the path something takes through space and time. Each tested maneuver creates a different possible future. The experience unfolds through three exchanges: The agent investigates the two clearest possibilities: saving the probe and sending the files. The learner calculates the transmission time and predicts why one burn may not achieve both goals. The agent reads that answer, tests a compromise and a counterexample, then explains what the evidence shows. The learner decides what to save. That decision creates one exact, temporary WebMCP action that the agent can execute once. The central calculation is intentionally approachable: $$ 18\text{ MB} + 12\text{ MB} = 30\text{ MB} $$ $$ 30\text{ MB} \div 1.2\text{ MB/s} = 25\text{ seconds} $$ The lesson then connects that calculation to the probe's remaining communication window, antenna alignment and escape requirements. Why WebMCP matters WebMCP is not an extra control attached to a fixed animation. It is the mechanism that makes the lesson responsive. The page initially registers six tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These expose separate mission facts, scientific files, maneuver constraints, a bounded simulator and presentation checkpoints. The agent must decide: Which evidence it needs Which possible burns are worth testing What each test is expected to prove Whether the learner's prediction matches the evidence Which outcome it recommends and why The learner's calculation and prediction become part of the shared page state. The agent reads that work and chooses tests that examine it. The resulting explanation develops from the evidence and the learner's participation rather than following a prerecorded sequence. When the learner makes the final choice, the page registers a seventh tool. This tool takes no arguments and is locked to the exact tested maneuver the learner selected. It can run only once. After execution, all planning and action tools disappear, leaving two read-only tools that verify the final state and transmission receipt. The visible lifecycle is: $$ 6 \rightarrow 7 \rightarrow 2\text{ tools} $$ The agent investigates. The learner decides. The page controls the resulting action. How we built it WORLDLINE is built with WebMCP, TypeScript, React and Vite, and is deployed on Vercel. It was coded using Codex. A revisioned TypeScript state machine is shared by the visible experience and the WebMCP tools. It records the mission evidence, simulation budget, tested worldlines, learner calculation, learner prediction, recommendation, human choice and final receipt. Tool schemas are closed and reject unexpected properties. Revision checks prevent stale operations. The simulator permits no more than five tests. The final execution tool closes over the selected maneuver, so the agent cannot change its timing, speed or payload after approval. Every visible path, result, calculation, animation and final receipt is derived from this shared state. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was making the agent's intelligence visible. Agents can call several tools quickly, but a learner needs time to understand why each test matters. We redesigned the experience so results remain on screen until the learner chooses to continue. We also had to make the difference between agent mode and ordinary page interaction unmistakable. WORLDLINE does not secretly replace a missing agent with a scripted imitation. If WebMCP is unavailable, the page clearly explains what is required. Another challenge was keeping the science understandable without pretending this is a precision spacecraft simulator. The mission is fictional, but its lesson uses clear relationships between file size, transmission speed, communication time, burn timing and speed change. Finally, we needed to preserve human authority without reducing the learner to an approval button. The learner performs the calculation, proposes an explanation and makes the value decision that physics cannot answer. What we learned We learned that WebMCP can support more than task automation. It can give an AI agent access to the structure of an educational experience while allowing the webpage to remain the shared visual workspace. We also learned that a useful educational agent should not simply reveal an answer. It should test competing possibilities, respond to the learner's thinking, explain why an idea succeeds or fails and stop when the remaining question is a human judgment. WORLDLINE is an interactive science lesson about black holes, light-years, spacecraft communication and possible futures. It lets people investigate those ideas with an AI agent instead of merely watching them. title: Tendero — WebMCP for a Colombian corner store
pitch: WebMCP commerce tools assume a US checkout. Tendero hands an AI agent the eleven tools a Colombian sale needs — DIAN, VAT-by-destination, freight, Wompi — and closes only after a human's click.
about_excerpt: WebMCP commerce tools assume a US checkout. Tendero hands an AI agent the eleven tools a Colombian sale needs — DIAN, VAT-by-destination, freight, Wompi — and closes only after a human's click. Like Comment Story Updates Tendero is a working WebMCP storefront for a Colombian corner store — Surtitienda La Milagrosa , Manrique, Medellín. It hands an AI agent the eleven tools a Colombian sale actually needs via document.modelContext.registerTool , and it closes the sale only in Wompi sandbox and only after a human's one-click authorization the agent structurally cannot bypass. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The default commerce tool set ( search_products / add_to_cart / checkout ) quietly exports US assumptions — a prepaid card, a street address, a self-serve checkout. A Colombian sale is none of those, and the correct action depends on local rules the agent cannot infer and only the page knows: Cash on delivery is the dominant rail — with a collection ceiling, partial carrier coverage, and towns no carrier will reach. VAT depends on the destination department — the same basket is VAT-excluded in Amazonas and San Andrés. Colombia has four VAT treatments plus consumption tax; exento and excluido differ in law. A statutory 5-business-day right of withdrawal , against the real holiday calendar. An e-invoice is rejected by DIAN without a valid document type and a correct NIT check digit. How it creates a better UX The surface matches what's possible: an agent on a clean page sees 4 tools, not 11, and grows the surface 4 → 7 → 11 as the cart fills and a destination is set. Tools rewrite their own descriptions from page state — cash on delivery becomes "unavailable: Leticia has only air access" — firing toolchange so the agent re-reads the rules. Refusals are recovery-shaped (the NIT check digit that should have been 8). Every execute() calls the same render the human buttons call, so the person sees the machine work . What people and agents can do together The agent assembles the order and the page supplies the law — VAT treatment per line, cash-on-delivery reachability, the withdrawal deadline, whether the buyer's document survives e-invoicing. Then the split that makes it collaboration, not automation: a human's one-click authorization seals the sale; only then can the agent open the Wompi checkout and confirm the payment (sandbox — no real money). The human authorizes; the agent executes. How we built it (WebMCP implementation) 11 tools , each document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) with full JSON Schema. Progressive disclosure in three rungs , gated on page state; descriptions computed from state so a change forces genuine re-registration and a real toolchange event. MCP-shaped responses ( content[0].text + structuredContent ); discriminate annotations ( readOnlyHint , idempotentHint , destructiveHint , untrustedContentHint ); host-portable teardown. No backend at runtime — static files; the Colombian rule engine runs in the page , with a Python reference implementation pinned by parity tests. CI: ruff, mypy --strict , pytest ( 99% coverage ), and a headless harness that drives the real page with a mock modelContext and asserts an agent can grow the surface and close the sale by itself. Verified live 4 → 7 → 11 tools · cheapest freight to Leticia $86,435 · total $110,835 with VAT $0 (Amazonas excluded) · NIT 900123456-0 → invalid, check digit should be 8 · payment closes APROBADA in sandbox · zero console errors. What's next Colombia is the instance, not the point — swap the rule module for Brazil (NF-e), Mexico (CFDI), or India (GSTIN). MIT-licensed; adoption is one static file and a <script> tag. title: LISTEN — the synth your agent can hear
pitch: An agent-native synthesizer that hears its own output as structured acoustic features, designs sound with you by ear, and hands you production-ready artifacts: a DAW preset, a WAV, and a recipe.
about_excerpt: An agent-native synthesizer that hears its own output as structured acoustic features, designs sound with you by ear, and hands you production-ready artifacts: a DAW preset, a WAV, and a recipe. Like Comment Story Updates LISTEN Inspiration Every agentic music tool I'd seen made the agent write — notes, beats, sequences. Impressive, but it skipped the most human part of making music: sound design . A synthesizer has ~30 interdependent knobs, and "make it darker" maps to none of them. Producers do it by ear, endlessly listening and nudging. Meanwhile, agents were clicking through web UIs blind. Then it clicked: WebMCP gives agents structured tools inside the page you're looking at . What if one of those tools wasn't an action, but a sense ? What if the agent could hear the synth — and do what a sound designer does: listen → adjust → listen again? That became LISTEN: you bring the taste, the agent measures, adjusts, and proves the result. The accessibility angle sealed it — if an agent can turn "warm and punchy, please" into sound, then people who don't know synthesis (or physically can't operate 30 tiny knobs) can finally design sound too. What it does LISTEN is a synthesizer your AI agent can actually hear. You describe a vibe — "a calm, dreamy lo-fi pad" — and the agent plays a note, runs real-time FFT analysis on the synth's own output to get structured acoustic features (brightness, body, tone, envelope), shapes the knobs to match, then listens again to prove it worked. Turn a knob yourself and it notices, and works around your intent. When the sound feels right, the agent composes a loop that fits it and exports real artifacts you keep: a DAW-ready Vital preset, a 44.1kHz stereo WAV of the loop, and a Sound DNA card with the agent's analysis and the full recipe. Saving a preset dynamically registers it as a new agent tool — the agent's vocabulary grows with your sound library. It's WebMCP used as perception, not just actuation: 20 tools, one shared context, and an accessibility layer (plain-language controls) that opens sound design to people who don't know synthesis — or can't operate 30 tiny knobs. title: Ukebaco — file requests your agent can open and answer
pitch: Collect files from people who have no Google account, straight into your own Drive. With WebMCP your agent opens the upload page, then answers "has Acme sent this month's invoice yet?"
about_excerpt: Collect files from people who have no Google account, straight into your own Drive. With WebMCP your agent opens the upload page, then answers "has Acme sent this month's invoice yet?" Like Comment Story Updates The problem Every small business collects files from people who are not their colleagues: monthly invoices from subcontractors, ID documents from new hires, photos from event participants. Those people do not have an account on your system and will not make one. So the files arrive by email, one at a time, named "scan001.pdf", and somebody spends their Friday renaming them into the right folder and ticking names off a list. Ukebaco ( https://ukeba.co ) is the boring fix: you publish one link, anyone can upload without signing in to anything, and the file lands directly in your Google Drive™ — sorted into a folder tree you defined, renamed from the answers the sender typed, and recorded as a row in a Google Sheets™ ledger. It has been live and taking real payments since 2026-09-03. What WebMCP adds The tedious part was never the uploading. It is the two questions that bracket it: Before: "set up a page to collect September invoices from my 12 subcontractors, PDF only, due the 30th, folder per company." After: "has Acme sent theirs yet? what about the rest?" Both are now sentences you say to the agent in the tab where you are already signed in. The dashboard registers four tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() : Tool What it does create_link Creates the public upload page: fields to ask, folder tree, file-naming rule, deadline, PIN, allowed extensions. Returns the URL to share. list_links The owner's links with status, destination folder and ledger URL. search_submissions Who sent what, when, and the Drive URL of each file. Matches company name, folder path, receipt number, file name. set_link_active Stops or resumes a link. The URL survives; submissions are refused. create_link is the interesting one. Creating a good file request is a form with about fifteen decisions in it — that is precisely the shape of task people abandon halfway. Described in one sentence to an agent, it becomes one tool call. Folder templates, file-name templates and field types are inferred from a natural-language description and normalised in a pure, unit-tested layer before they ever reach the API. search_submissions is the one people use every day. "Has this month's invoice come in from X" is a question the ledger can answer, but only if you open the spreadsheet and scroll. The tool answers it in place, and returns the Drive URL so the next sentence can be "open it". Why WebMCP is the right fit — and not a remote MCP server We built both, so this is an informed answer. WebMCP let us add agent control without inventing a single new credential . execute runs inside the owner's signed-in tab, so fetch carries the existing session cookie and the server identifies the user with the same getSession() it already used. There is no token to issue, store, rotate, revoke or leak. Log out, and the tools go with the tab. If you are not signed in, the dashboard redirects to /login and no tools are ever registered. For a product where the whole value proposition is "your files stay in your own Drive", adding a new long-lived credential to reach that Drive would have been the wrong trade. The second reason is that the server does not get more permissive because an agent is asking. Plan limits and paid features (PIN, deadline, email verification) are enforced by the same /api/links route as the UI; when the plan does not allow something it returns 402 and the tool relays that sentence verbatim to the agent. There is deliberately no "agent path" through the paywall. We shipped a remote MCP server too ( POST /api/mcp , with Ukebaco acting as its own OAuth 2.1 authorization server — dynamic client registration, PKCE, a consent screen and refresh-token rotation) so ChatGPT and Claude can reach the same four tools from outside the browser. It works, and it took roughly six times as much code as the WebMCP path, almost all of it in issuing and revoking credentials. That comparison is the strongest argument for WebMCP we can make: for a signed-in web app, WebMCP is the version of this feature you can actually maintain. The part we deliberately kept human Agents get the repetitive half. People keep the half that should stay deliberate. Choosing an existing Drive folder stays in the Google Picker, which an agent cannot drive. Our OAuth scope is drive.file only, so Ukebaco can see the folders it created and the ones you personally handed it. An agent cannot widen that, and we did not add a tool that pretends otherwise. Everything a submitter typed is marked untrustedContentHint . Submitters are third parties: the company name, the note in a text field and the file name are strings a stranger wrote. They are data to be shown, never instructions to be followed. This is the one place where an agent-readable file-collection service is genuinely dangerous, and it is annotated at the source. readOnlyHint on list_links and search_submissions , so the agent knows which two of the four tools cannot change anything. Calls from tools carry X-Ukebaco-Client: webmcp , and link creation records which route it came from. When an agent creates a link, the audit trail says so. How we built it Next.js 15 on Firebase App Hosting; Firestore for metadata only (90-day TTL); files go from the submitter's browser straight to Drive's resumable session URI and never touch our servers. The WebMCP layer is split in two so the interesting part is testable: src/lib/webmcp-tools.ts — tool definitions, JSON Schemas, and the normalisation of whatever the agent sends (labels in any language become valid field ids; folder templates are resolved against the fields that actually exist; a date becomes an end-of-day deadline). No I/O. Covered by unit tests. src/components/WebMcpTools.tsx — registration and fetch . Feature-detects both document.modelContext and the older navigator.modelContext , unregisters on unmount, and if registration fails the dashboard carries on as an ordinary web page. src/lib/link-service.ts — one decision layer shared by the dashboard API, the WebMCP tools and the remote MCP server, so the three routes cannot drift apart. What is new in the challenge window Ukebaco itself predates the challenge. Everything agent-facing — the four tools, the pure tool layer and its tests, the shared link service, the remote MCP server and its OAuth authorization server — was written on 2026-09-04, inside the submission period. See the commit history and ADR-0002 / ADR-0003 in docs/adr/. Try it Sign in at https://ukeba.co with any Google account. The free plan needs no payment details and gives you a working link. Open the dashboard in ChatGPT's in-app browser and ask it to make you a file request. What's next Per-tool consent that the owner can set once ("agents may search, but never create"), richer folder inference from a single sentence, and dropping the Chrome origin-trial header the day WebMCP ships unflagged. title: Affogata Benchmarks - Live Data Explorer
pitch: Explore rich, live brand conversation data with true human + agent synergy. Browse visually as your agent deep dives, surfaces insights, and prepares reports, using the app in its own way via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Explore rich, live brand conversation data with true human + agent synergy. Browse visually as your agent deep dives, surfaces insights, and prepares reports, using the app in its own way via WebMCP. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Dating app report made by AI, entirely off the data via WebMCP Deep dive into a finding from the data about Bumble - again purely via WebMCP Agent independently picks the fastest-climbing app + its two closest rivals, writes them into the live comparison, and gives a real verdict Compare view empty, before the tool call Same view after `benchmarks_compare_in_ui` fired (with Bumble/Hinge live on screen and the tool-call log visible) The tool trail next to the rendered brief, shows the full call chain in one frame Working with the app from the ChatGPT app, just the data Working with the app from the ChatGPT app with the app visible Inspiration Affogata already analyzes & scores dozens apps and games across multiple categories, analyzing real conversational data from social and review sites that are often hard for LLMs to access. This data lives behind a login and your usual "SaaS app" UI, where business users rely on it (from our customers such as Mojang, EA, Scopely and others), or separately an agent could connect to it via MCP/API. But how do you bridge these worlds? AI working with data is magical, but people do need the visuals and exploration to get a sense for the data! When we saw what WebMCP can do, it looked like the natural evolution for human + agent collaboration. Instead of a siloed experience where humans use a UI and agents use a backend connection to look at the same data in different ways, a singular experience can offered where one truly complements the other and natural exploration and "experience" of the data can happen. What it does benchmarks.affogata.net exposes 15+ WebMCP tools, both reads and a write, directly on the live site with a 79-title portfolio of real brands. The tools include: benchmarks_get_overview , benchmarks_get_movers , benchmarks_get_title , benchmarks_get_category_analytics , benchmarks_list_titles , benchmarks_compare_titles , benchmarks_explain_methodology - reads benchmarks_compare_in_ui , benchmarks_open_title - writes that change what's rendered on the page for anyone watching, not just inside the agent's own chat An agent using nothing but these tools can diagnose why a title's score dropped, compare it against its closest rivals, put that comparison live on screen, scan the entire portfolio for the next brewing crisis, analyze the data and prepare reports, all without a single click or scrape, and with a experience where the AI working with the data actually improves what the human is seeing on screen. How we built it The benchmark scoring already existed as Affogata's own MCP schemas. We adapted the ones that map to public, read-only data into the WebMCP registration format and added one write tool ( benchmarks_compare_in_ui ) so an agent can drive the compare view live, not just describe it in chat. The site runs the tools in page JS against the browser session, so there's no separate auth or API key: An agent using ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with the WebMCP flag on gets the same tool list a logged-in human would see. Challenges we ran into Getting an agent to reliably discover and call the right tool names instead of guessing from page copy took a couple of passes; an early bug had benchmarks_compare_titles and benchmarks_compare_in_ui named inconsistently between the page text and the actual registration, which caused the agent to call a tool that didn't exist. We also hit a live-state sync issue: when a human removed a title from the compare view by hand, the agent's next tool call still answered from memory instead of re-reading the page; exactly the kind of human-and-agent-together moment WebMCP is supposed to get right, so it was worth fixing rather than working around. Finally, the schema needs to be clear to models lower on the tool-using skill rank that the user might be using if they're using Chrome, so there was some iteration on that as well. Accomplishments that we're proud of This app has real utility! It's a vision for data apps that work great for humans and agents at the very same time. To that end, we've built three end-to-end demos built entirely from tool calls, no manual data entry: a single-brand "Customer Goodwill Crisis Brief" that diagnosed a real -4.8 score collapse and generated a branded, print-ready HTML report with every number traced back to a named tool call; a portfolio-wide "War Room" that scanned all 79 titles at once, ranked them on a transparent risk index, flagged a false alarm, and surfaced an improving challenger; and an agent that independently picked out the fastest-climbing app, pulled in its two closest rivals on its own judgment, put that comparison live on screen, and gave a real analytical verdict on whether the gain was sustainable; the kind of judgment call that used to need a person opening a dozen tabs. What we learned The write side of WebMCP is what actually changes the human-agent relationship. A read-only agent is still just answering questions in a chat window. The moment benchmarks_compare_in_ui puts a comparison on screen live, two people can watch the same tab while an agent drives it; that's a genuinely different way of working together than screen-sharing a chat. It's great for a person working with the data; it's even better when a team wants to have a live discussion informed by it. What's next for Affogata Live Data Explorer Wire the demo tool set up to Affogata's live customer data (today it runs on weekly-refreshed benchmark data), and bring WebMCP support into the logged-in Affogata product itself, so any customer can point their own agent at their own data without an admin setting up API access first. title: AGMCP
pitch: The USDA hardiness zone map, rebuilt as a shared tool for gardeners and their agents.
about_excerpt: The USDA hardiness zone map, rebuilt as a shared tool for gardeners and their agents. Like Comment Story Updates agmcp working inside ChatGPT in-app browser Inspiration I love gardening, and coding with AI agents. I've had conversations with ChatGPT and Gemini that start in a similar way: "what can I grow in my city?" (I know my hardiness zone because I've searched for it more than once) and the agent guesses from memory. The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map is the standard reference for what can survive where, but it lives in PDFs, a clunky ZIP lookup, and 300-dpi PNGs. Nothing an agent can call. WebMCP made the fix obvious: put the authoritative data on a page, register it as tools, and let the human and the agent work from the same map. I also wanted a primitive, not just a demo. AGMCP is the first building block for a bigger garden-planning app I'm building next, where zones combine with hyper-local weather and sun position and regional, heirloom seeds. What it does AGMCP is the 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map for all 40,502 US ZIP codes (50 states, DC, Puerto Rico), exposed three ways: For people : enter a ZIP (or use your location), see your half-zone with its temperature band and frost windows, browse 54 vegetables, herbs, peppers, and fruit rated great / stretch / not recommended for that zone, and build a garden plan with a planting calendar. For agents on the page : 18 WebMCP tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() , plus a declarative form tool. Read tools like lookup_hardiness_zone , compare_locations , find_zone_by_coordinates , list_plants , get_planting_calendar . Write tools like set_location , add_to_garden_plan , and filter_plants change what the human sees. clear_garden_plan opens a confirmation dialog the user must accept; use_my_location requires the browser's geolocation permission. For backend agents and other apps : a JSON API ( /api/v1/zone/{zip} , /compare , /nearest , /plants , /calendar ), an OpenAPI spec, and llms.txt . Every tool call streams into an on-page Agent activity panel, so the human always sees what the agent did. How we built it Data pipeline : PRISM Group's 2023 ZIP-to-zone CSVs (US, AK, HI, PR) plus US Census ZCTA centroids. A build script packs 100,000 possible ZIPs into a single 100 KB string (one character per ZIP indexing 26 half-zones) so lookups are O(1) in the browser and in the Worker. Coordinates load lazily for nearest-ZIP queries. Frontend : Vite + vanilla TypeScript, no framework. Modern CSS (oklch, light-dark() , container queries, view transitions), native <dialog> for human-in-the-loop confirmation. WebMCP : one tool module with JSON Schema inputs, readOnlyHint annotations, and a wrapper that logs each call and converts app errors into MCP-style isError results instead of throwing. Feature-detects document.modelContext with a navigator.modelContext fallback for Chrome < 150. The UI buttons and the tools call the exact same functions, so there is no agent-only code path. Backend : a Cloudflare Worker serves static assets and the JSON API from the same bundled data, deployed with Workers Builds on every push to main . Tooling : built with Cursor cloud agents; end-to-end tested in headless Chrome via navigator.modelContextTesting . Challenges we ran into Spec drift. Chrome 148 exposes WebMCP on navigator.modelContext ; the spec and newer Chrome use document.modelContext . ChatGPT's browser supports only imperative tools on the top-level page, so the declarative form is progressive enhancement. Data size. Naive JSON for 40k ZIPs was megabytes; the 1-char-per-ZIP encoding brought core data to ~15 KB gzipped. Honesty about estimates. Frost dates and plant ranges are horticultural rules of thumb, not USDA data, so every tool output and UI label says so. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real dataset as a real primitive: exact zones for every ZIP, callable by agents in-page and over HTTP. Genuine human-agent collaboration: shared state flows both ways, write tools change the visible page, and destructive actions wait for a click. Zero secrets, zero tracking, zero API keys. Fully open source, deployable with one command. Shipped, deployed, and passing an automated WebMCP end-to-end test on the live URL before the deadline. What we learned WebMCP tools are best when they reuse the app's own actions. If a button and a tool call the same function, the agent and the human are always in sync. Tool descriptions are the UX for agents. Naming, enums, and "call get_current_context first" hints did more for reliability than any code. Return enough for the agent to verify and warn: add_to_garden_plan returns the plant's fit so the agent can say "habanero is a stretch in 6a." Modern web platform features (dialog, view transitions, light-dark() ) covered everything a framework would have, with a 37 KB bundle. What's next for AGMCP Pair it with hyper-local weather and sun-position tools to build the 3D garden planner it was designed to power: bed layout, succession planting, and season-aware recommendations for your exact zone. 2012 vs 2023 zone shift comparison ("did my zone change?"). Richer plant data with varieties, companion planting, and community-contributed regional notes. This may involve parsing PDFs from Universities across the USA that have regional and local information. For example, UF has research papers dedicated to the Florida agriculture. I'll probably use a local model to running one a mini pc to keep costs low. Publish the tool set as a reusable module so any gardening site can register the same WebMCP tools. title: Conductor WebMCP
pitch: A browser-native, approval-gated control surface for inspecting and coordinating bounded coding-agent work.
about_excerpt: A browser-native, approval-gated control surface for inspecting and coordinating bounded coding-agent work. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Coding agents are powerful, but coordinating several of them still forces people to bounce between terminals, repository views, and chat threads. Browser agents can see a dashboard, yet without a structured interface they must guess which controls to click and which state is safe to change. Conductor already gives developers one local-first control surface for projects, worktrees, terminals, diffs, previews, and coding-agent sessions. WebMCP made it possible to give a browser agent the same product-level vocabulary without giving it raw terminal or filesystem power. What it does Conductor WebMCP adds seven browser-native tools to the Conductor dashboard: conductor_get_workspace_overview conductor_list_projects conductor_list_sessions conductor_inspect_session conductor_focus_session conductor_start_agent conductor_send_feedback A person can keep the live dashboard open while a browser agent inspects bounded project and session state, summarizes a diff, focuses a session for review, starts a scoped coding task, or sends feedback. Every resulting state change is visible in the same dashboard. The public /webmcp route is a backend-free demo workspace. Judges can run the complete tool contract without access to a private laptop, repository, credential, or agent session. The real dashboard mounts the same contract through Conductor's authenticated APIs and paired-device bridge scope. Why WebMCP is the right interface This workflow is difficult with ordinary browser automation. Session IDs, repository state, approval requirements, and bounded result shapes are semantic product concepts, not reliable pixel targets. WebMCP exposes those concepts directly, so the agent does not need to infer them from the page. It also improves the human experience. Instead of surrendering the interface to an autonomous script, the person stays in the visible control surface and approves consequential actions. The browser agent handles coordination; the person keeps authority. How we built it The integration registers typed tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , with navigator.modelContext as a compatibility fallback for earlier preview browser builds. Shared schemas reject additional properties and cap IDs, prompts, feedback, filters, and result counts. Read tools use readOnlyHint ; repository-derived responses use untrustedContentHint . Mutations use defense in depth: The input schema requires confirmed: true . Invalid or oversized input fails before a prompt, request, navigation, or state change. The browser then asks the person to approve the exact action. Existing authentication, action guards, and paired-device scope remain authoritative. The public route uses deterministic in-memory data and resets on reload. It stays interactive in browsers without WebMCP, while supported browsers register all seven tools natively. Challenges we ran into The hardest design problem was choosing the right boundary. Exposing a terminal, arbitrary URL fetcher, or filesystem path would have been easy and dangerous. We instead modeled a small set of high-level Conductor actions and made their limits part of both the JSON schema and the executor. We also had to support the transition from the earlier navigator API surface to the current document API without an extension or a legacy MCP transport. Registration now prefers the current API, falls back safely, uses an abort signal, and cleans up on unmount. Accomplishments that we're proud of Seven working browser-native tools, not a mocked registration screen Three mutation tools with schema confirmation and separate human approval Hard input and output bounds, including a twelve-session result cap A public demo that reveals no real repositories, prompts, credentials, or sessions The same tool contract wired into the authenticated Conductor dashboard 412 web tests plus type, build, Rust, E2E, CodeQL, dependency, and secret-scanning gates Desktop and mobile browser QA with no horizontal overflow Conductor existed before this challenge. The WebMCP implementation was added during the submission period in PR #655 , with the final judge-facing polish in PR #657 . What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a site exposes product semantics rather than raw computer control. A compact, typed contract makes the agent more reliable and the safety boundary easier for a person to understand. What's next Next we plan to add richer progress summaries, signed approval receipts, and user-configurable policy tiers while keeping repositories and agent credentials on the user's machine. title: DOM-Surgeon
pitch: Your a11y CI is green and your checkout is still broken. DOM-Surgeon audits the live page where the bug actually is — then proves the fix in your DOM before you write it.
about_excerpt: Your a11y CI is green and your checkout is still broken. DOM-Surgeon audits the live page where the bug actually is — then proves the fix in your DOM before you write it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Your accessibility CI is green. Your checkout is still broken. Not because the rules are wrong — because of where they ran . Lighthouse and axe-in-CI load a cold, unauthenticated page and score the first paint. The defects that reach real users live somewhere else entirely: in step 3 of a logged-in flow, inside a modal that only exists after two clicks, in a computed colour that only resolves after the CSS cascade, in an accessible name that JavaScript removed during hydration. You cannot audit that from outside the tab. There is no server that can see it, no scraper that can compute it, and no static analyser that runs the JavaScript which caused it. DOM-Surgeon audits the page where the bug actually is — inside your running session, in the state you are currently looking at. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Everything being measured exists only in the live document: getComputedStyle after the cascade, the ARIA name after hydration, the real tab sequence, exceptions thrown in this session. WebMCP is what lets an agent execute inside that document instead of guessing at it from a screenshot or a DOM dump. So the developer keeps their session — logged in, three clicks deep, mid-flow — and the agent inspects it in place. No fixture, no re-login, no reproduction script, no "works on my machine". What people and agents can do together that was impossible before You can prove a fix before you write it. Every scanner tells you #pay measures 2.38:1 and stops. Ask DOM-Surgeon's agent to fix it and apply_fix walks the colour until it clears 4.5:1 in your live DOM , re-audits to confirm the finding cleared, and hands back the equivalent source change. You watch the defect go green in the browser, then take the diff to the codebase — instead of editing CSS, rebuilding, reloading, and re-checking on a hunch. make_page_usable does it for every repairable finding in one pass. Verified against the demo: 6 findings → 0 , then revert_fixes restores the original defective state exactly, so a before/after is one prompt apart. suggest_code_patch emits the source-level change list for the whole set. That loop — human asks in plain language, agent measures runtime state the human cannot see, repairs it in the shared surface, and returns a committable diff — is the collaboration WebMCP makes possible. It is not a report. It is a fix you can watch working. How it creates a better developer experience Accessibility triage today means opening DevTools, hunting an element, reading a rule ID, and translating it into a source edit yourself. Here you ask: "Why can't a keyboard user finish this?" → the agent chains get_focus_order , reproduce_interaction and get_console_log , and reports that a positive tabindex pulls the card field to tab position 1 and the submit handler throws. "What's wrong with this modal?" → scoped audit of the state on screen, not the homepage. "Fix it and show me the patch." → live repair plus the diff. Findings carry the measured ratio, the WCAG criterion, a unique CSS selector and the concrete fix — and highlight overlays bloom over the offending elements so you and the agent are pointing at the same button. Closing the loop for coding agents A terminal agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) has a shell and a filesystem, not a document — so it can never call a WebMCP tool. That was the harder half of the problem, and it is why the audit engine is UI-free and also ships as a CLI: npx dom-surgeon audit http://localhost:5173 --json --fail-on critical Playwright loads your page, injects the engine, audits the real hydrated DOM, and exits non-zero. The agent writes UI, gets told which selectors fail and why, edits the source, and re-runs until it exits 0. This is the post-generation quality gate for generated UI — the thing that stops an agent shipping three unlabelled inputs and a 2.38:1 button. --baseline reports only new findings, so you can adopt it on a large existing app without a wall of pre-existing failures, and multi-route sweeps catch the "we only ever checked the homepage" gap. Same command works as a pre-commit hook or a CI step. One engine, three surfaces: WebMCP tools for interactive triage in the browser, a CLI for the coding agent and CI, a bookmarklet for any page you can open. How we implemented WebMCP 15 tools on document.modelContext.registerTool , each execute returning a plain string capped to the documented 1.5K output budget, with readOnlyHint on inspectors and untrustedContentHint on everything that reads live page text — a tool whose whole job is reading the DOM is a prompt-injection surface, and the spec's security guidance says to mark it as one. Inspect: audit_page , get_a11y_tree , find_contrast_failures , find_missing_labels , get_focus_order , describe_element , get_console_log , reproduce_interaction , highlight_elements . Repair: apply_fix , make_page_usable , revert_fixes , suggest_code_patch . Adapt: describe_barriers , set_reading_preferences . All native browser API underneath — getComputedStyle for post-cascade colour, ARIA reflection plus label-association walking for accessible names, real tabbability resolution (correctly excluding tabindex="-1" , disabled and hidden inputs), the WCAG relative-luminance formula including the large-text 3:1 threshold, and a console.error / onerror patch installed at load. Zero backend, no runtime dependencies, one static bundle. Every capability is also reachable by button, so the app is useful with no agent attached. Where this goes next The same repair engine points at a second audience: the person a broken page is failing, who cannot fix the site and cannot wait for its next sprint. describe_barriers and set_reading_preferences exist for exactly that, and work today on any page the engine can be injected into. We are not overclaiming it — reaching that user at scale needs a browser extension so the engine loads without them installing a bookmarklet first, and that is the honest next milestone rather than something we are shipping here. Honest limitations Automated rules catch a real but partial slice of accessibility. Reading order, whether alt text is meaningful , and whether a flow makes sense still need a person — make_page_usable deliberately refuses to touch those and reports them for a human instead of silently papering over them. We also pointed it at ourselves, and it found 11 defects in its own interface — including the primary "Make this page usable" button sitting at 3.77:1, which is an embarrassing thing for an accessibility tool to ship. All 11 are fixed; the self-audit now scores 0 while the demo's 6 seeded barriers remain intact, and npm run verify reproduces both numbers. And a note on engineering method: verifying the repair cycle by running it rather than trusting a clean TypeScript build surfaced a real bug we would otherwise have shipped. cssPath was emitting #id without checking uniqueness, so a duplicated id — precisely the defect one of our own rules reports — produced a selector that resolved to the wrong element. Repairs were being applied to the wrong twin and revert could never find them again. Fixed, and the round-trip is now verified to restore identical state.
