title: dug
pitch: Live DNS, TLS and mail diagnostics where your agent’s tool call renders on the page. It picks the lookups, you read the evidence. 27 WebMCP tools, one of which can’t exist on a server.
about_excerpt: Live DNS, TLS and mail diagnostics where your agent’s tool call renders on the page. It picks the lookups, you read the evidence. 27 WebMCP tools, one of which can’t exist on a server. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I asked a model why mail from a domain was going to spam. Got back a confident, detailed, completely stale answer. Which makes sense. Its weights hold the DNS and certificate state of whenever training stopped, and all of that changes without telling anyone. Giving an agent live lookups fixes half the problem. Here’s the half nobody talks about: when the agent runs six lookups and gives you a paragraph, you’re trusting the paragraph. You never see the SPF include tree that blew past ten lookups. The evidence existed for a second inside a context window and then it was gone. What it does dug is a command-driven terminal for domain and network diagnostics. One question per command, live, no key and no signup. DNS across six resolvers, TLS chains, RDAP registration, SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment, ASN and routing, plus a family of commands for how readable a site is to crawlers and agents. The full list is at https://dug.sh/llms.txt , generated from the same registry the app runs on, so it’s never out of date. Every command is registered as a WebMCP tool on document.modelContext. When an agent in the page calls one, the answer doesn’t go only to the agent. It renders on the page, as the same screen you’d have got by typing the command yourself. The tool I cared about most is the one that isn’t a command. dug_investigate takes a question, a target, and a list of commands the agent wrote itself: dug_investigate({ question: "why is mail from this domain going to spam", target: "acme.com", steps: ["MAIL acme.com", "SPF acme.com", "DIG acme.com MX", "RDAP acme.com"] }) It runs them in order and files every screen under the question, each one showing up as it arrives. You end up reading a case file instead of a summary. The header says “planned by your agent”, so you know which half of the room asked. Why WebMCP and not only MCP Because dug_investigate can’t exist on a remote MCP server. I shipped one so you can check. /mcp serves the same commands over Streamable HTTP. An agent there runs the same four lookups and gets the same four payloads. What it can’t do is leave them anywhere a person is looking. An investigation’s output is a page, and there’s nothing at the other end of an HTTP response to render onto. So don’t take my word for it. Call it over /mcp, you get JSON. Call it in the page, somebody watches the case get built. There’s a second reason that matters more than it sounds. Every tool is annotated readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint, because every answer here is built out of whatever some third-party nameserver or registry returned. A TXT record is attacker-controlled text. The page knows that. A scraper guessing at the DOM doesn’t. How it makes the thing better to use Typing “why mail acme.com” means knowing there’s a topic called “mail”. That’s exactly what you don’t know when you’ve got the problem. You know the symptom. I kept the keyword form for people without an agent, and the page says outright that it’s the worse path. Then I gave the prompt its own planner: type the sentence and dug asks a model to pick the lookups, and the case is headed “planned by dug” so it never pretends an agent was there. With a real agent you say “our invoices are landing in spam” and it plans through dug_investigate itself. Either way you didn’t learn a grammar, and you still get the evidence instead of somebody’s opinion about the evidence. What people and agents can do together now Read the same thing at the same time. That’s it. I think it’s new here. Before, an agent using a diagnostics API ate the output privately, and whatever you learned came through its summary. Scraping the UI is worse: the agent guesses at a DOM it doesn’t understand, and the site has no way to tell it a DKIM record is untrusted input. With dug, the tool call and the thing a human looks at are the same event. The agent gets structured payloads to reason over. You get a few thousand pixels of evidence to argue with it about. When it tells you SPF is fine, the include tree is sitting right there and you can see it at ten of ten lookups, one CNAME from breaking. There’s also a loop this challenge made possible, which I didn’t expect to build. WEBMCP checks whether some other site is wired for agents: the Origin-Agent-Cluster header native WebMCP needs, whether the page’s scripts reference the API, the remote MCP surface. It’s careful about what it can’t know. Tools register at runtime, so nothing fetched from outside a browser can list them, and the screen has a frame titled “what this cannot see” that says so. A checker printing a tool count off a curl would be making it up. How I built it WebMCP lives in lib/webmcp.ts, written against the current spec, not the February draft. That distinction cost me a day. Entry point is document.modelContext. navigator.modelContext is read as a fallback only, since it’s a deprecated alias as of Chrome 150. Registration is registerTool(tool, { signal }), one tool at a time, with a single AbortController for the whole set. provideContext got pulled from the spec because it replaces the entire list in one call, which on a page where two scripts register tools isn’t cooperation, it’s a takeover. Every response sends Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1. Without it Chromium disables the API and nothing you register works at all, which is a fun hour to spend. @mcp-b/global installs the API where the browser hasn’t shipped it yet. One command registry generates the tools, and the REST routes, the OpenAPI document and the MCP server all read the same registry, so the four surfaces can’t drift into describing different tools. A parity test fails the build if they do. Errors are made for agents too. A refusal is a 400 with a code the caller can branch on, and it says what would have worked: ask the DNS endpoint for a record type it doesn’t know and the hint lists the ones it does; send a command to an endpoint that doesn’t serve it and the hint names the ones that do. The plain-text form that curl and the MCP bridge get prints every block the page shows, and strips any control characters a page title or a TXT record might carry, so a hostile record can’t rewrite a terminal or slip an escape sequence to a model. Backend is Go on Vercel functions. The dialer validates every outbound destination right before connect, so a lookup can’t be aimed at private or loopback space, and it judges IPv4 wrapped in IPv6 by the address inside rather than the wrapper. What I learned Static analysis can’t see a WebMCP tool set. Obvious in hindsight, and it ended up changing the product. Building WEBMCP as a checker forced me to get precise about the difference between “this page’s scripts reference the API”, which you can observe, and “an agent is connected”, which nobody can observe from anywhere. The page never claims the second one, because nothing it could call would know. Things that were on the “next” list until yesterday A fleet in one case. dug_investigate takes a targets list, and a step written as MAIL {target} runs once per domain, in order, under one heading. WHY mail a.com b.com does the same from the prompt, and so does the planner: type “is mail set up right for a.com and b.com” and dug files one case for both. An agent asked about three domains files one case, not three. The server card as an MCP resource. SEP-1649 recommends it, so a client that’s already connected can read mcp://server-card.json and validate the tool set without a second fetch to .well-known. Both come from one builder, so they can’t disagree. Two more built-in investigations for people without an agent: “is this site down for everyone or only for me” and “is this domain’s registration and delegation healthy”. The whole point still stands, though: an agent doesn’t need me to write them. What’s next Whatever the judges break. Try it Live: https://dug.sh Code: https://github.com/zaidmukaddam/dug (MIT) Remote MCP: https://dug.sh/mcp Server card: https://dug.sh/.well-known/mcp/server-card.json For agents: https://dug.sh/llms.txt For judges: open https://dug.sh in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing turned on. Then ask your agent something like “why would mail from github.com go to spam?” or “is vercel.com readable by agents?”. No signup, no key, nothing to install. In an ordinary browser the tools register and nothing is listening, and the page tells you that instead of pretending otherwise. title: Every — real invoices from an AI browser, no sign-up
pitch: A marketing site that publishes 17 WebMCP tools, so an agent can make a real invoice for someone who has no account.
about_excerpt: A marketing site that publishes 17 WebMCP tools, so an agent can make a real invoice for someone who has no account. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT's built-in browser listing the 17 Site tools every.ai registers, beside the live generator page. Inspiration every.ai had two landing pages promising a free invoice generator and a free proposal generator to small service businesses. Neither had a generator behind it. We built one during the Challenge window, and made it agent-first from the first commit, because a generator is the one corner of a marketing site where "an agent fills in a form and gets a real result" is the whole product. Then we found the sharper reason to do it. Asked in plain language for "a free invoice tool I can use without making an account", ChatGPT recommended three competitors and then volunteered a correction about us: that Every requires a Google sign-up, so it does not qualify. It cited every.ai. Reading our marketing pages, that was a fair conclusion — the pages talk about trials and sign-in, because that is what the product needed before this week. That is the problem WebMCP actually solves. Search forms a view of what your site can do, and that view is stale the moment you ship. A page that publishes tools does not have to argue with the model. It just hands over the capability, and the agent updates. In our demo video you can watch that happen live : the agent tells the user Every needs an account, opens the page, and corrects itself on camera — "the earlier answer was indeed outdated: the page explicitly says no account is needed" — and then makes the invoice. What it does every.ai is a static Astro marketing site. It also registers 17 tools on document.modelContext , so an agentic browser can act for a visitor who has never signed up. They cover the whole arc of a visit. Decide. about_every and check_fit answer what Every is, what it costs from live pricing data, and whether it suits the business the visitor describes — including saying plainly when it does not. search_help answers from a build-time index of the site's own content and admits when it has no answer instead of guessing. Do. create_invoice , update_invoice , create_proposal , update_proposal , convert_estimate_to_invoice , get_document , list_my_documents and get_pdf create and revise real invoices, estimates and proposals. Not previews. Each one is created immediately, gets a public link, and is kept for 30 days. No account at any point. Leave. request_signup_link returns a single link that opens an Every account already holding everything the agent just made. open_app points existing customers at the right page. request_demo reaches sales. calculate_stack_cost and score_warm_lead expose the site's own calculators. get_more_tools records what an agent wanted and could not find, which becomes our roadmap signal. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP, and what is newly possible A free tool that only a human can operate sits and waits for a human. The visitor has to find the page, understand the form, and fill it in. WebMCP moves the tool to where the person already is — mid-sentence, in the conversation where they said "I need to invoice this client." Three things became possible that were not before: A stranger can transact with us. Not a demo account, not a sandbox: a real document at a real URL that they can send to their client, with no sign-up, created by their agent on their behalf. The page can correct the model. Our video is the proof. Static marketing copy loses that argument; a tool surface wins it, because the tool is the ground truth. We can hear demand. get_more_tools means an agent that wants something we do not offer tells us so, in the moment, in its own words. How we built it WebMcpTools.tsx is a headless React island mounted once on the site. It feature-detects document.modelContext (falling back to the deprecated navigator.modelContext ) and, on a browser without WebMCP, registers nothing and renders nothing. Each tool is registered with registerTool : a JSON Schema inputSchema , annotations ( readOnlyHint , and untrustedContentHint on anything relaying text a third party wrote), and an execute that calls the same typed API client the site's human-facing forms use — so a document created by an agent and one created by a person land in the same session and the same list. Two design rules shaped everything. Results are written to be read aloud. The agent, not our UI, is doing the talking, so every result is a short self-contained string that ends in a usable next step, and a test asserts each one fits the budget. Guest documents mirror the product. They live in a completely separate database whose every user-settable column matches the product table it will one day become, so claiming a document into a real account is an insert of the same columns — lossless, not a re-entry. Because no engineer has a WebMCP-native browser in CI, we wrote a small in-page polyfill that installs document.modelContext only when a page opts in with ?webmcp=polyfill and no real implementation exists. The same registration and execute() path then runs in ordinary headless Chromium, which gave us a node --test suite and a Python harness that hands the tools to a live Claude model and runs a real agentic loop against the page. Challenges we ran into Keeping the guest schema identical to the product's so that claiming is lossless rather than a reconstruction. Designing get_pdf to be genuinely useful while still capturing a lead. Writing results an agent can relay verbatim without a model misreading a phrase as a system error. The hardest one was restraint. Our first version of the sign-up tool emailed the link. An adversarial review called it what it was: an unauthenticated endpoint that sends mail from our domain to any address a caller names — roughly 1,200 sends an hour from one machine. We cut the send entirely. The agent already has the link in the conversation the person is reading, so delivery added nothing and risked our sending reputation. The tool returns the link and nothing else. Accomplishments we're proud of It runs on the real production data path, not a demo backend. Every document a tool creates is real and has a real claim path into the product. And the surface is honest under pressure: check_fit tells people when Every is not for them, and search_help says when it does not know. What we learned Designing for an agent is not designing an API. It is closer to writing for a colleague who will repeat what you said to a customer, word for word, without checking. That changes every string. What's next The Chrome origin trial, so Chrome and Gemini users can see the tools at all. Then WebMCP inside the signed-in product, so a customer's agent can operate their actual workspace in the same tab. New work vs prior work every.ai existed before the Challenge, and this submission is evaluated only on what was added during the Submission Period. All of it was built on 2026-09-02 and 2026-09-03 , inside the window, with dated commit history in the public repository: the tool layer, the polyfill, the test suite, the agent-simulation harness, the guest document store and its API, the generator pages, /for-agents , and llms-full.txt . Before this window, the two generator URLs were six-line landing stubs with nothing behind them and the site registered no tools at all. title: Favor
pitch: Favor lets browser agents turn Telegram work posts into trusted marketplace matches and reviewable deal drafts, while humans keep control of publishing and payments.
about_excerpt: Favor lets browser agents turn Telegram work posts into trusted marketplace matches and reviewable deal drafts, while humans keep control of publishing and payments. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Close a deal without leaving Telegram. Start where work already happens: in Telegram. GIF From Telegram post to contract, deal status, and verified review. Favor: Turn Telegram Work Into Trusted Deals Inspiration Online work already happens in Telegram. A photographer shows recent shoots in a channel. A tutor finds students in a neighborhood chat. A lawyer gets clients through recommendations. A designer sends a portfolio in private messages. Clients post requests in communities and ask friends whom they trust. The conversation is easy. The handoff into actual work is not. Useful posts disappear in the feed, terms stay scattered across messages, and a completed job often leaves no portable proof beyond "thank you" in an old chat. People do not need another place to talk. They need a reliable way to turn existing conversations into work that is searchable, structured, and trustworthy. That is why we built Favor: a Telegram-native marketplace where a post can become an opportunity, an opportunity can become a deal, and a completed deal can become reputation. What it does Favor serves both sides of online work. A professional can turn a public Telegram post into a service offer, then add a price, deadline, category, portfolio, and terms. A client can turn a post describing what they need into a client request. People can search both types, inspect profiles, ratings, reviews, portfolios, and completed work, then manage the deal within the Telegram flow. Optional on-chain escrow in TON or USDT can protect payment when both sides want it. For the WebMCP Challenge, we made this live workflow actionable for browser agents through four focused tools: favor_search_contracts searches public service offers and client requests by text, category, budget, deadline, rating, and escrow support. favor_get_contract returns one listing's terms, author reputation, reviews, completed-deal signals, and Favor URL. favor_read_telegram_post reads a public Telegram work post through Favor's existing import pipeline and returns its text and media metadata. favor_prepare_contract_draft turns the result into a draft with a Telegram review link that expires after 24 hours. A user can ask: "Find a TikTok promotion specialist under $300 who supports escrow, compare the strongest options, and turn my Telegram brief into a client request." The agent handles discovery and preparation. The user checks every field and decides whether to publish. How we built it Favor is a production Next.js 16 and React 19 application written in TypeScript, with Prisma and PostgreSQL, Zod validation, a Telegram Mini App and bot, and TON infrastructure for optional escrow. The product, its users, marketplace, deals, reputation system, and Telegram import flow existed before this challenge. During the challenge, we added a WebMCP extension using the imperative API. An application-level provider detects document.modelContext and registers the four tools once. This is progressive enhancement: without WebMCP, Favor works exactly as before. Registration failures are isolated, and React lifecycle cleanup removes registered tools safely. The tools reuse Favor's production clients and APIs instead of duplicating product logic. Inputs have strict JSON schemas and are validated again with Zod at execution time. Contract identifiers must match Favor's generated slug format and are URL-encoded before requests. Cancellation signals reach the network layer, so stopping a tool stops its underlying work. Trust boundaries are explicit. Public discovery tools declare readOnlyHint: true . Listings, reviews, and imported Telegram text declare untrustedContentHint: true , because user-written content must never become agent instructions. Search is rate-limited and scans a bounded candidate set. The only state-changing WebMCP tool creates a visible, expiring draft for human review. It cannot publish a contract, start a deal, fund escrow, release payment, or issue a refund. Those actions remain in explicit user-controlled Favor flows. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering a tool. It was deciding where an agent's authority should end. Turning a loose Telegram post into structured work is exactly where an agent helps, but the same flow touches identity, publishing, agreements, and eventually money. Full autonomy would look impressive in a demo and be wrong for a real marketplace. We designed the 24-hour review handoff so the agent removes repetitive work without impersonating the user or committing funds. Marketplace text and reviews created a second challenge. They are valuable context, but also untrusted user content. We had to keep responses concise, label content correctly, restrict slugs, validate inputs twice, rate-limit search, and preserve cancellation across every layer. Finally, this was not a greenfield prototype. We integrated WebMCP into a live Telegram product without breaking unsupported browsers or creating duplicate business rules that could drift from production. Accomplishments that we're proud of The demo uses the live Favor product, not a scripted chatbot over sample data. It shows Favor's four registered tools and a successful production marketplace search; we also verified live contract inspection and Telegram-post import. The private 24-hour draft handoff is implemented, while WebMCP registration, execution, cancellation, and cleanup are covered by automated tests. We deliberately did not create test data in the production account used for the read-only demo. The tools are small enough to be safe and composable, but together cover the tedious path from "I need help" to "this is ready for me to approve." Favor remains fully usable without WebMCP, while a compatible browser gains structured capabilities immediately. We are also proud of the boundary we did not cross. Every public or financial commitment stays human-controlled. Automated tests cover feature detection, registration, execution, cancellation, cleanup, and partial registration failure, alongside Favor's wider contract test suite and production build. To be transparent about challenge scope: Favor predates the event. The challenge-period work is the WebMCP runtime, four production-backed tools, application-level registration, schemas and safety annotations, tests, and documentation that make the existing product agent-ready. The exact source footprint and production checks are documented in the public challenge guide . What we learned The best agent integration is not a second interface pasted over a product. It is a precise set of capabilities attached to the product's existing source of truth. Small tools compose better than one oversized "do everything" tool. Search, inspect, import, and prepare each have a clear contract and permission level. We also learned that human approval is not friction to eliminate when identity, reputation, or money is involved. It is part of the product value. WebMCP can make a browser agent useful inside a real application without making the application dependent on the agent. That balance let us ship the extension into Favor instead of maintaining a separate hackathon demo. What's next for Favor Next we will improve intent-aware ranking and comparisons, expand the reputation signals agents can explain, and learn from real search-to-draft journeys. We want more kinds of Telegram posts to enter Favor while preserving the visible review step. As WebMCP evolves, we plan to expose more preparation and decision support around proposals and deal terms. Publication, deal acceptance, and every escrow action will continue to require explicit human approval. Try the live product at favor.deals or open @FavorDealsBot in Telegram. title: FloraLink
pitch: Turns messy field observations into structured ecological reports with WebMCP-powered AI staging and human submission!
about_excerpt: Turns messy field observations into structured ecological reports with WebMCP-powered AI staging and human submission! Like Comment Story Updates FloraLink Mobile-first workflow with ChatGPT Supabase Schema Inspiration Ecological reports are extremely important. We use them to identify environmental risks, ensure legal compliance for developments, and protect local biodiversity. Making one often begins with a simple moment on a trail when you notice an unusual insect, a damaged tree, or a plant growing where it shouldn't. Turning that observation into useful data, however, is difficult. A typical reporting portal asks for ten or more fields, including scientific names, exact coordinates, dates, ecological status, and photographic evidence. This process is frustratingly awkward when you're outdoors on a mobile phone. You may not know the formal species name, you might only be able to describe a relative location, or you may simply lose patience with a long form. The result is missing field data, especially regarding invasive species where early observations matter most. FloraLink attempts to solve this by asking: What if an AI agent could handle the research and structuring, without taking control away from the human observer? How I built it FloraLink is a mobile-first Next.js application built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Leaflet, and Supabase. I used the iNaturalist API for normalized taxonomy searches, turning generic observations into formal ecological classifications based on nearby occurrences. The browsing agent acts as a spatial data curator. FloraLink registers five narrow tools through direct document.modelContext.registerTool(...) bindings: taxonomy search, ecological verification, permission-based device location, sighting staging, and staged-draft reading. These tools are defined together in src/features/webmcp/register-floralink-tools.ts . https://github.com/ShreyanshMisra/floralink/blob/main/src/features/webmcp/register-floralink-tools.ts Importantly, there is no tool for agent driven submission. A hallucinated species ID or a fabricated GPS coordinate could pollute real-world conservation data, so I created a strict human-in-the-loop consensus model: The user describes what they saw and where they saw it. The agent researches possible taxonomy and sourced regional context. The agent stages structured data, including any uncertainty, in FloraLink. WebMCP writes the draft into a session-hydrated Zustand store. React immediately renders the draft as an editable review card and Leaflet map geometry. The human checks the fields, resolves location questions, attaches an evidence photo, accepts the acknowledgement, and clicks Confirm sighting. Agent actions remain temporary. Only the human-controlled confirmation path can call the server-side submission flow and create a durable report. Supabase provides anonymous authentication, private image Storage, PostgreSQL, and PostGIS. Anonymous authentication lets a contributor securely own a report without requiring account credentials. Challenges I ran into Preserving unresolved locations: Field descriptions are often relative (e.g., “two miles north of the trailhead”). Allowing an agent to guess this coordinate would create false precision. FloraLink accepts an explicit unresolved-location state. The human must intervene to use device location, drop a pin, or draw an approximate area before confirmation is enabled. Keeping WebMCP and React state in sync: WebMCP callbacks live outside React's normal component event flow, while our review interface needs to update the exact millisecond a tool finishes. I bridged the two using a Zustand store and its imperative getState() API. I also utilized an AbortController to clean up registrations during React 19 Strict Mode double-mounting, preventing duplicate tools and stale callbacks. Handling photo metadata safely: Photo GPS can recover a lost location, but uploading the original image exposes hidden personal metadata. FloraLink reads EXIF GPS locally before processing, offers it to the human as an explicit fallback choice, and then re-encodes the photo through a browser canvas. This completely strips the EXIF metadata before uploading to private storage. Accomplishments AI-assisted data collection is as much a governance problem as an interface problem. Ecological data influences conservation work, so unsupported confidence is actively harmful. I prioritized scientific integrity by preserving an unknown species, bounding an approximate area, and citing the source of a status claim, which I think is more valuable than filling every field with an AI guess. WebMCP also allowed me to build a totally different style of collaboration. The agent and the person work side by side in the same application. The agent researches and stages information, while the person sees each change instantly on the map and review card. There is no hidden transfer from a chat response into a separate form. Most importantly, this proved that useful AI autonomy can be bounded. FloraLink gives the agent enough capability to remove tedious research, but its tools stop at staging. The person supplies private evidence, corrects the draft, makes privacy decisions, and alone authorizes submission. That narrow boundary makes the workflow faster, safer, and highly trustworthy. What's next for FloraLink Scientific Data Export: Implementing Darwin Core data exports so our verified, human-confirmed reports can be seamlessly ingested by state conservation databases and global research networks. Civic Infrastructure Integrations: Expanding our verification tables to support local park services and municipalities for rapid anomaly and trail-damage reporting. Extensions The technology behind FloraLink has potential far beyond ecology. In fact, my original idea was "UFOLink", an anonymous sighting tracker where people could submit UFO reports using WebMCP tools. I quickly pivoted to biodiversity because it offered more testable, real-world use cases. That said, the core architecture remains incredibly versatile. Whether it is powering rapid citizen journalism, acting as a corporate field auditor for a "company brain", or intaking municipal infrastructure reports, this human-in-the-loop WebMCP model can be applied to almost any field that requires quickly turning unstructured data and field images into verified, database-ready information. title: Frontmend
pitch: Audit the site. Give your coding agent evidence it can act on.
about_excerpt: Audit the site. Give your coding agent evidence it can act on. Like Comment Story Updates Frontmend turns a public website audit into a clear recommendation list for people and an evidence-rich brief a coding agent can act on through WebMCP. The problem Frontend audit tools are good at measuring websites, and coding agents are good at working inside repositories. The handoff between them is the weak point. Most audit results are presented as score dashboards or lengthy reports designed for people. When a coding agent tries to use them, it has to scrape the page, interpret screenshots, follow buttons and reconstruct important context that may have been lost along the way. A copied recommendation such as “improve accessibility” is not enough. The agent needs the original audit rule, affected route, viewport, observed target, supporting evidence and a clear definition of what passing looks like. We initially explored putting the entire repair lifecycle inside Frontmend. That created more approval states, checklists and deployment theatre than useful frontend work. Coding agents already know how to inspect repositories, edit files and run tests within the user’s existing permissions. Frontmend should give them better evidence, not try to replace them. What Frontmend does A person enters one public URL. Frontmend runs an asynchronous PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse audit alongside bounded live-document analysis. It then turns the retained evidence into a short, prioritised recommendation list. Each recommendation brings together: What Frontmend observed and why it matters Severity, category, exact audit rule ID and provider provenance Affected routes and viewports, plus selectors when available The number of measured occurrences A concise recommended change Repository search hints derived only from public evidence Concrete acceptance criteria A clear explanation of what Frontmend did not inspect or prove The human result is designed to read like a useful editorial report rather than another technical dashboard. Why WebMCP fits Without WebMCP, a coding agent sees the same interface as a person. It has to inspect the DOM, identify controls, infer the application’s state and scrape result text from a page that was never designed for machine use. With WebMCP, Frontmend can describe its capabilities directly. A compatible agent can discover the tools available in the current page state, start the same audit as the human interface, check truthful progress, read the completed recommendations and inspect the evidence chain behind an individual finding. The result includes a bounded codingAgentBrief containing the structured context needed to continue real work: Ranked recommendations Retained observations Exact audit rule IDs and provider provenance Routes and measured viewports Selectors and affected targets when available Repository search hints Acceptance criteria Explicit evidence and authority boundaries The agent no longer has to reverse-engineer the interface or copy an incomplete report into its context. WebMCP does not perform the audit itself. Frontmend’s background audit service does that work. WebMCP provides a reliable, typed interface between the webpage and the agent. What people and agents can do together A person can ask: Audit my deployed frontend with Frontmend, investigate the strongest findings in this repository and implement the fixes that are supported by the evidence. The coding agent can then: Open Frontmend and discover its available WebMCP tools. Start an audit for the public URL. Poll the same durable job shown in the human interface. Read the ranked recommendations and supporting evidence. Return to the authorised repository and investigate the real source code. Implement justified changes and run the repository’s own checks. Frontmend remains useful without WebMCP. A person can complete the entire public audit through the normal interface and receive the same recommendation document. Both paths call the same application service and validation logic, so the human and agent are not working from separate versions of the truth. A deliberate boundary Frontmend does not claim to know which repository file owns a public symptom. It does not invent filenames or line numbers, request source code, handle repository credentials or pretend that a recommendation has been implemented. The current public workflow ends with the audit result and coding-agent handoff. Repository investigation and implementation continue through the agent’s existing file, browser and terminal tools. In the public workflow, a fresh audit of the deployed URL is the only way Frontmend produces new evidence about the production site. How it was built Frontmend uses: React 19 and Vite for the public interface Bun for package management, tests, linting and builds Socket’s Bun security scanner for dependency protection A Cloudflare Worker for the application and audit API SQLite-backed Durable Objects for asynchronous jobs, stable audit IDs, cancellation, retention and rate limits PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse behind replaceable evidence adapters Versioned, JSON-serialisable contracts shared by the human interface and WebMCP tools Contextual WebMCP registration, exposing only the actions that are useful in the current state Public URL handling is treated as a security boundary. Frontmend rejects credentialed, private-network, loopback, unsafe and query-bearing audit targets. Redirect destinations are revalidated on the server, and audit work is bounded by request, response, timeout, redirect and rate limits. Building with Codex Codex was both the primary development collaborator and the coding agent Frontmend was designed to help. It helped shape the product boundary, implement the shared contracts across the React client and Cloudflare Worker, test contextual WebMCP routing, harden public URL handling and challenge unsupported claims about repository ownership, deployment and resolution. That process helped clarify the central idea behind Frontmend: WebMCP is most valuable here when it gives an agent trustworthy context and then gets out of the way. Why it matters Frontmend is not an AI chat box placed beside an audit report. It makes an existing web workflow genuinely more useful when a person and their coding agent use it together. The person receives a clearer, more approachable audit. The coding agent receives structured evidence it can act on. Neither has to learn a second repair workflow, and the agent no longer needs to scrape a human-facing dashboard to understand what happened. title: GridBrief TR
pitch: An agent-ready bilingual workspace that turns public EPİAŞ Transparency Platform 2.0 data into explainable market, portfolio, and planning decisions through native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready bilingual workspace that turns public EPİAŞ Transparency Platform 2.0 data into explainable market, portfolio, and planning decisions through native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Türkiye's electricity-market teams must reconcile prices, system conditions, generation, consumption, and planning data before making a shift decision. Today that work often spans operator pages, spreadsheets, and chat. Each team rebuilds the same context, while the most important questions — which source, which timestamp, which scope, and how complete is the data — are easy to lose. GridBrief TR reimagines the public EPİAŞ Transparency Platform 2.0 as a bilingual, agent-ready decision workspace. It keeps the familiar market information architecture, but makes provenance, freshness, coverage, and missing data first-class product features. What it does GridBrief TR combines: a real-data market overview; the searchable Transparency 2.0 electricity catalogue; public organization and power-plant discovery; production and consumption planning views; English and Turkish interfaces; and a native WebMCP tool surface shared by the human user and browser agents. The production walkthrough uses a completed historical day and visibly shows EPİAŞ provenance, retrieval time, scope, coverage, and warnings. Examples include market price and imbalance context, 24/24 planning coverage, the public PURE ENERGY organization view and linked UEVÇB records, and an ACARSOY plant view that honestly leaves unavailable actual generation as null. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the interaction layer, not a chatbot bolted onto a dashboard. GridBrief registers eight structured tools on document.modelContext: set_analysis_scope get_market_snapshot find_market_entities compare_plan_actual stress_test_position draft_shift_brief search_transparency_datasets get_transparency_dataset A compatible browser discovers these tools and calls the descriptor returned by getTools() with schema-bounded arguments. Successful calls update the same visible workspace used by the participant, so the agent and human share the selected date, hour window, results, warnings, and sources. Our native Chrome 152 verification discovered all eight tools. It also executed search_transparency_datasets through document.modelContext and visibly synchronized the selected catalogue item. That is separate from the real-data production evidence: during the recorded native verification run, an upstream EPİAŞ live read timed out, so the harness failed closed, recorded the failure, and skipped downstream sensitivity and brief actions. It never substituted a synthetic observation. Example agent workflow A trading agent can retrieve price and imbalance context. An operations agent can inspect generation evidence and publication coverage. A planning agent can compare KGÜP, KUDÜP, EAK, load-plan, and actual series only at valid data levels. A portfolio-risk agent can apply a transparent local sensitivity after the live price reference passes validation. A management agent can turn the sourced evidence, risks, and proposed checks into an editable shift brief. These are role-specific uses of one WebMCP contract, demonstrated by a deterministic sample agent workflow in the repository. GridBrief does not claim that the runner itself is an LLM. It exposes no market-order, trading-account, message-sending, or upstream mutation tool. How we built it The application uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Vercel. A server-only EPİAŞ gateway obtains and caches the short-lived ticket-granting token without returning or logging credentials. Responses carry provider, retrieval time, scope, quality, coverage, and warnings. Partial data preserves nulls; live errors fail closed. The browser layer registers imperative WebMCP definitions for the lifetime of the workspace. A Node/CDP verification harness launches Chrome with WebMCP enabled, checks unique tool discovery, executes native descriptors, and writes bounded sanitized evidence and screenshots. The harness accepts no username, password, token, cookie, or authorization-header argument. Challenges and learnings The hardest part was preserving market-data integrity while making the experience useful to agents. EPİAŞ reports have different scopes and publication schedules; organization filters do not turn system-level actuals into organization data; and upstream availability can change during a demo. We therefore made data level explicit, preserved missing hours, withheld full-day deviation when coverage is not comparable, and separated catalogue availability from successful observation retrieval. We also learned that the current experimental Chrome implementation requires the descriptor returned by getTools() and JSON-stringified arguments. Testing that real boundary exposed issues a mock panel would have hidden, including duplicate registration risks, inclusive-versus-exclusive hour semantics, and upstream timeout handling. What's next Next steps are formal review of EPİAŞ report semantics and terms, organization-level audit retention, role controls, shared rate limiting, richer data-quality tests, and approved connections to internal portfolio systems. We will preserve the no-execution boundary unless a separately governed product is designed and authorized. It provides decision support only and does not place trades or provide financial advice. title: Legalize-KR WebMCP
pitch: People set the legal question. Agents retrieve and compare exact, source-linked Korean statute provisions through four read-only WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: People set the legal question. Agents retrieve and compare exact, source-linked Korean statute provisions through four read-only WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Korean Law Review Workbench with four read-only WebMCP tools ready for collaboration. The person selects the statute, article, archive dates, and review question before the agent retrieves evidence. Agent-generated review brief preserves the person's question, identifies the textual change, and provides verification checks and citations. A source-linked comparison shows that Article 1004-2 was added between the selected archive dates. Four structured WebMCP tools cover statute search, exact article retrieval, version comparison, and review-brief generation. Inspiration Korean legal review depends on exact text, exact dates, and verifiable sources. Finding only the current version of a statute is often insufficient. A reviewer must determine which text existed at the relevant time, identify what changed, and check the official source before drawing a conclusion. Browser agents normally have to infer the meaning of controls, scrape long documents, and guess whether visible text corresponds to the requested date. I built this project to explore a clearer division of responsibility: the person defines the legal question and review boundaries, while the agent performs structured and reproducible evidence retrieval through WebMCP. What it does Korean Law Review Workbench lets a person select: a Korean statute a specific article an earlier and later archive date a question that defines the scope of the review The page exposes four read-only WebMCP tools: search_laws finds matching Korean statutes for a requested archive date. get_articles retrieves one exact article with its official and archived sources. compare_versions classifies the article as added, removed, changed, or unchanged. build_review_brief prepares a deterministic, source-linked review memo around the person's question. Tool calls update the same visible workspace used by the person. The reviewer can inspect the exact text, dates, revision identifiers, and source links used by the agent. The default demonstration compares Article 1004-2 of the Korean Civil Act between January 1, 2020 and August 31, 2026. The archived versions show that the provision concerning the declaration of loss of inheritance rights was added during that period. The application performs textual and source comparison only. It does not provide legal advice or decide how a provision applies to a particular case. How we built it I created a new public, MIT-licensed repository and wrote the application from scratch during the WebMCP Challenge period. The project does not copy source code from the existing Legalize-KR production website. The application is built with TypeScript, Vite, and Vitest. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same legal-data and comparison functions so that agent results can be reproduced through the visible interface. Each tool is registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() with: a narrow JSON Schema readOnlyHint: true untrustedContentHint: true cancellation propagation for network requests compact results designed for agent context A bundled index contains 1,733 Korean statute titles and repository paths, but no statute bodies. At execution time, the app resolves the last archived Git revision available on or before the requested Korean calendar date. It then retrieves the statute Markdown from that immutable commit and extracts only the requested article. Every comparison includes the requested dates and links to the official Korean Law Information Center source and both immutable Legalize-KR revisions. The app requires no account and has no database, analytics, cookies, or personal-data storage. Its production build is designed for a static Cloudflare Pages deployment without Pages Functions, Workers compute, or paid storage bindings. Challenges we ran into One challenge was controlling the size of tool results. An early comparison response contained every parsed article from both statute versions. This produced an unnecessarily large agent context. I replaced the full snapshots with compact revision references and returned only the selected article. Historical-date resolution also required care. A requested date must resolve to the last revision available by the end of that calendar day in Korea, rather than returning the repository's current version. Another challenge was parsing legal Markdown conservatively. Article text must stop before the next article or structural heading. Real-data testing revealed a boundary case where the following section heading could be included in the final article. I added a regression test and corrected the parser. Finally, legal text presents a trust problem. Retrieved content must be treated as evidence, not as instructions or an automatic legal conclusion. The tools therefore remain read-only, mark external legal text as untrusted, and return explicit attribution and non-legal-advice notices. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that the project exposes four working WebMCP tools rather than adding a thin natural-language wrapper around an existing search interface. The human and agent paths share the same data functions and visible evidence state. When an agent performs a comparison or builds a review brief, the result also appears in the workspace for immediate human verification. The project uses real historical statute data and immutable Git revisions. The default scenario produces a reproducible added result for Article 1004-2 of the Korean Civil Act and provides direct links to the earlier archive, later archive, and official current source. I also added automated coverage for schemas, date handling, article parsing, comparison states, compact tool results, tool annotations, and visible-result publication. A deployment guard prevents Cloudflare Worker entry points, Pages Functions, routing files, and compute or storage bindings from being added accidentally. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it exposes meaningful domain operations instead of reproducing a general-purpose prompt box. Explicit tools for article retrieval, historical comparison, and source-linked brief generation reduce ambiguity and make the agent's work easier to verify. I also learned that human-agent collaboration requires shared state. Returning evidence only to the agent would make review difficult. Publishing the same result into the visible workspace lets the person inspect the sources, correct the scope, and retain control over the final judgment. Finally, compactness is part of tool quality. A legally accurate result can still be unsuitable for an agent if it includes an entire statute when only one article was requested. What's next for Legalize-KR WebMCP The MVP intentionally covers statutes only. The next improvements could include: paragraph-level and item-level change highlighting retrieval of supplementary provisions and transitional rules selection of multiple related articles for one review exportable review packages that remain local to the user improved handling of GitHub API rate limits Precedents, administrative rules, and local ordinances may be considered later, but each dataset requires a separate review of source rights, schemas, and attribution requirements. The core principle will remain unchanged: people control the legal question, scope, and judgment, while agents retrieve structured and verifiable evidence. title: Let your AI send letters and postcards on pieterpost.com
pitch: From prompt to post. Your agent writes it. Send invoices, cancellation requests, heartfelt letters and birthday cards through WebMCP on pieterpost.com.
about_excerpt: From prompt to post. Your agent writes it. Send invoices, cancellation requests, heartfelt letters and birthday cards through WebMCP on pieterpost.com. Like Comment Story Updates PieterPost WebMCP, Because apparently the future comes with stamps Inspiration Most AI actions end on a screen. But invoices, cancellation requests, important documents, heartfelt letters and birthday cards still need to reach a real mailbox. PieterPost already turns digital messages into physical post. WebMCP gave us a way to let an AI agent use that complete service directly. What it does From prompt to post. Your agent can write and prepare a letter or postcard, then pay through Stripe’s agentic payments or create a secure payment link for you. After payment, PieterPost prints, stamps and mails it. Your agent can check the delivery status at any time. The person stays in control of the recipient, message and payment. The agent handles the work needed to send it. Without WebMCP, an agent could help write a letter, but the person still had to copy the text, open a website, complete forms, upload files and return later to check the order. PieterPost’s WebMCP tools connect these steps into one conversation. How we built it We added seven structured WebMCP tools to the existing PieterPost website: Upload a document or image Prepare a letter Prepare a postcard Create a payment link Check an order’s status Cancel a prepared order List orders from the current session The integration uses document.modelContext.registerTool() with strict input and output schemas. It also supports cancellation, safe retries, clear tool annotations and structured results that agents can understand. The tools use PieterPost’s existing website and fulfillment system. People can continue to use the normal interface, while compatible agents get a direct and reliable way to complete the same workflow. The complete browser-side WebMCP integration is available as an open-source MIT-licensed repository. Challenges Sending physical post has real consequences. We had to make sure an agent could not accidentally create duplicate orders or expose private letter and address information. We have a complex .pdf rendering pipeline to support all languages, emoji's and various formats for many countries around the world. Preparing an order does not send it. Payment remains a clear approval step. Stable operation keys protect against duplicate actions, and status responses contain only the information the agent needs. We also had to turn a multi-step physical service into tools that are simple enough for an agent to use without losing the safeguards expected from a real checkout flow. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it removes the need for an agent to guess how a website works. The agent does not need to click through forms or interpret page layouts. It receives clear tools with known inputs, outputs and limits. The person still controls important decisions, while the agent handles the operational steps. The demo For the demo, Codex used PieterPost’s WebMCP tools to send a real thank-you letter to Tibo at OpenAI. Codex wrote the letter, prepared the order and created the Stripe payment link. After payment, Codex checked the order status, and PieterPost printed and mailed the letter. The product demonstrated itself: an AI agent sent a physical letter through WebMCP. Apparently, the future comes with stamps. title: Lyrashield AI — WebMCP Assurance tool
pitch: Find risky WebMCP tool definitions, review a proposed change with your agent and rerun the check. Source stays in your browser, you decide what to apply.
about_excerpt: Find risky WebMCP tool definitions, review a proposed change with your agent and rerun the check. Source stays in your browser, you decide what to apply. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Lyrashield AI homepage: release assurance for AI-built software. Workspace dashboard showing posture, active scans, and recent activity. WebMCP Assurance overview for reviewing browser-agent tool surfaces before release. WebMCP Security Lab: paste source and run 14 browser-local assurance controls. Lab results showing control states, evidence, and remediation guidance. Repository scan setup for an authorized target and assessment scope. Scan setup: choose a target and policy before creating a scan. Dashboard scan configuration with mode, scope, and review controls. Launch readiness view showing evidence, coverage, and next review actions. Launch readiness checks showing target coverage and remaining blockers. Human review dialog keeps an agent-assisted action visible for approval. Launch readiness report showing scope, evidence state, and review details. Why we built it The unsafe sample in Lyrashield's WebMCP Security Lab includes a tool named delete_user . It declares readOnlyHint: true , sends a DELETE request and sets exposedTo: ["*"] . We built WebMCP Assurance for developers adding browser-agent tools to their apps. A tool's description, input contract, permissions and implementation can disagree. We wanted developers to find those disagreements, inspect a proposed change and check the result before release. Try the review loop Open the free Security Lab . No account or API key is required. Load the unsafe sample and choose Check locally . The Lab parses the source in your browser and evaluates 14 deterministic controls. The sample produces seven controls marked DETECTED. Open Rewrite , select WEBMCP-03 , and prepare the change. The preview replaces exposedTo: ["*"] with exposedTo: [] . You review the diff, then choose Apply in memory and rerun . The exposure control becomes NO FINDING; six other detected controls remain. Undo restores the original sample. The change affects the local working copy. It does not edit a repository or establish that the tool is safe. How people and agents work together In a browser with WebMCP enabled, the Lab registers two page tools: analyze_webmcp_source analyzes the current local input or the built-in unsafe sample and returns a bounded summary. prepare_webmcp_rewrite prepares a change for a selected detected control and returns whether human review is required. The agent can work on the source already loaded in the page without asking the developer to paste it into a conversation. Raw source and the rewrite diff stay in the human interface; the tools return summaries and rewrite metadata. A visible activity record shows whether a call completed, failed or was cancelled. The developer keeps the Apply and Undo controls. WebMCP fits this workflow because the agent and developer use the same page state. The agent has named operations with defined inputs, and the developer can inspect the result in place. Browsers without WebMCP retain the manual workflow. The authenticated Lyrashield app also implements page-specific tools to review launch readiness, filter or explain visible findings and prepare a scan form. Preparation leaves execution to the human Start control and existing server authorisation. The public Lab is the no-login judging path. How we built it A shared TypeScript analyser discovers supported imperative registrations and declarative forms, builds a versioned tool inventory, and evaluates the controls. They cover behaviour and annotation mismatches, cross-origin exposure, confirmation, validation, data bounds, cancellation, cleanup, embedded credentials, instruction-shaped contract text and specification drift. The full analyser feeds the Lab, repository scanning, CLI/SARIF output, and WebMCP coverage receipts in reports. The self-contained GitHub Action runs a documented subset and blocks changed WebMCP mutation code it cannot structurally assess. The Lab loads its TypeScript and HTML parsers in a dedicated Worker when analysis begins. Its native tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool , validate inputs, support cancellation and return bounded results. Source selected or pasted into the Lab is processed locally. The public MIT-licensed repository contains the implementation. Start with the analyzer , the Lab tools , and the dashboard adapter . What we learned Rewrite safety required more work than generating a diff. The implementation checks that the source still matches the analysed inventory, limits edits to unambiguous wildcard-exposure cases, then analyses the proposed result before returning a patch. Unsupported cases remain unresolved. That constraint gives the developer a small change they can inspect. We also reduced the Lab from five overlapping agent tools to two focused operations. Apply, Undo, export and other human controls remain visible in the page. Codex helped with design review, implementation, regression tests, adversarial review, CI diagnosis, and release checks. The WebMCP controls and rewrite decisions run deterministically. Work added during the challenge LyraShield AI existed before The WebMCP Challenge. The pre-existing platform, billing, generic scanner, and dashboard are not claimed as hackathon work. During the submission period, we built and hardened the WebMCP-specific assurance layer: • A deterministic WebMCP analyzer and public browser-local Security Lab, where selected or pasted source stays in the browser. • WebMCP tools for local analysis and review-required rewrite preparation, including Chrome callback compatibility. • Repository scanning, CLI/SARIF output, and a fail-closed GitHub Action subset for structurally assessable WebMCP changes. • Page-scoped authenticated dashboard tools with visible activity records. Agents can prepare permitted state, but a human must explicitly start durable or resource-consuming work. • Fourteen controls covering annotation/behavior mismatch, exposure, origin isolation, confirmation boundaries, embedded credentials, prompt-injection text, specification drift, contract budgets, and related WebMCP risks. • A bounded rewrite path: only a statically checked, unambiguous wildcard-exposure case can produce a rewrite proposal. Applying it remains in-memory and human-controlled; all other cases stay review-required. We also extended the surrounding evidence workflow during this period: Launch Gate verdicts, signed shareable readiness reports, CLI readiness verdicts, an AI-built failure taxonomy, a server-generated fix and retest path, and explicit scope-limited results that never treat a partial assessment as launch-ready. Recent work improved judge usability and public clarity: WebMCP visibility in navigation, responsive navigation fixes, theme-token pricing and page polish, updated public explanation and control-count parity, plus refreshed demo and submission documentation. Key merged evidence includes WebMCP implementation and compatibility work in PRs #498, #499, and #512; launch-assurance work in PRs #555 through #561; WebMCP submission hardening in #569 and #570; and recent correctness and usability updates in #585, #587, #588, and #589. LyraShield reports bounded, deterministic evidence. It does not claim universal coverage, a security guarantee, or independent verification of every result. Scope and next work The Lab checks selected source. Dynamic behaviour, server authorisation, and obfuscated or unsupported registrations can remain outside its coverage. Results are deterministic detections, not independent verification or a security guarantee. Runtime drift protection remains future work. The next validation step is a recorded native-client invocation of both public tools, with their visible activity records and human Apply boundary. The completed manual Brave test covers analysis, rewrite, rerun and Undo. It does not establish native WebMCP execution. title: My Calendar Planner
pitch: My Calendar Planner (MyCP) is an agent-native shared calendar and planning tool that resolves scheduling conflicts, finds available times, and accounts for user preferences when proposing times.
about_excerpt: My Calendar Planner (MyCP) is an agent-native shared calendar and planning tool that resolves scheduling conflicts, finds available times, and accounts for user preferences when proposing times. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Scheduling meetings with large teams can be a pain, even when everyone is available. When you need to account for different schedules, locations, time zones, focus time, or other factors, things can get unwieldy very quickly. Existing assistants often force people to choose between manually coordinating everything and granting broad write access. We wanted to show a better default: give the agent just enough structured context to help, then keep the final decision visible and human-owned. What it does MyCP is a seeded shared-calendar demo for a distributed launch team. A browser agent uses WebMCP tools to inspect narrowly scoped context, find one-time or weekly availability, and rank meeting options. A weekly proposal checks every requested occurrence against private busy time, protected focus blocks, work patterns, travel buffers, and time preferences without revealing why another person is unavailable. When one weekly check-in conflicts with the manager’s existing meeting, it can stage one bounded reschedule for that instance without moving the existing event. The same pattern works for time away: the agent can prepare one compact change-set draft containing a private absence, proposed cancellation of the manager’s owned meetings, and a transfer to an approved delegate. It cannot apply any of those changes or send notifications. The person reviews a before/after diff in the calendar, opens a confirmation dialog, and explicitly adds the event. That API path requires the reviewed draft revision, a five-minute one-time confirmation, and an idempotency key. Private events remain generic Busy blocks outside the owner’s access. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite for the calendar interface. A Cloudflare Worker for static assets, same-origin API routes, and the WebMCP headers. Cloudflare D1 for persistent seeded-demo state with revision-checked writes. Zod schemas shared at the command boundary. WebMCP imperative tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Vitest coverage for scheduling, redaction, draft lifecycle, confirmation, idempotency, and rate limits. WebMCP Usage MyCP registers fourteen intent-level tools rather than exposing DOM selectors or database access. get_calendar_context provides bounded calendar/team identifiers, while get_user_scheduling_profile reads a purpose-limited profile with meeting preferences, recurring focus blocks, and office/remote work patterns—never a home address, live location, or private events. propose_recurring_schedule validates one weekly local-time slot across 2–26 occurrences and can return no more than four explicit, reviewable exceptions. get_events_in_range and propose_time_away_changes return only active events the user owns, while create_time_away_change_set_draft can only stage—not apply—cancellations and approved-delegate transfers. Read tools are annotated as read-only. Tool outputs carrying calendar content are marked untrusted and limited to 1.4 KB of UTF-8 data; the adapter returns compact events and candidate slots, or a safe truncation response. commit_event is intentionally blocked so an agent cannot bypass the human confirmation flow. Challenges we ran into The key challenge was making the agent useful without making it overly powerful. We separated recommendation, draft creation, and final commit; applied server-side ownership and revision checks; and designed bounded result shapes that still give an agent enough information to continue safely. Persisting the deterministic demo across Worker isolates also required an explicit D1 persistence boundary rather than relying on in-memory state. Accomplishments that we're proud of From a design standpoint, it took some time to really hone in on what would make this tool useful. At first it was basically a scheduling assistant that didn't do much more than what Outlook can do now. However, once I started experimenting with recurring meetings that need occasional alterations, I realized that there are scenarios I run into all the time in real life that MyCP would actually help with. What we learned I mostly got a much better understanding of what could be possible with WebMCP and I'm already thinking of other ways to implement it in my day job. What's next for My Calendar Planner One area where this tool could be incredibly useful is with room management as well as meeting management. Bringing in systems to manage space bookings and maintenance in a large organization, like a university, could really help alleviate pain-points for scheduling that involve lots of difference factors. From a technical standpoint, we could add real authentication, provider OAuth, per-user notification preferences, RSVP-aware recurrence exceptions, delegate acceptance, outbound notifications, and a normalized D1 schema. Those additions would preserve the same visible-draft and explicit-confirmation boundaries. title: Nearcast WebMCP
pitch: Nearcast is a WebMCP-powered cross-border hazard map that helps people and AI agents explore authoritative wildfire, severe weather, and earthquake data across Canada and the U.S.
about_excerpt: Nearcast is a WebMCP-powered cross-border hazard map that helps people and AI agents explore authoritative wildfire, severe weather, and earthquake data across Canada and the U.S. Like Comment Story Updates Map Overview Focusing on a specific region Human + Agent Shared State Cross-Border Hazard Comparison Inspiration Nearcast began as a Canadian iPhone app that pulls official hazard data. Hazard maps are exactly the kind of interface generic browser agents struggle with: hundreds of clustered markers, a dozen filter combinations, geographic bounds, a selection, and six agencies' worth of heterogeneous records. WebMCP lets the page say what it can do instead of making the agent infer it from the DOM. What it does Nearcast WebMCP shows current wildfires, weather alerts and earthquakes across Canada and the United States on one MapLibre map, normalized from six official sources (ECCC, NRCan CWFIS, Earthquakes Canada, NWS, NIFC, USGS) with explicit attribution and freshness. Every source fails independently; if a feed is down the app says so and keeps working. It exposes eight WebMCP tools that read and mutate the same application state the human is looking at: get_current_view — map bounds, zoom, filters, selected hazard, counts, source freshness get_visible_hazards — concise list of what is on screen after all filters set_focus_area — move the map to regions ( ["BC","WA"] ), bounds, or a point set_hazard_filters — countries, hazard types, minimum weather severity, minimum magnitude focus_hazard — select a hazard exactly like a human click (highlight, pan, details panel) get_hazard_details — full record with agency classifications and the official link compare_regions — deterministic counts for provinces/states create_situation_context — structured facts for an area; the agent writes the prose An Agent Activity panel logs every tool call, so people can see what the agent did. Why WebMCP fits this use case Map applications hold large amounts of visual state. Screen-scraping and clicking is brittle and slow. WebMCP gives the agent typed, described operations while keeping human and agent in the same visible workspace : the human zooms and clicks, the agent reads that through get_current_view , changes filters or focus, and the human sees it happen and refines by hand. Better UX Instead of manually toggling countries, filtering hazard types and scanning hundreds of markers, the user says "Focus on British Columbia and Washington and show only wildfires and important weather alerts" — and still sees and controls the resulting map. Verified live in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser with GPT-5.6. What humans and agents do together Human: explores visually, selects incidents, validates context, controls decisions. Agent: manipulates filters, compares regions, retrieves structured details, surfaces relevant information, writes the narrative. Application: authoritative normalized data, deterministic geographic calculations and counts, visual state — and never a "you are safe" claim. How we built it React + TypeScript + Vite + MapLibre GL (OpenFreeMap basemap, no tokens). One TypeScript Lambda behind API Gateway HTTP API with six source adapters ( Promise.allSettled , per-source timeouts, stale-snapshot fallback), a shared hazard model, and severity translation kept alongside raw agency classifications. CloudFront serves the SPA from a private S3 bucket (OAC) and routes /api/* to API Gateway so everything is same-origin; Terraform provisions all of it. Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() and wrap the app's own store actions — the same functions a click uses. No AI API keys anywhere: WebMCP is the AI integration. Challenges Government feeds are inconsistent: CWFIS's national fire layer is temporal (189k rows; only rows whose validity window includes "now" are current), most NWS alerts have no polygon (placed at Census county centroids and flagged approximate ), Earthquakes Canada is pipe-delimited text. Keeping severity honest: earthquakes and US wildfires have no agency severity, so we expose magnitude/hectares plus a clearly labelled display significance instead of inventing one. Demo robustness: per-source failure handling, stale snapshots, and a clearly labelled demo-data mode. Accomplishments Live cross-border six-source hazard workspace; eight well-described tools; shared state proven by get_current_view reflecting manual pans and clicks; 44 unit tests; reproducible Terraform deployment; verified end-to-end in ChatGPT's built-in browser. What we learned Tool descriptions and strict schemas matter more than tool count. Deterministic, structured outputs (counts, ids, source status) let the agent explain without hallucinating, and a visible activity log makes the collaboration legible to people. What's next Evacuation orders (BC first), air quality, time-windowed regional summaries, and Chrome origin-trial enrollment. Safety Nearcast is an awareness tool, not an emergency service. It always shows the issuing agency, timestamps and the official link, and reminds users to follow local emergency authorities. Built With amazon-api-gateway amazon-cloudfront amazon-web-services aws-lambda maplibre-gl node.js openstreetmap react terraform typescript vite vitest webmcp Try it out hazards.securitygeek.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo project. I designed the product and the human + agent experience, chose the government data sources (reusing what I learned building the Nearcast iPhone app), and built and deployed the full stack: React/MapLibre front end, TypeScript Lambda API, Terraform on AWS, and the eight WebMCP tools. I used Claude Code as a pair programmer throughout and tested the tools live in ChatGPT's desktop browser and Chrome. Biggest lesson: good tool descriptions and deterministic, structured outputs matter far more than tool count.
