title: Orgmemory
pitch: Company context and human control for engineering agents.
about_excerpt: Company context and human control for engineering agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI coding agents are becoming increasingly capable at understanding repositories and writing code, but production engineering depends on much more than code. The reason a service failed last time may be hidden in a postmortem. A critical constraint may live in Slack. Ownership information may be stored in a document, while the relevant architectural decision exists in another system. When an engineer or AI agent begins a change without this organizational context, it can repeat mistakes the company has already learned from. That inspired OrgMemory . I wanted to build a memory and governance layer that could answer a simple question before an agent acts: What does this company already know about the change I am about to make? OrgMemory began as a source-backed organizational memory system. For the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, I extended it into a browser-native context and governance layer that agents can access through the authenticated web application. The goal was not to give agents unlimited autonomy. The goal was to give them better context, make their actions observable, and keep consequential decisions under human control. How I Built It OrgMemory brings together incidents, decisions, dependencies, owners, runbooks, repositories, conversations, and documents. It converts this information into permission-scoped, time-aware company memory where every promoted fact remains connected to its original evidence. The application uses: Next.js 15 and React 19 for the workspace, WebMCP interface, approvals, and live agent activity. FastAPI and Python 3.13 for ingestion, retrieval, authorization, organizational operations, and the agent loop. SQLite and ArcadeDB for application state and organizational relationships. WebMCP for browser-native tool registration and execution. NDJSON streaming for live model steps, tool calls, arguments, and results. HttpOnly session cookies so browser agents never receive separate credentials. A separate MCP server, Python SDK, CLI, and REST API for agents operating outside the browser. I used document.modelContext.registerTool() to expose OrgMemory as a browser-native tool provider. WebMCP calls reuse the page's authenticated session, so the browser agent operates with the same permissions as the signed-in user. The authenticated workspace exposes 37 tools : 27 read-only tools 1 append-only outcome ledger tool 9 human-governed operations The focused Agent Operations page registers a 16-tool subset : 13 read-only operations 3 approval-gated operations The interface and WebMCP tools share the same backend handlers. This prevents the agent from receiving a separate privileged execution path. The demo follows a complete engineering workflow. The agent searches organizational memory, evaluates launch readiness, discovers a contradictory approval record, and proposes a correction. The proposal changes nothing until a person approves it. Once approved, the agent sends the plan to a coding IDE through MCP for implementation. It then checks launch readiness again and records the outcome. I also built a live activity view that shows the tools selected by the model, their arguments, results, durations, and citations. This makes it clear that the agent is calling real tools instead of replaying a scripted response. Challenges I Faced Separating capability from authorization WebMCP makes it possible to expose powerful operations to an agent, but access to a tool should not automatically authorize every use of that tool. I designed the write operations so agents can investigate and propose changes, while only a person can approve or decline them. There is intentionally no WebMCP tool that allows an agent to approve its own proposal. Designing an honest permission model The outcome ledger created an unusual case. Recording an outcome writes data, so it is not read-only. However, it does not modify company knowledge, so requiring human approval would make the feedback loop unnecessarily slow. I introduced a separate append-only permission tier for this operation. This allows the agent to report what happened without giving it the ability to change what the organization believes. Preserving history while identifying current truth Organizational knowledge changes over time. A task may still be marked open even though a newer decision says it was completed. Simply overwriting the old record would destroy useful history. OrgMemory preserves both records, connects them through relationships such as UPDATES , CONTRADICTS , and SUPPORTS , and creates a reviewable proposal for resolving the conflict. Maintaining security through the browser The browser agent needed access to organizational context without receiving reusable API keys or source credentials. WebMCP calls use the authenticated page session, while authorization is still enforced by the backend against the user's workspace, team, and project access. Making the system observable A judge or operator should be able to verify that the agent is calling real tools instead of replaying a scripted result. I built a live activity surface that displays tool calls, arguments, results, durations, citations, and approval requirements. The person can see exactly what the agent read, what it proposed, and where automation stopped. Explaining a large system in a short demo OrgMemory includes ingestion, retrieval, memory graphs, governance, multiple agent surfaces, SDKs, and an outcome loop. The challenge was reducing that scope to one clear story. I focused the demo on a single transformation: the agent begins with incomplete organizational context, finds a blocker, proposes a resolution, stops for human approval, and verifies the result after implementation. What I Learned I learned that browser-native tools are most useful when they reuse the identity, permissions, and state already present in the application. I also learned that tool annotations are helpful for communicating intent, but they are not a substitute for server-side authorization. Every permission boundary still needs to be enforced by the backend. Agents need more than semantic search. Before changing a system, they need an intent-specific briefing that includes constraints, previous incidents, dependencies, ownership, and potential blast radius. Human approval is most effective when it is visible. The agent response, approval interface, audit trail, and resulting state should all show exactly where automation stopped and where a person made the decision. Most importantly, I learned that organizational memory becomes more valuable when it records outcomes. The lasting advantage is not only knowing what the company learned, but also knowing which context led to successful action. title: PodHood — WebMCP for Podcasts & YouTube
pitch: Turn any podcast or YouTube library into a surface your agent can drive: 8 WebMCP tools that search, filter, read timestamped transcripts, and cue the player on the page you're both looking at.
about_excerpt: Turn any podcast or YouTube library into a surface your agent can drive: 8 WebMCP tools that search, filter, read timestamped transcripts, and cue the player on the page you're both looking at. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into* Live demo → https://aiengineer.podhood.com * — a real production library of 1,065 talks. Open it in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and just start asking. Inspiration Podcasts and conference talks hold an enormous share of what a field actually knows, and almost none of it is reachable. Search gives you an episode, not a moment. A transcript is a 20,000-word wall. "Where did she explain the eval harness?" is a question no podcast page can answer today. Agents don't fix this — they inherit it. An agent that lands on a podcast page can do one of two unpleasant things: swallow the entire transcript and burn its context on filler, or drive the UI by guessing at pixels. Either way it works around the page instead of with it. WebMCP changes where the agent is standing. It is already here, in the browser, next to the person, looking at the same screen. That turns out to change what a tool is even allowed to be. What it does PodHood turns any podcast or YouTube channel into a structured library — summaries, chapters, key moments, speaker-diarized and word-aligned transcripts, recognized people, companies and products — and then registers that structure as eight WebMCP tools via document.modelContext , across two surfaces. On the library page search_episodes — search the catalog by meaning or keyword; returns episodes with timestamped citation links filter_episodes — apply topic / person / company / product / collection / year filters; the visible list and the URL change list_episodes — read back exactly what the visitor is looking at right now, with IDs open_episode — navigate the visitor to an episode page On an episode page read_episode — summary, speakers, and the chapter + key-moment outline with timestamps search_transcript — find exact text and highlight it in the transcript panel read_transcript — speaker-labeled, timestamped transcript windows, by chapter or time range play_moment — seek the player to a moment and start playback play_moment is the whole thesis in one call. The agent is not handing you a link to go read later. It moves the playhead in the player in front of you, and you hear the thing. That is only possible because the agent shares the view with a human — which is exactly the shape WebMCP has and no other agent interface does. What a human and an agent do together here On https://aiengineer.podhood.com — 1,065 talks from the AI Engineer conference series, 86 collections, 1,033 speakers, 880 companies — the loop looks like this: "What's actually being said about evals at these conferences?" → the agent runs search_episodes , then filter_episodes on the Evaluation & Observability topic. Your screen changes. You are now looking at 83 talks, and so is it. "Only 2026, and only speakers from model labs." → filter_episodes narrows again. You watch it happen, and you can undo it by clicking, because they are the same filters you would have clicked. "Open the second one and find where he explains the harness." → open_episode , then search_transcript . The line lights up in the transcript panel. "Play it." → play_moment . The player seeks and starts. You ask a follow-up while it plays; the agent has read_transcript scoped to that chapter and answers with a citation that points at your domain, at the right second. No copy-paste, no tab-switching, no "here's a link, go find it yourself." The agent does the navigating; the human does the listening and the deciding. Why WebMCP is the right primitive for this We already run a hosted MCP server for podcast catalogs, so we can compare the two honestly. An external MCP connector is a good way for an agent somewhere else to query a catalog. It cannot touch the page a person is looking at. It has no playhead, no transcript panel, no filter rail. WebMCP inverts that assumption, and the tools change shape as a result. filter_episodes is not a query — it is a UI mutation the person watches happen. search_transcript is not a string match — it is a highlight. This is the only agent interface where "tell me" and "show me" are the same call. Three properties we deliberately locked in: Read and view-state only. No writes, no accounts, no purchases. An agent can only change what the visitor could already change themselves — filters, highlight, playhead — all visible on screen and reversible with a click. There is no state an agent can reach that a human cannot see it reach. Show-branded, not platform-branded. The tools present as belonging to the creator's show, on the creator's domain — not to PodHood. Domain-native citations. Every link an agent produces resolves to the creator's own domain with a timestamp. Agent traffic lands on the creator, which is the only version of this that is sustainable for the people making the content. Why this needs more than a transcript Every tool here is downstream of structure that has to exist before the tool can be honest: search_episodes needs a semantic index over the catalog, not ctrl+F. filter_episodes needs entities disambiguated — "Claude" the model versus a person named Claude, three different speakers named Chen. play_moment needs word-level audio alignment . A timestamp four seconds off makes the entire feature feel broken. read_episode needs chapters and key moments that were actually extracted, not guessed at read time. This is the part of WebMCP we think is under-appreciated: good tools are a consequence of good data modeling. You can bolt document.modelContext onto anything. You can only make it useful on top of a page that already knows what it contains. How we built it The tool layer registers on document.modelContext when each surface mounts, with JSON-schema'd inputs and compact, agent-shaped return payloads — never raw DOM, never a whole transcript. Tools are bound to the same client state store the UI reads from , so an agent's filter_episodes and a human's click on the filter rail go down one code path. There is no drift between what the agent believes is on screen and what is on screen — and list_episodes exists precisely so the agent can re-ground itself against the real view at any point. read_transcript is windowed by chapter or time range, because handing a model ninety minutes of speech is how you get a confident wrong answer. Tool names and descriptions were tuned hard. A model will reach for search_episodes when it wants search_transcript unless the boundary is stated explicitly in the description. Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. Our origins are registered for the Chrome WebMCP origin trial, so document.modelContext is available with no flags — including on creators' custom domains. Zero creator configuration. The tools ship automatically with every published PodHood library. Nothing to enable, nothing to write. Agents without WebMCP support see a completely normal page; nothing degrades. Challenges we ran into Sizing outputs. The first read_transcript returned everything and the agent drowned. Chapter-scoped windows plus a "next window" affordance fixed it. One state, two drivers. Making agent-driven and human-driven state genuinely the same object took a refactor. Anything less produced ghost states, where the agent was filtering a list the human was not seeing. Restraint. The tempting move is to expose thirty tools. Eight sharply-described verbs outperformed a larger surface every time we tested. Testing against a moving target. WebMCP is an origin trial. ChatGPT desktop plus Chrome flags plus a live registered origin is not a fast dev loop. What we learned The best WebMCP tools are not an API bolted onto a page — they are the page's own verbs, named. Everything that worked here was already something the site could do: filter, highlight, seek. WebMCP just let an agent do it on the human's behalf, in front of them. The tools that tried to be more than the page could do were exactly the ones models misused. What's next Cross-library tools, so an agent can work across a creator's entire network of shows at once. A compare_moments tool for putting two speakers' claims side by side with both timestamps. Publishing the WebMCP tool layer as a standalone open-source package, so any media site can adopt the same eight verbs. Prior work vs. work done during the submission period PodHood is an existing product. The ingestion pipeline, the Brief data model (chapters, key moments, diarization, entity recognition, word-aligned transcripts), the search index and the player all predate this hackathon. Everything in the WebMCP layer is new work built during the submission period (August 25 – September 3, 2026): all eight tool definitions and their schemas, the document.modelContext registration for both surf

title: Sky to Porch
pitch: Turn official environmental observations into shared, inspectable evidence for people and AI agents.
about_excerpt: Turn official environmental observations into shared, inspectable evidence for people and AI agents. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Ambiguous place? The Agent asks, the page shows the same choices, and the map waits for the person to decide. Official NYC air-quality evidence becomes a plain-English answer with sources and limitations beside the map. The Missions view traces Las Vegas drought evidence to the NASA and U.S. Drought Monitor products behind it. The Houston Beryl result shows validated NOAA wind observations, storm context, citations, and property-level limitations. The About view explains Sky to Porch’s evidence model, coverage, safety boundaries, and independent attribution. The catalog shows which NASA, NOAA, and regional satellite products are live, candidate, or require credentials. Inspiration After a wildfire or a storm, people ask whether smoke was recorded near their family that day. The records exist, but the hard part is tying a place and a date to what was actually observed. What it does Sky to Porch is a map-based evidence workspace where a person and an AI Agent investigate the same question on the same screen. The person gives a place, a completed date or range, a hazard, a radius, and a concern. The strongest supported assessment comes first, then the observations with times, official citations, confidence, limitations, and source status. Seven hazard families are covered, and a broad question runs related ones together. Fire & Smoke brings Air Quality. Extreme Heat brings Drought & Land. Earth & Volcanoes brings Air Quality and Extreme Heat. A plain storm question runs Wind & Storm and Flood & Heavy Rain. Naming one hazard keeps it focused. Chains never merge. Rainfall is not proof of wind damage, and a regional observation is not a verdict on one house or one person. Why WebMCP fits Sky to Porch WebMCP lets the person skip that setup and ask the question they actually have. "What environmental evidence was recorded near Los Angeles during the wildfire?" The Agent picks the tools, runs the Fire & Smoke and Air Quality chains, and summarizes in plain English what they support. Real questions also need cross-checking. A storm question means wind readings, rain totals, flood extent, and gauge levels from different agencies, on the same day, for the same area. A person doing that by hand runs each path and compares the results one at a time. An Agent is good at exactly this. It runs every relevant chain, reads all of them, and tells the person where the sources agree, where they differ, and what is still missing. This is collaboration, not hand-off. Human queries and Agent calls use one analysis service and update the same map, Meaning panel, and Evidence panel. The person can take over at any point, change the radius or the date, pick a different hazard, or click into a source. The person can also keep asking. "Which source failed?" or "Show me the exact gust reading" gets answered from the result already on screen, without rerunning anything. Every chain keeps its own button, so the Agent cannot hide a result, and the final judgment stays with the person. How I built it The stack is Next.js, React, TypeScript, and MapLibre GL. Adapters for NASA, NOAA, USGS, and EPA sources feed one deterministic analysis service that owns validation, retrieval, calculations, freshness, provenance, confidence, limitations, and safe display. The model chooses tools and explains validated results. It cannot invent an observation. The page registers eight WebMCP tools, covering hazard analysis, two-scenario comparison, active-result inspection without a rerun, source coverage, help and demos, a storm claim checklist, place lookup, and map layers. The Agent comes from a WebMCP-compatible browser. The site holds no model API key. Challenges I ran into Ambiguity. "Houston" matches several places, so the place tool lists up to five candidates with stable IDs and waits. The pick resumes the run with the original date, hazard, radius, and concern intact. Size. A result gets about 2,400 characters, so compaction drops optional detail first and keeps the strongest observations, provenance, limitations, and links to the visible result. Real Agent behavior. A valid schema does not mean the Agent picks the right tool or runs every chain, so I added live-source checks and model-scored evaluations of tool selection, ambiguity recovery, comparisons, and summaries. Accomplishments that I'm proud of User-specified locations, dates, and radii stay authoritative. Every result separates a valid observation from no observation returned, source failure, unsupported coverage, stale data, and inconclusive evidence. The Agent can answer a follow-up from the active result without rerunning it. The same experience works on desktop and mobile. The current build passes typecheck, lint, 1,617 unit tests, 133 integration tests, a 14-page production build, and the full desktop and mobile Playwright suite. What I learned Exposing tools is the easy part. The collaboration has to be visible on the screen. "No observation returned" is not the same as "no hazard," and a source failure must never disappear inside a confident summary. What's next I want more official-source coverage, portable evidence summaries, and contextual follow-up tools across the whole hazard catalog. Prior work and Challenge contribution Sky to Porch existed before the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge. The map, the human query interface, the source adapters, and the evidence contracts are prior work. Everything Agent-facing above is the Challenge contribution, along with more evidence for all hazards and the WebMCP testing. I built it solo with AI coding assistance. PRIOR_WORK.md in the repo documents the boundary. title: ToolForge
pitch: A human-in-the-loop WebMCP readiness inspector that turns existing website interactions into reviewable, testable agent tools.
about_excerpt: A human-in-the-loop WebMCP readiness inspector that turns existing website interactions into reviewable, testable agent tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a structured language for working with agents, replacing fragile visual guesswork with explicit tools. But the adoption challenge extends far beyond any single website or industry: every developer must still inspect their interface, identify meaningful actions, define schemas, make authorization decisions, and connect custom controls to real application behavior. ToolForge addresses that broader infrastructure gap. Rather than building another WebMCP-enabled storefront, we created a reusable, cross-functional developer tool that can audit many kinds of websites ranging from ecommerce and marketplaces to games, productivity tools and financial applications. It recognizes semantic forms, custom actions, composite workflows and uncertain elements, then converts them into evidence-backed candidates for developer review. ToolForge does not blindly expose everything clickable or pretend that business intent can be inferred from the DOM. It accelerates the repeatable parts of WebMCP adoption while preserving human control over meaning, safety and execution. The storefront is simply our end-to-end proof; the product itself is a general bridge between today’s websites and an agent-ready open web. What it does ToolForge is an injectable, development-mode readiness inspector for existing websites. It scans the live DOM including open Shadow DOM roots and accessible same-origin frames and organizes interactions into five groups: Declarative-ready native forms Form-like interactions Composite workflows High-confidence imperative actions Ignored or low-confidence elements For native forms, ToolForge drafts toolname , tooldescription , and toolparamdescription attributes from the page's existing labels and structure. The developer reviews every value, decides whether to enable toolautosubmit , applies the attributes to the live DOM for immediate testing, and can copy a minimal stable-ID attribute diff back to source. For custom JavaScript controls, ToolForge drafts metadata and a JSON schema but refuses to present the tool as complete until the developer provides a real function reference or execute body. Related controls such as separate price chips, region controls, and an “All filters” button can be grouped into one composite workflow instead of becoming dozens of tiny tools. Low-confidence elements are not silently discarded. Developers can search the ignored queue, inspect structural evidence, highlight the real page element, keep it ignored, promote it for review, or re-evaluate it after the page changes. Manual decisions persist across rescans for the current session. The repository includes a complete storefront that proves the result end to end. It exposes: search_products through the imperative WebMCP API add_to_cart through a declarative form with developer-approved autosubmit checkout through a declarative form without autosubmit, preserving human confirmation How we built it ToolForge is a static, dependency-free application built with semantic HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. It has no backend, framework, build step, runtime model call, or page-data upload. The finished storefront and the unannotated demo target share the same product rendering, cart state, and human interface logic. This creates an honest before-and-after comparison: demo-target.html contains no WebMCP surface, while index.html contains the reviewed declarative attributes and loads the imperative implementation from webmcp.js . The declarative tools reuse the forms' existing submit handlers. The imperative search_products tool uses document.modelContext.registerTool() and calls the same search function as the human interface. ToolForge's panel is isolated in Shadow DOM, observes dynamic page changes with a MutationObserver , records evidence for each classification, and gates every imperative export on a real developer-supplied handler. Automated Chrome DevTools Protocol tests cover tool discovery, execution policy, native forms, form-like controls, composite workflows, ignored-element review, dynamic content, open Shadow DOM, same-origin frames, duplicate collapsing, stable rescans, and the imperative export gate. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was staying honest about what the DOM can and cannot reveal. HTML can provide parameter structure, but it cannot reliably reveal private JavaScript behavior, business meaning, or authorization policy. ToolForge therefore does not invent handlers or automatically decide which actions are safe. Modern commerce pages presented another challenge because filters are often implemented as many independent buttons rather than native forms. Treating every chip as its own tool created noisy and misleading results. We added structural composite-workflow detection so related price and region controls become a single filter_listings candidate while product-card actions remain separate. We also had to balance filtering with developer control. A large ignored count was technically accurate but difficult to audit, so the ignored set became a searchable review queue with evidence, highlighting, promotion, persistent decisions, and re-evaluation. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working, polished storefront with three real WebMCP tools across both declarative and imperative APIs A clear safety demonstration: reversible add-to-cart can autosubmit, while checkout requires human confirmation A deterministic readiness inspector that works without AI inference or a backend Five evidence-backed readiness categories instead of an inflated list of clickable elements Composite workflow detection that groups related filters into a usable schema A fully reviewable ignored queue instead of silently discarding uncertain controls Automated browser regression coverage for the scanner and WebMCP execution policy Mobile Lighthouse scores of 100 for Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, and SEO What we learned Semantic HTML is already a strong bridge to agent-ready interfaces: a real form provides useful parameter structure and an existing execution path. The harder problems are meaning, authorization, and developer intent. Those cannot be responsibly inferred from labels alone. We also learned that WebMCP adoption tools should optimize for inspectability rather than maximum candidate counts. A smaller set of coherent, evidence-backed workflows is more useful than dozens of technically clickable but context-free actions. What's next for ToolForge Next steps include packaging the inspector as a browser extension, adding source-aware adapters that can produce framework-specific patches, supporting richer developer-defined workflow grouping. title: TrialBridge
pitch: A WebMCP powered ChatGPT and Chrome enabled agent that matches cancer patients to clinical trials in minutes - no filling forms, no endless clicks and no gatekeeping - for early therapy access.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP powered ChatGPT and Chrome enabled agent that matches cancer patients to clinical trials in minutes - no filling forms, no endless clicks and no gatekeeping - for early therapy access. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I (Vilay) started my career as a Clinical Research Coordinator at Stanford Cancer Center. Still the most formative experience working with patients at the end of their lives. I have since built award winning Palliative programs, but keep coming back to the same problem - how do we meet needs of patients who have exhausted all available FDA approved therapies. At that point, what most patients want is not survival for its sake, but to make it to an important life event - son's graduation, daughter's quincenera, or an anniversary. For these patients, clinical trials can be the only pathway that might increase their lifespan through a therapy that won't be on the market for years. Yet, the access is gatekept - geographically limited around academic medical centers who run the trials, or knowledge and bandwidth of community oncologists - all buried in CT.gov, a clunky government database that is difficult to navigate. Meanwhile clinical trials regularly shut down due to low enrollment. Patients who could have qualified never find a trial, and trials that can help many never fill and reach their endpoints. We built TrialBridge to close the gap on both directions. This is also the first project built together by us three brothers working across three different time zones and bringing experience from three very different fields: I, Vilay , am a healthcare executive with background in population health, high risk patient management and healthcare strategy and operations. He lived and breathed clinical trials for good portion of his career and brought the vision. Shobhit , based in India, conceived and created the application, designed the patient-facing workflow and built the WebMCP tools that connect an AI agent with TrialBridge. Harshit , based in New York and the most deeply technical member of the team, helped shape the application’s technical architecture, implementation and engineering reliability. TrialBridge emerged from the intersection of healthcare, technology and patient advocacy—and from three brothers wanting to build something useful together. What it does TrialBridge helps patients and caregivers discover clinical trials that may be worth discussing with their doctors. A patient can describe their situation to an AI agent in ordinary language—for example: “I have stage IV neuroendocrine cancer. I’m 58, live in Chicago, can travel 150 miles, and previously received Afinitor.” Through WebMCP, the agent can then interact with TrialBridge using structured tools registered directly by the webpage. The patient does not need to manually complete every field or navigate multiple filtering menus. However, the profile remains visible and editable, allowing the patient to inspect and correct what the agent entered. TrialBridge can: Convert a patient’s plain-language description into a structured search profile; Resolve supported medication brand names to their generic equivalents, such as Afinitor to everolimus; Search currently recruiting studies using the live ClinicalTrials.gov API; Distinguish the number of registry records checked from the number of trials eventually shown; Explain which records were filtered out and why; Show whether the search reached the end of the available registry results or stopped at an application limit; Compare age, location and supported prior-treatment information against published study details; Display what appears consistent, what appears inconsistent and what remains unknown; Allow the agent to shortlist potentially relevant studies with factual reasons; Open a full side-by-side comparison of shortlisted trials; and Support preliminary pre-screening against published inclusion and exclusion criteria. Importantly, TrialBridge preserves uncertainty. If a patient does not know their ECOG performance status or cannot answer another medical question, the application records that information as unresolved . It does not silently convert an unknown answer into a pass or a failure. TrialBridge does not determine eligibility, diagnose a condition, recommend treatment or provide medical advice. Only a clinical-trial study team can determine eligibility after medical screening. How we built it We began by developing the domain layer required to understand cancer terminology, treatment names and clinical-trial records. This included a curated cancer and treatment catalogue built from publicly available clinical sources and open clinical terminology, supported medication mappings, and brand-to-generic drug-name resolution. ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 provides the live public trial data used by the search. We then built TrialBridge using: Next.js React TypeScript ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 WebMCP Declared tool schemas and application-level input validation Browser-stored patient profile and pre-screening state Replit deployment The webpage registers ten structured tools using the current WebMCP imperative API: document.modelContext.registerTool() Each tool has: A defined name and description; A declared input schema; Structured parameters; Application-level validation before state changes are applied; A specific application action; and A visible result in the same interface used by a human. This means an AI agent does not have to scrape the page, interpret screenshots or guess which element to click. Instead, the webpage acts as an in-page tool server, allowing the agent to invoke capabilities that the application has explicitly exposed. Different tools handle different parts of the workflow, including: Reading and updating the patient profile; Searching conditions and trials; Retrieving trial details; Managing the shortlist; Opening comparisons; Starting pre-screening; and Recording preliminary criterion responses. Search and trial-data operations use the live ClinicalTrials.gov API. Patient profile, shortlist and pre-screening information are maintained within the browser so the patient can see and control the state being used. The agent and the patient share the same screen: when the agent changes something, the patient can see it immediately. Challenges we ran into Working with an emerging browser proposal WebMCP is still an emerging proposal, and its API, browser support and testing workflows continue to evolve. We had to ensure that TrialBridge could register its tools using the current API, expose understandable schemas and produce visible changes that both the agent and the user could verify. ClinicalTrials.gov API and browser restrictions Direct browser requests introduced CORS and preflight limitations. We addressed this through a server-side proxy while preserving live ClinicalTrials.gov data and transparent source attribution. Separating records checked from trials shown Registry metadata can be misleading if the application presents only the final number of displayed trials. We implemented explicit accounting for: Records returned and checked; Trials shown; Trials filtered out; Reasons for filtering; Pages retrieved; and Whether pagination reached the end. Translating complex eligibility language Clinical-trial inclusion and exclusion criteria are often long, inconsistent and written differently across studies. We needed to present them without pretending that TrialBridge could replace clinical judgment. Our solution was to treat the comparison as preliminary and preserve three distinct outcomes: Appears consistent; Apparent mismatch; and Still unknown. Preventing AI-generated certainty One of our most important challenges was ensuring that an agent could not guess an answer when medical information was unavailable. Unknown information remains unresolved, and malformed or unsupported responses are rejected rather than being forced into a pass-or-fail result. Protecting patient privacy We designed the demonstration so that it does not require a patient’s name, email address or date of birth. Search details and pre-screening responses remain visible and controllable in the browser. Accomplishments that we’re proud of Building our first project together as three brothers across three time zones and three industries: healthcare, technology and law; Creating a working clinical-trial discovery engine—not merely a static prototype; Compressing a process that can require hours of manual searching into a structured conversational workflow; Successfully connecting the application to an AI agent through ten WebMCP tools; Allowing the agent to operate the same visible interface that a patient can inspect and correct; Searching live, currently recruiting studies from ClinicalTrials.gov; Distinguishing records checked from trials shown and explaining why records were filtered; Supporting brand-to-generic medication resolution; Building a real preliminary comparison workflow for publis

title: webmcp.utlovat.se — Non-Partisan Election Fact-Checking
pitch: An agent-native election evidence layer where WebMCP exposes published sources, visible gaps, and human-in-the-loop verification directly in the browser. Just in time for the Swedish election 2026.
about_excerpt: An agent-native election evidence layer where WebMCP exposes published sources, visible gaps, and human-in-the-loop verification directly in the browser. Just in time for the Swedish election 2026. Like Comment Story Updates Utlovat.se WebMCP landing page explaining that agents can sort Swedish election evidence but cannot recommend a political party. tlovat.se research brief for healthcare, showing a recorded unclear position for Moderates, 12 evidence records for Social Democrats, Evidence cards in an Utlovat.se research brief, each with a Swedish quote, publication date, four-year cost range, source link, archive copy Inspiration During democratic elections, voters are inundated with conflicting claims, manifesto promises, and shifting party positions. When citizens in general, and first time voters in particular, turn to AI assistants for guidance, your average, I have and answer for everything, general-purpose LLMs present a dangerous hazard: they risk hallucinating plausible quotes, confusing past election cycles with current platforms, and inventing policy stances where parties are actually silent . In high-stakes civic decision-making, an AI summary is not enough. Citizens need evidence, not a verdict. And to be encouraged to question the feasibility of the "five minutes to Election Day" promises. utlovat.se (meaning "As Promised" in Swedish) is aims to be an independent, non-partisan election platform tracking over 2,000 promises and 700+ reviewed parliamentary actions for the 2026 general election. We (actually there is only me and my assisting agents) were inspired to build on OpenAI's WebMCP because it offers the missing piece of the agentic web: a standardized, browser-native protocol that allows a website to expose its immutable, verified evidence directly to AI agents . A perfect fit with how youths of today consume information. What It Does With WebMCP utlovat.se transforms from a static website into an active, agent-native truth layer. Through WebMCP, an AI assistant using a WebMCP-enabled browser gains access to 7 specialized tools in total (5 global + 2 contextual): Grounded Deterministic Search (search_verified_evidence): Queries exact manifesto commitments, returning verified quotes, publication dates, transparent cost approximations (≈), and linked Wayback Machine archive copies when available (we have set a 100% archive target and are very close to achieving it). Interactive Evidence Boards (build_research_brief): Generates side-by-side comparative cards on /granska and /webmcp without recommending any party. (Absolute neutrality in all aspects are paramount) Human-in-the-Loop Protocol Verification (get_evidence_board_status): Ensures that evidence remains strictly unverified until a human visually inspects the primary citations and marks the board as confirmed. Parliamentary Trail Tracing (trace_promise): Connects a 2026 election promise to Handlingsvågen's (our Swedish feature name) database of reviewed Swedish Parliament (Riksdagen) voting records and motion histories. Multi-Party Fiscal Matrix (show_party_comparison): Opens the interactive comparison matrix on /jamfor, accounting for joint coalition proposals without double-counting costs. Contextual On-Page Tools (trace_current_promise, build_current_question_brief): Dynamically activates contextual tools when browsing individual promise pages or topic questions. Honest Silence & Gap Transparency: Explicitly reports when a party has no recorded stance on a query, rather than treating a bounded empty result as proof of a position. How We Built It We built the WebMCP integration natively into utlovat.se using TypeScript, Astro, and Tailwind CSS: WebMCP Client-Side Tool Registry (site/src/scripts/webmcp.ts): We registered our 7 tools directly onto document.modelContext.registerTool, defining JSON schemas with strict parameter typing and non-partisan output structures. Cryptographic Data Hashing: Every tool response includes an authoritative data_hash (SHA-256), anchoring conclusions to a fixed, verifiable dataset snapshot. Web Archive Links: When available, a political quote includes a linked Wayback Machine archive copy, making the source trail inspectable and more resilient to link rot. (And also makes it possible to highlight a change in stance in any question). Parliamentary Open Data Bridge: We engineered client-side JSON API endpoints (/api/v1/promise-traces.json) linking election promises to Swedish Parliament document IDs (e.g. data.riksdagen.se/dokument/HB023145) and chamber voting roll calls. Dedicated English Surface (/webmcp): Built a dedicated English hub with the 5 global WebMCP tools, clear testing prompts and cost-range badges. The 2 contextual tools become available after navigation to an individual promise or topic page. Challenges We Faced Enforcing Strict Epistemic Neutrality: The primary challenge in election technology is preventing algorithmic bias. We designed tool descriptions and read-only output structures that explicitly instruct agents not to declare "kept/broken" verdicts, rank parties, or make subjective recommendations. Honest Silence Reporting: In standard RAG pipelines, an empty search return is ambiguous. We had to architect bounded search semantics so that if a party has no promise on a topic, the agent explicitly returns a structured gap report rather than extrapolating. Sometimes silence speaks a thousand words. Zero-Self-Certification for Human-in-the-Loop: We had to ensure agents could not fake human verification. The get_evidence_board_status tool queries the live DOM state, which only transitions to confirmed ✓ when the physical user clicks the inspection button. Anti-Double-Counting in Coalition Manifestos: Calculating joint party proposals required shared commitment keying so coalition proposals are not counted twice in fiscal matrix calculations. New Additions Developed Exclusively During the Hackathon (from August 25, 2026): 1. Prior Work (Before August 25, 2026): The core Swedish public-information website, Utlovat.se. Its foundational dataset of Swedish election commitments and public evidence, including data/promises.json and Handlingsvågen. Existing non-partisan calculations and Swedish public-facing comparison templates. 2. New Additions Developed During the Hackathon (August 25 – September 3, 2026): Browser-native WebMCP integration ( site/src/scripts/webmcp.ts ): Seven read-only client-side tools—five global tools and two page-contextual tools—registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . English Challenge Surface ( site/src/pages/webmcp.astro ): An English entry point, “Evidence, not a verdict,” with a testing guide and direct display of cost ranges marked with ≈ , their basis, and the four-year assumption where applicable. Visible Research Brief and Evidence Board ( /granska , site/src/pages/granska.astro ): A shared human–agent research surface that renders published quotes, dates, source links, archive copies where available, recorded unclear positions, and bounded gaps. It creates deep-linkable research briefs without recommending a party. Human review boundary ( get_evidence_board_status ): The agent can read whether the person has marked the visible evidence board as reviewed, but cannot mark it reviewed itself. Unread material remains explicitly unverified. Parliamentary action tracing ( /api/v1/promise-traces.json ): A read-only evidence chain from a published campaign promise to its source, archive copy, and recorded, human-reviewed parliamentary actions where available. The tool does not decide whether a promise was kept or broken. Automated WebMCP verification ( site/scripts/test-webmcp.mts , site/scripts/test-webmcp-retest.mts ): Tests of the published browser client, tool registration, evidence fields, archive filtering, visible uncertainty, neutral boundaries, English topic matching, shared links, and contextual tools. Open-source licensing : Apache-2.0 was added to the root repository during the hackathon. Frozen competition release : A separate public repository, bambapappa/utlovat-webmcp-challenge , preserves the final static competition build independently of the continuing election-information service. Its manifest records the selected source commit, data hash, and output hashes before the competition cutoff. Transparent implementation history : The public Git history records the WebMCP implementation commits from August 26 onward, while the separate snapshot repository records the freeze and release procedure. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Hackathon premiere: This marks the moment of my first ever participation in a Hackathon. Evidence-Bounded Civic Fact-Checking: WebMCP keeps tool outputs tied to published quotes, source URLs, archive copies when available, and a verifiable data hash. Complete 4-Step Parliamentary Accountability Chain: Users and agents can trace a promise from a party manifesto directly to permanent web archives and the official Riksdag voting prot

title: Aegis Operations
pitch: Aegis Operations is a human + AI security investigation workspace where browser agents use WebMCP to investigate real telemetry, build evidence, and help analysts decide.
about_excerpt: Aegis Operations is a human + AI security investigation workspace where browser agents use WebMCP to investigate real telemetry, build evidence, and help analysts decide. Like Comment Story Updates Human and agent collaborate to determine the answer. Investigate with an evidence-first workflow Prioritize correlated alerts Inspect and control detection content Inspiration Aegis Operations came from a question I kept running into while building security and AI-agent projects: What does useful human + AI collaboration actually look like inside a real security workflow? A lot of AI products still treat the model as a chatbot sitting beside the application. The human works in the actual product, while the AI works inside a conversation. Context gets copied back and forth, important state disappears into chat history, and the agent often receives far more information than it actually needs. That never felt like the right architecture to me. Over time, while experimenting with security agents, MCP tools, threat-intelligence workflows, and investigation systems, I became increasingly interested in a simpler principle: Deterministic systems should establish facts. AI should reason over those facts. Security makes this especially important. If an AI claims that an event exists, that a process executed, or that a user performed some action, I want that statement to resolve back to actual evidence. When I started exploring WebMCP, the interesting part was not simply that a webpage could expose tools to an agent. The interesting part was that the human and the browser agent could operate on the same application state . That became the foundation of Aegis Operations: Detection raises the question. Human and agent collaborate to determine the answer. Instead of building another AI security chatbot, I wanted to build an investigation workspace where both sides work with the same telemetry, evidence, hypotheses, and timeline. What it does Aegis Operations is a human + AI security investigation workspace built around evidence-grounded collaboration. The Complete Workflow: Security telemetry Ingestion and normalization Deterministic Sigma detection Correlated alerts Investigation Human + browser agent collaboration Evidence and hypotheses Human verdict The current demo processes 11,435 Sysmon events from three attributed Splunk Attack Data attack-range scenarios. Thirty official SigmaHQ rules are compiled and executed through pySigma. They produce 276 rule-event signals across 133 distinct events, which are deterministically correlated into 22 analyst-facing alerts. An analyst can: Inspect raw and normalized telemetry Search and filter security events Review Sigma detections Start investigations Pin events as evidence Create and revise hypotheses Review investigation history Decide whether activity is benign, suspicious, an incident, or inconclusive A compatible browser agent can participate in the same investigation through eight WebMCP tools. The agent can search telemetry, retrieve nearby event context, aggregate entity activity, add verified evidence, and create or update evidence-linked hypotheses. The agent does not have access to a verdict tool. It can investigate and recommend, but the final decision remains with the human analyst. How I built it Aegis Operations is intentionally built as a small modular monolith rather than a collection of unnecessary services. The Tech Stack: Frontend: React + TypeScript Backend API: FastAPI Persistence: SQLAlchemy Database: SQLite (for demonstration-scale operations) Rule Execution: pySigma (for deterministic Sigma rules) Agent Capabilities: WebMCP Deployment: Docker and Railway The application preserves each original Sysmon record and creates a pragmatic normalized representation containing only the fields needed for search, detection, and investigation. Detection is deliberately deterministic. Thirty official SigmaHQ rules are compiled through pySigma using the Sysmon processing pipeline and SQLite backend. No LLM decides whether an event matches a detection rule. The resulting rule-event matches are preserved individually and then correlated into analyst-facing alerts using deterministic source, host, process, and time relationships. The AI layer is intentionally much smaller. There is no embedded chatbot and no internal LLM runtime. Instead, the browser exposes eight WebMCP tools : get_workspace_status get_investigation_context search_security_events get_event_context aggregate_entity_activity add_investigation_evidence create_case_hypothesis update_case_hypothesis The agent does not receive the entire dataset. It retrieves bounded information when required, while the application remains responsible for searching, filtering, aggregation, validation, persistence, and audit history. Every event or evidence ID supplied by the agent is validated again by the backend. The core architectural principle became: Deterministic detection, probabilistic investigation. Challenges I ran into Avoiding Scope Creep: One of the biggest challenges was resisting the temptation to make the project larger than it needed to be. Security platforms can quickly turn into complex architectures before the first useful investigation even works. I kept coming back to a simpler question: What is the smallest architecture that can prove the complete idea using real data? That is why the project uses one backend, one frontend, one database, one deployment container, one browser agent, and eight carefully scoped tools. Credible Detections & Correlation: I did not want hardcoded alerts or fake responses created purely for a demo. The application had to ingest real attack-range telemetry, execute actual Sigma rules, retain exact event IDs, and allow every finding to resolve back to its original record. Because the Sigma rules produced 276 signals, presenting all of them as separate alerts would make the application less useful. I built a deterministic correlation engine that preserves individual signals but groups overlapping activity into 22 investigation-worthy alerts. WebMCP Compatibility Issues: Different browser implementations behaved differently around modelContext.getTools() . One environment exposed Promise-like behavior while another returned the tool list synchronously. A small assumption that .catch() could always be called managed to disable all the tools. I had to change the compatibility layer to support both synchronous and asynchronous implementations. Grounding the AI in Evidence: Rather than giving the model thousands of events directly, Aegis Operations exposes bounded search, context, and aggregation operations. The agent must deliberately retrieve information and work with stable event IDs. Unknown event IDs are rejected by the backend, and hypotheses cannot reference evidence outside the active investigation. Accomplishments that I am proud of The biggest accomplishment is that Aegis Operations is not a mocked security dashboard with an AI demo attached to it. The complete workflow operates over real stored telemetry and deterministic detections. The current reference environment contains: Component Count Real Sysmon events 11,435 Official SigmaHQ rules 30 Rule-event signals 276 Distinct detected events 133 Correlated analyst alerts 22 WebMCP tools 8 Accountability: Every alert resolves to the rules and events that produced it, and every evidence item resolves to an actual stored security event. Shared State: Every agent-created hypothesis must reference evidence belonging to the active investigation. Human and agent actions appear in the same persistent investigation state and audit timeline. Graceful Degradation: The application remains fully usable without an AI agent. If WebMCP is unavailable, the analyst can still perform all tasks manually. The AI is a collaborator, not a dependency. Human Authority: Keeping the final verdict outside the WebMCP tool surface was an intentional design decision. The agent can help investigate what happened; the human remains accountable for deciding what it means. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that an AI agent does not need to own the workflow in order to be useful. Before this project, a lot of my thinking around agents focused on runtimes, loops, memory, planning, orchestration, and tool execution. Aegis Operations pushed that thinking in a different direction. The most important part of the agent architecture turned out to be the boundary around the agent: The model reasons . The application retrieves facts, validates identifiers, stores evidence, and preserves provenance . The human owns consequential decisions . That separation makes the AI easier to trust and keeps the product useful even when the agent is unavailable. I also learned that conversation is not a good substitute for application state. If an agent discovers an important event, that fact should not live only inside a chat transcript—it should become evidence. If an agent develops an explanati

title: ChenChess live coaching board
pitch: Interactive live coaching sessions on chessboard with ChatGPT
about_excerpt: Interactive live coaching sessions on chessboard with ChatGPT Like Comment Story Updates ChenChess Coaching Board: Grounding a WebMCP Agent on a Live Chessboard Inspiration A player studying a game moves pieces with the mouse and asks questions by talking to a model. Those are two separate channels, and the language channel is full of pointers the model can't resolve on its own — why is this bad, what about that instead, is the line I tried still winning — all referring to board state the model never actually saw. WebMCP closes that gap: the page itself registers tools with document.modelContext , so an agent like ChatGPT or Claude can call them against the live page and the player's own session, instead of guessing from a transcript. The interesting problem wasn't wiring up tool calls. It was making sure an agent with real tools couldn't say anything about the board that wasn't true — the same grounding problem the rest of the coach has, now with a model that can also act . The coach-engine logic underneath Every WebMCP tool call ultimately reads from one deterministic pipeline, not from the model's own reasoning: Each position in a game is analyzed by Stockfish (objective best move and evaluation) and Maia-2 (what a human at a given rating would likely play) in parallel. A pure Rule Extractor compares the two and picks Critical Moments — plies where the position's win probability swung enough to matter. Evaluations are converted from centipawns to a win-probability curve first, since a swing means different things near equal and near winning: $$ \text{WinProb}(cp) = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{-cp/400}}, \qquad \left|\,\text{WinProb}(cp_{i+1}) - \text{WinProb}(cp_i)\,\right| \ge \tau $$ Each Critical Moment becomes a typed fact record (best line, refutation, verdict) before any prose exists, and a validator gate rejects any later explanation that doesn't match those facts ply-for-ply. The WebMCP layer doesn't get to skip this. Every board tool call returns a Coaching Board Snapshot — the same typed facts, plus which line is active and where the viewed ply sits on the game's own line — so the agent is handed grounded state on every call instead of being trusted to ask for it. How I built WebMCP support One authored map, not a second one. Coach tools already carried a coachToolSurface map of which tools the installed Coach App vs. the model may call. Adding the Coaching Board meant widening that map with a "web" target rather than maintaining a parallel list — the two surfaces share list_critical_moments , open_review_moment , and evaluate_player_line against the same data, distinguished by per-tool description, not by renaming. Register inside the auth gate, never at module load. Board routes pass through an asynchronous Beta Access check before a player is known. Tools register on an effect keyed by the authorized player ID and tear down through the AbortSignal registerTool accepts, so there's no window where an agent can discover and call board tools before identity resolves or after sign-out. Push the grounding policy into every result, not just instructions. Descriptions carry the rules once, at registration; each result also carries a constraint block for the facts it just returned, because nothing in WebMCP obliges an agent to re-read state before answering — an agent that skips the read produces fluent, confident, wrong coaching a player can't detect. Keep durable writes off the surface. The agent can stage a game import; only the player's own button press commits it. Challenges I faced Proving it actually grounds, not just that it compiles. A scripted deixis suite driving the board through a real WebMCP host measured 7/8 on referring expressions ( "that line," "the other one" ) but over-called tools on a non-deictic trap prompt roughly one run in five — enough signal to trust the mechanism, not enough to gate a release on yet. No production host to test against on demand. Storybook turned out to be a legitimate WebMCP host for driving the real board tools headlessly through Playwright with --enable-features=WebMCP , since neither ChatGPT's desktop app nor a locked devtools profile could be automated directly. A stale tab looks identical to a broken one. A board left open for hours answered every tool call with a bare "unavailable," which looked like a server-side bug; it was a client holding a dead connection. Fixing it meant turning any client-side throw into a typed unavailable result (rather than an opaque failure) so the agent — and future debugging — could tell "stale" from "actually broken." A withdrawn move can wedge every future write. A Slot Marker left behind by a since-withdrawn line kept blocking every Review Moment the board tried to write afterward; the fix surfaces the board's refusals in a banner instead of failing silently on the next unrelated call. The throughline: giving a model real hands on the board is only safe once every fact it can act on, and every fact it hands back, traces to the same deterministic pipeline the rest of the coach already trusts. title: Chinese Chess WebMCP: How to Win Grandpa’s Respect
pitch: Turn a chess game photo into an exact board, 20-move analysis, and your best shot at finally earning Grandpa’s respect. all in browser.
about_excerpt: Turn a chess game photo into an exact board, 20-move analysis, and your best shot at finally earning Grandpa’s respect. all in browser. Like Comment Story Updates Chinese Chess WebMCP: How to Win Grandpa's Respect Inspiration You see a Chinese chess match on TV, or two people playing in the park. You wonder what is happening and which move is better. Even a powerful AI may struggle to reconstruct every piece from a screen or photograph, and the image alone cannot reveal what a real chess engine sees many moves ahead. That everyday problem gave us the idea for Chinese Chess WebMCP. Many AI integrations help agents search across more information. We wanted to explore the complementary problem: going deeper into one interactive system, then making that depth easy for anyone to use. What it does Chinese Chess WebMCP is an interactive Chinese chess board with an actual chess engine running inside the browser. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can call the page for the exact position, legal moves, ranked candidate moves, scores, principal variations, and visible board annotations. The workflow can begin with the board already on the page or with a photograph of a real game. The AI converts the image into a proposed position, the page validates it, and the user confirms the result. From there, the same position becomes available for reliable engine analysis. The answer does not have to be a blunt command to play the top move. The AI can explain why a move works, compare alternatives, coach patiently, evaluate a move the user is considering, or find the best move for a particular piece. The page provides exact state and deep computation; the AI turns them into an explanation that fits the person asking. How we built it The application is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It includes Chinese chess rules and notation, a bilingual interface, position setup and validation, game review, and a Pikafish engine compiled to WebAssembly so analysis runs locally in the browser. The WebMCP layer registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool when the host supports it. Tool availability changes with the visible product state. For example, deep analysis is exposed only when the corresponding analysis and hint controls are enabled. Every tool execution checks that boundary again. For browsers without native WebMCP support, the page includes a visible compatibility panel that exercises the same tool contracts. GitHub Pages hosts the live demo, with a service worker providing the cross-origin isolation needed by the threaded WebAssembly engine. Challenges we ran into The photo workflow was not just an image-recognition problem. Real boards may be tilted, worn, partly obscured, or use unfamiliar handwriting. We needed a correction loop that could report invalid squares and let the AI repair only the uncertain parts instead of silently inventing a legal-looking position. The engine brought a different set of challenges. We had to reconcile board coordinates and notation, load a large neural-network file in the browser, make threaded WebAssembly work on static hosting, and present deep variations without overwhelming the user. The most important design challenge was deciding what the agent should be allowed to call. We made the WebMCP registry mirror the product's visible controls, so the agent works within the same boundary the person sees. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real Chinese chess engine runs entirely inside the browser, with no analysis backend. A photographed park or TV position can enter the same workflow as a native digital board. WebMCP exposes exact state and multi-move search, not a fragile interpretation of pixels. The AI can turn one structured result into direct advice, patient coaching, comparisons, move checking, or visible arrows on the board. The application is bilingual, open source, and available as a live demo with reproducible local tests. What we learned The most useful agent interface is not always the one with the most data. Sometimes the missing ingredient is depth: access to state and computation that exists inside an application but cannot be recovered reliably from its pixels. We also learned that exposing a powerful tool is only half the design. The page needs to communicate when that tool is available, what the user has enabled, and how the result maps back to something a person can see and understand. What's next for Chinese Chess WebMCP: How to Win Grandpa's Respect Next, we want to improve photo recognition across more board styles and camera angles, make the correction loop faster, and add richer coaching personalities without changing the underlying analysis. We also want to test the native WebMCP flow with more hosts as the API evolves, while keeping the in-page tool panel useful for anyone who wants to inspect the contracts today. Built With chess claude codex gemini onnx openai webassembly webmcp Try it out alexzhangji.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I designed and built the entire project, including the Chinese chess interface, in-browser engine integration, photo-to-board workflow, and dynamic WebMCP tools. I also created the bilingual experience, testing workflow, documentation, and demo video. The project taught me how WebMCP can expose not only more information, but deeper application state and computation.
