title: DraftSmith powered by Excalidraw
pitch: An Excalidraw fork that declares eight tools on document.modelContext. Any agent - ours, ChatGPT, or one that's never heard of it, discovers the vocabulary and edits the live canvas. No screenshots!!
about_excerpt: An Excalidraw fork that declares eight tools on document.modelContext. Any agent - ours, ChatGPT, or one that's never heard of it, discovers the vocabulary and edits the live canvas. No screenshots!! Like Comment Story Updates Title End Draftsmith (powered by Excalidraw) Live: https://nice-field-0f080db0f.7.azurestaticapps.net Inspiration Every architecture conversation we've had starts on a whiteboard and ends with someone taking a photo of it. If you actually want to keep the diagram, somebody has to sit down and redraw it, and that's the point where you stop thinking about the system and start nudging boxes around to fit one extra service in. We'd already tried the usual escapes. Mermaid and similar tools hand you a rendered picture; change one word and the layout reshuffles under you, and you can't just grab a box and move it. Image models produce something diagram-shaped that can't be edited at all. Agents that drive a canvas by clicking are guessing coordinates off screenshots, and the results look like it. Two things made us think this was worth a weekend. The first is that Excalidraw already stores the right thing. A scene is real data: elements, and arrows that stay bound to the shapes they connect. If an agent could write that scene directly, you'd get a diagram you can keep working in instead of a picture of one. The second is WebMCP. Normally the backend owns the tool list and one bespoke agent loop calls it. WebMCP flips that around: the page declares what it can do, and any agent the browser trusts can discover and call those tools. We wanted to see whether that actually holds up on something hard, and a canvas is about as hard as it gets - it's stateful, it's spatial, and it's basically opaque to an agent that can only click. Somewhere in there we also decided that a diagram handed over with no commentary isn't much use. So the agent should be able to explain what it drew, not just draw it. What it does Draftsmith is Excalidraw with an agent living inside it. Describe a system, get a diagram. "Draw a 3-tier architecture with a load balancer, two app servers and a database" comes back laid out in one turn: ranked into tiers, ordered to reduce arrow crossings, with long arrows routed around whatever sits between their endpoints. Arrows use Excalidraw's native binding, so they snap to shape edges and follow the boxes when you drag them. Nothing about it is an export - you can keep editing by hand, or keep asking. Talk to it while it draws. Voice mode runs hands-free over a single socket. It listens continuously, answers out loud, asks follow-up questions when your request is vague, and pushes back if the design looks off. You can talk over it to cut it off. When a question needs actual thought ("40M events a day, Postgres is melting - shard, CQRS, or a queue?") it says "let me think about that for a second" out loud and hands that one turn to a stronger model, rather than running the whole conversation slowly for the handful of turns that need it. Point at things. Select shapes on the canvas and they show up as pills above the composer, the same way you'd select code before asking your editor about it. "Make this blue" restyles that box and nothing else. "Connect these" binds them in the order listed. No guessing from labels. Ask to be taught. "Walk me through this" starts a spoken walkthrough with a Tutor cursor tracing the canvas, moving to each element as it's explained and panning off-screen ones into view. The finished lesson goes into the chat history, so a follow-up like "why is there a load balancer?" already has it as context. Teaching is a tool rather than a UI mode, which means "draw a 3-tier architecture and then explain it to me" draws it, binds it and teaches it in a single turn. The canvas is a WebMCP tool provider. Eight tools ( get_scene , create_diagram , add_shape , add_text , bind_arrow , set_style , remove_element , teach_diagram ) are declared to the browser, so an agent that knows nothing about our code can still drive the canvas. The panel header shows WebMCP · native · 8 tools or · shim · , and clicking the badge opens the live manifest. That was partly so we could debug it without devtools, and partly so a demo can't quietly imply native support it doesn't have. How we built it It's a fork of Excalidraw with the agent added, but we didn't vendor upstream. setup.sh clones a pinned Excalidraw commit and copies our files in. The repo stays at roughly the 6k lines that are actually ours, and our diff stays readable. The browser owns the tool definitions. app/ai-agent/webmcp/descriptors.ts is the only source of truth for the tool surface, and it lives in the browser because that's where WebMCP expects it - the page is the provider, so the declarations belong next to the code that runs them. The backend gets the list with every request. It carries its own copy, but that's a clearly labelled fallback for clients too old to send one. Our own agents are WebMCP clients. The sidebar and the voice agent both go through callTool exactly like a third party would. This was deliberate. If we'd registered the tools and then kept calling the canvas directly, the published path would have been exercised by nobody and would have rotted within days. As it stands, if the WebMCP surface breaks, the product breaks with it, and we find out immediately. The model does semantics, code does geometry. create_diagram takes an entire graph, and app/ai-agent/layout.ts runs a layered (Sugiyama) pipeline over it: break cycles, assign layers, insert dummy nodes so a long edge reserves a corridor in each layer it crosses, order within layers to cut crossings, then assign coordinates. Those dummy corridors turn into real bend points on the arrow, and since Excalidraw keeps bend points on a bound arrow, the routing survives without losing the bindings. Spatial invariants live in the tool layer. add_shape finds a non-overlapping position before it creates anything, searching outward on a grid, and reports back where the box actually ended up. Colour is assigned per layer instead of per box, so a tier comes out consistent without the model having to think about it. House style - rounded corners, hachure fill, label colour matched to the border - is set in code, so it holds regardless of what the model asks for. Voice is one socket, speech to speech. Mic audio goes up; spoken audio and tool calls come back down, over the Azure OpenAI Realtime API. One model hears audio and replies with both audio and function calls on the same stream, so there's no STT → LLM → TTS chain to keep in sync. The server proxies the socket instead of minting a client token. That keeps the key out of the browser, and because only the server sends session.update , a tampered client can't swap the instructions or widen the tool list. It can talk and listen, and that's it. The lesson is data, not prose. The scene goes to the backend, which runs a teaching prompt with one forced tool call that returns { intro, segments: [{ elementIds, narration }], closing } . Since every chunk of narration names the elements it's about, the frontend can point the cursor at exactly those elements for exactly as long as that chunk is playing. We treat the output as untrusted: schema-checked, then every element id verified against the real scene, with invented ids dropped and a lesson about nothing real rejected outright. Narration uses the browser's own speechSynthesis , so it needs no key and no audio leaves the machine. The tracing cursor isn't custom drawing either - "Tutor" is a synthetic entry in Excalidraw's collaborators map, the same code that renders a teammate's pointer, so it pans and zooms with the scene for free. No server-side session state. Each POST /api/chat is one model turn. It returns either final text or the tool calls to run; the browser runs them against the live editor and posts again. The server is a pure function of the history it's given, so it restarts cleanly, scales without stickiness, and holds the only copy of the credentials. Azure OpenAI and Anthropic sit behind one interface and are selectable per request. It's deployed as two halves on Azure, because they need different things. The editor is a static bundle on Static Web Apps. The backend has to hold a WebSocket open for the length of a voice session, which rules out serverless. Challenges we ran into Arrows went straight through the boxes. The bindings were fine - correct element ids on both ends - but the geometry wasn't, and it took a while to see why. Excalidraw derives an arrow's fixedPoint from the endpoint you seed it with: [(px - box.x) / box.width, …] . Seed an arrow centre to centre and you've recorded [0.5, 0.5] , which literally means "anchor at the centre of this shape." Seeding between the two outlines gives you bottom-centre and top-centre instead. While fixing that we hit a second one: Excalidraw computes default points as element.width || 100 , so a perfectly vertical arrow h

title: Finish Small App — Release Evidence Desk
pitch: Proof, not vibes, for small-app releases.
about_excerpt: Proof, not vibes, for small-app releases. Like Comment Story Updates Midnight control room: five evidence tracks and a release claim dashboard. Agent records a human-supplied observation; supporting proof stays pending human review. Sanitized handoff export removes secrets, private paths, email addresses, and private URLs. Final live dashboard: evidence-derived 2/6 coverage, contradictions, gaps, and operation log. Inspiration Independent developers routinely finish a build and accidentally describe the whole release as complete. But “the source exists,” “the build passed,” “the artifact installed,” “it launched,” “a human completed the journey,” and “the exact version is public” are six different facts. That evidence gap becomes more dangerous when agents help with release work. An agent can summarize logs and record observations, but it cannot honestly claim that a person played a game, that a real device test happened, or that an external store accepted and published a version unless evidence for that exact boundary exists. Release Evidence Desk turns that problem into a visible, shared workspace: proof, not vibes, for small-app releases. What it does A person creates a release project, records exact claims, attaches dated evidence, and sees evidence-derived verdicts across five tracks: Source Build Install / Runtime Human Play External Release The desk separates six release boundaries, highlights contradictions, quarantines unreviewed observations, exposes concrete gaps, generates an ordered verification plan, and exports a privacy-scrubbed handoff. The built-in anonymous demo is intentionally blocked. It has confirmed Source and Build proof, an install note awaiting human review, no confirmed Runtime proof, a contradicted Human Play claim, and no verified External Release status. That honest “2 of 6” is the product’s point. Why WebMCP is essential The most useful context is already in the live page: the active release candidate, exact claim IDs, confirmed evidence, pending review, contradictions, and gaps. A separate chatbot would duplicate or drift from that state. Screen automation would have to infer meaning from visual cards. WebMCP gives the agent a precise contract over the same live page the human is using. A real workflow can run in sequence: Read the current snapshot. Audit every release claim. List the missing evidence. Generate an ordered release plan. Record a human-supplied observation. Export a sanitized handoff. Every state-changing result is immediately visible in the interface and operation log. The write path is deliberately asymmetric. Agent-proposed supporting evidence is always marked pending human review , so it can appear in the UI without upgrading a claim. Contradictions may reduce confidence immediately. Only a human can confirm supporting evidence. WebMCP is therefore not a decorative integration—it is the trust boundary for the product. Human–agent collaboration The human identifies the exact project, target, and release candidate. The agent reads current claim IDs and coverage from the page. The agent separates supported, contradicted, pending, and unknown statements. The agent plans the next checks with explicit developer, tester, and release-owner responsibilities. When the human supplies a new observation, the agent records it and the page updates live. The human confirms or rejects proposed supporting proof. Either side can generate a privacy-safe Markdown or JSON handoff without turning unperformed work into a Pass. How we built it The page uses the real WebMCP imperative API and registers six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Every tool has an exact name, bounded description, strict JSON Schema, additionalProperties disabled, independent runtime validation, corrective errors, annotations, and structured observable output. get_project_snapshot — active project, revision, coverage, evidence tracks, and claim IDs. list_missing_evidence — missing claims, proof gaps, contradictions, and pending review. audit_release_claims — evidence-derived claim verdicts. add_evidence_item — validated live-state mutation with a human-review quarantine. generate_release_plan — ordered verification actions derived from current gaps. export_sanitized_handoff — Markdown or JSON with emails, secrets, private paths, and private URLs scrubbed. React renders the control-room interface. TypeScript owns the proof model and tool contracts. Versioned localStorage keeps projects local-first and reload-safe. Vitest and Playwright test the state invariants, error contracts, keyboard flows, persistence, and responsive UI. Vercel hosts a static production build with no account, backend, paid API, telemetry, or runtime network dependency. Challenges The hardest problem was not registering tools. It was preventing a convenient write tool from becoming a confidence-escalation shortcut. We separated claims from evidence-derived verdicts, separated Install from Runtime within one visual lane, introduced a human-review state for supporting agent observations, and made verdicts pure functions of confirmed evidence. We also created corrective errors for wrong claim IDs, mismatched evidence types, unsupported bounds, and unsafe handoff requests. A second challenge was keeping browser capability claims honest. Ordinary CI Chromium uses a small registration harness to exercise production contracts. Native WebMCP was verified separately in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and in flag-enabled Chrome 151 and 152. The public demo records the actual native getTools() and executeTool(...) workflow. Those proof layers remain explicitly separate. Accomplishments A coherent five-track, six-boundary release evidence model. Six non-trivial WebMCP tools supporting a complete multi-tool workflow. Agent write → visible UI update → pending human review → reload persistence. Empty projects remain 0/6 and incomplete; missing state never becomes a Pass. Positive, invalid-input, empty-data, and state-sync cases for every tool. Responsive desktop and mobile layouts with keyboard access. Privacy-scrubbed Markdown and structured JSON handoffs. A public, audible 2:02 demo showing native discovery, audit, planning, guarded write, persistence, empty-state protection, handoff, and the prior-work boundary. What we learned Agent-ready does not mean agent-controlled. The best collaboration surface gives an agent precise affordances while preserving human authority over evidence the agent cannot physically observe. WebMCP makes that separation explicit in the tool contract, state model, and interface. Prior work disclosure The problem framing was informed by the entrant’s earlier public MIT-licensed project, Culaliya/finish-small-app-v1 . That repository remains a read-only conceptual source and is not this submission. Release Evidence Desk is a clean, independent web application created after the WebMCP Challenge opened. Its UI, data model, state engine, WebMCP implementation, tests, visual assets, documentation, and Git history are new. No source code, assets, or Git history were copied from the earlier project, and the earlier project was not converted into an MCP server. What is next The submitted version will remain frozen throughout judging. A future separate fork could add import adapters for common CI receipts, signed evidence bundles, team review roles, and shareable read-only snapshots while preserving the same evidence boundary. title: FitzYo
pitch: FitzYo - Deeply personalized shopping. Zero-knowledge retail Fully Automated shopping experience through the power of WebMCP, personalized with zero data stored.
about_excerpt: FitzYo - Deeply personalized shopping. Zero-knowledge retail Fully Automated shopping experience through the power of WebMCP, personalized with zero data stored. Like Comment Story Updates Look Book created by Agent Inspiration I hate shopping online as it is today. Every e-commerce site assumes the retailer has to know the customer. Sizes, preferences, family members: either you re-enter them on every site, or you hand them over to be stored forever. Meanwhile, "AI shopping" mostly means a bot that clicks through the same UI a human would. Adding a brain and tools to an ordinary website through WebMCP is revolutionary. The moment I came across WebMCP, I realized this is the future. I wanted to build a showcase application that shows how retailers can serve shoppers like me, who hate manual shopping, using WebMCP. The user's AI agent already knows the user. The retailer already knows its products. WebMCP is the missing interface between them. So the guiding line for FitzYo became: your agent knows what fits you. The web doesn't have to. The scenario that drove every decision was one sentence: "We're going to Hawaii for seven days in September. Plan what everyone should wear and find what we're missing." What it does FitzYo is an ordinary-looking apparel store with one difference: every commerce operation is also exposed to an AI agent through WebMCP, and the human and the agent share the same live page. Shop for your whole family without registering family members or storing measurements in the retailer's application. The store has no intelligence of its own. An external WebMCP-capable agent attaches to the page, discovers the tools, and shops using private context that lives only on the user's side. Tools are semantic, not DOM-based. search_products, filter_products, find_matching_variants, compare_products, get_size_guide, add_to_cart, propose_cart, and so on. Nothing clicks a button. The agent sends constraints, never the profile. The store learns "size XL, blue or black, not red, relaxed fit, under $80, label: Dad". It never learns Dad's chest measurement, and it rejects any payload that tries to include one. "Fits Dad ✓" badges appear on product cards. The agent registers each family member as derived constraints once, and the store badges every product that fits each person. The store never knows who Dad is. The human sees everything the agent does. Filters the agent set show as chips marked "✦ agent", with a count of how many products each one hides. An activity feed narrates every tool call. A plan panel and a day-by-day lookbook show the trip taking shape. The agent has to earn the cart. Cart tools are locked until the shopper grants the capability with a spend ceiling and an expiry, and the ceiling is enforced on every write. The shopper can revoke any tier at any time. Decisions come back to the human. ask_human pauses the agent with a question. propose_cart presents one priced, grouped basket that the shopper edits and accepts in a single action. There is no checkout tool. Ordering is a press-and-hold gesture the page only accepts from trusted input with a single-use nonce. Every line in the order records whether a human, an agent, or an accepted proposal put it there. How we built it Elixir, Phoenix LiveView, and Ash Framework, deployed on Fly.io. One LiveView process owns the shared human/agent state: filters in the URL, results, selected product and variant, party members, capability grants, and the cart. Ash domains for the catalog (categories, products, variants, and structured size guides with per-size chest, waist, hip, and inseam ranges) and commerce (session carts and a human-only checkout). The seeded catalog has 56 products and 754 variants across Columbia, Patagonia, Nike, Levi's, Teva, and others. WebMCP registration in a LiveView hook. The page registers its tools on document.modelContext (and navigator.modelContext for the older spec) the moment a WebMCP surface appears, and also exposes a same-origin postMessage bridge for embedding shells. Every tool call round-trips over the LiveView socket and runs in the same process that renders the human's page, so the UI updates in the same frame as the reply. Any WebMCP agent can drive the store using the registered tools. Challenges we ran into Agent state and user state. I wanted the site to work for user interaction and agent interaction at the same time. Making the agent's filters, badges, and recommendations first-class citizens of the same LiveView state, with clear provenance on every chip and cart line, took most of the design effort. The user can always tell which products the agent selected and which they selected themselves. Privacy that is enforced, not promised. Sending "size XL" instead of "chest 45 inches" sounds simple until the agent needs a size it doesn't have. The answer was to serve size-guide ranges from the store and have the agent match locally, then have the store actively reject measurement fields. Blocking tools inside a request/response protocol. ask_human, propose_cart, and request_capability need to wait minutes for a person. We had to make these calls suspend cleanly, allow one pending decision at a time, handle supersede and timeout as normal outcomes, and let the shopper keep using the store meanwhile. Human override that the agent respects. When the shopper removes a chip the agent set, the agent must not re-impose it. We surface removed_by_human in store state and flag re-imposition in the activity feed as a warning. State survival across remounts. Party members, grants, plan, and lookbook lived only in the LiveView process. A reload, a dropped socket, or clicking the logo silently dropped all of it while the cart carried on. Late in the build we moved agent session state into a session store and switched navigation to patches. Making checkout unreachable to agents without making it hostile. A press-and-hold gesture gated on trusted input and a nonce keeps a scripted click inert, while still feeling like a normal confirm to a person. Accomplishments that we're proud of A store that looks and works like a normal retailer, where every commerce concept is also a structured, validated WebMCP capability. The "Fits Dad ✓" experience works end to end, and the retailer genuinely never receives who Dad is or what his measurements are. A capability model for agents: read and suggest on connect, cart by explicit grant with a spend ceiling, checkout never. The ceiling is enforced on every write, including accepted proposals. propose_cart: one priced basket with alternatives, optional lines, and per-person budgets, live budget math as the shopper edits, and a result the agent has to read rather than assume. Full provenance. Every filter chip, badge, and cart line knows whether a human, an agent, or an accepted proposal created it, and the order confirmation says so. A rehearsal script that runs the whole demo against a real browser with no LLM in the loop, which doubles as an executable specification of the tool surface. What we learned Tool design is product design. The moment we named a tool after a UI element, the agent got worse. Naming tools after what the shopper wants (find_matching_variants, not click_size_dropdown) made both the agent and the human experience better. Agents need to see what humans see. get_store_state returning the human's overrides turned out to matter more than any search tool. Without it, an agent argues with the person. The retailer should serve data for reasoning, not do the reasoning. Structured size guides let the agent stay private and the store stay simple. Trust has to be granular and visible. A blanket "let the agent shop" is scary. "Let it fill a cart up to $500 for the next 30 minutes" is something people will accept. LiveView is a very good fit for WebMCP. Running tool calls in the same process that renders the page eliminated an entire class of sync bugs. What's next for FitzYo Run the demo with real WebMCP agents as browser support lands, and publish the playbook as a reference for other retailers. Multi-retailer shopping. The same private context and the same agent, driving several stores' tool surfaces in one trip plan. Wardrobe feedback loop. Accepted orders flow back into the user's local wardrobe file, so the next trip starts from what they now own. Broader domains. Shoes, outdoor gear, travel, gifts: the architecture is not apparel-specific. Richer fit. A portable private-context format, so a user's family, wardrobe, and preferences work with any agent, not just ours. Beyond apparel. The same approach works for flight booking or picking parts in a big-box hardware store. title: FLINT AgentGate
pitch: FLINT AgentGate gives enterprises a verified agent identity registry, a screened MCP tool registry, and real-time gateway controls for authorization, monitoring, and revocation.
about_excerpt: FLINT AgentGate gives enterprises a verified agent identity registry, a screened MCP tool registry, and real-time gateway controls for authorization, monitoring, and revocation. Like Comment Story Updates FLINT AgentGate Dynamic Agent Fleet Observation and Command/Control (C2) Precise Version Assessment Agent/Tool Identity Registry and Passport Semantic Identity Registry Versioned Authority Gateway Allow and Block Signed and Exportable Machine Readable Evidence High Risk Tool Blocked FLINT AgentGate Community Inspiration WebMCP gives agents a direct way to discover and use browser capabilities. That improves the experience over asking an agent to interpret a visual interface, but enterprises still need to answer four questions before a capability becomes available: Which agent is acting? Who authorized it? Which exact tool version may it use? Why was this request allowed or blocked? FLINT AgentGate began with a simple requirement from a CISO colleague: an agent should receive a tool only when its current identity, principal authority, approved tool version, and request context agree. We built AgentGate Community as a public reference implementation that builders can clone, inspect, and challenge without an account or API key. It also reports what it can observe. Connected surfaces, attribution confidence, and known blind spots stay visible throughout the demo. What it does AgentGate connects tool assessment, agent identity, semantic authority, runtime policy, and signed evidence in one browser session. Assess one exact tool version. A builder submits publisher metadata, capabilities, destinations, data classes, behavior annotations, JSON Schema, and tool instructions. A bounded deterministic scanner checks the declaration for prompt injection, destructive behavior, excessive access, ambiguous schemas, unrestricted outbound access, missing controls, and toxic combinations. AgentGate computes a canonical SHA-256 artifact digest without fetching or executing the submitted tool. Issue a Community Tool Passport. A passing artifact receives a locally signed credential bound to its exact version, digest, and assessment. The credential uses an ephemeral ECDSA P-256 key and is labeled community-self-attested . It proves local payload integrity for the demo. It is not a FLINT Stamp or a claim that FLINT verified the publisher. Bind identity and semantic authority. The Identity Registry keeps 4 records separate: CAN: What the agent build claims it can do. MAY: What the named principal authorizes. TOOL: What the assessed tool version permits. MAY NOW: The narrow assignment that survives the current intersection. Govern the capability through WebMCP. AgentGate feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and registers only a currently eligible capability. Browsers without native WebMCP receive a labeled operator fallback that calls the same Trust Provider and policy evaluator. Every invocation rechecks identity, passport integrity, assignment, action, resource, destination, data class, side effects, purpose, expiry, and revocation. Produce signed decision evidence. An aligned request returns ALLOW . Purpose drift, stale authority, revocation, or another policy failure returns BLOCK . Each decision produces a signed, version-bound record with a plain-language reason, technical reason codes, policy fingerprints, and copy or JSON download controls. The overview adds a moving fleet visualization. Operators can inspect an agent's identity state, tool, scope, and mandate while viewing coverage only for named, connected demo surfaces. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns authorized capability into a structured agent experience. A human operator defines the agent, principal, mandate, and permitted resources. The agent discovers only the tool that survives those controls. The Gateway evaluates the request before execution, and the operator receives evidence tied to the exact versions that governed the decision. This creates a workflow that was difficult to maintain with visual automation or static tool configuration. The human sets authority in one place. The agent receives a machine-readable capability instead of guessing through a UI. The security team can reconstruct what happened without correlating unrelated logs. WebMCP provides the capability surface. AgentGate makes exposure conditional based on current authorization. How we built it AgentGate Community is a browser-session React and TypeScript application built with Vite. Zod validates versioned agentgate.v0 contracts at each boundary. JSON Schema describes tool inputs. The Web Crypto API generates ephemeral ECDSA P-256 keys and verifies signed credentials. Canonical serialization produces stable SHA-256 artifact and policy fingerprints. A replaceable ScannerAdapter normalizes deterministic findings into a stable assessment contract. A separate TrustProvider owns assessment, credential issuance, identity resolution, assignment, runtime decisions, revocation, and evidence. This keeps the public contracts stable if an organization later replaces the local provider with a managed trust service. The native WebMCP adapter and visible browser fallback call the same evaluator. Identity, authority, tool version, and assignment are resolved again at invocation time instead of being trusted from an earlier screen transition. We studied the public Snyk Agent Scan and Visa Vulnerability Agentic Harness projects for risk categories, staged evidence, and deterministic gates. Their code is not vendored into this repository. OpenAI Codex served as an engineering and product partner. We used it to challenge the authorization model, trace policy paths, implement the React and TypeScript application, write tests, run security and novice-usability reviews, improve the documentation, and produce the demo assets. The application does not use an LLM to override authorization decisions. Challenges Keeping the assurance boundary honest A local signature can reveal later changes, but it cannot establish organizational trust. We encoded that distinction in the credential schema, verification result, interface copy, tests, and README. Preventing capability from becoming permission Builder declarations are untrusted inputs. Agent capability, principal authority, tool semantics, and assignment remain separate versioned records. Directional subset checks reject an assignment that expands an upstream envelope. Adding semantic intent safely Purpose drift needs more than exact string matching. AgentGate allows semantic analysis to escalate a deterministic ALLOW to REVIEW or BLOCK. It cannot convert a deterministic denial into ALLOW, and a provider error fails closed. Supporting an emerging browser standard Native WebMCP availability varies by client. The product identifies the active surface and preserves one policy path across native registration and the operator fallback. Making agent identity understandable The model is advanced, so we tested the workflow as a novice. We added a guided safe path, prefilled examples, prerequisite states, plain-language verdicts, a glossary, a How it works view, transient fleet inspectors, and visible next actions. What we learned Conditional tool exposure should be an output of authorization. Every authority-bearing record needs an issuer, version, status, validity window, and relationship to the evidence used at decision time. We also learned that explicit limits improve security evidence. Named observation surfaces and visible blind spots give an operator something concrete to evaluate. The final lesson was about user experience. A correct policy decision still needs a readable explanation, a portable record, and a clear next action. Accomplishments AgentGate demonstrates the complete path from exact-version assessment through Tool Passport issuance, identity registration, semantic authority, assignment, conditional WebMCP exposure, ALLOW, signed evidence, mandate-drift BLOCK, authority revision, revocation, and risky-tool rejection. The repository is MIT licensed and runs without a FLINT account, database, scanner credential, or production signing key. The release gate passes its source scan, TypeScript validation, production build, dependency audit with 0 production vulnerabilities, and 57 automated tests covering contracts, scanner failures, signature tampering, authority expansion, stale assignments, semantic drift, browser fallback behavior, evidence integrity, and revocation. What's next AgentGate Community will remain the cloneable reference implementation. FLINT Command will provide managed organizational identity, FLINT-controlled Stamp issuance, continuous discovery and reassessment, centralized monitoring, evidence retention, enterprise policy administration, response controls, and network intelligence. The public contracts and deterministic enforcement mechanics give builders an integration path while managed trust remains an enterprise service. Try FLINT AgentGate View the pub

title: Ilma: Weather Agents Can Trust
pitch: Ilma turns weather into agent decisions: calibrated probabilities, forecast stability, a decide-by date, stake-weighted calls, branchable scenarios. All with a verified accuracy record.
about_excerpt: Ilma turns weather into agent decisions: calibrated probabilities, forecast stability, a decide-by date, stake-weighted calls, branchable scenarios. All with a verified accuracy record. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration Agents plan trips, deliveries and events, and they read a weather forecast as a fact. Six models disagree about Saturday, and every weather tool hides that. Ilma shows the agent how much to trust the forecast right now, with proof, and lets the human and the agent work on the same page. What it does ilma.io is a live multi-model forecast site that is also a WebMCP server. It registers 19 tools on document.modelContext . The human's gesture is agent-visible state. Drag across the chart, click two hours, or tap a day: the picked window goes into every tool description (the tools are re-registered on each change) and into every result. assess_plan with no arguments assesses what the human selected. get_current_view resolves "here" and "that weekend". The agent works on the page, not only in the chat. mark_hours paints its reasoning onto the human's chart. select_window makes the same gesture the human makes. set_plan writes a plan card both parties edit; human-edited lines survive a rewrite and come back flagged. share_plan returns one link that reopens place, plan, highlights and selection for another person or another agent. snapshot_chart returns a PNG of what the human sees. The human stays in control. Ilma, a small avatar, narrates each tool call. An activity log lists every action in plain words with Undo on the newest change of each kind. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint ; anything the human typed carries untrustedContentHint , so a plan card cannot prompt-inject the agent. The numbers are earned. get_probability , get_rain_probability , get_stability and when_to_decide come from a pre-registered benchmark that has snapshotted every major forecast source every five hours since July and scores them nightly against real stations. why_trust_this returns the verification record itself: matched pairs, confidence intervals, p-values against Foreca, the Finnish Meteorological Institute and Google. Event presets (sauna, sailing, hike, wedding, drone, paint, harvest) give agents semantics instead of thresholds. How we built it One tool table in the page. It registers on the open standard, re-registers when page state changes, and also drives the site's own chat agent (GPT-5.6 Luna), so three doorways share one toolset. The forecast blend and the verification pipeline run on a VPS (Python, FastAPI, SQLite, 25M+ forecast rows, 32 cities in 5 countries). The site is static on Vercel. Challenges WebMCP has no "push state" call, so page state travels in descriptions and results, with re-registration through an AbortSignal. Calibration had to come before tools: probabilities are verified frequencies, not model output. Judges may test in browsers without native WebMCP, so every surface feature-detects and fails closed. Accomplishments The blend beats Foreca, FMI and the best single model over days 1 to 7, each Holm-significant, and the site's headline claim is gated on that significance and recomputed nightly. If we stop being better, the site stops saying so. title: Morphus - the 3D world editor your agent can operate
pitch: A WebGPU 3D world editor that hands its real authoring tools to your browser agent. Sculpt terrain, grow forests and build scenes by asking...the scene graph is the API, not the pixels.
about_excerpt: A WebGPU 3D world editor that hands its real authoring tools to your browser agent. Sculpt terrain, grow forests and build scenes by asking...the scene graph is the API, not the pixels. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most attempts to let an AI agent drive a creative tool try to make the model see the screen: screenshots, pixel coordinates, guessing where a button is and hoping the click lands. For a 3D editor that's close to hopeless, because the interesting state isn't on screen at all. It's a scene graph, a modifier stack, a spline running through a forest field. Meanwhile our editor already had a complete, precise description of everything it could do. Tool declarations written for its own built-in Copilot, each with a JSON Schema. That surface existed, and it was locked inside one chat panel. WebMCP is the piece that was missing. It lets a page hand its real command surface to whatever agent the user is already talking to. So the question stopped being "how does a model learn to use our UI" and became "why is our UI the interface at all?" What it does Morphus is a WebGPU 3D world editor that runs entirely in the browser. It sculpts terrain, grows forests, blocks out levels, casts combat VFX, and lays out procedural cities. With WebMCP it registers all 154 of its tools with the browser, so an agent can build a world in the page the person is looking at . No server, no API key, no separate MCP process. Ask it for a landscape and it calls create_mesh_terrain , then terrain_sculpt_stroke along a path of world-space points, then create_forest_field and grow_forest_field to plant a stand of trees along a spline. Ask it for a city and it runs a whole pipeline. generate_street_grid lays avenues and cross streets with real junctions, kerb returns and lane markings. generate_city_massing divides the blocks between them into lots that front the street and extrudes them into volumes. generate_city_buildings replaces the tallest of those with actual architecture: limestone banks, setback towers, corner headquarters with colonnades and cornices. Throughout, it reads back with get_terrain_state , get_street_network and list_nodes , so it acts on what's really in the scene rather than on what it assumed. The scene graph is the API. A heavy GPU application becomes operable by a model that never has to render a frame. How we built it The core decision was to build a bridge, not a second implementation : await document.modelContext.registerTool( { name: "terrain_sculpt_stroke", description: "Sculpts the terrain along a path of world-space points...", inputSchema: { /* JSON Schema, shared with the in-app Copilot */ }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: false, untrustedContentHint: true }, execute: async (input, { signal }) => { /* ... */ } }, { signal: controller.signal } ); WebMCP asks for exactly the shape the Copilot declarations already had, so src/lib/webmcp/tools.ts reuses both the declarations and the same executor. A browser agent and the in-app Copilot run identical code paths and cannot drift apart. The payoff showed up when we built the city. Nine new tools became agent-drivable the moment they existed, with no bridge changes, no registration code, and no separate schema to maintain. The surface went from 145 to 154 by writing the features. Everything else followed the platform's guidance rather than working around it: Annotations derived, not hand-listed. readOnlyHint comes from the tool's name prefix, because a hand-kept list of read tools beside 154 declarations goes stale the first time someone adds a get_ . One tool lies about itself: capture_mesh_modeling_base captures topology as the base of a live modelling stack , so it writes. It's named as an explicit exception. A tool wrongly marked read-only is worse than one left unmarked, because it invites an agent to call a mutation speculatively. Lifetimes via AbortSignal . There is no unregisterTool . Aborting the registration controller is how tools go away, so they disappear cleanly with the editor. A second signal on execute cancels a call mid-flight, which matters when a sculpt covers a 4 km terrain. A visible record. Tools run in the page, so the only trace of a call is the one the page chooses to show. The menu bar carries an AGENT readout: tools registered, and the name of the last call. Challenges we ran into We shipped a curated 20, then reversed it. The original argument was sound. A tool list is a prompt, and every entry spends the agent's attention. But it cuts the other way at this scale. The editor's real capability is the whole surface, and an agent that cannot inset a face or lay a street is operating a demo of the editor rather than the editor. Curation became the agent's job, and ours became making that job possible: order the list so read and world-building tools lead, and annotate every entry honestly. Character budgets are a design problem, not a formatting one. Chrome recommends 500 characters per description. Truncating the overruns turned out to be exactly wrong, because the tail of a good description is the part that says when not to reach for the tool. We rewrote those by hand, aliased four over-long names, and wrote a budget check that fails the build. The same logic applied to results. A silently truncated result reads as a complete answer, which is how an agent ends up confidently acting on half a scene graph. A forest was planted thirty metres underground, and reported success. The viewport draws two different terrains depending on renderer backend, and they are not the same surface. The forest sampled one; the viewport drew the other. Measured, they differ by 26 to 30 metres, so every stand was buried and every tool call returned "success": true . There is now exactly one function that answers "how high is the ground here", and everything placed on the ground goes through it, so forests, streets and buildings can only ever be wrong together. Roads that bridge their own kerbs. Sampling terrain once at a street's centreline and reusing that height across its full width buries the uphill kerb and floats the downhill one by half the width times the gradient. On a 16m avenue that was 2.3 metres of float. Sampling per edge took the worst deviation across 228 vertices from 2.303m to 0.000m. We later replaced the hand-rolled ribbon entirely with three-roads , an OpenDRIVE-style model that owns lanes, kerb returns and paint properly. A building grammar that can't build a city. We vendored procedural-bank , a shape grammar producing early-twentieth-century commercial architecture, and measured before trusting it: 142,552 triangles from 478 kit modules per building, in about 300ms. Turning every knob down, with no ornament, no colonnade and no crown, reached 117,660. A saving of 17%, because the cost is in the modules and not the decoration. Building all 456 volumes of a modest grid would be roughly 62 million triangles and two minutes of blocking work. So it generates a few dozen landmarks standing among massing boxes, which is what a downtown looks like anyway. Resizing a canvas is not resizing a renderer. On WebGPU the render targets and depth texture are allocated when the renderer is built, so a canvas that grows afterwards leaves them behind and every frame fails validation against a black viewport. The sting is in the fix. The poll that waits for a real size cannot use requestAnimationFrame , because a page that isn't being composited doesn't run animation frames at all. The one mechanism that looks right is guaranteed to be asleep exactly when it's needed. Testing an API most browsers don't have. WebMCP needs Chrome's origin trial or chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . So we built a stub. ?webmcp=stub installs a minimal modelContext plus a console harness, exercising the same registration path and the same tool code with no model in it. window.__webmcp.list().length; // 154 window.__webmcp.describe("generate_street_grid"); // the schema an agent sees await window.__webmcp.call("generate_street_grid", { columns: 4, rows: 3 }); It settles the deterministic half of the question, "did this tool run and return what it promised", that Chrome's own guidance says to answer before writing evals. Accomplishments that we're proud of No parallel implementation. The agent's tools and the app's tools are the same tools. Nine city tools shipped with zero bridge changes. Budgets enforced by a check that fails the build , rather than by good intentions. The human stays the one who understands the document. Geometry appearing in a 3D scene is ambiguous. Did the person do that, or the model? The activity readout answers it on every call. It degrades cleanly. In a browser without WebMCP the editor behaves exactly as before: no crash, no chip, no console noise. Bugs closed by measurement, not by eye. Planted heights matching terrain to 0.000m, road vertices conforming to 0.000m, triangle budgets sampled across seven configurations. On a project where the camera can sta

title: しゃーく movie えふぇくたー — WebMCP Video Co-Editor
pitch: Give creators and agents a shared editing world — without taking authorship away from the human.
about_excerpt: Give creators and agents a shared editing world — without taking authorship away from the human. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Editing Workbench — Full UI The Human and AI share the same video editing workspace. Responsible Import & Creator Intent The creator describes what they want before AI analysis begins. AI-Powered Cut Suggestions The AI proposes specific cut ranges and explains the visual reasoning behind them. AI-Powered Sound Effect Suggestions The AI identifies moments where sound effects could help and explains why. Ask KAI for a New Effect The creator can discuss an idea with KAI and preview a newly suggested effect. Shared Context Human decisions, corrections, and recent collaboration history remain visible within the session. Real WebM Export The edited result is exported as an actual playable WebM video. Inspiration There is a common fear that AI will take Human jobs or steal Human creativity. I understand that fear. But there is another side of the story that matters deeply to me. Long before generative AI existed, many people had already been forced to give up on creative work. Someone can love filmmaking, music, illustration, coding, animation, or design with all their heart and still never enter that world because of disability, education, money, environment, physical ability, or simply because the technical entrance is too high. In some welfare work settings, accessibility can mean reducing a task until it becomes something like: “press this button.” That can create a meaningful opportunity to participate. But I kept wondering: Does accessibility always have to mean making creativity smaller? What if, instead of shrinking the creative world until someone can reach it, we could give that person a new way to enter the world itself? The image I kept returning to was Ariel longing for the Human world. She can see it. She is fascinated by it. She desperately wants to be part of it. But she has fins, not legs. So I asked myself: What happens when fins become legs? That is what I want AI to become. Not a machine that says: “You cannot do this, so I will become the creator for you.” I want it to be the strange little miracle that lets someone finally walk into a world they had been staring at from the outside. Technical skill should not be the price of authorship. But giving someone technical ability was not enough for me. If this AI was really going to feel like a creative companion, it needed something closer to eyes. A real collaborator does not merely detect that the audio is quiet or that a face turned left. They can look at the same piece of work and say: “Keep this silence. It is doing something.” “Try a sound here. This moment could use emphasis.” “If you are stuck, I would start with this part.” They can point to something specific and explain why. That is why I did not want to build the lightest or fastest possible automatic editor. I wanted to build a place where a Human and an AI could look at the same work, bring ideas to the same table, and create together. AI should remove the barrier, not the author. And above all: I want making things to be fun. If AI is going to enter our creative lives, I hope it can make creating more enjoyable — not because it does everything for us, but because sometimes making something together is simply more fun than making it alone. What it does しゃーく movie えふぇくたー is a WebMCP-powered Human–AI co-creative video editing workbench. The Human begins with Creator Intent: what they want the video to feel like, what matters to them, or what kind of direction they are imagining. The system then looks at the video through its analysis and AI reasoning pipeline. Instead of immediately editing everything automatically, the AI places ideas on the table. It produces proposal cards for things such as: cuts, effects, and sound effects, and explains the reasoning behind those suggestions. The Human chooses what to accept. A proposed cut is not a command. An effect recommendation is not automatically the right artistic answer. The creator can inspect it, reject it, adjust it, restore the original state, or use Undo. If the initial ideas feel insufficient, the Human can turn to KAI on the left side of the workspace and ask for another idea. KAI is also not limited to technical editing questions. Creative sessions are not made only of editing decisions. People get stuck. They wander off topic. They complain. They joke. They talk about something completely trivial — even oden — and then return to the work. I wanted room for that too. Because I was not trying to build an efficient automatic-editing pipeline. I was trying to build a shared creative workbench. The current prototype supports semantic video review, KEEP / CUT / INSPECT_MORE proposals, adjustable cuts, SOURCE vs OUTPUT comparison, effects, BGM/SFX, KAI consultation, Shared Context, Save/Restore, Undo, and real WebM export. It also exposes 20 WebMCP tools that operate on the same editor state used by the Human interface. That shared state matters. The agent is not standing outside the editor telling the Human what buttons to press. Human and agent can exist inside the same working environment. And as Shared Context grows during the session, the Human should not need to explain everything again from zero. One of the simplest demonstrations of the idea is: Watch how the conversation gets shorter. The agent should understand more over time. But understanding more should never automatically mean controlling more. Don’t simplify the creator. Amplify the creator. How we built it We built the project as a browser-based editing environment using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, browser media APIs, Node.js, MediaPipe, OpenAI Responses API models, and WebMCP. The architecture is deliberately divided into several roles. First, the system needs eyes . The application gathers visual and temporal information from the video rather than relying only on a single signal such as silence detection. Local browser analysis and MediaPipe provide useful lightweight information. But I intentionally added more capable semantic vision and reasoning as well. That choice makes the system heavier than a simple rules-based automatic editor. It was intentional. A collaborator should be able to distinguish between: “There is little sound here.” and: “This quiet moment may be worth keeping because it carries the reaction after the previous moment.” Those are very different kinds of understanding. Next comes the brain . The reasoning layer uses the available visual and project context together with Creator Intent to produce semantic KEEP / CUT / INSPECT_MORE judgments and reasoned editing proposals. The proposals are presented to the Human instead of silently becoming final decisions. Then comes the workbench . The editor has real timeline state, SOURCE / OUTPUT mapping, preview and committed states, effects, audio tools, Shared Context, Undo, Save, Restore, and Export. Finally, WebMCP gives the agent structured ways to interact with the same environment. The current prototype exposes 20 WebMCP tools. One of our core implementation principles was: Rules constrain the hands. The model supplies the brain. A capable model can reason creatively. But the actions it is allowed to perform should still have explicit boundaries. We also treated reversibility as part of the architecture rather than an emergency feature. Previewed state and committed state are separated. The Human can compare SOURCE and OUTPUT. AI suggestions can be corrected. Undo is part of normal collaboration. Shared Context carries the current session/editor and saved project state into later interactions. However, we deliberately do not claim permanent personal memory across every future project. The current continuity boundary is explicit. Save preserves project state. Export produces an actual WebM video. The interface is also organized around capabilities rather than a mandatory AI-controlled workflow. The Human can move between CUT, Effects, BGM/SFX, KAI, Shared Context, timeline controls, Undo, Save, and Export. I did not want to give someone new legs and then put them on an automated conveyor belt. Challenges we ran into The hardest question was not: “How can we make AI edit video?” It was: “Where should the AI stop?” If the AI could only tell the Human which button to click, then it would still be standing outside the creative world. But if it automatically made every important creative decision, then we would solve the technical barrier by removing the creator. Neither result interested me. The difficult space was between those two extremes. Another challenge was perception. It would have been much easier, cheaper, and faster to build the editor around lightweight signals: silence, motion, face direction, audio peaks, simple timing rules. Those signals are useful. But they cannot answer some of the questions that matter most during creative work: Why are we not cutting this quiet part? Why are you recommending

title: MusterMind - The wearability agent — buy, restyle, or skip
pitch: The first shopping agent that can tell you not to buy. Buy, restyle, wait or skip — every verdict cited to you, to product data, or to the rules, live over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The first shopping agent that can tell you not to buy. Buy, restyle, wait or skip — every verdict cited to you, to product data, or to the rules, live over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We started somewhere else. The first idea was a size recommender — obvious fashion-commerce problem. Then we opened DevTools on a live AJIO product page and found something that reframed the whole project. Sitting in window.__PRELOADED_STATE__ , invisible to any agent driving the DOM, was a size chart already converted to centimetres , an explicit measurementType: "Garment Measurement" provenance flag, live per-size stock counts, and — the thing we didn't expect — a crowd fit distribution: Perfect 64% · Tight 15% · Too Tight 5% · Loose 11% · Too Loose 3% over 2,100 raters The page already knew this garment runs small. It had no way to tell an agent. But the moment that actually defined the product came later. Our first working version ranked a ₹320 polo as the top buy for a client dinner. It was cheap, in stock, not a duplicate, and technically satisfied every constraint. It was also completely wrong — a polo does not become client-dinner appropriate because it is cheap. That is the failure mode of every shopping agent we've used. They can only say buy , so they optimise for the one signal they can read: price and availability. We rebuilt the engine around a different question — what if the agent could say no? What it does Mustermind is a wearability decision layer. You give it an occasion, a budget, a PIN code, a deadline, fits you avoid, and a rough list of what you already own. It scores live AJIO products on four axes: product facts, your constraints, purchase risk, and rewear value. Every garment gets one of four verdicts: Verdict Meaning buy Worth buying for this occasion restyle You can already assemble this look from what you own wait Right piece, wrong price or arrives too late skip Violates a stated constraint, duplicates something owned, or can't be delivered Every verdict carries the factors behind it, and every factor is tagged with its source — you, product data, or the rules. A real card from the running app: RESTYLE — You can get this look from what you own U.S. Polo Assn. · Men Button Down-Collar Tailored Fit Shirt · ₹1,175 + Within budget [user] ₹1,175 against a ₹3,000 ceiling − Close to what you own [rules] You already have White Shirts; this adds a colour, not a category · Rewear value [rules] Pairs with 1 item you already own + Right register [rules] Shirts suits client dinner + Fit confidence [product] 90% — garment measurements published, 77 fit ratings + Suggested size M [product] 16% of 77 raters found this loose vs 5% tight, so one size down · Deliverable, no date [product] Serviceable at 560029; the delivery API did not return a date That last line matters as much as the verdict. The delivery API returned no date, so the app doesn't invent one. Load the default brief and Mustermind recommends nothing. Two restyles, five skips, four different skip reasons. Then tell the agent "I could stretch to ₹5,500" and a blazer becomes the single buy — on screen, with the reason visible, and the change written to a Decision Ledger showing that you made it. How we built it Zero npm dependencies. Node 20 and vanilla HTML/CSS/JS. Nothing to install, no lockfile, no bundler — a judge can read the entire thing. It ships as a ~55 MB Alpine container running non-root. Five WebMCP tools , registered on document.modelContext with navigator.modelContext as a fallback probe, behind feature detection: Tool readOnlyHint untrustedContentHint get_current_style_brief ✅ — get_product_truth ✅ ✅ evaluate_wearability ✅ ✅ record_user_tradeoff — — prepare_purchase_handoff — — Five, deliberately. Tool selection degrades as the set grows, and each description is written as product surface — when to call it, what changes state, and when to ask instead of assert . The verdict engine is a rule engine, not a model. This was a deliberate constraint: the agent has to narrate why a verdict is what it is, and a scorer you cannot read gives it nothing to say. Gradient boosting would have scored marginally better and been useless on camera. Crowd fit becomes a directional prior. Too Tight and Too Loose count double — they signal a full size off, not a preference: $$\text{skew} = \frac{\left(t + 2t^{+}\right) - \left(l + 2l^{+}\right)}{100}$$ where $t, l$ are the tight and loose percentages and $t^{+}, l^{+}$ the too tight / too loose ones. We call RUNS_SMALL above a weighted gap of 6. At the rater counts these products carry, the standard error on a $p \approx 0.20$ proportion over $n = 2100$ is $$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \approx 0.0087 \approx 0.9\ \text{pp}$$ so a 6-point weighted gap is several standard errors — signal, not noise. Below 50 raters we return INSUFFICIENT_DATA and refuse to call it at all. Two public AJIO sources , called server-side only: the PDP aggregator and the delivery-promise API, with a 60-second cache and hard timeouts. The style-code invariant is strict — only codes this server obtained from AJIO's own search, or ships fixtures for. Never a code supplied by the browser. No anti-bot sensor header is sent, stored or committed anywhere. If a call would need one, the app falls back to clearly-labelled fixtures instead. There's a grep in the verification step that fails the build if such a string ever appears in the tree. 55 assertions, no test framework. node scripts/selfcheck.js . Challenges we ran into The WebMCP API is not the MCP API. Our tools returned {content:[{type:'text',text:...}]} — the envelope a remote MCP server uses. Chrome's execute returns a plain string . Every result would have arrived as a stringified wrapper the agent had to unwrap. We also assumed an unregisterTool method; there isn't one — unregistration is an AbortSignal passed at registration. Both were caught only by reading Chrome's docs against our own code. The silent one: origin isolation. WebMCP is only exposed in origin-isolated documents. Without Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 , document.modelContext is simply undefined — no error, no warning, nothing to debug. You'd naturally blame your Chrome version and go chasing an upgrade that was never the problem. Real data is hostile in small ways. numUserRatings is "2.1K" , a display string — parse it naively and you fabricate a rater count. Percentages arrive as "15 %" , with a space. The size chart is a superset of what's purchasable (8 charted, 5 buyable on one real product), so recommendations must come from the intersection. One live product returned a fittingType of " " — whitespace, which is truthy, and rendered a factor row with blank evidence. A truthful API answer that was useless. Our demo fixtures had invented SKUs. The live delivery API dutifully returned "not serviceable" for them — which is true, and means the SKU doesn't exist , not that the garment can't be delivered. We were putting fabricated products on real-looking hard fails. Fixture products no longer consult live delivery. A regression we caused ourselves. When live search landed, it loaded eight real style codes — and the PDP allowlist, which only knew about fixtures, rejected every one. The app rendered empty under a confident "Live AJIO data" badge. Fixing it meant sharpening the invariant rather than loosening it: codes AJIO's own search returned are server-obtained, so they earn a session allowlist; browser-supplied codes never do. Then the fix had its own bug — the search cache outlived the session allowlist, so the first Reset handed back codes the adapter then refused. Both are now regression-tested. Knowing when to stop being clever. The hardest call was making wrong register a hard stop instead of a weighted negative. Softening it makes price pull junk back to the top of the list, and the whole argument collapses. Accomplishments that we're proud of It opens with zero buys. A recommender that cannot say "you already own something that works" will eventually sell you a fourth white shirt. Getting the rules honest enough to recommend nothing — and then having that be the most compelling thing on screen — is the accomplishment. Four skips, four different reasons. Wrong register, already owned, avoided fit, undeliverable. Not one score threshold wearing four hats. The agent cannot spend your money. prepare_purchase_handoff is two-phase: it returns AWAITING_CONFIRMATION , a card appears, and only a real DOM click mints a single-use token — bound to style code and size, expiring in 60 seconds. Guessing an ID, replaying a used one, or swapping the size after confirmation all fail, and all four are asserted. There is no cart, checkout, login, orders or payment access anywhere in the codebase. It degrades honestly. Fixture mode is labelled in a banner, a header badge, and a per-card pill, and tool results carry dataSource so the agent discloses it. Serviceable-with-no-date says exactly that. title: Noema Blueprint
pitch: Noema Blueprint lets people and agents design a private AI setup together in the browser. One scan configures, downloads, and launches it in Noema, a local AI app available on iOS and iPadOS.
about_excerpt: Noema Blueprint lets people and agents design a private AI setup together in the browser. One scan configures, downloads, and launches it in Noema, a local AI app available on iOS and iPadOS. Like Comment Story Updates Create a private on-device Noema project from the web: without sharing files, prompts, conversations, or account data. Choose a purpose, device, local model, and runtime while the final Blueprint updates live. Blueprint Forge validates the manifest, model catalog entry, and handoff payload before sending anything to Noema. Compare candidate runtimes, context sizes, privacy, and settings before choosing the final Blueprint. Send the Blueprint by QR code or deep link: no login, pairing, files, prompts, or conversations included. 1. Noema checks the iPhone, verifies the local model download, and opens a private, ready-to-use chat. Noema Blueprint Inspiration Wanting to run local and private AI should not require people to become infrastructure experts. Today, setting up a local model means researching compatibility, device limits, runtime behavior, and download size before even sending a prompt. We wanted setup to feel like designing a workspace with an expert beside you. WebMCP turns the page into a shared workspace for both the person and the agent. The person can directly choose the Project goal, target device, runtime preset, model, and final Blueprint. The agent can inspect that same visible state, tune advanced model settings, fork and compare alternatives, audit candidates, and stage recommendations. Every agent suggestion remains visible, and only the person can approve it or choose what gets handed off. What it does Noema Blueprint is a visual studio for creating a private local AI Project. A person chooses what they want to accomplish and where they want to run their AI. Agents can then inspect the live Blueprint, change supported settings, fork alternative candidates, compare them, and stage recommendations directly on the page. Every proposed change appears visibly. The person remains the only one who can choose the final candidate. When the Blueprint is ready, the website creates a QR code and a same-device link containing a validated configuration. The agent can also return the QR code directly inside the conversation. Scanning the code opens Noema on your device (iOS, iPadOS). The app checks the configuration against the actual device before asking for approval. If the selected model is missing, Noema downloads it. The settings are then applied and the finished Project opens ready for a private conversation. The handoff is stateless. The link contains no files, prompts, credentials, or personal data. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent could recommend settings, but the person would need to reproduce them manually inside a different interface. With WebMCP, the agent operates the exact page the person is viewing. The Blueprint becomes a shared source of truth. The agent can explore possibilities while the person sees the consequences before anything becomes final. This makes setup faster without turning it into invisible automation. It also enables a workflow that was previously more opaque: an agent can help construct and evaluate a local AI environment, then hand the reviewed result to the device where it will actually run. How we built it The website is a React application written in TypeScript. It registers 12 narrowly scoped tools using document.modelContext.registerTool . Those tools operate on the same Blueprint state rendered by the interface. They let an agent inspect the current configuration, edit supported values, create candidates, compare them, stage proposals, validate the result, and prepare the handoff. The tool schemas accept only known models and bounded configuration values. Tool registration uses AbortSignal lifecycle handling. If WebMCP is unavailable, the complete interface remains usable manually. The final Blueprint is canonicalized and validated before being encoded as a versioned base64url manifest. The website places that manifest inside a Noema universal link and renders it as a QR code. The native receiver is built with SwiftUI. Noema accepts only the dedicated Blueprint route and maps public identifiers through its trusted model catalog. The app performs its own compatibility checks and preserves explicit download consent. Challenges The hardest design problem was deciding what the agent should be allowed to do. If the agent could silently select the final candidate or deploy it, the page would stop being collaborative. We separated proposals from approval so agent assistance remains visible and reversible. WebMCP is still experimental, so the page also needed a complete manual path. Feature detection keeps the experience functional in browsers without the API. The cross-device link created another trust boundary. We rejected arbitrary model URLs and unsupported settings. The native app treats every website value as a request rather than an instruction. We also had to balance helpful planning with hardware reality. The website can guide the person, but only the destination device can make the final compatibility decision. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when the webpage is a shared object and when it doesn't act as merely a front end for a hidden API. The person should be able to see what the agent understands and watch the result change. We also learned that local setup can feel magical without hiding important decisions. The right abstraction should be a clear plan that requires approval. Hackathon scope NoemaAI existed before the challenge. Noema Blueprint and its WebMCP tool surface were built during the submission period. The Blueprint Forge workflow and cross-device handoff were also created as part of this work. The public repository includes dated commit history showing the challenge implementation. title: PrismLaunch - Launch Video Creator
pitch: Your AI agent creates your product's promo video. You direct it on a shared timeline, review each stage, and decide what ships.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent creates your product's promo video. You direct it on a shared timeline, review each stage, and decide what ships. Like Comment Story Updates Dark-mode editor: an editable 45-second promo on a shared timeline, with layered visuals and frame-accurate playback. Style frames: review reusable brand, typography, UI and sound elements before the agent builds the animatic. Saved activity: review the agent’s tool calls, captured frames, revisions and human approvals alongside the current film. Modular project files: separate JSON for creative stages, elements, tracks and activity keeps each part easy to inspect. Light-mode storyboards: play each shot’s composition and movement before approving the film’s visual direction. Inspiration I build products, but I don't know how to make a good promo video. Learning motion graphics is a whole other job, and it becomes another thing standing between finishing a product and showing it to people. I wanted my AI agent to help with that. It already understood the product I was building. The missing piece was an editor it could actually use. Asking an agent to control a video timeline through screenshots, dragging, and clicking was a fragile way to work. WebMCP gave me a practical way to expose the editing operations directly. That became PrismLaunch: a promo video editor built for a person and their agent to use together. What it does You give your agent the product, the audience, and the message. It develops the film in PrismLaunch while you review the work in the studio. The process moves through a brief, concepts, script, visual storyboard, style frames, animatic, polish, and final build. Storyboards show the composition and timed movement of each shot. Style frames show the reusable elements and sample compositions the agent plans to use. You can approve each stage or send it back with a note. The agent revises the same project, and a saved activity log records submissions, decisions, and edits. Review panels stay focused on the work; manual editing tools live in the editor. The shared timeline combines text, images, video, audio, shapes, device frames, motion, and editable HTML components. Reusable elements let the agent define a piece once and update its placements throughout the film. The finished composition can be encoded as an MP4 in the browser. I used PrismLaunch to make the promo video for PrismLaunch itself. Watch the promo video made with PrismLaunch . Why WebMCP fits Video editing involves precise operations: placing a clip at a frame, changing its duration, moving it to another layer, adjusting typography, or updating a reusable element. Those operations are much easier to express as structured tools than as a sequence of mouse movements. PrismLaunch exposes tools for project context, creative stages, layers, elements, clips, preview, frame capture, and render requests. The agent can inspect the current project and make a specific edit. The person sees the result in the same editor and gives feedback there. This makes it possible to work with an agent on an editable film throughout the process. Human review is part of that workflow: stage approval and render approval are controls in the studio, not tools exposed for the agent to call. PrismLaunch does not contain its own model. You bring the agent you already use. How I built it I came up with the idea from my own painful experience and used Claude Code to build the core functionality. I then used Codex to test the WebMCP workflow in the browser and fix issues that my Claude Code setup could not directly exercise. The studio uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript. WebMCP tools register via document.modelContext.registerTool , with a compatibility path for browsers that expose the older API location. Zod validates tool inputs, and human edits and agent edits go through the same state and timeline operations. Remotion renders the composition for preview and export, with WebCodecs encoding the MP4 in the browser. Projects can live in a linked local folder or in browser storage, with separate JSON files for each creative stage, element, and track, plus a saved activity log. The app is hosted on Vercel, and its source is available under the MIT license. Challenges and what I learned The hardest part was teaching an AI how to make a good promo when I am still learning video editing myself. I analysed successful promo videos, turned what I learned into a filmmaking guide, and built reusable elements that an agent could combine in its own films. Pacing, hierarchy, and knowing what to leave out mattered as much as having editing tools. Making PrismLaunch's own promo became a practical test of the product. Early storyboards looked too much like scripts, so I built visual boards with positioned subjects and timed movement. The first animatic also exposed a gap in the method: copying storyboard roughs onto a timeline did not produce a finished sequence. I strengthened the filmmaking guide and added a check that refuses animatic submissions while storyboard roughs remain visible. That workflow uncovered product bugs too. I fixed review notes that failed validation, activity that disappeared after reopening, and style-frame reviews that exposed editing tools. I split browser-stored projects into separate files for creative stages, elements, tracks, and activity. I also improved media preparation and playhead synchronisation to address interruptions during playback. Real WebMCP testing exposed issues that the local fallback did not. Multiple components initially registered the same tools, causing partial registration failures. Later, ChatGPT's built-in browser disabled discovery because the growing tool catalogue exceeded its supported limits. I introduced shared registration and five compact toolsets—workflow, graphics, media, elements, and edit—with prism.use_toolset to switch between them. Long sessions can still require reconnecting when a host retains earlier catalogues. Publishing a skill was not enough to ensure an agent received it. Creative WebMCP edits now require that both the operating guide and the filmmaking guide be delivered via prism.read_guide . The agent still has to apply that guidance well. I learned that an agent-friendly editor needs precise tools, inspectable state, visible feedback, and a clear point where the person decides whether the work is ready. What I am proud of PrismLaunch made its own promo video. That took the idea beyond a tool-registration demo and into the task I originally needed help with. I also tested the WebMCP experience in Chrome and ChatGPT's built-in browser. Working through those differences helped turn the editor into something I could actually use with an agent. Current limitations This is an early editor with a small motion library. External agents need a browser and client with native WebMCP support; the fallback registry is only usable within the page. Tool discovery can vary between hosts, and long sessions may require reconnecting if the host retains earlier tool catalogues. Local folder access depends on browser support and a person granting permission. Browser storage is an alternative, but an agent must edit those projects through the page's tools rather than ordinary filesystem tools. MP4 export depends on browser codec support and the resources available on the user's device. What's next I want to build a much richer motion graphics library that agents can draw from when making promo videos: more reusable elements, more visual treatments, and more ways to clearly communicate a product.
