I developed the filmmaking guide and reusable elements, reviewed each creative stage, and used the app to make its own promo. title: Research Blackboard
pitch: Research Blackboard uses WebMCP to turn scattered research into a versioned map that humans and agents can inspect, update, and verify together—so useful work survives the chat.
about_excerpt: Research Blackboard uses WebMCP to turn scattered research into a versioned map that humans and agents can inspect, update, and verify together—so useful work survives the chat. Like Comment Story Updates Why I made this I am a mathematician, and the example project in the app comes from an actual problem I have been working on: the $N$-commutator problem for derivations, with the expected threshold $$ N=n^2+2n-2. $$ The project has accumulated many possible approaches: tree cancellation, representation theory, computations for small $N$, path decompositions, and threshold arguments. Some approaches overlap, some depend on unproved intermediate claims, and some looked promising before running into an obstruction. Keeping all of this in my head became difficult. A paper only presents the final linear argument. Ordinary notes record pieces of the process, but they do not make the relationships between those pieces easy to see. Chat conversations have the same problem: an agent can produce a useful observation, but it usually remains somewhere inside a long transcript. That was the starting point for Research Blackboard. How the idea changed The first version of the idea was much larger. I imagined groups of agents with roles, communication channels, and assigned research directions. We tested that idea and found no clear evidence that a complicated multi-agent system reasoned better than one capable agent using its own tools and subagents. It was also adding a lot of interface without solving the central problem. So I removed it. The final project does not try to run agents. It gives an agent a structured place to work. Ideas, lemmas, computations, obstructions, resources, and tasks live on a persistent map. An agent can read the relevant part of that map through WebMCP and add useful results back to it. Building it with Codex I built the project together with Codex. I made the product and research-workflow decisions, while Codex helped implement the application, debug it, write regression tests, and deploy successive versions. The process was very iterative. I would test the live site and notice something concrete: notes behaved strangely while dragging, relations were hard to read, the canvas could not move far enough left, the inspector occupied too much space, or an agent could edit a project but could not create or navigate between projects. Codex would inspect the implementation, make the change, test it, and deploy a new version. This was also useful for rejecting bad features. At one stage the application had agent groups, roles, activity feeds, and communication ideas. They made the product look more “agentic,” but they did not make it more useful. Most of them were removed. Technically, the application uses TypeScript, React, Vinext, Vite, and React Flow. It runs as a Cloudflare Worker. Cloudflare D1 and Drizzle ORM store projects, revisions, membership, and activity history. Mathematical notes use Markdown and KaTeX. The app exposes twenty typed WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . They cover project navigation, bounded branch reads, nested idea scopes, versioned node updates, directed relations, resources, and tasks. What was difficult The main challenge was making this more than a mind map. Containment and relations had to mean different things. A lemma may live inside one idea while still supporting something outside it. Resources should exist once at the project level but remain usable from many branches. Local notes should stay hidden until the researcher opens their parent idea. Cycles also needed a deliberate rule. A conceptual cycle can be meaningful: two approaches may refine or support one another. A dependency cycle is different. The application therefore permits ordinary relational cycles but rejects circular depends on chains. Agent writes introduced another group of problems. Repeated calls should not create duplicate objects. Two edits should not silently overwrite one another. Two agents should not claim the same task without noticing. I added operation identifiers, object versions, project revisions, and atomic task claims to address these cases. The visual board also took more work than expected. Dragging, resizing, zooming, negative coordinates, edge labels, nested scopes, and collapsible panels all had to work without losing the underlying research state. What I learned The most useful WebMCP applications may not be the ones where an agent completely replaces the human workflow. Here, the website remains useful on its own. WebMCP gives the agent access to the same objects and operations that the researcher already uses. The human still has an essential role. During one smoke test, an agent saved the standard parameterization of Pythagorean triples. I noticed that it had omitted the scaling factor and the conditions for primitive triples. The agent then corrected the existing resource in place. The corrected version and its history remained on the board. That interaction is close to what I wanted: the agent performs explicit work, the human checks the meaning, and neither has to reconstruct the project from an old conversation. Research Blackboard does not solve research problems automatically. It tries to preserve the structure of the attempt. title: Resolve Guard
pitch: A deterministic invocation-time policy gateway that makes routed MCP/WebMCP authority visible, blockable, exactly approvable, and replay-safe.
about_excerpt: A deterministic invocation-time policy gateway that makes routed MCP/WebMCP authority visible, blockable, exactly approvable, and replay-safe. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Browser agents can combine a person's intent, page content, tool metadata, tool results, credentials, and remembered context inside one decision loop. The individual pieces may look harmless, while the composed action quietly moves protected data to another origin, invokes a changed tool, presents a credential to the wrong resource, or turns a vague confirmation into a consequential side effect. Prompt-injection classification alone cannot reconstruct the authority that was lost. Advanced users and agent developers need one visible enforcement point that evaluates the actual invocation at the moment it would run. Solution Resolve Guard is an invocation-time security gateway and synthetic attack lab for one instrumented MCP/WebMCP client. Every protected call is normalized into an action envelope and evaluated by twelve deterministic checks: actor and client identity, browser origin, pinned MCP server, credential audience, least scopes, tool-manifest pin, schema pin, exact arguments, canonical destination, capability class, data-flow policy, and effect policy. The result is one of three explicit outcomes: Allow: bounded local work proceeds automatically. Block: a failed invariant stops execution and cannot be overridden by approval. Review: a policy-valid consequential action stops at a trusted, exact human approval surface. An approval is short-lived and bound to one normalized invocation, including its actor, client, origin, server, tool, effect, destination, data labels, argument digest, policy version, and expiry. Execution is at-most-once; replay returns the original operation instead of creating a second effect. The audit trail records correlated identifiers, decisions, and digests without raw protected content or credentials. Why This Matters WebMCP makes websites meaningfully agent-native: an agent can discover and invoke structured capabilities instead of guessing through a visual interface. That also creates composed authority across the person, browser, page, agent, MCP client, MCP server, credential, tool, and destination. Resolve Guard uses WebMCP to make that composition inspectable and enforceable. The agent can discover the security lab, inspect policy, run preflights, explain failures, and synchronize results into the same visual surface the person sees. The person retains the only approval surface for consequential work. Together they can investigate unsafe actions quickly without giving the agent a protocol tool that approves its own request. This proof of concept deliberately makes a narrow claim: it protects calls routed through one instrumented gateway. It does not claim to secure bypassed calls, compromised browsers or operating systems, dishonest providers after an allowed call leaves the boundary, or every future attack. How We Used AI The application itself demonstrates structured human-agent collaboration through imperative WebMCP tools. A WebMCP-capable agent can: list the seven deterministic attack scenarios; inspect the gateway policy and coverage boundary; run a scenario preflight; retrieve a redacted decision; and inspect the metadata-only audit trail. The agent cannot approve or execute a review decision through MCP or WebMCP. That omission is intentional: useful analysis remains agent-accessible, while the consequential boundary remains visible and human-controlled. All demo identities, documents, credentials, destinations, and effects are synthetic. Resolve Guard itself calls no external provider and uses no production credential. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the participant-directed security concept into a scoped proof of concept, threat model, policy engine, REST/MCP/WebMCP surfaces, adversarial scenarios, responsive attack-lab interface, tests, browser verification, and documentation. The process included an explicit product pivot: an earlier seller-operations concept was discarded after the participant clarified that the real goal was to restore disappearing security boundaries between people, browser agents, MCP clients, servers, tools, credentials, and side effects. Codex rebuilt the project around that corrected outcome rather than rewording the obsolete implementation. Codex also ran a real native WebMCP session in the in-app browser. That run exposed a runtime boundary gap: the browser surfaced additionalProperties: false to the agent but did not enforce it before calling the page handler. A regression test locked the defect, the page execution boundary was hardened with independent exact-key validation, and the invalid call was re-run with zero audit or operation side effects. The final automated suite passes 31 tests. Key Features Seven deterministic proof scenarios covering safe local work, injected exfiltration, parameter smuggling, destination confusion, tool drift, credential-audience mismatch, and exact approval/replay. Twelve ordered, explainable invocation checks with stable allow/block/review reason codes. Five same-origin imperative WebMCP tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Strict runtime validation in every page-defined tool before API I/O or UI mutation. Independent tool-manifest and input-schema pins. Default-deny protected-data egress and canonical exact-destination enforcement. Exact, short-lived, single-use, UI-only human approval. At-most-once sandbox execution with idempotent replay. Metadata-only correlated audit with canary-backed redaction tests. Dependency-free Node.js 22 implementation, responsive keyboard-accessible UI, local MCP HTTP/stdio transport, and a sealed synthetic public-demo mode. Architecture One in-memory domain service backs the visible browser UI, REST endpoints, MCP over HTTP/stdio, and imperative WebMCP tools, so every surface shares the same decision semantics. user goal + page/tool/result content | mixed trust with provenance v instrumented browser agent / MCP client | every protected invocation v Resolve Guard enforcement point normalize -> authenticate -> authorize -> data-flow check | allow | block | exact review v X v pinned sandbox tool visible approval surface | | +------ execute once <----+ The public demo is deliberately sealed: fixed fake identities, synthetic source data, in-memory effects, no credentials, and no outbound server request. Testing Instructions Public judge flow Open https://resolve-guard.vercel.app in ChatGPT's WebMCP-capable in-app browser, or Google Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and the browser restarted. Confirm the header reports five registered WebMCP tools. Run Safe local summary . Expect allow / LOCAL_FLOW_ALLOWED and one bounded synthetic operation. Run Injected exfiltration . Expect block / DATA_EGRESS_DENIED and no operation. Run Hidden callback parameter . Expect block / UNKNOWN_ARGUMENT . Run Publish sanitized status . Expect review / HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED and no operation before approval. Open the exact approval, enter the visible confirmation, execute, then replay. Expect the same operation to be returned and no second effect. Open the audit trail. Confirm it contains decision/approval/operation metadata and digests, not raw protected content or credentials. Suggested agent prompts “List the Resolve Guard security scenarios and state its coverage boundary.” “Run the injected exfiltration preflight and explain why it cannot execute.” “Run the sanitized publish preflight.” Confirm the agent stops at HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED and exposes no approval or execution tool. Local verification npm start npm run verify Requirements: Node.js 22.14 or newer. There are no package dependencies and no credentials to configure. Public Demo Link https://resolve-guard.vercel.app Public Repository Link https://github.com/VIVEHACKER/resolve-guard The repository is public, includes the complete MIT license at the root, and contains all source, assets, run instructions, tests, and WebMCP registration code. Anonymous HTTPS clone, raw-file access, the public main branch, WebMCP registration code, and GitHub's MIT license detection were verified after publication. Demo Video Public YouTube video: https://youtu.be/8uttf0gkMqE Visibility independently verified as Public. Duration: 2:30, below the three-minute limit. 1080p H.264 video with English AAC narration. Custom thumbnail and published English captions. Anonymous playback and audible playback were verified. The video is an uninterrupted, mouse-driven walkthrough of the real visual lab backed by the same policy engine. It shows the page reporting five registered native WebMCP tools and demonstrates allow, block, review, exact approval, at-most-once execution, replay, schema-smuggling rejection, audit evidence, and the honest protection boundary. title: Runbook Studio
pitch: Procedures that people and agents write, run and improve together. When a step no longer matches reality, the run records it, and the agent turns that into a fix.
about_excerpt: Procedures that people and agents write, run and improve together. When a step no longer matches reality, the run records it, and the agent turns that into a fix. Like Comment Story Updates A procedure held as structured data. Each step carries an instruction, a check saying what proof looks like, and an optional condition. Inspiration We run a small agency and a SaaS product on our own infrastructure, so we live on written procedures. Onboarding a client, restoring a backup, rotating a credential. They get written once, carefully, and then the software underneath them changes. A tab is renamed, a field moves, a step becomes somebody else's job. Within months a good portion of the document is wrong. What struck us is why that happens. The moment you discover a procedure is wrong is precisely the moment you cannot fix it. You are mid-task, under time pressure, and correcting the document is somebody else's job. So you work around it silently and move on, and the next person hits the same wall. WebMCP suggested a way out. If the procedure is something an agent can read and edit while you are standing in front of it, then finding the error and fixing it stop being separate jobs. What it does Runbook Studio holds a procedure as structured data rather than prose. Every step has a title, an instruction, an optional check stating what proof looks like, and an optional condition that sends the run to a different step when something is already true. Because the steps are data, three things become possible in one place. Write it with the agent. Ask it to split a vague step, add checks, reorder, or add a condition, and watch the document rearrange. Every change the agent makes is marked on the page. Run it with the agent. A run walks the steps in order, honouring conditions. At each step you confirm the check, or you record a blocker saying what you found instead. Improve it from the run. The blocker is pinned to the step that failed. Afterwards, the agent reads it and amends that step to match reality. That loop is the point. Documentation that gets better every time somebody uses it. The model is domain-neutral. Three examples ship with the app: onboarding a client into a CRM, restoring a database from a backup, and a cooking recipe. How we built it Next.js and TypeScript, client-side state, no database, no authentication. Self-hosted on our own infrastructure behind nginx-proxy. The only server-side component is an optional route that proxies to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for the built-in agent, rate limited and turn capped. 13 tools are registered on document.modelContext, covering the full lifecycle: reading the runbook, editing steps, setting checks and conditions, running, recording blockers, and turning blockers into amendments. Design decisions worth naming: Tool descriptions are the interface: they are written for a model to read, not a developer. We tested selection accuracy by giving the raw getTools() output to models with no other context and checking which tools they chose for real instructions. Descriptions were tuned until selection was reliable across independent models. The annotations are used properly. readOnlyHint on read tools, untrustedContentHint wherever user-written content flows back to the model. Chrome's budgets are respected: names under 30 characters, descriptions under 500, parameter descriptions under 150, and an output guard that trims oversized responses with a hint to use a narrower tool instead. Tools stay same-origin. exposedTo is unset, so no cross-origin frame can call them. Registration takes an AbortSignal: the execution-time signal is treated as optional, since it is not supplied in the Chrome build we tested against. The app also ships with its own agent, so it needs no browser flag and no ChatGPT to try. A built-in harness discovers the page's tools with getTools() and runs them with executeTool(), either manually or by sending a sentence to a model that chooses the tools itself. With no model configured, manual mode still works with zero setup. Verification was done against Chrome for Testing with native WebMCP, driving executeTool through Playwright and asserting on the resulting DOM, so no tool is reported working on the basis of code inspection alone. Challenges we ran into The API is new and the documentation moves. Older material uses navigator.modelContext; current Chrome uses document.modelContext. The API is undefined outside a secure context, which makes several obvious testing approaches fail silently rather than loudly. Steering a model reliably. Given only tool descriptions, a model would sometimes re-read every step, propose a change instead of making it, or keep editing after finishing. We fixed this with server-side guards rather than by making the tools more forgiving, because the tools have to behave correctly for any agent, not only ours. We could not test in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Our development machine is old enough that it is capped at a Chrome version predating WebMCP, and it cannot run the ChatGPT desktop app at all. So we never saw our own app inside the environment the judges will use. We compensated rather than hoped. Every tool was verified against Chrome for Testing 152 with native WebMCP, headless on our server, driving executeTool through Playwright and asserting on the resulting DOM. We separately tested tool-selection accuracy by giving the raw getTools() output to models with no other context, checking they chose the right tools for real instructions before we relied on the descriptions. The constraint turned out to be productive. Because we could not lean on ChatGPT, we built the app its own agent instead, which means anyone can try it with no browser flag, no desktop app and no API key. That is a better product than the one we would have shipped with easier hardware. Failure has to be as easy as success. If recording a blocker were harder than confirming a step, people would confirm and move on, and the loop would never close. Both controls sit together, same size, one click apart. Accomplishments that we're proud of The loop actually closes. A blocker recorded during a run becomes an amendment to the document, and the procedure is measurably more accurate afterwards than it was before somebody used it. Every tool was individually verified as firing and changing the page, not assumed correct from reading the code. The whole app is operable by keyboard, agent changes are announced through a live region, and it works with no browser flag at all. What we learned Naming is not cosmetic when a model is one of the readers. We renamed "branch" to "condition" throughout the interface, because "branch" is developer language borrowed from version control and told a first-time reader nothing. The tool kept its original name for the model. The two audiences did not want the same word. We also found that the work we did on semantic structure, accessible names and live-region announcements serves agent legibility as much as assistive technology. Both consume the page as structure rather than pixels. Building well for one turned out to be building well for the other. What's next for Runbook Studio Multiple checks per step, richer conditions, and shared runbooks so a blocker recorded by one person amends the procedure for everybody. I made the calls on how checks and conditions should read to someone seeing them for the first time, which led to renaming "branch" to "condition" in the interface while keeping the original name for the model. I wrote and recorded the narration. My first time building against WebMCP, and the most interesting part was discovering how much the wording of a tool description matters when a model is the one reading it. title: Streaming Lens — streaming market data, agent-native
pitch: Market research on streaming — micro-drama, African OTT, piracy, sports rights. Free WebMCP tools tell an agent what the paid data covers and how fresh it is, without returning a value.
about_excerpt: Market research on streaming — micro-drama, African OTT, piracy, sports rights. Free WebMCP tools tell an agent what the paid data covers and how fresh it is, without returning a value. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We already sell streaming-market research: 17,470 sourced datapoints on micro-drama, African OTT, piracy, the creator economy and sports rights, behind a paid MCP server with 194 tools. So the WebMCP question was never "what demo could we build" — it was sharper and more uncomfortable: what does a paywalled B2B product do when the visitor is an agent? Today, agents scrape sites like ours. They read the marketing pages, miss the data entirely, and invent the numbers. Blocking them is not an answer either: an agent that leaves with nothing never comes back, and never buys. Giving the data away ends the business. WebMCP allows a fourth option, and that is the whole submission: describe the asset precisely, withhold its substance, and always say where the substance lives. What it does Every page of lens.streaming-radar.com — 49 of them — registers tools on document.modelContext . Seven, all free, no key, no account, and no flag for the visitor to enable: we serve a first-party Chrome origin-trial token in <head> . ask_site — returns the page sections that answer a question, with canonical URLs. search_intelligence_archive — searches the published newsletter editions and analyses. check_data_coverage — the one that carries the idea. Ask about any company, country or topic and it returns how many sourced datapoints we hold, which report silos they sit in, which countries and years they cover, the confidence mix, when the most recent one was updated, and one sample datapoint — metric name, unit, source, confidence — with its value withheld . Asked about ReelShort: 408 datapoints, across five silos, 2022 to 2028, the most recent updated this week. get_market_signals — the live monitoring feed; it also re-renders the visible feed on the page. estimate_streaming_pnl — drives the on-page P&L calculator and returns the model output. Registered on /calculator only: a tool with no valid target is a broken contract. request_report_teaser — the conversion step. Requires an explicit consent argument and fills the page's own email gate, so the human sees what the agent did. browse_reports — the catalogue. Then the boundary itself. Until this week, a paid tool called without entitlement answered Authentication required — three words, a dead end. Now the JSON-RPC error carries error.data : what the silo holds (5,306 datapoints, 51 countries, 2004 to 2033 on our vertical-drama silo), one sample with its value withheld, the URLs to buy or authenticate, and the exact instruction to replay the call with a key. The refusal proves possession instead of ending the conversation. The same computation answers the free tool and the refusal, because they answer the same question and must answer identically. How we built it The site is static HTML with no bundler and no package.json , so the SDK is vendored as a pinned ESM asset and the module graph is injected by the site's page producer , never edited page by page. Tools are side-effect-free ES modules, registered once per document, unregistered on pagehide . The tools never reimplement the page. request_report_teaser calls the site's own email-gate API through a small public seam; estimate_streaming_pnl moves the calculator's real controls and lets the page compute; get_market_signals reads the same endpoint the visible feed reads. One behaviour, one implementation, whether a human or an agent triggers it. Agent traffic is measured server-side with a cookieless beacon — no cookie, no identifier, nothing to consent to — because GA4 only loads after a cookie banner and an agent never clicks Accept. Without it, agent traffic would be strictly invisible. Challenges we ran into A cache header that silently ate a release. Two new tools worked on the origin and reached no browser. Cloudflare Pages does not let a more specific _headers rule override a broader one — it concatenates them: max-age=31536000, immutable, public, max-age=300, must-revalidate . Browsers keep the first directive, so the modules stayed immutable for a year. The fix was to move the whole graph out of the /js/ prefix; there is no negation and no override. Short acronyms matching inside words. Our coverage counter used ILIKE '%ott%' and returned 109 rows; word-bounded, 78. Twenty-eight percent phantom matches in a number we use as a commercial argument. The same bug in our signal matcher had been filing Ridley Scott stories into the sports silo — ott inside Scott , mma inside summary . Both are bounded now, with regression tests. Bilingual pages. Our HTML carries French and English in the same DOM, hidden by CSS. In a detached document no CSS applies, so the first version of ask_site handed agents both languages glued together: "En brefTL;DR". A surface that switches off in silence. Without a valid origin-trial token, document.modelContext simply does not exist and the SDK no-ops — no error anywhere. Our pipeline health check now reads the token off the deployed page, decodes its expiry, and goes red fourteen days before. Accomplishments that we're proud of It is not a demo. It is a production B2B product, the surface is measured, and the independent webmcp.com directory grades the implementation A . 1,404 tests green, including three whose only job is to prove no datapoint value can escape through the free surface. What we learned An agent-native paywall is not a wall with an API. It is a boundary that explains itself. Publish the shape, withhold the substance, always say where the substance lives — everything else follows. What's next for Streaming Lens An agent-reachable checkout, so the handoff completes without a human copying a key. And per-call payment at the edge: our MCP already runs on Cloudflare, and a 402 with a machine-readable price is the same envelope we just built, with an amount attached. title: Finite Witness
pitch: Put a universal claim under pressure. Find the one graph that breaks it.
about_excerpt: Put a universal claim under pressure. Find the one graph that breaks it. Like Comment Story Updates One graph is enough: a ∀ → ∃ pressure rig for finite conjectures. Mobile repair loop keeps each rationale and next universal claim visible. The witness archive preserves the broken claim, search prefix, and deterministic certificate. Mobile witness view with exact graph metrics and certificate fw-b20670c4. Feed the witness back into three explicit repairs, then apply and retest. The first counterexample takes over the shared workbench: 4 vertices after 39 candidates. Finite Witness Inspiration Mathematical conjectures often fail for a small, concrete reason. A universal statement may survive a thousand examples and still end with one graph. Existing graph tools usually split the work: a person operates a visual interface, while an automated system works in a separate script or notebook. The two views drift apart. Finite Witness asks what becomes possible when a person and an agent share the same live mathematical workspace. Its ∀ → ∃ pressure rig makes the logic visible: the person frames the universal claim, the agent or person runs the declared search, and the first existential witness occupies the same sheet. The person can inspect every metric and decide what the mathematics means. What it does Finite Witness is an interactive conjecture laboratory for finite simple graphs. A user can combine assumptions such as connectivity, minimum degree, bipartiteness, parity, edge surplus, and diameter with one of several graph conclusions. The live header rewrites the resulting universal statement as controls change. The app then checks labeled graphs from three vertices upward and stops at the first counterexample or the selected upper bound. The result is an inspectable graph rather than a bare “false” answer. Finite Witness reports its vertices, edges, degree sequence, triangle count, diameter, and bipartite status, together with the exact number of candidate graphs searched. If no witness appears within the bound, the interface explicitly calls the result finite evidence rather than proof. Each witness also receives a deterministic certificate containing the normalized claim, labeled edge mask and edge list, metrics, enumeration order, and exact search counts. Experiments can be shared by URL, filed in the witness archive, and exported as a versioned JSON evidence bundle. Candidate repairs explicitly feed the current witness into the next claim before the rig runs again. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP turns the app from a visual calculator into a shared reasoning surface. The page exposes eight tools that let an agent read the current workspace, load a scenario, configure a conjecture, run the exhaustive search, save the witness, suggest stronger premises, apply a repair and retest it, and retrieve the counterexample certificate. Every agent action uses the same functions as the visible controls and updates the same graph on screen. This creates a useful division of work. The agent handles structured translation, exhaustive execution, and evidence bookkeeping. The human keeps visual control, checks the actual witness, and makes the creative mathematical decision about what to try next. Without WebMCP, the agent would have to guess at form controls or work in a separate environment whose state the person cannot directly inspect. How we built it The app is dependency-free HTML, CSS, and modern JavaScript. Graphs are encoded as integer edge masks. The search engine checks labeled simple graphs in increasing vertex and edge-mask order until it finds a counterexample or reaches the selected bound. It computes connectivity, degree sequence, triangles, bipartiteness, diameter, cycle structure, and perfect matching existence. A Web Worker keeps the interface responsive. WebMCP tools are registered in the top-level page with document.modelContext.registerTool . Their JSON Schemas keep inputs narrow, and tool responses include the resulting claim, graph, metrics, and search counts so an agent can verify the outcome. The human interface still works when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges The first challenge was making agent operations and human controls share one source of truth. Changing a visible assumption invalidates the earlier result immediately, so stale evidence cannot be mistaken for a result about the revised claim. The second was preserving mathematical honesty: an exhaustive search within a finite bound can refute a claim, but failure to find a witness is not a proof. The interface gives that outcome its own bounded-survival state. The final challenge was visual: every control, transition, and result had to express the same ∀ → ∃ argument instead of looking like a collection of dashboard cards. Accomplishments Eight working WebMCP tools with read, write, repair-loop, and certificate workflows. A complete visual product rather than a protocol demonstration. Exact ordered search across labeled simple graphs with three to six vertices, stopping at the first counterexample and recording the searched prefix precisely. Shareable experiments and deterministic witness certificates. Reproducible witness records stored locally and exportable as JSON. A dependency-free public deployment with no account or API key required. A responsive proof-sheet interface whose universal, witness, and repair states follow the actual search state. What we learned Agent-native design works best when tools expose meaningful domain operations, not copies of buttons. “Search for the smallest counterexample” is a stable mathematical action. The interface can then give that action a strong visual consequence without changing the tool contract. What's next The next step is a small declarative language for custom graph predicates, followed by canonical graph generation to extend exhaustive search beyond six vertices. A later version could support finite algebraic structures while preserving the same human-agent evidence workflow. title: Airlock: Agent-Native Data Workspace
pitch: AI analysis for file you can't upload. In-browser DuckDB plus WebMCP tools, every change staged for your approval, with a signed receipt of what the agent saw.
about_excerpt: AI analysis for file you can't upload. In-browser DuckDB plus WebMCP tools, every change staged for your approval, with a signed receipt of what the agent saw. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every team has a spreadsheet nobody is allowed to paste into ChatGPT: compensation, customer lists, finances under NDA. Yet people paste anyway — roughly 11% of ChatGPT pastes contain confidential information, a fifth of breaches now involve shadow AI, and AI chats have been ruled discoverable in court. We wanted the analysis without the upload: AI help with data that physically cannot leave the room. What it does Airlock is a data workspace in a single browser tab. Your file is read locally and queried with in-browser DuckDB-WASM — nothing uploads, ever. An AI agent works on it through WebMCP tools the page exposes: 8 read tools that run immediately and are logged, and 12 staged actions where every change (filters, derived columns, charts, flags, reports, redaction, export) appears as a visible diff that nothing applies until you press Approve. An activity ledger records every call with exact rows disclosed. A signed attestation receipt — hashes and counts, never values — verifies offline at /verify.html . God mode runs a Qwen model fully on-device via WebGPU for genuine airplane-mode analysis, or bring your own endpoint key, which never leaves tab memory. It also imports PDF, DOCX and images OCR'd on-device into queryable tables. How we built it React 18 + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind, npm workspaces. The reusable core is packages/webmcp-staged — a zero-dependency propose→review→commit primitive spanning WebMCP, OpenAI tool-calling and plain MCP transports. DuckDB-WASM, pdf.js, Tesseract and the model weights are all self-hosted same-origin; an egress monitor wrapping fetch/XHR/beacon/WebSocket proves zero bytes leave, live, in the top bar. 530+ tests, npm audit clean, Netlify deploy with COOP/COEP, WASM MIME types and origin-trial support. Challenges we ran into Honesty was harder than engineering: "data never leaves the browser" is false the moment a cloud agent reads query results, so cloud mode states plainly that slices travel (and counts them) while the fully-local loop makes the strong claim literally true. Small models were the second fight — 1.5B-parameter callers loop, invert comparisons and stuff GROUP BY into filter boxes — answered with schema-tolerant tools, corrective errors, repeat guards and a fail-fast circuit breaker. Third was host discovery: WebMCP gates on origin isolation and trial enrollment, which took real header and deploy work. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete loop the camera can verify: offline analysis with Seal at zero, every mutation human-gated, a signed receipt that verifies offline, and an agent surface ChatGPT, a local model, your own endpoint, or the built-in console can all drive unchanged. Plus a reusable MIT primitive any WebMCP app can adopt for the same propose→approve→commit safety. What we learned Agent UX is approval UX — the review queue, not the chat, is where trust happens. A privacy claim the code can't back is worse than no claim at all. And tiny on-device models are usable agents if the tool surface is tight enough to hold them. What's next for Airlock: Agent-Native Data Workspace Depth over breadth: the pay-equity workflow first (EU Pay Transparency deadlines make the receipt a requirement, not a nicety), then adjacent regulated-data reviews. On the tech side: richer provenance-linked reports, local folder and localhost-database sources, and a second independent implementation of the staged-authority protocol so the receipt becomes an interoperable standard, not a single-app artifact. title: Catchfly
pitch: See what agents do with your WebMCP app. Capture production traces, run Chrome WebMCP Evals from CI, and find regressions across app, model and tool versions.
about_excerpt: See what agents do with your WebMCP app. Capture production traces, run Chrome WebMCP Evals from CI, and find regressions across app, model and tool versions. Like Comment Story Updates Incidents | ChatGPT Incidents Releases Cases Inspiration I am an AI researcher and I fight with evals of my agent systems every day. When I heard about WebMCP, I thought it was a perfect fit for data analysis. I usually have a concrete question, and the road from the question to finding the data and visualising it is long. Then a deeper question appears, and I wander down a tree of questions looking for the answer. WebMCP and analytics dashboards are, in my view, a beautiful pair. What it does Catchfly is observability for WebMCP apps, built so an agent can run the investigation next to me. The @catchfly/sdk captures production traces of tool calls, while the @catchfly/cli runs Chrome WebMCP Evals in CI and uploads the report. The dashboard joins both sources per release: Incidents Releases Sessions Regression Explorer Cases The dashboard itself The dashboard itself is a WebMCP app with thirty-eight tools . I ask: "What broke in the latest releases?" The agent reads the incident overview. I ask: "Open the evidence." The view switches on my screen, attributed, with an Undo button. I ask: "Show me the production sessions that failed on this tool." The filters set themselves. I open one, the agent drafts an eval case from it, shows the draft and saves it after my approval. catchfly eval pull brings it into the repo. The tree of questions that used to take me an afternoon fits in one conversation. All of this is written in the lovely Catchfly UI . How we built it Catchfly is built as a TypeScript monorepo : React and Zustand for the dashboard API as Netlify Functions One route table shared with: a standalone server Vite middleware PostgreSQL via Supabase In the app, human clicks and agent tools call the same state actions. Every write returns the resulting state, every change has a source, the human can undo it, and the agent learns about the undo on its next call. Demo environment For the demo, I built a fictional Devpost Review Console with a real WebMCP surface so the Chrome runner has something to evaluate. I also created a deterministic synthetic world containing: 18 releases 25,000 sessions 27,000 eval attempts a deliberate latency false lead I also tested how the app worked in my previous projects using the Catchfly SDK, and everything worked perfectly. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge for me was to design the UI/UX in such a way that the application looks good and is easy to read, both for users and in the tools that support WebMCP, like ChatGPT Browser. At the same time, I’m racking my brains over WebMCP vs. security , but I haven’t come up with much yet. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m really pleased that it’s an end-to-end product . I’m posting it on Discord the day before the hackathon ends, and everyone can still use it because it works and looks cool. What we learned The most important thing: I discovered and learnt WebMCP . It’s great fun - but I wasn’t the only one to notice this, as basically everyone on Discord had a brilliant time collaborating with the agents via ChatGPT. What's next for Catchfly I would love to continue my journey with Catchfly. title: Cedarfield Clinic
pitch: An agent-ready clinic page for people who cannot race a booking form. The agent searches and holds through WebMCP. A press, a palm, or a spoken word is the only thing that books.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready clinic page for people who cannot race a booking form. The agent searches and holds through WebMCP. A press, a palm, or a spoken word is the only thing that books. Like Comment Story Updates Tagline A clinic page that gives your own agent real tools and never lets it book for you. Inspiration Someone in our family needs time to talk. Not to think, to talk. The web punishes that more every year. Cancelled appointments go up at 8:00 and are gone by 8:01. Course seats, visa slots, concert tickets, same story. If you use a switch, a head pointer, or voice control, you lose that race every time, and nobody who built the race was thinking about you. The odd thing is that this same person already has an assistant that understands them fine. It just cannot do anything on a clinic website except look at the buttons and guess. So we built the page we wished existed. Not an app you install and not the clinic's chatbot. A normal public booking page that, when you turn up with your own agent, tells that agent exactly what it may do for you and draws a line it cannot cross. What it does Cedarfield is a made-up clinic that releases cancelled appointments in waves, a few at a time. You open the booking page inside whatever agent you use. We recorded ours with Codex. Through WebMCP the page hands your agent the board, finds times, holds a slot for three minutes, lets it go, waits for whatever you say to the page, and asks you one question with two or three choices. You talk to the page however you can. Type. Speak. Press a phrase. Hold up a hand shape, and the camera reads it as a switch. If you cannot type your name, a scanning keyboard opens and you pick letters with a thumbs up, the way switch users have typed for decades. Your agent takes each request, searches, and holds a time, and when it needs a decision, it asks you on the page instead of in its own window. You answer with a button, a word, or a thumbs up. This is the part we care about most. When the page loads, there is no booking tool. None. Your agent can hold a slot, and it can ask, but it cannot book. A booking tool only comes into existence when you do something an agent cannot do: press a button yourself, hold an open palm to the camera, or say a word that is shown on your screen and nowhere else. Then the tool lives for ten minutes, works once, and disappears. You can watch it appear as a gold chip on the page and watch it die when you take permission back. Cancelling and moving are never handed over at all. If an agent tries to press the confirm button with a script, the press is refused and the count is shown on screen. Every call your agent makes is written on the page in plain English, and a small cursor travels to whatever it touched, so you can see your assistant working instead of taking its word for it. Cedarfield is fictional. The other patients you see taking slots are simulated, and the page says so in its footer. No real appointment is ever made, and your details never leave your browser. How we built it Next.js 15 on Vercel. The page registers tools with document.modelContext . The twelve tools that exist at load time are registered by an inline script in the HTML before any JavaScript bundle runs. We learned the hard way that an agent snapshots the tool list the instant a page opens, and would otherwise see nothing. The app takes over running those tools once it has hydrated. Three more sets of tools are born and die with the state of the page. The board is shared between every visitor and lives in Supabase. Row-level security and security definer procedures enforce the rules. One hold per person. Hold before you book. You can only cancel your own. A clever client cannot take someone else's slot. Hand shapes come from MediaPipe, served from our own domain. Speech is the browser's own recognizer. The scanning keyboard is a hundred-line state machine with tests. Every number you see on the page is measured by the code that displays it. One interaction from you. Three appointments left. Held for 2:41. We did not want a single decorative number. Challenges we ran into The first-call problem above cost us a whole audit round. Three fresh loads, three failures, all because React had not hydrated yet. Yes is a trap. It is the one word an agent can say too. So a spoken yes only counts when the page itself asked a visible question. The microphone is ignored while the page is talking. The page's voice client cannot run at the same time. For a noisy room, there is a word on screen you can say instead. We wanted to call the hand shapes sign language, and we cannot. Five shapes, not a language, and the page says exactly that. It stung. Claiming ASL with a gesture model would have been a lie to the people we built this for. Agents are slow. Ten to forty seconds per tool call in a chat client. Our forty-five-second hold kept expiring while the agent was still telling the user about it. Holds are three minutes now and the timer on screen is real. Accomplishments that we're proud of We got an agent to book an appointment for someone who never touched the page. That was the whole point, and it took twenty builds in one night to get there, because every time a real hand tried it, something real broke. The thumbs up never fired because our confidence bar was set for a lab and not a laptop camera. The palm met a closed lens because two cameras were fighting over one webcam. The agent never asked a question because nothing in our tool answers told it to. We found each of those with a person's hand in front of the screen, fixed the cause, and put it in front of the same hand again. The part we are most proud of is the line the agent cannot cross. There is no booking tool on this page until a person makes one exist, with a press, a palm, or a word only they can see. The tool then lives ten minutes, works once, and dies. We tried to break it ourselves with scripted clicks and a second agent auditing the live page cold, and it held every time. And it works for the person we built it for. Someone who cannot move their hands can open this page, type their name with two hand shapes, ask for a time with one finger, answer their agent's question with a thumbs up, grant permission with an open palm, and get a booking with a reference number and a calendar file. No touch. No voice. Nobody else in the room. What we learned Getting an agent to call tools is a weekend. Getting a page to decide what an agent may do for this person, right now, and to change its mind the moment the person does, is the actual work. We learned that the tool list is part of the page, not something you add after it loads. Agents snapshot the page the instant it opens. If your tools arrive a second later, the agent has already decided you have none. We learned that yes is a trap. It is the one word an agent can say too. A page that books on yes cannot tell its visitor from its assistant. So the page only listens for yes when it asks the question itself, ignores the microphone while it is speaking, and shows a word on screen for the room where that is not enough. We learned that a camera is a shared resource with one owner, that a hold has to outlive an agent's thinking time, and that agents follow the sentence you put at the end of a tool result far more faithfully than anything you put in a prompt. We learned to say no to our own idea. Five hand shapes are not sign language, and we took the words off the page. And we learned why WebMCP is different from an API. An API cannot see the visitor's palm. A scraper cannot see a tool that does not exist yet. A page that can make consent into a tool and unmake it is a page a person can trust with their own agent. What's next Three things, in this order. One. The pattern leaves the clinic. Everything that matters here is one idea: a page tells a visitor's own agent what it may do right now, and consent is a tool the person creates and the agent cannot. We are packaging that as a drop-in for any site, a few lines that register a born tool behind a trusted press, and we will propose the pattern to the WebMCP working group as a first-class annotation, so a booking tool that must not exist until a human acts can say so in the spec instead of in our code. Two. Real sign language, done properly. Five shapes are switches, not a language, and the page says so today. Next we train a recognizer for the fifty signs a clinic visit actually needs, on video from Deaf signers who are paid and named as co-designers, and we ship it only when they say it reads them. Not a demo of ASL. A vocabulary that works. Three. The people. A recorded session with a real switch user and a real AAC user, with their permission, and we change whatever they hate. Then the pages where people lose races they should never have had to run. Visa slots. Course registration. Ticket drops. Housing lists. We built one. The web needs all of them. Built with Next.js 15, TypeScript, WebMCP, Supabase, MediaPipe, We

title: Government Knowledge for Your AI
pitch: Your AI uses WebMCP to access government knowledge, while you can inspect the sources, provenance and limits behind every result.
about_excerpt: Your AI uses WebMCP to access government knowledge, while you can inspect the sources, provenance and limits behind every result. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP page Question, Answer and evidence Evidence trace Evidence trace Evidence trace Inspiration AI is becoming another way people find and understand public information. That raises a question I have been thinking about for some time: Does every government website need its own chatbot? Or could the AI a person already uses interact directly with authoritative public websites? That second possibility is what interested me about WebMCP. A personal AI may already understand the conversation and the user's circumstances. The government publisher, meanwhile, is better placed to say what information it provides, where it came from and what the boundaries of that information are. So I wanted to explore a proposed division of responsibility: the personal AI handles the conversation; a publisher defines the tools and evidence; and the person remains able to inspect the source before acting. This independent experimental prototype demonstrates that pattern using packaged public-source evidence. It is not GOV.UK, an official government service or an endorsement by the source organisations. Government information is a particularly useful test case because plausible answers are not enough. A result may depend on jurisdiction, date, eligibility, the authority of the source or information that is simply not present. The important question therefore becomes not just: Can an AI find an answer? but: Can I see the evidence behind what my AI is telling me? That became the guiding principle for the project: Provide the evidence with the answer. What I built This project demonstrates how a personal AI can use WebMCP to access structured government knowledge directly from a webpage. The site exposes six bounded WebMCP tools that can: search government knowledge; retrieve an exact resource; inspect its provenance; explore the evidence behind a claim in the packaged worked answer; compare claims in that worked answer with their evidence foundations; and present the evidence for a selected resource back on the webpage. There is deliberately no general-purpose answer_question tool. The website provides evidence rather than attempting to become the conversational AI. A compatible AI can use that evidence to help its user, while the human interface independently presents the same underlying information as an Evidence answer. That lets the person inspect: the recorded source; provenance; observation date; evidence level; access and reuse information; limitations; remaining unknowns; and the appropriate next check. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same underlying application actions, so there is not one implementation for people and another hidden implementation for AI. Where OKF fits WebMCP solves only part of the problem. It gives an AI a structured way to interact with a webpage, but government information also needs context. Finding a record is not the same as knowing: who published it; whether it is authoritative for the question; when it was observed; what has been transformed; what rights or access have been established; or what the evidence cannot tell us. I therefore used Open Knowledge Format (OKF) as the knowledge and provenance layer beneath the WebMCP experience. That gives the prototype three distinct parts: WebMCP — the interaction layer; OKF — the knowledge and provenance layer; and Evidence answer — the human verification layer. The demonstration includes 80 receipt-bound reviewed records together with 58,652 searchable source-snapshot records projected from 58,655 locked rows. The four federated OKF discovery collections cover A Life in the UK, Office for National Statistics metadata, the UK Government API catalogue and metadata-only HM Land Registry discovery. Those collections intentionally have different evidence levels. Discovery does not magically become verification simply because an AI can search it. How I built it The application is a static TypeScript web application. When the page loads, it validates its packaged knowledge artefacts before enabling search and registering its WebMCP tools. The WebMCP interfaces use bounded inputs, closed schemas and deterministic application actions. Source-derived text is treated as untrusted content rather than instructions for the AI. The site contains no embedded language model, user account or personal-profile database. That reduces what the page itself receives, but it is not a claim of complete privacy. Free-text searches can contain personal information, and a remote AI provider may receive the person's prompt, tool metadata, arguments and results. That was an intentional architectural choice. The experiment is not about building another AI service. It is about exploring what happens when an ordinary website becomes directly usable by the AI chosen by the visitor. I used Codex extensively as the implementation agent. I supplied the product direction, architecture, constraints and review decisions, while Codex implemented and repeatedly tested the TypeScript application, data pipeline, WebMCP tools, browser behaviour, schemas and supporting documentation. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini also helped with research, critique and evaluation design. Microsoft Copilot and a local Ollama model were used as experimental personal-AI hosts rather than as components of the application itself. Earlier OKF and GIS AI GO work supplied the design lineage. During the competition period I built this repository's six-tool WebMCP application, four-source federation, Evidence answer interface, tests, evaluation and protected public deployment. The biggest challenge The hardest part turned out not to be registering a WebMCP tool. It was deciding what we can legitimately claim happened. During testing, an AI could produce a convincing response that appeared to understand the website and even talked about tools. But that did not necessarily mean a WebMCP tool had actually been discovered and invoked. That distinction became important. I separated several questions that are easy to accidentally collapse into one: Did the browser expose the tools? Could the tool be called successfully? Did an AI choose the appropriate tool? Did the AI correctly interpret the tool result? Could the person independently understand the evidence? Those are five different tests. Direct testing through Chrome DevTools successfully exercised all six fixed WebMCP calls against deployed commit a4d2db44 , with matching tool and page Evidence answer digests. A model did not select those direct calls. An owner-operated ChatGPT Chrome extension journey visibly completed the ONS search-and-present flow. A later directed ChatGPT extension evaluation in Edge reported exercising all six page tools. Those host observations did not expose raw browser traces, and the Chrome journey did not expose an exportable exact call trace, host version or model identity. Testing with other personal-AI hosts was much less predictable. Microsoft Copilot could read and discuss the page, but no Site-tool invocation or Evidence answer update was observed; its call and page state remained unobservable. No Gemini Site-tool invocation was observed either. The local model produced a mixture of successful and unsuccessful tool-selection runs. Initially that felt like a limitation of the demonstration. It became one of the most useful things I learned. What I learned WebMCP changes the role of the website Most discussion about agents interacting with websites starts from the agent: How can the AI read the page? How can it find the button? How can it automate the browser? WebMCP lets us reverse the question: What capabilities should the website deliberately make available to an AI? That is a significant shift. Instead of an agent reverse-engineering the user interface, the publisher can define a small, explicit machine interface alongside the human one. Personal AI creates a different public-service architecture A public body does not necessarily have to own the entire conversational experience. There is another possible architecture: citizen-selected AI + publisher-defined tools + inspectable evidence The AI can remain personal to the user. The publisher can remain responsible for its information and tool boundaries. That separation seems particularly interesting for government. Provenance matters as much as retrieval It is easy to make a large body of information searchable. It is much harder to preserve the distinction between: authoritative information; publisher-declared metadata; transformed data; frozen discovery snapshots; inferred relationships; and things that remain unknown. OKF became important because I did not want the project merely to demonstrate retrieval. I wanted the AI and the human to be able to ask: What exactly is this evidence? title: Keep It Offline
pitch: A file workbench that doesn't upload your content. WebMCP lets an AI agent edit your PDFs, photos, video and audio through 29 tools. More upcoming!
about_excerpt: A file workbench that doesn't upload your content. WebMCP lets an AI agent edit your PDFs, photos, video and audio through 29 tools. More upcoming! Like Comment Story Updates empty bench photos loaded pdf pages redaction agent rotated audio video I got the inspiration from one of the many online tools that, unfortunately, force you to upload your documents in order to work on them. What it does This is file workbench for PDFs, photos, video and audio that runs entirely in the browser tab. It registers 29 WebMCP tools (more coming!) so an agent can drive all of it, but the tools return facts about your files, never their contents. You can ask it to black out every bank account and it gets back { matches: 10, pages: [4] }, never the numbers. Every tool also has a button, so you can use it without an agent as well. How we built it Vanilla JS, no framework and no build step, so the repo is what runs. Tools go through document.modelContext.registerTool(). The registered set tracks page state (2 tools on an empty bench, 29 with every file kind loaded), the agent and the UI share one state object, and Web Workers keep heavy work off the main thread. Every dependency is vendored, and a CSP with connect-src 'self' makes the browser itself block an upload. Challenges we ran into Redacting for real, since black rectangles leave the text extractable underneath, so pages are flattened to images. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent that redacts a document it is never allowed to read. The page runs the search locally and strips the matches out of the return value, so they never enter the model's context. What we learned That there are way too many things that could go wrong for such a "simple" app! What's next for Keep It Offline More type of files and more tools! title: Liha WebMCP Adapter
pitch: Make any website agent-ready with inspectable WebMCP tools—without changing the site.
about_excerpt: Make any website agent-ready with inspectable WebMCP tools—without changing the site. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP is powerful, but most existing websites will not implement it overnight. We wanted an adoption layer that works today while giving site owners a path toward native WebMCP tomorrow. What it does Liha WebMCP Adapter adds inspectable WebMCP tools to sites that have not implemented WebMCP themselves—without modifying the target website. People can install declarative adapters from the Liha Adapter Store, or record a real workflow once in Adapter Studio and turn it into a reusable tool. Agents discover named tools with JSON input schemas through WebMCP and invoke them like native tools. The runtime drives the site's real UI; it does not rely on screenshots or guessed selectors. How we built it A Manifest V3 Chrome extension injects a small runtime only into exact approved origins and registers tools through document.modelContext. Adapter JSON is validated against a closed schema. The recorder captures DOM intent, Studio turns recordings into parameterized steps, and the runtime replays them against the live UI. React and TypeScript power the extension, demos, and Store; Cloudflare hosts the public app. Safety by design Adapters are plain JSON with a closed step vocabulary: no scripts, no eval, and no wildcard origins. Users inspect origin, capability, selectors, and visible effects before installation. Ambiguous selectors fail closed. WRITE and DESTRUCTIVE actions can require explicit confirmation. Community adapters are submitted through public GitHub pull requests for review. Challenges The hardest part was preserving WebMCP's structured-tool model without creating an arbitrary-code channel. We also handled selector ambiguity, page-specific health states, React controlled inputs, confirmation gates, recording real workflows, and genuine out-of-page WebMCP invocation. Accomplishments The demo closes the full loop: discover an adapter, inspect permissions, install it, expose tools through WebMCP, invoke them from outside the page, record a new workflow, validate it, and install the resulting custom tool. A site with zero WebMCP code becomes agent-ready in minutes. What we learned Adoption and safety are the same design problem. Community tooling only scales when people can understand exactly where a tool runs and what visible actions it performs. What's next We will expand community coverage, add verified signing and version updates, improve multilingual registry metadata, and help site owners graduate popular adapters into native WebMCP implementations. title: TinCan WebMCP
pitch: Number of agent on websites is growing fast but they have no way to report issues. TInCan is a tool for agents to report website issues and unexpected behavior with otel compatible evidence attached.
about_excerpt: Number of agent on websites is growing fast but they have no way to report issues. TInCan is a tool for agents to report website issues and unexpected behavior with otel compatible evidence attached. Like Comment Story Updates TinCan WebMCP - streamlined method for agents to report issues TinCan WebMCP - workflow AI agents now use websites the way people do: navigating, filling forms, changing settings, checking results. When something goes wrong there is no site-native way for the agent to tell the website what happened. That covers every kind of issue an agent runs into: wrong results, unexpected behavior, failed actions, slow responses, and UI state that does not match what the tools report. The hardest cases are invisible to monitoring: a request returns 200 OK, there are no JavaScript errors, performance looks healthy, and yet the site completed the wrong action. WebMCP is the right layer for this because the agent already has a structured, browser-mediated channel into the page. TinCan adds one tool to that channel, report_site_issue, so the agent can report any problem to the site it happened on, with a category, a severity, and what it expected versus what it observed. No screen-scraping and no separate support integration. How it improves the user experience For the person using the agent: issues get reported and tracked instead of silently ignored or retried. The agent can verify a mutation with a read-only tool, notice a mismatch, and file a precise incident. Timeouts, errors, and slow operations can also be reported For the site owner: every report arrives with sanitized, bounded diagnostic evidence from the site's own browser flight recorder, metrics, and traces that map straight into an existing OpenTelemetry pipeline. No more "the AI said it didn't work" tickets with nothing attached. For privacy: Request and response bodies, credentials, cookies, storage, form values, keystrokes, DOM contents, and screenshots are never captured. The raw evidence is never returned to the agent, only a confirmation and an incident ID. What people and agents can accomplish together A person hands a task to an agent. The agent performs it through the site's WebMCP tools, verifies the persisted result, and whenever the site misbehaves it reports the category and severity, what was expected and observed, and which operation was involved. The site turns that into an incident with the technical context the engineering team needs. The human gets an honest outcome, the agent gets a way to escalate, and the site owner gets a bug report that arrives with evidence rather than a shrug. None of the three could do this alone before. Implementation approach Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , following the WebMCP Draft Community Group Report. The demo SaaS exposes add_licenses , remove_licenses , get_subscription , and export_usage_report . The TinCan package registers report_site_issue . report_site_issue accepts a category ( wrong_result , unexpected_behavior , action_failed , network_failure , performance , ui_state_mismatch , other ), a severity ( info , degraded , blocking ), a summary, and the expected and observed outcome. Agent input is treated as untrusted and cannot change what the site captures. The demo contains two deliberate defects in two different categories. A wrong result: adding n licenses persists n+1 while every request succeeds. A network failure: removing a license returns a 504 and leaves state unchanged. The agent detects both by reading back state, then reports them. A browser flight recorder built on OpenTelemetry fetch/XHR instrumentation, with a Resource Timing fallback, keeps the last 120 seconds of signals. On report, the site attaches a bounded, sanitized slice as logs, metrics, and traces. API validates and classifies each incident, sanitizes again server-side, and stores it. An admin view lets an engineer inspect incidents and their OTLP-compatible evidence. A developer harness at /agent discovers tools with getTools() and executes them with executeTool() for deterministic testing. title: Beat.Z
pitch: Beat.Z uses prompts and WebMCP tools to create custom audio-effect chains. Preview generated effects in-browser with AudioWorklet, then download working VST3 plugins in DAW—Ableton and Reaper tested.
about_excerpt: Beat.Z uses prompts and WebMCP tools to create custom audio-effect chains. Preview generated effects in-browser with AudioWorklet, then download working VST3 plugins in DAW—Ableton and Reaper tested. Like Comment Story Updates Beat.Z-generated VST3 “Pop Rush” running inside REAPER, with its custom multi-effect signal chain and mapped controls directly in the DAW. Beat.Z-generated VST3 “Electric Sweep” inside REAPER, with its custom multi-effect signal chain and mapped controls directly in the DAW. Beat.Z-generated VST3 “Slow Afterglow” inside REAPER, with its custom multi-effect signal chain and mapped controls directly in the DAW. Using @ComputerUse, you are able to forget about the downloaded file and open your DAW Once the Agent Creates plugin, you must approve changes and you can see how many changes the Agent made. The tool has full scope of project Inspiration I am self-taught and do not come from a traditional software-development background. I became passionate about AI through years of experimenting, learning, failing, and trying again. Beat.Z began as a challenge: could I use what I had learned to build a real product, not just another unfinished experiment? The inspiration came from JC, my younger brother—a college student, DJ, and producer. He had spent more than $1,000 on DAWs and plug-ins, but was still looking for new effects. When ChatGPT 5.6 came out, I told him I could probably build him one working plug-in. I did. Then I wondered: what if he could describe the sound he wanted, preview it immediately, and download it as a plug-in for his DAW? That idea became Beat.Z. What it does Beat.Z is a WebMCP-first sound-effect builder where a person uses plain-English prompts to work with an agent to create custom VST3 audio-effect applications for DAWs. Each application is a working sound-processing tool with its own effect chain, controls, and interface. AudioWorklets process the audio signal in real time in the browser, letting users preview the sound being shaped before exporting a working application as a VST3 plug-in. A user describes the sound they want. They could name the type of effect they want, describe how it sounds, reference familiar effects they want to recreate or take inspiration from, or include details about audio files and the exact changes they are after. For example, they might ask for a warm vintage delay, a wide chorus for vocals, or a punchier, more aggressive drum sound. Users can upload an audio file to hear how the effect shapes the sound before downloading the VST3. The agent can inspect the current plug-in, create or edit effects and controls, clear the builder, and start a VST3 download. The user can test the effect in real time in the browser, hear how it changes the sound, and refine it with the agent before downloading. Beat.Z maps creative intent—such as “make this warmer,” “give it more movement,” or “make it sound harsher”—into a specific sound-design chain. Beat.Z combines 14 audio-effect building blocks—including filters, distortion, delay, reverb, compression, modulation, EQ, limiting, stutter, and auto-wah—into custom signal chains. Faust, WebAssembly, and AudioWorklets power the browser preview. Once approved, the same effect design becomes a downloadable VST3 plug-in: a unique, working DAW tool that processes sound, not merely an AI-generated preview. I tested the workflow on macOS with Ableton and REAPER. How I built it Before this challenge, I had never written a line of code. I was curious about how Beat.Z could work, but I assumed it was too complicated to build. I spent a few months asking questions, researching, and teaching myself the architecture needed to connect AI agent tools, a browser audio engine, real-time preview, and a native VST3 build pipeline. When the WebMCP Challenge appeared, I found a way to implement the idea. I used Codex as my collaborator and teacher to turn that architecture into working code: building the WebMCP tools, integrating Faust effects, debugging browser audio, creating tests, and diagnosing native-build failures Challenges I ran into At first, the hardest challenge was keeping the AI from moving too far ahead of the actual goal. It was easy to generate too many ideas, add too much too quickly, or build features before the foundations were proven I worked through a loop of build, test, fail, diagnose, and rebuild until I was happy with the result. Managing my time was also difficult: I had no traditional coding background or development team backing me. But I had become highly capable with AI tools, asking the right questions, reviewing results critically, and turning a large idea into small, testable steps. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that I took an idea I had imagined for some time and turned it into a finished product I could submit. This challenge gave me the opportunity to finally take a shot at building Beat.Z, and I am proud that the result matches the original vision: a musician can describe a sound, preview it in the browser, and turn it into a DAW plug-in. Beat.Z includes 14 effect building blocks that can be combined into custom signal chains. I built focused WebMCP tools—inspect-builder, create-plugin, edit-plugin, clear-plugin, and download-plugin—along with custom browser AudioWorklet processing, real-time preview, and a VST3 build workflow tested on macOS with Ableton and REAPER. More than anything, I am proud that I built a working creative tool from the ground up, despite starting with no coding background. What I learned I learned how to use AI models at their best: when to use different models, how to set clear boundaries, and how to turn a vague idea into useful work. I learned systems architecture, audio design, browser audio, WebMCP tools, backend systems, open-source audio tools, and the Apple Silicon build challenges involved in creating VST3 plug-ins. Most importantly, I learned how to connect all of those pieces into a full-stack product. I built Beat.Z’s frontend, backend, browser audio experience, and native plug-in pipeline independently, using AI as a collaborator while staying responsible for the direction, testing, and decisions. I also learned that no one is going to come and build your idea for you. You have to do the work, keep asking questions, figure things out, and keep going when something fails. What's next for Beat.Z Next, I want to expand the effect library and add a sound-source library with options such as horns, frog sounds, and other creative samples. I also want to bring instruments into the builder: drums, pads, basses, leads, keys, and vocal effects. Users could create and download simple synths, instruments with custom effects, or more experimental ideas like a frog-inspired synth with a stutter effect. My main goal is to help musicians create with AI instead of feeling replaced by it.
