title: Didaction space
pitch: didaction space is a agent-enabled alternative jupyter frontend- enabling you to learn deeper
about_excerpt: didaction space is a agent-enabled alternative jupyter frontend- enabling you to learn deeper Like Comment Story Updates 1 Launch window Regular notebook Microscopes Inspiration LLMs have been a game changer for how we learn something new now. Autodidacts can satiate their curiosity to infinite bounds, ask however many question we would like within our token budgets. But it can also be very tiring when an LLM blurts out lot of text, and UIs are trapped inside boxes. For difficult concepts, I often find myself slowing down and trying to see things step by step, or illustrate visually wishing lesser friction between what in my head and what I can put down on something external- the monitor or on paper. This is an attempt to bring that to jupyter notebooks which are versatile in learning. For each cell, this is an attempt to slow things down and understand things step by step with some visualization, and play around with a segment of code deeper. What it does didaction space is agent-enabled Jupyter-kernel frontend centered on ability to do deep dive into each small snippet of code called a“cell”. An agent creates a “microscope” to create rich interactive walkthrough about the cell's contents through WebMCP. It provides the following primitives for agents: code examples with annotations animated graphics canvas to illustrate concepts executable playgrounds to spawn quick tests It can run in your browser completely locally executing Jupyter kernels in browser, or through self-hosted docker instances of kernels executing on your local platform. With server mode, you can also have multiple collaborators with one driver and remaining following the session. WebMCP allows you to bring your own agent and leverage your context/memory about knowledge, learning preferences, and technical interests. Conventional hosted segmented LLM wrapper tools have to learn that, and have to trust them with your data too. How we built it Most of the heavy lifting was done by Codex with hackathon skills and TDD skills. I gave it the architectural decisions, feedback and guidance. Frontend Jupyter's ecosystem has kernels for various languages, and documented protocol for interaction between frontend and backend. Instead of using Jupyter's existing frontend, we chose to use egui, a Rust based immediate mode GUI rendering to the frontend canvas. This was a decision due to familiarity with that ecosystem. The WebMCP calls hook through this Rust based frontend providing much richer client-side interactivity. "Backend" A rust based gateway handles communication with "backend". For local only mode, our "backend" leveraged JupyterLite's kernel implementation for in-browser kernels, through the gateway. For docker based server backend, the gateway is a sidecar to the language specific jupyter kernel streaming updates to all clients, and controlling who is the driver for the session & is allowed to send actions to jupyter server. Jupyter's architecture helped a lot, with common gateway code implemented to interact between frontend & backend . Challenges we ran into Things that were complex to keep in scope of hackathon: Using WebAuthn authentication, but that is currently not supported in Codex browser WebRTC to talk between collaborators directly, and server WebMCP design decisions: WebMCP design applied to jupyter model- idempotic actions, such as insert relative to cell-id rather than specifying index WebMCP orchestration with different collaborators - viewing is allowed by agents, but not active operations- controlled by central server For a complex multi-mcp invocation, WebMCP description should be given enough information to pick up context from it Local pyodide packages and constraints Accomplishments that we're proud of A fixed visualization API would be difficult to maintain. So we used an arbitrary AssemblyScript to provide more flexibility with a smaller host interface. So microscope graphics are dispatched as compiled wasm artifacts compiled using a inbrowser compiler. What we learned The important capability is not more agent control. It is shared access to the application’s concepts and state. For notebooks, agents should understand cells, execution, annotations, walkthroughs, Playgrounds, graphics, and notebook state—not reconstruct them from screenshots. For effective use, a SKILLS.md is still important and a mechanism to discover this would be a great addition to WebMCP. What's next for didaction space Microscopes are a first step toward software that can explain itself with an agent. We want to make walkthroughs richer by combining: code, narration, animation, graphics, experiments, domain-specific tools. The same approach could support mathematics, robotics, simulations, engineering, and scientific computing. The long-term goal is to reduce the distance between using a technical tool and learning how it works. title: DONE / PROVEN
pitch: Agents can challenge the definition of done. Humans keep authority. Proof stays current when reality changes.
about_excerpt: Agents can challenge the definition of done. Humans keep authority. Proof stays current when reality changes. Like Comment Story Updates Done is a claim. Proof is a state. AI agents are getting very good at producing work and increasingly good at reporting that the work is finished. The remaining trust problem is deeper: did the agent prove the right definition of success, did it have authority to act on that definition, and is that proof still valid after the world changes? DONE / PROVEN is a proof-carrying work layer for humans and agents. A human owns the mission and the semantic authority to decide what success means. An agent can inspect the mission and acceptance contract through WebMCP and can attack that contract by submitting a concrete counterexample: an outcome that appears to satisfy the current definition of done but should still count as failure. The system evaluates that counterexample deterministically. If the unacceptable outcome would pass, DONE / PROVEN surfaces a false-green contract defect to the human. The agent cannot rewrite the contract, approve its own fix, or impersonate the human decision. After the human admits a corrected contract, execution evidence can earn PROVEN state. If a dependency later changes, DONE / PROVEN invalidates only the proof that depended on the change. Unrelated evidence remains valid, and the system produces a minimum re-proof plan. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns the page from a dashboard into a structured human-agent collaboration surface. The release exposes seven tools that let an agent read the mission, inspect authority, inspect the candidate contract, list known contract risks, inspect evidence state, request a bounded human decision, and submit an adversarial counterexample. The key tool is submit_counterexample . It lets the agent actively pressure-test the human-owned definition of done while keeping semantic authority with the human. Better human-agent UX The point is not to make people write longer specifications. The system concentrates human attention on the few decisions automation cannot safely settle, gives the agent a typed way to expose loopholes, and keeps deterministic code responsible for evaluation and proof state. A later dependency change reopens only evidence that actually depended on what changed rather than discarding all prior proof or trusting a stale green checkmark. What people and agents can do together The agent can inspect mission, authority, candidate acceptance criteria, contract risks, and proof state; request a bounded human decision; and submit a concrete adversarial counterexample. The human owns unresolved meaning and admission. Deterministic code owns evaluation, proof validity, dependency impact, and minimal re-proof. Demo The demo begins with an agent claiming a landing-page task is DONE. The initial acceptance contract is deliberately wrong in two directions: False green: it forgets to require the waitlist signup to actually persist. False red: it requires one exact headline even though the human said wording does not matter. The agent submits a broken-waitlist counterexample. The deterministic engine returns EXPOSES_FALSE_GREEN , records the visible challenge, and leaves the active contract unchanged. The human resolves the genuinely semantic admin-privacy question, the corrected contract is admitted, and five requirements earn evidence-backed PROVEN state. Then a dependency changes. Exactly two of five proof receipts become STALE while three remain PROVEN. Re-running only the affected checks restores 5/5. WebMCP implementation Seven imperative tools register through the current document.modelContext surface when available, with the older navigator path retained only as compatibility fallback. submit_counterexample uses a narrow JSON schema, additionalProperties: false , runtime size/type validation, and an untrusted-content hint. It is non-read-only only because it records a visible challenge. It has no capability to edit or admit the acceptance contract. Evidence boundary This project does not claim that AI can automatically infer arbitrary human intent, that acceptance contracts themselves are novel, or that every verification problem is solved. The demonstrated contribution is narrower: an agent can adversarially falsify the human-owned definition of done without becoming the authority, and proof can remain dependency-aware after reality changes. The final licensed release passes 38/38 deterministic tests , TypeScript typecheck, static build, responsive browser verification, seven-tool WebMCP current-API harness registration, adversarial counterexample execution, agent-content injection probes, deployment-header verification, and zero unauthorized contract mutation. Existing-project disclosure Existing project, meaningfully extended during the challenge. The underlying contract-adequacy and continuous-validity research began before August 25. During the WebMCP Challenge submission period, the project was materially extended with the responsive human product surface, authority reconciliation, seven WebMCP tools, the agent-submitted counterexample mechanism, WebMCP trust boundaries and runtime validation, current-API harness verification, deployment-origin and permissions hardening, browser/mobile/injection verification, public-release packaging, and challenge-specific testing/documentation. Dated commit history and release evidence preserve that distinction. title: Playable
pitch: Learning an instrument shouldn't start with 40 beginner videos. Name a song to your agent, it researches the web, Playable verifies the facts and builds a version you can actually play, practice.
about_excerpt: Learning an instrument shouldn't start with 40 beginner videos. Name a song to your agent, it researches the web, Playable verifies the facts and builds a version you can actually play, practice. Like Comment Story Updates Playable For as long as instruments have been taught, beginners have started with the same generic exercises and the same simplified songs — not because those songs are motivating, but because adapting real music to a real beginner was too much work for any teacher to do per student. Now life moves faster than ever, attention is the scarcest resource, and the music people actually love is the best motivation they have. Playable closes that gap: tell your AI agent which song you want to learn, and it researches the song on the public web and submits what it finds through WebMCP. Playable verifies the evidence against music theory, compiles a version that fits your hands, and you practice it in the browser with real chord diagrams and a synthesized preview of exactly what you'll play. Why WebMCP is the right architecture A cover song can't be ingested: streaming links expose no analyzable audio, and downloading is off the table. But the musical facts exist everywhere in public — chord sites, BPM databases, music encyclopedias. Reading them is a research problem, and research is what LLM agents are exceptional at. Turning facts into a beginner-proof arrangement is a compilation problem, and that needs deterministic software: difficulty scoring, fingering search, audio synthesis. No single system has both. WebMCP is the first protocol that composes them without merging them. Playable exposes 24 real capabilities as tools; the agent orchestrates them and supplies the one thing the app lacks — live web research. Critically, the agent is a researcher, not an oracle: it submits compact facts with source URLs (never tabs, lyrics, or page dumps), and a deterministic resolver adjudicates them. The model proposes; the page verifies. That boundary is what makes the result trustworthy — and demoable — because every claim on screen traces to an accepted independent source. From facts to playable: the theory pipeline The resolver does what a trained arranger would do before trusting a source. Keys normalize enharmonically (G♯ ≡ A♭); chord symbols parse into root + quality family, so "Db" and "Dbmaj7" agree without erasing extensions. Guitar-shaped evidence becomes sounding harmony through the capo invariant — capo 1 "G Em C D" and "Ab Fm Db Eb" reconcile as the same progression. Metrical tempo claims cluster instead of averaging (63, 126 and 189 BPM are one pulse at different levels), transposition look-alikes become hypotheses rather than truths, and confidence is noisy-OR over independent source families — five pages from one database count once. Per-field confidence and conflicts stay visible; structure claimed by no source is labeled approximate. The verified blueprint becomes a SongGraph, then a compiler searches transformation chains — capo placement, chord-shape substitution, rhythm and tempo simplification, fingering optimization — re-scored against the player's profile (known chords, barre comfort, practice time) and Pareto-filtered over difficulty vs fidelity. Every accepted transformation is explainable: "why 27% easier for you" comes from real diagnostics, and if no capo and open chords are genuinely optimal, the system honestly says so. The same selected arrangement drives the diagrams, the capo mapping, and the Karplus–Strong synthesis you hear. The experience One sentence: "I want to learn Perfect by Ed Sheeran. I'm a complete beginner." No link, no upload. The agent follows a live research brief — what's missing, with search queries — submits evidence per independent source, resolves, sets the profile, compiles, and prepares a 20-minute practice session. The user watches confidence fill in field by field, conflicts resolve visibly, and the chord diagrams land front and center. The tool layer itself keeps agents honest: next-step suggestions with priorities, state-aware errors, and reporting guardrails. Agent and human share one state — every agent action is visible, every slider moves the controls the agent sees, and audio never autoplays. A human presses Play. Implementation Deliberately thin and native: tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool in plain TypeScript — no framework, no backend agent, no internal LLM. UI buttons and agent calls execute one shared action layer over one state object, so the page is a live, truthful mirror of the agent's work. Research fusion and compilation are fully deterministic; the agent is the only model in the loop. We didn't put a chatbot inside a guitar website — we made the guitar website agent-native. title: Root
pitch: Orchestrate real sites with WebMCP. Open several apps at once, watch the agent work on live pages, approve the steps that need you, and take control or stop any window when you want.
about_excerpt: Orchestrate real sites with WebMCP. Open several apps at once, watch the agent work on live pages, approve the steps that need you, and take control or stop any window when you want. Like Comment Story Updates root panel tab guide open root panel tab settings open root panel tab activity open root panel tab apps open root home page root in action. take control overlay over the active document sign in page home page when logout Inspiration Most WebMCP demos will be one site that registers a few tools. That is useful. It is also the obvious move. I wanted the harder surface: several real apps that stay themselves, each with its own origin and document, and one workspace where a person and an agent share those live apps. I built it so that Root does not sneak around the iframe and hit the child APIs itself. Cross-app work is what people already struggle with. Copy an id. Retype an email. Open the next tab. Hope the page still matches the plan. Agents are already strong at planning. What they cannot do, unless the sites hand them tools, is act on those live pages as part of one governed run. That is what Root is for: an orchestrator between Catalog, Customers, and Cases. Each app keeps its own tools on its own document. Root discovers and invokes them there, and the UI on that page is the evidence. What it does Root is a Mac-style desktop in the browser. Catalog, Customers, and Cases open as real provider windows. Lab can join after a human grant. Each provider is its own deployed site. Root loads it in an iframe with allow="tools" and only talks to tools that document exposes to Root. A person and an agent can run a pass across those windows: Search customers, products, or cases on the live lists Pause for a human row pick when there is a real choice Bind a later step to that selected snapshot (Root carries the object; it does not flatten Ada into a retyped email string) Open a record, or fill a create form and wait for a human persist on stage Keep other provider windows live instead of destroying them when work moves Notify when a wait needs you: after you grant it in inspect Settings, a pending-on-human pause plus a hidden Root tab shows a Notifications API toast (not Push, and not while Root is visible) Root’s own page registers the gateway the agent calls: list_providers , discover_capabilities , prepare_workflow , execute_workflow , invoke_granted_tool , plus inspect, cancel, and window chrome. Prepare freezes an allowlisted graph before anything runs. Execute opens or reuses each window, rediscovers, revalidates, and invokes on the live document. Take control stops the agent on that window. Custom tools never enter pass evidence. Try it: root.danieloyerinde.com with Customers , Catalog , Cases , and Lab . How I built it Four independently deployed Next apps (Root, Accounts, Shop, Support) plus Lab, one Express/tRPC API, and Postgres with tables owned by domain. No cross-domain joins. Support keeps its own copies of customer and order text. Root never mutates child domains through tRPC. On WebMCP: Each child registers tools on document.modelContext and exposes them only to Root’s origin Root’s Permissions-Policy delegates tools into those iframes Discovery uses getTools({ fromOrigins }) ; invoke uses executeTool in the child’s context Root is the author-provided agent that composes nested provider tools; the agent talks to Root’s gateway, and Root invokes tools inside each iframe The workflow layer is prepare then execute. Search, select, open, and create are allowlisted. A later argument may be a bind to an earlier selected snapshot. Create writes only after a human persist on stage. Agent lease is per window so one document serializes while another stays free. Rich fill, preview, and pick presentation run on stage on the live controls, not as a fake overlay of the whole desktop. Challenges I ran into The first hard truth was uniqueness. Multi-tab agents can already visit three sites. “Root opens three iframes” is not enough. The product only wins if the person and the agent share the same live documents under a freeze the agent cannot quietly rewrite. A core challenge was ChatGPT’s in-app browser. It only exposed top-level tools on Root. It did not discover tools registered inside provider iframes. That is exactly where Catalog, Customers, and Cases live. That gap is what pushed me onto a WebMCP-capable Chrome setup (testing flag / extension path) so nested getTools and executeTool could actually run against those documents. One stage window that remounted and killed the previous app made collaboration impossible. Search results and selections vanished when the next step switched providers. I moved to persistent independent windows so Customers can stay while Catalog runs. Binding looked simple until it was not. Typing Ada’s email into Cases again is not a handoff. Root has to deliver the selected snapshot intact and refuse graphs that invent ids from search results instead of an explicit selection. Human pauses were another edge. A pending pick, a create persist, Take control, and a silent timeout are different outcomes. Take control must fail closed as stopped by the user with no retry. A timeout with no gesture is not the same thing. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I shipped a real desktop, not a slide. Multiple provider windows stay live. Prepare refuses illegal tools and arguments. Execute rediscovers and fails closed on drift. The together loop is concrete: the agent fills a search, the person clicks Lin or Silent Mouse on the live list, Root binds that snapshot into a later Cases step without retyping her email, and Take control can stop the run on that window. Domain data lives in Postgres with SQL search. The iframe is not a picture over Root’s own API. Custom providers can still join behind a human grant without entering the typed pass. What I learned WebMCP tools belong to the open document. If Root calls the child’s API itself, the iframe is only decoration. An agent can run searches it already knows without the person. That is not much of a shared loop. Selection, bind, and create-after-persist are the parts where the person actually has to act on the live page. One allowlist scales cleaner than a prepare function per app. The step cap is only a safety limit. It is not tied to how many providers exist. Legal tools can repeat. Illegal ones still fail. Remounting the only window on every step wiped the previous app’s UI. Keeping separate windows open, with a lease per window, matched how people already keep a few apps around. What's next for Root As WebMCP leaves experiment and settles into real browser conventions, I expect clearer nesting rules, better host and agent tooling, and shared patterns for selection, grants, and multi-document work. Root will get simpler as those conventions land. Conclusion As of today, this principle gets shaky towards my final stages, after a final extensive check. A few things met me head-on. The agent can bypass Root. Even with a custom-tool setup where Root would in fact reject invoke when the tool is not granted, the agent could still go around me, because the underlying iframe exposes tools to the parent origin. That path is not quite spelled out in the docs the way you’d hope. Those tools would not show up when you list Root’s gateway tools, but Chrome still exposes them by name (direct invocation), so there is a direct bypass between Chrome and the providers. As WebMCP moves off experiment, the goal is that we get to conventions where this kind of multitasking is better supported, and where the tooling around it is better too. There is also usually a .map error that surfaces via the inspector. After extensive debugging, several bridges on my side were tested and still did not own the failure. The tools I had were limited, so I could not A/B the remaining layers cleanly (fresh tab vs stale session, inspector path vs gateway path, flag and extension in vs out) to confirm where it breaks. I treat that as outside Root: the experimental API or the extension. title: The Unattested Click
pitch: A shared record where every entry says which hand made it — or admits that nobody can tell.
about_excerpt: A shared record where every entry says which hand made it — or admits that nobody can tell. Like Comment Story Updates Four ways an act can arrive. Two name a hand; two admit nobody can. An act with no via is rejected, never filed as the human's. The store behind the tools: 767 append-only records from Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Mistral and one person, written over weeks. act-0001 and act-0002 are ours, and false: posted by curl from no page at all. act-0003 corrects them. Append-only, so both stand. The Unattested Click WebMCP Challenge submission Live demo: Relay attestation desk Repo: it-start/relay-ui — MIT Research notes: zaebee/p-e The problem WebMCP makes something new possible: an agent can interact with a web page using the same interface the page gives to a person. That's powerful. But it creates a surprisingly basic question: When something happens on the page, who actually did it? A person? Their agent? The page itself? Some JavaScript calling the same function? Today, WebMCP doesn't really give the page a way to know. We found this while looking at webmcp#288 . In the scenario described there, an agent called a tool on a deployment console. The proposed action wasn't automatically executed, so the agent clicked the page's own Approve button instead. The page recorded the approval as coming from the human operator. But the human never made that decision. That felt less like a UI bug and more like a missing piece of the web platform. What WebMCP actually tells the page A WebMCP tool gets its arguments and an AbortSignal . What it doesn't get is anything like: who initiated this action; whether an agent was involved; which session or conversation caused it; whether a person actually interacted with the UI. The browser creates an internal execution ID, but that ID is used for things like cancellation. It isn't exposed to the page as an identity or provenance signal. So from the application's point of view, several very different things can collapse into the same event: "This action happened." And that's the problem we're exploring. What we built We built Relay , a small append-only record system designed around provenance rather than pretending provenance exists. The live system already contains hundreds of records written over time by multiple participants, including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Mistral, and a person. They don't edit the history away when something turns out to be wrong. They argue with it. They add corrections. They issue errata. They leave the original record in place. That makes the provenance problem visible instead of hiding it. We added WebMCP to Relay Relay exposes six WebMCP tools: four tools for reading the existing corpus; two tools for proposing and approving new records. The important part isn't the number of tools. It's what happens when an action reaches the server. Every action has to say how we know it happened . We currently distinguish: via What it means Can we identify the actor? webmcp-tool The page says the action came through a WebMCP tool No ui-synthetic A scripted UI event ( isTrusted === false ) Not a person ui-trusted A trusted browser event Could be a person or an agent direct-http The request bypassed the page No There is deliberately no default . If an action doesn't tell us how it happened, Relay rejects it. A more honest UI Most applications would simply display: Approved by you We don't think the platform has earned the right to say that. Instead, the UI can say something closer to: A real browser input event arrived. We cannot determine whether a person or an agent produced it. That's less convenient. But it's true. And when agents and people can both operate the same interface, truth about provenance matters more than a reassuring label. The interesting part: the record is shared A person and an agent can both interact with the same Relay page. They write to the same append-only log. Every entry is hash-chained to the previous one. So if someone later changes an entry to make it look as though a different actor performed the action, the chain breaks. This doesn't magically prove who clicked the button. It does something more modest and useful: it makes the uncertainty explicit and makes later rewriting detectable. We also tried to break our own idea At first, we made a mistake. We assumed that because an action came through a WebMCP execute() callback, that callback itself could serve as an attestation boundary. It can't. registerTool() gives the page a callback authored by the page. That callback can potentially be reached by same-origin JavaScript, third-party code running in the page, or injected code. So the page saying: "This came from WebMCP" is still just the page saying it . We changed the design after discovering this. Records now explicitly distinguish: attested_by: "page" browser_attestation: "unavailable" a human-readable explanation of what the evidence actually tells us. We'd rather have an honest "we don't know" than manufacture a trustworthy-looking answer. Then we caught an even simpler problem Two minutes after deployment, we tested the API with curl . We submitted: via: "webmcp-tool" The server accepted it. There was no WebMCP page involved at all. So our first records were wrong. act-0001 and act-0002 are therefore false claims of provenance. act-0003 documents the mistake. We didn't delete them. That's the point of the experiment. An append-only provenance system should preserve the moment when we got provenance wrong , too. The missing primitive A real solution would need the browser to provide some execution context that: the page cannot forge; the agent cannot simply manufacture; the application can use to distinguish the origin of an action. WebMCP currently doesn't define such an attestation mechanism. We're not claiming Relay solves that problem. We're showing that the problem exists, what it looks like in a real application, and what information is currently missing. Why this matters Once agents can act on the web, "who clicked the button?" stops being just a UI question. It becomes a systems question. If an agent books something, approves a deployment, changes an account setting, or submits a form, the application may need to know not only what happened, but how it happened and what can actually be proved about the actor . Right now, the web has a gap there. The Unattested Click is our attempt to make that gap impossible to ignore. title: Agent Chess
pitch: One verified chessboard. Two native interfaces. Humans and AI agents share every turn through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: One verified chessboard. Two native interfaces. Humans and AI agents share every turn through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Opening Board Human-agent exchange WebMCP explainer Legal-move guidance Why I built it I wanted to test WebMCP on a task where success could not be hidden behind a convincing-looking interface. Chess is a good test because every action has an objectively correct result. An agent must know where every piece is, whose turn it is, which side it controls and which moves are legal. Misreading one square can invalidate the entire game. A normal chess website is designed for human eyes and a mouse. An agent using that interface must reconstruct 64 squares from pixels and translate its move back into screen coordinates. That is fragile and unnecessary—the page already knows the exact position and legal actions. Obsidian Chess explores a different model: give the person and the agent interfaces designed for their individual strengths while connecting both to the same game. What it does The person plays through a visual chessboard. The agent plays through four page-defined WebMCP tools. For example, the person can select Take White and move the pawn from e2 to e4 . An agent waiting through wait_for_turn wakes up and receives the updated FEN, move history, role ownership, game status and exact legal moves. The agent selects one of those moves and calls move_piece , optionally adding an explanation such as “I’m contesting the centre.” The move immediately appears on the board. The SAN history, FEN, turn indicator and Human + Agent Trace all update from the same position. This is a complete playable experience rather than a mocked tool demo. A person can claim either colour, full chess rules are enforced, games can be reset, promotions are supported and invalid actions recover safely. The board works with a mouse, keyboard or touch. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Most agent tools perform one action and finish. A chess match is different: it is a long-running collaboration where control alternates between a person and an agent. A person might think for five seconds or five minutes. Without WebMCP, the agent must repeatedly inspect the screen and guess whether anything changed. With wait_for_turn , it can wait, wake when the person moves and receive the new authoritative state. WebMCP also lets the application expose precise capabilities without giving up control of its rules. The agent can inspect the position and submit a move, but the page still verifies side ownership, turn ownership and chess legality before changing anything. If the agent acts out of turn, submits an illegal move or moves before the person has chosen a side, the request is rejected without changing the board. The response includes a stable error code, the unchanged state and a specific recovery instruction. The person keeps the expressive interface that makes chess understandable. The agent receives structured state, exact legal actions and explicit permissions. Neither participant operates on a copy. Who this helps Obsidian Chess is immediately a playable human-agent game, but it is also a reference for developers building applications where people and agents share responsibility. The same pattern appears in purchase approvals, document reviews, scheduling negotiations, incident response and simulations. A person reviews information and makes a decision; the agent waits, observes the resulting state and continues from an explicitly permitted set of actions. These workflows often rely on screen interpretation, repeated polling or separate custom integrations. Obsidian Chess demonstrates another approach: the website exposes its existing state and domain actions directly while retaining control over validation and permissions. Chess makes this pattern easy to verify. A move is legal or illegal, turn ownership is unambiguous and every transition can be compared with the visible board. This is also what makes the project different from a typical AI chess demo. It does not add a chatbot beside a board or connect a hidden chess engine. The agent discovers the page’s tools, reads the shared state, chooses an action, explains it and waits for the person. How I implemented WebMCP The application is built with React and Vinext. chess.js is the authority for legal moves, check, checkmate, draws, castling, en passant and promotion. The page registers four tools through the browser’s model context: join_game announces the agent and returns the collaboration contract. get_board returns the authoritative position, ownership, history and legal actions. move_piece submits one schema-checked, turn-gated and rules-validated move. wait_for_turn waits for the agent to gain control of the next turn. Every response includes a protocol version, success state, stable status code, suggested next action and current game state. This gives the agent enough information to continue or recover without guessing. The waiting system uses a bounded long poll tied to a session identifier and state version. Duplicate waits are rejected, and resetting the game invalidates older waits so a stale call cannot act inside a new match. The visible Human + Agent Trace shows tool discovery, board inspection, waiting, moves, resets and errors. I also published evaluation.json and llms.txt guides so automated evaluators can follow a deterministic testing path. Challenges and lessons The hardest part was keeping two different interfaces synchronized across human thinking time. An early bug allowed the person to claim White but left pawn interaction in the wrong state. Fixing it required treating side ownership, turn ownership and the chess.js position as one transition instead of separate UI events. I added regression tests for opening pawn moves with humans playing either colour, alongside tests for wrong turns, promotions, castling, en passant, checkmate and resets. Reset behaviour was another subtle problem. A waiting call started during one match must never wake up and act in a different match. Session and version checks now return an explicit reset result to stale calls. I also learned that agent interfaces must explain failure as carefully as success. Returning only “illegal move” leaves the agent guessing. Returning ILLEGAL_MOVE , the unchanged position and a specific next action lets it recover safely. The result is one person, one agent and two purpose-built interfaces sharing one precise, verifiable game. title: Boardspeak - See the tools your agent can use (in a game!)
pitch: An AI agent has 2 bad options for using a website: screenshot and guess or a separate MCP server. WebMCP is the 3rd way: the page itself tells you what you can do. Boardspeak is that, as a board game
about_excerpt: An AI agent has 2 bad options for using a website: screenshot and guess or a separate MCP server. WebMCP is the 3rd way: the page itself tells you what you can do. Boardspeak is that, as a board game Like Comment Story Updates agent plays boardspeak codex agent tools agent call trace Inspiration Today, an AI agent has 2 bad options for using websites: 1) it can take screenshots and guess or 2) the website owner can build a separate “MCP server” that the AI talks to instead of the website. WebMCP is a third way: the web page itself says, in plain JS, “here are the things you can do here and here’s exactly how” - that’s super powerful, especially if we imagine a future where AI does more for us. The specification names improving accessibility through agents as an explicit goal, and I wanted to test that goal on something pretty complex. A board game is the hardest thing I could think of in time for this challenge - the state is entirely visual, legality changes every single turn, and both players have to be looking at the same board state or it's not a game. What it does Boardspeak plays Breakthrough (Dan Troyka, 2000). 8x8, pawns only and pretty simple rules - get your pawn to the other side of the board, you can only go forward (diagonals+straight), and you can eat enemy pawns diagonally. In our scenario, White plays by mouse (a person, or the built-in bot if you're alone) and Black plays by talking or typing to the agent. The page publishes the live board to the agent as 9 WebMCP tools. Ask "what's on the board?" or "what's threatening my left flank?" and the answer comes from the game itself, not from a screenshot. Say "advance the pawn on e7" and the piece moves on the shared board state. Tools appear and disappear with the position. play_capture exists only while a capture is available. list_threats exists only while a pawn is one step from its goal rank. suggest_move exists only on the human's turn, and play_move only on the agent's. An agent that inspects this page mid-game sees a different set of tools than it saw 30 seconds ago, and that set is always exactly what is legal right now. An agent steering a game is not the new part; 2 players and an agent sharing one adversarial board, with the schema as the rulebook, is, and that's the really cool thing that WebMCP enables. Every agent call is logged on the page with its arguments and its result, so both players can see what happened without opening DevTools. The game is fully playable by mouse, in any browser, with no agent and no API key. In Chrome, Black can even play by voice with no agent at all: an on-page mic takes moves like "a7 to a6" and matches them against the same legal-move list, and saying "options" reads the legal moves out loud....but to play by talking to an agent you'll need ChatGPT's or Codex's built-in browser, or Chrome with the WebMCP flag! How I built it The idea: legality isn't checked inside the tool. The tool only offers legal moves in the first place. For example, play_move 's input schema is regenerated every turn to enumerate exactly the legal moves, so a schema-respecting client can't even form an illegal move. The schema is the contract so a client that ignores it meets the engine, which refuses anything outside of those rules and tells the agent why. I built this on Next.js 15 on Vercel. The game keeps no state on any server and there is no database; the only server code is the optional narration route (works without a key). One bridge component registers each tool on document.modelContext through GoogleChromeLabs' use-webmcp-tool hook, each with its own AbortController - a turn change aborts the old registration and registers the new one. The piece I am most happy about is the commit barrier. No mutating tool call resolves until React has committed the new board and the new tool surface, so that the agent's next getTools already reflects the move it just made and there is no moment where the screen and the agent can even disagree. Tool calls are serialized through a queue so 2 calls cannot interleave mid-turn. readOnlyHint is set on every read tool. Mutating tools return the full board text so the agent can verify what happened rather than assume. resign_game and start_new_game wait on an in-page confirmation. The page draws its own "are you sure?" dialog and waits for a real click, because the protocol does not have a built-in way to ask the human yet. Challenges I ran into WebMCP can't edit a tool after it's registered, and it refuses a second tool with the same name. So every turn the page has to remove the old move tool before adding the new one, in exactly that order, or it crashes mid-game. I wrote a test that plays 20 moves plus a full game reset against a fake browser that throws the moment any tool name repeats, and it finishes with zero errors. The other hard part was resisting the urge to make the agent the star. Every time I gave it a more powerful tool, the game got worse. suggest_move exists because the version where the agent could move the human's pieces was not fun to play against. Two limits I kept instead of hiding. The size check on tool responses runs before the board updates for the two move tools only; the others check after, which is fine today because their responses are small, but it is not the same guarantee. And the "are you sure?" step is a dialog my page draws itself, because the protocol does not have a built-in one yet. I would rather say that than pretend it does. Accomplishments that I'm proud of 9 tools that come and go with the position, so an illegal move is not even a choice the agent can make 82 unit tests, 9 full browser tests from a clean install, and 5 of 5 WebMCP eval cases A perfect 100 Lighthouse accessibility score on mobile and desktop, with the report in the repo Fully playable by mouse in any browser, no agent, no flag, no API key A live panel showing the agent's current tools, and you can watch it change as you play 2 people and an agent on one board, and the board + agent are fully aligned What I learned The list of tools a page offers does not have to be fixed. Publishing exactly what is legal right now, and nothing else, is the most useful thing a page can tell an agent. And it goes way past games: forms, wizards, checkout flows, anything with steps and rules. The harder lesson: the interesting question in building for agents is not what to expose. It is what to withhold, and when. What's next for Boardspeak Both colors by voice, with two agents sharing one board. More games behind the same engine contract. And a getTools -driven spectator mode, where a third agent can watch without being able to touch anything. title: Jhola - a trip finder whose slow searches you can stop
pitch: A trip finder with real, slow fare searches and a Cancel button that actually cancels - timers clear, nothing lands after, and the agent knows exactly what it never saw.
about_excerpt: A trip finder with real, slow fare searches and a Cancel button that actually cancels - timers clear, nothing lands after, and the agent knows exactly what it never saw. Like Comment Story Updates The trip finder: destinations, budget, and dates Tool console: get_brief tool called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: long-running tools accept execute(args, {signal}) and are genuinely abortable - a cancelled search stops mid-flight, not just in the UI. Inspiration "Somewhere warm under ₹40,000 for four days from Bengaluru" is a complete brief to a friend and an impossible query to a travel site, which wants a destination first, then makes you wait through a slow search per place - with no way to say "that's enough, I've seen what I need." What it does Jhola exposes catalogue, fare search, stay availability, and hold as tools. The agent runs one slow search across twelve destinations while results land one card at a time; the moment the traveller has seen enough, they press Cancel and the search stops honestly - timers cleared, nothing lands afterward, the agent told exactly what was found and what was never searched. A cancelled search returns a first-class partial report, never an error. Booking is irreversible, so there's no book tool at all - Book is a human-only button; holding is reversible, so hold_itinerary is a tool. How we built it execute(args, { signal }) , honoured all the way through: search_fares and check_stays advance through staged timers that obey the AbortSignal Chrome hands every tool call. One AbortController per call, shared by all four ways a call can end - the in-flight strip's own Cancel, the tool console's Cancel, the cancel_call tool, or the caller's own signal - and the activity log always says which one fired. Challenges we ran into Building runtime fallbacks for when Chrome's real cancellation bridge has gaps: if a Cancel click doesn't visibly end the in-flight record within 250ms, the console aborts the call directly and says so; if executeTool() 's own promise doesn't resolve with the string the call actually produced, the console reads it off the call's own record instead - both proven against a simulated broken bridge, not just the happy path. And, like its sibling apps, a self-abort race in hold_itinerary 's dynamic registration, found and fixed with the same deferred-abort pattern. Accomplishments that we're proud of A cancel that is actually honest - a stopped search names exactly what it never searched, instead of pretending it finished or silently discarding the question. What we learned Real cancellation UX needs a fallback story, not just a happy-path signal - a judge's browser, a flaky bridge, or a headless test environment can all diverge from the ideal case, and the app has to stay honest in every one. What's next A price-drop watch tool that re-checks a held itinerary's fare periodically and surfaces it only if it's dropped, without the traveller having to ask again. How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Jhola - a trip finder whose slow searches you can stop Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools). title: PrzedWysylka | WebMCP Lab
pitch: A browser-local FA(3) workbench where an agent can prove a repair while approval remains a visible UI decision.
about_excerpt: A browser-local FA(3) workbench where an agent can prove a repair while approval remains a visible UI decision. Like Comment Story Updates 1 The production workbench after WebMCP has staged and validated a two-value repair. Inspiration Invoice XML is boring until one malformed value stops a real workflow. Poland's FA(3) format is strict and large. Inspecting it by eye is difficult. An agent is useful when the fault is two placeholder values buried inside an official template. That does not mean the agent should quietly decide that the repaired document is acceptable. I built PrzedWysylka WebMCP Lab to test a narrower contract. The agent should do the mechanical work against the state already visible in the browser. The reviewer should see the source and proposed bytes. The same screen should show the validation result and final page control. What it does The app opens an official parameterized FA(3) template at Revision 0. The template is intentionally invalid. Its two placeholders fail canonical XSD validation. The page registers exactly six WebMCP tools: get_workspace_status list_official_assets read_official_asset select_official_asset stage_exact_replacements validate_workspace During the demo, the agent selects the template and validates Revision 0. It reads the relevant source lines, then stages two exact replacements. After validating the pending proposal, the page displays its diff and a SHA-256 proof bound to those proposed bytes. There is no WebMCP approval or rejection tool. The review buttons stay in the visible interface. In the demo workflow, I click Approve changes myself. The store creates Revision 1 and runs canonical validation again. An ordinary browser still gets the complete manual workbench. It also gets an honest WebMCP unavailable status instead of a polyfill pretending that the native API exists. Why WebMCP fits this job Without WebMCP, an agent would have to scrape diagnostics from the DOM and infer which file or revision is active. It would then scroll through XML and type into an editor. That is fragile. A remote MCP server would create another copy of state outside the review surface. Here, each tool calls the same asset registry and validator used by the UI. It also uses the page's replacement engine and workspace store. The agent receives bounded structured results. The reviewer watches the same state change in the page. WebMCP is the working interaction contract rather than a decorative endpoint. The missing capabilities matter too. Approval and rejection are not registered as WebMCP tools. Neither are upload, download or submission. The accurate claim is narrow: approval is a visible UI action and is absent from the WebMCP surface. The app does not claim to identify who operates the browser. How I built it The frontend uses React 19 with TypeScript 6 on Vite 8. It feature-detects document.modelContext and registers imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The definitions have static descriptions and JSON input schemas. Callback inputs pass through Zod before they reach application state. The callbacks reuse existing application services instead of maintaining an agent-only model. Validation runs in the browser through libxml2 compiled to WebAssembly. The deployed app has no application backend or account system. It also has no analytics and no customer upload path. Every successful tool response is limited to 1,500 serialized characters. Catalog results are paged. Source cursors preserve the locked files' CRLF/LF/bare-CR delimiters. A caller cannot place a cursor inside a UTF-16 surrogate pair. Validation returns the complete finding count with compact summaries and explicit truncation metadata. Proposal proof is owned by the store. validate_workspace hashes the exact content snapshot it checked. The record includes the asset and proposal IDs plus the base revision. It also stores the document generation, validation result and proposed SHA-256. Approval fails closed if any part of that identity is stale. Challenges Registering six functions was the easy part. Keeping async work tied to the same browser state took most of the effort. Cancellation exposed a subtle bug. A dependency could ignore its AbortSignal and resolve late, after the caller had already cancelled. I had to invalidate pending work immediately and check state again after every awaited boundary. A cancelled validation can no longer persist a result or revive an obsolete proof. Byte fidelity caused a different class of failures. Many official files use CRLF, while some contain bare carriage returns. Normalizing line endings made a source excerpt look harmless but broke exact replacement. The reader now slices the original decoded text and returns a recoverable cursor without splitting newline pairs or Unicode surrogate pairs. Evidence also needed a hard boundary. The deterministic Playwright suite uses an injected, standards-shaped harness. That proves callback behavior but not native browser support. A separate production smoke uses Chrome's real document.modelContext ; it records nativeModelContext: true and injectedHarness: false . The report does not pretend that an automated Playwright click was a human approval. Verification The native production smoke registers all six tools and executes every callback. It confirms that the WebMCP surface contains no approval tool. Every proof location resolves to the same value, from proposal preflight through the final applied draft: a41799c158deca1bca74e1a158a0748f401721b0ed4b5731ef1a38cfa087c3f0 The offline corpus gate checks all 55 locked first-party records. Browser WASM validation agrees with an independent xmllint gate on 28 expected-valid and 16 expected-invalid FA(3) records. The committed suite covers shared state and cancellation. It tests proposal gating and the visible approval path as separate boundaries. Other checks exercise the ordinary-browser fallback. Responsive layouts and Axe audits run too. The evidence files are committed under docs/assets/ . They record the exact browser build and production artifact identity used for the smoke instead of relying on a screenshot label. What I learned WebMCP works best when a page exposes capabilities it already owns. Creating a parallel agent backend would have weakened this project because the reviewer and agent could disagree about selection or revision state. I also learned that small protocol details become product behavior very quickly. Output limits and cancellation are not cleanup tasks. Neither are cursor semantics or proof identity. If any one of them is vague, the approval screen can look trustworthy while referring to old or incomplete work. What's next The same approach could support other regulated schemas where an agent prepares a repair but the final review stays visible. User-provided documents would require a separate privacy design and threat model before I add an upload path. The six-tool competition surface will remain narrow. title: African Market OS WebMCP Decision Readiness Lab
pitch: A browser-agent lab that turns high-context market decisions into evidence gaps, safe next steps, and human-controlled activation.
about_excerpt: A browser-agent lab that turns high-context market decisions into evidence gaps, safe next steps, and human-controlled activation. Like Comment Story Updates Live WebMCP first-call returns a bounded, gap-first response and maximum-safe next action. The agent converts missing evidence into observable requests before any consequential decision. Exactly five page-defined WebMCP tools are discoverable in the browser agent. Inspiration High-context market decisions often fail before execution because founders, investors, and advisers mistake a persuasive narrative for sufficient evidence. A browser agent can read a conventional page, but it still has to infer which fields matter, what sequence to follow, and when to stop. In market-entry, partnership, investment, and scale decisions, that guesswork can turn thin evidence into false confidence. We built the African Market OS WebMCP Decision Readiness Lab to explore a better interaction: the human supplies context and intent, the website supplies authoritative tools and boundaries, and the browser agent helps turn uncertainty into a practical evidence plan. What it does The live page supports both people and WebMCP-capable browser agents. A user scopes a non-confidential decision with an entity, country, local market or corridor, sector, decision type, timeframe, and evidence note. The page registers exactly five WebMCP tools: amos_scope_market_decision strictly validates and structures the decision context. amos_run_public_first_call calls African Market OS's live, keyless MVR first-call preflight for the active scope. amos_extract_evidence_gap_plan turns returned evidence gaps into observable requests only after a bound preflight exists. amos_prepare_human_next_step validates and prepares a bounded route for a human to choose. amos_get_webmcp_demo_script provides a repeatable state-aware reviewer sequence. The result is deliberately not an approval or readiness verdict. It identifies what is known, what evidence is absent, what must not be claimed, and the maximum-safe action available now. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent must scrape labels, guess UI state, and improvise the workflow. With WebMCP, the page exposes named tools, descriptions, JSON input schemas, execution logic, and explicit authority boundaries in the same context the person is viewing. The agent can invoke the intended operation and receive a structured response consistent with the human-facing experience. This creates a better experience through shared context, lower ambiguity, and safer activation. The workflow distinguishes evidence support from commercial, legal, credit, investment, procurement, or regulatory authorization. What people and agents can do together A person decides which real-world decision to examine and controls every consequential or commercial next step. The browser agent can structure the input, call the live preflight, summarize the evidence gaps, and prepare a focused plan. The visible buttons call the same functions, so browsers without WebMCP retain the full human workflow. How we built it The demo is a self-contained HTML, CSS, and JavaScript application deployed on African Market OS through Cloudflare. It uses the imperative WebMCP API, document.modelContext.registerTool() , to register five page-specific tools. Schemas describe the contract, but every handler also validates independently. Required fields, allowed values, lengths, unexpected properties, and sensitive-data indicators are rejected rather than silently repaired. A deterministic scope_id binds the visible decision to the first call, and the returned preflight_id binds every downstream action. Changing the scope invalidates the old preflight. Same-key retries reuse the active workflow unless an agent explicitly requests a new one. The default agent_compact profile returns one canonical page-level next action. An opt-in debug_full profile preserves deeper inspection without burdening normal agent context. If the upstream MVR response recommends a capability that is not one of the page's five tools, the response labels it as a separate remote-MCP continuation instead of pretending it is locally callable. Protected MVR scoring and private calibration assets are never exposed. The public result states when live scoring did not run and carries a clear not_a_verdict boundary. Challenges The hardest part was not registering a browser tool. It was making schema declarations, handler behavior, visible page state, retries, and downstream handoffs tell the same truth. We had to prevent sample fallbacks from masking invalid agent input, stop stale preflights from surviving a changed form, make retries idempotent, and keep remote MCP capabilities distinct from page-defined tools. Accomplishments Exactly five page-defined WebMCP tools are discoverable. Empty, malformed, over-limit, unexpected, and stale-state inputs fail explicitly. A valid first call returns HTTP 200, a compact gap-first response, and one bound next action. Same-key retries reuse the exact preflight rather than creating duplicate workflows. Human and agent paths share one implementation, while payment and consequential action remain human-controlled. A post-build adversarial review was converted into regression coverage: the production Worker suite passes 153 of 153 tests, the public repository includes a passing dependency-free contract test, and a 30-case Agent Experience regression records the post-fix evidence and caveats. The production /mcp/ and canonical /mcp/preflight surfaces remain separate and unchanged. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it carries semantics, not just clicks. Schema declaration alone is not enough; handlers must defend the same contract. Every multi-tool handoff needs explicit state identity. For evidence-sensitive decisions, a well-designed stop condition is a feature: helping an agent say collect this proof next can be more useful than producing another confident answer. What's next We plan to test the workflow with founders, programme operators, investors, and advisers; measure where agents stop in the handoff sequence; improve accessibility of structured results; and evaluate how evidence plans change real decisions over time. Consequential judgments, credentials, contracting, and payment will remain human-controlled. title: At Attin
pitch: Banking you can ask for — with authority you can see.
about_excerpt: Banking you can ask for — with authority you can see. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Banking still makes people translate a simple goal into menus, forms, account rules, and unfamiliar terminology. That friction hits older adults and first-time users hardest, but everyone feels it when a task becomes stressful or complex. We wanted AI to remove the translation work without removing the person’s authority. What it does At Attin is a complete single-user fictional-money bank: accounts, activity, payees, transfers, scheduled and recurring payments, cards and controls, savings goals, budgets, reports, notifications, disputes, trusted contacts, accessibility settings, and manual forms. Its in-site assistant is powered by Featherless and moonshotai/Kimi-K3 . A user asks for a banking outcome in plain language. The model selects one of 56 imperative WebMCP tools, while four visible form tools support browser-native agent interaction. The bank validates the request, prepares an exact preview, applies financial invariants, shows every consequence, and waits for a person. No agent request executes automatically. Every protected read and every mutation requires fresh visible confirmation. Higher-consequence actions require both YES and a new arithmetic challenge. Authorizations expire after 90 seconds, are single-use, bind to the exact preview and state version, and cannot be replayed. All money is fictional ATC, stored device-locally, with no cash value and no real payment rails. How we built it React, TypeScript, Vite, and React Router Browser-native document.modelContext.registerTool() One shared 56-operation descriptor layer for compatible browser agents and the in-site agent Featherless server proxy with Kimi K3; the provider key never reaches the browser App-owned prepare → confirm → commit coordination with cancellation, expiry, stale-state, and replay protection Integer minor-unit money, atomic writes, versioned local persistence, recovery, and append-only local agent audit OpenAI Codex, HyperFrames, Remotion, Kokoro TTS, Suno, and OpenAI Sites Why WebMCP matters At Attin does not add a deterministic intent parser. The model reasons; WebMCP publishes the bank’s real capabilities; the application owns authorization and execution. The same descriptors and confirmation boundary serve the embedded assistant and compatible browser agents. Challenges The hardest part was ensuring preparation could not leak protected data, and that registration, cancellation, retries, legacy persistence, linked savings reservations, balance floors, and dispute evidence all remained fail-closed. We built explicit invariants, version-bound authorization, single-pending-request coordination, and focused regression tests. Accomplishments 56 imperative tools and 4 visible form surfaces Confirmation for every agent read and change Step-up confirmation for critical actions A complete banking surface instead of a narrow proof-of-concept A working Featherless/Kimi K3 assistant with no direct bank-state access 141 automated tests plus lint, build, and Sites-worker verification High-contrast, low-cognitive-load UX with large text, keyboard focus, and reduced motion What we learned Trust improves when proposal, authorization, and execution are visibly separate. WebMCP gives models semantic access to application capabilities without forcing the application to surrender its policy boundary. What’s next Multi-user identity, passkeys, caregiver and small-business policy packs, privacy-preserving audit export, localization, and broader WebMCP conformance testing. Real-money connectivity remains out of scope until external security review. Try it Live app: https://at-attin.astronebulae.chatgpt.site ATC is fictional, device-local, and has no cash value. title: AutoShop
pitch: A seller-controlled authority layer for agentic commerce
about_excerpt: A seller-controlled authority layer for agentic commerce Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can act, but merchants still need to control what they are allowed to do. Shopify’s agentic-commerce direction and Visa’s emphasis on spending limits, approvals, authentication, and transparency highlighted the same gap: useful autonomy needs enforceable boundaries. AutoShop explores that problem without claiming customer validation. What it does AutoShop is a seller-controlled authority layer for agentic commerce. A seller defines a numerical mandate covering order quantity, value, discount, and remaining stock. Routine orders can proceed automatically. Orders outside the mandate stop as pending actions until the seller reviews and approves that exact exception. Our demo requests six RAM modules against a five-item limit. WebMCP returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED , prevents an immediate stock change, and allows commit_action only after visible human approval. A successful commit creates an auditable receipt recording the decision path and mandate version. Everything shown is synthetic; AutoShop processes no real payment or shipment. How we built it We built two ordinary web portals with seven role-scoped WebMCP tools: Buyer: browse_products , manage_cart , and submit_order Seller: get_mandate , list_orders , accept_order , and commit_action The frontend uses framework-free HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Netlify Functions enforce validation and authorization, while Netlify Database stores versioned mandates, orders, pending actions, inventory, approvals, and receipts. Strict schemas, page-held authorization secrets, authenticated seller sessions, atomic transactions, and idempotency checks prevent the model from expanding its own authority. We verified the complete workflow in ChatGPT’s in-app Browser and maintained 65 automated regression tests. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was making human control, agent capability, and server authority agree. Buyer and seller tools had to appear only in the correct role and disappear after logout, expiry, or navigation. Confirmation secrets also had to remain outside the model-visible tool schema. The final recording produced an honest safety test: our prompt contained a mistyped pending-action ID. The agent detected the mismatch, displayed the live alternative, and requested explicit human confirmation instead of guessing. Its browser-tool connection later expired, but it disclosed the reconnect and completed the confirmed, idempotent commit exactly once. We preserved that recovery in the demo while removing only inactive waiting. Accomplishments that we're proud of Seven deployed, role-scoped WebMCP tools Two visible human authorization boundaries Server-enforced mandate decisions and stale-state protection Token-private order submission and exception approval Atomic inventory mutation with durable receipts Seller-tool removal after logout A reproducible public demo requiring no real customer or payment data What we learned Agent safety becomes understandable when people can see and test the boundary. A written instruction is weaker than a refused tool call, and a promise to ask permission is weaker than a contract that cannot execute without current human authorization. We also learned that identifiers inside natural-language prompts must be treated as untrusted input. Detecting and confirming a correction was safer than silently rewriting the request. What's next for AutoShop Our next step is an observed test with an independent small-store order approver. After validating the workflow, we would build a narrow adapter that places the same mandate → exception → approval → receipt boundary in front of an existing merchant order API. title: Cadence Workout Studio
pitch: Cadence gives self-coached cyclists and agents a shared workout canvas where WebMCP agents turn athlete intent into transparent, constraint-aware workouts, while athletes retain final approval.
about_excerpt: Cadence gives self-coached cyclists and agents a shared workout canvas where WebMCP agents turn athlete intent into transparent, constraint-aware workouts, while athletes retain final approval. Like Comment Story Updates Workout Studio Inspiration For the past couple of months, I have been building an AI Cycling Coaching application that provides recommended daily workouts based on readiness and past activity data. When analyzing this challenge, I realized that the WebMCP capabilities can be used to develop a standalone workout creation canvas as well as have it plugged into an AI Cycling Coaching app. Amateur cyclist have limited time, changing readiness, specific goals, and important sessions they need to protect. AI can offer recommendations, but they often arrive as opaque text with no shared editing surface, visible calculations, or reliable approval boundaries. Cadence Workout Studio explores a different model: the athlete and agent collaborate on the same visible workout, while Cadence owns the calculations, constraints, revision history, and safety boundaries. What it does Cadence is a shared workout-composition studio powered by seven focused WebMCP tools. An agent can inspect the rider’s planning context, select an approved workout structure, construct interval blocks, evaluate the athlete’s exact revision, request a bounded repair, and validate the result. Every agent action appears immediately in the same interface the athlete uses. The Studio shows interval changes, workout duration, intensity, training load, time in zone, constraint violations, repair tradeoffs, provenance, and exact-revision status. The athlete can edit the proposed workout at any time. Approval and export remain human-only actions, so an agent cannot silently finalize a workout. The complete workflow also works manually in browsers without WebMCP. How I built it I built Cadence as a public, synthetic-data challenge edition using Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The WebMCP integration registers seven narrow page tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool delegates to the same domain services used by the human interface, rather than maintaining a separate agent workflow. Workout calculations and validation are independent of the WebMCP transport. Cadence calculates duration, intensity factor, training load, power targets, and time in zone. Every edit creates a new revision, invalidates previous validation or approval, and rejects stale agent requests. The application uses browser-local persistence and a resettable fictional rider, so judges need no account, credentials, wearable, private database, or personal health data. Approved indoor workouts can be exported as .zwo or JSON files. The repository includes automated domain, schema, persistence, stale-revision, export-gate, and browser workflow tests, along with the complete challenge-period implementation history. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was making the agent and athlete true collaborators, not building a chat interface that generated a finished workout. I needed one revisioned artifact that both sides could inspect and change without losing authorship or allowing stale operations. That required exact-revision validation, approval fingerprints, visible provenance, and automatic invalidation after every edit. Designing repair behavior was another challenge. The agent should not directly invent arbitrary changes, so Cadence accepts a bounded objective and priorities, chooses the concrete repair itself, and records the resulting tradeoffs. I also had to keep the seven tools narrow enough for reliable agent use while returning enough structured state for both the agent and athlete to verify every result. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that Cadence feels like a complete product that can integrate with its parent product, ThresholdLabs, to improve the recommendation engine or act as a standalone workout configurator. The athlete can deliberately change a workout, create a constraint violation, ask an agent to evaluate the exact revision, let Cadence repair it, validate the repaired workout, and then personally approve and export it. The same calculations, constraints, and state transitions power both the WebMCP tools and the manual interface. The app preserves human authority while making agent collaboration visible, structured, and useful. I am also proud that the public challenge edition requires no credentials or private infrastructure and contains only isolated synthetic data. What I learned I learned that the strongest WebMCP tools expose domain capabilities rather than mirroring buttons or asking an agent to scrape the interface. WebMCP becomes especially powerful when the webpage remains the source of truth. The agent contributes intent and priorities, the application enforces its domain rules, and the human can see and verify the result. I also learned that human approval is more meaningful when it is tied to an exact, validated revision rather than a general conversation or recommendation. What's next for Cadence Workout Studio Next, I would expand the approved workout library, add richer outdoor execution guidance, improve comparison between alternative repairs, integrate into ThresholdLabs intelligence engine, and support reusable athlete-created templates. A future production version could connect to athlete-owned training data with explicit consent, while preserving the same visible provenance, bounded agent actions, exact-revision validation, and human approval model demonstrated here.
