title: Countersign
pitch: An evidence room where WebMCP agents inspect and draft—but the publish tool literally does not exist until a human countersigns the brief.
about_excerpt: An evidence room where WebMCP agents inspect and draft—but the publish tool literally does not exist until a human countersigns the brief. Like Comment Story Updates The full evidence board: bounded claims, the human review queue, and the live WebMCP tool count. The seven baseline tools with their read and write annotations. Publication is not among them. Instruction-like evidence is labelled UNTRUSTED and given zero weight, yet preserved as quoted source material. Deterministic consistency findings, reproducible byte-for-byte across identical calls. An agent-staged assessment waits in the human review queue. No tool can approve it. Human approval is what exposes the publication capability. Eight tools now: publish_approved_brief carries the dynamic annotation. The approved brief, published unchanged and with its grounding chain intact. Inspiration Investigation leads often have to reconcile contradictory reports under time pressure. An agent can reduce the reading and drafting load, but an unreviewed synthesis should not silently become an official statement. I built Countersign to explore a stricter division of responsibility: software can inspect and propose quickly, while people retain accountable approval. The name describes the product rule. A consequential artifact needs a human countersign before an agent can receive the capability to release it. What it does Countersign is a fictional evidence room containing six claims and fifteen evidence records. A WebMCP agent can: inspect a bounded incident and list its claims; retrieve evidence through stable IDs and explicit trust metadata; run deterministic consistency checks; stage a cited assessment for human review; and create a brief from human-approved assessments. The agent cannot approve an assessment or brief. Those decisions exist only in the visible human interface. The final boundary is stronger than a disabled button. publish_approved_brief is absent from tool discovery until a person approves a brief. Approval changes the page's capability surface from seven tools to eight. The tool then releases only the unchanged approved artifact and disappears after the last eligible brief is published. Why WebMCP A vision-only agent would have to scrape cards, infer controls, and guess how evidence relates to claims. Countersign instead exposes a small typed contract through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . WebMCP is part of the governance model, not a wrapper around the UI: five baseline tools are genuinely read-only and perform no workspace mutation; two write tools can create drafts but cannot cross an approval boundary; claim and evidence responses carry untrustedContentHint ; schemas reject unknown fields, malformed values, and cross-claim citations; deterministic checks exclude instruction-like evidence from scoring; and human approval dynamically grants and revokes the one-shot publication capability. This lets a person and an agent share one workflow without sharing the same authority. Human review that is actually reviewable An approval screen shows the proposal alongside every cited excerpt, source, reliability label, trust boundary, and structured ID. Brief review shows the complete chain from approved assessment to claim and evidence. The released bulletin keeps that provenance visible and can be copied or downloaded as Markdown. The human gate therefore reviews evidence, not just an opaque agent conclusion. How I built it I built the application with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Zustand, then deployed it as a static Netlify site. The scenario and state are browser-local, so judges need no account, API key, external model, or private data. The seven baseline WebMCP tools are: get_incident_overview list_claims inspect_claim_evidence check_evidence_consistency get_review_status stage_claim_assessment create_brief_draft publish_approved_brief is the eighth, dynamic tool. Its handler rechecks live eligibility, accepts no replacement body, returns structured grounding, and becomes undiscoverable when no approved unpublished brief remains. Vitest covers validation, read-only purity, state gates, pagination, structured grounding, and deterministic logic. Playwright covers the visible human workflow, accessibility focus, responsive behavior, concurrent approved briefs, and the dynamic tool lifecycle. A separate Chrome harness exercises the native document.modelContext discovery and execution API against the production origin. Challenges The hardest problem was making capability registration follow application state without becoming fragile. Chrome 151 can omit the callback options argument, and aborting a registration synchronously during its own execution can cancel the result. I added compatibility handling, delayed technical removal while keeping business validation immediately one-shot, and a regression test for multiple eligible briefs so the page never races itself into a duplicate tool name. Another challenge was response size. list_claims now returns all six compact records in the normal path and also exposes offset , nextOffset , and hasMore for bounded pagination. Finally, I had to separate a security signal from a security claim. The application marks hostile text as untrusted and excludes it from deterministic scoring. The automated demo uses a deterministic native WebMCP client, not a language model, so I do not claim that it evaluates an LLM's prompt-injection resistance. What I learned WebMCP tool design is not only about choosing functions. It also requires deciding when a capability should exist, what state a read-only call may change, which outputs require distrust, and where human accountability belongs. I also learned that deterministic software and agent reasoning should not compete for the same job. Fixed code is better for replayable consistency checks and state enforcement; an agent is useful for navigating and drafting from bounded material; a person remains responsible for consequential release decisions. Potential impact The demonstrated workflow targets incident investigation leads who need to turn contradictory reports into one traceable, human-approved brief. The same capability-shaped consent pattern could support newsroom verification desks, compliance case reviews, research evidence synthesis, or incident postmortems. This prototype does not claim production readiness. A real deployment would need authentication, durable storage, role-based authorization, privacy controls, real source connectors, and domain-specific validation. The contribution here is a reusable WebMCP governance primitive: approval changes what the agent is technically capable of doing. title: DOMHamster
pitch: A human-in-the-loop AI dispatcher that helps coordinate volunteers without taking control away from the coordinator.
about_excerpt: A human-in-the-loop AI dispatcher that helps coordinate volunteers without taking control away from the coordinator. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are getting better at using websites, but many of them still have to guess what a page means from buttons, labels, and layout. That is usually fine for simple tasks. It becomes a problem when the agent is working with schedules, approvals, private information, or decisions that a person has already made. I wanted to explore a workflow where the agent could still do useful work, but where important decisions stayed clearly under human control. That idea became DOMHamster , a volunteer-dispatch demo built around WebMCP. What DOMHamster does DOMHamster helps coordinate a fictional, non-emergency volunteer operation with eight requests and five available volunteers. The agent can use WebMCP tools to: Read the current requests, volunteers, assignments, and audit history Create a complete assignment draft Check whether the draft is valid Repair scheduling conflicts Prepare a specific draft version for human review Commit the plan after the coordinator approves it Request one contact record when it is actually needed Review a sanitized history of important actions The agent does not have permission to do everything. It cannot approve its own draft, override a locked human decision, reset the application, or freely access every contact record. Those actions remain controlled by the person using the interface. How the demo works The agent starts by reading the current coordination data and creating a full assignment draft. The coordinator then changes request R-105 from volunteer V-01 to V-03 at 1:00 p.m. and locks that choice. This creates a scheduling conflict with R-106 . Instead of replacing the coordinator's decision, DOMHamster blocks approval and explains what went wrong. The agent is then asked to repair the plan while preserving the locked assignment. The repair keeps R-105 exactly as the coordinator selected it and moves only the conflicting request to another available volunteer. Once the draft is valid again, the agent prepares that exact version for review. The coordinator must approve it through the interface before the agent receives permission to commit it. The commit can only be used once. After the plan is committed, the commit capability disappears, and a repeated attempt is rejected. Contact information is also restricted. The agent can request the contact for one specific assignment only after the plan has been committed. The audit history records that contact access happened, but it does not copy the sensitive contact value into the log. Finally, the coordinator can reset the scenario and return it to the original READY state. How I built it I built DOMHamster as a state-driven web application and exposed its agent capabilities through the native document.modelContext WebMCP interface. The project includes 12 structured WebMCP tools. Each tool has: A clear purpose Structured inputs and outputs State requirements Predictable error responses A JSON Schema contract The available tools change depending on the current application state. For example, the commit tool is not available before human approval. Contact access is not available before the plan is committed. After a successful commit, the commit tool is removed so it cannot be used twice. I also tied approvals and mutations to the current draft version. This prevents an approval from being reused after the underlying plan has changed. I tested the tools with the ChatGPT browser extension , as well as Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. I also used Playwright and the Chrome DevTools Protocol to test tool registration, state changes, invalid actions, and replay protection. The application was built with TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, and deployed with Netlify. I used Remotion and FFmpeg to create and edit the project video. Challenges I faced The hardest part was keeping the WebMCP tool surface synchronized with the actual application state. A tool may be valid in one state but unsafe or meaningless in another. I had to make sure tools appeared and disappeared at the correct time, and that invalid or outdated actions failed in a clear and predictable way. Other challenges included: Preventing a stale draft from being committed Preserving human-locked assignments during an agent repair Making approval apply to one exact draft version Keeping commit authorization short-lived and single-use Rejecting repeated or out-of-order actions safely Restricting contact access until after commitment Recording useful audit events without exposing contact information Resetting the full scenario back to the same starting state for repeated testing Creating the demo video was also more difficult than expected. I had to keep the narration, subtitles, screen states, and timings aligned while still making the workflow understandable to someone seeing the project for the first time. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that giving an agent more tools does not automatically create a better experience. What matters is giving it the right tool at the right moment. Tool availability can work as part of the permission model. Instead of exposing every action all the time and relying only on written instructions, the application can remove capabilities that are not currently allowed. I also learned that approval is much safer when it is tied to a specific version. A general “yes” is ambiguous if the draft changes afterward. Approving an exact visible version creates a much clearer connection between what the person reviewed and what the agent is allowed to execute. Most importantly, the human-agent experience feels more trustworthy when the agent handles the repetitive coordination work, while important decisions remain visible and controlled through the interface. What's next The next step would be to test DOMHamster with more agent clients and expand the scheduling rules beyond the current deterministic scenario. I would also like to add server-backed authentication and authorization, improve accessibility, and explore how the same approval pattern could work in other coordination tools where agents need to act without silently taking control away from people. title: Github web mcp
pitch: If github implemented webmcp, this would help human and ai reviews co-exist with a better user experience
about_excerpt: If github implemented webmcp, this would help human and ai reviews co-exist with a better user experience Like Comment Story Updates After approval, the agent creates issue #3, opens it in the interface, and the WebMCP surface returns to seven tools. RepoScope shows the agent’s inline security finding, editable issue proposal, human approval, trace, and dynamically exposed 10-tool. ## Inspiration Repository review is usually split between a web interface and a detached AI conversation. Browser agents can attempt to interpret the DOM, while remote MCP servers can expose repository APIs, but neither naturally shares the exact transient workspace state the person is viewing. GitHub Web MCP, presented as RepoScope , explores a different approach: the webpage itself exposes structured, context-sensitive capabilities to the agent. The human and agent review the same file, findings, proposal, and approval state in one visible workspace. ## What it does RepoScope is a controlled GitHub-like repository review application demonstrating human-agent collaboration through WebMCP. A person opens a file and asks an agent to review the repository. The agent: Reads the live workspace context. Investigates relevant repository files. Identifies the most serious substantiated problem. Places a visible annotation on the relevant line. Prepares an editable issue proposal without creating it. The person can edit, approve, or dismiss the proposal. Approval authorizes one exact draft revision but does not execute it. After the person tells the agent “Approved,” the agent creates the reviewed issue and the result immediately appears in the interface. The page’s tool surface changes with its state: Fresh repository: 7 tools Reviewable file open: 9 tools Exact proposal approved: 10 tools Issue created or proposal dismissed: 7 tools This dynamic capability model demonstrates why the experience benefits from WebMCP instead of being a conventional API wrapper. ## How we built it RepoScope is a client-only React and TypeScript application built with Vite and deployed using Cloudflare Workers Static Assets. The React interface and WebMCP tools share one observable application service. This ensures that human actions and agent actions use the same application logic and produce immediate visible updates. The dedicated WebMCP adapter: Registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() Separates read-only and state-changing capabilities Reconciles registrations when workspace state changes Cleans up registrations with abort signals Verifies discovery using document.modelContext.getTools() Records agent calls in a visible activity feed Updates the interface before mutating calls finish The final issue-creation capability accepts only a reference to the exact approved proposal. It rejects pending, edited, dismissed, stale, unknown, or previously completed proposals. The project intentionally uses local fixture data rather than a backend or GitHub API. This keeps the demonstration focused on live page context, dynamic capabilities, and human approval. ## Challenges we ran into The first challenge was making WebMCP essential to the experience. An early version allowed an agent to inspect files and create an issue, but a remote MCP server could have provided the same functionality. We redesigned the workflow around live workspace state, dynamic tool discovery, visible annotations, and in- page approval. Designing a reliable approval boundary was another challenge. Clicking Approve and executing the action are intentionally separate. Editing an approved proposal revokes its approval, and the agent cannot change its contents during the final creation call. WebMCP is also an experimental browser API. We isolated all experimental integration code behind a small adapter, made the normal interface work when WebMCP is unavailable, and added visible discovery status and automated lifecycle tests. Finally, agent activity is normally difficult to demonstrate on video. We added a bounded activity feed so viewers can see the agent investigate, annotate, propose, and complete its work directly in the application. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete two-turn human-agent workflow that requires no tool names, schemas, or internal identifiers in the human conversation. The person can make a natural request, review the agent’s evidence in context, approve an exact proposal, and complete the action by saying only “Approved.” We are especially proud of: Dynamic discovery that visibly transitions 7 → 9 → 10 → 7 Inline findings connected to the relevant source line An editable and revocable approval workflow Exact-revision authorization for issue creation Immediate UI updates from agent actions A visible and safely summarized agent activity feed Graceful behavior when WebMCP is unavailable A native ChatGPT Site tools rehearsal of the complete workflow The automated suite includes 28 unit and component tests plus three Playwright browser scenarios, alongside TypeScript, ESLint, and production-build verification. ## What we learned Our main lesson was that WebMCP is more than a browser-accessible API. Its strongest value appears when an agent’s capabilities reflect the transient state, permissions, and workflow of the page a person is actively using. Dynamic discovery can provide both context and control. It reduces irrelevant options for the agent and ensures sensitive capabilities appear only when their prerequisites are satisfied. We also learned that successful tool execution is not enough for good collaboration. People need to see what the agent inspected, what it found, what it proposes, and exactly where human authority begins and ends. ## What's next for Github web mcp The next step is to evolve RepoScope from a focused competition demonstration into a reusable pattern for safe, context-aware repository collaboration. Potential extensions include: Optional integration with real GitHub repositories Persistent review sessions and findings Pull-request review workflows Line-range and multi-file annotations Multiple independently reviewable proposals Repository-specific authorization policies Richer evidence links between findings, code, issues, and pull requests Improved compatibility as the WebMCP standard evolves The approval model could also be applied beyond repository review. Document editors, design tools, administrative dashboards, and investigation workspaces could expose context-sensitive agent capabilities while preserving their existing human controls and authorization boundaries. title: Hubit
pitch: A storefront where you can hand an agent the shopping without handing over your wallet.
about_excerpt: A storefront where you can hand an agent the shopping without handing over your wallet. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration People will happily let an agent research a purchase. Almost nobody lets one finish it. The reason is not that agents shop badly. It is that "it can look but it cannot buy" has never been a mechanism, only a promise. Every guardrail on offer today is a server saying no, and a refusal is just a message. A model can retry a message, argue with it, or try again with different arguments. What it does Hubit is a storefront where you can hand an agent the shopping without handing it your wallet. You write your rules in plain language: under $1,200, I already have a laptop, prioritise quality. The agent searches the store, compares specs, finds cheaper alternatives, fills the cart, and types your delivery details. You watch every move it makes on screen while you edit the same cart yourself. Then it goes to check out, and checkout is not in its toolbox. Not refused. Not there. The agent has nothing to retry and nothing to argue with. Its only remaining move is to ask you: "$1,255 against your $1,200 budget. Raise it by $55?" You click approve, and checkout appears in the agent's toolbox, live, in the same tab, with no reload. Three things have to be true before that happens, and all three are visible on the page: the cart is inside your rules, your delivery details are complete, and you approved this basket. Change any of them and the approval goes with it. You approved a particular cart going to a particular address, so an agent cannot quietly redirect a parcel you already said yes to. How we built it A static storefront on Next.js, React and Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. Seventeen tools the agent can use. No backend, no database, no server anywhere in the project, which is the whole argument: there is no API for the agent to go around, because the authority lives in the page you are looking at. The agent writes to the same place your keyboard does. There is no separate agent path, which is what makes it honest rather than theatre. Every field the agent typed into your delivery form is marked on screen and tagged as agent-written, and you can overwrite any of it. That single screen carries the entire idea: the agent can type your address and still cannot spend your money. The store never just goes quiet on the agent either. It always says why checkout is being withheld, so the agent knows to come back and ask instead of retrying into a wall. Challenges we ran into Handing back a tool while you are using it. Checkout places the order, and placing the order is exactly what takes checkout away. The tool was pulling the rug out from under itself mid-call, so the agent saw an error on an order that had actually gone through fine. Accomplishments that we're proud of An uncoached model shopped the store on its own, in production. Given nothing but a plain shopping prompt, it compared desks, chairs, monitors and keyboards, built a $1,255 basket against a $1,200 budget, hit the missing checkout, went looking for cheaper alternatives, found the nearest one only saved $50, and proposed raising the budget on its own initiative. We never told it to do any of that. The full transcript is in the repo. 105 automated checks against the live site, all passing. They drive the real tools the way an agent would, and they open the gate by clicking the actual approve button on the page, not by flipping a flag in test code. Nothing in this project is faked. No mock agent, no simulated run, no fallback path. Everything in the demo is the real thing working. What we learned That the interesting part of WebMCP is not that a web page can offer tools to an agent. It is that which tools exist can change while the agent is working , and that it can change because a human just made a decision. We also learned to be precise about what we are claiming. This is a consent boundary, not a security boundary, and it sits one step earlier than a server check. A server saying no is something a model retries. A tool that is not there is something it never thinks to reach for. A real shop wants both, and WebMCP is what makes the earlier one possible at all. What's next for Hubit Real payments behind the gate , so both layers do their proper job: the missing tool stops the agent from ever forming the intent, the server stops anything that goes around the page. Approvals with shape, instead of one yes or no. Approve up to an amount, approve one merchant, approve for the next ten minutes. The mechanism already handles this, since each one is just a different question asked at the same moment. Approval that survives a refresh , tied to the exact basket so it cannot be reused on a different cart or a different address. The pattern beyond shopping. Nothing about this is specific to retail. Sending an email, filing a pull request, booking a flight, moving money: any page where an agent should do the whole job except the last irreversible step can hold back exactly one tool, and hand it over when a human says so. Why our use case is a strong fit for WebMCP People will happily let an agent research a purchase. Almost nobody lets one finish it. The reason is not that agents shop badly. It is that "it can look but it cannot buy" has never been a mechanism, only a promise. Every guardrail on offer today is a server saying no, somewhere behind an API. A refusal is a message, a message is an input, and a model can be argued into retrying an input. WebMCP has one property that no server-side guardrail can imitate: the tool surface is a live, mutable property of the tab. registerTool takes an AbortSignal , so a capability can be absent, then appear mid-conversation because a human decided something, then disappear again when they change their mind. Hubit registers checkout only while a gate is open. When that gate is closed the agent cannot call checkout , cannot retry it, and cannot argue with it, because there is nothing there. getTools() does not list it, and a stale handle captured before the abort is rejected at browser level. To be exact about what we are claiming: this is not a security boundary, and we have never presented it as one. It is a consent boundary, and it operates one layer earlier than a server check. A server refusal is a runtime "no" that a model retries, reasons around and argues with. A capability that is absent from the surface means the planner never forms the intent, so there is no retry loop to lose. In production both exist the server check is the security boundary, and this is what stops an agent from ever reaching it without you. WebMCP is what makes that earlier layer possible at all, because tools are registered per session in the page and can be revoked mid-conversation. How it creates a better user experience The tedious half of a purchase gets delegated. The half that needs judgment does not. The agent searches, compares specs side by side, finds cheaper alternatives, fills the cart, and types your delivery details name, email, address, postcode, country, delivery speed, courier notes. It writes to the same store your keyboard writes to. There is no separate agent path, and that is exactly what makes the provenance honest: every field the agent typed is outlined in the accent colour and tagged agent , and you can overwrite any of them. That one screen carries the whole thesis the agent can type your address and still cannot spend your money. You also watch it work instead of reading a transcript of it. Two tools move your screen filter_catalog changes the shelf you are looking at, focus_product opens a quick view and every call streams into a rail on the right with its real arguments. The rail renders from the tool host's own registry rather than from a hardcoded list, so if a tool ever failed to register it shows that instead of claiming it is live. And the store always tells you why checkout is withheld: over budget, no delivery address, or this basket is not approved. The agent's only remaining move is to ask you. propose_constraint_change queues a proposal and changes nothing by itself. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Grant a capability mid-conversation and take it back. Approve the basket and checkout appears live, in the same tab, with no reload. Then change the cart, move the budget, edit the delivery address, switch to express delivery, or click "Withdraw approval", and it leaves the surface again. Consent is per basket, not per session : you approved a particular cart going to a particular place, so any change to either withdraws it. Emptying a required delivery field withholds checkout , and restoring that field does not silently re-open it, because the approval left with the change. title: OpenDeal
pitch: Agent-native negotiation for the open web. AI agents discover, compare and negotiate structured offers via WebMCP while humans retain explicit authority over transactions.
about_excerpt: Agent-native negotiation for the open web. AI agents discover, compare and negotiate structured offers via WebMCP while humans retain explicit authority over transactions. Like Comment Story Updates OpenDeal OpenDeal is agent-native negotiation for the open web. It demonstrates how AI agents can discover suppliers, compare structured offers, negotiate price, verify delivery constraints, and recommend a transaction through WebMCP — while the human retains explicit authority over the irreversible financial action. The mission Buy 100 ANSI Z89.1 Type II safety helmets with four hard constraints: total budget ≤ $2,500 delivery by Friday no substitutions final purchase requires human approval Three supplier contexts expose WebMCP tools for inventory discovery, product specifications, quotes, counteroffers, and delivery checks. The deterministic negotiation produces: Alpha Industrial: $2,350, Friday — compliant Bravo Safety Supply: $2,325, Friday — compliant and selected Charlie Works: $2,290, Monday — cheaper, but rejected because it violates the delivery deadline The agent therefore optimizes for the buyer's actual constraints instead of simply choosing the lowest price. The core WebMCP idea: bounded authority OpenDeal does not treat human approval as a cosmetic modal. Authorization changes the browser's actual executable capability surface. Before approval, the suppliers' search, specification, quote, negotiation, and delivery tools are available — but bravo.create_purchase_order does not exist. When the human approves Bravo's exact $2,325 offer, OpenDeal dynamically registers the purchase capability. After the order executes, that capability is removed and replaced with bravo.get_order_status . A live Chrome/WebMCP run verified the lifecycle directly from document.modelContext : PRE-APPROVAL: 15 tools; purchase capability absent APPROVED: 16 tools; bravo.create_purchase_order present ORDERED: 16 tools; purchase capability absent; bravo.get_order_status present The workflow is: discover → evaluate → negotiate → recommend → human authorize → execute → observe Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent would usually need supplier-specific APIs, DOM scraping, brittle browser automation, or a centralized marketplace integration. With WebMCP, each website intentionally exposes structured actions using explicit schemas. The website controls which capabilities exist, their scope, and their lifecycle. The agent gets reliable machine-usable actions without guessing how to click through a UI. That creates a better user experience: the agent handles repetitive discovery, comparison, negotiation, and constraint checking, while the person keeps control over the action that commits money. What people and agents can do together The human provides the objective and authority boundary. The agent performs the multi-supplier work that would otherwise require repetitive browsing, quote collection, comparison, and follow-up. The human only steps back in when the transaction crosses the approval boundary. The important distinction is that the system does not merely say the agent lacks purchasing authority — the purchase operation is genuinely unavailable until authorization occurs. Implementation OpenDeal is intentionally dependency-light so the WebMCP behavior remains visible and auditable. It uses: modern JavaScript ES modules HTML and CSS browser Web APIs document.modelContext.registerTool() getTools() and executeTool() structured tool input schemas deterministic supplier pricing and delivery policies AbortController -scoped tool lifecycles an explicit transaction state machine a visible execution ledger and WebMCP inspector automated domain and lifecycle tests Each supplier registers five base capabilities. The selected supplier's purchase tool is dynamically registered only after approval, then removed after use and replaced by an order-status capability. The implementation also includes explicit buyer-origin allowlisting support for deployments where supplier contexts live on distinct origins; the challenge deployment is kept same-origin on Netlify for simple, reproducible judging. Why it matters Procurement is only the demonstration domain. The same capability-boundary pattern can apply to travel, logistics, reservations, insurance, professional services, or any workflow where agents need meaningful autonomy without unlimited authority. OpenDeal explores a web where agents do not need to imitate human clicking. Websites become intentional participants in agent-mediated transactions, and humans retain explicit control over the boundaries that matter most. title: Patchwork
pitch: A browser-native React workspace where people and Codex safely build, preview, recover, and export together.
about_excerpt: A browser-native React workspace where people and Codex safely build, preview, recover, and export together. Like Comment Story Updates Patchwork keeps files, code, preview, diagnostics, checkpoints, and activity in one browser workspace. Atomic multi-file WebMCP edit: one checkpoint, one revision, and the Roamly preview updated. The page becomes the tool: Patchwork exposes ten WebMCP operations while the human keeps the files, preview, and recovery controls in view. Inspiration Most AI coding tools bring the project into the agent's interface. We wanted to explore the inverse: what if the application itself could offer a precise, safe collaboration surface to the agent the user already has? Web development is a strong test case because the human needs visual context while the agent needs structured access to files, diagnostics, and mutations. Clicking through a file tree is possible, but it is slow and ambiguous. Patchwork keeps the project, preview, and recovery controls visible while WebMCP gives Codex operations with explicit schemas and outcomes. What it does Patchwork provides a browser-based workspace for small React projects. A user can load one of three deterministic starters, select and edit text files, inspect a live preview and available diagnostics, create or restore checkpoints, reset the current demo, and export the project as a ZIP. When the page is opened in a compatible ChatGPT browser, Codex can discover Patchwork's Site Tools. It can read workspace context and explicit files, apply a validated multi-file change, move or delete one explicit file, inspect preview diagnostics, manage checkpoints, and prepare an export. UI actions and agent tools call the same workspace services, so both participants see the same revision and result. Patchwork remains usable as a human-only application when WebMCP is unavailable. How we built it The host application uses React, strict TypeScript, and Vite. Sandpack provides the editor/preview runtime, IndexedDB stores local workspace state, and JSZip prepares local exports. The workspace domain normalizes relative POSIX paths, allowlists text formats, enforces per-file, per-batch, and total-workspace limits, and stages complete mutations before commit. An optional expected revision prevents silent stale overwrites. Every committed content mutation creates a checkpoint first and increments the workspace revision once. WebMCP is registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool() in the top-level host document after workspace services are ready. The Sandpack iframe does not register tools. An injected Playwright adapter captures those production registrations and invokes the real handlers for deterministic tests; it is not a second tool implementation. How WebMCP is used Patchwork exposes these stable tools: get_workspace_context list_files read_files write_files move_file delete_file inspect_preview create_checkpoint restore_checkpoint prepare_project_export Read tools return bounded, structured state without changing files, checkpoints, activity, persistence, or revision. Mutations validate the entire request before committing, create recovery checkpoints, and return stable receipts with revision and changed paths. Errors are structured and repairable, including stale revision, invalid path, collision, unsupported extension, and size-limit cases. Why WebMCP is load-bearing Without WebMCP, the agent would need to guess the application's state and manipulate files through pixels, focus, and keystrokes. That makes multi-file changes, concurrency, recovery, and verification fragile. With WebMCP, the page provides explicit schemas for reading selected files, applying one atomic batch, checking the observed revision, inspecting available diagnostics, and restoring a known snapshot. This is not a shortcut around the product UI: it is the collaboration layer that lets the person and agent operate the same live application with shared state and clear effects. Challenges The hardest design problem was making Site Tools useful without turning Patchwork into a remote shell. We constrained the workspace to small text projects, made paths and payloads narrowly valid, and separated export preparation from the user-triggered download. Another challenge was integrating an iframe-based preview while respecting current ChatGPT Site Tools limitations. Registration belongs to the top-level document, so the host owns the WebMCP boundary and receives only supported preview status and diagnostics from Sandpack. Patchwork does not claim visual understanding when it only has compiler or runtime signals. Finally, UI actions and agent calls had to stay consistent. We avoided parallel implementations by routing both through the same domain and persistence services. Accomplishments A browser-native collaboration model with no embedded chatbot or API key. A shared service layer for human and WebMCP operations. Atomic, revision-aware multi-file mutations with automatic recovery snapshots. Deterministic demo starters and reset behavior. Graceful human operation when Site Tools are unavailable. A production-handler test adapter that does not duplicate business logic. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a web product already has clear domain operations. The best tools are not generic clicks; they expose meaningful application actions with narrow inputs, honest side effects, and enough result data to verify the outcome. We also learned that local-first architecture is a useful fit for agent collaboration. It reduces setup and data movement, but it still needs explicit limits, persistence validation, concurrency control, and recovery. Finally, preview diagnostics and visual review are different evidence and should never be conflated. What's next After the challenge build is frozen, potential follow-ups include a small public-GitHub import with strict limits, a human-readable diff view, and a read-only share format. These are not part of the submitted MVP unless independently implemented and verified before the deadline. title: PlanOnIt
pitch: PlanOnIt gives a WebMCP agent real tools to plan your evening out — film, transport, dinner — while you keep the final approval.
about_excerpt: PlanOnIt gives a WebMCP agent real tools to plan your evening out — film, transport, dinner — while you keep the final approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted a small, concrete domain to actually test what WebMCP makes possible, instead of a demo that just claims an agent did something. Planning a night out — a film, then dinner after — is a real multi-constraint problem: the showtime fixes the cinema, the cinema fixes the route, the route decides how much time is really left before the table, and every one of those choices moves the total cost. It's exactly the kind of thing an agent is good at grinding through and a person is good at approving. Most "agentic" demos I'd seen were either a chat box bolted onto a UI it couldn't see, or an agent with unchecked authority to just click "book." I wanted the version where the agent gets real capabilities and the person still holds the only button that matters. What it does PlanOnIt plans a real evening out in Dhaka — a film, the trip across the city, and dinner after — with an AI agent doing the tedious cross-referencing through 13 WebMCP tools registered directly on the page. The agent can search restaurants and showtimes, build a plan, check feasibility, calculate cost, and repair a plan a human edit just broke. It can never approve or reserve anything — that stays a real click in the UI, every time. Once approved, reservation is a genuine sandboxed transaction: a compare-and-swap against shared inventory, idempotent on retry, and it fails closed on conflict instead of quietly double-booking. How we built it React 19 + TypeScript + Vite on the frontend, Zod for runtime validation, deployed as a static build to Vercel. The core decision was to build one domain layer ( src/domain.ts ) that both the human UI and the WebMCP tools call into — the same solver, the same nine feasibility checks, the same versioned mutations — so there's never a "friendly explanation for the person" that can quietly drift from "the raw check the agent gets." Every mutation carries an expectedVersion ; a stale write fails loudly with STALE_PLAN_VERSION instead of silently overwriting someone else's edit, whether that edit came from a human or another agent call. Same-origin tabs stay in sync through a Web Locks-backed compare-and-swap. Inventory sits inside a rolling two-week window computed off the real clock, so the demo never goes stale no matter when a judge opens it. Challenges we ran into The one I'm least proud of, and gladdest I caught before submitting: late in the build I found that a human could never manually pick a transport option — every click failed with "Transport option does not belong to the selected venue route." The agent's tools worked fine, and so did the auto-repair path, which made it easy to miss. It turned out the manual UI was resolving the cinema-to-restaurant route with the two location IDs swapped, and since each direction generates its own distinct set of transport-option IDs, the buttons on screen were always offering IDs from the wrong route object. It only ever broke the human path — a good reminder that "the agent's tools work" and "the manual UI works" are two separate claims, and testing one doesn't verify the other. I added a regression test that reproduces the exact failure so it can't come back silently. Building a reservation that's an actual transaction, not just a returned success string, was its own challenge: idempotency keys are bound to the reservation's content fingerprint, not just a request ID, so a retry after a dropped connection can't accidentally create a second booking, and a replayed or forged confirmation can't be pointed at a different reservation. And a last-minute one that had nothing to do with code: my original LICENSE restricted commercial use without permission, which meant it wasn't actually an open-source license, even though I'd always intended it to be. Caught and fixed to MIT before submission — "open source" has to be literally detectable, not just intended. Accomplishments that we're proud of 198 automated tests plus 21 real-browser Playwright tests, covering adversarial input, concurrency, the full reservation lifecycle, and idempotency — not just the happy path. The evaluation-symmetry property: the UI's "why isn't this plan valid yet" and the agent's validate_plan tool result are always the same function call against the same state. There's no second copy of the business logic that could quietly disagree with the first. Approval isn't gated by a permission check the agent could theoretically satisfy — it's architecturally absent from the tool surface. No WebMCP tool touches approval at all. Shipping with no login requirement, on purpose. It would have been easy to bolt on accounts to look more "complete," but this build doesn't actually need cross-device sync to do its job, so I didn't fake it. What we learned That "the agent works" has to be tested completely separately from "the human path works" — they share code, but a single reversed argument can break only one of them, silently. That documentation drifts fast: numbers like "12 tools" or "eight checks" written once during development go stale the moment the code moves on, and are worth re-deriving from the running code rather than trusting memory. And that the strongest trust story for an agentic feature isn't a more polite prompt — it's an architectural boundary the agent literally cannot cross, like approval never being expressed as a tool at all. What's next for PlanOnIt A real server-authoritative reservation boundary. The extension point already exists ( RemoteReservationAuthority in src/authority.ts ), but no concrete server ships in this build — a public browser bundle can't hold a shared bearer secret without a real per-user session, and I'd rather ship nothing than ship authentication theater. Real inventory behind the restaurants, cinemas, and routes, in place of the Dhaka sandbox data. A repair flow that explains the alternatives it considered and rejected, not just the plan it landed on. title: Redini-Atelier
pitch: A WebMCP design studio where agent actions arrive as editable ChangeSets you can preview, amend and undo before the canvas changes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP design studio where agent actions arrive as editable ChangeSets you can preview, amend and undo before the canvas changes. Like Comment Story Updates How it works—agent intent→one editable ChangeSet→human negotiates→receipt & history. Atelier is the product Redini is the transaction layer Inspiration Most AI agent demos mutate your app silently. You ask for a change, it happens, you hope it was right. Approval dialogs are binary — yes or no — while real design work is never binary. I wanted the opposite: what if every agent action arrived as a set of related, negotiable changes you can actually see together? A title, a background, a logo position — proposed at once, previewed as one coherent poster, edited one by one. That question became Atelier, powered by Redini . ## What it does Atelier is a WebMCP design editor where agent actions arrive as editable ChangeSets instead of silent mutations. ONE agent intent → ONE WebMCP call (design_update) → ONE ChangeSet → derived preview → amend / skip → atomic commit → receipt → Undo ↔ Redo One call can propose 3 or 6 operations at once. Before anything touches the live canvas you can preview the full result, amend any parameter with typed controls, skip any operation, and commit only the accepted subset. The receipt preserves the distance between what the agent intended and what you authorized: INTENDED / AMENDED BY YOU / SKIPPED BY YOU / APPLIED — STATE v0 → v2 Redini is the small, app-agnostic transaction layer underneath. Every commit, undo and redo advances the version — \( v_{n+1} > v_n \) — so a proposal that was staged on an old state becomes stale instead of being silently applied elsewhere. Live: https://redini-atelier.netlify.app — Try ?clean=1 for the focused agent path. ## How we built it Stack: TypeScript + Vite, native DOM/CSS, Netlify static hosting. No framework, no snapshots — forward operations + compensating inverses only. WebMCP: We use the native surface — document.modelContext.registerTool() , getTools() , executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify(args)) . The public app exposes 5 focused tools: design_update , list_templates , get_current_design , filter_templates , get_vendor_content . design_update stays pending while you negotiate and resolves with a concise result like {"status":"committed","appliedCount":2} . Undo/Redo are intentionally human-side only. Verified like a product: 104 tests, tsc --noEmit clean, production builds, and a real Chrome 149+ E2E that drives the true executeTool path — including PREVIEW — not applied yet , amend, skip, Commit N changes , receipt, Undo, Redo, keyboard ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z , and stale proposals. Deployed with explicit Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) so the experimental browser gate is unambiguous. ## Challenges we ran into WebMCP is still experimental. executeTool expects the tool object + JSON string , Chrome needs --enable-features=WebMCP , and documents must be origin-keyed or registerTool must reject with SecurityError . We found all three with a real Puppeteer spike on Chrome 149. Product challenges were harder: Preview without double-render: simulate() already gave the right derived state, but we rendered it as a translucent overlay on top of the committed poster. Fix: hide the committed canvas while previewing. Honest atomicity: if runtime.apply() mutates then throws without returning an inverse, the world may be partially changed. Redini never claims “nothing happened” in that case — it surfaces stateUncertain instead. Derived bounds: move {x:640,y:400} passes a per-field check but puts the logo fully outside the 640×400 canvas. Bounds are now validated on the sequential derived logo state and re-validated at commit. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, demo-ready loop that holds together under verification: agent proposes 6 changes in one call → you amend one, skip one, commit 2 of 6 → receipt → Undo → Redo → provenance shows Agent proposed vs You staged Template "..." , all with 0 console errors . We are proud of the small things judges can falsify: the badge names the proposal that owns the preview, Commit is disabled at 0 ops, templates are real <button> s, and the 104-test suite includes the exact repros from our external audits. And it works inside the real ChatGPT in-app browser — our final smoke was there, on the Netlify URL, with frame-ancestors allowlisted for it. ## What we learned A transaction layer does not need snapshots. Set-semantics + idempotent inverses are enough, and the hardest part is not the algorithm but making the UI tell the truth. We also learned to keep the agent surface small — 5 tools and one negotiable ChangeSet are more legible than a toolbox of approvals. Built solo for my first hackathon, it was also a crash course in reading specs before building. ## What's next for Redini-Atelier Redini stays a small, reusable guard. Next we want to make it a tiny npm module with a cleaner validate(op, priorOps?) contract, add opt-in persistence for history, and try the same pattern on other domains — dashboards, forms, planning tools — where one agent intent naturally touches several related fields. Code is MIT at https://github.com/cioffiAI/redini-atelier — v1.0.0-challenge is frozen, main stays open. title: OpenRepair
pitch: From photo to repair
about_excerpt: From photo to repair Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When something breaks, the hard part is rarely finding another generic tutorial. It is deciding what evidence matters, which component is implicated, what can be preserved, and when a repair should stop. OpenRepair creates that missing shared workbench. What it does OpenRepair turns a photo and symptom into visible evidence, confidence-ranked hypotheses, component context, clarifying questions, constraint-aware repair paths, and a checklist only the person can approve. The challenge build demonstrates the complete protocol with a reviewed bicycle repair pack. A person can correct observations and lock priorities such as budget or parts to preserve. A browser agent then works on the same live page state through eight WebMCP tools. Every change remains visible, stale writes fail, unsafe DIY paths stop, and incompatible replacements are rejected. In the core example, the user corrects an initial noisy-wheel interpretation: “Actually, the chain skips, but the wheel is straight. Preserve the cassette.” That correction changes the evidence revision, makes drivetrain skipping the leading hypothesis, shifts diagram focus, and reranks repair paths. Immediate cassette replacement becomes incompatible with both budget and preservation constraints. The agent can stage and validate a reversible indexing adjustment, but final approval remains a visible human action. Why WebMCP Repair is shared-state work, not a one-shot answer. The useful artifact is an evolving inspection containing evidence, uncertainty, constraints, alternatives, safety checks, and a plan. WebMCP lets the agent contribute directly to that artifact while OpenRepair remains the source of truth. The person supplies context, corrects observations, locks priorities, and retains final authority. The agent converts visual or conversational context into bounded evidence, focuses relevant components, compares paths, and prepares a validated draft. Without this shared state, owners must manually reconcile a chat diagnosis, diagrams, estimates, safety advice, and personal constraints. OpenRepair turns those fragments into one inspectable workflow. How WebMCP was implemented The React client feature-detects document.modelContext , with a legacy navigator.modelContext fallback, and registers eight narrow tools: get_repair_session reads bounded current state and the next legal action. initialize_repair_workspace creates a visible workspace for a user-identified object. set_inspection_context records bounded observations and confidence changes. show_component_diagram focuses known components without declaring a diagnosis. compare_repair_paths ranks options under locked constraints. stage_repair_plan creates a reversible draft and rejects stale revisions. validate_repair_plan checks evidence, constraints, verification, and safety. export_repair_checklist exports only a current plan explicitly approved on the page. Zod validates untrusted inputs. WebMCP handlers and visible UI controls use the same typed domain reducer. Raw image bytes never travel through tool results. There is no agent tool for approval, purchasing, booking, or repair execution. How we built it OpenRepair is a client-first React, strict TypeScript, Vite, Zod, and SVG application deployed on Vercel. Vitest covers the domain and WebMCP boundaries; Playwright and axe cover complete browser workflows and accessibility. Codex supported implementation, debugging, test development, WebMCP lifecycle hardening, contest audits, documentation, and submission preparation. ChatGPT with Terra demonstrated the real browser-agent workflow. AI text-to-speech narrates the demo video. Accomplishments Eight WebMCP tools support a non-trivial evidence-to-export lifecycle. Human corrections invalidate stale agent writes and rerank visible alternatives. Budget and preservation locks deterministically reject incompatible work. Agent tools can stage and validate but cannot approve. Safety stops prevent professional-only work from reaching approval. The product remains useful through reviewed fallback cases when WebMCP is unavailable. What we learned Agent-native UX works best when tool activity changes a durable visual artifact rather than only a transcript. Narrow schemas, visible revisions, bounded results, and explicit human gates make collaboration easier to understand and safer to trust. What's next Bicycles are the first reviewed repair pack. Future packs can cover appliances, electronics, furniture, vehicles, tools, and community repair knowledge while reusing the same evidence, constraint, revision, planning, and approval protocol. OpenRepair is an independent open-source project and is not an official OpenAI product. title: Reviewline
pitch: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. A WebMCP-native studio for evidence-backed autonomous-agent incident review.
about_excerpt: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. A WebMCP-native studio for evidence-backed autonomous-agent incident review. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The agent selects a critical incident and inspects synchronized, bounded evidence through WebMCP. A deterministic counterfactual replay keeps the $142K trigger blocked while the benign control remains allowed. After a clean replay, the agent drafts an evidence-backed gate and Reviewline transitions to human review. The human records the decision in the visible interface; the agent can verify the result but cannot create it. Inspiration Autonomous agents are great at analyzing large traces and evaluating many cases quickly. But incident response becomes risky when the same agent is allowed to both investigate an issue and authorize what happens next. We wanted to explore a safer and more practical model for human–agent collaboration: let the agent handle the evidence-heavy investigation, then stop at a clear decision point where a human reviews the same information and takes responsibility for the outcome. That idea became Reviewline’s core principle: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Incident review is a natural fit for WebMCP because the capabilities an agent needs change throughout the investigation. Early on, it may need tools for gathering evidence. After selecting an incident, it may need simulation tools. Only after a clean replay should it be able to draft a review gate. At no point should it gain control over consequential human decisions. What it does Reviewline is a WebMCP-native incident review studio designed for investigating failures involving autonomous agents. The main demo follows a synthetic procurement agent that encountered instruction-like content on a supplier page and attempted to make a $142,000 purchase , despite having a $50,000 spending limit . A deterministic mutation gateway blocked the transaction. Using WebMCP, a browser agent can: Find and list critical incidents. Select an incident and inspect a bounded set of trace and cohort evidence. Review instruction-like content that is clearly labeled as untrusted evidence. Replay a proposed guardrail against both the triggering incident and a named benign control. Confirm that the triggering purchase remains blocked, the benign control remains allowed, and no regressions are introduced. Draft an evidence-backed review gate for a human reviewer. Read the final decision recorded by the reviewer. The available tools change as the workflow progresses: Investigation: list_incidents , inspect_incident Incident selected: simulate_guardrail_patch Clean replay completed: draft_review_gate Awaiting human decision: the drafting tool is retired, and get_review_status becomes available Decision recorded: the agent can verify the result but cannot create or change it Tools such as approve , reject , activate , and deploy are deliberately never exposed through WebMCP. The human reviewer sees the same synchronized evidence as the agent. They must provide their identity, add a review note, confirm that they examined the evidence, and record their decision using consequence-specific interface controls. The blocked purchase remains unauthorized throughout the process, and the demo never deploys a real external policy. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to scrape a dense incident interface, infer relationships between records, and potentially interact with controls that grant more authority than the task requires. Reviewline replaces that approach with structured capabilities, deterministic evidence IDs, bounded results, explicit labels for untrusted content, a live capability manifest, and an append-only session timeline. How we built it Reviewline is a deterministic, client-only application built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. It uses the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API and falls back progressively to an in-page Tool Inspector when native WebMCP support is unavailable. The architecture separates: Deterministic domain actions and invariants Shared application state used by both the interface and WebMCP tools Strict runtime input validation Bounded outputs and structured errors Phase-aware tool definitions Lifecycle-safe native tool registration and retirement Every tool handler calls the same validated domain action used by the visible interface. JSON Schema helps the agent understand and invoke tools correctly, but the runtime implementation remains the final authority. The application updates the visible interface before a tool promise resolves. This ensures that the human reviewer and the agent always see the same resulting state. Tool calls, registration changes, results, workflow transitions, and the final human decision are all recorded in the session timeline. The registration layer also handles tool retirement carefully. It stops admitting new calls before retiring a tool generation, allows calls that have already started to finish, and prevents failed or timed-out registration attempts from leaving partially registered tools available. We tested the native browser contract using Chrome 152 rather than relying only on a polyfill. The deployed workflow discovers each dynamic capability manifest, executes the tools available at every phase, records the human decision through the interface, and verifies that forbidden authority tools never appear. The static application is deployed on GitHub Pages. A strict build verifier checks the project subpath, inventories active HTML resources, rejects external or inline executable content, and confirms that real, non-symlinked JavaScript and CSS artifacts exist inside the build directory. Challenges we ran into Defining a real authority boundary The hardest part was not deciding which tools to add. It was proving exactly when a tool should no longer be available. For example, drafting must remain unavailable until a clean replay has been completed. Once the workflow reaches human review, that drafting capability must be retired. Making this boundary explicit—and enforcing it throughout the entire lifecycle—was one of the project’s most important design challenges. Validating the complete state graph Validating only the selected incident or current proposal was not enough. Before retained tools could run safely, we needed to verify canonical IDs, references, actors, timestamps, simulation evidence, audit events, and timeline consistency across the full application state. Handling lifecycle races Native registration and browser testing revealed race conditions that happy-path tests did not catch. These included cancellation, timeouts, retained handles, process cleanup, and stale tool references. We added adversarial tests covering registration retirement, process-spawn failures, first and second termination signals, hanging browser shutdowns, stale tool handles, and fixture cleanup. Proving that the replay was meaningful Blocking the malicious trigger was only half the job. A guardrail that blocks everything would technically stop the incident, but it would not be useful. To avoid that outcome, Reviewline evaluates the triggering case alongside a named benign control. Drafting remains unavailable if the proposed guardrail causes any regression in the benign case. Making the GitHub Pages build portable and trustworthy GitHub Pages serves the application from a project-specific subpath. We needed to verify that every active script and stylesheet used the correct base path and resolved to a real build artifact. The verifier also rejects path traversal, malformed paths, external resources, inline executable content, and symlink escapes. Testing native WebMCP A test double can validate application logic, but it cannot prove that the browser integration behaves correctly. Native testing required us to account for Chrome’s serialized tool arguments and results, dynamic registration timing, cancellation behavior, and synchronization between tool execution and the visible interface. Accomplishments we’re proud of Built a complete WebMCP-native collaboration workflow rather than a generic CRUD-style tool surface Made the principle of least authority visible through a dynamic capability manifest Kept approval, rejection, activation, and deployment entirely outside the agent’s tool surface Added deterministic replay against both a malicious trigger and a named benign control Ensured that agent actions update the same visible state used by the human reviewer Added an append-only session timeline and a human-attributed audit record Preserved a complete human workflow in browsers without native WebMCP support Deployed a public, credential-free demo with no backend or production mutation endpoint Verified the project with: 303 unit, component, and integration tests 33 dedicated lifecycle, workflow, and portable-build tests 13 Playwright end-to-end tests TypeScript type checking and zero-warning linting npm audit with zero vulnerabilities actionlint workflow validation Native

title: Sundae Metrics
pitch: A sales dashboard that hands agents 6 WebMCP tools instead of a picture of a chart. Same question, same page: 4m 38s without the tools, 36 seconds with them.
about_excerpt: A sales dashboard that hands agents 6 WebMCP tools instead of a picture of a chart. Same question, same page: 4m 38s without the tools, 36 seconds with them. Like Comment Story Updates An agent just changed the dashboard: the amber WRITE entry in the Agent activity rail, with an Undo on it. Inspiration Ice cream chains are the smallest business that genuinely needs analytics: four shops, six flavors, wildly seasonal, and no data analyst. The products already sold to them - HioPOS, Sipos, GETPOS, Vendty - all ship the same dashboard, and every question that dashboard cannot answer ends the same way: an Excel export. An assistant looking at that screen is in a worse position than the owner. Ask it "how much did North's sales change between February and March?" and, without WebMCP, it has to drive the whole interface: find the store selector in the DOM, synthesize a click, wait for a re-render with no signal that it finished, set the month range through a native picker, read the values back and do the arithmetic itself. It gets there - and I measured that rather than assuming it, which is what the section below is about. What it cannot do is get there cheaply. An interface built for eyes makes an agent pay in clicks, re-renders and round trips for something the page already knows exactly. What it does Sundae Metrics is a sales dashboard for Glace , a fictional chain of 4 artisanal ice cream shops: 12 months x 4 locations x 6 flavors. It is a normal dashboard - KPI cards, a 12-month bar chart, a flavor breakdown, a compare-periods view. The product is the layer underneath. The page registers 6 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() : Tool What it does readOnlyHint list_stores Lists the locations on this dashboard true get_sales Exact units and revenue for one location in one month true compare_periods Percentage change between two months true get_top_flavors Flavor ranking - best sellers or slow movers true get_summary Revenue across every location over a date range true set_dashboard_view Changes what the user is looking at false The February-to-March question becomes one call: await compare_periods({ store: "north", monthA: "2026-02", monthB: "2026-03" }); // {"revenueChangePct":-17.1,"unitsChangePct":-15.4} And the dataset carries a case the chart actively hides. In January 2026 the North location's pistachio sales collapse from 2,099 units to 554 - down 74%, from the 3rd best seller to the 6th - a supply shortage. But January is also North's highest-revenue month of the year: the other five flavors each rise about 24% and absorb the gap, so the tallest bar on the chart is the one hiding the problem . Nothing on screen shows it. get_top_flavors({store: "north", month: "2026-01", limit: 3, order: "bottom"}) shows it immediately. set_dashboard_view runs the other way. Ask for the South location and the screen changes in front of you: the agent acts on the same interface the human is looking at, not on a copy of the data somewhere else. The measurement The demo video is not a mock-up. Both halves were filmed in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser - same model, same question, same page, changing only ?webmcp=off : Without the tools With the tools Time 4 min 38 s 36 s Work navigated the UI month by month, then asked permission to download the page's data file 5 tool calls Answer pistachio 2,099 -> 554 (-74%) same, "fell from third-best seller to last" Both are right, and that is the honest claim. Without the tools the agent still gets there - the chart prints its values as text, so it reads them. What it cannot do is get there cheaply. It also tried to escape the screen entirely: three minutes in, it asked to download the dashboard's JavaScript data file rather than keep reading the interface. That request was denied on camera, because bypassing the rendered page is precisely what a real app with a backend would not allow. How I built it Vite + React + TypeScript, client-side only, no backend. Plain CSS with custom properties, no Tailwind. The chart is twelve div s with percentage heights, no charting library. Two dev dependencies beyond the template: vitest and webmcp-types . src/lib/queries.ts is the only place in the codebase that computes anything. The dashboard and the tools consume the same pure functions, so a number on the chart and a number returned by a tool cannot drift apart. 39,871 is what get_sales returns, what is printed on the March bar, and what the KPI card shows - one function, three consumers. 56 tests cover that layer, the state and the tool definitions. State is a module-level store exposed through useSyncExternalStore - mutable from outside React, which is exactly what set_dashboard_view needs. The dataset is generated by a seed script with no randomness at all : running it twice produces a byte-identical JSON, and the test file is the only place in the repo where the expected figures are written by hand. If the seed drifts, the tests fail. Accomplishments I'm proud of order: "bottom" is not decoration. The KPI those POS products actually sell to ice cream shops is "best sellers and slow movers", because owners use the second half to decide what to drop from the menu. It costs one parameter, not a seventh tool. No tool carries untrustedContentHint , and that is a decision, not an omission. Every value comes from a committed seed file, so no tool output can carry third-party text an agent might read as instructions. The hint exists for tools that return content someone else wrote; claiming it here would be noise. The Agent activity rail is the security answer, not chrome. How much a site should have to reveal about what an agent did on it is still open in the standard - prompt injection ( webmcp#11 ) and hints for consequential actions ( webmcp#176 ) are both unresolved. This dashboard's response is to make every call visible as it happens: tool name, input, output, elapsed time, output size against Chrome's 1,500-character ceiling, and an Undo on the one call that changed something. Indigo means the agent read; amber means the agent wrote. Nothing an agent does here is invisible. Challenges I ran into Chrome drops a malformed tool without raising anything. Exceed the name limit (30 chars), the tool description limit (500), a parameter description (150) or the output ceiling (1,500) and the tool is simply not registered - no error, no warning. annotations placed as a second argument instead of inside the tool object is ignored the same silent way. The fix was to compare getTools() against the six expected names after registering and log the difference, and to route every execute through one helper that truncates output to 1,500 characters. The question you ask changes whether the agent finds the anomaly. Asked "look at the flavor breakdown and tell me if anything looks off", the tool-driven agent fetched January only and concluded the anomaly was passion fruit - the cheapest flavor per unit. It failed that way twice in a row. With one month of flavor data, 554 units is not remarkable; the agent without tools got it right precisely because navigating the UI forced it through December as well. Asking for the comparison explicitly fixes it without naming pistachio. That is a WebMCP design lesson, not a demo detail: a tool that answers one month invites a one-month answer. The wording that shipped, identical in both halves of the video: "For the North store, what happened to sales in January 2026? Compare the flavor breakdown against December and tell me if anything looks off." Agents are not deterministic. Across five runs of the same question the figures never moved - 15,826 units, $50,800, pistachio 554 against 2,099 - but the conclusion was worded differently every time. The narration was written to whatever the agent actually said, rather than re-asking until a nicer sentence came out. What I learned That the interesting half of WebMCP is not exposing data - it is deciding what a tool is allowed to be . Six tools with one write among them, each one answering a question an owner would actually ask, beats twenty tools that mirror the internal data model. And the write tool is where the standard gets genuinely new: it is the first time an agent and a person can be looking at the same screen, and the agent can change it. What's next for Sundae Metrics Hourly granularity, channel mix (counter / dine-in / delivery), and a real backend behind the query layer - the tool contracts would not change, which is the point. The interesting open question is the trust model: the activity rail is one answer, but the standard has not settled on one yet.
