title: Duel
pitch: The web page hands an AI agent a set of tools and says: play. Four minigames, every call visible live, and Pong proves a request/response protocol can survive a real-time rally.
about_excerpt: The web page hands an AI agent a set of tools and says: play. Four minigames, every call visible live, and Pong proves a request/response protocol can survive a real-time rally. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP landed in Chrome behind a flag and almost nobody at work had seen it. The pitch — a web page can declare tools that an AI agent calls directly — sounds abstract until you watch it happen. Slides weren't going to do it. So the goal was never "build a product". It was: make the mechanism visible in a room full of people in under five minutes. That single constraint decided everything. If a choice made the app more useful but the mechanism less obvious, the mechanism won. Games turned out to be the right vehicle, for a reason we didn't expect at the start: a game has rules the page can enforce. When an agent tries to move out of turn and the page answers { ok: false, reason: "it's not your turn" }, everyone in the room understands the trust model instantly. You can't get that from a to-do list demo. What it does Duel is a four-game arcade in the browser where your opponent is an external AI agent — and the agent doesn't see pixels. It plays by calling tools the page registers with document.modelContext.registerTool(). Minesweeper duel — a shared 9×9 board, 13 mines, turn-based. Claim a mine correctly and you keep playing. Connect 4 — turn-based, or a one-shot puzzle in single player. Pong — real-time. Yes, real-time, over a request/response protocol. More on this below. Towers of Hanoi — both sides race their own tower against one clock. Five discs, so $2^5 - 1 = 31$ moves is optimal. Nothing leaves the tab. No backend, no API key, no LLM call from the app. The page only registers tools; the intelligence is entirely on the other end of the wire. That's the whole point — the page is the tool provider, not the AI. The design exists to make three moments land: The page announces itself. Open the inspector and the tools are there with names and schemas. Nobody guessed anything. The agent plays, visibly. Every call lands live in the right-hand rail with its arguments and its response. That rail is what turns a game into a WebMCP demo. The tools change on their own. Switch games and an AbortController unregisters the old game's tools and registers the new one's. The inspector's list transforms live. How we built it Vite + TypeScript, no framework, no backend. Every module stays under ~200 lines, which is why each game is split into state / actions / query / render / tools. A dist/ you can serve from anywhere. The interesting engineering isn't the games — it's tool design, and three rules were earned the hard way: Give the agent constraints, not drawings. A tool that dumps the board makes the agent do vision work in text. ms_frontier hands it the deduction already worked out: these cells are provably safe, these are provably mines. c4_analysis does the same. Without those the agent plays badly and the demo falls apart. They are the real work of the project. The description is the code. When the agent plays badly, the fix is almost always in the description string, not the logic. We edited prose far more often than we edited functions. Stop the help short of solving it. Hanoi's hanoi_moves returns the legal moves and says outright that they are not the good ones. The optimal move is a four-line recursion — a tool that returned it would leave the agent nothing to do but transcribe, and the race would demonstrate nothing. Pong, the part that shouldn't work A tool call is request/response, and an agent round-trip takes seconds — longer than the ball takes to cross the court. Polling is hopeless. The answer was to make pong_read a blocking tool. It parks until the ball turns toward the agent, then returns the interception point. The agent's ordinary call-and-respond rhythm becomes the rally. The interception is computed analytically, because an agent reasoning about wall bounces from raw $v_x, v_y$ gets it wrong often enough to lose every point. Free flight to the paddle face: $$y_{\text{free}} = y_0 + v_y \cdot \frac{\Delta x}{|v_x|}$$ then folded back into the court by unrolling the bounces — a triangle wave over the span $s = h - 2r$: $$y_{\text{hit}} = r + \Lambda_s!\left(y_{\text{free}} - r\right), \qquad \Lambda_s(k) = \begin{cases} k' & k' \le s \ 2s - k' & k' > s \end{cases}, \quad k' = k \bmod 2s$$ And while the call is out, the page slows the ball to 12% speed. That pause is a round-trip to the agent, made visible — it's the moment the room actually sees what a tool call costs. The ball's speed isn't a playability number, it's a budget: $$t = \frac{\Delta x}{\sigma \cdot v}, \qquad \sigma = 0.12$$ There's a unit test asserting that budget stays above 8 seconds. If someone tunes a speed and that test goes red, the demo is what broke. Challenges we ran into The agent grabbed the human's mouse. Live. An agent whose client didn't surface the tools fell back on screenshot-and-click and started dragging our paddle around. Two fixes: Pong's paddle is now keyboard-only — keys are the human's channel, tools are the agent's, and the separation is the point — and clicking the board on the agent's turn no longer fails silently. It flashes the turn box and leaves a rejected line in the rail, because a silent swallow leaves both the agent and the room with no idea why nothing is happening. A hidden tab froze the game. The agent often drives from another window, so the tab is hidden exactly when the game most needs to run. Chrome throttles main-thread timers in a background tab to about one per second. We measured it — 5 seconds, setInterval(50ms): ┌─────────────────┬─────────────┐ │ Where │ Ticks in 5s │ ├─────────────────┼─────────────┤ │ Main thread │ 6 │ ├─────────────────┼─────────────┤ │ Inside a Worker │ 103 │ └─────────────────┴─────────────┘ So Pong's heartbeat moved into a Web Worker. Hanoi dodged the same class of bug differently: its clock is a timestamp, not a tally, so throttling can stutter the display but never slow the race. The bugs that only exist in the loop. Four separate Pong bugs passed every per-mechanism unit test and only appeared with the whole read → think → move → read cycle running at realistic latency. A shot could turn, arrive, and bounce entirely inside the gap between the agent's pong_move and its next pong_read — nothing parked to wake, so the trigger looked broken. There's now a test that drives the full loop across a sweep of simulated agent latencies, because the bugs it catches are properties of the sequence, not of any one function. The modal that made the agent give up. This one stung. On boot, the page used to ask the human "play vs agent, or solo?" — honest, because the WebMCP API has no "a consumer is attached" signal at all. But it registered nothing until someone clicked, and an agent attaching to the tab lists the page's tools immediately. It got an empty list, concluded there was nothing to call, and fell back to screenshots — the exact failure the whole demo argues against. We had asked the right question at the wrong moment. Now detection means duel mode with tools up first, and the human's escape hatch is a dropdown in the top bar. The honesty moved to after registration: the pill reads N tools · waiting for agent until a call actually arrives. The page that grew to 3907 pixels. The call rail gains a line per tool call. Nothing bounded it, so during a long Pong rally the page stretched past 3900px — which scrolled the board off the top of the screen while the agent was playing on it. The layout is now an app shell: board pane and rail scroll independently, the page itself never does. Accomplishments we're proud of Real-time Pong over a request/response tool protocol, with the latency turned into the most legible part of the demo instead of the thing you apologize for. Deduction aids good enough that the agent plays well — the demo lives or dies on this, and it's invisible when it works. 141 tests, and the discipline of writing a regression test at the level the bug actually lived at. What we learned A modal is a gate, and the agent is on the other side of it. Anything an agent needs must exist before a human interacts with the page. "Tools registered" and "an agent is playing" are different facts. The API can only tell you the first. Say so out loud, or a page that failed and a page nobody is calling look identical from the back of the room. Test the viewport the demo is actually watched in — inside the agent's own browser window, which is narrower and shorter than a desktop tab. Prose is load-bearing. Every Pong response ends with a next_action field naming the exact call to make next. Without it the agent answers one read, writes its user a progress report, and its paddle stands still for the rest of the round. Two things about the current Chrome that cost us an afternoon each and aren't documented anywhere: executeTool wants its arguments as a JSON string, not an object, and a subframe s

title: Islanding — Restore Critical Power W/o Energizing the Fault
pitch: A human sets safety priorities; an AI agent explores restoration plans; the page enforces exact approval before a synthetic switch is touched.
about_excerpt: A human sets safety priorities; an AI agent explores restoration plans; the page enforces exact approval before a synthetic switch is touched. Like Comment Story Updates Storm outage overview: feeder F1 faulted, 55% battery reserve, and nine WebMCP tools ready. The agent compares plans: the 18% reserve option is blocked and the 27% reserve option is valid. Human approval is bound to the exact switching sequence and held privately in the page. Receipt R-104 confirms one execution: hospital, shelter, and water restored with 26% reserve. Inspiration A grid diagram is readable to an operator but dangerously ambiguous to a general browser agent. The same switch icon can hide a fault interlock, transient state, capacity limit, and sequence dependency. Clicking the right-looking SVG control is not the same as understanding whether a plan is safe. We wanted to show WebMCP at its strongest: not as a faster form filler, but as the semantic control plane for a live professional digital twin. The human should contribute priorities and consent. The agent should contribute rapid constrained exploration. The page should remain the authority for rules, state, and consequences. What it does Islanding opens on a seeded storm outage. Feeder F1 is faulted; hospital and shelter are critical; battery reserve must stay above 25%. An agent uses nine page-hosted WebMCP tools to read exact incident state and topology, simulate two deterministic switching plans, compare their derived trade-offs, and put the best into visible preview. The operator then marks the water pump critical in the normal UI. That page edit increments the state version, invalidates the old draft, and revokes any approval. The agent sees a structured stale_state , re-reads the human choice, and computes a revised plan. The agent can prepare the exact sequence but cannot approve it. A normal page button creates a short-lived internal grant bound to the current draft hash and version. The grant never enters model context. Only then can the agent execute the synthetic sequence once. Retrying the same idempotency key returns the original receipt, not a second execution. The topology visibly restores hospital, shelter, and water pump while the fault stays isolated. The receipt records human approval, exact draft hash, operations, before/after state versions, and final reserve. How we used WebMCP The top-level document registers nine imperative tools through document.modelContext , with the deprecated navigator.modelContext only as a compatibility fallback: semantic reads: incident state and topology; compute: plan simulation and comparison; reversible collaboration: draft preview and current-state validation; trust boundary: exact preparation, page-held human authorization, idempotent execution; evidence: attributable execution receipt. Every registerTool is awaited inside try / catch , has a JSON Schema and explicit description, and is tied to an AbortController lifecycle. Inputs are validated again at runtime so malformed, extra, stale, and unsafe requests receive corrective structured errors before mutation. Each execute callback accepts the browser's independent cancellation signal. Calls that complete a domain operation write to the visible activity ledger, and simulations create candidates, so none is incorrectly marked read-only. Tool inputs never supply safety outcomes; the deterministic page engine derives them. Most importantly, the tools update the same visible UI a human uses. WebMCP does not create a hidden agent-only workflow. How it improves the user experience Without WebMCP, an agent must interpret SVG positions and click tiny controls while guessing at hidden constraints. With WebMCP, it can say exactly which stable operation it wants to simulate and receive exact consequences. The operator sees both alternatives, the winning preview, the stale-state correction after their own edit, and the final receipt. The result is faster than manual trial-and-error, more legible than autonomous clicking, and safer than giving the model a generic “execute” control. A new human-agent capability Islanding demonstrates co-operation on live shared state. The human is not reduced to writing the perfect prompt, and the agent is not reduced to driving the mouse. The person expresses contextual judgment through the interface and explicitly authorizes one exact consequence. The agent performs repetitive search, comparison, validation, and documentation. The website arbitrates both. That pattern can extend to infrastructure training, industrial digital twins, maintenance planning, emergency exercises, and other domains where consequential actions need semantic context and visible consent. How we built it The project deliberately has no framework, build step, backend, account, credentials, or live data. HTML and CSS render an accessible responsive command center. Three JavaScript modules provide a versioned domain engine, WebMCP contracts/registration, and UI wiring. A Node static server runs it locally. The mocked engine includes topology, priorities, deterministic candidate metrics, fault isolation, reserve rules, draft hashes, stale-state detection, 60-second page-held grants, approval revocation, idempotency, and receipts. Node's built-in test runner exercises the complete workflow and uses a fake modelContext to verify all registrations, schemas, annotations, lifecycle cleanup, and cancellation behavior. Challenges we ran into The hardest design decision was consent. An imperative WebMCP execute callback should not pretend it can securely ask the model for human approval, nor should a secret token be handed back to the model. We split preparation from execution and made authorization an ordinary visible page action. The execution tool can only ask the page whether its private grant matches the exact draft and current version. We also kept “simulation” honest. A tempting higher-coverage plan violates reserve; an unsafe S3 close energizes the fault; changing human priorities invalidates the previous plan. These are business-engine results, not claims generated by the agent. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is indispensable to the experience rather than bolted on. Human and agent paths use the same domain engine and visible state. The golden demo contains a genuine collaboration beat, a trust beat, and an attributable receipt. Unsafe, stale, unapproved, expired, and duplicate paths fail closed. The entire project remains tiny, deterministic, dependency-free, and easy for judges to run. What we learned Semantic tools are only part of agent readiness. A useful site also needs explicit versions, composable state transitions, corrective errors, visible effects, and a clear boundary between what the model can request and what the human must authorize. WebMCP turns the page from a picture an agent operates into a participant in the interaction. The most compelling agent experiences come from designing that shared contract alongside the human workflow. What's next Next steps would add a real optimization solver behind the same interface, multiple training incidents, richer electrical constraints, immutable exported evidence, and authenticated instructor/operator roles. Any real infrastructure integration would require an entirely separate safety, security, regulatory, and operational program; this prototype intentionally makes no such claim. Agents/clients tested Deterministic fake ModelContext harness: passed registration and execution contract tests. Standard human browser path: locally testable without WebMCP . OpenAI Codex desktop in-app Browser with native site tools: passed on the public deployment on 2026-09-02 . Exactly nine tools were discovered; successful calls included incident/topology reads, two simulations, comparison, and visible draft preview. AI tools used OpenAI Codex for research synthesis, implementation, tests, documentation, and submission preparation. webmcp skill from webmaxru/web-ai-agent-skills for current API, compatibility, lifecycle, and validation guidance. Known Limitations Deterministic synthetic training prototype, not a power-flow solver or operational grid-control system. No live utility data, equipment connection, backend, authentication, or persistence; page state disappears on reload. Human approval proves a local page action, not authenticated identity or cryptographic authorization. The visible activity ledger is demo evidence, not an immutable audit log. Native WebMCP support depends on the client/browser. The prior recorded native run and today's automated tests are distinct forms of evidence. Benefits such as faster exploration are design goals illustrated by the demo, not measured comparative performance claims. title: EpochX
pitch: Train an online classifier with your browser agent while humans control labels and model changes through WebMCP
about_excerpt: Train an online classifier with your browser agent while humans control labels and model changes through WebMCP Like 1 Comment Story Updates Label Loop Why we built it Software can rank uncertain samples, update a classifier, and calculate metrics. A person still needs to decide what an ambiguous example means. Most labeling interfaces expose this process as buttons and tables, leaving a browser agent to infer which actions are safe. We wanted the page to publish those operations directly while keeping label decisions under human control. Support-ticket routing gave us a small task with visible results. Label Loop classifies tickets as billing , bug , or access . What it does Label Loop runs an online multinomial Naive Bayes classifier in the browser. The session begins with nine seed examples, twelve unlabeled review candidates, and a fixed nine-item holdout set. The agent ranks unlabeled tickets by predictive entropy and can place up to three in the review queue. A person assigns each label through the page. The agent then trains a batch and evaluates the updated model. The interface shows probabilities, per-class F1, token weights, a confusion matrix, calibration, and log loss. A ledger records label provenance, while a separate trace records WebMCP calls. Model-setting proposals stay pending until a person accepts or rejects them. How we built it The project is a static Vite application with no backend or external model API. The classifier and session state run in page memory, so reloading creates a fresh deterministic session. For a document $d$ and class $c$, the model calculates: $$ P(c \mid d) \propto P(c)\prod_{w \in d}P(w \mid c) $$ Token likelihoods use Laplace smoothing: $$ P(w \mid c)=\frac{N_{w,c}+\alpha}{N_c+\alpha |V|} $$ $N_{w,c}$ is the count of token $w$ in class $c$, $N_c$ is the class token total, and $|V|$ is the vocabulary size. Each confirmed example increments these counts. Review candidates are sorted using normalized predictive entropy: $$ H(p)=\frac{-\sum_{c=1}^{K}p_c\log p_c}{\log K} $$ A value near one means the probabilities are close, so that ticket moves toward the front of the review queue. One-vs-rest log-likelihood differences show which tokens push the model toward each class. Holdout evaluation returns aggregate metrics without returning individual rows. How WebMCP is used The page registers nine tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : Tool Access Job get_training_state Read Model, queue, configuration, and metrics inspect_uncertain_samples Read Entropy-ranked unlabeled tickets inspect_model_diagnostics Read Features, confusion counts, calibration, and loss predict_ticket Read Probabilities, entropy, and route-or-review decision evaluate_model Read Aggregate holdout metrics inspect_training_history Read Checkpoints and label provenance queue_label_review Write A bounded request for human labels train_confirmed_batch Write Incremental training on confirmed examples propose_model_config Write A pending configuration proposal Each definition has JSON Schema and runtime validation. queue_label_review has no label input. Samples move through unlabeled , awaiting-human , confirmed , and trained states, and training accepts only confirmed examples. Configuration changes require a separate human action. Challenges WebMCP browser support was the first practical problem. We verified all nine tools in Chrome 152 and built a deterministic replay for ordinary browsers. Replay events are labeled local replay so they cannot be confused with external calls. The second problem was label provenance. Hiding a control in the interface would not prevent an agent tool from sending the same data. We removed labels from the review-request schema and made the training operation check sample state at runtime. Evaluation tools return aggregate metrics, feature weights, and confusion counts while omitting individual holdout examples and answers. We also corrected a misleading setting whose original name implied automatic training. It is now a review threshold. Predictions below it go to a person, and training remains limited to confirmed examples. What we learned Useful WebMCP tools matched domain operations instead of interface controls. queue_label_review gives the agent a clear capability and limit; a tool such as click_review_button would preserve the ambiguity of the page. Human approval also needs a technical boundary. Label Loop keeps label assignment out of the agent tool set and checks provenance again when training starts. Since the model runs locally, every displayed probability, token weight, and metric can be reproduced without an account or API key. title: LAST DOOR
pitch: When evidence changes, the WebMCP tools change with it.
about_excerpt: When evidence changes, the WebMCP tools change with it. Like Comment Story Updates Counterfactual: the same evidence leaves 9 static tools, 4 compiled tools, and removes 5 stale capabilities. System architecture: evidence compiles the live WebMCP surface while secrets and human authority stay outside. Live mission: three gates, current manifest, authority decision, evidence memory, and trace. Authority lifecycle: stale-event recovery, human handoff, and a structured completion receipt. The problem WebMCP lets a webpage expose useful actions directly to an agent. But stateful flows create a dangerous failure mode: a tool can remain callable after the evidence that made it safe has expired. An authentication challenge can go stale. A checkout can cross an approval threshold. A production change can reach the point where a person must take responsibility. Telling an agent "do not call that tool anymore" is weaker than removing the tool altogether. Teams building browser agents need a way to test whether the available tool surface still matches the current situation. What LAST DOOR does LAST DOOR is a WebMCP authority release test. It turns changing evidence into the exact tools an agent may use now—and removes everything else. The live identity-recovery mission has three gates. The agent completes a controlled link, encounters an expired challenge, rejects it safely, retries with a fresh event, and reaches a human-presence gate where it must stop. That final stop is the point of the project. The confirmation action exists only as a visible button for the person. It is never registered as a WebMCP tool. After the person acts, the agent can read a structured receipt explaining what happened. Why WebMCP is essential This is not a conventional interface with WebMCP added on top. The changing WebMCP manifest is the product being tested. After every meaningful result, LAST DOOR evaluates the current gate and a redacted evidence history. That decision names the responsible actor and the capabilities still allowed. The page then aborts its previous registrations and publishes a new tool surface. The agent does not merely receive a warning that an action is unsafe. The stale action disappears from the browser's callable tools. A better experience for people and agents The agent handles repeatable work and safe recovery. The person acts only when the decision genuinely requires human presence. Both sides can inspect the same rule, actor, evidence, capabilities, and final receipt. The person can see what the agent may do and why that changed. The agent gets a smaller, current tool surface instead of a permanent list padded with actions it should avoid. This makes a correct stop measurable. It is completion under the right authority rule, not a vague refusal or a failed run. The Live Policy Lab Judges can test the same authority compiler across three situations: Identity recovery: 09 → 04 High-value checkout: 10 → 04 Production change: 08 → 04 Across the three policy packs, 27 static capabilities become 12 current capabilities. Fifteen stale tools disappear, and zero human actions enter a manifest. Loading a new scenario revokes the previous registrations before publishing its four current tools. The browser then checks the live manifest and reports an exact 4 OF 4 TOOLS MATCH result. Checkout and production change are honest, read-only policy simulations. They do not touch a real order or deployment. How it works LAST DOOR is a dependency-free browser application built with the imperative WebMCP API: Mission events append symbolic facts such as STALE_CHALLENGE_REJECTED to page-owned Run Memory. A deterministic authority function evaluates the active gate and those facts. The decision returns allow , handoff , or complete , together with the actor, rule, and permitted capabilities. An AbortController removes the previous registrations. document.modelContext.registerTool() publishes only the current manifest. Tool results expose structured status and receipts; challenge values never leave the page. The explain_authority_decision tool lets the agent inspect the decision without receiving either challenge value. A native test bench uses getTools() and executeTool() to prove that the browser—not a mock list—contains the expected tools. What judges can verify The expired challenge is rejected and safely replaced. The rejected value is neither returned nor stored in Run Memory. Old WebMCP registrations disappear as the authority decision changes. The final rule is HUMAN_HANDOFF_PENDING and the responsible actor is human . No confirm_human_presence capability exists. After the visible human action, the receipt reports three completed gates, one safe recovery, one human handoff, zero unauthorized attempts, and RUN_COMPLETE . The released build passes nine deterministic domain checks, live 4/4 manifest verification for all three policy packs, and the complete native production path to the human boundary. How we used AI and Codex ChatGPT's in-app browser acted as the WebMCP agent under test. It discovered and invoked the live tools, recovered from stale evidence, inspected the authority decision, and stopped when responsibility moved to a person. Codex supported implementation, code review, adversarial testing, browser QA, release verification, architecture diagrams, and submission preparation. AI-assisted narration and editing were used for the demo video. Every generated claim was checked against the released product or repository evidence before publication. Scope LAST DOOR is an owned, deterministic test environment. It does not connect to real accounts, inboxes, phone numbers, orders, or production infrastructure. Real systems must still enforce authorization on the server. The project tests a narrower—and often overlooked—contract: when the situation changes, does the browser stop advertising actions that are stale or belong to a person? Try it No credentials are required. title: Pending: Human
pitch: A deterministic crisis simulator where AI investigates through WebMCP, compares interventions, and proposes plans—while humans retain final authority.
about_excerpt: A deterministic crisis simulator where AI investigates through WebMCP, compares interventions, and proposes plans—while humans retain final authority. Like Comment Story Updates The deterministic T+60 result compares the approved response with the do-nothing baseline. Choose one of three deterministic crisis missions and invite a WebMCP-enabled AI teammate. A live flash-flood response with graph-based vehicle movement, named roads, and human-impact forecasting. The AI reads structured city state while the human controls dispatch, routes, priorities, and approval. Full game view: live roads, facilities, incidents, city metrics, and synchronized AI activity. Inspiration Browser agents are usually asked to operate interfaces designed only for human eyes. That becomes fragile when an application contains a live model with more meaning than its visible controls can express. A crisis dashboard may show a blocked road, a failed power station, and an overloaded hospital, but the causal chain connecting them is difficult to reconstruct from pixels or DOM labels. We wanted to explore a different relationship: not an agent that simply clicks faster than a person, but a human and an agent operating the same complex system through complementary interfaces. What it does Pending: Human turns a sixty-minute urban crisis into a shared decision exercise. The deterministic simulation creates cascading infrastructure failures and tracks exposed residents, injuries, untreated critical cases, fatalities, hospital load, road travel time, emergency vehicles, and incident resolution. The AI teammate uses WebMCP to investigate structured city state, trace root causes, forecast the cost of doing nothing, compare three compound response plans, and stage one candidate for review. The player chooses the mission doctrine, dispatches vehicles and routes, can build an independent counterproposal, and makes the final decision. Simulating is never executing. A proposal remains pending until the human presses the visible approval control. There is deliberately no WebMCP approval tool. Why WebMCP Pending: Human is built around state that is richer than its visible dashboard. WebMCP gives the agent a semantic contract over the same facts used by the simulation engine: named roads and facilities, passability, power dependencies, hospital pressure, response routes, at-risk populations, and deterministic future outcomes. This avoids guessing from color, screen position, animation, or fragile markup. It also creates a stronger safety boundary. The agent receives deep investigative and counterfactual capabilities without receiving final authority to act. The tool surface changes with the stage. It begins with one entry capability, then exposes only what is useful at the current checkpoint. One integrated assessment call reads the evidence and issues three exact revision-bound previews; a second call lets the agent exercise judgment by selecting one. Short guidance tools explain and highlight the next human control without clicking it, and an event-wait tool keeps the shared session synchronized. A better human + agent experience The simulation, agent, and human have distinct powers: The simulation owns the facts. Every live and forecasted consequence comes from deterministic TypeScript rules. The agent compares possible futures. It connects evidence across infrastructure systems and explains trade-offs. The human owns the decision. The player sets values, accepts social costs, and authorizes consequential action. City time freezes while the agent analyzes and while a proposal awaits approval, so model latency cannot cause extra simulated deaths. Findings are mirrored into the page transcript, and the approval card shows benefits and costs before the player decides. The human can disagree by building a separate plan without erasing the AI proposal. Together, people and agents can identify a cross-system root cause, establish a shared no-action baseline, compare policy futures under human-selected values, and verify the result against the same rules. Doing this reliably through a human-only interface was previously slow and brittle. How we built it The project is a client-side React and TypeScript application. The road graph, casualty model, scenarios, incident clearance, vehicle travel, forecasts, and scoring all live in one deterministic simulation engine. A shared store manages the live clock, event queue, plan previews, human approval boundary, and teammate transcript. WebMCP tools are registered directly by the page and routed by the current simulation phase. The live workflow uses enter_pending_human_stage, analyze_crisis, propose_emergency_plan, post_next_guidance, focus_next_control, wait_for_city_event, and analyze_turning_point. Granular district, road, facility, hospital, power, routing, forecast, and simulation tools remain available for semantic diagnostics. There is no external AI API inside the application. The WebMCP-enabled browser supplies the agent. There is also no database, login, map API, or hidden backend simulation. Challenges The hardest design problem was keeping a continuous co-op experience responsive when an agent model could take tens of seconds to reason. We introduced time freezing, phase-aware tools, event waiting, and a two-call decision path that batches structured investigation while still requiring the agent to choose among candidates. Another challenge was visual causality. Response vehicles originally felt decorative. We rebuilt movement around the same road graph exposed to WebMCP, made congestion and closures change travel speed, anchored arrivals to visible nodes, and let on-scene units progressively resolve incident markers. Accomplishments Live play and forecasts share one source of truth. Simulating a plan never mutates the live city. Stale previews cannot execute after the city revision changes. AI and human plans remain visible together. High-impact actions cannot bypass human approval. Three difficulty-scaled missions are deterministic and replayable. Forty-two automated tests cover the engine, routing, approval boundary, and agent flow. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when it exposes meaning that cannot be reliably recovered from the human interface. It is also useful for defining what an agent cannot do. A good agent experience is not the largest possible toolbox; it is a clear sequence of meaningful capabilities, shared state, and explicit authority boundaries. What's next Future work could add a scenario authoring system, richer field observations, and deeper doctrine negotiation while preserving deterministic evaluation and human approval. The current version intentionally prioritizes one complete collaboration loop over an open-ended city model. Pending: Human is a fictional training and interaction-design prototype. All people, casualties, incidents, and outcomes are simulated. title: Pit Wall
pitch: A WebMCP-powered racing strategy game where humans and AI share the pit box—analyze live race conditions, make strategy calls together, or hand the race to an AI Crew Chief.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered racing strategy game where humans and AI share the pit box—analyze live race conditions, make strategy calls together, or hand the race to an AI Crew Chief. Like Comment Story Updates Pit Wall — A WebMCP-powered racing strategy game built around shared human + AI race control. Track & Control Selection — Choose the circuit and control model: Human, Co-Crew Chief, or a fully delegated AI Crew Chief. WebMCP Site Tools — 8 structured tools give ChatGPT live race intelligence plus controlled race actions. AI Race Analysis — ChatGPT reads live race state, evaluates strategy tradeoffs, and recommends a call without acting. Live Pit Wall — Position, fuel, tire age, running order, field strategy, and decision context evolve throughout the race. Shared Pit Wall — Human and AI Crew Chief calls coexist in one persistent race, with control passing between them. Decision History — Every Human and AI Crew Chief strategy call is attributed, timestamped by lap, and preserved. Race Recap — Stage results, strategy history, and major events create an auditable record from green flag to finish. Inspiration Race strategy is a constant sequence of decisions: tires, fuel, track position, cautions, pit timing, and when to sacrifice position now for an advantage later. Most AI experiences put an assistant beside an application. I wanted to explore something different: what happens when the AI has an actual role inside the experience? Pit Wall turns the player into a stock-car crew chief competing against autonomous rival pit walls. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can join that same pit box. The human can ask the AI to analyze the race, make one strategy call, manage a stage, or take responsibility for the entire race. Delegation itself becomes a game mechanic. What it does Pit Wall is a browser-based stock-car strategy game built around human-agent collaboration. Players race across five differentiated environments: Daytona International Speedway Bristol Motor Speedway Darlington Raceway Pocono Raceway Watkins Glen International The simulation models fuel, tire age, pit service, cautions, stages, track position, pace, strategy splits, and autonomous opponent pit walls. Players can interact with the race at several levels of autonomy. Observe ChatGPT can inspect the live race without changing anything. Advise The agent can analyze position, fuel, tires, stage context, field strategy, recent events, and deterministic Race Intelligence, then explain the strategic tradeoffs while leaving the decision to the human. Act The player can delegate exactly one strategy decision to ChatGPT. Delegate The player can hand over a bounded portion of the race—or the entire race through the checkered flag. Every strategy call records its provenance, so the interface shows whether a decision came from the Human or AI Crew Chief. The result is not a chatbot layered on top of a game. The agent and human participate in the same simulation, operate against the same race state, and can exchange control as the race develops. Why WebMCP Pit Wall is designed around a problem that ordinary browser automation does not solve particularly well. A visual agent would have to inspect the interface, infer what each control means, extract race state from rendered text, and manipulate UI elements. WebMCP gives the agent a semantic interface to the same live race the human is playing. Pit Wall registers eight Site Tools: get_race_state get_my_car_state get_field_state get_current_decision get_recent_events get_decision_history commit_strategy advance_to_next_decision Six are read tools and two can mutate the race. The read tools expose structured information about the race, player car, field, current strategic decision, recent events, and decision history. The write tools allow an authorized agent to commit a strategy call and advance the simulation to its next meaningful decision point. This means ChatGPT does not need to infer application state from pixels or simulate mouse clicks. It can reason over explicit race state and perform defined actions through the application's own interface. Human UI actions and WebMCP actions operate against the same canonical race session. Human + agent collaboration The central idea is not simply that AI can play the game. The player determines how much authority the AI receives. Ask: Analyze this situation and recommend a strategy, but don't execute anything. ChatGPT can inspect the race and act as an analytical crew chief while the human retains control. Or: Take this strategy call for me. ChatGPT can make exactly one decision. Or: Take the pit box through the end of this stage. The agent can manage a bounded portion of the race and return control at the stage boundary. Or: Take the pit box and call this race through the checkered flag. The AI Crew Chief can operate the race autonomously through successive strategic decisions. Control is therefore not binary. A player can move between Human, Co-Crew Chief, and AI Crew Chief behavior during one continuous race. Human and AI decisions remain attributed separately even as control passes between them. This creates an interaction model where a human and an agent can observe, reason, collaborate, transfer authority, and take control back inside the same stateful application. Race Intelligence Pit Wall calculates deterministic Race Intelligence for both the player and agent. It includes context such as: fuel margin to the next race boundary tire age relative to the field position trend stage context observable opponent strategy recent strategy consequences The simulation calculates the facts. ChatGPT interprets them. This separation is important. The agent does not invent the underlying fuel state, tire age, position, or field behavior. Pit Wall provides deterministic race information, while ChatGPT reasons about what that information means strategically. This allows the AI to explain why a decision matters instead of merely selecting an action. Strategy has consequences Pit Wall does not guarantee that either the human or AI will win. Pit service can sacrifice substantial track position. Staying out can gain immediate position while creating future tire or fuel problems. Short-pitting can create an undercut opportunity while temporarily sending the car backward through the running order. Different race environments also create different strategic conditions. The player's position, tire state, fuel state, pit history, field strategy, and race circumstances evolve as decisions are made. Completed WebMCP-controlled races have produced everything from victories to difficult finishes. Every decision remains visible in the strategy history, including: who made the call the lap on which it occurred the selected strategy the resulting position consequence Stage winners and the player's Stage 1 and Stage 2 results are preserved through the final race recap. The checkered-flag screen therefore becomes more than a finishing position. It provides a record of how the human and AI managed the race together. How I built it Pit Wall uses a React/Vite frontend, FastAPI backend, and deterministic Python race simulation. The architecture is: Human + ChatGPT → React/WebMCP interface → FastAPI → Pit Wall adapter → deterministic race simulation → user car + autonomous field The browser interface presents the same race state used by the agent. WebMCP tools are registered through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The application exposes eight WebMCP Site Tools directly from the live browser experience. The FastAPI layer provides the race-session API, while the simulation owns the canonical race state and advances the user car and autonomous field. The submitted application is self-contained and does not require an external database at runtime. The production build is packaged as a single-origin Docker application and deployed on Render. Reliability and integrity Giving an AI permission to mutate a stateful application introduces a different engineering problem from simply asking an AI for advice. A strategy call must apply to the correct decision. It must not execute twice. An agent managing a bounded portion of the race must stop at the requested boundary. And once the checkered flag falls, neither the human nor agent should be able to continue mutating the completed race. Pit Wall therefore includes protections for: stale decisions duplicate decisions decision-boundary overrun stage-boundary handling post-finish mutation actor provenance Human/AI control state Human and AI actions travel through the same underlying simulation rules rather than separate gameplay paths. A dedicated simulation exploit and strategy-integrity audit was completed before submission. The standalone test suite currently passes 46 focused tests covering the simulation, API behavior, WebMCP integration, decision handling, and race integrity. title: SAVS: Visual Proof for WebMCP Agents
pitch: A successful tool call is not a visual verdict. SAVS gives WebMCP agents revision-bound evidence for the interface humans actually see.
about_excerpt: A successful tool call is not a visual verdict. SAVS gives WebMCP agents revision-bound evidence for the interface humans actually see. Like Comment Story Updates 1 · Fresh R1 is blocked. The action succeeded. The rendered revision did not. 3 · Fresh R2 passes. Only a fresh audit of the repaired revision returns PASS. 2 · Four native WebMCP tools. State, action, audit, and repair are page-registered. 4 · Old evidence remains blocked. Visual evidence belongs to the exact revision it inspected. Inspiration WebMCP makes website actions explicit and reliable, but successful execution does not prove that the human-visible result is correct. An agent can invoke the right tool and still leave clipped text, a shifted baseline, an overflow, or another visual regression behind. People experience the rendered page; agents usually receive a structured action result. We built SAVS to connect those two meanings of success. What it does SAVS is an agent-native visual verification workbench for WebMCP. The workbench begins at approved reference revision R0. An agent invokes a valid compact-layout tool, which succeeds and creates immutable revision R1. R1 contains a small but visible two-CSS-pixel baseline defect in the metric strip. The agent then audits R1. SAVS rerenders the approved reference and requested revision, compares their pixels, and returns a fresh BLOCK verdict with visual evidence. A constrained alignment repair creates successor revision R2. The earlier R1 result cannot approve R2 because its evidence is bound to R1 and is now stale. Only a fresh audit of R2 returns PASS . Four native page tools expose this flow: get_visual_state reads the current immutable revision and audit state. apply_compact_layout performs the valid action that creates R1. run_visual_audit audits an explicitly requested revision and reports whether its evidence is fresh. apply_alignment_repair creates a successor revision using an allowlisted repair and an expected-revision precondition. The tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . They are semantic capabilities, not wrappers around screen coordinates. The visible controls use the same application endpoints, so the person and agent share one state, history, evidence surface, and set of verdicts. How we built it The reference app is self-contained. A Node.js server maintains isolated sessions, immutable revisions, idempotency receipts, and audit records. The browser renders the current revision and evidence while registering the four WebMCP tools. A controlled renderer produces approved-reference and candidate PNGs. The verifier checks exact pixel differences, protects a stable control region, limits accepted changes to the intended target, and binds every audit to its requested revision. The same R0 → R1 → R2 behavior is exercised through native WebMCP discovery and invocation in Google Chrome and through an independent verifier against the public Render deployment. The live app requires no account or credentials. The public repository contains the standalone source, tests, instructions, MIT license, and Challenge-period provenance. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not detecting that pixels changed. It was making the result trustworthy across time. An audit that was valid for R1 must not become approval for R2, and a repair must not overwrite the history that explains the failure. That led us to immutable revisions, freshness-aware verdicts, expected-revision checks, and idempotent action receipts. The demo also exposed a more human problem: a two-pixel baseline defect can be obvious to a viewer while looking harmless in code or DOM geometry. We made the rendered pixels—not styling intent—the final evidence boundary. Accomplishments that we are proud of Four real page-registered WebMCP tools form one coherent workflow. A technically successful action produces a visible defect and a structured fresh BLOCK verdict. Stale evidence remains blocked after the page advances to a new revision. A constrained repair creates R2 without erasing R1. A fresh R2 audit returns PASS with zero changed pixels. The same behavioral chain has passed against the public Render origin. The accepted 2:37 demo uses real native WebMCP calls, audible narration, and burned-in English captions. What we learned Structured tools solve action ambiguity, but agents also need structured evidence about outcomes. Visual approval is not a timeless property of a page; it belongs to a particular rendered revision. That small change in the contract makes failure, repair, and approval understandable to both the agent and the person supervising it. What's next This Challenge workbench proves the smallest complete loop. The longer-term direction is to generalize the same revision-bound visual contract across real applications, responsive states, and richer human-approved visual intent while keeping the evidence inspectable by both people and agents. Challenge-period provenance SAVS began as pre-existing visual-verification research. During the Challenge period, we built this self-contained WebMCP reference implementation: a new page-registered four-tool interface, immutable revision workflow, freshness-bound visual verdicts, constrained repair path, native WebMCP browser verification, public deployment, and Challenge demo. This repository does not import the private SAVS research runtime. title: SheetCanvas
pitch: A spreadsheet canvas ChatGPT can drive directly; no clicking, just tell it what to build
about_excerpt: A spreadsheet canvas ChatGPT can drive directly; no clicking, just tell it what to build Like 2 Comment Story Updates GIF SheetCanvas WebMCP Demo SheetCanvas.com Inspiration The real problem is that humans and agents don't have a place to actually work together on data. Ask ChatGPT to analyze something and it hands you a chart or a table inline; but that artifact is disposable. It lives in the scroll of one conversation, not anywhere sticky. Close the chat, come back tomorrow with a follow-up, and you're re-asking the same questions from scratch instead of building on what was already figured out. Existing BI tools don't fix this either, they were built for a person driving a mouse, and none of them have caught up to a workflow where an agent is a first-class collaborator rather than a text generator bolted on the side. Also most people isn’t good at data analysis, the tools has the data analysis knowledge built in, to write the best query, chose the suitable chart to tell the correct story. I built SheetCanvas to be that place: a canvas where a human and an agent cooperate on data analysis in real time, locally, the state persists, it's inspectable, and it's shared, instead of the agent's output vanishing back into a chat transcript the moment the conversation ends. I was building toward WebMCP specifically, before it existed. This tool is designed for an agent to drive the canvas directly, the same way a person does — and before document.modelContext was a real, shipped API, I got there with a workaround: a hand-rolled remote MCP server over a WebSocket, so an MCP-capable client like Claude Desktop could already act on the canvas. WebMCP isn't a feature I bolted on for this challenge; it's the primitive I was always building toward, and this challenge was the first chance to stop working around its absence. How I built it The reason this was cheap to build rather than a rewrite: SheetCanvas already had exactly one tool registry — 26 tools, defined once with zod schemas, covering everything from createSheet and setCells to chart creation and live connector queries — feeding a single executor. Three doors already used it: a person clicking around the UI, an in-app Copilot, and the WebSocket-based remote MCP server that had been standing in for WebMCP until it existed. WebMCP became a fourth door over that same registry — not a parallel build, but the door the other three had been waiting for. Concretely: document.modelContext.registerTool wraps every existing tool, converting its zod schema to JSON Schema with the identical call the backend already used, so the two doors can't quietly drift apart. A state-aware gating layer decides which of the 26 tools are registered at any moment — no point advertising queryConnection before a connection exists — keyed on durable facts (does a sheet exist? a note? a connector?) rather than conversation shape, since a tool that vanishes between the agent listing tools and calling one is an unrecoverable error, not a retry. A registration lifecycle manager reconciles the tool set on every relevant state change: diffed, coalesced, debounced, with one AbortController per registered tool (unregistering in WebMCP is only aborting a controller — there's no unregisterTool ). All four doors — clicks, Copilot, remote MCP, and now WebMCP — now route through one shared dispatch point, tagged by origin. That's what let me add a single activity trail that watches every tool call regardless of which door it came through, and a rewind control: "undo back to here," warning inline if it would also discard edits you made yourself in the meantime. Safety was the design question I spent the most time on, because there is no confirm() for an agent to hit — Chrome's own docs still reference a requestUserInteraction() primitive that was removed from the spec before it ever shipped. So instead of a dialog, safety became three structural properties: every tool is correctly annotated ( readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint on anything returning warehouse- or CSV-authored text back to the model), every mutation is undoable, and every mutation is visible in the trail as it happens — plus ChatGPT's own confirmation on top. title: Zada
pitch: The store that shops with you: a live storefront whose WebMCP tools let your agent search, check sizes, read reviews, track prices, and fill the bag while you watch and click in the same session.
about_excerpt: The store that shops with you: a live storefront whose WebMCP tools let your agent search, check sizes, read reviews, track prices, and fill the bag while you watch and click in the same session. Like Comment Story Updates Zada - the store that shops with you Zada is a live fashion storefront where people and AI agents shop together. The most important part is the human experience: shoppers still see real products, browse the grid, open product pages, compare options, and discover what they love. The agent works inside that experience, helping with the work around shopping instead of hiding the store behind a chat response. A shopper can say, “Find men's sport-elegant shoes for an event, size 42, under ₪200,” then watch the real items appear, navigate through them, open the ones that feel right, and save the products they love. The agent learns from those actions and becomes more useful as the session continues. Inspiration Shopping is personal. People do not only want an answer; they want to see the options, notice details, compare products, and have the small moment of finding something they genuinely like. Most AI shopping experiences reduce that to a text recommendation. We wanted to keep the discovery experience of a real storefront, while letting the agent remove the tedious work: filtering, size checks, price checks, review discovery, and finding similar products. and most important to understand what user love and what he want and give him inside the app a staph that he cant discover without agent that know what he loves What it does Zada supports a shared shopping session: The shopper sees and navigates a live product catalog at every step. The agent searches by intent, price, style, color, sale status, and size. Product pages remain fully clickable while the agent works. Shoppers can open products, linger on items, search, and mark products they love. get_shopper_signals lets the agent understand those real preference signals and recommend in the shopper's style. The agent checks exact size availability, finds similar products, surfaces reviews and price signals, and manages the bag. Checkout remains human-controlled and hands off to the retailer. The result is not “an agent that shops instead of you.” It is a store where the agent helps you shop better. Why WebMCP I have built hundreds of MCP servers, so I came into this challenge focused on the agent experience: progressive tool disclosure, tight token budgets, strong tool descriptions, validated inputs, and errors that agents can recover from. WebMCP changed the design question. The challenge is not only how to expose agent capabilities. It is how to add an agent to a web experience without taking the experience away from the person using it. With WebMCP, the page exposes the meaningful actions of shopping as structured tools: search products, check a size, save sizes, find reviews, check prices, discover similar items, understand shopper signals, and manage the bag. The agent can act reliably, but the person keeps the visual store, the product discovery, and the final decisions. How we built it We built one Node.js service with one shared shopping-tool layer across three surfaces: In-page WebMCP: 16 typed tools registered on document.modelContext , with compatibility fallbacks and a declarative search form. Remote MCP: The same tools are available through streamable HTTP at /mcp for Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and ChatGPT developer-mode connectors. Human UI: The storefront calls the same endpoints, so humans and agents operate on the same session state. Remote agent calls mirror into the open storefront over Server-Sent Events. Every action is visible in a live activity feed, attributed to either the shopper or the agent, and the UI stays interactive throughout. The catalog uses read-only public fashion data. Reviews combine public Reddit, YouTube, and web signals. A lightweight price-history store learns from product observations over time. We also built end-to-end tests for both real streamable-HTTP MCP calls and in-page WebMCP tool calls. Challenges and what we learned The hardest problem was designing for two users at once: the agent needs reliable, compact, recoverable tools; the person needs a rich, understandable shopping experience. We used progressive disclosure so agents see the right tools at the right moment, kept tool responses focused to avoid wasting context, and designed clear error responses so an agent can recover instead of getting stuck. But the bigger lesson was that agent capability is not the product by itself. The product is the experience around it. People need to see products, explore freely, and develop their own taste. Zada makes that discovery more personal by placing the agent inside the storefront, not between the shopper and it. Built entirely during the submission period. The repository history begins August 26, 2026. title: CoMapper - WebMCP
pitch: Make maps multiplayer.
about_excerpt: Make maps multiplayer. Like Comment Story Updates CoMapper Make maps multiplayer. CoMapper is a WebMCP reference implementation for shared spatial work. Users and agents explore, filter, inspect, style, and export the same live map state. Inspiration Maps shape our world. We use them to navigate, predict, plan, and understand the world around us. And yet, as the old saying goes: Tabula non est terra. (The map is not the territory.) For millennia, we've built tools for working with maps: the compass, sextant, surveying instruments, satellite imagery, GIS, spatial databases. Now agents can use those same tools. CoMapper asks: what happens when humans and agents collaborate on cartography? What it does CoMapper turns attributed GeoJSON into a shared spatial workspace. It validates mixed geometry, infers useful fields and controls, creates stable feature identifiers, and keeps the map, results, inspector, filters, and selection synchronized. Its WebMCP tools reflect the current page state. Dataset discovery and workspace inspection are always useful. Result-level actions appear once a search produces visible features. Styling and filtering accept fields declared by the active dataset. Feature actions accept visible result IDs. Agents can search, inspect, select, filter, style, and prepare CSV or GeoJSON exports. Their actions resolve into the same interface users are viewing. Prepared downloads appear as explicit controls in the workspace. Demo Scenario For the challenge demo, CoMapper includes a Toronto dataset with 269 features: 158 neighbourhoods, 86 technology-company locations, and 25 mobility, talent, and ecosystem anchors. The scenario gives the collaboration loop a focused question: build a shortlist for a potential OpenAI office. The first pass surfaces a density-led set of candidates. Users broaden the search beyond downtown, ask for a shorter list, inspect the evidence, and request an export. Each prompt continues from the state already visible on the map. The Toronto question is one worked example. The same interaction model applies wherever location, evidence, and human judgment meet: logistics, infrastructure, field operations, urban planning, environmental analysis, site selection, and emergency response. The demo also surfaces the limits of its evidence. A real property decision would require current rents, vacancy, floorplates, zoning, incentives, employee origins, and travel-time analysis. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the application expose the context it already understands. CoMapper registers page-bound tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and refreshes the available surface as the workspace changes. Each tool calls the same React action used by the interface. A search updates the result ledger and map. A selection opens the inspector. A filter changes the visible evidence. A prepared export reveals a download control. Users and agents remain synchronized around one state model. CoMapper demonstrates four reusable principles: Page state determines capability. Tools appear when their inputs and effects are valid. The interface remains authoritative. Tool actions resolve into visible application state. Schemas enforce scope. Fields, result IDs, limits, and spatial frames are validated. Users retain control. Evidence gaps stay visible and downloads require an explicit action. Stack CoMapper uses React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Zod, Cloudflare Workers, and the OpenAI Sites Vite plugin. The browser-side data pipeline accepts GeoJSON, validates its geometry, infers fields and controls, creates stable feature IDs, and normalizes the dataset into a shared search response. The bundled Toronto atlas follows the same path as an imported local dataset. The map, result ledger, inspector, and WebMCP tools all consume that response. The tool layer uses narrow JSON Schemas with Zod validation. Searches accept one spatial frame: radius, visible bounds, or a drawn polygon. Feature actions are limited to visible result IDs. Styling and filtering use fields declared by the active dataset. Connected text carries an untrusted-content hint. Tool registration follows page state and uses an AbortController for cleanup. Search calls receive the invocation cancellation signal. Tool results return updated visible state and provenance for the next step. The public demo runs entirely in the browser with its bundled fixture. Evaluation requires no account, database, API key, or paid model call. Challenges Three details shaped the implementation. First, tool state had to match page state. Result-specific tools need current rows, fields, and IDs, so registration changes as users move through the application. Second, spatial datasets mix geometry types and overlapping evidence. CoMapper keeps points and polygons legible together, gives points click priority where geometries overlap, and preserves the camera while layer state changes. Third, every agent action needed a visible and trustworthy boundary. Search limits, field allowlists, visible-ID checks, provenance, cancellation, and user-controlled download reinforce the same interaction model. Accomplishments Users and agents work with the same live application state. Tools adapt to the active dataset and current results. Follow-up prompts revise the evidence within the active workflow. Imported GeoJSON and the bundled fixture share one data pipeline. Inspection keeps source fields, provenance, and evidence gaps visible. Agent-prepared downloads remain explicit user actions. The public demo is deterministic, attributed, and ready immediately. Takeaways WebMCP is especially effective when a website is already an instrument. The most useful tools expose a few high-confidence operations, inherit the application's constraints, and return their effects to the interface. Shared state also changes the role of follow-up prompts. A correction becomes an input to the active workspace: users can see what changed, challenge the direction, and continue from the same evidence. The broader opportunity is software where visual interaction and agent action form one inspectable loop. What's next The next step is to develop the reference implementation into a reusable spatial-workbench pattern: pluggable dataset adapters and validation profiles; saved workspaces and collaboration history; richer spatial operators, joins, and travel-time analysis; reusable tool contracts for other MapLibre applications; and review flows for teams working with consequential spatial decisions. Use the bundled Toronto Office Placement Decision Atlas, or import an attributed GeoJSON file to exercise the same data pipeline. Ask the site tools to inspect the workspace or search the current map. For the bundled scenario, ask: “Build a shortlist of candidate locations for a new OpenAI Toronto office using site tools.” Follow with: “You're over-indexing on downtown. title: Duet
pitch: A browser design editor that a person and an AI agent operate on the same canvas, at the same time.
about_excerpt: A browser design editor that a person and an AI agent operate on the same canvas, at the same time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Making five platform versions of the same poster by hand is forty minutes of nobody's favourite work. Retyping every headline in a second language. Aligning twenty objects to a grid. Recolouring a layout to a new brand palette. This is the work designers actually complain about, and it is mechanical enough that a machine could do it correctly. So why hadn't one? Because a design document is a JavaScript object graph plus IndexedDB. There is no REST endpoint, no webhook, no export format an agent could round trip through. A server side MCP has nothing to connect to. An agent's only options were guessing at mouse coordinates, scraping the accessibility tree, or shipping a browser extension. All three are brittle, and none of them understand what a layer is. WebMCP changes the shape of the problem. It puts the tool registry inside the page, so a tool runs in the tab, against live in memory state, using the application's own code. For a design editor that turns out to matter in one very specific way: The agent can see what you selected. Not inferred from the DOM. The actual objects under your cursor, right now. An agent that merely generates designs could hand you a picture. It could never know that you just clicked two things and said "make these bigger." That is the whole idea, and it is not reproducible any other way. What it does Duet is a fork of an open-source browser design editor Avnac that adds WebMCP as a layer so a person and an AI agent can operate on the same canvas at the same time. Ask for something, get a real design. Say "design a flyer for my [cool] event" and the agent starts designing in real time using the WebMCP Point at something without naming it. Select two objects with your mouse, then say "make these bigger and line them up." The agent asks the page what you have highlighted and gets exactly that. This is the moment the idea justifies itself. Let it check its own work. Ask it to describe the layout and it reports what a person would notice: things that overlap, things outside the frame, edges that are almost but not quite aligned, and text that fails contrast against whatever sits behind it. Ask for an Instagram story version, the canvas grows, and the agent notices that the background no longer covers it and says so precisely. Approve or reject before anything changes. For anything involving taste, the agent proposes instead of acting. Its suggestions appear on your canvas as a ghosted preview with a dashed outline. You tick the ones you want, add a note back, and hit apply. Nothing lands until you say so, and the agent hears which changes you rejected. A tool that waits on a human decision inside the tab is the one thing a remote MCP server structurally cannot do. See exactly what happened. Every tool call is listed with its arguments, timing and result. Not a spinner. Seeing update_many { role: "headline", text: "Happy Birthday, Mum" } is how you tell a machine doing specific work from an animation pretending to. How we built it Duet is a fork of Avnac , an open source browser design editor. Avnac already had agent control of its canvas. It worked the only way that was possible before WebMCP: by embedding one specific AI vendor's SDK. Agent control required an account, an API key, a hosted service in the loop, and a hard dependency in the app's own package file. Only that vendor's agent could drive it. By the time I forked, that integration was paused and unreachable from the interface. Duet deletes that layer entirely and replaces it with an open browser standard. No account, no key, no vendor, no server. You send any agent the link and the tools are simply there. Before WebMCP, agent control of a browser design document meant choosing an AI vendor and marrying them. Now it is a property of the page. Fourteen tools , registered through document.modelContext.registerTool with an AbortController for teardown. The page feature detects and falls back to the deprecated navigator.modelContext . On Chrome 151 the two turn out to be literally the same object. Decisions that mattered: Registered once, reading live state through a ref. The editor's controller is rebuilt on every document change, so registering against it directly would register the whole surface again on every keystroke. Errors are returned, never thrown. An unknown id comes back as text naming what was wrong and listing the ids that do exist, so the agent corrects itself without another round trip. Every write returns the resulting state , never "ok". A tool that says "done" teaches the agent nothing. Readable ids at the tool boundary. The app uses UUIDs internally; the tools speak text_1 and rect_2 . Nothing inside the app was rewritten. Compact output built for a model to read. The scene comes back as a table rather than JSON, because it is read on nearly every turn. Descriptions that say when not to reach for a tool. That is where skilful use actually lives. Ghost previews needed no renderer changes at all. The editor's object component reads only its props, so a proposal renders through that same component in a sibling layer at reduced opacity, with the layer ignoring pointer events so a ghost can never take a click meant for the real object beneath it. Challenges we ran into A twenty second wait that hung forever. The proposal flow waits for a human decision. An early version used requestAnimationFrame to let React settle first. That works beautifully until the tab is backgrounded, at which point the callback simply never fires, and an agent driven page is backgrounded constantly. Caught it by actually switching tabs during a test rather than reasoning about it. The obvious proposal design is the broken one. The natural implementation is a single tool whose promise resolves when the human clicks approve. That hits the agent host's own tool call timeout long before a person finishes deliberating, and reads as a broken tool rather than a patient one. Splitting it into a call that returns immediately with an id and a second call that polls with a bounded wait keeps the human experience identical while making a timeout impossible. A layout checker that cried wolf. Every template has a background rectangle covering the whole canvas. A naive overlap check therefore reports one overlap per object on a perfectly clean design, and an agent that gets false positives once learns to ignore the tool forever. It now excludes full bleed backgrounds before any check runs, and separately reports the case where a background has stopped covering the canvas. Testing the implemantaion. I had intially planned on using Chatgpt's in-app broswer to drive the site and allow the agent to test out the tools, but unluckily for me i hit my free use limit on chatGPT so i ahd to improvise. I found and alternative: an extension that allows the user to use Gemini to test the project and connect to the WebMCP client directly. Silent failures are the whole genre. A tool can work perfectly when you invoke it by hand and never be chosen by an agent, with no error anywhere. That is not a bug you can debug; it is a writing problem. Accomplishments that we're proud of Selecting two objects by hand and having the agent know exactly what I meant. Everything else in the project supports that one moment. The proposal flow. Ghosted previews that track the live document rather than a stale snapshot, per-change approve and reject, a note that goes back to the agent, and the whole batch applying in a single commit. It is the part of the build that could not have existed a year ago. Being straight about the fork. It would have been easy to scrub every trace and present this as original. Saying "agent control already existed here, through one vendor's SDK, and I replaced it with a browser standard" is a better argument and it happens to be true. The tool descriptions I iterated multiple times on the tool descriptions before arriving at the current ones, which describe the tool adequately and allow the agent to call the right tool for the right action. What we learned Tool descriptions are the product. The difference between a tool an agent uses and one it ignores is almost never the code. A description that says what a tool does is half finished; one that says when to reach for it, and when to reach for something else instead, is the thing being graded. Give the agent a hand authored starting point. An agent placing objects by coordinate composes badly, because it cannot see the canvas. Templates removed that failure mode completely: the layout is a person's taste, and the agent only fills it in. Verify in the browser, not in the type checker. Every genuinely interesting bug in this build compiled cleanly. The background tab hang, the role that was silently dropped on save, the review card that read "move to same,620", the ghost that could not be told

title: Kuro Agent
pitch: Talk to your systems instead of managing them manually
about_excerpt: Talk to your systems instead of managing them manually Like Comment Story Updates Customer books through an AI agent, no forms Mimo clinic homepage Owner availability control room Inspiration I run a local digital presence here in Peru with Kurogrid, and I kept seeing Owners drown in dashboards. ERP tabs, CRM tabs, booking tabs, all day clicking. Talking it out solves a lot of things, so I started building an agent embedded straight into the system. The Owner talks, the system does, the Owner just checks. Developers today get two bad options for agents. Either the agent clicks around like a tourist with screenshots and DOM selectors, which breaks constantly. Or you build heavy API integrations with keys and OAuth that leak. WebMCP offered a third way, so I built Kuro Agent to prove it. What it does Kuro Agent is that idea in demo form. The vet clinic is just the example, do not get stuck on it. Think ERP, CRM, bookings, any system an Owner runs. A customer books a visit in one turn. The agent reads Saturday slots, prepares the request, the human confirms. On the Owner side, plain words plus a calendar conflict turn into an exact plan. Luna moves to a held 11:30, Max stays at 12:00, the Owner approves that exact revision, and the customer decides. Website, workspace, and agent read the same data the whole time. How I built it Next.js on the front, Supabase Postgres behind it. The page registers tools on document.modelContext based on role and state. Every consequential call runs same-origin against row level security, with one-shot approvals bound to a SHA-256 state hash, plus an audit trail. The heavy logic lives in Postgres procedures, so impact calculation and holds are atomic. Gemini powers the demo booking helper, Resend sends the customer emails, and the demo runs on isolated 30-minute sandboxes. Challenges we ran into Plenty. Concurrency for one, leases stepping on each other mid-demo. The plan hash covers that, any row mutating before approval aborts the apply. Two browser bugs ate my past few days. Registered tools carried circular window references that crashed JSON serialization, fixed with a schema sanitizer. And the inspector drawer got trapped under sticky headers until I portaled it to the body. But mostly the WebMCP invocation itself. Sometimes the agent prefers computer use over the tools sitting right there. And models return empty arguments whenever they feel like it, so the client heals that from the published list. The biggest call was deleting the Owner copilot entirely, since a page calling itself is theater, not WebMCP. Accomplishments that we're proud of One operation moves three places at once, nothing books or moves silently, and agents run admin operations without ever touching a credential. That is the whole bet. And I will keep developing and refining this idea, this is just the beginning demo. What we learned Cutting corners always bills you later. Every invented fallback and silent default I shipped came back as a bug during recording. Say the true thing, even if it is uglier. What's next for Kuro Agent Real email delivery on the deploy, asking for the email in Talk instead of fabricating one, and the same pattern on more verticals. The big one is a fully integrated voice system, specially on the backoffice Owner side. Talk everything out, check, done.
