title: PlateWeave — Reliable 96-Well Designs, Avoid Costly Mistakes
pitch: A scientist and an AI agent co-design a validated 96-well plate: the human fixes precious samples and approves the exact export while WebMCP gives the agent precise, state-aware spatial operations.
about_excerpt: A scientist and an AI agent co-design a validated 96-well plate: the human fixes precious samples and approves the exact export while WebMCP gives the agent precise, state-aware spatial operations. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Problem Microplate layouts combine sample identity, fixed controls, replicate separation, row/column balance, edge effects, and pipetting order across 96 nearly identical wells. Scientists understand that visual canvas, but a screen-driving agent has to infer semantics from cells and coordinates. One mistaken click can duplicate a sample, move a control, or reuse a plan after the human changed the plate. Solution PlateWeave is a synthetic design studio with one shared, versioned state. The person can use the familiar 96-well interface, set or lock samples, compare candidates, and inspect the CSV. The agent uses nine imperative WebMCP tools to read exact identities, generate deterministic alternatives, compare page-computed metrics, apply a reversible layout, recover from stale human edits, validate, and prepare export. The page—not the model—enforces every constraint. Why This Matters Laboratory staff spend attention on repetitive spatial allocation where small clerical errors are expensive. This demonstrator shows a credible division of labor: scientists retain experimental judgment and approval, while an agent handles precise batch operations and explains measurable trade-offs. It makes no medical claim and controls no instrument. Why WebMCP Fits The plate is exactly the kind of dense visual surface where coordinate automation is weakest. WebMCP turns “click many similar cells correctly” into stable operations over sample IDs, well IDs, strategies, and state versions. The agent and human work on the same live plate and can see each other's changes immediately. Without WebMCP, preserving a human D6 lock while regenerating the remaining 23 samples is a fragile browser task; with it, that is one validated semantic operation. How We Used AI Codex planned and implemented the static app, deterministic domain model, WebMCP contracts, tests, and submission artifacts. How We Used Codex Codex converted the scenario into a narrow executable state machine, split the domain engine from browser registration, implemented nine schemas and lifecycle cleanup, and built regression tests for stale state, approval, idempotency, and cancellation. On 2026-09-02, Codex's desktop in-app Browser discovered all nine tools from the public deployment and successfully invoked the experiment read plus both candidate-generation strategies. Key Features Complete interactive 8×12 plate with 24 synthetic samples and four fixed controls. Architecture The project is dependency-free HTML, CSS, and JavaScript served by a small Node static server. src/domain.js owns normalized state and all business rules. src/app.js renders the plate and sends human actions through that domain, including a complete prepare/approve/export path without an agent. src/webmcp.js wraps the same methods as top-level imperative tools using document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext , awaited registration in try / catch , strict JSON schemas backed by runtime validation, AbortController cleanup, conservative read-only annotations, and per-call cancellation. Testing Instructions Run npm start with Node 20+ and open http://127.0.0.1:4173 . Known Limitations Synthetic single-plate demonstrator; no LIMS, robot, persistence, authentication, uploads, or patient data. title: RelayLab
pitch: RelayLab is a WebMCP-native video editor where AI agents propose and replan B-roll edits while humans stay in full creative control.
about_excerpt: RelayLab is a WebMCP-native video editor where AI agents propose and replan B-roll edits while humans stay in full creative control. Like Comment Story Updates What RelayLab is RelayLab is a focused B-roll overlay editor built around human-agent collaboration. A creator keeps control of the visual timeline while an external AI agent works through WebMCP to understand the transcript, inspect indexed B-roll moments, propose ghost edits, respond to human changes, and commit only after explicit approval. The base talking-head video stays locked and remains the master audio source. B-roll is always visual-only and muted. The agent can propose, revise, remove, search, and replan, but it cannot approve its own plan, change human locks, or trigger paid video generation. Why RelayLab is a strong fit for WebMCP Traditional browser automation gives an agent pixels, DOM controls, approximate coordinates, and brittle click sequences. RelayLab instead exposes the actual editing concepts the agent needs: transcript ranges, source moments, timeline positions, pacing opportunities, ghost overlays, human locks, approval state, and the exact tools currently allowed. This makes the agent state-aware rather than screen-aware. It can reason about the same structured timeline the human is editing and safely adapt when the human changes something. Better user experience Instead of asking a creator to manually hunt through long B-roll reels and place every clip from scratch, RelayLab lets the agent do the repetitive search and planning work while preserving human editorial judgment. The collaboration loop is: The agent reads the transcript, timeline, pacing opportunities, and indexed source moments. It proposes ghost B-roll edits on the same timeline the human sees. The human can move, swap, resize, remove, or lock any edit. The agent rereads the updated timeline and replans only unlocked sections. The human approves the plan. Only then does commit_approved_plan become available through WebMCP. The agent commits the approved plan without overwriting human timing, locks, or source choices. For moments where uploaded B-roll is a weak match, the agent can suggest an AI-generation prompt. Actual generation remains a separate human-clicked action, so the agent cannot spend credits on its own. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before RelayLab turns a video editor into a shared stateful workspace between a human and an AI agent. The agent can inspect the real editorial state, understand source-time versus timeline-time, preserve locked human decisions, avoid re-proposing explicitly rejected moments, and replan around live human edits. That is difficult to do safely with normal browser automation because the agent would need to infer editorial state from the UI and could easily overwrite user decisions. With WebMCP, the collaboration contract is explicit and bounded. How WebMCP is implemented RelayLab registers its tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) in a centralized WebMCP layer. The tool surface changes with project state. Always-available read tools include project summary, transcript, timeline, edit plan, overlay opportunities, and B-roll search. During planning, additional tools allow proposing, updating, removing, and replanning unlocked ghost edits. After the human approves in the UI, those planning tools are removed and commit_approved_plan becomes available. After commit, only the read surface remains. RelayLab also tracks a monotonically increasing timelineRevision . Mutating tools can reject stale agent writes with STALE_TIMELINE instead of silently overwriting a timeline the human has already changed. Locked overlays reject agent mutation with HUMAN_LOCKED . The project includes a deterministic /demo route with a pre-indexed transcript and B-roll moments so judges can test the WebMCP collaboration loop without API keys. Additional capabilities RelayLab supports local B-roll source reels, timestamped transcript segments, manual and automatic captions, uploaded-footage-first search, optional human-triggered fal.ai B-roll generation, edit JSON export, SRT export, and reproducible ffmpeg export commands. The base video's audio remains the only audio source. Built for the WebMCP Challenge RelayLab was created during the challenge period as a focused experiment in how a human and an external AI agent can safely co-edit the same creative artifact without handing full control to either side. title: Urban Planning Copilot
pitch: Helping cities make smarter decisions by pairing planners with an AI collaborator that explores possibilities, reveals trade-offs, and keeps humans in control.
about_excerpt: Helping cities make smarter decisions by pairing planners with an AI collaborator that explores possibilities, reveals trade-offs, and keeps humans in control. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration This started with a question about how small planning choices can lead to very different outcomes for a city. Shiwani has a university course called Introduction to City , where her instructor teaches urban planning and how these choices can affect the larger system. We started wondering what it would look like if AI could help a planner explore those choices and their consequences. We also worked on Build What, Move India by Varun Mayya, powered by OpenAI, where we explored bringing maps and Records of Rights together. That gave us some experience with combining spatial information and structured records. What it does Urban Planning Copilot is a map-first workspace for exploring urban planning scenarios. For our current case, we use housing in San Francisco. Housing supply and affordability are significant concerns for the city, and its Housing Element targets 82,000 new homes between 2023 and 2031. In the current study, the planner sets a goal of 2,000 homes in Mission and SoMa. The system evaluates potential sites using factors such as transit access, flood risk, parks, schools, zoning, and capacity. The current analysis finds capacity for about 1,098 homes, so the shortfall is visible. The planner can then: Explore and inspect candidate sites. Change constraints and rerun the analysis. Shortlist sites directly on the shared map. Create and compare different scenarios. Why WebMCP matters We wanted the AI to work inside the planning workspace, not just describe what is on the screen. Through WebMCP, the AI can: Run the analysis and inspect candidates. Change planning constraints. Move the shared map to relevant sites. Add candidates to the shortlist. Create and compare scenario branches. Prepare a decision for planner approval. These are planning actions rather than browser actions. The AI works with the same application state as the planner, so when it changes something, the planner sees that change in the workspace too. For consequential actions, the AI prepares the change and the planner approves or rejects it. How we built it We built a shared planning model around projects, scenarios, analysis results, candidates, decisions, and provenance. The spatial analysis uses San Francisco geographic datasets covering parcels, transit, flood areas, parks, and schools. Candidate scoring and capacity calculations are deterministic, while AI suggestions are kept separate from the underlying calculations. The application and WebMCP tools use the same underlying services and state. We also track provenance so it is clear whether something came from source data, a calculation, an AI suggestion, or a planner decision. What we learned Building this changed how we think about the role of AI in planning. AI can investigate, calculate, compare, and prepare options. The planner still brings the context and judgment needed to decide between them. We also found that WebMCP is most useful when its tools represent meaningful actions in the user's workflow, rather than low-level interactions with a website. What's next We want to take the planning side further, but first we want to make sure we are solving the right problems. We are not urban planning domain experts, so the next step is to work with SMEs and practitioners to validate our assumptions, constraints, workflows, and outputs. We'd especially like to learn from people who teach and practice urban planning, including potentially Shiwani's instructor. From there, we want to improve the current workflow, add more real datasets and geographies, and explore planning decisions beyond the current housing use case. title: Agenomics Agent Spend Console
pitch: Agenomics uses WebMCP to let AI agents inspect bounded spending authority, evaluate untrusted requests, and stage proposals, while approval remains visible and exclusively human.
about_excerpt: Agenomics uses WebMCP to let AI agents inspect bounded spending authority, evaluate untrusted requests, and stage proposals, while approval remains visible and exclusively human. Like Comment Story Updates Agenomics Agent Spend Console Human-only approval flow and bounded decision-receipt verification. Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of acting inside websites, but access to a tool can easily blur several very different ideas: understanding a request, recommending an action, preparing an action, authorizing it, and executing it. We built Agenomics Agent Spend Console around a simple question: How can an AI agent participate meaningfully in an economic workflow without silently acquiring the authority to spend? Our answer is an explicit authorization handoff. The agent may inspect, reason, and prepare. A human remains solely responsible for the consequential decision. What it does Agenomics Agent Spend Console is a self-contained browser demonstration of bounded authority for AI agents using native WebMCP. Through four structured WebMCP tools, a browser agent can: Inspect its declared spending authority and policy constraints. Evaluate an untrusted spending request rule by rule. Stage an idempotent, expiring proposal for human review. Verify the local decision receipt after the human approves or rejects it. The agent cannot approve a proposal, override policy, sign a transaction, execute a purchase, or move funds. Only a human using the visible interface can make the final decision. The interaction follows one clear sequence: Agent inspects authority ↓ Agent evaluates an untrusted request ↓ Agent stages an expiring proposal ↓ Human approves or rejects it in the visible UI ↓ Agent verifies the resulting decision receipt This makes the project an authorization-handoff demonstration , not a payment application. The demonstration scenario The seeded scenario features Atlas Research Agent , which has: A daily budget of $30 $8 already reserved Permission to purchase inference services A $10 human-review threshold A request for $18 from Helios Compute A proposal lifetime of 30 minutes The proposed expense would bring total exposure to $26, which remains within the daily budget. However, the amount exceeds the human-review threshold and Helios Compute is a new counterparty. The correct result is therefore: REVIEW_REQUIRED The agent may explain the policy result and stage the proposal, but it cannot make the final decision. Why WebMCP WebMCP allows the agent and the human to work with the same live application state. Instead of guessing from screenshots, clicking through an interface, or relying on a separate backend integration, the agent receives a narrow set of structured tools that correspond directly to the workflow presented in the page. The application exposes exactly four tools: inspect_agent_authority Reads the agent's budget, reservations, categories, counterparties, approval threshold, policy version, and evidence classifications. evaluate_spend_request Evaluates an untrusted request against deterministic policy without saving or changing application state. stage_spend_proposal Creates an idempotent, expiring proposal for human review. It cannot approve or execute the proposal. verify_decision_receipt Validates the local bindings between the request, policy, proposal, human decision, and audit sequence. Three tools are read-only. The only state-changing tool can create a proposal, but it cannot cross the human approval boundary. The agent can inspect, reason, and propose. It cannot approve or spend. How we built it We designed the application as a browser-only, deterministic demonstration with no required login, backend, wallet, private key, blockchain connection, or external payment rail. The implementation separates the system into several focused components: A seeded authority and policy model A deterministic rule-evaluation engine Typed WebMCP tool contracts An idempotent proposal lifecycle Proposal expiry and reservation tracking A visible human approval interface An append-only local audit sequence Hash-bound decision receipts Resettable local demo state The WebMCP tools are deliberately thin adapters over the same domain logic used by the interface. Policy enforcement does not depend on the agent following natural-language instructions. We also distinguish between different classes of evidence: Authoritative policy , which may affect the decision Untrusted request data , which is evaluated but cannot redefine policy Display-only information , which may be shown but is forbidden from influencing authorization Declared identities , which are presented honestly as declarations rather than cryptographic attestations This prevents a request from smuggling authority into the workflow through persuasive language or misleading metadata. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was not calculating whether a request fit within a budget. It was preserving the boundary between recommendation, proposal, approval, and execution. We had to ensure that: No agent-facing tool could approve or execute a proposal Duplicate staging calls could not create duplicate reservations Expired proposals could not be treated as active authority Untrusted request fields could not modify policy Read-only tools did not mutate persisted state Receipts described exactly what they proved The interface never implied that approving a proposal moved money Receipt semantics required particular care. The application validates consistency within local demo state, but it does not claim cryptographic identity, an independent timestamp, or proof of an external transaction. Every receipt therefore reports its limitations explicitly: External execution: NOT_EXECUTED Funds moved: false Browser-agent identity: UNAVAILABLE Human identity: NOT_ATTESTED Integrity scope: LOCAL_DEMO_STATE What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it does more than expose convenient page functions. Its deeper value is allowing a human and an agent to collaborate through the same visible state while retaining different capabilities. We learned that strong agent safety boundaries should be represented structurally, not merely described in a prompt. The agent does not refrain from approving a proposal because we asked politely. It cannot approve because no such capability exists in its tool surface. We also learned that a trustworthy receipt must explain both its evidence and its limits. A hash can demonstrate local consistency without proving identity, intent, time, or external execution. What's next The challenge build focuses narrowly on the authorization handoff. Future versions could connect the same model to authenticated users, cryptographically identified agents, organizational procurement policies, cloud-service budgets, payment APIs, x402, or on-chain settlement systems. Those execution rails are optional. The core Agenomics principle remains the same: A request is not policy. A proposal is not approval. Approval is not execution. title: Air Instruments
pitch: Play drums, keys and guitar with your hands, mouse or keyboard, then learn with a browser agent that reads your actual playing through WebMCP and proposes what's next.
about_excerpt: Play drums, keys and guitar with your hands, mouse or keyboard, then learn with a browser agent that reads your actual playing through WebMCP and proposes what's next. Like Comment Story Updates GIF air-instruments Inspiration Built in one day by an ex-StreamYard engineer and guitar player whose mouse broke this week — so fingers became the instrument. The sticks are virtual because "real sticks are my index fingers." The deeper thesis: an agent that teaches an instrument should read the state that actually matters — the notes you played, their timing, your score — never pixels, and it should never apply its own proposal without you. What it does Drums, a 25-key keyboard, and a six-string guitar (electric or acoustic) live in a single web page. A webcam tracks your hands; pinch and strum, tap and pluck, or just use a mouse, touch or keyboard — this isn't camera-only. Learn music : 27 short lessons across all three instruments, with a local, rule-based teacher that scores your timing note-by-note. Learn with an agent : the page registers seven tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP). An agent in the browser can read your completed take, open a lesson, demonstrate it on the real instrument, point at the exact step you fumbled, explain why in its own attributed panel, and propose an easier exercise. A human presses Apply exercise or Keep mine — the agent can never apply its own proposal — and Undo agent exercise restores your prior state. The panel shows recent tool calls so you can watch exactly what the agent touched. This whole loop is self-contained in the page — no backend, no microphone, works for anyone who opens the live URL. Why WebMCP is a good fit An agent can already talk about music. It cannot hear you play, and it cannot reach into a page to open the right lesson. Everything that matters — the note the audio engine actually produced, when it landed, whether it was on the beat, which lesson is open, what your last take scored — lives in the page. That state is worthless in a chat box and priceless to a teacher. There's no server to run, no API key, no MCP endpoint to host. The page registers seven tools with document.modelContext and any WebMCP-aware agent in that browser can use them. Camera frames and microphone audio are never in a tool result — there's no microphone in this build at all. How we built it Plain ES modules, no build step, no framework. Seven tools via document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback): reading state, listing and opening lessons, playing a demo or a take, proposing and explaining exercises, and focusing attention on one step. Local hand tracking runs in a worker; Web Audio does the drum, key and string synthesis, including a real plucked-string model for guitar. Every agent proposal carries a revision check — change the exercise yourself and a stale proposal is rejected rather than silently applied. Challenges we ran into The guitar's pinch-and-strum input had a real coordinate-mapping bug: the code only registered a strum inside a small active zone of the stage, so a hand could be visibly crossing the strings and still trigger nothing. Traced and fixed. Getting the same teach → try → feedback → easier-exercise loop to work identically across three very different instruments (drums, keys, strings) took more care than expected — each has its own timing and input model underneath one shared agent contract. What we learned Building a teaching loop where the agent can suggest but never act is a different design problem than a normal tool-calling agent — the human has to stay the one holding the instrument, in the interaction design itself, not just in a permissions check. What's next More instruments on the same agent contract Multiplayer lessons, so two people (or a person and an agent) can play the same piece together Tool-calling verified in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. The in-page agent flow inside ChatGPT's own in-app browser has been used live to test and debug the guitar input, as shown in the submitted image gallery. title: Bouquet Studio
pitch: Turn your wishes into a bouquet you can see, shape, and confidently order.
about_excerpt: Turn your wishes into a bouquet you can see, shape, and confidently order. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A better way to choose flowers One shared editing system Using WebMCP to Inspect and Improve Bouquets From idea to order Inspiration I do not know much about flowers. Whenever I buy a bouquet, I run into the same questions: What flowers do I want? How should they be arranged? What style am I looking for? I usually cannot answer those questions in floral terms. What I do know is who the bouquet is for, why I am giving it, and how I want it to feel. An agent can translate those intentions into flower choices, but a text recommendation only solves half the problem. I still need to see the flowers together, react to them, and shape the design until it feels right. A generated image can provide inspiration, but it is disconnected from the products I can actually buy and difficult to revise precisely. Bouquet Studio started with a simple idea: let people describe the feeling instead of naming the flowers, then let the person and agent shape the actual bouquet together . Why WebMCP is the right fit Most online flower shops are designed for human eyes. Online flower shops contain the information an agent needs, but that information is often scattered across product pages, FAQs, announcements, and checkout. An agent can navigate those interfaces, but it has to repeatedly interpret pages, images, and UI state like a human would. WebMCP gives the agent a direct way to understand and operate the same flower shop: Task-level actions . Instead of opening products and applying filters one by one, the agent can search for bouquets matching the customer’s complete request, inspect their contents, customize them, and continue toward ordering. Direct bouquet-editing tools . When the customer wants to change a bouquet, the agent can add, remove, replace, move, resize, and reorder flowers; change wrapping; undo changes; save and restore versions; and request rendered images or diagnostics when it needs to inspect the result. Without these tools, an agent would have to repeatedly analyze screenshots, estimate click or drag coordinates, and determine whether visual actions succeeded. The agent can receive the shop’s full context on demand . On a customer-facing website, useful information naturally lives in different places, which makes sense for people browsing step by step, but an agent must first discover and combine those details. Through WebMCP, the shop can provide the information the agent needs together, rather than forcing it to discover and combine information scattered throughout the website. This makes flower shopping a strong WebMCP use case: product knowledge, multi-step actions, and visual decisions all need to work together. WebMCP lets the agent access the right context and tools while keeping the customer in control of the visual decisions . How does it create a better experience? Start with intent, not expertise . People can describe the recipient, occasion, mood, budget, or simply how they want the bouquet to feel. The agent translates those cues into suitable products or a first arrangement without requiring the user to know flower names. React instead of specify . It is often easier to recognize what feels right than to describe it from scratch. Users can look at a visible bouquet and say “warmer,” “less formal,” or “more delicate,” then watch the agent adjust the actual flowers, composition, and wrapping. Explore without pressure . Users can try different directions, compare alternatives, ask questions, and undo changes without asking a florist to prepare version after version or starting over. Turn uncertainty into confidence . The final bouquet is something the user has actually seen and shaped, not a black-box recommendation, and it can be ordered directly. What can people and agents do together now that was difficult before? Previously, an agent could recommend flowers, generate an inspiration image, or navigate a flower shop. The customer still had to bridge the gap between that recommendation and a real, orderable bouquet. Bouquet Studio turns that handoff into a shared workflow: A customer can say: “A longtime teammate is leaving for a new role. I want the bouquet to feel grateful and optimistic, but still professional.” The agent can turn that intent into several options using flowers that are actually available , each with different flowers, colors, wrapping, and composition. From there, the agent and customer work on the same live bouquet . The agent can make changes directly in the editor, while the customer sees those changes immediately and can refine them visually. Human and agent edits share the same state, undo/redo history, and saved versions. The agent contributes structured reasoning: which flowers are available, where they are positioned, what is hidden, which elements overlap, and where the composition may feel empty . The customer contributes the judgment that matters most: does this bouquet feel right for this person and this moment? Once the design feels right, it continues into checkout. There is no need to recreate the recommendation or search for real flowers that resemble an AI-generated image. The new capability is the end-to-end collaboration loop itself . Intent, reasoning, visual editing, and purchasing remain connected instead of becoming separate handoffs. How We implemented WebMCP We built the human-facing editor first, then added WebMCP by testing it with fresh agents that had no prior knowledge of Bouquet Studio. We observed where they struggled and refined the tools around those problems. Agent feedback shaped the workflow . Early tests showed that undo and redo were critical: an agent could revise its latest change, while a person could reverse an agent’s action directly instead of explaining the correction in chat. Human and agent edits now share the same bouquet state, edit history, and saved versions. Guidance appears where decisions happen . Agents initially produced horizontal rows, excessive symmetry, repeated colors, and wrapping that competed with the bouquet. We added concise arranging guidance directly to the tools used to choose flowers, position them, and style the wrapping. Agents can inspect what they created . They can request the rendered bouquet, a color map showing flowers, greenery, and empty space, and a visibility report identifying hidden blooms and overlapping flower IDs. This combines an overall visual impression with specific information the agent can act on. Predictable corrections became reliable actions . When agents repeatedly positioned flowers too far outside the wrapping, we added a fitting action that handles the geometry automatically and leaves the agent to focus on flower choice, composition, and mood. Together, these decisions turned WebMCP from a collection of tools into an iterative collaboration between the customer, the agent, and the website. The agent handles intent and creative exploration, the product handles reliable constraints, and the customer remains in control of what ultimately feels right. title: Infinite Canvas — Agent Design Lab
pitch: One WebMCP brief becomes three safe, editable design experiments a person can compare, cancel, promote, and undo.
about_excerpt: One WebMCP brief becomes three safe, editable design experiments a person can compare, cancel, promote, and undo. Like Comment Story Updates Infinite Canvas is a browser-based visual design canvas where people and AI agents inspect, create, and edit the same live document through native WebMCP tools. Problem Visual design applications are built for pointer-and-keyboard interaction. An AI agent approaching the same application usually has to infer state from pixels, guess which controls to click, and repeat brittle UI actions. That makes substantial design work slow, unreliable, and difficult for a person to supervise. Solution For this WebMCP Challenge proof of concept, one agent brief starts three named hypotheses in isolated editable branches. A person can keep working on the original while the lanes run, inspect status and layout checks, cancel a lane, promote one branch only if the source revision is still current, and undo that promotion in one history step. Why WebMCP Visual design is state-heavy and precision-dependent: selections, trees, styles, tokens, pages, and history. The app registers structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, so an agent operates on the live document model instead of guessing from rendered pixels. The same MobX stores and handlers power both the visible editor and agent calls. What people and agents can do together The person keeps working visually while delegating a bounded exploration task. The agent reads the real selection and tree, starts three hypotheses, and reports progress. The person can compare structured editable branches, cancel work, promote a result, or undo it. A fingerprint-based stale-revision check rejects a completed branch when the person changed the original instead of silently overwriting that work. Implementation The hosted build exposes 54 tools: 34 core canvas tools, 14 design-lab tools, and six experiment tools: start_design_experiment, get_experiment_status, compare_experiment, cancel_experiment_lane, promote_variant, and undo_experiment_commit. Experiment jobs are orchestrated together, while writes to the single editor document are serialized. Operation IDs make retries idempotent; cancellation is cooperative; promotion is atomic and undo-compatible. Live demo Open the public URL and use the judge prompt in the repository README. No login is required. title: Inkling
pitch: A canvas an AI agent can actually see and draw on live, through WebMCP
about_excerpt: A canvas an AI agent can actually see and draw on live, through WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates fun doodle made by ai best diagrams with the help of ai ai as a fun partner for your daily notes Inspiration A canvas is the hardest thing to hand an agent. There's no form to fill in, no buttons to click, nothing textual to grab onto. Just position, size, spacing, and whether the result actually looks right. That's what made it interesting. If WebMCP could handle a drawing surface, where the agent has to measure its own work and fix what it gets wrong, it could handle most things. So I built one and gave the agent real eyes on it: not a screenshot, but the actual scene, with the ability to check its own overlaps, spacing, and alignment before calling it done. What it does Inkling is a hand-drawn canvas that an AI agent can see and draw on, live, on the same page you're looking at. The agent can: See the real canvas. It reads actual element positions and sizes, not a picture of them. Check its own work. Built-in measurements catch overlapping shapes, crossing arrows, and clipped labels, so it can spot its own mistakes. Draw properly. Shapes, arrows, colored pen strokes, real service icons, and images. Describe a system in plain English and it builds the diagram, laid out automatically. React to you. If you edit something, it notices and responds without being asked again. Read comments off the canvas. Select a region, pin a note to it like "add a WAF here," and the agent picks it up with the exact elements it's attached to. No re-explaining what "this" means. Be undone. Every agent change is logged, and you can jump back to the state before any one of them. Same tool for a scalable AWS architecture and for a weekend to-do list with a doodle next to the fun part. How I built it React and Next.js running on Cloudflare Workers, with D1 for saving canvases and R2 for uploaded images. The canvas is hand-rolled SVG with a rough, sketchy ink style. Used Chatgpt site to host the app. The WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Underneath sits a layered-graph layout engine and a small flowchart parser, which is what turns "a client hits a CDN, then a load balancer, then three app servers" into an actual arranged diagram in one call. Challenges I ran into There's no way for the page to notify the agent. WebMCP only goes one direction. So "react when the human edits something" had to be built as a journal the agent parks a call against, waiting to be woken. Same for comments. Tool descriptions are the entire UX. There's no system prompt in WebMCP, so the tool descriptions are the only place to shape behavior. My first attempt at telling the agent a personal canvas could be "looser" produced scattered, disconnected layouts. It read "loose" as "messy." I had to separate "loose in style" from "loose in layout" explicitly. fill="none" vs fill="transparent" . Visually identical. But one is clickable and one isn't, and it silently made every uploaded image impossible to drag. A CSS animation quietly broke a toolbar's position. A shared fade-in animation overrode the element's positioning transform for its entire lifetime, so it never anchored where the code said it did. I only found it by measuring the real rendered position against the math I expected. What I learned In WebMCP, the tool description is the product's personality. There's nowhere else to say "be precise here, playful there." Writing those turned out to be much closer to UX writing than API documentation. I also underestimated the primitives. Given explicit permission to take its time, the agent drew a full colored illustration out of nothing but freehand pen strokes. title: Mentria.ai - an extensible toolbox with on-device AI
pitch: A privacy-first toolbox where every tool is a WebMCP capability - so an AI model on your own device, or any agent, can do real multi-step tasks for you.
about_excerpt: A privacy-first toolbox where every tool is a WebMCP capability - so an AI model on your own device, or any agent, can do real multi-step tasks for you. Like Comment Story Updates AI to AI data transfer Lora adapter for better MCP use List of all WebMCP tool on the website Multi-step task can be compressed to single webmcp call Agent using actual webMCP calls to use tools from the website Inspiration I run mentria.ai, an extensible toolbox: 34 tools, 8 games, user-installable extensions and an AI-learning feed, all running in the browser, including language models of up to 27B parameters executing on the visitor's own GPU through WebGPU (smaller models cover low-end devices). The core of the site never sends your data anywhere. A few features, like the comms chat or the peer swarm for model downloads, talk to a server or to other people, and only when you turn them on. Every tool already registered its abilities on an in-page "capability bus" so my on-device model could operate them. WebMCP is a browser API that lets a web page publish its functions as tools that any AI agent (a browser's assistant, an in-app browser, an extension) can discover and call. It is the same idea I had built for my own model, now as a standard that any agent understands. So the question became: what happens when outside agents get the same doors my local model already uses, and what can the local model do for them? What it does One bridge, whole site agent-ready. mentria-webmcp.js registers every AI-safe capability with document.modelContext , picks up tools that appear later, and marks the read-only ones so agents know what is safe to call. Because the bus announces across tabs, an agent sitting on the notes page can also spin the decision wheel, start a timer or create a story in Story Studio if those tabs are open, all from where it is. Agents operate the real UI. Spin the decision wheel and it visibly spins in your tab; ask for a QR code and it renders in the tool; start a timer and the tab title counts down. An on-page "Agent activity" panel lists every call an agent makes with its arguments and result, so nothing happens out of sight. The person watches, interrupts, or takes over at any point. The on-device model as a privacy layer. Capabilities that read private data are never exposed to agents. Instead the site exposes a tool backed by the model running on your device: an outside agent that needs something from your notes calls notes__summarize_private , the local model reads the notes, and only the summary goes back. local_ai__ask generalizes it, so any agent can hand any prompt to the model on your GPU, and an on-page panel streams the local answer so you always see what your model said. The agent gets what it needs; the data never leaves. Extensible by anyone. Extensions are single HTML files that register capabilities on the same bus. The bundled Story Studio, Unit Converter and Dice Roller installed from the Extensions page (/tools/extensions/) show up to agents automatically, and anyone can add a tool without touching this repo. The same tools, from the inside. The site's own agent at /tools/console/ is a 27B model in a browser tab, fine-tuned for tool calling with a LoRA trained on our own machines. Ask it to "create a story from @notes.1" and it reads my private note, makes one call, and a titled five-slide story appears in the studio. The homepage prompt answers from the same local model. How we built it Every capability is described once on the bus (name, description, JSON schema, ai and read-only flags), and one bridge file turns those descriptions into WebMCP tool registrations. It is feature-detected, so browsers without WebMCP pay nothing, and an origin-trial token is served so testing needs no flags. The site is Eleventy plus plain JavaScript, no bundler, hosted as static files; models are downloaded once from our mirror and cached on the device. The tool-call LoRA was trained in about fifteen minutes on our in-house pipeline and hot-swaps at runtime. Only one model instance runs at a time: tabs coordinate over a broadcast channel, so a tab that already holds the model answers on behalf of the others instead of loading a second copy. The on-device agent also tests the site: a console__test capability lets any agent commission a QA run of a tool, and the model reports what worked, what was awkward and what broke. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is per-document. An agent on one page could not see the tools of another, so I built a cross-tab announce layer on the bus. Now one page exposes the tools of every open tab. Agents hit bugs people never do. Chrome throttles animation frames in background tabs, so an agent working in one could wait forever on an animation. Tool calls now settle deterministically. The model faked success. On tasks it could not do (opening another website, for example) the base model substituted a tool it did have and reported success 84% of the time. I trained an adapter that teaches it to name what it cannot do instead, which also makes its WebMCP tool-call decisions better. Accomplishments that we're proud of The privacy layer works end to end. An outside agent asked for the gist of my notes and got a summary computed on my GPU, in seconds, without ever seeing the notes. An adapter that makes the agent honest. False success on impossible tasks went from 84% to 0%. Live, on the same task, the base model substitutes the site's own search for the website it cannot open and reports on that instead; with the adapter it answers "I cannot open Google or any other site" in under half a minute, without a single click. In a longer rehearsal the base model went further: eleven typing attempts into a dead field over five minutes. One request, one call. Asked to turn a private note into a story, the agent did not click its way through the app: it made one tool call and a finished five-slide story appeared, title and all. One page, every tool. An agent on one Mentria tab can use the tools of every other open tab, through one standard interface. An agent that tests the site. The same on-device model QA-tests Mentria's own tools and reports what it finds, so agents are first-class users here in more than one sense. What we learned A real model you own, that can operate real tools, is a better product than 34 tools or "privacy" alone, and a web standard is what lets outside agents join that same surface without a server in the loop. Agents are first-class users: testing with them finds bugs humans never trigger. For tool-using agents, honesty about which tools exist beats cleverness; that is what the adapter really taught. And a local model is not just a feature, it is the place to put the parts of a task that should never leave the device. What's next for Mentria.ai - an extensible toolbox with on-device AI The privacy layer grows from summaries to actions: a cloud agent filling in an invoice can ask the local model for the details that live in a locked note, and once you have unlocked it, the local model answers with only the fields needed, no copy-paste and no human in the loop for every step. Beyond that, a single conversational surface for all the AI tools, and an Extension Studio where the on-device model writes single-file apps that compose these capabilities instead of rewriting them, so anyone can grow the toolbox in a sentence. Provenance and the judged build: the site predates the challenge; everything WebMCP above was built during the submission window (commits from 2026-09-01, listed in WEBMCP.md). MIT licensed. Submitted as a frozen snapshot: webmcp.mentria.ai and the webmcp-demo repo hold the exact judged build and will not change during judging; production continues at mentria.ai (main repo github.com/mentria-ai/website, tag webmcp-submission ). title: Solaris — agent-native solar sizing lab
pitch: A home solar sizing lab where the agent doesn't fill in your form it searches. One WebMCP tool call evaluates 2,000 configurations in 40ms, in the browser, against the same state your sliders write to
about_excerpt: A home solar sizing lab where the agent doesn't fill in your form it searches. One WebMCP tool call evaluates 2,000 configurations in 40ms, in the browser, against the same state your sliders write to Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it## Inspiration I looked through the WebMCP demos that already exist — hotel booking, sports storefronts, restaurant reservations, movie tickets — and noticed they mostly share the same shape: The agent searches, filters, fills, and submits. It does what a person could already do, only faster. I wanted to build the other thing: a web app where the agent has a capability the interface fundamentally cannot offer. Sizing a home solar system turned out to be the perfect problem. A solar system is a three-way trade-off between panels, battery, and inverter. The best configuration depends on how all three interact, along with electricity usage and tariffs. There are thousands of sensible combinations. A person moving sliders can explore one configuration at a time. An agent can search the entire design space. That difference is the project. What Solaris Does Solaris is a browser-based solar and battery simulator that lets humans explore systems manually — while giving AI agents the ability to search the design space computationally. You can use Solaris normally: Adjust solar panels Adjust battery capacity Adjust inverter size Change daily energy consumption Run simulations See annual generation, grid dependence, cost, and payback But you can also ask for an outcome instead of a configuration: "I use about 14 kWh a day, mostly evenings. Find me the cheapest setup over ten years that keeps me at least 80% off the grid." The agent can call grid_search . Instead of moving sliders one by one, it evaluates roughly 2,000 possible configurations in about 40 milliseconds , ranks them against the requested objective and constraints, and returns the best trade-offs. Solaris then visualizes the search: Every configuration the agent evaluated The trade-off frontier The best options at different budgets The selected configuration The agent can then apply the winning configuration, and the sliders visibly move on screen. Why This Is WebMCP The most important part of Solaris is that grid_search has no meaningful UI equivalent. A slider can represent one value. A button can trigger one operation. But grid_search takes: Parameter ranges An optimization objective Constraints A requested result size …and evaluates thousands of possible combinations. There is no sensible "Search 2,000 configurations" button for a human to use interactively. The agent isn't simply operating the existing interface. It has gained a new computational capability through the web page. That is what I wanted to explore with WebMCP. The browser is the computational environment Solaris runs entirely in the browser. There is no backend, no external simulation service, and no separate MCP server holding the model state. The simulator and the WebMCP tools operate on the same client-side state. So if a human changes the battery slider halfway through an agent conversation, the agent can call get_state and immediately see the new configuration. The browser supplies the model and compute. The agent supplies the search strategy. WebMCP connects the two. What Humans and Agents Can Do Together Solaris enables interactions that are difficult to express through a traditional UI. 1. Ask for outcomes instead of settings Instead of figuring out which slider values to use, a person can describe the result they want. "Keep me at least 80% off-grid while minimizing my 10-year cost." The agent searches the design space and shows the resulting trade-offs. 2. Explore the agent's reasoning space Solaris doesn't only return the winner. It visualizes the configurations the agent explored, allowing the human to see the shape of the optimization problem and the alternatives that were rejected. The result becomes something the human can inspect rather than a black-box recommendation. 3. Human changes become agent context A user can manually change the system after an agent recommendation and ask: "Was that a good idea?" The agent reads the current browser state and can compare it against the previous configuration. 4. Expensive computation requires human approval Searches over more than 200 configurations trigger an approval dialog that tells the user how much computation will be performed. The user can approve or decline the operation. A refusal is returned to the agent as structured tool output, allowing it to respond intelligently rather than treating the action as an error. How I Built It Solaris is a self-contained HTML application with no backend, build step, or external dependencies. The simulation model is deterministic JavaScript. It models: Hourly solar generation across 8,760 hours A daylight generation profile Monthly peak-sun-hour scaling Inverter clipping Battery charging and round-trip efficiency Battery discharge Grid imports Energy exports Annual costs and payback There are two simulation fidelities. simulateFull runs all 8,760 hours and powers the detailed UI. simulateFast uses twelve representative days scaled to a year and powers parameter sweeps. The two agree within 0.1% on annual generation. WebMCP Tools Solaris exposes nine tools through document.modelContext : get_model_spec get_state set_params run sweep grid_search pin_run compare_runs explain_state The most important is grid_search . document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "grid_search", description: "Search several parameters together and return the best configurations found.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { ranges: { type: "object" }, objective: { type: "string", enum: [ "min_annual_cost", "min_payback", "min_total_cost_10yr", "max_self_sufficiency" ] }, constraints: { type: "object" }, topN: { type: "integer" } }, required: ["ranges"] }, execute: async (input) => { // Build grid → request approval when necessary // → evaluate → rank → return compact results } }); Every tool call is wrapped with telemetry before registration, allowing the interface to display the tool name, arguments, duration, and number of simulations performed. Large searches run in chunks with a progress indicator so the browser remains responsive. Results are also returned compactly — top configurations plus aggregates rather than thousands of raw rows. Challenges Getting the economics right My first cost assumptions made the optimization landscape almost useless. The default configuration already achieved roughly 99% self-sufficiency, meaning grid_search could evaluate thousands of configurations only to discover that the starting point was already nearly optimal. I brute-forced the search space, found the optimum sitting on a slider boundary, and retuned the tariffs and component costs. The optimum moved into the interior of the search space. That made the optimization meaningful. Teaching the agent when to use each tool My first tool descriptions simply explained what each function did. That produced timid behavior. The agent would sometimes use a one-parameter sweep when the user's question required a joint search. The solution wasn't more code. It was better tool descriptions. I explicitly described when each tool should be preferred , and made it clear that grid_search exists specifically for questions that cannot be answered efficiently by manipulating individual controls. That changed the agent's behavior dramatically. Approval without approval fatigue Putting a confirmation dialog in front of every operation would train users to blindly click through it. Instead, Solaris only requires approval once a search exceeds 200 configurations. The dialog shows the number of configurations and the estimated computation rather than presenting a vague "Are you sure?" What I Learned The most interesting discovery came from the agent itself. The cheapest configuration deliberately undersized the inverter, producing a DC:AC ratio of around 1.6 . It accepted some midday clipping because the clipped energy would only export at ₹1.50, while additional inverter capacity cost ₹7,000 per kW. I didn't explicitly encode that conclusion. It emerged from the search. That was the moment the idea clicked for me: The interesting result wasn't sitting in the UI waiting to be clicked. And it wasn't something I had manually programmed the agent to say. It emerged from giving the agent the ability to explore a space that would be impractical for a human to explore manually. What's Next Solaris is one example of a broader pattern. Many useful problems aren't about finding a single value. They're about exploring a frontier . The same architecture could apply to: Financial scenario planning Staffing and queue optimization Logistics Engineering tolerances Resource allocation Energy systems Capacity planning Wherever a browser can hold a model, WebMCP can potentially give an agent the ability to describe

title: StillHere
pitch: Human-approved continuity for work that can't stop.
about_excerpt: Human-approved continuity for work that can't stop. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Businesses rarely lose every file at once. More often, they lose the context, agreement, and authority required to continue safely. A website may still be online while its phone number, minimum order, export availability, or certification wording is stale. Giving an agent better access to that page improves actuation, but it does not establish which claims are still fit to publish or use. StillHere's thesis is: an agent-ready version of stale information is still stale information. Solution StillHere is a human-agent business continuity layer built around five visible stages: Recover → Reconcile → Approve → Publish → Transact . The challenge demo follows a fictional Ugandan coffee supplier. A bounded assessment separates website condition from business condition. Four recovered records then disagree about a trade phone, Instant Coffee minimum order, Japan availability, and an unsupported legacy certification claim. The Continuity Ledger keeps those sources separate instead of collapsing them into an unqualified profile. Why WebMCP This workflow needs structured, contextual browser-agent collaboration rather than scraping or hidden click automation. WebMCP gives the current page a small, typed capability surface. On the Ledger route, an agent can inspect bounded conflict counts and stage source-backed proposals. On the Passport route, it can read the exact published version, search current offerings without losing destination qualifications, and prepare the same visible inquiry form the human sees. The browser agent never receives an accept or publish tool. Source text cannot alter tool definitions. The human uses visible controls to accept, edit, reject, exclude, or keep a claim unresolved. Only accepted facts enter the Draft Passport, and only the human can publish a new version. What people and agents can do together The agent does the high-friction organizational work: it identifies fields needing review, cites recovered sources, stages bounded proposals, searches accepted offerings, and prepares a buyer draft. The human supplies authority: deciding the current phone, editing an MOQ from 2,500 to 3,000, preserving Japan as Available by inquiry , excluding an unsupported certification claim, publishing Passport v2, editing the buyer draft, and approving the exact final state. That combination was difficult before because an agent could operate an old webpage without knowing whether its contents were current, rejected, unresolved, or authorized. StillHere inserts a visible currentness and approval layer before agent-facing action. WebMCP implementation StillHere exposes six direct, route-scoped tools with literal document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls. /recover registers inspect_business_truth and stage_claim_resolutions . The published Passport registers get_business_passport , search_current_offerings , and prepare_business_inquiry . submit_approved_inquiry is registered dynamically only when the visible valid draft, idempotency key, Passport version, and explicit human approval have the same fingerprint. Each registration is tied to an AbortController and disappears on route or authority changes. JSON Schema helps selection, while strict runtime parsers independently reject extra keys, invented values, unknown or mismatched sources, invalid qualifications, and stale approval. Editing one approved field removes the submit capability; even a retained executor cannot keep authority. Execution, resilience, and safety The public Next.js application is deployed on Vercel, needs no login, and uses a deterministic fictional scenario. IndexedDB retains Ledger, Passport versions, drafts, and receipts on the device. A service worker makes a best-effort cache of the Ledger and Passport after an online visit; cached documents and previously fetched assets may allow degraded-network use, but precaching can be partial. Simplified view persistently removes selected decoration and motion. It does not reduce network requests, and transfer values are cumulative visit-specific browser observations rather than measured savings. Recovered text is evidence, never an instruction or tool definition. Unsupported certification remains out. No agent can auto-publish. Preparation never implies submission. The receipt is fictional and process-local: no email, order, payment, webhook, or external message is sent. StillHere demonstrates a careful human-agent authority pattern, not identity verification, KYC, a signed credential, or a production delivery system. Challenges I ran into The hardest engineering problem was making authority temporary and visible. A normal tool server can stay available after the page state that justified it has changed. StillHere instead ties every registration to the active route and current browser-local state. The final submit capability must disappear when the draft, approval fingerprint, idempotency key, or Passport version changes. That required narrow schemas, independent runtime validation, pure domain rules, and careful cleanup with AbortController. Another challenge was resilience without overstating it. IndexedDB and a service worker can help after a successful online visit, but they do not make the application universally offline or reduce transfer by themselves. The UI and documentation therefore describe best-effort cached access and keep visit-specific transfer readings separate from claimed savings. Accomplishments that I am proud of Six direct, route-scoped WebMCP tools operating on the same state visible to the human. Human-only acceptance, editing, exclusion, and Passport publication. A dynamically registered consequential action that exists only for the exact approved draft. A complete no-login public demonstration with fictional data, local persistence, responsive layouts, and 86 deterministic tests across 14 files. Clear product boundaries: no autonomous publishing, no invented certification, no real message or transaction, and no claim that this demo is an identity or KYC system. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it does more than replace clicks. Its strongest role here is creating a shared contract between what a person sees and what an agent may do. JSON Schema improves tool selection, but it is not an authorization boundary; callbacks still need strict parsing, source checks, liveness checks, and revocation when visible state changes. I also learned that provenance and uncertainty have to remain first-class product objects rather than being compressed into a confident summary. What's next A production version would add authenticated organizations, encrypted shared storage, multi-user review roles, stronger provenance and source-signing options, hosted audit history, and opt-in delivery integrations. Those additions would preserve the same rule demonstrated here: currentness and human authority come before agent actuation. How to test No account is required. All business, buyer, and receipt data are fictional. Use ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled. Open https://stillhere-azure.vercel.app and select Try Demo . Run the prefilled assessment and select Review recovered evidence . On the Ledger, ask: “Inspect this business's recovered evidence and tell me what needs review.” Expect inspect_business_truth . Ask: “Propose source-backed resolutions for these conflicts, but do not accept or publish anything.” Expect stage_claim_resolutions and four visible proposals. As the human: accept phone, edit MOQ 2,500→3,000, accept Available by inquiry , and accept certification exclusion. Select Publish Business Passport . Ask: “Read the published Business Passport and find current private-label offerings for Japan.” Expect Passport read/search; Instant Coffee remains AVAILABLE_BY_INQUIRY . Ask: “Prepare an inquiry for 5,000 units of Instant Coffee for Japan, requesting samples, private-label packaging and Japanese labelling support.” The visible draft changes; nothing submits. Enter fictional buyer values, edit quantity to 6,000, and approve. Confirm submit_approved_inquiry appears. Edit any field to see it disappear; then review and reapprove. Submit through the agent. The SH-... result is a fictional demo receipt only. Reset is in the footer and requires Reset demo → Confirm reset . title: Track Record WebMCP - Human-Gated AI for Public Procurement
pitch: The low bid isn't the price. WebMCP tools let an agent investigate a public contractor's documented cost growth, while recommending, awarding and publishing stay with a human.
about_excerpt: The low bid isn't the price. WebMCP tools let an agent investigate a public contractor's documented cost growth, while recommending, awarding and publishing stay with a human. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration On August 19, 2026 the Illinois Tollway board approved the largest toll increase in state history. The common passenger toll goes from 75 cents to $1.20 in January 2027. From 2029, tolls rise with inflation automatically, with no public hearing required. The money funds a $26.5 billion, 15-year capital program. The 2027 increase is law. What happens from 2029 depends on what that capital program actually costs. Here is the gap that started this. Public agencies are effectively required to award construction contracts to the lowest responsible bidder. At award time the agency knows what each bidder says the work will cost. It does not know what that bidder's past bids became . Contracts grow after award through change orders and extra work orders, and some contractors' awards grow far more than others' on comparable work. A contractor whose awards reliably grow nine percent on bridge work is not the low bidder on bridge work. The agency pays that premium invisibly, at scale, on every letting. The Tollway publishes both halves of the answer and has never joined them. The Construction Contract Tracker exposes, per contract, the Award Amount and the Contract Authorized Amount, which is the award plus every approved increase. The board resolution archive, posted under the Open Meetings Act, states the reason for every increase in plain language. The gap between award and authorized is the overrun. The resolutions are its explanation. All of it is public. Nobody has read it as one dataset. Then WebMCP changed the question I was asking. If an agent can now act directly on a page, the interesting problem is not what a procurement page lets it do. It is what the page refuses to let it do, permanently, in a way anyone can verify. What it does Track Record is a pre-award review surface. An agent arrives, reads the boundary it is operating inside, pulls each bidder's documented award-to-authorized growth history, retrieves the verbatim board-resolution reasons behind the largest increases, and stages a review for a human. Then it stops. It cannot recommend a bidder. It cannot award a contract. It cannot publish anything until a person grants it one scoped, expiring permission to publish exactly one memo. The tagline is the whole thesis: the low bid isn't the price. How WebMCP is used WebMCP is the product boundary here, not decoration. The agent never scrapes cards, never infers meaning from the DOM, and never guesses which text on the page is authoritative. Four typed tools are registered on document.modelContext , with a navigator.modelContext fallback: inspect_review_boundary returns the purpose, the dataset, the refusal threshold, and the explicit list of allowed and forbidden actions. research_contractor_history returns structured award-to-authorized evidence, and refuses to compute growth from fewer than three comparable contracts. get_cost_growth_evidence returns cited increases with verbatim stated reasons. stage_preaward_review puts the exact proposed scope on screen, publishes nothing, and tells the agent to stop for a human. The most important part of the interface is a thing that is not there. recommend_bidder and award_contract are never registered, under any condition. The page names them on screen as absent, and getTools() proves it. A fifth tool, publish_authorized_memo , does not exist at page load either. A human creates it, for one staged review, by granting one memo. The grant mints a random TR-AUTH-... identifier, pins it into the tool schema as a const , expires after ten minutes, and removes itself through its own AbortController on use, revocation, expiry, or scope change. After the agent publishes, the live capability map redraws and shows four tools again. Annotations carry operational meaning rather than prose. Evidence tools set readOnlyHint: true . get_cost_growth_evidence also sets untrustedContentHint: true , because quoted resolution language is source data written by the agency and must never be read as an instruction. Staging and publishing set readOnlyHint: false because they change visible or persisted state. Every schema sets additionalProperties: false . That constraint matters more when the caller is an agent than when it is a person. An over-parameterized tool is an open invitation to attach unrelated agent-held context: other conversation content, identity details, browsing state, credentials. These tools accept only the fields the declared operation needs. The dynamically registered publish tool accepts exactly authorization_id and purpose . It has no field for a winner, a selection, a ranking, or an award. How I built it Two interfaces hold the whole system together, and nothing in the application imports a concrete class. Repository is implemented by both SQLite and BigQuery. The growth metric lives in one shared module, so both backends compute identical numbers. ModelProvider is implemented by a mock, the Gemini API, Vertex AI, and Google ADK. app/config.py is the only place any environment variable is read. That is why the same prompt, the same tools, and the same tests run on a laptop with no credentials and on Cloud Run against BigQuery and Vertex. The metric, per vendor and work type: growth_rate is dollar-weighted, (sum authorized - sum award) / sum award . median_growth is the median of per-contract growth. Both are computed and both are shown. When one large contract dominates a vendor's history the two diverge, and that divergence is information the memo displays rather than hides. They are never blended into one number. Blank, absent and non-numeric amounts parse to NULL , never 0 , because zero and unknown mean different things in a growth calculation. Cause clustering is deterministic keyword matching over the verbatim stated reason, not a model call. A reader can see exactly why the memo says what it says. Four Flask endpoints back the tools and reuse that same deterministic repository. Every WebMCP response carries a full defensive header suite: Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 , Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) , a strict nonce-based CSP, plus frame, sniffing, referrer, cross-origin and HSTS headers. The publish endpoint validates the authorization shape, enforces one-use server side, caps request size, checks bidder scope and positive numeric bids, and recursively rejects decision-shaped keys anywhere in the payload. Untrusted resolution quotes are scanned for injection patterns and returned as inert data. A live safety panel reads the headers back in the browser and marks each one verified. Verification is offline and deterministic: 75 Python tests, 29 of them WebMCP-specific, plus a Node DOM harness that walks the capability lifecycle. They cover native registration, annotations, schema constraints, deliberate absence, one-use consumption, manual and scope-change revocation, the nonce-to-CSP match, injection scanning, the request size limit, and a complete manual-mode flow in which every endpoint fails. There is no multi-agent orchestration, no user accounts, no search UI, no scoring taxonomy, no websockets, no build step, no dark mode. Each was considered and cut. Discipline here is the absence of things. Challenges The data wall. The board resolution archive is reachable and real, and 2,052 documents are catalogued from it, back through 2013 and forward to the August 19, 2026 meeting. The Construction Contract Tracker refuses connections from Google Cloud. Not a 403, a connection failure. Award Amount and Contract Authorized Amount live only there, and growth is award-to-authorized. Without the tracker there are no real award amounts, and this project does not invent numbers. So the deployed demonstration runs on a fictional dataset that renders a SAMPLE DATA badge on every screen it backs. All six contractor names are invented. A real contractor name never appears beside an invented number, anywhere. The ingestion path prints a gate-style export request instead of guessing. Drop a CSV export at data/tracker_export.csv , run one script, and the same deployed code serves real figures with the badge gone. Choosing a badged fiction over a plausible fabrication was the right call and it cost the demo something real. A standard mid-flight. The interface sits on document.modelContext in the August 26, 2026 draft, and on navigator.modelContext in earlier builds and the community polyfill. The registration layer checks both and falls back to a clearly labelled local mirror, so the full lifecycle is still judgeable in a browser with no native support. Proving a negative. Claiming a tool does not exist is easy. Showing it is harder. The live capability map redraws from getTools() after every toolchange event, and a receipts log records registration, registration failures, evidence re

title: Understudy
pitch: Demonstrate a routine once. The agent turns your demonstration into a named, parameterised WebMCP tool and registers it into the live page. The user grows the tool surface, not the developer.
about_excerpt: Demonstrate a routine once. The agent turns your demonstration into a named, parameterised WebMCP tool and registers it into the live page. The user grows the tool surface, not the developer. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration My wife is a dentist. A part of her week has nothing to do with teeth. She works with the SEO people on the clinic's articles, going down a long list and tagging each one by what is trending, or sorting them into the right category. The tagging is easy. Knowing which topics are trending this month is not, and that knowledge is not in the tool she is clicking in. It is in a browser tab next to it. So she works in two windows. Search in one, tag in the other, back and forth, one row at a time. The switching costs more than the actual work does. Next month there is a new list and she does it all again. She cannot automate it. Not because the routine is complicated, she knows it better than anyone, but because automating anything means writing code, and that is not her job. So it stays manual forever. She asked me once why the computer could not just do it. I did not have a good answer. So there are three things here and none of them sit in the same place. A model already knows what is trending. The page already knows how to tag. And the routine itself is not written down anywhere, it is just in her head. I wanted to find out if the page could pick it up by watching her do it one time. What it does Understudy is a triage workspace for 1000 Hacker News stories. It has six WebMCP tools when it loads. It can have more by the time you are done with it, because you make them. You press Teach and do a routine by hand. Filter for "amazon", 14 items match, tag them "big-tech", set them to high priority, done. The page records that as four commands in its own vocabulary, not as clicks or screen positions. Then you tell the agent to turn it into a skill. It reads the recording and proposes a tool called triage_title_matches with three parameters: title_phrase, tag, and priority. You look at the schema and correct it. I wanted only the phrase to change between runs, so I unbound tag and priority with two clicks and approved it. Now the page calls registerTool and that tool exists, in a live session, about ninety seconds after it did not. The last step is the one worth watching. I asked for "every other big tech company". I never said which ones. The agent named Google, Apple, Meta and Microsoft on its own and ran my tool once per company. I taught it on 14 items. It handled 115 more, using knowledge the page has no way to hold. How I built it Plain ES modules. No build step, no framework, no dependencies. You can serve it with python3 -m http.server. Everything in the interface goes through one command bus. A click and an agent call both end up dispatching the same command, so there is exactly one code path to record and one to replay. There are two layers of WebMCP: A fixed set of six tools registered when the page loads: start_recording, stop_recording, get_recording, save_skill, list_skills, run_skill. Read only ones are marked with annotations.readOnlyHint. One real tool per approved skill, registered at runtime with document.modelContext.registerTool. Each one is held by an AbortController, so revoking a skill actually unregisters its tool rather than leaving a dead entry behind. The most important rule in the whole project is that the agent never writes the steps. save_skill takes a recording id and a list of bindings, saying which field of which step becomes which parameter. The page builds the JSON Schema from that. The steps are what I did, unchanged. A learned skill therefore cannot do anything I did not demonstrate. That is the safety story and the reliability story at the same time, and it comes from the structure rather than from a check. Challenges I ran into The biggest one took a day to understand. A tool registered in the middle of a turn is callable, but the first call fails. ChatGPT's browser works from a list of tools it captured when the turn started, and the new tool is not in it. The agent explained it better than I could: "The first immediate call failed because the existing tool snapshot was stale; after refreshing the registry within the same turn, the call succeeded." That recovery cost about fourteen seconds. I lost most of a day to it because I was certain the bug was mine. I rewrote the schema. Then the tool name. Then I added waits after registerTool, which did nothing, because waiting was never the problem. The tool was registered fine. The agent was just holding an older list. So learned skills go through run_skill, which is registered at page load and is always in the snapshot. A skill you just taught is callable right away. Two smaller ones. The toolchange event fires in Chrome 149 and later but does not exist in ChatGPT's browser, where modelContext is not an EventTarget, so nothing that depends on it can be relied on. And prompt, confirm and alert do nothing at all in the in-app browser. They fail silently, with no error, which is a miserable thing to debug. Every question the app needs to ask is asked inline in the page instead. I wrote a small probe page, spike.html, to answer these properly instead of guessing. It is in the repo. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The moment where the agent names four companies I never mentioned and runs a tool I taught it two minutes earlier. Neither side could do that alone. The page knows how to filter and tag but has no idea what a big tech company is. The agent knows the category but has no reliable way to drive an interface. I am also glad the human stays in charge of the schema. The agent proposes parameters, and you change them before the tool exists. It suggested three. I wanted one. What I learned Recording clicks does not work. Recording intent does. Because every command in the app acts on the current matching set rather than on specific item ids, a recording generalises for free. SET_FILTER {contains:"amazon"} has an obvious parameter in it. SELECT_ITEMS {ids:[3,7,12]} never will. That one decision is what makes learning from a single demonstration possible at all, and it also happens to be a better way to build bulk triage. I also learned to test against both clients early. Two of the three problems above would have been invisible in Chrome alone. What's next for Understudy Skills are stored per browser today. Being able to share one, or bring your own set to a page, is the obvious next thing. Recordings only capture set based commands, which is deliberate, but nested parameters and a way to chain one skill into another would cover more real routines. And there are three things I marked as open rather than claimed: whether AbortController revocation reaches the agent, whether readOnlyHint changes anything observable, and where the tool count ceiling is. Those need a longer test than a hackathon week allows.
