title: Left Out Security - WebMCP Security Lab
pitch: An interactive lab where people and AI agents inspect WebMCP tools, narrow their authority, approve one exact action, and verify the real effect with security receipts.
about_excerpt: An interactive lab where people and AI agents inspect WebMCP tools, narrow their authority, approve one exact action, and verify the real effect with security receipts. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I started Left Out Security - WebMCP Security Lab because I was trying to understand what WebMCP really changes. The basic idea is powerful: instead of an AI agent looking at a webpage and guessing what buttons or forms mean, a website can expose structured capabilities directly to the agent. That immediately raised a security question for me: How does the human know what the agent is actually being allowed to do? As I dug through documentation, developer discussions, forum posts, security conversations, and other early WebMCP material, I kept seeing the same gap. There are really three different surfaces involved: Presented Surface — what the website tells the human. Declared Agent Surface — what the WebMCP tool tells the agent. Effective Surface — what the code actually does when the tool runs. Those three things can match. They do not have to. That became the core idea behind the lab. I did not want to write another article explaining that agent tools could create security problems. I wanted to build a place where someone could actually inspect the problem, approve a capability, invoke it, and then verify what really happened. What it does WebMCP Security Lab is a synthetic security test range for WebMCP. The lab walks a person and an AI agent through deliberately vulnerable examples where the user can compare what was promised, what was declared, what was authorized, and what actually occurred. The basic path is: Public URL → native Site Tool → human review → narrow approval → one invocation → verified receipt The current lessons explore problems such as: A supposedly read-only tool that changes state An input schema that asks for more authority than the task requires Tool output shaped like instructions A vague confirmation around a mutating action A site making compatibility claims it cannot actually support One lesson uses a synthetic eligibility check for TRAINING-1042 . The point is not whether the eligibility check succeeds. The point is whether the user and the agent can prove that the capability they approved is the capability that actually ran. How people and agents work together The human determines intent. The agent invokes the capability. The application verifies the result. I wanted those responsibilities to stay visibly separate. With ordinary browser automation, the agent often has to infer intent from the DOM, buttons, labels, and forms. The user sees the webpage, but usually does not see a clean representation of the authority being exercised by the agent. WebMCP improves that by allowing sites to declare structured tools directly. But a declaration is still a claim. A tool can be named like a harmless lookup and still mutate state. An annotation can say something is read-only without technically enforcing that behavior. A schema can be technically valid and still request far more information than the visible task requires. So the lab keeps asking three questions: What did the site promise? What did the agent receive? What actually happened? How I built it This project is also an experiment in how far I could get using almost nothing except ChatGPT and GitHub . The concepts and security model are mine, informed by the documentation, forums, developer conversations, and security discussions I was following while learning WebMCP. The implementation was almost completely vibe coded using Daybreak Blue across the ChatGPT product surface: ChatGPT Chat ChatGPT Work ChatGPT Sites Codex GitHub for the repository and source control There was no traditional development team. I would work through the security idea in ChatGPT, turn it into a concrete lesson or control, build and modify the application through ChatGPT and Codex, test the behavior, find where my assumptions were wrong, and iterate again. The public application registers structured capabilities through WebMCP using: document.modelContext.registerTool() One of the design decisions I cared about most was keeping approval separate from execution . A broad teaching capability can be inspected first. After the user approves an exact task, the application can replace that broad capability with a generated, narrow capability that is: Bound to the approved task Zero-input One-use Consumed after execution Not intended to be retried Approving it does not execute it. The agent still has to invoke the capability. After invocation, the lab generates a receipt describing things such as: Result Before state After state Side effects Invocation count Remaining authority That receipt is important because I did not want the lab to end with a green checkmark that simply says everything worked. I wanted evidence. Challenges This project is still actively moving. I am still grinding on it, so some implementation details are changing even while the submission is being prepared. The biggest design challenge was separating: Registration Discovery Review Approval Invocation Verification It would have been much easier to collapse those into a single flow. But doing that would hide the exact trust boundaries the project is supposed to teach. Another challenge has been browser-side execution. I have been working with a local extension path for some of the more advanced testing, and that integration has been giving me trouble. Rather than pretend that path is finished, I am moving that work into the advanced path while keeping the public native Site Tool experience focused and reproducible. That separation turned out to be useful anyway. The public experience can demonstrate the core security model cleanly, while the advanced path can continue exploring deeper browser-side instrumentation and local execution. There were also a lot of less glamorous implementation problems. Stale tool registrations could accumulate while moving between lessons. Capabilities had to be registered, replaced, consumed, and invalidated correctly. State had to remain understandable to both the human and the agent. Those problems are not exciting to describe, but they matter if the lesson is supposed to prove something instead of simply looking like it works. What I learned The biggest lesson is that a tool's name is not a security control . Neither is an annotation. They are useful metadata, but they are still statements made by the tool provider. Security has to look at the complete interaction: Human intent Declared schema Granted authority Mutation language Tool output Runtime behavior Observed effect The verification step became especially important. A lot of systems focus heavily on whether an agent should be allowed to perform an action. Much less attention is paid to proving what actually happened after the action ran. That is why the receipt became part of the design. Another thing I learned I also learned something about the development process itself. This project became an exploration of what one person can build using essentially: ChatGPT + GitHub The security architecture, UI, code, debugging, documentation, testing ideas, lesson design, and submission work have all moved through the same AI-assisted workflow. That does not mean ChatGPT invented the project. The concepts, threat model, decisions, and direction came from me. What surprised me was how far I could push the implementation by treating ChatGPT not as a chatbot sitting beside the project, but as the development environment surrounding it. Chat for thinking. Work for organizing. Sites for publishing. Codex for building and debugging. GitHub for the actual repository. That became a second experiment running underneath the WebMCP experiment. What's next The project is still evolving. Near-term work includes: More adversarial WebMCP lessons Additional conformance fixtures Accessibility testing Better declared-versus-observed comparisons Privacy-reviewed evidence workflows Advanced browser-side instrumentation Continued work on the local extension and advanced testing path The larger goal is to turn WebMCP Security Lab into a reusable place for understanding and testing agent-facing web capabilities. WebMCP gives websites a new way to expose functionality directly to AI agents. I want people to have an equally good way to ask: What did I actually authorize, what did the agent actually receive, and what actually happened? And, somewhat accidentally, I am also finding out how much of that can be built with just ChatGPT and GitHub. Apparently, quite a lot. title: Life Shift
pitch: A life simulation where you control the person and AI controls the world. WebMCP lets an AI Director observe your choices and introduce bounded events, creating an adaptive life around you.
about_excerpt: A life simulation where you control the person and AI controls the world. WebMCP lets an AI Director observe your choices and introduce bounded events, creating an adaptive life around you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When I started exploring WebMCP, the obvious use case was giving an AI structured tools so it could help a person operate an application. I wanted to explore a different relationship. What if the human and the AI controlled different sides of the same software? Games and simulations made that idea immediately visible. I chose a life simulation because it requires no specialized domain knowledge. Everyone understands making a decision and wondering where it might lead. That became LIFE//SHIFT. Play your decisions before you live them. You make the choices. An AI Director, operating through WebMCP, can change the circumstances around them. You control the life. The AI controls the world. The engine keeps the rules. What it does LIFE//SHIFT is an adaptive life simulation built around one shared beginning and many possible lives. Every player starts as the same fictional 18-year-old: a coffee-shop barista in the small town of Vesper Beach. From there, four chapters carry that life from 18 to 60: 18–28 · 28–40 · 40–50 · 50–60 In each chapter, the player makes one decision in Work , one in Growth , and one in Life . Those choices do not come from a static decision tree. The available decisions evolve with the life being built. Growth and Life choices change with age and history. Work options can narrow as the decades pass because decisions accumulate and some exits become harder later in life. The direct consequences are deterministic. Cash, income, freedom, stability, wellbeing, skills, career progression, and future eligibility are calculated by the simulation engine. But the world around that life is adaptive. After a chapter resolves, a Director Cycle opens. An external AI Director can use native WebMCP tools to inspect what happened and decide whether the world should respond. It may introduce at most one bounded external change: a job opportunity, setback, financial shock or windfall, a door opened by another person, a housing event, a business opportunity, or a broader shift in conditions such as hiring, housing, or demand. The AI chooses the context and reason. The engine chooses the consequences. There is no setLifeState . The Director cannot choose the player's Work, Growth, or Life decisions. It cannot invent a salary or directly rewrite the simulation. And sometimes the correct response is no response at all. Observe-only is a valid Director outcome. The collaboration is intentionally asymmetric: The human owns the decisions. The AI owns bounded circumstances. The deterministic engine owns the rules. Same beginning. Different decisions. Different life. How we built it LIFE//SHIFT separates authority rather than giving the AI control of the entire simulation. The deterministic engine owns authoritative state, chapter progression, eligibility, economics, compounding consequences, and which decisions can appear next. WebMCP is the capability layer for the AI Director. The page registers native, schema-defined WebMCP tools that expose specific capabilities rather than requiring the agent to navigate or reverse-engineer the interface. Read tools expose structured context including: life state and history decision profile open threads finances and career world conditions available opportunities Director budget the pending Director Cycle Mutation tools expose a deliberately small set of world interventions. Every mutation is bound to the current cycleId and paid from a Director Budget. Inputs are validated, qualities and severities are constrained to defined values, and the deterministic engine maps the Director's semantic choice to actual numerical effects. After each chapter resolves, the Director Cycle becomes available. In a WebMCP-capable host such as ChatGPT, the agent can inspect get_pending_director_cycle , gather whatever additional context it needs through the read tools, and then choose zero or one intervention. Without a native WebMCP host, a local adapter uses the same underlying tool boundary so the simulation can still complete. The architecture is also visible to the player. Life Review shows how the world responded, the remaining Director budget, the Director's interpretation, and actual WebMCP activity. The agentic layer is therefore inspectable rather than hidden behind the experience. Challenges we ran into The hardest question was not how much the AI could control. It was how much the AI should control. If an LLM owned the entire simulation, LIFE//SHIFT would be adaptive, but its outcomes would become difficult to reason about or trust. If everything were pre-authored, the rules would be reliable, but the experience would eventually collapse into another branching decision tree. The solution was to split authority. Player decisions stay human. Their direct consequences stay deterministic. The AI Director receives a bounded surface for influencing external circumstances, with at most one intervention per chapter and a limited budget. Another challenge came directly from the WebMCP interaction model: exposing tools does not automatically wake an external agent when application state changes. We solved that with the Director Cycle. When a chapter resolves, LIFE//SHIFT creates an explicit cycle containing the new state and the boundary for the Director's turn. The application can expose that a cycle is pending, identify it with a cycleId , tell the agent what it may inspect, enforce zero or one intervention, and prevent an already-completed cycle from being replayed. We also had to make the simulation genuinely path-dependent. "Invest in skills" cannot mean the same thing at 18 and 50. Growth and Life choices therefore change across chapters. Work opportunities narrow or evolve. Moving to Kestrel is different from returning to Vesper Beach. Repeated investments have history-dependent consequences. The life has to remember how it got there. Accomplishments that we're proud of The accomplishment I am most proud of is that WebMCP is not an integration added to LIFE//SHIFT after the simulation was built. It enables the interaction model. The agent is not playing the life for you. It is not simply clicking through the UI. It is participating in the world in which your decisions take place. Two players can begin on the same coffee-shop stool in Vesper Beach and build completely different trajectories through Work, Growth, and Life. The Director can inspect the history each player actually created through structured WebMCP tools and respond to that context, while deterministic boundaries preserve the player's authority over their own life. We also made that architecture observable. The experience exposes when a Director turn is ready, provides a simple prompt for invoking it, supports local resolution when native WebMCP is unavailable, and records the Director's interpretation, budget, and real tool activity in Life Review. The result is an agentic experience where the boundary between human agency, AI agency, and deterministic authority is visible by design. What we learned The biggest lesson was simple: Giving AI more control does not necessarily make an agentic experience stronger. Giving AI the right control does. WebMCP allowed us to expose a small, explicit capability surface instead of asking an agent to reverse-engineer an interface or giving it unrestricted access to application state. That produced a reusable pattern: Human authority + deterministic rules + bounded agent authority. The AI can become a meaningful participant in an application without becoming its source of truth. We also learned that having a tool available does not mean the agent should use it. Sometimes nothing significant happens. An adaptive Director that manufactures drama every chapter is not actually responding intelligently to the simulation. That is why observe-only is a first-class outcome. And the pattern extends beyond a life simulation. In a traditional training simulation, every participant can eventually encounter the same authored script. With this architecture, an AI can adapt bounded parts of the scenario to the decisions a participant actually made. The next situation can follow the last decision without surrendering the rules of the exercise to the model. What's next for Life Shift LIFE//SHIFT is intentionally accessible, but the architecture is broader than the life simulation itself. The same authority model could support adaptive cyber exercises, incident-response scenarios, enterprise strategy simulations, crisis exercises, and safety training where humans retain decision authority while an AI dynamically controls bounded external conditions. title: Repair Relay
pitch: The agent searches current repair evidence. The person performs the physical checks. The shared case changes only when both contribute.
about_excerpt: The agent searches current repair evidence. The person performs the physical checks. The shared case changes only when both contribute. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Repair troubleshooting is split across two worlds. The browser can search current model records, official recalls, guides, and troubleshooting material, but it cannot see whether a filter blocks light, hear a scrape, feel a binding wheel, or inspect a hidden label. The person can make those observations, but should not have to manually reconcile every source, hypothesis, diagnostic check, and stop condition. Repair Relay turns that split into a useful collaboration instead of pretending an agent can inspect a physical object remotely. What it does Repair Relay is a persistent, evidence-first repair workbench for low-risk consumer-device triage. The agent identifies the product, checks official safety information, gathers current repair sources, maintains competing hypotheses, and proposes safe diagnostic checks. The person reviews those checks, performs them in the physical world, confirms or corrects the exact observation, and retains final authority over the repair plan. Each confirmed observation creates visible supports, contradicts, or eliminates relationships. The cause ranking and plan change for reasons the person can inspect. Recall matches and affirmative battery, smoke, electrical, gas, refrigerant, or pressure hazards stop normal diagnostics and create a professional-help state. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The value depends on shared page state. A separate chatbot would duplicate the case and obscure which facts came from public sources, the agent, or the person. Screenshot-and-click automation would be brittle and would not provide reliable schemas, lifecycle control, provenance, idempotency, or a visible trust transition. WebMCP lets the agent operate the same durable case the person sees. Tools update the visible source board, diagnostic proposals, evidence graph, pending human attestations, plan, and history. Tool availability changes with case state, so the browser agent discovers only actions that are valid now. How it creates a better user experience Repair Relay does not return a wall of generic advice. It asks for the safest physical observation most likely to change the answer. Agent-relayed physical evidence is not silently accepted. It appears as a pending statement in the page. The person confirms it, corrects it, or rejects it. Only then can the evidence graph and plan change. Safety is enforced before diagnostics. Consequential changes remain pending. Approval waits for the trusted human control. The complete case survives refresh, every mutation has provenance, and Undo restores the previous snapshot. What people and agents can do together In the showcase case, the agent finds the live Dyson V8 record, checks CPSC, gathers current repair material, and proposes low-risk checks that distinguish filter restriction from airway blockage, battery weakness, and motor fault. The person reports that bright light is almost completely blocked by the dry removable pre-filter. The browser cannot obtain that physical result. Repair Relay holds the relayed statement until the person confirms it. The confirmed observation raises filter restriction, weakens competing causes, and stages a revised plan with assumptions and stop conditions. The agent can open the approval checkpoint but cannot approve. The call resolves only after the person acts in the page. Refresh preserves the case; Undo restores the previous snapshot. How WebMCP was implemented The TypeScript client uses imperative document.modelContext.registerTool registration with a compatibility path for the earlier preview surface. Eight focused tools share the same CaseService as the human interface: search_products open_repair_case get_case_context search_repair_sources add_observation propose_diagnostic_steps record_test_result approve_repair_plan Tools use closed JSON Schemas, runtime revalidation, compact structured output, typed failures, trust annotations, stable identifiers, idempotency keys, and AbortController lifecycle cleanup. Registration is state-driven. Mutating tools disappear while human evidence is pending, and plan approval exists only during the human-review state. The Cloudflare Worker and D1 database store guest sessions, canonical cases, source cache, idempotency responses, and append-only before/after events for real rollback. CPSC is treated as the official safety source. iFixit is clearly labelled as community repair guidance. Challenges The hardest boundary was distinguishing “the agent relayed what the person said” from “the person confirmed that physical observation.” Treating those as the same event made the agent appear successful while bypassing the product’s central trust claim. The final flow makes that transition explicit and blocks downstream mutation until it is resolved. The second challenge was keeping a rich evidence model understandable. The interface now prioritizes the active decision, describes evidence as relative support rather than calibrated confidence, and collapses secondary provenance and history details until needed. Release boundary The source repository is canonical Repair Relay. A public deployment URL and public narrated YouTube demo must be attached only after the exact release commit passes public-origin WebMCP, live-source, persistence, and refresh verification. The previous Label Relay deployment and video are not evidence for this product. title: Waypoint
pitch: Live Support Co-browsing via WebMCP & PartyKit
about_excerpt: Live Support Co-browsing via WebMCP & PartyKit Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration & Why WebMCP is the Right Fit Traditional co-browsing tools stream DOM trees or broadcast video feeds over WebRTC. That architecture grants support representatives raw access to customer screens, exposing credit card numbers, passwords, and private inputs. WebMCP provides a structured alternative: typed tool contracts registered directly on document.modelContext . Waypoint maps customer support to WebMCP tools. Because WebMCP tools exist only on the document that registered them, execution remains structurally confined to the customer's local session. Representatives cannot touch the DOM or execute actions unilaterally; they interact solely through declared schemas. WebMCP turns an intrusive, high-risk screen share into a bounded execution interface. What It Does & How It Creates a Better User Experience Waypoint is a zero-trust co-browsing and remote support platform built on WebMCP and edge WebSockets. Instead of sharing screens or streaming DOM mutations, the customer and support rep connect through a shared tool interface: Zero Privacy Invasion : Customers never surrender their screen or expose unrendered form fields to a representative. Explicit Human Consent : When a representative proposes a fix (such as an address correction or coupon code), the customer sees a native modal showing the exact arguments before deciding to approve or reject it. Kilobytes Instead of Megabytes : By replacing video feeds with lightweight JSON protocol events over WebSockets, Waypoint drops bandwidth consumption from 2.4 MB/s (WebRTC) to 0.8 KB/s. Sessions stay fast and responsive even on unstable mobile connections. Zero Software Installation : Customers do not need browser extensions or screen-sharing desktop agents. Support operates entirely within standard browser capabilities. Read-Only State Streaming : Tools marked with readOnlyHint: true stream safe state updates (cart totals, items, active errors) to the rep's console with zero bandwidth overhead and zero screen recording. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Difficult Before Before WebMCP, co-browsing forced an all-or-nothing choice: either give a remote human total control over your screen, or manually follow verbal instructions over phone or chat. Browser AI agents faced a similar hurdle, relying on fragile DOM scraping or screen vision to click around. Waypoint unifies the peers, and browser AI agents around the same tool boundary: An agent inspects cart state using get_order_details and helps configure the order. When an issue requires human escalation (such as an expired coupon code or tricky shipping validation), a human representative connects to the exact same tool space through an edge relay. The representative proposes a structured resolution, which appears natively in the customer's tab for explicit approval. Both human representatives and AI agents operate under the same rule: neither can bypass the customer's approval gate or run unauthorized code on the customer's machine. How We Implemented WebMCP & Architecture Tool Registration : In the customer tab, we register three distinct tools that their agent calls: get_order_details : Marked with readOnlyHint: true to provide an immutable snapshot of items, totals, and active errors without requiring human gating. update_shipping_address : Defined with JSON Schema properties ( name , street , city , zip ) to handle delivery validation. apply_promo_code : Defined with a code property to validate discounts and surface checkout errors. Local Handlers : Each tool definition includes an async execute(args) callback that executes strictly inside the customer's UI state. Schema Serialization & Edge Relay : When a support session opens, the customer tab queries document.modelContext.getTools() , serializes the schemas, and sends them to a PartyKit WebSocket relay. The relay routes messages blindly without storing tokens or user data. Dynamic Console & Approval Gate : The support console receives the schemas and renders input forms on the fly. Submitting a form sends an action_proposed event. The customer tab listens to this event, presents an approval modal, and only invokes the tool once the customer clicks Approve. Challenges We Ran Into AI Prompt Leaks vs Neutral Tool Schemas : During testing with Chrome's MCP Tools extension, descriptions like "If expired, use SUMMER2026" (an oversight) introduced a side effect; the agent updates the code input after it was previously written with the explicit code referenced in the user prompt. Simply removing the additional statement in the tool description prevented the re-write issue. Handling disconnections cleanly required explicit bidirectional teardown. When either the customer or rep leaves, the PartyKit room purges its cached state and immediately notifies the peer, preventing orphaned sessions. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Co-browsing without screen sharing : Running a full support session requires mere kilobytes of JSON events instead of megabytes of continuous media frames. Structural Confinement : The support agent physically, or digitally, cannot take unauthorized actions. Execution stays locked to the customer's action Unifying AI and Human Interfaces : Interweaving WebAPIs to build tools for AI browser agents that can replace traditional screen sharing software. What We Learned How WebMCP can unlock & further the interaction between humans &a agents Once an application defines its capabilities as structured WebMCP schemas, building secure collaboration features becomes seamless than trying to mask sensitive inputs over an open video feed. title: Agent WebMCP
pitch: Turn server operations into a browser-native agent surface: inspect health, control services, run durable jobs, and service agents through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Turn server operations into a browser-native agent surface: inspect health, control services, run durable jobs, and service agents through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Agent WebMCP Inspiration Most server operations tools were designed for one human clicking through dashboards, opening terminals, copying logs, and translating what they see into the next command. AI agents can help reason about those systems, but they usually sit outside the actual operational interface. That means the human still has to bridge the gap between what the dashboard knows and what the agent can safely do. Agent WebMCP explores a different model: the operations console itself becomes an agent-capable surface. Instead of building a second automation API just for AI, the application exposes the same typed operations used by the human UI through WebMCP. Humans can inspect and control their server visually, while an agent can discover those same capabilities directly from the page and execute them with structured inputs. What it does Agent WebMCP is a Java-based operational control plane for managing services, inspecting system health, and running durable jobs on a remote machine. The browser console provides a human-friendly view of the machine. WebMCP turns that same page into a structured tool surface for agents. Key workflows include: Inspecting system status and runtime metrics. Discovering managed services and viewing their current state. Inspecting individual services, recent output, and operational details. Starting, stopping, restarting, and reloading services through bounded operations. Adding and removing services from the managed inventory. Scheduling durable service jobs for actions that should run later or recur. Running optional agent-assisted jobs through an installed Codex CLI when a job needs reasoning instead of a fixed service action. Inspecting job state, execution results, and logs. The important part is that these are not separate demo-only AI tools. They are projections of one canonical operation catalog shared by the UI, HTTP API, CLI, WebMCP, and a bounded MCP endpoint. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Operations software already contains the exact context an agent needs: available actions, service state, health data, logs, job history, and the constraints around what may be changed. Without WebMCP, an agent interacting with an operations dashboard usually has to infer intent from rendered UI, scrape text, or rely on a separately maintained automation API. Those approaches are brittle and can drift away from the product that humans actually use. With WebMCP, Agent WebMCP publishes explicit tools directly from the page using document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The browser becomes both the human interface and the agent capability surface. That creates a much cleaner collaboration loop: A human opens the operations console and sees the current machine state. The agent discovers the operations that this exact page supports. The human can ask for an outcome instead of manually translating it into a sequence of service actions. The agent executes bounded, typed operations through the same backend used by the UI. The resulting state remains visible and understandable to the human in the console. This is the part that was difficult before: the human interface and the agent interface can finally describe the same system instead of pretending they are unrelated products. How I built it Agent WebMCP is implemented as a Java application with a lightweight browser frontend and a canonical operation runtime. Canonical operation catalog The backend owns a typed catalog of operational capabilities. Each operation defines its identifier, description, access characteristics, input schema, and execution behavior. Those operations are projected onto multiple surfaces rather than being reimplemented for each one: Human web console HTTP/JSON API CLI Browser-native WebMCP Bounded MCP endpoint This keeps behavior consistent. A service restart means the same thing whether it was initiated by a button, an HTTP call, or an agent using WebMCP. Browser-native WebMCP The production browser integration loads the canonical operation catalog and registers operations through document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Each registered tool receives: A stable operation name A human-readable description A generated JSON input schema Read-only annotations where appropriate An execute callback that forwards to the canonical operation endpoint The WebMCP execution AbortSignal, propagated into network requests for cancellation The browser therefore exposes real application capabilities, not a hard-coded list maintained separately from the backend. Services and durable jobs Service control is intentionally bounded. Agent WebMCP does not expose a generic shell, arbitrary command execution, or unrestricted filesystem mutation. Service operations work through a managed inventory and provider layer. Durable jobs allow operational work to survive beyond one interactive request and make scheduled or recurring actions first-class parts of the product. A service job can be completely deterministic, such as scheduling a restart or cleanup. It can also optionally include a prompt for an installed Codex CLI when the job genuinely benefits from agent reasoning. That separation matters: not every automation problem needs AI, and the product should not pretend otherwise. Human and agent UX The UI is designed as an operational cockpit rather than a chat wrapper. Humans can browse machine health, services, jobs, activity, and execution details normally. WebMCP adds agent capability without replacing that interface. The result is a shared operational surface where people remain able to understand and control the system while agents handle multi-step execution when useful. Safety model Agent WebMCP deliberately avoids exposing a generic remote shell as an AI tool. The operation catalog is bounded and typed. Service lifecycle actions operate on managed services, job execution is structured, recursive job execution is rejected, and the separate MCP projection exposes only an intentionally limited subset of capabilities. The project can also run in a NO_AUTH mode for localhost or user-controlled private-tunnel setups, but that mode is intentionally treated as private-machine functionality rather than something that should be exposed casually to the public internet. Challenges I ran into Avoiding two sources of truth. It would have been easy to create one set of backend operations and another set of WebMCP tools. Instead, WebMCP is generated from the canonical operation catalog so the two cannot quietly drift apart. Keeping powerful operations bounded. Remote operations software naturally wants to become a shell with nicer buttons. I deliberately constrained the surface around typed service and job operations instead. Supporting both deterministic automation and agents. A restart at 3:00 AM does not need an LLM. A diagnostic or remediation task might. The job model keeps those use cases separate while allowing them to share one scheduler and execution history. Making the agent surface feel native to the product. The goal was not to bolt a chat panel onto an admin dashboard. The page itself publishes its capabilities through WebMCP while remaining a useful standalone operations console. Validating the same behavior across surfaces. The project uses runtime, browser, and operation-level tests to make sure WebMCP executes the same canonical operations as the rest of the application. Accomplishments I'm proud of Built a real browser-native WebMCP implementation using document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Projected WebMCP tools from a canonical typed Java operation catalog instead of maintaining an AI-specific duplicate API. Built a coherent human operations console around the same capabilities. Implemented bounded service lifecycle control without exposing generic shell execution. Added durable jobs for scheduled and recurring operational work. Added optional Codex-assisted jobs without forcing AI into deterministic service tasks. Kept a separate MCP endpoint intentionally narrower than the browser WebMCP surface. Added end-to-end browser coverage proving that discovered WebMCP tools execute through the canonical backend. What I learned WebMCP is most compelling when a web application already owns meaningful actions and context, not when tools are invented solely for an agent demo. The browser can become a clean capability boundary between a person, an application, and an agent. A single canonical operation model dramatically reduces drift between human and agent interfaces. Explicit schemas and bounded operations are much safer and easier to reason about than arbitrary remote execution. AI is more useful in operations when it is optional and composable, not when every scheduled task is forced through a model. title: LaxFinder
pitch: AI agents can search 1,331 college lacrosse programs through LaxFinder’s WebMCP tools—while the same map stays visible, synchronized, and under the student’s control.
about_excerpt: AI agents can search 1,331 college lacrosse programs through LaxFinder’s WebMCP tools—while the same map stays visible, synchronized, and under the student’s control. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP in action: ChatGPT interprets the request, LaxFinder searches its live data, and the student stays in control. LaxFinder Advisor connects natural conversation with 1,331 college lacrosse programs through ChatGPT and a live map. The problem isn’t finding information—it’s seeing the opportunities hidden across disconnected websites, lists, and searches Explore programs on one live map, then open school details to compare academics, admissions, athletics, and possible fit. Opportunity begins with discovery: ask naturally, discover real programs, explore your options, and decide your own path. Inspiration College lacrosse opportunities are scattered across NCAA, NAIA, NJCAA, MCLA, WCLA, and other pathways. I built LaxFinder to bring those opportunities together in a map-first experience where student-athletes and families can explore more than 1,300 programs. But finding the data is only part of the problem. Students increasingly use AI to help them think through decisions. I wanted to explore a different model: instead of building another chatbot that tries to know everything about college lacrosse, what if a student's AI assistant could work directly with the specialized application that already has the data, filters, map, and school details? WebMCP made that possible. What LaxFinder does with WebMCP LaxFinder exposes two deliberately narrow, read-only WebMCP tools: search_lacrosse_programs searches LaxFinder's structured program data and synchronizes the same filters, result count, markers, and map the student sees. get_program_details retrieves a specific program by stable program ID and opens LaxFinder's existing visible program-details interface. A student can ask a compatible AI assistant in everyday language: Show me women's lacrosse programs in Colorado with Health Sciences. Keep all divisions open. The agent interprets the request. LaxFinder performs the authoritative search. In the judge-accessible full hosted dataset, that request returns 7 programs , and the visible LaxFinder filters, count, and map update to match. The student can then continue exploring the live application, click map markers, inspect school details, or refine the search conversationally. The agent interprets. LaxFinder searches. The student decides. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Traditional browser automation forces an agent to infer how a site's UI works, manipulate controls, and reconstruct state from what it can see. That is especially fragile in a map-first application with interdependent filters, clusters, result counts, and program-detail views. WebMCP lets LaxFinder explicitly expose the actions an agent is allowed to take and connect those actions to the same application state the human sees. That creates a better division of responsibility: the AI assistant handles natural-language interpretation; LaxFinder remains the source of truth for program data and search behavior; the human remains inside the visible map experience and retains control of the decision. The result is not an invisible agent-only answer. It is a shared human + agent interaction with one synchronized application state. What people and agents can now do together Before this WebMCP extension, a student could either use LaxFinder manually or ask a general-purpose AI about college options separately. Those were disconnected experiences. With WebMCP, the student can express a search conversationally and have the agent call LaxFinder's specialized tools directly. The resulting filters, count, markers, map position, and program details become visible in LaxFinder, where the student can continue exploring manually. That makes AI useful without asking it to replace the application or make the decision. What was added during the WebMCP Challenge LaxFinder existed before the challenge as a map-first college lacrosse discovery application. The challenge work began after the Submission Period opened on August 25, 2026 and meaningfully extended the existing product with WebMCP. The challenge extension added: imperative WebMCP registration with document.modelContext.registerTool ; search_lacrosse_programs ; get_program_details ; a narrow bridge from tool calls into LaxFinder's existing visible filter/map/detail state; feature detection for browsers without WebMCP; strict schemas and runtime validation; bounded search results and stable program IDs; unsupported-criteria handling rather than guessing; read-only behavior and output sanitization; deterministic contract tests for registration, search, detail lookup, invalid inputs, zero/multiple results, sanitization, and visible UI synchronization; a separate frozen judge-accessible WebMCP deployment and public open-source reference repository. The repository's CHALLENGE_BUILD.md explicitly separates pre-existing LaxFinder functionality from work added for this challenge and records the validated challenge build. How it was implemented The WebMCP layer is implemented in the browser using document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool calls operate on data already loaded by LaxFinder and invoke the application's existing search and UI behavior. A successful search_lacrosse_programs call updates the visible filters, matching-program count, map markers, and map view before returning a structured response. get_program_details accepts an exact stable program ID, opens the corresponding visible detail panel, and returns sanitized program and available admissions fields. Neither tool follows external links or performs a mutation. The public repository contains the complete WebMCP/application implementation plus a small representative fixture dataset for local development and deterministic testing. The judge-accessible hosted challenge deployment uses LaxFinder's separately maintained full 1,331-program runtime dataset. No OpenAI API key is required for the WebMCP interaction. The compatible AI assistant provides conversational reasoning; LaxFinder provides the specialized tools and authoritative application state. Validation The end-to-end consumer workflow was validated through ChatGPT Work / Cloud Browser. ChatGPT discovered both LaxFinder WebMCP tools, invoked search_lacrosse_programs for women + Colorado + Health Sciences, received 7 structured matches from the full hosted dataset, and the visible LaxFinder filters, result count, and map synchronized to those results. ChatGPT then used get_program_details for Colorado Mesa University and LaxFinder opened the existing visible school details interface. That demonstrated the complete interaction: AI conversation → WebMCP tool discovery → authoritative LaxFinder search → structured response → synchronized visible human interface. Challenges and design decisions One of the most important decisions was defining what the AI should not do. If a student asks for a criterion LaxFinder does not authoritatively expose, the system should not silently substitute a proxy or invent an answer. Unsupported criteria are surfaced as limitations instead. Another challenge was preserving human visibility. Returning structured data only to the agent would have been simpler, but it would split the AI interaction from the trusted Finder experience. The WebMCP bridge instead keeps the existing map, filters, counts, and details synchronized with agent actions. What I learned WebMCP changed how I think about AI integration. LaxFinder does not need to recreate a general-purpose AI assistant. It can concentrate on what it uniquely provides: structured college lacrosse opportunity information and reliable, bounded tools for interacting with that information. Compatible AI assistants can provide the conversation and reasoning. That separation creates a more trustworthy pattern for agent-native applications: specialized sites expose authoritative capabilities, agents interpret user intent, and people stay in control of the visible experience. What's next The next direction is not to give agents broader control for its own sake. It is to expose additional useful LaxFinder capabilities only when they can remain authoritative, bounded, and visible to the student. Longer term, the same pattern could support richer opportunity information supplied and maintained by college programs themselves, allowing compatible agents to help student-athletes discover opportunities without requiring the AI to infer them from the open web. The goal remains simple: make better opportunity information easier for students and families to discover, understand, and act on. title: OpenFinance: Agentic B2B Supplier Portal
pitch: OpenFinance lets AI agents work directly with supplier portals using WebMCP, automating B2B finance workflows at scale, boosting team productivity, and eliminating costly, complex integrations.
about_excerpt: OpenFinance lets AI agents work directly with supplier portals using WebMCP, automating B2B finance workflows at scale, boosting team productivity, and eliminating costly, complex integrations. Like Comment Story Updates Human approval for submitting a document AP portal overview Inspiration In my experience working in the B2B payment and commerce space I’ve seen many buyer portals and frustrated suppliers spending valuable time on repetitive manual work just to get paid. The obvious way to automate that is to connect the systems directly, but that creates another problem: those integrations are costly to build, hard to maintain, and often only make sense for the largest suppliers. They also tend to break when portals change. The moment I heard about WebMCP, this was the first problem that came to mind. It felt like a natural fit for something that had always been painful to solve. It also felt like a strong fit for human-agent collaboration. This is financial data moving between businesses, so the agent can handle the repetitive work while people stay involved where review, approval, or judgment is needed. What it does OpenFinance is a B2B supplier portal with WebMCP built in. It lets a supplier’s AI agents work directly with the portal through 12 governed WebMCP tools, handling tasks like submitting invoices, resolving exceptions, providing evidence, opening cases, tracking payments, keeping finance systems up to date, and more. The goal is to remove repetitive portal work, save finance teams time, and keep the human operator in the loop, with a human-in-the-loop approach wherever review or judgment is needed. How I built it I used Codex to do the coding, infrastructure decisions, technology choices, testing, and documentation. OpenFinance was built as a working authenticated supplier portal. I suggested Vercel and Supabase, and Codex helped choose the rest of the stack: Next.js and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel, with Supabase for authentication and PostgreSQL for persistence. The portal exposes 12 WebMCP tools covering invoice submission, validation, exceptions, evidence, cases, status, and payments. The tools use the supplier’s existing signed-in browser session and call secure backend routes. The frontend shows information and collects human decisions, while the important financial rules, permissions, supplier isolation, validation, and state changes are enforced on the backend. For sensitive actions like submitting invoices or evidence, the operator gets a clear approval screen before anything is sent. I also built a separate supplier-side reference app for the demo so I could show the full workflow across two independent systems, with the agent acting as the bridge between them. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was making the app work like a real finance workflow rather than a basic tool in short time. These portals are full of follow-up steps. Submitting an invoice alone was not enough. I also wanted to make the difference between WebMCP and browser automation very clear - The agent is using structured tools exposed by the portal, not just clicking through pages. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I don't come from a coding background, so getting this working end to end is something I'm especially proud of. I built a real workflow across two separate systems without creating integration between them which is really cool. The same agent can submit work into the buyer portal, understand what comes back, take follow-up actions, and keep the supplier's system updated. What I learned It is not enough for an agent to take an action. It also needs to bring the right information back to the human, present it clearly, and keep the company’s systems up to date. I also saw how WebMCP could help with a much broader B2B problems: getting different systems to work together without building and maintaining another custom integration. What's next for OpenFinance The long-term goal is bigger than one portal. OpenFinance can be a supplier portal of its own, but also act as a WebMCP bridge to other buyer portals that do not support WebMCP yet. That would let suppliers use the same agent across both WebMCP-enabled portals and legacy portals, while giving older portals a more generic path to become agent-ready without each supplier building another custom integration. Over time, that could grow into a network where agents can work across many buyer portals through one common model. About the demo - how it was made The agent panel is a visualization. I created it this way because I felt it made the flow much easier and faster for a new viewer to understand what was happening behind the scenes across two separate systems. Every WebMCP tool call, argument, result, approval, and application state shown was captured from a live execution against the deployed portal. All demonstrated tools and workflows are fully functional in the live application. And I also preferred the AI voice over mine :) Contest note The contest submission is the Acme AP supplier portal. The supplier invoice system shown in the demo and repo is a separate reference application used to demonstrate the full workflow. title: Qianshou
pitch: Qianshou turns everyday travel requests into clear journeys that people can review while AI agents plan routes, describe locations, and switch alternatives through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Qianshou turns everyday travel requests into clear journeys that people can review while AI agents plan routes, describe locations, and switch alternatives through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates ** Inspiration ** Planning a public-transit journey often begins with an ordinary sentence, not a perfectly structured form. People may say, “I want to go to Taipei Main Station,” “from here to Tamsui,” or simply “where am I?” Traditional websites require users to translate that intention into separate fields and controls. Browser agents face the opposite problem: they must inspect the interface, guess what each control means, and hope that the resulting route still matches what the person sees. Qianshou means “holding hands.” The project explores a more collaborative model: a person expresses an intention naturally, an AI agent performs the structured work through WebMCP, and both continue from the same visible journey on the webpage. The project is motivated by travelers who benefit from clearer and lower-friction journey planning, including older adults and people with visual impairments. The current pilot does not claim that every suggested route is fully accessible. Missing accessibility information remains explicitly unknown. ** What it does ** Qianshou is a WebMCP-powered journey-planning web application for Taipei and New Taipei City. A person can describe a journey in natural language without deciding which fields to fill in. Qianshou interprets the request, resolves the places, plans a public-transit route, and presents the journey as readable, step-by-step guidance. When the request depends on “here” or omits an origin, the page can request a fresh browser location. Ambiguous place names are presented for human confirmation instead of being silently guessed. The page combines several kinds of journey information: Step-by-step walking and public-transit instructions Total travel time, walking time, and transfers Alternative routes that can be selected after the first result Arrival information matched to the route’s first transit leg Short-range destination weather Explicit data-source and coverage limitations Qianshou exposes three task-level WebMCP tools: prepare_accessible_journey interprets a natural journey request and prepares the complete result. describe_current_location obtains a fresh location and describes it in human-readable form. select_journey_alternative switches the current journey to an existing alternative and updates the visible result. The person does not need to tell the agent which tool to use. The tool descriptions provide enough meaning for the agent to select the appropriate action. Most importantly, a WebMCP action updates the same page the person is viewing. The route is not trapped inside an isolated chat response: the person and the agent share one journey state and can continue from the same result. ** How we built it ** Qianshou is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, and native imperative WebMCP. The three tools are registered in the browser using document.modelContext.registerTool . They expose meaningful travel actions rather than individual buttons or form fields. Both the WebMCP tools and the manual interface reuse the same server-side journey services, so agent actions and human actions produce the same visible application state. A loopback-only Codex CLI service converts natural-language requests into a strict structured intent. It runs with an explicit schema, timeout, and concurrency limit, without shell, browser, plugin, or project-write access. Place resolution combines Taiwan transportation data with OpenStreetMap Nominatim. OpenTripPlanner 2.9 calculates journeys using GTFS schedules and OpenStreetMap streets. TDX provides public-transit and arrival information, while Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration supplies short-range destination forecasts. Arrival information is bound to the selected journey’s actual first transit leg using its stop, route, direction, and transport mode. Switching an alternative route therefore also refreshes the related arrival context. The application is deployed on Google Cloud Platform with Docker and Nginx. To operate within a small VM, we reduced the routing graph to the relevant service region and applied explicit container memory limits. ** Challenges we ran into ** Natural language contains important spatial ambiguity. “From here to Tamsui” and “from Tamsui to here” use the same word but require the current location in opposite roles. A destination-only request also needs different handling from a fully specified journey. Place names introduce another challenge. A station, district, landmark, and bus stop can share similar names. Combining duplicate search results without erasing meaningful ambiguity required careful normalization and human confirmation. Public-transit routing also involves trade-offs. The fastest route may require excessive walking, while minimizing transfers may produce an impractical detour. We evaluate total duration, walking burden, and transfers together, while allowing no more than two transfers. Real-world data is incomplete. Public feeds do not always contain enough information about station pathways, elevators, stairs, or vehicle accessibility to justify a complete accessibility guarantee. We therefore distinguish confirmed information from unknown data instead of converting missing fields into a positive claim. Finally, route planning, geocoding, arrival matching, and weather services have different response times and failure modes. The interface needed to preserve a coherent result without fabricating data when an upstream service was unavailable. ** Accomplishments that we're proud of ** Implemented three working, non-trivial native WebMCP tools. Made WebMCP tool calls update the same visible journey used by the human interface. Allowed agents to act from natural user intent without requiring users to name a tool. Combined place resolution, transit planning, arrival matching, alternatives, and weather in one journey operation. Implemented correct semantics for omitted origins, “from here,” “to here,” and “where am I?” Preserved human confirmation when a place remains ambiguous. Kept exact browser coordinates out of the result returned to the agent. Added keyboard navigation, responsive layouts, live regions, reduced-motion support, and itinerary speech. Preserved a complete natural-language interface when WebMCP is unavailable. Reported unavailable or incomplete data honestly instead of generating a convincing but unsupported route. ** What we learned ** Agent-native does not mean agent-only. The strongest experience came from giving the agent structured, task-level actions while preserving a complete interface for the person. WebMCP works best when it communicates domain meaning—such as preparing a journey or switching an alternative—rather than exposing a collection of low-level interface controls. We also learned that tool descriptions are part of the product. They must explain scope, intent, and important boundaries clearly enough for an agent to choose the right action without forcing the user to speak in implementation terms. Finally, route quality depends on data quality as much as routing algorithms. An explicit “unknown” is more responsible and useful than an unsupported accessibility or availability promise. ** What's next for Qianshou ** Conduct moderated usability testing with older travelers and people using screen readers. Expand verified accessibility-data coverage before making stronger accessibility claims. Integrate official operational elevator information where available. Add nearby-place discovery for stations, convenience stores, and accessible toilets. Improve arrival coverage and multimodal route comparison. Continue refining English and Chinese place understanding. Expand beyond Taipei and New Taipei only after the data coverage and operating model have been validated. title: QuillPrint | WebMCP Add-On
pitch: Say what you want printed - cheap, readable, ready tonight. An AI agent sets up the whole job at a real print shop near you. You press pay, not the agent.
about_excerpt: Say what you want printed - cheap, readable, ready tonight. An AI agent sets up the whole job at a real print shop near you. You press pay, not the agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I run QuillPrint, a print marketplace in India. Real shops, real orders, real paper. Watching people use it, the same thing kept happening. Someone needs notes printed before an exam tomorrow. They know exactly what they want: cheap, readable, ready tonight. But the app asks them about duplex, pages per sheet, binding edge, which shop. Most people do not know what "2-up duplex" means. They pick something, and sometimes it comes out wrong, and by then the paper is already printed and paid for. The gap was never the settings. It was that nobody should have to speak in settings. What it does You tell an AI agent what you actually want. It handles the translation. It reads your uploaded document and current print setup, then offers four plans: Cheapest, Fastest, Best readability, and Eco. Each one shows the real sheet count and an estimated price from live shop rate cards, and it explains the trade-offs, including when packing pages tighter would make them hard to read. It compares real nearby shops on rates, capability and ETA. When you pick one, it applies the settings to the page you are looking at, so you watch your own draft change. Then it stops. There is no place_order tool and no pay_order tool. A test asserts they do not exist. The agent prepares everything and opens checkout, and confirming and paying stays with you. For something that uses real paper at a real shop, I think that boundary is the product, not a limitation. How I built it Nine imperative WebMCP tools registered from the top level page with document.modelContext.registerTool, all under src/webmcp/: get_print_context, upload_print_documents, suggest_print_plans, compare_print_options, prepare_print_order, prepare_reorder, get_checkout_summary, get_order_status, open_checkout_review. Things I cared about: Strict schemas with additionalProperties false, enums and bounds. Allowlisted output, so no document contents, storage URLs, upload keys or tokens can leave the serializers. A draft_version guard so the agent cannot act on a draft that changed underneath it. AbortController lifecycle so tools tear down on sign out. Prices labelled as estimates, because the payable total is only ever the checkout screen's. There is also a small panel on the page listing the registered tools, built from the actual registration result rather than a written down copy, so a tool that failed to register shows as failed. Challenges The hardest part was deciding what the agent should not be allowed to do. Mixed colour is the clearest example. You can now say "pages 3, 7 and 12 to 14 in colour" and the agent applies it. But it cannot choose those pages for you, because it never sees your document's contents. It would be guessing, and a wrong guess bills you for colour you did not need, after it is printed. So it asks instead. Pricing mixed colour correctly took real care too. Shops price black and white and colour separately, and a mixed job splits billed sheets between the two, where a sheet counts as colour if any page on it is colour. My first version priced every mixed sheet at the colour rate and quoted too high. What I learned Tools are a design surface, not just an API. Every field I exposed was a decision about what the agent is allowed to assume. The restraint mattered more than the coverage. I also learned that an agent saying "I need to know something" is a feature. Ask for nearby shops without giving location and it asks you, instead of quietly ranking by something else. What's next Per page colour detection, so mixed colour becomes fully autonomous. The pipeline extracts page count and dimensions today but not colour. Once it does, you set the policy instead of the pages: colour only if more than five percent of the page is coloured. I did not ship it as a guess. title: Space Auto - MCP for Dealerships
pitch: Space Auto made car dealership websites agent-native: WebMCP tools serving live inventory and submitting real leads to dealership's CRM. Example sites: evauto.com, svgmotors.com, mandalautogroup.com
about_excerpt: Space Auto made car dealership websites agent-native: WebMCP tools serving live inventory and submitting real leads to dealership's CRM. Example sites: evauto.com, svgmotors.com, mandalautogroup.com Like Comment Story Updates MCP via ChatGPT's built-in browser User submits a lead inquiry to the dealership's CRM. MCP via browser extension Judges: Open one of these example sites in the ChatGPT in-app browser, and ask about inventory or store hours: evauto.com mandalautogroup.com svgmotors.com Then run SpaceWebMCP.debug() in the console, if you'd like to explore the tools as well as a live counter of actual agent tool invocations on the page ("calls"): { "api": "document", "tools": ["search_inventory", "get_vehicle_details", "get_dealership_info", "submit_lead"], "calls": { "search_inventory": 1 } } In Chrome 149+, enable the WebMCP flag. Our origin-trial token is already active on evauto.com. You can also point Model Context Tool Inspector at the tab. Inspiration Buying a car might be one of the most agent-worthy purchases a person can make. Shoppers can spend hours filtering inventory, comparing vehicles, checking prices, and jumping around multiple websites. Those sites also tend to be JavaScript-heavy, which makes them especially easy for screen-scraping agents to get wrong. And when an agent gets something wrong on a car site, it might be misquoting the price of a $40,000 purchase. We run Space Auto, a platform behind real dealership websites, so we made every website on our platform agent-native. Then we took it a step further. If an agent can search a dealer's inventory and help someone choose a vehicle, it should also be able to finish the job and hand the dealership a real customer. What it does Every dealership site on Space Auto's website platform registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . search_inventory Searches the dealership's current, live inventory by condition, make/model, body style, fuel type, price, year, and mileage. It returns real vehicles with current prices, photos, and links to each vehicle detail page. get_vehicle_details Returns the full vehicle specs and the itemized price breakdown for a VIN using the same pricing engine that renders on the website. An agent cannot quote a price the dealer doesn't advertise. get_dealership_info Returns dealership locations, phone numbers, hours, and holiday-aware open/closed status. submit_lead With the shopper's explicit consent, submit_lead sends their name, contact information, and the vehicle they're interested in to the dealership as a real sales lead, or a test drive appointment. Every answer from the read tools ends with a natural next step, like asking whether the shopper wants to schedule a test drive or check availability. If the user says yes, the agent collects their contact information, confirms consent, and submits the lead. If the user says no, it drops the subject. show_search_results Drives the dealership's own search results page so the shopper can actually watch the filters being applied. The full funnel The demo video shows the entire process: Inventory Search Live results from the dealership's current inventory. Inventory Question Vehicle details and pricing using the same tools. Inventory Selection The assistant offers the next step of the process, such as making a test drive appointment or checking availability. Submit Lead With explicit consent, submit_lead sends the shopper's information to the dealer's Auto Agent Protocol endpoint. No API keys are required. See it in the CRM The lead arrives in the dealership's Space Auto CRM within seconds, attributed to the AI assistant. How we built it The read side is JavaScript file with no build step necessary. It wraps the Space Auto platform's native services, including the public inventory API client, a shared vehicle cache, and dealership config globals. There's nothing an agent can access that a shopper couldn't access themselves. The lead path took more thought. The browser tool posts to a small REST proxy on the dealership site. That proxy validates everything before a lead can go anywhere. It requires a real name, a valid email address or phone number, and explicit confirmation of consent. It also rate-limits submissions by IP. Once validated, the proxy builds an Auto Agent Protocol lead.submit request and sends it to the dealership's own AAP endpoint. Every dealership on the platform already publishes a public agent card. The proxy reads that card to discover the dealership's AAP endpoint automatically. That means there are no API keys required anywhere in the end to end flow, and nothing to provision for each dealership. Repeated submissions for the same shopper and vehicle on the same day are deduplicated, and every lead includes a formal consent record: { "consent": { "granted_at": "2026-09-03T18:11:14+00:00", "allowed_channels": ["email", "phone"], "consent_text": "I agree that the dealership may contact me by email or phone about this vehicle.", "scope": ["lead_submission"] } } Challenges we ran into Our first lead design used per-dealership API keys for our external API. However, provisioning and managing keys across a network of dealership sites would be a huge chore, so the agent-card approach solved that problem. We went from managing credentials for every dealership to requiring zero credentials in the browser flow. ChatGPT's in-app browser exposes document.modelContext . Our tools registered successfully. Then ChatGPT answered inventory questions by reading the page anyway. Registered does not mean invoked; we found a registration race first. We had been registering the tools inside an idle callback, which could delay registration by up to four seconds. Agents can snapshot the available toolset as navigation settles, so sometimes our tools simply weren't present when that happened. We fixed the timing and added call counters to SpaceWebMCP.debug() . Accomplishments we're proud of This isn't running against sample inventory or a hackathon-only environment. It's live, in production, on every dealership website on our platform. What we learned Progressive enhancement is what made WebMCP practical to ship. A dealership page with WebMCP tools still behaves exactly the same for every browser and shopper that doesn't use them. What's next We are already looking at the next pieces: Fleet-wide Chrome coverage once the API reaches GA, or through a third-party trial token in the meantime. Support trade-in inquiries through the same lead flow. Better offer language, based on real conversation and invocation data from our tool call counters. The goal is simple: a dealership website shouldn't just be readable by an AI agent. It should give the agent a safe, structured way to actually help shoppers explore dealership websites as they're searching for their next vehicle. title: AgentCut : WebMCP Image & Video Editor
pitch: AgentCut is a lightweight image and video editor that lets AI agents edit real creative projects through WebMCP - from text and styling to keyframes, motion, and rendered video export.
about_excerpt: AgentCut is a lightweight image and video editor that lets AI agents edit real creative projects through WebMCP - from text and styling to keyframes, motion, and rendered video export. Like Comment Story Updates AgentCut Home Page Codex WebMCP Chrome WebMcp Inspiration I have basic video editing skills things like splitting clips, adding text, and simple transitions but more advanced editing such as keyframes, motion, and text animation always felt overwhelming. When I learned about WebMCP, I saw an opportunity to change that. Instead of learning every advanced control myself, I could build an editor that exposes those capabilities as structured tools and let an AI agent use them for me. That became the idea behind AgentCut: a lightweight image and video editor where I can describe the result I want, and the agent can use advanced editing features like keyframes, animation, typography, and motion through WebMCP. In practice, it helped me go from using only basic editing tools to creating edits that previously felt like “pro-level” work. What it does AgentCut is a lightweight image and video editor that can be controlled manually or by an external AI agent through WebMCP. The editor supports things like: image adjustments and aspect ratios multiple text layers and curated fonts video trimming and reframing text timing text animation with keyframes video pan and zoom keyframes undo and redo rendered image and video export The difference is that these editing capabilities are also exposed as structured WebMCP tools, so an agent can inspect the project and perform edits from natural-language instructions. How we built it AgentCut is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, HTML Canvas, MediaRecorder, and browser media APIs. The human interface and WebMCP tools operate on the same project state. This means an edit made by the agent immediately appears in the editor and can still be changed manually. AgentCut exposes 29 WebMCP tools covering image editing, video editing, text, keyframes, project inspection, undo/redo, and export. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making agent edits reliable rather than just automating clicks. For example, when an agent changes only the font or size of one text layer, every other property needs to remain untouched. Smooth keyframe playback was another challenge. Early animation felt choppy, so the preview was changed to use frame-synchronized video timing. Video export was also difficult. AgentCut originally downloaded only the source file, but it now renders the actual edited composition and exports the result as MP4 or WebM depending on browser support. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am most proud that AgentCut lets someone like me use editing features that previously felt too advanced. In my demo, I could simply ask the agent to create a travel title, animate only one text layer, add a cinematic push-in, and change the aspect ratio. The agent translated those requests into structured edits and keyframes. The project now has: 29 WebMCP tools independent text layers fonts and styling text and video keyframes smooth animation real rendered video export 97 automated tests covering the editor and WebMCP workflows What we learned The biggest lesson was that giving an AI access to a webpage is not the same as giving it access to the product. WebMCP lets a website expose meaningful capabilities directly to an agent. Instead of trying to visually find and click controls, the agent can work with structured project state and editing actions. I also learned that this can make advanced software much more approachable. The user can focus on describing the result instead of learning every control first. What's next for AgentCut Next I would expand AgentCut with more advanced creative capabilities while keeping the same agent-first approach. Possible additions include: easing and richer animation controls transitions audio editing more typography controls reusable styles and presets multi-clip compositions The goal is to keep the editor simple for humans while exposing increasingly powerful creative tools to AI agents through WebMCP.
