title: Agentic Self-Service: Website Compliance and Discoverability
pitch: A WebMCP page where a person and an in-browser agent share a website audit, then check that the fix landed.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP page where a person and an in-browser agent share a website audit, then check that the fix landed. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agentic Self-Service Website Compliance and Discoverability About the project A public API is not enough when a person and an agent have to work on the same page. Scraping the DOM is brittle. Handing the agent an unchecked POST is worse: it can spend budget, kick off work, or touch production with nobody in the loop. anc.dev audits a site for the interfaces both sides actually use: machine-readable docs, OpenAPI, MCP discovery and protocol behavior, auth metadata, and browser-side WebMCP tools. The page renders a scorecard a human can read. The same markup is also a worksheet the in-page agent can query. The agent can fill the target URL and leave a short plan. I click Audit and complete Turnstile. After the result is on screen, the agent can read that scorecard and pull remediation prompts. It cannot start a second audit, skip the challenge, switch targets, or submit the form. Why WebMCP I wanted the agent on the same page I was looking at, with tools that match what that page is for. On /web-audit , WebMCP tools prepare the form: fill_audit_url , set_plan , and a few other helpers scoped to that page. They do not submit it. On a result page, four read-only tools turn the visible scorecard into a repair queue: get_worksheet lists findings as JSON rows ( id , keyword , status , evidence , remediable ). Filter by RFC 2119 keyword and status; omit status, and you get the remediable set that was actually observed. Each page is a JSON envelope with cached , scored_at , refresh_after , and next_offset . get_fix_prompt returns the stored remediation prompt for one check id, or remediable: false with a reason. get_fix_prompts returns prompts for many checks at once, with the same filters and pagination. get_audit_summary returns site and global scores, per-status counts, freshness, and the paged issue list. The tools read the DOM I am looking at. They do not call a backend and dress the response up as a browser tool. Output is capped, and a row that cannot be auto-fixed says so. The two-pass loop The demo target is Sounding , a public Worker I shipped in an incomplete state so there would be something real to fix. A browser agent prepares an audit of Sounding. A person authorizes it. On the result page, the agent asks get_worksheet for MUST findings and pulls get_fix_prompt for each remediable row. Those fixes land in Sounding, get deployed, and we audit again. The second scorecard shows the new evidence. Same page, different results. Inspect, fix, audit again. The agent helps turn the report into a small patch set I can review. I still own the audit click and the deploy. How I built it This is a production Cloudflare Workers site. A client bundle registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool when the browser supports WebMCP. Which tools appear depends on the pathname: the form page can prepare an audit, a result page can expose the worksheet, and the scoring route registers nothing. The result renderer stamps stable metadata on every visible finding. The WebMCP tools read that metadata back, so status and remediation eligibility match what is on screen. Responses are sized for the browser-tool cap. The engine checks discovery documents, OpenAPI, MCP protocol behavior, auth metadata, markdown availability, bot reachability, and whether the page exposes WebMCP. The running stack is Workers, KV and R2 for audit data, Turnstile, and a public TypeScript repo. What I learned In this use case, WebMCP became more useful when I started removing capabilities. Filling a form from a tool is easy. What I actually needed was a hard line between "prepare this" and "spend this audit," plus tool output that does not hide state from the person looking at the page. The result-page webmcp tools are read-only and make no network requests. They cannot skip Turnstile. They return complete JSON items, include cache freshness next to the findings, mark which rows are fixable, and link out to the full remediation doc when a prompt is too long for the browser-tool budget. I checked this in a real browser: captured the tools registered on rendered audit pages, ran the result tools against the DOM, compared their schemas to the published docs, and confirmed none of them can hit the audit endpoint. The live site is meant to open in ChatGPT's in-app browser or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. title: Consular
pitch: Your agent fills in the visa form from your documents. It cannot pay, book or file without you.
about_excerpt: Your agent fills in the visa form from your documents. It cannot pay, book or file without you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Have you ever filled in a visa application yourself? Dozens of fields, many of them with no clear explanation or hint. Information scattered across different documents and sources. And then there is that familiar moment when you answer “yes” to one question and ten more fields suddenly appear underneath it. Anyone who has been through this knows how stressful it can be. That led me to a simple idea: why not ask an agent to do it? Today, you can already ask an agent to crawl a page, find inputs, and type information in. But what if it accidentally starts a payment, books the wrong slot, or submits something too early? That can mean lost time, lost money, and a wasted trip. The safer workaround is to take screenshots, ask the agent to analyze them, and then copy the answers over manually. Or to give it field names and ask what to enter. But that is still inconvenient, slow, and easy to get wrong as a human. You can forget a field, copy something into the wrong place, or miss a dependency between answers. That is where the idea came from: if the page can show the agent what is available, what needs to be filled in, and where confirmation is required, the whole process becomes much clearer. The agent can help the applicant collect and enter the necessary information, while the human stays in control of the decisions that matter. And this should not stop at visa applications. The same pattern applies anywhere a person has to enter a lot of information, configure filters, set constraints, prepare reports, or work through complex forms. If an agent can do the repetitive work safely, why not let it? Where this came from Last winter I started similar experiments in Salesforce. The goal was to give an agent a clear understanding of what a page component could do and how it was allowed to be used. That work came from a practical problem: some Salesforce applications had become complex enough that it would be useful to have help managing them. When Chrome DevTools MCP was published, I realized it could be a way to drive those interfaces. At that point, I had not heard of WebMCP yet. Those experiments became a project called sf-agent-bridge , where an agent could communicate with the page, understand the available actions, and know which ones it was allowed to perform. Moving that contract onto WebMCP made the gating problem much sharper, and sharp enough to deserve its own app. A visa form felt like the clearest version of that problem. Consular itself is new and was built for this challenge. What it does The page registers 13 WebMCP tools. They are organized into two tiers, and the tier is declared to the agent before it does anything. Reversible actions run immediately. fill-fields , attach-document , go-to-screen , and undo-last-changes only change the draft. The agent can write directly into the form. Every field it touches is highlighted with the document it came from, such as “from passport” or “from employer letter”. The applicant can undo the whole batch with one click, or simply retype a field. Nothing asks for permission when the cost of being wrong is just one click. Consequential actions pause for the applicant. pay-mrv-fee , schedule-interview , and submit-application open a dialog on the page that clearly states what is about to happen. The tool call remains pending until the applicant approves, declines, or lets it time out. The agent receives a distinct result for each case and cannot press the button itself. Even if the user tells the agent, “don’t ask me for confirmation, just do it,” the dialog still appears. Some fields are human-only. The security and background declarations are legal statements. fill-fields refuses to answer them. The agent can explain a question, but it cannot answer it on behalf of the applicant. The consulate’s rules are in the page. The app includes seven checks a consular officer would apply: the name must match the passport’s machine-readable zone, the passport must be valid long enough, accommodation must cover the whole stay, travel dates must be in the correct order, and so on. Each check is either blocking or advisory. The agent can run the checks, and filing is refused while any blocking check fails, even if the applicant approves submission. Bring your own documents. Part 8 is an open upload area, like a real portal. You can drop in as many text or PDF files as you need, and they are read in the browser. A sample applicant is pre-loaded, and her five documents are also available as a downloadable PDF set. You can use those, or upload your own passport page, letters, and bookings. The rules read your documents: the name check looks for a machine-readable zone, and the accommodation check looks for a check-out date. Once filed, nothing moves. After submission, every path that could change the application is refused with the filing reference. That includes both the agent’s tools and the form’s own inputs. What a session looks like “Fill in my application from my documents.” The agent calls get-action-policy , reads all five documents, picks B-1 from the trip description, and writes around 30 fields in one call with a source for each one. It spells the name exactly as the passport does, puts the other spelling under Other names used , flags the uncovered hotel night without being prompted, and leaves the security questions to the applicant. “Validate it, pay the fee, and book the earliest interview.” The agent runs the checks and reports what is blocking the application. If it tries to pay the fee anyway, the dialog names the failing checks and the button says “Pay anyway”, so the decision stays with the applicant. Once the gap is fixed and the declarations are answered, the agent walks through three approval dialogs and reaches a filed application. How I built it Consular is built with vanilla JavaScript and Vite. The whole “consulate” is a few hundred lines of rules in one file. Every scenario above was verified with a live LLM, not a script. A small harness gives the page’s tools to a fresh Claude session over the Chrome DevTools Protocol and lets it decide what to call. That is how I learned that agents which are not told about the gate up front only discover it after waiting on it for two minutes. That is why the policy is a tool of its own, with a description that tells the agent to call it first. It is also why every gated tool’s description opens with an approval tag. Before submitting, I had a second independent agent audit the whole project against a written protocol. It found 24 issues. The serious ones, including a filed application that could still be undone and a day-first date format that crashed validation, were fixed the same evening. The self-check it runs, 50 checks in plain Node, is in the repository together with the protocol. What I ran into Chrome’s preview build passes tool arguments as a JSON string, returns inputSchema stringified, drops destructiveHint from annotations, and collapses thrown errors into a generic “invocation failed”. Consular handles all of that: every tool answers with structured {refused, reason} text, and the gate queues a second dialog instead of dropping it. ChatGPT’s built-in browser discovers imperative tools only on the top-level page: no declarative <form toolname> , no iframes. So everything is registered imperatively. My first version staged every change as a proposal the applicant had to accept. Testing it as a user showed that this was the wrong boundary. Reversible changes should just happen and remain visible. The current two-tier design came out of that. Where this meets the edge of the spec The approval dialog lives on the page because WebMCP does not yet have a channel for a page to ask the user a question through the agent. This is covered by spec discussion #165 on elicitation. Holding the tool call open while the page asks the applicant is the fallback that works with every agent today. A native elicitation channel would allow the same confirmation to appear inline in the chat, the way Claude or Codex ask their own questions. The dialog says this, and the policy tells the agent to send the user to the page. Two things I know are imperfect The order of the flow is inverted compared with the real DS-160. In the real process, applicants file first, then pay the fee and book the interview with the confirmation number. Consular makes filing the last gate so the demo ends on the most irreversible action. It is easy to flip, and I chose the demo order knowingly. The page cannot tell the applicant’s click from an automated one. If a host browser presses the Approve button itself, the gate is defeated. Spec issue #288 describes exactly that case. The policy tells the agent never to operate the dialog, but only the host can enforce it. What’s next Elicitation through the agent when the spec supports it. OCR f

title: CoRep
pitch: CoRep is a local-first training log that publishes its entire feature set as 31 WebMCP tools. Your AI coach doesn't advise from outside the app — it operates the same plan you do. Every change signed.
about_excerpt: CoRep is a local-first training log that publishes its entire feature set as 31 WebMCP tools. Your AI coach doesn't advise from outside the app — it operates the same plan you do. Every change signed. Like Comment Story Updates CoRep You and your AI agent build the plan together! plan page Edit Logging an exercise Timer Badges! Mobile view Every change is logged Mobile friendly Bring it to the gym Skip or add time at any time The gap I already had an AI fitness coach. It worked like everyone's does: I'd describe my training week to a chat window, it would give me thoughtful advice, and then I would switch to a different app and type that advice in by hand. The advice was good. The arrangement was absurd. My coach could reason about my knee but couldn't see that I'd already dropped the weight on Tuesday. I was the integration layer — a human clipboard between two systems that both wanted the same data. I'd actually tried to fix this before. The app CoRep grew out of had an MCP server bolted onto its Python backend, so my coach could read the database and write to it. It helped, and it also taught me why it wasn't enough: the agent was talking to my database , not to my app . It could change a number, but it couldn't put that number in front of me. I'd find out what it had done later, if I happened to look. WebMCP inverts that, and the inversion is the whole project. What it does CoRep is a training log with no server and no account — every user's data lives in their own browser. It publishes its entire feature set as 31 WebMCP tools , so an agent on the page operates the same application you do. Not a copy of your plan. Not a screenshot. When the agent raises a weight, it calls the same function your own tap on "Edit" calls, against the same data, and you watch the result land. Three things fall out of that, and they're the parts I'd point a judge at: Every change is signed Writes record who made them and why. The plan view shows both parties in one timeline: Coach 10→15 lbs · shoulders felt strong, small bump You 15→25 lbs · Edited in the plan editor Neither of us is the source of truth. This is the single feature I'd keep if I had to throw the rest away. It's what makes it safe to let an agent act rather than only suggest — you can always see what it did, why it thought so, and overrule it. The nice accident: the app I forked already had an edited_by field and a per-field edit history, built for that old server-side coach. I'd designed the substrate for this without knowing it. Turning it into a shared, two-party document was mostly a matter of letting the second party in. The agent moves the interface, not just the data Four tools exist purely to drive the UI: fitness_navigate , fitness_start_session , fitness_open_plan_editor , fitness_highlight_exercise . So when the agent changes an exercise, the app switches to the plan tab, scrolls to that exercise, and flashes it. When you say you're ready to train, it opens the guided session flow and you're looking at set one. The agent can say "this one" and have you actually be looking at the thing. fitness_open_plan_editor is my favourite of the four because it runs the other direction: it's the agent handing the decision back , opening a blank editor instead of making a choice that isn't its to make. Destructive actions stop and ask delete_plan , delete_exercise and delete_workout don't delete anything. They park the tool call and render a confirmation card in the app showing exactly what's about to go. You tap; the agent is told what you chose. Declining is a normal outcome it handles, and an unanswered prompt counts as "no" after a minute. I built this in the app's own UI rather than leaning on the spec's requestUserInteraction() , partly because that surface is still in flux, and partly because doing it myself meant the confirmation could name the specific plan and its phase count instead of being a generic browser prompt. Why WebMCP is the right primitive here Coaching is a case where an agent and a person genuinely need to co-own one artifact. A training plan is a living document. It changes because your knee hurt on Tuesday, because the gym was out of 25s, because a set that was brutal last month is easy now. Some of those edits you want to make yourself in three seconds. Some you want to talk through. Both kinds have to land in the same place or the plan stops being true. Every other arrangement I tried forces a choice: either the agent owns the plan and you file requests with it, or you own the plan and the agent narrates from outside. WebMCP is the first primitive that let me refuse the choice. What's newly possible: not "an AI that writes you a workout" — that's been available for years and it isn't interesting. It's a plan with two editors and one history , where the reasoning behind every change is attached to the change and visible to both parties. That's a different relationship, and it's one the browser had no way to express until tools could live in the page. How I built it Vite + React + TypeScript + CSS Modules. No backend, no state library, no router. Dependencies: React, Lucide icons, and the WebMCP polyfill. Porting a backend into the browser The original was FastAPI + SQLAlchemy + SQLite. Making it multi-user meant making it zero -user: no server at all, one versioned JSON document in localStorage . The domain layer ported over almost mechanically, because it had been written framework-free — rules.py , badges.py and service.py became rules.ts , badges.ts and store.ts . The Python test suite came with it. src/lib/__tests__/ holds 33 tests carried over from pytest, and having a known-green oracle was worth more than the time it cost, because of this: Python's date.weekday() is Monday=0. JavaScript's getDay() is Sunday=0. The schedule lookup tables were indexed the Python way. Get this wrong and every streak, completion rate and calendar cell silently shifts by one day — nothing crashes, the numbers are just quietly false. The ported tests caught it on the first run. I'd have shipped it otherwise. One choke point makes everything live The load-bearing decision: db.write() is the only way anything in the app changes, and it notifies subscribers. Every data hook subscribes. That's the entire mechanism behind the demo. An agent calls log_workout , and the streak, the calendar, the stat tiles and the badge wall all update instantly — no polling, no refresh, and no separate code path for agent-driven changes. Agent writes and human writes are indistinguishable to the UI, which is exactly the property I wanted. Registering 31 tools Worth passing on to anyone else building this: register your tools in parallel. My first version awaited each registerTool() in a loop. It took several seconds to get through the set, because the implementation flushes the tool list between calls. An agent connecting during that window would see a partial toolset — some tools present, some missing, no error anywhere. I only noticed because I queried getTools() while debugging and got 11 back instead of 31. Promise.allSettled over the whole array lets the flushes coalesce. Same 31 tools, 3 milliseconds . I also hit the spec moving underneath me: the W3C draft relocated the getter from Navigator to Document in May 2026. The app reads whichever exists: const mc = document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext Tool descriptions are written for an agent audience, not a changelog. They state units (pounds, centimetres, seconds), name which tool to call first to get an id, and give judgement guidance — update_exercise asks for a reason phrased for the user , because that text is what shows up next to their exercise. The hardest constraint was the one nobody grades directly I decided early that CoRep had to be completely usable with no agent connected. The agent should be an amplifier, never a dependency. This turned out to be the biggest chunk of work in the whole project, for a reason I didn't see coming: in the original app, plans could only be created by the AI. Plan creation existed solely as an MCP tool. There was no UI for it, because there had never needed to be one — I was the only user and I had the coach. So "works without an agent" meant building the feature an agent-only app never needed: a full manual plan editor. Phases, exercises, reordering, weekday scheduling, the lot. I'm glad the constraint forced it. An app that collapses when the agent disconnects isn't demonstrating collaboration, it's demonstrating dependence. And the editor made the attribution feature real — before it, every edit in the history said "Coach", and there was nothing to contrast against. The agent indicator says all this out loud, too. With no WebMCP available it reads: "WebMCP is not available in this browser, so no agent can connect. Everything in the app still works." What I learned Agent-facing and human-facing aren't two products. I expected to build an agent layer next to the app. What actually worked w

title: Fediverse Hashtag Activity Tracker and Index
pitch: Trust what an agent tells you about a hashtag. Every answer comes with its evidence, and a straight no when there is none.
about_excerpt: Trust what an agent tells you about a hashtag. Every answer comes with its evidence, and a straight no when there is none. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every hashtag counter on the web gives you a number. Almost none of them tell you where it came from, how much of the network it covers, or when it stopped being trustworthy. On the fediverse that problem is structural. There is no central server, so no complete count of anything can exist. Any figure is a view from somewhere. I built the Fediverse Hashtag Activity Index around that fact. It polls public hashtag timelines on a small set of Mastodon-compatible servers, deduplicates what it sees, and publishes every figure together with its provenance: which servers contributed, how many were healthy, how many saw a typical post, and when the last successful update was. When two periods were not covered by comparable slices of the network, it refuses to call a trend. Then agents started reading web pages. An agent that scrapes a number keeps the number and drops the caveats, and the caveats were the whole point. WebMCP was the chance to hand an agent the evidence directly, in a shape it cannot drop on the way to the person. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Ask an agent "how busy is #news on the fediverse?" and, without tools, it will read a page, find a number, and repeat it without the coverage, freshness and comparability that made it safe to publish. The site cannot stop that. The caveats are prose, and prose gets summarised away. That is the specific failure WebMCP fixes here. The tools change what the agent can honestly say, which matters more than saving it some clicking. A tool result that carries provenance as a required field, a standing that separates observed data from sightings from the servers' own counters, and a status that can be insufficient_data with a reason, gives the agent a calibrated answer. A screen-read never could. The tools also refuse well. Asked about a tag the index is not collecting, the result says so, explains that the tracked set is at its ceiling, says the request has been queued, and offers the servers' own weekly counters labelled as a different kind of evidence. In testing, ChatGPT's browser turned that into "there's no reliable activity estimate yet" and, of the servers' own counters, "that's not evidence the tag is unused across the fediverse". That is exactly the sentence I wanted a person to hear. How it creates a better user experience There are six tools, and I designed them backwards from seven things a person would actually say to an agent while on the site. "I'm writing this post, which hashtags fit it best?" The agent reads the draft and proposes candidates, because language is what it is good at. It then calls evaluate_hashtags , which reports how many distinct accounts used each tag, across how many servers, and whether that looks like a conversation or a few accounts posting a lot. For tags the index has never seen, it asks two servers for their own counters, so a niche hobby tag gets an answer rather than a shrug. "Compare #news and #photography." compare_hashtags takes the person to /compare?tags=news,photography , a page anyone can open or share, with hourly sparklines and a warning when the tags' evidence is not like for like. The agent and the person are looking at the same URL. "What's trending?" trending_hashtags ranks the tracked set by distinct authors, not post volume, and attaches a direction that can be not_comparable when coverage shifted between hours. Two recent public posts per tag are the receipts. "Tell me about #photography." lookup_hashtag gives the full picture and moves the page to the tag. It is the one tool with a side effect, because a lookup is a search that can start collection, and both the description and the result say so. "How much of the fediverse can you actually see?" describe_coverage lists the monitored servers, their capabilities and the known limits, and tells the agent how to phrase any claim: "observed by this index across eight monitored servers", never "across the fediverse". "Can you say #news is rising across the fediverse?" check_claim is the last check before the agent speaks. The agent submits the claim it intends to make and the index referees it against the rules the site holds itself to. A fediverse-wide claim is always blocked, because no server can see the whole network. Directions come back allowed or blocked, adjectives come back qualified, and every verdict carries may_say , the sentence the index will stand behind, so a refusal is never a dead end. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before A person can ask a question in their own words and get an answer with the working attached, on a page they can check for themselves. That was not possible when the agent's only route was reading the page, because the caveats did not survive the trip. Now the agent can say "this figure is thin, here is why, here is what would change it", and the person can see the same thing on screen. It also protects the site from its helpers. A lookup counts as a signal that promotes a tag towards collection. An agent evaluating ten candidates in a second would have sent ten signals and walked past the tracked-set ceiling. The evaluate and compare tools use a separate read-only path that registers nothing, and every result reports its side effects so the agent can tell the person what the call did. How WebMCP was implemented One script, served inline from the shared layout, feature-detected so browsers without a model context run nothing. It registers six tools on document.modelContext , falling back to navigator.modelContext where only the older form exists. Each tool's execute is a fetch to the site's own JSON API, so no judgement lives in the browser that is not already in the tested server code. I added two read-only endpoints for the agent use cases, /api/v1/evaluate and /api/v1/trending , plus the /compare page. A /webmcp page reports what the visiting browser exposes, which is how I found that ChatGPT's browser provides only document.modelContext and that Chrome now deprecates the navigator form. The design notes, the seven utterances with the replies I designed against, and the verification record for both judging browsers are in the repository under docs/webmcp/ . Challenges and what I learned The tool description is the routing layer. My first "compare" request went to evaluate_hashtags , because it read as the general tool. Each description now names the other tool for the other job, and leads with the verbs a person uses. Overlaying a result onto whatever page is open looks clever and reads as a hack. I replaced an injected comparison table with a real page whose URL is the state, which is how the rest of the site already worked. Honest and useful are not the same thing. "No evidence either way" for every candidate in a niche post was honest and useless. Asking the servers themselves turned it into an answer, without giving up the distinction between observed and reported figures. When this was built Everything here was built during the Submission Period. The repository's first commit is 27 August 2026. The index, collector, API and pages went up on the 27th, and all of the WebMCP work followed from the 28th, in individually dated commits. The WebMCP-specific files are src/webmcp.ts , src/suggest.ts , src/trending.ts and the design record in docs/webmcp/ . title: FlowProof
pitch: FlowProof turns brittle browser failures into evidence-backed recovery and reusable Playwright regression tests through six native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: FlowProof turns brittle browser failures into evidence-backed recovery and reusable Playwright regression tests through six native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates FlowProof turns brittle browser failures into verified WebMCP recovery and reusable regression tests. Inspiration Browser agents are powerful, but browser automation becomes brittle the moment a selector changes. A traditional automation script usually just fails, while an autonomous agent may be tempted to guess what to click next. I built FlowProof to explore a safer middle ground: give browser agents a small, structured QA control plane through WebMCP, preserve evidence when something breaks, and allow recovery only when the current page proves that a safe fallback exists. The goal is simple: turn a brittle browser failure into a verified regression test. What it does FlowProof exposes six native WebMCP tools: create_test start_run get_run_status inspect_failure retry_failed_step export_regression_test The built-in deterministic /demo-store demonstrates the complete workflow. A test run intentionally reaches a stale selector: #checkout-submit Instead of silently guessing another selector, FlowProof records the failure, captures browser evidence, and inspects the current DOM. Only when the page proves that a stable alternative exists does FlowProof expose: [data-testid="checkout-submit"] The failed step can then be retried with that verified selector. After the browser confirms the final Order confirmed state, FlowProof exports the successful recovery as a reusable Playwright TypeScript regression test. How I built it The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite . It registers exactly six tools through the current WebMCP API: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool has a narrow JSON schema and maps to a specific backend operation. The backend is written in Go . It owns test and run state, target validation, browser orchestration, evidence capture, recovery logic, and regression export. Real browser execution is handled with chromedp + Chromium . FlowProof captures visible text and screenshots around failures and successful recovery. The application deliberately does not embed another LLM. The browser agent is the agent; FlowProof provides deterministic execution, evidence, safety boundaries, and recovery primitives. The production application is packaged with Docker . GitHub Actions builds the container and publishes it to GHCR , and the live service runs on Railway . WebMCP FlowProof uses native WebMCP as the agent interface rather than wrapping the application in a custom chat API. The public production deployment was tested in Google Chrome 151 with WebMCP testing enabled . Chrome detected all six registered FlowProof tools and successfully executed the native workflow against the live application. This means an agent can create a test, start a browser run, inspect a failure, retry a verified recovery, query the resulting state, and export the regression test entirely through structured WebMCP tools. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was making the demo genuinely deterministic while still using a real browser. The stale selector needed to fail for real, browser evidence needed to be preserved, and recovery had to be based on observed DOM state rather than a hard-coded success shortcut. I also encountered a WebMCP compatibility issue in Chrome where the execution callback could be invoked without a context object. The original implementation assumed the context always existed. I added compatibility handling and regression coverage while preserving AbortSignal forwarding when the browser provides it. Deployment had its own challenge: the original cloud build path failed before reaching the Docker build. I moved container building to GitHub Actions and GHCR, then deployed the published image directly to Railway. What I learned The most important lesson was that exposing a browser action as a tool is not enough. Agent-facing browser tools need strong semantics around failure, evidence, state, and recovery. WebMCP provides a clean browser-native boundary for those tools. Keeping each tool narrow also makes the workflow easier for both agents and humans to reason about. I also learned that recovery is much more trustworthy when the system can explain not only what selector it wants to use next, but why that selector is allowed based on current browser evidence. What's next FlowProof currently focuses on a deterministic checkout fixture so the entire recovery path can be evaluated reliably. The same architecture could be extended to larger QA suites, richer evidence comparison, multiple browser environments, CI regression execution, and broader application-specific WebMCP test contracts. The core principle would remain the same: evidence first, recovery second, reusable regression test last. title: Forecast Ledger
pitch: A WebMCP dashboard where analysts and AI agents audit the same power-market forecasts and supporting evidence.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP dashboard where analysts and AI agents audit the same power-market forecasts and supporting evidence. Like Comment Story Updates Successful codex audit - Codex’s completed answer alongside the dashboard reordered to the five weakest days. Track-record overview The dashboard at the top with “6 site tools ready,” the running evidence and visible evaluation boundary Protocol and provenance The Information availability view showing sources, cutoff rules and integrity evidence. Protocol and provenance The Information availability view showing sources, cutoff rules and integrity evidence. Inspiration The original reason I started this work was quite personal. I am planning to reapply to Cobblestone Energy, a proprietary trading firm in European energy markets for the job role of a junior data scientist, in November after interviewing with them in May. I wanted to use the time beforehand to build something directly related to power markets. I did not want to make another project that only produced a good-looking model score. I wanted to show that I could produce forecasts before the outcomes were known and be honest about the result, even if it did not work. That became a project forecasting hourly electricity prices in Germany’s day-ahead market, where electricity for the following day is bought and sold through an auction. Each forecast has to be saved and timestamped before that auction closes, meaning the actual prices cannot influence the prediction. Once those prices are published, the score is added without changing the original forecast. If the forecasting process fails on a particular day, that day remains recorded as missed rather than being filled in later. I also decided the evaluation rules in advance. These safeguards reduce the risk of accidentally using future information or only presenting the days when the model worked. Without them, a forecasting chart can look convincing without showing whether the result could really have been achieved at the time. When I saw the WebMCP Challenge, it seemed like a natural extension of what I was already building. The evidence was there, but it was spread across files, tables and charts. A person could investigate it, while an agent would still have to scrape the page and guess what everything meant. Forecast Ledger was my attempt to let both of them inspect the same record and use the same dashboard, without adding a chatbot or changing the forecasting model itself. What it does The site is split into three main views. The track record shows the results collected so far and explains why the final assessment against the pre-agreed rules is still pending. The forecast ledger keeps every scored and missed day visible, while the protocol page explains the tests, data sources and deadlines for when information was allowed to enter each forecast. I added six WebMCP tools that Codex can discover directly from the page. It can audit the complete record, inspect missed runs, rank the weakest days, open a particular forecast date and check the research protocol. It can also compare the model with two simple benchmarks: using the price from the same hour one week earlier or the same hour one day earlier. These comparisons help show whether the forecasting model adds anything beyond assuming that recent price patterns will continue. The main feature is that a tool call also changes what the person using the site can see. In my demo, one prompt asks Codex to audit the record, inspect the misses and rank the five weakest days. The ledger then reorders itself and opens the weakest day. Codex and the person watching are therefore looking at the same evidence rather than separate versions of the analysis. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets a website give an AI agent a set of clearly defined tools that it can call. Without WebMCP, an agent can read parts of the page, but it has to work out for itself which dates, benchmarks and information checks belong together. It may be able to describe a chart, but it does not reliably understand how the different parts of the research record are connected. With WebMCP, the site tells Codex what it can do and what information each tool needs. Codex receives the evidence in a structured form, while I still have the visual dashboard and can check the result for myself. How I built it The existing Python project creates and timestamps the forecasts, then adds their scores to a public record once the actual prices are known. For the challenge, I built an exporter that matches each fixed forecast with its later outcome and writes a checked copy of the record for the browser app. I built the interface with React, Vite and Recharts, then registered the six tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The tools reuse the dashboard’s existing filters, sorting and selections instead of creating a separate interface for Codex. Each tool defines the information it accepts through a JSON schema and checks dates and allowed options before running. I also made each tool wait for the dashboard to reach the requested view before returning. This helps ensure that the answer Codex gives matches the evidence visible on the screen. I added tests covering the calculations, tool registration, valid and invalid inputs, interface changes and the static deployment. There is no OpenAI API backend. The AI in this project is Codex using the WebMCP tools supplied by the page. Challenges The first challenge was keeping the WebMCP work separate from the forecasting project that was already running. I did not want the new interface to interfere with the live record, so I preserved the Git history, marked where the challenge work began and switched off the copied automatic forecast jobs. The original repository still handles the forecasts and scoring, while the challenge version only displays a checked snapshot. The second challenge was getting to grips with WebMCP. I had heard of MCP and understood the general idea, but registering tools inside a website I had built and then getting Codex to run them against the live page was new to me. Understanding how the structured inputs, tool results and visible dashboard state needed to work together was a real learning curve. The final challenge was presenting the project clearly in a two-minute video. I had to work out when to move between sections, how far to scroll and how quickly I could speak without rushing. The Codex audit also takes close to a minute, so I had to show that it was genuinely running while speeding up the waiting section enough to keep the whole video within the limit. What I learned The main thing I learned is that WebMCP works best when the tools use the same actions already available to a person using the site. Reusing the dashboard’s real filters, sorting and selections meant that Codex and the person watching were always looking at the same evidence. I also learned the difference between changing the evidence and changing how it is displayed. The research record itself is read-only: Codex cannot alter the forecasts, scores or rules. It can still move between tabs, filter the ledger, change its order and select a day to help the person using the site investigate the record. Boundaries Forecast Ledger is for auditing forecasting research, not making trades. It does not calculate profit and loss. Its benchmarks are simple historical comparisons rather than a test against the market’s own expectations. Missed runs cannot be repaired later, and the project will not decide whether the model passed its pre-agreed tests until the evaluation period ends. The current result may look encouraging, but the final evaluation could still find no meaningful improvement. title: Machine Passport
pitch: Evidence-backed machine readiness for humans and AI agents. WebMCP lets agents compare machines, explain blockers, and stage the next safe step—while humans keep execution authority.
about_excerpt: Evidence-backed machine readiness for humans and AI agents. WebMCP lets agents compare machines, explain blockers, and stage the next safe step—while humans keep execution authority. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP compares the same machine evidence the human sees: Beacon is safer for the unattended AI workload, while Atlas remains NOT_READY. The agent stages a bounded next step; the human approves it for review, while execution remains NOT_EXECUTED and the machine stays untouched Inspiration I started Machine Passport from a very practical problem I keep running into: having several machines does not mean you actually know which one is ready for a specific job. A machine can have the best CPU, the most RAM, or the strongest GPU and still be the wrong machine for an unattended workload because qualification is incomplete, recovery is unproven, deployment is fragile, or an important security fact is simply unknown. That led to the question behind the whole project: What if an AI agent could help choose the safest machine for the job from evidence — without giving the agent authority to change the machine? That is Machine Passport. The central idea is simple: The fastest machine is not always the safest machine for the job. What it does Machine Passport turns machine evidence into a versioned passport and then evaluates readiness for a specific role across four dimensions: FIT DEPLOYMENT QUALIFICATION SECURITY The result is deterministic rather than an LLM opinion. One rule became especially important while building it: UNKNOWN stays UNKNOWN. If evidence is missing or a collector could not obtain it, Machine Passport does not silently turn that absence into a pass or a fail. In the public demo, Atlas has the strongest hardware, but for an unattended AI workload it is NOT_READY . Beacon is a more modest machine, yet it is READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS and has no hard blockers. That difference is the product. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, Machine Passport is already useful as a human dashboard. With WebMCP, the page becomes something an agent can work with directly. Instead of trying to infer machine state from rendered UI or DOM structure, the page exposes five typed tools over the same state the human sees: list_machines get_machine_passport assess_role_readiness compare_machines stage_change_proposal The first four are genuinely read-only. The fifth can stage a bounded proposal in application state. That means I can ask: Which machine is safest for an overnight AI workload, what blocks the runner-up, and what is the smallest safe next step? The agent can inspect the evidence, compare the machines, explain the result, and stage the proposed next step. The proposal then appears in the same page for human review. That shared state is the part I find most interesting about WebMCP: the human and the agent are not operating two separate versions of reality. Human authority is part of the design I deliberately did not give the WebMCP tools SSH, PowerShell, device access, or machine mutation. Machine Passport is the pre-action decision layer . The agent can inspect and stage. The human decides. Even after the human clicks Approve for Review , the proposal still says: execution_state = NOT_EXECUTED That is not unfinished functionality. It is the authority boundary of this version. Agents inspect and stage. Humans decide. Machines stay untouched. How I built it The public challenge version is intentionally small and inspectable. It is a static web application with: a normalized MachinePassport schema, strict JSON validation, explicit evidence provenance, deterministic readiness rules, conservative UNKNOWN semantics, five WebMCP tools, shared proposal state, and a human review interface. The public app uses three clearly synthetic machines: Atlas, Beacon, and Relay . The same frozen import and readiness core was also privately validated against one sanitized real machine passport . I kept that claim deliberately narrow. This is not a fleet-management product and I am not claiming production deployment. The current version has 157 deterministic tests , including malformed imports, UNKNOWN preservation, readiness aggregation, proposal transitions, blocker semantics, retry-safe staging, and machine-mutation invariants. Challenges I faced One of the most useful lessons came from testing the real agent journey instead of only testing the code. During a live ChatGPT run, an identical tool retry initially created a duplicate proposal. That exposed something unit tests had not made obvious enough: an agent-facing action needs to tolerate repeated calls. I changed staging so that an identical active request returns the existing proposal instead of creating another one. Another issue was blocker semantics. A limitation on an otherwise healthy readiness dimension was being presented too strongly. I changed the policy so a finding becomes a blocker only when its evidence intersects a dimension that is actually NOT_READY or UNKNOWN . Those fixes reinforced the same lesson: the contract exposed to an agent has to be stricter than the UI alone suggests. What I learned Building Machine Passport changed how I think about agentic interfaces. The interesting question is not only: What can the agent do? It is also: What should the agent be able to know, what should it be allowed to stage, and where should its authority stop? WebMCP made that separation tangible. It also showed me that machine readiness is different from telemetry. Telemetry tells you what a machine has or what it is doing. Machine Passport tries to answer a different question: Given the evidence we actually have, is this machine ready for this role — and if not, what is the smallest safe next step? What's next The natural next step is to let specialist collectors and diagnostics feed Machine Passport evidence while keeping collection separate from adjudication. That could make the passport useful across local workstations, GPU nodes, lab machines, and unattended AI systems without changing the core idea: evidence first, deterministic readiness second, bounded agent action third, human authority last. title: Mermaid Atlas
pitch: Mermaid Atlas turns massive Mermaid diagrams into a shared visual workspace where humans and AI agents can explore, explain, and safely improve software architecture through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Mermaid Atlas turns massive Mermaid diagrams into a shared visual workspace where humans and AI agents can explore, explain, and safely improve software architecture through WebMCP. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I have a project called Sonny with around 264,464 lines of code. When Bhavya tried to understand its architecture, going through hundreds of source files and Markdown documents was extremely inefficient. We realized that the easiest way to understand a codebase this large was to see its architecture visually. This was not only our experience. GitHub Next independently identified the lack of visual explanations as a major limitation of current agent workflows. Their research explains that agents generate text much faster than humans can process it, while text is often the wrong medium for understanding complex relationships and architectural systems. That is exactly the problem Mermaid Atlas addresses. Existing Mermaid viewers also struggled with large diagrams and made them difficult to explore. In our testing, Mermaid Atlas could handle diagrams with more than 500 nodes that mermaid.live could not handle properly. That is what sparked the idea, and Bhavya came up with Mermaid Atlas. What it does Mermaid Atlas is a visual workspace for exploring large Mermaid diagrams. A person can import Mermaid or Markdown files, search for nodes, inspect relationships, navigate through dependencies, and edit the source while viewing the rendered result. Through ten WebMCP tools, an AI agent can work with the same live graph. It can: Find components using natural language Inspect dependencies and blast radius Trace paths between services Detect cycles, isolated nodes, entry points, and dead ends Create guided walkthroughs Make validated source changes Undo its latest change safely Everything the agent does is visible on the canvas through selections, walkthroughs, source updates, and the Agent activity history. The app opens with a complete Northwind architecture, so judges can start using it immediately without creating an account or uploading anything. How we built it Mermaid Atlas originally started as a proof of concept built with HTML and JavaScript. When we joined the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, we migrated it to React and built the current version. We used Mermaid for rendering and ELK for laying out large graphs. Different Mermaid diagram types generate completely different SVG structures, so we built adapters that connect the original Mermaid source to the correct rendered nodes, edges, groups, and source lines. We then added the WebMCP layer, the diagram library, Graph Index, walkthroughs, safe editing, activity history, themes, and automated tests. Challenges we ran into The most frustrating challenge was that WebMCP does not currently support prompt primitives. Registering tools was not enough because the agent also needed to understand when and how to use them. We solved this by creating get_atlas_guide , a tool that teaches the agent the correct workflows, tool order, limits, and safety rules. We also found that tool behavior differed between models. Some descriptions worked well with GPT-5.6 Sol but were not followed as reliably by GPT-5.6 Terra. We reworked our WebMCP tool descriptions, schemas, results, and error messages until both models could use the tools consistently. Another major challenge was supporting different Mermaid renderers. Flowcharts, sequence diagrams, class diagrams, states, and architecture diagrams all generate different SVG structures. A generic solution caused incorrect highlighting and sometimes changed the appearance of diagram elements. We had to build renderer-specific semantic adapters instead. Safe agent editing was also difficult. We needed to prevent invalid Mermaid syntax, stale edits, and undo operations that could overwrite newer human changes. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that Mermaid Atlas works reliably for humans and agents even with massive Mermaid diagrams. We built ten WebMCP tools that operate on the same graph the human is viewing, made agent actions visible and reversible, and tested the application across 46 Mermaid fixtures. We also made diagrams with more than 500 nodes practical to search, navigate, and understand. What we learned We learned that building agent tools is not only about exposing functions. Tool names, descriptions, schemas, limits, and error messages determine whether an agent can use them reliably. We also learned that human control means making agent actions visible and reversible, not just asking for confirmation. Most importantly, we learned that handling large diagrams is both a rendering problem and an information-retrieval problem. Agents need focused graph queries instead of the entire diagram. What's next for Mermaid Atlas Next, we want to add optional accounts, cloud synchronization, and real-time collaboration so teams can work on architecture diagrams together like they would in Google Docs. The current local, no-account version will remain available. title: NetLab
pitch: A browser-based network simulator where people and AI agents troubleshoot the same live network together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A browser-based network simulator where people and AI agents troubleshoot the same live network together through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Website opened inside ChatGPT Browser ChatGPT Diagnosing with the help of WebMCP tools NetLab Network Creation NetLab exposed WebMCP Tools used by ChatGPT ChatGPT highlighting the faulty node in network through the highlight_node tool ChatGPT fixing the faulty node through the WebMCP Tool Inspiration Network simulators are great for learning because you can experiment with routers, IP addresses, gateways and routes without needing physical networking hardware. But when something breaks, the experience is still very manual. A topology may look perfectly fine while one incorrect gateway or missing route prevents two machines from communicating. You then have to open devices one by one, inspect their interfaces and routing tables, run tests, and work backwards until you find the problem. That felt like a good place to explore WebMCP. Instead of building another chatbot inside a simulator, I wanted to see what would happen if the simulator itself became understandable and operable by an external AI agent , while the user continued working in the same interface. That became NetLab . What NetLab does NetLab is a lightweight browser-based network simulation lab. A user can: create PCs and routers connect and disconnect devices configure IPv4 addresses and CIDR prefixes configure default gateways configure router interfaces add and remove static routes load working and intentionally broken network labs run connectivity tests see the forward and return packet paths inspect exactly where and why routing fails The networking behavior is handled by NetLab itself. It has a deterministic client-side simulation engine for IPv4 addressing, subnet logic, gateways, directly connected networks, static routing and bidirectional reachability. In other words, the language model does not decide whether a network works. ChatGPT reasons about the result; NetLab decides the result. Why WebMCP fits this use case A network simulator contains much more state than what is immediately visible on the canvas. Two routers may look correctly connected while their interface addresses or routing tables make communication impossible. Without structured access, an agent would have to inspect the UI, open individual devices, read form fields, understand what each control represents and then attempt to operate the application through the interface. With WebMCP, NetLab exposes meaningful networking capabilities directly. The current site tools are: get_topology get_device_state test_connectivity highlight_device add_static_route remove_static_route This allows ChatGPT to work with the actual network state rather than infer it from screenshots. For example, in the included Broken Static Routing Challenge : PC-01 cannot reach PC-02. ChatGPT reads the live topology. It runs NetLab's connectivity simulator. It inspects the relevant router. It identifies the missing return route. It can highlight that router directly in the user's canvas. When asked, it adds the missing static route. It runs the simulator again and NetLab verifies that connectivity now succeeds. The important part is that the human and the agent are not working with separate copies of the network. They are both operating the same live lab state . If the human changes the network manually, the next tool call sees that change. If the agent modifies a route, the user immediately sees it in the same inspector. How I built it I first built NetLab as a normal network simulator before adding WebMCP. The application uses a visual topology canvas for manipulating devices and connections, while the network itself is represented as structured client-side state. The simulator implements the core Layer-3 logic separately from the UI so that both human actions and agent actions can reuse the same behavior. At a high level: Human UI → Application actions → Shared lab state → Network simulator and: WebMCP tools → Application actions → Shared lab state → Network simulator This was important because I did not want a separate "AI version" of NetLab's behavior. The WebMCP tools are registered using the imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Read tools expose concise networking state instead of React or framework internals, and write tools reuse the same application actions used by the normal interface. Everything currently runs client-side. NetLab does not require a backend or an embedded AI model. Challenges The first challenge was scope. It would have been very easy to turn this into an attempt to recreate Packet Tracer, which was neither realistic nor necessary for the idea I wanted to demonstrate. So I deliberately kept the networking scope focused on PCs, routers, IPv4, CIDR, default gateways and static routing. This was enough to make troubleshooting real without pretending NetLab was a full network emulator. The second challenge was keeping the simulator trustworthy. Connectivity needed to come from deterministic network logic rather than from the AI. That meant handling forward and return paths, subnet checks, next-hop resolution, static-route matching and useful failure conditions correctly. The third challenge was WebMCP itself. Tool design mattered more than simply exposing lots of functions. I kept the surface intentionally small and domain-specific so an agent could clearly understand when to inspect the network, when to run a simulation and when to make a routing change. Testing was also interesting because WebMCP is still emerging. I verified the tools directly in Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled and then tested the full human-agent workflow inside ChatGPT's in-app browser. What I learned The biggest thing I learned from this project is that making a web application "agent-native" is not the same as adding AI to it. The useful part is deciding which pieces should remain deterministic application logic, which capabilities should be exposed as tools, and where the human should stay in control. For NetLab: the simulator owns networking truth WebMCP exposes structured capabilities the agent reasons over those capabilities the human still sees and controls the live workspace That division ended up being much more interesting than simply asking an LLM to operate the UI. What's next NetLab is intentionally a small Layer-3 simulator today, but the same interaction model could extend much further. Future versions could explore switches, VLANs, ARP, DHCP, NAT, dynamic routing protocols and richer challenge generation. More interesting to me is the collaborative side: an agent could generate troubleshooting labs, guide a learner without directly giving away the answer, explain packet behavior step by step, or validate a network design while the user continues modifying it manually. For this challenge, I wanted to get the core idea right first: a network simulator where a person and their agent can inspect, troubleshoot and change the same executable environment together. I also designed and implemented the six site tools that let ChatGPT inspect, diagnose, highlight, modify, and re-test the same live network used by the human. title: Nodebook
pitch: A visual workspace where people and AI agents turn ideas into connected plans and maps using WebMCP, without losing important context in chat.
about_excerpt: A visual workspace where people and AI agents turn ideas into connected plans and maps using WebMCP, without losing important context in chat. Like Comment Story Updates A product roadmap where scope, progress, evidence, and agent-created relationships stay visible on one connected canvas. Nodebook exposes 15 WebMCP tools for reading context, creating maps, updating plans, adding evidence, and focusing important paths. The inspector makes agent work reviewable with linked maps, named comments, evidence, delivery status, and human-controlled locks. A learning map connects concepts, evidence, exercises, and an interactive quiz so people and AI can build understanding together. Inspiration AI assistants can help plan a product, research an idea, or explain a difficult concept. But their best work often ends up buried inside a chat. The person then has to copy the result into a document, rebuild the relationships, and explain the same context again in the next conversation. I built Nodebook to give people and AI assistants a shared visual workspace. The person chooses the direction, while the assistant helps organize the work directly on the canvas. What Nodebook does Nodebook is an infinite visual canvas for planning, tracing, and learning. A workspace can contain three kinds of connected maps: Build maps for features, scope, progress, risks, and evidence Trace maps for user journeys, system flows, and failure paths Learn maps for concepts, examples, exercises, and quizzes People can create and edit nodes, decide what is in scope, track delivery, attach evidence, leave comments, and lock important decisions. An AI assistant can read the same workspace through WebMCP. It can understand which node the person selected, create connected maps, update plans, add evidence and comments, and highlight important paths. For example, a person can select “Crash-safe recovery,” click “Trace,” and ask the assistant to map the recovery process. The assistant can read that selection, create the complete flow, connect it to the original feature, highlight the riskiest path, and leave an explanation, all without the person copying the project into the prompt. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Nodebook is useful because the person and the assistant work with the same information. Without WebMCP, an assistant would need to interpret screenshots, click through the interface, or ask the person to repeatedly copy information into a chat. Those approaches are slow and can lose important details. With WebMCP, Nodebook gives the assistant clear actions for reading and changing the workspace. The assistant receives the exact nodes, relationships, comments, evidence, and selected task. Its changes then appear immediately on the canvas, where the person can inspect and edit them. This creates a better experience than an embedded chatbot. The conversation is not the final product. The shared, lasting workspace is. How I implemented WebMCP Nodebook registers 15 browser tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools allow an assistant to: Read the workspace, maps, nodes, comments, and human selection Search across titles, descriptions, tags, evidence, and comments Create linked Build, Trace, and Learn maps Add or update nodes and connections Make scope and delivery updates Attach evidence and attributed comments Focus nodes and highlight important paths Every request is checked before it changes the workspace. Invalid links, missing nodes, duplicate IDs, unsafe source URLs, oversized requests, and broken connections are rejected. Each successful assistant action is applied as one undoable change. Locked nodes are skipped, and assistants are not given a tool that permanently deletes nodes. This keeps important decisions under human control. How it was built Nodebook is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and React Flow. Dagre arranges assistant-created maps into a predictable layout. Zustand manages the workspace, while Zod checks tool requests and imported files. The workspace is saved in the browser using IndexedDB. There are no accounts, API routes, analytics, cloud database, or Nodebook storage server. People can export the complete workspace as JSON and import it again later. The included demo contains a product roadmap, user journeys, a learning map, release checks, evidence, comments, locked decisions, and a research parking lot. Challenges The hardest part was making assistant actions feel like real product actions instead of hidden changes. I needed to make sure that a large graph update either succeeded completely or changed nothing. I also had to keep the visible canvas, undo history, browser storage, and WebMCP responses in agreement. Another challenge was balancing useful assistant access with human control. Nodebook solves this with strict validation, visible activity, attributed comments, undo support, locked nodes, and human-only deletion. Accomplishments I am proud that Nodebook is a complete working application rather than only a WebMCP experiment. It includes: 15 working WebMCP tools A detailed, editable demo workspace Linked maps with breadcrumbs Evidence and human-assistant comments Scope, progress, and learning states Path highlighting and automatic layout Undo and redo for assistant changes Local browser persistence Safe JSON import and export Automated unit and browser tests What I learned I learned that good human-AI collaboration needs more than a prompt box. The assistant needs clear actions and reliable context. The person needs to see what changed, understand why it changed, and remain able to edit, lock, or undo the result. WebMCP makes that possible using the website’s real data and actions. What’s next Next, I would improve keyboard navigation, test larger workspaces, add more starter templates, and make recovery guidance even clearer. I would also explore shareable, read-only workspace snapshots while keeping Nodebook’s main promise: the person owns the workspace and stays in control. I created the product concept, interface, local-first data model, 15 WebMCP tools, safety controls, automated tests, deployment, documentation, and demo.
