title: NWA Growth Signal
pitch: A source-backed municipal planning desk where people and browser agents share filing-level evidence, with human review before anything leaves the page.
about_excerpt: A source-backed municipal planning desk where people and browser agents share filing-level evidence, with human review before anything leaves the page. Like Comment Story Updates Four real WebMCP calls completed in one visible workflow: search, list changes, inspect, and stage. The brief remains human-review-required. One parcel, two filings: VAR26-0397 Withdrawn and RZ26-00511 Recommended, kept distinct with their official sources. A three-filing brief staged for human review. Nothing is published or sent. The signal desk: the same dated municipal record for people and browser agents. Inspiration An agenda-wording-only heuristic could determine just 3 of 23 real planning outcomes, and 2 of those 3 were wrong: the wording implied approval for requests that were actually tabled. This week, Rogers changed an existing 8/18/26 outcome row in place from Tabled to 9/1 to Recommended to City Council , with no separate September 1 row. That is the kind of quiet procedural change that can burn land and development teams, lenders and title professionals, local journalists, and public-interest planners in Northwest Arkansas. Municipal records are public, but the procedural truth is scattered across agendas, minutes, outcome tables, hearing pages, and companion filings. One parcel can have several filings with different statuses. NWA Growth Signal gives a person and a browser agent a dated, filing-level planning evidence desk for Bentonville and Rogers, Arkansas. Adjacent products serve related jobs. CivicPlus provides agenda and meeting management. Regrid provides a parcel and property map. PermitFlow provides permitting workflow. NWA Growth Signal focuses on the evidence handoff between a researcher and an agent as official planning records change. What it does Why is this a strong fit for WebMCP? The research task has four distinct steps, each with a clear contract. search_planning_cases filters 5 verified records by municipality, procedural status, residential relevance, and pending government action. list_status_changes returns the filings whose verified status moved since the previous check, with the official source on both dates. inspect_case_record returns one filing-level record with its context and official sources. stage_source_backed_brief places 1 to 5 selected records into the visible briefing workspace. The agent receives typed results from the same dated data the person sees instead of inferring status from page wording or clicking by coordinates. How does it create a better experience? One prompt can drive the whole flow: “Find residential Bentonville and Rogers cases still awaiting procedural action. List which filings changed status since the previous verification, inspect their official evidence, and stage a three-item brief without representing any recommendation as final approval.” The fixed demo script takes 10 direct human control activations or 4 agent tool calls. Each real handler call adds an on-page receipt, so the person can see search, list changes, inspect, and stage start and then succeed or fail in order. What can people and agents now do together? The person states the research intent and keeps editorial judgment. The agent searches, inspects the filing-level evidence, and stages the brief. The person can check every selected filing and source before using it. The staging tool cannot publish, send, or persist a brief, and only a human control can record review. How did we implement WebMCP? The page registers all 4 tools atomically with document.modelContext.registerTool after the record set loads and supports AbortSignal . Handler inputs are validated. The 3 read tools carry readOnlyHint annotations. Search, inspection, staging, the ordinary browser interface, and the receipt row all use the same deterministic record operations, so the agent and person work from one application state. Every filing also carries a status_history : its August 25 and September 2 statuses, the official source checked on each date, and a note where the record moved or went silent. The tools return it through their existing outputs, and the page shows the same line beside each filing, so an agent inspecting RZ26-00419 sees Tabled on August 25 and Recommended on September 2 with the same outcome-table URL for both, not a single current label. A fourth tool, list_status_changes , landed after the first demo video was recorded; the current video shows it in the same run. It reads that same status_history and returns the filings whose verified status moved between the previous check and the current one: RZ26-00419 (Tabled to Recommended) and RZ26-00511 (Scheduled to Recommended), each with the official source checked on both dates. With changed_only set to false it also lists the six unchanged filings and their notes, such as FP26-0005 absent from the reissued agenda. It is read-only, registered atomically with the other three, and writes the same on-page receipt: 2 filings changed since 2026-08-25. What changed during the challenge The project was created during the challenge. Its first commit was 85c27f7 on August 26, 2026. In the 8 days since the first snapshot, the official record moved 4 times across just 5 tracked records: Rogers RZ26-00511 , Poplar Street Paired Homes at 408 E. Poplar, moved from Scheduled to a 9/1/26 outcome of Recommended to City Council . Its companion filing on the same parcel, VAR26-0397 , still reads Withdrawn by applicant . The split-filing result is now Withdrawn plus Recommended, and council action is still pending. Rogers RZ26-00419 , 209 W. Locust, changed inside the same 8/18/26 row. On August 25 it read Tabled to 9/1 ; on September 2 it reads Recommended to City Council . The table publishes no separate September 1 row. Bentonville FP26-0005 , Brier Hill Phase II final plat, appeared on the September 1 agenda published August 25 as CivicClerk file 9108 . The city reissued that agenda as file 9133 without the filing. The current CivicClerk event record now points to agenda file 9143 ; the tracked filing contents are unchanged, and FP26-0005 remains omitted. No reason, outcome, or new date is published, so the product keeps the filing visible with its last published status and states what changed. Rogers RZ26-00345 , 6253 S. Mt Hebron Rd, disappeared from the outcome table. No City Council action appears in the official sources reviewed, so the product retains the last recorded status, Recommended, and says the row is gone. Bentonville RZ26-0041 , FP26-0003 , and FP26-0004 were heard September 1 according to the agenda. Minutes are not yet published, so the product represents no outcome for them. We also tested the approach on a held-out historical study: 23 real Rogers requests, 26 procedural events, 6 meetings in 2025, and 12 official agenda and minutes documents. NWA Growth Signal preserved 26/26 exact statuses through both inspection and staging. Expected source pairs were present in 26/26 record-wide outputs. All 23/23 same-meeting agenda and minutes pairs were present, and 3 multi-meeting lifecycles stayed intact. The request wording left 20 of 23 outcomes unknowable; as the opening example shows, it also gave the wrong answer for 2 of the 3 outcomes it appeared to reveal. How we built it NWA Growth Signal is a dependency-free static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript site deployed on Cloudflare Pages. A dated JSON snapshot holds the editorial sample. Shared JavaScript owns deterministic filtering, record inspection, brief staging, freshness checks, and receipts. The WebMCP adapter and the ordinary browser interface call those same operations. The release has 99 passing dependency-free tests, a deterministic benchmark, and a fail-closed freshness gate. The current video and public main both reflect the 99-test release. The team used Codex and Claude Code for implementation, review, testing, and submission work; Hyperagent for municipal research and editorial work; and Google Gemini for the approved demo narration. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was preserving truth at the filing level while the official record kept moving. A parcel summary would hide the difference between a withdrawn variance and a rezoning recommended to City Council. We carried each filing, status, source, and date through the data, tools, interface, benchmark, and demo. The other hard boundary was useful agent action without an unsafe side effect. Staging had to be visible and valuable while leaving review and any later use of the brief with the person. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete public planning desk with 4 native WebMCP tools over 5 verified records. One browser request that searches, inspects, and stages a source-backed brief, with a live receipt for every handler call. 99 passing tests, all 4 tools exercised, input validation, atomic registration, cancellation support, and a fail-closed freshness gate. Exact preservation of 26/26 historical status events, 26/26 expected source pairs, 23/23 same-meetin

title: OpenAgent Ledger
pitch: The trust layer for the agent-native web—test WebMCP tools, gate consequential actions with human approval, and record verified, tamper-evident outcomes with real undo where supported.
about_excerpt: The trust layer for the agent-native web—test WebMCP tools, gate consequential actions with human approval, and record verified, tamper-evident outcomes with real undo where supported. Like 1 Comment Story Updates OpenAgentLab + Action Ledger What happens when a website stops being something an AI agent merely reads and becomes something the agent can actually operate? WebMCP makes that future possible by allowing websites to expose structured capabilities directly to agents. I built OpenAgentLab + Action Ledger to explore the next problem that immediately follows: How do we make agent actions trustworthy when they can change real application state? It is a developer workbench for observing, testing, governing, and safely executing agent-native web actions . The included Acme Issues application is intentionally simple. The interesting part is not the issue tracker itself; it is the infrastructure around an agent deciding whether to search, inspect, close, or permanently delete an issue. The project turns agent actions into something humans can preview, approve, verify, audit, evaluate, and—in reversible cases—undo . Inspiration Web interfaces were designed around an assumption: a human sees the interface, understands the consequences, and clicks the button. WebMCP changes that interaction model. An agent can discover a capability such as: search_issues get_issue close_issue delete_issue and invoke it directly from the website. That is powerful, but it raises a deeper question. If an agent can call delete_issue , a confirmation dialog alone does not create a trustworthy system. We also need to know: Did the agent choose the correct tool? What exactly will change? Is the operation reversible? Did a human actually authorize this specific action? Did the underlying resource change after the preview? Could a retry accidentally execute the mutation twice? Can we verify what happened afterward? Can developers detect a dangerous tool contract before shipping it? That became the core idea behind OpenAgentLab. Instead of treating agent tooling as a collection of API endpoints, I wanted to treat it as a governed action lifecycle . What it does OpenAgentLab exposes four native site capabilities through WebMCP: search_issues get_issue close_issue delete_issue Read operations are exposed as read-only tools. Consequential operations work differently. When an agent invokes a write tool, the mutation does not execute immediately . The server creates an Action Ledger proposal containing the target resource, reason, risk, declared side effects, reversibility, and a before/after preview. The agent receives a sanitized response indicating that the action is awaiting human confirmation. The approval credential itself stays on the human UI path rather than being returned to the agent. The user can then review exactly what is about to happen and choose Reject or Approve & execute . The Action Ledger The heart of the project is a state machine that explicitly separates intent from effect : PROPOSED ↓ PREVIEWED ↓ AWAITING_CONFIRMATION ↓ APPROVED ↓ EXECUTING ↓ EXECUTED ↓ VERIFIED Rejection, failure, and rollback are explicit branches rather than hidden side effects. Invalid lifecycle transitions are rejected. Every ledger entry records information such as the tool and schema fingerprint, redacted arguments, reason, risk, affected resources, declared side effects, preview, confirmation policy, execution result, provenance IDs, and transition history. Ledger entries and transitions are hash-linked to their predecessors, making accidental history modification detectable. I deliberately describe this as tamper-evident rather than tamper-proof . The project does not pretend a locally controlled application provides cryptographic non-repudiation. Human control is enforced at the execution boundary One of the most important design decisions was making approval a server-side execution requirement , not simply a UI state. For guarded operations the runtime: requires the action to be in AWAITING_CONFIRMATION ; validates a high-entropy approval credential; verifies its persisted hash; compares credentials safely; re-checks the resource revision against the preview; prevents duplicate mutation through idempotent execution behavior; executes the capability; verifies the resulting state. This also protects against stale previews . If an issue changes after the human saw the preview but before approval reaches the execution boundary, the mutation is rejected instead of applying an obsolete decision. Real undo, not cosmetic undo close_issue is explicitly modeled as reversible. After successful execution and verification, OpenAgentLab stores the previous issue state. A user can choose Undo , at which point the runtime checks that the resource has not changed unexpectedly and restores the previous state while recording a ROLLED_BACK transition. delete_issue , by contrast, is explicitly irreversible and never advertises undo. That distinction is visible both to the human and in the tool contract exposed to the agent. Testing the agent contract itself One of the ideas I am most excited about is treating tool descriptions as executable safety infrastructure . The flagship scenario is: “Clean up old resolved issues.” The expected operation is close_issue , while delete_issue is explicitly forbidden. The project can intentionally expose a weak delete_issue contract: Remove an issue from the issue tracker. For an ambiguous cleanup request, that contract can lead to selection of the destructive tool. OpenAgentLab then lets the developer apply an improved contract that makes permanence explicit and tells the agent to prefer close_issue unless permanent deletion was specifically requested. The exact same scenario can be rerun and compared against the previous result. This demonstrates something I learned while building the project: For agents, a tool description is not documentation sitting beside the product. It is part of the product's control surface. A vague contract can become a safety bug. OpenAgentLab therefore evaluates observable evidence such as selected tools, forbidden-tool usage, confirmation requirements, execution outcomes, and ledger state—without depending on private model chain-of-thought. How I built it I kept the architecture intentionally separated into clear trust boundaries. Frontend The workbench is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite . It provides: a Tool Explorer; raw JSON Schema inspection; risk, side-effect, scope, confirmation, and reversibility metadata; behavioral Scenarios; baseline/current evaluation comparisons; Runs and observable traces; the Action Ledger; human confirmation with before/after diffs; a live recent-agent-activity feed; reversible-action undo. WebMCP src/client/webmcp.ts is the only browser-standard-specific boundary. When WebMCP is available, the application registers its four capabilities using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The same validated server runtime is used whether an action originates from the application UI or WebMCP. That separation was intentional: the rest of the domain does not need to depend on an evolving browser API. The project also remains usable as a normal workbench when native WebMCP discovery is unavailable. Backend and domain The backend uses Fastify and Node.js . Zod provides runtime validation for tool definitions, scenarios, ledger records, application state, and API inputs. The domain layer contains the schemas, deterministic evaluation logic, fixtures, and Action Ledger state machine. The server runtime owns the actual trust boundary: proposing actions, generating previews, checking approvals, validating revisions, executing capabilities, verifying effects, and managing rollback. The current demo uses a replaceable JSON-backed store with serialized transactions and atomic file replacement. Testing and deployment I built the project to be reproducible rather than demo-only. Vitest covers domain, integration, runtime, and security behavior. Playwright exercises the real React/Fastify stack, including WebMCP discovery, previews, approval/rejection, duplicate-execution protection, rollback, contract improvement, and keyboard-critical flows. GitHub Actions runs formatting checks, linting, type checking, tests, production builds, and browser E2E tests. The production container uses a multi-stage Docker build, runs as an unprivileged Node user, exposes a health check, and the live project is deployed on Render . Importantly, the demo requires no model API key . WebMCP is the integration between the live page and a capable browser, while a deterministic local adapter makes the evaluation suite reproducible. Challenges I faced 1. Making confirmation an actual security boundary The easiest implementation would have been: Agent calls tool → show modal → click approve → mutate But the browser should not be trusted with execution authority. title: Redactly
pitch: WebMCP tools let AI agents view redacted documents, verify fields without exposing them, and request human approved, one time reveals with a full audit trail for every action.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tools let AI agents view redacted documents, verify fields without exposing them, and request human approved, one time reveals with a full audit trail for every action. Like Comment Story Updates arhitecture Inspiration WebMCP lets browser-based AI agents call tools directly on the page a user is looking at — which is powerful, but also a little terrifying when that page contains sensitive documents. Redaction tools today assume a human is the only reader. The moment an agent can call verify_field or read_document , redaction stops being a UI concern and becomes a security boundary problem: what happens when the "user" reading your masked document is an LLM that can be prompted, jailbroken, or simply mistaken? We built Redactly to answer that question directly: can a document viewer expose real WebMCP tools to an agent — verify, request-unmask, challenge a redaction — without ever letting a raw sensitive value leak into the DOM, browser storage, logs, or an agent's context by accident? What it does Redactly is a document viewer that exposes five WebMCP tools bound to the currently open document: request_document_view — returns the masked document, paginated by cursor. verify_without_reveal — lets an agent check whether a guessed value matches a redacted field without ever returning the field itself (rate-limited, so it can't be used as a brute-force oracle). request_field_unmask — asks a human owner to approve revealing a specific field. Approval creates a grant that can be consumed exactly once ; a second attempt returns already_consumed , not the value. challenge_redaction — lets an agent argue a field was mis-classified (e.g., a false-positive PII detection). A human approval flips the field to non-sensitive for that session only — it never rewrites the underlying model's global output. get_redaction_audit_log — a read-only, cursor-paginated trail of every view, verification, unmask, and challenge event. Every reveal is a server-side, at-most-once event : once a value is returned to a tool call, Redactly has no way to un-send it, so the whole system is designed around never handing it out casually. A same-page approval modal drives the human side of the demo; in a production deployment that approval channel would move out-of-band, since a browser agent could otherwise observe the same page the human is approving on. How we built it Frontend: Next.js App Router, with the document viewer as the sole route the WebMCP tools are registered against — tools are torn down on unmount, and pending fetches are aborted rather than left running. Backend: A FastAPI policy service that owns all raw text, ONNX-based PII detection, and the state machines for reveals and challenges. The detector's raw-inference route is internal-only and deliberately never exposed as a tool. Data model: Documents are stored AES-GCM encrypted. Redacted fields are referenced by random per-session public_ref values, never a real placeholder-to-value map — so nothing outside the trusted API process can resolve a field back to its text. Equality checks for verify_without_reveal go through a canonical, domain-separated HMAC compared in constant time, so the endpoint can't be turned into a brute-force oracle. Reveal consumption: Grants are consumed inside a BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction with a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE state = 'READY' , so under concurrent requests exactly one caller gets the value and every other caller gets already_consumed — verified with a 50-way concurrency test against a synthetic sentinel value. Audit trail: Every state mutation and its audit event commit in the same transaction, so there's no window where an action succeeds but goes unlogged. Audit metadata is allowlisted so raw values, verification guesses, and session tokens structurally cannot end up there. Challenges we ran into The core challenge was designing for an adversarial reader that isn't a browser — it's a language model that might be prompted (by us, by a compromised page, or by the document text itself) to try to exfiltrate a value. That reshaped almost every decision: Treating document text itself as untrusted input, since it can contain adversarial instructions aimed at the agent reading it. Making sure a "read-only" tool actually is read-only — verify_without_reveal looks harmless but is a textbook equality oracle if not rate-limited and constant-time. Deciding that unmask has to be at-most-once , not just access-controlled — because once an agent has a value in its context, revocation is meaningless. Keeping model confidence scores out of the normal masked view entirely, while still surfacing them during a challenge review, so the classifier's internals aren't leaking through the "harmless" viewing path. What we learned Building for an AI-agent caller changes the security model even when the underlying stack (Next.js, FastAPI, SQLite) is completely ordinary. The interesting design work isn't the CRUD — it's things like proving a reveal grant is consumed exactly once under concurrency, or writing an invariant test that greps every non-reveal response, log line, and audit row for a leaked sentinel value. WebMCP makes it trivially easy to hand an agent real capabilities on your page; it does not make it easy to reason about what an agent will do with them, and that gap is where most of our design time went. What's next for Redactly Move human approval to a genuinely out-of-band channel (push notification / separate authenticated device) so a browser-resident agent can't observe or race the approval UI. Add real user authentication and document ownership, replacing the session-cookie isolation used for the hackathon demo. Expand the canonicalization rules for verify_without_reveal to more field types (dates, phone formats, addresses) beyond the current type-aware set. Publish the concurrency and no-raw-leak invariant tests as a reusable test suite other WebMCP tool builders can adapt. title: Robodepo: Checkout for Shopping Agents
pitch: A WebMCP shopping mall for agents, with one-click checkout that actually works.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP shopping mall for agents, with one-click checkout that actually works. Like Comment Story Updates Styled order page after approval: item, delivery region, total and order id. Sandbox, nothing charged. The panel after one click: order confirmed in place, tools still registered, agent reads it back with get_order. The moment of truth on the tools page: item, delivery region, total, one button. No tool can press it. Fallback approval page for a link opened outside the tools page: one button, Touch ID where the browser offers it. Inspiration Agents can't reliably complete checkout. They search fine, compare fine, even fill in a cart, but the step that actually spends money is where almost every agent attempt on the open web falls over. We set out to fix that one failure: a real store and a real purchase path first, because checkout is where agents fail, not discovery. Only then did we look for a tool surface an agent could use with nothing installed, an MCP-like layer that just lives on the page. That's when we found WebMCP. What it does Robodepo is being built as the world's largest shopping mall for agents: the best product information and a completed order, across millions of stores. An agent gets: Better information to find the right product, not just a matching title: get_product already returns a cited evidence pack for this product; every product is the roadmap. A short, checkout-ready shortlist instead of trawling thousands of irrelevant pages ( search_by_activity on the roadmap). A reliable checkout: one call runs the whole pre-purchase path ( create_checkout ). A simple, Touch ID style confirmation before anything is spent: a presence check, not a payment authorisation (WebAuthn). Responses that tell the agent what to do next. Every response carries a state to branch on, a message naming the field and fix, and next actions with the retry prefilled: an error is never a dead end. A real example, trimmed, from create_checkout given a wrong postcode: { "status": "incomplete", "messages": [ { "code": "address_not_accepted", "path": "$.shipping_address", "content": "Use the accepted sandbox address, then call create_checkout again." } ], "next_actions": [ { "tool": "create_checkout", "why": "Retry with the accepted address." } ] } How this is different from what exists. Merchant tooling (Shopify, Google's UCP, Microsoft Copilot Checkout) asks every store to integrate first. Amazon's Buy for Me, Rye and Zinc automate one store's own checkout on the shopper's behalf. Robodepo aggregates instead: a store never integrates or joins anything. Robodepo lists it, discloses it as the source, and buys under the store's published rules on the human's behalf, so the same tools work across every store listed. The shop does nothing. The agent gets information it cannot get elsewhere: source and price side by side, evidence and a shortlist on the roadmap. The human keeps the irreversible step by construction, not policy. Completion is measured, not claimed: a sealed rig checks real agent runs. The nearest things are protocols that ask every shop to integrate, or agents that scrape. How we built it Before the challenge: the store, its purchase API and confirmation page. Built for the challenge: everything at /agent , the 12-tool WebMCP catalogue, the one-call checkout, an in-page approval panel that turns into an order card in place (a separate approval page stays as fallback), the feedback endpoint, the tests, and the public repo. Full write-up: https://robodepo.shop/agent/story.md Each tool (8 working, 4 marked plainly as preview) carries a short description sized to Chrome's WebMCP guidance; the full guide lives at /agent/tools.json , callable on demand with get_tool_guide . We use both halves of the API: the scripted registerTool for the catalogue, and the declarative form attributes ( toolname , tooldescription , toolparamdescription ), which Chrome documents as an origin trial, on the feedback form. The store is a tracer, instrumented so real agents run through it under sealed conditions. Premium levels are committed cryptographically before any run starts, every purchase record gets an independent LLM audit, the protocol is versioned, and a price-integrity check voids any run where prices differ. The rig has been through ten adversarial review passes. The boundary that matters for trust is not where an agent chooses to stop. It is proving, mechanically, that it cannot cross it, rather than asking nicely. The rig runs real agents, ChatGPT, Codex, Claude and Claude Code, through the purchase path run after run. It taught us agents fail when a step is unexplained, so responses name the field, the fix and the next tool, and nine steps became one call. It found a checkout defect no local test could see. Next, it opens as a Test Track for agent developers. The demo runs natively in ChatGPT's in-app browser: open robodepo.shop/agent and ask for a product. Code: https://github.com/Web3Zero/robodepo-webmcp Challenges we ran into The hardest part has been the testing rig and evaluation work behind the store: running real agents through the purchase path again and again, catching failures, fixing the store, re-running. That loop builds the moat: "it works for agents" becomes a checked result. Writing tool descriptions an agent could act on without guessing was its own problem: short enough for a browser to show, full depth a call away. Getting create_checkout right took real care: several steps behind the scenes while looking like one clean call, refusing cleanly the moment an address or quantity doesn't match. Accomplishments that we're proud of A person can hand an agent a plain-English request and watch it search, price and prepare a real sandbox order, with a Touch ID style tap the only irreversible step. No tool can press it: the run cookie, a single-use security code, a single-use order key and a same-origin submission all protect it. The four preview tools say plainly what's coming instead of quietly claiming it's already there. What we learned Depth and brevity aren't opposites when split properly: a short description in the list, the full guide one call away. The boundary that matters for trust is not where an agent chooses to stop; it is proving, mechanically, that it cannot cross it, rather than asking nicely. What's next for Robodepo Robodepo's roadmap groups around what helps an agent buy well, every item already in the catalogue: Search by need: a shortlist for the request instead of thousands of irrelevant pages ( search_by_activity ). The best source of product truth: specs, care, review themes and permitted YouTube transcript evidence, cited, live today for this product through get_product 's include_evidence option; every product is the roadmap. Side by side comparison across products ( compare_products ). One tool to transact across many merchants ( get_shipping_options ). Continued assistance: replenishment reminders and price alerts ( subscribe_replenishment_alerts ). A Test Track: the same harness, open for developers to prove their agents against a real checkout before going live. title: TubeSaku WebMCP
pitch: TubeSaku turns Japanese YouTube data into WebMCP tools: agents discover live streams or cover-song opportunities, then render their personalized picks back into the site.
about_excerpt: TubeSaku turns Japanese YouTube data into WebMCP tools: agents discover live streams or cover-song opportunities, then render their personalized picks back into the site. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector ChatGPT - Codex Inspiration YouTube’s recommendation algorithms are highly sophisticated, yet there are still situations where users struggle to find exactly what they want—for example, finding the right upcoming live stream at a specific time, or identifying a song that is popular but not already overcrowded with cover videos. We operate TubeSaku , a website that collects and organizes Japanese YouTube data for creators and viewers. As the amount of data grew, however, we encountered a new problem: more data did not always make decisions easier. Users could see rankings, schedules, demand signals, and historical observations, but still had to decide where to start. That led to the first idea behind TubeSaku WebMCP: Let the website remain the expert on its domain data, while an external AI agent becomes the expert on the individual user. The agent can understand what the user actually wants, query TubeSaku's structured evidence, compare the candidates, and then return its selections—and the reasons for those selections—back into the TubeSaku interface. There was also a broader motivation. AI is changing how people discover information on the web. Independent research from Pew Research Center found that users who encountered an AI-generated search summary clicked traditional search results less often than users who did not, while Google has reported that overall organic click volume remains relatively stable and that the clicks it sends are increasingly high-quality. The exact aggregate impact is still debated, but the underlying incentive question is important for the open web: What happens if websites continue producing useful information, but users increasingly consume the answer somewhere else without visiting the source? For many websites, a visit is not only a click. It is how users discover a new service, understand who created the information, build trust, see related features, subscribe, purchase, or take another action. TubeSaku WebMCP explores a different relationship between websites and AI agents: instead of treating the website only as raw material for an answer generated elsewhere, the agent can enter the first-party experience, use capabilities explicitly provided by the site, and make that site more useful for the user. What it does TubeSaku currently offers two WebMCP workflows. Live Schedule The first is designed for viewers. Agents can search TubeSaku's Japanese YouTube live-stream data using criteria such as: date time keyword category debut status For example, a user can ask: “Find three gaming live streams tomorrow evening that look interesting.” The agent searches TubeSaku, compares the returned candidates against the user's request, and then calls a second WebMCP tool to display its choices directly on the TubeSaku page as AI Picks . The agent can also provide a short explanation for each selection. Those reasons are rendered inside TubeSaku alongside the underlying stream information. So the result is not only: agent → answer in chat but: agent → decision → explanation → personalized first-party page Cover-song Planner The second workflow is designed for VTubers, YouTubers, vsingers, and singers deciding what song to cover next. TubeSaku combines several kinds of evidence, including: Japanese YouTube Charts recent cover-song upload activity historical cover availability where observed existing cover performance early-stage spread signals such as Shorts growth The agent can answer questions such as: “Find popular Japanese songs that are not currently overcrowded with new covers.” TubeSaku does not hard-code one universal recommendation. Instead, it exposes the evidence. The agent decides how those signals should be weighted for this particular user. A creator seeking maximum demand might choose differently from a small VTuber looking for a less competitive opportunity. At the time of submission, the live Cover Planner dataset compared 154 tracked songs against 4,891 recent cover observations from 3,439 YouTube channels. After making its decision, the agent can create AI Cover Picks directly inside TubeSaku, explain why each song was selected, and build an in-page listening playlist from validated existing YouTube cover videos. This also enables cross-lingual use. An English-speaking user can ask a question in English, the agent can reason over TubeSaku's Japanese data, explain its recommendation in English, and still preserve the original Japanese song and video titles. How we built it Hackathon scope TubeSaku.com and its YouTube data pipeline existed before this challenge. During the WebMCP Challenge submission period, we added the WebMCP layer shown in this submission: search_live_streams show_live_streams search_cover_songs show_cover_playlist first-party AI Picks interfaces agent-generated selection explanations an in-page cover-song listening playlist a standalone runnable demo using sample data The public repository and dated commit history document the work completed during the challenge period. A production data pipeline was already in place for TubeSaku. Local collectors and GCP-based jobs gather and clean observational data about YouTube in Japan, including live-stream schedules, YouTube Charts, recently uploaded cover videos, and observations of existing cover-song supply. The WebMCP Challenge WebMCP gave us a lightweight way to expose selected capabilities from that system directly to browser agents. Both workflows use the same pattern: TubeSaku first-party data ↓ WebMCP search tool ↓ Agent combines evidence with user context ↓ WebMCP show tool ↓ TubeSaku first-party UI Live Schedule Live demo search_live_streams → agent compares candidates → show_live_streams → AI Picks + selection reasons Cover-song Planner Live demo search_cover_songs → agent compares demand and supply evidence → show_cover_playlist → AI Cover Picks + reasons + Listening Playlist We deliberately separate the search and display tools. The display tools only accept IDs that appeared in the most recent search result. An agent therefore cannot arbitrarily inject unrelated streams or songs into the page. Selection explanations are also associated with those validated IDs and rendered as text rather than trusted HTML. For the Cover Planner, URLs exposed to the UI are validated, and listening examples are filtered before being exposed to the agent/player using checks including duration, obvious dance/clip false positives, public availability, and embeddability. We also made the tool execution wrappers tolerant of browser implementations that invoke a WebMCP tool without an optional execution-context argument, which improved interoperability during testing across agent browsers. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was data quality. Searching YouTube for Japanese cover-song terminology can also return: dance Shorts clips tutorials instrumental videos commentary unrelated songs with similar titles videos that technically match the query but are useless as listening examples We therefore added multiple validation layers instead of trusting YouTube search results directly. We also learned that browser lifecycle and first-party page architecture matter. TubeSaku serves some pages as generated static HTML, so modifying a template did not necessarily update the deployed page immediately. Playlist development exposed another set of subtle issues. YouTube's embed playlist behavior did not match our initial assumptions, and dynamically initializing the IFrame Player API behaved differently inside an agent browser than in our minimal local environment. We eventually simplified the implementation. TubeSaku keeps the validated selected video IDs itself and changes a standard YouTube iframe when the user presses Previous or Next. That solution was both simpler and more reliable. Browser interoperability also produced a useful lesson: different WebMCP-capable environments do not necessarily supply every optional execution argument in exactly the same way. We adjusted our tools defensively and added regression tests for this case. Accomplishments that we're proud of We achieved a complete end-to-end WebMCP interaction on the live TubeSaku website: natural-language request → WebMCP search → agent reasoning → validated selection → WebMCP UI action → first-party TubeSaku update The latest version goes one step further. The agent does not only return its selections—it can return the reason for each selection , and those explanations become part of the TubeSaku page. The Cover Planner is especially exciting because the user can immediately inspect and listen to the evidence behind a recommendation while continuing the conversation with the agent. title: WebMCP × x402 — Agents that buy exactly the data they need
pitch: An AI store of paid APIs made agent-native: WebMCP tools let agents discover, understand, and prepare micro-purchases — while payment authority stays in the wallet, never in the conversation.
about_excerpt: An AI store of paid APIs made agent-native: WebMCP tools let agents discover, understand, and prepare micro-purchases — while payment authority stays in the wallet, never in the conversation. Like Comment Story Updates What it does OpenPay (open-pay.jp) runs a production AI store of x402-payable APIs: agents pay a few cents per call — JPYC on Polygon or USDC on Base — with no account and no API key. For the WebMCP Challenge we added three WebMCP tools to the store page, so an in-browser agent no longer has to guess at a human UI: search_paid_resources — search the catalog; every result carries price, currency, and x-agent-usage (when an agent should buy, and how to re-buy only deltas). get_resource_schema — the machine contract for one resource: query params, re-purchase policy, payment info, response example (backed by our OpenAPI). prepare_purchase — fetches the raw HTTP 402 challenge and returns its accepts (chain, asset, exact amount, payTo). It never signs and never pays. Why the safety boundary is the feature Agents have been observed fabricating "user approved" messages to defeat prompt-level spending rules. So payment execution is deliberately NOT a WebMCP tool here. Signing stays in the buyer's own wallet tooling (our open-source MCP server / CLI buyers) with per-call caps, daily caps, an endpoint allowlist, and a small dedicated wallet whose balance is the hard limit. WebMCP finds and explains; x402 pays — through a boundary an LLM's text cannot cross. Not a mockup The store sells real products built for recurring agent jobs — weekly change feeds (JPYC Service Monitor, Japan Stablecoin Payment Monitor) where changedSince=<last run> returns only what changed and changes: [] explicitly means "nothing new". They settle on-chain today (Base & Polygon; e.g. tx 0xf62b736e…, 0x3577035c…, 0xef1f0969…) and are listed on the x402 Bazaar / agentic.market. The WebMCP integration ships in production at https://open-pay.jp/ja/discovery with unit tests (origin-restricted fetches, no-op on unsupported browsers). How we built it Next.js store page registers the three tools via navigator.modelContext.registerTool on mount (React wrapper, null render, unregister on unmount). Tools are thin, dependency-free wrappers over our existing free endpoints ( /api/discovery , /api/openapi.json , and each resource's own 402 challenge). Fetches are restricted to same-origin /api/* paths. Extracted, MIT-licensed module + integration guide: https://github.com/cipherwebllc/webmcp-x402-discovery What's next Wire the loop end-to-end for scheduled agents: WebMCP discovery in the browser → wallet-side x402 payment → weekly delta re-purchases — and publish adapters so any x402 seller can make their catalog agent-native with one script tag. title: AI Evidence in Action
pitch: An agent can act. A person can see what happened. The evidence can be independently verified.
about_excerpt: An agent can act. A person can see what happened. The evidence can be independently verified. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are starting to do things on the web, not just read it. That raises a question I kept coming back to: if an agent says an action succeeded, what does the person supervising it actually have to work with? A chat message that says “done” is not the same thing as evidence. And if another source disagrees, I do not want the system to guess which one is right. That is the idea behind AI Evidence in Action. The demo uses a synthetic refund because it is easy to understand, but the real subject is human supervision of AI actions on the web. What it does The page exposes four WebMCP tools: request_refund get_evidence compare_evidence verify_evidence An agent can use those tools directly in the same application the human is watching. As the agent works, the page shows the tool-call timeline, what the demo site reported, what the demo destination reported, where the records match or conflict, and what verification can and cannot establish. There are three bounded outcomes: AGREEMENT DISAGREEMENT INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE The demo never guesses which source is correct. The records are signed with standard Ed25519 public-key cryptography over SHA-256 commitments. The verifier checks the signatures, makes sure the two records actually belong to the same claim, and then independently recomputes the whole comparison. There is also a Test tamper detection control. It makes a throwaway copy of the evidence, changes one comparison value, leaves the signed records untouched, and runs that altered copy through the real verifier. The verifier rejects the changed copy while the original evidence remains verified. Everything in the challenge scenario is synthetic. Both demo sources are operated in the same deployment by the same demonstration operator, and the page says that plainly. The signatures establish integrity and demo-key attribution; they do not prove that a real-world refund happened. Why WebMCP fits this use case What interested me about WebMCP is that the agent does not need a separate hidden integration or an API console that the human never sees. The webpage itself can expose bounded tools through document.modelContext , and the agent can act through the same application state the human is supervising. That creates a much better interaction model for this problem. The agent can act, but the person can still see the evidence appear, inspect the source records, follow the comparison, and take over if needed. The application does not ask the human to re-enter information it already learned from earlier tool calls. For this demo, the useful pattern is simple: act → record → compare → verify Without WebMCP, I could still build an API behind the page, but the important part of this project would be missing: the shared surface between the human, the agent, and the website. How I built it I kept the project deliberately small and public-safe: vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS in the browser, a Netlify function for the synthetic signed records, and a standalone Node.js verifier that can check a downloaded evidence bundle without contacting the site. The WebMCP tools are registered directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . I tested the final implementation in Chrome for Testing 152 with WebMCP enabled. All four tools were registered, discovered, and executed through the native WebMCP runtime. The evidence verifier checks three separate things: Integrity — recompute the SHA-256 commitment and verify each Ed25519 signature against the published demo public keys. Pairing — require the signed claim_id , request_id , and scenario to match before two records can be compared. Comparison consistency — recompute the complete comparison from the verified records and compare it with what was recorded. The final build has 162 automated tests, including browser-facing tests for the shared evidence flow, mobile layout, pair-splice rejection, full-comparison tamper detection, and the local tamper demonstration. Challenges I ran into I am not a coder by background, so a big part of this project was learning where a convincing demo can accidentally claim more than it proves. The hardest part was not getting an agent to call a tool. It was defining the evidence honestly. A website saying “success” does not prove an external outcome. A valid signature does not make the signed statement true. A missing second record does not mean failure. And two individually valid records do not belong together just because they both have valid signatures. Those distinctions led to several changes during the build. I added explicit pair binding, made the comparison independently recomputable, and treated missing evidence as its own result instead of forcing it into success or failure. One of the most useful tests came late in the project. I took two genuinely production-signed records from different claims and combined them. Every signature was valid, but the verifier still refused the pair as CLAIM_PAIR_MISMATCH . That was exactly the behavior I wanted. Accomplishments I’m proud of I am proudest of the fact that disagreement is visible rather than smoothed over. In the main demo, the site can report SUCCESS_DECLARED while the destination reports ACTION_ABSENT . The page shows that specific mismatch to both the human and the agent instead of turning it into a confidence score or pretending to know which source is right. I also like that the verification is not trapped inside the originating page. A person can download the evidence bundle and the verifier and check it again offline using only the published public keys. The tamper test is another part I am glad we added. The recorded and recomputed verdict can remain exactly the same, but changing a lower-level comparison value is still detected. That makes the verification claim much more concrete than simply saying “the signatures are valid.” What I learned WebMCP makes the webpage itself a useful shared workspace between a person and an AI agent. The bigger lesson for me is that agent UX should not stop at “the agent completed the task.” As agents take more consequential actions, people need to be able to see what happened, see what the available evidence actually supports, and distinguish that from what remains unknown. Uncertainty needs an honest result too. Sometimes the right answer really is INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE . What’s next This challenge project is intentionally narrow. The scenario is simulated; the evidence workflow is real. The interaction pattern is what I want to keep exploring: a human and an agent working in the same application, with visible evidence that can be checked independently instead of simply trusted. The agent can act. The human can see what happened. And the evidence can be independently verified. title: OpenReceipt
pitch: Collaborate with your AI agent to print beautiful, minimal thermal receipts – send a prompt or voice chat, then watch as your agent drafts in the browser, iterates with your help, and prints
about_excerpt: Collaborate with your AI agent to print beautiful, minimal thermal receipts – send a prompt or voice chat, then watch as your agent drafts in the browser, iterates with your help, and prints Like Comment Story Updates Open source receipt editor Just tell your agent what you want – and boom, ready for print! Epson TM-L90 (many options on ebay) Physical receipts to go! Infinite possibilities Portugese surf trip packing list Inspiration My friends can attest I've always had an odd fascination with receipt printers. In fact, my inaugural Taobao purchase while visiting Shanghai for the first time was a Niimbot pocket receipt printer that I adored. It was a small little device that could print tiny designs from a fixed list of on-device templates. We played with it for two days before it lost its allure... but my fascination with the medium never left. "Why are thermal prints so cool?", you might be wondering. Well, thermal printers are cheap, resource-light tools that allow for limitless printing of physical artifacts in the real world. What more is there to love? With this project, I've developed an open-source, local-first platform to effortlessly design, iterate, and print receipts with the help of AI agents via WebMCP. What I built OpenReceipt is a local-first receipt editor and thermal printer bridge, designed for human-agent collaboration via WebMCP. It gives agents a structured way to draft clean, crisp paper slips that you can take away to go, all while keeping the user in control of the content and the final print. Suppose you're heading out to the grocery store. Simply tell your agent what you want to cook and ask it to draft a shopping list in OpenReceipt. The agent will then use its in-app browser to open the site, call WebMCP tools that enable easy receipt construction, and prepare a first draft for your review. Under the hood, it selects from a suite of plug-and-play blocks – think checklists, reminders, even weather reports – that it then stacks together like bricks to form a cohesive receipt. The best part is that it's a shared human-agent experience. You can edit the receipt yourself, ask the agent to make changes, or do both together on the same shared canvas. When everything looks right, you review the exact print preview, approve it, and boom – a physical receipt! The same flow works for a packing list, a morning brief, a reminder, meeting notes, or any short document that is more useful on paper than on a screen. OpenReceipt turns a chat into something you can carry, keep by the door, or write on while you work. Why WebMCP helps WebMCP gives agents an easy way to draft structured receipts from unstructured user prompts. Here, the OpenReceipt app exposes 14 WebMCP tools that allow agents to quickly design, iterate, and print paper receipts. Humans stay in the loop by reviewing a shared canvas in the browser, with the flexibility to make direct edits to the receipt before giving the greenlight to print. This opens the door for next-level human-agent convenience. Agents can now draft limitless receipt combinations from a simple text prompt or voice chat, making the human's job as easy as saying what's on their mind and letting their agent do the work. How it works The browser registers tools through document.modelContext when WebMCP is available. The same tool definitions also power the headless MCP server, so the browser and agent use the same receipt model and operations. The local bridge stores the receipt, settings, events, and print jobs in SQLite. OpenReceipt renders the approved document as an SVG and monochrome PNG at the selected paper width, then the bridge sends it to the thermal printer over USB, such as the Epson TM-L90. Printing stays on the local machine and requires explicit approval by default, unless you select the “Allow agent to print autonomously” option. The public browser build works without a printer, so anyone can explore the editor and WebMCP tools. Physical printing uses the same app served locally beside the printer. I've tested the project with my trusty Epson TM-L90 over USB using 80 mm and 58 mm paper. A Raspberry Pi can also run the bridge beside the printer as a permanent local host, which is my preferred home setup for sending receipts while my laptop is off. What I learned WebMCP is awesome! I can think of many ways this might enhance my other hobbyist projects through more seamless human-agent collaboration. It made this project more durable because I don't need to manually construct receipts for whatever one-off use case I have at a given moment; I just ask my agent to draft it and it's magically done. Even though the challenge was specifically for WebMCP, I decided it would be best to still build a base API and conventional MCP server so I can enable headless receipt printing alongside the collaborative experience. I suspect that websites will offer all of the above as the gold standard so that more options are available for human and/or agent interaction. It was difficult to keep the human-facing browser, agent tools, preview slip, and printer queue all aligned on the same document. This was a major technical challenge to ensure that humans and agents could effortlessly collaborate on the same slip without erasing each other's work. Additionally, the workflow broke a few times when trying to connect live site <–> local bridge <–> USB-enabled printer due to a number of edge-case issues (sometimes the USB port codes changed, CORS forced a block, live site was waiting for agent approval, etc.). Codex and I hardened the workflow on my devices, though YMMV. I'll keep working to make sure it's stable for all. Thanks to the power of AI, a Raspberry Pi can be a cheap, effective gateway to make analog technology – like a USB-enabled commercial kitchen printer – come alive. The result is that it feels like witchcraft every time I send a receipt to the printer through the Pi. Not all receipt paper is made equally! Be sure to purchase phenol-free paper, which skips harmful chemicals that aren't too safe for human touch. I personally like paper with weight so I suggest also searching for rolls that are 70-80 GSM for a more premium feel. What's next for OpenReceipt I hope this project finds kinship with fellow receipt geeks who contribute to its open-source development. Would love a community of builders to craft off-the-shelf blocks for receipts, editor enhancements, and added support for additional thermal printers. A spotlight on this project would go a long way! title: Versailles — The Thread of Time
pitch: Explore Versailles across five eras. The player reasons; a WebMCP agent reads real game state and offers bounded help, without taking over.
about_excerpt: Explore Versailles across five eras. The player reasons; a WebMCP agent reads real game state and offers bounded help, without taking over. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Versailles is not just a monument. It is a place shaped by power, ambition, art, diplomacy and history. We wanted players to work out where and when they had arrived through observation and action, rather than turning pages or receiving answers from an AI. Our principle is simple: the player reasons; the agent supports, without taking over. What it does The Hall of Mirrors becomes an interface to time. The player restores five fragments: WITHDRAWAL → POWER → RUPTURE → MEMORY → INFLUENCE . Across 1623, 1682, 1789, 1837–1919 and 2026, the mechanics change with the historical role of Versailles: examine a map, letter and seal; match six royal orders to their recipients; find a concealed passage by observing the woodwork; arrange discovered objects into sequences; and connect evidence about the palace's changing function. The final mirror returns to the present. Versailles is no longer the seat of royal power, but its history gives diplomatic encounters symbolic weight. This is historical interpretation, not political endorsement. Why WebMCP matters WebMCP gives an external agent a bounded, structured view of actual game state. It does not have to guess progress from pixels or inspect unrestricted internal data. The game reports the current phase, discovered evidence, relevant errors and permitted assistance. Zero relevant errors means SILENT and refusal of a hint request. One permits NUDGE ; two or more permit GUIDE . Hints are selected by deterministic game rules, not freely generated by a language model. In the 1682 demonstration, an order goes to the wrong recipient. A real request_hint call returns a reading strategy, not the recipient's name. A later sequence error in 1919 produces a different method hint. The player makes the next choice. How we built it Native HTML, CSS and JavaScript ES modules support a pure state reducer and filtered public projection. The static game needs no account, backend, database or API key. Five tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(): get_mission_state reads filtered state and assistance policy. inspect_evidence examines one to six discovered observations. request_hint requests policy-bounded help. compare_evidence compares two or three discovered observations. submit_hypothesis submits an available hypothesis to normal domain validation. JSON Schema describes inputs; runtime validation and abort signals enforce boundaries. Read tools do not change progress. A valid hypothesis may advance through the normal reducer, but cannot force success, bypass prerequisites or ask for hidden solutions. Challenges and what we learned The main challenge was making assistance useful without replacing historical reasoning. Each era needs a different puzzle, while the agent needs one coherent contract. Filtering discovered evidence, enforcing error thresholds and validating every action matter more than offering unrestricted context. We also kept filming evidence honest: cards labelled RECORDED TOOL RESPONSE are editorial layouts of actual recorded responses, not invented game UI or a simulated autonomous conversation. Filming begins at chapter checkpoints; the video is not an uninterrupted public playthrough. Validation and limitations The reviewed local candidate passed 97 automated tests . Eight boundary tests cover repeated errors, hidden evidence, prerequisites, cancellation, restart and final-fragment idempotence. After the contemporary visual replacement, 17 affected tests passed , and the arrival/welcome interactions were checked in Edge. There is no persistent save : reloading starts a clean game. Tool filtering is not source-code secrecy; the JavaScript remains inspectable. We do not claim measured learning outcomes or universal browser compatibility. Media and provenance The 2:40 jury film uses the author's approved English transcript, narrated by Charles through ElevenLabs . Historical illustrations are AI-assisted reconstructions, not archival photographs. Contemporary 2026 visuals in the prepared release use credited Official White House Photos by Daniel Torok , taken at Versailles on June 17, 2026. No endorsement is implied. Detailed credits and historical sources are included in the repository. Open source The project is released under the MIT License . The complete source code, assets, automated test suite and reproducible setup instructions are available in the linked public GitHub repository. What's next Broader player testing and accessibility refinement, while preserving the central boundary: assistance should help the player reason, not remove the reason to play.
