title: Agent-Native Newsroom Portal
pitch: An agent-native newsroom where editors and browser agents collaboratively move stories from draft to publication through 22 real WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An agent-native newsroom where editors and browser agents collaboratively move stories from draft to publication through 22 real WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates The Story Desk gives editors a complete view of the editorial pipeline, from draft and review through approval and publication. The Media Vault combines image discovery with licensing, allowed channels, attribution, expiration, and accessibility metadata. An approved story is blocked by an expired image license—a real newsroom problem that a WebMCP agent can detect and resolve. The Handoff Engine validates editorial, media-rights, attribution, accessibility, and publishing requirements before generating the handoff. A publishing payload is prepared through WebMCP and delivered only after the workflow passes validation and receives human approval. List of WebMCP tools available Inspiration A newsroom is a coordination machine. A story moves through many steps before it becomes publishable: assignment, drafting, editing, review, approval, media selection, rights verification, and finally handoff to a publishing system. Humans are good at navigating these workflows through interfaces. Agents face a different problem: a traditional website tells them what the interface looks like , but not necessarily what the application can do in a structured way. That led to a simple question: What would a newsroom look like if the website itself were designed for both people and agents? That question became Agent-Native Newsroom Portal . Instead of adding a chatbot to a newsroom, I built a newsroom whose actual capabilities can be exposed directly to external browser agents through WebMCP . What it does Agent-Native Newsroom Portal is an internal newsroom workspace built around three connected areas. Story Desk The Story Desk manages the editorial lifecycle from draft to publication. Editors can: Create and edit stories Assign stories to editors Submit stories for review Approve or request revisions Reorder the editorial run Track the complete story history The application enforces valid editorial state transitions instead of allowing arbitrary status changes. Media Vault The Media Vault manages newsroom images together with the metadata required to publish them safely. Each asset can contain: License information Allowed publishing channels Expiration dates Attribution requirements Photographer/source information Alt text This makes the workflow more useful than simply searching for an image. Can this image actually be used for this publication? The system can detect expired rights and identify usable replacement assets. Handoff Engine The Handoff Engine turns approved editorial content into publication-ready output. Before a story can be handed off, it validates: Editorial approval Editor assignment Headline and body content Media attachment Lead image Media rights Attribution Web publishing permissions Alt text Once the checks pass, the system generates a structured web publishing payload and can execute the simulated handoff. WebMCP The WebMCP layer is the core experiment. The application exposes 22 structured WebMCP tools covering newsroom operations such as: Finding and reading stories Creating and updating stories Approving stories Reordering stories Searching and inspecting media Checking media rights Replacing media Updating captions and alt text Renewing media licenses Validating publication readiness Preparing publishing payloads Executing the handoff There is deliberately no in-app chatbot . The website itself becomes agent-operable. A human editor can use the normal interface, while an external browser agent can use the same application capabilities through WebMCP. Both interact with the same underlying newsroom state. How we built it I built the application as a full-stack web product using: Next.js 16 React 19 TypeScript Tailwind CSS shadcn/ui Prisma SQLite for local development PostgreSQL in production Zustand The application is deployed on Vercel . The architecture separates the user interface, REST API routes, business logic, database, and WebMCP integration. One of the most important design decisions was to make the WebMCP tools use the same business-logic layer as the human UI . For example, approve_story , replace_story_media , and execute_web_handoff are not special demo-only operations. They perform real application operations and follow the same validation and workflow rules used by the normal interface. WebMCP tools are registered through the browser API: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool exposes structured inputs and structured results. I also seeded the application with realistic newsroom data, including expired media rights and valid replacement assets, so the agent workflow has real problems to discover and resolve. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering WebMCP tools. It was making them trustworthy . Once an external agent can change application state, the application needs strong rules around what the agent is allowed to do and when an operation should fail. For example: Editing an approved story should invalidate its previous approval. Expired media should not pass publication validation. Missing alt text should block publication. Invalid editorial transitions should be rejected. The final handoff should be validated again on the server. Another challenge was keeping human and agent interaction synchronized. When an agent changes the application, the human-facing UI must immediately reflect that change. Both paths therefore operate on the same underlying application state. Testing also uncovered a subtle bug in the media attachment flow. When isPrimary was omitted, it was being treated as false , which prevented the first attached image from automatically becoming the lead image. I fixed the API and WebMCP tool behavior and re-tested the workflow. For WebMCP testing, I used the Brave browser and the Chrome extension WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector while its free credits were available. I also used ChatGPT to help prepare the demo and GLM for additional WebMCP QA. I focused that external testing on the main workflow tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the project became more than a visual WebMCP demonstration. The application exposes a real, stateful agent workflow across the newsroom. The main publication path is: Create Story ↓ Update Story ↓ Editorial Review ↓ Approve ↓ Attach / Replace Media ↓ Check Rights ↓ Validate Publication ↓ Prepare Web Handoff ↓ Execute Handoff ↓ Published The agent can perform these operations through WebMCP without having to guess its way through the visual interface. We are also proud of the guardrails around agent actions. WebMCP is not treated as a back door around newsroom rules. Agent operations go through the same application logic and validation as human actions. The repository also includes an end-to-end WebMCP validation report covering the project's tool surface and failure handling. What we learned The biggest lesson was that building an agent-native application is different from adding AI to an existing application . The difficult question is not: “Where should I put the chatbot?” It is: “What should the agent actually be able to do?” Good WebMCP tools need meaningful boundaries, clear inputs, predictable outputs, validation, and safe failure behavior. I also learned that useful human-agent systems do not need to be completely autonomous. For a newsroom, the agent can investigate, prepare, validate, and execute structured work, while the human retains editorial judgment and final authority. That led to the interaction model at the heart of this project: The agent handles structured work. The human remains the decision-maker. Building the project also changed how I think about web applications. A website is not only a collection of screens and buttons. It can also expose a structured set of capabilities that other intelligent systems can understand and use. What's next for Agent-Native Newsroom Portal This project is a starting point for a larger agent-native newsroom. The next step would be to move beyond individual publishing tasks and let agents help coordinate the wider editorial operation. For example, a newsroom agent could: Monitor upcoming deadlines Identify stories at risk of missing publication Detect missing media or metadata Find unresolved workflow blockers Prepare recommended actions for editors Coordinate handoffs across publishing channels I would also like to connect the Handoff Engine to real publishing systems instead of the current simulated delivery flow. Another area I want to explore is agent permissions : allowing a newsroom to define which actions an agent can perform automatically and which actions always require explicit human approval. The long-term idea is simple: Don't build AI around the newsroom. Build the newsroom so humans and agents can work together inside it. That is the experiment behind Agent-Native Newsr

title: AgentWire
pitch: Dependency watch for production agents. Daily diffs of 48 MCP servers and the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini APIs, exposed as WebMCP tools so your browser agent and you work the same page.
about_excerpt: Dependency watch for production agents. Daily diffs of 48 MCP servers and the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini APIs, exposed as WebMCP tools so your browser agent and you work the same page. Like Comment Story Updates Six WebMCP tools on document.modelContext. Every agent call is logged with its arguments, latency and result, beside the human log. check_dependencies audits a pasted mcp.json in one call: 8 deps matched, 1 breaking. The page filters to that list, manifest redacted. The same function, called by an agent and by a person one click apart. Identical result, tagged HUMAN and AGENT in one log. What it is AgentWire watches the things production agents silently depend on — 48 MCP servers, the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini APIs, and the MCP spec, SDK and registry, 119 URLs in total — and diffs them every day: package manifests, tool lists in READMEs, JSON schemas, changelogs, deprecation pages. Each change is classified (version bump / schema / tools / changelog / content; info / notice / breaking) and stored with the line-level diff. Humans get a live change log and can save their own dependency list; the page immediately filters to its matches. Alert delivery ships with the pilot. With WebMCP, the agent running in your browser gets the same thing, from the same page, without an API key, an MCP server, or scraping. Why this use case fits WebMCP The people who need this data are already running agents, and the question they ask is naturally conversational and contextual: "did anything I depend on change since Friday?" , "is the Neon MCP server safe to bump?" , "show me the diff, then save this list." That is a tool-calling conversation, not a form-filling one. WebMCP lets the page itself be the tool surface: the six functions are registered on document.modelContext with JSON Schemas, use the same loaded data and PostgREST helper as the human UI, and the browser mediates the call. No separate MCP server to host, no credentials to hand out, no DOM scraping, and the page keeps working as a normal website for everyone without an agent. The read/write split also maps cleanly onto WebMCP's annotations: five tools are readOnlyHint: true and can be called freely; watch_dependencies is a write, is annotated as such, and its description tells the agent to confirm the email and list with the person before calling it. How it improves the user experience Audit your whole config in one call. The agent pastes your mcp.json into check_dependencies and gets back, per server, whether it is watched, what changed this week, and how many changes are breaking. The page filters itself to your list at the same time, so the person sees exactly what the agent is reasoning about. Fuzzy dependency lookup instead of scanning a table. check_dependency("claude-sonnet-4-5") resolves to the Anthropic API source; "github mcp" resolves to the official GitHub MCP server. The agent gets the last 30 days of changes and whether the most recent daily run fetched that source's URLs successfully, so "no changes" is distinguishable from "we couldn't check". Diff on demand. list_changes returns summaries; get_diff returns the stored - / + lines only when the agent decides a change matters. The agent can read the diff and tell you whether it affects your code path. Save and filter in one sentence. "Save these for me" becomes a watch_dependencies call with the deps the agent already knows you use. The list is stored and the page immediately filters to matching sources; alert delivery is not live yet and ships with the pilot. The page reacts to the agent. Tool calls mirror the relevant work into the UI: the severity chip flips, the matched source lights up, the diff row expands and scrolls into view, and a saved list fills the form and filters the change log. A small "Agent tools" panel lists the registered tools and logs every call live — tool, arguments, result, latency — so the person always sees what the agent did. What humans and agents can do together that wasn't possible before Before: a person opens the site, scans a table, copies package names into a form. Or an engineer builds a separate MCP server and API-key flow so an agent can query the data outside the browser, where the human can't see it. Now: person and agent share one page and one state. The person asks their browser agent "what changed in the MCP servers we use this week, and is any of it breaking?"; the agent passes the project's config to check_dependencies , reads anything important with get_diff , and the person watches each call land in the panel while the Mine filter shows the same list. The person decides, the agent saves their list with watch_dependencies , and the form shows exactly what was stored while the change log stays narrowed to matching sources. The panel's "▶ sample" buttons let a person run the same functions by hand, so both sides use one code path and one log. Potential impact The evidence pack records 25 changes across 13 sources since the Sept 1 baseline, including 2 classified breaking. One was change #19 for the official GitHub MCP Server, a tool-list change. The latest recorded daily run fetched all 119 watched URLs successfully with zero errors. Implementation Front end: a single static site/index.html (no build step). Data comes from Supabase PostgREST with a read-only publishable key; the only write is one insert into dependency_lists , guarded by row-level security. WebMCP: on load the page feature-detects document.modelContext (with navigator.modelContext as a fallback for older previews) and registers six tools with registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, annotations, execute }) . Input schemas use JSON Schema with enums, ranges and additionalProperties: false ; execute returns plain objects, which the browser serializes for the agent. Each tool's execute is wrapped so the call, arguments (with pasted manifest bodies redacted), result size and latency are appended to the on-page log, and so the tool can sync the UI (filter chips, Mine list, highlighted source, expanded diff, pre-filled form). Tools: list_changes({since_hours?, severity?, kind?}) , check_dependency({name}) (bigram + token-weighted fuzzy match across source name, id, npm and PyPI package names and model aliases; returns confidence and alternatives), list_sources({kind?}) , check_dependencies({deps?, manifest?, since_hours?}) , get_diff({diff_id}) , watch_dependencies({email, deps[], workflow?}) . Backend (unchanged for this challenge): a Deno edge function on Supabase fetches every watch URL daily via pg_cron, normalizes (npm/PyPI/registry JSON, HTML→text), hashes, multiset-line-diffs against the stored snapshot, classifies, and writes diffs rows. Testing: scripts/webmcp-smoke.mjs is a dependency-free script that launches Chrome with WebMCP enabled, asserts all six names, and has the browser invoke the five read tools plus structured-error cases through the DevTools WebMCP.invokeTool command — the same channel an agent uses. evidence/smoke_live_2026-09-03_final.txt is the current production transcript; docs/webmcp-test-log.md is historical four-tool evidence. Challenges The WebMCP docs disagreed on the namespace ( document.modelContext vs older navigator.modelContext ), so the page feature-detects both and was verified against Chrome 152 directly. Chrome's execute return value is JSON-serialized by the browser, which shaped the tools to return plain objects. Fuzzy matching model IDs like claude-sonnet-4-5 to an API source needed alias tables plus length-weighted token scoring so short tokens like "pro" don't outrank "gemini". Chrome also does not enforce a tool's inputSchema at runtime, so every tool re-validates its own arguments before building a query rather than trusting the declared enums and ranges. Prior work vs. work in the submission window The diff engine ( supabase/functions/run/index.ts ), schema ( supabase/migrations/0001_init.sql , applied 2026-09-01 per its header comment; the Supabase project was created 2026-09-01 22:36 UTC and took its first snapshots at 22:53 UTC, after the Aug 25 window start), the 48-source list and the original human page were built first. The WebMCP work is everything that touches an agent: the six current tools registered on document.modelContext , the UI mirroring and Mine filter, the Agent tools panel with its call log, the scripts/webmcp-smoke.mjs proof that has Chrome itself invoke the tools, and the real-agent demo pipeline in demo/ . All of it is in this repository's dated commit history, which starts 2026-09-02 10:38 CDT ( evidence/git_history.txt ). Limitations Severity is heuristic. "Breaking" is inferred from major version bumps, removed tools or schema fields, and changelog wording; it can over- or under-call. Every change links to the source line so a person can check. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Cadding
pitch: Cadding makes CAD as easy as describing what you want. Create, edit, and export 3D-printable parts with AI, directly in your browser.
about_excerpt: Cadding makes CAD as easy as describing what you want. Create, edit, and export 3D-printable parts with AI, directly in your browser. Like Comment Story Updates Wheel Iphone Cover WebMCP in action Inspiration Cadding was built to make real CAD work faster and more accessible for people who want to design real, 3D-printable objects without having to master complex traditional CAD software. Our goal is not simply to generate 3D meshes from text. Cadding is a browser-based CAD environment where users can create and modify precise, editable geometry, work with multiple parts, and prepare designs that can actually be manufactured and 3D printed. For the WebMCP Challenge, we wanted to take this one step further: make the same CAD environment accessible to external AI agents such as Codex . What we built For the challenge, we connected Cadding's CAD system to WebMCP and exposed 35 structured CAD tools to external agents. These tools give an agent access to a large part of the real Cadding modelling workflow. An agent can: Inspect the complete live CAD scene and understand existing parts Read exact dimensions, parameters, faces, edges and vertices Create primitives and profile-based geometry using extrusions, revolves, sweeps and lofts Change dimensions, positions, rotations and other editable parameters Add holes, fillets, shells and other features Perform boolean operations between parts Create linear and circular patterns Edit topology Align, assemble and mate multiple components Add mechanical connectors and joints Work directly with the same editable CAD scene that the user sees A typical agent workflow can look like: $$ \texttt{cad.get_scene} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.inspect_part} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.get_faces} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.add_profile_shape} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.edit_part} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.fillet_edges} $$ This is important because the agent is not generating an isolated mesh, and it is not trying to control Cadding by guessing where to click. Through WebMCP, the agent operates the actual modelling system using structured CAD operations. Every operation happens inside the live Cadding project, so the human and the AI agent are working on the same editable model . How we built it One of the most important parts of Cadding is the Cadding API . We originally developed this API to give our own AI agent a simple and reliable way to interact with the CAD editor. For the WebMCP Challenge, we extended that architecture so external agents could use the same modelling capabilities. Instead of building a small set of WebMCP-specific demo commands, we connected WebMCP directly to Cadding's canonical CAD API. The architecture is: $$ \text{External Agent} \rightarrow \text{WebMCP} \rightarrow \text{Cadding API} \rightarrow \text{CAD Engine} \rightarrow \text{Live Editable Scene} $$ This means the WebMCP integration is not a separate prototype sitting next to Cadding. It is an interface into the real CAD system . An external agent can first understand what exists: $$ \texttt{cad.get_scene} + \texttt{cad.inspect_part} + \texttt{cad.get_parameters} $$ and then act on that information using operations such as: $$ \texttt{cad.add_shape}, \quad \texttt{cad.add_hole}, \quad \texttt{cad.boolean_parts}, \quad \texttt{cad.mate_parts} $$ This allows agents to chain multiple operations together to build and modify much more complex objects. Biggest challenge The biggest challenge while building both the Cadding AI agent and the WebMCP integration was making every CAD step extremely easy for an AI model to understand and execute correctly. CAD becomes complex very quickly. An agent needs to reason about dimensions, coordinate systems, part relationships, faces, edges, transformations, feature order, boolean operations, assemblies and the constantly changing state of the model. In simple terms: $$ \text{Reliable AI CAD} \text{Clear Tools} + \text{Precise Geometry Context} + \text{Predictable Execution} $$ Because of this, we spent a significant amount of time improving the Cadding API itself . Our goal was to hide as much unnecessary CAD-engine complexity as possible and turn modelling actions into clear, predictable and structured operations. Instead of expecting an AI model to understand the internal implementation of a CAD engine, we expose actions that map directly to the modelling intent: Create a part Inspect its dimensions Get its faces or edges Add a hole to a specific face Resize an existing body Round selected edges Subtract one body from another Pattern a component Align two parts Mate two faces together We also worked extensively on stable identifiers, constrained parameters, clear tool descriptions, validation and useful execution feedback. This work was critical for making both Cadding's own AI agent and external WebMCP agents more reliable. What we learned One of our biggest learnings was that giving an AI model access to tools is not enough . The way those tools are designed has a huge impact on how capable the agent becomes. We found that: $$ \text{Agent Quality} \propto \text{Quality of the Tool Interface} $$ Complex software like CAD contains a large amount of implicit state and domain knowledge. If the interface presented to the AI is ambiguous, the agent quickly becomes unreliable. By spending months making the Cadding API easier for AI models to reason about, we were able to turn increasingly complex CAD workflows into structured actions that agents can understand and combine. WebMCP allowed us to take that same agent-friendly CAD interface and make it accessible to external agents. The result is a shared CAD workspace where humans and AI agents can work together on the same real, editable and 3D-printable models . title: CivicFlow: A WebMCP Public Benefit Portal
pitch: CivicFlow helps people complete complex public-benefit applications with a voice companion, while WebMCP lets browser agents assist safely through structured tools.
about_excerpt: CivicFlow helps people complete complex public-benefit applications with a voice companion, while WebMCP lets browser agents assist safely through structured tools. Like Comment Story Updates The first page of the CivicFlow Human Submitted Form Human Submitted Form Agent Companion Widget CivicFlow WebMCP Tool Registry Conversing with the Agent for a task Draft prepared by the Agent for Human Review Reviewable Agent Activity Inspiration I work at Optum as a software engineer, developing and maintaining the State of Massachusetts Health Care Exchange Portal. I know that system through and through, so I also know this: applying from start to finish takes hours of concentration and focus. That is true for individuals, assisters, and human agents alike. That is why it immediately clicked for me: this is a massive opportunity to upgrade US healthcare benefits sites, so faster eligibility submissions can lead to faster benefits for every citizen. I am going to showcase this demo I made for the hackathon to my project leadership as well. What it does CivicFlow is a demo public-benefits portal. A person can fill out six sections: About You, Household, Income, Current Coverage, Documents, and Review & Sign. A browser agent can work on that same form through WebMCP, instead of guessing from the page layout. The agent can check what is left, jump to a section, add a household member or income source, set current coverage, look at demo document status, and review what is blocking submit. There is also an optional Gemini Live companion for voice or chat. If the companion wants to change something, it has to wait for the person to click Save change, Need correction, or Cancel. Talking is not enough. This is a fictional local demo. Submit Demo is human-only, stays on the device, and does not call a real government system. There is no real eligibility, enrollment, document upload, or agent submit. How we built it I built CivicFlow with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The form, the WebMCP tools, and the Gemini companion all go through the same app state. That way the agent cannot take a side path the person cannot see. There are ten typed tools. Seven are always there. The other three only show up when they make sense, like when a household member is selected or the person is on Review & Sign. The page registers those tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , and it updates the list when the current section or selection changes. Gemini only sees the tools that are available right now. It still has to pass schema checks, and any write waits for a button click. The Gemini API key stays on the server. If WebMCP or voice is not available, the normal form still works. I used Vitest and Playwright to cover the main flow and the safety rules. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not adding more tools. It was making sure help never turned into silent control. The form, the browser agent, and the voice companion had to share one state, with no hidden shortcut around validation or human review. Contextual tools were also tricky. They have to show up and disappear as the person moves around the form. And a successful tool call means nothing if the person cannot see what changed, so I added the floating companion, a speaking cue, the current tool list, operation status, and an activity history. Keeping the Gemini key on the server, while still letting the demo work without voice, was another one. Accomplishments that we're proud of What I am most proud of is getting a realtime voice agent to talk to the site tools. You can ask for help out loud, and it can guide you through the form without typing. That is the part that feels closest to how I wish benefits sites worked. I also think this can help people with vision or other disabilities, because they would not have to hunt through a long form just to make progress. The other piece I really liked building is the draft popup during realtime voice. The companion can propose a change, but it does not silently write it. A confirmation card shows up first, and you still choose Save change, Need correction, or Cancel. That small pause is what kept voice helpful instead of scary. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it is part of the product, not a shortcut around the UI. Clear tool names, schemas, and contextual tools tell the agent what it can do. Visible confirmation and activity history help the person trust it, and step in if something looks wrong. I also learned that the page still has to be a good form on its own. If WebMCP or voice is down, a person should still be able to finish the demo by hand. What's next for CivicFlow: A WebMCP Public Benefit Portal Next, I want to put this in front of people who actually fill out long benefits forms, and keep improving accessibility and the “did that change what I think it changed?” feedback. I also want to take the demo to Optum leadership and talk about whether this pattern could help real healthcare benefits sites. Connecting to real program rules, identity, uploads, eligibility, or live submit is a much bigger security and policy project. That is not part of this hackathon demo. title: Co-Cart
pitch: An AI shopping decision assistant that uses WebMCP to compare live Shopify products, explain trade-offs, and propose the best choice—with voice-first accessibility.
about_excerpt: An AI shopping decision assistant that uses WebMCP to compare live Shopify products, explain trade-offs, and propose the best choice—with voice-first accessibility. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I asked an AI assistant to find wireless headphones under $50. It returned five polished recommendations: prices, brands, pros, cons, all written with confidence. Three of them did not exist. Not “out of stock.” Completely made up. That problem gets worse for people who cannot easily see a screen, use a mouse, or type a detailed search query. If shopping is already difficult to navigate visually, an AI assistant that invents products or silently makes decisions is not helpful; it is another barrier. Co-Cart began with two questions: How can an AI agent shop without inventing what it found? How can someone who cannot see or type comfortably still control that shopping experience? The answer is a shared human-and-agent shopping layer. For a person using the screen, Co-Cart provides simple decision cards and a verified shortlist. For a person who is blind, low-vision, has limited motor control, cannot type, or simply needs hands-free help, Co-Cart provides a voice-first path through the same experience. The agent reads choices aloud, accepts spoken answers, explains results, and prepares cart changes, but it never takes away the shopper's final decision. For a WebMCP-enabled browser agent, Co-Cart exposes 13 structured tools. Instead of scraping pixels, guessing which button matters, or inventing product details, an agent can read the visible shopping state, answer the same questions, run the verified search flow, inspect real results, and propose safe cart actions. The human sees the experience. The voice user hears the experience. The browser agent uses the experience. All three operate on the same truth. What it does Co-Cart is an accessible, human-in-the-loop shopping assistant for meals, gadgets, and clothing. When Co-Cart loads in a WebMCP-enabled browser or agent host, it silently registers 13 tools using navigator.modelContext . This lets an agent do useful work safely: Read the current shopping state ↓ Choose a category ↓ Answer the same visible decision cards ↓ Start the real OpenAI → Shopify search ↓ Read verified live results ↓ Highlight recommended products ↓ Propose a cart addition, removal, or swap ↓ Wait for the human to approve or reject it ### 2. A voice-first shopping flow for people who cannot see or type The hands-free mode is a core feature, not a voice-search add-on. A shopper can use speech to: - Hear what screen they are currently on - Hear each available choice read aloud - Answer decision questions without touching a keyboard - Start the live Shopify search - Hear the recommended products, prices, merchants, and tradeoffs - Ask the agent to repeat information - Create cart proposals safely - Approve or reject important actions with explicit spoken phrases This matters for blind and low-vision users, people with motor impairments, users with temporary injuries, and anyone unable to use a conventional screen-and-keyboard shopping flow. The microphone remains **off by default**. It only starts after the shopper explicitly enables hands-free mode. Most importantly, voice users are not pushed into a limited fallback experience. Voice mode uses the same live Shopify catalogue, the same verified product facts, the same WebMCP-style guarded tools, and the same human approval rules as the visual interface. ## What it does Co-Cart is a human-in-the-loop shopping assistant for meals, gadgets, and clothing. A shopper answers six simple questions, such as: - What are you trying to buy? - What matters most: best value, crowd favourite, hidden gem, or industry standard? - What is your budget? - Where should it arrive? Then Co-Cart: 1. Starts a real OpenAI shopping agent. 2. Searches Shopify Global Catalogue through MCP. 3. Verifies product facts from the merchant data. 4. Shows a short, explained list of options with tradeoffs. 5. Lets the shopper add products or approve/reject agent-made cart proposals. 6. Opens the real merchant checkout only when the shopper is ready. It also includes a hands-free voice experience for people who cannot comfortably see, point at, or type into a typical shopping interface. The voice agent can read options aloud, accept spoken answers, describe live results, and create proposals using the same guarded tools and safety rules as the visual experience. ## WebMCP: the agent action layer WebMCP is central to Co-Cart. WebMCP does **not** come with a fixed list of tools that every website must use. Instead, it gives a website a browser API — `navigator.modelContext` — for declaring its own safe, structured capabilities to an AI agent. Co-Cart uses WebMCP to register **17 custom shopping tools** designed specifically for this experience. They let a WebMCP-enabled browser agent: - Read the current shopping state - Choose Meals, Gadgets, or Clothing - Answer individual decision cards - Answer an entire shopping brief in one batch call - Start the verified OpenAI → Shopify search - Read live, server-verified results - Inspect individual products - Highlight recommended products for the shopper - Read the cart and its separate currency totals - Check dietary, allergen, or numeric constraints - Save shopping preferences - Propose cart additions, removals, and swaps The agent does not get a hidden admin mode. Every WebMCP tool maps to an action or state the shopper can see in the interface. The visual UI, voice mode, and WebMCP tools all use the same shared shopping state. ```text WebMCP itself Co-Cart ───────────── ─────── Provides the browser API Defines 14 shopping-specific tools Does not prescribe tool names Chooses only actions useful for shopping Connects page and agent Shares state with the visible UI ## How we built it Co-Cart is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, OpenAI, Shopify Global Catalogue MCP, WebMCP, and Netlify Functions. The main architecture is: ```text Human UI + WebMCP tools ↓ Shared Zustand state ↓ Netlify server function ↓ OpenAI Responses API agent ↓ Validated Shopify MCP calls ↓ Verified Shopify product data ↓ Shortlist, tradeoffs, and cart proposals The most important design choice is that the agent does not directly control Shopify or write product facts. The agent can select Shopify variant IDs and explain its reasoning. The server validates every tool call, retrieves the corresponding Shopify data, and reconstructs the product title, price, seller, image, and links from the verified response. For WebMCP, Co-Cart silently registers 13 browser tools through navigator.modelContext . A WebMCP-enabled agent can: Read the current shopping state Select a category Answer visible decision cards Start the live search Read verified results Highlight products Propose add/remove/swap cart changes Check cart constraints The key idea is that the human UI and agent tool layer use the same state. The agent does not get a secret admin mode. If it changes a decision, the UI updates accordingly. If it proposes a cart action, the shopper still approves or rejects it. For the demo experience, we also captured genuine live Shopify search results for three default paths. These replay in about two seconds with a visible search sequence. Any changed answer falls back to a real live search. Challenges we ran into Making AI recommendations trustworthy The obvious first version was to let the model return a JSON list with names, prices, and merchants. That was risky. Even a very capable model can produce plausible but inaccurate facts. We changed the design so that the model only chooses IDs from Shopify tool output. The server rejects any selected ID that Shopify did not return. Keeping agent autonomy safe An agent that can search should not automatically be able to buy. Co-Cart separates confirmed cart items from agent proposals. An agent can recommend an addition, removal, or swap, but the shopper must explicitly approve it. Checkout always goes to the merchant; Co-Cart never submits payment. Making voice genuinely accessible We did not want voice mode to be a weaker fallback. It uses the same live-search pipeline, verified product data, cart guardrails, and approval rules as the visual interface. The microphone also stays off until the shopper explicitly starts hands-free mode. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built a real WebMCP action layer with 13 guarded browser tools . Made the WebMCP tools invisible in the product UI, so the experience remains simple for regular shoppers. Ensured every displayed product fact is verified from live Shopify data rather than generated by the model. Added explicit human approval for every agent-initiated cart change. Built an accessible voice-first flow for people who cannot see or type comfortably. Prevented misleading multi-currency totals by keeping each currency subtotal separate. Added tests for the trust boundaries: rejected mod

title: CommerceGov: Governed AI Commerce via WebMCP
pitch: WebMCP lets AI agents interact with Shopify stores through a governed workflow - without giving them authority to change production. Capability is not authority.
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets AI agents interact with Shopify stores through a governed workflow - without giving them authority to change production. Capability is not authority. Like Comment Story Updates AI agent can inspect, but cannot change production. Inspiration (Why you built it) Capability is not authority. Shopify agencies want AI to draft catalog changes. They cannot afford AI that publishes them. One bad catalog change can hit a live store, paid traffic, and brand trust. That is a control problem, not a model-quality problem. WebMCP makes websites directly usable by agents through structured tools. But as agent capabilities expand, applications need a hard boundary between “prepare a change” and “write production.” CommerceGov focuses on that boundary. The agent gets enough capability to discover, inspect, and propose changes, but it does not get authority to change production state — it cannot approve or apply without human review. What it does (The core solution) CommerceGov puts a ChatGPT agent inside the same governed commerce workflow used by human operators — while keeping production authority outside the agent. The agent searches the shop, reads policy and governance state, proposes a change, and creates a Review proposal. Authorized operators review, approve, and apply according to CommerceGov’s workflow and role boundaries. Only then may CommerceGov’s worker write to Shopify. The agent cannot approve, apply, or mutate Shopify production. Those capabilities are not exposed through WebMCP. For Shopify agencies, this means AI can assist with daily catalog operations without receiving direct production authority. Agencies keep control over clearances, review, approval, and the history of governed changes. Live path: ChatGPT selects openai-webmcp-hackathon.myshopify.com , finds The Complete Snowboard , proposes changing the title to The Complete Snowboard — WebMCP Proof , creates a Review proposal, and retrieves its status and audit evidence. Production stays unchanged. How we built it (The technical stack) The backend is Python FastAPI. The operator UI is server-rendered, and Shopify writes go through a CommerceGov worker rather than the agent or browser. The application is hosted on Render at app.commercegov.io . We implemented WebMCP as a bounded tool surface, not a wrapper around the full CommerceGov API. The page's modelContext exposes five tools: search_products get_governance_context propose_change get_change_status get_audit_evidence We deliberately omit approve, apply, and Shopify production-write tools. The agent therefore has no WebMCP handle to invoke them. Each tool is bound to the authenticated shop and target. Proposal status and audit retrieval resolve to the exact proposal the agent created rather than silently switching to a newer object. Production-mutating tools are absent, not merely permission-gated after the fact. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was identity and authority: keeping tenant, shop, product, and proposal bound across tool calls while ensuring that a request for status or audit evidence cannot silently jump to a newer object. We addressed this by keeping the WebMCP surface deliberately small, excluding production-authority tools entirely, and resolving status and audit evidence against the exact proposal created by the agent. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent can perform useful catalog work while people retain risk, approval, and production control. The result is one collaboration workflow: agent discovers → agent proposes → human authority → governed apply → Shopify The WebMCP interaction ends before production authority begins. What's next for CommerceGov Next are richer policy explanations, stronger proposal diffs, and more governed mutation classes — under the same rule. WebMCP may add capability. It may not add production authority. title: Seedy Research
pitch: We make un-agentable archives agentable.
about_excerpt: We make un-agentable archives agentable. Like Comment Story Updates An agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser calls discover_research The agent calls build_research_path and the human's Research Path updates in place. Every supported claim resolves to a real page in a real NCCE volume. Verifiable, not generated — click through and read the Thai original. Inspiration Every AI agent shipping today can search the web. None of them can read Thailand's research output. Thailand's National Convention on Civil Engineering has run for decades. The proceedings exist as PDFs. Mixed encodings, no text layer on older scans, no cross-volume search, no API. To an agent, this archive does not exist. So a graduate student surveying prior work does it the 2005 way: download a volume, Ctrl-F, guess Thai keyword variants, repeat. Then their advisor asks "has anyone already done this?" and nobody can answer with confidence. Point a general-purpose agent at it and you get the worst possible failure mode: a citation that looks right. A fake page number inside a real volume survives review. It gets published. That's the wedge. Not "search is bad." The archive has no interface an agent can hold onto, and the substitute agents invent is dangerous. Three things made now the moment to build it: Agents got good enough to be trusted with research tasks — and therefore dangerous enough that unverifiable citations became a liability, not a quirk. WebMCP made the browser a distribution channel for tools. Before this, an agent-facing corpus meant getting into someone's MCP config. Now it means shipping a URL you can send to a professor. Retrieval got cheap enough to run at national scale. Our full stack runs under \$10/month. Archives held by underfunded institutions only get digitized if the running cost rounds to zero. ## What it does Seedy Research is a research workspace over an indexed Thai corpus — CE Project archives and NCCE Proceedings vol. 25, 26, and 29 — that exposes itself to any agent in the page. Surface What it does Agent-callable Explore Thai-first discovery; local = page-cited evidence, global = links only ✅ Chat Cited answers, paragraph-level retrieval ✅ Workspace Shared state: saved passages, comparisons, candidate gap ✅ read + write Research Path Evidence → connection → gap → testable next study ✅ Share & export Session URL, JSON export of the full evidence trail ✅ Every surface is agent-callable. That's deliberate. A workspace the agent can't write to is a workspace the human maintains alone. What people and agents can now do together that was hard or impossible before: Ask across 941 Thai PDFs and get a page you can open. The agent calls a tool, the passage renders with volume and page, and the human clicks through to the Thai original. Cross-language research without losing the source. The corpus is Thai. The agent reasons and answers in English while every citation still points at the Thai page. Co-author a gap statement. Human sets direction, agent fills evidence into the shared workspace, human prunes. Every line traceable. Hand off a session, not a transcript. JSON export or session URL — the next person, or the next agent, resumes with the same evidence set. ## How we built it We built the server-side MCP version first. It was the wrong product. A server-side MCP server hands an agent a database. It returns a string: "NCCE vol. 26, p. 412 reports a 14% reduction." The researcher then has two options — trust it, or go find volume 26 themselves. Neither one is research. WebMCP hands the agent the application . The agent calls our tool, the passage renders in the human's Evidence panel at that page in the original Thai, and then the tool returns to the agent. Verification stops being a task and becomes a glance. Same retrieval engine, completely different product. The tool layer. Next.js 15 on Vercel. Tools register client-side from a provider that mounts on session init. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "search_evidence", description: "Search the indexed Thai research corpus and return paragraph-level passages " + "with exact volume and page citations. Use for any claim that needs citing. " + "Do NOT use to find papers outside the indexed corpus — use " + "discover_related_research for that.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { query: { type: "string" }, collection: { enum: ["all", "ce_project", "ncce"] }, max_passages: { type: "integer", minimum: 1, maximum: 20 } }, required: ["query"] }, execute: async ({ query, collection = "all", max_passages = 6 }) => { const passages = await retrieve({ query, collection, max_passages }); setEvidencePanel(passages); // the human sees it first return { content: [{ type: "text", text: formatWithCitations(passages) }] }; } }); Two contracts hold the design together: Render before return. execute writes app state, then returns to the agent. One line of ordering separates a shared session from a remote control. We did not wrap our API. We shipped the verbs a researcher uses. Closed domains are enums, so agents produce a valid call on the first attempt instead of probing. Tool What it does for the agent search_evidence Page-cited paragraph retrieval over the local corpus answer_with_citations Cited answer through the bounded-context planner open_source_page Opens a document at a specific page for the human discover_related_research Metadata-only global discovery — no quotable field save_to_workspace Writes a passage into shared state list_workspace Reads back current shared state build_research_path Evidence → connection → gap → next study set_collection_filter Scopes the session to a collection export_session Full evidence trail as JSON Under the tool boundary. ChatGPT / Chrome agent │ document.modelContext.registerTool() ▼ Next.js 15 (Vercel) ── WebMCP tool layer ──► app state (Evidence, Workspace) │ ▼ FastAPI ── Bounded Agentic Context ──► planner → dedup → context budget │ → citation formatting ▼ Supabase pgvector — 49,965 chunks, page provenance preserved end to end The Bounded Agentic Context layer is our real engineering asset. A planner decides retrieval depth, deduplicates overlapping chunks, manages a context budget, and formats citations before anything reaches a model. The agent makes one call and gets clean, budgeted, citation-formatted results. All the expensive judgment lives inside the tool where we can guarantee it, instead of hoping the calling agent gets it right — and every future agent client inherits that for free. Collection PDFs Chunks CE Project Database 67 4,520 NCCE Database 874 45,445 Total 941 49,965 Auth, rate limiting, timeout control. Under \$10/month. Trust boundary and user control. Exposing tools means letting something else act inside a logged-in session, so we treated that as a product decision: Reads are free; writes are visible. Retrieval is frictionless. Anything that mutates shared state renders immediately and is reversible in one click. Nobody has to audit a log to learn what happened. No tool escalates scope. No generic fetch , no run_query , no arbitrary endpoint. Closed argument spaces, enums where the domain is closed. The surface an agent sees is exactly the surface we intend. Tools register with the session, not the origin. They mount after session init and unmount with the surfaces backing them. Nothing destructive is exposed. The worst outcome of a confused agent is a workspace with extra passages in it. Export is explicit. export_session returns to the human's session; it transmits nowhere. That posture is the precondition for institutional adoption. A university will not put its archive behind an agent that can delete things. When things go wrong. A demo that only shows the happy path isn't a product: Ambiguous requests get a question, not a guess. Scope-ambiguous queries return zero passages with an explicit note instead of weak matches. Agents route correctly on retry. Empty results are a real answer. "Nothing in the indexed corpus supports this" is returned as such. For a gap-finding tool, absence is the product. Budget overruns degrade rather than fail. Cap and deduplicate, never truncate mid-passage. Fewer complete citations, not more broken ones. Timeouts return partial evidence with a flag, so slow retrieval still yields something citable rather than an error the agent narrates as fact. ## Challenges we ran into Thai PDFs are hostile. Mixed encodings, no text layer on older scans, heading structure that shifts between NCCE volumes. Keeping page numbers alive through chunking, so a citation is actually clickable , was harder than retrieval itself. Page fidelity across the tool boundary. Volume and page must survive pgvector → planner → JSON tool result → UI panel. Any layer that drops that metadata breaks the only promise we make. Most retrieval systems lose citability here, and we had to rebuild our chunker to stop doing the same. Context budget versus completeness. Twenty passages makes an agent confident and wrong. title: Dust Off
pitch: An AI piano teacher that listens to your playing, gives feedback, and creates lessons you can practise anytime.
about_excerpt: An AI piano teacher that listens to your playing, gives feedback, and creates lessons you can practise anytime. Like Comment Story Updates Screenshot of site Inspiration A MIDI keyboard can sit unused because its owner doesn’t know what to practise or whether they’re improving. Dust Off turns that instrument into a shared workspace with an AI teacher that can demonstrate, respond to real playing, and prepare the next exercise. What it does Dust Off helps beginners learn through short, interactive exercises. The agent highlights notes with finger numbers, plays a demonstration, and reads the student’s notes, timing, and velocity to give feedback. It can also save personalised lessons. These stay in the library, where the app demonstrates, listens, and grades independently. Students can use a physical MIDI controller, computer keyboard, or on-screen keys. How we built it We built Dust Off with plain JavaScript, Web Audio, Web MIDI, and WebMCP, hosted on Netlify. WebMCP tools such as show_notes, play_notes, listen, and save_lesson let the agent work directly with the piano page. The page handles musical timing and analysis, while the agent decides what to teach. Lessons and practice observations are stored locally. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was browser compatibility: Codex’s in-app browser supported WebMCP calls but did not grant MIDI access, while Chrome supported our MIDI controller. We built a small local Node.js relay that forwards Chrome’s hardware input into the same Codex piano page where WebMCP operates. Real testing also exposed duplicate events from mirrored MIDI ports, premature phrase endings while beginners searched for keys, and outdated performance results after a listening window closed. Accomplishments that we're proud of We demonstrated a complete interaction with a real MIDI keyboard: the agent taught an exercise, demonstrated notes, read physical playing, gave feedback, and saved a personalised lesson. We also completed an independent chord lesson and reviewed its results with the agent. What we learned Musical timing belongs in the application, not in model round trips. WebMCP works well when tools represent meaningful actions—demonstrate a phrase, analyse a performance, save a lesson—rather than individual clicks. Testing with a real beginner also showed how important patience and clear feedback are. What's next for Dust Off We want to simplify hardware setup, improve phrase capture and progress tracking, and make saved lessons easier to share across browsers. We’ll also expand exercises for chord transitions, rhythm, and even touch while keeping practice approachable for beginners. title: Edgewright
pitch: A redirect console a human and an agent drive together, over WebMCP. Test, audit and fix routing across 11 hosts, then prove a migration never breaks a link.
about_excerpt: A redirect console a human and an agent drive together, over WebMCP. Test, audit and fix routing across 11 hosts, then prove a migration never breaks a link. Like Comment Story Updates Edgewright turns your redirect and rewrite rules into a live console a human and an AI agent work together, over WebMCP. Test any URL, catch the rule that shadows another, translate a config to another host, then prove nothing breaks, all in the browser. The problem: redirect rules are ordered and first-match-wins. A broad rule above a specific one makes the specific one dead code, so a link works locally then 404s in production. Edgewright makes that visible and fixable, by a person or by an agent on the same page. How the tools are used: the console registers fifteen tools with document.modelContext.registerTool. In the demo the agent runs test_url to find the 404, audit_rules to name the shadowed rule, reorder_rule to fix the order, then test_url again. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint so the agent runs them without a prompt. The tools that change rules omit it, so the agent asks first. The UI and the tools mutate one shared store, so a human clicking a button and an agent calling a tool run the exact same code. The product is three apps on one engine: the Console, Preflight (a pre-deploy gate), and Studio (migrate a config between hosts and prove every URL still resolves). Live: https://edgewright.vercel.app Source: https://github.com/zkasuran/edgewright Video: https://youtu.be/8Hry7ozQTe8 Built for the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge. The engine, @edgewright/core, covers eleven hosting platforms grounded in their own docs, with 148 passing tests, no build and no dependencies. For platforms whose routing is code, like Fastly and CloudFront, the engine resolves the trivial static patterns and labels the rest as not-simulated rather than guessing. Everything shown in the demo is the deployed product on the live URL or a real source file. The narration is synthesised speech. The design, the code, the review and the verification are the author's. title: GotPaid Agent Desk
pitch: An invoice-reconciliation dashboard humans and AI agents use together — agents query receivables, point at rows in your view, and draft chaser letters you review, via 8 WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An invoice-reconciliation dashboard humans and AI agents use together — agents query receivables, point at rows in your view, and draft chaser letters you review, via 8 WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates GotPaid dashboard — 8 WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool Agent calls a tool live — the human sees exactly what their agent just did Inspiration I run a Thai agri-export company that invoices Chinese buyers in USD/CNY. Every month a deposit lands with the wrong amount and a useless reference — "INWARD REMIT REF 88213" — and I have to guess which invoice it was, work out how much the bank silently skimmed, and remember which client always pays like this. I already built GotPaid to fix that. For this challenge, I asked a narrower question: reconciliation questions ("which buyer is slipping?", "why did this deposit match that invoice?") only really make sense pointed at a real row on a real screen — so what if the agent helping me could act inside the dashboard I'm already looking at, instead of just answering in a disconnected chat window? What it does GotPaid reconciles cross-border invoice payments against messy bank deposits — tolerant of hidden fees, batched payments, and split payments — learns each buyer's payment behavior over time, and surfaces what's still unpaid. The WebMCP layer adds 8 tools so a human and an AI agent can work the same dashboard together: the agent reads structured data (no screen-scraping — an embedded JSON island), switches tabs and flashes the exact row it's talking about in the human's own view, and drafts a chaser letter that opens on screen for review. Nothing is ever sent automatically — the agent proposes, the human decides, both looking at the same thing. That's the gap WebMCP closes: before, an agent could only describe what's on screen; now it can point at it. How we built it Python renders a static dashboard ( dashboard.py ) with all data baked into an embedded JSON script tag. On top of that, 8 tools are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() : 5 read-only ( list_companies , list_unpaid_invoices , get_buyer_profile , explain_match , get_dashboard_totals ) and 3 UI-action tools ( show_company , highlight_invoice , draft_chaser_letter ) that manipulate the DOM the human is looking at. Every tool call is echoed to an on-page "Agent activity" log so the human always sees what their agent just did. Deployed static on Cloudflare Pages — no server, no build step. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new — Chrome support is flag-gated ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), so I had to design a graceful fallback banner rather than assume every judge has it enabled. I also had to resist just exposing raw data dumps as tools; the ones that ended up mattering most act in the human's view (highlight, draft) rather than just answering questions in text. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working execute implementation behind every tool — not stubs — verified end-to-end (filtering, cross-company lookups, a chaser letter that actually reflects a buyer's real payment history) before ever opening Chrome's WebMCP flag. And keeping the human-in-the-loop boundary hard: the letter tool drafts and opens for review, it never sends. What we learned A "reasonable-sounding" tool surface (just dump every field as a tool) is worse than a smaller set of tools that do something in the human's view. Also: sponsor sandboxes don't always match their public docs — worth verifying the live account rather than trusting documentation alone when they disagree. What's next for GotPaid Agent Desk GotPaid already plugs into my company's deployed durian-export platform (2 awards at the Nanning ASEAN summit). This WebMCP layer is the template for making the rest of that platform agent-native — inventory, grading, logistics — all queryable and actionable by an agent working alongside the person actually running the business. Claude (via Claude Code) was my engineering execution partner throughout, including debugging the Chrome flag / managed-browser activation issue live. title: Gulawo Tendering Workspace with a Built-in WebMCP Agent
pitch: An AI agent lives inside Gulawo: it finds open tenders, scores fit, checks your document vault, flags disqualifying deviations, and drafts proposals you approve before anything is saved.
about_excerpt: An AI agent lives inside Gulawo: it finds open tenders, scores fit, checks your document vault, flags disqualifying deviations, and drafts proposals you approve before anything is saved. Like Comment Story Updates demo demo demo Inspiration East African SME contractors don't lose government tenders on price. They lose on a missing PPDA certificate. A deadline buried in a procurement portal. A compliance gap nobody caught until it was too late. That admin, the finding, the tracking, the checking, the paperwork, is exactly what beat the teams that could actually do the work. Gulawo exists to close that gap. What it does A contractor signs in, uploads a real certificate, hands a tender to the agent, and the agent works the whole pipeline inside the app. It searches open tenders, pulls the full brief, scores fit against the company's actual profile, checks the document vault against the compliance checklist, and scans the bid security against the stated guarantee so the fatal gap is caught before anyone submits. The agent proposes. The human approves. Nothing touches the bid until someone clicks Approve. How we built it Next.js and React for the workspace, and a WebMCP layer that declares six tools in the manifest and registers the same six on the page with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool dispatches to a typed function that runs real SQL against the live database, so the workflow is identical whether a human drives the cockpit in the browser or an agent calls the tools from ChatGPT's embedded browser with WebMCP enabled. It degrades gracefully if the API isn't there and is guarded by a session cookie. Challenges we ran into Making it watchable. The unbounded agent route we tried first was slow and unreliable, so we made the recorded path deterministic and database-backed, and bounded every step so one slow call could never blow the three-minute limit. A recording quirk taught us what the eye actually follows. A new tool's result is prepended above older ones, and an early cut scrolled the bottom card into view while the narration described the new one. Fixing the recorder to center the card it was talking about, and to actually reveal the proposal and the kanban, took more patience than the app itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of Credibility over confidence. Every WebMCP tool is deterministic. It returns structured JSON computed from real SQL against real tenders, the real compliance rule set, and the real uploaded documents. If the tool says a UGX 12 million bid security is short of the required two percent, that's arithmetic against an actual tender record, not a comforting guess. And human approval isn't a checkbox. Lookup tools run freely, but nothing persists until a person approves. What we learned For a contractor, credibility beats confidence. An agent that sounds sure about compliance is worthless if it's wrong and costs them a bid. That's why Gulawo doesn't guess. And we saw firsthand what people and agents can now do together that was hard before. Before, an assistant could only read whatever the page rendered. Now a small contractor gets a defensible answer in seconds. Is this tender worth it? Are we legally ready to bid? Is there a compliant draft held for sign-off? Instead of hours of paperwork or a disqualification. What's next for Gulawo Turn the six tools into a persistent compliance watchman. Let the agent monitor open tenders against the vault continuously, alert the contractor the moment a new tender matches, and keep draft proposals current as tenders change. Grow the readable tender pool beyond Uganda into Kenya, Tanzania, and Rwanda, and let the vault check itself against each market's rule set. And push deeper on the collaborative loop that WebMCP makes possible. The agent works the pipeline in the same session, with the human holding the final say, all the way to submission. title: kepler.gl webMCP
pitch: Empower AI agents like Codex to build, style, and explore interactive kepler.gl visualizations using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Empower AI agents like Codex to build, style, and explore interactive kepler.gl visualizations using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Kepler.gl WebMCP - demo 1 GIF Kepler.gl WebMCP - demo 2 (gif) Kepler.gl WebMCP - demo 3 Xun Li @Foursquare Inspiration Kepler.gl is a popular open source project for GPU-accelerated geovisualization, rendering millions of data points, trip animations, and flow maps via simple JSON configs. However, while modern AI agents like Codex/Claude code excel at spatial data preparation, preprocessing and analysis, they lack rich mapping tools—relying instead on flat, static plots. Bridging this gap used to require tedious manual friction: exporting data/results from the agent, opening kepler.gl, and rebuilding layers by hand. kepler.gl WebMCP eliminates that friction. Powered by the WebMCP standard, it exposes kepler.gl’s map controls directly to AI agents. Now, users can simply ask Codex(or Chrome webMCP puglin) to map their analysis and watch a live, interactive kepler.gl visualization build automatically with zero setup. What it does Open https://deploy-preview-3678--keplergl.netlify.app/demo in a WebMCP-enabled browser e.g. Codex browser and ask it to discover the site tools automatically. To create a map, ask in plain language and the agent composes the commands against the live map. Here are some examples: A map from your analysis data/results, in any style you can describe. "Get all roads in San Francisco and create a map using road types. Then make two more maps: 'winter SFO' using winter theme colors, and 'Van Gogh SFO' using Van Gogh Starry Night theme colors." The agent loads the data, feed to kepler.gl, add a new map layer, colors the roads by type — the skill turns "winter" and "Van Gogh Starry Night" into proper palettes. Animation with simulation/real data semantics. "Simulate 4 taxis moving on real driving routes in San Francisco, animate them on the map, and color them by company (Uber, Lyft, Waymo, Tesla)." The agent builds a trip layer by creating real driving routes along real streets, animates it over time, and colors each taxi by its company in kepler.gl. Everyday, personal data. "Create a flow map using the geotags and timestamps of the photos in my travel folder." The skill maps this to a flow layer, turning consecutive photo locations across a trip into origin–destination movements — a daily-life use case, not an expert feature. Here is a simulation that everyone can run: Every ask ends with a live, interactive kepler.gl map in the same browser — layers, colors, and animation all driven by the agent in real time. How we built it One contract, written once. Everything hangs on @kepler.gl/mcp package, which defines 12 map.* commands — data (load, save, create-table, add-column), layers (add-layer, update-layer-color), views (set-basemap, split-view, get-boundary), time filters, and dataset context. Each command has a ZOD input schema that converts once to JSON Schema (served to both MCP and WebMCP), policy metadata (read-only hints, risk), and results formatted as human-readable text for the model, not for an API. See the source code of kepler.gl/mcp at: https://github.com/keplergl/kepler.gl/pull/3678 Challenges we ran into Building on a moving target. WebMCP is an evolving draft standard with active UI, permissioning, and discovery developments. We mitigated this moving specification by shipping flexible adapters for both MCP and WebMCP API endpoints. The agent can’t see the map. Every command alters a visual surface where the ultimate source of truth is the rendered pixels. Right now, our tool outputs narrate the action taken rather than the visual result—closing that loop with screenshots and viewport deltas is our clear next step. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole kepler.gl map became a callable package. We extracted a mature map surface into @kepler.gl/mcp — twelve commands, dependency-light, with the kepler skill shipping inside. The same code now runs in a chat panel (kepler.gl AI assistant), an MCP relay, and browser WebMCP. What we learned Correctness comes from structure, not prompting. A structure with a combination of SKILL set and a limited number of tools is better than converting every function into tool. Write results for the model, not the API. Type-safe failures that die as an opaque UnknownError teach an agent nothing. It is better to return the details that say what went wrong to help agent work with the Kepler.gl webMCP. What's next for kepler.gl webMCP Close the visual loop. Let the agent see the map it's building — screenshots and viewport deltas as first-class command results — so it can verify its own work like a human would. Publish @kepler.gl/mcp to npm so any team can embed the same callable map surface in their own site or MCP server. Grow the ecosystem pipeline, so the "data processing → analyze → map → understand" conversation in Codex or other harness tools keeps expanding.
