title: KnownGate
pitch: The food verification layer for people's agents: state your family's rules and KnownGate rules products, menus, and plans against read-and-dated evidence. Four verdicts. Never "safe."
about_excerpt: The food verification layer for people's agents: state your family's rules and KnownGate rules products, menus, and plans against read-and-dated evidence. Four verdicts. Never "safe." Like Comment Story Updates A ruled answer: source and date attached Some lines can never be dropped We measured the difference the page makes The famous chain, answered honestly A refusal is an answer The agent works in the open The page speaks to agents natively. Why we built it People ask AI what they can eat, and a wrong answer has a cost. We asked GPT-5.2 directly, no tools: can a milk-allergic child have this chicken broth? It answered that it could not say: "the label is the only way to confirm," and asked us to photograph the pack. The model is right. Someone has to have read the label, and the web gives an agent no place where that reading lives. KnownGate is that place: the verification layer for people's agents. What it does Tell it your household's rules in plain words: "milk allergy, and keep sodium under 200 mg per serving." It turns them into typed rules you can see, then rules a product, a whole restaurant menu, or a week of meals against evidence: printed nutrition panels and published allergen charts, each with its source and the date we read it. Four verdicts can come back, and two of them are honest ways of saying "we don't know." The word "safe" never appears. Unknown counts as no. Nothing is stored unless you ask for a record, and a saved record is a permanent dated page you can hand to a school or a kitchen. We measured the difference the page makes On 2 Sept 2026 we ran one question three ways: "milk allergy, sodium under 200 mg per serving, Kroger 99% Fat Free Chicken Broth." Asked directly via the OpenAI API (gpt-5.2, no tools): no verdict in 9.7 seconds. "The label is the only way to confirm." A browser agent (Claude in Chrome) driving our human page with no tools: the correct conflict (780 mg, dated) in 1 minute 21 seconds and 6 counted actions, zero wrong turns, because the page is built to be legible to agents even without tools. Through the page's own engine, the same calls our WebMCP tools expose: the same correct verdict in 2 calls, under 5 seconds (median of three runs). One product, one question, single runs, not a benchmark suite. But the shape is the finding: the page supplies the trust; the tools supply the determinism. Why WebMCP fits this use case Food is the domain where an agent must not answer from training data, because a wrong answer carries liability. WebMCP lets the page hold the authority: knowngate.com registers its checking engine as tools on the page via document.modelContext (check an item, check a venue, check a plan, parse a premise). An agent that lands on the site calls the site's own engine instead of scraping it, and the human watches every call on a live step list on the same screen. We call the pattern the page as authority : the agent proposes, the page rules on evidence, and the human owns the premise. What people and agents can now do together An agent can rule a whole menu in one turn: 84 items at one chain, 72 conflicts, 12 that need one named kitchen question, plus a cross-contact caveat the site forbids any agent to omit, relayed word for word. It can save a dated record page a parent shares onward. It can answer for a famous chain honestly: In-N-Out returns 7 milk conflicts from the chain's own chart and "couldn't verify" where the chart is silent, never a clear the chart cannot support. And where there is no evidence at all, it refuses. That refusal is the part everyone else leaves out. How we built it Next.js and TypeScript on Vercel; Supabase Postgres holding a production evidence corpus: 67,791 products, 711,900 shelf records, 446,371 nutrition panels, 12 chains with 7,022 dishes ruled, measured 2 Sept 2026 and growing daily (current figures are published on the site's refusals page, along with how often we refuse). We also mapped 54,909 California venues so real places resolve; venues without evidence refuse honestly, and on our first recovery trial all 400 sampled venues resolved to a real place, 91% with a menu source. The same engine is exposed three ways: WebMCP tools on the page, an MCP server at mcp.knowngate.com, and plain REST with a free key. Agents without tool access get DOM-path directions published on every page, with stable element ids and a strict relay rule for must-not-omit lines. The MCP server is published in the official MCP Registry as com.knowngate/verify, DNS-verified to our domain Challenges we faced The hardest bugs only exist where agents live: document.modelContext exists only in agentic browsers, so our tool-registration crash never reproduced in a normal one. Reading evidence honestly was its own fight: In-N-Out's allergen chart draws its answers as red dots, vector graphics invisible to every text-extraction tool, and we had to render the page the way a person sees it before we could ingest a row. And we ingested that 12th chain 24 hours before this deadline: its one-sided chart structurally cannot prove an item clear, and the engine returned zero clears from it, exactly as the standard requires. The safety property held under deadline pressure, which is the only time it matters. What we learned A page that can say "couldn't verify" is worth more than one that always answers. Everything in our video runs on production; the rules of what counts as proof are published at knowngate.com/standard. The question we started with was whether an agent can be trusted about food. The answer we found is that trust doesn't live in the agent. It lives in what the page gives the agent to stand on. title: OpenSketch
pitch: OpenSketch is a free, open source alternative to paid editors for scientific figures depicting biological reactions and lab workflows.
about_excerpt: OpenSketch is a free, open source alternative to paid editors for scientific figures depicting biological reactions and lab workflows. Like Comment Story Updates Final screen Inspiration Scientific figure creation requires researchers to spend a lot of time finding suitable illustrations, arranging cells and molecules, connecting processes, adding labels, and fixing layouts. OpenSketch already existed as a browser-native scientific figure editor. For the WebMCP Hackathon, I wanted to make the user and AI agent collaborate inside one visual editor where both can create figures, make edits and refine each other's work. With advanced models and technologies the agent might be able to do this fully autonomously. What it does OpenSketch lets researchers build scientific figures from openly licensed biological and laboratory illustrations, such as NIH BioArt, combined with text, shapes, connectors, grouping, alignment, and publication-ready SVG, PDF, and PNG export. With WebMCP an AI agent can now do this work autonomously with the researcher approving and refining it's work. How I built it I added a typed semantic command layer between OpenSketch and WebMCP. Commands use stable object IDs, bounded schemas, structured errors, and the same editor transaction system used by the normal UI. The browser detects document.modelContext and registers the available tools through registerTool. The WebMCP layer covers scene inspection, scientific asset search and provenance, editing, semantic composition, layout planning, geometry-aware connectors, annotations, validation, and export workflows. Challenges I ran into The hardest problem was choosing the right abstraction level. Exposing only low-level move, resize, and click-like commands still leaves the agent reasoning in coordinates. To work reliably, the agent needs higher-level concepts such as stages, interactions, labels, geometry, connectors, and provenance. Another challenge was making human and agent editing interoperable. Agent actions needed to behave exactly like normal editor actions: visible immediately, undoable, persistent, and safe when the scene changed between inspection and execution. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The WebMCP integration is not a separate demo API. It works on the real OpenSketch editor state and uses the same history and persistence pathways as manual editing. An agent can understand and modify structured scientific content rather than blindly manipulating pixels, while the researcher can step in at any moment and edit the same figure manually. I also kept the application browser-native and privacy-preserving, with projects and imported media staying local to the user. What i learned The biggest lesson was that more actions do not automatically give an agent more understanding. For complex visual software, useful agent integration requires exposing meaningful application state, not just wrapping mouse interactions. WebMCP provides the transport, but the application still has to expose the right concepts. I also learned that the strongest human-agent experience comes from one shared state and one shared history, rather than building separate human and AI interfaces. What's next for OpenSketch The next step is expanding the semantic composition system to more scientific figure types and making agent-assisted layout and refinement even more robust. More broadly, I want OpenSketch to explore what agent-native canvas software can look like: humans keep the visual interface and final judgment, while agents get structured access to the same underlying artifact and can reliably help with complex multi-step work. title: Pathfinder
pitch: The vast amount of data on the internet makes analysis paralysis all too real. Pathfinder allows an agent to assist with one of the major decisions of many people's lives, where to go to college.
about_excerpt: The vast amount of data on the internet makes analysis paralysis all too real. Pathfinder allows an agent to assist with one of the major decisions of many people's lives, where to go to college. Like Comment Story Updates Pathfinder helps students turn overwhelming engineering-college research into a choice they can understand and explain. Start with a question in your own words. The agent researches the facts and organizes the decision visually. The agent narrows 75 sourced colleges into a focused shortlist shaped around the student’s actual priorities. Compare the differences that matter, including published cost, career outcomes, and engineering-program strength. Explore climate, walkability, campus scale, and nearby communities to understand what daily life could feel like. Open any school for a focused view of its program, costs, outcomes, admissions context, and surrounding area. Compare exact-major degree counts alongside clearly separated broader-field earnings, debt, and career context. Inspiration College research is not suffering from a lack of information. Students and parents already have access to costs, programs, outcomes, admissions data, weather, and campus-life details. The difficult part is organizing all of it into a decision they can understand and explain. I built Pathfinder to explore whether an agent could help with that actual decision, not just answer another isolated college question. What it does Pathfinder is an agent-first decision space for choosing an engineering school. A student can start with an imperfect question like: I’m interested in mechanical engineering. Show me a few reasonably priced schools with good career outcomes, and I don’t want somewhere brutally cold. The agent can search Pathfinder’s catalog of 75 colleges and 20 engineering majors, inspect supporting evidence, build a focused shortlist, and compose the website around the student’s question. Instead of returning a wall of text, the agent can create a visual comparison, explore campus life, open a focused school profile, or test a temporary “what if” scenario. The student supplies the priorities and judgment; the agent handles the research and organization. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns Pathfinder from a website beside a conversation into a workspace shared with the agent. Pathfinder exposes fifteen purpose-built tools for reading the student’s decision, searching colleges and programs, retrieving evidence, updating preferences, managing schools, creating temporary scenarios, and changing the visual workspace. The agent does not need to scrape the page or guess where to click. The student does not need to learn a complicated filtering system. Both work with the same decision state and see the same result. This also makes interactions possible that are difficult in either a traditional website or a standalone chat. A student can ask a natural follow-up, have the agent reorganize the relevant evidence visually, and continue refining the decision without starting over. How I built it I built Pathfinder iteratively with Codex. I would test realistic student scenarios, identify where the agent lacked the right tool or where the interface became confusing, and then work with Codex to redesign, implement, test, and refine the next version. The application uses React, TypeScript, Next.js, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, and OpenAI Sites. Its bundled catalog draws from public sources including College Scorecard, NCES IPEDS, NOAA, EPA, Census, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Visitors need no account or API key, and their personal decision stays in their browser. The hardest architectural problem was separating three kinds of state: The student’s saved decision A temporary what-if scenario The visual workspace currently being shown That separation lets the agent reorganize the page or explore a hypothetical situation without silently changing what the student has actually decided. What I learned The central lesson was that agent experiences are stronger when they are designed as shared environments. A chat response can explain a comparison. A WebMCP workspace can also preserve it, visualize it, expose the evidence, and support the student’s next question. Pathfinder is not meant to declare one objectively “best” college. It helps students reduce an overwhelming field of information into a focused choice they understand and can confidently explain. title: SameState - Redux_WebMCP
pitch: SameState makes Redux frontends agent-native: AI can use safe, real actions, inspect state transitions, test user flows, and consult a website's expert agent without exposing private backend tools.
about_excerpt: SameState makes Redux frontends agent-native: AI can use safe, real actions, inspect state transitions, test user flows, and consult a website's expert agent without exposing private backend tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The developer workflow: an agent receives scoped context, discovers declared tools, and tests a real frontend flow by intent. The customer-agent workflow: a customer agent reaches Breeze through a safe public WebMCP gateway. Codex uses a declared WebMCP storefront action to add Quiet Lamp through the same Redux command path used by a person. SameState makes an ecommerce frontend agent-native with structured tools, shared state, and observable progress. Breeze keeps durable conversation context while private catalog capabilities remain protected behind the website backend. Breeze returns a product recommendation backed by authorized catalog information and visible evidence. A live human-and-agent workflow where Codex operates the real SameState storefront through WebMCP. redux-webmcp gives an agent safe frontend context, typed actions, state inspection, and transition evidence. A website-owned service agent can help a customer agent without exposing private backend tools directly. Breeze provides concise, evidence-backed product advice in a shared consultation thread. SameState introduces two WebMCP use cases: developer-facing state-aware frontend control and customer-to-service-agent collaboration. Inspiration AI agents can already click around websites, but visual interaction alone does not tell them whether the application behaved correctly behind the screen. SameState was inspired by a simple question: what if a frontend could expose safe actions, useful context, and visible state transitions directly to an agent, while still keeping the human experience intact? We also wanted to explore a second idea: a customer agent should be able to ask a website's specialist service agent for help without being given direct access to private backend tools. What it does SameState demonstrates two WebMCP use cases. First, it helps developers let agents understand and test Redux-powered frontend flows. An agent can read application context, use declared safe actions, inspect Redux state, and see the transition created after every action. Second, it demonstrates customer-agent to service-agent communication. A customer-facing agent can ask Breeze, the website's product consultant, for advice through a public WebMCP gateway. Breeze uses authorized server-side catalog capabilities and returns a grounded answer with evidence, while private tools remain protected. The ecommerce app is a real shared interface. Humans can browse products, search, manage a cart, and ask Breeze for help. Agents can use structured WebMCP tools that perform the same meaningful actions and expose the resulting state changes. How we built it The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Redux Toolkit, and Vite. I built redux-webmcp , a package that wraps a Redux store with a scoped WebMCP layer. Developers declare the safe actions, state reads, semantic contracts, and frontend context that an agent can access. The package registers structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , validates inputs, dispatches through the same Redux path as the human UI, and records sanitized state transitions. The consultation service uses a TypeScript backend, persistent consultation threads, and authorized private catalog capabilities. Breeze receives requests through a public gateway, gathers only the permitted evidence, and returns a concise recommendation. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making human and agent behavior genuinely consistent. We solved this by routing both through the same Redux actions instead of creating a separate agent-only code path. Another challenge was making agent activity understandable during a live demo. A background tool call can otherwise look like unexplained UI behavior. We added visible tool-call notifications, an Agent View for Redux state and transition history, and an explicit action that opens the Breeze conversation. We also had to keep the public tool inventory focused. Rather than exposing every individual UI control, we combined overlapping capabilities into clearer semantic actions. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built and published redux-webmcp as a reusable package for Redux applications. Made human actions and agent actions use the same Redux state-transition path. Created visible evidence for WebMCP activity instead of hiding tool calls in the background. Built a safe customer-agent to service-agent gateway that keeps private backend capabilities off the public frontend. Delivered a working, deployed ecommerce experience with WebMCP tools, Redux inspection, transition history, and evidence-backed product consultations. What we learned WebMCP is more than a way for agents to avoid clicking buttons. Its greater potential is helping websites describe intent, safe capabilities, and application state in a way agents can reliably understand. We learned that useful agent tools need strong boundaries. They should be specific, validated, observable, and connected to the same business logic as the human interface. We also learned that agent-to-agent communication is most useful when it is mediated. A website can offer an expert service agent through a controlled gateway without exposing its private tools or internal data directly. What's next for SameState - Redux_WebMCP Next, we want to expand redux-webmcp with richer developer diagnostics, test-run reporting, replayable workflows, and broader framework support. For SameState itself, we want to improve the service-agent experience with more specialist workflows, richer evidence, and clearer approval boundaries for actions that should stay human-controlled. The larger goal is to help developers build frontends where people and agents can safely use the same product, understand the same state, and collaborate through well-defined capabilities. title: VocalApply - voice-driven job application
pitch: Talk directly to web pages! Watch a voice-driven AI agent navigate, filter, and fill out forms in real-time. Built with WebMCP, Gemini Live, and OpenAI Realtime to automate job applications.
about_excerpt: Talk directly to web pages! Watch a voice-driven AI agent navigate, filter, and fill out forms in real-time. Built with WebMCP, Gemini Live, and OpenAI Realtime to automate job applications. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Codex working screenshot 3 Codex working screenshot 1 Codex working screenshot 2 Chrome home WebMCP tools listed Application Page WebMCP tools listed VocalApply Inspiration If you watch a visual AI agent try to fill out a job application, it looks like someone trying to click a mouse while looking through a telescope. It takes screenshots, streams images to a vision model, guesses coordinates for dropdowns, misclicks, and retries. Now try navigating that same multi-step form with a screen reader. A screen reader reads top-to-bottom, line by line. When an application has five steps, dropdown menus, hidden accordions, and error labels, someone who is visually impaired has to tab through dozens of irrelevant links and labels just to find the next input. A task that takes a sighted user two minutes can take twenty minutes of listening to raw boilerplate. People also run into this when they have a broken wrist, severe carpal tunnel, or are multitasking with their hands full. Screen readers are slow, and vision bots keep guessing coordinates. We wanted to fix both: What if you didn't need a vision model watching your screen, and didn't need to tab through fifty links with a screen reader? What if you could just talk to the page, and the page exposed its buttons and inputs directly to your voice? At the same time, applying for a job is personal. It is your work history, your salary, and your name on a legal declaration. We wanted a tool that types the repetitive fields, asks you out loud when it needs your input, and deliberately refuses to press submit on your behalf . What it does VocalApply is a careers website paired with a voice agent that runs directly in your browser: Hands-Free Job Search: You speak naturally: "Show me what you have open." The page sets the filter bar, highlights the best match, and reads out why it fits your background. If you say "Not that one," it moves the ring to the next job on the shortlist. Visually impaired users can hear role summaries without tabbing through navigation menus. Form Filling: Say "Apply to that one and fill it in." The page opens the application and fills in your contact information, eligibility, and work history from a saved profile. Two-Pass Input: A profile cannot answer everything, and it shouldn't guess. When the form asks "Why this role, and why now?" or asks about relocation, the agent moves to that field, highlights it in amber on screen, and asks you out loud. You answer, it writes down what you said, and the highlight clears. Spoken Corrections: Say "My salary expectation went up to $130,000." It updates the field immediately and saves it locally for future applications. The Missing Submit Tool: When the form is ready, the agent focuses the submit button and prompts you to review your answers. It will not submit. There is no tool on the page that clicks submit, and no tool that checks the legal disclaimer checkbox. You have to read the declaration and click submit yourself. How we built it VocalApply runs entirely inside the user's browser tab. There is no intermediate application server storing resumes, voice recordings, or personal data. WebMCP ( document.modelContext ): Instead of a camera watching the screen, the page registers tools directly into the browser's model context. When the voice session starts, it asks the page what tools exist and runs them by name. Progressive Tool Scoping: On the job board, the model only has search and navigation tools (6 tools). It cannot access form tools until an application actually opens (9 tools). Keeping the two sets separate prevents the model from getting confused or calling form tools on a board. Live Voice Connections: The app connects directly to Gemini Live over a WebSocket (sending 16 kHz audio and receiving 24 kHz audio) and to OpenAI Realtime over WebRTC. You can interrupt the model mid-sentence without echo. Keyless Walkthrough: If you don't have an API key or microphone, a built-in walkthrough drives the same tools in the same order using the browser's speech synthesis, so anyone can test the full interaction immediately. Challenges we ran into Rethinking Accessibility Without Visual Clutter: Standard accessibility tools dump all content into audio sequentially. Building a voice assistant meant figuring out how to summarize jobs concisely so a user isn't forced to listen to five paragraphs of job descriptions just to compare titles and locations. Barge-In and Audio Echo: When using laptop speakers, the microphone picks up the model's own voice and cuts itself off. We had to tune audio threshold levels and scheduled playback queues so interruptions felt crisp without the model tripping over its own speech. Knowing Where to Stop Automation: It is easy to write a tool that ticks every checkbox and sends an application automatically. Deciding not to build that tool was an intentional design decision. We had to make sure the agent could prepare the application thoroughly without taking away user consent. Accomplishments that we're proud of A Better Experience for Low-Vision and Mobility-Impaired Users: Eliminating the need to tab through dozens of form elements or rely on clunky screen scrapers. You ask, it answers, and it fills the inputs cleanly. Safety as Code, Not Prompting: We didn't prompt the AI with "Please do not submit the form." We simply did not write a submit tool. The agent cannot submit an application because the capability does not exist. Direct Semantic Tools Over Computer Vision: Proving that connecting voice directly to web capabilities is faster, cheaper, and more reliable than streaming video to computer-vision bots. What we learned Voice Changes Web Accessibility: For people who rely on screen readers, conversational tools are a massive upgrade over linear DOM navigation. Asking a page to show relevant roles and hearing an immediate summary saves minutes of tedious keyboard navigation. Assistants Should Assist, Not Replace: Users don't want an AI that impersonates them or signs legal documents in their name. The most helpful tools handle mechanical data entry while leaving decisions and final consent to the person. Semantic Page Context Beats Pixels: Web automation that works with structured tools doesn't break when CSS classes change or buttons move. It provides a far more stable foundation than visual bot scrapers. title: Adamastor
pitch: The agent's output stops being a message and becomes something you can pick up and move.
about_excerpt: The agent's output stops being a message and becomes something you can pick up and move. Like Comment Story Updates Adamastor dashboard InspirationFor judges: the WebMCP tools require the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser (model GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra — Luna has WebMCP disabled), or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. The site works normally in any browser; the agent tools only appear in those. No credentials required — you get your own private workspace automatically. Signing in with ChatGPT is optional. Inspiration I have about 2,500 photographs from six years of hiking in the Western Cape — birds, fynbos, mountains, the sea — and I want to make a YouTube channel out of them. I am not a developer. So I asked an AI to help me plan it. It gave me nine hundred words. I read them once, and I never found them again. That is the whole problem in one sentence. An answer in a chat window is linear and undifferentiated, and it scrolls away. You cannot pick up idea four and put it beside idea eleven. You cannot fix line three and keep line four — you can only ask for the whole thing again and hope the new version's flaw is somewhere you'll notice. When the conversation ends, it is gone. Chat memory belongs to the AI. It is not yours, and you cannot rearrange it. I wanted the answer to be an object instead of a message. What it does Adamastor is a spatial canvas — notes, tasks, links, columns and files placed freely on a board. WebMCP lets an agent work on that board alongside you. The agent's output stops being a message and becomes something that stays where you put it, that you can move, edit, group and keep — and that the agent can read back later. Four things follow from that: You keep 90% and fix 10%. The agent lays out twenty shots for a film. You disagree with one. You drag it out and retype it, and the other nineteen don't move. In a chat window the equivalent is asking for the whole list again. The board is the briefing. Come back a week later, in a conversation that has never seen you, and ask what you'd done. The agent reads the board — your ticked tasks, your own edits — and picks up from there. You explain nothing. Structure survives. Ask it to re-cut twenty shots by what you could film this weekend versus what needs a trip, and it doesn't hand you a list you read once. It rebuilds the board. That structure is still there next month. Arranging stays yours. The agent composes; you place. Why this fits WebMCP A chat interface is the wrong shape for planning work, because planning work is spatial. But a spatial canvas has always been the wrong shape for AI help, because there was no way for a model to act on it without pretending to be a mouse. WebMCP closes that gap in the only place it can be closed — inside the page, where the application already knows what a board is, where the cards are, and how wide a column should be. The agent doesn't need to see pixels or guess coordinates. It says these items belong together and this group is called "This weekend", and the application does the geometry. The eight tools list-boards · read-board · search-items · create-board · open-board · add-items · update-item · group-items group-items takes meaning, not coordinates. The agent supplies groupings and labels; the application measures each card, sizes the columns to fit their contents, and grows the canvas to hold them. Chrome's WebMCP guidance is explicit that tools should not ask an agent to perform maths, and it produces a better result — the layout is consistent however the agent chooses to group things. add-items is batched, so one call can populate an entire board rather than twenty round trips. create-board opens the board in the same state update that creates it — no second call, no race, and the new board is on screen before the agent has finished speaking. Eight tools, not eighty. Each maps to one thing the product actually does — and one more was deliberately left out. What the agent deliberately cannot do It cannot delete your content. Notes, tasks, links and files are never removed by an agent, only regrouped. Column headings are structural labels and are replaced when a board is reorganised. There is no confirmation step in the WebMCP specification yet, and the read tools return user-generated content flagged untrustedContentHint — content the model then acts on. A delete tool in that context is a prompt-injection hazard, so it wasn't shipped. The agent groups what it suggests removing; the person removes it. It also cannot reposition individual cards. Composition is the agent's half of this product; arrangement is mine. What happened when I left a gap — and why it makes the case While testing, I asked the agent to move an image. There is no tool for that. Instead of refusing, it read the page, added a new image card through the toolbar, and pasted in a blob: address it had scraped from the rendered photograph. Then it reported: "Done — the bird image is now at the top of the board and synced." Nothing had moved. The new card was permanently broken — a blob: address dies with the page that made it. And "synced" was read off the interface, not returned by anything. That is what an agent does when it has no tool: it improvises with your interface and tells you it worked. With tools, every result across nineteen deployed versions was real, because a tool returned it. Without one, it scraped, clicked, and lied confidently. Every tool in this project exists to make that unnecessary — and update-item now says plainly when it has been asked to do something it cannot do, instead of reporting a success it never achieved. How I built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Cloudflare D1 and R2, deployed on ChatGPT Sites. The WebMCP layer is deliberately boring: the eight tool handlers are pure functions over the board array, in a file that imports no React and touches no browser API. That means they're unit-testable without a DOM, and the React layer only has to apply the result. Tool handlers read current state through a ref synced on every render, so they never act on a stale copy of the boards. Tools are registered with the imperative API on the top-level document. ChatGPT's browser does not discover tools inside iframes and does not support the declarative form API, so this approach runs in both browsers. readOnlyHint on all three read tools, untrustedContentHint on the two that return user content, outputs truncated to the recommended 1.5K budget, and errors written so the agent can recover on its own — "No board with that id. Call list-boards to see the available boards." Nineteen automated tests, including the output budget and the layout geometry. Challenges The thing I started from was broken in ways it did not admit to. This began as an AI-generated app that looked finished. It had one workspace, hardcoded, shared by every visitor — no concept of a user at all. The entire application state lived in a single database row. The file upload had never once worked in production, because of an undocumented ~1 MB request-body limit that nobody had measured. It was audited file by file before a single tool was written. Per-user workspaces had to come first. There was no point giving an agent tools to write into a workspace everyone shared. Authentication was added using a sign-in helper the original build had shipped and never called. Everything I guessed about behaviour, I got wrong. Not the structure — the behaviour. I guessed at the cause of a Safari error and was wrong. I guessed a storage binding was missing and was wrong. I predicted the agent would produce a scattered grid and it chained a second tool unprompted and produced a clean one. The lesson held every time: measure it, don't reason about it. A cached JavaScript bundle produced three false bug reports before I worked out that the embedded browser had to be quit entirely between deploys. What I learned That the interesting question isn't what tools to give an agent. It's what to withhold, and how a tool should behave when it's asked for something outside its remit. An agent with no tool doesn't stop. It improvises with your interface and reports success. So the honest failure message — "Items cannot be repositioned by a tool; a person drags them" — turned out to matter as much as any capability I added. And that latency belongs to the model, not the page. The tool calls return in milliseconds. The wait is the agent working out what to say — which is worth knowing before you design around it. What's next Per-item history, so you can see what the agent changed and undo one thing rather than everything. A read tool that returns a compact board summary for very large boards. And a delete tool, the day WebMCP has a confirmation step to hang it on. title: AIEndpoint - Service Discovery for the Agentic Web
pitch: AIEndpoint finds the right website. WebMCP operates it. An open standard and live registry that lets browser agents discover which service can do the job before they ever navigate.
about_excerpt: AIEndpoint finds the right website. WebMCP operates it. An open standard and live registry that lets browser agents discover which service can do the job before they ever navigate. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP integration docs: declare support in your manifest, promote it into page tools with @aiendpoint/webmcp DemoWeather: live Open-Meteo data. WebMCP tools generated from its /.well-known/ai manifest update this card when an agent calls them aiendpoint.dev - the open /ai standard: ~800 tokens of pure signal instead of 10k-50k tokens of page noise Registry search results with the ⚡ WebMCP badge - DemoWeather (verified, score 100) tops the results agents and humans both see Real Chrome with the WebMCP flag: tools registered, executeTool call received - the visible counter proves the loop works Inspiration WebMCP gives an agent structured tools for the page it is already on. But watching agents work, we kept hitting the step that comes before that: which page should the agent open in the first place? An agent that needs weather data or a currency rate still guesses URLs or scrapes search results. We had been building that missing step for months: AIEndpoint, an open standard where any site publishes a capability manifest at /.well-known/ai (an IETF Internet-Draft), plus a live registry indexing thousands of services. When WebMCP appeared, the two ideas snapped together: AIEndpoint finds the right website. WebMCP operates it. We are honest with ourselves: an independent project like this may never become the standard. The giants are drafting their own, and there is only so far one person can push. But robots.txt also started with one individual and an idea the web happened to need. We simply wanted to cut the traffic LLM agents waste crawling site after site just to figure out what each one can do - and we entered this challenge hoping more people will join us. What it does On aiendpoint.dev , an in-browser agent calls find_services ("a weather service with no auth"). The results the agent receives render as cards on the page the human is looking at. select_service opens the detail view with a live "Open service" link. One click later, on weather.aiendpoint.dev , the agent calls current_weather and the weather card in front of the user updates with live Open-Meteo data. Human and agent share one screen at every step. Nothing happens in a hidden console: every tool call has a visible consequence on the page. Before WebMCP, a service directory for agents could only be a server-side HTTP API, unreachable exactly where users work. Now discovery, selection, and execution all happen inside one browsing session, visibly shared between the user and the agent. How we built it @aiendpoint/webmcp (new package, ESM + IIFE): promotes a site's /.well-known/ai manifest into WebMCP tools. Tool names, descriptions, and JSON input schemas are derived from the manifest: the spec's compact parameter notation ( "string, required -- city name" ) is parsed into schema types and required lists. Execution stays in explicit per-capability handlers, so a site never exposes anything it did not consciously wire up. aiendpoint.dev (Next.js) registers find_services / select_service on every page; tool calls navigate the visible UI. A /webmcp/ping diagnostics page reports the browser's actual WebMCP surface and shows a live call counter. DemoWeather (FastAPI) serves its manifest, loads the adapter's IIFE bundle, and wires three handlers that drive the page's weather card, backed by live Open-Meteo data with a labeled stale-cache fallback. Challenges we ran into The API surface is still moving. Registration probes document.modelContext , navigator.modelContext (now deprecated), and older entry points, preferring registerTool with AbortSignal cleanup. We learned by experiment that executeTool takes the registered tool object plus a JSON string , so our handlers normalize both parsed objects and raw strings. provideContext replaces the whole tool set on every call , so independent components clobbered each other until we kept a page-wide union of registered tools. React Strict Mode silently unregistered tools in development via the register/cleanup/register cycle until we made registration fully idempotent. Making discovery honest: we rewrote our registry search to match capability keywords against descriptions, and fixed count/filter bugs the new browser-driven usage exposed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop is verified in a real browser , not just designed: tool registration, an actual executeTool call, and a visible UI change on the page. The discovery chain runs on live production data : the registry indexes 3,600+ services, and DemoWeather registers itself, passes our own validator at 100/100, and tops the "weather" search results agents actually see. One adapter call makes any /.well-known/ai site agent-operable - schemas included - while keeping execution in explicit handlers the site controls. We migrated the entire platform (registry, validator, CLI, MCP server, three demos, and every framework adapter) to the well-known location during the hackathon window, and cleared all 71 dependency audit vulnerabilities while we were at it. What we learned ogfooding an open spec against a second standard is the fastest way to find its weak points. Migrating /ai to /.well-known/ai (draft-01), parsing our own compact notation into JSON Schema, and watching a real browser call our tools taught us more in three days than months of design. What's next for AIEndpoint - Service Discovery for the Agentic Web Schema-typed params in spec v1.1, mutations with confirmation UI, auth-scoped tools, and a "WebMCP-ready" tier on the registry's verification badge, so agents can filter for sites that are operable , not just discoverable. title: API Canvas
pitch: API Canvas is a local-first WebMCP workspace where people and agents can discover public data, connect APIs,create reusable cards and visualizations,and reason across the resulting dashboard together.
about_excerpt: API Canvas is a local-first WebMCP workspace where people and agents can discover public data, connect APIs,create reusable cards and visualizations,and reason across the resulting dashboard together. Like Comment Story Updates Api Canvas build a dashboard Canvas View Inspiration Building a useful dashboard usually involves a surprising amount of repetitive work. You have to find an API, understand its documentation, construct the request, inspect the response, identify useful fields, create a visualization, connect those fields to a component, and repeat the process for every additional source. I wanted to see whether WebMCP could make that process dramatically more direct. Instead of only asking: "Can an agent operate this application?" API Canvas asks: "Can an agent help construct the application experience using primitives the website intentionally exposes?" What I Built API Canvas is a local-first workspace for turning public data into reusable connected cards. A dashboard can contain components such as: Tables Charts Maps Metrics Lists Notes Text and explanation blocks Search results Media Raw datasets API responses Question blocks Agent-generated answer blocks Sources and presentation are kept separate. That means one API response can power several different visualizations without repeatedly requesting the data. Users can also transform and combine information through declarative mappings including filtering, sorting, grouping, arithmetic, field selection, and joins. WebMCP Tools API Canvas exposes a large WebMCP tool surface covering dashboard and data workflows. An agent can perform operations such as: Create or switch dashboards Add data sources Request public API data Add cards Select appropriate visualizations Connect source fields to cards Transform data Update layout Resize or reorder cards Inspect dashboard state Read selected cards Answer questions using dashboard context Create new explanation blocks Export or present results This lets a simple request expand into a multi-step application workflow. For example: Build me an earthquake research dashboard. Find magnitude 5 or greater earthquakes from the past week, map the events, create a table, identify the strongest earthquake, and summarize it. API Canvas can break that request into structured operations and leave behind a real editable dashboard. Why WebMCP Dashboard construction is naturally compositional. The user usually knows the outcome they want but should not need to manually specify every intermediate API call and UI operation. WebMCP lets the application expose those intermediate operations directly. The agent gets structured tools instead of having to simulate: click Add Card → select source → open another menu → map a field → choose visualization → repeat. This makes workflows faster and substantially easier for an agent to reason about. Human + Agent Collaboration The most interesting part of API Canvas is that the resulting dashboard becomes shared context. Imagine the agent has created an earthquake dashboard containing a map, table, and several metrics. The user can then ask: Using all of the information currently on this page, which earthquake was strongest? The agent can inspect the existing structured cards, reason across them, produce an answer, and create another normal dashboard card containing that explanation. The workflow becomes: Data → Visualization → Context → Reasoning → New Visualization Everything remains editable by the human. How I Built It API Canvas is built with Vue 3, Vite, Pinia, IndexedDB, ECharts, AJV, and WebMCP. The workspace has a reusable block system that separates: data sources raw responses normalized values transformations bindings presentation The normal UI and WebMCP tools call into the same underlying workspace actions. AJV validates structured WebMCP inputs. IndexedDB stores larger browser-local response caches and workspace information. Public data adapters support structured formats including JSON, CSV, XML, feeds, permitted HTML tables, and embedded JSON. The application intentionally does not provide an unrestricted proxy or execute arbitrary supplied scripts. The /webmcp documentation page is generated from the same canonical WebMCP contracts used by the application. Challenges I Faced The largest challenge was building something generic without making it unpredictable. An unrestricted "call any API and run any code" tool would be powerful but would also make the application difficult to reason about. Instead, API Canvas uses bounded requests, validated schemas, explicit source handling, and declarative transformations. Another challenge was keeping data, provenance, presentation, and transformations sufficiently independent. That separation is what allows an agent to replace a chart with a table without losing the underlying source. What I Learned API Canvas changed how I think about agent interfaces. The visual dashboard does not need to be replaced by chat. Instead, the dashboard can become the persistent shared artifact that the human and agent construct together. WebMCP then acts as the structured editing and orchestration layer. What's Next I would like to expand API Canvas with more public data adapters, richer visualization components, reusable dashboard templates, local analytical queries, and collaborative sharing. The broader idea is an open, composable workspace where agents can assemble useful specialized interfaces on demand. title: ArchMorph
pitch: Browser-based architecture studio where a human and an AI agent design a building together on the same live canvas.
about_excerpt: Browser-based architecture studio where a human and an AI agent design a building together on the same live canvas. Like Comment Story Updates ArchMorph lets people and WebMCP agents shape, inspect, and validate the same live architectural model. A broad architectural perspective showing the finished envelope, outdoor spaces, and material palette. Connected living, dining, kitchen, guest suite, service core, and a clear daylit stair. Primary suite, sky lounge, garden suite, two baths, balcony, terrace, and aligned stair gallery. Balcony, entrance canopy, timber frame, slatted gate, and layered modern massing. Horizon House pairs exposed concrete with warm timber accents, deep shading, and framed glazing. Inspiration I have a dream of building a house for my family and being involved in designing it myself. For almost a year, I tried turning that dream into a floor plan using pen and paper and later Figma. I could imagine the house in my mind, but I was rarely satisfied with the result. Without architectural training, it was difficult to understand room relationships, circulation, dimensions, setbacks, and whether the design would actually feel comfortable. The biggest limitation was that a flat drawing could not show me what the finished house would feel like. I wanted to see it from the outside, walk through it from the inside, find problems, and keep improving it without needing years of training just to explore an idea. When I discovered the WebMCP Challenge, I realized I could build the tool I had been wishing for: an architecture studio where a person and an AI agent work on the same live building. That idea became ArchMorph . ArchMorph is intended for people who want to explore their future home visually before taking the design to a professional architect. It does not replace architects or engineers; it makes the early stage of imagining, testing, and communicating a home much more accessible. What it does ArchMorph is a Human + Agent Architecture Studio for designing residential buildings in the browser. A user can configure a plot, define its orientation and setbacks, and create a house using rooms, walls, doors, windows, stairs, floors, balconies, terraces, boundary walls, gates, and façade features. The design can be experienced through three connected views: Floor Plan for precise 2D planning and editing 3D Orbit for inspecting the building from different exterior angles Walk Mode for exploring the house from the inside ArchMorph also calculates architectural measurements in real time, including room areas, gross covered area, open-site area, plot coverage, and floor-area ratio. For example: $$ \text{Floor Area Ratio} = \frac{\text{Total Gross Covered Area}}{\text{Plot Area}} $$ The application can inspect circulation and identify early layout problems such as disconnected rooms, missing exterior access, invalid openings, overlapping geometry, and incorrect stair connections. These checks are meant to support early design decisions, not provide final building-code or structural certification. What makes ArchMorph WebMCP-native is that an AI agent can directly understand and operate the same project through 57 typed architectural tools . The agent can inspect the plot and existing design, create or modify elements, calculate measurements, validate the layout, control the 3D view, enter Walk Mode, capture snapshots, and export the project. The human and the agent are not working on separate versions. They share one live model, and every change made by either side appears immediately on the same canvas. How we built it I built ArchMorph using Codex as my main development partner . I used it to help shape the product, research architectural workflows, plan the system, implement the interface, debug geometry, design the WebMCP tools, test interactions, and refine the final experience. The foundation of ArchMorph is one canonical project model. The plot, floors, rooms, walls, openings, stairs, exterior elements, measurements, and validation results all come from the same structured state. The 2D plan and 3D building are different representations of that state. When a room is moved or resized, its walls, hosted doors and windows, measurements, validation results, floor-plan geometry, and 3D model update together. Each architectural element has a stable ID. This allows the agent to inspect a particular room, wall, door, window, or staircase and make precise changes to the correct object. The WebMCP layer is organized around clear architectural operations: Inspect the project, plot, floors, rooms, walls, openings, circulation, and exterior Design rooms, walls, doors, windows, stairs, floors, and façade elements Measure and validate areas, distances, coverage, access, and layout quality Present and export the design through 2D, 3D, Walk Mode, snapshots, SVG, and structured JSON Human edits and agent actions pass through the same operation system. This keeps the model synchronized and makes changes visible and understandable. Projects are also autosaved locally in the browser so users can continue working without creating an account. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was maintaining one reliable source of truth across the visual editor, WebMCP tools, calculations, layout checks, 2D plan, and 3D model. Architectural elements are strongly connected. Moving one room can affect several walls, openings, measurements, circulation paths, and both visual views. Doors and windows must remain attached to valid host walls, while staircases must connect the correct floors and respond to changes in storey height. Another challenge was making the WebMCP tools precise enough for an agent to use safely. The tools needed typed inputs, real measurement units, stable element IDs, useful inspection results, and clear errors. Invalid geometry had to be rejected without leaving the rest of the project in a broken state. I also wanted agent actions to remain visible. ArchMorph is designed around collaboration, so the agent should not silently modify a hidden data model. When it changes something, the result must appear on the human’s canvas, update the measurements, and remain available in the project history. Finally, balancing capability with simplicity was difficult. Architecture software can quickly become overwhelming, so I had to decide which controls should remain visible, which operations belonged in the inspector, and which details the agent could manage more efficiently. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that ArchMorph became more than a visual prototype. It is a working architecture environment where a user can create a measured floor plan, generate the corresponding 3D building, walk through it, inspect layout problems, and continue editing the same design. I am especially proud of the WebMCP integration. The agent can inspect the existing project before acting, reason about individual architectural elements, perform precise operations, and show the outcome directly in the live interface. Building 57 connected WebMCP tools during the hackathon was a major accomplishment. Together, they allow an agent to participate across the complete early design workflow rather than performing a single isolated demo action. Most personally, I am proud that I can now use ArchMorph to explore ideas for my own family home—the same need that originally inspired the project. What we learned The most important thing I learned is that WebMCP can turn a website from a human-only interface into a shared working environment for humans and agents. I also learned that useful agent integration is not simply about exposing many tools. An agent needs to inspect before acting, identify objects reliably, understand exact units, receive structured results, and make changes that the human can immediately see and verify. Building ArchMorph also gave me a much deeper appreciation for the complexity of architecture software. A simple-looking floor plan contains many connected systems: geometry, circulation, openings, measurements, floors, stairs, exterior features, and human experience. Codex helped me move much faster across product thinking, design, implementation, debugging, and testing. However, I also learned that the human still provides the purpose, judgment, creativity, and final decisions. That became the central idea behind ArchMorph: the best result comes from a human and an agent contributing different strengths to the same project. What's next for ArchMorph The next step is to make the collaboration more conversational. A user should be able to describe their family size, plot, lifestyle, privacy needs, climate, and budget, then ask an agent to create a thoughtful starting design through ArchMorph’s existing tools. I also plan to add deeper analysis for daylight, ventilation, accessibility, privacy, climate, and energy use. Location-aware planning guidance could help users make better early decisions while clearly distinguishing guidance

title: As I Am
pitch: The web adapts. You don’t have to. With WebMCP, your agent and participating websites plan an evening around your access needs.
about_excerpt: The web adapts. You don’t have to. With WebMCP, your agent and participating websites plan an evening around your access needs. Like Comment Story Updates A calm cinema view. Two seats together, with Alex at the aisle. The person can change and confirm the choice. Dinner before the film: three pictured dishes, including a favorite. Ingredient exclusions and kitchen questions stay visible. Inspiration “Plan a movie night for us next week. Dinner first would be lovely.” It is a small request, but the websites involved can ask a lot of someone: bright screens, moving content, crowded controls, a seat map to navigate and a menu to check. Having to explain your access needs again at each step adds more work. I wanted to show a different kind of assistance. An agent should be able to use preferences you have chosen to share, make the page easier for you to use and stay alongside you when you make a decision. What it does The demo follows Alex and Lea, a fictional couple with shared example preferences. Alex has a migraine today and wants his familiar calm view. He prefers an aisle seat beside Lea. She has explicitly shared peanut and avocado allergies. The cinema switches to dark, low-glare, still visuals. The agent finds a 20:15 showing next Friday and two seats with Alex at the aisle. Alex asks to move one row back; the pair moves together, keeping that arrangement. He reviews and confirms the demo tickets himself. Dinner comes next. An 18:00 table leaves time for a 90-minute meal, a short walk and arrival before the film. Three pictured dishes replace a long list, including Alex’s favorite mushroom risotto. Ingredient exclusions remain visible, and uncertain kitchen information stays a question. Alex can inspect the full menu, change the proposal and confirm the table. Why WebMCP Personal context becomes useful when an agent can act on the page. WebMCP exposes what each site supports: display changes, rendered measurements, available seats, dinner calculations and menu information. The agent can also ask the restaurant to show a smaller selection in its own interface. Each site owns its design and booking rules. The agent makes supported requests; the person sees the result. A display receipt carries only functional preferences between the venues. Names, diagnoses, allergies and booking details are kept out of that receipt. Final booking confirmation stays with the person. How I built it React, TypeScript and Vite power two participating venues. Their tools use document.modelContext.registerTool , with validated inputs and shared handlers for the visible interface and agent calls. The hosted version has separate cinema and restaurant pages on one HTTPS origin. The home experience is a labelled preset walkthrough. A real external agent can read the supplied example context and call the native tools directly. Both paths have been tested on the deployed site; the repository includes reproducible inputs and results. What I learned The most useful moment is a small correction: “one row further back.” Assistance should preserve what matters while making that change easy. I also learned to separate a supported preference from a promise: calm visuals are not a treatment, and matching recipe ingredients is not an allergy-safety guarantee. This is a working prototype for participating sites, with synthetic bookings and no production memory service. Validation with disabled participants is still ahead. The next step is learning which adaptations help people complete their own tasks. Built during the challenge The adaptive contract, participating websites, native tools, tests and demo were built during the submission period. The repository began on September 1, 2026. Existing building blocks include React, TypeScript, Vite, Fontsource, Vitest, Playwright and axe-core. Code and generated demo artwork are MIT licensed; fonts retain their own license notices. title: Attic
pitch: Attic is AI web-app that brings a family closer: the place your house keeps its memories, so everyone, and the AI agents they bring, can read and add to them.
about_excerpt: Attic is AI web-app that brings a family closer: the place your house keeps its memories, so everyone, and the AI agents they bring, can read and add to them. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted to build an AI tool my whole family would use together, every day. Something that connects every person in the household to one living memory and brings the family closer. Every home has one person who knows everything. The furnace filter size. The plumber who charges fairly. Where the water shutoff is. And, for the 53 million Americans caring for someone they love, who is taking Mom to cardiology on Thursday. When that person is busy, traveling, or gone, the household goes blind. Household knowledge leaks away because capture friction kills every tool built for it. The moment passes before anyone opens an app in the basement to type "check the anode rod in three years." Caregiver figure: National Alliance for Caregiving and AARP, "Caregiving in the U.S. 2020" (53.0 million adults, May 2020). What it does Attic is a living memory for one home, drawn as a cutaway house at dusk. Every lamp is one thing the house knows, glowing in the room it belongs to. A house is a private link you hand to your family. Everyone enters with the link alone. The people your family looks after live there too. The care circle holds Mom's appointments, her meds and refills, the rides still waiting to be claimed, and a journal siblings write to each other. Every family member's AI agent can read and write all of it through 17 WebMCP tools the house page publishes itself. Anyone in the house sees each change land as it happens, with a receipt they can press Undo on. How we built it The house is one hand-drawn SVG cutaway in React and Vite. Rooms, lamps, people, and the cat all sit on the same layout model, so a new memory knows which room it belongs in. Behind it is a Cloudflare Worker with one Durable Object per house. The object owns the state, applies every change as an op, stores the inverse op alongside it, keeps a 200-entry receipt log, and broadcasts to everyone connected over WebSockets. Every tool travels the same op channel as the buttons on the page. An agent's write lights a lamp in the right room on everybody's screen and leaves a receipt any family member can undo. Challenges we ran into Undo that survives other people. Working out how to reverse a change after the fact is guesswork. So every op stores its own inverse at the moment it is applied. Undo is a tool too. An agent can take back its own mistake by receipt id, and your sister can undo what your agent did from her phone in another state. Cloudflare answered before the Worker did. not_found_handling: "single-page-application" was serving index.html for API paths because the asset router sees navigations first. /api/* has to be named explicitly in run_worker_first . Making an agent's work legible. An agent quietly editing your family's records is unsettling. Every change lights the room it belongs to, writes a receipt with a name and a time, and stays undoable by anyone in the house. Accomplishments that we're proud of * An AI tool that connect people and agents, in two way network * A test suite that drives every tool and guards the spec. tests/webmcp-tools.test.mjs polyfills document.modelContext and calls all 17 house tools, both landing tools, and all three declarative forms. It also asserts that every annotation key is a member WebMCP defines. An invented hint fails the build. A two-browser test that proves the whole claim. One browser drives an agent, the other is a family member's screen. The suite watches the change cross the wire and watches the other person undo it. A demo a judge can run in any browser. The Agent tab runs the real execute() functions behind a button, so the entire tool surface is testable today, including on a phone. What we learned WebMCP changes what a page is for. The web was built for eyes and a pointer. Software reaching it has always worked from the outside: scrapers, separate servers, issued keys. WebMCP turns that around. The page itself offers what it can do, inside the user's own browser session, behind the security and permissions the site already enforces. The site stays in charge of its own rules. One codebase serves the person and the agent at once, with the agent surface designed in from the first line. I believe this is where web development goes: sites built for two audiences, with the second one treated as first class. Build the tool surface as a peer of the UI. Every tool goes through the same op channel as the buttons on the page. remember does what the add-memory panel does. claim_care_task does what the Claim button does. Once that was true, the design questions answered themselves: if a family member can do it, an agent can do it, and everyone in the house watches it happen. Tool names and descriptions are the interface. A model reads whats_coming_up , search_house_memory , claim_care_task , and undo_last_action the way a person reads menu labels. The names that work are verbs a family already says out loud. whos_here earns its place because an agent should know who else is in the house before it acts on their behalf. Returning both a receipt id and a record id from every write is what makes chained flows work: search, claim by id, then journal about it. The annotations are a vocabulary, and it rewards reading the dictionary. WebMCP defines three hints: readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint , and consequentialHint . destructiveHint and idempotentHint belong to MCP's separate server-side set. A conformant browser keeps the members WebMCP defines and silently discards the rest. Attic declares readOnlyHint on all 17 tools and sets it true on the seven that only read. untrustedContentHint goes on the twelve whose output can carry text another family member wrote. consequentialHint goes on the two an agent should confirm first. Attic ships the three WebMCP defines. Check the annotations in a browser, beyond the spec alone. I registered a probe tool in Chrome 152 under the origin trial with six annotation keys and read it back with document.modelContext.getTools() . Two survive today: readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . consequentialHint appears in the published dictionary but remains unimplemented, so it is dropped in conversion. Attic keeps it anyway. It is the correct member, and it starts working the day Chrome ships it. The same caution sits in the descriptions of forget and add_medication , which is the channel a model reads right now. That check takes five minutes and belongs in any WebMCP project. What's next for Attic I want Attic to become a real product. This submission is a hackathon build. The problem behind it is a solution, and it is the one I want to work on. The next step is putting OpenAI's newest models behind the house. An agent that holds a whole household in view can surface the refill that slipped and the appointment two siblings both booked. It can catch the pattern in a care journal that shows up only across months. Mostly I want Attic to be the answer when someone asks what these tools are actually for. Keeping a family close through a hard year is a real use for AI, and it is the one I care about. 1. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The thing that kills household memory is capture friction. An agent is the only thing that removes it. You say "gutters cleaned by ClearFlow, about $180" in passing to the agent you are already talking to. remember files it, dated, in the yard, with a reminder for next autumn. The knowledge gets captured at the moment it exists, which is the only moment it is ever free. Retrieval is just as agent-shaped. A year later you are in a hardware store and ask "what size filter does the furnace take?" Your sister, in another state, asks her agent "who is covering Mom this week?" Both of you want the answer where you already are, in the conversation you are in. A household memory needs structured tools. The data is small, highly structured, deeply personal, and it changes constantly from several directions at once. Attic hands agents 17 imperative tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool inside a house, and 2 more on the landing page so an agent can create or open one for you. All use JSON Schema inputs and annotations from the WebMCP ToolAnnotations dictionary, plus 3 declarative <form toolname> tools. 2. How it creates a better user experience Handing an agent write access to a family's shared memory is only tolerable if the family can see and reverse what it did. Every mutating tool call lands on the page as a receipt : who did it, through which tool, in plain language, with an Undo button any family member can press. title: BF scratch
pitch: Build your PC, but with your friend next to you, not a blind one that you need to teach and explain the context, but is right next to you, seeing the same thing.
about_excerpt: Build your PC, but with your friend next to you, not a blind one that you need to teach and explain the context, but is right next to you, seeing the same thing. Like Comment Story Updates Final result debugging process debugging process debugging process debugging process Github repo About the Project Inspiration The idea for BF scratch came from my own attempt to build a desktop PC for the first time. Right after finishing my military service, I wanted to know what the hype around the AI's were by myself. So I thought to start with a PC. I started comparing parts, watching YouTube, asking AI, and asking friends. The problem was that the recomendations were all so very different. Youtube videos focused on the general mass, naming phrases like frames per dollar for best optimal choices without fully understanding my needs on focusing on AI and development. Ai understood my context but gave outdated prices and has no idea what parts goes along with which. As someone who did not already understand PC hardware, especially when I was about to spend a significant amount of money, i just couldn't take the risk from anyone who doesn't understand mine or the market situation properly. In the end, I gave up on building a desktop and bought a laptop instead, paying an extra for the premium that I may not have needed if I had access to the proper tools. The issue was not that there weren't enough informatoin, it was the opposite. There were too many information, but nothing that I really needed. I needed to know the price, how the putting the parts actually seems like, where the cable goes, if the ram is compatiable with the CPU, do I have enough power supply before I buy this expensive hardware. When I learned about WebMCP, that old idea suddenly made sense. The biggest issue with AI assistants, when I tried to build a PC myself, I felt like getting advises from who is blind to the real world: whenever something changes, I have to explain the new situation again, paste a model name, or send another screenshot. I wanted the AI to feel less like a manager I had to report to and get confirmations from and more like a smart friend standing next to me, looking at the same PC and helping me build it. That became 'BF scratch', build from scratch, a name implying that this is going to be your friend to help you build, not a manager that you need to work for. What it does BF scratch is designed to tackle the exact problem that I described: the stress of not seeing the same page. The user can select, install, move, and replace PC components directly in an interactive 3D workspace. They can inspect compatibility, physical clearance, power requirements, cooling configuration, and component connections. At the same time, a WebMCP-enabled AI can access the same underlying build state. The AI does not guess the dimension of the GPU, or whether a power connector exists. It reads structured validation results, understands the user's intent, explains the problem, and helps choose or apply an appropriate solution. It is now, somethign that can give advice directly, looking at the same thing as the user. That is the highlight: both sides are working on the same build. A user can change a component manually, AI can see what changed, let the AI repair the configuration, and immediately see the changes in the same 3D workspace. No guessing from the AI and no prompts for the user. How we built it BS scratch is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Three.js, and React Three Fiber/Drei We deliberately separated the project into several layers: an authoritative build state shared domain commands for human and AI actions deterministic compatibility and readiness validation atomic simulation and mutation logic undo/history the React Three Fiber scene the WebMCP tool layer All live changes pass through the same command layer, regardless of whether they originate from the GUI or an AI agent. The agent can also simulate a set of changes before applying them to the live build. The current WebMCP interface exposes 16 tools, including build-state inspection, catalog and mount discovery, validation, component installation and movement, cable connection and disconnection, fan direction changes, simulation, case selection, auto-fill, and undo. This allowed us to treat WebMCP not as a chatbot feature, but as another structured interface into the same application. Challenges we faced We learned that building as a team/ and working on a time-constrained task is vastly different compared to self-ran projects. In my personal projects, I usually prefer to validate each layer carefully before moving on to the next part of the MVP. I actually make my AI agent go on it's self-validating loop until it reaches me to test it. sometime-to prevent hellucinations, I get a second agent to validate. This loop and seoncd validation, while it was able to get a better-bug free version, it was time costly as well; which was not a big issue in self-ran project. My teammate however, preferred to build visible functionality quickly and debug it afterward; which better suited not only in a team envorinment as I am not the only one working at the same given time-period, but also in a time-constrainted task as this hackathon. I think this difference came from our educational background of me being an economics student, and him being used of the debugging and time-constrained workflows due to his computer science background. That difference created some friction at first, I did not understand my friend's inital result as almost none of the functions were delivered, farcry from our MVP. We eventually found a compromise: we would not lower the quality bar of the MVP itself, but we would continuously produce visible, working milestones and refine them afterward. A mix of both of our workflows. We also had to define explicit contracts between components and responsibilities instead of relying on assumptions that would have remained in my head during a solo project. What we learned The biggest technical lesson was understanding what WebMCP can change about the relationship between an AI and a web application. Before this project, I mostly thought about AI assistance as a wish made to the monkey's paw: providing a prompt to just wish for the goal to be completed, the AI reasons about it, and the user hope for the optimual result that they may have to trust it, especially on a pricy enviornment that you cannot retireve, like buying PC parts. WebMCP made us think differently, the AI can participate directly in the workspace. I also learned a lot about the difference between building alone and building with another person. Team development required clearer contracts, more explicit ownership, and compromise about how quickly to move versus how deeply to validate. What made that moment especially meaningful was that I had not personally implemented or verified that part. My teammate had. When I saw their part of the system connect correctly with the architecture we had designed together, I felt a kind of satisfaction that was different from finishing an MVP alone. It was no longer just the feeling of, “I" made this work. It was the feeling of, “We" made this work. at that moment, did I feel like the name BF scratch was worthy for what it delivered.
