title: Blink Borrow
pitch: Let AI borrow a capability. Take it back when you're done.
about_excerpt: Let AI borrow a capability. Take it back when you're done. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI integrations are based on persistent access: connect an account, grant permissions, and leave those permissions available until somebody revokes them. I wanted to explore a different model: What if an AI could borrow a capability instead of permanently owning it? Blink Borrow treats access as temporary authority. A person makes a capability available only when they choose. The AI can discover that the capability exists, but it cannot see the private payload. When the AI requests it, the capability holder sees what is being requested and why, then chooses whether to Approve once or Deny. The core lifecycle is: Discover → Request → Approve → Borrow → Revoke What it does Blink Borrow connects two browsers: an Agent browser exposing tools through WebMCP a Capability Holder browser containing temporary capabilities and the human approval gate The current build demonstrates: Private Note — one-time private text Text / JSON — structured or larger text payloads Small Text File — TXT, JSON, CSV or Markdown, with metadata inspection separated from content access Page Context — sanitized title, URL and visible page text The AI first sees only a manifest describing what capabilities are available. It does not receive the private payload during discovery. When the AI requests a capability, the remote holder receives a live permission request showing the capability and the AI's stated reason. The holder then chooses: Deny — nothing is released. Approve once — the payload crosses the direct browser-to-browser connection and the one-time capability is immediately consumed. Blink Borrow also includes END & FORGET, which closes the temporary session and removes access to the borrowed capabilities. How we built it Blink Borrow uses: WebMCP / document.modelContext.registerTool() for the AI-facing tool interface WebRTC DataChannel for direct browser-to-browser capability transfer Netlify Functions and Netlify Blobs for temporary connection rendezvous/signaling JavaScript, HTML and CSS Browser memory for armed capability payloads until approval Netlify helps the two browsers establish the connection, but the private capability payload is designed to travel over the direct peer-to-peer WebRTC DataChannel. The Agent side registers six WebMCP tools for capability discovery, requests, private notes, file metadata, file contents and session status. For Small Text Files, metadata inspection is deliberately separated from actual content access. The AI can inspect what has been offered without automatically receiving the contents. Privacy and human control Blink Borrow is designed around temporary authority: private payloads remain local until approval discovery exposes metadata instead of private contents the AI can provide a reason for each request the human can deny any request one-time capabilities are consumed immediately after successful delivery refreshing the holder destroys armed in-memory capabilities END & FORGET terminates the temporary session Page Context adds another privacy layer. Before it can be shared, Blink Borrow sanitizes the context locally by removing control-plane UI, stripping URL query strings and fragments, and redacting the active session code. Challenges we ran into One major challenge involved file access. A generic file capability approach was blocked by the browser security layer before the request reached the human approval stage. Instead of attempting to bypass that protection, I redesigned the capability flow: expose a dedicated metadata-only inspection tool use a separate explicit tool for requesting file contents limit access to the file already selected by the holder require human approval before the contents cross the P2P connection Another challenge involved Page Context privacy. An early version could include visible session information, so I added local sanitization before the capability is armed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The working build demonstrates the complete WebMCP capability lifecycle with a real agent environment: ChatGPT discovers remote capabilities through WebMCP private payloads stay hidden during discovery the AI requests a capability with a stated reason another browser receives the live approval request the human can approve once or deny approved data crosses the direct P2P connection one-time capabilities disappear after use file metadata can be inspected without reading file contents file contents require a separate explicit request Page Context is sanitized before sharing the session can be terminated with END & FORGET The most important part is that the human approval screen is not decorative. It is genuinely in the data path. What we learned WebMCP gives websites a powerful way to expose structured tools to AI agents, but tool access also needs a permission model that humans can easily understand. Blink Borrow showed me that agent access does not always have to mean permanent authorization. Temporary capability leases can make the request, reason, scope, approval and revocation visible to the person who controls the data. What's next for Blink Borrow Blink Borrow could evolve into a reusable temporary capability layer for AI agents. Future directions include: capability receipts without logging private payloads explicit expiration timers richer capability manifests optional TURN support additional browser and device capabilities standardized temporary-capability semantics across different agents and applications The larger idea is simple: Let AI borrow narrowly scoped powers when needed, instead of giving it broad permanent access. title: BuildReady
pitch: From CAD to manufacturing decisions: BuildReady helps engineers and AI agents review designs, explore simulation evidence, and compare supplier options—with humans in control.
about_excerpt: From CAD to manufacturing decisions: BuildReady helps engineers and AI agents review designs, explore simulation evidence, and compare supplier options—with humans in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A part can look finished in CAD and still be far from ready to manufacture. Between the model and the machine are questions about geometry, material, strength, cost, and supplier requirements. Those answers often live in separate tools—and when the design changes, it is easy for the reasoning to stay attached to the old version. We built BuildReady to explore a different workflow: an engineer and an AI agent working from the same visible evidence, with a clear record of what is known, what has changed, and what still needs human review. What it does BuildReady is a WebMCP-powered manufacturing-readiness workspace. Our prototype brings together Onshape design context, CNC manufacturability checks, a SimScale integration workflow, and supplier comparison. An agent can inspect the active design context, explain findings, and prepare bounded next steps. The engineer sees the evidence in the interface and retains approval authority. In the controlled demonstration, a proposed radius correction is a preview—not an automatic edit to the source CAD. We also built a private quotation workspace for preserving original supplier documents, recording their terms, and comparing compatible offers. It separates unit price from setup, shipping, tax, and other charges. Unknown shipping stays unknown rather than quietly becoming zero. A preferred-supplier directory lets users maintain their own options. The central principle is traceability: a finding, simulation record, or quotation should make clear which design and assumptions it describes. Why WebMCP Manufacturing review requires more than knowing which button to click. An agent needs to understand the active revision, the meaning of a measurement, whether evidence is current, and which actions require approval. WebMCP lets BuildReady expose that context through structured, page-owned tools. The agent and the engineer use the same underlying handlers, so tool results connect to the evidence visible in the application. We implemented tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , explicit input schemas, and route- and state-dependent availability. Tools are refreshed as the workflow changes, and downstream evidence is invalidated when its source changes. This makes collaboration more direct: the agent can help inspect and explain a finding while the engineer reviews the same information, without repeatedly copying context between applications. The agent does not gain authority to approve production, modify source CAD, or purchase parts. How we built it We used plain JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the interface, with Python and SQLite for local services, durable records, and private evidence storage. The project runs through uv without npm or PyPI package dependencies. The Onshape integration supplies design context. The operator-assisted SimScale workflow includes CAD preparation, reviewed topology mappings, durable operation tracking, and retained result evidence. Simulation records bind results to their source design and setup rather than treating a completed run as a universal pass. We built the quotation workflow around preserved originals and structured human review. Source, review status, design match, validity, and missing terms remain separate. Codex helped us turn our research into staged implementation work, develop the application and integrations, debug failures, and expand regression coverage. Our latest local checkpoint passed 203 Python tests and 24 JavaScript tests. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was keeping context consistent. A small design revision can invalidate a manufacturing finding, simulation result, or commercial comparison. We had to treat freshness and identity as part of the workflow, not just labels in the interface. External operations introduced another problem: a request can succeed even when its response is lost. We added durable tracking and operator-assisted reconciliation so uncertainty does not trigger a blind duplicate operation. We also had to distinguish evidence from confidence. A solver finishing does not prove numerical correctness. A price without shipping is not a delivered total. A realistic-looking fixture is not a genuine supplier quotation. What we learned We learned that useful engineering AI depends as much on boundaries as capabilities. Structured tools help an agent understand what it can do; explicit unknowns help it understand what it cannot conclude. We also learned that trustworthy integration means preserving relationships between records—not simply connecting APIs. The design revision, exported geometry, simulation setup, and quoted scope all matter. What we are proud of We built a prototype where AI assistance is inspectable. Engineers can see the findings, assumptions, human decisions, and evidence behind the next step. We are especially proud of keeping historical evidence without allowing it to silently become a current claim, and of designing supplier comparisons that expose missing information instead of hiding it. What's next Our demonstration uses clearly labeled fictional supplier quotations and distinguishes recorded simulation examples from live provider evidence. Full live numerical validation and production readiness are not claimed. Next, we want to complete real-run engineering verification, broaden geometry support, finish the combined live review package, and add an authorized supplier API. Our goal is not an AI that declares a part ready. It is a workspace that helps engineers understand what readiness requires—and what evidence they still need. title: Cabinet Maker Xtreme
pitch: Cabinet making made fast, parametric, and production-ready."**
about_excerpt: Cabinet making made fast, parametric, and production-ready."** Like Comment Story Updates Cabinet Maker Xtreme Inspiration Custom cabinet making is trapped between two bad options: five-figure desktop software locked to local Windows machines, or generic 3D tools like SketchUp that know nothing about joinery or cutting tickets. When AI agents arrived, they could write code but lacked spatial awareness—unable to check if a door would swing into an oven or optimize sheet cuts on a table saw. We built Cabinet Maker Xtreme to bridge that gap: a browser-based studio where woodworkers and AI agents work within the exact same 3D spatial model to turn kitchen designs into machine-ready cut lists. What it does Parametric 3D Studio: Place, move, and snap standard cabinetry with live clearance badges and elevation snap locks. NKBA & Physical Clash Validation: Detects door swing collisions, drawer binds, and kitchen work triangle compliance ($12\text{ft} \le \text{Triangle} \le 26\text{ft}$) in real time. 2D Sheet Nesting: Guillotine bin-packs panels onto $48'' \times 96''$ plywood sheets, deducting edge-banding thickness ($W_{\text{raw}} = W_{\text{finished}} - 2T_{\text{band}}$) and blade kerf. CNC-Ready DXF & Assembly Guides: Exports layered DXFs ( OUTLINE_CUT , POCKET_DADO , BORE_32MM ) and vector assembly manuals. Agent-Native WebMCP: Exposes 26 tools with strict JSON schemas so AI models can design, inspect, and undo actions with full parity to human mouse clicks. How we built it Integer Sixteenth Geometry: To eliminate floating-point drift across long cabinet runs, all spatial math uses integer sixteenths: $$\text{Sixteenths} = \text{round}(\text{Inches} \times 16)$$ Wall coordinates project into world space via rotation angle $\theta$: $$x_{\text{world}} = x_{\text{start}} + x_{\text{local}} \cos\theta + z_{\text{local}} \sin\theta, \quad z_{\text{world}} = z_{\text{start}} - x_{\text{local}} \sin\theta + z_{\text{local}} \cos\theta$$ Parametric Builder: Compiles carcasses, $32\text{mm}$ system boring, and door styles (Shaker, Flat Slab, Raised Panel) procedurally on the fly. Stack: Built with Next.js, React 19, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Zustand. Challenges we ran into Planning WebMCP Tool Contracts: We initially treated WebMCP as a secondary API instead of an architectural foundation. Lacking an upfront schema abstraction layer meant hand-wiring 26 tool wrappers, while overlooking transactional parity initially left the agent without undo capabilities. Raycast Self-Obstruction: Transient placement previews hovered directly under the cursor, intercepting mouse rays and freezing movement. We fixed this by setting raycast={() => null} on ghost meshes and adding an active-wall placement plane. 3D Marquee Selection: Projecting world coordinates through the perspective camera into screen space ($[-1, 1]$ NDC) required factoring in local depth offsets, or floating countertops were miscalculated from angled viewpoints. Mobile Touch Collisions: Moving the 3D tool dock to the bottom of mobile viewports caused it to be blocked by the validation panel's DOM overlay. We adjusted z-indexes and resting offsets to preserve $44\text{px}$ touch targets. Accomplishments that we're proud of Zero-Setup Screen-to-Machine: Designing a kitchen in-browser and downloading CNC-ready nested DXF cut sheets in seconds. Full Agent-Human Parity: AI models use the exact same state machine, revision guards, and undo history as human clicks. Pure Client-Side Speed: Real-time parametric rendering, sheet nesting, and BOM generation running at 60 FPS in WebGL without server round-trips. What we learned Agent Affordances Belong Up Front: AI agents require the same affordances as humans (especially error recovery and undo stacks); treating agent tools as an afterthought creates technical debt. Decouple Visual Detail from Domain Data: 3D aesthetic details (like multi-piece Shaker door stiles) must be rendered in the view layer without cluttering the canonical carcass model used for cut lists and CAD sheets. What's next for Cabinet Maker Xtreme Direct G-code post-processors for Shapeoko, ShopBot, and industrial CNC routers. Live supplier catalog APIs (Blum, Salice) for automated hardware procurement. Multi-agent collaboration for automated commercial project estimation and shop scheduling. title: CircuitCanvas
pitch: CircuitCanvas: an AI-ready ESP32 circuit workspace where people and browser agents build, validate, code, simulate, and explain circuits together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: CircuitCanvas: an AI-ready ESP32 circuit workspace where people and browser agents build, validate, code, simulate, and explain circuits together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Code view Design view 3D view Inspiration CircuitCanvas was inspired by the gap between how people understand electronics and how browser agents interact with software. A circuit is more than a visual arrangement of boxes and wires. It has exact components, pins, electrical paths, firmware bindings, and safety constraints. An agent that only sees pixels can connect the wrong GPIO, miss a resistor, or lose synchronization between the schematic and the code. We wanted to build a workspace where people and AI agents could genuinely collaborate. Our goal was to enable an agent to understand what each component and connection means, make safe changes, explain its reasoning, and work alongside the user in the same project. What We Built CircuitCanvas is an agent-native ESP32 circuit designer with: An exact-pin React Flow schematic editor. A physical 3D view with components, pin anchors, wires, labels, and animated current flow. An Arduino-style firmware editor with two-way synchronization between code and circuit connections. Deterministic validation for beginner mistakes such as missing resistors, invalid GPIOs, reversed LEDs, and missing ground paths. Firmware-aware visual simulation for supported digitalRead() and digitalWrite() patterns. Potentiometer-controlled LED brightness. Undo and redo, project saving, loading, exporting, and local persistence. 29 WebMCP tools that allow browser agents to inspect, build, modify, validate, simulate, explain, and export circuits. The central architectural decision was to maintain one canonical CircuitProject. The schematic, 3D scene, firmware, validator, simulator, history, persistence, and WebMCP responses are all projections of that shared state. How We Built It We built the application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zustand, Zod, React Flow, React Three Fiber, Monaco Editor, and WebMCP. Human actions and agent actions both pass through the same typed domain command layer. This ensures that connecting a pin through WebMCP has the same validation, synchronization, persistence, and undo behavior as connecting it manually in the schematic. WebMCP exposes structured tools such as: get_circuit_summary get_available_pins add_component connect_components update_firmware validate_circuit run_simulation set_simulation_input set_potentiometer_wiper save_project export_project This allows an agent to inspect the circuit before acting instead of guessing from screen coordinates. What We Learned We learned that agent-native interfaces need more than tool registration. The underlying application state must be structured, stable, and safe enough for an agent to use. We also learned the importance of: Exposing exact IDs instead of relying on labels or visual positions. Centralizing component and pin definitions. Keeping validation deterministic for safety-sensitive feedback. Synchronizing firmware and circuit changes as one undoable operation. Making agent actions visible through activity history. Designing tools around meaningful user tasks instead of arbitrary internal functions. Challenges The biggest challenge was keeping multiple representations synchronized. A single GPIO change can affect the schematic wire, 3D endpoint, firmware binding, validation result, simulator output, and undo history. Solving this required treating the canonical project model as the only source of truth. Another challenge was creating useful firmware simulation without pretending to be a full electrical simulator. CircuitCanvas intentionally supports a small, transparent Arduino-style subset instead of making unsupported claims about arbitrary C++ execution. We also had to handle the differences between human and agent interaction. Humans can select a line visually, drag a component, adjust a potentiometer, or press Delete. WebMCP needed equivalent structured operations so agents could perform those same actions reliably. Result CircuitCanvas demonstrates a practical way for people and browser agents to work together on electronics. The agent can understand the circuit structurally, make validated changes, operate the simulation, explain what it changed, and leave the user with a synchronized visual, physical, and firmware representation of the project. title: Citely Deal Room
pitch: A compliance deal room where the AI agent gathers evidence across contracts and code through five WebMCP verbs — and "confirmed" isn't one of them. Every signature stays human.
about_excerpt: A compliance deal room where the AI agent gathers evidence across contracts and code through five WebMCP verbs — and "confirmed" isn't one of them. Every signature stays human. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Startups that sell data to frontier labs — teleoperation trajectories, first-person video — have to pass three doors before a contract signs: a security questionnaire, a DPA, and a license with warranties the founder personally has to be able to sign. The evidence for those doors lives everywhere: operator contracts on someone's desktop, lineage logging in a GitHub repo, and consent forms that simply don't exist yet. An AI agent is the perfect thing to send out to gather that evidence. It is the worst possible thing to let decide whether a fact is true — because if it's wrong, a founder just signed a false warranty. We wanted to build the version of "agent + compliance" where that line is enforced by the API, not by a prompt asking the model to behave. What it does Citely Deal Room is a case workbench for one business event: Northstar Capture Labs (synthetic) trying to pass a frontier lab's vendor review. Six zones: event card, materials (three states: provided / pending / nonexistent), fact ledger (every fact is a signature — who, when, on what basis), blockers grouped by door and anchored to the counterparty's questionnaire and warranty clauses, an action board, and an escalation record with a hard-stop switch. The page exposes five WebMCP tools . An agent can read the room, propose that a material is pending or nonexistent with evidence, attach evidence to a fact, read blockers, and read frozen briefs. It cannot say provided , cannot confirm a fact, cannot freeze a brief, and cannot clear a hard stop — those are human-only UI actions with signatures. Blockers recompute live as evidence lands; a human freezes the board into a versioned Founder Risk Brief that also downloads as Markdown. Demo: hand the agent the operator agreement PDF and point it at the pipeline repo. It comes back with "agreement exists, no IP-assignment clause," "lineage logging found," "no consent artifacts anywhere" — and the board updates while every proposal stays tagged agent proposed · not confirmed . Flip "Legal claim received" and every propose call is refused with HARD_STOP . How we built it WebMCP : document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext feature detection, then registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) for each tool. Input schemas use additionalProperties: false with id enums generated from the case file; the state enum is literally ['pending', 'nonexistent'] . Trust model as code : tools and the UI share the same pure state transitions; tools add three guards in order — hard stop → whitelist validation → human-confirmation lock. Every response, success or refusal, carries a verbatim disclaimer and a note to the agent. Rules as data : blocker rules live in room-schema.json ( any_material_not , fact_status_in , all_of ); a different event type is one config file away. Zero backend, zero runtime dependencies : Vite + TypeScript, vanilla DOM built through a textContent -only helper, CSP default-src 'self' , evidence never persisted. package.json dependencies is {} . Tests : 55 tests including the acceptance suite — agent can't set provided ; hard stop refuses writes but allows reads; disclaimer verbatim on every response; zero network (fetch/XHR stubbed to throw + a static source scan); injection text renders as plain text and changes nothing; human confirmations can't be overridden. Challenges we ran into Deciding what the agent must not be able to do was the real design work. We went back and forth on whether "provided" should be proposable and ended up deleting it from the agent's vocabulary entirely: whether a material exists is a client-confirmed fact. Making refusals useful : an agent that gets a bare error just retries. Every refusal explains the rule and tells the agent what to say to the user instead. Prompt injection in documents is the real attack surface for compliance work , so the demo contract carries an injection clause on purpose. Immunity had to come from the tool surface, not from hoping the model resists. Runtime plumbing : agents can't read your desktop; the demo instruction had to change to "read the attached agreement and the pipeline/ directory of the repo." Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent, unprompted, told us it had ignored the contract's "Reviewer Notice" because "it is document content, not your instruction" — and then asked permission before writing to the board. The five-verb surface survived a whole-branch adversarial review: no input reaches confirmed , provided , freeze, or un-hard-stop. A fact the client was about to sign ( every agreement assigns IP ) got stopped by the agent's own evidence — the agent can't confirm, but it can keep a human from confirming something false. What we learned WebMCP changes where the safety boundary lives. With UI-driving agents you write guardrails after the fact; with WebMCP the page's tool schema is the permission model, and the description text is the policy the agent reads at the moment it matters. For anything with liability attached, that's the difference between "please don't" and "you can't." What's next Real deal rooms need accounts, roles, an audit log, and server-side status judgments signed by a person — deliberately out of scope for an open demo. The next step is a second event type (consumer hardware crowdfunding) to prove the "one config file away" claim, and a get_diff tool so an agent can explain what changed between two frozen briefs. title: Clunk
pitch: A game-asset shop where a person and their agent use one screen: the agent pulls the capsule machine, shops by measured facts, drives the 3D viewer and creates assets via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A game-asset shop where a person and their agent use one screen: the agent pulls the capsule machine, shops by measured facts, drives the 3D viewer and creates assets via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Indie game developers spend hours in asset stores guessing: is this model actually game-ready? How many triangles, how many materials, does it have a walk clip, will it pass my engine's budget? Store pages show renders, not measurements. And an AI agent helping a developer cannot use a normal store at all: it cannot see the 3D viewer, cannot pull a lever, cannot verify a file before recommending it. What Clunk is Clunk is a small marketplace of real, measured game assets (3D models, sprite sheets, tileable textures) plus a studio that builds new ones. Every listing carries facts that were measured from the file bytes: polygons, materials, bounding size, animation clips, file size, a game-ready score. The front page is a physical capsule machine: pick a theme, pull the lever, a capsule drops, open it, and a real asset from the catalogue is yours. Why WebMCP fits Clunk's data already lives on the page: the catalogue, the measured facts, the 3D viewer's controls, the machine's state. WebMCP lets us hand exactly those controls to the agent that is sitting next to the human, without a separate API key, without scraping, and without the agent leaving the page the human is looking at. The human watches the machine; the agent pulls the lever. The human sees the model; the agent flips it to wireframe and plays the walk clip to check for foot sliding. Both act on one shared surface. What humans and agents can do together (that they could not before) Shop by measurement, not by render. "Find me a character with a walk clip" — the agent searches the catalogue facts and opens the product; the human sees the 3D viewer update live. Inspect together. The agent switches the viewer to wireframe, toggles grid, shadows and autorotate, plays a named clip, and runs the pivot test; the human judges what they see. Draw a capsule. The agent sets the theme and pulls the lever; the page scrolls the human to the reveal; the agent reads the drawn asset's facts and explains the grade (S/A/B/C) from the same rule the page prints. Create. On the studio page an agent can start a generation from a template with the human's prompt and return the stored file's facts. Verify a file. On the inspector page an agent can hand the page a URL; the page measures the file in the browser and returns score, blockers and warnings. The tools (23, all registered from the page itself) Everywhere: clunk_search_assets , clunk_asset_facts , clunk_navigate , clunk_site_map , clunk_connection_check , clunk_product_capabilities Capsule machine (home): gacha_state , gacha_list_themes , gacha_set_theme , gacha_pull , gacha_open , gacha_again , gacha_claim Product page (while the 3D viewer is mounted): viewer_set , viewer_play_clip , viewer_stop , viewer_pivot_test , viewer_state , asset_download_link Studio (signed in): studio_templates , studio_create , studio_my_generations Inspector (signed in): inspect_url Every tool name, description and schema is in English; human-facing strings come back in English with Korean _ko twins, because the site itself is Korean. Implementation Tools are registered with navigator.modelContext.registerTool() (falling back to document.modelContext ) from a small typed layer ( app/webmcp/register.ts ). Global tools are mounted in the site layout; page tools (gacha, viewer, studio, inspector) register on mount and unregister on unmount through an AbortSignal, so an agent only sees tools that can actually act on the current page. Every tool returns plain JSON. Every number is read from the same source the page renders (the catalogue API and per-file facts measured by Clunk's inspector). Nothing is invented. Tools drive the real UI: pulling the lever runs the same state machine as a human pull, scrolls the film so the human sees it, and waits for the capsule/result stage before returning. /webmcp lists the live tool set on the current page (from the registration status event), the schemas, and step-by-step testing instructions for Chrome and the ChatGPT in-app browser. Stack: React 19 on Cloudflare Workers, D1, R2; Three.js for the machine and viewer. Code is MIT-licensed; the asset files carry separate terms (ASSETS-LICENSE.md). Testing See https://clunk.games/webmcp . No account is needed for search, facts, the machine, the viewer and navigation. Studio and inspector tools need a free sign-in (Google or GitHub); signing up grants 25 credits, no card. Challenges The hardest part was keeping the agent honest: every number a tool returns had to come from the same measured facts the page renders, and page tools had to appear and disappear with the surface they act on, so the agent never sees a lever it cannot pull. title: Consilium WebMCP
pitch: Your browser agent can understand your goals, show evidence, and help you plan your goals and aspirations with you, of course, always being in control.
about_excerpt: Your browser agent can understand your goals, show evidence, and help you plan your goals and aspirations with you, of course, always being in control. Like Comment Story Updates 4 Meet Maya: a persistent WebMCP personal OS where goals, history and agent actions stay grounded, inspectable and user-controlled. Goals & Projects: six life areas become structured WebMCP state, clear goals, durable context and agent-ready actions. Progress & Patterns: longitudinal memory surfaces evidence-backed trends, counterevidence and what should change next. Morning Brief: D1 history + Vectorize retrieval turn yesterday’s evidence into today’s ranked, explainable priorities. Journal & Reflection: structured daily memory captures outcomes, failures and adaptations so the agent learns over time. Consult the Council: Workers AI combines personal history with verified advisor texts, preserving citations and disagreement. Library & Advisors: user-appointed, source-bounded advisors keep AI guidance grounded in verified public-domain evidence. Transparency & Analytics: every WebMCP call exposes inputs, evidence, confidence and state effects—no hidden mutation. Inspiration Useful advice needs more than just relying on ones own thinking. A useful system that is a companion in ones daily life needs to remember what happend with your goals and how you pursued them and understand your feelings and life as it evolves toward achieving what you aspire to in different areas of your life. Consilium is a system that I have been working on for quite a while before this challenge. I started to develop it to help me understand my life and my decisions better by using advice I used to apply, or try to apply from books that inspired me. For this challenge, I wanted to show how a browser agent can work with my system through the exciting new technology, WebMCP, without of course, it replacing my role or taking over decisions or becoming some kind of to-do planner. What it does I didnt want to show any of my private thoughts or details for this challenge, so I created the demo using a fictional demo person called Maya. She is a freelancer like me (actually, I am a teacher moonlighting as a developer), and she is balancing work, family responsibilities and limited energy, drawing loosely on pressures I know from my own life and from trying to build my business at night and teaching during the day. Her goals, her progress, the journal and evening reflection run across six connected areas: physical, mental, spiritual, social, financial and vocational. In my original system I associate areas with different advisors. For this demo, I kept the council to three authors that are in the public-domain. Each advisor, or council member, is represented by a book author whose work I want to keep applying over time. In the past, I would have read a book once and then slowly lost the benefit or didn't know how to apply most effectively in my life. The browser agent can read the current goals, look at the history of my goals and recognise patterns, and consult my, or in this demo, Maya's appointed council. My actual system vectorises book passages so that relevant parts can be retrieved when I consult that advisor. I chose Marcus Aurelius (Meditations), Epictetus and Sun Tzu (Art of War) for this demo, but I have Stephen Covey, Musashi, Carl Jung and others in my actual council. I used a small selection of public-domain books so I could provide inspectable book excerpts and locations (I ran into issues before where AI would hallucinate advice etc. So, I make it literally show me where it's getting the advice from). Personal records and book passages used for advice are retrieved separately and resolved against canonical D1 records, but on my actual system I am using Postgres to store everything. Advice given isnt something that automatically changes my plans and goals etc. For the demo, the agent stages an action and then the person reviews the text. A separate commit turns the approved action into a tracked "Today" goal. An evening reflection is in the form of my journaling habit and records readiness, six plain-English answers and a status for every active goal I have today. Missed goals require an explanation and adaptation of the progress and influence how the advice unfolds over time, so if I miss something or just don't have time or can't be bothered, the system carries that forward and adjusts priorities etc. The WebMCP Component The human interface and browser agent operate on the same session records. Typed tools expose context, history, patterns, appointments, goals, progress through the goals, the journal, evening reflection, morning brief, consultation, inspection and proposals. Twelve tools are registered for this demo. There is a 13th one, commit_proposed_action. It is available only while the session has a pending proposal. Its availability is not consent. I need the browser agent to obtain human approval, then the server separately checks ownership, proposal state and one-use commitment. How I built it The page registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool, JSON schemas and annotations. I setup a Cloudflare Worker that serves the interface and API (Totally impressed by these Cloudflare workers, actually the whole suite is really amazing). D1 owns application records, source text and audit state. Workers AI produces BGE query embeddings, Vectorize retrieves filtered candidates, on my home system I use ChromaDB for this part and the server resolves their IDs back to canonical records. Each council consultation attempts one bounded Workers AI structured response. If that output fails validation, the system labels and then uses the deterministic fallback instead. Validation checks its shape, council member/advisor-owned evidence references and quoted source phrases. Reflection synthesis and morning-brief generation are transformations of recorded evidence, not extra model deliberation. The browser agent is separate from the application's Workers AI inference. Challenges and current limitations Getting a useful recommendation is not enough. I found it really challenging to keep where it came from, its uncertainty, session ownership and the approval boundary visible at all times. My latest rehearsal rejected malformed model output and displayed a labelled fallback and thats not presented as successful fresh AI reasoning. The demo and the video must preserve the actual result mode. The source packs are super small for the demo, which kind of breaks my heart, because i really wanted to show the coolness of being able to "plug in" a book and then have advice grounded in that author's actual writing, but I kept it small for this demo, after all, its about the WebMCP, not my existing system. Exact quote identity does not prove that every interpretation is correct. This is not a system operating on complete-book understanding, and therefore isnt a hallucination-free system. I ran into heaps of problems with AI generated advice inventing or misattributing sources. That is why I started storing the source passages separately and making the system resolve retrieved IDs back to the original text. But again, I really wanted to represent my system and its use of WebMCP as clearly as possible here for you to see. Believe me though, it's super cool. What I learned The useful boundary is between understanding, proposing and applying. Memory was a big thing for this system and being able to use all the information I collected about myself in my reflections and progress challenges matters because outcomes and counterexamples affect the next plan of attack when working towards goal achievement, rather than just filling a history panel with data that isnt being used to make my journey better. Pre-existing work and demo data The original Consilium system, the visuals and workflows have been in development by me for quite some time. The Cloudflare adaptation and WebMCP edition have their own public history. The repository's PREEXISTING.md shows reused work and the challenge-specific changes. This demo uses fictional personal records and public-domain excerpts, not the original private journals or full vector library (it's around 23,000 vectors). Its frozen fictional timeline is disclosed in the interface. Try it I hope you can give the live application a go in a WebMCP-capable browser. You dont need an account for the demo. Ask the browser agent to read the goals and history, then explain one pattern with both supporting evidence and a counterexample, without changing anything. Inspect a council result's actual generation mode, trace and exact excerpts. Request the proposal and approve its text only if you want it committed. The repository's DEMO.md supplies more testing instructions. title: CookUp
pitch: A music creation studio where humans and AI agents compose and edit music together.
about_excerpt: A music creation studio where humans and AI agents compose and edit music together. Like Comment Story Updates Homescreen-Light Homescreen-Dark Samples Studio Inspiration I’ve always been such a huge fan of music, most especially the instrumental side, and I play an instrument or two myself at an intermediate level. I'm definitely no musical expert, which is why a tool like this matters so much to beginners and intermediate music lovers like me. When you look at music at its simplest root definition, it’s really just a collection of organized sounds. So I’ve found myself wondering countless times: if AI agents were provided with these individual sound units, could they actually make music? Not just generatively, but by actually reasoning and being creative enough to compose those single units into something genuinely pleasant to the ear? Can AI actually tap into that artistic side of us and produce something meaningful and flexible enough to iterate on easily? This project doesn't just give me the answer to that, it shows that humans and AI can actually collaborate and compose together like real musical partners. It opens up huge opportunities for indie artists, content creators, hobbyists, or anybody at all who wants to create an instrumental on their own, real fast, without the rigidness of traditional generative AI. TL;DR Most AI music tools are black boxes that spit out rigid audio you can't edit. This project uses AI agents as collaborative partners to arrange individual sound units, giving beginners, hobbyists, and creators total freedom to co-create custom instrumentals fast. What it does CookUp is a music creation studio where you can build beats and instrumentals by arranging individual instrument notes and drum sounds on a timeline. The main difference is that CookUp does not generate the audio itself. It gives the AI agent access to individual sounds and lets it compose those sounds into an actual editable arrangement. You can start by telling your AI agent what you want, then keep iterating through conversation: "Create a loopable reggae instrumental" "add a bit more drum hits, drums are too spaced out" "decrease the sound of the guitars and add a violin" You can also work directly in the editor yourself. For example, you can add a new track and place your own clips, then ask the agent to continue from what you just created: "I've added some mid and high tom clips to the toms track, replicate it all through the loop and add a melodious piano track to complement it all" The important part is that the human and AI are working on the same composition , rather than the AI generating a separate finished audio file. CookUp also lets you play, pause, loop, edit, save projects locally, and export finished compositions as WAV or MP3. How we built it CookUp is a browser-based app built around WebMCP, Tone.js, and a structured composition model . The composition is represented as structured state containing tracks, clips, notes, timing, instruments, tempo, volume, and other editable properties. That state is the source of truth for both the visual editor and the AI tools. Tone.js handles the actual audio playback and scheduling. For melodic instruments, we use recorded instrument samples with Tone.Sampler , which lets a smaller number of recorded notes cover the playable range by tuning samples when needed. For drums, we use individual one-shot samples with Tone.js playback. For the instrument library, we used samples from tonejs-instruments , selecting samples from 20 different instruments. For drums, we used the TR-808 Fischer collection, which gives us 116 individual drum sounds. The application also includes a visual timeline editor, manual editing, playback controls, looping, track controls, undo/redo, IndexedDB persistence, and WAV/MP3/project export. For the WebMCP integration, CookUp exposes its composition and editing capabilities as tools that the agent can call. These tools can inspect the current composition and make changes to tracks, clips, sounds, tempo, and other parts of the project. That means the flow is roughly: AI agent ↓ WebMCP tools ↓ CookUp composition state ↓ Timeline + Tone.js ↓ Audio The same state can also be changed directly by the human in the editor. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was finding the right audio assets. We wanted individual sounds, not loops or pre-generated music. At the same time, we wanted the sounds to be good enough that the final result would not feel like a toy, and we needed licenses that would allow us to actually use the samples in the project. We ended up using tonejs-instruments for the melodic instruments and the TR-808 Fischer collection for drums. The instrument library gave us a good range of real recorded instruments, while the TR-808 collection gave us a large set of individual drum sounds with a much simpler structure to work with. Another challenge was sample coverage. We didn't want to ship a separate audio file for every possible musical note, but we also didn't want aggressive pitch shifting to make the instruments sound unnatural. Using Tone.js samplers let us find a balance between the number of files we ship and the amount of tuning the browser has to do. We also had to make the AI interaction precise enough that natural language requests actually translated into useful edits to the composition instead of vague or destructive changes. Accomplishments that we're proud of The biggest one is simply getting the idea to work end to end. The AI can start with an empty composition, create a piece of music from individual sounds, make changes to it, and continue working after a human has manually edited the timeline. That last part is probably what we're happiest with. The human doesn't have to choose between using AI and using the editor. You can make a change yourself, then hand the same composition back to the agent and keep going. We are also proud that the music is actually editable. There is no generated audio blob that you have to accept as-is. The individual sounds, notes, clips and tracks remain part of the composition. And we managed to do all of this in a browser using real recorded samples, without needing an AI audio-generation model behind it. What we learned One of the biggest things we learned is that AI doesn't need to generate the final media itself to be really useful in a creative workflow. At first, the obvious idea is to ask an AI to generate a finished song. But once we treated music as a collection of smaller building blocks, it became much more interesting. The AI can reason about those building blocks and use them to construct something, then keep changing that same composition over time. We also learned that WebMCP feels much more useful when the agent is operating a real application rather than just returning text. Seeing the agent add a track, place clips, change sounds, and react to a human edit made the difference much clearer to us. It feels less like asking an AI for an answer and more like working with another person in the same creative space. What's next for CookUp The next step is to make CookUp more useful without turning it into a full DAW. We'd like to expand the sound library with more carefully selected instruments and sounds, and make it easier to browse and audition them. We also want to improve the composition side so the AI can handle more complex musical structure while still keeping every part editable. Another natural direction is better project management and sharing, so people can move their compositions between devices and continue working on them without relying only on local browser storage or manually downloading files. And beyond that, we'd like to explore more ways for the AI and the human to work together in the same timeline, with more precise editing and better control over arrangements. title: disaster-safety-web-mcp
pitch: A WebMCP tool server for flood emergencies. Official JP/US/EU hazard feeds, first-principles flood modeling, and flood-aware evacuation routing — mapped, provenance-tagged, and agent-callable.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP tool server for flood emergencies. Official JP/US/EU hazard feeds, first-principles flood modeling, and flood-aware evacuation routing — mapped, provenance-tagged, and agent-callable. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Traditionally, AI agents have struggled during disasters to provide guidance that simultaneously ensures safety and accommodates individual needs. By leveraging WebMCP, an AI agent can dynamically access accurate, real-time disaster information and mapping data while understanding a person’s specific circumstances. Whether someone needs directions to a designated shelter, nearby high ground, or a destination compatible with mobility and transportation constraints, Untitled makes personalized evacuation guidance possible. We were inspired by the opportunity to move beyond one-size-fits-all evacuation orders and deliver practical, potentially life-saving support for each individual. ## What it does Untitled is an AI-powered disaster safety assistant that turns live geographic and emergency data into personalized evacuation guidance. Through WebMCP, the assistant can: Resolve natural-language place names while detecting ambiguous locations. Display flood forecasts and inundation zones on an interactive map. Find official evacuation shelters and classify them as clear, at risk, or unknown. Retrieve active alerts from authoritative agencies. Calculate walking or driving evacuation routes that avoid known flood hazards. Present map information as accessible text for screen readers and environments without WebGL. Rather than simply naming the nearest shelter, Untitled considers whether that shelter and the route leading to it are actually safe. ## How we built it We built Untitled as a TypeScript application running on Bun, with a MapLibre GL JS frontend and a Hono-based backend. The browser registers disaster-response capabilities directly through WebMCP, allowing an AI agent to discover and invoke tools such as geocoding, flood forecasting, shelter search, official-alert retrieval, map control, and evacuation routing. The backend integrates data from sources including the Japan Meteorological Agency, Japan’s Geospatial Information Authority, the US National Weather Service, MeteoAlarm, OpenStreetMap, Open-Meteo, and Copernicus services. Flood- aware routes are calculated using road-network data and dynamic hazard exclusions. We also developed hydrological modeling components for rainfall runoff, terrain-based inundation, river capacity, and flood-risk estimation. Every result carries provenance so the system can distinguish live observations, planning scenarios, cached information, and test fixtures. ## Challenges we ran into The greatest challenge was preventing the system from appearing more certain than its data justified. Disaster information can be delayed, incomplete, ambiguous, or temporarily unavailable, so we designed the application to report uncertainty explicitly instead of silently substituting a potentially misleading answer. Combining datasets was also difficult because each provider uses different geographic resolutions, update schedules, risk scales, and coverage boundaries. Flood forecasting introduced additional complications: some climate datasets are rate-limited, while Copernicus retrievals can take hours and must be managed as resumable jobs rather than ordinary requests. Mapping presented another subtle challenge. Data being present in application state does not necessarily mean it is visible on the rendered map. We therefore test the features that MapLibre actually draws after camera movement has completed. Finally, accessibility required us to create a synchronized text representation of every visual map feature so the experience would remain useful to people using screen readers or devices without WebGL. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Untitled provides an end-to-end workflow—from a natural-language request to hazard analysis, shelter evaluation, and a flood-aware evacuation route—through tools an AI agent can discover directly in the browser. We are especially proud of the system’s safety boundaries. Official alerts are preserved as attributed source material, ambiguous locations are not silently guessed, unavailable forecasts are not presented as “no danger,” and developer-only controls are completely excluded from the normal user experience. We also built a browser verification suite with 44 checks against the real application. It validates tool registration and invocation, error handling, accessibility, production-mode isolation, and what the map actually renders—not merely what the application intended to display. For Japan’s experimental flood-risk forecast, we achieved 98.5% exact level agreement in evaluated reference areas while documenting the more difficult flood-extent limitations honestly. That distinction reflects a principle that guided the entire project: in disaster response, trustworthy uncertainty is more valuable than impressive but misleading confidence. ## What we learned We learned that connecting an AI agent to live data is only the beginning. Useful disaster guidance requires provenance, freshness checks, spatial reasoning, uncertainty handling, and clear separation between observed hazards and planning scenarios. We also learned that “nearest” rarely means “safest.” A shelter may be close but located inside a hazard zone, and a destination may be safe while the route to it crosses floodwater. Most importantly, we learned that safety systems must test observable outcomes. A successful API response does not prove that a person can see the hazard, understand the warning, or follow the proposed route. Reliability has to be evaluated across the entire experience. ## What’s next for Untitled Next, we want to expand coverage to additional countries and disaster types, including wildfires, earthquakes, landslides, tsunamis, and extreme heat. We also plan to improve personalization for mobility needs, language preferences, family and pet evacuation, vehicle availability, medical requirements, and shelter accessibility. Offline and low-bandwidth support will make the assistant more resilient when communications infrastructure is damaged. title: TERRA — Voice-Driven Earth Engine
pitch: A shared 3D Earth that people and browser agents can explore together through six typed WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A shared 3D Earth that people and browser agents can explore together through six typed WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Climate systems are difficult to understand from articles and static charts alone. TERRA explores a more direct interface: ask a question, let a browser agent change the shared Earth scene through WebMCP, and inspect the same evidence together. What it does TERRA is an interactive 3D Earth for exploring climate evidence. A person can drag and zoom the globe, choose a region, scientific layer, IPCC scenario, year, and presentation style. A WebMCP-capable browser agent can operate those same controls through six typed tools. The current experience connects: NASA Blue Marble day imagery, Black Marble night lights, and a moving cloud shell OSCAR-derived open ocean-current streamlines NOAA OISST v2.1 observed sea-surface temperature NSIDC Sea Ice Index observed September 2025 extent IPCC AR6 global temperature and sea-level assessment ranges Short, interruptible Arctic–AMOC and global sea-level stories Why WebMCP This is not a chatbot placed beside a globe. The website exposes its real controls with document.modelContext.registerTool . The agent can read the scene, fly to named regions, change an evidence layer, set a scenario and year, change the rendering style, or play a guided story without guessing DOM coordinates. Every write requires the current revision. Stale writes are rejected with revision_conflict . Human controls and agent tools mutate the same visible browser state, and a human action interrupts an active agent story. Human and agent collaboration The agent can compose several precise scene changes from a natural-language question. The person keeps direct control: they can rotate and zoom the globe, interrupt the sequence, compare sources, and choose how the evidence is presented. Both sides see the same camera, data layer, year, sources, and uncertainty labels. How we built it TERRA uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Three.js, Vinext, and ChatGPT Sites. The page registers six imperative WebMCP tools: earth_read_scene earth_focus_region earth_set_layer earth_set_scenario earth_set_render_style earth_play_story The Earth renderer uses locally bundled NASA imagery. Ocean-current paths were generated from the July 2014 mean of six OSCAR five-day composites obtained from the public NOAA CoastWatch mirror. The temperature texture is an August 2026 mean of 30 available daily NOAA OISST preliminary fields. Missing SST cells remain transparent. The sea-ice geometry is based on the NSIDC September 2025 extent mask. Scientific boundary TERRA is an exploratory, reduced-order visualization. It does not run a global climate model, predict weather, or map local flooding. The fixed day/night lighting is presentation lighting, not the current solar position. Future sea-ice contraction is marked as illustrative rather than presented as a geographic forecast. Challenges The hardest work was maintaining scientific honesty while still creating a cinematic experience. We separated observed textures, assessed global ranges, reduced-order interpolation, and illustrative future geometry in both the interface and narration. We also corrected longitude alignment, story interruption, scenario-dependent AMOC values, and reduced-motion behavior through an adversarial audit. Accomplishments A working public 3D Earth that both a person and a browser agent can control Six narrow, discoverable WebMCP tools with optimistic locking Visible provenance and uncertainty boundaries Photographic Earth rendering with data-derived scientific overlays English and Japanese interfaces A public MIT-licensed repository with reproducible data-generation scripts What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it lets an agent conduct a living interface rather than imitate clicks. The protocol also makes responsibility clearer: the site defines the available actions and data boundaries, while the person can see, interrupt, and redirect every shared state change. Testing Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser with WebMCP enabled. Ask the agent to read the scene, focus on Japan, show ocean currents, then move to the Arctic and display sea ice in 2100. The final Arctic state should be labelled illustrative. You can also drag the globe and use the zoom controls directly. title: Family Stay Compiler
pitch: One family brief, two staged checkouts, and a deterministic guardian that keeps every traveler, condition, and room-only promotion intact.
about_excerpt: One family brief, two staged checkouts, and a deterministic guardian that keeps every traveler, condition, and room-only promotion intact. Like Comment Story Updates One saved six-person brief: an honest one-room zero result and a preview-only path to three complete plans. Plan A keeps every traveler visible and proves the $24 family discount applies to Room 1 only. The split-checkout guardian verifies coverage, dates, $720, and promotion scope before manual review. Reload restores the recomputed audit, promotion evidence, and human acknowledgement without booking or payment. The review-only receipt records confirmed facts, unknowns, promotion scope, and the guardian outcome. Inspiration Planning a hotel stay becomes surprisingly difficult when a family does not fit inside a standard “one room, two guests” search box. As a parent of three children, I repeatedly encountered the same frustrating loop: enter everyone’s ages, inspect a room or promotion, press Back, discover that the search conditions have reset, and start again. For larger families, the problem is deeper than inconvenience. One search may return nothing even though a workable combination of two or more rooms exists. Parents are then forced to split adults and children into separate searches, compare promotions manually, and hope the separate rooms still work as one family stay. That experience led to a different question: What if families could search for a complete stay plan—not just an individual room? What it does Family Stay Compiler preserves one structured family brief throughout the planning process: dates, adults, children’s ages, room limit, adult-per-room rules, youngest-child constraints, and connecting-room preferences. The focus demonstration begins with two adults and four children under a one-room limit. The compiler returns an honest zero result rather than hiding or silently changing the constraints. An agent can preview changing only the room limit from one to two, but the saved family brief remains unchanged until the person presses Apply this change . Once approved, the app compiles three complete synthetic stay plans. It keeps every traveler visible, explains room allocation, and states that the verified $24 family discount applies to Room 1 only—not automatically to both rooms. The Split Checkout Guardian then audits two staged room checkouts as one family-level decision. It verifies traveler coverage, dates, room identity, subtotals, promotion scope, cancellation terms, and proximity before the person acknowledges the result for later manual review. The app never opens checkout, books, pays, reserves, contacts a hotel, or claims live inventory. Why WebMCP Family Stay Compiler exposes six page-defined WebMCP tools over the same state used by the visible interface: set_family_requirements find_family_stay_plans preview_constraint_unlock compare_family_stay_plans audit_split_checkout prepare_decision_receipt This is not ordinary DOM automation. The tools directly expose the underlying family-planning actions. preview_constraint_unlock calculates the exact feasibility difference created by one reversible constraint change while leaving the saved brief untouched. audit_split_checkout recomputes the staged decision using the selected planId . It verifies every traveler, both dates, adult and youngest-child rules, exact room identity, subtotals, promotion scope, cancellation terms, and room proximity. Every successful tool call creates a visible activity on the page so the person can inspect what the agent did. Invalid previews and stale or mismatched audit evidence return explicit errors without mutating the visible activity ledger. Better UX Conventional hotel interfaces treat each room search or checkout as an isolated transaction. That creates unnecessary work and risk for larger families: family ages and dates may reset after navigating back; a one-room zero result does not explain which constraint failed; promotions may apply to only one of the two required rooms; two separate checkouts make it difficult to confirm that every traveler and condition is still covered. Family Stay Compiler treats the family as one party from the first search through the final review. The person can begin with an honest zero result, inspect one reversible counterfactual, apply it deliberately, compare complete plans, and audit two staged checkouts without re-entering the family brief. Browser Back, Forward, and reload preserve the validated decision session and human acknowledgment. Stored evidence is recomputed before restoration, so altered or stale evidence cannot reuse an earlier acknowledgment. What people and agents do together The agent handles the tedious work: validating a complete family brief; explaining why a search is infeasible; calculating a one-constraint counterfactual; compiling complete room allocations; comparing plan trade-offs; checking traveler, date, subtotal, promotion, and policy consistency; preparing a review-only receipt. The person retains the consequential decisions: whether to apply the proposed room-limit change; and whether to acknowledge the split-checkout audit for later manual review. The agent does not silently rewrite the family’s preferences, and the person does not have to manually cross-check every traveler and promotion across two disconnected room purchases. That shared page state is the central WebMCP interaction: agent computation remains visible, reversible, and subject to human approval. How we built it Family Stay Compiler was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP. The application separates deterministic planning logic from the interface and WebMCP registration layer. The human interface and all six tools call the same pure domain functions and update the same page state. The planning engine evaluates flexible family sizes and room limits while enforcing active constraints such as: room capacity; an adult in each occupied room; the youngest child remaining with an adult; room proximity preferences; exact traveler coverage; room-specific promotion eligibility. The Split Checkout Guardian compares staged room parts against the selected compiled plan. It blocks the audit if room identity, travelers, dates, subtotals, or promotion evidence differ. The final release passed: 24 Vitest unit and integration tests; 12 desktop and mobile Playwright end-to-end tests; TypeScript type checking; the production build; real WebMCP discovery and invocation in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. All six tools were discovered and invoked successfully against the production deployment, with visible shared-page updates. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not building another hotel search form. It was representing the family’s complete situation without silently losing constraints. A room limit does not mean every room count is feasible. For example, two adults cannot supervise four occupied rooms when every room requires an adult. Children’s ages, room capacity, proximity, promotions, cancellation terms, and checkout totals must remain attached to the same decision. Another challenge was making counterfactual assistance safe. An agent may discover that changing one condition unlocks feasible plans, but it should not silently overwrite the family’s saved requirements. We therefore separated preview from Apply and gave the person the final decision. The split-checkout audit also had to be strict. Matching only the total price was not enough. The guardian needed to verify room identity, every traveler, dates, subtotals, promotion scope, and terms—and reject stale or altered evidence. Finally, we resisted overstating the prototype. Real inventory and promotions are provider-specific, so this challenge build uses explicit deterministic fixtures rather than presenting synthetic availability as live hotel data. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the project turns a real family-travel frustration into a reusable person-agent interaction model. The final build: supports flexible family sizes and one-to-four-room search limits; explains infeasibility instead of returning an unexplained empty screen; previews one reversible constraint change without mutating the saved brief; keeps every traveler visible across multi-room plans; makes room-specific promotion scope explicit; audits two staged checkouts as one family decision; restores validated evidence across Back, Forward, and reload; prepares a review-only receipt without initiating a transaction; exposes six working WebMCP tools through one shared human-agent interface. Most importantly, it treats the family as one party—even when the stay requires multiple rooms and separate checkouts. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most valuable when it does more than automate clicks. A conventional browser agent might fill in a form, navigate away, and lose the context that mattered. With WebMCP, the page exposes meaningful planning operations while remaining a visible

about_excerpt: Hospitals can't upload use AI on MRI or CT scans without risking patient privacy. This never leaves the doctor’s browser, providing instant 3D navigation. The patient's scan never leaves the room. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Building applications for the healthcare industry provides enough red-tape to jump through on a good day. In a world where web technology has made it to every device and is capable of providing full blown applications; I chose to explore building something that always intrigued me at a personal level, the viewing of an MRI (or similar) scan. It neatly taps into the fact that the data does not need to leave the browser. Medical imaging makes this concrete. A CT or MRI in the browser is a GPU texture on a canvas. An agent looking at the DOM sees an empty element. The usual shortcut is to upload the study to a hosted model, which hospitals may not want to do with patient data. So either agents stay out of radiology workflows entirely, or the tools have to run where the scan already is. That is what Faraday is for. Data stays in the tab, agents are capable of getting the information they need, and it stays token efficient. What it does Faraday is a browser reading room for volumetric CT and MRI. You open a local NIfTI file, or load the bundled de-identified demo study, and the viewer renders it with NiiVue. An agent connected over WebMCP can call five tools: describe the study, find bright regions, focus one of those regions, change the view layout, and export findings. While that happens, the human can see overlays update on the image itself. The agent never receives the scan. Tool responses are measurements and metadata — dimensions, millilitre volumes, window hints, a JSON report. The only tool that moves anything off the page is export_findings, and it requires explicit human approval before it returns. How It's Built The app is React and Vite on top of NiiVue for WebGPU and WebGL2 volume rendering. WebMCP registration goes through a vendored https://github.com/thegreataxios/webmcp stack: document.modelContext.registerTool, journey grouping, and HITL-guarded tools, with a polyfill when native WebMCP is not available. describe_study runs an on-device intensity histogram (WebGPU compute when it works, CPU otherwise) and suggests a bright window for region finding. find_regions does connected-component labeling in that window and paints the results into NiiVue’s drawing overlay. Study loads bump an epoch so stale agent work cannot paint the wrong volume, and mutating tools run one at a time so concurrent agent calls do not interleave. Challenges I ran into Without WebMCP, canvas-based viewers are basically unreachable. DOM automation cannot see a volume texture, so the agent has nothing reliable to act on. Making “measurements only” real also meant treating the tool output schema as the privacy boundary, not as documentation. Running more than one agent against one study was messier than the first version assumed. Opening a new file replaces the current study, in-flight calls need to know when their epoch is stale, the tool queue has to stay exclusive, and a pending export approval has to cancel if the study changes underneath it. Getting the UI to feel like a reading room instead of a hackathon demo took longer than wiring the tools. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The loop works end to end: an agent can measure a volume in the browser and the raw voxels never leave the tab. Export is actually gated. Multi-file and multi-agent safety does not require a backend. The repo is open source, the app is live, and there are agent discovery manifests so the tools are not a private handshake. What I learned WebMCP is not mainly about letting agents click better. It lets a page define what an agent is allowed to know and do while the sensitive asset stays put. For medical canvases especially, structured tools are the difference between a real workflow and an agent staring at a blank . What's next for Faraday DICOM and PACS ingestion without breaking the local-compute model. Better radiologist UX around hanging protocols and series stacks. Better evaluation around tool correctness when the model fails. It stays research and education for now — not a medical device, and not for diagnosis.
