title: Fashion Passport
pitch: WebMCP turns your style profile into a portable Fashion Passport, combining what suits you with what you love across compatible Shopify stores.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns your style profile into a portable Fashion Passport, combining what suits you with what you love across compatible Shopify stores. Like Comment Story Updates Fashion Passport logo Verdict Book helps user build ONE universal profile based on what suits them and what they love. Fashion Passport helps you shop across compatible Shopify stores, using WebMCP to apply one portable style profile to live products. Fashion Passport homepage Fashion passport on live retailer's website showing products that match user's choices ChatGPT Work uses WebMCP to search live Shopify catalogues with my Fashion Passport Inspiration As an avid online shopper of fashion products, I have spent thousands of hours browsing different catalogues, using the exact same filters and visual judgement again and again to narrow down choices to what I actually like and what suist me. This frustrates me because I need to keep doing the same thing every time. I know there are others like me who hate this repetition. A user who knows she wears a UK 10, avoids polyester, prefers midi lengths and stops looking above £100 still has to repeat that context at every retailer. Retailer profiles only work on their own websites, so you cannot take your preferences with you if you want to buy from a different store. Shopping search overwhelms users with endless options without fully understanding their specific colours, proportions and silhouettes, or the fact that personal taste should overrule every styling rule. Fashion Passport captures that judgment once and applies it across compatible stores. What it does Fashion Passport creates a portable personal style profile for womenswear. Its sub-two-minute "Verdict Book" fitting keeps three sources of truth separate: a.) a transparent starting point from body proportions and colour direction; b.) explicit Love, Avoid and Never choices across seven garment traits; c.) preference patterns learned from reactions to real retailer products. The ordering gives your preference greater weight than theory. An ordinary Avoid lowers rank while keeping the product visible, and repeated evidence is required before reactions create a learned preference. Once approved, an agent can use the Passport to search live retailer-owned Shopify catalogues, enforce the requested garment category, rank every product and explain why each item is Strong, Worth a look, another option or Held by a confirmed rule. The Chrome extension proves the same Passport on the retailer's own website and carries it to the next compatible retailer without another approval. This setup enables collaboration that was previously impossible: you supply subjective judgment, grant permission and can overrule; the agent handles catalogue breadth, category enforcement and reranking; the retailer remains source of truth for products, prices and availability. A single approval covers retailer, category, query and tab changes, eliminating the repetitive re-entry of context that defines current online shopping. Role of WebMCP Portability depends on a shared tool contract. WebMCP lets Fashion Passport expose typed tools to the agent while compatible retailers expose their own catalogue tools. The agent composes the two safely by obtaining approved user context, querying retailer-owned inventory and returning a personal, explainable ranking. People and agents do different work together: a.) you supply subjective judgment, grant permission and can overrule; b.) the agent handles catalogue breadth, category enforcement and reranking; c.) the retailer remains source of truth for products, prices and availability. WebMCP specifically enables the system to discover retailers as you browse without needing a central merchant directory, which standard APIs cannot provide because Shopify gives each store its own catalogue access only within individual store boundaries. The system combines this runtime store discovery with a verified comparison panel and shows you exactly where each piece of information comes from. The tool contract ensures that unknown attributes add no positive score, Avoid lowers rank, Never can hold a product, render batches control presentation, and catalogue-scanned counts remain separate from dress counts. How we built it The Next.js app registers five WebMCP tools: get_fashion_passport, find_personal_matches, compare_shopify_stores, request_passport_connection and record_style_signal. The Chrome extension registers an on-retailer surface and discovers compatibility at runtime. Before approval it sends only an anonymous capability check. After one-time approval, it reads the retailer's official Shopify catalogue data, normalises product information, applies the ranking engine and displays real retailer-hosted images and links. The ranking system applies: a.) category gate first; b.) hard rules only for explicit Never, hard query cap, strict budget and confirmed unavailable size; c.) explicit preference above learned preference; d.) styling theory at the lowest weight; e.) zero positive evidence for unknown attributes; f.) deterministic tie-breaks and evidence confidence separate from score. The web app and extension run against identical test data. The release requirements are lint clean, production-build clean, 36/36 tests passing, every extension script passing node --check, and browser verification at desktop and 390px mobile width. WebMCP tool registration differs from standard API integration by enabling the agent to discover retailer capabilities dynamically and invoke tools across domain boundaries while maintaining explicit user approval. The extension uses one browser engine and tests fail on any difference in evidence, score, tier, hard rule or ordering, ensuring the WebMCP-powered extension delivers identical ranking behavior to the web application. a.) category gate first; b.) hard rules only for explicit Never, hard query cap, strict budget and confirmed unavailable size; c.) explicit preference above learned preference; d.) styling theory at the lowest weight; e.) zero positive evidence for unknown attributes; f.) deterministic tie-breaks and evidence confidence separate from score. The web and extension run against a shared parity corpus. The release gate is lint clean, production-build clean, 36/36 tests, every extension script passing node --check, and browser verification at desktop and 390px. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was keeping recommendations accurate when retailer data is imperfect. Retailer search sometimes returns the wrong garment category. Those results must be filtered out rather than mislabeled as products that match your rules. Product information also varies across stores, so the system separates confidence from score and never rewards missing evidence. The second hard problem was consistency. An extension that behaves differently from the web app creates confusion. The extension now uses the same engine as the web app and tests fail on any difference in evidence, score, tier, hard rule or ordering. WebMCP introduces specific challenges around discovering stores and verifying compatibility as you browse. Shopify gives each store its own catalogue access without a central directory, requiring the system to discover stores at runtime while comparing them against a verified panel. The tool contract must show you exactly where each piece of information comes from so you understand when results come from live retailer data versus cached checks. Accomplishments that we're proud of The public application works without requiring you to log in, pay for API access, or manage any technical setup. The test panel includes eighteen directly verified fashion retailers on Shopify, with the system discovering additional compatible stores as you browse. The interface shows you exactly what is happening: which catalogues have been scanned, which items match your category, and how many results fall into each of four quality tiers. Every clothing evaluation uses real product photography from the retailer, and your reactions rerank results immediately with full Undo support. One approval covers retailer, category, query, and tab changes, and your saved Passports carry forward as the system evolves. The product combines WebMCP with a coherent shopping experience, demonstrating the ranking system on a real retailer's domain. Every count and product comes from live retailer data. Items you softly dislike rank lower without disappearing permanently, your personal taste can overrule theoretical styling rules, and the system requires repeated evidence before changing a learned preference. The Verdict Book visual system makes the whole process clear to shoppers. What we learned Shopify does not provide a central directory of all stores, so the system discovers compatible retailers as you browse and compares them against a verified panel. title: Feather Engine
pitch: Give browser AI agents direct control over a live 3D engine. Build scenes, configure physics, and test gameplay through natural language using the W3C WebMCP standard.
about_excerpt: Give browser AI agents direct control over a live 3D engine. Build scenes, configure physics, and test gameplay through natural language using the W3C WebMCP standard. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The hackathon prompt pointed me toward WebMCP, and I wanted to know the performance rate of agents when giving MCP tools to create games in a 3D engine. I am a Unity game developer, so I know firsthand how much manual work goes into coordinates, physics, and object placement. I wanted to see how much of that an agent could just take over. What It Does Feather Engine WebMCP connects browser-native AI agents directly to Feather Engine (React 18, Three.js, Rapier physics) using the W3C WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext ). Browser-native agent control: Agents auto-discover engine tools through document.modelContext . Zero plugins, zero CLI setup. Full 3D world building: Agents can spawn objects, sculpt terrain, generate wind, create water volumes, set lighting presets (cyberpunk, sunset), and tune rigid-body physics. Gameplay and controllers: Third-person character controllers, vehicle handling, and live Play mode to test games in place. Live agent HUD: A floating status bar shows real-time agent activity so you always know what it is doing. Tool inspector: A WebMCP modal lets developers explore tools, view input schemas, and copy executable snippets to test directly in DevTools. Human-in-the-loop: Every agent action goes through the engine's undo/redo history. You can tweak or roll back anything the agent does. How I Built It I registered tools onto document.modelContext.registerTool with fallback emulation and a global window.__featherWebMcp debug handle. The architecture runs on two tiers: 14 direct core tools covering high-leverage actions: create_new_project , create_object , set_physics , create_meadow , set_character_controller , set_vehicle , and more. 2 gateway tools ( search_engine_tools and execute_engine_tool ) that give agents on-demand access to the full 200+ tool catalog without loading it upfront. All tool parameters run through a Zod validation pipeline compiled to JSON Schema, preventing runtime crashes. Tool calls mutate the Zustand store directly, which triggers Three.js rendering and Rapier physics updates at 60 FPS. Challenges I did not plan the two-tier architecture upfront. I registered the full 200+ tool catalog and ChatGPT's browser agent rejected it outright. The schema payload came in over 150 KB and hit an undocumented size limit. I had to step back and redesign on the fly: strip the initial payload down to 14 core tools (about 7 KB), then build the gateway layer so agents could still reach the full catalog on demand. It worked, but it was not the plan going in. Everything else, including physics sync and history integration, held up through the demo without major issues. Accomplishments I Am Proud Of A visiting browser agent can take a high-level prompt, query the scene, build an environment, add physics, and start gameplay without human intervention. A web app with 200+ tools can operate within browser agent constraints using a dynamic gateway. That is a real architectural pattern other projects can use. What I Learned Browser agents have hard payload constraints most web apps are not designed around. If your application has a large tool catalog, dynamic gateway discovery is not optional. It is the only way to scale within browser limits. Exposing your app's core logic through WebMCP also changes how the tool feels to use. The engine stopped feeling like something you operate and started feeling like something you collaborate with. What's Next Visual blueprint generation: Agents inspect and wire visual scripting node graphs to create custom game logic. Multi-agent co-creation: Specialized agents (level designer, environment artist, gameplay scripter) working the same scene at the same time. WebRTC multiplayer + AI: Remote human teams and agents building 3D worlds together, live. title: Friction
pitch: Test the same task through human eyes and agent tools.
about_excerpt: Test the same task through human eyes and agent tools. Like Comment Story Updates Human-only patch review explains the evidence and proposed contract repairs. Baseline lab: paired human and agent traces expose a 50/100 parity score. Repaired scenario: clearer visible wording and a guarded completion contract. Ten real page-side WebMCP tools share state with the visible interface. Paired retest: the repaired human and agent journeys reach 96/100 parity. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Friction Inspiration WebMCP lets a live page publish named, structured actions instead of forcing an agent to infer buttons and forms. That creates a new usability question: does the agent receive the same information, consent gates, and final state that a person sees? Friction is a dual usability laboratory for answering that question. It pairs one visual journey with one WebMCP journey, exposes the differences, repairs both interfaces together, and proves the improvement with a retest. What it does The deterministic RelayConf event-registration scenario contains three intentional problems: a quiet-zone seat is hidden behind vague human-facing wording; the baseline agent result omits a $12 service fee and refund condition; an ambiguously described completion tool finalizes without the human review gate. Friction records both traces and scores outcome, information, consent, state, and effort parity. It produces evidence-backed findings and a four-part patch. A human must approve that patch through the visible UI—approval is intentionally not agent-callable. After approval, the human option becomes clear, the tool returns an itemized total and policy, and finalization requires a review token plus confirmed=true . The paired score rises from 50/100 to 96/100. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP generates one side of the experiment. The page registers ten tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ; these are not a remote MCP server and do not automate the DOM. Tool handlers and visual controls share the same React state and durable browser storage, so agent mutations immediately change the visible trace, findings, and comparison. Without WebMCP, Friction could test only visual automation. With WebMCP, it can inspect the explicit contract a site offers to agents and compare that contract against the human experience. How humans and agents work together People complete and judge the visual task, report hesitation, and retain approval authority. Agents exercise the structured contract, analyze traces, submit findings, and propose interface changes. Neither side replaces the other: the agent contributes speed and structured analysis, while the person supplies subjective usability evidence and approves consequential changes. How we built it Friction uses React 19, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, shadcn primitives, and ChatGPT Sites-compatible Cloudflare output. Ten page-owned WebMCP tools use restrictive JSON Schemas, runtime checks, read/write annotations, untrusted-content hints, feature detection, and registration cleanup with AbortController . The account-free demo persists locally in the browser, making the before/after experiment repeatable without credentials or external APIs. Deterministic tests cover the parity score, consent and information failures, approval transition, and repaired replay. Challenges we ran into The most important design challenge was avoiding a fake split between “human UI state” and “agent demo state.” Every interaction had to operate on the same live model. The second was expressing the repair as a real contract change: the completion tool’s description and JSON Schema are re-registered after human approval, and its handler independently enforces review and confirmation. Accomplishments that we're proud of A non-trivial ten-tool WebMCP implementation over shared visible state. A complete evidence → proposal → human approval → retest loop. A consent failure that is demonstrably blocked by the repaired handler. A polished responsive product requiring no accounts, secrets, or external APIs. Deterministic tests, type checks, linting, production build, and dependency audit. What we learned Parity is broader than whether both paths eventually produce the same record. A fast agent path can still be worse if it hides cost, weakens consent, or returns less context. Tool schemas, descriptions, results, and confirmation design are part of the product interface and need usability testing just as much as buttons and labels do. What's next for Friction Future versions could import OpenTelemetry-style traces, compare multiple scenarios, export regression suites for CI, and provide a lightweight SDK that lets other WebMCP sites embed paired parity tests while keeping approval policies application-owned. title: Future Doors
pitch: Future Doors turns a saved opportunity screenshot into an official-source-backed, human-approved career path that people and agents build together for one or more career futures.
about_excerpt: Future Doors turns a saved opportunity screenshot into an official-source-backed, human-approved career path that people and agents build together for one or more career futures. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Future Doors Your camera roll is full of possible futures. Future Doors turns a saved opportunity into a source-checked career path that a person and an agent can build together. The problem People who are exploring more than one career direction constantly save internships, fellowships, challenges, research calls, and communities from Instagram, LinkedIn, and group chats. Those posts disappear into a camera roll. Even when someone returns to one, they still have to find the official page, interpret eligibility and dates, check whether it fits their schedule, and understand what the experience would actually add to their longer-term direction. Most job products optimize for one role and one application. Future Doors is designed for people whose experience does not fit one label: a builder may also be a technical storyteller, researcher, or future education founder. What it does Future Doors turns scattered opportunity clues into a small, explainable plan: A person shares a saved screenshot or link. The agent finds the original official HTTPS source and stages the deadline, relevant rules, schedule, format, concrete outputs, and one unresolved fact for review. The same profile can hold several possible futures. AI product, hardware storytelling, and learning, for example, produce genuinely different recommended work. Source-checked cards are grouped as activities, projects, research, or credentials. Fit hearts represent verifiable alignment with the person's facts and preferences—not acceptance or hiring odds. The person chooses up to three near-term moves. The plan shows timing, prerequisite relationships, schedule conflicts, and which goal-specific evidence each move can create. Ineligible or unresolved opportunities remain visibly blocked. The agent can stage a separate source-backed path, but it cannot pretend that the original eligibility was restored. The result is not another ranked list. It is a visual evidence deck: what to do, when it fits, what it can produce, and what is still missing. Why WebMCP is essential Future Doors is a shared stateful surface, not a chatbot wrapper. Through WebMCP, an agent can read the same profile, futures, saved opportunities, constraints, timing, and proof gaps that the person sees. It can then focus a route, compare constrained paths, check a saved post, surface one missing fact, or stage a source-backed change directly on the page instead of guessing through visual controls. The live app registers 15 structured tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool inputs are schema-validated, read-only operations are identified, externally sourced text is treated as untrusted, outputs are bounded, and invalid dates or IDs return explicit errors. Most importantly, there is no WebMCP approval tool. An agent may prepare profile facts, an opportunity, a priority plan, an alternative route, or a work link, but the person must approve every consequential change in the interface. Source facts, agent inference, planned work, saved links, and verified proof are never presented as the same state. That boundary is the product: the agent prepares; the person decides. What is new Future Doors combines three ideas that are normally separated: a scrapbook for opportunities discovered outside job platforms; official-source and eligibility checking by an agent; a multi-future portfolio planner that shows how selected work can create reusable evidence. It does not force a premature career choice and does not manufacture a success score. It helps someone make a bounded decision across several plausible futures while keeping every important claim inspectable. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, and TypeScript Browser-native WebMCP via document.modelContext.registerTool 15 scoped tools for reading, staging, comparing, simulating, and explaining paths Vercel deployment with no account required for the judge demo Vitest regression tests covering tool registration, route-aware recommendations, invalid inputs, source requirements, bounded outputs, rule mismatches, and human-only approval boundaries Motion-based transitions that explain source checking, future-specific recommendations, card selection, and proof coverage The current automated suite contains 38 passing tests . The production site has also been verified to expose all 15 tools and return a successful live get_path_snapshot invocation. Try it Open the live app and choose TRY THE EXAMPLE . Switch between Maya's AI, Hardware, and Learning futures to see different work. Add cards to the plan and watch the evidence coverage change. Open HOW IT WORKS for two judge-ready WebMCP prompts and the visible human-approval boundary. No login or credentials are required. title: IMC Guardian
pitch: IMC Guardian is a tool designed to provide pilots with quick notifications and fast access to information about rapidly changing weather conditions using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: IMC Guardian is a tool designed to provide pilots with quick notifications and fast access to information about rapidly changing weather conditions using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates About the project IMC Guardian is the stretch project out of the two projects I built for the WebMCP Challenge. It is an aviation weather decision-support prototype for a solo pilot or private jet crew flying a longer route. The main goal is to save time and add a second pair of eyes when weather conditions begin changing. Pilots do not have a shortage of data. They have aircraft instruments, radar, dispatch, ATC, forecasts, advisories, and procedures. The harder problem is recognizing the exact moment when the picture no longer supports the plan. IMC Guardian is designed as an independent challenge layer, not a confirmation machine. A pilot can ask AI to check a proposed route in plain English. Fifteen site-owned WebMCP tools give the agent structured access to the route, airport observations, forecasts, advisories, risk factors, nearby alternates, configurable notifications, validated alerts, incident evidence, and decision options. The application does not tell a pilot that a flight is safe, issue a clearance, direct a maneuver, or replace an official briefing. It organizes the evidence and catches important changes, while the pilot remains in control. Inspiration The idea came from thinking about a long-route solo pilot or private jet pilot trying to keep up with weather while also managing everything else involved in a flight. Conditions can change quickly, especially ceilings and visibility. There can also be a lot of noise when the pilot only needs to know whether an important personal limit has changed. I wanted to see whether WebMCP could let a pilot ask one clear question, rapidly inspect the weather along the route, and configure a focused notification instead of repeatedly checking several different panels and sources. The phrase that kept making sense was “a second pair of eyes.” The interaction is almost as simple as asking, “Guardian, what do you see?” The AI helps watch, organize, and challenge the current picture. It does not become the pilot. Why this matters We added five investigation-backed case studies because the problem is real. Delta Flight 56 encountered severe turbulence in July 2025 after the crew had already discussed and adjusted around weather. The NTSB says the upset lasted about 2.5 minutes, two crew members were seriously injured, and the flight diverted to Minneapolis. Delta Flight 175 encountered a rapidly developing convective cell near Atlanta in 2023. The NTSB found that the low-precipitation buildup was not apparent on the aircraft's weather radar or ATC scopes. Four people were seriously injured and thirteen received minor injuries. The site does more than display that case. A WebMCP evidence replay loads the Delta 175 final-report record, reconstructs the weather timeline, compares the crew's concern with the recorded outcome, and explains what the evidence cannot prove. At 22:30 UTC the crew said conditions were about to get worse. Severe turbulence followed at 22:31:15 UTC. The result is deliberately precise: concern supported, action not judged. The NTSB found that near-real-time Graphic Turbulence Guidance Nowcast capability could have provided earlier awareness to secure the cabin, but the report does not establish that a different route choice or this prototype would have prevented the encounter. Singapore Airlines Flight 321 diverted to Bangkok in 2024 after an extreme acceleration change over developing convective activity. Air Europa Flight 45 diverted to Natal, Brazil after severe turbulence injured dozens of people. Air France Flight 447 is the foundational sensor-disagreement case. The BEA identified pitot-probe icing, erroneous speed indications, a stall, and impact with the ocean. IMC Guardian does not claim it would have prevented any of these events. The cases show why a concise, independent evidence check can matter when weather, workload, and human-machine interaction collide. What it does For the reproducible demonstration, a VFR pilot proposes a flight from Tampa to Tallahassee. Conditions deteriorate along the northern part of the route, the destination reports IFR, and a G-AIRMET for IFR overlaps the corridor. The agent can inspect the evidence, explain why the route risk increased, find comparatively better nearby airports, and compare delaying, diverting, or canceling. The pilot can also configure Second Pair of Eyes to watch a specific metric. In the demo, a 1,500-foot ceiling limit is crossed. WebMCP checks the threshold, forecast context, and overlapping advisory before presenting the alert. The project also includes a live Cesium globe with NASA satellite clouds, Apple WeatherKit context, and a Tampa-to-JFK weather corridor sampled across nine points. That gives the pilot and the agent a fast visual picture of changing conditions ahead. The globe stays focused on Florida so the demonstration supports the route instead of becoming a generic spinning-earth effect. The top of the experience now explains the interaction in three steps: ask once, let WebMCP double-check, and keep the final decision with the pilot. How we built it We built a React and Vite application with a deterministic aviation-risk engine and fifteen imperative WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . The user interface and the agent share the same route, assessment, alternatives, route watch, notifications, validation, historical replay, decision state, and live tool trace. NOAA Aviation Weather Center is the aviation-data foundation. Its data is reached through a scoped, cached Vercel server-side proxy with a custom user agent. Apple WeatherKit provides supplemental current conditions, cloud cover, temperature, precipitation, and wind. Its signing credentials stay on the server. CesiumJS provides the interactive 3D Earth. NASA EOSDIS GIBS supplies current GOES-East ABI GeoColor satellite imagery through a Web Map Service layer. The globe can animate roughly 90 minutes of recent satellite frames, focus on Florida, and display the demonstration route. Apple WeatherKit adds twelve global samples and nine cached checkpoints along the Tampa-to-JFK corridor. The frontend also includes a live natural-language demonstration using GPT-OSS 120B on Groq. The model interprets the pilot's sentence and chooses an ordered subset of allowlisted tools. The browser executes the actual WebMCP tools and shows every step, along with model token usage. Weather facts come from application tools and identified data sources, not the model's memory. The live session now exposes a safe server receipt so judges can see the complete connection path. It shows the browser request to /api/agent , the server-side call to Groq's OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint, the selected model, response mode, prompt size, 10-tool allowlist, request receipt, latency, and token usage. The Groq credential and hidden system instruction remain on the Vercel server and are never returned to the browser. The page also links Groq's API reference, OpenAI's gpt-oss announcement, and the public server implementation. We created a clearly labeled scenario mode so the judging flow stays reproducible even when live weather changes or a source is temporarily unavailable. Scenario values are never presented as current reports. We also created a historical evidence mode from the NTSB Delta 175 final report and public docket. Three WebMCP tools load the case, compare the documented concern with the recorded event and final findings, and expose the replay's limits. It is a structured investigation replay, not certified live telemetry. Challenges The hardest product challenge was deciding what the system must not do. It would be easy to make the demo dramatic by having AI say go or no-go. That would be the wrong product. The tools surface evidence and tradeoffs, but return no clearance, safety guarantee, or automated flight decision. The next challenge was keeping data provenance clear. Aviation Weather Center products are aviation evidence. Apple WeatherKit and NASA satellite imagery provide supplemental context. The interface identifies live information, scenario information, source time, and limitations instead of blending everything into one unsupported claim. The biggest missing connection is live aircraft tracking. RadarBox or another commercial aircraft-data API could add near-real-time position, pressure altitude, GPS-derived geometric altitude, ground track, groundspeed, vertical trend, and time-to-weather calculations. That access was too expensive for this prototype, so we did not fake it. The plane shown on the Tampa-to-JFK corridor is a clearly illustrative route animation. title: LivingTown
pitch: A town that learns from residents—and explains how verified knowledge changes an evacuation route.
about_excerpt: A town that learns from residents—and explains how verified knowledge changes an evacuation route. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The most useful evacuation knowledge often lives in everyday neighborhood conversations: “this crossing floods,” “this path is too narrow for a wheelchair,” or “this place is a safe waiting point.” Traditional maps rarely turn that local, changing knowledge into evidence that can safely affect a route. LivingTown explores a future where people and agents build a shared, verifiable memory of a town together. What it does LivingTown lets residents contribute local knowledge about barriers, flooding, darkness, narrow paths, and safe spots. Other participants can verify or dispute each item. Only verified knowledge can affect routing. In the evacuation drill, a person can register a privacy-safe household profile using only allowed constraints such as wheelchair, infant, elderly, or pet. LivingTown then calculates a deterministic route and explains exactly which verified knowledge changed it, which graph edges were avoided, and why. The production demo includes a long-distance wheelchair evacuation example: under flood + rain + daytime conditions, verified flood knowledge changes the route to a 1,330 m / 28 min evacuation to the existing shelter. The original canonical demo remains 440 m / 10 min for comparison. The experience is available in both 2D and 3D. A route-following 3D walkthrough moves from the household origin through the safe route, pauses at the avoided hazard with an explanation, and finishes at the shelter. Replay provides a KNOWLEDGE → ROUTE debrief so people and agents can review what changed and why. Why WebMCP LivingTown is a strong WebMCP use case because an agent should not have to guess how to operate a disaster-prevention UI. The app exposes structured, phase-scoped tools that let agents participate in the same workflow as people while respecting verification and privacy boundaries. MAP exposes contribute_knowledge , verify_knowledge , and query_area . DRILL exposes register_household , get_evacuation_route , and report_bottleneck . REPLAY exposes control_replay and get_debrief_summary . That is exactly eight WebMCP tools. The native adapter uses document.modelContext.registerTool , supports getTools() and toolchange , and uses per-registration abort handling. Native WebMCP was verified in Chrome 152. When the API is unavailable, LivingTown explicitly labels the local compatibility path as SIMULATED rather than presenting it as native evidence. Better user experience The user does not need to translate a vague request into a sequence of UI clicks. A person can ask an agent about an area, contribute or verify local knowledge, prepare an anonymous wheelchair household, calculate a route, and retrieve a debrief through explicit tool contracts. At the same time, the visual interface remains understandable for humans: pending → verified → affecting route is visible on the map, the avoided route is shown as a red dashed segment, the chosen route is shown in green, and the system explains why the route changed. What people and agents can do together Before LivingTown, community observations, accessibility constraints, route planning, and explanation typically lived in separate systems. LivingTown combines them into one accountable loop: Human observation → verification → agent-accessible structured knowledge → evacuation route → explanation → replay. An agent can help a wheelchair household without needing to know who that household is. The agent boundary is deliberately limited to anonymous labels, safe constraint enums, and temporary/demo locations rather than personal identity or exact private addresses. How we built it The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Vite. Mapping uses MapLibre for 2D and a Navara/Three-based 3D visualization with GSI/OSM data sources and Dynamic PLATEAU-supported city visualization where available. A deterministic graph routing engine makes route changes reproducible. Verified knowledge affects routing only when agreements minus disagreements reach the verification threshold. Avoided edges and reasons are returned as structured route evidence. Production runs in SUPABASE_SHARED mode using Supabase Anonymous Auth, Realtime, RLS, owner-scoped temporary drill households, and RPC-only protected mutations. Community knowledge is shared; private drill state is owner-scoped. The production database and client share the same trusted graph-node boundary. Production demo No credentials are required. Recommended flow: Explore MAP and inspect community knowledge. Open DRILL and choose Try long-distance example / 遠距離の例を試す . Calculate the flood + rain wheelchair route: 1,330 m / 28 min with a verified flood avoidance reason. Switch to 3D and use the route walkthrough to see the avoided hazard and reach the shelter. Open REPLAY for the knowledge-to-route debrief. LivingTown is a prototype. Moderation, retention policy, stronger identity/Sybil resistance, and broader real-world routing coverage remain future work and are documented in the public repository. title: Mantle Builder
pitch: Build WebMCP services from business workflows—agent-ready and Cloudflare-ready.
about_excerpt: Build WebMCP services from business workflows—agent-ready and Cloudflare-ready. Like Comment Story Updates Core ERP service graph generated from one Mantle Manifest. Typed data models include constraints, indexes, and agent-ready operations. A handoff package guides a coding agent from the backend contract to a deployable site. API, MCP, and WebMCP interfaces are generated and documented together. Mantle Builder uses WebMCP to rapidly create your own WebMCP-enabled business service and take it to Cloudflare. Describe the workflow in agent chat; the agent builds and validates the Mantle contract, previews its API, MCP, WebMCP, and Admin surfaces, then hands it to a coding agent to finish the frontend, authentication, and production deployment. Inspiration Companies adopting agent workflows quickly run into business-logic gaps. Agents can reason and browse, but the organization's real rules—who can do what, which records exist, how an order or request moves, and which operations are public or staff-only—are still trapped in documents and bespoke code. Conventional app builders also make the human perform every configuration step through a visual editor. We wanted a shared workspace where a person supplies intent and approval while an agent supplies structured implementation. What it does Mantle Builder lets a person describe a workflow and lets their agent build the service behind it through WebMCP. What is Mantle? Mantle is the open-source, config-as-code runtime beneath the Builder. An agent writes four atoms—Schema, View, Procedure, and Trigger—in one YAML Manifest; Mantle validates the contract and carries the runtime complexity. The same contract can power real consumer-facing services such as commerce, reservations, and application flows while immediately producing API, MCP, WebMCP, and Admin surfaces. Agents get the tools missing from their workflows, while operations teams get one place to manage customers, orders, requests, and queues. The agent works through four typed WebMCP tools: builder_get_started — inspect the active project, Mantle grammar, presets, and exact next calls. builder_apply_preset — start from a tested business workflow. builder_apply_manifest_patch — compile and safely activate confirmed changes. builder_execute_preview — run the service as a mock actor, inspect mutations, and follow the result in Admin. The prompt requires the agent to interview the user about actors, data, operations, permissions, and entry points, summarize the proposal, and wait for confirmation before changing the project. Every accepted change immediately appears inside an embedded Mantle Admin developer console. The person can inspect schemas, procedures, triggers, interfaces, and operational Admin views. The agent can execute the service as an anonymous visitor, member, or owner, compare canonical entries before and after mutations, and watch Admin follow the affected View, collection, or record. When the contract is ready, the user downloads a coding-agent handoff containing the complete Manifest, pinned Mantle references, a frontend WebMCP registration example, and deployment guidance. A coding agent can then add the consumer-owned frontend, authentication, provider configuration, and production wiring. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns Mantle Builder from a one-way generator into a shared control surface for people and agents. An agent can author the service, seed data, and exercise public, member, and staff workflows through typed preview tools. Each action updates the same persistent sandbox the human is viewing, while the embedded Admin console follows the affected page, collection, or record. The agent acts; the human can watch, inspect, and approve the result as it happens. This closes the loop from intent to implementation to verification. Teams can create MCP and WebMCP services that fill gaps in existing agent workflows, while operations still gets a trusted interface for managing customers, orders, requests, and queues. How we built it The React host registers Mantle-derived capabilities with document.modelContext . WebMCP calls enter one serialized mutation path where inputs and project revisions are validated. Valid Mantle resources compile into a runtime plan; a browser-hosted adapter and mock environment power the service preview. Mantle Admin runs in a same-origin iframe and talks to the host runtime over a constrained message bridge. Project Manifests and canonical preview entries autosave to IndexedDB. The production host is deployed as a Cloudflare Worker. What we learned A useful agent interface needs more than tool registration. The tools must expose enough grammar and current state for an agent to act reliably, mutations need optimistic revision checks, invalid candidates must never replace the last working project, and the human needs a visual way to verify what the agent created. Built during the challenge The implementation began on September 2, 2026. The WebMCP authoring flow, Mantle preview, project persistence, coding-agent handoff, browser testing, and Cloudflare production deployment were all created during the submission period. The public commit history distinguishes this work from the pre-existing Mantle Core dependency. Current limitations Builder project Manifests and preview records persist only in the current browser; they are not production data or synced across devices. Preview authentication is intentionally mocked. The Builder supports declarative Views and builtin Procedure handlers; custom handler refs, a consumer frontend, production authentication, and provider wiring are completed after the coding-agent handoff. title: MintPaw
pitch: Alibaba-sourced pet tech, sold across a border. Its WebMCP tools check your mains voltage, your LTE bands and your router — and refuse to cart what will not work when it arrives.
about_excerpt: Alibaba-sourced pet tech, sold across a border. Its WebMCP tools check your mains voltage, your LTE bands and your router — and refuse to cart what will not work when it arrives. Like Comment Story Updates Dog owner, 5GHz-only router. The agent fills in the store's own compatibility panel: Add to cart goes dead and express checkout disappears. Two cats with 2.4GHz available. Caveats instead of a block, and the buy buttons return - the gate is not a blanket no. Product copy rendered from the same record the agent reads, including a plain list of what MintPaw has not checked itself. The cross-border trap: plug variants for eight countries, and an input voltage the supplier never stated. The open questions put to the supplier, published on the product page instead of hidden. Inspiration Smart pet devices are returned at a punishing rate, and mostly not because they are broken. They come back because of a mismatch that was knowable before checkout and invisible while scrolling: a 2.4GHz-only device meeting a 5GHz-only mesh router — it will never finish setup a 4G tracker on LTE bands that do not exist in the buyer's country a companion app not published in the buyer's region a single-cat litter box arriving in a two-cat home Every one of those sits somewhere on the product page. Nobody reads it. So we built the store that reads it for you and then says no. What it does MintPaw is a live Shopify storefront selling five smart pet devices. Its WebMCP layer is not a faster way to buy — it is a gate. An agent records the shopper's household: species, weight, how many animals share the device, which Wi-Fi bands the router actually broadcasts , country, and willingness to add a cellular plan. It then returns, per product, a verdict of ok / caution / unknown / blocked with the specific reason in plain language. A blocked product cannot be added to the cart. The tool refuses, the Add to cart button goes dead and relabels itself "Not compatible with your home", and Shopify's express checkout button is removed from the page. A caution product is also held back until the agent has actually told the shopper the caveat and passed acknowledged_caveats: true . Informed consent, enforced in code rather than requested in a prompt. And the store says what it does not know. Our product data comes from Alibaba sourcing documents full of unconfirmed manufacturer claims. Instead of laundering those into spec, every tool returns them separately as notYetVerifiedByMintPaw — "the listing says 10000mAh, MintPaw has not measured it." unknown and ok are deliberately different verdicts. How we built it — and the discovery that shaped the whole project Partway in we found that Shopify's storefront now injects its own WebMCP adapter automatically ( cdn.shopify.com/storefront/webmcp/webmcp-0.1.1.js ). Out of the box our store already exposed ten generic commerce tools: search_catalog , get_product , get_cart , update_cart , cancel_cart , proceed_to_checkout , browse_store , show_variant , manage_orders and search_shop_policies_and_faqs . Our first draft had re-implemented five of those and collided with get_product outright — two tools with one name and an agent picking between them at random. We deleted it. That reframed the project: The interesting question WebMCP raises for a merchant is not "how do I expose my storefront?" — the platform now does that. It is "what do I know that the platform cannot?" For MintPaw that is compatibility: which device works in this home for this animal, and which claims we have not verified. That knowledge exists nowhere in Shopify's data model. So our seven tools are the layer above the platform, with zero name overlap: Tool set_household_profile always on pet, weight, count, Wi-Fi bands, country, SIM willingness get_household_profile always on read it back — the shopper may have edited it by hand clear_household_profile always on erase it, and withdraw the gated tools check_compatibility always on the core: per-product verdict and reason explain_product_fit always on one product in depth + every unverified claim find_compatible_alternative gated what works instead; "nothing does" is a valid answer add_compatible_to_cart gated refuses blocked items; holds caveats until acknowledged The two gated tools do not exist until a household profile does — without one they cannot answer honestly, so they are withdrawn rather than left to guess. On the live page the tool count goes 15 → 17 the moment a profile is set, and back to 15 when it is cleared. Registration uses AbortController , per the spec. Why cross-border sourcing makes this necessary Every product here is sourced on Alibaba.com and shipped to a buyer in another country. That is not incidental — it is the reason the gate has to exist. Cross-border sourcing produces a class of failure a domestic store never sees, and our own sourcing research (done with Alibaba Accio Work ) turned up exactly these: Sourced fact What it means for the buyer The feeder lists plug variants for 8 countries , input voltage not stated A plug adapter changes the pins, not the voltage. A 220–240V unit on 120V US mains is destroyed on first use. The tracker lists LTE 850/900/1800/1900 MHz — frequencies, no band numbers, no 700MHz US carriers lean on 700MHz for rural and in-building coverage. Bars on the street, nothing in the basement. Tuya companion app, regions not stated The app is published per app-store region. No app, no setup. "Waterproof" with no IP rating A word, not a specification. Both of the first two are live checks in check_compatibility , driven by the shopper's country. Provenance, not just "unverified" Every field carries where its value came from, and the verdict engine reads it: confirmed (supplier's written spec), platform_listed (on the Alibaba detail page), inferred_tbc (a conservative inference — a hint, not a fact), pending (no source; the supplier must be asked). Not one field in this catalogue is confirmed . No supplier has returned written specifications, and the store says so on the page, next to the price. The open questions we have put to each supplier and not had answered are published there too. An earlier version of this data asserted four products were 2.4GHz-only and that the litter box had a multi-cat limit. Re-checking the listings showed both were our guesses . We deleted them. That made the demo less dramatic and the store more honest — and we rewrote the tests to assert the honest behaviour instead. People and agents on the same object The product template already shipped an "AI Compatibility Check" block with five rows, rendered as static placeholders. Rather than bolt on a competing widget, we restructured the verdict engine around exactly those five axes — Network compatibility, Region lock, Power requirement, Pet profile match, Essential extras — so the agent fills in the storefront's own block. The shopper is not reading a chat transcript about the product. They are watching the product page itself change, row by row, with a panel in the corner logging every tool call and letting them clear the profile by hand. WebMCP's trust model assumes a human is watching; this is the watching part. One source of truth for the shopper and the agent Every product arrived with no description at all . The supplier gave us specification fragments, not marketing copy — and writing confident prose around numbers we have not verified is the exact thing this store exists to avoid. So the product copy is rendered from MINTPAW_COMPAT — the same record, the same fields, in the same order that check_compatibility reads. A shopper and an agent cannot be told different things about a product, because there is only one source for both. It also means the unverified claims appear on the page , under a heading that reads "What we haven't checked ourselves", rather than only inside a tool response the shopper will never see. The honesty is not a property of the agent. It is a property of the store. Challenges we ran into Not duplicating the platform. Described above. It cost a rewrite, and it was the best thing that happened to the project. A stale-verdict bug. Changing the household left the previous run's verdicts painted on the page. Our own test suite caught it, not a person. Dawn renders two forms pointing at /cart/add , and only one holds the submit button; the obvious selector picks the wrong one. The refusal was cosmetic at first. We disabled Add to cart, but Shopify's express checkout button sat right underneath, still live, one tap from payment. A gate with a hole in it is not a gate. Accomplishments we're proud of It is a real store, live, with a refusal you can trigger yourself in about thirty seconds. And it ships 29 headless tests that run the real theme asset against the real catalogue and assert the things that would make the store a lie if they broke — chiefly that a 2.4GHz device is never ok in a 5GHz-only home, and that a hard block cannot be acknowledged away. What we lear

title: NEXUS
pitch: The continuity layer for the Agentic Web. NEXUS lets a user's intent continue across independent WebMCP websites, with failure recovery, rerouting, and explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: The continuity layer for the Agentic Web. NEXUS lets a user's intent continue across independent WebMCP websites, with failure recovery, rerouting, and explicit human approval. Like Comment Story Updates Websites end. Human intentions don't. WebMCP gives agents tools inside a website. NEXUS lets the user's intent continue beyond it. NEXUS is a WebMCP-first proof of concept that explores a missing layer of the Agentic Web: intent continuity across independent websites. The problem Human goals rarely fit inside a single website. An agent might successfully buy furniture from one provider, but the user's actual goal could be much larger: open an entire office, organize a trip, launch a business, or plan an event. When one website reaches the boundary of what it can fulfill, the user's intent should not disappear with it. What NEXUS does NEXUS preserves the unresolved part of a user's goal and allows an agent to continue it across independent WebMCP-enabled providers. The demo proves the complete lifecycle: Fulfillment → Intent Handoff → Recovery/Reroute → Human Approval → Goal Complete It also introduces an important trust boundary. A user who starts with a specific provider remains in Brand Mode . NEXUS cannot silently divert that user elsewhere. Continuing through other providers requires explicit authorization into Broker Mode . The agent can discover, plan and recover autonomously, while the human retains authority over consequential actions. Hero mission Our deterministic challenge is: Open an office for 20 people in Guadalajara before October 1, 2026 with a MXN 500,000 budget. The mission crosses five independent providers: OfficePro fulfills desks and chairs → 40% The user explicitly authorizes an Intent Handoff TechSupply fulfills computers → 60% FiberMX can provide internet, but installation is October 8 — after the deadline NEXUS records the failure and reroutes the unresolved requirement to NetBusiness NetBusiness can install by September 25 → 80% SecureNow finds a valid security solution but reaches a commitment-class action NEXUS stops at REQUIRES_HUMAN Only after explicit human approval is the installation requested GOAL COMPLETE → 100% Final cost: MXN 410,000 Remaining budget: MXN 90,000 Deadline: Satisfied Why WebMCP matters NEXUS is not an agent calling one centralized REST API. Each provider is an independent website exposing its own genuine WebMCP tools and owning its own catalog, pricing, availability and actions. The production demo spans: 16 native WebMCP tools 5 independent providers 6 HTTPS origins Cross-origin WebMCP discovery and invocation Explicit permission boundaries Failure recovery and provider rerouting Human approval before commitment-class actions We also validated the complete mission end-to-end using ChatGPT's WebMCP experience. What we learned The most interesting challenge was not tool invocation — it was preserving intent safely across website boundaries. NEXUS treats failure as a first-class state. FiberMX is not hidden when it misses the deadline. The failure remains auditable while only the unresolved internet requirement is rerouted. We also learned that agent autonomy and human control do not have to be opposites. Agents can discover, compare, plan and recover autonomously while humans retain authority at consequential boundaries. Execution NEXUS runs as a deterministic production proof of concept across six independent HTTPS origins. Production Lighthouse scores: 100 Performance / 100 Accessibility / 100 Best Practices / 100 SEO Agent Readiness improved from 39 to 66 (+69.2%) , while the WebMCP-specific check remained 5/5 . We deliberately did not fabricate REST APIs, OAuth, MCP servers, A2A endpoints, SDKs, or other capabilities simply to increase a generic readiness score. The idea WebMCP makes websites agent-ready. NEXUS explores what happens next: What if the user's goal is bigger than the website? One intent. Many providers. Human stays in control. ## Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for NEXUS Built With chatgpt cloudflare css html javascript node.js openai pnpm typescript webmcp workers Try it out nexus.1expert.pro github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Gabriela Jimenez Like Share this project: Updates Gabriela Jimenez started this project — Sep 03, 2026 10:53 AM EDT

title: Perso-XXL
pitch: Perso-xxl is a web extension that allows you to personalize your experience of the web like never before using AI tools. UX/UI are optimized for the average people, You are not average ! Let fix it !
about_excerpt: Perso-xxl is a web extension that allows you to personalize your experience of the web like never before using AI tools. UX/UI are optimized for the average people, You are not average ! Let fix it ! Like Comment Story Updates After, analytics tools added by the agent. Before Inspiration Websites are built for the average user, but everyone has different preferences, accessibility needs, and workflows. We wanted users to ask their existing AI agent to adapt any webpage for them, even when they do not own the website. What it does Perso-XXL is a browser extension that lets AI agents safely personalize webpages. Agents can change styles, hide or move elements, add safe interface components, create shortcuts, and remember the user's preferences. Changes are local, reversible, and saved for future visits. With WebMCP, capable agents use Perso-XXL directly. OpenRouter is only a fallback for users without a compatible agent. How we built it Perso-XXL exposes WebMCP tools such as inspect_page and apply_page_plan . The agent first receives short-lived, opaque target IDs. It then submits a structured modification plan. Perso-XXL validates the plan, checks that targets are still fresh, and applies it atomically. The extension uses a secure bridge between the page and extension environments. It also supports confirmation, cancellation, rollback, persistent modifications, and dynamically registered shortcuts. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was giving agents useful control without allowing arbitrary JavaScript, HTML, CSS, or selectors. Modern pages also change constantly, so inspected elements can quickly become stale. We addressed this with one-use snapshots, fingerprints, navigation checks, and target revalidation. We also had to support both normal Chrome extensions and built-in agent browsers, which expose WebMCP differently. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Perso-XXL: Works on websites the user does not own. Lets existing agents personalize pages without another AI call. Rejects unsafe and stale modifications. Supports reversible and persistent changes. Turns saved workflows into callable WebMCP tools. Gives agents access to the user's style preferences. Includes automated browser, security, rollback, and adversarial tests. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when tools expose meaningful capabilities instead of raw DOM access. We also learned that data and presentation should be separate. A website can securely provide information, while the user and agent decide how to display it. Finally, reversibility is essential. Agents are more useful when users can safely experiment, inspect the result, and undo it. What's next for Perso-XXL Next, we want to: Move the OpenRouter fallback to a secure backend. Add encrypted preference synchronization. Improve accessibility-focused personalization. Expand the safe modification capabilities. Improve previews and explanations before applying changes. Support more browsers as WebMCP becomes widely available. Our long-term goal is to make web personalization belong to the user. title: Previz
pitch: Direct your vision. Let AI choreograph every frame.
about_excerpt: Direct your vision. Let AI choreograph every frame. Like Comment Story Updates Project Story About the project Previz is a browser-based 3D blocking and camera previsualization tool built for human–agent collaboration. Directors can stage characters, animate cameras, mark important positions, and describe creative goals in natural language. A WebMCP-enabled agent can then inspect the complete scene, propose a shot plan, calculate precise trajectories, validate them, and update the visible project. Inspiration Film previsualization tools are powerful, but turning an idea like “follow the character, hide the second performer, then reveal both in one continuous shot” into animation often requires manually editing hundreds of positions, rotations, and keyframes. We wanted to explore a more natural workflow: the human directs while the agent handles calculation. Instead of controlling the interface through fragile mouse coordinates, the agent receives structured access to the same scene the director sees. WebMCP made that relationship possible. What it does Previz provides a browser-based workspace for: Adding and positioning characters and cameras in a 3D scene Creating character and camera keyframes on a timeline Previewing the selected camera in real time Adding world-space and camera-space annotations Importing scene geometry and changing its visualization style Saving, importing, and autosaving project data Exporting camera previews as video Exposing the project to agents through WebMCP The accompanying previz-director Codex skill turns directorial intent into validated character blocking and camera motion. It reads the scene, discusses a creative plan with the user, calculates trajectories, checks continuity and safety, and writes the approved result back into the editor. How we built it The interactive editor uses Three.js and WebGL for the scene, characters, camera frustums, lighting, imported geometry, transform controls, and real-time camera previews. The timeline and editing interface are implemented with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The application is packaged with React, Vinext, Vite, and Cloudflare’s runtime tooling so it can run locally or as a hosted web application. WebMCP is implemented through two tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : read_state returns the complete project and its current revision. write_state accepts a complete project and an expected revision, validates the data, updates the editor, creates an undo snapshot, and autosaves the result. Both tools use JSON Schema. Revision checking prevents an agent from overwriting newer human edits. We also created the previz-director skill, which defines a two-stage workflow: Read the scene and agree on the directorial plan. Calculate, validate, and execute the approved character and camera trajectories. Challenges we ran into One major challenge was connecting creative language to exact 3D motion. A request can be visually clear to a director while leaving many mathematical details unspecified: timing, path shape, camera distance, target transitions, angle continuity, and collision clearance. Camera movement introduced additional problems. Smooth positions do not guarantee smooth framing, and direct look-at calculations can cause sudden rotations during close passes or near-vertical shots. We needed to consider speed, acceleration, angular motion, occlusion, and composition together. Another challenge was safe human–agent collaboration. The agent may spend time calculating a scene while the user continues editing it. Revision-based writes ensure that stale calculations cannot silently replace newer work. Finally, we had to keep the visual editor responsive while rendering multiple views, imported geometry, shadows, annotations, playback, and video exports. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that Previz does not treat WebMCP as a remote-control layer. The agent works with meaningful project concepts—characters, cameras, annotations, frames, and trajectories—instead of imitating clicks and drags. Other accomplishments include: Transactional, revision-protected project updates Immediate synchronization between agent writes and the visible editor Per-frame trajectory support for precisely calculated movement A reusable directing skill that separates creative approval from execution World-space and camera-space annotation workflows Browser-based video preview and export Automated coverage across 62 application tests A completely browser-based workflow with no traditional 3D application required What we learned We learned that the strongest agent experiences divide responsibility clearly. Humans are best at narrative intent, taste, rhythm, and deciding what an audience should feel. Agents are valuable when a creative decision expands into hundreds of dependent calculations and consistency checks. We also learned that structured state is much more reliable than visual automation. Giving the agent a small, well-described tool surface produced safer and more understandable behavior than exposing every interface control individually. Most importantly, planning and execution need a clear boundary. Having the agent present its interpretation before writing the scene keeps the user in control and prevents technically valid motion from becoming the wrong creative choice. What's next for Previz Next, we want to add: Adjustable focal length and camera sensor controls Look-at and subject-tracking constraints Editable easing and motion curves Motion paths and onion-skin visualization Keyframe copy and paste More detailed collision and occlusion diagnostics glTF and USD camera export Multi-user and multi-agent collaboration Additional WebMCP tools for targeted, incremental scene operations A reusable library of blocking and cinematography patterns Our long-term goal is to make Previz a shared creative surface where people direct ideas and agents turn those ideas into precise, editable cinematic motion. title: Prism
pitch: Tell Prism what a WebMCP is for, then test whether its tools actually deliver.
about_excerpt: Tell Prism what a WebMCP is for, then test whether its tools actually deliver. Like Comment Story Updates Prism turns a declared WebMCP purpose into an evidence-backed scorecard. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Prism Inspiration WebMCP evaluation can become a checklist of surface-level signals: did the page register tools, do they have schemas, and can the browser call them? Those checks matter, but they do not answer the product question. A commerce tool set, an editor, and a project workspace need different capabilities and different human-approval boundaries. Prism starts with the job to be done. It evaluates whether a WebMCP implementation covers that journey, whether mutations affect the same state a person sees, and whether consequential decisions remain visible and human-controlled. What it does Prism combines a purpose-aware evaluation dashboard with an open-source, local-first browser companion. A person selects Commerce, Project Operations, Content Editor, or defines a Custom contract. That contract states the intent, expected capabilities, and the action that must remain human-approved. The browser companion then runs on the target page, discovers its live WebMCP tools, executes only selected checks, and records schemas, annotations, timing, and privacy-preserving before-and-after evidence. Prism maps that evidence to four dimensions: purpose coverage; contract quality; observable mutation proof; and runtime hygiene. Every score includes journey-level evidence and a repair that can be tested again. A weak cart mutation, for example, does not merely lose points: Prism explains that the runner could not verify the visible state change and recommends returning a state revision plus a read-back check. Prism is itself a WebMCP app. Its four page-side tools let an agent read the selected contract, switch profiles, run a deterministic evaluation, and read the same score and evidence shown to the person. How we built it The dashboard is React and TypeScript on Vinext, deployed through ChatGPT Sites. Its scoring engine consumes a versioned runner snapshot and keeps the report deterministic and interpretable. The Manifest V3 companion uses the active page's document.modelContext.getTools() and document.modelContext.executeTool() APIs. It runs in the target origin because a hosted iframe or HTTP request cannot truthfully inspect another page's WebMCP tools. It hashes visible before-and-after state, supports an explicit read-back check, and exports only evidence metadata—not page text or tool output. The dashboard registers get_evaluation_context , choose_evaluation_profile , run_sample_evaluation , and get_latest_evaluation with narrow object schemas, annotations, validation, and lifecycle cancellation. The mutation tools update the same React state rendered in the visible interface. Challenges we ran into The hardest design constraint was the browser execution boundary. Cross-origin discovery would have been convenient, but it would also have been misleading. Separating collection from evaluation made the architecture more honest and gave us a useful privacy boundary. Behavioral evidence also needed careful calibration. A DOM digest proves that something visible changed, but not that the semantic change was correct. Prism therefore distinguishes visible-state evidence from stronger tool read-back evidence and does not claim either one proves the target application's human-approval policy. Accomplishments that we're proud of Purpose-specific contracts prevent irrelevant tool count from dominating the score. Every deduction is tied to visible evidence and an actionable repair. The companion is local-first, minimal-permission, and requires a fresh confirmation for mutation checks. Prism's own WebMCP mutations and reads agree with its visible UI. The dashboard, companion, source, tests, and judge guide form one coherent open-source release. What we learned WebMCP quality is not just API design. It is the relationship among intent, page state, agent authority, and the evidence available to a person. The most useful evaluator is therefore not a universal pass/fail scanner; it is a repeatable contract between the product team and the experience they intend to ship. What's next Next, Prism can add reusable contract packs, richer assertions for semantic read-back, shareable evaluation histories, and CI adapters that compare a new snapshot with a reviewed baseline. The same model could support accessibility audits, agent regression testing, and organization-specific approval policies.
