title: Project Notebook
pitch: A voice controlled notebook for agents and humans to use together via WebMCP: notes, diagrams, drawings, test prep, project tracking, code playground. The notebook is whatever you need it to be!
about_excerpt: A voice controlled notebook for agents and humans to use together via WebMCP: notes, diagrams, drawings, test prep, project tracking, code playground. The notebook is whatever you need it to be! Like 6 Comment 2 Story Updates 2 Live anatomy Test mode: section-specific recall questions across the head, thorax, pelvis, and lower limbs. Live skull coloring lab: saved surface paint with palette, brush, and labeled bone index. Project Notebook Why I built this I use ChatGPT Voice a lot, but the useful work usually ends up trapped in a chat that I forget about. I wanted to talk through an idea and have the agent build the actual notebook in front of me, with pages I can inspect, revisit, and correct. Project Notebook is a visual notebook that people and AI agents can work in together. I had tried to make the idea work a month ago before WebMCp, it never really worked though so I had to abandon the idea. The agent could produce an answer, but it could not reliably work against the page I was looking at and leave behind a useful artifact. Having the agent "see" the page allows a ton of control and interesting capability. The page can publish a small, typed contract that the notebook itself owns. An agent can create and revise actual pages, create original content, offline you can embed virtually anything in a notebook. That lets agents help me study, sketch ideas, and trace homework pages into interactable notebooks. That is why project notebook sort of turned into a nested set of tech demos, as I tried to make demos for my notebook the cool ideas kept just working! The live Instruction Notebook shows the same visible pages the agent can read, open, and revise. The anatomy notebook I wish I had in college The clearest example is Anatomy Exam Prep. When I took anatomy and physiology in college and had to learn human anatomy, studying for a lab practical was difficult because I did not have a skeleton model at home. I was looking at textbook diagrams and trying to memorize every bone in the human body. I also used a physical anatomy coloring book, which helped connect names and locations to the act of studying. I built the notebook I wish I had then. Its first page contains an interactive 3D adult skeleton with 206 logical bones and 208 source meshes. Models can use WebMCP to open the notebook and exact page. Once there, the anatomy lesson provides accessible controls for selecting and isolating a bone, orbiting and zooming the model, switching camera presets, and bringing the full skeleton back. The notebook also has Test mode. It gives me answer fields for a section, lets me move through the questions, scores the answers, and saves the latest result so I can try again. Fresh captures from the published site. Each panel shows the selected body section, the highlighted structure, and the answer fields used for practical-exam recall. The next six pages are 3D coloring labs for the head, spine, thorax, upper limbs, pelvis, and lower limbs. I can choose a color, paint a bone surface, erase a mark, clear a bone or section, and switch from visible labels to recall prompts. It recreates the part of my physical coloring book that helped me study, but ties it to the same explorable skeleton. Try having your agent drive through the test prep, or do like I did and try to have it color some bones for you! Fresh capture from the published site. The skull lab shows saved paint on the 3D model, the active palette, three started bones, the surface brush, and the bone index. The current challenge demo uses WebMCP to open the exact notebook and page. Bone selection, model orbit, zoom, Test mode, and coloring on the anatomy pages are direct accessible browser interactions. I keep that distinction visible because I want the demo to say exactly what the agent did. What a WebMCP tool is text WebMCP lets a web page publish named, typed capabilities to an AI client. Instead of hunting for buttons or manipulating the page's HTML, the agent asks the application for an outcome. The application validates the request, changes the notebook through its real data model, and returns a structured receipt.} - My agents definition Project Notebook tools: notebook_read Inspect notebook context without scraping the interface. notebook_open Move directly to the intended notebook, page, or view. notebook_apply Create and revise notebook content through validated actions. anatomy_context_read Inspect the anatomy atlas, current view, and test progress. anatomy_navigate Control the anatomy view and focus a bone or test question. anatomy_test Enter answers and submit an anatomy test for scoring. notebook_read This is the read path. It can return the agent guide, notebook shelf, current notebook, one exact page, or recent action receipts. The result contains structured text and figure information, page numbers, and stable references for later actions. It does not expose raw editor state or make the agent reverse-engineer the DOM. notebook_open This is the navigation path. It can open the shelf, open a notebook by title or id, open an exact page, move to the previous or next page, or reset the notebook view. Exact-page navigation matters. An agent can move from page 1 to page 7 directly instead of pretending to click Next six times. In my own testing, a navigation task that took roughly 90 seconds dropped to roughly 10 seconds after I tightened the agent instructions and removed unnecessary back-and-forth. That is an observation from my use of the app, not a controlled benchmark. notebook_apply This is the main workhorse. One typed action can: Create a notebook Write formatted headings, paragraphs, quotes, bullets, or numbered steps Add a semantic diagram or bounded editable drawing Trace validated vector ink Arrange a page element or a group of diagram nodes Add a page when the notebook needs more room Undo the latest agent change exactly The application computes identifiers, placement, pagination, and layout. It validates the content and geometry before saving. It rejects raw HTML, CSS, JavaScript, arbitrary URLs, raw SVG, and renderer-specific records. Every accepted change returns a receipt, and agent mutations participate in the notebook's real history. anatomy_context_read This is the read path for the Anatomy Exam Prep notebook. It returns the verified atlas state, current layout, Study or Test mode, skeletal section, camera position, isolation state, and the number of visible meshes. In Study mode, it can identify the selected and hovered bones. In Test mode, it returns question numbers, completion status, and score progress without revealing the hidden bone labels or entered answers. anatomy_navigate This is the navigation path for the 3D anatomy atlas. One action can set the page layout, switch between Study and Test mode, change the skeletal section, move the camera to the anterior, left, or right view, and control whether a bone is isolated. It can also focus a verified bone by id in Study mode or move directly to a numbered question in Test mode. Combining a section with Test mode starts a fresh test for that section. Setting isolation to false keeps the complete surrounding anatomy visible while the agent moves between questions. anatomy_test This is the test path. It can enter an answer for an opaque question number or submit the active section for scoring. Answer receipts confirm that the field was completed without repeating the answer back to the agent. When the test is submitted, Project Notebook scores it and saves the result through the application's own notebook path. The agent can operate the fillable test, but it cannot use the tool response to read the hidden answer key. The application computes identifiers, placement, pagination, and layout. It validates the content and geometry before saving. It rejects raw HTML, CSS, JavaScript, arbitrary URLs, raw SVG, and renderer-specific records. Every accepted change returns a receipt, and agent mutations participate in the notebook's real history. A trace test: from a reference page to editable notebook ink One test used a original scan of an Encyclopedia Britannica page as the source "traced" the page, create a 1:1 copy in html with images traced as SVG paths. It was a useful test because the formatting could be reapplied and the "tracing" for images gave me a nice workflow to create a hand drawn image effect by image generating and then tracing into SVG. The visible source page: Fig. 33 is the phyllotaxis diagram; Fig. 34 is a thirteen-leaf rosette; Fig. 35 is a Picea alba cone; Figs. 36–45 show leaf and bud forms. The trace skill lives in the agent environment. On the live site, notebook_apply accepts the resulting bounded trace through the figure.trace action. The page validates and stores the typed document. It does not scrape Britannica or perform the image-to-vector conversion. The workflow begins with a tight crop around the figure I actually want. The agent traces the visible ink into SVG paths, then render

title: SightSinger Copilot
pitch: Say the edit, hear the change. WebMCP fuses SightSinger and ChatGPT into one AI co-composer, precise score edits in plain language, and sing it back instantly. No DAW required.
about_excerpt: Say the edit, hear the change. WebMCP fuses SightSinger and ChatGPT into one AI co-composer, precise score edits in plain language, and sing it back instantly. No DAW required. Like Comment Story Updates SightSinger Copilot - Agentic AI Session Singer Edit score with natural language. Just tell AI what to edit. Not only lyrics. Just tell AI to update any notes just say "Sing the song", AI will complete generate all parts for you Inspiration SightSinger is a production score-to-singing tool with initial traction. Since launching in May 2026, it has reached 600 sign-ups, 200 active users, and MRR enough to cover my AI coding subscription. Our most requested features are a one-click "render all parts" button and cleanup of common score artifacts like redundant notes and misaligned lyrics. Both asks are harder than they sound. "Render all" means reliably orchestrating many long-running synthesis jobs. Score cleanup means running arbitrary code against user data. It requires a real sandbox to lock down which libraries and tools that code can touch. That's a security and infrastructure investment in its own, unrelated to the singing engine SightSinger was built to be good at. WebMCP solved the problem. Rather than building all by myself, I could expose only what SightSinger uniquely does well, like precise per-part synthesis and expressive singing, as narrow, callable tools, and let the requesting agent, already running under its own host's sandboxing and orchestration, handles the rest. The dangerous, generic work moves to systems already built to handle it. This isn't "let's add WebMCP because it's trending." The result is SightSinger Copilot: an edit, see, sing loop, where the agent handles precise editing and sequencing, and SightSinger handles the voice. What it does SightSinger Copilot turns a written MusicXML score into an agent-ready rehearsal studio. Instead of prompting for a generic song, musicians work from the notes, rhythm, lyrics, parts, verses, and instrumental arrangement already written in their score. A user can upload a score, or start with the built-in Happy Birthday demo, then ask an AI agent to inspect the score, make precise MusicXML edits, generate solfège lyrics, direct a vocal performance, synthesize a selected vocal part, and export the current vocal mix. The resulting vocal tracks sit alongside score-derived instrumental MIDI playback, so users can rehearse and iterate without DAW editing. WebMCP makes this workflow agentic and beyond a commodity score-to-singing tool. A musicXML score is structured text, any edit precise enough to describe, like "at bar 15, change the chord from D minor to F major 7th," becomes an exact change, not a lucky regeneration. How we built it We built an open-source React/TypeScript frontend hosted on Firebase Hosting. The frontend registers score-aware WebMCP tools at startup, letting an agent retrieve and edit the active MusicXML, add solfège, request synthesis, check credits, and export the current mix. The browser UI remains the visible workspace for score updates, rendering progress, multitrack playback, and downloads. A separate private Cloud Run backend handles authorization, score/session storage, and GPU-backed DiffSinger inference. It runs on an NVIDIA L4 GPU and turns the selected score part, lyrics or solfège, and performance settings into vocal tracks that return to the studio for playback and mixing. Challenges we ran into WebMCP tools do not currently provide a native way for an agent to attach a local file to the site or directly receive a downloaded audio file. That matters for a score-first music workflow. We designed around this with URL- and session-based handoffs. The musician uploads the initial score in the studio, then the agent retrieves and edits the active MusicXML through the current session. Synthesized tracks and exported mixes are returned as playback/download URLs, while the studio updates the visible score and multitrack player. This keeps every agent action grounded in the same active session without requiring unsupported file-transfer capabilities. Accomplishments that we're proud of I discovered this challenge only about two days ago, and the public repository was created just for it. In that short time, we learned WebMCP, exposed meaningful SightSinger capabilities as browser tools, and delivered a working, deployable demo. I'm proud that this is more than a tool-call showcase. It demonstrates a practical score-first workflow: an LLM can understand the active MusicXML score, make natural-language edits, prepare solfège or lyric renders, direct an AI singer, and help assemble a rehearsal-ready demo. All while keeping the musician in the visible studio loop. What we learned Before writing code, I asked which agent-integration approach actually fits: vision/screenshot control, DOM scraping, A2A, a hosted MCP server, a direct API, or WebMCP. WebMCP stood out for two reasons. It calls structured tools rather than clicking rendered pixels, so it's way more token efficient and accurate. And it runs the agent directly on our page, inheriting the user's existing logged-in session, no separate server, auth, or API keys to stand up. That also meant the riskiest part of this feature, an LLM freely editing a user's score, runs inside the agent's own sandbox instead of one we'd have to build ourselves. The lesson: there is no universally right integration approach. Only the approach that best fits the use case, constraints, and time. What's next for SightSinger Copilot Next, we want SightSinger Copilot to become a true co-director for score-based vocal production. It should understand a song’s musical context, including its form, phrasing, lyrics, harmony, vocal range, and emotional arc. It then translates that understanding into precise performance direction for the AI singer. For example, Copilot could direct: “bars 1–4: soft, peaceful, and clean,” “bars 5–8: gradually build intensity,” and “chorus: high-energy, emotionally open.” SightSinger would then translate the director’s or composer’s instruction into its voicing-curve parameter controls, shaping the singer’s delivery across the score. Rather than treating a whole part as one uniform render, SightSinger could create vocals that remain faithful to the written notation while carrying intention, contrast, and emotion. title: Tether
pitch: Teach one site, and a site that has never met you is already configured. A shared memory layer for the agent-native web, built on WebMCP. Delete a memory, and the next build forgets it.
about_excerpt: Teach one site, and a site that has never met you is already configured. A shared memory layer for the agent-native web, built on WebMCP. Delete a memory, and the next build forgets it. Like Comment Story Updates Logo Inspiration You tell one site you want dark interfaces, compact layouts, and TypeScript. Then you open the next tool and type all of it again. And again. Agents were supposed to remove that friction, but each one starts cold at the tab boundary, so the person ends up carrying context from site to site by hand. Being the integration layer is the last unautomated job on the web, and nobody was treating it as a problem. WebMCP changes what a website can hand an agent: real capabilities the page declares, instead of a DOM that was never built to be driven. That made one question worth answering. If every site can expose genuine tools, what is the single shared capability that would make all of them better at once? Memory. Not an assistant's private chat history sealed in a vendor cloud, but structured context that any participating site can read and write, with the person holding the delete key. What it does Tether is a shared memory layer for the agent-native web, plus two working sites that prove context survives the jump between them. DesignLab is the producer, a small design studio. Ask the agent to remember your preferences and its save_preference tool applies them to the canvas and writes them to Tether in the same call. DevForge is the consumer, a project scaffolder whose form has a project-name field and nothing else. Its create_project tool asks Tether what you prefer, then configures six things it never asked about: language, theme, layout density, framework, package manager, and styling, down to the lock file and the install command. The Tether control plane shows every memory with its source site, the tool that wrote it, tags, a confidence score, and a timestamp. Inspect, search, edit, add, or permanently delete any of it. Try it in 30 seconds Open DesignLab and ask the agent: "Remember that I prefer dark interfaces, compact layouts, and TypeScript." The studio turns dark and compact, and three structured memories land in Tether. Open the dashboard . They are already there, each carrying its full lineage. Open DevForge and ask for a starter project. It comes back TypeScript, dark, compact, with every value tracing back to the memory that produced it. Now delete the TypeScript memory and scaffold again. The language falls back to JavaScript. The others hold. Step 4 is the whole project. A cross-site demo can be faked with a hardcoded path, and a judge should assume it was until shown otherwise. So deletion is part of the demo: pull one row out of the layer, and a different site's output changes in front of you. None of this is limited to a fixed set of toggles. Both DesignLab and the control plane accept context in your own words through the same validated path. Say "I prefer pnpm over npm" or "I prefer Tailwind CSS for styling" , and the next scaffold picks it up, install command included. How we built it Next.js 15 App Router and TypeScript. Tailwind for a dark, high-density developer-tool surface. Zod on every boundary. Supabase Postgres for persistence, behind a pluggable store: with no environment variables at all, a fresh clone runs immediately on an in-process driver. Memories are structured rather than free text: content, category, tags, source, confidence, scope, timestamps. That schema is what makes the whole thing work. A pile of chat transcripts cannot be filtered, ranked, explained, or selectively deleted. Security got real attention for a hackathon MVP. The service-role key lives only in server-only modules, so an accidental client import fails the build instead of leaking a credential. Row-level security is enabled on both tables with no permissive policies. Memory content is rendered as text by React and never injected as HTML. Sessions are opaque random ids in an httpOnly first-party cookie, with no accounts and no PII. Challenges we ran into Making the memory falsifiable. The cross-site moment only convinces if it can visibly fail. Building deletion into the demo, and making the fallback path genuinely fall back rather than run a second hardcoded branch, is what turned a nice animation into evidence. Refusing to simulate. It would have been easy to fake tool calls when no agent is present and let the video imply otherwise. Detecting the absence and labelling every manual invocation cost a day and made the architecture clearer, because you can now see that the agent path and the button path run the same handler. Keeping retrieval interpretable end to end. Carrying matchedOn reasons from the matcher through the API into the UI constrained the entire pipeline. It ruled out the easy embedding approach, and it is the reason the product can show its work. Serverless state. The in-process store is perfect locally and wrong in production, because serverless functions do not share memory between invocations. The /api/health endpoint reports which driver is live specifically so a misconfigured deploy looks like a misconfiguration instead of a broken app. Accomplishments that we're proud of The delete-and-rescaffold moment. It is the rare demo that proves itself by breaking on purpose. You can verify our claims in ninety seconds. The test suite runs against the live deployment: curl https://tether-swart.vercel.app/api/health # {"status":"online","driver":"supabase"} git clone https://github.com/Dotman-Bei/Tether && cd Tether && npm install BASE_URL=https://tether-swart.vercel.app npm test It scopes itself to its own session cookie and cleans up after itself, so it is safe to point at production. It covers every route handler and, through them, the configured store driver: creation and defaults, numeric coercion, tag round-tripping, the duplicate guard, list ordering and filters, ranked retrieval with match reasons, update persistence, input validation, 404s, activity logging, session isolation, delete, and reset. No test framework and no dependencies. **A fresh clone runs with zero environment variables.** `npm install && npm run dev` and the whole demo works. **We did not overclaim the protocol.** WebMCP does not carry memory between unrelated sites on its own. It is the tool interface on each page, and Tether is the shared backplane those tools read from and write to. Saying otherwise would have been an easier pitch and a false one. ## What we learned **Structure is what makes memory shareable.** Category, tags, source, and confidence are what let a second site retrieve something specific, apply it, show its work, and let a person govern the result. Unstructured recall cannot do any of those four things. **Trust surfaces are product features, not compliance overhead.** The lineage drawer and the labelled telemetry stream are what make people believe the rest of it, and they were among the cheapest things in the build. **Explainability is a design constraint, not a feature you add later.** Choosing lexical matching over embeddings looked like a downgrade until we tried to render *why* a memory was applied. The interpretable pipeline turned out to be the product. ## What's next for Tether **Per-site scoped consent and real accounts.** The cross-origin story above, which is the difference between a demo and infrastructure. - **A small client library** so a site joins in a few lines instead of reimplementing the contract. - **Memory decay and conflict resolution.** Preferences change, and the layer should notice when a new statement contradicts an old one instead of accumulating both. - **Richer context types past preferences:** working conventions, project constraints, domain vocabulary. The two demo sites are an illustration. The direction is a shared memory layer that any experience can build on, where the person keeps the keys. Built With javascript lucide-react model-context-protocol next.js node.js postgresql react rest-api serverless supabase tailwindcss typescript vercel webmcp zod Try it out tether-swart.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Heisbei: Solo build. The thesis, the product design, the ten WebMCP tools, the memory layer and the API underneath are mine, with Claude Code as implementation partner. The decision I would defend hardest is the delete step. A clean cross-site handoff would have demoed fine, but a demo that cannot visibly fail proves nothing, so I made deletion part of the flow and let the scaffold fall back on camera. The second is making the app admit when no agent is present instead of faking the call. That cost a day, and it is the reason you can trust anything else on the screen. title: Tokuchu
pitch: Customize gifts for event attendees en masse using WebMCP + agents
about_excerpt: Customize gifts for event attendees en masse using WebMCP + agents Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Six years ago, I cofounded a cafe where much of our revenue has come from bulk orders for events. Event organizers often request customizations, from dietary restrictions to names printed on party favours. But the specifications for these customizations can be difficult to collect. Organizers may not yet know exactly who is attending, what each guest needs, or which details a vendor requires. That uncertainty creates a lot of manual back and forth. An intermediate source of truth gives agents somewhere to coordinate this information. I built Tokuchu to explore how WebMCP could connect an event’s attendee information with the requirements of a personalized purchase. What it does Tokuchu is a WebMCP-native application that helps your agent manage event participants and their needs. Its sister website, Customworks, is a Shopify storefront with WebMCP tools for configuring personalized merchandise and preparing a checkout. An organizer can ask ChatGPT’s browser to create an event and add attendees, then browse Customworks for a suitable gift. The store supplies the product’s customization requirements, which the agent brings back to Tokuchu. Tokuchu reconciles those requirements with attendee information and relevant shared event details. It identifies missing answers and validates the resulting values against the store’s constraints. After approval, the agent can prepare one personalized item per complete attendee, leave incomplete attendees pending, and save the checkout in Tokuchu. The organizer completes payment through Shopify. Tokuchu also supports scoped vendor access to fulfillment information, so a vendor can report an issue without receiving unrelated attendee data. How we built it I built Tokuchu with Next.js and TypeScript, with PostgreSQL persistence and deployment on Render. Its event, attendee, and vendor pages expose WebMCP tools appropriate to each page’s role. On Customworks, I added merchant tools to the Shopify storefront. get_customization returns a product’s required fields, constraints, and variants. add_customized_to_cart accepts the configured items and creates a separate personalized cart line for each included attendee. Tokuchu stores the product contract alongside the event’s records. Its validation and reconciliation logic produces a fulfillment manifest, and approvals reference a specific revision of that information. The main website entry uses ChatGPT’s browser. Tokuchu also has an interface that people and browser agents can manipulate, including an in-app chatbox that invokes its managed workflow. The final demo shows an agent entering prompts into that chatbox. A separate local Stagehand runner provides another way to exercise the cross-site WebMCP flow. Challenges we ran into It took time to configure the WebMCP tools and page instructions so ChatGPT could reliably discover and use them. Testing different scenarios also revealed edge cases that the data model did not yet account for, particularly when attendee information was incomplete or needed to be mapped to a product’s requirements. Working through those cases meant checking both what the agent understood and how Tokuchu recorded the resulting information. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m proud of building two live websites that work together to turn attendee information into personalized orders. Setting up Customworks also gave me practical experience with agentic e-commerce, including how product customization connects to Shopify’s cart and checkout. The store is configured to support real orders once test mode is turned off. An agent can prepare much of the personalized order through the browser, with the organizer reviewing the checkout before payment. That brings the project closer to the kind of ordering workflow I would want to use at our own cafe. What we learned I learned how much the initial setup of a website matters for agents. The page metadata and instructions directed toward them need to be clear and available when they first arrive, so they can understand what the site offers and how to navigate it. Making those entry points easy to discover can be just as impactful as refining the individual tools. A useful capability becomes much easier to work with when the agent can find it and understand when to use it. What's next for Tokuchu I’d love to continue experimenting with storefronts that provide useful information for agents to process, and explore how their requirements can inform what an event organizer asks attendees. I’d also like to develop an iteration of Tokuchu that helps us process orders at our own cafe, using what I’ve learned here to reduce the back and forth around bulk orders and customizations. title: Agent Escape Room
pitch: A 3D escape room built to benchmark AI agents through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A 3D escape room built to benchmark AI agents through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Just a look at the 21 WebMCP tools available to the agent. A look at the rankings of a couple agents that completed the escape room. A report card for an agent with relevant metrics used to evaluate the agent's performance. A look at the lobby as soon as the agent enters. Inspiration Most AI benchmarks test agents through text prompts, multiple choice questions, or isolated coding tasks. I wanted to explore a different question: Can an AI agent investigate an unfamiliar environment, use tools intelligently, connect evidence across multiple locations, solve a mystery, and reach a verified end state? That idea became Agent Escape Room , a 3D science fiction mystery designed for human exploration and structured AI agent interaction through WebMCP. The first mission, The Missing Researcher , places the player inside the locked down Helix Research Facility. Dr. Evelyn Vale disappeared shortly before announcing an important discovery. To escape, an agent must explore the facility, inspect objects, collect evidence, unlock restricted rooms, derive codes and passwords, investigate facility records, reconstruct what happened, and submit a supported final theory. What it does Agent Escape Room combines a navigable 3D environment with a deterministic mystery engine. Humans can explore the facility using the keyboard and mouse. Compatible AI agents can interact with the same underlying world through 21 registered WebMCP tools, including: identify_agent get_current_room get_available_actions look_around get_spatial_state observe_direction turn navigate_to_landmark move_to inspect search read take get_inventory use_item enter_code interact talk_to get_known_clues submit_solution escape The tools expose only information that an agent could legitimately know. They provide observations and actions, not hidden puzzle state or the solution. The mystery includes five interconnected locations: Lobby Research Lab Dr. Vale's Office Server Room Security Room Some doors remain locked until their requirements are satisfied. Important evidence is distributed across multiple rooms, so an agent must connect research notes, access records, security footage, system logs, and environmental clues instead of following a simple linear sequence. Before escaping, the agent must submit a causal explanation identifying what Dr. Vale discovered, why she disappeared, who was involved, whether she left voluntarily, and why the facility entered lockdown. The explanation must cite evidence collected during that specific run. How I built it I separated the application into three major layers. Deterministic game engine The engine maintains structured state for the current room, inventory, discovered objects, collected evidence, unlocked areas, solved puzzles, entered codes, conversations, final theory status, and escape status. Every action validates its prerequisites. An agent cannot read an undiscovered document, use an item it does not possess, access a locked room, or solve a puzzle through unsupported random guessing. Puzzle values are generated from the session identifier for each playthrough. This makes answers from previous runs less useful and creates a more meaningful benchmark. 3D exploration interface I built the facility as a navigable first person 3D environment with keyboard and mouse controls, interactive objects, locked doors, room specific environments, lighting, object labels, proximity detection, and contextual interaction controls. The interface also includes an evidence notebook, inventory, activity log, navigation guidance, interaction feedback, developer diagnostics, and a report card. WebMCP agent interface The game registers structured tools through Chrome's WebMCP Imperative API. Each tool maps to the same server validated actions used by the game engine, so agents and humans operate within the same world rules. I also built a Chrome Manifest V3 side panel extension that discovers the active page's WebMCP tools, sends them to the OpenAI Responses API, executes tool calls sequentially, displays live agent activity, and supports selectable models and reasoning effort levels. Agent identity is registered through identify_agent . Completed runs are added to the leaderboard only when the server verifies that the agent solved the mystery and escaped through WebMCP without using the visual interface. Agent evaluation Every playthrough records: Total actions WebMCP tool calls Incorrect attempts Navigation actions Observations Rooms explored Evidence discovered Important evidence missed Completion time Mystery solving status Escape status Successful agent runs appear on an efficiency leaderboard ranked primarily by the fewest actions required to escape. Incorrect attempts and completion time are used as tie breakers, while the score provides an additional diagnostic measure. This turns the escape room into more than a game. It becomes an environment for comparing agent reasoning, exploration strategy, tool efficiency, and reliability. Challenges I faced One of the biggest challenges was balancing difficulty with fairness. I wanted the mystery to require genuine multi step reasoning without making success depend on random guessing or obscure visual details. Building one shared experience for humans and agents was another major challenge. Visual interactions and WebMCP calls had to produce the same persistent state changes while preventing either interface from bypassing puzzle requirements. The experimental nature of WebMCP created several technical challenges. I worked through origin trial enrollment, browser flags, tool registration lifecycle issues, schema validation, agent client compatibility, and the differences between visual browser automation and true WebMCP tool usage. The 3D world introduced additional challenges, including lighting dark environments without losing the science fiction atmosphere, making interactive objects distinguishable, improving interaction distance, supporting reliable keyboard controls, and presenting contextual actions without interrupting movement. What I learned I learned that providing tools is not enough to make an agent successful. Tool descriptions, observation quality, error responses, state visibility, and prerequisite feedback all have a major effect on agent performance. I also learned that agents can become trapped in inefficient loops when an environment does not clearly distinguish between: Something that has not been discovered Something that is visible but out of range Something that requires another item Something that requires a derived password Something that cannot be interacted with Designing good agent facing feedback is remarkably similar to designing good human user experience. The system must communicate what changed, why an action failed, and what kinds of reasoning remain possible without revealing the answer. What's next Agent Escape Room is designed as the foundation for a larger AI agent evaluation platform. Future versions could include: Additional mysteries and environments Multiple difficulty levels Larger model comparison workflows Aggregate completion analytics Aggregate token and cost analytics Replayable agent action traces Standardized benchmark runs Custom escape room creation tools My long term goal is to make agent evaluation feel less like running a static test suite and more like watching an intelligent system investigate a living world. title: colorwake
pitch: A coloring studio for parents and kids where their own drawings come alive. Tell ChatGPT the story, and through WebMCP the characters walk, dance, and fly across the stage — imagination, extended.
about_excerpt: A coloring studio for parents and kids where their own drawings come alive. Tell ChatGPT the story, and through WebMCP the characters walk, dance, and fly across the stage — imagination, extended. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Canvas mode - select sketc Play mode Play mode - dance, fly, swim etc. colorwake in 20 seconds Kids color a character, then an agent directs it over WebMCP as it acts out their story onstage. A read-only get_guide tool works like a system prompt handed over by the page: an in-page playbook for guiding a child with choices, never a script. Successful write-tool results carry fresh, action-relevant context, while get_studio_state lets the agent resync after on-screen changes. No app backend or accounts: raw artwork stays local, and the agent receives only a compact state summary. A parent runs the agent; the child makes the art. Built solo by a first-time hackathon entrant with a product background. Inspiration Coloring apps end when the coloring ends. But the best part comes next, when a child holds up the drawing and says, “And then the rocket flies to the moon!” No app was listening. WebMCP changed that. The app’s state and tools live inside the page, letting a connected agent interact with the same canvas the child is touching and help the picture move as the child imagines. What it does Color — choose a sketch and paint it with a finger, mouse, or stylus. Play — finish coloring, and the same canvas becomes a stage. Tell ChatGPT the story — “The rocket flies to the volcano, and the robot dances!” — and through 10 WebMCP tools, the agent casts the characters, sets the place, time, and weather, and composes their movements. Young children shouldn’t need to formulate commands. The agent can read the state of play and offer one simple next choice — always choices, never a script. No artwork is generated for the child. The child makes the art; the agent plays inside it, in real time, on the same screen. Because ChatGPT is for users 13 and older (subject to local minimum-age requirements), colorwake is co-play by design: a parent operates the agent and relays the child’s ideas, while the child stays in charge of the art. How we built it colorwake is a static React 19 and TypeScript SPA built with Vite. It has no app backend or accounts; artwork and state persist in localStorage. Characters are rigged SVGs across five rig families, animated with the Web Animations API. Motion parameters are clamped to safe ranges for both whole-character and part-targeted moves. The WebMCP layer registers 10 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , typed with webmcp-types and validated with Zod: four read tools and six write tools. Three decisions mattered most: get_guide — an in-page playbook, delivered like a system prompt. A read-only tool can return more than app state. It can carry guidance: how the studio works, what the child can do in each state, and the house rules. An agent that reads it starts with a clear role as a playmate. A loop designed around WebMCP. On-screen button presses are not announced to the agent. Successful write-tool results provide current, action-relevant context, while get_studio_state lets the agent resync after manual interactions. The experience works best when the family continues through the protocol. Parity, with one boundary the agent cannot cross. UI-equivalent tools call the same actions as the on-screen controls, while motion tools drive the same play engine. The 20-picture and 8-step caps return actionable errors; the three-spot stage predictably swaps out the friend that has been there longest. There is deliberately no painting tool — coloring belongs to the child. Challenges I ran into This was my first hackathon, and I came to it with a product background rather than a traditional engineering one. The hardest part was translation : turning WebMCP’s technical properties into moments a family could actually feel. get_guide emerged from asking what happens when young children cannot type commands and turning that constraint into a feature. AI coding agents were my hands, but direction, taste, and QA were mine: round after round of on-device review, dozens of UI/UX fixes, and a 148-test verification chain. One technical lesson stood out: tool descriptions are UX writing. Agents behave only as well as the schemas and errors guiding them. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The promise works end to end: a picture colored a minute ago can walk across the stage beneath the weather the child chose. The page teaches the agent: get_guide gives it a playbook for becoming a good playmate. I shipped it solo for my first hackathon, with a local-first privacy model designed for families. What I learned Read-only tools can carry guidance — context, norms, and a role — not just app state. Designing for agents is UX design made of words: schemas, descriptions, and error messages are the interface. What's next for colorwake More sketches and motion families, sound, saved and replayable shows, and more languages — so more families can color together and more compatible agents can direct. title: ForgeMCP-Multi-Agent Research & Game Studio
pitch: Humans and AI agents use real WebMCP tools to observe Earth, test Cube Chess 512 AI, create 3D systems, verify evidence, and keep final decisions human-controlled.
about_excerpt: Humans and AI agents use real WebMCP tools to observe Earth, test Cube Chess 512 AI, create 3D systems, verify evidence, and keep final decisions human-controlled. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ForgeMCP — Multi-Agent Research & Game Studio ForgeMCP is an agent-native web platform where people and AI agents use real browser-native WebMCP tools to observe Earth, test a deterministic 8×8×8 chess engine, create verifiable 3D systems, and keep consequential decisions under human control. Core workflow HUMAN → COORDINATOR → SPECIALIST AGENTS → WEBMCP TOOLS → REAL DATA / ENGINE → VERIFICATION → HUMAN DECISION What it does ForgeMCP brings three working systems into one visible, auditable workflow: OBSERVE — Terra Observation System A user can select or search for an area of interest and investigate environmental change using public Earth-observation sources. Terra can retrieve location context, bounded research areas, representative satellite imagery, terrain/elevation context, hydrology signals and public hazard observations. Results return structured provenance, timestamps, confidence, uncertainty and a verification state. Terra never presents an AI-generated picture as satellite evidence. Missing or failed provider responses remain INSUFFICIENT_DATA or NOT_CONNECTED . Observations, anomalies, hypotheses, preliminary risk alerts and verified findings are kept separate. A hypothesis is not promoted to a fact without supporting evidence and, where required, field or in-situ verification. LEARN & COMPETE — Cube Chess 512 AI Cube Chess 512 is a deterministic three-dimensional chess laboratory with an 8×8×8 board and 512 addressable fields. ForgeMCP uses a pinned rules engine to execute a small candidate-versus-baseline benchmark with paired seeds and side swaps. The records contain replayable legal moves, results, termination state, legality checks, a deterministic material proxy and engine provenance. The application does not invent Elo ratings, game counts or training results. A candidate cannot be promoted merely because an agent recommends it: legality and regression gates must pass, a recorded result must exist, and literal human approval is required. CREATE — Game and 3D Creation Studio The Game Studio lets a person and agents configure procedural station concepts, generate deterministic low-poly glTF assets and PNG textures, inspect the exact generated geometry, compare visible results, run QA and export a manifest. It also includes a deterministic basic Capture Chess blueprint and a separate link to the playable Cube Chess 512 deployment. Concept artwork is labelled as concept artwork. A generated prototype is not described as manufactured hardware, an original satellite product or a production-ready model. How we built it The public application is built with React, TypeScript, Vite and browser-based 3D rendering. Real tools are registered through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool has a focused responsibility, a validated input schema, structured output, explicit error states and a traceable source or engine boundary. The coordinator is deterministic and does not claim that an LLM ran when it did not. The live tool inventory covers system status, place and AOI handling, Terra observation and verification workflows, the pinned Cube benchmark and promotion gates, visual QA, reversible actions and guarded commerce drafts. Chrome 149+ smoke tests discover and execute the native WebMCP tools in a real browser session instead of mocking document.modelContext . The dashboard exposes the human request, coordinator decision, active specialist, WebMCP tool, validated input, real source or engine, structured output, provenance, confidence, uncertainty, verification result, proposed action and human approval state. The hardest challenges The hardest problem was not adding more AI. It was defining where AI must stop. For Terra, the authority must be the original observation, provider metadata, measurement method and verification record. For Cube, the authority must be the deterministic rules engine, legal execution and saved game result. For mutations, the authority remains the human. A second challenge was integrating two projects that existed before the competition without presenting older work as new. The public repository therefore separates: PRE-CHALLENGE WORK: earlier Terra data integrations, Earth-observation research, Cube rules engine, self-play experiments, 3D models and game UI. NEW WEBMCP CHALLENGE WORK: ForgeMCP coordinator, browser-native tool registration, integrated Terra/Cube/Create workflows, structured provenance, verification timeline, approval gates, public dashboard, judge path and demo. A third challenge was making failures honest and visible. A provider timeout, missing image, unconnected service or unsupported browser must not quietly become a fabricated answer. Accomplishments we are proud of A public working web application with real document.modelContext.registerTool(...) handlers. Fifty registered central tools discoverable through the live capability inventory. Terra workflows grounded in public providers with provenance, uncertainty and strict evidence classes. A pinned deterministic Cube engine that executes the current-run benchmark and rejects illegal promotion paths. Real-browser Chrome 149+ WebMCP smoke testing. Visible PASS / WARNING / FAIL states, audit history, human approval and rollback boundaries. A free judge path with public source code, an open-source license, run instructions and a short demonstration video. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it lets a person and an agent operate a real application together, not when it merely adds another chat box. Small, single-purpose tools are easier to validate and audit than one oversized agent action. Structured results are safer than persuasive prose. Provenance and uncertainty must be visible at the same time as the result. Most importantly, an agent can coordinate and propose, but evidence, deterministic engines and human judgment must remain the final authorities. Why it matters My long-term goal is to use technology to help people and protect the environment. Terra approaches that goal through earlier investigation of water loss, rivers, lakes, terrain and environmental hazards. Cube Chess 512 approaches it through logic, spatial reasoning, competition and learning. The Creation Studio provides a practical space for turning ideas into testable visual systems. ForgeMCP connects those directions around one principle: AI should help humans observe, learn, create and verify — while real evidence and human decisions stay in control. What is next The next steps are to expand the audited Terra tool coverage, strengthen browser and regression testing, connect additional verified data adapters, run larger reproducible Cube candidate evaluations, improve accessibility and mobile performance, and keep every new mutation behind explicit approval, audit logging and rollback. The project will continue separating observations from hypotheses and challenge-period work from earlier research. The aim is not to claim certainty where it does not exist, but to help people reach better, faster and more transparent decisions with real tools. title: Handsfree — one line of WebMCP for voice & gesture
pitch: One script line turns any site's existing frontend into WebMCP tools you can speak to and point at — voice and hand gestures, no LLM in the loop.
about_excerpt: One script line turns any site's existing frontend into WebMCP tools you can speak to and point at — voice and hand gestures, no LLM in the loop. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Handsfree gives any website you can edit voice commands and hand-gesture control on top of WebMCP, with one command to your Claude Code and one <script> line in the page. WebMCP (the W3C Web Machine Learning draft, document.modelContext ) lets a page expose what it can do as tools : named functions with a description and a JSON schema. That is the half meant for agents. Handsfree is the other half, for people: a runtime that reads the same tools and drives them from speech and from a camera, with no LLM in the loop. Inspiration Every "agentic web" demo we saw ended with a chat box. But if a page has already declared its capabilities as tools, the input layer is free to be anything: a microphone, a hand, a floating sentence. We wanted to prove that the tool layer is the real product and the modality is a one-line add-on, and that the honest promise is "one command plus one line", not "one line". How we built it The tool layer. A demo shop ( webmcp-shop-demo.vercel.app ) where every capability is a WebMCP tool: ask , search_products , open_landing_page , focus_product , open_product , buy_now , scroll_page , refine_results , show_brands , browse_all , describe_focused , close_panel , help . The floating input box, the voice layer and the gesture layer are three clients of the same tools; a trace panel shows every call. Data comes from a public MCP catalog server ( search_global_catalog ) through a millisecond local index that the live catalog keeps growing. The Claude Code plugin. A skill that audits a codebase's existing frontend, wires the real actions to registerTool (never synthetic clicks when an API exists), marks one tool as the text-sink , one as scroll , gates money-moving tools with confirm , injects the runtime and verifies in the browser. Plus an idempotent injector CLI and a tool-authoring reference that quotes the draft precisely ( registerTool(tool, {signal, exposedTo}) , getTools , executeTool , toolchange ). The runtime ( handsfree.js , ~50 KB, zero dependencies). Discovers tools through the page's registry, by wrapping registerTool , or via a polyfill. Voice uses the Web Speech API and a rule router: built-in intents, tool phrases, tool names as words, then the text-sink. Gestures use MediaPipe HandLandmarker on-device: the index fingertip is a projected cursor, an air-tap clicks, the outer left/right bands scroll (faster towards the edge), an open-hand wave goes back or forward. Everything is drawn on a dot field that bulges under the cursor; a walkthrough tutorial starts the camera only at its last step. What we learned The current draft has no unregisterTool ; you abort the AbortSignal you registered with. execute gets (input, {signal}) and may return any JSON value. Only readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint are spec annotations, so our handsfree.* hints stay on the page-side registry and are stripped before forwarding to a native implementation. Rules beat models here. With good tool descriptions and phrases, 100% of our test utterances route correctly with zero model calls and zero latency; what a model would add is ambiguity handling, not the happy path. Gesture UX is about resting positions, not gestures: mapping the lower-left / lower-right of the camera frame to the whole screen so the arm can rest low mattered more than any recognizer tuning. Challenges Popups. A gesture or voice action carries no user activation, so window.open is blocked. The runtime navigates the current tab for synthetic clicks and asks the site for an in-page panel; "back" closes it first. Speech engines rewrite you. "landing page for cozy gifts under fifty dollars" arrives as "Landing page 4 cozy gifts under fifty dollars." We undo the common rewrites before matching and strip price phrases into max_price . Embedded browsers report a 0-height viewport , which put our fixed input box off screen; the page now measures the visual viewport and falls back to normal flow. A 12–70 s upstream search cannot sit on the render path, so every view paints from a local index in milliseconds and the live catalog tops it up in the background. Smooth scrolling never progresses in background tabs , which silently broke per-frame gesture scrolling until we forced instant steps. What's next Native document.modelContext on Chrome's origin trial, a real LLM fallback for the long tail of utterances, and a Shopify-theme recipe so the skill can instrument a store in one run. title: Sân Chơi
pitch: AI-hosted Vietnamese folk playground: Ô ăn quan, Bầu cua, Múa rối nước, Gióng's Iron Garage & Rồng rắn lên mây — 5 games, 21 hang-proof WebMCP tools. sanchoi.app
about_excerpt: AI-hosted Vietnamese folk playground: Ô ăn quan, Bầu cua, Múa rối nước, Gióng's Iron Garage & Rồng rắn lên mây — 5 games, 21 hang-proof WebMCP tools. sanchoi.app Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration My 3-year-old nephew loves hearing Vietnamese folk tales and watching water puppet shows during Tết. But these centuries-old traditions — Ô ăn quan (Mancala), Múa rối nước (water puppet theatre), Rồng rắn lên mây (dragon snake chase), Bầu cua tôm cá (Lunar New Year dice), and the legend of Thánh Gióng riding an iron horse — are vanishing from children's daily lives. I wanted to build a digital "sân chơi" (playground) where an AI agent acts as the Game Master (Người Xướng Trò), hosting these folk games for kids, in Vietnamese, with full cultural authenticity. The OpenAI WebMCP Challenge was the perfect catalyst: what if the AI doesn't just talk about folk games, but actually runs them — managing game boards, rolling dice, directing puppet shows, chanting call-and-response, and feeding Gióng's iron horse? How I built it Tech stack: Vite + TypeScript, Three.js (3D water puppet stage), GSAP (animations), Web Audio API (synthesized Đàn Bầu, festive drums, gongs), zero backend — fully client-side with localStorage persistence. Architecture: Each game follows a strict split: rules.ts (pure deterministic game logic, no DOM) and scene.ts (Three.js/GSAP visuals). Agent tools live in tools.ts and call rules directly, returning JSON state instantly — animations fire as fire-and-forget side effects. The WebMCP integration registers 32 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool following the standard JSON Schema spec with inputSchema , annotations, and AbortController -based cleanup. A fallback mode exposes tools at window.__debugTools for DevTools testing outside ChatGPT. For audio, I synthesized traditional folk instrument sounds using the Web Audio API — no external audio files needed for the core experience, just procedural Đàn Bầu melodies and percussion. Challenges 1. The hang bug. The first version of Ô ăn quan awaited GSAP animations inside agent tool handlers. In headless/backgrounded browser contexts, requestAnimationFrame is throttled, so the agent hung forever waiting for an animation that never fires. The fix: agent-facing tools ( isAgent: true ) return game state immediately; animations run as void animate().catch(...) fire-and-forget promises. This pattern was then retrofitted to all 5 games. 2. Bầu cua's async dice. The dice-roll scene awaited animateDiceRoll before resolving bets. Same class of hang. Refactored to split roll logic from animation, applied the fire-and-forget pattern. 3. Zero-backend persistence. With no server, game state survives refreshes through localStorage — but only the last active game is saved. I built a save_progress tool and a "flustered game master" easter egg: if the agent does 5+ actions without saving, Chú Tễu pops up with "Người xướng trò bị rối!" (The Game Master is flustered!). 4. Cultural authenticity in code. Every game had to feel Vietnamese , not just reskinned Western games. Ô ăn quan uses relay-sowing rules unique to Vietnam (when your last seed lands in a small pit with >1 seed, you scoop and keep sowing). Water puppetry required understanding the 11th-century thủy đình stage and iconic tales like Cóc kiện trời (The Toad Sued Heaven). Gióng's Iron Garage is rooted in the legend of Thánh Gióng — a folk hero who grew instantly, rode an iron horse, and defeated invaders. What I learned Building agent-native web apps requires a fundamentally different mental model from human-facing UIs. The agent needs instant, structured feedback — it can't "see" animations. This means: Game logic must be pure and synchronous. The DOM is for humans; JSON is for agents. Tool descriptions must be precise enough for an LLM to understand the game's mechanics and cultural context without ever seeing the screen. Easter eggs and "funny hooks" keep the experience playful even when the agent is driving: zero-capture moves in Ô ăn quan make the pit shake indignantly, matching dice in Bầu cua trigger a "XỐC! BA CON!" celebration, and the water puppet applause meter rewards dramatic timing. The result is a new kind of interactive cultural preservation — not a video about Vietnamese folk games, but an AI that can host them. title: TimeTrail
pitch: Create interactive hypermedia films with an agent, not just AI-generated video.
about_excerpt: Create interactive hypermedia films with an agent, not just AI-generated video. Like Comment Story Updates Time Trail Editor Inspiration TimeTrail is a browser-local interactive film studio where WebMCP agents can build and edit structured timelines, media, chapters, cards, annotations, quizzes, and branches while the human remains in control of the project. Agent changes remain editable and can be reviewed before becoming part of the approved timeline. AI can generate text, images, audio, and video remarkably quickly. But many creative AI workflows end with a problem: The AI generates the artifact, and then the user loses structured control over it. I wanted to explore a different model. Instead of having an agent return a finished interactive video, what if the application exposed the actual editing primitives to the agent? That would let AI accelerate creation while preserving the normal editing workflow. That idea became TimeTrail. What I Built TimeTrail is a browser-local studio for building interactive films and hypermedia experiences. Projects can contain: Video clips Images Generated cards Chapters Timed context Sources Captions Hotspots Quizzes Branches Maps Charts Checklists Persistent information panels Multiple screens Different player layouts The application includes a dedicated Studio for creation and a dedicated Player for experiencing the final project. Projects remain structured and editable instead of becoming a single opaque generated file. How WebMCP Is Used TimeTrail exposes creative editing operations through WebMCP. Agents can help: Create projects Create screens Build storyboards Add clips Add generated cards Add chapters Add annotations Add quizzes Add conditional branches Edit timing Update cues Search for usable media Populate project metadata Inspect the timeline Review a project Prepare corrections Control supported playback workflows This means a user can begin broadly: Create an interactive Apollo 11 experience. Then refine precisely: Find the Moon landing section and add a fact card explaining the Lunar Module. The agent operates on the existing structured project instead of regenerating the entire experience. Human + Agent Collaboration I did not want the agent to silently rewrite a creative project. TimeTrail therefore includes a proposal workflow. Agent-created changes can be assembled as a proposed revision. The user can inspect the changes before accepting them into the approved project. That creates a workflow where the agent can move quickly without removing human creative control. The person remains the editor. The agent becomes a collaborator capable of performing large amounts of structured editing work. How I Built It TimeTrail uses Vue, Pinia, Vue Router, IndexedDB, OPFS where available, Zod, WebMCP, and FrameTrail. FrameTrail provides part of the interactive playback foundation and runs in a same-origin integration. TimeTrail converts its own structured project data into compatible resources and annotations for the player. Projects, revisions, proposals, and most metadata stay browser-local. Local asset bytes can use OPFS with IndexedDB fallback. TimeTrail can also work with imported: Video Audio Images PDFs VTT captions SRT captions Existing TimeTrail projects Supported FrameTrail project data It can search sources such as NASA and Wikimedia Commons and retain attribution and source information. Projects can be exported in several forms, including structured project files and portable interactive experiences. Challenges I Faced The most difficult problem was giving an agent significant creative power without turning the application into a one-shot generator. That led to the proposal and approval model. Another challenge was coordinating browser-local media, playback state, portable project formats, timelines, annotations, and provenance without requiring a backend. Integrating an existing open-source hypervideo system while keeping the TimeTrail domain model clean was another significant architectural challenge. What I Learned The project reinforced that WebMCP is not limited to transactional workflows. It can also become an interface for structured creative software. Once an editor has clear domain operations, the same primitives can support: normal UI interactions WebMCP testing undo/redo validation documentation The result is much more controllable than one-shot AI generation. What's Next I would like to extend TimeTrail with additional media services, richer generation pipelines, more interactive component types, collaborative sharing, and more sophisticated agent-assisted editing. The long-term goal is a creative workspace where people can move fluidly between: "Build this for me" and "Change exactly this one thing." title: tobidas
pitch: Pop-up book-style web builder
about_excerpt: Pop-up book-style web builder Like Comment Story Updates tobidas — Pop-up book-style web builder GIF Exports a single HTML file containing asset images, audio, and video. Production is possible while switching between the editing and playback screens. It is not limited to works for children; free expression is possible. Inspiration Advancements in AI technology have made it possible to create increasingly complex and beautiful graphics. I realized that I could finally bring to life the kind of pop-up book visuals I had loved since childhood. Excited by the prospect of creating something even more imaginative and fantastical than the pop-up books I used to craft from calendar cardboard as a child, I decided to give it a try right away. What it does Tobidas is a web page builder inspired by pop-up books. Tobidas means "pop-up" in Japanese. It allows users to create web pages with a pop-up book aesthetic, combining visual elements with images, audio, and video. Projects can be exported as a single, self-contained HTML file containing all necessary image, audio, and video assets. How I built it I built tobidas as an online, browser-based builder that keeps project data and imported media in the user’s browser instead of uploading them to a server. I used React, TypeScript, and React Three Fiber to create the interactive 3D pop-up book canvas. Book projects are represented as structured data containing spreads, pages, elements, assets, timelines, and camera settings. For WebMCP, I register structured tools when the browser exposes document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext . These tools can read project state, inspect spreads and assets, place and edit elements, update timelines and cameras, assign audio, navigate between spreads, and use undo/redo. I designed the standard builder UI and WebMCP to use the same state-management, validation, and command paths. This allows people and agents to work on the same project with the same behavior, undo history, and autosave system. WebMCP does not directly modify the DOM or bypass the builder. I included the player used to preview and export finished works in the public build, which I deployed as a static application on Cloudflare Workers. Challenges I ran into I was committed to maintaining a "static delivery model" where the user-side agent could build the project directly within the browser. My goal was to enable sophisticated visual expression via a single URL, without requiring users to clone the Tobidas repository. One of my biggest challenges was figuring out how to provide the fine-grained controls required by the builder while keeping this model intact. Relying solely on direct DOM manipulation made agent interactions unstable and often resulted in long wait times and unreliable operations. Furthermore, previous implementations that used a dedicated DOM manipulation interface for AI—in addition to the standard human-facing interface—created a maintenance burden due to the need to manage two separate systems. Accomplishments that I'm proud of By integrating WebMCP, I was able to provide agents with highly reproducible and reliable control capabilities without significantly altering the human-facing UI. The dedicated AI DOM manipulation interface was completely eliminated, allowing the human UI to serve seamlessly for collaboration with agents. In short, this realized a production experience where agents handle complex operations—maintaining a high degree of creative freedom—while humans can intervene as needed via the UI for detailed visual checks and fine-tuning. Furthermore, the WebMCP tool list doubles as a feature catalog for "Tobidas." This has improved both explainability and maintainability, enabling agents and developers to understand the application's capabilities without relying solely on visual UI information. What I learned While AI and other tools can greatly enhance creativity, they aren't a cure-all. Although WebMCP was incredibly powerful and contributed to the evolution of tobidas , I also encountered areas within the ecosystem ripe for improvement, such as browser compatibility issues and varying levels of support across different agents. In an era where almost anything can be created, I have come to realize that the most critical decision for a developer is to constantly think for themselves: what to prioritize, what to express, and how to compete using the resources currently at hand. What's next for tobidas There is still plenty of room to expand the expressive capabilities of tobidas . I also found that a single prompt to an agent is often not enough to produce a truly satisfying result. I will continue exploring new interaction designs and integrations with external tools, with the goal of enabling people and agents to create higher-quality work with fewer instructions. title: AI Watermelon Smash
pitch: A co-op browser game where the human has the eyes and the blindfolded AI has the body. WebMCP lets the AI move, listen, decide whom to trust, and smash the watermelon.
about_excerpt: A co-op browser game where the human has the eyes and the blindfolded AI has the body. WebMCP lets the AI move, listen, decide whom to trust, and smash the watermelon. Like Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Most AI interfaces are still built around the same pattern: a human asks, and an AI answers. I wanted to explore a different relationship. What if the human and the AI shared the same visual world, but each had different abilities? What if the AI was not an assistant, NPC, or game master, but an actual player? That idea became AI Watermelon Smash . The human can see the beach, obstacles, and watermelon. The AI character is blindfolded, but WebMCP gives it a body inside the browser. The human has the eyes. The AI has the body. Neither can win alone. What it does AI Watermelon Smash is an asymmetric Human + AI co-op browser game. The AI can use five WebMCP Site tools: turn(degrees) for orientation walk(distance) for movement swing() for its arm get_self_status() for proprioception listen_to_guides() for social perception The tools intentionally do not provide the watermelon coordinates, target direction, obstacle map, shortest path, or which guide is correct. Instead, humans give natural-language guidance such as: “A little to the right.” “Careful, there is a rock.” “Now swing!” The AI decides how to act. Guide Chorus adds another layer: three human voices, A, B, and C, can give conflicting advice. Their messages are returned to the AI only as unverified testimony. A collision can become evidence. A previously reliable guide can become suspicious. The AI can change whom it trusts, ask for clearer information, take a cautious step, or choose to swing. The design principle became: Physical clarity, social ambiguity. How I built it The game is built with TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, DOM UI, and the imperative WebMCP API using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The gameplay simulation is kept separate from Three.js. GameState owns the actual gameplay state, while SceneView is only the visual representation. WebMCP tools call the same Game API used by the debug controls, so there is no separate agent-only version of the game. Guide Chorus uses a bounded message store. listen_to_guides() is read-only and returns recent A/B/C statements with sequence information. Tool outputs are intentionally minimized for the blindfolded role. They do not expose target coordinates, target direction, target distance, obstacle truth, guide truth labels, or route hints. The final game is deployed as static assets on Cloudflare Workers. Challenges The hardest problem was not implementing movement. It was deciding what the AI should and should not know. If the tools revealed too much, the AI could simply solve the board. If the controls were intentionally confusing, the difficulty felt artificial. That led to an important rule: Make the body clear. Make the information uncertain. I fixed the character's facing direction and swing so physical actions were unambiguous. Then I moved the uncertainty into human guidance. Another challenge appeared during playtesting: with only one helpful human, the AI could start to feel like a natural-language remote-controlled character. Guide Chorus changed that. Once humans could disagree, the AI had to make meaningful decisions about trust rather than simply execute commands. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The most exciting moment came during a real ChatGPT playtest. The AI followed advice that had previously been safe, collided with an obstacle, and then changed how much it trusted that guide. Later, it rejected suspicious guidance, switched between different guides, followed a concrete final instruction, and successfully smashed the watermelon. The final result was: “Direct hit! We smashed the watermelon together.” At that point, WebMCP was no longer just controlling a character. It was giving the AI experiences that affected later decisions. What I learned I expected the interesting uncertainty to be spatial: “Where is the watermelon?” Instead, the more interesting question became social: “Which human should I believe?” A collision is not just collision feedback. It can become evidence about a person's advice. That suggested a broader possibility for WebMCP: Web tools can represent an agent's body and senses, not just functions for completing tasks. The most interesting interaction appeared when the AI started asking humans to describe directions relative to its own current heading. The human had visual information. The AI had body-state information. They had to exchange both to coordinate. What's next A future version could connect several real human devices instead of entering A/B/C messages on one screen. Each human could have a different viewpoint, imperfect information, or different incentives. Lying could be possible without requiring a fixed “traitor” role. The AI would become an embodied participant inside a small human social system. The larger idea I want to explore is simple: We are not adding AI to a game. We are designing games for humans and AI to play together.
