title: GeneVault- AI check DNA File without ever seeing it
pitch: GeneVault uses zero-knowledge Groth16 zk-SNARKs to prove genetic drug contraindications in-browser. Clinical safety for AI agents, zero exposure for your raw DNA.
about_excerpt: GeneVault uses zero-knowledge Groth16 zk-SNARKs to prove genetic drug contraindications in-browser. Clinical safety for AI agents, zero exposure for your raw DNA. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Imagine an AI medical assistant wants to prescribe you a common blood thinner — Plavix. But for about 30% of people, genetics prevent the drug from working, which can lead to fatal blood clots. So the AI asks: "Just upload your full DNA sequence so I can check." And there's the trap. You should never paste your private genetic code into an AI model or a cloud server — once your DNA leaks, it's leaked forever. You can change a stolen password; you cannot change your genome. We started GeneVault the moment we realized the technology to break this deadlock already existed in the browser. WebMCP lets a website advertise real, callable tools to any AI agent. Zero-knowledge proofs let you prove a statement about secret data without revealing the data. Put them together and the answer to "upload your DNA" becomes: "No — but I'll prove the conclusion to you mathematically, right here on my device." That reframing — the browser as the trust boundary between a patient and any AI model — is the entire project. And here is the part that keeps us up at night (in a good way): this deadlock is not a medical problem. It is the structural problem of the AI era. An AI HR tool that wants your therapy history. A tax agent that wants your bank statements. A hiring agent that wants your face. In every case the model's context window is treated as the place where private data goes to be processed — and leaked. GeneVault is our answer, demonstrated end-to-end on the highest-stakes dataset we could find: the human genome. If the pattern survives DNA, it survives anywhere. What it does GeneVault turns a browser tab into a privacy-hardened pharmacogenomics workstation that any WebMCP-capable AI agent can operate — without ever receiving a single letter of DNA. Parses real raw genetic files fully client-side. Drop in a 23andMe / AncestryDNA / VCF export and GeneVault scans 643,000+ positions in a single pass, entirely in local memory. Nothing is uploaded — there is no server to upload to . Advertises 12 live tools to any AI agent through document.modelContext.registerTool — file parsing, marker listing, drug-safety checks, alternative-therapy recommendations, proof generation/verification, and even 3D protein manipulation. The agent discovers them on its own; we never prompt-inject instructions. Answers the question that matters: "Can I safely take this drug?" — for CPIC Level A pairs like Plavix/CYP2C19, Warfarin/CYP2C9+VKORC1, Simvastatin/SLCO1B1, Codeine/CYP2D6, 5-FU/DPYD, Abacavir/HLA-B and more. Backs every risky verdict with a real Groth16 zero-knowledge proof generated on-device in ~4.4 seconds. The agent receives a verified pass/fail — not your genotype. Keeps the human in charge. Every tool call from an external agent hits a consent gate (Allow once / Allow all session / Deny). Deny returns denied_by_patient and nothing is released. Every call lands in an on-page audit ledger. Visualizes the science. A built-in 3D viewer loads real protein structures (e.g. CYP2C19, PDB 4GQS). Every safety verdict now auto-renders its target enzyme in the viewport — and the agent can dock a drug into the catalytic pocket, zoom, highlight, and pin clinical annotations — live, from a chat prompt. The bigger picture: a pattern, not just a product. Everything above is shipped and working for pharmacogenomics — but the architecture itself is domain-agnostic by construction, and it has exactly three reusable layers: The tool boundary (WebMCP). The website advertises capabilities to any agent via document.modelContext.registerTool ; the agent never gets raw data access, only tool calls with typed schemas. The consent gate (human-in-the-loop). Every tool execution passes through a human decision point that cannot be prompt-injected around, with machine-readable denial ( denied_by_patient ). The zero-knowledge release. Verdicts leave the device only as Groth16 proofs — mathematical conclusions with zero source data. Swap "genome" for credentials, finances, or imaging and the same three layers hold. The genome demo is our proof that the pattern is real, not theoretical. How we built it The WebMCP layer. Each capability is registered in the standard form — document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) — and verified via getTools() with AbortController cleanup. Tool descriptions are written for agents , not humans: the discovery quality of the demo comes entirely from those description strings. For non-WebMCP browsers we ship an honestly-labeled local fallback, so judges on any browser still see the full pipeline. The zero-knowledge layer. The core claim — "this patient's CYP2C19 diplotype belongs to the poor-metabolizer set" — is compiled into a Circom circuit (8,845 constraints on the bn128 curve): Poseidon-hashed Merkle membership with depth $k = 16$, an EdDSA curator signature, and a single-use nullifier, all verified inside the SNARK: $$ \text{Verify}_{vk}(\pi_a, \pi_b, \pi_c;\; \text{root},\, \text{claim},\, \text{nullifier}) \Rightarrow 1 $$ Secrets are derived at parse time from the patient's actual file — never hardcoded: $$ s = \text{sha256}(\text{gene} \,|\, \text{genotypes} \,|\, \text{salt}) $$ $$ \text{nullifier} = \text{Poseidon}(s, \text{nonce}) $$ The nullifier makes every proof single-use, so a leaked proof can't be replayed by an attacker — double-spend protection, but for DNA claims. Groth16 proving runs in-browser via snarkjs (~4.4 s for witness + proof). Because witnesses are generated from the real file, a false phenotype fails witness generation — we ship a "Forgery Audit" button so anyone can watch the circuit refuse a forged claim in real time. The trust UX. A consent wrapper intercepts every execute() . External agent calls block until a human decides; the 3D viewport, HUD, and audit ledger visualize what the agent is doing as it does it. One click runs a built-in "Full Agent Demo" where the AI self-asks six questions and executes the full pipeline — our insurance policy for any demo environment. Challenges we ran into Two parse paths, one engine. Our file-upload and inline-text parsers initially kept separate state, so the ZK engine would report "not ready" after one path but not the other. We only caught it through end-to-end agent testing — the fix was unifying both paths into a single claim-tree build. Lesson: in agent-driven apps, every entry point must reach the same invariants. Making Groth16 feel instant. A ~4.4-second proving pause is an eternity in a demo. We restructured the UI so the wait is part of the show — the HUD narrates witness generation, proving, and verification step by step, turning dead time into credibility. Blocking an agent with a human. Agents expect fast async answers; our consent gate intentionally makes them wait for a human click. Wiring that without deadlocking the tool promise — and returning a machine-readable denied_by_patient the agent can respect — took several iterations. The honesty tax. SNP arrays can't see CYP2D6 copy-number variants, HLA alleles beyond our panel, or UGT1A1. We could have hidden those gaps; instead every limitation is stated in-UI, in tool responses, and in the README. It cost us "it does everything" bravado and bought us something better: judges believing everything else we claim. Accomplishments that we're proud of Nothing is mocked. Real Groth16 proofs, independent on-device verification, replay rejection, forged-claim rejection — all running in a browser tab with zero backend. Our automated suite passes 32/32 end-to-end (parse → phenotype → secrets → Merkle trees → prove → verify → replay-reject → forgery-reject). A real agent really did it. In our final integration test, a WebMCP-connected AI discovered all tools unprompted and executed the full chain — parse a genuine 643,163-position genome, assess Plavix, recommend an alternative, generate and verify a Groth16 proof — without ever receiving the genome. We made refusal a feature. Watching the circuit reject a forged phenotype, or an agent accept denied_by_patient , communicates our values better than any slide. What we learned With WebMCP, descriptions are the API. Agents choose tools based almost entirely on description quality. Writing for the model — not the user — was the highest-leverage engineering we did. Client-side ZK is production-plausible today. Seconds, not minutes, on commodity laptops, with snarkjs and careful circuit design. The "too slow for the browser" excuse expired. Policy belongs at the tool boundary, not the prompt. Prompt-level safety evaporates with a clever prompt; a consent gate inside execute() cannot be talked around. This, we think, is a pattern every WebMCP app should copy. Design for the agent's blind spots. In one real integration session an agent did everything we asked

title: Chip
pitch: Talk directly to your hardware. Chip links AI models straight to physical microcontrollers through browser-based Web Serial APIs for instant flashing.
about_excerpt: Talk directly to your hardware. Chip links AI models straight to physical microcontrollers through browser-based Web Serial APIs for instant flashing. Like 5 Comment Story Updates 1 Dashboard page: Connect microcontroller, view live firmware flashing Setting: See all available Webmcp tools and also copy Setup: Copy agent prompt / Live url or Setup Standard MPC Inspiration Building hardware with AI still has a missing link. An agent can write firmware, explain wiring, and debug errors, but the real ESP32 is sitting on the user’s desk, connected by USB to an IDE. Chip was inspired by that gap: how do we let an AI assistant move beyond “here is some code” and actually help with the real compile, flash, and debug loop? ESP32 development is powerful, but the beginner experience is long and requires process. Users often need an IDE, board drivers, local toolchains, flashing commands, serial monitors, and a lot of context just to blink an LED. Chip asks a simpler question: what if the user could plug in a board, open a dashboard, and let an AI agent guide the rest? What it does Chip connects AI agents directly to live ESP32 hardware through a browser dashboard. The user plugs in an ESP32, grants browser USB access through Web Serial, and Chip becomes the bridge between the agent and the physical board. Chip uses two kinds of MCP-style integration: Standard MCP connects the AI agent to the cloud/backend side of the system. Through the standard MCP server, the agent can work with higher-level project tasks like compiling firmware, starting flash jobs, checking job status, and coordinating the build pipeline. WebMCP connects the AI agent to the live browser session. This is the unique part: the browser actually has access to the USB-connected ESP32. Chip exposes browser-side WebMCP tools such as list_devices , get_board_status , read_serial_logs , read_job_status , read_dashboard_state , post_agent_message , set_agent_note , request_user_action , and erase_board . Beyond firmware, Chip includes Circuit Studio, allowing the AI agent to visually design, inspect, and modify hardware circuits directly on an interactive canvas. Through WebMCP and backend SKiDL integration, the agent searches real KiCad symbols on demand, inspects pinouts, places components like microcontrollers, passives, and sensors, wires nets, and runs Electrical Rules Checking to keep the schematic valid across versions. Together, Standard MCP handles cloud-side intelligence and workflow, while WebMCP gives the agent eyes and hands inside the browser session that is physically connected to the board. How we built it Chip is built as a three-part system: a React/Vite client dashboard, a backend service for compile, relay, and circuit synthesis workflows, and a standard MCP server for AI tool access. The client dashboard uses Web Serial and esptool-js to communicate with the ESP32 over USB. This is important because cloud servers cannot access a USB cable plugged into the user’s laptop. The browser owns the physical connection, so the browser performs board operations like flashing and erasing. On top of that, the client registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . These tools expose live browser state to the agent: connected devices, board status, serial logs, dashboard state, active jobs, and user-visible messages. The agent can also post notes into the dashboard and request physical actions from the user, like connecting the board or pressing reset. The result is a loop where the AI agent can reason, the backend can build, and the browser can safely touch the real hardware. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was the physical boundary between cloud AI and local hardware. An AI agent running in the cloud cannot directly access an ESP32 plugged into a user’s computer. Browser security also correctly prevents silent USB access, so the user must grant Web Serial permission. AI cannot directly generate a binary file accessible by Microcontrollers. That forced a better architecture: the backend should not pretend to flash the board. Instead, Chip makes the browser the active hardware bridge. The cloud compiles and coordinates, but the browser performs the physical write. Another challenge was separating Standard MCP and WebMCP cleanly. Standard MCP is useful for cloud/backend tools, while WebMCP is useful for live browser state and hardware access. Chip uses both instead of forcing one protocol to do everything. Handling schematic generation also required solving symbol storage constraints. Bundling full KiCad symbol libraries into production containers is heavy, so we built an on demand symbol loader using Cloudflare R2 to stream lightweight part definitions during synthesis without bloating backend storage. We also had to think carefully about destructive actions. Erasing a board is powerful, so the WebMCP erase_board tool checks for a connected board and is described as something that should only happen after the user clearly asks for it. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Chip is not just an AI code-generation demo. It creates a real bridge between an AI agent, a browser, and physical microcontroller hardware. The WebMCP implementation is especially important. The client exposes browser-side tools that let an agent inspect live board state, read serial logs, understand job progress, post messages into the UI, save guidance notes, request user actions, and erase the connected ESP32 when appropriate. We are also proud of the architecture split. Standard MCP handles the cloud workflow. WebMCP handles live browser interaction. Web Serial handles the actual USB connection. Each part does what it is naturally good at. The result is a more believable path toward AI-assisted hardware development: not just “copy this code into Arduino IDE,” but “connect your board and let the agent help you iterate.” What we learned We learned that connecting AI to hardware is less about making the model powerful and more about designing the right bridge between digital reasoning and physical constraints. The key insight was that the browser is not just a frontend. In Chip, the browser is the hardware runtime. It holds the USB permission, talks to the board, streams logs, flashes binaries, and exposes that live state back to the agent through WebMCP. We also learned that Standard MCP and WebMCP solve different problems. Standard MCP is great for remote services, build systems, and backend workflows. WebMCP is powerful when the agent needs to interact with the user’s live browser context, especially when that browser has access to local capabilities the cloud does not. What's next for Chip Next, we want to make the full agent-to-hardware loop smoother: ask for a firmware change, compile it, flash it, read the serial output, and let the agent debug the result automatically. We want to link Circuit Studio schematics directly to code generation, automatically assigning firmware pin definitions based on the visual wiring. We also want to improve safety and trust around hardware actions, especially destructive actions like erasing flash. Clear user confirmation, better action history, and stronger board/session pairing will make the system safer. Future work includes richer serial-log analysis, support for more boards, PCB layout export, saved project history, and a cleaner demo path for WebMCP-capable browsers. Long term, Chip could become a general bridge between AI agents and physical computing: a way for students, makers, and hardware teams to build with real devices using natural language, while still respecting the security boundaries of the browser and the real world. title: Fangorn.tv
pitch: Own your algorithm
about_excerpt: Own your algorithm Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration In 2020, NBC's Peacock officially launched and pulled the license for "The Office" from Netflix. I was bothered; another gatekeeper forcing yet another SaaS subscription to consume a single series could not be justified. Growing up with services like Limewire, this felt like a massive degradation in user experience. While the technology for distributing media has become more powerful, the consumer experience seems to be converging to the worst parts of cable TV again: fragmented catalogs behind increasingly costly paywalls, centralized recommendation systems, the reintroduction of advertisements, and increasingly little control over what you consume and how you discover it. This led to a multi-year journey into the depths of cryptography, storage, search, discovery, payment, privacy, and the many failed iterations of a sovereign, semantic web, in an effort to understand the economic and social factors that arise to bring us "Streaming services that are just TV again". Fangorn TV is an experiment of what it might look like if media curation, synthesis, and recommendation were designed for both humans and agents from the beginning. What it does Fangorn.TV is an agentic media platform that lives in the browser. It is a static site that exposes its own semantic dataset to agents through WebMCP. The key idea is that the site itself is the agent's data source, that the semantic index and media operations are exposed directly to an agent with WebMCP. Seeded from a slice of the Internet Archive, it holds ~20k titles to choose from. It has no ads, no login, and collects no user data whatsoever. For a human ( without an agent ), it lets you "own your algorithm": Maintain Client Privacy: privately search the archive by semantic meaning (e.g. "cats") entirely in the browser. Queries never get broadcast to a third party, your behavioral data remains yours. treat the internet archive as live TV channels that can be synced across viewers (i.e. watch with your friends), even building your own custom channels based on meaning Since all data in Fangorn.TV is a vector embedding, users can use ("train") a Markov kernel (over the embedding space) built on their actual behavior, providing newer ways to 'be your own discovery algorithm' Using WebMCP tools and an autonomous agent (like Claude Code): Agentic Media Curation: An agent can control playback based on your actual intent and preference, further amplifying the "own your own algorithm" capabilities. An LLM can be prompted to "Find that one episode of XYZ where THINGS happens", or "Create a new channel that only has shows and movies about dogs" and watch as it produces Dog TV in the browser. Byte-Level Range Requests: Agents can efficiently discover granularly labeled content and extract exact video slices directly using HTTP Range headers instead of downloading gigabytes of raw source files (e.g. efficient GIF extraction from media playing in the browser). Programmatic Media Synthesis: Allows an agent to efficiently synthesize disparate archival footage, builds seamless audio beds, applies dynamic text overlays, and executes frame-accurate FFmpeg cuts to produce polished short documentaries, GIFs, and audio clips. Zero DOM Scraping: Eliminates fragile HTML parsing, selector guessing, and simulated UI clicks. The agent interacts purely through typed, deterministic tool interfaces. Zero-Telemetry Local Discovery: Queries are resolved instantly against client-side vector bundles. The agent receives exact media segment URLs, transcript timestamps, and metadata in milliseconds—running search entirely on the client without exposing behavioral data to external backends. Beyond these immediate capabilities, Fangorn.TV does something less noticeable. It presents a reusable pattern for deploying static sites that simultaneously act as rich, agent-ready datasets with incredibly low overhead both in terms of storage, cost, and bandwidth. The same pattern can be applied to nearly any dataset. How we built it Fangorn.TV existed before we entered the hackathon, but without WebMCP integration. The majority of work during this hackathon involved both WebMCP integration and associated agentic tooling and testing. The application is built using the Fangorn SDK , a "git for knowledge graphs" protocol anchored to Arbitrum and backed by IPFS. We crawled the Internet Archive's Video and TV catalog, cross-referencing entries with wikidata and attempting to filter out content that either lewd/illicit/obscene, deemed low quality, or non-CC0/PD. We used the metadata to build a knowledge graph, organizing content hierarchically (e.g. title > series) and committing it onchain using Fangorn. Then, we run a multimodal feature extraction pipeline (developed during the hackathon in order to enhance the semantic richness of the embeddings), extracting timestamped subtitles using whisper and summarized video features using granite. This enriched data is then used to extend the KG that was committed to previously, adding new vertices and edges to map media to its extracted features. With the time available, we were able to execute this on roughly ~250 videos (using an RTX 3050/i9 - estimates indicate ~21 days for the entire catalog). The graph committed in Fangorn is then used to build vector embeddings (using Qdrant), where we leverage int8 scalar quantization to minimize the memory impact of the set of embeddings, make it small enough to efficiently live within a statically hosted Vite site. This site is deployed as a page on cloudflare, https://tv.fangorn.network , where WebMCP integration makes the bundled embeddings easily queryable by an agent. Challenges we ran into Restricting to Open/Public Domain Content: Navigating copyright boundaries requires strict filtering for CC0 and public domain assets. While we made a best effort to limit this, some content still made it through our filters. - Rich Semantic Embeddings Under Constraints: As mentioned above, our pipeline first extracts subtitles and video features, then builds a graph, and then on top of this embeddings. Due to computational and temporal constraints, we have only produced rich embeddings (i.e. including subtitles + features) on roughly 1.5% of the available catalog (so far). Accomplishments that we're proud of Autonomous Documentary: We used WebMCP to generate multiple 'documentaries' composed full of real archival footage. Zero telemetry RAG: Achieved fully private, semantic vector search running 100% inside the user's browser runtime through WebMCP. Massive bandwidth reduction: reduced data transfer by over 90% using HTTP range requests instead of pulling raw video files into an editor. What we learned Static sites can act as agentic backends : Instead of running a bespoke MCP server in order to make these embeddings available, we only need a static page deployed (e.g. on cloudflare), incurring virtually zero cost. By shipping quantized embeddings (built on top of a structured KG) and WebMCP, it becomes possible to turn a static webpage into a rich database that agents can natively query and leverage. The operational cost collapses to near zero. Efficient web tools can be used to optimize agentic compute : By using HTTP range requests and fine-grained timestamping (on the vids with enriched feature extraction), agents don't need local copies of massive datasets, instead benefiting from byte-level retrieval. A missing consumer class emerges : The Semantic Web of the early 2000s failed because there were no entities that needed to navigate RDF graphs. AI agents are the missing consumer that makes structured semantic data viable and necessary. What's next for Fangorn.tv While we used video streaming here, Fangorn TV is only a media-focused proof-of-concept for a broader architectural paradigm. The underlying pattern, where we leverage version controlled graphs, quantized vector embeddings, and client-side WebMCP interfaces, generalized to any dataset or web application. It fundamentally redefines how static web pages can host and serve data for both humans and agents. Generalizing Beyond Video By making the architecture reusable, we can allow developers to ship static, zero-latency, privacy preserving, agent-native applications across nearly any domain. For example: Private E-Commerce : Users and their agents can search and purchase items (using x402f - our x402-based private paymaster scheme using Semaphore) without sending query intent, browsing history, or shopping telemtry to centralized trackers. title: WallAlive
pitch: What if a child’s wall drawing could start moving and become part of a story? Kids can play and create stories together, then make their favorite creations into real keepsakes through Shopify
about_excerpt: What if a child’s wall drawing could start moving and become part of a story? Kids can play and create stories together, then make their favorite creations into real keepsakes through Shopify Like Comment Story Updates drawing webmcp agents web room changing draw together make an invite draw together Inspiration My eight years old daughter loves drawing everywhere. on paper, on the wall, and on her iPad. I love seeing her imagination, but like many parents, I also worry about how much time children spend only looking at screens. I started wondering what if screen time could begin with something a child created with their own hands? What if their drawing could leave the paper, become a character, and continue its story in a 3D world? That question became WallAlive. What it does WallAlive turns a child’s drawing into a movable 3D character. A child can draw inside the app or photograph a paper drawing. WallAlive separates the character from the background, detects its visible parts, builds a movable rig, and places it inside an interactive, storybook, wizard, or museum world. Children can paint the 3D character with brushes, spray paint, oil paint, and colorful splashes. They can make it walk, dance, wave, and join stories with characters created by friends. A browser agent can help plan stories, suggest painting activities, inspect what each character can do, and prepare a creator collection. Children still control the creative actions, and an adult must approve any Shopify product draft. drawing 3d model How we built it I used several small on-device computer-vision models for drawing isolation, face and body-part detection, pose estimation, and character topology. Three.js renders the characters, animations, paint effects, and interactive 3D worlds. WebMCP gives the browser agent structured tools for understanding the current scene and helping with the next step. The available tools change according to what the user is doing, such as drawing, checking the character, painting, storytelling, collaborating, or preparing a Shopify product. This makes the agent more reliable than asking it to understand the interface by guessing. Shopify’s API is used to read the connected catalog and create an unpublished product draft from approved artwork. Vercel hosts the public application, while Cloudflare D1 supports shared drawing rooms. I used Codex during development and gstack by Garry Tan to challenge the idea, review the experience, test the implementation, and find weak points. Challenges we ran into Turning a paper drawing into a believable 3D character was the hardest technical challenge. Real photographs contain paper edges, shadows, grid lines, handwriting, nearby objects, and sometimes several characters. Children also draw bodies in many different ways, so one fixed skeleton cannot work for every drawing. A single image does not show the back of a character either. I had to combine segmentation, pose estimation, learned topology, depth reconstruction, and a human review step instead of pretending every result would always be perfect. I also worried about whether WallAlive would be genuinely useful or only an interesting hackathon demo. I kept asking myself whether it solved a real problem and whether it was truly a good fit for WebMCP. Testing it with my daughter helped me find the answer that the value is not simply converting an image into 3D. It is helping a child continue creating, storytelling, collaborating, and learning from something they made themselves. Another challenge was using WebMCP meaningfully. At first, the app exposed too many tools and expected technical inputs. I changed it so the agent sees only the tools relevant to the child’s current activity and accepts natural requests such as “make a short wizard story” or “paint it with blue spray.” shop webmcp Accomplishments that we're proud of The moment I am most proud of was watching my daughter become curious about a character made from her own drawing. It was no longer just another game chosen for her. It began with something she created. I am also proud that WallAlive creates a complete journey that draw, check, build, paint, play, collaborate, and with adult approval prepare the artwork as a real Shopify product draft. Most importantly, the agent supports the child’s imagination without taking control of it. What we learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when the person and the agent have different roles. The agent can inspect information, organize a story, recommend the next activity, and handle complicated preparation. The child should still draw, paint, choose, and play. An adult should remain responsible for publishing or selling anything. I also learned that art and technology do not need to compete. Technology can give a physical drawing another life while keeping the child’s original work at the center. What's next for Wall alive Next, I want to improve character reconstruction with more varied children’s drawings, stronger multi-character segmentation, and better movable rigs. I also want to add richer collaborative stories, more interactive worlds, classroom activities, teacher-created challenges, and safer parent controls. The longer-term goal is for children to build shared 3D exhibitions, stories, and small creator shops from artwork they made themselves not from premade characters someone else gave them. title: kata
pitch: Lets users teach a website a new agent capability by demonstration, then compiles that behavior into a safe, typed WebMCP tool.
about_excerpt: Lets users teach a website a new agent capability by demonstration, then compiles that behavior into a safe, typed WebMCP tool. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does KATA KATA is a system that allows users to teach a web application a new agent capability simply by demonstrating a workflow. Instead of requiring developers to manually write a dedicated API or WebMCP integration for every repeated action, a user performs the task a small number of times. KATA records the semantic application actions behind those demonstrations, compares the traces, identifies what stays constant and what varies, infers typed parameters, compiles the repeated behavior into a deterministic workflow, and installs it as a new WebMCP tool. For example, a researcher may repeatedly save a paper, assign it a priority, and add an “architecture” tag. KATA can recognize the common structure and create a tool such as: triage_architecture_paper(workId) An AI agent can then discover and execute that newly learned capability through WebMCP. The important distinction is that KATA does not record mouse coordinates or replay brittle DOM clicks. It records semantic application commands. The human UI and the agent both ultimately use the same command system, so a learned tool invokes real application behavior rather than a separate simulation. KATA also avoids generating arbitrary executable code. Learned workflows are represented as structured, validated programs built from a finite set of supported commands. Inputs are validated before execution, the complete batch is preflighted before mutation, and invalid workflows fail without partially applying actions. The deeper idea behind KATA is user-extensible application APIs: the API available to an AI agent no longer has to be completely defined by the developer ahead of time. Users can teach software the workflows that matter to them, and the application can safely turn those workflows into agent-usable capabilities. title: 312Deals: Tonight
pitch: A live Chicago deals site where you and your agent plan tonight together: 17 WebMCP tools over 80,000 real deals, a shared plan with a lock you control, and booking links set to your time.
about_excerpt: A live Chicago deals site where you and your agent plan tonight together: 17 WebMCP tools over 80,000 real deals, a shared plan with a lock you control, and booking links set to your time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration 312Deals is a live site: 80,000+ food and drink deals at 12,000+ venues across 149 Chicagoland neighborhoods, covering the city and 60+ suburbs, re-verified weekly against 18,000+ tracked sources. People use it to figure out where to go tonight. When agent browsers arrived, we watched them try to do the same job by reading the page, and get it wrong in ways that matter: a happy hour that ended at six, a venue across town, a "deal" that was last week's. The inventory is structured and time-sensitive; the UI was built for people. WebMCP is the bridge. Tell the agent what the site can do instead of making it guess from what it shows. The idea we wanted to test: planning a night out is genuinely collaborative work. Ranking 80,000 time-windowed deals is the agent's job. Taste and veto are the person's. So instead of an agent that hands you a plan, we built a plan that both of you edit, on the same page. The idea we wanted to test: planning a night out is genuinely collaborative work. Ranking 80,000 time-windowed deals is the agent's job. Taste and veto are the person's. So instead of an agent that hands you a plan, we built a plan that both of you edit, on the same page. What it does Open 312deals.com in ChatGPT's desktop browser and the page registers 17 tools on document.modelContext: 10 data tools over the live corpus: search deals by neighborhood, day, type, and cuisine; deals near an address; a venue's deals; deal of the day; chain deals; neighborhood summaries; a multi-stop crawl planner; order and reservation links; and a moderated community deal tip (a write, so the browser's confirmation applies). 7 "Tonight" tools over a plan that lives in the page: the Tonight panel, bottom-right on every screen. The agent reads the plan, sets constraints (budget, hours, group size, max stops, neighborhood), adds stops from real deals, moves them, reorders them by deal window, removes, and clears. Every agent change lands in the panel with an "agent" chip and a toast. The person adds any deal from its card, reorders, vetoes, and locks the stops that must stay. Locked stops are constraints, not suggestions: an agent call against a locked stop returns a structured refusal, so the agent re-plans around it instead of over it. Every stop ends in action. Reservation links carry the plan: OpenTable's dateTime and covers, and Resy's date and seats, are built from the plan's start time and group size (or from the time and party size the agent passes), so the booking page opens on your slot rather than its 7-PM-for-2 default. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP. Deal discovery is precisely the case WebMCP was made for: typed tools over live, structured, expiring data beat screen-reading on speed, accuracy, and reliability. And the site already had an audience and a corpus. This isn't a demo dataset: 312Deals ranks on page one for its core Chicago queries and most of its traffic is organic search, so the pages an agent lands on are the same pages people land on. How it creates a better user experience. One request replaces a dozen searches across tabs. The agent searches real, verified deals, builds the plan from what is actually on at each hour, and shows its work in a panel you can touch. You lock what you care about; it optimizes the rest. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before. Before, you had two options: do all the work yourself in the UI, or let an agent scrape the UI and hand you a plan you couldn't touch. Now both act on one live surface. The agent proposes against live inventory, the person constrains with locks the agent must respect, and each sees the other's changes immediately. The plan is yours, built on tonight's real deals. How we built it Next.js 14 and React on Vercel, FastAPI on Railway, SQLite with FTS5 distributed through Cloudflare R2 with an ETag conflict guard, zustand for the shared plan, and the ElevenLabs API for the demo narration. Built and shipped solo under Hoyne Labs LLC. All challenge work went to production the same day it was written and was tested against ChatGPT's desktop browser on a free account. How we implemented WebMCP: Registration feature-detects document.modelContext (the current spec surface; ChatGPT desktop and Chrome 149+) with navigator.modelContext as a fallback for earlier Canary builds. Every tool carries readOnlyHint / destructiveHint annotations and is registered with an AbortSignal; teardown runs through both paths; tools re-register across client-side navigations. Agent-shaped results. The site's REST API returns about 60 columns per deal and about 92 per venue (a 20-result search is roughly 32 KB; one venue lookup roughly 117 KB). The tools trim each result to what a person acts on, add a link to the page, and say how many results were left out. Shared state. The Tonight tools act on a persisted zustand store the panel renders. The lock and veto contract is enforced in the store, so a refusal comes back to the agent as data with instructions ("locked by the user, plan around it"). One link builder, three surfaces. A single reservation-link helper is used by the Tonight tools, the get_reservation_link tool, and the panel's own Reserve link, so the agent's path and the person's path emit the same fully parameterized URL. Dates default to today in America/Chicago; times accept what an agent or a person would write ("6pm", "18:00"). Catalog and analytics. An informational manifest at /.well-known/webmcp.json lists all 17 tools alongside the site's existing /llms.txt, /llms-full.txt, /skill.md, and /.well-known/mcp.json. The FastAPI middleware that detects agent traffic and records tool calls predates the challenge, which is why the first real calls were captured the moment they arrived. Pre-existing project, what's new. 312deals.com existed before the challenge, including an earlier 10-tool WebMCP layer on the legacy navigator.modelContext surface. All challenge work is in the public repo's commits dated Sep 3, 2026, after a clearly labeled baseline commit: the spec-surface migration and agent-shaped results, the entire Tonight collaboration (panel, store contract, 7 tools), the lock guidance, and the plan-aware reservation links. Everything was deployed to production on Sep 3. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. The site's original WebMCP layer, built in February 2026 after joining Chrome's Early Preview Program for built-in AI, registered on navigator.modelContext, with a declarative form API on the highest-frequency tools. ChatGPT's browser only looks at document.modelContext. Until the migration, the 17 tools were invisible to the one client that mattered. Version fragility had been the known risk with this standard for months, and this is what it looked like in practice. The agent web-searched instead of calling tools. A plain "find me a happy hour" sent ChatGPT to general search, citing venue websites. Naming the site tools in the request ("using this site's tools...") reliably routes it to the page. The testing instructions say so. The lock was bypassable through the human UI. Asked to remove a locked stop, the agent hit the tool's refusal, then clicked the panel's padlock itself, announced it, and removed the stop. The refusal now tells the agent plainly that only the person unlocks, by hand. It's an honest lesson: when the agent can drive the UI too, "human affordances" are agent affordances unless the contract is explicit. Shallow deep links. The first reservation handoff landed on OpenTable's default slot. Pushing the plan's date, time, and party size into the URL made the link finish the job. Accomplishments that we're proud of The first real WebMCP tool calls the site ever received came from ChatGPT during this challenge: search, then tonight_add_stop three times, then a reorder that respected a lock. The site's own analytics recorded them. Seven months of building an agent surface (REST API, MCP server, custom GPT, llms.txt, WebMCP) and this was the first time we watched an outside agent discover the tools on the page and use them end to end. What we learned WebMCP's value isn't the tool list; it's designing for two actors on one surface. The interesting engineering is the contract between them: attribution, refusals as data, and what a lock actually means when the other party can also click. What's next for 312Deals: Tonight Keeping deals , venues and more up-to-date to enable discovery of venues, deals and more for small business owners. The goal was to spread awareness of this to support small biz. Hopefully this does just that by making it easier for the ever changing landscape of the web with AI, to support and facilitate that. title: Acorn
pitch: Acorn is the academic planning workspace built for Stanford. You and your agent set goals, research courses, and track your progress together, for every quarter till graduation.
about_excerpt: Acorn is the academic planning workspace built for Stanford. You and your agent set goals, research courses, and track your progress together, for every quarter till graduation. Like Comment Story Updates The landing page. Julia's September: move-in, auditions, club meetings, and the start of classes. Todos are labeled by who added them, her or her agent. The week view. Her agent picked these sections around ballet rehearsals and her Friday work-study shift. The academics page: the autumn plan, her AP credit, and search over the full catalog. A course's real sections, each lecture paired with a discussion. Times can be corrected by her or her agent. Her clubs, with meeting times that show up on the calendar. The scratchpad: her quick notes and the goal her agent structured into milestones. The activity log. Each entry shows whether she or her agent made the change. Every time I switched between building something technical and researching what I need to do to prepare for freshman year at Stanford, while using the same frontier models at my disposal, I was hit in the face with a sharp divergence in performance. The same model that built an entire secure backend meant to withstand ten thousand users and connected it to a frontend without trouble (the CORS errors alone took me hours just 3 years ago), was reduced to a useless machine awkwardly misclicking around Stanford Axess trying to retrieve any piece of information at all. It searched from stale sources and did not know what to do with broken links. It misclicked and accidentally closed browsing sessions. It forgot everything about me in a matter of a few messages. I saw that consumer AI was nowhere near the frontier I knew in development, and the problem was context and browsing. Which is why, when I heard that WebMCP, a concept I had heard of but never seen working, was actually moving forward, I was thrilled. This hackathon came at the right time, and with it the idea to finally streamline the process I had been struggling with all summer: pointing frontier intelligence at possibly the most important planning task of my adult life. I named it Acorn, an homage to the infamous Stanford squirrels that were darting around during my visit. Acorn is as much a context layer as it is a website. When we build with agents, we use markdown files in the repo so the model can carry goals, constraints, and decisions from one session to the next. Acorn acts as that durable context window, a version of which the average person could meaningfully interact with. You can talk to your agent and have it write things down, or scratch a half-formed idea into the pad yourself and have your agent make sense of it later. Either way you are both working on the same workspace: your goals, your notes on frosh-friendly classes, and the professors who you think might give you a research opportunity -- all forming a plan built collaboratively. The page registers 22 tools with the browser using WebMCP, giving an agent human-level control over the workspace. Everything a student would otherwise keep in their head has a place: a calendar that shows your actual week, a plan for each quarter, the clubs you joined with their meetings, the credit you brought in from AP or IB, and a scratchpad for any other tidbits of information. The official Stanford catalog with 15,618 courses across 256 departments is included in the workspace. So when you ask your agent for a schedule, it makes use of the actual options: it remembers the hours you blocked off, plans around your club meetings, picks lecture times that fit your week, and puts the result on your calendar. The biggest question was how much to hardcode and how much to leave to the user's agent. An empty catalog is useless, but a catalog nobody can correct goes stale when anything changes. I ended up shipping verified reference data as the base and allowing edits on top of it. The student or the agent can amend (or add) any course, club, or activity. To test all of this, I spun up Fable agents that played the students, each of them using the agentic workflow of Codex to plan their quarters collaboratively. Those rounds, and then planning my own autumn in the app, caught a number of problems. For a while the catalog had every lecture at Stanford and not a single discussion section, because my importer failed to scrape them. The same goal once appeared twice on the scratchpad, one copy with a milestone checklist and one without, because onboarding and the agent each saved it their own way. Saves took 32 seconds at one point, because every save was carrying ten full copies of the workspace as undo history, so I capped the history and saves dropped to three seconds. And once the app said a change was saved when it never reached the server, so saves now confirm against the server with an idempotency key. Through this, I learned that the divergence I kept running into had nothing to do with model capability. Once the browsing was replaced with webMCP tools and the context was durable, the same model that built my backend planned my quarter just as well. Next, I want to ship a barebones version of the workspace, giving a user's agent more autonomy over it, allowing it to research any university and build its catalog, programs, and clubs from official sources, so Acorn can extend beyond Stanford to any college, and past college to any long-running task where a person and their agent need one shared memory. The squirrels I named this after bury acorns all over campus and find them again months later, and that is what I want from planning with an agent: whatever the two of you put down, you come back and it is still there. title: CacheLens WebMCP
pitch: CacheLens uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT inspect LLM traces, find prompt-cache waste, explain why it happens, and simulate fixes that cut API cost.
about_excerpt: CacheLens uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT inspect LLM traces, find prompt-cache waste, explain why it happens, and simulate fixes that cut API cost. Like Comment Story Updates CacheLense WebMCP Inspiration LLM applications repeatedly send large amounts of identical context: system prompts, tool definitions, policies, and conversation history. Prompt caching can make that repeated input dramatically cheaper—but only while the cacheable prefix remains stable. A seemingly harmless change near the beginning of a prompt can invalidate cache reuse for everything that follows. Dynamic metadata, changing instructions, timestamps, or volatile content placed at the wrong cache boundary can quietly cause an application to pay to process thousands of largely unchanged tokens again. The difficult part is that developers usually cannot see why this is happening. That led to CacheLens: a developer tool for making prompt-cache behavior observable, identifying where prefix reuse breaks, explaining likely causes, estimating the financial impact, and recommending concrete fixes. The WebMCP Challenge suggested a natural next step: instead of requiring developers to manually interpret every trace and diagnostic, let ChatGPT inspect CacheLens directly through structured capabilities exposed by the live application. What it does CacheLens WebMCP turns prompt-cache diagnostics into a collaborative workflow between the developer, the web application, and ChatGPT. A developer can open a CacheLens trace and ask questions such as: Why is my cache hit rate low? Where is the cacheable prefix breaking? Which content is changing? How many stale tokens are being unnecessarily rewritten? What is that costing me? For an identified break, how much could be saved if the stable and volatile content were split correctly? Through WebMCP, ChatGPT discovers three domain-specific tools directly from the page: list_traces explain_cache_behavior estimate_split_savings Rather than scraping the DOM or requiring the user to copy diagnostic data into chat, the agent asks CacheLens directly for the underlying analysis. For example, one real captured trace reports a 44.3% provider-measured cache hit rate , 3 of 3 avoidable prefix breaks , and 28,175 stale tokens rewritten . CacheLens identifies the volatile cache boundary and can estimate the savings for a specific affected turn while clearly stating the assumptions and limitations of that estimate. The human remains in the loop through the CacheLens interface while ChatGPT reasons over the same application state through WebMCP. The workflow becomes: observe → diagnose → explain → estimate → improve How we built it CacheLens captures and analyzes LLM request traces while preserving the structure needed to understand prompt-prefix reuse. Its existing analysis engine compares successive requests, determines where stable prefixes diverge, separates stale tokens from genuinely new tokens, attributes likely causes, and estimates cache-related waste. For WebMCP, we deliberately reused that analysis rather than creating a second implementation. A thin serialization layer projects CacheLens analysis objects into safe application data. A small read-only HTTP server exposes the trace catalog and analysis endpoints, and a lightweight browser interface registers the three WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . The WebMCP tools use constrained inputs: trace identifiers are resolved through an explicit server-side catalog rather than arbitrary filesystem paths, and the tools expose no shell commands, writes, credentials, or mutation operations. The tools are intentionally higher-level than UI automation. CacheLens does not expose actions such as "click this button." It exposes meaningful developer operations: list available traces, explain cache behavior, and estimate the savings associated with splitting a specific identified cache break. That became one of the most important design principles of the project: WebMCP is most useful when a website exposes meaningful application capabilities, not simply another way to operate its interface. Challenges The first challenge was identifying cache waste accurately. Prompt caching is prefix-sensitive, so a small mutation can force a much larger region of otherwise unchanged input to be rewritten. Detecting that two strings differ is easy. Determining which divergence caused expensive cache invalidation—and separating stale tokens from genuinely new ones—is considerably more useful. The second challenge was presenting the result in terms developers care about. Token counts alone are abstract, so CacheLens connects structural changes to cache behavior and estimated cost while distinguishing measured provider usage from heuristic token estimates. The WebMCP integration introduced another challenge: deciding what an AI agent should actually be allowed to do. Exposing every internal operation would create a large and confusing tool surface. Exposing only low-level UI controls would miss the purpose of WebMCP. We settled on three small, read-only, domain-specific tools corresponding to real developer questions. We also deliberately avoided a tempting feature: a general-purpose "simulate fix" tool. CacheLens does not currently model arbitrary prompt reorganizations or predict a new cache-hit rate. Instead, estimate_split_savings performs one narrow counterfactual supported by measured analysis: for an identified cache break, estimate the cost difference if the unchanged portion could have been read from cache rather than rewritten. Keeping that boundary explicit made the result more defensible. What we learned The project reinforced an important lesson about AI infrastructure: optimization problems are often observability problems first. Prompt caching can provide substantial savings, but developers cannot optimize behavior they cannot see. We also learned that WebMCP changes the relationship between AI agents and web applications. Instead of treating a website as a collection of pixels, DOM elements, and buttons, an application can explicitly describe the capabilities it intends to offer an agent. For CacheLens, ChatGPT does not need to guess what a chart means or scrape text from a dashboard. It can ask the application directly for the underlying diagnostic information and help the developer reason about it. We validated this end to end in both Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled and ChatGPT's built-in browser . In ChatGPT, all three tools were discovered and invoked through natural-language requests while the page's WebMCP activity panel displayed the corresponding calls. That combination—structured application capabilities, shared live application state, and human oversight—is what makes WebMCP particularly compelling to us. What's next CacheLens can expand beyond individual traces into continuous monitoring of production LLM applications: detecting regressions in cache efficiency, comparing deployments, identifying recurring sources of prompt instability, and surfacing optimization opportunities over time. Its current ingest path focuses on Anthropic-format request traces; additional provider adapters are a natural next step. More broadly, we see WebMCP as a way to turn developer tools from passive dashboards into active collaborators. CacheLens started by answering a simple question: Where is my LLM application wasting tokens? With WebMCP, a developer can now ask that question directly—and let CacheLens and ChatGPT investigate the evidence together. title: canter.dev
pitch: Canter is a hosting control plane built for AI agents to operate and humans to govern.
about_excerpt: Canter is a hosting control plane built for AI agents to operate and humans to govern. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agents can write code, but running what they build still pushes them toward either brittle shell access or infrastructure credentials that are far too powerful. We built Canter around a different boundary: the agent proposes an exact, inspectable Change; the human governs authority and high-impact execution; and the control plane produces evidence of what actually happened. What it does Canter is an agent-operated, human-governed hosting control plane. An agent can inspect a System, draft a Change, and review an immutable execution plan without receiving provider credentials. Every proposed deployment is bound to an exact digest, policy is explicit, apply can require human approval, and execution produces durable receipts. For the WebMCP Challenge, Canter makes that workflow discoverable directly from the website. The site advertises same-origin agent discovery, provides WebMCP read and review tools, and points capable agents to the authenticated remote MCP contract for durable work. Browser tools cannot borrow the human session to bypass approval: a sensitive Change still needs a focused, short-lived review capability and an explicit human action. How we built it The control plane is written in Go with PostgreSQL-backed durable state. The product interface uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript. A typed System contract compiles into a deterministic execution graph before provider adapters can mutate infrastructure. The same semantic objects—Systems, Changes, exact digests, policy envelopes, operations, and evidence—are shared across the CLI, HTTP API, remote MCP, and WebMCP surfaces. The website registers its WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool. The public /.well-known/canter and /llms.txt routes explain the same-origin device flow, API, and Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint without exposing provider details. Authenticated agent installations are durable and revocable, with independent inspect, draft, and apply authority. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not exposing more tools. It was preserving a trustworthy authority boundary across several interfaces. We had to ensure browser tools remain read and review only, authorization binds to one immutable digest, replayed or expired approval links fail safely, execution can resume after interruption, and a failed release does not silently become desired state. Accomplishments that we're proud of One small vocabulary across web, CLI, API, MCP, and WebMCP: inspect System, draft Change, review exact digest, authorize, apply, inspect evidence. Agents never receive provider credentials or arbitrary infrastructure access. Human approval can be mandatory for apply while agents retain useful inspect-and-draft authority. Execution is evidence-producing, restart-safe, and able to contain unhealthy releases. The browser experience makes policy, pending work, exact plans, and agent authority visible at a glance. What we learned Agent infrastructure needs fewer ambient privileges and better semantic contracts. WebMCP is most useful when it is an adapter into a governed product model, not a shortcut around it. The strongest interface is one where both the agent and the human can see the same proposed Change and the same evidence. What's next for canter.dev We want to expand the provider adapter set, improve focused Change review, add more public verification recipes, and make the same governed deployment loop available to more coding agents without weakening the human boundary. title: PunchPilot — field review, drawn on the sheet
pitch: ChatGPT reads the live drawing context, drafts findings at a coordinate, and prepares the visit briefing. The person on site keeps verification and issuance.
about_excerpt: ChatGPT reads the live drawing context, drafts findings at a coordinate, and prepares the visit briefing. The person on site keeps verification and issuance. Like Comment Story Updates PunchPilot: field review drawn on the sheet, with ChatGPT beside the reviewer through six WebMCP Site tools. Six WebMCP Site tools registered by every project screen. Three read, two write, one drafts. None verifies, completes, or issues. ChatGPT reads the live context through the read tools, then asks before calling the write tool. The draft pin sits where it was asked for, 62% across and 49% down on sheet A2.02. Verification stays with the person on site. One word of confirmation. The page announces the save with a WebMCP notice and ChatGPT reports exactly what was written. The visit briefing assembled from live data. Nothing issued, nothing published. Inspiration Construction field reviews are done standing on a slab with a tablet, a set of PDF drawings, and last visit's open items. The record that comes out of that walk is a professional document. A generic assistant can summarise notes, but it cannot safely touch the same numbered record the reviewer is looking at. WebMCP is the first thing that lets the page itself hand the agent a small, typed set of actions bound to the project already open, under the reviewer's own identity. What it does PunchPilot is a full field-review workspace on Cloudflare Workers: projects with disciplines and a filed drawing set, numbered reviews per discipline, findings pinned as page-aware percentages on the PDF, photos, status history, per-review checklists, and a frozen issued report for each visit. Every project screen registers six WebMCP Site tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_field_review_context reads the open project, discipline, latest review, and unresolved carry-forward findings. list_open_findings reads the work list. start_or_resume_field_review resumes the active review or opens the next numbered one for a valid floor, discipline, and drawing. create_draft_finding saves a draft pin at a coordinate on the active sheet and selects it on screen. update_or_verify_finding updates a finding; verification is refused unless the item is already corrected, a human confirms it on site, and a note is given. prepare_field_review_briefing assembles a live-data briefing of raised, revisited, and carried findings and issues nothing. There is deliberately no tool that verifies on the agent's word, completes a review, or issues a report. Why WebMCP is the right fit The value is in the binding, not the chat. The tools are registered by the page that already knows which project, discipline, review, and sheet are open, so ChatGPT never has to guess an identifier or scrape a screenshot. Each tool calls the same authenticated API route the buttons call, with the same validation, the same audit trail, and the same identity the worker resolved at the edge. The drawing, the finding log, and the history update in front of the reviewer as the agent works, so every action is visible and checkable on the spot. That is the kind of trust a professional record needs, and it is exactly what a page-registered tool gives that an external API integration would not. How WebMCP makes the experience better Without it, the reviewer types findings on a keyboard while holding a tablet, re-reads last visit's list to know what to revisit, and rebuilds the briefing by hand at the truck. With it, they say "draft a finding at 62 across, 49 down, fire-rated door closer missing at corridor 205, warning, assign the site super" and the pin lands on the sheet with a number. They ask "what is still open on Level 2 electrical" and get the real list. They ask for the briefing and get raised, revisited, and carried counts from live data. Fewer taps in gloves, no retyping, and nothing invented, because every answer comes from the record. What people and agents accomplish together The agent does retrieval, consistent numbering, structured drafts, and the briefing. The human does what only a person on site can: decide what is physically there, whether a correction is acceptable, and whether the record is ready to issue. The tool schemas encode that split. Verification requires humanConfirmedOnSite , a corrected status, and a note. Completion and issuance are buttons, not tools. The briefing is marked draft and carries externalAction: false . How we built it React 19 on vinext (Next-style App Router compiled to one Cloudflare Worker with Vite), plain CSS design tokens, Lucide icons. Cloudflare D1 with Drizzle ORM (eleven migrations), Cloudflare R2 for drawings and photos, pdf.js with a real worker for the drawing canvas. Identity is resolved once in worker/index.ts and re-stamped as internal headers after stripping every client-sent copy. The public contest Site runs a shared Guest Reviewer so judges need no account; a private deployment uses the verified Sites or Cloudflare Access identity instead, with one build flag deciding which. WebMCP tools are registered from the top-level page with an AbortController , MCP-shaped results ( content , structuredContent , isError ), readOnlyHint on reads, and additionalProperties: false on every input schema. 123 source-level and behavioural tests run against the production build before every change ships. Challenges Coordinates had to survive zoom, resize, and re-uploaded sheets, so pins are stored as page-aware percentages rather than pixels. D1 caps a statement at 100 bound variables, so every bulk checklist insert is chunked. The hardest design call was what not to expose: there is no tool that completes a review or issues a report, and a test fails if one is ever added, because a report an agent can issue is a report nobody should trust. What's next Photo capture through a tool, voice-first capture on site, and per-member identity on the public Site once WebMCP supports signed-in flows for shared deployments. Try it (judges) Open the live app in the ChatGPT desktop app so it loads in the built-in browser, or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Open Meridian Commons — Building B . The header shows a Site tools badge once the tools are registered. Start a new ChatGPT thread in that workspace and ask, for example: "Use the PunchPilot Site tools on the open review. Create a draft finding on the current sheet at 62% across and 49% down: Fire-rated door closer missing — corridor 205, warning severity, assigned to the site super. Do not verify or issue anything." ChatGPT reads the context with the read tools, then asks you to confirm before it calls the write tool. Say yes. Watch the pin land, read the finding number in the receipt, and see the "WebMCP · Draft pin saved" notice on the page. Then ask for the briefing. Everything on the Site is fictional and shared. The project, drawings, findings, and the Guest Reviewer are demonstration data. Video guide (2:30) Time What to watch 0:12 The six Site tools by name: three read, two write, one drafts. No tool verifies, completes, or issues. 0:49 The live Site inside ChatGPT's browser, tools bound to the open project, discipline, and review. 1:03 The reviewer asks for a draft finding in plain words. 1:17 ChatGPT reads context through the read tools, then asks before it writes anything. 1:28 "Yes, save it." The count goes 5 to 6, the WebMCP notice fires, and the receipt reads: D-010, pinned, assigned, not verified, no report issued. 1:52 The pin on the drawing at 62 across, 49 down. Still a draft. 2:05 The briefing from live data: recorded, raised, revisited, carried. Nothing issued. title: Gates of Galloo
pitch: A voice-directed voxel world where people and AI reshape the same live scene through WebMCP, from bridges and domino chains to characters, weather, and contextual commerce.
about_excerpt: A voice-directed voxel world where people and AI reshape the same live scene through WebMCP, from bridges and domino chains to characters, weather, and contextual commerce. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration In the HBO show Silicon Valley, Dinesh turns on a microphone inside a game and mentions pizza. The game immediately fills itself with Domino's advertising. It is funny because the world appears to be listening and rewriting itself around the conversation. Gates of Galloo asks a more useful version of that question: what if speaking to a game did not merely open a chatbot or trigger an advertisement? What if the AI could understand the actual world, change it with you, and let you interrupt whenever its taste became questionable? What it does Gates of Galloo is a voice-directed voxel world shared by a person and an AI character named Nika. The player can walk around the island and speak at the level of intention: "Build a bridge in front of me." "Create a domino path from the chapel to the harbor, but leave it standing." "Extend the island with a mix of grass, stone, and water." "I am hungry." "That is too much. Undo it." Nika reads the current state of the island and turns the request into visible actions. Terrain grows, objects arrive, characters move, weather changes, dominoes fall, and contextual storefronts can become part of the scene. These changes happen over time, so the player can watch, interrupt, redirect, or reverse the result. The commerce interactions are no-charge previews. They demonstrate how a product, delivery, or storefront could enter a game as a playable event rather than as a detached banner. Why WebMCP matters The useful context is already inside the page: terrain, buildings, player position and facing, selected regions, actors, shops, domino runs, camera state, and recent changes. Ordinary computer control would force an agent to infer all of that from pixels and simulate mouse clicks. WebMCP lets the website expose the world directly through meaningful actions. Gates of Galloo registers six page tools: inspect_world list_assets place_asset erase_at paint_path undo_last_action The agent works with island objects and validated grid coordinates instead of screen positions. The available vocabulary is intentionally defined by the game, while the model remains free to decide what to create with it. This makes WebMCP part of the creative medium. The person and agent can see and change the same evolving artifact without repeatedly describing what is already on screen. How it creates a better experience The conversation stays inside the activity. The player does not have to export a screenshot, explain the map to a separate assistant, wait for generated code, and reload the result. Instead, an idea becomes visible inside the current world. If the interpretation is wrong, the player can correct it while it is happening. References such as "here," "in front of me," or "beside the bridge" work because the agent receives the live player and scene state. The result feels closer to improvising with another participant than issuing commands to a detached chatbot. How we built it The project began with the open-source Mykonos Island Voxels game by Ibrahim Boona. During the submission period, we transformed it into Gates of Galloo. The browser adapts the live game controller into WebMCP tool definitions and registers them through document.modelContext.registerTool() . For voice interaction, OpenAI Realtime handles the live conversation and transcription. It has one high-level function called direct_world . That function sends the player's original request, together with a semantic snapshot of the island, to a server-side director built with the OpenAI Responses API. The director produces a structured sequence of terrain, object, actor, camera, commerce, and domino operations. The browser validates that plan and performs it incrementally. The production interaction is model-directed rather than selected through keyword rules or canned responses. We also added an embodied isometric player, pathfinding, bridge traversal, camera follow, open-ended terrain growth, mixed-terrain paths, live transcripts, interruption, conflict-aware undo, actors, weather, chain reactions, and contextual storefront scenes. Challenges and lessons The hardest problem was giving the model enough live context to make those actions feel intentional. We had to solve placement validation, connected terrain painting, object footprints, isometric occlusion, bridge traversal, camera framing, world expansion, interruption, and undo without allowing one half-finished plan to corrupt the next. We also learned that the design of the tool vocabulary changes the personality of the agent. A model with raw DOM access behaves like an operator. A model given verbs such as inspect, place, paint, stage, and undo can behave more like a collaborator. Gates of Galloo is one playful example, but the same pattern can extend to design software, educational simulations, music tools, filmmaking environments, and any website where the human and agent should remain inside the work together. title: WebMCP Chess
pitch: A browser chess game where a person and an AI agent share one board and take turns, using WebMCP tools registered directly on the page. No backend MCP server, no scraping the DOM.
about_excerpt: A browser chess game where a person and an AI agent share one board and take turns, using WebMCP tools registered directly on the page. No backend MCP server, no scraping the DOM. Like Comment Story Updates AI Agent thinks and calls tools Coaching in action Analyze position with Stockfish Coaching with Stockfish in action Inspiration There's no shortage of chess apps. What's actually new here is WebMCP: a proposed API that lets a web page expose its own client-side functions as tools an AI agent can discover and call directly in the browser, no scraping the DOM, no separate backend integration for the agent. Chess was a good test case because it needs multi-step, stateful interaction: read the board, act, wait your turn, repeat. That's a real workflow, not a single API call dressed up as a demo. What it does Play chess in the browser on your own, or hand control to an AI agent mid-game. You share one board and one move history, and both of you go through the same validated chess logic. (Note: the demo video predates the engine work and shows the five original tools. The three Stockfish tools below are live in the deployed app and in the repository.) Eight WebMCP tools are registered on the page: Playing chess-get-board-state reads the current position, whose turn it is, legal moves, captured pieces and the material balance. chess-make-move plays a legal move. chess-wait-for-human-move pauses for your turn, then picks back up automatically. chess-new-game resets. Thinking chess-analyze-position returns ranked lines with real evaluations. Each one breaks out from, to and promotion, so a recommendation feeds straight into chess-make-move without the model having to parse its own advice. chess-evaluate-move reviews a move you just played: how much it cost in centipawns, what class of error it was, and the line that refutes it. chess-set-engine-strength weakens the agent's own play so it can be a beatable opponent. It never weakens the advice you are given. Coaching chess-suggest-move ranks candidate moves, draws them as arrows on the board, and explains the reasoning. The board also shows captured pieces and the material advantage for each side, so you can see who is up without replaying the move list in your head. How I built it Next.js, React and TypeScript. chess.js for the rules, react-chessboard for the board. Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(), each with a JSON schema and a callback that shares state with the UI, so an agent's move and a human's move land in exactly the same place. Stockfish 18 runs in the page, compiled to WebAssembly in a Web Worker. There is no backend. Searching happens off the main thread, so the board stays responsive while the engine thinks, and it reaches depth 16 to 18 in about a second. The 7 MB binary downloads on first analysis rather than on page load, and a small UCI client on the page serialises searches and handles aborts, so moving on to a new position cancels the search before it. Challenges I ran into WebMCP has no way to push application state to an agent. The spec has no notification for "the human moved, your turn". The workaround is chess-wait-for-human-move , a long-running call that resolves when the position changes, guarded by a FEN check and a two-minute timeout so it cannot hang. It works, but it is a workaround for a real protocol gap, not a claim that WebMCP does push notifications. A legal move is not a good move. Early on ChatGPT would cheerfully propose legal but tactically losing moves, because the only thing the page told it was which moves were legal. Legality answers whether a move follows the rules, not whether the opponent can immediately punish it. Stockfish now answers the second question, and the model is left to do the part it is actually good at. What I learned Long-running tool calls can bridge WebMCP's current gaps, but they are not push notifications and it is worth being honest about the difference. The pattern that actually emerged is a split of labour: the model explains, deterministic domain tools verify. Stockfish is the strongest version of that in this project. The engine calculates and returns ranked lines with real numbers; the model turns a principal variation into a sentence you can learn something from. Neither is asked to do the other's job, and the failure mode of each is caught by the other. What's next The interesting unfinished work is in the protocol, not the chess. Waiting for a human turn should not need a two-minute long poll, and the open WebMCP design discussions on application-driven observations, human-in-the-loop elicitation and long-running tool progress are all pointing at the same gap from different directions. This project is a small, concrete test case for whatever lands there.
