title: ArcadeOps Relay
pitch: Browser intent becomes a bounded mission, a human decision, and cryptographically verified delivery.
about_excerpt: Browser intent becomes a bounded mission, a human decision, and cryptographically verified delivery. Like Comment Story Updates The verified end state: four evidence checks pass and the accepted delivery receives a valid Ed25519 certificate. One shared Project Aurora workspace: browser agent, bounded worker, human authority, and evidence in the same state. Browser intent to verified delivery WebMCP mission control from browser intent to verified delivery. Inspiration Browser agents can understand the page in front of a person, while worker agents can execute substantial tasks. What was missing was the operational layer between them: a shared place to turn intent into a mission, keep work moving, bring in human judgment at the right moment, and carry trustworthy context through to delivery. We built ArcadeOps Relay as that mission control layer. What it does Relay gives a browser agent seven intent-level WebMCP tools on a live Project Aurora workspace. The agent inspects the objective and constraints, drafts a bounded mission, delegates a persisted internal worker, and follows authoritative progress. ArcadeOps coordinates the handoffs and surfaces one strategic release choice when human judgment adds value. The person sees the consequences and evidence in the same workspace, chooses whether to stage or postpone, and the exact run resumes with its context intact. The worker produces the release-readiness artifacts, ArcadeOps evaluates four required evidence checks, and a hash-bound Ed25519 certificate proves the accepted delivery. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the browser agent use the current page, scoped judge session, project, and human-visible state without DOM guessing or a separately installed MCP connector. Relay registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Tools appear only on the challenge page, use strict schemas, avoid duplicate registration, and disappear on navigation. Human-agent collaboration The human, browser agent, and worker share one authoritative workspace. The browser agent turns visible project context into a mission; the worker executes; ArcadeOps preserves progress, cost, decisions, and evidence; and the human guides the strategic moments. Together they can delegate real bounded work, resume safely after a decision, and prove delivery without losing context or letting an agent approve itself. How it was built Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Zod, native imperative WebMCP, server-side SQLite transactions, signed HMAC authority handles, canonical SHA-256 evidence packs, and Ed25519 certificates. Playwright covers desktop, dark theme, mobile, accessibility, isolation, tool lifecycle, and the complete visible workflow. Vitest covers state transitions and adversarial security cases. The app runs as a non-root Docker container behind TLS. The judge worker is intentionally deterministic. It performs real persisted state transitions and creates real hashed artifacts over synthetic Project Aurora data, but has no network, provider, production, email, calendar, financial, deployment, or destructive capability. Challenges Making WebMCP registration survive React Strict Mode without duplicate tools. Keeping server authorization authoritative while exposing useful browser intent. Binding decisions, resumes, and acceptance to exact signed targets and versions. Making retries safe under duplicate and concurrent calls. Distinguishing worker completion from evaluated evidence and accepted delivery. Providing a credential-free public demo without exposing production data or private source. Accomplishments Seven native, page-scoped intent tools. One genuine browser-agent → persisted worker → human decision → evidence → certificate loop. Zero approval bypasses and zero duplicate mutations in the reproducible five-run evaluation set. Signed, expiring, session-scoped handles and exact evidence-hash acceptance. A public, synthetic, resettable judge experience with no paid model calls. Automated unit, integration, browser, accessibility, evaluation, build, dependency, and secret checks. What was new for the challenge ArcadeOps existed before August 25, 2026 as a private agent operations platform with mission, approval, evidence, and certificate concepts. The challenge work is the self-contained WebMCP adapter; seven mission tools; Project Aurora judge workspace; live browser-agent/worker collaboration; deterministic challenge runtime; challenge policy; session isolation; authority and evidence binding; WebMCP evaluations; public deployment package; documentation; video; and submission materials. The private ArcadeOps repository and unrelated proprietary components are not published. What we learned The best browser tools describe product intent, not page mechanics. Shared state matters more than another chat transcript. A model response is not delivery truth. Human authority becomes usable when the page explains both the blocked action and the consequences, while signed handles let the agent safely continue afterward. What's next The same pattern can govern broader agent-native operations: richer workers, organization policies, external evidence attestations, and portable certificates—while preserving scoped authority, explicit human decisions, and honest cost and completion truth. Judge data All demo data is synthetic. No credentials are required. title: Ceiling
pitch: A WebMCP action gate that gives agents narrow tools, requires one-use user activation for changes, and produces a verifiable session receipt chain.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP action gate that gives agents narrow tools, requires one-use user activation for changes, and produces a verifiable session receipt chain. Like Comment Story Updates Universal adapter conformance across content, access, and spending policies. Seven-case Defense Matrix: authority, replay, concurrency, and receipt attacks. Hard policy denial: unsafe changes are refused before authority is considered. Unarmed effect control: an admitted proposal still cannot apply itself. Ceiling: a bounded WebMCP change gate with visible authority and evidence. Ceiling Why I built it Agents are getting better at working inside websites. That is useful, but it creates a basic problem: how do I let an agent help without handing it every action available in my signed-in session? Ceiling is my attempt to answer that question with something people can actually try. It is a small release-policy workbench where an agent can read the current state, prepare a change, and explain why it wants that change. The page decides whether the request fits its rules, and a person remains in control of the final action. I did not want the safety story to be a warning banner or a promise in a README. I wanted the boundary to be visible in the interface and testable from the agent side. What it does The demo follows four simple steps: The agent proposes one change. Ceiling checks the value and shows the difference. A person can authorize that specific change for a few seconds. The page applies or rejects it once and records what happened. Unsafe requests stop before the approval step. In the demo, an attempt to turn off signed artifacts is denied immediately. A safer request to change the rollback window from 30 to 45 minutes is allowed into review, but the agent still cannot apply it on its own. Approval is deliberately narrow. It is tied to the current policy, the proposed value, and the requested operation. It expires quickly and cannot be reused. Rollback follows the same rule instead of acting as an unprotected escape hatch. Every decision adds a linked receipt. The page can verify the chain again and export the session evidence as JSON. A built-in Defense Matrix also tries seven ways to break the boundary, including replay, expiry, parallel application, and receipt tampering. Why WebMCP fits Without a structured interface, an agent either has to guess from pixels or a site has to expose a broad action API. WebMCP gives the page a better option: it can publish a small, discoverable set of tools with clear inputs. Ceiling registers 11 tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Four are read-only. Seven cover the review workflow. An agent can inspect the available tools, read the policy, propose a change, test the safety boundary, and verify the receipts without being given deployment, credential, payment, messaging, or cross-origin powers. The result is a better experience for both sides. The agent does not have to guess what it is allowed to do, and the user does not have to trust a vague confirmation dialog. How I built it Ceiling is dependency-free HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The WebMCP tools use closed input schemas, and the interface reports whether registration succeeded, partly succeeded, or is unavailable. The release-policy demo sits on a reusable scalar-change core. I also tested that core against publishing, access-control, and spending-policy examples to make sure the pattern was not tied to one screen. The focused suite currently includes 78 tests, a 23-case policy evaluation, and 50 cross-domain adapter checks. I used OpenAI Codex during implementation, testing, adversarial review, and release packaging. A separate non-author review initially rejected the release because of three packaging and claim-boundary problems. I corrected those problems before preparing this submission. What was difficult The hardest part was defining what a click actually proves. Browser automation can produce trusted input, so Ceiling does not call a click proof of identity or proof that no automation was involved. It treats the gesture as short-lived permission for one visible operation and no more. I also found a concurrency bug in an earlier receipt implementation. Parallel writes could reuse the same sequence information. I kept that behavior as a regression fixture, serialized the active write path, and added full-chain verification. Chrome on my test machine did not expose WebMCP during the recorded fallback pass. The page says that plainly and keeps the fallback controls separate. The working WebMCP demonstration was verified in the ChatGPT/Codex in-app browser. What I learned The most useful lesson was that refusal is part of the product. A trustworthy agent interface should make denied actions, missing capabilities, and failed preconditions as clear as successful ones. I also learned that evidence is only useful when it is easy to inspect and hard to accidentally overstate. The final project deliberately claims less than the larger system I hope to build. What's next Ceiling is session-local by design. The next steps would be reviewed host adapters, optional signed or externally anchored receipts, and carefully scoped persistence. Each would need its own authority boundary rather than silently expanding the one demonstrated here. title: Doorman WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP authority demo where discovering a tool never means blanket permission to use it.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP authority demo where discovering a tool never means blanket permission to use it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP makes web apps easier for agents to use by exposing structured tools directly. Doorman explores a boundary that becomes important as soon as those tools can change state: capability_available != capability_exercised A tool being discoverable should not automatically mean an agent has blanket authority to use it. What it does Doorman is a small shared-board demo where the human UI and the WebMCP tool surface operate over the same local state. Four tools are normally registered: list_items , add_item , update_item , and request_approval . Their authority is intentionally narrower than their existence suggests. For example, update_item can only modify items created by the current agent session. The more interesting case is delete_item . It is not merely registered and then denied by policy. It is genuinely absent from the exposed WebMCP surface until a human approves one specific deletion target. Once approved, the capability is registered dynamically, can be used once for that approved target, and is then unregistered again. Each decision also produces a small local receipt that keeps policy decision and execution outcome separate. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer what the page can do from presentation-level UI. Doorman instead exposes an explicit tool surface while preserving a separate authority boundary. That creates a cleaner human-agent collaboration model: the agent can discover structured capabilities, application policy can constrain what those capabilities are allowed to affect, the human can grant a narrow one-shot capability when needed, and the capability can disappear again after use. The result is not "the agent can use everything on the page." It is a negotiated command surface whose available tools can change with human approval. How it works The implementation is deliberately small and inspectable. src/doorman.js wraps document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . The WebMCP callback and the local doorman.invoke() path share the same policy and execution boundary, so the demo does not maintain one policy for the UI and another for agents. Dynamic registration uses the AbortSignal lifecycle: aborting the signal unregisters delete_item . Registration is transactional, and a browser-registration failure rolls back the local entry. The one-shot delete grant is consumed at policy decision time rather than after the handler finishes. This prevents two concurrent invocations of the same approved target from both receiving authorization. The application is static and has no backend, account, or database. Board state and receipts live only in browser localStorage . Testing and evidence The repository includes Node tests, a browser probe that exercises real getTools() / executeTool() in a compatible browser, and a recorded interactive WebMCP cycle using the public URL: add, list, request approval, human approval, one-shot delete, then dynamic unregistration. That interactive run is treated as an integration result, not as evidence of an uncoached fresh-agent run. Security limitation Doorman is not a sandbox, IAM system, or strong browser security boundary. The page's own JavaScript could bypass its wrapper. The project demonstrates a cooperative application-level authority policy and the browser-visible distinction between a registered and an unregistered WebMCP tool. title: Incident Relay
pitch: A WebMCP-native SRE workbench where agents investigate incidents and stage mitigations, while an explicit operator approval gate prevents unsafe execution.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native SRE workbench where agents investigate incidents and stage mitigations, while an explicit operator approval gate prevents unsafe execution. Like Comment Story Updates The exact rollback plan and blast radius require explicit UI confirmation. WebMCP calls surface APPROVAL_REQUIRED before operator approval. Recovery restores p95 to 352 ms and errors to 0.4%, with replay protection visible. Inspiration AI agents are becoming very good at reading telemetry, correlating deployments, and proposing fixes. Production incident response still has a hard boundary, though: investigating can be autonomous, but executing a mitigation must remain accountable. We built Incident Relay to show what an agent-native SRE workflow looks like when that boundary is part of the product instead of an instruction in a prompt. What it does Incident Relay is a fully client-side incident response workbench built around a simulated checkout regression. A checkout-api v1.8.43 deployment raises p95 latency from 352 ms to 2.84 seconds and the 5xx error rate from 0.4% to 8.7%. The interface brings the complete response context into one place: service health, SLO charts, alerts, logs, deployment diffs, diagnostics, an evidence timeline, a staged rollback, and an agent-drafted postmortem. The page registers seven typed WebMCP tools: get_incident_summary query_logs compare_deployments run_diagnostic stage_mitigation execute_approved_mitigation draft_postmortem Together they support the full flow: detect → investigate → stage mitigation → operator approval → execute → recover. The approval boundary The most important part of the project is what the agent cannot do. There is no approval tool. stage_mitigation can prepare the exact rollback proposal, but only the visible UI can write an operator-ui approval. Execution then revalidates the current incident phase, the staged mitigation ID, the approved mitigation ID, and the approval source. Agent-supplied fields such as approved: true are rejected, and replay attempts fail after execution begins. This makes the human confirmation a real application invariant rather than a conversational convention. How we built it The workbench uses React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. Recharts renders the SLO and recovery timeline, while a pure incident state machine owns the six legal phases. A shared controller connects React's useSyncExternalStore to the WebMCP handlers, so agent actions immediately update the visible UI. The WebMCP adapter wraps document.modelContext.registerTool() with official TypeScript declarations, strict Zod runtime schemas, JSON-serializable results, secure-context feature detection, and AbortSignal-based cleanup. Unsupported browsers receive a clear notice while the normal UI remains fully usable. Vitest covers state transitions, input validation, immutable snapshots, approval provenance, exact plan matching, registration cleanup, and replay prevention. GitHub Actions runs the suite and deploys the static app to GitHub Pages. Challenges we ran into The hardest design problem was separating staging from authorization without creating a token that an agent could manufacture. We solved it by keeping approval out of the WebMCP surface entirely and tying execution to live, frozen application state. We also had to treat tool input as untrusted even when a browser advertises JSON Schema. The browser schema helps agents call tools correctly, but Zod validation inside every handler remains the security boundary. Finally, WebMCP support is still browser-dependent, so the demo needed to be useful both with and without an agent connection. The same state machine now powers both paths. Accomplishments that we're proud of Seven WebMCP tools registered and verified in the live Chrome build A human approval gate an agent cannot bypass or replay A live activity feed populated only by genuine WebMCP invocations A polished responsive English workbench with no backend or paid APIs 45 passing tests covering workflow and security invariants A public, MIT-licensed repository and reproducible GitHub Pages deployment What we learned Agent-native UX is not a chat box added to an existing dashboard. It means exposing meaningful, typed actions while making authority boundaries visible and enforceable. We also learned that good tool descriptions, runtime schemas, state provenance, and lifecycle cleanup matter as much as the UI when a page becomes an agent surface. What's next The MVP deliberately uses deterministic data. A production version could add read-only adapters for observability platforms, signed deployment-provider actions, multi-operator approval, and persisted audit trails while keeping the same approval invariant and WebMCP contract. title: Pocket
pitch: Poker for humans and agents: WebMCP gives each player’s copilot live, seat-safe game state and returns its advice to the table, while the human makes every move.
about_excerpt: Poker for humans and agents: WebMCP gives each player’s copilot live, seat-safe game state and returns its advice to the table, while the human makes every move. Like Comment Story Updates Pocket - WebMCP Poker Live Game With Staged Recommendation Bring Your Own Copilot in Multiplayer WebMCP Copilot in a Live Hand Inspiration Most web applications are built for people. When an AI agent tries to help someone use one, it often has to reconstruct what is happening from the page, or depend on the user to explain everything correctly. I wanted to explore a different model: what does an application look like when a user can bring their own agent with them, and the application is designed to work with it? Poker turned out to be a great environment for testing that idea. A poker decision can depend on public information like the board and pot, private information like your hole cards, the complete history of the hand, exact rules about which actions are legal, and a game state that may change while an agent is still thinking. There are also multiple people interacting with the same application, each with a different view of what they are allowed to know. But there is another kind of context too: information that belongs to the player rather than the poker application. Your agent might know how you like to play, strategies you've been working on, your appetite for risk, previous hands you've discussed, or your own observations about the people you're playing with. Pocket shouldn't need to own that information in order for it to be useful. That led to Pocket: a playable Texas Hold'em game where every seat can have two minds - the player and their AI copilot. What it does Pocket lets you play Texas Hold'em against bots or with other people while using a compatible AI agent as a copilot during the hand. Normally, asking an AI for poker advice means explaining your cards, the board, pot, stacks, previous betting, and what you can do next. Pocket already knows all of those things, so it exposes them directly through three WebMCP tools: get_current_situation gives the agent the exact current game state, including the player's private cards, board, pot, stacks, whose turn it is, and the legal actions with precise raise limits. get_hand_history gives the agent Pocket's authoritative record of how the hand reached the current situation. stage_recommendation lets the agent send its recommended move and explanation back into Pocket's Copilot panel. That creates a full application → agent → application loop. Pocket supplies the facts about the game, the agent reasons over them, and its recommendation comes back into the interface where the player is actually making the decision. The important part is that Pocket doesn't have to be the agent. A user can bring an agent that has its own context, preferences, memory, or way of reasoning and combine that with authoritative state supplied by the application at the moment it's needed. Pocket knows the table. Your agent can know you. That separation is especially interesting to me from a privacy perspective. Personal strategy, notes about other players, previous conversations, and other private context don't need to become part of Pocket's user profile or database just so an AI feature can use them. The application can expose what it knows, while personal context can remain with the user's chosen agent. I also deliberately did not give the agent a tool for folding, checking, calling, or raising. It can recommend a move, but the player still has to make it. The goal is a copilot, not an autopilot. How I built it Pocket is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. At the center is a Texas Hold'em game engine that owns the authoritative state of each hand and determines which actions are currently legal. One of the most important architectural decisions was creating a seat-safe view of that state. The engine itself needs to know everyone's cards, but a player's interface, and their copilot, should only receive the information that particular player is entitled to see. The visible game and the WebMCP tools are both derived from that same player-safe state. That means the agent isn't getting a privileged version of the game behind the scenes. I kept the WebMCP surface intentionally small. The three tools basically correspond to three useful questions: What is happening right now? How did we get here? What does the agent recommend? Pocket also tracks the game, hand, and state version. When the agent returns a recommendation, Pocket verifies that it still belongs to the current situation before displaying it. If someone has acted and the table has moved on, the old recommendation is rejected instead of being presented as current advice. Beyond the WebMCP integration, I built bot games, real-time multiplayer rooms, persistent game sessions, responsive table layouts, game history, visible copilot activity, and a deterministic demo flow so the complete interaction can be experienced reliably. Pocket is deployed on Vercel, with unit, integration, and browser tests covering the poker flow, privacy boundaries, WebMCP contracts, multiplayer behavior, and the end-to-end demo. Challenges I ran into Keeping private information private Poker made the permission problem impossible to ignore. The engine has to know everyone's cards, but a particular player obviously shouldn't. I didn't want to expose the raw game state and trust the agent not to use fields it wasn't supposed to see. Instead, I built a seat-specific projection that only contains information available to that player. There were some less obvious cases too, like showdown, where cards that were private earlier in the hand may legitimately become public. Multiplayer also made this feel like more than a theoretical concern. Every player can occupy the same shared game while still having a different private view of it, and potentially a completely different copilot with its own private context. Keeping recommendations synchronized with a live game Poker state can change quickly, and the game doesn't stop while the agent is thinking. A recommendation could be correct when the request starts but already be stale by the time it comes back because another player acted or the hand moved to the next street. I solved that by explicitly versioning the state and binding each recommendation to the game, hand, and exact state it was created from. Pocket validates that again before showing the recommendation. Keeping the WebMCP lifecycle stable This caused one of the more frustrating bugs during development. The table's React state changes constantly as players act, turns advance, and cards are dealt. My first implementation tied the WebMCP tool registration too closely to that changing state, which meant tools could be repeatedly removed and registered during normal gameplay. I eventually separated the stable tool lifecycle from the changing game data. The tools stay registered while the table is active, but read the latest authoritative state whenever they are invoked. Deciding what the agent should actually be allowed to do I could have exposed a tool that lets the agent make the poker move itself. Technically, that would have been pretty easy. But that isn't the interaction I wanted Pocket to demonstrate. There is an important difference between giving an agent useful capabilities and handing over every consequential action. stage_recommendation became that boundary: the agent can participate visibly in the live application, but the final move still belongs to the player. Making the integration visible without turning Pocket into a developer demo A technically correct tool exchange isn't automatically understandable to the person using the product. I spent a lot of time iterating on how the table, game history, player controls, WebMCP activity, and Copilot panel fit together. I wanted someone looking at Pocket to understand that an agent is actually participating in the application without making the entire product look like a tool inspector. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that Pocket doesn't just demonstrate an agent calling a tool. It demonstrates a much richer relationship between an application, a user, and the agent that user chooses to bring with them. Pocket is a real multiplayer game with real hidden information, changing state, history, rules, permissions, and decisions. That gave me a chance to explore several things I find genuinely exciting about WebMCP in one product. A player's copilot doesn't have to guess what is happening from the screen. Pocket can give it the exact state of the game and the exact actions that are legal. At the same time, that agent only receives the private information its player is entitled to see. In a multiplayer game, every person can be looking at the same shared table while their agent receives a different, permissioned view of it. title: Pursuit Permit
pitch: New facts need new authority.
about_excerpt: New facts need new authority. Like Comment Story Updates New evidence makes the £900k bid qualify, but the active permit survives: active_permit_conflict, 0h moved. The first permit call returns approval_required. No WebMCP tool can approve, and the page checkpoint still commits 0h. The flight recorder shows seven native WebMCP calls ending in a failed-closed capacity conflict. Pursuit Permit: recommendations can change without yesterday's approval drifting to a different bid. People approve snapshots; agents keep recomputing. Pursuit Permit lets recommendations update without letting permission drift. The £900k bid now qualifies. The active £750k / 32-hour permit does not change. active_permit_conflict . Zero hours moved. Inspiration A browser agent can discover new evidence in the same page where it can propose spending a scarce bid-team slot. The dangerous ambiguity is not ranking. It appears later: does yesterday's approval follow today's newly correct recommendation? Most approval demos end when approval is granted. Pursuit Permit starts where that becomes dangerous: after the facts change. It is a fixed, synthetic procurement replay of one narrow protocol—recommend, approve an exact revision, issue a bounded permit, and later re-prove the decision without inheriting yesterday's authority. What it does The demo gives every judge the same reproducible two-act decision: Five page-owned WebMCP tools search, compare, shortlist, issue, and retest. The apparent £900,000 winner fails two mandatory gates, so the eligible £750,000 alternative is proposed for the team's only 32-hour bid slot. issue_pursuit_permit returns structured approval_required . It creates no permit and commits no capacity. The registered tool surface intentionally exposes no approval endpoint. A visibly separate page checkpoint, labeled NOT AN AGENT TOOL , records an unverified reviewer label against the exact bid, allocation, evidence revision, and decision revision. Approval still commits zero hours. Only a matching WebMCP retry issues one idempotent, revision-bound permit and changes 32 hours from proposed to committed. A second page-only demo action revises the synthetic bidder evidence. Both reopening conditions stored in the historical receipt now pass, so the £900,000 bid becomes the better recommendation. retest_pursuit_permit(receiptId) re-proves the old receipt against the new facts and names the still-active permit the candidate would displace. It creates no new authority. A forced shortlist fails closed with active_permit_conflict . The original £750,000 permit survives. Zero hours move. The values, opportunities, evidence, and staffing hours are deterministic demo fixtures—not live procurement data, measured savings, staffing advice, verified identity, or production authorization. Why WebMCP This proof cannot live only in chat. The five imperative WebMCP tools and the React interface share one client-side controller. Every call changes the same opportunity rows, evidence panel, shortlist, capacity rail, checkpoint, receipt, and chain-of-custody ledger the reviewer sees. The built-in proof console exposes all five registered tools, the chronological invocation count, and selected request/response evidence. WebMCP therefore makes the state machine inspectable: an agent can re-evaluate and propose, encounter a machine-readable stop, retry after a visible checkpoint, and later discover that a better recommendation still lacks authority to displace an active permit. How we built it Pursuit Permit uses React 19, TypeScript, Vite, strict Zod schemas, and the official webmcp-types package. Motion provides causal rank transitions and checkpoint-to-receipt continuity; NumberFlow handles the changing leader value; Rough Notation marks the defeated pursuit and failed clauses. Locally bundled IBM Plex fonts keep the interface self-contained. The controller validates every tool boundary and produces immutable state shared by UI and WebMCP. Approval binds the shortlist, allocation, exact evidence content, opportunity details, bidder profile, evidence revision, and decision revision. Idempotency keys cannot replay across revisions, one approval fingerprint can create only one receipt, and relevant state changes invalidate approval. The active permit is stored separately from the new working proposal, so reopened evidence cannot erase or silently replace it. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was separating planned , proposed , approved , and committed . Comparison may calculate a 32-hour move; shortlist may propose it; the page checkpoint may record approval. Only permit issuance can change committed capacity. The second was making retest useful without making it dangerous. New evidence must be allowed to prove that the recommendation changed, but it must not rewrite history or let a reopened tender steal an already committed slot. The third was visual: the safety property had to be visible in seconds. We used an evidence thread, physical rank reversal, NO-BID stamp, capacity rail, distinct reviewer checkpoint, permit seal, green reopening thread, and a proof-mode flight recorder so the product demonstrates the boundary instead of merely claiming it. Accomplishments that we're proud of Five discoverable, page-owned WebMCP tools operating on the same state the judge sees. A structured approval_required stop with 0h committed and no exposed approval tool. One exact approved retry that issues a proof-carrying permit and commits 32 demo hours. A historical-receipt retest followed by active_permit_conflict , preserving the active permit and moving 0h . Keyboard-only operation, reduced motion, forced-colors support, focus-managed modal inspection, and 320px reflow. A verified release gate: 129 unit/integration checks, 42 applicable browser checks, 87.55% statement coverage, 80.56% branch coverage, production build, lint, typecheck, and zero dependency-audit vulnerabilities. What we learned An agent becomes more useful when its state transitions are narrower than its recommendations. ‘Approved’ and ‘committed’ are not synonyms, and a receipt is most valuable when it can be re-tested without becoming a blank cheque. What's next A production version would ingest licensed procurement data, use a permissioned company evidence library, attach source-level provenance, authenticate reviewers, integrate with real staffing systems, and define explicit revocation and supersession rules. Those are roadmap items, not capabilities claimed by this challenge build. title: ShopCanvas
pitch: ShopCanvas turns agent requests into visible, live changes on an adaptive bento storefront, making WebMCP feel like a conversation with the website itself.
about_excerpt: ShopCanvas turns agent requests into visible, live changes on an adaptive bento storefront, making WebMCP feel like a conversation with the website itself. Like Comment Story Updates ShopCanvas: a visual WebMCP storefront. compare_products presents key tradeoffs side by side. inspect_product expands product details within stable bento cells. show_reviews filters critical low-light feedback. search_products reshapes the catalog around the request. Inspiration Shopping online often means repeatedly leaving the product you are considering. Specifications live in one section, reviews farther down the page, comparisons somewhere else, and the cart on another route. That visual travel creates cognitive travel: shoppers must remember their original question while the interface continuously changes context. At the same time, browser agents can feel disconnected from the websites they operate. Actions happen in the background, and users only see the final response in a chat. ShopCanvas began with a question: what if using an agent felt like having a conversation directly with the website? We wanted every request to produce an immediate, understandable visual response on one shared surface. What it does ShopCanvas is a fictional camera store presented as an adaptive bento-grid workspace. Users can ask a browser agent to: Search and sort products Focus on a specific camera Compare multiple cameras Filter product reviews Update a local mock cart ShopCanvas exposes these capabilities through five imperative WebMCP tools: search_products , inspect_product , compare_products , show_reviews , and set_cart_quantity . Every tool call visibly affects the page. The relevant cells expand smoothly, receive a temporary highlight, and display an acknowledgement naming the agent’s action. An accessible live region also announces what changed. All seven cells remain mounted in permanent grid positions. They expand or contract without teleporting, reordering, or appearing from nowhere. Dense content scrolls inside its cell while the overall page remains fitted to the viewport. Manual controls and agent actions use the same state transitions, so the user and agent always share one source of truth. A Back control restores previous canvas states, while session data persists locally between reloads. How we built it ShopCanvas is a static React and TypeScript application built with Vinext, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Zustand, Motion, and AJV. The mock catalog, reviews, product names, and imagery are bundled locally. There is no authentication, backend database, payment processing, or checkout flow. WebMCP tools are registered from the top-level document using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool includes: A bounded JSON Schema Runtime AJV validation Rejection of unknown properties Cancellation support Concise, JSON-serializable results A visible UI acknowledgement A result returned only after the interface commits the change Both manual interactions and WebMCP calls dispatch the same semantic store actions. Session state is versioned and persisted in localStorage . Agent mutations are serialized, and cancelled operations use guarded rollback logic to avoid corrupting later changes. Because reviews represent user-generated content, review results are explicitly marked with untrustedContentHint: true . We used Playwright to validate the interface across desktop, tablet, mobile, and short-laptop viewports. Tests cover all five tools, persistence, malformed input, cancellation, concurrent calls, keyboard navigation, internal scrolling, fixed panel identity, responsive geometry, and visual regressions. A separate native-browser test discovers and executes the tools through the browser’s real document.modelContext implementation. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was preserving spatial continuity. Our early layouts replaced and reordered cells whenever the user entered a new state. Although functional, the result felt abrupt and contradicted the core idea of a stable workspace. We redesigned the grid so every cell has a permanent named slot. State changes now animate only the grid-track dimensions, allowing panels to expand and contract without being removed or moved. Fitting seven useful panels inside one viewport was another significant challenge. We avoided shrinking text until it became unreadable. Instead, each cell received a carefully bounded layout and its own keyboard-accessible scrolling region. We also had to coordinate asynchronous tool execution with visible feedback. Updating application state was not enough: the tool result needed to wait until the user could actually see the committed interface. Cancellation, overlapping calls, local persistence, and manual actions all had to remain consistent. Finally, WebMCP is still an evolving draft. We needed to accommodate differences between the current specification and native browser implementations while keeping the public tool surface small, predictable, and testable. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that ShopCanvas makes agent activity visible without turning the interface into a debug console. Every successful tool call has a clear visual consequence: The action is named The affected cells are highlighted The content changes on screen The grid resizes smoothly The tool waits for the visible commit The user can reverse the state with Back We also maintained the identity and position of all seven panels across every state transition. The same interface works from a 320-pixel mobile viewport through desktop layouts without introducing page-level scrolling. The complete application uses fictional data and original visual assets, requires no account, and remains fully usable through manual controls when WebMCP is unavailable. What we learned We learned that good agentic UX is not only about exposing capable tools. Users need to understand what the agent changed, where it changed, and whether the action completed. Tool schemas are also part of the user experience. Small, bounded tools produced more predictable behavior than one large tool with many ambiguous responsibilities. Another important lesson was that a state update and a visible UI update are not the same event. Waiting for the interface to commit made the interaction feel significantly more trustworthy. Most importantly, spatial stability matters. When panels retain their location, users can build a mental map of the interface even while its proportions change. What's next for ShopCanvas Next, we would like to explore: Additional fictional product categories and workspace compositions Optional adapters for real product data Agent explanations showing why an item matched a request User-defined layout constraints beyond cart pinning Saved comparison workspaces Collaborative sessions across devices Richer accessibility preferences for motion, contrast, and density More advanced multi-step shopping workflows We also want to continue refining ShopCanvas alongside the evolving WebMCP specification. The long-term goal is broader than e-commerce: to explore websites as adaptive, shared canvases where people and agents collaborate visibly instead of exchanging commands with hidden background processes. title: mimir
pitch: Where humans and ai study together - A local-first pdf reader workspace where the agent marks up the page with you, for you. Every edit is attributable and undoable.
about_excerpt: Where humans and ai study together - A local-first pdf reader workspace where the agent marks up the page with you, for you. Every edit is attributable and undoable. Like Comment Story Updates Opening a Pdf Landing Page Webmcp Usage - II Webmcp Usage - I Webmcp Usage - III Walkthrough Tour Inspiration Me and my friends have been using Preview (the macos app) extensively past years, where we are constantly reading research papers, lecture notes. Annotations, sticky notes, mind maps constitute a big part of our learning, but we have faced constant issues in Preview, ranging from random crashes, ram usage bloat, and biggest being inability to quickly search or modify any annotation. And there is no current satisfactory alternative available. So building a web alternative was something which was on my mind for a long time, and when I came to know about this webmcp challenge, I was excited by the ability to actually bring this vision to reality. What it does mimir (named after Norse God of Wisdom) is a local-native pdf reading workspace that runs entirely in your browser. You open a paper, highlight it, draw on it, pin sticky notes to it, and export an annotated copy anytime. But the interesting highlight, and which is relevant to the challenge, is that the opened document is a live tool surface. Your browser agent can do everything you can, much better and (for the most part) faster. It can search a pdf, read and navigate to specific pages, create any custom annotation you want. Sure, summarising and learning from pdf via chat tools like Chatgpt works, but there are a lot of people (researchers, lawyers, students preparing for their competitive exams, to name a few) who are visual learners, and value reading pdf the old fashioned way, but also want agentic capabilities to let their agent handle that part for you. mimir is built exactly for them, for this collaboration, and this is where browser native mcp in the form of webmcp holds a significant role. How we built it Tanstack start with react 19 and vite, typescript throught, bun for the toolchain, and tailwind v4 for styling interface. The initial cut was simple, pdf.js renders pages and extracts text in a web worker. pdf-lib draws annotations back into the original vector pages on export, so sticky notes come out as numbered pins with a comments appendix. As this is a local-first app, we heavily utilise IndexedDB (via Dexie) for the pdf and chat storage, while local storage is used to store user preferences etc. Zustand holds the editor state. Tools are registered in two scopes. Library tools ( list_documents , open_document ) are always live, so an agent that lands on the home page has somewhere to begin. 14 document tools register when a pdf is opened and deregistered on close - reading text, search, outline, navigation, annotation CRUD operations, context lookup around a mark, undo, export. Every tool's published json schema is generated from the zod schema that validates its input, so the contract it an agent reads is exactly the contract which is held. Ensures that agent never drifts from what it intended. Also, just wanna highlight, I felt there were 3 things it could achieve that a server-side MCP server could not, or atleast not that "beautifully". The tool surface is scoped to what is on screen. Document tools only exist while a document is open. An agent cannot annotate a file you closed, because the tool for it is not registered. Agent edits go through the human command path. There is no separate agent write path. create_annotations runs the same transaction a mouse drag runs, lands as one undo step, and is attributed. If the agent gets it wrong, ctrl+z. Consent stays where the consequences are. delete_annotations will not touch marks the reader made unless the caller explicitly opts in. prepare_export opens the export panel and stops. The human clicks save. The agent can do the tedious ninety percent and still cannot write a file to your disk on its own. Challenges we ran into Errors do not cross the agent boundary. A tool that throws hands the caller "the script function threw an error" and nothing else. An agent given no reason does not stop, it guesses, retries with a different irrelevant field, and then reports the guess to the reader as fact. Every tool in mimir now returns failures as data: a flag and one readable sentence with a recovery hint. Zod issues get flattened into field paths a model can act on. This one change did more for reliability than any prompt I wrote. Getting an agent to stay in bounds. Early on, asking for a summary would get me a summary plus eleven highlights nobody asked for. Some of that is prompting, but most of it is contract design: batch limits (twenty marks a call), geometry fixed by subtype through a discriminated union so a rectangle cannot arrive carrying line endpoints, and tool descriptions that say what to call first and what a failure means rather than just naming parameters. Availability. WebMCP needs a flag or an origin trial today, and a demo that only works on one machine is not a demo. So the tools are tracked locally as well as registered, and the app ships its own chat sidebar that calls the exact same tool objects through an in-page path. The sidebar reads the live catalogue with getTools() rather than a hardcoded list, so it is genuinely exercising the WebMCP surface and not a parallel API. The UI says which path a call took. Pixel-perfect PDF annotations Though not exactly related to WebMCP, working with PDF annotations and ensuring each annotation respects the render it is intended to be was pretty challenging in itself, more so forcing agent to do the same. Codex computer use plus webmcp debug logging helped a lot here. Accomplishments that we're proud of There were times when for some unknown reasons I wasn't able to properly test my webapp in the chatgpt app's in-built browser (stating it doesnt have access to webmcp capabilities). So I decided to build a built in webmcp chatbar in my web app as well. It was fun architecturing how to emulate webmcp there, but with couple of iterations I was able to achieve this. Essentially it follows a chat app using tanstack-ai to call gpt-5.6-luna api. For any user prompt, the LLM in itself has access to list_webmcp_tools mcp, allowing it to discover what all webmcp tools are present, and it returns relevant tool to call along with input args. Then on client side, the mcp toolcall execution takes place and output is relayed back to llm. In this way, entire processing works on client side only. Also so, I went one step further, and in case browser doesnt support webmcp, it is still artificially simulated (by calling tool function directly instead of going via document.modelContext route). So it makes the platform a beast. What we learned I learned a lot from the project. I had some experience building mcp agents before, but working with webmcp forces you to think mcp interactions from frontend perspective, how to achieve things in the DOM without relying on any backend call. So it was an extremely fun web design learning tbh. Plus this was my first time working with pdfs and vector graphic overlays, so I learned a lot of stuff about optimising the page renders and things to take care of for a seamless user experience. What's next for mimir I plan to build mimir to a fully fledged product in the coming days - few things like introducing file upload, voice chat, cloud storage and obsidian are on my mind, which would highly be beneficial for the target audience of the product. title: SignWise
pitch: AI contract review in the live signing workflow—without giving the agent authority to sign.
about_excerpt: AI contract review in the live signing workflow—without giving the agent authority to sign. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Electronic signing made the final click easy, but it did not make dense agreements easier to understand. Important terms such as automatic renewal, indemnification, liability caps, and data-retention requirements are still easy to overlook. We wanted to explore a specific question: what if an AI agent could help inside the signing experience itself, while the webpage—not the agent— continued to control consent and signature authority? That makes agreement review a strong fit for WebMCP. The agent needs more than a detached document API. It benefits from knowing which agreement and clause the person is viewing, the current review state, and whether an exact proposal has received human approval. ## What it does SignWise is a WebMCP-enabled agreement-review workspace built around a twelve-page fixture contract. A person can ask an agent to review the agreement in ordinary language. Through tools exposed by the live webpage, the agent can: Inspect agreement metadata and its clause index. Read individual clauses. Add evidence-linked risk findings beside relevant clauses. Prepare a concise, editable review. Record the exact review revision approved by the person. Every tool call appears in the page’s activity feed. When the agent flags a clause, the document scrolls to that page and displays the finding beside its evidence. The agent cannot accept terms, acknowledge clauses, approve its own proposal, or sign the agreement. The final signature control remains available only to the human through the interface. ## How we built it SignWise uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with local fixture data so the demonstration remains repeatable. The React interface and WebMCP tools call the same underlying application service. This avoids creating one behavior for humans and a separate simulated behavior for agents. When a tool changes application state, React updates immediately. WebMCP registration is isolated behind a small adapter using document.modelContext. The available tool surface changes with the live workflow: The agreement view begins with four safe inspection tools. Opening the review workspace adds flag_clause and propose_review. Human approval exposes record_approved_review for that exact proposal. After recording, the temporary capability disappears and the surface returns to four tools. The review record contains the approved revision, linked finding identifiers, timestamp, and agreement fingerprint. Editing an approved proposal revokes its approval, and recording is protected against duplicate execution. We tested the application service and WebMCP lifecycle with Vitest. Playwright tests exercise the complete browser workflow, including dynamic tool discovery, visible state changes, approval boundaries, mobile behavior, and operation without WebMCP support. The production application is deployed on Cloudflare. ## Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was deciding where useful agent action ends and legally meaningful human intent begins. Making every action require confirmation would weaken the workflow. Allowing the agent to approve or sign would make the experience unsafe. We separated investigation and preparation from consent: the agent may annotate and propose, while only a person may approve an exact revision or continue to signature. Dynamic tool registration also required careful lifecycle management. A tool being visible is not sufficient authorization, so every state-changing operation validates the current application state again when executed. Another challenge was keeping the demonstration honest. The agreement analysis comes from the agent reading clauses through WebMCP; it is not a hidden deterministic risk scanner. The fixture contract makes the run reproducible, while the visible activity feed shows the actual tool sequence. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that SignWise feels like a coherent human-and-agent product rather than a collection of tool callbacks. The strongest parts are: Evidence appears directly beside the clause that supports it. Agent actions visibly update the live interface. Tool availability reflects page context and human authorization. Approval applies to one exact review revision and is revoked by edits. The final record is bound to the agreement fingerprint. Signing remains an exclusively human action. The complete workflow runs through native ChatGPT Site Tools on the deployed application. The result is a practical example of an agent helping with a consequential workflow without impersonating the person making the decision. ## What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the webpage contributes context and authority that a detached API does not naturally possess. The important innovation is not simply exposing more buttons as tools. It is allowing the live application to offer the right capabilities at the right moment, publish their effects visibly, and withdraw temporary capabilities when their purpose is complete. We also learned that human approval should be treated as versioned state rather than a conversational assumption. “Approved” is meaningful only when the application can identify exactly what was approved and verify that it has not changed. Finally, visible agent activity is part of the product experience. It helps people understand what the agent inspected, what it changed, and where the evidence came from. ## What's next for SignWise The next step is replacing fixture data with real document parsing while preserving the same consent boundaries. Future versions could add: Organization-specific contract policies and playbooks. Suggested redlines and alternative language. Comparisons between agreement versions. Approval routing to legal, procurement, or security teams. Version invalidation when an agreement changes. Authorized integration with an e-signature sandbox. Persistent review records and signer-side identity controls. The long-term goal is not autonomous signing. It is a better informed signing process where agents investigate and prepare, applications enforce boundaries, and people retain authority over consequential decisions. title: CashLatch
pitch: Manage your money with ChatGPT- while CashLatch protects your limits and keeps you in control.
about_excerpt: Manage your money with ChatGPT- while CashLatch protects your limits and keeps you in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Managing money often means checking balances, remembering bills, tracking savings goals and doing the same calculations repeatedly. ChatGPT can help compare options, but a normal conversation does not automatically know what is currently saved in a financial tool. It may also continue using an old recommendation after the balance or bills have changed. I built CashLatch to connect these two parts. ChatGPT helps the user understand their options, while CashLatch keeps the current information, checks the user’s limits and requires approval before recording a recommendation. What CashLatch does CashLatch is a browser-based money workspace where users can: Track their current balance, expected income and expenses. Add monthly bills with amounts and due dates. Create savings goals and monitor their progress. Choose the minimum balance they want to keep. Limit how much one recommendation can put toward goals. See how their balance may change over 30, 60 and 90 days. Use different currencies and separate money workspaces. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can read the money workspace currently open in CashLatch. It can calculate what the goals need, estimate future balances, compare different funding options and prepare a recommendation on the webpage. The user can review the exact amount, where it will go and how much money may remain. ChatGPT cannot approve the recommendation for them. After the user approves it, ChatGPT can apply only that exact recommendation, and only once. If the balance, bills, goals or limits change, CashLatch cancels the old approval. ChatGPT must read the updated information and prepare a new recommendation. CashLatch is a planning workspace. Applying a recommendation updates its local records; it does not transfer real bank funds. How I built it CashLatch is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript modules. The interface is responsive and includes money workspaces, currency selection, monthly bills, savings goals, transactions, balance estimates, safety limits and recent activity. The app uses the WebMCP imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool . It provides tools that let ChatGPT: Read the open money workspace. Add or update savings goals. Add or update monthly bills. Record income and expenses. Estimate future balances. Calculate how much each goal needs. Check different ways to fund goals. Prepare a recommendation for review. Propose safety-limit changes without applying them. A recommendation cannot be applied immediately. When the user approves an exact recommendation on the webpage, CashLatch temporarily creates a one-time apply tool for it. Before applying, CashLatch checks the latest balance, bills and safety limits again. The approval expires after five minutes, disappears after one use and is cancelled by any financial change. A SHA-256 fingerprint helps CashLatch detect whether the information used for approval has changed. Money-workspace data is stored in the browser using localStorage . CashLatch does not require an external financial database or an OpenAI API key. Challenges I faced The biggest challenge was making WebMCP useful instead of simply adding chat controls to a webpage. The important difference is not that ChatGPT can calculate a recommendation. It is that ChatGPT can work with the information currently open in CashLatch, while the website independently checks the result and keeps the user in control. Another challenge was designing the approval flow. The first version used technical terms such as staging, allocation, authorization and stale state. These were difficult for normal users to understand. I replaced them with clearer terms such as recommendation, money added to goals, approve, apply once and needs an update. I also worked through browser permissions, dynamic tool registration, local persistence, responsive navigation, form contrast, graph readability and clear monthly-bill presentation. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when the website remains responsible for its own data and rules. ChatGPT is good at understanding a request and comparing options. CashLatch is responsible for checking the numbers, showing the exact result and requiring user approval. I also learned that approval should depend on current information. If the user’s money changes after approval, continuing with the old recommendation may no longer be appropriate. Finally, I learned that a technically correct workflow is not enough. The interface and tool responses must use language that non-technical users can understand. What I am proud of CashLatch demonstrates a complete WebMCP workflow: ChatGPT reads the open money workspace. It compares multiple ways to fund a goal. CashLatch checks the recommendation against monthly bills and safety limits. The user reviews and approves the exact recommendation. A financial change cancels that approval. ChatGPT prepares a new recommendation using the latest information. The newly approved recommendation can be applied once. The balance, goal progress, confirmation and recent activity are updated. This gives ChatGPT useful access without giving it unlimited control. What’s next The next steps are broader browser testing, improved accessibility and clearer first-time guidance. Future versions could also support optional encrypted cross-device sync and connections to external financial services. These would require proper authentication, consent and additional security controls. title: Dhwani - a support desk whose forms are the tools
pitch: A support desk built on WebMCP's declarative API - three of eight tools are plain HTML forms with no JavaScript, and one HTML attribute decides who submits.
about_excerpt: A support desk built on WebMCP's declarative API - three of eight tools are plain HTML forms with no JavaScript, and one HTML attribute decides who submits. Like Comment Story Updates The support desk: order-linked returns, warranty, forms Tool console: get_support_policy called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: three of eight tools are plain HTML forms using the declarative toolname / toolautosubmit API - no JavaScript tool registration for those three. Inspiration A customer with a fuzzy need - "my new headphones crackle, return or warranty?" - doesn't know which form applies. We wanted the site's own forms to answer that, instead of a chatbot re-explaining policy in prose. What it does The agent reads orders and policy, says which form applies and why, and fills it through the form itself. Three of the desk's eight tools are <form toolname tooldescription> elements whose controls carry toolparamdescription - Chrome derives the JSON schema straight from the markup and fills the controls; the page never writes those values. Whether a form submits itself is controlled by one attribute: request_return has no toolautosubmit , so a human must press Submit; file_warranty_claim and schedule_pickup carry it, because a click undoes either one. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript. The page handles submit with event.preventDefault() , and when event.agentInvoked is true, responds via event.respondWith(Promise) . Five imperative read tools share the same invoke() chokepoint the three forms' Submit handler uses. A getTools() probe shims any form Chrome doesn't register natively, so every judge's browser gets all eight tools regardless of native declarative support, and a status pill says which mode is active. Challenges we ran into Chrome fires toolactivated around a declarative tool call, but its exact target and bubbling behavior are undocumented - we ended up listening in two places (a capture listener on window and the identical handler on document.modelContext ) to catch it reliably either way. Separately, the very shim that covers non-native browsers had its own bug: getTools() can't distinguish a real native registration from the shim's own echo of itself, which caused a silent register/unregister oscillation - measured at roughly 145,000 cycles in three seconds before it was caught and fixed with an occurrence-count comparison instead of a name-presence check. Accomplishments that we're proud of A confirmation boundary expressed in markup - the presence or absence of one HTML attribute - rather than in a prompt instruction a model could ignore or a developer could forget to re-add. What we learned The declarative API pushes real complexity into event-timing edge cases (activation ordering, shim-vs-native detection) that don't exist in the imperative registerTool path - worth it for forms that need zero JavaScript, but not free. What's next Extending the declarative pattern to the pickup-scheduling calendar itself, so date/slot selection is also derivable straight from markup instead of a small script. How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Dhwani - a support desk whose forms are the tools Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content). title: Loomlace
pitch: Loomlace turns bespoke jewellery design into something you and your agent do together, live. It handles the precise geometry, you keep the taste, and nothing leaves your browser until you order.
about_excerpt: Loomlace turns bespoke jewellery design into something you and your agent do together, live. It handles the precise geometry, you keep the taste, and nothing leaves your browser until you order. Like Comment Story Updates Agent editing the design Agent made the order Inspiration We're actually running an early-stage jewellery business on the side with Shopify, so this isn't a random pick for a hackathon theme, it's a problem we already deal with. Bespoke jewellery design kinda bad right now, honestly. Two options we know: Fiddle with a rigid configurator by yourself till you give up, or Email a jeweller a description and wait days per round. Same root problem both times: the design lives in one place, and only one side gets to touch it at a time. We were also just tired of the usual "AI design demo" pattern, where the agent either describes a change and you go make it, or it takes the wheel completely and hands you a finished thing. That's not really collab, it's a queue with extra steps. WebMCP was the first thing we'd seen where a page could expose its live state + actions to an agent sitting right there in the browser w/ you, so both of you could actually have hands on the same object at once. A ring felt like a great test case because it's precise and parametric (agent territory) but still fundamentally about taste (very much not agent territory). Ask it for "three halo variants under £900 in white gold" and it's great. Ask it for "a bit more to the left, no less than that" and good luck. What it does Loomlace is a ring configurator where you and an agent design on one live canvas. Live at loomlace.vercel.app , go try it. You drag the stone, resize the band, pick metals, w/ your hands. The agent calls the same store actions for the parametric/combinatorial stuff: resizing, re-costing, generating variations. You keep the taste calls, it keeps the math. Nothing leaves the browser until you hit Review this ring and add to cart. That one matters more than it sounds like, bc engraving text is often the most private sentence someone types that month (a name, a date, an inside joke) and we didn't want any of that touching a server before you actually order. Why WebMCP, specifically A ring design is a rich, stateful, client-side thing, and that turns out to make it a bad fit for basically every other way an agent could touch it, but a great fit for WebMCP: Server-side MCP can't see it. The design lives in the browser as you're dragging things around. A server tool would either be working off a stale copy or forcing every drag through a round trip. A browser extension would just be DOM-poking. Generic click-and-scrape has no clue that widthMm is clamped 1.2 to 4.0mm, that x is a normalised position around the band, or that a halo needs a centre stone first. WebMCP lets us publish all that as actual schema instead of hoping a script guesses right. The data's personal. Again, engraving text, names, dates, jokes. Tools that run entirely in-page means nothing's transmitted until added to cart, and we say that on screen too, not just in a privacy policy nobody reads. The thing that actually decides it though is co-presence. The agent calls the exact same store actions the sliders call, so an agent edit and a human drag land on one surface instead of two copies fighting each other. What's actually new here Normally an agent either describes a change and waits for you to make it, or takes the wheel entirely and hands back a finished thing. Loomlace does neither. You drag the stone where it feels right. The agent reads the new position through get_design_state and builds the halo around it. Mid-demo proof: agent's partway through restyling, you drag the centre stone, and its next call sees the new spot and builds on it instead of overwriting it. Works because the design has one home and you both reach it through the same door. The tools themselves change as the design matures. add_engraving doesn't exist until a setting's been committed to - nothing to engrave otherwise. The agent gets a toolchange event and re-reads the list, so it only ever sees tools that actually make sense right now. How we built it Ten tools, wired straight into the page. Any agent visiting the site can see and call them - no separate backend, no config screen. The decision that mattered most: the ring's state lives in one place, always "live," kept deliberately outside our UI framework's normal state tracking. We didn't do this at first, and it bit us - an agent's instructions get built once but might not run for a bit, so reading state the normal React way meant it could act on a version of the ring that no longer existed. Moving the source of truth outside React fixed it: every tool call now reads the ring exactly as it is, not as it was when the agent's turn started. That one fix carries everything else: Pricing and rendering don't know or care whether a slider drag or a tool call triggered them - same code path, so the two can't drift apart. Tools register and unregister cleanly as the page updates, no stale ones left behind. Every agent input gets double-checked and clamped on our side, not trusted blindly. Stack: Next.js, React, TypeScript, three.js for the 3D ring. Challenges we ran into The worst bug was the one that never crashed. Silent stale state. If a human dragged the stone mid-agent-turn, the agent's edit could quietly build on the old position - no error, just a subtly wrong ring. We only caught it by testing that exact scenario on purpose. Fixing where state lived solved it; the scary part was how invisible it was. Chrome vs. spec. Chrome's actual behaviour didn't match WebMCP's spec for passing a tool's input, so calls failed with a vague error and no clue why. Took a while to realise it was Chrome, not us. Documented it once we knew, so it doesn't cost anyone else the hours. Accomplishments that we're proud of The co-presence demo isn't staged, it actually works. Human drags the stone mid-agent-turn, agent's next call reads the new position and builds around it instead of stomping on it. That's the moment the whole submission hangs on, and it's real, not narrated over in a voiceover. The tool surface grows up along with the design: add_engraving doesn't show up until there's something worth engraving. Small thing, but it's what stops the agent from ever offering something the app can't back up yet. What we learned The real problem in agent-native UI isn't "can the agent call a function." It's "does the agent see the same truth the human does, at the same time." Store location, the toolchange event, handlers returning resulting state - every real decision we made was that one question in a different costume. Co-presence beats capability. Also, the hard way: a browser's implementation of a spec ≠ the spec. Chrome 152's executeTool disagrees with the actual IDL, and the error doesn't tell you which side is "wrong." If you're building against WebMCP right now, test against the real browser, not just the doc. What's next for Loomlace More materials & cuts : catalogue's small on purpose for the demo, but pricing/rendering were built to scale up w/o new code paths. Multi-item designs : pairs (engagement + wedding band), matching sets, places where the agent's combinatorial side matters even more than on a single ring. Persisted, shareable designs : right now a design lives for one browser session. Letting someone send a link to a jeweller or partner is the obvious next move, just needs doing carefully so it doesn't wreck the "nothing leaves the browser till checkout" thing. A real store integration , swapping out the current placeholder NEXT_PUBLIC_STORE_URL so add_to_cart actually goes somewhere. Voice as a second input , alongside typing and dragging, for when both hands are busy turning the ring on screen.
