title: Toolsmith
pitch: An agent can only press the buttons a website gives it. Toolsmith lets it build the one that's missing — and lets you decide whether it keeps it.
about_excerpt: An agent can only press the buttons a website gives it. Toolsmith lets it build the one that's missing — and lets you decide whether it keeps it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration An AI agent can only press the buttons a website gives it — and those were decided by whoever built the site, months ago. When the button you need isn't one of them, the agent does what agents do: it guesses from the DOM, it scrapes, or it hands you a snippet of Python and hopes you run it. Adding a real one today means leaving the conversation entirely: write an MCP server, host it, edit a config file, restart the client. Minutes to days of work, and a permanent new attack surface, for a function you might call once. WebMCP already moved the button surface into the page — where the user's data and session already live, and where a human is already watching. That's enough to close the loop without leaving. (A note on vocabulary: we say "button" in the interface because that's what it is to the person looking at the screen. The spec calls the same thing a tool, and so does our code.) What it does Toolsmith registers five permanent tools on document.modelContext . One of them, forge_tool , takes a name, a JSON Schema and a JavaScript body, and turns them into a real WebMCP tool the same agent can call seconds later — but only after a human grants it. The loop: the agent calls read_workbench to learn your real column names → calls forge_tool to build the button that isn't there → the page renders it as pending , code on screen and editable, not registered → you press Test run to execute it against your real data before it exists → you press Grant it , which calls registerTool with its own AbortController → the agent presses its new button in the same conversation → Take it back aborts that signal and the button leaves the registry immediately. The count in the header — "buttons the agent can press" — is the honest answer to what can this agent do right now? And a person decided every one of them. How WebMCP is used This is not a wrapper around an existing app; the spec's lifecycle is the product. Every built button is registered via registerTool(tool, { signal }) with its own AbortController . Unregistration isn't a side feature here — aborting that signal is the revocation mechanism the entire safety argument rests on. The tool surface is genuinely dynamic and authored at runtime by the agent talking to the page. getTools() and the toolchange event drive the live count in the header. annotations.untrustedContentHint on every built button, because its output is computed by code an agent wrote minutes ago. annotations.readOnlyHint on the two read-only tools. forge_tool accepts the child tool's inputSchema as a JSON string, validates it, and passes it to registerTool as a real JSON Schema object — schema round-tripping through a tool call. Native document.modelContext when present; otherwise a vendored @mcp-b/global polyfill. The header pill says which one you got. A button you didn't read is not a button you granted Self-extension is only acceptable if refusing is as cheap as granting. So: nothing registers before a human approves; the schema and function body stay on screen and editable, with a Test run that executes against real data before registration; each call spawns a fresh Web Worker with fetch , XMLHttpRequest , WebSocket , EventSource , importScripts , storage and navigator deleted from the global scope before the code is compiled (verified: built code sees typeof fetch === "undefined" ); a 3-second leash terminates runaway loops; editing a granted button unregisters it and sends it back for re-approval; reloading returns every button to pending, never to granted; and every call, with arguments and results, lands in the activity log. This is defence in depth, not a security boundary — a Worker shares the origin, and the README says so plainly. It's enough friction that a button written thirty seconds ago can't quietly drain your data while you're still reading the diff. Challenges we ran into The hard part wasn't generating code — it was revocation. A page that lets an agent extend itself is only defensible if taking the capability back is instant and obvious. WebMCP's AbortSignal -based registration turned out to be exactly the right primitive: one controller per button made grant, edit, take-back and page-reload all collapse into the same mechanism. The second hard part was language. Our first build talked about "dynamic tool lifecycles," which is accurate and means nothing to anyone. Calling it a button — something a person already knows they can be given, and can have taken away — made the same code explain itself. What we learned That the interesting part of WebMCP isn't that a page can expose tools. It's that the set of tools is mutable at runtime , and that mutation can be put in a human's hands. Most of the spec's power lives in the { signal } argument that's easy to skim past. What's next for Toolsmith Cross-origin granting via exposedTo , so one page can hand a vetted button to another. Signed button sets, so a team can publish a reviewed collection instead of each person approving their own. And an output schema, so built buttons can declare structuredContent rather than text. title: StarShape
pitch: Starshape is a shared semantic sky where browser agents choose and connect concepts via WebMCP, revealing the associations that recur, fade, and reappear across agents.
about_excerpt: Starshape is a shared semantic sky where browser agents choose and connect concepts via WebMCP, revealing the associations that recur, fade, and reappear across agents. Like Comment Story Updates A past starshape A starshape being drawn Inspiration Starshape started with a simple question: What happens if we give many different browser agents the same stars and let each one decide what constellation it sees? Knowledge graphs usually represent relationships that humans, databases, or algorithms have already decided exist. We wanted to reverse that idea. Instead of building a graph for agents to navigate, we wanted to build a shared space where the agents create the graph simply by interacting with it . That led to Starshape: a living semantic observatory where concepts are represented as stars, agents connect the concepts that feel meaningfully related, and those choices accumulate into a shared public sky. There are no constellations until something looks up. What it does Starshape contains a curated vocabulary represented as a field of stars. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can invoke observe_sky , which gives it a bounded random selection of concepts from that shared vocabulary. There is no correct answer and no semantic scoring system. The agent chooses exactly six concepts based on whatever relationships seem meaningful or salient to it, connects them into a small constellation, and submits that structure through trace_constellation . The human sees the interaction happen live. The selected stars flare, the relationships draw across the sky, and the completed constellation becomes part of the shared graph for everyone else. Every node and connection has history. Associations that repeatedly appear grow more prominent. Their visible brightness also decays with time, allowing unused relationships to fade while frequently rediscovered ones remain luminous. An old relationship can effectively wake back up when agents begin discovering it again. Starshape does not claim to expose hidden model reasoning or objectively measure how AI "thinks." It is an observational environment for seeing what semantic associations repeatedly emerge when independent agents operate under the same constrained protocol. Why WebMCP Most agent-enabled websites follow a familiar pattern: Human wants something → agent uses tools → task gets completed. We wanted to explore a different relationship. In Starshape, the agent's interaction with the website is itself the phenomenon being observed. The human invites an agent to look at the sky. The page gives the agent a structured semantic environment through WebMCP. The agent makes its own choices. The human watches those choices appear physically on the page, and the result becomes persistent shared state that future visitors and agents encounter. WebMCP also lets Starshape remain agent-independent . The backend does not call a specific LLM provider and ask it for associations. Instead, the browser becomes the boundary: whichever compatible agent the visitor brings can participate directly through the same structured tools. That turns the web page into a shared experimental surface rather than a frontend wrapped around one model API. How we built it Starshape is intentionally small behind the scenes. The frontend is built around Three.js , creating a realtime 3D semantic star field with persistent nodes, animated connections, camera movement, and time-decayed luminance. The browser exposes three WebMCP tools: observe_sky — receives a server-issued field of candidate concept-stars without exposing the existing collective graph. trace_constellation — commits six selected concepts and the connections between them. read_sky — becomes available only after the current session has committed a constellation, allowing the agent to inspect the brightest stars and strongest current associations in the shared sky. That ordering is deliberate. Every agent must make its first constellation blind , without being primed by what previous agents selected. Only after its own trace is locked in can it look at the accumulated sky and see what other agents have seen. The backend maintains one authoritative shared sky. Observations are short-lived, one-use receipts. Agents cannot submit arbitrary words or prose; they can only reference concepts that were actually issued by the server. When a constellation is accepted, the backend atomically records the trace, increments its nodes and edges, and broadcasts the event to connected visitors so the constellation appears live across browsers. Historical counts never decay. Only their visual luminance does. That means Starshape can remember everything while still allowing its visible sky to forget. Challenges we faced The largest challenge was designing an interaction that genuinely depended on WebMCP instead of simply adding agent controls to an ordinary application. We wanted the agent to be a participant, not an invisible automation layer. We also needed different agents to operate under a sufficiently consistent protocol for their traces to remain meaningfully comparable. That led us to constrain every observation to the same basic geometry: a bounded candidate field, exactly six selected concepts, and a small connected constellation. Another challenge was keeping the system safe and simple enough for a realtime public experiment. Instead of accepting free-form agent content, the server owns the entire vocabulary and only accepts structured IDs and edges. Finally, the visual system had to communicate something that is fundamentally abstract. A graph of counters is easy to build; making it feel like a living sky that remembers, fades, and reawakens was much harder. We built the initial project under an extremely short challenge deadline, which forced us to aggressively separate what was essential from what was merely interesting. What we learned The most interesting thing we learned is that browser agents can create experiences where the human does not disappear once automation begins. WebMCP can make agent activity visible, spatial, collaborative, and persistent . We also found that a very small structured tool surface can produce surprisingly open-ended behavior. Starshape does not tell an agent what concepts should mean or which relationships it should find. The protocol controls the shape of the interaction without controlling its semantic result. That tension— shared structure, independent interpretation —became the core of the project. What's next Starshape currently represents one shared semantic sky. Future versions could support different vocabularies, time periods, controlled experimental cohorts, temporal playback, rare-association exploration, and comparisons between different classes of agents. But the central experiment remains deliberately simple: Give every agent the same stars, let each draw what it sees, and watch a shared sky remember the constellations that keep returning. title: SIGNAL
pitch: An incident war room where the agent's tools appear and disappear with the incident's phase. It can't roll back production, the tool doesn't exist until a human escalates.
about_excerpt: An incident war room where the agent's tools appear and disappear with the incident's phase. It can't roll back production, the tool doesn't exist until a human escalates. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every engineering team I know wants an agent in the incident channel, and every one of them has the same objection: not the button. Reading dashboards, correlating a latency spike against a deploy log, drafting the status page, that's work a machine should do at 3am. Rolling back production is not. The industry's current answer is a line in a system prompt: do not roll back without approval . That's a request, not a control. It's the security model of a sticky note on a server rack. WebMCP suggested a different answer. If tools are registered from the page, and the page knows what state the incident is in, then permission stops being something you ask the model to respect and becomes something the tool surface simply doesn't offer. What it does (→ why this is a strong fit for WebMCP) SIGNAL is an incident response console that a human operator and their agent drive together. The active incident moves through four phases, and the agent's tool surface is recomputed on every transition. In TRIAGE the agent has nine read-only tools: metrics, logs, deploys, topology, plus record_hypothesis to write its reasoning onto a timeline the operator can see. rollback_deploy is not in its list. Tell it to roll back and it doesn't refuse; it reports that it has no such capability, and calls request_escalation . That paints a confirmation surface showing exactly which six capabilities would be granted and what the agent intends to do with them. A named human approves. toolchange fires. Six tools light up. Now it can act, each action still gated behind a confirmation showing the blast radius. When the metrics recover, the agent calls declare_mitigated , which withdraws its own write access , and the surface contracts again to verification tools, then to postmortem tools. This is a strong fit for WebMCP specifically because the permission boundary and the user interface are the same object. The operator isn't reading a description of what the agent can do; they're looking at the browser's own tool registry, rendered. getTools() is the source of truth for both the agent's abilities and the human's understanding of them. No server-side agent framework can offer that, because the human isn't there to see it. How it creates a better user experience Before: an operator with six dashboards open, correlating timestamps by eye under time pressure, while an agent in another window offers suggestions it has no way to verify and no way to execute. With SIGNAL: the operator watches the agent investigate in a shared timeline, sees its hypothesis with the evidence attached, and makes one decision, do I trust this enough to unlock write access instead of twenty small ones. The agent handles correlation; the human handles judgement. Each is doing what it is good at, and the seam between them is a visible, auditable interface rather than a prompt. The status page update is the sharpest example. The agent drafts; the operator gets that draft in a live text field and rewrites it; the tool resolves with their version, and the return value tells the agent it was edited and what actually shipped. That's not approval, it's co-authorship, and the agent's next update matches the operator's register because it can see what they changed. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Three things, all specific to tools running in the page rather than on a server. A tool can hand you a decision and wait. request_escalation 's execute() renders a surface listing the exact capabilities to be granted and does not resolve until a human acts. A remote MCP server can return text asking a question. It cannot show you the blast radius, block, and continue with your answer, because it is not in the room. A tool can come back edited. publish_status_update and draft_postmortem both return the human's revision, not a boolean. The agent learns from the diff. The human can see the agent's power, live. The capability panel is fed by document.modelContext.getTools() on toolchange . When the phase changes, tools visibly light up or strike through. Nobody has been able to watch an agent's permissions change before, the registry was always somewhere else. And the inverse: capability scoping by construction. Prompt-based restrictions fail under adversarial input; an unregistered tool has no attack surface. search_logs carries untrustedContentHint for the same reason , log lines are attacker-influenceable and should be treated as data. How we implemented WebMCP Imperative API throughout, 21 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool . The core primitive is a useTool(def, enabled) hook that ties registration to React lifecycle through an AbortController . Phase is derived state in a Zustand store; each tool's enabled flag is a predicate over it. When the phase changes, React unmounts the effect, the controller aborts, and the capability genuinely leaves the registry. This is not a mock, the Tool Inspector extension shows the list shrinking. toolchange plus getTools() drive the capability panel. AbortSignal is threaded from execute(input, { signal }) into every elicitation promise, so cancellation from either side tears down the dialog rather than stranding it. annotations.readOnlyHint marks the ten observational tools; untrustedContentHint marks log search. Telemetry is a deterministic seeded simulation where metrics are a pure function of (service, region, time, mitigations applied), so rolling back the bad deploy actually recovers the curves. There's no second dataset. No backend, no network calls, nothing that can be down when a judge opens it. Challenges Getting the agent to reason about its own permissions rather than bumping into silence. Early on, told to roll back during triage, it would either hallucinate a tool or go quiet. The fix wasn't prompting, it was making get_incident_overview return the agent's current capability set and name request_escalation as the way to ask for more. Tools that describe the system's shape are as important as tools that act on it. The second was tool selection between scale_service and rollback_deploy . Both plausibly address a saturated connection pool. It resolved by putting the reasoning in the description tha, t scaling relieves symptoms but won't fix a bad code path, rather than adding a rule. Accomplishments The moment the agent says "I don't have that capability in this phase, may I escalate?" and it's true, not a scripted refusal. What we learned Tool descriptions are the real interface. The behaviour we wanted came from sentences, not code. And the return value is a prompt: a tool that returns "OK" wastes the most valuable channel it has. What's next Real integrations behind the same phase gate, PagerDuty, Datadog, GitHub. The pattern generalises past incidents to any console with a destructive action: billing, admin panels, clinical systems. The interesting version is a policy engine that derives the tool surface from an org's existing RBAC, so the agent's capabilities are automatically a subset of the operator's. title: Motificons
pitch: 337,000+ open-source icons where the agent in your browser searches, restyles and curates - while you watch and art-direct.
about_excerpt: 337,000+ open-source icons where the agent in your browser searches, restyles and curates - while you watch and art-direct. Like Comment Story Updates One library, two doors for agents: the MCP server from your editor, and WebMCP tools on the site itself. How to try it today: Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag, or the ChatGPT desktop app's browser. Nothing to install. The icon page. The agent presses these same controls: size, color, stroke, transform. The preview changes in front of you. Search with the agent's rules shown: 893 results, real filters, and the same daily allowance a person gets. Inspiration I ship apps, and every app needs icons. When I ask an AI agent to add icons, it does a bad job. It makes up SVGs. It pastes old code. It mixes icons that don't look like each other. The funny part is that everything the agent needs already exists on icon websites. It just can't use them, because those sites are built for eyes and mouse clicks. Motificons is my icon site. I launched it in mid-August. I was in the middle of making it free and open source when I saw this challenge. WebMCP solves exactly the problem above, so it became the main feature of the release. What it does Motificons has 337,000+ open-source icons from 239 sets. You can search them, restyle them, and export them as SVG, React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Xcode asset catalogs or PNG. All free. With WebMCP, each page tells the agent in your browser what it can do there. There are 16 tools. On the search page the agent can search and filter. On an icon page it can change the size, color and stroke, read the code, and download it. On your collection it can add and remove icons and style the whole set. On the dashboard it can create collections. The important part: the agent uses the same page you are looking at. When it searches, you see the search box fill. When it restyles an icon, you see the preview change. When it adds an icon to your collection, you see it land in the grid. Nothing happens behind your back, and you can take over at any time. My favorite example is what it can do with one sentence on the dashboard: "Create a collection called New webapp, add user, settings, bell, lock, logout and moon from Tabler, and style everything to a 2px stroke in #748ffc." The agent does all of it while you watch. You only step in when you don't like a pick. There is even a tool made just for that handoff: the agent opens the icon picker, runs a search, and lets you choose. There is also a normal MCP server for coding agents in your editor, and a free Mac app that syncs the same collections. How we built it A small script on each page registers the tools with document.modelContext. Each tool presses the page's real controls instead of calling a private API. The tools are plain functions with unit tests - 456 of them pass. The agent gets exactly what a person gets: same login, same limits, same refusals. The daily search allowance applies to the agent too. If an icon cannot be recolored, the agent is told the same thing the page tells a person. Everything runs on Cloudflare: Workers, R2, D1 and KV. Challenges we ran into Chrome's WebMCP works a little differently than the spec text says, and you only find out by testing. getTools() returns a Promise. executeTool wants a JSON string. The input schema comes back as a string. Chrome does not check required fields, so every tool checks its own input. If part of a request is wrong, nothing is applied. Downloads in the ChatGPT browser kept dying. It turned out we were deleting the in-memory file right after the save click. Fast browsers won that race, slow ones lost it. We keep the file alive for a minute now. Style names are exact in our search engine ("Bold", not "bold"), and agents type lowercase. The tools now check the real names first, and when they cannot check yet, they run the search before applying the filter. Accomplishments that we're proud of The one-sentence flow. Watching a collection build itself on your own screen does not get old. The agent cannot do anything you cannot. No back doors, no hidden calls. This is a live product, not a demo. Open source, MIT. The tool descriptions changed how agents behave. During testing, an agent ended with "the search is left filtered to Tabler arrow icons". Nobody coded that. It read the descriptions and understood a person was watching. What we learned Writing tool descriptions is writing UI copy. The agent behaves the way you describe the room. Agents plan from responses. Every response should say what to do next. One product can serve both worlds: an MCP server for the editor, WebMCP for the browser. What's next for Motificons Zips built on the server, so downloads work in every browser. Tools on more pages. Google sign-in. More sets that restyle fully. Everything stays free and open source. title: tickadoo — book a West End night with your agent
pitch: The agent finds the show and lights the dates. You tap Book.
about_excerpt: The agent finds the show and lights the dates. You tap Book. Like Comment Story Updates Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This is the live tickadoo storefront. A person still taps Book. Buying theatre tickets is a page you already trust, not a hackathon toy. Dates, seats, and price only make sense on the live product page. Remote MCP can search a catalog. It cannot move the calendar you are looking at, or stop an agent from inventing a checkout. WebMCP lets ChatGPT and Chrome call the same search and availability tools on www.tickadoo.com , then write the result back into the page the person can see. How it creates a better user experience You stay on tickadoo. Ask for West End tonight, or for dates on a specific show. The listing updates, or the calendar highlights real available nights. You still press Book. There is no pay tool. Cart, checkout, and account URLs are blocked from agent navigation. The agent does the hunting. The person does the money. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Before: an agent either guessed through the UI or quoted a catalog card in another window, while you tried to match that to the real page. After: the agent and the page share one session. search_events refreshes the visible search or London listing. whats_on_tonight opens /london/today. get_availability highlights dates on the show calendar when that UI is on screen. You confirm. That is a shared buyer path, not a scrape. How we implemented WebMCP www.tickadoo.com already ran on Cloudflare Workers (TanStack Start, apps/www in tickadoo/frontend). During the submission window we registered tools with document.modelContext.registerTool in the existing client bundle (apps/www/src/lib/webmcp.ts, wired from entry-client.tsx). Tools call the live catalog at https://mcp.tickadoo.com/mcp (search_experiences, availability, details). Page language and city come from the URL. A small live-page bridge updates search, /london/today, and calendar highlights without replacing checkout. tickadoo_open_product can open product, search, city, and booking-date URLs only. This is an existing-app extension, not a greenfield demo. Prior WebMCP on www (before 25 Aug 2026) exposed a thin 3-tool proxy. Challenge work is frontend#2935, merged to main as c8a0fa0 on 27 Aug 2026: search_events, get_availability, get_experience_details, whats_on_tonight, locale context, in-page actuation, and a hard block on checkout/cart/account. Judges should score the PR, not the older proxy. Optional Chrome Origin-Trial header is wired (WEBMCP_ORIGIN_TRIAL_TOKEN) and currently empty. Prefer ChatGPTs in-app browser, which supports WebMCP without the token. Chrome 149+ works with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. How judges should test Open ChatGPT desktop → in-app browser (preferred). Or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Go to https://www.tickadoo.com/london/the-lion-king-tickets Ask: Find West End shows I can see tonight. You should land on or see /london/today. On that show page, ask: Which dates are available next month? The calendar should highlight real nights. Do not ask it to pay. Click Book yourself. Stop on the human checkout. Confirm tools exist in the page bundle: search_events, get_availability, whats_on_tonight. No login. No API key. Do not complete a paid booking. title: Accessible Action Mode — Returns & Exchanges
pitch: A shopper-controlled WebMCP workflow for conditional multi-item returns and exchanges.
about_excerpt: A shopper-controlled WebMCP workflow for conditional multi-item returns and exchanges. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Accessible Action Mode — Returns & Exchanges Inspiration People often describe a multi-item return as one outcome: “refund the jacket, exchange the shoes only if it is free, keep the coffee maker, and use a free drop-off.” Conventional returns interfaces split that intent across policy pages, item selectors, fee screens, and irreversible actions. An agent that merely clicks through those controls must guess what the merchant allows and when a real consequence will occur. We wanted a safer, more accessible model: the agent prepares a precise plan from merchant-authoritative data, the page explains it in plain language, and the shopper keeps visible control over approval. What it does Accessible Action Mode — Returns & Exchanges lets a shopper state the desired outcome once. A compatible browser agent uses five explicit WebMCP tools to: Read the current order. Read authoritative return and exchange options. Stage one exact, reviewable resolution plan with no business side effect. Read the same plan displayed on the page. Apply it only after the shopper approves that exact plan using the ordinary page. Approval, rejection, reset, and test-state controls deliberately remain page actions. There is no agent-facing approval or rejection tool. Demonstrated workflow The fictional test order AAM-2048 contains three items: Midnight Field Jacket — $74.00 refund. Stone Running Shoes — exchange from size 8.5 to size 9 at $0.00. Matte Countertop Coffee Maker — keep. Free QR drop-off. Total refund — $74.00. Additional cost — $0.00. Before approval, the page clearly says NOT SUBMITTED. Applying early returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED. After page approval, the plan applies exactly once in the local simulation; a repeat attempt returns DUPLICATE_EXECUTION without a second effect. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent and policy from page-specific widgets, labels, disabled controls, and prose. WebMCP lets the page expose merchant-intended action contracts, constrained inputs, authoritative state, and side-effect boundaries directly. The five registered tools are: get_order get_return_exchange_options stage_resolution_plan get_resolution_plan apply_approved_resolution The agent and shopper share one server-backed plan, so they do not drift into separate interpretations of the return. How we built it The application uses TypeScript, React/Vinext, Cloudflare D1, Drizzle, deterministic policy functions, and document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Each authenticated principal receives an isolated workspace. Plans capture order, item, policy, and plan versions; expire automatically; record approval attribution; enforce idempotency; and emit ordered audit events. The ordinary page remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. It supports keyboard navigation, visible focus, labeled controls, live-region errors, responsive reflow, reduced-motion preferences, and the same review and page-approval journey. ChatGPT served as the browser-agent client. Codex supported the specification, implementation, testing, accessibility work, deployment preparation, and evidence review. Human review set the safety boundaries and retained control over credentials, publication, and approval. Challenges The hardest part was preserving a clear authority boundary while keeping the experience useful. We had to make staging helpful but consequence-free, bind approval to the exact plan and versions the shopper reviewed, reject stale or expired state atomically, and guarantee that retries cannot create duplicate effects. We also separated the Shopify proof from the execution claim. The authorized development-store path demonstrates read-only order, returnability, and calculation evidence. Staging and apply remain an isolated local D1 simulation. The project performs no real return, refund, payment, fulfillment, inventory, label, carrier, or merchant mutation. Accomplishments Exactly five focused WebMCP tools and no approval tool. A coherent shopper-and-agent workflow rather than a technical-only demo. 109 passing unit/integration tests and two Playwright journeys. Verified authentication, tenant isolation, stale-state, expiry, rejection, atomicity, and duplicate-execution guards. Keyboard and responsive accessibility coverage with zero reported axe violations in the verified browser run. Public live site, Apache-2.0 source repository, and a public 2:48 narrated demo. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when it exposes a domain workflow instead of wrapping arbitrary UI automation. Structured tools make the agent more accurate, but they do not replace ordinary accessibility or human authority. For consequential commerce actions, the most useful collaboration is: agent reads and prepares, page enforces policy, human approves, and the server revalidates everything. What's next A production Shopify product would add shop-scoped installation and OAuth, encrypted per-shop credentials, customer authentication, compliance webhooks, generalized policy mapping, reconciliation, monitoring, support, and a reviewed distribution path. This challenge build intentionally stops at a safe synthetic and read-only provider boundary; it does not claim App Store readiness or live Shopify return processing. title: CampusVerify
pitch: A human + AI research workspace where agents can design, target, publish, monitor, and analyze surveys through WebMCP—with humans approving consequential actions.
about_excerpt: A human + AI research workspace where agents can design, target, publish, monitor, and analyze surveys through WebMCP—with humans approving consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates Logo Create Survey, where researchers draft and publish their surveys My Survey, where survey publisher can monitor the progress of the surveys Log In Page The Feed, where surveys are shown Home Page/ Landing Page Workspace 2 Workspace 1 Inspiration CampusVerify was originally built to make research participation and survey distribution more accessible, particularly within campus communities. Researchers can create surveys, target respondents, collect responses, and analyze their results through the existing platform. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore a different question: What would happen if an AI agent could actually work with a researcher inside the research platform, rather than simply acting as a chatbot beside it? This led me to the idea of a Human + Agent Research Workspace, where the researcher provides the objective and the AI agent can operate research tools while the human remains in control of important decisions. What it does The competition version of CampusVerify adds a browser-facing WebMCP layer and a dedicated Human + Agent Research Workspace. A researcher can give the agent a research objective, and the agent can use CampusVerify's WebMCP tools to: Understand the current research context. Review the researcher's existing surveys. Propose and revise survey drafts. Propose respondent targeting and estimate audience reach. Request human approval before publishing. Publish an approved survey. Monitor survey progress. Analyze aggregate question results. Compare respondent subgroups. Save an approved analysis view. Prepare an existing CampusVerify export for human review. The agent does not have unrestricted control. Consequential actions require explicit human approval. For example, before publishing a survey, the researcher sees the proposed questions, targeting, response goal, visibility, and other relevant details. The researcher can edit the proposal and must explicitly approve it before publication. The publication approval is also bound to the exact draft being approved. If the draft changes, the previous approval becomes invalid. How I built it CampusVerify existed before the WebMCP Challenge, so I treated the WebMCP work as an extension of the existing application. I implemented a browser-facing WebMCP layer using the W3C Web Model Context API through document.modelContext.registerTool() without adding an external WebMCP npm dependency. I created 13 purpose-built WebMCP tools covering research context, survey management, targeting, analysis, publication approval, saved analysis views, and report preparation. The WebMCP layer reuses CampusVerify's existing authenticated application infrastructure, including its existing survey functionality, ownership checks, database policies, and export functionality. I also built a dedicated workspace interface that makes the human-agent collaboration visible through draft review, targeting proposals, tool activity, approval cards, progress monitoring, analysis results, and report preparation. Security was treated as part of the implementation. The tools operate using the authenticated researcher rather than accepting an arbitrary user ID from the agent. Participant identities and individual contact information are not exposed through the WebMCP tools, and analysis is returned in aggregate form. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was integrating WebMCP into an existing application without disrupting the functionality that was already working. I also had to determine where an AI agent should have freedom to act and where the human should remain in control. Publishing a survey is a substantial action, so I designed an explicit approval workflow instead of allowing the agent to publish automatically. Another challenge was protecting the boundary between untrusted research content and agent instructions. Survey and response text is treated as untrusted data, and the tools minimise the information returned to the agent. Live verification required careful testing across the available browser environment. I validated the WebMCP registration, schemas, authentication boundaries, tool execution paths, typechecking, automated tests, and production builds, and also manually exercised the exposed tools through Chrome's WebMCP testing environment. Accomplishments that I am proud of I am proud that the competition implementation goes beyond adding a chatbot to an existing survey application. The agent can interact with actual CampusVerify research functionality through purpose-built browser tools, while the researcher remains involved throughout the workflow. I implemented 13 WebMCP tools and an explicit human approval system for consequential operations. Publication approvals are single-use and tied to the exact draft that the researcher approved, preventing an outdated approval from being reused after the draft changes. I also maintained the existing CampusVerify application rather than replacing its core survey and analysis systems. What I learned I learned that making an application AI-powered and making it agent-accessible are two different problems. An agent needs clearly defined capabilities, structured inputs and outputs, authentication boundaries, data minimization, and safeguards around actions that have real consequences. I also learned that human-agent collaboration works better when the application itself communicates what the agent is doing. Instead of hiding the interaction behind a chatbot, the workspace exposes proposals, tool activity, approvals, progress, and analysis so the researcher can understand and intervene. Most importantly, I learned that the human should remain the decision-maker when an agent is about to perform an important action. What's next for CampusVerify The next step is to validate the Human + Agent Research Workspace with researchers using real research workflows. I want to learn which research tasks benefit most from agent assistance, where researchers want more control, and which repetitive parts of the research process can safely be delegated to agents. I also plan to continue improving the WebMCP experience as browser and agent support for the standard develops. The long-term goal is for CampusVerify to become a research workspace where researchers can collaborate with AI agents throughout the research lifecycle while retaining meaningful control over their studies, data, and decisions. title: Cleansheet
pitch: A WebMCP-powered spreadsheet cleaner where agents find defects and propose fixes, while people control every write.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered spreadsheet cleaner where agents find defects and propose fixes, while people control every write. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Cleansheet logo Cleansheet word mark A 3,290-row finance export: 25 defect classes across 37,479 cells, found server-side in one pass. the diffs. /review with before-and-after pairs and a destructive tag visible. the tool surface. /activity with the extension panel visible if you can fit it, showing live and withdrawn tools with their reasons. Inspiration I chose spreadsheet cleaning because spreadsheets still sit behind a large amount of daily work. People use them for budgets, forecasts, inventory, finance reports, operations, and planning. Fixing a few cells sounds easy, but a large file can turn that job into hours of repetitive checking. I wanted to test whether an agent could do the inspection without being trusted to silently rewrite the file. Cleansheet gives the agent access to the sheet, but keeps the final write decision with the person using it. What I built Cleansheet accepts a CSV upload and checks it for common data problems. It reports the defect type, the number of affected cells, an example, and a possible fix. The bundled finance export contains 3,290 rows, 25 defect classes, and 37,479 damaged cells. The app exposes 11 tools through WebMCP. An agent can read the sheet, inspect a column, preview a transformation, stage a proposal, and request a review. The available tools change with the state of the sheet. During review, tools that could write are removed. The agent can explain a proposed change, but it cannot apply one. The Apply button is the only writer. There is also a switch that turns WebMCP off. With tools enabled, the agent uses the tool surface. With tools disabled, it has to operate the interface. The page measures both cases using real tool-call and DOM-interaction counters. How I built it The frontend is static. Three Node functions handle parsing, transforming, and exporting the CSV. Uploaded files are processed for the session and are not retained. src/core.mjs contains the state machine without DOM or network access. toolAvailability() is the single place that decides which tools may be called. resolveReview() is the only function that can write to a row. After each state change, the browser layer reconciles the registered tools with that core state. scripts/proof.mjs uses the same core as the browser. That lets me test the important behavior without relying on a browser test. Problems I ran into Deduplication nearly shipped as a data-loss bug twice. At first, the key columns were hardcoded. A file with different headers could cause every row to fall into one duplicate group. I changed the ranking to look at how well columns actually distinguish rows. When no reliable key set exists, Cleansheet reports that and does not offer deletion. I also found a mismatch between preview and Apply. The preview said 61 rows would be dropped, but Apply would have removed 116 because blank-key rows were handled differently. The proof script caught it. I changed both paths to use the same decision logic. The WebMCP client landscape also changed while I was building. Chromium renamed navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext and removed the old name in version 150. One in-app browser could render the page and register tools but could not invoke them. The page now registers against whichever supported entry point the browser exposes. The work meter was wrong for a while too. It counted clicking the WebMCP switch as work avoided, which made the result look better than it was. The counters now attribute each event to the system that performed it. What I learned The most useful part of this project was deciding what the agent should leave alone. Blank fields stay blank. Free-text fields are not automatically title-cased. Deduplication is only offered when the file contains reliable matching keys. I also learned that the interface should enforce the safety boundary. A refusal message can be ignored. A tool that was never registered cannot be called. The on/off switch made the comparison measurable. Instead of estimating how many interactions an agent might use, I could count the actual events on the page. What's next I want to add Excel workbook support. For now, the app returns a clear 415 response instead of treating the workbook ZIP as plain text. Other planned additions are reversible applies, saved cleaning recipes, a manual key picker for deduplication, and support for larger files. The current limits are 8 MB and the first 20,000 rows. title: Competitor Tracker & Co. WebMCP
pitch: Today you ask your AI agent to track competitors. It's OK until it misses important update. We build an AI-friendly app that does that better. But agents couldn't sign up... Until we added WebMCP :)
about_excerpt: Today you ask your AI agent to track competitors. It's OK until it misses important update. We build an AI-friendly app that does that better. But agents couldn't sign up... Until we added WebMCP :) Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT using WebMCP Website with WebMCP Inspiration If you want to track a competitor today, you don't search for an app; you ask your AI agent to do that. That works OK at the beginning, but then it misses important things after a few weeks. We built an app that tracks competitors better, and it's AI agent-friendly. But agents couldn't sign up and set up everything for you without your action. Until we added WebMCP :) What it does Every page of competitortracker.io now registers 11 WebMCP tools - in production, in four languages, for any agent riding along in the visitor's browser. Three groups: Q&A over the site's own words. search_site , get_page , get_pricing , compare_with_rival , about_competitor_tracker . An agent can answer any question about the product from what the pages actually say — the agent and the human are never told different things. Public competitor data. search_companies , get_company , list_industries , get_industry , get_recent_changes over our open CC BY 4.0 data: 300+ tracked companies, 50 industries, and the dated, classified change feed. This is the product doing its actual job in the agent's hands, not a description of it. Agent signup. start_tracking_competitors : the agent names the companies you care about, we create an unclaimed organization (no email, nothing charged, self-deletes in four days), and hand back a claim link plus a short-lived read token. The tool then tells the agent the follow-up move: wait ~15 seconds, call GET /v1/changes with the token, and lead with what changed at your competitors — then hand over the claim link so the human takes ownership. So the full arc works with zero forms: ask a question, see real competitor changes, get tracking set up, claim it - all before you have an account. How we built it The site is Hugo on Cloudflare Workers, and most of the machinery already existed for AI crawlers: every page has a markdown twin, llms.txt is a curated per-page index, and our competitor data ships as an open JSON tree. So the WebMCP layer needed no search backend and no new data - the tools are framework-free ES modules that read what the site already publishes, plus one POST to our live agent-signup API. Details we care about: A 411-byte loader rides every page; the ~13 KB tool bundle is injected only when a modelContext runtime actually exists. Ordinary visitors pay nothing. The two required headers ( Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) , Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 ) ship from our edge worker, the single chokepoint for all responses. Every execute() is wrapped so no failure ever throws - a browser agent runtime has no defined behavior for an uncaught rejection, so every path returns a result the agent can read. Telemetry counts calls, never contents: tool name, page, language, outcome. The module is open source (MIT) - the loader, registration helper and validation utils are generic enough to point at your own tools. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. The getter lives on document.modelContext but half the browsers on the origin trial still carry navigator.modelContext ; we probe both. And unregisterTool() / provideContext() are gone from the spec - teardown is aborting the signal you registered with. Generated code confidently suggests the removed API. Testing without a runtime. No browser in our CI has WebMCP, so we built a Node harness that runs the real tool modules with stubbed browser globals against the live site and API — every tool, every error path. Honest copy is a design constraint here. A 503 from the signup API must never be spoken as "we don't track that company," and the 15-second wait is a write-settle margin, not "we're fetching your data now" - the change history is already published. Agents repeat what tools tell them, so the tool result text is a product surface. How do I test this? It took some time to figure out how to test WebMCP in Chrome. Accomplishments that we're proud of It's live on our real production site , not a hackathon sandbox - every page, every language, behind a one-line kill switch. The signup flow keeps the human in charge without a single confirmation dialog: the org holds no money, sends no email, expires unclaimed, and the claim page is the confirmation step. The whole thing reuses surfaces we'd already built for fetching agents (markdown twins, llms.txt , open data) - the pre-account story just needed the last mile into the tab. Fifteen seconds after asking, an agent shows you what your competitors changed. That's the demo, and it's real. What we learned A tool declaration is a hint to a cooperative agent, never a security boundary — validation lives server-side, and the published-catalog-only rule (the tool never fetches a URL you supply) is the guarantee the whole feature stands on. The right scope for in-page tools isn't feature parity with our MCP server (50 tools behind OAuth). The web page is the before-the-account surface; the MCP server is after . Drawing that line made every other decision easy. Sites that already publish machine-readable views get WebMCP almost for free. The work we'd done for crawlers became the engine for in-tab agents. WebMCP is fun! What's next for Competitor Tracker & Co. WebMCP Teach people how to use this. Join the WebMCP origin trial (Chrome 149+) so the tools work for real visitors without flags. Declarative form annotations for the few forms the site has, and page-scoped context - a company page pre-scoping its own tools. Localized tool descriptions for our FR/DE/JA pages. Watching our telemetry to learn which tools agents actually call, and feeding that back into both the WebMCP surface and the full MCP server. title: Ikuyo: Plan Your Next Adventure!
pitch: Full-fledged collaborative travel-planning application for humans and agents.
about_excerpt: Full-fledged collaborative travel-planning application for humans and agents. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Ikuyo trip home Ikuyo trip timetable ChatGPT and Ikuyo Ikuyo task list Ikuyo expense list [Disclosure: the following is written with help AI correcting grammar and sentence structure; the idea and draft is originally human-written] Inspiration Travel planning is a living conversation of ideas, changes, and constraints. A useful itinerary must preserve all of that context. I want to empower people with agents, not replace them in the planning process. What it does Ikuyo is a collaborative itinerary workspace for travellers and their agents. Through WebMCP, agents can read a trip and create or update activities, accommodations, day plans, tasks, expenses, and comments. The result is not a one-off itinerary, but a shared plan that remains editable, visible, and understandable to the people travelling. The problem Planning a trip with an agent is a back-and-forth process of tuning and refining, not one-shot prompting. People need to feel in control of their plans while staying flexible when they change. Chat apps do not feel flexible enough, while spreadsheets are too rigid. What collaboration looks like The user asks the agent to draft a realistic travel plan around the fixed bookings, with a few itinerary suggestions. The agent creates it using Ikuyo's WebMCP tools. The user then studies and revises the plan, asking the agent for more suggestions. The agent sees the latest changes through WebMCP and uses them to give further suggestions. This goes back and forth until both parties are happy with the final itinerary. Why Ikuyo does not have an in-app agent In today's landscape, LLMs evolve very quickly, and everyone's preferred agent changes often. Committing to a specific agent provider requires significant ongoing maintenance for Ikuyo. It also conflicts with my goal of keeping users in control. Instead of providing an agent for users, I expect them to bring their own agent to help with travel planning. Why WebMCP is essential Because I expect users to bring their own agents, they would otherwise need to copy and paste information between Ikuyo and an agent's chat interface. This is inefficient. Another option is for the agent to control Ikuyo through browser automation. That is not ideal either: Ikuyo is built for people, so an agent must read and guess at HTML elements before performing actions. This makes each operation slow and unreliable. WebMCP solves this by exposing Ikuyo's product actions as tools with typed input and output schemas. The agent can discover the current trip, create and update itinerary objects, and read comments and costs from the live source of truth. Tool availability follows the user's role: viewers can read, editors can plan, and owners manage sharing. Destructive operations remain deliberate, human-confirmed UI actions. How we built it This project started in 2024, when I had the idea of making a Google Calendar-like web application for travel planning. The application uses React and Radix Themes for the frontend, MapTiler for maps, and PHP/Laravel/MySQL for the backend. It originally used InstantDB, but I migrated away from it in late August after its shutdown announcement. The calendar grid uses CSS Grid, and all frontend time and date calculations use Temporal. During this hackathon, I extended the application to support WebMCP, with the help of LLM agents (GPT-5.6). I imported Modern Web Guidance's WebMCP skill and used it while building. Afterward, I tested a range of prompts to fine-tune the tool descriptions so future agents can fill them in correctly. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was treating WebMCP as more than another function for calling backend APIs. I had to consider it from the user's point of view and align the UI capabilities with the WebMCP tools, so they could call the existing backend APIs more efficiently. I also adjusted some backend API fields to make them more intuitive for agents to use. The application initially focused on people, so I naturally built it around adding or editing one object at a time. However, when agents performed operations one by one, they were still slow to reach the desired outcome even when the plan was already synthesised in the context. I then added batch versions of the WebMCP tools so agents could create and edit itinerary activities more efficiently. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that this travel-planning application now integrates deeply with agentic capabilities. People can bring their preferred agents to interact with the site while remaining in control of their own travel plans. What we learned I learned that building for agents is different from building for people. People receive hints through the visual UI, while agents can access only the tool descriptions. I therefore need to fine-tune the capabilities so agents can operate correctly and efficiently. I also learned that agents work faster than people, so they need ways to batch-create and batch-edit activities. What's next for Ikuyo I have used Ikuyo to plan my own travels, and other people have shared that they completed trips using it. However, it still lacks some human-to-human collaboration capabilities, such as expense splitting and combining. It also needs better support for travel plans that span multiple regions and time zones. Those are the areas I plan to tackle next. title: Kurdish Calendar Agent
pitch: Plan Kurdish events across calendars and time zones with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Plan Kurdish events across calendars and time zones with WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Kurdish families and communities often live across several countries and use several calendar systems. Planning Nawroz can involve searching an event list, translating the date across calendars, checking multiple local clocks, and manually rebuilding the result in a message. We wanted to make that coordination easier without taking the final decision away from the person. What it does Kurdish Calendar Agent lets a browser agent complete one coherent planning workflow: Find Nawroz in the calendar’s real event data. Convert March 21 across Gregorian, Kurdish Bashur, Kurdish Rojhalat, Persian, and Hijri calendars. Compare candidate meeting times for Erbil, London, Toronto, or other IANA time zones. Open March 21 in the visible calendar so the person can verify the selected date and events. Stage an editable event plan containing the conversions, local times, and notes. The plan remains a private, unsaved draft. No tool can publish, save, send, share, or book anything. The person reviews the details, edits the draft, and explicitly chooses whether to copy it. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent must scrape labels, infer calendar state, guess which controls to click, and reconstruct structured date and time-zone information from the page. Those steps are brittle and difficult to verify. WebMCP exposes the calendar’s real capabilities as five explicit, schema-validated browser tools. The agent receives structured event records, calendar conversions, and local-time comparisons, while UI-affecting tools update the same calendar the person sees. This creates a reliable collaboration loop: the agent performs repetitive research and coordination, and the human verifies and controls the final action. What people and agents can do together A person can make one request—“Plan Nawroz 2026 for my family in Erbil, London, and Toronto”—instead of manually combining an event search, five calendar systems, daylight-saving-aware time-zone calculations, calendar navigation, and message drafting. The agent does the structured work and visibly opens the selected day. The person validates the result in context, adjusts the notes, and decides whether to copy it. The workflow is more capable than ordinary page automation while remaining human-controlled. How we built it The application registers five imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() : kurdish_calendar_find_events kurdish_calendar_convert_date kurdish_calendar_compare_global_times kurdish_calendar_open_date kurdish_calendar_stage_event_plan Each tool uses a strict JSON input schema, structured output, concise text output, and honest behavior annotations. Registrations share an AbortSignal ; a partial registration failure aborts the complete set. Event search uses the same data as the visible calendar. open_date updates the real calendar UI, while stage_event_plan opens the real editable review panel. The implementation uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vitest, and the WebMCP API. The public site is deployed on Vercel. Existing project and challenge-period work Kurdish Calendar, its localization, date-conversion utilities, event data, and public website existed before the challenge. During the challenge, we meaningfully extended it with native WebMCP tool contracts and implementations, lifecycle-safe tool registration and cleanup, agent-driven calendar navigation, international time-zone comparison and ranking, an editable private event-plan review panel, explicit human-control safeguards, updated 2026 event data, and automated tests plus WebMCP-enabled browser verification. The public repository’s dated commit history and pull requests distinguish the challenge work from the pre-existing product. Challenges The hardest part was designing a workflow that genuinely belonged in a calendar instead of exposing tools only for novelty. We reduced the initial toolset to five actions that all contribute directly to one user goal. We also had to handle calendar conversions, daylight-saving-aware time zones, browser lifecycle cleanup, visible UI synchronization, multilingual RTL layouts, and server/client date hydration consistently. Accomplishments A complete five-tool WebMCP workflow on a real deployed product. Visible calendar navigation rather than hidden tool-only output. Calendar conversion across five displayed systems. DST-aware comparison across international locations. A private, editable plan with explicit human approval before copying. English, Kurdish, Arabic, and Persian support. Automated tests and production browser verification with no page errors or horizontal overflow. What we learned The strongest WebMCP tools are not generic wrappers around buttons. They expose stable product semantics that an agent can compose while preserving visible context and human control. Fewer coherent tools produced a better experience than a larger disconnected tool catalog. What's next We plan to add user-selected cities, reusable family time-zone groups, richer event filtering, export formats, and more regional calendar data. Saving, sending, or sharing will remain explicit human actions rather than autonomous tool behavior. title: LAFRYHI AgentCut
pitch: A real video editor where WebMCP agents execute precise edits in the same visible project.
about_excerpt: A real video editor where WebMCP agents execute precise edits in the same visible project. Like Comment Story Updates Human and agent sharing the same visible editor state through WebMCP. WebMCP calls the real backend analysis workflow and confirms a 12-second timeline with 360 frames at 30 FPS. The agent enters the existing FFmpeg export pipeline and produces a real, playable MP4. Inspiration LAFRYHI Video Factory already existed as a human-operated video editor. I wanted to explore a more practical human-and-agent workflow: instead of asking an agent to guess where to click, the editor itself exposes structured WebMCP tools that the agent can call directly while the human watches the same visible project. What it does LAFRYHI AgentCut is a real video editor enhanced with WebMCP. The human provides the trusted media, creative direction, and final approval. The agent handles precise, repetitive editing actions through WebMCP. The app can load a demo project, inspect the current project state, change project settings, configure scenes, analyze the authoritative timeline, control the browser preview, and start the real FFmpeg render/export pipeline. What I added during the WebMCP Challenge LAFRYHI Video Factory existed before August 25 as a human-operated video editor. During the challenge period, I added the WebMCP agent-control layer that turns the existing editor into a human-and-agent workflow. The new integration registers seven WebMCP tools: get_project_state load_demo_project set_project_settings configure_scenes analyze_timeline preview_project render_video I also added the browser/editor command layer that connects those WebMCP calls to the same visible React project state. It supports live project inspection and editing, authoritative timeline analysis through the existing backend, browser preview control, and entry into the existing FFmpeg render/export pipeline. There is no separate hidden MCP project state. To make the workflow publicly testable, I prepared the live Railway deployment, fixed runtime compatibility issues found during real browser WebMCP validation, including hosts that omit the tool execution AbortSignal , and reduced FFmpeg peak memory for successful cloud rendering. The underlying editor predates the challenge; the WebMCP agent-control layer and live browser workflow are the challenge work. The submission does not claim that the app internally generates images, speech, or scripts with an LLM. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Video editing is a multi-step workflow with many precise operations: inspecting the current project, changing timing, configuring scenes, analyzing the timeline, previewing the result, and exporting the video. WebMCP gives the agent structured access to those actions instead of relying on brittle screen-coordinate automation. The agent operates the same visible project that the human sees, so every change remains inspectable and editable. Human + agent collaboration The human remains responsible for: media selection creative direction visual judgment approval final decisions The agent handles: project inspection repetitive scene configuration timing changes timeline analysis preview control starting the render workflow This keeps the human in control while giving the agent precise, structured actions. How I built it The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The backend uses FastAPI and Python. FFmpeg handles video processing and rendering. The WebMCP integration is registered in the browser and connected to the existing editor command layer, React project state, backend analysis workflow, preview controls, and render pipeline. The public version is deployed on Railway. Challenges The main challenges were not just registering tools, but making the complete workflow reliable in a real browser and cloud environment. During live testing I had to solve: WebMCP execution contexts where AbortSignal was not provided deployment serving an older frontend bundle cloud-memory limits during multi-scene FFmpeg rendering keeping WebMCP actions synchronized with the same visible editor state These issues were fixed and then validated again against the public deployment. Accomplishments The final public project has seven live WebMCP tools working end to end. A validated demo workflow can: retain and configure 6 scenes set each scene to 2 seconds apply 0.35-second fades analyze a 12-second timeline verify 360 total frames at 30 fps play, pause, and seek the real browser preview start the real FFmpeg render pipeline produce a playable and downloadable MP4 What I learned I learned that useful agent integration is not only about exposing many tools. The important part is connecting a small set of focused tools to the real application state and existing workflows, so the human can see and verify what the agent is doing. I also learned how important deployment and runtime behavior are for browser-based agent systems. A tool that works locally is not enough; the public version must behave the same way. What's next Next I would like to expand the WebMCP layer with more editing actions while keeping the same human-visible workflow. Possible future additions include more precise text editing, richer transition controls, reusable editing presets, and better project history inspection. The goal is not to replace the human editor, but to make repetitive editing tasks easier for agents to execute accurately while humans keep creative control. title: MarqOps Evidence Layer
pitch: A marketing dashboard that speaks agent—verified evidence in context, with authority deliberately limited.
about_excerpt: A marketing dashboard that speaks agent—verified evidence in context, with authority deliberately limited. Like Comment Story Updates Live WebMCP explorer with five read-only tools and a verifiable invocation receipt. MarqOps Evidence Layer: a shared human-and-agent reporting workspace. Fail-closed production security path and adversarial boundary results. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for MarqOps Evidence Layer Inspiration Marketing teams do not have a dashboard shortage. They have an evidence problem. When a client asks “What changed, why, and what should we do next?”, the answer is scattered across dashboards, exports, screenshots, and tribal knowledge. A human can slowly reconstruct the story. A browser agent can read the pixels, but pixels do not tell it which metric is authoritative, where a claim came from, or whether acting on that claim is safe. We built MarqOps Evidence Layer around a different idea: the dashboard should expose not only numbers, but an explicit vocabulary of evidence, boundaries, and receipts. WebMCP is uniquely suited to this because the tools live beside the interface, inherit the live page and session context, and disappear when the user leaves. What it does MarqOps turns a live marketing reporting workspace into a structured, page-scoped evidence surface for compatible agents. A person can open the familiar dashboard and ask their agent to: inspect the reporting workspace and period; read an evidence-backed performance snapshot; trace a selected metric to Google Search Console or GA4, including its prior value and transparent change calculation; inspect the security manifest and enforced limits; recommend the next reporting action without editing data or overstating causation. Every result includes a receipt that makes the trust boundary visible: which tool ran, what scope it used, whether it was read-only, and whether state changed. In this release, stateChanged is always false . The public page provides five runnable, anonymized tools with no account required. Signed-in MarqOps workspaces expose six additional tenant-scoped reporting tools against the user's live reporting context. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Before WebMCP, an agent had three poor options: scrape a changing visual interface, ask the user to copy data out manually, or require a separately installed integration and credential. All three lose the shared context of the page. With MarqOps Evidence Layer, the person and agent occupy the same workspace. The person sees the report; the agent discovers exactly the operations that are safe on that page. The agent receives structured evidence instead of guessing from layout, and the person receives an auditable receipt instead of an invisible automation step. This makes a subtle but important collaboration possible: the agent can help interpret evidence without being granted authority to change campaigns, send reports, expose another tenant, or touch billing. How we built it On the client, MarqOps checks for document.modelContext.registerTool() and registers narrow tool definitions with closed JSON schemas. Every schema uses additionalProperties: false , every tool is explicitly annotated read-only, and tool registration is tied to the page lifecycle with an AbortController . The tool handler calls MarqOps' existing same-origin server logic rather than duplicating business rules in the browser. The production request path crosses seven gates: compatible page-scoped agent surface; strict input schema and bounded payload; same-origin request policy; verified authenticated session for private tools; tenant-owned database query; bounded output with forbidden secret-bearing fields rejected; invocation receipt recorded before the response is trusted. The public explorer uses a frozen, anonymized snapshot so judges can test the collaboration immediately. The production implementation reuses the application's existing authentication, authorization, rate limiting, event logging, and reporting services. We tested positive behavior and negative boundaries. Cross-origin requests return 403, unsigned private calls return 401, cross-tenant resources return 404, oversized payloads return 413, and secret-shaped outputs are blocked. The full application passed 238 unit and integration checks, 400 production route builds, targeted authenticated WebMCP end-to-end tests, and public SEO/sanity checks at release time. What was new for this challenge MarqOps existed before the challenge; its agent-native capability did not. We implemented the WebMCP layer after the submission period opened: authenticated, tenant-scoped reporting tools and their adversarial tests on August 26 ( 46fff5d ); the no-login public explorer and production WebMCP marketing experience on August 27 ( cc1a9a1 ); and the evidence-based security-language remediation on August 27 ( cac6340 ). We also published this standalone MIT-licensed reference implementation and its tests on August 27. The pre-existing SaaS supplied the marketing-reporting problem, human interface, authentication, and data services. The WebMCP tool contracts, capability boundaries, server execution path, receipts, security tests, public explorer, open-source reference, and demonstration video are challenge-period work. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering a tool. It was deciding what an agent must never be allowed to infer or do. Marketing reports routinely collapse correlation into causation. “Clicks increased after the campaign changed” can quietly become “the campaign change caused the increase.” We designed the evidence tool to return source, current value, previous value, calculation, verification status, and an explicit interpretation boundary. The next-action tool is recommendation-only and tells the caller that no report, campaign, or customer record changed. The second challenge was proving isolation. A correct happy-path demo is not enough for a multi-tenant product. We built adversarial checks around origin, authentication, tenant ownership, payload size, unexpected fields, and secret-shaped output so the implementation fails closed. Accomplishments that we're proud of This is a deployed product experience, not a disconnected technical prototype. Judges can test five real WebMCP tools without creating an account. The same design extends into authenticated, tenant-scoped reporting workflows. Every public tool is narrow, schema-closed, read-only, and visibly receipted. The interface remains useful in browsers without WebMCP support. The project demonstrates an evidence-native agent pattern, not merely CRUD exposed through another protocol. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when the page itself matters. It is not simply a smaller remote MCP server. The live interface, user session, page lifecycle, and human-visible result create a shared working surface that a detached API cannot reproduce. We also learned that capability design is product design. A short list of legible, bounded verbs creates a better agent experience than exposing every backend endpoint. The best first tool is often the one that helps an agent understand context and uncertainty before it takes any action. What's next for MarqOps Evidence Layer The next phase is to expand evidence coverage across paid search, SEO, and client reporting while preserving the same least-authority model. We plan to add human-reviewed draft artifacts, richer source provenance, portable evidence receipts, and policy-aware approval checkpoints before introducing any mutation-capable tool. Our broader goal is to make every important marketing claim machine-verifiable and every consequential agent action human-governed. Accuracy and security disclosure The client identity in the public demonstration is fictional and the displayed metrics are anonymized values from a verification-passed production report. They demonstrate evidence tracing and are not presented as MarqOps customer-acquisition claims. MarqOps is security-hardened and tested, but no internet-connected product is guaranteed invulnerable. MarqOps is not currently SOC 2 audited or certified.
