title: OpenBento
pitch: A living intelligence dashboard where humans and AI agents organize the web together.
about_excerpt: A living intelligence dashboard where humans and AI agents organize the web together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web is still mostly designed around humans opening tabs, searching pages, and manually organizing what they find. AI agents can answer questions about the web, but they usually operate in a separate chat experience rather than inside the same persistent workspace as the user. OpenBento explores a different model: what if humans and agents could work on the same web-native intelligence dashboard? What it does OpenBento is a persistent dashboard for following topics as they evolve. Each Canvas contains one live Dashboard where users can combine persistent WatchBots, web/news Cards, X posts with rich media and engagement data, playable YouTube Cards, notes, structured Columns, financial Cards, and AI assistance. A WatchBot owns a dedicated Column. New discoveries appear at the top of that stream instead of endlessly expanding the workspace. When something matters, the user can drag that Card out of the live feed and place it directly onto the Dashboard, preserving it while the WatchBot continues monitoring. The result is somewhere between a live research desk, TweetDeck, an intelligence dashboard, and an AI workspace. Why WebMCP is a strong fit OpenBento is fundamentally about shared state between humans and agents . Without WebMCP, an AI assistant can describe what the user should do, but it cannot naturally operate the same web application the user is already working in. With WebMCP, OpenBento exposes meaningful application actions directly to compatible agents. An agent can work with the same persistent Canvases, Cards, WatchBots, and Dashboard state that the human user sees. The agent is not controlling the application through screenshots or brittle coordinate-based browser automation. It interacts through explicit tools published by the website itself. That makes agent actions more reliable, understandable, and aligned with the application's own permission and domain model. What humans and agents can do together A person can ask an agent to create or modify parts of the workspace while continuing to interact with the same Dashboard manually. For example: A user asks an agent to create a WatchBot for Apple news. OpenBento creates a persistent WatchBot and its dedicated live Column. The WatchBot begins collecting relevant web, X, and YouTube developments. The user pulls an important Card out of that stream and pins it elsewhere on the Dashboard. A WebMCP-capable agent can later create Cards, move content, update the Canvas, or manage the WatchBot. Both the human and the agent continue working against the same persistent state. This turns the agent from an external chatbot into a participant in the user's workspace. How WebMCP is implemented OpenBento registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . The WebMCP layer maps a safe set of snake_case tools onto the same authoritative domain action system used by the application's own UI. Current tools cover retrieving Canvas state, creating and switching Canvases, creating/updating/moving/resizing Cards, managing viewport state, fullscreen Dashboard presentation, creating and managing WatchBots, and reading WatchBot status. OpenBento currently exposes 15 WebMCP tools . The WebMCP implementation does not maintain a separate privileged mutation layer. Authentication, ownership checks, validation, and persistence pass through the same shared domain executor used by the human UI. Architecture OpenBento uses Next.js 16, React, TypeScript, Supabase PostgreSQL/Auth, Railway, XYFlow, OpenAI, X API, YouTube Data API, Sentry, and Resend. The application runs as a web service plus dedicated background workers for different monitoring providers. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was making background AI activity coexist with a persistent spatial interface. An early version placed every newly discovered Card directly onto an infinite Canvas. That quickly became unusable. We redesigned OpenBento around a finite Dashboard with dedicated streaming Columns. WatchBots continuously update their Columns while users can pull important information out into the persistent Dashboard. We also had to make WebMCP a genuine part of the application's architecture instead of a demo-only wrapper. WebMCP actions use the same domain action catalog, authentication, validation, and persistence layer as the human UI. What we learned The most interesting lesson was that agent-friendly websites benefit from exposing intent-level operations , not reproducing mouse and keyboard interaction. A tool like create_watchbot or move_card communicates much more useful application semantics than asking an agent to infer coordinates and manipulate the UI visually. WebMCP makes that model native to the website. What's next OpenBento can expand into a broader personal intelligence environment with richer market Cards, more social/news providers, AI-generated layouts, configurable Dashboard templates, team collaboration, and additional WebMCP actions. AI organizes the story. Sources remain the story. title: PrepWise Lite
pitch: Smart pantry tracking and recipe management web application that helps you keep track, manage and generate your inventory, shopping lists, and recipes with a privacy first approach.
about_excerpt: Smart pantry tracking and recipe management web application that helps you keep track, manage and generate your inventory, shopping lists, and recipes with a privacy first approach. Like Comment Story Updates Using Chat GPT MacOS Desktop app for testing, Chat GPT is reasoning through and doing tool calls. Confirmation modal for user after Chat GPT did its work Recipe view that shows the new recipes from Chat GPT The first expanded recipe from Chat GPT The second expanded recipe from Chat GPT Inspiration My wife asks if we have ...breadcrumbs, After checking all four obvious spots I said no, later after she returns with freshly purchased groceries she finds the breadcrumbs in another spot that I didn't think to check. This was not a "we need an app" problem so much as "nobody knew what we had in our pantry and kitchen", and it is exactly the kind of question an AI assistant should be able to answer instantly, if it could ever actually see the pantry. I started building PrepWise Lite earlier this month on my free time as a local-only, privacy first pantry tracker with zero backend by design. when the WebMCP challenge landed, it was the first time there was a legitimate way to let an agent read that data without breaking the one promise the app makes: nothing leaves your device unless you say so, What it does PrepWise Lite tracks a pantry, a cookbook, and food allergies, entirely in the browser's localStorage, no accounts, no backend, no network calls once loaded. Beyond the usual inventory/recipe/shopping-list/expiration features, it now exposes 13 WebMCP tools so an agent open in the same tab can: summarize the pantry and shopping list, find what's expiring soonest, check what's missing (and by how much) from a recipe to help ground a substitution suggestion, rank recipes for weekly planning by what rescues an expiring ingredient, batch several recipes' timing so an agent can sequence them across limited stovetop/oven/air-fryer capacity, check a recipe against a recorded allergy, propose new inventory from a fridge photo, and write up a whole recipe with per-step timers, propose new inventory from a fridge photo, and write up a whole recipe with per-step timers. Every write is staged as a preview the user must confirm, never applied automatically and that preview is a refining pass rather than a yes/no gate: a quantity the model misread off a photo gets corrected in place, and any row dropped, before anything lands. How PrepWise was built Vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, no framework, no bundler, no runtime dependency. The CSP is connect-src 'none', so the app is structurally incapable of making a network call. "assets/js/webmcp.js" registers each tool via "document.modelContext.registerTool();" handlers run in the page next to the same state object the UI already renders from, so exposing a tool is a local function call, not a new attack surface. The governing rule: reads are answered directly, writes are staged. Every write tool builds a backup-shaped payload and routes it through the exact "validateBackup()" to "sanitizeBackup()" then to "import-preview" gate a hand-edited backup file would go through. An agent gets no shortcut a hostile file wouldn't get. The whole feature is off by default; registering nothing until the user intentionally ticks one Settings checkbox. Challenges I ran into Real agents find real bugs static tests miss. An early run against a live agent returned every recipe with a blank method the step text lived in content, and the code read .text. The existing test only asserted "Ingredients:" appeared, so it passed on a recipe with an empty method. Fixed, and the test now checks for actual step text. Keeping "an assistant can propose, never apply" airtight under UI tampering. It's not enough to hide the "replace everything" radio button for agent-sourced imports the confirm handler independently re-checks the source of the import regardless of what the (hide-able, script-editable) radio says. Resisting the urge to fake domain expertise. A few tool ideas we considered such as calculating food-safety timelines during a power outage, flagging "nutritional gaps," reverse-engineering a spice blend, would have required PrepWise to invent plausible-sounding heuristics from a bare item name, with zero temperature, storage-location, or nutrition data behind them. For a food-safety context, a confidently wrong heuristic is a real harm, not just a bug. We scoped those down to "PrepWise hands over the real data it has; the agent's own food/nutrition knowledge does the actual reasoning" instead. Testing an API that doesn't exist yet in a test browser. WebMCP is a moving W3C Community Group draft behind a Chrome flag; Playwright's bundled Chromium doesn't support it at all. Lots of trial and error. Making the preview editable without turning the sanitizer into decoration. The whole point of staging a write is that nothing reaches the pantry unchecked, so adding form fields to that screen is exactly where a safety property quietly dies. The rule we settled on: an edit is still input. Edits land on the staged payload, and the confirm handler re-runs the same sanitizer over all of it before applying — nothing is trusted for having been in the page. The item's name deliberately stayed read-only, because changing it changes whether the merge sees a duplicate, so the row would have to re-decide between "will add" and "already in your pantry" as you type. Accomplishments that I am proud of Added a full agent-facing tool surface without loosening the CSP by one character, connect-src 'none' on day one is still connect-src 'none' today. Every single write path, file import, sample data, or an agent's proposal goes through the identical "validate/sanitize/preview/confirm" gate. There is no separate, quieter door for a model to walk through. Allergy severity is never disclosed to an agent, matching exactly what Settings promises a human user and it's pinned by a test that stages a real conflict and asserts the severity string never appears in the output. 13 tools, off by default, verified against a real agent in real Chrome. The human-in-the-loop gate is a refining pass, not a rubber stamp. A vision model miscounts what it cannot see like six oranges in the photo is eight in the bag once the buried ones are counted. So an agent's proposed rows carry an editable quantity and unit and an Add tick: correct what it misread, drop what you don't want, then confirm, which is more efficient than throwing all the work away and doing a new call. What I learned The right mental model for handing an agent access to a personal-data app isn't "sandbox what it can see" it's "answer freely, stage everything that changes something" which turned out to generalize cleanly across a dozen tools built weeks apart. A local-first architecture, which we'd built for privacy reasons that had nothing to do with AI, turned out to be exactly what makes an app trustworthy to hand to an agent: there's no server in the loop to leak to in the first place. The most valuable thing a tool can do for a model is supply ground truth the model has no other way to get such as what's actually on your shelf, what's actually about to expire, and then get out of the way not try to out-reason the model on things it already knows better such as food chemistry, nutrition, spice profiles. "Approve or reject" is the wrong shape for a human-in-the-loop gate when the model's mistake is small and numeric. Forcing a binary choice on a proposal that is 90% right means the user either accepts a number they know is wrong or discards work that was mostly correct, and the first of those is what actually happens. Letting them fix it in place is better UX and a stronger safety argument: the human stops being a rubber stamp and becomes the one who ultimately decides and approves the unit and value. What's next for PrepWise Lite More refining, and more agentic testing to try and catch anything a real agentic conversation surfaces that a test suite wouldn't. Beyond that: the two other ideas from the original design such as starting a timer, and switching views are still unbuilt, and a couple of the scoped-down ideas from this new round of edits like an honest "storage-location-aware version of the outage/storm tools" would need a deliberate data model addition rather than another heuristic, worth designing and iterating on it properly rather than rushing in under deadline pressure. title: Relay
pitch: An ops console where every UI action has a matching tool, enforced by CI, so it's fully operable by an agent alone, no mouse required.
about_excerpt: An ops console where every UI action has a matching tool, enforced by CI, so it's fully operable by an agent alone, no mouse required. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Complex professional software is where accessibility fails hardest. Dispatch boards, scheduling grids, drag-and-drop conflict resolvers, all of it leans on spatial interaction: drag this, hover that, click a target that's twelve pixels wide. Someone who can't use a mouse gets locked out of exactly the tools where their judgment would matter most. We wanted to build the sharpest possible counterargument to that, a real operations console where an agent has full authority to do everything a mouse user can, with nothing held back. What it does Relay is a logistics-dispatch console: jobs, drivers, vehicles, time windows, and the double-bookings and coverage gaps that inevitably come with all of that. Its core claim is enforced parity. Every action in the UI has a matching WebMCP tool with identical authority, and the reverse holds too. No tool exists that the UI can't also trigger, and no button exists that only a mouse can reach. Ask an agent to close a coverage gap, resolve a scheduling conflict, or preview a bulk reassignment before committing to it, and it does real work against real schedule state, the same reducer the UI itself writes through. simulate_change is a genuine dry run: it calls that reducer, discards the result, and hands back only the diff, so an agent can show you what a reschedule would do before anything actually happens. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite on the client, Cloudflare Workers plus a Durable Object as the backend, the same pattern as our other two entries. src/shared/reducer.ts is the single mutation path for assign, reschedule, swap, and bulk reassign, and it throws a real SkillMismatchError when someone tries to put a driver on a job they're not qualified for. src/shared/derive.ts computes conflicts and coverage gaps against live state, not canned examples. The part we're actually proudest of is scripts/check-tool-parity.ts . It asserts that Relay's mutating tools and the UI's mutating actions are the exact same set, not a superset in either direction, and it runs as the first step of every build. Ship a button with no matching tool, or a tool with no matching control, and the build just fails. That's not a design principle we're asking you to trust. It's a gate. The seed schedule ships with a real conflict (two jobs double-booked onto one driver, overlapping by an hour) and a real coverage gap (a hazmat job with exactly one qualified driver, and that driver's marked unavailable), so list_conflicts and find_coverage_gaps have something to actually find the moment you open the app. Challenges we ran into Enforcing parity mechanically turned out to be harder than just building the tools. It's easy to write a tool and a button that do roughly the same thing and call it done. Building the CI check that fails the build the moment they drift apart took real thought about what counts as "the same action", is reschedule_assignment the same capability as dragging a job on the timeline? We decided yes, and the registry in src/shared/ui-actions.ts reflects that decision, not just a list of function names that happened to match. We also hit a real validation gap the hard way. reschedule_assignment originally accepted any two numbers as a time window, so an agent that meant "6am" as a time-of-day offset instead of an absolute timestamp could silently corrupt a job's schedule into 1970. We added an assertValidWindow check and clearer schema descriptions after catching this from a live activity-feed log, which was a genuinely useful reminder that a tool's input schema saying "number" isn't the same as it saying what the number means. And the same shared-board demo-state problem we hit on our other two apps showed up here too: because a Durable Object's seed loads exactly once, repeated testing consumed the same live board every time. Fixed with per-visitor isolated schedules and a visible reset button. Accomplishments we're proud of A parity guarantee that's mechanical, not aspirational. check-tool-parity.ts isn't a claim in a README, it's a build step that fails loudly the moment someone adds a UI action without a paired tool. simulate_change as a real dry run, not a description of one. It runs the actual reducer and throws the result away, so the diff an agent shows you is the real diff, computed the real way. A schedule view built as a genuine <table> with proper <th scope="col"> and labeled controls instead of a drag-and-drop grid, specifically so it's screen-reader operable from day one rather than retrofitted later. What we learned Accessibility and agent-operability turned out to be the same problem wearing different names. Once every capability in an app is expressed as a named, described tool with a real schema, that description is simultaneously a machine interface and the clearest possible explanation of what the app does, for a screen reader, for a voice interface, for anyone who's never seen the UI. Building for agents and building for accessibility pulled us in exactly the same direction the entire time. That surprised us going in and feels obvious in hindsight. What's next A full WCAG 2.2 AA audit to sit alongside the enforced-parity guarantee, since right now the table-based schedule view is built with accessibility in mind but hasn't been formally verified. And a client-side undo stack for mutations, matching what Cadence already has, since Relay currently only has the audit log for accountability, not reversibility. title: SkyRingAI-WebMCP
pitch: Run your AI receptionist from ChatGPT with secure analytics, transcripts, appointments, and preview-before-publish configuration updates.
about_excerpt: Run your AI receptionist from ChatGPT with secure analytics, transcripts, appointments, and preview-before-publish configuration updates. Like 3 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Small-business owners using an AI receptionist accumulate valuable context across call analytics, transcripts, appointments, and assistant settings. Answering a question like “Which qualified callers need follow-up?” normally means navigating several screens and then switching to another workflow to act on the answer. Conventional browser agents must guess at controls and page state, which is brittle and especially risky when changing a live voice assistant. What it does SkyRingAI-WebMCP turns the authenticated SkyRingAI customer portal into a structured, agent-operable workspace. After the existing Supabase session resolves an active customer, the portal registers seven private WebMCP tools: get_dashboard_summary search_call_history get_call_details list_upcoming_appts get_assistant_config preview_assistant_update publish_assistant_update A customer can ask ChatGPT to summarize performance, find qualified calls, inspect a bounded transcript, list upcoming appointments, read the full receptionist configuration, and propose changes. Configuration changes use an explicit preview-before-publish workflow: the preview returns field-level differences and a short-lived ID; only a separate publish request saves the reviewed change. The production demo uses a dedicated non-admin judge account with isolated fictional records, a disposable VAPI assistant, and a live inbound demo number. The public repository contains the complete WebMCP contracts, seven-tool implementation, registration lifecycle, fixture provider, tests, and runnable sanitized demo—not the private commercial SaaS. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a strong fit because the useful unit is a trusted business operation, not a page click. An agent receives bounded tools with explicit schemas, read/write annotations, and authentication-derived scope instead of guessing how to traverse a dashboard. This lets a person and agent combine analytics, call discovery, transcript review, appointment context, and controlled action in one conversation. Tool inputs cannot select a customer or tenant. Stored transcript and database text is treated as untrusted, phone output is masked, and ranges, transcript size, pagination, and configuration fields are bounded. How we built it The tool layer is organized around a provider interface. The portal resolves the authenticated Supabase user and active customer, constructs a provider bound to that trusted context, validates tool inputs, repeats customer filters on production reads, and normalizes privacy-bounded results. An abortable lifecycle removes every private tool when the authenticated session ends. Assistant updates first read the complete current configuration so list replacements can preserve stable IDs. Greeting-only changes use the existing direct assistant path. Every effective non-greeting change must complete the authenticated N8N preview workflow before a publishable ID exists. Publishing accepts only that short-lived preview ID, and the server resolves the customer again before saving and requesting the downstream VAPI update. Challenge-period enhancement SkyRingAI existed before this challenge and briefly experimented with one small public, read-only WebMCP pricing tool plus declarative form annotations. During the submission period I built a substantial new authenticated customer-portal capability with Codex: seven tools spanning dashboard analytics, call search, bounded transcripts, appointments, complete assistant configuration, and preview-before-publish updates. I added the customer-scoped production provider, validation and privacy boundaries, lifecycle cleanup, controlled N8N mutation path, automated tests, dedicated production judge tenant, and separate open-source challenge repository. This expands the early experiment into a coherent, working business operations workflow. How I used AI and Codex ChatGPT is the runtime conversational control surface. VAPI powers the voice receptionist, and N8N powers the existing non-greeting configuration generation and update workflow. Codex was the primary engineering collaborator for architecture inspection, scoping, implementation, debugging, tests, security hardening, production verification, and open-source packaging. Lovable helped provision and verify the isolated production judge tenant through its connected Supabase and existing server integrations. The feature was tested live through ChatGPT from another machine. Accomplishments Seven authenticated WebMCP tools working in production. Customer identity derived from the trusted session, never a tool argument. Bounded outputs, masked phones, safe errors, strict schemas, and untrusted-content hints. Human-reviewable, single-use preview-before-publish assistant mutations. Real N8N preview/publish integration for non-greeting changes. Verified RLS isolation and a dedicated fictional judge environment. Runnable fixture-only open-source edition with no production credentials or customer data. Passing automated tests and production build. What I learned The most important lesson was that exposing more tools is not automatically better. Agent-native product design is about creating trustworthy operational boundaries: give the agent enough structured context to be useful, keep identity outside caller-controlled input, label untrusted data, constrain outputs, and separate “show me what would change” from “make the change.” What's next After the challenge, I plan to expand customer-controlled WebMCP workflows while keeping the same authentication, tenant, privacy, and preview-before-publish model. Likely next areas include controlled follow-up actions, broader analytics questions, and additional assistant lifecycle operations. title: Toban
pitch: Turn one plain-language request into a structured, editable duty roster.
about_excerpt: Turn one plain-language request into a structured, editable duty roster. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Toban is a WebMCP app that turns a single natural-language request into an editable duty roster, reducing the effort and errors in schedule creation. Inspiration Duty rosters look simple, but the request behind one is usually scattered across names, duties, dates, rotation intervals, exceptions, presentation choices, and sharing rules. Toban already gave people a visual way to create and manage these rosters. The WebMCP Challenge made it possible to add a faster path: describe the whole intent once, let an agent translate it into typed product actions, and keep Toban responsible for validation and rotation math. What it does With a WebMCP-capable client connected to Toban, a person can ask for a complete roster in ordinary language. The request can include members, separate duties, a start date, an automatic or manual rotation, weekends and Japanese holidays to skip, a Table, Calendar, or Wheel view, and a visual style suited to the setting. The agent calls Toban's page-defined tools. Toban validates the structured input, calculates the roster, saves it, and displays the result as a normal editable schedule. Follow-up requests can change one duty, adjust appearance, restrict task eligibility, query a future assignment without changing state, advance a manual rotation, or rename a member while preserving unrelated settings. Public sharing stays under human control. The agent can prepare the share step, but Toban opens its own confirmation dialog and waits for a person to decide whether to publish. How it was built Toban is a React and TypeScript application served through Cloudflare Workers. For the challenge, I extended its WebMCP interface to 18 typed page tools around the existing roster domain: create, read, target, refine, present, calculate, print, and prepare sharing. Tool schemas use stable roster identifiers and structured results so an agent can operate on product concepts instead of guessing through DOM clicks. The roster engine remains the source of truth for validation, eligible-date calculation, Japanese public-holiday handling, rotation state, and persistence. The agent interprets intent; Toban performs deterministic application logic. The demo was captured in the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser, which the official Challenge rules list as a WebMCP testing method. During the capture, the agent calls those real tools on the live page. Challenges The hardest part was making follow-up language safe. A request such as “replace Plant Care with Supply Check” should update one duty without silently changing members, dates, rotation rules, view, or appearance. The implementation adds stable target resolution, typed partial updates, explicit errors, idempotent mutation behavior, structured read-back, and verification after meaningful writes. Another challenge was drawing the right publication boundary. Sharing has an external effect, so the WebMCP tool prepares a reviewable confirmation but does not publish. That keeps the final decision visible and human-controlled. Accomplishments One natural-language request creates a complete, styled roster. The same typed roster model supports Table, Calendar, and Wheel views. Calendar assignments account for weekends and Japanese public holidays. Narrow follow-ups preserve fields the person did not ask to change. Read-only tools answer assignment questions without mutating the roster. The agent stops at Toban's sharing confirmation; publication requires an explicit click in Toban. The public repository includes the full challenge-period commit history and an MIT license. What I learned WebMCP works best when the page exposes domain actions rather than a catalog of UI gestures. The agent is useful at interpreting a flexible request, while the application is better at enforcing invariants, calculating dates, storing state, and presenting the result for human review. What's next Next steps include more locale-aware holiday calendars, richer rule explanations, and additional verification views for complex eligibility constraints, while preserving the same typed-tool and human-confirmation boundaries. title: WebMCP Portfolio Kit
pitch: An evidence-first WebMCP portfolio kit: agents inspect published work, identify gaps, and prepare human-reviewed next steps.
about_excerpt: An evidence-first WebMCP portfolio kit: agents inspect published work, identify gaps, and prepare human-reviewed next steps. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I'm a freelance WordPress/WooCommerce and Shopify developer, and I already had a portfolio site built for an earlier dev.to Gemini hackathon. What stuck with me from that event wasn't the winning entries — it was one unranked submission: an MCP-enabled portfolio where an agent could actually query someone's CV instead of just reading it. It never won anything, but it was the only project I actually remembered months later. The WebMCP Challenge was the excuse to finally build that properly — and to fix what I think was the real gap in that original idea: answering "what are his skills" is a parlor trick. Answering "does he actually fit this job, and where are the gaps" is what a technical buyer actually needs. What it does WebMCP Portfolio Starter Kit exposes 8 WebMCP tools on a normal-looking portfolio site. An agent — acting for a recruiter, a CTO, whoever — can hand it a real brief and get back a transparent requirement → evidence → gap map: evidence found, or no direct evidence, stated plainly. It's never a forced "95% match" score. From there the agent can compare engagement options (migration / optimization / audit / advisory), save a session-only discovery brief, and prepare a contact request. A human reviews the draft; the core kit never sends a message. It's also a starter kit, not just a personal site: config, content, and code are cleanly separated, so anyone can fork it, drop in their own skills and projects, and deploy their own copy to Vercel with one click and zero required environment variables. How we built it I extended my existing Vite/React portfolio rather than starting from scratch, restructuring it into config/ (the fork surface), content/ (skills, case studies, engagement options), and generic src/lib/ tool code that never hardcodes a name. All 8 tools use the WebMCP Imperative API with explicit input schemas. Evidence tools are read-only; the remaining tools only update the visible page or create an unsent, reviewable draft. The core kit needs no backend. The one optional exception is a /setup Profile Bootstrapper that uses Vercel AI Gateway to help a forker draft their profile.json from raw material — off by default behind an explicit env var, output validated against a strict schema, and prompted to treat source text as data, never as instructions. Testing wasn't just manual clicking: validate-content checks the profile data against a schema, test:forkability runs the matching logic against a completely unrelated fixture persona, and a production run of the official webmcp-evals suite passed all eight tools against the live deployment. Challenges we ran into The hard trade-off was breadth versus coherence. I kept all eight tools, but prioritised their shared evidence model, clear side-effect boundaries, and production testing over extra visual polish and stretch features. Avoiding a false-precision "fit score" was a real design problem, not just a copy choice — early versions of the matching tool risked implying certainty the underlying logic didn't have. I settled on a plain requirement/evidence/gap map with an explicit disclaimer field on every response instead. And I didn't want "forkable" to just be a claim in a README. Proving it meant building an actual unrelated test persona and a smoke test, not just asserting the code was generic. Accomplishments that we're proud of The forkability test genuinely passes against a persona with nothing to do with cloud infrastructure — it surfaces a real skill match, a real project match, and an honestly stated unmatched requirement, for a profile that shares nothing with mine. Zero required environment variables to deploy the core kit — fork, edit two JSON files, click deploy. The optional AI-assisted drafting path is off by default and explicitly designed against prompt injection in its own source material, not just in theory. And map_requirements_to_evidence stating a gap plainly, instead of forcing a match — that's the single behavior the whole project is really about. Existing-work disclosure The visual portfolio and its self-authored project history existed before the challenge. During the submission period, I meaningfully extended it with eight WebMCP tools and schemas, the requirement-to-evidence interface, source-labelled outputs, the reusable config/content/code split, the Bootstrapper, and automated validation and evaluation. The public repository’s dated September 2–3 commits document that WebMCP-specific work. What we learned That a "never overclaim" constraint has to be enforced in the code itself, not just promised in a README — stating a gap instead of forcing a match, and never wiring up an auto-send path for the contact tool. That deterministic, auditable matching is a legitimate design choice against a generative one, not just a corner cut when you're short on time — every match traces back to real data instead of a model's guess. And that two small automated tests, plus one production evals run, are worth more than an evening of manual clicking when there's no time left to re-verify everything by hand before a deadline. What's next for WebMCP Portfolio Starter Kit Support importing authorised structured exports or pasted profile material — for example from a PeoplePerHour export — into profile.json , instead of a one-time manual copy. Semantic, embedding-based matching via Vercel AI Gateway as an option — making the matching smarter while keeping every match's underlying evidence fully auditable, not replacing it with a black box. And more real forks, to prove this out beyond the one alternate-persona fixture. title: yesmcp: agent-native booking, the human keeps the click
pitch: A real booking service an in-browser agent can use through WebMCP. It checks live availability and prepares a booking. The page then asks the human to press Confirm.
about_excerpt: A real booking service an in-browser agent can use through WebMCP. It checks live availability and prepares a booking. The page then asks the human to press Confirm. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What it is yesmcp ( https://yesmcp.com ) is a live business. It builds companies their own MCP connectors so their customers can book, order and ask directly inside AI chats. Its own site now practices what it sells at a deeper level: the site itself is agent-native through WebMCP. The home page registers six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Every other page registers four of them: the entrance gate and the demo driver exist only on the home page, and a tool that cannot work on a page is never registered there. get_services : the authored services catalog. The answer carries an explicit degradation flag, so an agent never presents a stub as the catalog. check_availability : genuinely bookable 30-minute windows with slot ids. Every label carries an explicit UTC offset, never a bare wall-clock time. book_consult : prepares a REAL booking, then opens a confirmation card on the page. The request is submitted only after the human clicks Confirm. Decline is a first-class answer returned to the agent, not an error. get_live_status : live proof numbers from the production connector. answer_entrance_check : the site asks arriving visitors one question at the door. This answers it, so an agent can open the page for its human instead of stalling at a dialog it cannot see past. drive_demo (home page only): drives the interactive hero chat demo through the same controls a finger taps, so the visitor can watch the story the agent is telling. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP A services business's page is exactly where "humans and agents together" stops being a slogan. The agent does the tedious part: find the catalog, check the calendar, fill the form. The human does the human part: decide, and press the one button that commits their calendar and their inbox. Before WebMCP an in-browser agent had to guess at our DOM and click blind. One redesign and it breaks. With WebMCP it gets the same honest API our own page uses, and the page stays a normal website for everyone else. No modelContext API means no behavior at all, so all of this is progressive enhancement. How it creates a better user experience The visitor never has to translate between two systems. They say what they want in their own words, the agent turns that into two tool calls, and what comes back on screen is the server's own label for the slot, not the agent's paraphrase of it. The one irreversible step stays with the person: a card rendered by the site itself, with a button the agent cannot press. What people and agents can do together that was hard before A visitor tells their browser agent "find me a slot Thursday afternoon and set up the call". The agent checks real availability, fills the booking, and the visitor confirms with one click on a card the site rendered. The confirmation email and the owner's notification run the same production path every other door uses. The agent can also show things, not only tell them. drive_demo replays the landing's scripted chat story (browse, pick a time, booked, reschedule) in front of the visitor, driven through the same controls a finger would tap. It is labelled as a scripted demo, and the real tools sit right beside it. This is not a prototype It is a running production service. Bookings are atomic: the confirmation email is sent inside the transaction, so if the send fails the slot is released. A booking nobody was told about is not a booking. There is rate limiting, an origin allow-list on the browser endpoints, a public status endpoint reporting since 2026-08-21, and a test suite that runs green on every change. The public counter deliberately excludes bookings made from test domains, so the number it reports can only ever mean real customers. The demo booking recorded for this submission does not inflate it. The same capability already runs as a remote MCP server at https://mcp.yesmcp.com/mcp , which works today from Claude and ChatGPT. WebMCP is the third door into the same real system. How I implemented WebMCP Imperative API: document.modelContext.registerTool , with a provideContext fallback for hosts that shipped the earlier surface. Plain JavaScript, no dependencies, no framework. Tool results use the MCP content shape. Verified end to end in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, and with the Model Context Tool Inspector extension driving the tools through a real agent loop. Safety, in this order: the page never books without a human click; no modelContext means no behavior at all; agent input is never parsed as markup, because the confirmation card is built with createElement only. Server-side validation, rate limits and junk filters are shared verbatim with every other door. title: AgenticRoom
pitch: Your room. Your agent. One shared canvas.
about_excerpt: Your room. Your agent. One shared canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a room gets messy fast. Products live in one tab, measurements in another, and the budget usually ends up in a note or spreadsheet. By the time the pieces come together, the sofa may not fit or the total may no longer make sense. AgenticRoom started with a simple idea: let the person and the agent work on the same room instead of passing suggestions back and forth. What it does AgenticRoom puts a furniture catalog, an editable 3D room, budget tracking, and a shopping cart in one workspace. Start with the room you have, describe the room you want, or share an inspiration image with a compatible browser agent. The agent can inspect what is already in the room, search the catalog, place and move furniture, compare cheaper alternatives, check the layout, change the finishes, track the budget, add selected products to the cart, and save the design. Nothing happens in a hidden result. Every change appears on the same canvas and remains editable by the person. You can let the agent handle a full furnishing pass, step in to move one chair yourself, then ask it to finish the room without losing context. Why WebMCP fits A room plan is a chain of connected decisions. A sofa changes the remaining space and budget. A window limits placement. Replacing an expensive item should preserve its position while changing the total. Free-form recommendations alone are not enough. WebMCP gives the browser agent precise actions for those decisions. It can ask what fits, search within a price range, place a product in a valid zone, validate the layout, or add the selected marketplace pieces to the cart. The person makes the taste calls. The agent handles the searching, placement, and arithmetic. Both see the same room and the same result as it changes. How I built it I built AgenticRoom as a browser-only Next.js application using React, TypeScript, React Three Fiber, Three.js, and Zustand. I deliberately kept one source of truth: the human interface and the WebMCP tools call the same Zustand store actions and the same deterministic domain rules. The page registers 31 WebMCP tools through the browser's Model Context API: 11 read tools and 20 mutation tools. Those rules check furniture footprints, placement zones, doors and windows, locks, stock, prices, budgets, room resizing, saved designs, finishes, and cart behavior. If an action is invalid, it returns a structured error and leaves the room unchanged. There is no backend, account requirement, payment processing, API key, or remote runtime data. The furniture catalog and room rules are hand-authored and run entirely in the browser. Features Shared human-and-agent 3D room planning Image-inspired room direction Furniture search by category, style, color, material, price, dimensions, and stock Layout and opening-clearance checks Budget-aware furnishing and cheaper alternatives Editable room dimensions, openings, and finishes Integrated furniture catalog and shopping cart Saved room designs Privacy-conscious agent activity feed 31 structured WebMCP tools for reliable agent actions Testing The project has 135 deterministic domain tests covering placement, validation, pricing, alternatives, resizing, appearance, saved designs, and cart behavior. I also tested the deployed app in ChatGPT's in-app browser with a connected browser agent. No credentials are required. The README includes local setup instructions and reproducible WebMCP workflows. title: ArtSoul  Agent-Native Art Auctions
pitch: An agent can read a live ArtSoul auction on Base bids, deadline, provenance through declared tools instead of guessing at pixels. It prepares the bid. You sign it.
about_excerpt: An agent can read a live ArtSoul auction on Base bids, deadline, provenance through declared tools instead of guessing at pixels. It prepares the bid. You sign it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Available site tools 2 Available site tools 4 Available site tools Available site tools 3 Available site tools 5 Inspiration ArtSoul is an art auction protocol I have been building on Base. The basic idea is simple: an artist can publish a work without minting an NFT first. Collectors discover the work and bid in an auction. Every bid has real commitment behind it through a deposit. Only after the auction settles is the NFT minted to the First Collector. While testing ArtSoul through an AI agent, I noticed a problem. A human can look at the page and usually figure out what is happening. An agent has to infer it from buttons, labels and whatever happens to be visible on screen. But things like the current auction state, the exact deadline, the owner of an artwork or whether a wallet is allowed to bid are not visual guesses. ArtSoul already knows the exact answers. That made WebMCP a very natural fit for the project. Instead of teaching an agent how to navigate ArtSoul visually, I used the challenge to expose the protocol itself to the agent. What it does ArtSoul now exposes eleven WebMCP tools: search_artworks - search published works by text, creator, lifecycle state or artwork number find_active_auctions - return auctions that are actually open for bidding, ordered by deadline get_artwork - return the public record for one artwork get_auction_state - return the current auction state, bids, bidder and timing get_artwork_provenance - return Creator, First Collector, current Owner and the event history behind them explain_settlement - explain where an artwork is in the publish → auction → settlement → mint lifecycle open_artwork - open the correct artwork for the user prepare_bid - check the current state and prepare the user for a bid place_bid - hand the transaction to the user's wallet for approval end_expired_auction - finalize an auction whose bidding period has ended prepare_artwork_registration - validate artwork details and open the publishing flow This lets someone ask normal questions such as: “What auctions are open right now?” “Who created artwork 19, who was its first collector, and who owns it now?” “Can you place a bid for me?” The answers come from ArtSoul's own data and Base state instead of from the model trying to interpret the page. ArtSoul currently runs on Base Sepolia. Mainnet is planned after an independent contract audit. The read tools do not require a wallet. The line the agent does not cross The most important part of the integration is what the agent cannot do. It cannot sign a transaction. In my demo, I ask the agent to place a bid. Before doing anything, it checks the live auction state and gives me the current terms. During testing, the first wallet I used was the creator of the artwork. ArtSoul detected that and refused to send me into a transaction that the contract would reject. I then connected another wallet as a collector. The agent checked the auction again, found the current valid minimum bid, and prepared the transaction. My wallet opened with the transaction details. And that is where the agent stopped. I had to review and sign it myself. That separation matters because a bid locks a deposit. I do not want an AI agent, browser page or tool to have authority to make that financial decision for me. Reading can be automatic. Signing stays with the person. No second source of truth I also made a deliberate decision not to copy ArtSoul's economic rules into the WebMCP layer. Things like: bid increments deposits auction duration settlement timing belong to the protocol and its contracts. The WebMCP tools read the current state instead of maintaining another JavaScript version of those rules. That means the agent layer cannot silently drift away from the protocol. The contracts remain the source of truth. Building the agent surface found real bugs One of the most useful parts of the challenge was unexpected. Making ArtSoul answer an agent precisely forced me to check whether every answer was actually correct. That exposed bugs that were much easier for a human using the interface to overlook. Provenance The first implementation returned empty provenance fields because I had assumed the shape of an API response instead of validating the actual production payload. I fixed the parser and changed the test fixture to use the real response structure. Creator bidding The contract already rejects a creator bidding on their own artwork. But before the WebMCP work, a user could still get far enough in the interface to attempt that transaction. The tools now check the connected wallet first and explain the restriction before opening the wallet. Artwork IDs versus auction IDs Artwork IDs and auction IDs are separate counters. Because the numbers can overlap, an artwork lookup could accidentally resolve to an older finished auction with the same numeric ID. That caused a live artwork to appear as if its auction had already ended. The resolver now prefers the live auction belonging to the artwork. This was not just an AI problem. It affected normal bidding too. WebMCP exposed it because an agent cannot compensate for an ambiguous answer the way a person sometimes can. How I built it The integration is intentionally small. The site registers its WebMCP tools through: document.modelContext.registerTool() using JSON Schema inputs. The tools reuse endpoints that ArtSoul already had. I did not create a second backend for the agent and I did not change the protocol contracts for the challenge. The WebMCP implementation is isolated from the main application logic and the tool definitions are built from injected dependencies, which lets me test them against mocked responses in the existing Node test suite. The repository currently has 831 tests, with CI running on Ubuntu and Windows. For visitors using a normal browser without WebMCP support, the integration does effectively nothing. The bootstrap exits before registering tools or making extra requests. Challenges The biggest challenge was deciding where automation should stop. It would have been easy to make the demo look more impressive by pushing more logic into the agent layer. I deliberately went in the opposite direction. For example, an early version of the bidding helper calculated bidding values itself. I removed that. If the contract controls an economic rule, the agent should not maintain its own copy of it. Another challenge was working inside an existing product rather than a clean hackathon prototype. ArtSoul already has contracts, an indexer, APIs, UI flows and tests. I wanted WebMCP to sit on top of that architecture without changing how the protocol itself behaves. Most of the integration therefore lives in new code rather than rewriting existing application logic. What I learned The most interesting WebMCP question for me became: What should the agent not be allowed to do? Giving an agent more tools is easy. Knowing where to stop is harder. For ArtSoul, the boundary is clear. The agent can search, read, explain, verify and prepare. It can help a person reach the correct transaction. But it cannot make the final financial decision. I also learned that exposing an application to an agent is a surprisingly effective correctness test. A human can look at a slightly confusing interface and work around it. An agent asks for a precise state. If the application gives the wrong answer, there is nowhere for that ambiguity to hide. What's next The next step is making auction state more reactive so an agent can receive changes as they happen rather than only fetching them on request. I also want to improve the bid handoff so the prepared amount can move directly into the bidding interface while keeping the exact same security boundary: the agent prepares the person signs. ArtSoul is currently running on Base Sepolia, and the next major protocol step is an independent contract audit before Base mainnet. For this challenge I designed and shipped the agent layer — which tools to expose, what each one is allowed to answer, and the decision that the agent prepares a bid but never signs it. The refusal to let an agent sign is the part I care about most. title: Atinamos Agent Shop
pitch: A live WebMCP storefront where ChatGPT can discover and request paid AI services, while x402 payments remain explicitly human-controlled and results return directly to the agent.
about_excerpt: A live WebMCP storefront where ChatGPT can discover and request paid AI services, while x402 payments remain explicitly human-controlled and results return directly to the agent. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT sees the live Atinamos WebMCP site tools exposed directly by the Agent Shop The paid request lifecycle: human approval required, Base wallet connected, x402 payment settled, and service completed Human-readable view of the completed JSON Repair result after the 0.005 USDC payment settled Inspiration Atinamos Agent Shop already existed before this challenge. It was an experiment in whether one AI agent could actually find and buy a small service from another AI-facing service. I already had a catalogue, paid x402 endpoints, REST/OpenAPI and an external MCP endpoint. When the WebMCP Challenge appeared, the obvious question for me was, could we make the website itself usable by ChatGPT, rather than expecting the agent to know about our API or MCP server beforehand? The other question was payment! I didn't want WebMCP to suddenly mean that an agent could spend from a wallet without the person using it knowing what was happening. So the aim became quite simple, let the agent find the service, understand the price and request the work, but stop when money is required. The human should still control the payment. What was built The Agent Shop now exposes eight WebMCP tools from the live website. ChatGPT can list the services, inspect their inputs, check prices, search our observed service market, start a paid request and check the result afterwards. For the demo I used our JSON Validate / Repair service, which costs 0.005 USDC. ChatGPT sends deliberately broken JSON to the real service endpoint. The endpoint returns HTTP 402 because payment is required, at that point WebMCP stops. The request also appears in the Agent Activity panel on the website, where the human can choose to continue and pay using their own Base wallet. Once I approved the payment, x402 verifies and settles it, the existing JSON service runs, and the result becomes available to the agent and to the human result page. The important bit for me is that the agent can initiate the transaction without being given control of the wallet. How it works The existing Agent Shop is built with FastAPI and already had the service catalogue, paid routes, OpenAPI, MCP and x402 support. During the challenge we added browser-native WebMCP tools using 'document.modelContext.registerTool(...)' The tools use the same live catalogue and endpoints as the rest of the service. We did not make a separate demo backend. I added the Agent Activity panel so the person using the site can see what the agent is doing and where the payment boundary has been reached. The responsibilities are deliberately split. The agent can discover, quote and request a service. The human connects the wallet and approves the payment. WebMCP does not hold wallet keys, sign the payment itself or automatically retry a paid request. What went wrong along the way Quite a lot of the useful work came from things not behaving as expected. I found that read-only WebMCP tools and the purchase tool did not always behave the same way between ChatGPT model configurations. The embedded browser could also lose state during the wallet hand-off, so safe request recovery was added. The first result viewer was too complicated and actually crashed the embedded browser. Rather than keep patching it, most of it was removed and that made the result button navigate to a simple dedicated result page. That ended up being much more reliable. What I learned The interesting part of WebMCP for me is not just that an agent can click fewer buttons. The website can actually tell the agent what it can do, what something costs and what inputs are required instead of asking the agent to infer all of that from HTML. The payment experiment also reinforced something i had already been thinking about with AI-agent commerce, the ability to act and authority to spend should not automatically be the same thing. This project now demonstrates that separation with a real payment and a real service rather than a mocked checkout. What's next I have other live services in the shop, including Render Check, Buyer Check and Technical SEO Crawl, so the same WebMCP pattern can be extended across those. The wider experiment is still the same one that started Atinamos Agent Shop. Understanding how AI agents will actually discover, select, buy and verify small machine services in the real world. title: Companion Sketch
pitch: Skribbl.io or Pictionary, but with all your friends and all their AI agents 🤖
about_excerpt: Skribbl.io or Pictionary, but with all your friends and all their AI agents 🤖 Like 1 Comment Story Updates OWL?! Inspiration Companion Sketch started with a simple question: what would a game look like if an AI was not just generating content for a human, but was actually another player? Most AI games treat AI as a tool, narrator, or content generator. We wanted to experiment with something more direct: a shared game where a human and ChatGPT could draw, guess, chat, and participate in the same gameplay loop. Drawing games felt like the perfect test because they depend on creativity, interpretation, imperfect communication, and humor. Those interactions become much more interesting when humans and AI share the same canvas. What it does Companion Sketch is a real-time multiplayer drawing and guessing game for humans and AI agents. A human creates or joins a room, then ChatGPT can join the same visible game through native WebMCP Website Tools. Players take turns choosing secret prompts, drawing them, and guessing what other players are creating. The current version includes: Real-time drawing and game synchronization through Socket.IO Shared multiplayer rooms with clear, copyable room codes Human and AI players participating as equal game participants Three private candidate words for every drawing turn Native WebMCP Website Tools for ChatGPT gameplay A REST API fallback for other agents and testing Touch-friendly mobile drawing with pointer support A compact drawing toolbar with expandable tool, brush-size, and color palettes A mobile-first dark glass-style interface Background and reload recovery that preserves the current room, round, timer, score, chat, and canvas Graceful fallback when WebMCP is unavailable The result is a social game where the interesting part is not simply “AI-generated art,” but what happens when humans and AI try to understand each other’s drawings. How ChatGPT plays through WebMCP The page registers eight top-level imperative Website Tools using document.modelContext.registerTool: companion_sketch_status — Read the current viewer-safe game state companion_sketch_join — Join the visible room as the ChatGPT companion companion_sketch_pick_word — Choose a drawing prompt companion_sketch_draw_paths — Submit bounded normalized drawing paths companion_sketch_clear_canvas — Clear the canvas when authorized companion_sketch_guess — Submit a guess companion_sketch_chat — Send a chat message companion_sketch_leave — Leave the room and invalidate the session ChatGPT does not need to manually manage a bearer token. The page adapter keeps the agent session inside tab-scoped storage and sends only the structured action required by each tool. Drawing requests are intentionally bounded. The agent submits normalized polylines instead of arbitrary canvas commands, and the server validates colors, sizes, coordinates, and stroke counts before accepting them. The tools are registered only in the top-level page, matching the current WebMCP integration requirements. The same game still works normally for human players in browsers that do not support WebMCP. How we built it We built Companion Sketch from scratch as a web application. The backend uses Express for the application server and Socket.IO for realtime communication. Socket.IO handles room membership, drawing updates, chat, readiness, turn changes, timers, and game-state broadcasts. The game engine is server-authoritative. It controls: Player identities and room membership Turn order and timers Private drawing words Stroke validation Guess scoring AI guess windows Canvas clearing permissions Human reconnect and resume behavior The WebMCP layer sits on top of the same game services as the REST API, so ChatGPT and human players follow the same rules instead of using a separate simulation. On the frontend, we rebuilt the interface around mobile play. Room codes are prominent and tap-to-copy. The drawing controls are now a small icon rail: one button for the current tool, one for brush size, one for color, and one for clearing. Each control expands into an overlay palette so the canvas keeps as much space as possible. Human sessions use a private resume token stored by the page. If a phone is backgrounded, suspended, or reloaded, the player can reconnect to the same room and continue from the current game state. The game is deployed over HTTPS so it can be opened directly in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and tested as a real WebMCP experience. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was supporting two very different types of players. Humans interact visually through a touchscreen and canvas, while an AI agent needs structured state and explicit actions. We had to design one gameplay system that could support both without making the AI feel like an external controller. WebMCP introduced another challenge. The tools had to be registered in the correct top-level document, use strict input schemas, expose only safe actions, and remain useful when the browser does not support the protocol. Realtime drawing also created synchronization problems. A canvas produces many rapidly changing points, so we had to keep drawing responsive while preventing duplicate strokes, invalid coordinates, oversized requests, and unauthorized actions. Privacy was important as well. The active drawer can see the selected word, but other players and agents receive viewer-safe state. The server never exposes a private drawing prompt to someone who should be guessing. Mobile playtesting exposed additional issues. Drawing with a finger behaves differently from drawing with a mouse, and mobile browsers may pause or reload tabs when they are placed in the background. We added pointer handling, canvas fitting, reconnect logic, and state restoration to make those interruptions recoverable. We also redesigned the toolbar after testing revealed that a full row of controls consumed too much canvas space. The new expandable palettes keep the controls available without sacrificing the drawing area. Accomplishments that we’re proud of The thing we’re most proud of is that Companion Sketch became a real playable human-and-AI game rather than just an AI concept demo. We successfully built: A complete realtime drawing and guessing loop Multiplayer rooms with human and AI identities A functioning WebMCP integration with eight native Website Tools An AI player that can join, choose words, draw, guess, chat, and leave Shared server-authoritative state between the human UI, WebMCP, and REST fallback Private word handling and validated drawing actions A responsive mobile interface with a large canvas and compact controls Recovery from phone backgrounding and page reloads A deployed HTTPS version that can be played from ChatGPT’s browser Automated coverage for state, authorization, privacy, WebMCP registration, and reconnect behavior We also verified the game on a phone-sized 390×844 layout and tested the deployed WebMCP page directly. Seeing people play the game has been especially rewarding. Early playtesters created surprisingly strange drawings, guessed in unexpected ways, and made it clear that the most interesting part of the project is the shared interaction between human creativity and AI interpretation. title: Execution Receipt
pitch: Turn “done” from an agent claim into a verifiable artifact.
about_excerpt: Turn “done” from an agent claim into a verifiable artifact. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI-assisted workflows can fail one step before the visible answer. An agent says a file was attached, a package was built, or a submission was completed, and that unsupported claim becomes input for later work. The rest of the workflow may look coherent even though its trace is already false. Execution Receipt turns that failure into a small, inspectable product. It asks what bytes were actually created, from which source revision, and whether later source changes made the earlier result stale. What it does Execution Receipt gives a person and an agent one shared, revision-aware workspace. Required document slots expose what is present and missing. An incomplete build is rejected with a concrete reason. A successful build creates real ZIP bytes, a manifest, per-document SHA-256 hashes, and a package SHA-256 receipt. Repeating an unchanged build returns the same receipt instead of inventing another execution. Changing a source document preserves the old package but marks its receipt stale. A download request is recorded only as a request; it is never reported as a confirmed save, submission, receipt, or acceptance. The manual interface and WebMCP tools operate on the same state-transition logic. Why WebMCP This is a strong WebMCP use case because the human and the agent operate on the same visible application state and the same guarded transitions. The agent can inspect requirements, add a document, build the package, and read the receipt. The human can inspect the manifest, see the execution trail, and download the artifacts. Neither side has to trust a conversational claim that an action happened. The application exposes four tools through document.modelContext.registerTool: get_case reads requirements, the current revision, receipts, and the execution trail. attach_document attaches or replaces UTF-8 text in a fixed slot using the current expected revision. build_package creates the actual ZIP and receipt or returns a precise missing-evidence or revision-conflict result. get_receipt reports whether a receipt is current or stale. WebMCP is feature-detected, and the application remains usable manually when it is unavailable. How it was built The prototype uses dependency-free HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. core.mjs owns requirements, revisions, ZIP creation, hashing, receipts, and the execution trail. webmcp.mjs registers the agent tools and adapts their inputs to the same core operations used by app.mjs. Documents exist only in the active browser session. Codex helped implement the application, ZIP and hashing logic, WebMCP adapter, mobile presentation, tests, documentation, and public deployment. It also helped design adversarial tests for stale revisions, idempotency, cancellation, and competing builds, and verified ZIP output with an independent Python zipfile reader. Challenges The central challenge was defining a narrow proof boundary. A hash proves that specific bytes were hashed; it does not prove that a document is true or legally valid. Creating ZIP bytes does not prove that the user saved them. A WebMCP handler call identifies the application path used, not an authenticated agent identity. The interface and receipt wording preserve these distinctions. Concurrency was another important failure mode. An older build can finish after a source change. The application performs a final revision check before committing a receipt, so obsolete work cannot become the current result. Accomplishments Real package bytes and inspectable manifest, not a simulated success state. Idempotent builds and preserved stale receipts. Optimistic revision checks for manual and agent-driven changes. Cancellation and concurrent-build protection. Binary-safe manual file attachments up to 2 MiB. 21 automated tests, including 50 deterministic chaotic sessions with 6,000 mixed operations and an independent archive verifier. Testing Open the live app. It initially shows two present documents and one missing approval document. Attempt a build and confirm the missing evidence is named. Add a clearly synthetic approval document, build again, inspect the receipt and manifest, then download the ZIP and Receipt JSON. Replace the project brief and confirm the prior receipt becomes stale. For automated verification, run node --test tests/*.test.mjs with Node.js 22+. The suite passes 21/21 tests. What we learned The strongest reliability boundary is not a longer explanation from the model. It is a product state that makes unsupported transitions difficult, exposes missing evidence, and carries the exact source revision into the result. Execution Receipt does not promise universal truth. It proves the execution that the application actually performed. Real WebMCP validation The public HTTPS deployment was tested in the ChatGPT Work cloud Chrome browser. The browser discovered all four page tools. A build with the missing approval was rejected, attach_document added a synthetic approval at the current revision, build_package created a 1,655-byte ZIP with SHA-256 3bd4de89043b067e3a8c2c5d9fe811f72d92b8673ea4010039befb02fba4d814 , and get_receipt returned the resulting receipt as current. title: Gatherwire
pitch: Turn browser-agent actions into visible, source-linked handoffs your team can verify and continue.
about_excerpt: Turn browser-agent actions into visible, source-linked handoffs your team can verify and continue. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For product and engineering teams using multiple AI assistants, the expensive step is often not generating an answer—it is moving a decision or finding to the next person or agent without losing its source, owner, or next action. Copying a summary into another chat strips away that provenance and makes the handoff hard to verify. Gatherwire explores a simple answer: give a person and a browser agent the same visible workspace, then make a handoff a durable, source-linked product object instead of another disposable chat message. What it does Gatherwire is a public WebMCP collaboration workspace. A person can use it like a compact team room. From that same top-level page, a compatible browser agent discovers seven structured site tools: gatherwire_list_spaces gatherwire_read_messages gatherwire_search_messages gatherwire_list_project_agents gatherwire_publish_handoff gatherwire_post_message gatherwire_create_space The main demo is a five-call mission. The agent lists the spaces, finds a seeded handoff note, reads its source room, finds the available demo project agent, and publishes a handoff to Atlas in the product room using the source message ID as evidence. The result appears immediately in the human interface: a visible capsule with a summary, one next action, the receiving agent, linked evidence, source room, task ID, and correlation ID. A separate receipt panel records the tool call, and clicking the evidence returns to the exact source message. The page marks the mission 5/5 , so evaluators can verify progress without opening a separate transcript. Gatherwire's completed challenge boundary is the handoff layer, not an external agent runtime. Atlas is synthetic and no external agent is started; this keeps discovery, shared state, provenance, and safe write behavior directly testable without implying a production bridge exists. Why WebMCP This experience depends on the page and visitor session the person already has open. A traditional remote API can expose backend functions, but it does not automatically give an agent the exact workspace, on-page progress, or visible receipts that the person sees. WebMCP lets the site declare a narrow capability layer directly: The browser agent does not have to guess where to click or scrape the interface. Human actions and agent calls use the same operations and the same HTTP API. Agent writes refresh the visible product state instead of disappearing into an isolated tool transcript. Inputs, side effects, and boundaries are explicit and inspectable. Without a page-native tool layer, this workflow typically means brittle UI automation or a separately installed integration, plus manual copying between chats. Gatherwire exposes the workflow from the page itself and turns a found message into a traceable collaboration artifact in one bounded flow. How we built it The page registers seven imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each definition has a focused description, a bounded JSON Schema, read/write annotations, and JSON-safe output. We intentionally avoided a single all-powerful “operate the workspace” tool. The human UI and WebMCP handlers call the same API. A dependency-free Node.js service serves the application and manages an isolated sample workspace for each visitor. Session IDs are opaque and host-only; unknown caller-supplied IDs are rotated instead of adopted. The handoff endpoint accepts only the synthetic agent returned by the demo. Every evidence ID must exist in the selected source space. Successful writes return stable task and correlation IDs. A caller-supplied request ID makes a retry idempotent; reusing the same ID with different content is rejected. All user-controlled content is length-bounded and rendered as text, never HTML. The live app runs on Google Cloud Compute Engine behind a dedicated Cloudflare Tunnel at gatherwire.vistua.de . The repository includes the complete source, deployment files, MIT license, verification record, and 15 automated tests covering session isolation, evidence validation, idempotency, security headers, tool contracts, and registration. Challenges The hardest question was not how to register a tool. It was how much authority a public demo should honestly give it. A useful handoff needs enough context to be actionable, but an unconstrained “run an agent” endpoint would be unsafe and misleading. We separated discovery, reading, searching, posting, room creation, agent listing, and handoff publication. We allowlisted the destination, required source-local evidence, and kept execution outside the challenge demo. The second challenge was legibility. A successful tool call is not enough if the person cannot tell what happened. That led to the five-step mission, visible receipts, evidence links, stable identifiers, and the handoff capsule itself. Accomplishments Seven native WebMCP tools are discoverable and executable from the live page. The complete mission was run in ChatGPT's in-app browser using native WebMCP. The final handoff was read back from the target room with matching task and correlation IDs. Repeating the same write request returned the existing capsule instead of creating a duplicate. Fifteen automated tests pass with zero failures, errors, or skips. Every visitor gets an isolated workspace; no account or credential is required. No customer data, private repository, production conversation, or external agent participates in the demo. What we learned WebMCP makes tool design part of product design. A good tool is not only callable; it has a truthful name, a narrow contract, understandable side effects, useful output, and visible feedback. We also learned that provenance can be a collaboration primitive. A summary is easy to lose or distrust. A source-linked artifact with evidence and stable IDs can survive the chat that created it and support the next person or agent. Challenge-period work The broader idea of Slack-like collaboration between people and project-bound agents, plus private experiments with backend orchestration, existed before this challenge. Gatherwire itself is a new standalone WebMCP app created during the submission period. The public commit history documents the seven browser-facing contracts, isolated workspace, handoff ledger, visible mission and receipts, validation rules, tests, deployment, and documentation added for the challenge. What's next The next layer is a real, permission-aware project-agent bridge behind the same handoff contract. Organizations could connect their own apps and runtimes while keeping the interaction stable: discover context, select an authorized destination, publish a source-linked task, and follow its status from the shared workspace. The longer-term goal is not another closed chat app. It is a modular context and handoff layer that helps existing web apps become safely usable by people and agents together.
