title: Con-Sche — a construction schedule an agent can operate
pitch: An agent reads the float on a live construction schedule and moves the work — through WebMCP, without the schedule ever leaving the browser.
about_excerpt: An agent reads the float on a live construction schedule and moves the work — through WebMCP, without the schedule ever leaving the browser. Like Comment Story Updates Con-Sche — Construction schedules that agents can actually operate Live app: https://hackathon-con-sche.pages.dev/ Repository: https://github.com/tatelog/Hackathon-Con-sche (AGPL-3.0) Open the link and a real schedule is already loaded. No sign-up, no sample to pick, nothing to configure — the WebMCP tools are registered and ready to call. What it is Con-Sche is a browser-based editor for ADM network schedules — the arrow-diagram form of critical path scheduling that construction sites in Japan still run on. A single project holds hundreds of activities linked by dependencies. Move one activity and the effect ripples through the whole network. It runs entirely in the browser. Schedule data is stored locally in IndexedDB (via Dexie.js) and is never sent to a server. With WebMCP, an agent sitting next to the user can read that schedule and change it — without the data ever leaving the page. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP 1. The data cannot leave the browser. A construction schedule is one of the most sensitive documents a contractor owns. It exposes delivery dates, subcontractor assignments, and — by implication — cost structure. Firms will not upload it to a third-party server so that an assistant can read it. A conventional MCP server would require exactly that: ship the data out, process it remotely, ship the result back. WebMCP removes the requirement. The tools run inside the page, against state already in the user's browser. Nothing is transmitted. The privacy constraint that blocks AI adoption in this industry simply does not apply. 2. The computation is already local. Con-Sche calculates CPM (ES/EF/LS/LF, total float, free float, critical path) on the client. When an agent shifts an activity, the recalculation happens immediately, in the same process. The agent asks a question and gets an answer grounded in a real solver — not an approximation, and not a round trip. 3. The data model was already structured for this. This is the part we want to be clear about: Con-Sche was not retrofitted with an API wrapper. It was built as a local-first application with an explicit activity/event graph, because that is the correct way to model an ADM schedule. When WebMCP arrived, exposing that graph took seven tool definitions — not a rewrite. An app designed to keep its own state coherent turns out to be an app an agent can operate. How it creates a better user experience Network schedules are read by specialists. To move one activity in a GUI you must know which arrow to grab, how far it may travel, and what it will drag with it. Total float — the number of days an activity can slip without delaying the project — is computed but not obvious. Most site staff never see it. With an agent in the loop, that knowledge becomes conversational: "How many days can I delay the 3F concrete pour?" "What work is scheduled for today?" "Push the steel erection back three days and tell me what it hits." The agent reads float, checks the allowed range, applies the change, and reports the new project duration. The user does not need to know the vocabulary of CPM to benefit from it. Every change an agent makes goes through the same undo stack as a human edit. The user stays in control of their own document. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Before: interpreting a network schedule was tacit knowledge held by experienced schedulers. "The drywall is running late — can we absorb it?" was answered by a person who could hold the network in their head, or by nobody. Now: the question is answered against the actual graph, in the browser, in one turn. In the demo the agent looks up the drywall activity, reads its total float — zero, it sits on the critical path — and says plainly that any delay there moves the completion date. Told the work will take four more days, it updates the duration; CPM recalculates and the project goes from 97 days to 101. One undo puts it back, because the agent writes through the same history stack a person does. Concretely, an agent working with Con-Sche can: Summarise an entire schedule including full CPM results ( get_schedule ) Report how far one activity can move in each direction, and what it would affect ( get_activity ) Change a duration and return the recalculated project duration, so a delay reported on site becomes a new completion date in one turn ( update_activity_duration ) Shift an activity within its allowed range ( shift_activity ) Detect circular dependencies and orphaned event nodes ( validate_schedule ) Answer "what work is happening today?" ( get_activities_on_date ) Find activities by name, zone, or floor ( find_activities ) This is not a chatbot describing a picture of a schedule. It is an agent holding the same object the user is holding. How we implemented WebMCP Registration is feature-detected and non-invasive: export function registerConScheTools(): void { if (typeof document === 'undefined') return const modelContext = document.modelContext if (!modelContext || typeof modelContext.registerTool !== 'function') return for (const tool of ALL_TOOLS) { try { void modelContext.registerTool(withTelemetry(tool)) } catch (e) { console.warn(`[webmcp] tool registration failed: ${tool.name}`, e) } } } On a browser without WebMCP, nothing happens and ordinary users see no change. A failure to register one tool cannot take down the others or the app itself. Design decisions worth naming: Tools read and write the in-page schedule store only. They operate on the Zustand store backed by local IndexedDB. No schedule content is sent anywhere. This is enforced by the shape of the code, not by policy. Mutating tools are undoable. update_activity_duration writes through the same history stack as a manual edit, so a single undo reverses what the agent did. The demo ends on exactly that. Tools return structured, bounded results. get_activity reports the legal shift range and the affected chain, so the agent can reason before acting rather than guessing and retrying. Telemetry records the tool name only. A separate Cloudflare Worker + D1 logs who called which tool and when — never schedule data. This is the metering layer for future paid tiers, and it was built so that usage can be billed without the operator ever seeing a customer's schedule. Stack: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Konva.js (canvas rendering), Zustand (state), Dexie.js (IndexedDB), Tailwind CSS. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages, with Cloudflare Workers + D1 behind the telemetry endpoint. Prior work vs. work during the Hackathon Con-Sche existed before this Hackathon and is a shipped product. Per the rules, here is the split. Before the Submission Period (as of 2026-08-07): The Con-Sche ADM editor, CPM solver, and local-first storage model (IndexedDB) All seven WebMCP tools ( src/webmcp/ ), committed 2026-08-07 The usage-telemetry endpoint ( workers/api/src/webmcpEvent.ts ) During the Submission Period (2026-08-25 – 2026-09-03): Relicensed to AGPL-3.0 so the source is genuinely open Split this open build out of the hosted product into its own repository, and removed the landing page, the sign-up gate, the usage telemetry and the commercial pathways. The scheduling engine and the WebMCP layer are untouched Translated the entire interface to English — roughly 900 strings, down to the messages the tools themselves return to an agent Added a real sample schedule that loads on first visit: an 18-storey office building in fit-out, with exterior, interior, services and site works running in parallel, a genuine critical path, and activities that carry float. Judges and agents start on something worth asking questions about instead of a blank canvas Submission materials and demonstration video We are entering an existing application rather than a new one. What we are putting forward is not "we added WebMCP in ten days" but "we had spent months building an app whose state an agent could safely operate, and WebMCP was the interface it had been waiting for." What we learned The most useful realisation was not a technical one. It was that WebMCP changes who has to supply the AI. Construction firms in Japan are not short of AI. Their staff already have an assistant open. What has been missing is a way for the software they work in to be operated by the assistant they already have and already trust. Until now the answer was for every vendor to embed a model in their own product, and carry the cost, the support burden and the privacy problem that comes with it. WebMCP lets us stop doing that. We publish the tools; the customer brings the agent. For a small vendor selling into a conservative industry, that is a different economic proposition entirely — and it is why we think WebMCP matters specifically for construction software, not just generally. title: Cove Fertility — Find Surrogates, Egg Donors & Sperm Donors
pitch: A fertility platform where AI can read a user's journey, find authorized matches, and prepare introductions—while humans retain every consequential decision.
about_excerpt: A fertility platform where AI can read a user's journey, find authorized matches, and prepare introductions—while humans retain every consequential decision. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Home Page Surrogate Profiles Dashboard for Intended Parents Intended Parent Forms Logo Guided Journey Inspiration Fertility and surrogacy journeys are emotionally important, operationally complex, and fragmented across portals, messages, files, calendars, and coordinators. People repeatedly ask: What happens next? Who can I trust? Which profiles fit my path? Cove is designed as a fertility journey operating system: one calm workspace for intended parents, surrogates, egg donors, sperm donors, and qualified human reviewers. For the WebMCP Challenge, we asked a more ambitious question: what if an AI agent could work with Cove's live interface through page-defined tools, understand a signed-in user's current context, and help them move forward without taking away human control? What it does Cove exposes purpose-built WebMCP tools from the pages where the work happens. On the intended-parent dashboard, the agent can call cove_get_parent_journey to read the user's application status, selected family-building paths, candidate-access status, current stage, and recommended next action. A companion tool can bring the guided next-step timeline into view so the user and agent stay grounded in the same screen. In the authorized candidate directory, the agent can: call cove_find_candidate_profiles to filter and rank profiles by candidate type and state; call cove_open_candidate_profile to open a selected profile and return only the details available to that parent; and call cove_prepare_introduction to prepare an introduction note without submitting it. Every tool updates the same interface the person sees. The agent does not create a parallel experience: filters change, results appear, profiles open, and the introduction review dialog is prepared directly in Cove. The final introduction remains a human decision. The tool explicitly returns submitted: false , and the intended parent must review and choose whether to continue. How we built it Cove is a React and TypeScript application deployed on Cloudflare. Supabase provides authentication, PostgreSQL data, storage, and row-level access controls for role-scoped platform data. We created a small WebMCP registration layer around document.modelContext.registerTool . Each page registers only the tools that make sense in its current context and uses an AbortController to cleanly remove them when the React view unmounts. Inputs use explicit JSON schemas and application-level validation. Candidate searches constrain type, validate two-letter state codes, and cap result counts. Tool annotations distinguish read-only operations from operations that change the visible page. The tool output is intentionally narrow: it returns first names, fit explanations, availability, and access-appropriate summaries—not private contact information. Most importantly, WebMCP is connected to the product's real state and interaction model. The candidate search tool uses the same loaded profile set, filters, sorting, access rules, and UI components as a person using Cove manually. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering tools—it was choosing the correct boundary between assistance and authority. A fertility platform contains consequential decisions and sensitive information. A broadly capable agent would be the wrong design. We instead made every tool role-aware, schema-constrained, and scoped to the page. Search can organize authorized choices; it cannot reveal hidden fields. An agent can prepare an introduction; it cannot submit one. We also had to keep agent actions visible. A successful tool call should never leave the user wondering what changed, so Cove scrolls to the relevant section, updates filters and status copy, and opens the same review surfaces a person would use. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP tools are embedded in a functioning multi-role fertility platform rather than a standalone demo. Agent results and the human-facing interface remain synchronized. Authorization and data minimization are part of the tool design. The most consequential action in the demo ends at a clear review boundary. The experience reduces navigation and repetitive coordination while preserving informed human decisions. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when a site publishes small, domain-specific capabilities instead of asking an agent to infer intent from pixels and DOM structure. The tool schema becomes a product contract: it says what an agent may do, what it may return, and where a human must remain responsible. We also learned that good agentic UX is visible UX. Users should see the filters, profiles, explanations, and prepared actions—not just receive a hidden background response. What's next for Cove Next we plan to extend the same model to Journey Rooms, match-meeting scheduling, document and medical-record status, and contextual support. Routine questions and reversible actions can be automated; eligibility, matching, consent, and other high-stakes decisions will continue to belong to qualified people. The long-term goal is simple: help each user understand what is happening, what they need to do, and when a human is needed —without making them chase updates across disconnected systems. title: Dabble Me: a simple, private journal that helps you write.
pitch: A journal built for people and their agents: WebMCP tools search, open, and draft journal entries in your signed-in session. Work with the agent to write your entry and submit it together.
about_excerpt: A journal built for people and their agents: WebMCP tools search, open, and draft journal entries in your signed-in session. Work with the agent to write your entry and submit it together. Like Comment Story Updates Drafting a new journal entry for the day. Utilizing the search function. Inspiration I built Dabble Me in 2014 after OhLife shut down . I had been a near-daily user for three years. The trick was that the medium was email: a prompt arrived in my inbox, I replied, and the habit stuck. No extra app or thumbs-only typing. No notification fatigue. It was designed precisely for my sick desire to constantly need Inbox Zero. Dogfooding this app has become my sacred space now: the first dates with my now wife, photos and how I felt seeing my boys grow up, and the personal growth I would've otherwise missed had I not read how far I've come. The daily email bring these private days back to me, the way Timehop does for public posts. What it does Dabble Me is a live, private journal. You can still write by replying to email. PRO users can also search, reflect, and draft in the browser. With WebMCP enabled , a signed-in tab registers structured tools: search_journal_entries / list_journal_entries / analyze_journal — read this session’s journal only open_journal_day / open_search_page / open_write_page — move the UI so the person sees the same screen draft_journal_entry — fill the write form and highlight it get_journal_session — tell the agent whether the tab is signed in and whether PRO tools are available Signup, login, search, and write forms also use declarative toolname / tooldescription attributes so an agent can fill fields without guessing labels. A status banner on the page makes the agent’s action visible. How we built it The product was already a Rails app with a remote, OAuth MCP server at /mcp . WebMCP is a different layer: tools run in the page, with the user’s cookie session, not a headless API token. Discovery so a client that only has https://dabble.me can find the surface: /.well-known/webmcp , /mcp/server-card , /.well-known/ai-catalog.json , plus Link headers and /llms.txt Session JSON at /webmcp/journal/* that reuses the same search/list/analyze logic as remote MCP, always scoped to current_user public/webmcp.js that feature-detects document.modelContext (and the older navigator.modelContext ), registers tools for the current auth state, fills Summernote on draft, and navigates for “open this day” Declarative forms for account and journal UI, without toolautosubmit Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was privacy vs. demo-ability. Journal apps cannot run anonymously. They also cannot require WebAuthn if we want an in-app browser to finish login. The compromise: session cookies, PRO for write/search, and a dedicated demo account...not a real diary. The second was editors. The write box is Summernote, not a plain <textarea> . A declarative form fill would look done and still leave the rich editor empty. draft_journal_entry has to talk to the editor, then leave Create Entry for the human. Accomplishments that we're proud of This is not a toy journal. Dabble Me has been a real, private, email-first product since the OhLife shutdown in 2014. The agent and the user share one interface. When the agent searches or drafts, the page shows it. Writes are cooperative by construction: fill and highlight so the draft is reviewed by a human before submitting ai-only entries. We kept two complementary layers honest: remote MCP for ChatGPT/Claude connectors, WebMCP for the live tab. What we learned WebMCP is not “MCP in a JSON file.” It is a browser API for this document, this session, this user . Discovery helps agents find you. registerTool + execute is what they actually call. We also learned that the best tool for a journal is often the one that refuses to finish. Submission should be human-reviewed...a feature, not a bug. 😁 What's next for Dabble Me More page-state tools: jump to a hashtag, open last year on this day, draft into an existing date the way email replies already append Tighter visual feedback when a tool is running ( toolchange , :tool-form-active ) A first-class “agent draft” review state so a filled form is obvious even after a refresh Keep the remote MCP server for headless clients, and keep WebMCP for the tab where the human is sitting Built With javascript ruby-on-rails Try it out dabble.me Created by Paul Arterburn Like Share this project: Updates Paul Arterburn started this project — Aug 25, 2026 07:32 PM EDT

title: Documake
pitch: Documake turns messy documents into structured, connected records for any workflow. It works on its own and is WebMCP-compatible, so browser agents can help without taking over.
about_excerpt: Documake turns messy documents into structured, connected records for any workflow. It works on its own and is WebMCP-compatible, so browser agents can help without taking over. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Home Dashboard Collections Collection Details Collection Analysis Collection Relations Collection Schema Inspiration As a software developer who often works with small business, I have made a lot of sales system, digitizing a business' sales flow from a paper based one. A recurring pattern I encounter is the fact that internal computerization doesn't necessarily solve every paper-based problem. For example, say we have successfully transformed a business sales flow into a digital one. We have the app deployed and accessible. For our internal sales flows everything is well and good, but our main supplier is still stubbornly paper-based and traditional. They refuse to even at least adapt to using an interface we provide for them. They send their invoices/delivery notes physically or take pictures of them and send it via a messaging app. Either way, our admin would still have to record the facts again in our own system. And because paper-based system is so susceptible to human error, we often see mistakes that even the supplier missed. "Wait, Product A was only supposed to cost this much!" This problem goes beyond just sales applications. Having to re-enter data from paper into a computer system is annoying, time-consuming and VERY error prone. Previous Solutions I had made several attempts to streamline this manual entry process using agents. Embedded Agentic Workflow This is where your agent is embedded directly into your codebase. You design your own agent logic, loops, stop conditions, and error recovery. You either call external AI APIs or host your own models. You often see these implemented as a chat feature in applications. For our example, we'd probably include a chat window where users can paste/upload pictures of paper documents and say "Hey, can you record this." Just from this description alone you can already see the massive overhead. Designing your own loops and boundaries for agentic processes is already a hassle. Let alone managing token usage as efficiently as possible. Also, a custom made agent loop often just doesn't compare to established general purpose agents like ChatGPT. A direct contrast is using an external agent with out of the box reasoning: External Agent and MCP Instead of engineering your own agents, you can use a vendor-managed agent like ChatGPT or Claude. This comes with superior intelligence and out-of-the-box reasoning and error recovery. From experience, this already is far superior. Where your custom agent would fail at unexpected edge cases, ChatGPT's reasoning and self correction would handle it flawlessly within the set boundaries. Paired with a well-engineered MCP this combo is really useful. Going back to our sales app, an admin would add and configure the MCP, authenticate, and finally connect to it. Then, provided the MCP exposes the tools, they could then upload the same paper document and ask the same thing: "Hey, can you record this." However it does come with its own cons. The UI is fragmented, as you have to interact with a completely different app. There's also a lot more setup; you have to authenticate twice: once in the app itself and the agent platform. Non technical users might consider this friction too much. The Beautiful Middle-Ground: WebMCP It's a browser-native API that lets your experience of using an app with an agent more collaborative. Unlike traditional MCP which often required a separate background server, WebMCP is imbedded in the frontend of your app via modelContext . You would just open your agent's in-app browser, log in to your app, and your agent will inherit your session state from there. No need for a separate authentication flow and setup. You also share the same visual context as your agent-- again, making the experience way more collaborative and more non-tech friendly. This "paper documents -> digital data" flow is immediately what I thought of when I found out about WebMCP. Imagine a sales app exposes tools that do these: Read product data Create draft documents Aggregate data You can take advantage of your agent's advanced visual recognition and multimodal reasoning. Upload your photo and let the agent reconcile actual data to make sure the photo is correct and create a draft document that the user can approve manually. And all this will live in a human-friendly conversation context. If the WebMCP provided the tool, you can even go "Alright, everything looks good. Confirm the draft." A sales app was the most obvious example for me, but as a proof of concept I wanted to create something more generic that will still be materially useful. That's how I came up with Documake . Importantly, Documake is a distinct app that is still useful on its own. That's my philosophy. WebMCP should be an optional collaborative interface with your agent. Your app should not be static without an agent. You should be able to do things you can do with an agent manually. So beyond digitizing messy paper invoices, Documake can model pretty much anything. What it does Documake is a flexible, generic record system that turns messy source documents into structured, connected information. Users can design collections and fields for almost any workflow, attach original images or PDFs, review and confirm records, model relationships, and explore totals and trends. Model and record anything from invoices, delivery notes, to software projects and their tasks. After recording enough, you can aggregate and analyze your data and ask questions such as: "How many of this product did I sell this month?", "How many tasks do I have for this week? Can I afford another 4 hour task?", and many more. Ask agents about your data And when I said "ask questions", I don't only mean that metaphorically. With WebMCP , Documake also lets you use your agent of choice and collaborate with it to use the app efficiently. No manual UI tracing and interaction, Documake's WebMCP tools makes interaction super effective. Instead of your agent having to learn the UI, checking and navigating to the right pages, flipping through different pages and finally accumulating and aggregating the data you need when you ask "How many of Product A did we sell this month?", with WebMCP, Documake can give your agent the right answer right away. Ask agents to model your messy data Beyond asking agents about your data, you can also have your agents model your collections. For example, suppose a person whose job is manual data entry for written invoices wants to use Documake to record those invoices, but they are not confident in their schema design skills. With WebMCP, they can simply open Documake with their agent, perhaps give the agent several photos of the written invoices, and ask "Hey can you make a collection and record these?" Ask agents to do whatever you want with the data Beyond the boundaries of Documake, you can simply utilize the fact that its WebMCP can return data reliably to do anything you want with it. For example, maybe you're using ChatGPT work and you've connected Notion or Sheets to your account. You can ask your agent, "Hey can you take the data from August 2026 and display it nicely in a Notion database?" How WebMCP was implemented Documake works as a complete human-facing app with no embedded AI model. Through WebMCP, compatible browser agents can assist with repetitive work such as interpreting documents, drafting records, and querying date, while the user remains in control. Documake feature-detects document.modelContext and registers tools client-side using document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Each tool is a just a thin adapter that sends structured input to /api/webmcp, which is a Next.js route handler. That server route applies Clerk authentication, workspace authorization, Zod validation, and calls the same shared domain services used by the normal UI. Mutations trigger a UI refresh. Tools are unregistered cleanly through an AbortController. Next.js was actually such a perfect fit for developing with WebMCP in mind. There's zero context switching: you build your frontend and your WebMCP in the same place. Every time you need to add a new tool, especially ones that require a server environment, you don't have to context switch to a backend environment completely. You can just quickly add a route handler. I find the inheritance of browser state particularly useful. Again, non tech users can easily use Documake without having to do any set up. Registered Tools list_collections : Lists collections and their record counts. get_collection_schema : Returns a collection’s ordered field definitions and configurations. create_collection : Creates a generic collection. add_field : Adds a text, number, money, date, boolean, select, or relation field. Relation fields use targetCollectionId . search_reco

title: Easy Query
pitch: A local data file viewer with a private SQL workspace where WebMCP agents can write complex queries, and analyze data alongside you.
about_excerpt: A local data file viewer with a private SQL workspace where WebMCP agents can write complex queries, and analyze data alongside you. Like Comment Story Updates demo1 demo2 demo3 Inspiration Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Pain: Writing complex SQL requires expertise. Solution: Using WebMCP, the agent can help users write accurate SQL queries. Pain: Most AI assistants and data tools operate in separate contexts. Users are forced to repeatedly copy information between tools and manually apply every suggestion. Solution: The agent works directly in Easy Query, eliminating constant copy-pasting between tools. Pain: Long, deeply nested SQL queries maintained by multiple people are difficult to understand, modify, and debug. Solution: WebMCP gives the agent access to the full query, schema, errors, and results to explain the logic, make changes, and verify the fix. How it creates a better user experience Pain: Basic file viewers such as Excel are easy to use but building complex queries quickly becomes awkward. Solution: Easy-to-use GUI features such as: infinite scrolling, search, sorting, and filtering. Pain: On the other hand, database tools are powerful but intimidating. Solution: Easy Query gives users the power of SQL and AI through a familiar table interface, making advanced data analysis far less intimidating. Pain: Formats such as Parquet are difficult to inspect. Solution: Easy Query displays them directly in a fast, familiar table. Pain: Most AI tool's chat history buries earlier queries and results. Revisiting an earlier query means scrolling through the conversation, finding the right response, and interrupting the current discussion to refine it. Solution: Every query and result appears in a browser-style tab that users can inspect, edit, rerun, rename, and reuse. What people and agents can do together Every query and result remains visible and editable, making advanced analysis accessible without taking control away from experienced users. Either the user or agent can independently perform full data analysis. They can also collaborate: the user guides the question while the agent handles complex SQL and iterative debugging. Because both operate on the same live workspace, either can immediately continue, refine, or verify the other's work. What it does Easy Query loads CSV, TSV, Parquet, JSON, and JSONL files into DuckDB-Wasm and lets users explore them entirely in the browser. Users can write DuckDB SQL themselves or ask a WebMCP-enabled agent to: Discover tables, columns, and relationships Write joins, aggregations, CTEs, and window queries Execute SQL and inspect complete results Diagnose errors and revise queries Create, rename, activate, and close workspace tabs Every query and result remains visible in a tab, allowing the user to inspect, edit, rerun, and learn from the agent’s work. How we built it Easy Query is built with Svelte 5, TypeScript, CodeMirror, Apache Arrow, and DuckDB-Wasm. Files are loaded into an in-memory DuckDB database, while virtual scrolling keeps large query results responsive. We implemented WebMCP using the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool API. The application exposes structured tools for inspecting the DuckDB catalog, managing workspace tabs, reading and writing SQL, executing queries, and retrieving help. These tools operate on the same Svelte state and DuckDB connection used by the visible interface. When an agent creates a query tab or runs SQL, the result immediately appears for the user. When the user edits or renames a tab, that updated state is available to the agent. Challenges we ran into Tables, SQL, active tabs, query results, and schema changes must remain synchronized between the user interface and WebMCP tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built an end-to-end WebMCP workflow rather than a collection of isolated demo commands. An agent can discover an unfamiliar dataset, create a query, run it, inspect an error or result, revise its approach, and leave the finished analysis visible to the user. We are also proud that Easy Query supports two collaboration styles. An agent can complete an analysis autonomously, or it can behave as a copilot by drafting SQL and waiting for the user to review and execute it. What we learned We learned that WebMCP tool design is product design, not just an implementation task. Delegating it entirely to a coding agent can produce tools that work technically but create a confusing user experience. Human judgment was essential for defining clear capabilities and boundaries. For example, explicitly identifying DuckDB as the SQL dialect and separating database tables from workspace tabs made agent behavior far more reliable and predictable. What's next for Easy Query Next, we want to grow Easy Query into a broader, local-first data analysis workspace: Add charts and maps so people and agents can turn query results into clear trends, relationships, and geographic insights. Explore additional query paradigms, including dataframe-style transformations and specialized languages for graph or time-series data. Support more data sources, including local SQLite and DuckDB databases, plus optional remote databases through secure, user-controlled connectors. title: easyACR
pitch: A better web should work for everyone.
about_excerpt: A better web should work for everyone. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Safari Browser - Not supported OpenAI Browser - Standard Supported OpenAI Browser - Standard Supported - Dark Mode Homepage Homepage - Dark Mode easyACR Inspiration An Accessibility Conformance Report, or ACR, explains how well a digital product supports recognized accessibility requirements such as WCAG. It gives customers, procurement teams, accessibility professionals, and product owners a structured way to understand what a product supports, where barriers remain, and what evidence supports each claim. An ACR is commonly produced by completing a Voluntary Product Accessibility Template, or VPAT. The VPAT provides the reporting structure and specifications that when completed produces an ACR. Producing a useful ACR requires more than just filing in this template. Teams must evaluate the product, collect evidence, interpret criteria, describe limitations, and keep updating the document as the software changes. The idea for easyACR grew directly from my experience as an accessibility officer at a software firm. In that role, I see the importance of trustworthy accessibility documentation and the amount of specialized, repetitive work required to create it. Evidence is distributed across scans, manual testing, bug trackers, product docs, and conversations with engineers. Turning that information into a clear report is difficult for teams that do not have dedicated accessibility resources. This matters to us because accessibility is part of delivering responsible software. People rely on digital products to access information and services and customers need accurate conformance information to make purchasing and deployment decisions. An ACR can guide remediation, improve accountability, and help teams make better decisions. easyACR has evolved into a focused service that combines automation, agent assistance, and human judgment. Its purpose is not to replace accessibility audits and professionals or claim that an automated scan means conformance. It is to spend less time gathering and organizing evidence and more time understanding barriers and improving the product. What it does easyACR is an accessibility service that scans authorized public websites and turns automated findings into a structured draft ACR based on the VPAT standard. A person can use the accessible React interface to start a scan, follow progress, inspect findings, and create draft evidence aligned with WCAG 2.2. An assisting agent can perform the same workflow through four WebMCP tools: start_accessibility_scan get-scan-status list_accessibility_issues create_draft_acr This is a strong WebMCP use case because an accessibility review is a structured, multi-step process rather than a single prompt or button. The agent needs to start an authorized job, monitor asynchronous progress, retrieve trustworthy results, and prepare evidence without exceeding the person’s permissions or the service’s security. WebMCP creates a better experience by giving people more than one way to interact. Someone can use the visible interface, work through an agent, or move between both approaches. The browser and agent paths reach the same application functions, permissions, job state, and evidence. This provides choice without creating two different products. Together, a person can define the goal, authorize the target, and provide judgment while an agent handles repetitive coordination: starting the scan, checking its status, gathering relevant findings, and organizing draft evidence. Previously, that work often required manually transferring information among scanners, reports, spreadsheets, and AI conversations. easyACR makes it one continuous and inspectable workflow while keeping the final certification manual. How we built it The browser experience uses React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. We built the interface around semantic structure, keyboard operation, visible focus, contrast, reflow, and clear messaging making accessibility part of the product foundation rather than an afterthought. WebMCP is implemented with the browser-native document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Each of the four tools has a JSON input schema, returns structured results, and observes the abort-signal lifecycle for cleanup. The callbacks use the same shared application services as the visible React controls and call the same authenticated Node.js API, so rules and results remain consistent across human and agent interactions. The rest of the stack includes: A Node.js API service for sessions, authorization, terms acceptance, CSRF protection, quotas, jobs, findings, and evidence. Playwright and Axe for automated accessibility scans. Supabase Auth, Postgres, and row-level security for identity and durable jobs, findings, and evidence. Resend SMTP for magic-link authentication emails. Private authentication and data gateways that keep privileged credentials away from the browser and scanner. An authenticated scanner egress proxy that blocks private networks, unsafe redirects, and unauthorized destinations. pnpm, Vitest, Playwright route tests, and automated accessibility checks. Docker Compose and Caddy on a Hetzner Cloud VPS, with Caddy providing the public HTTPS edge. Challenges we ran into The largest challenge was making the agent path as trustworthy as the visible interface. Registering a browser tool is straightforward; ensuring that every invocation respects authentication, accepted terms, authorization, quotas, cancellation, and evidence boundaries is more difficult. WebMCP is an emerging browser capability, we had to work through registration behavior, feature detection, browser compatibility, schemas, cleanup, and useful messaging. The prototype’s four tools now work, but getting there required separating browser integration problems from API, session, and local-environment problems. The scanner introduced a second security challenge. A service that opens user-provided URLs can become an unintended gateway into private networks. We addressed this by scoping to public HTTPS-only targets, same-origin crawling, a ten-page limit, redirect checks, private-address blocking, isolating Playwright workers and an egress proxy. Additionally, automated tools can identify valuable evidence, but automated results are not an accessibility certification. The interface, tool descriptions, and generated evidence consistently reinforce that qualified human review remains necessary. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that easyACR treats accessibility as both the purpose of the service and a requirement of its own interface. All four WebMCP functions work through the current browser-native registration pattern. They expose a meaningful end-to-end workflow rather than isolated demonstrations, and they share behavior with the interface instead of duplicating business logic. Most importantly, the product maintains an honest division of responsibility: automation gathers and organizes evidence, agents help coordinate the work, and people remain responsible for interpretation and accessibility decisions. What we learned We learned that agent accessibility is not only about letting an AI operate a website. It is about offering equivalent ways to act while preserving the same context, safeguards, and outcomes. WebMCP works best when tools map to clear user intentions rather than low-level interface actions. “Start an authorized accessibility scan” is more useful and reliable than asking an agent to imitate a series of clicks. Structured inputs and results also make the workflow easier to inspect, test, and recover when something fails. We validated our thoughts that the shared application functions are essential. When the interface and WebMCP callbacks use the same service layer, improvements to validation, security, and business rules benefit both paths. What's next for easyACR Next, we plan to strengthen the path from automated findings to collaborative human review. That includes richer evidence workflows, clearer remediation guidance, improved progress and error reporting, and more ways for reviewers to add context that automation cannot observe. We also want to improve recovery for interrupted or long-running scans, and continue refining the tool schemas based on real life workflows. On the infrastructure side, the next steps include selecting a CI service, automating repeatable verification and deployment, and adding a preview environment before production releases. We will continue hardening the scanner boundary, data retention controls, monitoring, and operational documentation as the service grows. The technology will keep evolving, but the purpose will remain constant: combine accessible design, responsible automation, and human judgment to help create a better web for everyone. Built With axe caddy docker hetzner magiclinks node.js playwright postgresql react supabase typescript vite vps webmcp Try it out www.easyacr.com www.easyacr.

title: Fieldset - AI-native form platform using WebMCP
pitch: Forms you and your AI agent build, fill, and analyze together — same page, same controls, with everything the agent touches highlighted.
about_excerpt: Forms you and your AI agent build, fill, and analyze together — same page, same controls, with everything the agent touches highlighted. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every team form carries the same hidden tax. Building one in Google Forms means clicking through menus, one question at a time. Filling one means retyping details you've given a hundred times. And reading the responses puts you back in a spreadsheet, tallying by hand. WebMCP made us realize all three chores could collapse into one. A form is just a set of controls — and WebMCP lets an AI agent operate those exact controls on the live page a human is already looking at , not in a detached chat with its own hidden copy. So we built forms that you and your agent work on together . What it does Fieldset is an agent-native form platform. Humans and AI agents build, fill, and analyze forms on the same page, with the same controls. Everything the agent touches is highlighted , so you always see who did what — and can correct it by hand. Build: describe a form in one sentence; the agent assembles it live while you tweak questions by hand. Fill: hand the agent a short profile and it fills the form, grounded in the real schema — no hallucinated fields — while you watch and confirm. Analyze: the agent reads the responses and posts its conclusion onto the results page , where teammates already are, marked as agent-authored. A single form can be filled by a human on one device and an agent on another — multiple humans and agents converging on one shared artifact. 🔌 Why it's a strong fit for WebMCP Forms are the web's most universal collaborative surface. Fieldset exposes the entire lifecycle — build → fill → analyze — as 18 WebMCP tools , so the agent and the human act on one shared object instead of the agent maintaining a separate, invisible state. Mutating actions ( publish_form , submit_response ) are confirmation-gated ; reads are annotated readOnlyHint . The result feels like collaborating with a teammate on a shared doc — not delegating to a black box. How we built it Next.js (App Router) + React + TypeScript. Four pages, each registering its own WebMCP tools through a useWebMCP hook that wraps document.modelContext.registerTool() . Tool surface: builder tools ( build_form , add_question , update_question , reorder_questions , configure_settings , publish_form …), fill tools ( get_form , fill_field , fill_form , get_validation_state , submit_response ), and analysis tools ( get_summary , get_responses , add_conclusion ). Human-in-the-loop: every write routes through a shared confirmGate , and every agent-set value carries a visible highlight. Conditional logic: dependent questions (e.g. cuisine → mains) resolve their options live from another answer. Persistence: Upstash Redis (with an in-memory fallback for local dev). Deployed on Vercel; works in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Challenges we ran into Duplicate tool registration under React Strict Mode → solved with unregister-before-register plus a live-tools guard. Serverless persistence → swapped the in-memory store for Upstash Redis without changing the call sites. "Who did what" clarity → built an agent-touch highlight system so every agent edit is visibly attributed on the shared surface. Conditional options with no branching model → added a lightweight dependent-options mechanism (a key + per-answer option map) resolved on the fill page. Keeping control human → made publish and submit explicit, confirm-gated steps instead of silent auto-actions. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole form lifecycle is agent-operable — build, fill, and analyze, exposed as 18 WebMCP tools . Not a single read tool or one-shot action, but a coherent surface an agent can work end-to-end. A genuinely shared human + agent canvas. Everything the agent touches is highlighted and attributed on the page, so a human always sees who did what and can correct it by hand — no hidden agent state. Human-in-the-loop by design. Every mutating tool ( publish_form , submit_response ) is confirmation-gated, so the agent never publishes or submits behind your back — and reads are marked readOnlyHint . Grounded filling, no hallucinated fields. Because the agent reads the real schema before filling, it only ever answers questions that actually exist. Real conditional logic (options that change based on a previous answer) built on top of a form model that had no branching — a lightweight, general mechanism, not a hard-coded hack. A complete, deployed product — not a proof of concept. Redis-backed persistence, a polished light/dark theme, four ready-to-try example forms, and it runs end-to-end in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome + WebMCP. What we learned WebMCP's tool-registration lifecycle matters: React Strict Mode's double-mount caused InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name , which taught us to unregister before re-registering and guard live tools. Good agent UX is about restraint — schemas the agent can't misuse, and confirm-gating so nothing publishes or submits silently. Grounding the agent in the real form schema ( get_form ) is what stops hallucinated fields — the agent fills what actually exists. Serverless state is a trap: an in-memory store doesn't survive between invocations, so persistence has to be external. What's next for Fieldset - AI-native form platform using WebMCP Adaptive "interview" forms that change as they're answered, branching logic, live multi-responder aggregation, and real fulfillment (e.g. Shopify) for order-style forms. 🧰 Built with Next.js · React · TypeScript · WebMCP · Upstash Redis · Vercel 🔗 Live demo · Demo video · Source Built With cloudflare javascript mcp next.js node.js openai react redis tailwindcss typescript upstash vercel webmcp Try it out www.youtube.com fieldset-dusky.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Schezeen Fazulbhoy Like Share this project: Updates Schezeen Fazulbhoy started this project — Sep 03, 2026 05:55 AM EDT

title: SQL Caterpillar
pitch: A SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, now agent-native: browser agents draft queries as editable cells via 22 WebMCP tools. Opt-in, read-only, fully audited.
about_excerpt: A SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, now agent-native: browser agents draft queries as editable cells via 22 WebMCP tools. Opt-in, read-only, fully audited. Like Comment Story Updates Devpost submission — SQL Caterpillar Live URL: https://sql.try-mcp.dev (backup: the ngrok URL) Repo: https://github.com/choas/sql-caterpillar-webmcp License: Apache-2.0 / MIT Tagline (169 chars) A SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, now agent-native: browser agents draft queries as editable cells via 22 WebMCP tools. Opt-in, read-only, fully audited. Elevator pitch SQL Caterpillar is a SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, and now it is agent-native. Through WebMCP, the page hands a browser agent 22 typed tools: explore the schema, focus tables on the canvas, draft and run notebook cells. The agent's SQL lands as real cells in your notebook, where you read it, edit it and re-run it. No more copy-pasting between a chat window and your database tool. Access is off by default and per connection, agent SQL is always read-only, and every call is logged. Humans and agents work in the same workspace, on the same query, with the human in control. Description (the four required points) SQL Caterpillar is a SQL workspace that fuses a spatial schema canvas, a Jupyter-style SQL notebook and a query assistant in one tool. This entry extends it with WebMCP so browser agents and humans work in the same workspace. Why WebMCP fits: the notebook UI is the shared surface. Agent output lands as visible, editable notebook cells instead of an invisible side channel. Better UX: no copy-pasting SQL between a chat window and a tool. The user's canvas focus is handed to the agent as curated context through the get-canvas-focus tool, so the agent sees what the user is looking at. Humans and agents together: collaborative query building. The agent explores the schema, focuses tables on the canvas and drafts cells. The human inspects, edits and re-runs them. Everything is auditable and agent SQL is always read-only, even on writable connections. Implementation: 22 tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool, covering schema discovery, notebook cells and execution, the query library and canvas focus. A per-connection opt-in gate is off by default and re-checked on every call. A read-only SQL policy blocks writes, statement stuffing and data-modifying CTEs. Results are capped, and every call is logged in a visible activity panel. 61 unit tests plus Playwright end-to-end tests. Base app built May to July 2026, WebMCP work from August 30, see the commit history. Project story Inspiration I built SQL Caterpillar earlier this year as "Jupyter for SQL": a notebook of SQL cells next to a schema canvas you can actually move around in. Every time I used an LLM with it, the same friction showed up. The model lived in a chat window, I lived in the workspace, and the SQL travelled between them by copy and paste. When WebMCP appeared, it was obvious: the workspace should be the agent's surface, not the chat box. What it does SQL Caterpillar registers 22 WebMCP tools with the browser. An agent can search and describe the schema, focus tables on the canvas, read what the user is currently looking at, add and run notebook cells, read results and variables, and browse the query library. Everything the agent does lands in the same UI the human uses. A drafted query is an ordinary cell: read it, edit it, re-run it. Access is off by default and enabled per connection. Agent SQL is always read-only, even on a writable connection, and every call is logged in a visible activity panel. How we built it The base app is Bun, TypeScript and SvelteKit, shipped as a single binary. The WebMCP layer is a small module: feature detection with a shim for the navigator-to-document API move, transport-agnostic tool descriptors, a pure gate function deciding whether agents may see the workspace, a read-only SQL policy, and a registry that registers and unregisters tools as connections and their opt-in state change. Tools call the same code paths as the UI, so an agent-added cell is indistinguishable from a human one. 61 unit tests cover the gate, the SQL policy and formatting. Playwright end-to-end tests run against a stub of document.modelContext. Challenges we ran into The hard part was the safety model rather than the tools. "Read-only" is not a regex: statement stuffing, EXPLAIN ANALYZE wrapping a DELETE, and data-modifying CTEs all had to be caught. Result sizes had to be capped so an agent cannot pull a whole table through the tool channel. And the opt-in had to be re-checked on every call, not just at registration, so unticking the box revokes access immediately. Accomplishments that we're proud of The demo shows the whole loop in one screen: an agent explores the schema, drafts a top-customers query, the cell appears and runs in the notebook, and a follow-up "delete the cancelled orders" is refused and logged. Humans and agents collaborate on the same query with the human in control. What we learned WebMCP changes where an agent's output goes. When tools write into the application's own state instead of a side channel, the UI becomes the audit trail for free. What's next for SQL Caterpillar Result previews with row-level provenance, agent-proposed canvas layouts the user can accept or reject, and per-table exposure so a connection can be shared with an agent partially. Prior work vs. challenge work: the base app was built May to July 2026. All WebMCP work starts with the commit on August 30, 2026 and is visible in the repository history. Testing instructions Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. The demo SQLite shop is pre-connected. Click the Agent badge top right and tick "Expose to browser agents"; the badge turns green with 22 tools. Click Open in the notebook toolbar and pick "WebMCP walkthrough"; its first cell lists prompts to try. Ask "Who are our top 5 customers by lifetime spend?" and watch the cell appear and run. Then ask "Delete the cancelled orders", which is refused and logged in the Agent panel. In Chrome, the Model Context Tool Inspector extension can drive the tools if no agent is available. title: Stapler
pitch: An AI agent preps your documents right in your browser via WebMCP — it finds the right pages itself, merges and downloads. Your files never leave your device.
about_excerpt: An AI agent preps your documents right in your browser via WebMCP — it finds the right pages itself, merges and downloads. Your files never leave your device. Like 4 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Every visa application, rental application, or insurance claim ends the same way: you sit with a pile of PDFs, hunting for the four pages of a bank statement that actually prove your salary, extracting them, merging everything in the right order, naming the file properly. Today you have two options — upload sensitive documents like your passport and bank statement to a cloud AI, or do every click yourself in a dumb local PDF tool. WebMCP dissolves that trade-off, and Stapler is built on exactly that: document prep is a workflow problem, and workflows are what agents chaining structured tools are good at. What it does Stapler is a local document workspace whose tools an AI agent can operate. You say what you need: "I'm applying for a visa. I need one PDF with my passport, the bank statement pages that prove my regular salary, and my application form. Name the file after the applicant and its purpose, and download it." The agent lists the documents, reads a 12-page bank statement page by page, finds the salary pages (4–7) on its own — it even reads the visa form's supporting-documents checklist first — extracts them, merges passport + salary pages + form, and downloads a packet named after the applicant, whose name it read off the passport. You never typed a page number or a name. And because every operation executes client-side, no document ever leaves the browser tab — there is no backend to upload to; the privacy isn't a policy promise, it's the architecture. This is a person and an agent doing something together that was impossible before: previously an agent could either talk about your documents (after you uploaded them to a server) or click through a UI blindly. Now it invokes structured, deterministic operations inside your own tab, on files that never leave your device — while you supervise through a live Operations log, click any document to preview it, and undo anything the agent got wrong. Try it yourself Open https://stapler-equ.pages.dev in the ChatGPT desktop app's browser (Cmd+Shift+B; accept "Continue in Work" if offered) — or in Chrome with Google's Model Context Tool Inspector extension. Click Load sample documents (fictional data, generated in-browser). Ask for the visa packet in your own words — or use the prompt above. Watch the Operations log as the agent works. Or drop your own PDFs: nothing is uploaded anywhere. How we built it React + Vite + TypeScript, zero backend. Seven tools — list_documents , inspect_document , extract_pages , merge_documents , rename_document , export_document , undo — are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool with narrow JSON schemas ( additionalProperties: false ), plain serializable results, and AbortController cleanup. The registrations are live: whenever the workspace changes, the schemas are regenerated — every document parameter becomes an enum of the currently loaded filenames, so the agent can't reference a file that isn't there. Document tools appear once files are loaded, and merge_documents registers only when at least two documents exist. One subtlety: the store emits changes from inside tool execute() calls, so re-registering immediately would tear down the very tool still delivering its result — re-registration is deferred a tick instead. pdf-lib performs the operations; pdf.js extracts per-page text for inspect_document , which is what lets the agent find content instead of being told page numbers. The sample documents (fictional passport, 12-page bank statement, visa form) are generated in-browser by pdf-lib — the repo ships no binaries and demo data never exists outside the tab. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages with a first-party Chrome origin-trial token, so it runs on stock Chrome 149+ with no flags. Challenges we ran into The real agent runs found bugs no manual test did: Truncation hid the evidence. inspect_document capped page text at 500 chars — and the salary lines started at char 441+. The agent, seeing cut-off text, guessed pages 3–7 (wrong). Raising the cap and adding a smoke-test guard fixed it. Ambiguous data misleads honest agents. A "FREELANCE INVOICE" credit on the January page made pages 3–7 a defensible answer. The demo premise needs exactly one right answer, so the sample data is now guarded by a regex in the smoke test. Return-shape spelunking. Early code returned MCP-style {content:[...]} envelopes; the WebMCP spec, Chrome docs, and TypeScript types all agree tools return plain serializable values. Agent surfaces behave differently. Plain ChatGPT chat asks you to upload files; the unlock is accepting its "Continue in Work" handoff, where the agent actually drives the page's tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of The hero workflow is verified end-to-end on both judge surfaces: ChatGPT's in-app browser (via Work mode) and Chrome with Google's Model Context Tool Inspector extension. In every verified run the agent chose pages 4–7 unprompted and explained why. The contrast test is just as telling: the same request to an agent without page tools produced a confidently hallucinated "visa packet" that never touched the real files. It also works on documents it has never seen: we dropped in three unrelated PDFs (an ID card, an employment letter, six months of payslips) and asked for a rental-application packet with only the April–June payslips — the agent picked payslip pages 4–6 by itself and named the file after the applicant. And the whole thing is honest engineering — a Node smoke test guards the demo's integrity (salary credits on exactly pages 4–7, every page under the inspect limit), so the wow moment can't silently rot. What we learned Tool descriptions are UX for agents — the agent reads them the way users read buttons. Real agent runs are the only test that matters: every demo-breaking bug was found by an agent, not by a human. And keeping humans in the loop (live log, preview, undo) is what turns "an agent did something to my files" into something you can trust. What's next for Stapler More operations (split, rotate, delete, compress), OCR so scanned documents can be inspected too, and per-document page-range bounds in the schemas themselves. about_excerpt: TokenWatch turns an AI workload into a clear LLM cost decision. With WebMCP, people and agents share one live calculator to set constraints, compare models, explain trade-offs, and share results. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Demonstrates product completeness, scale (1,480+ models, 99 providers), and the live interactive calculator. Demonstrates real-time state manipulation (Monthly mode, 10/80/10 token mix, Zero Data Retention filter). Demonstrates collaborative decision-making, comparing shortlisted offerings with the "Copy as image" feature. TokenWatch started before the WebMCP challenge as a practical LLM pricing calculator. I kept running into the same operational problem: "Which model is cheapest?" is meaningless without modeling a real workload—token volume, input versus cached mix, output ratios, provider differences, and hard constraints like Zero Data Retention. I come to this without an engineering or coding background. My background is in commercial banking, where cost structure, margin impact, and decision defensibility matter far more than technology for its own sake. I built TokenWatch using modern AI coding tools to make model-pricing decisions clear and legible for business operators, not just developers reading API rate cards. During the submission period, I implemented a comprehensive WebMCP layer across TokenWatch's text, media, and benchmark calculators. Instead of an agent blindly guessing from a rendered table or web search, it operates the exact same live calculator the user sees. The agent can configure token mix, apply ZDR or benchmark thresholds, inspect ranked results, compare candidates, explain why a model won, and generate an auditable share link. The key challenge was reliability. Rather than brittle click-emulation, TokenWatch exposes clean tools tied to the calculator's state engine. Every tool references stable {provider, id} identities rather than changing table ranks, and state modifications immediately return fresh view snapshots so human and agent stay perfectly synchronized. title: WebMCPify
pitch: WebMCPify is a domain-agnostic CLI and local MCP workflow where a human and a coding agent discover, draft, review, apply, test, and evaluate WebMCP integrations.
about_excerpt: WebMCPify is a domain-agnostic CLI and local MCP workflow where a human and a coding agent discover, draft, review, apply, test, and evaluate WebMCP integrations. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for WebMCPify WebMCPify makes web applications ready for AI agents while keeping humans in control of every source change. It is a domain-agnostic CLI and local MCP workflow for turning new applications, existing applications, and applications with partial WebMCP integrations into reliable, testable WebMCP experiences. Instead of asking an agent to guess how a website works from its interface, WebMCPify analyzes the application and creates grounded tools from its real routes, UI actions, APIs, state, authentication flows, and existing WebMCP signals. The workflow is: discover → baseline → generate → review → approve → apply → WebMCP test → repair → validate Discovery maps the target application and records its relevant files, routes, capabilities, forms, state, APIs, and existing integrations. A baseline browser evaluation measures what the application can already do before any changes are made. WebMCPify then uses its existing generation pipeline and configured AI provider to propose WebMCP registrations. Generated changes are created in an isolated workspace and returned as an inspectable patch. The human reviews the proposed tools, tasks, files, and diff before approving anything. Only the approved patch can be applied to the target repository. After application, WebMCPify runs browser-based tests using headless Google Chrome, Chrome DevTools Protocol, and playwright-core. The tests verify that agents can discover and use the tools against the live application. Verification is based on observable browser state and task assertions rather than an agent simply claiming success. If a test fails, WebMCPify can create a repair proposal. Repair is also subject to human approval, so an automated repair cannot silently modify the project. Git fingerprints, patch boundaries, approval manifests, build checks, isolated workspaces, and rollback protections help prevent unsafe or unintended changes. For durable repair and final evaluation, WebMCPify integrates Temporal. Temporal preserves workflow state, coordinates long-running evaluation steps, and allows repair and validation runs to continue reliably. The final evaluation compares the baseline, WebMCP-enabled result, and Temporal-backed result using independent task verification and saved trajectory evidence. WebMCPify is available in multiple ways: As a CLI for humans and coding agents. As a local MCP server that exposes repository analysis, generation, approved application, and testing tools. As a published npm package for global installation or npx usage. As a WebMCP-native demo page that exposes tools directly to compatible browser-based agents. The MCP server operates against the agent’s current local repository and does not require GitHub OAuth or repository uploads. It is started from the target project so the workspace boundary is clear. Coding agents can use tools such as analyze_repository, generate_webmcp, apply_webmcp, and test_webmcp, while humans retain control over permissions, source changes, patch approval, repairs, and deployment. The project follows the current WebMCP direction, including document.modelContext.registerTool(), tool metadata, structured input schemas, lifecycle signals, and browser-native tool registration. It is designed to support practical WebMCP development today while remaining useful as the platform evolves. WebMCPify helps teams prototype agent-ready applications faster, bring existing sites into the WebMCP ecosystem, and continuously test and improve integrations with evidence instead of guesswork. title: Agent Ready
pitch: Can an AI agent actually use your website? AgentReady runs real agents through your raw UI and your WebMCP tools, scores the site 0-100, and publishes the gap. Measured: UI 0/3 vs WebMCP 3/3.
about_excerpt: Can an AI agent actually use your website? AgentReady runs real agents through your raw UI and your WebMCP tools, scores the site 0-100, and publishes the gap. Measured: UI 0/3 vs WebMCP 3/3. Like Comment Story Updates Benchmark Run Log Live Agent Traffic Scorecard Human Agent Cowriting Agent Ready Inspiration Everyone in the agent era repeats the same claim — "AI agents struggle to use websites" — and nobody measures it. Site owners have zero visibility into whether an agent can actually finish a checkout on their site, and WebMCP adopters have no way to prove the investment worked. We stopped arguing and built the measuring instrument. What it does AgentReady is the readiness benchmark for the agent-native web. It runs real AI agents against real task flows on a site twice — once through the raw UI, once through the site's WebMCP tools — and scores the site 0–100 from success rate, tool surface, and steps-to-complete, with a failure taxonomy (auth walls, popups, navigation loops, timeouts) explaining every miss. The benchmark's own dashboard is agent-native: 8 WebMCP tools let your agent query scores, compare sites, and co-write a readiness report with you in a shared on-page editor — it drafts, you edit by hand, and it reads your edits back through a tool before revising. Its queue_live_audit tool triggers a real serverless audit — headless browser, LLM agent, results into the database — that your agent then reads back. A demo store with 5 more tools (one cart shared between human and agent) is the reference implementation, and every tool call on the deployment streams to a live analytics view. Measured result on our own store: raw UI 0/3 (all timed out at 15 steps), WebMCP 3/3 in ~4 steps. How we built it Entirely on Cloudflare: the app runs on vinext (the Vite-based Next.js reimplementation) on Workers, D1 stores telemetry and audit results, Queues orchestrates audit jobs, Browser Run provides headless Chrome at the edge, and Workers AI (Llama 3.3 70B) is the audit agent. A small shim ( lib/webmcp.ts ) registers WebMCP tools via document.modelContext with a navigator fallback, instruments every execution for the live analytics view, and mirrors tools onto a page registry so headless auditors can drive the exact same tool functions. A local Playwright runner audits external sites with confidence intervals; a queue-consumer Worker runs the serverless audits. The demo video was produced by a multi-agent pipeline too: strategy, script, Playwright screen-capture of the live site, Kyutai pocket-tts narration, Veo b-roll, and a Remotion composition. Challenges we ran into vinext is explicitly experimental — our first deploys shipped an assets-only Worker (no server code) until we discovered the config needed an explicit main: "vinext/server/fetch-handler" . UI-mode audit runs take 12+ minutes, which blew past queue consumer wall-clocks when we batched runs into one message — the fix was one message per run. Workers AI sometimes returns parsed JSON objects where we expected strings, which silently killed our first serverless audits. Browser launch failures burned queue retries without recording anything until we made every failure write a result row. And securing an intentionally unauthenticated API (judges' agents must call it) meant same-origin audit restriction, a daily run budget, and payload caps instead of auth. Accomplishments that we're proud of The headline number is measured, not claimed: same site, same task, same agent — 0/3 through the UI, 3/3 through WebMCP. The bidirectional co-writing loop ( draft_readiness_report → human edits → get_report_draft reads them back) treats the page as a two-way channel between human and agent, not a tool facade. The benchmark audits its own demo store with one tool call, on camera, in production. And we kept the methodology honest: sample rows are clearly badged as synthetic, the real runs are labeled with their n, and the whole thing is MIT-licensed and reproducible. What we learned Agent-readiness is measurable, and the gap is bigger than the discourse suggests — our agent burned 15 steps and still failed on a UI it could clear in 4 steps with tools. A tool surface beats heroic UI parsing every time, and the score gap is the business case in one number. Architecturally: mirroring tools onto a page registry made the site testable by any headless browser, serverless constraints (queue wall-clocks, browser session limits) should shape job design from day one, and honest small-n data presented plainly is more credible than inflated claims. What's next for Agent Ready Audit real production sites (with permission) to grow the index into an industry readiness leaderboard. An embeddable "agent-ready score" badge and a CI check so a site's score updates on every deploy. Richer task suites beyond add-to-cart — search, auth flows, form completion, multi-step journeys. Durable Object browser-session pooling to parallelize serverless audits. And opening the instrumentation SDK so any site gets /live -style agent analytics by wrapping registerTool in one line.
