title: Aidra
pitch: Bridging the web accessibility gap with structured agent collaboration.
about_excerpt: Bridging the web accessibility gap with structured agent collaboration. Like Comment Story Updates Completed schedule booking screen aidra Inspiration Every year, WebAIM publishes the Screen Reader User Survey . In every edition, the #2 most cited barrier for screen reader users is "Interactive elements such as menus, tabs, and dialogs that don't behave as expected," second only to CAPTCHA. Compounding this, the WebAIM Million annual analysis tracked an average of 56.1 accessibility errors per home page in 2026, a 10.1% increase over the prior year. Inaccessible patterns such as drag-and-drop calendars, nested custom comboboxes, and unlabelled canvas widgets continue to create barriers for assistive technologies. Generic computer-use agents inherit many of these same failure modes. An agent that relies on vision, DOM inspection, clicking, or coordinate-based dragging can fail just as unpredictably when a complex widget has unexposed state or requires interactions that are difficult to interpret programmatically. I was inspired to build aidra to show how WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) can become an accessibility bridge. By exposing clean, typed, high-level tools directly inside the webpage, an AI agent can execute complex workflows without interacting with broken widgets. At the same time, every action can be narrated live through aria-live regions so the human remains informed and in control. What It Does aidra is an appointment booking portal built around one deliberately difficult interaction pattern: a drag-and-drop-only scheduling calendar with no click-to-select fallback. A user can complete the entire booking flow manually using a mouse or keyboard. They can also hand the workflow to an agent using natural language, such as: "Book me the earliest Tuesday morning appointment with Dr. Chen and add a note about my insurance card." Instead of trying to drag or click the calendar, the WebMCP agent uses 7 typed in-page tools: search_providers list_available_slots select_slot fill_intake_form submit_booking reschedule_booking cancel_booking These tools allow the agent to search providers, retrieve available slots, select an appointment, populate the intake form, and manage existing bookings without directly manipulating the inaccessible calendar widget. Every tool call is announced through an aria-live region and mirrored visually through an Agent Activity sidebar for sighted collaborators. Human Confirmation Is Enforced The agent cannot finalize an appointment. submit_booking only stages the appointment and opens an accessible confirmation dialog. The booking can only be finalized through an explicit human click on the Confirm button. This is enforced in the application logic, not simply described as a rule for the agent. Even if an agent calls submit_booking repeatedly, it cannot bypass the confirmation step because the only code path that marks an appointment as confirmed is the human-facing confirmation action. The agent handles the difficult interaction. The user retains authority over the action that matters. Why WebMCP? Without WebMCP, an AI agent has to perceive and manipulate the same interface a user does. That means guessing through pixels, DOM structure, focus states, and interaction patterns. With WebMCP, the webpage exposes semantic capabilities directly to the agent. Instead of asking: "Where is the calendar and how do I drag this appointment?" the agent can ask the page: "What providers are available?" "What appointment slots are available?" "Select this slot." The interaction becomes structured, typed, observable, and reviewable. This is what makes WebMCP particularly interesting for accessibility. The same abstraction that makes an agent more reliable can also make its actions easier for a human to understand and trust. How I Built It I designed aidra with a zero-build-step architecture for fast iteration, transparency, and auditability. Markup and UI: Semantic HTML5, Tailwind CSS via CDN, vanilla CSS custom properties, and native browser APIs. State Management: A centralized reactive store synchronizes manual DOM interactions and WebMCP tool executions through the same state and rendering pipeline. WebMCP Registration: I registered all 7 tools using document.modelContext.registerTool({...}) with strict JSON schemas and JSDoc @typedef annotations for editor-level type checking. WebMCP Compatibility: I built a small polyfill that detects whether document.modelContext is available natively and falls back to a local tool registry when it is not. Input Normalization: Tool arguments are normalized so each execute() function receives the same input shape across different invocation environments. Speech Pacing: I paced announcements so screen readers have time to finish communicating one action before the next tool executes. Live Observability: An in-page Agent Activity console streams tool invocations, parameters, and status changes so sighted collaborators can observe the agent working in real time. The shared state architecture was particularly important. Both manual interactions and agent tool calls write through the same state layer. This means the manual and agent-assisted experiences are not separate implementations that can quietly drift apart. Challenges I Faced 1. Modal Dismiss and ARIA Live Race Condition Problem: Closing the confirmation modal returned focus to the general page body. This caused screen readers to begin announcing unrelated page content at the same time the booking result was being announced. Solution: I gave the booking status region a tabindex="-1" focus anchor and moved focus there before triggering the announcement. This gives the screen reader a stable and meaningful landing point after the modal closes. 2. Form Input Cursor Jumping Problem: The render pipeline re-synced input values from state on every state change. During manual typing, this caused the cursor to jump to the end of the field after each keystroke. Solution: I added diff-checking guards so DOM values are only overwritten when they have actually diverged from the current state. 3. Cross-Environment WebMCP Tool Invocation Problem: Chrome's experimental WebMCP implementation and other agent-driven environments did not always pass tool arguments in the same shape. Some contexts provided objects while others provided JSON strings. Solution: I added an input normalization layer that parses and normalizes incoming arguments before they reach the tool execution logic. This keeps the tools consistent across environments. What I Learned 1. WebMCP Can Be Accessibility Infrastructure WebMCP should not only be viewed as an automation mechanism. Structured tools can provide a semantic interaction layer for web applications that would otherwise be difficult for both agents and assistive technologies to navigate reliably. 2. Co-Navigation Can Build More Trust Than Black-Box Delegation An agent performing actions on behalf of a user should not mean that the user loses visibility into what is happening. By combining WebMCP tools with live aria-live narration and a visual activity stream, aidra keeps the human involved throughout the workflow. The agent acts, but the user can hear and observe what it is doing. 3. Human Authority Should Be Architectural The confirmation gate taught me that trust is stronger when it is enforced by the system rather than communicated as an instruction. The agent can prepare the appointment, but it cannot cross the final confirmation boundary. That distinction makes the human's authority a property of the application itself. 4. Zero-Build Architecture Has Real Advantages Using native ES Modules, vanilla DOM APIs, and JSDoc typing gave me extremely fast iteration while working with an experimental browser API. There was no build pipeline between changing the code and testing the result, which made debugging and experimentation much faster. What's Next for aidra Multi-Domain Extension: Generalize the WebMCP co-navigation pattern into a browser sidecar that could support historically difficult interfaces across government portals, travel booking, insurance, and healthcare. In-Page Voice Interface: Integrate the Web Speech API so users can provide prompts and receive narrated feedback without leaving the page or relying on a separate agent surface. Complex Form Assistance: Expand the tool layer to handle custom comboboxes, multi-step forms, and other interaction patterns that are difficult for assistive technologies and computer-use agents. Multi-Step Verification: Explore safer ways for agents to assist users through complex verification workflows while preserving explicit human control over sensitive actions. title: AssetsCurator
pitch: AssetsCurator is an app built for automatically collecting assets like images,videos,audio voiceover and background music,based on video script and arranging them in downloadable zip folder by scene
about_excerpt: AssetsCurator is an app built for automatically collecting assets like images,videos,audio voiceover and background music,based on video script and arranging them in downloadable zip folder by scene Like Comment Story Updates architecture app home page Inspiration Assembling a shot list, mood board, or pre-viz pack for a short video means juggling a dozen tabs — an AI image tool, two or three stock sites, a YouTube search, a text-to-speech page, a royalty-free music library — and then renaming every file into numbered folders by hand. Agents are great at the fetching, but curation is visual and iterative : a human has to see the board while it fills up and say "no, swap the hero of scene 2." WebMCP made a different shape possible. Instead of bolting a chatbot onto a website, the website exposes tools and ChatGPT itself becomes the operator of a live canvas . That reframed the whole product: no in-app chat, no copy-paste — the human watches the board, the agent fills it. What it does AssetsCurator is a WebMCP media bin . Open the board in ChatGPT's in-app browser and ChatGPT gains ~23 registered tools to build a shot list scene by scene: Generate AI stills, short clips, and audio (voiceover, score, SFX) Search & attach royalty-free photos, footage, and music Pin YouTube references (links and embeds only, never downloaded) Surgically edit — replace a single asset in place, reorder scenes, set roles Export a shot-ordered folder ( 01-open/ , 02-pour/ …) with audio files, attribution, and .url shortcuts Every write tool updates the visible UI before it returns , and the whole board works in 16:9, 9:16, or 1:1 . With no agent present, the same actions are plain buttons — progressive enhancement. How we built it Next.js 15 (App Router), TypeScript, Tailwind v4. Tools register on the top-level document via document.modelContext.registerTool() . A Zustand store is the single shared source of truth (persisted to IndexedDB). The agent's tools and the human's buttons call the same action layer, so their views can never diverge. API routes proxy keys and run a free-first fallback router ( firstOk() + a circuit breaker): each modality has a provider chain that cools a failed source and tries the next, so the board is never empty. A cinematic prompt layer + higher generation resolution lift AI output from "AI default" to production-looking frames. JSZip assembles the shot-ordered export. Challenges we ran into Top-level registration only. WebMCP hosts discover tools registered on the top-level page; iframe and declarative-form approaches didn't surface, which shaped the whole client architecture. Free providers are fragile. During the build, HuggingFace retired FLUX from its free serverless inference (HTTP 410), Together's free tier began requiring a paid deposit, and a keyed Pollinations endpoint ran out of credit (402). Rather than chase one "good" provider, we leaned into the circuit-breaker + fallback design — the fragility became resilience . Vertical video. Most free image generators emit a fixed square frame; only Pollinations honors arbitrary width/height, so it anchors the 9:16 / 1:1 feature end to end (generation, stock orientation, and display). A silent zero-result bug. A Jamendo include parameter returned an empty (but "successful") result set and masqueraded as a provider failure until we traced it. Accomplishments that we're proud of A genuinely agent-native UX : no chatbot, the page is the canvas, and single-asset replace_asset proves the model is doing typed mutation on shared state , not DOM scraping. Runs end to end on free providers with graceful degradation — a judge with zero keys still gets a full board. Conflict-free human + agent co-editing through one optimistic store. One-call export that drops straight into CapCut or Premiere. What we learned WebMCP rewards designing tools as verbs over shared state , where every write returns the new project so the agent can verify ids and self-correct. Optimistic UI + a single store is what makes human-and-agent co-editing feel live. Fallback architecture matters more than any single provider. Assume every free API will fail, quota out, or get deprecated mid-hackathon — and design for it. What's next for AssetsCurator Sequence/timeline export (EDL / Premiere XML) and per-shot duration trims. More aspect-native video and a Ken Burns motion pass for stills. Collaborative, multi-viewer boards. Optional paid-tier providers behind the same router for higher-fidelity generation, with the free chain as the always-on floor. title: CarePortal
pitch: A patient portal built for patients, caregivers and their agents. Agents handle appointments, meds, results and messages in signed-in session; users confirm what matters and sign what only users can.
about_excerpt: A patient portal built for patients, caregivers and their agents. Agents handle appointments, meds, results and messages in signed-in session; users confirm what matters and sign what only users can. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Anyone who has managed a parent's care knows the portal. Appointments in one tab, medications in another, lab results in a third, messages in a fourth, consent forms somewhere in a fifth. One question — is Mom okay this week? — takes twenty minutes and a lot of clicking to answer, and most caregivers give up halfway. Hospitals will never fix this by issuing API keys to your agent. Liability, HIPAA, bot defenses. But you are already signed in. That gap — a site that will never expose an agent API, and a user who is already authenticated — is exactly what WebMCP fills. What it does CarePortal is a patient portal with proxy access, built for caregivers and the agents they bring with them. You sign in, switch to the family member you're managing care for, and say one sentence to your agent. The agent works across four modules in your signed-in session — appointments, medications, results, messages — and the page follows it: every tool call navigates to the relevant screen and highlights what the agent is looking at. A rail on the right logs each step in plain English. Writes are split into three tiers, decided by the portal, not the agent: Read anytime. Appointments, medications, results, unread messages, who you're acting for. Confirm in-page. Refill requests, replies to a provider, rescheduling. The agent prepares the action; a confirmation card opens in the portal; nothing is submitted until you approve. Message drafts are editable before sending. Not exposed. Signing consent forms, opening full records, changing proxy permissions. There is no tool for these. The agent can only tell you they exist and bring you to them. The demo runs on realistic seed data. The data layer is an interface with a documented SMART on FHIR mapping for the production path. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The session is the trust boundary. A remote MCP server would require the hospital to build agent authentication, a new API surface, and still couldn't ask for consent inside the page. WebMCP reuses the login the portal already has and the frontend logic it already runs. The portal decides what agents may do. DOM-driving agents can't distinguish "help with this" from "this needs a human." A tool set can. The not-exposed tier is a first-class design decision, and it's only possible when the site defines the tools. Patient-access FHIR is read-only by law. The 21st Century Cures Act forces hospitals to expose reads to patient-authorized apps. It does not — and likely never will — expose act-as-the-patient writes. That half exists only inside the portal, which is precisely where WebMCP lives. How it creates a better experience Before: five tabs, ~40 clicks, no way to ask "what's affected this week." After: one sentence. The agent traverses the modules; you make two decisions and one signature, each in the place where the action actually lives. You never leave the portal, never paste anything into a chat box, and never wonder what the agent did — the page moved with it. What people and agents can now do together Cross-module reasoning. "Her blood pressure med is low, the cardiology follow-up is next week, and the lab result the PCP flagged needs a reply" — portals are organized by department, not by situation. Agents aren't. Consent where the action is. The confirmation card is the portal's own UI, with the portal's own copy, not a generic "allow?" in the agent's chat window. A visible line the agent can't cross. what_requires_me returns the consent form and says, in its own description, there is no tool to sign documents . The agent hands off; the human finishes. Context switching that agents understand. Switch from your own account to your mother's and every tool re-registers with her name in its description. The agent knows whose records it's touching before it decides which tool to call. How we built it Vite + React + TypeScript, Zustand for state, deployed on Vercel. WebMCP via document.modelContext , with a status badge that tells judges how to enable it if the browser doesn't have it. Ten tools in three scopes , each scope an AbortController : Scope Registered when Tools auth before sign-in get_login_status patient after sign-in; rebuilt on every patient switch get_patient_context , get_upcoming_appointments , get_medications , get_recent_results , get_unread_messages , request_refill , send_message_to_provider , what_requires_me route only on /appointments/:id reschedule_appointment Page-follow. Every execute begins by navigating and highlighting, so the human and the agent are always looking at the same thing. Confirmation protocol. Confirm-tier tools return a Promise that resolves when the user clicks. Agent harnesses have tool-call timeouts and humans don't, so after 60 seconds the tool returns pending_user_confirmation , the card stays open, and a later approval is applied directly. Every confirm-tier tool shares one status vocabulary: submitted | declined_by_user | pending_user_confirmation | busy | requires_provider_approval . document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "request_refill", description: "[Acting for Margaret Lee via proxy access] Requests a refill for one medication. Opens a confirmation card the user must approve; nothing is submitted until they do. ...", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { medication_id: { type: "string" } }, required: ["medication_id"] }, execute: async ({ medication_id }) => { follow("/medications", { kind: "medication", id: medication_id }); const r = await showConfirm({ title: "Request refill", detail: "...", onLateApprove: () => ds.requestRefill(medication_id) }); if ("timeout" in r) return text({ status: "pending_user_confirmation" }); if (!r.approved) return text({ status: "declined_by_user" }); ds.requestRefill(medication_id); return text({ status: "submitted" }); } }, { signal: patientScope.signal }); Challenges Deciding what not to expose was harder than deciding what to expose. The temptation is to make everything a tool. The portal's credibility comes from the line it draws. Timeouts. A confirmation card is a human-speed operation inside a machine-speed protocol. The 60-second pending state and onLateApprove came out of that mismatch. Descriptions are the product. An agent that picks the wrong tool or skips get_patient_context isn't a model problem; it's a description problem. We rewrote every description three times, always answering: what does this do, when should you call it, what does it return, when should you not call it. Hot reload. Re-registering a tool name throws InvalidStateError . Scopes are torn down in import.meta.hot.dispose . What we learned WebMCP isn't a way to make agents autonomous on the web. It's a way for a site to say exactly how far an agent may go — and for the human to stay in the page for the part that's theirs. For healthcare, that part is small, non-negotiable, and legally required. Designing around it turned out to be the whole project. What's next Implement FhirDataSource against a SMART on FHIR sandbox for the read tier. Add more human-only patterns (identity verification, payment authorization). Talk to a hospital. title: CargoMesh
pitch: Autonomous Agentic Freight Orchestration for Cross-Border B2B Logistics
about_excerpt: Autonomous Agentic Freight Orchestration for Cross-Border B2B Logistics Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Moving heavy freight across Latin America is complex and fragmented. Shippers juggle multiple carrier portals, emails, spreadsheets, and phone calls just to verify route coverage, check truck capacity, get rate quotes, and confirm bookings. Traditional automation relies on fragile web scraping or custom APIs that smaller carriers cannot maintain. We asked: what if carrier websites could directly publish typed, structured capabilities to an authorized browser agent through the open WebMCP standard? CargoMesh makes this possible. What it does CargoMesh is an agent-native B2B freight orchestration platform: Canonical Intake : Shippers define or load freight requests (e.g., FR-1042 Callao, Peru → Santiago, Chile). Dynamic Discovery : Discovers 0..N compatible carriers from an open registry without hardcoded lists. Native WebMCP Execution : The browser agent visits carrier portals (Andes, Inca, Pacific) and consumes 5 structured tools via document.modelContext : check_service_coverage , check_capacity , quote_freight , book_freight , and get_provider_booking_status . Result Bridge : Validates and persists commercial responses without client-side data tampering. Deterministic BALANCED Engine : Scores offers mathematically (25% cost, 25% reliability, 20% transit, 10% availability, 10% route experience, 10% org history). Recovery : If a carrier rejects a booking, CargoMesh offers authorized alternatives (e.g., Andes rejection → Inca confirmed). How we built it Frontend & Provider Portals : Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet for explicitly planned route corridors, and EN/ES support. WebMCP Runtime : Browser-side document.modelContext.registerTool with strict JSON schemas, abort handling, and tool cleanup on provider navigation. Backend & Security : Supabase PostgreSQL, Supabase Auth, RLS, and optimistic concurrency through draft_version . Result Bridge & Auditing : Server-side validation of tool envelopes, origin/classification, request correlation, and commercial responses. The Judge Drawer exposes auditable inputs, outputs, timestamps, and origin evidence. Challenges we ran into Separating browser execution from database truth : WebMCP tools execute in browser memory; we built the Result Bridge to validate signatures before persisting commercial offers. Dynamic 0..N provider identity : Preserving exact matchingServiceId across dynamic navigation without breaking idempotency. Clean context management : Ensuring active WebMCP tools are completely removed from document.modelContext when navigating away from a provider. Technical honesty : Avoiding artificial GPS simulation; planned corridors are explicitly labeled as planned references. Accomplishments that we're proud of Native WebMCP tool surfaces through document.modelContext . A deterministic, explainable BALANCED ranking for the canonical FR-1042 fixture: Andes 89, Inca 84, Pacific 72. Repository and client-bundle checks with no detected secret exposure, plus RLS-protected organization-scoped access. A demonstrated recovery flow: Andes rejection, explicit human selection of Inca, then confirmed replacement booking. What we learned We proved that WebMCP fundamentally shifts how B2B platforms interact: websites can expose clean, agentic tool surfaces without breaking the visual human interface, eliminating the need for brittle web scraping. What's next for CargoMesh Onboarding additional real-world carriers across the Pan-American corridor. Integrating independently hosted provider origins with external WebMCP adapters. Multi-modal freight orchestration (maritime and air freight handoffs). title: ChessUp
pitch: ChessUp shows what learning tools gain from WebMCP. Our progress and mistakes become data, and from that data, we can get a customized learning experience.
about_excerpt: ChessUp shows what learning tools gain from WebMCP. Our progress and mistakes become data, and from that data, we can get a customized learning experience. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A colleague mentioned, that he had never learned to play chess. Every app he tried gave him the same puzzles as everyone else and told him a move was bad without explaining why. I believe that WebMCP will be beneficial in learning for anything, not only chess. What it does You play a builtin bot. The app records every move and scores it with in-browser Stockfish. Ask your browser agent for help and it reads the position and your mistakes, marks the key error on the board, and builds a drill starting from your own position. ChessUp gathers data for AI, that can be helpful in your journey. The key here is to know, when you did a mistake that you can chat with AI about. Thats why i added Stockfish to the project. How we built it Next.js, chess.js, react-chessboard, Stockfish 18 in a Web Worker, and 20 WebMCP tools sharing one store with the UI. Tools are registered in groups with abort signals, so the set shrinks to what is relevant. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is pull-based, the app cannot wake the agent. So i needed to inverted the design. The chess bot plays instantly, the page records events, the agent catches up when spoken to. And agent-written puzzles can be wrong, so every solution is checked for legality and verified by Stockfish before the learner sees it. Accomplishments that we're proud of That i learned more about WebMCP and how can i use it with our clients at your company. What we learned Good tools expose meaningful actions and return enough state to verify the result. What's next for ChessUp I want to add a free registration for the tool so you can store your progress, save more data. The tool could be really good for learning chess. title: ClaimDesk | Agent-Native Lost Property Recovery
pitch: ClaimDesk turns airline lost-and-found into an agent-led investigation, using WebMCP to search, match, and verify lost property while keeping humans in control of recovery.
about_excerpt: ClaimDesk turns airline lost-and-found into an agent-led investigation, using WebMCP to search, match, and verify lost property while keeping humans in control of recovery. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The idea came from a very simple situation — you lose something while travelling. Suppose I leave my backpack somewhere after a flight. First question itself is confusing: did I leave it inside the aircraft or somewhere at the airport? Then I have to figure out whether to contact the airline or airport, find the correct lost-and-found page, fill forms and keep checking for updates. I thought, why can't I simply say: "I lost my black backpack on my Mumbai to Delhi flight. I'm not sure where I left it. Please help me find it." And let an AI agent handle the investigation. That's how ClaimDesk started. What I built ClaimDesk is a lost-property portal for AeroOne, a fictional airline I created for this project. It works like a normal website where passengers can report and track lost items. But using WebMCP, the same website also exposes its recovery capabilities as tools that an AI agent can use. In my demo, I tell ChatGPT that I lost a black backpack on flight AO-123. From that one request, the agent creates a claim, checks the flight, searches found inventory and compares possible matches. I intentionally added multiple similar backpacks. One is from the wrong flight, one is a partial match at the airport, and one is a strong match from the aircraft. So the agent actually has to investigate instead of simply getting one perfect search result. Ownership and human control Finding a black backpack doesn't automatically mean it belongs to me. For this, I added private ownership evidence. The correct backpack has an identifying detail which is not shown publicly and is also not given to the agent. ChatGPT has to ask me for something only the owner would know. I tell it there was a small red keychain inside , and ClaimDesk verifies this against the private record on the server. Even after ownership is verified, the agent cannot release the item automatically. It can prepare the recovery, but I have to explicitly approve the final release. This rule is enforced by ClaimDesk itself, not just through instructions given to the AI. How I used WebMCP I didn't want to build another chatbot inside the website. ClaimDesk remains a normal web application. I used WebMCP to expose capabilities like creating claims, searching inventory, comparing matches, verifying ownership and preparing recovery directly to the agent. The UI and WebMCP tools use the same application state and business logic. So when ChatGPT investigates a claim, I can see the same claim getting updated on the ClaimDesk website. Challenges and learnings One challenge was deciding what the agent should control and what the application should control. I finally kept it simple: the agent can decide how to investigate, but ClaimDesk decides what is allowed. Another challenge was making the demo realistic. Having only one perfect matching item was too easy, so I added wrong and partial matches and made ownership verification a separate step. The biggest thing I learned from this project is that an agent-friendly website doesn't need to become an AI chatbot. With WebMCP, the website can continue working normally for humans while also exposing meaningful capabilities to agents. With ClaimDesk, instead of understanding the complete lost-and-found process, the passenger can simply explain what happened and let the agent take it from there. title: Cleanroom
pitch: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero.
about_excerpt: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero. Like Comment Story Updates Cleanroom What it does Cleanroom is a data-cleaning workbench for messy CSVs. You drop a file on the page and an agent in your browser profiles it, finds the concrete problems, queries and charts it, and proposes the fixes — without the file ever being uploaded anywhere. The design rule is one sentence: reads are free, writes are proposals. No tool mutates your table. When the agent wants to change something it computes the exact before/after diff, puts a card in front of you with its reasoning, and stops. You click Approve or Reject. undo is deliberately not exposed as a tool — the ability to walk a change back belongs to the person, not the model. The problem it solves Every analyst has the same bad afternoon. A CSV arrives and before you can answer one question you have to fix it: regions spelled five ways, amounts stored as ¥39,545 , four date formats in one column, duplicate rows silently doubling your revenue. An LLM is excellent at spotting exactly these problems. But letting one help has meant either uploading your data to a server or code interpreter — a non-starter the moment the file has customer names, salaries or anything your compliance team has an opinion about — or pasting a sample and hand-applying the suggestions yourself, which is the automation you wanted, gone. Cleanroom is the third option: the agent gets tools, not your data. Why this is WebMCP and could not be a server MCP This is not a remote MCP server with a web page bolted on. It structurally could not be one. The agent and the human operate on literally the same JavaScript object . One store is the single source of truth; the UI renders it and the tools operate on it. When the agent proposes a change the approval card appears in the human's rail in the same tick — no sync, no polling, no second copy that can drift. A remote agent cannot have that property, because a remote agent needs a copy. And everything a server MCP would need — upload, storage, auth, per-seat infrastructure — is simply absent. It's already your browser and already your session. The whole app is a static file. The privacy receipt The claim is "your data never leaves this tab," and a claim is worth nothing, so the page proves it. Before any other module loads, Cleanroom instruments fetch , XMLHttpRequest , sendBeacon and WebSocket and counts every outbound request. The count is in the header, and the agent can read it too, via a get_privacy_receipt tool — so when you ask "did my data go anywhere?" it answers with a verifiable number instead of a promise. It reads zero because there is nothing to send it to: no analytics, no CDN, no webfont, no charting library. Even the sample dataset is inlined as a string rather than fetched, specifically so the ledger stays honest. The deployed site also ships connect-src 'none' in its CSP, so the browser enforces it independently of our own code. Being straight about the limit: this counts requests the page makes. It cannot police the browser itself or a malicious extension, and it isn't a substitute for a security review. How I built it Vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, no framework and no runtime dependencies — a dependency that phones home would undermine the entire premise. Roughly 1,800 lines across eleven modules: a RFC-4180-tolerant CSV parser, type inference and column profiling, an issue detector, fifteen pure transform operations with a diff builder, the store that holds the undo stack, the WebMCP tool layer, the UI, and hand-rolled inline SVG charts. 14 tools are registered — eight read-only, six human-gated. Three implementation details did the most for how well an agent actually performs here: Every detected issue carries a suggested_fix — a ready-to-use propose_transform payload. The agent goes from "what's wrong?" to a queued, reviewable fix in one hop instead of guessing at an API shape. This cut the model's flailing more than anything else I tried. Errors are instructions. Every failure names the valid inputs — Column "reigon" does not exist. Available columns: order_id, order_date, region, … — and is returned as text rather than thrown, so the agent reads the recovery path instead of hitting an opaque host error. Results are context-window shaped. Profiles and aggregates are summaries by construction; raw rows are returned only on request and hard-capped at 200. A 100,000-row file is fully workable without a single row entering the model's context. Challenges WebMCP's API moved while it was being standardised — some hosts expose navigator.modelContext , the current spec draft uses document.modelContext , and earlier builds took a batch provideContext({tools}) instead of per-tool registerTool . Rather than bet on one, the registration shim feature-detects all of them and reports which it found, so the header tells the user the truth about their browser instead of failing silently. Tool results are returned in three shapes at once — MCP-style content , structuredContent , and a bare data object — so the same tool behaves identically across hosts. The harder problem was designing the pause . An agent that has to stop and wait is easy to build badly: it either blocks forever or barrels ahead assuming approval. propose_transform returns pending_human_approval with an explicit next_step , and a separate await_decision tool blocks on the human with a timeout and tells the agent what to say if it expires. Getting the agent to reliably not assume its change landed was most of the prompt-shaped work. What I learned Designing tools for an agent is interface design, and the same thing that makes an API pleasant for a junior engineer — good names, errors that say what to do next, results scoped to what you actually need — is what makes a model competent instead of erratic. The suggested_fix field was the clearest demonstration: same model, same data, dramatically better behaviour, purely from shaping the return value. The second thing: an approval gate makes an agent more useful, not less. Once a change is reviewable before it lands, you stop hedging your prompts and start letting it try things. What's next Multi-table joins under the same proposal model — the agent proposes the key and shows you the match rate before committing. Recipe export — the change log is already ordered and structured; emit it as a runnable script so a one-off clean becomes a repeatable pipeline. Approval policies — "auto-approve whitespace fixes, always ask about dropped rows." The gate exists; this is a rule layer on top of it. Try it In ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, open the page and ask: "What's wrong with this data? Don't change anything yet — just tell me what you'd fix and why." "Clean it up. Propose each fix separately so I can review them, and ask me before you touch anything that's a judgement call." In any other browser the built-in Agent Console calls the same registered tool objects a host calls — an inspector, not a mock — so you can see exactly what the agent sees. title: ClearRights
pitch: Agents prepare privacy changes. People approve them. Websites apply and verify the result.
about_excerpt: Agents prepare privacy changes. People approve them. Websites apply and verify the result. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A privacy banner detects WebMCP access while keeping every choice visible and human-controlled. WebMCP prepares an exact plan and explains the effects; human review is still required.” A deliberate human hold unlocks only the exact unchanged plan for application. The host applies the reviewed plan, reads it back, and issues a verified receipt. The timeline separates agent preparation and application from human review and direct choices. Reversible display preferences add extra-large text and dark mode without changing privacy state.” Inspiration Living in Italy, and more broadly in Europe, made privacy controls feel like an everyday problem rather than an abstract one. Almost every website presents a cookie banner or some form of privacy choice, but those decisions are often fragmented across banners, account settings, policy pages, and support flows. I also noticed a new problem while using browser agents: when a website places an intrusive banner in front of the content, an agent may simply accept it so it can continue with the task. That is convenient, but it may not reflect what the person actually wants. I could not find a simple developer tool that lets an agent understand a website's real privacy controls, prepare a safer configuration, and still leave the consequential decision visibly in human hands. That became the starting point for ClearRights Privacy. The goal is not to replace privacy laws, consent platforms, or legal review. It is to give websites a structured layer that can connect their existing controls to both people and agents, while keeping a clear history of what was prepared, approved, applied, and verified. The central question was: What if a website exposed its privacy controls as a structured, agent-readable model while keeping final authority visibly with the person? This led to one simple principle: Agents prepare privacy changes. People approve them. Websites apply and verify the result. What it does ClearRights Privacy is a headless SDK and reference implementation for privacy settings that people and compatible agents can use together. A developer describes the website's controls once: what each setting does, whether it is required or optional, what data it uses, and what changes when it is enabled or disabled. The human interface and the WebMCP tools then use the same structured model. I built Waypoint Travel, a fictional travel website, to demonstrate the complete flow. An agent can inspect the current configuration, explain individual settings, identify the required services, and prepare a plan based on a natural request such as: Keep booking and account security, but disable personalised recommendations, location suggestions, and partner offers. The proposed plan opens in the same interface the person can use manually. It clearly shows each change and its consequences, but it does not modify the product yet. The agent marks the plan as prepared, while the human check remains separate. The person must hold the visible control to confirm that they reviewed that exact plan. Only after this step does apply_privacy_plan become available as a WebMCP tool. When the tool is invoked, Waypoint applies the complete approved state through an adapter and reads it back from the target system. If the result does not match the plan, the operation fails closed. If it matches, ClearRights creates a verified receipt containing the decision, revision, approval method, adapter, and readback result. The effect is also visible in the product itself: recommendations become generic or personalised, and optional surfaces such as nearby suggestions and partner offers appear or disappear. Preparing a plan alone never changes the experience. Waypoint is a local fictional demonstration, not a compliance product. The same architecture could later connect to a real consent platform, backend, feature-flag system, or data pipeline through host-owned adapters. title: CommandDeck
pitch: AI builds the right retail workspace for each task, while staff review, edit, and approve every change through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: AI builds the right retail workspace for each task, while staff review, edit, and approve every change through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In my own work, I often ask AI for help, but I still have to move the result into the actual admin screen by hand. I built CommandDeck because I wanted the AI's plan to appear directly as a workspace that staff could review and use. Retail staff often use separate screens for products, prices, inventory, and storefront content. When old stock must be cleared, staff have to find products, check margins, prepare discounts, and review the customer view by hand. We wanted one simple request to prepare the right workspace for the job. What it does CommandDeck turns a business request into a task-ready workspace. In the demo, a staff member asks for a clearance plan. The agent finds slow-moving products and creates a workspace with product photos, prices, stock levels, and margin checks. The staff member can remove a product and ask to see what customers will see. The agent then changes the same workspace into a storefront preview. CommandDeck also supports price reviews, inventory replenishment, and storefront editing. Each task gets the tools and layout it needs. The agent prepares the work, while the staff member can edit, lock, review, and approve it. How we built it CommandDeck is built with React and TypeScript. It uses Zustand for state management, Zod for validation, and native document.modelContext.registerTool() calls for WebMCP. WebMCP lets the agent inspect the demo catalog, create a workspace, add trusted interface blocks, and change the layout when the task changes. The agent chooses from 11 trusted React blocks and five layouts. The visible controls and WebMCP tools use the same service layer. We also added English and Japanese interfaces and responsive layouts for desktop and mobile. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was allowing the workspace to change without losing human edits and approvals. We added revision checks, locks, and separate review groups. We also separated previews from applied results, so staff can see what is planned and what has actually changed. Accomplishments that we're proud of A single request can create a complete workspace and then reshape it when the job changes. The human and the agent work with the same information on the same page. Staff do not need to copy AI advice into several admin screens. CommandDeck keeps important actions under human control. Emergency rollback is human-only. The public demo uses browser-local sample data, so it does not place real orders or change a real store. What we learned WebMCP can do more than automate clicks. It allows an agent to prepare the right interface for the current job while the human keeps final control. This makes AI assistance easier to understand and more useful for everyday store operations. What's next for CommandDeck Next, we want to connect CommandDeck to real commerce systems with secure authentication and audit logs. We also want to add more operation templates, team roles, and saved work histories. title: Consequence
pitch: An agent can fill out your visa application, but it can't sign your name. High-stakes paperwork with a permission boundary enforced in code, not just the UI.
about_excerpt: An agent can fill out your visa application, but it can't sign your name. High-stakes paperwork with a permission boundary enforced in code, not just the UI. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most WebMCP demos we looked at treat "the agent" as strictly upside: it fills things in faster, it clicks buttons for you. Nobody was building the other half of the story, the part where an agent's authority has to have a hard edge somewhere. High-stakes paperwork is the clearest place to make that argument: a visa or residency application has dozens of fields an agent can genuinely help with (dates, addresses, transcribing from a passport) and a handful it categorically should not be able to touch, because they're attestations. Signing your name is not a transcription task. So we built a fictional application (the invented "Skyward Residency Program," no real agency or form referenced anywhere) specifically to make that boundary concrete and testable, not just asserted in a README. What it does Consequence is a long, branching application where every field carries a permission class: agent_fillable , human_only , or evidence_required . An agent can fill addresses, employment history, and dates directly. If it calls answer_question on an attestation field, it doesn't fail quietly, it gets back a structured error naming the field and telling it to hand back to the human. For evidence_required fields like a bank-balance summary, the agent can only propose_answer , which lands as pending confirmation, never as answered, until the human accepts it. Every field also carries provenance (who set it, when, from where), and the whole mutation history is hash-chained and replayable, so a final review screen can show exactly who filled what. Conditional branches make the same point about tool existence . Answering that the applicant is self-employed reveals a Self-Employment Details section, and only then do fields like business_income_summary become part of what get_section and list_open_questions read from. The tool surface reconfigures itself based on answers already given. How we built it React + TypeScript + Vite on the client, Cloudflare Workers + a Durable Object as the authoritative backend, same architecture as our other entry, Cadence. webmcp-kit for tool definitions, shared across both apps. ~63 fields across 9 sections (7 base, 2 conditional), each declaring a PermissionClass in seed/schema.ts . One reducer ( src/shared/reducer.ts ) enforces the permission class on every mutation path, client UI, Durable Object, and every WebMCP tool call alike, so there's exactly one place the boundary is defined and no path that can skip it. check_consistency does real cross-field validation: an expired passport, overlapping employment dates, an unexplained income gap, checks that are genuinely tedious for a person and genuinely tractable for an agent, run against real answers in src/shared/derive.ts . submit_application is confirmation-gated and independently refuses while anything required is still open, on top of the per-field refusals. Challenges we ran into Making the refusal mean something. It would have been easy to add a client-side check that just hides the "sign" button for agents. That's not a real boundary, it's a UI suggestion. The actual fix was routing every write, human or agent, through the same reducer, so the refusal is enforced at the one place a mutation can happen, not duplicated (and driftable) across the UI and the tool layer. Seed data with nothing to catch. Early on, the seed application started blank, so check_consistency had zero contradictions to ever find, meaning the tool looked broken on every fresh demo even though the logic was correct. Fixed by seeding two fields that genuinely overlap (an employment start date before the prior job's end date), so the tool has real work to do the moment a judge opens the app. Shared-board demo entropy , the same problem we hit on Cadence: because a Durable Object's seed loads exactly once, repeated testing against one shared instance permanently consumed the demo state. Fixed with per-visitor isolated application instances plus a visible in-app reset button. Accomplishments we're proud of A refusal that's actually structural, not cosmetic: answer_question against a human_only field is rejected by the same reducer a human's own edit goes through, verifiable by reading src/shared/reducer.ts directly rather than taking our word for it. A tool surface that changes shape based on the application's own content, not just page navigation, extending the same dynamic-registration idea from Cadence into conditional business logic. A tamper-evident provenance trail (hash-chained mutation history) that answers "who actually filled this field" with cryptographic backing, not just a database column that could silently be edited later. What we learned The interesting design constraint wasn't "what can the agent do," it was "what can the agent be structurally prevented from doing, in a way that can't be bypassed by a differently-worded tool call." A permission check living only inside one tool's execute function is trivially circumvented by any other code path that touches the same state. Putting the enforcement in the shared reducer instead of the tool layer was the difference between a real guarantee and a suggestion. What's next A real evidence-extraction pipeline behind read_evidence (currently a clearly-labeled stub), a dedicated multi-party reviewer invite flow (the data layer already supports scoped reviewer tool grants), and extending the consistency checks beyond the current date/income rules. title: Cooktree
pitch: Give an AI the kitchen. Keep the keys. CookTree hands an agent thirteen functions and withholds four — your card, your address, your order history, your spend limit.
about_excerpt: Give an AI the kitchen. Keep the keys. CookTree hands an agent thirteen functions and withholds four — your card, your address, your order history, your spend limit. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Native Meal Planning, built for humans and agents. Inspiration There are only two ways to let an AI act for you on a website today. Hand it your browser, and it inherits your entire logged-in session — every page, every saved card. Or issue it a token, which outlives the session and can be replayed somewhere you'll never see. There is no third option that says "just a little bit." WebMCP is that third option, and we wanted to build the smallest thing that makes the difference obvious. Meal planning turned out to be perfect: it's a dependency graph pretending to be a list, and a grocery account holds exactly the things an agent has no business touching — a card, an address, an order history, a spend limit. What it does Tell CookTree what you want for dinner. It plans the week, works out what's already in your kitchen, dedupes ingredients across dishes, rounds up to real pack sizes, and gives you a list of things to actually buy. Twenty-one ingredient requests collapse into sixteen ingredients and eight purchases. Say "drop the mapo tofu" and it returns the diff — three lines gone, −$14.70 — not a page you have to re-read. Say "I used up the garlic" and the buy list grows to match. Describe a dish it has never heard of, in English or Chinese, and it generates a real recipe with quantities, cookware, and a photograph, then plans it through the same engine as the built-in dishes. Then ask it to change your delivery address. It can't. Not blocked, not password-protected — the site never registered that function. Thirteen tools exist; that isn't one of them. How we built it One static HTML file, no build step. Thirteen tools defined once in §4 TOOLS[] and registered individually with document.modelContext.registerTool(), falling back to navigator.modelContext and to provideContext({tools}) where registerTool is absent. Every tool body — and every button in the UI — routes through a single invoke(name, args) function, so there is no separate agent path that can drift out of sync with what people see. Clicking an ingredient fires explain_shortage; clicking a dish fires plan_week. It all shows up in the on-page agent console as tool calls, because it is all the same layer. Two Vercel Functions sit behind it so provider keys never reach the browser or the repo: one turns free text into a plannable dish (DeepSeek for the recipe, Nano Banana 2 Lite for the photo, in parallel), the other turns shortages into live Shopify Global Catalog listings and real merchant carts. We chose the tool set with one question per candidate: if this fired a hundred times by mistake, what happens? Nothing → expose. A draft gets messy → expose. A retailer handoff is created → expose, but gate it on a human. Money moves → keep the final action on the retailer's page. The account becomes someone else's → never expose. That last answer is why update_delivery_address, update_payment_method, read_order_history and update_spend_limit have no tool. Challenges we ran into The spec is still moving. The context object has lived on both document and navigator during the draft, and both spellings are still in the wild, so we probe for both. registerTool returns a promise, which a synchronous try/catch will not catch — a registration failure could leave the status pill claiming success. We trusted the model's numbers once, and shouldn't have. A generated recipe asked for 3 g of onion. An onion is a 200 g pack. Now the site validates every quantity against its own pack sizes and says in the console when it corrects one. The model is a source, not an authority. A hardcoded string nearly lied to the judges. The console header shipped with 8 tools registered, which JavaScript overwrites at load. When we opened the live site in ChatGPT's plain browsing — which reads rendered text without executing the page — it reported eight tools. Anything that doesn't run the script saw the wrong number. Deployment split in half. GitHub Pages auto-deployed but has no /api routes; Vercel had the routes but kept serving a stale build, because the Vercel GitHub App was installed on the account without being authorized for this repository. Diagnosing that took a cache-busting fetch and reading response headers, not guessing. Accomplishments that we're proud of We verified the argument in someone else's agent. ChatGPT's Cloud Browser opened the live site, enumerated all thirteen tools by name, and called get_kitchen successfully. Then we asked it to change the delivery address, and it came back with: → update_delivery_address {"address":"42 Mission St"} ✕ no such tool — 13 registered, this is not one of them the site never exposed it · a click-agent would open Settings and change it That refusal is not our demo script talking to itself. A real third-party agent tried, and the site had nothing to give it. We're also proud that checkout stops where it does. CookTree sends product names and quantities to Shopify, gets back real listings and real merchant carts, and then stops — the person pays on the merchant's own page. That boundary is the design, not an unfinished edge: a version of this that took payment would be a version that had to hold a card. What we learned Splitting is what buys the site choice. The interesting granularity isn't categories, it's scope. get_order_status is registered — it covers handoffs this agent created in this tab. Reading the retailer account's order history is a different scope and has no tool. The same noun splits into an exposed half and a withheld half, and you only get that by registering functions instead of handing over a session. And an honest boundary: this is least privilege, not a security perimeter. An agent that already has DOM access can go around all of it. The point isn't that the site is armored. It's that a cooperating agent never needs that access in the first place, and the site — for the first time — gets to define the surface it's willing to support. Cooking is just the version you can understand in ninety seconds. The mechanism matters most in banking, health portals, and internal admin consoles, where the list of things a site must not hand over is long. What's next for Cooktree Make the Agent/Manual switch real. Right now it only disables the chat box. The spec's registerTool(..., { signal }) means a site can revoke its tool layer with an AbortController — so the toggle could genuinely withdraw all thirteen tools and drop the pill to zero. A site that can choose what to expose should also be able to choose when. Surface the withheld set as a first-class thing. Today the four unregistered functions are visible in the account panel and in the docs. They should be part of the protocol conversation: a site should be able to tell an agent "this exists and I'm not giving it to you," so the agent can say so to the user instead of failing blind. Take it somewhere with real stakes. The same shape — a small set of typed functions, a human gate on the one that reaches outside, and a withheld list you can point at — is what a bank or a patient portal would need. Groceries were the version we could ship in three days. title: Countersign
pitch: It lets you use an AI agent to fight a denied insurance claim, without having to trust the agent.
about_excerpt: It lets you use an AI agent to fight a denied insurance claim, without having to trust the agent. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT screen Interface Inspiration Roughly 95% of denied health insurance claims are never appealed. Not because people accept the decision — because the process is slow, jargon-heavy, and exhausting by design. A letter arrives saying CO-97 , and most people put it in a drawer. An AI agent is almost perfectly suited to that problem. It can decode the denial code, check the appeal window, and draft the letter in seconds. But 2026 is a bad year to hand an agent your paperwork. OpenAI has said prompt injection is "unlikely to ever be fully solved," ChatGPT Atlas was retired partly over security, and researchers have tricked six different AI browsers into leaking credentials. Meanwhile 68% of organizations can't distinguish agent activity from human activity in their own logs. An insurance workspace is the worst possible place to put an agent, because the agent must read letters written by the opposing party . If the insurer can put text in front of your assistant, the insurer can talk to your assistant behind your back. We didn't want to build a safer agent. We wanted to build an app where the agent's safety doesn't have to be load-bearing. What it does Countersign is a workspace for appealing a denied claim, with an agent you don't have to trust. The agent does real work: it reads your denial letters, explains what CO-97 actually means and what evidence overturns it, checks how many days you have left, and drafts the appeal. Every tool the page exposes sits in one of three capability tiers, and the tier decides what happens — not the agent's judgment : read — runs immediately, changes nothing write — runs immediately, always attributed, always revertible consequential — submit_appeal , accept_settlement , withdraw_claim . These never run on an agent's say-so. The agent can only propose them. When the agent proposes something consequential, it doesn't execute and apologize later. The page stops it and raises a consent card showing the exact capability, the exact arguments, and what it would cost you in plain language — "Close CLM-4471 for $0 against $2,840 billed, giving up the right to appeal." You approve or reject. Everything either of you does lands in a provenance ledger — actor, tool, arguments, timestamp, outcome — and anything the agent changed can be undone. What's now possible that wasn't: you can let an agent operate on something that actually matters — money, a legal deadline, a waiver of your right to appeal — without auditing its reasoning, because the actions that can hurt you were never in its reach. Not withheld by instruction. Structurally absent. How we built it WebMCP is what makes this possible. Because the site declares exactly what an agent can do, the site also gets to decide what it can't. Ten tools registered imperatively via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Risk annotations that are honest and test-enforced : readOnlyHint on every read tool, untrustedContentHint on read_correspondence (which returns insurer text), and destructiveHint on the three consequential ones. Tests assert no consequential tool can ever claim to be read-only. Chrome's character budgets enforced in CI, not by hand — 500 chars per tool description, 150 per parameter, and tool output capped at 1.5K before it reaches the model. Staged execution. A consequential call returns a machine-readable NOT EXECUTED result telling the agent to stop and wait, so a well-behaved agent explains rather than retries. An actor-agnostic gate. workspace.invoke(tool, args, actor) takes an actor, so a human clicking a button and an agent calling a tool go through the identical enforcement path. WebMCP is how the agent reaches the rule, not where the rule lives. Rollback via state snapshots taken before any mutating call. Vite + React + TypeScript, no backend, no accounts, no keys — all state lives in the page, so it deploys as a static site and judges need nothing to test it. 49 tests. Challenges we ran into The agent refused to propose anything. Our first tool descriptions were written as warnings — "this leaves the workspace and cannot be unsent." A well-aligned model read that and simply declined to touch those tools at all, telling the user it wouldn't "create an external claim action." The consent gate never fired, because nothing ever reached it. The fix was to lead with the safety rather than bury it: "Propose filing the appeal. Calling this sends nothing." Proposing had to be framed as the safe act it actually is. Capping tool output without making tools useless. The 1.5K budget is easy to blow with a list of claims. We had to truncate structurally — dropping whole records and telling the agent to ask for a specific one — rather than slicing strings into invalid JSON. Making consent legible. A card that says accept_settlement {"amount": 0} is not informed consent. It had to say what you're giving up, in dollars, against what you were owed. The demo problem, honestly. When we tested the planted injection, the model recognized it and refused — which is the outcome you want and the wrong outcome for a video. We could have escalated the attack until something broke. We didn't. The test suite proves the claim can't settle even when a model is fooled, and that felt like better evidence than a staged hijack. Accomplishments that we're proud of The spec's Issue #165 is still deciding how a tool should elicit user confirmation, and Chrome's own tool security guidance currently offers no pattern for it at all . Countersign is one working answer, built entirely with today's shipped API: consent as a page-owned capability tier, rather than a prompt the agent is trusted to raise. We're also proud that the safety claims are checkable rather than asserted. The character budgets, the annotation honesty, and the injection defense are all covered by tests — including one that plants a real prompt injection in the seed data and proves the claim still can't settle. What we learned Tool descriptions are product surface, not documentation. They're the only thing standing between your intent and the model's behavior, and a single reframing — warning versus invitation — completely changed what the agent was willing to do. Safety language that scares the agent away from safe actions is a UX bug. Alignment is not a substitute for capability control. Our model resisted the injection. That was luck we don't want to depend on, from a model we don't control, against an attacker who gets to iterate. What's next for Countersign Skills ( Issue #161 ) to give the agent workflow-level guidance, not just a list of functions. Adopt requestUserInteraction() natively once the spec settles, replacing our page-level staging with the browser-mediated primitive. Consent policy — spending thresholds, auto-approve for low-stakes actions, step-up confirmation for irreversible ones. Cross-origin delegation via exposedTo , so a patient advocate or legal aid worker's agent can be granted a scoped subset of tools. Real claim import from EOB documents, and lifting the gate out into a library any site can adopt — the pattern isn't specific to insurance. title: DataSweep Pro — agent-human data cleaning on WebMCP
pitch: An AI agent and a person clean the same spreadsheet through the same 15 WebMCP tools. Every change is previewed on real tables, approved by a human, attributed, and reversible.
about_excerpt: An AI agent and a person clean the same spreadsheet through the same 15 WebMCP tools. Every change is previewed on real tables, approved by a human, attributed, and reversible. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "AI cleans your data" demo we'd seen had the same shape: a chat box, a spinner, and a table that changed. You never saw what the model was about to do, you couldn't check its arithmetic, and if it was wrong you started over. WebMCP changes what's possible there. If a page can publish real tools on document.modelContext , an agent doesn't need to guess at your UI — it calls the same functions your buttons call. That reframes the problem. The interesting question stops being "can a model clean a spreadsheet" and becomes "what has to be true before you'd let one write to your data?" Our answer: it has to show you what it measured, ask before it writes, record who did it, and let you undo it. So we built the execution environment for that, rather than another chat wrapper. What it does DataSweep Pro is a data cleaning studio where an agent and a person work on the same messy spreadsheet through the same 15 WebMCP tools . Load a CSV. Eight analyzers run concurrently and find what's actually wrong — mixed date formats, duplicates, currency strings that won't sum, whitespace that breaks joins, outliers, and rows the parser silently dropped. Each finding carries the measurement behind it and a suggested fix. An agent can do the same thing through the same tools. The load-bearing property: There is no separate "agent path" that could behave differently from the buttons. Everything runs locally. Your file is parsed and queried by DuckDB compiled to WebAssembly, in the tab. External communication — a model API, a desktop MCP client, a GitHub pull request — is opt-in and separately gated. How we built it Four layers, each testable without the one above it. Arrows point one way only: the domain layer knows nothing about tools, and the engine knows nothing about MCP. The WebMCP surface. 15 tools registered via @mcp-b/global . Each is one ToolDefinition — name, description, JSON Schema, annotations, execute — and that single object serves three consumers: WebMCP registration, the in-app Tool Inspector, and the agent loop. That's what guarantees the schema a reviewer inspects is the schema an agent is offered. Bridgeable to Claude Desktop with @mcp-b/webmcp-local-relay . The approval gate. A mutating tool called without a confirmation_token runs the transformation against scratch tables, measures exactly what changed, drops the scratch tables, and returns a token. Your data hasn't moved. The token is bound to a fingerprint of the exact arguments, single-use, and expiring — so an agent can't preview something harmless and reuse the token for something else. Enforced once in middleware, not per tool. A mutating tool declared without a preview() throws at construction rather than silently skipping the gate. Prompt injection. A spreadsheet cell is attacker-controlled text. Cell content leaves every tool inside a fence carrying a per-call random nonce, so injected text can't forge the closing tag and escape into the instruction region. Pattern detection also runs, but it's treated as advisory — the structural defence is what holds for payloads no rule matches. Testing. 380 tests. The integration and security-eval suites run real DuckDB-Wasm through its Node bindings, not a mock, because the interesting bugs live in the SQL. title: DeepTrail
pitch: An evidence-first WebMCP workspace where humans and browser agents research, challenge conclusions, and make inspectable decisions together.
about_excerpt: An evidence-first WebMCP workspace where humans and browser agents research, challenge conclusions, and make inspectable decisions together. Like Comment Story Updates DeepTrail Most AI research tools optimize for producing an answer. DeepTrail optimizes for making the path to that answer inspectable. DeepTrail is a local-first research and decision workspace where a human and a WebMCP-aware browser agent work against the same visible state. Instead of burying reasoning inside chat history, DeepTrail structures an investigation into questions, sources, claims, evidence relationships, counterarguments, confidence changes, research gaps, comparisons, and decisions. Why WebMCP is essential DeepTrail needs the human and agent to operate on the same application state. Copy/paste or generic DOM automation would lose stable entity IDs, provenance relationships, tool intent, attribution, and the distinction between supporting, contradicting, and qualifying evidence. The site exposes explicit research actions through WebMCP. A browser agent can inspect the active workspace, identify unresolved research gaps, add web sources with provenance, create or refine claims, link evidence, challenge conclusions, update confidence with a reason, compare alternatives, and record a draft or final decision. Every mutation becomes immediately visible in the same interface the human is using. This makes WebMCP the collaboration layer of the product rather than an optional wrapper around a chatbot. A better research experience A normal research session often ends up fragmented across tabs, notes, and chat threads. Later it becomes difficult to answer basic questions: Which source supported this claim? What contradicted it? Why did confidence change? What remains unknown? What evidence would change the decision? DeepTrail keeps those answers in one durable, inspectable workspace. Critical-thinking features Attack this conclusion turns adversarial research into a product workflow. DeepTrail captures a confidence baseline and asks the agent to search specifically for evidence that could falsify or materially qualify the current conclusion. What would change my mind? lets the investigation record explicit reversal criteria before more evidence arrives. Research Debt is a deterministic score that surfaces unsupported claims, thin provenance, unresolved questions, and missing counterevidence. The evidence graph makes relationships between sources and claims visible, while confidence history records why confidence changed rather than silently overwriting a number. What humans and agents can do together A human creates an investigation and defines the question or decision. The browser agent reads the structured workspace through WebMCP. The agent researches the web and writes credible sources, claims, evidence links, gaps, counterarguments, comparisons, and decisions back into DeepTrail. The human sees the same state update immediately and can challenge, edit, or redirect the investigation. Both sides can keep unresolved uncertainty visible instead of forcing a premature answer. WebMCP implementation DeepTrail uses the imperative WebMCP API with document.modelContext.registerTool() and a state-aware toolset. Tool availability changes with the workspace state so the agent receives only relevant actions. The implementation includes strict execution-time Zod validation, bounded inputs and outputs, HTTP(S)-only source URLs, same-origin tool exposure, WebMCP annotations, AbortController lifecycle cleanup, compact tool results, stable entity IDs, actor attribution, and local persistence in IndexedDB. External research text is treated as untrusted content. DeepTrail includes advisory prompt-injection risk checks and does not grant external content authority over tool behavior. Reliability and privacy DeepTrail requires no paid LLM API, search API, database, or backend. Research state is stored locally in IndexedDB. Users can export and restore validated JSON backups, and workspace integrity checks reject broken references and malformed imports. Judge quick start Open the live /judge route. It contains an evidence-backed seeded investigation, production-readiness diagnostics, and the exact agent prompt for the demo. Load the seeded workspace, send the prompt to a WebMCP-capable browser agent, and watch the agent research a real gap, add evidence, challenge the current draft conclusion, and update the same visible workspace. The seeded investigation is intentionally imperfect: it includes supporting evidence, a qualification/counterargument, confidence history, explicit falsification criteria, and unresolved production-verification gaps rather than presenting a pre-baked perfect answer. Built for the WebMCP Challenge DeepTrail was built during the challenge as a WebMCP-native product focused on human-agent collaboration, inspectability, adversarial thinking, and evidence-backed decisions. The goal is not more generated prose; it is a durable research trail showing what supports a conclusion, what weakens it, and what remains unknown.
