title: Dependency War Room
pitch: An adaptive WebMCP workspace that simulates API changes, measures downstream dependency risk, traces critical paths, and helps maintainers and AI agents plan safer software releases together.
about_excerpt: An adaptive WebMCP workspace that simulates API changes, measures downstream dependency risk, traces critical paths, and helps maintainers and AI agents plan safer software releases together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Dependency War Room Inspiration Dependency registries answer the forward question well: “What does this package depend on?” The harder operational question is the inverse one: if a package changes, who downstream is exposed, what evidence do I have, and what should I migrate first? What it does Real-time Dependency Graph Analysis Platform combines dependency graph data, API-change analysis, declared version-range exposure, security evidence and explicit human review in one War Room. For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended the existing platform with a browser-native War Room where a developer and an agent operate the same application workflow. WebMCP exposes constrained product actions for graph inspection, blast-radius analysis, human review, critical paths and migration planning instead of giving the agent raw database or GraphQL access. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Dependency-impact analysis is naturally multi-step: opening a package graph, summarizing topology, calculating blast radius, tracing a dependency path, simulating an API change, reviewing version exposure, applying human business priority or exclusions, recalculating the scenario, inspecting critical paths and generating a migration plan. With WebMCP, the application exposes those operations as explicit, schema-constrained product actions. The user remains in the visual War Room while the agent works through the same application workflow. Human and agent collaboration There is no separate agent-only copy of the workflow. If the developer changes scenario priority or explicitly excludes something from migration scope, the agent continues from that same reviewed state. The agent coordinates the investigation, while deterministic application logic remains responsible for breaking-change analysis, version exposure, blast-radius calculation, compatibility-related evidence and migration-plan generation. Human review remains explicit for business priority and exclusions. How WebMCP is implemented The application uses document.modelContext and registers a catalog of 16 canonical WebMCP tools. The runtime surface is adaptive: the application does not expose all 16 tools at every moment, but only tools relevant and executable for the active War Room phase. A verified initial runtime surface for cargo:tokio included open_package_graph , summarize_graph , calculate_blast_radius , trace_dependency_path and focus_graph_nodes . As the workflow advances, actions such as recalculate_scenario and generate_migration_plan become relevant. Both human UI actions and WebMCP actions call the shared WarRoomActions abstraction. WebMCP does not expose raw SQL, raw Cypher, arbitrary GraphQL, arbitrary scripts, arbitrary URLs or unrestricted backend operations. Better user experience The developer can inspect facts visually, make a business decision, and then ask the agent to recalculate the scenario and generate the next migration plan from the updated state. This shared-state collaboration is difficult to achieve reliably with ordinary DOM automation or a standalone chatbot. Real production environment The public deployment uses Vercel for the Next.js frontend, Render for the Rust/Axum API, Memgraph Cloud for the dependency graph, Redis for runtime cache/state, PostgreSQL/Neon for relational metadata, Qdrant for semantic search/vector data and OSV.dev for vulnerability evidence. The production demo is intentionally a seeded environment rather than claiming live registry ingestion. The graph and API interactions demonstrated in the submission video are real production application state. Existing-project disclosure The dependency analysis platform existed before the WebMCP Challenge. The challenge submission is the meaningful WebMCP extension and War Room integration added during the competition period, including shared WarRoomActions state, phase-adaptive runtime registration, constrained browser-agent actions, explicit human review, critical-path inspection and deterministic migration planning. What I learned WebMCP works best when a website exposes meaningful application actions rather than generic backend capabilities. The important design question is what the application should allow the agent to be authoritative about. Keeping deterministic evidence, human decisions and agent coordination separate made the WebMCP surface clearer and safer. What's next The next step would be expanding the same WebMCP authority model to larger dependency graphs and additional package ecosystems while keeping the adaptive tool surface small, with stronger browser-level WebMCP regression coverage and richer source-compatibility evidence. title: Duet
pitch: Turn the music you love into a piano lesson made for you.
about_excerpt: Turn the music you love into a piano lesson made for you. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Duet Piano Studio Agent created lesson Inspiration Duet began with a gap we kept running into: an agent could give us a good music lesson, but it could not reach the piano. We could ask, “Can you help me practise these four bars?” and receive sensible advice—slow the piece down, isolate the right hand, repeat the difficult section—but the useful part stopped at the chat box. We still had to find the music, change the tempo, set the loop, remember the notes and rebuild the lesson ourselves. We wanted the agent to meet the learner inside the instrument. That became Duet: a browser piano where the learner and their agent work on the same piece, using the same transport and seeing the same lesson change in real time. What it does Duet turns a natural-language request into a visible, playable music lesson. A learner can ask: Load Minuet in G. Keep only the right hand, slow it to 70 per cent, loop bars 1–4, add a one-bar count-in and metronome, highlight the opening phrase, and start practice. Through WebMCP, the agent can carry out each part of that request directly. The piece loads, the tempo changes, the left hand is removed, the loop and count-in appear, the requested keys light up and practice mode begins. The learner does not receive another list of instructions. They receive a lesson they can immediately play. Duet includes: A responsive browser piano playable with mouse, touch or A–Z/0–9 keys Fourteen public-domain pieces and exercises Demo, Play Along and Practice modes Tempo changes, transposition, simplification and hand isolation Bar-level slicing and looping Count-in, metronome, seeking and hand-mix controls Visible key highlights and expected-note practice Agent-supplied structured musical arrangements Microphone permission and monophonic phrase-capture support A shared activity history showing what the learner and agent changed Why WebMCP matters This would be a much weaker product if the agent were simply clicking buttons. Music has meaningful concepts: pieces, bars, beats, notes, hands, tempo, loops and phrases. Duet exposes those concepts through 21 structured WebMCP tools. The agent can ask what Duet supports, inspect the active piece, read a bounded section of the score, transform the music and verify the resulting transport state. It does not need to guess screen coordinates or depend on fragile DOM selectors. The learner stays in control. Sound still requires a human gesture because of browser audio rules, and microphone access still requires explicit browser permission. Duet reports those boundaries honestly instead of pretending an action succeeded. How we built it Duet is a React and TypeScript browser application. The interface and WebMCP tools share one Zustand command and state layer, so an agent action produces the same visible result as a human action. Zod validates tool inputs before they reach the music engine. Playback uses the Web Audio API with an audio-clock transport. This supports reliable play, pause, resume, seek, looping, count-ins, metronome clicks and separate left- and right-hand mix controls. The 21 tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool . They cover capability discovery, state and score reading, playback, transformations, highlighting, practice, transport configuration and captured phrases. We tested the WebMCP experience with both OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude. This was important to us: Duet should present a clear musical tool surface to any compatible agent, not depend on behaviour unique to one client. Challenges The hardest part was keeping three realities synchronized: what the learner sees, what the agent reads and what the browser is actually playing. Browser audio also introduced constraints that a normal interface can hide. Audio must be unlocked by a human interaction, scheduled voices must stop cleanly and pause/resume must preserve the real musical position. Another challenge was returning enough score information for an agent without exceeding the WebMCP response budget. We added bounded pagination so an agent can read longer pieces safely rather than receiving silently truncated data. We also had to resist adding visual effects that looked impressive but distracted from practice. The final interface focuses on a realistic keyboard, the active musical phrase and the controls a learner genuinely needs. What we learned The biggest lesson was that WebMCP works best when a website exposes the language of its domain rather than a list of UI actions. “Click the third button” is brittle. “Loop bars 1–4, isolate the right hand and start practice” is understandable, verifiable and useful. We also learned that agent actions need immediate visual feedback. When the tempo, loop, highlights and practice state change on screen, the learner can understand what happened and continue from there. The agent becomes a collaborator rather than an invisible automation layer. What is next We would like to add MIDI and MusicXML import, score-image recognition, timing and dynamics feedback, richer sampled piano sounds, and saved practice history. The current microphone pipeline handles monophonic phrases and has automated signal coverage, but real-world pitch recognition still needs broader testing across devices and environments. Duet is our first step toward a music lesson that does not end when the agent finishes speaking. title: EZI ChemLab
pitch: A 3D chemistry and physics lab where an AI agent runs the experiment. Through WebMCP it mixes reagents, switches modes and writes the lab report, for schools without a safe lab.
about_excerpt: A 3D chemistry and physics lab where an AI agent runs the experiment. Through WebMCP it mixes reagents, switches modes and writes the lab report, for schools without a safe lab. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Many schools in Indonesia teach chemistry without a laboratory that is safe or complete enough for students to run experiments themselves. Teachers describe reactions on a whiteboard, and students memorise colour changes they have never actually seen. The missing piece is not information. It is the instructor standing beside you who pours the reagent, points at the bubbles as they form, and stops you before you make an unsafe combination. We wanted to find out whether an AI agent could take that role, and WebMCP is the first thing that makes it possible. A chatbot can describe a reaction. With WebMCP, it can run one. What it does EZI ChemLab is a 3D chemistry and physics lab that an AI agent drives from inside the browser. The student talks to the agent, and the agent operates the bench. There are three practical modes, mapped to Phases D, E and F of the Indonesian national science curriculum: Acids and bases , with indicator colour change and gas evolution Electrolyte and non-electrolyte solutions , tested with a conductivity lamp Density and buoyancy , the classic egg in fresh water against salt water The agent can switch topics, mix substances, read the current state of the bench, explain each stage, raise an educational safety warning, reset the experiment, and write up the observation report at the end. Reagents are not teleported into the beaker. Each one is measured out into its own graduated cylinder first, or lifted on a spatula if it is a powder, and only then poured in one at a time. The amount_ml the agent asked for is something you can read off the glass rather than take on trust. How we built it Seven tools are registered client side through the browser model context API: switch_experiment_mode , mix_substances , get_lab_state , explain_reaction_step , trigger_safety_alert , reset_experiment and render_lab_report . The frontend is Next.js with React Three Fiber. Every object on the page is built from geometric primitives in code, with no third party assets: the glassware is turned on a lathe from a profile the way real glassware is, and the floor tiles and the room the glass reflects are drawn to a canvas at runtime. Bubbles are capped at 110 instances so the simulation runs on the standard school laptops we are aiming at. The backend is Rust with axum, acting as a proxy so that no API key ever reaches the client. One decision shaped everything else: reaction outcomes come from a static lookup table, never from a language model. The visual result of a reaction is a scientific fact, and a hallucinated colour change would teach a student something false. The model writes prose. The table decides the chemistry. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP specification moved the API from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext in July 2026, and browsers in the field are still split across both locations. Every registration goes through a resolver that checks both, because a page that registers nothing looks exactly like a page that was never built. Refracting glass nearly cost us the experiment. The renderer builds the buffer that transmissive glass reads from opaque objects only, so anything marked transparent inside a beaker is not merely faint, it is absent: the liquid, the bubbles and the electrodes all disappeared behind the very glass that was meant to show them. Worse, our whole browser test suite stayed green while the beaker was empty on screen, because every check ran at 900 pixels and refraction only switches on from 1024 up. We now have a check that runs wide, hides the interface panels so that a text update cannot stand in for a reaction, and insists the contents are actually visible. We also had to design for a judging period that runs for weeks. An API quota running out in mid September would leave the lab looking broken, so step explanations are generated once, reviewed for scientific accuracy, and served as static content. Only the lab report, which depends on what the student actually did, calls a model at run time, and the backend accepts several numbered providers and moves to the next one when a call fails. That is not a claim on paper: in production the first provider currently fails on every request and the second answers, and the report still arrives. Every remaining failure path returns vetted static text with a 200 response rather than an error. Accomplishments that we're proud of Every execute handler returns a structured result containing the visual state, the temperature change and a plain language observation, so the agent narrates what actually happened instead of guessing. Unknown reagent pairs return a structured error listing the valid pairs, which lets the agent correct itself without the student ever noticing. We also built the lab so that it stays usable when WebMCP is not available. A status badge reports what the browser supports, a manual panel calls the exact same handlers rather than mock versions, and the topic buttons in the header run switch_experiment_mode the same way an agent does. The tool layer is genuinely separate from the interface. What we learned Reading matters as much as writing. get_lab_state returns the same view of the bench that the interface shows, so the agent can check what is actually there before it acts rather than assuming its last call succeeded. Together with the structured errors, it is what keeps a long conversation from drifting away from the simulation. We also learned that visible tool call indicators are not decoration. Every call is written to an activity console with the tool name, the outcome, and whether it came from an agent or was run by hand. Watching that line appear at the exact moment the liquid changes colour is what makes the whole thing legible, both to a student and to anyone evaluating it. What's next for EZI ChemLab Reaction rate is the next topic, and it is the one that rewards an agent most. It has four variables to manipulate and two beakers to compare, so the agent stops triggering effects and starts designing an experiment. Thermochemistry follows closely behind, since temperature data already flows through mix_substances . Beyond that: teacher accounts with printable worksheets, offline packaging for schools with limited connectivity, and coverage extending into Phase F electrochemistry. I designed the product and made the calls on how the lab should behave: measuring each reagent before mixing so the amounts are visible, building the room and glassware as 3D geometry rather than using imported assets, and keeping reaction outcomes in a static table so the science cannot be hallucinated. I set up the infrastructure, VPS, domains, Dokploy, and the provider chain behind the lab report, and I tested the whole session in the ChatGPT desktop app. The implementation was written with AI coding agents working to those decisions, and I reviewed and tested what it produced. title: Firebro
pitch: A WebMCP incident console where agents investigate production failures and humans stay in control of remediation.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP incident console where agents investigate production failures and humans stay in control of remediation. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Incident response is one of those workflows where an AI agent could genuinely save time, but it is also a workflow where giving an agent unrestricted control would be a terrible idea. During an outage, engineers jump between service health, deployments, logs, traces, alerts, runbooks, and incident timelines while trying to answer a few basic questions: What changed? What is actually failing? What evidence supports that diagnosis? And what is safe to do next? I wanted to explore what incident response looks like when the agent can work inside the same operational console as the human instead of operating through a separate chatbot or a disconnected API. That became Firebro . The design principle behind the project is simple: Agent capability, human authority. What it does Firebro is an incident response console built around WebMCP. An agent can investigate an active incident by checking service health, dependencies, recent deployments and changes, logs, traces, alerts, metrics, runbooks, and the incident timeline. It can correlate that evidence, identify a likely cause, and propose a remediation. For example, one incident starts with degraded checkout performance after a bad deployment. The agent can compare service metrics, inspect traces and logs, find the deployment that introduced the regression, and propose rolling it back. But the agent cannot simply execute a consequential remediation on its own. Actions such as a rollback can require an approval tied to the exact proposed action. The approval has to come from a real human interaction in the console before the action can proceed. Once remediation starts, the simulated production environment reacts. Metrics recover, logs change, and the incident moves through recovery and monitoring before it can be resolved. Firebro includes multiple deterministic incident scenarios so the correct response is not always "roll back the latest deployment." Some incidents involve resource exhaustion, feature flags, memory leaks, or even third-party failures where the best action may be to wait rather than make an unnecessary production change. How I built it Firebro is built as a web-based incident console with a WebMCP capability layer on top of the same operational state visible to the human operator. The system exposes tools across the full response workflow: incident discovery, service health, dependencies, deployments, recent changes, logs, traces, metric comparisons, alerts, runbooks, incident notes, remediation actions, approvals, and incident resolution. One of the main implementation goals was avoiding a separate "agent version" of the application. When an agent investigates something, the console reacts too. A service can be highlighted in the topology, log views can focus on relevant entries, metric comparisons become visible, traces can be surfaced, and approval requests appear next to the operational evidence the human needs to make a decision. Tool availability also depends on context. Capabilities can change based on the selected incident, current incident state, and what actions are currently valid. The backend runs a deterministic incident simulation. Each scenario has a known underlying cause, but that ground truth is intentionally hidden from the WebMCP tools. The agent has to diagnose the incident using the same observable evidence available through the console. Mutations and incident events are persisted so the UI and tool layer stay synchronized as the incident evolves. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the environment realistic enough that the agent actually had to investigate. If every incident simply had an obvious error message pointing to the answer, there would be no real diagnostic workflow. Firebro includes misleading signals and plausible alternatives so the agent has to correlate evidence instead of choosing the loudest symptom. Another challenge was tool design. Returning thousands of raw log lines or metric samples makes an agent less useful, not more useful. The tools needed to expose enough evidence to support a diagnosis without turning every response into an unstructured data dump. I also had to think carefully about approvals. A generic "approved: true" flag would not be enough for a real operational workflow. Approval has to be tied to the exact action being proposed so an approval for one operation cannot silently authorize another one. Keeping the simulation deterministic was another important challenge. The same incident needs to behave consistently enough for automated evaluation while still looking like a live operational system. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that Firebro feels like one shared workspace rather than a dashboard on one side and an agent on the other. The agent works with the same incident, graphs, logs, services, and actions the human is looking at. Investigation has visible consequences in the interface, and consequential actions pass through an approval workflow instead of bypassing the operator. I'm also proud of the incident simulation itself. Different scenarios require different forms of reasoning, and remediation does not always produce an immediate perfect recovery. Some actions only partially help, some have no effect, and the system can regress if the diagnosis was wrong. That makes it possible to evaluate more than whether an agent can successfully call a tool. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that agentic interfaces need more than a large tool list. The useful part is the structure around those tools: when they are available, what evidence they return, how their effects appear to the human, and what happens when the agent is wrong. I also learned that human approval is much more useful when it happens next to the evidence supporting the action. Asking someone to approve a rollback in isolation is very different from asking them while they can see the deployment, affected metrics, traces, and the agent's proposed action in the same console. WebMCP also made browser context much more important than I originally expected. The agent is not operating a remote service in the abstract. It is operating the application the human currently has open. What's next for Firebro The current version uses deterministic simulated infrastructure so incidents can be reproduced and evaluated reliably. The next step would be connecting the same interaction model to real observability and incident-management systems while keeping the approval boundary intact. I'd also like to expand the scenario set, add more complex multi-service failures, improve automated agent evaluations, and explore richer policy controls for actions with different levels of operational risk. The long-term idea is not an autonomous system that replaces the incident commander. It is an incident console where an agent can do far more of the investigation and coordination work while the human keeps authority over decisions that can affect production. title: GenScape WebMCP
pitch: A persistent creative run that people and browser agents can inspect, pause, resume, and move into Canvas together.
about_excerpt: A persistent creative run that people and browser agents can inspect, pause, resume, and move into Canvas together. Like Comment Story Updates Creative work is not a single prompt. It moves through intent clarification, skill selection, model routing, asynchronous generation, review, and revision. Screen-driven agents are brittle in this environment: they can click the wrong model, lose a long-running job, repeat a paid request, or expose internal execution prompts. We wanted people and browser agents to share the same visible, recoverable workflow while the human keeps control of consequential creative choices. What it does The page registers six WebMCP tools for the current authenticated user: discover professional skills by workspace; start one real Agent, image, video, or audio run; read bounded public run status and result asset IDs; answer a pending Human-in-the-Loop question and resume the same run; list recent Canvas projects; create a visible Canvas project and return its stable URL. Mutating calls appear in the normal GenScape interface. Status recovery reuses the original run identity instead of silently creating another paid request. Tool results exclude system prompts, planning prompts, optimized execution prompts, provider channel IDs, credentials, routing diagnostics, and hidden model reasoning. How we built it We added a dependency-injected WebMCP layer on top of GenScape's existing authenticated client APIs. The imperative tools use document.modelContext.registerTool() , JSON Schema inputs, WebMCP annotations, one registration AbortSignal , and per-invocation cancellation signals. A React bridge owns registration for the signed-in page identity. Persistent Agent Run IDs connect start, status, Human-in-the-Loop answer, and resumed status. The Apache-2.0 public repository contains the competition adapter, clean standalone reference runtime, tests, and documentation. The existing VOZEB-PRO-derived GenScape host predates the challenge and remains under its existing BUSL/proprietary boundary; it is not copied or relicensed in the competition repository. The hosted demonstration integrates the new adapter with that existing host. The standalone runtime is explicitly a schema and lifecycle fixture and does not claim to generate paid AI media. Challenges The hardest boundary was returning enough state for an agent to make progress without leaking internal planning content. Long-running creation also required stable run identities, idempotent request identities, explicit Human-in-the-Loop state, and cancellation that stops pending browser requests without pretending an already accepted upstream task never happened. Accomplishments Six discoverable tools backed by the same visible workflows as the human UI. A complete start -> status -> answer -> status loop on one persistent run. Canvas creation with a stable URL. Registration removal on logout or page-owner change. Invocation cancellation forwarded through AbortSignal . Public result shaping with tests proving internal fields stay isolated. What we learned WebMCP works best when tools map to durable domain actions rather than UI controls. A reliable creative tool returns stable identities and visible state transitions, while the page remains the review and control surface. Browser-native tools are also a useful privacy boundary: the agent receives the public workflow state it needs, not the host's internal execution context. What's next Add tools scoped to the active Canvas selection, browser-mediated confirmation before high-cost generations, standardized output schemas when the proposal stabilizes, and progress notifications for long-running media work. title: Happy Coffee: The Agent-Native Data Developer Portal
pitch: Turning a data portal into an agent-native workspace: agents explore, query, test, and stage data products through WebMCP while developers see every result, lineage, and run in real time.
about_excerpt: Turning a data portal into an agent-native workspace: agents explore, query, test, and stage data products through WebMCP while developers see every result, lineage, and run in real time. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Dataset details Costs Development Quality checks Home page Sources Inspiration Data developers spend too much time moving between catalog pages, lineage graphs, SQL editors, quality dashboards, and pipeline runs. This project shows what changes when an agent can use a data developer portal directly - not by guessing from the UI, but through explicit WebMCP tools. Happy Coffee is built around the idea that the agent does the routine development work while people can see, understand, and control the outcome. What it does Happy Coffee is an agent-native data developer portal powered by WebMCP. It gives AI agents structured tools to understand and operate the portal without relying on screenshots, DOM scraping, or UI automation. An agent can: discover the portal’s capabilities and safeguards; search datasets, sources, quality checks, pipeline runs, logs, lineage, and costs; inspect schemas and preview bounded samples of data; open a browser-local DuckDB workspace and write or run SQL; create temporary derived tables and data-quality checks; prepare a table for publication with metadata, field descriptions, transformations, schedule, and attached quality checks. At the same time, the portal gives people visual feedback for every meaningful step. They can inspect the source data, review the SQL, see result grids, follow lineage, understand quality-check failures, and observe mocked staging runs. On critical decisions, such as publishing a table to production, the agent is not doing it automatically. A human must intentionally review and approve it. How we built it Happy Coffee is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. The development experience runs on DuckDB-Wasm inside the browser. Generated catalog data is loaded into the happy_coffee schema, while temporary derived data is created in a local workspace schema. This means the SQL experience is immediate, portable, and does not require a server-side database. The portal registers structured tools through document.modelContext , and each tool returns a versioned contract with stable IDs, bounded data previews, navigation context, and explicit safeguards. This lets an agent reason about the portal as an application—not as a collection of pixels. The app is deployed on Cloudflare Pages. Every merge to main produces a new production deployment, and pull requests receive preview deployments. It was tempting to expose one more tool that would publish a table automatically, for example. Instead, we made publishing a deliberate boundary. The agent can do all preparatory work, but it cannot cross the final line without a person. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a portal that an agent can understand through structured capabilities rather than visual inference. We made the human-agent experience observable: the agent acts, while the portal explains and visualizes the work. We designed a complete development arc—from catalog discovery to SQL, quality checks, publishing preparation, and mocked execution. We added data-integrity guarantees specifically because agent workflows need trustworthy relationships, not merely realistic-looking data. We kept DuckDB-Wasm local to the browser, making the SQL workspace fast, private, and easy to deploy. We established a meaningful safety boundary: agents can prepare a publishable table, but people retain the final publishing decision. What we learned We learned that agent-native UX is not about adding a chat box to an existing product. The real work is deciding what an agent should know, what it should be able to change, what context it needs to make safe decisions, and how the human can verify the result without reading a wall of tool output. We also learned that visual feedback is not a fallback for agents - it is the collaboration layer for people. Sample rows, lineage graphs, quality cards, result tables, and run logs turn invisible agent actions into something a developer can inspect, challenge, and trust. Finally, we learned that safe autonomy is a design advantage. The human publish step does not weaken the agent experience; it makes the experience credible. What's next for Happy Coffee: The Agent-Native Data Developer Portal Next, we want to make the collaboration model even richer: reusable agent workflows for common data-development tasks; visual explanations for query plans and quality-check failures; richer staging and production simulation; shared ephemeral workspaces for team review; better ways to compare an agent’s proposed data product against existing catalog assets. title: JurisMind — Private legal desk
pitch: A private legal desk in the browser. ChatGPT uses the site’s own WebMCP tools to save holdings with your note and build a support map — only from what you already saved.
about_excerpt: A private legal desk in the browser. ChatGPT uses the site’s own WebMCP tools to save holdings with your note and build a support map — only from what you already saved. Like 1 Comment Story Updates tools maps zero I built JurisMind because I am a lawyer, and I do not want a chatbot inventing case law for me. I also wanted something I can use case by case, not one giant dump of everything I have ever read. The job is simple. I save a source together with why it matters for this case (any case; the demo is just an example). That library lives in my browser, not on a server. That matters because this is where I already work, next to Word and the rest of my case tools. When I ask a question (or when ChatGPT asks it for me), JurisMind builds a "mapa de sustento": excerpt, my note, and the gaps, kept apart. If the library has nothing on that question, it says so. My sources stay organized per case. The rule I actually work with: I decide what enters; the source decides what can be claimed. The UI is in Spanish; I am a lawyer in Colombia, so I built it first for a lawyer who works in Spanish. This page is in English so judges (and you 😅) can read it. Why WebMCP I am not going to paste a whole expediente into a chat window. I am also not going to let an agent invent a back door into my file. WebMCP is the controlled window: the site publishes two tools. ChatGPT can call those tools — review the library, save a holding with my note, build a map — without me uploading the case to someone else’s server. The page stays the source of truth. (A browser agent can still see what is on screen; WebMCP is not magic privacy. It is an honest tool access.) What we can do together now I open https://jurismind-five.vercel.app . ChatGPT looks at the origin and finds the real tools — capturar_recurso and buscar_y_armar . It does not invent an API. Then, in ordinary language (the demo is caso Ramírez: high-cost medicine, EPS delay): it reviews what is already in mi biblioteca it finds an official Corte Constitucional judgment, opens it, and saves it with my note it builds the map only from what is saved — and it flags when a card matches the note but has no excerpt yet I ask something the library cannot support ( caducidad de la reparación directa ) and I get 0 fuentes . No invented sentencia. That is the feature. 🙂 Before this, either I clicked the UI myself or I hoped the model would not hallucinate the rest. Those were the options. How it is wired document.modelContext.registerTool on this origin only. capturar_recurso — write. Needs url and nota . Optional title, excerpt, collection. buscar_y_armar — read. Needs query . Opens the map in the page. IndexedDB per origin. Production and localhost are not the same library. No case-file backend. Chrome production has a WebMCP origin trial. ChatGPT Desktop works with Sol or Terra (not Luna). Gemini Nano / Prompt API can classify if the device has it; there is a fallback that does not depend on it. Repo: https://github.com/cristianbdev/jurismind (MIT). Video: https://youtu.be/2MnIFDTDRkE Test it like a lawyer, and you'll see what I see Open the live URL in ChatGPT Desktop. Optional: “Probar el caso Ramírez” loads three official Colombian sources you can delete. Then talk to ChatGPT the way you would talk to a junior: look at the file, go get a sentencia, save it with a note, arm the argument, then ask something that should come back empty. title: La Bàn - Career Guidance for Vietnamese AI Transition webmcp
pitch: La Bàn turns a career-guidance website into an in-browser MCP server: the AI agent a Vietnamese worker already trusts reads our verified occupation database and research library...
about_excerpt: La Bàn turns a career-guidance website into an in-browser MCP server: the AI agent a Vietnamese worker already trusts reads our verified occupation database and research library... Like 1 Comment Story Updates A screen demo of chatGpt in-app Note: the app is hosted on Render's free tier, so the server spins down after 15 minutes of inactivity - the first request may take up to a minute while it wakes up. Once warm, everything responds quickly. Inspiration The ILO estimates generative AI could impact more than 20% of jobs in Vietnam — and nearly 80 million workers across ASEAN are in occupations likely to be affected. Millions of them are asking the same question: "Will AI take my job - and what should I learn?" The answers they get online are generic, and when LLMs write them, the citations are sometimes fabricated. We measured it: across 12 Vietnamese worker personas, a single-prompt baseline produced 2 fabricated citations out of 26 - fluent, confident, and unverifiable. For decisions this life-altering, that's disqualifying. La Bàn (Vietnamese for The Compass ) already existed as a career-guidance platform with a curated Vietnam occupation database and research library. The WebMCP Challenge gave us the missing piece: instead of being a destination the worker visits once, the site could become the evidence engine behind every agent conversation about their career. Existing tools are either static career sites (no agent) or chatbots (no verifiable data, no persistence, no human gate) — La Bàn brings the three together: the page supplies the evidence, the agent reasons over it, and the human holds the pen. What it does La Bàn is an in-browser MCP server . Open it in ChatGPT's in-app browser (or Chrome with the WebMCP flag) and your agent immediately gets 12 tools in three layers: Evidence (client-side, works with zero API keys): lookup_occupation reads a curated Vietnam resilience database with MOLISA/O*NET codes and task-level automation exposure; search_research returns verifiable sources from WEF, ILO, the World Bank and more. Analysis : analyze_career_transition runs a verified multi-agent pipeline (Profiler → Evidence Gatherer → Analyst → Verifier) where only what the tools return can be cited , and every citation is checked against the corpus. Workspace (writes): save_career_plan , add_milestone , update_milestone_progress , share_plan_to_community - every single write opens an approval modal inside the page . A rejection means the agent asks what to change; it never retries blindly. The human and the agent share one page. What used to be tab-switching between a chatbot and a static website — with nothing saved or tracked — becomes a single conversation: the agent looks up the occupation, pulls the research, scores the risk, and drafts an editable 90-day plan; the human edits it in a modal before it's saved, both track progress across sessions, and an Agent Activity Panel shows every tool call in real time. Writes never happen without explicit human approval. How we built it Progressive enhancement : tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool with JSON Schema inputs and readOnlyHint annotations. In a normal browser the app runs unchanged; in an agent's browser it becomes a workspace. The honesty layer : when an occupation isn't in the database (a watch repairer, for example), lookup_occupation says so - and the agent falls back to research evidence instead of inventing a resilience score. Verification-first pipeline : the Verifier checks schema, guardrails and every citation; on failure, the analyst repairs its own output. Ablation showed the interesting part: tools alone changed nothing on grounding - the verifier loop is what eliminated fabrication (91.7% → 100% grounding, 2 → 0 hallucinated citations, 12/12 valid schemas). Stack : React 19 + Express + Gemini (multi-agent pipeline), localStorage workspace persistence, deployed on Render's free tier. 119 unit tests cover the agents, verification and every WebMCP handler. Challenges we ran into requestUserInteraction is not universally supported. During rehearsal on the real ChatGPT in-app browser, the Codex WebMCP shim exposed the API but threw on every call, breaking all workspace writes. The fix: treat the wrapper as best-effort with a try/catch fallback to the in-page modal - the human gate stays intact in every runtime. Free-tier reality. Our analysis endpoint was "timing out" in ChatGPT - but measured directly it returns a full verified result in ~16 seconds warm. The real culprit was Render's spin-down after 15 idle minutes. Cold start, not code. Teaching an agent to say "I don't know." The database covers 10 occupations. Designing tools whose no-match response is genuinely useful - and watching ChatGPT relay that honesty instead of hallucinating - was the most satisfying moment of the project. Accomplishments & what we learned A baseline with measurable fabrication became a demo where the agent refuses to invent data in front of a live audience. Writing WebMCP tools is really API design for a new kind of user - the tool descriptions we wrote read like prompts, and the agent followed them ("call this FIRST", "cite these instead of guessing"). Retrieval alone doesn't stop fabrication. Verification that can send work back does. Try it: open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser and ask "I'm an accountant in Hanoi, will AI replace me?" - then say "Save me a 90-day plan to become a data analyst" and approve it in the page. title: Lattice
pitch: A better way to review architecture with your agents.
about_excerpt: A better way to review architecture with your agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am a designer and engineer, so naturally, I love whiteboarding ideas. Especially today, as the implementation of software can be abstracted more than ever, I find it both necessary and enjoyable to diagram architectures before I build my ideas with agents. However, the revision loop has lately felt more drawn out that it needs to. I tried a bunch of whiteboarding apps before landing on the excellent tldraw , but as advanced as it is, it's still tedious to use it in conversation with an agent about a given diagram. I often turn to Computer Use, which relies on the slow process of screenshots and imprecise whiteboarding editing, and the alternative is building a custom API with an unnecessary amount of complexity just to allow and agent and I to collaborate on a whiteboard. WebMCP seemed like an excellent fit to make this workflow more efficient. What it does Lattice is an infinite canvas that functions similarly to tldraw, which it's built on, but specialized for reviewing architecture diagrams with your agents. It exposes WebMCP tools to view, create, and edit diagrams, so you can ask it to explain code concepts in an instant. Where Lattice really excels, though, is in its comment tool. Just like Figma, you can easily mark up any node or area on the board, and the agent connected to Lattice is able to understand exactly what you annotated without any screenshots or even any semantic references in your comments. How I built it Each Lattice board is stored in the browser via localStorage, so it persists with no accounts or exports needed. The underlying architecture is stored as a semantic graph, where every node, edge, and comment has metadata labeling exactly what and where it is (ID, type, label, connection, position). This is what allows the connected agent to make targeted edits without screenshots and without editing unrelated parts of the board. Challenges I ran into While dogfooding the first version of this app, I found myself constantly telling the agent, "I added a few comments, check them." It became a bit tedious, so I thought this back-and-forth could be improved with a simple keyword, like "Lattice." A skill was a perfect fit here, so I wrote a lightweight one that explains what the user is trying to do when they say "/lattice create" or just "/lattice" (to edit). Accomplishments that I'm proud of Lattice is not just a demo for me. I've started using it every day in the Codex in-app browser, and it truly has made me more productive, allowing me to understand concepts better and churn out higher quality code more efficiently. What I learned Before this challenge, I hadn't heard of WebMCP, so I learned all about how it works and where it works best (hoping more companies begin integrating it into their apps!). I also learned how to maximize an agent's capabilities not by necessarily giving it more tools, but rather by improving its existing set of tools through more narrow typing, better tool descriptions, and more. What's next for Lattice I plan on sharing this app with a few friends to see if/how it fits into their workflows. I suspect that many of them use whiteboards for more than just diagramming architecture, and the great part about Lattice today is its simplicity and its foundation (tldraw) that can be expanded in countless ways to support more use cases. Along with potentially expanding its feature set, I hope to find more ways to integrate it into my own workflow, like I did when I made the Lattice skill. I can imagine that instructing the agent to automatically create new diagrams when relevant would be useful, and I could even see some sort of cross-board context coming in handy as I work on one project across multiple Codex threads. title: Lessonique
pitch: An agent-guided coding classroom where ChatGPT teaches through safe, structured WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An agent-guided coding classroom where ChatGPT teaches through safe, structured WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates The agent prepares the lesson and configures the learning workspace. A focused explanation connects a variable declaration to its name and value. The learner completes a variables exercise and receives validation feedback. Lessonique waits for a WebMCP connection before opening the classroom. Code highlighting connects undefined and null to concrete examples. The guide highlights a const declaration while explaining its behavior. Inspiration When I first started learning programming, I did not have the kind of guidance I needed. It was difficult to know where to begin, how the concepts connected, or whether I was really understanding what I was doing. Those first steps could feel confusing and frustrating. Lessonique grew from that experience. I wanted to build the kind of learning companion I wish I had: something that explains a concept, shows exactly where it applies, and gives you a small opportunity to practice before moving on. The goal is not to let AI do the learning for you. It is to make learning to code feel more approachable, with clear guidance and less frustration. What Lessonique does Lessonique is an agent-guided coding classroom for learning HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. ChatGPT uses WebMCP to turn a learning request into a workspace with examples, a learning plan, visual explanations, and practice exercises. Instead of reading an explanation in one window and figuring out where it applies in another, the learner can follow the explanation directly in the classroom. The agent guides; the learner practices. Connect your AI guide Open Lessonique in a WebMCP-capable client. The application detects the connection, and the agent discovers which classroom tools and learning environments are available. No Lessonique account is required. From a request to a classroom Ask to learn a topic from scratch. As the agent prepares the lesson, Lessonique shows the setup stages: understanding the goal, preparing the lesson, and configuring the classroom. Understand one concept at a time Lessons break concepts into small explanations with examples. The guide can focus attention on the relevant code while the learning plan keeps the broader topic sequence visible. In this example, a JavaScript variable is introduced through its name, value, and assignment operator. Follow the explanation in the code The visual guide connects explanations to specific code targets. Here, the learner explores a const declaration and when to use it. Previous and Next controls let them review the lesson at their own pace. Make abstract ideas concrete Concepts such as undefined and null are easier to discuss when the learner can see the exact declarations being compared. The companion, highlight, and guide work together to keep that connection visible. Practice and check your progress The learner writes code in the editor and validates it against the lesson's declared requirements. The screenshot shows a completed exercise using string, number, and boolean values. Guidance supports the learner without replacing the practice itself. Why WebMCP is essential A coding classroom needs more than generated explanations. An agent must be able to configure the workspace, present a lesson, point to relevant code, and request meaningful feedback about progress. Lessonique exposes those operations through 13 structured WebMCP Site Tools registered in the top-level document with document.modelContext.registerTool. The tools use closed schemas, Zod validation, and capability checks. Semantic targets describe what to highlight instead of requiring the agent to supply CSS selectors or screen coordinates. This lets the human and agent share a coherent learning workflow: ChatGPT coordinates the lesson, Lessonique handles presentation and validation, and the learner controls the exercise code. The agent does not need to reconstruct the classroom through fragile UI automation. How I built it Lessonique uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with Monaco for editing and Sandpack for the runtime, preview, and console. A provider-neutral core separates the WebMCP tools, lesson orchestration, workspace management, teaching scenes, and validation. Codex helped implement the specification-driven architecture, debug interactions, build tests, assemble visual assets and sprites, and verify the deployed experience. ChatGPT Create Image produced the source visual references for the companion. Asset provenance and third-party notices are documented in the repository. ChatGPT is the teaching agent. Lessonique has no built-in chatbot or custom AI backend. Challenges and what I learned The difficult part was coordinating the lesson with a changing workspace: keeping visual guidance attached to the right code, handling learner interactions, cleaning up a replaced lesson, and keeping exercise requirements consistent with validation. This project taught me that an agent-friendly application needs explicit contracts, not unrestricted control. It also reinforced a teaching principle: a clear explanation, a small exercise, and useful feedback belong together. What I am proud of Lessonique brings the explanation and the practice into the same experience. WebMCP is part of the teaching workflow, not an extra feature layered onto a chatbot. The project includes automated unit and browser tests, a development panel for the registered tools, and an open-source MIT-licensed repository with setup instructions and asset provenance. Try it yourself Open https://lessonique.com/ in a WebMCP-capable client. The experience was tested with the Codex in-app browser. Ask: "Teach me JavaScript variables, data types, and functions from scratch using the current tab with WebMCP. Build an interactive step-by-step lesson with examples and exercises." Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jzit0TkxBmM Source code: https://github.com/GilbertrdzDev/lessonique What is next The current release supports HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. Future work could extend the provider model to additional languages and refine the learning experience based on beginner feedback. Those extensions are not implemented in this release. title: Modelo
pitch: A notebook where the calculations and the narrative live in one place. Collaborate with your agent on building deterministic and interactive models.
about_excerpt: A notebook where the calculations and the narrative live in one place. Collaborate with your agent on building deterministic and interactive models. Like Comment Story Updates Notebook Page Homepage Inspiration Modelo is directly inspired by Decipad, a product I worked on in the past. At the time, LLMs were far less advanced, and few products had useful AI features. The project did not work out, but I always believed it was a great idea that needed agentic collaboration to feel complete. For this challenge, I rebuilt a minimal version of it. What it does Modelo is a local-first notebook. You can write prose with headings, paragraphs, and lists, as in any other rich-text editor. Between paragraphs, you can add model blocks: a number, slider, select, toggle, or formula. Each block declares a named variable. Typing @ in a paragraph inserts the value as an inline chip that reacts to model changes. This lets you build deterministic, interactive models and add a narrative around them. You can also create and save scenarios with predefined values to compare different outcomes. Everything you can do manually is also available through WebMCP tools. An agent can list notebooks, open them, read a model, set an input by name, or rename a variable and update every formula that uses it. Each writing tool reports what changed, what remains broken, and how well the page reads. How we built it Modelo uses React 19 and Vite, with no backend. BlockNote provides the editor and acts as the only source of truth. The document you see is the same document that the tools edit. MathJS evaluates the formula graph based on its dependencies, while Zod validates every argument at the boundary. WebMCP registration uses Chrome’s use-webmcp-tool hook. A single table in src/webmcp/tools.ts defines all 23 tools: their names, scopes, Zod schemas, descriptions, and run functions. The React layer loops through the table and registers each tool with document.modelContext.registerTool . The interface buttons call the same runTool function that the agent uses. Challenges we ran into Currency algebra was difficult. Registering each currency as a separate MathJS unit makes mixed-currency formulas return an error. In the future, we would like to add FX rates to support currency conversion. More generally, units require careful handling and many design decisions. Agent-written prose was another challenge. By default, agents focus on building the model rather than creating a clear and visually appealing narrative. I added sections to the tool calls to improve this. A section is more than a set of blocks: its paragraphs can mention variables that do not exist yet. The section tool resolves @names against variables declared in the same call, so a sentence can reference a formula that appears later. Accomplishments that we’re proud of I created one portable format for seeds, storage, exports, and agent payloads. The application is highly testable. Most importantly, a person and an agent can edit the same paragraph without either needing to know who made the previous change. What we learned A tool should always report what it changed. Without this feedback, agents make more mistakes than they should. The mutation report became the most useful information an agent receives. I also learned that tool descriptions are prompts. Two sentences explaining when to use write_section instead of insert_blocks changed agent behavior more than any schema did. What’s next for Modelo Next, I want to support sharing notebooks by link, which will require a small backend. I also want to add charts as a block type, so users can see scenario comparisons as well as read them. Other ideas include importing spreadsheet ranges as inputs and building a richer unit system that can convert values instead of only formatting them. title: MOOD: A system for creative thinking
pitch: MOOD helps turn references and half formed ideas into a clear creative direction. The agent helps connect the dots, suggest what could work and refine it. You still make the calls.
about_excerpt: MOOD helps turn references and half formed ideas into a clear creative direction. The agent helps connect the dots, suggest what could work and refine it. You still make the calls. Like Comment Story Updates Cover Why I made MOOD The beginning of a creative project is usually the messiest part. You have a brief. Screenshots saved in five different places. References you love but cannot quite explain why yet. And very useful thoughts like "softer, but still bold" or "I know what I mean, I just can't explain it." That messy part is also where a lot of the actual creative thinking happens. I built MOOD because I wanted to explore what happens when an agent joins that process without trying to take it over. References become directions. Directions become decisions. Decisions slowly become a design system, and the agent helps along the way. The goal was never to let AI make the creative decisions. It was to give it enough context to be genuinely useful while I make them. What MOOD does A project starts with a brief and visual references , then moves through four stages: Stage What happens Explore Collect, organise and react to references Direction Turn those references into possible visual directions Refine Test choices, compare ideas and make actual design decisions System Bring the approved direction into colors, typography, principles and a reusable design system The System view is not a separate document generated at the end. It is a live projection of the selected direction and the decisions made along the way, so the different parts of the project cannot quietly drift away from each other. The same goes for the agent. It works with the same project state as the designer. It can understand which references were kept, which direction is selected, what has already been decided, what is locked and what still needs work. Then it can actually help. Why WebMCP This was the part of the project that really clicked for me. Creative work carries a ridiculous amount of context. A screenshot can show an agent what is on screen, but it does not explain why I kept one reference and rejected another. It does not know which decision I already approved. And it definitely does not know that changing one palette should update three different parts of the project. With WebMCP, MOOD can expose that context directly . The site currently registers 43 WebMCP tools , including 17 read only tools , through document.modelContext.registerTool() . They allow an agent to understand the live project before deciding what to do with it. A few examples: get_project_context get_selected_references get_selected_direction get_design_decisions get_design_system evaluate_palette create_suggestion update_palette navigate_to_phase So instead of guessing its way through the interface or asking me to explain the whole project again every time, the agent can simply ask MOOD . It can: inspect the current creative context understand the references behind a direction read existing and locked design decisions evaluate palettes and visual choices suggest changes with supporting evidence add or organise references create and refine directions update parts of the live design system move through the workflow itself And these are not shortcuts sitting on top of the product. WebMCP and the UI use the same underlying actions and the same state. If I change a palette in the interface or an agent changes it through update_palette , MOOD handles the result through the same system. Direction, Refine and System update together inside the running application. No separate "AI version" of the project floating somewhere else. The agent is not sitting next to the product. It can actually work inside it. The human part I really did not want to build another "AI does the creative work for you" tool. Taste is subjective. Context matters. And sometimes a suggestion can make perfect sense on paper and still just feel wrong. So MOOD treats suggesting and deciding as two different things. A suggestion contains: the reasoning behind it the references used as evidence the exact scope of the proposed change the mutation it would perform if applied The suggestion itself does not need to change the creative work. It can be inspected first, applied, rejected or simply ignored. Important design decisions can also be locked , so they cannot quietly be overwritten later. That separation became one of the most important ideas behind MOOD. The agent can contribute to the process without becoming the owner of it. You can disagree with the agent. That matters. The goal is not less human involvement. It is less time spent translating creative context back and forth . How I built it MOOD is built with React, TypeScript, Vite and Zustand , and deployed on Vercel. Project data lives locally in the browser. The architectural rule behind almost everything else is simple: There is one project state. The designer and the agent interact with the same thing. The visual interface and WebMCP tools dispatch the same domain actions against the Zustand store. For example, keeping a reference manually in the UI and calling keep_reference through WebMCP both update the same underlying project state. I documented that relationship in docs/action-parity.md , mapping: Human action → WebMCP tool → Domain action → Shared state That helped me make sure the agent was not getting special shortcuts that behaved differently from the actual product. Every WebMCP input is validated with Zod and exposed as JSON Schema . Mutating tools also return the current projectVersion , so changes to the shared state can be tracked consistently. I also built a WebMCP debug mode that exposes: API and registration state expected and registered tools available tool names execution results errors a guarded self test It started as something I needed while debugging and became one of the fastest ways to understand what the browser and the agent were actually seeing. The tricky bits 1. Deciding what an agent should actually be allowed to do Registering tools was not the hardest part. Deciding what those tools should be allowed to do was. There is a meaningful difference between: "What do you think about this palette?" "Suggest a better palette." "Change the palette." They sound almost identical in a conversation. Inside a creative product, they absolutely should not behave the same way. That meant thinking carefully about reads, suggestions and direct actions , and about where the human needs to remain in control. 2. Keeping one source of truth An early version allowed the System view to hold its own version of palette and typography. That worked until something changed somewhere else. The moment an agent updated a color, the selected direction and the generated design system could start telling two different stories. So I changed the model: the selected direction became canonical, and System became a synchronized projection of it. It sounds like a technical decision, but for me it was really a product decision. If a designer and an agent are genuinely working on the same project , they cannot be looking at two different versions of the truth. 3. Translating creative language into structure Creative feedback is rarely neat. It sounds more like: “This is too clean.” “I like this, but not for this project.” “It needs more personality.” Or the timeless classic: “Something feels a bit off.” Turning those kinds of thoughts into something both a designer and a browser agent can meaningfully work with turned out to be a surprisingly fun design and data modelling problem. What I learned I came into this project as a web designer first , and that shaped the way I approached MOOD from the beginning. One thing became very clear while building it: if you want a design system that actually feels specific to a project, a brand or an idea, the human part still matters a lot . AI is incredibly useful in the creative process, but on its own it can easily move toward something technically good and visually coherent, yet still very generic and basic. The harder decisions, the ones about taste, personality, context, what feels right and what does not , still need human judgement. Where I found AI genuinely powerful was in everything around those decisions. During Explore , it can connect references, spot patterns and suggest directions I might not have considered. Later, while shaping the design system, it can analyse choices, surface inconsistencies, suggest alternatives and help turn a direction into something much more complete, much faster than I could alone. That changed the way I started thinking about the relationship between human and AI. They are not simply two different ways of doing the same job. They are good at different parts of it. Human Agent Taste Speed Context Pattern finding Personality Analysis Creative judgement Alternative directions Final decisions A second point of view The designer still decides what the project should feel like. title: Music Synth Creator
pitch: Iteratively create music synths with AI. The agent constructs a synth in the app - you listen and give it feedback to iterate on. Since all state is in the browser, WebMCP is the perfect solution.
about_excerpt: Iteratively create music synths with AI. The agent constructs a synth in the app - you listen and give it feedback to iterate on. Since all state is in the browser, WebMCP is the perfect solution. Like Comment Story Updates Full-size web application open in Chrome Web application open in ChatGPT Inspiration I am a hobbyist music producer. Every time I produce a track, I spend hours trying to find the perfect synth for my idea, either by searching through online libraries or by trying to make my own. By the time I have found the right sound, the inspiration has faded and I have usually forgotten what I wanted to compose. I was also inspired by these two example applications: Field Beat Machine: https://developers.openai.com/showcase/ko-field-beat-machine Codex Modeling Studio: https://developers.openai.com/showcase/codex-modeling-studio What it does The app is a music synthesizer: you tweak the controls to configure the sound it makes, then press a key to produce a sound. The WebMCP layer allows the AI to interact with the controls and create synths according to your description. You can listen to the sound and give some feedback for the AI to modify the configured synth. Finally you can export the synth as an open source .vital file for use in music production software. How we built it I built a compact, visually informative synthesizer app which is easy to navigate. I compiled Vital's open source wavetable synth engine with WebAssembly to produce sounds from the patch configured in the UI. I built a canonical synth patch object as the state for the application's visual and audio components, as part of which I had to create mappings to .vital format parameters. I added WebMCP tools so that agents can inspect and interact with the application state directly, without needing to manually interact with the browser. Challenges we ran into I started by creating my own digital signal processing functionality for the synth, until I realised that I would spend too much time developing each feature. Eventually I ported Vital's open-source C++ engine and built an interface around that. I created a simple and restricted interface around Vital's complex sound engine. This may have been fine if I hadn't tried to make the app compatible with any .vital file import, which requires a lossy re-construction of their format into my canonical patch object. I also started with very low level WebMCP tools, which slowed down and confused the agent. To solve this, I created high level abstractions for the agent to use which improved the sounds it could create. I had to add safeguards for when the agent creates a synth with high feedback due to poorly configured effects. Accomplishments that we're proud of I can create synths in my app, that I can then import into my music production software! They sound good and the agent responds creatively to my input. I am also very happy with the visual polish of my app. What we learned Digital signal processing is hard! Don't try to create too many features! Focus on the core elements. I think there might be many exciting WebMCP-enabled apps in the future I have started to wonder if there is another possible protocol that could allow for agents to interact with native desktop applications. What's next for Music Synth Creator I want to use it properly - so far I have just been developing it. I want to reduce the startup delay when the first note is pressed I want to reduce the delay in transitioning between synth variations A and B I want to improve the .vital import feature to work with more existing presets I want to improve the WebMCP interactions, and add more elements for visual feedback (such as a parameter diff when the agent makes a change) I want to add a help section with common music producer jargon to help users better describe the sound they want.
