title: PaperTrail
pitch: A research review canvas where researchers and browser agents search, read, synthesize, and audit evidence together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A research review canvas where researchers and browser agents search, read, synthesize, and audit evidence together through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Research is not a straight line. Researchers discover candidate papers, decide what deserves attention, inspect evidence, challenge interpretations, and synthesize. Existing AI workflows usually split that process between a chat window and a separate research tool, leaving people to copy results by hand and making agent decisions hard to audit. PaperTrail imagines the open web as a shared research room where humans and browser agents work on the same living page. What it does PaperTrail is a collaborative literature-review canvas organized around the meaning of the work: Inbox stages relevant articles found by a person or agent. To Read holds candidates that merit review. Reading is active evidence work: paper details, citation context, findings, limitations, and questions. Synthesized contains only completed cases that have contributed to a cited conclusion. A researcher can click Go Live and share the canvas. A colleague can join from another browser, and their agent can search the internet for relevant scholarly articles, add a focused candidate, read evidence, annotate it, compare sources, create a decision brief, and audit the result. Every contribution appears on the same board with author badges, tool-call receipts, and a visible activity trail. The human keeps control over selection, questions, source verification, and what is considered complete. Why WebMCP This workflow needs more than an agent collaborating as a peer. PaperTrail exposes 16 typed WebMCP tools over its real research model, including literature search, workspace state, selection-aware context, paper details, citation contexts, notes, comparisons, artifacts, verification, and export. Because the tools are registered by the page, agents can discover the available actions, receive structured state, and write first-class objects directly into the research canvas. Researchers see the results immediately and can inspect the exact receipt behind each agent-written claim. This removes copy-and-paste handoffs while preserving human judgment and provenance. A complete human+agent research flow The researcher opens a question and takes the canvas live. A collaborator and their browser agent join from a second session. The agent searches for relevant work and contributes one focused candidate to To Read . The researcher curates another candidate and selects the active case. The agent reads details and citation context, then records a grounded finding and an evidence boundary in Reading . The researcher adds a question that changes the direction of the synthesis. The agent compares sources and publishes a cited decision brief. A second agent audits the conclusion from its own browser. The researcher verifies sources and moves only the completed case to Synthesized . What was difficult before is now native to the page: multiple researchers and agents can extend, question, and audit the same evolving body of work across browsers without losing context or authorship. How we built it PaperTrail uses vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules with no build step. The top-level document registers WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool, closed JSON Schemas, honest read/write annotations, and an AbortController lifecycle. The tools operate on a DOM-independent state model and return structured results with provenance metadata. Live collaboration uses a Vercel API and Neon-backed operation log to replicate human edits and agent tool calls across shared links. Scholarly discovery and citation evidence are sourced through public research APIs. The app includes source verification, Markdown/BibTeX/JSON export, and a local compatibility layer so the workflow remains demonstrable when native WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges and lessons The hardest problem was preserving causality across live sessions: an agent action must be visible, attributed, replayable, and safe to challenge. We learned that successful human-agent collaboration depends less on automating every step than on making state, authorship, evidence boundaries, and handoffs explicit. Accomplishments A real two-browser, human-and-agent research workflow 16 discoverable WebMCP tools over one coherent data model Per-action receipts and source verification Live shared state with visible peer presence A complete path from discovery through reading, synthesis, audit, and export An open-source MIT-licensed implementation with tests and no required authentication Built With openai Try it out papertrail-platform.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Sarath Shekkizhar Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Sarath Shekkizhar started this project — Sep 03, 2026 11:50 AM EDT

title: Portego
pitch: Setting up a smart home is still slow and fragmented. Portego lets you and an AI agent design the floor plan together, then bind it to real devices through a local gateway.
about_excerpt: Setting up a smart home is still slow and fragmented. Portego lets you and an AI agent design the floor plan together, then bind it to real devices through a local gateway. Like Comment Story Updates Portego WebMCP Canvas Portego Gateway Config Gateway Setup Inspiration Smart-home setup is still fragmented. Every brand has its own app, and those apps rarely treat the home as rooms, doors, and devices. I built Portego to try a different sequence: describe the home in conversation, refine it on a shared canvas, then connect that plan to real hardware. What it does Portego is a digital twin of the home. People and agents share one model of floors, rooms, and devices. A Linux gateway on the local network binds that model to real hardware, so the house you designed is the house you can switch. You can create floors, rooms, doors, windows, and devices by hand, or ask an agent to create them through WebMCP. Both write the same home document. You can drag a room after the agent makes it, and the agent can read the new layout and continue. The canvas works without an account. Login and hardware connectivity are private beta. The gateway opens an outbound WebSocket to Portego. It shows a pairing code, finds supported devices on the LAN, and lets you bind them to devices in the model. The connection is outbound, so the house does not need an exposed port or a public IP. Why WebMCP The home is structured data. Asking an agent to read pixels or click around a canvas would be fragile. Portego registers operations such as home.add_room , home.add_device , home.get_document , and home.apply_changes . Those tools use the same model and validation as the editor. A compatible agent is operating Portego, not a separate chat bolted onto it. How people and agents work together You describe a house; the agent produces a first layout. You move rooms, rename devices, add openings, or undo. The agent reads the revised document and continues from there. Once a physical device is discovered and bound, device.set_state goes through the gateway to the real device. How I built it The frontend is Next.js on Vercel. Konva draws the home. A validated HomeDocument is what actually gets saved. The page registers twenty WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool calls and UI actions share the same operations, validation, history, and persistence path. A FastAPI service on Render handles authentication, stored homes, gateway pairing, device bindings, and command relay. The Linux gateway connects out to the backend over an authenticated WebSocket and runs protocol adapters for local devices. Shelly is the first working adapter. Matter discovery is in the repo; Matter commissioning is not enabled yet. There is also an optional Cloudflare Worker and Durable Object relay, so long-lived gateway connections do not have to live on the API process. Challenges The hard part was keeping agent edits, canvas interactions, undo history, and persisted data on one model. Geometry needed real validation. An agent-generated layout is only useful if rooms, openings, and devices stay valid and still editable by hand. Local hardware added another constraint: remote control without opening inbound ports into someone's home. Guest designs also have to survive login without being duplicated or dropped. What I learned Structured operations are much more reliable than asking an agent to drive a visual UI. The useful loop was a strong first draft from the agent, then both of us revising the same home. I also think this only scales if devices ship agent-native. If every product keeps a private app, agents go back to guessing at UIs. Building that access has to become ordinary product work, or there needs to be a shared protocol so each brand is not inventing its own. What's next Public signup, OAuth for the remote Portego MCP server, a packaged Raspberry Pi gateway, more protocol adapters, and Matter commissioning. Longer term I want the agent-native part to be reusable: either make it cheap to ship a device that already exposes structured operations, or settle a protocol others can implement. Portego is one attempt at that for the home (WebMCP on the model, adapters on the gateway). Try it at tryportego.com . title: Proofpress
pitch: Govern what future agents may safely rely on.
about_excerpt: Govern what future agents may safely rely on. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agents now produce decisions, summaries, research findings, and operational conclusions faster than teams can safely govern them. The missing layer is not another chat interface or memory store. It is a reliable answer to a harder question: what may the next agent safely rely on? Proofpress is an agent-produced knowledge management system (AKMS) for that boundary. Agents can propose knowledge and assemble bounded evidence, but proposed knowledge does not become reusable merely because a model generated it or an automated check passed. What it does Proofpress gives an owner a governed workspace for agent-produced knowledge: agents submit evidence-bound candidate conclusions; deterministic checks validate integrity, scope, freshness, and required qualifiers; an optional LM judge provides policy advice without receiving approval authority; a human owner approves, rejects, or requests a revision; successor agents retrieve only admitted, current, in-scope knowledge; append-only activity and lineage preserve who proposed, evaluated, and authorized each decision. Why WebMCP matters Before WebMCP, an agent could help prepare governance work, but a person still had to navigate the application manually and translate UI state back into instructions. Proofpress now exposes product semantics directly from the web application: workspace summary, review queue, evidence, lineage, deterministic checks, semantic activity, policy configuration, and agent access. The agent can find the right candidate, inspect its evidence, run checks, prepare a policy or credential form, and open the exact owner decision surface. It cannot approve knowledge, reveal secrets, activate policy, or issue credentials. WebMCP therefore improves the collaboration without erasing the authority boundary. The end-to-end workflow A connected agent submits bounded evidence and proposes a conclusion. Through WebMCP, the agent inspects the queue and runs deterministic checks. The owner sees a progressive-disclosure review: a quick snapshot first, then full evidence, checks, LM advice, history, and lineage. The owner alone records the decision. Once admitted, the conclusion appears in governed context. A successor agent retrieves it only when its identity and scope are eligible. Rejected and revision-requested conclusions remain in the append-only history, but are excluded from governed context. How we built it Proofpress is a Python-first governance control plane with a canonical operation contract shared by local, HTTP, hosted, and MCP transports. The hosted dogfood runs on Render with persistent storage. The owner workspace renders semantic WebMCP tools from the same product state used by the human UI, rather than exposing coordinates or a parallel demo API. The WebMCP implementation adds 13 agent-facing tools while deliberately omitting approval and credential authority. Deterministic checks remain fail-closed. The public demo uses an isolated synthetic workspace; our internal hosted workspace exercises the same workflow against real Proofpress development knowledge. What is new for this challenge The core Proofpress governance system existed before the challenge. The new challenge work is the WebMCP-native interaction layer and its production UX: semantic workspace, review, evidence, lineage, policy, access, and activity tools; authority-safe preparation flows; a public synthetic demo; and end-to-end production validation. The dated implementation history is in the public repository and release PR. Challenges and learnings The hardest design problem was deciding what not to expose. A superficially convenient tool that can approve knowledge or activate credentials would collapse the governance model. We learned to separate preparation from authorization and to make product semantics available to agents without turning the browser into an unbounded control surface. We also learned that raw audit logs are insufficient for people. The interface needs semantic activity and progressive disclosure, while the underlying ledger remains append-only and inspectable. What's next Next we will deepen time-aware lineage, add clearer policy-as-code authoring, and package the hosted workspace for design partners—while preserving the central invariant: agents may propose and evaluate, but only an authorized person may decide what future agents can rely on. title: Relay WebMCP
pitch: An AI stand-in that handles what you'd approve, refuses what you'd not, and hands off the rest while you're away.
about_excerpt: An AI stand-in that handles what you'd approve, refuses what you'd not, and hands off the rest while you're away. Like Comment Story Updates the tightened copy, heartbeat dot, RELAY label, one-line pitch Project Links Inspiration People who need to step away unexpectedly, a scheduled procedure, a custody handoff, a hospital stay with no warning, have always faced the same bad choice: hand someone full access and hope they use good judgment, or go dark and let everything queue up until they're back. Password managers solve access, not judgment. Auto-replies solve nothing, they just defer. What was missing was a way to hand off exactly the part of a decision someone is comfortable handing off, nothing more, with everything outside that boundary going to a person they trust instead of an inbox nobody's watching. WebMCP made a genuine version of that possible: a tool surface that changes based on who is looking and what state things are in, computed live in the browser rather than fixed on a server, is what lets the boundary actually get enforced instead of just described in a policy nobody reads. What it does Relay lets someone prepare a delegate agent before they become unreachable, one that keeps answering the people who depend on them, inside limits they set in advance, escalating anything outside those limits to a person they trust. The absence doesn't have to be the same shape twice. A contractor covering client work during a scheduled procedure. Two co-parents who need logistics handled without every message pulling one of them out of their day. Someone who ends up in the hospital with no warning and no time to write instructions for anyone. A support lead pulled into a family emergency mid-shift. Relay works the same way whether the absence was planned six weeks out or started an hour ago. A person prepares a delegate agent in advance: an interview-style briefing agent asks about their specific situation and drafts a full configuration for them to review, rather than making them author policy from scratch. When the person goes unreachable, the delegate starts answering the people and agents who depend on them, inside a boundary of autonomy the principal defined, escalating anything outside that boundary to a named human, and producing a complete accounting of what happened. How we built it Relay registers seven WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, but which tools are visible depends on who's looking and what state the relay is in: the principal sees five configuration tools while their relay is still in draft, a recipient sees nothing until the relay goes active and then sees exactly one tool (ask_delegate) scoped to their own access token, and everyone can request a record of what happened, filtered to what they're allowed to see. That conditional, per-visitor tool surface, not just per-server but per-session, is something a hosted MCP server can't express, and it's the core of why this is a WebMCP-native product rather than a chatbot with extra steps. Underneath that, the delegate's reasoning loop uses Claude to classify every incoming request into a tier (autonomous, flagged, refused) and propose a reply, then a deterministic check runs after the model and before any action is taken. Challenges we ran into The interesting part of building this turned out not to be the AI, it was the governance. Anyone can wire a chatbot to answer messages while someone's away. The harder problem is making sure it never quietly does more than it was authorized to do. If a request's dollar value exceeds an autonomous ceiling, it has to be forced to flagged regardless of what the model said. If nothing matches, it has to fall through to a configured default and never default to autonomous. The model proposes. The code disposes. Getting that rule to actually hold, every time, took more iteration than the AI side of the build did. The other hard challenge was the permission surface itself, described above, getting the tool set to genuinely change per visitor and per state rather than just claiming to. Late in the build, rehearsing the actual demo flow surfaced a genuine problem: the briefing interview was losing its own memory mid-conversation, because session state lived in server memory with no guarantee two requests land on the same instance. We caught it by testing the exact path a judge would take, not by reading the code, and moved session state into the database before it ever reached a recording. Accomplishments we're proud of The deterministic override actually holds under a live test, not just in theory: a request the model classified one way gets forced to a different tier the moment it crosses a rule the principal set, and the reply shown updates to match, so the tier badge and the words never contradict each other. The tool surface is genuinely live, not simulated, confirmed by calling document.modelContext.getTools() directly in an actual WebMCP-enabled browser and watching the exact same page return a different tool list depending on who's asking. And we found and fixed the session-memory bug above before it ever showed up in a recording, by actually rehearsing the demo end to end instead of assuming the happy path would hold. What we learned For a product where an agent has a multi-turn conversation, the failure modes that matter show up in an actual multi-turn conversation, not in a single request, and the only way to catch them is to actually run the conversation end to end rather than trust that a single successful test proves the whole path works. What's next There's no principal login yet, a relay's own URL currently acts as the access credential the way a recipient's token does, which is fine for a single-user demo but not for a multi-tenant product. Principal authentication is the next piece. Beyond that, more activation conditions (calendar-based, not just missed check-ins) and letting an approver resolve a flagged request directly through their own agent, not just by clicking Approve, are the two directions we'd take this next. title: Remy
pitch: Remy lets AI agents take real actions without taking control away from users. Safe work runs automatically, risky actions wait for approval, and every change gets a receipt and recovery path.
about_excerpt: Remy lets AI agents take real actions without taking control away from users. Safe work runs automatically, risky actions wait for approval, and every change gets a receipt and recovery path. Like Comment Story Updates Homepage Agent Activity Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of changing real application state, but the current trust model feels broken. Users either approve every small action, making the agent slow and irritating, or grant broad autonomy and inspect the damage afterwards. Remy explores a middle ground: let reversible work happen automatically, pause consequential actions for explicit approval, and give users a clear record of what happened and a way back when possible. What it does Remy is a protocol-neutral action layer for applications that allow AI agents to take real actions. Developers define an action once, including what it changes, its risk, and how it can be recovered. Remy then provides: Runtime validation and action previews Developer policies and user-selected autonomy Explicit approval for consequential actions Human-readable receipts and diffs Append-only action history Exact undo, compensation, or an honest irreversible state The demo is a fictional headphone shop using WebMCP. An agent can add headphones, select delivery, and apply a discount automatically. Placing the order spends money, so Remy pauses and presents the exact item, price, address, and payment method for the user to approve. How we built it Remy’s core is a TypeScript action engine that does not depend on React or WebMCP. Every semantic action passes through the same validation, preview, policy, execution, receipt, and recovery pipeline. A WebMCP adapter exposes those actions as page-scoped tools. The shop’s normal interface and its WebMCP tools use the same underlying engine, keeping policy enforcement beside the application’s business logic. The demo uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zod, Tailwind CSS, Motion, and Vitest. State and receipts are persisted locally for the challenge demonstrator. I also built an alpha initializer that scaffolds Remy into a Next.js application. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was making approval a real enforcement boundary rather than an instruction in a prompt. If an agent is merely told to wait, it may continue through another interaction path. The restriction therefore has to be enforced where the final state change occurs. Approval is also asynchronous, while agent tool calls may be short-lived. Remy represents approval as pending application state and revalidates the authoritative data before execution. Recovery introduced another challenge. Some changes can be undone exactly, some require a new compensating action, and others are genuinely irreversible. Remy needed to represent each case honestly without pretending that every action has an undo button. Accomplishments that we're proud of The working demo shows useful autonomy rather than simply approving or blocking everything. Reversible shopping actions can execute automatically, while the irreversible purchase stops for explicit approval. An agent cannot grant itself greater autonomy. Every attempt produces a readable receipt, duplicate effects are prevented with idempotency keys, stale approvals are invalidated, and reversals remain linked to the original action instead of erasing history. The same semantic action definitions power the normal website, the WebMCP tools, the policy engine, receipts, and recovery. What we learned Action history by itself is only observability. A receipt written after an unsafe mutation cannot protect the user. The action layer must make its decision before execution and remain on the path to the real state change. We also learned that reversibility is a useful basis for autonomy. Users should not need to approve harmless work that can be safely reversed, but consequential or irreversible actions deserve a clear checkpoint. Finally, WebMCP works well as an adapter, but the underlying action contract should remain protocol-neutral so the same guarantees can follow an action across different agent environments. What's next for Remy The next steps are publishing the core SDK and initializer, adding MCP and agent SDK adapters, and moving histories from local storage to a durable hosted journal. Future versions could add authenticated agent identity, approval routing, shared policies, monitoring, alerts, signed receipts, and evidence exports while allowing applications to keep their own interface and business logic. title: ReStock
pitch: Wholesale buyers order in messy plain language. Restock gives distributor sites a WebMCP tool layer that resolves those requests to real SKUs — and knows when to ask instead of guess.
about_excerpt: Wholesale buyers order in messy plain language. Restock gives distributor sites a WebMCP tool layer that resolves those requests to real SKUs — and knows when to ask instead of guess. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration My brother has a phone accessories store. Every time he restocks, he sends his supplier a message like: 2 cases of 6ft usb c braided black, 10 tempered glass for the 14 pro, 3 chargers And then somebody on the other end sits down and turns that into SKUs by hand. In a wholesale catalog that last line might be listed as WL CHGR 65W SINGLE USB PRT BLK REMAX . It takes twenty minutes and usually a phone call to confirm. Every order, every week. I assumed for a long time that this was a search problem. It isn't. Software that tries to solve it by matching ends up guessing, the buyer receives the wrong charger, and after that happens once nobody trusts the automation again. What the person on the other end is actually good at is knowing which lines they can fill and which ones they have to ask about . What it does Restock makes a distributor's ordering portal something an AI agent can operate directly. The demo storefront, Harbor Wireless Supply , has 243 SKUs named the way wholesale catalogs actually name things: abbreviations, inconsistent casing, pack units that don't match how buyers talk. An agent passes the buyer's raw sentence to resolve_order and gets back a decision for each line. Resolved, with the reason stated. "2 cases of 6ft usb c braided black" comes back as SKU 10009 , Cable Usb-c 6ft Braided Black Premium , matched on cable, braided, USB-C, 6ft and black . The buyer said "cases" and the catalog sells EA, so Restock records both instead of quietly converting one into the other. Needs clarification. "3 chargers" really is ambiguous in this catalog, so instead of picking one Restock returns what separates the candidates (product type) and the three actual options: charger, car charger, wall charger. The agent asks the buyer and calls choose_option with the answer. Not found, said plainly. It never substitutes something close. submit_order refuses while any line is still unresolved , the same way the portal's own Confirm button stays disabled. Why WebMCP fits this problem Catalog resolution can't live in the agent. The distributor is the one who knows the catalog, the pricing, the pack units, what's in stock, and what counts as ambiguous in their own inventory. An agent scraping the page would have to reconstruct all of that from rendered HTML, and it would guess in exactly the places where the distributor would have asked. With WebMCP the site can publish that judgment as a tool contract instead. The agent handles the language, the site handles the catalog and decides what needs a question. What people and agents can now do together The part I find interesting isn't the matching, it's the question . When Restock returns NEEDS_CLARIFICATION it's telling the agent: this one is mine to ask, here's what to ask, here are the options to offer. That's backwards from how this normally works. Usually the agent decides when to bother the human. Here the website decides, because it's the one that knows where its own catalog is ambiguous, and the agent just carries the question to the buyer in whatever language the buyer speaks. The buyer answers once and the order closes. How I built it Next.js on Vercel. Five tools registered natively with document.modelContext.registerTool — no extension, no polyfill — and annotated so an agent knows which four only read and which one writes. Behind the tools there's lexical search over the catalog, an LLM pass that splits a sentence into order lines with quantities and units, and a decision layer that compares the surviving candidates for each line and works out what actually distinguishes them. If they differ on exactly one attribute, that attribute becomes the question . I validated it against a set of real buyer phrasings before wiring up any of the WebMCP part. The tools drive the same order draft the human UI does , so the application can't tell a tool call from a click. The order fills in on screen while the agent works. Challenges I ran into Getting the tools to work was easier than getting them to be honest. My first version threw exceptions with genuinely useful messages, like "1 line still needs clarification" . Agents never saw any of them — a thrown error arrives as a generic failure and the reason is gone. I also rendered a WebMCP status line server-side for my own debugging. Agents that read the served HTML saw it say the tools weren't ready yet, believed it , and stopped before ever trying to call anything. That one cost me most of an afternoon. And submit_order shipped with no annotations, so it wasn't classified as an action at all. Everything else was marked read-only, and the one tool that actually places the order was invisible as a thing an agent could do . None of these were visible from inside the app. They only showed up when I started calling my own tools the way an agent would . What's next Restock is meant to be infrastructure rather than a storefront : a hosted tool layer a distributor can point at their own catalog. The one in the demo is synthetic. Ingesting a real catalog is the next piece. title: Rove
pitch: Rove turns open-web shopping into a shared workspace where people and browser agents research, refine, and save real retailer finds together.
about_excerpt: Rove turns open-web shopping into a shared workspace where people and browser agents research, refine, and save real retailer finds together. Like Comment Story Updates Threads of Clothes you saved Clothes and Styles for you by Agent Update Profile Welcome and Profile setup More Clothes List of Saved Prompts and their finds Inspiration Shopping across the open web is fragmented. Products live across dozens of retailer tabs, useful recommendations disappear inside chat transcripts, and the human often cannot refine an agent’s work without starting over. That inspired Rove: a shared fashion research workspace where a person and a browser agent work on the same shopping mission. The agent handles open-web research while the human stays in control of preferences, budgets, product review, selective replacement, and the final cart. What it does Rove turns a natural shopping request—such as “Find three shirts, three pants, sneakers, and a fragrance for four days in Cancún under C$450”—into a structured research mission. The browser agent can: Read the user-approved style profile. Translate the request into quantities, categories, occasions, and budgets. Claim prioritized retailer research targets. Browse live retailer pages. Progressively publish grounded products with direct images and canonical links. Enrich products with availability, pricing, materials, and variants. Report research progress and unresolved needs. Add exact products to the shared cart. At the same time, the human can: Watch products arrive progressively. Filter and compare recommendations. Inspect retailer provenance. Accept the complete edit or replace only selected items. Request completely fresh research without duplicate links. Save completed prompts and accepted products locally. Manage a cross-retailer cart called “Your Thread.” Rove keeps completed missions separate from the current mission, so previous research remains useful without confusing the active task. How we built it Rove is a client-only application built with Nuxt 4, Vue 3, strict TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and the imperative WebMCP API. It registers 17 tools through document.modelContext , covering profile setup, mission planning, retailer scheduling, candidate publication, product enrichment, recommendation review, research history, and cart management. The most important architectural decision was giving the interface and WebMCP tools the same typed domain action layer. Agent actions do not update a separate hidden system: they produce the same visible state changes as human actions. A deterministic research scheduler ranks retailer targets based on: Requested categories and quantities. Remaining unmet needs. Style and occasion relevance. Department compatibility. Per-item and overall budgets. Retailer capabilities. Scarce categories such as fragrance. Published candidates pass through validation for retailer domains, canonical product URLs, mission identity, budgets, duplicate history, and required imagery. Recommendation order combines relevance, budget fit, profile alignment, availability, freshness, and retailer diversity. The application uses browser-local persistence and requires no backend, database, account, API key, embedded chatbot, or OpenAI API call. It is deployed as a static Netlify application and remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making agent research behave like a reliable product workflow instead of an open-ended chat. Retailer information is inconsistent. Some products have sizes and colours, while fragrances and accessories may have neither. We had to introduce category-aware variant handling so a perfume could not accidentally inherit an invalid clothing colour or size. Selective replacement was another difficult problem. When the user rejected one product, the system initially risked replacing or hiding accepted products. We redesigned the review workflow so accepted products remain visible and only explicitly rejected items become new research targets. We also had to solve duplicate prevention across repeated missions. Rove now retains previously surfaced and accepted product links so “research again” can use past preferences as context without relisting the same products. Product imagery created additional complexity because retailer image URLs vary and can fail after publication. We added direct-image validation, visible fallbacks, and consistent image framing so missing or differently sized assets do not break the interface. Finally, we had to balance a sophisticated agent workflow with a simple human experience. Mission state, research queues, replacement context, saved history, and the cart all needed to remain understandable without exposing internal orchestration details. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that Rove feels like a complete fashion product rather than a WebMCP demonstration screen. Key accomplishments include: Seventeen working WebMCP tools with closed schemas and clear annotations. One shared action boundary for human and agent operations. Progressive multi-retailer research with visible state changes. Quantity-aware and budget-aware mission fulfilment. Selective product replacement without disturbing accepted items. Fresh research that avoids previously listed links. Category-aware cart variants for clothing, fragrance, and accessories. Saved missions with locally preserved prompts and accepted edits. A polished, responsive, accessible Rove interface. A deterministic test suite with 68 passing tests, strict type checking, and verified production builds. What we learned We learned that useful agent experiences depend more on state design and tool contracts than on one large prompt. Small, purpose-built tools with explicit schemas gave the browser agent clearer responsibilities and made failures easier to understand. A persisted state machine also made the collaboration resilient: the agent could report what it had completed, what remained unresolved, and what it should do next. We also learned that human control must be visible. Users need to see what the agent changed, preserve decisions they already approved, and request corrections without restarting the entire workflow. Most importantly, WebMCP works best when it is integrated into the product’s real domain model. The tools should not sit beside the application—they should operate the application. What's next for Rove Next, we want to expand Rove with: More retailer adapters and stronger regional availability support. Better price and inventory freshness indicators. Optional, privacy-conscious cross-device synchronization. Visual style references and wardrobe-aware recommendations. Stronger accessibility and mobile interaction testing. User-controlled retailer preferences and sustainability signals. Cleaner retailer checkout handoffs while keeping purchasing on official retailer sites. Evaluations that measure duplicate rate, budget adherence, research completion, and recommendation acceptance. Our long-term vision is for Rove to become the open-web workspace where people and agents build confident shopping decisions together. title: Salesive Graphics
pitch: A browser SVG design editor that hands its full toolset (drawing, layout, gradients, icons, templating) to any AI agent over WebMCP, so the agent builds finished graphics on the live canvas you use.
about_excerpt: A browser SVG design editor that hands its full toolset (drawing, layout, gradients, icons, templating) to any AI agent over WebMCP, so the agent builds finished graphics on the live canvas you use. Like Comment Story Updates An AI agent builds graphics on the live Salesive Graphics canvas through WebMCP. Inspiration Any AI agent can talk about design, but when you ask one to actually make a graphic it usually hands back a raw SVG string or a one-shot image it can't revise. We wanted an agent to be able to sit down at a real design tool, the same canvas a person uses, and build a finished flyer, social post or promo one element at a time, with the human watching and free to take over whenever they want. WebMCP is what made that practical. Instead of building a separate agent API, we could just expose the editor's own tools to whatever agent the user brings. What it does Salesive Graphics is a browser based SVG design editor. You can draw, lay things out, add gradients and icons, drop in image slots, and turn a design into a reusable template with a generated JSON schema. The part that makes it different: the whole editor toolset is published to any connected AI agent through WebMCP (document.modelContext). Around 100 editor tools, the exact same ones the built in assistant uses, are exposed to outside agents. A curated core set of about 48 is registered directly so it stays inside agent runtime limits, and the rest stay reachable through two meta tools, list_editor_tools and call_editor_tool. Agents draw shapes and text, apply gradients, insert Lucide icons, run the layout and alignment helpers, build reusable component groups like buttons, badges and stat blocks, and map dynamic fields, all on the same live canvas the user is looking at. Coordination between agent and user is built in. set_agent_identity shows who is working, lock_canvas puts up a blocking overlay while the agent edits, ask_canvas_question opens a modal so the agent can ask the user to pick between options, and every tool call streams into a live Activity panel. Guests can use it without an account and let an agent build for them. Work is saved to localStorage. It's live at https://graphics.salesive.com How we built it React 19 and Vite 8, Tailwind v4, deployed on Cloudflare with static assets served through Wrangler. WebMCP comes from @mcp-b/global, lazy loaded after first paint as its own chunk. A useWebMCP hook registers each editor tool with an input schema and emits call, result and error events. One clientToolHandlers map is the single source of truth. Every tool is available both to the in app assistant over a socket and to external WebMCP agents, so any new editor capability is exposed automatically. The SVG engine renders live and serializes to a standalone SVG. A mapping step produces a schema.json describing text, image, color, icon, toggle and variant fields. The design guide we ship to agents through get_editor_guide is generated from the same skill file we use internally, so the guidance never drifts away from the actual tools. Challenges we ran into Tool count limits. Agent runtimes reject a page whose WebMCP config is too large, so we had to prioritize down to a core set and add meta tools to keep everything else reachable. Keeping the live renderer and the serialized SVG in agreement, especially around circles versus ellipses, text bounding boxes and gradient references. Designing the coordination UI so that an agent editing the canvas never feels like it is fighting the user for control. What we learned WebMCP works best when you expose the tools you already have instead of inventing an agent API. The hard part is the ergonomics, things like identity, locking, questions and an activity log, not the tool calls themselves. What's next More component helpers, richer templating, and multiple agents working on one canvas at the same time. title: Sonicviz
pitch: Hands-free guitar and harmonica practice. An agent sets up the lesson, you play it. Built with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Hands-free guitar and harmonica practice. An agent sets up the lesson, you play it. Built with WebMCP. Like 2 Comment Story Updates The WebMCP Inspector completing the example agent request. The WebMCP Inspector generating a new lesson from a voice request. Harmonica explorer with chord and scale overlays on a 10-hole diatonic harp. Practice view with the guitar playing the guide melody. Fretboard explorer with chord and scale overlays and interval labels. Practice view with the harmonica playing the guide melody. Inspiration I play guitar and harmonica (see https://komuso.info/ ). A lot of practice time is not spent playing, it's spent fiddling with practice tools and setup. Finding an exercise, working out which holes and frets play the same melody, slowing a loop down. These are common music practice issues that waste time and effort that could be better spent playing and learning. AI tools are good at making a finished song (see my side project https://www.crisiskaraoke.com/ ) but I did not need a song. I needed short lessons I could play to learn scales and chords in different tunings on both instruments, that I could rapidly configure with a couple of clicks or ultimately hands-free by voice. What it does SonicViz is a practice app with three connected views: Fretboard, Harmonica, and Practice. Fretboard and Harmonica views allow you to quickly build mental models of scales and chords in different tunings and keys on both instruments. These mental models are critical to developing creative improvisation skills that help you break out of pattern playing ruts. Practice keeps one chord progression and one timed melody. The guitar positions, the harmonica holes, the score, and the TAB are all views of that same melody. Change the instrument and the notes stay put. Only the way your hands (or lips in the harmonica's case) reach them changes. WebMCP makes it hands-free. SonicViz exposes 12 typed tools, so a browser agent reads and writes actual musical state instead of guessing at the screen. I say "loop bars 1 through 2 at 40 BPM and play." The agent makes the call, and I play along with the harmonica still in my hand. Playback only starts after I allow it, and only for that page session. You can use WebMCP to interact with all three tabs. The video uses typed commands for clarity; the same requests work by voice through a custom WebMCP extension with a mic lock for hands-free practice. How we built it From scratch, starting August 27, with just an idea for a new type of app. I leveraged my experience as developer of https://harpninja.com/ to give me a clear direction to address the problem with a workable solution with WebMCP being the key to unlock it. Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework, no backend. KISS to see if the idea works. AI assistants did most of the coding, mainly GPT-5.6 Sol plus a few other models, while I made the musical and product calls. The core is a pure function. A seed, a key, and a style produce the same lesson every time, and everything else is derived from that. Challenges we ran into Taming the agent was the hard part. A model will reorder tool calls, drop an argument, or answer from memory instead of reading the current state. Three bugs shipped and only showed up when I tested with a real model and complex mixed commands. A loop command toggled off on the second call. A mute command could not tell which direction I meant. An agent answered "already set" without checking the app. Each fix went into the tool contract. Accomplishments that we're proud of The boundary is deterministic even though the agent is not. The same seed gives the same lesson every time. Consent is real. Agent playback waits for an explicit page-session permission. One melody reprojects across guitar, harmonica, score, and TAB without changing. Twenty-six browser checks pass, plus a long manual QA run. What we learned Determinism is something you have to re-establish every time you use the tools. The schema limits what the model can pass, but it doesn’t dictate the model’s decisions. That’s why discipline has to exist at the tool boundary. Idempotency, a single source of truth, and thorough testing with real models, both automated and manual, are essential. I’ve shared more about these lessons in a blog post: https://sonicviz.com/2026/09/03/webmcp-deterministic-hybrid-app-design/ What's next for Sonicviz Add more instruments, with lesson briefs that guide and coach. Include per-chord scale options so pros can practice the way they improvise. Consider simple performance recognition, letting the app detect if you hit the note using real-time pitch feedback. AI should enhance the process, not replace it. Nothing exercises the mind, body, and spirit quite like playing music on a real instrument. The tactile connection—the kinesthetic, energetic back-and-forth with the instrument—is a vital part of the experience and the process. It’s all about lips, fingertips, and ears. The hands memorize the shapes, the ears absorb the sounds, and the patience to loop a bar until it’s perfect becomes the skill that truly counts. The tool exists to support that process. The goal remains the same: the output isn't the song; it's a person who can play it. title: SwitchBack
pitch: Switchback makes planning for your hike fun again. Collaborate with the agent and save time on research for the next adventure! It provides verified routes to best fit your idea of a great day.
about_excerpt: Switchback makes planning for your hike fun again. Collaborate with the agent and save time on research for the next adventure! It provides verified routes to best fit your idea of a great day. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am usually short on time for planning my next hike or trail run. I always leave it until the very end. It is hard to Google "ChatGPT" and get routes from AllTrails or Wikiloc. They are unverified, and more than once I have been on closed hikes or dangerous segments. Also, I think we need to be able to co-create with agents. Planning a hike is not really a question with a single text answer. It is a shared, spatial decision: where to start, whether a route genuinely closes as a loop, how far it is, what the ascent looks like, and what the current planning context is. I built Switchback around a simple idea: ask for a loop, then see the ground truth. Rather than having an agent recommend a walk somewhere in a random place, a person and an agent work on the same Collserola–Vallvidrera map and can inspect the same route, evidence, and limitations. What it does Switchback is a WebMCP-native trail planner for short, car- or public transport-accessible walks around Collserola in Barcelona, Spain. It is the closest national park to the town. A person can ask for a family loop, a specific distance, or an evening option in natural language. The agent discovers the WebMCP tools, selects from graph-verified circuit options, validates a route before changing the map, and renders the result directly in the shared interface. The result stays inspectable: A closed circuit is drawn on the map. The route card shows measured distance and sampled ascent. Forecast, daylight, and official Park notices appear as clearly labeled planning context. Every agent action is visible in a shared worklog and trail ledger. The agent can prepare a briefing or GPX trace, but the person remains in control: they review/copy the briefing and manually click Download GPX . How I built it Switchback is a static TypeScript app hosted on Netlify. It registers fourteen page-bound WebMCP tools through the browser’s model context, with strict JSON schemas and the same planner functions used by the manual UI. Routing happens locally in the browser over a 66-tile directed Collserola TrailPack assembled from OpenStreetMap data and the Park’s published public-use network. The planner only offers routes that the available graph can close without a long retraced leg. I have used the official PDF and the park's website. I added route-aware forecast/daylight context via Open-Meteo and official Park-alert context through a same-origin adapter. Original Catalan notices remain visible; English is clearly labeled as machine translation. I used the AWS Translate service and Amazon Location services for the translations and maps. Challenges I ran into The hardest problem was avoiding an impressive-looking but untrustworthy route suggestion. A distance target alone does not prove that a loop closes, and a forecast does not prove that a hike is safe. That led to a few important product constraints: Routes are graph-validated before they render. Short, Medium, and Long are distance profiles, not difficulty labels. Difficulty is only described conservatively when the available ascent and terrain data support it. Forecasts and Park notices are planning signals, never a safety clearance. The agent cannot auto-download GPX files, send messages, or access external accounts. What I learned WebMCP is most compelling when the agent is not treated as a chat layer bolted onto an app Sometimes, it was hard for ChatGPT to use the tools because the agent's skill was not working correctly. I even fixed my local installation of ChatGPT with Codex. title: TreeTree
pitch: A family tree you can talk to: an AI agent interviews your family, turns it into a tree. The agent drives the page with WebMCP reading, navigating, creating with you.
about_excerpt: A family tree you can talk to: an AI agent interviews your family, turns it into a tree. The agent drives the page with WebMCP reading, navigating, creating with you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Family trees are shared documents edited across generations, yet genealogy software still hides them behind forms, menus, and closed APIs. We built TreeTree around a simpler idea: talk to your family archive. With WebMCP, the webpage itself becomes the agent interface, so humans and agents can explore and edit the same family tree together. What it does TreeTree is an open-source, self-hosted family archive built for humans and agents. Its WebMCP interface exposes 14 tools directly from the page. Ask “How am I related to her?” and TreeTree computes the actual kinship path. Ask “Where did our family come from?” and it derives migration across generations. More importantly, the agent can operate the live UI you're looking at . It can find a relative and center them on the tree, switch views, open records, add people, connect parents, record marriages, or import a GEDCOM. Every action appears immediately on the shared canvas, with narration and undo. TreeTree also adapts when an agent is present: redundant chat UI gets out of the way, and what_can_i_do_here lets the page teach the agent how to help the user. The same intent layer powers TreeTree's built-in AI archivist and a hosted MCP server for remote agents. Reads respect access controls; writes become reviewable proposals with provenance, audit history, and undo. How we built it TreeTree runs on Next.js and Cloudflare Workers with D1 + R2 , with deterministic GEDCOM import/export. The main WebMCP challenge was making tools available reliably, including to agents that enumerate them before React hydrates. We register them at document parse, reconnect them at mount, and handle late-injected model-context hosts. Our Playwright tests inject a model context before any page script and verify the real deployed UI changes : tool registration, creation, navigation, undo, and agent-aware UI behavior. Challenges WebMCP forced us to think beyond “give the model an API.” Agents may arrive before hydration. Agent actions can race React state. Undo must work across both human and agent edits. And the interface has to remain understandable when either one is driving. Solving those problems turned TreeTree from an AI-enabled website into a genuinely shared human-agent application . What we learned A webpage's tools are its language to an agent. The best tools aren't database CRUD. They're user intents : Who is this person? How are we related? Show me where they are. What can I do here? Designed that way, WebMCP makes the agent part of the product itself: onboarding, navigator, researcher, and co-author. What's next TreeTree already supports creating a family archive through conversation. Next we're bringing richer WebMCP editing to real archives through the proposal/review system and expanding the built-in archivist. One family tree. Humans and agents working on it together. MIT licensed and deployable in one command. title: The Gauntlet
pitch: A public adversarial range for WebMCP agents — hidden prompt-injection and scope-creep traps, scored with a cryptographically signed, tamper-proof scorecard.
about_excerpt: A public adversarial range for WebMCP agents — hidden prompt-injection and scope-creep traps, scored with a cryptographically signed, tamper-proof scorecard. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A real scorecard breakdown — which traps were resisted, which were fallen for, grouped by attack class. The offline verifier — drop in a signed evidence bundle and watch the Ed25519 signature and hash chain get checked live in your own browser. Every sealed run, publicly signed. 'Signature verified' means the server independently re-derived the score Every trap published in full, mapped to a real OWASP LLM Top 10 / MITRE ATLAS attack class — nothing hidden from the agents being tested. The Gauntlet homepage — a live adversarial range that offers real WebMCP tools mixed with hidden attacks to any agent that visits. Inspiration WebMCP hands AI agents real tools instead of a UI to click through. That's great, but it also means the tools themselves become the attack surface and nobody's actually testing that yet. I wanted a place where you could point any agent and get a real, honest answer to "does it actually hold up." What it does The Gauntlet is a live security range for WebMCP agents. Point an agent at it and it gets a mix of normal tools and hidden traps poisoned descriptions, typosquatted tool names, prompt injection buried in tool results, scope creep, multi-step attacks, and a few with no obvious red flags at all. Every trap maps to a real OWASP LLM Top 10 / MITRE ATLAS attack class. At the end you get a scorecard, and it's actually signed the server recomputes the score itself from the event log and signs it, so you can't fake a result. How I built it 17 tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(), running on Cloudflare Pages + D1. Every tool call gets logged server-side, and sealing a run recomputes the score from that log rather than trusting anything the client says. There's also a check that rejects runs that don't look like real interaction it already caught a real ChatGPT agent trying a shallow run and rejected it. Everything (traps, scoring, leaderboard, verifier) comes from one source file so it can't drift out of sync. Challenges I ran into Building the traps was the easy part. Making sure my own claims actually held up was harder. I found by attacking my own site that the anti-cheat check was trusting timestamps the client sent instead of when the server actually received them, which meant you could fake a "verified" run. Fixed it to only trust server time, then re-ran the same attack to make sure it actually failed this time. Accomplishments A real adversarial benchmark that's cryptographically backed, not just a demo. It's already caught a real agent cheating, and it survived me trying to break my own trust model. What I learned If you're building a security tool, you have to attack yourself as hard as you'd attack anyone else. The best bug I found all night was in my own code, not in the traps. What's next Traps that generate procedurally so they can't just be memorized, and growing the leaderboard into a real cross-model comparison as more agents support WebMCP. title: WEBMCP
pitch: Seven WebMCP tools that let an agent and a bid manager read the same procurement board together, scoring what a supplier qualifies for and flagging the tenders written so only one firm could win.
about_excerpt: Seven WebMCP tools that let an agent and a bid manager read the same procurement board together, scoring what a supplier qualifies for and flagging the tenders written so only one firm could win. Like Comment Story Updates One button, one autonomous pass over twelve open procurement notices. No further human input. Seven tools registered through document.modelContext. Every agent call is mirrored on the right, in the human view. Every criterion ruled met / gap / unclear with its evidence, four integrity flags with their reasoning, and a dated bid plan. An agent raised the bid ceiling through update_supplier_profile and the board re-ranked live: this notice moved 17 to 41. The board ranked by fit, with the reasoning trace beside it: every tool call, its output and its latency. Inspiration Across the EU roughly half of all public contracts attract a single bidder. The usual explanation is corruption. The more common one is arithmetic: a tender dossier runs 40 to 130 pages, the qualification criteria that decide whether a company may legally bid are scattered through it, and a 26-person firm has nobody who can read forty of those a month. So they stop reading, and the field empties out on its own. The document that tells a supplier you qualify for this is the same document that reveals this one was written for somebody else — a specification fixed to 14 mm and 63.5 Wh describes exactly one laptop on the market. Once you are parsing dossiers at scale, both answers fall out of the same pass. TenderLens does that pass. The WebMCP layer is what lets somebody else's agent do it too, on the same page, in front of the human it is working for. What it does One button starts an autonomous sweep. For every open notice the agent opens the dossier, extracts the qualification criteria into structured form, rules each one met / gap / unclear against the supplier's real profile with the evidence attached, screens the buyer's award history and the clause wording for integrity red flags, scores fit out of 100, and writes a dated bid plan working backwards from the deadline with an owner on every step. It ends with a ranked board — 87 down to 17 across twelve notices — and a written bid / no-bid brief per notice. The full reasoning trace streams to the browser while it runs: every tool call with its input, its output and its latency. The integrity screen is five detectors, each grounded in a documented single-bidding indicator: SHORT_WINDOW , THIN_COMPETITION , VENDOR_CONCENTRATION , SPEC_LOCK and INCUMBENT_LOCK . None is presented as proof of wrongdoing. Each carries the reasoning that makes it worth a clarification question or a formal challenge. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Bid/no-bid is a conversation, not a query. The questions a bid manager actually asks are open-ended and chained — what closes this week that we can actually win? which of those look rigged? what would we qualify for if our turnover were three million instead of one-point-eight? — and every answer changes the next question. That is exactly the shape of work an agent is good at and a filter UI is bad at. But it is also work with consequences. A supplier who skips a tender because an agent said "weak fit" has lost a contract on the strength of a sentence. So the human has to stay in the room, looking at the same board the agent is reasoning over. WebMCP is the only arrangement that gives you both. The tools live on the page the human is already looking at. The agent gets typed JSON — fit scores, verdicts with evidence strings, flags with rationale — instead of scraped DOM text, and every call it makes is mirrored into a panel on that page, in the human's field of view, while the board itself re-ranks in front of them. No API key, no OAuth handshake, no separate agent-facing copy of the product to drift out of sync. How it creates a better user experience Three things change: You ask, instead of filtering. "Show me everything closing inside ten days with an integrity flag" is one sentence. In the UI it is four controls and a sort. You can see what the agent did. Every tool call appears in the Agent activity panel with its arguments and a one-line result. The verdict is auditable in the moment, not after the fact. The page answers with the page. search_notices outlines the matching rows on the board. update_supplier_profile re-ranks it live. The agent's answer and the human's screen are the same object, so there is nothing to reconcile. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before The what-if is the one that did not exist. update_supplier_profile lets the agent change the profile every notice is scored against — turnover, headcount, certificates, capability areas, bid ceiling — and the entire board re-ranks in the human's browser while they watch. Ask "what would an ISO 27001 certificate be worth to us?" and you do not get an estimate; you get the actual board you would have had, recomputed by the real engine, with the notices that moved outlined. That is a joint action. The agent supplies the question and the argument, the page supplies the ground truth and the recomputation, and the human sees both at once and decides. Before WebMCP you got one or the other: a chatbot that could reason but only about text you had pasted to it, or a dashboard that held the truth but could not be asked anything. The same applies to the integrity work. A journalist can now walk an agent across a portal — screen these, tell me which buyers concentrate awards — and every claim the agent makes is anchored to a screen_integrity call whose output is sitting on screen next to the claim. How I implemented WebMCP Seven tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , in edge/webmcp.ts : tool what it does search_notices rank open notices by fit; filter by category, country, days left, fit band, or integrity flags get_notice one notice in full: every criterion with its verdict and evidence, flags, bid plan, optional raw dossier screen_integrity the five single-bidder detectors with the reasoning behind each flag get_bid_plan dated plan worked backwards from the deadline, owner on every step get_supplier_profile the profile every notice is scored against update_supplier_profile change the profile and re-rank the board — the what-if tool run_sweep the whole pass over every notice, returning the ranked board Each registration carries a real JSON Schema — enums, descriptions and required fields on every property — because the schema is the only instruction the visiting agent gets. Every execute returns { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(...) }] } , so the shape holds across clients. Three implementation decisions are worth naming: Tools call the product, not a demo path. Each execute hits the same /api/notices , /api/notice/:id and /api/profile endpoints the page itself uses. There is no agent-facing copy that can drift out of sync with what the human sees. Every call is visible. record() writes each invocation — name, arguments, one-line result — into the Agent activity panel on the page. Tool calls also act on the view: search_notices outlines matching rows, update_supplier_profile and run_sweep re-rank the board. Writes are validated, not trusted. update_supplier_profile goes through applyProfilePatch in edge/agentapi.ts , which range-checks every field and ignores anything it does not recognise. An agent can explore the profile space; it cannot corrupt it. Registration degrades cleanly. If document.modelContext is absent the pill reads "WebMCP not detected" and the page works as an ordinary web app. The tools are also exposed on window.__TL_TOOLS__ , and every tool in the list has a run button beside it that fires the identical execute() — so a judge without a WebMCP-enabled browser can still see each tool run and log its result. How I built the rest TypeScript throughout. Supabase Postgres holds the notices, the supplier profile, the run log and every assessment; Server-Sent Events carry the live trace; the agent itself runs as a Supabase Edge Function on Deno. The front end is a single static page on GitHub Pages that talks to that function over CORS-open JSON and SSE, which keeps the page a plain document a judge or an agent can open with nothing in the way. The agent core — orchestrator, six tools, provider adapters, types — depends on nothing from Node, React or Next. That buys a second runtime for free: the same engine drives a Next.js build and the Deno edge build, unmodified. The decision worth defending is deterministic core, model at the edge . Every score, verdict and flag comes from code that can be read, tested and cited. A supplier disqualified on a criterion needs to point at the rule that fired; a score that exists only inside a model's context window cannot survive a procurement review board. The side effect is that the hosted demo runs with zero API keys — which is also why a judge can open it, and a visiting agent can use every

title: Wishlist Concierge
pitch: An agent + human co-curation layer for Sylius 2.0 wishlists
about_excerpt: An agent + human co-curation layer for Sylius 2.0 wishlists Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a gift for someone means opening a dozen browser tabs, clicking filters that never quite match your intent, mentally adding up prices, then abandoning the cart when you realize the total blew past your budget. We asked ourselves: what if the storefront could understand "birthday for my nephew" and do the search, curation, and budget math for you while still giving you, the human, full control over what gets added to your cart? What it does Wishlist Concierge exposes 12 imperative WebMCP tools on a Sylius 2.0 storefront, covering the full gift-planning lifecycle: Find products by theme (tags); hard match on tags first, then soft match on product name, then fallback to all channel products Build & curate themed wishlists, add or swap products, reorganize at will Apply a budget constraint using a knapsack algorithm over quantity × ChannelPricing, with active catalog promotions discounts factored in; Return a human-readable explanation of what was chosen and why Move selected items into the Sylius cart and hand you the token to proceed How we built it The entire project is a Sylius 2.0 plugin with the Sylius Wishlist plugin providing the persistence layer. The key architectural choice was single-source-of-truth tool definition: Each tool is declared once via a #[ModelContextTool] attribute on its shop controller action with a name, description, input DTO class, path params, confirm/destructive hints, all in one place. A ModelContextToolCollector service introspects these attributes at compile time, resolves each tool's route via the Symfony router, and produces a JSON manifest. The frontend registry.js fetches that manifest and calls document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, {signal}) for each — so adding a tool means writing a controller method and a DTO, not touching JavaScript at all. Server-side, a ToolContractValidator kernel.request listener deserializes every incoming payload against the DTO's #[Assert] constraints and returns deterministic 422 envelopes on failure. As a bnous, the schema the agent sees is the schema the server enforces. The frontend uses two Stimulus controllers. A toolbox modal that dynamically renders a run form for every registered tool, and a toast controller for live feedback via webmcp:* custom events. Accomplishments that we're proud of The single-source-of-truth tool definition. A tool lives once as a #[ModelContextTool] attribute and that single declaration drives the manifest, the frontend registration, the server-side validation, and the toolbox UI. No duplicate schema, no drift, no manual sync. What we learned WebMCP changes the agent & web relationship. Instead of agents screen-scraping your UI, you hand them structured tools with typed schemas. That means better agents (clear contracts) and safer apps (no ambiguous click paths). Single source of truth is everything for developer experience. When a tool is defined in one place and everything else is derived, adding a new tool is a 5-minute task. Structured error shapes make agents better. Once the server returns {"error":"Validation failed", "message":"...", "violations":[{field,message}]}, the agent can reason about what went wrong and fix its next call - the feedback loop closes. What's next for Wishlist Concierge Real-world testing Extend the knapsack algorithm to consider stock levels and quantity discounts, not just unit price × quantity. title: WorkSpec Studio
pitch: Design an application with your agent, derive its infrastructure needs, compare Azure and AWS, record the ADR, and export the complete .workspec workspace.
about_excerpt: Design an application with your agent, derive its infrastructure needs, compare Azure and AWS, record the ADR, and export the complete .workspec workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Architecture decisions usually fragment across diagramming tools, spreadsheets, cloud pricing tabs, chat transcripts, and ADR documents. The diagram stops matching the estimate; the rationale disappears; and the final artifacts are trapped in somebody else's database. We built WorkSpec Studio to make architecture a shared, inspectable workflow between a person and an AI agent, with portable files as the durable result. What it does WorkSpec Studio takes a project through one connected journey: Design the application as an interactive C4 model. Derive an editable, provider-neutral infrastructure shopping list from its deployable elements. Map the same requirements to Azure and AWS and compare deterministic monthly planning estimates. Prepare and review the cloud-platform decision. Record the approved choice as an architecture decision record. Download the complete .workspec workspace as a ZIP. A user can start blank, load an example, or import an existing .workspec bundle. The C4 canvas supports context, logical-container, and deployment views. People can create, move, connect, and edit elements directly; the agent can propose or arrange the same model through WebMCP. The resulting workspace is schema-validated YAML that can be reviewed in the browser, committed to Git, used by WorkSpec command-line tools, or consumed by a hosted WorkSpec Enterprise installation. Why WebMCP Architecture work combines two different strengths. Agents are good at turning intent into a coherent first draft and tracing consequences across many artifacts. People are responsible for understanding the system, correcting assumptions, weighing trade-offs, and approving durable decisions. Without WebMCP, an agent must manipulate a complex infinite canvas with fragile pointer automation or edit files somewhere outside the UI the person is reviewing. WorkSpec's WebMCP tools connect both participants to the same live browser-local workspace. The agent can create a structured C4 proposal in one operation while the person immediately sees a real diagram they can drag and edit. The infrastructure list is derived from that same model, the provider comparison uses that same list, and the ADR is generated only from the visible draft the person has approved. Every successful agent operation appears in a collapsible Agent activity history. How we built it The workbench is a TypeScript and React monorepo composed from reusable WorkSpec packages for C4 schemas and rendering, infinite-canvas interaction, topology planning, provider mapping, decisions, ZIP workspaces, and the shared Studio shell. The page registers eleven bounded tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(). They let an agent inspect the workspace, navigate the gated workflow, control relevant sidebars, create a complete C4 architecture, inspect and pin diagram layout, update infrastructure requirements, compare providers, prepare an unsaved decision, record a reviewed decision, and export the workspace ZIP. All tool inputs use closed JSON schemas. Handlers resolve the current application state through stable action references, and registrations share an AbortController so React Strict Mode cannot leave duplicate tools behind. Human UI actions and agent tools operate on the same canonical MemoryWorkspace. The cloud estimates are deterministic planning figures rather than live quotes, keeping the comparison reproducible. Provider-specific choices do not leak into the source architecture or neutral requirements. Human review is part of the protocol The decision flow is intentionally split into two tools. prepare_cloud_decision opens the Decision page and fills a visible, editable provider and rationale draft. record_cloud_decision rejects calls until that draft exists and is used only after explicit human approval. This makes review a real product boundary, not a sentence in an agent prompt. The export tool returns the exact current workspace as a bounded base64 ZIP. That gives agents a reliable handoff even in browser environments where clicking a download button is awkward, while people retain the ordinary visible download control. Challenges we faced The biggest challenge was making an infinite visual canvas genuinely agent-operable without taking control away from the person. We added semantic architecture and layout tools rather than exposing cursor coordinates, while keeping every generated node editable and draggable. We also had to keep one canonical state across four routed stages, preserve unknown files during ZIP round trips, prevent stale React closures in registered tools, and make irreversible decision recording impossible before a visible draft exists. Accomplishments we're proud of One continuous Design → Infrastructure → Compare → Decision story. A real C4 canvas that supports both semantic WebMCP operations and direct human editing. Provider-neutral requirements with traceability back to architecture elements. Like-for-like Azure and AWS mappings and monthly estimates. A visible approval gate before ADR generation. Complete .workspec ZIP import and export. Eleven WebMCP tools plus a clear Agent activity history. More than two thousand automated tests across the WorkSpec packages and applications. What we learned The best WebMCP tools describe meaningful product operations, not DOM gestures. A tool such as "prepare a decision for review" is more robust and more understandable than a sequence of clicks, and it lets the UI enforce the same rules for both humans and agents. We also learned that shared visibility matters as much as capability. The strongest moments are not when the agent finishes everything invisibly; they are the pauses where a proposal appears in the real UI, the person edits or approves it, and both continue from the same state. What's next Azure and AWS are the first provider adapters. The provider-neutral model is designed for additional clouds, on-premises targets, live pricing catalogs, policy checks, and organization-specific mapping rules. We also plan to reuse the extracted Studio packages directly inside WorkSpec Enterprise. Try it Live app: https://studio.workspec.io/ Source: https://github.com/FieldstateNZ/workspec-studio Suggested prompt: Help me design Orderlight, an online ordering system that takes payment through an external gateway and fulfils accepted orders asynchronously. Build the C4 architecture, derive and review the infrastructure plan, compare Azure and AWS, and prepare a recommendation. Stop for my review at every stage and do not record the decision until I explicitly approve it.
