title: 0x1 Expedition Vault
pitch: A WebMCP learning roguelike where humans and browser agents share one branching expedition state.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP learning roguelike where humans and browser agents share one branching expedition state. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most learning apps expose a human UI and leave agents to scrape the DOM. We wanted the opposite: a learning world where the human and browser agent share one explicit game state and can genuinely take turns. What it does 0x1 Expedition Vault turns a topic, YouTube lecture, public article/PDF, pasted notes, or uploaded text into a branching learning roguelike. Learners study sources, answer quizzes, build causal chains, defend models in adversarial dialogue, choose risk/recovery branches, accumulate strikes, fail runs, recover, and defeat a final systems boss. The branching map is not cosmetic: unresolved splits expose multiple selectable paths. A route is marked taken only after the learner or agent commits to it; same-row alternatives become skipped for that run, matching the source expedition semantics. Why WebMCP The page registers four tools directly on document.modelContext : ingest_learning_material explore_module submit_solution inspect_progress The key point is that these tools do not maintain an agent-only copy of the course. Human clicks and agent tool calls mutate the same expedition graph, active room, checkpoint, belief trajectory, strikes, branch choices, mastery, and failure state. An agent can forge a course, inspect progress, choose a branch, submit a solution, fail the same run, or advance the same map the learner sees. Better together A human can watch a source video and clear a checkpoint; the agent can then inspect the resulting state and continue from the newly available branch. Or the agent can ingest a new topic and generate an expedition that appears immediately in the learner UI. WebMCP removes the brittle layer of DOM guessing and makes the collaboration explicit, structured, and inspectable. Cognition, not keyword recall Generated expeditions separate source study from hidden cognition checks. Later rooms test causal transfer, source-vs-inference separation, falsification, adversarial prediction, and integrative defense. Hidden checks conceal their rubric and discount terms already present in the prompt. Human and WebMCP text answers use the same semantic evaluator; verbose nonsense cannot clear a checkpoint. How we built it The app uses SvelteKit/Svelte 5, Vite, native document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , a deterministic source-grounded curriculum generator, serverless-native PDF extraction, opportunistic YouTube transcript extraction with source-honest metadata fallback, and persistent browser-local expedition state. The map runtime ports the original expedition engine's seeded node/edge geometry and explicit path-choice semantics. Reliability The deployed build was tested end-to-end on Vercel: source ingestion, branching path selection in both directions, three-strike run failure, restart, staged Back-EMF causal chain, Lenz adversarial dialogue, five-variable boss system model, WebMCP failure parity, and visible progression all pass. title: ADAPT
pitch: A behavioral trust layer that checks what WebMCP tools actually do.
about_excerpt: A behavioral trust layer that checks what WebMCP tools actually do. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration ADAPT actually started before this hackathon as a completely different project: an adaptive browser privacy and content-blocking system. When we started looking seriously at WebMCP, though, one thing kept bothering us. WebMCP gives websites a much cleaner way to expose tools directly to AI agents. Instead of an agent guessing where to click or trying to understand a page visually, the site can simply say: here is a tool, here is what it does, here are the arguments it accepts. That is a huge improvement. But it also means the agent is trusting a description written by the same page that controls the code behind the tool. So we asked a pretty simple question: What happens if a WebMCP tool lies? We made one. It described itself like a harmless cart-viewing action. When it was executed, it attempted payment-like network activity, changed local payment state, and navigated to an order-success page. That experiment became the new direction for ADAPT. What made us take the idea even more seriously was seeing that the WebMCP specification itself discusses this problem as misrepresentation of intent . At that point, it stopped feeling like an artificial demo attack and started feeling like a real trust problem that the agent-native web is going to have to solve. What it does ADAPT is a behavioral trust layer for WebMCP. Instead of trusting only what a tool says it will do, ADAPT compares that declaration with what actually happens when the tool runs. The basic flow is: Declare → Classify → Observe → Compare → Decide When a WebMCP tool is exposed, ADAPT builds a declared contract from information such as its name, description, schema, annotations, and expected capabilities. During execution, ADAPT observes browser-visible effects such as network writes, storage mutations, and navigation. It then compares the two. If the observed behavior stays within what the tool declared, the result can be marked SAFE . If the tool behaves in a way that does not match its declaration, ADAPT can surface the mismatch and QUARANTINE the result. For actions that are already known to be consequential, ADAPT can take a different path entirely: execution is HELD before it happens and a human has to explicitly approve or deny it. That distinction was important to us. A deceptive low-risk tool and an openly high-risk tool should not be treated as the same problem. We also generate an auditable trail of what was declared, what was observed, what decision ADAPT made, and how the action was executed. The idea is simple: Trust the behavior, not just the label. How we built it The WebMCP work lives in the ADAPT Trust Lab and a reusable trust core under src/webmcp . We use the real document.modelContext WebMCP surface where it is available, including tool registration and discovery. Around that lifecycle, we built several pieces: declared tool contracts consequence classification runtime behavior observation declared-vs-observed capability comparison guarded execution human approval for consequential actions trust receipts and an audit trajectory tool-surface change detection adversarial scenarios for deceptive and benign tools One thing we cared about a lot was keeping the security logic separate from the demo UI. The Trust Lab is just the place where you can see the system working. The actual decision and trust logic lives in standalone modules that can be tested independently. We also built a deterministic WebMCP-compatible test path because relying only on live browser behavior would have made the security tests flaky and hard to reproduce. The current build has 526 unit tests , 24 E2E assertions plus 2 harness meta-checks , adversarial scenarios, repeated stress runs, receipt-chain verification, and a real Chromium WebMCP surface check. The live version is deployed as a static site and can be opened in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not detecting that "something happened." The hard part was deciding whether what happened was actually outside the behavior the tool had declared. Early versions of ADAPT were much too simple. A read-only tool performing a write was easy to classify, but real tools are not always that clean. A legitimate write-capable tool may make a network request, change state, or navigate as part of its intended behavior. That forced us to move away from a basic read-only vs. write check and start thinking in terms of declared capabilities versus observed effects . Another challenge was being precise about the word "blocked." For a consequential action that ADAPT holds before execution, "blocked" really can mean nothing happened. For a deceptive tool that has already started running before ADAPT observes the mismatch, that is different. In that case we describe the result as quarantined rather than pretending ADAPT somehow reversed an arbitrary side effect. We spent a surprising amount of time fixing that language because we did not want the demo to claim more than the implementation actually guarantees. Real WebMCP testing was another challenge. Browser support is still experimental, so we needed both a real WebMCP path and a deterministic test harness to make development and CI reliable. And because this is a page-level prototype, the observer currently shares a JavaScript context with the page it is observing. A fully hostile same-context script can bypass some instrumentation. We treat that as a real limitation, not something to hide. Accomplishments that we're proud of The thing we are most proud of is that ADAPT stopped being just an interesting security idea and became something we could actually demonstrate end to end. A judge can see: a normal WebMCP tool behave as declared and pass as SAFE a deceptive tool produce a visible declared-vs-observed mismatch a consequential action get HELD before execution for a human decision a decision leave behind an auditable trust receipt We are also proud of how much effort went into proving the demo rather than just polishing it. The trust core is covered by hundreds of tests, adversarial cases, repeated browser runs, tamper checks, and reproducible evidence tied to a specific build. We also kept the history of the original ADAPT project in the same repository instead of pretending everything existed only for this challenge. The WebMCP Trust Lab and trust runtime were added during the challenge period, and the repository history makes that separation visible. What we learned The biggest thing we learned is that metadata is useful, but metadata is not enforcement. A tool name, description, schema, or annotation can help an agent understand what a tool is supposed to do. But if the system never compares that promise with reality, the declaration is still just a claim. We also learned that "security" gets much harder the moment you try to describe exactly what you guarantee. It is easy to say: "ADAPT blocks malicious tools." It is much harder, and much more useful, to say: "This action was held before execution." or: "These effects were observed, they exceeded the declared capability, and the result was quarantined." That distinction changed a lot of the design. Finally, WebMCP made us think differently about the browser itself. Once websites expose callable capabilities directly to agents, trust can no longer live only at the UI level. The relationship between declaration, execution, user intent, and evidence becomes part of the product. What's next for ADAPT The current challenge build is a research prototype, not a complete browser security boundary. The next step is moving more of the enforcement into a trusted browser or extension context so observation cannot be bypassed by code running in the same page. We also want to make the behavioral model richer. Today ADAPT focuses on a small set of high-value effects such as network writes, storage changes, navigation, and consequential actions. A production system could reason about much more specific capabilities: payments, deletion, account changes, credential access, file actions, identity changes, cross-origin effects, and more. We would also like the trust receipts to become portable evidence that an agent, browser, user, or external policy system can inspect independently. WebMCP makes the web callable. We think the next question is whether those calls can also become accountable. That is the part of ADAPT we want to keep building. title: Aergebra
pitch: Aergebra is a shared geometry workspace where humans edit shapes and AI reads and acts on the exact same geometry, relationships, and constraints through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Aergebra is a shared geometry workspace where humans edit shapes and AI reads and acts on the exact same geometry, relationships, and constraints through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The name Algebra comes from al-jabr — "the reunion of broken parts." Aergebra reunites the two broken halves of agent–human work on the web: what the agent sees (screenshots) and what you see (prose about your own screen) — into one live drawing both of you can touch. Inspiration Watch an agent help a human with anything spatial and you see the same failure twice: the agent "sees" the page by screenshotting it and squinting; the human "sees" the agent's work as prose ( "I placed a vertex near the top-left" ). Neither is looking at the thing. We wanted one shared object both kinds of hands can touch: live geometry . What it does Aergebra is a geometry workroom — points, segments, circles, polygons, groups, photo/SVG underlays, a live algebra Inspector — where the document is the truth and the canvas is its projection. With WebMCP the page registers 16 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() , so an agent in a WebMCP-capable browser gets the whole kit as structured tools: Construct — points/segments/circles/polygons, groups, frames — including over an imported photo. Mean — attach meanings ; the board labels things by what they ARE, never arbitrary letters. Tools accept a meaning as the name: {name: "Table 2"} . Point — aergebra_highlight lights objects up so the human sees exactly what the agent means. No more "the circle on the left". Read as data — aergebra_get_algebra returns the construction as algebra; aergebra_get_view returns the camera as data. The agent never screenshots. Status in colour — a four-colour status vocabulary (at rest / blocked / ready / willing), visible in a legend on the board, so "Nan's path is blocked till Thursday" is one brown line everyone can read. Every mutation — human tap, typed command, or agent tool call — goes through the SAME façade and lands on the same append-only receipt line. Agent calls echo live in the same command-line output a human's typed calls use. One board, one history, two kinds of hands. The demo is a real session The middle of the video is an actual conversation: Andrea tells the agent Saturday's wedding floor plan in plain words ("table 2's nan… speaker cable till thursday… table 4 on hold"); the agent builds, labels, colours and reads the board back — every board change a real WebMCP tool call, captured live. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Geometry is the worst case for pixels-in/prose-out and the best case for WebMCP: the page's internal model is already structured, so exposing it as tools is lossless. And it's bidirectional shared state : the agent reads the model as data, writes through receipted tools, and points at what the human is looking at. The human's UI and the agent's tools are projections of one document. Who this is for Anywhere a page's model is already graph/geometry: entity-relationship and data modelling, event floor plans and seating charts (our own business), process and project maps, tutoring. Any canvas-like app — whiteboards, CAD, slides, maps — can copy the pattern. How we built it TypeScript + Vite + JSXGraph, no frameworks. A receipted document model ( src/model.ts ) is the single source of truth; a typed façade ( src/toolapi.ts ) is the ONLY write path; src/webmcp.ts maps it onto document.modelContext.registerTool() (navigator fallback, late-injection retries) with JSON-Schema inputs. A badge reports WebMCP · 16 tools live when a model context is present; without one the page runs unchanged. Tested against native WebMCP in Chrome 152. Built during the submission period Everything in the repository was built during the Challenge submission period; the commit history is the evidence — the engine first, station by station, then the WebMCP integration on top. Challenges One façade kept honest (if the agent's path and the human's path diverge, receipts lie); resolving objects by meaning, not letters; auto-fit that never clips; Windows shells mangling --base=/aergebra/ mid-deploy. What's next User-declared colour meanings ("red = check on nan" is your board's meaning), outline detection over photos, .scu / .acu exports for agents, and a live mission clock — shared geometry applied to time. title: Ribband
pitch: Source-backed personal decisions for shopping, gifts, dates, vacations, and project staffing.
about_excerpt: Source-backed personal decisions for shopping, gifts, dates, vacations, and project staffing. Like Comment Story Updates Ribband: About Inspiration Most recommendation tools begin with a category and a search box. People rarely make decisions that way. A good vacation can echo a childhood memory. A good gift depends on who it is for, what they already love, and the occasion. A good date balances two people and avoids repeating what they have already done. A project crew needs the right roles, credentials, equipment, location, and schedule. At the same time, most of the web is designed to be seen, not understood by an agent. Important facts are buried inside presentation markup, forcing agents to infer controls and reconstruct evidence out of sight of the person who asked for help. Ribband explores a clearer contract for the next era of surfing the web: let an agent understand the personal context a person deliberately shares, move quickly across explicitly authorized sources, preserve the evidence, and keep consequential actions with the person. The name nods to the Blue Riband, the historic distinction associated with speed records on Atlantic passenger crossings. What it does Ribband is an open-source, source-backed personal decision agent for five everyday needs: Shopping: compare products for yourself using goals, preferences, exclusions, existing items, and a budget. Gifts: recommend options using the recipient's age, interests, occasion, deadline, dislikes, and whatever else the shopper chooses to provide. Dates: balance two people's interests, constraints, prior activities, and desired mood across low-cost, balanced, and special-occasion ideas. Vacations: turn visited places, fond memories, desired novelty, dates, party size, and budget into value, balanced, and signature packages containing lodging, transportation, dining, and activities. Project staffing: assemble eligible laborers, technicians, and creatives by role, credential, equipment, geography, schedule, and quote mode while surfacing coverage gaps instead of inventing a match. A person can begin with a sparse goal and budget or share richer context. One read-only plan_decision WebMCP tool routes an explicit vertical through a fixed deterministic strategy and returns a DecisionEnvelope containing the selected strategy, exact context projection, evidence state, ranked options, tradeoffs, price range, revision linkage, and available next actions. General shopping is self-directed; gifts add recipient and occasion context rather than disguising every purchase as a gift. Ribband also preserves its original evidence workspace. Ten WebMCP tools let an agent list and select allowlisted origins, search and rank Offers, inspect product pages as stripped Markdown plus structured data, compare products, build a grounded brief, assemble a planning-only activity itinerary, and stage a purchase review. Both surfaces use the same normalized Offer protocol and the same visible workspace as the person. The agent can prepare, explain, and revise a decision. It cannot silently buy, book, contact a provider, request a quote, sign a contract, or save personal memory. Purchase handoff, provider-source opening, and memory approval remain separate visible human controls. How I built it Ribband is a TypeScript application running on Cloudflare Workers. The primary Worker serves the human workspace, same-origin APIs, security controls, diagnostics, and WebMCP handlers. A separate controlled public Worker serves original goods and service fixtures over live HTTPS. Every source adapter compiles into one Offer graph. Product feeds and page JSON-LD reconcile price, availability, condition, shipping, and returns. Service Offers add provider, location, duration, price basis, party limits, published windows, cancellation terms, credentials, service radius, and itinerary or staffing eligibility. Decision fields preserve canonical source links and are labeled verified , single-source , or conflict . The unified orchestrator projects only the context needed by the chosen vertical. Hard exclusions are applied before scoring. Deterministic strategies then expose their factors, reasons, tradeoffs, unknown costs, and source state rather than hiding the ranking inside an opaque model response. Revisions resubmit the complete visible context and link to the prior page-memory decision id; the Worker stores neither request. Vacation packages combine lodging, transportation, dining, and activities with category totals, contingency, and explicit unknown costs. Staffing plans combine controlled provider Offers, fail closed on missing roles or unverified geography, and require a second human review showing the destination and transmitted information before a provider source can open. Trust boundary Ribband never accepts an arbitrary upstream URL. Every upstream request must use HTTPS, match an exact authorized hostname and path, remain within byte and time limits, and reject off-origin or out-of-scope redirects. Each origin has a validated authorization manifest describing capabilities, response limits, freshness policy, and review date. Expired origins fail closed before an upstream request is made. The current controlled catalog intentionally demonstrates guitars rather than claiming arbitrary retail coverage. The controlled service directory contains 20 original fixtures: 5 activities, 1 wellness service, 1 home service, 3 lodging Offers, 2 dining Offers, 2 transportation Offers, and 6 professional services. These fixtures prove the data contract, provenance, planning, and action boundaries; they do not claim live inventory, measured travel time, reservations, messages, contracts, orders, or payments. Date and vacation outcomes can create a tentative memory proposal, but only a visible human approval can save the exact reviewed fact in that browser. Saved facts remain unselected until the person chooses them for a later decision, and the person can correct or delete them. There are no cookies, analytics identifiers, hidden profile reads, or hidden approval paths. Challenges and learning The central challenge was making personalization genuinely useful without turning personal context into invisible surveillance or giving the agent irreversible authority. Extending one Offer protocol from products into dates, vacations, and staffing also required separating facts that can be normalized from actions that remain specific to a vertical. The strongest lesson was that an agent interface should expose more than tools. Trust improves when the person can see the context used, authorization, source state, ranking factors, uncertainty, conflicts, activity, and the exact point where automation stops. A safe refusal is part of the product: Ribband should stop when evidence is stale, contradictory, out of scope, or insufficient. Current verification The deployed release passes strict TypeScript checking, 217 automated tests across 28 test files, eight running-Worker release checks, deployment dry runs for both Cloudflare Workers, and 30 production checks. Browser acceptance exercises all five strategies through WebMCP, the complete outcome-memory consent cycle, eligible and ineligible staffing source review, the homepage entry point, and a 390-pixel mobile layout with no horizontal overflow or console errors. The public /health response exposes the exact deployed Git commit and Worker version. title: BeatForge for Beatsaber
pitch: BeatForge uses WebMCP to let people and agents co-create Beat Saber maps: humans set intent, agents configure and review, and only humans certify playability.
about_excerpt: BeatForge uses WebMCP to let people and agents co-create Beat Saber maps: humans set intent, agents configure and review, and only humans certify playability. Like Comment Story Updates Interface for people/agents Generated beatmap for Tame Impala's Is It True Inspiration I'm a top ranked player in Beatsaber and I got tired of playing the same tracks over and over again. Beat mapping sits between music, interface design, and safety engineering. A mapper has to hear a song, decide how its energy should move through space, and check hundreds of technical rules. I built the BeatForge Beat Saber level-generation pipeline alone. In my own testing, MCP access reduced generation setup and iteration time to roughly one-tenth of my previous manual process. I estimate a roughly 100x improvement in consistency and usable output quality compared with that earlier workflow. These are my project observations, not a controlled industry benchmark. What it does BeatForge is designed for any full-length song that the user owns or has permission to use. The complete mastered track is uploaded locally as an MP3, WAV, OGG, FLAC, M4A, or MP4. The public WebMCP connection has a separate rights-safe preview path. It can find metadata, album artwork (which it then takes the color palette of the artwork and applies it to the level environment) , and a permitted short preview of about 30 seconds. That preview is only for discovery and the browser demo. It is not a full-recording downloader. Complete level generation uses the user's full local audio file. The agent can read studio context, find song metadata, apply a mapping plan, start generation, review timing and safety results, and record human playtest evidence. It cannot claim that it played the map. Human headset judgment remains essential. How we built it FastAPI handles full audio uploads, background jobs, progress events, validation, packaging, and the local Beat Saber workflow. The analyzer converts the full song to a 44.1 kHz integer-sample timeline. Demucs is used for audio separation. BeatForge uses the htdemucs_6s model to separate the song into drums, bass, guitar, piano, vocals, and other stems. This helps identify which musical layers drive each section. Full-mix timing consensus still has to pass strict timing gates, so stem analysis never hides uncertain timing. The generator independently creates Easy, Normal, Hard, Expert, and Expert+ maps. It checks hand reach, saber paths, recovery, collisions, walls, bombs, lighting, and structural validity. A generated chart remains a playtest_candidate until a human completes VR and fresh sight-read checks. The WebMCP layer registers eight typed JSON-Schema tools through document.modelContext.registerTool. The interface displays tool activity, mapping state, album artwork, generation status, and safety results. The public GitHub Pages demo uses a synthetic groove so judges can test the collaboration loop without copyrighted audio or local setup. I spent a full week running BeatForge in local reinforcement-learning environments. Each environment stepped through a beat grid while exposing Demucs-separated stem energy, audio features, red and blue hand kinematics, difficulty targets, and lookahead context. A PPO policy selected idle or note poses for each hand. Rewards encouraged onset alignment, musical energy, readable density, natural flow, and safe two-hand coordination. Penalties covered repeated cuts, insufficient recovery, handclaps, saber-path collisions, vision blocks, and other unsafe transitions. These training runs improved candidate search and helped the generator produce more musical and playable patterns before validation. The RL policy could never override the hard safety contract. Deterministic timing checks, map validation, and human VR playtesting remained mandatory before release. The RL implementation is included in skills/beat-saber-mapping/scripts/rl/. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is still experimental, so BeatForge needs to work both with and without native WebMCP support. In supported browsers, it registers its tools. Elsewhere, it remains usable and explains how to enable WebMCP. Another challenge was adapting a local music tool for public judging. The full pipeline depends on local files, model availability, and Beat Saber-specific paths. Demo mode gives judges a complete collaboration loop without requiring that setup. The hardest product decision was defining what an agent must never claim. A chart can pass structural checks and still feel uncomfortable or unsafe in a headset. BeatForge keeps software validation and human playability evidence separate. Accomplishments that we're proud of Agents can now change a real mapping plan through typed operations instead of fragile UI guesses. People see those changes immediately and can accept, reject, or revise the direction. The activity panel makes the collaboration inspectable. We are also proud that the WebMCP work preserved BeatForge’s existing safety behavior. Timing uncertainty, mapping failures, and missing human evidence remain visible. The repository now includes the WebMCP implementation, browser tests, setup instructions, an MIT license, and a deployment definition. What we learned WebMCP tool descriptions are part of the product experience. A useful schema tells an agent what an operation means and tells the person what will change. Demucs showed me that source separation can provide better evidence about which musical layer should drive a phrase, while full-mix timing verification remains necessary. What's next for BeatForge for Beatsaber Next, I want agents to compare mapping plans, explain why sections failed safety gates, and turn human headset notes into structured revision requests. Longer term, BeatForge should feel like a rehearsal partner. The person brings taste and physical knowledge. The agent tracks decisions and helps turn a musical idea into a chart that someone can actually play. title: Cascade
pitch: A shared decision canvas where people and agents map hidden assumptions, stress-test plans against real world shocks, and turn uncertainty into resilient action.
about_excerpt: A shared decision canvas where people and agents map hidden assumptions, stress-test plans against real world shocks, and turn uncertainty into resilient action. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When working on an app launch, we found ourselves sending planning docs back and forth between us and our agents. That was very problematic. We wanted to move beyond asking an AI, “What could go wrong?” and getting another list to read. What if the agent could work inside the plan itself, connecting assumptions, exploring consequences, and proposing alternatives that a person could inspect and challenge? That became Cascade: a shared decision canvas for people and their agents. What it does Cascade turns a consequential plan into a connected map of objectives, assumptions, dependencies, constraints, risks, and outcomes. Our demo starts with a product launch: six weeks, 500 teams, and a $12,000 budget. What happens if billing arrives three weeks late? An agent can create a separate what-if branch, apply the disruption, and trace modeled downstream effects. It can then stage possible responses, such as launching a free beta first. The human can inspect the map, drag cards with their connections following, compare scenarios, and accept or reject proposed factors and relationships. Applying a shock is allowed inside a what-if branch; proposed mitigations remain drafts awaiting review. Promoting a branch is a human action. Product launch is the starter. Cascade also includes a community tool-lending scenario and a blank workspace for other plans. Why WebMCP Cascade is built around a shared working surface, not a separate chat transcript. WebMCP lets the agent read and act on the structured model behind the page. Tool actions update the same interface the person is watching: branches appear, shocks enter the map, and proposals arrive for review. This makes an otherwise awkward workflow practical: the agent explores alternatives inside the live application while the person retains an inspectable record of the model and controls which proposals are accepted. There is no need to copy the plan into a chat and manually translate the answer back into a diagram. How we built it Cascade uses TypeScript and React, with a Next.js-style App Router implemented through vinext on Vite. React Flow provides the draggable node-and-edge canvas. Custom CSS and a Tailwind CSS build pipeline support the visual design. The app registers 11 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). They cover reading the workspace, staging factors and relationships, creating branches, applying shocks, proposing mitigations, running stress tests, and comparing or explaining results. Tools use structured schemas and bounded inputs. Version checks on scenario-editing tools help reject stale writes when a person and an agent are working on the same model. Draft revision is limited to unlocked draft factors. A local TypeScript engine propagates shocks through accepted relationships to produce deterministic sensitivity metrics and impact paths. Its outputs are modeling aids. Vitest tests cover stable metrics, shock propagation, draft exclusion from cost and schedule totals, and graph layout. The workspace is stored in browser localStorage and can be exported as JSON. The app does not need its own AI API key; a connected agent uses the page's tools. That agent still receives the workspace data exposed through those tools. Cascade is hosted on ChatGPT Sites with a Cloudflare Workers-compatible build, with source code on GitHub under the MIT license. Challenges we ran into One challenge was making the graph behave like a genuine working surface: cards needed to move freely while their connections stayed anchored. Another was separating exploration from commitment. An agent needs room to test a disruption without silently rewriting the baseline, and people need a clear distinction between proposed and accepted changes. Rehearsing the demo exposed a subtler problem: an agent created a scenario whose description mentioned a delay, but did not actually apply the delay to the model. That reinforced an important lesson: a success message is not proof of a state change. Reliable collaboration needs outcome verification, not just well-described tools. Accomplishments we're proud of We built a working shared canvas where agent actions become visible, reviewable changes rather than suggestions trapped in a conversation. The same decision model supports both the product-launch and community examples, and the app remains usable by a person when WebMCP is unavailable. Most importantly, human review is part of the interaction itself: proposals, locks, scenario branches, and promotion controls make the collaboration boundary visible. What we learned Agent-native design is as much about accountability as capability. Giving an agent tools is only the beginning; the application must make its actions understandable and checkable. We also learned to distinguish a useful model from a confident-looking number. Cascade's purpose is to expose assumptions and explore consequences, not claim certainty about the future. What's next Stronger end-to-end evaluations that verify actual model changes after agent actions. More explicit feedback when a scenario has been created but no disruption has been applied. Improved mitigation-effect modeling, uncertainty handling, and explanation of score contributions. Shared team workspaces with durable persistence. Evidence links and richer review history for the assumptions behind a decision. title: Codex Ascend
pitch: Turn one real goal into a living expedition shared by a human and an AI agent.
about_excerpt: Turn one real goal into a living expedition shared by a human and an AI agent. Like Comment Story Updates Mission state becomes mountain geography: camps, routes, confidence, moving weather, and WebMCP activity share one living world. A real blocker fractures the route and changes the weather. Cosmetic progress stops until the obstacle is actually resolved. The agent asks; the human decides. Only the user can authorize repair or bypass at Camp III before the agent continues. Evidence before Summit. Completion activates only after every dependency, blocker, and success criterion passes deterministic verification. What Codex Ascend does Codex Ascend turns long-running agent work into a living mountain shared by a human and an AI agent. Camps are verified outcomes, fog is uncertainty, crevasses are blockers, route forks are consequential choices, and the Summit stays locked until every required proof passes deterministic verification. Codex Ascend is for developers and technical leads supervising long-running AI execution, where blockers, approvals, and proof should never disappear inside a chat log. Why WebMCP is essential Most agent interfaces split the model’s plan from the person’s understanding: the agent sees tool state while the human gets a chat log or decorative progress bar. Ascend gives both sides one execution model. The page registers 18 native WebMCP tools with closed JSON schemas and structured results. An agent can inspect mission state, discover topology, advance stages, report blockers, propose routes, request a human decision, attach evidence, verify completion, and finish the mission. These tools manipulate mission semantics—not pixels—and run through the same validated command engine as the human UI. The centerpiece is a genuinely bidirectional loop: The agent reports a persistence blocker and proposes repair or bypass routes. The mountain fractures at that exact geography and renders the choice. Only the human can authorize the consequential route inside the website. The agent reads the structured decision through WebMCP, resolves the blocker, and continues. New required work can reveal another ridge; evidence finally unlocks Verified Summit. There is intentionally no agent tool that can resolve the human decision. WebMCP makes collaboration safer and clearer because authority remains explicit while state stays machine-readable. How it works A neutral TypeScript Mission Engine validates commands and records a versioned event journal. React provides the accessible HUD and geography-bound scenario cards; PixiJS renders the living scene and elevation topology. An Ascend projection layer maps mission truth into camps, waypoints, weather, camera focus, narration, and generated imagery. A Cloudflare Worker uses Workflows and R2 for reviewed OpenAI GPT Image 2 generation. Provider credentials stay server-side, retries require explicit operator intent, and only accepted candidates enter the public world. Rendering can never mutate mission truth. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when the website owns an action the agent should not silently take. Structured inspection matters, but the memorable moment is the round trip: the agent surfaces a real decision, the human answers it in context, and the agent continues from shared structured state. Built with WebMCP, TypeScript, React, Vite, PixiJS, Zod, OpenAI GPT Image 2, Cloudflare Workers, Workflows, R2, Vitest, and ESLint. title: Enactive Brand Portal
pitch: Brand Portals explain brands to humans working in marketing, who then prompt their AI systems. In this project we expose the brand rules directly via WebMCP to agents as tools they can directly call.
about_excerpt: Brand Portals explain brands to humans working in marketing, who then prompt their AI systems. In this project we expose the brand rules directly via WebMCP to agents as tools they can directly call. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Brand portals are built for human reading. When someone wants an AI assistant to apply their guidance, the usual workflow is surprisingly fragile: find the relevant page, interpret it, copy fragments into a prompt, and hope the important context survives. This especially leads to errors and failures when external suppliers, such as marketing agencies interpret the Brand Portal of their clients. Enactive Brand Portal explores a different model. The website remains a real, human-readable brand book, while WebMCP makes the active page available to a visiting assistant as structured capability. The goal is to remove the repeated manual retransmission of brand guidance without removing human intent, factual responsibility, or judgment. What it does The public site presents Enactive Wonderland, an original Carroll-inspired fictional creative house. Visitors can browse its brand foundation, core voice, six character communication modes, and pen-and-ink image world like an ordinary brand portal. On applicable pages, a compatible browser exposes Site Tools derived from that exact page. For the canonical language journey, the person opens the Cheshire Cat page and supplies a communication goal and source facts. The assistant: retrieves the active-page guidance; prepares a structured Language Studio brief; writes one complete draft; stages the result back in the portal. The Studio then displays the original source, proposed draft, material changes, applied rules, rationale, warnings, and ordinary human controls. The person can edit, keep, discard, copy, or reset the work. No tool approves or publishes anything. The same pattern is implemented for visual work. The assistant can prepare and stage a generator-neutral image prompt package containing positive guidance, negative constraints, composition, alt text, and applied rules. The portal does not pretend that it generated or approved an image. Why WebMCP WebMCP tools change the ontological status of the brand rules from static text to executable affordances by the agent. These can be offered context dependent, so that the right tool is available on the right page of the brand portal. Opening Cheshire Cat provides strategic reframing. Opening White Rabbit provides lucid urgency. Opening Image World provides linework, composition, colour, and provenance guidance. WebMCP lets the assistant use that structured active-page context without DOM scraping or requiring the person to reconstruct the brand rules in every prompt. Page and session state determine which tools are available. After a copy brief is prepared, the staging tool appears as the next session affordance. Without Site Tools, the website remains a useful brand book and manual briefing and review surface. With Site Tools, the assistant can perform the substantive transformation and return it to the same browser session for visible human review. How we built it Enactive Brand Portal is a static React and Vite application written in TypeScript. Its source of truth is a four-layer JSON-LD knowledge model: Brand meaning; portal-edition content; generic product and WebMCP contracts; traceability and acceptance evidence. The top-level page registers exactly nine browser Site Tools using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Five tools provide read-only brand and guidance access. Four prepare or stage session-local work. Local-effect tools update visible React state and sessionStorage only. There is no remote MCP server, backend, API route, database, CMS, authentication layer, embedded model, or runtime network dependency. Challenges I ran into The hardest product challenge was keeping the brand and the technology separate. An earlier version technically worked but made the public experience feel like a WebMCP demonstrator rather than a useful brand portal. I rebuilt the content architecture so that Enactive Wonderland remains the subject and WebMCP appears only as a restrained application capability. Other challenges included route-specific tool availability, dynamically adding the staging affordance after preparation, cancellation handling, output-size limits in a real host, preserving context across Studio navigation, and distinguishing native browser evidence from a local handler harness. I also had to keep every claim honest: deterministic copy checks are partial, staged image work is a prompt package rather than an image, and the assistant proposes while the person decides. Accomplishments A coherent human-facing brand portal that works without WebMCP. Nine page- and session-aware browser Site Tools. A real compatible-host copy journey covering discovery, guidance retrieval, brief preparation, dynamic staging, visible review, and reload persistence. A fully static architecture with immutable brand knowledge. Human-readable source, diff, rule, rationale, and warning inspection. Automated graph, schema, architecture, layer-separation, unit, accessibility, and browser checks. A public Vercel deployment with ten working direct routes. A public Apache-2.0 repository with recorded content and asset provenance. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when the active page is not merely navigation but meaningful task context. The strongest interaction was not “an agent can click the website.” It was that the website could expose purpose-built, state-aware affordances while remaining understandable and useful to a person. We also learned that local tool execution is not equivalent to native browser proof, and that agent capability should stop before consequential human decisions such as approval or publication. What's next Next steps include reproducing the complete image-prompt journey in additional native hosts, testing compatibility across more WebMCP-enabled browsers, extracting the generic portal engine for other governed knowledge systems, and measuring the effect on task time, omitted rules, correction count, and reviewer confidence. The same pattern could be applied to design systems, policy portals, learning systems, editorial standards, and other websites whose knowledge currently stops at reading and downloading. Creator and provenance Enactive Brand Portal is an independent experiment by Sven Spöde, a Specialist GenAI for Marketing & Communications. Enactive Wonderland is an original fictional brand inspired by the public-domain works of Lewis Carroll. The project contains no brand assets, internal data, proprietary guidelines, or endorsement. Research, writing, design exploration, and implementation were AI-assisted under my direction and final conceptual, editorial, architectural, licensing, and release authority. title: First Key
pitch: A WebMCP apartment desk where an AI clerk flags costly lease clauses, while the app withholds send, agree, and countersign tools until two humans approve.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP apartment desk where an AI clerk flags costly lease clauses, while the app withholds send, agree, and countersign tools until two humans approve. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Renting a first apartment is a high-stakes moment. A student or first-time renter often has to understand a dense lease quickly, while a parent wants to help without taking over. We wanted to explore a sharper question for WebMCP: what if AI safety came from the product architecture itself, not just from asking the model to behave? What it does First Key is a first-apartment desk for a tenant and parent. An AI clerk can read the listing, inspect the lease, flag costly clauses, and draft a landlord letter. The important part is what it cannot do: the app never exposes tools for sending email, agreeing, paying, submitting, or countersigning. The demo follows Maya Chen and her parent through a shared rental packet. The clerk can identify costly lease terms like a non-refundable pet fee, early termination fee, automatic renewal, and rent increase. The letter can be staged, but it only becomes downloadable after two separate human seats agree in two different tabs. How we built it We built First Key with React, TypeScript, and WebMCP page tools. The app registers different tools depending on the current stage: listing, lease, application, or outbound. This makes tool availability part of the UI state. For example, the clerk can use tools like pull_listing_terms , run_playbook , pin_finding , and stage_outbound . But tools like send , agree , and countersign are intentionally never registered. The interface shows this directly with active tools and withheld tools side by side. We also built a deterministic clerk playbook evaluation. The app reports costly-clause recall, precision, and boilerplate silence across development, held-out, and adversarial lease fixtures. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was resisting the temptation to make the AI do everything. Many rental demos would let the agent email the landlord, submit the application, or sign the document. We chose the opposite: the AI can prepare work, but irreversible actions require humans. Another challenge was evaluation. A lease scanner can look good if it only checks one hand-written example. We added held-out fixtures, adversarial decoys, and a regression probe so the project has a measurable claim instead of just a nice demo. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that First Key demonstrates WebMCP as a product boundary, not just an integration layer. The app can say: these tools are available now, these tools are withheld forever, and this action requires human agreement. We are also proud of the evaluation page. It shows 1.00 costly-clause recall, 1.00 precision, and 1.00 boilerplate silence on development, held-out, and adversarial extractive labels. It also openly shows the 0.00 paraphrase robustness result as a deliberate boundary: the clerk prefers silence over speculative guesses. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most powerful when the site is opinionated about capability. Instead of giving an agent a broad instruction and hoping it follows policy, the application can expose a small, stateful set of tools that match the current workflow. We also learned that restraint can be a feature. The best demo is not an agent doing everything. It is an agent helping at the right moments while the app protects the actions that should stay human. What's next Next, First Key could support more lease templates, clearer state sync for families, and richer jurisdiction-specific playbooks. The same architecture could also apply to other high-stakes workflows: medical forms, insurance claims, school financial aid, or any process where AI should assist but not act alone. title: Grand Adventure Engine
pitch: Grand Adventure Engine brings tabletop worlds to life. With WebMCP, ChatGPT becomes a safe Co-DM—reading campaign lore, messaging players, and proposing consequences that stay under human control.
about_excerpt: Grand Adventure Engine brings tabletop worlds to life. With WebMCP, ChatGPT becomes a safe Co-DM—reading campaign lore, messaging players, and proposing consequences that stay under human control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates AI Co-DM cockpit Co-DM cockpit, showcasing an approval Player view Inspiration I’ve been thinking a lot about how we’re naturally wandering back toward old-school terminal interfaces. Games like Zork amazed me as a kid because it felt like I could do almost anything, even though everything still operated within certain boundaries. I’m a huge fan of old-school MUDs, D&D adventures, and good storytelling. When I was ten, I connected through Telnet and played games that way. Grand Adventure Engine draws from all of that: it’s a retelling of an old idea, now guided by an LLM so the world can react when I decide to do something clever, unexpected, or just plain dumb. What it does Grand Adventure Engine turns a text-adventure campaign into a shared workspace for players, human Dungeon Masters, and browser agents. Players explore and act through natural language while the AI narrator maintains the story and game state. Meanwhile, a WebMCP-enabled Co-DM can inspect live scenes, search campaign lore, examine characters and quests, message players, and propose mechanical interventions. High-impact changes—such as applying conditions, adjusting health, or correcting suspicious actions—remain queued for human approval, combining the speed of an agent with visible, accountable DM control. How we built it We extended an ASP.NET Core and PostgreSQL RPG engine with five browser-native WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool: scene inspection, world search, entity inspection, player messaging, and governed mechanical-change proposals. The vanilla JavaScript dashboard provides a real-time DM console and player view through SignalR, while server-side authorization, ownership checks, typed schemas, bounded searches, audit receipts, and human approval gates protect the game state. The application is containerized, deployed over HTTPS through Azure Container Apps, and backed by automated unit, integration, security, and browser tests. The original project was build a few months ago, mostly over the course of a week. I sat on it, doing occasional work, and popping in to update it, play with it, or test it on a newly released model. Originally the plan was to set it up for local LLM use only, but it naturally progressed into using Codex OAuth (on a local node) and it worked really impressively and quickly. When I decided to join the hackathon, I added the admin console, and updated the site to handle the incoming changes. I opened it up to (hopefully) allow the admin to do basically anything they wanted to from Codex. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was flexibility—specifically, finding the right balance between hands-on and hands-off control. We needed a way for the DM—or God, depending on how dramatic they’re feeling—to step into a scene, rebalance an encounter, influence an outcome, or simply monitor the game to make sure everyone is having a good time. It’s frustrating when you give an LLM a basic command and it simply says “no.” At the same time, even with strict guidance, players will inevitably find ways to break things. I can’t justifiably blame them for that. If a character wanders off the edge of the map, that’s the developer’s problem—not the player’s. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m especially happy that I originally architected this project in a way that could be meaningfully extended for this hackathon. I’m proud that I found a balance between giving players free rein and preserving human control when intervention is necessary. The project is also bootstrapped: I designed it to be inexpensive to operate and straightforward to manage. Finally, I’m proud of how quickly I was able to iterate, incorporating the latest WebMCP guidance into an existing project under an extremely short deadline. What we learned The biggest lesson was the difference between having a cool idea, merely bolting WebMCP onto it, and creating something where WebMCP is genuinely useful. This competition forced me to assess ideas honestly and pivot quickly when something wasn’t coming together. ChatGPT provided valuable feedback throughout the process, helping me turn the project into something fun and functional while still aiming for a creative and novel use of the technology. What's next for Great Adventure Engine Honestly: playtesting and gathering interest. This is an iterative project, and so far it has only been playtested by me—which means someone else will almost certainly discover an imaginative new way to break it. The plan is simple: playtest, study the logs, fix the problems, and keep going. I’m particularly interested in bringing it into Discord communities, where I can host the engine from my own machine and let the AI respond directly in Discord. That would make it an inexpensive, accessible way for groups to run persistent adventures together. title: HeatGrid
pitch: A shared heat-emergency operations board where people pin local reality and WebMCP agents build accountable, stress-tested plans.
about_excerpt: A shared heat-emergency operations board where people pin local reality and WebMCP agents build accountable, stress-tested plans. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Extreme-heat response is a coordination problem disguised as a map. A coordinator must balance neighborhood risk, cooling-center capacity, shuttle routes, budget, accessibility, bridge conditions, and facts that often live only in people's heads. Traditional dashboards make humans compare every option manually. A chat assistant, meanwhile, can suggest ideas but cannot reliably see or change the live planning state. HeatGrid explores a better pattern: the human pins local reality; the agent handles the combinatorics; the human keeps authority. What it does HeatGrid is a shared human-agent operations board for the fictional Harbor City. It is a planning prototype—not a live dispatch or medical system—and all data is synthetic. A coordinator can set the budget, choose priority districts, lock cooling centers, and mark the North Bridge open or closed. A WebMCP-capable agent can then use six focused tools to: read the same operational context visible to the human, inspect individual centers and shuttle routes, apply explicit planning constraints, draft a deterministic allocation plan, stress-test that plan against disruptions, and request human review. The resulting plan appears immediately on the map and dashboard, with allocations, route usage, cost, coverage, equity, constraint checks, and a visible audit trail. The agent can prepare and test a decision, but only the human can approve it ; HeatGrid deliberately exposes no approval tool. In the demo scenario, the planner produces plan HG-001 with 97.7% coverage, 98% equity coverage, a $40,700 spend, a 2.7-mile average trip, and zero constraint violations. It then survives a bridge-closure stress test before stopping at human review. Why WebMCP matters HeatGrid is not a chatbot attached to a dashboard. WebMCP turns the website itself into a structured, agent-ready workspace: Tools operate on the live state the coordinator sees, not a stale copy. Typed inputs reduce ambiguity around budgets, districts, locks, and disruptions. Small, non-overlapping tools let an agent inspect before it changes anything. Structured results are concise enough for model use and rich enough for UI updates. Every consequential action remains visible and attributable in the audit trail. The missing approval tool is intentional: tool design is also permission design. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer controls from pixels, scrape the page, or work in a separate chat disconnected from the operator. With WebMCP, the page publishes a purpose-built operational interface while remaining fully usable by a person. How I built it HeatGrid is a dependency-light Node.js and browser JavaScript application. The WebMCP layer uses the imperative navigator.modelContext.registerTool() API and exposes: read_heat_context inspect_heat_option set_heat_constraints draft_heat_plan stress_test_heat_plan request_plan_review Each tool has a narrow responsibility, JSON Schema inputs, concise descriptions, appropriate read-only and untrusted-content annotations, strict validation, and abort-signal handling. Tool actions update the same in-memory state model used by the visible interface. A deterministic local planner scores feasible allocations against coverage, equity, travel distance, capacity, budget, route availability, locks, and priority districts. The interface is built with semantic HTML, responsive CSS, an SVG operations map, and accessible form controls. The server adds origin isolation, a restrictive Permissions Policy for WebMCP, a Content Security Policy, and other security headers. The UI also works normally when WebMCP is unavailable. Automated tests cover default planning, tight budgets, locked centers, bridge closures, and invalid constraints. I additionally exercised the complete six-tool flow against the deployed site through a WebMCP-capable browser. Challenges The biggest challenge was designing tools that are useful without being dangerously broad. A single “optimize everything” tool would hide important choices; dozens of tiny tools would burden selection. The six-tool sequence became a legible planning protocol: observe, inspect, constrain, draft, stress-test, review. A second challenge was making agent actions trustworthy. HeatGrid treats every tool call as a visible state transition, returns validation failures instead of silently relaxing constraints, and makes approval explicitly human-only. The third challenge was working against an emerging browser API while preserving a graceful non-WebMCP experience and a small, auditable codebase. Accomplishments A real, live WebMCP implementation rather than a mocked tool transcript Six composable tools with typed schemas and safety annotations Deterministic, reproducible planning and stress testing Immediate shared-state UI updates and a complete audit trail A hard human-approval boundary encoded in the tool surface Five passing planner tests and a deployed public demo Zero runtime dependencies in the application itself What I learned The best agent tool APIs are also good interaction design. Names, schemas, outputs, and missing capabilities all teach an agent how to collaborate. I also learned that “human in the loop” is strongest when it is architectural—not a warning in a prompt, but an action the agent literally cannot perform. Collaboration This is a solo submission by SSHDotCodes, developed with Codex as an AI implementation and testing partner. The demo narration uses Qwen Audio 3.0 TTS Plus. Product direction, safety boundaries, tool design, verification, and final submission decisions remained human-controlled. What's next The next step is to connect validated municipal data sources such as center inventories, GTFS transit feeds, and OpenStreetMap travel times; add signed scenario imports and multi-user incident rooms; and evaluate the workflow with emergency managers. The longer-term idea is a reusable pattern for accountable human-agent operations—not only heat response, but shelter planning, supply distribution, and other high-stakes coordination work. title: Heap-4
pitch: Heap 4: Agents recover unfinished workflows, one verified step at a time.
about_excerpt: Heap 4: Agents recover unfinished workflows, one verified step at a time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Something I dread, as a solo founder, is the potentially overwhelming amount of comments or fixes that need to happen within a short period of time for user retention and enjoyability in an app. I initially wanted something that would scrape the web or bug that user submitted, then fixed them for me. However, this is very security-vulnerable and not good practice. I did see a future product in this though, so I determined the next steps would be to create a minimal yet compliant demo that did some variation of this. That variation landed to be: a user does something, something else goes wrong --> how do we still get it to work? Well, the intention was still there (evidence, what went wrong, why--like an obvious invoice needing to be sent). Heap 4 was inspired by that gap: applications preserve errors, but often lose the user’s intention, partial progress, and safe next steps. *Quick side note on the name: I typically utilize random DSA terms with a number because it sounds cool on miscellaneous projects. AI did not come up with this name (however apparent it may or may not be). The core idea is: Developers define what is legal. The agent discovers what will work. Heap 4 verifies every step. --> define a set of parameters, let the agent do the rest so you don't over-engineer the app with a load of try/catch or if/else statements. What Heap 4 Does Heap 4 is a runtime for unfinished workflows. It captures: The user’s desired outcome What has already succeeded The failed route and runtime evidence Available capabilities Policies and constraints Invariants that must never be violated An agent can then inspect the situation, choose and sequence available actions, observe failures, and replan. The agent does not receive unrestricted access or authority to mutate arbitrary state. Every action is verified by deterministic application code. The Demo The concrete example is invoice delivery. The user wants Acme Corporation to read invoice INV-2841 for $4,850. The invoice is successfully persisted, but the email provider fails with an HTTP 500. Retrying the whole operation could create a duplicate invoice, so Heap 4 preserves the existing invoice and marks the workflow as interrupted. The agent then: Inspects the interruption, customer policy, and available contacts. Attempts Acme’s preferred procurement portal. Observes that the portal is unavailable. Selects Dana Lee, the designated acting AP approver, rather than an archival mailbox. Requests approval for a temporary one-hour, read-only access grant. Creates the scoped grant. Discovers that creating authority alone does not deliver it. Sends a policy-compliant notice without attaching the invoice. Continues monitoring the original email route while Acme remains unblocked. Resumes the existing invoice after a human approves the bounded repair. Revokes the temporary share link. Verifies that the invoice was sent, no duplicate was created, and temporary access has stopped. The application does not contain a single recover_invoice button or a hardcoded “if portal fails, send a link” branch. It exposes smaller primitives whose availability changes with server-authoritative state. How I Built It Heap 4 is built with TypeScript, React, Vite, and native WebMCP. Moreover, help with agents (Codex, GitHub Copilot), although strictly code-only, nothing with idea development. The system is split into three responsibilities: The agent interprets evidence, chooses parameters, sequences primitives, and replans. Heap 4’s runtime preserves intent, exposes state-gated capabilities, and coordinates recovery. The server enforces policy, authorization, state transitions, and invariants. The invoice workflow uses a server-authoritative state machine: active → blocked → mitigated → resumable → completed The alternate route is deliberately staged. Creating a share grant does not satisfy the outcome. A separate send_access_notice capability must verify the recipient, message, attachment choice, and current customer policy before delivery is recorded. The share link is implemented as a real capability: Scoped to one invoice Limited to read_invoice_only Expiring Revocable Stored server-side only as a SHA-256 digest Returned as plaintext only once Tracked with a server-stamped first-access timestamp The repair path is separately bounded. A repair worker reproduces the failure, validates a narrow candidate change, and prepares it for review. Deployment requires explicit human approval. Once deployed, the agent can resume only the unfinished delivery step. The application runs locally through Express and is also deployed as a Cloudflare Worker with D1-backed session state. Native WebMCP registration is used where supported. For browser-agent hosts that can inspect the page but cannot invoke native WebMCP tools, the application provides clearly labeled, parameterized compatibility controls that call the same server-verified transitions. What I Learned I was able to answer a tough question: when does something go form: "a human could engineer this"; "an architecture's best practices should contain fallbacks"; and whatnot. It led me to: a route selector is not enough to demonstrate useful agency. A workflow becomes meaningfully agent-native when the agent must compose multiple independently verified operations whose sequence depends on policy and runtime evidence. Challenges As stated before, I struggled a lot. Not with "what do I want this to be", but rather: "where does agency really belong in a website/workflow?" I had to really separate authority from agency. It was obvious that an agent cannot be responsible for actions, nor should it. However, what use does it bring if it cannot do what's convenient nor has the authority to do so? The second issue I had to tackle was the limitation of the nature of WebMCP: "what can an agent do for me that might be something I don't want to do for myself?" I'm under the impression that an agent with WebMCP strictly does the things you can but with slightly more knowledge and efficiency. Both of the issues were resolved with agency belongs in orchestration; authority belongs in deterministic application code. The agent is allowed to inspect evidence, choose parameters, compose legal primitives, react to failures, and replan. Heap 4 remains responsible for authorization, policy enforcement, state transitions, invariants, and human approval for deployment. The agent can propose and initiate actions, but it cannot directly mutate arbitrary state or make an unsafe action legal. The second question was harder because, for one workflow, a human can often do the same things. A human can select a contact, choose a duration, click a button, and revoke a link. WebMCP does not make the agent magically capable of actions a user could never perform. The value is continuity and coordination. In a normal system, someone would need to notice the failure, understand what already happened, interpret the customer’s policy, choose a valid recovery, monitor the repair, return later, resume only the unfinished step, revoke temporary access, and verify the final state. That is manageable once. It becomes expensive and unreliable across thousands of interrupted workflows. In this project, the agent handles that orchestration while Heap 4 keeps it bounded. It does not receive a single “fix everything” capability. It receives specific tools whose availability changes with the workflow state. It must inspect the situation, attempt the preferred route, react to the outage, request approval for a disclosure change, compose the grant and notice steps, and clean up afterward. <--The earlier defined 'parameters'. A final issue: browser support. The testing browser could report that native WebMCP was unavailable and could not invoke page-defined tools. I intentionally did not install a fake production polyfill. Instead, I added a transparent compatibility path and kept its controls parameterized, so the agent still has to choose the contact, duration, message, attachment handling, and sequence. title: Weaponised Ecommerce: The Hyphosphere Observatory
pitch: Hyphosphere uses WebMCP to help researchers and AI agents trace the hidden commercial infrastructure behind online information operations, inspect cited evidence, and retain promising leads.
about_excerpt: Hyphosphere uses WebMCP to help researchers and AI agents trace the hidden commercial infrastructure behind online information operations, inspect cited evidence, and retain promising leads. Like Comment Story Updates Working concepts: The six level source ecology A number of possible reporting outputs WebMCP research brief Save as you go: the research notebook The Atlas Relay map and evidence demo A thesis proof of concept - creating purpose built tools for the project The agent manages a live feed Inspiration My thesis research asks how ordinary commercial systems such as platforms, data services, advertising tools, registries, domains, hosting, payment services, and ecommerce infrastructure, might be co-opted to help information operations travel, scale, and persist. Public reporting often begins and ends with the most visible elements of these activities: a post, advert, account, headline, campaign, or a platform takedown. But the less visible enabling relationships remain scattered across datasets, platform disclosures, investigative reporting, archives, registries, and infrastructure records. I had already been imagining a larger online observatory project that could connect these traces, but the WebMCP Challenge supplied the missing interaction model. Rather than placing a chatbot beside a static dashboard, I wanted a researcher and an AI agent to work on the same inspectable terrain. That way the agent could search, organise, follow relationships, and surface current reporting, while the human researcher retained control over the provenance, uncertainty, and interpretation of evidence, and what deserved to enter the research record. This Hyphosphere project grew from that junction of needs and observations. It is a proof of concept for the thesis, as well as an experiment in research methods: a way to make the enabling ecommerce assemblage visible, without treating every single suggestive pattern as a conclusion. It helps to prevent premature closure on a messy and interesting problem. What it does Hyphosphere presents a human–agent research environment for tracing the commercial infrastructure behind online information operations. A visitor can: follow a reproducible investigation across cases, services, datasets, and reporting; distinguish verified, supported, inferred, and disputed relationships; inspect each research artifact’s provenance, original citation, reason for inclusion, and ecommerce-stack position; explore six layers of the enabling commercial stack; search curated records and linked source collections; ask an agent to assemble a compact, visible research brief; receive current, directly linked reporting through an agent-mediated signal feed; pause the feed, inspect citations, and retain selected leads; save discoveries and agent briefs in a device-local notebook; export retained research notes in Markdown; and preview possible outputs such as timelines, cluster summaries, micro case studies, and network visualisations. The project is deliberately not just a dashboard of troll posts. It begins with what is publicly visible, but then it helps the researcher examine the wider field of services, platforms, data, interfaces, and infrastructure that may enable an operation. How I built it The application was built as a responsive React research console and iterated with Codex. Its data model connects research objects through typed relationships, while preserving separate evidence states and six ecommerce-stack levels. A deterministic demonstration corpus supports the principal Atlas Relay investigation, so that judges can reproduce the same path. The page registers twelve WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . These tools can: follow a relationship; open supporting evidence; change the evidence threshold; reveal the source terrain; save a discovery; draft a possible research output; list source collections; search curated and linked sources; assemble a research brief; save an agent brief; publish current signals; and save an individual signal to the notebook. Human interface controls and WebMCP tools call on the same underlying React actions. This means an agent does not operate an invisible parallel system: its actions produce visible changes in the interface that the researcher can inspect and guide. The live signal feed is also agent-mediated rather than presented as an autonomous page crawler. A connected agent finds current material relevant to the research topic, as defined by the researcher, and supplies constrained, HTTPS-linked records through publish_signal_feed . The page then validates and displays those records with labels for source, relevance, information-warfare, and ecommerce-stack. The prototype notebook uses browser-local storage, with Markdown export providing a portable research trail. These are materials a researcher may later cite and repurpose in their work. Challenges I ran into The central challenge was balancing agent initiative with evidentiary caution. If automation silently produced a polished conclusion, it would undermine the very research method the application was intended to support. I therefore made agent actions visible, preserved citations, labelled with levels of uncertainty, and left final decisions about retention and interpretation with the researcher. A second challenge was how to use this to communicate a complex research idea to people who might be unfamiliar with information operations or online commercial infrastructure. The interface needed to explain the research problem, but without becoming an extended essay. Stable tabs, progressive disclosure, a guided investigation, interactive stack levels, and recurring visual cues helped make the concept navigable. I also encountered practical interaction problems: controls that changed content outside the viewport, competing menus, inactive-looking buttons, responsive layouts that concealed summoned material, and panels that obstructed the evidence beneath them. Repeated browser walkthroughs helped to consolidate the navigation and make interactions produce visible, comprehensible responses. Finally, WebMCP’s emerging implementation required careful debugging. Tool registration initially produced promise rejections until execution handlers were placed correctly inside each tool definition. The repaired implementation now exposes and executes all twelve tools. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Twelve functioning WebMCP tools operate a meaningful shared page state. Agent actions are visible and inspectable rather than hidden behind a chat response. A reproducible investigation, and an agent-mediated current-research path, co-exist without being confused. External leads retain direct citations, provenance, stack positions, and reasons for inclusion. The notebook brings discoveries, research briefs, and current signals together. The six-level stack model makes largely invisible enabling infrastructure easier to understand. The interface gives newcomers several ways to explore the topic, without forcing any pre-determined conclusions. The project has developed a distinctive visual identity based on branching relationships, layered infrastructure, and colourful research artifacts. What I learned Building the instrument has become part of the research discovery for the wider project. Designing the WebMCP actions revealed where agent assistance is genuinely valuable: searching, structuring, comparing, labelling, and bringing scattered material into a common field. It also clarified where human judgement must absolutely remain explicit: assessing provenance, interpreting relationships, recognising context, and deciding whether a lead actually belongs in the research record. I learned that an agent-native interface needs more than just exposed functions. Tool descriptions, input schemas, visible state changes, reversibility, and clear feedback, all shape whether people and agents can work together successfully. Most importantly, the project demonstrated that the commercial infrastructure surrounding information operations can be made more legible without reducing uncertainty or turning a recurring pattern into an automatic verdict. What's next for Weaponised Ecommerce: The Hyphosphere Observatory This challenge entry is the first glimpse of a much larger online observatory. Future development will include: a production database for durable research records; authenticated and collaborative researcher notebooks; automated ingestion from suitable public datasets and archives; a larger reusable collection of case studies; researcher-contributed records and annotations; richer temporal and geographic analysis across local, regional, and transnational relationships; tools for observing how actors and assemblages change over time; expanded network, timeline, and stack visualisations; stronger WebMCP evaluations and security annotations; and carefully governed access to private or sensitive research collections.
