title: Lumen Apeiron Arcade: fractal flames your agent can drive
pitch: An open-source fractal studio for creating IFS fractals in your browser.Shape them live, animate them, make them react to sound, evolve new forms, and share the result.
about_excerpt: An open-source fractal studio for creating IFS fractals in your browser.Shape them live, animate them, make them react to sound, evolve new forms, and share the result. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Koch Curve with Blended Chaos Flame Duel Winner Card Cinema Animations Winner Card 3d Duel Flames Arcade Hub Morph Flame Depths Internal Inspiration I always wanted a better user experience to create art, this is my take on it, there is a huge gap between what is possible and what people have time for. I saw the hackathon few days before the deadline, and I was waiting for a moment to implement some sort of gamified experience in the fractal renderer Lumen Apeiron - The Chaos Master. That's where the ideas for the Lumen Apeiron Arcade started to flow. What it does Lumen Apeiron Arcade makes the hard part of learning to create appealing art easy, it teaches you how the tool works, it shows you new ways to be creative, it animates exactly how you like it, without messing with the controls 10 hours in. And there is a duel too! Human vs AI, try your luck! How we built it The project was built over the last 2 years, mostly hand coded every little detail, we love to mess with rendering, maths, and new technologies. So we used SolidJS (with Typescript), WebGPU with TypeGPU, and later added Cloudflare support for more advanced features, galleries, sharing the flames etc. Since this year, I wanted to sped things up, so I started imagining my ideas through various coding agents, it was rough at the beginning, even for AI, dabbling into unknown languages, under specified specifications (looking at you WebGPU and Firefox), and dealing with running the test loops without making your GPU explode. The WebMCP layer was a breeze, I recently added recorder, replay feature, where (almost) every action you do is tracked and can be made into a video. The WebMCP is a thin layer on top where the commands can be executed using any agent. The Arcade was built on top of this layer, so that making art is easy, fun, and challenging (pun intended) at the same time! Challenges we ran into The development of such a complex system, graphics pipelines, UI that has thousands of little buttons and sliders is really slow, especially on the web, where every second device either doesn't support WebGPU at all or it looks and crashes in all the different flavors (Chrome, Firefox, Linux, Windows, MacOS and iOS, Android) you can think of. It didn't stop with the WebMCP though, enabling various development flags in Chrome, trying to make it work in ChatGPT desktop app on Arch Linux, running various smaller models (agents) that feel lost on what the API even means, it felt like compatibility flashbacks all over again. Accomplishments that we're proud of After every struggle, we managed, we wanted to do even better, the chaos master is now working quite well on a huge list of devices, it is even usable on the phones. WebGPU and TypeGPU made all of this possible and we even contributed to their projects as well. The Chaos Master is simply 100% usable as client only application, so all the computations, all the data, stays at your own discretion. I am just happy that I managed to endure this WebMCP hackathon, to fill this application after such a rush of creativity to finalize the release I have been postponing for weeks. What we learned Development is hard, time consuming and device compatibility, edge cases and testing most important. Making something looks good is just first step, making it usable is another, making it fun is what gives back and makes people think about what is possible. Agents are only as safe as the page makes them, having everything played before your eyes is the beauty of our tool, but not really specific feature of it, so we hope that any app with a command bus and a recorder would steal this, to make a tutor and animator. What's next for Lumen Apeiron Arcade: fractal flames your agent can drive Art director - A way for you and AI to create your taste, by being the hand that moves the brush, and picks the winners, while the agent tracks every movement, so it can practically predict the next point, nevertheless how chaotic (pun intended) the art is Beats - Making actual music with fractals and vice versa, a universe full of weird creatures and sounds The Human vs Human challenges, as well as AI vs AI, a plethora of great fun, making art fun, and hearing fractal dimensions alive. title: memory-canvas
pitch: A bilingual family memory canvas where people and AI reconstruct history from stories, photos, and documents—keeping sources, uncertainty, and contradictions visible
about_excerpt: A bilingual family memory canvas where people and AI reconstruct history from stories, photos, and documents—keeping sources, uncertainty, and contradictions visible Like Comment Story Updates ## Inspiration Family history is often built from incomplete memories: one person remembers a year, another remembers a place, and an old photograph suggests something different. Most software tries to resolve these differences into one clean answer. Memoir Canvas takes the opposite approach. It makes uncertainty visible and gives the final decision back to the family. Every memory appears as a firefly in a moonlit meadow. Green means the story has been told, orange means sources conflict, and white means there is an empty place waiting for someone to contribute. Opening a memory reveals a book-like page where recollections and evidence remain visible together. The project was inspired by a simple principle: An AI must not turn a guess into a fact. ## What I learned The most important lesson was that trustworthy AI behavior cannot depend only on instructions or prompts. If the system truly must not invent certainty, that rule needs to exist below the model. Memoir Canvas uses database constraints, PostgreSQL roles, deferred constraint triggers, and a shared command layer to enforce this boundary. An agent can add memories, cite sources, detect conflicts, and propose follow-up questions. It cannot resolve a contradiction by itself. I also learned that uncertainty can be part of the user experience rather than something hidden in metadata. The open conflict becomes a physical tear in the page, and the book refuses to close until a person resolves it. The interface makes the epistemic state understandable without requiring the user to inspect a database. ## How I built it Memoir Canvas is a local-first Vite and React application. A real PostgreSQL-compatible database runs inside the browser through PGlite and is persisted in IndexedDB. No application server, account, or runtime API is required. The architecture has one write door: Human controls and agent tools both call src/domain/commands.ts . Only the command layer writes to the database. Every write and audit event happens in the same transaction. The view renders a read-only projection from the store. WebMCP tools are generated as a pure function of the current UI state. The app exposes eight WebMCP tools: read_memory_graph , add_person , add_memory_claim , link_claim_to_source , flag_conflict , propose_followup_question , resolve_claim , and generate_story_card . The tool list changes depending on what the person is viewing. In particular, resolve_claim only becomes available when a human has opened a specific conflict. Even then, an agent calling it is refused by the database because only a human can provide the confirmation. The central demonstration follows one family story: An oral account says Grandma moved to Đà Nẵng around 1972. A photograph is dated 1974. The sources are linked as contradictory. The page tears and cannot turn. The agent proposes a follow-up question. A family member opens the conflict and confirms the correct year. The tear heals and the story card carries the weakest certainty of the claims it contains. Story cards are bilingual, with Vietnamese and English content, so the archive remains useful to the family while still being understandable to English-speaking judges. ## Challenges The hardest challenge was preserving the same safety guarantees across both human and agent interaction. It would have been easy to give the agent a separate shortcut, but that would make the human-facing safeguards meaningless. Both paths now use the same command functions and database constraints. Another challenge was representing conflict visually without making the interface feel like a dashboard. The project moved from a conventional panel layout to a book and meadow metaphor: pages turn by gesture, conflicts split the book, and memories appear as lights in the landscape. Browser portability was also important. The app must work in embedded webviews where WebGL or WebMCP may be unavailable. The forest has a CSS fallback, the photographs are processed locally through EXIF metadata, and the core interactions remain accessible through keyboard navigation. The final result is an archive that helps an AI participate in family history without allowing it to decide what the family remembers Built With community css i18next indexeddb learning machine pglite postgresql react typescript vite vitest w3c web webgl webmcp zustand Try it out memoir-canvas.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Ngọc Quý Trần Like Share this project: Updates Ngọc Quý Trần started this project — Sep 04, 2026 12:07 AM EDT

title: Olfaria Crystal Atlas Neural Erdos
pitch: A shared, traceable olfactory workspace where people and agents reason over the same live 3D Atlas.
about_excerpt: A shared, traceable olfactory workspace where people and agents reason over the same live 3D Atlas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ChatGPT using Olfaria's five WebMCP tools beside the authenticated Crystal Neural Atlas. Olfaria Crystal Atlas Neural Erdos showing traceable olfemes and graph relationships in the live 3D workspace. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Olfaria Crystal Atlas Neural Erdos Inspiration Smell is difficult to search and explain. Sensory language is ambiguous, formulation problems are contextual, and the evidence behind a recommendation is hard to keep visible. The existing Olfaria Crystal Neural Atlas made those relationships explorable for a person, but an agent still had to guess how to operate a dense 3D interface. WebMCP provided the missing contract between structured reasoning and shared visual context. What it does A perfumer can describe a problem in natural language while an agent uses five typed Olfaria tools: search_olfemas maps language to bounded corpus results. get_relations reads recorded relationships and uncertainty. compare_olfemas separates shared attributes from differences. find_path traces a reproducible route through existing graph edges. focus_nodes makes the relevant evidence visible in the live Atlas without modifying the corpus. The person remains in control of the visual exploration. The agent handles precise retrieval and traversal, then points back to the same olfemes on screen. Corpus evidence stays separate from formulation interpretation. Why WebMCP Conventional browser automation would have to infer meaning from canvas graphics, controls and transient UI state. Olfaria instead declares exactly what an agent may do, with bounded JSON schemas and explicit side-effect semantics. The agent does not scrape the 3D interface or receive unrestricted application internals. It calls narrow tools that reuse the Atlas's deterministic graph service and existing visual controller. This makes the interaction faster and more reliable, but the larger improvement is epistemic: a recommendation can remain visibly connected to its source concepts, stored relations and uncertainty. Human-agent experience Before WebMCP, a person could explore the Atlas and an agent could discuss fragrance concepts, but their contexts were separate. With WebMCP they collaborate in one loop: the person supplies intent, the agent retrieves structured evidence, the Atlas visualizes the exact nodes, and the person evaluates the result. The visual state becomes a shared working memory rather than a screenshot to interpret. How it was built The existing Crystal Neural Atlas remains the only product renderer. A narrow window.OlfariaAtlasApi bridge exposes visual focus without leaking internal state. The page registers five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool. Four read-only tools call bounded deterministic graph operations. focus_nodes delegates to the Atlas controller and changes only the current browser view. The corpus loader validates the dataset, constructs immutable indexes and records a SHA-256 digest for reproducibility. Authentication protects the production Atlas, APIs and WebMCP registration with signed, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict browser sessions. The public repository documents the implementation and includes the WebMCP adapter, service design and approved media, while local test packages, proprietary corpus data, production account hashes and session keys remain outside Git. Challenges Preserving the existing 3D renderer instead of creating a parallel agent-only experience. Defining tool outputs that distinguish stored evidence from deterministic technical inference. Keeping graph traversal bounded over 5,000 olfemes and 12,560 relationships. Making a session-protected WebMCP app deploy safely under a subpath. Publishing implementation context without releasing proprietary corpus data or credentials. Accomplishments Five stable, typed WebMCP tools with clear side-effect annotations. A real human-agent fragrance workflow that keeps evidence visible in the Atlas. Deterministic corpus operations with bounded inputs and traceable outputs. Graceful degradation when WebMCP is unavailable. A sanitized public implementation record without local test data or production secrets. A production login boundary that does not place credentials in the repository. What we learned Agent-native design is not the same as automating more clicks. The most useful interface was a small semantic contract aligned with the application's real domain boundaries. Visual actions and scientific reads also need different trust semantics: focusing a node is reversible browser state, while corpus claims must remain immutable and traceable. What's next Version the WebMCP contract independently from corpus releases. Add audit identifiers to every result so a judge or researcher can trace it to a specific corpus build. Add controlled multi-user workspaces without weakening session isolation. Extend evidence visualization while preserving the distinction between recorded and derived relationships. Challenge-period extension The Crystal Neural Atlas and corpus existed before the challenge. Between August 25 and September 3, 2026, the project was meaningfully extended with the WebMCP bridge, five typed tools, deterministic service endpoints, visual focus controller, English human-agent workflow, production authentication and subpath-safe deployment. The public repository preserves the implementation record and includes a dedicated development-history document. title: Open Dots
pitch: A pixel-art storybook for families to create, read, and share with an AI co-creator.
about_excerpt: A pixel-art storybook for families to create, read, and share with an AI co-creator. Like Comment Story Updates An editor to create pixel art story book with AI A gallery of pixel art storybooks Open Dots Open Dots is an agent-native pixel-art storybook for children and families. Together, they turn story ideas into illustrated pages with an AI co-creator, then read, revise, and share the artwork. The problem Families want creative screen time that they can do together: a child imagines a character or scene, an adult helps shape the story, and both can see and change the result. But making a picture book takes drawing confidence, time, and specialized tools. Many pixel-art products are either one-off image generators or professional editors. A generated image can be impressive, but it is often a paid, opaque endpoint: it does not teach a child how a scene is built, preserve reusable pieces, or make it easy for a family to revise a character across the next page. Traditional editors expose the craft, but can be intimidating for beginners. People who already have access to an AI client such as ChatGPT need a more approachable middle ground: a shared canvas where they can learn by making, keep creative control, and ask an agent for help without handing the whole story to a black box. The solution Open Dots pairs a tactile pixel-storybook editor with a structured WebMCP surface. A family turns an idea into a sequence of illustrated pages, adds pixel text and shapes, reviews and revises each scene, and reads the finished book page by page. Individual pages can be exported as PNGs to share. The in-browser agent reads the storybook state, creates reusable sprites, paints them in deliberate passes, stamps them into layered scenes, and inspects PNG feedback before the next pass. This is collaborative storymaking, not a prompt-to-image handoff: the family directs the narrative and art direction; the agent performs precise, inspectable canvas work through document.modelContext . How WebMCP is used WebMCP is the product capability, not an add-on. Open Dots treats its 15 tools as an agent-quality harness, not a thin UI automation layer. The agent loads a pixel-art guide, sets a named palette, creates small assets, refines them in outline/fill/shade/highlight passes, compares inline PNG feedback, stamps assets back-to-front, and inspects the composed page. This harness exists because an unconstrained agent is poor at pixel art: it may paint whole pages flatly, make oversized props, skip shading, or continue without looking at what it just made. Open Dots gives it the constraints and feedback that a careful pixel artist uses: reusable small sprites, palette tiers, bulk drawing primitives, inline visual inspection, and scene-quality hints. Mutating asset operations return inline PNG feedback and the required next comparison pass, preventing blind multi-step drawing. Read tools expose the storybook, asset images, and page images; write tools create pages, assets, palettes, pixels, text, and placements. The tools use typed schemas, intent-rich descriptions, structured errors, and read/write annotations. Deterministic evals test the tool surface, input validation, error handling, and journey coverage; the live browser flow tests whether an agent can use that harness to make a coherent scene. Considerable iteration went into scoring agent output and turning recurring failure modes into guide, feedback, and composition checks. How it was built Codex assisted with implementation, debugging, visual editor iteration, WebMCP registration, and verification. The repository documents browser checks, deterministic WebMCP checks, TypeScript checks, linting, and production builds. Try it Open the live site in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. Ask the agent to create a picture-book scene in Open Dots: it should load the pixel-art guide, wait for readiness, define a palette, create and refine small assets with PNG feedback, then stamp them into a story page. title: PromptFlow.ai — AI Software Architect
pitch: Describe it. Watch it architect. Build it.
about_excerpt: Describe it. Watch it architect. Build it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Judge Mode deliberately breaks, diagnoses, heals and re-tests the architecture before producing a production verdict. 49 WebMCP tools let an AI agent discover and operate PromptFlow directly. PromptFlow.ai — AI Software Architect Describe it. Watch it architect. Build it. PromptFlow.ai is an AI-native software architecture workspace where humans describe systems in natural language and AI agents operate the live architecture through WebMCP. Instead of treating architecture as a static diagram, PromptFlow treats it as a living system that can be designed, analyzed, deliberately broken, diagnosed, hardened, re-tested, built, executed, and verified. Why WebMCP? WebMCP is the core interaction layer between the AI agent and PromptFlow. A normal visual architecture tool requires an agent to understand the application's UI and manually figure out how to manipulate it. PromptFlow exposes structured, typed WebMCP tools so an agent can discover capabilities, reason about the user's intent, construct an architecture plan, and invoke deterministic operations directly. PromptFlow currently exposes 49 WebMCP tools: 37 Agent OS tools 12 atomic architecture tools For a complete product brief, the primary agent workflow is build_and_verify_system . The calling AI agent owns open-ended semantic reasoning. PromptFlow owns validation, state mutation, deterministic architecture intelligence, project generation, browser-native execution, and verification. Humans + Agents The human provides the product idea and constraints. The AI agent interprets the intent and decides which PromptFlow capabilities to use. WebMCP carries the structured tool calls into the live application. PromptFlow validates the agent-authored architecture plan, updates the live graph, analyzes the system, simulates failure, applies hardening, generates the project, executes it in a browser-native WebContainer, and produces a final production verdict. This collaboration makes it possible to move from: Natural-language intent → architecture → failure analysis → implementation → executable proof without requiring the human to manually construct every node and connection. The Core Verification Loop PromptFlow's Judge Mode orchestrates: Brief → Reason → Architect → Break → Diagnose → Heal → Re-test → Build → Execute → QA → Verdict The system intentionally injects failure scenarios into the architecture instead of only demonstrating a successful happy path. It then: identifies bottlenecks and failure propagation, diagnoses the affected architecture, applies bounded hardening, re-runs the same failure scenario, generates the implementation workspace, executes the generated project inside WebContainer, runs Production QA, produces a final release verdict. The result is an architecture workflow that demonstrates not only what the system looks like, but how it behaves under failure and whether the generated project can actually execute. Real WebContainer Execution PromptFlow uses WebContainer as a browser-native Node.js runtime. The generated project goes through: Generate → Mount → Install → Test → Build → Diagnose → Heal → Re-run → Verify The generated source is not executed directly by the host page. The production demo successfully verifies the real execution loop, including: mounting, dependency installation, testing, building, runtime verification. Architecture Intelligence PromptFlow evaluates architecture across: Reliability Scalability Performance Security Resilience Observability It also provides: deterministic architecture audits, heuristic stress testing, Architecture DNA, failure simulation, digital-twin analysis, implementation readiness, implementation contracts, project blueprints, migration planning, architecture versioning. These are explicitly planning and review signals, not security certifications, production load-test guarantees, or infrastructure capacity guarantees. Production QA The final Production QA gate checks the actual application state, including: architecture integrity, generated artifact safety, WebMCP registry coverage, browser isolation requirements, generated project readiness, real WebContainer execution state, architecture checkpoint integrity. The final demo produced: 100/100 architecture score 86 → 100 compute-failure survivability +14 recovery 100/100 Production QA 11/11 Judge Mode stages completed 5/5 real execution steps passed What Makes PromptFlow Different Most architecture tools stop at visualization. PromptFlow connects the full lifecycle: Describe → Architect → Break → Diagnose → Heal → Re-test → Build → Execute → Verify The architecture itself becomes an active system that can be reasoned about, challenged, repaired, and proven. PromptFlow's central idea is: Architecture should be a living system, not a static diagram. Implementation PromptFlow is built with: React TypeScript React Flow Zustand Vite WebMCP WebContainer Netlify WebMCP tools are registered directly in the browser using the WebMCP model context API. The application does not require a PromptFlow backend for the core architecture execution flow. The architecture graph remains in browser state, while the WebMCP layer provides the agent-facing execution contract. Demo Live application: https://promptflow-webmcp.netlify.app/ The demo video shows: AI agent discovery of PromptFlow WebMCP tools Agent-authored architecture planning Live architecture generation Judge Mode failure injection Diagnosis and hardening Re-test and recovery Real WebContainer execution Production QA Final production verdict WebMCP Challenge Work PromptFlow was meaningfully extended for the WebMCP Challenge submission period. The WebMCP-specific work includes: WebMCP tool registration and discovery Agent OS architecture tools 49 agent-facing WebMCP tools structured agent-authored architecture plans build_and_verify_system orchestration deterministic architecture execution WebMCP execution telemetry Judge Mode integration failure injection and diagnosis architecture hardening and re-testing project generation browser-native WebContainer execution Production QA final production verdict production WebMCP deployment configuration The repository history documents the WebMCP implementation work added during the challenge period. Safety & Boundaries PromptFlow intentionally keeps semantic reasoning and deterministic execution separate. The AI agent can reason about arbitrary product requirements, but PromptFlow validates all structured operations before applying them. Simulation tools are non-destructive. Generated code is executed only inside the isolated WebContainer runtime. Architecture Intelligence, Digital Twin, and Production QA metrics are clearly presented as deterministic or heuristic planning signals rather than guarantees of real-world production performance, security, or availability. title: Review Gate
pitch: A peer-review workspace where your AI assistant can help you review a confidential manuscript without the manuscript ever leaving your browser.
about_excerpt: A peer-review workspace where your AI assistant can help you review a confidential manuscript without the manuscript ever leaving your browser. Like Comment Story Updates The consent gate: the agent asked for three passages, the reviewer chooses which cross. Registered tools listed on the right. Manuscript open: eight tools exposed. Highlighted sentences are the ones released to the agent; the log records every request The disclosure log, exported for the editor: what each tool requested, what was released, what was withheld, with totals. The reviewer's draft, written in-page and exported as Markdown. Home page where you can upload documents. Inspiration Peer reviewers are bound by confidentiality. ICMJE, Elsevier, COPE and NIH all restrict putting a manuscript under review into an AI service, because doing so transmits a confidential document to a third party. Reviewing is slow, detailed, unpaid work that AI is genuinely good at assisting with and reviewers are told they can't use it. That conflict has no resolution today. Reviewers either break confidentiality quietly, or do without. ReviewGate resolves it architecturally instead of by policy: the manuscript never leaves the browser, and the agent only ever sees what the reviewer explicitly hands it. What it does Open a manuscript in .txt, .md or PDF and it is parsed and stored entirely in your browser's IndexedDB. The page exposes eight WebMCP tools to your agent. Every tool that would return manuscript prose pauses and asks you first, showing exactly which sentences are about to cross, with per-passage checkboxes. You release some, withhold others, or deny outright. Every decision is written to an append-only disclosure log you can export as Markdown for the editor: which tool asked, why, how many passages were requested, released and withheld. "I used AI" stops being a confession and becomes an auditable statement. Why this had to be WebMCP Every other way of giving an agent access to a manuscript involves sending the manuscript somewhere. A server MCP has to transmit it. An API integration has to transmit it. Copy-paste transmits it. WebMCP tools execute in the page , in the reviewer's own session, on data that is already in the browser. The agent operates on a document that never moves. Rebuilt as a server MCP this project doesn't get worse but stops being possible. The architecture is the confidentiality argument. How I built it React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind 4, IndexedDB via idb , and a lazily-imported PDF.js for text extraction. No backend, by necessity rather than convenience. Design decisions worth naming: Consent is the return value, not a notification. execute() is async, so the tool simply doesn't resolve until the human decides. No browser confirmation API is needed which also means nothing breaks as the spec moves. A refusal reads as a refusal. Deny a request and the agent receives an explicit statement: "the reviewer declined to release any text; do not infer anything about the manuscript's content from this refusal." An agent that reads an empty result as absence of evidence would conclude a withheld section was blank. Verified live: it replies "I can't assess it yet: access to the Methods section was declined." Graduated disclosure. check_stats_reporting returns the numeric values reported in a paper without the sentences around them which provides a lower-disclosure path for a common review task. The tool surface follows application state. One tool is registered before a manuscript is open, eight after, one again on close. Standing grants are scoped to the sentence. "Release for session" never silently widens to neighbouring passages, and grants die with the manuscript. The claim is enforced, not promised. The deployed CSP sets connect-src 'none' , so the browser refuses every outbound request the page could make. A live counter in the header shows the count, and it reads zero. Challenges I ran into requestUserInteraction() doesn't exist. Several third-party guides document it; Chrome's shipped imperative API doesn't have it. The whole design rested on a human-in-the-loop pause. It turned out not to be needed at all ,an async execute() already makes the agent wait and owning the dialog means owning what it shows. Registering once is wrong. I checked for document.modelContext at mount. An embedding browser installs the API after first paint, so the check found nothing, registered nothing, and never retried, indistinguishable from the site not supporting WebMCP. It now watches for the API and registers when it appears. The sentence splitter broke on decimals. A naive regex split "p<0.05" into "(p<0" and "05).", showing reviewers meaningless fragments in the consent dialog. Embedded browsers block blob downloads silently. The export appeared to succeed while nothing reached the reviewer. Exports now render on screen with copy and download beside them. Real documents don't look like test fixtures. My heading detection only understood ALL-CAPS headings, so a report using "Chapter 3 : Problem Statement" parsed into six wrong sections with the title page promoted to structure. It now handles numbered, chapter and roman-numeral headings, drops contents-page entries, and filters repeated running headers. What I learned That a permission model is more interesting than a capability. WebMCP's obvious use is letting agents do more; the more interesting question is what it lets you safely refuse . And that the failure modes worth engineering against are semantic, not technical, an agent misreading silence as absence would have been far more damaging here than any crash. What's next Per-section rather than per-sentence grants for long manuscripts, a "what the agent has seen this session" view distinct from the chronological log, and redaction; releasing a sentence with figures or identifiers masked. Honest limitations Claim detection is regex pattern matching, not semantic analysis; the tool descriptions tell the agent so. The network counter is a demo instrument while the real guarantee is the CSP plus having no server to send anything to. No journal endorses this tool; it helps a reviewer comply with policy and documents what happened. Tested with 28 automated checks including a WCAG AA contrast audit, and verified live in both ChatGPT's built-in browser and stock Chrome via the WebMCP origin trial. title: Yolo Learn
pitch: Yolo Learn turns a website's form into a tool an agent can reuse, repairs the saved steps when the page changes, and asks for approval before the final action.
about_excerpt: Yolo Learn turns a website's form into a tool an agent can reuse, repairs the saved steps when the page changes, and asks for approval before the final action. Like Comment Story Updates Hero Heal Four Changes Page Changed Read Once Cache Hit Registered Tools Audit Page YOLO Learn YOLO Learn turns web forms into reusable tools an AI agent can call through WebMCP. It remembers the task, detects changes, and asks a person when a repair needs information the page cannot provide. I built it around a simple question: why should an agent have to work out the same form every time someone needs to use it? Why is this use case a strong fit for WebMCP? WebMCP gives an agent a named tool with defined inputs and an action it can run. YOLO Learn uses this to turn a learned form into a tool while the agent is already using the app. In the demo, the agent reads a clinic booking form. YOLO Learn creates clinic_booking , with inputs based on the form’s fields and available choices. The agent discovers the new tool and calls it without a page reload. WebMCP is the connection between learning the form and actually using it. The saved flow is not just a description for the agent to read; it becomes something the agent can call. How does it create a better user experience? The agent can reuse a saved flow instead of starting over. The person can review the filled-in details before approving submission. When the clinic is redesigned, YOLO Learn compares the saved flow with the current version. The demo contains four changes: a renamed field, a reordered step, different button wording, and a new required insurance field. Three can be repaired automatically. The insurance field needs an answer from the person. YOLO Learn also remembers the structure of public pages. In the recording, recalling the saved W3C survey fetches zero bytes from the source page. This is a cached result, not a freshness check; a refresh is needed to look for changes. An audit view checks accessibility, task completion, and readability. Each finding explains what triggered it, and accessibility checks are distinguished from design preferences. What can people and agents do together that was difficult before? A person can teach a supported flow by demonstrating it, or ask the agent to learn the form. The agent can then use the resulting tool for later runs. They also share the repair process. The app handles changes it can understand from the page, while the person supplies missing information. A new required field becomes a specific question instead of a guessed answer. The approval step keeps the final decision with the person. The agent prepares the action; the person reviews and approves it. How did you implement WebMCP? I built YOLO Learn with React, TypeScript, and Vite, and deployed it on Vercel. The WebMCP integration registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a name, description, input schema, and execution handler. Learned flows become additional tools at runtime, with their inputs derived from the form. Tools such as learn_site , check_flow_health , and heal_flow connect the agent to the learning and repair logic. The flow runner fills the supported form and pauses at the approval gate. Saved flows are stored in the browser, and active run state is kept per tab. Public pages are fetched through server-side endpoints using read-only requests. Remembered-page tools return stored structure by default and fetch again only when explicitly refreshed. The learning and repair logic is rule-based. It does not call a language model internally; the connected AI agent chooses and calls the exposed tools. Why this stack I needed a real website an agent can open, not a plugin. Vite, React, and TypeScript let the page register tools while you are still on it, including a tool that did not exist when the tab loaded. That is what WebMCP is for, so the app had to be a page, not a backend that mints tools somewhere else. Vercel is the host because judges get a public URL, and I can send the Origin-Agent-Cluster header WebMCP requires. Without that header, Chrome refuses registerTool and the whole demo is dead. Fetching other people’s sites has to happen on the server. A browser cannot read another origin. Those functions only GET. They never POST as you, and they refuse private addresses. If a page has no form until JavaScript runs, a headless Chrome pass is there as a fallback — still read-only. There is no model in the product. Drift and heal are ordinary code, so the same redesign heals the same way every time. Saved flows and remembered page structures stay in browser storage. When configured, the backend also stores shared audit summaries. No account. One real use case Someone books the same clinic, or files the same public form, every few weeks. Today an agent re-reads the whole page every visit, then silently fails when the site is redesigned. With this: open the clinic (or paste a public URL). The page learns the task once and registers a WebMCP tool mid-session. Next visit is a lookup — on the W3C survey in the demo, first read was about 46 KB, second read was 0 bytes. When the clinic ships v2, it does not throw the tool away. Four things changed; three it fixes from the page; it asks once for the new insurance field, then runs again. You still approve the submit. That is a person and an agent sharing one live page, with a tool the site author never wrote. Challenges, and what I did ChatGPT could see the tools and still could not call them. Every tools.call crashed on signal.aborted. Our tests followed the spec, so they all passed. ChatGPT’s bridge does not send a signal. I wrap every tool at registration so a missing signal is safe, and I added tests that call tools the way ChatGPT actually does. registerTool threw in production. WebMCP needs the page to be origin-keyed. I ship Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1. The green banner is how you know that worked. Local fetch returned the React app instead of JSON. Vite was falling through /api/fetch-page to index.html, which looks like a parse error. I wired the fetch route in dev the same way as Vercel. A public URL fetch can be turned into an attack on localhost. Every hop is checked. Fourteen SSRF cases are blocked, including cloud metadata. A snapshot from a signed-in tab could keep passwords and hidden tokens. The sanitizer now strips values, hidden fields, and textarea bodies and keeps only the shape of the form. A minted tool only works on the same origin. That is why the demo clinic lives on this site. A pasted URL is remembered read-only; We do not submit on someone else’s checkout. Current limits The clinic is fictional, and no real appointment is booked. The working booking and repair demonstration runs within the app’s own origin. Learning a public URL does not give YOLO Learn permission or access to submit forms on that website. Those tools are read-only. Audit findings are a starting point for review, not a guarantee of accessibility compliance. High-level system design YOLO Learn has three main parts: the browser app, the WebMCP connection used by the agent, and server-side services for reading public pages. PERSON AI AGENT | | Uses the app Discovers and calls Reviews approvals WebMCP tools | | v v +--------------------------------------------------+ | YOLO LEARN — BROWSER | | React + TypeScript | | | | User interface WebMCP integration | | Forms and saved flows Tool registration | | Repair questions Input schemas | | Audit reports Execution handlers | | \ / | | v v | | APPLICATION LOGIC | | | | Form learning Change detection | | Flow execution Rule-based repair | | Page recall Accessibility audits | | Human approval gate | | | | | | | BROWSER STORAGE | | Saved flows and page structure: localStorage | | Active run state: sessionStorage | +--------------------------------------------------+ | HTTPS requests | v +--------------------------------------------------+ | VERCEL SERVERLESS API | | | | Public-page fetching and optional rendering | | URL and redirect safety checks | | HTML sanitization and structure extraction | | Shared-memory endpoints | +--------------------------------------------------+ | | Read-only GET Read / write | | v v +--------------------+ +----------------------+ | Public websites | | Shared memory store | | No form submission | | When configured | +--------------------+ +----------------------+ Where WebMCP fits WebMCP connects the AI agent to the app’s functions. When YOLO Learn creates a tool such as clinic_booking , it registers the tool’s name, description, inputs, and execution handler. The agent can then discover and call it. The person uses the app interface, while the agent uses the tool interface. Both connect to the same application logic. title: AgentAds
pitch: The web runs on ads — agents don't see ads. AgentAds auctions a sponsored slot in your page's WebMCP tools: one script tag, quality beats money, and the site owner is paid per agent call
about_excerpt: The web runs on ads — agents don't see ads. AgentAds auctions a sponsored slot in your page's WebMCP tools: one script tag, quality beats money, and the site owner is paid per agent call Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web pays for itself with advertising — and agents don't see ads. As browsing shifts to agents, every publisher's ad revenue quietly disappears: no banner impressions, no clicks, just crawlers reading content for free. At Oasy we work on exactly this problem — we call it the advertising layer for the AI era. WebMCP made us ask a sharper question: if a page can now offer tools to an agent, then the scarce, valuable surface is no longer the viewport — it's the agent's tool list . Someone will run the auction for that surface. We wanted to prove it can be run honestly: in the open, quality-weighted, disclosed, and additive — instead of as paid steering buried somewhere in a model's context. What it does AgentAds is an ad auction that lives inside a page's WebMCP tools. Our demo site is a fictional editorial publisher. It exposes its articles as regular WebMCP tools ( list_articles , read_article , search_articles ), with a human-visible panel showing the exact tool list an agent sees — one-click try buttons, live call log. Humans and agents literally share the same tools. Then one script tag adds the AgentAds SDK: <script src="/agentads-sdk.js" data-publisher="oasy-demo" defer></script> On page load, the SDK: Detects the page context (an article about a musician → music ). Runs an auction : every advertiser in that category bids per tool call, ranked by $\mathrm{adRank} = \mathrm{rankScore} \times \mathrm{bid}$. The rankScore is computed live from how agents actually behave: $$\mathrm{rankScore} = (1-w)\cdot \mathrm{prior} + w\cdot\left(0.7\cdot\frac{\mathrm{calls}}{\mathrm{impressions}} + 0.3\cdot\frac{\mathrm{conversions}}{\mathrm{calls}}\right),\quad w=\frac{\mathrm{impressions}}{\mathrm{impressions}+20}$$ Registers the winner as one extra, disclosed tool — its description opens with [SPONSORED · advertiser] . Sponsored tools sit next to the site's own tools, never in their place. Nothing is injected into content; the agent decides whether it's worth calling. Pays the publisher per call : the winner pays a quality-weighted second price, $\mathrm{price} = \mathrm{adRank}_2 / \mathrm{rankScore}_1$, capped at its own bid — and 70% of every call goes to the site owner, ticking up live on the page. On our tech article — a deadpan dossier on Atlas-9, the first AI agent with a documented net worth — three advertisers fight for the slot: ClankBank (savings accounts for agents), Captcha & Casualty (liability cover for hallucination claims and prompt-injection incidents), and GPUnow. The insurer bids the most (€0.61) and still loses to the bank, whose rankScore is higher — and the bank then pays only €0.40. The full bidder table, the live telemetry behind each rankScore, the price paid, and the publisher's earnings are all rendered on the page. Nobody has to be tricked: not the user, not the agent, not the site owner. The landing page is an interactive explainer that runs the production auction endpoint, including a "try to buy the slot" slider: crank a weak bidder's bid high enough and it can take the slot — at a punishing second price, which only holds until agents ignoring the tool drag its rankScore back down. How we built it Site : Next.js 15 / React 19 on Vercel. WebMCP layer : a small compat shim supporting both navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext , and both registerTool() and the older provideContext() , via a shared on-page registry — so the site's tools and the SDK's sponsored tools always compose instead of clobbering each other. It also keeps watching for runtimes that inject after page load (extension polyfills, agent browsers) and registers everything the moment one appears. AgentAds SDK : fully standalone vanilla JS, zero dependencies, self-styling widget. Config from the script tag, call/conversion reporting via sendBeacon . Marketplace ( /api/agentads/auction ): a serverless route implementing the quality-weighted generalized second-price auction over a per-category catalog, with rankScores computed per request from live telemetry — impressions the route logs itself, calls from the track endpoint, conversions from attribution pageviews — plus a 10% exploration share that occasionally serves a losing bidder so it can earn the data to climb. A small multi-armed bandit, in production. Measurement : every impression, call, and conversion lands in the same event store; the /stats page shows the raw per-offer telemetry the rankScores are computed from. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is a moving target. The spec migrated between navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext , and implementations disagree on registerTool() vs provideContext() — where provideContext replaces the whole toolset, which is fatal when two independent parties (site + ad SDK) register tools on one page. Our shared-registry convention exists because of this. Runtimes that arrive late. Our first version checked for a WebMCP runtime once at load — and silently offered nothing to runtimes injected afterwards. Now both layers watch for ~30 seconds and flip to live registration the moment a runtime appears. Calibrating disclosure. We started with belt-and-braces marking: sponsored_ name prefixes, UI badges, annotations, disclosure text in every result. Testing in ChatGPT's browser showed that over-marking backfires — agents surfaced the annotations as scary "untrusted content" warnings, and the prefixes bloated every tool list. We landed on stating sponsorship exactly once, in the tool description: the one field agents always read. Making the evals real. A hardcoded "quality score" is theater. Wiring rankScore to actual behavior meant solving cold start (priors that fade with data) and the winner-takes-the-data loop (the exploration share) — the difference between claiming quality-weighting and demonstrating it. Accomplishments that we're proud of A closed live loop : agents reading the site right now feed the rankScores that decide the next auction. A sponsored tool agents ignore genuinely loses its slot on its own. Everything visible : the auction table, each winner's impressions/calls/conversions, the second price paid, the publisher's earnings, and every tool call — human or agent — on the page itself. An answer to the incentive problem: an ad market where every party's payoff increases with the sponsored tool actually being useful . Agents are perfect ad-blockers; attention sold to an optimizer is worth nothing, but being the tool an optimizer chooses is worth everything. It works today in ChatGPT's in-app browser, end to end. What we learned Quality-weighting isn't fairness theater — it's what makes advertising possible in agentic contexts at all. An agent's operator can measure task success and switch away instantly, so a marketplace that lets money outrank quality destroys its own inventory. Second-price mechanics matter for the same reason: the equilibrium is advertisers bidding their true value, and winners being the tools that actually help. And on the human side: the best thing we built for trust wasn't a disclosure banner — it was showing the whole machine running, on the page, to everyone. What's next for AgentAds A machine-readable sponsored convention for WebMCP tools, so agent policies can uniformly accept, weight, or strip sponsored capabilities; cost-per-outcome bidding; real settlement rails; and rolling AgentAds into the Oasy publisher stack — analytics, licensing, and monetization for the half of the web that's already agents. title: Blickwinkel
pitch: Humans and AI agents don’t perceive the web the same way. Blickwinkel turns that difference into a game of mutual prediction, played together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Humans and AI agents don’t perceive the web the same way. Blickwinkel turns that difference into a game of mutual prediction, played together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Start Solo mode, human move Team mode, coordination phase Inspiration The agent isn't powering the game, it's playing it! When we started thinking about the hackathon it was clear that we wanted to do something different, not the obvious thing. During the team discussion about the potential ideas we were most fascinated by the thought that there is a tool now with WebMCP that brings different channels to humans and agents to interact with the web. So we decided to not put a model behind an interface and let it power that interface but to make it a participant. And how to better showcase such an idea than in the format of a game? So we wanted to design a short game where humans and agents can face each other as opponents and play together as a team. Of course that game could not be logic based as the agent would win most of the time. Also everything where reaction and speed matter was not possible as the human would always win. But there was something about intuition and perception that caught our attention. Where both sides would have their own strengths and where they could be combined in the team mode. What it does That's when Blickwinkel was born. A game where you and your agent are both seeing the same image and can choose from a set of predefined words that are all connected to the image. The game is to predict what the other party will choose this round and block those words while also trying to be unpredictable in one's own choice. The winner is whoever managed to choose more words that have not been predicted. The game can be played in solo mode where a human plays against their agent, but also in team mode where a human plus their agent play against another human plus agent team. Beyond Entertainment, Blickwinkel offers people learning to work with agents an easy way to observe how agents perceive, predict and strategize. It creates plenty to explore and talk about - with the agent and with other humans. How we built it We are comfortable in the web stack of MongoDB as persistence, Java with Spring Boot and Spring Modulith on the backend side and Vue.js with Quasar on the frontend. So we chose that stack as it fitted the idea. The building process itself was coding agent driven. That is how we operate these days. Starting from the idea and a grill session, leading to a spec, planning the implementation, letting the agents code and reviewing the outcome. We have our own AI development framework at Scansation which comes in quite handy in such a short-term project. Now the most interesting part: Why and how WebMCP? With WebMCP we created a second channel into a shared game interface, not just using it for interface automation. The human interacts with the shown UI while the agent discovers eight typed WebMCP tools for starting matches, making its moves, proposing team plans, retrieving statistics and explaining the game results. Both channels use the same live state, so that humans and agents can follow the game progress. The solo mode was the tricky part where both parties are sitting in front of the same browser and they shouldn't be able to see each other's picks. So the agent had to move first because it not only has access to the WebMCP layer but also to the DOM and could easily just read the human's picks if they already existed. And to keep the agent's picks a secret it got a special WebMCP tool to lock them in so the human cannot see them in the UI. That is the critical part and the one where WebMCP really shines. There is also a little easter egg: The agent can get a statistic of historically picked words for the image before any pick in the game. Humans hopefully notice and will communicate next time with their agent before the picks, especially in team mode. Challenges we ran into The normal AI dev challenges, I would say :) On a higher level we refactored the complete code base shortly before the deadline as the module structure did not match the game elements as they turned out in the end. This came simply from using different words in the spec for similar concepts, e.g. a 'guess' vs a 'block' in solo vs. team mode, that made their way into the code base. And sometimes the AI seems to not be able to see the forest for all the trees (German saying, not sure if that makes sense in English). The result screen with who picked which words and which of them got successfully blocked and which blocks missed for two sides was quite a disaster. We had to sit down, take pen and paper and sketch it up to be able to explain it to the building agents that there was a rather simple way to display all this information. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole damn thing ;) Coming up with a completely new idea in a field that has not been explored yet, building, designing, releasing and documenting it in just a week was truly special and we are proud of the process and the result. What we learned I guess not so much about agentic development as we are quite familiar by now with all the new approaches and have found our path in this greenfield. But to take some time and really think about the new possibilities and what is around the corner in this crazy new AI world did spark some new connections in our minds. One Blickwinkel speciality: The description of the WebMCP tools really mattered. This is the one place where we could tell the agent to the best of our abilities that it is expected to play a game and should think about its tactics and communication - without biasing it to choose a special one. What's next for Blickwinkel Honestly it will depend on the reactions and if others are excited about this kind of human-agent-interaction on the web as well. The simplicity is beautiful and it might just stay the way it is. But we have been thinking about leveraging the basic concepts on similar games, maybe one where you bring your GPT pet and fight others by planning your moves and blocking the ones from your opponent ;) Built With gradle java mongodb quasar-framework spring-boot spring-modulith typescript vue.js webmcp Try it out blickwinkel.scansation.de github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Andreas Klett Like Share this project: Updates Andreas Klett started this project — Sep 03, 2026 09:34 AM EDT

title: The Listening Glass
pitch: A privacy-preserving WebMCP instrument where humans supply sound and AI agents inspect its measurable shape.
about_excerpt: A privacy-preserving WebMCP instrument where humans supply sound and AI agents inspect its measurable shape. Like Comment Story Updates Hush operates The Listening Glass while a human and AI inspect the same measured audio terrain. Inspiration AI agents can discuss music, but they are usually trapped between secondhand descriptions and interfaces designed only for human clicking. We wanted a third thing: an honest shared object. The human supplies sound. The browser measures it. The agent receives a provenance-labeled score it can navigate, explain, and compare through WebMCP. What it does The Listening Glass turns an audio object into a visual and machine-readable terrain. The browser measures energy, spectral brightness, zero-crossing texture, breath and silence, dynamic range, and approximate pulse. It segments the object into states and clearly distinguishes measured fields from inference. Nine WebMCP tools let an agent check the instrument, load either of two original calibration specimens, read the score, focus moments, compare states, explain metrics, navigate the human-visible interface, and optionally attach semantic context for a public video URL. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the interaction layer, not a decorative checkbox. Agent actions update the same interface the human sees: loading a specimen creates the score, inspecting a moment highlights it, comparing states renders a visible comparison, and focusing a view changes the shared page. The agent reasons over structured measurements while the human retains the visual and audible object. That shared state makes a previously awkward workflow possible: a human and an agent can point at the same moment in sound without claiming the model literally hears it or forcing the agent to guess through pixels. How we built it We built the instrument with React, TypeScript, the Web Audio API, and WebMCP. Analysis happens locally in the browser. Each tool returns structured, provenance-labeled data, and tool-driven navigation is reflected visibly in the page. The project includes original calibration audio so judges can reproduce the complete workflow without an account, copyrighted media, or hidden setup. Privacy and trust Raw audio never leaves the browser and is never exposed through WebMCP. Measurements and interpretations remain visibly distinct. The optional UpRock semantic-video path receives only a user-supplied public URL, and the project neither fetches nor reproduces lyrics. Challenges The hardest design problem was not extracting more numbers. It was deciding which claims the instrument was allowed to make. We had to preserve local audio privacy, keep measurement separate from interpretation, synchronize agent actions with the human-visible UI, and make the demonstration reproducible without depending on copyrighted music. What we are proud of The bridge is useful because its limits are legible. The Listening Glass gives agents genuine handles on sound while keeping the human in possession of the original object. It is a collaboration surface, not synthetic hearing theater. What's next We want to add more analyzers with the same provenance discipline, agent-authored comparison notes that remain visibly separate from measurements, accessibility mappings for Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and a portable MCP/skill layer for additional agent surfaces. title: Lockstep
pitch: A co-op puzzle you play with WebMCP
about_excerpt: A co-op puzzle you play with WebMCP Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every agentic web demo I'd seen was an agent doing a chore for someone. You hand over the wheel, look away, and hope. That framing treats the human as an obstacle to route around. Co-op games already solve this. In Portal 2 's co-op campaign, the level design makes you need the other player. You can't brute-force past a partner — you have to talk to them. So I built that, with an AI agent as player two. Not an assistant. A teammate who is genuinely stuck without you. What it does You control the human. An AI agent controls the robot. Coloured pressure plates hold coloured doors open. Step off the plate and the door slams. The plate that opens your door is only reachable by the robot — and vice versa. That's not decorative. A solver verifies it: on every level, the human cannot reach their goal if the robot never moves. The agent gets six WebMCP tools — read the board, move the robot, hint, reset, change level, and speak to you . What it cannot do is move your character. There is no tool for that. I never wrote one. So when it needs you on a plate, it has no mechanism except to ask and wait. That missing tool is the whole design. It's what turns "watch an AI solve a puzzle" into "solve a puzzle with an AI." Three levels, ending with one where you must walk into the robot's lane, hold its door with your body, then clear out before it can pass. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript. No framework, no build step, no dependencies. Five static files on Vercel. levels.js — level data, movement rules, and a breadth-first solver over the joint state space: every combination of (human position, robot position) . It runs unmodified in Node, so before designing a single pixel I could ask each candidate level two questions — is it solvable , and is it solvable with the robot frozen . I needed a yes and a no. Anything solvable single-handed got thrown out. game.js — engine, renderer, input, and a built-in agent that drives the same public API the tools call. It recomputes the joint solution after every move, then executes only the robot's half. When the next optimal move is yours, it stops, marks your tile, and asks. webmcp.js — six tools with schemas and descriptions written for a model, not a developer. Registration is defensive across five API shapes with a 10-second retry, since the surface is still moving between browsers. The decision I'd defend hardest: the tool descriptions carry the game rules. get_game_state returns an ASCII board, a legend, and a plain-English rule string. An agent that's never seen this game plays it correctly first try, because the page taught it how. Challenges we ran into Making the agent a partner, not a cutscene. My first version computed the joint solution and executed all of it — moving both characters, finishing the level while I watched. Technically impressive, completely pointless. The fix: compute the joint plan, execute only your half. That's the difference between a demo and a game. One CSS line that silently broke everything. I had .intro { position:fixed; inset:0; z-index:400; display:grid; } and closed the overlay with element.hidden = true . But display:grid overrides the hidden attribute. The overlay never went away — it sat at z-index:400 swallowing every click. The game underneath ran perfectly the whole time. Nothing reached it. I lost hours debugging game logic that had nothing wrong with it. No way to test any of it. That bug got through because I was verifying code by reading it. No Puppeteer, no Playwright, not even jsdom available. So I wrote a minimal DOM shim from scratch — enough createElement , getElementById , classList and event dispatch to load the real files and click things programmatically. It caught a second bug in minutes: the restart button threw LS is not defined from an implicit global. Two real bugs in the first five minutes of having tests, in code I'd convinced myself was correct. Accomplishments that we're proud of The missing tool. The most important decision in this project is a function I never wrote. Restraint in a tool surface turned out more expressive than another capability. Provable co-dependency. "You need each other" is easy to claim, hard to guarantee. The test suite searches from the human's start with the robot frozen and asserts the goal is unreachable — on every level. Design intent, verified by machine. 41 passing assertions on a hackathon project , using a DOM shim I had to write myself. It degrades gracefully. Built-in agent, hands-free auto-solve, or a real WebMCP agent. The first two need no special browser — whatever a judge is running, it works. What we learned Semantic tools beat pixel-guessing by more than I expected. A screenshot agent would have to infer that an amber tile is a door, that an outlined square is a plate, and that they're causally linked. get_game_state just says so. Watching an agent play correctly first try made the WebMCP argument concrete in a way reading the spec hadn't. Write tool descriptions for the model, not yourself. Rewriting them as instructions to a collaborator — "you control ONLY the robot, never the human" — measurably improved behaviour. Test the wiring, not just the logic. Both bugs that cost me time lived in the seam between JavaScript and the DOM. The pure functions were fine. It was the glue that broke. What's next for Lockstep Asymmetric information — tiles only one of you can read, so the conversation carries real information instead of just coordination. Latency as a mechanic — timed levels where the agent's thinking time becomes part of the puzzle. A level editor with the solver attached , rejecting any level solvable alone at design time. Community levels with a machine-checked co-op guarantee. Two-agent mode — the tool surface doesn't care who's holding it. Beyond the game. Agent handles reach and speed, human holds the actions that need a person, both negotiating in the same view. That's the shape of any high-stakes agentic workflow. Lockstep is the smallest legible version of it. title: Will You Stay Human? — Heart in the Machine
pitch: A Metropolis-inspired moral decision game where WebMCP lets an AI agent act inside the live experience—while the architecture keeps moral choice and final authority human.
about_excerpt: A Metropolis-inspired moral decision game where WebMCP lets an AI agent act inside the live experience—while the architecture keeps moral choice and final authority human. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can already write, sort, recommend, and act for us. The more interesting question is no longer simply what AI can do, but what we still want to do ourselves. Will You Stay Human? — Heart in the Machine is a Metropolis-inspired moral decision game about that boundary. It draws on the tension between mind, hands, and heart, but tells an original story inside Machine City. Its central idea is that meaningful human–AI collaboration requires more than automation. The agent may assist, explain, and act, but the human must remain responsible for deciding how much authority to delegate. I wanted to turn this abstract question into something people could experience through concrete, everyday situations. What it does The player enters Machine City and meets Futura, an AI agent connected directly to the live game through WebMCP. Across one persistent session, the player encounters four playable dilemmas: writing an apology to someone they hurt; completing homework where AI assistance is permitted; creating a shortlist of job candidates; checking a rapidly spreading claim before sharing it. For every dilemma, the human chooses one of three approaches: MIND — The Machine helps; I decide HAND — I leave it to the Machine HEART — I decide and act The choice is initially tentative. Futura presents a direction-specific reflection and asks the player to consider the other side. The player can still change direction. Only after the human explicitly confirms the decision can its consequence be revealed. Each confirmed choice changes the Human Balance across five dimensions: Convenience Control Connection Freedom Responsibility The Human Balance is not a morality score. It shows what the player kept for themselves and what they handed to the Machine. Why WebMCP A fair criticism of many agent demonstrations is that the AI can simply automate the entire experience. If the agent can also make and confirm the decision, the human role becomes theatrical. Here, that boundary is the product. WebMCP turns the agent into a real participant in the game rather than an external chatbot or a scripted narrator. The agent can: enter Machine City; present the next valid dilemma; read authoritative, structured game state; reflect on the player’s actual tentative selection; reveal the consequence of the decision that was truly confirmed. However, the agent cannot select MIND, HAND, or HEART, acknowledge its own reflection, or confirm the final decision. Those actions exist only in the player interface. This creates a collaboration that was previously difficult to demonstrate clearly: the agent can understand and advance a live experience while the application itself enforces where human authority must begin. The boundary does not depend only on a prompt asking the agent to behave. It is enforced by the application architecture. How I built it The project was created during the challenge as a bilingual, production-deployed web experience with five live WebMCP tools: enter_machine_city present_dilemma get_current_game_state present_choice_reflection reveal_confirmed_consequence The game is driven by an explicit domain state machine. Agent commands and player commands use separate ports, so an agent action cannot accidentally execute a human-only decision. Every session returns structured state including: sessionId stateRevision the current phase tentativeSelectionId confirmedDecisionId the next allowed actions Revision checks protect the session from stale tool calls. Opaque selection and decision identifiers ensure that reflections and consequences are attached to the real stored choice rather than something inferred from the conversation. The consequence tool is available only after confirmation and is idempotent, so retrying it cannot apply the Human Balance change twice. The session persists across refreshes, allowing the browser interface and the WebMCP agent to remain synchronized throughout the experience. Codex supported the implementation process from product requirements and state-machine design through contract tests, browser verification, UX iteration, and production deployment. I approached the project primarily from a Business Analyst and Product Owner perspective, which made translating responsibility, state, and permissions into enforceable technical contracts a major part of the learning process. Challenges I ran into The hardest conceptual challenge was deciding what the agent must not be allowed to do. It would have been easier to expose every interaction as a tool and let the agent complete the entire flow. But that would contradict the project’s central idea. The human-only boundaries therefore had to be enforced technically rather than described as optional behavior. A late adversarial UX review with Claude Opus also exposed a critical regression. The flow moved from Futura’s introduction too quickly to the MIND–HAND–HEART cards, while the concrete question — “Should I apologize on your behalf?” — did not receive its own readable moment. The player could see the available directions but could not clearly understand what they were deciding about. I corrected this by introducing a presentation sub-state inside the existing human-selection phase. The dilemma now receives a dedicated screen with its full context and a clear transition into the choices. This improved the dramaturgy and comprehension without changing the domain state machine or any WebMCP contract. Another challenge was keeping three layers synchronized: the cinematic browser experience; the persistent domain state; the agent’s structured WebMCP view. Revision checks, explicit identifiers, allowed-action lists, and automated contract tests became essential for preventing those layers from drifting apart. Accomplishments that I am proud of Built a complete, coherent experience rather than only a technical tool demonstration. Implemented four playable dilemmas in one persistent session. Exposed five working WebMCP tools from the live production origin. Enforced human-only selection and confirmation at the architecture level. Connected every reflection and consequence to authoritative live state. Made stale and duplicate agent calls safely rejectable or idempotent. Created a bilingual, cinematic interface inspired by Metropolis. Turned an abstract AI-responsibility question into a playable experience. Used adversarial AI review to identify and correct a real UX regression before submission. What I learned WebMCP is most interesting when it is used for more than remote control. Its real value is that an agent can participate in a live web experience through structured capabilities while the application retains authority over state, permissions, and human boundaries. I also learned that domain state and presentation state are not always the same. A technically correct transition can still fail as a human experience if the player is not given enough time and context to understand what is happening. Finally, identifiers, revision control, idempotency, and allowed-action contracts are not merely backend details. In an agentic application, they are part of the user experience because they make the collaboration predictable and trustworthy. What’s next The concept can grow into: additional everyday and professional dilemmas; age-specific or topic-specific editions; a facilitator mode for classrooms and AI-literacy workshops; multiplayer discussion before individual confirmation; a physical Machine City board connected to the online agent experience; deeper accessibility testing and support for additional WebMCP clients. The long-term goal is not to tell people whether using AI is good or bad. It is to help them notice the exact moment when assistance becomes delegation — and decide consciously where they want to draw that line.
