title: Counterfactual
pitch: See your future before you choose it. Name a big decision, watch it branch into possible paths, protect what matters, and decide with an agent by your side.
about_excerpt: See your future before you choose it. Name a big decision, watch it branch into possible paths, protect what matters, and decide with an agent by your side. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Dynamic paths Home page Flight Recorder for tool calls Decisions, assumptions, and goals Testing with WebMCP tools Chrome extension Tutorial mode Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of taking actions across the web, but users do not always get a clear picture of the consequences before those actions happen. A decision like buying a car can affect several competing goals at once, yet most financial tools reduce that complexity to a single static calculation. I built Counterfactual around a simple question: what if an agent could show you several possible futures before asking you to commit to one? Instead of immediately executing an action, Counterfactual gives the agent and user a shared space to explore alternatives, revise assumptions, understand tradeoffs, and decide together which future—if any—should become real. What it does Counterfactual is a WebMCP-powered decision simulator and permission layer for the agentic web. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can discover structured tools exposed by Counterfactual, read the user's financial assumptions, create alternative scenarios, simulate their outcomes, and compare them. Counterfactual turns those scenarios into explorable futures with dynamic visualizations that show how each decision affects the user's finances and protected goals. Users can change an assumption at any time and immediately see every future recalculate. A built-in WebMCP Flight Recorder makes the agent's behavior visible by recording each tool it discovers and invokes, along with its arguments, risk level, origin, status, and results. Rather than receiving only the agent's final recommendation, users can inspect the actual sequence of actions that produced it. Most importantly, Counterfactual distinguishes between exploring a future and making it real . Read-only and simulation tools can run freely, but when an agent attempts a consequential action, Counterfactual pauses execution and requires explicit human approval. The result is a simple principle: agents can explore autonomously, but humans retain control over commitment. How I built it I built Counterfactual with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and client-side state . Its scenario engine uses deterministic calculations so the agent's conclusions and the visual interface always operate from the same source of truth. Counterfactual exposes structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . These include tools for reading financial state, defining a decision, protecting goals, creating scenarios, comparing outcomes, simulating purchases, and committing to a selected scenario. Each tool has a natural-language description, JSON Schema input definition, validation, and metadata describing its behavior and risk. To support browsers that do not yet implement WebMCP natively, Counterfactual uses the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill package. A thin compatibility layer detects the available context—native, polyfilled, legacy, or fallback—and registers the same tool surface against it. Every invocation, whether initiated manually or by an external agent, passes through the same execution and logging pipeline. Calls are timestamped and risk-tagged before appearing in the Flight Recorder. Consequential actions go through an additional policy and approval layer before they can modify committed state. The approval is tied to that specific proposed action, preventing an agent from silently turning a simulation into a real commitment. I also tested the WebMCP integration end-to-end using Google's webmcp-evals CLI. That testing uncovered an issue that was invisible through Counterfactual's own UI but appeared when a tool was invoked through the actual WebMCP path. Fixing it helped ensure the project works through the protocol itself rather than only through a scripted demo. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was building against an experimental standard whose API and browser support are still evolving. Counterfactual needed to target the current document.modelContext API while remaining usable in browsers and agents relying on earlier or unsupported implementations. Another challenge was maintaining a single source of truth across the agent, editable controls, scenario calculations, visual branches, and Flight Recorder. A tool call could not simply generate an answer—it had to operate on the same live state the user was seeing and immediately update the rest of the experience. The final challenge was designing meaningful human oversight without making the agent feel unnecessarily constrained. Requiring approval for every tool call would defeat much of the value of an agent, while allowing every action to execute automatically would remove meaningful user control. Counterfactual therefore treats risk as a gradient: agents can read, simulate, fork, and compare independently, while actions that create real commitments stop at the point where human judgment matters most. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that Counterfactual uses WebMCP as a core interaction model , rather than adding it as a superficial integration. The agent does not simply fill out a form or operate a scripted demo—it collaborates with the user inside a shared decision environment. I also built a complete flow from tool discovery → simulation → comparison → recommendation → approval . Users can see what the agent is doing, inspect how it reached its recommendation, modify the assumptions themselves, explore alternative futures, and ultimately reject or approve the proposed action. Most importantly, Counterfactual turns an abstract AI safety problem into something tangible: consequential agent actions become forkable futures that people can inspect before making them real. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is more than a reliable way for agents to interact with websites. It can enable entirely new forms of human-agent collaboration . Structured tools allow an agent and an interface to share the same capabilities and application state without relying on fragile DOM interpretation or browser automation. I also learned that confirmation alone is not enough to provide meaningful user control. Before approving an action, people need to understand what they are approving, which goals may be affected, what alternatives exist, and whether the action can be reversed. Building Counterfactual showed me how structured tool schemas, deterministic application logic, risk classification, and visual design can work together to make agent behavior more transparent, understandable, and trustworthy. Why my use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Many agent experiences focus on reading the web: searching, summarizing, and answering questions. Counterfactual focuses on the harder problem— what happens when an agent can act on something that matters? That is where WebMCP becomes especially valuable. Counterfactual's decision process maps naturally onto a set of well-defined tools such as get_financial_state , define_decision , set_protected_goal , fork_scenario , compare_scenarios , and commit_scenario . Those tools also span a genuine risk gradient. Reading financial state is fundamentally different from simulating a hypothetical decision, and both are fundamentally different from committing to one. Counterfactual uses that distinction to determine when an agent can proceed independently and when control must return to the user. Instead of bolting permissions onto a chat interface after the fact, the application's capabilities, schemas, risk levels, and guardrails are part of the same structured tool environment the agent discovers and uses. How it creates a better user experience Instead of interacting with a black box that eventually reports, "I looked into it and think you should wait," Counterfactual lets the user see what the agent actually explored. Each hypothetical future becomes a visible branch with its own projected balance, goal impact, and explanation. The Flight Recorder shows the sequence of tool calls that produced those futures, including their arguments, risk levels, and results. That makes questions like "Why did the agent recommend this?" answerable by inspecting what actually happened rather than trusting a secondhand explanation. Counterfactual also includes a Manual Tool Console that lets users invoke the same tools themselves through the same schemas and Flight Recorder pipeline. The human and the agent are therefore operating the same system rather than two separate interfaces. And when an action would turn a hypothetical future into a real commitment, execution stops. Counterfactual shows the consequences and requires explicit approval before anything changes. The user sees the future before they inherit its consequences. title: AI Delegation Boundary
pitch: A WebMCP-powered system for defining, challenging, and approving where agent autonomy ends and human authority begins.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered system for defining, challenging, and approving where agent autonomy ends and human authority begins. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT works through WebMCP tools while the web app retains delegation state and human authority. The workspace guides each Human-Agent handoff while keeping the delegation boundary and approval state visible. Inspiration AI agents are increasingly able to make decisions and take action across real workflows. As their autonomy grows, a harder question follows: Where should agent authority end, and where should human authority begin? AI Delegation Boundary began as a way for us to understand WebMCP by building with it. While developing the project, we realized that WebMCP could support more than letting an Agent operate a web page. The web application could hold the current boundary, constraints, human judgments, and approval state, while the Agent reasons and acts through tools exposed by that page. That led to the core idea: Make AI delegation itself something a human and an Agent can examine, challenge, revise, and approve together. What it does AI Delegation Boundary helps a human decide what an AI Agent may do on its own. A human first defines the work being considered. The Agent then uses WebMCP tools exposed by the page to: Inspect the current delegation boundary. Propose a revision. Challenge that revision with a concrete scenario. Re-test it against Guardrails and previous human decisions. Inspect the revision history and current state. When the Agent finds a case that requires judgment, it stops and returns control to the human. The human decides whether that case should be: Agent-only Human review Not delegated That judgment becomes a regression test for future revisions. The collaboration loop is: Proposal → Challenge → Human Judgment → Re-test → Human Approval → Apply The Agent cannot approve its own revision. Only the exact revision explicitly approved by the human can be applied. How we built it AI Delegation Boundary is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP, and is deployed on GitHub Pages. The web application holds the delegation boundary, Guardrails, human judgments, revision state, approval, and applied state. WebMCP exposes five normal tools to the Agent: Inspect the delegation workspace Propose a boundary revision Challenge the current revision Review the current revision Inspect revision history After the exact current revision receives explicit human approval, an additional apply capability becomes available. There is no dedicated AI backend. The conversational Agent works directly through the WebMCP tools exposed by the page. Our architectural principle is: Conversation is the Agent; state and authority live in the web app. Review combines three different controls: Guardrails — deterministic invariants that must not be violated Known Decisions — previous human judgments preserved as regression tests Agent Challenges — concrete scenarios generated to actively challenge the current boundary Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not exposing tools to an Agent. It was designing the authority model around them. We needed to ensure that the Agent could propose and challenge changes without granting itself additional authority. We also had to make sure that: human judgments became reusable tests, a changed boundary required a fresh Agent Challenge, approval referred only to the exact state the human reviewed, and an Agent could never silently approve or expand its own authority. Another challenge was the Human-Agent handoff. We did not want users to type tool names, revision numbers, or challenge scenarios manually. The browser therefore tells the user what happens next, where the next action takes place, and provides copy-ready handoffs when control moves back to ChatGPT. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete Human-Agent governance loop through WebMCP. The Agent can inspect, propose, challenge, and re-test changes to its delegation boundary, while the human retains final judgment and approval. Human judgments do not disappear after one decision. They become regression tests that constrain future revisions. We also made the Agent capability surface depend on human authority: five normal tools are available during collaboration, and the apply capability becomes available only after explicit human approval of the exact current revision. Most importantly, WebMCP is not used here simply as a remote-control layer for a website. It is part of the mechanism that separates Agent action from human authority . What we learned Building AI Delegation Boundary changed how we think about WebMCP. The interesting part is not simply that an AI Agent can operate a website. A web application can hold state, constraints, and authority while an Agent reasons and acts through that surface. This allows the collaboration itself to be designed: what the Agent may change, what it must challenge, when it must stop, what only a human may decide, and when additional capability may become available. For us, WebMCP became a way to connect Agent reasoning with a governed web surface. What's next for AI Delegation Boundary AI Delegation Boundary is a focused implementation of a broader problem we are exploring through SOLIFAN and ReadinessOps: How can organizations expand the practical use of AI Agents while deliberately retaining the judgments and authority that should remain human? Next, we want to connect this model to real organizational workflows, richer evidence, additional delegation factors, and reusable governance patterns across different Agent environments. The long-term goal is to make Agent authority something organizations can deliberately: Design → Test → Approve → Evolve Built With chatgpt github react typescript vite vitest webmcp Try it out solidfdn.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I conceived AI Delegation Boundary and built the project end to end, from the Human-Agent authority model and WebMCP architecture through implementation, testing, UX refinement, documentation, and the final demo. title: Ordering an Endotoxin Assay from My Lab Notebook
pitch: Allowing agents to order and interpret the results of a routine biochemical assay.
about_excerpt: Allowing agents to order and interpret the results of a routine biochemical assay. Like Comment Story Updates "Notebook paired". This means a session exists between the lab notebook and chatGPT browser ClearSignal. The price from the website is quickly found and quoted via webMCP `quote_endotoxin_tests`. The lab notebook can receive status updates. Order ID available for confirmation. Results page shows actionable data and the standard curve. All in the lab notebook. Inspiration Life sciences labs sell services to other labs. One of those services is the endotoxin detection assay. An assay is a test. Endotoxin is a molecule from bacteria that can cause fevers in humans and other animals. Labs producing a product like a vaccine or a protein want to ensure their product is free of endotoxin. Detecting endotoxin is a routine, well-known biochemical assay that uses horseshoe crab blood or a protein from horseshoe crab blood. The problem is that this simple test is encumbered with difficulty. 1) A researcher who wishes an endotoxin test must search online for a provider. 2) The researcher "reaches out" through a site request form or by email or by phone calling another human. 3) The researcher and provider discuss terms: how many samples, how often, customization, etc. 4) The providers gets back in a few days with a quote. 5) The researcher agrees to the quote, signs it, sends it back. 6) The researcher prepares the samples and mails them 7) Samples are received and processed, usually 3-5 business days. 8) Provider sends email saying samples have arrived and are being processed. 9) Results are sent, usually by email, in a pdf. Fancy provider labs have the researchers create an account and sign in to download a pdf. 10) Researcher combs through 5-8 pages of lot numbers and temperature settings to find the 3 or 5 datapoints that are actionable, i.e. "Endotoxin < 0.05 EU/mL". I want to condense the above steps to one step: A researcher uses their lab notebook to order an endotoxin test. And then I want every lab in the world to join us. Every lab selling their specialized assay order-able, update-able and interpretable with webMCP-enabled sites. This is the Federated Cloud Laboratory Network. Materials Needed 1) chatGPT desktop with browser and webMCP enabled. 2) Obsidian, https://obsidian.md/ 3) Obisidian plugin, "ClearSignal Lab Assistant", https://github.com/har1eyk/clearsignal-lab-assistant 4) Lab notebook page for testing (any markdown file will do!) 5) ClearSignal access, https://clearsignal-gray.vercel.app/ 1) user: endo@toxin.com 2) pass: horseshoe What it does A researcher keeps a lab notebook in a markdown file. A markdown viewer like Obsidian is used. Obsidian can use plugins for beyond-markdown functionality. I created a plugin that allows a researcher to call for an endotoxin assay test from their lab notebook using three backticks. After the backticks, "clearsignal" is typed and a researcher can request: Order an endotoxin assay on two samples if the price is less than <$500. The sample IDs are: "ID-0001 and ID-0002". Then, the plugin begins a session with chatGPT's browser and the ClearSignal site. The webMCP-enabled site can easily find the endotoxin-per-sample-cost and report it. The quote is provided to the lab researcher in their notebook! Additionally, the researcher can also ask questions in their original prompt like: Can I send in plasmid samples? (Plasmids are circular pieces of DNA purified from bacteria.) The webMCP-enabled site answers it directly from the FAQ. No hunting and clicking for the page and the question. Save those tokens with webMCP. Lastly, the researcher's samples are loaded and the price is visible. The final "submit" creates the order. Order information is transmitted to the lab notebook. Status updates are also provided. In this demo version, status updates occur every few seconds. In real testing conditions, the status updates occur every few days. I like that when the testing is "complete", that endotoxin concentration and standard curve data is sent to the lab notebook so the researcher can take actionable next steps. Table 1: Time Savings with WebMCP-enabled ClearSignal Site With WebMCP Without WebMCP Calls quote_endotoxin_tests with two sample IDs Has to navigate forms, locate fields, type IDs, submit, and inspect the rendered result Receives exact fields such as unit_price: 375 and total: 750 Extracts prices from page text and infers which numbers represent unit price and total Automatically returns structured events to the Obsidian note Require a separate copy/paste or integration workflow How we built it 1) Building landing page. Paper and ChatGPT desktop 2) Build backend (postgres, Supabase) 3) Create login page 1) successful via chatGPT sites 2) successful via localhost 4) Create user dashboard or login landing page 5) Create order page, make it webMCP enabled 1) Human successfully order via chatGPT site? 2) Human successfully order via localhost? 3) Bot successfully order via chatGPT site? 1. Logged in (success) 2. Not Logged in (success) 4) Bot successfully order via localhost? 1) Logged in (can't get chatgpt plugin to use webmcp; uses navigation.) 2) Not Logged in 6) Build Obsidian plugin 7) Publish website (Vercel) 8) Use Obsidian plugin chatbot to order via published clearsignal site 1) get status updates from backend 2) Upon status update "Complete", Obsidian plugin connection automatically closes. 9) Generate supabase cronjob to process all the order sequences steps for demo purposes. Real testing takes days/weeks. 10) Next Steps: Use Benchling plugin to order via published clearsignal site Challenges we ran into Lots of hard parts here. Some we overcame, some we patched, and some we're leaving for later. Overcame 1) How do we get markdown to chat with a website? Answer: The Obsidian plugin routes with chatGPT desktop session which connects to the webMCP-enabled site. 2) How do we get so much sci-knowledge into webMCP? Even a simple test like the endotoxin assay can have dozens of questions from researchers, e.g. Do samples need to be aqueous? Do you perform dilution series? What about inhibition? Answer: this one was easier to solve than expected. Having a FAQ list and then loading the questions and answers into get_endotoxin_faqs was a nice, quick way to help find answers. I imagine an entire page of FAQs with every question a researcher has every asked easily navigable with webMCP. 3) How do we show a quote, order updates and results? Answer: we instantiate a session between Obsidian plugin and chatGPT desktop. Quotes, results and updates are added to the lab notebook. Patch 1) Chrome chatGPT extension with sites-enabled still did not invoke some of webMCP items on ClearSignal. For isntance, sometimes I would ask "What is the cost per sample?" and the extension would show a pointer and click around until it found a price. Lots of troubleshooting later, I realized that chatGPT desktop web interface behaves different than Chrome websites with chatGPT extension enabled. So, I continued to use chatGPT desktop. Future Work 1) The site still relies on chatGPT desktop. Can we make an Obsidian Plugin chatGPT API and bypass chatGPT desktop? Still, how do we sign off on the ordering step. 2) Right now the order status come in a few seconds after each other, e.g. "in_preparation", "in_testing", etc. These updates typically occur every couple of days. How do I keep a Obsidian-plugin-chatGPT session going that long? I probably can't. I need to build out the plugin to do periodic polling probably via REST API or webhook. 3) I would love to see this in popular Lab notebook like Benchling and Notion. Custom plugin for each? Chrome extension? 4) What would it take to let every biotech lab sell and describe their assays to researchers and their agents so that they can be ordered from a lab notebook? Accomplishments that we're proud of Two that I'm proud of: 1) Quotes, ordering, questions, updates and results are all incorporated into the lab notebook. Having all these timestamped updates and results in one place with a collapsible menu is so fun! 2) Using webMCP on a science site as a way to quickly arrive at answers like cost and sample criteria will save days of back-and-forth clarification and negotiation. What we learned 1) The FAQ lives on. 2) All scientists should be keeping a lab notebook in mardown. 3) Obsidian is a fabulous markdown viewer. 4) There are important webMCP differences between chatGPT desktop browser and Chrome chatGPT extension. What's next for Endotoxin Let's help all researchers order all assays via their lab notebooks! title: EventReady
pitch: Hiring vendors for an event is the part everyone knows how to do, and EventReady helps. The harder part is whether all of it holds together on the day, and that is what it keeps track of.
about_excerpt: Hiring vendors for an event is the part everyone knows how to do, and EventReady helps. The harder part is whether all of it holds together on the day, and that is what it keeps track of. Like Comment Story Updates Developer docs covering the nine WebMCP tools, the session they share with the UI, and the trust boundary that keeps vendor text as data. Source compares real service plans built from eight provider contracts, showing coverage, cost and coordination burden for each. A plan chosen through the WebMCP tools rather than the UI. The agent selected it and the interface you are watching updated with it. Describe an event and EventReady plans it, then tells you whether all the pieces actually work together on the day. The run of show after an agent assigned every open responsibility. Readiness reached Ready to run and the day has a real timeline. Inspiration I was inspired by my day job and my hobby, as they both played a part to this idea. I work for a major grocery retailer that does catering, and we'll be launch a AI concierge chat bot soon. Watching that come together, I ultimately thought I could do better. It helps you build a basket inside one catalog, and you make a purchase. Easy peasy right, but what if your event requires purchasing and coordination across multiple vendors? You've got food from one vendor, tables from the venue, a friend driving warming trays across town, and there's no single place that knows whether all of it adds up. The other half comes from concert photography. I shoot live music, which puts me in the parts of a venue an audience never sees, watching how a show actually gets run. Big events don't go well because every vendor is good. They go well because somebody's holding and coordinating across the seams. Who's where at what time, what happens when the truck's late, who owns the thing nobody put their name on. That work is coordination, and it's almost never written down anywhere. EventReady points those two observations at the same problem. Hiring people for your event is the part everyone already knows how to do. The part that goes wrong is everything between them. What it does You describe the event, and EventReady walks it through five phases. Shape the brief, source the services, coordinate the owners and the money, close the gaps, then run the day. The piece I care about most is the readiness layer. It reads what each provider has actually committed to, works out what that leaves uncovered, and tells you plainly what isn't going to work. Nobody's bringing the warming trays. The transport window doesn't fit the service time. Four responsibilities don't have an owner at all. Coordinate shows that as two columns, everything without an owner on the left and everything settled on the right, and a card crosses over the moment somebody takes it. Run turns the whole thing into a printable run of show with a real timeline. The agent side isn't a second product. Nine WebMCP tools sit on document.modelContext , and they mutate the same EventSession the visible interface renders. An agent can assess readiness, compare plans, change the service level, assign an owner, or pull the run of show, and you watch it happen in the UI. Every change writes a decision receipt with before and after cost, coverage, ownership and readiness, so you can see what a tool call actually did instead of trusting that it did something. How I built it Using a combination of Codex and Claude Code. Deployed onto Vercel. Challenges I ran into Mostly compounding defects working across two different agents and environments. I have multiple setups and the commits and merges kept colliding. So I had to hand a lot of the refinement and polish more to Claude Code as Codex was really churning. Codex was mainly where I tested the WebMCP protocol in the in app browser. Accomplishments I'm proud of I was able to get a viable working concept up and running pretty quickly. Even though it's not perfect, with some additional tuning it could be really helpful with tons of integration potential across a variety of cases and industries. What I learned Most of what an agent does on the web today is guesswork. It reads rendered text, infers structure that was never declared, and hopes the number it pulled off the page is the number the page actually meant. That's slow, it burns context on markup that carries no meaning, and it's wrong often enough that you can't trust it with anything that matters. WebMCP flips that. The page declares what it can do and what it knows as narrow typed contracts, so the agent reads a structure instead of reverse engineering one. Nine outcome shaped tools replaced what would otherwise be thousands of DOM nodes to crawl and guess at. The agent doesn't ask what's on the screen, it asks whether the event is ready, and gets back a typed answer with coverage, blockers, ownership and timing already resolved. The accuracy gain matters more than the speed. Because the tools mutate the same session the interface renders, the agent and the person are reading one number, not two that drifted. There's no second pipeline to keep in sync and no chance the agent reports a total the screen disagrees with. I built a source gradient demo to check this properly, comparing what's knowable from WebMCP tools against schema.org markup, a plain price table, a document transcript, and a provider that publishes nothing. The difference isn't subtle. Structured capability is the only one of those that lets you act with confidence rather than infer and hope. The part I didn't expect is that structure is also what makes safety possible. When provider data arrives in fixed declared fields, you can draw a hard line between data and instruction, because you know exactly which bytes are which. Free text gives you nothing to defend. My hostile vendor fixture is only defeatable because its blurb is a field with a known role, so a sentence aimed at the agent can be quarantined instead of obeyed. Standardizing the shape of the data is what made the trust boundary enforceable at all. What's next for EventReady Scale to make it functional end to end. Full catalogs and payment processing? Provenance on every row, so you can see which obligations the engine derived from a contract and which ones a person added. Real provider handoffs behind the copy-the-checklist step. And multi-device collaboration, which is honestly the whole point of coordination work and the one thing this build deliberately doesn't claim to do yet. title: Form Less
pitch: Turns a complex service into a personal interface built for the user's needs.
about_excerpt: Turns a complex service into a personal interface built for the user's needs. Like Comment Story Updates The initial form The simplified version based on the agent's contextual understanding of the user The final submitted version with MCP logs Inspiration I feel like most people who are technically oriented have at some point - and maybe with increased frequency - have found themselves frustrated with tech interfaces they encounter in their daily lives. Custom car interface software is a classic example, a needlessly long web form is another (as someone with ADHD I could go on for hours about other examples personal to me). But what if the interface adapted based on the personal facts about you, as well as your current intention? Most commercial consumer AIs have a memory feature these days, and most consumers are starting to get the reflexive habit of treating their AI not just as a chatbox, but as a companion that can be present when they need - so how can we get the agent to help in the example of a confusing interface that sits between a user and the problem they need solved/communicated? What it does Form Less shares the website's rules and structure with the user's agent, so that the agent can adapt its interface around what the user actually needs to do. To better demonstrate the functionality of Form Less, I built an example site/form: an application for repair support in the fictitious area of Alderwick. The default form - being a relic from days where the application was manual and has just been directly ported to a web version - can appear quite intimidating and confusing. But Form Less, via WebMCP, can take the user's specific situation into account and show them only what's necessary and what they need to understand and submit their application. The user would describe their situation to their agent, e.g. showing it a photo of the damage/what needs repairing, and the agent would The purpose isn't to complete the form for the user - not to 'remove thought' - but to present it and communicate it in a way that helps the user understand exactly what's being asked, and what they're submitting. So Form Less is the reusable WebMCP pattern behind that helps an agent to help its human navigate UIs How we built it It's a static React/Typescript application in 3 layers: The JSON schema defines the 34 questions and answer types The UI schema defines the complete form and the focused layouts that are permitted A rules document handles the expansions and checks with more complex conditional branches. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was product design, and thinking about the wider nature of the interaction between a human and their agent. It would be technically trivial to also expose submission tools to the agent, but I explicitly scoped it behind this. I didn't want it to be a 'form completer' kind of tool, but something to help the user better understand the issue I also wanted to make it technically easy for a site to implement - so the form and the agent's understanding is driven by the form's schema, so it learns the rules and requirements from the form's rules itself, so that a human 'deploying' it doesn't have to think and basically rewrite the rules of the form - no additional thinking/labour required here. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud of the general idea and design of the execution. It's not just a one-time form-restyler, or 'get an agent to fill out a form for you', but a general approach that bridges the human-agent connection and the agent-browser connection, which I think is exactly what WebMCP enables. Providing the agent with structured JSON gives it the form's design and its rules, so that if a site wanted to adopt it, they wouldn't have to spend extra time explicitly rewriting the form's rules, and also passes the principle that if the form is correctly built, the agent will correctly understand it. What we learned I realised that the difficult/interesting part of webMCP is deciding what tools you want to expose, and how they relate to the visible interface and the authority they should share. My initial conception of WebMCP was that it was just a more reliable way for an agent to do browser tasks like fill in fields. But then I realised you can communicate a lot more in terms of structure and logic that unlocks a lot more possibility for the agent to enhance the experience for the user. What's next for Form Less Alderwick's one example of making it easier for people to fill out a complex form, but the whole point of Form Less is that the general approach can be applied to many other areas Built With react typescript vite webmcp Try it out fortydegrees.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Pratt Like Share this project: Updates David Pratt started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:59 AM EDT

title: Gigr
pitch: Verified people. Safe payments. And an AI that makes hiring as easy as texting.
about_excerpt: Verified people. Safe payments. And an AI that makes hiring as easy as texting. Like Comment Story Updates Gigr home screen dashboard Autonomous AI agent performing tasks for user. Mobile view of dashboard. Mobile view of services. Profile of a user. ChatGPT using the WebMCP in Gigr to do tasks. Inspiration Two experiences I had in my country made me build this project. The first: my leaking bathroom sink and a phone full of unanswered "does anyone know a plumber?" messages. Nobody I knew around me could name a plumber they trusted, and the strangers I found online did not seem trustworthy enough to complete the job without me fearing, as I had been scammed by a plumber before. The second is on the other side of the proverbial freelancing coin. I was also an animator who delivered a finished project, only to never get paid on the fully agreed on price after all my hard work. It turns out trust is broken on both sides of the market: clients fear being scammed by someone they hired, and workers fear doing the job and never seeing the money. I built Gigr for both of those people: the client who wants to know they can trust who they hire, and the worker who wants to know they'll actually get paid for work they've done. What it does Gigr is a neighborhood marketplace where trust is the core product: Verified people: Every provider carries real reputation history, plus on-chain "vouches" from neighbors who actually hired them. Safe payments: When you hire someone, the money goes into an escrow program that nobody can touch. It's released to the worker only when you confirm the work is done: so workers get paid, and clients only pay for work they're happy with. Easy to use: You don't browse and click through endless forms. Your AI assistant finds a trusted provider, posts the job, holds the payment, and releases it when you're satisfied: all in plain language. Gigr works for both sides of the market: hire someone trustworthy, or be hired: your agent can list the service you offer, field requests, and protect your payment the exact same way. How I built it I built a modern full-stack app with these: Frontend: React + TypeScript + Vite, deployed on Vercel. Backend: FastAPI + Postgres/PostGIS (deployed on Koyeb), which powers proximity search: "find providers near me" is ranked by real distance. Real escrow: Payments are locked in a Solana smart contract. Funding, releasing, and completion are genuine on-chain transactions, not mockups. Real reputation: Completed jobs mint vouches as on-chain tokens, making history tamper-proof and fully portable with the provider. Agent-native (WebMCP): I exposed Gigr as a set of 14 WebMCP tools ( get_user_location , search_providers , post_job , post_service , fund_escrow , release_escrow , accept_job , and more) inside the user's logged-in browser, so an AI agent can act on the user's behalf with no separate agent login. Sensitive tools are only visible when you're signed in. Challenges I ran into The hardest lesson was understanding how an agent should act for a real user. At first, I assumed the agent had access to the logged-in session; I learned that WebMCP tools only work when they run inside an authenticated tab. Any request made from outside that context can't carry your login: that took a few frustrating debugging sessions to nail. From there came a subtler design problem: WebMCP has no built-in way to unregister a tool, so I had to tie every sensitive tool to an AbortSignal and tear it down the moment the user signs out: ensuring a signed-out session cannot make escrow calls. I also built the escrow state machine to refuse invalid state transitions (e.g., "you can't release a payment that was never funded") with clear explanations, so the agent guides the user instead of erroring out. Finally, building for both sides of the market effectively doubled my workload: I had to serve both "I want to hire" and "I want to be hired" flows, each with its own tailored agent interaction model. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A client can move seamlessly from "find me a verified plumber near me" to real USDC sitting safely in an on-chain escrow: all directly from a chat interaction. A provider can ask their agent to get them hired: listing services, fielding requests, and accepting jobs autonomously. Reputation is genuinely on-chain and ungameable, not a superficial star rating that can be inflated or bought. The agent's "sense of the user": location, currency, and preferences: comes dynamically from the app context itself rather than repeatedly asking the user. The agent can also call the user when a task is done but this uses Twilio's free tier for now so it only works for me (the tester). What I learned Authentication and identity are the real product surface: The most impressive-sounding agent features collapse the moment the agent can't act safely as the user with explicit human consent. Signing in stays a crucial human moment. Escrow is a product feature, not just a crypto feature: I used a blockchain because it provides what traditional databases cannot: a trustless payment execution that nobody can quietly reverse. However, end users never need to care about the underlying tech. Build for both sides: A marketplace only thrives when both the hirer and the worker feel completely protected: most platforms historically only cater to one. What's next for Gigr Move escrow contracts to Solana mainnet and integrate real ₦ (Naira) and other currency payments on/off-ramps so local currency seamlessly swaps to USDC inside the app. Expand the agent's capabilities to handle multi-step negotiation and automated dispute resolution (with human-in-the-loop oversight). Grow the vouch graph so reputation seamlessly follows providers across cities and platforms. Launch a dedicated mobile experience and expand into more service categories: from plumbers to digital animators who, this time, always get paid. title: GridPact
pitch: Where people and agents agree when compute should run.
about_excerpt: Where people and agents agree when compute should run. Like 1 Comment Story Updates arch Inspiration Carbon-aware schedulers already move jobs into cleaner hours, but they decide silently. The constraints that actually matter: this backup stays in Frankfurt, that training must finish by 8 AM and live in people's heads and never reach the scheduler. WebMCP made it possible to turn that into a conversation. What it does Shows your workloads on a timeline against the grid carbon forecast. You state a goal, the agent plans against it. When the goal is impossible, GreenWindow names the colliding constraints and offers the smallest trade that unlocks most of the benefit: shift one deadline by 45 minutes, get 38% of the reduction, keep region and cost untouched. You accept or reject each trade. Anything you lock stays locked. The output is a carbon execution contract: what was preserved, what was relaxed, and the resulting savings. How we built it TypeScript, React, Vite, static, no backend --> WebMCP tools run in the user's own browser session. The planner is a constraint solver over discrete time slots optimizing carbon and cost. Infeasibility explanations come from tracking which constraint killed which window, so the solver can name culprits instead of returning "no solution". Carbon and price forecasts are a bundled 24-hour dataset, so the demo needs no API key. Challenges we ran into The first version let the agent apply schedules directly. It produced better plans that no operator would ever run, because it had no idea which constraints were negotiable. Rebuilding around locks and single-constraint trades was the turning point. Explaining infeasibility properly meant instrumenting the solver, not bolting on a message afterwards. Accomplishments that we're proud of The infeasibility explanation: it tells you exactly why your goals don't fit and what the cheapest way out is. And the demo is honest: state really changes, plans recompute live, and the savings come from the same solver that produced the schedule. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when tools aren't remote controls for existing buttons. The useful ones here have no button at all: test a hypothetical constraint set, find the minimum relaxation. Those are questions, not clicks. What's next for GreenWindow Export contracts in a form the Carbon Aware SDK and Kubernetes schedulers can consume. Real grid forecast APIs with fallback. Multi-region contention when two teams want the same clean window. A review mode, so contracts can be approved by someone other than the negotiator. title: HealthBook
pitch: Healthbook: Your private health companion - meds, labs, and care connected in one vault.
about_excerpt: Healthbook: Your private health companion - meds, labs, and care connected in one vault. Like Comment Story Updates Doctor Patient Chart Patient Lab Biomarker Trajectory Patient Weekly Medication Planner Doctor Triage Dashboard WebMCP Agent Tools Family Care Circle Patient Medication Reconciliation Patient Clinical Dossier Inspiration We kept seeing the same gap after discharge. Patients leave the hospital with three different medication lists, follow-ups get lost, and family members end up doing double-entry on scratch paper. An eighty-year-old patient comes home holding a stapled discharge summary, trying to remember if their new blood pressure pill clashes with their morning grapefruit, while their primary doctor has no idea what got stopped during the hospital stay. Most medical software solves this by throwing more forms at the user. Chatbots go the other direction, spitting out three paragraphs of generic advice that you still have to manually retype into another app. We wanted one place that remembers where each clinical fact came from, tracks biomarkers across visits, and gives doctors and caregivers a shared view of the actual pill routine. What it does HealthBook runs in the browser and gives both people and agents tools to work on the exact same records. PillMap organizes medications into a seven-day by four-slot grid for morning, noon, evening, and bedtime. You can drag pills around, spot red interaction arcs between conflicting drugs, and check meal timing flags like taking with food or avoiding grapefruit. LabStory takes five years of lab PDFs at once, normalizes different units like mg/dL and mmol/L, and plots them on individual biomarker charts. Medication start and stop dates sit directly on the chart, so you can see if a drop in kidney function happened right after starting a new drug. RxBridge compares pre-admission, in-hospital, and discharge lists side by side. It marks each pill as Continued, Dose Changed, Stopped, New, or Held, and explains the reason in plain language. HomeLab tracks lab rechecks with countdown cards, lets patients photograph outpatient slips, and gives doctors a way to propose dose changes directly into the patient's queue. Safety and calendar lets patients report acute symptoms with photos, runs a basic triage check, and exports lab due dates and follow-ups to standard calendar files. Care Circle allows family members to act on behalf of a patient with view, manage, or full permissions, keeping an audit log of every change. Dossier pulls meds, labs, and danger reports into an emergency snapshot where each line links back to the original PDF highlight. How we built it We built the interface with React 18, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. State lives first in the browser vault, with optional background sync to Supabase Postgres for multi-profile access and doctor-patient links. Instead of writing a chatbot that talks about medical records, we wired forty-seven WebMCP tools directly into document.modelContext . When an agent connects, it does not just suggest advice in a chat window. It inspects the actual client state, runs interaction algorithms, and calls functions like suggest_schedule , propose_dosage_change , or correlate_meds . Any action that changes a schedule or modifies a dose routes through an approval gate in the UI. The agent stages the change, the user sees the preview on the canvas, and nothing updates in the vault until the user clicks approve. For clinical verification, we use deterministic local checks for drug-drug and food-drug rules, combined with Exa search proxies for medical fact verification and optical character recognition for lab slips. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making tool execution safe when dealing with real medications. An agent suggesting a schedule tweak might look reasonable on paper, but moving a pill from morning to bedtime can trigger an interaction with an evening drug. We had to build strict dependency checks so the agent cannot silently move pills without the client validating contraindications first. Normalizing lab data was also surprisingly difficult. Different labs report the exact same test under slightly different names, and reference ranges fluctuate between hospitals. We had to map disparate units into consistent internal standards so five years of historical draws would render on a single chart without breaking the scale. Getting WebMCP tools to behave cleanly across both native model contexts and polyfilled browser environments took several iterations. We had to make sure tool schemas remained strict, arguments validated cleanly, and tool cancellation signals properly cleaned up background operations. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the agent actually works on the page instead of living in a side box. Watching an agent take a prompt, inspect a messy medication list, shift a morning pill load, and paint a red interaction arc across the weekly grid feels like how software should work. What we learned We learned that agent tools are only as good as the approval interfaces around them. If an agent changes state in the background without clear visual feedback, users immediately lose trust. Giving the user a clear before-and-after ghost preview on the pillbox turned out to be far more important than making the agent faster. We also learned that clinical workflows have very little tolerance for vague summaries. Doctors and patients do not want a model to tell them that kidney markers improved; they want to click a point on a chart and verify the exact draw date and reference range from the original slip. What's next for HealthBook We want to expand the optical character recognition pipeline to handle poorly lit, handwritten clinic notes and multi-page discharge packets more reliably. We also plan to add direct FHIR export so patients can download their compiled records and hand them directly to hospital electronic health record systems without manual transcription. Finally, we want to refine the doctor review queue so specialists can handle batch approvals across multiple linked patients even faster. title: Mirror WebMCP Secure
pitch: Mirror lets AI agents use private website data through native WebMCP tools without copying the raw data into agent context. Only the minimum approved information crosses the boundary.
about_excerpt: Mirror lets AI agents use private website data through native WebMCP tools without copying the raw data into agent context. Only the minimum approved information crosses the boundary. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP makes websites actionable by AI agents, which is powerful, but a lot of useful actions depend on private user data. The problem is that the easiest way to build these workflows is often to give the agent the raw data it needs. That can put sensitive information into model context, logs, traces, or downstream systems. We wanted to see if there was a better way: let the agent act, without giving it the full private record. What it does Mirror WebMCP Secure adds a privacy boundary around native WebMCP Site Tools. Our demo is a procurement workflow. A buyer wants to purchase GPUs. The buyer has private requirements, and the seller has private pricing rules. Instead of copying the buyer's full record into ChatGPT, the website seals that private state into a short-lived, context-bound capability. ChatGPT can then use native procurement Site Tools through that capability. Only the information needed for the action is passed across, and sensitive steps still require explicit user approval. The end result is that the agents can find a product, request a proposal, release it, and accept it without either side getting the other's full private context. Why WebMCP is a good fit This is more than a chatbot reading a webpage. The agent needs to discover structured actions from the site and then use them to: find compatible products request a seller proposal release an offer accept it WebMCP gives us that action layer. Mirror sits around those actions and controls what private data they are allowed to receive and what result they are allowed to return. Better user experience Without this kind of boundary, the user either has to expose sensitive information to the agent or do more of the workflow manually. With Mirror, the user keeps the private data on the website and lets ChatGPT handle the workflow through Site Tools. The user only steps in when something important needs approval. That means the agent can still be useful, while the user keeps control over what gets disclosed and when. How we built it The website exposes four native procurement Site Tools: procurement.find_private_matches procurement.request_seller_proposal procurement.release_proposal procurement.accept_proposal The buyer form is sealed into a restricted mirrorh_... capability instead of being copied into agent context. Mirror acts as the boundary between the private website state, the user agent, and the seller-side action. The seller receives only the minimum approved handoff needed to make the proposal. The seller-side inference also runs through Mirror using ciphertext compute. ChatGPT discovers and invokes the tools natively through WebMCP rather than relying on visual page automation. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was making the workflow useful without leaking more private data than necessary. We also wanted to avoid a fake-looking demo where everything happens through a local button. The actual flow had to work through native Site Tools. Another challenge was approvals. Releasing a proposal and accepting it are different decisions, so we treated them as separate approval steps rather than collapsing them into one. We also wanted the privacy claims to be visible, not just something we said in the description. So the demo includes a proof view showing what each side actually received. Accomplishments that we're proud of We got the complete native WebMCP flow working end to end. Two agents can collaborate on the procurement task while each side keeps its private context. At the end of the demo: the seller does not receive the buyer's budget the seller does not receive the browser handle the seller's private price floor is not returned buyer fields returned: 0 At the same time, the workflow still produces a real usable offer. That balance between usefulness and privacy is the part we're most proud of. What we learned One thing that became very clear while building this is that tool access and data access are not the same problem. WebMCP defines what the agent can do. Mirror focuses on what private data that action can receive, and what result is allowed to leave the boundary. We also learned that approval works better when it is tied to meaningful user decisions rather than added as a generic confirmation step. What's next for Mirror WebMCP Secure This procurement flow is just one example. The same pattern could be useful in finance, healthcare, legal, and enterprise workflows where agents need to act on sensitive information without directly owning the raw data. Next, we want to explore richer tool policies, stronger capability binding, more multi-agent workflows, and an easier integration path for developers who want to add privacy-preserving WebMCP actions to existing sites. title: Ninth Tool
pitch: Runs your page's WebMCP tools in a real browser and shows which promises it silently drops, with the command that reproduces each one. Twenty behaviours, twenty reproductions.
about_excerpt: Runs your page's WebMCP tools in a real browser and shows which promises it silently drops, with the command that reproduces each one. Twenty behaviours, twenty reproductions. Like Comment Story Updates The Silent Drop Problem: Demonstrating how browser engines silently drop destructiveHint, error envelopes and signals. Live 20-Behaviour Catalogue: all six groups, from the six rows a page author can act on to the fourteen that are facts about the host. Defect Inspection & Remediation: Exact reproduction command and standard gap analysis per behaviour row. Live In-Browser Audit: Running all 20 probes in Chrome with WebMCP enabled, scoring 13 broken, 5 kept, 1 by design, 1 unsettled. Dynamic Tool Mutation: The nt_get_findings tool appears only when findings exist and is withdrawn when cleared. Headless DevTools CLI Runner: Running the same twenty behaviour probes from a terminal, with zero dependencies. Architecture and behaviour matrix: two transports, twenty rows in six groups, and the tools the page publishes to an agent. Ninth Tool: A Reproducible Behaviour Probe for WebMCP Ninth Tool executes your page's WebMCP tools in the browser and shows which promises the browser silently drops, with the command that reproduces each one. Live, no account: https://upgradedev.github.io/ninthtool/ Code (MIT): https://github.com/upgradedev/ninthtool Compatibility: Chrome or Edge with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . Inspiration I was adding WebMCP to a page, writing the shape I knew from building MCP servers. I marked a tool destructiveHint . I returned { isError: true } when it refused. I passed a signal on the descriptor so it would withdraw. All three were accepted without complaint and none of them did anything. Nothing threw, nothing reached the console, and the tool list carried no warning. Existing checkers read the declarations a page publishes and told me the page was fine, because by the only thing they look at, it was. The gap is not in what a page declares. It is in what the browser does with the declaration, and reading cannot see that. What it does It runs twenty behaviours against a live WebMCP tool surface and reports each one with the exact command that reproduces it. Six rows read the tools the page publishes, snapshotted before the probe registers anything of its own. Fourteen rows are facts about the host: 3 where the browser diverges from the W3C draft, 5 the draft cannot express, 3 silent traps, 1 by design, 2 that hold. On its own page, in Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled, the reading is 13 broken, 5 kept, 1 by design, 1 unsettled, 20 tested . It labels that run PARTIAL rather than rounding the unsettled row up. Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The subject being tested is WebMCP itself. Whether a host honours destructiveHint , whether a refusal survives the boundary, whether a tool registered with a signal actually withdraws: none of it is visible from outside a browser, and none of it can be read off a declaration. This is not a page that uses WebMCP to deliver something else. WebMCP is the thing under test, so the only place the work can happen is inside a page that speaks it. How it creates a better user experience A page author gets what their browser actually did, next to the one command that reproduces it, instead of a linter's reading of their source. No account, no install, and nothing about their page is uploaded anywhere. The audit runs in the tab they already have open, against a subject document in a same-origin frame. Every row that could not be run says so, with the reason, rather than counting as a pass. A run with one unobserved row reports PARTIAL . That is the difference between a result you can act on and a green tick you have to trust. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before This page publishes its own WebMCP tools, so an agent can run the audit, list the twenty behaviours, explain one row in full and read the findings without touching the screen, while a person watches the same rows fill in beside it. The nt_get_findings tool does not exist until a run has produced findings, and it is withdrawn when they are cleared. An agent that asks for findings which are not there is answered by the tool surface itself rather than left to guess. That is the behaviour this suite is named for, demonstrated on itself rather than described. The auditor is a WebMCP page, so it is also a subject. How WebMCP was implemented document.modelContext.registerTool publishes three tools from this page at rest and a fourth while findings exist. Three carry readOnlyHint . The one that runs the audit deliberately does not, because it drives forms. The subject page it drives is a separate document in a same-origin frame that promotes two ordinary forms to tools through the declarative HTML attributes, so both halves of the standard sit on one surface. The probe registers its own throwaway tools with a signal in the options bag and withdraws them when it is finished, which is how the withdrawal row gets measured at all. How I built it Gathering is not deciding. The probe runs inside a document and records what happened, with no opinion about what a pass is. The judge is pure, runs deterministically, and cannot reach a browser. 533 unit tests and 97.95% line coverage across 57 files at commit 231c45f , counting each file once against an 85% floor for lines, branches and functions. Eleven below-floor metrics occur across six files, and the gate names every file instead of averaging it away. Reproduce it with node --experimental-test-coverage --test tests/unit | tee coverage.txt then node tests/unit/coverage_gate.mjs coverage.txt --per-file --threshold=85 . Dual transports. The in-browser runner, plus a zero-dependency headless Chrome DevTools Protocol client. No bundler, no test framework, no lock file, no runtime dependencies. Run it against any page from a terminal: npx --yes https://github.com/upgradedev/ninthtool/tarball/main https://your-page.example The package is not published to npm, so the tarball URL is the whole install. Safety By default it calls no tool of yours and submits no form. Calling your read-only tools needs an explicit flag you pass yourself. Submitting a form runs only against the fixture this tool serves itself. It is not invisible, and that is stated rather than hidden: registering a probe tool is a document-level event that your page can see. Honest limits A preregistered study on thirteen independently authored WebMCP pages has run, and its hypothesis failed . Five of twenty rows told those pages apart, and every one of them was already readable from the tool list. Taking it apart afterwards showed why: at most two rows could ever have told one of those pages from another, against a threshold of three fixed before anyone looked, and both were switched off by the run's own read-only default. The bar could not be cleared by any result. That is a defect in the protocol, not a measurement of what this tool reaches. Two findings it did report about strangers' pages were checked against their own source and retracted as defects in this tool , with the handler lines cited. One page had rejected the missing argument at its first line. On the other, this tool's own control call was as malformed as the one it meant to break. That is the thing worth reading. Any suite that runs against pages it does not own will produce false findings. The useful question is whether it catches them and publishes the retraction beside the claim, in the same generated file. It did. One of the two study-specific oracle weaknesses behind those retractions is now closed. The other stays open on purpose: the obvious fix was built, measured against a copy of the tree, and it turned this suite's own flagship true positive into an abstention. That measurement is published rather than the fix. The protocol was written and committed before any page ran, the failure is published in evidence/impact/results.md , and the primary metric was not changed afterwards to make it read better. Five rows have known fail-open paths, and P2 is only partially closed. They were found by external review and reproduced before publishing: P4 treats unreadable provenance as local because it filters only fromThisDocument === false . P3 walks only top-level schema.properties , so an undescribed nested parameter passes. D1 accepts any toolchange event without proving that the target tool caused it. P5 removes only required[0] , always uses the same good/bad/bad/good order, and later resolves the snapshotted tool by name. Later required keys, position-dependent behaviour, or a same-name replacement can produce a false pass or misbound call. P6 also resolves by name, stringifies answers, is order-sensitive, and counts every resolved value, including an error envelope, as an answer. A replacement writer can be called, distinct structured states can collapse to the same text, and a resolved refusal can satisfy the

title: Ohmni
pitch: Ohmni exposes hardware diagnostics as WebMCP tools, so an AI agent can measure a device, run approved tests, gather evidence, request physical changes, and verify the repair.
about_excerpt: Ohmni exposes hardware diagnostics as WebMCP tools, so an AI agent can measure a device, run approved tests, gather evidence, request physical changes, and verify the repair. Like Comment Story Updates the landing page Inspiration I’m learning robotics, and one of the most frustrating parts has been getting an AI to understand what is actually happening on the board in front of me. I was constantly taking screenshots, copying serial logs, and pasting telemetry into ChatGPT just to explain the physical world. The WebMCP Challenge gave me a different idea what if the browser itself could become the bridge between the agent and the hardware? Ohmni came from that. Using WebMCP and Web Serial, the agent can inspect the board through real tools in real time and you see the result of your action in front of you instead of relying on screenshots and copied logs. What it does Ohmni is a browser based hardware debugging workbench where AI agents and humans diagnose physical device problems together. Using WebMCP, Ohmni exposes hardware capabilities as structured tools an agent can call directly. The agent can inspect reset history, measure supply voltage, read telemetry, run controlled diagnostic tests, collect evidence, and build a diagnosis from real measurements instead of guessing from screenshots or pasted logs. For safety, read only tools can run autonomously, while actions that can affect hardware require explicit human approval. When a physical change is needed, such as moving a jumper or reseating a connection, the agent hands that step back to the human and then retests the device to verify whether the fix actually worked. Ohmni also supports real hardware through Web Serial apis , alongside a deterministic virtual ESP32 environment that lets anyone experience the full diagnostic workflow without needing a physical board. How we built it We built Ohmni with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Bun, using WebMCP as the core interface between the AI agent and the hardware workbench. Device capabilities are exposed through document.modelContext as structured tools. Read-only tools can run directly, while actions that may affect hardware pass through a human approval gate before execution. A device adapter handles both the deterministic virtual ESP32 environment and real hardware over Web Serial. Telemetry is streamed into the browser in real time, and each diagnostic action produces evidence that the agent can use to form, test, and verify hypotheses. We also added dynamic tool registration, capability filtering, safe disconnect handling, and an evidence trail so the system stays useful, inspectable, and safe throughout the debugging process. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making agent access to hardware useful without making it unsafe. Some tools only read data, while others can actually change device state, so I had to design a clear safety boundary and pause physical actions for human approval. Another challenge was making the diagnosis trustworthy. The agent should not simply guess the fault, so Ohmni hides the underlying problem, exposes only measurements and test results, and requires the diagnosis to be built from evidence. Accomplishments that I am proud of I built a full debugging loop instead of just a WebMCP demo, An agent can inspect the device, run controlled tests, collect evidence, form a diagnosis, ask the human to make a physical change, and then rerun the test to verify the fix. And the diagnosis is not just a chat response. Ohmni keeps an evidence trail so every conclusion can be traced back to actual measurements and test results. What i learned i learned that giving an AI access to hardware is not just about exposing more tools. The real challenge is deciding what the agent can do autonomously, what requires human approval, and how every conclusion can be grounded in evidence. WebMCP made that separation much clearer. It let us treat the browser as a trusted bridge between the agent and local hardware, while keeping the human in control of physical actions. I also learned that the strongest agent workflows are collaborative: the agent measures and reasons, the browser enforces safety, and the human handles the physical world. What's next for Ohmni I want to grow Ohmni into a broader hardware debugging tool that works across more boards and devices. The next step is expanding the Web Serial layer so more microcontrollers can connect over USB, expose their own diagnostic capabilities, and use the same WebMCP workflow for measurement, testing, human intervention, and verification.
