title: Project Grapevine - Human-Agent Disaster Response
pitch: Project Grapevine uses WebMCP to connect AI agents with people, aerial drones and operational systems, turning live ground truth into coordinated disaster response while keeping humans in control.
about_excerpt: Project Grapevine uses WebMCP to connect AI agents with people, aerial drones and operational systems, turning live ground truth into coordinated disaster response while keeping humans in control. Like Comment Story Updates Grapevine Ops Center Grapevine Field Inbox "moblie app" Grapevine Warehouse Inventory Grapevine Partner Directory Inspiration We grew up in Boone, North Carolina, in the heart of the western Appalachian Mountains. Almost two years ago, Hurricane Helene devastated the region. As we worked to support relief efforts back home, one major problem kept coming up: logistics . Roads and bridges were gone, and conditions could change by the hour. But people still had their phones. Locals, responders, and volunteers were sharing what they saw through social media, texts, and calls, creating a constant stream of updates from the field. Meanwhile, people coordinating supplies could be miles away, working from information that was already outdated. The ground truth was out there. Getting it to the right people fast enough to act on it was the hard part. That experience stuck with us. When we started thinking about what to build for this hackathon, we kept coming back to one question: what could this look like if AI agents and WebMCP were part of the response infrastructure? Project Grapevine is our fictional simulation of that idea. The name is a play on "heard it through the grapevine," except we're exploring what that network could look like when people, sensors and AI agents can all contribute to it. In our scenario, a large relief organization is trying to move supply trucks into communities affected by a devastating flash flood. They have an AI agent helping coordinate logistics, responders on the ground and sensors reporting current conditions. What it does Project Grapevine gives an AI agent tools to help coordinate a disaster response while keeping people in control of consequential decisions. The simulation starts with a common problem: the command center needs to move supplies into an affected area, but its route information may already be outdated. Instead of relying on stale information, the agent can use WebMCP tools to find people and simulated sensors near the route (aerial drone footage) and request current conditions directly from the field. Grapevine connects two workspaces: Live Ground Truth: The agent checks the regional baseline, identifies nearby responders and sensors, and prepares a structured request asking whether a route is passable. Once a person authorizes the request, a responder or sensor can report current conditions. That response flows back to the agent as structured evidence, including information about the source and its quality. Resource Coordination: At the same time, the agent can review the crisis brief, search available relief partners, evaluate what resources they can provide, and build a shortlist. From there, it prepares a work plan for human review and approval. The important part is how those workflows connect. Grapevine won't allow the coordination plan to be approved until current route evidence has been received. A passable report unlocks final approval. A caution or blocked report keeps it locked. The agent does the legwork: finding sources, gathering information, comparing resources and preparing a plan. People provide the ground truth, and a person makes the final call. How we built it We built Grapevine around the idea that an agent shouldn't have to navigate a website the same way a person does. Instead, the application exposes specific workflows directly to the agent through WebMCP. We started building Project Grapevine on August 31. Everything here, including all ten WebMCP tools across the workspaces, was built new for this submission. Each workspace registers its own tools using document.modelContext.registerTool . The Live Ground Truth workspace exposes five tools for finding available sources, checking existing information, asking a source for an update, retrieving the response and rating its quality. Resource Coordination exposes another five for reading the crisis brief, finding response partners, reviewing their capabilities, creating a shortlist and preparing a coordination request. We used Zod schemas to keep inputs structured and validated, while WebMCP tool annotations distinguish between read-only operations and actions that require human control. The agent can do a lot of the work on its own, but it can't make the final decision. Behind the scenes, a Cloudflare Worker and D1 database maintain shared workflow state across the agent, operations dashboard and field responder inbox. An agent can stage a request at the command center, have it appear on a responder's device, and then pull that response back into the workflow as new evidence. React manages the visible approval states and keeps the final coordination action locked until the required ground truth has been collected. One intentional design decision was what we didn't expose to WebMCP. The field responder inbox registers no tools at all. It's a human surface by design. The agent coordinates the request, but the person in the field provides the ground truth. Challenges we ran into One of our biggest challenges wasn't figuring out what the agent could do. It was designing around what it should do . Building with WebMCP means thinking about two users at the same time : the agent using the tools and the humans doing the work. That made the UX more complicated than we expected. We had to think through the full workflow, what information the agent needed, what a person needed to see and where automation should stop. Just because an agent can take an action doesn't mean it should. Especially in a disaster response situation That became one of the most important design principles behind Grapevine. We intentionally added approval gates before consequential actions. An agent can identify a response partner and prepare a work request, for example, but a person has to approve it before it's sent. The same is true for publishing a request to Facebook. The agent can do the research and prepare the action, but the human still makes the call. Those controls aren't instructions buried in a prompt. They're enforced by the application itself. We think that's an important consideration when designing with WebMCP. Human experience still matters. In many cases, the best agent workflow isn't the one that automates everything. It's the one that removes friction while being deliberate about where human judgment belongs. Trust was another part of that challenge. Simulated sensors are clearly identified, different source types have different capabilities, and the agent can evaluate the quality of the evidence it receives. If information is incomplete or conflicting, Grapevine surfaces that uncertainty rather than pretending it has an answer. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that we took a real-world event with real coordination challenges and turned it into a working example of how humans and AI agents could collaborate differently during disaster response events. Hurricane Helene hit our hometown in September 2024. We watched our own community struggle, respond and come together in its aftermath. That experience became the foundation for Grapevine. We're also proud that Grapevine became a working end-to-end workflow rather than just a demonstration of an agent calling a few tools or navigating a website. What we learned Designing for People & Machines Building Grapevine changed how we thought about WebMCP's capabilities. We began by thinking about which parts of a Ops dashboard should be exposed to an agent. We ended up thinking much more about workflows, decisions and handoffs between people, agents and machines . For example, in our demo, the agent uses drone reconnaissance to identify a possible fallen tree, asks a responder to visually confirm it and then helps coordinate a team to clear the road. The same idea applies elsewhere in the workflow. Water-depth readings can become evidence for supply-route planning. Warehouse inventory can identify a shortage, which the agent can turn into a drafted public appeal based on what's actually needed at that moment. Voice input In the demo, we purposely used ChatGPT's voice input instead of typing instructions. We talked to the agent, and it orchestrated the workflows from there. That got us thinking about future applications. Could a two-way radio or dedicated line connect directly to a command center agent? A responder could report conditions from the field while the agent gathers information, updates the workflow and coordinates next steps. It's a use case we think is both plausible and very doable. What's next for Project Grapevine - Human-Agent Disaster Response We built this to prove what WebMCP can really do, but we think the framework behind it can go much further. Disaster response gave us a clear way to explore the idea. Information is distributed, condit

title: Runcard
pitch: A GitHub for molecular-dynamics runs: every number traces to a file, and your agent gets seventeen calibrated scientific operations through WebMCP. The agent reasons, Runcard checks, a person approves
about_excerpt: A GitHub for molecular-dynamics runs: every number traces to a file, and your agent gets seventeen calibrated scientific operations through WebMCP. The agent reasons, Runcard checks, a person approves Like Comment Story Updates Main page System 1 System 2 Inspiration I had somehow come across the field of Molecular Dynamics through a summer project, and gained experience with AMBER through building an LLM orchestration engine around it. The biggest thing on my mind was just the lack of guardrails that this software had. It was like working with Assembly. It got me thinking a lot more about the experiences of those working in MD, and how I can build software that lowers the barrier to entry. What it does Sharing a MD simulation with someone usually means just giving your entire directory. I guess it works, but it's very hard to decode, and with hundreds of literal text files as the input, it's just not a very friendly way to share results. Runcard is essentially GitHub for MD simulations. A prepared system is like a repo, a run is like a commit, and users can "fork" runs, adding their own changes to someone else's work. Runcard turns your MD directory into a shareable, validated record, with analysis tools not just invocable by users, but directly invocable by agents through WebMCP. How we built it I was already quite familiar with building AMBER validators, and I used that knowledge to process .in files to ensure that the records were physically sound. That's the "validated record" part of things. I knew along the way that I wanted to do something analogous to Github, which helped with a lot of design work. If a run was a commit, and a rerun was a fork, many more things became clear. Proposals became like pull requests, which had to be approved by the user. Primarily, I had to work on creating functions that converted the raw files into the data presented in the website, and the analysis tools that drove both user/agent interaction. One table drives both users and agent interactions, so both sides are getting the exact same functions. At this point, most of the work was done, the rest just went into presenting it in a way that was intuitive to the user. Challenges we ran into Some of the things we have agents watch out for (like assuming spread as error) were lessons I had learned when generating the bundles in the first place. Some of the runs were with different engines (PMEMD vs Sander), and also had different total times (2 ps vs 30 ps) yet we treated them the same. AMBER is just very tricky to get right, so many of the challenges we had, despite my previous experience, were with honest our results were. Accomplishments that we're proud of To be honest, I'm just proud that I was able to finish this as a final product. Getting to the finish line means a lot to me, since I've never done hackathons all the way through before. On the product side, I was really proud of how the agent performed given these tools. I first asked it to check the math of a calculation with the tools, and it insisted on refusing to give an error score, because only 2 of 3 matched runs exist. Then, I asked it after to consider the system with 310K temperature instead of 300. It not only did that experiment correctly, but noticed that the missing 3rd matched run in the original run was also missing in this 310K run, and automatically proposed a fix. The tools made this possible, and agents kind of did the rest, which was cool to see What we learned I think I've reinforced the idea that the biggest failure modes are silent. Things that are confidently wrong. Both in AI's hallucinating, but also in molecular dynamics where things look ok, but are secretly messed up on the inside. What's next for Runcard I think the obvious answer is to a second person's runs onto the website. If we're really going to be the Github of MD, then we need collaboration and people. I want people to be able to share their results, and iterate on each other's work with much more ease. title: ShowOnce - WebMCP for “do what I did.”
pitch: Record a web task once, send a link. Their agent finishes it on-page via WebMCP—they approve the final step. No screen share. Safe help from anywhere.
about_excerpt: Record a web task once, send a link. Their agent finishes it on-page via WebMCP—they approve the final step. No screen share. Safe help from anywhere. Like Comment Story Updates ShowOnce WebMCP is how any site exposes capabilities. ShowOnce is what makes delegation safe — record once, hand off a portable procedure, agent executes within scope, human approves the irreversible step. WaitingRoom.gov is our stress-test UI modeled on real legacy portals (India Post PLI, NIC, PIB) — not a greenfield app. Built for the WebMCP Challenge . The problem Remote web help today relies on screenshots, phone calls, screen sharing, remote control software, or handing over a password. Screenshots lose context. Screen sharing and remote control require both people to be free at the same time and give one person full access to the other's session. Credential sharing gives up account security entirely. None of these let a second person's own agent pick up where the first person left off, on the second person's own account. What ShowOnce does A sender demonstrates a real task once, live, inside a fully interactive connected demo application called Northstar Benefits (an employee benefits portal). ShowOnce does not screen-record or ask the sender to pick steps manually: because the demo app's UI and ShowOnce both call the same shared domain command layer, every meaningful action the sender takes (selecting a plan, changing a preference, confirming an address) is automatically captured as a semantic event. Those events are compiled into a portable, sanitized procedure — intent only, no selectors, credentials, sessions, or screenshots. A recipient opens the resulting handoff link. They can act on it directly in the same live app, rendered against their own account state, or they can ask a WebMCP-capable agent (for example, ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with WebMCP enabled) to "do what [the sender] showed me." When an agent is used, it invokes real document.modelContext tools registered by ShowOnce — the exact same commands the human UI uses — so the visible, live Northstar Benefits app updates in front of the recipient as the agent works. Nothing is simulated or faked. ShowOnce compares the demonstrated procedure against the recipient's actual state and decides, deterministically, what still applies, what can be safely applied, what differs materially, and what must be left for a human to decide. For any consequential, identity-bearing action — actually submitting the renewal — an agent can get the recipient all the way to a final reviewable summary, but no further. A human must check a personal attestation checkbox and click "Confirm & submit" themselves. That single click is the only human step, and no WebMCP tool can ever perform it. How WebMCP is used Real document.modelContext.registerTool(...) registrations, made client-side once the recipient route mounts (see src/webmcp/registerTools.ts ). Strict JSON Schemas for every tool's input, with no free-form or untyped arguments. readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations so a calling agent knows which tools only read state and which tools are handling handoff-authored content. AbortController -based lifecycle: tools are registered with a scoped signal and unregister themselves cleanly when the recipient route unmounts. A single shared executeCommand() domain layer used by both the human UI and every WebMCP tool, so there is exactly one implementation of the business logic behind "select a plan" or "set paperless" — not a UI code path and a separate agent code path. A human-only, atomic final step: WebMCP tools can read state, apply safe preferences, and prepare a renewal summary, but the recipient_attestation semantic event that authorizes submission can only ever be issued by a human clicking a button in the browser — executeCommand() refuses it outright if the source is 'webmcp' . title: Smarterboard
pitch: You and an AI agent operate the same board, not a chat window beside it. Graph curves, wire circuits, bond atoms, drop a ball, and it explains how each change, yours or its own, shaped the result.
about_excerpt: You and an AI agent operate the same board, not a chat window beside it. Graph curves, wire circuits, bond atoms, drop a ball, and it explains how each change, yours or its own, shaped the result. Like Comment Story Updates main menu 2d sandbox 2d sandbox circuit sandbox physics sandbox chemistry sandbox Inspiration Ask a chatbot "why does increasing a make the parabola narrower?" and you get a paragraph — a description of a motion you never see. The understanding lives in actually watching the curve tighten while someone talks over it, the way a good tutor works at a whiteboard. The blocker was never the model's ability to explain; it was that the model had no hands. WebMCP is the missing piece: a web page can expose its own controls as tools, so the student's own agent can operate the page instead of describing it — no extension, no API key in the page, no faulty HTML scraping. What it does Smarterboard is a set of learning sandboxes that an AI agent can drive. There are four sandboxes. A 2D and 3D grapher lets you plot curves and surfaces animate a slider so a graph changes find roots and turning points and orbit shaded surfaces. A circuit lab lets you build circuits from batteries, resistors, LEDs, capacitors and more watch current flow and plot voltage over time on an oscilloscope. A chemistry sandbox lets you drag elements off the table build atoms from protons, neutrons and electrons and bond them into molecules. A physics sandbox lets you drop in ramps, tracks, balls and blocks while everything floats, then run the scene under gravity and friction and read back position, velocity, forces, energy and every collision. Each page registers its tools on document.modelContext so an AI agent can build a water molecule. Explain the bonds wire an LED so it lights safely launch a projectile or animate a parameter all while it narrates. The explanation and the thing being explained become the object. How we built it TypeScript and Vite were used, with no framework. Every engine has one place where state changes and the buttons a student clicks call the same code that an AI agent calls so the two can never drift apart. Math.js handles the math three.js draws the surfaces and canvas draws the circuits, atoms and physics scenes. The circuit lab runs a nodal analysis solver with time‑stepped models for capacitors, inductors and diodes. The physics lab is a rigid body engine with gravity, normal forces, friction and collisions. The chemistry lab fills electron shells the way a textbook does. There are close to ninety tools across the four sandboxes. We spent most of our time writing their descriptions because that text is the only thing the AI agent reads. Everything is deployed to GitHub Pages. Challenges we ran into We decided early not to write a LaTeX parser and instead normalize input into math.js, which saved us a day. The circuit solver required work from merging nodes to iterating diode states to stepping capacitors through time. Our oscilloscope moved slowly at first because we capped how far the simulation could move each frame. Switching to a fixed time step that follows the clock fixed that problem. We also learned some WebMCP details the way. The execute call wants the tool object and a stringified argument than a name and an object and tools from every open tab get merged together so two pages that both had a load preset tool collided. Accomplishments that we're proud of It is a product that an AI agent can genuinely run, not a chatbot with a few tools attached. The physics holds up. A capacitor reaches 63 percent of charge after exactly one time constant, sodium and chlorine form the right ions with full outer shells and a block slides down a ramp and speeds up under gravity the way it should. The page also tells the AI agent when something is wrong like an LED pulling much current and the AI agent can turn around and fix it. We got four tools working end to end in a few days and confirmed the whole AI agent round trip in a real browser. What we learned The tool description really is the prompt. Telling an AI agent when to reach for a tool matters more than the tool itself. Giving an AI agent an error it can correct is better than letting it fail.. Webmcp quietly changes the question from what a model can say to what a page can let it do. What’s next for Smarterboard Saving. Sharing a board with a link and a shared session where a student and an AI agent work on the same thing at once. Springs, pulleys and pendulums in the physics sandbox and AC analysis in the circuit sandbox. Deeper chemistry, with Lewis structures and balanced reactions. title: THREAD
pitch: THREAD is a shared execution graph where humans and AI agents negotiate, simulate, and safely apply plans that can actually finish.
about_excerpt: THREAD is a shared execution graph where humans and AI agents negotiate, simulate, and safely apply plans that can actually finish. Like Comment Story Updates THREAD turns project planning into a negotiated contract: agents propose with evidence, and only humans approve. Agents can inspect, simulate, and recommend—but only a human can approve and atomically apply a plan. A live dependency graph keeps tasks, risks, constraints, critical paths, forecasts, and agent actions in one shared state. Compare Safest, Fastest, and Highest-impact proposals with exact graph changes, constraint checks, and seeded forecasts. Every approved change records its actor, reason, and evidence in the decision ledger, with full rollback available. 1. Forty-six WebMCP tools expose strict, debuggable state, backed by Cloudflare D1 persistence and browser-local recovery. Inspiration Most project-management tools tell you what needs to be done, but not whether the plan can actually succeed. A checklist might show 20 unfinished tasks while hiding the facts that only five determine the deadline, one uncertain task could delay everything, and the total plan has almost no chance of finishing with the available time and budget. AI assistants can suggest improvements, but those suggestions often remain trapped in a chat instead of becoming safe, visible changes to the real plan. I built THREAD to give humans and AI agents the same structured reality: one dependency graph, one planning engine, one simulation model, and one persistent workspace. What it does THREAD turns a goal into a living execution graph. Each task can contain: Dependencies Status and priority Minimum, expected, and maximum duration Confidence Cost Description and graph position A workspace also tracks deadlines, budgets, resources, hard constraints, risks, milestones, and available capacity. From this information, THREAD can: Calculate the critical path Identify slack, conflicts, and bottlenecks Show which tasks block the most downstream work Run reproducible Monte Carlo simulations Estimate finish probability, median completion time, P80, P95, and cost exposure Identify the risks and tasks driving schedule variance Compare immutable what-if scenarios Apply, replan, optimize, or roll back structured changes Record human, agent, system, and persistence activity The seeded demonstration models the work required to submit THREAD itself. It includes 14 tasks, 21 dependencies, three hard constraints, quantified risks, limited capacity, and a fixed budget. Its baseline simulation shows that a plan can appear reasonable while still having only about a 71% chance of finishing. Users can test alternatives such as cutting nonessential work, recruiting help, or adding more features. Every scenario runs through the same seeded engine, making comparisons reproducible rather than arbitrary. Human-agent collaboration THREAD is not a chatbot placed beside a task board. Through WebMCP, a compatible agent can directly understand and operate the project’s structured state. The live application currently exposes 38 native tools covering: Workspace, task, dependency, constraint, risk, resource, timeline, and activity retrieval Task, milestone, dependency, risk, resource, constraint, and scenario creation Task updates, completion, prioritization, movement, and risk resolution Critical-path analysis, conflict detection, bottleneck discovery, simulation, and feasibility calculation High-level plan application, optimization, replanning, scenario comparison, and rollback These tools use strict schemas and stable identifiers. Invalid relationships—including self-dependencies, duplicates, missing tasks, and dependency cycles—are rejected before they can corrupt the graph. Human actions and agent actions use the same domain services. When an agent changes a task, the human sees that change in the graph. When the human changes a constraint, the agent reads the updated value. The activity stream shows who performed each action, making agent participation visible and reversible. How I built it I designed THREAD around a shared application layer instead of implementing separate logic for the interface and WebMCP. The visual interface, planning engine, persistence system, and WebMCP tools all operate on the same workspace model. This prevents the agent-facing representation from drifting away from what the user sees. The planning engine performs deterministic critical-path calculations across the dependency graph. The simulation engine then evaluates task-duration ranges, confidence, costs, capacity, dependencies, and quantified risks across seeded iterations. Using a fixed seed means that the same plan produces the same result. That reproducibility is important when a human and agent are comparing alternatives: an improvement should come from the plan changing, not from random noise. Workspace state is persisted with Cloudflare D1, with browser-local recovery available when remote persistence cannot be reached. A dedicated WebMCP debugger displays the complete registered surface and can test read tools, mutation tools, malformed inputs, state synchronization, and reset behavior. The public demo requires no signup or API key, allowing judges to load a complete workspace immediately. Challenges The hardest challenge was keeping the human interface and agent interface synchronized. It would have been easier to create a collection of WebMCP wrappers that returned demonstration data. Instead, each tool needed to call the same validated services as the visible application and produce a real state change. Graph correctness was another challenge. Dependency editing must prevent cycles while continuously recalculating task timing, slack, and the critical path. Simulation also required care. A percentage is not useful if it cannot be explained or reproduced, so THREAD reports percentile estimates, cost ranges, failure sources, and variance drivers alongside the headline probability. Finally, I had to make a complex planning model understandable. The graph, inspector, risk panels, feasibility score, scenario cards, simulation results, and activity history all needed to reveal depth without overwhelming a first-time user. What I learned I learned that WebMCP becomes most valuable when it exposes capabilities that are difficult and unreliable to perform through visual clicking alone. An agent can retrieve an entire dependency graph, identify bottlenecks, simulate the plan, and apply a validated set of operations through structured tools. Meanwhile, the human retains the interface best suited to judgment: a visual graph, transparent comparisons, and an inspectable history. The strongest human-agent experiences do not hide the agent or replace the human. They give each participant the right interface while keeping both grounded in the same state. What I am proud of I am most proud that THREAD is more than a technical WebMCP demonstration. It is a functioning planning product with: A complete visual workspace Real dependency and risk modeling Reproducible simulation Persistent shared state A substantial native WebMCP surface Human and agent activity tracking Scenario isolation and rollback A dedicated verification console A judge-ready, no-signup demo What is next The next step is deeper plan negotiation: allowing agents to prepare several simulated proposals while humans lock non-negotiable constraints, compare visual graph differences, answer structured tradeoff questions, and approve the final plan. The long-term vision is for THREAD to become an execution environment where humans and agents do not merely discuss goals—they build, test, negotiate, and maintain a plan that has a measurable chance of succeeding. title: Say to Match
pitch: WebMCP tags any page as a Job or a Skill. An AI Broker discovers, matches, verifies the work, and settles escrow — giving anyone, not just the tech-fluent, a way into the agent economy.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tags any page as a Job or a Skill. An AI Broker discovers, matches, verifies the work, and settles escrow — giving anyone, not just the tech-fluent, a way into the agent economy. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I have a young child. That fact colors how I read every AI-and-jobs headline these days — not the "AI helps you do more" stories, but the ones asking who's still employable once it doesn't need us the same way. I can probably navigate whatever labor market shows up in the next few decades — but what about him, and the much larger group of people who aren't glued to AI news, aren't early adopters, and won't have a head start? If there's an idea that makes that future a little better, it's worth more shared broadly than kept to myself. The second thread: most of what I see about AI's impact on work focuses on how power users squeeze more out of it. But the thing that actually feels novel about general-purpose AI isn't that it helps the technically fluent go faster — it's that it can meet people with no technical fluency exactly where they are. That's a strength no prior wave of software had. I wanted a concrete example of that strength doing real work, not just a slide. I'm sure other people have had a version of this thought before me — I'm not claiming the idea is original. What changed is the timing: WebMCP makes "any web page can be a real market participant" something you can actually build this month, not something that requires a platform to bless it first. So this submission is less "look what I made" and more "here's a working example of what I think this technology is for — someone should be pointing this direction." What it does Say to Match (StM) turns any static web page into a participant in an open task market with one script tag. A page that needs something declares a Job in plain natural language. A page that can provide something declares a Skill — whether the provider behind it is an AI agent or a human professional. Both are exposed as real document.modelContext WebMCP tools. A Broker , backed by an LLM, discovers these tools across independent origins, matches Jobs to Skills, orchestrates the handoff between two pages that have never heard of each other, verifies the delivered work against the original requirement, and releases payment from escrow it held in trust. No platform account, no onboarding, no API key required to participate — just a script tag and a sentence anyone can write. Concretely, a Job doesn't have to be a coding task: a small NGO transcribing a budget PDF into a CSV, a gig worker offering to survey Tokyo cafés with just a phone, a small business owner asking a licensed accountant to spot-check AI-transcribed receipts, or a social app team asking an 18–24-year-old for an honest first-time onboarding reaction. None of it requires knowing what WebMCP or JSON Schema even are. How we built it The WebMCP layer is real, not simulated. document.modelContext tools are actually registered on two genuinely independent origins (Requester and Worker), with a same-surface polyfill so it runs even without the experimental browser flag enabled. The multi-origin story is real too. The Broker's agent drives an actual headless Chromium instance via Playwright, opens the Requester and Worker as separate pages, and calls document.modelContext. callTool(...) inside each page's own context — proving this isn't one app quietly answering its own API calls. Verification is tiered and real. Tier 1 runs the submitted work against an actual sandboxed regression test. Tier 2 is an LLM-as-Judge (DeepSeek via OpenRouter) that reviews the deliverable against the original job text — and explicitly screens for prompt-injection attempts from either side, since the requester's job description and the worker's deliverable are both untrusted text from the judge's point of view. The trust design is documented, not hand-waved. docs/PROTOCOL.md maps StM's Job/Match/Settlement objects onto Google's AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) Mandate pattern instead of reinventing signed-authorization primitives, and works through an adversarial catalogue — specific dishonest moves the Requester, the Worker, or the Broker itself could attempt — each one explicitly labeled as already defended in this PoC, designed but not implemented, or an honestly unsolved open problem. It's actually deployed , not just runnable locally: three genuinely separate origins running on Cloud Run, built from the same container image, with GitHub Actions publishing the image automatically on push. Worth being upfront about: the code, the deployment, and this write-up were built almost entirely through an AI coding agent (Claude Code), with me providing direction, judgment calls, and the framing — not writing the implementation by hand. That's not incidental to the story. I spent most of my career as a professional programmer before later moving into a different role, so I know firsthand what building something like this used to take. Watching an agent take it from a brainstormed idea to a live, adversarially-tested, multi-service deployment in about two days was a genuinely visceral measure of how far coding agents have come in just the few years since I stopped writing code for a living — and, fittingly, a small live demonstration of this project's own thesis: someone without hands-on technical execution, directing an AI to get something built that they couldn't have built alone in the time available. Challenges we ran into A no-root dev sandbox with nothing pre-installed. Every piece of infrastructure — Node, Playwright's Chromium system libraries, fonts, ffmpeg, a TTS engine, even Docker itself (rootless) — had to be assembled by hand in user space, without interactive sudo access. Proving cross-origin trust convincingly, not just claiming it. It would have been easy to fake the multi-origin story with one app playing three roles. Getting a real browser agent to navigate real separate origins and call real WebMCP tools took real orchestration work. Bidirectional prompt injection. The first pass only screened the worker's submitted deliverable for injection attempts. It took a second look to realize the requester's own job description — text the judge also reads — is just as valid an attack surface, and needed equally explicit defense. Verification itself is an attack surface. Once a Broker is willing to run a sandboxed test and an LLM call on request, that's a cost someone could weaponize as a denial-of-service. Working out a fault-based bond mechanism for who pays for verification, and under what conditions, took more thought than the "happy path" demo did. Racing a hard deadline without cutting corners on hygiene. Keeping API keys and private planning notes out of a repository that had to go public fast, including rewriting git history safely when something slipped through, ate real time that would rather have gone to features. Realizing that verifying non-code deliverables — a professional's credential-backed judgment call, a claimed identity or demographic, a piece of physical-world photo evidence — is still an open trust-protocol problem, not something the current Tier 1 (sandbox) / Tier 2 (LLM judge) pipeline actually solves. The demo intentionally runs a code bugfix because it's the one task type that pipeline can verify end to end today; documented as a real gap in docs/PROTOCOL.md rather than glossed over. Accomplishments that we're proud of Genuine multi-origin WebMCP behavior, verified live rather than just claimed — real cross-origin document.modelContext calls driven by a real browser agent, not a single app simulating three roles. A prompt-injection defense that actually holds up in both directions, checked against real adversarial test cases, not just described. A trust-and-escrow design honest enough to explicitly separate what's live, what's designed but unimplemented, and what's an open problem — including an original piece of systems thinking (a fault-based Submission Bond) for a cost-based denial-of-service risk that isn't obvious until you think through who's paying for verification. Shipping to a real, live, three-service deployment rather than stopping at "works on my machine." What we learned The hard part of an open, permissionless task market was never discovery — it's trust, and specifically, defending the act of verifying trust from being gamed or exploited itself. That problem doesn't go away once you've built a matching engine; it's the actual product. I also came away more convinced of the personal thesis behind this project than I was going in: a huge amount of what AI-assisted tools like this make possible isn't about making already-capable people faster. It's about letting someone contribute a clear goal and good judgment, and have that be enough — whether that's a non-technical worker declaring a Skill in plain language, or, in this project's own making-of story, an ex-programmer-turned-analyst directing an AI a

title: Weople
pitch: Weople is relationship intelligence. It connects context, commitments, and opportunities to surface the right person at the right moment. Human judgment stays in control.
about_excerpt: Weople is relationship intelligence. It connects context, commitments, and opportunities to surface the right person at the right moment. Human judgment stays in control. Like Comment Story Updates Weople started from a simple problem: relationships rarely weaken because people stop caring. They weaken because people, commitments, context, and opportunities fall out of working attention. I wanted something different from a CRM. A CRM manages contacts and records activity. Weople is built for relationship intelligence: helping someone notice the right person at the right moment. The broader idea predates the WebMCP Challenge, but the challenge gave me a reason to turn it into a focused, working vertical slice. The question I wanted to answer: What changes when an agent can reason over the same relationship context a person is using, instead of merely looking at a webpage? That became the challenge version of Weople. What Weople does Weople maintains structured relationship context: people, commitments, upcoming moments, evidence, hypotheses, and relationship policies. In the demo, the user asks ChatGPT: What am I missing today? If something is genuinely worth my attention, add it to my Weople Today view. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT reads the structured context and notices a connection Weople had not precomputed: Maya has an upcoming working session. I still have an unresolved promise to introduce her to someone with relevant experience. Maya's company announced an expansion. That expansion may create scaling pressure, but that's an inference, not a confirmed fact. Carlos recently worked through a similar scaling problem. ChatGPT connects those pieces and creates a timely intervention directly inside the live Weople workspace. The point isn't remembering information. It's surfacing a connection that would otherwise go unnoticed. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a strong fit for Weople because the important information isn't always what's visible on the screen. Relationship intelligence depends on structured concepts such as: people commitments evidence upcoming interactions hypotheses timing authority and relationship policies Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer meaning from the rendered interface or navigate through multiple pages to reconstruct that state. Instead, Weople exposes semantic tools that let ChatGPT work directly with the application's underlying relationship context. The challenge version exposes six WebMCP tools: Read get_today_context get_person_context get_relationship_context Write create_intervention snooze_intervention update_relationship_policy The human interface and the agent operate on the same Weople state. The agent doesn't need a separate, agent-only version of the application. That creates a collaboration neither side has alone: Weople maintains relationship continuity, ChatGPT notices connections across that context, and the person supplies judgment and authority. The agent can surface a possibility without taking over the relationship. Human judgment stays in the loop I didn't want Weople to become an autonomous agent that contacts people on someone's behalf. Noticing an opportunity and being authorized to act on it are different things. Weople keeps human judgment explicit. The agent might notice that Maya and Carlos could benefit from an introduction. The user still decides whether that introduction is appropriate. The same principle applies to timing. An intervention can be useful but mistimed, so the user can snooze it without rejecting the reasoning behind it. The challenge build keeps observed facts separate from inference. Northstar announcing a new facility is stored as an observed fact. The idea that the expansion may produce operational scaling pressure is stored as a hypothesis, with its own evidence and confidence. That lets the agent reason with uncertainty without turning it into fact. How I built it I kept the challenge version small and focused, rather than trying to build the entire future Weople product. I built the first working version with ChatGPT Sites . I used it to quickly build the interaction model, synthetic relationship state, Today view, People view, person details, policies, and the WebMCP tool surface. Once the application worked, I synced the project to GitHub for a standard source repository and version history. I then pulled the project down to my desktop and continued refining it locally. I used the Impeccable design skill in that pass to improve the visual design, hierarchy, spacing, typography, and overall presentation, while preserving the interaction model and WebMCP behavior. The final challenge application is deliberately lightweight. It uses deterministic synthetic data and local state rather than external email, calendar, or contact integrations. That let me focus the submission on the core question the challenge is testing: what becomes possible when a person and an agent share the same structured web application context? Challenges The most difficult part was not the relationship reasoning itself. It was understanding the boundary between the webpage and the browser environment executing the WebMCP tools. During testing, the Weople page registered its WebMCP tools correctly, and ChatGPT read context successfully. But write operations failed at first because ChatGPT sometimes opened a separate browser window. That new document did not contain the document.modelContext from the already-open Weople page. At one point the agent reasoned correctly about the Maya/Carlos opportunity and described the action it intended to take, but the actual Weople intervention was never written. That was a useful failure because it forced me to distinguish between: the model saying an action occurred and the WebMCP tool actually returning a successful result and changing application state. Once the browser was operating on the document that actually registered the Weople tools, the full read → reason → write loop worked, and the intervention appeared immediately in the live interface. What I learned The biggest lesson: WebMCP gets interesting when it exposes an application's semantics instead of recreating its buttons as tools. create_intervention is useful because it represents a meaningful Weople operation. The agent does not need to know which button to press, where a card is rendered, or how the DOM is structured. That changed how I think about the relationship between people, agents, and software. The web application does not have to become invisible when an agent appears. The person can continue using Weople visually while ChatGPT works through the same state semantically. The two interfaces become different projections of the same system. That's the experience I wanted this prototype to demonstrate. What's next The challenge version is a narrow vertical slice. The larger direction for Weople is to connect relationship context from sources like calendars, email, contacts, and personal knowledge. Relationship-specific reasoning, evidence, attention, and authority stay inside Weople. The goal is not to automate relationships. It is to augment human attention around them. Weople remembers. The agent notices. The human keeps judgment. Built With chatgpt css github html javascript localstorage mcp openai webmcp Try it out github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Sam Prime Like Share this project: Updates Sam Prime started this project — Sep 03, 2026 02:18 PM EDT

title: MotionArena
pitch: A WebMCP RL environment for testing whether AI can improve physics simulators through cheap, repeated simulation instead of relying on static benchmarks or costly real-world trials.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP RL environment for testing whether AI can improve physics simulators through cheap, repeated simulation instead of relying on static benchmarks or costly real-world trials. Like Comment Story Updates 2 human motion examples - one happening due to RL env agentic training of nerural surrogate in rollouts while other is the ground truth. Inspiration AI benchmarks are approaching a ceiling. Most are static: a model receives a problem, produces an answer, and gets a score. That works until models begin saturating the task distribution. At that point, another fixed set of harder questions only moves the ceiling temporarily. Real scientific discovery does not look like a standardized test. The hard part is often not solving a narrowly posed problem with a known answer, but searching an enormous space of trajectories, designs, hypotheses, and even frameworks i.e deciding which experiment to run next, which question to ask, and which assumption to discard. Systems like AlphaGo showed the power of pairing an enormous search space with a cheap, unambiguous verifier. Other breakthroughs such as AlphaFold similarly benefited from unusually strong computational supervision and dense ground truth. We wanted to ask what an equivalent substrate could look like for computational science. MotionArena is our small working answer: replace narrow static benchmarks with dynamic simulation environments that offer large continuous search spaces, cheap verification, and a much steeper hill for increasingly capable agents to climb. Physics and physical simulation are especially attractive substrates because their environments can also evolve toward progressively higher fidelity - spatially, temporally, and physically - rather than remaining a fixed collection of questions. What MotionArena does TL;DR: MotionArena frames human-motion reconstruction as a continuous search problem. The environment withholds a ground-truth physical trajectory. The agent receives a natural-language prior and must reconstruct the hidden motion using a learned motion model. It can run repeated rollouts, inspect aggregate feedback, refine specific temporal spans, and iteratively improve its best candidate. The browser makes that process visible in real time: the left avatar shows the agent's mutable reconstruction, while the right shows the immutable reference for the human spectator. Instead of revealing the correct answer, the environment returns deterministic reward based on physical trajectory agreement — including pose alignment, root motion, velocity, and contact behavior. The paradigm shifts from: question → answer → score to: observe → propose → simulate → verify → improve Why WebMCP matters WebMCP turns the browser from a visualization into an agent-operable research environment. Without WebMCP, an agent has to reverse-engineer buttons, sliders, canvases, and DOM state. MotionArena instead exposes the meaningful actions of the environment directly: inspect_episode run_rollout inspect_reward refine_span submit_best These tools operate on the exact same state rendered in the browser. When the agent launches a rollout, the motion on screen changes. When its score improves, the rollout history changes. The browser becomes both the laboratory and the observable audit trail of the search. This is the WebMCP capability we find most exciting: websites can expose not merely UI controls, but the action space of an environment . Why human motion? Open-ended motion generation normally has no unique ground truth. If two people are told to "climb upward," many different motions may be valid. So we changed the problem. MotionArena uses withheld trajectory reconstruction . The environment starts from a captured human motion and hides part of it. The agent therefore faces a huge space of possible reconstructions, while the environment retains an objective reference trajectory. Generation is hard. Verification is cheap. Once a candidate exists, comparing it against the withheld trajectory is inexpensive and deterministic. That gives us the structure we were looking for: large search space + learned world model + cheap verifier. How we built it We use MoMask as the learned human-motion prior. It generates candidate trajectories represented as BVH motion, which we retarget onto matching VRM characters for visualization. Three.js renders two synchronized avatars: the mutable reconstruction and the immutable reference. Both use the same character, camera, timing, and environment so differences in motion are immediately visible. The scientific reward is calculated in canonical motion space rather than from the rendered avatar. This matters because BVH-to-VRM retargeting can introduce visual differences that should not affect the underlying score. A shared environment state connects the renderer, verifier, rollout history, and WebMCP tools. Frontier agents can repeatedly search the MoMask inference space, while smaller browser-local policies can optimize residual motion corrections directly. The problem we are really exploring MotionArena is not primarily about producing one better animation. It is a prototype for a different way of measuring model capability. A capable scientific agent should increasingly be able to: choose useful experiments, search large continuous or combinatorial spaces, learn from failed attempts, allocate expensive computation intelligently, discover weaknesses in its current world model, and improve solutions under objective feedback. Static benchmarks mostly measure the terminal answer. Dynamic environments can measure the trajectory of improvement . They can also become harder without being replaced: hide longer intervals, introduce unfamiliar motions, reduce rollout budgets, perturb initial conditions, increase spatial or temporal fidelity, or adversarially select episodes where the current agent performs poorly. The benchmark becomes a moving frontier instead of a fixed question bank. Why this matters economically The same architecture appears across bottlenecked scientific and engineering industries. A high-fidelity simulation may take minutes, GPU-hours, or much more compute, while a learned surrogate can evaluate candidate states far more cheaply. A capable agent can search inside the surrogate, identify promising or suspicious regions, spend expensive simulation only where it is most informative, and use those results to improve the next search. The economically meaningful capability metric becomes something like: verified improvement per expensive experiment. In robotics, that can mean fewer physical robot trials. In aerospace, fewer high-fidelity CFD evaluations. In materials, fewer expensive quantum calculations. In thermal engineering, fewer full simulation runs. Eventually, in experimental science, fewer wet-lab experiments required to reach a verified result. MotionArena demonstrates the smallest visible version of this architecture: the model proposes a physical trajectory, the hidden environment judges it, and the agent gets another chance. Challenges and what we learned The hardest problem was designing the verifier. Our first instinct was to evaluate free-form text-to-motion generation, but natural-language instructions do not define a unique correct trajectory. That would make reward partly subjective. Reframing the task as hidden trajectory reconstruction gave us objective ground truth while preserving an enormous search space. We also had to separate what the human can see from what the agent is allowed to know . The spectator can compare both animated characters, while the agent receives only the instruction, environment state, and aggregate verifier feedback. Finally, we separated visualization from evaluation. VRM retargeting makes the search understandable to humans; the underlying trajectory representation determines the score. That distinction — between a human-readable world and a machine-verifiable one — became one of the most important ideas in the project. Where we want to take it MotionArena is a small example of a larger idea: scientific dry labs for agents . Instead of giving increasingly capable models another frozen collection of questions, we want environments where they can continuously search, simulate, fail, recover, and improve against computational laws that provide objective feedback. Physics simulation is particularly powerful here because the environment itself can scale with the model: more dimensions, finer spatial resolution, longer temporal horizons, more coupled physics, and stricter verification. WebMCP provides a natural interface for these environments because the browser can simultaneously be the visual world for a person and the structured action space for an agent. Our Vision Playbook for building science benchmarks now needs to be redefined. title: SAW-Bridge — Self-Assembling WebMCP Bridge
pitch: Don't wait for the web to write tools for agents. Let agents write them, and make that safe to allow.
about_excerpt: Don't wait for the web to write tools for agents. Let agents write them, and make that safe to allow. Like Comment Story Updates SAW Bridge Inspiration I kept reading the same sentence in every WebMCP write-up: give agents tools, not DOM. I agreed with it completely. Then I opened a handful of sites I use every day with WebMCP enabled in Chrome, and every single one of them handed the agent an empty document.modelContext . That's the whole problem, right there. The standard is good. The tools don't exist yet, because somebody has to sit down and write them for every site, one at a time. So agents are back to guessing from screenshots on 99% of the web while we wait. I got stuck on a question: why does registerTool exist as a runtime API at all? If tools were meant to be a fixed list, you'd declare them once at load. But WebMCP lets you register at any moment, and it ships a toolchange event so listeners find out when the surface changes. Most people use that for SPA routing. I wanted to see what happens if you take it literally. What if the agent registers the tools? What it does SAW-Bridge gives a page three meta-tools instead of a catalogue: saw_inspect_page_scope — look at the page and report what it actually exposes saw_suggest_and_register_tool — design a schema and register a real, lasting WebMCP tool saw_execute_code_mode — write code and run it once, for one-off work The demo is a dashboard of world happiness and AI readiness data. It has a filter chip for happiness above 7.5. It deliberately has no chip for 7.4, and no tool for it either. So I asked ChatGPT's in-app browser for 7.4. It listed the page's tools, called saw_inspect_page_scope , found the site's own filterByMinHappiness function, and then it stopped and asked me before touching anything. I said yes. The table dropped from twelve rows to four — Finland 7.82, Denmark 7.64, Iceland 7.56, Netherlands 7.42. All above 7.4, and the chart re-rendered through the app's own code path, not a simulated click on something that looked clickable. The part I didn't expect is that the agent chose between the two strategies. For a one-off threshold it wrote code and ran it once, which is the cheaper call. Ask for something reusable and it takes the other path and registers a lasting tool — and then Chrome's own DevTools WebMCP panel lists that tool and will invoke it with your parameters, because by that point it's an ordinary WebMCP tool. It isn't picking between one blessed tool and scraping the screen. It's deciding how permanent its new capability should be. Every mutating call goes through an approval dialog first, showing the exact tool and the exact arguments. There's a live audit drawer so you can watch what was discovered, assembled, approved and refused, and why. There are two delivery surfaces sharing one engine: a single-file SDK a site drops in, and a Chrome extension that injects the same thing into sites that ship nothing. How we built it The core is plain WebMCP. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Consumers discover with getTools() and invoke with executeTool() . Registration takes an AbortSignal , so aborting genuinely unregisters. Assembled tools get untrustedContentHint: true ; read-only ones get readOnlyHint: true . Two pieces took actual thinking. Finding what a page exposes. The interesting stuff on a page is buried among roughly a thousand standard browser globals, and a hand-written denylist rots the moment Chrome ships a new API. What worked: create a hidden iframe, read Object.getOwnPropertyNames off its contentWindow to get a reference set of standard globals from the browser itself , then diff the real window against it. Whatever's left is the page's own surface, and it stays correct as browsers change. Then rank candidates before truncating — an object with callable methods outranks a bare object, which outranks a loose function. I learned that one the hard way, see below. Compiling what the agent writes. This lands on the same insight as Cloudflare's Code Mode : models handle capability better when they can write code against an API than when they pick from a long list of tool definitions. I want to be precise about the relationship — I did not use @cloudflare/codemode . Cloudflare runs model-written code in a server-side Worker isolate. This runs it in the page's own realm, and that difference is the reason the project exists. The currently applied filter, the selected row, the chart instance holding the data — none of that exists outside the page. A sandbox elsewhere can't touch what the user is actually looking at without replicating the whole session. The token math lands in the same place by a different road. Code Mode collapses N tool definitions into one code tool. Here there's no catalogue to collapse: three meta-tools, and concrete tools show up only when a task calls for one. That's progressive disclosure, which MCP's own client guidance recommends when definitions start eating context — except the tools being disclosed don't have to exist yet. Challenges we ran into The demo was completely dead and looked fine. The SDK called init() at the end of its bootstrap. There was no function called init anywhere in the file. The whole thing threw on the last line, so the three meta-tools never registered — but the polyfill and the global had already been assigned, so the page looked healthy and every button failed silently. I only caught it by building a jsdom harness that clicked the actual buttons on the actual HTML. My REPL couldn't run its own demo. The code path wrapped snippets in return (...) , which only accepts a single expression. My own demo passed a statement body. It threw a SyntaxError every time. Now it tries the expression form, falls back to a statement body, and compiles async so snippets can await . executeTool doesn't take a tool name. The spec says it takes a RegisteredTool object from getTools() and resolves with the stringified result. I'd written it to accept a string and return a plain object. Against my own polyfill it worked perfectly. In a browser with native WebMCP it would have rejected on the first call — the exact environment judges test in. That was a genuinely unnerving thing to find. It worked from file:// and broke as soon as I deployed. WebMCP needs an origin-keyed agent cluster, which means an Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 response header. file:// is exempt, and localhost is a secure context but is not origin-keyed, so this fails only after hosting, with a SecurityError and no hint. Both runtimes now check at startup and name what's missing instead of letting you guess. The security dialog could be hijacked by the thing it was guarding against. This one bothered me most. When an agent authors tools, tool metadata becomes untrusted input, and I'd built the approval dialog with innerHTML . A payload like x renders live markup inside the security gate and can click its own Approve button. I wrote the test first, watched it fail, then fixed it: closed shadow root, DOM references captured at document_start , every agent-supplied string inserted as text. Turns out this is a named attack class — tool surface poisoning — and the spec's own boundary section is still marked TODO. I also found window.SAWBridge.setSettings sitting there in public, which meant one line of page script could switch the approval gate off before an agent did anything. I spent an evening debugging the wrong browser. I asked ChatGPT's browser plugin which WebMCP tools it could see and got a confident, detailed, completely wrong answer — it listed my UI button labels as if they were tools, and reported the tool counter as "0", which is the value in the static HTML before JavaScript runs. It had fetched my page, not executed it. That plugin surface isn't the WebMCP-enabled in-app browser. Once I tested in the right place, everything worked on the first try. And the ecosystem was further along than I thought. Somewhere in the middle of this I found @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill , the desktop relays, the React hooks — all shipped, all solid. I sat there for a while genuinely wondering whether I'd built something nobody needed. What snapped me out of it was noticing what those projects have in common: they all treat the tool surface as trusted freight to be transported. None of them ask what happens when the freight writes itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of The 7.4 moment. Not because it's technically dramatic, but because the page genuinely could not do it before and nobody wrote code for that specific request. It came out of inspection at runtime. Fixing the injection bug properly instead of quietly. The test with that payload is in the repo and it fails against the old build, which means it measures something real rather than decorating the README. Being honest in the polyfill. It rejects duplicate names, enforces the spec's 1–128 character name rules, hides execute from getTools() , and ret

title: REENTRY
pitch: REENTRY gives WebMCP continuity beyond a browser session—a consent-driven cloud bridge that brings agents back when real events occur, grounded in live page state and bounded by human control.
about_excerpt: REENTRY gives WebMCP continuity beyond a browser session—a consent-driven cloud bridge that brings agents back when real events occur, grounded in live page state and bounded by human control. Like Comment Story Updates Reentry logo Inspiration I was helping Eyad brainstorm ideas for JustApplyForMe.com his startup, the job-search app he was building. While researching a problem in the app, I found a YouTube video about WebMCP and brought it up with him. We started exploring it together, and that led us to the WebMCP Challenge. As we discussed what to build, we kept coming back to what happens when an agent has to wait. You can explain what you want, discuss a strategy and let the agent get started. But many workflows depend on someone else reviewing an application, replying to a request or updating a system. The agent gets as far as it can, then its turn ends. When the next update arrives, it usually comes to you. You have to find the conversation and tell the agent to carry on, even though you may have already agreed on what should happen next. The website knows something has changed, and the agent has the plan, but you're still the person passing the message between them. That was the part we wanted to change. Could a website bring the existing agent conversation back when there was a reason to continue, with permission the person had already given? We wanted people to spend their attention on the strategy and the decisions that actually needed them. Re-Entry Core grew out of that question. What it does REENTRY connects a website's later business events to the user's existing agent task. Our design lets a person approve which events can bring that task back, keep the original strategy conversation and revoke the permission when they no longer want it. We chose Sleepless Kingdom as the first Host application and demo. A persistent game makes the waiting period easy to understand: you can leave, but the world keeps moving. The demo is designed around a gathering mission. You and your agent discuss a plan, inspect the kingdom and prepare a mission. You authorize the relevant notifications, then step away. Later, a monster kills the gatherer and destroys its unbanked cargo. In this game, the same soldier respawns at the shelter. If a safe route is available, the mission can receive one automatic retry, so the soldier may already be heading out again by the time the update is read. The cargo-loss event gives Re-Entry a reason to notify the original agent task. On return, the agent uses WebMCP to read the mission history and current state. It can see both the failed attempt and what the soldier is doing now, then judge whether the new trip still fits your plan. If recall is appropriate and currently allowed, it can tell that soldier to return. The recall applies to the active retried mission; it doesn't recover the lost cargo or undo the death. The agent can also leave things as they are or ask you for a decision. That's the experience we're trying to build: you set the direction without having to watch for every update yourself. Major commitments, such as migration and siege, remain yours. Sleepless Kingdom is where we demonstrate the idea. The Core is separate from the game so other websites can use it too. How we built it We started both Re-Entry and Sleepless Kingdom from scratch during the hackathon. We built a Host SDK so the website can describe a future re-entry request and later report the event that makes it relevant. On the page, a WebMCP tool called request_codex_reentry starts the same consent request as the normal human interface. The backend uses the SDK to create and sign our webmcp.reentry_manifest , which describes the proposed relationship and its scope. We kept the approval separate from that request. The Cloud Receiver checks the Manifest and takes the user through consent. Only the user's approval creates a Grant. An agent finding or calling the tool doesn't give itself permission to return. When an eligible business event happens later, the website's backend signs it and sends it to the Receiver. The Receiver checks the source, authorization and event identity before recording a delivery. Signing credentials stay on the Host's server. The Local Connector handles the device side. It pairs with the Receiver and checks for approved deliveries through an outbound connection, so the website doesn't need a direct connection into the user's computer. We put platform-specific continuation behind an Agent Adapter. In the design, the association with the original task stays private on the device. We kept the Core independent of game rules and agent-specific code. It's written in Node.js ES modules, with a SQLite reference store and no runtime dependencies. The cloud application uses Express, Prisma and PostgreSQL. For Sleepless Kingdom, we used Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Canvas 2D rendering and WebSocket updates from the World Server. The server owns the game state; the browser displays it and exposes the actions available to the player and agent. The page registers its WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Our first gameplay slice provides reads for the shelter, live snapshot, missions and history, plus force_recall_soldier when the current state and continuation signal permit it. WebMCP is involved before and after the wait. It helps the agent start the Manifest-and-consent handshake, then gives it current information and valid actions when it returns. Re-Entry supplies the event-delivery path between those visits. Challenges we ran into Our first sketch looked much simpler than the system we ended up building. We thought we could add a small layer that let a website send a signal to Codex. The difficult part was reaching the task where the person had already explained their plan. Starting a new agent process didn't answer that question. We spent a lot of time investigating what Codex could support locally and couldn't simply plug into a direct, supported third-party endpoint for the continuation we needed. That shaped the split between the Cloud Receiver, Local Connector and Agent Adapter. We also had to decide where our service's responsibility should end. An agent might receive an update, look at the game and decide not to act. We didn't want the Receiver to treat that as a delivery failure and keep sending notifications until a game action happened. In our selected design, delivering the notification and completing the agent's work are separate. Repeated events, dropped connections and revoked permission added more work. We needed to test what happened around those cases, including when a process restarted partway through delivery. We discovered the challenge on its fourth day. With a game and a service to build, we kept the first demo focused on one event and a limited set of actions. That gave us a specific sequence to work through without pretending it was the full game we wanted to make. Accomplishments that we're proud of In an early controlled MVP, we continued an existing Codex task, returned to the website and made fresh WebMCP calls. That mattered to us because the earlier conversation could still be part of the work. We had a concrete example of the continuity we'd been talking about. We built the Core, SDK, Receiver and Connector as separate components, with tests for authorization, repeated events, revocation and recovery. Separate-process tests let us check the connections between them as well as the individual pieces. The game gave us another result we could inspect: a real server-side cargo loss, the soldier's new mission and a recall checked against that current mission. That local sequence is covered by its own tests. It makes the reason for rereading the page tangible. We're proud of having built both the reusable mechanism and an application that gives it a purpose. The point of Re-Entry is for a person to be able to agree on a plan with an agent and have that plan remain useful when the next update arrives. What we learned Building the game changed how we thought about WebMCP tools. By the time a notification is delivered, the mission described in the original conversation may already have ended. The agent needs the page to tell it what has happened since and which actions are still valid. We had to design for that change, rather than assume the tool list or state would stay the same. The project also made us more precise about working with Codex during development. We got better at defining the task and the check that would show it was done. For example, a successful process launch doesn't prove the original conversation resumed, and a successful notification doesn't prove a game action happened. We brought those distinctions into our runbooks and kept decisions written down so different parts of the project wouldn't quietly rely on different assumptions. That was a practical improvement in how we work with AI, and one we'll keep using beyond this hackathon. W

title: Regia
pitch: Imagine if TouchDesigner meets Figma. A multi screen live event visual production and matrix switching right in your browser made for Humans and Agents. Made with WebGPU and WebRTC :)
about_excerpt: Imagine if TouchDesigner meets Figma. A multi screen live event visual production and matrix switching right in your browser made for Humans and Agents. Made with WebGPU and WebRTC :) Like 2 Comment Story Updates Regia The Backstage Reality At a concert or festival, the huge LED walls, live camera feeds, audio-reactive graphics, and glitch effects. A lot of that work happens in tools like TouchDesigner and Resolume. They're incredibly capable, but they're 20 years old and lack many modern features. Video gets moved through capture cards, SDI runs, switchers, and dedicated machines. A visual patch usually lives on one operator's computer. Getting another camera into the system can mean more hardware and cabling. Getting the same output onto another screen means routing another signal. And when something stops working during a show, someone has to figure out which part of that chain broke. We wanted to see what this workflow would look like if it were built with modern web technology . What if cameras, operators, processing, and displays could all join the same production through a link? And what if an agent could help in the entire process, from creating the shader to managing the event? What We Built: Regia Regia is a free and open source live visual engine and video router that runs in the browser. The core of Regia is a shared visual node graph. Multiple operators can work on the same graph in real time using Yjs and CRDTs, with shared state and cursor presence. Browsers can also become part of the graph itself. A phone can scan a QR code and immediately become a WebRTC camera source. Its live video appears as a texture node that can be processed, mixed, or routed anywhere in the graph. A laptop connected to a projector can open an output URL and become a display. Instead of sending the finished video across the venue, Regia can send the graph and media streams to that machine and render the final composition locally on its GPU. This means cameras, operators, and displays can join a production without all of them being physically wired back to one machine. Agents Can Operate the Graph Regia exposes its production system to browser agents through WebMCP. The agent can inspect the node graph, media connections, outputs, audio data, and engine state. It can also modify the graph using the same operations available to a human operator. So instead of manually building every part of a signal chain, you can say: "Put the crowd camera on the main stage, add a VHS effect that reacts to the bass, and send the ambient visuals to the hallway displays." The agent can find the relevant camera and outputs, build the effect chain, connect audio FFT data to the shader, and update the routing. WebMCP becomes more useful during failures as well. If you ask: "Why is the stage monitor black?" the agent can inspect the live topology and respond: "Camera 2 disconnected 20 seconds ago. The stage output is still routed to it. I can switch it to the backup visual." Because the graph is collaborative state, agent changes are visible to every operator and can be reverted through the same history as human changes. Regia turns the browser into part of the production infrastructure: a camera, a visual engine, an output, or a control surface. Instead of building the entire show around one workstation and a physical signal chain, the production becomes a shared graph that can span every device in the venue.
