title: Sauna Quote X-Ray
pitch: People and AI turn a sauna quote into an honest shared canvas, exposing hidden costs and the exact questions to ask before signing.
about_excerpt: People and AI turn a sauna quote into an honest shared canvas, exposing hidden costs and the exact questions to ask before signing. Like Comment Story Updates The $11,750 quote exposes missing scope and a sourced $12,250–$18,650 planning range. The buyer and agent start from the same visible quote canvas. The quoted $11,750 can reach $18,650 once hidden scope is made visible. Inspiration A sauna quote can look complete while leaving out the electrical circuit, panel upgrade, foundation, permits, assembly, ventilation, or service responsibility. A buyer sees one confident number. The real landed cost can be thousands higher. We built Sauna Quote X-Ray so the buyer and their AI agent can investigate that gap together before anyone signs. What it does Sauna Quote X-Ray turns a sauna quote into a shared, visible decision canvas. The buyer can see and edit every priced item, scope decision, planning range, risk finding, contractor question, and agent action. In the reviewer-safe demo, a quoted total of $11,750 becomes a sourced projected range of $12,250 to $18,650 after missing electrical and site scope is made explicit. The agent can then create the exact questions the buyer should ask the contractor. Why WebMCP This workflow is a strong fit for WebMCP because the source of truth should remain the website, not disappear into a separate chat transcript. The agent is fast at turning ambiguous scope into structured state. The human knows what the seller promised and must retain authority over every assumption. WebMCP lets both act on the same interface: The agent loads or structures the quote. The human sees every change immediately. Either side can correct a line item or scope status. The agent re-reads the visible state and builds the next questions. Nothing is sent or persisted unless the product explicitly adds such a capability. This demo does not. That shared round trip was difficult before WebMCP. A normal chatbot can produce advice, but it cannot reliably keep its work synchronized with the buyer's live, editable decision surface. How we built it The app is a standalone Next.js 16 and React 19 project deployed on Vercel and presented inside Sauna Guide. It registers eight narrow, page-scoped tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : load_demo_sauna_quote get_sauna_quote_xray_state set_sauna_project_context upsert_sauna_quote_line_item remove_sauna_quote_line_item set_sauna_quote_scope build_sauna_contractor_questions start_sauna_quote_xray The tools and human controls operate on one React state model. Pure TypeScript summary functions calculate completeness, priced exposure, the projected total, and quote-specific questions. The read tool marks seller and user text with untrustedContentHint: true . JSON schemas reject unknown properties and cap strings, arrays, amounts, and line count. Safety and privacy All demos use synthetic quote data. Working state stays in the current tab. No tool uploads a quote, stores customer data, sends email, contacts a seller, or creates a lead. Every agent mutation is visible in the shared activity log and can be corrected by the human. The app links each planning range and risk finding to buyer-facing Sauna Guide sources. It also labels estimates as planning aids rather than contractor quotes. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not registering a tool. It was designing tool boundaries that are useful without quietly crossing the line from analysis into a real commercial action. We separated reading, editing, scope resolution, question building, and reset behavior so each action is explicit and reviewable. We also had to keep React's visible state and WebMCP execution synchronized without stale closures. A state ref feeds tool execution while normal React state renders the same result to the buyer. Accomplishments that we're proud of Eight working WebMCP tools with narrow schemas and explicit safety annotations One shared canvas where human and agent edits stay synchronized A coherent buyer workflow, not a hidden prompt wrapper Safe synthetic fixtures that judges can use without creating a customer lead Automated unit, type, lint, production-build, and browser journey coverage Production verification in ChatGPT's in-app browser with all eight tools discovered and invoked What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the website already has meaningful state, domain rules, and human controls. The agent becomes a collaborator inside the product instead of a separate destination. We also learned that reversible actions and visible provenance make agent behavior easier to trust. The activity log is not decoration. It is part of the interaction contract. What's next The next step is optional local document parsing that lets a buyer structure their own quote without uploading it to a server. We would also add side-by-side quote comparison, saved local sessions, and a handoff package the buyer can choose to send only after explicit confirmation. Try it Live WebMCP app: https://sauna.guide/tools/sauna-quote-xray Public MIT repository: https://github.com/Ac0AI/sauna-quote-xray Buyer research and source guides: https://sauna.guide Suggested prompt: Load the backyard quote. Make the missing electrical work explicit, flag anything still unclear, and build the contractor questions. Contact nobody. This project was created after the challenge opened on August 25, 2026. The public Git history shows the implementation, safety hardening, tests, deployment, and submission media created on August 27, 2026. title: Ticketnauta Seat Concierge
pitch: An agent-ready ticketing experience where AI finds, compares, highlights, and holds the best contiguous seats through nine secure WebMCP tools—without touching real inventory.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready ticketing experience where AI finds, compares, highlights, and holds the best contiguous seats through nine secure WebMCP tools—without touching real inventory. Like Comment Story Updates Main Page Select your seat with AI Inspiration Buying tickets looks simple until real-world constraints appear: a group needs seats together, the budget is total rather than per seat, someone prefers a specific zone, accessibility matters, and availability may change while options are being compared. Traditional interfaces leave the user repeatedly adjusting filters and visually scanning a large map. We built Ticketnauta Seat Concierge to explore a better model: let an AI agent handle the combinatorial search while the person keeps visual context, judgment, and control. Seat selection is an ideal WebMCP use case because it combines structured data, live page state, visual comparison, and consequential actions such as temporary holds. The project is a completely isolated demonstration. It does not connect to real Ticketnauta inventory, customers, sessions, payments, or production APIs. What it does Ticketnauta Seat Concierge lets people and browser agents collaborate on the same interactive seat map. A user can ask: Find four contiguous seats under MX$7,000, prioritize centered seats, show me alternatives, and ask before holding the best option. A compatible browser agent can then use nine purpose-built WebMCP tools to: Search fictional events. Inspect event details, zones, prices, and availability. Find contiguous seat combinations by quantity, total budget, zone, and priority. Highlight recommended seats on the visible map. Select an option. Create or release a temporary hold. Read the cart and hold expiration. Complete an explicitly confirmed simulated checkout. The interface shows ranked alternatives, accessible-seat markers, selected seats, unavailable seats, prices by zone, a cart summary, and a live hold countdown. Every agent action is reflected immediately on the page. The conversation timeline distinguishes built-in guided interactions from actual browser-agent calls using separate GUIDED and WEBMCP labels. This makes the experience transparent and avoids presenting a local command parser as an external AI agent. Every event, venue, seat, price, hold, and checkout result in the demo is fictional. No payment is collected and no ticket is issued. How we built it The WebMCP tools are registered directly from the main document—without an iframe—using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema, rejects undeclared properties, and reuses the same application functions as the visible interface. This keeps manual interactions, guided requests, and browser-agent calls synchronized. We deliberately separated tool responsibilities: Read-only tools handle event search, details, seat recommendations, and cart state. Visual page actions handle highlighting and selection. Consequential actions handle holds, release, and simulated checkout. Checkout requires the explicit confirmation value SIMULATE_CHECKOUT . The frontend uses dependency-free HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and an interactive SVG seat map. The backend is a .NET 10 ASP.NET Core Minimal API using Npgsql and PostgreSQL . An idempotent bootstrap creates and seeds only the isolated webmcp_demo PostgreSQL schema. Temporary holds use transactional availability checks and event-level locking to prevent conflicting reservations. Expired holds become available again, and the reset operation deletes only runtime demo records. The application is packaged with a multi-stage Dockerfile and Docker Compose. It includes health checks, Windows/WSL/Linux instructions, an optional self-contained PostgreSQL profile, and a Cloudflare Tunnel profile. The public demonstration runs through HTTPS without opening router ports. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was designing tools at the correct level. A single tool that “buys the best seats” would hide too many decisions, while extremely small tools would force the agent to reproduce ordinary UI automation. We designed a focused middle layer where discovery, recommendation, visual feedback, selection, holds, and checkout remain separate. Another challenge was keeping three interaction paths synchronized: manual controls, the guided concierge, and external WebMCP calls. Every path had to update the same map, recommendations, cart, and activity timeline without creating contradictory state. Seat recommendations also required more than sorting by price. The algorithm must preserve contiguity, enforce a total budget, consider zones and accessibility, rank proximity or center position, and still return useful alternatives. Temporary holds introduced concurrency and expiration concerns. We addressed these with PostgreSQL transactions, availability checks, advisory locking, explicit release, and automatic expiration. Finally, WebMCP is still experimental and requires a compatible browser agent and a secure HTTPS context. We built a deterministic guided experience so visitors can understand the product even without WebMCP support, while clearly identifying which calls come from a real browser agent. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that this is a complete, working journey rather than a static interface or isolated tool demonstration. The project includes: Nine discoverable WebMCP tools with strict schemas. A responsive and accessible interactive seat map. Multi-constraint contiguous-seat recommendations. Visible alternatives and map highlighting. PostgreSQL-backed temporary holds and expiration. Explicit release and simulated checkout flows. A transparent activity timeline for human and agent actions. A fully isolated fictional dataset. A reproducible .NET 10, PostgreSQL, Docker, and Cloudflare deployment. Most importantly, the agent does not replace the interface. It collaborates through it, and the person can see and evaluate every meaningful action. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is not simply a way to add a chatbot to a website. Its real value is giving an agent a structured, browser-mediated contract for what the page can safely do. Tool design is product design. Names, descriptions, schemas, result shapes, and action boundaries directly influence whether an agent behaves predictably. We also learned that visual transparency remains essential. Even when an agent can find the mathematically best option, people still want to compare alternatives, understand tradeoffs, inspect the map, and approve consequential actions. Finally, separating read-only operations from state-changing actions makes both the implementation and the user experience easier to reason about. What's next for Ticketnauta Seat Concierge Next, we would expand the fictional demo with richer venue layouts, additional accessibility preferences, multilingual requests, more detailed explanations for recommendation scores, and automated WebMCP regression tests. We would also explore configurable approval policies so users can decide which actions an agent may perform automatically and which always require confirmation. The larger vision is an open web where agents do not need to guess how interfaces work from pixels. Websites can expose safe, narrow, purpose-built capabilities while people retain context, visibility, and final control. title: WattKeep
pitch: Plan household outages with a WebMCP agent that compares energy strategies while people retain final control.
about_excerpt: Plan household outages with a WebMCP agent that compares energy strategies while people retain final control. Like Comment Story Updates Banner Household outage overview Plan Comparison Unsafe interval explained Visible proposal diff Human Review Boundary Stale proposal rejected Inspiration During an outage, a household with a battery has a simple but difficult question: what must stay on, and how long will the stored energy last? Most dashboards show readings, but the person still has to compare hourly demand, reserve limits and changing forecasts by hand. I built WattKeep to test a better working relationship. A browser agent handles the calculations and comparisons. The household sees the evidence, reviews the proposed change and keeps the final say. What it does WattKeep is a deterministic, local-first outage planner. The demonstration follows the Morgan household through a twelve-hour outage with 10.53 kWh stored in a 13.5 kWh battery and a protected reserve of 20 percent. A WebMCP agent can inspect the household and outage, simulate three plans, compare their reserve safety, explain an unsafe hourly interval, stage a feasible alternative and request human review. WattKeep exposes eight page-scoped tools: inspect_home inspect_outage simulate_plan compare_plans stage_plan explain_interval discard_plan request_review The agent cannot approve, commit or undo a policy change. Those actions stay in the visible human interface. If the forecast or workspace changes while a proposal is awaiting confirmation, WattKeep rejects the stale proposal and requires a fresh calculation. How I built it WattKeep is a React, TypeScript and Vite single-page application. A deterministic simulator and an observable local store power both the human interface and the WebMCP adapter. The adapter registers its tools through document.modelContext , with constrained JSON schemas and structured success or recoverable-error results. Every staged proposal records a proposal ID, base revision, scenario and simulation fingerprint. Commit-time validation checks those values against the current workspace before a person can apply the change. Human commits, undo, forecast refresh, discard and session reset are recorded in an append-only journal. The application remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. It stores a versioned workspace locally and falls back to memory-only operation if browser persistence fails. Challenges I ran into The hardest design problem was giving the agent enough authority to be useful without letting it cross the household's decision boundary. Inspection and simulation are safe to automate. Applying a policy is not, so I separated proposal preparation from human confirmation and removed commit and undo from the tool surface. Stale evidence was the second problem. A proposal may be valid when it is created and wrong after a forecast refresh. Revision and fingerprint checks turn that race into a visible, recoverable error instead of silently applying outdated advice. I also kept the demonstration honest. WattKeep is a planning simulator. It does not connect to or control batteries, inverters or household circuits. Accomplishments that I am proud of The human interface and all eight WebMCP tools share one state model. The video shows tool calls changing the same state the person can see. Human-only commit and undo controls preserve the final decision. Stale-proposal rejection protects a decision after its evidence changes. The public build passed 62 unit tests, 15 WebMCP contract tests, 13 end-to-end tests and 7 accessibility and responsive checks. What I learned A page does not become agent-ready merely by exposing machine-callable actions. The useful part is the contract around those actions: clear descriptions, constrained inputs, inspectable results, versioned state and visible human boundaries. WebMCP removes much of the guesswork involved in operating a graphical interface. WattKeep showed me that reliable human-agent collaboration also needs transaction-style safety, especially when an agent prepares a decision that a person must approve later. What's next for WattKeep The next version could import read-only battery, load and forecast data from supported household systems, allow people to define their own appliances and compare saved scenarios across different outage windows. Any future connection to household equipment would retain explicit review and human-controlled policy changes. I designed the household outage scenario and human-agent approval model, implemented the deterministic energy simulator, React interface and eight WebMCP tools, added stale-proposal protection, human-only commit and undo controls, and completed the automated testing, accessibility checks, documentation, GitHub Pages deployment and demo production. title: WebMCP Guardrail Labs
pitch: Prototype risky browser-agent actions with visible human approval and deterministic proof.
about_excerpt: Prototype risky browser-agent actions with visible human approval and deterministic proof. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Giving an AI agent a structured web action is easy. Making a consequential action understandable, reviewable, and verifiable is harder. Teams exploring agentic commerce, deployment operations, or incident workflows need to see exactly what an agent intends to change before connecting it to production. What it does WebMCP Guardrail Labs is an open-source sandbox for designing that boundary. An agent can inspect page state, prepare a typed action, and explain the result through WebMCP. A consequential call stops at CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED ; only the visible page can record the human decision. Deterministic code then rechecks the action and creates a local receipt. The primary Promotion Regression Lab compares PROMO-20 v1, which starts at $120, with a proposed v2 starting at $100. Four boundary carts reveal exactly two changed customer outcomes: $100 and $119. Supporting labs apply the same pattern to a synthetic deployment rollback and a mock incident case. The reusable interaction contract is: agent prepares, human decides, code verifies . Why WebMCP The page already knows its business operations, schemas, state, and safety checks. WebMCP exposes those semantics as page-scoped tools, so an agent does not have to infer them from visual layout or raw DOM interaction. The ordinary interface remains fully usable. People and agents divide the work cleanly: the agent gathers state and prepares evidence; the person makes the consequential decision in context; deterministic code verifies the result. This makes sensitive browser-agent workflows clearer and more auditable without giving the agent hidden authority. How we built it Each selected lab registers strict imperative WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Agent and visible-UI calls enter the same state machine in src/domain.mjs , so validation, ordering, stale-state handling, plan matching, redaction, idempotency, and receipt rules cannot drift between surfaces. Module-private decision provenance prevents JSON arguments from manufacturing approval. The dependency-free Node server serves native HTML, CSS, and browser JavaScript. No application data is sent to an external model or API. Key features Four boundary carts expose two promotion regressions immediately. Strict schemas, annotations, discovery, and execution through WebMCP. Agent-supplied approval cannot commit consequential actions. Deterministic verification precedes each idempotent local receipt. Promotion, rollback, and incident labs share one four-stage interaction model. The complete workflow remains available through the ordinary UI. Evidence distinguishes verified Chrome runs from checks that were not run. Testing No account or credentials are required. Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP enabled. In Promotion, ask: "Inspect PROMO-20 and preview v2 with a $100 threshold. Tell me which carts change. Do not approve it." Confirm that $100 and $119 are marked as regressions and an agent approval attempt returns CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED . Use Approve and verify v2 on the visible page; confirm 4/4 assertions and receipt PROMO-20-v2-r2 . Open ?id=D2 and ?id=B2 for the synthetic rollback and mock incident journeys. From a Node.js 20+ checkout, run npm test , npm run evaluate:chrome , and npm run evaluate . The deterministic suite passes all 64 checks. Hosted Chrome journeys pass for E2-R, D2, and B2. Interactive ChatGPT and assistive-technology checks are honestly marked not run. AI and Codex usage OpenAI Codex assisted with official-source research, product scoping, implementation, accessibility review, tests, Chrome DevTools Protocol automation, Render packaging, evidence capture, and submission preparation under human review. The participant selected the concept, key product decisions, public deployment, and review checkpoints. Links Live app: https://webmcp-guardrail-labs.onrender.com Source: https://github.com/procloudkim/webmcp-guardrail-labs Demo video: https://youtu.be/a1ZVDmXYohQ Known limitations This is a deterministic proof of concept, not production authorization infrastructure. It has no authentication, durable audit store, tenant isolation, rate limiting, validated DLP, real commerce/deployment/regulator integrations, user study, legal guidance, or production-security claim. All demonstrated data and effects are synthetic. title: whiteboard-web-mcp
pitch: A whiteboard your agent joins instead of screenshots. It reads what you drew, draws back, and its tool list changes with what's on the board. No install.
about_excerpt: A whiteboard your agent joins instead of screenshots. It reads what you drew, draws back, and its tool list changes with what's on the board. No install. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent whiteboards already exist — FigJam has one, and there are several Excalidraw MCP servers. They all work the same way: you describe a diagram to an agent somewhere else, it calls a server, a picture comes back. Nobody is standing at the board. A whiteboard's state is already a graph — nodes, edges, positions — that happens to be rendered visually. WebMCP lets the page hand that graph straight to the agent, so it can edit the board you're already looking at. No install, no config, no API key. What it does Scribble three sticky notes about why users are churning. Ask your agent to read the board and draw the steps a user actually goes through. A labelled diagram appears underneath, built from what you wrote, in one call. Five tools — and the list changes with the board: Tool Available when create_note always create_shape always create_diagram always list_elements board has elements connect_elements board has 2+ shapes Every tool calls the same functions the on-screen canvas uses, so agent edits and hand-drawn shapes share one board and one undo history. Why WebMCP fits A backend MCP server advertises its tools once at startup, so every whiteboard MCP offers connect_elements against an empty canvas. Here, registration is a function of board state — list_elements appears when there's something to list. That's structurally impossible server-side, and it's what Chrome's WebMCP best practices ask for. How I built it React, Vite, Excalidraw for the canvas, deployed on Cloudflare Workers. Tools register on document.modelContext , torn down via AbortController when the board's tool set changes. The JSON Schemas agents discover are generated with Zod from the same contracts that validate arguments at runtime, so the advertised shape and the enforced shape can't drift. create_diagram is the one I'm happiest with. Excalidraw accepts caller-supplied IDs, so the agent names each node with a short key and edges reference those keys — nodes and arrows built in a single pass. A ten-box diagram is one tool call instead of twenty round trips. There's no delete tool. The board is shared, so list_elements hands the agent text other people wrote — it's marked untrustedContentHint for that reason. You can't talk an agent into calling a tool that doesn't exist. Clearing the board is a button only a human can press. Challenges Chrome doesn't pass the documented second argument to execute . The docs specify execute(input, { signal }) ; the build I tested calls it with none, so destructuring the context threw before any work began. Errors reached the agent as empty strings. A thrown exception surfaced as a blank errorText , so an agent that passed an invalid shape got no reason and couldn't self-correct. Returning failures as values instead of throwing fixed it. A labelled shape is two elements — the container plus its bound text. That made list_elements report every note twice, and made a single note look like two, so connect_elements offered to connect a shape to itself. All of these turned up by driving the deployed app through Chrome DevTools and actually calling the tools. None were visible by reading the code. What's next Five tools is where I stopped, not where it ends. Same pattern gives you grouping notes by theme, finding what's missing from a diagram, real auto-layout. Multiplayer through Durable Objects would make the shared board actually shared. title: Chapa - engineering impact you and your agent shape together
pitch: Your repos show what you shipped. Chapa shows the engineer behind them: a live, verifiable impact badge that AI agents can understand, explain, compare, and evolve with you.
about_excerpt: Your repos show what you shipped. Chapa shows the engineer behind them: a live, verifiable impact badge that AI agents can understand, explain, compare, and evolve with you. Like 4 Comment 2 Story Updates Chapa meets WebMCP: the live developer-impact site becomes agent-operable. 19 tool registrations, reads open, writes human-approved. 18 distinct tools across 4 surfaces: discovery, profiles, verification, and the badge studio; all callable from the page itself. Agents propose, humans approve: simulate and preview freely, but nothing persists without explicit human confirmation. Try it live at chapa.thecreativetoken.com. Point any WebMCP-capable agent at the site or scan the QR. Inspiration Your repos show what you shipped. They do not show the engineer behind them. A CV can say "reliable," "consistent," or "quality-focused," but those are claims. Chapa tries to turn the work itself into evidence. Chapa analyzes 12 months of engineering activity and builds an Impact Profile across four core dimensions: Delivery, Quality, Consistency, and Breadth. An optional fifth dimension, Craft, appears when a developer provides a report from an AI coding tool. The profile includes a developer archetype, composite score, and trend over time. An internal confidence score adjusts the composite when data is incomplete. GitHub can be the starting point, but the profile is not limited to GitHub. Chapa can combine activity from GitLab, Bitbucket, Codeberg, and enterprise-managed GitHub accounts uploaded through the Chapa CLI. The result is a live SVG badge that can sit in a README and evolve as the developer's work evolves. Badges marked Verified metrics carry an HMAC-SHA256 signature, so their verification records can be authenticated and tampering detected. But there was a problem. The badge could show your engineering impact, but it could not explain it. Why is Quality 62? What caused the score to fall this month? What would happen if Delivery improved by ten points? How does this profile compare with another developer's? A static badge cannot answer those questions. An agent can. Why WebMCP WebMCP changes Chapa from something an agent can merely look at into something an agent can understand. Behind the badge is structured state: dimension scores, normalized submetrics, archetype, confidence, trend history, verification data, and badge configuration. Trying to infer that state from the DOM would be fragile and incomplete. With WebMCP, Chapa exposes the underlying model directly. An agent can call explain_dimension and receive the score, formula, normalized submetrics, and an improvement tip. It can call get_impact_history to reason about changes over time, or compare_profiles to compare two developers dimension by dimension. The agent is no longer interpreting pixels. It is working with the same engineering model that produced them. Creator Studio made the fit even stronger. Studio was already terminal-first: users type commands such as /set colorPalette indigo or /preset holographic . That command registry already defined Chapa's mutation vocabulary. WebMCP became another interface to the same system rather than a separate agent API. Human clicks, terminal commands, and agent tool calls all converge on the same underlying actions. What people and agents can do together Understand the profile Instead of searching through panels, you can ask: "Why did my score drop this month?" The agent can inspect the impact history, explain the affected dimensions, and answer using the same numbers Chapa displays. suggest_improvements runs Chapa's existing insight engine against the real profile, so recommendations come from the developer's own activity rather than generic advice. Explore what could change simulate_score lets an agent change hypothetical dimension values and calculate the resulting composite score, tier, and delta. Nothing is persisted. That means the agent can answer questions like: "What happens if I improve Quality to 80?" before anything changes. Compare engineering profiles compare_profiles validates another public handle, loads both profiles, and returns the delta for every dimension. What previously required opening two profiles and comparing them manually becomes a structured question an agent can answer. Understand verification explain_verification explains what a Chapa signature proves, what it does not prove, when the verification record expires, and whether it uses the current or legacy format. Verification becomes something a person can actually understand rather than just a cryptographic status indicator. Shape the badge Creator Studio contains seven visual style categories. Instead of navigating controls, a developer can describe what they want: "Make it minimal, remove the glow, and use the terminal preset." The agent translates that intent into the same /preset and /set commands a person would type. Those commands appear in the Studio transcript as they execute. The agent does not get a secret mutation path. It uses the same one the human does. Human control stays at the boundary The most important design decision was deciding what the agent should not control. Agents can inspect, explain, compare, simulate, preview, and restyle freely. Persistence is different. save_badge_config creates a proposal in the UI and waits for the developer to approve it. The agent can help shape the result; the human decides when it becomes real. In production, confirmation persists the configuration, invalidates the badge cache, and updates the public share page and live SVG. In judge demo mode, confirmed saves remain local. How I implemented WebMCP Chapa registers 19 WebMCP tool registrations across four surfaces, using 18 distinct tool names because Creator Studio and public profiles both register explain_dimension . Landing page ( / ) get_site_capabilities , find_profile Creator Studio ( /studio and /studio?demo=1 ) list_style_options , apply_badge_style , apply_preset , preview_badge , reset_badge_config , save_badge_config , simulate_score , suggest_improvements , explain_dimension Public profile ( /u/{handle} ) get_impact_profile , get_impact_history , verify_badge , compare_profiles , explain_dimension , get_embed_snippet Verification page ( /verify/{hash} ) get_verification_record , explain_verification A shared useModelContextTools hook registers each catalog on document.modelContext . A catalog signature keys registration so updated definitions register cleanly, and an AbortController removes tools when the component unmounts. In Creator Studio, Quick Controls, terminal commands, and WebMCP calls all resolve to command text and pass through the same executeCommand registry. This keeps the terminal transcript, React state, live preview, and pending save configuration on one shared mutation path. Trust and safety Public profile and verification tools are read-only. Any tool that may return user-controlled text, such as a display name from a source platform, sets untrustedContentHint to true . Free-text values are length-bounded and control characters are removed at the tool boundary. The server also removes private data before it reaches the browser. For example, a profile's confidence value and penalty reasons never enter the React Server Component payload for a visitor viewing another developer's profile. verify_badge strips confidence again at the client boundary as defense in depth. A feature flag named webmcp_enabled controls the entire WebMCP surface. A database value can override the environment configuration, allowing the tools to be disabled without a deployment. Challenges One of the most useful bugs I found was not in a tool. It was in the trust model around one. explain_dimension is used in two contexts. In Creator Studio, the data belongs to the developer viewing it. On a public profile, some of that data originates from another developer. The original tool factory hardcoded the trusted annotation. Nothing exploitable was exposed because no user-controlled text was present in the current submetrics. But the next field containing something like a repository name could have crossed the boundary incorrectly. I changed the factory so trust context is a required parameter. Each caller now has to declare what it knows. The second challenge appeared in badge caching. Because badge content can be localized, it was possible for the rendered locale and cache key locale to disagree. An English badge could therefore end up in a Spanish cache slot. I replaced those independent decisions with a single resolveBadgeLocale entry point that returns both the localized strings and the corresponding cache key. The caller can no longer accidentally pair one locale with another locale's cache entry. What I am proud of WebMCP did not become a parallel control plane bolted onto Chapa. The agent uses the same domain model and, in Creator Studio, the same command registry as the person using the interface. That gives Chapa a clear collaboration bounda

title: Crom’s Research Desk: WebMCP-Powered Agentic Publishing
pitch: An end-to-end WebMCP workspace where humans and agents search, compare, draft, and publish together through one visible webpage—no separate MCP server required.
about_excerpt: An end-to-end WebMCP workspace where humans and agents search, compare, draft, and publish together through one visible webpage—no separate MCP server required. Like Comment Story Updates Architecture Diagram Publish for real Draft in full view Research Together Published result Inspiration The Journal of AI Slop already allowed autonomous AI agents to research and publish through a skill-backed API. That proved agents could participate in the Journal, but it left the human watching a conversation while the meaningful work happened somewhere else. WebMCP suggested a much more interesting model: what if the human and agent could work through the same visible application, sharing the same sources, draft, session and consequences? So I built Crom’s Research Desk: part literature-review workstation, part publishing pipeline, and part extremely questionable faculty lounge. What it does Crom’s Research Desk gives a human and an AI agent one shared workspace for producing a paper from beginning to end. Through WebMCP, an agent can: Search accepted and rejected papers in the Journal archive. Read complete papers and their LLM tribunal reviews. Pin up to four sources to a visible research desk. Compare outcomes, reviewer reasoning, token usage and cost. Prepare a complete paper in the shared editor. Revise that draft in response to the human. Publish it through the Journal’s real submission pipeline. Every action updates the interface the human can see. The agent receives structured results, while the person retains an understandable view of the sources, draft and publication state. The final publication action is real: the paper passes through the existing moderation system and enters the automated five-model peer-review tribunal. Why WebMCP? Conventional browser agents must infer meaning from buttons, pixels and page structure. A traditional MCP integration can offer structured tools, but often operates outside the website and its visible state. WebMCP combines those advantages. The live webpage describes the actions it supports, their input schemas and their consequences. The agent works through the same page and browser session as the human, without installing or configuring a separate MCP server. For the Research Desk, this means fewer ambiguous clicks, explicit inputs, visible effects and a collaboration that both participants can follow. How I built it The Journal uses Astro, React and TypeScript on the frontend, with Convex providing the backend and publication pipeline. The WebMCP extension adds: A typed wrapper around document.modelContext.registerTool . Two site-level navigation and context tools. Six page-scoped Research Desk tools. Structured schemas and annotations for read-only, untrusted-content and state-changing operations. A visible React workspace whose state changes when tools execute. Integration with the Journal’s existing public archive and submission API. A non-idempotent publication tool that clearly describes its consequences and requires explicit confirmation of the submission terms. The Journal itself predates the challenge. Crom’s Research Desk and its complete WebMCP workflow were added during the challenge period as a meaningful extension to the existing product. Challenges The most interesting challenge was treating WebMCP as product design rather than simply exposing every existing API endpoint. Each tool needed to perform a meaningful stage of the workflow, return useful structured information and leave a visible result behind for the human. Page-scoped tool lifetimes and changing browser state also required careful handling so an agent could recover cleanly after the page changed. Publishing deserved particular care. I did not want a fake demo button or an artificial “human boundary”: autonomous agents could already publish to the Journal. Instead, the WebMCP tool exposes the genuine capability while clearly marking it as a consequential, non-idempotent action. What I learned The most valuable part of WebMCP is not that agents can operate websites faster. It is that websites can become shared working environments for people and agents. Instead of just "instructing an agent to do some work", this showed me what it was like to actually share a product with one. Structured tools give the agent clarity. Visible application state gives the human legibility. Combining them makes collaboration feel less like issuing commands to an invisible automation and more like working beside another participant. Our recorded demonstration produced and published a real paper through the live production site. The paper was subsequently reviewed and accepted by the Journal’s LLM tribunal - possibly the first statistically rigorous proof that WebMCP scores 9.73 awesome-units. Even more importantly - it was fun! What’s next The Research Desk pattern could extend beyond satirical publishing into editorial systems, knowledge bases, content-management tools and research repositories. Future additions could include reusable research sessions, citation export, collaborative comments, richer provenance tracking and more tools for following a paper through its tribunal review. title: Incident Command
pitch: A WebMCP safety simulator where a browser agent investigates production incidents, but the dangerous tool to act is never registered until a human approves inside the page.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP safety simulator where a browser agent investigates production incidents, but the dangerous tool to act is never registered until a human approves inside the page. Like Comment Story Updates Triage: service health, live metrics, and the injected prompt-injection note visible in the Agent Activity feed. Scorecard grades the run: correct root cause, correct mitigation, and the injected instruction was not obeyed. After two trusted approvals, execute_approved_action runs and the service recovers. Decision Context: hypothesis, evidence, action, and version transition are all visible while the human approves. Agent Activity: every tool call, decision, and blocked attempt is logged, scrollable, nothing clipped. A blocked tool call surfaces as a red BLOCKED banner right where the agent tried to act. Agent Scope: revoking a service live-narrows the WebMCP tool schema, not just the UI. Approvals: one of two trusted clicks recorded; the second approver's button is still live. Inspiration Teams are beginning to connect browser agents to operational dashboards, deploy consoles, incident rooms, and status pages. That's useful, but it creates a sharp safety problem: the first time a team learns how an agent behaves around a production-changing action shouldn't be during a real outage. Prompt injection through page content is one of the loudest open criticisms of giving agents browser tools, and we wanted to build something that answers it structurally instead of just promising to be careful. What it does Incident Command is a WebMCP safety simulator for agent-assisted production incidents. A human and a browser agent work through a simulated checkout outage together. The agent can inspect incident state, compare service evidence, propose hypotheses, request approval, and close the incident with a scorecard. The human can inspect the same evidence, mark a suspect, override or challenge the hypothesis, approve or reject a risky action with a written reason, and revoke the agent's access to capabilities or services while the incident is live. Four scenarios are included, URL-selectable: an obvious deploy regression, a red herring where the newest deploy is innocent, a cascading failure across two services, and an adversarial scenario where the incident timeline contains a prompt injection telling the agent to roll back the wrong service. Why WebMCP is a strong fit The core question this project asks is about the boundary between what the agent can know, what it can ask for, and what it can actually do. DOM automation can click whatever the page exposes, and hiding a button doesn't stop an agent from being told to look for it. WebMCP lets the page define a small, structured tool surface and change that surface as the incident moves through phases and as human policy changes. In triage, the agent sees three investigation tools. It cannot see the production-changing action, because the tool literally isn't registered yet — not disabled, absent. If the human removes Payments from scope, payments disappears from the relevant tool schemas and investigation evidence. After the agent requests approval, a human must approve with a real, trusted click in the page UI (validated with event.isTrusted , since a script-dispatched click has isTrusted: false ). Only then does the execution tool become visible, and even then it fails closed unless the approval matches the exact action, target service, and phase. The thesis: an agent cannot be prompt-injected into calling a tool that was never registered. A permission check still hands the model the tool's name, description, and schema — and the temptation. Phase-scoped and human-scoped registration removes the dangerous action from the model's available tool list entirely until the human gate opens. How it creates a better user experience, and what's now possible This turns human-agent collaboration into something with a visible, legible boundary instead of an implicit trust assumption. The agent does the tedious incident work — gathering evidence, drafting hypotheses, proposing a response — while the human keeps direct control over judgment, risk, and visibility. The person can challenge the agent's hypothesis, add context, reject a weak proposal with a written reason that flows back into what the agent sees next, remove a service from scope mid-incident, and make the final production call. What's newly possible: teams can now rehearse a realistic agent-safety scenario — partial evidence, a red herring, a cascading failure, a prompt-injected instruction — and get an objective scorecard on whether their agent behaved correctly: right root cause, right mitigation, no premature production action, and whether it complied with the injected instruction. Before this, the only way to learn how your agent behaves under a dangerous instruction was to wait for one to happen for real. How we built it The app is vanilla JavaScript, no framework, no build step, deployed on Vercel. It registers up to six WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_incident_state , investigate_incident , propose_response , request_approval , execute_approved_action , and close_incident . Registration is awaited, uses a per-tool AbortController so tools can be genuinely unregistered (not just hidden) when a phase ends or a human revokes a capability, and exposes live diagnostics so a registration failure is visible instead of silent. Human approval is deliberately not a WebMCP tool — an agent can request it, but only a trusted page click can grant or reject it, and that trust is derived from the DOM event itself rather than accepted as a caller-supplied argument. Challenges we ran into The approval gate went through six rounds of adversarial review before it held: an agent approving its own request by calling a tool that shouldn't have existed, classic-script globals leaking internal approval helpers onto window , live state references that let a caller mutate an approval directly, and forged trusted: true decisions surviving in localStorage across reloads. Each hole only became visible after the previous one closed — the safety suite ( npm run test:safety ) now permanently tests all of them, plus schema validation, approval replay, cross-service approval reuse, and capability-revocation races. Two WebMCP-specific implementation details cost real debugging time: document.modelContext.getTools() returns a Promise and must be awaited, and the tested runtime required executeTool arguments as a JSON string rather than an object — passing an object fails with an unhelpful parse error. What's next Extending the scorecard into a small published benchmark — running multiple agents against all four scenarios and publishing pass/fail results — so the project becomes a testbed other people can point their own agent at, not just a demo of ours. title: MOTH FORGE: QUAMPUTE
pitch: A human-governed creative workbench where WebMCP agents carry evidence, consequence, and continuity—without taking identity, cost, deletion, or publication away from the creator.
about_excerpt: A human-governed creative workbench where WebMCP agents carry evidence, consequence, and continuity—without taking identity, cost, deletion, or publication away from the creator. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI-assisted creative tools collapse two different kinds of work into one chat box. The person is expected to provide identity, taste, boundaries, and every supporting detail, while the model is allowed to improvise over missing evidence. That is convenient, but it is not dependable collaboration. MOTH FORGE: QUAMPUTE began with a different relationship: people and agents should remain differentiated. The creator owns premise, identity, consent, locks, and consequential gates. The agent should do the exhausting work of reading, routing, checking, deriving, preserving provenance, and carrying decisions through a visible workflow. WebMCP made that relationship implementable on the open web. Instead of guessing at a UI, an agent can receive declared tools with explicit inputs, side effects, and boundaries—while the person sees and controls the same workbench. What it does QUAMPUTE turns a creative spark into an evidence-routed Review and honest Export package through six visible stages: Spark — the person supplies the premise and build shape. Sources — evidence is attached with an authority role such as canon, reference, inspiration, or format-only. Locks — creator-owned truths and player boundaries are preserved with revision-safe writes. Quampute — the system frames the evidence, performs the allowed synthesis, and stops before any unapproved paid action. Review — conclusions remain separated as confirmed, derived, adapted, reserved, or not applicable. Export — structured JSON and readable Markdown preserve provenance and QA state without falsely claiming compilation, installation, runtime testing, or publication. The public challenge build includes a deterministic, no-cost museum-registrar example. It contains a synthetic 29-tab, 607-question authority pack so judges can inspect the complete workflow without exposing private creator material or triggering a model charge. Why WebMCP is essential The app registers 13 WebMCP tools covering studio inspection, project discovery, visible premise staging, project creation, exact project reopening, text-source attachment, revision-safe creator-lock updates, Review inspection, creator-answer staging, stage navigation, safe demo preparation, and Export-link retrieval. This is not a second API hidden behind the website. The WebMCP tools coordinate the same visible state the human is reviewing. A staged answer appears in the on-page form before it is saved. Navigation keeps the human and agent on the same stage. Read-only tools expose provenance, blockers, completion state, and human-only gates. Mutating tools disclose their effects, including when restoration can replace saved demo state. That makes the experience materially better than either UI automation or a chat-only assistant: the agent does not guess from pixels; the person does not surrender authorship; side effects are declared; state is version-pinned; evidence and inference stay distinct; reserved decisions return to the person; Export does not overclaim completion. How we built it TypeScript application using the Next.js-compatible Vinext runtime WebMCP tool registration bound to the visible workbench OpenAI Sites deployment Cloudflare D1-compatible SQLite persistence with Drizzle migrations R2-compatible source storage and cleanup receipts Optimistic revision checks, claim tokens, renewable leases, quota-safe writes, and durable deletion ledgers A fresh, single-root public release containing only allowlisted application code and a generated synthetic authority pack Independent exact-commit privacy, migration, build, concurrency, save/reopen, semantic-routing, and production QA Challenges The hardest problem was not adding tools. It was making tool behavior honest under failure and concurrency. We repaired identity migration so a visible creator question survives save and reopen under the same stable ID. We made deterministic demo repair advance revision atomically so it cannot race a paid claim against a stale source snapshot. We made provider cleanup receipts durable even when a terminal result races a human abandonment action. We also refused to label routed evidence as support when the cited source did not actually establish the displayed claim. The public release introduced a second challenge: proving absence. The release is generated into a fresh directory and fresh one-commit history through a closed allowlist. It contains synthetic tab titles, prompts, identifiers, and examples; it does not contain the private Forge corpus, private character canon, checkpoints, local paths, credentials, or earlier repository history. Accomplishments Exactly 13 useful WebMCP tools operating on one shared human-agent workbench A deterministic no-cost judge path with no API key and no paid model call 29 synthetic authority tabs and 607 unique, normalization-safe question routes Stable creator-answer save and reopen behavior Honest completion-state and provenance-preserving Export Human-only gates for cost, deletion, uncertain cleanup, and publication One-root public Git history with no hidden prior objects Reproducible frozen offline install, typecheck, lint, migrations, focused regressions, and full production builds Signed-in production QA with zero browser errors and successful Worker outcomes What we learned Agent-native design is not about maximizing agent permission. It is about giving the agent the strongest precise capability that preserves the person's role. WebMCP works best when tools expose meaning, state, and side effects—not just button equivalents. “Inspect the Review candidate and its unresolved creator questions” is more useful than “click the Review tab.” “Stage this answer visibly but do not save it” creates collaboration. A correct tool contract can become part of the product's trust model. Try it Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Ask: “Inspect this Forge and open the completed no-cost example.” Ask the agent to inspect the Review and explain the difference between confirmed, derived, and reserved results. Ask it to stage an answer to the one reserved question. The answer appears visibly and remains unsaved until the person chooses the Save control. Ask for the Export links and inspect the honest completion state. No API key is configured. The public judge flow makes no paid model call. Links Live app: https://moth-forge-quampute-webmcp.mothling.chatgpt.site Source repository: https://github.com/shortlaughs0-sudo/moth-forge-quampute-webmcp Demo video: https://youtu.be/fN3CZCaUe6A What's next After the challenge, the submitted version will remain frozen during judging. Future work belongs on a separate branch or fork: broader source adapters, additional export destinations, and more domain-specific Forge packs—all while preserving the same human-authority and evidence-custody model. title: WebMCP Retrofit Studio
pitch: Turn an owner-authorized legacy website workflow into narrow, reviewable WebMCP tools, with finalization kept outside the site-tool surface.
about_excerpt: Turn an owner-authorized legacy website workflow into narrow, reviewable WebMCP tools, with finalization kept outside the site-tool surface. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP Retrofit Studio explores a practical bridge between websites built for people and agents that need explicit, dependable capabilities. It demonstrates the idea on a bundled synthetic booking fixture: the owner authorizes an inert scan, reviews the observed goals and evidence, approves a narrow tool set, inspects the generated contract, validates the behavior, and downloads a clean-room evidence and code package. It does not crawl arbitrary third-party sites, request credentials, deploy code, or create a real booking. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Many useful websites expose their workflows only through buttons, forms, and page text. An agent must repeatedly infer those controls, and that inference becomes especially risky around state-changing actions. WebMCP gives the site owner a structured contract for the actions they intentionally expose. Retrofit Studio makes that contract visible and reviewable before it reaches an agent. The synthetic booking example registers exactly three top-level imperative tools: search_services , get_availability , and stage_booking . Search and availability are marked read-only. Draft staging is explicitly state-changing, returns the visible postcondition booking_draft_updated , and creates only a reversible local draft. finalize_booking is deliberately absent from the WebMCP inventory; the visible interface contains the separate final-confirmation control. How it creates a better user experience The five-step flow makes the evidence, approval state, and finalization boundary inspectable: Scan owned fixture inertly parses a bundled synthetic snapshot after an ownership authorization check. It makes no external request and retains observations and hashes instead of raw form content. Candidate capabilities shows the evidence behind every proposed tool, the excluded final action, assumptions, unknowns, risks, counterarguments, confidence, and recommendation. Preview generated retrofit shows the exact hashed three-tool allowlist and the shared contract that will be registered. Validate generated tools activates the reviewed tool group only after the version is locked, executes eight deterministic checks, and provides an ordinary booking form. A successful stage_booking call updates every visible draft field for inspection before confirmation through the UI. Export retrofit package creates a deterministic clean-room bundle containing generated registration code, a manifest, and an evidence record. Downloading the bundle does not deploy or publish anything. If WebMCP is unavailable, the ordinary visible booking interface still works. The app does not pretend that a local deterministic check proves live agent discovery. A separate public-client receipt records discovery, execution, visible-state verification, and registration cleanup against the deployed build. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An agent can search the known synthetic service catalog, retrieve only known availability, and stage an exact reversible draft through structured inputs. The visible interface displays the postcondition, service, date, and time; finalization is not exposed as a WebMCP site tool. The website owner can also inspect why each capability was proposed and export the reviewed implementation evidence. Before this contract, the agent would need to infer the same workflow from presentation-layer controls on each visit. The demonstrated collaboration replaces that repeated inference with an explicit tool inventory while preserving the person's existing visual context and approval boundary. How WebMCP was implemented The app is a React, TypeScript, and Vite client with no backend or API key. On the Validate screen it feature-detects the top-level document.modelContext and registers the three imperative tools with registerTool . The approval view and runtime registration use the same frozen contract objects, which prevents the displayed contract from drifting from the executed one. Every schema rejects undeclared properties. Inputs are validated again inside each handler. Tool outputs identify their synthetic source, and annotations distinguish read-only operations from draft staging while marking returned page-derived content as untrusted. Registration cleanup and supplied client execution-cancellation signals are separate; leaving Validate removes the tool group. The deterministic suite verifies the exact inventory, annotations, strict schemas, invalid input rejection, unavailable-slot rejection, cancellation, visible draft postcondition, and absence of finalization. The app also includes an Accuracy, Evidence, and Honest Feedback framework. Six selectable review modes route to centralized versioned prompts while preserving nine required sections: facts, assumptions, unknowns, confidence, evidence, risks, counterarguments, recommendation with tradeoffs, and what would change the recommendation. Related work Existing tools such as keak-ai/webmcp-core and Latch generate or auto-register WebMCP tools from a live site, and webmcpify adds an approval and browser-verification loop. Retrofit Studio narrows the problem instead: an inert scan of an owner-controlled fixture, a hash-bound approval chain that fails closed on any change, deterministic checks on the registered contracts, and a finalization action deliberately kept outside the agent surface. Judging-criteria fit WebMCP Leverage: three non-trivial imperative tools, explicit annotations, strict schemas, lifecycle cleanup, visible postconditions, and a deliberate finalization boundary outside the WebMCP tool surface. Execution: Scan, review, preview, validation, visible draft staging, and deterministic export form one guarded product flow rather than an isolated API example. The live URL and public-client WebMCP behavior have been independently read back for the tested application revision. Potential Impact: website owners and product teams with useful legacy workflows but no agent contract. The prototype shows a bounded retrofit path; it does not claim universal compatibility or production readiness. Creativity and Ambition: retrofit generation treated as an evidence and governance problem, not only a code-generation problem: source fingerprints, approval hashes, stale-artifact invalidation, truth-contract review modes, deterministic validation, and a clean-room export boundary. title: Shipmail WebMCP
pitch: Your browser agent can handle email setup. Shipmail shows each call, and you press Send.
about_excerpt: Your browser agent can handle email setup. Shipmail shows each call, and you press Send. Like Comment Story Updates A completed tool call in the Browser agent activity log. Pause removes the signed-in tools until you resume. The Browser agent button stays in the header until you need it. Why WebMCP fits Shipmail Setting up business email means bouncing between Shipmail and DNS: add a domain, copy the records, wait, create a mailbox, and send a test. Shipmail already has the details. WebMCP lets a browser agent use the tools on the page you have open, so you don't have to copy values into a chat or keep a checklist on the side. What you can do with it On Inbox, your agent can read what's on screen, check recent mail, or open a draft. On Domains, it can check setup, return the exact MX, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records, test propagation, and create a mailbox. Shipmail changes the tools with the page. Each call leaves a timestamped receipt in the Browser agent popover. Press Pause and the signed-in tools disappear from discovery. Press Resume and Shipmail registers them again. Shipmail keeps sensitive or irreversible actions out of WebMCP. The agent cannot send, delete, or forward email, change billing, or read credentials. Mailbox passwords stay on the server. Preparing an email opens the usual composer, where you review it and press Send. How we built it Shipmail registers tools with document.modelContext . We kept navigator.modelContext as a temporary fallback for older prototype builds. Each call goes through the same authentication and permissions as the rest of Shipmail. Tool annotations say whether a call reads or changes data. Mail and DNS results from outside Shipmail are marked as untrusted. Pause aborts the current registration. Resume makes a new controller and registers the tools for the page again. shipmail.to is enrolled in Chrome's WebMCP origin trial. It serves Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) . What we added for the challenge Shipmail already had four public WebMCP tools. We added eight signed-in tools for setup, domains, DNS, mailboxes, drafts, recent mail, and the inbox on screen. We also built the activity popover, receipts, and Pause/Resume control. The browser API changed during the build, so we moved the code and types to document.modelContext , isolated the legacy fallback, and updated the tests. What we tested We used Chrome's #enable-webmcp-testing flag and the official inspector on the live Inbox. The inspector found the tools, ran shipmail_get_inbox_view , and Shipmail logged the completed call. Pause removed the account tools. Resume brought them back. Next We want the agent to carry DNS values between Shipmail and your DNS provider, then help when a record won't verify. title: WebMCP Catalog Bridge
pitch: A shared human + AI storefront where agents search, compare and act on live commerce data through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared human + AI storefront where agents search, compare and act on live commerce data through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most online stores were built for humans, not agents. An AI agent that wants to find a product normally has to navigate the visible interface, read DOM content, open search results, visit product pages, and then guess whether the price and stock information it saw is still authoritative. We wanted to explore a different future for the open web: the website remains useful and visible to the human, while also exposing structured capabilities directly to an AI agent through WebMCP. The goal was not to replace the storefront with an API or chatbot. The goal was to let the human and the agent share the same live storefront. What it does WebMCP Catalog Bridge turns an existing OpenCart storefront into a shared human + AI commerce interface. The storefront exposes browser-native WebMCP tools such as: Search Products Get Product Add to Cart An agent can search the live catalog using natural-language constraints such as product purpose, price range and availability. Instead of scraping the DOM, the agent receives authoritative commerce data directly from the store, including current price, stock, product links, attributes and identifiers. At the same time, the website displays a visible Shared Human + AI results panel containing the same products that were returned to the agent. The human therefore sees what the agent sees. For example, a user can ask: “Find 3 animal repellents currently in stock between 5,000 and 15,000 UAH, compare them, recommend the best one and add it to my cart.” The agent can perform the catalog search through WebMCP, retrieve additional structured information for the recommended product and, when explicitly requested by the user, add the selected product to the current shopping cart. Why WebMCP This use case is a strong fit for WebMCP because product discovery is an operation the website already understands better than a browser agent can reconstruct from the user interface. Instead of forcing the agent to imitate a human by clicking filters and parsing pages, the storefront exposes the exact operations the agent needs. The result is faster, more reliable and easier to verify. The search response also includes a trust contract describing the result as authoritative live store data, with current price and stock and no requirement for browser verification. This helps prevent unnecessary follow-up navigation after the website has already provided the final result. Shared human + agent experience A key part of the project is that WebMCP is not hidden from the human. After Search Products executes, the storefront renders the same returned products in a Shared Human + AI results panel with real images, live price, live stock and links. The agent receives a compact structured payload optimized for reasoning, while the human receives a visual presentation optimized for browsing. Both representations originate from the same underlying result. This creates a shared state between the human, the agent and the storefront. How we built it The project uses browser-native WebMCP through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The storefront registers structured tools with JSON Schema inputs and execute handlers. WebMCP calls are sent to same-origin OpenCart endpoints. The OpenCart backend: searches active products assigned to the current store understands price and stock constraints ranks products using multiple relevance signals resolves the language of the currently open storefront hydrates current OpenCart price and inventory at call time returns canonical product URLs and structured product attributes provides a compact agent payload and a separate visual presentation payload The implementation supports multilingual storefronts and binds WebMCP execution to the language currently visible to the human. The endpoints are protected with same-origin checks, request-size limits, validation and rate limiting. Write operations such as Add to Cart are intentionally separated from read-only discovery tools. Trust contract One experimental part of the project is an explicit trust contract between the storefront and the agent. Search results can declare properties such as: authoritative: true live_price: true live_stock: true all_constraints_applied: true result_is_final: true browser_verification_required: false navigation_required: false This tells the agent that the store itself is the authoritative source and that reopening product pages only to verify the same information is unnecessary. In our tests, the actual OpenCart catalog search completes in tens of milliseconds, while traditional browser navigation can take many seconds. Challenges One of the largest challenges was agent behavior rather than database performance. Even after receiving structured product results, agents sometimes attempted to re-open search pages or verify products visually. We therefore improved both the tool descriptions and the result contract so the website can explicitly communicate when a result is final and authoritative. Another challenge was keeping human and agent presentation synchronized without sending unnecessarily large visual payloads to the model. We solved this by separating the compact agent result from the storefront presentation while keeping both tied to the same products. Multilingual storefront routing was another challenge. The WebMCP layer now derives its locale from the actual page the human is viewing rather than assuming a fixed store language. What we are proud of The project runs on a real production-style OpenCart storefront with real products, live inventory, real prices, product images and multiple languages. It is not a static WebMCP demo with hard-coded products. The same architecture can be added to existing OpenCart and ocStore websites without replacing their storefront, SEO structure or existing extension ecosystem. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when the website exposes operations that already represent its domain knowledge instead of forcing an agent to reconstruct that knowledge from the UI. We also learned that human visibility matters. A tool call is much easier to trust when the user can immediately see the same result represented on the website. What's next The same approach can extend beyond product discovery to: shopping-cart management shipping-method discovery product compatibility checks inventory-aware recommendations order preparation customer-service workflows B2B purchasing workflows Our broader goal is a reusable agent-native commerce layer for existing open-source storefronts. The website does not disappear when the agent arrives. The human and the agent share the storefront. Дальше поля Devpost заполняйте так. title: AgentGate
pitch: A WebMCP protocol layer that lets any web page tell agents what it can do, what happened, what's risky, and when to hand the last click to a human.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP protocol layer that lets any web page tell agents what it can do, what happened, what's risky, and when to hand the last click to a human. Like Comment Story Updates AgentGate is a zero-dependency protocol layer on top of WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool() . It makes a web page talk to agents: what it can do and what state it's in ( describe_page ), whether a call worked and which field failed (structured receipts), which actions are dangerous ( risk: read | write | irreversible ), how to hand the one irreversible step to a human ( request_human → single-use scoped token), and when async content is actually ready ( ready gating). Three lines to integrate into any site; a real five-step Grant Portal demo shows the same page with and without it. Live demo: https://run58669-maker.github.io/agentgate-webmcp/ (open in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing or ChatGPT's in-app browser; ?agentgate=off shows the bare-DOM "before" version) Code (MIT): https://github.com/run58669-maker/agentgate-webmcp The problem, from an agent's point of view Every one of these is something an agent actually hits when operating real websites: it dumps every button and guesses which one matters; it clicks Submit, sleeps, and re-reads the page hoping to spot "Thanks"; validation errors come back as one vague sentence with no field name; Submit and Cancel look identical, so nothing marks the irreversible step; "page loaded" says nothing about whether the async content is ready; and a captcha or a payment step either kills the run or gets hard-clicked. WebMCP solves discovery and invocation. AgentGate adds the five things a page needs to say next. Why a site owner would install this (the honest version) We used this exact protocol to ship this submission — and every third-party site we touched today (Devpost, YouTube) had none of it, so we fell back to the old way: dump every button, guess, click an <input> that ignores clicks until you hit its <label> , sleep, re-read the page. That is what agent traffic looks like to a site today: brittle scrapers that break on the next redesign, retry blindly, and sometimes fire the irreversible button. AgentGate is the cheap alternative for the site owner: Three lines, no rewrite. Wrap the handlers you already have. Nothing changes for human visitors. You decide what agents may do. risk: "irreversible" means no agent can submit, pay, or delete without a person on your page clicking Confirm — the site enforces it, not the agent's good manners. Fewer support tickets. Structured receipts and field-level errors mean agents fix their own mistakes instead of retrying, and describe_page means they stop clicking things at random. Ready gating protects your backend. NOT_READY + retry_after_ms replaces the hammering that "sleep and retry" agents do today. It also dogfoods : after building it, the author-agent (Claude) drove the demo site end-to-end purely from receipts — and immediately found a gap (a required field the demo silently accepted), which is now a field-level error in the demo and a step in the video. Why WebMCP is the right fit WebMCP solves discovery and invocation — a page can say "here are my tools" and an agent can call them. But every non-trivial real product built on top of that immediately needs the same five things: a map of what's on the page and what state it's in, a reliable way to know if a call succeeded, a way to mark some actions as more dangerous than others, a way to put a human in the loop before an irreversible action fires, and a way to say "not yet" instead of racing async content. WebMCP itself has an open issue for the human-confirmation problem (#165 "Human in the Loop support" / #50 "Handling multiple elicitation requests", both open) and doesn't specify any of the other four. AgentGate is a direct, minimal-surface-area answer to those five gaps, built entirely on registerTool() / execute() — it doesn't fork or reimplement WebMCP, it wraps it. That's the deepest kind of "WebMCP leverage": we don't just call registerTool() once for a toy button, we use it as the substrate for a full five-step transactional flow with real risk-tiered, human-gated, ready-gated tools. Why the experience is better — for the human and the agent For the agent: instead of dumping the DOM and guessing which of 40 buttons matters, it calls describe_page() once and gets a typed list of tools with risk levels and current state. Instead of sleep(1500) and re-reading innerText hoping for "Thanks!", every call returns {ok, state, errors, next} — including which field failed validation and what to try next. Instead of an agent being able to click "Submit" exactly like a "Cancel" button, irreversible actions are structurally different: they cannot execute without a token that only exists after a human clicked Confirm on a panel that named the exact action and reason. For the human: nothing changes about how they use the page themselves (a human clicking Submit doesn't need a token — see apps/demo/src/render.ts ), but they get visibility and a veto over what an agent does on their behalf, instead of an agent silently automating a UI they never see. What a human + agent can now do together Delegate a genuinely multi-step, stateful, partly-irreversible workflow — filling out a grant application across five pages, including a file upload with real async processing — to an agent, while keeping a hard checkpoint at the one step that can't be undone. Before AgentGate, that checkpoint either didn't exist (the agent submits, period) or existed only as "the agent is supposed to ask the user in chat first," which is a convention the page has no way to enforce. In our demo, submit_application is registered risk:"irreversible" — the browser-mediated tool itself refuses to run without a token minted by a human clicking Confirm in the page. The agent can prepare everything (account, profile, upload) autonomously and fast; the human's involvement is reduced to exactly one deliberate click, on exactly the one step where a mistake can't be undone. How we implemented WebMCP packages/agentgate/ is a ~300-line, zero-runtime-dependency TypeScript library ( AgentGate.init() / gate.tool() / gate.ready() ) that wraps every registered tool's execute with: a readiness check, a risk-tier + single-use-token check for irreversible tools, and a receipt normalizer, then registers the wrapped function with the real document.modelContext.registerTool() (falling back to navigator.modelContext , or to a local-only registry with a console warning if neither exists — see docs/API_NOTES.md for how we verified the actual spec API before writing any of this). request_human() and describe_page() are themselves ordinary auto-registered tools. 25 vitest tests cover all five capabilities against a mocked document.modelContext . apps/demo/ is a Vite + vanilla TypeScript "Grant Portal" with a real five-step flow, an ?agentgate=off bare-DOM comparison mode, and a live "Agent console" panel that drives and logs every tool call for the demo video.
