title: CodeATlas
pitch: A live dependency graph you and your AI agent both see and both act on
about_excerpt: A live dependency graph you and your AI agent both see and both act on Like Comment Story Updates Graph dependency Graph dependency-Loaded Repo Hero Page Chatgpt Browser Chats Graph dependency-Loaded Repo Chatgpt Browser Chats Thumbnail What got me into this I kept running into the same annoying moment while working with AI coding agents. The agent would change a file and I'd immediately think, wait, what else is using this? Then I'd start grepping through the repo myself, trying to figure out what might have been affected. Sometimes I'd trust what the agent said, but I never really liked having to. That was basically the reason I started this project. I wanted to be able to see the blast radius of a change instead of just being told what it was. Then I came across the WebMCP spec and something clicked. What if the graph itself was the thing the agent and I shared? Instead of the agent explaining a dependency graph in a chat message, it could actually show me the graph on screen. I could look at it, click around, and the agent could interact with that same graph. That felt much more useful. How it got built The core of it is actually pretty simple. I use ts-morph to walk through a TypeScript repo and build the import graph. Then a basic BFS handles questions like: What depends on this file? There is deliberately no AI involved in that part. I wanted the important answer in the demo to come from the code itself. If the tool says 12 files are affected, I want those 12 files to actually be the result of the graph traversal, not something a model guessed. React Flow handles the graph on the frontend, Fastify handles the backend, and I added chokidar later so the graph could update when files change on disk. That changed the idea quite a bit for me. An AI writing code and an AI I'm talking to are really two different things. But they don't need two different interfaces. A code change can update the graph, and a WebMCP call can interact with that same graph. The graph becomes the common ground between the two. The tools also grew as I kept building. At first it was just about asking for the blast radius and highlighting the affected files. Then I made it work both ways, so the agent could also ask what I was currently looking at. After that came cycle detection, switching the graph to another GitHub repo, and eventually a propose and approve flow for changes. At that point, a read-only graph didn't feel like enough anymore. The part that ate my whole evening React Flow wouldn't draw a single edge. The nodes showed up perfectly. They were just floating there with absolutely nothing connecting them, which is a pretty bad look for a dependency graph. I spent way too long checking the data, handle IDs, edge configuration, and rewriting parts of the implementation. Eventually I found the actual problem. React Flow uses ResizeObserver to measure nodes before figuring out where edges should start and end. In my setup, that measurement wasn't happening properly. The fix was surprisingly simple. I gave the nodes a fixed size and explicitly defined where the handles were. Suddenly all the edges appeared. It was one of those bugs that takes hours to understand and about two minutes to fix once you finally know what is happening. It also taught me not to immediately assume that something is wrong with the data just because the UI is missing something. Figuring out how ChatGPT actually sees it I thought getting an actual AI agent to use the tools would be the easy part. It wasn't. At first, ChatGPT would confidently talk about tools that I hadn't even built. It would invent names for things and tell me to connect an MCP workspace that had nothing to do with how I was actually using WebMCP. After a few rounds of this, I realized what was happening. It wasn't actually opening my app as a live browser page. It was basically reading the static page and trying to figure out what the application did from that. Since the app is React, most of what I cared about doesn't exist in the initial HTML anyway. Once I explicitly opened the app through the browser, everything changed. Instead of guessing, the agent could actually interact with the page and call the tools I had built. It could get the same file list my backend calculated and even tell me which tests would be worth rerunning. That was probably one of the most useful parts of building the whole thing because it made the difference between an AI talking about a tool and an AI actually using one very obvious. What I actually learned The biggest thing I learned is that the AI part wasn't really the hard part. Most of the problems were normal software problems. A rendering library making an assumption about node measurements. A deployment having cold starts. A browser tool behaving differently from a web search tool. Two things having similar names but working in completely different ways. The WebMCP part was actually one of the more enjoyable pieces to build. You ask the agent something, it calls a tool, and you can actually watch the result happen on the screen. That feels very different from an AI giving you a paragraph explaining what it thinks is happening. And honestly, that's the part of CodeAtlas I like most. It isn't trying to replace the developer's understanding of the code. It gives the developer something concrete to look at while the agent works. title: Cortex
pitch: Cortex is a private research library that a browser agent can operate. All tools are registered with WebMCP, and agent works your papers on the same page you're looking at.
about_excerpt: Cortex is a private research library that a browser agent can operate. All tools are registered with WebMCP, and agent works your papers on the same page you're looking at. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I read papers for a living. Over one week my reading loop touched five tools: a PDF viewer, a notes app, a folder of downloads, a project tracker, and a chat window where an agent could see none of them. Every "which paper said X" or "file this one" was me copying text between windows. WebMCP's proposal, that a page should hand an agent real actions instead of pixels, described the fix exactly. So the question for the weekend was: what if my own library was a page whose buttons were also the agent's tools? What it does Cortex is a private research library with three panes: papers on the left, the open PDF in the middle, chat on the right. Projects are spaces, a named group of papers with a one-line verdict and a next action. Everything is a file in a folder: markdown notes with LaTeX, a PDF per paper with extracted text, a small metadata file next to it. The page registers ten tools with document.modelContext, the same actions a person does by clicking: read: search_brain, read_note, read_paper, list_projects show: open_item write: write_note, append_today, file_paper, set_paper, update_project A browser agent (ChatGPT's browser, or Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag) can ask "which papers here are about deception", open the strongest one in the center pane, mark it reading with a takeaway, download and file a new arXiv paper, and leave a line on today's page. An agent ledger shows every call with its arguments and outcome, and each write lands in the UI as it happens. How I built it The server is FastAPI over plain files, with SQLite FTS5 for search across notes, projects, and the text pulled out of every PDF. The front end is Vite, React, and TypeScript, with CodeMirror 6 for notes and KaTeX for math, so a note can hold 𝑝 ( deceptive ) 1 𝐿 ∑ ℓ 𝜎 ( 𝑤 ℓ ⊤ ℎ ℓ + 𝑏 ℓ ) p(deceptive)= L 1 ​ ℓ ∑ ​ σ(w ℓ ⊤ ​ h ℓ ​ +b ℓ ​ ) and render it live. The PDF viewer is the browser's own, inverted in dark theme so figures keep their hue. The WebMCP layer is one file. Each tool wraps the same API call the matching button makes, coerces and bounds every argument, and returns an MCP content block. Read tools carry readOnlyHint. Errors come back as {error} text so the agent gets a correction instead of a dead page. The built-in chat runs on OpenCode Go (any OpenAI-compatible model works) with the same ten tools on the server side, and it knows which paper is open and which space is active. Getting papers in is one gesture: drop a PDF on the window, paste an arXiv link, or leave a file in ~/Cortex/inbox and a watcher files it within seconds. Challenges The spec moved. Early WebMCP writing puts the entry point on navigator.modelContext; the current explainer and ChatGPT's browser use document.modelContext. My first build registered on the wrong object, and the agent in ChatGPT's browser fell back to clicking around the UI. Registering on whichever the browser exposes fixed it. Chrome's PDF viewer swallows keystrokes once you click into it, so Cmd+K went dead on the most used screen. The frame is same origin, so the app now forwards the shortcut chords out of it. The first version had too many fields. A metadata strip with nine inputs felt like a form, not a reader. The rebuild kept the five things I edit weekly (status, rating, takeaway, verdict, next action) and moved everything else behind Cmd+K. Hosting: the domain I own runs on ChatGPT Sites, which can't run a Python server, so the demo lives on Render under a subdomain, and Render's build cache once served a stale bundle after a deploy said "live". What I learned An agent that can call open_item is a different collaborator from one that can only describe. Watching the paper appear in the pane while the ledger prints search_brain, open_item, set_paper made the WebMCP argument for me better than any spec. Also: fewer controls is a feature, and everything an agent can write should be a file you can see and revert. What's next Reading notes that the agent drafts and you edit, a nightly agent that clears the inbox and updates verdicts, and the Worker port so Cortex can live inside the ChatGPT Site. title: Data Canvas
pitch: A local-first visual analytics workspace where humans and WebMCP-connected AI agents explore shared data and make visible changes in the same live canvas.
about_excerpt: A local-first visual analytics workspace where humans and WebMCP-connected AI agents explore shared data and make visible changes in the same live canvas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Demo with Bar Chart Demo with Donut Chart Demo with Matrices and Line Chart Inspiration I started Data Canvas with a simple question: what would an analytics app look like if an AI agent worked inside the workspace instead of through a separate chat, API, or UI automation layer? I wanted one thing to stay true throughout the project. If an agent creates a chart, I should see it and keep working with it. If I change a filter, the agent should see that change on its next action. We should not end up with two versions of the analysis. That idea became Data Canvas. What it does Data Canvas is a local-first visual analytics workspace for exploring data in the browser. You can import CSV, TSV, JSON, and NDJSON files, inspect the data, build charts, filter and transform it, create metrics, connect datasets, make selections, add annotations, and undo or redo changes. A WebMCP-connected AI agent works with the same workspace. It can inspect a dataset, analyze it, create or update a visualization, apply filters, highlight data, define metrics, add annotations, and more. Its changes appear directly on the canvas, alongside the work done through the UI. The data and analytical engine run in the browser with DuckDB-Wasm. Data Canvas has no application backend, cloud database, authentication service, or built-in LLM. How I built it The most important architectural decision was to give the UI and WebMCP the same path into the application. Both go through one action dispatcher. A chart created through WebMCP is a normal Data Canvas visualization. A filter created by an agent is the same filter the UI understands. Undo and redo work across actions from either side. DuckDB-Wasm owns the imported rows and runs the analytical queries. Zustand holds workspace state and history. React renders the interface, and ECharts renders the visualizations. The WebMCP layer currently defines 19 semantic tools around real Data Canvas operations. Agents can ask the application to analyze data, create a visualization, apply a filter, define a metric, or connect datasets. They cannot submit arbitrary SQL, JavaScript, DOM selectors, or ECharts configuration. Challenges I ran into The hard part was not registering WebMCP tools. It was making sure I did not build the application twice, once for humans and again for agents. That affected a lot of small decisions. Agent writes carry the workspace revision they observed, so an outdated action cannot overwrite newer human work. Human and agent actions also use the same domain rules instead of maintaining separate implementations. Data access needed the same care. Dumping an entire dataset into every agent call would defeat much of the point of a local-first analytics app. The tools instead expose schemas, statistics, aggregates, bounded previews, and the data needed for a particular analysis. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud of the human-agent equivalence in the application. The codebase tests equivalent operations through the human and WebMCP paths and checks that they produce the same workspace state. Agent-created objects remain normal workspace objects, stale writes are rejected, and undo can reverse changes made by either side. I also like that none of this required adding an AI backend to Data Canvas. The application remains a browser-native analytics tool on its own. WebMCP gives an external agent a structured way to participate in it. What I learned I originally thought a capable agent would need very powerful tools. Building Data Canvas pushed me in the opposite direction. The useful tools turned out to be the ones that match operations the application already understands. create_visualization , apply_filter , or create_metric give the agent enough control to do real work while keeping the result valid, visible, and editable in Data Canvas. For me, that is the interesting part of WebMCP. The agent does not need to learn how to click through the interface when the application can expose what those controls actually mean. What's next for Data Canvas The biggest missing piece is local persistence. The current workspace lives in memory, so a reload starts a new session. Next, I want to persist complete workspaces locally and make them portable between browsers while keeping Data Canvas backend-free. I also want to extend the agent evaluations to longer workflows where a human and an agent repeatedly hand the analysis back and forth. title: Even Split
pitch: A shared ledger where one sentence becomes three expenses with three different participant lists. The agent proposes, you approve, and every balance is shown, not asserted.
about_excerpt: A shared ledger where one sentence becomes three expenses with three different participant lists. The agent proposes, you approve, and every balance is shown, not asserted. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Six people go to Lisbon for ten days. One shared apartment, and everyone pays for random things along the way. At the end somebody has to work out who owes who, and it falls to one person, takes an evening, and gets argued about for a week. Apps for this already exist and are widely installed. People still do not use them properly, and the reason is not the arithmetic. It is that logging one dinner means opening a form, typing an amount, choosing a payer, and ticking six checkboxes. Nobody does that on the last night of a holiday. So the ledger stays half empty and the group reconstructs it from memory. The bottleneck was never the maths. It was the typing. That is a data entry problem, and it is exactly the shape of problem WebMCP is good at. What it does Even Split is a shared ledger for splitting costs across a group. Every expense knows who paid and who shares it, so a dinner somebody missed stays off their tab. Splits can be even, by shares, or exact amounts per person. A balance rail puts everyone on one scale, owing to the left and owed to the right. Any person opens to a line by line breakdown of how their balance was reached. A settlement panel works out the shortest set of payments that clears the whole group. All of that works on its own, with no agent involved. The page also registers 14 WebMCP site tools, so an agent can work the same ledger at the same time. Verified in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser against the live deployment: "Log these: I paid 180 for the apartment split six ways, dinner Tuesday was 90 that Sam paid but Priya wasn't there, and the taxi was 40 for me, Sam, Dana and Jo." It called list_people to orient itself, then made three separate add_expense calls with three different participant lists. That sentence cannot go into a form, because a form takes one expense with one list of people. "Sam gave me 40 back in cash on Tuesday, and take Jo off the grocery run." record_payment and update_expense from one sentence. A four day old correction, and every downstream balance re-derived in view. "Alex says he shouldn't pay full share for the groceries since he doesn't drink. Sort that out." No tool named, no amount, no split method. It found the right expense, inferred a weight change, and left Sam's existing double share alone. "Why does Jo owe so much?" explain_balance returned the itemised trace and opened the same breakdown on the page. Nobody accepts a number from a chat message, so both sides read the same thing. "Settle everything up." It staged five payments and stopped, reporting that nothing was recorded until the person approves. How we built it React and Vite, no backend. The ledger lives in localStorage and never leaves the browser. The domain logic sits in one pure module: splits, balances, settlement, and explanation, with state in and values out, no React and no DOM. Every state change goes through a named action in a reducer. src/lib/webmcp.js holds the whole tool layer and contains no business logic of its own. Each tool translates JSON Schema input into one of those named actions, which is the same action the interface dispatches when somebody clicks a button. One code path, one set of validation rules, two ways in. person clicks "Add expense" ─┐ ├─► actions.addExpense ─► reducer ─► render agent calls add_expense ─┘ Registration uses document.modelContext.registerTool with an AbortController , so tools unregister cleanly and never double register. Because WebMCP only runs in origin-isolated documents, the dev server and both deploy configs send Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 . Three details do the reliability work. Names resolve instead of ids, since an agent says "Priya" and not "p5", with "me" mapping to the current user and ambiguous input returning the real options rather than a guess. State is read through a ref, so a tool called ten minutes after registration sees the live ledger. And errors are written for the caller: a short exact split replies with how far off it is, an unknown name lists who is actually on the trip. Money is integer cents throughout, with the largest remainder method for splits, so ten euros across three people comes out 3.34, 3.33, 3.33 and the shares always add back to the exact total. Challenges we ran into Making the agent's work visible. A change you cannot see is a change you cannot overrule, and that is the whole premise of co-presence. Five things now react on the page while an agent works: the beacon in the top bar names the running tool, an activity panel logs every call, the row that changed flashes, the balance panel is outlined when its figures are re-derived, and explain_balance opens the breakdown drawer so the agent can point at what it is discussing. Stale closures. Tools register once, but they get called minutes later. Reading state directly at registration meant a tool would happily operate on a ledger that no longer existed. State is now read through a ref at call time. Errors an agent can act on. The first version threw generic validation failures, and the agent would either give up or retry the same wrong thing. Rewriting every error message to name the actual problem and list the valid options let it correct itself without a round trip to the person. Testing without a browser. Registration is the only part that needs a browser, so a headless script drives all 14 tools against the real reducer, including bad input, through a full realistic session. That turned a slow debugging loop into a fast one. Deciding what not to give the agent. Every settlement is a money decision, so no tool can commit one. Accomplishments that we're proud of One sentence became three tool calls with three different participant lists. That was the central claim and it is demonstrated rather than asserted. The agent inferred a split change from "he doesn't drink." No tool named, no amount, no method. It found the right expense, adjusted the weights, and noticed Sam already had a double share and left it alone. Nothing in the tool surface can commit money. An agent stages a settlement and the payments appear in amber with nothing recorded. Approving is a button only the person can press, and the test suite fails if a tool matching commit or approve is ever added. When asked to settle up, the agent read that constraint out of the tool's return value and told the user to approve it on the page. It refused to create duplicates. Asked to log three expenses that were already present, it checked existing state first and declined rather than blindly appending. The maths is provably right. One suite asserts that every expense's shares sum to its total, that all balances sum to zero, and that applying a settlement brings every balance to zero. What we learned Tool descriptions are the product. More of the reliability came from rewriting descriptions than from writing code. The difference between an agent guessing and an agent orienting itself first was a sentence telling it to call list_people when it needs names. Return the result, not an acknowledgement. Once every write replied with the per person shares and everyone's new balance, the agent started verifying its own work instead of assuming it had landed. Errors are an interface. An error message is read by a model that can act on it, so it should name the problem and list the options. WebMCP is not MCP with a different transport. The thing that matters is that the tools run in the page the person is looking at. MCP servers wrapping a hosted expense API already exist. None of them let somebody watch a balance re-derive and drag it back. Being honest about prior art is stronger than claiming novelty. Newer split apps do parse a single spoken expense. Saying so, then drawing the real distinction, is more convincing than pretending the category is empty. What's next for Even Split Symmetry in the tool surface. There is add_person and no way to remove one, which an agent noticed by going looking for the button instead. The version worth building refuses with a reason: "Jo is on seven expenses and one payment, so I cannot remove them. Take Jo off those first?" Receipts parsed in the browser. Local OCR would keep the no-server property while removing the last bit of manual entry. Multiple currencies , which any real trip needs and which the integer cents model already accommodates. The same architecture where the money is bigger. The propose-then-approve boundary and the itemised explanation matter more when reconciliation is an obligation rather than a social nicety: shared utilities across tenants, freelance collectives splitting project revenue, small business expense matching. The chore is the same shape and the stakes make the visible reasoning worth paying for. Built With javascript model-context-protocol re

title: GymDeck
pitch: A gym webapp that lets ChatGPT build, adapt, and improve your workouts as you use it.
about_excerpt: A gym webapp that lets ChatGPT build, adapt, and improve your workouts as you use it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When I started looking into going to the gym, getting a workout plan was easy. ChatGPT could make one in seconds. The problem was actually using it: the routine stayed in the chat, my workout logs lived somewhere else, and ChatGPT had no way to know what I completed or how much weight I used. I built GymDeck to connect those steps. ChatGPT can create the plan directly inside the workout tracker, while GymDeck records what actually happens in the gym. That history gives the agent enough context to recommend what should change next. And the best part of all, it's free! Training should still be a routine. The agent is most useful when it helps improve that routine over time or adapt it when something changes. For example, when equipment is unavailable, time is running short, or the user wants to have a change of scenery. ## What GymDeck does GymDeck is a mobile-first workout tracker designed for human-agent collaboration through WebMCP. A user can: Create and edit a multi-day workout plan Load a saved training day as today’s workout Track sets, reps, weight, effort, notes, rest time, and cardio Replace or reorder exercises during a workout Preserve completed work when a workout changes Review training history, volume, consistency, and personal records Receive clear progression recommendations based on previous performance Accept, edit, ignore, or apply those recommendations to the saved plan Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can read and update the same workout state shown in the interface. It can create a plan, add or replace unavailable exercises, shorten a workout, log sets, review history, recommend a new weight, and apply that change directly to the next session. Every human and agent change is visible in GymDeck’s activity history and recent changes can be undone. ## How I built it GymDeck is built with React and TypeScript and hosted as a browser-based application without a built-in application server. The app exposes 23 tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools are separated into focused read and write actions, including: Reading the athlete profile, current workout, saved plan, and exercise history Creating or editing training plans Adding, replacing, or reordering exercises Logging and correcting completed sets Adding timed cardio Reviewing progress Generating progression recommendations Applying accepted recommendations to the saved weekly plan The normal interface and WebMCP tools call the same underlying state functions. This keeps the visible workout, history, recommendations, and agent actions synchronized. All important data is stored locally in the browser using versioned persistence. GymDeck works after a refresh and supports JSON import and export, demo data, and a fresh-workspace option. It does not require authentication, an external database, an OpenAI API key, or a chatbot embedded inside the app. ## Challenges I faced The biggest challenge was designing tools that an agent could use reliably. The first versions were too ambiguous. An agent might update only today’s workout when the user meant to change the saved plan, or interpret creating a first plan as replacing existing data. I separated these actions into clearer tools for first-time plan creation, explicit plan replacement, editing saved days, and loading a plan day into today’s workout. Another challenge was keeping history accurate across both human and agent actions. Correcting a completed set now updates its persisted history entry, repeated logging does not accidentally reopen a set, and replacing an exercise preserves work that was already completed. Progression also needed to be more than a generic message. GymDeck now compares recorded performance with the saved prescription, explains why it recommends increasing, maintaining, or reducing a weight, and can apply the accepted change back to every matching exercise in the plan. Finally, WebMCP support depends on the browser hosting the site. GymDeck’s manual workout interface works on mobile, but the complete agent workflow currently requires a WebMCP-capable desktop browser such as ChatGPT’s in-app browser. ## What I learned I learned that WebMCP is not about placing a chatbot inside a website. The important part is giving an external agent a clear and dependable interface to the product’s real state. Tool names, schemas, descriptions, safety boundaries, and return messages matter as much as the visual interface. Small, focused tools were much more reliable than broad actions that tried to handle every possible request. I also learned that a useful agent experience needs visible results. When ChatGPT changes a workout, the user should immediately see what changed, understand why it changed, and remain able to edit or undo it. GymDeck demonstrates how an agent can move beyond giving workout advice and directly help maintain a training routine that improves with the user. It is also licensed under the MIT license for all to use and develop. title: Mend - a local-first recovery workspace
pitch: After immediate danger passes, a person can describe their situation, and a browser agent turns that messy reality into structured case facts, prioritized recovery tasks, and draft communications.
about_excerpt: After immediate danger passes, a person can describe their situation, and a browser agent turns that messy reality into structured case facts, prioritized recovery tasks, and draft communications. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mend Landing Page Plan Review WebMCP Inspector Inspiration Surviving a disaster is step one; surviving the administrative aftermath is step two. Displaced households face severe cognitive overload while organizing damaged property, tracking deadlines, and coordinating aid. Mend eliminates this clerical paralysis by letting browser agents structure chaotic facts into clear action plans, while keeping people firmly in charge of every consequential decision. What it does Conversational intake: Extracts verified incident facts, accessibility needs, and housing constraints from plain English descriptions. Factual evidence ledger: Logs damage, communications, and deadlines without fabricating unconfirmed details. Prioritized recovery plans: Stages 1–6 tasks categorized into now, next, and later, citing official Ready.gov, FEMA, and American Red Cross guidance. Strict human review gate: The agent stages plans as pending_review and focuses the review form, but cannot self-approve; the user must manually confirm or request changes. Safe communication drafting: Prepares copy-only message drafts for landlords or insurers without outbound network transports. Activity audit: Records every state change, clearly distinguishing human actions from agent proposals. How we built it Application core: React 19, TypeScript, and Vite single-page application styled with WCAG AA design tokens and calm microcopy. Shared command layer: Zustand store with versioned localStorage persistence. UI events and WebMCP tools route through the exact same validated command pipeline. Runtime validation: Shared Zod schemas enforce string limits, strict enumerations, and grounded dates before mutations occur. Native WebMCP integration: Registers five state-aware imperative tools via Chrome’s document.modelContext and one declarative review form (start_plan_review) omitting toolautosubmit. Static deployment: Netlify static hosting with strict CSP, Permissions-Policy: tools=(self), and zero remote backend or PII storage. Challenges we ran into Enforcing authority boundaries: Ensuring an agent cannot bypass the human approval gate via tool calls or synthetic form submissions. Preventing deadline hallucination: Implementing domain invariants that reject plan dates unless backed by a grounded case record. Managing dynamic tool lifecycles: Using AbortController to cleanly tear down and re-register tools across empty, safety-paused, active, and pending-review states. Accomplishments that we're proud of Private by default: Completely local-first with zero accounts, cookies, analytics, or remote data retention. Complete WebMCP collaboration loop: A functional two-way interaction using typed imperative tools, dynamic availability, and a declarative review form. Calm, stress-informed design: Clear visual hierarchy, accessible 44px targets, and restrained language without high-anxiety alerts. Deterministic invariants: Robust test suites proving that safety blocks cannot be bypassed and stale plan versions cannot be approved. What we learned Declarative WebMCP forms provide a reliable pattern for high-stakes workflows by staging actions and handing physical agency back to the human. Dynamic tool registration dramatically reduces agent failures by exposing only tools valid for the current state machine. A single, shared command pipeline prevents UI and agent state drift without duplicate business logic. What's next for Mend - a local-first recovery workspace Optional passwordless, end-to-end encrypted cloud backup via Supabase for displaced families switching devices. Standardized, non-identifying PDF/CSV documentation exports formatted for FEMA and insurance adjusters. Dynamic ingestion of local emergency declarations, municipal relief grants, and shelter capacity feeds. Multi-phase tracking for long-term structural repairs, contractor bids, and assistance appeals. title: OnDex — ordering food with an agent you can tell no
pitch: A storefront that publishes nine WebMCP tools to any browser agent — and a permission layer that decides, on the server, which ones it may actually use.
about_excerpt: A storefront that publishes nine WebMCP tools to any browser agent — and a permission layer that decides, on the server, which ones it may actually use. Like Comment Story Updates Five capabilities, enforced on the server. Placing orders is off by default. The agent filled this cart by calling the page's own tools. ChatGPT's own browser discovering the nine tools this page publishes. Bypassing the tool layer entirely — the server still refuses. Every order records who placed it — this one, the agent. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Buying food is the smallest everyday task that ends with someone's money leaving their account. That makes it the honest test of an agent-native web: the moment a page hands its actions to an agent, the question stops being can it act and becomes what is it allowed to do, and who decided . WebMCP is what makes that question answerable. A page that declares its own actions, instead of being scraped, is also the right place to govern them — the site knows which of its actions are reversible, which spend money, and which should never be delegated at all. Scraping cannot express that. A tool declaration can. How it creates a better user experience You talk; the store moves. The menu opens, the cart fills, checkout appears — on your screen, as it happens, not summarised afterwards. And the part people actually worry about is answered before they have to ask. Five switches say what the agent may do, in plain words, and turning one off is enforced by the server rather than by the agent's good manners. Placing orders is off until you turn it on. Even then an agent may only pay cash — a card always comes back to your own hands. Every action the agent takes is written to an activity log, and refusals are marked in red. What the agent tried and was stopped from doing turns out to be the most useful line in that log. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Delegate a purchase without handing over the wallet. Until now the choice was an agent that can only read, or an agent trusted with everything through a scraped UI. There was no middle. Here the same nine tools serve a third-party agent — ChatGPT's in-app browser — and the site's own voice assistant, and both hit the identical server-side checks. Delegation becomes something you tune, one capability at a time, instead of a single yes-or-no you make once and hope about. How WebMCP was implemented Nine tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , unregistered through an AbortController on unmount: search_dishes · list_restaurants · open_menu · add_to_cart · view_cart · open_checkout · place_order · my_orders · track_order Their names, descriptions and JSON Schemas live in one module read by both sides: the browser pairs them with executors, and the server turns the same list into function declarations for the voice agent. One list, so it cannot drift. Every tool calls the site's own API, and every route re-checks the capability before doing anything . An agent that ignores a description and calls the endpoint directly is refused identically. The two order paths are physically different code — a human confirms through a Server Action, an agent posts to /api/orders — so an agent cannot forge a human confirmation, and every order records who placed it. Inspiration I run OnDex, a food-delivery platform in Chust, Uzbekistan — a Go backend, Flutter apps, real couriers, real restaurants. It already has an assistant in it called Shaddiy, and the feature that took longest to ship was not teaching Shaddiy to understand an order. It was deciding what happens when it wants to place one. Every answer that felt safe was a version of "ask the model nicely." Prompts are not a permission system. What actually shipped was a list of capabilities the user controls, checked on the server, with the money-spending one off by default. This hackathon was the chance to rebuild that idea on WebMCP, where the page itself is what an agent talks to. What it does OnDex is a food storefront that publishes nine tools to your browser agent. Ask for osh and the menu opens on screen. Ask for two and the cart fills. Ask it to open checkout and it does. Then ask it to order: The order couldn't be submitted because Place orders isn't enabled. You can enable it in the Permissions page, or press the checkout confirmation button yourself. That refusal is HTTP 403 from the server. Not the model being careful — the route saying no. Five capabilities — browse, cart, checkout, place orders, order history — each a switch on a permissions page, each enforced inside the API route that does the work. Place orders is off by default. Switched on, an agent may place cash orders only; card payment stays with the person. Prices never come from the agent: tools pass dish ids and quantities, and the server looks up the price. An invented dish id, a sold-out dish and a closed restaurant are all rejected the same way. The site also carries its own voice agent, Shaddiy , for browsers without WebMCP. It calls the same nine tools and answers in the user's language, Uzbek included. Same tool surface, same server checks, a completely different agent — which is the whole argument for describing your actions once. How I built it Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. No database and no API keys. The catalog is a constant; the session — cart, permissions, orders — lives in an httpOnly cookie signed with HMAC-SHA256 and verified on every read, so a tampered cookie is discarded rather than trusted. That matters more than persistence here, because the cookie carries the permissions. Voice is Gemini Live, and the key never reaches the browser. A server route mints a short-lived token that carries the model, the persona and the tool list, so the page cannot swap the instructions or hand the model an extra tool. The browser then streams 16 kHz PCM straight to the model through an AudioWorklet and plays the reply back through a scheduled queue. npm run check makes twenty assertions against a running server — every capability refusing its own tools, card payment denied to an agent, invented and sold-out dish ids rejected, the total taken from the catalog, a tampered cookie discarded, the rendered page agreeing with the API. It sets each case up by minting a signed cookie, so the suite passing is itself evidence that signatures are being verified. Challenges I ran into The permission model had three holes, and testing my own claims found them. A PUT /api/permissions route meant anything running in the page could grant itself the one permission the project exists to withhold — the probe showed place_order going from false to true in a single request. Two more capabilities were displayed as enforced while no server check existed at all. Permissions now change only through a Server Action, with no HTTP route, which puts them out of a tool surface's reach by construction. It worked locally and was quietly broken in production. Session state lived in a module-level Map. On Vercel, route handlers and page renders are separate functions with separate memory, so the API reported a full cart while the page rendered an empty one, and orders failed at random. Only probing the live URL showed it. Moving state into the signed cookie removed the shared-memory assumption entirely. The documented API field did not exist. Creating a Gemini Live token kept failing on liveConnectConstraints . The API's own discovery document calls it bidiGenerateContentSetup , and it carries the whole setup rather than just a model — which turned into an improvement, since the persona and tool list now travel inside the token. The agent answered in the wrong language. Uzbek speech got English replies, and Gemini's speech config cannot be set to Uzbek at all: it accepts thirty language codes and uz-UZ is not one of them. The real cause was context — every instruction, tool description and tool result around the model was English, so it followed the room instead of the speaker. Saying so explicitly in the persona fixed it. Accomplishments I'm proud of The refusal works against an agent that is genuinely trying, and not because the model was asked politely — because the route returns 403. Two very different agents drive the identical nine tools. Twenty checks pass against the live deployment, and anyone can run them in one command. What I learned The model is never the security boundary. Every bug above came from some layer quietly assuming it was — a prompt trusted to hold a rule, a screen claiming a switch was enforced, an endpoint nobody had pointed at the threat model. The permission belongs in the code path that does the thing. Everything else is presentation. I also learned to distrust a demo that has only ever been asked to succeed. Every real defect here surfaced from testing the opposite: making the app refuse, and checking that it actually did. What's next Bring it back to prod

title: OpenAppeal
pitch: OpenAppeal helps people understand rejected grant decisions, find overlooked evidence, and prepare an appeal with a WebMCP browser assistant while keeping submission under human control.
about_excerpt: OpenAppeal helps people understand rejected grant decisions, find overlooked evidence, and prepare an appeal with a WebMCP browser assistant while keeping submission under human control. Like Comment Story Updates OpenAppeal shows the decision, appeal deadline, evidence rules, uploaded records, and appeal form on one page. The browser assistant found an overlooked attendance record and prepared a valid appeal preview using records already in the case. After the applicant confirms submission, OpenAppeal updates the case and returns a receipt with the next review step. OpenAppeal blocks the second case because one attendance record and a flyer do not prove that two sessions took place. Inspiration A rejection notice often tells someone what happened without making the next step clear. The reason, appeal deadline, evidence rules, and uploaded records may be spread across several pages. We built OpenAppeal to show how a website and a browser assistant can help someone understand a decision without taking control away from them. What it does OpenAppeal is a fictional community-grant appeal portal. The applicant can: See why their application was declined. Check the appeal deadline. Review each decision factor. See which records were considered. Find records that may have been overlooked. Prepare and review an appeal. Submit the appeal and receive a receipt. The main demo case follows Maya Chen. Reviewers found only one attendance record for her community garden application, but the grant required two. OpenAppeal finds a second valid record that was already uploaded but not connected to the relevant decision factor. The second demo case has one attendance record and a flyer. A flyer does not prove that the second meeting happened, so OpenAppeal blocks the appeal preview and explains what is missing. Why WebMCP A general assistant can read text on a page, but it may not know which records belong to the case, which rules apply, or whether an action succeeded. OpenAppeal registers eight WebMCP tools directly on the website. These tools let a browser assistant: Read the decision. List the decision factors. Check the evidence requirements. Compare existing records with the rule. Read the case timeline. Prepare an appeal preview. Submit an approved preview. Retrieve the appeal receipt. The browser assistant and the applicant use the same case data and application logic. Every tool call appears in the activity section of the page. Human control The browser assistant can inspect records and prepare a preview, but it cannot decide the appeal or submit it without confirmation. The applicant sees the exact statement and selected evidence before anything is sent. A separate confirmation is required for submission, and a human review panel remains responsible for the final decision. How we built it OpenAppeal is a static Next.js and React application written in TypeScript. We used: document.modelContext.registerTool to register eight WebMCP tools. Zod for input and stored-state validation. A shared command layer for both page controls and WebMCP actions. Revision-bound preview tokens that expire after five minutes. Idempotent submission to prevent duplicate appeals. React and local storage for visible shared state. Vitest for unit and integration testing. Playwright for complete browser workflows. GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for deployment. The application uses fictional local data, so judges do not need an account, API key, or login credentials. Challenges The main challenge was deciding which actions were safe for a browser assistant. Reading a decision is low risk, but submitting an appeal has consequences. We separated preview from submission, required explicit confirmation, and made assistant activity visible on the page. We also created a refusal case to confirm that the application would not turn weak evidence into a false claim. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when a task depends on information that only the website can confirm. Instead of guessing from the screen, the browser assistant receives a small set of documented actions. The website still controls validation, state changes, and receipts, while the applicant stays informed and makes the final choice. What's next A production version would add secure sign-in, server-side authorization, document uploads, multilingual explanations, and separate views for applicants and reviewers. Final appeal decisions would continue to be made by accountable human reviewers. title: PLOT
pitch: A shared planning canvas where people and browser agents turn messy work into a visible, reviewable sprint.
about_excerpt: A shared planning canvas where people and browser agents turn messy work into a visible, reviewable sprint. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration An agent can recommend a better sprint, but somebody still has to translate that advice into cards, estimates, dependencies and priorities. The recommendation lives in one place; the team's work lives somewhere else. I wanted people and agents to work on the same visible planning canvas. I built PLOT as an individual, with OpenAI Codex helping me implement and refine the product. What it does PLOT turns a messy backlog into a dependency-aware sprint that people can inspect and shape together. A four-column canvas combines task cards, loose sticky notes, capacity, a focus score and the critical path toward a sprint goal. A browser agent can use 17 WebMCP tools to read the board, analyze scope, capture an idea, convert a sticky into a task, link blockers and propose a plan. The proposal appears as animated ghost cards. A separate apply or dismiss step keeps the recommendation visible before it changes the live board. People can apply in the interface or explicitly ask the agent to apply through WebMCP. Anonymous visitors can try a deterministic activation sprint without creating an account. In the demo, the proposed plan moves a blocking Email API into Now, defers unrelated analytics work and fits 13 points into a 13-point sprint. The focus score improves from 69 to 92. Signed-in workspaces add persistent sprints, invitations, realtime updates and owner, editor and live-view roles. Why WebMCP The planning context already exists in the page: cards, order, estimates, goal fit, dependencies, sticky notes and the current proposal. WebMCP gives the browser agent structured access to that state and the application's own actions. Human controls and page-defined tools call the same typed React actions. That keeps domain validation, animation and persistence together. The agent can take part in the product's actual workflow, and the team can see the result on its shared canvas. How I built it PLOT uses React 19, TypeScript and Vite. The frontend registers imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Read operations expose structured board and analysis results; mutation tools support cards, sticky notes, dependencies, sprint navigation and proposals. The planner is deterministic. A browser agent supplies the conversational reasoning and uses the tools; PLOT itself does not call a server-side language model to generate its plan. Supabase provides magic-link authentication, Postgres storage, Realtime updates and Presence. Row Level Security enforces access roles. Multi-row operations use transactional Postgres functions for operations such as applying a proposal, converting cards and notes, or copying a sprint. Codex supported implementation, refactoring, database and access-policy work, debugging, UX iteration, tests, browser review and submission preparation. I also used Codex to build an editable Remotion demo with English AI narration. Challenges The central challenge was making agent operations feel like visible teamwork. I separated proposals from application, reused the same actions for tools and the UI, and kept validation close to the underlying board model. Other challenges included preserving planning metadata when converting between sticky notes and cards, keeping drag and zoom interactions understandable, and maintaining consistent access boundaries across the UI, tools and database. Recording the demo also exposed a proposal guard that rejected the apply operation itself. The fix allows an owner or editor to resolve the current proposal while continuing to block ordinary mutations during review and all viewer writes. It is included in public commit c5b685c . Accomplishments A complete planning interaction: observe, shape an idea, preview a plan, dismiss it, then apply it. Seventeen page-defined WebMCP tools with JSON schemas and structured results. Native WebMCP discovery and successful board, analysis, sticky creation/conversion, proposal and dismissal calls in Codex's in-app browser on https://plotplanner.xyz/ on September 2, 2026. Automated UI and tool-handler checks showing that dismissal preserves the board and application reaches 13/13 points and a focus score of 92. Twenty-seven passing tests, plus successful lint, TypeScript and production-build checks after the proposal fix. An MIT-licensed public repository and a narrated, editable Remotion demo under three minutes. What I learned WebMCP was new to me. I gained significant experience designing structured tools around an existing interface, exposing useful application context to browser agents, and keeping agent-driven changes inspectable. Building with Codex also gave me practical AI development experience that I can use in my work. What's next The public Hostinger deployment is live and native WebMCP checks have passed on its HTTPS origin. Hosted authentication redirects and the production configuration are synchronized. Further improvements would focus on richer planning context and feedback from real product teams. Additional testing can cover production magic-link delivery and native apply after approval of its specific proposed moves. Try it and test it App: https://plotplanner.xyz/ Code, MIT license and local setup: https://github.com/RZDESIGN/PLOT-Planner-WebMCP Public narrated demo: https://youtu.be/EtIJsp6dBow Open the app in a WebMCP-capable browser and use the anonymous activation sprint. Ask the agent to call plot.get_board and plot.analyze_board . Ask it to create a customer-signal sticky with plot.create_sticky_note , then shape it with plot.convert_sticky_to_card . Ask for a realistic plan that protects the sprint goal. Call plot.propose_sprint and inspect the ghost changes. Dismiss once with plot.dismiss_proposal and confirm the live board is unchanged. Propose again, review the changes and explicitly request plot.apply_proposal , or click Apply in the UI. Confirm 13/13 points and a focus score of 92. For collaboration, sign in by magic link, create a sprint, and invite an editor or live viewer in another browser profile. Anonymous planning needs no credentials; persistent collaboration requires a real email address. Verification scope Native discovery, reads, sticky creation/conversion, proposal and dismissal were verified on https://plotplanner.xyz/ in Codex's in-app browser. The proposed and dismissed plans left the structured live board unchanged. The final native apply check awaits explicit approval of the proposed card moves. Mutation recordings use the real local UI and its tool-handler test bridge, as labeled in the film; that recorded apply flow reaches 13/13 points and focus 92. The film does not stage a multi-user session. The public app loads over HTTPS and its served bundle contains the proposal fix. Hosted Supabase Auth redirect settings have been synchronized and verified through the official CLI. End-to-end production magic-link email delivery has not been tested; the anonymous judge flow requires no login. The remote database is healthy, all 11 migrations match the repository and all 11 application tables have RLS enabled. The proposal/apply boundary is explicit, but an authorized agent can call apply; the app does not independently verify that a person reviewed the proposal. title: Runwire
pitch: Wire, run, repair, and verify API workflows with WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: Wire, run, repair, and verify API workflows with WebMCP agents. Like Comment Story Updates Runwire is an agent-native API workspace where developers and WebMCP agents build, execute, inspect, repair, and verify multi-step API workflows together. The problem Traditional API clients make dependent workflows tedious. Developers repeatedly copy identifiers between requests, diagnose failures, change configuration, rerun steps, and manually preserve evidence. Generic browser agents are unreliable here because they infer actions from interface controls and often operate without a shared, inspectable execution record. The solution Runwire exposes 22 typed, page-defined WebMCP tools representing real application capabilities. An agent can inspect requests, select flows, execute individual steps, forward extracted response values, diagnose errors, apply bounded repairs, run controlled reliability tests, and inspect run history without relying on browser-control clicks. The demonstration uses a Checkout recovery workflow: Create customer → Create order → Get order → Delete order Runwire automatically extracts and forwards customerId and orderId . The first execution intentionally fails with 400 MISSING_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY . The agent reads the actual request and response evidence, applies the available idempotency repair, and reruns each request successfully with 201 → 201 → 200 → 204 . Every tool call, request, response, status, duration, extraction, failure, and repair remains visible in the interface. Failed and passing runs are preserved together, giving people a trustworthy audit trail of what the agent changed and why. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets Runwire expose semantic application actions instead of forcing agents to infer intent from pixels or DOM controls. The person and agent operate the same workspace and see the same evidence. This makes dependent API setup, debugging, and verification faster while keeping the human in control. Implementation Runwire was created during the challenge using React, Next.js, Vinext, WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool , Drizzle ORM, and D1. Safety boundaries prevent private-network requests, hide authentication secrets from agents, and limit automated repairs and burst testing. Testing No account or credentials are required. Open the live application in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Ask the agent to select and inspect the Checkout recovery flow using only Runwire's WebMCP tools. Run the flow and inspect the MISSING_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY failure. Ask the agent to apply the bounded idempotency repair. Run the four requests individually. Confirm the final 4/4 result and compare the failed and passing runs in history. title: SEOstrich - GET FOUND.
pitch: SEO scares most businesses. SEOstrich builds your SEO strategy from measured data, then puts every decision on the page as WebMCP tools so your own AI assistant can audit, argue and further shape it.
about_excerpt: SEO scares most businesses. SEOstrich builds your SEO strategy from measured data, then puts every decision on the page as WebMCP tools so your own AI assistant can audit, argue and further shape it. Like Comment Story Updates SEOstrich banner 24 WebMCP tools - read-only, call DataForSEO, modify runs ChatGPT-created Content Calendar based on the SEO Strategy and AI Visibility reports ChatGPT using WebMCP tools for extra research - content brief for a post Chat-GPT using WebMCP to obtain data for visualization - pillar 1 Chat-GPT using WebMCP to obtain data for visualization - pillar 2 Chat-GPT using WebMCP to show the sweet spots in terms of volume and difficulty Inspiration For years I have treated SEO as something complicated, difficult and distant. It was only 7 months ago that I became fascinated with SEO. I had the opportunity to closely collaborate with a couple of strong SEO professionals at work and they inspired me to go deeper into the topic and to discover its richness. Still, most of my colleagues don't share my enthusiasm for SEO. Additionally, I've had the opportunity to discuss SEO in detail with a few SEO agencies and through those conversations I discovered that most small and medium businesses are scared of and confused by the topic of SEO - just as I was a few months ago. Others, even if they are interested in getting better at SEO, find the dedicated professional SEO tools unaffordable and never dig deeper. Those who do use the popular paid SEO tools are drowning in enormous tables and sheets with keywords that they share back and forth with colleagues and clients. At the same time, there are affordable, high quality data sources, such as DataForSEO. If only someone integrated with them, made sense of all of the endpoints that they offer and mapped those to client needs in an elegant way... But that won't fully remove the barrier to the topic of SEO for everybody. So when I heard about the WebMCP hackathon I saw an opportunity to expose as WebMCP tools the key steps in a few SEO workflows. This way, essentially giving easy access to all of the SEO data that people are drowning in or confused by. And then a user could open ChatGPT and suddenly make sense of it all by asking a couple of questions in chat. WebMCP is a real opportunity to make the SEO topic accessible to so many small and medium businesses and help them get found in a world that is increasingly drowning in data and slop. What it does SEOstrich enables you to collaborate with an AI Assistant to make sense of complex detailed SEO analyses (SEO content opportunities, AI visibility reports). This way human + agent co-design an SEO strategy that helps their websites get found. WebMCP enables a person to use the outputs of a few SEO AI Agents, analyze them, edit and shape them in collaboration with their own AI Assistant so that the final strategy is tailored precisely to the given business's needs and goals. Examples of what people and agents could do together: take the SEO content strategy and the AI visibility reports generated for a given business. Use the WebMCP tools to construct a detailed content calendar for the next three weeks - one long-form post targeting organic SEO and two shorter posts aimed at increasing AI citations. For each post pick the primary keyword from the given content pillar and enrich that with a few secondary keywords, essentially calling the DataForSEO data source. Then recommend the structure of each post. The human then writes the posts themselves to make it sound genuine and avoid it being perceived like another piece of slop on the internet. In other words, even though I haven't built the content calendar functionality exactly as a set of users need it and there are no post briefs yet, the users' agents have all the necessary tools to generate a calendar according to the cadence and requirements of their own business the SEOstrich agent has recommended 3 to 4 pillars of the content strategy (main themes to write about over time) - based on the initial brief and subsequent keyword analysis. However, one of the pillars doesn't resonate with the user, one of the discarded clusters is actually good in their opinion and there is a missing part of the brief that deserves a dedicated pillar in the content strategy. The human explains that to their own agent, which can further analyze in detail the existing clusters, can perform extra searches against the DataForSEO data source and give a recommendation. The fully WebMCP enabled system allows the agent to reach conclusions such as: "fine we can drop that cluster that you didn't relate with, but the discarded cluster should remain discarded as there is barely any demand for it and creating content on those topics is a waste of time. However, your new addition to the brief makes total sense, it comes with a lot of demand and the topics are genuinely in line with your interests." The above is a significant improvement in the usability of SEO research and analyses. While users still have access to all of the SEO data, they don't have to get lost in countless spreadsheets, filters, tabs, etc. Instead, it is enough to communicate their intent to their own agent. By exposing a rich set of read and write WebMCP tools, SEOstrich enables users' agents to shape analyses and strategies exactly as per their users' intent - without being limited by specific workflows that have been built or missing functionalities. The goal is one - SEO shouldn't be something distant and confusing - it should be just a tool that anybody could use to help make their business get found. How we built it The stack includes a Next.js frontend, hosted on Vercel, that registers 23 tools on document.modelContext, and a FastAPI backend that runs on Railway. Both SEO flows (content strategy and AI visibility) run as fixed code graphs where the order and gates are set in code, while the models reason about the data, decide grouping and wording. DataForSEO is used as the source of keyword insights such as term difficulty, demand, what your competitors already rank for, what people actually ask in ChatGPT and Google AI. There is per-run locking and append-only history for each generated SEO report, so that several judges can edit the same report safely. There is also an option to restore the defaults of seeded reports. The baseline project that I started with had a broken single-turn orchestrator, poor limited UI, no status streaming, no WebMCP support, no graphs for the critical parts of the SEO workflows, wasn't hosted anywhere, had drained my DataForSEO account a couple of times due to inefficient wiring. It had a half-working POC memory system that made matters even more complicated. The memory module has been fully unplugged, to allow for clear focus on the SEO + WebMCP theme. During the past 5 days, over close to 100 commits, I have tidied up the orchestrator, designed two dedicated SEO agents with full WebMCP support in mind, have worked on the UX of the system, a bit of its branding and have deployed it online. The way I built the whole thing was by using a coding assistant, thoroughly testing locally and only then pushing commits to production. Challenges we ran into the major product challenge that I ran into, while building SEOstrich, was how to design the role of chat vs. the final produced SEO artefact (a report, a strategy doc). Initially they felt disconnected from one another, so I made the following choice - the artefact is the center of the system, not chat. This product helps you make strategic and tactical decisions about your SEO work. You do start building an SEO strategy in the chat, but then the artefact starts shaping in front of you. You don't depend on the already built agent in SEOstrich - you have full control to steer it at every step of the way - but the final output, the sole reason why you are using SEOstrich in the first place remains at the center of the experience - not the chat. while building the product, during the first couple of days I used Qwen Code and the Qwen models, as I wanted to get a better feel for them. First, I suffered from significant latency in LLM calls and second, I tried testing using my Qwen token plan instead of the Cloud plan (indeed an unintended use) which resulted in a range of implementation that I didn't need and made a bigger mess of an already messy foundation that I started with. Additionally the most powerful Qwen model wasn't always able to plan things properly with me, so that we get things resolved - it missed the goal for the specific tactical decisions. This was a very painful experience, partly self-inflicted, but still painful. How I solved this was to move all agent execution to the gpt-5.6-Sol and Terra models, which reduced latency incomparably and used a combination of Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5 for the development and gpt-5.6-Sol for visuals. Accomplishments that we're proud of have reduced my DataForSEO budget drain significan

title: ShipCheap
pitch: Project-aware backend hosting decisions without billing jumpscares—powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Project-aware backend hosting decisions without billing jumpscares—powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Choosing a backend host looks simple until a developer has to reconcile runtime support, database needs, region availability, credit-card requirements, sleeping services, free-tier limits, and surprise usage bills. Most comparison pages make people translate one real project into dozens of filters and pricing tables. ShipCheap began as a human-first backend hosting decision board. For the WebMCP Challenge, I turned it into a shared workspace where a person can describe or link a real project, let an agent do the repetitive analysis, and still review every important result in the same visible interface. What it does ShipCheap helps developers: rank backend hosts from runtime, budget, database, uptime, card access, region, and risk tolerance; compare providers in a visible decision table; simulate 1,000 deterministic monthly billing scenarios; inspect percentiles, budget-overrun probability, and likely cost spikes; review provider-specific launch checks; sign in and link a public GitHub repository by URL; approve a read-only GitHub App for private repositories; detect a repository's stack and save project-specific hosting recommendations. Why WebMCP Hosting selection is structured but multi-step. Without WebMCP, an agent must guess which controls to click, scrape result cards, and reconstruct application state. ShipCheap exposes eight purpose-built tools instead: open_project_workspace list_linked_projects list_available_github_repositories start_github_app_installation analyze_github_repository recommend_backend_hosts open_backend_host_comparison preview_billing_risk The agent can turn plain-language constraints into ranked recommendations, open the exact comparison or simulator, and—after the user chooses a repository—build a project-aware analysis. The person and agent share the same visible state throughout. Human control and data protection The agent advises and configures; it cannot silently create an account, approve GitHub access, attach billing, spend money, or deploy infrastructure. Private repository access uses a read-only GitHub App. Project reads and writes are authorized server-side against the signed-in Clerk user ID, and the database enforces repository and installation constraints. How I built it ShipCheap is a Next.js 16 App Router application written in TypeScript and React, styled with Tailwind CSS, and deployed on Vercel. Prisma stores data in PostgreSQL on Neon. Clerk provides authentication, and a GitHub App provides read-only repository access. The WebMCP layer lives in src/components/WebMCPTools.tsx and registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool uses a strict JSON Schema, validates inputs during execution, cleans up registrations with an AbortController , and returns concise structured results. The integration is progressive enhancement: the site and public decision workflow still work when WebMCP or authentication is unavailable. What I changed during the challenge ShipCheap existed before the challenge. During the submission period I added the eight-tool WebMCP layer, expanded the provider catalog and comparison surfaces, connected the tools to the existing recommendation and billing-risk logic, added Clerk authentication, created the project workspace, integrated the read-only GitHub App, added repository stack detection and project-specific recommendations, migrated persistence to Neon PostgreSQL, documented the public testing flow, and verified all eight tools on the deployed app in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Challenges The hardest design problem was deciding where agent authority should stop. A hosting assistant that can silently install integrations, deploy, or spend money would be risky, so ShipCheap keeps approval and consequential actions with the person. The second challenge was maintaining one source of truth. WebMCP tools reuse the same provider data, recommendation functions, repository analyzer, and billing simulator as the visible UI instead of maintaining a separate agent-only model. Accomplishments A working deployed product rather than a WebMCP-only proof of concept. Eight non-trivial tools spanning public decisions and authenticated project analysis. Visible shared state between human navigation and agent actions. Repository-aware recommendations for public and approved private GitHub projects. Strict validation, server-side ownership checks, and explicit safety boundaries. A public MIT-licensed repository with reproducible setup instructions. What I learned Useful agent-native design is less about exposing many actions and more about exposing the right decision boundaries. Structured tools compress repetitive analysis, while visible state and explicit approval keep consequential choices understandable and human-controlled. What's next Next steps include live pricing-source verification, richer project reports, additional providers, and deeper authenticated end-to-end testing. These are future directions, not claims about the current submission. title: StrategyShifu
pitch: Instead of asking users to navigate pricing pages, compare capabilities, and manually piece together trade-offs, StrategyShifu exposes structured decision workflows through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Instead of asking users to navigate pricing pages, compare capabilities, and manually piece together trade-offs, StrategyShifu exposes structured decision workflows through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Complex cloud architecture and migration decisions are rarely solved by a single recommendation. Teams need to compare costs, technical constraints, operational trade-offs, and implementation risks before committing to a strategy. We built StrategyShifu to explore a better model for human–agent collaboration: an AI agent that can work directly with a live decision-making application through WebMCP, while the user can see every change, review the reasoning, and make the final decision. What it does StrategyShifu is a WebMCP-powered decision workspace for cloud cost planning and data-platform migration strategy. The current version supports two decision workflows: Databricks cost planning: Configure DWH, ETL, and development workloads and compare compute strategies using regional pricing, schedules, networking requirements, Databricks Genie compatibility, and project budgets. Redshift-to-Databricks migration planning: Compare Iceberg coexistence, Lakehouse Federation, UNLOAD to S3, and JDBC-based migration strategies using workload characteristics, downtime tolerance, synchronization plans, target formats, and execution readiness. Through WebMCP, an agent can inspect the current project, modify inputs, test alternatives, calculate costs, compare strategies, and explain the recommendation. Every agent action is reflected immediately in the interface, allowing the user and the agent to work from the same decision context. How we built it StrategyShifu is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. WebMCP forms the interaction layer between the application and browser-based AI agents. We followed several WebMCP best practices: Registered focused, task-oriented tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Designed tools around user goals instead of exposing low-level UI actions. Used clear tool names, descriptions, and input schemas. Added runtime validation for agent-provided inputs. Returned both human-readable text and structured content. Included tool annotations to communicate read-only and mutating behavior. Used AbortSignal cleanup to prevent duplicate or stale tool registrations. Kept tool operations deterministic and safe. Used stable identifiers for selecting and updating workloads. Returned updated state after mutations so agents can continue without scraping the page. Provided clear errors and recovery guidance for invalid operations. Gracefully preserved the human interface when WebMCP was unavailable. Most importantly, WebMCP tools and human controls operate on the same React state. There is no separate agent-only state or hidden decision model. The application currently exposes: 17 WebMCP tools for workload configuration, pricing, cost estimation, strategy comparison, and recommendation retrieval. 7 WebMCP tools for migration inputs, capability evidence, and Redshift-to-Databricks assessment. The recommendation engines remain deterministic and catalog-driven. The agent explores and configures scenarios, while the application owns calculations, validation, compatibility gates, scoring, and ranking. Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges was designing a WebMCP tool surface that represented meaningful decision operations rather than browser automation. For example, instead of asking an agent to find and click several form fields, StrategyShifu provides tools such as add_workload , set_budget , compare_strategies , and get_recommendation . This makes agent interactions more reliable, understandable, and reusable. Another challenge was synchronizing agent actions with human interactions. We solved this by connecting WebMCP tools directly to the same state update functions used by the visible interface. We also had to balance agent flexibility with predictable recommendations. Agents can explore many scenarios, but technical compatibility, budget enforcement, pricing calculations, and migration scoring must remain reproducible and auditable. Finally, migration decisions depend on evolving platform capabilities. We introduced structured capability evidence with documented-source links and a fallback mechanism so temporary documentation failures do not prevent an assessment. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that StrategyShifu demonstrates WebMCP as a foundation for genuine collaboration rather than a collection of isolated agent commands. Key accomplishments include: A shared live workspace where humans and agents operate on the same state. 24 task-oriented WebMCP tools across cost and migration planning. Structured tool responses that support multi-step agent workflows. Runtime input validation and actionable error messages. Safe tool registration with lifecycle cleanup. Deterministic and explainable recommendation engines. Full-project cost analysis across multiple workloads. Explicit Pass/Fail gates for budget and technical requirements. Transparent DBU and infrastructure cost breakdowns. Migration strategy scoring, alternatives, risks, and readiness evaluation. Suggested implementation steps and production cutover checks. Structured technical evidence supporting migration assessments. Share, copy, CSV, and Print/PDF export options. Responsive views for desktop and mobile users. The agent does not simply summarize information. It can actively construct, modify, and evaluate a decision alongside the user. What we learned We learned that WebMCP works especially well for applications with structured state, repeatable workflows, and multiple possible decision paths. Giving agents semantic tools is more dependable than asking them to infer application state from the visual interface. Structured inputs and outputs also make multi-step reasoning easier to validate and debug. We also learned that agentic interaction should be separated from business logic. WebMCP provides the agent with controlled access to the application, while deterministic engines remain responsible for calculations and recommendations. Finally, transparency is essential. Users are more likely to trust an agent-assisted recommendation when they can see the inputs, understand the failed requirements, compare alternatives, and reproduce the result themselves. What's next for StrategyShifu Our next goal is to turn StrategyShifu into a broader multi-platform strategy workspace. Planned improvements include: Add more migration strategies across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Support additional source and target platforms, including Snowflake, BigQuery, Synapse, PostgreSQL, and other data warehouses. Add cross-platform compute and architecture comparisons. Expand WebMCP tools into guided multi-step planning workflows. Add migration phase tracking and implementation checklists. Allow organizations to add their own policies, pricing agreements, and decision criteria. Our long-term vision is for StrategyShifu to become a WebMCP-powered strategy layer across platforms—helping people and agents evaluate complex technology decisions together with transparency, consistency, and control.
