title: TagTitan Listing Studio
pitch: A listing studio for print-on-demand sellers where the agent presses the same buttons you do, in the same grid, with every action visible and overridable.
about_excerpt: A listing studio for print-on-demand sellers where the agent presses the same buttons you do, in the same grid, with every action visible and overridable. Like Comment Story Updates The grid, and the activity log that stamps every action as agent or human. Inspiration A print-on-demand seller with forty designs does the same chore forty times, multiplied by every marketplace they sell on. Etsy allows a 140 character title and 13 tags. Amazon Merch allows 60 characters, no price claims, and two bullets. Redbubble wants 15 tags of up to 30 characters each. The work is not creative. It is compliance, and it eats a day. Handing it to an AI has always meant choosing between two bad options. Either the agent described what to write and the seller pasted forty listings by hand, or the seller handed an opaque tool their credentials and hoped. One is dictation. The other is abdication. Neither is collaboration. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP changes the shape of the problem, because the tools live on the page the seller is already looking at. The studio is a grid. Designs down the side, marketplaces across the top, one listing per square. It publishes twelve tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Ask the agent to fill the grid and the squares fill in front of you. Every field stays editable. Every action, yours or the agent's, lands in the same activity log stamped with who did it. The design rule the whole project follows is that a tool is never a private back door . Each one is a thin wrapper over an action that a button in the interface also calls. One store, one set of mutations, one log. buttons (app.js) ---+ +---> studio.js ---> live TagTitan API tools (webmcp.js) --+ | +---> one grid, one activity log That symmetry is what makes the collaboration legible. The agent cannot do anything the seller cannot see, undo, or do themselves. How it creates a better user experience The seller never leaves the page, never pastes anything, and never loses sight of what was done on their behalf. They can interrupt at any square. A batch that would have been forty context switches becomes one instruction and a grid they supervise. It also degrades honestly. With no agent connected the studio is a complete tool you can drive by hand, and the header states plainly which mode you are in. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Supervised bulk work. "Take all four designs, do Etsy and Redbubble, premium voice." The agent calls the same actions the buttons call, and the seller watches each square resolve, fixing anything wrong in place. A critique loop against a real scorer. The agent calls grade_listing , reads back a 0 to 100 score broken into title, tags, description and readability with concrete fixes, then calls update_listing to apply one. It checks its own work against the same grader the seller sees. Marketplace rules as shared context. list_marketplaces returns live character and tag limits for 18 marketplaces, so the agent reasons about real constraints instead of guessing. Correction without restarting. "The Etsy title is too generic, make it about cottagecore." One field changes. Nothing else regenerates and no context is lost. Knowing when to stop and ask. account_status reports remaining quota, so before a large batch the agent can tell the seller to sign in rather than burning what is left. How we built it The front end is deliberately plain: no build step, no framework, no dependencies. studio.js holds all state and every mutation. app.js renders it and wires the buttons. webmcp.js registers the tools. The last two are peers, and neither can reach past the store. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "generate_listings", description: "Write full listings for products across the selected marketplaces...", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { /* ... */ } }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }); Every execute is wrapped so a thrown error becomes a readable tool error rather than a crash, and each call writes to the shared activity log before returning. The listing engine behind it is the live TagTitan API, a shipped commercial product, so the output is what real sellers actually publish rather than demo filler. The twelve tools Tool What it does read_studio Full state: products, marketplaces, listing status, scores account_status Whether the seller is signed in and how much quota remains list_marketplaces 18 marketplaces with live title, tag and content limits add_product Add a design as a new row remove_product Drop a row and its listings set_marketplaces Choose which marketplaces are columns set_tone Set the brand voice for everything generated after suggest_keywords Real buyer search phrases for a seed term generate_listings Write listings across the grid grade_listing Score a listing 0 to 100 and return fixes update_listing Rewrite one field of one listing export_csv Every finished listing as bulk-upload CSV Challenges we ran into The API restricts CORS to an allowlist. Calling it from a new origin returned 400 with no allow header. Rather than widen the allowlist we proxy /api server-side, so the browser only ever makes same-origin requests and the backend needed no change at all. That also let the session cookie ride along without any SameSite juggling. The free tier allows one listing per browser, in total. Cookie tracked, and it silently truncates a multi-marketplace request to a single marketplace. Anyone opening the site cold got one square filled and then a wall, which made the whole studio look broken. Adding sign-in fixed it, and signed in the API writes every marketplace in a single call. The backend sleeps. It runs on a free instance that takes about 23 seconds to wake. A judge whose first click hangs that long assumes the project is broken, so a scheduled function now pings it every ten minutes. What we learned The interesting constraint in WebMCP is not what the agent can do. It is what the human can still see. It would have been easier to give the agent a fast private path to the API and let the UI catch up afterwards. Everything good about this project came from refusing that and making both paths identical. What's next Unifying the studio session with the main TagTitan app, image-driven listings so a design can be dropped straight in, and pushing finished rows to marketplace APIs directly instead of exporting CSV. title: Tandem
pitch: Tandem is a spaced-repetition study board where students and AI agents share live context, improve weak topics, and build lasting study plans through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Tandem is a spaced-repetition study board where students and AI agents share live context, improve weak topics, and build lasting study plans through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Study apps remember what a student has practiced, while AI assistants are good at explaining difficult ideas. The problem is that these two sides usually do not share context. A chat assistant cannot reliably see the card on screen, understand which topics the student repeatedly misses, or make its explanation available during the next study session. I built Tandem to explore what happens when a study app and an agent work on the same persistent state instead of communicating through copied text or brittle interface automation. What it does Tandem is a working spaced-repetition study board for students and their AI agents. The student can create decks, study flashcards, reveal answers, grade recall, inspect weak topics, and follow a revision plan. Through WebMCP, an agent can directly access the structured learning state and help with the same workflow. For example, the agent can: Rank topics using real lapse counts and difficulty data Start a study session focused on the weakest material See the exact card currently on screen Check whether an earlier explanation actually improved the student’s results Replace an ineffective explanation and save the new one directly on the card Build a revision plan from the exam date and weak-topic history Request permission to remove a card without being able to approve the deletion itself Agent actions and human actions appear together in a visible activity feed, so the collaboration remains understandable rather than happening invisibly. Why WebMCP This use case needs more than an agent clicking through a website. A student should not have to repeatedly explain which deck, topic, or card they are viewing. Tandem exposes that information as typed WebMCP tools. When the student says “the card currently on screen,” the agent can call get_study_state and receive the exact card, session position, reveal state, and study progress. WebMCP also lets the agent work with durable application state. An explanation written with annotate_card becomes part of the card and remains available in future sessions instead of disappearing in a chat transcript. The tool surface changes with the application state. Tandem exposes 16 live tools on the dashboard. When a study session begins, session-specific tools such as reveal_answer , grade_current_card , queue_cards , and end_session become available, bringing the live surface to 19 tools. They are withdrawn again when the session ends. Human and agent collaboration Tandem deliberately keeps important decisions with the student. For destructive actions, delete_card does not delete anything. It creates a permission request in the interface and returns a pending result. The student sees exactly which card would be removed and how many recorded reviews would be lost. Only the student can press the confirmation button. The agent can later read the decision through get_approval , but it cannot approve its own request. This creates a clear division of responsibility: the agent can inspect, explain, organize, and propose, while the student remains responsible for studying, grading, and irreversible decisions. How I built it Tandem is built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite and deployed on Vercel. Study data is stored locally in the browser, so the project requires no account or backend. The WebMCP adapter registers tools through document.modelContext , supports contextual registration and withdrawal, and reads current application state when each tool executes. Every tool has a typed input schema, a detailed agent-facing description, structured output, and safety annotations. The app includes 20 tools covering deck inspection, card search and editing, study sessions, note-impact analysis, revision planning, interface highlighting, and human approval. Challenges One challenge was ensuring that tools never operated on stale React state. The executors therefore read the current store at call time instead of capturing an old snapshot when they are registered. Another challenge was designing a dynamic tool surface without duplicate registrations. The registry compares the tools that should currently exist with the tools already registered and changes only the difference. The most important design challenge was human approval. A simple confirm: true argument would only be the agent claiming that permission had been given. Tandem instead separates requesting, deciding, and reading the result into different actions, with the actual decision taking place in the user interface. Accomplishments I am especially proud that Tandem is a complete study product rather than a static WebMCP demonstration. The same structured tools used by the agent affect the real interface and persistent study data. The project includes automated coverage for the spaced-repetition scheduler, tool schemas, contextual tool registration, note-impact calculation, revision planning, approval boundaries, accessibility states, and an end-to-end agent simulation. What I learned Building Tandem changed how I think about agent-enabled websites. A useful tool description is not just API documentation; it explains when an agent should use the tool and where the human boundary begins. I also learned that WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes domain logic and live context that would be difficult to reconstruct from screenshots or interface automation. What’s next Next, I would add optional cross-device synchronization, richer study analytics, document-to-deck importing, and longer-term measurements of whether agent-written explanations improve retention across multiple review cycles. title: Tax Pundit
pitch: Tax Pundit lets people and browser agents turn scattered tax records into a cited, review-ready case to file tax return - while every consequential tax decision stays with the person.
about_excerpt: Tax Pundit lets people and browser agents turn scattered tax records into a cited, review-ready case to file tax return - while every consequential tax decision stays with the person. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP processes tax documents while results appear live in the shared workspace. Profile-based onboarding creates a personalized tax preparation plan. Transparent WebMCP audit trail showing every agent action and case revision. Pundit summarizes case progress, completed actions and the next review step. The agent pauses safely when mileage needs human confirmation. A clear review handoff showing preparation status and unresolved questions. Inspiration Tax filing often means sending the same income slips, receipts, mileage records and personal details to an accountant every year. The harder part is knowing what information is missing and which deductions or benefits may apply to your job, province or family situation. During the busy filing season, it is difficult for taxpayers and accountants to discuss every possible opportunity. We built Tax Pundit to make this preparation more organized and proactive. What it does Tax Pundit is a shared tax-preparation workspace for a person, their browser agent and their tax professional. It organizes records, identifies missing information, performs bounded calculations and surfaces relevant deductions, benefits, CRA forms and official guidance. Through WebMCP , a browser agent can work directly with the application using 15 structured tools . Each action produces a visible document, calculation or decision in the center workspace, while the WebMCP panel shows the live tool sequence. The agent can gather information, calculate vehicle expenses and prepare recommendations, but it cannot approve a tax treatment. Important decisions and final export remain human-controlled. The current demo uses synthetic Ontario and British Columbia cases and creates a cited, review-ready brief for a tax professional. It does not file a real return or calculate a complete refund. How we built it We built Tax Pundit with TypeScript, React, Vinext and Vite , then deployed it through ChatGPT Sites . The interface and WebMCP tools share one canonical case store, so human and agent actions always update the same information. We added strict tool schemas, profile-based workflows, official CRA references, visible agent activity and human approval controls. The project includes 40 automated tests covering all 15 WebMCP tools, calculations, invalid inputs, changed facts, approval invalidation, undo, reset and export behavior. Challenges we ran into Our main challenge was making agent activity easy to understand. Early versions looked like technical commands running in the background. We redesigned the experience so the current result stays in the user’s eye line while the WebMCP panel provides a transparent record of the supporting actions. We also had to manage shared state safely. Reading a case should not change it, while editing an important fact—such as mileage—must invalidate an earlier approval. We deliberately prevented the agent from approving decisions or filing anything. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created a complete human-agent workflow rather than only a WebMCP technical demo. Tax Pundit exposes 15 functional tools , adapts the preparation flow to different profiles, presents agent results visually and stops for human approval when judgment is required. The application is publicly available, requires no login for the demo and has a complete open-source repository with tests and setup instructions. What we learned WebMCP works best when tools have narrow responsibilities, strict inputs and clear limits. We also learned that users need to see what an agent produced—not just that a command ran. Most importantly, agentic experiences become more trustworthy when responsibilities are clear: the agent handles repetitive preparation, while the person retains control over facts and consequential decisions. What's next for Tax Pundit Next, we would support secure document uploads, OCR and confirmation of extracted information. We would also add persistent user accounts, more Canadian tax scenarios and an accountant portal for reviewing evidence, calculations and unresolved questions. The long-term goal is to make Tax Pundit a secure preparation layer between taxpayers, browser agents and tax professionals. title: WebMCP Forge
pitch: Turn existing portfolios into agent-ready WebMCP sites with one script—scan, map, install, verify, and even use WebMCP itself to build WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Turn existing portfolios into agent-ready WebMCP sites with one script—scan, map, install, verify, and even use WebMCP itself to build WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP Forge scans an existing portfolio, maps its content, lets owners choose agent capabilities, and generates one install snippet. Five-step flow: paste a portfolio URL, scan the site, choose agent capabilities, install one snippet, then verify the live runtime. WebMCP Forge itself exposes WebMCP tools, so an AI agent can scan a portfolio, change capabilities, and generate the integration. ChatGPT discovers WebMCP Forge's 8 Site Tools and uses the builder through WebMCP to update the portfolio URL live. One ChatGPT request reads the current permissions, changes multiple capabilities through WebMCP tools, then verifies the updated state. WebMCP Forge doesn't merely generate WebMCP. The Forge builder itself is an agent-operable WebMCP application. Inspiration WebMCP immediately stood out to me because it changes an important assumption about the web. Most websites are designed entirely for people. An AI agent that wants to use one usually has to interpret the page, find the right controls, and interact with the interface almost like a person would. WebMCP gives a website a much cleaner option: it can explicitly describe the useful things an agent is allowed to do. While experimenting with that idea, I realized there was still a practical problem. Adding WebMCP to an existing website is straightforward for a developer who understands the site's code, but it is a much bigger ask for someone who built a portfolio in Framer, Wix, Webflow, or another site builder. A designer should not have to learn document.modelContext , JSON Schema, CSS selectors, or tool-calling conventions just to make a portfolio usable by an agent. That became the idea behind WebMCP Forge : Point it at an existing portfolio, let it understand the site, choose what agents should be able to do, install one snippet, and verify that the integration is actually live. I chose portfolios as the first use case because they are a good example of a website that contains useful structured information but is still primarily built for human browsing. Projects, experience, skills, education, contact information, and navigation all map naturally to useful agent capabilities. What it does WebMCP Forge provides a guided five-step workflow for turning an existing portfolio into a WebMCP-enabled site. 1. Point it at your portfolio The user enters the URL of an existing portfolio. WebMCP Forge fetches the site and analyzes its structure rather than asking the user to describe how the site was built. 2. Review what was found The scanner identifies useful portfolio content such as: projects skills work experience education navigation profile information contact information The interface shows a simple summary of what was detected so the owner can verify that the site was understood correctly. 3. Choose what agents can do The site owner decides which capabilities should be available to an agent. For example: learn about me browse my projects inspect a specific project search my projects show my skills read my experience read my education share my published contact information navigate my portfolio focus a particular project on the page The normal interface deliberately avoids exposing WebMCP implementation details. A portfolio owner chooses capabilities in plain language while WebMCP Forge handles the underlying tool definitions. 4. Install one snippet WebMCP Forge generates a small script tag that can be added to the website once. The runtime loads the site's published WebMCP configuration and registers the appropriate tools in supported browsers. The owner does not need to regenerate the integration every time a project or skill changes. The runtime reads the current live site rather than maintaining a separate copy of the portfolio content. 5. Verify the real installation I did not want the product to stop at "here is some generated code." WebMCP Forge can check the actual deployed website and report whether: the runtime is installed the configuration loaded correctly content mappings are still valid WebMCP is available in the current browser tools were registered projects, skills, experience, and education can still be found on the live site This gives the owner a concrete answer to a much more useful question: Is my website actually agent-ready? Why WebMCP fits this use case A portfolio already has two audiences. The first is a person who wants to look around the site normally. The second can now be an agent trying to answer a question such as: Which of this person's projects demonstrate backend development? Without WebMCP, the agent has to derive that information from the visual website or page structure. With WebMCP, the portfolio can expose a small set of intentional capabilities such as: list_projects get_project search_projects get_skills get_experience The portfolio remains the same website for a human visitor, while an agent gets a structured interface designed specifically for the task. Some tools can also affect what the human sees. For example, focus_project can bring a requested project into view instead of only returning text to the agent. That is the part of WebMCP I found most interesting: the agent and the person can work with the same live interface rather than having separate copies of the application. Use WebMCP to build WebMCP One feature I particularly wanted to include was making WebMCP Forge itself WebMCP-enabled . A compatible agent does not have to operate the builder by guessing where its buttons and switches are. The builder exposes its own tools for actions such as: setting a portfolio URL starting a scan reading the scan result reviewing available capabilities enabling or disabling a capability generating the installation checking verification status That means a user can work with an agent to configure WebMCP for another website. For example, the user could say: Scan my portfolio. Then: Do not expose my contact information. Then: Generate the integration. The corresponding WebMCP Forge interface changes as those tool calls occur. So WebMCP is both what the product generates and part of the interface used to generate it . How we built it WebMCP Forge is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui. The backend performs a bounded scan of a public portfolio rather than crawling the entire web. The scanning pipeline has two stages. Deterministic site analysis The first stage uses normal parsing and extraction to inspect things such as: page metadata headings navigation links repeated DOM structures semantic HTML internal routes contact links likely project collections platform fingerprints This gives the application a compact representation of the site before any model is involved. Semantic interpretation Some portfolio layouts are obvious to a person but difficult to identify from markup alone. For those cases, Google Gemini is used to interpret the extracted structure and map it onto WebMCP Forge's known portfolio concepts. The model does not generate arbitrary JavaScript for the user's website. Instead, WebMCP Forge owns a fixed capability catalogue and validates the structured result before using it. The application also has model fallback and retry handling so a scan is not tied to one model being available. Runtime The script installed on a portfolio is framework-independent browser JavaScript. It can: load the site's published configuration inspect the current page understand the active route read current portfolio content register allowed tools through WebMCP expose diagnostics for verification Normal portfolio visitors do not trigger a Gemini request when an agent calls one of these WebMCP tools. The portfolio itself remains the source of truth. Challenges we ran into Portfolio websites are not standardized The largest practical challenge was that two websites can present the same information with completely different markup. One portfolio may have a clear /projects page and semantic <article> elements, while another may be a single dynamically rendered page with generated class names. I did not want the system to depend entirely on model-generated guesses, so the scanner combines deterministic extraction with semantic interpretation. Avoiding stale portfolio data An early architectural temptation was to scan the website, copy its projects into WebMCP Forge, and have the generated tools return that stored data. That would have made the demo easier, but it would also mean the WebMCP representation became outdated as soon as the owner changed the portfolio. Instead, the configuration stores information about how to find the content , while the runtime reads the live site. title: Accessibility Repair Studio
pitch: A human-in-the-loop workspace
about_excerpt: A human-in-the-loop workspace Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Small web teams struggle to understand and fix common accessibility failures without losing human design control. Existing tools either automate too aggressively (risking design integrity) or require deep accessibility expertise. We saw an opportunity to use WebMCP's structured semantic context to let AI agents manipulate accessibility intent more reliably than visually clicking unfamiliar pages, while keeping humans in full control of every change. What it does Accessibility Repair Studio provides a four-part collaborative workspace: Left panel : Page templates and component semantic outline Center : Responsive live preview with selectable elements and viewport controls Right panel : Issue list, issue inspector, patch editor, and approval controls Bottom : Keyboard path, screen-reader-style narrative, audit comparison, and agent activity The product loop: audit → inspect an issue in context → stage a constrained repair → preview visual and semantic changes → obtain human approval → apply → test keyboard and narrative behavior → compare audits → export a patch manifest The studio includes a seeded "Field Notes" event-registration page with eight deliberate accessibility issues: unnamed icon-only navigation, skipped heading level, insufficient text contrast, form error without input relationship, positive tabindex changing focus order, ambiguous link text, unhelpful image description, and unannounced registration status. Two clean reference templates are also included. How we built it Tech Stack: React, TypeScript, and Vite for the frontend framework Next.js for deployment and server-side billing integration axe-core for documented subset of automated accessibility checks Custom deterministic checks for the seeded component model Vitest, Testing Library, and Playwright for comprehensive testing Polar for paywall and benefit entitlements Remotion for demo video rendering Architecture: Typed component schema with safe renderer (no arbitrary HTML) Versioned state reducer with patch history Safe finite repair DSL with 10 allowed operations WebMCP tool registry with state-scoped capabilities Device-local persistence and one-click reset Apple-inspired studio UI with translucent surfaces, careful typography, high-visibility focus rings, and reduced-motion support Safety Model: Preview isolation until human approval Version guards and approval token expiration Rejection of raw HTML, CSS, JavaScript, event handlers, URLs, arbitrary ARIA Finite allowlists for element, content, color, relationship, and ordering values apply_accessibility_patch registered only after visible human approval Challenges we ran into Balancing automation with human control : Designing a safe repair DSL that's powerful enough to be useful but constrained enough to prevent dangerous changes required careful iteration on the operation allowlist. WebMCP integration complexity : Implementing state-scoped tool registration where apply_accessibility_patch only appears when a preview has human approval required understanding the evolving WebMCP spec and handling edge cases like stale approvals. Truthful audit representation : Avoiding claims of complete WCAG conformance while still providing actionable insights meant carefully labeling automated results as partial checks and preserving issues requiring human judgment. Studio accessibility : The interface itself had to be keyboard accessible and pass its own core audit, which required rigorous focus management and testing. Embedded git repository : During initial commit, the studio directory had its own .git folder, which required removing it to properly commit as part of the main repository. Accomplishments that we're proud of Safe collaboration model : Successfully implemented a human-in-the-loop workflow where AI agents can suggest repairs but humans always approve before application Comprehensive tool surface : 11 WebMCP tools covering the full audit-inspect-repair-apply-compare-export loop Truthful limitations : Clear labeling of partial checks, manual-review requirements, and screen-reader narrative as approximation rather than emulator Beautiful accessible UI : Apple-inspired studio design that itself passes accessibility audits with excellent focus management Full test coverage : Vitest, Testing Library, and Playwright tests covering safety, approval, version guards, and keyboard operability Real demo : Three-minute narrated walkthrough showing the complete product loop with real screenshots Production-ready : Polar integration for paid features, admin allowlist, and static deployment configuration What we learned WebMCP's potential for accessibility : Structured semantic context allows agents to understand accessibility intent much better than visual inspection alone State-scoped tool registration : Dynamic tool availability based on UI state is a powerful pattern for safety-critical operations The importance of version guards : Approval tokens must expire on any relevant state change to prevent stale approvals Partial audit honesty : Being transparent about what automated checks can and cannot prove builds trust DSL design trade-offs : Finite operations are safer but require careful selection to remain useful Studio self-auditing : Building accessibility tools requires the tools themselves to be accessible What's next for it Additional repair operations : Expand the safe DSL to cover more common accessibility patterns More title: Agent Operations Center
pitch: An AI agent investigates a production outage — then its tool call suspends mid-execution until a human clicks Approve.
about_excerpt: An AI agent investigates a production outage — then its tool call suspends mid-execution until a human clicks Approve. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Production incidents are difficult because engineers have to investigate metrics, deployments, dependencies, and logs while customers are still affected. I was interested in the idea of letting an AI agent help investigate production incidents without giving it full control. That led me to build Agent Operations Center, where the agent investigates the problem and I stay in control of the actual fix. What it does Agent Operations Center is an incident-response control room where a human engineer and an AI agent work the same production outage together. The page exposes nine WebMCP tools the agent uses to investigate — but it cannot apply the fix itself. The agent investigates: service health against 7-day baselines, deployment timing against the incident, dependency direction for blast radius, and its own log queries. It records findings with cited evidence, so the human audits reasoning rather than a summary. The dashboard reacts live, with nobody touching the mouse. Cards highlight as it inspects them, the log panel narrows to its query, every call appears in an activity feed. The reasoning is genuinely the agent's. Tools return evidence, never conclusions — there is no "find the root cause" function. The scenario includes a decoy: a healthy service deployed more recently than the guilty one, so blaming the newest deploy gets it wrong. Then a human approval gate that is structural, not advisory. propose_remediation suspends mid-execution inside the browser until someone clicks APPROVE. The agent has no path to production — the click is what changes state, bound to the exact service and version proposed. One approval, one execution. The agent then verifies recovery and resolves the incident. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, deployed on Vercel. A simulated production backend — services, deployments, dependencies, logs, metrics — lives in an in-memory store exposed to React through useSyncExternalStore, since tool calls originate outside React and there's no render pass to hook into. Nine tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool. Five read, two write the agent's reasoning back into the UI, one gates approval, one verifies recovery. The design rule that mattered most: tools return evidence, never conclusions. There is no analyze_incident(). get_service_health returns p95Ms: 8.13× baseline and stops. The diagnosis has to happen in the model, or the demo is just a scripted animation. Challenges we ran into The API isn't documented yet. I guessed wrong three times. There's no unregisterTool — registration is one-way for the document's lifetime, so React StrictMode's double-mount collides with InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name; a window-level flag is the only guard that survives both StrictMode and Fast Refresh. And executeTool takes a RegisteredTool handle from getTools(), not a name, with arguments as a JSON string — an object throws Failed to parse input arguments. I found that by writing a probe that tried six encodings. The hardest problem wasn't technical. My rollback worked perfectly when I called it by hand, and the agent refused to call it. It would investigate, propose a plan, get approved — then ask "May I execute the rollback?" and end its turn. Assistants won't invoke destructive tools without re-confirming in chat, and no amount of rewording the tool description changed that. So I inverted it. The rollback now runs inside approvePlan — the click handler. The agent proposes; the human's click executes. That turned a limitation into the better architecture: the agent has no path to production at all. Accomplishments that we're proud of The approval gate is structural, not advisory. The agent has no path to production at all — a human's click is the only thing that changes system state, and approval is bound to the exact service and version proposed. The agent's reasoning is actually part of the workflow. The scenario includes a decoy: a healthy service deployed more recently than the guilty one. An agent that blames the newest deploy gets it wrong. Ours rules it out by combining deploy timing, service health, and dependency direction in the demo scenario. The dashboard reacts to the agent, not the mouse. Service cards highlight as it inspects them; the log panel narrows to its query. That works because the WebMCP tools run inside the page and can update the same state the dashboard displays. I documented an undocumented API. executeTool's signature, the absence of unregisterTool, and the JSON-string argument encoding are all recorded in webmcp.d.ts with the console output that proves them. ## What we learned Tool descriptions are prompts, not documentation. Writing "get valid ids from get_system_status" inside an inputSchema field is what produces tool chaining instead of the agent guessing an id and failing. Return errors, don't throw them. { error, knownIds: [...] } lets an agent self-correct on the next call. An exception dead-ends it, and a stalled agent is the fastest way to lose a demo. External state needs useSyncExternalStore. Tool calls originate outside React, so there's no render pass to piggyback on — and mutating state in place means React never re-renders and the dashboard silently goes stale. Design around the model's caution, not against it. Fighting it cost hours. Accommodating it produced a stronger safety guarantee than the one originally designed. ## What's next for Agent Operations Center More scenarios, randomized — config errors, dependency outages, resource leaks — so the agent can't pattern-match its way to the answer. Competing remedies. Restart, feature flag, and rollback all viable, so the agent has to choose the safest one rather than having only one option. Real backends behind the same tools. Swapping the simulated store for Kubernetes wouldn't change a single tool description. Policy tiers. Low-risk actions auto-approved, high-risk requiring two approvers. title: BeatScope Director
pitch: An in-browser WebMCP music workspace where AI agents can inspect timing, find visual moments, compare sections, and control playback using BeatScope’s deterministic local audio analysis.
about_excerpt: An in-browser WebMCP music workspace where AI agents can inspect timing, find visual moments, compare sections, and control playback using BeatScope’s deterministic local audio analysis. Like Comment Story Updates GIF WebMCP Director focusing and comparing measured visual ranges inside the BeatScope player. Inspiration BeatScope started from a simple problem: music visualizations often look impressive, but the timing logic behind them is usually locked inside one demo. I wanted to turn musical timing into reusable, deterministic data that could drive different visual systems — and also be understood by coding agents. The WebMCP Challenge made it possible to take that idea one step further: instead of making an agent inspect the DOM or guess how the player works, BeatScope can expose its musical state directly as structured browser tools. What it does BeatScope Director adds an in-browser WebMCP collaboration layer to BeatScope. An AI agent can inspect the loaded track, query timing and energy at any moment, read bounded musical events, find visually interesting ranges, compare sections, focus the timeline, control playback, and create loops — all inside the same player the user is watching. It currently exposes eight WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() , including: get_project_context get_state_at_time get_events find_visual_moments compare_ranges focus_range control_playback set_loop_range The agent does not receive the source audio. It works from BeatScope's already-computed analysis, while the user's normal local upload and playback workflow remains unchanged. How I built it I kept BeatScope's existing architecture and analysis pipeline intact and added WebMCP as a separate browser integration layer. Both the existing stdio MCP server and the new WebMCP Director read the same Rhythm IR and deterministic runtime, so they describe the same track with the same semantics; only the transport and lifecycle are different. The WebMCP layer is split into schemas, queries, actions, responses, and registration lifecycle code. Read-only tools are explicitly separated from tools that modify the page. Agent actions are visible in the UI and can be reversed by the user. I also built a reproducible WebMCP demo with rights-safe synthesized audio, browser smoke tests, snapshots, benchmarks, and CI coverage. Challenges The hardest part was keeping the agent useful without letting it invent musical meaning. BeatScope deliberately reports measurable facts such as beats, transients, frequency-band energy, and neutral structural repetition. It does not pretend that an onset is a kick or snare, or that a repeated section must be a verse or chorus. Another challenge was browser control. Playback actions have to respect autoplay restrictions, variable-tempo timing, cancellation, page lifecycle, and user ownership of the final state. I also wanted WebMCP to fail gracefully: if document.modelContext is unavailable, BeatScope still behaves like the normal player instead of breaking. What I learned WebMCP works best when it is not just a wrapper around buttons. The most useful tools expose the application's actual domain model. In BeatScope, that means giving the agent direct access to deterministic rhythm, structure, energy, and playback state instead of forcing it to reconstruct those concepts from the interface. I also learned that human-agent collaboration feels much safer when agent actions are visible, bounded, and reversible. The user still owns the player; WebMCP simply gives the agent a structured way to participate. title: CanvasOps
pitch: CanvasOps is a shared cloud architecture canvas where developers and AI design, analyze, and safely modify infrastructure together in real time using WebMCP
about_excerpt: CanvasOps is a shared cloud architecture canvas where developers and AI design, analyze, and safely modify infrastructure together in real time using WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates working interface 20 live tools Inspiration Cloud architecture is often designed visually on canvas-based tools, but AI usually only sees the conversation. This creates a disconnect: developers have to explain their architecture, copy configurations, and constantly switch between diagrams, cost tools, policies, and AI chats. CanvasOps was inspired by the idea that humans and AI should be able to work on the same live architecture. With WebMCP, the canvas becomes a shared workspace where both understand the same resources, connections, costs, regions, and policies. What it does CanvasOps is an agent-native cloud architecture canvas where humans and AI agents design and improve infrastructure together. Users can visually build architectures using services, databases, caches, queues, storage, gateways, load balancers, workers, authentication services, and other components. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can understand the live canvas, validate architecture decisions, analyze cost and resilience, add or modify components, connect dependencies, simulate regional failures, and suggest improvements. Important changes never happen silently. CanvasOps shows the proposed changes and their cost before execution. The user approves the plan, watches each operation happen live on the canvas, and can pause, cancel, roll back, or undo the entire change. How we built it CanvasOps is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, React Flow, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and WebMCP. We exposed 20 browser tools: 19 typed tools using @mcp-b/react-webmcp and one human-approved provision_and_pay tool using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools operate directly on the same React Flow state shown to the user. We added strict schemas, architecture fingerprints, policy validation, cost previews, approval flows, rollback, undo/redo, and an activity console that records agent actions. Cloud provisioning and x402 payment are mocked for the hackathon MVP. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making agent-driven changes feel safe instead of unpredictable. An architecture can change while an AI-generated plan is waiting for approval, so we introduced architecture fingerprints to reject stale plans. We also had to make multiple agent operations behave as one transaction: cancellation restores the original architecture, while successful execution becomes a single Undo action. Another challenge was converting free-form AI intent into predictable visual operations. We solved this using strict schemas, semantic component types, stable node references, validated connections, and deterministic layouts. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built 20 browser tools that let agents meaningfully understand and operate a live architecture canvas. Created a shared source of truth where human edits and AI actions affect the same architecture. Added human approval, cost checks, stale-plan protection, rollback, and atomic undo. Built architecture analysis for cost, connectivity, replicas, regions, failover readiness, and resilience. Created Judge Mode and a WebMCP Activity console so every agent interaction is visible and easy to demonstrate. What we learned We learned that making a website agent-native requires more than exposing simple CRUD actions. Agents need structured tools, semantic context, predictable references, and clear safety boundaries. For consequential actions, the best model is proposal and approval: AI handles analysis and planning, while the human keeps control over execution. What's next for CanvasOps Next, we want to connect CanvasOps to real infrastructure-as-code and cloud provider APIs so an approved architecture can move from design to actual deployment. We also plan to add Terraform import/export, collaborative projects, architecture versioning, richer policy systems, architecture diffs, and real signed x402 payment flows. title: CoCanvas
pitch: Chat is a bad place to move a box. You write the brief. A WebMCP agent draws on the same board. If the draft is a mess, undo it. No screenshot guessing.
about_excerpt: Chat is a bad place to move a box. You write the brief. A WebMCP agent draws on the same board. If the draft is a mess, undo it. No screenshot guessing. Like Comment Story Updates Astra from the announcement. Drawn on this board. Payment skipped. The page finds it. Try it. Link in the description. Inspiration When I try to map a product flow with an agent, the work happens in chat. I ask it to add payment between address and success. It returns a paragraph, or a table of labels. I still rebuild the diagram by hand. Exporting a PNG is not a better contract. The model infers from pixels, and I cannot undo a node. I wanted the brief and the board in the same tab, and I wanted the agent to edit that board the way I do. WebMCP is how I tried that. What it does CoCanvas is a product-flow canvas that stays in the browser. You write a brief. You and an agent add nodes, arrows, and pins to the same document. There is no account and no server. The board is stored in localStorage . Connect an agent and it receives 25 tools on that store. It can draft from the brief, connect two element ids, run a review owned by the page, and pin a note on a real node. Every change is tagged You or Agent. Undo reverts the last turn. Find the gap is the short path. The page sets a grocery-checkout brief, draws cart, address, and success, and omits payment. review_canvas reports the gap and pins it on Success. You add Payment in the UI and export a PNG. Astra from the source is the longer ChatGPT prompt. It opens the GPT-6 Astra announcement and draws a product map: a hub, four children, score bars for figures that appear on the page, and pins on what is still rolling out. If the tab has no host, the header reads Not connected. The Agent panel still runs the same tools. Once a host is connected, tool results can enter its context, and writes stay undoable either way. How I built it The tools run in the page, against the same store the UI writes to. The tools register on document.modelContext after the store loads, then navigator.modelContext , then window.modelContext . ChatGPT injects the host after first paint, so registration retries. The Agent panel uses a private polyfill that does not occupy document.modelContext , which leaves room for a late host. Availability follows board state. draft_from_brief and review_canvas require a brief. connect_elements requires two nodes. Each tool has its own AbortController . When a tool leaves the gate, that signal aborts and the host removes it. review_canvas is application code. It reads the brief, the nodes, and the connectors. It reports a missing step, an unlabeled shape, an arrow between siblings that already hang from a hub, and an arrow attached to a score bar. await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "review_canvas", description: "Page-owned review of the live board against the brief.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {}, additionalProperties: false }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, untrustedContentHint: true }, execute: () => { const report = reviewCanvas(store()); return { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(report, null, 2) }] }; }, }); Challenges I ran into The agent kept producing layouts that did not read as a diagram: a table of labels, a row of colored cards, a hub stretched across the page so every arrow could stay vertical, then a side arrow from API into Rollout that appeared to pass through the box. Those constraints now live on the page: arrows bend from a compact hub, sibling links and score-bar links are rejected, and review reports them when they slip in. Site tools failed the same way they did on Glassbook. The Microsoft Store build of ChatGPT desktop left document.modelContext undefined. The installer from the ChatGPT website worked. The connect guide now names GPT-5.6 Sol and Terra, and notes that Luna and Light do not expose site tools. What I'm proud of The Astra board is what I wanted out of this. It comes from the announcement, and it stays a map I can still edit. Find the gap is simpler, and it is the clearest proof. The page catches the missing step, pins it on the success node, and I add Payment in the UI without leaving the board. What I learned If the page does not own the review, the model will accept a table of labels as a finished board. If the last turn cannot be undone, it is hard to let the agent draft. The pin on Success did more useful work than another write tool. What's next for CoCanvas Too much of the diagram guidance still lives in the prompt. I want more of it enforced by the tools. Sharing is not built. localStorage covers one tab, which is enough for a demo and not enough for a workshop. title: CommonGround Travel
pitch: CommonGround lets an agent reconcile every traveler's budget and must-haves through 27 WebMCP tools, then select a fair hotel and prepare a human-reviewed booking draft.
about_excerpt: CommonGround lets an agent reconcile every traveler's budget and must-haves through 27 WebMCP tools, then select a fair hotel and prepare a human-reviewed booking draft. Like Comment Story Updates Codex explains trade-offs, selects a zero-violation hotel, and prepares a reviewable draft using CommonGround’s Site Tools. The agent prepares a €380 hotel draft and stops at human approval. Nothing is booked, purchased, or charged automatically. Live workspace with 27 WebMCP tools, traveler constraints, visible agent activity, conflicts, and fair hotel rankings. Inspiration Planning a group trip rarely fails because there are too few hotel options. It fails because the important details are scattered across messages and held by different people. One traveler needs step-free access. Another has a hard nightly limit. A parent needs a suitable family room. Someone else cares most about reviews, location, or a gym. The organizer ends up acting as a human spreadsheet, and the loudest preference often wins. We built CommonGround to make that negotiation explicit, fair, and inspectable. The goal is not to let an AI choose a holiday for everyone. It is to let people and an agent work on the same decision, while preserving each traveler’s constraints and keeping the final commitment with a human. What it does CommonGround is a shared hotel decision workspace for groups of up to 30 travelers. Each person has a budget, preferences, and locked must-haves. The workspace detects conflicts, normalizes hotel inventory, and scores options under three transparent strategies: Group Consensus, Best Value, and Balanced Compromise. An attached agent can use 27 WebMCP Site Tools to read the live workspace and act on it. In one request, the agent can: identify every traveler by name; read their budgets, preferences, and locked requirements; explain concrete conflicts between them; search the available hotel inventory; compare all three decision strategies; select the fairest zero-violation result; and prepare a complete booking draft for human review. In the public Lisbon demo, that flow considers Maya’s step-free requirement, Diego’s €130-per-night limit, Sana’s family-room requirement, and Leo’s higher-budget preferences. It identifies budget gaps of €80, €100, and €140, then selects Pensão Lumen at €95 per night—€380 for four nights—with zero locked must-have violations. The agent stops there. The final Approve draft button remains untouched. CommonGround has no autonomous purchase path, and the tool response reports purchaseOccurred: false . Why WebMCP is essential A screenshot or scraped page is not enough for this problem. The agent needs structured access to shared state: who owns a requirement, whether it is a preference or a lock, which hotels violate it, which scoring strategy is active, and what the agent is permitted to change. WebMCP turns the website itself into the agent interface. The agent and the travelers use the same workspace, the same scoring logic, and the same visible controls. There is no separate chatbot database that can drift away from the page. When the agent selects a scenario or prepares a draft, the board changes in front of the group and the action appears in the activity and telemetry surfaces. This replaces a multi-screen, copy-and-paste workflow with one auditable request. More importantly, it gives the agent useful power without hiding its actions or surrendering human control. How we built it CommonGround feature-detects document.modelContext and registers 27 typed Site Tools. Every tool has a strict JSON schema, read/write annotations, cancellation support, and structured success or error results. Eight read tools expose workspace identity, onboarding and collaboration state, invitations, named traveler constraints, normalized inventory, scenario comparisons, and conflict explanations. Nineteen permission-aware action tools cover workspace creation, scoped invitations, trip and capacity settings, traveler-profile changes, priorities, locks, vetoes, scenario and hotel selection, and booking-draft preparation. The tools call the same React state transitions and scoring functions as the human interface. Writes are immediately visible. Invitation tokens are scoped to a traveler and stored as hashes. Supplier responses are treated as untrusted data. There is deliberately no reservation or payment endpoint behind the draft action. The application is built with React, TypeScript, Vite/vinext, Zod, Cloudflare Workers and D1, and Codex Sites. Vitest and automated browser verification exercise the scoring, permissions, tool contracts, state synchronization, and the no-purchase safety boundary. For a reliable judging experience, the deployed challenge build uses six clearly labeled curated Lisbon hotel records. The inventory layer is provider-based, so a licensed TravelWithWadjet, Booking.com Demand, Expedia Rapid, or other hotel supplier adapter can replace the demo provider without changing the consensus model or the WebMCP interface. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering tools; it was keeping three things synchronized: the state returned to the agent, the state visible to people, and the permission boundary between reading, changing, and committing. We also had to make subjective fairness explainable. A single “best hotel” score hides who is being asked to compromise. CommonGround therefore shows individual satisfaction, hard violations, group conflicts, and the effect of each scenario rather than presenting an unexplained recommendation. Browser support for an emerging technology was another practical challenge. We added capability detection, clear connection status, deterministic demo data, strict tool outputs, and a Chrome verification path so a judge can distinguish a product problem from a missing browser capability. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that CommonGround is a complete shared product experience rather than a chatbot wrapped around a static demo. A real external Codex agent can discover 27 typed Site Tools, identify four travelers by name, explain their specific conflicts, compare three decision strategies, choose a zero-violation hotel, and prepare a human-review draft in one request. The same actions immediately update the board the travelers are looking at. We are especially proud of the safety boundary. The agent is useful enough to complete the difficult research and negotiation work, but it cannot quietly cross into a purchase. The interface shows zero autonomous purchases, the draft explicitly says that no purchase is made, and the final approval remains a deliberate human action. We also built beyond the single demo path: organizers can create private workspaces for up to 30 travelers, invite people with scoped links, configure the trip, manage priorities and locks, and follow a guided onboarding flow. Automated tests and browser acceptance checks cover the tool contracts, permissions, fairness scoring, state synchronization, and booking-draft boundary. The result is something judges can use as a coherent product, not merely inspect as a technical prototype. What we learned Agents are most useful when they can operate on the same structured state as people—not when they merely describe what appears on a page. We also learned that visible actions are a product feature, not debugging decoration. People trust an agent more when they can see what it read, what it changed, why it made a recommendation, and where its authority ends. What's next for CommonGround Travel The next step is to connect licensed live hotel inventory through the provider adapter and carry the same model into flights, itineraries, and group expense decisions. The larger opportunity is a reusable negotiation layer for any shared decision where several people have different constraints and an agent should help without taking control away from them. title: CommonMesh
pitch: Human-approved community coordination through structured WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Human-approved community coordination through structured WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I didn’t want to build another chatbot. I wanted to see whether WebMCP could help with a messy, practical task: coordinating volunteers and shared resources for a community event. An agent can save time by comparing schedules, capacity, distance and requirements. But assigning a person or a vehicle creates a real commitment. That decision should stay with the organizer. CommonMesh is my attempt to split those responsibilities clearly. What it does CommonMesh runs one fixed demo: Saturday Community Day at Riverlight Hall in Gothenburg. The event has 7 needs and 15 possible resources. A browser agent can inspect the workspace, find compatible resources, validate a complete plan and stage it for review. The proposal then appears in the same interface the organizer is using, marked PROPOSED . If the agent tries to commit too early, CommonMesh returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED and records the failed attempt in the activity trail. The organizer can review the assignments and approve that exact plan. Only then can the agent commit it. The demo then breaks the plan on purpose by making the assigned van unavailable. CommonMesh flags that assignment without making everything else look broken. The repair keeps 7 existing assignments and replaces 1. Why WebMCP CommonMesh registers 9 browser tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Seven are read-only. The two write tools can stage a proposal and commit an approved plan. There is no WebMCP tool for approving a proposal, resetting the demo or changing resource availability. Those actions stay in the human interface. The agent receives stable resource IDs, strict input schemas and structured errors instead of trying to infer state from page text or screenshots. The tools and the interface use the same CoordinationStore , so the organizer can immediately see what the agent proposed, what failed and what was committed. How I built it The app uses React, TypeScript and Vite. A shared domain layer checks availability, timing, capacity, distance, licences and double-booking. Approval is tied to the normalized assignments and current workspace revision with a SHA-256 digest. Before committing, CommonMesh calculates the digest again and validates the plan against the latest state. Reloading the page also clears pending approval, so it must be given again. A late code review found a persistence edge case where an inconsistent saved state could lose its commit history. I tightened the loader and added regression tests for approvals, rejected repairs and completed repairs. The final suite has 57 tests and runs in GitHub Actions. I used OpenAI Codex throughout the project for implementation, UI iteration, testing, review, documentation and demo production. The app itself does not embed a model or require an API key. Runtime AI comes from the browser agent using WebMCP. ElevenLabs Eric v2 was used only for the English video narration. What I learned Structured agent tools are boring in a good way. The agent knows what operations exist and what data they require. The application still decides what is valid, and the person can see exactly where their approval is needed. The hardest part wasn’t finding a matching van. It was making approval mean “this exact plan” rather than “whatever plan happens to exist when the agent commits.” Current limits CommonMesh is a client-side prototype with fixed demonstration data. It does not yet have user accounts, server-side authorization, multi-user synchronization or live community-resource integrations. The next step would be moving the trust boundary to a server and testing the workflow with real organizers and real data. title: Counterparty
pitch: Let AI agents negotiate with competing sellers—while humans control the final deal.
about_excerpt: Let AI agents negotiate with competing sellers—while humans control the final deal. Like Comment Story Updates homepage Inspiration Most shopping assistants stop after recommending a product. But for many purchases, finding the product is only the beginning. People compare several sellers, look at price, warranty, delivery, and reputation, and sometimes negotiate for better terms. This work is repetitive, so it is a good fit for an AI agent. But the final purchase is still an important human decision. That led me to one question: What if an agent could handle the negotiation, while the person stayed in control of the deal? That is why I built Counterparty. What it does Counterparty is an agent-native marketplace where an AI agent can: search for products using structured requirements; open negotiations with multiple sellers; submit counteroffers for price, warranty, and delivery; compare the latest offers; respond when the human changes their priorities; prepare an agreement for review. The agent cannot complete a purchase by itself. When it tries to commit an agreement before approval, Counterparty returns HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED . The human must review and approve the exact terms before the transaction can succeed. In the demo, the agent initially recommends GearFrame because it has the lowest price. The human then changes the priority to warranty. The agent compares the same offers again and recommends ForgeBook instead. This is the main idea behind Counterparty: the agent does the repetitive work, while the human provides judgment and authority. Why WebMCP Negotiation is stateful. The agent needs to understand products, sellers, offers, negotiation rounds, accepted terms, and approval status. Trying to infer all of this from buttons and page structure would be unreliable. Counterparty exposes six semantic tools through WebMCP: search_products start_negotiation submit_counteroffer get_negotiations prepare_agreement commit_agreement These are real product capabilities, not instructions for clicking the interface. Each tool uses a strict JSON Schema. Tool calls update the same application state shown in the human interface and activity feed. How I built it I built Counterparty with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The application has three main domain layers: A catalog service for products and public seller information. A deterministic negotiation engine for offers, counteroffers, acceptance, rejection, and negotiation rounds. An agreement service for preparation, approval, integrity checking, and commitment. Each seller has a different private negotiation policy. This creates meaningful tradeoffs between price, warranty, delivery, and reputation. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same domain services. This means an action performed by the agent immediately appears in the interface. For the approval boundary, Counterparty creates a fingerprint of the exact agreement terms. If those terms change after approval, the approval becomes invalid. The marketplace data and final transaction are simulated so the demo remains reliable. The WebMCP tools, negotiation flow, shared state, recommendations, and approval checks are real. Challenges I faced The hardest challenge was deciding what the agent should and should not be allowed to do. I wanted the agent to be useful enough to negotiate independently, but not powerful enough to make an important purchase without the user. Another challenge was keeping the human interface and WebMCP actions synchronized. I solved this by making both surfaces use the same catalog, negotiation, recommendation, and agreement logic. I also needed the demo to be reproducible. Real seller integrations could fail or return unpredictable results, so I created deterministic seller strategies that still produce different and meaningful outcomes. Finally, I had to design tools around business actions instead of page actions. A tool such as submit_counteroffer is much more useful to an agent than a tool such as “click the counter button.” What I learned Building Counterparty changed how I think about web applications. A website designed for agents needs more than a good visual interface. It also needs a clear capability interface, structured state, useful errors, and explicit authority boundaries. I also learned that human-agent collaboration becomes more valuable when the two participants have different responsibilities. The agent is good at repeated comparison and negotiation. The human is better at deciding which tradeoff matters and whether the final deal should happen. Accomplishments I am proud of Six working semantic WebMCP tools Parallel, stateful seller negotiations Recommendations that respond to human preference changes A visible activity trail for agent and human actions Human approval required before commitment Approval invalidation when terms change A complete deployed product rather than only a technical demo 18 automated tests covering the critical flow What's next The next step would be connecting Counterparty to real businesses that expose negotiation capabilities through WebMCP. The same model could eventually support electronics, travel, vehicles, freelance contracts, subscriptions, and business procurement. A production version would also add authenticated users, durable server-side state, real seller integrations, inventory reservation, and payment processing. title: Countersign
pitch: Your agent drafts. You countersign. A WebMCP billing ledger an agent can really work - but sending an invoice or marking one paid stops for your approval first.
about_excerpt: Your agent drafts. You countersign. A WebMCP billing ledger an agent can really work - but sending an invoice or marking one paid stops for your approval first. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A billing ledger is the one place where "let the agent do whatever it wants" is not an acceptable default. An agent that drafts an invoice is useful. An agent that sends one, or marks one paid , on its own authority is a financial incident waiting to happen. Today freelancers get one of two bad options: keep the agent out of billing entirely, or give it the same access a human has and simply trust it. Countersign is the third option - your agent drafts, you countersign. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The baseline value is obvious: instead of an agent scraping a DOM and hoping the button it clicked was the right one, the site declares an explicit, typed contract. For money, "hoping" is not a strategy. But the deeper fit is a gap in the platform. The published WebMCP IDL has no confirmation or consent primitive. requestUserInteraction() appears in Chrome's own tool-security guidance as a draft idea, but it does not exist in the published spec - I checked the IDL, and cross-party consent management is still an open discussion . So an agent-native app that touches money has to answer that question itself, today, using only the primitives that do exist: AbortSignal , annotations , and ordinary application state. Countersign is a concrete answer rather than a wait for the platform to catch up. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Hand an agent real financial authority while keeping a hard, site-owned veto on the two steps that actually move money. The agent can read the ledger, draft invoices, edit drafts, add clients, schedule reminders, chase late payers, and log client replies - on its own. Sending an invoice and marking one paid always stop and ask. That trade-off barely exists today; it's normally all-or-nothing. Two mechanisms make it inspectable rather than a trust exercise: 1. Tiered confirmation. send_invoice raises a light, single-screen approval - sending is routine. mark_invoice_paid always raises a heavier one, and if the amount the agent reports doesn't match the invoice, the approve button stops saying "Approve" and instead says "Accept $2,400 instead of $3,000." You cannot wave the mismatch through without reading it. Decline, and the tool returns a plain DECLINED - ... string instead of throwing, so the agent reports back honestly rather than silently retrying. 2. Untrusted-content quarantine. Client replies are third-party text arriving as ordinary business data - a perfect prompt-injection vector. log_client_reply and read_client_replies both carry untrustedContentHint , and every reply runs through a pattern scanner ( ignore previous , disregard , system: , mark ... as paid , you are now , override , and similar). A flagged reply is stored, never dropped , but rendered with a visible amber "Quarantined - not acted on" badge listing exactly which patterns matched - and the tool's own return string tells the agent plainly: this is data, not instructions. Three layers of defence: the protocol annotation, the in-band tool response, and the human-visible badge. How it creates a better user experience The confirmation isn't a modal that nags you - it's the only place the agent can't proceed, and it shows you the exact amounts before anything happens. Every gated call, every decline, and every quarantined reply lands in a live activity feed and tool-call console, so the agent's work is auditable after the fact instead of taken on faith. It also works with or without an agent. The invoice panel has human Your actions buttons that dispatch the same reducer actions the WebMCP tools dispatch, carrying actor: 'human' instead of 'agent' - identical guards, identical audit log, attributed separately. Open it in a plain browser and it's still a working billing desk. How I implemented WebMCP The Imperative API directly - no third-party wrapper library. 11 tools , registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . StrictMode-safe registration. registerTool rejects with InvalidStateError on a duplicate tool name rather than replacing (confirmed in the spec's own algorithm steps), so React's double-invoke would break naive registration. A fresh AbortController is created inside each effect pass and only ever aborts its own registrations. No stale closures. Tools are built once and read live state through a ref, so a tool registered at mount never sees a frozen ledger. Abort-aware confirmation broker. The gated tools park on an in-page requestConfirmation() that settles on human approval, human decline, or the tool's own AbortSignal firing - an aborted agent call can never leave a dialog hanging and deadlock later calls. Annotations used deliberately: readOnlyHint: true on reads, explicit false on writes, untrustedContentHint on both tools that carry client-written text. Chrome's character budgets respected - every tool name <= 17 chars (limit 30), every description <= 196 (limit 500), every parameter <= 61 (limit 150), and outputs clamped to 1.5K. No backend, no auth, no database: one reducer is the only place ledger data mutates, persisted to localStorage . Both the human path and every agent tool dispatch through it. Challenges I ran into useSyncExternalStore compares snapshots by reference, so returning a freshly-mapped array from getSnapshot sent React into "Maximum update depth exceeded." The snapshot is now recomputed only when the queue actually changes. The tool-call log went silently empty in development: a tool's execute() closes over the logger at registration time while the console subscribes at render time, so Vite HMR re-instantiating the module left registered tools writing into an orphaned copy. Anchoring the store to globalThis makes both halves agree however many times the module is evaluated. A hand-written -webkit-backdrop-filter made Lightning CSS ship only the prefixed property - which current Chrome doesn't support - so the frosted UI silently did nothing. Removing the manual prefix let the compiler emit both. What I learned - and the limit worth naming An in-page checkpoint can be clicked by an agent that also drives the browser. Approval now requires a trusted event, so script-dispatched clicks ( button.click() from a content script or console) are refused. But an agent acting at the input layer via CDP or WebDriver produces clicks indistinguishable from a human's by design , and no page-level code can close that gap. That's not a footnote - it's the argument. In-page consent gets you real, inspectable protection against the realistic threats: a confused agent, an over-eager one, and injected instructions arriving as client data. Going further requires a browser-mediated prompt that a page can request and no page-level actor can synthesise - exactly the requestUserInteraction() primitive WebMCP still lacks. Countersign shows how far in-page consent can go, and precisely where the platform has to take over.
