title: Dispatch
pitch: A shared decision memo for an ad account. Agents file findings through the page's own WebMCP tools — every claim must cite a number, and the number is verified before the finding lands.
about_excerpt: A shared decision memo for an ad account. Agents file findings through the page's own WebMCP tools — every claim must cite a number, and the number is verified before the finding lands. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every week, somebody writes the memo for each ad account. It is asymmetric work: a media buyer can tell in seconds whether a reading is plausible, but pulling the numbers that justify it across five campaigns and thirteen ad sets is an afternoon. An agent is the reverse — it reads every line instantly, but it has nowhere to put what it finds, and no way to be held to the numbers it quotes. Today that gap is bridged by copy-paste. The agent writes a summary in a chat window, the buyer retypes the useful parts into a document, and the link back to the specific metric is lost on the way. That matters more than it sounds: "CPM is climbing in Creative Testing" is worth nothing if nobody can check it, and a memo full of unverifiable claims is worse than no memo, because people act on it. What it does Dispatch is a room built around one shared decision memo for one ad account. Open it, send the link to a colleague, and both of you — plus any agent driving either browser — work the same memo live. Agents call file_finding , and the finding appears in the memo as a claim with a citation you can click through to the numbers behind it. The claim is verified before it lands. file_finding re-reads the cited metric from the account and refuses the finding if the value is wrong. An agent that cannot point at the number does not get to make the claim. A human accepts or dismisses each finding. Dismissed findings stay visible, struck through, with the reason — so next week's memo can be read against this week's argument. Press Send the analyst team and three agents join: an Analyst files findings with citations, a Skeptic rules on each one, and a Strategist files what happens Monday. In a real run the Skeptic dismissed a rip-current claim as "single-period snapshot; cannot verify a rising CPM trend" , and accepted a scale recommendation on evidence of 8.40x ROAS and $10.27 CPA. Two agents disagreeing in front of the person who has to act — that argument had no natural home on the web before. How we built it A useWebMcpTool hook wraps document.modelContext.registerTool : one tool per component lifetime, registration tied to an AbortController so unmounting unregisters, and execute held in a ref so tools read current state without re-registering on every render. Ten tools are registered from src/components/memo-tools.tsx — get_account_summary , get_breakdown , check_metric , file_finding , set_finding_status , read_memo , dispatch_analyst_team , set_focus , join_room , list_participants . The UI and the tools call the same endpoints, so a number an agent cites is the number on the buyer's screen, not a second implementation that can drift. Shared room state lives in Upstash Redis. Because judges cannot connect a Meta ad account, the room runs on a seeded deterministic account — 5 campaigns, 13 ad sets, 28 days — shaped so each situation in the taxonomy actually occurs. Every visitor sees identical numbers, which is what makes a citation checkable. Challenges we ran into Concurrency was the real one. Modelling the room as a single JSON document with compare-and-set lost 4 of 10 concurrent writes in testing. Splitting the state into separate Redis structures — RPUSH for findings — held 20 parallel writes from three agents. Safety was the other. There is no free-form query tool, so a steered agent has no vocabulary beyond the fixed shapes; campaign names written by people outside the buyer's organisation are fenced in guillemets so the model reads them as data, never instruction; every tool validates its own input; and nothing writes to an ad account. Accomplishments that we're proud of Fabrication is refused, not caught later. A finding citing a CPM of $4.10 when the real figure is $20.88 is rejected with the true number, at the moment it is filed. What we learned Putting the tools in the page changes what an agent is for. A conventional MCP server can fetch these metrics; it cannot put a finding in front of you, take your verdict, and let a second agent argue with it. What's next for Dispatch A live Meta Marketing API connection behind the same tool surface, so the citation check runs against a real account; and memo history, so this week's argument is read against last week's. title: Duet
pitch: A local-first piano roll where people and AI compose together through safe, visible, undoable WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A local-first piano roll where people and AI compose together through safe, visible, undoable WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Duet lets people sketch music while an AI agent reads the live session, adds deterministic harmony or bass, and explains every reversible change. Inspiration Music software can be powerful but intimidating: theory vocabulary, dense interfaces, and opaque “AI generate” buttons often put the person outside the creative loop. I wanted to explore a different interaction: what if an AI agent could work inside a music editor, see the same live project as the person, and make small musical changes that stay understandable and reversible? That became Duet. What it does Duet is a local-first, browser-based piano-roll editor for collaborative human–AI composition. A person can draw notes, play from a MIDI keyboard or computer keyboard, set chords, select bars, and hear the result. In a compatible browser, ChatGPT/Codex discovers Duet’s WebMCP site tools directly from the page. The agent can then: Read a concise summary of the live project or the exact selected notes. Analyze harmony deterministically. Set a chord progression with validated voicings. Add precise notes or generate bass, counter-melody, and pad material. Quantize, humanize, transpose, or remap a selected phrase. Change tempo and instruments. Create auditionable drafts and alternatives instead of silently overwriting music. Verify the resulting state after every action. Every persistent AI edit appears in the app with a plain-language explanation and a one-click Undo action. How I built it Duet is a client-only React + TypeScript app powered by Vite and Zustand. The editor uses Pointer Events so drawing, dragging, stretching, and erasing notes work across mouse, touch, and pen input. Musical rules are deterministic rather than model-generated. I use Tonal for chord and scale logic, Tone.js for browser playback, and @tonejs/midi for MIDI export. Optional Web MIDI support allows class-compliant keyboards to control the editor. For WebMCP, Duet registers narrow site tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools read the current browser state, validate every mutation, and create serializable inverse patches. That makes changes inspectable, reproducible, and undoable without a backend, API key, account, or cloud project storage. Browser and MIDI constraints A practical constraint shaped the product flow: ChatGPT/Codex’s built-in browser can discover and call WebMCP site tools, but it does not expose a connected physical MIDI device to the page in the same way a regular Chrome session can. I designed Duet around a shared live-session model to bridge that gap. The musician can open Duet in a WebMCP-enabled Chrome session, connect and play a MIDI keyboard there, while ChatGPT/Codex accesses the same live project through the connected WebMCP session. The agent does not need direct MIDI hardware access: it reads the resulting notes and project state, then proposes or applies visible, undoable musical edits. This separation keeps the human performance layer local and hardware-friendly while preserving the agent’s ability to collaborate through the browser. Challenges I ran into The core challenge was not simply generating musical material—it was making agent actions feel safe and legible. I designed the tools around a few principles: The agent receives compact state summaries before acting, rather than a flood of raw notes. Music theory remains in pure deterministic functions, so harmony does not depend on model guesswork. Write operations validate their inputs and preserve an inverse patch for Undo. The person can see what changed, why it changed, and which bars were affected. Drafts let the person hear alternatives before committing them. I also had to balance expressive composition tools with small, precise schemas that are useful to WebMCP clients. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A live browser session where a person and AI can compose on the same page. WebMCP tools that support both reading context and making safe musical edits. Agent-authored notes are visually distinct from human-authored notes. Every AI mutation has a human-readable explanation and one-click Undo. Deterministic harmony, voicing, bass generation, and mode transformations. No backend, authentication, analytics, API keys, or remote project storage. An end-to-end test: read a person’s notes, add accompaniment, undo it, then reapply a different arrangement through WebMCP. What I learned I learned that agentic interfaces become much more trustworthy when they expose small, contextual tools instead of treating the app as a black box. In creative software, reversibility is not a safety feature added at the end—it is part of the creative experience. Clear diffs, explicit intent, deterministic musical rules, and visible state make it easier for a person to stay in control while still benefiting from an AI collaborator. What's next for Duet Next, I would like to add richer MIDI export/import workflows, more arrangement patterns, stronger visual auditioning for draft variations, and broader browser support as WebMCP availability grows. Acknowledgements Special thanks to my wife, a pianist and piano teacher, who performs in the demo video. Her musician’s perspective, feedback, and willingness to test the human side of the workflow were essential to shaping Duet. This application would not have been possible without her. title: ELANE - Agent-Ready Fashion Shopping with WebMCP
pitch: ÉLANE lets shoppers and AI agents build an outfit from trusted product data, then create a personal concept preview without uploading the customer’s photo to the store.
about_excerpt: ÉLANE lets shoppers and AI agents build an outfit from trusted product data, then create a personal concept preview without uploading the customer’s photo to the store. Like Comment Story Updates What inspired me Online fashion shopping involves many small decisions. A customer may know the occasion, budget, size, colour, and style they want, yet still need to move between product pages, filters, the shopping bag, promotional details, and policy pages. An AI agent can help, but relying on screen navigation alone is not always reliable. The agent may have to infer product details, selected sizes, garment images, prices, and the current bag state from different parts of the interface. I wanted to create a shopping experience in which the customer and agent work with the same visible state. I was especially interested in personal outfit previews. This led to a simple idea: bring your own agent to preview your personal look . The customer can keep a full-body photo inside their own agent conversation. ÉLANE provides the agent with references to the exact garments staged on the website. A compatible image-generating agent can then create a personal outfit concept before the customer decides what to buy. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP ÉLANE uses WebMCP to give an agent structured access to the same catalog, Style Studio, shopping bag, promotions, and store policies that the customer can see. After an outfit is staged in the Style Studio, the agent can call the read-only read_look_render_kit tool. The tool returns one public garment image for every staged item, together with the selected size, garment layer, and a concise generation brief. The agent therefore does not need to guess which clothes are present by examining a screenshot. It receives structured references directly from the website and works with the same Style Studio state that is visible to the customer. The customer also does not need to upload their photo to ÉLANE. The photo stays inside the customer’s agent conversation and is never received or stored by the website. The generated image is presented as a visual concept, not as evidence of exact fit, sizing, material, proportions, texture, or drape. This demonstrates the value of WebMCP clearly: the website supplies trusted product information and controlled actions, the customer supplies their personal context, and the agent connects the two. How it creates a better user experience Instead of manually working through filters and comparing numerous products, the customer can describe the result they want in natural language. In the demo, the customer asks for a polished smart-casual outfit for OpenAI DevDay 2026 in San Francisco, with a budget of CAD 1,500. The agent searches the live catalog and stages a complete four-piece men’s outfit in size M. The selected look costs CAD 1,100 and appears in the visible Style Studio. At this stage, the shopping bag remains empty because staging an outfit is only a preview. The customer then attaches a clear full-body photo to the agent conversation and asks for a personal preview of the staged outfit. The agent calls read_look_render_kit , receives references to the four exact garments, and creates the concept inside the conversation. The customer’s photo is never sent to ÉLANE, and the shopping bag remains unchanged. After reviewing the concept, the customer makes a separate request to add the outfit to the shopping bag and apply an eligible promotional offer. The agent rechecks the staged look and current bag, adds the four items in size M, evaluates the promotion terms, and applies ATELIER15. The visible total changes from CAD 1,100 to CAD 935 after a CAD 165 discount. The demo stops before checkout. No payment is collected, and no order is placed. The agent can also read ÉLANE’s current shipping, return, refund, delivery, and promotional policies. This allows it to explain store terms accurately without leaving the shopping experience or changing the customer’s bag. What people and agents can do together The customer provides the personal part of the decision: the occasion, budget, style preference, photo, size, and final approval. ÉLANE provides structured catalog information, the current Style Studio state, exact garment references, controlled shopping actions, promotion rules, and policy information. The agent connects these two sides. It can understand the request, find compatible products, stage an outfit, create a personal concept using its own image capability, and perform only the shopping actions explicitly approved by the customer. The customer and agent share one visible working state. When the agent stages an outfit or updates the shopping bag, the customer can see the same result on the page. This workflow would be difficult to make dependable through screen navigation alone. An agent would otherwise need to infer product information, selected items, sizes, garment images, prices, and bag state from multiple parts of the interface. WebMCP provides structured results, allowing both the customer and agent to understand what was selected, what was visualized, what changed, and what still requires approval. How I built the project I built ÉLANE with React 19, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, with Codex assisting throughout development, debugging, testing, and documentation. The website functions as a complete human-operated storefront in browsers without WebMCP. Compatible clients receive an additional native, page-scoped tool layer. ÉLANE registers 22 imperative WebMCP tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool : eight read tools and fourteen write tools. These tools cover catalog discovery, natural-language search, Style Studio state, outfit staging and refinement, exact garment references, shopping-bag operations, promotions, and store policies. Each tool uses a closed input schema, side-effect annotations, runtime validation, and lifecycle cleanup. Tool handlers read or update the same React state used by the human interface, helping the agent’s response remain consistent with what the customer can see. Read operations and state-changing operations are deliberately separated. Catalog, bag, promotion, policy, and render-kit reads do not change the shopping experience. Staging an outfit changes the Style Studio but not the bag. Adding products or applying a promotion requires a separate, explicit customer request. The automated verification suite checks all 22 storefront registrations, the two policy-route registrations, 20 output-budget boundary fixtures, and one generated preview asset for every product in the 88-item catalog. It also runs TypeScript validation, linting, WebMCP contract checks, and a production build. Challenges I faced The first challenge was keeping the Style Studio and shopping bag separate. A visual preview should never quietly become a purchase action. I designed the flow so that staging and refining an outfit are safe and reversible, while bag and promotion changes require clear customer intent. The second major challenge was personal image generation. There are many possible garment combinations, but I did not want the website to collect customer photos. I addressed this by creating the read-only read_look_render_kit tool. It returns references to the exact staged garments, allowing the customer’s own compatible agent to use those references with a photo already present in the conversation. Another challenge was natural-language catalog search. Customers do not always use exact product names. I added ranked search, aliases, stop-word handling, optional collection and price filters, and deterministic pagination to make product discovery more reliable. I also had to keep tool results compact enough for dependable agent reasoning. The implementation uses bounded responses and output-budget checks while still providing enough information for the agent to verify that it has reached the end of a result set. What I learned I learned that WebMCP works best when it improves an existing website instead of replacing it. Customers should still be able to browse normally, while agents receive structured tools for the same visible experience. I also learned that tool boundaries are as important as tool capabilities. Reading information, creating a preview, changing the shopping bag, applying a promotion, and beginning checkout should not be combined into one operation. Customers need to understand what changed and what still requires their approval. Another important lesson concerned privacy. Personalisation does not always require sending private information to every website involved in a workflow. In ÉLANE, the customer’s photo can remain with their chosen agent while the boutique provides only the selected garment references. Finally, I learned that smaller and more specific tool outputs make agent behaviour more reliable. title: FinalPick
pitch: FinalPick turns human choices between AI generated text and image option into reusable decision memory, while 6 WebMCP tools help agents prepare reviews without taking final authority away from people
about_excerpt: FinalPick turns human choices between AI generated text and image option into reusable decision memory, while 6 WebMCP tools help agents prepare reviews without taking final authority away from people Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI gives creative teams more options than ever, but the reasoning behind a final choice often disappears in chat, spreadsheets, or handoff notes. The next teammate or model sees the result without knowing the brief, rejected alternatives, or why the decision made sense at that moment. We built FinalPick around a question raised by agentic browsing: how can an agent reduce review work without quietly taking over human judgment? What it does FinalPick is a browser-based decision workspace for reviewing actual text and image candidates. Each round contains one medium, a brief, constraints, and evidence, so options are compared on equal terms. A person selects a candidate, records reasons and an optional note, and saves that context as decision memory. In later rounds, FinalPick requires a current assessment before revealing compatible past decisions as useful, non-binding precedent. Six WebMCP tools let an agent inspect the review and candidates, retrieve precedent, and stage a comparison or follow-up question in the same visible interface. The agent can commit only after a person creates a short-lived, one-time approval in the page. How we built it We built FinalPick as a static top-level web app using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules, with localStorage for versioned rounds, staged work, and decisions. When a browser exposes document.modelContext.registerTool , the page registers six narrow WebMCP tools; without it, the complete human workflow still works. Tool schemas reject extra fields, read tools are annotated as read-only, and UI actions and tool handlers share the same validated state layer. We used Codex in a recursive improvement loop: define a small slice, implement it, run unit and Playwright browser checks, inspect responsive captures and UX feedback, then use those findings to shape the next slice. This loop expanded the prototype from built-in image examples to user-created text and HTTPS-image rounds while preserving the authority boundary. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making WebMCP essential rather than decorative. A chat recommendation alone would not improve the product, so agent work had to appear visibly in the review and reduce copying between systems. We also had to make chained tool calls reliable by returning the candidate, analysis, decision, and approval identifiers needed by later calls. Human approval introduced edge cases around changed selections, expiration, cancellation, and token reuse. Finally, early screens felt like dense metadata dashboards, so we progressively disclosed evidence, agent staging, and history while keeping the creative artifact and decision controls prominent. Accomplishments that we're proud of The prototype supports complete create, select, save, and reload flows for real text and image candidates. It registers exactly six WebMCP tools in the local integration harness, keeps staged agent work visibly separate from committed decisions, and rejects missing, revoked, expired, or reused approvals. Decision memory preserves the brief, chosen artifact, reasons, note, and later superseded revisions. The current verification suite reports 27 passing unit tests, a successful static build, six registered tools in the browser roundtrip, responsive desktop and mobile captures, and no browser console errors. What we learned Structured tools are most useful when they act on the same state people can see, not when they create a second agent-only workflow. Human control is stronger when enforced by application state—here, an approval that no WebMCP tool can create—rather than by prompt wording. We also learned that memory should provide context, not automatic preference: showing what changed between then and now makes precedent useful without turning it into a hidden scoring model. What's next for FinalPick Next, we want to harden hosted-browser interoperability across supported ChatGPT configurations and test the workflow with more first-time users. Beyond the prototype, we would add collaborative persistence, accounts, richer asset versioning and uploads, and explicit review or dispute states only after designing the necessary permission, privacy, retention, and conflict-resolution rules. title: Firebreak
pitch: Fast incident response for browser agents, with exact human authority over every consequential action.
about_excerpt: Fast incident response for browser agents, with exact human authority over every consequential action. Like Comment Story Updates GIF Firebreak in five frames: investigate, block unsafe recovery, require exact human authorization, and verify the result. Firebreak Agentic demos ask: How much can the agent do? For incident response, I think the question becomes How much should it be allowed to do? Speed is useful. Standing authority is not. Firebreak separates the two. What it does Firebreak gives a browser agent nine intent-level WebMCP tools to investigate a checkout outage. The agent gathers evidence, correlates recent changes and tests recovery options. A payment-database restart gets rejected because it threatens protected outcomes: payments and accepted orders. Similarly, a safer checkout rollback becomes an Action Contract bound to the system state, evidence, blast radius, expiry, verification and compensation plan. The human authorises that exact contract. Only then can the agent execute. If state changes, the authority becomes stale. If execution is retried, it remains idempotent. If verification fails, compensation is required instead of declaring false success. The result is a complete chain: investigate - propose - authorise - execute - verify - receipt Why WebMCP Incident response is an incorrect place for agents to infer intent from pixels. It is urgent, stateful and potentially destructive. Firebreak exposes intent. The agent can inspect, simulate, prepare, execute and verify through narrow typed tools. The UI and WebMCP tools use the same deterministic application service, so there is no privileged agent path around the controls visible to the human, but one capability is deliberately missing: human authorisation . The agent can request authority, but it cannot grant authority to itself. Better human-agent collaboration The agent handles the repetitive work: investigation, correlation, simulation and proposal. The human makes the consequential decision. They see before approving anything. And the approval is not: “let the agent operate.” It's: this action, against this state, under these constraints.  That's the core of Firebreak. Intelligence can stay flexible. Authority should be precise. Who can use it The current implementation is a checkout recovery scenario, though the pattern extends to SRE, security, commerce, data and regulated operations where agents can investigate and prepare consequential work without receiving standing authority. The important abstraction is a proper roadmap from investigation to proposal - authority - execution - verification. Other domains would still require their own identity, provider adapters, telemetry, policy and tested rollback paths. How it was built Firebreak uses React and TypeScript with a deterministic domain engine. That engine owns revisioned state, protected outcomes, constraints, expiring Action Contracts, idempotent execution, verification, compensation and receipts. Nine WebMCP tools sit on top of the same service used by the human interface. Vitest, Playwright and deterministic journey fixtures test the system from foundation through workflow and stress cases. The demo requires no API key, cloud account or production credentials. Making approval mean something is harder. If state changes after approval, should the old approval still work? No. If execution retries, should the action happen twice? No. If the command runs but recovery fails, should we call it success? No. If the agent can approve itself, was there ever a human boundary? No. Firebreak turns those answers into system properties instead of UI promises. What we learned Agents do not need more buttons. They need better abstractions like Raw controls, implementation and intent-level tools for meaning. And once intent is explicit, we can attach evidence, policy, authority and verification to it. That makes agents easier to guide. Try it Live app: https://neel-error404.github.io/firebreak-webmcp/ Source: https://github.com/Neel-Error404/firebreak-webmcp The intended flow: inspect - correlate - reject unsafe recovery - prepare rollback - human authorisation - execute - verify - recept What's next Firebreak is a prototype; production would require signed identities, durable audit storage, isolated real connectors, stronger policy authoring, broader evaluations and staged deployment evidence. We want to explore & make capability bounded, legible and accountable. title: FlowLens
pitch: Workflow intelligence, in focus
about_excerpt: Workflow intelligence, in focus Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration FlowLens was built for the WebMCP hackathon to solve a core problem in automation debugging: most debuggers require humans to manually translate visual context back into text. We wanted to turn human focus into a typed, temporary tool surface where selecting a failed execution path automatically bounds the evidence an agent can inspect, enabling precise diagnosis and safe repairs without copying node IDs, payloads, or timestamps. What it does FlowLens is a deterministic workflow flight recorder that allows operations specialists to: Run automation workflows and visualize execution traces on an interactive canvas Select exact failed execution paths (normalization and condition steps) Expose selection-bound WebMCP tools that capture immutable run, step, node, selection, and workflow versions Let browser agents inspect bounded evidence and propose the smallest safe repair Preview patches with visible diffs before any mutation occurs Apply approved patches with single-use tokens, rerun fixtures, and prove results with before-and-after comparisons Maintain a complete audit trail with undo capability The hero defect demonstrates a subtle bug: normalization emits customer.segment while the condition reads customer.tier , causing VIP customers to reach the standard queue without throwing errors. How we built it FlowLens is a static React application built with: React + TypeScript for type-safe component architecture @xyflow/react for the interactive workflow canvas with finite node types Vite for fast development and production builds Zod for strict JSON Schema validation Lucide React for consistent iconography @polar-sh/checkout for embedded Pro feature paywall The architecture follows a clean domain-driven design: Domain layer ( src/domain/ ) contains workflow types, validation, simulation, patches, and redaction Application layer ( src/app/ ) manages state through a typed reducer with command facade Feature layer ( src/features/ ) provides canvas, header, panel, paywall, and sidebar components WebMCP adapter ( src/webmcp/ ) handles dynamic tool registration with AbortController cleanup The deterministic simulator traverses directed graphs producing bounded trace steps without real side effects. The repair engine accepts only restricted operations (like replace_condition_field ) with preview, approval tokens, version guards, and reversible history. Challenges we ran into WebMCP API evolution : The specification was still evolving, requiring feature detection for both document.modelContext and optional toolchange events independently Selection lifecycle complexity : Managing selection-bound tools that need to abort on workflow edits, selection changes, or component unmounts required careful AbortController coordination Security boundaries : Implementing bounded outputs, secret-like field redaction, version guards, and single-use approval tokens while maintaining usability Deterministic simulation : Building a simulator that produces realistic traces without actual side effects, queues, or network operations Paywall integration : Balancing a local admin bypass for demo purposes with production-grade Polar checkout that requires trusted backend authentication Accomplishments that we're proud of Complete WebMCP integration : Successfully implemented 16 tools (10 base, 4 selection-bound, 1 approval, 1 conditional undo) following Chrome security guidance Deterministic testing : 19/19 Vitest unit tests and 2/2 Playwright E2E tests passing, including real in-app WebMCP calls Apple-inspired UI : Dark graphite interface with glassy chrome, crisp hierarchy, restrained color, and reduced-motion support Safe mutation model : Non-mutating preview, visible diffs, human approval, single-use tokens, and reversible history Production-ready build : TypeScript strict mode passing, static bundle deployable to Vercel or any static host Comprehensive documentation : Architecture, security model, WebMCP inventory, and eval corpus all documented What we learned WebMCP patterns : The imperative API requires careful lifecycle management—tools must register dynamically, capture closure state, and clean up with AbortController Selection as context : Turning visual selection into typed API boundaries is more powerful than traditional copy-paste debugging Deterministic simulation : A bounded simulator can provide sufficient evidence for diagnosis without requiring real integrations Security by design : Version guards, bounded outputs, and single-use tokens prevent many classes of attacks while maintaining usability Static architecture : A well-designed static app can deliver complex functionality without backend dependencies What's next for FlowLens Additional workflow types : Expand beyond the CRM escalation hero flow to support more automation patterns Richer patch DSL : Add more safe operations beyond replace_condition_field while maintaining boundedness Authentication backend : Implement trusted server authentication with Polar webhook verification for production entitlements Multiplayer collaboration : Enable shared workspaces with real-time collaboration on workflow debugging Advanced analytics : Add workflow performance insights, failure pattern detection, and optimization suggestions Expanded WebMCP coverage : Support additional WebMCP features as the title: Forkline
pitch: Forkline lets an AI agent rehearse disposable operational futures through native WebMCP tools, while a human keeps exact-state approval over anything that can become real.
about_excerpt: Forkline lets an AI agent rehearse disposable operational futures through native WebMCP tools, while a human keeps exact-state approval over anything that can become real. Like Comment Story Updates Main UI Inspiration The dangerous part of an agent is not simply that it can be wrong. It is that it can be fluent while it is wrong, and then something irreversible happens. We kept seeing the same shape: a model explores a messy situation, picks a plan, and the UI treats “the agent said so” as permission. The human either rubber-stamps it or fights the interface. There is no clear place where the agent is allowed to be ambitious and forbidden to make its answer real. Forkline started from that split. Let the agent try every recovery. Do not let it touch the live world. The human sets the non-negotiables in the open. The only thing that becomes real is one exact state a person approved — not a vibe, and not a checkbox the model can invent. The Port Azure / St. Anne story is the sharpest version of that: hospital kits, a closed port, and a tempting air-freight cheat. If the agent can talk past “no air,” the whole thing is theater. What it does You open a disruption. The rules are on the page: protect hospital orders, keep critical fill above the floor, and use no air freight. An agent (via WebMCP) reads the network, forks disposable futures, reroutes, switches suppliers, reallocates stock, simulates, and compares. Bad futures stay useful. Emergency air looks fast and expensive, but it is illegal under the human rule . Regional stock-preserve starves the hospital. Those branches do not get a secret override. The agent can still ask to commit. Forkline says no until a human selects a branch and approves that exact state . Change the fill floor after approval, and the old yes is dead. Then you approve again, or you don’t. Six tools: get_network_state , fork_scenario , apply_intervention , simulate_scenario , compare_scenarios , commit_scenario . They use the same engine as the dashboard. If WebMCP is off, the page says so and still lets you walk the futures by hand. How we built it A small deterministic runtime in the browser handles the network, interventions, KPIs, violations, branch identity, and approval fingerprint. Then we put two faces on it: the ops UI and document.modelContext . Approval is not a field on the tool. The page mints a one-shot token bound to the scenario and the current human rules. Commit checks that fingerprint again. If the agent could mint “approved,” we would have built a liar. Challenges we ran into Making “the agent cannot authorize” actually true, not just a prompt. That meant fail-closed commit, stale tokens, and tests that try to cheat. WebMCP is still behind a flag, so a normal Chrome tab has to stay honest instead of fake-registering tools. The demo had to show a rejected commit, not just a pretty graph. That is the product. It is also the part people are most likely to skip when rushing a video. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent can be wide. The human is narrow. You can watch both. You can watch an illegal recovery fail in public instead of getting smoothed into a recommendation. You can watch a feasible recovery still get refused until a person binds themselves to that exact snapshot — and watch that binding die if they move a slider. What we learned More tools do not create safety. A gate the model cannot write creates safety. If the human rules live in the prompt, they are decoration. If they live in the page and the commit path, they are real. Disposable futures only matter if commit is expensive. Cheap commit, and you have just built a faster way to ship a bad plan. What's next for Forkline Same protocol, nastier decisions: anything where “try it” should be free and “make it live” should not — config, money, clinical, deploys. Tighter WebMCP as the API hardens. Keep the map small until the gate is obviously the point, not the supply chain. title: GeoMart
pitch: An AI agent reads your live, unsubmitted VES site brief via WebMCP, flags physical depth/resistivity mismatches, builds your comparison tray, and drafts your quote. No REST fallback.
about_excerpt: An AI agent reads your live, unsubmitted VES site brief via WebMCP, flags physical depth/resistivity mismatches, builds your comparison tray, and drafts your quote. No REST fallback. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration The WebMCP Challenge's own rules ship search_products , compare_products , and request_quote as the example tool names. That's the obvious shape for almost any submission, and it's the wrong shape to build on top of if the goal is to show WebMCP doing something a REST API couldn't. I have a geophysics background, specifically Vertical Electrical Sounding (VES) and resistivity survey work, and picking that domain over another generic storefront meant the physical constraints in the tool logic would be real instead of decorative. What it does A human fills in a site brief on the page: target depth, expected resistivity range, terrain, and budget. That data lives only in the browser's memory until someone explicitly submits a quote. An AI agent connected via WebMCP reads that live brief, scores a given instrument against it using physical limits (can this unit's depth range actually reach the target depth, will its resistivity ceiling saturate on this site), writes results into a visible comparison tray in real time, and drafts quote justification text that a human has to review and submit themselves. The agent can propose a quote. It cannot send one.Before this, matching a site's physical constraints to the right instrument meant manually cross-referencing depth ranges, resistivity ceilings, and budget against 25 spec sheets, or explaining the same constraints over again to a salesperson. Here, a human states the constraints once, in a form that never leaves the browser until they choose to submit it, and the agent does the cross-referencing: reading the live brief, scoring each instrument's actual physical fit, and rejecting the ones that can't do the job, with a stated reason. The person still makes every decision that matters (which instrument, whether to request a quote), but skips the manual lookup work, and the reasoning behind each recommendation is visible on the page, not buried in a chat transcript. How I built it Cloudflare Workers serves the storefront and a plain REST catalog listing. Cloudflare D1 holds 25 real VES/resistivity instruments from ABEM, AGI, IRIS Instruments, GF Instruments, Geometrics, Megger, and Zonge, with depth ranges, resistivity specs, and estimated market prices. The client is plain TypeScript bundled with esbuild, no SPA framework, so document.modelContext registration timing stays simple. The app registers five tools: read_site_brief , assess_site_fit , flag_depth_mismatch , update_comparison_tray , and draft_quote_notes . Challenges I ran into The original design called for fit-scoring to run inside a Cloudflare Worker, kept off any public route. That doesn't work: a tool's execute() handler runs in the browser, and a browser can only reach Worker code over HTTP, so any such route is curlable whether or not it's documented anywhere. The fix was moving the scoring functions into the browser bundle itself, operating on an already-fetched public catalog cache, so no request ever carries the site brief anywhere. The second problem was subtler. Two of the five tools, assess_site_fit and flag_depth_mismatch , originally just returned JSON to the calling agent. That meant an agent holding only read_site_brief plus the public catalog listing could work out the same score itself, without needing either tool at all. The fix was having both tools also write a visible fit badge onto the product's own catalog card, so the result lands on the page a human is looking at, not just in the agent's own reasoning. The WebMCP proposal spec describes agent.requestUserInteraction() as the built-in way to pause a tool for human confirmation. Chrome's own developer documentation describes it as not yet implemented. Rather than build the quote-submission gate around an API that might not fire, the plain-button commit gate outside the tool surface became the primary mechanism, with requestUserInteraction() wired in as an upgrade that no-ops safely if the browser doesn't support it. Live testing through a real agent (Codex, via the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser) confirmed it: the API silently did nothing, and the plain button carried the whole gate. The hardest problems didn't show up until adversarial testing started, using Google Antigravity with both the source code and the live site open at once. The first pass found an XSS: agent-supplied text (the quote reasoning, tray product IDs) was going into the page via unescaped innerHTML. It also found that the commit endpoint, POST /api/quotes, had zero protection at all. A bare script outside any browser could submit a quote directly, bypassing the human-approval button entirely. Both got fixed: HTML escaping everywhere agent-supplied strings render, and an isTrusted check on the submit button's click handler so a script-simulated click (element.click(), dispatchEvent) can't fire it, only a real one. A second adversarial pass immediately broke the second fix. The isTrusted check only guards the button's own handler; it does nothing against a request that skips the browser entirely. The interim mitigation, checking the request's Origin header, turned out to be checking a public value: this repo is open source, so a script reading it knows exactly what Origin to send, and Node's fetch() has no browser-level restriction against forging that header. Closing it for real took Cloudflare Turnstile, verified server-side against a secret that lives only in a Worker secret, never in the repo or the client bundle. That's the one piece of the whole flow a script reading the source still can't derive. A third retest confirmed the original bypass now returns 403, and separately caught two smaller bugs in the Turnstile wiring itself: a race where the ready-callback was defined inside the ES module and could run after Turnstile's own script had already looked for it, and a missing hostname check on the verification response. What I learned Checking a spec claim against the primary source instead of a blog summary caught a bug before it shipped: two different search results disagreed about whether requestUserInteraction() even exists in the current draft. A second lesson came from the security arc: a check that looks like it closes a gap can still be trivially defeated if the thing it validates (an Origin header, a value read from public source code) isn't actually a secret. The only thing that closed it for real was a value a reader of this repo could never find. The broader lesson about the tools themselves: returning a computed value to an agent is not the same as making that computation something only WebMCP could have produced. If the same result is derivable from data already available through legitimate channels, the tool isn't pulling its weight. What's next A few things worth doing beyond the hackathon. agent.requestUserInteraction() is worth revisiting once Chrome ships it, since the tool already checks for it and falls back safely, no rework needed on that side. The same physical-constraint pattern used for VES/resistivity gear would carry over to adjacent survey equipment: ground-penetrating radar's depth of investigation is even more terrain-dependent than VES's (clay soils can cut penetration from tens of meters to under one), and seismic refraction has its own hard depth limit set by spread length and source energy rather than soil conductivity. Both map onto the same "does this equipment's spec sheet reach my target depth" tool logic. And right now a submitted quote just lands in D1; connecting that to a distributor contact would turn this from a demo into something a geophysicist could use in the field. title: GomiMCP
pitch: Municipal waste rules that AI agents can understand and act on—without guessing, while humans retain control of final decisions.
about_excerpt: Municipal waste rules that AI agents can understand and act on—without guessing, while humans retain control of final decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Japan has highly organized waste-disposal systems, but the rules differ between municipalities. The same object may be classified differently depending on the city, quantity, size, material, or safety risk. People also rarely use exact official category names. They say things like: “I have ten of those transparent things sold at convenience stores for rainy days, something I put on the floor to sleep on, and a portable battery for charging my phone.” An AI agent can understand what the user probably means, but it should not invent municipal rules or automatically complete a potentially unsafe action. GomiMCP separates those responsibilities: The municipality declares the rules. The agent interprets the user’s language. The human makes the final decision. What it does GomiMCP is a static WebMCP-powered interface that exposes structured municipal waste rules directly from a webpage. The page registers three WebMCP tools: resolve_item converts ordinary or indirect wording into a canonical waste item. get_disposal_rule returns the municipality’s declared rule for that item. prepare_bulky_pickup prepares an eligible bulky-waste request without finalizing it. In the demo, the agent interprets one indirect Japanese request as ten umbrellas, one futon, and one mobile power bank. It makes eight real WebMCP calls: resolve_item ×3 get_disposal_rule ×3 prepare_bulky_pickup ×2 Under Aoba City’s fictional test rules, ten umbrellas and the futon are classified as bulky waste. GomiMCP prepares both requests and displays a Human Confirmation Gate totaling 800 yen. The mobile power bank is classified as high-risk. Automated preparation is refused, and the result is marked manual_review_required . The agent can prepare eligible requests, but it cannot press the final confirmation button. Nothing is booked until a human explicitly confirms it. How we built it GomiMCP is a static JavaScript application deployed with GitHub Pages. Its tools are registered using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool provides a name, natural-language description, JSON input schema, execution logic, and safety annotations. The implementation separates: Item aliases and canonical identifiers Municipality-specific classifications Conditional rules such as quantity thresholds Fees and reservation requirements Risk levels and automation permissions Human-confirmation requirements Rule provenance and version information The LIVE WEBMCP TRACE displays only actual tool calls made through the page, making the interaction visible and auditable. No backend, database, authentication system, payment integration, or real municipality booking is used. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was deciding where language interpretation should end and authoritative decision-making should begin. Natural language is flexible, while municipal rules must be precise. Allowing a language model to invent a disposal category would be unsafe. Passing an entire ambiguous sentence directly into a rule engine would also be unreliable. We solved this with a staged flow: The agent interprets each description as one ordinary item concept. GomiMCP resolves that concept to a canonical item. The page applies the selected municipality’s declared rules. Risk policies determine whether automation must stop. Consequential actions stop at a visible Human Confirmation Gate. Another challenge was proving that the tools were actually called. The LIVE WEBMCP TRACE records real page-level tool activity rather than displaying a simulated agent response. Accomplishments that we're proud of We successfully demonstrated: Semantic interpretation of indirect Japanese descriptions Eight real WebMCP tool calls Deterministic results based on municipality and quantity Automatic refusal for a high-risk mobile battery Preparation of two eligible bulky-waste requests A mandatory human-confirmation boundary A visible and auditable trace of every tool call A complete product experience running as a static website We are especially proud that the demo shows a useful division of responsibility: the agent understands the user, the page owns the rules, and the human retains control of the final action. What we learned AI does not need to own every decision to be useful. The model is best used for understanding human intent. The authoritative source should still own the rule, the safety constraint, and the final action boundary. WebMCP makes this division practical. It allows an ordinary webpage to expose structured capabilities to an agent while preserving the page’s existing logic, state, and user interface. We also learned that observability matters. Showing the real tool-call trace makes the system easier to test, explain, and trust. What's next for GomiMCP The current version uses fictional municipalities and test rules derived from official municipal open-data structures. It must not be used as real-world disposal advice. Future work includes: Importing and validating real municipality-maintained rules Expanding rule provenance and version tracking Supporting more item conditions, such as dimensions and remaining contents Adding multilingual municipality-maintained descriptions Providing reusable schemas for additional municipalities Exploring Remote MCP and SDK integrations Testing the same contracts across more WebMCP-aware agents and browsers Our longer-term goal is simple: municipalities should be able to declare their rules once and make them safely usable by people, websites, and AI agents. title: Home Gym Creator
pitch: Design a home gym with an AI agent. Edit one shared room through WebMCP while the app checks space, access, training goals, and budget.
about_excerpt: Design a home gym with an AI agent. Edit one shared room through WebMCP while the app checks space, access, training goals, and budget. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I first tried Codex Modeling Studio and was fascinated by the idea of designing something together with an AI agent in a shared visual workspace. It made me want to explore the same kind of human-agent collaboration in a domain I care about personally. Strength training is my hobby, so I started wondering whether the same approach could help design a home gym around real spatial, training, and budget constraints. That question became Home Gym Creator. What it does Home Gym Creator helps people design a home gym that fits their actual room, training goals, and budget. Users can model the room in 2D or 3D, add furniture, doors, windows, and unavailable areas, then choose equipment from a catalog of 24 fictional products. An AI agent can read and modify the same project through WebMCP. It can configure the room, search the catalog, add and arrange equipment, react to manual changes, and validate the finished layout. Every agent action is immediately visible in the editor and uses the same undo and redo history as manual edits. The application validates the layout by checking collisions, room boundaries, exercise clearance, access paths, ceiling height, wall mounting, training-goal coverage, and total cost. The agent respects these validation results and uses them to improve the design together with the user. How I built it I built Home Gym Creator with Next.js, TypeScript, Zustand, Zod, and React Three Fiber. Manual actions and WebMCP tools use the same project commands, state, validation, and undo history. I used Codex and Cursor throughout development for planning, implementation, debugging, and testing. The app runs entirely in the browser and is deployed on Vercel. Challenges I ran into At first, the agent placed equipment too close to furniture or blocked paths from the door to the wardrobe and bed. I introduced collision detection, equipment and furniture use zones, and access-path validation to model these practical constraints. I did not want placement tools to contain rigid rules that removed the agent’s freedom. Instead, I added a tool that suggests suitable positions before placement and another that validates the complete layout afterward. Modeling realistic combinations was also challenging: for example, a wall-mounted pull-up bar can remain usable above a low object, and people can still walk underneath it. Representing these height-aware rules required careful iteration. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that the agent can use deterministic tools to check its own work and respect the user's room, budget, and training requirements. Selecting equipment often requires combining several products: for example, a strength setup for squats and bench press may need a rack, bench, barbell, and weight plates. The agent can choose that combination within the available budget, arrange it inside the room, and verify that it fits without collisions or blocked access paths. Making this complete workflow work reliably was one of my biggest accomplishments in the project. What I learned I learned about the current limitations of AI-generated 3D assets. My first attempt was to generate 50 equipment models at once, but it did not produce usable results. Generating one model at a time and improving it iteratively worked much better. I also learned how to guide an agent without adding rigid instructions to every tool. Instead, I gave it dedicated suggestion and validation tools, allowing it to explore solutions, check its own work, and improve the layout based on deterministic feedback. What's next for Home Gym Creator If I continue developing Home Gym Creator, I would add protective floor-mat planning, wall and floor customization, and more equipment options with additional 3D models. I would also expand the concept beyond home gyms toward commercial facilities, supporting multiple rooms and floors, changing rooms, and more complex equipment layouts. title: Host Whisperer
pitch: When your cloud host fails, your customers’ agents can fix it.
about_excerpt: When your cloud host fails, your customers’ agents can fix it. Like Comment Story Updates Why I built it A checkout error is a dead end for a customer. They do not know whether to refresh, wait, or contact support. The website often knows what failed, but that context never reaches the customer's agent. I built Host Whisperer to make that moment useful instead of frustrating. What it does A developer connects their host and downloads one JavaScript file for their website. That file contains a small WebMCP runtime and the exact recovery actions the developer has allowed. In the demo, Big Pink's checkout returns a 503 because its checkout service is unhealthy. Host Whisperer offers help beside the error. The customer asks ChatGPT to fix checkout, and ChatGPT makes one WebMCP tool call. Host Whisperer checks the incident privately, applies the approved recovery, and verifies checkout before reporting success. The customer sees simple progress instead of infrastructure logs. Their cart is preserved, and ChatGPT never places the order for them. If the problem is unsupported or verification fails, the tool escalates it instead of pretending it worked. The hosting operation is simulated so the demo is repeatable. The WebMCP handoff, state changes, recovery flow, and verification all run in the browser. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an assistant has to guess from the page or from whatever the customer can describe. Here, the website exposes one purpose-built support handoff tied to its current state. The customer supplies the intent, ChatGPT carries it through a structured tool call, and Host Whisperer uses the website's private diagnostics and developer-approved recovery. No one part can safely do the whole job alone. How I built it The setup experience is React and TypeScript. It generates a self-contained, origin-bound plugin. The host token is never stored in the browser or included in the downloaded file. The runtime registers one tool with document.modelContext.registerTool(...). It includes a small incident state machine, a Shadow DOM support panel, context sanitization, single-use recovery, replay protection, progress updates, and post-recovery verification. WebMCP is registered only on the customer website. What I learned The hardest part was deciding what the agent should actually do. Giving a customer's assistant raw logs or general infrastructure access would be unsafe and confusing. I ended up with one high-level delegation tool and kept the technical work behind Host Whisperer. My main takeaway is that WebMCP can let a website define a narrow support contract: what evidence is safe, what action is allowed, and what must be verified before success is returned. title: Jipsa
pitch: A real local cake marketplace where people shop visually and AI agents compare, configure, quote, and prepare the same order through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A real local cake marketplace where people shop visually and AI agents compare, configure, quote, and prepare the same order through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Jipsa Inspiration Custom cake shopping is surprisingly difficult. Price changes with size, filling, lettering, and extras. Pickup inventory differs by maker, and every local shop supports a different set of options. People usually open many pages and manually reconcile those constraints. We built Jipsa to show what becomes possible when a polished human storefront and an AI agent share the same commerce state. What it does Jipsa is a real visual marketplace for 20 independent cake makers. Shoppers can browse stores, inspect current availability and policies, personalize a cake, receive an itemized quote, and review the exact order before confirmation. Through WebMCP, an agent can perform the same workflow with ten focused tools: search_local_stores , get_store_details , search_products , get_product_options , check_availability , configure_product , get_quote , prepare_order , place_order , and get_order_status . A single natural-language request can check all 20 makers against distance, exact configured price, servings, ingredients, supported cream colors, lettering, and pickup inventory. Jipsa returns three ranked candidates and exposes criterion-level rejection counts so the recommendation is inspectable. Why WebMCP This use case is full of structured but inconsistent constraints. Traditional visual automation has to repeatedly navigate cards, menus, forms, and calendars. WebMCP exposes those capabilities directly while preserving the same interface for the person. The result is not a detached chatbot or a single opaque automation endpoint. The agent composes purpose-built tools across search, comparison, availability, configuration, quoting, confirmation, ordering, and status. Every mutation remains visible to the shopper. If the agent changes lavender cream to light pink, the product photography and selected option update immediately while the lettering, flavor, filling, size, and pickup time remain intact. How we built it Jipsa is a React and TypeScript app using the WebMCP imperative API. src/webmcp.ts registers the ten English-language tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with JSON Schema inputs, focused descriptions, annotations, validation, structured output, and recoverable errors. src/marketplace.ts is the shared domain layer used by both the UI and WebMCP callbacks. It owns catalog search, ranking, pickup availability, partial configuration updates, exact pricing, confirmation tokens, local prototype persistence, and the developer audit trail. src/data.ts provides 20 distinct sample makers. Search price, quote, final review, and the persisted prototype order all use the same pricing engine. prepare_order only creates a short-lived confirmation token and opens human review. place_order requires that exact token plus confirmed: true . The production build is deployed on ChatGPT Sites with the headers required for WebMCP discovery. The app also includes a clearly labeled preview drawer for browsers where WebMCP is unavailable, without pretending that the protocol is connected. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping search ranking, visual state, and order safety consistent. A candidate price is only useful if it reflects the same configuration used at checkout. We solved that by centralizing validation and pricing instead of duplicating estimates in the UI and tool handlers. We also designed partial updates so a follow-up request changes only the named field rather than resetting the order. Accomplishments that we're proud of A compound request evaluates 20 makers and explains both matches and rejections. Ten small, composable WebMCP tools cover the complete workflow. Human and agent actions update one shared, visible order state. Exact configured pricing remains consistent from search through confirmation. Ordering is confirmation-gated and produces no external payment or real-world order. The deployed app, public repository, automated tests, and a sub-three-minute narrated demo are ready for judges. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools are narrow, descriptive, and composable. The human interface remains essential: it provides context, trust, and final control, while structured tools give agents reliability. The strongest experience comes from letting both sides take turns on the same task rather than creating separate human and agent products. What's next for Jipsa A production version would connect maker inventory, secure checkout, live pickup calendars, and verified merchant onboarding. The same pattern can extend beyond cakes to florists, tailors, caterers, and other local businesses whose products are highly configurable and time-sensitive. title: Jobly: turn a resume into a completed application
pitch: Give Codex your resume. It finds matching jobs on Jobly and completes applications on two structurally different ATS portals via WebMCP tools - you keep control of the choices and the final submit.
about_excerpt: Give Codex your resume. It finds matching jobs on Jobly and completes applications on two structurally different ATS portals via WebMCP tools - you keep control of the choices and the final submit. Like Comment Story Updates Jobly Inspiration Job applications often fail before a candidate can make their case. A promising role becomes a relay of unfamiliar portals, repeated resume uploads, and long forms asking for information that already exists in the resume. By the last page, the candidate has spent their attention on administration instead of the opportunity. We wanted to show how WebMCP changes that: the candidate keeps the consequential decisions, and the agent does the repetitive work between them. What it does Jobly turns a resume into a completed application. The candidate gives Codex their resume and preferences. Codex identifies relevant roles on Jobly (an Indeed-style job board), the candidate chooses which opportunity is worth pursuing, and Codex uses each employer portal's explicit WebMCP tools to carry the application forward across two simulated ATS sites: Greenhold — a Greenhouse-style ATS with a five-step application wizard Leverly — a Lever-style ATS with a single-page form The journey: Codex uses Jobly's list_jobs / get_job tools to build a shortlist with each role's applyUrl . For each approved role it opens the ATS, signs in, inspects the real form via get_application_form / get_page_fields , fills it from the resume with fill_fields , attaches files, validates, pauses for human approval, and finally submit_application returns a confirmation ID — verifiable under My applications . The WebMCP surface This is not a UI-scraping demonstration. Jobly exposes structured search and job-detail tools ( get_filter_options , list_jobs , get_job ); the two ATS sites expose their jobs, form schemas, page state, file attachment, validation, and submission actions directly ( sign_in , start_application , fill_fields , attach_resume , attach_cover_letter , goto_page , next_page , prev_page , validate_application , submit_application ). Greenhold and Leverly expose the same agent contract but render structurally different forms . That difference is intentional: the agent must inspect and adapt to each application experience instead of replaying a hardcoded sequence of clicks. How we built it Monorepo (npm workspaces): three Vite + React + TypeScript apps and three shared packages. packages/webmcp — WebMCP registration glue, tool helpers, and an Origin-Agent-Cluster Vite plugin (WebMCP requires origin isolation). packages/convex — one shared Convex backend ( jobs + applications ) that all three apps point at. packages/ats-core — a config-driven form engine (store, validation, submit mapping, WebMCP tools, React renderer) shared by both ATS sites. WebMCP tools call Convex imperatively ( convex.query/mutation ), so the agent path and the React UI share one backend and, in the ATS apps, one in-page form store — the visible human view stays in sync with the agent's progress. Challenges we ran into Designing one tool contract that works for both a multi-page wizard and a single-page form, so the agent adapts by inspection rather than memorized flows. Keeping the human UI and the agent's mutations in perfect sync through a single in-page form store. Origin isolation requirements for WebMCP, solved with a reusable Origin-Agent-Cluster Vite plugin. What we learned WebMCP is at its best when the site tells the agent what it can do instead of the agent guessing at the UI. Structured form schemas plus validation tools let the agent complete real multi-step workflows safely, while explicit human approval before submit_application keeps the person in control of the consequential choices. What's next for Jobly Richer candidate profiles, more ATS form archetypes (Workday-style multi-section forms), and employer-side WebMCP tools for reviewing incoming applications. title: KineticFlow: AI Motion Design Studio
pitch: An agent native motion design workspace bridging visual timeline editing with WebMCP driven key-framing, SVG orchestration, and real-time animation.
about_excerpt: An agent native motion design workspace bridging visual timeline editing with WebMCP driven key-framing, SVG orchestration, and real-time animation. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Motion design tools are powerful, but even small animation changes often require repetitive timeline editing, precise layer targeting, and multiple export steps. Browser agents usually struggle with these tools because they must guess what the user selected and interact through fragile screen coordinates. I built KineticFlow to explore a better model: the designer points to what they mean, while the AI agent handles the structured motion work. WebMCP makes this possible by giving agents direct, typed access to the application’s canvas and timeline state. Live app: kinetic-flow.netlify.app Source code: github.com/SamyakJ05/KineticFlow Demo video: Watch on YouTube What it does KineticFlow is a browser-native vector motion design studio where humans and AI agents work on the same canvas. A designer can select a layer and ask an agent to: Inspect the complete scene and current human selection Add rectangles, circles, hearts, stars, and sparkles Refine a layer’s position, size, color, rotation, scale, or opacity Generate multi-track animation keyframes Apply easing curves and spring physics Load polished motion presets Play, pause, or seek the live preview Export the animation as CSS, animated SVG, or Lottie JSON Every operation appears in a live Tool Stream with its inputs, structured result, status, and execution time. Designers can continue editing manually, drag objects, adjust properties and keyframes, or undo an agent’s changes. When WebMCP is unavailable, an in-page co-pilot and manual tool tester use the same underlying handlers, making the complete experience accessible in standard browsers. How I built it KineticFlow is built with: React TypeScript Vite Zustand Tailwind CSS SVG Netlify The WebMCP integration registers seven imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool includes: A focused name and human-readable title A natural-language description A strict JSON Schema inputSchema Input validation Structured return values Cancellation-signal support Read-only annotations where appropriate The main architectural component is a shared Zustand editor store. The canvas, timeline, property controls, in-page co-pilot, and browser agent all read and update the same state. The getCanvasScene tool returns more than a scene snapshot. It also provides: The layer selected by the human The current playhead position Playback status Loop state This enables natural handoffs such as: Make this coral, add a spring pulse, and play it. The user does not need to find or provide an internal layer ID. A requestAnimationFrame loop drives the live preview, while a custom interpolation engine evaluates position, scale, rotation, opacity, width, and height tracks. The exporter compiles the shared scene into reusable CSS and HTML, standalone animated SVG, or Lottie JSON. The application is deployed on Netlify with SPA routing, security headers, asset caching, and an explicit tools=(self) permissions policy. Challenges I ran into WebMCP is an emerging specification, so one major challenge was keeping the implementation aligned with the latest API. Earlier experiments used navigator.modelContext and a parameters field, while the current specification uses document.modelContext and inputSchema . I migrated the primary implementation while retaining a compatibility path for earlier experimental builds. Another challenge was designing tools that were useful to an agent without removing control from the designer. Small atomic tools were precise, but agents also needed enough context to understand the user’s intent. Returning the current human selection alongside the scene created a much more natural collaboration model. I also had to ensure that tool responses reflected the updated state rather than a stale snapshot. Playback and animation handlers now read the store again after mutations before returning structured results. Finally, animation exports required translating the same internal motion model into three different formats while preserving timing, transforms, opacity, and layer geometry. Accomplishments that I’m proud of Built a complete motion-design product rather than only a technical proof of concept Implemented seven structured WebMCP tools Created a shared-context workflow between human selection and agent action Added multi-track keyframes, easing curves, and spring-motion interpolation Made agent operations visible through a real-time execution stream Produced CSS, animated SVG, and Lottie exports Added a fallback co-pilot and manual tester powered by the same handlers Created automated smoke tests that register and execute all seven tools Deployed the application publicly with WebMCP-compatible permissions What I learned I learned that agent-native applications work best when agents receive semantic actions and meaningful application state—not just access to buttons and screen coordinates. WebMCP is especially valuable for creative software because human intent is often communicated through selection. A designer clicking a layer is already providing useful context. Exposing that selection to the agent allows short, natural instructions to become precise structured operations. I also learned that tool descriptions, schemas, validation, and return values are part of the product experience. Well-designed tools make agents more reliable while making the system easier for humans to understand and trust. What’s next for KineticFlow: AI Motion Design Studio Planned improvements include: Agent-generated motion plans that designers can preview before applying Multi-layer selection and batch animation operations Natural-language editing of easing curves and spring parameters SVG import and advanced path manipulation Collaborative history with agent-versus-human change attribution Reusable brand and motion-style systems Additional production exports and framework integrations Declarative WebMCP support as the specification matures The long-term goal is to make KineticFlow a creative workspace where humans provide taste, direction, and final judgment while agents handle repetitive, structured animation work. title: KoKo
pitch: A trip itinerary with no edit UI: you change plans by talking to your browser's agent. Sharing a URL grants permissions to someone's AI - edit link gets write tools, view link is read-only.
about_excerpt: A trip itinerary with no edit UI: you change plans by talking to your browser's agent. Sharing a URL grants permissions to someone's AI - edit link gets write tools, view link is read-only. Like Comment Story Updates Koko (ここ, "here") is a live, shared map itinerary with no edit UI. The page registers its capabilities as WebMCP tools, and the only way to change the plan is to talk to the agent in your browser — while looking at the same map the agent is changing. Why WebMCP, not a remote MCP server? I designed a remote-MCP version of this app in August. It collapsed the moment I realized my family would have to complete an OAuth flow to let their agents in. WebMCP inverts that: sharing a URL is granting permissions to someone's AI. The edit URL and the view URL serve the same document, but register different tool sets — 12 tools on the edit page, 8 read-only tools on the view page. A viewer's agent doesn't get its write calls rejected; the write tools don't exist in its world. The server enforces the same split on PUT, and a rotate_share_links tool revokes a leaked view link. Because the tools live in the page, the agent shares the user's context: get_current_view makes "add a lunch option around here" work, search_places biases to the visible map, and get_travel_time draws the route it just computed and compares it against the travel slot you planned. The itinerary stores decisions — stops, stay times, reserved travel slots with route notes, a wishlist — while live facts (current drive time, what's next, how late we're running) are computed on demand, so the plan never goes stale. Every tool call pans the map, opens a popup and appends to an on-page activity log: the UI is the confirmation. Try it: the live URL creates your own shiori (edit + view link pair) from a sample 3-day road trip. Open the view link in a second window and watch your agent's permissions change. Built on Cloudflare Workers + Hono + Leaflet: one Worker, one KV namespace, a Durable Object for atomic saves, valibot validation on every agent input, CSP with per-request nonces, 209 tests. MIT.
