title: LabMCP
pitch: A chemistry lab where humans and agents work side by side to learn and explore, sharing the same tools. Mix, measure by hand, experiment, or let an agent use WebMCP tools to accomplish your tasks.
about_excerpt: A chemistry lab where humans and agents work side by side to learn and explore, sharing the same tools. Mix, measure by hand, experiment, or let an agent use WebMCP tools to accomplish your tasks. Like Comment Story Updates Titrating an unknown acid to the endpoint Mixing silver nitrate and sodium chloride forms a white silver chloride precipitate Four unlabeled samples dosed with acid to find which one reacts Oversaturating potassium nitrate leaves visible undissolved crystals at the bottom of the beaker Diluting a 1.0 M sodium chloride stock down to exactly 100 mL of 0.10 M What's LabMCP? LabMCP is a virtual chemistry lab where a person and an agent can work in the same area. Both humans and agents can do the exact same actions, like dragging glassware, dispensing chemicals, finding the pH of a liquid, or heating a beaker. While the human clicks buttons and drags stuff around, the agent does this via exposed WebMCP tools that we've created! Our hackathon project comes with seven scenarios, which include titration, precipitation, neutralizing, dilution, watching a solid dissolve and crystallize, and a reaction mystery. It also includes a sandbox to work on other experiments. You can use it with ChatGPT's desktop app using its WebMCP tools, or with Chrome's. Inspiration In high school we often used tools like PhET, interactive simulations designed to teach science concepts through virtual actions. One problem they have is that without a teacher or a packet guiding you through what to do, they often feel confusing and very restraining. We wanted that guidance to come from AI agents, acting as a partner and a teacher at the same time. While computer use can already make this possible, it's very slow and clunky, and you need some prior knowledge of how it works. WebMCP solves this issue by giving agents the exact tools to emulate humans. How we built it We built LabMCP in Next.js on top of a chemistry engine written in TypeScript. The engine tracks what is in each container, has a small set of reactions (acid and base, precipitation, carbonate fizz, indicators, solubility), and finds pH by solving the charge balance. Every action, whether from a mouse or an agent, goes through this engine and returns a new state plus a set of events. LabMCP has 25 tools on document.modelContext , and each result an agent receives has a redacted summary of the lab so it only shows what a person could see. The frontend is styled with Tailwind and shadcn/ui. The glassware is drawn as SVGs. Challenges we ran into Originally our project had a much larger scope: 3x more chemicals, more glassware, and 10+ more experiments. We started this hackathon late, so we had to cut down our scope a lot and focus on the popular chemicals and experiments, most of which we had seen in our high school AP classes. Other than scope, our biggest challenge was making the system feel intuitive and inviting to use. Essentially it had to have taste and be playful. Our initial design was a 3D chemistry lab where the glassware sat on a bench. This worked somewhat, but it was: Laggy inside of ChatGPT's browser. Dragging and placing items required a perfect position, so it didn't feel intuitive or easy to use. It didn't look playful or modern. It seemed like we were using 3D just for the sake of it "looking cool." Because of these issues we switched to a 2D bench with snapping and more playful icons and glassware SVGs. This solved all three issues we had with the 3D bench and actually made us want to play with it. What we learned Firstly, we learned how cool a service WebMCP is. Before this competition we both thought MCP was for APIs, and that the only way to get work done reliably in a browser was by burning tokens on computer use, so this definitely introduced us to a new technology. In terms of actually building the project, we learned how to decompose our huge scope into tickets for a swarm of agents to implement and test in parallel (using GPT 5.6 Sol as an orchestrator and GPT 5.6 Luna as an implementer). What's next for LabMCP Right now LabMCP is quite limited in terms of experiments and elements. We want to expand past first-year chemistry into a more open sandbox engine with a huge number of experiments and tools, so that eventually it can be used by labs that might not have access to equipment, or even for testing potentially dangerous experiments. title: LooPROOF
pitch: Product truth, callable by agents.
about_excerpt: Product truth, callable by agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Enterprise buyers rarely encounter one product surface. They compare a marketing page, pricing matrix, docs, trust center, contract language, and actual product behavior. Those surfaces drift. A browser agent can describe each page, but it still has to guess which statement wins. LooPROOF turns that hidden governance problem into a WebMCP-native collaboration surface. The website exposes not only controls, but the product claims, evidence provenance, authority boundary, and claim ceiling an agent needs to reason safely. What it does This challenge build includes a synthetic enterprise SaaS evidence graph with customer-facing claims and authoritative runtime, contract, and repository evidence. LooPROOF deterministically classifies each claim as BLOCK , REVIEW , ALIGNED , or NOT_EVALUATED . A human and an agent can work through the same visible state to: inspect the product-truth summary; find claims blocking an enterprise sales gate; trace every source, locator, value, provenance class, and authority level for a claim; focus the dashboard on the same claim the agent is investigating; stage canonical copy changes in a local-only sandbox; re-run the deterministic gate and reach STAGED_CONSISTENT_NON_ISSUING . LooPROOF deliberately refuses to call a sandbox change “fixed.” Production verification remains a separate authority. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent must infer the purpose of rows, badges, filters, and buttons from the visual interface. More importantly, it cannot reliably infer LooPROOF's domain contract: runtime evidence outranks marketing copy; model-proposed evidence cannot bind a verdict; a missing evidence edge is NOT_EVALUATED ; and a sandbox patch has a strict claim ceiling. LooPROOF registers 7 imperative WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . Closed schemas give the agent stable claim IDs, explicit inputs, side-effect annotations, and compact structured outputs. Tool execution updates the same state the human sees, creating a shared workspace rather than hidden backend automation. How we built it The app is dependency-free JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. A deterministic TruthEngine evaluates a bundled evidence graph and overlays sandbox patches in memory. The WebMCP adapter registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() , uses AbortSignal for lifecycle cleanup, declares read-only and side-effect annotations, and normalizes outputs to compact MCP text content. Node's built-in test runner verifies verdict binding, provenance boundaries, sandbox isolation, reset behavior, and tool-contract limits. GitHub Actions runs the complete verification suite. What is new for this challenge LooPROOF existed as a broader verification-engine concept before the submission period. During the challenge period, it was meaningfully extended through a new standalone public implementation containing: the complete imperative WebMCP tool surface; a shared human-agent state model; a provenance-preserving product-claim evidence graph; the local resolution sandbox; the deterministic re-verification path; a new responsive interface, test suite, security boundary, and challenge documentation. The repository contains synthetic evidence and does not copy or expose the private production implementation. Challenges The central challenge was not exposing more tools. It was preventing agent convenience from weakening evidence semantics. The implementation had to make the useful path easy while refusing unsupported claims. We therefore separated evidence alignment, staged consistency, and production verification into distinct states. Accomplishments 7 working imperative WebMCP tools. A coherent human-agent product experience rather than a wrapper around a chat box. Shared visible state between tool calls and the dashboard. Deterministic verdicts with provenance and authority ordering. A local sandbox that performs zero network, repository, or deployment writes. Explicit refusal to overclaim success. Dependency-free tests and CI validation. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when a website exposes its domain semantics, not merely its controls. Tool schemas can encode the decisions an interface is designed to support, while the visible page preserves human oversight. The difficult design work is defining claim boundaries and side effects precisely enough that an agent can help without becoming a new source of product drift. What's next The production direction is to connect the same WebMCP surface to versioned proof packets generated from real product surfaces, repository policy, and observed runtime flows, while keeping final verification capability-separated. title: MCPation
pitch: A browser-native WebMCP gate that lets Codex inspect one explicitly granted workspace, explain drift, and apply supervised, reversible cleanup—without installing an MCP server.
about_excerpt: A browser-native WebMCP gate that lets Codex inspect one explicitly granted workspace, explain drift, and apply supervised, reversible cleanup—without installing an MCP server. Like Comment Story Updates What I built MCPation is a browser-native WebMCP pre-flight gate for Codex. It is a deliberately scoped MVP exploring a new category of agent-native DevTools: many of the useful, structured interactions people associate with an installed MCP can happen directly in a web page, without installing a server, daemon, extension, or API key. The user grants access to exactly one workspace folder, and the agent works inside that visible boundary. Why WebMCP is a good fit Agent configuration tends to grow quietly. Duplicate MCP servers, disabled entries, invalid endpoints, package drift, and layered Codex instructions can make it hard to know what an agent will inherit before it runs. MCPation turns that uncertainty into a shared, inspectable pre-flight step. The first pass is read-only: it reads an allowlisted set of configuration, package, and instruction metadata, then returns a readiness score, concrete findings, and an evidence graph connecting artifacts to those findings. This creates a better experience for both sides. A person gets an understandable report instead of guessing through configuration files. Codex gets a structured tool surface instead of having to click through an unfamiliar UI. They see the same state, while the person stays in control of every write. What the real demo shows The demo workspace is intentionally seeded with reproducible problems so the workflow has something meaningful to solve. The browser flow itself is real, not a mocked result: MCPation scans the selected folder, identifies duplicate JSON server entries, an invalid endpoint, and a disabled server, explains the evidence, and builds a supervised hardening plan. I choose the exact duplicate cleanup, explicitly approve it, grant the browser write permission, and MCPation creates one sibling backup before removing only those selected keys. It then rescans and shows the new readiness score and the restorable snapshot. More complex commands, TOML, policy, and instruction changes remain review items rather than being silently changed. The important collaboration is that a person can decide what is safe while an agent can inspect, explain, and verify the result through the same page. That combination would be difficult with a normal UI-only workflow and risky with an unbounded local tool. How WebMCP is implemented The page registers a concrete document.modelContext surface with tools for scanning the workspace, reading the declared MCP/package inventory, reading the instruction chain, explaining findings, building a hardening plan, requesting a bounded host handoff, submitting a sanitized host snapshot, applying the selected deterministic cleanup, verifying the result, and explaining the exact access scope. Read-only tools are annotated with readOnlyHint; the apply tool accepts only action IDs from the latest plan and requires confirm: true. The visible browser control owns the permission prompt, backup, write, and rescan. When a browser cannot expose native WebMCP, MCPation says so explicitly and shows a local preview instead of pretending that native tools are available. The same app works in Codex's in-app browser and in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Scope and honesty This is a deliberately scoped MVP for a new category of agent-native DevTools, built under a short hackathon deadline. I chose one deterministic, reversible cleanup and a strong evidence trail instead of pretending to support every possible workspace utility. With more time, the same pattern could extend to onboarding, compliance checks, migrations, review gates, and other supervised workflows. The point is that a useful MCP-like experience does not necessarily need installation when WebMCP can publish a scoped page surface and the user grants explicit permission. A note about the English text English is not my native language. I understand and speak it fluently, but expressing myself precisely in written English takes me much longer. I used AI to help draft, translate, and polish this description so it would be clear to the judges; the product decisions, implementation, testing, and claims in this submission are based on the project that is actually running. I am genuinely grateful to be able to participate in this hackathon. I discovered it rather late and would have loved more time to explore richer utilities, but I am very happy to share this concept and what I managed to build. title: Meridian Voyager
pitch: A car configurator where the agent and the human edit the same build. Nine WebMCP tools let it explain every constraint and solve for the cheapest valid car.
about_excerpt: A car configurator where the agent and the human edit the same build. Nine WebMCP tools let it explain every constraint and solve for the cheapest valid car. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Car configurators are one of the most frustrating interfaces on the web, and it isn't because they're badly designed. It's because the options genuinely interact. The tow package needs all-wheel drive. Sport suspension drops the ride height below legal hitch clearance. The 21-inch wheels are locked to trims you may not want to pay for. Every real configurator has a hidden constraint graph, and the only tool it gives you for exploring it is clicking and backtracking. So when someone asks the question they actually care about — "what's the cheapest build with all-wheel drive and a tow hitch that still comes in under fifty thousand?" — the interface has no answer. You brute-force it by hand. That's a constraint-satisfaction problem behind a UI that can't express one. It seemed like exactly the shape of problem WebMCP exists to solve. What it does Meridian Voyager is a car configurator where an agent and a human edit the same build. Not a chat widget stapled to a product page — the page registers nine tools on document.modelContext, and the agent reads and writes the exact state the human is looking at. You can click paint colours yourself and the agent sees your choice on its next read. You can ask the agent for the cheapest build meeting your constraints, and the car on screen changes while you watch. An activity log labels every change You or Agent, so the collaboration is legible rather than magical. The centrepiece is find_cheapest_build. It enumerates the full option space against every compatibility rule and returns an exact cheapest answer, which the agent can then apply in one call. That's the question the UI could never answer. The other half is that constraints get explained, not just enforced. Every rule carries a human-readable reason, and tool responses hand those sentences back: ▎ "The Tow Package needs the front motor for low-speed traction under load, so it requires Dual Motor AWD or Performance AWD." A blocked set_option teaches the agent something instead of erroring. It can then offer a real trade-off — "I can add the hitch if we move you to Dual Motor AWD, which is $5,000 more and costs 12 miles of range" — which is exactly the conversation a good salesperson has and a form never can. How we built it React and Vite, with the domain deliberately separated from the tool layer: src/domain/catalog.ts — the option catalog as pure data src/domain/rules.ts — the constraint engine, pricing, and the exact cheapest-build solver src/store.ts — the single shared configuration src/webmcp/register.ts — the nine document.modelContext tools src/components/CarView.tsx — layered SVG that reacts to paint, wheels, and ride height The catalog and the rules are plain data, so adding an option or a constraint never means touching tool code. The tools describe the catalog to the agent from the same source the UI renders from, which is what keeps the two views honest. The nine tools: get_configuration, list_available_options, check_compatibility, get_price_breakdown, find_cheapest_build, set_option, remove_option, apply_build, reset_build. One store, two writers. The click handlers and the tool implementations both go through store.ts. There's no separate agent-facing model to drift out of sync — that's the whole reason the demo reads as collaboration rather than automation. Read and write get different trust. Read-only tools are marked readOnlyHint, so an agent can explore the entire option space and price out alternatives freely, and only needs the user's confidence when it's about to change the build. Native first. The app waits for a native document.modelContext and uses it directly on Chrome 149+. Only when the browser hasn't shipped the API does it load @mcp-b/global, a polyfill of the same W3C spec, so anyone evaluating it on another browser still gets the full experience. A badge in the header shows which one is active. Challenges we ran into Getting the tool responses right mattered more than getting the tools right. The first version returned bare success and failure, and an agent driving it would just retry the same blocked option. Moving every constraint's rationale into the response — and adding a hint pointing at find_cheapest_build — changed the agent from something that poked at the form into something that reasoned about trade-offs. The solver also had to be exact rather than greedy. A greedy walk produces a plausible build that isn't actually the cheapest, and a wrong confident answer is worse than no answer. The option space is small enough to enumerate honestly, so it does. Detecting the native API was subtler than expected. Registering against the polyfill because document.modelContext hadn't appeared yet silently downgrades a native browser, so the app waits for the host's implementation before falling back. Accomplishments that we're proud of scripts/verify.mjs drives the app through the tool layer in headless Chromium — the same path an agent takes — and asserts the page moves with it. Nineteen checks, all passing, covering tool registration, constraint enforcement, the solver (including a deliberately impossible request it must refuse), agent writes reaching the UI, and human clicks becoming visible to the agent. What we learned WebMCP's real leverage isn't letting an agent click things faster. It's that a page can expose the reasoning behind its own interface — the constraints, the trade-offs, the search space — which is precisely the part a visual UI throws away. The tow-hitch rule exists in every real configurator; WebMCP is the first time the page can explain it rather than just enforce it. What's next for Meridian Voyager Multi-vehicle comparison, financing as a tool so the agent can optimise on monthly payment rather than sticker price, and tightening the transport's allowedOrigins from the demo's permissive setting to a real allowlist. title: mock exams for your AI agent
pitch: Cheap model or expensive one? More skills, or a better prompt? More tools or fewer? Sit both on a real benchmark in a browser tab — and keep the record, so you know which version to go back to.
about_excerpt: Cheap model or expensive one? More skills, or a better prompt? More tools or fewer? Sit both on a real benchmark in a browser tab — and keep the record, so you know which version to go back to. Like Comment Story Updates How I switch my ChatGPT's MBTI. lol ChatGPT gets better result without using tools Inspiration There are so many AI tools and agents, we don't know which one to choose. And most people are not researchers. I'm not either. I build things. The evaluation that exists is expensive and heavy for us normal people. I don't need an academic, precise number. But I don't want to vibe-pick my AI either. I need to answer, for my task, in a practical way: the expensive model, or the cheap one, or a mix? another skill, or a better prompt? more tools, or fewer? And I need the answer written down. AI isn't like software. When a change breaks software, you find out straight away and roll back. When a change makes an agent worse, you find out weeks later, and by then you've forgotten which version was the good one. WebMCP is what makes this light enough to actually use. If the benchmark is a web page, and the page hands the agent its tools, then the agent you already have sits the exam directly. Nothing to install, nothing to log into, no API key. What it does mocks puts 15 live benchmarks in a browser tab. Open one, tell your agent to sit it, and watch it work. Each answer is scored by that task's own judge.py , fetched from the exact commit its leaderboard grades against and run unmodified in the browser. Not a copy of the scoring. Name the setup you're running, and the result goes on the board under that name. Run it again with one thing changed, and you have a comparison you can still read in a month. How we built it Six WebMCP tools. start_run , get_next_case and submit_answer run the exam. list_case_files , search_pdf_text and read_pdf_page_text exist because one task's answers are inside a 17-page PDF. They exist because the page is open — not because you installed anything. You get them by visiting a URL and lose them by leaving. get_next_case hands over the question and nothing else. The page holds every expected answer, because the judge can't run without them, and never lets them out. submit_answer returns recorded: true — not whether the case passed. On a 23-case task a per-case mark isn't a verdict, it's feedback for the next answer. There is no per-task code anywhere in this repo. Every task ships the same contract, so a task published tomorrow works the day it lands. Today that is 12 of 15 tasks and 297 cases. The three refusals are worked out from each task's own judge, not from a list we wrote. Two of them are graded on what the solution says about itself, backed by a video, and typed into an anonymous page that would be a claim rather than a result. Challenges we ran into Every real bug was the same one: we assumed something the data doesn't actually guarantee. And the fake data in our tests was tidier than the real thing, so the tests passed. The scoring scripts don't say "passed". They print a number — 1.0, or 0.4. We assumed they also printed a true/false. None of the 53 do. So the page put FAILED next to every correct answer, while the overall grade right beside it said passed. The database gives times back as dates, not text. We sorted the board by time, comparing them as text. With one run on the board there's nothing to sort, so it looked fine. The second run crashed the page. The database doesn't keep the order things were written in. The MBTI scoring script prints several things — the four-letter type, the percentages, and a label saying what kind of task it is: "personality". We showed the first one. The database reorders by name length, so "personality" came out first, and the board announced a model's personality type as "personality". Accomplishments that we're proud of A task's own judge.py runs in the browser, unmodified. Not a port, not a reimplementation — the same file its leaderboard grades with, fetched from the same commit and executed in Pyodide. That's what makes a score here mean the same thing it means there. You can watch it work. Every tool call the agent makes lands on the page as it happens — took the case, found the document, opened page nine, committed to a number. The page never touches the model. It only writes down what came through its own front door. What we learned The site measured our own tools and found them wanting. On the PDF task, GPT-5.6 scored 14 of 23 using the text tools we built. We ran it again and told it to ignore those PDF tools and just open the PDF and look. It scored 17 . The gain wasn't spread out. Every question that needed reading a length off a chart went from failed to passed, all three! So the page stopped recommending those tools for chart questions. They're still there, because they're the right instrument for the other PDF task, which is all tables. But a value plotted in a figure isn't text, and no amount of text extraction will find it. That is the site doing the job it exists to do, on itself. What's next for mocks — your agent sits a real exam, in a browser tab Server-side judging. Worth saying, because the whole point is that a number should mean what it says it means. Judging happens in your browser. The page runs judge.py client-side and then posts the result. So the board records what a browser claimed it scored. A curl can post a perfect score without answering anything. The fix is server-side judging, but we ran out of time for this challenge. Then sign-in , so a name on the board means something. Then per-case views — which cases a change broke, not just whether the average moved. title: Moshimo Tag
pitch: Add a what-if layer to any plan.
about_excerpt: Add a what-if layer to any plan. Like Comment Story Updates Start a Project and build the expected Plan Attach What-ifs to the Plan moments they affect Review Situations, countermeasures, and Plan B options Review only the responses selected by the human Inspiration When I first heard about WebMCP, the first thing that came to mind was a stage I once performed on. In that Japanese-style stand-up comedy performance, I had to change which line I delivered depending on the audience’s reaction. At every branch, I made sure to prepare at least three lines: one for a good reaction, one for a bad reaction, and one for a reaction that was hard to read. I had not always worked that way. Countless times, when the audience did not respond as expected, I forced myself to continue with the material exactly as I had prepared it and lost heart partway through. The method above grew directly from reflecting on those failures. Strangely, once I began preparing responses for several plausible cases, I sometimes found that I could hold the audience’s attention with improvisations I had not prepared at all. However, that kind of advance planning had several drawbacks. Writing down all the branches in text documents or data files was cumbersome. Listing several options at a single branch point quickly made the page cluttered. I could not always cover all the Situations that might arise at each branch point. From one person’s perspective, it is easy to overlook things. I thought WebMCP might be exactly the right mechanism for solving these problems. That idea led me to create Moshimo Tag: I felt that if this kind of preparation could be applied to a broader range of events, it might help many people. Most people do not examine multiple scenarios carefully enough. Even among the performers who shared the stage with me, many imposed a self-centered, single-track script that created a divide between the stage and the audience. People in general likewise tend to write schedules around the path where everything goes as planned and stop there. Yet even in real events such as trips, interviews, and dates, lateness, forgotten items, weather, and reactions that differ from expectations often force plans to change. Even when people understand the importance of advance planning, it takes effort to think through these possibilities beforehand, identify where each one relates to the Plan, and write a countermeasure for each. It is only natural that people would rather avoid such meticulous preparation. If WebMCP can make it easier, I believe more people may be able to avoid failure. What it does In Moshimo Tag, the user creates a Project and arranges schedules, procedures, scripts, and similar content as a Plan in chronological or execution order. Project: Flight to San Francisco. Plan 1: Research airlines. Plan 2: Book a seat. Plan 3: Leave home. Plan 4: ... Each Plan item can contain the following structure. Plan └─ What-if ├─ Situation 1 │ ├─ main countermeasure │ ├─ Plan B 1 countermeasure │ ├─ Plan B 2 countermeasure │ └─ ... └─ Situation 2 ├─ main countermeasure └─ ... For example, the user can attach the What-if “What if I leave late?” to the Plan “Leave for the venue.” Under it, the user can separate Situations such as “I am 15 minutes late” and “I am more than 30 minutes late,” then prepare a main countermeasure and Plan Bs for each. Users can enter all of this manually. Compared with writing in a blank notebook, it is much easier to build a plan in an organized form. Alternatively, when asked, a WebMCP-capable agent can read the current Project and add or edit Plans, What-ifs, Situations, and countermeasures on the same screen the user already has open. This is far faster and easier than entering everything by hand. However, everything the agent creates remains a candidate. The agent cannot edit or save the following final decisions: Already covered Accept risk Prepare Dismiss That is because the most important part of advance planning is for the human to review the candidates, edit the wording when necessary, and decide how to respond. After the user has decided each item, opening View final plan removes the noise of candidates and undecided items. It displays only the countermeasures the human selected alongside the original Plan, making the result easy to review. When useful, the final state can also be passed to an agent as a structured projection and reused as a CSV, spreadsheet, summary, Situation matrix, runbook, or similar output. Why WebMCP Of course, even without WebMCP—or without Moshimo Tag itself—you could ask an AI to “list the risks,” and it would probably produce similar What-ifs. But an ordinary chat response can easily become a long list with more detail than necessary. It does not preserve which point belongs to which Plan item, what the human chose to adopt, or what became outdated after the Plan changed. Even if the result is saved to a file, unless you have a heavily customized system, the information will still tend to become scattered and cluttered, and organizing it will take additional effort. This is where WebMCP becomes useful: it takes the AI’s answer out of the chat and connects it directly to the same Plan the human is viewing. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can read the structured state of the Project currently open on the page and use stable IDs to add likely What-ifs at the exact points in the Plan they affect. It does not need to risk typing into the wrong field or clicking a button at the wrong moment. Because the agent uses structured page tools and performs its work as direct, visible, verifiable state changes, the human and the agent share the same screen, the same Project, and the same saved state—not separate copies or chat logs. The format of the plan does not change because of an AI’s whims or memory lapses. It can be created in the same form every time, providing a consistent user experience. WebMCP also allows permissions to be deliberately constrained. Instead of relying only on promises in a system prompt, Moshimo Tag enforces the boundary through capabilities the tools simply do not have: the agent may prepare candidates, but it cannot take away the human’s decision about how to respond. This is essential to Moshimo Tag’s core UX of helping people feel adequately prepared before an event. How we built it Moshimo Tag is a web application built with TypeScript, React, Next.js, and Vite/Vinext. It is deployed and publicly available through ChatGPT Sites. I used ChatGPT Pro to discuss the concept and draft the implementation plan. Before this challenge, I had already created guideline skills for developing implementation plans with ChatGPT and Codex for my personal projects. I used those skills to turn the draft into an implementation plan. Codex handled most of the implementation. My main role was to review key points, request corrections, and create the SVG graphics used in the app. I also edited the code myself for design adjustments. I made trade-offs between development time and different aspects of quality with the hackathon’s timeframe in mind. Time was not unlimited, so I do not claim that the implementation is flawless. I expect to improve it incrementally as needed. The WebMCP tools use document.modelContext.registerTool() in src/webmcp.ts . The current implementation registers 12 tools, covering: listing, creating, updating, and opening Projects, as well as switching views reading, adding, editing, reordering, and deleting Plan items managing What-ifs and impact managing Situations and their main countermeasures managing Plan B countermeasures preparing non-binding response candidates reading final and export projections The human UI and WebMCP mutations use the same application command path. There is no separate hidden state that only the agent can manipulate. Every mutation validates IDs, entity versions, text lengths, operation limits, state, and idempotency keys. Read tools return projections bounded to their purpose rather than raw browser storage. Project data is stored in the browser’s localStorage . The app requires no account, API key, or dedicated backend. Challenges we ran into Even now that I have a working version, I still wonder whether I could have found a UI and design that were easier to read and manage. In other words, designing an excellent UX was my greatest concern from the earliest stage of the project. WebMCP testing presented another challenge. Because I let an AI agent work autonomously, parts of the verification process became something of a black box. Did the agent really use WebMCP to make the update, or did it enter the content by manipulating the DOM through a browser-control skill? I had to distinguish between the two carefully several times, which was nerve-racking. In fact, an agent once followed an editing instruction through DOM manipulation instead of WebMCP, and I nearly missed it. title: Mysynote
pitch: A browser synth where you and an AI agent share one live Web Audio graph — lock what's yours, the agent patches the rest through real WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A browser synth where you and an AI agent share one live Web Audio graph — lock what's yours, the agent patches the rest through real WebMCP tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Default startup interface Click on play and see the synth in action. Message sent to live AI agent. WebMCP tools verified. Confirmation of agent not changing things manually locked by hand. One single source of truth. Self-testing. Inspiration Every AI-powered creative tool right now works the same way: you describe what you want in a chat box, and the model either generates a static result or silently mutates state you can't see happening. Sound design tools especially suffer from this — either the agent is a chatbot bolted onto the side of a DAW, guessing its way through a UI it wasn't built to understand, or it just spits out a finished audio file with no room for you to steer it mid-process. WebMCP flips that. Instead of an agent scraping a UI, the app itself declares exactly what it can do — real, typed, callable tools. That felt like the right foundation for something more interesting than "agent generates a sound": a studio where a human and an agent operate the same live instrument at the same time, each able to see and change what the other just did. What it does Mysynote is a browser-based modular synthesizer built on the Web Audio API. You patch together oscillators, filters, distortion, delay, reverb, and a sequencer on a live canvas, exactly like a hardware modular rig. An AI agent (Gemini or Claude, bring your own API key) sits alongside you with access to the same graph through WebMCP tools — it can inspect the current state, spawn and remove modules, patch and unpatch cables, tweak parameters, and read the live spectrum, all through structured tool calls rather than by describing changes in text. The part I care about most: you can lock any parameter by hand. Once locked, that boundary isn't a suggestion sitting in a system prompt the model could talk itself around — it's enforced in the tool implementation itself. If the agent (or a WebMCP-enabled browser calling the tools directly) tries to write to a locked parameter, or even tries to call unlock_parameter on a lock you set, the call is rejected with a structured error before it ever reaches the audio graph. You define the boundaries; the agent works freely inside them. How I built it The frontend is Next.js/React/TypeScript, styled with Tailwind. The audio engine is hand-written against the raw Web Audio API — no framework wrapping it — with a reconciler that diffs a plain-object graph state against the live AudioNode graph and patches only what changed, so the agent's tool calls and your own dragging/clicking stay in sync against one authoritative source of truth instead of two. WebMCP tools are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool : get_audio_graph_state , spawn_module , remove_module , patch_cable , remove_cable , set_module_param , lock_parameter , unlock_parameter , get_spectrum_analysis , get_sequencer_state , set_sequencer_step , and clear_graph . The in-app agent console (Gemini/Claude, BYOK) drives these exact same tools, so what you see the agent do in-app is identical to what any WebMCP-aware browser or agent could do against the live site. Challenges I ran into The hardest bug wasn't a crash — it was a bug that looked like everything worked. Early on, a locked parameter really did block direct writes, but the agent could still call unlock_parameter on itself with no restriction, defeat the lock, and then set the value anyway. Nothing crashed; it just quietly broke the entire premise of the project. Fixing it meant tracking who set a lock (human vs. tool) and rejecting a tool-sourced unlock of a human-set lock at the enforcement layer — plus adding it as a permanent regression check in the app's own self-test, so it can't silently reappear. I also hit a nasty reconciler bug where removing a module threw an uncaught exception mid-cleanup (a plain string field was being treated like an AudioNode ), which left orphaned nodes that kept crashing every subsequent state change. Chasing a bug that hides behind unrelated symptoms — a stuck test button, a sequencer step failing — down to one bad property check was the toughest debugging of the project. What I learned Building the "hard boundary" wasn't a UI problem, it was an authorization problem — the interesting design work in an agent-native app isn't the tools you expose, it's deciding which of your own tools the agent is allowed to call on itself. And that a feature can look completely correct in every manual test and still have a real security-shaped hole in it until something actually tries to defeat it on purpose. What's next Multiplayer patching (multiple humans + one agent on the same graph), saved/shareable patches, and exposing the sequencer's per-step modulation as its own lockable, agent-modifiable surface. title: Neighbors Decide
pitch: An AI agent plans a whole neighborhood budget through WebMCP tools. It has no tool to adopt the plan, so the decision stays with a named human by design.
about_excerpt: An AI agent plans a whole neighborhood budget through WebMCP tools. It has no tool to adopt the plan, so the decision stays with a named human by design. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The reflex in agent tooling right now is to expose more actions. Give the agent another tool, another capability, let it do more. That has a blind spot: some decisions are not ours to delegate. Whether a patient consents to a procedure, whether a family's loan is refused, how a neighborhood spends public money. Each has to be attributable to a named person and contestable afterwards. An agent can and should do the work around such a decision. It should not be the thing that makes it. We wanted a WebMCP project that took that seriously. Not a confirmation dialog the agent could talk its way through, but a structural boundary. The setting is participatory budgeting, inspired by the gram sabha and ward committee, Kerala's People's Plan Campaign, and Pune's ward budgets, where residents themselves decide how a local fund is spent. What it does One resident splits a fixed hypothetical fund of ten lakh rupees across exactly eight local public works that cannot all be funded. An AI browser agent assists. The agent gets seven WebMCP tools: get_budget_state : the whole board in one call. Fund, priorities, protected works, the active draft and its validity, revision numbers. list_projects : the eight works with costs, funding rules, dependencies, incompatibilities, and the full numeric scoring model. list_strategy_options : three valid budget directions, each scored against the resident's current priorities. simulate_allocation : run the shared validator on a hypothetical and get every rule violation at once, each with a machine readable fix. propose_allocation : file a draft as the agent's own, after validation. An invalid draft is still stored, visibly, as a rejected draft. explain_tradeoffs : what changed between two plans, and what it costs. request_allocation_review : hand the draft to the resident. It cannot accept or adopt. Five read only, two that write, none that commits a decision. There is deliberately no tool to set priorities, protect a work, accept, reject, adopt, or reset. Those are the resident's, through visible buttons on the page. The agent can model the entire budget and draft a valid plan. It cannot make the call, because the function that would make it was never registered. When the resident protects a work the agent left out, a flood prone riverside park where her children play, the agent's draft goes stale on screen and it has to read the budget again and rebuild around that choice. The machine adapts to the person's decision. It does not get to freeze one. How we built it A pure domain engine in TypeScript, framework free, with no DOM and no globals: the eight project dataset, one deterministic allocation validator that returns every issue in a stable order and never repairs anything, a benefit scoring model that is fully disclosed so the agent can reproduce every number, and a deterministic rebuild that keeps protected works and trims the rest to fit. One in memory store, with React bindings through useSyncExternalStore. The manual UI and every WebMCP tool handler dispatch into the same store instance and call the same validator, so displayed values and tool output cannot diverge. A human budget change bumps a revision counter and stales any active proposal. Only the reducer writes actor labels, derived from the action prefix, so the final record has trustworthy authorship. The WebMCP adapter registers the seven tools against whichever the runtime provides, navigator.modelContext or document.modelContext, using a shared AbortController so aborting unregisters every tool. Handlers return the MCP result shape with structuredContent, and rule violations come back as data, not errors, so a failed plan stays inspectable. React 19, Vite, Vitest. No backend, no API keys, no external data calls, no persistence beyond the browser tab. Deployed as a static site. Challenges we ran into Registration under React StrictMode. StrictMode double invokes effects, and our first version registered three of seven tools before the second pass cancelled the first. The fix was a caller owned AbortSignal and a deferred registration pass, so the setup, cleanup, setup cycle collapses to one real registration. Two runtimes, one adapter. The editor draft and ChatGPT expose document.modelContext; Chrome's preview build exposes navigator.modelContext. A judge on Chrome would have seen no assistant at all. We now feature detect and prefer navigator. Keeping the boundary honest. What we built governs the cooperative structured tool surface a WebMCP style agent negotiates with the page. It is not a privilege boundary: an agent driving the raw DOM could still click the resident's buttons. We say so plainly, in the app and the README. What omission actually buys is that a cooperative agent has no function to call, and the decision record has a human author by construction. Deployment. Our host froze production deploys mid event on a plan limit, leaving the live site several commits behind. We moved continuous deployment to GitHub Pages, switched to relative asset paths so the build works under a project subpath, and verified the full agent loop against the new URL. Accomplishments that we're proud of The boundary is visible, not asserted. The app shows a live trace of every WebMCP call the agent makes, labelled read or write, and a permanent list of the actions no tool can perform. Ask the agent to adopt the plan and nothing happens: no refusal, no error, no tool call. The absence is the proof. One validated state, shared byte for byte between the human UI and the agent tools. The agent literally cannot be shown a different number than the resident sees. It degrades gracefully. With no WebMCP runtime present, every flow still works by hand, including the rebuild around a protected work. What we learned The interesting lever in WebMCP is not only which tools you add. It is which you withhold, and whether that omission is legible to the agent and to the person. Our get_budget_state returns a structuralLimits field that tells the agent, in plain terms, the things no tool will do. An agent that reads it stops asking. Enforced by omission beats a confirmation dialog for decisions that must stay human. There is no rubber stamp step to automate, no injection target, and a decision record with a named author by construction rather than by policy. What's next for Neighbors Decide Extract the pattern as a small reference other WebMCP builders can adopt: an agent does the preparatory work, the act of deciding stays human and attributable, both sides read the same validated state, and the boundary is a tool that was never registered. The same shape fits clinical informed consent, lending decisions, hiring, content moderation, and legal filing. The budget scenario is a vehicle. The pattern is the point. title: Nivra: shared architecture for humans and AI
pitch: A shared visual architecture workspace where humans and AI agents uncover hidden coupling, propose safer alternatives, and validate architecture together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared visual architecture workspace where humans and AI agents uncover hidden coupling, propose safer alternatives, and validate architecture together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Nivra: result of changes Nivra: issue found Nivra: HLD view Nivra: proposal solution Nivra: final cut Nivra: LLD view for Checkout Inspiration Software architecture is usually spread across diagrams, documentation, tickets, and conversations. Humans can understand the visual context, while AI agents often receive only screenshots or incomplete text descriptions. We wanted to explore a different model: what if the architect and the agent could work inside the same structured architecture workspace? That idea became Nivra. What it does Nivra is a shared visual architecture reasoning workspace for humans and AI agents. The human works with an interactive architecture map. Through browser-native WebMCP tools, an agent can read the same underlying model, inspect components and dependencies, navigate between high-level and low-level views, record findings, create proposals, and validate architecture against explicit policies. The demo begins with a Commerce Platform where Checkout appears to be independently deployable. Deeper inspection reveals hidden runtime coupling: Basket Adapter directly shares Product Store state across a deployment boundary without an explicit contract. The agent surfaces the evidence, but the architectural decision remains with the human. The architect defines the required policy, and Nivra validates the Current Architecture deterministically. Current fails two of four rules. Nivra then creates a separate remediation proposal that replaces the shared-state dependency with an explicit Checkout Snapshot Contract. The Proposal passes all four policies, while Current Architecture remains unchanged. Why WebMCP Nivra is not an AI assistant discussing a screenshot. WebMCP allows the application to expose structured architecture operations directly to an agent inside the same live page and browser session. Nivra exposes seven WebMCP tools for: reading the active architecture; inspecting elements and relationships; opening and focusing architecture views; recording architectural findings; defining deterministic constraints; creating patch-based proposals; validating Current or Proposal architecture. This makes agent actions inspectable, repeatable, and visible to the human through the Agent Activity timeline. How we built it Nivra is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, React Flow, Zustand, and browser-native WebMCP. The architecture domain model is kept independent from the UI. React Flow renders the visual workspace, while Zustand manages interaction and persistence. WebMCP tools call the same validated workspace actions used by the human-facing interface. Current Architecture is treated as immutable. Proposals are represented as patch-derived alternatives rather than destructive edits. Validation is deterministic and runs against the same policy rules for both Current and Proposal. The project also includes automated unit tests and a repeatable browser-level WebMCP workflow that exercises the complete scenario multiple times from a canonical reset state. Challenges we faced One of the hardest challenges was making the agent experience meaningful without removing human control. The agent needed enough capability to inspect evidence and propose changes, while the architect still had to own policy and approval decisions. We also had to ensure that: repeated agent calls remained idempotent; Current Architecture could never be accidentally overwritten; high-level and low-level views represented the same model; validation results were deterministic; agent operations were visible and understandable; the complete product story remained clear in a demo shorter than three minutes. Working with an experimental browser API also required careful feature detection and graceful behavior in browsers where WebMCP is unavailable. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete human-agent workflow rather than a technical proof of concept. Nivra can move from architecture discovery to evidence, human policy, remediation proposal, deterministic validation, implementation planning, and a saved verified architecture branch—all inside one coherent workspace. The original Current Architecture remains available throughout the entire process. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-native applications need more than a chat interface. Agents become more useful when applications expose precise domain operations, stable identifiers, validated inputs, and observable outcomes. We also learned that a strong human-agent experience is not about maximizing autonomy. It is about giving each participant the right responsibility: the agent discovers and structures evidence, while the human owns intent and architectural decisions. What's next for Nivra Future versions could add architecture imports, collaborative multi-user workspaces, durable server-side storage, real delivery-system integrations, and connections to source control, ADRs, and work-management platforms. The long-term goal is to make architecture a living shared context for engineering teams and their agents. title: Northstar
pitch: An editable software-improvement decision workspace where humans and browser agents turn source-linked evidence, constraints, and trade-offs into a human-owned Improvement Plan.
about_excerpt: An editable software-improvement decision workspace where humans and browser agents turn source-linked evidence, constraints, and trade-offs into a human-owned Improvement Plan. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI coding tools can help non-developers build software, but deciding what should change next is still difficult. In an ordinary chat, hypotheses, counter-evidence, constraints, rejected options, and trade-offs become buried across messages. The AI may produce an answer, but the human cannot easily inspect or revise the decision that produced it. Northstar explores a different interface: a shared, visual software-improvement decision that both a person and a browser agent can work on. The controlled prototype starts with a familiar problem: “I built a RAG chatbot, but the answer quality is poor.” What it does Northstar turns software-improvement reasoning into an editable workspace. A person can: inspect competing explanations and the evidence behind them; add supporting or contradicting evidence; mark an approach as already tried; reject or deprioritize hypotheses; activate constraints; compare improvement alternatives by benefit, complexity, cost, latency, and risk; and select a preferred direction. The actual output is not a chat transcript. It is a structured Improvement Plan containing the problem, important evidence, selected explanation, selected improvement, rejected options and reasons, constraints, risks, implementation steps, and acceptance criteria. Why WebMCP WebMCP makes the workspace meaningfully better because the human and agent operate on the same structured decision state. The page exposes eight semantic tools: inspect_improvement_workspace list_code_files read_code_file add_evidence update_hypothesis record_decision begin_analysis complete_analysis A browser agent can inspect the current decision, read shared source files with numbered lines, add only source-linked evidence, and complete a review. Human changes—such as counter-evidence, rejected options, and active constraints—become inputs to the agent's next analysis instead of remaining trapped in a separate conversation. The agent cannot silently take ownership of the decision. An agent-selected alternative remains a proposal until the human confirms it. How we built it Northstar is a React and Vite single-page application deployed on Vercel. The site registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Human controls and WebMCP tools dispatch domain actions into the same reducer state. Presentation components derive the diagnosis, recommendation, alternatives, and Improvement Plan from that state. Tool contracts validate revisions, decision ownership, source file IDs, and exact one-based line ranges. The prototype intentionally has no backend, database, external API, or site-owned LLM. Code context and decision state remain in browser memory. The page supports controlled sample files as well as pasted or uploaded text-based source files. Human and agent workflow Parsing begins as the strongest explanation because several failed examples involve tables. The human adds counter-evidence: failures also happen on plain-text PDFs. The human marks prompt changes as already tried, rejects multimodal parsing because of cost, and activates a simplicity constraint. A browser agent reconsiders the current revision through WebMCP. The agent verifies claims against exact source line ranges and updates the shared decision. Retrieval becomes the leading explanation and a reranker becomes the recommended experiment. The human reviews the trade-offs, chooses the direction, and receives an updated Improvement Plan. Challenges The hardest design problem was avoiding a chatbot, admin dashboard, or RAG monitoring interface. The core visual object needed to remain a decision . We also had to make agent activity trustworthy. Northstar tracks code-context and decision revisions, hides stale recommendations, requires exact source ranges for source-derived evidence, and prevents an agent recommendation from masquerading as a human selection. Accomplishments that we're proud of A coherent human-facing product experience, not only a tool-registration demo. Eight working WebMCP tools mapped to domain concepts instead of UI button clicks. Source-linked evidence with exact file and line ranges. Visible revision and analysis states that prevent stale conclusions from appearing current. A human confirmation boundary around the preferred improvement direction. A structured Improvement Plan that can be reviewed without reading an agent transcript. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools expose the meaning of an application rather than imitate mouse interactions. The agent does not need to guess how the UI works, and the human does not need to translate every judgment back into a prompt. Both can collaborate through the application's domain model while the interface preserves context and ownership. What's next for Northstar This submission is deliberately a controlled RAG prototype, not a universal code analyzer. Next steps would include persisted decisions, broader project-context adapters, reusable decision templates, and integrations with development tools—while keeping source edits and final direction explicitly under human control. title: PDX ReviewDesk
pitch: Humans and agents review a regulated dossier in one tab. WebMCP tools call ProDocuX checks and PDX digest-bound approvals, while source PDFs never change.
about_excerpt: Humans and agents review a regulated dossier in one tab. WebMCP tools call ProDocuX checks and PDX digest-bound approvals, while source PDFs never change. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A product specification, an approved formula, and a certificate of analysis can disagree, and they often do. The specification still names formula revision 2 while the master formula is already revision 3. The certificate reports a pH the specification does not allow. A human reviewer can see that if the three PDFs are on one desk. An agent usually cannot: it scrapes a UI, invents a side channel, or silently edits the wrong bytes. WebMCP is the missing control surface. The page should be the MCP server. The agent should call the same actions the reviewer sees, on the same documents, with the same results. Checks should not live in the frontend. Approvals should bind to digests, not to a screenshot of a button. That is the inspiration for PDX ReviewDesk: one tab where humans and agents share a regulated dossier, while published ProDocuX and PDX Artifact Engine do the work the page must not invent. What it does As a MVP showcase, ReviewDesk is a WebMCP workspace for dossier review. The live demo is Harbor Calm Serum: the product specification is the subject; the formula and certificate are references. The page walks Documents → Findings → Corrections → Close. Start the demo. ProDocuX verifies a typed evidence bundle and flags the planted disagreements (formula revision, pH range). PDX opens a digest-bound checkpoint. The agent focuses a finding and opens the governing source PDF in the same tab. A correction rewrites normalized evidence only. Source PDF bytes and digests never change. Commit re-runs ProDocuX and replaces the PDX checkpoint. An observed fact (the pH) can be confirmed without rewriting the certificate. Human-only approval stays on the UI. There is no WebMCP tool that approves the checkpoint. Registered tools include start_demo_audit , get_workspace_state , select_finding , open_source_document , propose_correction , commit_correction , and confirm_observed_fact . execute() hits the same FastAPI routes the page uses, so the workspace updates in place. No login. Judges can open https://pdx-reviewdesk.onrender.com/ in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or in Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled. How we built it The UI is Vite and React. On every run-state change it aborts the previous registration and calls document.modelContext.registerTool for the tools that are currently enabled. Each tool’s execute() function is a real workspace mutation, not a prompt that describes the UI. The API is FastAPI. It consumes published PyPI packages: prodocux==0.3.0rc4 for verify_evidence_bundle pdx-artifact-engine==0.3.0a4 for checkpoint open/replace and the approval ledger GET /health publishes those installed versions. CI asserts they load from site-packages . Authorization does not trust JSON actor or channel . The page session cookie plus a capability header decide whether a call is treated as UI or WebMCP. Human-only approval at the current demo is a channel boundary, not cryptographic proof that a person pressed the button. The hosted app is one Python process that serves /v1 , /health , and the built SPA on Render. Challenges we ran into Keeping WebMCP honest was harder than registering tools. If execute() does not change the page, the agent is just narrating. If the API trusts a body field named actor , the agent can pretend to be the human. We had to make the session cookie and capability header the only authorization, and keep approval off the tool catalog. Render’s Free plan does not attach a disk, so runs are ephemeral and the service spins down when idle. That is acceptable for judging. It is not how a durable review desk would store an approval ledger. Accomplishments that we're proud of A WebMCP tool call updates the same documents, findings, and checkpoint the human is looking at. Verification and digest-bound checkpoints come from published products, not from a page-local reimplementation. Source PDFs are immutable. Corrections cannot launder a new file in as the original. The tool surface cannot approve. The human gate is visible and boring, which is what we wanted. The live URL, public Apache-2.0 repository, and /health pins are all checkable without a login. What we learned WebMCP is not a second kernel. It is how an agent holds the same desk as the human. The valuable tools are state-dependent: you cannot commit a correction that does not exist, and you should not be able to approve through the agent channel. On the other hand, the security claim is important. A channel boundary is not a hardware attestation. It has to be emphasized before talking about “human in the loop.” What's next for PDX ReviewDesk Review is the first slice, not the final product. The desk should become a place where humans and agents co-author the packet, not only argue about PDFs that already exist. Next, an agent will fill important documents from files the human names or from search results it is allowed to use. The human stays on the same page, watches the draft appear, corrects it, and accepts it. When the packet is agreed, ReviewDesk exports the specified formats - the durable path for verification and digest-bound artifacts is already the published ProDocuX and PDX Artifact Engine stack. The review tools stay. They become the acceptance pass over a jointly written dossier, instead of the whole story. title: Pixael
pitch: A pixel-art sprite studio where humans and AI share one canvas.
about_excerpt: A pixel-art sprite studio where humans and AI share one canvas. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Watch your animation Edit your frames Manage your assets Edit your sprites Pixael!! Connect your AI Inspiration I've spent more hours redrawing walk cycles pixel-by-pixel than actually building the games they were for. Sprite work is one of those things everyone assumes is quick, it isn't. At the same time, AI has gotten genuinely good at generating pixel art, but every tool treats it as a one-shot image: no memory of your last frame, no shared palette, no way to nudge a single pixel afterward. It generates around your project, not inside it. WebMCP looked like a real answer to that gap, a way to let an agent work inside the same live tool a human uses, instead of handing back a disconnected PNG. Pixael is what that looks like for pixel-art sprites specifically. What it does Pixael is a pixel-art sprite studio for creating, animating, and exporting 2D game assets — and every meaningful action in it is also a WebMCP tool, so a human and an AI agent can work on the same live canvas. Full pixel editor: pencil, eraser, bucket fill, eyedropper, lines, rectangles, undo/redo, zoom, onion skinning Multi-state animation system (Idle, Walk, Attack, Hurt, etc.) with per-state frame timelines and adjustable-FPS playback Multi-asset project management with categories, palettes, and PNG/sprite-sheet export Zero login, zero backend everything saves locally via IndexedDB, works the moment you open it 37 WebMCP tools spanning asset management, animation states, frame editing, three tiers of pixel manipulation, palette control, and export registered through document.modelContext.registerTool An agent can create a character, add an animation, edit specific pixels, fix a visual bug, or export a sprite sheet using the exact same operations the UI calls, nothing simulated or faked. How we built it React + TypeScript on Vite, with a strict layered architecture: UI components never touch state directly, they call a pure, deterministic domain layer ( assetOperations , animationOperations , frameOperations , pixelOperations , paletteOperations , exportOperations ), which sits on top of an authoritative project store with full undo/redo, plus isolated stores for playback and editor tool state so a 60fps animation preview doesn't re-render the whole app. Persistence is IndexedDB with debounced autosave and a graceful in-memory fallback if it's unavailable. The WebMCP layer was built as a thin registration module wrapping that same domain layer. Two design decisions mattered most: pixel data is transmitted as palette-index + run-length encoding rather than raw pixel arrays or images, keeping a typical frame read to roughly 100–300 tokens instead of 600+; and pixel editing is split into three tiers (full-frame rewrite, targeted coordinate patches, and shape/transform operations like flood fill and line draw) so an agent picks the cheapest tool for the job instead of rewriting an entire canvas for a one-pixel fix. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is genuinely new. The flag needed for testing ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) only works on recent Chrome builds, and even the correct API surface shifted under us mid-build ( navigator.modelContext vs. document.modelContext across different docs and spec drafts). Chrome's native tool-result contract also turned out to be string-only no structured image content blocks like backend MCP supports which meant redesigning how the agent gets visual feedback, leaning on the compact RLE pixel format as the primary channel instead of images. And with a hard four-day runway from architecture decision to submission, we had to be disciplined about which tools were "genuinely useful agent capability" versus "nice to have" to hit both breadth and reliability in time. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full 36-tool surface actually works end-to-end, verified through both the Model Context Tool Inspector extension and ChatGPT's in-app browser not a demo of one tool, a real one covering asset creation, animation, pixel editing, and export. It's held up across different model sizes too, including smaller/cheaper models, which we take as a sign the tool schemas carry enough signal on their own rather than relying on a large model to compensate for ambiguity. And in testing, agents completed genuinely non-trivial multi-step tasks in a single instruction resizing a sprite and adding a held item consistently across four animation frames, or diagnosing and correcting a specific pixel-level bug in an existing sprite without us hand-holding the request. What we learned Schema clarity matters more than model size the clearest signal came from watching a smaller model succeed at multi-step tasks because the tool contracts left little room for ambiguity, not because it was a bigger model doing more inference work. We also learned the token economics of data representation are a real design constraint for agent-facing tools, not an afterthought RLE vs. raw pixel arrays was a multi-hundred-token difference per call, which adds up fast across an editing session. And architecting the domain layer for automation from day one before WebMCP was even in the picture made the actual integration almost mechanical; retrofitting agent tools onto UI-coupled logic would have been a much harder rebuild. What's next for Pixael Batch and multi-select operations so an agent can act across several frames or assets in one call instead of one-at-a-time. Undo-aware agent tools that can reason about and revert their own multi-step changes. Broader testing across WebMCP-capable surfaces as the standard matures beyond Chrome and ChatGPT's in-app browser. And of course improving the quality and performance. title: Places
pitch: A live floorplan you share with an agent. You pin what's non-negotiable. Then you rearrange the room together, the agent cannot move anyone you pinned.
about_excerpt: A live floorplan you share with an agent. You pin what's non-negotiable. Then you rearrange the room together, the agent cannot move anyone you pinned. Like Comment Story Updates Places is a live floorplan. You pin what's non-negotiable. Then you and an agent rearrange the same room, the agent cannot move anyone you pinned. Inspiration Seating a company dinner is still a spreadsheet and an argument. The room matters. The rules matter. HR stays away from engineering. The CEO sits at the head of the center table. A few people need the aisle. A plus-one is still on the way. By the time the chart leaves the sheet, it is already wrong. A constraint solver dumps a list. A group chat dumps a thread. Neither is the room. I wanted one canvas where the host and the model share the same seats, and where “Mabel stays at the window” is not a prompt. It is a pin. Because she is pinned, move_guest is gone. WebMCP is a capability bus for a live page, not a cart API. Pins, aisle seats, and “do not sit together” pairs are page state. Scraping the SVG drops them. The agent has to call tools, and the tool list itself is the contract. The hundred-person problem is the category. The demo is twenty-two, same job, at a scale the canvas can prove. How I built it The page is ground truth. Drag, pin, plus-one, and every agent write go through the same executeCommand() in web/lib/places/commands.ts . A tool call moves a place-card on the SVG you are looking at. There is no backend, no login, and no API key. State lives in sessionStorage for the current tab. document.modelContext.registerTool exposes a stable read/rule set: get_room_state , list_violations , explain_guest , add_guest , list_constraints , add_constraint , remove_constraint . Selection, pins, and open violations abort the previous AbortController and register only the tools that make sense now. When Tools the agent can see A table is selected seat_guest_here , set_capacity , leave_empty_seats An unpinned guest is selected pin_guest , move_guest , swap_guests A pinned guest is selected unpin_guest only The room has violations fix_violations (never moves pins) There is no always-on move_guest(guestId, tableId) . You choose the contract. The agent works inside it. If document.modelContext is missing, the human controls still work. The header badge says so. The seed is a fictional Thursday: four tables, pixel-art guests, rules you can point at. Rex and Vivian cannot share a table. Arthur needs the aisle. Two chairs are held empty. Each load picks one of four opening problems ( ?seed=0 through ?seed=3 ) so a judge can share a messy room, not a blank grid. The solver is a deterministic hill-climb over pairwise swaps. It scores the room as $$S = \sum_{v} w(v),\quad w(v)=\begin{cases}10 & \text{hard}\ 3 & \text{preference}\end{cases}$$ then reports why it stopped: solved , blocked_by_pins , infeasible (with a proof), or no_arrangement_found . Same room, same answer, every time, which is what the tests and the timeline need. The stack is a Vinext/React page on ChatGPT Sites. Domain logic is isolated under web/lib/places/ . CI runs unit tests, WebMCP eval fixtures, typecheck, lint, and format. The evals replay tool traces against the real registrations without calling a model or spending a key. Challenges The tool list had to be the lock. A prompt that says “don't move pinned guests” is a suggestion. Unregistering move_guest is a lock. Getting that to update on every pin and selection, without racing the previous AbortController , was the WebMCP work. The fixture respect-pin-when-reflow-is-blocked forbids unpin_guest , move_guest , and swap_guests , and expects blocked_by_pins . Honesty beats a pretty rearrange. Hill-climbing gets stuck. A better arrangement may exist only if you move a pin. I had to distinguish “the pins are in the way” from “the hard rules are impossible” from “the search gave up.” The solver runs once with pins respected, once with pins relaxed, and only then returns blocked_by_pins with the guests at fault. It never overrides the host. The room had to stay a product. An empty grid is a proof of concept. A messy dinner is a job. Building a cast, a floorplan, a timeline, undo/redo, JSON import/export, and a PNG save took as much care as the tools. If the human half is a toy, the shared room is a toy. CI cannot pretend it is ChatGPT. Model selection is probabilistic and costs money. The eval fixtures describe representative journeys (read the room, fix it, pin blocks, plus-one, add a rule) and replay them deterministically. Live-browser trials still matter. They are not the merge gate. What I learned WebMCP is not “expose every action as a tool.” It is exposing the right contract at the right moment. The interesting part is what the agent cannot see. People are good at naming constraints. Models are good at searching a room. That split only works if both hands write to the same state. Same executeCommand() whether I drag a seat or the agent calls a tool. A pin is stronger than a system prompt. blocked_by_pins is a feature. The host stays in charge. Pin what's non-negotiable. Rearrange the rest together.
