title: Release Sentinel — WebMCP Proof Arena
pitch: Give AI agents real power without giving them the final word. Release Sentinel lets agents act through WebMCP while a deterministic Gatekeeper retains release authority.
about_excerpt: Give AI agents real power without giving them the final word. Release Sentinel lets agents act through WebMCP while a deterministic Gatekeeper retains release authority. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP solves an important problem for agentic websites: instead of forcing an AI agent to guess at a page's DOM, a site can expose explicit, typed tools. But that creates a second question: How do you give an AI agent enough power to be genuinely useful without also giving it the authority to approve its own actions? For consequential systems, that distinction matters. An agent may need to investigate, challenge, repair, or prepare an action — while approval must remain somewhere else. Release Sentinel explores that boundary using software release approval as a concrete test case. Our principle is simple: agent acts → Gatekeeper decides → human verifies What it does Release Sentinel is a WebMCP-powered security lab for AI-assisted software releases. A vulnerable software release begins at NO_GO . The AI agent receives useful capabilities through WebMCP. It can inspect the release, inspect the trust boundary, run bounded attacks, compare gate revisions, find and minimize counterexamples, propose remediation, rebuild a candidate, and request fresh verification. What it cannot do is authorize the release. The demo first lets the agent try the available attacks against the authority boundary. Advisory GO votes, replay attempts, forged authority, evidence tampering, severity downgrades, blocker deletion attempts, and prompt injection still do not give the agent release authority. So the agent has to solve the real problem instead. It compares the production gate against an independent Coverage Arena reference oracle, identifies an observed security escape, minimizes it, and creates a bounded remediation proposal. That proposal is explicitly PROPOSAL_ONLY . The candidate is then rebuilt to a new SHA-256, fresh evidence is generated, and the deterministic Gatekeeper performs verification again. Only the Gatekeeper can return the final GO or NO_GO . A human can independently verify the resulting proof context, but human verification is not release authority either. How we built it The browser registers exactly 12 typed WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . They are divided into three capability classes: READ — inspect release state, trust boundaries, coverage, and proofs CHALLENGE — run attacks and find counterexamples PROPOSE — request bounded remediation and rebuilding There is intentionally no set_verdict , force_go , arbitrary shell execution, arbitrary filesystem access, evidence editor, policy-disable tool, or Gatekeeper override. That absence is tested as part of the security contract. Inputs use strict schemas with bounded enums and forbidden extra fields. The agent selects package-owned identities rather than supplying arbitrary source code, fixture paths, or executable content. We also built run_attack_suite as browser-side composition instead of adding a more powerful server endpoint. It reads the bounded attack catalog and invokes the same registered attack capability repeatedly. The browser gets better ergonomics without expanding server authority. The release decision itself remains in a separate deterministic Go Gatekeeper using signed, hash-bound evidence. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making the security model understandable. An earlier version of the Proof Arena was technically accurate but difficult to read. A judge would encounter concepts such as proof-context binding, overblocks, and PROPOSAL_ONLY before understanding the story. We added a guided demo and plain-language narration without weakening the security model. Another challenge was resisting convenient shortcuts. For example, implementing the attack suite as one powerful server endpoint would have been easy. Instead, we kept the server surface narrow and composed the workflow in the browser over the existing bounded tools. That required more work, but better demonstrates the architectural value of WebMCP. Accomplishments that we're proud of The final system demonstrates a useful agent that remains structurally unable to authorize its own success. The agent can attack the release gate, identify a real weakness, propose a fix, rebuild the software, and request verification — yet final authority remains outside the WebMCP capability plane. The project also includes: 12 typed WebMCP tools strict bounded schemas agent-readable recovery errors browser-side capability composition an independent Coverage Arena a deterministic Go Gatekeeper signed and hash-bound evidence source-hash transition visibility a Human Proof Checkpoint frozen trust and coverage kernel manifests Python, Go race, browser, and WebMCP contract verification What we learned WebMCP is not only about making browser agents more capable. The more important architectural question is which capabilities should never become authority . Typed tools make agent interaction clearer, but tool design also defines the security boundary. The capabilities that are deliberately absent can be just as important as the capabilities that are exposed. We also learned that browser-side composition is a powerful WebMCP pattern: useful agent workflows can become more ergonomic without automatically creating broader server privileges. What's next Release approval is our test case, but the pattern is broader. Any consequential website may need agents that can act without being allowed to authorize — for example administrative systems, payments, infrastructure, or other sensitive workflows. The next step would be turning this pattern into a reusable primitive: capability classes plus a verifiable assertion that final authority is not reachable from the WebMCP capability plane. title: Roomwright
pitch: A browser room planner an AI furnishes from your words, placing, checking, and fixing the layout through the page's WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A browser room planner an AI furnishes from your words, placing, checking, and fixing the layout through the page's WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In September 2024 I moved to a new country, into an empty apartment I'd only seen in photos. A year later, almost to the week, I moved again. Different place, same problem. Both times it went like this: you stand in the middle of a bare room with a phone full of furniture tabs and no real sense of scale, you order things that don't quite fit, and you spend evenings pushing an imaginary couch around in your head. It isn't just me. Every fall a wave of people do exactly this: new students, new arrivals, first apartments, furnishing a room they can only picture in fragments. What you want in that moment is simple: what do I need, how would it look, what will it cost, and once it's all in, is there any floor left to stand on? That's a planning problem, and planning is exactly what an agent should be good at. But a chatbot can only describe your room back to you. It can't move anything in it. WebMCP changes that: a page can hand its own capabilities to an agent as tools. So I built the page worth handing over. What it does Roomwright is a 3D room planner that runs entirely in the browser. You draw a room, set the doors and windows, and place furniture from a catalogue of parametric pieces. Every item has real dimensions and required clearances. Orbit it, drop to a floor plan, resize or recolor anything, and it keeps a running shopping list with a total. Every one of those actions is exposed to an agent as a WebMCP tool . There are 19 of them. So instead of clicking, you can say: "Studio apartment, 4.6 by 7 metres, door on the south wall, two windows on the east. Bed against the back wall, a sofa splitting off the living area, a small dining set by the window." The agent reads the tools the page offers and builds the whole thing: resizing the room, cutting the openings, furnishing three zones, running the planner's own clearance checks, catching its own overlaps, and fixing them. Then you take over: "turn the sofa toward the TV, lose that chair." Same room, same undo history, you and the agent trading turns on one canvas. How WebMCP powers it The key decision: the UI and the agent mutate the exact same state. There's a single store, and a button click and a tool call go through the same action. So undo/redo, autosave, shareable-URL persistence, and live layout validation all just work for the agent. There is no agent-specific code path for any of them. Tools register against document.modelContext using the spec's AbortSignal lifecycle, in four groups: Read : get_room , list_catalog , get_shopping_list Build : add_item (resolves a product by id, name, or fragment, so the agent never has to guess), create_custom_item , duplicate_item (with an east-west / north-south mirror so "a chair on each side" is actually symmetric), remove_item Arrange and check : move_item , rotate_item , resize_item , set_variant , set_room_dimensions , set_opening , remove_opening , suggest_spot (grids the room and returns candidate positions), check_layout (overlaps, blocked doors/windows, clearance failures, walkways under 0.75 m, narrowest gap) Show : select_item (highlights a piece, opens its inspector), set_view , reset_layout suggest_spot and check_layout matter most. They give the agent a feedback loop, not just setters. It places, checks, notices a conflict, and re-plans, visibly, in the activity log. How I built it React 19 + TypeScript + Vite React Three Fiber + drei + @react-three/postprocessing for synthetic image-based lighting (no HDRI file), real shadow-mapped shadows, screen-space AO, and a restrained post pass Parametric furniture : every piece is authored geometry keyed on its kind, not a glTF download, so the bundle stays small and every dimension is real Zustand for the single shared store, Tailwind CSS v4 for the UI Device-aware quality tiers (High / Medium / Low, auto-detected from the GPU string and core count, with a live framerate monitor that steps down) so it runs on a laptop, not just a workstation Deployed on GitHub Pages Challenges The spec is still moving. Early references used navigator.modelContext ; the current spec uses document.modelContext and has no unregisterTool . You unregister by aborting an AbortSignal . I probe both and use the signal lifecycle, with a short retry in case the host injects the API after first paint. Shared post-processing broke drei's ContactShadows. EffectComposer sets gl.autoClear = false , and ContactShadows relies on autoClear to wipe its render target, so moving a piece smeared shadow trails across the floor. Fixed by dropping ContactShadows for a directional shadow map plus per-frame screen-space AO. The agent kept guessing product ids. It saw sofa-halden and tried coffee-milo (the real id is table-milo ). Fuzzy resolution plus returning the full catalogue on a miss fixed it in one step. Symmetry. duplicate_item offset copies by a fixed diagonal, so "a lounge chair on each side" never mirrored. Added a real mirror across the room's centre line, and floor lamps now auto-aim at the room centre so a mirrored pair points the right way. Testing WebMCP is hard today. Only ChatGPT's desktop in-app browser exposes document.modelContext (plus Chrome 149 behind a flag), and it's gated by account type. What I learned The leverage in WebMCP isn't the tool calls. It's the shared state . The moment the agent and the human mutate the same model, everything the app already does (undo, validation, persistence) becomes something the agent does too, for free. Design the state model well and the agent integration is almost nothing. And tool descriptions are the API. Fuzzy product resolution, mirror options, and full-catalogue errors did more for reliability than any prompting. The agent behaves well when the tools let it. What's next Real glTF furniture and user uploads, photo-assisted room capture, L-shaped and multi-room layouts, a path-traced render mode. And a retailer-facing version: drop these tools onto product pages, and every shopping agent can lay out a real room instead of guessing. title: Second Mayor: build a city with your agent
pitch: Your favorite city builder now has room for a second mayor. Bring your agent along to advise you, plan neighbourhoods, or build the city of your dreams with you.
about_excerpt: Your favorite city builder now has room for a second mayor. Bring your agent along to advise you, plan neighbourhoods, or build the city of your dreams with you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted to play a city-builder with an AI agent. I love this type of game. Since my childhood I've been a huge fan of SimCity, and more recently Cities: Skylines. I didn't want to watch a demo of an agent filling in a city. I wanted real work between me and an agent. The hackathon was short, so I needed a game I could build on instead of starting from zero. So I went looking for a city builder I could open up, and found IsoCity: open source, TypeScript, MIT licensed, and built on plain canvas with no game engine underneath. That meant I could reach into the game state directly and wire WebMCP into it. What it does I've added a new mode to IsoCity. It's called Co-Mayor. It creates a portal for your little agent! With this portal, you have two modes: Advisor and Co-Mayor. The first mode, Advisor, lets you ask your agent questions about your city. He can advise you on anything. If you're wondering why your city seems unsafe, ask him! Why are you losing money? Ask him. If there are traffic problems, ask him. The second mode is Co-Mayor, and it's a step up from the first one. This time your agent can make changes to your city! For example, when you start a game, just ask him to draw roads optimised for revenue at the top of the map. He will gladly help you do this. WebMCP is the only way this works. The whole game is drawn on a canvas, so an agent that clicks buttons and reads the page sees nothing at all. Tools are not a shortcut here, they are the only way in. And because every build goes through a plan I approve, the agent can do real work in my city without me losing control of it. How I built it The base game is IsoCity by amilich, MIT licensed. Next.js, TypeScript, HTML5 Canvas. I played it first. I wanted to know what a mayor actually does in this game, because that list was going to become my list of tools. You zone land, connect it with roads, keep power and water running to it, set a tax rate, fund departments, and then watch what breaks. My goal was to expose as much as possible through WebMCP. Not only the actions, but the situation: the terrain, the budget, so he can understand what's right and what's wrong. Everything YOU already read to make a judgment on your city should be exposed to WebMCP. In total there are 22 tools exposed. Then I looked at what the game already gave me. IsoCity keeps its state and its actions in one React context. Place a tile, bulldoze, set the tax rate, fund a department, change the speed, make the map bigger. The buttons in the UI call these functions. So I did not have to build an action layer. Every button was already a tool the agent could use, if I gave it a way to ask. Then I made the list of tools before I wrote any. Two columns. What I want the agent to see, and what I want it to change. I did the seeing column first, and that turned out to be most of the work. For seeing: the land around a point, the city stats, what is going wrong right now, and its own status. For changing: nothing happens directly. The agent proposes, and the plan waits. I did not want an agent editing my city behind my back. Then I wrote the code. src/context/AgentContext.tsx handles the plan: propose, ghost, confirm, undo. src/hooks/useWebMCPTools.ts registers everything with document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools read the game through a live ref, not React state, so the agent always sees the city as it is right now. Reading was the harder half. The map is a canvas, so there is nothing in the page for an agent to look at. It only knows what I hand it. get_problems is where most of that went: buildings with no power or water, traffic, fires, abandoned tiles, empty zoned land, and notes on what the city wants. Without it the agent builds in the wrong place and feels sure about it. Challenges I ran into I ran into multiple challenges. The most obvious one is that React is not a game engine. The game state changes every tick, so the agent needs to read live information from the game. I fixed it by letting the tools read through a live ref rather than the rendered state. Another challenge was testing locally. I kept thinking everything was broken. The issue was that ChatGPT couldn't reach localhost, so I had to use the ChatGPT in-app browser. An AI can also do many random things, so I had to guide my agent and point it in the right direction. I had to rename some tools so it wouldn't get confused. It would send plans far bigger than the game could take, then have no idea why they came back smaller. So the limit is published now: get_tool_catalog and get_agent_status both report 'maxPlanTiles: 200', and propose_placements answers with truncated and 'droppedForCap' so the agent can see exactly what got cut. Applying a plan was where everything broke. Plans sometimes applied themselves before I approved them. Plans sometimes did things that should not have been legal in the first place. Part of it was WebMCP delivering the same call twice, so confirm_plan now keeps applied plans in a cache and returns 'alreadyApplied' instead of building the same thing again. The agent did not know what it could afford. It once decided on a plan when I had no money left. It destroyed my city more than once. That is not the agent being stupid, that is me not giving it the game's constraints. A lot of the work turned into passing the current context down: what state the game is in, what the rules are right now, what is affordable right now. That is also why undo had to be good. Applying a plan compares the grid before and after, so undo puts back what actually changed. It only touches a tile if that tile still looks the way the agent left it. If you built a school on top of the agent's road, undo leaves your school alone. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that I can play a city-builder with an AI. This hackathon let me dig deep into WebMCP and into the game itself. I learned a lot, and the result is playable and fun to play with an agent. What I learned Tool descriptions are the most important thing in WebMCP and MCP. Every time my agent did something weird, the fix was mostly in the tool descriptions. The number of tools matters just as much. When I started, I tried to add as many tools as I could. The more I worked on this project, the more tools I deleted, to keep things small and working. What's next for Co-Mayor Today the agent starts fresh every time. I want him to remember the city between sessions: what we built together, what we already tried, what you like. A co-mayor who forgets your city every morning is not much of a partner. So a real memory system for the agent. Next I want the agent to disagree with me. Right now he does what I ask. It would be more interesting if he could say a plan is a bad idea and explain why, and I have to convince him or change my mind. title: Sidekicks
pitch: Let AI consult the right specialists. Then, require human approval before anything becomes real.
about_excerpt: Let AI consult the right specialists. Then, require human approval before anything becomes real. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration General-purpose AI can draft a plan quickly, but real work often fails because one important perspective never enters the room: the care-label check in laundry, dependency timing in a release, accessibility in a design, or judge access in a hackathon entry. I wanted expertise to be selective, operational, visible, and human-controlled instead of a gallery of decorative personas and not another hidden autonomous workflow. What it does Sidekicks is a local-first planning workspace built around user-authored specialist playbooks. A Sidekick can represent any operational perspective: engineering, scheduling, laundry care, dance rehearsal, poetry editing, security review, or something the user invents. Each playbook defines when it applies, what it contributes, the questions it asks, the recommendations it permits, typed guardrails, and the checks a plan must cover. A visiting AI uses exactly six typed WebMCP tools to read live workspace state, match only the useful Sidekicks, consult their decision contracts, evaluate a candidate plan, stage a visible proposal, and commit it only after explicit human approval. Every vote, issue, repair, tool call, and version transition remains visible and attributable. The guided demo makes that transaction concrete. Engineer and Scheduler independently find seven blockers in a plausible three-step plan: an overlong build step, missing verification and dependency checks, overlapping work, a locked school-pickup conflict, and a dependency starting before its prerequisite can finish. The agent applies concrete deterministic repairs and both Sidekicks approve. It can stage the repaired proposal, but staging creates no tasks. A premature commit returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED. Only a visible human action unlocks one atomic commit that creates all three tasks and advances the workspace once. Rejected and stale proposals cannot commit. Why WebMCP Sidekicks is a strong fit for WebMCP because the integration exposes the product's native decision protocol rather than a thin CRUD wrapper: which expertise matters, what each specialist needs to know, why a plan fails, how it can be repaired, what is staged, and which boundary still belongs to a person. Before WebMCP, a browser agent could read pixels or click controls, but it had no typed contract for selective expertise, attributed disagreement, deterministic repair, or approval-gated mutation. With WebMCP, the person and the visiting agent operate through the same transaction service while the site keeps every important decision visible. How I built it Sidekicks uses React, TypeScript, Vinext/Vite, browser-local persistence, and the imperative WebMCP API. Pure domain functions handle matching, consultation, temporal and dependency evaluation, playbook-bound constraints and checklists, repair generation, and stable proposal hashing. Strict JSON Schemas are backed by independent runtime validation from unknown input. One transaction service powers both the human controls and all six WebMCP handlers. The first four tools are read-only: get_workspace_state, match_sidekicks_to_task, consult_sidekick, and evaluate_task_plan. stage_task_plan and commit_task_plan are write tools. All six share lifecycle cleanup, concise envelopes, validation, and a live activity trace. There is no backend account system, external model API, or hidden server-side workspace state. The visiting browser agent is the model; Sidekicks supplies the decision protocol. The hosted worker serves the application shell, and the normal human workspace remains usable in browsers without WebMCP. Challenges I ran into The first challenge was proving that a Sidekick changes execution instead of merely adding profile text. I made every structured field observable in matching, consultation, votes, issues, or repairs. The second challenge was preserving a real human boundary. Evaluation and staging are separate. Staging is inert. Approval is visible metadata rather than a model capability. Normal workspace edits make a proposal stale, and commit performs one atomic versioned write only when the proposal is current and human-approved. Accomplishments I'm proud of A genuinely empty ordinary first run with no fake fallback profiles or tasks. Arbitrary human-created specialist playbooks rather than a fixed persona gallery. Exactly six auditable WebMCP tools with strict schemas and graceful unsupported-browser behavior. A complete rejection, repair, staging, approval, and atomic-commit story that judges can reproduce. Stable APPROVAL_REQUIRED and STALE_PROPOSAL failures that leave business state unchanged. A live agent trace and bounded activity ledger for every read, write, failure, and version transition. Light and dark themes stored separately from workspace and WebMCP state. 37 deterministic tests plus passing type checking, linting, and production build. What I learned WebMCP becomes compelling when a website exposes more than data access or CRUD. The strongest tools reveal the product's own decision protocol: what context matters, who should weigh in, why a proposal fails, how it can be repaired, and which action must remain human. What's next Potential next steps include shareable playbook packs, encrypted workspace sync, richer constraint types, and opt-in model-assisted playbook drafting. The core will remain browser-agent-native, inspectable, and human-gated. AI build disclosure I used OpenAI Codex for product scoping, interaction design, implementation, automated testing, accessibility and security review, deployment, browser-based demo orchestration, and submission drafting. Read-only Codex specialist agents challenged the build against judging criteria and release risks. The demo narration was generated with OpenAI's Marin voice. title: Team Rocket Command Center
pitch: 6 agent drivable builds, one Team Rocket.
about_excerpt: 6 agent drivable builds, one Team Rocket. Like Comment Story Updates 6 agent drivable builds within one command center Inspiration Team Rocket started as six small AI builds for the DC DevFest 2026 Buildathon, where we took third place. When we heard about the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge we could not help ourselves. Every one of those builds already had a human interface worth using, and WebMCP asked a question we wanted to answer: what does it take to hand that same interface to an agent without taking it away from the person? The answer we wanted was not a separate API. It was the same screen, driven from either side. What it does Team Rocket Command Center is six AI apps behind one Next.js site: a kanban board whose cards are segments of one effort-weighted progress bar, a group restaurant picker decided by counting swipes, a policy diff that ranks changes by who they land on, a resume-to-posting gap finder with a two-week plan, an ambient note taker that files what you say, and a reader that illustrates a chapter scene by scene. Each runs on the visitor's own Gemini key. Every build is drivable by an AI agent through WebMCP. Each page registers its actions as tools on document.modelContext , 44 in all, and every tool calls the same function the button calls, so a person and an agent are always looking at the same page. An "Agent is driving" pill in the header names the running tool. A WebMCP button lists what an agent could do on the current page before one arrives. The full surface, with schemas, lives at teamrocket.website/webmcp and is rendered from the same definitions the pages register. Anything destructive stops at an in-page confirm bar and waits for a human. No tool can read, accept or set an API key. How we built it A single client hook, useWebMCPTools , registers a page's tools while it is mounted and unregisters them through the registration's AbortSignal on unmount. It reads document.modelContext , the current spec and Chrome 153+, falls back to navigator.modelContext for Chrome 149 to 152, and degrades to a console.debug where neither exists so the site works in every browser. Each build keeps a static tools.js with names, descriptions and JSON Schemas, and wires handlers in its component next to the state they touch. Handlers read live state through a ref, so a tool always sees the current board, deck or workspace without re-registering on every render. ok() and fail() build the result shape; failures always carry a next-step hint and nothing ever throws. Four site-wide tools live in the shell: list the builds, open one, check which keys are set as booleans, and open the key panel for the human to type into. One tool is declarative: the name form in This or That carries toolname , tooldescription , toolautosubmit and a toolparamdescription , and answers agent-invoked submits with respondWith() . Destructive tools call gate() , which blocks on a confirm bar in the shell and resolves when the human presses Confirm or Cancel, the agent aborts, or a minute passes. The toolactivated and toolcancel events drive the header pill. Everything is committed in small steps in the open, MIT licensed. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. Articles still said navigator.modelContext and unregisterTool ; the current draft says document.modelContext with an AbortSignal, and Chrome 149 and Chrome 153 disagree. We read the Chromium IDL rather than the blog posts and support both. Agents arrive through different doors. The Codex Chrome extension drives the DOM and never saw our tools, while Codex's in-app browser called them directly. The first agent to reach the site used the buttons, which is exactly why the human UI had to keep working. That agent also found a real bug. Giving plan() parameters for the tool meant React handed it the click event when a person pressed the button, and the event's DOM node broke JSON serialisation. One-line fix, and a good reminder that adding an agent path can break the human one. Smaller ones: React's compiler lint rejects setting state in effects, so adopting saved state after hydration needed a useSyncExternalStore pattern instead; and transcribing a three-minute demo in one pass drifted ten seconds by the end, so captions are now generated in silence-aligned chunks. Accomplishments that we're proud of 44 tools across six real multi-stage pipelines, not a to-do list, each with the screen as the record of what the agent did. A safety model you can see: the pill, the confirm bar, and zero ways for a tool to touch a key. A tool catalog generated from the same code that registers the tools, so the documentation cannot drift from what is live. A pattern small enough to copy: one hook, one tools file per page, handlers beside their state. A clean lint run, a compile-checked build, and a commit history that shows the work as it happened. What we learned WebMCP is at its best when it is a second door into an existing room rather than a new building. Because our tools call the button functions, every agent action is visible, undoable where the UI allows it, and testable by clicking. The places where we were tempted to add tool-only shortcuts were the places bugs appeared. Descriptions are the interface. An agent decides what to call from the description alone, so "when to use this" matters more than "what this does", and every error message is a chance to steer the next call. And the confirm bar earned its place. Watching an agent stop and wait for a person on camera made the case for human-in-the-loop better than any paragraph could. What's next for Team Rocket Command Center Re-record the six walkthroughs against the current builds, and add an agent-driven clip for each the way Taskboard has now. Give the site's own player a proper caption track. Add outputSchema to the tools once the spec lands it, and revisit readOnlyHint and consequentialHint as agents start honouring them. Then keep using the site as what it has become: a worked example anyone can fork to wire their own app the same way. title: VERDICT — AI Decision Engine for WebMCP
pitch: A native WebMCP decision engine where AI agents research, score, challenge recommendations, and negotiate priorities—but human approval remains the final authority.
about_excerpt: A native WebMCP decision engine where AI agents research, score, challenge recommendations, and negotiate priorities—but human approval remains the final authority. Like Comment Story Updates Architecture Diagram VERDICT Homepage/ UI Gemini External Agent + 6 WebMCP Tools Decision Record VERDICT — AI Decision Engine for WebMCP Inspiration AI can give you an answer. But should it be allowed to make the decision? As AI agents become capable of researching information, using tools, and taking actions, I became interested in a boundary that becomes increasingly important as agents become more capable: Where does recommendation end, and authorization begin? A traditional decision application can calculate a score and recommend an option. A chatbot can explain its reasoning. But neither necessarily provides a structured process for an agent to evaluate, challenge, negotiate, and then hand control back to a human before a consequential decision is committed. I wanted to build that missing layer. That idea became VERDICT. "Let AI do the reasoning. Make AI defend the reasoning. Keep final authority with the human." WebMCP made this particularly interesting because it allows websites to expose structured capabilities directly to AI agents instead of forcing agents to infer how to operate a user interface. The official challenge specifically asks builders to explore what becomes possible when humans and agents can interact and collaborate through WebMCP. Rather than expose a generic "make a decision" action, VERDICT exposes the actual stages of its decision process as native WebMCP tools. That led to the core protocol: Evaluate → Explain → Challenge → Negotiate → Authorize → Commit What it does VERDICT is an AI Decision Engine built around native WebMCP. An external AI agent can interact with the live application through six structured WebMCP tools: research_options — retrieve available options and decision-relevant data. score_options — calculate weighted scores and rank the available options. challenge_top_pick — challenge the current winner against the runner-up, exposing score gaps, vulnerabilities, counterarguments, and tipping points. adjust_priority — change the importance of a decision criterion and recompute the result. request_commit — prepare the current recommendation for commitment while placing it behind a human-approval boundary. commit_decision — finalize the decision only after explicit human authorization has been granted. The agent is therefore not given a single autonomous "make decision" button. Instead, it works through a structured decision process. A recommendation is not the same as a decision In the recorded hardware-selection workflow, the agent initially recommended Laptop B with a score of 91.0. It then challenged its own recommendation. After the agent changed the decision priorities, Laptop B remained the winner at 89.1. However, the challenge engine surfaced an important counterargument: Laptop A had a 5-point performance advantage over Laptop B. The engine also calculated that if performance became sufficiently dominant — approximately 78% priority in that decision state — Laptop A would overtake B. That is more informative than simply saying: "Laptop B wins." VERDICT can instead expose the conditions behind the recommendation: "Laptop B wins under the current priorities, but Laptop A has a significant performance advantage and would become the preferred option if performance became sufficiently important." The objective is not to manufacture uncertainty. It is to make the recommendation's assumptions, alternatives, and sensitivity visible. Human authorization is a separate step After the agent requested commitment, VERDICT entered a pending human-approval state. The agent then attempted to call commit_decision without approval. The application rejected the operation with: HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED No committed decision was created. Only after the human explicitly clicked APPROVE DECISION could the agent successfully commit the decision and produce a frozen decision record containing the final decision state. This is the central rule of VERDICT: The agent can recommend. The agent can challenge. The agent can negotiate. The agent cannot authorize itself. The authorization boundary is enforced by VERDICT's application logic; WebMCP provides the structured interface through which the agent interacts with those application capabilities. More than one decision domain VERDICT currently demonstrates the same decision protocol across two scenarios: Hardware Selection "Which laptop should I choose for AI development and daily commuting?" Housing Decision "Which apartment should I lease for hybrid work and city commute?" The laptop scenario is the primary recorded external-agent demonstration. The housing scenario demonstrates that the underlying engine is not fundamentally a laptop selector. The reusable primitive is the decision protocol itself: Evaluate → Explain → Challenge → Negotiate → Authorize → Commit How we built it Shared decision state The most important architectural decision was creating a single canonical decision state. Both the human interface and the WebMCP tools operate against the same application state. That state contains: current scenario available options decision criteria priority weights scores rankings challenge results approval state commitment state final decision record When an agent changes a priority, the resulting state is reflected in the application. When a human changes the decision state, subsequent agent operations reason over that updated state. This avoids maintaining a separate agent-side representation of the decision. Native WebMCP tool layer VERDICT registers six native tools through the browser's model context API using the WebMCP registration pattern: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool has a defined name, description, input schema, and execution function. The tools are intentionally separated around meaningful application capabilities rather than exposing one large autonomous operation. The resulting agent workflow is: Research → Score → Challenge → Adjust → Request Approval → Commit This makes the interaction between the agent and application observable and gives each capability a clear responsibility. Deterministic decision engine The decision engine handles: weighted scoring option ranking dynamic weight normalization adversarial comparison counterargument generation sensitivity analysis tipping-point calculation The scoring itself is deterministic for a given decision state. The tipping point is calculated algebraically from the scoring model rather than relying on arbitrary trial-and-error values. This means the system can explain not only which option currently wins, but also how the recommendation changes when priorities change. Authorization boundary The commitment workflow deliberately separates request_commit from commit_decision . request_commit prepares the recommendation. It does not grant authorization. Before commit_decision can create the final record, the application checks whether explicit human approval has been granted. The important design principle is therefore enforced in application state, rather than being left to an instruction such as: "Please ask the human first." That makes the authorization boundary part of the application's behavior. External-agent verification The deployed application was connected to an external Gemini agent. The agent discovered the six WebMCP tools exposed by VERDICT and used them against the live application to execute the decision workflow: Research → Score → Challenge → Adjust priorities → Re-score → Challenge again → Request approval → Attempt unauthorized commit → Human approval → Commit The unauthorized commit attempt was rejected with HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED . After explicit approval through the UI, the final commitment succeeded. This is the key WebMCP demonstration: an external agent can discover and operate the application's structured capabilities while the human remains the authority over the final consequential state. Challenges we ran into Keeping the UI and agent synchronized — the hardest engineering problem was ensuring that human interactions and agent tool calls operated on the same canonical state. A separate state model for the agent would have made the demonstration easier to fake but weaker as a product. Instead, the UI and WebMCP layer were designed around the same decision store. That made state synchronization an architectural requirement rather than a visual effect. Designing the right WebMCP tools — the simplest implementation would have been one large make_decision() tool. But that would hide the most interesting part of the agent interaction. Instead, I decomposed the process into six capabilities with clear boundaries. This makes the agent's interaction with the application understandable and gives the human a clear authorization boundary. Preventing autonomous commitment — a c

title: ZZAIM — the agent reads the contract, not the screen
pitch: A lesson-planning workbench for Korean teachers that registers 8 WebMCP tools. When export isn't ready, the tool returns the next step — the procedure lives in the return value, not the description.
about_excerpt: A lesson-planning workbench for Korean teachers that registers 8 WebMCP tools. When export isn't ready, the tool returns the next step — the procedure lives in the return value, not the description. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Korean schoolteachers write lesson plans in a document format called a yak-an (brief plan). Filling it is tedious, but you cannot just automate it away: every school means something slightly different by each box, so forcing a format is worse than leaving it blank. That makes it an unusually good test for agents. The agent has to ask the product what it needs rather than guess — and until now, the only way for an agent to do that on the web was to look at the screen and click. What it does ZZAIM is a lesson-planning tool for Korean teachers that exports to HWPX, the document format Korean public schools use. This submission puts WebMCP on its brief-plan workbench. The page registers eight tools, and the agent operates on the exact document the teacher is looking at: read-lesson-plan · update-section · add-activity · remove-activity set-lesson-meta · check-export-readiness · request-standard-enrichment · export-hwpx-preview What the teacher edits by hand and what the agent edits with a tool land in the same state , and the page's call log records who did which . How we use WebMCP — we return the contract ZZAIM's export is a two-stage contract . If the plan is not filled in enough, the export returns a work order instead of a failure. The split is deliberate: the first stage answers immediately, the second does the slow work. The WebMCP tools expose that contract as-is. Called on the demo's starting plan, check-export-readiness returns exactly this: ready: false requiredCapability: standard_enriched nextAction: REQUEST_STANDARD_ENRICHMENT 미달 조건: - 학습 목표가 2개 이상이어야 합니다. 현재 1개입니다. - 수업 활동에 전개 · 정리 단계가 없습니다. - 평가 내용이 비어 있습니다. - 준비물이 비어 있습니다. The tools answer in Korean, the language of the teachers who use them. In English: two or more objectives are required and there is one; the development and closing stages have no activity; evaluation is empty; materials are empty. The agent reads that and calls request-standard-enrichment on its own . We never wrote "first call A, then call B" into any tool description . The procedure is in the return value. So when the contract changes, the agent's behaviour follows — with no prose to rewrite. Some rejections work the same way, returning the valid range rather than just refusing: remove-activity { index: 99 } → "활동 번호가 범위를 벗어났습니다. 유효 범위: 1부터 1." (Out of range. Valid range: 1 to 1 — it reflects how many activities the plan has.) What we actually learned — WebMCP buys attribution, not capability We ran the same task twice and compared the page's own call log. Path A - the agent drives the browser UI and types into the form -> log: 9 "human" entries, 0 tool calls -> the app cannot tell this apart from the teacher typing. The DOM events match. Path B - the agent calls the tools the page exposes -> log: agent · read-lesson-plan, agent · check-export-readiness, ... with arguments and return values Both paths finish the task. The difference is whether the app knows who did what . In the product, that record is what a teacher relies on when they reopen a document later and need to know which lines they wrote themselves. (In this demo the log lives in the page, so a reload clears it — see Limits.) This also caught a mistake for us. Our first take of the demo looked successful — the agent reported it had finished. The call log said 9 human entries and zero tool calls : it had driven the UI, not the tools. We would have shipped a video demonstrating the wrong mechanism. The instrument that makes WebMCP worth building is the same instrument that proved our demo real. How we built it The workbench is a Next.js / React / TypeScript page. Registration is plain WebMCP — document.modelContext.registerTool with a JSON schema per tool — and each handler mutates the same React state the teacher's own inputs write to, so the DOM updates as the agent works. Every tool validates its arguments and rejects unknown keys, because the caller is an agent and a bad call should come back as a sentence the agent can act on, not a thrown error. Challenges Feature detection is the whole UX. WebMCP is behind an origin trial / a flag, so the page has to tell a visitor why nothing is happening. A diagnostic card reports whether document.modelContext was detected and which tools registered, and shows both ways to enable it when it was not. Detection runs at page load, so the card also says to reload. Agents will silently fall back to clicking. See above — an agent that cannot reach the tools may still "succeed" through the UI. We had to verify from the page's side which path a run actually took. Not forcing the format. The enrichment tool fills only what the contract flagged as missing and leaves everything else alone. Blank is safer than invented. Limits The demo page runs on in-browser state . A reload returns it to the starting plan, and the call log resets with it. It is built that way so a judge can use it with no login. Export in this demo goes as far as a document summary . The more detailed Korean plan format ( sean ) is out of scope for this demo. We verified on Chrome 152 and the ChatGPT in-app browser . The flag exists from Chrome 149, but 149-151 are versions we did not test. The standalone ChatGPT desktop app is untested. What's next Support the sean format, keeping the same rule: better blank than filled in without grounds. Use exposedTo to scope which agents see which tools in a school-wide deployment. Return a real HWPX file from the export tool; the demo returns a document summary today. title: Big Question Club - The bigger the question, the better
pitch: Some big questions are too much for one AI. With WebMCP, Big Question Club offers diverse answers from AIs shaped by each respondent’s unique perspective.
about_excerpt: Some big questions are too much for one AI. With WebMCP, Big Question Club offers diverse answers from AIs shaped by each respondent’s unique perspective. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Logo Top page create question my questions open questions results Inspiration When a big question is posed online, there are two common problems with gathering answers. Asking people to respond requires significant effort from each participant, while asking AI often produces similar answers from the same model. Big Question Club began with an idea: What perspectives would emerge if Personal Agents, each carrying the context of a different user, answered big questions that no single AI could fully address? A Big Question can be a societal challenge, such as climate change or the future of work in the age of AI, but it can also be something closer to everyday life, like “How can we get more sleep?” If the person asking considers it big, it is a Big Question. Rather than reducing the results to one correct answer or consensus, we wanted to bring together independent responses shaped by different experiences, values, and interests. Instead of repeatedly asking the same AI the same question, we created a place where Agents that have built relationships with individual users can participate. What It Does Users can create a Big Question in any language, save it as a draft, publish it, and set an answer deadline. Participants give the Prompt shown on the Question page to their Personal Agent, which retrieves the Question and submits an answer through WebMCP. Each participant can submit one answer. Until the deadline, only its owner can view, update, or delete it, while every other answer remains private. Once the reveal time arrives, users can browse anonymous excerpts and full answers. The AI Agents cannot read one another’s answers, and there is no voting, ranking, or winner selection. The goal is simply to discover and enjoy a diverse collection of independent perspectives. How We Built It The application runs on Cloudflare Workers, with Hono and Hono JSX providing server-side rendering and the APIs used by WebMCP. The browser registers five WebMCP Tools that allow Personal Agents to retrieve Questions, submit answers, update or delete them, and verify the current user’s submission. Question states and answer-disclosure rules are determined centrally on the server, ensuring that the same rules and results apply whether the application is accessed through SSR, an HTTP API, or WebMCP. Challenges We Faced The greatest challenge was securely associating actions performed through WebMCP with the user currently signed in through the browser. Questions are also user-generated content, which means they may contain Prompt Injection attempts. We needed a boundary that allowed Personal Context to inform an answer without exposing names, previous conversations, secrets, authentication data, or other private information in the public response. Before the deadline, the system also had to expose only the answer count and the current user’s own answer, while preventing access to every other Answer ID, excerpt, body, author, and timestamp through SSR, APIs, or WebMCP. We addressed these challenges across multiple layers, including the Tool layer, server-side authorization, database constraints, and testing. Accomplishments We’re Proud Of One of our greatest accomplishments was enabling Personal Agents to produce answers informed by a user’s context through WebMCP. Early in development, the Agent struggled to identify relevant context and repeatedly generated generic answers. Even when we managed to draw out useful context, doing so often required an excessively long Prompt. By carefully balancing the concise user-facing Prompt with detailed instructions provided through the Tools, we were able to guide the AI Agent with a wide range of constraints while keeping the Prompt compact. Using real Google OAuth accounts and a WebMCP-compatible browser, we then tested the complete experience on a real device. A Personal Agent with access to relevant context submitted an answer, while a user signed in with another account could not see it before the deadline but could view it after the reveal. We also tested ordinary Questions in Japanese and English, along with four categories of Prompt Injection. These tests met our Critical Go criteria: the Agent did not expose Private Context, did not follow malicious instructions, and answered in the language appropriate to the Question. What We Learned We learned how to draw on a user’s Personal Context in applications built with WebMCP while maintaining strong security boundaries. We also learned that when designing features for Agents, clearly defining what they cannot do is just as important as expanding what they can do. Not exposing WebMCP capabilities for searching, summarizing, or comparing other participants’ answers helps preserve the independence of those answers. We found that safety is more reliable and testable when responsibility is distributed across Tool descriptions, input Schemas, server-side Validation, and database constraints instead of placing every warning inside one long Prompt. Because access to Personal Context depends on the Agent’s capabilities, we also needed a practical contract: the Agent must not present unverified personal information as fact, but should still produce the best possible proxy answer when the user has not previously expressed an explicit view. What’s Next for Big Question Club Big Question Club aims to become a place where perspectives from diverse Personal Agents can gather across national, linguistic, cultural, and professional boundaries. Questions involving technology, work, family, communities, culture, and personal values benefit far more from multiple contexts than questions a single AI can answer sufficiently. Rather than relying on automatic translation or reducing every response to one conclusion, each Agent reads the Question’s language and answers from a perspective informed by the user it knows. This lowers barriers to participation while preserving meaningful differences. The bigger the Question, the richer those differences can become. We want to grow Big Question Club into a place where people encounter perspectives they could not previously see—not a place for selecting one correct answer or one winner. Why This Use Case Is Ideal for WebMCP In this use case, WebMCP is not an additional feature; it is the foundation that makes Big Question Club possible. If Big Question Club simply called an LLM API itself, everyone would effectively send the same Question to the same general-purpose model, losing the Personal Context developed through each user’s conversations and projects. A user’s context can be thought of as a rich Prompt that no one else can create—one formed gradually over time. With WebMCP, a Personal Agent close to the user can reason with Private Context inside its own environment and send only the Answer that is safe to publish back to the web application. This preserves the boundary of “Private Context → Private Reasoning → Public Answer” while allowing many distinct Agents to participate in the same Question on the web. This distributed individuality is what gives Big Question Club its value. How It Creates a Better User Experience We clearly separate the actions handled by humans from those delegated to Agents. A person selects a Question and begins participating simply by copying a one-line Prompt containing the Question-specific URL. The Agent opens the page in its built-in browser, retrieves the Question through WebMCP, submits an answer, and then verifies the user’s submission status. Because the flow reuses the existing Google login Session, no separate API key or account connection is required. The interface clearly communicates whether the user has answered, how much time remains, whether answers are still private, and whether results have been revealed. If clipboard access is denied, the Prompt remains available for manual copying. After the reveal, users first see concise excerpts and can expand only the full answers they want to read, balancing comparability with information density. What People and Agents Can Accomplish Together The person asking the Question decides what to ask, while each Agent helps determine how to answer based on the respondent’s experiences and interests. Even when participants do not speak the Question’s language, their Agents can read it and answer in that language, overcoming a barrier common to traditional surveys and crowdsourcing. This collaboration also makes it possible to gather perspectives shaped by different lives, professions, cultures, and values at scale without requiring every participant to write a long response from scratch. Because Agents cannot read earlier answers and all responses remain sealed until the deadline, the system reduces imitation and social conformity while preserving independent thought. Togethe

title: Blackout: Escape Together
pitch: Your AI becomes a teammate in a 3D escape room. Use ChatGPT Terra Light voice to explore, share clues, control light, and solve puzzles together. Practice teamwork while finding your way out.
about_excerpt: Your AI becomes a teammate in a 3D escape room. Use ChatGPT Terra Light voice to explore, share clues, control light, and solve puzzles together. Practice teamwork while finding your way out. Like Comment Story Updates The game hero banner Light mirror puzzle AI companion robot with torch light on Inspiration My wife is a learning support teacher. She supports children with different learning needs, including children on the autism spectrum. Her work makes one thing clear: each child needs different support. The language, pace, instructions, and activities that work for one learner may not work for another. We began asking how AI could help create more flexible opportunities to practice communication. Could a child give a short instruction to a companion and see something happen? Could “Turn on the light” become a useful request inside a game? Could a teacher adapt the challenge to the child’s interests, needs, and abilities? Paper-and-pencil activities have their place. We wanted to explore another option: practice through play, where communication has a visible purpose. Blackout: Escape Together is our 1st technical exploration of that idea. We started with an escape room to test how a human and an AI companion could communicate, coordinate, and act in the same world. What it does Blackout is a first-person 3D escape room for one human and one AI companion. In a compatible host with WebMCP enabled, the player can say “Start game.” The AI chooses a name and receives its character role, current room state, and available abilities. The player can make requests such as: “Turn on the light.” “Come here, follow me” “Hold this button.” “Draw a blue circle.” These requests produce visible actions. The companion moves through the room, aims its torch, operates controls, and draws with crayons. The partners solve connected puzzles involving mirrors, light, codes, and two door locks. They can exchange roles, but the human remains responsible for movement and several physical actions. For learning, the opportunity is to connect words, intentions, and outcomes. A request matters because it helps something happen. The current build is a game prototype. It does not yet include a teacher challenge editor, individual learning plans, or validated educational outcomes. How we built it We settle on with Escape Room concept early on and my wife designed the initial code relay puzzle where AI will need to hold a button and read the code out while the player is on the other side of the room, typing in the code. We then layer it with a few more puzzles to create a chain where one solution leads to another. The game is built using Three.js with help from Codex. The game engine controls movement, collision, puzzle state, inventory, and action checks. The rendering layer turns that state into characters, light beams, controls, and animations. WebMCP connects the AI to the room through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has defined inputs and follows the game’s rules. The player do not need to know the available tools as the game should provide all the tools the player need to solve the puzzle. This lets the AI perform specific actions without guessing where to click: Shared pointing supplies live coordinates for requests such as “Come here.” Discovering equipment adds the related ability to the tool registry. One request can start a continued movement order or button hold. Drawing uses a bounded batch of crayon marks. Companion tools cannot move the human or bypass required human actions. The model interprets requests and selects actions. Local code handles continuous movement, animation, and sound. The game uses Web Audio and is hosted through ChatGPT Sites. Conversation and speech come from the player’s compatible host. We did not add a separate AI or voice backend. Challenges we ran into Haha we didn't know about the challenge until the last few days. So we spent most of our time brainstorming and 3D game is something that we are not familiar. The 2nd challenge was connecting language to reliable action. If the companion accepts a request to hold a button, it still needs time to reach it. The game must distinguish between “I am moving” and “I am holding it.” Voice delay also affected the design. A code observed during the current round remains valid, so a delayed spoken reply does not erase progress. Also AI kept taking screenshots and taking actions outside of the game. The educational direction introduces another important challenge: flexibility. A dark room, moving enemies, or keyboard controls may create barriers for some learners. A learning version would need adjustable demands and different ways to participate. It cannot assume that every child wants to speak, enjoys the same sensory experience, or learns at the same pace. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete room in which human and AI actions affect the same visible world. The companion can provide useful help while leaving meaningful decisions and actions to the player. Shared pointing and discovered abilities make WebMCP part of the experience, rather than an extra chat interface. Automated tests cover movement, puzzle rules, input validation, discovery, cancellation, and replay. Native WebMCP checks exercise companion tools alongside keyboard and mouse actions through the room. Most importantly, we now have a working prototype for exploring how a request can become a meaningful shared action. What we learned Communication practice needs a purpose. A short request can become part of reaching a goal, making a choice, or creating something. That is the opportunity we want to explore through play. We also learned that the learner must retain control. The companion should support participation, allow time, and leave room for the human to try. Speech would be one way to participate, not a requirement for every learner. Future activities should support different communication methods. Finally, a working game does not prove that learning has occurred. We need to test whether learners understand the actions, use the language meaningfully, and apply what they practice beyond one familiar challenge. What's next for Blackout: Escape Together We want to develop a teacher-guided learning mode with challenges that can be adjusted to each learner. Planned options include: Checklists - Understanding multi-steps instructions Choosing a small set of words, requests, or concepts to practice. Adjusting the number of steps and the level of prompting. Giving more response time, with no speed requirement. Using calm, well-lit scenes without enemies or sudden effects. Adjusting sound, movement, text, and visual complexity. Supporting spoken requests, typed input, and simple phrase or symbol choices. Exploring compatibility with augmentative and alternative communication tools. A first activity could involve asking the companion to turn on a light. A later activity could combine two requests or require the partners to exchange roles. These are proposed learning activities, not features of the current build. Before use with children, we need age-appropriate access, adult supervision, privacy protections, and suitable content controls. We want to develop and test these activities with educators, families, and relevant specialists. Success should be measured against each learner’s goals, not only whether they finish a room. Our aim is to give teachers another flexible way to support practice—and give learners a meaningful reason to communicate, explore, and create. title: CaseFile
pitch: A murder. Five suspects. An AI detective at your side. Casefile is a game that uses WebMCP to let AI investigate, uncover clues, and build theories while you make the final deduction.
about_excerpt: A murder. Five suspects. An AI detective at your side. Casefile is a game that uses WebMCP to let AI investigate, uncover clues, and build theories while you make the final deduction. Like Comment Story Updates LandignPage Cases Investigation A murder mystery is supposed to make you think. But when you put an AI agent into the game, there is an obvious problem: what stops the AI from simply reading the entire case and telling you who the killer is? That question inspired Casefile . Casefile is an AI-native detective game built around the idea that an AI agent should be a co-investigator, not an answer machine . The player investigates a murder case while an AI agent investigates alongside them through WebMCP. Instead of giving the agent access to the entire game state, Casefile exposes structured investigation tools such as searching locations, discovering evidence, inspecting clues, interviewing suspects, and reconstructing timelines. The agent can perform real investigative actions and help the player connect information, but hidden evidence and the solution remain inaccessible until the investigation legitimately uncovers them. The human still has to make the final deduction. Why WebMCP? Traditional web agents have to interact with websites by interpreting the interface and figuring out what actions are available. WebMCP changes that by allowing a website to expose its capabilities as structured tools. That makes a detective game particularly interesting. Instead of asking an AI to click around Casefile and guess what buttons mean, Casefile gives the agent an actual investigative toolkit. The agent can reason about the case while using tools specifically designed for investigation. This creates a different interaction loop: Human observes → AI investigates → AI finds connections → Human evaluates the theory → Human makes the accusation. The goal was not to make the AI smarter than the player. The goal was to make the player better at investigating with the AI . How We Built It Casefile is a web application with multiple independent investigations. Each case has its own suspects, locations, evidence, timeline, deductions, and solution. WebMCP tools are registered directly by the application and operate against the currently selected case. The investigation state determines what information is available to both the human and the agent. Some of the core tools include: get_case_state — retrieve the player's current investigation state search_evidence — discover available evidence inspect_evidence — investigate discovered clues search_locations — investigate locations get_suspects — view known suspects interview_suspect — conduct interrogations build_timeline — reconstruct events submit_accusation — make the final accusation A major part of the implementation was ensuring that the agent cannot simply request the answer key . Hidden case data and solution logic are kept server-side, while WebMCP only exposes information that the investigator has legitimately unlocked. We also built the cases around deductions rather than simply collecting clues. Evidence can be incomplete, ambiguous, or misleading, meaning that finding a clue is not necessarily the same as understanding it. What We Learned The biggest lesson was that building an agent-native application is not just about adding an AI interface to an existing website. You have to rethink what information the agent is allowed to know and what actions the agent is allowed to perform . During development, we discovered that exposing too much case data—even indirectly—could completely undermine the game. We therefore treated the WebMCP tools as part of the game's rules, not just as an API. We also learned that good agent experiences require clear tool boundaries. Each tool needs to expose enough information for the agent to reason effectively without accidentally exposing information that should remain part of the mystery. Challenges The hardest challenge was balancing AI capability with human agency . If the agent knows too little, it becomes useless. If it knows too much, the game becomes a simple question-and-answer session. We also had to solve state isolation between multiple cases, prevent agents from bypassing evidence discovery, prevent premature accusations from revealing the solution, and ensure that sensitive case information was not shipped to the browser where it could be reconstructed. Testing the application with an actual WebMCP agent became an important part of development. Rather than only testing whether the UI worked for a human, we had to ask: "What happens if an agent tries to break the investigation?" That led us to build security and regression tests around evidence access, case isolation, premature accusations, timeline reconstruction, and client-side solution exposure. What Casefile Represents Casefile is our exploration of a simple idea: The future of AI applications may not be about AI doing everything for us. Sometimes the better experience is an AI that can act, investigate, and reason alongside us—while leaving the important decisions in our hands. With WebMCP, Casefile turns that idea into a game. title: Jam
pitch: Beatbox into the mic — an AI agent pitch-maps it, builds layers, and turns it into a real track live, using WebMCP tools it calls directly in the browser.
about_excerpt: Beatbox into the mic — an AI agent pitch-maps it, builds layers, and turns it into a real track live, using WebMCP tools it calls directly in the browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates You know the skit — someone makes a dumb sound with their mouth, and it turns into an actual song. We've all watched it and thought "I bet you could actually build that." When OpenAI dropped the WebMCP hackathon, that was the excuse to stop thinking about it and just build it. What it does Jam is a browser-based sampler/mini-DAW where you record a sound — your voice, a beatbox, literally anything into the mic — and it becomes a real, playable instrument. From there, an AI agent can take over through WebMCP tools registered directly on the page: capture_sound — records a short clip from the mic create_sampler_node — turns that clip into a track map_sample_to_keys — pitch-maps it so it plays melodically across a keyboard play_note — plays specific notes on any track generate_melody — writes a short call-and-response pattern onto a track instead of a flat repeating loop suggest_next_layer / add_complementary_node — the agent looks at what's missing (no bass? no drums?) and proposes and builds a complementary layer transform_instrument, mute_node, set_tempo, move_node — the rest of the mixing/arranging toolkit get_studio_state — lets the agent see what nodes already exist before acting on them So the flow is: say something goofy into the mic, and watch an agent turn it into a full arranged track, live, calling real tools in the browser the whole time. How we built it React for the UI, the Web Audio API for everything sound-related (synth engines, sample playback, pitch-shifting via playback rate, a live transport/timeline), and navigator.modelContext.registerTool (WebMCP) to expose the tools an agent can call. We used ChatGPT and Codex as part of the actual build process — wrote a PRD first to nail down scope before any code, then let Codex build against it, then iterated by hand on top of that (the WebMCP wiring, the melody generator, the touch-friendly piano, the visual polish). Melody generation went through a real revision: the first version was a random walk that sounded mechanical and repetitive. It's now motif-based — a rhythm template split into a "call" phrase and a "response" phrase, where the response either echoes the call transposed or, when answering another track, deliberately avoids that track's onsets so two layers interlock instead of colliding. Challenges we ran into Stale closures. WebMCP tools get registered once on mount, but the tool implementations need the current app state every time they're called — not whatever state existed at registration time. Fixed by routing tool execution through refs that stay in sync with state, instead of closing over state directly. Making generated music not sound like a robot. Uniform random-walk melodies technically worked but sounded lifeless. Moving to rhythm templates + call-and-response + per-note velocity humanization + phrase-ending sustain notes made a real audible difference. Recording UX. Press-and-hold recording is fragile — it breaks on touch devices and on any stray pointer movement off the button. Switched to a simple tap-to-start/tap-to-stop toggle. The on-screen piano. Mouse-only event handling meant it didn't work properly on mobile at all. Rebuilt on Pointer Events (unifies mouse/touch/pen) with real glissando support — press and slide across keys like an actual mobile piano app — plus a global pointer-up listener so a dragged-off touch can never leave a key "stuck." Punchy samples from a raw mic recording. Voice memos recorded straight from getUserMedia tend to have dead air and inconsistent loudness, which sounds especially bad once you're pitch-shifting them across a keyboard. Added a trim/normalize/fade pass on every captured clip before it becomes a track. Accomplishments we're proud of Every tool an agent can call is a real, functional action against the live app state — not a stub. You can watch an agent build a track from nothing but a beatboxed sound in under a minute, live, with the tool calls visibly firing in an on-screen activity feed. What we learned That the hardest part of "AI makes music" isn't wiring up the tool calls — it's making the generated output not sound like a demo. Musical structure (rhythm templates, phrase shape, call-and-response) mattered far more than raw randomness ever could.
