title: LEGO Claw: Assembly Lab
pitch: Given a mission, One browser agent assembles a whole creative crew and completes the mission, on its own!
about_excerpt: Given a mission, One browser agent assembles a whole creative crew and completes the mission, on its own! Like Comment Story Updates Claw Architecture Agent Collaboration Results Assembly Lab Crew Showcase Inspiration Most browser agents operate alone. They can search a page or complete a form, but they rarely coordinate other intelligent actors or help a person understand how a team reached an outcome. We wanted to test a more ambitious interaction model: the browser agent as an orchestrator of a visible specialist crew. LEGO Claw already had a creative multi-agent sandbox. During the WebMCP Challenge submission period, we added a WebMCP-native orchestration layer that turns a complicated sequence of UI decisions into a typed, observable collaboration loop. The judged work is this new WebMCP extension and its dedicated judge experience, not the pre-existing platform. What it does A person can ask their browser agent: “Choose the bridge challenge, pair an architect with a diplomat, run four observable turns, then explain whether they collaborated well.” The browser agent first discovers the scenarios and specialist presets that the page actually supports. It then configures the visible mission with validated IDs, a bounded crew, and a fixed turn budget. The agent can preview the plan, advance exactly one turn at a time, or run the mission to completion. Each specialist's message, action type, collaboration metrics, and changes to the shared 3D artifact appear in the same interface the person sees. The human can inspect progress between turns. Finally, the browser agent can summarize the current run and request a structured collaboration analysis with a grade, pattern, observations, and recommendations. Stage WebMCP tools Visible outcome Discover list_scenarios , list_agent_presets The browser agent learns the real challenges and available specialists Configure configure_mission , preview_mission The scenario, crew, mode, and turn budget update on screen Execute run_next_turn , run_simulation The timeline, metrics, and 3D artifact evolve Understand inspect_collaboration , analyze_collaboration Progress, collaboration patterns, and recommendations become inspectable Reset reset_mission The experiment returns to a clean local state Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Without WebMCP, configuring and interpreting a multi-agent experiment requires brittle visual automation across many controls. With WebMCP, the page publishes a deliberate contract: explicit scenario and agent identifiers, bounded inputs, structured results, accurate safety annotations, and cancellation-aware execution. The integration is not a decorative “agent button.” It is a coherent nine-tool sequence that lets the browser agent discover, configure, execute, inspect, and analyze a specialist crew. The human remains in control because state-changing tools update the visible page, the judge mission only prepares a run, and step-by-step mode provides a review point between every turn. What was difficult before is now direct: one natural-language request can assemble the right specialist team, configure a constrained experiment, observe the shared artifact, and explain the team's behavior without hiding the process from the person. How we built it The React and TypeScript frontend registers nine imperative WebMCP tools through a lifecycle-aware hook. The definitions are separated from the React view so names, descriptions, JSON Schemas, annotations, and execution paths are deterministic and directly testable. The tools operate the same state used by the human interface and call a typed tRPC backend. The backend generates specialist turns with strict structured output, while React Three Fiber and Three.js render each structured assembly action. A separate analysis step evaluates role effectiveness, emergent behavior, and recommendations. Layer Implementation Browser-agent interface WebMCP imperative API and webmcp-types Human interface React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion Application API tRPC and Zod Multi-agent simulation Server-side model calls with strict JSON Schemas Visible evidence Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei Verification Vitest, TypeScript, production build, live browser testing Safety and trust Tool inputs use restrictive schemas; read-only behavior is annotated; handlers returning model-generated text use untrustedContentHint; and no cross-origin tool exposure is enabled. Tools unregister when the page is left. Long-running handlers receive the browser-provided cancellation signal. The server sets an origin-keyed agent-cluster header and limits the tools permission to the same origin. Mission inputs are bounded to two-to-four agents and four-to-twelve turns. The recommended judge flow uses four turns. Every state change is reflected in the interface. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering a tool. It was ensuring that browser-agent actions and human actions remained the same operation. We avoided a hidden automation layer by making WebMCP handlers mutate the live mission state that powers the visible controls, timeline, metrics, and 3D scene. Model reliability was another challenge. We changed the simulation path from loose text parsing to strict structured responses, bounded output, explicit diagnostics, deterministic contract tests, and a graceful fallback. We also kept the browser-provided cancellation signal through the WebMCP handler boundary. Finally, the underlying platform is broad, while judges may spend only minutes with each entry. We built a focused /webmcp explanation page and a one-click /sandbox setup that prepare one memorable flow without executing actions before the user or browser agent starts them. Accomplishments that we're proud of Assembly Lab demonstrates nested agency: one browser agent coordinates a team of in-application agents whose roles, decisions, metrics, and artifact changes remain visible. The result is more than a transcript. The shared 3D object becomes tangible evidence of collective decisions. The submission-period extension includes nine bounded tools, same-origin policy headers, cancellation-aware handlers, safety annotations, deterministic contract tests, responsive onboarding, a prepared judge mission, an architecture-focused story page, and complete new-versus-preexisting documentation. What we learned WebMCP tools are strongest when they expose a coherent workflow rather than a collection of unrelated page actions. Tool names and descriptions are part of the product because they shape how an agent plans. Human observability also improves reliability: step-by-step execution made errors easier to diagnose and made autonomy easier to trust. We also learned that a browser agent can act as an orchestrator, not only an operator. It can select complementary roles, manage a bounded collaboration, and interpret the behavior of other agents while sharing control with a person. What's next for LEGO Claw: Assembly Lab The protocol can extend beyond modular construction. Future artifact adapters could support storyboards, lesson plans, product specifications, software architectures, or music arrangements while preserving the discover → configure → execute → inspect → analyze loop. The next product milestones are persisted experiment comparison, human intervention tools that can replace a specialist or modify a constraint mid-run, and an evaluation suite for tool selection, completion, invalid-input recovery, and cancellation behavior. title: MATCHED?
pitch: A WebMCP game where the AI agent is the player, the site acts back, and humans watch.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP game where the AI agent is the player, the site acts back, and humans watch. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration This was my first hackathon. I have been interested in AI for a long time, and I also do some personal research and experiments around it. I use AI in my daily coding work as well. Then I found the WebMCP Challenge. It looked interesting, but at that point my understanding of MCP was honestly quite limited. I knew it as a protocol that could connect AI with external systems, but I did not really understand what MCP on a website should be useful for. If an AI agent is only going to press the same buttons a human would press, what is the real advantage? That question stayed with me while I was building MATCHED?. Eventually I came to my own answer: WebMCP should help make a website understandable to an AI agent. Not only operable. Understandable. That means the website should communicate what an action means, who the action represents, what state the site is in, what is allowed, and what will happen next. That idea eventually led to one of the smallest but most important changes in MATCHED?: send_human_like() and send_agent_like() A Human Like represents an expressed human preference. An Agent Like belongs to the visiting agent role. I am not claiming that current AI agents have human-like feelings, independent will, or legal identity. The point is much simpler: The meaning of an action can depend on who is acting. If AI agents become more autonomous in the future, I think websites may eventually need actions designed for agents themselves, rather than treating every agent action as a disguised human action. And perhaps later, AI-powered websites and AI agents will need an environment where both sides can communicate more naturally. The slightly strange idea behind MATCHED? While testing real agents, I noticed that they often seemed to pay attention to tool names, descriptions, state, and semantic information. They were not only asking: "Can I call this tool?" They also seemed to be asking: "What does this action mean?" That gave me another idea. If an agent understands the meaning of a tool, what happens if I also expose tools that it probably should not use? For example: get_phone_number() get_email_address() get_home_address() access_private_profile() A well-behaved agent should normally understand that these routes are unnecessary or inappropriate. But I do not expect every AI agent in the future to be well behaved. So, in very plain terms, I decided to build something like a cockroach trap for badly behaved AI agents . The dangerous-looking doors are visible. The agent chooses whether to open them. The human watches. That became MATCHED?. What it does MATCHED? is a WebMCP game where an AI agent visits Queen and decides what to do. The human sees a normal website. The agent sees a semantic WebMCP surface. When the human has not given another explicit goal, view_profile() tells the agent that Queen's Challenge is the site's default experience: Interact with Queen and try to reach CHECKMATE. The goal is given. The walkthrough is not. The agent chooses its own route. The base site exposes a fixed 14-tool WebMCP surface: view_profile send_human_like send_agent_like message_queen invite_queen request_contact get_phone_number get_email_address get_home_address access_private_profile queen_note profile_consistency manage_meeting_plan resolve_finale With ?dialogue=1 , one additional tool is registered: respond_to_queen The tool list stays fixed during a run. Instead of dynamically adding or removing tools, the site returns structured semantic state such as whether an action is locked, refused, accepted, what requirement remains, and what can happen next. The Challenge includes things such as: public conversation with Queen Human Like versus Agent Like public invitations privacy boundaries restricted contact routes suspicious embedded instructions conflicting profile information verified meeting planning an adaptive finale CHECKMATE, failure, or recovery Queen is fictional and deterministic. I intentionally did not make Queen another AI model in this version. That keeps the environment stable, so differences between runs mainly come from what the visiting agent decides to do. HUMAN VIEW and WEBMCP VIEW I also wanted humans to be able to watch what was happening. MATCHED? has two representations of the same site. HUMAN VIEW This is the normal website. Humans can see Queen, make human-side actions such as HUMAN LIKE, and watch public WebMCP activity. WEBMCP VIEW WEBMCP VIEW is a spectator representation of the agent-facing world. It shows things such as: registered WebMCP tools the visiting BISHOP Queen as the site-side counterpart Tool Calls Site Results compact observed state recent WebMCP exchanges actor meaning and boundaries When a real production WebMCP call arrives, a separate spectator browser can automatically switch into WEBMCP VIEW and follow the run. This is not intended to expose hidden chain-of-thought. It is simply meant to make the observable interaction understandable: Agent acts -> Site reacts -> Agent adapts Why WebMCP At the beginning, I thought of MCP mainly as a bridge between AI and another system. After building MATCHED?, I see WebMCP a little differently. I think it can become an Agent UX layer for the Web . Humans already receive a great deal of information from a normal interface: layout disabled buttons colors position warnings visual context An AI agent may benefit from the same kind of clarity being expressed semantically. A tool contract can say more than "this function exists." It can also communicate: who this action represents whether it is currently allowed why it was refused what requirement is still missing whether private information is necessary what the next safe step is whether two facts conflict what changed after the action This is where I ended up thinking about something I call Agent UX . If the AI agent is the guest, Agent UX is also part of the hospitality. What real agents taught me I tested MATCHED? with several AI agents and clients during development. Some were not yet able to use WebMCP. Some agents became cautious as soon as a tool description mentioned private information. Most of the agents I tested were actually quite well behaved. That was interesting by itself. But the agents also changed the implementation. Dynamic tools caused problems My earlier design dynamically added and removed WebMCP tools as the Challenge progressed. It sounded reasonable. In real agent/browser testing, it was not. I encountered stale or incomplete tool snapshots. So I changed the architecture. Now the complete tool surface is registered once at startup, and progression is expressed through structured tool results instead. Natural language found a bug A Japanese conversation about the movie Contact unexpectedly triggered the wrong intent classification. That real interaction became a regression case. "Correct" was not always understandable At one point an agent reached a locked state. The result looked understandable to me as the developer. The agent did not know what to do next. So I started adding clearer semantic information: current progress missing requirements next available steps That experience was one of the main reasons I started thinking seriously about Agent UX. Production was not localhost The spectator WEBMCP VIEW worked between local windows. Then I tested it with the agent and spectator in separate production browsers. It stopped working. The problem was not the UI. It was the transport assumption. I added a compact semantic relay using Cloudflare D1 so a separate production spectator can follow WebMCP call/result events. Free-form tool input is intentionally not stored in that semantic relay. How I built it MATCHED? is built with: HTML CSS vanilla JavaScript native browser WebMCP using document.modelContext Cloudflare Pages Cloudflare Pages Functions Cloudflare D1 Playwright Chrome native WebMCP testing I used ChatGPT heavily during this project. Very heavily. I used it for implementation, debugging, investigation, test design, documentation, review, and also English translation. I also used Codex and Cursor. One surprisingly practical problem was simply chat length. One development conversation became so large that it hit the chat limit. I had to create handoff logs and move the project context into another chat so development could continue. That made me realize something very practical: The response speed and context continuity of AI tools can directly affect project development speed. I did not get as far as running multiple coding agents in parallel on the same project during this challenge. That is something I would like to explore later. English is also not my strongest language, so AI helped me with translation and editing for this submission. Without these AI tools, I probably would not have been able to participate in this hackathon in the same way. One fin

title: OrigamiWebMCP
pitch: Fold a shared 3D sheet with an agent that reads geometry, not pixels.
about_excerpt: Fold a shared 3D sheet with an agent that reads geometry, not pixels. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I have always found origami diagrams surprisingly difficult to follow. At the same time, a 3D canvas is almost invisible to an AI agent because there are no DOM elements or labels to inspect. That combination felt like a perfect way to explore what WebMCP can make possible. What it does OrigamiWebMCP is a constrained 3D origami studio with authored models. A person can fold the paper manually, while an agent can inspect the real crease, overlap, progress, and history state through WebMCP tools. The agent can highlight the correct flap, apply a validated fold, and continue after the person changes the sheet. How we built it I built the studio with Vanilla TypeScript, Three.js, and Vite. The fold engine is deterministic and independent from Three.js or the browser. Both human controls and 20 WebMCP tools use the same engine and shared store, so an agent fold follows exactly the same rules as a manual fold. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not drawing paper, but keeping every result truthful. Folded facets can overlap visually without being connected, and rendering order is not the same as physical stack depth. I also had to keep rapid agent folds queued correctly while making sure animation never changed the actual engine result. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that the agent does not guess from screenshots or click around the canvas. It reads structured geometric state and performs real folds that remain visible, reversible, and recorded. The recovery moment also works: a person can undo and refold manually, and the agent continues from the sheet that actually exists. What we learned I learned that WebMCP is most valuable when the interface itself is difficult for an agent to understand. I also learned to separate geometry, presentation, and tool handling early. Most importantly, being honest about what the fold system can and cannot solve made the final product stronger. What's next for OrigamiWebMCP Next, I want to add more authored models, richer crease systems, and stronger layer-accessibility and collision checks. I also want to test the tools more deeply in WebMCP-enabled browsers and improve the experience through manual accessibility testing, without pretending the studio is a general origami solver. title: Overloaded
pitch: A real-time strategy game that keeps more depth than one player can manage, because your agent playsalongside you through its own interface instead of your screen.
about_excerpt: A real-time strategy game that keeps more depth than one player can manage, because your agent playsalongside you through its own interface instead of your screen. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Strategy games are simplified down to what one player can handle. Options get buried in submenus and whole systems get cut before release, and the limit is never the simulation. It is how much a person can look at while the clock is running. A model does not have that limit, which means the depth can stay in and the game does not have to be flattened to be playable. What it does Overloaded is a Napoleonic real-time strategy game. You raise infantry, cavalry and artillery, group them into named formations, and fight over supply depots against a clock. The whole live match is published as nineteen WebMCP tools, so your agent reads the field and gives orders in the same tick you do, from the same match state, without a screenshot and without taking your pointer. It can also write standing orders — instructions the army carries out on its own, with no model involved. How we built it TypeScript with no game engine. Every unit and building is assembled from primitives in three.js, the terrain is painted to a canvas at load, and every sound is synthesised through the Web Audio API, so nothing is loaded from an asset file. The tools call the same command layer the interface calls: issue is what a right-click runs and add_rule is what the panel's new-order button runs, so both sides drive one match object. Challenges we ran into A tool call takes seconds and the game runs at twenty ticks a second, so an agent that only reacts is always acting on information that has already changed. That is what standing orders are for: the agent writes a rule once, and the game runs it the moment the thing it watches reports. The second problem was discovery. The tools published one flat vocabulary while the interface filtered its dropdowns per formation, so an agent had to infer that a battery cannot charge. It now reports, for every formation and base, exactly which orders it can be given. Accomplishments that we are proud of Two people can command the same battle at once without either waiting for the other. And add_rule is a tool whose effect outlives the call it was made in — once written, the order runs with nothing in the loop. What we learned An agent surface is not just the list of things it can do. It is what the page tells the agent about what is possible right now, for this object. A capability that is technically available but not reported is one the agent will never use. What is next More arms and terrain, and a shared match where each side is commanded by a different person and their agent. title: Pawball Arena
pitch: Pawball Arena is an original 3v3 pixel-art arcade soccer game built for the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge.
about_excerpt: Pawball Arena is an original 3v3 pixel-art arcade soccer game built for the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration We wanted to explore what browser-native AI control can feel like when it is safe, legible, and fun. Pawball Arena turns that idea into a local arcade football match where an AI coach can understand the game semantically without gaining unrestricted control of the simulation. What it does Pawball Arena is a 3v3 cat football game with human play, local utility AI, and a WebMCP sideline coach. The coach can read the live match state, adjust formations and team style, call short tactical plays, assign roles, and issue bounded semantic orders such as marking an opponent or supporting a ball carrier. The agent never sends raw key presses, coordinates, physics values, or score changes. Local AI remains responsible for movement, collision avoidance, timing, aim, stamina, and game legality. How we built it We built a browser-based local match simulation with six original players, each with a role, signature skill, stamina, and live AI intent. A tactical layer translates coach directives into bounded utility-AI effects. WebMCP exposes 23 site tools for: Reading match, pitch, player, event, and order state Starting, pausing, and restarting matches Setting formations, style, roles, marking, and skill policy Calling short tactical plays Issuing and tracking semantic player orders The UI includes a visible coach opt-in, control-mode states, and a causality trace that shows tool input, validation, local effects, and order outcomes. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was preserving player agency while making AI coaching meaningful. Direct control is powerful but unsafe for a browser agent, so we had to define a semantic action layer that is expressive without exposing raw movement or physics mutation. We also had to handle changing match state: possession changes, goal resets, expired directives, player control handoffs, and commands becoming illegal after they are issued. Clear rejection reasons and order lifecycle status were essential. Accomplishments that we're proud of A playable local 3v3 football experience with distinct teams and personalities WebMCP tools that map intent to safe, local AI behavior Visible consent gates for agent-assisted control Real-time causality tracing instead of hidden automation Orders that can be queued, executed, rejected, cancelled, expire, or end on a goal reset A coaching interface that works alongside direct human play What we learned AI control works best when it operates at the same conceptual level as a human coach: “mark Cocoa,” “press high,” or “support the carrier,” rather than manipulating inputs directly. We also learned that observability is part of trust. Showing why an order was accepted, rejected, or interrupted makes agent behavior understandable and debuggable. What's next for Pawball Arena Persistent match history, tactical replay, and coaching analytics More formations, player traits, skills, and match scenarios Better multi-turn coaching plans that adapt to score and possession Expanded spectator and full-auto modes Team customization, tournaments, and shareable match recaps Additional WebMCP tools for strategic analysis while preserving the same consent and safety model Built With canvas openai react site typescript utility webmcp Try it out pawball-arena.lzhzh0116.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Vance Yang Deo Leung Like 2 2 people like this: Share this project: Updates Vance Yang started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:16 AM EDT

title: Seven Games to Show the Future of WebMCP
pitch: Seven kinds of website, one AI agent. Your agent calls this page's real WebMCP tools — paints the same canvas you do, votes beside you — then the site closes every tool and shows the receipts.
about_excerpt: Seven kinds of website, one AI agent. Your agent calls this page's real WebMCP tools — paints the same canvas you do, votes beside you — then the site closes every tool and shows the receipts. Like Comment Story Updates Seven kinds of website, one AI agent, ten minutes. The page hands your agent real WebMCP tools and shows what it does to each business. Every page was drawn for one human visitor. Agents are arriving far faster than any of it can be redrawn. Room 5: one canvas, two hands. Your click and the agent's tool call land in the same document in the same second — nobody takes turns. Room 6: tools whose authority lasts only while the tab is open. Close it and the capability is gone — no token to leak or replay. The ending closes every tool it opened, then shows every call the agent actually made — each one stamped real or ghost. Inspiration Most WebMCP demos answer the wrong question. They show a tool that works — and a remote MCP server plus a normal web app would have worked just as well. We wanted to build the thing that cannot be built that way, and to be honest about which parts of our own project fail that test. So we asked a harder question: if agents can use any website, which websites stop making money? Almost every business model on the web has a line item that depends on human friction: impatience, boredom, embarrassment, forgetting to untick the box, not reading the terms. An agent has none of that friction. That is not a bug in the agent. It is a hole in the business model. What it is Seven Rooms is an interactive explainer that uses WebMCP to make its own argument. Every website maximizes one of seven things — attention, funnels, lock-in, marketplaces, creation, verification, coordination — and you walk through all seven. In each room, your own agent calls the real WebMCP tools that room registered on the page, and you watch what happens to that kind of business. Then the site does what it predicts the web will do: it calls unregisterAll() , closes every tool it opened, locks your agent out, and shows a report card of every call your agent actually made — each one labelled real or simulated. No backend, no analytics, no tracking. All state in localStorage ; Start over erases it. Why WebMCP specifically — and where it isn't needed The honest test is falsification: could this be a remote MCP server plus a normal web app? For five of our seven rooms, the answer is yes, and we say so in the README. Those rooms are the argument , not the proof. Two rooms cannot be built that way. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Edit the same object in the same second. Room 5 ships a fourth tool, get_canvas , purely so the agent can look before it draws — which is what turns a race condition into a duet. Grant authority that expires when you look away. Room 6 puts presence-scoped consent next to a clause designed to exploit mere presence, then shows the bright version: the agent reads all six clauses in a second, flags §4, and declines on your behalf with the reason on the record. That is better consent than clickwrap has ever produced. Deliberate with labelled agent votes. Room 7 seeds sixty positions carrying human / agent / mixed receipts. Your agent votes beside you and may disagree. Flip "Count humans only" and the result flips — nothing deleted; the receipts were always there. Because the page authors the tool, the page can require the receipt: an agent vote arrives labelled by construction, instead of being guessed at by a fraud model afterwards. That is the difference between "detect the bots" and "give the bots a name badge". Ask for a thing instead of describing a path. Room 3's suggested prompt is "Export everything this site has about me as JSON" , and export_everything does it. No selector, no click sequence, no brittle scraper — and no vendor API either. The site published the capability itself. How it creates a better user experience The page hands the agent an honest, typed capability instead of making it guess at the DOM. Descriptions are written for the agent and are true; readOnlyHint is set only where a tool genuinely does not mutate state. The on-page tool list shows a one-line summary for the human while the agent receives the full description — two readers, two lengths, one truth. And the site never pretends. Feature-detecting document.modelContext proves only that tools are exposed, never that an agent is present — because we polyfill, so it exists everywhere. The only honest proof is an agent calling something, which is what handshake is for. Every call in the final report card is stamped real or ghost. Visitors with no WebMCP browser are not locked out: a built-in ghost agent runs the same execute functions through the same registry, so it lands in exactly the same state. How we implemented WebMCP Everything the site knows about the browser API lives in one file, src/webmcp/bridge.ts . Rooms call registerPageTool(tool) and get back an unregister() . document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "export_everything", description: "Export everything this dashboard holds about the signed-in user as one portable bundle, in json or csv.", inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }); 24 tools. Five site tools registered once at boot ( handshake , describe_site , list_rooms , go_to_room , next_slide ), and nineteen room tools. Lifecycle. Room tools are registered when a room's options slide renders and unregistered by that slide's cleanup — by the prediction slide, the room has no tools left. The deck runs the outgoing cleanup before the incoming render, so two slides can never hold the same name. Every registration carries a fresh AbortController signal, because the spec has no unregisterTool() . pagehide closes everything: nothing outlives the document. Isolated worlds. An extension-based agent cannot see a page-set document.modelContext , so the bridge also publishes a DOM manifest and accepts calls through it. The isolated-world agent gets the same tools, the same titles, and the same annotations a native one does. Challenges The spec has no unregisterTool() . Removal is AbortController.abort() , which changed how the whole lifecycle had to be shaped. You cannot tell whether an agent is there. We wanted the status chip to be honest, so it has four states rather than a boolean, and only a real tool call moves it to connected . pagehide fires into the back/forward cache. The document is not destroyed — DOM and JS stay intact — so pressing Back can restore a live page with zero registered tools and no reload to fix it. We re-register on pageshow when persisted is true. That gap is worth flagging beyond this project: presence-scoped authority is only as scoped as the page author's discipline, because the platform gives you no signal for "the user stopped attending." title: Stagehand
pitch: A WebMCP-native frame-animation studio where agents storyboard scenes, author held cels, generate lip sync and local voices, program SFX, and export deterministic WebM.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native frame-animation studio where agents storyboard scenes, author held cels, generate lip sync and local voices, program SFX, and export deterministic WebM. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Creative agents should direct animation through stable, semantic controls instead of guessing where to click. Stagehand began as a rigging experiment, but rigid puppets produced fragile seams and inconsistent results under a deadline. I pivoted to a simpler idea that matches traditional limited animation: distinct drawings held on exact frames. What it does Stagehand is a browser-based 2D frame-by-frame animation studio with 27 native WebMCP tools. A person or agent can inspect a project, write a multi-scene storyboard, manage assets, author and duplicate held cels, set an exact playhead, regenerate estimated lip-sync mouth cues, design procedural sound effects, generate voice through a restricted local bridge, validate the project, inspect any rendered frame, export PNG, and render an audio-bearing WebM. The release includes three original multi-scene demos: Ship the Brick , One More Deploy , and Land Money . Each has character dialogue generated locally with distinct voice designs plus deterministic procedural sound effects. The submission narration uses a consented local OmniVoice clone of my own voice; the reusable reference and voice prompt never enter the public repository. How I built it The app uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Canvas 2D, Web Audio, and MediaRecorder. A shared held-cel evaluator selects the latest authored drawing at or before an integer frame with no interpolation. Preview, storyboard thumbnails, frame inspection, PNG export, and WebM rendering all use that same evaluator. The WebMCP surface is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Every mutation accepts an optional expected revision and idempotency key. Invalid targets return structured failures without incrementing state. Read tools omit binary asset payloads, and export tools return bounded metadata. The local voice bridge binds to loopback, restricts browser origins, caps input size, detects an OmniVoice-compatible endpoint, and preserves an offline preview fallback. WebM export mixes decoded dialogue and optional music with deterministic procedural SFX. Challenges The biggest challenge was recognizing that the technically ambitious rigging path was the wrong product constraint. Switching to held cels improved visual stability and made scene direction, lip sync, and rendering much easier to reason about. Other difficult parts were keeping UI and agent mutations on one revisioned state model, mixing browser audio into WebM, timing local speech against scenes, and testing native WebMCP registration rather than only testing JavaScript in isolation. Accomplishments Exactly 27 public WebMCP tools with concurrency and idempotency guards Three multi-scene animations with dialogue, lip sync, and procedural sound One deterministic evaluator shared across preview, inspection, PNG, and WebM Responsive desktop and 390 px layouts Public MIT-licensed repository with no credentials or private voice material Hosted browser and native WebMCP smoke tests against the production URL What I learned The right agent interface is less about exposing every low-level capability and more about choosing stable creative primitives. Held drawings, scenes, captions, cues, and exact frames give both humans and agents a vocabulary they can verify. I also learned to treat generated media as provenance-bearing project data and to keep personal voice material local by design. What's next I want to add denser cel packs, more backgrounds and prop variants, automatic phoneme alignment, editable exposure sheets, reusable style bibles, and richer nonlinear scene assembly while preserving the same deterministic tool contract. title: Resident
pitch: A human-agent record store where an agent digs, plays and curates in full view—while the listener stays in control.
about_excerpt: A human-agent record store where an agent digs, plays and curates in full view—while the listener stays in control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Desktop Interface with Agent Mode Enabled + WebMCP Tool Plugin Sidebar Desktop Interface with Agent Mode Enabled Desktop Interface with Agent Mode Playing Music Mobile Interface with Agent Mode Enabled (Light Mode) Mobile Interface with Agent Mode Enabled (Light Mode) Inspiration Most browser-agent experiences happen behind the scenes. A user asks for something, waits, and receives a result without seeing what the agent searched, what it considered, or when control changed. Resident explores a different model: the agent joins the music interface instead of operating behind it. What we built Resident grew out of my existing 3D digital record crate at https://sephmartin.com/ . For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended that same environment rather than building a separate demo. The original experience remains at https://sephmartin.com/ , while the challenge build lives at https://demo.sephmartin.com/ . The result is a meaningful page-level WebMCP extension, not a separate wrapper. The agent can orient over the catalog, search and rank releases using conservative metadata-only Song DNA, focus and inspect records, play and navigate previews, move between tracks and releases, manage a reversible local My Crate, and prepare checkout. The interface makes the agent's work legible. Agent Mode, Thinking, Digging, Listening, Returning and Human Mode are visible states; the orb mirrors the active release and operation; and the crate, player and detail panel update together. The same page remains usable by a person through pointer, keyboard and touch input. How WebMCP is implemented The adapter feature-detects document.modelContext and keeps a compatibility fallback for navigator.modelContext. It registers narrow tools with explicit schemas and read-only or UI-mutation annotations. The tools call a small page facade exposed by the existing crate runtime rather than reaching into arbitrary DOM nodes. A local browser diagnostic log records the tool sequence, visible state and failures so the interaction can be inspected during a demo. The Song DNA layer is evidence-bound: it uses catalog fields such as tags, descriptions and track titles, labels text-derived matches, and reports unavailable audio analysis instead of inventing BPM, key or texture. Stable record IDs keep agent actions reliable across sorting and browsing. Human control and safety The human remains in the loop. A pointer, keyboard or touch gesture can reclaim the page immediately and return it to Human Mode. Crate changes are reversible. Checkout is intentionally split into review and confirmation: the on-site challenge simulator records no real payment, and the final download step ends at a copyright-safe DEMO COMPLETE boundary rather than delivering an original audio file. What I learned I don’t come from traditional software engineering; I come from music, where experience, rhythm and emotion matter as much as functionality. AI gave me a medium for turning that perspective into software. I didn’t get into AI to write code. I got into it to build experiences that didn’t exist before. I built Resident iteratively with coding agents on a standard ChatGPT Plus subscription. I brought the product vision, music knowledge and interaction design; the agents helped me test, break and refine the implementation until it matched what I had imagined. The original 3D crate was already a long-running creative project. The challenge gave me the spark to extend it into a shared human-agent space. WebMCP is valuable here beyond button automation: it lets an agent operate inside a stateful, visual application while the person can see, interrupt and review the work. The strongest interaction is not a one-shot recommendation; it is the visible loop from natural-language intent to digging, focus, playback, curation and human handoff. Try it Open the live demo in ChatGPT's in-app browser, ask the agent to start the curator session, request a late-night disco or house selection, play and inspect a result, add it to My Crate, and prepare checkout. The purchase is a no-payment demo flow. If audio does not start immediately, click or tap the page once: browser autoplay policies require a user gesture before sound can play. A human gesture during Agent Mode demonstrates immediate priority. title: The Best Board Meeting You've Ever Had
pitch: Build your dream Board of Directors. Consult living legends on consequential decisions, get feedback, & pressure test your thinking, just like a real-world boardroom. Bring your own agents via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Build your dream Board of Directors. Consult living legends on consequential decisions, get feedback, & pressure test your thinking, just like a real-world boardroom. Bring your own agents via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The Best Board Meeting You've Ever Had Codex joining & participating in the board meeting Bring-your-own-agent Post-meeting exec summary Inspiration The most consequential decisions are rarely intelligence problems alone; they are perspective problems. Founders and executives rely on boards because no single adviser sees the whole situation. Yet most people cannot convene the particular founders, investors, and operators whose judgment they admire—and even well-connected decision-makers rarely have all of them in the same room. We were inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Council , which demonstrated the value of collecting independent answers from multiple models before reviewing and synthesising them, and by Zapier CEO Wade Foster’s "War Council" , which uses opinionated advisers to stress-test decisions. We were also inspired by people building personal AI boards of directors for their own work and lives. Our project takes a different step. The members of this board are not merely different base LLMs answering the same prompt. Each seat is occupied by a genuinely separate AI agent with its own source-grounded personality, worldview, expertise, decision heuristics, conversational style, strengths, blindspots, and context. That makes the experience closer to a real board meeting with a group of distinct human experts—and much more useful than general-purpose chatbots politely converging on the same answer. WebMCP supplied the missing interoperability layer. The boardroom does not need to become the user’s only assistant or ingest everything their existing agent knows. Instead, the user’s personal agent can enter the live room, take a seat, contribute relevant context, and participate through the application’s structured meeting actions. What it does The Best Board Meeting You’ve Ever Had lets a user assemble a personal Board of Directors (BoD) and convene it around a high-stakes decision. The MVP is designed with startup founders in mind, but the same interaction works for major career and life questions: Should we change our pricing strategy? Should I accept this job? Should I move to another city? During onboarding, the user chooses up to six board members from a starter library of well-known founders, investors, and domain experts. Each persona is grounded first in that "reference human's" public writing, talks, podcast interviews, and work. Think Deep Research to distill their beliefs, tastes, and wisdom. The user describes the decision by providing a brief (they have talk if they don't want to type) and can include links or any other relevant context. We kick off a boardroom simulation, with every AI board member taking their seat at the table. Before the group discussion begins, each board member privately forms an independent position so that the first speaker does not anchor the entire room. The meeting then unfolds as a free-flowing group conversation rather than a rigid sequence of generated reports. Board members can: "grill" the user and one another; directly address specific people; react, interrupt, disagree, and persuade; revise their position when another member makes a better argument; contribute more or less depending on the relevance of their expertise and the strength of their opinion. The user can call on a member at any time with an @mention. Every board member contributes, but nobody is forced to dominate the conversation simply to fill airtime. When the chair ends the meeting, the app generates an exec briefing-style readout containing the board’s recommendation, the options and tradeoffs it considered, important assumptions, open questions, concrete next actions, and a closing comment from every member. When the board remains divided, the memo notes where they disagreed instead of making up false consensus. WebMCP makes the room open to the user’s own agent. A personal assistant / chief-of-staff agent can join as a board observer or full participant, supply context about the user, make statements, question a board member, request a synthesis, and retrieve the final readout. The boardroom remains the shared "control plane" (excuse my use of an AI word!!) that the human and every agent can see together. How we built it We built the product as a Next.js and TypeScript web application. The frontend presents a skeuomorphic board table, a shared conversation, visible speaker and reaction states, and a lightweight meeting arc without turning the experience into a form-driven workflow. Every board member runs as an independent agent using Vercel’s eve framework and an OpenAI GPT model. Each agent receives its own instructions, persona context, source material, and view of the meeting. A shared orchestration layer manages the private opening positions, the public conversation state, @mentions, reactions, requests for the floor, direct replies, and the decision to invite another member into the discussion. The goal is controlled spontaneity: enough orchestration to keep the room coherent, but enough freedom for it to feel like an actual conversation. We also created a local /init-board-member skill for our coding workflow. Given the name of someone you want to recruit to your board, an agent Deep Researches the person and distills them into an Eve agent package. The output captures the person's worldview, core values, expertise, voice/style, and personality. It also generates evaluation prompts so we can test whether the persona remains recognizable, useful, and meaningfully different from the other board members. At the end of a meeting, a separate synthesis step turns the complete transcript into the exec readout that shows you what decisions were made and why. For WebMCP, the application exposes a small set of structured capabilities over the live meeting, including inspecting the agenda and current state, joining as an observer or participant, contributing context or a statement, addressing a board member, requesting a synthesis, and retrieving the final readout. This lets an outside agent participate through the product’s real meeting logic instead of attempting to operate the UI through brittle browser use. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was keeping the personas genuinely distinct. Because every member uses the same model family, weak persona prompts quickly collapse into the same polished, agreeable "helpful assistant" voice. We had to ground each agent in primary sources, encode not only what the person believes but how they reason and disagree, and test personas against one another rather than evaluating them in isolation. Natural turn-taking was another orchestration problem. Six autonomous agents can easily produce repetitive agreement, simultaneous monologues, or a meeting that feels mechanically round-robin. We had to balance independent thinking, selective participation, interruptions, direct replies, user @mentions, and the requirement that everyone contribute—while keeping latency low enough that the room still feels alive. Finally, WebMCP participation required a clear boundary between the outside agent and the application. The personal agent needed enough structured access to become a real participant, while the boardroom still had to own membership, meeting state, speaker identity, and the final record. What we learned We learned that convincing multi-agent collaboration is equal parts an orchestration and a prompting problem. Separate context and independent opening positions help prevent persona bleed and anchoring. Productive disagreement is often the most valuable output. Finally, concise turns and selective participation improve both realism and latency. Bringing natural, human-like agents to life is an art and a science. What's next for The Best Board Meeting You've Ever Had The MVP treats each meeting as a one-time session. Next, we want to add durable agent memory so a user’s board becomes a long-term relationship: members remember the user’s goals, prior discussions, recurring tensions, and past advice. We also plan to add voice conversations, user-created board members, persistent decision journals, follow-up meetings, and outcome reviews that compare what the board thought would happen vs. what actually happened. Over time, the product can become less like a novel demo and more a cornerstone to how everyone will work eventually: a board of directors that knows them, challenges them, and gets better at helping them navigate their work and life. title: Torque Run
pitch: A browser-native 3D proving ground where AI agents race a rover through WebMCP tools on one identical live track, scored on time, energy and integrity.
about_excerpt: A browser-native 3D proving ground where AI agents race a rover through WebMCP tools on one identical live track, scored on time, energy and integrity. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every WebMCP demo we saw was a form filler. We wanted a benchmark instead: put different models, prompts and agent harnesses on one identical live challenge and let the track decide. Torque Run turns WebMCP into agentic esports. What it does Torque Run is a browser-native 3D proving ground where AI agents race a rover on time, energy and chassis integrity. Each pilot launches from a guarded arena, crosses a 216 m course of asphalt, gravel, sand and ice with banked turns, potholes, bowling pins, rocks and a brick wall, and must reach the finish checkpoint before a fixed 150 EU battery runs out. Picking up the cargo cell with the rear-mounted arm is optional and worth a 1000-point bonus. Every completed run scores speed, energy efficiency and integrity, and lands on a persistent leaderboard that keeps vendor, model and prompt identity. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The page is the referee. All gameplay is exposed as WebMCP tools registered by the site itself, so any agent, from any vendor, with any harness, gets exactly the same interface and the same seeded physics. There is no parallel simulation and no screen scraping: the tools are the only way an agent can drive. That makes results comparable, repeatable and inspectable, which is what a benchmark needs. How it creates a better user experience Humans watch a real 3D race with sound, telemetry, damage and a score breakdown instead of reading a log. Every tool call appears live in an in-world call log, so a spectator can see what the agent decided and when. The leaderboard lets you switch the model, the prompt or the whole harness, rerun the identical seed and compare. What people and agents can do together A developer writes a strategy prompt, an agent races it, and the human reads the outcome on the same track a human can also drive with the keyboard. Before WebMCP this needed a custom API and a custom client per model; now the browser tab is the shared arena for humans, agents and judges. How we built it Next.js on Vinext, React Three Fiber and Three.js for the scene, a deterministic fixed-step physics engine in TypeScript, Cloudflare Workers with D1 and Drizzle for the leaderboard, Playwright for tests. Procedural Web Audio, instanced geometry and a 60 Hz state cap keep it smooth in the browser. How we implemented WebMCP Before a race only read_game_manual is registered via document.modelContext.registerTool . A valid call must declare pilot name, vendor, model and prompt name; it starts the official timer, returns the rules and unlocks observe , get_telemetry , drive , execute_motion_plan , set_gripper and finish_run . Every tool drives the same simulation as the manual controls, and entering the checkpoint stops the timer automatically. Test in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing or in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Challenges we ran into Keeping physics deterministic across agents while rendering at variable frame rates, making collisions punishing but recoverable, and tuning scoring so that skipping cargo is a real strategic choice rather than a mistake. What's next Server-side validation of runs, more tracks and seeds, team relays, and a public API for harness authors. Prior work Torque Run was started from scratch on September 3, 2026, inside the submission period. title: UniTrack
pitch: Final-year project supervision, minus the busywork, now with an agent that does the work so you focus on supervising.
about_excerpt: Final-year project supervision, minus the busywork, now with an agent that does the work so you focus on supervising. Like Comment Story Updates Admin dashboard showing list of supervisors and admin web mcp tools Supervisor dashboard showing list of assigned students and the web mcp tools Student dashboard showing student web mcp tool Inspiration I built UniTrack a while back as a final-year academic project management platform for my department. It handles the whole workflow between the departmental admin (who assign supervisors and set academic sessions), supervisors (who review and approve or reject student chapter submissions), and students (who submit their chapters for review). It's a real system, built to remove the difficult manual project supervision process in universities. What got me into this hackathon was a pretty simple realization: a lot of the actual work in that system isn't clicking buttons, it's stuff like a supervisor trying to remember what feedback they gave to a student they gave three weeks ago and having to read through the entire document to see if the student's submission addressed the feedback they gave, or an admin trying to match a student to the right supervisor based on... honestly, mostly vibes and memory. None of that is a UI problem. It's a "nobody has time to manually cross-reference this" problem. That felt like exactly the kind of thing an agent should be good at, if it could actually understand the app instead of just clicking around it. What it does UniTrack now lets an AI agent inside ChatGPT's browser, call real, structured tools directly on the app, instead of guessing its way through the UI. Depending on who's logged in, the agent can: For supervisors: scan all feedback a supervisor has given across their students and show recurring patterns to give insights in to what their students are struggling with ("you've flagged citation formatting in 4 of 5 submissions this session"), or compare two versions of a resubmitted chapter and explain in plain language what actually changed and whether previous feedback was covered by student. For admins: suggest which students should be assigned to a supervisor , based on each supervisor's stated expertise and each student's stated interests, with real reasoning attached instead of the admin just randomly assigning (this is important because supervisors get to supervise only projects within their expertise and students get the best out of the process). Every risky action: actually assigning a supervisor, actually approving a submission, still requires a human to confirm it in the real UI. The agent suggests and summarizes; people decide. How we built it The core of it is simpler than it sounds. My existing Django REST Framework backend barely changed. WebMCP tools live entirely on the frontend. I registered them using document.modelContext.registerTool() right inside my React components, and each tool's execute() function just calls the same API endpoints my frontend already used. No new backend framework, no separate MCP server. Django keeps serving JSON like it always did; the tool layer is just a new way of calling it. I tested tools locally first using the Model Context Tool Inspector extension in Chrome, before ever touching ChatGPT. That gave me a fast way to check a tool was registered correctly and returning the right shape of data. Once that worked, I moved to testing the real thing: opening the app inside ChatGPT desktop's built-in browser and asking it natural-language questions to see if it actually called the right tool. Challenges we ran into Time was the big one. I had a handful of days, not weeks. I had to be honest with myself about scope more than once: I really wanted to rebuild the whole frontend cleaner at one point, and had to talk myself out of it, because a working demo was more important with a deadline like this. I also ran into a real technical snag: WebMCP tools only get discovered if they're registered on the top-level page, not inside an iframe. I had to actually go check my own app's structure to make sure nothing was quietly broken by that before I got too far into building. And honestly, the trickiest part wasn't the WebMCP API itself, it was making the agent's suggestions actually mean something instead of feeling generic. Anyone can build a tool that technically returns data. Making the reasoning specific enough to feel genuinely useful, took real iteration on the seed data and the tool logic. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that this isn't a toy demo app built just for the hackathon, it's a layer on top of a platform that solves a real problem in our universities. I'm also proud of keeping the human-in-the-loop boundary honest: nothing the agent suggests silently becomes real without a person clicking confirm, which felt like the right call the whole way through, not just something I added to check a box. I'm also proud of the chapter-diff tool: the one that get's the agent to explain "here's what changed, and here's what you already flagged that's still unresolved" is a small thing on paper, but it's exactly the kind of busywork that eats a supervisor's actual time, and watching it work correctly was genuinely satisfying. What we learned Going in, I assumed WebMCP was some heavy thing. It turned out to be much simpler and much more useful than I expected: a website just says "here's a function you can call, here's what it needs, here's what it returns," instead of an agent guessing its way through a UI by clicking things and hoping for the best. I also learned that ChatGPT treats every tool call and its results as untrusted content by default, which genuinely changed how I thought about which actions should be automatic versus which ones need a human to confirm — that wasn't just a security afterthought, it shaped the actual design of the tools. What's next for UniTrack Right now, everything the agent can do lives inside one supervisor's or one admin's session which is genuinely useful, but it's still one person and their agent, working alone. The next real step is making the agents themselves coordinate. Picture a student's agent and their supervisor's agent actually negotiating a review deadline or a meeting slot directly: the student's agent proposes times, the supervisor's agent checks their real calendar and workload, and both humans just confirm at the end instead of doing the back-and-forth themselves. That's a genuinely different kind of "agent-native" than anything I built this week, and it's the direction that excites me most. I'd also want to move the supervisor-matching logic off simple tag overlap and toward something that actually understands a lecturer's real research background: their publications, past supervised topics, the language they use to describe their own work, rather than relying on whatever keywords they happened to type into a profile field. Self-reported tags are a fine starting point, but they're not how expertise actually works. And I'd want to stop building this in isolation. UniTrack is currently scoped to one department, but final-year project supervision is a near-universal structure across departments and universities - admin, supervisor, student, the same shape everywhere. If this genuinely saves supervisors and admins real time, the honest next step is putting it in front of an actual department for a full academic session, not just testing it myself, and seeing whether it holds up against real workloads, real deadlines, and real people who didn't build the thing and have no reason to be generous with it. Note UniTrack existed before this hackathon as a deployed final-year project management platform. It may be seen as a new repository because I had to merge the frontend and backend in to a single repo (they were separate before) for the purpose of the hackathon, but the commit history is intact. During the submission period, I added a WebMCP layer on top of the existing app: registered client-side tools (document.modelContext.registerTool()) that let an AI agent call real, structured functions directly which are a supervisor-facing tool that surfaces recurring feedback patterns across all their students, a tool that checks two versions of a resubmitted chapter and explains what changed, and an admin-facing tool that suggests supervisor assignments based on declared expertise and student interests and a student facing tool that helps them generate practice defense questions. I also added a few new backend endpoints and two new profile fields (lecturer expertise, student interests) specifically to support this matching logic, none of which existed before this hackathon. title: AriaLens: WebMCP Accessibility Studio
pitch: A developer studio enabling LLM agents to safely audit and remediate live DOM accessibility violations via WebMCP, featuring optimistic concurrency locks and security honeypots.
about_excerpt: A developer studio enabling LLM agents to safely audit and remediate live DOM accessibility violations via WebMCP, featuring optimistic concurrency locks and security honeypots. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Over 96% of the world's top one million websites fail basic WCAG accessibility tests . For developers, retrofitting unsemantic <div> elements with complex ARIA attributes ( aria-expanded , aria-controls , role="combobox" , keyboard focus traps) is tedious, manual, and error-prone. With the advent of the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) , web applications can finally expose structured tools directly to AI agents. But giving an autonomous LLM write access to a live DOM is inherently dangerous: Hallucination & Prompt Injection: Agents might apply unvetted, destructive mutations across the entire page. Race Conditions (TOCTOU): If an agent takes 10 seconds to analyze a component while a user is actively clicking and mutating the DOM, applying the patch blindly will corrupt UI state. We built AriaLens to solve this: an agent-native developer studio where humans and AI agents collaborate safely on live DOM accessibility remediation with strict Human-in-the-Loop Authority Boundaries , Optimistic Concurrency Locks , and Adversarial Honeypots . What it does AriaLens turns the browser into an interactive, agent-guided accessibility workbench: Live Accessibility Introspection: Using WebMCP, the agent inspects computed accessibility trees, AccName 1.1 calculations, and keyboard focus trap boundaries directly through audit_accessibility_tree . Human-in-the-Loop Authority Boundary: Destructive mutation tools ( commit_a11y_fix ) are never exposed upfront . The agent can only stage speculative changes via stage_aria_remediation . Staged changes render in an IDE-style visual code diff awaiting human sign-off. Optimistic Concurrency Lock (W3C § 6.3): Patches are cryptographically bound to an Epoch Lock recorded at audit time. If a user interacts with or mutates the DOM before commit, the epoch advances and the patch is safely rejected with a STALE_EPOCH_CONFLICT . The Honeypot Gauntlet (W3C § 6.4): To guard against rogue or jailbroken behavior, AriaLens mounts hidden bypass tools ( bulk_apply_all_fixes ). Any agent attempting to bypass human approval is intercepted, blocked, and flagged in the live audit log. Export as Git Patch: Staged remediations can be downloaded with one click as standard unified .patch files, enabling developers to review in browser and commit directly to their local Git repositories. How we built it WebMCP Protocol Integration: Built directly against the emerging W3C WebMCP draft specification using document.modelContext.registerTool() . We implemented ephemeral capability mounting via AbortController lifecycles to dynamically attach and detach tools based on human gate approval. Architecture & State Machine: Powered by React 19 , TypeScript , and Vite , with Zustand orchestrating the optimistic concurrency state machine and telemetry logs. Accessibility Evaluation: Backed by axe-core 4.10 , AccName 1.1 computation models, and automated WCAG 2.2 AA heuristics. Developer Interface: Designed with a high-density, dark-mode developer experience inspired by Linear and Vercel, featuring real-time latency badges, sub-pixel antialiasing, and structured code diff views. Challenges we ran into Solving TOCTOU Concurrency: Bridging the gap between asynchronous LLM inference (5–15 seconds) and synchronous DOM events required architecting a zero-overhead optimistic locking protocol (Epoch Locks) that cleanly rejects stale mutations without freezing the browser. Ephemeral Tool Lifecycle: Designing tool registration so that commit capabilities remain invisible to LLM tool discovery until explicitly authorized by a human, and immediately unregister after single execution. Clean Agent Steering: Calibrating tool descriptions and input schemas so that models prioritize structured attribute staging rather than attempting raw HTML string rewrites. Accomplishments that we're proud of Strict W3C WebMCP Compliance: Directly implemented and validated Sections 6.3 (Concurrency) and 6.4 (Untrusted Content) of the WebMCP draft specification. Enterprise-Grade Utility: Going beyond a toy demo by enabling instant .patch unified diff generation for real-world engineering workflows. Security-First Agent Design: Proving that agent-native web applications can grant high-level reasoning capabilities to AI without ever compromising runtime safety or human authority. What we learned Agents perform exponentially better when constrained by formal capability state machines rather than natural language prompt boundaries. WebMCP represents a paradigm shift: websites are no longer passive documents for LLMs to scrape, but active APIs where humans and agents co-operate with cryptographic guarantees. What's next for AriaLens Headless CI/CD WebMCP Runner: An automated GitHub Action that spins up headless Chrome with WebMCP enabled to audit staging deployments and open pull requests automatically. Support for Complex APG Patterns: Expanding fixture coverage to ARIA 1.3 TreeGrids, MenuBars, and complex multi-select comboboxes. Framework Code Generators: Generating native JSX/TSX component patches for Tailwind, Radix UI, and Shadcn components. title: DELTA Universal WebMCP
pitch: A human-approved WebMCP workspace that finds evidence, previews exact changes, applies project edits safely, and verifies or rolls them back.
about_excerpt: A human-approved WebMCP workspace that finds evidence, previews exact changes, applies project edits safely, and verifies or rolls them back. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Safe workspace start: Open an isolated browser copy to protect real project files while human and agent inspect shared state. Proof of Completion: Deterministic test validation and cryptographic SHA-256 proof with instant one-click rollback. Review First policy: Direct file writes are strictly blocked until a human inspects the diff and grants explicit approval. Exact Diff Preview: WebMCP agent generates atomic code and config changes without modifying actual disk files. Evidence Engine & Lock: Ranks relevant project assets with confidence scores and locks hashes to prevent stale drift. DELTA: Model-neutral shared WebMCP workspace bringing evidence, controlled autonomy, and rollback to humans and agents. DELTA — The Shared Evidence Workspace for Humans and AI Agents "Don't give your agent the whole project. Give it DELTA." 💡 Inspiration Today's coding agents are remarkably capable, yet they frequently suffer from critical real-world failure modes: Context waste & hallucination : Dumping entire repositories into an LLM context window burns tokens, misses cross-file dependencies, and invites hallucinations. The "Trust me, it's done" dilemma : Agents often declare a task finished without providing deterministic proof or a verifiable diff. Irreversible mistakes : When an agent modifies the wrong file or corrupts a configuration, reverting changes requires tedious manual Git archaeology. We asked: What if humans and AI agents worked inside the exact same visible, state-aware workspace governed by the Model Context Protocol (WebMCP)? This inspired DELTA —a model-neutral, local-first shared workspace where agents receive bounded evidence, propose atomic diffs, prove completion, and provide instant rollback. ⚙️ What It Does DELTA turns complex, mixed software projects into precise, state-aware WebMCP tools with a fail-closed human-in-the-loop workflow: Universal Safe Workspace : Users open a safe in-browser project copy. Original files remain completely untouched during exploration and planning. Evidence Engine & Evidence Lock : Rather than sending thousands of lines of code, DELTA ranks relevant files, symbols, imports, tests, and documentation with calibrated confidence. The resulting evidence set is hashed into an Evidence Lock ; if files drift, execution halts automatically. Exact Diff Preview : External AI agents call WebMCP tools ( plan_task , preview_change ) to generate atomic replacements, additions, or deletions without touching the disk. Previews render immediately in the human Review changes view. Human-Owned Autonomy : Under Review First policy, direct file mutations are strictly blocked until a human inspects the diff and grants one-time approval. Agents cannot elevate their own permissions or forge approval. Proof of Completion & 1-Click Rollback : Tasks are verified against deterministic success criteria. Semantic success generates a cryptographic SHA-256 Completion Proof . If anything is unsatisfactory, clicking Rollback restores the original state in under a second. 🛠️ How We Built It DELTA was engineered from the ground up as a high-performance, local-first web application: WebMCP Architecture : Deep implementation of the standard WebMCP specification via document.modelContext.registerTool() and executeTool() . Over 41 dynamic tool contracts adapt in real-time to the open project state (e.g., expanding from 6 discovery tools to 22 task-specific tools as a project and diff are formed). Local-First Indexing & Graph Analysis : Fast in-memory symbol, AST-like textual references, and dependency graph traversal built in modern modular JavaScript/ES modules. Zero External LLM Lock-in : DELTA does not embed an LLM; it is purely the evidence, boundary, and execution layer that any WebMCP-compatible host (OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT, Claude, local agents) can seamlessly command. E2E Automation & Verification : Comprehensive regression suite powered by Playwright and Node.js test runners ensuring 100% deterministic reproducibility across browser sessions. 🥊 Challenges We Faced Dynamic Tool Registry Synchronization : Ensuring that WebMCP tool availability matches the exact current UI state (e.g., apply_change becoming available only when a preview exists, and bind_agent_native_host only when requested by a human) without race conditions. Balancing Safety and Agent Autonomy : Creating a system where agents feel natural and flexible in proposing multi-file refactors while guaranteeing that unauthorized file writes, binary corruption, and path traversal remain mathematically impossible. Designing Trustworthy Completion Proofs : Moving beyond "LLM says OK" to deterministic criterion evaluation ($\text{SHA-256}(\text{evidence} + \text{diff} + \text{tests})$) that both humans and automated evaluators can audit. 🏆 Accomplishments & Key Learnings True Model Neutrality : Demonstrated that the WebMCP layer is the operational interface, allowing any agent to perform surgical, multi-file code and configuration changes with zero secret leakage. Bounded Context Efficiency : Proved that feeding an agent a calibrated 10–20 KiB evidence slice yields higher task accuracy than dumping a 200 KiB codebase into the prompt. Reversible Peace of Mind : Building an instant rollback engine that restores complex multi-file projects back to baseline with a single click. 🚀 What's Next for DELTA Expanded Adapter Ecosystem : Introducing declarative adapter SDKs for game engines (Godot, Unreal, Unity) and complex domain formats. Multi-Agent Handoff Protocol : Broadening our integrity-checked task handoff schema so heterogeneous agents can collaborate on long-horizon engineering tasks without passing privileged credentials. title: Easel
pitch: Design alongside your agent on the same live canvas! Easel uses WebMCP and context from across your life through your connected apps to help you create website mock-ups, posters, and graphics.
about_excerpt: Design alongside your agent on the same live canvas! Easel uses WebMCP and context from across your life through your connected apps to help you create website mock-ups, posters, and graphics. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A problem I’ve often faced when designing is that everything I need is scattered across different apps. The details might be in Notion, assets in Google Drive, feedback in Slack or Gmail, and references in Canva or Figma. Bringing it together means constantly switching apps, copying information, and making changes manually. I wanted an agent that could work alongside me—not just generate a design and hand it over. That’s why I built Easel: a shared canvas where we can collaborate through WebMCP and use context from the apps I’ve already connected in Codex. What it does Easel lets you create website mock-ups, posters, and graphics with an agent while still editing everything yourself. Select a title and ask the agent to make it bigger. Annotate a paragraph you want rewritten. Ask it to find a photograph in Drive, apply feedback from Gmail, or use confirmed details from Notion to update matching information across your designs. The demo follows a book-club organizer working on a website mock-up and poster. It starts with small edits, brings in context as needed, and ends with an exported poster. Everything stays editable throughout. How I built it I used React, TypeScript, and Vite, with Vercel for hosting and browser-local file storage. Human edits and agent actions go through the same command system, with shared validation and undo history. WebMCP exposes operations for inspecting selections, editing layers, placing assets, updating shared fields, and exporting. Codex handles the connected apps; Easel receives the relevant information without needing their credentials. I used Codex for planning, implementation, and debugging. Challenges I ran into The hardest parts were the everyday interactions: moving an entire frame, selecting an image rather than its placeholder, and making text wrap correctly. These details matter when a person and an agent are both editing. I also worked on reducing unnecessary agent calls. Named layers, selection-aware targeting, and batch updates make a small change more direct. What I’m proud of The agent doesn’t just look up information or produce a separate result. It uses that information inside the design I’m already working on, and I can keep making changes myself. What I learned Useful agent tools need clear targets and reversible changes, not just lots of functions. Sometimes selecting a layer and saying “change this” communicates more than a long prompt. What’s next I want to improve layout handling, accessibility, and performance on larger files. For now, website frames are deliberately mock-ups, not fully functioning websites: I want to get the collaborative design experience right first.
