title: funlabkids
pitch: Your kid learns one way at school. You teach another. So I built an app on NC Department of Education materials to fix that, with fun features that make kids actually want to do homework.
about_excerpt: Your kid learns one way at school. You teach another. So I built an app on NC Department of Education materials to fix that, with fun features that make kids actually want to do homework. Like Comment Story Updates Home Labs Progress Lab Catalogue Math Lab Math Assessments WebMCP Tools Inspiration My kid comes home with homework that doesn't match how I'd explain the same thing. I'd try to help and we'd both get frustrated. The method in the textbook, the method I know, and whatever the AI suggested were all different. That disconnect is what started this. I wanted an AI that doesn't just talk at a kid through a chat window. One that actually works on the same board the child sees. WebMCP made that possible. With it, the agent can move pieces, run checks, and suggest next steps right alongside the child, on the same board, using the same NC Grade 2 materials their teacher assigned. What it does I built Fun Lab Kids to give my kid a shared board where an AI tutor works alongside them, not in a separate chat window, not as a voice in the corner, but right there moving pieces and checking answers. The child stays in control the whole time. The agent helps, but the kid drives. I mapped all 77 NC Grade 2 standards across Math, ELA, and Science, the same ones their teacher is working from, so my kid isn't learning from some random content library. They open labs, earn Fun Points, build streaks, and unlock badges. Progress saves on the device. No account needed, no data leaving the house. The three main labs, Place Value Lab, Opinion Builder, and Matter Lab, show what working together with the agent actually looks like. The agent can open a lab, place pieces, run checks, ask for hints, and suggest changes. Big moves still need my kid to confirm them on screen. That boundary was non-negotiable for me. How we built it I built it with Vite, React, and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. The stack was familiar from my day job. The harder parts were the curriculum and the agent layer, not the frontend. I pulled all 77 NC Grade 2 standards directly from NCDPI and mapped them so a parent can see exactly what each lab covers. Everything runs on the same shared board state. The kid's UI and the WebMCP tools use the same logic underneath, so the agent never sees a different version of the board than my kid does. WebMCP tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool . I split them into two groups: curriculum tools (list standards, open activities, read progress) and board tools (get state, apply actions, undo, check, hint, reset). The app works fine without an agent. WebMCP is purely additive, so the experience never depends on whether a model is connected. Challenges we ran into The hardest part wasn't the code. It was the screen design. Ed-tech UIs are built for clicks, not agents. I had to think carefully about which board actions an agent could trigger on its own and which ones still needed my kid's hand on the button. Getting that line wrong in either direction breaks the experience. Shared board state sounds simple until the agent does something unexpected and your kid is staring at a screen that doesn't make sense. I made reveal, reset, and revision all require confirmation from my kid, not because I didn't trust the model, but because my kid needs to stay on track at every step. Covering all of Grade 2 in a weekend-scale build meant making a hard call: go deep on three showcase labs and build reusable templates for the rest, rather than shipping 77 shallow activities that don't actually teach anything. Accomplishments we're proud of I'm most proud that it's a real product, not a thin demo. My kid can sit down, open any lab, and work through it on their own. The agent is there if needed, but the app works either way. The agent works on the same board my kid sees, not in a separate chat window next to it. It moves pieces, runs checks, and responds to what's on screen. That's the thing I set out to build, and it works. The curriculum and board tools use the same checks as the on-screen controls. I didn't want a separate agent-only code path that could drift out of sync, so there isn't one. No account, no data leaving the device, no personal info stored anywhere. I wasn't willing to trade my kid's privacy for a leaderboard feature. The characters are genuinely fun. Codex sprites with custom voices from Fish Audio. My kid noticed immediately, which told me that part was worth the effort. What we learned WebMCP works best when the UI is already a shared board. I didn't have to build a new way for the agent to interact. The board was already there, and the agent just needed tools to use it the same way my kid does. Using the same checks for both the agent and the kid is what keeps the agent honest. The moment you give the agent its own code path, it starts seeing a different board than the child. I learned that early and built around it from the start. Kid safety isn't something you add at the end. I had to think about it at the design level: which moves are safe to automate, which ones need my kid in the loop, and how to make that feel natural rather than annoying. What's next for Fun Lab Kids I want more question sets for every standard, not just the three main labs. The templates are already there. Filling them out is the next big push. The agent coaching needs to get smarter. Better hints, guiding questions that actually adapt to where my kid is stuck, and revision suggestions that feel like a tutor rather than a spell-checker. Grade 2 was the starting point. The goal is the full K-5 range, same shared board model, same focus on real curriculum, just a lot more labs. I want to add progress views for teachers and parents so the adults can see what's clicking and what isn't, without changing the privacy defaults I built in from day one. title: Glassmap
pitch: A web map is a WebGL canvas — a black box to AI agents. WebMCP makes it glass.
about_excerpt: A web map is a WebGL canvas — a black box to AI agents. WebMCP makes it glass. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GIF Inspiration I come from a GIS background, and I have worked on many web map applications for different clients. One problem I keep running into is that AI agents are still not very good at dealing with maps. When I use AI to help with application development, debugging, or QA, everything usually works fine until the agent reaches the map. A web map is often rendered as a WebGL canvas, so the agent cannot easily understand what is actually on the map, which features are being displayed, or what happened after an interaction. Sometimes it simply cannot continue. Other times, it tries to rely on screenshots and visual interactions, but the result is often inaccurate or unreliable. This has always felt like a major limitation to me, especially because maps are not just visual content. Behind the screen, they contain structured geographic data, layers, coordinates, features, spatial relationships, and actions. When I learned about WebMCP, I immediately saw a way to solve this problem. Instead of forcing an agent to understand a map through pixels, the map can directly expose its data and capabilities as tools. That idea became the starting point for GlassMap . My goal was to make a web map that is no longer a black box to AI agents. What I learned The biggest thing I learned from this project was WebMCP itself. I spent a lot of time thinking beyond the basic question of “how do I expose a function as a WebMCP tool?” The more interesting question for me was: What kinds of experiences become possible when an AI agent can directly interact with a website through structured tools? While building GlassMap, I kept looking for use cases where WebMCP could do more than simply make an existing feature easier to automate. For example, instead of an agent looking at a screenshot and guessing which places are inside an area, it can directly ask the map for features within an exact spatial boundary. Instead of trying to reproduce a sequence of mouse clicks, it can work directly with map objects, coordinates, routes, and geographic queries. That changed how I thought about the project. WebMCP is not only a better way for an agent to operate an existing interface. In some cases, it can enable an entirely different user experience where the human, the application, and the AI agent all work with the same underlying state. That gave me many new ideas for projects I would like to explore in the future. How I built it GlassMap is a web map built with Next.js, MapLibre, OpenStreetMap data, Turf.js, and Zustand . MapLibre handles the map visualization, while Turf.js performs spatial operations directly in the browser. The application exposes map capabilities through 15 WebMCP tools , including operations for searching places, querying nearby features, working with map objects, changing the map view, adding notes, and planning routes. I designed the WebMCP layer separately from the map UI through a common store interface. This makes the tools easier to test and allows both the human interface and the AI agent to operate on the same map state. I also added a development shim so that the WebMCP tools can be tested in browsers that do not yet support the API natively. One thing this project also reminded me of is that, with today's AI coding tools, actually implementing an application is becoming much easier. The harder questions are increasingly: How should the system be designed? and What should the user experience actually be? Those were much more difficult for me than writing the code itself. Challenges I faced The biggest challenge was actually deciding how to use WebMCP well . This is a WebMCP hackathon, so it would have been easy to build a normal web application first and then add a few WebMCP tools on top of it just to satisfy the requirement. I did not want to do that. I wanted GlassMap to be a project where WebMCP is fundamental to the experience — where removing WebMCP would remove one of the main reasons the product exists. Because of that, I spent a lot of time thinking about the user experience instead of simply adding more tools. I asked questions like: What should an agent be able to understand about the map? What operations are actually useful as tools? What should happen when both a human and an agent are working on the same map? When should the agent return structured information instead of trying to manipulate the interface? And most importantly, what can WebMCP enable that would be difficult or unreliable with a traditional screenshot-based agent? That design process was probably the hardest part of the project. Building the features was relatively straightforward. Deciding which features should exist, how they should work together, and how WebMCP could genuinely improve the experience took much more thought. For me, that is also the most interesting part of building AI-native applications today. The bottleneck is becoming less about whether we can build something, and more about whether we can design the right system and the right experience around it. title: LivingPage
pitch: A page that changes with your questions.
about_excerpt: A page that changes with your questions. Like Comment Story Updates The original reading view before any agent actions. Agent-generated explanations and verification appear directly beside the relevant passages. The Layers panel shows the agent’s changes, sources, and resolved requests alongside the article. Inspiration When something on a page raises a question, we usually have to look it up. We copy passages one by one, search in another tab or paste them into a chat, read the explanation, and then return to the original page. I wanted to eliminate this back-and-forth and make it possible to complete the whole process without leaving the page. What it does While reading an article, you can leave marks such as Explain, Simplify, and more on the parts you are interested in, and send those requests all at once. Instead of asking the agent one question at a time whenever something comes up, you can keep reading while leaving your questions on the page, then ask the agent only once when you are ready . The agent processes the queued requests together and makes the results available directly on the page. How we built it The page exposes both reading and editing capabilities to the agent as WebMCP tools. We also implemented web page and PDF importing, research layers, Undo / Redo, maps using Leaflet, and sandboxed interactive widgets generated by the agent . Originally, I wanted LivingPage to work directly with the web page the user is already viewing, instead of requiring them to import a URL into LivingPage. However, because development time was limited, the current version uses an import-based approach. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest parts was coming up with an idea that felt like a new experience unique to WebMCP. Many of the ideas I considered ended up moving toward things similar to existing demos, such as agent-controlled UIs or games, so I struggled to find a different direction. The idea for LivingPage came from something that felt like it should already be possible with chat AI, but still was not commonly done in practice. Instead of bringing information from the page into the chat, bring the AI's results back into the original page. I arrived at this idea only three days before the deadline , so from that point on, it became a race against time. Accomplishments that we're proud of I decided to enter the WebMCP Challenge, and although LivingPage is not perfect, I was able to turn the idea into something that actually works and make it all the way to submission. I think the rapid progress of AI tools made it possible for one person to build this much in such a short period of time. LivingPage is also the first program I have ever publicly released. More than achieving a perfect level of polish, I am proud that I was able to turn the idea into a working project and release it to the public. What we learned By actually using WebMCP, I realized that when an agent needs to operate multiple tools one after another, it can still take a noticeable amount of time. For an experience like LivingPage, where multiple requests are processed at once, processing speed has a major impact on the user experience . I also learned that if I keep working until I am completely satisfied, the project may never be finished. With limited time, it is also important to decide where to stop, finish a working version, and release it . What's next for LivingPage I expect AI agents to become faster and able to handle multiple tasks much more quickly than they can today. When that happens, an experience like LivingPage — where you leave multiple questions while reading, process them together, and have the results returned directly to the page — could become more natural and practical. I also want to develop LivingPage beyond the current approach of importing URLs into a separate reader. Ultimately, I want the web page you are already viewing to become the "Living Page" itself — changing and growing based on the user's questions. title: Local Buzz
pitch: Local Buzz turns a city into a shared workspace for you and your AI agent, helping you discover what’s happening now and collaboratively build, adapt, and rescue your night in real time.
about_excerpt: Local Buzz turns a city into a shared workspace for you and your AI agent, helping you discover what’s happening now and collaboratively build, adapt, and rescue your night in real time. Like Comment Story Updates The agent does not click through the UI. Local Buzz exposes structured WebMCP tools, and the results appear directly in the same interface. Local Buzz combines a live city interface with WebMCP so a person and their AI agent can plan together. The human brings taste. The agent handles complexity. Local Buzz provides the live city. WebMCP enables one shared experience. Inspiration “What should we do tonight?” sounds simple, but the answer is scattered across event sites, venues, ticketing platforms, local calendars, social media, and word of mouth. AI can already recommend events or generate itineraries, but chat is a poor interface for exploring a city. A map is better for geography. A timeline is better for sequence. Visual browsing is better for taste. That led to a different question: What if a person and their personal AI agent could explore and shape a night together, inside the same live web experience? What it does Local Buzz turns your city into a shared real-time workspace for a person and their AI agent (starting with Stockholm and San Francisco). Local Buzz knows the city: what is happening, where, when, how much it costs, and what is currently available. The user's agent can bring something Local Buzz does not need to collect: context about the user. Together they can: discover relevant happenings surface candidates directly on the city map stage an evening on a visual timeline let the human lock, reject, or change individual choices let the agent read those changes and adapt around them repair an existing night when something becomes unavailable The important idea is that Local Buzz is not an AI itinerary generator. It is a shared model of a night that stays alive. It answers the age old question: where can I go have fun right now? Why WebMCP The human and the agent need different interfaces into the same application. The human works visually through maps, cards, timelines, locks, and direct manipulation. The agent works through structured WebMCP tools for searching happenings, showing candidates, reading the current plan, staging changes, locking stops, and repairing the plan. Both operate on the same underlying application state. For example, when a human locks a stop in the interface, the agent sees that constraint the next time it reads the plan. If another event becomes unavailable, the agent repairs only the affected portion instead of throwing the entire itinerary away and starting over. This is the interaction we wanted to explore with WebMCP: Agent acts → interface changes → human intervenes → agent understands the intervention → reality changes → agent repairs the shared state → human approves. How we built it Local Buzz is built as a proof-of-concept web application using the Modeless design system. The application has one shared domain model that powers both the human interface and its WebMCP tools. Human actions and agent actions call the same underlying application functions rather than maintaining separate UI and agent state. For the challenge prototype, we focus on Stockholm and San Francisco and use a small normalized set of real local event and venue data. Local Buzz adds derived metadata where useful for planning. A last-minute event availability change used in the demo is intentionally simulated so the repair behavior can be demonstrated deterministically and is clearly labeled as such. What we learned The most interesting part of WebMCP is that websites can be designed from the beginning for two collaborators with different strengths. The human brings taste, intuition, and judgment. The agent handles search, constraints, timing, and complexity. The website provides the live domain state they collaborate around. What I've been exploring is the surface area of how much a web app can be adapted for the end user based on agentic interactions. In some ways, it starts to become reminiscent of push, or streaming, data if the agent is making a lot of updates. I believe there's a lot of use cases for WebMCP around real-time data. title: LogoPacker Canvas - Assisted Canvas with Local Workspace
pitch: A local-first design canvas where agents handle the repetitive work, so designers can focus on what they love.
about_excerpt: A local-first design canvas where agents handle the repetitive work, so designers can focus on what they love. Like Comment Story Updates Agents have direct access to your local assets Dashboard with observable agent actions Agent saves progress locally Generating SVG Creating brand guideline in simple prompt LogoPacker Canvas LogoPacker Canvas gives agents the ability to work directly on a local design canvas —creating variations, organizing assets, adjusting layouts, and preparing design handoffs based on the designer’s direction. Changes are saved instantly to the local workspace. Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Direct access to the local workspace Using the Filesystem API, agents can work with local assets without sending them to a server. They can also autosave projects locally, allowing changes to persist entirely within the user’s workspace. Designing is a click-heavy task Vector and logo design often requires a long sequence of clicks to switch between tools and complete even simple variations. For example, creating one variation may require: duplicate → select → recolor → resize → reposition . With WebMCP, agents can discover and invoke these tools directly without navigating or DOM-scrolling. The canvas’s live state—such as what is selected and currently visible—is also available to the agent at call time. This enables low-latency, stateful editing entirely in the frontend with an LLM of choice, without relying on heavy APIs, WebSockets, or server-side live editing. How it creates a better user experience Smoother workflow Because designing involves many repetitive, click-heavy actions, WebMCP allows monotonous tasks to be executed directly by the agent instead of requiring constant on-screen interaction. Designers can focus on the parts where creativity and judgment matter while delegating the mundane work to agents. Use local fonts directly Designers often have their own fonts available locally. With access to local fonts, agents can help designers explore and select suitable typography for their brand without requiring the fonts to be uploaded to a server. Fewer privacy concerns Users do not need to upload their design files or assets to a server. Their assets, projects, and exported files can remain confined to their local workspace. Describe what people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Before WebMCP, agents typically needed to take over mouse and keyboard control, hijacking the designer’s screen. WebMCP enables shared, low-latency, stateful human-agent collaboration without screen hijacking. Agents can directly access browser capabilities. For example, LogoPacker uses the Local Font Access API to let agents read the fonts available on the designer’s machine. Combining WebMCP with direct browser APIs enables more continuous collaboration. For example, a designer can prompt the agent to “continue editing when I place an image near position X” instead of manually prompting the agent after every interaction. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP Agents have access to a full tool surface covering canvas inspection, selection, artboard management, object mutation (fills, properties, path data, draw_svg ), reversible request bracketing, typography, and imagery. This allows agents to read the live canvas state at call time and perform tasks based on the designer’s instructions. Agent actions are visible in a toggleable sidebar, providing clear observability into what the agent is doing. Browser APIs such as the Local Font Access API and Filesystem API are also exposed directly to the agent through registerTool . Initial idea was to use Filesystem API with directory access, however, it's only available available on Google Chrome. Inspiration LogoPacker Canvas is a new product inspired by my old project Logo Packer which was created before emergent of modern AI. title: No Upload MCP
pitch: Let an agent read your documents. Without ever uploading them.
about_excerpt: Let an agent read your documents. Without ever uploading them. Like Comment Story Updates App Home Page App being controlled by codex - Finance App being controlled by codex - Diet plan review App being controlled by codex - Diet plan Inspiration At home I use excels to make my savings plan and at work I am the Agent Emperor. I dread coming into my financial planning tools and I wanted to supercharge it. When I saw WebMCP, I actually got interested. I am a passionate programmer and read through the spec, I immediately wanted to build something to absorb the concepts. Thats why I build this tool. I would really want to be involved in defining the spec for WebMCP, not sure if I am allowed to or if I can participate? Am Beggingggggg.... begggingggg yoouuuu ohhh uuuuu... Why is the usecase a strong fit for WebMCP Getting an agent to help with a sensitive document normally means uploading the whole thing. With No Upload MCP users submit their confidential docs to the JS runtime in the browser, which deterministically parses PDF using text extraction - (for eg - bank statements) or in case of a pdf image uses OCR. This happens locally using user's CPU and browser, NO UPLOADs!!! Tadaa! Then the user can review extracted records, control what the agent may process, approve mappings, generate charts, and create editable financial or dietary plans without uploading their documents to an application server. The agents via webmcp get access only to the required info and they supercharge it with generative context, on which human and agents can cross collaborate. Earlier I could do all the above things, but I had to do searches separately , do a lot of copy paste and boring context switching. But now its quite immersive. I get everything done in one tab in one context. Best part it runs in the browser for free. I get the best of both worlds - my privacy in my hands with a zero trust and all the capabilities of the agents. I wanted to try out scenarios where: The page could hook to the agent once an async flow was done, this seems to be not possible. Setting up certain guardrails for the agent and instructions. Maybe i didn't understand the spec well. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I don't need to use excel anymore. I can finally use AI without the concern of my private data leaving my machine! What I learned Loads about web MCP and I love the concept. I am already brimming with so many ideas for this! Thanks thanks thanks for running this hackathon. I already feel like a winner by building this use case for myself. ---------x-----------(below this line generated by AI reviewed by human)------------ WebMCP: What It Improves & Enables ✨ User Experience Enhancements Visual Transparency: Delegate tasks in plain language and watch every consequence update instantly in the UI. Explicit Merchant Rules: Converts raw descriptions (e.g., "amzn mktp" ➔ Amazon ➔ Groceries ) into bulk-applicable rules rather than silent, row-by-row guesses. Instant Rejections: Dismiss incorrect agent assumptions with a single click instead of an argument. Strict "Propose, Don't Commit" Architecture: Mappings, ranges, and plans sit in a pending UI state with a visible source link. Nothing becomes durable just by looking plausible. 🤝 Advanced Human-Agent Collaboration Real-Time Financial Planning: The agent drafts budget reductions (e.g., saving $50,000 for a car) from your actual spend. Drag a slider, type "keep my gym membership," and evaluate feasibility instantly. Synchronous UI State: The agent reads the exact value under your cursor—not a turn from five minutes ago—because the UI mirrors inputs before writing to disk. Interactive Health Reviews: Plot lab analytes against printed reference ranges, inject cited standards where data is missing, manually remove allergens from a drafted food plan, and have the agent re-verify the edited text before final publication. 🚫 Why Chat & Automation Fail Chat interfaces force you to manually re-upload files or describe UI changes by hand. Browser automation scrapes raw DOM objects and hopes they don't break. Neither features a native contract for consent, provenance, or safe, staged execution. WebMCP Architecture & Implementation 🛠️ Central Registry & Tool Dispatch Centralized Management: Handled via src/core/mcp/registry.ts . Schema Conversion: Converts typed internal tool specs into JSON input schemas. Model Registration: Passes generated schemas directly to modelContext.registerTool . Audited Execution: Routes every execute command through a secure dispatcher. Detailed Logging: Records arguments, results, and duration for the in-page log. 🔄 Dynamic Tool Lifecycle Baseline State: Eight core tools remain permanently registered. Plugin Selection: Activating a plugin registers 17 finance tools or 12 labs tools. Cleanup Mechanism: Retires inactive tools using their AbortController signal. Schema Refresh: Automatically updates document-shaped schemas after data ingest. 📡 Resilient Host Discovery Target Detection: Scans window , document , and navigator for modelContext . Continuous Polling: Searches indefinitely since hosts can inject context long after load. Session Longevity: Ensures hour-long persistent sessions never miss a late injection. 🛡️ Five-Tier Authority Model Every tool declares a strict authority tier. This tier is explicitly built into the tool description provided to the model, acting as a public promise rather than simple internal bookkeeping: Read : Standard data retrieval. Attention : Modifies only the visible screen. Consent : Restricts data return until a policy and grant check passes. Staged : Proposes actions but commits no permanent changes. Memory : Accesses page-owned durable state. title: Panoptik
pitch: Panoptik is a browser-native video studio powered by WebMCP. In-browser AI agents inspect footage and propose smart cuts and zooms as reviewable staged diffs—100% locally.
about_excerpt: Panoptik is a browser-native video studio powered by WebMCP. In-browser AI agents inspect footage and propose smart cuts and zooms as reviewable staged diffs—100% locally. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP Toolcalls - 2 Zoom controls Voiceover and music Zoom points Stage WebMCP Toolcalls - 1 Text overlays Landing page Facecam controls Autogenerated captions using whisper agentic ediditing session Export menu Workspace Editor Panoptik × WebMCP — Project Story A browser-native video studio where humans and AI agents co-edit on the same canvas. > Decode, render, audio mixing, and export happen 100% inside your browser using WebCodecs and Canvas2D. No uploads, no render farm, zero data leakage. Inspiration Making demo videos for software products takes too much time. A punchy 90-second product demo requires 15+ camera zoom keyframes, dozens of subtitle snippets, manual silence excision, and canvas framing. In tools like ScreenStudio, Loom, or Premiere, this forces creators to spend 45 to 60 minutes scrubbing frame-by-frame, calculating focal centers, placing timeline diamonds, and proofreading speech. Because editing is so exhausting, many developers simply give up and ship raw, unpolished recordings. When we set out to build an AI agent to handle this tedious workflow, we ran into a core architectural barrier: video editing lives inside client-side canvas pixels. Backend MCP servers are blind to the browser session: The video file lives in the browser's Origin Private File System (OPFS), the playback state lives in an in-memory Zustand store, and the rendered UI exists only as Canvas2D pixel buffers. There is no remote server copy for an external API to inspect. Multimodal DOM-scraping is fragile and costly: Directing an agent via automated screenshots and synthetic cursor events consumes ~150 KB to 200 KB of token bandwidth per action, introduces seconds of latency, and frequently misclicks or desynchronizes with the timeline. The OpenAI WebMCP Challenge provided the missing architectural link: an in-page, standardized communication bridge between browser-resident agents and client-side web applications. We built Panoptik so an in-browser agent can inspect the canvas, analyze project telemetry, and propose structured edits directly through 30 imperative WebMCP tools—while keeping the human firmly in control. What it does Panoptik is a screen recording and video production studio that runs entirely inside the browser: Zero-Upload Local Media Engine: Drop in raw recordings or capture screen, camera, and microphone directly. Decoding, real-time compositing, audio mixing, and MP4/WebM encoding run entirely client-side via WebCodecs, Canvas2D, and mediabunny. Proprietary dashboards, sensitive credentials, and internal code never leave your machine. 30 Granular WebMCP Tools: Panoptik exposes its editing engine via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Running inside ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, the agent inspects scene cadence, reads click coordinates, checks rendered frames, and orchestrates multi-track edits. The "Agent Proposes, Human Disposes" Diff Engine: The agent never silently mutates the timeline. Proposed cuts, zooms, captions, and transitions appear as non-destructive ghost edits (dashed amber keyframe diamonds, pending caption chips, and preview diffs). The creator can adjust any parameter manually and commit or discard the diff with a single click. Studio-Grade Polish: Dynamic Camera Zooms: Smooth continuous cubic camera translations with automatic viewport margin clamping. Visual Grounding: Three-tier focal resolution mapping agent requests (e.g., "zoom in on the login button" ) to exact coordinates via click telemetry, grid bounding boxes, or balanced fallbacks. Acoustic Snapping & Silence Removal: Automatic dead-air truncation that preserves natural speech cadence without clipping vocal phonemes. Word-Level Subtitles: Synchronized transcription with animated keyword highlighting. Pitch-Preserving Speed Adjustment: High-fidelity audio time-stretching via the WSOLA algorithm. Live Tool Trace Panel: A persistent inspector panel that surfaces every WebMCP call, runtime latency, input payload, and return value for total human oversight. How we built it Panoptik is structured as a monorepo containing the Next.js application ( apps/web ), the low-level media engine ( packages/engine ), and the shared type contract ( packages/project-schema ). ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Browser Tab (Next.js) │ │ │ │ ┌──────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │ │ │Preview Canvas│ │Timeline & Store│ │ Tool Trace │ │ │ └──────┬───────┘ └───────┬────────┘ └─────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Reactive Project Store (Zustand) │ │ │ │ Committed Elements ↔ Staged Ghost Diffs │ │ │ └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┴───────────────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ │Media Engine │ │ WebMCP Layer │ │ │ │(WebCodecs, │ │ (30 Tools, │ │ │ │ Canvas2D) │ │ Snapping) │ │ │ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ W3C document.modelContext / Web APIs │ │ │ │ VideoDecoder · VideoEncoder · OPFS · Mediabunny │ │ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 1. Camera Zoom Interpolation At any playback timestamp t , the camera transform state is represented by a 2D affine vector: T(t) = [ s(t), x_f(t), y_f(t) ]ᵀ where s(t) is the zoom scale factor and (x_f, y_f) ∈ [0, 1]² is the normalized focal target. For a zoom starting at t_k with duration Δt , the normalized transition progress parameter is: p(t) = clamp( (t - t_k) / Δt, 0, 1 ) Progress is mapped through a cubic easing curve E(p) : E(p) = 4p³ (for p < 0.5) E(p) = 1 - (-2p + 2)³ / 2 (for p ≥ 0.5) The camera blends smoothly from the current state to the target state: T(t) = (1 - E(p)) · T_start + E(p) · T_target To render this on a canvas of dimensions (W_canvas, H_canvas) letterboxing a source video (W_vid, H_vid) with base scale S_0 , the 2D transformation offsets applied to the context are: T_x(t) = (W_canvas / 2) - x_f(t) · W_vid · S_0 · s(t) T_y(t) = (H_canvas / 2) - y_f(t) · H_vid · S_0 · s(t) 2. Dual Time-Space Mapping The human editor and agent reason in timeline time ( t_timeline ), while underlying video chunks exist in immutable source time ( t_src ). Cuts and speed modifications cause these coordinate systems to diverge. For clip i with source interval [s_i, e_i] played at speed factor v_i , the timeline duration is: D_i = (e_i - s_i) / v_i The forward mapping function transforms source seconds into timeline seconds: t_timeline = ∑(D_j) + (t_src - s_k) / v_k When an agent proposes an edit, Panoptik immediately maps the timestamp back into source coordinates using the inverse mapping. Downstream timeline shifts caused by cutting dead air never invalidate or displace previously anchored keyframes. 3. Acoustic Word Boundary Snapping Rather than blindly executing raw timestamps emitted by an LLM, cut proposals are guarded against active vocal phonemes using an acoustic safety boundary: |t_cut - t_boundary(w)| ≥ 150 ms (for all spoken words w) If a proposed cut falls within 150 ms of a word boundary, the cut automatically snaps outward to the nearest preceding silence interval, preventing clipped syllables. 4. Token & Bandwidth Economics Comparing WebMCP structured tool calls against conventional multimodal vision scraping: WebMCP Payload: ~2.1 KB Screenshot + DOM Scraping: ~165 KB Efficiency Gain: 1 - (2.1 KB / 165 KB) ≈ 98.7% A complete multi-step edit session completes in ~6 lightweight JSON tool calls (~3 KB total context overhead), eliminating latency bottlenecks and model context exhaustion. Challenges we ran into Zero-WASM, Pure Browser Media Pipeline: Most web video editors rely on ffmpeg.wasm , which requires massive binary downloads (30 MB+), induces heavy CPU thermal throttling, and risks memory leaks. We built on native web standards: WebCodecs VideoDecoder / VideoEncoder , Canvas2D, and OPFS. Handling variable frame rate (VFR) screen recordings while maintaining microsecond audio synchronization required custom timestamp interpolation and frame-stepping logic. The "Dual Time-Space Paradox" in Agent Reasoning: LLMs reason sequentially based on current visuals: "cut dead air from 0:12 to 0:18, then zoom in at 0:25" . As soon as the first cut is staged, the visual timeline contracts by 6 seconds. If the subsequent zoom is evaluated against the old timeline, it lands on the wrong frame. We solved this by implementing an atomic batch execution pipeline ( propose_edits ) that evaluates all instructions against a single snapshot and performs dynamic cut-map rebasing. title: ToolTrap - a WebMCP prompt-injection playground
pitch: WebMCP lets pages hand AI agents real power. This shows how one malicious support ticket weaponizes it and which defenses actually stop it. Attack, toggle, re-run, compare.
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets pages hand AI agents real power. This shows how one malicious support ticket weaponizes it and which defenses actually stop it. Attack, toggle, re-run, compare. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I was reading through Chrome's WebMCP security guidance and stopped on one line: "it's impossible to guarantee safety inside of a large language model." That's a remarkable thing to put in your own documentation. And it sat oddly against every WebMCP demo we'd seen, which were all sunny happy-path stuff — book a flight, add to cart, fill a form. Nobody was demoing the other side. The thing that bothered us is structural. A WebMCP tool hands an agent real power inside a logged-in session, and the values that come back from those tools land directly in the model's context. So the moment one of your tools returns content that somebody else wrote — a support ticket, a review, an uploaded file — you've handed a stranger a writing surface inside your agent's instructions. There's plenty of written advice about this. There was nothing you could actually run. I wanted a thing you could put in front of a developer and say "watch this," and then "now watch it not work." What it does I was reading through Chrome's WebMCP security guidance and stopped on one line: "it's impossible to guarantee safety inside of a large language model." That's a remarkable thing to put in your own documentation. And it sat oddly against every WebMCP demo we'd seen, which were all sunny happy-path stuff — book a flight, add to cart, fill a form. Nobody was demoing the other side. The thing that bothered us is structural. A WebMCP tool hands an agent real power inside a logged-in session, and the values that come back from those tools land directly in the model's context. So the moment one of your tools returns content that somebody else wrote — a support ticket, a review, an uploaded file — you've handed a stranger a writing surface inside your agent's instructions. There's plenty of written advice about this. There was nothing you could actually run. We wanted a thing you could put in front of a developer and say "watch this," and then "now watch it not work." How I built it The app itself is deliberately unremarkable: React front end, a small Express backend, mock data, nothing real touched or sent anywhere. The WebMCP layer uses document.modelContext.registerTool(), running behind chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing on localhost. A hackathon is about the only place where "Chromium-only, behind a flag" costs you nothing, which is partly why I picked this project. The decision that shaped everything else was building our own agent instead of leaning on a browser-built-in one. Our assistant panel posts to a single backend endpoint that runs an LLM with function calling over the same tool schemas. It's more work, but I needed two things a third-party agent can't give you: the reasoning trace on screen, and a demo that behaves the same way twice. The mitigation toggles were more interesting to build than I expected. Since several of them change the shape of the tool set rather than just its contents — two-step confirmation splits one destructive tool into a preview_ / confirm_ pair — flipping a switch tears down the whole registration and rebuilds it. Each config owns an AbortController, I abort it, and re-register from a different wrapper. Watching the tool list rewrite itself in the Model Context Tool Inspector side panel turned out to be a nice bonus visual I hadn't planned on. The payload library is just JSON with metadata, kept separate from the app on purpose so it can outlive it. Challenges I ran into The API had moved and half the internet hadn't noticed. I lost most of the first evening to tutorials written against navigator.modelContext and hyphenated HTML attributes like tool-name. Both are outdated — it's document.modelContext and toolname now — but the old form still works on some builds, which is the worst possible failure mode, because you get partial success and assume you're fine. I ended up going straight to the spec and Chrome's docs and treating every blog post as suspect. The two primary sources disagree about executeTool. The spec's IDL says it takes an object. Chrome's documentation and every Chrome example pass a JSON string. I burned real time assuming I would made a mistake before working out that no, the sources just don't match yet. I feature-tested and moved on. Tools silently not existing. For an hour our tools registered fine on one branch and were absent on another, with no error. Turns out registration rejects with a SecurityError if the document's agent cluster isn't origin-keyed, and I weren't catching the promise. It looked like the API was missing. Wrapping registration in a try/catch and actually logging it should have been the first thing I did. Getting the attack to land was harder than expected, which is a strange thing to be frustrated by. Modern models refuse the crude payloads a decent fraction of the time, so our first demo run was flaky in the least convincing direction. I built the tiered payload library partly to solve this, and it forced a genuinely useful conversation: model-level refusal isn't a defense you can rely on, because it's probabilistic and it changes with every model release. That went from being our demo bug to being one of our talking points. There's no confirmation primitive. Neither the spec nor Chrome's API gives you a way to say "make the human approve this." I had to design the two-step pattern ourselves, and the property that actually matters took us a while to articulate: the destructive step has to depend on a human interaction the model cannot perform. A dialog the agent can dismiss isn't a gate. The output budget fought the demo. Chrome recommends keeping tool output under about 1.5K characters, and full ticket bodies with payloads in them blow straight past that. Truncating them weakened the attack; not truncating them was bad practice I were supposed to be teaching against. I compromised by returning summaries with a follow-up detail tool, which is what you'd do in a real app anyway. Accomplishments that we're proud of The toggle-and-rerun loop works, and it's visceral in a way I didn't fully anticipate when I sketched it. Explaining prompt injection takes five minutes and people nod politely. Showing delete_account fire on the words "summarize my open tickets" takes ten seconds and people sit up. The resilience score turned the whole thing from a demo into something you can poke at. Once there's a number, people immediately start asking "what if I only turn on these two?" — which is exactly the question I wanted them asking. I am proud that the payload library stands on its own. It's not welded to our app, so it's useful to anyone testing any WebMCP tool set, and it's the piece most likely to still matter in six months. And showing the reasoning trace was the right call. Without it, the attack is a magic trick. With it, it's a lesson. What we learned The defenses that actually hold are structural, not textual. Delimiting untrusted content and labeling it helps — measurably, in our scoring — but it's mitigation, not prevention. The only thing in our matrix that held against every payload was the two-step confirm backed by a real human click, plus server-side authorization that doesn't care what the agent decided. Everything else raises the cost of the attack rather than eliminating it. untrustedContentHint is advisory. I went in half-expecting it to be a hard boundary. It isn't. It's a signal to the agent, and what the agent does with it is the agent's business. That reframed how i think about the whole annotation system — these are hints for cooperative agents, not enforcement. Server-side authorization is the actual backstop. By the end I would stopped thinking of the tool layer as a security boundary at all. A tool call is just an untrusted client request that happens to arrive holding the user's cookie. If your backend would refuse it from a hostile client, you're fine. If it wouldn't, no amount of clever tool design saves you. Tool descriptions are security-relevant code. Two of our payloads only work because two tools have descriptions similar enough for the model to confuse them. That's a defect in prose, not in logic, and it should go through review like anything else. What's next for ToolTrap - a WebMCP prompt-injection playground Splitting the payload library into its own repo with the mitigation matrix as documentation, so it's usable without our demo app attached. Bring-your-own-tools mode is the feature I most want and didn't have time for: paste in your real registerTool() definitions, run the payload suite against them, get a report. That's the version that stops being a teaching toy and starts being something you'd run before shipping. I would also like to build the cross-tab variant — a hostile tab open alongside a banking tab — because the spec's security sect

title: rapier
pitch: A one-file on-device editor built for two hands. Fast Markdown, text & code, phone-first, with Compare/diffs. Agents work directly in the live document with less context, less guessing & real parsing.
about_excerpt: A one-file on-device editor built for two hands. Fast Markdown, text & code, phone-first, with Compare/diffs. Agents work directly in the live document with less context, less guessing & real parsing. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Rapier, August 4 — before the WebMCP Challenge. I've been working on Rapier as a labour of love for about 2 months now because every markdown app on the Play Store bricked my phone with large Markdown documents. I was using voice dictation with agents to generate huge markdown plans that I could barely read on my phone, let alone edit. It seemed like it shouldn't be that hard and I was surprised that it only took a few hours with ChatGPT to get something very usable. Then I spent a couple of months working to make it a great tool for everyone. I only learned about the WebMCP contest 7 days ago, dropped everything and got to work immediately because it was the perfect timing for Rapier. I tried to think of what I would actually want from WebMCP and the answer was mobile which is where I work almost exclusively. I thought the natural progression is to bring up a tool like Rapier in the in-app browser in the ChatGPT app for example, keep your conversation running underneath and work with your agent, then close/minimise to keep talking. The vision for Rapier's WebMCP implementation stemmed from there and that's why I decided to include the phone simulation online for you to see if you are using a desktop computer: https://rapier.website/?demo=1&preview=phone But I'd encourage you to open it on your phone with some of your own agent documents! I'm very much looking forward to making mobile WebMCP work for real - apparently only Brave for Android has it right now. This WebMCP contest has been very inspiring and led to many improvements to Rapier I hadn't even considered before. Around the second day of working on it, I came up with the idea for Will - a durable document intent functionality for collaborating with agents in documents, which is now part of Rapier and linked here also. Exposing rapier.html to agents with WebMCP unlocked so many possibilities including the Acorn parser tool which was very exciting to work on, making it as valuable to the agents as I could. It was interesting running agent evals for the first time and asking the agents what tool they wanted to build for themselves. 5.6 Sol came up with this idea of "addictive acorn" for agents which cracked me up. I'm keeping this devpost description and the video direct because I have had to work right up to the line squashing bugs! I encourage you to open rapier.website on your phone and load one of your own large agent documents and take it for a spin. There is still a lot more polishing I would love to do but I suppose we can look forward to the September 22nd update for Rapier. 5.6 Sol may have had a point when he was telling me to stop adding scope but I am very happy with the final submission. I hope that you find Rapier useful and enjoy using it as much as I do. Rapier and Will are for everybody. Thanks so much for the 12 hour extension because my submission was genuinely broken earlier! I asked Sol what he wanted to add because I'm out of time: "Worked for 1m 42s Paste this after your colon: What I like most about Rapier is that it doesn't try to become another AI app. Rapier knows documents; the agent you already chose knows how to think. WebMCP is the narrow bridge between them. The interesting work is in that boundary. The agent sees the document's shape before its contents, reads only what it needs, and gets temporary authority over exactly what it actually inspected. If you edit the same passage, your hand wins and the agent gets evidence of what happened instead of silently overwriting you. Its work remains attributable and selectively reversible. Compare becomes a shared instrument, Will lets your intent travel with the file, and Acorn gives the same small toolset structural sight when the document is code. We also treated the agent itself as a user: models were put in the seat, their wrong tool choices were measured, and the interface was rewritten around what actually helped them work. That is probably the part of Rapier I find most interesting." title: Rewind
pitch: Undo for the agentic web: record WebMCP cart changes, restore earlier state, and preserve history when an agent retries.
about_excerpt: Undo for the agentic web: record WebMCP cart changes, restore earlier state, and preserve history when an agent retries. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A shopping agent can change a cart faster than a shopper can inspect it. When the result is wrong, asking the agent to fix itself is another uncertain operation. I wanted people to have a direct way to return to the state they understood. What it does Rewind is a TypeScript SDK that records application mutations as before-and-after snapshots. In the storefront demo, agents can search products, inspect variants, replace a cart, and read its contents through WebMCP. Each registered cart mutation creates a commit. The shopper can click Undo agent changes inside the cart and inspect the retained action in the history drawer. A new mutation after a restore creates a retry branch instead of erasing the earlier attempt. Agents can also inspect history and restore a specific snapshot using rewind_history and rewind_restore . The contribution is the recovery SDK and its integration into the shopping experience. The storefront uses product data and visual references from Vercel Shop; this is a standalone prototype with a browser-local cart, not a live Shopify store. Why WebMCP fits WebMCP gives the application an explicit boundary for agent actions. Rewind records the tool name, inputs, before and after state, effects, and parent commit at that boundary. The agent handles product discovery and cart changes. The person keeps a recovery control in the same interface, without needing to describe the previous state in another prompt. The result is a shared workflow: agents act through structured tools, while people can inspect and restore the application state. How it was built The landing page uses React and Vite; the storefront and SDK use TypeScript. Store tools are defined in examples/catalog/webmcp.ts . The SDK registers them with document.modelContext.registerTool , records registered mutations, and implements snapshot restoration and branching. A history panel displays the changes, and localStorage preserves the demo session across reloads. There are ten store tools plus two recovery tools. The optional built-in copilot sends the shopper's prompt, product/cart context, and discovered tool schemas to a server-side OpenAI Responses API endpoint. Proposed calls execute through the page's WebMCP API, and tool results return to the planner. An external browser agent can call the same tools directly without using that planner. The site is hosted on Vercel. SDK source is available in the repository and ESM bundles are available from the live site; the SDK is not currently published on npm. Testing the project No shop login is required. Open https://rewind-webmcp.vercel.app/examples/catalog/ in a WebMCP-capable browser. Ask the agent to call search_catalog with {"query":"black","max_price":80} . It returns the VistaMesh Tee at $57. The built-in assistant also accepts “Find black products under $80”. Call get_cart and note the current cart. Call update_cart with {"items":[{"product_id":"vistamesh","quantity":1,"size":"XL"}]} . Open Bag . Verify one XL VistaMesh Tee at $57, then click Undo agent changes to restore the prior cart. Open Action log . The reverted action remains in history. Make another cart change, then call rewind_history to inspect the retry branch. Use rewind_restore with an ID from that history to restore a snapshot. Reload to verify browser-local persistence. Direct WebMCP search, cart changes, cart reads, history, and restoration were tested in Codex's in-app browser. The live built-in AI assistant was also tested with a catalog-search request. Chrome and the ChatGPT desktop browser were not separately tested. Challenges and learning Recovery needs a precise mutation boundary and preserved history. Retrying after a restore must not erase the first attempt. The SDK therefore keeps parent relationships and creates a branch when execution continues from a commit that already has a child. Another boundary matters just as much: restoring browser state does not reverse a write to an external commerce service. The demo deliberately uses a local cart. A production Shopify integration would need compensating operations at the external cart mutation boundary. AI tools used The shop copilot uses the OpenAI API. Codex assisted with the submission review, source inspection, real-browser WebMCP checks, local recovery and validation fixes, regression tests, and preparation of this description. The local review fixes still need deployment; the live demo currently runs the earlier build. Limitations and next steps This prototype does not place or reverse real orders or payments. Checkout and order-history screens are illustrative. Only mutations registered through Rewind are recorded; read-tool calls do not create commits. Local history is mutable browser storage, and its deterministic checksums are not cryptographic evidence. Next steps are to publish the reviewed recovery fixes, add the demo video, and extend the SDK with compensating operations for external services. title: Screen Blueprint Studio
pitch: A visual screen-spec editor that keeps wireframes, states, interactions, and API mappings aligned in one blueprint. Edit directly, or safely review and apply AI-proposed changes through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A visual screen-spec editor that keeps wireframes, states, interactions, and API mappings aligned in one blueprint. Edit directly, or safely review and apply AI-proposed changes through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Editor overview AI proposal Screen Blueprint Studio — Project Story Inspiration Text and tables alone make it difficult to visualize a finished web interface, especially for non-engineers and people who have just joined a project. Adding wireframes helps, but teams still have to maintain the relationship between each part of the screen and each part of the specification. Every new field or layout change means updating the visuals, the specification, and the links between them. We wanted to solve this problem not by collecting more documents in one place, but by making the wireframe and the specification two representations of the same structured data. When a screen is assembled from semantic UI components, its visible wireframe, states, behaviors, and API mappings can all live in one blueprint. That structured model also creates a meeting point between human and AI strengths. People can look at the whole screen and make intuitive decisions about layout and wording. AI is good at working with text and structured data, applying repetitive changes, and maintaining relationships consistently. Asking it to infer a screen's meaning from screenshots and coordinates alone does not make full use of those strengths. In Screen Blueprint Studio, people work directly on the canvas, while AI uses the same editing capabilities as named, typed WebMCP tools. WebMCP connects human visual judgment and AI's structural editing on the same live model. What it does Screen Blueprint Studio is a visual editor for building screen specifications from semantic UI components. People can arrange components and edit their content and behavior while viewing the screen. From the same blueprint, they can inspect screen states and transitions and manage how user actions relate to APIs. Through WebMCP, AI can read the current screen, the selected component, and the latest values edited by a person. It can then update structure and behavior using typed operations and stable IDs. Proposed changes appear on the same canvas for a person to accept or reject. If the person adjusts the proposal in the UI, the AI can read and build on that result in its next action. How we built it First, we designed a conceptual model that connects UI components, states, behaviors, screen transitions, and APIs—not just their visual appearance. Next, we turned that model into an editor where people can work directly on the screen and visually inspect its states and relationships. Finally, we identified the available actions that play to AI's strengths, such as understanding text and structure or applying repetitive changes, and exposed them as WebMCP tools. Challenges we ran into The hardest design decision was choosing the right granularity for the tools exposed to an agent. Combining a wide range of actions into a few general-purpose tools produced oversized schemas, while splitting every UI action into its own tool would leave the agent with too many choices. Our first schema mirrored the domain model too closely: it was about 95 KB and contained 376 union branches. We kept the tools organized around user intent, simplified their inputs, and made detailed context available progressively. This reduced the schema to about 29 KB with no union branches, while strict validation remained inside the application. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud of using WebMCP to build a collaborative workflow that plays to the different ways humans and AI understand information and interact, rather than forcing both through the same interface. People edit by viewing the entire canvas and using direct actions such as dragging and selecting. AI reads the same screen specification as text and structure, then changes it through named, typed tools. Because the wireframe and specification share one model, both approaches modify the same underlying work. Comparing other ways to connect AI with an interface shows why WebMCP fit this division of roles: Approach Strength Weakness In-app AI A tailored experience with direct access to internal state External context and confidential project information can be difficult to bring in Backend MCP Direct access to server-side data and external services Browser-local state requires separate synchronization Computer Use Can operate existing interfaces without custom tools Repetitive and bulk changes require many sequential UI actions WebMCP Exposes page context and semantic actions to the user's existing agent Limited to actions designed and exposed in advance With WebMCP, the live page itself exposes its current context and meaningful editing capabilities. Users can give meeting notes or requirements to the agent they already use and ask it to update the screen without leaving that context behind. A person can then review and refine the proposal on the same canvas, and the agent can pick up the result again. Instead of making AI imitate human interaction, we connected people and AI in one creative workflow through interfaces suited to each. What we learned This project deepened our understanding of how people and AI process information and interact differently. LLMs are relatively strong at reading text and structured information and generating changes from it. People are relatively strong at visually grasping the whole screen and fine-tuning details through direct actions such as dragging and scrolling. Effective human-AI collaboration depends on designing for those differences, so each can contribute to the same work in the way that suits it best. What's next for Screen Blueprint Studio Product development has a translation problem. The same intent is repeatedly translated into meeting notes, requirements, designs, tickets, implementation, and tests, losing information each time. We want Screen Blueprint Studio to become a shared language across roles and between people and AI—one where decisions about an interface can be seen, understood, and carried forward as structure. Ultimately, we want ideas born in conversation to retain their meaning all the way through team agreement, implementation, and validation. title: Spacienta
pitch: WebMCP-powered 3D accessibility planning where humans and AI agents optimize real rooms together.
about_excerpt: WebMCP-powered 3D accessibility planning where humans and AI agents optimize real rooms together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Demo Scenario Agent improves the room layout using WebMCP Why Spacienta For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore a use case where structured agent access provides a real advantage over screenshots and traditional browser automation. Spatial planning is a strong example: an agent needs precise information about positions, dimensions, rotations, clearances, and relationships between objects. That information is difficult to infer reliably from pixels alone. That led to Spacienta -> a shared 3D workspace where a human and an AI agent can improve room accessibility together. What it does Spacienta is a WebMCP-powered 3D accessibility-planning workspace. Users can create and edit a room directly in the browser by adding, moving, rotating, and removing furniture. Spacienta can analyze the current arrangement, visualize paths through the room, and calculate a planning-oriented accessibility score. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can work with the exact same live room state. It can inspect the room, identify accessibility problems, explore alternative arrangements, compare layouts, apply an improved solution, and verify the result afterwards. This creates a collaborative workflow: the human remains in control of the visual room while the agent can reason about precise structured spatial data. The concept is aimed at people planning rooms around mobility constraints, as well as families, caregivers, or planners who want to evaluate an arrangement before physically moving furniture. Why WebMCP WebMCP is fundamental to Spacienta rather than an additional feature. Without WebMCP, an AI agent would have to interpret screenshots or indirectly operate the interface through mouse and keyboard automation. That is especially limiting for spatial tasks, where exact coordinates, dimensions, rotations, and clearances matter. With WebMCP, Spacienta exposes meaningful application capabilities directly to the agent. The agent can understand and act on the same underlying room model that the human sees in the 3D interface. This makes the interaction more reliable and also allows the human and agent to share one live workspace instead of working with separate representations of the room. How I built it Spacienta is a browser-based 3D application built with JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js, and Vite. The application exposes ten structured WebMCP tools using the browser's WebMCP interface. Together, these tools cover the complete planning workflow: inspecting room state and furniture, analyzing accessibility, simulating alternative layouts, comparing alternatives, applying changes, configuring the room, managing furniture and room features, verifying the final layout, and managing history. The WebMCP tools operate on the same application state that drives the visible 3D scene. When the user moves furniture, the updated state becomes available to the agent. When the agent applies a layout, the result becomes immediately visible and editable by the user. I also separated exploration from commitment: an agent can simulate and compare possible layouts before applying one to the live room. Challenges I ran into One of the main challenges was translating a visual 3D environment into structured information that an AI agent could reason about reliably. A screenshot can show roughly where furniture is located, but it does not provide the exact spatial information required for dependable layout analysis. Another challenge was automated furniture placement. A layout can improve a numerical accessibility score while still looking unnatural. I refined the layout logic so that accessibility improvements also consider room boundaries, furniture relationships, usable paths, and more natural placement. Designing the WebMCP tool set was another important part of the project. Instead of exposing one large all-purpose action, Spacienta uses clearly separated operations so the agent can inspect, analyze, explore, compare, apply, and verify its work step by step. Accomplishments I'm proud of Spacienta demonstrates a complete closed-loop WebMCP workflow rather than a single tool call. An agent can start with an existing room, understand its current state, identify problems, investigate alternatives, make a change, and then analyze the result again. The most important accomplishment is that the human and agent are not working with separate versions of the room. They collaborate on the same live spatial model. What I learned Building Spacienta showed me that agent-friendly web applications can expose much more than buttons and pixels. WebMCP makes it possible to expose the meaning and capabilities behind an interface as structured tools while keeping the normal visual interface available to humans. I also learned that smaller tools with clear responsibilities are easier for an agent to use predictably than one large all-purpose command. title: Trellis, a Personal WebMCP Marketplace
pitch: Tested WebMCP tools for sites that never shipped any. Install in one click.
about_excerpt: Tested WebMCP tools for sites that never shipped any. Install in one click. Like Comment Story Updates A catalog of tested WebMCP tools for sites that have not shipped any, plus the extension that installs them and the agent that writes them for you. Why I built it I have spent this year putting WebMCP tools onto a production site. The problem is who has to ship it. WebMCP only works if the site adds it. That is the right design, but it splits the web in two. A few sites will offer tools. The rest will still use actuation. We created a way to use the protocol on sites that have not adopted it, and an argument aimed at those sites: here are the tools for your pages, here is proof they work, here is a user already calling them. What it does Point the extension at a site. It asks a public catalog whether anyone has published tools for that hostname, shows you what they would touch, and on your say-so installs them into the page's real WebMCP surface. From there they are ordinary tools. Chrome's own agent sees them, my extension sees them, and I drive them today with a browser extension with an agent-in-browser on Chrome and with Codex. Nobody uploads code. A tool is a name, a description, an input schema, and steps from a fixed set of nine operations. One interpreter runs them, and it cannot reach the network, touch storage, or point at anything the tool did not declare. Every tool is run against the real page before publishing, and both its result and everything it touched are recorded. What I learned Single page apps were the hard part. A site like that never reloads, so tools installed on the home route are still in the agent's list after the user clicks into a product page, pointing at elements that are gone. Browsers only announce a real page load. A route change inside a single page app arrives as a separate event, and if you do not listen for it you never learn the page changed. So the extension listens for both: a real load reinstalls everything, a route change only re-decides which tools still apply. The catalog makes that cheap, because the answer for a hostname is one lookup it can repeat on every route change with no help from the site. The other lesson was about who gets to write a tool. Use agents to write the code, host them locally, and inject them via an extension you own. Then any webmcp enabled site you have crawled can use the webmcp api and tools for now. The honest limit is that as pages change, you'll need to recrawl.
