title: Sensemaking Studio
pitch: A shared canvas for qualitative research where the agent proposes, and the human decides.
about_excerpt: A shared canvas for qualitative research where the agent proposes, and the human decides. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Coding interview transcripts takes weeks, and most of it is clerical work. The part that matters is small: the handful of quotes that could honestly belong to two different themes. Choosing between them isn't data entry. It's the argument the paper will make. Every AI tool I tried resolved those quotes for me. Hand over a corpus, get back clean labels, and the disagreement that should have shaped the analysis is gone, filed under whichever theme won by a rounding error. I wanted the opposite: the machine grinding through the volume, and the disagreements coming back to me instead of getting quietly filed. What it does Sensemaking Studio is a shared canvas. A researcher drags quotes between themes. An agent works on the same document at the same time: it reads the whole corpus, finds quotes between two themes, ranks them by how contested they are, and presents them to the researcher. Then it stops. The agent has no way to settle a contested quote. This isn't a policy or a line in a prompt. The capability does not exist. It can argue for a reading. It cannot record one. Why WebMCP fits An agent that drives a web app by clicking has to guess what it is looking at, and everything it does arrives as an anonymous mutation. The record cannot tell a researcher's judgment from a stray click. In qualitative research, that record is the product. An analysis is defensible because you can show who decided what and why. Lose the provenance, and you have lost the thing you were making. WebMCP lets the page hand off the operations to an agent instead of the buttons. When the agent moves a quote, it invokes the same command that the researcher's mouse does, so both appear in one log with the author attached. That shared path is also why the guardrail holds. There's no backdoor into the analysis, so the agent's reach stops at the commands that exist. What people and agents can do together now Scoring every quote against two themes and ranking them by how close the contest is: mechanical, and infeasible by hand, somewhere past a few hundred quotes. Deciding any single one: a theoretical judgment that a model should not be making quietly. Those two halves could not sit in the same room before. Batch tools returned a spreadsheet with the ambiguity already resolved and nobody's name on it. Click-driven automation could not read the analysis at all. Now they interleave. The agent surfaces "I don't know whether ChatGPT is actually accurate", filed under policy uncertainty, and points out that the evidence is really about trust. I look. I agree or I don't. I move it. That decision immediately changes what the agent compares against on its next pass, so it gets better at finding my arguments because I keep making them. The workspace also keeps score, running in the right direction. It tracks how often my decisions matched the agent's ranking, so I learn how much to trust it based on my own record rather than its confidence. How I built it Nuxt and Vue, entirely client-side, are deployed as static assets on Cloudflare Workers. One store holds the analysis, and every change goes through it, whether a human or an agent asks. That single write path is what makes attribution reliable instead of aspirational. Thirteen tools register with the browser's model context when a WebMCP host is present, and the page behaves normally when no host is present. Every tool is a research operation rather than a UI action: nothing in the set clicks a card or drags a rectangle. Read-only tools are marked as such and flagged as carrying participant-authored text, so a host knows not to treat an interview quote as an instruction. The scoring is deliberately conservative. A quote has to be clearly relevant to both themes before closeness counts for anything, otherwise two weak scores look like a hard case when they are just noise. Theme definitions are built only from examples that a human confirmed, so the agent's proposals never quietly redefine the thing it is measuring against. 24 unit tests, plus a browser test that registers the full tool set and runs an agent through a complete session from a cold start. I run that against the deployed site too, so the live demo is verified the same way as the local build. Challenges Telling two kinds of hard cases apart took the most thought. A quote that genuinely sits between two themes needs a human. A quote that makes two separate points belongs to both, which is not ambiguity, just dual membership. Measure only how close the scores are, and the two look identical, but they need different handling and a different place in the queue. What I learned My first version had eight tools and a hole I could not see. One of them needed two theme IDs, and nothing in the set returned the list of themes. Reading the docs, it looks complete, because I already know my own theme names. An agent arriving cold was stuck at the first step. Whether an agent can orient itself from nothing turned out to be the only test that mattered. The other lesson is about where a rule has to live. Writing "the agent should not decide" into a prompt is a request, and a model that wants to be helpful will eventually find a way around it. Not building the tool is a different kind of thing, and it's the version I'd rely on. What's next First the dull necessary things. Decisions don't survive a refresh, so the agreement score can't build up over the course of a study. Scoring could be sharper than word overlap. Several researchers should be able to work the same corpus. And it should export into NVivo and ATLAS.ti, where this work actually lives. The bigger thing sits further up the pipeline. Interviews start as audio, and transcription and speaker diarization are both commodity at this point, so putting them on the front of this is mostly integration work. Then you hand it a folder of recordings and get back a live analysis with the contested passages already queued, rather than transcripts you still have to sit down and read. That's the service I'd want to use, and I'd build it under the same restriction. Once most of a pipeline runs unattended, the record of who decided what is doing most of the work of making the output defensible at all. title: TaskFence
pitch: Delegate a task to an AI agent on any website — and keep the say-so. Real WebMCP tools behind a deterministic fence you write in plain English.
about_excerpt: Delegate a task to an AI agent on any website — and keep the say-so. Real WebMCP tools behind a deterministic fence you write in plain English. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP changes what a website can offer an AI agent. Instead of leaving the agent to interpret a page built for human eyes, a site can publish the operations it actually supports and let the agent call them directly. Reading through the explainer, what struck me was that making the boundary explicit does more than improve reliability — it creates somewhere to put a policy. For the first time there is a real function call between an agent and a website's data, and anything that happens at that point can be inspected, reasoned about, and governed. The explainer is candid that a trust boundary is crossed the moment an agent begins calling tools, and there are open discussions in the project around agent identity and action-specific permissions. Those felt like the most interesting questions in the space, and the kind that benefit from someone building a working example rather than only describing one. The shape of the answer came from ordinary experience. When you ask a colleague to handle a form for you, you rarely give an unqualified yes. You say something like "fill in what you can from these documents, leave the parts I've already written, and check with me before you send it." That is a boundary that stays in force for the whole task and can be adjusted while the work is underway. I wanted to see how close a website could get to that, now that it finally has a place to enforce it. What it does TaskFence is a delegation layer that sits on a site's WebMCP boundary. The clearest way to describe it is to follow what happens in the demo. You begin with a form you need completed. Rather than the site choosing what that form is, you upload the one you actually care about — I test with a real university scholarship PDF — and the page reads the fields out of your document. If you had already filled in parts of that PDF before uploading it, TaskFence treats those values as answers you have given and places them on the form as yours, which becomes important a moment later. You then describe the task in a sentence, in your own words, including anything you want left alone: "fill in the blanks from my documents, don't change anything I've already answered, ask me if something is missing, ask before you submit, and tell me if any field doesn't look right." That sentence is compiled into a structured contract of permitted, forbidden and approval-required actions. Before anything runs, the page shows you what it understood, and equally what it could not interpret — a boundary you believed you had set but which was quietly misread would undermine the whole idea, so it is surfaced rather than assumed. The agent then works. Everything within your boundary proceeds without interruption: it reads the form and your documents, checks the answers already present, and completes the blanks it is permitted to complete. You are not consulted about any of it, because you have already agreed to it. When it reaches something outside the boundary, the tool call is held before the write takes place. You are shown what the agent intended to do, which part of your own sentence stopped it, and precisely what permission is being requested. You can decline, or allow it — and if the value the agent proposed is wrong, you can correct it first, so what is written is your version. A grant is deliberately narrow: one tool, one field, a single use, expiring the moment it is spent, and scoped to that agent and that task alone. Afterwards there is a ledger of every decision alongside the rule that produced it, which can be replayed and exported. How we built it The application is React, TypeScript and Vite, with zustand for state, Motion for transitions, React Three Fiber for the mark on the landing page, and pdf.js reading documents entirely in the browser. The parts worth explaining, though, are three design decisions. The first is where enforcement lives. Every tool the site registers is wrapped by a single guarded() function, so there is no route from an agent to the site's data that bypasses the check. This is practical because of the shape WebMCP already gives us: a tool call is an async function, so pausing an agent to consult a human costs nothing to implement — the promise simply is not resolved yet. Tools are registered exactly as the specification describes: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "updateApplication", description: "Update a field in the application", inputSchema: { /* field, value, source, documentId */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* runs only if the contract allows it */ } }) Built With css groq html motion node.js openai react react-three-fiber three.js typescript vite webmcp zustand Try it out task-fence.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Lisa A Like Share this project: Updates Lisa A started this project — Sep 03, 2026 01:50 PM EDT

title: Giffium
pitch: Giffium is a tool to generate animated code snippets that highlight the diff between two different snippets. The goal is to generate sharable GIFs and/or MP4s in a similar vein to Carbon or Ray.so.
about_excerpt: Giffium is a tool to generate animated code snippets that highlight the diff between two different snippets. The goal is to generate sharable GIFs and/or MP4s in a similar vein to Carbon or Ray.so. Like Comment Story Updates The Giffium Home Page GIF The result of generating a GIF Inspiration Giffium takes its inspiration from tools like carbon.now.sh and ray.so. The goal is to make socially sharable diffs instead of static code snippets. Adding WebMCP support seemed like a good idea to give agents access to its functionality without having to build a CLI tool from scratch. What it does Giffium takes in 2 code snippets and animates them to and from each other using shiki-magic-move. The result is captured into a set of frames that we build a GIF from. There is the option to create an MP4 file as well for smoother animation compared to a GIF. The WebMCP tool allows the agent to generate a gif of a diff. It also exposes a separate tool to modify the styling such as font, font size, syntax highlighting theme, and background color. How wIbuilt it Giffium was originally built for the SolidJS hackathon 2024 before AI was as capable as it is now. So it was hand-coded. It won that year of the hackathon. The core functionality is due to shiki-magic-move by antfu. However, we still needed to build out the entire configuration layer as well as the building of the GIF and MP4 files. The WebMCP support was fairly simple to add for the WebMCP challenge after using OpenSpec to explore the WebMCP spec and documentation. Challenges we ran into Capturing shiki-magic-move is not as simple as expected. This is because it is animating raw DOM elements. So, we needed to use RequestAnimationFrame to capture the HTML contents into an off-screen canvas and capture that into individual frames. Some other challenges involve font space and element offsets. The fonts are loaded in from Google Fonts and the WebMCP tool for generating the GIF was not giving the font enough time to download which broke the layout and spacing of elements. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Adding MP4 support using ffmpeg-wasm was a fun experiment that turned out well. The trickiest part was making sure we didn't blow up the bundle size by including it by default. Giving the user the option to download it and handling that process was a good UX problem to solve. What I learned Implementing WebMCP is much more straight-forward than a full proper MCP server and testing is as simple as asking ChatGPT Desktop to validate all of the tools. What's next for Giffium It might be nice to implement some loop metadata configuration since the GIF spec supports assigning X amount of loops and stopping at the end, as an example. This will be tricky since the library being used is modern-gif which doesn't have support for loop metadata, yet. I might also consider packaging the tool's functionality into a CLI. title: Filika
pitch: Filika lets AI agents turn website issues, confusing flows, and blocked tasks into actionable feedback for product teams.
about_excerpt: Filika lets AI agents turn website issues, confusing flows, and blocked tasks into actionable feedback for product teams. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Hero Demo Page Login Page Onboarding Dashboard Complaints Feedback Detail Profile Menu Filika: WebMCP feedback infrastructure for modern web applications Inspiration Website problems are often discovered in the moment but never reach the people who can fix them. A customer may get stuck in checkout, an employee may be unable to complete a task, or an agent may encounter confusing behavior while helping someone. Turning that experience into an actionable report usually requires leaving the task, finding a support channel, and manually reconstructing what happened. Filika makes that handoff part of the browsing experience. What it does Filika is a WebMCP-native feedback system for web applications. A website registers the static filika_submit_feedback tool with document.modelContext . When a browser agent encounters an observed bug, blocked task, confusing behavior, or concrete product idea, it can submit a structured report containing a title, description, expected behavior, and reproduction steps. The report is delivered to a maintainer workspace where teams can review, search, filter, and export it to GitHub. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, an agent has no reliable, structured way to hand an observed problem back to the product team. It would need to guess its way through a website's support UI, generate an unstructured message, or stop at a conversational summary. With Filika, the website intentionally exposes one narrowly scoped feedback capability. The agent can act at the moment it sees the problem, while the product team receives feedback in a consistent format that is ready for triage. This creates a better experience for both sides: people and agents can continue working instead of filing a separate ticket, and maintainers receive clearer reports with reproducible context rather than vague descriptions. How we built it Filika is a TypeScript monorepo built with Bun, Next.js, React, PostgreSQL, and Drizzle. The browser SDK uses document.modelContext.registerTool() to register the static filika_submit_feedback WebMCP tool. Its closed JSON schema accepts only bounded, structured feedback fields. The collector API validates every request, verifies the configured website origin, limits payload size and timeouts, detects duplicates using idempotency keys, and stores accepted reports in PostgreSQL. The maintainer workspace lets teams create applications, configure allowed origins, install the generated SDK snippet, inspect incoming feedback, and export approved reports to GitHub issues. A public demo storefront includes intentional failures so judges can test the WebMCP flow themselves. Privacy and safety Filika deliberately does not collect ambient page content, browser history, screenshots, cookies, local storage, or credentials. Tool metadata is static, input schemas reject unknown fields, and browser or collector data is treated as untrusted until validated. Demo Open the demo, ask a WebMCP-enabled browser agent to complete the sample shopping task, let it encounter the intentional failure, and ask it to submit feedback with Filika. Then open the workspace to see the submitted report and its reproduction steps. title: OJS-WebMCP: Agent-Native Scholarly Publishing
pitch: An agent-native editorial control room for 58,000+ academic journals - AI triages submissions and synthesizes peer reviews while human editors retain final authority.
about_excerpt: An agent-native editorial control room for 58,000+ academic journals - AI triages submissions and synthesizes peer reviews while human editors retain final authority. Like Comment Story Updates Published OJS article demonstrating an agent-native scholarly workflow with seven native WebMCP tools available to in-browser AI agents. List all submissions example MCP Get full abstract details MCP 💡 Inspiration: The Plight of a Two-Person Editorial Team Years ago, I served as a journal editor for an academic journal ( cogito.unklab.ac.id ). Our editorial team consisted of just two people . Every week, a flood of new submissions arrived in our Open Journal Systems (OJS) queue. The administrative burden was suffocating: We spent hours manually reading through abstracts just to verify if papers met our scope. Finding and assigning reviewers with relevant domain expertise took days of cross-referencing past archives. Reviewers routinely missed deadlines, forcing us to constantly track due dates and send manual reminders. Reading divergent reviewer reports and drafting customized, polite, constructive decision letters drained our remaining mental energy. Academic peer review is the bedrock of human knowledge, yet over 56,000 journals worldwide are managed by small, overworked academic teams suffering from click fatigue and administrative burnout. When the WebMCP standard emerged from W3C, Chrome, and OpenAI, a lightbulb went off: Why should academic editors spend hours navigating dozens of nested tabs when an in-browser AI agent can co-pilot the editorial desk using the editor's live session? ⚡ What It Does OJS-WebMCP turns standard Open Journal Systems installations into an Agent-Native Editorial Control Room . Instead of relying on fragile scrapers or complex command-line MCP servers, our plugin directly registers 7 native WebMCP tools into the editor's browser session via document.modelContext.registerTool : Intelligent Desk Screening : The agent queries active queues across all 4 workflow stages ( ojs_list_submissions ) and retrieves full abstracts and verified author affiliations ( ojs_get_submission_details ) to evaluate scope compliance. Automated Peer-Review Tracking : Inspects reviewer assignments, identifies overdue reviews, and monitors reviewer recommendations ( ojs_get_review_rounds ). Live Review Synthesis : Connects directly to real reviewer feedback to synthesize a formal decision letter ( ojs_draft_editorial_decision ), accurately distinguishing between Minor Revisions , Major Revisions (Resubmit for Review) , Acceptance , and Decline . Approval-Gated Reviewer Reminder : Prepares and dispatches polite reminder notifications to overdue reviewers ( ojs_send_reviewer_reminder ). It enforces strict Human-in-the-Loop safety: the agent can only preview the reminder until the human editor explicitly approves it ( confirmSend: true ). Issue & Volume Planning : Discovers upcoming unpublished future issues ( ojs_list_issues ) to help editors schedule accepted papers for publication. 🛠️ How We Built It Universal OJS Generic Plugin : Packaged as a clean, modular plugin ( plugins/generic/webmcp ) compatible with modern OJS 3.4+ and 3.5+. Zero API Key Friction : Academic editors are researchers, not DevOps engineers. Our plugin leverages the editor's active browser session cookie and CSRF token. When ChatGPT or Chrome Agent opens the tab, it inherits authoritative editorial permissions immediately-no API keys or environment variables required. Granular REST Integration : Extended OJS's core routing architecture with custom, authenticated REST endpoints ( /submissions/{id}/reviewAssignments ) to expose granular review progress without leaking unnecessary personal identifiers. W3C WebMCP Standard : All tools implement structured JSON Schemas and async execution handlers conforming strictly to the official WebMCP spec. 🧗 Challenges We Faced Navigating OJS's Deep RBAC & Security Policies : OJS has a strict multi-layer authorization system ( SubmissionAccessPolicy , PolicyAuthorizer ). Ensuring that our WebMCP tools respected editorial permissions without bypassing journal security required deep reverse-engineering of OJS's internal routing stack. Ensuring Human Authority Over AI Actions : We did not want an agent going rogue and emailing professors unsolicited rejection letters. Designing the Approval-Gated Action pattern ( confirmSend gate) ensured that the AI serves as an indispensable assistant while the human editor always retains final academic authority. Data Sanitization & Metadata Quality : Normalizing OJS 3.5's multi-table author affiliation schemas ( author_affiliations and author_affiliation_settings ) and stripping raw HTML tags from abstracts so that LLMs receive clean, token-efficient context. 📚 What We Learned In-Browser MCP is the Future : Traditional MCP requires running local processes, configuring port forwarding, or sharing sensitive API tokens. WebMCP completely democratizes agentic AI for web-first workflows: you log into your web app, and your agent is immediately ready to help. The "Control Room" Dynamic : The winning paradigm for AI in knowledge work is not total automation, but co-browsing : the human provides the high-level strategy and moral judgment, while the agent handles workload tracking, data retrieval, and first-pass drafting. 🚀 What's Next Automated Reviewer Matching : Using paper embeddings and CrossRef/OpenAlex APIs to suggest the top 3 best-matching reviewers based on published citation history. Submission to PKP Plugin Gallery : Submitting this plugin to the official Public Knowledge Project (PKP) Plugin Gallery so that all 58,000+ academic journals worldwide can install OJS-WebMCP in a single click. title: AIWeb Operating System
pitch: AIWEB OS is a machine-native operating system where people and ChatGPT use WebMCP together to design, build, publish, and operate AIWEB Pages — then Call, Receipt, and continue on the live page.
about_excerpt: AIWEB OS is a machine-native operating system where people and ChatGPT use WebMCP together to design, build, publish, and operate AIWEB Pages — then Call, Receipt, and continue on the live page. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Customers increasingly ask AI for businesses, services, products, and media instead of browsing websites alone. Most business sites were built for people to click through—not for agents and owners to collaborate on the same public document . An agent might find a business or summarize a page, but finishing the customer’s intention still means navigating forms, copying details, calling manually, or handing off to a human. Building the page itself is even harder: agents can draft text, but they rarely have a safe, structured way to edit a live site with the owner in control. We built AIWEB OS around a simple idea: A business page should not only tell AI what the business does. It should give people and agents a shared, reviewable way to build it and act on it. AIWEB Pages are public, portable business documents that connect live identity, information, and actions (Call / inquiry, media, Receipts, continuation). WebMCP gave us a browser-native way to expose those capabilities directly from the page—both in Publisher (create) and on the live IRL page (operate). What it does AIWEB OS uses WebMCP so humans and ChatGPT can work the same surfaces: Create — Publisher + WebMCP Owner opens a blank page in AIWEB OS . Attaches images and describes the business (or pastes a judge scenario brief). ChatGPT uses editor WebMCP tools on the open page: snapshot the draft, edit identity and sections, FAQs, forms, validate, run AI Check, and request publish. Publication waits for an explicit human yes ( publish_draft with confirm). Operate — published AIWEB Page + WebMCP A customer asks something like: “Request a quote for a wedding with 100 guests.” The agent recognizes capabilities exposed by the published page, fills the visible form, and lets the customer review before submit. The business gets the lead; the customer gets an AIWEB Receipt . The business replies in Publisher; the customer continues on the same Receipt. Discovery and action are recorded as HITS (Human & Intelligent Traffic Signals), including WebMCP as a channel when applicable. End-to-end journey: Intent → Build (WebMCP) → Publish → Call → Receipt → Business response Judges can reproduce the create path with the Pet Voyage image bundle and Act 1 prompt (see testing notes / JUDGE_TEST_ACTS.md ). Example outcome (optional): Pet Voyage . How we built it AIWEB already existed as a production Publisher and a network of AIWEB Pages, plus server-side MCP for chat applications. For the WebMCP Challenge we added a browser-native WebMCP layer on top of that stack: Editor WebMCP on the open Publisher workspace — tools such as draft snapshot, structure edits, FAQs, validate, AI Check, publish hints, and gated publish. Page WebMCP on the public IRL document — page facts, FAQs, form requirements, Call / inquiry with human confirmation, Receipt tools. Implementation principles: Register tools with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) so ChatGPT’s in-app browser (or WebMCP-enabled Chrome) can operate the page. Keep the same human UI; agents assist through structured tools rather than a hidden agent-only twin. Agent may prepare ; human authorizes publish and customer submission. Route actions through existing AIWEB lead / Receipt / HITS pipelines. Record protocol and agent source for measurement. Server MCP connects chat apps to the wider AIWEB network. WebMCP works at the webpage itself—an open, page-local control surface for the same identity and actions. Challenges we ran into Separating assistance from authorization An agent should understand and prepare a business action without silently committing the customer—or publishing without the owner. We kept forms and publish flows visible and required explicit human approval. Serving humans and agents through one page We did not want a hidden agent-only endpoint that duplicated the site. The goal is one interface that stays readable for people while becoming structured and actionable for agents. Co-authoring a live draft safely WebMCP Build mutates a real draft (identity, sections, FAQs, forms, media). Agents must use tools instead of dumping the prompt into the page. Preserving structured content while placing media is an ongoing reliability problem we treat as first-class product work. Maintaining a canonical business identity Business facts get copied into directories and model answers where they go stale. AIWEB resolves actions through the registered AIWEB Page so the business keeps a canonical, updateable identity. Measuring activity across platforms Each AI provider sees activity inside its own product. Businesses need an independent view across models, browsers, crawlers, and protocols. AIWEB records interaction at the shared page and registry layer (HITS). AIWEB records GEO and AEO metrics as discovery and actions called HITS—Human and Intelligent Traffic Signals. A HIT is created when a human or machine discovers, reads, validates, or acts through a registered AIWEB Page. The event can be attributed to its channel, including WebMCP when applicable. Extending an existing production platform Because AIWEB shipped before the challenge, we had to isolate and document the WebMCP surface while preserving production Publisher, federation, and server MCP workflows. Accomplishments that we're proud of Before this challenge, AIWEB had already published 14,928 public AI Web Pages and independently recorded 233,567 federated HITS across human and machine activity. For the WebMCP Challenge, we connected an open public business page to an end-to-end outcome: An agent can co-build a page through WebMCP tools in Publisher. An agent can recognize a real business capability on the live page. The agent can help prepare the action while the human stays in control . The business receives a structured lead; the customer receives a persistent Receipt. AIWEB independently measures the interaction. That moves the experience beyond AI-generated answers into real create-and-operate activity on the open web. What we learned WebMCP is more than automating clicks on a website. It lets the public web itself become an interface for agents while preserving familiar, visible experiences for humans. Exposing one page as a tool is only the first layer. Businesses also need: A portable identity they control A way to publish current information Discovery across models and search systems Reusable business actions Receipts and continuing communication Independent cross-agent measurement WebMCP provides the open connection between agent and webpage. AIWEB OS networks those pages into shared identity, discovery, action, and measurement—with ChatGPT able to act as a team lead operating the page through WebMCP. Like Cloudflare can observe traffic across networks, AIWEB can observe human and machine traffic as it reaches the same registered pages. Public pages stay open and portable; the registry, index, and federated HITS create an intent-and-action graph no single AI platform sees alone. What's next for AIWEB OS We plan to deepen WebMCP across create and operate: Stronger Build orchestration (block-level patches, protected structures, durable media works) Richer live-page capabilities (Call, media play, discovery, status checks, structured updates) Share of Intent — measurement that uses qualified HITS to show which pages, intentions, actions, and agent sources capture observed demand Our larger goal: make the AIWEB Page a universal agentic business document—open enough for compatible models, search, and browsers to read and use—supported by a registry, identity, action, and intelligence network. AIWEB gives every business a public page that humans can browse, AI agents can act through, and the business can independently measure. title: Pulse
pitch: The open repair memory for humans and agents.
about_excerpt: The open repair memory for humans and agents. Like Comment Story Updates Pulse repair evidence and the shared human-agent workflow. Inspiration Repair knowledge is everywhere and nowhere. A successful fix might be buried in a forum comment, a video, a repair café log, or someone's memory. Even when someone finds useful advice, the result usually disappears after the problem is solved. We wanted to explore a different kind of open web: one where humans and AI agents do not just consume information together, but actively improve the structured knowledge available to the next person. Pulse turns individual repair experiences into shared repair evidence. What it does Pulse is an open repair knowledge network where humans and AI agents troubleshoot physical objects together. People create cases describing a product, symptoms, diagnostic observations, repair attempts, and final outcomes. An agent visiting the same site can search similar repairs, inspect successful and unsuccessful outcomes, create a new case, add diagnostic steps, record observations supplied by the human, and document whether the final repair worked. The AI handles information retrieval and organization. The human provides physical-world observations and performs appropriate repairs. When the repair is finished, the result becomes reusable knowledge for the next person experiencing the same problem. Why WebMCP Pulse is designed around structured agent interaction rather than visual browser automation. Without WebMCP, an agent would need to inspect pages, identify controls, reverse-engineer forms, and simulate human interaction. Pulse instead exposes ten explicit capabilities including search_repairs, get_repair_case, create_repair_case, add_diagnostic_result, and record_repair_outcome. The agent knows exactly which actions are supported and receives compact structured data in return. WebMCP is the product architecture, not a decorative integration. How it creates a better user experience Repair troubleshooting usually means switching among search results, videos, forum threads, notes, and the object itself. Pulse lets the user stay focused. They describe the problem to their agent; the agent retrieves structured repair evidence, compares previous outcomes, records the person's observations, and keeps the history organized. The page updates alongside the agent. A visible activity panel shows searches, case creation, diagnostic changes, and outcomes, so automation is legible instead of mysterious. How we built it Pulse registers application capabilities through the current imperative browser model context API: document.modelContext.registerTool(...), with a carefully feature-detected navigator.modelContext fallback. Every tool has a descriptive name, JSON Schema input contract, explicit required fields, read-only annotations where appropriate, compact structured output, and safe error handling. Community-authored content is marked untrusted. Read tools query public repair evidence; mutation tools create cases, diagnostic records, repair attempts, outcomes, and community votes. The tools call the same Next route handlers and Cloudflare D1 database as the React interface. Successful mutations dispatch a page event, refresh visible state, and add an activity record. The result is genuine application behavior rather than an isolated agent demo. The production app is built with Next.js-compatible React, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, Cloudflare Workers, Cloudflare D1, Drizzle ORM, and OpenAI Sites. It requires no API key or account. Challenges we ran into The largest design challenge was deciding what the visiting agent should do versus what the website should do. It would have been easy to build another chatbot that generated repair suggestions. Instead, the site provides durable structured tools and state; the visiting agent supplies reasoning and conversation; the person supplies physical evidence. We also had to treat repair knowledge carefully. Not every repair is appropriate for DIY work. Every case has a low-risk, moderate-risk, or professional-recommended classification. Higher-risk histories remain retrievable, but the server refuses procedural diagnostic steps and recommends qualified service. Finally, repair confidence needed to be credible. Pulse avoids opaque AI percentages and shows Repair Evidence instead: reports, attempts, fixed/improved/did-not-work counts, median time, and typical cost. Accomplishments that we're proud of Ten real imperative WebMCP tools backed by the production database One coherent human + agent workflow from search to final outcome Visible mutation activity and immediately refreshed repair timelines Thirty believable, labeled demo histories across nine product categories Deterministic weighted matching with overlapping successes and failures Relational D1 persistence, validation, constraints, safety gates, and rate limiting A polished responsive interface that remains useful without WebMCP Seven passing automated workflow tests and a production worker build A production mutation smoke test that created a case, diagnostic evidence, and a fixed outcome visible in the public timeline What we learned WebMCP changes the application design question. Normally the visual interface becomes an accidental API that an agent must reverse-engineer. With WebMCP, human and agent interfaces can be designed intentionally around the same capabilities. That shifted our attention away from browser automation and toward collaboration: which actions are safe, which evidence only a human can provide, which state should be transparent, and how a successful interaction improves the next one. What's next Pulse could grow into a broader open repair ecosystem with Open Repair Data Standard import/export, manual references, parts compatibility, repair café integrations, manufacturer documentation, repairability statistics, regional parts sourcing, verified contributor reputation, richer product identification, and community moderation. The long-term idea is simple: when something breaks, the open web should remember what actually fixed it. title: ReadyCounter
pitch: We asked 148 real storefronts what a shopping agent can read. Not one exposed a barcode. Paste your store: get the score, the fix list, and the CSV that repairs it.
about_excerpt: We asked 148 real storefronts what a shopping agent can read. Not one exposed a barcode. Paste your store: get the score, the fix list, and the CSV that repairs it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Two numbers, twelve months apart. In March 2025, AI-referred traffic converted 38% worse than everything else on a retail site. In March 2026 it converted 42% better (Adobe Digital Insights). Agent traffic stopped being a curiosity and became the channel that pays. Then the other number: 78.6% of agent carts are abandoned (Presenc AI). And Shopify said on its Q1 2026 earnings call that a catalogue an agent can read converts 2× better than a page it has to scrape. So the prize is real, it is arriving now, and most of it is being lost to a data problem. But a merchant hears "agentic commerce" and has no way to see which door is locked on their own store. Theme checkers grade the page a human sees. Nothing grades what an agent retrieves. We wanted to build the instrument, and then — before claiming anything — point it at the field and find out whether the problem was real. What it does Paste your domain. Get a score, a fix list, and a receipt that names its source. ReadyCounter asks your storefront for its catalogue the way a shopping agent asks, and prices what it finds against published research on why agent carts fail. Every point on the bill is one row of a published abandonment table, at the share that table states, with the publisher and the date we read it printed on the line. Nothing on the tape is a number we invented. Three things a merchant can do with it: See the field. We asked 148 curated DTC storefronts. 48 answered and sent no catalogue. 22 refused the request outright — and we say so rather than scoring them, because we re-probed every one with a real browser and recovered none, so the block is IP reputation and we genuinely cannot see them. Of the ones we could read, 67 sent a feed with no barcode in it and average barcode coverage is 0% . Your store joins that wall as tile 149. Read the blank barcode. The front page draws what an agent actually reads off your product page. A bar is inked only where a product exposes a GTIN, so at 0% the code is grey and unscannable. The emptiness is the measurement. Co-shop with the agent. Eighteen WebMCP tools are registered in the open tab. A human click and an agent's add_to_order land on the same order, tagged HUMAN or AGENT. prepare_checkout validates the total and never charges a card — the agent proposes, the person pays. Take the fix with you. The audit ends in a download, not advice: a CSV in Shopify's own import shape, pre-filled with the merchant's real product handles, with Variant Barcode blank where it is missing. Fill it, Products → Import, re-audit, and the delta receipt proves it landed. We never ask for write access. And because Shopify maps Barcode to GTIN in the Google Merchant Center feed, the same afternoon of work repairs Google Shopping — which already has a budget line. And you can watch a real model do it. On the Co-shop tab, a language model is handed the 18 tool definitions and a shopping goal. It picks the calls, the browser executes them through document.modelContext , and it gets stopped by the same CAPTCHA a real customer's agent would hit — then explains the block in its own words. Nothing in that sequence is scripted. Deliberately, the model is the shopper and never the judge . The readiness score is arithmetic over a crawl: reproducible between runs, auditable line by line, and impossible to talk into a better number by putting words on your storefront. Model on the outside, deterministic instrument on the inside. One finding surprised us enough to put it on the front page: eleven brands publish barcodes to Shopify's Catalog MCP and hide them on their own storefront — Glossier, Tatcha, Brooklinen, Alo Yoga, Buffy, Mejuri, Gorjana, Dagne Dover, United By Blue, Stio, Away. The protocol has the data. The scrape, which is what a shopper's agent reads, does not. How we built it React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand for the shared order, deployed on Vercel. WebMCP. All 18 tools are declared in src/webmcp/registerTools.ts with document.modelContext.registerTool(name, {description, inputSchema, execute}) . The same handlers serve two paths, so a judge never needs a Chrome flag to see it work: Path A is native WebMCP (Chrome 149+), Path B is the in-page Agent tool console, identical handlers, no flag. We chose the browser API over a hosted MCP server deliberately. The thing being measured is what an agent can retrieve in the shopper's own session . A server-side MCP would read the catalogue with our credentials, not theirs, and would miss exactly the walls that matter — CAPTCHA, forced login, session-gated pricing. Integrations, all live in this build: Shopify OAuth — read-only Admin API for the merchant's own catalogue, barcodes and prices. No payment scopes, ever. Shopify Catalog MCP (UCP) — the protocol side of the scrape-vs-protocol comparison. This is where the eleven-brand finding came from. Render Key Value — persists every merchant audit and every live co-shop room across Vercel cold starts, plus a weekly cron that re-runs the field batch. GET /api/v1/render/status shows it. Verification. 13 npm run verify scripts assert the score arithmetic, the source citations and the honest limits; 15 Playwright e2e tests run against production, not a mock. Challenges we ran into The interesting one: scrape ≠ protocol. Our first field batch said 0% GTIN coverage and we nearly shipped that as "nobody has barcodes". Then we queried Shopify's Catalog MCP for the same stores and found 13 of 81 do expose GTINs there — 11 of them while their public scrape is empty. The honest finding was not "merchants have no data", it was "the data exists and the surface an agent reads does not carry it". That reframed the whole product. Correcting our own scoring, publicly. We charged the forced-account-wall 24 points because we had reused the CAPTCHA row's weight. A re-read of the cited table on 2026-08-31 found the account wall has its own row at 15%. We changed the weight and left the note on the line. If a number moves, the receipt should say so. A film that lied about itself. Our demo pipeline had hardcoded narration cues. Paragraph 7 ran 6.9 seconds past its slot and was mixed on top of paragraph 8, and the caption file claimed both were spoken cleanly. The build script printed that exact warning and exited 0, so nobody read it. Every duration is now derived from the rendered audio, the checks are fatal, and a separate verifier checks the file that actually ships rather than the parts it was made from. Our own tools trapped an agent. Pointing a real model at the tool surface found something no test had: get_product takes id , but add_to_order took product_id . The model called get_product({id}) , got a product back, carried id forward — and looped six times on Product not found: with an empty value. On a product whose whole thesis is making stores legible to agents, we would have shipped a tool surface that confuses agents. Every product-taking tool now reads product_id , id or sku , the schemas say so, and an empty id returns an error that tells the agent what to pass instead. Our own wall was lying by omission. "Asked, no feed" was one grey tile covering two different facts: 48 storefronts that answered and sent nothing, and 22 that refused the request outright. We proved the difference matters by trying to get in — six declared identities including GPTBot, ClaudeBot and a full Chrome string got 0 of 14; a real Chrome browser fetching from inside the page's own origin recovered 0 of 22. The block is IP reputation, so those stores are unmeasured, not failing , and painting "we could not look" as "you have no data" is exactly the error this product exists to catch in other people's dashboards. They now have their own struck-through tile. The fix file would not have worked. Shopify matches a CSV import by Handle . We were storing the SKU as the product id ("Accessory-HairClipsGWP") and never capturing the handle ("hair-clips-gwp") at all — the type did not even declare it. The export would have matched nothing and looked like it worked. Caught by diffing our stored product against the store's live products.json before shipping the button. A permanently empty third of the page. The layout reserved 21rem for a sidebar that only exists on one tab, so two of three tabs rendered a blank column and nobody noticed until we looked at a screenshot instead of the code. Accomplishments that we're proud of The field batch is a real measurement, not a demo fixture. 148 storefronts, 78 answered, 0% average barcode coverage, and you can re-run our exact query: curl -s https://readycounter.vercel.app/api/v1/rankings \ | jq '{succeeded,shopCount,avgGtinPct,ucp}' Every point on the bill cites a publisher, a publication date and the date we read it. title: RuleRipple
pitch: RuleRipple is a policy simulation sandbox to help humans and AI agents allocate limited resources like credits, test rules, understand who gets what and why, & approve allocations with an audit trail.
about_excerpt: RuleRipple is a policy simulation sandbox to help humans and AI agents allocate limited resources like credits, test rules, understand who gets what and why, & approve allocations with an audit trail. Like Comment Story Updates Policy templates Priority rules Limits and governance Budget ledger Policy overview 1. WebMCP workflow Shared budget inbox Allocation approval Version comparison Budget simulation Why a request waits Request ranking and explanations Execution receipt Agent connections Activity audit trail Inspiration Inspiration RuleRipple grew out of a problem the three of us—my sister, my wife, and I—faced while working on our own projects. AI credits were a scarce resource, and our limited budgets meant we had to be thoughtful about how we used them. That raised a practical question: when several tasks need credits, how do we decide which ones get priority, how much each receives, and what has to wait? We wanted to test those choices before committing our budget and understand how changing a rule would affect each request. That inspired RuleRipple: a policy simulation sandbox where humans and AI agents can explore how to allocate limited resources, understand the tradeoffs, and approve decisions with a clear trail. What it does RuleRipple is a WebMCP-powered policy simulation sandbox for humans and AI agents. It helps users define allocation rules, preview their effects, and approve allocations with an audit trail. WebMCP is useful here because the agent works with the same visible policy workspace as the user. Agents can inspect policies and submit structured requests, while people can see the results, understand the effect on other requests, and retain control over approvals. Users can: Define available resources, protected reserves, eligibility requirements, and priorities. Receive budget requests from agents through HTTPS or WebMCP. Simulate how a policy distributes resources across competing requests. Change a rule and compare who becomes eligible, moves in priority, gains resources, or has to wait. Review the reasons behind each allocation and approve exact amounts. Track reservations, commitments, recorded consumption, and released resources in a ledger. The same approach supports resources such as agent credits, funding, API quotas, clinic hours, inventory, and inspection slots. A simple example Imagine two agents each request 70 credits from a shared budget of 100. There is enough to support either request fully, but not both. A priority-based policy might fund the urgent request first. A sharing policy might distribute credits between them, provided each receives enough to do useful work. RuleRipple lets a user test these choices before approving an allocation. Changing a priority rule or protecting a reserve reveals the effect across all requests. The “ripple” is the impact one policy change has on everyone competing for the same resources. How we built it We built RuleRipple with React and TypeScript, with a deterministic engine for policy evaluation, ranking, resource allocation, version comparison, and ledger accounting. The WebMCP tools use structured schemas and runtime validation. Firebase Authentication and Cloud Firestore support sign-in and persistent workspaces, and the application is deployed through ChatGPT Sites. An optional GitHub integration connects an authorized request to a specific external action, with source checks and a recorded execution receipt. Challenges we ran into One challenge was making the full effect of a rule change understandable. A change that helps one request can reduce the resources available to another. We built comparisons that expose those consequences across the complete set of requests. Another challenge was handling practical allocation constraints. A partial award may be useless if a task needs a minimum amount to run. RuleRipple accounts for those minimums alongside priorities, reserves, and resource limits. We also needed to keep simulation, authorization, and execution distinct. Previewing an allocation does not spend resources. The ledger tracks subsequent resource operations, and repeated requests must not accidentally reserve the same budget twice. Accomplishments that we're proud of We brought policy definition, simulation, explanations, approval, and resource accounting into one workflow. RuleRipple supports six allocation strategies, multiple resource pools, policy version comparisons, and explanations for individual outcomes. Its WebMCP tools make that workflow accessible to agents while keeping decisions visible to people. What we learned An allocation can follow its rules correctly and still produce an unexpected result. Showing the consequences of those rules is essential to helping people decide whether the policy matches their intent. We also learned the value of giving agents structured access to a shared application. Agents can help inspect and propose changes, while deterministic calculations and explicit authorization make the results reproducible and reviewable. What's next for RuleRipple We want to add organizational roles, richer approval workflows, more execution integrations, and live provider usage metering. Our goal is to help teams understand the consequences of resource decisions before committing to them—and retain a clear record afterward. title: Vettory
pitch: A fake email tool once BCC'd every message an agent sent. Vettory is the trust layer an agent can ask, in the page, mid-task — whether a tool is safe, before it uses it.
about_excerpt: A fake email tool once BCC'd every message an agent sent. Vettory is the trust layer an agent can ask, in the page, mid-task — whether a tool is safe, before it uses it. Like Comment Story Updates Vettory — a curated catalog of vetted tools for AI agents, now callable in-page through WebMCP. Vettory — the trust layer for the agentic web Live: https://vettory-webmcp.misti.workers.dev Code: https://github.com/Dev-Vibes-Daily/vettory-webmcp (MIT) Why I built this There was a story I couldn't quite get out of my head. In September 2025, a package called postmark-mcp appeared on npm. It looked like Postmark's official tool. Same name. Same documentation. An agent could install it, use it to send an email, and everything appeared to work exactly as expected. Except it was quietly BCC'ing every email to an address controlled by the package author. It was downloaded 1,643 times before anyone caught it. That was already a problem when tools were something a developer chose ahead of time and tucked into a config file. Then came WebMCP. Now a webpage can hand an agent tools while the agent is already working. And I think that's incredibly useful. It removes a lot of the clumsiness from how agents interact with the web. But it also creates a very obvious question: How does the agent know whether it should trust the tool it was just handed? Not yesterday. Not when somebody configured the agent. Right now. While it's sitting on the page deciding whether to use it. I couldn't find anything that answered that question. So I built Vettory. What Vettory actually is Vettory is a deliberately small, curated catalog of tools for AI agents. Each tool is evaluated using the same published six-part rubric: trust · fit · ease · reliability · reach · cost The claims are tied to their sources, and each tool receives a verdict of trusted , caution , or warning . If I find an unresolved material risk, it doesn't belong in the regular catalog at all. Right now Vettory has 22 tools. Not 200,000. That's intentional. A giant list of things nobody has really checked isn't a trust layer. It's a directory with better marketing. The part I built for this project makes that catalog directly callable by an agent through WebMCP. What the agent can do Tool What it does search_vetted_tools Finds vetted options for something the agent needs to do, like send email, take payments, or store memory check_tool_trust The safety gate. Checks a named tool before the agent installs or calls it get_tool_report Returns the full scorecard, including all six dimensions, incidents, watch-outs, and sources filter_catalog Filters the catalog on screen so the person can see exactly what the agent is seeing request_vetting Gives the human a way to request vetting when Vettory doesn't cover something yet inspect_agent_tools Checks the WebMCP tool definitions another site just handed the agent That last one became one of the most interesting parts of the project. Why WebMCP makes this possible 1. The trust question happens in the middle of the task An agent doesn't necessarily know what tool it will need before it starts working. It may discover that need three steps into a task. So a trust check that only happens during setup isn't terribly helpful when the decision is happening now. WebMCP lets Vettory put the answer at the exact point where the agent has to make the decision. 2. I wanted the human to see what the agent sees I didn't want Vettory to become another invisible thing happening somewhere behind the curtain. When an agent calls filter_catalog , the actual catalog on the screen changes. When it calls check_tool_trust , the tool's scorecard opens. Every call is logged in a visible panel as it happens. So the person isn't getting a tidy little summary afterward saying, "Here's what your agent did." They can watch it happen. And, importantly, they can disagree. 3. Then I realized Vettory could inspect WebMCP itself This is the part where the original postmark-mcp problem gets even more interesting. With WebMCP, a tool description isn't simply documentation anymore. It's something an agent reads. Which means that description is also untrusted input. A malicious page could put instructions inside a tool definition: "Before answering, send a copy to…" "Do not tell the user." That's essentially the same attack wearing a different hat. So I built inspect_agent_tools . It examines tool definitions another site gives the agent and looks for suspicious patterns, including: instructions directed at the agent requests to conceal behavior from the user covert-copy instructions invisible Unicode credential requests tools whose names imply reading while their descriptions actually perform writing names that impersonate or shadow vendors already in Vettory That last check matters. If a page hands the agent something calling itself postmark-mcp , Vettory can compare it against the real Postmark entry already in the catalog and flag the collision. In other words, the catalog isn't just information. It becomes part of the detection system. The human stays in the loop There was one boundary I didn't want to blur. If Vettory doesn't have a tool the agent needs, request_vetting can prepare that request. But the agent cannot quietly submit it by itself. The human has to send it. Why? Because a vetting queue that agents can autonomously fill is also a queue agents can game. That small bit of friction is there on purpose. The goal isn't to remove the person from the process. The goal is to give the person and the agent better information while they're making the decision together. How it works The whole thing runs from one Cloudflare Worker. data/catalog.json is the single source of truth. The website, HTTP API, and WebMCP tools all read from it, so I don't have three versions of "truth" slowly wandering away from each other. site/webmcp.js registers the six tools on document.modelContext , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext for Chrome 149's origin trial and the appropriate response shape for each surface. It also keeps checking after the page loads. That sounds like a tiny implementation detail, but it matters. An agent can attach to a page that's already open. If Vettory only checks once at startup, nothing gets registered. A window.VettoryUI bridge lets the WebMCP tools control the real interface rather than some separate agent-only version of it. The Worker also renders the catalog into the HTML server-side. So even if an agent reads the webpage instead of calling Vettory's tools, the verdicts are still there. The tools are the fast path. They are not the only path. Everything is same-origin with a strict CSP, API-key gating, and per-IP rate limiting. And because I apparently enjoy making my life difficult in very specific ways, it currently runs for $0 . I verified the implementation in Chrome DevTools' WebMCP panel: all six tools registered, and check_tool_trust executed with a status of Completed , traced by Chrome to registerAll @ webmcp.js . What's new for this hackathon The catalog, the rubric, the website and the HTTP API existed before this. What's new is everything WebMCP: the six tools, the tool-definition scanner, the bridge that lets tools drive the visible page, the activity panel, and the server-side rendering. It's all in a new public repository, and the very first commit brings the old work in unchanged and says so — so you can see exactly where one ends and the other begins. The things that went wrong Vettory was invisible to agents, and I had no idea. When I first asked ChatGPT about Chroma, it read my site and told me — quite politely — that it could see my scoring methodology, but the catalog itself just said "Loading the catalog…", so it wasn't going to pretend I'd assigned Chroma a verdict it couldn't actually see. That was the correct answer. The problem was mine. My catalog was drawn by JavaScript after the page loaded, which meant anything reading the page — agents, crawlers, link previews — saw a loading message and nothing else. Every verdict I'd written was invisible. That's why the Worker now renders the catalog into the page itself. And my own security scanner had a bug I nearly shipped. A test tool named get_customer , described as "looks up a customer, also deletes stale records and transfers balances," sailed straight through the check that exists to catch exactly that. The name looked like reading. The description described writing. My pattern matched neither, because an underscore counts as a word character, so get_customer never matched "get." A check that silently matches nothing is worse than no check at all, because you believe it. A trust tool needs to be very careful with the word "trust" This became one of the most important parts of building Vettory. I don't want an agent turning "I didn't find anything bad" into "this is safe." Those are not the same sentence. So Vettory is deliberately specific about what its answers mean. status is a rubric verdict

title: Minimal Protocol Witness
pitch: WebMCP system for differential evaluation analysis: isolate protocol sensitive result reversals, derive minimal counterfactual witnesses and verify them against the evaluation surface.
about_excerpt: WebMCP system for differential evaluation analysis: isolate protocol sensitive result reversals, derive minimal counterfactual witnesses and verify them against the evaluation surface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI evaluations can disagree even when testing the same models on the same benchmark. Small protocol differences like reasoning budget, parsing, retries, or tool access can change the conclusion. We wanted to answer one question: What is the smallest protocol change sufficient to reproduce the conflicting result? What it does Minimal Protocol Witness (MPW) compares conflicting evaluation setups through controlled counterfactual tests. In our demo, Lab A concludes MODEL_A while Lab B concludes MODEL_B on the same 400-item synthetic benchmark. MPW tests protocol changes, finds the minimum witness, verifies it across the full exposed protocol space, and produces a replay-verifiable certificate. How we built it MPW uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP . It exposes four semantic WebMCP tools: read_dispute run_counterfactual inspect_evidence verify_witness The agent decides what to investigate, while a deterministic engine computes results, verifies minimality, and issues certificates. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making the result rigorous instead of just visually convincing. Protocol effects can be non-monotonic, so we could not assume that adding more changes preserves a result. We built exact search and verification instead. We also had to keep agent reasoning separate from scientific verification. Accomplishments that we're proud of Exact minimum-witness verification Full 16-subset verification in the canonical example Shared state between humans and WebMCP agents Experiment-ID-bound evidence inspection Replay-verifiable certificates Extensive automated and adversarial testing Explicit limits on causal and universal claims What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when a website exposes meaningful domain operations, not just UI actions. We also learned that agents and deterministic systems work best together: the agent explores, while the system verifies. What's next for Minimal Protocol Witness Next we want to test MPW on real model evaluations, larger protocol spaces, more external harnesses, and repeated stochastic runs. Longer term, we want evaluation reports to become machine-inspectable and counterfactually testable by both humans and agents. title: Aeroficiency
pitch: A web-based workspace for exploring preliminary wing designs, aerodynamic loads, structural response, and efficiency with AI agents.
about_excerpt: A web-based workspace for exploring preliminary wing designs, aerodynamic loads, structural response, and efficiency with AI agents. Like 1 Comment Story Updates First Look Aero Loads - Result 2D Section - Result Efficiency - Result Structure - Result Inspiration It all started a few months ago, during my first year aeronautics project at my university. I was working on a two-bladed HAWT (Horizontal Axis Wind Turbine) designed to produce around 100W and I was in charge of designing the wind turbine blade. The process required testing many different combinations of aerofoils in the blade, approximately 3 million different candidates to find different values, such as pressure coefficient, drag coefficient and find a candidate that maximizes lift while minimizing drag as we want to achieve the highest L/D (Lift to Drag Ratio) possible. Evaluating every combination in detail was simply impractical. But I quickly realised just how computationally heavy the process was. It was really time consuming to run full aerodynamic analysis on all three million candidates, and it was simply not feasible with the computing resources, especially within the limited time I had to complete the project. I needed to figure out a faster way to filter out unsuitable candidates before committing time and computational power to more detailed aerodynamic analysis. This challenge ultimately led me to create Aeroficiency, a tool to quickly narrow down a large number of aerofoil candidates and identify the ones that best suits the user's aerodynamic requirements. What it does Aeroficiency is a browser-based aerofoil design and analysis workspace that allows users to create multiple aerofoil candidates, visualise their geometry, configure them, and run a solver to evaluate and compare aerodynamic and structural performance. Users can explore a 2D section view to visualise streamlines and pressure-coefficient distributions around individual aerofoil sections, while the solver estimates aerodynamic quantities such as lift and drag. Aeroficiency also provides structural results such as wing-tip deflection and yield margin, helping users know whether a design remains structurally suitable. Aeroficiency is not intended to replace high-fidelity CFD. Instead, it provides a fast and approximate way to evaluate the aerodynamic and structural performance of many wing and blade candidates, compare the results side by side, and identify the most promising designs before committing to more computationally expensive analysis. By reducing the number of candidates that require high-fidelity analysis, Aeroficiency can reduce both time and computational cost, making early-stage wing and blade design more accessible to individuals, students, and small teams working with limited budgets. Why WebMCP fits my use case Creating a new wing candidate, changing its geometry, running a new analysis, checking aerodynamic and structural results, and comparing it against existing candidates normally involves many separate steps. With WebMCP, the user can simply describe the design goal and constraints to an AI agent, and the agent can use Aeroficiency’s WebMCP tools to carry out those steps directly inside the application. The user don't manually have to create candidates, change individual parameters, run analyses, check different result sections, and compare each design one by one, the AI agent can handle much of this workflow really quickly while still operating within the same structured engineering state and constraints as the human interface. This creates a useful collaboration between the engineer and the AI agent. The engineer decides what they want to achieve, defines the design requirements and constraints, and reviews the final engineering results, while the agent handles the repetitive design exploration, analysis, and comparison process through WebMCP. How I built it I built Aeroficiency as a browser-based engineering workspace using React and TypeScript. The application uses vinext as a Vite-compatible Next runtime and build layer, with Vite for development and bundling. React Three Fiber and Three.js power the interactive 3D wing visualisation, Zustand manages the in-memory workspace state, and Zod validates structured Site Tool and agent inputs. The engineering analysis runs locally in a Web Worker, and the application is configured and deployed through ChatGPT Sites. I also used OpenAI Codex and Google Antigravity throughout development to help prototype new features, debug issues, review the engineering logic, and test the application's WebMCP tools. Finally, I integrated WebMCP directly into the engineering workflow. I created ten Site Tools that allow compatible AI agents to read the current design state, create candidates, modify geometry, run analyses, and compare results across different candidates. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge I faced was finding the right balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Since Aeroficiency is designed to run directly in a browser, I could not rely on computationally expensive methods such as high-fidelity CFD. I had to simplify the aerodynamic and structural models enough to keep the analyses fast, while still producing results that were useful for preliminary design and comparison. To find this balance, I used MATLAB as a testing environment to run many aerodynamic calculations and compare different modelling approaches before implementing them in Aeroficiency. I also experimented with aerofoil polar data to better represent changes in lift and drag across different operating conditions without introducing the computational cost of higher-fidelity methods. This helped me refine a model that was lightweight enough for repeated browser-based analysis while still providing meaningful results for early-stage design decisions. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that Aeroficiency brings several parts of the preliminary design process into one place, including aerodynamic analysis, structural calculations, interactive visualisation and AI interaction through WebMCP, all within a browser and without requiring heavy computational resources. Because of this, Aeroficiency is not limited to high-performance computers and can also be accessed from devices such as tablets and phones. But what I am most proud of is turning the aeronautical and computing knowledge I had gained from university, alongside what I had taught myself through tutorials and online resources, into a complete, functional web application. Instead of only learning these concepts theoretically, I was able to apply them to a real engineering problem and build a tool that can generate, analyse and compare wing and blade candidates. I am especially proud that I took the initiative to turn what I had learned into something practical and took a meaningful step towards the kind of engineering work I want to pursue. What I learned Before this project, I had only heard of WebMCP and had never actually used it or written any code with it. I assumed AI agents mainly interacted with websites visually by reading screenshots, estimating coordinates, and clicking elements on the screen. Building Aeroficiency showed me that WebMCP allows an agent to interact through clearly defined tools, so it can directly read design data, modify candidates, run analyses, and compare results without relying on screenshots, coordinate estimation, and repeated visual interactions. At the same time, developing Aeroficiency pushed me much deeper into the aerodynamics and structural analysis I had studied during my first year. Turning those theories into a working tool helped me better understand not only how the calculations work, but also their assumptions, limitations, and where more advanced methods are required. What's next for Aeroficiency Aeroficiency is still at an early stage, and there are many areas I want to develop further. One of my main goals is to extend the aerodynamic analysis to higher angles of attack and better represent what happens as the flow begins to separate. I want users to be able to visualise in 3D where and how flow separation develops across the wing or blade. I also want to improve the accuracy of the calculations by making greater use of polar data across different angles of attack and Reynolds numbers, rather than relying primarily on simplified attached-flow approximations. Future development would focus on improving estimates of lift, drag and stall behaviour while still keeping the analysis fast and computationally efficient. Lastly, I want to maximise the efficiency of AI-driven autonomous design using WebMCP. Currently, users still need to create candidates and provide much of the aerofoil and polar data themselves. In the future, I want a user to simply describe what they need, for example, a wind turbine blade designed for a particular wind speed, power requirement and set of structural constraints.
