title: The Agentic Textbook
pitch: Learn anything, with the help of your favorite agent
about_excerpt: Learn anything, with the help of your favorite agent Like 3 Comment Story Updates The Agentic Textbook The textbook that builds itself around you. Learn any concept, with the help of the agent that already knows you Agentic Textbook turns the AI agent you already use into a live teaching partner, creating the exact explanations, visuals, exercises, and learning paths you need inside a shared WebMCP canvas. Inspiration Most training around tech products/concepts are outdated before they even goe live. We see this constantly while onboarding customers onto frontier AI tools—especially Codex. New capabilities appear almost every day, while users still need a simple place to understand what changed, why it matters, and how to use it well. We needed a learning surface that could keep up. Not another static academy, but a place where every learner could generate the exact training they need, the moment they need it. What it does Agentic Textbook makes the textbook as dynamic as the technology it teaches. It also explores a bigger question: what should learning become when every learner has an AI agent? The system has two deliberately separate parts: The agent brings intelligence and context. It understands the learner’s goals, prior knowledge, interests, and current questions, and can generate explanations, diagrams, examples, code, or exercises on demand. The Agentic Textbook leverages coding agents capabilities to create new and exciting content. The textbook brings pedagogy and structure. It provides an open, editable canvas with lesson sequencing, remediation paths, learning-science-informed components, and clear learner controls. Think of it as the pedagogical authority, based on learning sciences, that harnesses the agent's infinite potential. This creates a BYOA model: Bring Your Own Agent. Learners keep the agent they already trust, while WebMCP turns the browser into a shared workspace where human and agent can build the lesson together. And adapt it on-demand to the learner's needs. Ask for another explanation. Add a formula. Generate a diagram. Create a code exercise. Slow down, go deeper, or approach the concept from another angle. The agent can update one focused part of the textbook without rebuilding the entire experience. How we built it We wanted to understand what WebMCP makes possible at its core. The key primitive is surprisingly powerful: the browser becomes a shared place where humans and agents can read, act, and create together. We wanted to apply this concept to something that was both important for us in our day-to-day, and could also change the broader picture of web based learning experiences. That insight shaped the entire product. The learner prepares a brief and reviews the context being used. The agent authors a structured lesson. The app validates and renders it. From there, the learner and agent can keep refining individual regions of the canvas together. Once the interaction model clicked, Codex helped us turn it into a working product through tight iteration. Under the hood, topic-neutral lesson schemas can combine prose, formulas, diagrams, governed media, exercises, and executable code labs, without hard-coding a course for each new subject. Challenges we ran into The hardest part wasn’t implementation. It was making the idea legible to a coding agent. First, we had to understand what WebMCP really changes compared with standard MCP, and how it relates to inline MCP apps inside products such as ChatGPT. Then we had to steer Codex away from familiar patterns. Coding agents are excellent inside known territory. Asking them to help invent a genuinely new interaction model is much harder. We had to make the underlying idea extremely precise before the implementation became coherent. If you let a coding agent loose on an innovative concept, it tends to bring it back to known patterns, which destroy the originality of the idea. Personalization introduced another tension: context is valuable, but privacy is non-negotiable. Codex was rightly cautious about exposing sensitive information. We designed a consent-scoped, local-first context lane where learners review minimized signals before they enter a lesson. That became our biggest lesson: implementation is getting easier; steering agents toward reliable novelty is not. The main bottleneck today is speed. At Cerebras-class inference speeds, the delay between asking for a change and watching the textbook transform could almost disappear. That’s when the experience becomes magical. Accomplishments that we’re proud of A small set of primitives created a surprisingly large design space. We’re proud that the product feels simple despite what is happening underneath: structured lesson generation, contextual adaptation, interactive exercises, targeted revisions, and learner-controlled publishing. We’re especially proud of the UI and interaction model. The agent can do powerful work, but the learner always has a clear, understandable surface in front of them. Our favorite technical detail is the JSON Render integration. Codex can author structured components while the textbook progressively renders them on the canvas. Pushed further, this could become one of the product’s defining capabilities. What we learned WebMCP isn’t simply MCP inside a browser. It’s a new interaction model. The browser is no longer just the destination where an agent’s output appears. It becomes a shared, live workspace where humans and agents can think, create, inspect, and revise together. We also learned how powerful a clear division of labor can be: the agent brings context and generative ability; the application brings pedagogical constraints, trust boundaries, and learner control. What’s next for Agentic Textbook AI education now has a shelf life measured in days. On September 2, while finishing this project, we discovered OpenAI’s new ChatGPT Training hub , with practical learning paths for ChatGPT Work and Codex. The timing felt almost comically perfect. For teams like ours, keeping clients current with products such as Codex is already a daily challenge. We need a way to create tailor-made training capsules as quickly as the product itself evolves. Next, we’re pushing in two directions. For businesses, we want organizations to bring their own curricula, terminology, policies, and role-specific knowledge into the same consent-scoped learning experience. For learners, we want to make the agent-to-canvas loop dramatically faster. The long-term goal is simple: learning experiences that move as fast as the technology they teach. title: Corotum
pitch: Corotum helps you keep AI agent skills consistent across every machine and AI agent. Instead of copying and fixing drift, you manage one desired state and sync it safely through Git or Corotum Cloud.
about_excerpt: Corotum helps you keep AI agent skills consistent across every machine and AI agent. Instead of copying and fixing drift, you manage one desired state and sync it safely through Git or Corotum Cloud. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I use multiple AI agents on different machines, and I kept running into the same problem: their skills were never quite the same. A skill would be installed on my Mac but missing on a VPS. Another would be outdated somewhere else. Sometimes I had changed a skill locally and forgot about it. The usual solution was copying folders around and trying to remember which version was the right one. That became the starting point for Corotum. I wanted one place to define which skills I use, which versions should be installed, and which agents should get them. I also wanted to see how far I could take the idea during a 7-day build challenge for the WebMCP Challenge. What it does Corotum manages and synchronizes AI agent skills across machines and agents. It keeps a desired state and compares it with what is actually installed on a machine. From that comparison it works out what needs to change, applies it, and verifies the result. There are two sync modes. Git Sync uses your own Git repository and does not require a Corotum account. Corotum Cloud hosts the desired state and adds a dashboard, devices, revisions, sync status, and WebMCP. The CLI can add, remove, adopt, update, restore, and target skills to specific agents. Versions are locked to exact Git revisions, so running sync does not unexpectedly update a skill to whatever happens to be latest. Corotum also treats local changes carefully. If a managed skill was modified by hand, it is marked as drifted instead of being overwritten. Skills that Corotum does not manage are not deleted during normal synchronization. How I built it Corotum is a TypeScript monorepo using Bun workspaces. The CLI runs on Bun and is compiled into standalone binaries. The web app uses Next.js with vinext on Cloudflare Workers, with D1 for the hosted state. The main sync flow is: Desired State + Actual State → Diff → Reconcile Plan → Apply → Verify Git Sync and Corotum Cloud use the same synchronization model. The dashboard, API, and WebMCP also use the same application services instead of having separate implementations of the same operations. For private repositories, Corotum uses Git credentials already configured on the user's machine. Those credentials are never sent to or stored by Corotum Cloud. Challenges Most of the work was not actually copying files. It was deciding exactly what every operation should mean when several machines can be in different states. For example, remove and unmanage both remove a skill from the desired state, but they cannot behave the same way. remove should eventually delete the managed copy from every device. unmanage should stop managing it but leave the local files in place. Drift was another case that needed explicit rules. If somebody edits a managed skill locally, a normal sync should not silently destroy those changes. Offline devices made this harder. A machine might reconnect several revisions later, so looking only at the newest snapshot is not always enough to understand what should happen locally. Private repositories had a similar constraint. The Cloud can coordinate the desired state, but it cannot assume that it has access to the repository. Resolution sometimes has to happen on a device that already has Git access. What I learned The project started as a fairly simple "sync skills between computers" idea. Most of the complexity turned out to be around ownership and state. Once I separated the shared desired state from the actual state of each device, a lot of the behavior became easier to define. Locking skills to exact Git revisions was another important decision. It keeps sync and update as two separate operations: sync reproduces the selected state, while update intentionally changes it. What's next The first version is deliberately limited to AI agent skills. The same model could later be used for other parts of an agent setup, such as MCP servers, prompts, rules, profiles, agent configuration, and team policies. title: Verified Giving Protocol | Agent-readable Donate pages
pitch: A standard JSON for donate pages built for agents. The problem: A nonprofit's donate button is JavaScript and a hero image. PayPal Giving Fund has an API and will route agents to their pipes.
about_excerpt: A standard JSON for donate pages built for agents. The problem: A nonprofit's donate button is JavaScript and a hero image. PayPal Giving Fund has an API and will route agents to their pipes. Like 1 Comment Story Updates donate page of powerpoetry.org with info about webmcp Generate a file based on standards verify a page Inspiration A nonprofit should decide where its own donations go. This is going to matter as AI Agents begin to take over web actions like donating. Tell an AI agent "donate $50 to this nonprofit" and it routes to whatever it can parse. That is structurally almost never the nonprofit's own donation page. It's an aggregator, an outdated page, or a third-party fundraising page set up on the organization's behalf without its knowledge. Those pathways can hold funds for weeks before disbursing — some intermediaries take up to 90 days — introducing float, intermediary risk, and a donor record the nonprofit never sees. The organization gets the money once and loses the relationship. Two trends are making this worse at the same time: Agents are being locked out. Cloudflare challenges, bot rules, and hardened forms mean the legitimate path is often the hardest one for an agent to complete — so it takes the easy path, which is somebody else's page. Donation forms are unreadable by design. Most are cross-origin iframes. An agent looking at a real nonprofit donate page cannot see the amount, the frequency, or who receives the money. It's a black box, so it guesses. The result is an agent doing the reasonable thing with bad information. We wanted the nonprofit to be able to state, in a way a machine can act on, this is where our money may go — and have that statement come from the one domain nobody else controls. What it does The Verified Giving Protocol lets a nonprofit publish a machine-readable declaration at https://their-domain.org/giving.json naming the giving destinations it authorizes — and exposes that to AI agents as WebMCP tools. The protocol turns on one distinction: Statement Who makes it Authorizes? benefits — "proceeds go to Organization X" anyone no confirmed — "evidence consistently identifies this destination" a discovery process no authorized — "we declare this an approved destination" the organization yes No amount of evidence converts confirmed into authorized . A human at the nonprofit types a fixed affirmation verbatim , and that's the only route in. It's enforced as a const in the JSON Schema, in the Python approval script, and in the WebMCP tools — not as a UI check. A paraphrase is refused. The nonprofit's own page then registers four WebMCP tools built entirely from that declaration: giving_verify , giving_options , giving_designations , and giving_prepare . An agent asks instead of scrapes. The reference implementation is live. Power Poetry ( https://www.powerpoetry.org/donate ) publishes a declaration naming To Be Heard Foundation Inc, EIN 13-3648963, verified against the IRS Business Master File. An agent starting from the donate page alone can determine who legally receives the money, that the organization authorized it, and construct a working prefilled donation URL. How we built it The standard — a specification, a JSON Schema, and a stdlib-only Python validator and approval script. No dependencies, so a nonprofit can run the tooling without a toolchain. The WebMCP layer — giving-tools.js , generated from a reviewed template by generate_webmcp.py and byte-compared against a fresh generation in CI. The tools cannot drift from the template, and hand-editing them to say something the declaration doesn't is caught by the test suite. The site — verifiedgiving.ai, an Astro build with an in-browser generator and a live validator. The site pins the standard as a git submodule and renders the specification and publishes the JSON Schema from it at build time, so no copy can drift from the source. The discovery agent — vgpify , a Claude skill that crawls a nonprofit's site, extracts organization identity and giving pathways, flags conflicts, and produces an evidence-backed review document. It proposes ; it cannot publish. 54 tests , and most of them assert refusals rather than successes. Challenges we ran into There is no payment API to route to. We assumed one existed. Givebutter — the processor behind our reference implementation — publishes 42 API endpoints and none of them creates a checkout session, payment intent, charge, or token . POST /v1/transactions requires a past timestamp and has no payment-instrument field: it records a gift that already happened. The capability exists one layer down (Givebutter settles through Stripe), but no nonprofit-facing platform exposes it. We're now in conversation with people interested in changing that, and published an open request ( https://verifiedgiving.ai/providers ) describing exactly what we'd need and — importantly — what we would not ask a processor to take on. Publishing is not discovery. We deployed a correct declaration, at the correct path, with the correct media type, plus the link relation and the WebMCP script — then pointed ChatGPT at the page. It found almost nothing. Every discovery mechanism we'd built required the world to have already adopted VGP: nobody probes /giving.json , nothing parses rel="giving" , and ChatGPT's browser provides no document.modelContext so the tools never register. That five-minute test reshaped the project. The cold start. VGP has one adopter and zero consumers . A standard nobody consumes is invisible, and a nonprofit that does everything right and sees no effect concludes the standard doesn't work. That's the likeliest way this dies, and we'd rather say so than imply an ecosystem that doesn't exist. Platform documentation isn't platform behaviour. Givebutter documents frequency=quarterly ; it's not enabled on our campaign and is silently ignored. once works and is undocumented. Amounts over 999 are silently dropped from prefill. Every one of those was found by testing the live widget, and each would have failed in the worst place — a donor believing they'd set up a monthly gift that wasn't. Accomplishments that we're proud of The tools fail closed, and it's provable. If a declaration is missing, unapproved, or wrongly served, the page registers no giving tools at all . An agent is told "this site exposes no authorized giving pathway" rather than handed a plausible form. Flip one boolean and watch it happen: node --test webmcp/harness.test.mjs . Authorization cannot be faked, and you can check in ten seconds. In the live generator, type a paraphrase of the affirmation — authorized_destinations stays empty. Type it exactly — the destination is authorized. A live reference implementation , end-to-end verified: an agent derives the receiving legal entity, its EIN, the authorization record, and a prefilled donation URL that drives the real payment widget to the right state. giving_prepare never charges. It returns payment_completed: false and requires_human_payment_authorization: true . VGP routes; the donor authorizes; the nonprofit's existing processor charges. We shipped the honest version. The site states its own adoption position rather than implying consumers exist. What we learned Absence of a tool is safer than presence of an ambiguous one. The most valuable thing our WebMCP integration does is decline to appear. Infrastructure ahead of its consumers is invisible, not broken — and the escape is to speak a vocabulary that already has consumers while the new one accumulates them. We added schema.org ( legalName , taxID , nonprofitStatus , DonateAction with an EntryPoint.urlTemplate ) and a plain visible link to the declaration. That turned "a couple more details" into an agent that could name the receiving entity and build a working donation URL — with no change to the underlying declaration. Rank discovery mechanisms by how little the world must change: a visible link needs nothing; schema.org needs a vocabulary that already has consumers; llms.txt needs a spreading convention; your own new mechanism needs adoption. Ship them in that order. The declaration belongs at the document root, not /.well-known/ . /.well-known/ is for protocol metadata; the root is for owner policy — robots.txt , sitemap.xml , ads.txt . VGP is the second kind, and ads.txt is the near-exact analogue: a domain owner naming who may act on their behalf, published to defeat unauthorized intermediaries. The test is what absence means. Declare, never infer. Every platform parameter is declared by the organization with an explicit vocabulary and bounds. A guessed parameter fails silently where it costs most. What's next for Verified Giving Protocol A payment endpoint worth declaring. We've specified what we'd need from processors: a checkout session an agent can create, a required idempotency key (agents retry, and a dropped response on a donation charges someone twice), published amount and currency rules, status and receipt — and explicitly

title: Agent Process
pitch: Agent Process lets teams turn repeatable browser tasks into reusable workflows that run directly in Chrome. It exposes them as WebMCP tools so assistants like ChatGPT can trigger them on the page.
about_excerpt: Agent Process lets teams turn repeatable browser tasks into reusable workflows that run directly in Chrome. It exposes them as WebMCP tools so assistants like ChatGPT can trigger them on the page. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Running List of processes - Tools History of execution No-code Recording using Inline Manual Builder No-code Recording using Inline Manual Builder Inspiration AI assistants are getting better at using websites, but they still often have to figure out the interface from scratch every time. We wanted to make it easy for anyone to teach their AI assistant a repeatable process on top of any website, regardless of whether that website has MCP or WebMCP implemented. Even when a website already exposes MCP functions, users are still limited to the tools and workflows the developer decided to provide. We wanted users to be able to create their own personalized workflows around the way they actually work. Instead of asking an agent to understand the whole UI and decide what to click every time, a user can record a process once and reuse it. This can be useful for repetitive internal workflows, sharing processes between colleagues, making execution more predictable, reducing token usage, and making tasks faster and easier to debug with an execution log. We also wanted the creation side to be completely no-code. We reused the Inline Manual Builder so a user can simply record what they are doing in the browser and turn that workflow into an Agent Process. What it does Agent Process is a browser extension that lets users turn repeatable workflows on almost any website into WebMCP tools that AI assistants can use. A process can be created in two ways: by importing a JSON definition with the individual steps, or by recording the workflow using the Inline Manual Builder. The user can also define inputs that the AI assistant should provide when the process is executed. For example, you can create processes such as: Create a lead Add a customer Create a ToDo Publish an article Update a record in a CRM The Agent Process extension then exposes these processes as WebMCP tools directly in the browser. When an AI assistant calls one of these tools, Agent Process executes the predefined browser interactions instead of requiring the AI to inspect the interface and figure out every step again. Processes can include parameters, for example values that should be entered into forms, so the same process can be reused with different data every time it runs. This effectively lets users create their own personalized WebMCP tools on top of existing websites. The website itself does not need to implement WebMCP, expose an API, or be modified in any way. How we built it We built Agent Process as a browser extension that combines WebMCP with our existing Inline Manual process-recording technology. The Inline Manual Builder acts as the no-code recorder and editor. It captures the individual steps of a workflow, the elements being interacted with, and the parameters that can be provided when the process is executed. These processes are exported as JSON and imported into the Agent Process extension. The extension registers them as WebMCP tools, executes the predefined browser interactions when a tool is called, and records the result in an execution history log. We used Codex extensively to build the browser extension, with supervision, testing, and product decisions from our team. Our previous experience building browser-based product guidance with Inline Manual helped us move quickly, especially around reliable element targeting, working with dynamic web applications, handling overlays and different browser behaviors, and executing interactions on third-party websites. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was discovering that the ChatGPT browser extension does not currently automatically discover or use WebMCP tools in the way we initially expected. To make the integration work reliably, we currently need to add custom instructions telling ChatGPT to look for and use the available WebMCP tools. That made testing the complete experience slightly different from our original assumption, but it also gave us a much better understanding of how WebMCP discovery currently works in practice and where some of the limitations are for browser-based AI assistants. Our use of MCP is also slightly different from the typical implementation. We are not adding tools to an application we own; we are adding them on top of any existing website. While exploring the architecture, we even built our own MCP server before realizing that a traditional MCP server was not the right fit for what we wanted to achieve. WebMCP running directly in the browser turned out to be the key piece. Without browser-level WebMCP support, exposing personalized tools on top of arbitrary websites in this way would be much more difficult. On the Agent Process side, development went relatively smoothly thanks to our previous experience building Inline Manual and working with browser applications. Browser automation itself still comes with the usual challenges: every website behaves differently, with dynamic interfaces, overlays, delayed elements, and different frontend frameworks. Those are challenges we already know well from Inline Manual, though, and are separate from the WebMCP API itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that we managed to make WebMCP useful on top of websites that were never designed for it. A user can take an existing website, record a process without writing code, turn that process into a reusable WebMCP tool, and let an AI assistant execute it with parameters. We are also proud that the process remains fully under the user’s control. Instead of being limited to whatever MCP tools an application developer decides to expose, users can create workflows that match the way they actually work. Another accomplishment is that we were able to reuse our existing Inline Manual recording technology in a completely new way. Something originally built for creating product guidance can now also be used to teach AI assistants how to perform tasks. The early feedback has been especially encouraging. People immediately understand the idea of recording a process once and then letting an AI assistant reuse it, which makes us think there is something genuinely useful here beyond the hackathon. What we learned We learned a lot about how WebMCP works in practice, how tools are exposed inside the browser, and how AI assistants currently discover and use them. We also learned that our use case sits somewhere between traditional MCP and browser automation. We are not exposing backend capabilities from an application we own. Instead, we are giving the user a way to define their own tools on top of an existing interface. One of the most important things we learned is that AI does not always need to figure out how to complete a task from scratch. If the user already knows the exact process, it can be more efficient to record that process once and let the AI decide when to use it and what parameters to provide. In our testing, this approach can make execution faster, transparent and more predictable, reduce the amount of page analysis the AI needs to do, and potentially save tokens. It also gives us better control over what actually happens in the browser and provides a clear execution log when something succeeds or fails. That changed how we think about browser agents. Full autonomy is useful when the path is unknown, but for repetitive and well-understood tasks, a reusable process can often be the better tool. What's next for Agent Process The current version supports a limited set of browser interactions, so one of our next priorities is expanding the types of actions that can be recorded and executed reliably across different websites. We also want to make the recording experience much smoother. The goal is that a non-technical user can simply open the Inline Manual Builder, perform a task once, and end up with a reusable Agent Process without needing to understand selectors, JSON, or WebMCP. Sharing is another big part of what we want to build next. Today, processes are exported and imported manually. We would like to create a backend where teams can maintain a shared library of processes and make them automatically available to colleagues and their AI assistants. From there, we can see Agent Process becoming a form of team process memory: a shared collection of repeatable workflows that captures how a team actually works, not just what individual applications expose. We would also like to explore a public process library or marketplace, where people can publish and reuse processes for common applications instead of recording everything themselves. Another direction is composable processes. A larger workflow could be built from several smaller Agent Processes, allowing users to combine existing actions into more complex workflows. title: CalmKitchen Designer
pitch: Validate your commercial kitchen design by pressure testing the dinner traffic or walking the setup in 3D. Find gaps before you build and let AI explore competitive alternatives.
about_excerpt: Validate your commercial kitchen design by pressure testing the dinner traffic or walking the setup in 3D. Find gaps before you build and let AI explore competitive alternatives. Like Comment Story Updates Configuration Comparions Service Simulation Space Designer Walk Kitchen / First Person View Landing Page w/ instructions for agentic use Equipment Fit-out Split View (Realtime Rendering) Inspiration My partner and I build hotels and also write the software to operate them. We're currently building a new hotel and debating how we should order the kitchen equipment for maximum efficiency. We typically use cutouts of the equipment and just move it around the architectural drawing during the brainstorming session. One of my favorite scenes from the movie 'The Founder' (about McDonald's) was when they drew out the industrial kitchen on a basketball court to help figure out opportunities for efficiencies (" Speedee Service System "). What if we didn't have to do it manually and could actually get better results by running more advanced simulations in parallel? What if the effort to get the results of such a simulation were minimal, due to AI agents already having the context and details to help carry out the busy work with minimal supervision? What it does Design your floor plan, fit out your equipment and then simulate peak traffic. It provides a flat view of the plan, a 3D view and a Split view to make changes in your plan while seeing the effect in realtime. I also added a 'Walk Kitchen' option to get a first person / third person view of walking around the kitchen. This feature has been remarkably popular with my friends, as it gives so much more context about the space than a floor plan or other hand drawn drawing. There are options to auto-fix issues (equipment not having enough clearance, etc.) at all of the stages. In the simulation, it is possible for the agent to tweak the parameters for better reflection of the actual dishes used in service. The sim mode also provides a service scorecard and the option to compare the performance of different layouts. Since this is a tool we're leaving open for restauranteurs/hoteliers, it requires no login and allows users to save their layout with changes locally. How we built it We used our actual floor plans to help drive the requirements. Since my partner is not an engineer, she prefers to use ChatGPT's in-built browser with WebMCP to implement the changes / drive the results with minimal manual work. The base product had revisions built into it. We went from 2D -> 3D -> Simulations. The project was done in a little over 2 days. Challenges we ran into Spatial conflicts, in term of clearance for opening freezers, etc. and adding validation in both the 2D and 3D spaces. WebMCP within ChatGPT was also interesting in the sense that it did not check for availability and had to be explicitly informed about it. Accomplishments that we're proud of 'Walk Kitchen' option. It's basically the same as playing Doom with a spatula. Building a restaurant is hard - let us have a bit of fun :-) What we learned Small changes go a long way, when we impose additional modifiers such as staff calling in sick, etc. What's next for CalmKitchen Designer Our core product is HotelOS.ai, with CalmKitchen running as the operating layer for restaurants that are on-prem. We'll continue improving CalmKitchen Designer so that hoteliers and restauranteurs can hopefully save a few of their nine lives before they step into the arena. title: XACT FOUNDRY
pitch: Xact Foundry turns natural-language intent into governed, deterministic agent capabilities—where ChatGPT understands, Xact decides, and consequences stay under explicit control.
about_excerpt: Xact Foundry turns natural-language intent into governed, deterministic agent capabilities—where ChatGPT understands, Xact decides, and consequences stay under explicit control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Xact Foundry: Open-Ended Understanding. Governed Execution. Inspiration Most enterprise tools have to be anticipated and built in advance. Xact Foundry asks a different question: What if a worker could describe the WebMCP Tool they need, and the system could safely build it on the spot? A worker can simply say: "Show urgent work orders that have no available qualified owner, ordered by due time." ChatGPT acts as the conversational Boss . It interprets the request and can propose a structured capability. But understanding is not authority. Deterministic X-Nodes decide whether that proposal qualifies to become a governed WebMCP Tool. The Boss can clarify and reason, but it cannot override Xact . The Boss determines what you mean. Xact determines what may become real. What We Built Xact Foundry turns ordinary human intent into governed WebMCP Tools. Instead of requiring thousands of prewritten natural-language intent patterns, Xact works from a governed business vocabulary : customers, support cases, work orders, owner availability, due time, escalation eligibility, credit history, evidence freshness, permitted operations, roles, confirmation requirements, and authority boundaries. The architecture is: Stable governance primitives ↓ Reusable governed business vocabulary ↓ WebMCP Tool compositions A request can resolve to five outcomes: ALREADY_GOVERNED --- Xact already knows the composition. COMPOSABLE --- the exact tool is new, but every required component is governed. NEEDS_RESOLUTION --- a genuine semantic question remains, so the Boss asks for clarification. NOVEL_BOUNDARY --- Xact understands the request, but the governed vocabulary does not yet support part of it. UNAUTHORIZED --- the request is understood, but the required authority does not exist. The Boss proposes structure. Xact has the final say. Why WebMCP WebMCP gives websites a structured way to expose capabilities directly to agents. Xact Foundry explores what happens when those WebMCP Tools do not all have to be manually anticipated and built ahead of time. A worker describes what they need. ChatGPT interprets it. Xact determines whether it can be constructed from governed business concepts. If it qualifies, Xact builds the governed WebMCP Tool. If it does not, Xact fails closed. And building a tool is not permission to use it consequentially. Permission to construct a tool is not permission to execute it. A consequential runtime action still requires fresh Xact authority and an explicit Commit. In short: WebMCP provides capability. Xact provides authority. The Hard Part: Evidence Is Not Authority The hardest part was not making successful requests work. It was making ambiguous and unsafe requests fail truthfully. During testing we found cases where: "escalated" could be mistaken for an instruction to escalate; "owner unavailable" could be mistaken for a reassignment request; "service credit" in an evidence view could be mistaken for a credit mutation; and historical or possible actions could be mistaken for requested actions. We turned those failures into regression tests and reusable governed business concepts. That led to a core invariant: A consequence mentioned as history, eligibility, evidence, policy evaluation, hypothetical outcome, or a possible next action never implies intent or authority to perform that consequence. Or more simply: Evidence about a consequence is not authority to cause that consequence. Governed Self-Service for the Enterprise The larger vision is employee self-service without uncontrolled agent authority. Instead of IT trying to anticipate every report, workflow, and agent tool employees may need, a company can govern its business vocabulary, data boundaries, roles, operations, and authority rules. Workers then describe the combinations they need in ordinary language. Some requests resolve immediately. Some can be safely composed. Some need clarification. Some require new governance. Others are understood perfectly and still refused. Give workers freedom to ask for what they need without giving agents freedom to do whatever they want. In a production deployment with authenticated identity and durable audit storage, the architecture can preserve evidence of who requested a capability, what was built, who invoked it, what was authorized, what was committed, and whether the consequence was verified. How We Built It Xact Foundry uses TypeScript, React, Model Context Protocol, an OpenAI Apps SDK-compatible MCP surface, and a public Sites deployment . The demo uses fictional, public-safe business data rather than claiming a production CRM or ticketing integration. To make the workflow easy to explore, we also created a set of pre-made example requests that users can run directly. These are not canned responses or separate demo paths. They are realistic business requests designed to exercise the same Foundry pipeline a user's own request would use. The examples let a first-time user quickly experience different behaviors: an already-governed tool, a newly composable tool, a read-only evidence view, a request requiring clarification, and a request Xact must refuse. After seeing the workflow, users can simply write their own request in ordinary language. The control flow is the same for both the example requests and custom requests: Human intent ↓ ChatGPT / Boss ↓ Structured proposal ↓ Xact resolution ↓ Clarify or compose ↓ Validate ↓ Authorize construction ↓ Commit ↓ Build WebMCP Tool ↓ Observe and verify ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## What We Learned The biggest lesson was that open-ended understanding does **not** require open-ended authority. We also learned that reusable governed business vocabulary scales better than thousands of prompt-specific rules. When a novel composition is validated, governed, and activated, future requests for that composition can take the deterministic **ALREADY_GOVERNED** path. That creates a governed learning loop: > **Reasoning discovers. Governance approves. Xact absorbs.** Reasoning can reduce the future need for reasoning without giving the reasoning model authority to expand its own permissions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The Proof Already-governed capabilities can resolve and construct with **zero LLM inference tokens**. In a browser benchmark, **10,011 deterministic construction operations** were exercised with parallel execution reaching approximately **6.1× speedup** while preserving a **bit-identical checksum**. Parallelism changed speed, not the result. Separately, the reference Xact implementation measured approximately **9 microseconds mean decision latency** on a single CPU. That is a reference measurement, not a claim about the live browser demo. The important idea is not simply that deterministic execution can be fast: > **The language model does not need to sit in the middle of work that > has already become exact.** ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The Vision Xact Foundry changes the enterprise tool model from: > **Build every tool someone might need.** to: > **Govern what may be built, then let workers describe what they > need.** **ChatGPT provides open-ended understanding. WebMCP provides structured capability. Xact determines what qualifies to be built and what is authorized to become consequential.** ## Built Around Your Business No two businesses operate exactly alike. Their data models, workflows, roles, policies, terminology, and backend systems are different. That is where the combination of **Xact Foundry and WebMCP becomes especially powerful**. Instead of forcing every company into a predefined set of tools, an organization can give Xact a governed description of its business: the resources that exist, what they mean, the approved connection points, who may access them, and what actions are permitted. WebMCP provides the structured connection to those capabilities. Xact provides the governed construction and authority layer around them. Once that foundation exists, workers do not need developers to anticipate every useful combination in advance. They can describe what they need in ordinary language, and Xact can determine whether that capability can be safely constructed from the company's own governed business vocabulary. > **Your business defines the vocabulary. WebMCP connects the capabilities. > Xact governs what may be built and what may become consequential.** The result is not one generic toolset for every company. It is a Foundry that can adapt to the shape of each business without relaxing the boundaries that business has established. > **Reason when necessary. Execute Xactly.** Built With cloudflare-d1 cloudflare-sites cloudflare-worke

title: Signoff - the agent proposes, you decide
pitch: A refund-approval queue where the agent proposes decisions with written reasons - and the tool that applies one doesn't exist until a human approves it.
about_excerpt: A refund-approval queue where the agent proposes decisions with written reasons - and the tool that applies one doesn't exist until a human approves it. Like Comment Story Updates The refund queue: risk signals and proposals Tool console: get_policy called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: the apply_proposal tool doesn't exist in the registry until a human approves the agent's proposal - enforcement lives in tool existence , not a runtime permission check. Inspiration Working a refund queue is judgment sandwiched between drudgery: read the ticket, weigh the amount against the risk, write a defensible reason, repeat forty times. The judgment is the human's job. The reading, weighing, and drafting shouldn't be. What it does The agent reads a written refund policy and every request's evidence, proposes approve / deny / partial decisions with a written reason each, and stages them as cards next to the requests they concern. Nothing applies until a human clicks Approve - and apply_proposal , the tool that actually applies a decision, is registered only while at least one approved-but-unapplied proposal exists. Approve nothing, and the tool to apply anything simply isn't in the agent's list. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript, no framework. Every tool and every UI button call the same mutation through one invoke() chokepoint that also writes the shared activity log. apply_proposal dynamically registers/unregisters via an AbortController tied to whether a pending approved proposal exists - a permission boundary expressed as which tools exist, not as an instruction a model could ignore. Challenges we ran into Two rounds of adversarial testing against real Chrome (not headless mocks) found two distinct bugs in that dynamic-registration path: first, a self-abort race where the tool's own disarm logic cancelled the very call it was running under; then, after fixing that with a deferred abort, a second race where a fast Approve → Revoke → re-Approve cycle could silently desync the tool from Chrome's real registry - no error, but the tool had actually vanished. Root-caused via page.mouse.click() (real coordinate clicks reproduced it 12/15 times; Playwright's polling clicks never did), then fixed by tracking and synchronously draining any stale pending abort before re-arming. Accomplishments that we're proud of An approval boundary enforced by the browser's own tool registry, not by prompt instructions - and proven against the actual WebMCP bridge under adversarial, rapid-clicking conditions, not just the happy path. What we learned "It passed headless Playwright" and "it's correct against real Chrome" are different claims. The riskiest bugs in a dynamic-tool-registration pattern only show up under real, synchronous, same-tick timing. What's next A written audit trail export per decision, and richer risk-signal explanations sourced from order history across the whole account, not just the single request. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools). title: Presence
pitch: The trust layer for live human-agent software.
about_excerpt: The trust layer for live human-agent software. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent requests a seat Human and agent share live state The boundary is real Work stays provisional You decide what becomes real Every session leaves a receipt Give agents a seat. Not the keys. Browser agents can now understand and act inside live software. But there is a problem: once an agent enters a shared workspace, what is it actually allowed to touch? Presence is a trust layer for live human agent collaboration. Instead of giving an agent the same authority as the human, Presence gives it an explicit seat with bounded capabilities. Humans and agents can work in the same live state without silently sharing control. The idea Presence reduces agent collaboration to four primitives: Seat Where an agent may be present. Scope What the agent may do. Revision The state the agent observed before acting. Receipt What actually happened during the session. Together they create a simple rule: Presence does not trust an agent to respect a boundary. The application enforces the boundary. The demo The demo uses one responsive project with three live surfaces: Desktop is the reference. Tablet is the agent's seat. Mobile belongs to the human. A browser agent discovers Presence through WebMCP and asks to join as a responsive collaborator. The human can inspect the requested capabilities before admitting it. Once admitted, the agent can inspect the project and propose work for Tablet while the human continues editing Mobile. Then comes the important part. The agent attempts to modify Mobile. Presence rejects the operation because Mobile is outside its granted scope. The same agent can successfully propose a Tablet change because Tablet belongs to its seat. Its work remains provisional: even the agent itself cannot publish it. Only a human acceptance can make the proposal canonical. Presence also tracks the revision an agent observed. If the human changes the project while the agent is acting on older state, the stale operation is rejected before it can mutate canonical state . The human's newer work remains untouched. Every significant action is recorded in a structured audit trail. Accepted proposals produce a verification receipt containing the agent identity, granted scope, revisions, operations, protected surfaces, and before/after state fingerprints. Finally, the human can revoke the seat. The agent loses its authority while accepted work remains part of the project. Why WebMCP WebMCP makes the website itself an agent interface. Presence exposes semantic operations for discovering the workspace, inspecting available roles and constraints, requesting admission, inspecting project state, proposing scoped changes, reviewing state, and releasing a role. The agent does not need DOM coordinates or a scripted sequence of clicks. It can reason about the application's actual concepts while Presence remains responsible for authorization and state integrity. How I built it Presence is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, and WebMCP. The UI and WebMCP tools operate on the same domain model. Mutations pass through the Presence domain layer, where admission, scope, ownership, and revision rules are enforced before canonical state can change. Agent proposals are provisional by default. Agents cannot publish their own work. Humans retain final authority. Presence also records structured audit events, computes deterministic state fingerprints, and generates verification receipts after accepted proposals so the collaboration can be inspected and verified after the fact. Challenges The hardest part was not exposing tools to an agent. It was deciding what should happen after an agent discovers those tools. A useful agent needs enough authority to accomplish real work, but giving it unrestricted access destroys the distinction between assistance and control. That led to the central design principle behind Presence: Authority should be explicit, scoped, temporary, and visible. Another challenge was concurrency. If an agent begins working from one revision while a human continues editing, the system cannot simply trust that the agent's eventual change is still safe. Presence revalidates the expected revision at mutation time and blocks stale operations before they reach canonical state. Presence explores what software could look like when agents are not merely chatbots beside an application, but participants inside it with boundaries the application can actually enforce. What's next The responsive workspace is one demonstration of the model, not the limit of it. Presence already applies the same collaboration model to a second application, demonstrating that the security model is not tied to responsive design. The same Seat, Scope, Revision, and Receipt primitives could govern agents working inside operations software, content systems, developer environments, and other collaborative applications. The larger idea is simple: As agents enter live software, applications need a way to decide not only what agents can understand, but where they may act. I focused on exploring how humans and agents can safely collaborate in the same live software without giving agents unrestricted control. title: Lumos: Human-First WebMCP for Transparent AI Collaboration
pitch: Lumos lets people and AI agents collaborate through explicit consent, scoped tools, clear action previews, and user-controlled execution—built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Lumos lets people and AI agents collaborate through explicit consent, scoped tools, clear action previews, and user-controlled execution—built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates For WebMCP Challenge judges Live URL: https://welockai.com/panel/ Repository: https://github.com/candasoz01-cmd/lumos-core License: Apache-2.0 Open in: ChatGPT’s in-app browser, or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Lumos exposes three task-board tools through document.modelContext : lumos-list-tasks , lumos-propose-task , and lumos-complete-task . Reading requires explicit session-scoped sharing consent. Every write is previewed and confirmed inside Lumos. Declining writes nothing, and completing a task cannot be used to discover task existence without consent. The recorded native proof used Chrome 152. ChatGPT’s in-app browser was not used as the recorded native proof; the live Lumos panel is the judge-facing surface. Inspiration AI agents can move quickly through software, but speed without visible authority boundaries can undermine trust. Lumos already had a task board and a human approval flow. For the WebMCP Challenge, we explored a focused question: how can an agent use a real product surface without taking the final decision away from the person? What it does Lumos exposes three task-board tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : lumos-list-tasks reads the task board only after the user explicitly approves sharing it with agents. The permission is session-scoped, visible in the panel, and revocable. lumos-propose-task proposes a task but does not create it until the user approves the panel's own confirmation dialog. lumos-complete-task requires board-sharing consent first, then a separate approval before changing a task's status. The confirmation preview shows the exact fields involved, including title, priority, schedule, status, source, and status transition. Cancelling produces no write. If WebMCP is unavailable, Lumos fails closed, registers no tools, marks the surface unsupported, and continues as a normal panel without a shim or polyfill. How we built it The public Lumos panel is built with Astro and browser-native JavaScript. A narrow bridge in the existing panel runtime connects WebMCP tools to the established task workflow. The tools return MCP-compatible content payloads and reuse the same task persistence and confirmation paths as the human-facing interface. The implementation includes source-contract tests and a Playwright end-to-end harness that exercises tool registration, consent refusal, approval, cancellation, task creation, and completion. The harness simulates the browser's agent-side WebMCP host so it validates the page implementation without pretending to be native browser proof. The public panel is deployed on Vercel, and the source is available under the Apache-2.0 license. What changed during the challenge Lumos, its panel, task module, and approval flow existed before August 25, 2026. The WebMCP-specific layer was added during the challenge period. That work added the three tool registrations, session-scoped read consent, per-mutation approval, full-field action previews, fail-closed behavior, and automated verification. Security review also led to concrete fixes: task data is no longer returned without sharing consent; task-completion lookups cannot reveal whether a task exists before consent; and a stale dialog-close event can no longer cancel a later approval prompt. Challenges we faced The hardest part was treating privacy and consent as implementation details rather than slogans. A read-only task list can still contain sensitive personal or work information. A confirmation that hides priority or schedule is not meaningful consent. Different error responses can also leak whether a task exists. WebMCP is emerging, so we also had to keep three kinds of evidence separate: source behavior, harness-based end-to-end verification, and native browser-agent invocation. Lumos does not add a compatibility shim when the platform API is missing. What we learned Read-only does not automatically mean safe to share. Approval must show every field that will be written. Refusal and failure need different machine-readable results. Unsupported environments should fail closed without changing the ordinary product. Human control works best when it is part of the product flow, not an agent-side promise. What's next Next we will expand native live-origin verification as supporting browsers expose WebMCP, preserve raw evidence for agent discovery and invocation, and continue testing consent revocation and approval behavior across clients. The goal remains the same: useful agent collaboration with authority, privacy, and final control kept visibly in human hands. title: Polkaswap
pitch: Browser agents discover assets, quote routes, and build fresh swap plans without wallet access.
about_excerpt: Browser agents discover assets, quote routes, and build fresh swap plans without wallet access. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a swap involves identifying assets, reading precise amounts, comparing routes, and checking fees, price impact, and freshness. We wanted browser agents to obtain those facts directly from the exchange and explain them through a structured, inspectable interface. Polkaswap already connects people to SORA liquidity. WebMCP lets an agent use that same application to build a useful plan while wallet access remains a separate decision. What it does Polkaswap exposes nine public WebMCP tools for capabilities, status, readiness, asset search and resolution, common assets, quotes, unsigned swap plans, and pool information. An agent can respond to “Plan swapping 1 XOR for VAL with 0.5% slippage” by calling polkaswap_plan_swap directly. It waits for the node, resolves assets, obtains a fresh quote, and returns the route, amount bounds, fee estimate when available, warnings, expiry, network context, and unsigned SDK-call metadata. Unavailable fees produce an explicit warning. No wallet connection or prior quote-button click is required. People can inspect the same planning workflow in the agent playground. Changing the pair or amount refreshes the plan automatically; visible pages also refresh expired plans. A switch stops automatic planning. The interface prevents older responses from overwriting newer inputs. Public tools cannot expose account identity or balances, connect a wallet, create an executable intent, sign, submit, transfer funds, or change liquidity. Plans return mode: "unsigned" , canExecute: false , and requiresWallet: false . The preview is SDK-call metadata, not a SCALE-encoded transaction. This entry provides autonomous planning, with no unattended trading. How we built it The implementation uses Vue 3, TypeScript, Vite, the existing SORA SDK and node connection, and FPNumber for precise token amounts. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool() when WebMCP is available. The playground registers its tools at the top level and forwards calls into its same-origin application iframe. Strict schemas require decimal-string amounts and reject additional properties. Public result projection excludes wallet and provider details. Cancellation, bounded errors, network-context checks, and five-minute expiry keep planning results predictable. No executable authorization is stored by planning. Everything ships as static assets suitable for IPFS, without hosted command middleware. An optional local Node.js stdio MCP bridge shares the same public catalogue. Humans use visible controls and agents use named tools, with both reaching the application's existing planning logic. Challenges we addressed Browser agents do not discover tools registered inside the playground iframe, so discovery needed a top-level adapter. Useful market results also needed careful separation from the application's broader wallet-aware API. Planning introduced timing problems: inputs can change during a quote, results can expire, and pages can become hidden. The scheduler serializes requests, ignores superseded results, pauses while hidden, and bounds retries for transient failures. Accomplishments Native verification of the published build discovered all nine tools and directly invoked polkaswap_plan_swap . It returned an unsigned live SORA plan without wallet access. The page planner also refreshed from 1 to 2 XOR and stopped automatic refresh when disabled. The clean submission passed 306 focused tests across 21 files, 13 translation tests across four files, and nine preview-helper tests. The official Node MCP stdio check discovered all nine schemas. A separate browser registration-harness smoke verified planning and input-change replanning with zero captured console, request, or HTTP errors. Existing project and challenge contribution Polkaswap is an existing open-source exchange. Its exchange UI, SORA integration, wallet workflows, static deployment infrastructure, and earlier browser-agent foundation predate this contribution. The August 25–September 3, 2026 challenge contribution adds the public WebMCP catalogue and adapters, wallet-independent swap planning, the agent playground and automatic replanning behavior, and supporting tests and documentation. The linked public comparison identifies the changes from baseline 893783b to submission commit 4955eb0 . What's next We want clearer multi-route comparisons, more useful public market reads, and better explanations when node data is temporarily unavailable. Signing and execution remain outside the public WebMCP tools. title: GhostLayer — Agent Speed, Human Authority
pitch: GhostLayer gives agents fast, typed WebMCP tools while keeping consequential actions behind a visible human decision.
about_excerpt: GhostLayer gives agents fast, typed WebMCP tools while keeping consequential actions behind a visible human decision. Like Comment Story Updates A consequential call waits with zero drafts until human approval. Approval creates one tab-local fictional invoice; replay stays at one row. Two page-owned WebMCP tools are live and discoverable. Pause removes both tools from the agent surface; resume restores them. Inspiration Browser agents usually have to infer intent from interfaces designed for people: find the right control, interpret changing DOM structure, and guess whether an action is harmless or consequential. WebMCP changes that relationship. A website can publish an explicit capability with a typed contract instead of making an agent reverse-engineer the screen. We wanted to explore the product-design consequence of that shift, not only the reliability benefit. If an agent can act faster through declared tools, the application should become equally explicit about where human authority begins. GhostLayer asks a simple question: what if the agent could discover and prepare structured work immediately, while the website retained validation, effect preview, approval, rejection, lifecycle, and recovery at the point of consequence? What it does GhostLayer is a human-authority layer for product and platform teams exposing commerce, finance, support, and administrative actions through WebMCP. It keeps consequential work behind a human-owned commit boundary instead of giving an agent unchecked authority. The public Challenge Edition proves that product pattern in a fictional, client-only CRM sandbox with two page-owned WebMCP tools: find_customer performs an exact read-only lookup over three clearly fictional customer records and returns structured output. create_invoice_draft accepts a returned customer ID, a 1–160 character description, and a fictional amount from $0.01 to $5,000. It validates the input, then keeps the tool call pending while the site shows the exact effect for human review. Nothing is created while approval is pending. Rejecting, cancelling, expiring the two-minute window, pausing the agent surface, or resetting the sandbox creates no draft. Approval creates one tab-local demo draft. Repeating the same normalized approved request returns the existing invoice with replayed: true instead of adding another row. The human can pause the entire agent surface, which disposes both WebMCP registrations, and resume it to publish the same bounded contract again. Reset clears all fictional state in the current tab. Visible forms provide a transparent manual path through the same lookup, validation, approval, rejection, replay, pause, and reset behavior when native WebMCP is unavailable. The public challenge build intentionally contains no real customer data, login, application credentials, application API, D1 database, R2 bucket, external CRM, payment flow, or durable persistence. Reloading, closing, resetting, or opening a new tab starts clean. It demonstrates a governed interaction pattern; it does not claim durable or globally exactly-once execution. From sandbox to a production app A production team keeps its existing identity, policy, database, and business API. The request path becomes: agent request → typed WebMCP contract → GhostLayer review → authenticated, policy-checked backend commit → durable receipt returned to the agent. The public app proves the complete visible decision loop; production adopters connect server-side RBAC, durable idempotency, and audit storage at the same boundary. How we built it The challenge Site is a TypeScript application built with React 19 and Next.js 16 through Vinext/Vite for the OpenAI Sites runtime. The bounded adapter schema and WebMCP bridge began in the earlier GhostLayer 0.5 private prototype and are reused transparently here. The new challenge-period work is the standalone public native WebMCP experience: its judge sandbox, page-owned registration, visible approval, rejection and expiry semantics, replay protection, Pause/Resume lifecycle, Reset behavior, deployment isolation, and verification. The private owner application, extension, control plane, and credentials are not part of this submission. The tool contract in app/challenge-contract.ts defines the fictional records, exact-origin adapter, typed input and output schemas, and separate read and confirm risk levels. A shared WebMCP bridge feature-detects secure document.modelContext , registers the page-owned tools, validates adapter configuration and exact-origin availability, validates provider inputs and outputs, limits serialized tool results to 1,536 bytes, and uses an AbortController to dispose registrations with page or human-controlled lifecycle changes. The React application owns the consequential boundary. create_invoice_draft returns a promise that stays unresolved while the approval panel is visible. The panel shows the customer, description, amount, and two-minute decision window. Approval resolves the call after creating one in-memory draft; rejection, cancellation, expiry, pause, reset, or teardown rejects it without a write. A stable replay key is derived from the normalized customer ID, trimmed description, and amount in cents. State and a short eight-entry activity log remain in React memory, with an eight-draft-per-tab cap. Vitest uses deterministic fake timers to verify the exact two-minute expiry and tests schema validation, normalization, and replay-key stability. Playwright covers route isolation, absence of application API calls, tab isolation, zero-write rejection, approval, and the native WebMCP discovery/execution/replay/pause/resume chain in a compatible Chromium build. GhostLayer had an earlier private adapter/extension prototype. This standalone public Challenge Edition was created during the submission period as a new directly testable WebMCP application. The challenge-period work comprises the client-only judge sandbox, direct page-owned native tool registration, governed approval/rejection/expiry, same-tab replay, Pause/Resume and Reset controls, deployment isolation, and the accompanying automated verification. The dated public commit history records this package; the earlier owner-only prototype is not included or required to run the submission. Challenges we ran into An evolving API surface. WebMCP is experimental, and the current draft and available Chromium implementation can expose slightly different provider callback shapes. The bridge supports both without weakening validation or lifecycle cancellation. Waiting safely for a person. A consequential tool had to remain pending across visible review without silently committing, leaking an unresolved invocation, or writing after cancellation, expiry, pause, reset, or teardown. Replay without overclaiming. The demo needed to prevent duplicate rows for the same normalized request while staying honest that this is tab-local behavior, not durable cross-device idempotency. A genuinely safe public judge target. The experience had to be fully interactive without credentials, private routes, production data, persistent storage, or application API calls. Progressive availability. Native WebMCP is not available in every browser, so the manual forms needed to explain and exercise the same application-owned behavior without pretending to be an agent call. Accomplishments we are proud of A real WebMCP tool invocation remains pending until the person approves or rejects the exact effect. The visible invoice count stays at zero during review, and rejection or expiry creates nothing. An approved replay returns the same tab-local invoice rather than adding a duplicate row. One human control removes both tools from agent availability and can restore the bounded contract. Input and output validation, exact-origin checks, bounded provider output, and cancellation are enforced inside the provider path. The judge sandbox is useful without collecting or persisting user data and includes a manual fallback for incompatible browsers. Browser tests exercise both the visible safety behavior and the native WebMCP chain. What we learned Typed tools remove UI ambiguity, but the schema is only the beginning of a trustworthy WebMCP product. The application still needs to own validation, effect previews, approval semantics, cancellation, lifecycle disposal, replay behavior, and recovery. We also learned that human control is most convincing when it changes the capability surface itself. Pausing GhostLayer does not merely disable a button; it removes both registered tools. Finally, safe replay semantics must be described at their real scope. The current sandbox can prove same-tab duplicate prevention, while durable idempotency, authorization, and multi-tenant isolation belong in a separately reviewed server-backed system. What's next Test the provider bridge against additional browser implementations as the WebMCP draft evolves. Extract the visible governed-approval bound

title: MCP, Meet PCM
pitch: PCM turns Mohit's portfolio into a context manager where people and agents find relevant proof, create a tailored takeaway, and prepare the next conversation together.
about_excerpt: PCM turns Mohit's portfolio into a context manager where people and agents find relevant proof, create a tailored takeaway, and prepare the next conversation together. Like Comment Story Updates Title MCP, Meet PCM Subtitle: Portfolio Context Manager — a WebMCP-powered portfolio that turns visitor context into evidence, a durable takeaway, and a human-reviewed project brief. One-line Summary PCM turns Mohit's portfolio into a context manager where people and agents find relevant proof, create a tailored takeaway, and prepare the next conversation together. Problem Professional portfolios are designed for browsing, not collaboration. A founder, CTO, recruiter, or design leader must scan several pages, infer which projects matter, verify whether the evidence truly supports their need, remember the useful parts, and then repeat the context in a blank contact form. An agent can help, but without a structured interface it must scrape presentation-oriented pages, reconstruct the site's meaning, and guess which claims are canonical. The website knows the facts; the agent knows the visitor's context. Conventional portfolios give them no reliable way to work together. Solution PCM adds five WebMCP tools to the existing portfolio. The agent can establish a canonical profile, rank relevant work with evidence and honest gaps, create a visible visitor-specific briefing, save selected work as a durable web/PDF takeaway, and prepare an editable project brief. The human stays in the loop. Page-changing actions are visible and reversible. A takeaway is created only after the visitor confirms that anyone with its unguessable link may view it. An inquiry is prepared and the contact form is prefilled, but the tool never sends it. This produces a better experience than either side can create alone: the site contributes reviewed, structured evidence; the agent contributes the visitor's already-known goals and priorities; the human sees, edits, saves, or rejects the result. Why This Matters The same pattern applies far beyond portfolios. Today, useful web experiences repeatedly ask people to translate context from their agent back into forms and filters. A structured website capability layer can let agents do the broad comparison work while the website retains authority over facts, validation, presentation, persistence, and side effects. MCP, Meet PCM demonstrates that future on a familiar, high-friction decision: “Could this person help us?” Instead of producing a generic summary, the collaboration ends in inspectable evidence and an actionable—but deliberately unsent—next step. Why This Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP The agent needs reliable access to facts and actions owned by the live website, not a second copy of the portfolio in an external database. Visitor context is what makes the experience valuable, but that context should not need to be permanently uploaded to the site. Read-only research and state-changing actions have meaningfully different contracts and safety boundaries. The best result is visible on the web page: a human can inspect what the agent selected, edit it, reset it, save it, or continue manually. The five tools form a coherent journey rather than a decorative one-tool integration. How We Used AI The visitor's agent supplies the reasoning. The website supplies canonical public data, strict tool contracts, deterministic matching, evidence boundaries, visible UI state, and durable artifacts. No embedded chatbot or paid model call is required. AI is useful here because it can combine the visitor's nuanced intent with a larger evidence set, explain why specific work is relevant, and carry context between research, personalization, saving, and inquiry preparation. The site's deterministic layer prevents that reasoning from becoming an excuse to invent credentials, project outcomes, or client claims. The implementation was tested through Codex's in-app browser and with GPT-5.6 Terra. GPT-5.6 Luna completed page, saved-artifact, and injection baselines, but its available browser runtime did not expose document.modelContext or the WebMCP tool-list operation; that limitation is reported rather than treated as a pass. How We Used Codex Codex was a working product and engineering partner throughout the WebMCP extension. It helped: turn the initial concept into product, development, and browser acceptance specifications; define bounded tool contracts and the human/agent safety model; implement the five tools, canonical content layer, relevance engine, browser state, storage API, and PDF output; write regression tests and exercise complete browser flows rather than checking registration alone; inspect desktop and mobile UI, identify the unfinished modal-like experience, and redesign it into a polished editorial briefing and project-brief surface; validate persistence, confirmation gates, error states, privacy boundaries, response headers, deployment storage, and rate limiting; prepare the demo narrative and Devpost materials while keeping unverified claims and release blockers explicit. Key Features Canonical understanding — a concise, bounded profile and service overview from reviewed site content. Evidence-based matching — deterministic project ranking with approved evidence, stable links, and explicit evidence gaps. Visible portfolio context — an editorial briefing tailored to the visitor's role, goal, and priorities, with reset and persistence behavior. Durable takeaway — an immutable public-by-link page and server-generated PDF, created only after confirmation. Human-reviewed inquiry — an editable brief that prefills the existing contact form while remaining clearly unsent. Progressive enhancement — the normal portfolio remains complete when WebMCP is unavailable. Architecture PCM is an Astro 7 application with React islands deployed on Vercel. A browser adapter checks for document.modelContext.registerTool and registers exactly five tools. Zod validates bounded inputs; outputs are compact structured results. The human pages and tools consume the same canonical content under src/content . Relevance matching is deterministic and uses curated capabilities, audiences, problem types, roles, outcomes, evidence, and evidence gaps. Personalized views and inquiries use versioned sessionStorage and custom events to keep state changes visible. Confirmed takeaways are written through an Astro API to private Vercel Blob storage. IDs are opaque, stable, HMAC-derived values; exact retries are idempotent. Public records exclude identity, email, transcripts, and hidden reasoning. Saved pages are no-index and offer a server-generated PDF. Public Demo Link https://mohittater.in/ Public Repository Link https://github.com/mnttnm/mohit-freelance-portfolio Known Limitations WebMCP support varies across experimental browser and agent runtimes. The available GPT-5.6 Luna browser runtime did not expose the required page model context, so real Luna routing remains blocked by that runtime. Preview deployments remain owner-protected; the production judging URL is public and was verified separately. Saved takeaways are public by unguessable link and do not yet have an account-based library or revocation UI. Inquiry preparation intentionally stops before external communication. Real email delivery, timed cancellation, and timed storage-failure recovery were not exercised against production.
