title: Hustl
pitch: Hustl connects your training, recovery, nutrition, and progress in one adaptive coaching system—where you collaborate with AI while keeping every change under your control.
about_excerpt: Hustl connects your training, recovery, nutrition, and progress in one adaptive coaching system—where you collaborate with AI while keeping every change under your control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I’ve been skinny for most of my life. I tried apps like Strong to track my workouts and MacroFactor to manage my nutrition. Both were useful, but each understood only one part of what I was trying to achieve. I still relied on ChatGPT or Claude for advice. That meant repeatedly explaining my training history, diet, recovery, and goals, then manually carrying their suggestions back into each app. I built Hustl because I wanted those pieces to work together. The same problem exists whether someone wants to gain muscle, improve performance, or lose weight without sacrificing strength: good coaching needs the full picture. What it does Hustl connects training, recovery, nutrition, progress, and AI coaching in one app. It also brings in health and activity data from outside Hustl through Apple Health and Health Connect on Android, including data shared by compatible apps such as Google Fit. This gives the coach a broader view of the athlete’s workouts, sleep, heart rate, recovery, and daily activity. An AI assistant can understand what the athlete has trained, how their exercises are progressing, whether they have recovered, what they have eaten, and what their current goals are. It can then help with practical tasks such as: reviewing workout and exercise history; interpreting readiness, sleep, HRV, and resting heart rate; comparing food intake with calorie and macro targets; logging or correcting meals; proposing nutrition targets; building and revising workout templates; adapting a workout when recovery is poor; and showing proposed changes inside the Coach inbox. Hustl supports both MCP and WebMCP. MCP lets compatible assistants work with Hustl directly. WebMCP gives an assistant tools related to the Hustl screen currently open in the browser. The important part is the collaboration. The assistant studies the evidence and explains its recommendation. Hustl turns that recommendation into a concrete proposal. The athlete reviews, refines, accepts, or rejects it. How I built it Hustl is a Flutter application backed by a TypeScript and Next.js API, Supabase and PostgreSQL, native Apple Health and Android Health Connect integrations, and an MCP server. For WebMCP, I built a coordinator that registers tools according to the visible route. Train exposes training and progression tools. Recover exposes readiness data. Nutrition exposes the food diary and nutrition proposals. Coach exposes trends and pending changes. Templates and active workouts expose their own focused capabilities. When the user changes screens, the old tool handles become stale. This prevents an assistant from retaining a capability simply because the user visited that page earlier. Actions use strict schemas and explicit outcomes. Coaching changes normally become pending proposals rather than being applied silently. They appear in Hustl’s regular Coach interface, where the athlete can inspect the rationale and proposed values. For the challenge, I also created a public evaluator using Hustl’s real Flutter interface and WebMCP coordinator. Private services were replaced with deterministic, in-memory data. It contains no production credentials, personal health records, analytics, or backend connection. Its runtime also blocks unexpected network and browser-credential access. Challenges I ran into The first challenge was resisting the temptation to build a small, isolated demo. Hustl is meant to support the whole coaching loop, so the WebMCP experience needed to work across the real training, recovery, nutrition, Coach, template, and workout screens. Navigation was harder than it appeared. The visible screen, browser URL, and registered tool catalogue all needed to agree. I found cases where a detail screen opened without correctly taking ownership of its route. I also had to ensure that tools disappeared and old handles failed safely after navigation, reloads, and account transitions. Proposal state required similar care. A successful request might be pending, applied, duplicated, dismissed, reverted, or rejected by validation. Those outcomes needed to remain distinct in both the tool response and the interface. Finally, I needed to make the source inspectable without publishing Hustl’s private backend or user data. The public evaluator therefore uses synthetic fixtures, explicit no-op integrations, source manifests, and checks for private paths, credentials, and unexpected network origins. Accomplishments that I’m proud of The public evaluator exposes 20 route-scoped WebMCP tools across training, recovery, nutrition, coaching, templates, and active workouts. Those tools support a complete coaching story. An athlete can describe a goal, let the assistant study twelve weeks of training and exercise progression, account for a poor recovery day, compare nutrition with current targets, and receive concrete changes for review. I am especially proud that the safety model is visible in the product: tools follow the screen the athlete is using; stale handles fail closed; proposal status is explicit; duplicate requests do not create duplicate changes; workout and nutrition-target proposals require human review; and the public evaluator cannot access production systems or personal data. This is not a separate interface made for the challenge. It is a safe, deterministic version of Hustl’s real Flutter experience and coaching architecture. What I learned More autonomy does not automatically make an AI coach more useful. Better context and a clear review process matter more. I also learned that the interface can act as a meaningful permission boundary. Route-scoped tools make the assistant’s access easier to understand because its capabilities follow what the athlete can currently see and do. Most importantly, AI collaboration works better when the result becomes part of the product’s normal workflow. A recommendation should not disappear inside a chat transcript. It should become something the athlete can inspect, refine, follow, and revisit. What’s next for Hustl The next step is to make the collaboration continuous rather than limited to a single planning session. I want Hustl to support richer long-term recovery analysis, clearer progression explanations, and weekly coaching check-ins that compare the plan with what actually happened. I also want the same experience to work consistently across web, desktop, and mobile assistants through MCP and WebMCP. The principle will remain the same: Hustl provides the evidence, AI helps interpret and propose, and the athlete controls what changes. title: Keep
pitch: Remember people. Don’t impersonate them. Keep turns messy relationship notes into visible promises, attention rankings, and editable drafts while the human stays in control.
about_excerpt: Remember people. Don’t impersonate them. Keep turns messy relationship notes into visible promises, attention rankings, and editable drafts while the human stays in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I talk to enough people that promises disappear into notes, calendars, and guilt. Traditional CRMs optimize deals and reporting. I wanted a quieter tool for the relationships where the real question is: what did I say I would do? What it does Keep is a local-first relationship desk. It stores fictional demo contacts in the browser, turns raw call notes into owner-labelled promise chips, ranks people who need attention, and creates editable follow-up drafts. Keep never sends a message. The human remains responsible for anything another person receives. Why WebMCP This workflow depends on live page state: which person is selected, their last interaction, unresolved promises, pipeline position, and whether a draft exists. Screen scraping makes an agent guess. A backend integration separates the agent from the interface where the human reviews the result. Keep registers narrow tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Those tools call the same store as the human UI, so cards, timelines, promises, suggestions, and drafts update in front of both participants. The active tool set changes with page state. With no selected card, the agent sees discovery tools. Selecting Priya adds her relevant actions. Promise and draft tools appear only when those objects exist. Human and agent together After a call, the human gives the agent one messy sentence. The agent logs the original words, extracts commitments, and moves the card. On Monday morning, who_needs_attention ranks relationships using cadence, overdue promises, and the Waiting on me column. The agent can draft a follow-up, but it cannot send one. mark_sent only records an action after the human confirms it already happened. How I built it The app uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and a small useSyncExternalStore state layer persisted to localStorage . It exposes 14 WebMCP tools with JSON Schema inputs. Read operations use readOnlyHint ; promise extraction marks raw notes with untrustedContentHint . A deterministic commitment parser and draft generator keep the live demo independent of API keys or inference availability. Archiving, dropping a promise, and recording a sent message have in-page confirmation gates. The repository includes eight unit and WebMCP contract tests plus browser acceptance coverage for desktop and mobile. OpenAI Sites hosts the public production build used for judging. Challenges The hardest choice was deciding what the agent must not do. Auto-sending would look powerful in a demo, but it would turn a relationship tool into an impersonation tool. Keep makes the handoff visible instead. The agent can organize, recall, and draft. The person decides what is true and what leaves the browser. The second challenge was keeping agent calls and human actions consistent. Both paths now mutate one store and produce the same visible UI changes. Dynamic registration also required careful cleanup with AbortController as selection and object state changed. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when the browser is not a thin shell over an API. It lets an agent participate in a stateful visual workflow without bypassing the product or duplicating authentication and client state on a server. The best tools are narrow verbs with visible effects. What is next Calendar context is the next useful input, followed by optional encrypted sync. Sending integrations are not on the roadmap. Keep should become better at helping a person remember, not better at pretending to be them. title: LingoMargin
pitch: LingoMargin turns any text into a personalized language lesson where learners and agents collaborate through contextual annotations, grammar missions, and review practice powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: LingoMargin turns any text into a personalized language lesson where learners and agents collaborate through contextual annotations, grammar missions, and review practice powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Language learners increasingly use AI to understand given texts, but the usual workflow is fragmented: read in one place, copy a confusing sentence into chat, receive an explanation elsewhere, and manually save useful vocabulary. I wanted to explore a more natural model where the learner and agent share the same reading workspace. The learner stays focused on the text while the agent understands the current passage, proficiency level, annotations, exercises, and learning progress. What LingoMargin does LingoMargin turns any passage into an interactive, level-appropriate language lesson. Learners can paste their own text or request a new passage by specifying a language, level, length, and topic. They can select unfamiliar phrases, save vocabulary, inspect contextual explanations, complete Grammar Detective missions, review mistakes, and export learning material. The agent can directly update the workspace by: Adding selective vocabulary, grammar, and cultural annotations Creating hidden-answer Grammar Detective missions Generating contextual review activities Leaving feedback in the margin Producing new level-appropriate passages Every agent action creates a visible change in the interface. The learner decides what to study and can undo passage replacements when needed. How I built it LingoMargin is built with React, TypeScript, Vinext, and WebMCP, and is deployed using ChatGPT Sites. The application registers six tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_learning_context annotate_text create_grammar_mission create_activity add_feedback create_generated_passage These tools give the agent structured access to the current lesson and allow it to make precise, verifiable updates. Mutating tools return confirmation describing what changed, while the learner immediately sees the result in the passage or margin. The workspace is stored locally in the browser. Passage content and learning state are shared with an agent only when the learner asks for help through a WebMCP tool. Challenges The main challenge was designing genuine human-agent collaboration instead of attaching a chatbot to a reading app. Annotations had to remain anchored to exact character ranges while preventing duplicates and overlaps. Grammar missions needed to accept the complete intended phrase without incorrectly accepting tiny fragments. Agent-generated activities also required validation so malformed exercises could not enter the interface. Another challenge was preserving learner control. Replacing a passage clears lesson-specific state, so I added confirmation, recovery, and one-step undo. I also had to make the relationship between the page and adjacent agent chat understandable without filling the interface with technical WebMCP terminology. Finally, the workspace needed to remain usable on mobile, where the mission must appear before a potentially long passage. What I learned WebMCP changes interface design, not just integration code. A useful agent-native application needs carefully scoped tools, observable outcomes, reliable validation, and clear boundaries between human and agent responsibilities. The best result came from giving each participant a distinct role: the agent analyzes and adapts the lesson, while the learner notices, selects, answers, and decides what becomes knowledge. title: LiquidHR Agent Workspace
pitch: A state-aware HR workspace where a browser agent uses WebMCP to prepare grounded development conversations while the manager retains the final decision.
about_excerpt: A state-aware HR workspace where a browser agent uses WebMCP to prepare grounded development conversations while the manager retains the final decision. Like Comment 1 Story Updates 1 Inspiration I am a product manager, not a software engineer, and I am building an HR application called LiquidHR using AI-assisted development with Codex (luna model only). I was preparing to explore a traditional MCP server for LiquidHR when the WebMCP Challenge appeared. I decided to change direction and spend a day answering a different question: What happens if the web application itself can teach an AI agent what it is allowed to do? LiquidHR Agent Workspace is the result. What it does The project demonstrates a people manager and a browser agent preparing the same employee development conversation together. The application initially exposes three WebMCP capabilities: find an employee within the manager's scope retrieve that employee's development context prepare a grounded development-conversation draft The manager can ask, in natural language, for a development conversation to be prepared for Sophie. The agent uses the capabilities exposed by the LiquidHR website to find Sophie, retrieve her current goals, open actions and skill-development signals, and create three grounded discussion topics. The manager sees that exact same draft in the human interface. This is not a chatbot creating a separate copy of HR data. The human interface and the agent operate on the same application state. State-aware WebMCP capabilities One of the ideas I especially wanted to explore was whether the capability surface itself could follow the workflow. Initially, the application exposes three tools. Once a valid conversation draft exists for the currently selected employee, LiquidHR dynamically exposes a fourth WebMCP capability: add_follow_up_action The agent can then add a bounded follow-up action to the existing draft. When the manager finally reviews and saves the conversation, that temporary capability disappears again. The capability lifecycle is therefore: 3 → 4 → 3 The application's state determines what the agent can do next. Human judgment remains human Final save is deliberately not exposed as a WebMCP capability. The agent can retrieve context, organize information, prepare the draft and add a follow-up action, but the manager must perform the final Review & save action in the human interface. That creates a deliberate human-confirmation boundary around the judgment-bearing transition. The agent doesn't bypass the application. The application teaches the agent how to use it safely. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, a general-purpose assistant often has to work through a second interface, copied data, brittle browser interaction or a separately designed API. WebMCP lets the web application expose a structured capability contract directly to the browser agent. The tool names, descriptions, input schemas, annotations, authorization rules and lifecycle are defined by the application itself. That means the agent does not have to guess which buttons to click or infer hidden application state. It receives capabilities that reflect what the application can safely do at that moment. Shared application architecture The human UI and the WebMCP callbacks use the same: workspace facade → actor and manager-scope policy → domain service → shared draft state → synthetic repository Employee lookup is restricted to the fictional manager's authorized scope. Direct employee context access is validated again before information is returned. The project also contains an out-of-scope synthetic employee for authorization testing. All company, employee and activity data is fictional. Implementation The project uses the imperative WebMCP API through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The application uses object JSON Schemas, tool descriptions, annotations, structured results and lifecycle-managed registrations. The first three capabilities remain available for the workspace lifecycle. The fourth capability is dynamically registered only when a valid matching draft exists and is removed after the draft is discarded or saved. The application is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript and deployed publicly on Vercel. No production HR backend, real employee data or external AI API is embedded in the challenge application. What I proved The live end-to-end flow demonstrates: real WebMCP capability discovery and execution natural-language interaction with application-defined tools scoped employee access grounded development context shared state between human and agent dynamic state-aware capabilities a visible activity trail a deliberate human confirmation boundary The complete natural-language flow was also tested against the public application using ChatGPT's browser with a WebMCP-capable runtime. Potential impact Managers frequently spend time gathering goals, open actions and development signals before a useful conversation can even begin. An agent can remove much of that repetitive retrieval and preparation without taking over the manager's judgment. The same pattern can extend far beyond HR: applications can expose safe, contextual capabilities to agents while retaining their own business rules, permissions, workflow state and human approval boundaries. Human judgment. Agent speed. One shared HR workspace.## Inspiration Built With chatgpt next.js react typescript vercel vitest webmcp Try it out liquidhr-agent-workspace.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I conceived, designed, built, tested, deployed and documented LiquidHR Agent Workspace as a solo project. As a product manager rather than a software engineer, I defined the product concept, WebMCP workflow, authorization boundaries, shared human-agent state and human confirmation model, and used AI-assisted development with Codex to turn those specifications into the working application. I also performed the end-to-end WebMCP testing, prepared the public demo, and created the challenge submission. title: Mend: Safe, verified website repairs with WebMCP
pitch: Mend helps you find website problems, review safe AI fixes, and verify the results, while WebMCP and security safeguards keep your source code and workflow under your control.
about_excerpt: Mend helps you find website problems, review safe AI fixes, and verify the results, while WebMCP and security safeguards keep your source code and workflow under your control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Scan: find the issues that matter most Mend landing page: safe, verified website repairs Read-only source viewer mapped to the issue Understand: trace audit evidence to the source Proposed diff waiting for human approval Performance finding: hero image is larger than rendered Audit dashboard with performance, accessibility, SEO, and link scores Accessibility finding: email field without an associated label Connected repository with WebMCP tools ready Verify: compare results and prove the fix worked Inspiration Website audits tell you what is wrong, while coding agents can edit source code. The difficult part is the handoff between those systems. Mend turns that gap into one human and agent workflow. What it does Mend scans a website for accessibility, performance, SEO, and broken-link issues. It keeps evidence tied to pages and selectors, maps findings to authorized source hints, proposes a bounded patch, shows an exact diff, waits for explicit approval, records a branch-first change, and verifies the before-and-after result. Why WebMCP This is a structured sequence of actions, not a chatbot guessing which pixels to click. Mend registers 13 compact tools through document.modelContext: scan, summarize, list and inspect issues, inspect source, propose a fix, review the diff, request approval, apply the approved fix, verify, and compare audits. The agent and human see the same state, and the tools work in WebMCP runtimes that omit optional execution context. How we built it The app is Next.js and TypeScript with server-side bounded HTML checks, normalized audit models, a controlled demo repository, and deterministic fix and diff generation. WebMCP is feature-detected so the manual UX works in browsers without it. Human approval and applied state are bound to signed HTTP-only receipts, the browser workspace recovers after reload, and verification reruns checks against the actual patched source snapshot. The approval guard rejects unapproved changes and the checked-in main fixture remains untouched. What we learned The hard part was making the workflow trustworthy and legible. We kept evidence, confidence, diffs, approval status, and verification together, and added SSRF protections, timeouts, size bounds, safe path validation, reload recovery, and regression checks. Try it The deterministic demo repairs missing hero-image alternative text: Accessibility moves from 74 to 89, one issue resolves, and zero regressions are reported. The production workflow was verified end to end from scan through source-backed comparison. title: Meridian Bank — a WebMCP banking demo
pitch: Banking where the AI does the homework and you keep the pen: an agent compares, checks eligibility, and applies inside your session, on your page but only a human can hit submit
about_excerpt: Banking where the AI does the homework and you keep the pen: an agent compares, checks eligibility, and applies inside your session, on your page but only a human can hit submit Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "agent browses the web" demo we'd seen worked against the page screenshotting, scraping the DOM, guessing which button to click. Meanwhile, the tasks people actually want help with (like picking a credit card) depend on private, session-bound data an outside agent can't see: your income, your credit score, what you already hold. WebMCP flips the model the page itself tells the agent what it can do. We wanted to build the strongest possible case for that flip: a bank, where the data is personal, the answers must be grounded, and the final action is too consequential to leave to an AI. What it does Meridian Bank is a retail-banking portal where an AI agent works inside your authenticated browser tab through 15 WebMCP tools the page registers: Search & compare — full terms sheets for 21 products across 8 categories, with a side-by-side comparison matrix Grounded recommendations check_eligibility runs the bank's real rules engine against your profile and returns per-requirement verdicts (ELIGIBLE / NOT_ELIGIBLE / REVIEW_REQUIRED) with reasons and alternative products the agent recommends from the same source of truth the bank uses Visual co-presence highlight_differences lets the agent light up the exact rows of the compare table that drove its recommendation and dim the rest, with its note shown above the table. The agent literally points at the page Acting on your behalf it assembles a multi-product application basket, picks card designs, applies your loyalty offer, and the UI updates live as it works Human-in-the-loop by construction submit_application never submits. It opens an in-app approval dialog with the full basket summary and blocks until the human clicks Approve or Reject. Even a misbehaving agent cannot submit, because the guardrail lives in the tool's implementation, not in a prompt Tool availability mirrors the session: 3 tools logged out, 15 logged in the browser's tool list itself reflects auth state. Try it: https://meridian-bank-client-production.up.railway.app in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. How we built it The app is built with Wasp (React + Express + Prisma/Postgres), deployed on Railway. Every tool is registered through the browser's WebMCP API: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "check_eligibility", description: "Check whether the user qualifies for a product…", inputSchema: { /* JSON Schema / }, execute: async (input) => { / … */ }, }); …via a small React hook that handles register/unregister on mount and auth gating with an enabled flag. Each tool's execute delegates to the same typed RPC operations the UI uses, so Wasp's automatic query invalidation makes the interface update live after every agent action — zero extra wiring. The eligibility engine is a pure, fully unit-tested module (16 tests); the approval flow is a promise that only resolves when a human clicks a button. We tested with Claude connected over chrome-devtools-mcp in a WebMCP-flagged Chrome. Challenges we ran into React lifecycle vs. browser API. Tools registered from React must survive StrictMode double-mounting and never close over stale component state every execute reads through the RPC layer instead of captured props, and aborted registrations had to be handled as expected lifecycle noise rather than errors. Designing for a non-human user. Tool descriptions are UX writing where the "user" is a model. Getting the agent to reliably check eligibility before recommending and to never submit unprompted — came down to careful naming, descriptions, structured error messages, and returning effect fields that tell the agent what just changed on screen. Making approval un-bypassable. The tempting version is "tell the agent to ask first." The robust version is a tool whose result the agent can't have until a human acts designing that blocking flow (with a timeout, and honest reporting of rejected vs timed out) was the most interesting part. Accomplishments that we're proud of A structural safety guarantee, not a prompted one: no sequence of agent calls can submit an application without a human click and the agent gets an honest account of what the human decided. The agent explains itself in the page: highlight_differences turned "trust me, pick the Voyager" into a compare table where the decisive rows are glowing and everything else is dimmed. A complete, working product 21 products, a real eligibility engine, offers, applications history live on the open web, where the full three-prompt demo (compare → apply → approve) runs end-to-end against the deployed site. What we learned The biggest lesson: safety and UX come from tool design, not prompt engineering. A well-shaped tool result (verdicts with reasons, an effect field describing what changed) steers an agent better than any system prompt. We also learned that exposing state-reading tools (get_compare_list, get_my_holdings) matters as much as actions "which of these two?" only works because the agent can see what the human is looking at. And practically: WebMCP is genuinely host-agnostic it's a client-side browser API, so the same tools worked identically on localhost and on Railway. What's next for Meridian Bank — a WebMCP banking demo Streaming progress into the page while the agent works, per-tool scopes the user can grant and revoke (a "permissions drawer" for agents), and multi-tab flows imagine the agent comparing your bank's offer against another site's, with both pages exposing tools to the same assistant. pitch: Learn cooking one dish and one technique at a time. Your assistant adapts the real recipe; you control saved preferences and completed practice.
about_excerpt: Learn cooking one dish and one technique at a time. Your assistant adapts the real recipe; you control saved preferences and completed practice. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A simple tomato pasta can be the start of learning to cook, not just a recipe to finish. Mise explores how to make the next action manageable and add a cooking technique when the learner is ready. What it does Four cooking lines—pasta, rice, potato and one-pan oven—each contain ten recipe versions. Servings and dietary preferences change ingredients and directions together. People choose guidance, use one-step mode, pause and return, and keep approved preferences in their account. Why WebMCP The assistant acts on the same cooking workspace the person sees. Eleven page tools read current state, compose a session around multiple constraints, propose smaller actions, and request human confirmation. The assistant cannot award completed cooking through a tool call alone. Suggested memory stays pending until the person approves it. How it was built React, Vinext, Cloudflare Workers and D1, with imperative document.modelContext.registerTool registration. Runtime schemas reject malformed inputs. Context tokens prevent stale recipe changes; per-account storage and revision checks protect saved progress. Challenges and lessons Testing found that paused sessions could be changed invisibly and that pending completion could outlive a servings change. Both were fixed and retested. A final beginner-rice correction made adding water, boiling and switching heat off explicit. Shared state and learner control matter more than simply awarding levels. Validation and boundaries 36 automated tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. Actual browser checks covered shared state, persistence, pending approvals, invalid tools, mobile layout and keyboard navigation. Six cooking personas are simulations, not real-user research. Recipes are not professionally cook-tested or allergy-certified. This is browser WebMCP while Mise is open, not a remote connector in every GPT or Claude chat. title: Offroof
pitch: Evidence before action for suspicious job offers—shared safely by people and WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: Evidence before action for suspicious job offers—shared safely by people and WebMCP agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Job offers often mix ordinary details with missing context, urgency, payment requests, and invitations to move to unofficial channels. Under pressure, it is easy to confuse what a message actually says with an assumption. We built Offroof as a calm evidence workspace that preserves the wording, explains why a phrase deserves verification, and keeps the person in control of every consequential change. What it does Offroof accepts fictional or privacy-cleaned offer text by paste or browser-local .txt , .md , and simple plain-text .eml import. It detects deterministic verification signals, attaches each signal to its exact supporting excerpt, and separates: what the message literally says; the limited inference a reviewer may draw; what Offroof cannot conclude; the next verification step. Offroof never labels an offer as fraudulent or safe. It never opens a link or attachment, contacts an employer, sends money, or files a report. Instead, it creates an inspectable case record and a reversible verification checklist. Why WebMCP Offroof exposes the same visible case as six semantic, page-native tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : get_case_summary — read a sanitized case snapshot and safe next actions. inspect_offer_signals — run browser-local deterministic inspection. build_verification_plan — create a visible checklist after explicit user consent. update_verification_step — update one current step with case/version guards. get_official_resources — read an allowlist of official Korean guidance. get_action_receipts — inspect filtered, privacy-safe activity receipts. WebMCP is central to the product. The person and agent share the same visible state; read, analysis, and mutation operations are separated; mutations require on-page consent; stale case versions are rejected; and operational calls leave visible receipts without storing the original offer text or raw tool arguments. The manual interface still works when no WebMCP client is connected. How we built it Offroof is a static React, TypeScript, and Vite app. Signal inspection, privacy masking, file-intake validation, state transitions, WebMCP adapters, and receipts all run in the current browser tab. No backend, account, API key, or real personal data is required. The six tools use bounded JSON schemas, enums, additionalProperties: false , stable error codes, conservative annotations, and compact structured results. Mutation tools validate both explicit consent and the latest case ID/version. The app has three state-preserving views—Overview, Review offer, and Case record—plus a Korean/English switch that does not reset the active case. Safety and trust boundaries Offer text is treated as untrusted content, never as agent instruction. Files are read locally and never executed. HTML, multipart, binary, encoded, archive, PDF, Word, and executable inputs are rejected. Links and attachments are never opened automatically. Evidence is masked before it is returned to an agent. Offroof provides verification signals, not a fraud or malware verdict. What we verified On the deployed public build, a native WebMCP client discovered all six tools. Using only the fictional built-in sample, we verified the complete flow: six evidence-backed signals, a blocked mutation before consent, a six-step plan after consent, one checklist update, and a newest-first action receipt trail. The visual interface updated from the same domain state after every call. The project also has 43 automated tests, a passing production build, and zero production dependency vulnerabilities. Challenges The hardest part was defining a truthful safety boundary rather than merely detecting keywords. A checklist mutation must not silently operate on stale state, untrusted offer text must never become agent instruction, and a read-only receipt query must not recursively create another receipt. We also made the manual and agent paths converge on the same domain transitions so the demo is not a separate mock. What we learned WebMCP works best when the webpage is already trustworthy for a person. Semantic tools can then expose the same bounded operations to an agent, with schemas, consent, state guards, visible effects, and receipts. The protocol does not replace product safety boundaries; it makes them machine-operable and auditable. What's next Future work could add an opt-in browser extension or approved mail-provider integration for pre-click mailbox review. A separate isolated service—potentially implemented in Python or Java—could inspect deliberately selected attachments by signature, hash, metadata, and safely extracted text. Those capabilities are intentionally outside this browser-only submission and would never silently open or execute content. title: Outcome Network
pitch: WebMCP turns business websites into capabilities agents can safely compose. Outcome Network coordinates providers, checks constraints, requires human approval, and uses reversible holds.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns business websites into capabilities agents can safely compose. Outcome Network coordinates providers, checks constraints, requires human approval, and uses reversible holds. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most web agents still interact with websites indirectly: read the page, inspect controls, then infer what action to take. WebMCP provides a cleaner model. A site can expose structured capabilities while still owning its UI, state, permissions, and business rules. Outcome Network explores what that looks like for a real multi-provider business workflow. What it does The demo coordinates opening a 15-person Toronto office with two constraints: CAD 12,000 maximum budget Everything ready by Friday Three providers supply furniture, networking, and facilities services. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can search offerings, check inventory and availability, and create temporary resource holds after the user approves the plan. Those holds are reversible. ChatGPT can release them and restore provider availability without changing the approved plan. Every action is recorded in a visible audit trail with the capability, provider, result, and whether it came from WebMCP or the human workspace. How we built it The app uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vercel, and the native document.modelContext WebMCP API. The production workflow exposes six tools, including: search_products check_inventory check_service_availability reserve_outcome_resources release_outcome_reservations WebMCP calls use the same domain logic and state as the UI rather than separate mock handlers. The production path uses same-origin WebMCP for reliability. I also built an experimental cross-origin implementation using allow="tools" , explicit exposedTo origins, and getTools({ fromOrigins }) . Challenges we ran into The main challenge was working with an emerging browser API. WebMCP support behaved differently across local Chrome, public HTTPS, and ChatGPT's in-app browser. Rather than hiding those differences behind a polyfill, I added runtime diagnostics and kept the reliable production path separate from the experimental cross-origin path. The other challenge was authority and failure handling. Approval is tied to the current plan, so changing the plan invalidates stale approval. Multi-provider reservation failures also trigger compensating releases so partial holds are not left behind. Accomplishments that we're proud of The WebMCP integration is part of the application rather than a demo wrapper. In the deployed app, ChatGPT can: invoke real provider capabilities mutate the same state shown in the UI create six temporary holds across three providers release those holds and restore availability leave a visible WebMCP audit trail The project also supports deterministic supplier failure, replanning, and rollback after partial reservation failure. What we learned Tool discovery is only the beginning. Once agents can change application state, the harder questions are around authority, stale approvals, partial failure, reversibility, and auditability. That led to explicit approval boundaries, typed schemas, shared state, reversible operations, and compensating rollback. What's next for Outcome Network The next step is connecting the same model to real independent WebMCP-enabled businesses across different origins. The goal is not to build another marketplace. Businesses should be able to keep their own applications and rules, expose the capabilities they choose, and let agents coordinate those capabilities into useful outcomes. title: PaperPilot
pitch: An AI assisted grant form that checks eligibility and pre-fills answers, keeping the applicant in full control to review and approve every detail before submitting.
about_excerpt: An AI assisted grant form that checks eligibility and pre-fills answers, keeping the applicant in full control to review and approve every detail before submitting. Like Comment Story Updates PaperPilot is an open-source, secure grant application built to solve a glaring problem in the AI space: grant websites are where AI agents usually break down. They screenshot buttons, guess labels, and occasionally submit data the applicant never even reviewed. Paperwork is high-stakes, and trust matters far more than speed. We noticed a major mismatch: people are already chatting with assistants in side panels, but the forms in the main tab have no structured way to let that assistant help without taking the wheel entirely. WebMCP was the missing link for us. Instead of forcing an external automation script to crawl the page, WebMCP puts tools directly inside the page , running against the same session cookie as the human while the applicant watches the live UI. We built a mock Small Business Recovery Grant for our demo because it has real-world rules (revenue caps, headcount limits, drops in sales) and heavy jargon (EINs, fund allocation) that people actually need help navigating. The goal wasn’t to build a bot that says, "Look, the model filled out 11 fields!" The goal was to build a system where the model physically cannot silently commit those fields. What it does PaperPilot is a clean, three-step grant application (business details → financials → applicant profile) complete with a review page, a dashboard, and a home-page pre-qualification widget. In a standard browser, it acts as a normal FastAPI and Jinja form. But open it in Chrome with WebMCP enabled (via flags or the Model Context Tool Inspector), and the page exposes tools like explain_field , check_eligibility , flag_issues , propose_fields , and extract_doc , alongside step-save tools. Eligibility isn't left up to a vague "vibe check"—it’s driven by a strict rules engine. A business qualifies if their revenue is at most $\$5{,}000{,}000$, their headcount is at most $500$, and their year-over-year revenue drop ($d$) is at least 15%. The award estimate is tiered based on that drop, plus a workforce bonus: $$B(d) = \begin{cases} 50000 & d \geq 50 \ 25000 & d \geq 30 \ 10000 & d \geq 15 \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad A = B(d) + \min(500 e,\, 10000)$$ where $e$ stands for full-time employees. Because human reviewers always make the final call, the UI displays this as a calculated range (roughly $0.6A$ to $A$). Crucially, any fields proposed by the agent are saved as FieldValue rows with committed=False . Only a human-triggered CSRF POST can flip them to committed=True . The final Submit application action is never exposed as a WebMCP tool. Try it out: Live Demo · GitHub Repo How we built it The Stack: Powered by Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLModel/SQLite, Jinja2, and vanilla JavaScript in webmcp-tools.js (no React bloat). Document parsing uses pdfplumber and optional Tesseract, passing uploaded files through the exact same validators as typed input plus an injection-phrase filter. Raw OCR data never flows back to the agent. Two WebMCP Surfaces: We utilized both declarative tools (Steps 1 and 2 use <form toolname="..."> so the browser automatically synthesizes submission tools) and imperative tools ( document.modelContext.registerTool() for explanations, eligibility checks, flags, and extractions). Communication & Security: Every execute call makes a same-origin fetch() to /api/... , returning JSON when Accept: application/json is requested so the agent doesn't crash trying to parse an HTML redirect. Security-wise, we shipped HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookies, HTTPS cookie enforcement, CSRF protection, strict same-origin checks on mutating JSON APIs, rate limiting (20 calls / 60s / session), and audit logs. Best of all: no server-side LLM API key . The Inspector's Gemini key stays securely in the browser. Deployment: Containerized via Docker (Python slim + Tesseract) and deployed on Google Cloud Run , with secrets managed through Google Secret Manager. Challenges we ran into Navigation vs. the Inspector: Saving Step 1 by changing window.location.href or pushing to history kept killing the agent mid-turn—tools would vanish, Chrome would crash with mysterious bad-message errors, and traces threw empty responses. A full-page iframe preview was even worse because it registered duplicate tools and threw connection errors. The boring, correct fix? Never change the active tab's URL during a tool turn. Saves return quiet JSON, and the human opens the review page in a new tab when they're ready. HTML vs. JSON Confusion: The agent's fetch() calls kept blindly following human 303 redirects and blowing up on JSON.parse("<!DOCTYPE html>") . We fixed this by cleanly splitting responses based on the Accept header. Human-in-the-Loop as Data, Not Copy: Anyone can write UI text saying "the user confirms." Enforcing that committed=True is structurally impossible to reach from an agent tool path took careful hook design backed by automated tests. Cloud LLMs in the Backend: We initially experimented with server-side Azure OpenAI for field explanations before ripping it out entirely. Grant copy should be deterministic, and document parsing belongs to regex and strict validators. Keeping the LLM solely as the browser agent kept our deployments lightweight and kept API keys out of Cloud Run. Ephemeral SQLite on Cloud Run: It’s fine for a hackathon demo, but a real-world program would need Cloud SQL. We documented the limitation transparently instead of faking persistence. Accomplishments we're proud of Getting a fully functioning WebMCP grant form live on Cloud Run that a Chrome Inspector agent can drive seamlessly with a single prompt—handling explanations, eligibility checks, estimates, and proposals—while leaving final submission strictly in human hands. Successfully blending declarative <form> tools and imperative registerTool() workflows under a single session. Engineering the uncommitted-values pattern where agents draft data, but only human-driven CSRF actions can commit it. Writing 99 automated tests covering validators, rules logic, hooks, and API contracts. What we learned WebMCP isn’t just "ChatGPT that can click." It’s about capability discovery on a document —handling schemas, respecting read-only hints, and avoiding automatic submissions unless explicitly intended. The hardest product problem is lifecycle management: figuring out what happens to modelContext when a document navigates. We also learned to treat the Chrome Inspector like a fragile integration partner: keep it to one tab, don't reload mid-turn, and register tools exactly once. On the domain side, we realized that while eligibility rules are just basic math, applicants feel them as intense anxiety. Presenting awards as a calculated range rather than a hard promise made the whole demo feel like an authentic, reassuring government portal. What's next for PaperPilot Persistent Cloud Storage: Migrating from ephemeral SQLite to PostgreSQL/Cloud SQL to support multi-session draft recoveries. Expanded Document Support: Adding automated parsing for corporate balance sheets, W-2s, and 1099s to speed up financial verification. Enterprise Agency SDK: Packaging our WebMCP components into a drop-in SDK so local and state governments can modernize their legacy portals without compromising security or compliance. title: Paperwork - a form your agent fills while you watch
pitch: A gnarly insurance form the agent fills from plain language while you watch - pending until you accept, and the legal attestations have no tool that can touch them.
about_excerpt: A gnarly insurance form the agent fills from plain language while you watch - pending until you accept, and the legal attestations have no tool that can touch them. Like Comment Story Updates The renters-insurance form: six steps, one pending layer Tool console: get_form called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: three legal attestations are structurally unreachable by any tool - human-only fields enforced in the data model itself, not by prompt instruction. Inspiration Nobody's brain fails at forms; their patience does. A renters-insurance application asks forty questions, a third of which only appear conditionally, in the form's own order - even though the applicant already knows all of it. What it does Tell the agent what happened in plain language; it drafts answers onto the real six-step form, in front of you. Nothing the agent writes is an answer yet - every draft lands in a pending layer, highlighted, tracked by provenance (empty / human / pending / accepted / uncertain), and only counts once you accept it. Three legal attestations - fraud acknowledgement, an animal attestation, final accuracy - are marked human-only in the data model itself: no tool can reach them, structurally, not by instruction. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript. Every tool writes through the same setField() the inputs commit through via one invoke() chokepoint, so conditional fields, repeaters, and validation behave identically whichever side acted. fill_field / fill_section draft into the pending layer; review_submission is read-only and there is no submit tool at all - Submit is a human-only button. Challenges we ran into An edge case in add_repeater_item : when a conditional trigger (e.g. "any claims in the last 5 years?") auto-spawned an empty repeater row, the tool would add a second row instead of reusing the empty one the UI had already created - a subtle UI/agent-state drift caught by explicit testing of the conditional-field interaction, not the isolated tool call. Accomplishments that we're proud of A form where the agent can genuinely say "I'm not sure" - a flagged, visible uncertainty on a field, not a silent guess - and where three specific legal fields are unreachable by any tool, not merely discouraged by one. What we learned Provenance tracking (who wrote this field, and is it still pending) turned out to be the real product, more than the fill-from-text trick itself - it's what makes it safe to let an agent write into a legal document at all. What's next Multi-document support (a second insurer's form with a different question set) to prove the provenance model generalizes beyond one carrier's application. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools). title: PART / NER
pitch: Shop for PC parts with an AI assistant that shares your live build, understands your goals, explains compatibility and trade-offs, and keeps you in control of every choice.
about_excerpt: Shop for PC parts with an AI assistant that shares your live build, understands your goals, explains compatibility and trade-offs, and keeps you in control of every choice. Like Comment Story Updates Browse PC parts while the shopper and AI assistant share the same live build and goals. AI recommendations appear directly in the storefront with goal impact, compatibility, and trade-offs. Agent-proposed changes are staged as a preview. Only the shopper can approve and apply them. Inspiration Choosing PC parts is difficult, especially for people who do not already understand hardware. There are three problems at the same time: Compatibility: Will this CPU work with this motherboard? Will this GPU fit in the case? Is the power supply sufficient? Understanding specs: Numbers like VRAM, wattage, clock speed, and dimensions do not directly tell a shopper what they mean for the games they want to play. Trade-offs: Every choice affects performance, budget, aesthetics, and the parts that can be selected next. Traditional compatibility checkers can tell you whether parts work together, but they do not feel like shopping with a knowledgeable person who understands what you are trying to achieve. We wanted to explore a different experience: what if the AI assistant you already use could shop with you , directly inside the storefront? What it does PART / NER is a PC parts storefront where a shopper and their AI assistant work on the same live build . The shopper can browse and select products normally. The AI assistant can: understand the current PC build and the shopper's goals recommend products directly inside the storefront explain expected game performance in terms of the shopper's FPS targets explain compatibility problems and trade-offs compare options based on performance, budget, and aesthetics prepare multi-part build changes as a preview The shopper always remains in control. The AI cannot directly apply a staged build change. Agent-proposed changes appear as a before/after preview, and only the shopper can apply them by clicking Approve & apply preview on the page. A key WebMCP interaction is that the shopper can ignore the AI's recommendation, manually choose a different part, and the assistant can continue from that updated live build on the next turn. This is not an AI that shops for you. It is an AI that shops with you. How we built it PART / NER is a frontend-only React application. The React UI and WebMCP tools operate on the same shared Zustand store, so human actions and agent actions always refer to the same build state. The app exposes WebMCP tools for: reading the current build setting shopping goals finding products displaying recommendations in the storefront staging build changes resolving compatibility issues For example, recommend_products ranks and renders product candidates without selecting anything, preview_build_changes stages multi-part changes for human review, and resolve_build_issues is dynamically registered only while a compatibility error exists. The application owns deterministic domain logic for: compatibility rules budget calculations fictional benchmark estimates goal evaluation recommendation ranking The AI does not invent prices, compatibility facts, or FPS numbers. Those values come from the application. There is no backend, database, authentication system, retailer API, or model API in the app itself. The catalog contains 30 fictional PC products and fictional games so the demo is reproducible and does not depend on third-party product data. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was deciding where the boundary between the AI and the application should be. It would have been easy to let the model reason about compatibility or generate performance claims, but that would make the experience unreliable. Instead, the application owns the facts and deterministic rules, while the AI focuses on understanding intent, comparing options, and explaining trade-offs. Another challenge was making WebMCP visibly useful rather than simply exposing CRUD-style tools. The key was treating the live build and storefront UI as a shared workspace between the shopper and the assistant. We also deliberately removed the agent's ability to apply build changes directly. An assistant can stage a preview, but only the shopper can approve it on the page. This made the human-agent boundary much clearer. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that the demo shows a genuine collaborative loop between a person and an AI assistant. The AI can recommend the best-value GPU, but the shopper can choose a different GPU for aesthetic reasons. On the next turn, the assistant reads the updated build and continues naturally from the shopper's decision. Recommendations are rendered directly in the storefront instead of existing only as chat text. Compatibility, game-performance goals, budget impact, and trade-offs are presented together so the shopper can make the final decision with useful context. We also implemented versioned previews so an old agent proposal cannot overwrite a newer human choice. What we learned The most interesting part of WebMCP is not automating a website. It is enabling a human and an agent to collaborate through the same interface while each uses what they are good at. The AI can process constraints and explain options quickly. The human can make subjective decisions about appearance, priorities, and preferences. The web application becomes the shared workspace connecting the two. We also learned that meaningful WebMCP tools should expose semantic actions and live application state, rather than reproducing low-level UI automation. What's next for PART / NER A real version could connect to retailer catalogs and verified benchmark sources, support more PC component categories, and incorporate live inventory and pricing. It could also use the shopper's existing AI context and preferences, when available, to make the experience more personalized without requiring the user to start from scratch in every shopping session. The same interaction model could extend beyond PC parts to other purchases where products depend on one another, such as cameras and lenses, home networking equipment, audio systems, or DIY electronics. Build together. Choose with confidence. title: PixelForge
pitch: An agent-native pixel art studio where humans and AI agents operate the same editor through WebMCP — 19 tools, one shared canvas, every action visible and undoable.
about_excerpt: An agent-native pixel art studio where humans and AI agents operate the same editor through WebMCP — 19 tools, one shared canvas, every action visible and undoable. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The PixelForge brand: a pixel anvil where human and agent strokes meet, forged in the app's own 32×32 pixel style. The PixelForge mascot — a slime blacksmith, born in PixelForge and drawn entirely in 32×32 pixels with WebMCP tool calls. Live demo: ChatGPT drawing a green slime inside PixelForge — every tool call visible in the Agent Activity panel, every edit undoable. PixelForge — humans + agents, one canvas. An agent-native pixel art studio where ChatGPT operates the editor through 19 WebMCP tools. Inspiration AI "editors" today are one-shot generators: you prompt, you get a file, and you fix it by hand. The agent never touches the actual software. We asked the opposite question — what if the agent could operate a real creative tool, the same way a human does? A pixel editor turned out to be the perfect answer. Pixel art is 100% structured state — a grid of colors, layers, frames, a palette — which maps exactly onto tool schemas. No vision models, no guesswork: an agent can read the canvas as exact pixel data and edit it through the same primitives a human uses. What it does PixelForge is a complete, Aseprite-inspired pixel art studio: pencil / eraser / flood fill / color picker, brush shapes (circle, square, line) from 1–64px with pixel-perfect strokes, layers (duplicate, merge down, flatten), a cel-based animation timeline with playback, onion skinning, palette sorting & gradients, canvas resize, and PNG / animated GIF / sprite-sheet export. The same studio is also an agent workstation . ChatGPT — or any WebMCP client — can inspect the canvas, batch-draw hundreds of pixels, manage layers and frames, recolor entire animations, and export finished assets, through 19 structured WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool . Try it: open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser and ask: "Create a cute green slime with a simple face, then turn it into a 4-frame idle animation." How we built it React + TypeScript + Vite + Zustand + Tailwind — fully client-side, no backend. The core rule: one action layer, two users. All 19 WebMCP tools call the exact same store actions as the mouse and keyboard. There is no separate "AI drawing" code path — so every agent edit is history-tracked, replayable, and undoable by the human. Tools use strict JSON schemas with batched operations ( draw_pixels takes an array of pixels — no one-call-per-pixel) Layer/frame references resolve by id or name , so agents never need to track internal ids Every tool returns structured JSON: {success, operation, detail} or {success:false, error:{code,message}} — so the agent can reason about failures instead of guessing Read-only tools ( get_editor_state , get_region ) let the agent see the canvas as exact pixel data before acting A live Agent Activity panel shows every tool call with HUMAN/AGENT badges — and every mutation, human or agent, is undoable 38 unit tests cover the editor actions and the tool contracts (schema validity, batched draws, structured errors, undoability of agent mutations). Challenges we ran into Making agent tool calls render live on the canvas while still committing as one undoable step Keeping agents effective across animation frames: layer references are remapped by name, so "draw on the Eyes layer" keeps working after frame switches Designing batched pixel operations that survive strict JSON-schema validation Testing across environments (ChatGPT in-app browser, Chrome with the testing flag) — plus building an honest debug bridge for browsers without WebMCP, clearly labeled so nothing is faked Accomplishments that we're proud of The full creative pipeline runs on WebMCP. A judge can ask ChatGPT: "Create a green slime → make the eyes smaller → turn it into a 4-frame idle animation → make the palette warmer → export a sprite sheet" — and watch every step execute as real tool calls on the live canvas, including 411 pixels placed in a single batched call . A complete product, not a tech demo. In 9 days we built an entire Aseprite-style studio from scratch: cel-based animation timeline, onion skinning, brush shapes with pixel-perfect strokes, palette tools, three export formats — all sharing one action layer with the agent. Trust by design. Every agent operation appears in the activity feed with an AGENT badge and sits in the same undo history as human edits. The human can take back anything the agent did — visibility and control are built in, not bolted on. Verified, not claimed. 38 unit tests cover the editor actions and tool contracts, and the 19 tools were confirmed live in both target environments: ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with the WebMCP testing flag. What we learned Strict schemas beat clever prompts. Because every tool has precise input validation and returns structured errors ( INVALID_COORDINATE , LAYER_NOT_FOUND , NO_SELECTION ), the agent self-corrects instead of hallucinating. And sharing one action layer between human and agent turned out to be the cheapest possible way to earn trust: visibility + undoability come for free. What's next for PixelForge Declarative WebMCP tool registration, agent-driven tileset workflows, multi-sprite projects — and WebMCP support for tiled drawing mode. I leaned on an AI coding agent for scaffolding and iteration, but the core architecture — one shared action layer so the agent and I use the exact same tools — was designed and verified by me. This was my first time building for the WebMCP standard. title: My Project Desk
pitch: A local-first project workspace where people and AI plan, create, reconcile evidence, and review work together, while consequential decisions and completion remain human-controlled.
about_excerpt: A local-first project workspace where people and AI plan, create, reconcile evidence, and review work together, while consequential decisions and completion remain human-controlled. Like Comment Story Updates The Project Desk Dashboard Workspace Options: manage portable copies, local references, and this browser's workspace data. Tasks the agent and human have added to the project Decisions the agent identified the human needs to make Deliverables the agent created based on the tasks and decisions A working record of facts, assumptions, and missing information. Human, agent, and system actions in a shared history. About Project Desk AI agents can create plans, recommendations, and drafts quickly, but the work often remains scattered across chat. People have no durable shared surface for seeing what is verified, what is inferred, what is still unknown, what needs their judgment, and what has actually been approved. Project Desk was built to make that collaboration legible. It gives a person and an agent one project workspace with tasks, decisions, evidence, deliverables, and activity history. What it does A person creates a browser-local workspace and describes an objective. They may add tasks or references themselves, then ask ChatGPT to plan through the open app. The agent inspects the workspace, creates only necessary tasks, records clearly classified evidence, and requests human decisions where judgment is required. After the person answers, the same reusable handoff starts another work pass. The agent reads the latest decisions and references, reconciles stale or answered evidence, and saves substantial plans, briefs, checklists, drafts, or other work products directly into the relevant tasks. The person can request changes, accept a deliverable while keeping the task open, or accept and complete it. Project Desk is local by design. Workspace data stays in the current browser unless the person deliberately exports it, restores a backup, uploads a bounded reference, or asks ChatGPT to work with the open page. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, the agent would have to guess at page meaning from buttons and layout, rely on coordinate clicks, or return work to chat where it becomes detached from project state. Project Desk exposes eleven typed domain actions against the same live workspace the person is reviewing. The agent can inspect state, read references and approved decisions, add necessary work, submit deliverables, record and reconcile evidence, and request judgment. The tool boundary deliberately withholds workspace selection, deliverable acceptance, unrestricted task editing, and human completion. The linked GitHub repository includes the WebMCP tool reference, implementation details, and testing documentation. Instead of repeatedly copying plans, decisions, and revisions between ChatGPT and a separate project tracker, the person and agent can keep the work in one shared workspace. After the person supplies decisions or references, the agent can inspect the updated project, reconcile outdated evidence, advance multiple tasks, and save reviewable deliverables, while the person retains control over acceptance and completion throughout repeated work-and-review rounds. That creates a safer and more useful human-agent loop: the agent can contribute work to a structured application, while evidence, uncertainty, decisions, and final authority remain visible to the person. How it was built Project Desk is a React and TypeScript application packaged for ChatGPT Sites. It uses imperative document.modelContext.registerTool registration for eleven WebMCP tools, explicit JSON schemas for tool inputs, and browser-local storage for project state. Vitest covers workspace isolation, prompt behavior, evidence reconciliation, deliverable review, stale approvals, backup validation, and progress calculation. Challenges The hardest design problem was defining where the agent power should stop. The workflow went through repeated usability tests to remove circular approval steps, distinguish task review from completion, make unanswered evidence actionable, reconcile stale claims after a person supplies information, and explain how repeated work passes are started. Accomplishments Eleven discoverable WebMCP tools with meaningful project-level actions. A complete planning, decision, work, reconciliation, review, and completion loop. Substantial agent deliverables saved in the app rather than stranded in chat. Evidence classifications and history that distinguish verified facts, reports, assumptions, and open questions. Explicit human control over workspace selection, acceptance, and completion. Local backup, restore, export, reset, and bounded reference-file support. What I learned I learned that effective WebMCP tools require more than connecting an agent to an app. The tools need clear descriptions, predictable state changes, visible feedback, and thoughtful approval boundaries so people understand what the agent did and what still needs their judgment. The importance testing by humans still plays in this world where AI can do much of the coding and testing themselves. Testing Project Desk also showed me how important guided onboarding and shared, reviewable work products are for making agent-assisted workflows feel trustworthy and useful. I would not have gotten there without human testing being in the process. What's next for Project Desk After the challenge, Project Desk will become a free Everyday AI Made Simple resource. I have a free resources hub where I provide thoughtful resources to people learning how to use AI tools. Future work may include a version with optional account-based synchronization and templates while retaining the current local-first mode and human-approval boundaries. title: RELAY — One Intent. Many Websites.
pitch: One moving-home request becomes a permissioned, auditable plan across multiple WebMCP-enabled services.
about_excerpt: One moving-home request becomes a permissioned, auditable plan across multiple WebMCP-enabled services. Like Comment Story Updates One intent. Many websites. Moving home is not one task. It creates repeated updates across council, energy, water, postal, insurance, broadband, and employer websites. People re-enter the same information, compare consequences, remember which services changed, and trust that nothing outside their intent was touched. RELAY is a one-screen coordination workspace for this life event. A person enters their current address, destination, move date, forwarding period, and approval threshold once. RELAY converts that intent into an explicit delegation policy and coordinates six fictional services through structured WebMCP tools. A better human-agent relationship Low-risk changes run in order. Actions outside the policy are refused. When Wavelength proposes a broadband transfer that raises the monthly price from £36 to £42, RELAY stops at a visible human checkpoint. The person reviews the exact provider, action, plan, price, contract, date, and one-use scope before approving. Every successful mutation creates an append-only receipt. Rejected actions create separate refusal evidence proving that provider state did not change. The result is useful automation without unlimited authority. Why WebMCP Conventional browser automation guesses from pixels and page structure. RELAY instead exposes 27 focused tools through document.modelContext. An agent can inspect the move plan, read permissions, preview provider effects, execute allowed changes, request a human decision, retrieve receipts, and run controlled safety challenges through structured inputs and outputs. The agent and visible interface share the same browser-local domain state. Mutations pass through the same policy regardless of whether they originate from the interface or a WebMCP call. High-risk internet-plan changes require an exact, unexpired, single-use approval grant bound to the provider, action, proposal, plan, price, contract, move date, and postcode. Changed terms, replay, expiry, wrong-provider use, wrong-action use, and out-of-order actions are refused before mutation. What people and agents can do together A person can express one outcome and its boundaries once. An agent can coordinate the dependent work across multiple service surfaces, stop for a precise decision, resume with narrowly scoped authority, and return a coherent record of what changed. This preview → policy → human approval → scoped commit → receipt pattern can extend beyond moving home to starting university, changing jobs, travel, government services, financial administration, and other multi-provider workflows. Key features Six fictional service providers sharing one move plan 27 structured WebMCP tools on the main workspace Standalone WebMCP surfaces for provider sites Explicit allow, ask, and never-change delegation boundaries Preview-before-commit mutations Exact human approval for a recurring price increase Ten-minute, single-use, replay-safe approval grants Six append-only action receipts Five executable adversarial safety challenges Visible activity trace with tool names, scoped inputs, results, and receipt IDs Responsive, accessible mission-control interface Implementation RELAY uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Vinext, and ChatGPT Sites. The shared domain layer owns the move plan, service ordering, policy decisions, approval grants, receipts, and refusals. A dedicated tool-definition layer exposes testable WebMCP contracts, while the registration lifecycle registers and unregisters them through document.modelContext. The main workspace and provider pages use the same browser-local fictional service ledger, preventing human actions, agent actions, receipts, and visible state from drifting into separate demonstrations. Verification The release includes 29 automated tests, ten isolated tool-driven rehearsals, ten production-interface rehearsals, a five-image evidence set, and a narrated 2:47 public demonstration. Lint and production builds pass, the production dependency audit reports zero vulnerabilities, and the public app, repository, and video have all been verified without private-session access. All displayed people, addresses, providers, accounts, and transactions are fictional. No credentials are required.
