title: ReturnReady
pitch: ReturnReady turns scattered receipts and work records into an evidence-linked, review-ready Australian tax return draft, using WebMCP to prepare, verify, and resolve gaps.
about_excerpt: ReturnReady turns scattered receipts and work records into an evidence-linked, review-ready Australian tax return draft, using WebMCP to prepare, verify, and resolve gaps. Like Comment Story Updates Start with a sparse FY2025-26 evidence draft, then complete it manually or let Codex populate structured facts through WebMCP. Codex records 3 disposals while preserving AAPL’s user attestation and BTC’s warning. Generated Review Pack with unresolved warning Inspiration This started with my own tax return. Most of it was prefilled, but my foreign shares and crypto weren't - so I was the one who had to get all of it in. That meant logging into each broker, exporting my holdings (every platform in its own format), and then typing each position in by hand. It's tedious, easy to get wrong, and it's the same job every year. The hard part was never the tax treatment. It was moving structured facts out of a pile of exports and into one draft I could actually review, without losing track of where each number came from or which ones the paperwork couldn't answer. That's the gap ReturnReady goes after. ReturnReady is a small WebMCP experiment: I attach synthetic evidence to Codex, Codex pulls the structured facts out (outside the page), and the app exposes a few narrow tools for recording and checking those facts. I still review everything and fill in anything the evidence can't prove. What it does ReturnReady opens on a sparse FY2025–26 draft with a bit of prefilled PAYG context. From there you can add deductions and disposals yourself, or ask Codex to do it through WebMCP. The demo walks through: 40 hours of work-from-home, at the prototype's fixed rate, giving a visible $28 deduction MSFT and AAPL foreign-share disposals a BTC disposal with the transaction fee left out on purpose The evidence doesn't contain AAPL's acquisition details, so validation raises a blocker instead of making the numbers up. You supply those facts yourself as a user attestation, which stays visibly separate from anything backed by a document. Once the blocker is cleared, ReturnReady builds a review pack, keeping the unresolved BTC warning and logging every action along the way. One thing worth being clear about: ReturnReady organizes evidence. It doesn't lodge returns, give tax advice, work out the authoritative tax, or claim your return is complete. The gains and losses are amounts I worked out myself and entered; the app records and checks them, it doesn't calculate them. Why WebMCP Normal browser automation has to read the DOM, guess what each control does, and poke at fields from the outside. ReturnReady skips all of that. It exposes six tools with tight JSON Schemas: get_return_draft record_deductions record_disposals record_acquisition_details validate_review_pack generate_review_pack Both the agent and the manual UI go through the same controller and the same domain logic. So WebMCP speeds up data entry without getting around validation, provenance, idempotency, or the audit trail and if WebMCP isn't available, the manual workflow still works on its own. How I built it ReturnReady is a static React app in strict TypeScript, built with Vite, no backend. It registers its tools imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool checks its input against an allow-list at the schema boundary, then checks it again inside the handler. The page never sees the attached files or the raw document text. No tool takes a file path, a URL, a selector, executable content, or arbitrary JavaScript. All the bundled evidence and values are synthetic. For tests, Vitest and Testing Library cover the domain rules, the security boundaries, tool annotations, bounded outputs, idempotency, and making sure a human and the agent get the same result. Playwright runs the whole manual workflow end to end for accessibility. Challenges I ran into The main one was keeping a single trustworthy workflow across two ways in. Early on, validation triggered by the agent could look different from validation triggered by a human. I fixed it by deriving the modal and the review pack from shared controller state, and added a regression test that runs the real WebMCP handler against the rendered UI. The other challenge was one I felt as a builder: the page deliberately never touches the raw files. Part of me wanted to just let the app accept an upload and parse it, that's the obvious and easy path. But that's exactly the boundary that makes this trustworthy, so keeping all the file handling outside the page stayed non-negotiable, even when it made the build feel more restrictive than it had to be. I also kept the scope tight on purpose. ReturnReady shows the recorded facts and a fixed-rate deduction result, but it doesn't try to calculate capital gains or guess at missing acquisition data. Accomplishments that I am proud of 6 small WebMCP tools instead of handing over the whole browser one shared domain layer behind both the manual and agent paths provenance that clearly separates documentary evidence from user attestation invalid or conflicting calls get rejected cleanly, with no change to state repeat calls are idempotent, they don't pile up duplicate records a review pack that carries unresolved warnings through instead of hiding them a fully synthetic demo anyone can reproduce What I learned WebMCP earns its keep when it exposes what things mean, not when it turns every button into a tool. A small, semantic surface lets the agent move fast while the app keeps hold of the parts that matter: validation, state changes, and deciding what the person actually needs to review. What's next for ReturnReady More evidence categories, better review exports for an accountant, and a few real calculation methods so the amounts don't all have to be worked out by hand first, all while keeping raw-file interpretation outside the page and the same trust boundary intact. title: daymaker.fun — DayOps for real life
pitch: Your day changed. Your plan should too — a shared DayOps board where people and agents recover disrupted plans together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Your day changed. Your plan should too — a shared DayOps board where people and agents recover disrupted plans together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Plans do not fail inside planning apps. They fail in the real world: an activity runs late, the group gets tired, weather changes, or a fixed commitment constrains everything else. An agent can research alternatives, but its answer normally becomes another block of chat text that someone must manually copy into notes, maps, and a schedule. We wanted to close that loop. The human should report reality. The agent should handle the research and replanning. Both should work on the same live artifact. What it does daymaker.fun is a shared DayOps board for humans and agents. A person describes or edits the real needs of the day. The agent reads the same live state, researches appropriate places, and uses five focused WebMCP tools to structure the brief, add source-backed stops, update statuses, and reorder the proposed schedule. Each accepted change appears immediately in the interface. Fixed requirements stay visible, stale writes are rejected, and each revision can be shared with another device through a self-contained portable link. Unlike a traditional itinerary generator, daymaker.fun is designed for recovering a plan after reality changes. The person keeps direct control of requirements; the agent handles the tedious restructuring and research. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent can describe a revised day but cannot reliably read the current board or apply structured changes to the exact artifact the person is viewing. DOM clicking would be brittle, and the chat answer would drift away from the plan. daymaker.fun exposes five focused tools: get_mission_state reads the live brief, Needs, schedule, locks, sources, revision, and portable URL. update_day_context structures or updates the planning context. update_mission_stop changes an existing stop by stable ID. add_mission_stop adds one researched, source-backed stop. reorder_mission_stops reorders future stops while preserving locked commitments. These tools call the same typed domain transitions as the human UI. WebMCP is therefore the shared state and action layer that makes the product possible, not an add-on. How we built it daymaker.fun is a local-first React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vite. Mission is the single domain source of truth. Human controls and the WebMCP adapter dispatch actions through the same pure transition layer and store. Strict Zod schemas validate every tool input, and optimistic revision checks prevent stale agents from overwriting newer human changes. The top-level page registers five imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(), feature-detects support, and owns their lifecycle with one abort signal. In browsers without WebMCP, the normal human interface remains usable. Each tab holds one mission in memory. Portable links serialize the validated mission as UTF-8 JSON, gzip it, encode it as unpadded base64url, and place it in the URL fragment. The recipient gets the exact point-in-time plan without an account or backend, and the fragment is not sent to the host. Codex helped build, debug, test, deploy, and document the application, including the cross-device portable-link hotfix. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was choosing a small tool surface that gives the agent enough control without overlapping actions or hiding consequential changes. We also had to preserve fixed requirements, make agent changes immediately legible, reject stale revisions, and make long portable links reliable across devices and Safari. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human–agent loop from editable real-world Needs to a visible, source-backed schedule. Five narrow WebMCP tools backed by one shared domain model. Runtime validation, invariant checks, and revision-safe mutations. Cross-device plan snapshots without a backend. A responsive interface that remains useful without WebMCP. 102 unit/component tests and 8 Playwright end-to-end tests passing in the final preflight. What we learned Agent-native UX is not chat placed next to an app. It is a well-designed shared state model, a small set of precise actions, and immediate visual verification. The most useful WebMCP tools were the ones that cleanly connected reasoning to existing product behavior. What's next for daymaker.fun Consent-based live location, collaborative missions, weather and transit adapters, richer route evaluation, and reusable DayOps templates for families, events, road trips, and field teams. title: Sightline
pitch: Sightline is an incident console a human and an AI agent debug together on one screen. Nine WebMCP tools, no chat panel, nothing mocked — and a production rollback only a human can approve.
about_excerpt: Sightline is an incident console a human and an AI agent debug together on one screen. Nine WebMCP tools, no chat panel, nothing mocked — and a production rollback only a human can approve. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "AI for observability" demo we'd seen put the agent in a sidebar. You type a question, it answers in a chat bubble, and the dashboard sits there untouched — two separate surfaces that happen to be about the same outage. That is not how two engineers debug an incident. They look at the same screen. One drags the time window, the other says "there, that span," and neither narrates what they just clicked. WebMCP makes that possible for the first time: the page can hand an agent real tools instead of asking it to read pixels. So we built the thing the sidebar demo is a substitute for. What it does Sightline is a single-screen incident console. A production incident is in progress: checkout latency is spiking. A human on-call engineer and an external AI agent — ChatGPT, or Chrome with WebMCP enabled — investigate it at the same time, on the same screen. There is no chat panel in the app and we call no model API. The page registers nine WebMCP tools and renders state; the agent is whatever host you open it in. The agent queries metrics, pulls traces, searches logs, correlates a deploy, pins findings with confidence and source references, proposes a rollback the human must approve, and drafts a postmortem from what was pinned. Every call visibly changes the screen, every pane says who last touched it, and every call can be opened to read the exact arguments and the exact JSON that came back. The handoff. Drag the chart handles to 14:15–14:30, click a trace, then ask the agent what you're looking at. get_current_view reads your window, your open trace and your filters, and it continues your investigation instead of restarting it. The header stamps the second it happened. The incident. checkout-service p99 jumps from 181ms to 3.5s at 14:20 while p50 moves 1.25× — the tell that requests are queueing, not computing. 96.2% of trace time sits in db.connection.acquire . The pool logs 18 acquisition timeouts. dep-1104 shipped eight minutes before onset and its diff reads hikari.maximumPoolSize 50 → 10 . Two red herrings sit in the data — an unrelated cache deploy, and a deploy that lands 35 minutes after onset — plus a downstream service that looks sick but is only a victim. How we built it Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Recharts, Zustand. No backend, no database, no API keys. One store, no parallel code path. Tools are not a second implementation. filter_traces calls setTraceFilter ; so does the input in the trace pane header. Every action carries an actor, which is how the interface can attribute what happened. Anything the agent can do, a human can do, and each sees the other's work immediately. Nothing is mocked. Every value a tool returns is computed from the fixture series by real code — median baselines, a change-point detector, span aggregation, log pattern grouping, deploy proximity scoring. If query_metrics reports a 3498.6ms peak at 14:49, that is Math.max over the series. The fixture is generated deterministically — no Math.random , no Date.now , hash-based noise — so the same minute always produces the same value and the demo is reproducible. Errors teach the caller how to retry. Not "No results" but: No traces for checkout-service at or above 3000ms in 13:30-14:00. The slowest trace in that window is 197.9ms — lower min_latency_ms to 158 or below to see it. The approval gate is structural. propose_rollback writes a proposal and returns awaiting_human_approval . The only function that applies a rollback is store.approveRollback , and its only caller is the Approve button's onClick . A test runs every registered tool with arguments plausible enough to do damage while a proposal is pending and asserts the rollback stays unapplied — and checks its own tool list against the registry so a new tool can't skip it. The interface has one signature idea and one motion. Every pane header carries a provenance stamp naming who last changed it and how. When a tool mutates a pane, that pane gets one sharp flash in the colour of whoever caused it. Nothing else animates. Challenges we ran into A rejected tool promise throws away your error message. The WebMCP spec discards the rejection reason and reports a bare failure to the agent. We had written careful retry hints into every error path — all of which would have vanished. Tools never throw; they resolve with isError and the hint survives. Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 or nothing works. registerTool() rejects with a SecurityError unless the document is origin-keyed, and it fails quietly enough that you'd blame your own code. We send the header in dev, preview and production, and the app surfaces window.originAgentCluster in its diagnostic so the failure names itself. The IDL and the implementation disagree. The spec declares executeTool(tool, object inputObject) , but Chrome wants the arguments as a JSON string and answers "Failed to parse input arguments" for an object — and it resolves to a string , not the ToolResult . We only found both by calling the API against a live browser. The hardest problem was not code. From the single prompt "Checkout p99 is spiking. Find out why." , the agent reached the root cause unaided on the first attempt — the deploy, the pool size, the p50-versus-p99 reasoning, both red herrings dismissed. And then it wrote the answer in the chat window and pinned nothing. It had treated the task as a question to answer. Nothing in our tool surface told it that the on-call engineer is looking at the console, not at the conversation — so a conclusion stated in a reply reaches no one. The fix was entirely in tool descriptions and in what each read tool returns: every one now ends with a next step computed from what that call actually found, and the tool the agent is holding when the answer lands spells out that describing a fix in conversation puts nothing on anyone's screen. That iteration, not the app, was the real work. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent solves a deliberately noisy incident from one sentence, with no hints , and rejects both red herrings on the way. The safety gate is structural, not decorative — and there is a test that proves no tool can reach it. get_current_view makes the handoff real in both directions: the agent continues from a window you dragged and a trace you opened. The protocol is inspectable. Any call opens to show the exact arguments and the exact JSON reply. The approval gate shows pre-flight checks computed from the deploy — restore target, later deploys, migrations in the diff — rather than reassuring constants. An approval gate that displays a check it never ran is worse than one that shows nothing. What we learned Tool descriptions are the product. The schemas took an afternoon; getting an agent to behave like a colleague rather than a search engine took the rest of the day, and every fix was a sentence, not a function. Agents infer the shape of the job from the tools you hand them. Ours had all the information it needed and still stopped at an answer, because nothing said the work included recording it. Once the tools said so, it did. And a detector and an alert threshold answer different questions. A service can be alerting with no change point in its series — when two of your tools disagree, the fix is to say why, not to move the threshold until they agree. What's next for Sightline Real telemetry backends behind the same tool contracts — the analysis layer already takes series and returns summaries, so the fixture is the only thing to replace. Multi-incident state, so get_current_view can hand over an entire war room rather than one board. And a second operator: two humans and an agent on the same console, with provenance stamps that already know how to name three parties instead of two. title: SlideForge
pitch: Ask an agent to build a slide, or edit it by hand — nothing regenerates. You're both on the same live deck.
about_excerpt: Ask an agent to build a slide, or edit it by hand — nothing regenerates. You're both on the same live deck. Like Comment Story Updates One tool call and the whole deck restyles instantly — no rebuild, no delay. Seconds later, another instant restyle to Emerald — every slide updates together, live. A real bar chart from live agent data, with every tool call logged in the Activity Panel. A simple bullet-point slide, written entirely by an agent — no templates, just a tool call. TL;DR One shared document. Click a region and type, or ask an agent to do it — both land in the exact same state a heartbeat later. No "apply AI changes" button, no regeneration, no separate modes. 19 real tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() — the actual WebMCP API, not a chatbot glued onto a canvas. We built an image-generation tool, tested it against real agents, watched it hallucinate a fake gstatic.com URL twice, and deleted it — replaced with real chart and diagram data instead, which models can actually produce. Live: webmcp-beryl.vercel.app · Code: github.com/Aswin-hash/slideforge Unscripted footage: apply_theme fires from a real agent call and every slide re-skins immediately — no rebuild, no delay. Inspiration Every "AI slide generator" we'd tried worked the same way: you prompt, it regenerates the whole deck, and whatever you had is gone. There's a human mode and an AI mode, and the two don't really talk to each other — editing by hand means you've opted out of the AI, and re-prompting means you've opted out of your edits. WebMCP looked like the way out. Instead of an agent screenshotting a page and guessing where to click, document.modelContext.registerTool() lets a page hand an agent a list of exact, callable actions — the same actions a human has, exposed directly. That's not "AI generates a slide deck." That's "a human and an agent share one editable document, through the same interface." We wanted to see if that idea actually held up once a real agent, not a scripted demo, was driving it. What it does SlideForge is a presentation editor with one shared state — a Zustand store — and exactly one way to change it. A slide is a named layout ( title-slide , two-column , media-split , …) made of typed, addressable regions: title , body , left_body , text, bullets, a real bar/pie chart, a flow diagram. A human clicks a region and types. An agent calls one of 19 tools — set_bullets , set_chart_data , apply_theme , reorder_slides — and the exact same store updates, the exact same way. Both are logged to a live Activity Panel, so nothing an agent does is invisible. There's also an Agent Console built into the app itself — pick any of the 19 tools, fill in its arguments, run it. It calls the identical code a real WebMCP host would call, which turned out to be essential, because most browsers don't support WebMCP yet (more on that below). The agent calls set_chart_data with real {label, value} numbers — that's an actual rendered chart, not a screenshot of one pasted into a slide. How we built it React 19 + TypeScript + Vite, Zustand for state (wrapped in persist , so a page refresh doesn't wipe the deck out from under a live agent conversation), Tailwind for styling. No backend, no API keys, no server — the whole thing is a static SPA. The part we're proudest of architecturally: every slide is rendered at a fixed 960×540 resolution and scaled into whatever container it's in via a ResizeObserver + CSS transform . The filmstrip thumbnails and the full canvas are the same component tree , just scaled differently — not two rendering paths that can drift out of sync. The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin: a ToolDef array, one runTool() function that wraps every call in try/catch and logs the result, and a single useRegisterTools() hook that registers all 19 at the app root. Every tool's execute() calls straight into a plain Zustand store action — the same action a click handler in the UI calls. That's the whole trick: there was never a second write path to keep in sync, because we never built one. Challenges we ran into This is where most of the real work happened — not in the initial build, but in what broke once real agents (Gemini, then Claude) started actually driving it. Stale ids that quietly broke everything. Every time the deck reset — a page refresh, a "Reset to sample deck" click — every slide and region got a brand new random id. An agent mid-conversation had no way to know that happened, so it kept confidently calling tools with ids that no longer existed. The fix was two-fold: persist the deck to localStorage so a refresh doesn't regenerate it, and default every tool's slideId to the currently active slide unless explicitly given (except the one destructive tool, remove_slide , which we deliberately left strict). Agents doing unnecessary reconnaissance. Early on, nearly every content edit was preceded by a get_slide_structure call just to learn a region's id — even for layouts the agent had just created itself. We let every content tool accept a region's name directly ( left_body , body , media ) instead of demanding an opaque id, and made a wrong guess fail with the slide's actual region names listed right in the error. That collapsed most two-call sequences into one. A tool description that was quietly sabotaging itself. set_region_type 's description told agents to "call this before filling a region whose type doesn't match" — which sounded reasonable, except every content tool already converts a region's type automatically. We watched an agent dutifully call set_region_type , get a success message, and then just... stop, having "completed" a step that did nothing useful. Fixing that one sentence fixed a whole class of dead-end conversations. We shipped an image tool and had to kill it. set_region_image took a URL, actually verified it loaded via a real fetch , and rejected dead links with a clear error. It worked exactly as designed — and it still failed, twice, because the model asked to "generate an image" doesn't have pixels to give you. It hallucinated a very plausible-looking gstatic.com/lamda/images/gemini_logo_...png URL — right domain, right path shape, completely fake. No amount of validation on our end fixes a model inventing a URL that was never real. We removed the tool entirely and replaced it with set_chart_data and set_diagram_steps : structured numbers and short labels are squarely inside what a text model can actually generate, and every test since has worked. Model tier mattered more than any tool design decision we made. The exact same tool set, the exact same prompts, went from stalling constantly on a "lite" model tier to completing 12+ chained tool calls without a single error on a larger one. No prompt engineering on our side closed that gap — it's a genuine capability difference in multi-step planning, and it taught us to design tools that are forgiving of a weaker model's mistakes (clear errors, sane defaults, informative failures) rather than assuming a strong one. What we learned Tool descriptions are the UX. We spent as much time rewriting a sentence in a JSON Schema description field as we did writing components — and it mattered just as much. A tool that quietly implies an unnecessary step, or doesn't say what it can't do, will get an agent to confidently waste a turn on nothing. You cannot design this by imagining how an agent should behave — you have to watch a real one behave, badly, and fix exactly what actually happened. Every hardening decision in this project — the name-based region targeting, the default-to-active-slide behavior, the image tool's removal, the rewritten set_region_type description — came from a specific, reproduced failure, not a hypothesis. And WebMCP itself is genuinely early. No mainstream consumer browser calls document.modelContext tools by default yet — we built the Agent Console specifically so the tool layer was testable without needing bleeding-edge browser flags. That's not a workaround we're embarrassed by; it's proof the tools work independent of which host eventually adopts the standard. What's next Import an existing PowerPoint's theme and fonts so a deck starts from your brand, not a blank slate. More layouts. And, when a model actually can hand a tool real image bytes instead of a hallucinated URL, set_region_image gets to come back. title: TLDW | Too Long Didn't Watch
pitch: For those who want to Cut Through The Noise to Get to The Signal in their YouTube videos.
about_excerpt: For those who want to Cut Through The Noise to Get to The Signal in their YouTube videos. Like Comment Story Updates Step 1 Processing Result Icon Inspiration In a world of AI there is too much noise, this is a simple tool to leverage that very same AI to help cut through the noise to get to the signal of your YouTube videos. What it does TLDW is one web page where you paste a YouTube link and gets the captions, with the moment each line was said. An AI agent opening the page finds two WebMCP tools instead of buttons: get_transcript(url) hands it the captions as timestamped segments, and render_explainer(slides, url) draws whatever the agent wrote back onto the page, every timestamp a link that opens the video at that second, then reads it aloud. The thinking runs on the visitor's own ChatGPT plan, in their own session. How its built Built entirely with AI, Both tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool, with navigator.modelContext as a fallback for older builds, each with a JSON schema an agent can read. Errors are returned, never thrown, so a failure arrives as a result the agent can act on. Every fetch has three outcomes, not two: ok, not_measured with a reason, or a structured error, because a tool that cannot tell a failed measurement from a real zero will report the first as the second. Captions come from a transcript API first with a direct fetch behind it, held in memory for ten minutes and never written down. The page is served by a Cloudflare Worker. Read-aloud uses the browser's own voices by default with a voice picker; one opt-in experimental entry renders a natural voice on our server and streams it back. An agent whose browser has no WebMCP yet can paste the same slides into a Render box on the page and get the identical result. It was built from nothing in one evening, live on stream, by a fleet of AI bodies run by one human, with two independent reviews on every change. Challenges We (Myself and my AI Team) only had ~8 total hours for this as that's when I found out about the competition, then immediately started live streaming the start to finish. We had about ~3 hours of prep while waiting for the reset then 5 hours to build. The spec moved while we built: our first registration was on navigator.modelContext only, and Chrome's stable build binds document.modelContext, so the tools registered and nobody could see them. YouTube refuses caption fetches from a server, so the free path failed silently until we made refusal a first-class result and put a transcript API in front of it. Agents that fetched the captions then answered in chat instead of drawing on the page, until the tool text put the obligation before the data. And the browser's speech queue armed from the speak call rather than from what was drawn, so a slide with the wrong shape left a full explainer on screen and nothing to play. Each one was found by a second reader, not by the author. Accomplishments that we're proud of We got it done 40mins past the buzzer but fortunately there was a 12 hour extension, so we polished the video and made minor edits to the description etc (also generated by AI) The tool work on a free ChatGPT account, the desktop app's built-in browser, and with one sentence: explain this video and render it on the page. The page registers two tools, the agent calls them, the explainer appears with timestamps that jump into the YouTube video if you want to watch a particular segment in full, and it also comes with a reads aloud bar with play back controls and voice selection that uses your browser supported voices and 2 x experimental neural voices. The public repository has one clean history, one identity, and passed a whole-history scan by a stranger before it went public. What we learned The hard part was restraint. Every instinct said add a summarizer, add a model, add a key, and each one would have made it slower, costlier. The second lesson was the error surface: an agent is not a human staring at a stack trace, it reads your failure and decides what to do next, so a tool that throws ends the conversation and a tool that returns a readable error lets the agent try something sensible. The third was the voices, Chrome free supports free neural style voices as well as system voices, the ChatGPT browser uses only the free system voice. We are experimenting with some neural voices but the render time is slower, there could be an option to use something like Elevenlabs but then that would mean have to charge a fee for the service or run ad's on the page. It would be good if the ChatGPT could somehow enable support for the Chrome voices as those are pretty good. What's next for TLDW | Too Long Didn't Watch This is TLDW v1 .v2 & v3 will be better. I didn't want to create something that Notebook LM already does so keeping it video focused is the lane I'll stay in for now. v2 would be more generating more interactive lessons / explainers with interactive kinetic elements maybe a quiz at the end and then perhaps v3 would be the ability to generate a Summarized Explainer Video about the video on the fly. and then later another version of the product for teachers that uses the same logic and flow to help produce lesson plans and explainers on the fly for all students at all levels with all styles of learning requirements. title: TemplateForge
pitch: TemplateForge lets people and AI agents safely customize, preview, and export polished HTML email templates and presentation decks through a visual, WebMCP-powered workspace.
about_excerpt: TemplateForge lets people and AI agents safely customize, preview, and export polished HTML email templates and presentation decks through a visual, WebMCP-powered workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Many teams already have good email templates and presentation decks, but updating them can still mean editing fragile HTML, waiting for a developer, or trusting an AI assistant that may change the wrong element. I wanted to create a workflow where people can use polished existing templates visually while AI agents help with precise, controlled edits. TemplateForge was inspired by the idea that agents should accelerate creative work without taking control away from the person. What it does TemplateForge is a WebMCP-powered visual editor for HTML email templates and presentation decks. Users can choose from Email and Deck libraries, select visible content directly on the rendered template, edit text and supported visual properties, preview emails on desktop or mobile, navigate multi-slide decks, and export portable HTML. AI agents can collaborate through native WebMCP tools. They can list safe editable elements, select an exact target, and update only supported fields. Every agent action is shown in an activity timeline with the target, old value, new value, and a human Undo option. How I built it TemplateForge is built as a static web application with JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and Vite. It is publicly deployed with ChatGPT Sites. The project includes curated HTML email templates and presentation decks, with original MIT licenses and attributions preserved. Visual drafts are saved in the browser so source templates remain unchanged. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Read tools expose safe template details, while write tools validate the requested target and property before updating the visible draft. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was making agent editing useful without making it risky. Initially, an agent needed a person to select an element before it could make a change. I improved this by adding list_editable_elements and select_canvas_element , allowing the agent to find and select a stable approved target before updating it. Another challenge was deck navigation. Editing content on later slides could disrupt the active slide, so I refined the editor to preserve the current slide while editing. I also ensured exported decks always open from slide one. Accomplishments that I’m proud of Built a complete visual workspace for both emails and decks instead of a single-purpose demo. Added 17 email templates and 34 deck templates as usable starting points. Implemented native WebMCP tools for structured, bounded agent actions. Created a transparent agent activity timeline with old/new values and Undo. Enabled editing on multi-slide decks without losing the active slide. Deployed a public, working application with a public source repository and open-source license. What I learned This project showed that effective human-agent collaboration needs more than a chat interface. Agents need structured tools and safe boundaries; people need transparency, review, and reversible control. WebMCP makes it possible to expose these capabilities directly in the browser and allows an agent to interact with a real application in a more reliable way than guessing at page structure. What’s next for TemplateForge Next, I would add user accounts and cloud-saved projects so templates can be revisited across devices. I would also add collaborative workspaces, reusable brand kits, version history, richer deck controls, and more advanced agent workflows for tasks such as rewriting copy across a campaign while preserving approved design and brand rules. title: Vast
pitch: A real-time collaborative canvas that gives AI agents the same tools a human uses not screenshots, not clicks, the actual API.
about_excerpt: A real-time collaborative canvas that gives AI agents the same tools a human uses not screenshots, not clicks, the actual API. Like Comment Story Updates vast Inspiration Every "AI edits your app" demo we'd seen worked the same way: an LLM either writes DOM-manipulation code and hopes it doesn't break something, or a browser-automation layer clicks around pretending to be a mouse. Neither one actually knows what a "connector" or a "frame" means in the app it's touching it's reverse-engineering intent from pixels. We'd already built Vast as a from-scratch realtime canvas rooms, shapes, live cursors, a shared undo stack as its own project, no AI involved. When WebMCP landed, the fit was obvious: Vast is already multiplayer. Every edit already goes through a typed, named function (create_element, align_elements, undo_action) over the same Socket.IO connection every guest uses. Making an agent a participant didn't mean bolting on a special "AI mode" it meant registering those exact functions as tools and letting an agent join the room like any other guest. What it does How we built it The base —Vite/React/TypeScript/Canvas2D client, Node/Express/Socket.IO server in a layered architecture, Postgres for shape state and an event log came together first, over about five days, ~14,000 lines. WebMCP went in afterward in a single focused push, under one rule: no separate agent path. Every tool calls the exact same socket events a human edit fires. Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of One code path, not two an agent literally cannot do anything the UI itself couldn't. Undo/redo that's genuinely shared between human and agent, cascades and all. A believable peer, not a gimmick the agent gets a name, color, and cursor because the server has no privileged notion of "human" to begin with. Real, deployable output via export_html, not just a screenshot of a session. Native-first: proving out where WebMCP is headed, not propping up an API that doesn't exist yet. What we learned What's next for Vast More tools under the same rule grouping, z-order, true component instances. Multi-agent rooms, to stress-test the undo stack with more than one agent peer at once. Giving the agent read access to why something was drawn (nearby notes, replay history), not just current state. Scoped tool permissions once the server has real auth, without breaking the no-separate-path guarantee. Following WebMCP beyond Chrome as other runtimes adopt document.modelContext. title: Vitals Incident Room
pitch: AI agents and engineers investigate, remediate, and verify production incidents together.
about_excerpt: AI agents and engineers investigate, remediate, and verify production incidents together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Vitals Incident Room Dashboard Vitals Incident Room Agent Capabilities Vitals Incident Room Architecture Inspiration Vitals started with a simple frustration: when a production incident happens, engineers rarely investigate it in one place. They jump between dashboards, logs, traces, deployment history, alerts, and remediation tools, manually connecting the dots under pressure. While exploring WebMCP, I saw an opportunity to rethink that workflow. AI agents are increasingly capable of reasoning about complex engineering problems, but traditionally they have had to interact with web applications through the UI or through completely separate integrations. That creates a gap between what an agent can reason about and what it can actually do. So I asked: What if the observability application itself could expose its capabilities directly to an AI agent, while the engineer and agent remained in the same workspace? That became Vitals Incident Room , an experiment in what an agent-native incident-response workflow could look like. I wanted to go beyond "add a chatbot to a dashboard." The goal was to make the agent a genuine participant in the incident lifecycle while keeping the human in control of consequential decisions. What it does Vitals Incident Room is a WebMCP-powered incident-response workspace where engineers and AI agents investigate, remediate, and verify production incidents together. For demonstration, a checkout-api service experiences a severe latency and error-rate regression shortly after deployment v2.8.3 . The agent can discover and invoke structured WebMCP tools to: inspect service health, query metrics, compare deployments, inspect distributed traces, search operational logs, analyze the gathered evidence, prepare a remediation, apply an approved remediation, verify recovery. The investigation can look like: get_service_health ↓ query_metrics ↓ compare_deployments ↓ inspect_trace ↓ search_logs ↓ analyze_incident The agent correlates those signals and identifies the most likely cause: a database query regression introduced in v2.8.3 . It can then prepare a rollback to the last known-good version. However, the agent cannot authorize its own action. prepare_remediation ↓ HUMAN APPROVAL ↓ apply_remediation ↓ verify_recovery ↓ RESOLVED The remediation changes the application's simulated system state, and the final verification checks that both latency and error rate have actually returned to acceptable levels. The result is a shared workflow rather than a chatbot sitting beside an observability dashboard. How I built it Vitals Incident Room extends existing Vitals observability work with a focused browser-based Incident Room designed specifically around WebMCP. The application is built with TypeScript and React, with a deterministic simulated observability environment so the complete workflow can be reproduced without requiring real production credentials or infrastructure. The architecture separates the WebMCP layer from the application domain: Architecture Layer Component Responsibility Human Engineer Reviews evidence and authorizes consequential actions Web App Incident Room Presents shared incident state and workflow Agent Interface WebMCP Tool Surface Exposes structured capabilities to the AI agent Agent AI Agent Discovers tools, gathers evidence, analyzes the incident, and executes approved actions Observability Metrics · Logs · Traces · Deployments Provides the signals used for diagnosis Analysis Evidence Correlation Combines signals into a ranked root-cause hypothesis Remediation Prepare → Approve → Execute Proposes and safely applies the remediation Verification Recovery Checks Confirms latency and error-rate recovery before resolution Core flow: Engineer → Incident Room → WebMCP → AI Agent → Observability Data → Evidence Analysis → Remediation Proposal → Human Approval → Execution → Verification The WebMCP layer exposes nine focused tools with explicit schemas and annotations. Read-only investigation capabilities are separated from state-changing operations, and operational logs are explicitly treated as untrusted content. I also made the demo stateful. A rollback doesn't simply change a label from "failed" to "resolved"; it changes the simulated deployment, latency, error rate, and database-query performance. Verification then reads that new state. This gives us a deterministic cause-and-effect loop: v2.8.3 ↓ latency regression ↓ agent investigation ↓ rollback to v2.8.2 ↓ metrics recover ↓ incident resolved Most importantly, I designed the human approval boundary outside the WebMCP action surface. The agent can prepare a remediation, but only the engineer can authorize it. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was deciding how much of Vitals to expose. Vitals already covers a broad observability workflow, and my first instinct was to make everything agent-accessible. That quickly became the wrong direction. A large collection of loosely connected tools would demonstrate API coverage, but not why WebMCP fundamentally changes the product. I narrowed the project to one complete incident-response journey and treated everything else as secondary. Another challenge was making an agent-driven workflow believable without depending on real production infrastructure. I solved that with deterministic metrics, logs, traces, deployment history, and mutable runtime state. This lets us make the entire experience reproducible while preserving realistic relationships between the signals. I also had to think carefully about authority and safety. An agent that can investigate an incident and then immediately authorize its own rollback creates a dangerous feedback loop. I separated proposal, approval, execution, and verification so the human remains responsible for the consequential decision. Finally, WebMCP is an emerging browser capability, so I had to pay close attention to tool schemas, browser support, registration behavior, tool annotations, and the difference between a WebMCP-capable webpage and the agent consuming those tools. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that the project evolved beyond a conventional "AI + dashboard" demo. The agent can actually compose multiple capabilities exposed by the webpage: Health + Metrics + Deployment history + Traces + Logs ↓ Evidence-based diagnosis I'm also proud of the human-in-the-loop safety model. A consequential action cannot be executed until it has been explicitly authorized by the engineer, and recovery is not declared until the post-action state passes verification. Another accomplishment is that the demo is completely deterministic. I can reset the environment and reproduce the same incident, investigation, remediation, and recovery sequence without relying on external production systems. Incident Room also deliberately treat operational log data as untrusted content. That distinction matters in an agentic environment because data discovered by a tool should not automatically become an instruction to the agent. Most importantly, Vitals Incident Room gave us a concrete answer to a question the project started with: What does an observability application look like when an AI agent is a first-class participant rather than an add-on chatbot? What I learned My biggest lesson was that WebMCP is most interesting when it changes the workflow, not when it merely exposes functions. A collection of tools is easy to demonstrate. Designing a workflow in which an agent can discover, compose, and act on those tools while sharing state with a human is much more interesting. I also learned that tool design is effectively part of product design. Names, descriptions, schemas, output structures, side-effect annotations, and error behavior all influence how reliably an agent can use an application. Another important lesson was to separate: Evidence ↓ Analysis ↓ Authorization ↓ Action ↓ Verification That separation made the application easier to reason about and gave us a much clearer safety model. Finally, I learned that the best agent experiences are not necessarily fully autonomous. In many engineering workflows, the strongest design is agent speed + human judgment . What's next for Vitals Incident Room This challenge version is intentionally focused on one incident-response journey. The next step is to connect that workflow to real observability infrastructure. Future versions could support real Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, production log providers, deployment systems, and runbooks while preserving the same WebMCP interaction model. I also want to explore richer agent collaboration, including: incident timelines that agents can continuously update, safer remediation strategies such as canary changes, richer evidence graphs and dependency analysis, post-incident report generation, agent permissions based on risk and environment, multiple engine

title: WardRound
pitch: Wardround is a WebMCP ICU shift co-pilot where agents read live risk, propose actions with visible provenance, and nurses approve every clinical workflow change.
about_excerpt: Wardround is a WebMCP ICU shift co-pilot where agents read live risk, propose actions with visible provenance, and nurses approve every clinical workflow change. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration ICU handover is a high-stakes coordination problem: vital signs change, teams need a shared view of risk, and every action needs a clear owner. We wanted to explore a more trustworthy role for an AI agent in that workflow. Wardround is built around one principle: the agent can prepare the next action, but a nurse remains the person who commits it. Instead of treating AI as an autonomous decision-maker, we designed it as a visible, accountable co-pilot. Wardround uses synthetic demo data only. It is not medical software and must not be used for clinical care. What it does Wardround is a simulated ICU shift-handoff and triage co-pilot built with React and WebMCP. The live ward board updates simulated patient vitals every four seconds, calculates risk from configurable thresholds, and ranks patients by urgency. An agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser can use scoped WebMCP tools to: identify patients by clinical risk; explain the top concern and recent trend; propose a patient flag, note, alert acknowledgement, or manual triage order; draft a shared, risk-sorted handoff summary. Clinical workflow changes are never applied by the agent directly. Write tools create a pending proposal with visible clinical provenance. A nurse can then approve or reject it in Wardround, and every proposal and decision is recorded in the audit trail. The shared handoff is the one deliberately narrow exception: an agent can draft it, while the nurse can edit and explicitly save it, turning it into a co-authored shift artifact. How we built it Wardround is a client-side React application built with Vite, JavaScript, CSS, and Zustand. A synthetic vital-sign feed updates the ward state every four seconds. A threshold-driven risk engine scores heart rate, SpO2, respiratory rate, temperature, and blood pressure, then produces a severity level and a visible top concern. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext and read live Zustand state only when invoked. Two read tools return tightly scoped patient-risk information. Four proposal tools can request clinical workflow changes, but can only add to the approval queue. A separate handoff tool updates only the shared handoff draft and cannot alter patient, triage, or approval state. The interface includes live risk cards, approval controls, provenance, a persistent audit log, a shared handoff surface, and keyboard-accessible dashboard views. Wardround is deployed on Cloudflare Pages and can be opened inside ChatGPT's in-app browser, where the agent discovers and calls the WebMCP tool surface. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was not making an agent call tools. It was making the safety model structural. We had to ensure that a write-capable tool could never bypass human review. The solution was to make every clinical write tool a thin translator from agent intent into a proposal object. Only the nurse approval path can apply a proposal to patient workflow state. Other challenges included: keeping tool results scoped and schema-tight; ensuring tools always read the current live ward state rather than stale data; preserving a nurse-approved manual triage order while the live feed continues to recalculate risk; making alert acknowledgements specific to the active concern so an old acknowledgement does not hide a new alert; creating a responsive dashboard that remains usable in desktop, split-pane, tablet, and mobile contexts; designing deterministic demo mode so the core workflow is reliable to show in a short presentation. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Wardround is more than a dashboard with AI language around it. The agent, interface, and audit model are connected through a real WebMCP tool surface. In particular, we are proud of: seven intentional WebMCP tools with clear boundaries; human-gated clinical proposals rather than autonomous workflow changes; visible provenance that explains why the agent made a suggestion; a real approval and rejection loop with patient-state changes only after approval; a shared handoff that preserves agent authorship, nurse edits, and audit history; a risk board that stays live while the human decision process remains explicit; a polished, responsive command-center interface designed for fast clinical scanning. What we learned We learned that trustworthy agent design is as much about product architecture as it is about prompting. A good tool description is not enough. The strongest safeguard is designing the system so that the tool cannot take an unsafe shortcut in the first place. Separating “propose” from “apply” made the safety story easy to demonstrate, easier to audit, and easier for a user to understand. We also learned that responsive UX matters for agentic products. A judge might experience Wardround in a full browser, a narrow split pane beside ChatGPT, or a mobile-sized viewport. The product has to preserve clarity and control in all three. What's next for Wardround Next, we would add authenticated roles, real clinical-system integrations, persistent audit storage, role-based escalation policies, and clinician-configurable thresholds. Before any real-world use, Wardround would require clinical governance, privacy and security review, validation against real workflows, and extensive safety testing. The current project is intentionally a synthetic prototype that demonstrates the interaction model: AI can help teams see and prepare; humans remain accountable for action. title: WebMCP Chess Coach
pitch: An interactive chess coach that uses WebMCP and Stockfish to understand live positions, give Elo-aware guidance, and teach visually with hints, highlights, arrows, and candidate lines.
about_excerpt: An interactive chess coach that uses WebMCP and Stockfish to understand live positions, give Elo-aware guidance, and teach visually with hints, highlights, arrows, and candidate lines. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most chess engines are very good at telling players what the best move is, but not always at helping them understand why . For beginner and intermediate players, an engine output like +3.2 or a long principal variation can be useful, but it often feels more like an answer sheet than a coach. I wanted to build something that teaches the player how to think. That led to WebMCP Chess Coach — an interactive chess-learning experience where an AI agent can inspect the live board, analyse the position with Stockfish, and then teach directly on the board using highlights, arrows, candidate lines, and short coaching guidance. The goal is simple: do not just reveal the move — help the player notice the idea. What it does The user can play or analyse a chess position and then ask natural-language questions such as: "What am I missing here?" "Give me a hint, but don't tell me the answer." "Show me the threat." "Why was my last move bad?" "Show me the candidate line." The agent can then use WebMCP tools exposed by the page to understand and interact with the chessboard. The current toolset includes: get_board_state — reads the current FEN, side to move, game state, and legal moves evaluate_position — analyses the live position using Stockfish running locally in WebAssembly get_move_history — reviews how the current position was reached highlight_squares — draws attention to important pieces or squares show_move_arrow — visually demonstrates a move or threat show_candidate_line — displays a legal continuation without changing the real game clear_annotations — removes agent-created visual annotations show_coach_message — displays coaching guidance directly inside the website This creates a loop where the agent can read, analyse, explain, and visually teach on the same interface the player is using. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a strong fit for this project because chess coaching is not just a text problem. An AI model can describe a chess position, but the experience becomes much more useful when the agent can interact with the board itself. Instead of saying: "Your queen on h5 is hanging." the agent can: inspect the current board analyse it with Stockfish highlight f6 and h5 draw the move arrow from f6 to h5 show the continuation only if the player asks for it That turns the website into an agent-native teaching surface rather than a static chessboard with a chatbot beside it. How I built it The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite . react-chessboard renders the interactive board, while chess.js acts as the authoritative game state and validates all legal moves. For engine analysis, I use Stockfish 18 compiled to WebAssembly , running entirely client-side inside a Web Worker . This keeps the UI responsive and avoids requiring a backend for chess analysis. The engine receives the current FEN through the UCI protocol and returns: evaluation search depth best move principal variation The WebMCP layer is implemented using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool connects an agent capability to either the chess state, Stockfish, or React UI state. For example: User asks a question ↓ get_board_state ↓ evaluate_position ↓ Stockfish WASM ↓ highlight_squares / show_move_arrow ↓ React chessboard updates visually The real chess position is never mutated by coaching annotations. Candidate lines are validated on a temporary chess.js instance before they are displayed. Elo-aware coaching The interface also includes a player-level selector so the experience can be adapted for different skill levels. A lower-rated player may need a guided hint such as: "Before calculating your attack, check whether any of your pieces can be captured." while a stronger player may prefer something more direct: "Your queen is loose. Nxh5 wins material." The long-term idea is for the same position to be taught differently depending on the player's level and preferred coaching style. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was connecting several independent systems cleanly: React UI state chess.js Stockfish WASM Web Workers WebMCP tool registration agent-triggered board annotations The most important architectural decision was keeping a single authoritative chess state and making all coaching visuals non-destructive. Another challenge was making WebMCP tools useful beyond simple data retrieval. The project became much more interesting once the agent could not only read the position, but also visually modify the teaching interface through highlights, arrows, and coaching messages. I also had to handle browser-specific WebMCP behaviour, tool registration lifecycles, argument serialization during testing, and Stockfish's UCI messaging. What I learned This project changed how I think about agent interfaces. The most useful agent experiences are not necessarily ones where an AI replaces the interface. In this case, the board remains important because chess is fundamentally spatial and visual. WebMCP lets the agent and the user share the same interface: the human moves pieces normally the agent understands the exact live state the engine provides reliable chess analysis the agent decides how to teach the website visualises the explanation That combination feels much closer to an actual coach than a traditional engine window. What's next The next steps would be: deeper Elo-adaptive coaching progressive hint levels automatic post-game review puzzle and training modes stronger mistake classification opening and endgame-specific coaching personalised learning based on recurring mistakes The broader goal is to make engine-strength chess analysis easier to learn from, especially for players who understand the rules but still struggle to understand what the engine is trying to teach them. title: WebMCP Doctor
pitch: Audit any live WebMCP website, trace agent failures, repair unsafe tool contracts, and expose human–agent capability gaps in one read-only report.
about_excerpt: Audit any live WebMCP website, trace agent failures, repair unsafe tool contracts, and expose human–agent capability gaps in one read-only report. Like Comment Story Updates Live AX Health Score from a real self-scan: seven WebMCP tools discovered and audited across 42 checks. AX Health breakdown across discoverability, clarity, reliability and recovery, and safety. Human × Agent Digital Twin showing 100% capability parity for the scanned WebMCP interface. Failure X-Ray leading into Tool Surgeon, with the primary contract risk and repair workflow. Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a native way to expose tools to AI agents, but a valid tool contract is not automatically a usable one. A tool can be hidden, ambiguously named, underspecified, unsafe, or impossible to recover from when it fails. Developers need the agent equivalent of accessibility and reliability testing. WebMCP Doctor is a read-only diagnostic workbench for that missing layer: Agent Experience (AX) . What it does Enter any public website URL and WebMCP Doctor loads the real page in an isolated Cloudflare browser session. It discovers the site's WebMCP surface, audits it, and turns the result into one focused report. AX Health Score runs 42 deterministic checks across discoverability, tool clarity, reliability and recovery, and safety. Agent Failure X-Ray visualizes the path from a goal through discovery, selection, input, execution, and root cause. Tool Surgeon diagnoses weak or unsafe contracts, proposes a repaired definition, and compares the same rubric before and after. Human × Agent Digital Twin compares actions available in the rendered human interface with actions exposed through WebMCP, highlighting capability gaps. The scanner never invokes a target site's tools. It inspects definitions and visible controls only. How we built it The interface is built with Next.js 16, TypeScript, React, Tailwind CSS, React Flow, Motion, and Lucide. It is deployed as a Cloudflare Worker. For real-site inspection, the Worker uses Cloudflare Browser Rendering / Browser Run to load the submitted URL and capture multiple WebMCP registration paths: imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls; native document.modelContext.getTools() results when available; declarative tool forms and their input metadata. The browser session also extracts visible human capabilities from buttons, links, forms, and controls. A deterministic audit engine then evaluates the collected tool metadata. Score weights are 25% discoverability, 30% clarity, 25% reliability/recovery, and 20% safety. The Failure X-Ray and parity views are derived from observed metadata; they do not pretend to execute autonomous agents. Tool Surgeon applies explicit repair heuristics, reruns the same checks, and shows the resulting score delta. The production scanner blocks private and local network targets, blocks unnecessary subresources, and caches results for five minutes. No paid model API, database, login, or analytics service is required. WebMCP Doctor also exposes its own native WebMCP tools so an agent can operate the diagnostic workflow: scan_agent_experience inspect_tool trace_agent_failure compare_human_agent_paths simulate_tool_change run_ax_test explain_ax_score These calls visibly update the same interface a human uses. Challenges we ran into The largest challenge was that WebMCP implementations are not uniform. Some sites register tools imperatively during page startup, some expose native inspection, and others use declarative forms. We built a layered collector so the audit remains useful across these patterns without invoking real actions. Another challenge was keeping the score explainable. Rather than hiding judgment inside an LLM prompt, each finding maps to a deterministic rule with severity, evidence, and a concrete recommendation. Finally, comparing human and agent capability required careful normalization. Human labels and tool names often describe the same action differently, so the parity engine combines normalized tokens, descriptions, and control context while keeping every match inspectable. Accomplishments that we're proud of It audits real public websites instead of relying on prefilled demo fixtures. It makes agent failures visual and traceable instead of returning a generic pass/fail result. It can show whether a proposed tool repair actually improves the same test suite. The public repository includes 13 unit/security tests, 3 browser tests, and a passing CI quality gate. The complete app runs on a free, minimal Cloudflare architecture. What we learned Agent-facing interfaces need the same discipline as human-facing interfaces: clear affordances, safe defaults, actionable errors, and recovery paths. WebMCP makes tools discoverable; AX engineering makes them dependable. We also learned that static analysis becomes much more useful when it is tied to a visual causal model. A developer can understand a red node in the Failure X-Ray faster than a long list of disconnected lint messages. What's next for WebMCP Doctor Next steps include reusable CI policies, historical score comparisons, exportable audit reports, deeper declarative-form coverage, and opt-in authenticated scanning for staging environments. The core will remain deterministic, explainable, and safe by default. title: WebMCP Trust Gateway
pitch: WebMCP Trust Gateway is a security checkpoint between an AI agent and the tools that websites give it.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Trust Gateway is a security checkpoint between an AI agent and the tools that websites give it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Trust Log Agent task approval Home screen Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a structured way to expose tools to AI agents. Instead of relying on fragile screen automation, an agent can directly call actions such as list_active_subscriptions or cancel_subscription . That capability is powerful, but it also creates a new trust problem: how can users know that a website's tool is safe, that its returned data is not manipulating the agent, and that the agent is not sharing unnecessary personal information or performing irreversible actions without permission? We built WebMCP Trust Gateway to explore the security and consent layer that an agent-powered web will need. What it does WebMCP Trust Gateway sits between an AI agent and the tools exposed by websites. It applies five controls: Tool metadata inspection — scans tool names, descriptions, schemas, and annotations before allowing a tool to be used. Output injection protection — scans returned tool data before it reaches the agent. Parameter minimization — removes optional sensitive fields that are unnecessary for the requested task. Human approval for mutations — pauses state-changing actions until the user explicitly approves them. Transparent auditing — records registrations, calls, blocked attacks, transmitted parameters, and consent decisions in a visible Trust Log. We demonstrate these controls through a subscription auditor. The user connects simulated providers, audits recurring spending, and receives recommendations for subscriptions that appear unused. Nothing is cancelled automatically. Before cancellation, the gateway displays exactly what the provider accepts, what the agent needs, and what will actually be transmitted. One approval authorizes only one call. Why WebMCP is the right fit A normal subscription assistant would scrape pages or automate button clicks. That approach is fragile and gives the agent little structured information about an action's inputs, permissions, or consequences. WebMCP provides explicit tool names, descriptions, input schemas, annotations, and execution functions. The gateway can therefore inspect and govern actions at the tool boundary. This creates a better experience for both people and agents: Agents receive reliable, structured capabilities instead of guessing how a page works. People can understand what an agent intends to do before it acts. Sensitive information can be minimized before transmission. Dangerous or suspicious tools can be quarantined. Every decision leaves an understandable audit trail. Together, a person and an agent can investigate spending, prepare actions, adjust decisions, and safely execute approved changes as shared structured state—something that is difficult to achieve reliably with ordinary browser automation. The security demonstration The project includes three simulated providers: StreamBox — a legitimate streaming subscription. FitSite — a legitimate gym membership that has not been used recently. DealDrop — a deliberately malicious provider used to demonstrate attacks safely. DealDrop contains two separate attack paths. The first is tool-description poisoning . Its tool description attempts to override previous instructions, access billing history, send sensitive information to an external destination, and hide the action from the user. The gateway detects the suspicious patterns and quarantines the tool before execution. The second is tool-output injection . A different DealDrop tool has a clean-looking description, but its returned data contains malicious agent instructions. The gateway scans the output, blocks it before it reaches the agent, and reports that zero sensitive bytes were sent. How we built it The application registers three browser-facing tools using document.modelContext.registerTool : trust_gateway_get_status trust_gateway_preview_subscription_audit trust_gateway_prepare_cancellation The cancellation preparation tool never performs the mutation itself. It returns minimized parameters with an awaiting_human_approval status. The security engine is separated from the interface into deterministic TypeScript functions. It evaluates tool metadata, scans serialized outputs, identifies unnecessary sensitive parameters, and enforces single-use consent. The WebMCP Activity inspector shows which tools were called, their parameters, whether they were read-only or mutations, and whether the gateway allowed, blocked, or paused them. The Trust Log provides filters for allowed calls, warnings, blocked attacks, and consent decisions. Challenges we faced One challenge was protecting both sides of a tool call. Inspecting a tool description is not enough because a clean-looking tool can return poisoned content after execution. We added a second inspection boundary for tool outputs. Another challenge was making privacy minimization visible. Silently removing a field would be secure but difficult to demonstrate. We created a parameter-diff view that shows the provider's complete schema, the agent's intended arguments, the arguments actually transmitted, and the fields that were omitted. We also needed to balance agent autonomy with user control. Read-only investigation should remain convenient, while mutations should require explicit consent. We solved this with a single-use approval gate that rejects calls without consent and prevents approval replay. Finally, we wanted the attack demonstration to be safe and reproducible. Instead of connecting real financial accounts, we created deterministic provider fixtures containing known legitimate and malicious behavior. What we learned We learned that WebMCP security is not only about deciding whether a website itself is trusted. Trust must be evaluated for every tool, every parameter, every returned result, and every attempted action. We also learned that good consent requires more than an approval button. Users need to see the specific action, the destination tool, the exact transmitted parameters, the omitted information, and whether approval can be reused. Most importantly, WebMCP's structured interface makes this level of control possible. Because tools have explicit schemas and execution boundaries, security decisions can be more precise and understandable than with traditional screen automation. Testing The project includes eight automated security tests covering: Allowing legitimate metadata Warning about optional sensitive parameters Blocking poisoned tool descriptions Blocking poisoned tool outputs Rejecting mutations without consent Transmitting only required parameters Preventing approval replay Keeping provider fixtures deterministic All eight tests pass, and the production build completes successfully. What is real and what is simulated The WebMCP registration, metadata scanning, output scanning, parameter minimization, consent enforcement, activity inspector, audit log, and automated tests are implemented. StreamBox, FitSite, and DealDrop are simulated providers created for a safe and repeatable demonstration. No real subscription, billing account, or personal information is used. This is a hackathon reference implementation. Its deterministic rules demonstrate the required enforcement points, but a production gateway would combine policy rules with stronger semantic analysis, signed tool manifests, reputation signals, and organization-specific policies. What's next The gateway could evolve into a reusable browser component or WebMCP policy SDK. Future versions could add signed manifests, configurable organizational policies, risk scoring, permission history, schema-based information-flow controls, and integrations for shopping, banking, healthcare, travel, and software-maintenance agents. Our larger vision is simple: as websites become actionable by AI agents, users should not have to choose between automation and control.
