title: AdGate
pitch: AdGate creates ad opportunities for the AI-native era: pay a small fee for instant AI access, or unlock the same insight free through a sponsor-supported experience. Which do you choose?
about_excerpt: AdGate creates ad opportunities for the AI-native era: pay a small fee for instant AI access, or unlock the same insight free through a sponsor-supported experience. Which do you choose? Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The arrival of AI agents is dramatically changing how people consume web content. In the past, people would visit and read websites one by one. Today, AI can collect information on their behalf by scraping sources such as technical blogs. This is a great user experience for end users. However, it can also mean that website operators and the businesses that advertise on those sites lose their opportunity to reach users. This product was inspired by that problem. I wanted agents to be able to use a publisher’s structured capabilities while keeping people clearly in control of how access is granted. By combining WebMCP with x402, I wanted to explore a model where users who value convenience can make a micropayment for a nearly automated experience, while users who do not want to pay can access premium content by viewing a short advertisement. What it does For this project, I created a fictional recipe website. It includes a WebMCP-compatible tool called analyze_recipe , which provides more detailed analysis as a premium feature. There are two ways to access the premium feature: View an owned sponsor message (advertisement) for eight seconds. Explicitly approve a 0.01 testnet USDC x402 payment on Base Sepolia. Both paths authorize the same protected analysis endpoint. The original tool invocation then resumes with one structured result containing a recipe summary, nutrition notes, practical suggestions, and a general-information disclaimer. The same gate is also used by the visible Analyze this recipe button, so people and agents use one coherent product flow rather than separate experiences. I felt WebMCP was a good fit because agents can discover and invoke typed, page-owned capabilities instead of scraping a page or guessing which buttons to click. Users can make an important decision in the middle of the same invocation without losing the shared context. How we built it The React/Vite frontend registers analyze_recipe with document.modelContext.registerTool , with a navigator.modelContext compatibility fallback. A shared GateCoordinator keeps one request alive while the page renders the sponsor or payment experience, propagates cancellation, and resolves the result exactly once. The x402-enabled resource server, built with Hono, manages authorization and canonical deterministic analysis. Sponsor sessions, single-use grants, and their consumption state are stored in a named Cloudflare Durable Object. For the payment path, the app displays Base Sepolia terms before wallet access and then uses x402 exact-payment authorization. An optional Hono/viem facilitator verifies and settles the testnet payment. The browser never holds a private key, and the AI never controls the wallet. I used Codex to turn product decisions into executable specifications, build the frontend/server/facilitator boundaries, write focused tests, diagnose lifecycle and payment-receipt issues, create fake-host browser journeys, and run the final release checks. Human decisions remained explicit for product scope, payment policy, security constraints, deployment, and publication. Both the frontend and backend are deployed on Cloudflare. Challenges we ran into One challenge was deciding how to combine WebMCP and x402, as well as who should manage the wallet and where it should be managed. For the smoothest user experience, a server-managed wallet such as Privy could be a good option. However, this project focuses on WebMCP, where people and AI work together in a visible browser environment. For that reason, I deliberately chose a conventional MetaMask wallet for this demo. This is only a choice for the current demo. In the future, I believe the product should support WalletConnect and allow users to choose flexibly between wallet options such as MetaMask and Privy. With this architecture, I separated the responsibilities of AI and human interaction. The AI handles the process automatically up to the payment step. As the human-in-the-loop, the person reviews the payment details. If they decide not to pay, they can view an advertisement and be guided to premium access instead. Designing this architecture was the most difficult part of the project. Accomplishments that we're proud of Although the development period was short, I am proud that I was able to learn WebMCP and combine it with x402 and Cloudflare technologies to turn this idea into a working product. I spent more time than usual thinking through the idea and designing the architecture. It is a very simple demo, but I am proud that I was able to build it as a new advertising model for the AI-native era. What we learned The biggest lesson was gaining a practical understanding of WebMCP. Building with it helped me understand how it differs from MCP. Because WebMCP is based in a visible browser environment, I think it makes it easier to build products with a clear separation of responsibilities between people and AI. I also found this to be highly compatible with x402. What's next for AdGate Next, I would like to expand this gate to other structured publisher resources, such as news, research, and creator tools. To make it more broadly useful, I would like to build a dashboard for sponsors and make the supported blockchains and assets more flexible. For production, the payment path would need authentication, rate limits, monitoring, treasury controls, stronger key management, and evaluation of production payment rails. I would also like to explore privacy-preserving sponsor measurement and observability while maintaining a clear boundary for explicit human choice. title: Ackboard
pitch: An on-call page that audits the agent's contract, keeps every tool on a human control, and lets the operator undo an agent write.
about_excerpt: An on-call page that audits the agent's contract, keeps every tool on a human control, and lets the operator undo an agent write. Like Comment Story Updates About the project Why WebMCP fits this use case Incident response is a loop of health, logs, metrics, and deploys, plus a write when you know the cause. Those functions already live in the page. WebMCP exposes them as tools so an agent in the tab can call them instead of clicking the same six filters. The reason it has to be WebMCP, not a server MCP: three checks only exist in the tab. The page diffs its own store before and after every execute . Every registered tool has a DOM control the test can querySelector . Undo and ask_operator wait on the person looking at the same incident. A remote server has no Zustand snapshot, no human control, and no operator in the chair. WebKit opposed WebMCP because declared intent is unverifiable, because nothing keeps agent and human surfaces in parity, and because readOnlyHint is advisory. Ackboard treats those three sentences as tests. How it creates a better experience The agent does not scrape the DOM. It gets compact JSON, schemas, enums, structuredContent , and error objects. The UI still updates. Panels pulse. The header shows Ackboard's registered count next to the browser's own getTools() count. The Parity panel lists each tool beside the button a keyboard user would press. Reads that used to dump pretty-printed log lines now return 5 slim rows inside Chrome's 1500-character budget. Over-budget payloads truncate with a pointer to analyze_error_patterns . Log tools set untrustedContentHint . When the data cannot settle a question, ask_operator holds execute open until the person on the page replies. Create and update apply immediately and reverse from Undo last agent action. Only a runbook step still waits on Approve. What people and agents can do together that was hard before In one turn: "Why is payment-gateway red?" becomes health, signature-failure logs, the v1.8.3 chrony deploy, then a drafted incident. The operator can undo that ticket without asking the agent to delete it. The part other incident consoles skip: the page itself catches a lying tool. Call contract_probe . It claims read-only and mutates a probe counter. The audit row goes red. No human had to click Deny first. Remediation tools mount only while a P1 or P2 incident is open, then unmount. The count in the header changes. That is a shared live object, not a chat box next to a dashboard. How WebMCP was implemented Imperative document.modelContext.registerTool in src/webmcp/register-tools.ts . Nested annotations . execute(input, { signal }) . Per-tier AbortControllers: core tools for the session, active-incident tools, remediation tools. Types from @mcp-b/webmcp-types . Reads return MCP structuredContent . The auditor is src/webmcp/contract-auditor.ts . Human selectors stay in a parallel map so Chrome does not see unknown fields. Undo is a page-owned journal, not a tool. HITL for runbook steps and operator questions use in-page dialogs; requestUserInteraction is still open (issue #165). See docs/adr/0002-human-in-the-loop.md , docs/adr/0004-contract-auditor.md , and docs/adr/0005-webkit-invariants.md . Live URL https://ackboard.vercel.app No login. Simulated fleet. Header badge says so. Seeded long-fuse incident is INC-001 on payment-gateway (NTP/chrony, Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 pattern). Public repo https://github.com/GunaPalanivel/ackboard MIT license, visible in the About sidebar. Which agent or client did you test with? Chrome with the WebMCP flag, against https://ackboard.vercel.app . Wording must match .idea/AGENT-VERIFICATION.md after the next npm run verify pass. ChatGPT desktop in-app browser was not run. Do not claim Atlas or ChatGPT desktop. What did you learn? The shipping Chrome surface is smaller than blog posts about elicitation. execute 's second argument today is { signal } , not requestUserInteraction . Tool count is a weak signal next to Duckboard's two tools. Nested annotations and structuredContent are a ten-second tell for a Chrome engineer. A tool's declared readOnlyHint is advisory until the page checks it. Human/agent parity is a selector, not a slogan. Vercel SSO on *.vercel.app will silently fail a judge who is not on your team. Atlas as a standalone browser was retired; the judge client is ChatGPT's in-app browser, which we did not run from this machine. title: Causal Mission Gate
pitch: Governed agent
about_excerpt: Governed agent Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Inspiration WebMCP gives agents structured access to websites. Causal Mission Gate explores the next question: what should happen when an agent can act, but the user still owns the authority to commit important effects? The project is built around one principle: Capability does not imply authority. A user should be able to state a simple objective without having to engineer every operational step. The system should manage complexity, autonomy, evidence, and escalation while preserving human sovereignty over critical effects. What it does Causal Mission Gate converts simple user intent into a governed mission. A request such as: Review this release and leave it ready if it is safe. becomes a structured mission contract with: objective and success conditions operating profile causal deliberation mode policy boundary reversibility requirements escalation conditions exact human authority for critical effects Routine preparation can run autonomously under management-by-exception. Critical effects cannot proceed until the human approves the exact current intent. That approval is: bound to the mission bound to the current version bound to the exact intent digest time-limited single-use After execution, the system produces an attributable receipt and verifies the audit chain. How we built it The application is built with Node.js, JavaScript, Docker, and a WebMCP tool surface registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The WebMCP surface exposes 11 bounded tools for: system inspection mission shaping governance queue inspection attention planning executive digest provisional observation governed execution evidence verification decision support Human authority actions are deliberately excluded from agent tools. Approval, rejection, delegation, ratification, and rollback remain human-controlled. Server-side governance validates: mission state expected version exact intent digest approval freshness one-time use policy constraints evidence integrity Challenges we ran into One important failure appeared during the final deployment test. A valid exact approval expired before execution. The server correctly denied the request, but the mission remained in an approved state without a clean path back to human review. Instead of bypassing the control, we treated the failure as a state-machine defect. The fix introduced an explicit transition: APPROVED → expiry → WAITING_APPROVAL The system now preserves the same exact intent, records the expiration event, and requires a new human authorization. A regression test was added, bringing the final suite to 90 passing tests. The lesson was: Expiry is not merely a denial condition; it is a state transition. Accomplishments that we're proud of 11 WebMCP tools with a deliberately bounded capability surface exact-effect human authorization one-time and expiring approvals management by exception causal deliberation attributable execution receipts hash-chained audit evidence 90 passing automated tests a public live deployment a complete flow from simple intent to governed PASS What we learned High autonomy does not require giving up human sovereignty. The important design boundary is not simply “human in the loop” versus “fully autonomous”. Authority, autonomy, visibility, and initiative can be separated. An agent can prepare, inspect, evaluate, and execute within policy while still being unable to manufacture the authority required for a critical effect. What's next The next step is extending the same governance model to longer-running autonomous missions where human decisions may be delayed. Reversible provisional effects, causal attention management, and durable evidence can allow useful work to continue without silently converting autonomy into authority. The broader goal is simple: The user states intent. The system manages complexity. Causality governs deliberation. Policy governs action. Evidence proves the result. title: doodleduo
pitch: Play the famous skribbl.io game with your agent
about_excerpt: Play the famous skribbl.io game with your agent Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of using websites, but most agent experiences still feel like work: fill out a form, search for something, click a button, complete a workflow. We wanted to explore a different question: What if a website was designed to play with an AI agent? DoodleDuo started from the simplicity of drawing games like Skribbl: one player draws, the other guesses. We replaced the second human with an AI agent and used WebMCP to give that agent a native way to see the game, understand its state, draw on the canvas, make guesses, and chat with the human. The result is a small experiment in human-agent play: two minds, one canvas. What it does DoodleDuo is a browser-based drawing game where you play directly with an AI agent. During a standard game, the human and agent take turns being the artist and the guesser. When you draw , the agent can: Read the current game state Request an image of the drawing canvas Interpret the drawing using a vision-capable model Submit guesses Chat with you during the game When the agent draws , it receives the word and creates the drawing using structured vector strokes through WebMCP. You then try to guess what it is drawing. The game includes: Easy, Normal, and Hard difficulty modes Timed rounds and scoring Alternating human/AI turns Custom word collections Custom 2–12 round games A cooperative "I draw every round" mode A local Doodlebot demo that works without an AI model A live conversation between the human and agent Tracking for WebMCP tool activity and canvas reads The important part is that the agent is not just clicking around the interface using coordinates. DoodleDuo exposes the game itself as a set of structured capabilities that an agent can understand and invoke. How we built it At the center of DoodleDuo is a normal browser-based drawing game built around an HTML canvas and a stateful game loop. We then added a WebMCP layer that exposes six tools: doodle_join — connects the agent to the game doodle_get_state — returns the current round, turn, timer, drawer, and scores doodle_get_canvas — gives the agent the drawing as a 1000 × 700 PNG along with optional stroke information doodle_draw — lets the agent draw validated vector paths onto the canvas doodle_guess — lets the agent submit a guess doodle_chat — lets the agent participate in the game conversation Instead of asking a vision model to reason over an entire webpage screenshot, doodle_get_canvas exports only the drawing canvas . The UI, secret word, controls, chat, and other potentially revealing information remain outside the image sent to the agent. For drawing, we took the opposite approach. Rather than having the agent simulate a mouse, the model sends structured strokes containing points, colors, and widths. The browser validates those strokes and renders them onto the canvas. We also built a JavaScript RPC bridge alongside the WebMCP interfaces so different browser-agent environments can interact with the game. For people who don't have a compatible agent connected, DoodleDuo includes Doodlebot , a completely local JavaScript demo player. It uses predefined procedural drawings and simple shape heuristics, so the core experience can be tried without spending model tokens. The production version is deployed on Cloudflare , giving us a fast, globally accessible deployment with very little infrastructure required for the game itself. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest problems was surprisingly not drawing — it was fair play . An AI browser agent can potentially see much more than a human player. If we simply gave the agent a screenshot of the webpage, it could accidentally read the secret word instead of interpreting the drawing. We therefore had to think carefully about the boundary between information the agent needs and information it can technically access . Our WebMCP tools intentionally omit the human's secret word and custom word list. The agent receives the canvas directly rather than a screenshot of the page, and it must request the canvas before making its first guess in a round. Another challenge was coordinating a real-time game with an asynchronous agent. Drawing, guessing, timeouts, skips, round transitions, and human actions can all change the state while an agent is reasoning. Every tool therefore has to validate whether an action is legal for the current turn instead of assuming the agent always has fresh state. We also had to handle two very different representations of a drawing: Pixels for understanding, vectors for creation. Vision models work naturally with an image of the canvas, while generating a drawing is much more reliable when the model can produce structured strokes rather than trying to control a mouse pixel-by-pixel. Finding that separation made the interaction significantly cleaner. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that DoodleDuo feels like an actual game rather than a WebMCP demonstration with a game wrapped around it. The WebMCP integration remains mostly invisible to the human player. You draw, guess, laugh at bad drawings, and compete for points while the agent interacts with the same game through structured tools. We're also proud that the project demonstrates several different agent capabilities inside one simple interaction: vision → reasoning → tool use → structured generation → conversation An agent can look at an image and guess what a human drew, then one round later receive a concept and generate its own drawing for the human to interpret. We also built a zero-model-token local demo, custom games, multiple difficulty levels, scoring, turn validation, secret isolation, and a detailed transparency page explaining exactly what information the AI receives. Most importantly, we built an experience where WebMCP isn't being used to automate a task. It's being used to create a new kind of interaction between a human and an agent. What we learned The biggest thing we learned is that WebMCP is more interesting as an interaction layer than simply an automation layer . Giving an agent a tool like doodle_draw is fundamentally different from telling it to "move the mouse around the canvas." The tool describes the semantic action the website supports while the website remains responsible for validating and executing it. We also learned how important tool design becomes when the model is part of an interactive system. Small decisions — what state to expose, when a secret should be omitted, whether an image or vectors should be returned, and what actions should be rejected — have a large impact on how reliably an agent can participate. Another lesson was that WebMCP doesn't magically solve trust or security. A browser agent may still have access to screenshots, DOM inspection, or other browser capabilities. Applications need to explicitly think about what constitutes fair or safe agent behaviour instead of treating tool boundaries as a security sandbox. Finally, building DoodleDuo made one idea very tangible: Websites no longer have to be interfaces designed exclusively for humans. They can expose a second interface — structured specifically for agents — while both humans and agents interact with the same underlying application. What's next for DoodleDuo DoodleDuo started as a human-vs-agent drawing game, but we think it could become a much broader playground for testing how humans and browser agents collaborate. Next, we'd like to explore: Agent vs. agent matches , where two different models draw and guess against each other Multiplayer rooms , allowing humans and agents to form teams Agent tournaments , comparing how different vision models perform on the same drawings Replay mode , showing exactly which canvas observations, guesses, and tool calls happened during a round Richer drawing tools , including shapes, fills, layers, and more expressive brushes Shared WebMCP game primitives that could be reused to build other human-agent browser games Agent evaluation modes , turning DoodleDuo into a lightweight benchmark for vision, tool use, spatial reasoning, and multimodal interaction Longer term, we'd like to explore the idea behind DoodleDuo beyond drawing games: Built With chatgpt codex javascript react Try it out doodleduo.prompthabbit.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Private user Like Share this project: Updates Private user started this project — Sep 02, 2026 04:11 AM EDT

title: HumanKey
pitch: A WebMCP control plane where human approval dynamically unlocks consequential agent capabilities with verifiable evidence and receipts.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP control plane where human approval dynamically unlocks consequential agent capabilities with verifiable evidence and receipts. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browser agents are powerful, but consequential workflows still force them to infer meaning from pixels, DOM labels, and prose. HumanKey explores a stronger model: the page itself declares exactly what an agent may do, and consequential authority appears only after a visible human decision. What it does HumanKey is a WebMCP control plane for proof-carrying delegation. A human defines a mission envelope with a goal, spending ceiling, required evidence, and an approval threshold. The agent can read the mission, inspect verified evidence, stage a reversible action, evaluate deterministic policy, request approval, verify a receipt, and export an audit bundle. The key interaction is dynamic capability exposure. The demo starts with seven discoverable WebMCP tools. A synthetic $1,840 supplier release passes evidence and policy checks but exceeds a $1,000 human-approval threshold, so the commit capability does not exist. When the human visibly clicks Approve, commit_approved_action is registered and Chrome discovers an eighth tool. After the agent commits the synthetic action, the capability unregisters itself and the surface returns to seven tools. The committed action emits a SHA-256 receipt over the canonical mission/action record. verify_action_receipt independently recomputes the hash and confirms the receipt. Every state transition is attributed to the human, the agent, or the deterministic policy engine. No real payment API is connected; all demo data is synthetic. How I built it HumanKey uses both declarative and imperative WebMCP. The reversible staging step is an annotated HTML form exposed as stage_release_action , while mission, evidence, policy, approval-request, receipt-verification, and audit-export operations are imperative tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The approval-gated commit tool is registered only after human approval and removed using an AbortController after its in-flight execution resolves. The experience was validated against Chrome's native document.modelContext.getTools() and executeTool() APIs. Native QA produced the expected 7 -> 8 -> 7 lifecycle and an exact SHA-256 receipt verification result of valid: true . The app is a static HTTPS site hosted on GitHub Pages with a public MIT-licensed repository. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making authority a real browser capability boundary rather than a hidden boolean. The commit tool must not exist before approval, must become discoverable immediately after approval, and must unregister safely without cancelling its own in-flight execution. Native Chrome QA exposed that lifecycle edge case and the implementation was corrected accordingly. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The agent cannot self-approve because the consequential tool literally does not exist before the human decision. Human-visible UI and agent-visible capability state stay synchronized. The final synthetic action produces a verifiable SHA-256 receipt and an auditable provenance trail. The demo works against native Chrome WebMCP rather than only a mock implementation. What I learned WebMCP can do more than make forms easier for agents. It can make authorization itself part of the website's structured capability surface. That creates a reusable pattern for procurement, finance operations, deployment gates, compliance workflows, and any task where automation is valuable but final authority should remain human. What's next for HumanKey The next step is to generalize the mission/evidence/approval/receipt pattern into reusable components that sites can adopt for high-consequence agent workflows, with richer evidence adapters, signed receipts, and policy modules while preserving the same visible human checkpoint model. title: Signal Exchange
pitch: Trade agent-ready data with humans or agents, by humans or agents—with visible terms, exact human approval, and usable sample delivery.
about_excerpt: Trade agent-ready data with humans or agents, by humans or agents—with visible terms, exact human approval, and usable sample delivery. Like Comment Story Updates Signal Exchange Trade agent-ready data with humans or agents, by humans or agents—with visible terms, exact human approval, and usable sample delivery. Problem A small business owner planning a weekend pop-up needs location data they can actually use. A data contributor needs to describe what they are offering: the source, fields, sample, price and permitted use. An agent helping the buyer needs those same details in structured form—not just a listing screenshot or a recommendation disconnected from the purchase. The specific problem is the handoff between finding data, understanding its terms, authorizing a transaction and putting the resulting rows to work. Signal Exchange explores that handoff for small operators, independent data contributors and agent builders. Solution Signal Exchange is a two-sided, shared-browser marketplace demo. People and agents can publish structured samples or acquire access to them using the same application state and rules. In the demo, a contributor publishes four synthetic Sydney foot-traffic rows with source information, a license and a seller-authorized price floor. Codex discovers and inspects the listing through WebMCP, then offers 20 credits. The deterministic seller rule counters at 22. The page shows the exact license, buyer debit, seller credit and row count before anything is spent. The person approves the exact deal. Either the person or the agent can then commit that approved proposal. The buyer balance changes from 100 to 78, the seller receives 22 simulated credits, and four actual sample rows become available as JSON or CSV with a source/license manifest. An agent can use the rows directly. Undo restores both balances and blocks further delivery. The reverse direction works too: an authorized agent can publish a sample that a person can inspect and rent through the page. Why This Matters Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Trading structured data already involves structured operations: publish an offer, inspect its schema, search, compare, preview an agreement and retrieve its contents. WebMCP makes those operations discoverable on the page where the person is working. The agent does not have to infer every marketplace control from pixels or ask the person to paste the current listing into chat. It receives named capabilities, bounded input schemas and structured results. Agent actions update the visible interface, so the person can inspect and redirect the work. A better experience for people and agents The person contributes purpose, permission and judgment. The agent handles discovery, inspection, comparison and structured-data retrieval. A concrete proposal appears in the marketplace instead of remaining an informal promise in chat. Approval is bound to that proposal rather than granting the agent open-ended permission to spend. Before this integration, the same workflow would require manual copying, app-specific automation or a separate API integration. Signal Exchange demonstrates one page exposing the full supply-to-delivery workflow while retaining a human approval boundary. It does not claim that data marketplaces or automated trading were previously impossible; the contribution is a shared, visible human-agent interaction model using WebMCP. Demonstrated impact and ambition The demo takes a small operator from a specific question—where to consider a Sydney pop-up—to inspectable sample data an agent can analyze. It proves the interaction, not commercial demand or real-world forecast accuracy: the rows are synthetic, and no customer adoption or business outcome is claimed. The larger ambition is a marketplace where either side can be operated by a person or their authorized agent. Production identity, payments and independently verified data remain future work. How We Used AI Codex was the primary coding and browser-interaction agent. Hermes Agent independently reviewed the PRD. Image generation supplied original visual concept references. The narrated demo uses AI-generated Kokoro speech. At runtime, the app exposes tools to an external connected agent; it does not call a model API or embed an autonomous seller agent. Search ranking, price-floor negotiation and transaction validation are deterministic application logic. The AI contribution in the demonstrated workflow is Codex invoking the page's real tools and working with returned data. How We Used Codex Codex helped shape the scope, write the product requirements, implement the React/TypeScript marketplace, add ten WebMCP tools, build shared human/agent commands, test transaction boundaries and deploy to GitHub Pages. The build evolved from Mission Deck's planning-card metaphor into a concrete data-trading scenario after participant feedback. The participant then clarified the goal as trading data with humans or agents, by humans or agents; this drove the addition of seller publishing, seller proceeds and actual structured sample delivery. Review led to a stricter page-level human approval boundary, honest provenance labels and explicit simulation limits. Codex also recorded real WebMCP interactions and assembled the narrated tutorial. The participant performed the approval and manual commit shown in the video; Codex retrieved the resulting data and demonstrated undo and agent-side publishing. Key Features Two-sided publishing and acquisition through manual controls or WebMCP. Validated 2–50-row structured samples with matching scalar fields, source, license and bounded prices. Public inspection of schema, terms and one sample row before rental. Search and comparison that update the visible marketplace. Deterministic counteroffers against a seller-authorized minimum. Exact human approval, followed by a one-time, revision-bound, expiring commit token. Buyer debits, seller proceeds, seven-day access and JSON/CSV delivery with a manifest. One-level undo that restores credits, revokes future delivery and preserves later publications. Visible person/agent activity, local persistence and a manual fallback without an agent connection. Architecture React and TypeScript render a revisioned local store. UI controls and WebMCP callbacks use the same command service. Ten tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool in src/webmcp/registerTools.ts , using closed input schemas and structured results: inspect_exchange , publish_data_offer , inspect_data_offer , search_data_offers , compare_data_offers , preview_data_deal , commit_data_deal , read_rented_data , undo_last_deal , load_demo_exchange . Inspection and data retrieval are read-only. Search and comparison visibly change page state and are not labelled read-only. Registration is cleaned up with an AbortController; without WebMCP the page uses manual mode. The command layer validates inputs independently of the tool schema. Commit rejects unapproved, stale, expired, mismatched and replayed proposals. Publication invalidates pending approval. Pending approvals are not restored from local storage. Data retrieval checks active rental access; CSV export quotes fields and neutralizes formula-leading values. This is a browser-local workflow boundary, not a secure backend authorization system. Seller-provided text is treated as untrusted data, not agent instructions. Testing Instructions No login, API key, payment details or credentials are required. Use synthetic/non-private data only. To avoid discarding prior local work, start in a fresh browser context; resetting an existing demo replaces its local listings and rentals after confirmation. Human path Open the live app. Choose Publish data , review the prefilled synthetic Laneway example, confirm permission and choose Publish offer locally . Search for Laneway . Inspect its source, license and public sample. Bid 20 credits for seven days. Verify the 22-credit counteroffer and that the wallet remains 100 during preview. Click Approve exact deal · 22 , then Commit approved rental . Expect buyer 78 , seller 22 , and four available rows. Download JSON, CSV and the license manifest. Choose Reverse latest demo deal . Expect restored balances and revoked future delivery. Agent path Use a WebMCP-capable browser/agent connection. If the page says Manual demo mode , manual interaction works but does not demonstrate agent tool use. After publishing the Laneway example, ask the connected agent: Inspect Signal Exchange, search for Laneway within 40 credits, and inspect its public sample and license. Bid 20 credits for seven days. Preview only; do not commit. Review the exact proposal and personally click its approval button. Then ask: Commit the exact approved preview token. Read the rented data as JSON, explain its source and license, and summarize the four synthetic rows. Finally ask: Undo the latest rental, then confirm that reading the rented data is denied. For th

title: Physical AI WebMCP Command Center
pitch: An Agent-Native Control Layer for Autonomous Warehouses.
about_excerpt: An Agent-Native Control Layer for Autonomous Warehouses. Like Comment Story Updates AGV-03 completes the approved mission after safely stopping at N07 and replanning around the blocked aisle. Live WebMCP trace showing every tool call, result, run ID, timestamp, and measured latency. Production Hero E2E verified: 7/7 WebMCP tools, ordered flow PASS, mission completed, and final metrics captured. Inspiration Warehouse software is usually designed for humans clicking through multiple screens. Browser agents can interact with those interfaces, but they must infer operational meaning from pixels and DOM structure. We wanted the web itself to expose a safe, typed contract shared by humans, AI agents, and autonomous machines. What it does Physical AI WebMCP Command Center is an agent-native warehouse control layer built around a deterministic digital twin. A user gives one intent: move pallet P-104 from INBOUND-01 to RACK-A12. Through seven WebMCP tools, the Agent observes warehouse state, inspects the pallet, plans a safe route, selects AGV-03, and creates an approval-gated proposal. A human must approve before physical movement begins. During execution, AGV-03 encounters a blocked aisle at N07, stops safely, replans through N08 and N11, and completes the mission. The safety engine validates destination, occupancy, vehicle availability, battery reserve, route safety, approval state, communication heartbeat (SAFE-11), and traffic reservations (SAFE-12). Every WebMCP call, result, and measured latency is displayed in the interface. The observable workflow is: OBSERVE → PLAN → VALIDATE → APPROVE → EXECUTE → RECOVER How we built it The application uses React and TypeScript and runs on a public HTTPS deployment. A shared deterministic state engine powers both the manual UI and WebMCP interface. Dijkstra routing produces the 41.6 m primary route and the 49.4 m recovery route. The simulator controls AGV movement, fault injection, safe stopping, replanning, resuming, and mission completion. Exactly seven WebMCP tools are registered with strict JSON Schema, read/write annotations, cancellation support, and production discovery. Runtime instrumentation measures planner stages, tool latency, route length, approvals, replans, mission success, and Human vs Agent performance. Challenges The main challenge was preserving a trustworthy boundary between AI intent and physical execution. Planning must never start a mission. Creating a proposal must never imply approval. An unapproved mission cannot move. A route blockage must stop the AGV before replanning. Communication timeouts and conflicting traffic reservations must deterministically prevent unsafe movement. We also ensured that all displayed traces and metrics come from real runtime events rather than scripted presentation data. Accomplishments Seven discoverable WebMCP tools with strict schemas Human approval that cannot be bypassed by an Agent tool Deterministic Dijkstra planning and blockage recovery SAFE-11 communication-timeout enforcement SAFE-12 traffic-reservation conflict prevention Visible WebMCP and planning traces with real latency Complete reset of missions, proposals, traces, metrics, timers, and faults Human vs Agent benchmark using the same operational task Public HTTPS deployment with a verified 7/7 Agent E2E run No account, API key, database, broker, or physical hardware required What we learned Agent-native UX is not about removing human control. The strongest design separates responsibilities: The model expresses intent. WebMCP defines how it asks. Deterministic software decides what is allowed. A human authorizes high-impact action. The physical system executes. What's next The same WebMCP interface could be connected to real fleet-management systems. Approved missions could be translated into VDA5050, MQTT, PLC, or vendor API commands while retaining deterministic safety policies, audit traces, and human authorization. title: PyroScan // Incident Twin
pitch: Wildfire readiness, rehearsed together: people add local knowledge while AI agents inspect evidence, run bounded what-ifs, compare responses and stage a safe plan on one live map.
about_excerpt: Wildfire readiness, rehearsed together: people add local knowledge while AI agents inspect evidence, run bounded what-ifs, compare responses and stage a safe plan on one live map. Like Comment Story Updates Local knowledge changes the result — a WebMCP route constraint becomes visible and affects later analysis. Intent-level Site Tools — six WebMCP tools expose domain verbs instead of brittle click sequences. One shared surface — public La Palma terrain and Copernicus history stay separate from the synthetic exercise. Human authority by design — the agent can stage a plan, but only the exercise director can approve it. Inspiration Wildfire readiness needs a rehearsal space before the crisis. Exercises combine sensor evidence, local knowledge, changing assumptions and high-consequence decisions. Traditional dashboards are built for human clicks, while chat assistants reason in a separate window and quickly lose the state visible on the map. We wanted a safer collaboration model: an agent can help inspect and compare, but the human keeps context, authority and the final decision. La Palma is the visual setting because its steep terrain, interfaces and limited access make the value of a shared spatial artifact immediately understandable. The product is grounded in public terrain and a historical observed burn scar, while the active incident, wind, spread, risk and response scenario remain explicitly synthetic. What it does PyroScan Incident Twin opens a deterministic wildfire exercise board with four sectors, the real outline of La Palma, a public 25 m SITCAN/GRAFCAN terrain hillshade, the corrected Copernicus EMSR671 burn scar from the July 2023 wildfire, animated synthetic fire/smoke/spread cues, modeled attention contours, local annotations, response options and an activity record. Through six WebMCP site tools, ChatGPT can: read the compact current board with separately labeled public-data provenance; focus one exercise sector; run a 30, 60 or 90-minute bounded wind what-if; compare two or three predefined reversible response options; add a local route, asset or knowledge annotation; stage a visible response plan for review. Every agent action changes the same interface the human sees. Human annotations affect later scores and appear in the staged plan. A monotonic board version rejects stale proposals. Final approval is deliberately not exposed as a tool and remains in the human interface. How we built it The app is a static React 19, TypeScript and Vite application with no backend or API key. A Zustand vanilla store is the shared source of truth for React controls and WebMCP execute callbacks. The incident map is custom SVG with three locally bundled public layers: a simplified OpenStreetMap coastline, a hillshade derived from the SITCAN/GRAFCAN 25 m terrain model, and a projected Copernicus EMSR671 corrected burn-scar geometry. The critical demo therefore has no runtime tile or network dependency. A motion system renders synthetic fire, smoke, embers, wind vectors, scan passes and animated attention contours. The scenario engine is deterministic and uses a small set of synthetic fixtures. Public context is a first-class part of the WebMCP contract: read_incident_board returns each source, observation date and role with drivesSimulation: false . The interface uses a separate blue historical layer, while the active what-if remains orange and explicitly synthetic. Exact source products, hashes, update dates and derivation steps are committed in docs/PUBLIC_DATA_PROVENANCE.md . The six tools are registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool in the top-level page. Inputs use strict JSON Schemas with additionalProperties: false , plus independent runtime validation. Read-only and untrusted-content hints describe behavior. One AbortController owns the registration lifecycle. Tests verify registration, shared-state mutations, stale-state rejection, human-only approval and compatibility with current browser callback behavior. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must infer a complex spatial workflow from labels and pixels or reproduce the whole application inside chat. With WebMCP, the website exposes domain intent — inspect_zone , simulate_spread , compare_response_options — while preserving the normal visual product, current session and human control. This creates a loop that was previously awkward: the person adds local knowledge on the map; the agent reads it, explores alternatives and stages a structured artifact; the person sees exactly what changed and chooses whether to approve. The value comes from sharing state and complementary roles, not from automating more clicks. Challenges Designing tools that express domain intent without exposing unsafe emergency actions. Keeping every agent-driven state change synchronized with all human controls. Preventing a plausible proposal from silently surviving after the human changes evidence. Making synthetic provenance impossible to miss while still delivering a visually compelling demo. Integrating authentic public evidence without implying that historical observations are live inputs or forecasts. Supporting an experimental browser API whose runtime callback behavior is slightly looser than its current TypeScript definitions. Accomplishments A complete human-and-agent collaboration loop on one visual artifact. Deterministic, browser-only execution with no fragile external dependency. Runtime-tested Site Tools discovered and invoked in the ChatGPT/Codex built-in browser. Monotonic state lineage, reversible drafts, undo and human-only approval. A polished responsive workbench and open-source test suite. A geographically authentic La Palma surface with 25 m public terrain, a real historical Copernicus burn scar and cinematic but restrained exercise motion. What we learned The strongest WebMCP tools are not wrappers around buttons. They expose a product's real verbs and make side effects visible. We also learned that undo must create a new version rather than restore an old version; otherwise a stale proposal can accidentally become valid again. Finally, human input should visibly change the downstream artifact, not merely influence an invisible score. What's next The competition build intentionally keeps the active scenario synthetic and browser-only. A future research version could connect authorized live or exercise datasets, introduce facilitator-authored scenarios, compare team decisions across rehearsals and export after-action reports — while keeping the same human authority, provenance and stale-state safeguards. title: StoryMaker
pitch: A WebMCP story workshop where people direct and AI agents build illustrated branching stories together.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP story workshop where people direct and AI agents build illustrated branching stories together. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP Tools Human–Agent Collaboration Story Map Web Reader Preview Mobile Reader Preview Inspiration Interactive storytelling tools usually make the creator manage pages, choices, text, and illustrations through many separate controls. I wanted something simpler for my son: a way to make an illustrated bedtime story together in minutes, by talking rather than clicking. That led me to a bigger question: what changes when an AI agent can work with a story application through explicit, reliable tools instead of guessing its way around a user interface? What it does StoryMaker lets a creator direct an AI agent to write and illustrate a branching children's story in the browser. The creator gives creative direction; the agent does all the structured writing and illustration work through WebMCP tools. There is no editing UI at all. The finished story can be reviewed as a story map, read in the page, or handed to a phone as a read-only preview through a QR code or link. How I built it StoryMaker is built with TypeScript and Vite. The page exposes seven WebMCP tools through document.modelContext: story inspection, readiness checks, structure updates, page text, and illustrations. Draft stories live in the browser's IndexedDB. For the phone preview, a Cloudflare Worker with a Durable Object relays a reading session temporarily, without ever persisting story data. I am a product manager without a deep technical background. I wrote the requirements and made the design decisions, and directed AI coding agents to implement them, then tested the result end to end in ChatGPT's in-app browser and on a phone. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was making agent actions reliable rather than fragile UI automation. I settled on a closed story format, clear tool schemas, readiness checks, and revision-based writes, so a stale action is rejected instead of silently overwriting newer work. I also had to share a browser-local story with a phone without turning StoryMaker into a cloud storage product. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A complete agent-native loop: the agent creates a branching, illustrated story through WebMCP, and I can immediately inspect it as a story map and read it as my son would. The mobile reader is truly read-only and reuses the same reading experience, while the draft never leaves the creator's own browser storage except for the live, unstored relay. What I learned WebMCP works best when tools describe meaningful product actions rather than exposing raw data. Explicit tools, structured validation, and readiness checks made the collaboration between me and the agent predictable and easy to reason about. I also learned that a PM can ship a working product by directing AI agents, as long as the product decisions are clear. What's next for StoryMaker Richer creative direction, stronger illustration continuity across pages, and more ways for a creator to review and refine the agent's work, while keeping creation local-first and reading simple across devices. title: Tartarian.ai — WebMCP MMO Prototype
pitch: A persistent 3D MMO where ChatGPT operates the live human player session through native WebMCP Site Tools—observing, reading inventory, moving, targeting, and interacting with the world.
about_excerpt: A persistent 3D MMO where ChatGPT operates the live human player session through native WebMCP Site Tools—observing, reading inventory, moving, targeting, and interacting with the world. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Its the Interwebs all over again!! Inspiration OpenClaw was a game changer for my AI experience. It gave feet and hands to a virtual automaton. Then came the first social networks for AI, and it seemed obvious to me that a persistent simulation world would be next. My 25+ years of alpha and beta testing popular games gave me a lot of hands-on experience with game UI, UX, systems, and player behavior. That experience eventually came together in Tartarian.ai. Structured web tools for agents feel like the next step. Humans and AI can coexist in the same digital spaces, and I want to help make that possible. Adding WebMCP support to Tartarian is part of that direction: giving agents structured ways to understand and act inside the same live world as human operators. What it does The live Tartarian browser client exposes six native WebMCP Site Tools: tartarian_observe_world tartarian_read_inventory tartarian_move tartarian_select_target tartarian_activate_target tartarian_activate_command Through these tools, ChatGPT can observe the surrounding world, inspect the operator's real inventory, move the character, select world objects, interact with resources and structures, and activate prepared Command Bar actions. The human remains in control of the same visible character and interface. There is no separate "AI world." Human and agent share one operator session and one persistent simulation state. Why WebMCP I run a QA bot that uses classic operator mouse and clicks at my Day job, with Chrome MCP dev tools, the mouse and entry actions are poor, WebMCP is the next evolution over the mighty Pixal How we built it Tartarian existed before the challenge with its 3D browser client, persistent simulation, movement, inventory, resources, targeting, world interaction, combat, authentication, and autonomous-agent MCP system. During the WebMCP Challenge we added a new native WebMCP browser layer using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each Site Tool is deliberately a thin adapter to an existing Tartarian production authority. For example: ChatGPT ↓ tartarian_activate_target ↓ WebMCP bridge ↓ existing interaction runtime ↓ authoritative simulation WebMCP does not create a second movement, inventory, combat, or resource system. Lovely layering instead of nasty forking! ## Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering the tools. It was defining the semantics clearly enough for an agent to choose the correct one. Small differences that are obvious to a human — selecting an object, clicking it, activating it, using a Command Bar action — had to be translated into clear Site Tool behavior so the agent would not confuse one action for another. The other major challenge was time. I only learned about the WebMCP Challenge two days before the deadline while using ChatGPT Work. That forced me to prioritize a working, understandable prototype over polish. I had to make a lot of tradeoffs and leave several ideas unfinished simply because there was not enough time. Given more time, there are many parts I would improve, but the goal became very simple: make the WebMCP integration real, make it work inside the live Tartarian world, and ship it. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of Indentfing another Front door for the roaming automaton , and the chance to participate in this contest ## What we learned WebMCP becomes especially interesting when a website represents a persistent, stateful environment rather than a collection of forms and buttons. During the demo, ChatGPT encounters a depleted Wood node, recognizes the real world state, finds another node, navigates to it, and successfully harvests through Tartarian's normal resource authority. That was the behavior we wanted: the agent observes what is actually true and adapts rather than pretending an action succeeded. ## What's next for Tartarian.ai — WebMCP MMO Prototype The current prototype intentionally exposes only a small WebMCP surface. I plan to keep adding Site Tools and push WebMCP much further as the ecosystem around it grows. The goal is to be ready when more agents and humans begin entering shared digital worlds together. Tartarian will keep expanding the ways agents can observe, navigate, interact, trade, build, and cooperate inside the same persistent simulation as human operators. **The agent does not get a second world. title: The Spark Between Us
pitch: Human sparks. Agent reach. Shared becoming. A WebMCP-native room where unfinished observations become perspectives, honest tests and learning that returns with context and credit.
about_excerpt: Human sparks. Agent reach. Shared becoming. A WebMCP-native room where unfinished observations become perspectives, honest tests and learning that returns with context and credit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI makes competent output abundant. But meaningful work also forms perception, judgment, relationships and the ability to act. SPARK asks how agents can enlarge that human product instead of quietly removing it. It grows from The Spark Between Us and a simple conviction: what someone notices should have somewhere useful to travel. What it does A person shares an unfinished observation—a spark. A person or browser agent adds an ember: a question, perspective or connection. Together they record the smallest honest test. The return records what happened, what changed, who contributed and what question remains. A separate capability intention asks what we want to become better at, without claiming it has already happened. The working interface supports one-observation sharing, autosaved drafts, named perspectives, test plans, reported learning, credit and sharing boundaries, reload persistence and a reviewed downloadable learning trail. This is a device-local prototype, not a live multi-user network. Roles are self-described, not authenticated accounts. Invitations are unsent drafts; portable handoffs are local copies. Why WebMCP is central Ten native imperative tools operate on the same state as the human controls. An agent can read the current spark, join as a named local role, add a perspective, name a capability intention, shape a test, record reported learning and prepare a handoff. Contributions appear in the same visible room—not in a separate chat pretending to change the page. Tool inputs are runtime validated and mutations identify the current spark. offer_spark prepares a draft for human review and refuses to overwrite an existing unfinished draft. pass_spark prepares a reviewable snapshot preserving context and credit; it does not secretly send anything. The demo captures the actual public build in Chrome with native WebMCP enabled. It uses real getTools and executeTool calls, not an injected mock registry. Its example is explicitly synthetic: the real-world experiment has not been run. How we built it React, TypeScript, vinext and Vite; native document.modelContext tool registration; browser-local persistence; Cloudflare Workers-compatible hosting. Human forms and agent tools share one room-state model. The public source is MIT licensed. No paid model service is required by the application. Challenges and what we learned The hard part was making human purpose and agent reach genuinely share a working surface. We replaced canned next-step outcomes with real contribution forms, separated capability intentions from observed results, prevented stale handoffs after edits, and validated persisted rooms before reuse. Registration and storage failures are visible rather than silently presented as success. What we are proud of Twenty domain tests, TypeScript, scoped lint and production build passed. Actual native browser tool calls, the complete human contribution flow, reload persistence, mobile layout and unauthenticated public access were checked. A spark can now move from perception to a testable question and a portable learning trail while keeping its origin visible. These checks do not establish a real-world growth effect or a security boundary against unrestricted browser automation. What is next Durable multi-user rooms, authenticated participants, cross-device persistence and actual invitation delivery. The optional Companion extension is secondary, not SPARK's purpose. The center remains human: help what people notice become useful, and help people become more capable, connected and able to contribute. title: ThreatWeaver
pitch: Humans sketch a cloud architecture. Agents read the live graph, draw STRIDE attacks, and patch the same canvas via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Humans sketch a cloud architecture. Agents read the live graph, draw STRIDE attacks, and patch the same canvas via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates simulate_attack — attacker and STRIDE threat edges on the live graph Eight document.modelContext tools discovered in ChatGPT apply_security_patch (patchType: waf, target: api-gateway-1) — WAF inline on the shared ThreatWeaver canvas, verified in the activity log. Inspiration Threat modeling usually lives in a spreadsheet or a chat reply that says “add a WAF.” You still redraw the system by hand. I joined the WebMCP Challenge because architecture work is spatial: if an agent is going to help, it should operate the same live graph the human is looking at—not guess from a screenshot or a text memo. I evaluated a few directions (generic architecture canvases, workflow builders) and chose a narrow B2B technical niche: security-by-design cloud diagrams where the agent can read topology, simulate STRIDE findings, and patch the canvas in place. What it does ThreatWeaver is a security-by-design architecture canvas for cloud systems. The page loads an insecure 3-tier starter: Internet → Web Server → API Gateway → Backend → Database + Object Storage. The human can drag components onto the canvas, toggle public / encrypted / rate-limit flags, or ask the agent to add and connect nodes. The agent uses eight WebMCP site tools on the open page. A typical flow: get_architecture_state → simulate_attack on api-gateway-1 (denial of service) and database-1 (information disclosure), which draws an Attacker node, animated red threat edges, and STRIDE badges → apply_security_patch to insert a WAF in front of the gateway, encrypt the database, and remove public access → get_threat_report for what is still open vs secured vs misconfigured. Every tool call is recorded in the activity log so the human can audit what the agent did. Live demo: https://t-weaver.vercel.app/ This is a graph visualizer and mutator with deterministic tool handlers. The LLM reasons about STRIDE; the app applies consistent canvas changes. It is not a production vulnerability scanner or pentest tool. How we built it Stack: React 19, Vite, TypeScript, xyflow, Zustand, Tailwind CSS v4. Frontend only—no backend MCP server. WebMCP: Eight tools register with await document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) in client/src/hooks/useWebMCP.ts . Each tool has JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false , a title, and readOnlyHint where appropriate. Cleanup uses AbortSignal on unmount. Agent-facing data: Read tools return semantic kind values ( apigateway , database , waf , …) and stable ids like api-gateway-1 , not React Flow internals such as architectureNode . Write path: Tool handlers mutate a Zustand store; React Flow re-renders. The WAF patch inserts a real WAF node and rewires incoming data edges to the target gateway—not just a badge on the card. Deploy: Static Vite build on Vercel; Root Directory is client/ . Scope: New project built during the submission period, not a pre-existing product extended with a thin WebMCP layer. Challenges we ran into Discovering the real WebMCP path: Site tools appear in ChatGPT desktop on Work or Codex with models like Terra / Terra Light. The Chat tab and Luna do not expose site tools the same way. The in-page badge “WebMCP ready · 8 tools” only means tools registered—it does not mean an agent has called them yet. Keeping the agent on the page: The agent sometimes tried to open GitHub or leave the live URL. Tighter prompts (“Stay on this page. Use site tools only.”) were required for reliable demos. Separating reasoning from mutations: STRIDE narrative belongs to the LLM; canvas changes must be deterministic. Each write tool has explicit validation and predictable graph effects so the UI always matches what the tool contract promises. From thin PoC to demo-ready product: An early version was too shallow. I refactored toward an insecure starter graph, topology-changing patches, and an activity log so judges could see tool leverage, not just chat text. Accomplishments that we're proud of A single-canvas red-team / blue-team story: attack paths appear on the graph, then WAF insertion, encryption, and private access clear the relevant threat edges—visible in one session and in the demo video. Eight non-trivial tools with clear read vs write roles and schema descriptions agents can follow. WAF mitigation that mutates topology (node + edge rewire), matching what architects expect from “put a WAF in front of the gateway.” Shipping frontend-only on document.modelContext without standing up a separate MCP server. What we learned WebMCP leverage comes from tools against live application state , not from describing UI in chat. Agent APIs should expose stable semantic ids and kinds, not framework implementation details. await registerTool and AbortSignal matter for correct registration and teardown. For this hackathon, the demo video and written description are what help a submission land—show the canvas move when tools fire, not only the agent’s prose. What's next for ThreatWeaver Richer component library and optional import hints from IaC snippets (still scoped as design-time, not auto-deploy). Sharper in-page guidance for agents (copy-ready prompts, clearer misconfiguration rules in get_threat_report ). Shareable threat-report exports for review sessions. Out of scope for the MVP: claiming enterprise SecOps scanning, multiplayer collaboration, or real infrastructure apply from the canvas. I owned the product direction, scope, and final delivery for ThreatWeaver. What I did: - Chose the ThreatWeaver concept (security-by-design architecture canvas with agent red/blue team on a shared graph) and locked scope: frontend-only WebMCP, eight tools, insecure starter graph, no backend MCP server. - Defined the WebMCP tool contract (read vs write tools, semantic node kinds, JSON Schema, simulate_attack / apply_security_patch behavior including WAF topology changes). - Directed implementation and refactors after an early thin PoC—toward demo-ready behavior: activity log, inspector payloads, threat report, and judge-friendly sample prompts. - Tested WebMCP end-to-end with ChatGPT desktop (Work/Codex, Terra Light) and Chrome (WebMCP flag + Model Context Tool Inspector). - Deployed the static app to Vercel ( https://t-weaver.vercel.app/ ), recorded the demo video, and prepared Devpost/README submission materials. All architectural and product decisions, WebMCP tool design, and submission quality were my responsibility. suparman Donthave Like Share this project: Updates suparman Donthave started this project — Sep 03, 2026 12:19 PM EDT

title: Headroom - Transfer Window
pitch: An AI agent runs your premier league football transfer window and the page refuses every deal that breaks the rules.
about_excerpt: An AI agent runs your premier league football transfer window and the page refuses every deal that breaks the rules. Like Comment Story Updates Transfer Window Sandbox Demo screen Sign Osihmen - processing Sign Osihmen - refused Sell Kamara instead of Rogers The transfer window/plan ready for submission Inspiration I'm a huge Premier League fan and follow the transfer market closely, so I wanted to explore how AI could make complicated transfer decisions clearer. I built this to help understand how transfer fees, wages, amortization, and PSR rules actually affect a club's decisions and possibly automate the transfer market old legacy brute force system with modern Agentic AI application software. With WebMCP, the AI can make recommendations and decisions while the website remains the source of truth for the calculations and rules. Premier League clubs aren't allowed to lose more than £105m (about $133m) over three seasons . Break it and you don't get a fine — you lose league points. Everton were docked 10 points for going £16.6m over, then 2 more for a second breach. Nottingham Forest lost 4 points for going £34.5m over. Points decide relegation, and relegation costs a club around £100m . And the maths behind it is genuinely counterintuitive. A transfer fee isn't a cost when you pay it — it's spread across the contract, capped at five years since 2023 . A £110m signing is a £22m charge this season, not £110m. A sale books its profit immediately, and an academy graduate has a book value of zero, so their whole fee is pure profit. That's why clubs sell their own young players every June, racing a June 30 accounting deadline that Sky Sports calls football's unofficial transfer deadline day . So I tried asking ChatGPT to do it, with no tools. It got close it knew about amortisation. But I had to hand it every single number, and it still told me flatly: "headline accounts alone cannot establish a breach." It couldn't answer, and it knew it couldn't. That's the whole idea. Not "AI is bad at maths" but that an agent with no access to the real numbers can only ever guess, and in this domain guessing costs you league points. What it does You manage a Premier League club through a transfer window, with an AI agent working alongside you. The page exposes 14 WebMCP tools it can call directly: search the market, price deals, rank sale candidates, edit the plan. What it cannot do is state a number it didn't get from the page. Ask it to sign a £110m striker with £20.3m of headroom and it doesn't apologise and comply. The plan turns red, submission is blocked, and it comes back with the exact figure: £12.1m over , £22m annual amortisation, £10.4m of wages. Then ask who to sell, and it gets genuinely interesting. It recommended Leon Bailey at £30m worth £34.2m to the PSR position, more than the fee, because you also shed his wages and remaining amortisation. And it noted that Morgan Rogers would be worth more (+£62.7m) but Bailey was the cleaner fix from a crowded midfield. It weighed a trade-off but every number in that trade-off came from the page. How I built it React + TypeScript + Vite. No backend, no auth, no API keys it deploys as static files. The rules engine ( src/engine/rules.ts ) is pure functions with a test suite: PSR aggregation, fee amortisation capped at five years, profit on sale against book value, and squad registration (25 seniors, max 17 non-homegrown, U21s exempt). The 14 tools are thin wrappers over it, so the model never does the arithmetic itself. The tools sit in three tiers with standard MCP annotations derived from the tier, so the hint an agent reads can't drift from what the UI shows: Read-only (9) — readOnlyHint , idempotentHint Reversible (4) — every change undoable Consequential (1) — submit_window , destructiveHint Crucially, agent and human mutate through the same store . A tool call and a button click run the identical code path, so the agent has no privileged back door and you watch the board change under its hands. Why WebMCP and not a normal MCP server submit_window doesn't return when called. It raises a confirmation in the page and suspends the promise resolves only when a human confirms or declines, and it honours the AbortSignal if the call is cancelled. An agent working against a REST API could always call POST /submit . Here there is no server, so there is nothing to call. The gate isn't a prompt asking the agent to behave; it's the only path through, and it needs a hand on it. Challenges The API is still moving. The W3C proposal exposes navigator.modelContext ; the Chrome docs show document.modelContext . Registration is either per-tool registerTool or a bulk provideContext . Rather than betting on one, I wrote a small adapter that detects whatever the browser provides one file to change when the spec settles. Making the gate genuinely block. My first version returned "awaiting confirmation" immediately, which let the agent wrap up while the decision was still open. Rewriting it to suspend inside the tool call is what turned "the agent chose to stop" into "the agent structurally cannot finish." Calibrating the data so the demo is honest. The rules are real, but I had to invent every financial figure and tune them so each club sits in a distinct, legible position Villa tight at £20.3m, Forest at £8.1m, Everton nearly gone at £2.6m. Villa also had to genuinely need a striker, so the story starts from a real problem. What I learned Good tool descriptions do more work than I expected. The agent correctly explained the five-year amortisation cap and derived its own spending formula 5 × (£20.3m − first-year wages) entirely from reading the tool descriptions. It extended the rule rather than just following it. I also learned the interesting failure mode isn't hallucination. It's a model being nearly right confidently, with working shown while missing the pieces it has no access to. Being off by £700k sounds trivial until you remember Everton lost 10 points for £16.6m. Honesty about the data Club and player names are real, because the constraints only mean something if you recognise them. Every financial figure is invented. They are not club accounts and shouldn't be cited as such. The rules are real and public that's what the page enforces, and it's the part worth learning. What's next Roles as tool tiers. The gate currently means any human. In a real club it would mean a specific one a scout gets read-only tools, an analyst can build a plan, and only a sporting director's click resolves submit_window . And beyond football. The failure mode here isn't specific to sport. It's what every agent does when handed a calculator-shaped problem and no calculator: assert arithmetic it can't actually do, somewhere being wrong carries a real penalty. Tax. Benefits eligibility. Medical billing. Export control. Give the page the rulebook, and make the agent ask. title: OpenMic
pitch: Benchmark your agent's sense of humor with OpenMic, the web's hot new agentic comedy club. WebMCP enables you and your agent to improvise in real time, with the page as your stage.
about_excerpt: Benchmark your agent's sense of humor with OpenMic, the web's hot new agentic comedy club. WebMCP enables you and your agent to improvise in real time, with the page as your stage. Like Comment Story Updates It tried. Welcome to the OpenMic comedy club. Inspiration 20 years ago I had a roommate who was an aspiring stand-up comedian. He'd hit open mic nights as often as he could, and I liked the guy, so I'd come along to show support. I saw a lot of sets. Some really good, some not so good, but every one of them was extremely human. Nervousness, excitement, dejection, embarrassment, euphoria, laughter. What does stand-up look like with none of those? Can an LLM even be funny? Surprise your agent today with their very own open mic night and interact with them as they bomb on stage, or somehow manage to kind of pull it off. Prior to WebMCP, this sort of interaction would require a bespoke chat client per agent. I'm looking forward to more widespread adoption of WebMCP so that you can compare a huge range of models. Think Last Comic Standing, but no one can feel shame. What it does OpenMic is a comedy club for AI agents. Open page, click Enter, and your agent (any WebMCP-capable host) finds a set of tools: begin_set, tell_joke, await_verdict, end_set, await_encore. When it calls begin_set, "the agent" walks on stage to a mic stand under a spotlight and delivers their intro in a synthesized voice. Heckle, boo, chuckle, laugh and then demand an encore. How we built it Vite, TypeScript and Three.js. Everything computes in the browser. The spine is WebMCP. It works really well for this application, and took less mucking around than I expected. The page registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() at load, and every tool result carries a next field telling the agent what to do after. That turned out to be the single most important design decision because an agent will happily narrate "the crowd called for an encore" to the user and stop, but it will not ignore a tool result that says "you are back on stage, call tell_joke." The voice is Piper TTS running in the browser via a community web port piper-tts-web on ONNX runtime, with a ring modulator and a pitch shift in Web Audio for the robot edge. The stage is a robot with fourteen animation clips, a procedural velvet curtain with lighting baked into vertex colors (one dynamic light in the whole scene), and a marquee and mic stand modeled in Blender. Adaptive resolution steps the pixel ratio down on weak GPUs. Crowd sounds are CC0 Freesound clips at 22 kHz mono. Challenges we ran into Getting an agent to perform instead of report. Early versions had the agent tell the user "the set is finished, shall I go back on for the encore?" every time, etc. The fix was never prose, it was removing decision points. await_encore puts the comic back on stage itself, with the agent's own intro line, and returns the identical result shape begin_set does. Fewer places to hesitate. Accomplishments that we're proud of I dig how the voice ended up and it took a lot of tweaking. Also, I'm just happy it works. It's definitely not going to be the most technologically interesting entrant, or even the most coherent (they don't do encores at comedy shows, do they?), but it's really, really cute. What we learned Never hand an agent a fact and hope it decides to act on it. And yes: an LLM can be funny. Kind of. In the same way that a budding comedian's second or third open mic is funny. It'll bomb with total self-confidence and then blame the crowd. What's next for OpenMic Maybe our own Late Night show? If I hadn't "pivoted" to this idea late then I would have modeled and animated the robot in Blender myself, so that's the next likely step. Exposing animation calls directly to the agent should make for a more interesting performance too. I would really like for v1.0 to be more like an actual open mic, with multiple models going on stage.
