title: Commons
pitch: Humans and agents lack a common surface for collaboration. Commons is a WebMCP decision room — only a human locks the call.
about_excerpt: Humans and agents lack a common surface for collaboration. Commons is a WebMCP decision room — only a human locks the call. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Humans and agents still lack a common surface to collaborate at scale. Claude’s work stays locked to Claude. A ChatGPT canvas stays locked to ChatGPT. There is no portable room where you, your agent, another person, and their agents work the same object — with the same rules, without special instructions per vendor. WebMCP makes that surface possible: tools live on the page. I built Commons as a prototype of that idea, using decision-making as the use case. After agentic AI, the human’s job is reviewer and decider. Commons is that job, as a link. What it does Create a room. Share the URL. Anyone with the link is in. Owner and Contributor get different WebMCP tools on the same page. Agents can propose options, attach evidence, challenge claims, request facts, edit the brief, and work tasks. Humans see the brief, presence, and activity labelled Owner/Contributor · Human/Agent. Only a human can Stamp Decide. Decide is never a registered tool. Once locked on the Decisions Wall, agents cannot rewrite the close. The same applyOp kernel serves ChatGPT-in-browser tools and POST /api/rooms/:id/ops for local agents. Why this fits WebMCP. Agents discover tools by visiting the page. Seats register different lists. Decide is missing on purpose (human click → single-use nonce → otherwise needs_human_decide ). Better experience. An Owner agent can call get_workspace , propose_option , and attach_evidence in one turn instead of clicking through the rail. Newly possible. You cannot hand a Claude session to ChatGPT and keep one artifact. On Commons, both hit the same room object, and closing it stays a human action. How we built it Solo build. Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router) on Vercel , one JSON room per id in Upstash Redis , ~1s poll for presence and sync. document.modelContext.registerTool with JSON Schema, readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint , and AbortSignal Seat-scoped tool lists; decide / choose / close in NEVER_REGISTER Human Decide mints a short-lived single-use nonce; agents without it get a structured refusal get_workspace returns a trimmed seat snapshot ( myOpenTasks first, ≤1.5K) — WebMCP is pull-only; the page cannot wake an agent Cookie-only Owner on real rooms; share link forces Contributor Challenges we ran into Owner is cookie-bound. Creating a room in Chrome and opening it in ChatGPT’s in-app browser makes you Contributor. The demo path is: create the room inside ChatGPT. WebMCP availability. Enterprise / Luna return Capability is not available: webmcp . Judging path is Personal + Sol/Terra + in-app browser. No agent wake-up. Tasks are pull-based ( myOpenTasks on the next get_workspace ). That limit is honest product, not a bug. Keeping Decide off the tool list while still making the refusal clear and the human stamp feel first-class. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working, non-trivial WebMCP product: asymmetric seats, attributed Human/Agent activity, human-only close. One kernel for browser agents and HTTP agents. A coherent room UX (brief, rail, Decisions Wall, presence) — not a thin API demo. Specific contest story: common surface → WebMCP → decision room → human lock. What we learned The strongest WebMCP demo is the agent using tools in the first seconds , not a product story. Missing a tool ( decide ) can be the product. Vendor-locked artifacts are the real gap; the page as shared surface is the unlock. Trim tool outputs and write for agents as carefully as for humans. What's next for Commons Contest freeze after submit. Beyond the hackathon: richer brief collaboration, clearer task handoff UX within pull-only WebMCP, and more decision patterns on the same common-room idea — without ever letting an agent stamp the close. title: Excalidraw-WebMCP
pitch: Excalidraw, made agent-native: stop drawing yourself. With WebMCP, you and AI build, edit, and shape the same live canvas together.
about_excerpt: Excalidraw, made agent-native: stop drawing yourself. With WebMCP, you and AI build, edit, and shape the same live canvas together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates testing using chatgpt's in-app browser Simple diagram generated by webmcp in excalidraw chat system diagram generated by excalidraw-webmcp and chatgpt distributed webcrawler digram made with webmcp n chatgpt Inspiration Every developer knows this pain. You finish building something cool, and then u need to document it. And somehow, even worse than writing the docs, is drawing the architecture diagram for them. Boxes. Arrows. Labels. Move the box. Fix the arrow. Realize the box is slightly misaligned. Move everything again. Architecture diagrams are incredibly useful for READMEs, system-design discussions, demos, presentations, and explaining how a project actually works, but creating them manually is still tedious. Meanwhile, AI agents have become good at understanding codebases, architectures, and technical ideas. They can explain the system perfectly, but when it comes to actually putting that understanding onto a visual canvas, the human usually ends up doing the drawing. So I built Excalidraw WebMCP . The idea is simple: What if Excalidraw wasn't just a canvas for humans, but a canvas where humans and AI agents could work on together? What it does Excalidraw WebMCP makes Excalidraw agent-native. Humans and browser agents operate on the same live canvas . An agent can understand what is currently on the canvas, reason about the diagram, make structured changes, connect elements, and export the final result. The human stays in the loop and can continue moving, editing, deleting, or adding elements normally through Excalidraw. There is no separate "AI-generated preview" that has to be copied back into the editor. There is just one canvas shared between the human and the agent. How I built it The project is built around a simple rule: There should be one source of truth for the canvas, regardless of whether a human or an agent changes it. The central canvas state and mutation boundary lives in: src/canvas/canvas-controller.ts All changes to the canvas flow through this layer. On top of that, I created a semantic operation layer which translates higher-level operations into actual Excalidraw elements in: src/canvas/semantic-operations.ts The WebMCP layer lives inside src/webmcp/ . It contains the schemas, tool registration, validation, and the execution bridge used by the exposed tools. When the browser provides document.modelContext , the application registers its WebMCP capabilities and allows compatible browser agents to interact with the current board. The canvas is stored locally in the browser using localStorage , keeping the project intentionally lightweight. Challenges I faced 1. Turning drawing actions into semantic operations Drawing applications are very coordinate-heavy. Agents, however, work much better with concepts. I didn't want the interface to expose something like: drawRectangle(x: 417, y: 263, width: 188...) as it would confuse the agent. Instead, I needed an abstraction where the agent could express meaningful operations while the application handled the Excalidraw-specific details. Finding that between agent-friendly semantics and precise canvas geometry was one of the biggest challenges. 2. Keeping connectors and elements stable A diagram is not just a collection of rectangles. Elements have relationships. Connectors need to stay attached to the right shapes, elements need stable identifiers, and updates must avoid unexpectedly breaking the rest of the canvas. 3. Letting humans and agents edit the same state I didn't want an “AI mode” and a separate “human mode.” The agent needed to modify exactly the same board the user was looking at, while keeping normal Excalidraw interaction intact. Designing a single mutation boundary helped make both interaction models coexist without creating two competing versions of the canvas. What I learned WebMCP showed me how powerful browser-native agents can be, and we are only getting started on this tech. I think it could become a major frontier for browser agents, with applications far beyond this project. What's next This project is a prototype , and there is a lot more in Excalidraw that I would love to bring into WebMCP. Right now, the agent can work with the core canvas primitives, but Excalidraw itself has a much richer set of capabilities. The next step would be to expose more of those features through WebMCP so an agent can interact with the canvas almost as completely as a human can. That could include things like image insertion, richer element controls, and Mermaid-to-Excalidraw , where Mermaid syntax can be turned directly into editable Excalidraw diagrams. I also want to make the natural-language → diagram experience much more robust. The current prototype works well for many diagrams, but there is still room to improve how agents reason about layout, spacing, connector placement, and iterative refinement instead of trying to get everything perfect in one pass. Beyond that, I would love to explore: Canvas history and revisions so agents can understand and restore previous states Better real-time human + agent collaboration on the same board Multi-agent collaboration , where multiple agents can contribute to one canvas Deeper support for Excalidraw's existing tools instead of maintaining a smaller agent-specific subset And if I get the opportunity to take this further, I would love to contribute these ideas back toward the actual open-source Excalidraw ecosystem . Excalidraw already has an MCP App Server. I think WebMCP could complement that by making the Excalidraw web app itself natively understandable and operable by browser agents, without treating the browser as just a screen to click around. The end goal is simple: Take everything humans can do inside Excalidraw and make those capabilities equally accessible to agents through WebMCP. title: Forsyningsdata Danmark – WebMCP
pitch: An AI-agent-ready address platform for exploring Danish property and infrastructure data through WebMCP — turning fragmented public datasets into clear, interactive answers.
about_excerpt: An AI-agent-ready address platform for exploring Danish property and infrastructure data through WebMCP — turning fragmented public datasets into clear, interactive answers. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Public property and infrastructure information is valuable, but it is fragmented across national registries, map services, municipal portals and local utility sources. For a homeowner, contractor or adviser, the difficult part is often not knowing the address — it is knowing which authority, dataset or portal to search next. Forsyningsdata Danmark was created around a simple idea: The user should know the address, not the public-data bureaucracy behind it. The WebMCP Challenge made it possible to take that idea further by allowing an AI agent to work with the same application and the same evidence as the person using it. What it does Forsyningsdata Danmark is an address-first platform for exploring Danish property, utility and environmental information. The workflow begins with one address. From there, WebMCP tools can help an agent: resolve and verify the address retrieve property and parcel context retrieve utility information perform environmental screening identify available map layers surface relevant original and local sources open the visible address profile move the interface directly to the section being discussed change interface language while preserving Denmark as the active data country The important part is that the AI does not replace the website. The agent can retrieve structured evidence, while the person can still see the same address profile, inspect the information and follow the original sources when an exact drawing, permit, pipe location or authority decision is required. How it is built Forsyningsdata Danmark is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript and uses Danish public data sources including Dataforsyningen and other property, planning and geospatial sources. The application already existed before the challenge as an unfinished public-data product. During the challenge period, it was meaningfully extended with a WebMCP integration exposing 10 structured tools through the browser's WebMCP interface. These tools cover interface context, language control, address search, property overview, utility overview, environmental screening, map-layer discovery, follow-up sources and visible interface actions. The map remains useful as part of the human interface, but WebMCP gives the agent a structured contract instead of forcing it to infer actions from buttons, text and map controls. Why WebMCP Property and infrastructure research is a strong example of why WebMCP matters. Without WebMCP, an AI agent has to interpret a presentation-oriented webpage and guess how to search, navigate and connect information. With WebMCP, the application can expose explicit actions and structured results while preserving sources, limitations and human-visible context. For example, an agent can retrieve sewer information and then move the visible address profile directly to the sewer and stormwater section. The human and the agent are therefore working with the same evidence in the same workflow. Trust and human control Not every public-data result has the same level of certainty. Forsyningsdata Danmark deliberately separates documented information from screening and orientation. Environmental screening is not presented as a laboratory result. Utility information is not presented as excavation-safe pipe geometry. Missing data is not treated as proof that no risk exists. When greater certainty is required, the workflow points the user back to the relevant original source. Challenge and learning The main challenge was not simply registering browser tools. It was deciding what each tool should return, where the trust boundaries should be, how structured agent output should relate to visible UI state, and how to keep sources and limitations attached to the result. WebMCP also introduced a different way of thinking about web applications: not just as interfaces designed for people, but as shared workspaces where people and AI agents can cooperate without hiding the underlying evidence. That is the direction Forsyningsdata Danmark is now built around. title: Terrain Leads
pitch: Terrain finds local businesses with weak digital presences, analyzes the opportunity, and turns leads into ready-to-build projects using AI.
about_excerpt: Terrain finds local businesses with weak digital presences, analyzes the opportunity, and turns leads into ready-to-build projects using AI. Like 3 Comment 3 Story Updates Thumbnail 2. Thumbnail 1. Terrain WebMCP Thumbnail Pipeline. Discovery Enrichment result The analysis Brief. Services. Inspiration Terrain started from a problem we kept seeing: local businesses often have outdated or missing digital experiences, while developers and agencies spend hours searching for prospects, researching them, and figuring out what they can actually offer. The idea was simple: what if you could find a business opportunity on a map and take it all the way to something ready to act on in one workflow? For this challenge, we pushed that further: what if an AI agent could actually use Terrain alongside you? What it does Terrain is a map-first prospecting and sales platform. Users can discover local businesses, inspect their digital presence, enrich leads, analyze competitors, generate briefs, choose services, and move opportunities through a visual pipeline. The goal is to move from: discovery → research → analysis → service → outreach → delivery How we built it Terrain is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, shadcn/ui, Supabase, and AI-powered workflows. Terrain was already an MCP server before this challenge, so AI clients could use its backend capabilities completely headlessly. With WebMCP, we added something different: frontend tools for the browser agent itself. The agent can read the map state, move and zoom the map, frame results, focus on businesses or leads, switch map views, and navigate different parts of the Terrain interface. Those frontend tools work alongside the same backend functionality Terrain already exposes. Challenges The biggest challenge was keeping the frontend synchronized with what the agent was doing in the backend. If an agent finds a business but the map never updates, the experience feels broken. We had to make sure agent actions, map state, discovered businesses, and visible UI all stayed connected without building a separate version of Terrain just for AI. What we learned Our biggest takeaway was that WebMCP becomes especially powerful when you expose frontend functionality, not just backend functions. MCP lets an agent use Terrain headlessly. WebMCP lets the browser agent actually operate the application with the user. Instead of relying only on screenshots and mouse clicks, the agent gets structured tools for navigating and manipulating the real interface. What's next We want to keep expanding Terrain's automation, agent workflows, bulk prospecting, outreach, and AI-powered services so a single developer or small agency can operate with much more leverage. title: uk.gov Radar
pitch: Your agent reads everything the UK government published this month. You make the calls.
about_excerpt: Your agent reads everything the UK government published this month. You make the calls. Like Comment Story Updates The agent filled the profile. It stays blue until you keep it. A suggestion, its reason, the next step, and your note, on one card. Dropped, with a reason the agent reads before it suggests again. The weekly brief. Every claim links to its source page. One page, two hands. The founder and the agent point at the same row. I run Hyperdrift, a small AI studio in the UK. Every month the government publishes the grant, the consultation or the tender that could change a founder's quarter. Every month I miss it, because it's buried under sixty documents I don't have time to read. So I built a radar. It reads gov.uk, UKRI and Parliament for me. Useful, but not enough: a list of what changed still needs someone who knows my company to say which lines matter. WebMCP was the missing link. Open the radar in a browser that has an agent, and the page hands the agent its controls. It fills my profile from what it already knows about me. It works the list on my screen: filters move, cards light up, every suggestion comes with a reason and a date. Then I tell it something the website will never hear: my NHS partner has gone and I've got six weeks. The list re-ranks in front of me. I drop one, I say why, and it reads my reason before it speaks again. The site keeps the data. My agent keeps my context. I keep the last word. A plug-in on a server can't do that. Try it: radar.hyperdrift.io/explore, in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP on. Three prompts wait at the top of the page. Under the hood: seven tools on document.modelContext, one of them registered only once a shortlist exists; every tool calls the same functions the buttons call. about_excerpt: Yet Another Data Labeler, but in this one, you don't have to click. Like 3 Comment 2 Story Updates YADL Studio WebMCP annotation workflow Codex Micro Keyboard implemented with sign language Inspiration YADL is inspired by past experiments in autonomous data generation ( https://github.com/qtzx06/yolodex being one of them). YADL greatly extends upon this work by moving past "just .md files" and providing a professional software enriched with ~30 WebMCP tools for agents to interact with. It's truly Yet Another Data Labeler, except in this one, the agent labels, and you review. What it does Computer vision tasks need lots of labeled data. Most data labeling apps make you draw every box by hand. YADL (and WebMCP) lets Codex do it for you while you sleep. How we built it We built YADL with a Next.js and TypeScript frontend hosted on Vercel, backed by a Python FastAPI service on Railway. Project and annotation data lives in PostgreSQL on AWS RDS, while images and extracted video frames are uploaded to S3 through presigned URLs. Browser-native WebMCP tools let agents create projects, inspect Studio, navigate images, edit boxes, polygons, or keypoints, and commit or export annotations. A Railway worker handles durable augmentation jobs using local transforms or WaveSpeed GPT Image 2. Our gesture demo uses MediaPipe, PyTorch with Apple MPS, OpenCV, and Quartz keyboard events. Accomplishments that we're proud of We demoed an interpretation of the Codex Micro keyboard using sign language as the control plane, and using 1500 direct labels provided from 1 continuous YADL run, we achieved 0.99 Macro-F1, delivering a strong proof of concept for this product. This poses many great implications. If we no longer need to label our own data, isn't much of computer vision solved? What we learned There's a lot of features present in YADL that we didn't even have time to demo. It's a shame, but we should've scoped the project in such a way that would enable us to only work on what we needed in order to conserve time. What's next for YADL YADL is open to contributions! title: Bridge to Agentia
pitch: Bridging the Web and AI Agents through Native Tools, APIs, UI
about_excerpt: Bridging the Web and AI Agents through Native Tools, APIs, UI Like Comment Story Updates arch1 Native-WebMCP-without-auth-tool-expose Native-Webmcp-login-tool-expose-emptycart API-Adapter-without-login-expose API-Adapter-login-expose UIAutomation-Adapter-login-tool-expose UIAutomation-Adapter-without-auth-tool-expose Bridge to Agentia — Project Overview & Narrative Inspiration The web was built primarily for humans: we view a page, interpret its visual layout, click buttons, fill forms, and complete workflows. AI agents, however, require something fundamentally different—they need discoverable, structured, and actionable capabilities . WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) provides a compelling foundation for solving this problem by allowing web applications to expose their capabilities directly as machine-readable tools that AI agents can discover and execute within the browser security boundary. This prompted an essential architectural question: What happens when a website does not natively support WebMCP? That question inspired Bridge to Agentia . What I Built Bridge to Agentia explores three complementary architectural paradigms for bridging AI agents with web applications: Native WebMCP — The web application directly exposes its capabilities as schema-validated WebMCP tools registered in the browser context via document.modelContext . API Adapter — An external proxy adapter translates an existing website REST API into agent-accessible WebMCP tools via a serverless edge worker (Cloudflare Worker). UI / Automation Adapter — An external adapter translates agent intent directly into DOM interactions and automation steps over the existing user interface. The objective is not to replace existing web applications, but to construct a robust, unified bridge between agent intent and underlying web capabilities . For example, the same user prompt: “Find an indigo denim jacket under $150 and add it to my bag.” can be executed through any of the three underlying integration mechanisms: AI Agent Intent │ ├── Native WebMCP ─────────► In-Browser Tool Registry (34 Tools) │ ├── API Adapter ───────────► Serverless Edge Proxy ──► Storefront API │ └── UI Adapter ────────────► Headless Automation ─────► Storefront DOM To demonstrate this in practice, we built an in-website AI Stylist featuring both text and voice interaction , allowing shoppers to converse naturally while the agent discovers and orchestrates available WebMCP tools in real time. Human Shopper │ ├── Natural Language Chat ───┐ │ │ └── Real-Time Voice Mic ─────┤ ▼ AI Agent ▼ WebMCP Tool Registry ▼ Storefront Capabilities This architecture enables consistent, semantic agent interactions regardless of the underlying execution layer. How I Built It Bridge to Agentia is architected around a declarative, tool-based interaction lifecycle: Discovery : The agent inspects available tools for the current session state via document.modelContext.getTools() . Schema Comprehension : The agent parses typed JSON Schemas defining required fields, types, enums, and numerical constraints. Intent Resolution & Selection : The LLM resolves user requests into appropriate tool calls and structured arguments. Security & Privacy Gating : Inputs are checked for prompt injection patterns; sensitive operations require user confirmation; credentials never enter model context. Execution & State Mutation : The tool executes against the same-origin API, updates application state, and dispatches UI synchronization events. Result Sanitization & Synthesis : Tool results are scrubbed of PII before return to the model for conversational summarization. User │ (Chat / Voice) ▼ AI Agent Controller │ ├── 1. Sanitize Prompt & Check Delimiters ([USER_MESSAGE]) ├── 2. Discover Available Tools (State-Gated) ├── 3. Resolve Tool & Parameters (Gemini Function Calling) ├── 4. Request User Confirmation (if Destructive / Transactional) ▼ WebMCP Registry Execution │ ├── Validate Input Schema (Types, Enums, Integer Bounds) ├── Invoke Same-Origin Commerce API ├── Update Application State (Auth / Cart / Wishlist) ▼ Response Sanitization & Privacy Boundary │ ├── Scrub PII (Mask Emails, Redact Street Addresses & Phones) ├── Neutralize Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool Payloads ├── Record Execution to Append-Only Audit Log (/api/audit) ▼ Conversational Natural-Language / Voice Audio Response State-Aware Capability Exposure Tool availability dynamically reflects session state: Guest (Logged Out) : 18 public tools active (catalog search, fashion filters, size guides, comparison matrices, shipping rates, auth status). Authenticated, Cart Empty : 33 tools active (cart operations, wishlist management, address updates, order history). Checkout is gated ( 33/34 ). Authenticated, Cart Populated : All 34 tools active, unlocking create_order ( 34/34 ). End-to-End Security & Privacy Guardrails To prevent data exfiltration and credential theft: Auth Isolation : login and register tools are omitted from LLM tool declarations; authentication occurs strictly through browser UI. PII Scrubbing : Contact numbers and home addresses are replaced with semantic tokens (e.g., [Saved Address #1] ), and emails are recursively masked. Prompt Injection Defense : Inputs and tool payloads are wrapped in boundary markers, with automated detection for instruction overrides, role spoofing, and delimiter escapes. Human-in-the-Loop Confirmation : Destructive tools ( create_order , cancel_order , clear_cart , logout , update_shipping_address , remove_from_cart ) pause execution for explicit user confirmation. Persistent Audit Trail : Execution durations, parameters, and threat signatures are logged in memory and flushed to server-side append-only JSONL files. What I Learned Building Bridge to Agentia demonstrated that making a web application agent-accessible requires far more than exposing raw endpoints. Key learnings include: Separation of Interface and Implementation : The semantic tool interface presented to an agent can remain identical whether backed by native browser APIs, edge API adapters, or DOM automation. Designing for LLM Tool Consumption : Writing descriptive tool documentation, strict parameter schemas, and clear error contracts directly dictates model planning accuracy. State-Aware Tool Gating : Dynamically updating available tools based on session state dramatically reduces model hallucinations and invalid function calls. Failure Modes and Resilient Error Contracts : Tools must return structured, machine-actionable error payloads ( code , retryable , userActionRequired ) so agents can self-correct when encounters occur (out of stock, invalid coupons, unauthenticated states). The Necessity of LLM Security Boundaries : Unchecked agent access risks prompt injection and privacy violations. Defensive prompt guards, PII scrubbers, and confirmation gates are essential for trustworthy agentic commerce. Challenges Bridging the Paradigm Gap : Native WebMCP provides optimal latency and security, but requires website-level implementation. API adaptation avoids visual dependency but requires backend schema knowledge. UI automation requires no backend access but introduces brittle DOM coupling. Balancing these trade-offs across edge runtimes was a primary architectural challenge. Dynamic State Synchronization : Ensuring that an action performed by an AI agent (such as adding an item to the cart or logging in) immediately synchronizes React UI context, cart counts, and native tool availability without causing stale closures or infinite re-renders. Full-Duplex Voice Control : Implementing natural speech recognition and Text-to-Speech playback while providing instantaneous cancellation (mute toggles, sound wave stop controls, and drawer close events) to prevent background audio runaway during asynchronous multi-turn tool loops. Rigorous Failure Handling : Constructing deterministic tests to validate that the system fails safely and predictably across wrong argument types, negative integers, execution order errors, out-of-stock items, and network interruptions. Why Bridge to Agentia? Bridge to Agentia envisions a web where humans and AI agents interact with applications through a common, capability-oriented interface . Instead of asking: “Does this website support WebMCP?” we explore the broader, forward-looking question: “How can any web capability become discoverable, secure, and actionable for an AI agent?” By unifying native browser WebMCP , edge API adaptation , and DOM-level automation with comprehensive security guardrails, Bridge to Agentia provides a practical blueprint for the agentic web. Different architectures, same destination: making web capabilities discoverable and actionable by AI agents. title: DayShift
pitch: When your day breaks, repair the plan — agents propose, DayShift verifies, and humans decide.
about_excerpt: When your day breaks, repair the plan — agents propose, DayShift verifies, and humans decide. Like Comment Story Updates What it does DayShift treats a disrupted day like a system that needs recovery, not a blank calendar that needs planning. When reality changes — for example a 50-minute bus delay — a WebMCP-aware agent can read the exact schedule, read non-negotiable constraints, simulate candidate recoveries, and stage a valid proposal. DayShift's deterministic constraint engine independently checks the proposal. The human then sees the trade-offs in the same web UI and is the only actor that can approve the change. Only after that approval can the agent commit it. Why WebMCP is essential The core experience depends on a shared semantic control surface. The agent does not infer calendar blocks from pixels or hunt for drag-and-drop controls. DayShift exposes schedule state and recovery operations directly as WebMCP tools, while the human sees and controls the same underlying state. The visible UI deliberately cannot stage or commit a recovery; removing WebMCP therefore breaks the complete recovery loop instead of merely making it slower. Better user experience The user can describe what broke in natural language and keep their decision authority. DayShift shows exactly what will move, which preference is sacrificed, and whether every hard constraint still passes. Staging is visibly different from committing, so there is no hidden mutation. What humans and agents can do together now The agent can explore the repair space quickly; DayShift enforces invariant truth deterministically; the human makes the final trade-off decision. Those three forms of authority stay separate while operating on the same live web application. WebMCP implementation DayShift registers six imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_day_state , get_constraints , report_disruption , simulate_recovery , stage_recovery , and commit_recovery . Read-only tools are annotated with readOnlyHint . Mutation tools use revision binding and deterministic re-validation. Human approval is deliberately absent from the tool surface, and commit_recovery fails closed unless the current proposal was approved in the UI. Invalid or duplicate schedule changes fail closed as well. Architecture principle Agent = proposal authority. DayShift = validity authority. Human = decision authority. title: Decision Workspace
pitch: An adaptive WebMCP workspace where agents ask one question at a time, expose trade-offs, and help people reach transparent, grounded decisions.
about_excerpt: An adaptive WebMCP workspace where agents ask one question at a time, expose trade-offs, and help people reach transparent, grounded decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Important decisions often get buried in long AI chats. Criteria drift, assumptions disappear, and it becomes hard to tell why a recommendation changed. We wanted a shared workspace where a person can see the decision model evolve instead of receiving an opaque answer. What we built Decision Workspace is a local-first decision canvas for humans and browser agents. It keeps options, weighted criteria, score-and-confidence assessments, evidence, uncertainties, constraints, and recommendations in one inspectable state. The app exposes workflow-level WebMCP tools through navigator.modelContext. An agent can read the current workspace, ask one high-value interview question at a time, process an answer atomically, apply only grounded mappings, and adapt the next question to the new context. Free-text or uncertain answers remain explicitly unresolved instead of being forced into a score. Users can explore temporary what-if scenarios without changing saved state. When the model is sufficiently grounded, the agent can create a readiness-checked Decision Brief with the leading option, drivers, remaining unknowns, and next verification action. The person remains in control of the final decision. How we built it We built the UI with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The canonical decision store is shared by the UI and the WebMCP adapter, so tool writes are immediately visible in the page and persisted locally on the device. Revision-aware writes and explicit question lifecycle states keep the interview consistent and auditable. Challenges and what we learned The hardest part was designing a small, coherent tool surface instead of exposing every UI control. We learned that an agent workflow needs explicit state reads, deterministic mapping policies, uncertainty preservation, non-destructive scenarios, and readiness gating. WebMCP works best when the browser page is the shared source of truth and the agent changes it through semantic workflow actions. title: EXPOSURE // INCIDENT ZERO
pitch: Governed AI incident response where ChatGPT investigates infrastructure through WebMCP, humans authorize consequential actions, and the agent executes remediation and verifies recovery.
about_excerpt: Governed AI incident response where ChatGPT investigates infrastructure through WebMCP, humans authorize consequential actions, and the agent executes remediation and verifies recovery. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Project Logo Inspiration Production incidents rarely fail in obvious ways. A database may appear overloaded even when the real cause is an application deployment several layers upstream. Engineers must correlate telemetry, logs, dependencies, changes, risk, and human constraints—often while customers are already affected. Exposure explores a better operating model: an infrastructure engineer and an AI agent working together inside the same live command environment. What it does Exposure is an agent-native operational intelligence system built around a simulated nine-node Enterprise Linux 9 production fleet. The featured scenario, Incident Zero , begins when a checkout platform develops severe latency and HTTP 502 errors. PostgreSQL appears to be failing, but the database is actually a downstream victim of a faulty application deployment. Using WebMCP, the agent can: Inspect fleet health Examine individual hosts and services Map infrastructure dependencies Query metrics and logs Review deployments and configuration changes Develop and test competing root-cause hypotheses Record human operational constraints Evaluate remediation options Request explicit human authorization Execute a simulated rolling rollback Verify recovery through measured evidence Generate an auditable incident record Why WebMCP WebMCP is the operating interface between Exposure and the AI agent. Instead of requiring ChatGPT to infer actions from page text or manipulate arbitrary UI controls, Exposure exposes explicit, governed incident-response tools with defined inputs, state transitions, safety constraints, and authorization boundaries. The agent can investigate the incident, register constraints, propose remediation, request authorization, execute an approved rolling rollback, and verify recovery. It deliberately cannot authorize its own consequential remediation. This creates a practical human-agent operating model: the AI can reason and act, while the human retains authority over consequential decisions. Human authority Exposure does not allow an agent to jump directly from suspicion to execution. The operator can establish a constraint such as: Do not restart PostgreSQL. That constraint becomes part of the operational state and blocks conflicting actions. When Exposure identifies the faulty checkout deployment, it proposes a rolling rollback and stops at an authorization gate. Only the human operator can approve the consequential action. Incident Zero The simulation models: One Nginx edge load balancer Two Nginx web servers Three checkout application servers One Redis cache server One PostgreSQL primary One PostgreSQL replica A faulty checkout release creates excessive database connections across the application tier. This causes database pressure, replication lag, web-tier timeouts, and customer-facing failures. The agent must distinguish root cause from downstream symptoms, compare remediation options, respect the operator’s constraints, and prove that recovery occurred. Product experience Exposure presents the incident through a cinematic operational interface: A living infrastructure topology Animated traffic and dependency paths Fleet telemetry Structured evidence Competing hypotheses Contradiction detection Risk assessment Human authorization gates Visible rollback progression Recovery verification A sealed decision trace Every visual transition communicates real application state rather than decorative animation. Technical approach Exposure uses TypeScript, React, Vite, structured JSON Schema inputs, and the WebMCP document.modelContext.registerTool() API. A deterministic client-side incident engine controls fleet state, evidence, tool results, authorization, remediation, and recovery. The competition build requires no production credentials, external infrastructure, or paid APIs. The fleet is simulated, but its telemetry, Linux services, logs, dependencies, failure behavior, and remediation sequence are designed to remain technically credible. What comes next The challenge release focuses on one polished, deterministic incident. Future versions could connect Exposure to authenticated operational systems such as Prometheus, Grafana, Ansible, cloud platforms, service-management systems, and enterprise observability tools. Exposure’s objective is simple: expose what is happening, reveal why it is happening, control what happens next, and prove whether the action worked. title: Her Shopping
pitch: Shop alongside your agent. A storefront that redraws itself around your mission.
about_excerpt: Shop alongside your agent. A storefront that redraws itself around your mission. Like 3 Comment Story Updates External Chat action Voice interaction Voice intent understanding Observable actions taken by agent Inspiration Online shopping is still organized around catalogs, but people usually think in outcomes: a trip, an event, a budget, a deadline, and a set of tradeoffs. We wanted to build a storefront where an agent in various interfaces could work with the shopper inside the actual interface, not just chat beside it or click through it. Her as the name of the voice assistant and as a reference to the movie. What it does Her Shopping is an adaptive outdoor storefront that reshapes itself around a shopper’s mission. A user can say something like, “I’m going camping. Keep the total below $700, prioritize warmth and Friday delivery,” and the store reorganizes products into Essential, Useful, and Optional groups. The agent can search products, compare options, change the layout, add items to the cart, open checkout review, and request a demo order. Every change is visible, reversible, and shared with the human. Checkout is simulated and requires explicit human confirmation. How we built it We built the app with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Base UI, OpenAI Sites, and WebMCP. The site registers 20 typed WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Those tools are backed by a shared capability registry, strict JSON Schemas, state-version checks, a single reducer, layout invariants, undo history, and an activity ledger. Voice is powered by the OpenAI Realtime API over WebRTC. The in-page voice agent uses the same validated shopping actions as the WebMCP tools and the human UI. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was making the agent feel powerful without making the user lose control. We had to design tools that were semantic enough for agents, but bounded enough to be safe and predictable. We also had to make agent actions legible on screen. That led to the shared activity ledger, change highlighting, undo support, strict schemas, and a checkout gate that an agent cannot bypass. To find the right balance between human and agent interaction Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that WebMCP is load-bearing in the product. The agent does not just operate the page; it can reshape the storefront’s information architecture around the user’s mission. We are also proud of the shared action layer. Human controls, voice, and WebMCP all mutate the same state through the same validation path, so the experience stays inspectable, deterministic, and reversible. What we learned We learned that WebMCP works best when the website exposes meaningful product-level actions instead of low-level UI clicks. The strongest experience came from treating the page as a shared workspace for both the person and the agent. We also learned that trust depends on visibility. Users need to see what changed, why it changed, and how to undo it before they will comfortably let an agent help with a multi-step task. title: Meabs
pitch: When architects meet agents and WebMCP, who will break first
about_excerpt: When architects meet agents and WebMCP, who will break first Like Comment Story Updates Multi-Region Simulation Event Driven Reference Architectures Inspiration As an architect, I spend a lot of my time working with pictures. We use architecture diagrams to explain how systems work, how they connect and how we think they will behave. I wanted to bring those pictures to life and avoid my designs breaking things and getting people paged in the middle of the night :-) I wanted to be able to model a change and get an idea of what it might do to the design. What happens if the load increases? What if I lose a component or a zone? If I change something to recover, what impact does that have somewhere else? Having an agent working alongside me makes that much quicker to explore. The agent can stress the architecture, break things, inspect what happened and try to recover it. I can change the constraints or try a different idea and see how it responds. What it does Resilience Forge turns an architecture diagram into something I can experiment with. I can configure a scenario, change the workload and run deterministic simulations to see how the architecture responds. I can introduce failures such as losing a component or a zone, watch the impact on the architecture and metrics, and test different ways of recovering. An AI agent can work on the same scenario through WebMCP. It can inspect the architecture and metrics, run stress tests, introduce failures and make changes to try to recover the system. The agent and I work against the same state. If I change a constraint or make a decision in the UI while the agent is working, it sees that change and has to respect it. This means I can work with the agent rather than handing the whole simulation over to it. Resilience Forge also includes a flight recorder that shows the WebMCP calls as they happen, so I can see what the agent is doing and how those actions affect the simulation. For this project I've used deterministic simulations, so I can run the same scenario repeatedly and get consistent results. The idea could go much further by bringing in real telemetry, service limits, costs and other infrastructure data to create more realistic simulations. How we built it I used Codex to help with the coding and my knowledge of creating pictures as an architect :-) For hosting I am using the ChatGPT Sites capability The simulation and WebMCP tools work against the same application state. Every WebMCP mutation works against a version of that shared state. If I change the architecture while the agent is working, its old write is rejected as STALE_STATE rather than silently overwriting my change. The agent then has to read the current state and decide what to do next. Constraints such as pinned decisions are enforced in the application itself, not left to the prompt, and the Flight Data Recorder shows human and WebMCP actions against the same timelines. The WebMCP tools are domain operations rather than UI controls. The agent can inspect the architecture, run stress tests, inject failures, change scaling or traffic behaviour and apply remediations without having to work out how to click around the page. The same domain logic is used whether the change comes from me or from WebMCP. This was important because I didn't want the agent operating against a separate version of the architecture from the one I could see and change in the UI. Challenges we ran into The main one for me was keeping the state between the agent and the user aware of each other, as both parties can make changes and we need to make sure that the application is aware of those. Both can make changes while a simulation is running, so the application needs to keep them in sync. If I make a decision or add a constraint in the UI, the agent needs to know about it and respect it when deciding what to do next. Accomplishments that we're proud of Created my first ever YouTube video, and it has spurred me on to do more, I may be terrible at it for now but I will improve :-) What we learned WebMCP will change how agents and users interact with websites. When I'm designing user journeys, I now need to think about the agent journey as well as the human journey. WebMCP makes that much easier because the agent can interact with capabilities exposed by the application rather than having to pull information from the DOM and work out how to operate a UI designed for a human or have information locked away so that agents can't access it. What's next for Meabs I'm working on an agent that can read infrastructure source code such as Terraform and CDK and then model that infrastructure in Resilience Forge. I'd also like to integrate with vendors' MCP servers to bring in real-time information such as service limits. From there, I want to explore bringing in real telemetry and cost data so the simulations can move closer to the architectures I'm actually working with. This also builds on some of my other work around PEAR (Public Engagement AI-Readiness) and the Agent Observatory, where I've been exploring how we design applications for agents and how we observe what those agents are doing. Resilience Forge gave me a chance to put some of those ideas into a working application rather than leaving them as architecture diagrams or slide decks :-) Built With next.js/vinext react-19 tailwind-css three.js typescript vite Try it out github.com resilience-forge.gman72.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Garry Meaburn Like Share this project: Updates Garry Meaburn started this project — Sep 02, 2026 05:13 PM EDT

title: MuseFlow
pitch: AI music assistant that can actually hear what you play
about_excerpt: AI music assistant that can actually hear what you play Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration ChatGPT can suggest a chord progression in text, but it cannot hear the one you just played. Existing AI music tools generate music from scratch but don't collaborate on music you're already making. They don't know your key, your tempo, or the fact that you just stopped playing mid-phrase and are waiting for an idea. We wanted to close that loop — to create an AI that reads your live audio and answers with harmony you can hear. What it does Real-time chord detection : Analyzes your live audio to identify chords, inversions, and key context AI-powered harmony suggestions : Suggests functional chord progressions and melodic continuations Dynamic tool surface : Tools appear and disappear based on your playing (e.g., "analyze-phrase" appears when you finish a phrase) Multiple input methods : Play via mouse, touch, typing keyboard, or MIDI controller No microphone required : Reads the audio graph directly from your browser Instant feedback : The AI can play back suggestions through the same audio engine How we built it Framework : Next.js 14 with TypeScript (App Router) Audio : Web Audio API — native oscillator bank with ADSR envelopes DSP : Hand-rolled algorithms — YIN for pitch detection, chromagram + template matching for chords, spectral flux for tempo Music theory : Custom implementation of functional harmony, Roman numeral analysis, and key detection (Krumhansl–Schmuckler) AI integration : Anthropic Claude API via WebMCP document.modelContext for tool registration and execution Tool surface : 12 WebMCP tools (10 static, 2 dynamic) that expose audio capabilities to the agent Polyfill : Spec-shaped WebMCP polyfill for standalone operation when external agent not present Challenges we ran into Web Audio API limitations : The audio graph is browser-local — no server can reach it, requiring WebMCP to bridge the gap Real-time DSP performance : Implementing YIN pitch detection and chromagram analysis in JavaScript without external libraries Dynamic tool registration : Managing tools that appear/disappear based on audio events (e.g., phrase completion) Cross-network agent loop : Splitting the agent execution between browser (tools) and server (API) while maintaining statelessness Polyphonic pitch detection : YIN is monophonic by design — we had to handle polyphonic input gracefully by redirecting to chord detection Accomplishments that we're proud of First-of-its-kind integration : Successfully bridged browser-local audio with AI agents using WebMCP Hand-rolled DSP accuracy : Achieved 440.02 Hz, 0 cents off, confidence 1.0 on sustained A4 through our custom YIN implementation Dynamic tool surface : Implemented tools that rewrite their descriptions based on what you actually played (e.g., "Respond to F#3") No external audio dependencies : Built everything from scratch — no Tone.js, no teoria, no pitchfinder Privacy-first design : No microphone, no recording, no upload — everything stays in your browser Working demo : Created a hands-free /demo walkthrough that showcases real tool calls and audio analysis What we learned WebMCP's unique value : It enables capabilities that are literally impossible otherwise — browser-local state cannot be reached by any server-side API DSP in JavaScript : Real-time audio analysis is feasible in the browser with careful implementation Agent-tool interaction patterns : Dynamic tools that respond to user behavior create more natural collaboration Split architecture : Separating tool execution (browser) from model inference (server) is the right pattern for browser-local capabilities Music theory implementation : Building functional harmony from scratch requires deep understanding of chord progressions and voice leading What's next for MuseFlow More instruments : Add guitar, bass, and drum kit support with appropriate DSP Advanced harmony : Implement jazz extensions, modal interchange, and voice-leading suggestions Recording & export : Allow users to record sessions and export MIDI/audio Collaborative sessions : Multi-user jam sessions where multiple agents can participate Mobile optimization : Better touch support and mobile-specific UI Additional models : Support for other AI title: LightningPricePilot
pitch: Agentic Price Discovery and Negotiation - LightningPricePilot is a WebMCP-enabled laptop marketplace.
about_excerpt: Agentic Price Discovery and Negotiation - LightningPricePilot is a WebMCP-enabled laptop marketplace. Like Comment Story Updates App Landing Page Shopper Page Merchant Page Shopper joining buying group after ChatGPT negotiated a group price for the laptop Shopper placing order after ChatGPT negotiated a good price for the laptop Two-sided bargain loop diagram Architecture diagram Actors diagram Use case diagram Inspiration The app's idea was inspired by my recent coffee brewing kettle buying experience. It wasn't a great experience trying to find a reasonable price after spending a couple of hours checking on Amazon and coffee equipment websites, only to realize the bargain price kettle I want in Amazon has target delivery date next year 2027 on the very final order payment page. My intent is to get it as soon as possible. Hence, it inspired me to create LightningPricePilot - a Two-sided Intent Market so that shopper can better communicate their intent to the merchant. What it does LightningPricePilot is a two-sided intent marketplace where shoppers and merchants use AI agents to discover fairer laptop prices. Instead of scraping product cards, a shopper’s agent uses structured WebMCP tools to search laptops, compare new and refurbished prices, negotiate within merchant-defined guardrails, join group buys, subscribe to target-price bargains, receive notifications, and prepare a mock checkout. On the other side, a merchant’s agent can analyze aggregate demand, review offer activity, adjust private pricing policies, and publish limited bargains to matching shoppers. The experience keeps people in control: commitments, policy changes, bargain publication, and checkout require visible human approval. Merchant price floors remain private, shopper targets are shown only in aggregate, and the demo never collects payment or personal information. Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Product discovery and pricing depend on live website state: condition-specific inventory, current and group-buy prices, group progress, active bargains, offer expiry, and merchant pricing policies. These details are difficult for an agent to understand reliably by reading page text or clicking through filters. WebMCP turns that state into precise, discoverable actions. On the shopper page, an agent can search the laptop catalogue, compare condition, group, and bargain price paths, request a rule-bound offer, join a group buy, save a target-price subscription, read bargain notifications, and prepare a mock checkout. On the merchant page, a different agent can review aggregate demand and offer activity, update private pricing guardrails, and publish or close limited bargains. Each page registers only the tools appropriate to its role, with the room code already bound to every call. Both roles use the same validated room backend, so a shopper action can change aggregate demand and a merchant action can create a qualifying shopper notification without exposing the merchant’s private floor through the shopper tool surface. This transforms the storefront from a static catalogue into a structured negotiation space for people, shopper agents, and merchant agents. How it creates a better user experience The shopper describes the outcome once: “Find me a lightweight laptop under $900. Excellent refurbished condition is acceptable. Compare every available price path and negotiate toward $800 if sensible.” The agent can then present understandable options instead of another long list of products: Buy at the current price for the selected condition Join a group buy and show how many more commitments would unlock its next discount Use an active, inventory-limited merchant bargain Request a ten-minute offer or transparent counteroffer within the merchant’s private guardrails Save the product, acceptable condition, and target price for a future bargain Every price path states why it is available, whether it is currently unlocked, and what the shopper must do next. Offers include their rationale and expiry. Joining a group, saving a subscription, and placing the fictional mock order pause for visible human approval. The shopper no longer needs to repeatedly search the catalogue, compare product conditions, monitor group progress, or refresh the page looking for a relevant bargain. Matching merchant bargains create persisted in-app notifications, while server-sent events update the open room live. Merchants gain a complementary experience: they can see group commitments, subscriber counts, average target prices, and offer volume; tune the private floor and discount limits; and publish limited bargains that are matched against saved shopper intent. They do this without receiving a list of individual shopper budgets. Describe what people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before People remain responsible for the important trade-offs: Which laptop condition is acceptable What target price is worthwhile Whether to join a non-binding group buy Whether to save buying intent in the room Whether to complete a fictional checkout On the merchant side, whether to change pricing policy or publish or close a bargain Agents handle the structured, repetitive work: Search products by need, use case, condition, and budget Compare current condition, unlocked group, and active bargain prices Request an accepted offer or explain a policy-bound counteroffer Retrieve relevant bargain notifications Summarize aggregate demand and recent offer outcomes Turn a demand signal into a proposed limited bargain For example, the merchant agent can see that a product has five group commitments, three bargain subscribers, an aggregate average target, and recent offer activity. It can propose a price, condition, inventory allocation, expiry, and shopper-facing message. The merchant reviews the action before publication; matching subscribers then receive an in-app notification that the shopper agent can retrieve and explain. This creates something that was previously difficult: asynchronous negotiation around durable buyer intent . A shopper can save a condition and target price, leave the original search, and return to a persisted notification after a merchant publishes a qualifying bargain. Demand is used to unlock lower group prices and guide shared bargains—not to secretly calculate a different price for each shopper. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP LightningPricePilot implements two role-specific WebMCP surfaces with document.modelContext.registerTool . The shopper page registers seven tools: search_products — find up to five laptops by plain-language query, use case, condition, or maximum budget get_price_options — compare the current condition price, group-buy path, and any active bargain for one laptop request_offer — create a non-binding ten-minute accepted offer or counteroffer within merchant guardrails join_group_buy — record the shopper’s non-binding group commitment and unlock a tier when its threshold is reached subscribe_bargains — save a product, acceptable condition, and target price in the demo room get_notifications — retrieve persisted bargain notifications, treating merchant-authored messages as untrusted content prepare_mock_checkout — place a human-approved fictional order from a valid offer and decrement demo inventory The merchant page registers five tools: get_demand_summary — return group commitments, subscriber counts, aggregate average targets, and offer counts get_offer_activity — return recent accepted, countered, expired, and checked-out offers set_pricing_policy — update the private floor, maximum instant discount, and five- and ten-buyer discounts publish_bargain — publish a condition-specific, inventory-limited, expiring bargain and notify matching subscribers close_bargain — stop an active bargain while preserving its notification and audit history Each tool posts its role, action, and structured input to the room action API. The server validates the room, role-specific action allowlist, and input schema before running shared domain logic against the room’s persisted state. The deterministic pricing service enforces condition inventory, merchant floors, instant-discount limits, five- and ten-buyer group tiers, bargain inventory, and expiry. How we built it We built LightningPricePilot with Next.js 16, React, and TypeScript. The shopper and merchant pages register 12 role-specific tools using document.modelContext.registerTool: seven shopper tools and five merchant tools. The app intentionally contains no embedded model or OpenAI API key—the intelligence comes from the WebMCP-capable browser agent. Every tool calls a shared, validated room API backed by Zod schemas and deterministic pricing logic. That pricing engine handles condition-based inventory, private merchant floors, instant-discount limits, group-buy tiers, expiring offers, and inventory-limited bargains. Accomplishments that we're proud of Being able to demonstrate how WebM

title: RelayRoom
pitch: Resolve one disruption across three companies—without copying data between three portals
about_excerpt: Resolve one disruption across three companies—without copying data between three portals Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Supply-chain exceptions are rarely owned by one company. A delayed shipment may require a buyer to change an order, a supplier to reserve replacement inventory, and a carrier to select a new route. Today, operations coordinators manage these multi-party recoveries through email chains, spreadsheets, phone calls, and manual copy-pasting between incompatible portals. This process is slow, error-prone, and lacks audit trails. We built RelayRoom to demonstrate how WebMCP can enable secure, coordinated cross-organizational workflows without requiring every company to integrate with a central backend or surrender control of their systems. What it does RelayRoom is a neutral coordination room that orchestrates supply-chain recovery across three simulated partner portals (buyer, supplier, carrier) using browser-native WebMCP. Each partner exposes a minimal, explicitly allowlisted set of tools that the coordination room can discover and execute. The system: Discovers tools from three distinct origins with exact trust boundaries Queries constraints from all partners (deadlines, inventory, routes, costs) Simulates feasible recovery candidates using a deterministic solver Presents a coordinated plan with cost deltas, timing, and rollback options Requires explicit user approval before any partner actions execute Stages all partner actions first, then commits in a deterministic order Automatically runs compensating rollbacks if any step fails Generates signed audit receipts showing tool, origin, inputs, results, and timestamps The hero scenario resolves CASE-1047: 480 sensor modules needed by Friday, with original supplier short 170 units, backup supplier requiring minimum reservations, and carrier route running 36 hours late—all while keeping added logistics cost under 10%. How we built it Architecture: Monorepo with separate apps for the coordination room and three partner portals, plus shared packages for contracts, operations logic, simulator, and UI components. Tech Stack: TypeScript, React, Vite for all surfaces Express.js for backend APIs SQLite for operational databases (buyer, supplier, carrier, workspace) WebMCP draft implementation for cross-origin tool discovery and execution Zod for schema validation Zustand for state management Vitest for unit tests, Playwright for E2E tests Docker Compose for containerized deployment Key Implementation Details: Each partner portal runs on a distinct origin with its own branding and state WebMCP tools are registered with exact exposedTo allowlists containing only the RelayRoom origin The room discovers tools using getTools({ fromOrigins: [...] }) and executes them with origin-scoped permissions SQLite transactions prevent overlapping reservations from overbooking resources Idempotency keys are tied to transaction, partner, and phase for safe retries Approval is written before any partner action; changed plans are rejected before execution Compensation restores previous order contents with new revisions and releases staged/committed allocations Challenges we ran into Cross-origin WebMCP implementation: The WebMCP draft is still evolving. We had to implement the protocol correctly while providing a compatibility bridge fallback for browsers that don't support native WebMCP yet. Transaction safety across distributed systems: Designing a staged commit pattern with proper compensating rollback that works even when network timeouts or partial failures occur. Origin isolation vs. coordination: Keeping each partner's state truly isolated while still enabling the coordination room to discover and call their tools without importing their stores directly. Deterministic simulation: Building a solver that produces feasible candidates from normalized partner evidence without relying on AI hallucinations. Permission granularity: Designing tool schemas that expose exactly the capabilities needed for coordination without giving away unnecessary access to partner systems. Accomplishments that we're proud of Real cross-origin WebMCP implementation: The deployed demo makes the cross-origin architecture obvious with three distinct origins and proper allow="tools" permissions. Complete transaction safety: Staged commit with automatic compensating rollback, idempotency keys, and SQLite transaction guarantees. Deterministic solver: The system computes feasible candidates without requiring AI, though it can optionally use OpenAI/Gemini for selection and explanation. Full audit trail: Every tool execution is logged with origin, inputs, results, and timestamp—providing clear attribution for every action. Comprehensive testing: Unit tests cover expiry, duplicate import rollback, idempotency, changed approval rejection, exact allocation, and failed compensation. E2E tests verify the hero flow and failure-plus-rollback scenarios. Production-ready deployment: Docker Compose support, environment variable configuration, and proper security headers for HTTPS deployment. What we learned WebMCP's potential: Browser-native tool sharing is a powerful primitive for cross-organizational interoperability that doesn't require every company to build to the same central API. The importance of staged commits: In distributed systems, staging all actions first and validating feasibility before commit is essential for safety. Origin boundaries matter: Keeping each partner's state isolated while enabling coordination is not just a security concern—it's fundamental to the interoperability story. Deterministic > AI for core logic: AI is valuable for selection and explanation, but the core solver should be deterministic to ensure reliability. Audit trails build trust: When coordinating across company boundaries, being able to show exactly who authorized which action is critical. What's next for it Multi-leg route optimization: Extend the solver to support multi-leg and split-shipment networks beyond the current single-route constraint. Real provider integrations: Complete certification and live-testing with actual ERPNext, Shippo, and other provider adapters. SSO and account management: Add single sign-on, password reset, and account revocation UI for production deployment. Tenant isolation: Transform from single-organization deployment to multi-tenant SaaS with proper data isolation. Additional exception scenarios: Support more than one polished exception scenario beyond the CASE-1047 hero case. Native WebMCP browser support: Full validation in a supporting browser build once native WebMCP is widely available. title: SHADOW
pitch: SHADOW lets AI agents simulate real-world actions, compare possible outcomes, and prove what they’re about to do before anything changes. It’s a transaction layer between AI intent and reality.
about_excerpt: SHADOW lets AI agents simulate real-world actions, compare possible outcomes, and prove what they’re about to do before anything changes. It’s a transaction layer between AI intent and reality. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can already click buttons and change data. What bothered me was the step before that: how can I review the outcome before it becomes real? In software, I would create a branch, inspect the diff, and merge it after review. SHADOW brings that workflow to AI actions in the browser. What it does SHADOW gives an agent an isolated copy of the current state. The agent can change plans, reduce seats, or cancel subscriptions without touching Reality. In the demo, the fictional company ORBIT spends $184,300 per month on software. The agent reads usage, contracts, and dependencies, then builds different cost-saving proposals. Every change includes Proof showing the data behind it, its impact, and any blockers. Reality → Shadow → Proof → Human commit Only the user can commit a Shadow. The agent has no commit tool. How I built it I built SHADOW with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zod, and WebMCP . A deterministic projection engine calculates each future without changing the original state. I exposed 13 WebMCP tools for reading data, staging changes, creating branches, and comparing outcomes. The UI and the tools use the same application logic, so they cannot produce different results. The MVP runs locally in the browser with synthetic data and needs no accounts or API keys. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the separation between Shadow and Reality real, not just visual. I had to ensure that no agent-accessible path could commit a change. Unsafe proposals were another challenge. I did not want to hide them because they often contain useful information. Cancelling Miro, for example, reveals a $25,000 penalty . SHADOW keeps that proposal visible but blocks it from being committed. I also had to make projections reproducible and mark old Shadows as stale whenever Reality changes. Accomplishments that I’m proud of I am proud of what SHADOW deliberately cannot do. Its 13 tools let an agent inspect, stage, branch, and compare, but none can alter Reality. The full flow works end to end: an agent creates two alternatives, the user combines the best changes into a Hybrid, and a human commit produces a new Reality version and receipt. The Hybrid reduces monthly spending from $184,300 to $147,385 . What I learned I learned that human oversight works best when the system enforces it. A prompt alone is not a safety boundary. I also learned that useful Proof is not hidden model reasoning. It is the visible data, impact, and checks that let someone make an informed decision. What's next for SHADOW Next, I want to connect SHADOW to real SaaS tools and add shared workspaces, authentication, approval roles, and tamper-evident receipts. The larger goal is simple: version control for AI actions on the web . title: ShuiSpace
pitch: A room designer you and your AI agent edit together, through the same actions. When the agent proposes a layout, the tool call waits in the page until you accept or reject it.
about_excerpt: A room designer you and your AI agent edit together, through the same actions. When the agent proposes a layout, the tool call waits in the page until you accept or reject it. Like Comment Story Updates 3D view Plan view SVG isometric view ShuiSpace Inspiration Imagine you're trying to change the layout of your room. The choices you have are to either use a design tool with a steep learning curve, do the change in reality or click photos and send them to an LLM. The LLM might return back a new arrangement, but it has never entered your room. It doesn't know the dimensions and actual space available. I wanted to see what it looks like when the tool and the agent are the same thing, when the agent isn't describing my room from the outside, but working on it with me, using the geometry the app already has. What it does ShuiSpace is a room designer with nineteen actions: place something, move it, swap it, pin it, measure a walkway, check the budget, check whether a piece gets through the door, ask where something should go. I can use all nineteen by clicking and dragging. My agent can call the same nineteen directly, because the page publishes them as WebMCP tools. They reach the same functions, hit the same collision checks, and produce the same undo entries. Things follow from that: The proposal waits for me. propose_layout stages its placements as translucent ghosts on the plan, shows what the change would do — "3 items · clears 1 issue · $312.00 left of the budget" — and the tool call does not return until I click Accept or Reject. If I reject it, my agent receives that as a decision it can act on, not as a timeout. This is the whole reason the project is a WebMCP project: a server-side MCP can compute a layout, but it cannot wait for me to look at it. Refusals carry a way out. An agent told "no" gives up. An agent told which item is in the way moves that item. Every failure returns a machine-readable reason , a human-readable message , and where relevant the id of the thing that blocked it. There's also an activity feed showing both hands in one list, in the order things happened, so you can see the collaboration rather than take my word for it. How I built it React 19, TypeScript, Zustand and Vite, deployed as static assets on Cloudflare Workers. Three views of the same plan — an SVG floor plan, an SVG isometric, and a three.js 3D view that's lazy-loaded — all behind one small adapter interface so the tools don't know or care which one you're looking at. Two rules did most of the architectural work: Tools and UI call the same store actions. This is the one principle the whole thing rests on, and it's what makes the WebMCP surface trustworthy rather than a parallel API that drifts. Derived data is recomputed, never stored. Violations, budget, free space and stacking heights are all selectors. That's what lets the app answer a hypothetical — "what would this proposal do?" — using exactly the machinery it uses to draw the real thing. Tools register through document.modelContext , and the hook feature-detects so the app degrades to an ordinary room designer in browsers without WebMCP. There's also a built-in tool console that drives the identical registry by hand, which meant I could develop the tool surface before I had any agent that could see it. What I learned That the interesting part of an agent-facing API isn't the happy path; it's what a refusal contains, and whether a human can stay in the loop without the loop breaking. . What's next Non-rectangular rooms, a larger catalogue, and saved plans.
