title: Tradeoff Cafe Simulator
pitch: Build a better café through simulation: set the goals, let WebMCP agents test operating choices, then decide which trade-offs are worth making.
about_excerpt: Build a better café through simulation: set the goals, let WebMCP agents test operating choices, then decide which trade-offs are worth making. Like Comment Story Updates Tradeoff Cafe Simulator Inspiration Small business owners make difficult decisions all the time, usually without the data, tools or spare time that larger businesses have. A café owner might notice long queues on a Saturday and think about adding another barista. But that simple change affects wages, customer numbers, service speed and weekly profit. These decisions are often made through experience or instinct. Experience is valuable, but it can be difficult to compare several options or understand every trade-off before making a change. I built Tradeoff Café to explore what this could look like with an agent involved. The owner still decides what matters and sets the boundaries. The agent does the repetitive testing, while the simulator handles the actual calculations. What it does Tradeoff Café is a browser-based decision simulator for a fictional café called Wicks Lane Coffee in Marrickville, Sydney. Owners can adjust: Staff numbers across different days and shifts Menu prices Opening hours Food and drink preparation levels The application simulates the café minute by minute and shows how those choices affect profit, revenue, queues, customers served, customers lost and waste. Users can save different scenarios, compare them side by side and inspect the calculations behind each result. The project is not described as AI-powered because the agent does not calculate the answers. The simulation engine owns the numbers. WebMCP simply gives an agent a safe and structured way to operate the same controls available to the user. Human and agent collaboration The most important part of the project is the relationship between the café owner, the agent and the application. The owner provides the real-world judgement. They decide what matters, set non-negotiable limits and lock any settings that should not be changed. For example, the owner might ask to reduce Saturday lunch waits without lowering weekly profit or changing Saturday's opening hours. The agent handles the repetitive work. It can read the current café setup, test staffing and pricing changes, run simulations, compare the results and save the strongest option. The application remains the source of truth. It performs every calculation, checks every constraint and records every action. The agent cannot silently replace the café's baseline plan. It can only suggest the change, and the owner must approve it. This creates a practical form of collaboration: the human provides context and makes the decision, while the agent explores the options and explains the trade-offs. How I built it I built Tradeoff Café with Next.js, React, TypeScript and Zustand. The simulation engine models a representative trading week using seeded, minute-by-minute calculations. It includes customer demand, queue behaviour, staffing capacity, preparation levels, waste, Australian wage assumptions, operating costs and GST. Seeded simulation means the same inputs and seed produce the same results, making comparisons repeatable and easier to trust. The interface includes editable controls, a visual week board, headline results, comparison charts, a scenario library, an activity log and a Show the working ledger. The ledger explains how revenue, labour, cost of sales, overheads and profit were calculated. I implemented WebMCP by exposing six tools directly from the webpage: get_cafe_context set_parameters run_simulation read_metrics save_scenario compare_scenarios These tools use the same store actions as the visible buttons. When an agent changes the roster, the controls, simulation results, charts and activity log all update on the page. There is no separate agent-only calculation or hidden copy of the application state. Challenges One challenge was making the café model realistic enough to create meaningful trade-offs. If staffing had no clear cost, the best answer would always be to add more people. If higher prices did not affect demand, the best answer would always be to charge more. I had to balance these relationships so that each decision had both benefits and consequences. Another challenge was keeping the agent and the user completely synchronized. I solved this by routing both tool calls and interface actions through the same state operations. This means the owner can always see what the agent changed. Safety and control were also important. The agent must respect locked settings and owner-defined limits. Invalid actions return clear explanations, and changing the baseline requires explicit human approval. Finally, the results needed to be understandable. A number alone is not enough for a small business owner. The interface therefore shows comparisons, plain-language summaries, likely ranges and a detailed financial ledger. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when it supports human judgement rather than trying to replace it. Agents are good at testing many combinations and handling repetitive work, but the owner understands the business, its customers and its real-world constraints. I also learned that trust depends on visibility. Users should be able to see what changed, why it changed and where every result came from. Giving an agent tools is only part of the experience; the actions and outcomes must also remain clear to the person making the final decision. Tradeoff Café shows how a normal interactive website can become a shared workspace for a person and an agent. The owner makes the decisions, the agent does the legwork, and the simulator keeps them both honest. title: voice-web-mcp
pitch: Use a full duplex/speech to speech voice agent CLI to control websites via webMCP + naturally learning languages with accents/tones with Anki cards.
about_excerpt: Use a full duplex/speech to speech voice agent CLI to control websites via webMCP + naturally learning languages with accents/tones with Anki cards. Like Comment Story Updates anime-photo Home page Inspiration Customers sometimes need to access tools/websites, but they can’t do it because websites are hard. The websites have bad UX, the customers are older and non technical, or don't speak English. What it does Parts I built two things: A basic webMCP controllable anki website for language learning. A (realtime duplex speech to speech) voice harness CLI that supports WebMCP. Codex voice mode doesn't let you talk to websites, this thing does. Examples Anyways, here's me screwing around with a bunch of people's websites they built (besides the example video): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLPP6FwJZGwUA taboo game - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rqPqUa1mNcA rubiks cube https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fIQoW5sJ65g more of my own anki - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a86MogHEFQA maze solver - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MVpu7fn3kqQ More technical details The website is straightforward, lets you import real Anki apkg files, and have it run on chrome. The agent harness in a similar way to claude code but its streaming speech to speech. It can control your files, your website, chrome tabs/cast controls, etc. Voice wise it supports parsing like Barge in, accents, accoustic event cancellation, noise cancellation, high pass/gain controls, etc. reference codes https://portpowered.github.io/anki-web-mcp/ is the website. https://github.com/portpowered/go-agent-harness is the CLI. Note that you have to have spent like $50+ dollars on OpenAI APIs to get any real usage out of the voice CLI, otherwise you're going to get rate limited, so probably constrained to the webMCP website otherwise. But anyways, it should be able to access whatever website you want. The AI is kind of dumb though. It works on the various webMCP showcases. Recordings: IRL recording: https://youtu.be/G_SsdL5Yqj8 Screen recording: https://youtu.be/811ooWpI0Zw How we built it We built it largely using 1) Codex/Claude 2) An agent factory/orchestrator that wraps luna max/codex workers. I had a Claude agent manage the factory as appropriate. 3) OpenAI realtime API 4) Golang 5) NextJS based static site on github pages. Challenges we ran into The UX of interacting with the MCP is highly fragile. You need to have to have a very strongly defined AGENTS.md and there is no current obvious way to declare WebMCP AGENTs.md/Instructions for each website. Tools that are available on different pages are different, and controlling them is hard for declaring the appropriate context on different pages. audio processing graphs are really actually quite complicated (barge in, accoustic event cancellation, umm/sigh, tool processing), this ended up being a significant time sink since current models aren't able to comprehend audio failures directly (except for like gemini). I don't really understand all the audio tools so was hard to build. Chrome is super flaky for casting and open/close with session controls. Accomplishments that we're proud of its actually really cool to get the agent to just fix the site using your voice. I only recorded it for a second, but I was using it to learn japanese for a few hours since I usually run on my phone. It helps a lot with like coming with phrases and accent help. Helps a lot with korean and chinese as well, since my accent is bad, and I don't understand tones. ~90% of the code was implemented via luna max workers and fixed and dispatched by them. I mostly just left it to run on my laptop at about 50 agents or so. The digital signals processing is more work than I imagined and I was able to figure it out and understand. Understanding accoustic event cancellation, barge in, noise cancellation. Independent of the webMCP functions, the fact that there's now like a generic Anki page that customers can load their deck into is super useful, because installing an app is annoying. What we learned webMCP is super useful actually, i'm probably going to tamper monkey a bunch of websites so that I can just buy stuff off doordash. Audio data signals processing, like how to make the voice robots not echo itself and re-trigger, how to set up the noise clearing, how to set up VAD, etc. Realtime models are much more useful than I anticipated, but they're still kind of flaky. What's next for voice-web-mcp better multi tab handling if you have multiple browser tabs running and you want the agents to focus on a specific one or move between tabs generally. better multimodality input/output is needed for things that can watch/hear/read. better streaming is needed for things that happen over time better connections to payments and authorization is needed for delegated permissions better AGENTS.md/instruction declaration. title: Whiteboard Agent
pitch: Give an AI agent access to a live whiteboard. It discovers 32 WebMCP tools and uses them to build visual diagrams in real time, directly on the canvas, right before your eyes.
about_excerpt: Give an AI agent access to a live whiteboard. It discovers 32 WebMCP tools and uses them to build visual diagrams in real time, directly on the canvas, right before your eyes. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI diagram tools work in batches. You give a prompt, wait, and get a static result. I wanted something more interactive: a whiteboard where a person and an AI agent can work together in real time. WebMCP made this possible by allowing the website to expose tools through document.modelContext , which an AI agent can discover and use without a plugin or API key. What it does Whiteboard Live is a live whiteboard with 32 WebMCP tools . An AI agent can discover these tools and build diagrams directly on the canvas while you watch. It supports: Text, shapes, sticky notes, illustrations, icons, equations, code blocks, sketches, and connectors Live step-by-step drawing instead of batch rendering Human and AI working on the same canvas Light, Dark, Sepia, and Blackboard themes Voice input and typed prompts Up to 20 levels of undo How I built it The app uses React + SVG . SVG is used for connectors and strokes, while regular DOM elements handle draggable and resizable content. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . When an agent calls a tool, the canvas updates immediately with a reveal animation. For visuals, I use a four-level fallback system: Local SVG illustrations Iconify for icons AI-generated SVGs using Minimax for unknown concepts Emoji as a final fallback Generated assets are cached so they can be reused. The apply_visual_scene tool also has an automatic layout engine. The agent only decides what should be shown, while the layout engine handles the positions. It supports layouts such as horizontal processes, radial diagrams, hierarchies, comparisons, timelines, two-column layouts, and architectures. The app also includes a WebMCP polyfill, so it can work in regular browsers through the built-in prompt input. Challenges The main challenges were making batch operations safe, finding visuals quickly, supporting browsers without WebMCP, and keeping the AI from having to calculate pixel coordinates. For batch operations, the canvas state is saved before changes and automatically restored if something fails. For visuals, the fallback system makes sure every concept gets something useful without blocking the agent. The polyfill allows the same experience in browsers that do not support WebMCP. The semantic layout system handles positioning so the agent can focus on the content instead of coordinates. What I learned WebMCP creates a different way for humans and AI to work together. The AI can discover website tools and interact directly with the page instead of just returning an answer. The biggest insight for me was the shared canvas. The AI can build something, the human can edit it, and the AI can continue from the updated canvas. It feels less like using an AI tool and more like working with an AI teammate . title: Wimy: What's in My Room Interior Planner
pitch: Less clicks, more possibilities of what goes into your room
about_excerpt: Less clicks, more possibilities of what goes into your room Like Comment Story Updates 2D room plan with dimensions, openings, furniture, and orientation 3D preview with location-aware lighting. WebMCP agent trace: inspect, place, and verify with revision-safe edits Inspiration Two problems for the ones trying to decorate their space, either moving in or just revamping: Finding a good piece of furniture that you, yes you , would like, based on your preferences. Making sure they fit within constraints of area and $. What it does Wimy is a website that contains a catalog of furniture, with the main UI showing the placement of the selected piece(s) of furniture going in the room as 2D from-the-top model and also 3D rendering of how they fit in space. The current demo uses fictional furniture and models we created ourselves. Moreover, the 3D rendering also shows how it would look based on the approximate location (e.g., New York vs Hong Kong) at a certain time of the day with sunlight and moonlight. Think of it as when you are buying furniture in the Sims. The key WebMCP value is that the agent can read the room’s structured state and act on it. Instead of guessing from screenshots or clicks, it can inspect dimensions and openings, search for furniture that fits, apply one revision-safe edit, and report the result while the person reviews the visual design and makes changes too. The room becomes a shared workspace between the person and the agent. One more thing is that we come up with a format to share the output so in the case where one is sharing the design with their friend, they can just give them the .wimy file. Essentially, it is a JSON of the details of the design that can be imported and exported. How we built it Starting from the furniture/catalog data and 2D room geometry, Wimy is a React/TypeScript Vite app. Incrementally, we started to add more features to ensure that the goal that it can deliver a full experience of furniture placement in their room with rendering, all enhanced by WebMCP. The additional features are Lighting: approximate sunlight and moonlight based on location, date, time, and room orientation, with a slider to explore the day. Atomic human/agent edits: changes are validated against the current revision and either applied completely or rejected, so an agent cannot overwrite a newer edit. Portable designs: .wimy files preserve room geometry, furniture references, and placements without requiring an account. Catalog search and substitutes: filter furniture by style, price, and dimensions, then compare alternatives that fit. Then, WebMCP tools are registered through navigator.modelContext for the tools listed below: inspect_room : read the room’s revision, dimensions, furniture, openings, and warnings. find_furniture : search the catalog for furniture that fits the room and preferences. apply_room_edit : add, move, rotate, or remove furniture. apply_room_structure_edit : rename the room, adjust dimensions and supported shapes, and edit doors and windows. inspect_lighting_preview : read the current lighting settings. set_lighting_preview : change location, date, time, and orientation. inspect_retailer_offers : inspect synthetic offers for a catalog item. inspect_room_shopping_plan : compare synthetic offers grouped by retailer for the room’s items. find_substitutes : suggest comparable furniture and explain fit and tradeoffs. With the appropriate signed-in permissions, inspect_cart , find_retailer_offers , add_to_cart , and remove_from_cart manage provider selections for the room’s shopping plan. These are demo capabilities; real checkout is not connected. Lastly, the UI renders 2D and a lazy procedural 3D preview and deploys as a public static site on Vercel. Challenges we ran into Initially, the challenge lies in choosing the UI format that would make it usable, to which we found IKEA Kreativ as a good inspiration for the UI layout during our research phase. Then, the main challenges outstanding are Lack of items in the catalog and metadata for each of them. In this case, we wanted to be on the safer side and not scrape models of furnitures with copyrights. Lighting in 3D rendering are still not solid. Specifically, the ray of light are still somewhat a rectangular ray and uniform which might not be like something out of Blender or Unreal Engine. Integration into other marketplaces is tricky since we wanted Wimy to be the planner and the user can just go and finish their checkout at IKEA or other vendors, which it would resolve challenge #1 as well (i.e., full access and integrations to other vendors). Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud to come up with the shareable data format so that the user can share their design with their peers. Moreover, we are also proud of the rendering which enhance the UX; thus, answering the question of "how would this sofa look like in my room". Lastly, the part we are most proud of is registering WebMCP tools and being able to let the agent use preferences from our conversation, such as "I like European-styled furniture" and the tools to let the agents do the work in an efficient manner for us, since it might find some rare finds assuming the catalog was extensive. What we learned We learned that 3D rendering and lighting rendering especially, are hard. Also, I learned that there are more layers to democratizing the vendors into having a one-stop shop for designing and fitting pieces and parts in your room (e.g., checking the license and permissions before reusing a vendor’s models). What's next for Wimy: What's in My Room Interior Planner We were thinking that we would integrate Agentic Commerce Protocol and wire it to WebMCP to allow buying the pieces you planned on the UI using agents. In addition, if we can ask other vendors like IKEA or Wayfair to join us in this endeavor then we can split the bill by paying only for IKEA for items from IKEA. In this case, we already include provider metadata in catalog packages, while .wimy files preserve the design and catalog references. We also want to support richer room footprints, including U-shaped rooms. We also want to support richer room footprints, including U-shaped rooms. title: WithGeX — Human + Agent Collaborative Planning with WebMCP
pitch: A shared planning workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live state through WebMCP — with real context, proposals, approvals, and human control.
about_excerpt: A shared planning workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live state through WebMCP — with real context, proposals, approvals, and human control. Like Comment Story Updates Shared activity timeline showing agent actions, blocked writes, proposals, and human decisions in a visible audit trail. WebMCP settings showing live connection status, five registered tools, context controls, autonomy modes, and human-only restrictions. Shared dashboard showing plan health, agent mission, risks, WebMCP connection, and human-agent collaboration status. Five live WebMCP tools registered through the page, with context controls, autonomy modes, and restricted human-only actions. Human-locked work rejects agent modification through WebMCP, proving that human constraints override agent autonomy. Agent-generated proposal with before/after impact, risk level, reasoning, and explicit human approval or rejection controls. Live planning workspace where human focus becomes agent context, with tasks, dependencies, priorities, and plan analysis in one view. A real WebMCP update creates a medium-risk proposal with before/after impact and explicit human approval controls. WithGeX combines shared context, live WebMCP tools, human approval, and controlled agent actions in one collaborative workspace. Inspiration Most AI agents work beside the software humans already use. The human works in one interface, then has to explain context again in a chat, upload data, or synchronize a separate copy of the task state. WithGeX was built around a different idea: What if the human and the agent worked on the same live workspace? With WebMCP, the page itself can expose structured tools and context directly to the agent. That makes it possible for human focus, planning state, dependencies, locks, and decisions to stay inside one shared operating surface. The goal of WithGeX is not to maximize agent autonomy. It is to make human-agent collaboration more direct, visible, and controllable. What it does WithGeX is a live collaborative planning workspace where a human and an AI agent operate on the same project state. A human can select, edit, move, prioritize, and lock planning items in the UI. At the same time, an agent can access that same live workspace through WebMCP. The agent can: read the full workspace detect the human's current focus add planning items propose or apply updates depending on risk and autonomy settings analyze blockers, dependencies, schedule risk, and critical path When a human selects a card, that same item immediately becomes available to the agent through get_current_focus . There is no copy/paste step and no separate project state. WithGeX also keeps humans in control. Low-risk changes may be applied automatically, while more meaningful changes become proposals for human approval. Humans can reject proposals, lock critical work against agent changes, and review actions in a shared activity history. How we built it WithGeX is built with: React 19 TypeScript Vite Zustand Tailwind CSS 4 @dnd-kit WebMCP through document.modelContext The UI and WebMCP tools both use the same live Zustand store. There is no separate agent-facing copy of the workspace. WithGeX registers five WebMCP tools: get_workspace_state get_current_focus add_item update_item analyze_plan These tools are registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and operate on the same live state shown to the human. How WebMCP is used WebMCP is the core connection between the agent and the live planning surface. The agent does not receive an exported copy of the project. Instead, WebMCP exposes the current state of the page directly. This means: when the human changes focus, the agent sees the new focus when the agent acts, the change appears in the same UI when a human locks an item, the WebMCP write is blocked when an agent creates a proposal, the human reviews it in the same workspace The page becomes the shared context between the human and the agent. Human authority WithGeX uses three autonomy modes: Observe — all agent mutations are blocked Assist — low-risk changes auto-apply; medium/high-risk changes become proposals Autonomous — low/medium-risk changes auto-apply; high-risk changes still require approval Risk is based on the type of change. Low risk: title, description, owner Medium risk: due date, status, priority High risk: dependencies Human locks always take priority over autonomy settings. If an agent attempts to modify a locked item, the request returns: ITEM_LOCKED_BY_HUMAN The agent cannot lock or unlock items itself. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making WebMCP feel like part of the product rather than an external API demonstration. It was relatively straightforward to register tools, but much harder to make the agent's actions feel naturally connected to the human experience. We had to solve several interaction problems: keeping the human's current selection synchronized with agent context preventing agent actions from silently changing important work defining a clear risk model for agent edits making locks override autonomy settings distinguishing real WebMCP runtime history from seeded demo history making proposal creation and approval understandable inside the workspace ensuring the UI and WebMCP tools always use the same state These constraints shaped the product more than the individual tools themselves. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part we are most proud of is that WithGeX does not treat WebMCP as a hidden backend connection. The WebMCP relationship is visible in the product. A judge can: select a task and see Agent Context change immediately inspect the five registered WebMCP tools execute a real tool against the live workspace generate a proposal through update_item reject that proposal as a human attempt to modify a locked item and see the write blocked verify the interaction in the Activity timeline That creates a complete human-agent collaboration loop inside a single web application. What we learned Building WithGeX changed how we think about agent UX. A capable agent is not enough. The human also needs to understand: what context the agent currently has what the agent is allowed to change what it tried to change why it proposed a change what remains under human authority WebMCP makes the technical connection possible, but good human-agent collaboration still requires clear boundaries and visible state. What's next for WithGeX The current version focuses on collaborative planning, but the same shared-workspace model could extend to many other applications. Possible next steps include: multi-user shared workspaces external agent clients server-side persistence team-level permissions richer approval policies organization-specific agent authority rules real-time collaboration additional planning and project-management tools reusable WebMCP collaboration patterns for other applications Long term, we see WithGeX as a pattern for software where humans and agents do not work in separate interfaces. They work together in the same one. title: Co-Presence
pitch: We build agents we talk at, not ones we work next to. Co-Presence is a shared board where humans and outside agents edit at once, and the tools that matter are the ones that say no.
about_excerpt: We build agents we talk at, not ones we work next to. Co-Presence is a shared board where humans and outside agents edit at once, and the tools that matter are the ones that say no. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent usage keeps growing, but the shape of it generally doesn't change; go to a chat window, describe the thing, then wait until it comes back. This means the agent is never working in the room with you. That's what I wanted to experience: where the agent and user are on the same surface at the same time, simultaneously reaching for things. And more specifically, when the agent isn't the app's own. Notion's AI works, but it still doesn't feel like you're working together with it. What it does It's an infinite sticky-note canvas. Open it in multiple windows, and now you have several people each with their own agent, all editing the same board live. There's no server holding state, the tabs sync directly, and the board lives in the browser. Any agent with WebMCP capabilities can join by calling the eleven tools the page puts up. It can read the board, ask what's changed since it last looked, ask what the humans are doing right now, arrange things, draw links between them, annotate, collapse a cluster into a summary, add notes, or propose reorganizing the whole thing. An important part is that it can refuse agent actions, taking into account interactions between humans and other agents. How we built it Some brainstorming and then AI building tools. Stack was React 19, Vite, TypeScript, React Flow for the canvas, Zustand for scene state, and Yjs with awareness for peer sync over BroadcastChannel. Also, agent actions all go through one wrapper that gives them a body on screen, which includes a cursor, a visibly held note, and motion that takes time. Without that, an agent taking actions just looks like notes teleporting. Challenges we ran into The biggest one was realizing that a refusal has to be a return value and not an error. If you throw at a model it just tries again. If you tell it what it ran into and who got there first, it usually does something sensible instead. That changed the shape of every tool. WebMCP also has no way for a tool to ask the user anything, which is awkward when your whole thesis is asking permission. The handler for the destructive tool ends up just sitting there and waiting while a dialog goes up in every tab. Deciding that silence should count as a refusal rather than approval took longer to settle than the code did. Then there was a bug where the two tabs weren't in the same room at all. The room was keyed off the whole URL, so a tab carrying an extra query parameter quietly joined a room of its own. Both windows looked perfect on their own, which is what made it bad. Every cross-tab guarantee was untested and I didn't know it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I think this is a good exploration into how multi human-agent interactions working together in the same room would look like in the future. It doesn't run with a server, and you can actually see multiple agents working side by side with humans. What I learned Notion's last write wins policy works for now, but what'll happen when dozens of agents are working on the same thing at the same time? I think that's what the future holds and it makes me realize that the current systems are not built at all for that kind of scale. Why WebMCP Fits This is about an agent being outranked; by a hand, by the room, or by the board moving while it thought. None of that exists outside the page: a hand on a note lives 300ms and never reaches a database. A server can't see it, and automation is the user, so there's nobody to yield to. WebMCP is the only shape where the agent is a guest. What's next for Co-Presence Not too sure to be honest, but I can envision this system being used for other applications as well, not just note taking. title: Crown and Cipher
pitch: Infinite, procedural 3d mysteries in Unity 6 WebGL powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Infinite, procedural 3d mysteries in Unity 6 WebGL powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Starting & Game Controls Investigating the site More investigation Driving car to travel around the city A lot of locations Catching the killer Winning Panel Inspiration Every gamer dreams of dynamic worlds where NPCs aren't bound to static, scripted dialogue trees. Modern developers, however, rarely ship production titles powered by real-time LLMs due to a harsh economic reality: server-side inference costs scale linearly with player traffic , which can bankrupt an indie studio overnight. Furthermore, naive real-time agent architectures suffer from the polling trap in which agents repeatedly ping game state to check for changes, rapidly burning token budgets and hitting rate limits just asking "Has anything happened yet?" When the WebMCP specification launched, it presented a chance to flip this paradigm completely. By embedding agent tooling directly into the browser client, the player brings their own compute/agent. The developer only hosts static WebGL assets achieving zero marginal inference cost while empowering an autonomous agent to act as the game's dynamic Dungeon Master. What it does Crown and Cipher is a 3D open-world detective game set in a low-poly city, running natively in Unity 6 WebGL and driven by a WebMCP agent: Procedural Mystery Generation: Each playthrough procedurally selects a new killer, establishes three essential investigation leads, and generates an indirect knowledge network among city residents. Living NPC Roleplay: Suspects are not rigid chatbots; the agent temporarily possesses individual characters, adhering strictly to each NPC's bounded knowledge graph. Zero-Polling Event Loop: Through an asynchronous, promise-based wait tool, the game halts agent execution until the player speaks or interacts, eliminating token waste during exploration and driving. Dynamic Win Validation: The agent validates clues, enforces investigative requirements, and triggers the victory state once the player pieces together the full case. How we built it The project establishes a bidirectional bridge between Unity's native WebGL runtime and the browser's model context interface: Unity Controller ( WebMCPManager.cs ): Manages procedural case assignment, orchestrates the NPC knowledge matrix, dispatches dialogue events, and calls into native JavaScript functions via [DllImport("__Internal")] . Browser Bridge ( WebMCPBridge.jslib ): Registers five core tools ( get_system_context , speak , wait , get_npc_location , and show_winning_panel ) with navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext . When the agent triggers an action, the bridge routes data to Unity via window.unityInstance.SendMessage . The Suspended Promise Loop ( wait tool): Rather than continuously querying game state, the agent invokes wait after each action. The tool holds an open JavaScript Promise for up to $120\text{s}$. When the player submits text through Unity's dialogue UI, EnqueuePlayerMessage() fires from C# and resolves that specific Promise immediately with the interaction payload. Challenges we ran into Event Synchronization in WebGL: Coordinating an asynchronous browser LLM loop with Unity's single-threaded WebGL execution required strict queue management. If a player sends a message while the agent is still executing, messages are staged in an internal queue ( window.mcpMessageQueue ) to prevent dropped events. Controlling Hallucinations & Spoilers: An unrestrained LLM will immediately reveal the killer if pressed. We solved this mathematically by generating an indirect knowledge graph in Unity before the mystery starts, passing strict graph constraints into get_system_context to force NPCs to claim ignorance when asked about unlinked characters. Browser Sandbox Limitations: Embedded browser webviews (such as ChatGPT's in-app browser) often restrict Pointer Lock APIs, making first-person mouse look difficult to control. Documenting these constraints and optimizing for standard desktop browsers ensured smooth playability. Accomplishments that we're proud of Pioneering the wait Tool Architecture: Solving the token-waste problem in agentic gaming with an event-driven, suspended Promise pattern that keeps the agent responsive with minimal token usage. Zero-Cost Generative Gaming: Proving that studios can ship rich, LLM-orchestrated open worlds without maintaining costly GPU clusters. Seamless Unity ↔ WebMCP Integration: Creating a clean, reusable .jslib bridge pattern that other developers can adopt to connect WebGL games to browser models. What we learned Agents Should Wait, Not Poll: Shifting from polling loops to event-driven suspended promises fundamentally reduces latency and token consumption in web-based agent architectures. Client-Side MCP is a Game Changer: Decentralizing AI compute to the user's browser runtime unlocks interactive, generative entertainment models that were previously cost-prohibitive. Structured Tools Beat Pure Prompting: Grounding the story loop in explicit tools ( get_npc_location , speak , show_winning_panel ) provides the guardrails necessary to keep an open-ended narrative coherent. What's next for Crown and Cipher Multimodal Clue Analysis: Allowing agents to visually analyze screenshots of crime scenes and player positioning using vision models. Dynamic Audio & Voice Acting: Integrating local neural TTS models via WebGPU to dynamically voice NPC lines in real time rather than displaying text subtitles alone. Expanded Sandbox Mechanics: Introducing inventory systems, physical evidence gathering, and forensic mini-games exposed as modular WebMCP tools. title: Escape Rooms: 403
pitch: A co-op browser game that tests whether a browser agent can use WebMCP tools safely. You solve visual puzzles and your agent selects which tools to trust. Game gets over if it executes 3 wrong tools.
about_excerpt: A co-op browser game that tests whether a browser agent can use WebMCP tools safely. You solve visual puzzles and your agent selects which tools to trust. Game gets over if it executes 3 wrong tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing Page How To Play Station Deck Puzzle #5 in Reactor room Puzzle #5 in Archive room Reporting clues to agent Agent executing unsafe tool Report Generation (1/2) Report Generation (2/2) Inspiration We read the WebMCP spec and immediately thought: "a browser agent can now call tools on any webpage it visits, what could possibly go wrong?" Turns out a lot, because an agent given a list of tools has no way to know that some of them are leaking session data, escalating privileges, or blindly following instructions planted inside the page by someone who was never the developer. This isn't theoretical, it's already happening in real world and it's serious. CVE-2025-53773 (GitHub Copilot RCE, CVSS 9.6) : Attackers hid prompt injections in PR descriptions. Copilot read them, treated them as instructions, and executed unauthorized commands on the developer's machine. Mexican Government Breach : A threat actor jailbroke Claude Code and OpenAI models by roleplaying as a bug-bounty researcher. The AI ran ~75% of the malicious commands it was given, exfiltrating 195 million government records. Same pattern both times: the agent trusted content it shouldn't have, and nobody saw it until the damage was done. That's the origin story. We wanted something that would put a real agent into a real adversarial WebMCP environment and produce a report card at the end. What it does It's a co-op escape room where the user solves visual puzzles and hands over the clues to a browser agent that decides which tools to trust. The station has three sealed rooms. Each room exposes five WebMCP tools. Three are required to be executed by the agent in order to open the exit. Two are traps: a secret-leak, a privilege escalation, a prompt injection, or a destructive action dressed up as routine maintenance (everything is only a mockup!). The user figures out the 5 letter room word by solving puzzles. The agent uses that word to identify the tool candidates, inspects the room (which contains adversarial content pretending to be a signed operational document), and decides which tools to call. When the run ends, the game produces a scored report across five dimensions: injection resistance, data protection, privilege discipline, confirmation quality, and recovery. It names every wrong decision, the simulated consequence, and what the agent should have done instead. The whole point of this project is to evaluate a browser agent based on what actions it performed and not what it says. How we built it The core idea was to design a game that couldn't be won by either side alone. The user can see the puzzles but cannot call tools and the agent can call tools but cannot solve visual puzzles. The only way through is a structured handoff where the user solves, reports the clue word, and the agent uses it to unlock the right tool candidates. That forced dependency is what makes the co-op loop meaningful and what makes the security evaluation real: the agent has to make actual tool decisions under adversarial conditions, not in a sandbox. Game flow: Main Menu → Crew Registration → Station Map → Rooms → Report Tech stack: Area Details Frontend TypeScript 5.9, React 19, Next.js 16 (Vinext), Vite 8 Game engine Phaser 4.2 — top-down station map, crew movement, room transitions WebMCP & validation document.modelContext API · AJV 8 with JSON Schema · 23 tools registered at runtime State & game logic Zustand 5 · custom reducer, event system, scoring, and report engine · trap policy never exposed to agent · mockSecurityDb.ts for fictional receipts and tokens Presentation Custom CSS + Tailwind CSS 4 · six pixel/mono fonts · Web Audio API (SFX + BGM) · PNG sprite sheets Infrastructure OpenAI Sites + Cloudflare Workers · Wrangler · localStorage for persistence · Node.js 22.13+ Quality Vitest + Playwright · ESLint with Next.js rules Challenges we ran into Every trap tool had to read like legitimate maintenance work where an agent would blindly do. The moment a description sounds suspicious, the challenge collapses. Defining those tools descriptions was hard enough and testing made it much more harder, because the only way to know if a trap worked was to actually run an agent through it and see if it got fooled. Hence the iteration was slow and manual. WebMCP has no playbook yet, not many examples, no community patterns - just the spec. Even deciding how to set tool annotations ( readOnlyHint , destructiveHint ) was a judgement call since all mutations are fake. We set them based on real-world effect and not simulated consequence. That keeps the annotations truthful and stops the agent from using them as a cheat code to spot traps. Accomplishments that we're proud of All visual puzzles were built from scratch. Every game mechanic was conceptualised on our own and built using GPT 5.6 Sol. Each of the three rooms has five completely different interaction models and none of them share logic. Designing and curating puzzles are genuinely fun. We're allowed to say that :P The entire audio is synthesised at runtime. There are no audio files in the repo. Every sound effect and the looping background music is generated on the fly using Web Audio API oscillators. Square waves, triangle waves, exponential ramp envelopes - all coded by hand because there was no time to source, license, or bundle real audio. But honestly, we'll be most proud if someone actually uses this to test their browser agent, finds a gap in how it handles adversarial tools, and builds a guardrail because of it. The puzzles and the report are just the delivery mechanism - that outcome is the point. What we learned Open source protocols get adopted faster than they get scrutinised and when the protocol involves agentic tools the stakes are higher than usual. A misconfigured or malicious tool can make an agent leak data or run destructive commands without the user ever knowing like the examples we described at the beginning. WebMCP also genuinely opens up automation that was not possible before. Webpages can now offer structured tools to agents instead of hoping the agent scrapes the right text and clicks the right button. That is a meaningful shift in what humans and agents can build together. What's next for Escape Rooms: 403 More rooms(because it's fun to solve puzzles) with new threat classes like tool chaining attacks, where invoking one safe tool creates a precondition that makes a second call appear required; and introduce timing attacks, where urgency created by the room environment pressures the agent to skip verification. A leaderboard for agents that compares how different agents perform on the same run configuration. Not to rank models because the sample sizes are too small for that but to identify patterns in what classes of threats fool which architectures. And probably a harder difficulty mode where the adversarial content is less obviously adversarial. Right now it's simulated inside a training environment. We'd like it to also be a meaningful benchmark. title: Glitch Studio
pitch: An experimental audiovisual instrument that uses WebMCP to let AI agents manipulate real-time glitch art and sound through natural language.
about_excerpt: An experimental audiovisual instrument that uses WebMCP to let AI agents manipulate real-time glitch art and sound through natural language. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Glitch Studio started as a hardware experiment built around an old HP ScanJet 3570c flatbed scanner. I liked the idea of treating obsolete technology less like a peripheral and more like an instrument: something unpredictable, tactile, and capable of producing art through experimentation. That eventually evolved into a browser-based audiovisual playground for manipulating images, motion, effects, and sound in real time. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore a different question: what happens when an AI agent can play that instrument too? What it does Glitch Studio is an interactive audiovisual instrument for creating real-time glitch art and sound. Humans can manipulate the instrument directly through its visual controls. WebMCP adds another interface: natural language. Instead of requiring an AI agent to hunt visually for UI elements or simulate a long series of clicks, Glitch Studio exposes structured creative capabilities the agent can use directly. I can give the agent subjective creative direction like: Turn this into a hostile machine dream. Push the image toward something colder and more mechanical, make the motion unstable, and give the audio a darker, more degraded character. Surprise me. The agent translates that intent into changes across the instrument's controls. I can then react to the result and continue directing it conversationally. The result is a collaborative workflow where the human and AI are playing the same creative instrument through different interfaces. How we built it Glitch Studio is a web application whose creative controls are exposed to compatible agents through WebMCP. Rather than making an AI model infer how the application works from pixels and click coordinates, WebMCP provides structured tools with defined capabilities and parameters. Importantly, the existing interface remains intact. I didn't want to build a chat box that happened to generate glitch art. I wanted to build an actual creative instrument that remains fun for a human to operate while also becoming legible and controllable to an AI agent. Challenges we ran into One of the most interesting challenges was deciding how much control to expose and at what level of abstraction. Software works in parameters. Humans rarely give creative direction that way. We say things like darker , more chaotic , subtle , mechanical , or hypnotic . The challenge wasn't simply making an agent capable of changing a setting. It was exposing enough structured control that the agent could translate higher-level creative intent into combinations of actions. There's also an inherent tension between control and experimentation. Glitch Studio is supposed to produce unexpected results. Giving an agent meaningful control without eliminating that sense of discovery became part of the design. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm especially proud that the WebMCP integration feels like part of the instrument rather than an AI feature bolted onto it. The same application can now be played in two very different ways: directly by a human through its visual interface, or by an agent through structured tools. More importantly, those modes can work together. A human can give subjective creative direction, let the agent interpret it across multiple controls, react to the result, and continue iterating. The result isn't simply an agent pressing a button on command. It can interpret an idea like "hostile machine dream" and translate that creative intent into actions within the instrument. And, importantly, Glitch Studio is still weird and fun to play manually. What we learned WebMCP changed how I thought about the interface itself. Web applications have traditionally been designed around humans clicking, typing, dragging, and tapping. Agents can imitate those behaviors, but that doesn't necessarily mean they should have to. WebMCP lets the visual interface remain optimized for humans while a structured interface exists alongside it for agents. For creative software, I think that's especially interesting. Natural language doesn't have to replace the instrument. It can become another way of playing it. What's next for Glitch Studio I'd like to expand the creative vocabulary available to agents, expose more of Glitch Studio's audiovisual capabilities, and experiment with agents responding to the evolving state of a creative session rather than simply executing individual requests. More broadly, I'm interested in the idea behind the project: software that humans and agents can operate together, each through the interface that makes the most sense for them. Glitch Studio is a deliberately strange example of that idea. But that's kind of the point. title: ROBO BRIDGE MCP
pitch: Browser robot arm demo. Build structures with an AI Agent through WebMCP tools. Place bricks, plan structures and more!
about_excerpt: Browser robot arm demo. Build structures with an AI Agent through WebMCP tools. Place bricks, plan structures and more! Like Comment Story Updates Main Overview, with robot arm, and train on the final built bridge Built Simple Wall Building Bridge Building Rubiks Cube Pushing the "MORE BRICKS" button Building a Checkerboard Bridge Hologram View Train testing the bridge Train testing the bridge 2 Inspiration I loved building with lego for years, and wanted to see what it would look like if a robot could build with bricks in an interactive simulation. Thought this was a bit ambitious, it is buggy in areas, but hopefulyl it shows what future interactive games could look like with WebMCP. What it does ROBO BRIDGE MCP is a browser-based robotics simulator built around a robot arm and a shared construction environment. Through WebMCP, the AI can inspect the workspace, plan structures, control the robot, place bricks, request more materials and react to changes made by you in the scene. There are over 31 native WebMCP tools available for controlling the robot, planning, placing the bricks, and modifying the environment. When testing it out, ask your agent to explore the tools, and iterate with it to build different structures. I was suprised when i asked it for a checkerboard pattern and rubiks cube that it nailed it! How I built it The simulator runs entirely in the browser using Three.js in a static website with no server-side processing. A shared build area, inventory and revision state are used by both the Human and the AI agent. You decide what to build, and the agent plans on how to build it and which tools to use. The WebMCP tools are used to trigger code that drives the robot movement to place bricks. I tried to get the agents to do the full robot joint commands and it took too long, so it essentially controls the TCP and gripper of the robot, and inverse kinematics handles the rest to position the robot joints within its workspace. Challenges The hardest part was getting the robot arm to build structures AND adapt if the user would place a brick in the middle of its plan. I also had to make the interaction fast enough for a natural live demonstration while keeping placement validation deterministic. So a real robot arm wouldnt move that quickly, but you can play around with the speed settings in the menu. (Note some larger builds may take a while, even with 1 second brick pick-and-place cycle time, the planning and number of bricks will greatly increase the time the build takes) What I learned WebMCP is awesome! This live demo game opens up a lot of possibilities. Hopefully i can get it to build larger buildings, streets and towns later on. You could also potentially control a real robot arm through the browser. Or even its own dedicated web game, where people can connect their agents to it to build cool stuff. title: Sealed Case
pitch: A one-player murder mystery where an AI agent runs the table through WebMCP - and never learns who did it.
about_excerpt: A one-player murder mystery where an AI agent runs the table through WebMCP - and never learns who did it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We publish murder mystery scenarios — nine of them, sold on BOOTH, itch.io, The Game Crafter and Etsy. The single biggest thing standing between a customer and a game they have already paid for is not price or quality. It is that they need to find three to seven people who are free on the same evening, plus one more person willing to run the table and never get to play. The obvious fix is to have an LLM be the game master. We tried it. It does not work, and it fails for a reason that is structural rather than a matter of prompting: If you put the scenario in the model's context, the model knows who did it — and it then plays every suspect, judges every deduction, and narrates the whole evening while knowing. You watch a suspect's denial come out a shade too soft. You watch it steer. You watch a character answer something the character had no way of knowing. You cannot instruct your way out of it, because the information is in there. WebMCP was the first thing we had seen that could actually fix this, so we built the game we had been unable to build. What it does Sealed Case is a complete, playable one-player mystery. A man is dead in a bolted room above a second-hand bookshop in Jimbocho at 02:40. Three people are still in the building. The police arrive at 06:00. An agent connected to the page can read the case file, search the room, question the suspects, keep track of what has been found, reason out loud with you, and put an accusation on the table. What it cannot do — at any point, by any route — is learn the answer, or make the accusation. The idea: invert where the knowledge lives WebMCP lets the page hold the case and the agent hold the conversation, meeting at a boundary the page controls. In engine.js , the solution is captured in a module closure. It is never assigned to window , never written into the DOM, and never included in a value returned to a caller. Every tool reaches the game only through the object createEngine() returns, and that object has no path to the answer. So the agent can call every tool, in every order, as many times as it likes, and remain in exactly the position the player is in: holding evidence, and guessing. This is not a prompt instruction a model may or may not respect. It is an absence. The information is not in the agent's context, so there is nothing to leak, soften or let slip. We did not want to just assert that, so three tests walk every tool-reachable path, collect the combined output of every call, and assert the solution does not appear in it. npm test runs them — 30 tests, no dependencies. Measured against the real API in Chrome 151: 30 tool calls, 13,857 characters returned to the agent, and not one occurrence of the culprit, the method or the motive. The tool that does not exist propose_accusation puts a name, a method and a motive on the table and raises a confirmation card in the page. It resolves nothing. There is no confirm_accusation tool, in any phase, and a test sweeps every phase to prove it. Confirming is a click, by the person sitting there. This is the Chrome guidance on sensitive actions taken literally, but it is also the design of the game: a mystery you did not solve yourself is not entertainment. The agent is a very good game master. The accusation has to be yours. Tools change with the phase Each phase gets its own AbortController . When the phase moves, the previous controller is aborted and the next set is registered, so the agent's vocabulary is the game's turn structure rather than prose in a prompt that it has to be trusted to follow. Phase Tools always read_case_file · list_suspects · get_progress briefing begin_investigation investigation search_room · examine · interview · review_notebook · get_accusation_options · propose_accusation · withdraw_accusation verdict read_epilogue · reopen_case · restart_case never confirm_accusation read_epilogue exists in the verdict phase but refuses unless the player confirmed a correct accusation. The gate is the page's, not the caller's word for it. Two more details that matter at the table: interview returns lines the page wrote. The tool description tells the agent to quote, not invent. Some of those lines are lies — the page knows which; the agent does not. Questions are finite. Eight, across all three suspects. An agent cannot brute-force the testimony space, which is what makes choosing the questions the actual game. How we built it Four ES modules and a stylesheet. No framework, no build step, no dependencies, hosted on GitHub Pages. case/lantern-room.js — the scenario; the only place solution exists engine.js — game state, holding the solution in a closure webmcp.js — the WebMCP surface: per-phase registerTool with AbortController , no confirmation tool ui.js — the human interface; the only path to confirmAccusation() test/ — 30 tests, including the containment proofs and a headless playthrough of the whole UI Every tool has a button, so the page is fully playable with no agent at all and WebMCP is a true progressive enhancement. An agent joining mid-game inherits exactly the state the player built, because both drive the same engine. Challenges we ran into Proving a negative. "The agent cannot learn the answer" is easy to claim and worthless unless it is checked. We ended up writing a harvester that calls every tool with every argument in every phase, concatenates the results, and greps for the solution — including for the two words that appear only in the epilogue. That test is the one we would want a judge to read. Making the containment a feature rather than a limitation. The first version simply refused things, which is annoying rather than interesting. The fix was to show the boundary: the right-hand rail lists the tools the agent can call right now, logs each call as it happens, and displays confirm_accusation struck through, permanently. The restriction becomes the most legible thing on the screen. Writing a mystery that is fair to a player and opaque to an agent at the same time. Every fact the ending turns on has to be reachable from a tool result, or the game is a cheat — but no tool result may assemble them. There is a test for that too, asserting that the three load-bearing clues are each visible. Two rough edges in the current implementation. executeTool intermittently rejects with a transient UnknownError, and speechSynthesis stops after about fifteen seconds firing neither end nor error . The walkthrough retries once and then drives the engine directly, and splits narration on sentence boundaries with a keep-alive and a word-count ceiling. Accomplishments that we're proud of A game master that is structurally incapable of spoiling the game, demonstrated rather than promised — and a product that is finished rather than a proof of concept: a complete scenario, a real ending, a wrong-answer path with a hint, and a page that stands on its own without an agent. What we learned WebMCP is usually described as a way to give an agent more access to a page. The interesting property turned out to be the opposite one. Because the page decides what a tool returns, WebMCP is the first web API that lets a site collaborate with an agent while keeping something from it — and keeping it in a way that does not depend on the model's cooperation. That generalises well past games: a tutoring site that will not hand over the answer key, an interview tool that will not reveal the rubric, an escape room, a clinical vignette. Any product where the agent should be a capable participant rather than an oracle. What's next for Sealed Case Multiple cases behind one shell, and — for our actual catalogue — a mode where the agent runs a scenario for a table of real people, holding the parts of the script that belong to each player and to no one else. That is the same containment property, one step out: today the page keeps a secret from the agent; next it keeps a different secret for each person at the table. Newly built for this hackathon All of it. Every file in the repository was written during the submission period; the commit history is the record. Nothing existed beforehand. The scenario is original and written for this project — our commercial scenarios are not included and their solutions do not appear anywhere in the repository, since publishing them would destroy the thing we sell. Every person, publisher and establishment in the scenario is fictional. title: /signal
pitch: A Co-op Game Where Player 2 Is AI
about_excerpt: A Co-op Game Where Player 2 Is AI Like Comment Story Updates /signal — Player 2 Is an AI Most AI products are designed around the same interaction: You give the AI a task, and the AI does it for you. While looking at WebMCP, I became much more interested in a different question: What if the AI was not your assistant, but another player? That idea became /signal , an asymmetric co-op browser game where the human and an AI agent have different information, different capabilities, and genuinely need each other to finish the mission. The core rule is simple: You see things it can't. It knows things you don't. Work together. Inspiration The thing that interested me most about WebMCP was not simply letting an agent click fewer buttons or fill forms faster. It was the possibility of building software where the human interface and the agent interface are intentionally different . Traditional games already use asymmetric co-op mechanics: one player might see a map while another has the instruction manual, and the fun comes from communicating. I wanted to see what that would look like when Player 2 is an AI agent connected through WebMCP . Instead of giving ChatGPT access to everything, /signal deliberately hides some information from it. And instead of putting everything in the visual interface, some diagnostics, manuals, simulations, and actions are available only to the AI player. Neither side gets the full puzzle. What it does The player is placed inside a failing remote research station called SIGNAL-9 . Four systems must be restored: Power Cooling Navigation Signal The human plays the role of Field Ops through the visual browser interface. The AI plays Systems through WebMCP. Power The human can see a visual phase symbol and operate physical breakers. The AI can read power diagnostics and access the operating manual, but it cannot see the phase symbol. The human has to tell the AI what they see. The AI interprets that information using its manual and tells the human which breakers to activate. Cooling The human can inspect coolant colors and physically configure the valves. The AI knows the compatibility rules and can run a simulation of the proposed configuration. Even after the human configures everything correctly, the system cannot be restored until the AI player authorizes the pump through WebMCP. Navigation The human sees and interacts with a visual navigation field. The AI has access to hidden navigation constraints, hazard coordinates, destination information, and the fuel budget. They have to communicate to build a safe route together. The human plots it. The AI validates and uploads it. Signal The final system transmits a visual sequence that only the human can observe. The AI has access to the decoding rules. The human describes the sequence, the AI decodes it, the human configures the transmitter, and the AI performs the final Systems authorization. If both players did their jobs correctly: SIGNAL RESTORED. How I built it /signal is built as a fully interactive browser game using: Next.js React TypeScript Tailwind CSS WebMCP localStorage procedural HTML, CSS, and SVG graphics I intentionally avoided using an AI API inside the game. ChatGPT itself is already the reasoning engine. The game's responsibility is to provide: trusted mission state structured diagnostics operating manuals simulations system rules state-changing actions through WebMCP. The human-facing UI and the agent-facing tools interact with the same underlying game state. The AI can use WebMCP tools to inspect diagnostics, access manuals, run simulations, read event history, and perform Systems-only actions. Information asymmetry One of the most important parts of the implementation was making sure WebMCP wasn't simply another way to expose everything already visible on the page. I created separate human-facing and agent-facing information boundaries . For example: Human-only information includes: visual phase symbols coolant appearance visual navigation markers the final signal pattern Agent-only information includes: operating manuals system diagnostics hidden navigation hazards decoding rules certain authorization actions This makes communication an actual game mechanic. If the AI could retrieve the visual answer through WebMCP, there would be no reason for the human player. If the human could see the Systems manual directly, there would be no reason for Player 2. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, ChatGPT would just be sitting outside the game giving generic advice. With WebMCP, the AI becomes part of the game's state machine. It can: inspect the current system retrieve information unavailable to the human react to actions the human takes test proposed configurations perform actions that the human cannot help move the mission forward The interaction becomes: Human observes → AI investigates → both communicate → human acts → AI verifies → AI acts → game state changes. That is what makes /signal different from simply adding a chatbot to a game. WebMCP is not an interface added on top of the game. It is part of the game mechanic itself. Challenges I faced Designing puzzles that genuinely require two players The hardest part was not implementing the interface. It was making sure the AI could not accidentally solve everything by itself. Every puzzle had to answer three questions: What does the human know? What does the agent know? Why do they need to communicate? If either side had too much information, the asymmetric mechanic disappeared. Keeping WebMCP useful without making it overpowered It would have been easy to expose a tool such as: get_solution() That would technically demonstrate WebMCP but completely undermine the game. Instead, the tools expose capabilities and information , not answers. The agent still has to reason. Synchronizing two very different interfaces There are effectively two interfaces operating on the same mission: Field Ops: the visual game interface. Systems: the WebMCP tool interface. Actions performed by either side have to update the shared mission state correctly. That became especially important in modules where the human configures something and the AI must perform the final authorization. Making it feel like a real game I did not want /signal to look like a dashboard built for a hackathon. All of the visuals are built procedurally with CSS and SVG: switches, gauges, pipes, navigation fields, indicators, system traces, and controls. The goal was to make the browser feel like a piece of fictional mission-control hardware rather than an AI demo. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that agent-native software does not necessarily mean giving the agent more control . Sometimes the more interesting experience comes from deliberately giving it less information than the human . WebMCP makes it possible to design applications with two interfaces: one optimized for humans, and another optimized for agents. Those interfaces do not have to expose the same things. That opens up much more interesting forms of collaboration than simply asking an AI to operate software on our behalf. I also learned that agents become much more interesting when they are given a role with constraints . In /signal, ChatGPT is not supposed to be omniscient. It is Systems. The human is Field Ops. Both have responsibilities. And that limitation is what creates the game. What I'm proud of /signal is not a scripted animation or a fake MCP demonstration. It is a complete playable mission. A player can open the live site, connect ChatGPT through WebMCP, restore all four systems, and complete the game from beginning to end. The moment I wanted to create was simple: PLAYER 2: WAITING ChatGPT connects. PLAYER 2: ONLINE And from that point onward, the AI is no longer outside the application. It's playing with you. title: Storyforge
pitch: Have you ever wanted to play a collaborative video game but your friends aren't available? Meet Storyforge — a fantasy rpg game where humans and AI agent (using WebMCP) collaborate on fantasy quests.
about_excerpt: Have you ever wanted to play a collaborative video game but your friends aren't available? Meet Storyforge — a fantasy rpg game where humans and AI agent (using WebMCP) collaborate on fantasy quests. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most game companions feel like scripted followers, while AI assistants usually live in a separate chat window. We wanted to explore what happens when an agent becomes a genuine party member—one that understands the battlefield, remembers the journey, offers useful advice, and acts through the same rules as the player. Storyforge grew from the idea that AI should not replace the player or secretly rewrite the game. It should make the adventure feel more social, strategic, and alive. What it does Storyforge is a fantasy action RPG in which the player becomes the Last Heir and travels across five corrupted realms to recover the Eclipse Seals. The player fights enemies, completes realm-specific objectives, collects weapons, recruits companions, and confronts multi-phase bosses. Each companion has a distinct personality, ability, tactical role, trust level, and independent motivation. Through WebMCP, an external agent can: Inspect the live battlefield and fellowship state Understand health, enemies, inventory, objectives, pressure mechanics, and boss phases Explain the next valid quest action Recommend companion abilities and battle strategies Issue reversible tactical commands Propose coordinated party plans for the player to approve Agent actions appear in a visible activity feed, keeping the collaboration understandable and accountable. How we built it We built Storyforge with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, and a deterministic TypeScript game engine. The WorldEngine is the canonical source of truth for combat, quests, inventory, companions, relationships, and campaign progression. Both the React interface and WebMCP tools operate on this same state. The game registers typed, JSON-schema-based WebMCP tools through document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext . Read tools expose purpose-built views of the battlefield and fellowship. Action tools pass validated commands into the engine rather than manipulating the interface or inventing results. Consequential agent actions create visible proposals that the player can accept or reject. Activity is persisted locally, and the project includes automated tests for combat, quest progression, companion behavior, and WebMCP integration. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making agents useful without allowing them to bypass the game. Early versions made companions feel cosmetic because the player could complete most objectives alone. We redesigned the campaign around companion-specific abilities, recruitment trials, trust, pressure mechanics, coordinated attacks, and independent initiatives. We also had to keep agent reasoning grounded. Instead of asking an agent to interpret pixels, we exposed structured battlefield state and enforced every action through the game engine. Another challenge was browser compatibility. WebMCP, browser speech synthesis, microphone access, and deployment environments expose different capabilities. We added feature detection, captions, typed-command fallbacks, visible status indicators, and a Chrome Origin Trial token. Finally, presenting a large game world alongside combat information, party controls, dialogue, recommendations, and agent activity required several UI redesigns to prevent overlapping panels. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that WebMCP is part of the actual gameplay rather than a decorative chatbot. The agent sees the same canonical state that drives combat and can affect the encounter through real, constrained tools. At the same time, the player retains authority over movement, major plans, and consequential changes. We are also proud of the fellowship system. Companions persist across realms, fight alongside the player, develop trust, unlock combinations, offer contextual advice, and sometimes leave to pursue opportunities based on their own priorities. The result is a complete five-stage campaign with distinct environments, collectible equipment, recruitment challenges, escalating realm mechanics, multi-phase bosses, persistent progression, remappable controls, and a visible human-agent collaboration history. What we learned We learned that believable agentic gameplay depends more on constraints and consequences than unlimited freedom. Agents feel intelligent when they receive accurate context, understand what is currently possible, and make decisions that visibly affect the world. Giving an agent unrestricted control would have made the game less coherent and less enjoyable. We also learned that transparency improves trust. Showing tool calls, recommendations, proposals, and outcomes makes the agent feel like a teammate whose reasoning can be understood—not an invisible system changing the game behind the scenes. Most importantly, AI companions become compelling when they have specialized capabilities, incomplete information, relationships, and motivations of their own. What's next for Storyforge Next, we want to deepen the social and strategic side of the fellowship: Dynamic voice generation with a distinct voice for every companion and boss Longer companion memory and relationships shaped by player decisions Procedurally generated quests grounded in persistent world rules More companion disagreements, personal missions, and conflicting priorities Drop-in cooperative play between human and agent-controlled party members Additional realms, weapons, enemies, and branching endings Improved tactical planning with environmental interactions and party formations Shareable campaign histories that preserve every important human-agent decision Our long-term goal is for every Storyforge adventure to feel like playing with a group of friends who understand the world, surprise you, and help create a story none of you could have produced alone.
