title: StudyTree
pitch: Play a learning game with an AI that can talk but can't cheat. A human and a voice agent alternate turns growing a knowledge tree, and the agent moves only through WebMCP tool calls.
about_excerpt: Play a learning game with an AI that can talk but can't cheat. A human and a voice agent alternate turns growing a knowledge tree, and the agent moves only through WebMCP tool calls. Like Comment Story Updates GamePlay chatgpt image gen inspiration Inspiration I'm a lifelong learner, and I've always loved the idea of studying new topics with tech. Over the last few years I've tried just about every way there is to learn with AI. The seed for this project goes back further than the challenge. Years ago I bought the domain studytree.ai (I'm a bit of a domain freak) and it's been rattling around in my head ever since. The original concept was a way to organize your ChatGPT history: a folder system with interconnected nodes so you could go back and actually study what you'd learned in conversation. The problem was keeping that data in sync, so I could never make it seamless. (err proprietary systems) So I pivoted toward a pure studying tool, but I never quite knew what it wanted to be. I even tried wiring in backend MCP servers to prototype it. It wasn't until WebMCP came out that I saw the real unlock: the agent could live inside the page and act through tools the page exposes, no backend required. That's what turned a vague study tool into a game you play with an AI. I mean I had experimented with somewhat of a complex node system here https://app.studytree.ai but I never was truly satisfied. What it does StudyTree is a turn-based learning game on a shared canvas. A human and an AI agent take turns building a knowledge tree around a single learning question. The human clicks and types. The agent can only change the board by calling registered tools. Voice is the agent's controller. Node types: 🌱 Root (the learning question) · 💡 Concept · 📚 Resource · ⚡ Skill · ❓ Gap Moves: Plant, Branch, Prune, Mark Gap, Mark Clear, and a human-only Undo of the agent's last move. Rules: 10 moves total, alternating turns. Win with 5+ nodes and zero gaps remaining when the moves run out. Lose if gaps are still open. The game works through two agent surfaces, and both go through the same six tools: WebMCP an in-browser agent (like ChatGPT's built-in browser) calls tools registered on document.modelContext . ElevenLabs voice an on-canvas voice panel connects to a public ElevenLabs agent that invokes the same moves as client tools. get_board is read-only and free; the other five are the legal moves. Tool arguments accept a node's label as well as its id, so a voice agent can say "branch from First Principles" instead of spelling out n3 . How I built it The build was almost entirely agent-driven, in stages: Voice dump. I started by talking the idea out loud with a Grok voice bot and let it spit the concept back to me. Cloud agent scaffold. That spec went into a Cursor Cloud agent, which spun up the first version. I pulled it down and tested it on a local port inside the Codex browser. Refinement. I brought in Claude Opus 5 to refine the architecture and tighten the tool layer. Redesign. When Claude 5.1 dropped yesterday, I had it re-evaluate the whole design. I pulled visual references from Cosmos for inspiration and had it pick apart the game mechanics. That's where it evolved from "a tree you build" into a real turn-based pairing between human and agent. Stack: Vite · React 19 · TypeScript · React Flow (canvas) · Zustand (state) Architecture: there is exactly one implementation of each move, in the Zustand store. Three entry points reach it: human buttons ──┐ WebMCP tools ──┼──→ applyMove() ──→ store action ──→ React re-render voice tools ──┘ Neither agent surface can touch the DOM or skip a rule, because both call the identical store actions the human's buttons call. Adding a move means adding it once in moves.ts , and both surfaces pick it up. WebMCP registration is feature-detected, so nothing breaks in browsers without it, and the ElevenLabs SDK is code-split so the board is interactive before the voice stack loads. Challenges I ran into Getting the agent to take its turn on its own. Right now the agent moves when you prompt it. I want true back-and-forth: I make a move, and the agent immediately responds without me nudging it. I don't think I've solved this yet. My current thinking is a polling or event loop that watches get_board and triggers the agent when the turn flips. Keeping the agent honest. The agent needed real agency without being able to cheat. Routing every move through the same applyMove dispatcher the human uses, and giving the human an undo, was how I solved that. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Two completely different agent surfaces (WebMCP and ElevenLabs voice) driving one shared rule set, with zero duplicated game logic. No API keys, no backend, fully static deploy. The whole thing runs in the browser. A concept I've been circling for years finally has a shape I can actually play. What I learned WebMCP is far more powerful than I expected. Exposing a handful of well-defined tools on the page is enough to turn a static app into something an agent can genuinely collaborate in. The Codex browser is going to change how people use the internet. Once the general public starts adopting agent-driven browsers, the interactions are going to get profound. Voice-first, agent-first workflows (talk the idea out, let cloud agents scaffold it, iterate with frontier models) are a real way to build now, not a gimmick. What's next for StudyTree Autonomous turn-taking. Finish the polling/event system so the agent moves the instant the human does. Real back-and-forth, no prompting. Fold it into StudyTree. Finished trees persist as study maps, resource nodes become live links, and the 10-move game becomes the on-ramp to a longer learning session. This is the studytree.ai vision I've been sitting on, finally with a front door. Classroom mode. Make this fun for younger students: a whole class builds one tree together with the agent as a co-player, taking turns to plant concepts, spot gaps, and fill them. The game format already has the ingredients (a shared board, clear turns, a win condition) to turn "what do we know about this topic?" into something kids actually want to play. title: Business Central WebMCP
pitch: Turn Business Central into an agent-native ERP
about_excerpt: Turn Business Central into an agent-native ERP Like Comment Story Updates bc-webmcp in action bc-webmcp in action Inspiration ERP software runs entire companies—yet to an AI agent, it can still look like a wall of buttons. BC WebMCP lets Business Central tell the agent exactly what record is open and what it can safely do. Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central manages customers, suppliers, products, finances, and documents. Browser agents can navigate its interface visually, but they must infer context from a complex UI. Traditional backend integrations have the opposite problem: they can access data, but do not naturally know what the user is viewing. WebMCP offered a compelling third option: expose small, structured tools directly from the active page. What it does BC WebMCP adds a lightweight FactBox to the standard Customer, Vendor, and Item cards. It follows the current record and dynamically exposes relevant tools to a WebMCP-enabled browser agent. An agent can retrieve basic and financial information, recent ledger entries, and related sales or purchase documents. It can also identify the current record through a generic primary-key tool. One deliberately limited write tool records when WebMCP last accessed the record. The extension does not expose unrestricted database access. Every request is handled by Business Central itself, so the current user’s permissions and Business Central’s application rules remain in force. How we built it We combined a Business Central AL extension with a JavaScript control add-in. JavaScript registers tools through the experimental document.modelContext API, then sends each invocation into AL using a correlated asynchronous request. Inside Business Central, a generic dispatcher validates the current record and routes the request to a typed Customer, Vendor, or Item provider. Results return as structured JSON. Tool definitions change automatically with the page context, configurable limits prevent oversized queries, and public integration events allow other extensions to add their own tools. Challenges we ran into The biggest question was architectural: could a WebMCP tool registered inside a Business Central control-add-in frame actually be discovered and invoked by a browser agent? We also had to handle lazy-loaded FactBoxes, navigation between records, timeouts, page closure, missing or deleted records, duplicate documents, composite keys, and the different roles records can play—for example, a customer being either the sell-to or bill-to party. Most importantly, we had to make something agent-friendly without weakening the security model of an ERP system. Accomplishments that we're proud of The original end-to-end MVP successfully proved that a browser agent could request the primary key of the Customer currently open in Business Central. From that small experiment, BC WebMCP grew into a reusable architecture supporting Customers, Vendors, Items, ledgers, financial details, and eighteen types of sales and purchase documents. Version 0.2 and its separate AL test extension compile against Business Central 28/runtime 17, with the broader browser acceptance matrix ready for sandbox testing. What we learned Page context is just as important as data access. An agent becomes much more useful when it knows what the user is already looking at. We also learned that narrow, semantic tools—such as “get this customer’s ledger entries”—are safer and more reliable than giving an agent a generic database interface. Business Central should continue enforcing permissions, validation, and business rules; WebMCP should provide a well-defined doorway into them. What's next for Business Central WebMCP Next, we want to complete the expanded browser test matrix, add more Business Central pages, and introduce carefully governed actions such as checking item availability, creating a sales quote, or previewing a posting. The larger goal is simple: make Business Central agent-native without replacing its interface, duplicating its logic, or compromising its safeguards. title: Forge
pitch: Forge is an open-source, browser-based IDE where humans and AI agents can work on the same project.
about_excerpt: Forge is an open-source, browser-based IDE where humans and AI agents can work on the same project. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Forge An agent-native web IDE for humans and AI agents Inspiration AI coding agents can generate impressive amounts of code, but generating code is only one part of software development. A real development workflow also involves creating projects, managing files, installing dependencies, running applications, reading console output, debugging errors, rebuilding, and eventually deploying the result. Most AI coding experiences handle these tasks through a chat interface, while the actual development environment remains separate. Forge asks a different question: what if the development environment itself could be used by an AI agent? Forge is a browser-based IDE where humans and AI agents can work on the same project. Instead of asking an agent to generate code and then manually moving that code into an IDE, Forge exposes its development capabilities directly through WebMCP. The agent can operate the IDE itself. Why WebMCP? Forge is a particularly strong fit for WebMCP because its core functionality is already organized around meaningful actions that an agent needs to perform. An IDE is not just a page to read. It is an environment to operate. Before WebMCP, an agent interacting with a browser-based IDE would need to rely on indirect mechanisms such as simulated clicks, keyboard input, or copying and pasting code. With WebMCP, Forge can expose its capabilities as structured, semantic tools. The agent can discover what Forge can do and directly invoke those capabilities. This transforms the IDE from a human-only interface into an agent-accessible development environment . What agents can do in Forge Forge exposes meaningful development operations through WebMCP, including: Create and manage projects List project files Read files Write and modify files Run projects Inspect console output Build projects Deploy projects These tools are connected directly to Forge's underlying application logic. The WebMCP layer is therefore not a separate demonstration layer. The agent and the human interface operate on the same project and the same underlying state. For example, an agent can be asked to: "Create a React landing page for a fictional company." It can then: Create the project. Create and modify the required files. Run the development server. Inspect the result. Check the console for errors. Modify the code when necessary. Build the project. Deploy it. The agent is not merely generating a code snippet. It is operating the development environment. Human + Agent collaboration Forge is designed around collaboration rather than replacement. The human developer remains inside the IDE and can see the project, preview the application, inspect the code, and make manual changes at any time. The agent can perform repetitive or complex development operations through WebMCP while the human remains in control. A developer can ask an agent to create a project, modify multiple files, run it, inspect an error, fix the problem, and build the result. The developer can then review the changes, edit the code themselves, and ask the agent to continue. Both human and agent can work on the same project without leaving the development environment. This is the experience that WebMCP makes possible. What was difficult before? Without WebMCP, an AI assistant could generate the code for a project, but the developer would still need to transfer that code into the development environment and manually perform many of the surrounding operations. The workflow becomes: Ask AI → Copy code → Open IDE → Create files → Install dependencies → Run → Find errors → Go back to AI → Copy fixes → Repeat Forge changes this interaction into: Ask agent → Agent operates Forge → Review → Iterate The important difference is not simply that AI can write code. It is that the agent can use the tools of the development environment itself. Built for the browser Forge runs directly in the browser using WebContainers, providing a real development environment without requiring a local installation. The editor is powered by Monaco Editor, giving developers a familiar coding experience while keeping the entire workflow inside the browser. Forge is built with: React TypeScript Vite Monaco Editor WebContainers WebMCP Tailwind CSS WebMCP implementation Forge registers its capabilities using the WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a clear name, description, structured input schema, and execution function. The tools call Forge's actual application logic rather than simulating interaction with the UI. This architecture allows both the human interface and AI agents to work with the same underlying functionality. The result is a genuine WebMCP integration rather than a chatbot placed on top of an existing application. Execution and agent-native design Forge was designed around the idea that WebMCP tools should represent meaningful operations , not low-level interface actions. Instead of exposing tools such as "click button" or "type text", Forge exposes higher-level development operations such as create_project , read_file , write_file , run_project , get_console , build_project , and deploy_project . This makes the interface understandable to an agent while keeping the application usable for humans. The result is an IDE that has two interfaces: A visual interface for humans. A structured tool interface for agents. Both operate on the same environment. Potential impact Forge explores a future where web applications are not only designed for people, but are also designed to be used by AI agents. For developers, this could reduce the friction between AI-generated code and a working application. For AI agents, it provides a structured environment where they can move beyond generating text and actually perform meaningful software development tasks. The same principle could extend beyond IDEs to other professional web applications: design tools, data platforms, project management systems, scientific software, and more. Forge is therefore an experiment in a broader idea: What happens when the tools we use every day become directly accessible to AI agents? Creativity & ambition Forge is not simply an online code editor with AI assistance. It explores the idea of an agent-native IDE : an environment where AI agents are first-class users of the application rather than external assistants sitting beside it. WebMCP provides the bridge between the agent and the application. The goal is not to make AI better at pretending to be a developer. The goal is to give AI agents the tools they need to actually participate in the development process. Open source Forge is open source and designed to be transparent and inspectable. The project demonstrates how a complex browser application can expose useful capabilities to AI agents through an open web standard. Built for the WebMCP Challenge Forge was created for the WebMCP Challenge to explore the future of the open web, where humans and AI agents can interact, collaborate, and create together. The central idea is simple: The future of agentic software may not be an AI sitting beside an application — it may be an AI working inside it. Forge — The IDE that agents can use. title: GroundTruth
pitch: Post-disaster damage assessment where the agent's tools are scoped to what's on your screen. Ask "what's the flood exposure here?" and here means your viewport, your selected building, right now.
about_excerpt: Post-disaster damage assessment where the agent's tools are scoped to what's on your screen. Ask "what's the flood exposure here?" and here means your viewport, your selected building, right now. Like Comment Story Updates The problem After a flood or an earthquake, the first 72 hours are triage. Someone sits in front of aerial imagery deciding which blocks get the trucks. The imagery tells you what a roof looks like. It does not tell you how many people live under it, whether the road in is passable, or whether the building you just clicked is a clinic. That context exists — building footprints, population rasters, road networks, critical infrastructure — but it lives in files nobody opens during a crisis. What it does GroundTruth is a damage assessment console. You pan aerial imagery and select buildings. An agent sitting inside the page answers questions about what you are looking at right now: population exposure in this viewport, road access to this polygon, which critical facilities fall inside the affected area. You ask "what's the flood exposure here?" and here is unambiguous — it is the current viewport, the current selection, the imagery date currently loaded. Why WebMCP and not a server MCP This is the whole argument. A remote MCP server can query the same datasets, but it has no idea what "here" means. It cannot see your viewport, your selection, or your map state. It would need you to describe your screen in words before it could help. WebMCP puts the tools in the page, so they close over live application state. The agent does not receive a bounding box you typed — it reads the one you are looking at. The tools are the app's own functions, which means the agent and the human operate the same console and see the same thing. How we built it A Next.js map console over MapLibre, with a WebMCP tool surface exposed from the client. Each tool is scoped to live UI state rather than taking free-floating parameters. A data pipeline pre-processes building footprints, population and infrastructure layers into tiles the browser can query without a round trip. What we learned Designing tools that close over UI state is a different discipline from designing REST endpoints. The temptation is to expose one powerful tool with many parameters. That performs worse than several narrow tools that each read the current state, because the model stops having to reconstruct context it cannot see. What's honest about it The datasets are pre-staged for the demo region rather than fetched live, and the damage signal comes from imagery the operator reads, not from an automated classifier. Both are deliberate: the point of the entry is the agent-to-page interface, not a damage model. Live data ingestion is the obvious next step. title: pact
pitch: Gives agents only the exact authority needed for one approved transaction, with stale-state protection, verification, auditability, and receipts.
about_excerpt: Gives agents only the exact authority needed for one approved transaction, with stale-state protection, verification, auditability, and receipts. Like Comment Story Updates PACT PACT is a transaction and authority protocol for AI agents performing consequential actions inside web applications. Most agent systems give an AI broad access to application tools and rely on instructions such as “only change these resources” or “do not touch billing.” PACT treats that model as insufficient for high-impact operations. Instead, PACT turns every consequential task into an explicitly scoped transaction. The workflow is: Intent → semantic preview → exact-plan approval → scoped authority → commit → canonical verification → receipt. Before any mutation occurs, PACT determines the exact effects required by the task. The human sees precisely what will change and what will not change. Approval is bound to the specific plan, its hash, and the canonical state on which it was created. If the underlying state changes after approval, the plan becomes stale and commit authority disappears. The agent must re-plan and obtain approval for the new state instead of silently executing an outdated operation. PACT includes protections for stale state, duplicate commits, idempotency, version conflicts, approval expiry, negative invariants, post-condition verification, audit integrity, rollback conditions, and transaction recovery. Its key WebMCP contribution is that agent capability is not equivalent to permanent administrative access. Mutation capabilities can appear only after an exact transaction has been approved and disappear when the authorization is no longer valid. The reference implementation demonstrates this through operations such as contractor offboarding, ownership transfer, access revocation, and protected resources such as billing or deletion. The broader thesis is that agents should not receive permanent authority. They should receive narrowly scoped, temporary, verifiable authority for a specific approved transaction. title: WebReform AI
pitch: WebReform AI lets users to reshape real websites around their intent—using WebMCP to focus, simplify, reorganize, and restore any webpage.
about_excerpt: WebReform AI lets users to reshape real websites around their intent—using WebMCP to focus, simplify, reorganize, and restore any webpage. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web has become incredibly powerful, but most websites still expect humans to adapt to their interfaces. Every site has its own navigation, layout, sidebars, recommendations, ads, and information hierarchy. We wondered: what if the interface could adapt to what the user is actually trying to accomplish? That led to WebReform AI. Instead of building another AI that simply tells you what to click, we wanted to build an interface layer where an agent can understand a webpage and safely reshape it around the user's intent. WebMCP made this idea especially interesting because it gives agents a structured way to interact with real web capabilities instead of relying entirely on brittle browser automation. What it does WebReform AI lets users express what they want to accomplish on a webpage in natural language. An agent can use WebMCP tools to understand the current page and perform actions such as: Focusing on the most relevant content Hiding distracting elements Reorganizing information Creating a task-focused view Highlighting useful content Restoring the original interface The important part is that these operations happen on the real webpage. WebReform AI analyzes the page into a semantic representation, generates a structured transformation plan, validates it, and applies the changes through a deterministic transformation engine. Every transformation is designed to be reversible, so the user remains in control. How we built it WebReform AI is built as a Chrome extension with a lightweight, dependency-free architecture. The main pipeline is: User Intent → AI Planner → Semantic PageModel → Transformation DSL → Validator → Transformation Executor → Real DOM The extension analyzes webpages into a bounded semantic PageModel rather than sending an entire raw DOM to the model. The planner produces structured transformation operations instead of arbitrary JavaScript. We integrated WebMCP through document.modelContext.registerTool() and exposed structured tools for page analysis, querying, focusing, hiding, reorganizing, creating focused views, and restoring the original page. We also built a deterministic fallback planner so the core transformation system can still be demonstrated without depending entirely on an external AI model. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making the concept work across different websites without building a separate integration for every website. Modern websites have constantly changing DOM structures, dynamically loaded content, nested layouts, and very different ways of representing similar information. A transformation that works perfectly on one page can easily break another. We therefore had to build around semantic page understanding rather than relying on fixed website-specific selectors. Another major challenge was making AI-generated actions safe. We didn't want the model generating arbitrary JavaScript and directly modifying the page. Instead, we created a strict transformation DSL with validation and a controlled executor. Getting WebMCP, the extension messaging layer, the semantic analyzer, the AI planner, and the real DOM to work together reliably was another significant part of the project. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that WebReform AI goes beyond simply describing webpages or automating clicks. The agent can interact with structured WebMCP capabilities that cause actual, visible changes to the webpage. We built a complete pipeline from natural-language intent to semantic page understanding, structured planning, validation, real DOM transformation, and restoration. We're also particularly proud of the reversible transformation system. The user doesn't lose control of their original interface—changes can be rolled back and the original page can be restored. Most importantly, we built the system to be generic. The goal isn't to make one perfect GitHub demo; it's to create a reusable interface layer that can adapt different kinds of websites around different human goals. What we learned We learned that making an AI agent useful on the web isn't only about giving it more powerful actions. The representation of the webpage matters just as much. Giving the agent a bounded semantic representation makes it easier to reason about the page while also reducing the amount of raw information that needs to be processed. We also learned that safety and reversibility are essential when an agent is allowed to modify a user's interface. A powerful agent should not mean an uncontrollable interface. Most importantly, WebMCP changed how we think about agent-to-web interaction. Instead of treating websites as something an agent has to mechanically operate, structured web capabilities can give agents a much cleaner way to understand and interact with them. What's next for WebReform AI The hackathon version is only the beginning. Next, we want to make WebReform AI substantially more robust across complex websites and dynamic applications, improve its semantic understanding, and expand the types of transformations agents can safely perform. We also want to explore deeper agent-driven workflows where the interface continuously adapts as the user's goal changes, while still keeping the human in control. Longer term, the vision is bigger than a browser extension: WebReform AI could become an adaptive interface layer for the web, giving websites a way to expose structured capabilities to agents while allowing those agents to reshape the experience around individual human intent. title: PowerForge.Web - Verified WebMCP for Static Sites
pitch: Turn generated documentation sites into verified, agent-native applications without adding an application server.
about_excerpt: Turn generated documentation sites into verified, agent-native applications without adding an application server. Like Comment Story Updates OfficeIMO exposes the read-only search_site Website Tool. PowerForge.Web generates and verifies the complete WebMCP contract. Codex invokes search_site and leaves matching results visible. One opt-in engine capability serves seven independent documentation sites. Inspiration Documentation search is usually designed for people clicking through a page. An agent must either imitate that interface, scrape the rendered HTML, or bypass the site's intended search experience entirely. Those paths are harder to validate and leave the person with little visibility into what the agent actually did. WebMCP provides a cleaner contract: the page can expose a small, typed capability that works inside the current document. We wanted that capability to be reusable across generated static sites rather than implemented as custom JavaScript for one showcase page. What it does On a participating site's search route, PowerForge.Web registers a read-only search_site Website Tool. The tool accepts a bounded query and result limit, searches the site's generated JSON index, and returns structured results containing titles, descriptions, collections, tags, languages, and URLs. The same invocation also updates the visible search page. The agent receives structured data while the person sees the corresponding query and result cards, can inspect the choices, refine the search, and open a result normally. Browsers without WebMCP continue to use the ordinary search page. The live judging target is OfficeIMO: Live application: https://officeimo.com/search/ Demo video: https://youtu.be/xIPtNwYBO58 Public source: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule Why WebMCP is a strong fit Search is a good first agent journey because it benefits from structure without requiring broad authority. WebMCP removes UI guessing, gives the agent an explicit schema, and keeps the action bound to the page the person is already viewing. The tool is read-only, the query is bounded, and the result remains visible. The improvement is not only faster retrieval. The person and agent now share one observable state: the agent can perform the structured search, and the person can immediately review the same results in the website's normal interface. How we built it PowerForge.Web is a .NET static-site engine. A site opts in through the engine's typed agent-readiness configuration and declares a route-scoped WebMCP tool. During generation, the engine: Builds the site's normal search route and JSON search index. Emits a same-origin WebMCP runtime. Registers search_site through the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API. Connects the tool to the visible search UI through a reusable adapter. Verifies the rendered route, executable script ordering, same-origin index and runtime, asset integrity, schema, and declared tool metadata. Advertises WebMCP readiness only when the complete generated artifact passes those checks. The runtime supports cancellation, bounded input, cached index loading, explicit cache invalidation, and theme-owned ranking through an adapter. The current shared implementation intentionally supports a read-only site-search journey; future write or product-specific actions will require separate authority and product contracts. What people and agents can do together Before this addition, a person could search the documentation, but an agent had no explicit contract for using that experience. It had to infer controls or search elsewhere. Now the person can open the OfficeIMO search page and ask Codex to find Word-to-PDF resources using the page's Website Tool. Codex invokes search_site , receives three structured matches, and leaves the OfficeIMO results visible. The person can verify the query, inspect the result cards, and continue browsing from the same page. Challenges we ran into Generated static sites create a different reliability problem from server-backed tools: configuration may look correct while the deployed page is missing its route, index, script, or fingerprinted asset. We therefore treated rendered output as the contract and added both local and remote readiness checks. We also needed to keep structured agent results synchronized with the theme's human-facing search behavior. PowerForge.Web provides a fallback search surface and an adapter that lets richer themes own ranking and rendering without replacing the shared WebMCP runtime. Accomplishments One reusable implementation in the PowerForge.Web engine rather than seven unrelated site scripts. A live, read-only Website Tool recognized and invoked by the ChatGPT/Codex integrated browser. Fail-closed verification of the actual generated and deployed artifact. Visible synchronization between the structured tool call and human search page. Opt-in deployment across seven independent Evotec documentation sites: evotec.xyz, evotec.pl, OfficeIMO, HtmlForgeX, IntelligenceX, CodeGlyphX, and TestimoX. Normal search behavior remains available in browsers without WebMCP. Work completed during the challenge PowerForge.Web existed before the challenge. The WebMCP capability was added as a meaningful extension during the challenge period on September 2-3, 2026. PR #860, Add verified WebMCP site search support: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/pull/860 PR #865, Define safe WebMCP portfolio rollout: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/pull/865 Registration runtime: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/blob/main/PowerForge.Web/Assets/WebMcp/site-search.v1.js Implementation and operating documentation: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/blob/main/Docs/PowerForge.Web.AgentReadiness.md The dated pull requests and commit histories distinguish this WebMCP work from the pre-existing engine and websites. What we learned Adding registerTool is the small part. A reusable implementation also needs truthful discovery, bounded inputs, same-origin resources, script-order guarantees, browser fallback behavior, visible state synchronization, and validation of the final deployed files. Treating those pieces as one contract made the feature safe enough to enable across multiple sites. What's next The next phase is to add richer read-only journeys where a site has a real domain-specific task, such as navigating API surfaces or comparing documented capabilities. Write tools will remain opt-in and will be designed per product rather than enabled across the portfolio by default. Testing instructions Open https://officeimo.com/search/ in ChatGPT's integrated browser. Open the address-bar Site tools menu and confirm that search_site is available as one read tool with no write tools. Attach Browser to a Codex request. Ask: "Use the current OfficeIMO page's search_site Website Tool to find three resources about converting Word documents to PDF. Use only the Website Tool exposed by the page and leave the matching results visible." Confirm that Codex returns structured links and the OfficeIMO search page displays the corresponding query and result cards. No account or credentials are required. title: transcriptly
pitch: Clean, timestamped transcripts from any video URL, built for AI agents: MCP server, WebMCP tools on the page, REST API, and CLI. Whisper on the audio, not scraped captions.
about_excerpt: Clean, timestamped transcripts from any video URL, built for AI agents: MCP server, WebMCP tools on the page, REST API, and CLI. Whisper on the audio, not scraped captions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agents can read almost anything, but they can't hear a video. Every workflow that touches YouTube, TikTok, or a recording hits the same wall: captions are missing, auto-generated, or wrong, and "transcribe this" becomes a manual detour. I wanted one small, honest tool that turns any video URL or file into a clean transcript and exposes that single capability everywhere an agent or a human might need it, including directly on a web page through WebMCP. What it does Paste a YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, X, or Reddit link, or drop a video or audio file, and get a clean, timestamped transcript as Markdown, plain text, SRT, or JSON. It runs Whisper on the actual audio, so it works on videos with no captions at all. One core, four surfaces: CLI and npm library : npm i -g transcriptly , then transcriptly "<url>" . Whisper runs locally on your machine; the first run checks your tools and lets you pick a model with arrow keys. MCP server : claude mcp add --scope user transcriptly -- npx -y transcriptly mcp gives Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT, Copilot, or any MCP client two tools: get_transcript and get_video_info . Hosted API at transcriptly.dev: a free tier with honest limits, live progress streamed as server-sent events, and curl, TypeScript, and Python examples in the docs. A waitlist gauges demand for a paid, generous tier. WebMCP : the landing page registers get_transcript , get_video_info , and transcribe_file through document.modelContext . A browser agent can transcribe a video right on the page, and even transcribe a file the human dropped into the page's drop zone. An agent panel shows every tool call and its progress as it happens, and the human sees the same transcript the agent got. How I built it TypeScript throughout. The core resolves a source with yt-dlp (or ffprobe for files and direct media links), extracts audio with ffmpeg, runs speech recognition through whisper.cpp locally or Groq's whisper-large-v3-turbo in the hosted tier, normalizes the segments, and formats the result. The CLI runs on plain Node 20 with the MCP SDK as its only runtime dependency. The MCP server uses the official SDK over stdio. The API is a small Bun server with a transcript cache, sliding-window rate limits, a daily transcription budget, and a single shared pipeline that serves both plain responses and progress streams. The site is Next.js with a static export, hand-built animated SVG illustrations, light and dark themes, deployed with Caddy on a Hetzner box through GitHub Actions. The WebMCP layer is deliberately thin: the page's tools call the same API the human uses, so the agent path and the human path share one implementation and one cache. The transcribe_file tool exists because of a WebMCP-specific idea: the human drops a private file into the page, and the agent gets to work with something that never had a URL. Challenges YouTube, Facebook, X, and Reddit block or login-wall datacenter IPs. The hosted tier routes those platforms through a residential proxy and pre-warms a transcript cache; the CLI on your own machine has none of these problems. Instagram exposes only video-only streams to yt-dlp without a login, so it is listed honestly as unsupported rather than half-working. Groq caps uploads at 25 MB, which raw 16 kHz audio exceeds after 13 minutes; the engine re-encodes to compact MP3 before uploading. Agents don't discover things the way people do: an agent asked for "the file" tried the page's download buttons instead of calling the tool with format: "md" . The fix was better tool descriptions, which is where most WebMCP polish actually lives. Accomplishments Four working surfaces from one core, all live and tested end to end: the npm package, the MCP server inside Claude Code, the hosted API, and the WebMCP page with real tool calls from an agent browser. MIT licensed and documented for someone who has never seen it. What I learned WebMCP makes "the page is the tool" feel natural: once the tools exist, an agent uses the page the way a person would, and the same UI can show the person what the agent is doing. Most of the hard work was not the AI part but the plumbing around platforms, limits, caching, and honest error messages. What's next A paid hosted tier for longer videos if the waitlist says so, speaker labels, translation, and more platform-specific care where yt-dlp needs help. title: YallaQueue Agent Desk
pitch: WhatsApp booking meets an agent-native live queue for local service businesses.
about_excerpt: WhatsApp booking meets an agent-native live queue for local service businesses. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Many small service businesses manage appointments through WhatsApp and then manually transfer those bookings into a schedule or queue. This wastes time, creates booking conflicts, and makes it difficult to keep customers and staff working from the same information. I created YallaQueue to connect WhatsApp booking, a live business dashboard, and an AI agent. What it does YallaQueue converts natural WhatsApp messages into confirmed appointments. It can: Check whether an appointment time is available Prevent conflicting bookings Assign a queue number Save the appointment Send a WhatsApp confirmation Display the appointment on a live shop dashboard The signed-in shop owner can also use two WebMCP tools through a browser agent: get_queue_summary returns the current queue without exposing customer phone numbers. update_queue_status changes one appointment to confirmed, completed, cancelled, or no-show. For example, the owner can ask: “Summarize today’s queue.” “Mark queue 1 completed.” The dashboard immediately shows the updated state. How we built it YallaQueue uses Next.js and React for the dashboard, Supabase and PostgreSQL for authentication and appointment data, and n8n with the WhatsApp Cloud API for messaging automation. The dashboard registers two browser-native WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool calls a protected server route using the owner’s active login. The server checks authentication, shop membership, input validity, appointment ownership, and database row-level security before returning data or making a change. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was giving the agent useful access without bypassing security. The agent must only access appointments belonging to the signed-in owner’s shop. Customer phone numbers must not appear in tool results, and an appointment must not be changed without a clear user request. Another challenge was keeping WhatsApp, the database, the dashboard, and the agent synchronized so they all display the same queue state. Testing WebMCP also required enabling its experimental Chrome flag and using ChatGPT Work so the browser agent could discover the registered tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of Connected a real WhatsApp booking flow to a live dashboard Built and deployed two working WebMCP tools Used structured tool data instead of visual browser guessing Protected every tool route with server-side authorization Excluded customer phone numbers from agent responses Successfully tested both reading and updating the live queue through ChatGPT Work What we learned I learned how websites can provide structured tools for both humans and AI agents. I also learned that WebMCP does not replace application security. Agent actions must still pass normal authentication, authorization, input validation, ownership checks, and database security rules. What's next for YallaQueue The next steps are adding more carefully controlled tools for availability searches, creating appointments, rescheduling, and cancellations. I also plan to add clearer confirmation screens for sensitive actions, support multiple shops and staff members, and improve reporting for business owners. title: Scout
pitch: Know the market before you make the offer — transparent card deal evidence for people and agents through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Know the market before you make the offer — transparent card deal evidence for people and agents through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Side-by-side Scout listing comparison with acquisition cost, 90-day market delta, trust, and alerts. Scout market overview with exact-tier pricing, robust comps, Deal Score, and Seller Trust. Scout Deal Score, Seller Trust, confidence, and normalization methodology. Scout provider capability matrix and explicit separation of synthetic demo data from live integrations. What Scout is Scout is a transparent Pokémon card buying assistant for people and agents. It normalizes the exact card, printing, condition, grading company, and numeric grade before comparing any price. Buyers can inspect current availability, total acquisition cost, the latest exact comparable sale, robust 30- and 90-day medians, Seller Trust evidence, listing warnings, and a fully explained Deal Score. The Phase 1 judge build is deliberately synthetic-only. Every card, seller, marketplace, listing, and sale is fictional and visibly labeled. This lets judges test the complete workflow without fabricated API claims, scraping, credentials, or accidental mixing of demo and live records. Inspiration Collectible-card buyers often have to reconcile ambiguous listing titles, asking prices, shipping, grade-specific sales, and seller evidence across several tabs. A PSA 10 is not a PSA 9; a raw Near Mint card is not a slab; and one extreme sale should not define the market. We wanted an assistant that shows its work and is as comfortable saying “insufficient evidence” as it is ranking a deal. What it does Searches normalized card identities and exact raw/graded market tiers. Compares current total acquisition cost with the latest exact sale and robust 30/90-day market statistics. Detects duplicate exposures and flags extreme price anomalies without hiding the audit trail. Produces an inspectable Deal Score and platform-specific Seller Trust Score, withholding either when evidence is inadequate. Surfaces listing risks such as stock photos, weak seller history, title/description conflicts, no returns, high shipping, and missing certification evidence. Compares two to five listings and shows raw versus graded markets without pooling unlike tiers. Registers six read-only WebMCP tools: search_cards , get_card_market_state , assess_listing , compare_listings , find_deals , and compare_raw_vs_graded . Lets a WebMCP tool result update the visible collector workspace, so the person can inspect the same evidence the agent used. How we built it Scout is a strict TypeScript and React application built with Vite and deployed through OpenAI Sites. A provider-adapter boundary maps catalog, listing, sales-history, and seller sources into canonical domain records. Deterministic engines handle identity, deduplication, exact comparable matching, median/MAD statistics, Seller Trust, listing risk, and Deal Score. The React UI and imperative WebMCP registrations call the same CardMarketService , preventing agent and screen results from drifting. Responses carry data mode, synthetic status, source capabilities, retrieval time, limitations, methodology version, and suggested UI state. A service invariant rejects any attempt to introduce non-synthetic records into Phase 1. The disabled eBay configuration contains only server-side environment placeholders—no fake endpoint or fallback data. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was refusing false equivalence. Marketplace titles are loose, but market estimates must be strict enough to keep variant, language, raw condition, grading company, and numeric grade separate. We also needed robust statistics that keep anomalies auditable while preventing them from distorting the estimate, plus score coverage rules that do not turn missing evidence into false certainty. The other challenge was designing WebMCP as the product interface rather than a demo wrapper. Each tool has strict schemas, read-only annotations, structured provenance, honest limitations, and UI-state metadata, while using exactly the same service as the human interface. Accomplishments we are proud of Six WebMCP tools are discovered from the live page and covered by tests. Exact-tier rules prevent PSA 10, PSA 9, BGS 9.5, CGC 10, and raw condition data from being pooled. The 90-day engine uses shipping-inclusive medians, recency weighting, dispersion, and log-price median absolute deviation anomaly flags. Scores explain every weighted component and are withheld when evidence coverage is too low. Synthetic/live isolation, capability-scoped sources, security headers, CI, strict schemas, and a zero-known-vulnerability audit are part of the repository foundation. What we learned Agent-ready commerce tools need more than a convenient function signature: they need provenance, confidence, exact identity boundaries, and a path back to inspectable human evidence. We also learned that withholding a score is a feature. A trustworthy assistant should expose uncertainty instead of manufacturing precision. What's next Phase 2 moves adapters, credentials, rate limits, caching, persistence, and scheduled ingestion behind a server boundary. We will re-verify current provider terms and enable one approved live source at a time, starting only where documented access can support the fields we display. PostgreSQL/Prisma storage, an identity-review queue, sandbox provider contract tests, authentication, saved searches, and alerts follow. No marketplace will be enabled through scraping or an undocumented workaround. title: AlertKick: agent-native website and server monitoring
pitch: Websites and server monitoring that ChatGPT can operate directly on the page. Start with a URL, no agent required. WebMCP exposes website, ssl, domain checks and account specific monitors and alerts.
about_excerpt: Websites and server monitoring that ChatGPT can operate directly on the page. Start with a URL, no agent required. WebMCP exposes website, ssl, domain checks and account specific monitors and alerts. Like Comment Story Updates Listing of WebMCP tools Creating different monitors using the WebMCP Creation of http monitor using webmcp with json output creation of other dns monitor and email monitor Final output of the agent interface after creating all monitors through WebMCP Inspiration I built AlertKick to make monitoring websites and servers dead easy with as little config as possible. In all my previous jobs monitoring and setting up alerting is a lot of moving parts and a lot of config. Even a URL monitoring requires, type a URL, pick an interval, pick a region, pick who gets paged. When something breaks at 3am the person on call then clicks through five more screens to find out what is failing, acknowledge it, and record what they changed. We already run a hosted MCP server so Claude can do all of this over an API key. WebMCP lets the agent already sitting in the user's browser tab do the same thing in the user's own session, with the browser enforcing confirmation on anything risky. That is a much shorter path from "watch my site" to a working monitor, and the user needs nothing except to be logged in. What it does AlertKick monitors websites and servers. Website monitoring needs nothing installed: uptime and response time from multiple regions, TLS certificate and domain expiry, DNS records and cron heartbeats. Teams running their own hosts add the Linux/Windows agent for metrics, Docker and eBPF security detections. Alerts route through on-call scheduling, escalation policies and change control. With WebMCP, two surfaces register their capabilities as page tools: Public free tools at alertkick.com/tools (SSL checker, DNS checker, domain expiry, security headers, website check). Each page registers one read-only tool. "Check the cert on example.com" runs the checker and hands the agent structured JSON instead of a rendered table. The tenant dashboard. On login the app registers the same tool set our hosted MCP server exposes: create and manage HTTPS, TCP, DNS and domain-expiry monitors, heartbeats, list/acknowledge/resolve alerts, inspect servers and containers, and create/approve/start/verify/complete change records. Example flows in the ChatGPT desktop browser: New user with only a URL: "add uptime, DNS and cert-expiry checks for example.com" creates three monitors in one turn. During an incident: "what is paging right now, ack the critical ones and open a change for the fix" becomes list_alerts , acknowledge_alert (confirmed by the user) and create_change . On a free tool page, no account needed: "is example.com's TLS chain valid and when does it expire?" Read tools carry readOnlyHint: true . Every write goes through requestUserInteraction() and the app's own confirm dialog. The agent proposes, a person approves. How it's built One manifest, two tool builds. Our MCP server is written in Go and already defines 34 tools with JSON Schema inputs. A generator dumps name , description and inputSchema to a JSON manifest that the React dashboard imports. The UI supplies only the execute() bodies, each tool is a small call through the same authenticated /api/v1 client which UI already usages. Both MCP and WebMCP share one source of truth, so they cannot drift. Session-scoped registration. Tools register when the auth context resolves a logged-in user and unregister on logout. An unauthenticated tab does not exposes anything. The server side has tenant isolation on every request the same way as for the normal UI calls, so the agent can reach only what the user can. Website tools. I use the same to provide tools on the main site. main site registers per free-tools page via a shared component that wraps the existing /api/tools/* endpoints (Cloudflare rate limited to 10 requests per 10 seconds per IP). Testing. Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and navigator.modelContextTesting.executeTool() for unit-style checks, then end to end in the ChatGPT desktop app against staging and production. Also my MCP server is all tested using MCP Inspector and is also available on the Claude Connectors directory so it's well tested from there as well, and it usages same request parameters. Open source. The manifest generator, registration helper and execute adapters are published as a standalone package so any product with an MCP server can expose it in-page the same way. Challenges we ran into Write safety. A tool that deletes a monitor or approves a change is one sentence away from an accident. Every non-read tool now calls requestUserInteraction() , which opens confirm modal for clicking the button we see. The tool result reports this too, whether the user approved or cancelled. Schema fidelity. Go MCP tool schemas use enums and nested objects that our first manifest export flattened. The generator now emits the schema verbatim and a test asserts the browser manifest equals the server's tools/list response. Spec churn. provideContext() disappeared from the spec in March and the attribute location changed mid-year. We wrote to registerTool / unregisterTool only and kept detection defensive. Registration timing in an SPA. React re-renders and route changes re-registered tools and hit InvalidStateError on duplicates. Registration now lives in a single effect keyed on user id, with a module-level registry that unregisters before re-registering. Accomplishments A user with only a domain name gets uptime monitoring, DNS checks, and cert-expiry monitoring by typing one sentence. Zero duplicated tool definitions between the hosted MCP connector and the in-page WebMCP surface, as we using same manifest for both to avoid drift between them. A human in the loop on every write without adding a single new backend endpoint or permission model. The public free tools work with ChatGPT for anyone, no account, no API key. What we learned Agent traffic is one more client of the API you already have. If tenant scoping and authorisation live server-side, WebMCP costs little to add and adds no new attack surface. If they live in the UI, the agent will reach things it should not. Tool descriptions are very important and needs to explain what it is. The model picks tools by reading them. "List monitors" performed badly compared to a sentence explaining when to use it and what comes back. This becomes more important with more tools you add. readOnlyHint matters. Without it the agent asked for confirmation on every read and the experience felt slower than clicking. Backend MCP covers automation with no human present. WebMCP covers the person already on the page. What's next We'll expose on-call and escalation tools in-page (who is on call, override a shift, page a person). get_current_view() and navigate_to() so the agent can reason about what the user is looking at. Incident summaries and after-action reports generated from list_alerts and list_changes context. add the WebMCP layer to the mobile web view and status pages. Looking at adopting the declarative <form webmcp-tool> variant when it's available, this will help so the monitor-create form can register itself without any Javascript. Overall, I learned a great deal from this. Given my background as SRE and Devops backend systems comes easy to me and can write backend APIs and systems processes all day long but working with React/Node and browser side is always challenging but it was fun to add this and I believe it'll add value to the product and to users. title: Bizgrid
pitch: Bizgrid is an AI commerce platform for African sellers. With WebMCP, any agent can search products across every live store on Bizgrid and add to the correct merchant’s cart without scraping the UI
about_excerpt: Bizgrid is an AI commerce platform for African sellers. With WebMCP, any agent can search products across every live store on Bizgrid and add to the correct merchant’s cart without scraping the UI Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Starting an online business in Africa is still harder than it should be. Many small businesses rely on social media because building an e-commerce website requires technical skills, time, and money. Existing platforms often expect merchants to understand themes, hosting, product management, and website design before they can even make their first sale. We asked a simple question: What if building an online store was as easy as describing your business to an AI? That idea became Bizgrid, this an AI-powered commerce platform that lets anyone create, customise, and launch a professional online store through natural conversation. What it does Bizgrid is an AI commerce platform for sellers and SME's. With WebMCP, any agent can search products across every live store on Bizgrid and add to the correct merchant’s cart ,without scraping the UI. Why our use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Bizgrid is an AI-first commerce platform for African sellers: dozens of independent merchants each run their own storefront, with their own catalog, inventory, prices, and Paystack checkout, all hosted on one platform. That shape many sellers, one marketplace is exactly where WebMCP shines, because commerce is fundamentally structured data. Stores, products, prices, stock levels, variant options, and carts all have well-defined schemas. WebMCP's tool model lets us expose that structure directly, instead of forcing an agent to reverse-engineer it. Before WebMCP, an agent trying to shop on Bizgrid would have to scrape HTML fragile, slow, and blind to the rules that matter. It wouldn't reliably know whether a product is in stock, how many units can be purchased, what currency the merchant prices in, or which variant options are required. It certainly couldn't know that a "cart" on Bizgrid is scoped to a specific merchant, and that putting an item in the wrong cart means paying the wrong seller. Those are business-critical rules, not UI details. With WebMCP, we encode them once, as typed tool contracts: every tool response carries a store_slug, every add_to_cart validates stock, purchase limits, and variant options against the merchant's real data before writing. The agent can no longer guess wrong about who gets the money the platform itself enforces correctness. There's also a natural symmetry in our product story: Bizgrid merchants already run their shops with an AI assistant on WhatsApp. WebMCP completes the loop on the buyer side. Merchants sell through an agent; now buyers shop through an agent, too with Bizgrid as the structured layer that connects them. How it creates a better user experience Imagine a shopper in Lagos who wants a vitamin C serum under ₦20,000. The old way: they'd discover Bizgrid stores one at a time, open each storefront in a new tab, search each shop's catalog separately, compare prices by hand, and repeat the whole ritual for every product. The new way: they open ChatGPT (or any WebMCP-capable browser) on the Bizgrid homepage and say one sentence: "Find me a vitamin C serum under ₦20,000." The agent calls search_products with budget_max, gets back structured results from every published store at once — name, store, price, currency, stock status, and a direct product link and presents a ranked comparison. The shopper says "add the one from GlowSkin to my cart," and the agent calls add_to_cart with the correct store_slug, where the platform validates stock and variants and writes to that merchant's cart. The shopper then clicks one checkout link and pays normally with Paystack. What makes this a better experience, not just a different one: the human stays in the familiar, trusted flow the same storefront cart and checkout they already know while everything upstream (search, comparison, decision fatigue) becomes conversational. And because tools are typed, the agent quotes real prices in the right currency, never hallucinates a product, and never sends a shopper to a checkout that doesn't contain what they asked for. Discovery becomes instant; trust stays human. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before The genuinely new capability here is platform-wide shopping with a human-held checkout. Before WebMCP, an agent could only operate inside one website at a time, scraping one storefront's HTML. Cross-store comparison meant running one agent per tab, and adding to a cart meant custom per-merchant integrations that no small African seller could afford. There was no way for an agent to say "search all of Bizgrid" the marketplace existed in the URL structure, not in any machine-readable interface. WebMCP collapses that. A single tool layer registered on the platform homepage exposes every published store, every product, and every cart as first-class, callable operations. One agent can search across merchants, compare, negotiate the shopper's preferences, and fill the correct seller's cart then hand the same browser cart to a human for the final, money-moving step. That handoff is the heart of it: a division of labor that didn't exist before. The agent does what machines are good at exhaustive search, structured comparison, remembering constraints, enforcing rules. The human does what humans insist on reviewing, confirming, and paying with the checkout they trust. Agent discovers and carts; human reviews and pays. That collaboration was impossible with scraping, and it's exactly the human-agent partnership WebMCP exists to enable. How we implemented WebMCP We extended Bizgrid's Next.js frontend with a WebMCP tool layer, all client-side, no agent-specific integrations: Registration: src/lib/webmcp/bootstrap.ts polls for document.modelContext (up to 120 animation frames, so registration works even if the WebMCP runtime initializes after page load), registers all tools through registerTool, dispatches a toolchange event so agents re-discover them, dedupes via a single bootstrap promise (protecting against React Strict Mode double-invocations), and cleans up on pagehide. An app-wide provider (src/components/webmcp/platform-webmcp-provider.tsx) plus an instrumentation hook register the tools on every page, early. The seven tools (src/lib/webmcp/platform-tools.ts) — list_stores, list_catalog, get_store_info, search_products, get_product, add_to_cart, get_cart — each with a JSON Schema inputSchema, descriptions written to guide agent tool selection (e.g., "prefer search_products when the shopper has a specific query"), and readOnlyHint annotations so agents can reason about side effects. Data layer — tools call Bizgrid's existing catalog APIs (store listing, full catalog with pagination, search with budget filters, per-product lookup), so agents get live, real prices and stock, never static HTML. Shared cart, shared checkout — add_to_cart writes to the same per-store localStorage cart keys the storefronts already use (src/lib/webmcp/platform-cart.ts), with validation of stock, purchase limits, and variant options (src/lib/webmcp/shared.ts). Every response includes cart_url and checkout_url, so the human opens the exact checkout the agent filled. Agents and humans share one cart and one trusted Paystack flow nothing is simulated or sandboxed. No server changes required because everything is structured client-side on top of existing APIs, the entire WebMCP surface ships with the normal frontend bundle, live at https://www.bizgrid.shop today. title: Murph Food Lab
pitch: Compare 2M+ foods with clear grades, lab evidence, and WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Compare 2M+ foods with clear grades, lab evidence, and WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Murph Food Lab compares more than two million foods with ChatGPT and WebMCP. ChatGPT sees four typed WebMCP tools exposed directly by the Food Lab page. Murph compares exact products in one normalized nutrition table. Open the grade, ingredients, and product-level lab evidence behind each result. Inspiration Food labels make simple choices hard. Serving sizes differ, ingredient lists are difficult to scan, and lab results rarely tell a shopper what matters. We wanted a child, a parent, or an AI agent to compare real products and understand the tradeoffs in seconds. What it does Murph Food Lab searches more than two million branded foods and compares up to four exact products side by side. It normalizes nutrition to the same basis, shows a clear A-E Murph grade, calls out useful and concerning ingredients, and links exact product-level lab evidence when it exists. The person and the agent share one visible workspace. The agent can search for foods, add exact products, read the current comparison, and open the evidence drawer. The person stays in control and sees every result the agent used. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the interaction layer, not a wrapper around a chatbot. The Food Lab page registers four typed tools: search_food_products searches the public catalog and returns exact product references. compare_food_products places selected products into the visible comparison. get_food_comparison reads the same normalized metrics and grades shown to the person. show_food_evidence opens the visible evidence view for one selected product. Each tool has bounded input, structured output, and shares the current page state. This lets an agent act through the real interface instead of using a separate hidden backend. How we built it We built the experience with TypeScript, React, Next.js, WebMCP, PostgreSQL, Vercel, Brandfetch, and Codex CLI. Murph reuses its public product search and exact-evidence APIs. Nutrition comparison and grading use deterministic code. WebMCP exposes those same results to compatible agents. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping the result useful without pretending that one food is universally healthy. We kept nutrition, ingredients, and lab evidence separate. Missing lab data stays unknown instead of becoming a safety claim. We also filtered generic database rows that look like products but do not identify a real consumer product. Accomplishments that we are proud of A shared human-agent comparison instead of a separate AI chat result. More than two million searchable food records. Clear A-E grades with plain-language reasons. Exact product-level evidence when available. Stable layouts across loading, empty, mobile, and four-product states. Brand matching without exposing the Brandfetch credential to the browser. What we learned WebMCP works best when tools control a useful page that already makes sense to a person. Typed tool inputs, exact product references, and shared visible state made the agent behavior easier to trust and debug. What is next We want to add barcode scanning, more exact lab sources, regional product catalogs, and personal comparison preferences. We also want agents to explain why two similar products received different grades without hiding the underlying label or evidence. title: moodle-webmcp
pitch: Students can use their familiar ChatGPT interface to get grounded answers and help, fast, with no setup, via a WebMCP integration for Moodle.
about_excerpt: Students can use their familiar ChatGPT interface to get grounded answers and help, fast, with no setup, via a WebMCP integration for Moodle. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In my time at university, which used an OpenLMS deployment based on Moodle, course content was often scattered and hard to dig through. When OpenAI announced The WebMCP Challenge, the lightbulb went off. WebMCP moves tool execution right into the browser. So instead of fighting IT firewalls or using API keys, tools run inside the student's active browser session. I wanted to build a real WebMCP enablement plugin that turns standard Moodle course pages into active, agentic workspaces for both students and instructors, requiring no additional setup from them. What it does moodle-webmcp is a Moodle plugin that enables a number of useful WebMCP tools primarily for students, with some extra tools useful for course admins. When you open course pages in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 146+, the plugin automatically declares structured AI tools directly on the web page to: Retrieve upcoming assignments and labs in chronological order Fetch relevant lecture summaries and course materials Generate an adaptive day-by-day study schedule based on available daily hours Critique a student's draft essay based on the assignment's official grading rubrics How we built it Moodle Plugin Core : Developed local_webmcp in PHP, integrating with Moodle's navigation hooks and AMD loader. Deployment : Packaged Alpine Linux with PHP 8.3, Moodle 5.2.2, and SQLite3 on Render with persistent disk storage and a custom domain ( moodle-webmcp.akashgpt.me ). Development Tooling : Built and debugged the full stack with Codex and Chrome DevTools MCP. Challenges we ran into Minimal issues overall. The main hurdles involved working through Moodle-specific quirks and container setup, such as aligning with Moodle 5.x's public document root structure and ensuring database gradebook items were properly registered for assignment activities. Accomplishments that we're proud of True Zero-Token Authentication : No API keys required. Tools inherit the student's existing authenticated web session and CSRF tokens automatically. Real, Live Moodle Environment : Built and deployed a full Moodle 5.2.2 LMS with seeded courses and working student/teacher roles rather than a static mockup. Practical Student Utility : Tools like adaptive study scheduling and rubric draft critique solve real, everyday student problems. What we learned WebMCP vs. MCP : For web applications, in-browser execution is fundamentally more secure and accessible than backend daemons for everyday users. Defense-in-Depth in the Browser : Constraining tool inputs with strict JSON schemas and enforcing read-only boundaries protects against indirect prompt injection from untrusted course forums or scraped HTML. Moodle Plugin Internals : Deepened our understanding of Moodle's local plugin architecture, AMD modules, and database hooks. What's next for moodle-webmcp Expanding the number and types of tools available and integrating deeper with Moodle, including: Two-Way Action Tools with Confirmation Gates : Adding safe, human-confirmed write capabilities like save_assignment_draft and post_forum_reply . Discussion Board & Workshop Integration : Extending WebMCP tools to summarize peer reviews and handle complex forum threads. Official Moodle Plugins Directory Release : Packaging local_webmcp for official submission to the Moodle Plugins Directory so LMS administrators worldwide can install it in one click.
