title: AgentReady.js: Instant WebMCP for Every Website
pitch: Turn any website into safe, structured WebMCP tools with a single script tag. Progressive enhancement for AI agents with built-in human-in-the-loop safety.
about_excerpt: Turn any website into safe, structured WebMCP tools with a single script tag. Progressive enhancement for AI agents with built-in human-in-the-loop safety. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Send "Search for Keyboard" in WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector Watch the AgentReady tool calling logs Fill the form using WebMCP Find a product Inspiration The promise of autonomous AI agents browsing the web has collided with a painful reality: modern agent browsing relies heavily on computer vision, screenshot parsing, or dumping massive DOM trees into LLM context windows. This approach is slow, brittle, and expensive. When an agent consumes raw HTML or high-resolution screenshots, the signal-to-noise ratio is dismal: $$\text{Efficiency Ratio} = \frac{\text{Semantic Information}}{\text{Token Overhead}} \ll 1$$ The emerging WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) standard solves this by allowing web applications to declare structured, high-level tools directly to AI clients via document.modelContext. However, expecting developers to rewrite millions of legacy websites and single-page apps (SPAs) with custom WebMCP implementations will take years. We asked ourselves: Why can't existing websites become instantly agent-ready with zero code changes? That question inspired AgentReady.js — a progressive-enhancement JavaScript runtime that extracts semantic meaning from standard HTML and instantly exposes safe, structured WebMCP tools to any AI browser or in-page agent. What it does With a single tag, AgentReady.js transforms any standard web page into an AI-accessible powerhouse: Automatic Semantic Discovery & Synthesis: Scans the DOM tree, analyzes forms, buttons, navigational structures, and accessibility attributes (aria-label, placeholder, label), and automatically derives typed JSON Schema tools (e.g., transforming a search form into search_products({ q, category, max_price })). 7 Core Built-In Primitives: Provides foundational tools including get_page_context, find_on_page, read_target, activate_target, set_field, fill_form, and submit_form. Multi-Platform WebMCP Bridge: Exposes all synthesized and registered tools natively via document.modelContext (and navigator.modelContext), while providing an identical in-page shim (getTools() and executeTool()) so ChatGPT desktop browsers, Chrome 149+, Firefox, and in-page AI companions work seamlessly. Three-Tier Progressive Enhancement: Level 0 (Zero Code): Drop in the script; tools are synthesized automatically. Level 1 (HTML Metadata): Refine tools using declarative data-agent-* attributes. Level 2 (Native Tooling): Register bespoke business logic via window.AgentReady.register({...}). Human-in-the-Loop Safety Engine: Quarantines sensitive fields (passwords, tokens, CVVs, cc-* credit card data) and pauses consequential actions (purchases, deletions, form submissions) with an interactive Approve / Decline panel. How we built it AgentReady.js is crafted with modern TypeScript and Bun for high performance and zero external runtime dependencies: ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Web Browser │ └───────────────────┬────────────────────┘ │ ┌────────────┴────────────┐ │ AgentReady.js │ │ (Zero-dependency Shim) │ └────────────┬────────────┘ │ ┌───────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌───────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐ │ Semantic Analyzer │ │ Safety Policy │ │ Runtime Adapter │ │ • WeakRef Cache │ │ • Regex Redactor │ │ • document. │ │ • Form Synthesis │ │ • Token Budget │ │ modelContext │ │ • MutationObserver│ │ • Approval Dialog │ │ • In-Page Fallback│ └───────────────────┘ └───────────────────┘ └───────────────────┘ Runtime & Adapter Layer (src/runtime.ts): Listens to native engine events, dynamically registers schemas, and manages tool life cycles. When native WebMCP is absent, it seamlessly provides spec-compliant getTools() and executeTool() methods. Semantic Engine & Stable Ref Pool (src/semantic.ts): Indexes interactive elements using WeakRef to eliminate memory leaks. Elements are queried via natural language token matching without mutating the original DOM. Dynamic Resynthesis (src/index.ts): Leverages a debounced MutationObserver (\Delta t \approx 100\text{ms}) to detect route transitions in SPAs and re-synthesize available tools on the fly. Shadow DOM Inspector (src/inspector.ts): An isolated UI widget attached via Shadow DOM with closed encapsulation, preventing CSS collisions with host websites while rendering real-time execution logs and safety confirmation dialogs. Strict Testing Suite: Over 43 automated unit tests run with Bun's test runner, combined with full end-to-end Playwright tests on real Chrome. Challenges we ran into 1. The Dynamic SPA Problem & Memory Leaks Single Page Applications (SPAs) frequently tear down and rebuild DOM subtrees. Storing direct references to DOM nodes caused memory leaks, while relying on static selectors resulted in StaleElementReference failures. Solution: We implemented an ephemeral reference registry backed by JavaScript WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry, pairing fuzzy text queries with structural paths to gracefully recover when elements re-render. 2. Output Budgets and Context Poisoning LLMs can easily be overwhelmed if a tool returns an entire table containing thousands of rows. Solution: We designed a strict output-budget clamp enforcing an upper bound: $$L_{\text{output}} \le 1500 \text{ characters}$$ This truncates large payloads gracefully while informing the agent that additional pagination or targeted querying is required. 3. Divergent Browser Implementations During testing across Chrome 149+ builds and ChatGPT's in-app browser, we encountered differing WebMCP draft implementations (e.g., JSON schema strings vs. parsed schema objects, document.modelContext vs. navigator.modelContext, and register-only environments). We engineered a resilient normalization layer that detects engine quirks and provides a consistent interface across all clients. Accomplishments that we're proud of True Zero-Configuration: Simply adding immediately enables a ChatGPT browser or WebMCP agent to navigate, search, add products to cart, and prepare checkout on a standard e-commerce storefront. Radical Token Reduction: Replacing raw HTML DOM dumps with structured JSON tool schemas achieves up to a 90% reduction in token consumption per interaction turn: $$\text{Token Savings} = 1 - \frac{\text{Tokens} {\text{WebMCP Tool}}}{\text{Tokens} {\text{Raw DOM}}} \approx 85\% - 95\%$$ Zero-Compromise Security: Full proactive redaction of type="password", autocomplete="cc-*", hidden CSRF tokens, and sensitive credential fields ensures agent actions remain transparent and strictly supervised. Lightweight Footprint: The entire runtime bundles into a standalone, minified script under 25 KB with zero third-party dependencies. What we learned Semantic HTML is AI's Best Friend: Modern accessibility primitives (aria-*, label, form method, semantic button labels) already contain almost all the structural metadata needed to synthesize high-quality AI tool definitions. Building for accessibility naturally creates AI-ready applications. Deterministic Tools Beat Autonomous Spelunking: Agents provided with 5–8 high-level, strongly-typed semantic tools consistently outperform agents forced to guess low-level click coordinates or query selectors. Safety Must Be Default, Not Configurable: Autonomous tools that can submit forms or make payments must demand human confirmation at the platform level, making safe behavior the default rather than an afterthought. What's next for AgentReady.js: Instant WebMCP for Every Website Framework Adapters & Components: Native bindings and wrapper components for React, Vue, Svelte, and Next.js for even easier declarative tool mapping. Multi-Modal Spatial Grounding: Integrating semantic bounding box data so agents combining visual and WebMCP modalities can visually correlate tools with UI components. Public CDN & npm Package: Distributing @agentready/core via npm and global CDNs (Cloudflare, cdnjs, unpkg) for one-line deployment across the web. Community Tool Templates: Pre-built semantic profiles for popular web platforms like Shopify, WordPress, WooCommerce, and Webflow to instantly expose rich store and CMS actions out of the box. title: AgentReady
pitch: Your site works for humans. Can an agent finish the job? The WebMCP app that helps devs quickly find out if their site/app is agent ready. If you aren't agent ready, you ain't gonna make it.
about_excerpt: Your site works for humans. Can an agent finish the job? The WebMCP app that helps devs quickly find out if their site/app is agent ready. If you aren't agent ready, you ain't gonna make it. Like Comment Story Updates The WebMCP vision: From Page Chaos to an Agentic Open-door Inspiration Recent discussions online about agentic traffic exceeding human traffic alerted me to the concept that if your site/app isn't agent ready, you ain't gonna make it. I also realized that what's needed during development is a lightweight web app to provide quick check with easy to understand results, and, in line with being agent ready, this app needed to be readily available to one's coding agent. Why WebMCP is the right fit for this use case WebMCP's hardest problem isn't technical — it's adoption. Almost every page an agent visits today declares zero tools. AgentReady attacks that directly, twice over. First, it is a WebMCP app: open it in ChatGPT's browser and the agent discovers audit_site , a declared-and-registered tool that audits any public URL and returns the score, grade, coverage and top finding — human and agent reading the same report on the same page. Second, its output creates more WebMCP : for every audited page, it generates a working tool from that page's own first form — the declarative toolname / tooldescription / toolparamdescription attributes and the document.modelContext.registerTool code with a correct JSON schema — ready to paste. Every WebMCP app improves one site; AgentReady is built to recruit the rest of the web. How it improves the user experience For a site owner, an invisible problem becomes a number in ten seconds, and the number comes with the fix: six evidence-backed checks (discovery, structure, renderability, forms, actionability, WebMCP), a "Do this first" list, copy-paste remediations, and a computed "+N with WebMCP" showing exactly what declaring one tool is worth. For an agent, the site is a first-class user: the audit works as a WebMCP tool call, a plain GET /report?url= (fully server-rendered — the entire report works with JavaScript disabled), or POST /api/audit described by /openapi.json . The report is honest by construction — unobserved evidence never counts against a site, coverage and confidence are always visible, and a blocked fetch yields "no score", never a fake grade. Novel collaborative capabilities The human pastes a URL; the agent calls the same action as a tool; both land on one shared report. In ChatGPT's browser you can ask the agent to audit a site, then expand the findings it summarised and copy the generated stub yourself — a genuine division of labour on a single page. The demo bistro ( /demo ) completes the loop: a reservation form an agent can book through, next to a deliberately gorgeous-but-broken page ( /fixtures/soup , 28/F) that shows what agents face everywhere else. And the tool teaches: what helps agents (labels, landmarks, real buttons, schemas) is what helps assistive technology, so every fix serves both user bases. How it was built Next.js 16 App Router on Vercel, TypeScript, zero database — URL in, report out. A hardened safe-fetch (SSRF-proof: pinned DNS, per-hop robots.txt enforcement, streaming caps) acquires one page plus its discovery sidecars; six pure check modules score it against a published rubric (weights in one file, methodology in /docs and docs/INVARIANTS.md ); a stub generator turns the page's own form into spec-correct WebMCP code ( document.modelContext , plain-value execute returns, the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill@5.1.0 pinned with a verified SRI hash). 348 tests, including an SSRF bypass corpus and a runtime test that executes generated tool code against a real DOM. Built entirely within the submission window — the git history is the timeline — by a human directing a multi-agent AI team with adversarial cross-review on every merge. AgentReady audits itself at 96/A , and the one point category it drops is documented as "we don't run an MCP server, and won't pretend to for points." Accomplishments that I'm proud of This whole thing was done in an afternoon, which is the first time I've essentially one-shot a finished, useful, deployed app in a single day. What I learned Just how crazy easy it is to incorporate WebMCP. Now I'll be making sure to go back into other apps I'm working on and add it. What's next for AgentReady Circulate v1 in some communities I'm part of & get any feedback. Next version should include detection of dynamic WebMCP. title: Meshful
pitch: Learn anything and make it stick. Your AI agent prepares the material and grades answers in your own words, while Meshful schedules each concept for the right time.
about_excerpt: Learn anything and make it stick. Your AI agent prepares the material and grades answers in your own words, while Meshful schedules each concept for the right time. Like Comment Story Updates How Meshful was Born A study system should test your memory, not your patience. Spaced repetition works, but using it can feel like building the course before taking it. You start by deciding what matters and how to organize ideas you do not understand yet. Then you grade yourself. You might reveal the answer before trying to recall it, think “Oh, I knew that!” only after seeing it, or explain the right idea in different words and still doubt yourself. Meshful removes deck setup and self-grading, but you still do the work that makes learning stick. An agent prepares the material and evaluates your answers while you recall each idea, explain it in your own words, and learn from honest feedback. Meshful schedules every review, tracks your progress, shows what comes next, and brings each idea back when it is time to try again. What Meshful does Meshful turns that burden into one clear study loop. Choose a course from the Deck Library or ask an agent to build a custom deck on your topic. For custom decks, the agent draws on its own knowledge and runs Meshful's validator to catch missing definitions, duplicate cards, and broken prerequisite links. The validator checks the deck's structure. It cannot verify every fact. Once the deck is ready, all you have to do is click Study and give each term your best attempt. Study shows you one term without its definition. You explain it in your own words in chat. The agent checks your answer against the card's built-in rubric and rates your recall as Again, Hard, Good, or Easy. Through WebMCP, it sends the grade to Meshful, which saves it and updates your FSRS schedule. Meshful reveals the definition while the agent explains what you got right or missed. Then the next term appears. The agent handles judgment and teaching, so the experience can improve as models improve. The site owns the decks, review history, schedule, progress, and interface. Choose a Deck Library course or have an agent build a custom deck ↓ Click Study ↓ Give your best answer in your own words ↓ The agent grades your recall and sends the grade to Meshful ↓ Meshful saves the grade and updates your FSRS schedule ↓ See the definition and get feedback ↓ Move to the next useful idea ↺ Finish today's reviews or continue with eligible new material Due reviews come first. When they are done, Meshful continues with eligible new material. Ideas you miss return sooner. Strong answers earn longer gaps. As you earn Good or Easy on prerequisite ideas, later ideas open. You move toward mastery without leaving older knowledge behind. How I built Meshful I started with the study loop and worked backward: what must the agent understand, and what must the site make exact? One shared deck model. Every course uses the same structure, whether it comes from the Deck Library or an agent. Each card stores a term, a hidden definition, a grading rubric, and links to the ideas that should come first. This gives learners one consistent study experience instead of a different format for every subject. A learning map, not a pile. The prerequisite links form a map of how the ideas fit together. That map decides which new cards are ready to appear. It solves a different problem from the memory schedule: prerequisites control what you are ready to learn, while FSRS controls when you should review it. FSRS sets the pace. Meshful gives each grade to FSRS, which updates when the card should return. Missed ideas come back sooner, strong answers earn longer gaps, and reviews that are due come before new material. WebMCP closes the loop. The agent reads the active card and its rubric, understands the learner's own words, chooses a grade, and explains the gap. It sends one grade to Meshful through WebMCP. The site checks the active session and card, records one review, runs FSRS once, and moves forward once. WebMCP lets the agent work with the same study state the learner sees while Meshful remains the source of truth. Challenges I ran into 1. Keeping the agent flexible without letting study state drift The problem. Agents are good at understanding the different ways people explain an idea, and that judgment should improve as models improve. A study site has a different job. It must know exactly which card is active, save one grade, update the schedule once, and show the right next step. If those roles blur, a retry or model mistake could create duplicate reviews or conflicting progress. The solution. I split the work at a clear boundary. The agent reads the learner's answer, applies the rubric, explains what was missing, and proposes a grade. Meshful validates and commits every exact change through WebMCP. Why it works. The learning record stays deterministic while the intelligence can keep improving. The boundary leaves room to trade speed for deeper reasoning as agent models improve, without changing the rules of the deck, schedule, or progress. 2. Making generated decks and grading trustworthy The problem. A deck can look complete while hiding a weak definition, a broken prerequisite, or a rubric that grades normal wording unfairly. Free-form grading is just as difficult. A correct answer may use different words, while a confident answer may still miss the key idea. Structural checks alone cannot prove that the content is right or that the grader is fair. The solution. I used deterministic validation to catch missing fields, duplicate cards, and broken references. Then I built small benchmarks with synthetic learner answers that ranged from wrong to partly right to correct in different words. I compared each grade with a frozen reference judgment, reviewed the feedback for mistakes, changed the instructions, and ran the same cases again. Why it works. The validator tests the deck's structure, while the benchmark tests the judgment built on top of it. The current benchmark is small, so it does not yet prove broad accuracy. It does give me a repeatable way to improve performance as I add more subjects, answer styles, and models. Why Meshful matters Meshful matters to me because it turns curiosity into a study system I can act on. A new subject can begin with an honest attempt, useful feedback, and a clear next review instead of hours of setup and uncertain self-grading. As the Deck Library grows and agents improve, the same trusted loop can support more subjects and stronger feedback. Meshful is more than a demo. It is a foundation for making serious study easier to begin, continue, and measure honestly. What's next for Meshful I see two main paths for Meshful. A broader Deck Library. I want to add law, medicine, history, and more advanced courses in the subjects already covered. This would save more people from having to build every deck themselves. I also want to explore deck publishing, so people can easily share what they make while keeping the source and quality of each deck clear. Practice beyond terms. I want to move from recall into questions and problems. Math and coding are learned by doing. The agent could review a solution, explain where the reasoning or code went wrong, and bring back focused practice later. The hard part is adapting an FSRS-like schedule to work with many valid paths and several skills at once. Rather than repeat one problem, Meshful could schedule a problem type and create a fresh version each time. This would bring the same loop of practice, feedback, and well-timed review to richer challenges. title: Move Board
pitch: An agent's property research dies with the chat. Move Board turns it into a board the agent fills and you keep - searching 15.79M UK sold prices, right in your browser.
about_excerpt: An agent's property research dies with the chat. Move Board turns it into a board the agent fills and you keep - searching 15.79M UK sold prices, right in your browser. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Hero Nine tools Board Code About the project Inspiration Deciding where to live in the UK means holding a dozen things in your head at once: what a street actually sold for, whether an area is rising or flattening, what your current place is worth, how far it is from work. The data exists. It is scattered across a dozen tabs and comparable only in a spreadsheet. An AI agent can do that research today and then hands you back a wall of prose. You cannot sort it, cannot pin two candidates side by side, cannot come back to it tomorrow. The research dies with the conversation. What it does Move Board gives an agent nine tools, and they split into two kinds. That split is the whole idea. Four tools look things up in rielty's public property corpus is 15.79M UK sold-price records and 1.96M commute journey times: search_properties , property_details , area_report , estimate_value . Five tools edit the board itself , and have no server behind them at all: add_to_board , remove_from_board , get_board , compare_on_board , annotate_card . A conventional MCP server could serve the first four. Only WebMCP can serve the other five , because they act on a surface the person is looking at, in their browser, in their session. There is nothing to authenticate and no state to sync. Ask, inside ChatGPT's in-app browser: "I'm moving to Yorkshire on a £400k budget, 3 beds minimum - research it and keep the three best on the board, with a note on each." Findings appear as it searches. Cards land on the board only when it decides they are worth keeping. Notes get written onto them explaining why. When it finishes you will have a board and you can drop the one you never liked, and the agent sees your edit next time it calls get_board . How we built it Deliberately boring. No framework, no build step, no dependencies: index.html , styles.css , app.js and one serverless function. Tools are declared as data and registered in one loop: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "add_to_board", description: "Pin a finding to the board so it survives the conversation…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { … }, required: ["card_id"] }, execute: async (input) => { /* mutate the board, re-render, reply */ } }); Every execute() mutates state and re-renders before it resolves, so the human sees the result at the same moment the agent receives it. No polling, no websocket. readOnlyHint is declared per tool rather than inferred from the name - search_properties is not read-only, because it changes what is on screen even though it writes no data. Challenges we ran into The browser cannot call an MCP server directly. We assumed a static page could talk to rielty.co.uk/mcp/v1 and found otherwise: it sends no CORS headers, answers OPTIONS with a 405, and does not expose the mcp-session-id header its own handshake depends on. Hence one serverless function that speaks MCP server-side - initialize , notifications/initialized , tools/call . It allows only the four tools rielty publishes, so it cannot be used as an open relay. A page full of tools looks broken. Our first deploy was correct and felt dead: open it in Safari, or Chrome without the flag, and you get two empty boxes and nothing to click, because there is no agent present. Correct behaviour, indistinguishable from a bug and judges would open it exactly that way. So we added Watch it work and ?demo=1 , which run the same nine tools in the order an agent calls them. Nothing is faked; every card is live data. Saying where the agent actually is. Our copy read "ask your agent something like…" beside a page with no input box. The agent is not in the page - it is whatever is browsing it. That sentence had to be rewritten to teach the model, not just describe the feature. API details that are easy to get wrong. The spec says document.modelContext ; some write-ups say navigator . Chrome 152 has it on document , so we feature-detect both. And executeTool takes the tool object from getTools() plus a JSON string - passing a name throws not of type 'RegisteredTool' , passing an object throws Failed to parse input arguments . Accomplishments that we're proud of The honesty survives the trip to the agent. rielty's corpus is predominantly sold history, not homes for sale, so every card is labelled "Sold record", and estimate_value returns no figure at all where there are too few local sales. The tool descriptions tell the agent to check listing_type before calling anything available. It would have been easy to ship something that quietly implies 15.79M homes are for sale. What we learned WebMCP changes what a page is for. We started thinking of it as a second transport for an API we already had, and finished thinking of the page as a shared workspace - the agent's tools and the human's hands acting on the same DOM. The moment that clicked was writing get_board : an agent has to be able to ask what the person changed, because they are editing the same thing. What's next The same nine tools are already built into rielty's own Phoenix/LiveView app and verified in Chrome, where search_properties runs the page's real typed-search path - so the map pans and the result list repaints as the agent works. That branch is not deployed yet. Beyond it: outbound tools (price alerts, enquiring with an agent) behind an explicit human confirmation step, since an agent reading a property description is reading attacker-controllable text. title: Nagara
pitch: Bengaluru civic reporting where people and WebMCP agents share one visible, actionable map.
about_excerpt: Bengaluru civic reporting where people and WebMCP agents share one visible, actionable map. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Civic failures are experienced locally but reported through fragmented, repetitive workflows. A resident may have the strongest evidence—a photo and a locality—but still needs to identify the issue type, find the correct ward, avoid filing a duplicate, and connect the report to relevant public works. A general browser agent can try to click through that process, but DOM guessing is brittle and makes it hard for the resident to see or trust what changed. WebMCP turns civic reporting from a fragile sequence of inferred clicks into a legible collaboration. People retain judgment and visual confirmation; agents handle structured lookup and repetitive coordination. The result is faster reporting, fewer duplicates, better geographic routing, and a clearer connection between a resident's evidence and the city's published work. What it does Nagara is a public Bengaluru civic-voice map designed as a shared workspace for a person and an agent. The resident supplies context and evidence. A WebMCP-enabled agent discovers the current page's actions, fills the same visible form, classifies the issue, resolves the GBA ward, files or supports a voice, focuses the matching map pin, and retrieves related public records. Human and agent actions use one command layer and one local state model, so the interface never drifts into a hidden agent-only workflow. Key features Route-aware list_ui_actions manifest covering every meaningful control Shared human/agent form with visible field, category, reset, and filing updates Public evidence-photo attachment by URL or human file upload Bengaluru locality or coordinate lookup to a GBA ward and corporation Issue classification across flooding, water, lakes, works, encroachment, footpaths, lights, waste, and other Duplicate-aware voice filing and community support Shared MapLibre pin selection and focus Related civic-record discovery with bundled OpenCity/news data and optional Firecrawl refresh WebMCP readiness indicator and on-page agent activity trail /llms.txt , a public UI-to-tool coverage matrix, and reproducible judge instructions How we built it Nagara exposes 19 structured WebMCP tools on every route. list_ui_actions gives an agent a route-aware manifest of meaningful controls. set_draft , select_category , classify_issue , resolve_ward , use_current_location , and file_voice form a complete filing workflow. focus_voice and support_voice preserve shared follow-up. list_related_tenders , refresh_tenders , and enrich_source connect the selected voice to public information. Each mutation returns explicit stateChanges and updates the visible UI and activity log. The implementation uses JSON Schema enums and URI formats, readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint , titled tools, structured error results, and AbortSignal-based lifecycle cleanup. Unsupported browsers retain the full human workflow. Next.js 16 / React 19 / TypeScript: public application and route handlers WebMCP bridge: lifecycle-safe document.modelContext.registerTool registrations with titled tools and structured schemas Tool registry: 19 descriptors plus route-aware UI mappings and a single execution dispatcher Voice command layer: one command surface used by both React controls and WebMCP tools MapLibre GL: shared geospatial map and focused pins UploadThing: optional public evidence-photo hosting Firecrawl: optional refresh/enrichment of allowlisted civic sources Local-first state: browser persistence keeps the public demo usable without an account or backend setup How we used Codex Codex was used as an engineering partner to inspect the existing Next.js application, fetch the current WebMCP and Next.js documentation, audit every visible interaction, implement the missing semantic tools, refactor the shared state provider for React 19, add lifecycle-safe tool registration, write judge-facing documentation and tests, and exercise the resulting tools from the Codex in-app browser. The browser verification caught an intentional-unregistration promise rejection that ordinary unit tests did not; the registration wrapper was then fixed and rechecked against a production build with a clean browser console. Testing instructions Open https://nagara-webmcp.vercel.app/create in ChatGPT's or Codex's in-app browser. Confirm the page displays WebMCP ready . Call list_ui_actions ; it should return 10 mapped interaction groups for /create . Call get_workspace_state to inspect the same selected voice and form visible on screen. Call set_draft with areaName: "HSR Layout" , a factual title , a short body , and any public image URL in photoUrl . Watch the form fill. Call select_category { "category": "flooding" } , then resolve_ward { "areaName": "HSR Layout" } . Call file_voice . A new pin should appear, become selected, and show a timeline and related records. Call focus_voice or support_voice with a returned voice ID. The same visible pin/rail should update. Call clear_draft ; the visible filing form should reset. No account or credentials are required. Optional live UploadThing and Firecrawl paths have bundled/local fallbacks, so the core WebMCP demo remains judge-testable. Product screenshots Bengaluru landing experience Shared civic overview Filing workspace, live map, and public records Known limitations and next steps Voice data persists in the current browser rather than a shared production database Ward lookup is a focused demo dataset of Bengaluru localities, not a complete authoritative city GIS Live UploadThing and Firecrawl behavior depends on deployment credentials; core filing and bundled records continue to work without them get_link_target returns external URLs for deliberate agent navigation instead of forcing a popup or navigating away from the active tool context Next we would add a shared production database, expand ward resolution against authoritative Bengaluru GIS data, provide moderation and provenance workflows for evidence, and deepen civic-record matching across budgets, tenders, work orders, and service-level commitments. title: ONE
pitch: An open lab where humans and agents build, test, and improve voice AI together.
about_excerpt: An open lab where humans and agents build, test, and improve voice AI together. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Make it YOU Inspiration Voice AI demos can feel magical. Then someone interrupts, stays silent, speaks over background noise, reaches voicemail, or loses their connection, and that magic can disappear. After years of helping organizations turn APIs and SDKs into dependable customer experiences, I became fascinated by the gap between an impressive voice demo and a system people can genuinely trust. Building voice AI meant navigating fragmented providers, hidden events, incompatible interfaces, unpredictable costs, sensitive credentials, and failures that were difficult to reproduce. I started ONE as a local learning lab where I could see the entire system working: authentication, payloads, transcripts, realtime events, latency, interruptions, recovery behavior, and the connection between an audio interaction and its intended human outcome. As I explored more providers, a larger problem became clear. Creators are often asked to choose a platform before they have enough evidence to know whether it fits their needs. Provider comparisons tend to flatten everything into leaderboards, even though the best combination depends on language, latency, privacy, accessibility, geography, budget, and the experience being created. ONE grew from a personal voice AI lab into a larger mission: give humans and agents an open place to understand the ecosystem, test it honestly, and assemble the combination that works best for them without surrendering control to a single vendor. What it does ONE is an open, provider-neutral lab for learning, building, testing, and improving voice AI. The lab makes normally hidden system behavior visible, including: Realtime conversation states and event timelines Speech-to-text, reasoning, text-to-speech, and transport layers Interruptions, crosstalk, silence, latency, voicemail, and reconnect behavior Controlled failures, fallback paths, and recovery decisions Provider capabilities and implementation status Structured evaluation evidence Authentication and payload construction Explicit execution and provider-spend controls Reusable voice-agent architecture patterns For the WebMCP experience, ONE exposes a focused workflow through four structured tools: list_voice_scenarios configure_voice_replay start_deterministic_replay get_replay_evidence A person can ask their agent to test how a voice system handles an interruption or lost connection. The agent can discover the available scenarios, configure a deterministic replay, request execution, and retrieve the resulting evidence without guessing where to click. The browser remains the shared workspace. Configuration changes appear visibly in ONE, consequential actions require confirmation, the test unfolds through the interface, and the resulting timeline and scorecard remain available for human review. The agent handles repetitive discovery, configuration, and evidence gathering. The person retains intent, judgment, approval, and the final decision. How we built it ONE began as a local React-based voice lab and evolved into a modular system with provider adapters, realtime inspection tools, deterministic scenarios, evidence capture, and an extensive browser regression suite. The most important architectural decision was creating one capability layer shared by the human interface and WebMCP. The agent does not operate a hidden copy of ONE or maintain a separate version of its state. WebMCP invokes the same capabilities, updates the same interface, and produces the same evidence that a person sees. The collaboration loop works like this: The person defines the goal and constraints. The agent discovers an appropriate test. The agent configures the scenario. ONE makes the proposed configuration visible. The person approves execution when required. The replay runs inside the shared interface. The agent retrieves and helps interpret the evidence. The person decides what to investigate next. I built deterministic local replay so reliability failures can be reproduced without requiring a live provider call or spending API credits. Live, simulated, experimental, and proposed capabilities are labeled separately so ONE never implies that something is operational when it is not. Provider credentials remain server-side, while execution gates prevent a browser agent from silently initiating billable activity. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was not teaching an agent how to operate ONE. It was deciding what the agent should be allowed to do, what must remain under human control, and how every action could be inspected afterward. Realtime voice is also inherently difficult to test. Network conditions, timing, microphones, background noise, provider behavior, and human speech can all change the result. Deterministic replay became the bridge between realistic failure scenarios and repeatable evidence. Another challenge was translating a complex laboratory into a small set of meaningful WebMCP tools. Exposing every button would only recreate the interface as an API. I instead designed tools around complete intentions: discover a scenario, configure it, run it, and inspect what happened. ONE also began as a substantial local project rather than a challenge-sized prototype. Preparing it for the web required disciplined scope, deployment hardening, browser validation, security boundaries, and careful separation between what is truly implemented and what remains part of the roadmap. Accomplishments that we're proud of ONE grew from a provider-specific learning experiment into a provider-neutral system for studying the complete voice AI stack. I am especially proud of: Building deterministic reliability scenarios for interruption, crosstalk, silence, latency, reconnects, and other real-world conditions Creating a zero-provider-spend path for testing system behavior safely Making agent execution visible instead of allowing agents to act silently Preserving explicit human confirmation before consequential or billable actions Separating live, adapter-backed, experimental, simulated, and proposed capabilities Producing structured timelines and evidence instead of relying only on subjective impressions Building a shared capability layer that serves both the human interface and WebMCP Growing an extensive automated regression suite around a fast-moving experimental project Building this as an independent creator while keeping the architecture open to an entire ecosystem The accomplishment I value most is that ONE does not treat human control as friction. Human judgment is part of the architecture. What we learned The biggest lesson is that voice quality is not a single model score. It is an end-to-end property of the system, including timing, turn-taking, transport, recovery, observability, permissions, cost, and human expectations. I also learned that provider neutrality requires more than displaying several logos. It requires consistent capability descriptions, honest implementation states, comparable evidence, provenance, and the freedom to combine services rather than accept an entire bundled stack. Agent-native design is not simply automation. An effective agent needs structured capabilities, but a trustworthy agent also needs bounded authority, shared state, visible history, and clear moments of human approval. WebMCP creates that relationship inside the web experience. The agent does not replace the interface or move the work into an invisible backend. The person, page, and agent remain together. Finally, I learned that hosted access and local sovereignty are not opposing ideas. The web can support discovery, education, and collaboration, while local execution can preserve privacy, resilience, portability, and user control. What's next for ONE Almost everything. The long-term vision is for ONE to include every meaningful provider across the voice AI ecosystem: speech recognition, speech generation, speech-to-speech models, language models, telephony, orchestration, evaluation, translation, accessibility, observability, and supporting infrastructure. The goal is not to identify one universal winner. It is to let any human or agent assemble the right system for a particular need and budget. Someone might choose one provider for transcription, another for reasoning, another for voice, another for telephone transport, and a separate evaluation layer to verify the result. Another creator might prioritize local processing, a specific language, low latency, accessibility, regional data handling, or the lowest sustainable cost. ONE should help both of them construct an evidence-backed stack. Agents will help people navigate this growing ecosystem by translating human requirements into testable configurations. They will compare current capabilities, identify missing evidence, run approved experiments, explain tradeoffs, and help assemble portable blueprints. People will remain res

title: Pokefinder.app WebMCP
pitch: Pokémon cards scattered across stores and priced differently. We built the agent-driven marketplace that turns 30min of tab-switching into a 30sec conversation: search, compare, buy, all by asking.
about_excerpt: Pokémon cards scattered across stores and priced differently. We built the agent-driven marketplace that turns 30min of tab-switching into a 30sec conversation: search, compare, buy, all by asking. Like 4 Comment 2 Story Updates Adding card to a basket Getting card details Listing top 10 Pokemon sets Analyzing card image and identifying card by its image Inspiration PokéFinder started because my son wanted to track down a few rare Pokémon cards. We tried eBay first and quickly ran into the usual problems: noisy listings, inconsistent naming, and the same card priced differently across a dozen stores. So we built PokeFinder.App to make the search easier. It brings live listings from Shopify Catalog together in one structured place through UCP, then enriches them with set, rarity, and grading data from the Pokémon TCG API. When the WebMCP Challenge was announced, the idea immediately made sense to us. The hard part of buying Pokémon cards is not simply finding listings. It is knowing enough about the hobby to make sense of them: holo versus reverse holo, set codes, grading, and which cards were released last week. An LLM can close that knowledge gap, but only if it can do more than answer questions in a chat window. It needs to work with the page alongside the user. That is what made WebMCP so interesting to us: it turns “AI can help you shop” into “AI can shop with you.” Whether someone is a lifelong collector or a complete beginner, the experience can meet them where they are. What it does PokéFinder is a single-page marketplace where humans and AI agents shop the same catalog side-by-side. A user can browse trending cards or every connected store, search by card name, set, or rarity, snap a photo and let AI identify it, filter by country, currency, price, or grading, compare prices across stores, save cards to a wishlist, sign in with magic link or Google or Discord or Shopify, and check out. An AI agent can do all of the same things by driving the page directly. PokéFinder registers thirteen tools through WebMCP. They split into three categories: Data queries (also exposed via MCP for external agents): search_pokemon_cards —> search the live catalog across every connected store browse_card_database —> browse all cards with full pagination get_card_details —> fetch the full detail page for a specific card list_sets —> list every Pokémon card set currently in the catalog find_cards_in_set —> find all cards within a specific set get_filter_taxonomy —> return the filter fields with brief explanations for non-experts get_featured_cards —> return the curated featured / trending cards compare_prices —> compare prices for the same card across every connected store Image / AI (also exposed via MCP): analyze_card_image —> extract set, rarity, grading, and condition from a card photo identify_card_image —> identify the card from a photo, then return matching listings Page actions (WebMCP-unique, these are what the agent-driven web unlocks): highlight_card —> light up a specific card on the live page so the user sees exactly which one was selected apply_filter —> filter the visible grid by price, country, rarity, or grading add_to_basket —> add a chosen card to the cart The data and image tools give the agent everything it needs to reason about the catalog. The page-action tools give it the ability to drive what the user actually sees. How we built it We started with the PokéFinder backend we had already built: a Cloudflare Worker in front of the UCP catalog, plus a D1 mirror of the Pokémon TCG database for metadata enrichment. That foundation already gave us a strong search experience. The WebMCP layer was the new part. We registered the same tool set through WebMCP for in-browser agents and through MCP for external agents such as ChatGPT, Claude, and custom MCP clients. The tools keep the same names and arguments on both surfaces, and they share the same underlying backend logic. Through WebMCP, however, the browser-facing tools can also update the page the user is looking at. That distinction became central to the project. A catalog search can return the same listings through MCP or WebMCP. But with WebMCP, the agent can also highlight its recommendation, apply the requested filters in real time, and add the chosen card to the basket. MCP gives the agent data; WebMCP lets the agent use that data with the user on the live page. One part of the build that we particularly enjoyed was resurfacing capabilities we already had. The server already knew how to search the catalog. We exposed that same capability through WebMCP, then connected it to the result grid so the agent could work with actual items on the page instead of returning a block of text. We used the same approach for filtering and highlighting. We only added a page action where changing the page genuinely helped the user. Our stack is Cloudflare Workers, D1 for the Pokémon TCG mirror, KV for search caching, Workers AI with Llama 3.2 11B Vision for image identification, and the UCP catalog endpoint. The frontend is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was making the tools feel like a natural part of the page. WebMCP is not just a chatbot sitting beside a website; the agent needs to interact with the experience itself. The hardest design decision was deciding what should be a data query and what should be a page action. The rule we eventually settled on was simple: if the agent needs the result to reason, it is a data tool. If the action changes what the user sees or does on the page, it is a WebMCP page action. Turning backend results into page actions A search endpoint normally returns a JSON list. On the page, that list also needs to be rendered in a way the agent can work with. We built a thin layer that gives each result a stable ID. Follow-up actions such as highlighting a card or adding it to the basket can then target the exact item the user and agent are discussing. Making image identification reliable The vision model sometimes produced a confident but incorrect identification when the photo was low resolution. Instead of pretending that uncertainty did not exist, we added a confirmation step so the user can correct the result before the Worker searches for listings. What began as a reliability problem ended up becoming a useful part of the experience. Keeping the experience fast Browser-side tool calls introduce a network round trip. When an agent makes five calls in sequence, the delay adds up even if every individual call is reasonably fast. We cached aggressively and pre-rendered what we could so the experience would still feel responsive. Accomplishments that we're proud of Thirteen WebMCP tools now cover the full catalog journey, including search, comparison, image identification, filtering, highlighting, and adding to the basket. The same underlying capabilities are also available to external agents through MCP. A discovery-to-purchase journey that once meant opening ten browser tabs can now happen in one conversation in around 30 seconds rather than 30 minutes. We tested PokéFinder with people who knew very little about Pokémon TCG, including some very patient family members. They could find specific cards simply by describing what they wanted in plain English. The interaction becomes more useful as the agent learns what the person is actually trying to find. That makes the hobby much more approachable for beginners without getting in the way of experienced collectors. The image search works as a real shopping tool: take a photo of a card and get matching listings from every connected store. What we learned The page actions are what make WebMCP feel genuinely different. Highlighting, filtering, and adding to the basket turn an agent from something that gives advice into something that can work alongside the user. Resurfacing is a powerful pattern. Many useful agent actions do not require a completely new backend feature; they require an existing capability to be exposed with a stable, UI-addressable ID. Latency compounds quickly. Caching and pre-rendering matter just as much for a WebMCP experience as they do for any other real-time interface. When an LLM can work directly with the page, conversational clarity becomes part of the UX. Some of our best improvements came from simplifying the interface and letting the agent handle the complexity. Context makes the experience accessible. The agent can explain unfamiliar terms and narrow the catalog at the same time, which helps beginners shop with much more confidence. What's next for Pokefinder.app WebMCP More agent surfaces. Today, WebMCP connects to ChatGPT in the browser. We would love to see first-class integrations with tools such as Cursor, Claude, and Comet. Built-in chat. We want to add a “search with AI” experience directly to the site so people without a separate AI assistant can shop in the same way. Promoted placements through UCP. When the Shopify program

title: RocketTurtle
pitch: RocketTurtle gives coding agents focused repository context through WebMCP, helping them understand, locate, inspect, check, and verify changes before they edit code.
about_excerpt: RocketTurtle gives coding agents focused repository context through WebMCP, helping them understand, locate, inspect, check, and verify changes before they edit code. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am a business student, not a traditional software engineer. For the last two years, I have been following AI and AI agents out of curiosity. As I started building things myself, I kept running into the same thing: almost everything eventually exists in the form of a repository. AI can write 1,000 lines of code in the next five minutes. But before changing an existing open-source project, a human still needs answers to much simpler questions: Where do I begin? Which files and folders matter? Which files are safe to inspect first? Which file is responsible for the exact function that I want to change? What can break if I touch it? That is where RocketTurtle was born. It started with an MVP and my own brainstorming sessions. I wanted to paste a public GitHub repository into a simple application and get a useful map of what was actually inside it. I built the first version of RocketTurtle around that idea: help someone understand an unfamiliar repository before they start changing it. Then I wanted to improve it. Around that time, I found the Devpost WebMCP Hackathon and started learning what WebMCP actually was. That immediately made the original RocketTurtle idea more interesting. RocketTurtle already reduced how much of a repository a human needed to inspect. With WebMCP, I realized that the same idea can apply to an agent . Why must a coding agent read an entire repository before it can understand where to work? That question became the basis of the WebMCP version of RocketTurtle. What It Does RocketTurtle is a repository understanding layer for humans and AI agents. For the WebMCP extension, I went back to first principles and asked: If an agent is about to work inside an unfamiliar repository, what does it need to know before it writes code? That produced five steps: Understand → Locate → Inspect → Check → Verify Those five steps became five WebMCP tools. 1. analyze_repository — Understand Before anything else, the agent needs a map. This tool analyzes the repository structure, technologies, complexity, important files, risks, and supporting evidence. 2. map_change_surface — Locate Understanding the repository is not enough. If the goal is to change authentication, fix a feature, or update some behavior, the agent needs to know which parts of the repository are likely connected to that goal. This tool maps the requested change to likely relevant files and risky areas. 3. inspect_file_context — Inspect After finding a likely file, the agent needs focused information about that file. This tool inspects one selected text file and returns useful structural context without requiring the agent to explore the complete repository first. 4. validate_change_plan — Check Before an agent edits code, it can explain what it plans to change. RocketTurtle checks that plan against the available repository context and identifies risks or missing evidence. RocketTurtle does not make the code change. The coding agent remains responsible for the code. 5. get_verification_context — Verify Finally, the agent needs to know how the repository expects changes to be tested. This tool finds existing tests, scripts, build commands, lint commands, CI signals, and other useful verification context. Together, the five tools create one workflow: Understand → Locate → Inspect → Check → Verify The user provides the goal. RocketTurtle provides focused repository context. The coding agent uses that context before it acts. How I Built It I extended the existing RocketTurtle MVP instead of creating a separate application for the hackathon. The WebMCP layer reuses RocketTurtle's existing: GitHub access logic Repository analyzer Types API routes Vercel deployment I then added the logic required for the five WebMCP tools. Each tool has: A clear tool name A defined input schema An execution function Structured output Error handling Input and output boundaries The browser exposes these tools through document.modelContext , which lets a WebMCP-capable client discover and invoke RocketTurtle's repository tools. I kept one boundary throughout the project: RocketTurtle understands and checks. The coding agent writes the code. RocketTurtle does not: Generate code Edit repository files Create pull requests Replace the coding agent It gives the agent focused repository context before the agent starts changing code. Challenges I Faced One of the hardest problems was deciding how much repository information each tool must return. If RocketTurtle returns the entire repository, it defeats the purpose. If it returns too little information, the agent cannot make a useful decision. I had to design each tool around one specific question in the agent's workflow. Another major challenge was safety. Repository content is untrusted input. The WebMCP layer therefore needed boundaries around: Repository access File paths File types File sizes Tool inputs Tool outputs Testing also became much more important than I initially expected. Seeing five registered tools in a browser was not enough. I tested cases such as: Valid inputs Invalid inputs Missing repositories Missing files Unsupported files Large inputs Tool output limits Tool cleanup behavior The complete five-tool workflow I also had to make these changes without breaking the existing RocketTurtle application. That forced me to keep the WebMCP extension focused instead of redesigning the entire product around the hackathon. What I Learned The biggest thing I learned is that giving an AI agent more context is not always the answer. A better question is: What is the minimum useful context that the agent needs for its next decision? That idea now defines how I think about RocketTurtle. AI can generate code extremely quickly. But before generation comes understanding. An agent still needs to know: What already exists? Where does the relevant functionality live? What files are connected? What can break? Does the proposed plan make sense? How does this repository verify a change? WebMCP gave me a way to turn those questions into tools that an agent can call directly. I also learned that building a useful agent tool involves much more than exposing a function. The input boundaries, output limits, untrusted content, error handling, cleanup behavior, testing, and evidence all matter when another agent depends on that tool. What's Next The current RocketTurtle WebMCP implementation focuses on public GitHub repositories and one clear five-step workflow: Understand → Locate → Inspect → Check → Verify The next goal is not to make RocketTurtle another coding agent. I want to improve the quality and precision of the repository context that RocketTurtle provides while keeping the same separation of responsibilities. The original RocketTurtle MVP helped a human understand a repository . WebMCP gave me a way to extend that same idea to AI agents . And that is the direction I want RocketTurtle to continue exploring: Let RocketTurtle understand the repository. Let the coding agent write the code. Accomplishments That I'm Proud Of The accomplishment I am most proud of is that RocketTurtle started as my own question, not as a hackathon idea. I am a business student who became curious about AI and agents. I went from trying to understand repositories myself to building a tool that can help both humans and agents understand them. I am especially proud that: I took RocketTurtle from an MVP to a working WebMCP implementation. I designed the five WebMCP tools from first principles instead of adding unrelated features. I kept one clear workflow: Understand → Locate → Inspect → Check → Verify . I made all five tools work together against real public GitHub repositories. I tested the tools with a real WebMCP-capable browser instead of relying only on local tests. I kept the original RocketTurtle application working while adding the WebMCP layer. I learned enough about WebMCP to turn an existing idea into something that an AI agent can directly use. Most importantly, I built something that I personally wanted when I first started exploring unfamiliar repositories. That feels like the best accomplishment of the project. title: AdapTab
pitch: Inject prebuilt WebMCP adapters to turn any website into an agent-native interface. Use your existing browser session. Create your own, too.
about_excerpt: Inject prebuilt WebMCP adapters to turn any website into an agent-native interface. Use your existing browser session. Create your own, too. Like Comment Story Updates AdapTab WebMCP for every tab AdapTab comparison with standard web use GIF AdapTab mechanism animation AdapTab architecture Inspiration We have been building browser automation tools and skills for faster, cheaper agentic web use. Our previous open-source project, Showrun, taught us that known network requests executed inside an authenticated browser are often faster and more reliable than visual UI automation. While experimenting with WebMCP, I noticed that most websites do not support it. This is especially limiting for authenticated and legacy platforms, where agents must repeatedly inspect and navigate the interface. Even when a website provides MCP or WebMCP tools, users may still need operations the official tools do not expose. Based on these lessons, I built AdapTab from scratch for this hackathon. What it does AdapTab turns network-first knowledge and deterministic methods into injectable WebMCP adapters. It uses the browser session the user already trusts, reducing navigation, token usage, and execution time. It is expandable, configurable, and requires no per-site setup. The user gives their agent one bootstrap URL. AdapTab then: resolves the target website, route, and task. selects the smallest compatible public or private adapter. returns a versioned installer with origin checks and a SHA-256 hash. uses an approved browser bridge, currently Chrome CDP, to inject it. registers the adapter as native WebMCP tools on the target page. executes known requests inside the authenticated tab without exporting credentials. The current catalog contains a small set of demonstration adapters. AdapTab also provides a private workspace for personal, internal, or custom tools. Custom source is encrypted in the browser, and the key remains in that browser profile. If no adapter matches, the agent can submit a privacy-minimized request to the AdapTab backlog. This helps us and the community decide what to build next. How I built it I initially explored a browser extension, but it added installation and permission overhead. Live JavaScript injection through Chrome CDP worked without an extension, so I focused AdapTab on providing the adapters, metadata, and activation instructions. AdapTab separates three trust boundaries: Netlify selects and delivers adapter metadata and bundles. An approved browser bridge injects the adapter into the target tab. The injected runtime registers WebMCP tools and uses the page's existing session. I built it with TypeScript, React, Vite, and Netlify. Netlify Functions handle resolution and delivery, Netlify Blobs stores private records and requests, and Netlify Identity provides authentication. Private source is encrypted with AES-GCM through the Web Crypto API. Adapters are route-aware, versioned, origin-guarded, and integrity-addressed. Vitest covers resolution, security boundaries, private access, lifecycle behavior, and adapter execution. Challenges I ran into WebMCP tools belong to the current document, so refreshes and full navigations remove injected tools. AdapTab currently handles this through lazy reinjection. A hosted page cannot inject into another origin directly. An approved browser bridge such as CDP must perform that step. Authenticated platforms required keeping sessions inside the page while safely handling confirmation and ambiguous writes. Combining public and private discovery required strict owner checks without leaking private metadata or source. The biggest optimization came from small details: a lightweight agent bootstrap, explicit single-tab instructions, and guidance that tells agents to use injected requests instead of opening unnecessary pages. Accomplishments that I'm proud of In one LinkedIn test involving four profiles, AdapTab used about 70% fewer tokens and completed the workflow 1.8x faster than standard agent web use. The multi-step adapter performed better than having the agent discover and coordinate every operation independently. One bootstrap URL replaced per-site installation and setup. Public and private adapters work through the same discovery flow without exporting website credentials. Private custom source stays encrypted outside the user's browser. The project ships with six tested adapters and 69 passing automated tests. What I learned WebMCP and CDP solve different parts of the problem. WebMCP provides typed discovery and invocation, while CDP provides the privileged injection and lifecycle bridge. Together, they can bring WebMCP to existing websites without requiring those sites to modify their code. Page-context execution is also a useful authentication boundary. The browser remains the cookie jar, and AdapTab never needs the user's website credentials. Deterministic network requests reduce navigation, token consumption, and execution time. Tool descriptions alone are not enough, though. Adapters should also declare tab strategy, URL behavior, concurrency, side effects, and the reasons for any limits. What's next for AdapTab A CDP supervisor engine for automatic reinjection after navigation A browser extension for environments without a CDP bridge An adaptab-author workflow and community contribution system Shareable links for public or private adapters Team workspaces for sharing internal workflows More private templates and workspace controls Native WebMCP conflict detection A general multi-step workflow engine Privacy-preserving analytics for adapter and website developers Shareable adapters could let someone turn a successful browser workflow into a WebMCP tool and send it to a teammate's agent with one link. title: AetherDraw
pitch: An agent-native infinite whiteboard that turns visual canvases into structured spatial playgrounds for autonomous AI agents via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An agent-native infinite whiteboard that turns visual canvases into structured spatial playgrounds for autonomous AI agents via WebMCP. Like 2 Comment Story Updates One-shot AI Inference Pipeline generated via create_diagram with automated Dagre layout, smooth cubic Bezier routing. Bi-directional co-creation: Agent detects human-drawn Auth Service and routes a smart Bezier connector from API Gateway in 1ms. WebMCP Inspector drawer displaying all 11 registered browser tools, JSON parameter schemas, and real-time execution telemetry. Console inspecting document.modelContext.getTools(), exposing typed WebMCP tool definitions directly to AI agents. Autonomous diagram synthesis running directly inside the browser runtime via native WebMCP tool invocation. Full AI inference architecture on infinite canvas with responsive camera auto-framing and zero shape collisions. Spatial introspection via get_canvas_state followed by instant atomic connector routing using connect_elements. One-click visual styling: apply_theme restyles the entire canvas into the handcrafted Nordic Frost color palette. Hierarchical Microservices Architecture template with multi-tier services and obstacle-avoiding edge routing. Public open-source repository on GitHub (ShreyashChaurasia/AetherDraw) with full source code, MIT license, and tests. In-app architecture modal detailing the 4-layer WebMCP tool suite, W3C protocol integration, and Excalidraw attribution. Project Story: AetherDraw Inspiration Visual whiteboards like Excalidraw, Miro, and FigJam are the ultimate playground for human thinking. Whenever I need to design a backend architecture, trace a data pipeline, or brainstorm an idea, I immediately open a blank canvas. Spatial thinking feels natural to humans because our brains process relationships, hierarchies, and groupings through physical distance and layout. However, for AI agents, these visual canvases have always been a complete black box. Today, if you want an AI model to interact with a spatial whiteboard, you are forced into one of two terrible compromises: The Vision Approach: Taking screenshots, feeding them into a multimodal LLM, and hoping the model can approximate pixel coordinates. This is slow (taking several seconds per step), costly, and prone to severe spatial hallucinations. The Brittle Automation Approach: Simulating fragile mouse drag-and-drop events on raw HTML5 <canvas> elements that easily break whenever the viewport pans, zooms, or resizes. When I saw the WebMCP specification, the lightbulb turned on. WebMCP provides the exact missing bridge: instead of forcing AI agents to squint at canvas pixels from the outside, the web application can expose its internal scene AST, geometric bounds, and layout engines directly to the browser runtime via document.modelContext . I wanted to build a whiteboard where AI agents and humans collaborate as equals: an agent-native infinite canvas where an AI can read, build, style, and route complex diagrams in single-digit milliseconds with deterministic precision. That is why I built AetherDraw. What It Does AetherDraw is an open-source, agent-native infinite whiteboard powered by WebMCP. It extends Excalidraw core with a suite of 11 schema-typed tools organized into four functional layers: Spatial Inspection (Layer A): get_canvas_state , get_selected_elements , and find_elements serialize the visual canvas into a structured abstract syntax tree (AST). The agent receives bounding boxes, node types, text labels, and connection graphs without needing a single pixel screenshot. Algorithmic Synthesis (Layer B): create_diagram takes high-level intent (nodes, roles, connections, title, and direction) and executes automated graph layout in a single call, dynamically framing the result to the viewport. Fine-Grained Mutation (Layer C): add_elements , update_elements , delete_elements , and connect_elements allow agents to perform atomic edits, relabel nodes, modify styles, and route smooth Bezier arrows that snap to human-drawn shapes. Layout & Styling (Layer D): apply_auto_layout reorganizes messy hand-drawn clusters into clean hierarchical structures; apply_theme transforms palettes across 7 themes (Classic, Nordic Frost, Cyberpunk Neon, Pastel Dream, Blueprint, Minimal Dark, Solarized); and export_canvas creates high-res PNG or SVG artifacts. Crucially, AetherDraw enables bi-directional co-creation . A human can sketch a couple of boxes and type "Auth Service". The agent calls get_canvas_state , detects the human's shapes, understands where they sit in space, and uses connect_elements to hook up the rest of the backend architecture seamlessly. How I Built It I built AetherDraw as a solo developer using React 19, TypeScript 5, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. 1. Canvas Engine Foundation I chose Excalidraw core ( @excalidraw/excalidraw ) because it represents the gold standard of hand-drawn collaborative canvases. However, Excalidraw was built strictly for human input. To make it agent-native, I wrapped the imperative canvas API with an adapter layer that tracks non-deleted scene elements, manages selection state, and coordinates camera zoom. 2. WebMCP Protocol Implementation I integrated @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill to register all 11 tools directly on document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool defines a strict JSON Schema for its parameters, validates inputs, and reports structured telemetry. In addition to the runtime polyfill, I published a static discovery manifest at /webmcp.json following the official WebMCP specification. 3. Automated Graph Layout Theory Rather than asking the AI model to guess coordinates, AetherDraw uses battle-tested layout algorithms: Dagre (Sugiyama Hierarchical DAG Method): Computes vertex layers, minimizes edge crossings, and assigns discrete ranks. ELK.js (Eclipse Layout Kernel): Handles orthogonal graph layouts and complex topologies. The agent simply specifies the relational graph $G = (V, E)$. The layout engine solves the layering and coordinate assignment in $O(|V| + |E|)$ time, placing each node $v_i \in V$ at an optimal coordinate $(x_i, y_i)$ with zero shape collisions. 4. Organic Cubic Bezier Arrow Routing Connecting boxes with straight lines looks messy and cuts across neighboring elements. I wrote a dedicated router that calculates smooth cubic Bezier curves: $$B(t) = (1-t)^3 P_0 + 3(1-t)^2 t P_1 + 3(1-t) t^2 P_2 + t^3 P_3, \quad t \in [0, 1]$$ Where: $P_0 = (x_{\text{start}}, y_{\text{start}})$ is the anchor point on the source shape. $P_3 = (x_{\text{end}}, y_{\text{end}})$ is the anchor point on the target shape. $P_1$ and $P_2$ are dynamically computed control points offset along the primary flow axis. The router detects intervening obstacle nodes within the direct corridor. If an obstacle exists, the route dynamically diverts through outer gutter channels to avoid line crossings. For horizontal peer nodes sitting side-by-side, it routes directly from the right border of the source to the left border of the target without piercing the shape boundary. 5. Viewport Fit-Screen Mathematics When generating large diagrams, placing shapes off-screen ruins the user experience. I implemented a dynamic framing calculation that computes the total bounding rectangle of all diagram nodes: $$x_{\min} = \min_{i} (x_i), \quad x_{\max} = \max_{i} (x_i + w_i)$$ $$y_{\min} = \min_{i} (y_i), \quad y_{\max} = \max_{i} (y_i + h_i)$$ Given available viewport dimensions $W_{\text{avail}} = W_{\text{window}} - 2 \cdot \text{pad} x$ and $H {\text{avail}} = H_{\text{window}} - 2 \cdot \text{pad}_y$, the camera zoom factor $z$ is computed as: $$z = \text{clamp}\left(\min\left(\frac{W_{\text{avail}}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}, \frac{H_{\text{avail}}}{y_{\max} - y_{\min}}\right), z_{\min}, 1.0\right)$$ The canvas camera pans directly to the center coordinates: $$(x_{\text{center}}, y_{\text{center}}) = \left(\frac{x_{\min} + x_{\max}}{2}, \frac{y_{\min} + y_{\max}}{2}\right)$$ This ensures the entire diagram immediately fills the screen at crisp resolution with proper toolbar clearance. 6. Developer Telemetry & Inspector To make WebMCP observable, I built a slide-out Inspector drawer that lists all registered tool schemas, streams live invocation events, and displays execution duration timers down to the millisecond. Challenges I Faced Imperative Canvas State vs. Asynchronous Tool Calls: Excalidraw maintains its own internal React reconciliation cycles, selection maps, and rendering loops. Bridging asynchronous WebMCP tool executions into Excalidraw's imperative API required careful synchronization so that rapid sequential tool calls wouldn't cause state tears or canvas flickering. Smart Arrow Routing without Box Penetration: Early prototypes had arrows that routed straight through boxes or connected to the far side of target nodes. Writing the horizontal peer detection logic and obstacle corridors required extensive coordinate geometry and edge-case testing, especially ensuring that arrowheads snap flush

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation.
