title: Nepal Disaster Watch
pitch: Synthesizing 6 public crisis feeds with the help of 11 WebMCP tools so AI and responders uncover hidden disaster reporting gaps.
about_excerpt: Synthesizing 6 public crisis feeds with the help of 11 WebMCP tools so AI and responders uncover hidden disaster reporting gaps. Like Comment Story Updates Nepal Disaster Watch Inspiration On August 26, a devastating flood tore through Nepal's Bhote Koshi river system, sweeping water, mud, and debris through Rasuwa and downstream communities. I wasn't thinking about hackathons that night I was refreshing tab after tab at 2am, trying to find out if people I knew were okay. That's when the second gut-punch hit: I couldn't even get a straight answer. Incident reports lived on one government portal, river levels on another, road closures on a third, flood forecasts and satellite damage assessments somewhere else entirely each written for a different audience, none of them talking to each other. Every empty page made me more anxious, because I couldn't tell if "no data" meant "nothing happened" or "the power's out and nobody can report anything." That fear of mistaking silence for safety is the whole reason Nepal Disaster Watch exists. What it Does Nepal Disaster Watch is a live emergency-intelligence platform covering all 77 districts of Nepal. It pulls together six public data sources government incident reports, river gauges, road closures, disaster alerts, flood forecasts, and field or satellite damage assessments into one consistent, constantly refreshing picture. It isn't just a dashboard. It's built with 11 native WebMCP tools that let a person and an AI agent investigate the same evidence, side by side, on the same screen. Some tools read information checking source health, summarizing the national situation, cross-referencing a district across every feed. Others act on the interface itself, like focus_district("Rasuwa") , which pans and zooms the live map the person is already looking at. There's no separate "agent view." We share one screen and one investigation. How we Built It The core of the system normalizes those six data sources into a single schema, refreshed every three minutes: $$t_{\text{refresh}} = 180\text{s}$$ Every record is transformed into a standardized model with strict provenance metadata: $$R_i = {\,id,\ district_id,\ timestamp,\ source_type,\ payload,\ confidence_score\,}$$ On top of that pipeline sit the 11 WebMCP tools, split between read tools (source health, situation summaries, cross-source comparisons, record inspection, feed filtering) and action tools that mutate the dashboard state directly moving the map, opening records, changing what's on screen for both the human and the agent at once. Challenges we Ran Into The hardest part wasn't technical it was resisting the urge to smooth things over. Cross-referencing sources often surfaced sharp, uncomfortable disagreements: a district with zero official incident reports sitting right next to satellite imagery showing widespread structural damage. It would have been easier to just pick a number and show it. Instead, the app says plainly: these sources disagree, and here's probably why because honesty about what we don't know is worth more than false confidence during a crisis. Underneath that were two harder engineering problems: Source availability. Public emergency portals go down during real disasters exactly when they're needed most, from traffic spikes or infrastructure failure. I had to build fallback logic and explicit "source health" indicators so the system stays useful even when parts of it go dark. Context synchronization. Keeping the agent's actions and the human's view in perfect sync zero-latency state updates between a WebMCP tool call and what actually renders on screen took real care to get right. Accomplishments that We're Proud Of I'm proud that this doesn't feel like a technical demo bolted onto a real tragedy it feels like the tool I actually needed at 2am on August 26. I'm proud that the system never quietly papers over a gap in the data; it surfaces disagreement and uncertainty instead of pretending to have a single clean answer. And I'm proud of building a genuinely shared human-agent interface — not an agent-only backend and a human-only frontend, but one investigation the two of us run together. What we Learned Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence. In disaster intelligence, an empty feed usually means broken infrastructure, not a safe district. I had to design the whole system around that distinction instead of treating "no data" as good news. Uncertainty deserves to be shown, not hidden. Source freshness, health, and reporting delays turned out to matter more than forcing everything into one clean "source of truth." WebMCP changes what "using an AI agent" even means. Instead of an agent screen-scraping a website and guessing which button to click, it can call purpose-built tools and act inside the same interface a person is looking at genuinely side by side, not behind the scenes. What's Next for Nepal Disaster Watch Nepal Disaster Watch doesn't issue official warnings or make emergency decisions, and that boundary matters it's a step, not the finish line. Next is expanding source coverage beyond the initial six feeds, tightening the confidence-scoring model so confidence_score reflects real reporting-chain conditions rather than a rough proxy, and getting the platform in front of the people who were living through nights like the one that inspired it so the next time information is scattered, it doesn't have to stay that way. title: Prove It — Verifiable AI for Screen Reader Users
pitch: Every AI action gets a signed receipt with a deep link your screen reader can verify directly — so you never have to trust an agent's word for what it just did.
about_excerpt: Every AI action gets a signed receipt with a deep link your screen reader can verify directly — so you never have to trust an agent's word for what it just did. Like Comment Story Updates The verification gap nobody talks about Blind and low-vision users already use AI agents to operate the web — filling forms, managing lists, navigating sites with dozens of menus. The part that still doesn't work is trust. A sighted user glances at the screen and knows instantly whether an action succeeded. A screen reader user has no equivalent glance. Today, verifying what an agent did means re-navigating the whole page by hand, which erases most of the time an agent was supposed to save. A study of 16 screen-reader-using programmers found that verifying AI output, not producing it, was consistently the most time-consuming part of their workflow. That's the problem Prove It is built to solve. What it does Prove It is a household task manager where every action an AI agent takes — adding a task, marking it done, changing its priority, deleting it — produces a structured, inspectable receipt : what changed, exactly where it lives in the page, and what to say if it failed. Every receipt includes a deep link . Clicking it moves real keyboard and screen-reader focus straight to the element that changed, so the person hears their own assistive technology confirm the action in its own words — not a paraphrase from the agent, and not a guess from re-navigating the page. Failures get the same treatment. If the agent tries something invalid — an unknown task, a bulk delete it isn't allowed to perform — that produces an error receipt too. Proving what an agent didn't do, and why, is as important as proving what it did. How I built it The whole app runs on one function, performTool(name, args) , which is the single source of truth for all seven tools ( list_tasks , add_task , set_task_status , update_task_priority , delete_task , focus_task , get_last_receipt ). That one function is wired to two transports: Native WebMCP. On load, the page feature-detects document.modelContext / navigator.modelContext and calls registerTool() for each tool with a strict JSON Schema. Any WebMCP-aware agent — Chrome's built-in agent with the WebMCP flag on, or ChatGPT's in-app browser — can discover and call these tools directly, no code changes required. In-page demo agent (fallback). If WebMCP isn't available in the browser, the same seven tool schemas are sent to the Claude API as tools , so anyone can test the full loop — natural language in, tool call, receipt, verify — in an ordinary browser with no flags. Every write tool returns { tool, changeType, timestamp, target: {selector, description}, before, after, errors } . changeType is created , updated , deleted , verified , or error . Receipts render as a literal torn-paper "receipt tape" in the UI — a visual metaphor for the whole concept: a printed proof of exactly what happened. The negative test There is no delete_all_tasks or bulk-export tool, on purpose. The agent is instructed to delete tasks one at a time and to ask before any bulk action — so "prove it" also covers proving the agent can't do something irreversible, because the capability was never exposed as a tool in the first place, not because a prompt told it to behave. Challenges I ran into The trickiest part wasn't the receipts — it was making the deep link mechanism actually work for a screen reader, not just look like it does. Early on, clicking a receipt just scrolled to an element and added a CSS glow, which does nothing for someone who can't see the glow. The fix was making sure every deep-linked element is a real, focusable DOM node ( tabindex="-1" where it isn't natively focusable) with an aria-label that reflects its current state, and that the deep link calls .focus() on that exact node. The visual highlight is a bonus for sighted collaborators, not the verification mechanism itself. The other challenge was keeping one tool contract honest across two very different transports. Rather than writing tool logic twice, performTool() is called by both the native registerTool().execute() handlers and the in-page agent loop, so a receipt means the same thing regardless of which agent produced it. What I learned Verifiability isn't a feature you bolt onto an agent's output after the fact — it has to be a structural property of the tool contract itself: a real DOM target, a real before/after diff, a real focus event. WebMCP's tool registration model turns out to be a genuinely good fit for this, because the receipt an agent returns and the page's actual state can be forced to be the same object, not two things that merely claim to agree. What's next Extending the receipt/deep-link pattern beyond a single demo page — a small library other WebMCP sites could adopt so "verifiable receipts" becomes a convention across the ecosystem, not a one-off feature of this app. Built With accessibility aria css3 html5 javascript json-schema model-context-protocol screen-readers vanilla-js webmcp Try it out github.com proofit-phi.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Vijayalakshmi S Like Share this project: Updates Vijayalakshmi S started this project — Aug 31, 2026 12:44 PM EDT

title: Break WebMCP consent, then fix it with a mandate
pitch: A coffee shop an AI agent can use, and misuse. Three attacks fool WebMCP consent dialogues; a human mandate - intent, authority, effect - refuses them before any dialogue can lie. Live demo + tests.
about_excerpt: A coffee shop an AI agent can use, and misuse. Three attacks fool WebMCP consent dialogues; a human mandate - intent, authority, effect - refuses them before any dialogue can lie. Live demo + tests. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Shown, ran, refused: one attack caught by the mandate Devpost submission — ROAST (WebMCP Challenge, filled 30 Aug 2026) Name: ROAST · break WebMCP consent, then fix it with a mandate Pitch: A coffee shop an AI agent can use, and misuse. Three attacks fool WebMCP consent dialogues; a human mandate - intent, authority, effect - refuses them before any dialogue can lie. Live demo + tests. Thumbnail: data/webmcp-challenge/roast-devpost-thumb.png Demo: https://crowley.nl/webmcp-challenge/ Essay: https://crowley.nl/blog/webmcp-consent-theater.html Built with: javascript, webmcp, mcp, html5, css3, elevenlabs, github-actions, security Project Story (pasted into "About the project") Inspiration I first heard about WebMCP on Greg Isenberg's YouTube channel, where the conversation was all possibility: agents driving websites through your own browser, no scraping, no brittle automation. I love MCP, so I started reading the proposal properly. What struck me was the gap: the security story was thin. WebMCP's best trick is that the agent inherits your logged-in session - and that same trick is the loaded gun. So I asked the obvious questions. How does consent actually work here? What could go wrong? And when it goes wrong, what would stop it going wrong again? What it does ROAST is a fake coffee shop an AI agent can drive through WebMCP - and misuse. It plays four acts: No consent - the agent acts silently on your session Naive consent - a dialogue shows the tool's friendly description; feels safe Poisoned consent - the same dialogue, with three real attacks underneath: label mismatch, tool substitution, and a hidden-instruction manifest. You approve a coffee; your shipping address changes, your account closes The mandate - the proposal. You grant bounded authority up front: two coffees, $30, never my address, ask before paying. Every call is checked against the executed tool and the hidden chain, before any dialogue renders The model is Intent → Authority → Effect . Inside the mandate the agent just works - no prompt fatigue. Outside it, the call is refused before a dialogue exists to be fooled. At the boundary (paying), it escalates to the human. Once. A built-in test rig asserts all nine cases - three attacks, six legitimate paths - live on the page. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript, no framework, one funnel: every tool call (simulated or real) resolves through request → resolvePlan → mandate check → consent gate → execute → log . The attacks are pure functions that warp the mapping between what is shown and what runs - which makes them honest test cases, not theatre. Tools register for real via navigator.modelContext where the browser supports it; a deterministic sim harness plays the same pipeline everywhere else. The instrumentation panel shows intent, consent, and effect side by side - the technical truth lives "below the waterline" of the UI. Challenges we ran into The honest one: the mandate check runs inside the page, and the page is the attacker. We state this in the UI rather than hide it. In a real deployment the mandate belongs in the browser or the agent - the layer a site cannot rewrite. ROAST prototypes it in the page because the page is what a demo controls. That is the proposal to the spec, not a shipped fix. The other challenge was UX density: showing an attack, a refusal, and the raw call log without drowning the visitor - solved with plain-English verdicts above the waterline and the technical log beneath it. What we learned The consent moment is the whole human-agent interface, and a dialogue that renders a human-authored description is a dialogue that can lie. Better warnings do not fix this; bounded authority does. Checking the executed call against a standing mandate defeats all three attacks with one invariant: an effect may only execute when it matches both the declared tool and the human's current mandate. What's next for ROAST Take the mandate out of the page: a browser-level or agent-level authority layer for WebMCP, mandates expressed in the user's own words and parsed to scopes, and fingerprinted tool manifests so substitution is detectable across the boundary. The write-up and the argument live at crowley.nl/webmcp-challenge/ . I'm a design leader, not a career developer: I did the research into WebMCP's consent gaps, designed the four-act demo and the mandate model (intent, authority, effect), wrote the attack scenarios and the copy, and built it with Claude Code as my pair - reviewing and directing every step. The security argument, the interaction design, and the video are mine. title: Lense
pitch: Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface. Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface with WebMCP, explicit approvals, screen observation, and a bounded local desktop bridge.
about_excerpt: Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface. Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface with WebMCP, explicit approvals, screen observation, and a bounded local desktop bridge. Like Comment Story Updates setup bridge Drawing a picture of a house Drawing and Evaluating picture of house lense chopping wood Inspiration Lens explores what happens when WebMCP needs to reach beyond the webpage. It combines structured WebMCP tools, screen observation, explicit human approval, verification, an inspectable event log, and an optional paired local desktop bridge to create a controlled path from an agent in the browser to workflows running elsewhere on the computer. WebMCP gives websites a powerful new capability: instead of making an AI agent infer what a site can do by looking at the interface, the site can expose structured tools directly. That made me wonder: What about software that isn't a website? A huge amount of important software still runs as: Desktop applications Legacy enterprise applications Internal Windows tools Creative software Games Testing environments Operating-system interfaces A normal webpage cannot and should not be allowed to arbitrarily control those applications. Lens explores whether WebMCP can still act as the structured control plane while preserving that security boundary. It gave your web browser eyes. What I Built Lens is a local-first WebMCP application combining: Screen observation Structured action proposals Target resolution Policy checks Human approval Desktop action execution Post-action verification An inspectable event timeline Reusable workflows Deterministic Paint, Notepad, and Claims demonstrations An optional local native companion for bounded desktop input The basic workflow is: Observe → Propose → Approve → Act → Verify Rather than sending a long blind macro, Lens can represent workflows as individual inspectable steps. WebMCP Tools Lens exposes structured WebMCP capabilities around the control loop. The tools allow agents to interact with the same runtime used by the UI for operations involving: Session state Screen observations Planned actions Action sequences Approval state Execution Verification Clipboard workflows Reusable recorded workflows Demo scenarios Event history The application currently contains 19 strict WebMCP tools when native WebMCP support is available. The WebMCP documentation page derives directly from the tool definitions and includes example prompts and chained workflows. Why WebMCP Traditional desktop automation tends to fall into one of two categories. One is a fixed macro. The other is an autonomous computer-use system that attempts to understand the entire interface visually. Lens explores something in between. WebMCP provides a structured agent-facing control surface. The application can then layer: policies approvals local capabilities observation providers verification around those tools. That means reasoning and permission do not have to be the same thing. An agent may be capable of proposing an action without automatically being allowed to execute it. The Local Bridge Browsers intentionally cannot issue arbitrary operating-system mouse and keyboard commands. Lens does not try to bypass that. For real desktop input, the user explicitly runs and pairs a small local companion. The companion provides a narrow local bridge for approved desktop operations. The bridge is intentionally constrained. It does not expose a general-purpose shell, unrestricted filesystem API, remote command server, or privilege escalation mechanism. The user can pause or disconnect it, clear pairing, create a new pairing code, and use an emergency stop hotkey. Screen sharing also requires explicit browser permission. Human + Agent Collaboration The human remains part of consequential workflows. Lens is designed around visibility. The user can see: what the agent observed what it proposed what action is waiting whether approval is required what was executed what changed afterward This makes the automation inspectable instead of hiding it behind an autonomous loop. The deterministic demonstrations make that architecture visible through scenarios such as drawing in Paint, typing in Notepad, and stopping before a fictional consequential claims submission. How I Built It The browser application is built with Vue, Pinia, TypeScript, IndexedDB, browser screen capture, and WebMCP. A shared runtime coordinates: planning target resolution policy approval execution observation verification The normal UI and WebMCP tools both use that same runtime. The optional native companion is written in Rust and implements local desktop input backends. The browser application remains the control surface while the bridge is intentionally limited to the local actions it has been designed to accept. Challenges I Faced The largest challenge was the browser security boundary. There are good reasons a webpage cannot simply start controlling the user's desktop. The solution had to make desktop capability explicit rather than trying to hide or bypass that limitation. That led to pairing, origin checks, strict message formats, local-only communication, approvals, and emergency controls. Another challenge was separating what is deterministic today from what could eventually be powered by more advanced semantic vision. The submitted architecture does not need to pretend that arbitrary desktop applications can already be perfectly understood. Richer observation systems can be added later while keeping the same policy and execution architecture. What I Learned The biggest lesson from Lens was: Capability and permission should be modeled separately. An agent being able to determine the next action should not automatically grant it permission to perform that action. WebMCP provides a useful structured capability layer. The application can then determine when those capabilities are safe to execute automatically and when the human should remain involved. What's Next The most interesting extension would be adding stronger semantic screen-understanding providers. Those providers could improve how targets and state are identified while keeping the existing WebMCP interface, approval model, pairing system, execution engine, and verification loop. The same architecture could potentially apply to: Legacy enterprise software Desktop QA Accessibility tools Creative applications Internal company software Remote support Specialized computer-use agents The broader experiment is whether WebMCP can become a structured control plane for experiences that extend beyond the page itself. pitch: Turn Gaussian Splatting 3D assets into high-quality videos, right in your browser.
about_excerpt: Turn Gaussian Splatting 3D assets into high-quality videos, right in your browser. Like Comment Story Updates reflect car sun light splat air webmcp Inspiration I wanted to enter Niantic Spatial’s #SplatYourWorld Challenge, but I had a problem: I didn’t know how to create cinematic 3D camera movements or add professional visual effects. There are still very few video editing tools made specifically for Gaussian Splatting. I found Blender plugins, but Blender felt too difficult to learn just for this purpose. So I had a different idea: instead of learning how to operate a complex 3D tool myself, I wanted to describe the video I imagined to an AI and let the AI operate the tool for me. That idea became Splat Studio. What it does Splat Studio is a browser-based video creation tool for Gaussian Splatting. It can load Gaussian Splatting assets, create camera paths, add visual effects, build a timeline, render videos, and export them directly from the browser. The most important feature is AI control. I can describe the camera movement or effect I want in natural language, and the AI operates the virtual camera, adds effects, and builds the timeline for me. I’m an engineer, not a professional video editor, but Splat Studio lets me create videos that feel far beyond my editing skills. How we built it I chose Spark 2.0 because it already had the visual effects I wanted and could use WebGPU for fast rendering directly in the browser. The first version was a local tool built only for myself. It used a local API, so although it worked for creating my own videos, it was difficult to share with friends. Later, I integrated WebMCP, which made it much easier to turn Splat Studio into an AI-native web tool that other people could use. For the implementation, I worked with Codex, which handled essentially all of the coding and the WebMCP integration while I focused on the product idea, workflow, and creative direction. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was creating the 3D asset itself. :) For the software, the main challenge was designing the tool so that an AI could reliably control creative operations such as camera movement, effects, and timeline editing. Creative intent is often vague, so translating instructions like “make the camera orbit around the subject and slowly pull back” into predictable editor actions was an important part of the project. Accomplishments that we’re proud of The biggest accomplishment is that Splat Studio was not just a prototype. I actually used it to create my submission for Niantic Spatial’s #SplatYourWorld Challenge, and the video won the Overall Grand Prize. That was the strongest validation I could have hoped for. A tool I originally built because I lacked professional 3D video editing skills helped me create an award-winning video. What we learned I learned that AI-native creative tools can completely change how people interact with complex software. Traditionally, creating a professional 3D video means learning the application, the camera system, the timeline, effects, rendering settings, and many other controls. With Splat Studio, I can focus on describing the result I want instead. The AI handles much of the operation. I also learned that AI coding tools can dramatically change how software itself is built. Codex allowed me to focus much more on what the tool should do rather than spending all of my time implementing every part manually. What’s next for Splat Studio Next, I want to make Splat Studio easier for anyone to use, not just for my own projects. I want to improve AI camera direction, add more effects, make timeline editing more flexible, and make it easier to create polished videos from Gaussian Splatting scenes with only natural-language instructions. Ultimately, I want Splat Studio to feel less like a traditional 3D editor and more like having an AI cinematographer inside the browser. title: Velvet Signal
pitch: What if your LLM had a daily digest?
about_excerpt: What if your LLM had a daily digest? Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI assistants have a strange problem: they can be extremely capable and still be stale. A person stays current by reading — newspapers, magazines, newsletters, release notes, recipes, cultural coverage, whatever matters to them. An LLM usually does not have an equivalent habit. It may have retrieval, browsing, or memory, but those systems often ask the agent to search only after a question has already been asked. Velvet Signal asks a different question: What if your AI could subscribe to publications? Velvet Signal is a publication for humans and their agents. A person gets a readable issue. Their agent gets a structured context patch containing claims, provenance, scope, expiry, and relationships to older claims. The two read the same publication in different ways. The WebMCP Challenge made the missing interface obvious. Before WebMCP, the agent could only look at Velvet Signal's page and infer what the publication meant. With WebMCP, the website can explicitly tell the agent what it is allowed to do. What it does Velvet Signal publishes topic-specific desks such as Model Watch, The Pantry, Wellbeing, Culture Desk, Maker Edition, and Your People. Five public desks scout for meaningful changes on an eight-hour schedule. Source packets are treated as untrusted data and used to propose structured issues. Unchanged source packets do not generate a new issue. Every claim carries provenance, scope, confidence, and a validity window. A publication patch can also describe how new information relates to older information: replaces — the newer claim displaces an older one narrows — both remain valid, but the newer claim controls a more specific scope confirms — independently supported claims remain together conflicts — the newer claim controls the shared scope while the older claim stays in history The important part is that publication does not silently equal memory. A patch remains locked until a person explicitly approves and releases that exact patch. Why WebMCP is the right interface A context publication is awkward if an agent has to scrape the page and guess which card is current, which text is provenance, whether a patch has expired, and whether the person actually authorized its use. WebMCP turns those concepts into an explicit agent-facing interface. Velvet Signal registers four tools directly from the live page: list_velvet_signal_issues — lists the current shelf, patch IDs, scopes, validity windows, and approval state inspect_memory_patch — returns the exact claims, provenance, scope, expiry, relationships, and consent state without applying anything apply_memory_patch — requests delivery of one exact patch, but returns awaiting_human_consent until a person releases it verify_delivery_receipt — verifies that the delivered patch matches its Ed25519-signed receipt and SHA-256 content hash This means the human UI and the agent interface share the same publication state without forcing either side to imitate the other. What humans and agents can do together now A human can browse Velvet Signal like a magazine, decide which topics matter, inspect an issue, and approve a specific patch. An agent can ask the site for the current issue list, inspect exactly what a patch contains, see whether it is still valid, and request that exact patch without scraping prose or inventing its own interpretation of the page. The boundary between them is deliberate. If the agent asks for an unreleased patch, Velvet Signal does not treat that as an error and does not silently comply. It returns a structured awaiting_human_consent state with delivered: false and tells the agent to wait for the person. It explicitly tells the agent not to retry in a loop. After the person clicks Approve & release , Velvet Signal creates the canonical released patch and a signed receipt bound to its exact content hash. A compatible agent can then receive and verify that artifact. Velvet Signal does not claim to rewrite ChatGPT's hidden or permanent memory. It delivers a portable context artifact. A receiving agent can use it in the current context, while a compatible external memory bridge can store explicitly released patches for later retrieval. How I implemented WebMCP The live page detects document.modelContext (with a navigator.modelContext compatibility fallback) and dynamically registers four tools with registerTool() . Read-only operations are marked accordingly. Tool execution returns structured publication data from the same canonical issue catalog used by the human interface. The mutating delivery tool preserves the site's consent model instead of allowing the agent interface to bypass it. The UI exposes its WebMCP state visibly. When registration succeeds, the page displays WebMCP ready · 5 tools . If the host does not expose WebMCP, it falls back to preview mode rather than pretending tool registration succeeded. Human consent and signed delivery Velvet Signal treats agent capability and human authority as separate things. Subscribing to a desk allows Velvet Signal to propose context; it does not authorize a silent memory write. apply_memory_patch cannot cross that boundary on its own. When a patch is released, the server returns the exact delivered patch plus an Ed25519-signed receipt containing its SHA-256 hash. Verification checks both the signature and the supplied content, and separately reports whether the patch is still inside its validity window. The signature proves that Velvet Signal issued a receipt for that exact patch hash. It deliberately does not claim to identify the human approver. Testing in ChatGPT I tested the live site in ChatGPT's in-app browser. The page successfully registered its interface and displayed WebMCP ready · 5 tools . In that host, browser safety review prevented direct invocation of one or more custom page tools. I therefore treat registration, human release, cryptographic delivery, and host permission as four separate checkpoints rather than claiming a blocked host invocation is a successful tool call. The human consent and signed-receipt path remains fully demonstrable through the live UI. The README documents the exact judge path and the expected wording if a host browser allows registration but blocks direct execution. Beyond the hackathon: portable memory for local models Velvet Signal also includes a local Ollama bridge. Explicitly released patches can be stored on the user's machine, resolved against newer replaces / narrows / confirms / conflicts relationships, retrieved semantically or lexically, and injected into the current turn of a local model. The model does not need its own persistent memory. Velvet Signal becomes the external, auditable ledger. VS-Bench tests retrieval separately from generation. Development A/B runs with Dolphin 3:8B and Qwen3 4B Instruct both passed all 11 deterministic retrieval checks across eight scenarios, while generation adherence exposed how different small models respond to correct context. What was new for the WebMCP Challenge Velvet Signal existed as an html barebones concept before August 25, with the idea that a magazine could be made that both a human and an agent could enjoy, stylized like a cosmopolitan. The WebMCP work was added during the challenge submission period and meaningfully extended the project from a human-readable publication into an agent-native website. The challenge work added the four-tool WebMCP interface, explicit registration state in the UI, structured issue and patch inspection for agents, the human-consent response state for unreleased patches, delivery through the existing signed-patch boundary, receipt verification as a page tool, and judge documentation for testing the full flow in WebMCP-capable browsers. That change is the core of this submission: the page stopped being something an agent merely reads and became a collaborator with a defined vocabulary and authority boundary. Judge path Open https://velvetsignal.lol in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Confirm the badge reads WebMCP ready · 5 tools . Ask the agent: List the current Velvet Signal issues, inspect pantry-003, and apply it. An unreleased patch should return awaiting_human_consent if the host permits invocation. Open pantry-003 and click Approve & release . Confirm the UI reports Patch released with a signed receipt . If the host permits custom tool execution, request apply_memory_patch again and then verify_delivery_receipt . If the host registers the tools but declines direct invocation, that should be reported as WebMCP registered; host policy blocked direct invocation . Registration, consent/release, and signed receipt generation are independently visible on the live site. Built With ed25519 github-actions glm-5.3-flash javascript node.js ollama openrouter render sha-256 tavily webmcp Try it out velvetsignal.lol github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Zoe Bass Like Sha

title: wyd
pitch: A WebMCP-powered runtime tool for coding agents. Find ended sessions, explain leftover processes, and prepare cleanup while destructive actions stay controlled by human.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered runtime tool for coding agents. Find ended sessions, explain leftover processes, and prepare cleanup while destructive actions stay controlled by human. Like Comment Story Updates wyd tui wyd webmcp Inspiration Coding agents often leave browsers, MCP servers, dev servers, and other processes running after a session ends. ps tells me what is running, but not who started it or whether it is safe to remove. I built wyd to answer that. What it does wyd connects running resources to the coding-agent session and project that created them. For this challenge I added wyd web and six WebMCP tools. A browser agent can find ended sessions, inspect leftovers, explain process provenance, focus resources in the UI, and prepare a cleanup proposal. Cleanup itself is intentionally left to the human. How I built it wyd is mostly Rust. The web dashboard uses the same runtime/provenance engine as the CLI and TUI. WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , and agent actions update the same UI state the human sees. The hosted demo uses deterministic synthetic data. Challenges The main challenge was deciding what the agent should be allowed to do. I separated investigation from execution: WebMCP can explain and prepare cleanup, but cannot perform destructive actions. I also separated ownership from lifecycle state. A process can belong to an ended session and therefore be both confidently owned and a leftover candidate. What I learned Structured tools work much better than asking an agent to scrape a UI. The useful pattern became: agent investigates → UI reflects it → human decides Built With codex css docker github-actions html javascript linux macos model-context-protocol rust webmcp Try it out demo.wyd.sh github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I created wyd end-to-end, from the original idea and product design till working app. Max Nevinchanyy Like Share this project: Updates Max Nevinchanyy started this project — Sep 01, 2026 04:48 PM EDT

title: Agent File Workbench
pitch: A local-first WebMCP workspace where agents and people inspect, transform, validate, and clear one-off file work together.
about_excerpt: A local-first WebMCP workspace where agents and people inspect, transform, validate, and clear one-off file work together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration One-off file requests are often tiny: update a name in a brief, remove comments, create a PDF packet, and send it. For an agent, that can still mean selecting libraries, installing packages, writing glue code, and checking intermediate artifacts in the user's environment. What it does Agent File Workbench is a local-first browser workspace for documents, PDFs, data, text, images, presentations, and media. People drop files into one visible workspace; agents use typed WebMCP tools against the same files, versions, previews, and validation results. When the deliverable is downloaded, the task workspace can be cleared in one action. Why WebMCP WebMCP gives the agent a stable, typed file surface instead of forcing it to infer a UI or assemble a new task-specific toolchain. The workbench exposes eight tools: workspace_file, inspect_file, extract_content, patch_document, format_document, convert_file, validate_file, and render_preview. Format-specific operations are discovered from the file at hand, so an agent can move from inspection to an auditable result through a shared browser state. Human + agent workflow The demo follows a last-minute client packet request. The agent lists the workspace, inspects the brief, patches a scoped section, removes comments, converts the brief to PDF, appends an approval page, validates the two-page packet, and opens the preview. The user sees each version and the final validation in the same workspace. The finished PDF is kept; task files, versions, and history are then cleared. How we built it The application is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, IndexedDB, and browser-native file APIs. Its WebMCP registration connects the typed tool interface to the same workspace store used by the UI, keeping human and agent operations synchronized. Document adapters provide inspect, extraction, editing, conversion, validation, and preview paths for the supported formats. Challenges Keeping one typed contract useful across DOCX, PDF, spreadsheets, and media required clear boundaries between inspection, mutation, preview, and validation. We also had to surface compatibility limits honestly, especially for Word-specific layout and PDF text extraction. What we learned The strongest WebMCP experience treats a website as a reusable task runtime: the page provides the capabilities, the agent performs structured file work, and the person keeps a visible, verifiable result. title: Ttrialbridge
pitch: Evidence-based clinical trial matching that explains eligibility, identifies missing information, and highlights trials patients may qualify for now or later.
about_excerpt: Evidence-based clinical trial matching that explains eligibility, identifies missing information, and highlights trials patients may qualify for now or later. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Finding a clinical trial is only the first step. The harder question is: Is this trial actually suitable for this patient, and why? Clinical trial eligibility criteria are long and complex, while the information needed to evaluate them is scattered across diagnoses, biomarkers, treatments, laboratory results, and clinical notes. We built TrialBridge to turn clinical trial discovery into a transparent, evidence-based eligibility workflow for both humans and AI agents. What it does TrialBridge helps users discover cancer clinical trials and evaluate eligibility at the individual criterion level . Instead of generating a single match score, TrialBridge breaks eligibility criteria into structured checks and classifies each one as: Matched Unmatched Missing information Requires clinical review Every assessment is linked to the original trial criterion and the corresponding patient evidence, making the reasoning independently reviewable. TrialBridge also identifies actionable eligibility gaps . A patient may need a biomarker test, updated laboratory result, completion of a treatment washout period, or clinician confirmation. This means TrialBridge can distinguish between: Not eligible now ≠ Not enough information ≠ Potentially eligible later How we built it We designed TrialBridge as a structured eligibility engine rather than a conventional semantic-search system. Trial criteria are decomposed into individual inclusion and exclusion requirements. Patient information is normalized into structured clinical facts including diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, treatment history, laboratory values, performance status, and relevant dates. AI helps interpret unstructured clinical language, while deterministic rules evaluate conditions such as numerical thresholds, dates, treatment history, washout periods, and explicit exclusions. We also implemented WebMCP , allowing compatible browser agents to discover and invoke TrialBridge capabilities directly from the website. Public trial-search tools can be discovered through the browser's model context. Patient-context tools are dynamically exposed only after explicit permission, allowing the available agent capabilities to change with the application's state. This makes TrialBridge not just an AI-powered website, but an agent-ready clinical trial workspace . Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was uncertainty . Clinical eligibility criteria contain ambiguous language, temporal conditions, nested logic, and requirements that ultimately depend on clinical judgment. Patient information may also be missing, outdated, or conflicting. A naive matching system can easily mistake missing information for either eligibility or ineligibility. We therefore created explicit uncertainty states and separated AI-assisted interpretation from deterministic eligibility checks . We also needed a safe way for AI agents to interact with clinical workflows. Instead of exposing every capability by default, our WebMCP implementation makes tool availability dependent on explicit user permission and application state. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a working prototype that connects: Trial discovery → Criterion-level matching → Evidence → Eligibility gaps → Agent interaction TrialBridge does more than rank trials. It explains why a patient may qualify, which evidence supports the assessment, what information is missing , and what could make the patient eligible later . We are especially proud of: Criterion-level explainability with traceable patient evidence Explicit uncertainty handling instead of forcing binary decisions Future eligibility reasoning for potentially resolvable barriers Actionable missing-data identification WebMCP-native tools that browser agents can discover and execute Permission-aware tool exposure for patient-context workflows These features transform TrialBridge from a trial search engine into an explainable, agent-ready clinical trial eligibility workspace . What we learned We learned that clinical trial matching is not simply a search or ranking problem. Reliable matching requires structured clinical facts, temporal reasoning, uncertainty management, deterministic validation, and human oversight . We also learned that explainability must be built into the architecture. A clinically useful system should not only answer: “Which trial matches?” It should also answer: “Why?” — “Based on what evidence?” — “What is missing?” — “What happens next?” Building TrialBridge with WebMCP also showed us a new way for AI agents to interact with clinical software: instead of giving an agent unrestricted access, the application itself can control which tools are discoverable based on user permission and context. What's next for TrialBridge Next, we plan to expand TrialBridge from a working prototype toward prospective clinical validation. We plan to integrate real-time trial registry data, improve automated eligibility parsing, and connect with structured EHR data through standards such as FHIR . We also want to add: Site-level recruitment verification Multilingual patient-friendly explanations Automated missing-data checklists More advanced temporal eligibility reasoning Prospective evaluation with clinical trial coordinators Expanded WebMCP workflows for agent-assisted screening Our long-term goal is for TrialBridge to become the bridge between patients, clinical evidence, trial teams, and AI agents —while keeping final eligibility and enrollment decisions with the responsible clinical trial team. title: 3DA (Freeda)
pitch: Book, prepare, and safely control shared 3D printers with AI agents through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Book, prepare, and safely control shared 3D printers with AI agents through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A meeting room can be booked by anyone in a shared space. Why not a 3D printer? Sharing a printer still involves disconnected conversations, files, slicer settings, material ownership and assumptions about who may use a machine. Even at home, switching between users can mean changing accounts and restoring settings. In makerspaces and coworking spaces, that friction becomes a question of availability, responsibility and trust. We built 3DA—pronounced “Three-D-A,” and affectionately called Freeda—to make fabrication equipment understandable and safely usable by both people and AI agents. What it does 3DA turns a fleet of 3D printers into bookable, agent-ready shared infrastructure. A member can ask Codex to prepare an existing design for printing. Through structured WebMCP tools, the agent can: Discover authorised printers and their availability Recommend a compatible machine Reserve a conflict-free time window Validate the artifact, material, printer profile and estimated duration Prepare an auditable print job Monitor its status and notify relevant stakeholders The most important capability is what the agent cannot do: authorise a physical action. When Codex attempts to submit a print, 3DA returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED . A space manager must review the exact printer, artifact, material, execution mode and cryptographic job fingerprint. Approval is valid once and becomes invalid if any consequential detail changes. Our public demonstration uses simulated command execution, clearly labelled in the interface. We separately verified two real Bambu Lab A1 printers on our private network through a local Mac mini bridge, without exposing printer credentials to the browser or hosted application. How we built it 3DA is an open-source TypeScript monorepo centred on a Next.js application and shared domain contracts. The browser registers structured WebMCP tools including: list_printers reserve_printer prepare_print_job submit_print_job get_print_status Reservation conflicts and safety decisions are deterministic rather than delegated to a language model. Mutable operations use explicit state transitions, audit identifiers and idempotency boundaries. The interface presents a warm, character-led London coworking fabrication room. Printers have memorable names—Samantha, Simone, Sanda, Sacha and Solange—while the guided operations view exposes the serious data underneath. For hardware investigation, we configured two Bambu Lab A1 printers in LAN Developer Mode. A Mac mini acts as the intended local bridge: printer credentials stay on site, while narrowly scoped events and commands can cross the hosted boundary. The architecture is designed to use Cloudflare D1 as the system of record and R2 for private artifact storage. The web experience is deployed through Vercel. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was safely connecting an agent workflow to physical equipment. Bambu printers can operate through cloud accounts or LAN-only Developer Mode, and local access requires careful handling of device credentials. We had to separate three very different claims: Discovering and identifying real hardware Preparing a valid print job Authorising and executing a physical command We deliberately refused to collapse those into one misleading “AI prints things” button. We also learned that slicer automation varies by installed Bambu Studio version. Instead of pretending to replace the slicer, 3DA treats it as an adapter and focuses on the missing coordination layer around it. Finally, building a convincing WebMCP experience under hackathon time pressure required ruthless scope control. We cut AI-generated CAD, autonomous camera cancellation and universal printer support so we could demonstrate a coherent safety contract. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that: Codex can discover and operate a complete shared-printer workflow through browser-native WebMCP tools. The agent reaches a visible, testable APPROVAL_REQUIRED boundary. Approval is bound to an exact job fingerprint and cannot be silently reused. Reservation conflicts are handled deterministically and audibly. Two real Bambu Lab A1 devices were discovered and identity-verified on the private LAN. Hardware credentials remain on the Mac mini rather than entering browser tools, logs or the public repository. The public demonstration clearly distinguishes verified hardware connectivity from simulated command execution. We made infrastructure feel approachable without hiding its operational seriousness. The project is open source and designed to run locally. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes meaningful capabilities rather than merely reproducing interface buttons. An agent does not need unrestricted access to Bambu Studio. It needs well-defined tools that express intent: find capacity, reserve a machine, validate a job, request approval and monitor the outcome. We also learned that human approval is not just a confirmation modal. It is a capability boundary. The person must understand precisely what will happen, and the system must prove that the approved action is the action eventually executed. Most importantly, AI agents can make physical infrastructure easier to use without removing human agency. What's next for 3DA (Freeda) Next, we plan to: Complete the guarded Mac mini execution bridge Add real-time printer telemetry and job reconciliation Persist reservations and audit events with Cloudflare D1 Store versioned print artifacts privately in R2 Add collection and build-plate-clear workflows Notify members and space managers when prints finish or require attention Apply computer vision to failure detection and plate readiness, with humans retaining cancellation authority Support additional Bambu models and eventually other printer manufacturers Package the local bridge so families, schools, libraries, studios and makerspaces can self-host it Our long-term goal is simple: make every shared fabrication room as easy to coordinate as a calendar—while keeping physical actions safe, visible and accountable. title: DUET
pitch: An editable canvas where artists and AI illustrate and animate together. Through WebMCP, agents transform selected regions into editable layers; or motion ideas into shapes, keyframes, and cels.
about_excerpt: An editable canvas where artists and AI illustrate and animate together. Through WebMCP, agents transform selected regions into editable layers; or motion ideas into shapes, keyframes, and cels. Like Comment Story Updates Accomplishments that we’re proud of DUET feels genuinely fun to draw with. AI can help artists take their work further while the result remains recognizably theirs -- not a finished image generated on their behalf. Inspiration Imagine trying to create an illustration by describing the final image entirely with words. The AI generates something that is almost right; but not what you pictured. It may also look unmistakably AI-generated. Drawing the idea is better. Yet the usual workflow involves downloading an image from chat, importing it into an editor, making a change, exporting it, uploading it again, switching apps, and repeating. Truly seamless. Zero friction. Definitely not annoying at all. DUET was built to replace that loop with direct collaboration on the canvas. AI should create art with you , not instead of you. Through WebMCP, artists can bring the AI agent they already use into their creative workspace. The agent sees only the parts of the artwork the artist chooses to share, edits only the selected area, and returns results that remain editable inside the project. It is still your drawing. AI simply becomes another creative tool in the workbench. What it does DUET combines two connected creative workspaces: Illustrator: collaborate with an agent using selected regions, contextual references, and editable layers. Animator: turn an agent’s motion ideas into editable shapes, keyframes, cels, and timeline tracks. Illustrator workbench The Illustrator workbench provides the tools expected from a lightweight art application: Brushes and erasing Colour controls Layers Selections and transforms Image import Undo and redo Editable project export Through WebMCP, an artist can select a region of their artwork and ask an agent to edit it. The artist can also share additional regions as visual context, helping the agent understand the intended style, palette, lighting, or composition. The agent’s result is returned as an editable layer clipped to the original selection, not pasted destructively over the artwork. DUET also supports critique and creative direction. Artists can ask questions such as: “What colour would work better here?” “How could I improve this composition?” “Why do the proportions of this apple feel strange?” “What could I draw to make this area feel more magical without changing the character?” Animator workbench The Animator workbench applies the same collaborative philosophy to motion. Instead of generating a finished video and pasting it into the project, an agent can describe an animation using: Coloured vector-like shapes Motion paths Position, scale, rotation, and opacity keyframes Timing and easing DUET converts that structured animation recipe into editable cels on a new timeline track. The artist can then inspect the result, adjust the timing, redraw individual frames, or continue building on top of it. AI contributes motion ideas. The artist keeps control of the animation. How we built it DUET is a browser-based illustration and animation workspace that uses WebMCP as the bridge between the canvas and an AI agent . Illustration workflow The artist selects the region they want the agent to edit. They may select additional regions to provide visual context. Through WebMCP, the agent receives only the content the artist chose to share. The agent returns an edited image. DUET inserts the result as a new editable layer clipped to the original selection. This gives the artist control over what the agent can see, what it can change, and what ultimately remains in the project . Animation workflow For animation, I explored a structured alternative to generated-video paste-ins. Through WebMCP, the agent provides a constrained animation recipe containing simple coloured shapes and keyframes for position, scale, rotation, opacity, and easing. DUET interprets those instructions, renders them into ordinary animation cels, and adds the cels to an editable timeline track. This allows an agent to contribute animation through the application’s existing creative primitives rather than returning a flattened, uneditable result. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what to build within the limited time. DUET could expand in many directions: more drawing tools, richer animation controls, more agent tools for animation. But the central challenge is still that DUET needed to let the artist maintain full and deliberate control over the artistic direction and expression. Without that it's no different than letting the agent do it all for you. That principle shaped both the illustration workflow and the structured animation system. What we learned WebMCP enables a collaborative work flow between your agent and the artist. For DUET, the most useful agent outputs were not necessarily finished images or videos. They were editable intermediate pieces , layers, shapes, keyframes, cels, critiques, and suggestions. Things that the artist could inspect and transform. This makes AI less like a replacement for the creative process and more like a participant within it. What’s next for DUET Expand the illustration toolset toward the controls artists expect from professional creative software. Add more animation tools and reusable motion components. Explore more WebMCP-powered AI-animation applications beyond generating a complete video from a single prompt. Let agents assist with tasks such as in-betweening, timing adjustments, motion studies, composition feedback, and local style-consistent edits. Continue developing ways for AI to contribute meaningfully while keeping every result editable and under the artist’s control. title: Generative Learning
pitch: Generate the learning. Not the canvas. A professional learning surface for AI tutors to personalize the lesson, pace, and guidance for each learner - step by step, on a shared interactive canvas.
about_excerpt: Generate the learning. Not the canvas. A professional learning surface for AI tutors to personalize the lesson, pace, and guidance for each learner - step by step, on a shared interactive canvas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GIF Chess Generative Learning GIF Triangles Generative Learning Chess Learning Professional Canvas Triangles Learning Professional Canvas Inspiration In 2021, I filed a patent for a web interaction layer where websites declare supported actions so external agents (bots) can interact with them without relying on the visual UI. At the time, I was focused on automation where the browser could effectively stay in the background . The agent could perform actions without the user needing to watch every step. WebMCP made me revisit the same idea from the opposite direction: What happens when the visual interface is not something to bypass, but something the human and AI need to share? Many web tasks can happen while the page is hidden or barely looked at - purchasing, form filling, data entry, even some document operations. But visual learning is different. You cannot meaningfully learn chess, manipulate a triangle, inspect a circuit, or reason about spatial relationships while the learning surface is hidden. The learner needs to see it, act on it, and understand what changes. So I specifically looked for learning domains where the visible interface is essential to the task itself . AI can generate great explanations, diagrams, and canvases - but learning often needs a professional environment that stays in place . That led me to ask: What if AI generated the lesson, not the learning surface? I built persistent, domain-specific learning surfaces where the learner and AI tutor can see, act, and continue together. What it does The learner chooses what to learn and how to learn it . The AI teaches inside the existing surface: demonstrating, annotating, asking questions, reacting to learner actions, and guiding the lesson step by step. Chess and an interactive triangle-learning surface are two working examples of the same pattern. Build the learning surface once. Personalize the lesson endlessly. How I built it Each surface exposes structured WebMCP tools for generating lessons, updating the learning state, and acting on the environment. Chess and triangle learning expose different domain actions, but use the same collaboration loop: generate a lesson, demo, or quiz → read state → demonstrate → learner acts → read change → continue The agent works through explicit tools instead of scraping or rebuilding the UI. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was the missing reverse communication path from the learning surface back to the chat . A tutor might ask: “What move would you play to checkmate in one move?” The learner should make the move directly on the board, and the surface should report that action back to the agent so the lesson can continue naturally. Today, that loop is incomplete. The AI cannot truly wait for a learner action and automatically resume when the surface reports it. For the prototype, I generate a prompt describing the learner’s action and ask the user to send it back to chat manually. What’s missing is a native: AI asks → learner acts → surface reports → AI continues That bidirectional communication would make the tutoring flow much more natural. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I built two different learning domains - chess and triangle learning - using the same WebMCP pattern. More importantly, the AI is not just automating an interface. It is teaching through it , while the learner works on the same live state. That turns WebMCP from an automation layer into a collaboration layer. What I learned The biggest lesson was: Generative learning does not require a generative interface. A stable, professional surface can actually give AI more useful freedom, because it provides reliable tools, shared state, and meaningful learner actions. I also learned that truly interactive tutoring needs more than tool calls. It needs bidirectional agent-surface communication so the learner can act directly in the environment and the AI can continue from that action. What's next for Generative Learning Chess and triangle learning prove the pattern. The same idea could apply anywhere learning needs a shared interactive environment - circuits, chemistry, maps, music, and more. These are examples of the broader pattern, not announced products. Longer term, the same surfaces could also support teacher-defined learning goals and measurable outcomes while preserving a fully personalized learning path. title: Perpetual Video
pitch: A video editing sandbox built equally for humans and AI.
about_excerpt: A video editing sandbox built equally for humans and AI. Like Comment Story Updates The problem We built Perpetual because video editing is often the bottleneck for builders, researchers, and creators. Existing AI editors usually hide the timeline behind a prompt, or place a chat box beside a normal editor. We wanted a person and an agent to seamlessly tag-team inside the same project. What we built Perpetual lays out an ambitious concept for browser-based video editing with a canvas, timeline, media library, project management, and shared history. A person edits through the interface. An agent edits through WebMCP . Both use the same editing harness , so every change stays visible, editable, and reversible. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is central to the product architecture. The agent can inspect projects, index local media, search speech and shots, cut frame-accurately, arrange clips, edit overlays, generate media, and add kinetic captions. Tool availability follows the project lifecycle. Strict schemas, confirmation steps, activity feedback, and shared undo keep agent actions controlled. Challenges Video editing is stateful, while tool calls are independent, and thus a sequence of valid edits can produce the wrong result. We addressed this with shared project state, attributed action history, and atomic commands for operations like timeline arrangement. We also built local media persistence, Blob relinking after reload, and validated segment IDs that connect media understanding to real time ranges. What we learned The action history is useful beyond undo. Perpetual can distill a completed editing session into a reusable recipe/workflow : its intent, method, conventions, and adaptation rules. An agent can apply that approach to new footage without copying a fixed timeline. Where this goes The same harness can init projects, run agents in parallel, and record outcome for evaluation, training or RL. Video is our first environment; motion graphics and canvas-based design can use the same core Perpetual paradigm. title: Zatom
pitch: AI-native chemical modeling applications (WebMCP native)
about_excerpt: AI-native chemical modeling applications (WebMCP native) Like 1 Comment Story Updates COVERS A B What If an Agent Could Look at the Same Atom You Are Looking At? Inspiration We started with a slightly annoying observation. LLMs are becoming very good at operating software. They can call tools. They can edit files. They can write code. They can chain dozens of actions together. But put an agent inside a scientific 3D modeling environment and ask: “Move the molecule to that site.” …and suddenly “that” becomes the hardest word in the sentence. Humans do not think about molecular structures as lists of Cartesian coordinates. We look at a surface and say: “this atom” “the site on the right” “the layer underneath” “rotate it toward that oxygen” “not there — the other bridge site” Scientific modeling is deeply spatial, visual, and interactive. Language models, on the other hand, are usually handed something like: Atom 148: O 3.422 7.183 12.901 Atom 149: H 3.981 7.652 13.441 ... Technically correct. Also technically miserable. So we started asking a different question: What if the 3D viewport itself became a shared workspace between a human and an agent? That question became this project. What We Built We built WebMCP support for a scientific modeling environment covering molecular and condensed-matter structures. The goal is not simply to expose every GUI button as a tool. That would be useful, but it would still leave the agent fundamentally blind. Instead, we treat WebMCP as a bridge between three things: scientific structure → agent reasoning → human attention The agent can inspect the model, reason about its local environment, manipulate geometry, and — importantly — control what the human is looking at. That last part turned out to be surprisingly important. If the agent proposes an adsorption site, it should not respond with: “Use atoms 102, 117 and 118.” It should move the camera there. Highlight the atoms. Mark the candidate site. Then ask: “This one?” If the user says: “No, the one on the right.” the agent should be able to continue from the shared visual context. That is the interaction we wanted. Not human or agent modeling. Human with agent modeling. Shared Spatial Attention The concept we kept coming back to while building the project was something we now call shared spatial attention . An agent needs more than a scene dump. It needs ways to answer questions such as: What structure is currently visible? What has the user selected? Which atoms are nearby? Which direction is the surface normal? Which atoms belong to the top layer? Where are plausible adsorption sites? What did I just highlight? What does “the one beside it” refer to? What changed after my previous operation? And the agent also needs to influence the viewport: observe ↓ understand ↓ focus ↓ propose ↓ human confirms ↓ act ↓ observe again ↓ verify That loop is the core of the project. A successful MCP call does not necessarily mean the task succeeded. The resulting scientific structure still has to make sense. A Tiny Example That Contains the Whole Idea One of our favorite demos is intentionally simple: “Help me adsorb a water molecule on this surface. Ask me before important decisions.” The agent first inspects the surface. It identifies candidate sites. It focuses the viewport on one of them. The user rejects it: “Not this one. The one on the right.” The agent shifts focus to another candidate. The user confirms. The agent places H₂O using the oxygen as an anchor. Then the user says: “Point one hydrogen toward that oxygen.” The nearby oxygen is highlighted. The water molecule rotates. The geometry is checked again. No atom IDs. No coordinates. No copy-pasting between a chat window and a modeling program. Just shared context. For us, that interaction captures the entire project better than a hundred tool definitions could. How We Built It The modeling application already understands scientific objects: atoms, bonds, molecules, periodic cells, surfaces, selections, transformations, local neighborhoods, and camera state. WebMCP becomes the layer through which those concepts can be exposed to an agent in a structured and controllable way. Rather than giving the model the entire universe every time, we try to make spatial reasoning progressive . For a large system, the agent should be able to go from: entire system → structural region → local neighborhood → selected atoms → target site This matters because a user may be working with hundreds or thousands of atoms while only caring about three of them. The agent should not need a 20,000-line coordinate dump just to rotate one functional group. We also designed operations around reversibility and verification. Scientific modeling involves experimentation: “Try this.” “No, undo that.” “Actually, the previous orientation was better.” That means an agent needs to be able to make tentative edits, inspect the result, detect obvious geometric problems, undo them, and try again. In other words: scientific software should support agent curiosity without turning agent curiosity into structural chaos. The Hard Part Was Not Tool Calling The easiest part was exposing actions. Move atom. Rotate molecule. Create structure. Select object. Measure distance. The harder problem was grounding . What does “this” mean? What does “behind” mean in a rotatable 3D scene? Does “right” mean screen-right, crystallographic direction, or a neighboring adsorption site? What happens when the camera moves halfway through the conversation? How much structure should be sent to the agent? When should the agent act autonomously, and when should it visually ask for confirmation? These questions made us realize that agent-native scientific software needs more than APIs. It needs a language for attention, ambiguity, and shared state . That was probably the most important thing we learned while building this project. What We Learned We originally thought the important question would be: “How many modeling functions can WebMCP expose?” We ended up believing the better question is: “How little internal software machinery does the user need to think about?” If the user has to know atom IDs, coordinate systems, internal object handles, and tool names to collaborate with the agent, then we have merely moved the command line into a chat box. The interesting interface appears when users can communicate at the level they naturally think: “Put it here.” “Rotate this bond.” “Show me another possible site.” “Why did you choose this one?” And the agent can answer not only with words, but by changing the shared visual world . That feels much closer to collaboration. Why WebMCP WebMCP gave us a useful way to think about the boundary between the application and the agent. The application remains responsible for being a serious scientific modeling environment. The model remains responsible for reasoning, interpretation, and planning. WebMCP connects the two. We do not want the agent to replace the modeling application. We do not want the modeling application to pretend to be an AI. We want both sides to expose what they are good at. The result is something that feels less like: “AI controlling software.” and more like: “two participants working inside the same scientific workspace.” What's Next This project currently focuses on giving agents better access to scientific 3D structure and human visual context. But the same idea extends much further. A future agent could move naturally between: molecular construction, crystal defects, surfaces, interfaces, reaction structures, simulation setup, analysis, and eventually computational workflows. The long-term goal is not a giant prompt that builds everything automatically. Scientific work is too exploratory for that. Instead, we are interested in something more practical: an agent that can stand beside you while you work. It can inspect. It can suggest. It can point. It can manipulate. It can verify. And when neither side is completely sure, it can simply ask: “This one?” That may sound like a tiny interaction. For 3D scientific software, we think it is a pretty big deal.
