title: Reflex
pitch: Agentify the web you already use.
about_excerpt: Agentify the web you already use. Like Comment Story Updates ## Inspiration WebMCP gives a website a way to hand an agent real tools instead of making it guess at pixels. The catch is that every website that already exists was built before it. Adapting each one by hand means a developer identifying capabilities, naming tools, writing descriptions, authoring JSON Schemas, implementing handlers and maintaining registrations — which is exactly the adoption barrier that keeps agents stuck clicking through user interfaces: fragile, slow, and ambiguous. Then I noticed something. Those sites are not silent about what they do. A form that carries aria-label="Search claims" , an aria-description explaining itself, and <label> s on every field has already declared everything a tool definition needs — a name, a description, and a typed parameter list. That metadata exists on millions of pages because accessibility law required it, not because anyone was thinking about agents. Accessibility metadata is already a capability contract. Nobody was reading it as one. ## What it does Reflex is a Chrome extension. Open it on a page and it reads the DOM's forms, buttons, labels and ARIA attributes, then proposes WebMCP tools from what it finds — generating the tool name, a description, a full JSON Schema, a risk classification and a confidence score, and recording the exact attributes that produced each one as evidence. You review that evidence and approve what you want. Approved capabilities are registered through WebMCP: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "search_claims", description: "Find a claim by reference number, claimant name or policy number.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { query: { type: "string", maxLength: 60 } }, required: ["query"] }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true }, execute: async (input) => executeCandidate(document, candidate, input) }); The point is that Reflex writes that object for you , from markup the page already had. When an agent calls the tool, Reflex fills the site's own form, dispatches input / change so frameworks notice, submits with requestSubmit() so the page's own validation runs, and returns the text of the region the page updated — so a read-only tool returns real data, not "submitted". It ships with a fictional government claims service to demonstrate against, and a scanner that runs the discovery engine against any live URL. ## How we built it A TypeScript monorepo where the discovery engine has no extension dependencies, so it can be pointed at any page: capability-model — the CapabilityCandidate type, schemas, and the typed message protocol discovery-engine — form and button scanners, ARIA and label resolution, tool naming, ignore rules, keyword risk classification, confidence scoring, stable selectors and semantic fingerprints schema-generator — HTML controls to JSON Schema: enums from <option> , radio groups, checkbox groups, min / max , formats, required webmcp-adapter — the only file that touches modelContext , plus the DOM executor The extension is split across the two JavaScript worlds Chrome gives you, because a content script cannot reach the page's own modelContext . The content script (isolated world) does discovery and holds the user's decisions; a page runtime (main world) registers tools and executes them. Everything between them is a typed message on a private channel. The content script never touches WebMCP; the page runtime decides nothing. Testing was the backbone: 183 unit tests in jsdom and 25 end-to-end tests that load the real built extension into a browser, approve capabilities through the real message protocol, and call the registered tools the way a WebMCP client would. CI runs all of it on every push. ## Challenges we ran into The 242-row wall. Pointed at YouTube, Reflex found 242 candidates, all scoring 55%, named 1_reply , 150_replies , 166_replies — the button on every comment. Discovery wasn't the hard part; review was. A list that long is worth exactly what an empty one is. The obvious fix — raise the confidence floor — was wrong, and I nearly shipped it. Real working capabilities on well-built government forms also score 50–60%, because those pages never wrote an aria-description . Companies House and the NHS pharmacy finder both score 50%, and both work. What separates them from noise isn't the score, it's the source : a form arrives with a typed schema, which is evidence in itself; a button is an unparameterised action inferred from two words of label. Two floors — 50% for forms, 70% for buttons — cut YouTube from 57 candidates to 0 while keeping every real one. Risk classification kept lying. Three separate false positives, each found by pointing the engine at something real: "Find an employee by name or email " was flagged sensitive because email was a keyword; "Search pay ments" was flagged sensitive because prefix-matching pay hit payments ; and "View claim record " was classified as a write because record is also a write verb. Fixes: separate consequential actions (authorise, send, grant) from sensitive subjects (password, bank, role), match short verbs as whole words only, and resolve read-versus-write by position , since these labels are imperative phrases and the leading verb is the action. Two JavaScript worlds racing. The content script's handshake could arrive before the page runtime was listening, leaving the panel convinced the page had no WebMCP host. And when the popup re-injected, a second runtime appeared with its own registry — so one approved tool registered twice and executed twice. Fixed with a readiness announcement, a retry, and making injection idempotent. Reloads dropped everything. activeTab is revoked the moment a page navigates, so refreshing took the registered tools with it. Approvals were never lost — they're stored per origin — but nothing re-attached. Rather than requesting blanket host permissions, a site can now be granted individually, registering a dynamic content script for that origin alone. Tooling fought back. Stable Chrome 151 refuses --load-extension , so the e2e suite runs on Playwright's Chromium. Playwright's Chromium ships without H.264, so a video check hung for two minutes and looked like a broken page. GitHub strips <video> from READMEs entirely — I verified all four embed forms through their API before settling on an animated GIF. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of It works on sites nobody built for it. GOV.UK search scores 95% and yields a ten-parameter filter form; the NHS pharmacy finder 90%; Companies House 89%; GitHub's advanced search produces a tool with 25 typed parameters from one form. All three of the top sites were verified end to end — approve the tool, call it through navigator.modelContext , and the site performs the real search. Their Content-Security-Policy is no obstacle, because Chrome injects the runtime through a privileged path. It fails closed. Every candidate stores a semantic fingerprint — tag, role, accessible name, expected field names — re-verified before anything actuates. Relabel a form while keeping its id and execution refuses with "accessible name changed" rather than driving the wrong control. It refuses to be glib. On a page with nothing worth reviewing, the panel says so and explains why, instead of showing thirteen rows of noise. Password fields are never exposed. Destructive tools ask a human, in the page, on every single call. Five panel designs over one component tree — every row renders each design's parts and the stylesheet decides which are visible, so the review logic cannot drift between looks. ## What we learned Discovery is the easy half. Generating tool definitions from markup turned out to be straightforward. Making a human able to review them was the actual product, and it's where most of the engineering went. Measure, don't guess. The highest-leverage thing I built was a 60-line scanner that runs the engine against a live URL. Every significant design decision — the two floors, the classifier rewrites, the ignore rules — came from pointing it at a real page and being wrong. A warning that fires wrongly is worse than no warning. Flagging search_payments as sensitive teaches people to click past the flag that matters, authorise_payment . Accessibility quality is bimodal. Public services are excellent, because they were made to be. Consumer apps with 227 interactive controls can yield nothing at all. The readiness score exists to say which signal is missing rather than just "didn't work". ## What's next for Reflex Teach mode — record a human performing a multi-step workflow and propose a single higher-level capability from it, moving from UI operations to domain actions. Network correlation — observe the request behind a click and execute against that instead of the DOM, for a far more robust executor. A capability graph — lift discovered operations into entity-level capabilities (an employee can be searched, viewed, transferred) and then into workf

title: a11y-mcp
pitch: Speak Thai, fill any English web form by voice. a11y-mcp reads forms aloud, fills them from your speech, and self-corrects — powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Speak Thai, fill any English web form by voice. a11y-mcp reads forms aloud, fills them from your speech, and self-corrects — powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Two failures, stacked. First, AI agents "use" the web by guessing which pixel is a button — and guess wrong. Second, accessibility tooling is built for English. Our lead user is a Thai person in front of an English-only visa, university, or airline form: it's well-marked-up and completely unusable if you don't read English, and nobody translates it. Screen readers mangle code-switched Thai. The same tool helps blind, low-vision, motor-impaired, and elderly users — so we built it as a capability, not a special-needs product. What it does a11y-mcp turns any semantically sound web form into typed tools an AI agent can call (via WebMCP / document.modelContext), then lets a Thai speaker read, fill, correct, and submit that form entirely by voice. You press a microphone, speak Thai, and GPT-4o-mini calls the page's tools while the page answers with structured, typed feedback instead of a red border. It reads the form aloud in Thai, fills each field from your speech (keeping names in Latin script, translating free text to English, matching dropdown options), self-corrects from typed validation errors, asks you in Thai when it isn't sure, and never submits without an explicit confirmation. How we built it TypeScript + Vite + @crxjs/vite-plugin, with Zod defining the tool boundary once for both JSON Schema and runtime validation. It's an MV3 extension with two content scripts bridged over postMessage: a MAIN-world script that reaches document.modelContext, registers the four tools (describe_form, read_form, fill_form, submit_form), and runs the GPT brain; and an ISOLATED-world script that owns the microphone and calls Paxa. GPT-4o-mini function-calling turns Thai speech into tool calls; Paxa Labs handles Thai text-to-speech (voice "yoyo") and translation; the Web Speech API handles voice input. Both APIs allow direct browser calls, so there's no proxy in the demo path. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP spec is unstable. The API had movedext to document.modelContext (deprecated in Chrome 150), so nothing worked at first. We instrumented the live Chrome 152 surface and dct: registerTool is async, there is no unregisterTool, duplicate tool names throw, getTools() returns inputSchema as a JSON strinarguments as a JSON string — none of which the docs said. We rebuilt against that. We also had to get the failed-vs-needs_human distinction righit, and work around audio autoplay needing a user gesture. Accomplishments that we're proud of The failed vs needs_human split: "failed" is reactive (the page rejected a value, so the agent retries), while "needs_human" is prensure, so nothing is filled and the agent must ask). A confidently-wrong value on a visa form is the failure mode that actually hurts peoplet. Error speech comes from stable Thai templates keyed by an enum — never model prose. And the read-back: a blind Thai user can finally percejust fill it. We verified the whole loop live in Chrome — one Thai sentence filled eight fields, translated the free text, matched a dropdown, rrected a bad ID number, and correctly left an unlabeled field empty. What we learned Don't trust the docs for an unstable API — instrument the runtime; it's the only truth. WebMCP's real value is constraint feedbnt can act on, versus a red border a human has to interpret. And accessibility and agent-usability turn out to be the same problem — a well-markeh. The Thai angle isn't a bolt-on; it's exactly the audience Western accessibility tooling has never served. What's next for a11y-mcp It works on sites with reasonable semantics, aells the truth when a site's markup is bad rather than filling wrong values silently. Next: move the API keys server-side and ship it publicly oncehind the Chrome flag. Deliberately out of scope for now — cross-page memory (a privacy design problem) and custom non- widgets. Everything in it is accurate to what we actualnt me to tighten any section, or add yourteammates / a "Built with" tech list (Devpost usually has a separate "Built with" tags field — I'd suggest: typescript, vite, chrome-extension, webmcp, opabs, zod, web-speech-api)? title: Virgil
pitch: Pin what matters while you browse. Learn it now or later, wherever you work.
about_excerpt: Pin what matters while you browse. Learn it now or later, wherever you work. Like Comment Story Updates Virgil beside the browser: pin the exact source, then learn now or return later. Learn from one grounded Pin, check understanding, or continue in another surface. One board across subjects turns scattered Pins into clear next actions. Check work against explicit criteria without rewriting it. A deliberate Google Notebook handoff through learner-approved source documents. The complete learning loop from browser capture to evidence-led recommendations. Detailed production architecture across Google Cloud, Gemini, ADK, Notebook, WebMCP, and Gemma 4. Inspiration Learning rarely arrives as a neat course. It appears while you browse: a useful passage, a difficult idea, a deadline, feedback on your work, or a source you know will matter later. Bookmarks preserve links, but not why they mattered. Chat can answer the current question, but it rarely stays connected to what you saved, what you understood, and what you should do next. We built Virgil to close that gap. What it does Virgil is a learning manager that stays beside you while you browse. When something matters, highlight it and press Pin . Virgil preserves the exact passage, source page, surrounding context, and your reason for saving it. You can keep browsing, learn it immediately in the side panel, or return when you have more time. The same Pin can move across several learning surfaces: Learn with Virgil in the browser side panel or full web application Continue with the grounded context in Gemini Use Virgil's bounded WebMCP study tools Send selected material to Google Notebook Return later through Board, Learn, My studies, Plan, Check, or Insights Learners can choose a one, three, or five minute path. Virgil keeps the source visible, checks understanding, accepts corrections, and records useful evidence. A wrong answer, correction, completed task, or recorded outcome can change the next recommendation for a visible reason. Longer work continues after the browser closes. Virgil can research, organise sources, identify gaps, update the learner model, prepare a lesson, and verify that the result remains grounded in the original material. It also supports an explicit local model route using Gemma 4. The learner chooses Cloud or Local deliberately. Virgil never silently changes providers. How we built it Virgil combines a Chrome Manifest V3 extension with a hosted TypeScript and Node.js application. The extension provides selected-text capture, a toolbar popup, and a persistent side panel. The hosted application gives the learner a larger workspace for Pins, studies, plans, reviews, outcomes, and background processing. The deployed model route uses Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite . Durable background work runs as an eleven-stage Google ADK SequentialAgent workflow: Intake Forage Cluster Survey Analyse Comfort Statements Prospect Garden Compose Verify The workflow runs in a Google Cloud Run Job , separate from the Cloud Run service that hosts the browser product. This allows work to continue safely after the learner closes the tab. Firestore stores durable, isolated learner state. Firebase Authentication identifies the learner, while the server verifies identity before accessing Firestore. The browser never talks directly to the database. Secret Manager , scoped IAM, and deny-all Firestore client rules protect the server-owned boundary. Each background run uses checkpoints, idempotency controls, and terminal receipts. Gemini calls retain the exact model and token record, and Virgil checks the learner's Cloud limit before sending a request. Google Notebook export is an explicit, one-way handoff through stable Google Drive documents for material to learn now, items on the board, and archived material. Virgil does not read Notebook responses back or silently treat them as learner evidence. Virgil also exposes four bounded WebMCP study tools and a read-only guide over visible product surfaces. For local processing, an authenticated hosted-to-local connector implements a fast text route using gemma4:12b-mlx . It does not open an inbound laptop port, does not silently replace Gemini, and preserves the same learning contract across providers. Data sources Virgil does not use a third-party training dataset. It works from material the learner deliberately supplies or approves: selected browser text, public source links, notes, documents, PDFs, images, syllabi, rubrics, deadlines, drafts, answers, corrections, and explicitly recorded outcomes. Virgil preserves source provenance and does not ingest private browsing history. Challenges we faced The first challenge was making capture genuinely lightweight. If saving a passage requires organisation, waiting, or an immediate model call, the extension becomes another interruption. We separated capture from processing so a Pin is saved first and learning can happen now, elsewhere, or later. The second challenge was keeping background work trustworthy. An eleven-stage workflow is only useful if the learner can see what ran, what changed, and whether it completed. We added durable checkpoints, retry-safe execution, stage receipts, and an independent verification stage before material can be promoted. The third challenge was maintaining one coherent product across several surfaces. The side panel, full Virgil page, Gemini, WebMCP, and Google Notebook could easily become disconnected features. We designed them around the same grounded Pin and made every transfer deliberate. The fourth challenge was privacy and provider control. Cloud and Local needed to be real choices, not labels over hidden fallback behaviour. Identity, storage, budgets, model routing, and provider selection are enforced in code rather than left to model judgment. What we learned The most important product lesson was that capture must stay almost free. The value appears later, when saved material becomes a useful next move rather than a larger pile. The most important agent lesson was that generated content is not a result by itself. A useful run needs a visible control, a durable receipt, a resulting product surface, and stored evidence that all agree. We also learned that adaptation should follow evidence, not a guessed learning style. Virgil changes its recommendation based on what the learner answers, corrects, postpones, and achieves. Finally, we learned that models work best inside clear boundaries. Gemini handles the deployed reasoning and teaching work, while deterministic code controls identity, persistence, budgets, ranking, provider selection, and recovery. What we are proud of Virgil is not a chat window attached to a bookmark manager. It is a working learning loop: See something. Pin it. Learn now or later. Record what changed. Get the next useful move. Virgil was conceived, designed, and built in full during the Google All Things Agentic Hackathon contest period. It contains no pre-existing product code. title: Documesh
pitch: One endpoint for agents to all documentation available: match any multi-stack error signature to the closest official documentation — cited, versioned, attributed. Every time.
about_excerpt: One endpoint for agents to all documentation available: match any multi-stack error signature to the closest official documentation — cited, versioned, attributed. Every time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Documesh WebMCP App Inspiration When something breaks at 2 AM, the fix is buried somewhere in dozens of doc sites, each with its own search, its own format, and its own idea of what "current version" means. And when an AI agent hunts for that fix, it's even worse: crawling page after page, scraping prose built for humans, burning thousands of tokens to find one config key. Then WebMCP shipped in Chrome, and I surveyed the ecosystem it created: 322 sites exposing 1,817 agent tools. The pattern was impossible to miss, more than thirty ship near-identical shallow search_docs wrappers, every one locked to a single vendor. Not one could answer a cross-vendor question, cite a doc version, or let an agent act on an answer safely. The docs layer of the agentic web was stuck in 2019: prose for humans, scraped or ignored by agents. The insight that became Documesh had two halves. Agents are the new visitors. When they arrive at a debugging problem, they need one declared, machine-actionable interface to all the official documentation, not thirty-eight walled gardens. And attention is the real cost, every scraped page dumped into context is tokens spent on noise, when one structured call should return exactly the doc section that matters, with the version and license attached. So I built the mesh I wanted my agent to have: one WebMCP endpoint for the whole stack. What it does Documesh gives agents a single endpoint for debugging multi-stack applications: match any multi-stack error signature to the closest official documentation, cited, versioned, attributed. Every time. Federated search of 47 sources synced for now (from a 555-source verified registry), 36,000+ doc sections. Every result carries source, version, license, attribution, canonical URL, and last-updated. Error → docs bridge paste a stack trace; explain_error extracts error signatures and returns the closest official doc sections, with an honest disclaimer: closest matches, not a diagnosis. Chainable answers: every result carries a machine-actionable object: exact config keys, language-tagged code snippets, runnable CLI commands, version applicability. The agent orchestrates; Documesh makes answers reliable enough to chain. An act surface with one rule: verify configs against documented keys, compare config conventions across vendors, check provider status ("is it down, or is it me?" anw, it caught a real Cloudflare outage during testing), report outdated docs. Every write is an append-only proposal, agents never mutate the mesh directly. All exposed as 9 tools across three protocols: WebMCP in the browser, MCP over Streamable HTTP, and plain REST. How we built it License-aware from the first byte: a Python indexer crawls docs through five ingestion patterns only via vendor-consented interfaces (llms.txt) or permissive licenses (CC-BY-4.0, MIT, Apache-2.0). Terraform (BUSL) and copyrighted docs are documented exclusions, license awareness as a feature. Always Search lives in the indexed, lived on Cloudflare. The extraction path has no LLM. deterministic extraction means excerpts are data, not instructions, and a hostile docs page can't prompt-inject through results. Provenance is enforced by schema audit (100% coverage), and search quality is CI-gated at ≥80% on real-world errors. Challenges we ran into The legal maze, most vendor docs are copyrighted with no agent interface; the rule that resolved it: vendor-consented interfaces or permissive licenses, excerpts + canonical links, never mirrors. Search architecture hit a wall 47 static shards loaded into Worker isolate memory (~65 MB) per query; D1 FTS5 dropped per-request memory to ~0. Honest machine-actionability the obvious shortcut was LLM extraction; deterministic is harder but never hallucinates a config key. Testing agents inside someone else's browser. WebMCP verification ultimately required a human, which is why the three-layer eval suite exists. Accomplishments that we're proud of 47 sources / 36k+ sections / 555 registry 100% response provenance agent-readiness score 89/A eval gate 5/5, the act surface caught a real Cloudflare outage during testing three protocols, one mesh an npm SDK so others can chain on it. All solo, all on $0 infra. What we learned Declared contracts beat scraping, the agent doesn't break in, it's invited. Provenance is a feature, not overhead -> "cited, versioned, attributed" became a schema rule instead of a slogan. The agent is the orchestrator, tools should be structured enough to chain, not call each other. Honest abstention survived every skeptical reading. And every constraint became a documented next step instead of a dead end. title: CityDefense: Fork the Future
pitch: The chat is temporary. The city remembers.
about_excerpt: The chat is temporary. The city remembers. Like Comment Story Updates The authenticated top-level page exposes exactly two WebMCP tools: get_city_context and place_stamp_bundle. One bounded WebMCP write updated the visible map and Activity Feed; the same D1-backed state survived reload. Live CityDefense in the Codex in-app browser with Site Tools READY and durable Branch v1 state. Inspiration Stateful work often outlives the AI chat that performed it. We wanted to explore a web-native collaboration model where the application—not a model-specific memory layer—owns the durable role, object identifiers, event history, and current state. A city-defense surface makes that problem visible. An agent can inspect a district and leave a canonical signal in the same live interface the human is watching. The signal remains after the interaction and after a normal page reload. What CityDefense does CityDefense is a focused, working WebMCP vertical slice. An authenticated Planner seat exposes exactly two Site Tools: get_city_context reads the active Branch, Central Ward state, current Branch Version, persistence mode, and recent activity without changing state. place_stamp_bundle performs one bounded, typed city action: placing a canonical confirmation stamp on district:CENTRAL_WARD . A successful write creates stable Event and Stamp identifiers, increments the Branch Version, updates the visible city and Activity Feed, and persists the result in Cloudflare D1. A normal reload restores the same state. Why WebMCP is a strong fit An agent should not need to infer button positions or reconstruct application state from pixels. WebMCP lets the authenticated top-level page expose the meaning of available operations, their input schemas, and stable application identifiers. The tools are bound to the same live Seat, Branch, and page state the human is viewing. Human and agent therefore work against one authoritative application state. How it improves the UX Typed inputs remove ambiguity about the target, operation, scope, and expected Branch Version. The human gets immediate visual feedback in the same page, while server-issued Event and Stamp IDs make the change auditable. Optimistic version checks prevent stale writes. A request ID prevents accidental duplicate mutation. Server-backed persistence means the result survives a normal reload instead of remaining only in the chat transcript or temporary browser state. What people and agents can now do together A human can authorize a temporary browser-agent thread to inspect a live, authenticated city Branch and perform a precisely bounded application action. The human immediately sees what the agent changed and can verify the durable record in the same interface. This establishes a reusable pattern for web applications where temporary agent sessions operate durable, human-inspectable state. How we implemented WebMCP The authenticated /play page registers two tools from the top-level document using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . No iframe is used. Both tools call the same server query and command paths used by the application. The server authenticates the Seat, authorizes the role and Branch, validates canonical IDs, checks the expected Branch Version, enforces request idempotency, writes the Event and Stamp to Cloudflare D1, and returns compact structured results. The flow was exercised in the Codex in-app browser: exact available tool set: get_city_context , place_stamp_bundle ; read operation invoked without mutation; one bounded write invoked; Branch changed from v0 to v1 ; visible game surface and Activity Feed updated; persisted=true ; normal reload restored the same state. Challenges The hardest part was keeping one trustworthy chain of evidence across WebMCP registration, authenticated Seat authorization, optimistic concurrency, idempotency, D1 persistence, browser-host behavior, human-visible feedback, public-source sanitization, and the deployed login path. We also had to ensure the submission described only the live vertical slice rather than future design work. Accomplishments and lessons learned We proved the complete loop: a real WebMCP host discovered the exact two-tool set; the browser agent invoked both the safe read and the bounded write; the write issued stable Event and Stamp identifiers; the visible page updated; and a normal reload restored the same D1-backed result. The key lesson is that durable human-agent collaboration is not only a model-memory problem. A web application can own continuity through authenticated roles, stable object references, typed actions, Event history, and visible state—while WebMCP connects an ordinary temporary agent session to that authoritative layer. What’s next The documented design extends this foundation with persistent Sentinel and Planner roles, structured city signals, crisis telemetry, semantic replay, owner-controlled branching, transport systems, and a data-driven crisis catalog. These are development directions, not claims about the current live submission. title: AI Governance Watch: A Source-Grounded WebMCP Briefing Desk
pitch: Source-grounded AI governance intelligence for humans and agents.
about_excerpt: Source-grounded AI governance intelligence for humans and agents. Like Comment Story Updates AI Governance Watch turns source-backed AI governance research into a shared briefing workspace for people and browser agents. Inspiration AI governance information is scattered across legislation, agency announcements, standards, procurement records, civil-rights proceedings, and technical guidance. Government leaders and policy professionals often need a concise briefing, but the distinctions behind that briefing matter. A proposal is not an enacted law. A publication date may differ from the underlying event date. An official announcement is not proof of an outcome. A general AI summary can easily blur those boundaries. We built AI Governance Watch to explore a more trustworthy model. The website remains the authority for its research and actions, while a browser agent helps the user search, verify, compare, and organize the information. What it does AI Governance Watch is a public, standalone WebMCP Briefing Desk built around a dated governance snapshot and a 62-entry Source Ledger. The application exposes four focused WebMCP tools: search_updates searches the locally bundled governance report using text and structured filters. get_source_record retrieves an exact Source Ledger entry by its registered identifier. compare_updates compares developments while preserving their dates, jurisdictions, statuses, confidence labels, and sources. build_briefing assembles selected records into a visible, session-only briefing for human review. A user can ask a browser agent to find developments relevant to a government leader, verify the underlying sources, compare the most important records, and construct a briefing focused on implementation, procurement, or public accountability. The resulting briefing appears directly in the application. The human can review, reorder, remove, or clear its contents before relying on it. This is a strong use case for WebMCP because traditional browser agents must interpret layouts, cards, filters, and buttons to determine what an application can do. That approach can be fragile when a page contains legally or operationally significant distinctions. WebMCP allows AI Governance Watch to expose its real domain functions as structured tools. The agent receives validated parameters, stable record identifiers, bounded outputs, and explicit fields for status, confidence, jurisdiction, event date, publication date, and source. How we built it The project uses the WebMCP Imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool . The four tools register only on the public /webmcp route. No tools register on the application’s unlock page or protected monitor routes. Each tool has a strict JSON Schema and repeats validation at runtime. Every registration promise is awaited before the interface reports that the tools are available. An AbortController manages the registration lifecycle and removes the registrations when the React component unmounts, preventing duplicate tools during remounts. The three research tools are read-only. The briefing tool changes only visible session-level React state. It does not write to a database, publish content, send messages, download files, or contact an external service. All tool results are returned as valid, bounded JSON strings. A single JSON.parse() exposes the top-level ok field and the applicable results, source record, comparison items, or briefing details. The implementation uses the application’s locally bundled August 22, 2026 report and Source Ledger without adding a crawler, external AI provider, or autonomous publishing system. AI Governance Watch treats source-derived material as untrusted content and labels every WebMCP tool accordingly. The implementation includes strict validation, same-origin exposure, read-only annotations, bounded outputs, exact identifiers, visible and reversible state, registration cleanup, and no database or network writes. The standalone route includes dated-snapshot and independence disclosures. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, sponsored by, or published by the Maryland Responsible AI Council, the State of Maryland, or any government body. If WebMCP is unavailable, the human interface continues to function and explains how to use a supported browser. Existing project disclosure The base Maryland AI Governance Monitor was created on August 22, 2026. Verified pre-challenge baseline commit: c5543d31d7cfc9bd4492bc539112c8801bada8b9 The WebMCP tools, standalone Briefing Desk, shared human-agent state, validation, tests, documentation, and public challenge interface were added during the WebMCP Challenge submission period. Final deployed challenge implementation: 310114de0dfcc426b19f9f2b438b9e7c54dbd487 Public standalone repository commit: 95b584f512cf27ca1ef9a3244f0121626f7a1799 Only the WebMCP extension and human-agent briefing workflow added during the challenge period are presented as challenge work. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was enabling useful agent action without weakening the information boundaries that make a governance monitor trustworthy. Search results needed to remain compact while preserving their status, confidence, source, jurisdiction, and two distinct date fields. The state-changing tool also needed to create meaningful collaboration without producing a hidden or irreversible external side effect. We also needed to separate the challenge project from the broader credential-protected Maryland monitor. The final /webmcp route is publicly accessible and uses a dedicated AI Governance Watch shell, while every existing monitor route remains protected. The resulting design keeps the agent workflow deterministic, inspectable, reversible, and under human control. Accomplishments that we're proud of Converted a human-first research interface into a genuine agent surface. Exposed a complete research-to-briefing workflow through four focused tools. Preserved exact sources, dates, statuses, and confidence labels. Created shared application state between the browser agent and human reviewer. Made the challenge desk publicly accessible without exposing the protected monitor. Demonstrated practical human-agent collaboration beyond a technical proof of concept. Added security annotations, runtime validation, output limits, failure handling, and lifecycle cleanup. Required no new backend, database, crawler, or external AI service. Published a clean standalone repository with no credentials, runtime secrets, authentication implementation, or unrelated application code. Verified all four tools in the live production application using Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP testing enabled. Confirmed that build_briefing creates visible state that a human can reorder, remove, clear, and reset on reload. Documented the exact pre-challenge baseline and challenge-period extension. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes an application’s real domain capabilities instead of turning every button into a tool. Four carefully designed functions were enough to let an agent complete a meaningful governance research workflow while keeping the website responsible for its evidence, validation, and state. We also learned that human-agent collaboration does not require unlimited autonomy. A narrow, visible, and reversible action can provide significant value while preserving trust. The project demonstrated that a website can remain the authority for its data and actions while giving agents a structured, safer way to assist the person using it. What's next for AI Governance Watch: A Source-Grounded WebMCP Briefing Desk Future versions could add versioned governance snapshots, user-approved exports, role-specific briefing formats, change detection between reports, claim-level evidence tracing, and additional vetted records. A private editorial pipeline could monitor an approved source registry, identify candidate developments, and route them for human verification before they enter a published snapshot. Any live ingestion, persistent storage, customer-specific workspace, or external action would require separate security, privacy, and editorial review. title: AyMateo Tickets
pitch: An agent-native ticketing experience where people and AI agents discover, compare, reserve, and prepare tickets for Bolivian cultural events together using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An agent-native ticketing experience where people and AI agents discover, compare, reserve, and prepare tickets for Bolivian cultural events together using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Initial WebMCP state — the demo event is loaded and the shared cart starts empty. WebMCP reserves tickets and the human-visible Shared Cart updates with the temporary hold. Checkout prepared — the agent stops before payment and explicit human confirmation is required. Human experience — users can open the full seating map and select seats manually without WebMCP. 1. Three seats selected and reserved in the standard human checkout flow before payment. Inspiration Ticket buying is usually designed for only one kind of user: a human clicking through a website. But AI agents are increasingly helping people search, compare options, and complete multi-step tasks. We wanted to explore what ticketing could look like if a website were designed for both humans and agents from the beginning. AyMateo already had a pre-existing ticketing platform with event pages, seat inventory, temporary holds, carts, and checkout infrastructure. For the WebMCP Challenge, we extended that platform with a structured agent-native interaction layer instead of building a disconnected chatbot or a demo that only returns static data. Our goal was simple: let an AI agent help a person discover a Bolivian cultural event, compare tickets, reserve real inventory, and prepare checkout while the human can see and understand every action happening on the same page. What it does AyMateo Tickets exposes seven WebMCP tools directly from the website: search_events get_event_details get_ticket_options add_tickets_to_cart remove_tickets_from_cart get_cart_summary prepare_checkout An agent can search for cultural events using natural language, retrieve structured ticket information, reserve tickets, inspect the cart, and prepare an order. The important part is that these actions are not isolated from the normal website. When the agent adds tickets, the human-visible Shared Cart updates too. The same browser session contains the ticket hold, prices, expiration state, and prepared checkout. The Agent Activity panel also makes the agent's actions visible instead of hiding them behind an invisible automation. Humans can still use the normal ticketing experience, including the full seating map. Payment is intentionally excluded from the WebMCP action surface. prepare_checkout only creates a pending order, and final payment still requires explicit human confirmation. How we built it The project uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Prisma, Docker, and WebMCP's imperative API. On the /webmcp page, the application registers tools through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool connects to real server-side ticketing logic rather than mocked frontend state. Event discovery reads published events and current ticket availability from PostgreSQL. Ticket mutations create real temporary seat holds using the same transactional inventory system used by the human ticketing experience. The WebMCP page and the normal website share the same browser checkout session, which allows human and agent actions to stay synchronized. For the challenge deployment, we created an isolated WebMCP environment with its own PostgreSQL database and fictitious Bolivian cultural-event data. The demo is publicly available over HTTPS at: https://webmcp.aymateo.com/webmcp The public submission repository is also separated from the private development history and was scanned for secrets before publication. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was making WebMCP interaction truly stateful. Searching for an event is easy, but reserving tickets means the agent must interact with temporary inventory holds, browser-session state, expiration rules, backend validation, and the same cart the human sees. We also encountered browser lifecycle issues while registering imperative WebMCP tools. Tool execution needed to remain stable even when React state changed, so registration and handler lifecycles had to be carefully separated. Another challenge was natural-language discovery. A strict substring search worked for controlled test inputs but could fail when an agent sent a phrase such as "Find me a Bolivian cultural or folklore event under Bs 100." We improved the search logic so it remains deterministic while handling meaningful words from natural agent requests. Finally, we wanted the agent to be useful without giving it unsafe authority. That led us to draw a clear boundary: agents may search, compare, reserve, and prepare checkout, but they cannot complete payment. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that WebMCP is not just decorative in this project. The agent can perform a complete, visible journey: event discovery → ticket comparison → real temporary reservation → shared cart → prepared checkout. The ticket reservation is backed by actual PostgreSQL inventory and transactional seat-hold logic rather than a fake demo cart. We also built the experience so that human and agent interactions remain inspectable. The Shared Cart and Agent Activity panels show what the agent changed, while the normal seating-map experience remains available for people who prefer to interact manually. The complete WebMCP flow is deployed publicly and has been tested end-to-end using the Model Context Tool Inspector. What we learned The biggest lesson was that agent-native websites should not necessarily replace human interfaces. WebMCP is most interesting when the agent and human can collaborate with the same application state. Structured tools give an agent a safer and more reliable way to interact with a website than interpreting buttons and rendered text, while the visual interface still gives the human context, control, and confidence. We also learned that tool design matters as much as implementation. Clear schemas, read-only annotations, untrusted-content boundaries, backend validation, and explicit limits on high-impact actions are essential when an agent can mutate real application state. What's next for AyMateo Tickets The next step would be expanding the agent-native experience beyond a single-event demo. Future work could include richer event discovery, multiple performances, accessibility preferences, price and seating recommendations, and agent-assisted seat selection on the visual seating map. We would also like to explore standardized confirmation flows for actions with higher impact while preserving the principle demonstrated here: AI agents can do the repetitive searching, comparing, and preparation, while humans remain in control of the final decision. title: RelayGrid
pitch: Safe, explainable WebMCP workflows for enterprise data grids.
about_excerpt: Safe, explainable WebMCP workflows for enterprise data grids. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Enterprise teams spend too much time constructing nested filters, checking why records were selected, and safely applying repetitive actions across dense operational tables. Natural-language filtering alone does not solve the risky part: understanding the interpretation, reviewing the impact, and reversing a mistake. What it does RelayGrid turns a natural-language goal into a visible, deterministic query tree over 7,500 synthetic radiology records. It shows the matching records and explains why each one matched. Stage-aware actions are processed in visible batches of at most 50 records: Preview separates permitted and protected records, explicit confirmation executes the saved plan, every action is audited, and the latest batch can be undone. Unsupported or out-of-order requests are rejected without changing data. Why WebMCP is essential RelayGrid exposes six high-level tools directly from the active page instead of asking an agent to scrape the DOM or guess which controls to click. WebMCP publishes the grid's real fields, supported operators, input schemas, and live context. ChatGPT constructs a schema-grounded Query AST; WebMCP invokes the requested tool; RelayGrid validates and evaluates it deterministically. The tools and the human interface share the same active query, Preview plan, workflow stage, status colors, and audit history, so every agent action is immediately visible and reviewable. The tools are: describe_grid apply_query explain_record preview_batch_action execute_batch_action undo_last_batch How we built it The page registers imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . A canonical JSON AST supports nested AND, OR, and NOT groups, comparisons, dates, Boolean values, enums, and sorting. A deterministic query engine validates and evaluates the AST against the full dataset. A shared transition engine powers both non-mutating Preview and confirmed Execute, while a workflow state machine exposes only context-valid operations and returns precise errors for invalid stages. The interface is built with React, TypeScript, Next.js, and Tailwind CSS. The public app is hosted with OpenAI Sites, and the complete MIT-licensed source is available on GitHub. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making natural-language intent safe without hiding the interpretation. We separated the agent's structured intent from the application's deterministic matching logic, then added stale-preview protection so execution can only use the exact reviewed plan. We also had to keep filtering global while limiting mutations to the current visible batch, preserve the active query as the next eligible batch loads, and make every scenario reset to a reproducible state. Accomplishments Non-trivial nested filtering over a realistic enterprise dataset Shared state between WebMCP tools and the visible grid Record-level explainability Preview, policy exceptions, confirmation, audit, and undo Safe 50-record batch progression Stage-aware command gating and a visible invalid-input test Four guided judge scenarios with exact prompts and expected outcomes Native Chrome WebMCP verification of all six tools against the published site What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a page exposes domain capabilities and safety contracts, not low-level UI gestures. A strong tool result should update the same state the human sees and leave enough evidence to verify, approve, or reverse the operation. How to test Open the live app and follow the sticky Judge Demo Guide . The Main scenario covers Filter, Verify, Preview, Confirm, Next batch, and Undo. Additional tabs demonstrate Review to Approve, Cancel to Undo, and invalid-input rejection. The repository includes exact judge instructions and verified QA results. All records are synthetic. No GitHub account, deploy key, access token, or project credential is required. What's next The same schema and action engine can support insurance claims, inventory exceptions, CRM worklists, and ERP approvals without building a separate copilot for every application. title: Relay
pitch: One plan for you and your agents.
about_excerpt: One plan for you and your agents. Like Comment Story Updates Relay command center with shared task board and live workspace metrics. Human Inbox for deliverable review and clarification decisions. Activity History records the full human, agent, and system handoff. Human approval completes RP-104 and unlocks dependent task RP-106. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Relay Inspiration People increasingly ask separate AI agents to research, build, write, test, and review, but conventional task boards were designed only for humans. They rarely expose whether a task has enough context for an agent, whether dependencies are actually complete, which agent has capacity, or which result still needs a human decision. We wanted a control center that makes delegation legible without handing away authority. What it does Relay combines a command center, six-column task board, Human Inbox, agent coordination roster, structured task packets, and complete activity history. It shows human-owned, agent-owned, unassigned, locked, blocked, review, and completed work. Agents can read the same workspace, find eligible Ready tasks, claim work, post progress and blockers, ask questions, and submit evidence-backed deliverables. Deliverables stop at Human Review; only the visible human interface can approve or reject them. Approval completes the task, records the handoff, and automatically unlocks eligible dependencies. How we built it Relay uses React 19, TypeScript, Vinext/Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, and ChatGPT Sites. A page-side WebMCP provider feature-detects the Model Context API and registers six schema-constrained tools exactly once. Both the interface and tools call the same /api/workspace service and pure domain-rule engine. A Cloudflare D1 table stores a versioned workspace aggregate; optimistic writes prevent silent lost updates. Runtime validators reject unknown fields and enforce input limits. The UI reacts to successful tool mutations through a shared browser event and remains fully usable without WebMCP. How WebMCP is used Relay registers get_workspace_context , list_ready_tasks , claim_task , update_task_progress , submit_deliverable , and request_human_input in the top-level page through document.modelContext.registerTool . Read tools are annotated read-only. Write tools explain their side effects, validate narrow closed schemas, mutate durable visible state, return verifiable transition metadata, and append activity events. Approval, rejection, clarification answers, deletion, and project finalization are deliberately not exposed as agent tools. Why WebMCP improves the experience Without WebMCP, an agent must infer a project from pixels or copied text and cannot safely act on it. Relay turns the website's own semantics into a structured, in-context capability layer. The agent can ask the page what is Ready, receive the exact task packet, perform a rules-checked mutation, and immediately show the person the same updated board. That removes brittle screen automation while preserving visible human oversight. What humans and agents can do together Humans set goals, own sensitive tasks, answer ambiguities, inspect evidence, request revisions, and make final decisions. Agents discover structured work, claim it within capacity, report progress and blockers, request missing context, and submit deliverables. Relay coordinates the handoff: dependency rules decide what becomes Ready next, the Human Inbox concentrates decisions, and Activity History makes every transition interpretable. Challenges we ran into The hardest design problem was making the page genuinely agent-operable without letting agent tools bypass human authority. We centralized every transition in one domain-rule layer, constrained schemas and ownership checks, and made deliverable submission terminate at Human Review. We also needed production state to be the same state judges see, so we used durable D1 persistence and optimistic workspace versions rather than a disconnected WebMCP mock or per-tab local storage. Accomplishments that we're proud of Six real page-side WebMCP tools sharing visible durable state Human-only approval and rejection enforced at the tool boundary and rule layer Structured task packets with dependency, capacity, and completeness checks Immediate visible updates plus a full before/after activity history Responsive, keyboard-friendly planner that still works when WebMCP is absent Deterministic demonstration reset, JSON export, D1 persistence, runtime validation, tests, green CI, deployment documentation, and a public MIT-licensed repository What we learned WebMCP works best when tools map to domain actions instead of generic clicks. Read tools should reveal enough context for good decisions; write tools should be small, auditable, and return proof of the exact state transition. Human control is strongest when it is structural—missing from the agent surface—rather than a warning agents are expected to obey. What's next for Relay Next we would add user-created projects, validated JSON import, role-based accounts, signed agent identity, scoped permissions, notifications, richer revision threads, project templates, and multi-workspace search. We would add real-time collaboration only after implementing and validating appropriate conflict resolution and authorization. Try the WebMCP flow Open the live app in a WebMCP-capable ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome evaluation environment. Confirm the lower-left activity dock reports six registered WebMCP tools. Ask: "Read this Relay project and give me a brief summary. Do not modify anything." Ask: "Show me the Ready tasks that the Research Agent can claim." Claim RP-104 , post progress, then submit a deliverable with evidence and a known limitation. Confirm the task stops at Human Review and appears in the Human Inbox. Approve it through the visible UI; confirm RP-104 becomes Completed, dependent RP-106 becomes Ready, and Activity History records the handoff. Refresh to verify the mutation persisted, then use Reset demo to restore the starting state. title: Waypoint — plan trips with your agent, beside you
pitch: A trip planner where your AI agent works INSIDE the page with you — visible, constrained by your 🔒 locks, and corrected by the app's own math
about_excerpt: A trip planner where your AI agent works INSIDE the page with you — visible, constrained by your 🔒 locks, and corrected by the app's own math Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Trip planners are single-player, and AI travel agents that book through a backend leave your screen behind — the agent works on a hidden copy of your data while you stare at a chat window. We wanted the third model: an AI agent that works INSIDE the page, beside you — visible, correctable, and constrained by your decisions. WebMCP made that possible, so we built Waypoint for The WebMCP Challenge. What it does Waypoint is a trip itinerary planner where you plan in the UI and an AI agent (ChatGPT desktop's built-in browser) works on the same board through 8 tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() : The agent reads the itinerary, adds/updates/removes activities, re-orders days, audits conflicts and budget. You keep hard control: activities you 🔒-lock are enforced in the tool contract — reorder_day refuses to move them and explains why. The agent literally cannot touch your locked lunch. The app does the math, the agent does the judgment: overlap detection and budget totals are computed deterministically and returned as JSON from every mutation, so the agent verifies its own changes in one turn. A shared activity feed logs every human and agent action — you watch your agent work beside you. In the demo video, the human resets the board mid-session, the conflict reappears, and the agent catches it and fixes it live on screen — leaving the locked lunch untouched. How we built it React 18 + TypeScript + Vite 6 + Tailwind v4 — a static site with zero backend and zero API keys : the browsing agent is the AI. src/webmcp.ts registers all 8 tools per the WebMCP spec , with JSON-Schema inputs and agent-oriented JSON returns (post-change schedule + new conflicts + budget deltas + actionable hints). Both WebMCP APIs in one app: set_trip_budget is also a real HTML <form> carrying the spec's proposed declarative attributes ( toolname / tooldescription / toolparamdescription / toolautosubmit ). Flag-enabled Chrome auto-registers the form as a tool — we watched it happen ("Duplicate tool name" was the happy error). An in-app agent simulator executes the identical tool implementations, so visitors without a WebMCP browser still experience the collaboration. State lives in a pure reducer + localStorage; tool mutations apply synchronously so a tool's return value always reflects its own change. Deployed on GitHub Pages; the Devpost video's voiceover is Deepgram TTS and the edit was scripted with ffmpeg. Challenges we ran into Chrome 152 expired the #enable-webmcp-testing flag — "Enabled" was a silent no-op until we also enabled the "Temporarily unexpire M150/M151 flags". Then "modelContext" in document returned true and all 8 tools registered. ChatGPT's regular chat only "searches" pages — Site tools attach only in the desktop app's built-in browser with Codex/Work (on GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra). Finding that flow took real debugging. A sneaky HTML5 validation bug: the budget form had step=5 + min=1 , silently rejecting round numbers like 150 — caught only because we functionally tested every form before recording. Hosting hurdles: a leftover CNAME in a GitHub user-pages repo was redirecting all our Pages URLs, and Git Bash mangled Vite's --base=/WebPoint/ into Program Files/Git/WebPoint/ on the first deploy. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full human + agent loop works end-to-end in the judges' environment: green "WebMCP live" chip, agent fixing conflicts live on screen, lock refusals, budget checks — verified, not mocked. The collaboration contract (human locks as tool-enforced constraints, app-returned math) is implemented exactly as designed. What we learned WebMCP flips the integration model: instead of the agent bypassing your UI, your UI becomes the agent's API — and that makes human control a schema-level feature , not a hope. Returning rich post-state from mutating tools lets agents self-correct in one round trip. Test the boring paths (HTML forms!) as hard as the shiny ones. What's next Multi-trip support and shared trips (multiple humans + agents on one board). A lock-approval flow: agent proposes, human accepts — one click at a time. Shipping a small "site tools" badge pattern other sites can copy. title: PantryPilot
pitch: Meal planning a human and an AI agent do together, live through real WebMCP tools, not clicks.
about_excerpt: Meal planning a human and an AI agent do together, live through real WebMCP tools, not clicks. Like Comment Story Updates PantryPilot High-Level Architecture PantryPilot Low-Level Architecture Diagram banner Inspiration Most "AI meal planning" demos are a chatbot that describes a plan in a text box - you still have to go copy the ingredients into a shopping list app yourself. WebMCP flips that: instead of an agent guessing at button selectors or a chat window narrating what you should do, a page can expose its actual capabilities as tools an agent calls directly. Meal planning turned out to be a good fit to prove that out. It's a genuinely tedious, recurring chore with real constraints - dietary restrictions, a grocery budget, food already sitting in the fridge about to go bad - the kind of multi-step, stateful task that's tedious for a human to do by hand and awkward for a chatbot to do by description, but a natural fit for an agent that can actually read and write app state. What it does PantryPilot is a meal planner and shopping list. A household sets dietary preferences (vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, dairy-free, nut-free, or a free-form avoid-list), tracks what's in the pantry (including expiry dates), and optionally sets a weekly grocery budget. From there: Search and rank a 16-recipe catalog by pantry match ("what can I make with what I already have"), by what's about to expire, by cost, by prep time, or by calories/protein. Plan a single day, or hand the whole week to plan-week , which fills every empty day under whatever constraints you give it - tags, max prep time, a calorie/protein ceiling, the remaining budget, and a "use up what's expiring" priority - while never overriding an active dietary restriction and never repeating a recipe in the same week. Get a shopping list generated automatically from the plan, aggregated across recipes and offset by what's already in the pantry. See a per-day and weekly nutrition summary. See exactly what happened and who did it - every action is logged and tagged human or agent - and undo the most recent change with one click, by either party. All of that is exposed as 19 WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() , so a human using the page and an agent acting on it are working in the same live session, not two separate experiences. How we built it Plain JavaScript, ES modules, no framework and no build step - the whole app is static files. The core design decision was a single shared domain module, js/actions.js , that owns every mutation (planning a recipe, updating the pantry, regenerating the shopping list, undo). Both the human-facing UI and every WebMCP tool's execute() call the exact same functions in that module, tagged with who's calling ( "human" or "agent" ), so there's no separate, more-powerful "agent path" that could drift out of sync with what a human can do. State lives in a small reactive store backed by localStorage ; the UI and the tool layer both subscribe to its change event, so a change from either side re-renders the page immediately. Since this session's sandbox had no WebMCP-capable browser to test against, we built an in-page "Agent Console" that drives the identical document.modelContext tool handlers through a plain form (pick a tool, edit the JSON arguments, run it) - the same code path a real agent would hit, just reachable without the Chrome 149 origin trial or ChatGPT's browser. It became a first-class part of the app rather than a throwaway test harness, since it also lets anyone verify every tool works without installing anything. We also wrote a node:test suite (32 tests) against js/actions.js directly, covering dietary-conflict enforcement, shopping-list aggregation, budget math, and the undo system, and ran full Playwright end-to-end passes over every tab and every tool before each push. Challenges we ran into No native WebMCP runtime to test against. We couldn't rely on trying it in a real agent client during development, so correctness had to come from the domain layer itself (validation, tests, the Agent Console) - the tool registration is thin by design, and almost all of the actual logic lives in code we could run and test directly. Keeping the agent from being more powerful than a human. It would have been easy to write a fast "agent path" that skips validation for convenience. Instead every tool routes through the same functions the UI uses, which meant designing actions.js first as a proper API, not as UI glue. Undo without duplicating history. A single logical action like "add a recipe to Monday" cascades into a second internal update (the shopping list regenerating). A naive undo implementation would push a separate history entry for that cascade and undo the wrong thing. Snapshots are taken immediately before the actual mutating store.update() call inside each action, and the shopping-list regeneration that happens as a side effect of another action is marked silent and skipped by the snapshot - so one user-facing action is always exactly one undo step, verified with a dedicated test. Shopping-list aggregation. Merging ingredient quantities across multiple recipes, scaling by servings, subtracting whatever's already in the pantry, and preserving which items are already checked off across a regeneration all had to work together without double-counting or losing state. Accomplishments that we're proud of 19 WebMCP tools that are genuinely load-bearing - plan-week does real constraint-based selection (dietary safety, no repeats, budget, expiry priority), not a lookup table dressed up as a tool. An architecture where an agent provably can't do anything a human couldn't do by clicking around, because they're the same code. A working undo system - a real implementation of the reversibility idea in WebMCP's own security guidance, not just a line in the description. 32 passing unit tests plus a full Playwright pass over every tab and every tool, run before every push. Zero backend, zero build step, deployable to Netlify, Vercel, or Cloudflare Pages in minutes. What we learned WebMCP's imperative API is small on purpose - registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) is most of it - which pushes the real design work down into the domain logic underneath, where it belongs. Tools that compose ( plan-week reusing search-recipes 's own ranking logic) produce much better agent behavior than a flat pile of unrelated CRUD tools would. Trust in a page an agent can write to has to be built into the architecture - one shared code path, validation at the domain layer, and reversibility - not asserted after the fact in a description. What's next for PantryPilot Testing against a real WebMCP origin trial browser and ChatGPT's browser once broadly available, beyond the in-page Agent Console. Redo (undo is currently one level deep, with no way back). Recipe ratings/favorites and multi-week history ("plan like last week"). A substitution tool that suggests a swap when an ingredient is missing or newly avoided. Optional lightweight sync so a plan isn't tied to one browser's localStorage . Exploring WebMCP's declarative API and cross-origin exposedTo , e.g. a grocery-delivery origin reading the shopping list directly. title: WebMCP Course Planner
pitch: A course planner where student and AI work from one live WebMCP state, so the AI builds valid schedules, adapts to manual edits, and leaves registration to the student.
about_excerpt: A course planner where student and AI work from one live WebMCP state, so the AI builds valid schedules, adapts to manual edits, and leaves registration to the student. Like Comment Story Updates UI Guesswork → WebMCP → Shared Live State AI SAW THE CHANGE Biology Semester Planner one live state Inspiration Course planning looks simple until you actually try to make everything fit. A student might want to stay under 15 credits, avoid early classes, keep Friday free, make progress toward their degree, and still protect time for work. One small change can make a schedule that looked fine stop working. That made me think about how an AI agent could help with this kind of problem. The obvious approach is to let the agent look at the webpage, figure out which buttons to use, click around, and check whether the result looks right. But that still leaves the agent guessing how the interface works. WebMCP suggested a different idea: what if the website could give the agent a structured way to read and work with the same live state the human is already using? That became WebMCP Course Planner. I wanted a small but convincing example of a future where a human and an AI agent don't take turns controlling a webpage, but collaborate through it. Human changes the website, the live state changes, the AI sees that new state through WebMCP, and the work continues. What it does WebMCP Course Planner is a fictional Biology semester-planning application where a student and an AI agent work on the same live course plan. The student gets a normal visual interface where they can choose courses, review a weekly timetable, set a maximum credit limit, avoid 8 AM classes, keep Friday free, block Tuesday from 11:00 AM to 12:00 PM, review conflicts, and make the final fictional registration decision. The website also exposes WebMCP tools that let an AI agent read the current planner state and update the selected courses. The interesting part happens when the human changes something directly. In the demo, the agent first creates a schedule containing STAT 210. Then I manually block Tuesday at 11 AM inside the planner. I don't tell the agent what I changed. When the agent reads the planner again, it sees the new blocked time and the conflict with STAT 210. It can explain the trade-off and help build a new plan while keeping the preference I set myself. The human and the agent aren't working from separate copies of the data. They're working with one live planner state. How I built it The application is built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, the WebMCP Imperative API, and Vercel. I kept the WebMCP surface very small. The production application exposes two tools. get_course_plan is the read-only tool. It gives the agent the current planning context: the student's preferences, selected courses, credit total, remaining requirements, available catalog information, conflicts, and whether the plan is ready for review. It reads the latest planner state, so if the student changes a preference directly in the webpage, the next call sees it. set_course_plan is the write tool. It lets the agent replace the selected course set using valid course IDs. Its authority is deliberately limited: the agent can change the course selection, but it cannot change the student's scheduling preferences and it cannot perform the final registration confirmation. Both the visual interface and the WebMCP tools connect to the same canonical React state. When the human changes something, the tools see it. When the agent changes something, React renders the result for the human to inspect. The planner calculates conflicts deterministically in application code rather than asking the language model to decide whether a schedule is valid. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what not to build. A university registration system gets enormous fast. I could have added prerequisites, live seat availability, authentication, registration windows, student databases, full degree audits, multiple semesters, and real registrar integrations. Those are interesting, but they would have made the most important WebMCP interaction harder to demonstrate reliably. So I kept coming back to one question: what is the smallest workflow that shows why WebMCP matters? That led to one student, one semester, one planner state, one read tool, one bounded write tool, and one strong human edit. The other challenge was deciding how much authority the AI should have. I didn't want a demo where the agent simply takes over the website. The student owns their preferences. The agent can read them and adapt the selected courses around them, but it can't quietly rewrite what the student wants. Final confirmation stays with the human. Finding that boundary made the project better. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The thing I'm most proud of in this project is Miu. As AI systems get more capable, they also get harder for normal users to follow. A student might ask ChatGPT to fix a schedule, see the timetable change, and know that something happened without understanding what the agent did in between. I wanted to make that interaction visible. Miu is a small on-page companion that gives WebMCP activity a personality. She isn't another AI agent and she doesn't hold her own state. She reacts to real events happening between ChatGPT, the WebMCP tools, and the planner. When ChatGPT reads the current planner through get_course_plan, Miu reacts as if she's checking the schedule. When set_course_plan updates the selected courses, she reacts to the planning work. When a human edit creates a conflict, her expression changes. When the plan becomes ready again, she responds to that too. So instead of an invisible tool call happening somewhere behind the interface, the student gets a visual cue for the current stage of the interaction. Without Miu, the workflow feels like: "AI, fix my schedule," and then something changes. With Miu, the student can follow it: the agent is reading, something changed, there's a conflict, the agent is adapting, the plan is ready. That mattered to me because I don't want agentic software to get less understandable as it gets more powerful. I want the human to stay aware of what is happening. I'm also proud of the smaller technical moment underneath all of this. I can change Tuesday at 11 AM from available to blocked without telling the AI what I changed. The next time ChatGPT reads the planner, it finds the newer state and reacts to the STAT 210 conflict. That's where the project stopped feeling like an AI operating a website and started feeling like a human and an agent sharing a workspace. And the whole thing only needs two focused WebMCP tools: read, act, human edits, read again, adapt, human reviews. Miu makes that invisible loop visible. What I learned Building for AI agents is not the same as giving an AI more control. Clear boundaries can make an agent more useful. A small tool with one responsibility is easier to understand, test, and trust than a generic tool that can manipulate everything. I also learned how much shared state matters. The most interesting part of WebMCP for me wasn't structured function calling. It was that the website can stay the source of truth while both the human and the agent work against that same current state. That creates a different relationship between an agent and a web application. The human doesn't have to stop using the interface because an agent is helping, and the agent doesn't have to pretend to be a human clicking through it. What's next for WebMCP Course Planner For this challenge I kept the project focused on one semester-planning workflow. There are plenty of directions it could grow: prerequisite checking, live seat availability, persistent student profiles, multi-semester planning, richer degree requirements, and eventually integrations with real university systems. I'd want to add those carefully rather than just increase the number of tools. The principle I want to keep is the one that shaped this version: the website stays the source of truth, the agent gets clear and bounded capabilities, and the human has a real role in the final outcome. This is a small experiment, but building it made the future of the web feel more concrete to me. Instead of asking whether AI agents will replace web interfaces, I think the better question is what humans and agents can do when the web is designed for both. Main changes: removed the mechanical bolding and the dramatic one-sentence-per-paragraph rhythm, cut lines that only existed to say the idea mattered ("That moment is the heart of the project", "Finding that boundary made the project much stronger" trimmed), joined the fragmented bullet list into prose, and dropped words like "genuinely", "intentionally", "completely", and "entirely" where they were just emphasis.
