title: Agent Native Portfolio
pitch: Recruiters get an instant, job-specific candidate fit—no digging or guessing. WebMCP lets agents bring the role, verify portfolio facts, and surface the strongest matches live.
about_excerpt: Recruiters get an instant, job-specific candidate fit—no digging or guessing. WebMCP lets agents bring the role, verify portfolio facts, and surface the strongest matches live. Like Comment Story Updates A portfolio that screens, tailors, and pitches itself to any AI agent — live, on the page, in front of you. Inspiration Recruiters spend ~30 seconds on a portfolio, and increasingly they browse with agents that have to scrape and guess. Meanwhile every developer sends the same static site to every visitor. WebMCP lets both sides collaborate instead: the agent brings the job, the site brings verified facts about the candidate, and the human watches the two work together in real time. What it does Built on top of my existing personal portfolio site (live since early 2026). Everything WebMCP-related — all 11 tools, the AgentBridge island, the scoring engine, the two Netlify Functions, and the /agent-traffic, /agents, /profile.json, and /llms.txt surfaces — was added entirely during the submission period (Sept 1–2, 2026). Nothing about the pre-existing site's design or unrelated content is part of this submission. This portfolio exposes 11 typed WebMCP tools that a visiting agent can call while its human watches the page respond: get_profile / search_projects / get_experience — structured facts: skills with honest self-assessed levels and years, projects with measured outcomes, not tech-tag lists get_evidence — verifies a specific claim ("has HIPAA experience") against the record, or says plainly that no evidence exists match_role — deterministically scores a pasted job description against the candidate's real skills; a visual fit report renders on the page live, gaps included tailor_view / reset_view — the live page reshapes itself for a role: a prominent, highlighted banner appears under the name, projects reorder by relevance, unrelated work dims generate_resume — a role-targeted résumé assembled from the same structured data, downloadable as a PDF at /resume compose_inquiry — drafts a message into the contact form with an "AI-composed, review before sending" banner; the human always reviews and clicks send — it never submits on its own sign_guestbook / get_guestbook — agents leave notes under their own identity, visible on a public dashboard Every tool call is logged (anonymously) to a public /agent-traffic dashboard — live agent analytics for a personal site, showing which tools get used and what agents have signed the guestbook. Why WebMCP fits this use case A portfolio's entire job is to be legible to a stranger fast. Static HTML forces every visitor — human or agent — through the same generic narrative. WebMCP lets the site expose structured, callable truth instead: an agent doesn't have to scrape and infer whether a candidate fits a role, it can ask, and get a deterministic, evidence-backed answer. How it improves the experience For the visitor's agent: verifiable answers instead of scraped guesses. For the human on the other end: they watch their agent's work land live — a fit report appears, the page visibly reshapes around their role, a résumé is ready — instead of reading a wall of text summarizing what happened elsewhere. What people and agents can accomplish together that wasn't possible before A recruiter pastes a job description into their agent. Together, in one session: the agent gets a scored, honest fit assessment (not a sales pitch — real gaps are called out); the page itself re-prioritizes around that role in front of the recruiter; a tailored résumé is ready to download; and if there's a fit, the agent drafts an outreach message that the recruiter reviews and sends themselves. None of this — live personalization driven by an external agent, with the human co-present and in control of every outward action — was possible with a static site. How we built it Astro 5 (static output) + React 19 islands + Tailwind v4, on Netlify. A single persistent island ( AgentBridge , mounted with transition:persist ) registers all 11 tools once and survives Astro View Transitions, so tool state (a tailored view, a fit report) persists across page navigation. Matching is deterministic — no LLM call, no hallucination risk — reading a structured skills/projects/experience dataset ( bio.json + content collections). Two Netlify Functions with Netlify Blobs power the guestbook and the public analytics dashboard, rate-limited and PII-free. Non-WebMCP agents get the same data via /profile.json and /llms.txt. Challenges we ran into Netlify Blobs' list() reads are only eventually consistent — new guestbook entries took ~40s to appear. Fixed by switching to a maintained index at a fixed key (strongly-consistent get/set), the same pattern already used for the analytics counters. Early tailor_view changes were functionally correct but visually easy to miss (a small badge and a secondary paragraph changed, while the name headline — the most visually dominant element — never did). Fixed by adding a prominent, pulse-highlighted banner directly under the name. The résumé PDF export (browser print-to-PDF, no PDF library) silently rendered several headings invisible when the browser was in dark mode. Fixed by forcing solid ink on every element inside the résumé under @media print . A legacy ng build override left in Netlify's dashboard settings (from before this was ever an Astro site) silently broke every PR's deploy preview for months — found and fixed as part of this work. Deploy previews and production turned out to share the same Netlify Blobs store rather than being isolated per deploy context — test writes during development leaked into the live public guestbook. Built a secret-protected admin endpoint to clean that up, which now also serves as basic spam moderation going forward. Accomplishments that we're proud of A fully working, evidence-based fit report an agent can trust, live page personalization that's actually visible without scrolling, and an agent-facing guestbook + public analytics dashboard — nobody else appears to have built "agent SEO" analytics for a personal site. What we learned A correct tool isn't the same as a convincing one — tailor_view tool worked perfectly but was almost invisible until we made the change land somewhere a human would actually notice. Trust boundaries need to be designed, not just enforced in code: compose_inquiry tool drafts and discloses, but a human always has to click send. And "agent-native" means building to the open navigator.modelContext standard, not to any one agent's quirks — testing across ChatGPT, Chrome, and a separate coding agent made that concrete fast. What's next for Agent Native Portfolio Extracting the reusable core (context detection, registration manager, generic read tools, deterministic scorer) into a standalone open-source Astro integration package, so any developer can make their own portfolio agent-native by defining one structured data file. title: AgentDesk
pitch: Human-agent workspace built with WebMCP. Agents can analyze, compare, and propose; consequential decisions require human approval. Every action is visible and auditable.
about_excerpt: Human-agent workspace built with WebMCP. Agents can analyze, compare, and propose; consequential decisions require human approval. Every action is visible and auditable. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration As browser agents become capable of taking real actions, the important question is not only what an agent can do, but what it should be allowed to commit. We built AgentDesk around one principle: Agents get real tools inside the workspace. Humans keep the decisions that matter. Instead of building another chatbot that only recommends actions, we wanted to explore a practical human-agent boundary using WebMCP. What it does AgentDesk is a shared human-agent workspace where an agent can operate on structured workspace state through real WebMCP tools. The agent can: Read workspace state with get_workspace Analyze requirements with analyze_plan Compare options with compare_options Create or update tasks with create_or_update_task Prepare consequential decisions with prepare_decision The final decision boundary is human-only. resolve_decision rejects attempts from an agent or system with human_approval_required . The rejection does not mutate workspace state. A human can then approve or reject the pending decision through the AgentDesk UI. Once approved, the workspace state changes and the Decision Ledger records the resulting chain. How we built it AgentDesk uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Zod, and WebMCP through the native document.modelContext API. The shared workspace state is the source of truth for both the UI and WebMCP tools. Six WebMCP tools expose different capability levels: reading, changing, proposing, and human-only resolution. The domain layer contains the actual workspace operations, budget calculations, option comparison, task mutations, and decision lifecycle. The human-approval invariant is enforced at the domain layer as well as at the WebMCP boundary. This prevents the authority rule from being merely a UI restriction. The Decision Ledger is derived from the workspace decisions, options, budget state, and activity history to provide an auditable view of proposal, approval, and commit. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making the human-agent boundary real rather than cosmetic. It would have been easy to add an "Approve" button and call the project human-in-the-loop. Instead, we separated proposing from committing. prepare_decision can create a pending proposal with rationale, cost impact, and projected budget effects without changing consequential state. When an agent attempts to resolve that decision, the system explicitly returns human_approval_required and states that no workspace state was changed. We also had to ensure that the UI, WebMCP tools, domain layer, budget calculations, and Decision Ledger all remained consistent around the same source of truth. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that the core security boundary is enforced by the application rather than simply demonstrated visually. The agent can genuinely interact with the workspace through WebMCP, but it cannot cross the human-only decision boundary. We also built the Decision Ledger to make the complete chain visible: Agent proposed → decision held at the gate → agent could not commit → human approved → workspace updated. The project includes automated tests covering the tool layer, domain behavior, decision authorization, persistence behavior, capability boundaries, and presentation. What we learned We learned that giving an agent tools is only half of the problem. A useful agent interface also needs explicit capability boundaries and enforceable authority boundaries. We also learned that proposals and commits should be separate operations. An agent can prepare a meaningful recommendation without receiving authority to execute the consequential decision. WebMCP made this model particularly interesting because the agent interacts with real application capabilities rather than simply exchanging text with a chatbot. What's next for AgentDesk The current project demonstrates the core human-agent execution model using a concrete event-planning scenario. Next, we would generalize the workspace beyond event planning and support more domains where agents can perform useful work while humans retain authority over consequential actions. We would also expand the capability and audit model, add richer workspace integrations, and explore more granular policies for different types of decisions. The long-term goal is a reusable human-agent control plane for applications where agents can do the work without silently becoming the decision-maker. title: AI Boardroom
pitch: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide.
about_excerpt: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide. Like Comment Story Updates One COO and 6 Ai Assistant Agents Inspiration Founders often need to make consequential decisions with incomplete evidence, changing constraints and too many disconnected conversations. AI Boardroom puts a founder and a browser assistant in one shared decision room where specialist perspectives, evidence and trade-offs remain visible. What it does AI Boardroom gives one browser AI six specialist perspectives: Product, Evidence, Commercial, Operations, Technology and Chair. WebMCP lets the assistant read the live brief, request named roles, post evidence-linked contributions, respond when constraints change, and retrieve the exact decision record. The central interaction is deliberately human-controlled. A fictional launch budget changes from R20,000 to R8,000; the previous recommendation becomes stale, the assistant reads the new revision, and a new recommendation can be prepared without rewriting the earlier record. The founder reviews alternatives and reservations, then approves, rejects or requests revision in the visible page form. This is stateful collaboration rather than a detached chatbot transcript. The app does not run six independent AI workers or call a model API. One browser assistant adopts the roles and the human retains the final decision. How we built it The app is built with the OpenAI Sites React and TypeScript scaffold, Vinext and D1. Native document.modelContext.registerTool exposes seven WebMCP tools: start_session, get_boardroom_context, update_agenda, request_perspective, add_contribution, prepare_recommendation and get_decision_record. UI actions and WebMCP tools share the same API and persistence logic. Mutation inputs use expectedRevision for optimistic concurrency and operationId for safe retries. Evidence is stored with the relevant contribution and rendered as untrusted text. The visible review channel is a workflow boundary, not proof of human identity. Challenges The design challenge was making an AI council useful without pretending that six hidden agents or automatic consensus exist. We made the roles explicit, preserved disagreement, invalidated recommendations when the brief changed, and kept approval out of the WebMCP tool surface. A second challenge was handling uncertain browser or network outcomes without duplicating or overwriting decisions. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the agent can operate on the same visible, stateful interface as the human. Structured tools make the collaboration legible, while revision checks, evidence snapshots and a human review stop make the limits legible too. What's next Production use would require stronger identity and access controls, consent design, privacy and retention rules, abuse and rate-limit controls, independent security review, and integrations governed by explicit human approval. Disclosure All briefs, budgets, evidence and decisions in this project are fictional. The app does not make purchases, send messages, or change external systems. Browser-generated council text is created at runtime and is not preseeded consensus. title: Booksy reloaded
pitch: Booksy Reloaded lets an AI compare Tampa professionals, securely use a customer's history, book exact matches within preset limits, and ask only when a substitution needs a decision.
about_excerpt: Booksy Reloaded lets an AI compare Tampa professionals, securely use a customer's history, book exact matches within preset limits, and ask only when a substitution needs a decision. Like Comment Story Updates About the project Booksy Reloaded is our answer to a simple question: if a customer already knows who they like, what they normally book, how they pay, and how much they are comfortable spending, why should booking the next appointment still take so many steps? We built an original two-sided marketplace where a customer can ask an AI to find or rebook an appointment through WebMCP. The customer can set practical limits once, such as using the usual provider and service, paying in person, and staying at or below $50. If the appointment fits those rules, the AI can complete the repetitive work. If the provider is unavailable, the service changes, the requested time changes, or the price goes above the limit, the system comes back and asks the customer what to do. The project also shows the provider side. Once an appointment is created, the exact same appointment appears in the provider's calendar and activity feed. That makes this more than an AI filling out a booking form. It demonstrates how a customer, an agent, and a provider can share one visible workflow. Inspiration I am an avid Booksy user, especially when I want to get a haircut. That made it a good starting point for thinking about WebMCP because it is a real consumer habit I already understand. Even when I know the barber I want, I still have to open the app, find the provider, check availability, and repeat a decision I have made before. I wanted to see what this experience could look like if I could simply ask AI to handle it. The goal was not just to make booking faster. It was to let the website give the AI structured, reliable information while the customer stays in control of the rules that actually matter. What we built Booksy Reloaded is an original bilingual marketplace for six fictional beauty and wellness professionals in Tampa, Florida. Three customer profiles see the same provider pool ranked differently. Returning customers can ask for their usual service in natural language without starting over. An AI agent can use fifteen WebMCP tools to inspect authenticated relationship history, find rebooking options, weigh goals, specialties, proximity, budget, review themes, language, accessibility, promotions, and availability, explain every score and tradeoff, and prepare an appointment. The customer sets a practical policy: use the usual provider and service, pay in person, and stay at or below $50. Exact matches can be booked when the customer asks. A different provider, service, requested window, or higher price returns a structured exception and requires a new customer choice. The final tool creates one idempotent sandbox appointment. Switching to the provider account shows that same appointment on the professional's calendar and activity feed. Why WebMCP The website owns provider facts, services, prices, availability, and booking policy. The person owns intent, preset limits, and exception choices. The agent handles the tedious comparison across those constraints. WebMCP lets all three responsibilities meet in one shared visible state without making the agent rediscover cards, buttons, and calendars through visual browser automation. This is not a generic booking form. It is a two-sided marketplace demonstration. The agent's completed action becomes visible to both the customer and the fictional provider, while any material change invalidates stale availability, review, approval, and booking state. How we built it Booksy Reloaded registers fifteen top-level imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Human controls and agent tools call the same deterministic marketplace engine. The recommendation score is inspectable and has no paid placement. A new med spa can compete through price, specialty fit, and availability while its shorter review history remains visible. Returning-customer history is explicit site data, not invisible model memory. Closed JSON schemas limit every input. Read-only actions are annotated, customer history is unavailable before the site-owned demo session is established, and the final booking tool requires confirmed: true plus either an exact policy match or explicit exception approval. The English and Spanish interface uses the same provider and appointment state. All marketplace records and generated portraits are original fictional demo assets. A small browser-local database keeps the public project credentialless and lets a booking created in the customer account appear in the provider calendar without exposing a public production backend. Challenges The first challenge was getting the entire project up to spec while still making it visually appealing and easy to understand. It needed to feel like a real consumer marketplace, not a technical screen built only to show tool calls. We also needed to show what happens after the booking, so we built the customer account, the provider workspace, the provider calendar, and the activity feed around the same appointment state. The biggest design challenge was security. While building this second project, the AI kept returning to security and confirmation. That was useful, but asking the customer to approve every familiar appointment would defeat much of the reason for using an agent. We wanted something secure but also smart. Our answer was parameter locking. The customer can approve a reusable policy for an exact match and change the price ceiling from the account. The workflow fails closed if a provider, service, time window, or price changes. We considered building a real passkey server for exception approval, but this public demo is hosted as a static site. A real passkey requires server-generated challenges and server-side signature verification, so we decided not to fake that security step. Instead, the demo clearly shows the secure boundary we could connect to a production authentication service later. What we learned We learned that security does not have to mean asking the same question every single time. A customer can define clear limits in advance, and the agent can act inside those limits while still pausing for the decisions that are actually different. That is a much more useful version of customer control. We also learned that WebMCP is strongest when tools describe the customer's goal instead of browser mechanics. search_providers , compare_providers , find_rebooking_options , and request_booking are more reliable and understandable than asking an agent to repeatedly scan cards and click through calendars. Finally, we learned that the provider side matters. The agent should not stop after making a recommendation in chat. The completed action should become visible to both sides of the marketplace. Seeing the same confirmed appointment in the customer account and provider calendar made the project feel much closer to a real-world workflow. Results The current policy-aware benchmark uses ten engine calls through final booking status. Across 25 reproducible runs, all 25 completed successfully. The latest artifact measured approximately 84 input plus 1,968 output JSON I/O tokens, for an estimated serialized payload footprint of 2,052 tokens. These are transparent JSON-size estimates, not provider-billed model tokens, and the benchmark excludes rendering, networking, native WebMCP transport, and model inference. Booksy Reloaded is a sandbox. It contacts no real provider, collects no payment, sends no notification, and consumes no production inventory. What was built during the challenge The Booksy Reloaded application, original interface, fictional marketplace data, generated provider portraits, bilingual experience, personalized and returning-customer flows, customer and provider views, browser-local persistence, fifteen WebMCP tools, tests, native browser verifier, benchmark, and submission materials were created during the challenge. title: CallReclaim: Agent Rescue Desk
pitch: WebMCP turns a missed-call inbox into a cited rescue plan and editable reply—while the owner keeps every approval and nothing can send.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns a missed-call inbox into a cited rescue plan and editable reply—while the owner keeps every approval and nothing can send. Like Comment Story Updates Five WebMCP tools are ready. The agent compares authorized calls and stages a cited one-slot rescue plan; only the owner can accept it. After owner acceptance, draft revision 1 enters the owner checkpoint. The reply stays editable and unsent; stale edits cannot be queued. Caller text is marked untrusted. It cannot create approval, review, or send capabilities. Why I built it A detailing shop owner can miss a call while working on a car. The hard part is not writing a text. It is deciding which call deserves attention when several people have different deadlines, job values, and follow-up permissions. I built CallReclaim around one rule: the agent can prepare an editable reply, but only the owner can accept the plan and complete review. Nothing is sent. What it does The demo opens with five fictional missed calls. The owner starts by saying how many replies they can handle in the next 30 minutes. A WebMCP agent can then: Compare the inbox and read the current owner brief. Stage a rescue plan that fits the owner's capacity. Link each choice to exact facts recorded on the page. Open an accepted lead and inspect its conversation. Draft an editable reply after the owner accepts the plan. Queue the current draft revision for owner review. The plan and draft appear in the same desk the owner is already using. The owner can accept or clear the plan, edit the reply, mark the draft reviewed, discard it, or reset the demo. The agent cannot accept its own plan. It cannot approve a draft. It cannot complete review. It cannot send a message. Those capabilities do not exist in the tool surface or the application. Why WebMCP fits A normal interface is good for reading one conversation. The harder task crosses several calls and constraints. WebMCP lets the agent compare the calls, cite the records, and stage a plan in the same live desk the owner sees. The owner and agent also need a safe way to take turns. If the owner changes the reply capacity, the previous plan no longer applies. If the owner edits a draft, the old revision cannot be queued. Agent drafts also remember which accepted plan and owner brief authorized them. Without this handoff, the owner has to compare the calls and rebuild the context alone. Here the agent does that cross-record work while the owner keeps the customer decision. How I built it The challenge app is a one-page React and TypeScript project built with Vinext and deployed on OpenAI Sites. The top-level page registers five imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : list_demo_leads inspect_demo_lead stage_rescue_plan draft_owner_reply queue_for_owner_review The tools and visible controls use the same state rules. Inputs are bounded with JSON Schema and runtime checks. Tool registration is page-scoped and cleaned up with AbortSignal . Caller transcripts are marked as untrusted content. The records are deterministic and fictional. There is no database, model API, authentication, telephony provider, tracking, secret configuration, or messaging backend. The hard parts The first hard part was capability design. A warning that says "do not send" is weak if a send capability still exists. CallReclaim has no send tool and no messaging backend. The second hard part was protecting the owner's edit. When they change the plan or draft, the old agent version is rejected. The third hard part was caller text aimed at the agent. One fictional caller tries to give the agent an instruction. The app treats that as caller text, not as a command. The demonstrated inspection creates no plan or draft. What I tested The frozen release passes 14 focused tests, lint, TypeScript checking, production build, dependency audit, and public CI. The tests cover schemas, output budgets, capacity limits, unauthorized leads, unsupported citations, stale plans, owner acceptance, draft gating, owner edits, stale revisions, reviewed work, tool cleanup, and browsers without WebMCP. I also ran the prompt matrix through fresh public in-app-browser sessions. Direct requests staged the same cited proposal. Ambiguous requests made no changes. Unsafe send requests stopped at the owner gate. Missing follow-up requests stopped before drafting. Stale queue requests preserved the owner's edit. The adversarial reference test found one real identifier bug, which was fixed and re-run before submission. What I learned The important decision was what to leave out. The agent can prepare a reply. It cannot approve or send it. Revision checks protect the owner's latest work in code. The agent sorts the inbox. It stages a plan linked to recorded facts. It prepares an editable reply. The owner completes review. Nothing is sent. What I built during the challenge CallReclaim's broader missed-call concept existed before the challenge. During the challenge, I built a separate WebMCP edition with an owner capacity check, a cited plan, five page tools, and revision checks that stop stale work. What's next This submission stays fictional. A production version would require customer authorization, secure tenant data, verified messaging consent, provider integrations, audit logging, and a separate operational rollout. title: Campaign Arena
pitch: AI agent searches KOC creators and proposes deals via WebMCP Site tools. Policy violations pause the tool call until you decide — approve, reject, or let it self-correct.
about_excerpt: AI agent searches KOC creators and proposes deals via WebMCP Site tools. Policy violations pause the tool call until you decide — approve, reject, or let it self-correct. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Influencer marketing is a $32.5 billion industry growing at 33% annually — and the #1 investment priority for marketers in 2026 is AI-powered creator matching. Yet most campaign tools still treat the agent and the human as two separate systems: the agent guesses through a UI, the human reviews a report afterward, out of context and too late to change anything. Influencer campaigns have a split-second problem: the agent that's fast enough to search hundreds of creators and score them against policy is the same agent you don't trust to commit ¥12,000,000 without asking. We built Campaign Arena to close that gap — not by slowing the agent down, but by giving it a shared workspace where both agent and person operate on the same live page. What it does Campaign Arena is a KOC (Key Opinion Consumer) campaign workspace where an AI agent and a human operator work side-by-side through four WebMCP Site tools: searchKOCs(platform?, category?) — filters the creator roster and updates the dashboard KOC grid in real time proposeDeliverable(kocKey) — proposes a deal; auto-confirms if safe, or blocks until the human decides if a policy violation is detected getTrustScore() — returns the current AEGIS trust score, autonomy tier, and factor breakdown endSession() — closes the session, locks all mutations, and writes the final trust report A policy engine enforces five rules: blacklist, platform allowlist, campaign budget ceiling (hard limit), split-deal detection, and single-deal approval threshold. An AEGIS trust score tracks the agent's behavior across the session — LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH autonomy tiers control how much the agent can auto-confirm without asking. Every event — proposed, blocked, rejected, corrected, confirmed — is recorded in order in the Session Ledger. After a rejection, the agent suggests a policy-safe alternative. That suggestion is a nudge, not an automatic commit. How we built it Single HTML page using React 18 (via CDN) and JSX compiled to vanilla JS at build time — no framework build chain, no server. All WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool directly in the top-level page. The production build strips runtime Babel using esbuild and is served as a fully static site on Vercel. The core of proposeDeliverable is a Promise-based human-in-the-loop gate: waitForDecision(kocKey) stores a resolver in a Map . The tool await s that Promise. The human's Approve or Reject button resolves it — and only then does the tool return its result to the agent. ChatGPT is correctly suspended while the dialog is open and cannot proceed until the person has acted. Challenges we ran into Making the approval flow genuinely transactional was the hardest part. The tool result must be truthful about what happened — not what was intended — so the agent's next action is always correct. Concurrency edge cases required the most attention: double-clicking Approve or Reject, closing the session while a simulation is mid-flight, an orphaned Promise resolver when an intermediate await throws. Each of these could silently corrupt the ledger or committed spend. We addressed them with synchronous instance flags and careful finally cleanup — the part that took longest to get right. The policy engine also required precision: split-deal detection depends on cumulative confirmed spend across proposals, which must account for prior session history to trigger correctly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The proposeDeliverable tool genuinely blocks as a Promise until the human decides. This means the agent's next tool call is always based on the real outcome. Agents using Campaign Arena cannot accidentally double-spend, propose the same creator twice, or close the session while a decision is pending — these return bounded error objects instead of hanging or corrupting state. The shared-page model is the real accomplishment: the agent does not guess through visual controls, and the person never loses context or authority. Both see the same ledger, the same trust score, the same mission progress — in real time. What we learned Designing for agents and people simultaneously forces contract clarity that is easy to skip in ordinary apps. Every tool needs a precise description, strict input schema ( additionalProperties: false , enum for allowed values), and a result that accurately reflects state — not just the happy path. We also learned that the shared-page model is fundamentally different from building an API. The tool and the UI must stay in sync: what the ledger shows and what the tool returns must always agree. Getting that right is a design problem as much as an engineering one. What's next for Campaign Arena Persistent session ledger so campaigns survive a reload Multi-agent support: a planning agent hands deals to an execution agent, with the human overseeing both Audit export: the session ledger as a signed, timestamped record for compliance review Expanded policy rules: geo restrictions, budget pacing, and creator exclusivity windows Built With css html javascript react vercel webmcp Try it out campaign-arena-webmcp.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I led the WebMCP integration and policy engine design, built the human-in-the-loop approval flow, and handled all bug fixes and hardening before submission. My teammate handled UI design, character design, and initial project scaffolding with ChatGPT. title: Kopilotti Sales — Kopilotti WebMCP Challenge build
pitch: A 24/7 digital sales channel—not a chatbot—where an agent can research and prepare, but only a human can approve deterministic price evaluation and its auditable receipt.
about_excerpt: A 24/7 digital sales channel—not a chatbot—where an agent can research and prepare, but only a human can approve deterministic price evaluation and its auditable receipt. Like Comment Story Updates Kopilotti WebMCP turns a fictional car storefront into a 24/7 digital sales channel—not a chatbot. Car shopping is repetitive enough for an agent, but consequential enough that a human must stay in control of the commercial outcome. WebMCP is a strong fit because the page exposes the safe parts of the journey—search, comparison, condition review, draft preparation, and approved evaluation—as explicit, schema-constrained tools. The agent calls those capabilities directly instead of scraping the page or guessing at controls. Every action updates the same visible workspace and activity log the person can inspect, which makes the experience clearer, more reliable, and easier to correct. Together, the person and agent can move a sales conversation forward outside dealership opening hours. The agent can find vehicles, compare factual fields, retrieve condition facts, and prepare a €90,000 non-binding discussion draft independently. It cannot cross the consequential boundary by itself: approval for deterministic evaluation is a page-native human action that is never registered as a tool. A scripted .click() has no effect. After approval, a fixed public policy evaluates €90,000 against the fictional €95,000 asking price as exactly 9,473 basis points, returns COUNTER at €92,150, and resists an agent policy-override attempt. The resulting JSON receipt records the policy and approval evidence with binding: false and transmittedToDealer: false. The implementation uses five narrowly scoped WebMCP tools—search_vehicles, compare_vehicles, get_vehicle_condition, prepare_price_discussion, and evaluate_price_discussion—over fictional in-memory inventory. WebMCP and manual controls call the same application functions, while the activity log labels the real invocation source as webmcp, manual, or human-ui. When a browser does not expose WebMCP, a persistent readiness banner immediately offers the complete, honestly labeled manual path rather than presenting the application as broken. Inspiration Car shopping is a useful test case for agentic browsing: the research is repetitive, the facts are structured and the commercial consequences matter. A useful agent should accelerate the research without silently gaining authority to negotiate, contact a dealer or create a transaction. Kopilotti WebMCP explores that boundary. The browser agent gets explicit, schema-constrained tools. Every result appears in the same workspace the person sees, and the final commercial action remains outside the agent's authority. What it does The demo registers five WebMCP tools: search_vehicles filters and sorts a fictional six-vehicle inventory. compare_vehicles returns a factual side-by-side comparison without choosing a winner. get_vehicle_condition selects a vehicle and displays its versioned condition facts. prepare_price_discussion creates a pending, local and non-binding discussion draft. evaluate_price_discussion evaluates only the exact draft that received page-native human approval and creates a machine-checkable receipt. Approval is deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. The page also contains a numbered manual fallback for browsers that do not expose WebMCP; it uses the same application functions and labels each invocation honestly as manual. How we built it The project is a dependency-free static web app using semantic HTML, modern CSS and JavaScript modules. WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() and include bounded JSON Schemas, descriptive titles, explicit annotations and abort-signal handling. Tool execution calls small, independently tested domain functions and then updates the visible UI. A page-native approval gate binds the human action to the current draft context. The public demo policy produces deterministic ACCEPT, COUNTER or ESCALATE results and an in-memory JSON receipt. There are no production APIs, external data sources, customer records or hidden production pricing rules. Why WebMCP matters here Visual automation would have to infer search controls, card layouts and state transitions. WebMCP gives the agent stable named capabilities with typed inputs and clear safety boundaries. The user can watch the same workspace change after each tool call, making the process observable and correctable. Safety and responsible design All vehicle data is fictional. No tool accepts personal data. Search and comparison are explicitly read-only. Preparing a price discussion creates only pending local UI state. No tool can grant human approval, set or override policy, submit an offer, contact a dealer or create a transaction. Evaluation runs only after page-native human approval and produces a non-binding, unsent demo receipt. The repository contains no proprietary Kopilotti Sales decision logic or production data. Challenges The main design challenge was making price evaluation genuinely useful without allowing the agent to authorize itself. The solution was a reversible drafting step, a page-native approval action that is absent from the tool manifest, context-bound validation and a deterministic receipt. What we learned Agent-native design is not just adding an API to a page. The tool contract, the visible UI and the authority model must agree. A narrow tool with an honest description can be more useful than a broad tool that leaves the user uncertain about what the agent actually did. What's next Test the tool contracts against additional WebMCP-capable agents. Expand manual assistive-technology and cross-browser regression coverage. Explore dealer-approved, explicitly confirmed handoffs without giving the model pricing authority. Built with WebMCP, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Node.js test runner AI-assisted development disclosure Development was AI-assisted with OpenAI Codex. Product scope, trust-boundary decisions, verification and submission remain human-directed. This open challenge build is separate from the private production Kopilotti Sales engine and contains none of its source code, data or private pricing rules. title: Patchwork WebMCP- let people and AI agents discover projects
pitch: Turn good intentions into neighborhood action. Patchwork lets people and AI agents discover projects, build plans while keeping them human-approved. Use any AI browser to query it, like ChatGpt.
about_excerpt: Turn good intentions into neighborhood action. Patchwork lets people and AI agents discover projects, build plans while keeping them human-approved. Use any AI browser to query it, like ChatGpt. Like 2 Comment 1 Story Updates 1 Patchwork WebMCP Small actions. Shared momentum. Patchwork is an open-source neighbourhood planning workspace where people and browser agents discover opportunities, build practical plans, and draft new community needs together—while every publication or commitment remains under human control. Project links Live application: https://patchwork-webmcp.pages.dev/ Source repository: https://github.com/lsantos2000/patchwork-webmcp Demo video: https://youtu.be/so9sDOxzeJY Browser testing guide: resources/docs/browser-test.md Visual evidence: README.md#visual-evidence License: MIT Created by Leonardo Santos-Macias as an individual submission to the WebMCP Challenge. Inspiration People often want to help their neighbourhoods but struggle to turn good intentions into a practical plan. Finding opportunities, comparing them, and deciding what fits into a free afternoon takes effort. The push to actually build it was personal. Our newborn, Ellie Victoria, arrived premature—a fighter from the first day—and is growing into a wonderful child. Watching my wife become a mother, with our other children and our family around us, changed how I think about spare time: it stopped being an afternoon and became the gaps between feeds, school runs, and appointments. That is what most volunteering asks you to have, and what a new parent never does. So Patchwork starts from a smaller question: what if an agent did the searching, comparing, and fitting-it-together work, and handed back something small enough to actually do—while the person kept every decision that mattered? Small actions. Shared momentum. What it does Patchwork is a WebMCP-powered neighbourhood action prototype. People can explore example community projects, filter opportunities, and assemble a plan that fits their interests and available time. A compatible browser agent can work with the same project data and the same visible plan through structured tools. Instead of merely describing what someone could do, it can help organize those opportunities inside the application. The Discover tab covers intent-aware project search, an editable weekend plan, device-local persistence, community-project drafts, and draft-only pledges. Plan together adds negotiated planning: the person sets a time budget, selects and pins projects, and reviews the agent's proposed before-and-after revision. Action history records accepted and rejected planning actions without pretending a real-world pledge was sent. The boundary is deliberate: preparing a plan is not making a commitment. An agent can propose changes, draft a new local need, and prepare a pledge draft, while approval remains a separate step in the interface. The prototype does not send pledges to real organizations. Why WebMCP This workflow maps naturally to declared website capabilities: search project records, combine selected IDs into a plan, inspect a shared workspace, propose a revision, structure a new community need, and prepare a pledge draft. Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer meaning from visual pages, scrape text, or automate fragile click sequences. Patchwork instead exposes typed operations and structured results through the website itself. The agent works with the application's real records and constraints, while its results update the same interface the person is viewing. This creates a continuous human-agent experience. A person can inspect an agent-created plan, adjust it manually, preserve a pinned choice, reject a proposed revision, approve a community-project draft, or undo an accepted workspace change without transferring information between a chat response and another form. How I built it I built Patchwork with React and TypeScript, using Vinext for the Cloudflare Pages production build. Project-domain helpers provide deterministic catalogue search, planning, constraint checks, and persisted-data validation. A reusable React hook registers WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool({...}), falls back to navigator.modelContext, and unregisters tools during cleanup. Each handler validates or normalizes its input, calls the relevant domain helper, updates shared React state, and returns a structured response—so agent actions and manual interactions stay connected. The WebMCP integration exposes six tools, scoped to the active workflow. Discover provides: search_neighborhood_projects build_action_plan propose_neighborhood_project pledge_support Plan together and Action history provide: get_workspace propose_plan_revision Proposal results include revision information and a before-and-after comparison. Stale revisions and impossible constraints produce explicit conflicts rather than silent compromises. The human-control boundary is built into the results. propose_neighborhood_project returns human_approval_required with published: false; only the visible approval control adds the draft to the browser-local catalogue. pledge_support returns confirmation_required and never delivers a pledge. Local browser storage preserves the Discover plan between visits on the same device. I also added automated tests, browser-testing instructions, screenshots, and submission documentation. The source is publicly available under the MIT license. Challenges I ran into One challenge was making agent actions understandable. A successful tool response is not enough—the person needs to see what changed and keep the ability to review it. WebMCP handlers therefore update the same React state as the human controls, so both participants share one visible source of truth. Another was distinguishing discovery from planning: finding projects that each fit a time limit does not automatically produce a combined plan within that limit. State synchronization also required care. A plan must stay consistent when it is edited manually, created through a WebMCP tool, restored from local storage, or revised in the negotiated workspace. The implementation validates persisted records and uses workspace revision numbers so a stale agent proposal cannot overwrite a newer human choice. I also fixed production styling problems and state disappearing after navigation. Throughout, I worked to distinguish actual browser evidence from automated tests and edited demonstrations. Accomplishments I'm proud of I'm proud of building a shared interface where people and agents work with the same plan, rather than two separate experiences. Patchwork demonstrates why WebMCP is useful here: structured tools let an agent use the application's own data and actions without relying on fragile page scraping. Review and consent are part of the design, alongside persistence, testing, and documentation. A deployed, open-source WebMCP application that stays fully usable without an agent. Six structured tools across two scoped workflows. Explicit approval, rejection, conflict, and undo behaviour. Device-local persistence with validation and graceful storage-unavailable messaging. A responsive interface with production styling on Cloudflare Pages. Automated coverage plus separately recorded native WebMCP evidence. Clear prototype boundaries: demonstration data, browser-local publication, and no real pledge delivery. What I learned I learned that useful agent integration depends as much on clear boundaries as on capability. An agent should understand what an action changes, what stays a draft, and when approval is required. WebMCP is most compelling when it exposes meaningful domain actions rather than recreating low-level clicks. Small, well-described tools give an agent enough structure to help while keeping the application's rules in the application. Honest constraints also improve the agent experience. A structured conflict response is more useful than silently dropping a pinned project or exceeding a time budget, and revision tokens protect a person's newer decisions from stale proposals. I also learned that a convincing demonstration must make those distinctions visible. Good documentation and reproducible tests help explain both what works and what remains a prototype. How AI tools were used Patchwork does not embed its own model or chatbot. It exposes browser-local WebMCP tools that a compatible external agent can discover and invoke. Codex assisted with React and WebMCP implementation, debugging, automated testing, documentation, browser evidence, and demo production. Google Gemini was also used during the project. Piper generated the synthetic narration for the demo, and FFmpeg assembled and validated the final video. ChatGPT WebMCP discovery query A ChatGPT conversation was used to query the live application with the request: Discover tools at https://patchwork-webmcp.pages.dev/ The query identified six WebMCP tools across Patchwork's workflows. title: Port Authority
pitch: A browser-only workbench for documenting and auditing the tool contracts a page exposes through WebMCP. It turns the page’s agent-facing surface into something a developer can inspect.
about_excerpt: A browser-only workbench for documenting and auditing the tool contracts a page exposes through WebMCP. It turns the page’s agent-facing surface into something a developer can inspect. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it# PORT AUTHORITY The harbor master for WebMCP. No agent docks on vibes. Port Authority is a browser-only workbench for documenting and auditing the tool contracts a page exposes through WebMCP. It turns the page’s agent-facing surface into something a developer can inspect, redline, approve, and export. An agent may inspect contracts, run deterministic checks, stage one bounded revision, and preview documentation. It cannot approve its own proposal. Only the visible human controls can grant clearance, return a revision, or reset the manifest. Live application: port-authority-webmcp-preview-0904a.mjohnson1307.workers.dev The working loop ARRIVE → INSPECT → REDLINE → CLEAR → EXPORT The accepted registry starts at revision 1 with six deterministic findings. One is a deliberate, concrete contradiction in the documented propose_contract_revision example: - baseRevision: "1" + baseRevision: 1 The schema requires an integer, but the seeded example supplies a string. The golden path is real application state, not a scripted mock: The agent lists the five registered tools. The agent audits the accepted manifest and receives six findings. The agent inspects propose_contract_revision and confirms INVALID_EXAMPLE from declared contract data. The agent stages the smallest allowed revision: the same example array with only baseRevision changed from "1" to 1 . The accepted registry remains unchanged while the revision waits in DRY DOCK . A human reviews the exact payload and selects GRANT CLEARANCE — Accept this exact revision or RETURN TO SHIPPER — Reject without changing registry . After clearance, the accepted revision becomes 2, the audit count becomes five, and INVALID_EXAMPLE disappears. SHIP’S PAPERS opens four synchronized projections of the accepted registry. Demo prompt Audit the loaded Port Authority manifest. List the WebMCP tools, run the deterministic contract inspection, and inspect propose_contract_revision. If the declared data confirms that its example uses a string where baseRevision requires an integer, stage the smallest bounded revision that changes "1" to 1. Do not infer runtime behavior and do not grant your own clearance. After the human grants clearance: Reinspect the cleared manifest, report the remaining finding count, and open the four accepted artifact projections. Confirm whether the repaired example now matches its declared schema. To reset the demo, select RESET LOCAL CATALOG and confirm the browser-local reset. Reloading the page also starts a new in-memory session. Five registered berths WebMCP tool What it may do list_tool_contracts List the five accepted contracts, revisions, annotations, side-effect classes, and finding counts. get_tool_contract Inspect one exact accepted contract and visibly select it in the workbench. audit_tool_contracts Run deterministic checks over declared contract data and populate CUSTOMS INSPECTION . propose_contract_revision Validate and stage one fixed-name, allowlisted metadata revision for human review. It cannot accept it. preview_contract_bundle Open four projections generated from the currently accepted registry. The tool names are fixed. Revision patches reject unknown fields, stale base revisions, invalid schemas, empty changes, and attempts to rename executable tools atomically. One accepted source src/contracts/registry.ts is the canonical contract registry. That one accepted source drives: top-level document.modelContext.registerTool() metadata; the visible HARBOR MAP and registration explorer; deterministic audit findings; staged before/after revisions; registration metadata; the canonical JSON manifest; the Markdown reference; and the OpenAPI 3.1 documentation chart. Output schemas, examples, recovery guidance, lifecycle states, prerequisites, privacy notes, and side-effect classifications are Port Authority documentation extensions. They are not presented as native registerTool() fields. The OpenAPI artifact is documentation only. Synthetic paths carry explicit x-webmcp-* , x-documentation-projection: true , and x-network-endpoint: false markers. It creates no HTTP routes or network endpoints. What the audit proves Port Authority checks only facts supported by the accepted contract data, including: missing, malformed, or vague contract fields; missing, open, or internally inconsistent input schemas; examples that do not validate against their declared schemas; conflicts between read-only annotations and declared side effects; missing untrusted-content hints for developer or external output; missing recovery guidance; duplicate tool names; and disagreements between the accepted registry and generated projections. It does not prove runtime behavior, actual side effects, privacy, security, or semantic truth. Those remain developer-review responsibilities. No model call or external service is used by the deterministic audit. Agents may inspect, audit, stage, and preview. Only visible human controls may accept, reject, or reset. WebMCP is progressive enhancement. The visible workbench remains usable when document.modelContext is unavailable. Runtime registration is imperative on the top-level document.modelContext ; there is no WebMCP polyfill or dependency on introspection APIs. title: Repro Ledger
pitch: An evidence desk where agents turn synthetic vulnerability evidence into validated reports while humans keep approval and export control.
about_excerpt: An evidence desk where agents turn synthetic vulnerability evidence into validated reports while humans keep approval and export control. Like Comment Story Updates RL-101 awaiting human review after the agent completed evidence-bound validation. The redesigned review gate binds four evidence signals to the exact report revision awaiting human approval. why this exists Vulnerability reports often fail at the boring boundary between evidence and claims. A reproduction may be real while the impact is unsupported, the asset is out of scope, or the final report quietly overstates what the evidence proves. Repro Ledger makes that boundary visible. It is an editorial evidence desk where an agent can inspect synthetic vulnerability evidence, draft a structured report, validate every claim category, and request review. A person still controls approval and export. Everything in the demo is fictional. Northstar Cloud, its .invalid assets, the cases, requests, responses, and program rules are synthetic. what people and agents can do together The seeded workspace contains three deliberately different cases: RL-101 is in scope and has evidence for scope, reproduction, impact, and a negative control. RL-102 is in scope but lacks impact and negative-control proof, so review remains blocked. RL-103 is reproducible but explicitly out of scope, so review remains blocked. An agent can list the cases, inspect the program rules and evidence, write a report draft, run deterministic validation, and request human review. Those edits appear in the same workspace the person is viewing, without a reload. The person can edit the draft, approve the exact revision, and download the approved report as Markdown. Approval and export are intentionally not agent tools. Any later edit returns the report to draft and invalidates the previous approval. why WebMCP is the right interface DOM automation would make an agent infer the task from labels, layout, and click targets. That is brittle, and it blurs the permission boundary between drafting and approval. Repro Ledger exposes six imperative WebMCP tools with strict inputs: list_cases, get_case_context, get_evidence, update_report_draft, validate_report, and request_human_review. Read operations are annotated as read only. All tool results are marked as untrusted content. Unknown IDs, cross-case evidence IDs, malformed inputs, and invalid transitions fail with actionable errors. The WebMCP surface is deliberately narrower than the interface. The agent gets the actions it needs to assemble an evidence-backed report, but it cannot approve, export, reset fixtures, or mutate program scope. Unsupported browsers still get the complete manual workflow. how it was built The app uses React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind/Kumo, Zod Mini, Vitest, Testing Library, and Cloudflare Workers. React state and a versioned localStorage record back both the human UI and the WebMCP tools. Canonical program rules, scope verdicts, evidence text, and evidence coverage signals are compiled fixtures rather than trusted browser storage. A shared reducer keeps human and agent edits on the same transition path. Validation is deterministic. A reviewable report needs a bounded title, summary, impact, severity, three to ten reproduction steps, an in-scope verdict, and linked evidence covering scope, reproduction, impact, and negative control. Approval is a session-only grant bound to the current report revision. Markdown export escapes untrusted structure before download. challenges and lessons The hard part was not registering tools. It was keeping the trust boundary honest when local state, evidence content, and agent output are all potentially untrusted. That led to strict persisted-state parsing, cross-case ownership checks, revision-bound approval, cleanup for partial tool-registration failures, bounded schemas, export escaping, and tests for forged approval state and invalid transitions. The main lesson is that WebMCP works best as a small command surface, not a second copy of the UI. The site should define the task model, validation rules, and permissions. The agent should operate inside those rules, and the person should keep the decisions that require judgment or accountability. try it Live demo: https://repro-ledger-webmcp.repro-ledger.workers.dev/ Source: https://github.com/StressTestor/repro-ledger Demo prompt: Review the open cases in Repro Ledger. Select the strongest in-scope finding with sufficient evidence, produce a concise evidence-backed report, validate it, and request human review. Do not approve or export it. title: Saturate
pitch: Saturate is a system design and LLM serving simulator that exposes its canvas to ChatGPT over WebMCP. You describe a change, the agent makes it on the graph, and you both watch where it saturates.
about_excerpt: Saturate is a system design and LLM serving simulator that exposes its canvas to ChatGPT over WebMCP. You describe a change, the agent makes it on the graph, and you both watch where it saturates. Like Comment Story Updates Home Idle Collapsed Sustaining Held Inspiration System design is part of my daily job as a software engineer. I built Backpressure first, for the same reason: I wanted to see how a design behaves under load without waiting for production to tell me. Saturate is the version I wrote for OpenAI's WebMCP challenge. Different codebase with a small version of the engine engine. What it does You drop components on a canvas, wire them up, and push load through. The example I used: 40 inbound requests, 12 tool calls each, is 480 calls dumped on a pool of 4 workers. Queue cap is 50. Parallel fills that queue and the run dies. Serialize the loop (one tool at a time) and the same 480 drain. I see nodes, heat, ERROR on the wires. ChatGPT sees queue depth, utilization, a verdict. We edit the same session. How we built it Vite, React, TypeScript. The sim is a deterministic tick engine in the tab: no API, no auth. Burst -> Agent -> Pool (plus whatever you drag) compiles to { burst, fanout, mode, poolSize, queueCap } . The buttons and the WebMCP tools call the same handlers. Tools register on document.modelContext when it exists. Always-on: get_board , run . State-gated: list_parts , add_component , set_burst , set_agent , then apply_fix and explain_verdict after a collapse. Eight tools, and serialize / widen pool / batch only exist when the board is actually dead. Cloudflare Pages hosts it. The header that made modelContext exist is Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 . Skip origin isolation and the API never shows up, flag or not. Challenges we ran into The integration itself was the easy part. I already had MCP running on my machine, so once I found the right browser (the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in one, ⌘⇧B, Terra) the tools registered and got called on the first try. The real work was cutting Backpressure down. The original has a full component library, a general system design mode, and an LLM serving model with TTFT and KV-cache math. None of that fits a single-board demo where the point is watching an agent fix one bottleneck. Deciding what to delete took a few hours, and most of that was resisting the urge to bring one more node type along. Two things did catch me. document.modelContext never appears without Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 , so origin isolation is a hard requirement and the failure is silent. And after a held run the card printed 0, because it was reading the last tick's empty queue. The number that matters is completed: 480. Accomplishments that we're proud of Eight tools, same path as the UI, gated on board state. The agent and I hit identical handlers, so there is no separate agent surface to drift out of sync with the buttons. Same board plus same load always gives the same result, which means a fix the agent suggests is actually verifiable rather than a plausible-sounding guess. What we learned I over-registered on the first pass. Gating tools on board state came out of that: an agent offered apply_fix on a healthy board will reach for it. The WebMCP surface is narrower than the spec reads. Origin isolation and the right browser are both hard requirements, and neither failure mode announces itself. What's next for Saturate The loop I wanted is working (read the board, run it, watch it collapse, serialize, run again). Before adding node types I want that loop to hold under boards the agent builds itself rather than ones I hand it. Backpressure is already live and in use, with the full component library, general system design, and the LLM serving model. Saturate was the small board I needed to prove the WebMCP surface out on. Now that the eight tools work against the same handlers the UI uses, the plan after the challenge is to bring that WebMCP into Backpressure, where there is a lot more for an agent to actually reason about. title: Seating Repair
pitch: A WebMCP workspace for repairing constrained plans while keeping humans in control
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workspace for repairing constrained plans while keeping humans in control Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A surprising number of everyday operational problems are really placement problems in disguise. You have a set of people, tasks, items, vehicles, or events, a limited number of places or resources, and a collection of rules that determine what can go where. We see this everywhere. Guests need to be assigned to tables. Patients need beds. Employees need shifts. Classes need rooms. Aircraft need gates. Jobs need machines. Inventory needs storage locations. In every case, the basic question is the same: how do you put the right thing in the right place while respecting all the constraints around it? Creating the first plan is only part of the challenge. The harder part often comes later, when reality changes after the plan has already been accepted. A guest suddenly needs an accessible table. Two people can no longer sit together. A VIP needs a specific position. A resource becomes unavailable. A manager makes a last-minute decision that should not be undone. At that point, the goal is not to throw everything away and optimize from scratch. It is to repair the existing plan while preserving as much of what already works as possible. Traditional optimization systems are good at solving structured problems, but people do not usually describe operational changes as formal constraints. They say things like "keep these two apart", "do not move this person", or "this group needs to stay together". An AI agent can help translate that kind of natural-language intent into structured constraints, but there is another problem: the agent may be working from an older version of the plan while a person is still editing the live page. That creates a very real failure mode. A person can make an important manual change, and the agent can later overwrite it simply because it is still acting on stale state. We wanted to explore a collaboration model where that cannot happen silently. We chose seating because it makes the larger idea easy to see. A guest represents an entity that needs to be assigned. A table represents a limited-capacity resource. "Together" and "apart" rules behave like clustering constraints. Accessibility and fixed-table rules represent eligibility and placement requirements. A locked guest represents a human decision that the agent is not allowed to override. Seating Repair is our way of exploring how WebMCP can bring these pieces together: natural-language agency, deterministic constraint solving, live application state, and direct human control, all operating on the same shared planning surface. What it does Seating Repair is a WebMCP application for solving and repairing constrained placement problems while a person and an agent are both working on the same live plan. The demo uses 12 fictional guests and three tables because that makes the idea easy to understand at a glance. But underneath the seating interface, the application is dealing with a more general planning problem: limited-capacity resources, people who must stay together or apart, fixed placements, eligibility requirements such as accessibility, decisions that a human has explicitly locked, and the need to keep as much of the existing plan unchanged as possible. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can read the exact current state of the board, understand the active constraints, add new hard constraints from a person's request, repair the plan, and then validate the result. The goal is not simply to press an "optimize" button and generate a completely new seating arrangement. In a real planning workflow, many existing decisions are already correct and should stay that way. A useful repair needs to preserve what still works, respect every hard constraint, treat human-locked placements as authoritative, change only what is necessary, and verify that the final result is actually valid. This becomes especially important when a person and an agent are working at the same time. If the agent reads the board and a person then moves or locks a guest, the agent is no longer allowed to write using the old version of the plan. That stale write is rejected with STATE_CHANGED. The agent has to read the page again and continue from the decision the person actually made instead of silently overwriting it. In the demo, this is easy to see: a person can move Grandma Rose to a different table and lock her there. The agent can then add another constraint, repair the remaining conflicts, and validate the board while leaving Grandma Rose exactly where the person placed her. Seating is the domain we chose to demonstrate the idea, but it is not the limit of the underlying pattern. The same kind of constrained allocation and repair appears in restaurant and event operations, protocol seating, workforce scheduling, room and resource allocation, patient-to-bed assignment, airport gate reassignment, and many other situations where a working plan has to adapt as constraints and human decisions change. The current build is intentionally focused on demonstrating that shared coordination model clearly. It is not meant to pretend that one seating demo is already a complete product for every one of those industries. Instead, it shows the core interaction pattern: an AI agent can help repair a constrained plan, while the live application remains the source of truth and human decisions remain in control. How we built it We built Seating Repair as a lightweight TypeScript app with Vite. Everything runs in the browser, with no backend and no separate database for the agent. The seating board that the person sees is the same state the WebMCP tools work with. We kept the WebMCP side intentionally simple and exposed only four tools. One reads the current seating state, one adds hard constraints, one repairs the plan, and one validates the result. That was enough to cover the full interaction we wanted to demonstrate without turning the project into a large collection of overlapping tools. We also did not want the language model itself to be responsible for deciding whether a seating plan is correct. The agent can understand a request such as "keep these two apart" or "do not move this guest", but the actual planning is handled by deterministic application code. The repair logic runs in the browser and searches for an arrangement that satisfies all of the current constraints. It checks table capacity, together and apart rules, fixed-table requirements, accessibility, and human locks. When there is more than one valid solution, it prefers one that changes as little of the current plan as possible. Human edits are treated as first-class state changes. A person can move a guest manually and lock that placement. Once a guest is locked, the agent cannot move them during a repair. There is no hidden tool option that lets the agent ignore the lock; the person has to unlock that guest first. One of the main things we wanted to get right was what happens when the human changes the board while the agent is working. Every change to the seating plan increments a revision number. When the agent tries to change the plan, it has to provide the revision it previously read. If the board has changed since then, the write is rejected with STATE_CHANGED. That means the agent cannot quietly apply an old plan over a newer human decision. It has to read the current board again and continue from there. Repairs are also atomic. The solver works on a snapshot first and only updates the live board after it has found a complete valid solution. If the constraints cannot be satisfied, the current plan stays as it was instead of being left in a partially changed state. The manual UI and the WebMCP tools share the same store, validation logic, and constraint model. We wanted there to be one source of truth rather than one version of the plan for the person and another version for the agent. For the demo, state is stored in browser localStorage, which keeps the project self-contained. We also added tests for the behaviors we considered most important: constraint validation, deterministic repairs, minimum-change solutions, human locks, unsatisfiable plans, stale revisions, invalid tool input, and WebMCP tool execution. The overall design is fairly simple on purpose: the agent handles natural-language intent, WebMCP gives it structured access to the live application, and normal deterministic code is still responsible for enforcing the rules and deciding whether the final plan is valid. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not the seating solver itself. It was deciding how a person and an agent should safely work on the same plan without one silently undoing the other. At first, it is tempting to treat the agent like a normal automation flow: read the state, calculate a better arrangement, and write the result back. That works until the person changes something in the meantime. Once we started testing that interaction

title: Thought Amplifier — Evidence Workspace for WebMCP
pitch: Turn a messy brain dump into a source-grounded, inspectable, human-approved decision with your existing browser AI.
about_excerpt: Turn a messy brain dump into a source-grounded, inspectable, human-approved decision with your existing browser AI. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can clarify difficult decisions, but a chat answer is easy to detach from its source, blur facts with assumptions, or accept without a reviewable trail. We wanted a shared workspace where an agent can reason, the application enforces structure and freshness, and the human keeps the final word. What it does Thought Amplifier is a subject-independent WebMCP decision workspace for bounded plain-text brain dumps. A compatible browser agent invokes real page-defined tools to read the current source, revision, and fingerprint, then stages a structured amplification: objective, success criteria, facts grounded in exact source excerpts, assumptions, unknowns, options and trade-offs, a recommendation, reversal condition, and next actions. The result appears in the same visible page. The app validates the payload, binds it to the source revision, records the tool transition, rejects stale writes after the source changes, and exposes no agent approval tool. Only the human-facing UI can approve the exact displayed proposal. Our demo makes the product test itself: it analyzes the real decision between three challenge ideas—an MCP-readiness auditor, a residential concept coordinator, and Thought Amplifier. The workflow itself is general and supports clarify, decide, plan, diagnose, create, and learn modes. How we built it We built a React and TypeScript client with imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool. Three typed tools share live application state: read_thought_source, stage_amplification, and read_thought_workspace. Closed schemas and runtime validation reject unexpected, malformed, duplicate, or out-of-bounds data. Every staged proposal must match the current source revision and fingerprint; changing the source invalidates the old result. Human approval remains outside the WebMCP tool surface. The public repository includes architecture and tool-contract documentation, a reproducible real-host verification receipt, a demo runbook, screenshots, tests, and an MIT license. Challenges The hardest part was making the integration genuinely useful without turning WebMCP into an unrestricted write channel. We also had to make the manual and agent paths converge on the same state, keep evidence and inference distinct, and ensure a plausible result based on an older source could never silently replace newer work. Accomplishments A compatible browser host discovered and invoked all three real page tools in a local end-to-end run. It read the exact live source, visibly staged a complete proposal, read it back, and received STALE_SOURCE when an old payload was replayed after an edit. The registered tool surface contains no approval, publication, submission, or arbitrary-action endpoint. What we learned Useful agentic browsing is not just more autonomy. It is precise semantic operations inside software that owns state, validates transitions, exposes provenance, and preserves a human authority boundary. Structured reasoning becomes more credible when the source, transformation, freshness check, and approval are visible together. What's next Next: source-span citations, multiple text sources, private document and image ingestion with visible extraction provenance, persistent branches and locks, exports, and permissioned collaboration. This submission deliberately remains a focused prototype: plain text only, session-local state, no embedded model, no autonomous approval, and no claim of production or universal browser certification.
