title: Blindspot
pitch: A five-minute bomb-defusal game where a human sees the bomb, an AI agent gets seven WebMCP tools, and neither can win alone.
about_excerpt: A five-minute bomb-defusal game where a human sees the bomb, an AI agent gets seven WebMCP tools, and neither can win alone. Like Comment Story Updates The bomb has a blind spot Blindspot is a five-minute cooperative bomb-defusal game built around a capability split. The human can see the bomb: its wire colours, keypad symbols, button markings, casing, and the coloured strip that appears during a hold. The AI agent gets the manual and seven WebMCP tools: two read tools for rules and progress, plus five narrowly scoped actions. Neither side has the complete answer in the intended tool-only run, so they must talk before the timer reaches zero. Why WebMCP is the mechanic, not a checkbox Most agent demos try to expose as much page state as possible. Blindspot asks the opposite question: what should a good tool contract deliberately withhold? get_bomb_status reports the countdown, strikes, module types, and progress, then explicitly lists the visual facts it refuses to return. The action tools can cut, press, hold, and release, but they never reveal the bomb's appearance. This makes least-privilege interface design playable. If one tool leaks a wire colour or keypad symbol, the co-op game collapses because the agent no longer needs its human partner. This is a tool-contract demonstration, not a claim that WebMCP is a browser sandbox. An agent separately granted vision or DOM access could inspect the rendered page. The mission prompt therefore asks the agent to use only Blindspot's WebMCP tools, making the seven contracts the complete interface for the run. The human-agent experience The agent calls get_bomb_status and get_manual . It asks the human for only the visual facts required by a rule. It acts through typed WebMCP calls while both participants watch every call and result appear live. On the button module, the agent holds the button, a strip lights up only in the human view, the human reports its colour, and the agent schedules the correct release digit. A successful run ends in a mission report with time left, strikes, and tool-call count. The page includes a physical bomb-console interface, responsive human and agent views, an enlarged handoff state, opt-in synthesized sound, accessible redundant colour labels, and a replayable deterministic judge seed. Implementation Blindspot is intentionally small: vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no runtime dependencies or build step. src/tools.js declares the seven real contracts and registers each one with document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext , including name , description , JSON inputSchema , annotations, and execute . The same instrumented handlers update the live call feed. A fallback console is generated from those schemas only when native WebMCP is unavailable. Native sessions keep the executable controls with the connected agent. The public repo includes an MIT license, complete run instructions, a deterministic judge walkthrough, and 26 headless checks. The suite covers rules, clock throttling, all seven registration descriptors, partial registration reporting, hostile call-feed input, audio opt-in, schema-driven fallback accessibility, and bomb-appearance leak probes across fresh seeded games. GitHub Actions runs the suite and syntax checks on every push. Verified live I tested the production deployment in ChatGPT's in-app browser. It registered all seven tools from the production origin, completed the deterministic bomb through native WebMCP, and ended DEFUSED with zero strikes. title: Dungeon Crawl
pitch: An AI Dungeon Master that doesn't narrate your game it plays it. Five registered WebMCP tools are its only way in, and the page can refuse them.
about_excerpt: An AI Dungeon Master that doesn't narrate your game it plays it. Five registered WebMCP tools are its only way in, and the page can refuse them. Like 3 Comment Story Updates 01-the-broken-gate 02-agent-spawned-fight 03-difficulty-changed 04-advanced-story-with-reward 05-a-room-the-dm-wrote 06-the-ending 06-on-a-phone Inspiration Every AI dungeon master I have played with does the same thing: it describes a world it also controls. If it says you took six damage, you took six damage until it forgets, and then you didn't. There is nothing underneath the sentences. The model is the referee, the rulebook, the dice and the narrator all at once, so none of those things quite exist. WebMCP changes what an agent is on a page. It stops being a thing that writes about your app and becomes a thing that operates it, through controls the page itself defines. That felt like the right shape for a Dungeon Master: someone who can genuinely act on the world, but who does not own the rules. So I built the underneath first a real game with real state and then gave the AI five ways in, and no other way at all. What it does Dungeon Crawl is a single-page text adventure with a chapel to explore, a lamplighter to find, and an AI Dungeon Master sitting beside you. You play with buttons: Attack, Explore, Talk, or a free-form line of your own. The DM plays with five registered WebMCP tools: it reads the game state, spawns encounters, resolves combat rounds, awards items, and moves the story on. Every call it makes changes the screen you are looking at, in the moment it makes it. Dungeon-Crawl-how-it-works: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1j55D6dXDGQCK6EJ541I9T9pUSiPNuVqW/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=116709698709972850916&rtpof=true&sd=true Flow of the Dungeon : https://drive.google.com/file/d/1K_KQOtsLircpPqm4rHiFApVwMvjwydnH/view?usp=sharing Three things make it more than an AI with a game attached: It can be refused. Ask for a second fight while one is still alive and the tool returns "The turned verger is already fighting you here. Resolve that first." That is the game's rule, inside the tool, refusing the call not the model being polite. It can be overruled. The page keeps its own opinion about what you can survive, computed from health, level and how many rounds have gone badly in a row, and treats it as a ceiling. The DM may always go gentler, never harder. Ask for hard while hurt and you get "You asked for hard; the player is hurt (12/20), so this came out easy." It can write. Once the seven hand-written rooms are exhausted, advance_story lets the DM invent one and the prose arrives as tool arguments, styled by a house voice brief carried in the schema itself. Rooms the DM wrote appear on the map with a ✦, so you can always see which parts of the dungeon were written for you and which were written on the spot. How I built it React 19, Vite and Tailwind v4. No backend, no database, about 1,850 lines of source. The architecture is one idea: there is exactly one way to change the world, and both players use it. A room's Attack/Explore/Talk verb is a pure function of state returning an effects bundle { dm, hp, xp, item, reveal } . A tool call builds the same kind of bundle from its arguments. Both go into applyEffects(state, effects) , which is the only mutation in the application, and into the same reducer. Combat narrows further: combatRound() is a single resolver, and the Attack button and the resolve_combat tool both call it. A test asserts the button and the tool leave the player and the enemy on identical health from the same starting state, because "the agent plays by the same rules" ought to be a property you can run rather than a claim in a README. The prose the DM writes comes through the tool schema, not a side-channel API call. This is a static page in a public repo, so a model API key shipped in the bundle is a key published and the agent calling the tools is already a language model, so asking it for the sentences removes the secret, the round trip, and the second voice that would have to be matched to the first. What it sends is sanitised (markdown stripped, whitespace collapsed, length capped) and shown to the player verbatim. Challenges I ran into A try/catch that caught nothing. React StrictMode double-mounts effects in development, so the second pass met tool names the first pass had registered, and the console filled with InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name . I wrapped registration in a try/catch and moved on and the errors kept coming, because registerTool returns a rejecting promise , not a thrown error. A try/catch around an async call catches nothing. The fix is await , and it is now covered by four tests against a mock context that rejects duplicates the way the real one does. A difficulty curve that killed the player. My first heuristic gave a healthy level-1 player "hard" and the hard enemy deals 7 a round against 20 health while taking four rounds to kill. The playtest died in four rounds. Hard now requires level 3 as well as health. A finale nobody could pick up. Seven rooms hand out eight items against a six-slot pack, so a thorough player filled it before the last room and the game silently refused them the item the whole story points at. Only found it because the playtest logged inventory counts. A backspace character in a regular expression. A \b got mangled into a literal 0x08 byte, so a word-boundary test never matched and free-form input produced room names like "The And Light Every". It was invisible in every editor and grep od -c found it. Dried blood is unreadable on deep ink. The palette's accent scored 1.80:1 against the background, and it was carrying the combat numbers. I computed every text style in the app and added a fifth token the same blood with a lamp on it, at 4.60:1 used only for the system voice. What I learned The tool descriptions are the product. They are the only thing the model ever sees: not the code, not the UI, not the state. A tool that behaves perfectly and describes itself vaguely is a tool an agent will use wrongly, and the fix is always writing, never logic. I also learned how much better refusals feel than validation. Every tool that says no says what to do instead, in a sentence and an agent that is told why it was refused corrects itself on the next call rather than retrying the same thing. What's next Multiplayer, with two agents and one human the same pipeline already supports more than one actor. And an authored campaign format, so someone who cannot write JavaScript can drop in rooms of their own and let the DM extend them. title: ElijahOS
pitch: Portfolios are built for one visitor. ElijahOS gives the second one, your agent, typed WebMCP tools to search evidence and act inside the same OS a human is exploring.
about_excerpt: Portfolios are built for one visitor. ElijahOS gives the second one, your agent, typed WebMCP tools to search evidence and act inside the same OS a human is exploring. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I rebuilt my portfolio for a web where every visitor brings an agent. ElijahOS already existed as a personal website with two human interfaces: a windowed desktop OS and an intentional one-app-at-a-time mobile shell. But like most portfolios, it was still designed for one participant. A visitor could browse it, or an outside agent could summarize rendered text, but the agent could not reliably understand the site's capabilities, distinguish evidence from presentation, or act inside the same interface the person was using. That felt like the right problem for WebMCP. Instead of adding another chatbot, I wanted the website itself to become natively operable by the visitor's agent while the human experience remained intact. What it does ElijahOS now gives each participant the interface it needs: The person explores a playful personal operating system, opening apps, arranging windows, reading projects, and controlling the music player. Their agent receives ten narrow, typed, page-scoped WebMCP capabilities over the same public content and live workspace. Both operate on shared, visible state. Agent actions appear inside Agent Workspace, and bounded human changes can be read back through a workspace-state tool. A visitor's agent can bring in a distilled, session-only objective; search and inspect evidence; surface unsupported terms instead of guessing; and compose the actual ElijahOS apps that show the selected material. The person can inspect the sources, edit or clear the objective, change the workspace manually, and remain the decision-maker. The agent can then continue from a narrow snapshot of that human action. The site does not generate fit scores, rankings, hiring verdicts, or automated recommendations. It supplies candidate-authored evidence, provenance, contribution scope, limitations, and documented gaps. The visitor or their agent performs the interpretation. Why WebMCP is essential This is more than machine-readable portfolio data. The core experience is coordinated action inside a page both participants can see and change. Static metadata can describe content, scraping can recover text, and a detached API can return records. None of those creates the same page-local handoff: the agent can make its objective visible, investigate typed evidence, place the supporting artifacts into the existing UI, let the person redirect the workspace through ordinary navigation, and then resume from bounded shared state. WebMCP turns the website from something an agent merely reads into an environment the visitor and agent can use together. The normal interface remains fully usable without WebMCP. The capability surface is progressive enhancement, not a replacement for the site. How I built it ElijahOS is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Zustand, Three.js, and Vercel. One client-side provider registers ten tools through the browser's available ModelContext host after the shell becomes interactive. Five tools carry the core journey: set_visit_intent, search_evidence, inspect_evidence, compose_workspace, and get_workspace_state. Three read-only tools expose the public profile, resume, and contact data. Two visible action tools open an allowlisted app and control the on-page music player. The WebMCP adapter is isolated in src/lib/webmcp. It detects the available browser host, validates narrow JSON-schema inputs, uses accurate read-only and untrusted-content annotations, returns structured failures, and records each call in an in-memory activity feed. It has no database, analytics, provider credential, persistent query log, or server-side agent. Evidence is derived from the same typed sources that render the public portfolio rather than maintained as a second biography. Each record includes a canonical route, authorship provenance, documented contribution scope, limitations, displayable app artifacts, and first-hand links where available. Workspace actions reuse the existing app registry, shell-neutral launcher, desktop window store, and separate mobile opener. What people and agents can now do together Previously, a person could navigate ElijahOS while an external agent reasoned in a separate conversation. The agent could summarize the page, but it could not reliably know what the person had opened, place the exact supporting artifacts into the OS, or make its objective visible inside the site. DOM automation was especially brittle against overlapping windows, focus state, minimization, anchored project sections, and the separate mobile shell. Now the agent can investigate the structured evidence and visibly compose a workspace. The person can verify each claim in context, review the activity feed, change the workspace by hand, and hand control back without exposing the rest of their private conversation. That agent action → human correction → agent continuation loop is the collaboration WebMCP unlocked. Challenges I faced The hardest part was preserving ElijahOS instead of flattening it into a recruiter dashboard or a chat transcript. Every capability had to pass through existing app and shell boundaries so desktop and mobile behavior stayed coherent. The second challenge was trust. Portfolio claims are easy to overstate, so I designed the evidence layer to preserve sources, contribution scope, limitations, and explicit unmatched terms. “No documented evidence on this site” had to remain a useful result rather than a gap for a model to fill creatively. The third challenge was verification across an experimental browser surface. I kept source tests, injected-host browser tests, native discovery, deployed execution, and model-selection claims separate. A successful HTTP response is not WebMCP proof, and deterministic Playwright coverage is not proof that every agent will choose the same tools. What I learned I learned that a good agent interface is less about exposing everything and more about designing a small set of semantic capabilities with honest boundaries. Visible, reversible actions build more trust than invisible automation. Structured uncertainty is a feature. And a shared workspace only works when both sides can understand what changed without transferring the person's entire private context. Most importantly, WebMCP changed how I think about personal websites: the human interface can stay expressive while an agent receives a completely different native interface over the same state. Challenge provenance ElijahOS predates the challenge. The public challenge-baseline tag preserves the sanitized pre-challenge desktop/mobile OS, app system, public portfolio content, and original Ask concept. The meaningful post-baseline work includes the WebMCP adapter, ten-tool surface, typed evidence projection, session-scoped visit intent, shared workspace bridge, Agent Workspace and activity feed, anchored evidence navigation, focused tests, public release documentation, and the separately deployed challenge edition. Try it Open https://webmcp.elijahos.com in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. No account or credentials are required. The complete MIT-licensed source and testing instructions are available at https://github.com/juulsverne/elijahos-webmcp . title: Pokémon JS: One Trainer, Many Agents
pitch: Gen-1 Pokémon in the browser, where you and your agents drive the same trainer at once. WebMCP exposes the map, party and battle as tools, so an agent plays from game state, not pixels.
about_excerpt: Gen-1 Pokémon in the browser, where you and your agents drive the same trainer at once. WebMCP exposes the map, party and battle as tools, so an agent plays from game state, not pixels. Like 7 Comment 2 Story Updates Tools exposed in Chrome WebMCP Game Screen Inspiration Twitch Plays Pokémon . In 2014, tens of thousands of strangers played a single game of Pokémon Red together by typing commands into a Twitch chat. One avatar, one party, one save file, and a crowd all pressing buttons at once. It took over two weeks to finish, it produced its own mythology — the Helix Fossil, Bird Jesus — and it was gloriously, famously chaotic. The trainer spent whole hours walking into walls. The chaos was not a bug in the crowd, it was a missing capability. Those players had no way to coordinate and no way to see the game as anything but a video stream . They could not check whose turn it was, could not read the party's HP as data, could not agree who was driving. All they could do was mash inputs and hope. It got so bad they had to invent "Democracy mode" — a voting system — just to get through a maze. So we asked: what if the crowd were agents, and what if they could actually read the game? That question runs straight into the reason WebMCP exists. A Game Boy is the hardest possible surface for an agent: 160×144 pixels of sprite work, no DOM, no ARIA labels, no semantics. A battle menu is four words drawn onto a tilemap. A wall is a pixel that happens to be dark. Tall grass and a decorative bush look identical and behave completely differently. A crowd of agents watching a video stream would be exactly as lost as the crowd in 2014. So we took an existing open-source Pokémon Red/Blue recreation and made it expose what it knows instead of what it draws — then let many agents into the same save file at once. Twitch Plays Pokémon, if the crowd could read the game and talk to each other. What it does Gen-1 Pokémon in the browser, playable by a person, an agent, or both at the same time. Thirteen tools on document.modelContext cover the whole game, shaped for a reader rather than a renderer: The map arrives as an ASCII grid with a legend — @ you, ~ tall grass, D door, T trainer — plus the notable tiles in view with absolute coordinates you can pass straight back to walk_to . The battle's 52-step animation state machine becomes a named phase : choose-move , opponent-fainted , animating . Agents never see a stage number. Menus report their entries and where the cursor sits, so choosing is select_menu_item("BULBASAUR") instead of three arrow presses and a hope. Every screen that holds input reports waitingFor — dialogue , menu-open , wild-encounter — so a frozen screen is never a dead end. And it is one world, not one session per player — the Twitch Plays part. Every tab that joins a room drives the same trainer . Game and battle actions are broadcast over Supabase Realtime and applied everywhere, so a person on the D-pad and an agent calling tools are in the same fight, on the same party, and either can take the turn. The difference from 2014 is that this crowd can coordinate. get_party_agents shows who else is connected and what they have been doing; tell_agents leaves a note to claim a task before starting something long, so two agents do not both walk into the same trainer. One tab is elected driver — oldest peer, tie-broken on id, derived from presence so it needs no negotiation and hands over on its own — which is what stops every tab rolling its own wild Pokémon. No Democracy mode required. The room is the save file. A world survives everyone disconnecting, and handing a playthrough to a friend, or to another agent, is sending a URL. How we built it The registration is the easy part: webmcp-react , a WebMCPProvider , and a useMcpTool call per tool. The real work was making the game legible. src/webmcp/snapshot.ts — one read model for everything: position, ASCII map, notable tiles, party with types and PP, bag, on-screen state, battle phase. src/webmcp/pathfinding.ts — BFS over the reducers' own walkability rules, so a path we return is a path the game will actually accept. No separate model of the world to drift out of sync. src/app/use-menu-registration.ts — mirrors on-screen lists into Redux so a tool can read the cursor and pick by label. src/state/session.ts — the shared world: action broadcast, presence-based driver election, room persistence. src/state/battleSlice.ts — battle state lifted out of component state, which is what lets every agent watch one fight. Writes go through the same event bus as the on-screen buttons, so an agent cannot reach a state a player couldn't. Challenges we ran into We found most of these by actually playing it with an agent, not by reading the code. A battle read cost 37,000 tokens. The battle payload included the trainer object, which carries a portrait and twelve walk sprites — inlined by the bundler as base64 data URIs. Every single read of a trainer fight shipped all of it. Replacing it with {name, canBattle} took the payload to ~600 tokens, a 60× cut. The party screen was a blind spot, and it cost us a run. PokemonList kept its cursor in component state and never mirrored it anywhere, so get_game_state reported no menu at all while the party was on screen. The agent picked by arrow presses it could not verify — and sent out a Pokémon that had already fainted, because the voluntary switch had no guard on it. The party wiped shortly after. That one bug taught us more than anything else on this list. Presses were landing on deaf frames. Battle choreography ignores input while animating, so a burst of A presses mostly hit nothing. Tools now wait for a phase that actually wants input before spending a press. Pathfinding refused to walk onto items. The game's canWalk treats an uncollected item as solid but stepping onto it is exactly how you pick it up. Item tiles are now valid destinations, though never intermediate steps, so paths stay ones the reducers accept. Battles rewound themselves. The intro effect depended on the driver flag, which is recomputed on every presence sync, so a peer joining or leaving mid-fight replayed the choreography from step 0, rewinding the battle under everyone. Then battles froze instead. Fixing the rewind exposed the deeper problem: the choreography runs on setTimeout chains that do not survive a reload, so a fight restored from the save had no timer left to advance it. It now resumes at the last stage that accepts input. Deploys did not reach anyone. The service worker precached the app shell cache-first, so a browser that had loaded the game once kept booting the old bundle — the stale build even re-registered the worker after we removed it. The worker is gone entirely now; a shared world is worse off stale than offline. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are equally proud of the boring parts: a 60× reduction in the cost of reading a battle, and a test suite that pins the agent-facing behaviour, that pathfinding only routes through tiles the reducers accept, that no sprite data can leak back into a battle payload, that every driver election is unanimous without negotiation, that a frozen screen always says what it is waiting for. What we learned Agent-facing state is a product surface, and it needs the same care as a UI. Every place we had kept state in a component was a blind spot : invisible to a tool, and therefore a place an agent would guess and get it wrong. Lifting it into the store was consistently the fix. A frozen screen with no explanation is the cardinal sin. A human sees a text box and presses A. An agent sees frozen: true and nothing else, and has no move. Every refusal we return now names its cause, and the snapshot and the refusal are computed by the same function so they can never disagree. Cheap reads change how an agent plays. When reading the game was expensive, the agent guessed to avoid looking. When it got cheap, it looked before acting, and played far better. And the tools should encode the game's own rules, not a copy of them. Pathfinding over the actual reducers, phases named from the actual state machine: every place we duplicated a rule instead of reusing it, the two drifted and the agent paid. What's next for Pokémon JS: One Trainer, Many Agents Collaboration, and it turns out to be a stranger problem than we expected. There is only one avatar. You cannot parallelise a single body walking through a single world — two agents cannot grind in two places at once, and a third cannot go shopping while the other two fight. So "many agents" can never mean dividing the labour, which is what we assumed at the start and had to throw away. What's left, once you drop division of labour, is everything that happens around the one person holding the thing. Three shapes we want to try: The second player who isn't holding the controller. Your little brother on the couch, watching you play and telling you where to go. The friend who read the strategy guide and

title: Taste Gate
pitch: An explainable WebMCP preview gate where agents plan queues and people choose what to reveal.
about_excerpt: An explainable WebMCP preview gate where agents plan queues and people choose what to reveal. Like Comment Story Updates Four narrow WebMCP tools expose previews and proposals — never full post content. The agent proposes an order; the person independently selects and reveals stories. Judge's 45-second path Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Ask for a preview-only two-card queue. Inspect the four discovered Site tools and the visible proposed queue. Select cards yourself and press Reveal my selected stories . The agent can propose and explain; only the person can choose a reveal. Inspiration Project .taste already proves that a social card can begin as a compact, deterministic 16-byte preview packet. Taste Gate asks a different question: when an agent and a person share the same live page, can the agent help plan attention without silently deciding what the person must open? What it does Taste Gate exposes a preview-only view of a live feed through WebMCP. The agent can inspect media shape, text geometry, engagement heat, visual seed, and existing interaction flags; it can then explain and write a proposed queue. The user sees that proposal in the same page but must select cards and press Reveal my selected stories themselves. The gate filters muted or blocked cards before they reach the agent-facing preview list. It does not infer author identity, topic, timestamp, or full text from a packet. How I built it I reused the existing zero-dependency TypeScript .taste decoder and built a small static JavaScript app around it. The top-level page conditionally registers four WebMCP site tools: get_gate_state list_previews explain_preview set_proposed_queue The normal UI remains fully usable without WebMCP. Full sample content is fetched only when the user uses the ordinary Reveal action. The app labels this honestly as a coordination contract for the demo, not server-enforced privacy. The demo video voiceover is generated with macOS text-to-speech (Samantha). Challenges I ran into The hard part was defining a useful agent boundary without inventing meaning that the 16-byte protocol does not contain. A packet gives layout, media, coarse heat, and social-state signals; it does not justify a claim about a post's topic, author, or relevance. The tools therefore return field-level reasons and explicit non-inferences instead of a hidden recommendation score. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A shared-page agent workflow that stays inspectable by the person using it. Four narrow tools, including a state-changing proposal tool that cannot reveal content or alter the human selection. Tests that reject gated, unknown, and repeated cards and verify that the agent-facing list contains no author, topic, timestamp, or full text. A normal UI fallback and a live ChatGPT desktop-browser check that discovers all four tools. What I learned WebMCP becomes most compelling when it exposes application state that a person can see and review immediately. Narrow, verifiable operations are more useful than a broad agent action that obscures how a decision was made. What's next for Taste Gate Replace the demo content source with an application-controlled hydration endpoint, retain the same packet-only agent contract, and evaluate whether users find proposed queues more understandable than automatic ranking. title: ShipASO
pitch: WebMCP tools for safe App Store Optimization: agents research, explain, draft, and stage proposals; people retain approval.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tools for safe App Store Optimization: agents research, explain, draft, and stage proposals; people retain approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for ShipASO Inspiration App Store Optimization is a high-leverage workflow with a sharp boundary: an agent can do the research and drafting, but a person should retain the approval decision. What it does ShipASO watches app listings, keywords, and competitors. When a change matters, it prepares a proposal: title, subtitle, keywords, and promotional text at their exact character limits. On a run page, WebMCP tools let an agent read the queue, explain why a proposal exists, draft an alternative that preserves the brand, and stage it for review. The agent never gets an approval, publish, ship, or push tool. Staging changes what a person will review; it leaves the run awaiting approval. How it uses WebMCP ShipASO declares 14 page-scoped WebMCP tools. The browser reads the live tool list after registration, so the interface distinguishes a declared manifest from tools the browser actually received. Read and draft tools are available where they make sense; run-specific tools appear only on a run detail page. The boundary is also enforced on the server. Approval requires a single-use challenge issued when a run is opened and consumed with the approval update. That prevents replay and makes bulk approval follow the same per-run protection. What we learned Tool descriptions are not a security boundary. WebMCP makes the page's intended contract legible to agents, but server-side enforcement is still required for consequential actions. We deliberately built both: helpful tools for analysis and drafting, and a separate human decision point. title: Promise Gate
pitch: A WebMCP safety layer that lets AI agents test commitments against real capacity, propose honest alternatives, and finalize only after explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP safety layer that lets AI agents test commitments against real capacity, propose honest alternatives, and finalize only after explicit human approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing tasks, but there is an important difference between doing work and making a promise . An agent can draft a response in seconds, but accepting a deadline may silently overload the user, delay existing work, or affect other people. Most productivity tools show what is scheduled; they do not stop an agent from creating an unsafe commitment. I built Promise Gate to explore a simple principle: An AI agent may analyse and prepare a commitment, but a human should retain authority over the final promise. What it does Promise Gate is a capacity-first commitment system powered by WebMCP. The demonstration begins with a request from Northstar Studio for twelve hours of homepage work by Friday. Promise Gate shows that twenty of the user’s twenty-four safe hours are already promised, leaving only four hours available. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can: Structure the incoming request. Read the user’s available capacity and existing commitments. Test whether the original promise is feasible. Identify the exact deficit and the commitments that would be threatened. Generate honest alternatives. Stage a feasible option for human review. Finalize only an option that the human explicitly approved. In the demo, the original request is blocked because it exceeds safe capacity by eight hours. Promise Gate then offers three transparent alternatives: Deliver a smaller four-hour risk audit by Friday. Move the complete redesign to Tuesday. Explicitly displace existing work, requiring separate consent. Nothing is silently rearranged, and the agent cannot approve its own recommendation. How I built it Promise Gate is a responsive React and TypeScript application built with Vite. The page exposes six WebMCP tools: structure_incoming_request get_capacity_context reserve_original_request generate_counteroffers stage_counteroffer finalize_commitment The tools operate on a deterministic commitment model containing safe capacity, existing promises, deadlines, staged alternatives, human approval state, and schedule versions. The workflow separates reversible agent actions from irreversible human decisions. Human approval is deliberately not exposed as a WebMCP tool. The finalization tool rechecks capacity and verifies that the approved option still matches the current schedule version before creating a receipt. The interface acts as a visible decision ledger. Every tool call changes the page state and adds an entry explaining what happened, so users can understand what the agent did and why. Challenges The biggest challenge was making the safety boundary real rather than decorative. It would have been easy to add an “Approve” button while still allowing an agent to bypass it through another tool. I designed the state model so that finalization fails unless an exact staged option has been approved by a human. It also refuses the original request with a structured OVER_CAPACITY result containing the deficit and threatened commitments. Another challenge was making agent activity understandable on screen. Promise Gate therefore translates tool results into clear visual states such as Blocked by Gate , Awaiting Decision , and Committed , supported by a visible action ledger. Finally, I needed the experience to work both as an agent interface and as a normal responsive website without hiding the important decision behind generic dashboard elements. What I learned I learned that a useful WebMCP integration is not simply a collection of website buttons exposed as tools. The tool surface can encode authority, reversibility, and policy. Tool descriptions and schemas also influence how an agent reasons about a workflow. Separating “generate,” “stage,” and “finalize” creates a much safer interaction than exposing one broad “accept request” action. Most importantly, human-in-the-loop design works best when the human decision is specific. Promise Gate does not ask the user to approve a vague AI plan—it asks them to approve an exact scope, deadline, capacity allocation, and schedule version. What's next The current hackathon demonstration uses transparent fictional data so the complete safety model can be evaluated without requiring an account. The next step would be connecting Promise Gate to real calendars, project-management systems, and communication tools, allowing the same commitment gate to protect real schedules before an agent sends a consequential reply. title: Sigmora Live Relay
pitch: Stay live while an agent builds, reviews, and verifies the launch moment with you.
about_excerpt: Stay live while an agent builds, reviews, and verifies the launch moment with you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Sigmora Live Relay Inspiration Going live is when creators most need cross-platform promotion—and when they can least afford to leave the stream to edit, rewrite, upload, and check posts. Sigmora Live Relay turns one selected live event into a reviewable 12-second vertical campaign on a shared release board. What it does The page exposes eight narrow WebMCP tools. An agent reads the visible brand and destination context, finds or declares the source live event, drafts the relay, polls generation, revises copy, queues exact destination accounts, releases the human-approved revision, and checks each destination independently. Every tool call updates the same board the creator sees. The consequential checkpoint remains human. Queue items are bound to exact account IDs and one immutable revision. The creator reviews those items in the UI and approves them there; approval is deliberately not exposed as a tool. Any revision invalidates the receipt. Release requires that receipt plus an idempotency key, and partial failure can never be reported as total success. Why WebMCP This is a strong WebMCP fit because the useful context and collaboration live on the open page: current creative state, selected destinations, approval, and receipts. Without WebMCP, an agent must infer buttons and duplicate state. With WebMCP, it uses an explicit contract while the person keeps visual control. People and agents can now share one live workspace: the agent handles multi-step coordination while the creator remains present with the audience and retains authority over publication. How we built it The challenge implementation is framework-free TypeScript built around document.modelContext.registerTool(...), closed JSON Schemas, typed result envelopes, an observable shared controller, page-scoped teardown, a strict HTTP adapter, and a deterministic local provider. The normal manual interface continues to work when WebMCP is absent. The eight tools cover context, source discovery, drafting, job polling, revision, exact destination queuing, approved release, and independent status verification. Unit and end-to-end tests exercise schemas, lifecycle cleanup, revision invalidation, idempotency, partial failure, and the manual fallback. Challenges The hardest design problem was preserving human authority without making the agent workflow brittle. We solved it with an immutable approval receipt bound to an exact revision and destination set, plus clear state transitions visible to both sides. Another challenge was truthful partial failure: each destination receives an independent receipt, so a mixed outcome stays mixed. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when it is not simply a hidden automation API. The shared page should remain the source of truth, and the tool contract should expose exactly the capabilities that benefit from agent reasoning while keeping consequential consent visible and human. What's next The public reference is intentionally simulated and says so throughout the UI and tool results. Next we would connect the strict provider adapter to real publishing APIs, preserving the same approval, idempotency, readback, and partial-failure guarantees. title: MarketPane
pitch: Bring your AI agent along to explore financial products and test your screener ideas.
about_excerpt: Bring your AI agent along to explore financial products and test your screener ideas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 This is our design goal for a grid and widget based editable UX Inspiration MarketPane, is an AI assisted research workbench for doing stock price analysis. Our goal is to build a tool that removes the barriers between an AI and the research canvas, so that a user can spend more time developing their hypothesis, and less time copying charts data back and forth. By putting the tools directly into the hands of an AI, we are basically shortening the iteration loop, allowing you to get to your goal faster. What it does MarketPane is a WebMCP-powered stock screener and research workbench shared between a human and an agent. Either one can define a screener over a universe of instruments (asset class, exchanges, sectors), build a filter tree of typed conditions, set a ranking, and run it to get a pinned, stable set of results. Results land in a panel grid: a results table the agent or the human can inspect, and — via drag-and-drop or a tool call — individual rows become live price charts on the same canvas. Every panel, chart, and result the agent creates is visible and rearrangeable by the human in real time, and vice versa. How we built it The frontend is SvelteKit 5 (SPA) with a browser-side panel/grid system and a workspace document that both the UI and the WebMCP tool layer read and write. WebMCP tools ( define_screener , run_screener , get_screener_results , create_panel , resolve_ticker , search_catalog , get_canvas_state ) operate on that same document, so an agent's actions show up as first-class panel changes instead of hidden side effects. The backend is a FastAPI service (Python, pandas) that evaluates screeners against an OHLCV panel of real market data (EODHD-sourced, object-store backed) and exposes a stateless /api/screener/run endpoint. A typed catalog of fields, operators, and universes keeps every filter condition validated rather than arbitrary code — the agent composes screeners out of known building blocks, it doesn't write expressions the backend has to trust blindly. Challenges we ran into There was a series of challenges that we ran into along the way. Firstly, we ran out of coffee half way through development and had to make an emergency trip to Costco. There were also a number of WebMCP specific challenges that we resolved: The browser was not aware of any WebMCP tools being available and kept trying to use UI elements. The agent has to query a document schema to know that the tools exist, and if it does not suspect them to be there it does not do this. We had to add specific UI elements to notify the agent. The browser did not support the number of tools that we initially created, and blocked them entirely. We had to minimize our implementation. It was very difficult to debug issues with the tools, especially in prod where we don't have all the BE logs handy. This is because issues are not just "bugs" in the app code, but problems with the sequence of actions that the agents take over time. Accomplishments that we're proud of We got a late start on the hackathon and had to build everything very quickly. Our AI enabled development platform has allowed us to achieve the capacity necessary to deliver a POC in time. We managed to add some not-so-simple features, and will continue to expand the feature palette. What we learned Building agentic tools is more than just developing the right workflow and backend scalability. It is also very much about giving the agent the proper awareness and context for the tools that you build. Without clean, self-explainable interfaces, agents will spend extra tokens going on detours or producing errors. What's next for MarketPane Next, we want to widen the live tool surface back toward the fuller design we already built and tested: similarity search ("find setups like this one"), chart annotation and capture, computed fields and custom studies, watchlists, alerts, and backtesting are all implemented behind feature flags today and just need to be wired back into the live composition root. We also want richer chart controls (timeframes, overlays, multi-ticker comparison) and stronger measurement tools so a user can move from spotting a pattern to testing it across cohorts, outcomes, and market regimes. title: Tandem
pitch: The grocery store where your agent does the shopping within your budget, your diet, your rules and buys nothing until you tap Approve.
about_excerpt: The grocery store where your agent does the shopping within your budget, your diet, your rules and buys nothing until you tap Approve. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Everyone is talking about agentic commerce, but almost nobody is comfortable with it. Would you hand an AI your credit card and walk away? Today's agents either scrape websites blind, clicking through UIs they were never meant to understand or they get access with no visibility and no control for the person they're acting for. We built Tandem to prove there's a third option: a storefront designed for both audiences at once the human who owns the money, and the agent who does the work. WebMCP makes this possible because the app can speak to the agent in structured tools instead of hoping it guesses the UI correctly. What it does Tandem is an agent-native grocery store where you and your AI shop together: Give your agent a mission, not clicks: "Dinner for 4, gluten-free, under $60." It searches the catalog, reads product details, and builds a cart using its WebMCP tools. Guardrails are enforced by the app, not the prompt. add_to_cart refuses items that break the budget or dietary rules. The agent can't prompt its way past policy, the store itself is the policy layer. Every agent action is visible. Each tool call renders as a human-readable card in a shared Activity Timeline. Shopping with an agent stops being a black box. You can talk back. Drop a note like "no cilantro" — the agent reads it via get_shopper_notes and re-plans. Async human→agent communication, inside a web app. Nothing is bought until you tap Approve. request_checkout returns a pending_human_approval card. The agent fills the cart; only you can greenlight it. Swaps, not surprises. When the agent wants to replace an item (out of stock, over budget), it calls propose_swap and you accept or reject in one tap. How we built it The storefront is a React (Vite) app with a product catalog, cart, notes panel, activity timeline, and approval flow. We registered 7 WebMCP tools using the standard browser API: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "add_to_cart", description: "Add a product to the shopper's cart. Enforces budget and dietary guardrails.", inputSchema: { /* JSON Schema / }, execute: async (input) => { / validate policy, mutate cart, log to timeline */ }}); Full tool set: search_products, get_product_details, add_to_cart, get_cart, get_shopper_notes, propose_swap, request_checkout. Each execute() returns structured JSON (prices, remaining budget, refusal reasons) so the agent can plan its next move and also updates the UI so the human sees the same story in real time. Guardrails (budget cap, dietary exclusions) live in app code, evaluated inside tool executions, the same rules apply no matter what the agent's prompt says. A built-in Dev Tools panel can invoke any registered tool manually, a fallback demo path and a debugging aid. Deployed on Vercel; tested in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Challenges we ran into Tool descriptions are the agent's entire documentation. We rewrote them repeatedly; vague descriptions produced hesitant agents, precise ones with explicit constraints produced confident, correct plans. One action, two audiences. Every execute() must mutate UI state for the human and return clean structured data for the agent. Getting that dual contract right was the core design problem. Policy vs. persuasion. The agent would "ask" to exceed the budget. We learned to encode refusals as first-class structured responses ({ added: false, reason: "over_budget", remaining: 4.50 }) so the agent recovers gracefully instead of failing. Testing across two WebMCP surfaces (ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome's flag) surfaced small schema strictness differences we had to normalize. Accomplishments that we're proud of In testing, the agent completed a full mission 11 items, gluten-free, $58.40 of a $60 budget on its first attempt, with zero unauthorized purchases. Not because we asked nicely, but because the app makes it impossible. The human's Activity Timeline is generated from the exact same tool-call events the agent generates one source of truth, two audiences. A pattern we believe generalizes across the web: propose → enforce → approve, applicable to expenses, bookings, emails, and deploys. What we learned Designing tools is designing an API for a new kind of user. Schema and description quality mattered more than anything else we wrote. The best agent UX isn't full automation, it's delegation with visibility. Humans stay sovereign; agents do the labor. Rich structured responses (remaining budget, reasons, alternatives) make agents dramatically more capable than bare success/fail returns. What's next for Tandem Real payments behind the approval gate (Stripe), making the pattern production-safe. A roaming agent that shops across multiple WebMCP-enabled stores in one mission. Shared household carts with per-person budgets. A spec proposal: a standard human-consent / approval tool pattern for WebMCP, so every agent-native app can implement trustworthy checkout the same way. title: TestPilot
pitch: Agent-native QA mission control that turns release risk into traceable evidence.
about_excerpt: Agent-native QA mission control that turns release risk into traceable evidence. Like Comment Story Updates 01-initial-dashboard-at-risk 02-webmcp-14-tools 03-req-003-coverage-gap 04-ai-created-tc-004 05-exe-004-negative-inventory 06-def-001-traceability 07-final-not-ready Inspiration A green test dashboard does not always mean a release is safe. Important requirements can remain untested, execution evidence can be scattered across different tools, and defects can lose their connection to the tests and requirements that exposed them. QA leaders and release managers often spend more time assembling this context than making the release decision itself. I built TestPilot to demonstrate a better model: one shared release workspace where a human can review the evidence visually while an AI agent can discover and invoke the same QA capabilities as structured WebMCP actions. What it does TestPilot is an agent-native QA Mission Control application for requirements, test cases, executions, defects, traceability, and release readiness. The demonstration starts with fictional e-commerce release 2.4. All existing tests pass and there are no critical defects, but the release is still AT RISK because REQ-003 - the critical requirement preventing concurrent customers from purchasing the final inventory item - has no test coverage. The user asks: “Check whether version 2.4 is safe to release.” The agent then: Inspects the release and its requirements. Detects the missing REQ-003 coverage. Creates TC-004 for two simultaneous purchases of the final item. Runs the new test. Observes both purchases succeeding and inventory reaching -1 . Diagnoses a non-atomic concurrent inventory update. Creates a critical defect with structured evidence. Links the defect to TC-004 and REQ-003. Reassesses release 2.4 as NOT READY . Every action immediately appears in the human-facing dashboard, producing a complete evidence chain from requirement to test, execution, defect, and release decision. How I built it TestPilot uses React, Next.js, strict TypeScript, and Vinext for the application interface and server endpoints. It is hosted publicly on OpenAI Sites, with Cloudflare Workers and Cloudflare D1 providing persistent, isolated demo state. Drizzle ORM manages the data model, Zod validates inputs, and Vitest verifies the important release logic. The page registers 14 semantic tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . These include get_coverage_gaps , create_test_case , run_test , inspect_failure , create_defect , link_defect_to_test , and get_release_readiness . These are business-level QA actions, not low-level instructions such as clicking buttons. The UI and WebMCP tools use the same domain services, APIs, and persistent state, so there is no separate agent-only version of the data. Each browser receives an isolated anonymous workspace. This allows judges to run and reset the deterministic demonstration without creating an account or interfering with another evaluation. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was keeping the human interface and agent workflow synchronized around one authoritative state. An agent-created test or defect needed to appear in the dashboard without duplicating business logic or maintaining a second data model. Another challenge was making the demonstration deterministic. A real concurrency failure can be timing-dependent, which is unsuitable for a short judging session. I designed TC-004 to reproduce the negative-inventory result reliably while keeping the evidence realistic and structured. I also needed to expose meaningful semantic tools with clear descriptions, typed inputs, validation, predictable JSON responses, and useful errors. Finally, the public application had to support anonymous access while keeping every visitor’s mutable demonstration data isolated. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that TestPilot demonstrates an end-to-end agent workflow rather than adding a chatbot beside an existing dashboard. The agent can discover missing coverage, create and execute a test, diagnose a failure, create a critical defect, link the evidence, and produce a release recommendation using structured WebMCP actions. At the same time, the human sees every state transition and can inspect or reset the workflow. The final result is a clear trace: REQ-003 → TC-004 → failed execution → DEF-001 → NOT READY The entire TestPilot project - including its concept, interface, application code, WebMCP integration, automated tests, documentation, and deployment - was created during the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge hackathon period. What I learned I learned that agent-native applications should expose intent rather than presentation details. A tool such as create_defect remains meaningful even if the website’s layout changes, while DOM-based automation can break when a button label, loading state, or responsive layout changes. I also learned that trustworthy agent workflows require shared state, input validation, deterministic evidence, explicit error responses, and visible human oversight. A release verdict is much more valuable when the user can trace exactly how the agent reached it. What's next for TestPilot The current e-commerce system and test runner are intentionally simulated to provide a reliable competition demonstration. A production version could connect the same domain and WebMCP boundaries to real CI/CD pipelines, automated test runners, requirements platforms, defect trackers, source-control checks, and deployment approval systems. Future versions could also add organization authentication, role-based access, configurable release policies, audit retention, notifications, historical risk trends, and human approval gates. title: Three in the Loop
pitch: A WebMCP research workbench where agents do the legwork and humans decide what counts as evidence.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP research workbench where agents do the legwork and humans decide what counts as evidence. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 3-in-the-loop-human-agent-research-workbench how-it-works human-approve-reject-retry-sourcing-method human-approved-artifact-ready flow-chart Inspiration Three in the Loop began with a practical question: what should research look like when a human, an agent, and a website work together in the same live workspace? We began with the WebMCP specification, Chrome developer and agent/tool security guidance, OpenAI developer demonstrations, community/practitioner demonstrations, and repeated internal dogfooding. Together, those sources made the website-declared tool model concrete. Our product question was what should remain under human control. Research was the test case we kept returning to. It rewards speed in gathering and punishes speed in judging. So we built the smallest workbench that could test the boundary between useful research delegation and human evidence judgment. Repeated dogfooding refined that boundary until it matched the workflow. What it does Three in the Loop is for researchers, analysts, and technical teams doing fast-moving evidence-based research where recency, authority, and provenance matter. It is a research workspace shared by a person and a WebMCP-enabled agent in the same live browser workspace: Human defines → Agent researches → Human curates → Agent synthesizes → Human approves You set the research question, audience, and evidence limit. The agent reads the workspace, searches OpenAlex, inspects sources, and proposes evidence. Then it stops. You accept or reject each proposal in the Workbench and control evidence membership. The agent drafts an Evidence Brief whose findings may cite only human-accepted evidence. You edit and review the brief, mark it reviewed, approve it, and download the approved Markdown. The Research Cycle shows whose turn it is at every stage. A WebMCP activity readout records real tool calls as they land, so agent work is visible without exposing private reasoning. The application embeds no model and makes no OpenAI API calls; intelligence comes from a compatible external agent using the site’s bounded tool surface. Why WebMCP The interesting question was never whether an agent can search. It was which operations the site should expose as structured tools and which decisions should remain in the human workflow. WebMCP lets the site declare that boundary on its structured tool surface. Three in the Loop exposes exactly five tools: get_research_workspace search_sources get_source_details propose_evidence draft_evidence_brief Accepting evidence and approving the brief are deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. They are buttons, not tools. For the operations the site does expose, the agent can use structured calls instead of scraping the interface or imitating human clicks. Both actors work against the same bounded browser workspace. It is the same page, with the turn changing hands. Challenges The hard problem was not building tools. It was deciding where useful delegation should stop. We began with read-only tools and added exactly two state-changing operations when the workflow needed them: propose_evidence can stage a proposal, and draft_evidence_brief can place or replace a review-required draft. Evidence acceptance or rejection, evidence membership, brief editing and review, and final approval remain outside the WebMCP tool surface. That boundary looks obvious in hindsight. It took repeated use to find it. Two smaller problems followed. The site cannot know that a person has spoken to an agent or that the agent is thinking, so it only reports AGENT WORK IN PROGRESS after a real WebMCP call lands in the current stage. And persistent rehearsal state kept reviving old missions, so the workspace now uses session-scoped browser storage: same-tab refreshes survive, while a new browser session starts clean. What we learned We began by treating the tool as the main unit of WebMCP design: name it well, type it well, keep it narrow. That is necessary. It is not what made the product work. What made it work was the handoff. The agent works until evidence selection returns control to the human. The human changes the evidence set. The agent continues from that decision, not from scratch, and drafts from the accepted evidence. The human reviews and signs off. Each time we clarified one of those transitions, the product became simpler and more useful. Looking at tools in isolation never explained the workflow as clearly as the handoffs did. Next time, we would design the journey between the person, the agent, and the page first; the tool set should follow from that journey. The final product does not try to show how much the agent can do alone. It shows how clear the responsibility is at every step. What's next The application is frozen for submission. What follows is evaluation before expansion. Planned assurance work includes deterministic checks of workflow invariants, WebMCP registration and cancellation lifecycle testing, response and serialized-output measurement, model-facing indirect prompt-injection evaluations, browser-agent evaluations of human-authority boundaries, and adversarial retesting after approved hardening. Product directions remain open too: richer evidence comparison without a fake credibility score, additional structured research providers, reusable research sessions, and collaboration. Expansion follows evidence from the evaluations while preserving the principle that made the product useful: The agent gathers. You decide what counts. I handled product design, WebMCP workflow design, implementation, deployment, dogfooding, validation, and submission preparation. title: WATCH//FLOOR
pitch: WATCH//FLOOR is an analyst-first security operations workbench where a connected agent investigates through bounded WebMCP tools while the human retains every consequential decision.
about_excerpt: WATCH//FLOOR is an analyst-first security operations workbench where a connected agent investigates through bounded WebMCP tools while the human retains every consequential decision. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I’m a security practitioner, and I keep seeing investigations reduced to an LLM summary. The summary helps, but it can leave the analyst a step away from the evidence. Meanwhile, people are building personal agent setups with their own models, memory, skills, and runbooks. I wanted a workbench where you could bring that agent into the case without giving it the final say. What it does WATCH//FLOOR is a visual WebMCP workbench for escalated cases. The agent runs approved skills, shows the exact KQL and raw records, and adds evidence to a live graph as it works. It can investigate, model impact, and prepare a response. Evidence sufficiency, restricted telemetry, response approval, and case closure stay with the analyst. How we built it I registered page tools with document.modelContext.registerTool and tied them to the current case and revision. Fixed KQL contracts stop the agent from quietly widening a query. The app is TypeScript and React on Cloudflare Workers with D1. It uses synthetic data and records response actions instead of contacting real systems. I used Codex to build and test it in a couple of days. Challenges we ran into The hard part was deciding what the agent should do and what must remain human. I also had to keep a growing graph readable and make real WebMCP activity easy to follow in a three-minute video. What’s next for WATCH//FLOOR Next I want to connect real SIEM, EDR, identity, and cloud data, add team policy around the gates, and make skill packs portable. Bring your own harness; keep authority with the analyst. title: WebMCP Angular KIT tool
pitch: Enterprise Angular 22 toolkit for W3C WebMCP — uniting browser AI agents with 3D WebGL CAD, reactive BI analytics, and a dynamic SubAgents SDK.
about_excerpt: Enterprise Angular 22 toolkit for W3C WebMCP — uniting browser AI agents with 3D WebGL CAD, reactive BI analytics, and a dynamic SubAgents SDK. Like Comment Story Updates Most AI browser agents today are essentially screen-scrapers: they take screenshots, guess button coordinates, or try to parse messy DOM trees. That approach is slow, breaks the moment a CSS class changes, and fails completely when interacting with a canvas element or stateful WebGL scenes. When the W3C published the WebMCP draft, we saw a much cleaner path: expose typed, client-side functions directly from the browser runtime to the model. Instead of treating the web app like a static document an external bot has to inspect from the outside, the user and the agent can mutate the exact same application state in real time, whether that means extruding a 3D CAD mesh at 60 FPS or running financial risk analytics without backend roundtrips. The showcase is built with Angular 22, Three.js, and Bun, organized into four primary layers: First, Angular 22 signals and directives. Rather than wrapping tools in heavy abstractions, we built directives like webmcpTool that bind directly to reactive signals. When a user adjusts an input or the agent calls a tool, state updates synchronously with zero change-detection penalty. Second, the Three.js spatial engine and push-pull extrusion. We built a SceneActionBus to decouple asynchronous tool promises from the Three.js render loop. The agent can draw planar 2D profiles and extrude solid 3D geometry along the face normal vector, while camera movements interpolate across spherical coordinates for smooth transitions. The agent can also call a screenshot tool to pull the raw WebGL drawing buffer and visually verify its own modifications. Third, in-browser memory with IndexedDB and BM25. Rather than standing up an external vector database, we built an episodic memory store on IndexedDB paired with a pure TypeScript BM25 search implementation. Relevance scoring runs standard Robertson-Spärck Jones IDF directly on the client using tuned parameters (k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75), allowing the agent to retrieve user preferences and historical actions in sub-millisecond lookups completely offline. Fourth, a dynamic SubAgents SDK and multi-domain business intelligence. Injecting dozens of tool schemas into every prompt quickly blew through token budgets. We created an SDK that dynamically filters tools per domain, allowing the main agent to delegate tasks to specialized workers (such as analytics or 3D specialists). These workers run isolated multi-turn loops, compute normalized anomaly risk scores across metrics, and return concise execution receipts signed with a client-side SHA-256 hash. We tackled several technical hurdles along the way. Calling Three.js mutations straight out of asynchronous HTTP promises caused frame drops, so we created a queue in SceneActionBus that holds incoming tool commands and executes them strictly on animation frame ticks. Exposing every tool simultaneously caused models to hallucinate arguments or hit context caps; scoping tools dynamically by route and delegating to subagents cut token usage by roughly 85%. Additionally, server-side rendering under Node and Bun crashed whenever code referenced browser globals like window, navigator, or IndexedDB. We resolved this by building an in-memory emulator (WebMcpEmulator) that activates during SSR and in browsers lacking native WebMCP support, eliminating hydration mismatches. Through this process, we achieved 511 unit and integration tests passing on Bun in under 1.5 seconds. The project demonstrated that agent autonomy does not require a heavy backend or remote vector database; native browser primitives like IndexedDB, WebGL, and Signals are remarkably capable when wired directly to function calling. Furthermore, Angular's dependency injection model fits WebMCP tool registration naturally by treating tools as standard injectable providers. Moving forward, our next steps include publishing the webmcp-angular library as an open-source npm package, adding WebXR support to let agents interact with 3D scenes in headsets like Apple Vision Pro and Meta Quest, and compiling OpenCASCADE geometry routines to WebAssembly for true solid modeling directly in the browser. title: WebMCP Design Studio
pitch: A studio where a person and an AI agent co-create flyers, posters and social posts on a live canvas. Agent-driven through WebMCP tools, images generated on-device via WebGPU.
about_excerpt: A studio where a person and an AI agent co-create flyers, posters and social posts on a live canvas. Agent-driven through WebMCP tools, images generated on-device via WebGPU. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every design tool is a wall of menus, and every "AI design" demo is a black box that hands you a finished picture. We wanted the third thing: a person and an agent at the same canvas, where the agent does the tedious work and the person keeps the final say. WebMCP made that buildable. A page can declare exactly what an agent may do, so the agent does not have to guess at the UI, and the human's consent can be part of the protocol instead of a dialog bolted on afterwards. What it does WebMCP Design Studio is a live canvas for flyers, posters and social posts. Say "make a spring yard sale flyer, Saturday 8am to 2pm, 14 Orchard Lane" and the agent creates the design, generates the artwork, sets the type and lays it out. Nothing is committed until you approve it. Every edit lands in a pending batch, approve-batch exists as a tool only while there is something to approve, undo appears with it, and a toolchange event fires as they come and go, so any agent can see the moment a human is required. Seventeen tools cover the whole loop: designs, elements, image generation on-device or through the fleet, background removal, restyling, export, memory of your preferences, and a production log that lets the agent tell you what the studio has made this week. A protocol feed shows every registration and call as it happens. How we built it Vite, React and TypeScript, with a fabric.js canvas. One ToolRegistry reconciles the design state onto document.modelContext when the native API is present and onto a spec-shaped polyfill when it is not, so the same tools work in ChatGPT's browser, in Chrome with the WebMCP flag, and everywhere else. The studio's own in-page agent drives the page through the same getTools and executeTool surface an external agent would, so the WebMCP surface is exercised by real traffic. The consent controls are also registered declaratively as a , the spec's second path. Images come from an on-device WebGPU model or from Sana on our fleet through the studio's own proxy; text comes from Bonsai 27B with an automatic fallback lane. It deploys as a static site on GitHub Pages with 205 tests behind it. Challenges we ran into Making consent a protocol object rather than a UI element took the most design work: the batch, the disappearing tools and the toolchange events had to agree exactly. The fleet side fought back too. Under load, the 27B text model crashed and the image lane timed out behind Cloudflare's 100-second cut, so we built a second text lane with automatic fallback, moved image generation onto a resident GPU path, and set honest timeouts everywhere. The demo itself was re-shot after the first cut used artwork from an unrelated production pack instead of the flyers the studio actually makes. Accomplishments that we're proud of The consent boundary lives in the tool surface itself, so any WebMCP agent inherits it. The app eats its own protocol. Image generation runs fully on-device when the browser can do it. And the studio is used for real work: its production log is a week of actual pieces, readable by the agent through a tool. What we learned Declaring capabilities changes how you design the app. Once every action was a tool with a schema, the pending batch and the approve step became obvious, and the UI got simpler rather than more crowded. We also learned that a demo built for agents is judged in the agent's environment: cross-origin, preflight and timeout behavior matter as much as the tools. What's next for WebMCP Design Studio Print-ready export with bleed, richer declarative tools for the whole rail, a daily production routine that keeps the log growing on its own, and the studio as a room inside the Aitherium playground, where the same agent that drafts your flyer can also hand it to your community. title: WebMCP Studio
pitch: WebMCP Studio turns existing websites into agent-ready experiences by discovering actions, generating structured WebMCP tools, and letting AI agents safely interact with live web apps.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Studio turns existing websites into agent-ready experiences by discovering actions, generating structured WebMCP tools, and letting AI agents safely interact with live web apps. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We were inspired by the upcoming availability of WebMCP tools and noticed that many production websites still do not expose agent-native capabilities. WebMCP Studio helps developers detect useful capabilities from existing websites, then compose them into reusable workflows. This can reduce agent tool calls and make agentic workflows easier to understand and maintain. What it does WebMCP Studio discovers native WebMCP tools and infers potential tools from a website’s semantic DOM, forms, and visible actions. Developers can review the evidence, drag actions into a workflow, generate a higher-level tool such as buy_best_product, and test it on a controlled page. The hosted Studio provides a simple judge path. An optional Chrome MV3 extension supports advanced discovery and execution on eligible live pages. How we built it We built the project in TypeScript with a dependency-light browser architecture: A discovery engine scans semantic HTML, forms, controls, Shadow DOM, and same-origin frames. A capability graph stores discovered tools, schemas, locators, evidence, confidence, and effects. A structured workflow interpreter composes primitive actions using validated JSON bindings. A hosted Studio provides the visual discovery and drag-and-drop workflow builder. A versioned postMessage bridge connects Studio to controlled commerce and travel target pages. Generated tools are registered through the browser’s document.modelContext API when WebMCP is available. External URLs remain potential-only in the hosted flow; the extension handles approved live-page instrumentation. The demo workflow searches products, filters by price, views details, and adds the selected product to a cart. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP ecosystem is still evolving. Browser support, Permissions Policy, secure-context requirements, and agent-provider capabilities vary, so successfully registering a tool on a page does not automatically prove that ChatGPT can discover and invoke it. We also had to distinguish native tools from inferred suggestions. Inferred tools may be useful, but they need evidence, confidence, schema validation, stable locators, and human review before execution. Dynamic websites introduced additional challenges, including SPA updates, Shadow DOM, iframes, weak accessibility semantics, stale elements, and potentially unsafe actions. We addressed these with bounded discovery, structured validation, explicit activation, session checks, and clear native-versus-preview states. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built an end-to-end workflow from: Discover → Compose → Generate → Inject → Test We are especially proud that the product remains honest about capability status: Native WebMCP tools are clearly separated from inferred tools. Unsupported browsers receive an explicit preview path instead of a simulated native claim. Generated workflows produce structured traces and visible page effects. The project includes unit tests, Playwright end-to-end tests, deterministic target fixtures, and an optional browser extension. What we learned We learned that making websites useful to agents requires more than finding buttons or API requests. A reliable tool also needs a meaningful name, typed input schema, evidence, permissions, stable locators, and understandable failure behavior. We also learned that page-level WebMCP registration and agent-level WebMCP consumption are separate compatibility problems. Finally, structured workflows make agent behavior more reusable and auditable than repeatedly asking an agent to perform low-level website actions. What's next for WebMCP Studio Next, we want to validate the complete native ChatGPT/browser connection in a supported environment. We also plan to improve inference accuracy, add more site-specific adapters, support more dynamic and authenticated workflows, and make generated projects easier to reuse across websites and sessions. title: WebMCP Vision

about_excerpt: An agent-native shopping experience that uses structured commerce tools and targeted product imagery for visual decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP Vision WebMCP Vision is an agent-native shopping experience for visual product decisions. It combines fast, structured commerce actions with focused product imagery, so an AI agent can answer questions about appearance without relying on full-page screenshots or guesswork. Problem Shopping agents can search product data, but questions such as “which finish fits my room?” or “which of these looks best in a minimalist kitchen?” require visual context. Full-page screenshots are noisy, slow, and force an agent to locate the relevant product before it can reason about it. Solution WebMCP Vision exposes two deliberate tool tiers. Structured tools handle catalog discovery, specifications, compatibility, cart actions, and checkout. Five vision tools return bounded product-image references and, when explicitly selected, a temporary browser photo URL so a multimodal agent can make a visual judgment without pretending the server is an image model. People and agents can collaborate on a decision that was previously difficult to express through structured product data: a person supplies a style or space, while the agent compares relevant visual candidates and explains visible trade-offs. Routine actions remain fast and deterministic, and visual context is used only when it helps. WebMCP implementation The existing structured commerce tools remain the default. The vision tier adds getProductImage , compareProductAesthetics , highlightVisualDifference , matchToUserPhoto , and pickBestFit .
