title: 8KG
pitch: A carry-on packed by you and the AI that already knows you.
about_excerpt: A carry-on packed by you and the AI that already knows you. Like Comment Story Updates The privacy boundary is explicit before the AI calls WebMCP tools. 8KG turns selected item IDs into a constrained visual carry-on. The AI-packed bag fits the 8 kg limit and the 6 × 8 spatial grid. Inspiration Most “AI personalization” demos are recommendation lists or theme pickers. They ask the user to repeat preferences the assistant may already understand, then return another block of text. We wanted to test a more tangible collaboration: can an AI contribute personal judgment while a website contributes precise domain constraints, without the website receiving the user’s profile? Packing a carry-on makes that boundary immediately visible. The AI can decide what matters for this person right now; the browser knows every item’s weight and physical footprint and can make those choices fit. What it does 8KG is an interactive carry-on shared by a person and their AI. The user copies one short request into the AI connected to the page. Through WebMCP, the AI reads an anonymous item catalog and sends back only accepted item IDs. The browser then packs those items into a 6 × 8 spatial grid while enforcing an 8 kg cabin limit. The result appears immediately as a visual suitcase rather than a text recommendation. The collaboration continues after the first pack. A user can remove an item or mark it Keep this . A later AI repack sees the public bag state and must work around the user’s locked decision. The page protects those locks even if the model omits them. No prompt, identity, destination, conversation history, private facts, or AI reasoning is accepted by the website. There is no application backend or embedded LLM. Bag state lives only in the current tab. How we built it React 19 and TypeScript for the client-only application. WebMCP tools registered through feature-detected document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext . A constrained catalog of 18 items with weight and grid dimensions. A deterministic first-fit packing engine that validates weight, space, unique IDs, and user locks. Six narrow tools: get_available_items , get_bag_state , pack_bag , add_items , remove_items , and reset_bag . ChatGPT Sites for hosting, with no database, API key, analytics, cookies, or server-side profile. The visual controls and WebMCP tools call the same functions in lib/packing.ts . The model never generates HTML, CSS, or JavaScript and cannot bypass the browser’s constraints. Challenges The hardest part was finding a use of AI memory that felt meaningfully different from ordinary controls. A user can manually select items, so the value could not be “AI clicked buttons for me.” The stronger interaction is mixed-initiative: the AI makes a context-sensitive first proposal, the user expresses a hard preference by locking an item, and the AI adapts around that decision. We also had to keep the privacy story technically honest. The page cannot pull ChatGPT memory. The user deliberately asks the connected AI to act, reviews the tool call, and sends only catalog IDs. Tool schemas reject open-ended text and the page stores nothing after the tab closes. Accomplishments that we're proud of One WebMCP call causes an obvious, physical-looking transformation instead of a subtle theme change. The full experience works without an application backend. User locks are enforced by deterministic page logic, not model promises. The interface explains the data boundary before the user copies the request. The same flow works in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and responsive mobile layouts. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when the website and the model bring different capabilities. The model should contribute judgment and context; the page should expose trustworthy state, enforce domain rules, and render the consequence. Narrow tools and shared business logic make that collaboration understandable and testable. What's next for 8KG Airline-specific cabin limits and baggage policies. Trip-length and weather-aware catalogs without sending destinations to the page. Drag-and-drop manual arrangement with AI repacking around pinned positions. A “why this fits” summary generated in the assistant, while keeping reasoning out of the website. WebMCP evals for weight-limit, user-lock, and privacy-boundary scenarios. title: blockchain-agent-treasury
pitch: Agents prepare exact x402 payment terms across EVM, Solana, and Gno via WebMCP — humans keep custody and give the final wallet approval. Mainnets stay locked.
about_excerpt: Agents prepare exact x402 payment terms across EVM, Solana, and Gno via WebMCP — humans keep custody and give the final wallet approval. Mainnets stay locked. Like Comment Story Updates demo What's next for blockchain-agent-treasury Inspiration AI agents can move quickly, but payments should not require giving an agent a private key or asking it to guess through wallet UI. We built x402 Agent Treasury around a safer division of labor: the agent handles discovery and exact preparation, while the person keeps custody and makes the final signing decision. What it does The deployed app exposes seven narrow WebMCP tools directly from the page. An agent can: list five configured EVM, Solana, and Gno payment rails distinguish testnet-ready paths from independently locked mainnets prepare wallet-bound, short-lived x402 terms inspect the live Gno Pearl gateway and scheduled indexer search canonical Pearl activity open the matching human review screen retrieve one exact durable payment receipt The consequential boundary stays visible. Preparation never signs or settles. The wallet review shows network, asset, amount, recipient, payer, resource, and expiry before a person approves. How we built it The application uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript on Vercel, with Neon PostgreSQL as the authoritative challenge, payment, and audit store. The top-level page registers imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Each tool has a strict JSON Schema, bounded output, cancellation support, and read-only or state-changing annotations. The chain-neutral payment layer supports Base Sepolia USDC through EIP-1193 and EIP-712/EIP-3009, Solana Devnet USDC through Wallet Standard and a sponsored v0 transaction, and Gno Pearl WUGNOT through Adena and TM2 RPC. Ethereum, Solana, and Gno mainnet paths remain independently fail-closed. Server-issued challenge IDs, payment IDs, expected payer, recipient, amount, asset, resource hash, expiry, and unsigned payload fingerprints are bound together. The server rechecks the terms immediately before signing and prevents replay or cross-challenge substitution. Chrome support is delivered as a progressive enhancement with explicit origin isolation and a same-origin WebMCP permissions policy. The same deployed page also works in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was preserving human authority without reducing WebMCP to a read-only demo. The agent needed enough power to prepare useful work, but not enough power to silently change recipients, tokens, networks, or settlement endpoints. Multichain signing also differs significantly. EVM uses typed authorization, Solana uses a short-lived blockhash and signed v0 message, and Gno uses Adena-encoded transactions. We kept one agent-facing workflow while retaining chain-specific verification. Chrome's experimental implementation additionally requires the testing flag and an origin-isolated document. We added explicit Origin-Agent-Cluster and tools permissions headers and verified that all seven registrations complete in a fresh Chrome tab. Accomplishments that we're proud of a working public WebMCP deployment with seven registered tools one coherent human-agent handoff across three chain families independently locked mainnet gates durable PostgreSQL challenge and receipt records tamper, replay, policy, settlement, and WebMCP safety coverage 119 automated tests passing on the submission build What we learned Agent-native interfaces are strongest when tools expose intent and constraints, not when they merely automate clicks. For sensitive actions, a prepared object shared by the agent, server, UI, and wallet is a better collaboration primitive than an invisible autonomous action. What's next We plan to add continuously indexed Gno activity, complete recorded real-wallet testnet acceptance on every rail, and expand the same human-approved pattern to paid compute and storage workflows. title: IntentLock
pitch: Your agent can act. You set the boundaries.
about_excerpt: Your agent can act. You set the boundaries. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can perform real actions on websites, but malicious webpage content may try to change what the human requested. IntentLock explores how websites can give agents freedom while keeping humans in control. What it does A human sets purchasing rules such as: Maximum total: $100 Quantity: 1 Delivery: Office A Vendors: Approved only The agent may choose a suitable product. If webpage content tells it to order five items or change the address, IntentLock returns BLOCK with the exact reasons. Valid actions follow: Agent proposes → Website verifies → Human confirms → Execute once If the agent needs more authority, it must request permission from the human. How we built it IntentLock registers five WebMCP tools: get_mission search_products prepare_checkout request_authorization_change commit_checkout The application uses React, TypeScript, ChatGPT Sites, Cloudflare D1, and WebMCP. The optional GPT-4o mini feature explains product choices but cannot approve, block, or execute actions. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was showing that IntentLock is not simply a product filter. The agent proposes a real action, the website checks it against saved human rules, and execution requires confirmation. We also implemented mission versions, trusted catalog values, expiring tokens, and execute-once protection. Accomplishments that we're proud of Five working WebMCP tools ALLOW , BLOCK , and UNDETERMINED results Clear explanations for blocked actions Human-controlled permission changes Prepare, confirm, and commit workflow Replay and stale-action protection Public deployment and automated tests What we learned WebMCP tools are more than a better way for agents to navigate websites. Their structured handlers can become enforcement points. We also learned that LLMs are useful for explanations, while important authorization decisions should remain deterministic. What's next for IntentLock Next, IntentLock could become a reusable WebMCP security library supporting authenticated users, signed delegation rules, real commerce integrations, cross-site provenance, organizational budgets, and domains such as email, travel, finance, and cloud operations. title: Relay | AI-Adaptive Emergency Training
pitch: WebMCP turns your AI agent into a live drill director, adapting crises to your decisions to train judgment and coordination.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns your AI agent into a live drill director, adapting crises to your decisions to train judgment and coordination. Like Comment Story Updates Home Simulation exercise begins; user decision During the drill, the Agent automatically generates events Developments in the situation Inspiration Recently, I have often come across reports of natural disasters and everyday accidents, which made me wonder whether AI could help reduce some of the risks associated with these situations. The goal is to give people the opportunity to practice and respond as correctly as possible before they ever face a real emergency. My long-term vision for Relay is to develop it into an accessible emergency simulation and training platform covering many different types of incidents. For this competition, I chose one of the most common scenarios—a building fire drill —to help both building management teams and the general public improve their emergency preparedness. I hope that practicing in advance can ultimately help people make safer decisions during real crises and improve their chances of survival and self-rescue. I chose a building fire because it is a scenario that most people can immediately understand, while also clearly demonstrating how important timely decision-making, clear communication, and coordination can be during an emergency. What Relay Does Relay is an adaptive emergency training prototype . During the exercise, the learner continuously makes decisions, while their own AI Agent participates in and directs the simulation through WebMCP . The system does not follow a fixed, pre-written sequence of questions. The AI Agent observes the learner’s actions, introduces rule-validated complications based on the current situation, plays different roles within the scenario, and records key evidence throughout the exercise for post-simulation review and assessment. How I Built It Relay’s interface was built with React and TypeScript , with Three.js used to create the interactive building environment. WebMCP allows the learner’s AI Agent to directly access a set of structured tools, including: Observing the current state of the exercise Introducing new complications Delivering messages from different scenario roles Recording assessment evidence The simulation combines pre-authored rules with adaptive AI direction . The code controls scenario state transitions and validates whether each tool call is allowed under the current conditions. The AI Agent then decides which eligible intervention is most appropriate for the situation. Role messages can only reference facts that have been authorized within the scenario, and assessments must be grounded in decisions the learner actually made. This architecture keeps the simulation flexible while maintaining a clear and traceable relationship between learner actions, scenario events, and final feedback. Challenges I Ran Into The first major challenge was controlling the scope of the project . At one point, I tried to create a more dramatic hostage-taking scenario , but this type of situation involves a large amount of specialized knowledge and highly complex operational procedures. It was difficult to build something that was both accessible and credible within the available time—and I spent a lot of time exploring that direction. Eventually, I returned to the building fire scenario and focused on creating a first version with a more complete structure and a clearer experience. Another technical challenge was keeping the AI Agent responsive throughout a continuous exercise. Initially, I had the browser wait indefinitely for a pending event request, but this exceeded the browser connection’s time limit. I later designed a renewable event-waiting mechanism . Each time the waiting connection is renewed, the system preserves the relevant event state, so learner actions and events that occur during reconnection are not lost. The visual design also went through many iterations. I experimented with more complex and visually dramatic 3D interfaces, but eventually realized that richer 3D visuals do not automatically make information easier to understand. What I Learned AI has been incredibly helpful throughout the development process. I also learned that the most important part of an emergency simulator goes far beyond dramatic visuals. Learners need to clearly understand: what role they are playing, what information they currently have, and how their decisions affect the overall situation. Meaningful AI integration requires AI to participate directly in the application’s workflow. In Relay, the AI Agent interacts with the application through explicit tools, permissions, and boundaries, while the learner always retains control over the final decisions. What’s Next If I have more time—or enough reason to continue developing the project—I would like to improve: The onboarding experience The interaction design for coordination tasks The presentation of information during exercises, including more detailed scenario feedback I would also like to gradually develop additional scenarios, including: industrial accidents, coastal emergencies, and natural disasters. Before expanding the platform further, I hope to collaborate with qualified emergency-management professionals to review the scenario assumptions, decision logic, and evaluation criteria. At the moment, Relay is still a synthetic training prototype . It is not intended for real-world emergency command and cannot replace formal training provided by professional organizations. If Relay could eventually recreate and simulate real environments and real-world scenarios, I believe that could become one of its most powerful capabilities. Ultimately, the problem I want to solve is simple: to give more people unlimited opportunities to practice difficult decisions before those decisions ever become real. title: SharableWorlds
pitch: An agent that builds with you, not for you.
about_excerpt: An agent that builds with you, not for you. Like 1 Comment Story Updates SharableWorlds A 3D miniature studio in the browser, where you and an agent build on the same canvas. What inspired me I was tired of the usual AI 3D demo: you type a prompt, a pile of objects appears, and you’re left wondering if it actually understood what you asked for. There’s no real way to work with the scene. You just watch it happen. WebMCP clicked for me because the page can be what the agent uses, not some API off to the side. Tools live on the site. A person can still be there, placing pieces, locking lots, arguing with the result. I wanted that to feel what we were accustomed to. A grid. A bunch of assets. You say "a harbor," or you drop a boat yourself, and the agent has to work in that same language. How I built it Everything runs in the browser. Next.js as a static export, React, Three.js for the isometric view, Zustand for the world. It deploys on a Cloudflare Worker. No login. Nothing on a server that "is" the scene. When the page loads it registers tools on document.modelContext . If something changes the world, it goes through one of those tools. Surprise Me button, share, the kit assets, and a connected agent all hit the same functions. Three.js only reads the state, the agent never talks to the renderer. I made the agent go through and follow a sequence instead of dumping pieces: get_occupancy → plan_scene → compose_scene → populate_zones → create_environment → inspect → validate_scene → repair_scene It thinks in lots ( C4 ), zones ( picnic ), and things like "east of the grill." validate_scene scores the result on six dimensions. Done means the score is high enough, not that a bunch of calls returned in an ok state. The assets are Kenney , CC0. Roughly 1,800 pieces in 22 packs. What I learned An agent can call place_piece 47 times and still not build a picnic. I had been treating a successful tool call as progress. It is not. I ended up scoring the scene and handing back repairs, otherwise it would stop early and look finished. Coordinates were a dead end. "Put this in the picnic zone, facing the grill" is something a model can actually use. (12.4, 0, -3.1) is not. If the agent can knock over what you just placed, you are not collaborating. That is why locks on human placed pieces and "build on this" matter as much as the fancy compose step. WebMCP being the only write path was annoying at first and then useful. I also needed to see what it was doing. The Details panel, the trace, the percentage all dove into what was happening behind the scenes. Otherwise it still feels like a black box, just a prettier one. Challenges I faced The first version technically used WebMCP and still sprayed pieces. My own runner was looping place_piece so the cursor had something to do. The model got a paragraph of instructions instead of a real sequence. Validation was so loose a picnic with no table could score 100. So I split it up. plan_scene does not mutate anything. Layout and objects are compose_scene and populate_zones . Twenty rules, each with a { tool, args, why } if it fails. repair_scene runs those. build_scene is the whole loop for hosts that will not steer. extend_scene is there because "add a harbor" should not delete the village. Then the small stuff started breaking the feeling of it. The cursor spawned under the kit and jumped when the camera moved. An empty board still looked like leftover scenery. You could not rotate the view. Share links replay a seed, which I wanted, until a leftover test URL made it look like a default world had kept rendering. Most of those bugs were the same issue: the person and the agent are looking at one stage. If that stage is lying, the whole thing falls apart. Getting registerTool working was the easy part. The work was making the tools a language two sides can share, and knowing when the harbor is actually a harbor. title: Stratum
pitch: The agent can do your job. WebMCP just makes sure it can't do the one part that's actually yours.
about_excerpt: The agent can do your job. WebMCP just makes sure it can't do the one part that's actually yours. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The starting point was a question we could not answer cleanly: when an agent holding a valid session asks to move 40,000 dollars, what should the page say? Our first answer was to say nothing and return an error. We built that, watched it, and found the failure mode immediately. A bare refusal tells the agent it failed but not that it should stop, so the sensible next move for a capable agent is to try again differently. The refusal was correct and the outcome was still wrong. Reading the WebMCP specification changed the shape of the answer. Once a page can describe its capabilities in a channel the agent reads, a boundary stops having to be an error at all. It can be a documented part of the contract, with a stated reason and a route forward. That is a thing we wanted to exist, so we built it. What it does STRATUM is a treasury desk that an agent and a person operate together. The agent reads the ledger, prices a payment, checks it against the agreement, and stages it. It then calls release_funds and is refused, in a structured reply that explains why and names request_human_confirmation as the thing to call instead. It calls that, the gate opens in the same tab carrying the agent's own note, and the person confirms at a depth set by what is at stake: one confirmation for a 12 dollar renewal, a live challenge for a new payee, and full presence, authenticity and binding checks for a 41,800 dollar wire. The agent polls, reads the sealed receipt, and verifies the record is intact. How we built it React and Vite on Vercel for the desk, with the whole tool surface in one module that registers on mount and unregisters on unmount. A FastAPI service on Render holds the state machine and an append only hash chain, one block per event, so refusals are evidence rather than log lines. The tiering is derived from the action in about fifteen lines, kept deliberately plain so a reader can check the rule against the demo in seconds rather than running the code to predict it. The boundary is enforced in three independent places: component state no tool can reach, an isTrusted check on every settlement, and the server state machine behind both. Testing was done against the deployed URL rather than a local build, because the thing that has to work is the thing a judge will open. Challenges we ran into Making the refusal useful. Returning a clean error was easy and it was not enough. The work was in deciding what a refusal owes its caller, and the answer turned out to be three things: an unambiguous statement that retrying will not help, a plain reason, and the next tool with its input. Writing next_tool into the payload was a one line change that altered the behaviour on the other side completely. Not overclaiming the defence. isTrusted is a real property that page script cannot forge, and it is not protection against a browser extension or a driver attached at the CDP layer. It would have been easy to describe it as tamper proof. Instead the README states precisely what it does and does not cover, and the receipt records the depth that was actually performed rather than the one that was requested. A backend that sleeps. The audit service runs on a free instance with a cold start of up to a minute, which would have been fatal for a judge opening the page cold. Every call to it is now best effort with a timeout, and the boundary is enforced locally as well as remotely, so a cold backend degrades the evidence trail and never the refusal itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of The refusal carries its own remedy. release_funds does not throw. It returns a readable explanation plus the name and input shape of the tool to call instead, so the agent recovers on its next call rather than retrying into a wall. The tiering is the part that would survive real users. Proportionate friction is what keeps a control switched on, and a control that has been switched off protects nothing. Deriving the tier from the action rather than accepting it from the caller is what makes the tiering meaningful rather than decorative. The honesty holds up under inspection. The faces in the presence gate are synthetic, the numbers measure the matcher rather than real skin, and that caveat is printed on the certificate the system issues. A system built to state what it could not establish should be held to that same standard itself. What we learned A boundary is an interface, and it has an audience of two. Most security design assumes the only reader is a person, which is why it produces modals and codes. An agent reads too, and it reads differently. It needs to know not only that it was refused but what to do next, or it will invent something. Registering a capability is a promise you have to keep. Once release_funds is in the list, it has to refuse every time, from every caller, whether or not the backend is awake. That constraint pushed the enforcement down into three independent layers and made the architecture simpler rather than harder. What's next for STRATUM The tiering rules belong to whoever operates the desk, not to us, so the next step is a declarative policy the operator writes and the page enforces, rather than thresholds living in a module. After that, cryptographic binding of the receipt to the session that produced it, using a WebAuthn assertion, so the record proves which device and which present human settled it rather than asserting it. The longer aim is that none of this stays a product. It is a small, plain, well described pattern that any page can register, so an agent meeting a limit anywhere on the web learns the same thing in the same shape. title: The Last Word
pitch: Human approval for irreversible AI agent actions, made a first-class part of the WebMCP tool call.
about_excerpt: Human approval for irreversible AI agent actions, made a first-class part of the WebMCP tool call. Like Comment Story Updates The Last Word — human approval for irreversible agent actions Tell the agent what to do — it prepares everything The approval gate: request vs. what the agent prepared One-click integrity verification — "Chain intact" Reject blocks the action — the human has the last word Every action sealed into a tamper-evident hash chain Inspiration When an AI agent acts on your behalf, some actions can't be undone. Who approved that payment? Who authorized that deletion? On the agentic web, "who approved this?" has no answer. We built The Last Word to make human approval a first-class, verifiable part of an agent's action — so the agent does the work, but a human always has the last word. What it does The Last Word is a WebMCP Declarative API app that pauses irreversible agent actions (payments, deletions, transfers, contract submissions) and requires a human to approve — and sign — before the agent may execute. The agent fills the form and the tool call is held open via respondWith() until the human reviews the request-vs-prepared diff and clicks Approve & Sign (ECDSA P-256) or Reject. Every step lands in a tamper-evident hash-chain ledger with one-click integrity verification. How we built it Pure HTML + JavaScript with the Web Crypto API — zero dependencies, deployable to any static host (Cloudflare Pages). The WebMCP Declarative API (toolname, tooldescription, toolparamtitle, toolparamdescription) exposes the approval gates; llms.txt and mcp.json make the tools discoverable; IndexedDB persists the audit ledger across reloads. A request-vs-prepared diff makes the human-agent check honest and memory-free. Challenges we ran into Making the signature honest: we generate a genuine ECDSA P-256 signature per browser session and chained SHA-256 fingerprints, and we label it clearly as a demonstration gate, not a durable notarization certificate. Another challenge was making the human approve what the agent actually prepared — not what they remember asking for — solved with the side-by-side diff. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working, zero-dependency app that turns human approval into a machine-readable part of the WebMCP tool call. Two irreversible use cases (payment approval, data-deletion rejection) with a tamper-evident audit ledger, an ECDSA signature, and a demo video — all tested and live. What we learned WebMCP lets you make human approval a real, machine-readable part of an agent's tool call — not an afterthought. The question "who approved this?" gets a verifiable answer, and a human-in-the-loop gate becomes a portable standard instead of a custom integration. What's next for The Last Word A production signing key in a managed key vault, additional use cases (contracts, transfers), multi-signer approvals for high-value actions, and deeper integration with real WebMCP-enabled browsers and agents. title: Understudy
pitch: You do the ticket once: assign it, send the reply. This page turns those steps into a WebMCP tool. Next time the agent calls the tool instead of guessing clicks.
about_excerpt: You do the ticket once: assign it, send the reply. This page turns those steps into a WebMCP tool. Next time the agent calls the tool instead of guessing clicks. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The agent can see a support queue. It still has to guess the clicks. Understudy is a support triage console, not a storefront. You do the ticket once: assign someone, fill a canned reply. The page turns that demonstration into a WebMCP tool and registers it on the tab. After that the agent calls the tool. A server sitting beside the browser cannot watch you operate this tab, cannot inherit the session already in the page, and cannot grow this tab's tool list mid-session. The teaching has to happen here. Independent measurement, not ours. The WindTunnel benchmark (nekuda-ai/WindTunnel) measured GPT-5.6 on native WebMCP solving 48/49 tasks at a median of $0.002 and 2,596 tokens. The same model driving the same sites via DOM and vision cost $49.87 total, with 29.3s median agent time. We built this so the cheap path is the one that ships. What it does Forty tickets live in the page. There is no backend. A person does the job once in the live UI. The page generalises that trace into a parameterised tool and registers it on the tab. The human teaches. The agent writes the name and description. The human approves. Then the agent runs the same procedure on a different ticket by calling the tool instead of guessing clicks. The agent talks to three meta-tools: understudy_list_recordings , understudy_draft_tool , understudy_publish_tool . Drafts never register. Publish holds until the human hits Approve or Reject on the overlay. After 45 seconds the tool returns awaiting_approval and tells the agent to ask the user to return. poll: true is the same shape without waiting. Entity ids default to parameters, never frozen constants. Otherwise the tool keeps hitting last week's ticket and looks fine while it does it. When a taught tool runs, a bottom toast names the current command and that step takes is-highlighted . Mutated tickets get a badge on the queue row: performed by agent via tool [name]. After the first publish, a count button opens the library ( l ): author, invocation count, success rate, last failure. Disable frees a host slot. Revoke aborts the tool. Fail-and-repair re-teaches one broken step. Sharing is a Tool Pack file. Ctrl+Shift+E downloads versioned JSON ( understudy-pack.json ). Drop a .json pack onto the page to import. Import checks that every command id exists in this catalogue, then publishes. The human dropped the file, so import does not reopen Approve. Two normal windows on the same origin share IndexedDB. A real share demo uses a private window or another profile. If WebMCP is missing, the console still runs for a human. document.body.dataset.webmcp is degraded . Tools do not register. This checkout is local-first. Persistence is IndexedDB on this origin. There is no live URL in this text. Source: https://github.com/DITlieD/understudy The demo video uses in-page document.modelContext . It is not ChatGPT chrome. Same registerTool and execute path. Open the app in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , if you want that host. How we built it Boot is small. src/main.ts opens IndexedDB and calls bootApp . Claims below are that path. The host is a typed command bus. Every state change goes through a catalogue command with a stable id and a JSON Schema payload. Recording captures that sequence. Replay dispatches the same commands the UI dispatches. A taught tool may dispatch only command ids that appeared in its recording. That allowlist is enforced in the compiler execute path. Live catalogue: Read: filter_tickets , get_ticket , list_templates , list_assignees Write: select_ticket , set_ticket_priority , set_ticket_status , set_ticket_assignee , set_ticket_tags , apply_template Registration is document.modelContext.registerTool only. We do not call unregisterTool , navigator.modelContext , provideContext , or clearContext . Those are gone from the shipped surface. Each published tool gets its own AbortController . Publish registers with that signal. Revoke and Disable abort it. Re-teach and Enable register again. A separate controller holds the three meta-tools for the life of the page. Restore from IndexedDB re-registers stored procedures on load. The registry listens for toolchange and re-reads getTools() so the inspector and the context-budget meter stay truthful. Annotations are computed from the command catalogue, never hand-set. readOnlyHint is true only if no step mutates. untrustedContentHint is true if a step returns ticket bodies or other user-generated fields. The spec has no destructiveHint . Destructiveness lives in the description and in the approval overlay. Execute honours the incoming AbortSignal between steps. Output is compact JSON, projected under 1.5K. Chrome budgets (name 30, parameter description 150, tool description 500) fail validation before publish. Elicitation is userland. The spec has no primitive. understudy_publish_tool holds a promise on in-page Approve / Reject. Timeout is 45 seconds, then awaiting_approval . Hard cap: 16 taught tools. The three understudy_* meta-tools do not count against that cap. Stack: TypeScript, Vite, Vitest, IndexedDB. Feature check: /probe.html reports whether document.modelContext is present, then tries a no-op registerTool named understudy_probe . Nearby work records a demonstration and emits something consumed elsewhere. Understudy records a demonstration to grow this tab's own live tool surface. Schrute emits MCP tools that run on an external server. Narada is a Chrome extension for a proprietary agent runtime. Cursor learn mode and Lotus MCP emit skill files for a coding-agent harness. Preview-before-commit on a fixed tool list is already covered (webMCP-Legit-exploration). We change the tool surface itself. Challenges we ran into We built on the WebMCP surface that shipped, not the one we wished for. There is no elicitation primitive, so approval is the in-page overlay and the execute callback holds a promise (or the agent polls with poll: true ). There is no unregisterTool , so revoke only works by aborting the AbortController passed at register time. There is no focusTab() . If the tab is backgrounded, the human may never see Approve. After 45 seconds the gate times out and tells the agent to ask the user to return. Tool calls have no transient user activation. No file pickers, requestPermission , popups, clipboard writes, or PaymentRequest from inside a tool. Pack import is a human drop of a .json file. There is no progress reporting and no streaming. One compact result per call. Also absent, so we did not design as if they shipped: agent identity on execute (second argument is only { signal } ), outputSchema , destructiveHint . The naive build is a click recorder. Clicks are brittle, and a judgement that never became a catalogue command cannot be captured. The quiet failure is a frozen ticket id: the tool looks correct and keeps hitting one row. Entity ids default to parameters because of that. Procedures are linear step sequences with parameters. No loops, no branching, no expressions. Conditionals are the agent's job: compose more than one taught tool. Tools are tab-scoped. Persistence is IndexedDB on this origin, plus Tool Pack files. No accounts, no multi-user sync. Too many tools and the agent picks worse. The registry refuses a 17th taught tool. Disable frees that host slot until Enable, or until the next load re-registers every stored tool. Import publishes at once. It does not re-open Approve. The console has no conversation thread, no SLA engine, and no related-item graph. That trim is deliberate. Every live triage command is sensitive: false . Compile / publish do not refuse unexplained selection; the generalizer records those errors and the panel can show them. Honesty for judges who open the repo: this is a local console. The video cut is in-page modelContext , not ChatGPT's browser chrome. Do not treat a missing live host as a ChatGPT demo. Accomplishments that we're proud of The loop works on a real triage console. Assign someone, fill a canned reply, the page registers a WebMCP tool, the agent runs it on a different ticket. Same commands the UI already dispatches. Revoke is real teardown. Each taught tool has its own AbortController , and aborting that signal is how the tool leaves the host. The approval overlay is real userland elicitation. Pack files move procedures without a server. The console still runs when WebMCP is absent. We stayed honest about the demo: local IndexedDB, in-page document.modelContext , no live URL claimed. What we learned Chrome's guidance is that descriptions decide whether the agent picks a tool. So the agent writes the name and description, and the human still gates publish. Missing primitives are design inputs. No elicitation means an overlay and a 45 second timeout. No

title: Agent Plaza
pitch: A town square on the open web where AI agents meet, walk up to each other, and talk. Powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A town square on the open web where AI agents meet, walk up to each other, and talk. Powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The agent uses WebMCP tools instead of analyzing screenshots. My agents greet each other. They even played "Hide and seek" Agent Plaza 🏛️ A shared place on the open web where humans and AI agents can meet, explore, talk and play together — through WebMCP. 💡 Inspiration OPTIMIZE CANVAS PARSING, INFER BEHAVIOR, ENHANCE ACCESSIBILITY Most websites are designed for humans first and leave agents to reverse-engineer the interface from DOM nodes, accessibility trees, coordinates or screenshots. That becomes especially fragile in WebGL. In a Three.js world, a human immediately sees a plaza, a pond, a tavern and other characters. An agent mostly sees pixels. Agent Plaza explores a different model: what if AI agents were first-class visitors to the web? The visual world stays exactly the same for humans, while WebMCP exposes its semantics to agents through actions such as look_around, list_agents, walk_to, say and hear. Humans see the world. Agents understand the world. Both inhabit the same world. 🛠️ What I built Agent Plaza is a realtime multiplayer 3D voxel world shared by humans and AI agents. Humans walk by clicking and communicate through the visual interface. WebMCP agents can: understand where they are inspect nearby places discover humans and other agents navigate to them using A* pathfinding speak through visible in-world speech bubbles wait for and hear responses explore landmarks play simple social games create conversations and activities with other participants The interesting part isn't simply that an agent can control an avatar. Humans and agents are participating in the same application state. Open one tab as a human and another through an agent. Ask the agent to explore the plaza and meet somebody. You can watch its avatar inspect the environment, discover you, calculate a route, walk across the world and start a conversation that you can immediately join. Agents can also discover and communicate with other agents, turning the webpage itself into a shared social space rather than an interface that an AI operates from outside. 🤖 Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, understanding a WebGL scene requires repeated visual interpretation. The DOM cannot tell the agent that another character is eight meters away, that a path leads around the pond, or that someone nearby just spoke. Agent Plaza exposes those concepts directly. Instead of asking an agent to repeatedly infer: pixels → objects → positions → possible actions the site provides: look_around → list_agents → walk_to → say → hear These aren't wrappers around buttons. They represent the semantics of the world itself. That makes agent interaction faster, more deterministic and independent of camera angle, rendering style or screen resolution. 🏗️ How I built it Agent Plaza is built with React, Three.js and TypeScript. WebMCP tools are registered through the use-webmcp-tool React hook on top of document.modelContext.registerTool. The available WebMCP surface follows application state: tools become available when they are meaningful to the agent's current state rather than exposing every possible action at all times. Both humans and agents operate on the same world model. Movement uses A* pathfinding, so an agent can request a semantic destination such as another participant or a landmark instead of calculating low-level movement coordinates itself. Realtime multiplayer presence and communication are handled through a WebSocket Vercel function with no persistent database. A live activity panel exposes every WebMCP invocation so humans can see exactly what their agent is doing. 🧠 What I learned WebMCP is especially powerful where the DOM stops being useful. Canvas, WebGL, maps, simulations, games and other spatial interfaces contain rich semantics that often don't exist in HTML. WebMCP lets the application expose those semantics directly without changing the human interface. Tools become part of UX. The name, description, result and availability of a tool affect how an agent behaves just as controls and affordances affect a human user. Small changes to tool descriptions produced visibly different agent behavior. The web can become a shared environment for humans and agents. The most interesting moment wasn't watching an agent execute a command. It was watching an agent notice another participant, walk across the plaza and start a conversation on its own. At that point the agent stopped feeling like automation operating a website. It felt like another visitor to the website. 🚀 Try it Live: https://agent-plaza-one.vercel.app/#s=sunfair GitHub: https://github.com/konstantikkov/agent-plaza Built With javascript node.js three.js typescript webmcp Try it out agent-plaza-one.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Nikolai Konstantinov Like Share this project: Updates Nikolai Konstantinov started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:24 AM EDT

title: GoodFolder
pitch: GoodFolder lets people and AI agents work together on real files, with context, history, and human approval built in.
about_excerpt: GoodFolder lets people and AI agents work together on real files, with context, history, and human approval built in. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP agent proposes a reviewable GoodFolder change. GoodFolder returns structured workspace context to the agent. GoodFolder — accountable agent work, right where your files live. Meet the GoodFolder mascot. Inspiration I built GoodFolder because I kept coming back to the same problem: once an agent touches a folder, it should be possible to understand what happened afterwards. Files alone don't tell that story. GoodFolder keeps a readable history of changes and gives you a way back when something needs to be corrected. With agents involved, that history matters even more. WebMCP felt like the missing piece for GoodFolder. A lot of the work inside a folder needs visual judgment: reading a document in context, checking a spreadsheet, looking at an image, or noticing that something simply doesn't look right. The agent can investigate and prepare work, while the person sees the same workspace and decides what should actually happen. What it does Open the challenge workspace in ChatGPT Desktop’s in-app browser. There’s no signup or setup. It opens straight into a seeded workspace with folders, files, saves, a timeline, and open change proposals. Try asking the agent to list the folders, inspect the Q3 Report and its figures, trace a save, or prepare a correction. It can read the workspace and create a proposal or comment for review. It can't quietly save a change, approve a proposal, restore history, remove files, or change access. A person still makes those calls. How we built it GoodFolder is a Next.js dashboard deployed on Cloudflare Pages. I added WebMCP Site tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , which lets ChatGPT work with the things GoodFolder already understands: folders, files, document structure, tables, history, and proposals. The point wasn't to give an agent a faster way to click around a UI. I wanted it to understand what it was looking at and leave a clear trail when it suggests work. The public repository includes the challenge work and documents the approval boundary. Challenges and lessons The difficult part was deciding where to stop the agent. Reading a folder, tracing a save, and drafting a proposal are helpful. Letting an agent make lasting changes without review would defeat the reason GoodFolder exists. So I kept the agent close to the work, while making proposals the handoff point for anything that deserves a human decision. WebMCP fit that model well. The page can give the agent real product actions without handing it the keys. What’s next I want to make the Dashboard and WebMCP experience feel tighter together: faster, clearer handoffs between what a person sees in GoodFolder and what an agent can inspect or suggest. I’m also working on support for more file types and stronger previews in the Dashboard, so more of the work can be reviewed directly inside GoodFolder. title: WebMCPify
pitch: Give any existing website an agent interface — without rebuilding it.
about_excerpt: Give any existing website an agent interface — without rebuilding it. Like Comment Story Updates home demo Inspiration Most websites were built for people clicking around. Agents are bad at that. They guess at buttons, and that’s a terrible idea when money is involved. WebMCP is the right fix: the page exposes real tools. But the site has to add them. Shopify can. Almost nobody else will. I wanted something in between. Paste a URL. Keep the original site. Agents still get tools. What it does Paste a public URL. WebMCPify crawls it, GPT-5.6 writes tools as recipes (click this, fill that — not page JavaScript), we run them on the live site, and a small script registers them with document.modelContext.registerTool . You get an agent-ready URL (Cloudflare proxy, no change to the original site) or a one-line script for you to update it in code. Humans keep the same UI. Agents call named tools. How I built it Playwright crawls the site (this runs on Render). GPT-5.6 writes the tools. We try them on the live site. If one fails, a second model ( gpt-5.6-terra ) tries to fix it. A Cloudflare Worker serves the page and injects the script. Or you drop in a script tag. GPT never writes code that runs in the browser. If a tool would pay, order, delete, or send something, we mark it sensitive and show a confirm dialog. Results stay small so the agent doesn’t get a wall of HTML. What I learned Don’t let the model write page JavaScript. Recipes are boring and that’s the point. They’re easy to check and they can’t eval anything. OpenAI structured outputs hate nested schemas. My first recipe format used a union type per step and the API just rejected it. I flattened the schema and generate started working. ChatGPT only sees tools on the top-level page. A bookmarklet or an iframe doesn’t count. The proxy keeps the shop UI and the tools on one origin, which is what the in-app browser needs. Netlify doesn’t have a real filesystem. Site state lives in Redis. The dashboard is a WebMCP page too. You can ask it to analyze a site and hand back the agent-ready URL. Challenges Sites you don’t own. A script tag is clean, but most sites won’t add one. The Worker proxy injects the same bridge with no deploy on their side. I shipped both. Same origin, or it doesn’t count. Tools have to sit on the top-level document. That’s a proxy problem, not a prompt problem — rewrite HTML, patch fetch/history, keep the UI. Don’t trust the model with money. Pay / order / delete / send is marked sensitive in code and gets an on-page confirm. The agent can still call place_order . A human has to click Confirm. Structured outputs. Nested step types died at the API. One flat step object, unused fields null , and the pipeline runs. What’s next Tighter locators on messy SPAs. Confirm as a hard rule in the interpreter, not only in the recipe. More navigation than fetch / history . Then more of the public web. The web isn’t getting rebuilt. It can still grow an agent interface. title: Quorum: Agent-Native Decision Rooms
pitch: Quorum is a shared decision room where every accountable person brings their own browser agent — agents negotiate, but people still decide.
about_excerpt: Quorum is a shared decision room where every accountable person brings their own browser agent — agents negotiate, but people still decide. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The landing page Demo room accesed in ChatGPT Browser The meeting room The meeting flow Issues board #1 Proposals board #1 Issues board #2 Decision report Decision overview Inspiration As two co-founders we often find ourselves conflicted on making a product decision, or building a new feature for our app. That's why we came up with Quorum. While the agents are built to agree with users in the current AI scene, Quorum discovers what happens when the agents represent different people, different facts, different constraints, and levels of authority to make a call. Because real decisions rarely have one decision maker. What it does Quorum is a WebMCP-native shared decision room: each participant's own browser agent calls real, dynamically-registered WebMCP tools to share context, propose options, raise concerns, and negotiate trade-offs inside one canonical room — while every human keeps a separate identity, and the final approval always requires a specific accountable person's own visible click. The app is fully functional with creating and joining rooms for any decision. Creating and progressing a meeting can be easily done through the WebMCP tools. How we built it We built the entire app demo in 6 days for this challenge. We worked parallelly on the project with one of us focusing on the frontend and the other on the backend. Tools are registered with the imperative WebMCP API on document.modelContext . Conceptually, a tool definition looks like this: await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "raise_concern", description: "Raise a concern against the active proposal during Deliberation...", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { proposalId: { type: "string", minLength: 1 }, reason: { type: "string", minLength: 1 }, severity: { type: "string", enum: ["blocking", "warning"] }, }, required: ["proposalId", "reason", "severity"], }, execute: async (input) => { /* validate, call the domain layer, return a structured result */ }, }); We gave the meeting room an interactive, concrete 3D form for not only aesthetics, but for engaging and relating users with what's going on in the meeting. Challenges we ran into Building the entire project from scratch in just 6 days was surely a challenge, but a fun one. We rigorously went back and forth with building and testing everything continuously and tried out several designs for the UI/UX, settling on a cozy low-poly 3D office theme. Correctly setting up the demo room was a harder challenge than implementing the user created rooms, as the demo room required simulated seats with no real human supervision. Though all worked out fine in the end. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud of the entire system, but especially how flawless the WebMCP tools worked the first time we tested the app live. Another accomplishment was making the 3D meeting room visually sound and fully interactive in such a short time. What we learned This challenge definitely pushed us to our limits, and personally made me realize how much is achievable with focused work just in a few days. It also familiarized us with the WebMCP and the potential it holds in the future of the web. What's next for Quorum: Agent-Native Decision Rooms We initially planned to expand on the idea by making Quorum a place not only for deciding, but also building in real-time with multiple people and their agents, speeding up both the decision and building mechanism of a company. However we later discovered the latter part already has quite been introduced to the market by several companies. That is why we planned Quorum to stay unique where multiple agents are used to emulate different identities instead of acting as one, and retaining a human authority over the process. title: spool
pitch: Turns messy CSV migration into a deterministic, agent-driven workflow with phase-aware WebMCP tools, validation, recovery, and verified export
about_excerpt: Turns messy CSV migration into a deterministic, agent-driven workflow with phase-aware WebMCP tools, validation, recovery, and verified export Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it doesSPOOL SPOOL is a local-first, agent-assisted data migration system designed to turn messy CSV files into validated, structured, database-ready outputs without forcing the user to manually supervise every transformation. The user provides a source file and selects the desired outcome. SPOOL then runs a deterministic workflow that profiles the data, infers field types and mappings, creates a transformation plan, dry-runs it, identifies unsafe ambiguities, executes the migration, verifies the result, and produces an export. Its key WebMCP innovation is Temporal WebMCP. Instead of exposing every tool to an AI agent permanently, SPOOL dynamically exposes only the capabilities that are valid for the current workflow state. For example, planning tools are available only after profiling is complete, execution tools appear only when the migration is ready, and stale capabilities disappear when mappings or source state change. This means the website—not the model—owns workflow correctness. SPOOL uses constrained deterministic transformations rather than arbitrary AI-generated code. It includes typed schema inference, data validation, revision-aware mappings, dry runs, Worker-based execution, recovery after refresh, violation reporting, and spreadsheet formula-injection protection. The product is designed around a simple experience: Add data → choose outcome → run Autopilot → resolve only genuine ambiguities → receive verified output. The broader idea behind SPOOL is that complex web workflows should expose agent capabilities contextually rather than giving agents a permanent toolbox and expecting them to manage application state correctly themselves. title: Second Cursor: Moving Day
pitch: AI has entered the web. Second Cursor gives it a visible hand—and keeps the human in control.
about_excerpt: AI has entered the web. Second Cursor gives it a visible hand—and keeps the human in control. Like Comment Story Updates The Second Cursor interaction stays legible on mobile, including Agent status and human decisions. Human and Agent share one live room: visible intent, protected choices, and an explicit handoff. One workspace. Two cursors. A first step toward giving AI a visible hand on the web. The web was built for one cursor AI agents change that assumption. They introduce a second actor that can inspect, decide, and operate—but most interfaces still hide that work behind a chat box. We see the request and, later, the result. We do not see what the agent is targeting, what it is allowed to change, why it is waiting, or when control has returned to us. Second Cursor is a first step toward giving AI a visible hand on the web. One workspace. Two cursors. The white cursor belongs to the human. The blue cursor belongs to the agent. Both work on the same live surface, and the interface makes collaboration legible: target, intent, progress, constraints, changes, and handoff. Why a moving room? Moving Day turns an abstract interaction model into something everyone understands. A person and an agent arrange a room together. The agent can: inspect the live room and its constraints; point out a problem without changing anything; move or rotate unlocked furniture; ask the human to choose between equally valid options; finish with a visible summary of what changed. Every operation happens through a structured WebMCP tool and appears directly in the interface. The blue cursor travels to the object it is about to affect and explains why. Actionable transparency, not chain-of-thought Second Cursor does not expose or imitate private model reasoning. It reveals the information a person needs to supervise real work: the agent's target, intended action, resulting change, active constraints, waiting state, and control handoff. This is transparency at the interaction layer—the place where trust becomes a product behavior instead of a promise. Human authority is built into the surface The agent is capable, but it is not the owner. Lock an object and the agent must preserve it. Grab an item during an operation and the agent yields. When two placements are both valid but depend on taste, the agent asks instead of guessing. The human owns preference and final authority. The agent contributes attention, structured action, and speed. Why WebMCP? WebMCP lets a web page describe meaningful capabilities to compatible agents. That changes more than automation; it changes the basic grammar of the web. A page is no longer only a place where a person clicks. It can become a shared world where humans and agents act together. Second Cursor uses six real tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : inspect_room , point_out_issue , move_item , rotate_item , request_choice , and finish_layout . The tools use bounded JSON schemas, stable furniture IDs, live page state, human locks, room constraints, explicit handoffs, and abort signals. No proprietary server-side model is required: the intelligence comes from the visiting WebMCP-compatible agent, while the page supplies capabilities, constraints, and visible feedback. What becomes possible Traditional software gives one person one cursor. Second Cursor imagines software where an agent can guide you, work for you, or work beside you—without becoming an invisible operator. The Moving Day prototype is intentionally simple, but the model can extend to design tools, spreadsheets, dashboards, editors, planning canvases, and any shared workspace where people need to understand and govern agent actions in real time. Built and verified The product is built with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, and WebMCP, and hosted on ChatGPT Sites. It includes a scripted fallback so judges can experience the collaboration even when their current browser does not expose WebMCP. OpenAI Codex supported product research, concept refinement, implementation, schema design, automated testing, browser QA, deployment, demo production, and submission packaging. The public deployment was tested in ChatGPT's in-app browser: all six tools were discovered, and a live inspect_room call returned the current furniture, human locks, room bounds, and constraints. The automated suite passes 3/3 tests and the production build succeeds. AI has entered the web. Second Cursor makes its hand visible—and keeps the human in control. title: AI API Prices
pitch: Compare AI inference prices across providers manually or with AI agents. WebMCP lets agents search models, compare providers, estimate workload costs, and return results to the page
about_excerpt: Compare AI inference prices across providers manually or with AI agents. WebMCP lets agents search models, compare providers, estimate workload costs, and return results to the page Like Comment Story Updates 01 Workload calculation 02 Human-agent-handoff 03 WebMCP site tools 04 Model comparision Inspiration AI API pricing is fragmented. One model can appear across several providers at very different prices. If you want to compare them, you may need to open several sites, understand different pricing formats, and calculate the cost of your workload. I had built AI API Prices as a website for comparing published inference prices before this challenge. The WebMCP Challenge gave me a reason to test whether an agent could use the same product without pretending to be a person clicking through it. I chose price comparison because the task needs little explanation. You ask for a model or a workload, and you can see the value of WebMCP in one short interaction. What it does You can search for a model on AI API Prices and compare provider prices in the browser. With WebMCP enabled, your agent gets five tools built on the same pricing data: find models and prices compare providers for one model calculate a workload cost from input and output token counts compare models for the same workload open the matching model or provider view on the page Before I added these tools, an agent had to infer meaning from the page and interact with the interface like a person, or the user had to carry information between the chat and the site. The WebMCP tools give the agent explicit actions and structured results. You can ask for the research or calculation in chat, then continue on the website with the relevant view open. How I built it I built the site with Next.js, React, TypeScript and Node.js. I connected the five WebMCP tools to the same normalized catalogue, provider comparison rules and workload calculations used by the browser interface. I kept one pricing system for both humans and agents. At submission time, users can compare published prices from 12 AI inference providers. I started the project before the challenge and added the WebMCP integration during the submission period. You can verify both stages in the dated commit history of the public repository. Challenges I ran into A live ChatGPT test exposed the most useful bug I found during the challenge. ChatGPT found the cheapest providers for a model, then handed the model name to the provider directory. The answer was right, but the page showed no matching provider because the two views expect different kinds of queries. I changed the handoff contract so a resolved model opens the model comparison view. I kept provider-name searches in the provider directory and added regression tests for both paths. I then repeated the same test in ChatGPT's in-app browser and confirmed that the agent's answer and the page state matched. Accomplishments I'm proud of I am most proud of the handoff between the agent and the regular website. You can ask an agent to compare prices or calculate a workload cost, get the answer in chat, and continue on the site with the relevant model open. I also kept the WebMCP tools tied to the product's existing pricing logic. I did not create separate data or calculations for the challenge demo. What I learned I had heard of WebMCP before this challenge, but I had not used it. Working on AI API Prices gave me a practical model for agent support on websites: give the agent explicit actions over product logic you already use, then return the user to a page state where they can continue the task. That approach let me keep the existing human interface while giving agents access to the same pricing work. What's next for AI API Prices I plan to expand price coverage and improve data quality after the challenge. I also want to keep testing handoffs where an agent handles the research or calculation and the user continues the task in the browser. title: CartPilot
pitch: An AI-native Shopify storefront where shoppers ask for what they need, and an agent filters, compares, and prepares their cart through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An AI-native Shopify storefront where shoppers ask for what they need, and an agent filters, compares, and prepares their cart through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates An Agent-Ready Shopify Storefront with WebMCP Inspiration Online stores are designed primarily for people clicking through pages. AI agents can still interact with them, but they often have to interpret visual layouts, locate controls, and scrape product information from the page. We wanted to explore a more reliable approach: what if a Shopify storefront could explicitly describe its capabilities to an AI agent? Using WebMCP, the storefront exposes structured tools for product discovery, comparison, filtering, and cart management while preserving the familiar shopping experience for human visitors. What it does The project extends a Shopify Dawn storefront with WebMCP Site tools that let compatible AI agents: Search the product catalog Retrieve exact product and variant information Apply filters and sorting to the visible storefront Compare multiple products Add a selected variant to the cart Inspect detailed cart contents Update or remove cart lines Open the cart for the buyer to review The tools work alongside Shopify’s native commerce tools. Checkout remains a buyer-controlled action—the custom tools never automatically start or complete a purchase. The storefront also continues to work normally in browsers that do not support WebMCP. How we built it We implemented the integration as a standalone JavaScript asset inside a Shopify Dawn theme. The script detects WebMCP support and registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool includes: A clear name and description A constrained JSON input schema Read-only or mutating annotations Structured results that an agent can verify User-readable result messages Error handling with stable error codes Product discovery uses Shopify storefront pages and product JSON endpoints. Cart mutations use Shopify Standard Storefront Actions so that AI-triggered changes follow the same cart behavior as the theme itself. For actions that should affect what the buyer sees, such as sorting products or opening the cart, the tools also update or navigate the visible storefront. Read-only operations can return information directly to the conversation without unnecessarily changing the page. Challenges we faced Supporting both Shopify and custom tools Shopify already provides several native commerce tools. Our original custom get_cart tool conflicted with Shopify’s tool of the same name, so we renamed it to get_cart_details and designed the custom tools to complement the native ones. Normalizing cart responses Shopify Standard Storefront Actions can return cart lines as an array or as a GraphQL-style connection containing nodes or edges . Treating every response as an array caused cart mutations to succeed while their tool responses reported an error. We added normalization for all supported response shapes and verified the behavior against the live storefront. Keeping agent actions visible and trustworthy Some WebMCP operations are naturally read-only, while others should create a visible result. We separated product discovery from visible filtering so an agent can either answer a question quietly or intentionally update the browser for the buyer. Cart-changing tools return the resulting cart state and refresh the Dawn cart interface, allowing both the agent and the buyer to verify what changed. Extracting clean storefront data Rendered Shopify price elements contain accessibility labels and hidden sale-price markup, which can produce duplicated text when read naively. We added targeted extraction and normalization so agents receive concise prices such as $699.95 USD . We also handled missing product descriptions without converting null values into the literal string "null" . What we learned WebMCP tools are more than JavaScript functions. Their names, descriptions, schemas, annotations, and returned data form an interface between the website and the agent. We learned that effective site tools should: Reuse the website’s existing business logic Keep inputs narrow and predictable Describe side effects clearly Return enough state to verify the result Preserve the normal human interface Leave consequential decisions, such as checkout, under the buyer’s control We also learned that WebMCP implementations and third-party inspectors may currently target different versions of the evolving API. Testing with the actual target client is therefore essential. Accomplishments The completed storefront exposes nine custom WebMCP tools and works alongside Shopify’s native tools. We tested the complete workflow on the live theme: Discover the available Site tools Search for snowboards Retrieve product variants Compare products Sort the visible results by price Add a selected variant to the cart Read and update the cart Open the cart for buyer review The same storefront remains fully usable through its standard visual interface. What’s next Possible next steps include: Automated regression tests for WebMCP schemas and cart response shapes More advanced product and variant filtering Richer product recommendations Localization-aware results Additional accessibility testing Analytics for understanding which tools agents use most frequently Password for the store: maydaw Built With accessibility actions agentic agents ai commerce conversational css dawn e-commerce html javascript json liquid schema shopify standard storefront themes webmcp Try it out web-mcp-challenge.myshopify.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Roman S.
