title: Clip Magic- WebMCP on an Existing Contact Form
pitch: A live business website where a user’s AI agent prepares a contact form enquiry for human review and submission.
about_excerpt: A live business website where a user’s AI agent prepares a contact form enquiry for human review and submission. Like Comment Story Updates Using WebMCP on an existing website Clip Magic: making a real-world SMB website agent-ready Inspiration Most small businesses do not need another chatbot. They need fewer obstacles between a potential customer deciding, "I need help with this," and actually taking the next step. That was the attraction of WebMCP. The interesting part for me is that the user owns the AI agent . A business website does not have to create its own assistant, replace its existing workflow or force visitors to learn a new interface. Instead, it can expose a small number of safe, useful capabilities that a person's chosen agent can understand and use. Clip Magic is a real small-business website, so I deliberately chose a practical task for this challenge: preparing a website-review enquiry. I chose a pragmatic approach rather than a dramatic one. The problem is familiar: people often know what they need, but do not know which service label to choose or how much detail to type into a set of fields. For some users, especially those who find dense, field-by-field interfaces difficult, a conversational route can be useful. It is not a replacement for accessible form design, and it does not remove human choice. The ordinary form remains available; the agent simply helps a user reach the same workflow and leaves the final decision with them. Most people I know would rather explain what they need than fill in boxes on screen or on paper. The opportunity extends well beyond one website. Small and medium-sized enterprises represent around 90% of businesses worldwide , yet reliable data about the proportion of websites they operate is not generally available. What is clear is that there is already a large installed base of small-business websites: in 2025, 76.67% of EU small enterprises with 10–49 employees reported having a website ( Eurostat e-business data ), while 17% reported using AI, compared with 55% of large enterprises ( Eurostat AI statistics ). That suggests a practical path between the old web and the AI-first web. Most small businesses are not going to abandon their CMS, rebuild their website, or become AI companies overnight. They may, however, be able to add small, useful, standards-based capabilities to the websites and workflows they already rely on. The question behind the project was simple: Can a user's AI agent understand that Clip Magic may be able to help, gather the minimum missing information, and prepare the existing enquiry form without bypassing the human or creating a separate AI workflow? The aim was not to build the most elaborate WebMCP demo. It was to see whether WebMCP could remove friction from something businesses and customers already do every day. What it does The live Clip Magic website exposes one bounded WebMCP capability: request_website_review A user can describe what they want in natural language. Their agent can inspect the public website, determine whether the request is relevant, ask for missing information, open the existing Contact workflow and populate the visible form. The important part is what happens next: nothing is submitted automatically . The user can read the completed form, change anything they want, and decide whether to click Submit. The human and agent therefore use the same underlying workflow: Contact dialog → existing FormBuilder form → existing validation and spam controls → human review → human submission WebMCP does not bypass that process. It progressively enhances it. If WebMCP is unavailable, the standard human form still works exactly as before. How I built it Clip Magic is an existing ProcessWire website. Its Contact form is managed by the commercial ProcessWire FormBuilder module, which already handles validation, spam filtering, storage and email delivery. Rather than duplicate any of that logic, I kept FormBuilder authoritative and added a thin WebMCP layer around the existing form. The implementation has two parts. First, the rendered form carries declarative WebMCP metadata describing the capability and its parameters. This keeps the agent-facing schema close to the real form instead of maintaining a separate copy of the business rules. Second, I added a small imperative compatibility bridge. During testing, Chrome's WebMCP client could discover the declarative tool, but ChatGPT's in-app browser did not. The bridge derives its name, description, parameters and required fields from the rendered declarative form, so it provides compatibility without becoming a second independent schema. WebMCP tools are discovered at the document level, so the capability is available as soon as the page loads. The Contact form remains the existing destination for the agent's prepared data, and the existing FormBuilder workflow remains unchanged. The capability is not tied to the Contact dialog's open or closed state. The dialog can be opened and closed normally without changing WebMCP availability; when the agent uses the capability, it opens the existing Contact workflow and populates the visible form. The live implementation was tested in both ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Challenges The biggest challenge was not creating the tool. It was making WebMCP coexist safely with a real website that already had years of working behaviour and production constraints. Working with an existing form The challenge was to add an agent-facing capability without rebuilding the Contact system or duplicating its business rules. The solution was to keep the WebMCP layer close to the existing visible form while leaving the shared dialog system and FormBuilder workflow intact. Different WebMCP client behaviour Declarative WebMCP worked in Chrome testing but was not discovered by ChatGPT's in-app browser during development. Even Google's public declarative demo showed the same limitation in that environment. Rather than abandon the declarative implementation, I kept it as the primary definition and added the small compatibility bridge. This let both clients exercise the same capability without duplicating the schema manually. Preserving human control It would have been easy to make the demo look more impressive by allowing the agent to auto-submit the form. I chose not to. Sending an enquiry is a consequential action. The useful boundary for this project is that the agent can do the repetitive preparation work, but the person sees the actual values in the real form and remains responsible for submission. Testing beyond the happy path Because this runs on a real production website, successful population was only the start. The workflow was tested for cancellation, required-field validation, stale tool reuse, rapid double-submission, unexpected parameters, honeypot handling, email-header injection, unsafe URL schemes, prompt-injection text, session/token behaviour and controlled network failure. The supplied website URL is treated as form data only. The site does not fetch it, and no CMS, customer, authenticated or administrative capability is exposed through WebMCP. What I learned The most useful lesson was that WebMCP does not have to mean rebuilding a website for agents. For an existing business site, the better approach may be to identify a useful customer outcome, find the authoritative workflow that already handles it, and expose the smallest capability needed to help the user's agent reach that workflow reliably. I also learned that progressive enhancement matters just as much for agents as it does for browsers . The human path should not become dependent on WebMCP. The WebMCP path should not gain privileges the human path does not have. Both should meet at the same validation, security and business rules. Finally, testing natural-language requests reinforced an important distinction: the website does not need to encode every sales or qualification decision as another tool. The agent can reason from public website content. The site only needs to expose the capability that benefits from a reliable machine-readable contract. What comes next This prototype uses a website-review enquiry, but the same pattern applies to many everyday service-business tasks: checking whether a business services a location; preparing a quote request; checking suitability for a service; finding relevant booking options; preparing an appointment or reservation. The commercial opportunity is not "install WebMCP." It is helping businesses identify where a customer's AI assistant can remove friction from an existing journey, then integrating that capability into the systems the business already trusts. For Clip Magic, this challenge was a small proof of that idea: customer intent → less hunting and fewer clicks → the same trusted business workflow Source Public challenge repository: https://github.com/clipmagic/webmcp-challenge Built With formbuilder html javascript php processwire

title: Olos-AI Mini Budget Planner
pitch: A simple local-first budget tracker where people use a clear visual interface and agents use structured WebMCP tools against the same deterministic financial logic.
about_excerpt: A simple local-first budget tracker where people use a clear visual interface and agents use structured WebMCP tools against the same deterministic financial logic. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted a personal budget tracker because I'm generally hopeless (like most people) at controlling my spending and having something like this app allows me to be accounting for each and every dollar I spend, yes there are hundreds of them in the app store but I don't think people need to spend more money for a subscription and lose their privacy for a basic tracker. I used AI to assist in the development and writing to assist with expressing the story clearly Personal budgeting should be simple: record money coming in or going out, then immediately understand what remains. Many budgeting products instead introduce subscriptions, user accounts, bank connections, advertising, telemetry, and increasingly complex dashboards. Olos-AI Mini Budget Planner was built as a deliberately small alternative. Its normal experience remains a fast, visual, local-first budget tracker. The WebMCP Challenge presented a different question: can this existing application become agent-native without embedding a chatbot, adding an LLM dependency, or surrendering its financial rules to an AI model? What it does The planner records income, expenses, bills, savings, recurring commitments, revolving credit, Pay Later balances, and estimated fixed loans. It shows actual and projected monthly cashflow while keeping available cash, available credit, and loan liabilities clearly separate. People use the normal responsive interface. Compatible agents receive eleven structured WebMCP tools for reading budget information and performing explicit, validated actions. An agent can: Read the monthly budget summary List upcoming commitments Search recent activity Inspect credit and loan balances Read calendar projections Record a confirmed transaction Create or record a recurring item Record a credit payment Correct an existing transaction Delete an identified transaction with deliberate confirmation Agent-created changes appear immediately in the same interface the person uses. How we built it The application uses FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLite, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and PWA APIs. The WebMCP layer is a thin adapter. Each tool is registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) with a strict JSON schema, clear description, bounded inputs, and appropriate read-only or mutating behaviour. Tool callbacks call the same FastAPI endpoints used by the visual interface. All validation, recurrence handling, credit balances, fixed-loan calculations, and no-double-counting rules remain in the existing deterministic application logic. Financial calculations are not duplicated in prompts or delegated to an LLM. Why WebMCP improves the experience Without WebMCP, an agent must interpret labels, click controls, and infer meaning from page layout. With WebMCP, the application directly explains what actions are available and the exact structure each action requires. A person can say, “Record an $87.40 grocery expense paid with my credit card,” and the agent can submit one validated transaction using typed fields for amount, date, category, payment method, and facility ID. The result then appears in Recent Activity and updates the monthly figures. The application itself does not contain an AI assistant and does not send financial data to a third-party AI service. WebMCP lets the browser and a compatible agent collaborate with the application at its boundary. Challenges The most important challenge was preserving one financial authority. It would have been easy to create simplified financial behaviour inside the WebMCP callbacks. Instead, the tools reuse the same tested API and domain rules as the human interface. The hosted demonstration also required a strict privacy boundary. The public Render deployment uses synthetic data and isolated disposable browser sessions. It has no connection to anyone’s personal local database. Accomplishments Eleven meaningful WebMCP tools rather than a ceremonial integration Exact decimal-string money inputs Structured separation of cash, credit availability, and loan liabilities Immediate visual refresh after agent mutations Idempotent recurring-payment recording Protection against double-counting credit and loan repayments A useful application that remains fully functional without an agent Disposable, session-isolated public demonstration data What we learned Agent-native does not have to mean “put a chatbot in every application.” A deterministic web application can preserve its normal human interface while exposing a second, structured interface designed for agents. That approach makes agent interaction more accurate while keeping the application’s own rules authoritative. What’s next The immediate goal is to keep the project small, understandable, and dependable. Future work would focus on wider WebMCP browser compatibility and further usability testing, without turning the application into banking software or a financial-advice platform. title: OrbitFlo.co
pitch: Your Mission Control for Productivity
about_excerpt: Your Mission Control for Productivity Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP flips the usual agent story. Instead of an agent living in a separate tab with its own copy of your data, the page itself offers tools and the agent works in your session, on your screen. Orbit Flo was already built so that every domain operation is a plain async function over an authenticated Supabase client, with row-level security as the real boundary. That made it the right app to hand to an agent: the agent could only ever do what the signed-in person could do, by construction rather than by prompt. What it does Orbit Flo takes software projects from idea to done: kanban boards that run Docked → Ready to Launch → Launching → In Orbit, a daily flight plan with one primary item, milestones, markdown notes with orbit: links between tasks, an inbox for stray thoughts, mind maps that autosave and convert nodes into tasks, notes or milestones, and shared workspaces with link invitations, roles and assignment. All of it inside a live WebGL galaxy. Through WebMCP it registers thirteen tools with document.modelContext , so a browser-hosted agent can read today's plan, capture thoughts, file them as tasks, move cards, add work to the plan, write notes, add milestones and search the workspace. Each mutating tool invalidates the right queries, so the human watches the agent's work land on the board live. Tool What it does list_projects Projects in the current workspace, with ids get_flight_plan Today's daily plan and due work create_task New task on a project's board move_task Move a task between status columns search_workspace Search tasks, notes, projects, milestones capture_thought Drop a thought into the inbox complete_plan_item Complete a flight-plan item (with the launch animation) list_inbox Read unprocessed inbox captures file_capture_as_task Turn a capture into a task on a board add_to_flight_plan Put a task on today's plan list_notes List the workspace's notes create_note Write a note (ideas, decisions, risks…) create_milestone Add a milestone to a roadmap How we built it React 19, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind on the front; Supabase (Postgres, auth, row-level security) behind it; TanStack Query owns server state. The WebMCP layer is one module, src/features/agent/agent-tools.ts , that wraps the existing domain functions: each tool validates its input, calls the same function the UI calls with the same client, and ends with a query invalidation. Registration is feature-detected and scoped to an AbortController , so a browser without WebMCP runs the app unchanged and switching workspaces re-registers the tools against the workspace on screen. The privilege model is machine-verified: CI replays every migration onto a fresh Postgres and runs catalog assertions over grants and policies on every pull request, so a tool can never exceed what the database allows. Challenges we ran into No browser on the development machine exposed document.modelContext , so the tool layer was built against the specification and a recorded fake, with the absent-API path tested first. The first real integration run happened days before the deadline. Making the agent's work visible instantly meant auditing which query keys every mutation touches; the demo moment depends on it. Autosave for mind maps surfaced a latent server bug: the graph-replace RPC dropped conversion links on every save. It shipped with a migration that snapshots them first. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent and the person share one workspace, one session and one screen, and the board updates as the agent talks. Nothing destructive is exposed: no deletes, no member or role management, and a test pins the tool list so a fourteenth tool is a failing build. The whole thing is open source, including the schema and the CI that guards its privilege model. What we learned Agent tooling is cheapest when the app already has clean, client-scoped domain functions and a real authorization boundary underneath them. The tool layer then becomes wiring plus validation, and the security story is the same one the UI already tells. What's next Streaming page context to the agent ( provideContext ), tools for maps and the crew (assign, mention), and a guest mode so judges and visitors can try the agent without shared credentials. title: StackKits Planner
pitch: Humans and browser agents plan self-hosted infrastructure together: module-level compute profiles, honest capacity checks, and a read-only CLI handoff.
about_excerpt: Humans and browser agents plan self-hosted infrastructure together: module-level compute profiles, honest capacity checks, and a read-only CLI handoff. Like Comment Story Updates Choose your workloads: visual use-case tiles, declared kit defaults and explicit module alternatives. Declare capacity: CPU, RAM and storage sliders with a transparent per-axis assessment. Review and copy: individual terminal commands or a complete Markdown handoff for your agent. Nothing runs in the browser. Inspiration Planning a self-hosted system should not require a browser agent to guess what a website means. StackKits already provides CUE-defined infrastructure blueprints and a standalone CLI. We built the WebMCP Planner to make those declared product facts directly usable by people and browser agents, in one visible workflow. What it does At https://stackkit.cc/planner , choose a StackKit, select compute profiles independently for its modules, and declare available CPU, RAM and storage with numeric inputs and sliders. The planner compares that capacity against declared requirements and prepares a reviewable CLI handoff. Four read-only WebMCP tools share the same implementation and planner state as the human UI: stackkits_list_catalog stackkits_get_module_profiles stackkits_assess_capacity stackkits_prepare_handoff Agent choices and results appear in the planner immediately. A small host can use a lighter module profile without forcing every module into one global tier. Missing declarations remain unverified; below-minimum capacity blocks the handoff. This is declared-capacity assessment, not a promise of host compatibility. Why WebMCP fits The useful action here is structured planning, not scraping prose or giving an agent a shell. Native document.modelContext.registerTool exposes narrow, validated operations with explicit read-only annotations. People can inspect and change the same selection an agent is working with. Without native WebMCP support, the complete human planner remains usable and explains why agent tools are unavailable. How we built it The public implementation includes JSON Schemas, generated TypeScript types, a deterministic catalog projected from the OSS CUE authority bundle, source and digest provenance, shared core logic, and a Svelte planner with a reproducible reference host. The production site is a thin host of that same component. Tool execution is local and deterministic: no model inference, provider call, or per-request server analysis. Capacity checks are simple comparisons, and bounded outputs avoid repeating the full UI explanation. Targeted local benchmarks measured sub-millisecond p95 core execution for the four tools; that excludes page loading and browser-agent transport and is not an end-to-end latency guarantee. The handoff describes init, validate, resolve, generate and plan commands. The browser executes none of them. Target-side stackkit compat remains mandatory, and apply is excluded from the executable handoff and requires a later owner decision. Challenges and lessons The most important architecture correction was separating per-module compute profiles from the kit's product selection. A uniform low or standard switch does not describe a real mixed workload. Another challenge was keeping incomplete capacity declarations honest rather than treating missing information as success. We also separated native API availability, catalog verification and registration failures in the UI. Unsupported browsers must not be made to look agent-ready, and native integration must not be replaced with a production polyfill. What is new for this challenge StackKits, its CUE definitions and standalone CLI predate this entry. The contest work adds the shared WebMCP planner, browser-tool contract, module-profile workflow, capacity UI, read-only handoff, public reference host, and focused validation and performance evidence. The public source and commit history distinguish the existing platform from this extension. Try it Open https://stackkit.cc/planner . No account is required. Choose Basement Kit to load its declared default core module. Declare 4 CPU cores, 8 GiB RAM and 32 GiB free storage, assess capacity, and prepare the CLI handoff. Copy an individual Bash/POSIX or PowerShell command, or copy the complete agent Markdown including choices, notices and provenance. Nothing is executed by copying. Add optional workloads with the visual use-case tiles and inspect their module-local profiles. Lower an axis below its declared minimum to see a blocked result, or leave it empty to see an incomplete assessment. Native WebMCP tools and the manual planner share the same implementation and visible state. The complete manual workflow also works without WebMCP support. What's next Broader declared module requirements and more agent evaluations can improve coverage without turning the browser into a second infrastructure compiler or installer. title: Tree Radar
pitch: Explore real city trees with AI. WebMCP lets agents search public tree data and turn results into an interactive map you can explore.
about_excerpt: Explore real city trees with AI. WebMCP lets agents search public tree data and turn results into an interactive map you can explore. Like Comment Story Updates Explore 118,403 official street-tree records across Taichung on an interactive map. Search by species and inspect matching trees with their official record details and locations. Inspiration Cities publish valuable information about their trees, but that data is often difficult for ordinary people to explore. Tree Radar began as a way to turn official municipal tree datasets into a searchable, visual map that makes urban trees easier to discover. The WebMCP Challenge raised a different question: what if an AI agent could work with the same interface instead of requiring a separate API or agent-only application? The goal became to let people explore trees visually while allowing an agent to understand the available city data, search it through structured tools, and bring useful results back onto the same map. What it does Tree Radar is an interactive city tree map built from public municipal data. For the WebMCP Challenge, it exposes three browser-native tools: get_city_coverage — lets an agent understand which city datasets are available find_trees — searches the tree dataset using structured criteria show_trees_on_map — turns selected search results into visible state on the map The current WebMCP demo includes more than 118,000 Taichung street-tree records. Together, the tools create a human-agent loop: a person can ask about trees in natural language, the agent can discover and call the appropriate tools, and matching trees can then be shown on the same interactive map for the person to explore. How we built it Tree Radar is built with Next.js, TypeScript, React, and MapLibre GL JS. The WebMCP implementation registers three explicit tools through the browser's model context. Each tool has a bounded responsibility and structured inputs and outputs. The workflow is deliberately separated into three steps: discover available city coverage search for matching trees explicitly choose which results to display on the map This keeps information retrieval separate from state-changing behavior: searching does not unexpectedly change the map. The production build was tested in a WebMCP-capable browser to verify tool discovery, structured calls, tree search, and the final map transition. Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges was deciding what should become an agent capability and what should remain normal application behavior. Exposing too much would make the integration harder to understand and less predictable. The three-tool design came from keeping the agent surface small and making state-changing behavior explicit. Municipal tree data also contains variations in species naming. Search behavior was refined to support useful partial species matching while keeping results bounded and predictable. Accomplishments that we're proud of The result is not a separate AI demo layered beside Tree Radar. The agent and the existing web interface participate in the same task: the agent handles structured discovery and search, while the map remains the shared visual surface where people can inspect the result. The WebMCP flow has been validated end to end in production with all three tools discoverable and callable. Tree Radar existed before this challenge as a city-tree exploration product. The WebMCP integration is a new extension built specifically for the WebMCP Challenge. The challenge work includes the browser-native WebMCP tool layer, the three-tool discovery/search/map workflow, WebMCP-specific acceptance testing, and a dedicated challenge repository whose commit history documents this work separately from the pre-existing product. What we learned The most important lesson was that WebMCP is useful for more than retrieving information from a website. It can create a bridge between agent reasoning and an existing visual interface. In Tree Radar, the agent does not replace the map. It helps a person reach meaningful results, then hands those results back to the interface where spatial context becomes visible. Designing a small, explicit tool surface also made the interaction easier to reason about than exposing every possible application action. What's next for Tree Radar Tree Radar is expanding toward broader city coverage while keeping the same principle: official public data should be easier for people to explore and understand. The WebMCP experiment also points toward a larger possibility for Tree Radar: as more city datasets become available, agents could help people navigate increasingly large collections of urban tree data without replacing the visual and geographic context that makes that data meaningful. title: Formulate
pitch: Your AI agent fills forms, explains jargon, and asks before it submits , powered by 12 WebMCP tools and a natural language data vault.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent fills forms, explains jargon, and asks before it submits , powered by 12 WebMCP tools and a natural language data vault. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration 67% of people abandon government forms at the first confusing field. We've all been there — staring at a 40-field form that asks for your CIN number, your GSTIN, your TDS rate, and nobody explains what any of it means. In India alone, 900 million voters interact with the Election Commission's Form 6. Millions fill out business registrations, insurance enrollments, and rental applications every year. Most people either pay someone to fill these forms or give up entirely. We asked: what if an AI agent could fill the form for you — explain every confusing field — and you just approve at the end? What it does Formulate is a WebMCP-powered form assistant with three parts: 1. Natural Language Data Vault You describe yourself in plain text: "My name is Mohammed, I work at TechVentures in Bengaluru, my PAN is ABCPM1234K." The vault extracts your data using pattern recognition — PAN format, Aadhaar format, phone numbers, PIN codes, email, employer, job title, city, state. No form to set up a form-filler. 2. Smart Form Engine Five real-world forms with 172 total fields: Rental Application (39 fields), Health Insurance Enrollment (27 fields), Small Business Registration (25 fields), Airtel Business Enterprise Registration (40 fields), and India's Election Commission Voter ID Form 6 (41 fields). Every confusing field has an inline plain-language explanation. 3. 12 WebMCP Tools Registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() — the agent calls structured tools instead of scraping the page: get_form_fields — reads the entire form structure fill_field — fills a text/number/date/phone field select_option — selects from a dropdown check_checkbox — toggles a checkbox explain_field — returns a plain-language explanation validate_form — checks for empty required fields get_form_progress — returns filled/total counts review_form — summarizes all values before submission clear_field — removes a value autofill_from_vault — checks what can be auto-filled apply_vault_suggestions — fills all matching fields from vault submit_form — requires human approval before proceeding How we built it Next.js 16 with App Router and TypeScript Tailwind CSS v4 with shadcn-style design tokens (2 colors: foreground and muted) WebMCP — supports both document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext for Chrome compatibility Pattern recognition vault — regex-based extraction for PAN, Aadhaar, GSTIN, CIN, Udyam, phone, email, PIN codes, plus keyword extraction for name, employer, job title, address Playwright — 30 end-to-end tests covering tool registration, field filling, validation, approval flow, and activity panel Vercel for deployment The execute function returns { content: [{ type: "text", text: "..." }] } per the Chrome WebMCP spec. Input parsing handles both JSON strings and parsed objects so it works regardless of how the host agent calls the tools. Challenges we faced The biggest challenge was WebMCP spec compliance. The API migrated from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext in July 2026, and different hosts (Chrome vs ChatGPT) may use either surface. We had to support both. We also discovered that executeTool sends arguments as a JSON string in some hosts but a parsed object in others — so we added defensive input parsing. The natural language vault was tricky because names, cities, and job titles don't have fixed formats. We combined regex patterns for structured data (PAN, Aadhaar, GSTIN) with keyword-based extraction for unstructured data (name, employer, address), with confidence scoring to show users what was extracted and how sure we are. What we learned WebMCP changes the relationship between websites and AI agents from "scrape and guess" to "structured collaboration." A form that registers 12 tools gives the agent complete understanding of what's possible, what's required, and what needs human approval. That's fundamentally different from an agent trying to parse HTML and click buttons. title: innpilot hotel pms
pitch: Hotel PMS with WebMCP tools for AI agents
about_excerpt: Hotel PMS with WebMCP tools for AI agents Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 innpilot landing page dashboard Inspiration Hotel management involves constant operational work: checking room availability, making reservations, updating room status, checking guests in and out, and monitoring occupancy and revenue. We built InnPilot because we wanted to explore a different question: what if a hotel management system was designed to be used by both people and AI agents? Instead of adding an AI chatbot that only answers questions, we wanted the agent to interact with the actual hotel system through structured capabilities. WebMCP gave us the opportunity to make InnPilot's hotel operations directly discoverable and usable by agents while keeping the application responsible for enforcing its business rules. Our goal was simple: make hotel software something an agent can actually operate, not just talk about. What it does InnPilot is a multi-tenant hotel management platform for hotel owners, managers, and staff. Through WebMCP, InnPilot exposes real hotel operations as structured tools that agents can use directly. An agent can: View hotel rooms and their current housekeeping status Check room availability for specific dates Filter availability by room type Create reservations List and filter reservations Check guests in and out Cancel reservations or mark no-shows Update room status, including Cleaning, Maintenance, and Out of Service Retrieve occupancy information Retrieve revenue and financial performance The tools are designed around hotel-domain actions rather than generic database operations. For example, an agent doesn't get a generic "write reservation" function. It gets a purpose-built innpilot_create_reservation tool with a defined schema and hotel-specific validation. This also means the agent cannot simply bypass InnPilot's rules. Overlapping reservations are rejected, and rooms under maintenance or out of service cannot be booked. The result is a collaboration model where: Human intent → AI agent → WebMCP tool → InnPilot business logic → Result How we built it InnPilot is a web-based multi-tenant hotel management application. We integrated WebMCP by registering structured tools that expose important hotel capabilities to agents. Each tool provides: A unique tool name A clear description explaining when it should be used A structured input schema An execution handler connected to InnPilot's existing application logic We deliberately exposed domain-level operations such as innpilot_check_room_availability, innpilot_create_reservation, innpilot_set_room_status, innpilot_get_occupancy, and innpilot_get_revenue. This allows the agent to interact with InnPilot through well-defined capabilities instead of trying to navigate buttons, forms, or pages. The underlying application continues to perform validation and enforce hotel rules, so WebMCP becomes a reliable agent interface to the existing product rather than a separate parallel system. Challenges we ran into: The biggest challenge was making agent interaction reliable enough for real hotel operations. Reservations aren't just simple database writes. Availability depends on dates, existing reservations, room status, and operational constraints. We had to make sure that: Availability reflects the requested stay rather than only the room's current status Existing and legacy bookings are considered Maintenance and out-of-service rooms cannot be sold Reservation creation rejects conflicting bookings Reservation status transitions are handled correctly Tool inputs are strictly validated Agents receive useful results after each operation Another challenge was deciding what should become a tool. We learned that exposing too much low-level functionality can make an agent interface harder to use. We focused instead on meaningful hotel actions that map directly to tasks a manager or staff member would actually perform. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that InnPilot is more than a WebMCP proof of concept. We connected WebMCP to an actual hotel management workflow with real operational state and business rules. An agent can go from: Finding an available room → creating a reservation → managing the reservation lifecycle → updating housekeeping → checking occupancy → analyzing revenue. We're particularly proud of the validation layer. If an agent tries to book an occupied room or create an overlapping reservation, InnPilot doesn't blindly execute the request. The application rejects the operation according to its hotel rules. That demonstrates what we believe agent-native applications should look like: agents get powerful capabilities, but the application remains responsible for correctness. What we learned WebMCP changed the way we think about web applications. We learned that a website can be designed not only as a visual interface for humans, but also as a structured capability layer for agents. The most useful agent tools are not necessarily complex. A small collection of well-designed, domain-specific tools can allow an agent to accomplish an entire workflow when those tools compose naturally. We also learned that agent-native design requires more than exposing functions. Tool descriptions, schemas, validation, error handling, and business rules all become part of the experience. Most importantly, we learned that human + agent collaboration can be a product feature in itself. What's next for InnPilot We're continuing to develop InnPilot as an agent-native hotel PMS. Next, we want to expand the range of workflows that hotel staff can delegate to agents while keeping humans in control of important decisions. We see opportunities for agents to coordinate more complex workflows across reservations, housekeeping, restaurant operations, conferences, payments, reporting, and hotel administration. Our bigger vision goes beyond InnPilot. Today, most websites are built primarily for humans to navigate. We believe the next generation of the web can expose structured capabilities that agents can discover and operate safely. InnPilot is our exploration of what happens when a real-world business application is built for both humans and agents from the start. title: MAC Inventory Workbench
pitch: A WebMCP workbench where you and a browser agent triage a network's MACs on one surface: paste raw ARP/DHCP dumps, enrich every address against macadress.com, filter, and export an allowlist.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workbench where you and a browser agent triage a network's MACs on one surface: paste raw ARP/DHCP dumps, enrich every address against macadress.com, filter, and export an allowlist. Like Comment Story Updates Mac Inventory WorkBench Sample Data Mac Address Enrichment Export Options ChatGPT Agent Interaction Inspiration Anyone who has done network cleanup knows the loop. You pull an ARP table off a switch, or a DHCP lease file, or a page of nmap output, and you are staring at 150 MAC addresses. Which ones are real devices? Which are VMs? Which are phones cycling through randomized addresses so they never look the same twice? Which OUI was never registered with the IEEE at all? The honest answer is usually a spreadsheet on one monitor and a vendor-lookup site on the other, and an hour of alt-tab. The WebMCP Challenge asked for something specific: a page where a human and a browser agent work the same surface, not a chatbot bolted onto a UI. Network triage turned out to be a near perfect fit. The task is tedious, it is full of small judgment calls, and it produces an artifact someone actually applies afterward: a firewall allowlist. macadress.com already solved the hard part behind an API (OUI and IEEE registration data, device-class inference, virtualization fingerprints, randomization scoring), so the workbench itself could stay thin and honest. What it does Paste raw text. The app extracts every MAC in any common format (colon, hyphen, Cisco dotted, bare hex), enriches each one against macadress.com, and drops the results into a table you can slice by vendor, device category, virtualization platform, "randomized," or "unregistered." When the slice looks right, you export it as an nftables set, a Zeek annotation file, or CSV. Every button on the page is also a WebMCP tool. There are eight: add_mac_addresses , load_sample_data , lookup_mac , enrich_inventory , summarize_inventory , filter_inventory , export_filter_list , clear_inventory . The agent and the person edit one inventory. There is no separate agent view and no "agent mode." If the agent filters to virtualized hosts and builds an nftables set, the human watches it happen in the same table and export box they would have used by hand. How we built it Two pieces, no build step. web/ is static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The design rule was one shared state object. app.js defines an ops object with the actual operations. The on-page buttons call ops . The WebMCP tool handlers call ops . Because both paths mutate the same Map of rows and the same listener set re-renders the table, the human sees the agent's work land row by row, and the reverse. web/wmcp.js is the only file that touches the WebMCP spec, on purpose. It resolves the host object ( document.modelContext , falling back to navigator.modelContext ) and supports both the modern registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) shape and the older bulk provideContext({ tools }) shape. It wraps every handler so a handler can return a plain JavaScript object and the adapter stringifies it, since execute is required to resolve to a string. worker/ is a Cloudflare Worker that proxies api.macadress.com . The API key lives as a Wrangler secret and never reaches the browser. The Worker also enforces a route allowlist (single lookup and a capped batch only), a per-IP rate limit, and a CORS origin pin. The math that matters A MAC address is 48 bits, so there are 2^48 of them, roughly 2.8 x 10^14. The IEEE hands out the top 24 bits as the OUI and the vendor owns the bottom 24, which is 2^24, or 16,777,216 addresses per registration. Randomized addresses are the reason a hand-built allowlist rots. The naive detector is a single bit: the locally-administered bit, the second-least- significant bit of the first octet. Write b for that octet and use the wedge for bitwise AND: $$b \land \mathtt{0x02} \neq 0 .$$ That flag is necessary but not sufficient, because plenty of legitimate hardware is locally administered. macadress.com layers a confidence score on top, and the workbench only marks a row as randomized when the API returns potentially_randomized with confidence possible or likely . Enrichment runs in batches of 40, so the cost is one upstream call per 40 addresses, with a per-row fallback if the batch endpoint misbehaves. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP surface is still moving. Different runtimes expose different objects and different registration methods. Isolating every assumption into wmcp.js meant the rest of the app never had to care, and a spec change is a one-file diff. Tools have to return strings, but useful strings. A handler that returns { found: 12, added: 9 } is easy to write. Making sure the agent gets back something it can reason about took a pass over every return value and every tool description. The descriptions are the real API, so they say when to call a tool, not just what it does. Percent-encoding broke lookups. The upstream API does not decode %3A , so a MAC sent as 00%3A11%3A22... fails. The Worker forwards the colons and dashes intact and only decodes a caller that pre-encoded, so both callers end up identical. A public Worker URL cannot hold a real secret. The answer was layers instead of one wall: a dedicated low-quota key, an edge WAF rule that rejects any request whose Origin is not the demo page, a rate limit, and a rotatable friction token shipped in config.js . None of them is cryptographic alone. Together they make an abused URL cap out fast. Demo limits during judging. Testing burned through the shared key more than once, so we added a bring-your-own-key path: paste a macadress.com key into the header, it is stored in that browser only and sent as X-Macadress-Key , and the Worker forwards it upstream while skipping the demo gate and the shared rate limit. Accomplishments that we're proud of One surface, zero duplicated logic. Eight buttons and eight tools route through a single ops object. There is no code path the agent can take that a human cannot, and none the human can take that the agent cannot. It degrades cleanly. With no WebMCP host present the page is a fully working manual tool. Open it in a WebMCP runtime and the same eight actions become agent tools, no reload. The spec coupling is one file. wmcp.js already absorbs two different host API shapes without the app noticing. The output is real. nftables sets, Zeek annotation files, and CSV that you can apply, not a demo-only artifact. A public demo that is safe to share , because the proxy leans on layered defense rather than a secret in the page, with BYOK as the escape hatch. What we learned The value of WebMCP is not "give an agent your API." It is that the agent and the human share one DOM-backed state, and the interesting design work is refusing to fork the view. Once ops existed, the tool layer was almost free, and progressive enhancement fell out for nothing. We also learned how much weight tool descriptions carry: with a good description the agent sequences filter_inventory then export_filter_list on its own, and with a vague one it guesses. What's next for MAC Inventory Workbench diff_inventory , so an agent can compare a fresh capture against last week's allowlist and report only what changed. More export targets : Suricata datasets, EdgeOS and MikroTik address lists, a Prometheus textfile for alerting on unknown MACs. Persist inventories so a triage session can be reopened, and so the diff has something to diff against. Push the same tool set through the other macadress.com integrations so the workbench and those connectors share one vocabulary. title: OpenAssist Daily Workspace
pitch: One visible workspace where people and agents safely organize daily work together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: One visible workspace where people and agents safely organize daily work together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates OpenAssist turns scattered work into one visible, voice-enabled WebMCP workspace. OpenAssist brings email, tasks, and calendar into one calm WebMCP workspace. A clear multi-account inbox keeps urgent mail visible while treating external content as untrusted. A Shopify catalog gives the agent structured product search with visual results. Every change pauses at an exact preview before anything is applied. The approved cart update is executed once, read back, and visibly verified. The activity view separates agent reads from user-approved changes for a complete audit trail. The movable voice agent uses the same WebMCP tools while the workspace stays visible. Inspiration My work is spread across several accounts, inboxes, task lists, calendars, notes, ideas, and projects. I wanted one calm place that could organize my day, remember useful context, and let agents help without hiding what they are doing. What it does OpenAssist Daily Workspace brings email, tasks, calendar, notes, memory, accounts, and activity into one clear workspace. The public judge workspace uses safe synthetic data. In normal use, the OpenAssist ChatGPT app connects Gmail, Tasks, Calendar, Drive, and other Google services, bringing a user's information into this same workspace. Through WebMCP, an agent can search, focus, organize, and act on that information while the user sees the result. Changes remain behind clear approvals. The Shopify example uses the same WebMCP approach. The agent can search the connected catalog, show product images and details, and prepare a cart action for approval. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent has to guess how a page works or use a separate system the user cannot see. OpenAssist exposes clear tools for the actions available on the page, so the person and agent share the same context. Reads happen immediately. Changes first show an exact preview. The user approves the action, OpenAssist runs it once, verifies the result, and records it in Activity. Email, attachments, and website content are treated as untrusted and cannot approve actions. How I built it The ChatGPT Site uses document.modelContext.registerTool and a shared registry for tool schemas, safety rules, demo behavior, and private Workspace mappings. The site is hosted on ChatGPT Sites. Cloudflare Workers and D1 provide isolated demo storage. The private workspace connects to OpenAssist Workspace and Composio-managed Google services without copying private Google content into the demo database. The voice agent runs in an isolated Cloudflare Container using Codex and my ChatGPT subscription for the demonstration. It calls the same WebMCP tools as the browser, so every result, preview, approval, and completed action remains visible in the workspace. Challenges The biggest technical challenge was streaming Codex voice from an isolated Cloudflare Container into the live site while keeping the browser, voice session, and WebMCP tool results in sync. A spoken request had to reach Codex, call the correct site tool, update the visible workspace, show any required approval, and return a spoken response without losing context. I also had to keep judge data separate from private data and prevent email or other outside content from becoming instructions. Accomplishments OpenAssist gives the agent useful tools while keeping every important action visible. The same interface works for personal daily planning and for demonstrating safe actions across connected services. What I learned An agent-friendly website needs more than automation. People and agents need a shared view, clear limits, and visible proof of what changed. What's next I want OpenAssist to become a practical second brain that organizes projects and research, remembers useful context, plans active work, and helps people safely assign prepared work to agents. title: Organize hackathons using Codex with WebMCP
pitch: Imagine not having to juggle excel sheets, Notion docs and complicated Devpost UI as a hackathon organizer. Instead, stay in Codex and manage a full hackathon end-to-end.
about_excerpt: Imagine not having to juggle excel sheets, Notion docs and complicated Devpost UI as a hackathon organizer. Instead, stay in Codex and manage a full hackathon end-to-end. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Organizing hackathons is a lot of putting out fires because there are many "sources of truth" and interfaces to learn for those involved. I run two dozen hackathons a year with AI Tinkerers / AGI Ventures Canada. Our volunteers used to juggle between Notion, Devpost, Excel and stressed out about attendees, prizes, judging, etc.. So a while back I built hackathon.new and it had allowed our team to manage hackathons through a CLI, with a nice web GUI. But the non-technical volunteers couldn't use it. Now with WebMCP added during this hackathon, anyone can use the platform to host hacks (including non-coding ones) and without having to know the GUI. What it does hackathon.new allows anyone to organize hackathons and manage them from their agent. This means one can stay in Codex, ask how many people have singed up, start judging phase, ask how many had submitted projects, pull project ABC down to run and judge locally, send mass email notifications to attendees about schedule changes, invite judges, and more without even learning how the website works. How we built it A while back I built it with Next.js + Vercel, Resend for emails, Clerk for authentication, and Supabase for database. I also built a CLI for our volunteers to use, but that left out the non-technical volunteers from levveraging the platform to the max. As of today, they can too by using Codex to just go to Challenges we ran into The built in browser in Codex had troubles detecting the available tools through WebMCP when hitting the site. So I added these changes so Chrome could recognize hackathon.new as a website that supports WebMCP: a WEBMCP_ORIGIN_TRIAL_TOKEN environment variable, an Origin-Trial response header for the correct hostname, and scripts that register the site’s tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). I first placed the token in a page meta tag, then moved it to the HTTP response header because browsers detect the WebMCP trial more reliably that way. Also seems like gpt-5.6 luna doesn't support WebMCP from using Codex's built in browser, but sol does. Finally, when testing with Codex's built in browser, it's very eager to just use computer use and browser use to accomplish the task. I'd have to explicitly tell it to use WebMCP tools, otherwise it wouldn't know to do that automatically. Accomplishments that we're proud of It was great thinking through ways an organizer, judge or attendee would use the platform. Initially I had it so the majority of tools are discovered as the agent / human navigates to different pages, but then realized that for power users like myself, we'd want to use the critical tool (create new hackathon event, check what happened in the last few hours in this event, etc..) from anywhere in the app. So I rejigged it so there are quite a few global tools that users can call even from the root of the domain (and even when user is not logged in too) What we learned WebMCP makes it even easier for non-technical folks to not have to set up anything. this is amazing because if you ever had to explain step-by-step how to set up something a bit complicated like an MCP server, a plugin (let alone a CLI), you know its a painful experience for non-technical folks. With WebMCP I don't have to tell them anything. I'd just say, "go to hackathon.new" in your codex and tell it what you want done. What's next for Organize hackathons using Codex with WebMCP We're helping AGI House in San Francisco host the next hackathon and I've been blowing up their Whatsapp about my new WebMCP addition. They're pretty versed with the CLI I built so the WebMCP will allow the house managers who don't code as much to use it as well. We've had the government of Alberta hosted hackathon on this platform as well, and they're very AI-forward, so I might just email the deputy there again about this (he'd be excited). title: RESCASAP.UY
pitch: RESCASAP.UY uses WebMCP to let AI agents discover, compare and prepare discounted surplus-food reservations, while people keep control of the final confirmation.
about_excerpt: RESCASAP.UY uses WebMCP to let AI agents discover, compare and prepare discounted surplus-food reservations, while people keep control of the final confirmation. Like Comment Story Updates RESCASAP.UY WebMCP experience: AI agents discover, compare and prepare surplus-food reservations while humans keep final control. Inspiration Every day, local businesses end up with perfectly good food that must be sold quickly or goes to waste. At the same time, people are looking for more affordable ways to buy food. RESCASAP.UY was created to connect those two realities: helping businesses recover value from same-day surplus while giving people nearby access to food at reduced prices. The WebMCP challenge gave us the opportunity to take that idea one step further: instead of making people manually browse, filter and compare every option, we asked what would happen if an AI agent could interact directly with the marketplace on their behalf. What it does RESCASAP.UY is a surplus-food rescue marketplace built for Uruguay. Businesses can offer discounted rescue packs before food goes to waste, while users can discover available options and choose what works best for them. For the WebMCP experience, RESCASAP exposes a small set of purpose-built tools that allow an AI agent to: Find and rank available rescue packs using constraints such as price, food weight, category and urgency. Compare multiple packs by price, savings, estimated weight, pickup window and neighborhood. Prepare a selected pack for reservation by opening the checkout experience for human review. The agent handles the repetitive discovery and comparison work, but the consequential action remains human-controlled: it never completes the final reservation or initiates a payment by itself. How we built it The WebMCP integration is implemented directly inside the RESCASAP web application through typed, imperative site tools. Three WebMCP tools power the challenge experience: find_rescue_packs compare_rescue_packs prepare_pack_reservation Their inputs use bounded schemas, their outputs are concise and verifiable, and every agent action is reflected visibly in the interface. The application is built with TypeScript, React, Vinext and Cloudflare infrastructure. The production architecture includes Cloudflare D1/SQLite with Drizzle ORM, Supabase authentication and Mercado Pago marketplace payments. For judging, we created a dedicated /demo route that requires no account, API keys, database setup or payment method. It uses an isolated in-memory dataset while running the same product interface and WebMCP tool implementation. This makes the complete agent experience immediately testable by evaluators without touching real customer, merchant or payment data. Human–agent collaboration A core principle of the project is that AI should remove mechanical work without hiding important decisions from the person using it. The agent can search, filter, rank, compare and prepare an action, while the user remains in control of the final commitment. The demo itself was produced through human–agent collaboration: while I recorded the experience, an AI agent operated the web workflow being demonstrated. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was deciding where agent autonomy should stop. A food marketplace contains time-sensitive inventory and potentially consequential actions such as reservations and payments. Instead of giving the agent unrestricted control, we designed a clear boundary: discovery and preparation can be automated, while the final reservation remains a human decision. Another challenge was making the experience easy for judges to reproduce. The WebMCP demo therefore runs without authentication, secrets or payment credentials and resets automatically with the browser session. We also had to make agent actions visible in the actual interface so users can verify what the agent found, compared or prepared instead of trusting an invisible automation. What we learned WebMCP changes the relationship between an AI agent and a website. Instead of relying on visual interpretation or fragile browser automation, a website can expose a small set of intentional, structured capabilities designed specifically for agents. We learned that the most useful agent experience is not necessarily the one that automates everything. It is the one that gives the agent enough capability to remove repetitive work while preserving transparency and human control where it matters. What's next The next step for RESCASAP.UY is to continue developing the real marketplace in Uruguay: onboarding more local businesses, increasing available rescue inventory and improving location-aware discovery. The WebMCP layer can evolve alongside the marketplace, giving people an increasingly natural way to discover and compare surplus food through AI while keeping reservations and payments safe and user-controlled. RESCASAP.UY turns a simple idea — rescue food before it becomes waste — into an experience that humans and AI agents can navigate together. title: Scholarship Scout
pitch: A source-transparent WebMCP workspace where students and agents find, explain, compare, and plan scholarship applications together.
about_excerpt: A source-transparent WebMCP workspace where students and agents find, explain, compare, and plan scholarship applications together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Scholarship Scout turns fragmented scholarship research into a structured human-and-agent workflow. Students provide a lightweight profile, search a curated catalog of 30 named programme records, inspect match, mismatch, and unknown evidence, compare up to three candidates, and turn a selected route into a planning checklist. A catalog record is not automatically presented as an open application or a verified match: each result exposes its official provider link, review date, evidence scope, cycle status, and unresolved facts. WebMCP is central to the experience. Six typed page-defined tools expose search, eligibility, comparison, shortlisting, checklist generation, and checklist updates to an agent. The tools use the same deterministic TypeScript domain layer and browser-local state as the visible interface, so agent actions and student actions stay synchronized. State-changing tools require explicit student confirmation, and the app never submits a scholarship application. This improves scholarship research because agents can filter and normalize structured evidence while students retain the judgment calls: resolving country or course rules, choosing among tied candidates, verifying the official source, and approving saved work. Unknown facts add no ranking points, so missing evidence cannot silently become a recommendation. The release was tested on the live Vercel deployment in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. All six tools were discovered. A clean Nigeria + Computer Science + any-level + any-funding run returned 25 candidates, preserved unknown criteria in the top-three eligibility checks, populated a three-way comparison, and generated three source-aware Chevening planning tasks. Built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, browser-native document.modelContext.registerTool registration, deterministic domain functions, local browser persistence, and Vercel. The public repository contains the complete source, demo assets, setup instructions, automated tests, and MIT license. Codex helped scope the product, implement and test WebMCP, audit all 30 catalog records against official-source evidence, correct high-risk facts, harden persistence and confirmation boundaries, verify the live workflow, and render the narrated demo. title: ShopNearMe
pitch: Help your agent shop for you
about_excerpt: Help your agent shop for you Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Home Page - Desktop Home Page - Mobile Product Search 2 - Mobile Searching... Filters Menu Choosing Location Product Search 1 - Mobile Product Search 2 - Desktop Inspiration Shopping for a product often means repeating the same research across search engines, marketplaces, local-store websites, maps, and second-hand listings. ShopNearMe was built around a simple idea: product comparison should work equally well for people and for AI agents. Instead of forcing an agent to interpret buttons, filters, dropdowns, and result cards visually, WebMCP lets the website expose those capabilities directly as structured tools. What it does ShopNearMe searches for products around a selected location and combines several ways of buying them into one interface: Buy in store — nearby physical stores relevant to the product. Order online — online offers, including shipping in the total price when available. Second hand — used or pre-owned offers when available. Users can search for arbitrary products, use their current location or choose another location on an interactive map, sort by total price, and apply filters derived dynamically from the current product results. The filters therefore change with the product. For example, a clock search can expose clock-specific attributes such as clock type or movement, while other products expose different facets. ShopNearMe also distinguishes between verified product prices and nearby stores where a reliable price could not be obtained. Unverified offers are hidden by default and can be explicitly enabled. Why WebMCP Product research is naturally multi-step. A request such as “Find desk clocks near Tel Aviv and show me the cheapest options” normally requires an agent to understand the page layout, operate the location selector, submit a search, inspect dynamic results, find the sort control, and extract the results. ShopNearMe instead exposes those operations through WebMCP. The application registers five tools: search_products get_visible_results set_search_location filter_results sort_results This gives agents a structured contract instead of requiring them to guess how the visual interface works. WebMCP is especially useful here because ShopNearMe is highly dynamic: products, categories, filters, locations, prices, and available offers can all change between searches. Human and agent collaboration The human and the agent use the same application state. An agent can search, change the location, filter results, or change the sorting order, and those actions are reflected in the visible ShopNearMe interface. The user can then inspect the results visually, compare prices and stores, change filters manually, or follow a retailer link. This creates a useful division of work: the agent can handle repetitive product research while the person retains the visual context and final purchasing decision. How I built it ShopNearMe uses React, TypeScript, and Vite for the frontend. Live product and local-store data are fetched through server-side search endpoints so provider credentials are not exposed to the browser. Search data includes Google Shopping and Google Maps local results through SerpApi. The location picker uses Leaflet and OpenStreetMap, with geocoding and reverse geocoding for address search and direct map selection. Search results are normalized into a shared offer model. ShopNearMe calculates total prices including shipping when available, derives product-specific filters from the returned data, separates different purchase methods, and handles offers whose prices cannot be verified. WebMCP is implemented directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The tools operate on the same state used by the normal interface rather than functioning as an unrelated API layer. The project is deployed on Vercel. GitHub Actions runs linting, TypeScript checking, tests, and a production build. Challenges I ran into One of the main challenges was normalizing inconsistent commerce data. Different listings provide different levels of information about shipping, price, availability, attributes, location, and store details. Local shopping also behaves very differently from online shopping. A local store may be highly relevant to a product even when no trustworthy price is available. Instead of presenting that data as equivalent to a verified listing, ShopNearMe exposes unverified local offers separately. Another challenge was making product filters truly dynamic. Hard-coded filters would only work for predefined products, so ShopNearMe derives useful facets from the actual results. The WebMCP integration also required keeping agent actions synchronized with the visible interface so that the user and the agent are genuinely operating the same application. Accomplishments ShopNearMe is a working, deployed WebMCP application rather than a WebMCP proof of concept. Its five WebMCP tools cover the core shopping workflow and operate on the same state as the human-facing application. The project also includes: Live arbitrary-product search Nearby physical-store results Online and second-hand offers Shipping-aware total prices Dynamic product-specific filters Two-way price sorting Current-location support Searchable interactive map selection Explicit handling of unverified prices Responsive desktop and mobile interfaces Automated tests and CI A live desk clock search around Tel Aviv, for example, returned local stores together with online and second-hand offers. What I learned The main thing I learned is that an agent-native website does not need a separate AI interface. WebMCP can expose the semantics behind an existing human interface while keeping both interaction models synchronized. I also learned that useful WebMCP tools should represent meaningful user actions rather than simply wrapping backend API endpoints. The project also required learning more about normalizing commerce data, location-aware search, dynamic filtering, geocoding, handling uncertain data, and testing agent interactions in a real browser environment. What's next A production version of ShopNearMe could add more commerce providers, direct retailer integrations, stronger stock verification, better cross-store product matching, broader international support, and improved ranking of physical stores. Future WebMCP tools could also support saved comparisons, watchlists, product availability monitoring, and multi-product shopping plans. title: Simple Post
pitch: Your AI writes. SimplePost publishes. Turn ideas into platform-specific posts and schedule them across social networks from your favorite AI assistant.
about_excerpt: Your AI writes. SimplePost publishes. Turn ideas into platform-specific posts and schedule them across social networks from your favorite AI assistant. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI assistants are already great places to develop ideas and write social posts. But getting those posts published often means copying text into another tool, adjusting it for each network, uploading media, and scheduling everything separately. SimplePost closes that gap. Instead of adding another AI writer to a social media scheduler, it brings publishing to the AI assistant you already use. The idea is simple: Your AI writes. SimplePost publishes. What it does SimplePost is an open-source social publishing platform for people, AI agents, and applications. It lets you preview, validate, publish, and schedule content across 11 social platforms, including X, LinkedIn, Instagram, Threads, and Bluesky. You can work through an AI assistant using MCP, use the web scheduler directly, or integrate publishing into your own workflows through the TypeScript SDK, HTTP API, and CLI. The goal is not to copy the same message everywhere. One idea can become several platform-specific posts, with different text, media, and thread structures. Where WebMCP fits WebMCP brings the person and their agent into the same visual workspace. SimplePost’s free social media preview tool exposes structured tools that let a browser agent read the current drafts, render platform-specific versions, edit individual previews, configure profile details, and bring a particular preview into view. For example, a user can ask: Turn this launch announcement into posts for X, LinkedIn, and Instagram, then show me the previews. The agent prepares the versions and renders them on the page. The user can edit them directly or ask for changes, such as shortening the X version or making the LinkedIn post more technical. Both work with the same underlying content. The preview experience requires no signup or connected social accounts. Its WebMCP tools do not publish anything. After the user approves the content, the agent can retrieve a structured handoff for a separate, authenticated SimplePost publishing workflow. WebMCP handles the shared browser workspace; the remote MCP server handles authenticated publishing and scheduling. How I built it SimplePost is built around a shared TypeScript SDK that handles platform-specific publishing. The web scheduler, HTTP API, CLI, and MCP server build on that foundation. The web applications use Next.js and React, with PostgreSQL and Prisma supporting the scheduler’s persistent data. OAuth connects AI clients to the user’s SimplePost account without exposing raw social platform credentials to the assistant. Social previews come from a separate open-source rendering library shared across the product. It supports platform-specific layouts, profile identities, text, images, videos, and threads. The WebMCP integration connects structured tools directly to the preview page’s React state. Tool inputs are validated before changes are applied, and manual edits are reflected in the state the agent can read. Challenges One challenge is keeping a consistent publishing interface across platforms with different authentication flows, media requirements, content limits, and error responses. A shared SDK centralizes those differences without pretending every network works the same way. Another is coordinating human and agent edits. The preview page needs to remain an ordinary, usable editor while also exposing meaningful operations to an agent. Both interaction paths update the same drafts, and changing a preview clears its previous approval. A third challenge is separating experimentation from external actions. Preparing a preview should not accidentally publish a post. The public WebMCP tools stay local to the preview experience, while publishing requires a separate authenticated action. What I learned Building SimplePost reinforced that generating content is only one part of an AI-assisted workflow. Reviewing it, adapting it to its destination, and controlling what happens next matter just as much. The WebMCP integration also highlighted the value of shared, visible state. An agent can do the repetitive work while the person sees the result, makes direct edits, and guides the next step. That is the experience SimplePost aims to create: keep the AI assistant you prefer, make the publishing work easier, and stay involved in what goes out under your name. title: 2D Room Planner
pitch: "Move the desk toward the window for the light, stay 80 cm from the bed, don't block the door." WebMCP lets the agent check that in centimetres, not pixels, then show you the floor plan.
about_excerpt: "Move the desk toward the window for the light, stay 80 cm from the bed, don't block the door." WebMCP lets the agent check that in centimetres, not pixels, then show you the floor plan. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most layout tools give the person and the assistant different information. The person sees a plan drawn to scale. The assistant sees a screenshot and guesses from it. That is how you get a wardrobe door that cannot open, a walkway 12 cm too narrow, or a desk that looks centred but sits a few centimetres to one side. I wanted the agent to work from the same measurements a designer would use, and I wanted the person to watch it work and step in whenever they want. WebMCP is how the agent gets the model the page draws from instead of a picture of it. What it does Room Planner is a 2D layout tool in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. You create a room by size or from a template, add furniture from presets or as custom rectangles, and arrange it by dragging, by typing exact coordinates, or with the keyboard. It puts doors and windows on any wall, flags collisions, out-of-bounds objects, and blocked door clearances, and lets you add rules such as "keep 80 cm between the bed and the wall" that turn green or red as you edit. Measurements are in centimetres and the plan persists to localStorage . How I built it Room Planner is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no build step and no dependencies. The floor plan is one JavaScript object that everything reads from. An SVG renderer draws it, and the WebMCP tools change it, both through the same update and validation code, so an agent edit and a hand edit are the same operation underneath. The geometry, including footprints, overlaps, distances, and clearances, is plain functions working in centimetres. The WebMCP layer registers on navigator.modelContext or document.modelContext when a host is present and falls back to a built-in shim otherwise, so the tools behave the same either way. I used several AI models and providers while building this, each on the parts it handled best, from writing code to checking the geometry to finding edge cases. Challenges I ran into Rotation math caused the most rework. xCm and yCm mark the top-left corner before rotation, but at 90 and 270 degrees width and depth swap for collision and distance checks. Getting that consistent across the renderer, the geometry module, and the tool schemas took several passes. Keeping the agent and the UI in sync was subtler. Any mutation that bypassed the shared update code could leave a layout that passed the validity badge while breaking a constraint. I routed every WebMCP tool through the same store mutations the UI uses. WebMCP itself is experimental. Neither the spec's document.modelContext nor the browser's navigator.modelContext is widely available, so I wrote a shim, a simulated host, and a console bridge that all call the same execute functions. Exporting a clean SVG took some care. It renders correctly outside the page only after every CSS class is inlined and every oklch() colour is converted to sRGB, with the capture clipped to the plan and no app chrome. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am a perfectionist, and I have lost whole evenings to a single floor plan. There is always a constraint you cannot see coming, or a sequence of moves that checks out at every step and then wrecks something you fixed earlier. Chatting with an agent that could actually reason about the geometry while I watched the plan take shape on screen was the best part of building this. What I learned Grounding did more for reliability than autonomy did. Once the agent had exact geometry, ordinary requests started working, and once every change animated on the canvas, people trusted the agent because they could see and undo what it did. Returning the validation result with every mutation removed most of the "did that work?" follow-up calls. Building against an unshipped spec is workable when the shim and the simulated host share code with the real path. What's next for the room planner? A 3D preview beside the 2D plan, from the same model. More constraint types: sight lines, traffic flow, natural-light scoring, accessibility clearances. Multi-room plans with shared walls and doorways. Agent-proposed layouts, such as "give me three arrangements that seat six people," with the person picking one to refine.
