title: CareerCompassAI
pitch: CareerCompass AI uses WebMCP to let AI agents safely connect degree progress, courses, skills, scholarships and internships—while keeping every important student decision under human control.
about_excerpt: CareerCompass AI uses WebMCP to let AI agents safely connect degree progress, courses, skills, scholarships and internships—while keeping every important student decision under human control. Like Comment Story Updates CareerCompass AI Inspiration Career planning tools fail students in two opposite ways. Dashboards dump everything at once — majors, courses, internships, scholarships, research labs — and leave a 19-year-old to figure out which of forty things matters this semester. Chatbots do the reverse: they accept any free-text goal, including ones the system has no real data for, and generate confident advice on top of nothing. We wanted a third shape. A student should make one supported choice at a time , and each choice should visibly narrow what comes next — the way a good advisor works through a conversation rather than handing over a catalog. The WebMCP challenge gave us the other half of the idea. If a page can register its own tools with the browser, then an agent doesn't have to scrape our UI or guess at our data model. It can call explore_career_path or simulate_degree_plan directly, with real schemas, while the student stays in control of anything consequential. That's a much healthier division of labor than an agent clicking buttons on a student's behalf. What it does CareerCompass AI is a browser-native, agent-ready career planning journey with 33 WebMCP tools registered on the top-level page . The student moves through nine dependent steps: Direction — pick 1 of 6 broad career areas (or browse all 20 supported fields) Role — pick a field, then a role that actually exists inside that field Priority — internship readiness, research, portfolio proof, or graduation protection Academic route — is the current degree direct, adjacent, or a real pivot? Next semester — pick a workload, review one prerequisite-safe term, approve it Skill sprint — choose one of at most three role-specific gaps Experience — internship, research, or portfolio proof (at most two options shown) Funding — optionally add one relevant funding lead Roadmap — milestones assembled only from the choices actually made Nothing is preselected, and there is no free-text career box in the primary journey, so an unsupported entry like "singer" can never silently enter the planning engine. The catalog covers 20 fields and 54 roles , grouped so every role appears exactly once. The six starting areas are: build software and digital products; work with AI, data, and advanced computing; protect and connect systems; build hardware, robots, and physical systems; design human and immersive experiences; and apply technology to health and biology. Underneath, an agent connected through Chrome's WebMCP API can call any of the registered tools. The split is $25$ read/reason tools and $8$ approval-gated writes, so $25 + 8 = 33$ total: Read/reason — list_career_fields , explore_career_path , recommend_career_paths , compare_career_paths , check_prerequisites , simulate_degree_plan , identify_skill_gaps , find_internships , find_scholarships , find_research_opportunities , build_personalized_pathway , and more Approval-gated writes — create_degree_plan , add_course_to_plan , save_internship , save_scholarship , save_research_opportunity , express_research_interest , update_internship_status , update_scholarship_status The write boundary is the part we care most about: every write tool returns a pending approval, never a persisted change. An agent can propose a degree plan. Only the student pressing Approve plan in the interface applies it. Formally, for any agent-initiated write $w$, the applied state satisfies $$S_{t+1} = \begin{cases} \text{apply}(S_t, w) & \text{if the student approves } w \ S_t & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ Selections are not cosmetic. Area, field, and role set the career anchor used by every later step; priority changes how courses are ordered and which proof type is emphasized; the approved plan becomes the context for skill-gap and opportunity reasoning; and only the selected experience and funding survive into the final roadmap. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, no framework — a deliberate choice so the WebMCP registrations are plainly readable in the repository rather than buried in a build artifact. Architecture: src/webmcp.js — the 33 shared tool contracts (schemas, handlers, annotations) plus a local runtime for browsers without WebMCP src/site-tools.js — 33 literal document.modelContext.registerTool({ ... }) calls, one per tool, each forwarding the browser-provided AbortSignal through to the shared handler src/app.js — top-level page startup, registration, and approval gating src/buddy-journey.js — the nine-step state model and the six catalog-backed career groups src/career-catalog.js — JSON loading, normalization, exploration, and comparison src/engine.js — prerequisite resolution, term planning, skill-gap matching, roadmap assembly src/store.js — student-controlled state and the pending-approval queue src/dom-patch.js — keyed in-place reconciliation, so re-rendering a step doesn't flicker or reset scroll Data: the career catalog JSON holds the 20 fields, 54 roles, learning paths, scholarships, internships, universities, and research contacts. src/data.js holds curated demonstration student, degree, and course records. Where the catalog has url: null , we left it null and labeled the record Verify in the UI instead of inventing a link. Registration: every tool is registered imperatively from the top-level page during startup — not from an iframe — with the browser's cancellation signal threaded into the shared handler: await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "explore_career_path", description: exploreCareerPath.description, inputSchema: exploreCareerPath.inputSchema, execute: async (input, options = {}) => exploreCareerPath.execute(input, { signal: options.signal }), title: exploreCareerPath.title, annotations: exploreCareerPath.annotations, }, { signal }); Browsers without WebMCP run the exact same handlers through the local runtime, so the journey never depends on the agent being present. Challenges we ran into Proving registration instead of claiming it. Our first version generated the 33 registrations in a loop. It worked at runtime, but a reviewer reading site-tools.js couldn't see a single tool name. We rewrote it as 33 explicit literal calls, so the mapping from source to registry is one-to-one and visible on the page — because "trust the loop" isn't a submission. Accomplishments that we're proud of 33 of 33 direct document.modelContext.registerTool({ ... }) registrations, literal and visible in source A real write boundary , not a disclaimer — 8 write tools, zero of which can persist anything without a student action A refusal to fake coverage — unverified catalog URLs stay null and get labeled, and unsupported career fields simply cannot be entered Clean at $390 \times 844$ and on desktop , with no horizontal overflow Progressive disclosure enforced in code , not by convention: at most three skill gaps, at most two experience options, one active decision card, later steps locked until dependencies resolve Catalog coverage that partitions cleanly — six areas covering all 20 fields and 54 roles exactly once, with no duplicates and no orphans What we learned WebMCP rewards honest schemas. The moment tools are callable by an agent, vague inputs stop being a UI problem and start being a correctness problem. Writing strict inputSchema definitions forced us to sharpen the data model itself. Cancellation is not optional. Forwarding options.signal into every handler seemed like boilerplate until an agent abandoned a long compare_career_paths call mid-flight. Plumbing the signal through from the start is far cheaper than retrofitting it. Untrusted content needs a marker. Catalog-derived tools carry untrustedContentHint: true . Third-party records flowing into an agent's context are a prompt-injection surface, and labeling them is the minimum. Constraint is a feature. We expected students to want more options. Testing the journey, the opposite held — cutting to at most three skill gaps and two experience options made the tool feel like advice instead of a search result. Deterministic beats plausible for an MVP. Our reasoning engine is local and rule-based, not LLM-backed. Every recommendation traces back to a catalog record and a selection, which is exactly what a career tool ought to be able to show. What's next for CareerCompass AI Real institutional data. The biggest gap between demo and product: authenticated SIS integration and per-institution degree adapters, so prerequisite checks run against a student's actual transcript instead of curated records. Verified, live opportunity feeds. Replace the null-URL entries with verified sources and freshness dates for scholarships, internships, and research postings — with an as-of timestamp on every record. Server-side authorization and audit. Right now approval gating

title: ClauseProof
pitch: A source-grounded contract decision room where people and agents can analyze and propose together without collapsing human approval into AI output.
about_excerpt: A source-grounded contract decision room where people and agents can analyze and propose together without collapsing human approval into AI output. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for ClauseProof Inspiration Contracts rarely fail because nobody summarized them. They fail because risk, authority, and action get blurred together. ClauseProof explores an open web where a person and an AI agent can inspect the same contract state without allowing fluent model output to masquerade as human approval. What it does ClauseProof turns a high-stakes agreement into a source-grounded decision room. Documents are read locally, including OCR for image documents. Deterministic rules keep the exact governing clause beside each finding. A human can resolve or explicitly accept risks, record a case-specific approval, and prepare an unsigned signature-packet receipt. The synthetic Northstar supply agreement demonstrates auto-renewal, exclusivity, payment, cure, and liability findings. Uploaded bytes and extracted text stay in the browser. Why WebMCP The live page exposes six narrow tools over the same state the human sees: get_case_summary list_open_risks propose_risk_resolution record_human_risk_decision approve_case_decision prepare_signature_packet Each tool is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , uses a closed input schema, describes its effects, and returns a structured receipt. An agent proposal remains a proposal. Approval requires a visible human decision, and signature preparation always reports sent: false and signed: false . How we built it React and TypeScript power the shared browser workflow. PDF.js and Tesseract.js handle local text and OCR. Xano provides the durable synthetic case, audit events, evidence receipts, idempotent bootstrap, and five deployed endpoints. SerpApi runs one bounded server-side counterparty query through Xano; the live proof returned nine organic results and evidence receipt 1 without exposing the key to the browser. Vitest covers the authority boundaries and deterministic extraction. Netlify serves the public HTTPS build. Challenges The hardest problem was making agent actions useful without collapsing capability into authority. We separated analysis, proposal, human risk decisions, case approval, signature preparation, sending, and signing into independently verifiable states. Accomplishments One shared human-and-agent workflow instead of an agent-only chatbot Exact-source findings with local OCR Six working WebMCP tools over real product state Explicit approval and non-action receipts Live Xano and SerpApi integration Public MIT source and reproducible deployment artifacts What we learned WebMCP is strongest when it exposes a product's real workflow, keeps effects narrow, and makes meaningful transitions independently reviewable. The best agent experience is not maximum autonomy; it is useful capability with trustworthy authority boundaries. What's next Add authenticated private rooms, versioned redlines, provider-backed PDF generation, and a human-controlled e-sign handoff. Those providers will not be claimed until their live calls and terminal receipts are proven. title: Cogsmith
pitch: CogSmith helps gearheads turn old bikes into modern single-speeds. Making cool bikes for everyone!
about_excerpt: CogSmith helps gearheads turn old bikes into modern single-speeds. Making cool bikes for everyone! Like 8 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I started CogSmith because I needed a calculator to do some garage math for me. In my downtime I’ve started converting older MTBs into cool single-speed bikes, I find the tinkering in my garage really relaxing. The challenge is I'm constantly trial-and-erroring to figure out good combinations of gears to use, and I don't have a million gears to select from. I only have what the bike came with. There is math to help with this, but after crunching these numbers manually one too many times, I built a tool to handle it. I ended up fully fleshing out CogSmith because the calculator worked incredibly well for my own projects, and I was looking for a practical excuse to learn about vibe coding. What it does A rider enters information about their project bike, including wheel size, chainstay length, available chainrings and rear cogs, desired gearing, and dropout adjustment range. CogSmith then evaluates the possible combinations and calculates the Goldilocks combination for the rider. Instead of only calculating a gear ratio, CogSmith tries to answer the more useful question: "Can I actually build this combination on my bike?" CogSmith also supports WebMCP, allowing AI assistants to interact directly with the calculator. This is great as sometimes in the garage, your hands are filthy and the AI assistant can do lookups for you. How I built it I have a background in DevOps and infrastructure type scripting, so I wanted to use this as a chance to learn some vibe coding. For tools I wanted to do this as cheaply as possible so the best fit was to build this on GitHub, for its CI/CD pipelines and its static page hosting. It also integrated well with workflows I had used in the past AND worked well with GPT Work and Codex. CogSmith was built as a static web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It slowly grew from an all-in-one HTML file into something broken out into components, ultimately getting to a point where resources were broken up into testable pieces and I started using GitHub releases. As the project matured so did its architecture. It focuses on two areas now. A tool for humans and a tool for robots. Human interface → CogSmith calculation engine and AI through WebMCP → CogSmith calculation engine Both paths use the same underlying logic, so an AI recommendation is based on the same calculations that appear in the browser. CogSmith exposes WebMCP tools that allow an AI to read the current bike configuration, calculate possible gearing combinations, and display a selected setup back in the user interface. One of the core measurements CogSmith uses is gear inches: G = D × (T_f / T_r) where: G is gear inches D is wheel diameter T_f is the number of teeth on the front chainring T_r is the number of teeth on the rear cog CogSmith then combines that gearing calculation with chain-length and axle-position calculations to determine whether the setup will physically fit within the available dropout range. We also added automated tests and CI validation around the calculator and WebMCP interfaces so changes can be tested before being deployed. Challenges I ran into Honestly most of the infrastructure and pieces of the website were well understood and commonly used, however I started to face challenges with understanding how MCP worked and pivoting to how WebMCP works. WebMCP isn't well documented yet and honestly the test frameworks aren't great for it right now. That was the hard part, learning MCP :) Accomplishments that I'm proud of I love everything about CogSmith, I've used it for 3 different bikes so far and it saves me from fiddling around with gears. I'm most amazed and proud of learning about WebMCP. I'd been familiar with taking a function and exposing it as an API, but I never knew you could do something similar like taking a math formula and passing it to an AI. I think that's cool. It's like APIs for LLMs :D What I learned I had already learned that the voice assistant was useful in the garage, like "tell me the wheel lug nut torque rating for a 2018 GMC 1500 truck" or "I need 50:1 fuel mix for my outboard motor, I have 5L of gas, how much oil do I add" , but I never knew I could build a tool and plumb it into GPT. I had always thought GPT needed to search the internet to find this knowledge. What's next for CogSmith CogSmith is gonna simmer for a bit, it's Fall soon and I have some bike projects to finish. Other than that, I think I might do some repo cleanup, create some linting (I love linting) for the repo, and probably patch things as they need it. I need to see how popular WebMCP gets :) Built With chromium ci/cd css3 github html5 javascript opensource playwright pwa Try it out cogsmith.bainer.ca github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I rode the bikes! title: Consensus
pitch: Human + AI decision workspace powered by WebMCP, where agents research, score, flag conflicts, and propose rankings while humans retain final control.
about_excerpt: Human + AI decision workspace powered by WebMCP, where agents research, score, flag conflicts, and propose rankings while humans retain final control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration - AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of researching, analyzing, and making recommendations, but important decisions still require human judgment. We wanted to build a workspace where humans and AI could work together on the same decision instead of the AI simply giving a final answer. Consensus was inspired by the idea of making AI an active collaborator while keeping humans in control of important decisions. What it does - Consensus is a shared decision and research workspace for human + AI collaboration. In Decision Mode, AI agents can use WebMCP tools to read the board, add options, score options, flag conflicts, resolve flags, and propose rankings. Humans can independently score options, review AI reasoning, dispute evaluations, and lock the final decision. Consensus also includes Research Mode for extracting claims, checking evidence, identifying contradictions, and building citation relationships. All important actions are persisted and can be reviewed through activity history and provenance. How we built it - The frontend is built with React and Vite, with WebMCP integrated through document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The backend uses FastAPI and is deployed on Google Cloud Run. Firestore stores shared board state, evaluations, flags, and activity history. Vertex AI with Gemini 2.5 Flash provides AI-assisted analysis. The WebMCP tools connect to the same real backend operations used by the application, so agent actions update persistent state rather than a simulated demo. Challenges we ran into - A major challenge was deciding what AI agents should be allowed to do and what should remain under human control. We wanted the agent to be useful without allowing it to silently make consequential decisions. We also had to make WebMCP tool registration reliable as the application changed between different modes and states. Finally, connecting the React frontend, FastAPI backend, Firestore, Vertex AI, and WebMCP into one working deployed application required careful coordination. Accomplishments that we're proud of - We are proud that Consensus is a real deployed WebMCP application with persistent state, rather than just a prototype or mock demonstration. The live application exposes six Decision-mode WebMCP tools that can interact with the shared workspace. We are especially proud of the human-agent boundary: agents can investigate, evaluate, flag issues, and recommend actions, while humans retain control over scoring, overrides, and locking the final decision. Our backend verification tests also pass checks for persistence, provenance, conflict handling, evaluation history, overrides, and locking. What we learned - We learned that WebMCP becomes much more powerful when tools operate on real shared application state. We also learned that human-AI collaboration is not only about giving agents more capabilities. It is equally important to define the actions they should not control. Building Consensus also taught us how browser-native agent tools can work together with a persistent cloud backend and an AI reasoning layer. What's next for Consensus - Next, we want to expand Consensus into more complex collaborative workflows. We plan to explore multi-agent debate, stronger evidence and citation verification, configurable decision rubrics, richer provenance, and approval workflows with different levels of human confirmation. Our long-term goal is to create a workspace where humans and AI agents can work together on complex decisions while keeping the reasoning, evidence, actions, and final authority visible and auditable. title: CUF
pitch: Deterministic trust for agentic systems
about_excerpt: Deterministic trust for agentic systems Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration CUF is a WebMCP-powered security verification demo built around one core rule: agents can run the test, but they cannot grade themselves. As agents gain more ability to interact with software directly, I wanted to explore a simple question: how do you let an agent perform useful verification work without also giving that same agent authority over whether the test passed? CUF Challenge Edition demonstrates that separation. What it does The demo verifies a synthetic multi-tenant authorization boundary. A Support actor in Tenant A may access Tenant A tickets, but must never access Tenant B tickets. Through WebMCP, an agent can discover CUF’s tools, run verification cases, retrieve evidence, inspect the latest result, and export a sealed challenge artifact. The agent never supplies the final verdict. CUF’s deterministic kernel returns: PASS when the expected boundary is enforced FAIL when a cross-tenant regression is observed INCONCLUSIVE when the authorization outcome cannot be established The most important safety property is that missing evidence never becomes a false PASS. For the challenge, I built a standalone public CUF WebMCP edition with five browser-registered tools: cuf_list_cases cuf_run_case cuf_get_latest_verdict cuf_get_evidence cuf_export_seal How we built it The challenge edition is intentionally small, public, and inspectable. It uses a browser-based JavaScript application, WebMCP through document.modelContext, a deterministic verification kernel, synthetic authorization scenarios, Web Crypto for the sealed challenge artifact, and a Node.js test suite. I verified the deployed application end to end in a WebMCP-capable Chrome build. The browser discovered the production tools and invoked them through the WebMCP interface rather than by directly calling the application JavaScript. The verified results were: Healthy → PASS Regression → FAIL Unavailable → INCONCLUSIVE I also tested attempted verdict overrides. The run tool does not expose a verdict input, and attempts to force a verdict did not change CUF’s deterministic result. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was preserving the separation between orchestration and judgment. It would have been easy to let the agent inspect evidence and then decide whether the system passed. That would undermine the entire point of the demo. Instead, CUF mechanically classifies the observations and applies deterministic verdict rules outside the agent. Another challenge was proving that the WebMCP implementation actually worked through a real browser environment, not just proving that the underlying JavaScript functions worked. The final deployment was tested in a WebMCP-capable Chrome build, where the tools were discovered and executed through document.modelContext. One hardening detail also surfaced during testing: Chrome accepted an undeclared verdict property instead of rejecting the whole call. CUF ignored it and still preserved the correct deterministic verdict. Accomplishments that we’re proud of The project now has a real browser-level WebMCP implementation with five production-origin tools. The live deployment successfully demonstrated all three deterministic outcomes: PASS for a healthy boundary FAIL for a cross-tenant regression INCONCLUSIVE when the evidence could not be established Evidence retrieval also worked through WebMCP, and attempted verdict overrides were unable to change the result. I’m also proud that the demo keeps the human and agent working against the same visible state. The agent can do the operational work, but the human can still see what happened and why. What we learned The biggest lesson was that WebMCP is most useful when it exposes product semantics instead of UI mechanics. The agent does not need a tool that means “click this button.” It needs a typed capability that means “run this verification case.” That makes the interaction more reliable and lets the application keep control over the rules that should not be delegated. For CUF, that rule is verdict authority. What’s next for CUF CUF as a broader private project predates this challenge. This submission is a separate public challenge edition using synthetic data and an intentionally small, inspectable deterministic kernel. The next step is to apply the same WebMCP orchestration model to CUF’s broader provider and evidence architecture while preserving the same invariant: agent capability can expand, but verdict authority remains deterministic and auditable. title: DemoMotion × WebMCP — Collaborative Demo Studio
pitch: A human and an AI agent build, refine, and export a narrated product demo together—the agent drives DemoMotion through structured WebMCP tools while you keep control of the same workspace.
about_excerpt: A human and an AI agent build, refine, and export a narrated product demo together—the agent drives DemoMotion through structured WebMCP tools while you keep control of the same workspace. Like Comment Story Updates ## Inspiration Product demo videos are painful to make, and AI agents are surprisingly bad at making them: an agent staring at a demo-generation UI has to guess which button does what. WebMCP flips that around — a website can expose its real actions as structured tools. We asked: what if a human and an agent could build a demo video together , in the same workspace, instead of the agent flailing at a UI or taking over completely? ## What it does DemoMotion AI turns a web app URL and a goal into a narrated product demo video (it plans a scenario, records the browser with Playwright, writes and voices the narration, and renders an MP4 with ffmpeg). For the WebMCP Challenge we added a shared /webmcp workspace where a human and a browser AI agent collaborate through five WebMCP tools: get_demo_state — read the current demo (read-only) create_demo — start an editable draft (title, steps, first-pass narration) update_demo_narration — rewrite the narration/title; the UI updates instantly generate_demo — run the real pipeline to a narrated MP4 export_demo — local-only download, gated on explicit human approval The human can edit the exact same fields by hand, a "WebMCP enabled" badge and an agent/human activity log make every tool call visible, and every call actually executes against the same backend as the main dashboard — nothing is faked. ## How we built it WebMCP is a thin adapter , not a rewrite. Tools register on document.modelContext (native in Chrome 149+ and the ChatGPT desktop browser, polyfilled elsewhere via @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill ) and call the existing FastAPI services rather than duplicating pipeline logic. A tiny shared store lets the React UI and the agent's tools mutate one source of truth, so agent actions are immediately visible and the human keeps control. We added just enough backend surface for real collaboration: a lightweight POST /v1/demo-drafts that reuses the existing planner + narration writer (no recording), and optional title_override / narration_override on the job API so a narration edited before generation actually reaches the rendered video. Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript Backend: FastAPI, Playwright, ffmpeg, gTTS / Google Cloud TTS, optional Vertex AI (Gemini) for planning Ops: Docker Compose, Terraform, Google Cloud Run ## What's new vs pre-existing The generation pipeline, the dashboard, the demo-app, the REST API, and the deploy tooling existed before 2026-08-25 . Everything under apps/web/app/webmcp and apps/web/lib/webmcp (the 5 tools, shared store, strict schemas), plus the /v1/demo-drafts endpoint and the override fields, is new for this challenge . ## Challenges we ran into Making edits real. An agent rewriting narration is meaningless unless it changes the output. We threaded a narration override through the pipeline so the edited script is exactly what gets voiced and rendered. Treating WebMCP as an external interface. Every tool uses a strict allow-list schema, returns structured errors ( INVALID_INPUT , PROJECT_NOT_FOUND , GENERATION_FAILED , EXPORT_NOT_READY , EXPORT_REQUIRES_CONFIRMATION ), accepts only http/https URLs, and never leaks secrets or stack traces. Keeping the human in control. Export is a local download only and requires explicit confirmation — the agent can never publish or share on its own. Runtime quirks. Tying tool lifecycle to an AbortController surfaced an expected AbortError under React StrictMode's dev double-mount; we handle it cleanly. ## What we learned WebMCP shines when a site exposes creative actions with sharp boundaries. Shared state between human and agent — not full autonomy — is the interesting design space, and strict schemas plus human-gated side effects make an agent safe to hand real controls. ## What's next More editable dimensions (scene ordering, pacing), and richer live progress in the workspace — while hosted projects, sharing, and team features stay in DemoMotion Cloud. WebMCP stays an open ecosystem feature. title: Night Sky Atlas
pitch: A shared, visible observing route for people and their AI agents.
about_excerpt: A shared, visible observing route for people and their AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a short stargazing session asks a beginner to combine an observer's place and time, target visibility, object types, and a comfortable route. That is more than a list of astronomy facts: changing the observer or advancing the clock changes what the person sees. Night Sky Atlas makes that work collaborative instead of opaque. What it does A person can explore the planetarium manually, edit an observing plan, and save it locally. With WebMCP, an agent can query the same live sky context, find observable catalog targets, and propose a timed route. The agent's proposal appears in the same planner rail as an Agent preview . Previewing does not change observer location or time, so the person can inspect the route before approving any mutation. After approval, the agent can visibly set the observer, save the route, and advance the shared tour target by target. This is a good fit for WebMCP because visual sky state is the product: the person and agent need the same map, time, location, selected target, and plan. The site exposes ten strict, top-level imperative tools that reuse the manual application actions rather than a parallel automation path. It remains a zero-build static site with local browser persistence; no account, backend, or API key is required. How I built it The July 22, 2026 baseline at commit 81672ede79762cbf3aadfe23a8dc9eee32013f94 was an interactive planetarium. During the challenge I added a persistent, human-editable observing plan and ten WebMCP tools. The tools reuse the same catalog, altitude calculations, validation, persistence, application actions, and visible state as the manual interface. The intended safety sequence is read, find, preview, inspect, mutate, save . In particular, preview_observing_plan makes a proposed New York route visible while the current London observer and time stay unchanged; only an explicit location or time action mutates them. Challenges I ran into Designing tools that share exactly the same state and validation as manual controls without creating a hidden agent-only path. Keeping location and time changes visible and reviewable while still making the agent route useful. Computing and preserving per-slot altitude constraints for a timed route. Making a dense planner rail work at desktop and mobile sizes with usable keyboard focus, live progress, and reduced-motion behavior. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A preview-first workflow that visibly proposes a route before observer mutation. Ten narrow, strict-schema WebMCP tools: three read tools and seven visible write tools. A manual planner that remains useful without an agent, plus a saved guided tour that frames targets and advances time. Browser verification of an altitude-constrained New York demo route. 81 automated tests covering astronomy, planning, persistence, UI, and WebMCP integration. What I learned WebMCP is most compelling when it gives an agent a deliberate application surface while the person can still see and steer every result. Tool descriptions and schemas clarify what an agent may ask for, but the visible UI is what makes the collaboration legible. Separating preview from commit made the location change understandable instead of surprising. What's next Add weather, darkness, and equipment-aware recommendations with clearly labeled data sources. Let people compare alternative plans side by side before saving one. Export plans as printable or calendar-friendly observing cards. Broaden accessibility testing across assistive technology and real devices. title: OCHECK — Agent-Ready Official Guides
pitch: OCHECK turns official information into personalized, verifiable action. With WebMCP, agents help users plan, complete, and confirm trusted steps without altering the official source.
about_excerpt: OCHECK turns official information into personalized, verifiable action. With WebMCP, agents help users plan, complete, and confirm trusted steps without altering the official source. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every experience already has an integrator. Today, that integrator is usually the customer. People reconstruct events from emails, chats, PDFs, maps, deadlines, providers, partner offers, and last-minute changes. Organizers may publish information across multiple channels, but participants must still assemble it into a usable path. OCHECK changes who performs that integration. It creates an organizer-governed official experience in which people and AI agents work from the same live, verifiable outcome state. It represents a new mindset and an INNOVATIVE approach to e-commerce: not simply getting things done, but doing them well—and making them OFFICIAL . What OCHECK does OCHECK transforms fragmented event information into one official, sequenced experience that integrates rules, timing, AI assistance, verified progress, optional partner value, and shareable achievements. The Challenge Edition presents three connected perspectives: Organizer + AI: An agent reads a fragmented creation brief, identifies sources, actors, services, and open loops, and stages an official guide. The guide is validated and cannot become official until the organizer separately confirms its publication. Participant: The participant receives an official path instead of having to reconstruct the event. An agent can create a personal plan without modifying the official source of truth. Verified completion brings readiness to 100% and unlocks a Ready Pass. Sponsor Impact: Sponsored utility reaches a genuinely interested, specialized audience. Sponsors gain actionable insight into the audience segments that viewed and purchased their products, while preserving participant privacy. Their offerings are not merely presented as items for sale; they are integrated as useful components of the official experience. The Ready Pass is not a reward purchased through commercial interaction. It is a verified, shareable achievement. Its clean referral link opens a new official guide for another participant without transferring any personal progress. Why WebMCP? OCHECK is a strong WebMCP use case because the challenge is not simply to generate an answer. The agent must understand and act on the authoritative state of a live web experience and its relationship with the event sponsors’ products. Without WebMCP, an AI assistant can discuss an event, but it cannot reliably inspect which guide is official, what remains incomplete, whether a participant is eligible for a Ready Pass, or which action a person has authorized. Through WebMCP, the browser page exposes 13 narrowly scoped Site Tools: Six read tools inspect the official outcome, creation brief, draft validation, participant progress, sponsorship opportunities, and commercial impact. Seven action tools stage a guide, publish the official source of truth, create a personal plan, verify completion, activate an optional benefit, claim a Ready Pass, and undo the last confirmed mutation. This gives the agent structured access to the same state visible to the person while keeping authority within OCHECK. What people and agents can do together The demonstrated workflow is: ChatGPT reads the organizer’s fragmented brief through OCHECK Site Tools. The agent identifies the intended outcome, sources, actors, and unresolved questions. The agent stages an integrated guide proposal. OCHECK validates governance, deadlines, evidence, source traceability, sponsorship disclosure, optionality, and Ready Pass logic. The organizer decides whether the validated proposal becomes official. The participant’s agent creates a personal execution plan without rewriting the official guide. Human-confirmed completion unlocks a Ready Pass, while the audit history and Undo function preserve human control. The agent provides interpretation and execution leverage. The organizer retains authority. The participant controls personal actions. OCHECK preserves one official source of truth. How we built it The Challenge Edition is a standalone, dependency-free web application built with HTML, CSS, and modern JavaScript and deployed on Vercel. The tools are registered directly through the browser-native API: const tools = buildSiteTools({ store, confirmAction }); for (const tool of tools) { await document.modelContext.registerTool(tool); } Read operations use narrowly defined schemas and readOnlyHint . Every state-changing operation opens an in-page confirmation showing the proposed action and its exact data before any state changes. A dedicated state layer separates: the official guide as the source of truth; staged AI proposals; participant progress; personal planning; sponsored interactions; Ready Pass eligibility; audit activity; and reversible mutations. The repository contains the complete source code, synthetic demonstration data, execution instructions, a BSD 3-Clause license, trademark boundaries, challenge provenance, and an automated test suite. Sixteen tests cover the complete human-agent experience, including validation, authority, privacy, Ready Pass rules, referral behavior, sponsorship separation, and Undo. No login, private service, production database, third-party runtime SDK, or real participant information is required. Challenges The hardest challenge was not registering the tools. It was defining trustworthy boundaries between agent capability and human authority. We had to ensure that: an AI-generated draft could not automatically become official; personal planning could not rewrite the organizer-controlled source of truth; commercial interaction could never purchase completion of, or satisfy, an official requirement; a Ready Pass could not be claimed before readiness had been verified; every consequential action required human confirmation; and the previous state could be restored through Undo. We also designed the tool schemas to remain narrow enough for reliable agent use while supporting a complete product experience rather than merely a technical proof of concept. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools expose meaningful product state instead of merely duplicating interface buttons. A strong agent-ready experience requires three elements working together: structured access to authoritative state; explicit authority and confirmation boundaries; and visible outcomes shared by both the person and the agent. We also learned that personalization does not require changing the official source of truth. The official guide can remain stable while the agent creates a contextual path for each participant. Challenge-period work OCHECK existed before the challenge as a product concept, brand, business model, and private MVP for official guides. The WebMCP Challenge Edition was created during the submission period as a separate, standalone implementation. Work completed during the challenge period includes the 13 browser-native tools, AI Guide Forge, explicit outcome contracts, draft validation, human-confirmed publication, separate organizer, participant, and partner perspectives, Ready Pass verification, privacy-preserving sponsor signals, audit history, Undo, synthetic data, and automated testing. The public repository includes a timestamped commit history and HACKATHON.md , which clearly distinguishes OCHECK’s previous work from the new WebMCP implementation. Potential impact Events are the first use case, but the underlying problem arises wherever people must reconstruct an official process from fragmented information: events, education, travel, onboarding, public services, healthcare preparation, compliance, and professional workflows. OCHECK proposes a web in which agents do not replace authority. Instead, they help people understand and act upon a governed source of truth provided directly by the organizer. Founder OCHECK was founded and is led by Gustavo García Figueroa, a Colombian lawyer without a traditional background in software engineering. Gustavo contributed the original idea, product judgment, governance model, privacy boundaries, commercial logic, and testing decisions. ChatGPT and Codex accelerated execution by translating those decisions into workflows, source code, tests, and rapid iteration. The project uses generally available tools and does not claim endorsement, investment, or preferential support from OpenAI, Vercel, or any other challenge sponsor. One experience. One official truth. Human intent. Agent execution. Verified growth. This is OCHECK. title: λ-SPEC WebMCP
pitch: Resilience you can delegate. Evidence you can audit.
about_excerpt: Resilience you can delegate. Evidence you can audit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Rich analytical web apps are easy for humans to use but brittle for agents. A browser agent normally has to infer intent from forms, synthesize clicks, and scrape charts back out of the DOM. λ-SPEC explores a better contract: a scientific web application that exposes its real domain capabilities directly to an agent while keeping the human in the same visible workspace. What it does λ-SPEC measures observed system–environment coupling and asks what remains when environmental support is progressively withdrawn. It computes coupling λ, complementary fragility Φ, rolling λ and dλ/dt, an environmental-withdrawal stress envelope, ranked measured environmental drivers, confidence, limitations and exportable evidence. For the WebMCP Challenge, λ-SPEC was extended with eight typed WebMCP tools. An agent can discover datasets, load and configure a demo, run the resilience analysis, inspect the current evidence, inspect the withdrawal envelope, ask an evidence-bounded interpreter and run an end-to-end collaboration workflow. Why WebMCP is essential The agent is not clicking buttons or scraping charts. document.modelContext.registerTool(...) exposes the underlying analysis contract with constrained JSON schemas, read-only annotations and explicit validation. Tool calls update the same in-page state the human sees. A person can manually change the method, rolling window or column roles and then ask the agent to continue from that exact revised state. That human→agent handoff is the core improvement: both sides operate on one visible scientific state instead of maintaining separate hidden automation contexts. How we built it Challenge-specific implementation lives in lambda_spec/static/webmcp.js . The registered tools are: list_resilience_demos load_resilience_demo configure_resilience_analysis run_resilience_analysis get_resilience_state inspect_environmental_withdrawal ask_resilience_evidence run_resilience_collaboration Inputs are bounded with enums, limits, uniqueness constraints and validation against the active dataset. WebMCP progressively enhances the app: if document.modelContext is unavailable, λ-SPEC still works normally for a human. Existing project vs. challenge work λ-SPEC v1.2 existed before the challenge with its analysis engine, demos, charts, CSV workflow, exports and evidence interpreter. The WebMCP layer was added during the challenge period beginning at commit b40ec1f6ff4d2ff2f506b08331f69fe678754499 . Subsequent challenge commits add tool registration, shared human/agent state, tests, deployment configuration and judge materials. How to test Open the live app in a WebMCP-capable browser/runtime and ask: Analyze the orbital telemetry demo. Tell me whether measured coupling is strengthening or weakening, inspect the environmental-withdrawal envelope, identify the strongest measured environmental drivers, and tell me what to investigate next. Stay within the measured evidence. Then manually change the coupling method or rolling window and ask: Inspect the current resilience state again and continue from the state I changed. The floating WebMCP · human + agent workspace panel reports agent activity visibly. Scope and limitations λ-SPEC measures observed coupling. It does not establish causality, provide clinical diagnosis, certify engineering safety, make financial suitability determinations, or guarantee forecasts. The withdrawal curve is a controlled signal-removal stress envelope, not a literal simulation of every real-world intervention. Built With css html javascript numpy openai python scipy webmcp Try it out lambda-spec-webmcp.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by As the project lead and principal developer, I conceived and built λ-SPEC WebMCP from the ground up. My contribution covered system architecture, AI workflow design, WebMCP integration, UX/product design, implementation, testing, and demonstration. I designed the human-agent interaction model so AI agents can understand available web capabilities, execute structured actions, and return useful results while preserving human oversight. I focused the platform on health and education use cases, translating complex workflows into accessible, explainable, agent-ready experiences. title: Redline
pitch: Your AI agent reviews an employment contract through tools the page registers in your browser and the blurred document snaps into clarity as you decide each redline.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent reviews an employment contract through tools the page registers in your browser and the blurred document snaps into clarity as you decide each redline. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration You get an offer. The salary is great — and the contract is 22 pages of fine print with a 48-hour signature deadline. About 30% of US workers are bound by non-competes, and most people sign without understanding what they're signing. A lawyer costs $400/hour. The alternative used to be asking an AI "is this enforceable?" and getting a confident essay you then had to reconstruct into something actionable. Redline is for the person who actually has: a document, a deadline, and an AI agent they already use. What it does Paste an employment contract (or open one of three deliberately overreaching samples) and it loads blurred — the way a 22-page contract actually feels. Your AI agent then works inside the page: it reads every clause, flags the risky ones with severity and grounded reasons, and proposes concrete redline language. Each proposal lands as a decision card under the exact sentence it modifies. You decide each one — Keep as-is, or Redline it — and accepted changes roll up into a negotiation email, Current vs Proposed side by side, one click to copy. As the agent assesses each clause, it snaps into clarity — but clarity is computed, not decorative: a clause only clears once it's assessed and every redline on it is decided. Reset a verdict and it re-flags. The blur is the progress bar. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP A contract-review tool needs an agent to see inside the document, clause by clause, and write back into it. That is exactly what WebMCP enables: Redline registers seven tools on document.modelContext — get_sample_contract , get_document_state , extract_clauses , get_clause_text , assess_clause , get_enforceability_context , export_negotiation_email . Two-phase dynamic registration: at boot only a get_sample_contract tool exists; once a document is loaded, the app retires it via WebMCP's signal-based lifecycle and registers the six analysis tools. The tool list always matches what is meaningful right now. Grounded analysis, not vibes: get_enforceability_context hands the agent real data — non-compete enforceability across 20 US states (earnings thresholds, void-by-default rules, notice requirements), training-repayment-agreement traps in 5 states, and heuristic families for NDAs, arbitration, and IP assignment. When Redline says a five-year worldwide non-compete is high-severity in Washington, it quotes RCW 49.62. No API keys, no backend, no scraping. The page is the tool provider and the browser is the whole stack (static assets on Cloudflare Workers). What people and agents can do together now The old pattern: ask an AI, get an essay, copy fragments into a text editor, lose the structure. Here the agent proposes and the human decides — and the boundary is enforced by the data flow itself: agent tools write proposals and assessments into clause threads, but redline verdicts can only come from the UI. What was six screens of copy-paste is now one grounded pass with the human keeping the pen on every change. Because all state is derived (blur, completion, the email draft are computed from assessments and verdicts — never stored as flags), the UI can't claim progress the human didn't actually make. How we built it React 19 + TypeScript (strict), Vite, Cloudflare Workers static assets — no backend, no keys. All tool reads go through a live session ref (tools never read stale React state); writes flow actions → store → UI in one direction. The email composer is deterministic: the page and export_negotiation_email emit byte-identical output. The decision UI (FlagBadge, RedlineCard, ClauseChat) renders proposals inline in the document; a 500ms transition snaps each clause from blurred to clear as decisions land. Challenges we ran into WebMCP's registration lifecycle has no unregister API — tools are retired through abort signals, which shaped our two-phase registration design. Making blur honest took a derived rule: early versions cleared clauses on assessment alone; the shipped version requires every redline on the clause to be decided. Keeping page and tool output identical forced us to make the email composer a pure function both paths call. Live agent testing caught real bugs (duplicate redline proposals on re-assessment, chat auto-expand behavior) that we fixed with a pure redline-planning function and better thread state. What we learned The WebMCP model inverts the usual architecture: the app doesn't call the model, the agent calls the app. Designing tools for another developer (the agent platform) forced us to make state readable, actions explicit, and UI claims derived from data — which made the app better for humans too. What's honest about this demo The samples are drafted overbroad — that's the test. But nothing is scripted: the app ships data and heuristics, not verdicts, and accepts whatever a competent model actually produces through the tools. Different model, different analysis — same structure to hold it. Try it: https://redline.kangyow.workers.dev/ — paste your own contract, or start with "The Offer Letter": a $128k role in Seattle with a five-year, worldwide non-compete. Washington law is not impressed. Now the app says so, with the citation. Not legal advice — a hackathon demo. The document lives in your browser session; only what the tools return reaches your agent. title: Nexo RUTIC
pitch: Every button in this Colombian telecom registry has an AI-agent twin — same validation, same logic, same authority. A WebMCP Challenge entry.
about_excerpt: Every button in this Colombian telecom registry has an AI-agent twin — same validation, same logic, same authority. A WebMCP Challenge entry. Like Comment Story Updates Attaching the three bundled sample documents through the canonical manifest — the same files whether clicked or registered by the agent. Every step names both paths at once: the button to click, and the exact sentence to tell the agent instead. The Spanish interface, with an explainer panel describing what WebMCP is and how each action maps to a tool. The agent creates a dossier, is blocked from skipping a step, then submits it — all through the page's own validated logic. Review step: every extracted field cites the exact document and page it came from, before a human approves submission. Inspiration What it does How I built it Challenges I ran into## Inspiration We wanted to test a real, unglamorous shape of task against the WebMCP standard: a government procedure. A trámite is a bounded set of well-defined actions with real validation and real consequences — exactly the kind of task where an agent guessing at buttons or screen text is not an acceptable failure mode. RUTIC is a synthetic GovTech app: a public telecom-provider registry for Colombia where every action a person can do with buttons, an AI agent can also do, through the same page-owned logic, never around it. What it does RUTIC lets a person create a dossier by uploading three documents, which the page extracts and validates locally — no PDF ever reaches the AI model. From there they review or edit nine typed fields, submit with an explicit human-approved code, modify a submitted dossier without re-uploading anything, cancel an edit and keep the last submitted version untouched, list and check their dossiers, and switch the interface between Spanish and English. Every one of those actions is reachable two ways: a button, or a sentence to the agent. "Modify my dossier" resolves to the one submitted dossier without asking for its code back; "the second one" or "el segundo" resolves against a list the agent just showed; "envíalo" is accepted as the explicit approval without repeating a code already on screen. The task takes the same number of real steps either way — talking removes the cost of finding the right control, and a person can switch between clicking and talking mid-task because both paths write to the same state. How we built it Every dossier action is a real, imperative document.modelContext.registerTool call, not a static list — the set of registered tools is recomputed from the page's own state machine on every change, so the agent can only ever see and call what's actually valid at that moment. Gemini (gemini-3.5-flash-lite) receives a fresh summary of the true page state on every turn and is instructed to reuse only values it has actually seen: it never receives PDF bytes and never invents a claim value, a dossier code, or an approval code. The page keeps the authority; the agent only routes intention to it. Challenges we ran into We built and load-tested a declarative variant — an annotated form the browser fills and submits directly — for the one task that looked like a natural fit, editing form fields, and reverted it. Our full-page re-render recreates the form's DOM node on every state change, and the browser's declarative discovery treated that as a brand-new tool appearing each time, causing a runaway feedback loop. We're documenting that attempt rather than hiding it, because it's a real, useful finding about the standard's current rough edges, not just a footnote. Accomplishments that we're proud of Nothing the agent can do is something the page can't already validate and execute on its own — the agent only ever decides which action, never how it runs. That guarantee holds across nine typed fields, a document manifest, and a state machine with an explicit human-approval gate, and it's backed by 45 tests covering the state machine, the WebMCP bridge, the Gemini boundary and its retries, extraction, and localization. What we learned The clearest lesson came from the failure: WebMCP's declarative discovery assumes a form's DOM identity is stable, and a framework that re-renders the DOM on every state change breaks that assumption outright. The imperative registerTool path, recomputed from the same state machine, doesn't have that problem — for a UI built around frequent re-render, the imperative API is the one that composes safely with real application state, not just a fallback. What's next The pattern holds past this one registry: any administrative procedure with well-defined actions, real validation, and real consequences can be built this way — clicked through as usual, or described in plain language, with every check the process requires staying exactly as strict either way. The submission step here is intentionally local and simulated, and always reports externalTransmission: false; the natural next step is wiring that same page-owned logic to an actual government backend without loosening any of the guarantees the demo enforces today. title: Serendipity
pitch: An AI-powered city planner that uses WebMCP to discover, combine, and book a personalized night out across independent local services.
about_excerpt: An AI-powered city planner that uses WebMCP to discover, combine, and book a personalized night out across independent local services. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I started Serendipity because planning a free evening in Tokyo kept turning into admin. I would find an interesting place, look for dinner nearby, check when both closed, open a map, and then discover that the route did not fit. A simple night out could leave me with ten tabs and no actual plan. The first version was a technical reservation-network demo. It worked, but it did not answer the question a normal user would ask: why would I use this? I kept the reliable parts and rebuilt the product around a simpler job. Give it the evening you have, and get back one plan whose times and prices you can check for yourself. What it does You choose Shibuya, Shinjuku, or Ikebukuro, then set the group size, time, per-person budget, walking limit, and the kind of night you want. Dinner can be included or left out. Serendipity builds one route with two or three stops. It shows when to visit, how long the walks are, what each stop should cost, and the estimated total for the group. If three stops do not fit, it says why it returned two. If nothing fits, it does not quietly loosen the request. It shows the closest option and waits for the user to approve the change. Each stop has a sources section with the publisher, checked date, published hours, official menu, and official link. This is planning from published information, not a live booking service. Serendipity does not claim a seat is available and does not send anything to a venue. Why WebMCP is a strong fit This kind of planning often starts as a conversation: “Plan a calm Ikebukuro evening for three, include dinner, and keep it under ¥4,000 each.” Then comes the follow-up: show me where the meal price came from, or change one stop. An assistant can try to operate the form like a person, but it has to interpret the layout and guess whether the page really changed. WebMCP gives it five actions instead: find a plan, show the evidence for a place, change one stop, save the plan, or delete it. Those actions use stable plan and place IDs, and the result appears on the same page the user is watching. I stopped at five tools. Finding a plan, checking evidence, and changing a stop are read-only. Saving and deleting are the only write actions, and they only affect this browser. Opening a restaurant or venue website is still a normal link the user chooses. How I built it The app is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript and deployed on Vercel. The planner is deterministic. It checks combinations of activities and meals against published opening hours, visit length, closing time, budget, and walking limits. Restaurant budgets use the highest price in the official menu range. Walking time is marked as a coordinate-based estimate. I reviewed 21 places across the three hubs: four activities and three meals in each area. Every place in a route needs support for its name, address, coordinates, hours, public access, and price. I wrote the short descriptions myself and used official pages instead of copying marketplace reviews or photos. Google enrichment exists behind a server flag, but it is off in the submitted version. The live app works from its reviewed data and official menu pages. The human controls and the five Site Tools call the same controller. I did not want an agent demo sitting beside a separate, less reliable product. If a request is stale, malformed, cancelled, or unsafe, both paths reject it in the same way. Challenges The hardest part was deciding what the app was allowed to say. It is easy to make a schedule look convincing. It is much harder to prove that a place is actually open at that time and that the displayed price came from a menu. I spent more time removing weak data than adding new places. Parks without published hours, prices inferred as zero, stale closure calendars, and unclear reuse rights all forced changes to the data model. The UI went through several bad versions. One was two dashboards side by side. Another had oversized type and decorative cards that made the route harder to follow. Feedback on those versions was blunt, but correct. I removed most of the explanation from the main path, gave the route the full page, and kept source details behind disclosures. The agent and the human also kept finding different edge cases. A late response could overwrite a newer search. Browser Back could make the URL disagree with the plan. A damaged saved record could break reopening. Fixing those bugs led to one shared state controller instead of two implementations. Accomplishments The live app covers three Tokyo hubs, with four reviewed activities and three official-menu meals in each one. Codex discovered all five Site Tools in the ChatGPT desktop browser and used them to build a real plan and open its meal evidence on the visible page. A strict request can return an honest no-result. The app only offers a relaxed search after the server has verified it and the user chooses it. What I learned A difficult technical demo is not automatically a useful product. The first version proved that several sites could coordinate, but people still asked, “What is this for?” Rebuilding it around one understandable job made the engineering choices much clearer. Good Site Tools are closer to product actions than UI controls. The agent does not need a tool for every button. It needs a few useful verbs, clear limits, and enough evidence for the person to check the result. WebMCP worked best when the agent and the user could look at the same updated plan, not when the agent disappeared into a background workflow. What’s next I would add more neighborhoods only after reviewing them to the same standard as the current three. The next practical improvements are transit-aware travel, shareable saved plans, and an optional live Google check controlled by the user. I would not add booking or payment until a venue provides real booking authority and there is a safe way to handle the transaction. title: Suede Agent Studio WebMCP Storefront
pitch: A browser-native marketplace where agents discover, inspect, and safely preview paid services before a person authorizes purchase.
about_excerpt: A browser-native marketplace where agents discover, inspect, and safely preview paid services before a person authorizes purchase. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Visual marketplaces are designed for people, but browser agents still have to infer meaning from buttons and page layout. A service marketplace becomes meaningfully better when the browser exposes a small, stable set of structured tools: the agent can search by intent, inspect exact terms, and preview safely while the person retains the payment boundary. What it does Suede Agent Studio exposes six curated services from its 31-listing public directory through four page-scoped WebMCP tools: find_services searches the published service shelf by job-to-be-done. get_service returns the current price, exact input contract, review policy, data-handling statement, and worked examples. preview_service records a free dry-run receipt without model inference or payment. buy_service uses only prepaid workspace credit after server-side origin, rate-limit, buyability, and exact-price checks. The fixed tool set stays constant as inventory grows, avoiding one tool per service and keeping the browser agent's context bounded. How people and agents work together The agent handles discovery and contract reading. The person keeps control over the meaningful boundary: whether to preview and whether to authorize a purchase. The challenge demo uses synthetic purchase-order and invoice data, stops after a free preview, and performs no purchase or model inference. How we built it The existing Next.js application was extended during the challenge window with a browser compatibility layer, four fixed tool descriptors, page-scoped registration, bounded result formatting, a server-owned purchase contract, mutation guards, and focused regression coverage. Tools are mounted only on /agents and /a/[slug] . Creator-authored catalog text is marked as untrusted. Purchase authority never moves into page JavaScript. The public history preserves the pre-WebMCP baseline ( f4943a1 ) and the challenge implementation ( e2c3b11 ), followed by hardening and evidence commits. The focused WebMCP suite contains 71 tests covering protocol compatibility, shelf parsing, descriptors, preview budgets, server guards, and mount scope. Challenges we ran into WebMCP's shipping namespace changed across Chrome versions, so the compatibility layer supports the current document-scoped API while retaining the origin-trial alias. Registration also handles both synchronous browser bridges and Promise-returning native APIs; a regression test confirms that an undefined return still registers all four tools. We also had to keep every descriptor and result inside strict field budgets, distinguish a durable preview from a read-only operation, and ensure no client-side tool could bypass server-side price and payment authority. Accomplishments we're proud of Four stable tools serve a growing marketplace without context bloat. The agent receives terms and examples before acting. Free preview is honest about what did and did not run. Purchase uses exact-price binding and prepaid credit only. The public demo uses synthetic data and cannot accidentally spend money. The implementation is public, MIT-licensed, and separated from the pre-challenge baseline in Git history. What we learned The strongest WebMCP experiences do not copy every button into a tool. They expose the smallest task-oriented contract that helps the agent reason while preserving human control where risk or irreversible action begins. What's next Expand the service shelf without expanding the tool namespace, add more contract-first preview patterns, and continue testing the same human-agent boundary across compatible browsers. title: Suede Agent Studio WebMCP Storefront
pitch: Agents discover services, inspect exact contracts, and run free previews in the browser while people control purchases.
about_excerpt: Agents discover services, inspect exact contracts, and run free previews in the browser while people control purchases. Like Comment Story Updates Why WebMCP fits A service marketplace asks people and agents to make the same decisions: find a service for a job, understand its inputs and price, and decide whether to proceed. An agent that only sees a visual page has to infer buttons, fields, and changing layouts. Suede Agent Studio exposes the storefront as four structured tools in the visitor's current browser page: find_services, get_service, preview_service, and buy_service. The tool set stays constant as the catalog grows. Agents search by intent, then inspect the selected service instead of loading a separate tool definition for every listing. A better experience for people and agents The agent handles discovery and contract reading. The person can review the service's exact price, input schema, review policy, data handling, and worked example before deciding whether to act. Creator-authored catalog text is marked as untrusted content, and returned results are bounded. The demo follows a concrete purchasing-operations task: find a service that compares a purchase order with an invoice, inspect PO Match Gate, and run a free preview using synthetic documents. The worked example illustrates a $15 discrepancy. The actual preview is explicitly a dry run: it records a run and returns a receipt without model inference, payment, or settlement. It is not presented as a fresh model-generated discrepancy analysis. How WebMCP was implemented The existing Next.js, React, and TypeScript application was extended with page-scoped WebMCP tools on /agents and /a/[slug]. Browser registration and same-origin tool execution live in StorefrontTools.tsx; typed tool contracts and result formatting live in src/lib/webmcp. Discovery and contract inspection are read-only. Preview is correctly labeled as a write because it records a durable run. The separate purchase route retains server-side authority, validates origin and request size, applies rate limits, checks service availability, and rechecks the exact accepted price before spending prepaid workspace credit. Purchase receipts preserve the run identifier and charged amount. The public demo does not execute buy_service. Challenges and lessons The central design challenge was making useful agent actions available without turning catalog text into instructions or treating a preview as a purchase. Explicit tool contracts, bounded results, untrusted-content markers, and server-side price checks make those boundaries inspectable. A dry run still changes state when it records a receipt, so preview is labeled as a write even when no funds move. Work completed during the challenge Suede Agent Studio predates the challenge. This entry focuses on its WebMCP storefront extension added after August 25, 2026. The public MIT-licensed repository preserves the pre-WebMCP baseline and separate feature and hardening commits, with an implementation map and reproducible validation instructions in CHALLENGE_EVIDENCE.md. The September 1 verification passed type checking, lint, the production build, and 70 focused WebMCP tests. Try it Open https://agents.suedeai.ai/agents in ChatGPT's in-app browser or a compatible Chrome browser with WebMCP enabled. Ask the agent to find a service for comparing a purchase order with an invoice, inspect po-match-gate-mkgu0, and run its free dry-run preview using synthetic documents. Do not buy anything. The preview receipt should show status done, totalCostUsdc 0, settled false, and mode dry-run. README.md, DEMO_SCRIPT.md, and CHALLENGE_EVIDENCE.md in the public repository provide the full walkthrough and local setup. The remade 2:29 live-interface demo is https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZR1At7lX6-E .
