title: An AI Agent and webMCP Walked Into a Museum...
pitch: Museum collections shouldn’t stay behind glass. Search major art museum collections, build a private gallery, and let an AI agent create curated art exhibitions for you. For the art historian inside.
about_excerpt: Museum collections shouldn’t stay behind glass. Search major art museum collections, build a private gallery, and let an AI agent create curated art exhibitions for you. For the art historian inside. Like Comment Story Updates Search across 3 museums for any art or artist Add art to your gallery Your Gallery Your AI Agent curates your gallery The Agent lets you review and completes the gallery build A completed exposition Inspiration Museum collections shouldn’t stay trapped behind four walls. I wanted to liberate art from institutional silos by aggregating masterpieces across major institutions - The Met, the Art Institute of Chicago, and the Cleveland Museum of Art - into a unified workspace. By pairing this open collection access with WebMCP, I set out to explore how browser-native AI agents can act as collaborative co-curators, helping everyday art lovers organize visual narratives. Let your agent surprise you with the patterns it finds! WebMCP lets your app be manageable by the AI so that it can rearrange your gallery, annotate it, and create an educational narrative about your selections. What it does The Museum Media Grouper and Exposition Builder is an Astro and Cloudinary-powered studio for searching, saving, and curating cross-museum artwork. Universal Search & Ingestion: Allows users to perform live queries across three major museum APIs simultaneously, saving selected pieces into a personal Cloudinary gallery organized by artist. The system is designed to quickly onboard new APIs as we discover and vet them. Agentic Exposition Builder: Integrates 8 custom WebMCP tools through document.modelContext so a browser-based AI agent can search saved assets, initialize draft exhibitions, sequence artwork, and write wall-card narrative captions using what it knows about the art and the connections it discovers while curating it. Human-in-the-Loop Curation: Keeps the human curator in complete control. An agent can assemble and propose a story layout, but setting a project as ready_for_review and issuing the final publication requires explicit human verification. How we built it Framework & Storage: Built using Astro for fast server-side asset handling and dynamic rendering. Ingested museum objects are stored and transformed in Cloudinary under a structured museums/* namespace, with story drafts managed locally via a modular StoryRepository pattern (localStorage). WebMCP Architecture: Exposed 8 structured tools via document.modelContext (search_saved_assets, create_story_draft, add_story_items, arrange_story_items, edit_item_text, preview_story, delete_story_draft, and request_story_review). Dual-Path Execution: Designed UI controllers (storyBuilderController.ts) as thin DOM wrappers over shared, dependency-injected handlers in toolHandlers.ts. A user clicking a button and an AI calling a tool run the exact same function, preventing behavior drift. Lots of help from Claude and Lovable for design inspiration. Challenges we ran into Every museum API, when you can find them (not every museum has an open one - sadly Boston's MFA does not!), has a slightly different shape. This project began initially as a museum explorer, to see how easily I could ingest art into Cloudinary and use tagging as a way to build a database of metadata attached to the art. I also found that discovering a demoable use case for webMCP was more challenging than originally anticipated. I originally wanted to attach a webMCP routine to a curriculum I'm developing, but it helped only to make quizzes auto-completable, which is an antipattern. So I pivoted this project, which was inspired by work I did at Microsoft with the Cooper Hewitt Museum and, more recently, as a contractor with Microsoft Philanthropies working to stand up the new Roosevelt Presidential Library. Accomplishments that I'm proud of It was a delight to watch the AI Agent clicking around, arranging items, and filling in the field to create the exposition. It was able to detect patterns and I found myself learning about art as I worked with the tool. I didn't know Sonia Delaunay was from Ukraine, for example. It might turn out to be a useful tool for fledgling art historians. What I learned WebMCP Simplicity: Exposing client-side browser tools directly through document.modelContext eliminates fragile DOM scraping, allowing agents to interact with web apps cleanly and deterministically. But we'll have to see where the spec lands and how browsers adopt it. What's next Cloudinary Search API Migration: Upgrade verification logic from in-memory collection filtering to native Cloudinary Search expressions to scale beyond the initial asset cap. Server-Backed Persistence: Swap the local StoryRepository interface for a multi-user database backend, allowing real-time collaborative curation across multiple devices. Individual auth and login would allow users to save their own galleries and share them via microsites. Currently the cool archives don't persist. title: Agent Has to Ask
pitch: Our agent can pick the cart. You still own the charge. The store sees what you allowed, checks the limit and only opens checkout after that check passes.
about_excerpt: Our agent can pick the cart. You still own the charge. The store sees what you allowed, checks the limit and only opens checkout after that check passes. Like Comment Story Updates GIF knowyouragent webmcp demo Inspiration Checkout with an agent usually collapses into one click: the agent talks to the page, asks to buy, and a session appears. The person whose card is about to move never sees a clean “this is what it asked for.” The merchant never has a clean “this is why we said yes.” We split that into three questions a human can actually answer: What did the agent ask to buy? What will this store allow? Does the server still say yes? Until those are separate, an agent shopping for you is a blank check. What we built Agent has to ask is a public KnowYourAgent demo for agent-assisted checkout. The agent can request a purchase. It cannot approve one. The page shows a short-lived signed permission: who the agent is, which cart, which wallet, what it may buy, when it expires, and the spend cap. A browser agent gets two tools: kya_validate_trace — check that permission in the browser kya_verify_agent — send the cart to the merchant for a read-only preflight The server checks the signature, audience, agent, scope, expiry, currency, cart, wallet, and amount. Then it says one of three things a person can read: Accept Review Decline Checkout runs the same check again on the server before it creates a simulated session. No card is captured. No production order is written. After the decision you can inspect the record: trace ID, preflight ID, cart fingerprint, and why it landed where it did. How we built it Next.js, TypeScript, React, signed JWT traces, Web Crypto, and WebMCP tool registration. The page registers tools on the browser’s model context. The merchant adapter stays on the server and keeps the last word. Challenges The hard part was not wiring tools. It was refusing to let the browser become the thing that authorizes payment. A browser tool can help an agent ask . It must not be the authority that charges . We also kept the flow usable when WebMCP is missing: a person can still read the permission and run the same server preflight by hand. What we learned Agent checkout needs a human-shaped boundary. The agent files a request. The merchant enforces policy. The server decides. The record has to explain what happened and why — to the shopper, not just to the protocol. title: MOHAE · Explore Korea
pitch: Explore unknown, get random but curated events. Talk and share context with agent. Plan own agents with all participants in travel.
about_excerpt: Explore unknown, get random but curated events. Talk and share context with agent. Plan own agents with all participants in travel. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Three travelers choose independently across Explore, the shared room, and the map. Four WebMCP tools registered on the live MOHAE page in Chrome’s Tool Inspector. The Agent searches MOHAE’s structured Korea place catalog through WebMCP. Inspiration Inspired by exploration vs exploitation in RL. Nowadays people are mostly locked in their everyday routine (exploitation). I wanted people to explore lot more to find possibilities beyond and what they really want to do. I'm the first user of this project mohae. This web gives me events, places, opportunities that I can try. With agent I can put in my context like where I live, current place, what I want right now like cafe or food or events. I can see and get inspiration from given cards and see them in map. Also you can get all random events for exploration. This can also help people who came to korea, and when evolved it will help me traveling other country. You can also put own agent's result in the web and see your result in our template and map. Finally you can share link and plan travel within all the participants in the travel. What it does MOHAE is a mobile-first Korea place discovery product. A traveler can swipe to save or pass places, inspect candidates on a Naver map, and ask a WebMCP Agent to search and render visible candidate scenes. For a shared trip, a host creates an expiring invite link. Travelers join from their own devices, make independent save/pass and map choices, tell their own Agent natural-language needs, and mark their selection complete. The host Agent then reads the accumulated evidence and proposes an approximate ordered plan. Demo flow Open MOHAE and explore Korea place cards by saving or passing. Inspect candidates on the map and save useful places. Create a shared trip and send the expiring invite link. Join from another device, make independent choices, and add a raw trip note through an Agent, such as ‘must-visit food’ or ‘less walking.’ Mark that traveler’s selection complete. Ask the host Agent to read the room context and present an ordered candidate scene. Switch to route mode to see the Agent-supplied order numbered with a guide line. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets an Agent read and change the currently visible shared product state while humans continue choosing in the UI. The browser page is not just a chat attachment: it exposes explicit tools for catalog search, scene rendering, preserving traveler language, and reading room evidence. Agent actions remain visible and inspectable in the same interface the group is using. MOHAE deploys four WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : search_mohae_places : read-only catalog search. present_exploration : renders ordered deck/map scenes and can publish them to the shared room. add_group_trip_note : preserves a joined traveler’s raw natural-language note. get_group_trip_context : reads travelers’ save/pass/map choices, notes, readiness, anchors, and candidates. Provenance and scope Agent-researched external candidates stay provenance-tagged and separate from catalog admission. Route mode displays the Agent-supplied order and a guide line; it does not claim route optimization or travel-time calculation. MOHAE does not provide booking, live queue data, or full realtime presence. How we built it The product uses vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Supabase Postgres stores shared-trip data behind protected RPCs and row-level security, with append-only room events. The app is deployed on Vercel and uses the Naver Maps JavaScript SDK. Challenges and lessons The central design challenge was making Agent side effects visible, scoped, and auditable while several people continue using ordinary UI controls. We learned that coordination works better when the product preserves behavioral evidence and each traveler’s original words instead of compressing everyone into a single averaged profile. title: OpenQuest
pitch: OpenQuest turns unused AI agent capacity into useful public work through an open WebMCP network.
about_excerpt: OpenQuest turns unused AI agent capacity into useful public work through an open WebMCP network. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration OpenQuest started from a pretty simple idea. A lot of us already pay for capable AI agents and we dont always use all of that capacity. Tokens reset, credits expire, whatever. At the same time there is basically infinite useful public work that could use more intelligence. Open source, research, education, climate, accessibility, science etc. So the question was: what if people could point some of that unused agent capacity at useful open problems? Not donate API keys or send credits somewhere. Just bring the agent you already use. Thats OpenQuest What it does OpenQuest is an open public network where independent AI agents can work together. The structure is pretty simple: Quest → Challenge → Contribution → Review → Result A Quest is a big goal. It gets split into smaller Challenges that are actually manageable for an agent. An agent can come in, see what work exists, pick something useful, do the work and submit a Contribution. Then another independent agent can review it. If the work is good it becomes the Result. If not the Challenge stays open and someone else can improve it. Everything is public so the work doesnt just disappear inside another chat window. Why WebMCP This is probably the most important part. We didnt want to build another platform with our own agent inside it. The idea is that you bring your own agent . WebMCP gives that agent a structured way to understand OpenQuest and actually participate in it, instead of scraping the page or clicking around blindly. OpenQuest currently exposes five tools: observe the network find useful work submit work review work propose new work Humans use the UI. Agents use WebMCP. Both are working against the same shared public state. That felt like a pretty natural use case for WebMCP. How I built it The frontend is React + TypeScript and the backend runs on Cloudflare Workers. Shared state is stored in D1 and we use Durable Objects + WebSockets so the UI updates when agents change something. We also added a simple rule where an agent session cant review its own Contribution. Another session has to do it. It sounds small but this is quite important because otherwise "review" doesnt really mean anything Challenges and what we learned The hardest part was mostly figuring out how little we could build. It would have been very easy to turn this into some huge agent orchestration system with 40 tools and a lot of abstractions. I tried to do the opposite. What is the minimum information an agent needs? What are the minimum actions it needs? What should the server control? How do you keep it understandable for humans and predictable for agents at the same time? One thing I learned from this is that the website itself starts becoming a different kind of thing with WebMCP. Its still a UI for humans, but its also an interface that can explain its capabilities directly to an agent. You dont necessarily need to put an AI assistant inside every product. Sometimes the better model is to make the product legible and usable by the agents people already have. Whats next The bigger idea is that eventually a research lab, open source project, university, nonprofit or whoever could publish useful work as Quests. Then people around the world could point their own agents at parts of that work. One agent contributes, another reviews, another builds on the result and so on. The network doesnt need to own the intelligence. title: Paqly
pitch: Plan, preview, and pack with AI. Just tell ChatGPT what you're bringing, and through WebMCP it automatically generates a physically optimized 3D packing plan broken down by layers and order to pack.
about_excerpt: Plan, preview, and pack with AI. Just tell ChatGPT what you're bringing, and through WebMCP it automatically generates a physically optimized 3D packing plan broken down by layers and order to pack. Like Comment Story Updates Labled Layers Packed, labeled Empty Closed Duffel bag Backpack Inspiration I always procrastinate packing until the very last minute, then struggle to find what belongs where even if I already have a packing list in mind. After I guess where everything should go and then rearrange my suitcase a dozen times, I finally come to find that it doesn't fit. With AI becoming good at understanding what we need through context and chatlogs, I wanted to create a tool for ChatGPT to express a simple request into something physical and visual that we could actually use. What it does Paqly turns any packing list into a 3D packing plan that you can breakdown into clearly labeled layers. Instead of organizing and planning what to put and where, you can simply tell ChatGPT what you want to bring or even just ask ChatGPT to create a list for you. ChatGPT would then communicate with Paqly directly through WebMCP and create a 3D visual based on the specified suitcase and items. With Paqly, you are able to see where each item should go, which layer it belongs in, the order in which each item should be packed, how much of the suitcase is filled and whether the packing list actually fits. How I built it The core of Paqly is a WebMCP integration that exposes packing functionality directly to AI agents. Rather than requiring an agent to navigate the website like a human and click through forms, Paqly exposes structured tools that allow ChatGPT to send packing information directly to the application. From there, the packing system takes the item dimensions and suitcase constraints, determines an arrangement, groups the result into packing layers, validates the placement, and passes that result into the interactive 3D visualisation. A lot of the work also went into making the output understandable. A mathematically valid arrangement is not very useful if a person cannot tell what they are looking at, so the 3D view includes item labels, separated layers, a re-playable packing order and an interactive suitcase view. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the packing plan physically believable rather than just visually impressive. Early versions could technically place objects inside the scene while still producing obviously bad results: items could overlap, float, extend outside the suitcase or leave large amounts of wasted space. This meant I had to treat validation separately from visual rendering and continuously check that the generated arrangement actually made sense. Another challenge was the WebMCP integration itself. I wanted the AI to interact with Paqly through structured WebMCP tools rather than simply using browser automation to click around the interface. Finally, 3D packing is much harder than displaying a normal list. Different objects have different dimensions, orientations and levels of compressibility, while the final result still needs to be simple enough for someone to reproduce with a real suitcase. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that Paqly goes beyond giving packing advice. You can describe what you are trying to pack like thinking aloud and get back an actual spatial plan showing where everything should go, and the combination of AI, WebMCP and interactive 3D makes the result easier to obtain and follow. I'm also proud of how much the physical packing and visualisation improved throughout development. What started as basic object placement became a layered system with packing order, fit validation and a much clearer 3D representation of the suitcase. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that giving AI tools is much more interesting than simply putting an AI chatbot inside a website. WebMCP lets the AI interact with the actual functionality of Paqly. The AI handles the vibes, while Paqly handles the specialised packing logic and visualisation. I also learned how quickly a 3D system can look correct while being physically wrong. Building this forced me to think much more carefully about constraints, validation and the difference between generating something that looks good and generating something that actually works. What's next for Paqly The next step is making Paqly understand more about the real world. I want it to support a much larger library of real items, better modelling of soft and compressible objects, different suitcase types and more advanced physical optimisation to better simulate a real packing environment. I want it to be able to mathematically find not just the optimal placement for each item, but the optimal fold, the optimal angle, and other features that make a paq perfect. title: Precidra Viewer
pitch: Let AI agents reason about precise drawing geometry, not screenshots.
about_excerpt: Let AI agents reason about precise drawing geometry, not screenshots. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Technical drawings contain precise geometrical information, but AI agents usually encounter them as screenshots or opaque user interfaces. From pixels alone, an agent cannot reliably determine exact distances, intersections, containment, adjacency, or object geometry. Building a fully semantic model from the ground up for every drawing is expensive and often unnecessary. Precidra Viewer explores a different approach: expose the drawing's existing geometry directly through WebMCP and let an agent derive useful spatial understanding from it. What it does Precidra Viewer is an open-source, read-only companion for .prec technical drawings created with Precidra . Humans can view a drawing, pan and zoom, inspect objects, and toggle layers. At the same time, an AI agent can query the same document through seven focused WebMCP tools. The agent can: summarize the document and its layers; list and inspect individual objects, using nearby annotations and layer names as semantic hints; retrieve exact contour and vertex geometry; measure minimum distances; test intersections; discover containment, adjacency, overlap, proximity, and disjoint relationships; evaluate hypothetical geometry without modifying the drawing. This enables questions such as: Which rooms share a real wall edge rather than only a corner? How far is an object from the nearest obstacle? What objects are contained inside this area? Would a proposed shape intersect existing geometry? Why WebMCP WebMCP lets Precidra expose domain-level capabilities instead of asking an agent to interpret pixels or automate toolbar controls. The tools return deterministic geometric results from the same model rendered for humans. This creates a clear division of work: a human selects and visually verifies the drawing, while the agent searches, measures, compares, and explains its spatial structure. The interface is intentionally read-only, so agents can investigate freely without accidentally changing the document. What changed for the challenge Precidra existed as a drawing application before the challenge. During the submission period, I created the standalone open-source viewer and added the WebMCP interface for querying document structure, exact geometry, measurements, intersections, and spatial relationships. How it was built The viewer is implemented in dependency-free HTML5 and JavaScript and runs as a static site on GitHub Pages. It reuses a small set of Precidra's geometry, model, parsing, and rendering modules inside a new standalone viewer shell. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The tool layer provides document orientation, compact object summaries, detailed geometry on demand, exact distance and intersection operations, and spatial predicates including contains , within , touches , overlapping , close , and disjoint . Tool descriptions guide the agent to begin with compact document metadata, inspect only the necessary objects, account for document-specific coordinate units, and distinguish meaningful shared edges from incidental point contact. Challenges The main challenge was turning raw geometry into useful agent semantics without requiring drawings to contain a complete semantic model. Spatial relationships also need to remain reliable across open and closed shapes, modeling tolerances, different coordinate scales, and drawings in which a shared corner has a very different meaning from a shared wall. Another challenge was designing responses that provide enough precision for reasoning without overwhelming the agent with every coordinate in the document. The tools therefore use progressive disclosure: summaries first, exact geometry only when requested. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes the underlying domain model rather than reproducing visible UI actions. A relatively small set of carefully designed geometric tools allows an agent to answer questions that would be unreliable or impossible through screenshot interpretation alone. Open source and full editor The submitted project is the open-source Precidra Viewer, licensed under AGPL-3.0. It includes all code, assets, instructions, and a sample drawing required to run and test the submission. The full Precidra editor, including DXF and SVG import, can be used freely without an account. It remains separate from this open-source submission. title: Corealm
pitch: Corealm is a browser based medieval RPG built for an AI agent to sit beside you using WebMCP, whether that means guiding you with suggestions and overlays or playing the game itself.
about_excerpt: Corealm is a browser based medieval RPG built for an AI agent to sit beside you using WebMCP, whether that means guiding you with suggestions and overlays or playing the game itself. Like Comment Story Updates Corealm Inspiration This game is inspired by Runescape, Runelite, and Knight Online. There both games fight against bots while offering pay to win mechanics. Corealm takes a different stance and builds "botting" as part of the game. You can also choose to only use the agent as a guide in a similar way Runelite works, which uses overlays. What it does Its a browser based RPG where your ai agent can play alongside you. The agent can help you plan what's next, show you the steps for a quest, or grind away at tasks you might just not have the time for. How we built it Vite + TypeScript + Three.js, with Rapier for physics and Recast for navmeshes. The agent API is a thin WebMCP tool layer using the same functions the UI calls. The docs are generated from the same data the game runs on and is exposed two ways: the Astro site for humans, and corealm_search_docs that agents query directly. Challenges we ran into Honestly the WebMCP was the easy part, making a game in less than a week was the hard part. title: EasyTax - Your convenient tax WebMCP
pitch: Turn complex tax forms into a conversation. WebMCP lets ChatGPT help populate a visible draft, while users stay in control of review and submission.
about_excerpt: Turn complex tax forms into a conversation. WebMCP lets ChatGPT help populate a visible draft, while users stay in control of review and submission. Like Comment Story Updates The Problem Filing an annual individual tax return (1770 S) under Indonesia's centralized Coretax system creates a learning curve for salaried workers. Translating personal life events into rigid government tax classifications creates a high burden and confusion across generations. Knowing your salary or family situation is different from knowing which tax field or classification it belongs in. While the system offers spreadsheet bulk uploads to bypass manual entry, they frequently fail due to minor error, forcing users back to rework manual entry or exposing them to server timeouts during peak traffic. Independent sentiment analysis of over 53,000 digital conversations during the early rollout Coretax system revealed that 39% of user sentiment was negative, driven by procedural confusion and system navigation (Source: Journal UII / 2025 ). Despite these points, the submission is massive. By late April 2026, over 13 million annual tax returns were filed following the activation of nearly 12.9 million individual accounts (Source: Tempo.co ). The Solution: Human-Agent Collaboration via WebMCP This project demonstrates how WebMCP can turn a complex tax administration portal into a collaborative interface. Rather than hiding the form's complexity or forcing users to navigate hidden form logic, the browser exposes section-level tools directly to the assistant, keeping the detailed form visible to ensure user review control capability. The Workflow Conversational Extraction: The assistant conducts a plain-language interview to extract necessary tax facts such as salary, deductions, and family status without requiring users to memorize form codes or tax classifications. They can use their own ways to describe their condition and an AI assistant will translate it. For example, when a user says, “My employer was PT Nusantara Digital, gross salary 180 million for the year, 6 million in pay deductions,” WebMCP translates it into: “Records the employment slip, derives net income, recomputes the tax.” Deterministic State Updates: As facts are confirmed, the assistant invokes section-level WebMCP tools (such as updating taxpayer profiles, recording employment, or adding cash and assets). The website itself handles all validation, calculation, and conditional branching, deriving fields like PTKP (e.g., K/1) and recomputing the tax balance automatically. Manual Submission: Final review, resolution of data conflicts, declaration, and submission remain strictly manual. No tool can execute a final filing, and the assistant explicitly states this if asked. title: Commonplace
pitch: A WebMCP workspace where agents stay current and people retain authority.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workspace where agents stay current and people retain authority. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Important shared decisions get stale as evidence changes. Commonplace turns that drift into a visible collaboration loop: people can see the decision, its evidence, the agent's reading, and the exact moment a person must decide. What it does Commonplace is a shared human-agent workspace built around a Freshness Protocol. A human records new evidence; the affected decision becomes paused; the agent re-grounds on the decision context and evidence objects; it proposes a new, cited decision; and a human alone confirms what becomes canonical. The shipped Project Aurora workspace gives judges a complete, fast demo path: Record the “Monday sensor reconciliation” update. Watch decision P-014 pause because its support is no longer fresh. Let the agent read structured decision/evidence context and create P-015. Confirm the human authority gate to make the revised date canonical. Why WebMCP A browser agent should not have to infer whether a decision is stale, which evidence supports it, or whether it may finalize a decision from visual UI. Commonplace exposes six browser-native WebMCP tools for those exact capabilities: get_decision_context get_evidence_changes get_evidence_objects get_decision_history propose_decision_update request_human_confirmation The agent receives structured, bounded context and must use a separate human-confirmation tool before any decision becomes canonical. This is not a generic chat layer: the agent has an explicit, inspectable role in the workspace’s state machine. Better together Humans contribute judgment and retain final authority. Agents handle the repetitive but high-risk reasoning work of grounding a proposal in current evidence, citing what changed, and keeping the activity trail legible. The result is a workspace where collaboration remains understandable after the moment has passed. Implementation Commonplace is a React + TypeScript + Vite web app deployed to Cloudflare Pages. It registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool when the browser exposes WebMCP, validates every input, derives freshness and citations from workspace state, and refreshes the visible workspace after a tool action. It also provides a clear fallback mode in unsupported browsers. title: Symbiosis
pitch: Symbiosis is a shared control plane where AI agents and humans work together. Agents do the work while humans monitor, make judgments and approve key decisions - all in one visible workflow.
about_excerpt: Symbiosis is a shared control plane where AI agents and humans work together. Agents do the work while humans monitor, make judgments and approve key decisions - all in one visible workflow. Like Comment Story Updates Human direction, agent execution Inspiration AI agents are becoming dramatically more capable. At the same time, the services we use every day are becoming increasingly agent-friendly through technologies like MCP. That creates a new problem: as agents become capable of doing more work on our behalf, we need better ways to give them work, set priorities and boundaries, step in when human judgment is needed, and review what they have done. Chat is great for giving an agent one task. It is less suited to overseeing an ongoing workload. Then came WebMCP. WebMCP gives us the tooling we need to make this relationship work particularly well. What it does Symbiosis is built around the symbiotic relationship between a human and their AI agent companion. The human plans the work, prioritizes tasks, defines constraints, reviews results, and makes the decisions that require human judgment. The agent works through that queue autonomously using the tools and capabilities it already has. It reports progress, records results, and pauses for a decision when necessary before continuing. In short: The agent executes. The human oversees, prioritizes, and decides. Symbiosis makes that relationship visible in one shared workspace, with tasks moving between Backlog, Working, Needs Decision, and Done as the human and agent collaborate. How we built it Symbiosis itself was built collaboratively with AI, which felt particularly appropriate for the project. I used ChatGPT to explore and challenge the original product idea, gstack to turn that concept into a detailed product and engineering design, and Codex to help implement and test the application. A major design goal was keeping the architecture deliberately small. Symbiosis is the coordination layer - it does not try to duplicate the reasoning, web access, coding tools, email integrations, or other capabilities the agent already has. Challenges we ran into Our first iteration was built around a single workboard. It worked, but it quickly became clear that the model was too limited. Jobs could not be reused easily, workflows were difficult to compose, and the overall experience lacked the flexibility we wanted. Through further iteration, we developed a three-level system of flows → workboards → jobs. Flows orchestrate workboards, and workboards execute jobs. That hierarchy gave us a much more elegant and reusable way to model agent workflows. Instead of rebuilding a process from scratch every time, users can define small reusable jobs, group them into workboards, and then combine those workboards into larger flows. The challenge was finding a structure that stayed simple enough to understand while still being powerful enough to support loops, delays, schedules, human decision points, and more complex workflows. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are particularly proud of the flows → workboards → jobs system. Its reusability is one of the most powerful parts of Symbiosis. Jobs can be defined once and reused across different workboards, while workboards can become reusable building blocks inside larger flows. This turns agent interaction from a sequence of one-off prompts into something that can be structured, repeated, refined, and reused over time. We are also proud that WebMCP feels fundamental to the product rather than being added simply for the hackathon. Symbiosis relies on WebMCP as the coordination layer between the human-owned workflow and the user's existing AI agent. What we learned The biggest thing we learned was where WebMCP is genuinely useful. WebMCP works extremely well as a bridge between a conversational AI agent and a website. It allows the agent to understand structured application state, take actions, update progress, request decisions, and continue working while the human interacts naturally through chat. We also learned what it is less suited to. Trying to make the entire agent experience happen inside the webpage itself weakens one of WebMCP's biggest advantages: the agent already has its own context, identity, tools, and conversational interface. The strongest pattern we found was to let the website act as the structured control surface while allowing the agent to remain where it already lives. That separation became one of the core design principles behind Symbiosis. What's next for Coop Queue The immediate focus would be UI and UX refinement, clearer and richer tool outputs, and more advanced flow-control capabilities. One particularly exciting area is intelligent conditional loops, where a flow can evaluate the result of a completed job and decide what should happen next based on that data. We would also like to add better reporting, notifications, execution history, and visibility into long-running workflows. Beyond that, the most important next step is user testing. We want to see how people actually use persistent agent workflows in practice, where they want more control, and where they are comfortable giving their agents more autonomy. Like Comment Story Updates Overview Debugging electronic circuits is often a slow and fragmented process, especially when the problem is not immediately obvious or the person working on it does not have deep experience with the specific hardware. AI can assist with the diagnosis, but the usual workflow of sending screenshots, measurements, and explanations back and forth through chat quickly becomes confusing and loses context. empeirik was built to bring that process into one shared workspace. The circuit, measurements, hypotheses, diagnostic steps, and proposed fixes all remain visible in the same environment while the AI works directly with the current state of the problem. It can inspect the circuit, decide which measurements are useful, narrow down likely causes, propose repairs or directly implement them, and verify them in simulation instead of repeatedly reconstructing the situation from a conversation. The project is built on top of CircuitJS1 for circuit rendering and simulation, with an additional diagnostic layer for measurements, hypotheses, repair testing, a shared activity timeline, and WebMCP tools that let the AI interact directly with the workspace. One of the main challenges was turning a traditional circuit simulator into a structured environment that both the user and the AI can operate at the same time while keeping every diagnostic step synchronized and visible. Learning and building electronics made it quickly clear how much context is lost when AI assistance is limited to a separate chat window. Giving the agent direct access to the same tools, state, and visual environment as the user makes the debugging process much more continuous and practical. title: ExceptionOSMCP
pitch: The agent-operable command center for resolving business exceptions safely.
about_excerpt: The agent-operable command center for resolving business exceptions safely. Like Comment Story Updates ExceptionOS Inspiration Operational teams spend hours resolving supplier delays and other business exceptions by moving between dashboards, spreadsheets, policies, and approval systems. AI agents can help, but traditional websites only expose interfaces designed for humans. Agents must interpret visual elements, guess which buttons to press, and operate without clear authority boundaries. We built ExceptionOS to explore a different model: operational software that exposes structured capabilities directly to agents while keeping humans in control of material decisions. What it does ExceptionOS is an agent-operable operations command center centered on a realistic supplier disruption. Pacific Components has reported that a battery-module purchase order will arrive nine days late. The disruption threatens a production order, a customer delivery, and $84,000 in revenue. Through WebMCP, an agent can: Retrieve the structured exception. Trace affected production and customer orders. Read its spending and approval policy. Search for qualified alternative suppliers. Compare recovery strategies. Simulate a resolution without changing business records. Request human approval when the plan exceeds its authority. Execute the approved supplier change. Verify that the customer commitment is protected. Produce an auditable evidence ledger. The recommended recovery plan changes the supplier to Northstar Cells for an additional $3,400, protecting the delivery date and $84,000 in revenue. Because the agent’s autonomous spending limit is $2,000, ExceptionOS blocks execution until a human explicitly approves the plan. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP ExceptionOS is not a conventional dashboard with an AI chatbot added to it. WebMCP is the application’s structured agent interface. Without WebMCP, an agent would need to interpret cards, tables, buttons, and changing application state visually. With WebMCP, it receives purpose-built tools with typed inputs, structured results, safety annotations, and clearly defined authority boundaries. The experience demonstrates a complete operational workflow: Observe → Investigate → Compare → Simulate → Ask → Act → Verify WebMCP makes the workflow faster and more reliable while letting the application control what the agent can read, simulate, and change. How it improves the user experience Humans no longer have to manually collect information from multiple screens, calculate the consequences of each option, or reconstruct what an agent did. The agent handles structured investigation and comparison. The human concentrates on the decision that requires judgment and authority. ExceptionOS also keeps the user informed through a live agent-activity panel. Every tool invocation visibly updates the interface, making the agent’s work understandable rather than invisible. After execution, the evidence ledger records the complete human-agent decision trail for accountability and review. What humans and agents can do together Before WebMCP, operational applications were largely human-operated, while agents had to approximate human interaction through screenshots and browser automation. ExceptionOS enables a safer partnership: The agent investigates structured operational data. The agent compares and simulates recovery plans. The application enforces organizational policy. The human approves consequential actions. The agent executes only within that approval. The system independently verifies the outcome. Both parties receive an auditable evidence trail. This combines machine speed with human authority. How we implemented WebMCP The browser application registers ten tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(): get_exception get_impacted_orders get_policy search_alternative_suppliers compare_recovery_options simulate_resolution request_approval execute_resolution verify_resolution get_evidence_ledger These tools invoke the same stateful application logic used by the visible interface. Agent activity therefore changes the application in real time. ExceptionOS also exposes the same capabilities through a Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint at /mcp. It supports initialization, tool discovery, tool calls, structured results, and safety annotations. Read and simulation operations are marked read-only. execute_resolution is marked destructive and requires explicit human confirmation plus an approver name. Calls without approval are rejected. How we built it Suggested “Built With” tags: WebMCP Model Context Protocol TypeScript React Next.js JSON-RPC Streamable HTTP ChatGPT GitHub Challenges we ran into The central challenge was designing tools that represented operational capabilities rather than simply exposing UI controls. We separated the workflow into read, plan, act, and verify capabilities. We also needed to ensure the agent could investigate and simulate freely without gaining unrestricted execution authority. The approval boundary became a core part of the architecture: requesting approval does not grant approval, and execution is rejected unless explicit human authorization is supplied. Another challenge was making agent activity visible enough for users to understand. We addressed this with synchronized interface state, a live tool-call feed, execution status, and an evidence ledger. Accomplishments that we're proud of Implemented ten meaningful WebMCP tools. Created a complete, stateful agent workflow rather than isolated tool demonstrations. Added a genuine human approval boundary. Blocked unapproved destructive operations. Made every agent action visible in the user interface. Added post-execution verification and an auditable evidence ledger. Exposed the capabilities through both browser WebMCP and remote MCP. Produced a polished, deterministic scenario that judges can understand quickly. What we learned Agent-native websites require more than tool discovery. They require carefully designed authority, observability, verification, and evidence. We also learned that the best division of responsibility is not to make agents omnipotent. Agents are strongest at structured investigation and comparison, while humans should retain control over consequential decisions. WebMCP provides the bridge between those roles. What's next for ExceptionOSMCP ExceptionOS could expand to additional operational exceptions, including inventory shortages, logistics disruptions, quality incidents, invoice discrepancies, and customer-delivery risks. Future versions could connect to real ERP, procurement, logistics, and policy systems. The same authority model could support role-based approval limits, multi-stage approvals, organization-specific policies, and cryptographically signed evidence records. The broader vision is an agent-operable layer for enterprise software in which every action is structured, policy-aware, observable, and verifiable. title: MetaEdit
pitch: Edit live websites with your team and a browser agent. Annotate elements, review before/after, approve, and open a GitHub pull request, all inside the website. Cool, huh?! 😎
about_excerpt: Edit live websites with your team and a browser agent. Annotate elements, review before/after, approve, and open a GitHub pull request, all inside the website. Cool, huh?! 😎 Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I was heavily inspired by React Grab by Aiden Bai for this project, but I wanted to make it such that the live prod website could be malleable by anyone on the team who has suggestions and who probably don't know how to use GitHub or Figma or an IDE to make edits. What it does MetaEdit turns a live website into a shared review space. A visitor opens the normal site. A collaborator adds metaedit. to the hostname, enters the shared demo token, and can click an element or draw a freeform region over several elements. A WebMCP-capable browser agent can read those annotations, inspect the selected UI, and propose a preview-only revision. Collaborators see the request, the proposed result, reactions, approvals, and history together. The eye control switches between the current page and the proposed result. Upon approval of those changes, they can publish a pull request (PR). Under the hood, MetaEdit creates a GitHub branch, commits the revision evidence, and opens a PR. The live site is not changed directly. How I built it This is a React/Vinext app served by a Cloudflare Worker. Cloudflare D1 stores annotations, revisions, approvals, and activity. A Durable Object keeps presence and page-space cursor positions live over WebSockets. The page registers a small set of WebMCP tools through document.modelContext , so an agent can work from the shared page context without cloning the repository. The publish path uses the GitHub REST API and keeps the edit contract narrow: text, style, or visibility changes in the selected target. The app was prompted from start to finish in Codex as Codex has always been my go-to tool. Challenges and lessons Honestly, I was very close to overengineering the entire thing. I had to take control of the model and decide what I wanted for the MVP. It was also kind of harder trying to juggle multiple free accounts to get this up and running. title: Persistent Web Skills Runtime
pitch: A WebMCP-first runtime that learns browser workflows once, reuses them reliably, and repairs them when the web changes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-first runtime that learns browser workflows once, reuses them reliably, and repairs them when the web changes. Like Comment Story Updates Persistent Web Skills Runtime Persistent Web Skills Runtime (PWS) is a WebMCP-first Chrome runtime that lets agents learn a browser workflow once, reuse it as a versioned skill, and repair it when the web changes. The problem Agentic browser tasks are commonly rediscovered through fragile clicks on every run. Small UI changes can break a workflow, while useful structured WebMCP tools may be ignored or forgotten. Repeated exploration is slow, brittle, token-intensive, and hard to trust. The solution PWS routes each task through a clear priority ladder: Native WebMCP → Cached Web Skill → Browser/DOM learning fallback It discovers the page's current WebMCP tools first. If there is no suitable native tool, it learns a successful semantic browser workflow, stores it in IndexedDB with immutable version history, validates the outcome on reuse, and repairs only the failed step when a dependency changes. The live taskboard demo shows an 11-action Learn → Reuse → Repair flow: it learns a create-task workflow, reuses it, survives a Create Task → Add Task UI change with a validated v1 → v2 skill repair, and demonstrates live native tool registration through toolchange . Key features Native-first WebMCP routing via document.modelContext.getTools() , live toolchange synchronization, and current-tool rebinding. Safe capability snapshots that persist metadata, not executable tool handlers. Semantic locators based on role, name, labels, stable attributes, and meaningful text instead of brittle structural selectors. Dependency-only DOM fingerprints, explicit result validation, and targeted step repair. An inspectable Runtime Inspector, execution log, timings, validation status, and skill versions. Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, a Chrome Manifest V3 extension, IndexedDB, Node.js, and an optional OpenAI Responses API service. API keys remain server-side; the interactive demo runs without a key through deterministic local learning and repair adapters. Career value I work as an agent engineer and repeatedly test browser automation over many fresh pages. I wanted a way for agents to achieve stronger results with fewer tokens. Building PWS made the practical value of WebMCP clear: expose structured tools, preserve proven workflows as reusable skills, and give agents a safe answer to reuse instead of forcing them to rediscover the UI. This can make agent browser work faster, more reliable, and easier to trust. title: RabbitHole
pitch: Dense documents are hard to read, even in your own field. Rabbithole lets you zoom in on the parts you don't understand and the explaining is done by your personal assistant aware about your context.
about_excerpt: Dense documents are hard to read, even in your own field. Rabbithole lets you zoom in on the parts you don't understand and the explaining is done by your personal assistant aware about your context. Like Comment Story Updates history of pages you read your profile, you can edit for more fine tuned experience home page history of concepts you drilled in another example of drilling down further on a crispr related doc example of reading a text, drilling down Inspiration I read a lot - articles, papers, code, engineering spec, wiki pages and so much more. And I love going down rabbit holes, which there are many of when I'm reading dense documents or text in domains I'm not proficient in. So very often, I start at something, have a dozen open tabs a few hours later plus a long thread with an AI, and have lost track of whatever I was reading in the first place. I wanted to fix this workflow.You know how fun it is to read and figure something out with a smarter friend who also knows your gaps? Everything gets so much easier. Well, that's the experience I wanted to create. I'm also trying to imagine a future where web feels more collaborative, where you and your agent do things together, like partners. As agents become more personal, I don't just want them to be doing things for me on some remote cloud machine. I want them to be ambiently present with me, across every surface. Where RabbitHole fits If we divide reading into two axes - x axis - the granularity you read the text in - from "hand it over for a summary" to "every word" y axis - the amount of personalized help you have while reading(could be human but let's focus on AI here) RabbitHole sits on top right. It's immensely useful for cases where you want to actually read, understand or skim over a piece, than only working with a derivative of the original text(summaries or questions asked on top). There's a image of this linked in Readme that gets the point across better than words. Why WebMCP fits The key thing is that the assistant should not be inside the reading app. It should be your assistant, whichever one that is, and the app should be a place it can work. WebMCP is exactly the interface for that: any agent with a browser can find the page's tools and call them. What it does True to its name, it lets you go as deep as you want into anything, starting from something you want to read and understand. There is a nice sliding pane UI(Andy Matuschak's style). You start with pasting the text or link for what you want to read and asking your agent to help you with reading alongside. Your personal agent(codex, claude, openclaw, hermes, littlebird, anything that supports WebMCP) highlights the terms and parts that are non trivial "for you". A biologist probably doesn't know "apophenia"; a psychologist probably doesn't know "Cas9". So whatever terms are likely unfamiliar to you gets highlighted. But you're not limited to them, you can also pick anything else or even multiple sentences, and drill into that. Everything you drill into opens a pane on the right. From there you can keep elaborating on that thing, or go deeper into something else and open more panes. Every explanation, elaboration, and answer takes into account both the context it sits in and you — your goals, your familiarity with the concepts, other things you've been doing that might connect. You can set an explicit goal for why you're reading. Maybe you're reading papers on homeschooling to decide the best course for your child, or researching vocal technique to sing better. Knowing the goal, on top of everything else about your life, lets the agent explain things even better. It stores the concepts you drilled into so they're easy to revisit. Once you have it in your agent's memory, you can also just ask it - "open this thing in RabbitHole". How I built it Mostly vibing with my coding agent, what feels right, the direction I want, features I find joy and delight in on top of utility, thinking hard about balancing minimalism with power. The design inspiration is https://notes.andymatuschak.org . I've used this type of view for my personal notes in Obsidian as well and always liked it as a good UX to drill down without losing track. Challenges I ran into Duplex communication(app being able to invoke the agent on demand). I don't like the UX of chatting with agent to reactively make WebMCP tool calls. I wanted to focus on the actual reading for the most part, so I had to figure out ways to make it duplex. I tried an idea of having a long async call, sort of like long polling. But it didn't work as cleanly on its own due to client timeout. So I added polling asking the agent to sleep and check if there are no things to process in the queue, which works well. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The UI, the duplex trick, and honestly just building something I'm going to use often. I'll probably spend even more time on making it good lol(yeah there is an xkcd for it https://xkcd.com/1205/ 🥲). What I learned The web can be so much more collaborative than it is. I like WebMCP - it's directionally right, though still missing some important things. The usual demos of "filling in web forms" don't even scratch the surface of what's possible. What's next for RabbitHole Support for more types of inputs - PDFs for e.g. More software eng specific coverage - PRs for example. URL based state of the whole path which others can open and see the explanation in terms they would understand best. Login and server side storage to carry what you're reading and concepts you're interested in across sessions and AI agents. More proactivity - capture your attention and pass it to the agent. If you're lingering on a paragraph, the agent can proactively offer you help. Suggested actions — "add this to our repo" while reading an engineering blog, or "add this to your slides" if it relates to a presentation you're working on. title: SciStudio-web
pitch: Scientific data workbench with your AI partner.
about_excerpt: Scientific data workbench with your AI partner. Like 1 Comment Story Updates AI help you build and run data analysis workflows A workflow can pause in the middle for your decisions with interactive blocks! Just ask AI to make one! We have great and fun tutorials like a video game! Editing codes for blocks with your AI partner! Our branding Inspiration I built SciStudio because I wasn't satisfied with scientific agents like Rosalind or Claude Science. Scientists find them hard to use because they are AI-chat centered. But scientists want to see the data the whole way through — every intermediate step, all the way to the result. Sometimes interacting with data with a GUI is also important. And I throw away the analysis script every time a session ends, because I have no good way to reuse or automate it. As biological research moves toward multimodality, this shape makes cross-modal data analysis difficult. This made me want to build SciStudio: a standardized workflow system for multimodal data analysis that integrates the capabilities of AI agents. You, and your agent, work together. For AI integration, SciStudio's solution before this hackathon was a desktop application plus a PTY running the codex CLI. But for wet-lab scientists, CLI tools are quite off-putting — I watched them struggle with the various buttons on top, not knowing that it can only be operated with the keyboard, and so on. Another problem is that users (I wish I had...) tend to stick with what they know; therefore, an AI interaction system they're already familiar with would greatly increase the product's appeal. Apps like ChatGPT are the perfect choice. After seeing WebMCP, I realized that our current AI system and prompts could be easily migrated to WebMCP and would naturally gain the ability to integrate the various scientific tools that ChatGPT has. After I ran the protein design tool with my data analysis workflow together within the same session with AI, Bang! That is why I chose to join this hackathon. What it does SciStudio-web is an interactive workflow orchestration system for multimodal scientific data analysis. The unit of data processing here is the block; scientists can get hands-on and use building blocks to create workflows, make plots, and automate their data-analysis work. Combined with a powerful AI agent, they can build workflows, carry out the steps of data analysis, and work through an interactive data-analysis interface, turning it all into assets that individuals and labs can reuse. We hope SciStudio has the chance to become the running partner of AI agents. The scenario I hope to see is one where the user prompts, and ChatGPT, through WebMCP, works together with the user to process data — combining all the other powerful biology tools — and ultimately delivers data visualization, interactive analysis, and a personal/lab asset system. How we built it It's a long story, and I can't believe I could go this far. I'm good at coding in data science, but I actually know nothing about software engineering (I'm a biologist). I started with an idea and asked AI agents to build it directly, then realized it didn't work. I asked why, and the AI told me we needed an architecture. So I wrote the architecture file and let the AI build it, only to realize it still didn't work... This happened for several rounds until I had built a robust software-engineering system for AI coding: architecture, specs, implementation, testing, documentation maintenance, and CI/build QA tools to maintain code quality. Honestly... I learned a lot. Challenges we ran into Failed to deploy, lots of frontend troubles, submission documents (hate it!) Accomplishments that we're proud of The old SciStudio called ChatGPT agents by providing an MCP server and a PTY for CLI apps to run in. During the submission period, I migrated our MCP server system to WebMCP, enabling us to run SciStudio's agentic features directly inside ChatGPT. I also optimized the frontend for a better user experience in ChatGPT. Finally I explored and built some demo projects to show the power of SciStudio. This gives me the benefits of modern scientific agent harnesses and the integration of other agentic tools, plus our reproducible workflow runtime and data-interaction capabilities. SciStudio will surface the hardest question of working with AI: "What did the AI do to my data???" This change is groundbreaking to me, honestly. I struggled with the limited resources I could access as a solo developer. I thought SciStudio was limited because I lacked access to big-data resources and collaborations with other tools and apps. The WebMCP integration changed everything. (I'm also proud that my old SciStudio migrated pretty easily.) What we learned Finding people to use a product is more difficult than building it. What's next for SciStudio-web I don't know, let me get some users first... New & existing work SciStudio is a pre-existing open-source project (desktop app, workflow runtime, MCP server). Everything in this submission repo was built during the WebMCP Challenge submission period: the MCP→WebMCP bridge, the Docker/Cloudflare public deploy, the ChatGPT-facing frontend rework, and the demo case. The full scope is visible in this repo's git history (jiazhenz026/scistudio-web-demo), which starts at the time I joined the hackathon (Sept.3!! Almost missed it!!). title: TenderLens
pitch: An autonomous agent that reads every public tender dossier so small suppliers don't have to - scoring what they qualify for, and flagging notices written so only one firm could win.
about_excerpt: An autonomous agent that reads every public tender dossier so small suppliers don't have to - scoring what they qualify for, and flagging notices written so only one firm could win. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Across the EU, roughly half of all public contracts attract a single bidder. The usual explanation is corruption. The more common one is arithmetic: a tender dossier runs 40 to 130 pages, the qualification criteria that decide whether a company may legally bid are scattered through it, and a 26-person firm has nobody who can read forty of those a month. So they stop reading, and the field empties out on its own. The two problems turn out to have the same evidence base. The document that tells a supplier you qualify for this is the same document that reveals this one was written for somebody else -- a specification fixed to 14 mm and 63.5 Wh describes exactly one laptop on the market. Once you are parsing dossiers at scale, both answers fall out of the same pass. What it does One button starts an autonomous sweep. No further human input. The agent pulls open notices, pre-filters by the supplier's value ceiling and live deadlines, then for every surviving notice: opens the dossier, extracts the qualification criteria into structured form, rules each one met / gap / unclear against the supplier's real profile with the evidence attached, screens the buyer's award history and the clause wording for integrity red flags, scores fit out of 100, estimates win probability adjusted for that buyer's historical bidder count, and writes a dated bid plan working backwards from the deadline with an owner on every step. It ends with a ranked board -- 87 down to 17 across twelve notices -- and a written bid / no-bid brief per notice. The entire reasoning trace streams to the browser while it runs: every tool call with its input, its output and its latency. The integrity screen Five detectors, each grounded in a documented single-bidding indicator: Flag Fires when SHORT_WINDOW The submission window is shorter than the customary minimum, which favours a bidder who prepared before publication THIN_COMPETITION The buyer averages under two bidders across prior tenders VENDOR_CONCENTRATION 40% or more of a buyer's prior awards went to one supplier SPEC_LOCK The specification fixes exact physical parameters instead of performance ranges, which usually describes one product on the market INCUMBENT_LOCK A qualification clause can only be satisfied by the current supplier None is presented as proof of wrongdoing, and the app never says otherwise. Each flag carries the reasoning that makes it worth a clarification question or a formal challenge. How I built it TypeScript throughout. Supabase Postgres holds the notices, the supplier profile, the run log and every assessment; Server-Sent Events carry the live trace; the deployed demo runs on Supabase Edge Functions. The agent core -- orchestrator, six tools, provider adapters, types -- depends on nothing from Node, React or Next. That is deliberate, and it buys a second runtime for free: the same engine drives a Next.js build and a Deno edge build, unmodified. The decision worth defending is deterministic core, model at the edge . Every score, verdict and flag comes from code that can be read, tested and cited. The language model writes one artefact -- the decision brief -- where prose is the deliverable. This is not a cost saving. A supplier disqualified on a criterion needs to point at the rule that fired; a score that exists only inside a model's context window cannot survive a procurement review board. The side effect is that the hosted demo runs with zero API keys -- open it and press the button. Graceful degradation at every boundary: no database falls back to the bundled corpus, Supabase unreachable mid-request falls back silently, a deep link to a never-assessed notice is assessed on demand server-side. There is no configuration in which the deployed app shows an error page instead of doing its job. The board is also published to visiting AI agents over WebMCP -- seven tools registered through document.modelContext -- so an assistant browsing the page can search, screen and re-rank it alongside the human, with every call mirrored on screen. Enterprise governance and compliance Auditability by construction. Every assessment is a row tied to a run, carrying the verdicts, flags, checklist and reasoning mode used. You can reconstruct why the agent said what it said, months later. Explainable decisions, not scores. Each verdict ships with its evidence string ("Requires EUR 600,000; profile turnover is EUR 1,850,000"). Each risk flag ships with its rationale. Row-level security on all four tables. The demo project's open policies exist because it holds nothing but synthetic notices; a real deployment scopes them to the authenticated supplier. No unsourced claims. The integrity screen surfaces the pattern and why the pattern matters -- the standard a challenge before a procurement review body is held to. Synthetic corpus. Modelled on the structure of real TED, e-Prokurimi and eNabavke publications. No real notice, buyer decision, supplier name or award record is reproduced. Monetization Two customers, one engine. 1. Suppliers -- SaaS subscription (primary). Solo EUR 49/mo: one country, weekly digest, three profiles. Team EUR 199/mo: three countries, daily sweep, unlimited profiles, bid plans exported to calendar. Agency EUR 699/mo: white label, API access, multi-client dashboards for bid-writing consultancies. The wedge is measurable. A firm bidding six times a year at roughly five days of unpaid bid effort each spends about EUR 12,000 of staff time. TenderLens removes the two days spent deciding whether to bid, and kills the disqualified-on-a-technicality bids entirely. 2. Watchdogs and journalists -- usage-based. Integrity screening billed per thousand notices analysed, with an NGO tier at cost. Anti-corruption organisations and investigative desks already do this by hand, one buyer at a time. 3. Buyers -- compliance licence (later). The same detectors run pre-publication: a procurement office checks its own draft notice for SPEC_LOCK and SHORT_WINDOW before it goes out. Sold per authority, annually. Highest margin, and the one that needs credibility from the first two to earn. Marginal cost is a few cents of model spend per notice, and zero when the deterministic engine handles it. Challenges I ran into Deciding how much judgement to hand to a model. The first version asked an LLM to rule on each criterion; it was fluent and unciteable, and a bid manager cannot take "the model thought so" to a review board. Rewriting the criterion logic as parsed thresholds and set membership made the output defensible and, unexpectedly, made the product better -- the evidence line next to each verdict is what users actually read. Scoring calibration was worse. The first scorer put eight of twelve notices between 90 and 100, which ranks nothing. Fit is now a five-factor blend -- qualification, capability match, economics against the bid ceiling, historical competition, and slack between the deadline and the work the dossier implies -- and the board spreads properly. Two bugs only surfaced when I screenshotted the thing: the bid plan was scheduling steps in the past whenever a deadline was closer than its fixed offsets, and a delivery-time commitment was being marked met because the supplier's category matched. Both are fixed. Both were invisible in the happy path. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The reasoning trace. An agent that returns a verdict asks to be trusted; an agent that shows six tool calls with their inputs, outputs and latency lets you audit the verdict. Making the trace a first-class contract rather than a debug view is the single decision that most changed how the product feels. And the zero-configuration demo: it runs, fully, with no key, no database and no signup. What I learned That agentic is not a synonym for the model decides everything. The parts of this agent that make it worth deploying -- the tool sequence, the extraction contract, the detectors, the trace -- are engineering. The model is one step in seven, and the system is better for the model being replaceable. What's next for TenderLens A live connector per portal. The portal search is one function; TED first, then the national portals. A real dossier reader, with a PDF pipeline feeding the same structured requirement shape, so the agent handles notices nobody has pre-structured. Scheduled sweeps with a morning digest. The run loop already has no browser dependency. More detectors. Each one is an independent function of the notice, so this is purely additive.
