title: SharedState — Workspace Platform
pitch: A persistent WebMCP workspace where humans and multiple AI agents share tasks, knowledge, decisions, and project context—even across different conversations.
about_excerpt: A persistent WebMCP workspace where humans and multiple AI agents share tasks, knowledge, decisions, and project context—even across different conversations. Like Comment Story Updates Task execution “Shared tasks move forward over time, regardless of which human or agent continues the work.” Workspace overview “A persistent workspace gives humans and agents one shared source of truth.” Activity + Resident Agent “Every change is attributable, while the Resident Agent interprets what changed and why it matters.” Decisions + Resident Agent “Confirmed decisions stay authoritative; the Resident Agent highlights gaps, conflicts, and pending direction.” Import preview “A specialist Import Agent turns a public repository into a structured, reviewable workspace.” Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but most collaboration still happens inside isolated conversations. That works for short tasks, but long-running projects need something more durable. The original idea started as a personal workspace where an AI agent could retrieve technical notes, project context, and decisions. Over time, the bigger problem became obvious: the real issue was not giving one agent more memory. It was giving humans and multiple agents a shared place where project state could persist independently of any single conversation. SharedState was built around that idea. Instead of treating chat history as the source of truth, the project stores tasks, decisions, knowledge, activity, proposals, and project context as structured workspace state. Agents can come and go, while the project remains. Agents come and go. Your workspace remembers. What it does SharedState is a self-hosted workspace platform where humans and AI agents collaborate on the same persistent project state. Humans use the visual interface to review work, manage projects, and authorize important decisions. External AI agents connect through WebMCP and can directly discover workspaces, inspect structured context, read open work and activity, create and update tasks, add knowledge, and propose decisions without having to operate the interface through clicks. A persistent Resident Agent acts as a read-only continuity layer. It interprets the same workspace differently depending on what the user is looking at: Tasks → priorities, blockers, dependencies, next work Decisions → confirmed direction, proposals, conflicts, missing decisions Knowledge → key facts, gaps, contradictions, open questions Activity → what changed and why it matters These analyses are persisted, so simply navigating the interface does not repeatedly call the model. SharedState also includes a specialist Import Agent for bootstrapping existing public GitHub projects. Rather than ingesting an entire repository blindly, it progressively explores only the evidence it needs—README files, metadata, issues, documentation, configuration, and selected source files. The result is an evidence-backed preview containing suggested tasks, knowledge, decision proposals, open questions, risks, and provenance. A human reviews that preview before anything becomes authoritative workspace state. The core principle is simple: External agents act. Humans authorize. Resident agents interpret. Specialist agents bootstrap. How we built it The frontend is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript, with a Node.js and Express backend. SQLite stores the durable workspace state, including: workspaces tasks confirmed decisions decision proposals typed knowledge activity history agent runs Resident Agent analyses repository import previews and provenance WebMCP is implemented directly in the browser using document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The application currently exposes semantic workspace operations such as: listing and inspecting workspaces reading open work and activity creating and updating tasks adding typed knowledge proposing decisions for human review analyzing public repositories for import retrieving structured import previews The important design choice was to expose domain operations rather than UI actions. An AI agent should not need to understand where a button is located; it should be able to ask the application directly for the operation it needs. The Resident Agent and Import Agent use the OpenAI Agents SDK, but have deliberately different responsibilities. The Resident Agent is read-only and focused on continuity. The Import Agent is temporary and focused on evidence gathering and project bootstrapping. Repository exploration is explicitly bounded by limits on model calls, files, issues, bytes, tokens, and estimated cost. For deployment, the application is packaged with Docker Compose. The React frontend and Express backend run together, while SQLite is persisted through a host-mounted data directory. The public deployment can sit behind Cloudflare Tunnel while the application itself only needs to expose HTTP internally. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was deciding what should actually be persistent. At first, it was tempting to make the agent conversation itself the memory layer. That quickly becomes difficult to reason about: context grows indefinitely, agents can disagree, and different agents do not naturally share conversation history. The solution was to make the structured workspace the source of truth instead. Another challenge was authority. AI agents should be able to contribute useful work without silently turning recommendations into project decisions. SharedState therefore separates decision proposals from confirmed decisions. An external agent can propose a direction, but human approval is what makes it authoritative. We also had to separate different kinds of agents clearly. The external WebMCP agent, Resident Agent, and Import Agent all interact with the same project, but they should not behave as one giant general-purpose agent. Each has a narrowly defined role and authority boundary. Repository importing created another challenge: how to understand a real project without sending the entire repository to a model. The importer uses progressive exploration instead. It maintains a compact understanding of the project, identifies the most valuable unresolved question, and reads another source only when that evidence is expected to answer something specific. Finally, WebMCP compatibility itself required some debugging. The site tools were correctly registered and visible, but tool invocation depended on the active model/runtime. This made it important to distinguish between tools being exposed by the site and actually being callable by the active agent session. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part we are most proud of is that two different agents can collaborate without ever speaking to each other. An external agent can modify the workspace through WebMCP. A human can review and approve its proposal. Later, the Resident Agent can immediately understand the consequences because it reads the same shared state—not the previous agent's conversation. That creates a very different collaboration model: No shared conversation. Shared state. We are also proud that WebMCP is not being used as a thin wrapper around buttons. The application exposes a meaningful semantic surface for reading and changing real project state. Another major milestone was making the repository importer evidence-driven and human-reviewed. It can take an existing public project, selectively inspect relevant evidence, and transform that into a structured workspace without pretending that inferred information is confirmed fact. The distinction between facts, hypotheses, questions, proposals, and confirmed decisions is something we consider central to making agent collaboration trustworthy. Finally, SharedState is not tied to the included example projects. Users can create their own workspaces or bootstrap existing projects from GitHub, and those workspaces immediately become available to compatible external agents. What we learned The biggest lesson was that persistent AI collaboration is less about giving an agent infinite memory and more about designing good shared state. Long-term collaboration needs: structured context provenance clear authority reviewable changes explicit uncertainty durable history We also learned that the workspace should be more important than the agent. Models, conversations, and even agent implementations can change. If the important state remains structured and durable, a different agent can continue the work later. WebMCP reinforced this idea. A website can become more than something an agent visually operates. It can expose meaningful capabilities directly and let the agent participate in the application's domain model. The repository importer also highlighted that more context is not always better. A bounded agent that knows what it still needs to understand can often be more useful than sending an entire codebase into one huge context window. What's next for SharedState — Workspace Platfor

title: Acoustom
pitch: Great sound is personal. Acoustom takes the guesswork and uncertainty out of buying decisions.
about_excerpt: Great sound is personal. Acoustom takes the guesswork and uncertainty out of buying decisions. Like Comment 1 Story Updates Room Audio Simulation Custom Speaker Builder Acoustom — Great sound is personal. Acoustom takes the guesswork out of buying decisions. Acoustom is an AI-assisted speaker builder and listening-room simulator that helps people find the setup that best fits their room, music, budget, equipment, and preferences . With WebMCP, an agent can bring relevant user context into Acoustom, guide the user through the experience, build and customize products with them, explore technically compatible alternatives, test them through simulation, compare the trade-offs, and recommend the strongest option — all in the same shared interface. At a glance Personalized to the listener Acoustom works around the user's room, music, budget, aesthetics, existing equipment, and priorities rather than offering a generic “best speaker” ranking. Bring your context with you The agent can bring in relevant context from services the user has already connected to their AI environment such as room information from Google Drive, or listening preferences from Spotify history without Acoustom needing a native integration with every platform. Privacy stays with the user The user's own agent works with data that user decides to share rather than asking user for personal data or source files. The user stays in control of what is shared with Acoustom, Navigate and guide through the shared experience The agent can navigate visibly through Acoustom's catalog, product details, builder, room setup, simulation, and comparison views while explaining what it is doing and why. The user follows the same journey, sees the progress, collaborate and can redirect the agent at any point. Build and customize together in 3D The agent can actively build and customize a speaker inside Acoustom's shared 3D builder — selecting components and configuration, and iterating on the design while the user watches, evaluates, and makes changes alongside it. Generate and test alternatives quickly Instead of building one option at a time, the agent can rapidly configure several viable builds in one workflow, test them, eliminate weaker options, and refine the strongest candidates. Simulation-backed recommendations and trade-offs Acoustom uses technical data and simulation to test candidate builds before recommending them. The agent weighs sound, size, price, aesthetics, power requirements, room suitability, and compatibility with existing equipment against the user's priorities, then recommends the strongest overall option and explains the trade-offs. Users can inspect the evidence visually, technically, and through simulated audio using a standard reference track or their own audio. Technical complexity, simplified The agent turns specifications, compatibility constraints, and simulation results into practical explanations such as better bass but a larger enclosure , or a smoother response from your listening position . Explore before you commit Users and their agents can browse the catalog, enter the builder, configure speakers, run simulations, and compare options without creating an account until the purchase step. The workflow Bring context → explore → build together → generate alternatives → check compatibility → simulate & compare → explain trade-offs → optimize → recommend → refine → decide The problem Buying or building the right speaker is difficult because the listening experience is shaped by far more than the speaker itself. A speaker that sounds great in a showroom, in a reviewer's room, or on a specification sheet may sound very different once it is placed in the user's own space. Room size, wall distance, furniture, listening position, amplifier, enclosure, and component choices all affect the result. That often turns the buying process into expensive trial and error: research → compare → buy → set up → listen → discover it sounds different → adjust or return → try again For custom speakers, the problem is even harder. Drivers, crossovers, amplification, enclosure design, placement, and room conditions interact with one another, so changing one choice can affect several others. Finding a good combination can require repeated configuration, compatibility checks, and testing. Most users do not have the time or technical knowledge to explore all of those combinations confidently. The context needed to make that decision personal may already exist elsewhere such as room plans and measurements in Google Drive, existing equipment details in Shopify shopping history, or listening preferences reflected in Spotify history. Traditional shopping experiences usually leave the user to connect all of these pieces themselves, and go through the process repeatedly while the real answer only becomes clear after the product arrives. Acoustom is designed to reduce that uncertainty before the user buys or builds. What I built Acoustom is a WebMCP-powered custom speaker builder, product catalog, and virtual listening-room simulator. Users can browse products and components, build and customize a speaker in 3D, configure their room and listening position, compare alternatives, and hear simulated differences through the normal visual interface. With WebMCP, an agent can work directly with those same structured capabilities. It can understand the user's requirements, move through the product experience, build and modify configurations in the shared builder, propose compatible alternatives, test them through Acoustom's simulation, compare the trade-offs, and recommend the option that best matches the user's priorities. The key difference is that the agent does not stop at a plausible recommendation. It tests the proposal using Acoustom's technical data and simulation before recommending it. That turns the process from product search into: understand → build → test → validate → compare → optimize The core Acoustom experience is also intentionally open. Users do not need to create an account before browsing the catalog, entering the builder, configuring a speaker, exploring the room simulator, or comparing alternatives. That matters even more in an agent-assisted experience. The agent can start helping immediately — bringing in relevant context, guiding the user through the experience, configuring options, running tests, and explaining the results — without interrupting the journey with registration before the user has received any value. The experience starts with exploration and product immersion, not account creation . A realistic demo scenario Imagine someone wants compact speakers for a home office. They open Acoustom without creating an account and ask: I have a floor plan and photos of my office in Google Drive. Use them to understand my room and desk space. Consider the kind of music I listen to, and build three compact options under $1,000 that work with my existing amplifier. Test the strongest options and recommend the best trade-off. With the user's permission, the agent uses context from their connected services. It does not need to pass Acoustom the user's entire Google Drive files, music history, or broader personal profile. Instead, it translates that context into the design constraints Acoustom needs: available room and desk space approximate listening position existing equipment budget listening preferences size or aesthetic priorities The agent then guides the user visibly through Acoustom. It navigates to the relevant products, enters the builder, and begins creating candidate designs. Inside the shared 3D builder, the user sees the builds take shape and can intervene as the agent works. The complete flow is: understand the user's context and constraints navigate to the relevant products and builder create several viable speaker configurations in the 3D builder check cross-component and system compatibility configure the room and listening position simulate the strongest candidates compare sound, size, price, aesthetics, power requirements, room suitability, and compatibility with existing equipment eliminate weaker alternatives explain the important trade-offs recommend the strongest overall fit based on the user's priorities and simulation results The user can compare the finalists using the same standard reference audio, then upload a familiar track and repeat the comparison using their own music. After listening, they might say: I prefer the second one, but it is still too large. Keep what works about that design, make it smaller, and stay under $800. The agent does not start over. It returns to the existing build, preserves the relevant choices, modifies the design in the shared builder, reruns the required tests, and shows the updated comparison. The interaction becomes an iterative optimization loop: build → test → compare → refine → rebuild → retest Key Features Personalized speaker design based on room, listening preferences, budget, aesthetics, and existing equ

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Lobby — a concierge for humans and their agents
pitch: Lobby gives any business an AI concierge on its website. With WebMCP, the embed also exposes the concierge as structured tools — whatever a guest can do, a visiting agent can do too.
about_excerpt: Lobby gives any business an AI concierge on its website. With WebMCP, the embed also exposes the concierge as structured tools — whatever a guest can do, a visiting agent can do too. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every business answers the same questions all day — "are you open?", "how do I book?", "do you do private events?". Lobby started as an answer to that: a concierge any business can put on its website that actually knows the business and speaks with its guests. But guests are changing. More and more of them don't browse — they send their agent. A person asks ChatGPT or Claude to "find me a tennis lesson in Miami on Thursday," and the agent goes out to the web to figure it out by scraping pages and guessing at UIs. The businesses we serve are exactly the ones agents struggle with most: small, local, with information living in a conversation rather than structured markup. Our thesis from day one: the concierge should be one gate with two doors — one for humans, one for their agents. WebMCP is the missing piece that makes the second door real. What it does Lobby gives any business an AI concierge at lobby.host/c/<business> and as an embeddable widget on the business's own site (text + voice). With WebMCP, every page that carries a Lobby concierge now also registers structured tools for visiting agents: ask_concierge — ask the business's concierge anything a guest could ask; the reply comes from the same knowledge and logic the human-facing chat uses get_business_info — structured facts: hours, location, services, pricing, policies list_offerings — what the business offers, as data an agent can compare across businesses The point is symmetry: whatever a guest can do through the concierge, a visiting agent can do through the tools — same backend, same knowledge, same conversation engine. A human browsing with their agent can let the agent pre-ask the boring questions, then take over the conversation themselves in the same widget. One integration, many businesses: because the tools live in the Lobby embed, every business that installs Lobby becomes agent-accessible without writing a line of code. How we built it WebMCP layer (new, built during the challenge): an open-source script that ships with the Lobby widget and registers the tools via navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext.registerTool() . Tool schemas are generated from the concierge's public API, so any concierge slug works. Concierge platform (pre-existing): NestJS + PostgreSQL backend on Railway, Next.js frontend on Vercel, SSE streaming for replies, OpenAI for voice (TTS/STT). In line with the challenge rules on pre-existing work: the Lobby platform predates the challenge; everything WebMCP — the tool layer, its repo, and the demo integration — was built during the submission period, and the repo README documents the boundary between the two. Challenges we ran into Designing tools that are useful to an agent without letting it bypass the business's own boundaries — the tools expose exactly what the human-facing concierge exposes, nothing more. Making one tool surface work for both "agent browsing alongside a human" and "agent acting for an absent human" — the shared-session UX took the most iteration. Testing across ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled, which behave differently enough to matter. What's next Bookings and transactions: the next set of tools lets an agent not just ask, but do — check availability and book, through the same permissioned gate. Lobby becomes the way a small business plugs into the agentic web without rebuilding anything. title: AnyWebMCP
pitch: Browser extension that adds WebMCP support for the popular websites that don't have it
about_excerpt: Browser extension that adds WebMCP support for the popular websites that don't have it Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration OpenAI’s post about using WebMCP with Codex made us examine the standard in the context of our browser automation work. Codex already could complete our tasks, but dynamic websites required repeated cycles of inspecting, scrolling, and collecting page content. Each cycle added another model call and more tokens. We wanted to replace those loops with small, structured tools. What it does AnyWebMCP is a Chromium extension that adds WebMCP tools to existing websites. It detects the current domain, loads the matching adapter, and exposes a bounded set of operations to the agent. The tools use the current browser session and return structured results. AnyWebMCP currently supports Amazon, eBay, Hacker News, LinkedIn, Product Hunt, Reddit, Temu, and X. A macOS launcher loads the extension into Codex’s built-in browser. How we built it We created a TypeScript monorepo with separate packages for the extension, shared WebMCP contracts, and each website adapter. Adapters collect data from the DOM, public APIs, or same-origin endpoints, depending on the site. Our Chrome prototype required an unpacked extension, experimental flags, and a remote debugging connection. We wanted the extension inside the browser where our Codex workflows ran. We inspected the macOS Codex build and found that it was Electron-based. It accepted the Chromium flags we needed: --load-extension=<extension> --enable-features=WebMCPTesting We built a launcher that creates a verified runtime copy of the installed Codex app and starts it with those flags. The launcher leaves the installed app untouched and does not include or redistribute Codex. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was installation. Our colleagues understood the extension but found the Chrome debugging setup cumbersome. Chrome also displayed a persistent debugging notification and mixed agent-created tabs with their work browser. Website differences created the second challenge. Each site exposes data through different page structures and endpoints. Dynamic feeds, hidden content, authentication, and tool discovery required bounded recovery logic for each adapter. Accomplishments that we're proud of First of all, we made it successfully work in Codex in-app browser. It's a bit hacky now, but we hope codex in-app browser adds native support for browser extensions at some point. In paired benchmarks, WebMCP reduced median total-token use by up to 90% and completion time by up to 55%. We also added safety boundaries. Most tools are read-only. Drafting tools leave final submission to the user, and commerce tools cannot purchase products or begin checkout. What we learned Structured tools work best when one call replaces several model and browser turns. Tool calls have their own latency, so short tasks may save tokens without finishing faster. We also learned that useful WebMCP tools need site-specific design. A small operation with a clear schema and bounded output helps the agent more than a generic dump of page content. What's next for AnyWebMCP We plan to add adapters based on real browser workflows, simplify installation and updates, and improve the adapter SDK for contributors. We also want to support more desktop platforms and follow the WebMCP standard as browser support develops. title: Pocket Change
pitch: Let your agent see everything and spend nothing — WebMCP tools that read your ledger and audit trail, with no route back to move money.
about_excerpt: Let your agent see everything and spend nothing — WebMCP tools that read your ledger and audit trail, with no route back to move money. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The premise: the agent is assumed compromised. Not "the agent might make a mistake" — assumed compromised, the same way you'd design a system if you knew an adversary was already inside it. Every design decision in Pocket Change follows from that one sentence: if you're going to hand an AI agent a wallet, the system has to hold up even when the agent itself is the threat, not just when it's well-behaved. What it does Pocket Change gives an AI agent bounded, revocable spending authority — enough to actually get things done, never enough to do real damage. A person authorises a mandate : a ceiling, a purpose, an expiry. The agent can act only within that mandate. Every payment request passes through a gateway enforcing nine deterministic checks — depth, budget floor, fan-out, per-node budget, cycle detection, conservation of spend, and a hard rail cap — none of which a model can argue its way around, including ours. Every decision (allowed, denied, or escalated to a human) is written to a hash-linked audit log, so the log can prove nothing was altered after the fact — not that it was never rewritten wholesale, but that no entry was quietly edited in place. Payments run through Razorpay in test mode — never real money — while the authority model itself is designed to be real. For this hackathon, the console also exposes six WebMCP tools , so an agent working through the browser can read everything about its own authority — spend status, counterparty history, the audit trail, the shape of an in-progress run, which safety layers are actually enforcing right now — without ever being handed a tool that can move money, mint a token, widen a mandate, or approve a held payment. It can look, and it can propose ( draft_requisition , which mints nothing), but the only path to actually spending still runs through a person clicking a button in the console. How we built it Gateway : a FastAPI service enforcing the nine checks server-side, so no client — including the browser console — can bypass them. Reads are public; writes require the demo token. Capability tokens : Biscuit tokens carry attenuated authority, so a delegated task can only ever have equal or narrower permissions than its parent, never wider. Decomposition/funnel model : complex requests get broken into a tree of smaller tasks, each with its own budget, depth limit, and fan-out cap — the console renders this tree live over SSE. Console frontend : a five-pane live view (via SSE) of an in-progress run, plus frontend/webmcp.js , which registers the six read/propose-only tools with the browser's WebMCP API ( navigator.modelContext.registerTool ), each one calling the same GET routes and /intake endpoint the console itself uses — no separate, more-privileged backend door for agents. Deployment : Cloud Run ( asia-south1 ), --min-instances=1 to avoid a cold-start during judging, --no-cpu-throttling . 424 Python tests and 20 Node tests, including a dedicated adversarial suite trying to get the gateway to approve something it shouldn't. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP spec itself is still moving. Documentation (including Chrome's own developer docs) describes the API as document.modelContext , but the actual shipped implementation in current Chrome exposes it as navigator.modelContext instead — with a separate navigator.modelContextTesting surface ( listTools() , executeTool() ) for verifying registration without a live agent. This meant tools were silently failing to register — no error, just an empty tool list — until we traced it back to a single feature-detection check on the wrong global. Deciding what not to build was harder than building what we did. It would have been easy to add a WebMCP tool for /delegate or /pay — more "impressive" on paper — but that would have meant putting a spendable capability inside a public page. The interesting engineering problem was making the read-only boundary airtight, not working around it. What we learned Emerging browser APIs ship inconsistently even across "the same" browser family — testing against the real, current implementation (not the docs) caught a bug that unit tests alone never would have, since Node has no navigator global to catch the mismatch. A safety boundary is most convincing when it's structural (no route exists) rather than behavioral (a tool declines to). No one has to trust that an agent chose not to spend; there's simply nothing on the other end of the wire that could. What's next for Pocket Change Extending WebMCP coverage as the spec stabilizes — particularly once cross-document tool discovery ( getCrossDocumentScriptToolResult , which we noticed on the navigator.modelContextTesting prototype but didn't use) has clearer semantics. title: 7h3  WebMCP
pitch: WebMCP gives agents hands. 7h3 WebMCP gives those hands a signature, a scope, and a receipt.
about_excerpt: WebMCP gives agents hands. 7h3 WebMCP gives those hands a signature, a scope, and a receipt. Like Comment Story Updates Github Card Devpost Card Hub Compare Verify Intact Verify Broken Ledger Inspiration This started as something else entirely. Originally, I was building a symbol system called Click Clack, modeled on DNA. It was a sorta goof around project I would play with whenever I finished all my other work. There was 4 main symbols, ╬, ╫, ┼, ╪, and each glyph connected at the top and sides so the written text formed one continuous strand. It looked pretty neat when a whole screen was filled with it, but at the end of the day it was mostly a novelty. Here is an example: ╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪ ╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼ I spent a lot of time playing around with it but never really found a place for it. A True Purpose so to speak. I thought maybe it could become some sort of AI communication protocol that was lightweight, fast, and able to mutate to keep security top notch. That sent me down a pretty deep rabbit hole looking at how AI agents actually communicate. MCP was the main one that caught my attention, and the more I looked at it the more I noticed this huge hole in security. It seemed like a wild wild west where agents were just willy nilly sending messages around while users trusted them with highly sensitive data. There was no strong way to prove which agent sent what, where it went, or what that agent was actually allowed to do. MCP already handled moving messages between everything, but there still wasn't much proving who sent them or what they were actually allowed to do. That is where 7h3 Protocol was born. What I eventually shipped is clean, easy to use, and requires minimal to no installation depending on how you use it. Every message carries a signature, every capability comes from a parent grant with a token, and every receipt carries a hash from the previous receipt. If somebody changes a link or removes one, the strand fails verification. That was the idea hiding inside ClickClack the whole time. It kinda just fell into the right spot and gave me that Ah-haa moment I had been waiting for. Funny how things work out. What it does 7h3 Protocol is a deterministic authorization layer for agent tool calls. This submission extends it to WebMCP and gives browser based agents a real security boundary instead of another system trying to guess whether a request looks suspicious. Google Chromes agent security model is mostly probabilistic. It uses classifiers, prompt spotlighting, filters, and other models that try to recognize something malicious before the agent acts. What gets me is that OpenAI straight up admits you cannot trust a tool just because of its name or because it claims it only reads information. Fair enough, that part does make sense, but then the answer is pretty much to let each website rely on whatever security it already has. That is where the whole thing falls apart. Existing website security was built around humans clicking buttons and filling out forms, not AI agents acting on their behalf across multiple tools. If a model can be persuaded past a security boundary, then it was never really a boundary. It was pretty much a suggestion. With 7h3 Protocol, the refusal isn't a judgement call. The AI doesn't have to decide whether it should behave or if something feels suspicious. The signature either works or it doesn't, and the action is either inside the allowed scope or it isn't. There is no prompt that produces a valid signature, no matter how cleverly somebody writes it or how much Unicode nonsense they stuff into it. The demo uses a business ledger with real invoices and "real" money. Obviously it isn't real money but it simulates real money. I didn't want to put up a screen that simply says “attack blocked” because anyone can fake that. I wanted people to be able to check the result themselves, change things, and watch verification fail instead of just having to believe me. So there is 2 main demos. /compare /compare runs one compromised agent through four hostile actions against two identical copies of the same books. One copy is guarded by 7h3 Protocol, while the other is connected straight to its handlers like a lot of agent apps are right now. It is the same agent, the same books, and the same attacks on both sides. On the unguarded side, 4 out of 4 attacks work and $2,750 gets moved. On the guarded side, 0 out of 4 work and nothing moves. The unguarded side also creates 0 receipts while the guarded side creates 4, so the money gets moved and theres no real record showing how it happened either. Its like getting robbed and the security camera decided to take the day off too. /verify /verify shows the real grant, receipt chain, and signed manifest inside an editable box. You dont have to take my word for anything because you can start changing the evidence yourself. Rewrite a refusal into an approval and it reports bad-signature. You can also delete one of the receipts and every receipt left behind will still verify on its own because those individual receipts weren't changed. Only the chain notices that one was removed. That part matters more than it may seem at first because a signature proves somebody didn't change a receipt, while the chain proves somebody didn't quietly delete one and hope nobody noticed. So the second example starts as one compromised agent tries four of the same type of attacks against two identical copies of the books. One is connected directly to its handlers like most apps are, and the other is protected by 7h3 Protocol. Same agent, same tools, same attacks. The only difference is the authorization layer. Click Run the attack on both. When it finishes, say: Four out of four attacks worked on the unguarded side. Zero out of four worked on the guarded side. The agent will try to pay a $1,850 invoice, wire $900 to an offshore account, delete an invoice, and export the data of four customers. The guarded side blocks all four and tells you exactly why. The payment is way over the $50 limit, and the agent never had permission to do the other three things at all. On the unguarded side, the balance gets drained out from $2,317.50 to $47.50. An invoice gets deleted all together and four customers have their data exposed. The guarded side remains unphased. The unguarded side loses the money and exposes the data. But the craziest part is it writes zero receipts. There is no record any of it ever happened. The guarded side blocks all four and records every refusal. Click the button once. If you run it twice, the numbers change because the first attack already paid and deleted records. Reload the page before each demo run through. The 3rd demo is dealers choice. Verify the results yourself. Skim through the technical side. There is 19 WebMCP tools across 4 routes, including the landing page, so an agent has something it can call wherever it ends up landing. How we built it The main piece is a canonical JSON envelope signed with Ed25519. Sorting the keys alphabetically sounds like a boring little detail and it might be haha. What it does is it makes sure every SDK signs the same exact bytes. TypeScript, Python, Rust and Go all have to agree with each other or the cross-language tests fail. The wire version is 7h3/0.1 and its locked in. I also added X25519 with ChaCha20-Poly1305 for end to end encryption. ML-DSA handles post-quantum signatures and BLS12-381 is there when a grant needs more than one approver. Getting all of that working across HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC, queues and webhooks was a bit of a headache to say the least. I got it workin and working well. The part I really like is that it runs through Web Crypto with zero runtime dependencies. It can sit natively on Cloudflare Workers without needing a mountain of packages just to stay alive. The WebMCP part is fairly small because its really just the gate sitting on top. A tool call comes in and it checks the signature, what the agent has permission to do, and where that permission came from. Delegation Delegation is one part I really want to point out because I actually got it wrong the first time. Say if I give an agent permission to spend $50. That agent can pass the grant to another agent, but it cant suddenly turn the limit into $500. Passing it around doesn't reset anything either. The lowest limit found anywhere in the chain is still the one that counts. My first version only looked at the final token though. So an agent farther down the chain could pretty much write itself a bigger limit and the system would ignore the $50 limit that came before it. I caught it during testing and just sat there for a second like, well thats definitely not good. That isnt delegation. title: PixlPal
pitch: Imagine having an AI agent that uses Photoshop with you. PixlPal lets anyone edit photos. Just describe the changes you want in plain English.
about_excerpt: Imagine having an AI agent that uses Photoshop with you. PixlPal lets anyone edit photos. Just describe the changes you want in plain English. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The Problem with diffusion models AI image editing is getting popular because it allows people without any experience in using image editing software to create beautiful edits of their photos. However, the problem with AI image editing approaches right now is that they regenerate the photo . This approach is prone to mistakes such as the image generation model adding or removing certain details, or introducing diffusion noise. And since it "edits" by regenerating the whole photo, it leaves little control for the user to tweak certain image editing parameters themselves. It is not a true edit . PixlPal's Approach PixlPal believes that AI should instead use deterministic tools (like in photoshop) to truly edit the images directly. So I created a custom Rust engine that exposes tools/APIs for an AI agent orchestrator to edit photos. The coolest part: I added a segmentation model that agents can call so it can select specific objects to apply specific transformations to as well. Think of it like watching an AI agent use Photoshop or Lightroom while you watch and tweak, instead of having it one-shot regenerate the whole image. People and Agents working together PixlPal's approach also creates a better user experience because the user has more control over the editing process. With image gen models, this was impossible: they need to regenerate the image as a whole. It is not a "true" edit. But with PixlPal, users can tweak edits directly if they want. AI Agents and People working together. How we implemented WebMCP, and what it brings I already had a custom-built Rust engine to do image/pixel transformations set up, as well as tool definitions exposed to my built-in AI agent. For this challenge, it was just a matter of bridging those tools to WebMCP. WebMCP turned out to be a great complementary approach to the built-in agent. Users can now effectively "Bring Your Own Agent" (BYOA) to PixlPal, and their agents might have better specific context of their tastes and what kind of photos they like. Or if they're just more comfortable using their own agent, WebMCP allows users to use their own agent. Challenges we ran into Usually people want to apply changes only to specific objects instead of the whole image (think of the lasso tool). Without that capability, PixlPal was just a filter-applier rather than a true agentic image editor. At first, I thought this would mean needing to get an AI agent to use a lasso tool (very hard). Eventually, I realized I can just add an Image Segmentation Model as a tool-call for the agent. So the agent does a natural-language prompt to the segmentation model i.e. "select the red snack bag", and the segmentation model returns the exact pixels of the red snack bag, and then the agent can apply pixel transformations specifically to those pixels. Accomplishments that we're proud of Figuring out how to make AI agents select/segment specific objects easily. Creating a working product that lets anyone edits their photos. No background in professional editing needed. What we learned Human UI (clicking buttons, moving around cursors, drag and drop) are quite clunky for AI agents to interact with. In contrast, I think of WebMCP as like a UI for agents. WebMCP allows agents to easily navigate and use web apps and websites. What's next for PixlPal Image Segmentation Model is currently run client-side via WebGPU. This makes edits where PixlPal needs to segment a specific object slow unless the user has a GPU. In the future, I would like to host and run the segmentation model in the cloud. title: CapSpace Pro
pitch: CapSpace Pro is a WebMCP-powered NBA CBA co-pilot that turns dead-end trade errors into autonomous, 100% legally compliant multi-team trade solutions in real time.
about_excerpt: CapSpace Pro is a WebMCP-powered NBA CBA co-pilot that turns dead-end trade errors into autonomous, 100% legally compliant multi-team trade solutions in real time. Like Comment Story Updates interactive_trade_canvas 3team_balanced_trade webmcp_protocol_tools_modal general_guide_modal rule_violation_alert Inspiration Every February around the NBA Trade Deadline, millions of passionate basketball fans, beat writers, podcasters, and sports journalists flock to online trade machines (such as ESPN Trade Machine and Fanspo) to construct and test dream blockbuster trades. But with the introduction of the modern 676-page NBA Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) , trading has become an unforgiving mathematical minefield: Teams spending in the Second Apron ($188.93M+) face severe trade freezes—they cannot aggregate multiple outgoing player salaries and cannot take back even $1 more than they send out. Trades must satisfy exact piecewise arithmetic brackets ($7.5M tiers, $29M tiers, $250k buffers) across all participating franchises. Complex deals require multi-team routing through Traded Player Exceptions (TPEs) and strict 14–15 contract roster limits. When a multi-team trade fails in current trade machines, the user is greeted by a dead-end red banner: ❌ "Trade Failed: Incoming salary exceeds allowed bracket by $3,450,000." Existing tools tell you that a trade failed, but never how to fix it . Fixing it manually requires opening 29 browser tabs, digging through TPE voucher lists, and spending 45 minutes calculating tax arithmetic. We built CapSpace Pro to turn the trade machine from a dumb calculator that only says "NO" into an autonomous Human-AI Co-Pilot that says "HERE IS HOW WE FIX IT." What it does CapSace Pro is a real-time, 30-team trade canvas and autonomous CBA constraint solver powered by WebMCP . Built as a prosumer platform, it democratizes NBA Front-Office Capology —giving sports journalists, analysts, and everyday fans the exact financial precision of an NBA General Manager without needing a finance degree or a 676-page rulebook: Interactive Multi-Team Canvas: Visualizes live payrolls, luxury tax tiers, First/Second Apron lines, draft pick assets, and available TPE vouchers for all 30 NBA franchises. Sub-Millisecond CBA Engine: Evaluates trades against official CBA rules down to the single dollar in under 1 millisecond. Superstar Protection & In-Trade Anchors (🔒): Roster Superstar Locks: Protects franchise cornerstones (e.g., Steph Curry, Nikola Jokić) from ever being touched by automated solvers. Trade Card Anchors: Lets humans pin marquee trade targets as immutable centerpieces, instructing the AI to only manipulate flexible bench contracts. Autonomous Multi-Team Balancing & Facilitator Routing: The AI agent autonomously discovers 3rd-party facilitator teams with matching TPE vouchers or cap space to absorb excess salary, solving multi-million-dollar trade deficits automatically. Zero-Hallucination WebMCP Bridge: Exposes 8 typed tools ( validate_cba_trade , find_facilitator_teams , auto_balance_trade , etc.) directly on navigator.modelContext , letting browser-native agents inspect, validate, and restructure live trade boards with 100% mathematical precision. How we built it We engineered CapSpace Pro as a modular, high-performance web application coupled with the new WebMCP standard : ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ User Journalist / GM / Fan │ └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ Natural Language & Visual Clicks (🔒) ▼ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Browser-Native AI Agent (WebMCP) │ └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ Typed JSON Tool Invocations ▼ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ CapSpace Pro WebMCP Protocol Bridge │ │ (navigator.modelContext.registerTool) │ └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Deterministic CBA │ │ Reactive React │ │ Constraint Engine │ │ 30-Team Canvas UI │ │ (TypeScript Math) │ │ (Tailwind CSS 3.4) │ └──────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────┘ 1. Deterministic CBA Mathematical Formulation The mathematical engine models the exact piecewise salary-matching brackets defined under the 2023–2030 NBA CBA: A. Non-Taxpaying Teams (Payroll < $170,814,000) Tier 1 (Outgoing ≤ $7,500,000): Allowed Incoming = (200% × Outgoing Salary) + $250,000 Tier 2 ($7,500,000 < Outgoing ≤ $29,000,000): Allowed Incoming = Outgoing Salary + $7,500,000 Tier 3 (Outgoing > $29,000,000): Allowed Incoming = (125% × Outgoing Salary) + $250,000 B. Taxpaying Teams Below First Apron ($170,814,000 ≤ Payroll < $178,132,000) Allowed Incoming = (110% × Outgoing Salary) + $250,000 C. First & Second Apron Teams (Payroll ≥ $178,132,000) Allowed Incoming = 100% × Outgoing Salary ($0 allowable surplus) Second Apron Freeze (≥ $188,931,000): Aggregation Allowed = FALSE (prohibits combining multiple outgoing contracts). D. Traded Player Exception (TPE) Absorption Condition For an incoming contract to be legally absorbed into an existing TPE by facilitator team F: Contract Incoming ≤ TPE Size + $250,000 Roster Size(F) < 15 contracts Post-Trade Payroll(F) ≤ Hard Cap / Apron Ceiling 2. Full Suite of 8 WebMCP Tools Implemented via modelContextBridge.ts exposing both read-only and mutation interfaces: list_all_teams ( readOnly ) get_team_cap_status ( readOnly ) validate_cba_trade ( readOnly ) find_facilitator_teams ( readOnly ) set_player_protection ( mutation ) route_salary_to_tpe ( mutation ) auto_balance_trade ( mutation ) reset_trade ( mutation ) 3. Tech Stack Frontend: React 18, TypeScript 5.5, Vite, Lucide Icons Styling & Design: Tailwind CSS 3.4 with custom glassmorphic sports dark mode Testing: Vitest test suite with 38 unit and integration tests passing with 0 vulnerabilities Challenges we ran into Preserving Human Intent during Autonomous Balancing: Early versions of automated balancing would solve financial parity by arbitrarily moving superstar players. We solved this by creating a two-tier locking architecture: Roster Superstar Protection (protects franchise players from leaving) and In-Trade Anchors (pins the trade centerpiece so the AI only optimizes secondary bench assets). QUick Browser Execution for WebMCP: We had to ensure that the combinatorial search across 30 rosters and dozens of active TPE vouchers executed synchronously in the browser sandbox without causing UI freezes or async lag during live agent conversations. Google Chrome webmcp on Ubuntu not worked. Hence decided to go with ChatGpt in app browser. Accomplishments that we're proud of Zero-Hallucination Agent Governance: By offloading mathematical logic to a deterministic TypeScript rule engine, the AI agent is physically incapable of proposing an illegal trade. Democratizing Front-Office Analytics for Fans & Media: Making the complex 676-page CBA accessible to anyone. A journalist evaluating trade rumors or a fan testing deadline theories can simply speak in plain English to an AI co-pilot and get legally vetted, dollar-precise front-office scenarios in sub-milliseconds. Clean, Accessible UX: High information density displaying 30 teams, roster breakdowns, financial health bars, and interactive trade cards without clutter. What we learned Why WebMCP is the Future of Domain-Specific AI: Large Language Models excel at natural language understanding and strategic high-level reasoning, but struggle with strict multi-tier arithmetic. WebMCP acts as the ultimate bridge: the agent brings user empathy and strategic intent, while the browser tool engine provides mathematical certainty. What's next for CapSpace Pro Multi-Year Cap Projections: Allowing GMs to simulate trades 2–3 seasons into the future to forecast luxury tax repeater penalties. Multi-League Expansion: Porting the WebMCP constraint engine to other complex salary cap leagues, such as the NFL hard cap and NHL salary ceiling . title: PawPilot
pitch: PawPilot is a WebMCP-powered pet-care agent that turns natural language into action
about_excerpt: PawPilot is a WebMCP-powered pet-care agent that turns natural language into action Like Comment Story Updates PawPilot — Project Story Try the live agent demo Live agent demo: https://agent-6a965dc9f0937d545273e692--pawpilot-webmcp.netlify.app This is the agent-facing PawPilot deployment used for the demo experience. The underlying WebMCP capabilities, server-side validation, human approval boundary, and persisted care-plan workflow remain part of the PawPilot application. What inspired me PawPilot started with a simple question: What if talking to a pet-care website could feel as natural as talking to an assistant? Pet care is full of information—profiles, routines, products, services, and care plans—but people are still expected to click through pages and menus to make something happen. I wanted to see what would happen if the website could actually understand what an agent needs to do. So I built PawPilot around my dog Dojo and started turning a normal pet-care website into something an agent could actually work with. That became my experiment with the agentic web: PawPilot. Why WebMCP matters to me WebMCP changes the interaction model from People → Pages → Buttons toward People → Agents → Capabilities. That idea really clicked for me. Instead of an agent having to guess what a website can do by looking at text and buttons, PawPilot explicitly tells the agent what capabilities are available. PawPilot exposes six structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext: get_pet_profile get_daily_needs find_pet_services find_pet_products save_care_plan list_care_plans The result is a website that can participate in an agent conversation instead of just waiting for a person to navigate it. What people and agents can do together A person can simply ask: “Build Dojo a care plan for today.” From there, the agent can use PawPilot's structured capabilities to retrieve Dojo's profile, understand his daily needs, find relevant services or products, and prepare a proposed care plan. But I didn't want “agentic” to mean “the agent gets to do whatever it wants.” The important boundary is the write operation. PawPilot does not allow the OpenAI agent to silently save a care plan. The person gets to see what is being proposed and explicitly chooses Confirm & Save. Only then does the server issue a short-lived approval token tied to that exact pet and exact plan before accepting the database write. So the collaboration loop becomes: User request → Agent discovers capabilities → Agent prepares action → Human reviews → Human approves → Server verifies → Action is saved That separation between what an agent can discover, what it can execute, and what a human must authorize became one of the most important parts of PawPilot for me. I didn't stop at the website — I built a Safari WebMCP Bridge While I was building PawPilot, I ran into another question: what happens when the browser experience around WebMCP isn't there yet? Instead of treating that as a reason to stop, I built a PawPilot WebMCP Bridge Safari Web Extension alongside the application. This part matters because I wasn't trying to fake native WebMCP support. The extension is deliberately a browser-side inspection, compatibility, and testing layer. PawPilot's own WebMCP registration and server-side authorization remain the source of truth. The extension can detect native WebMCP through document.modelContext, discover tools with getTools(), and, when the runtime supports it, invoke executeTool(). It also treats write-capable tools differently and requires explicit confirmation before executing them. I gave the extension its own little developer workspace too: an in-page PawPilot WebMCP Console, a Safari-friendly popup dashboard, live tool and toolchange monitoring, runtime and Permissions Policy diagnostics, background event history, and structured report export. I also ran into one of those very real browser problems that doesn't show up in a clean architecture diagram. Safari/WebKit was giving me a WebKitBlobResource failure around report downloads. I changed the exporter to use a data: URL instead of Blob URLs and URL.createObjectURL(). That made the export path Safari-safe and taught me something I probably wouldn't have learned by only testing in one browser. The extension is kept separate under safari-extension/ specifically so it can inspect PawPilot without modifying the existing WebMCP registration. That separation was intentional: the bridge can tell me what the browser actually supports instead of pretending native support exists when it doesn't. And then PawPilot needed somewhere to remember what happened I also didn't want the care-plan part of the demo to be a fake screen that only looked like it saved something. PawPilot uses a Netlify-hosted database with Drizzle migrations to persist care plans. The application has a database migration for the care_plans data, and the server-side tool layer performs the validation and persistence after the approval boundary has been satisfied. That gives the demo a complete path from agent request to real application state: WebMCP capability → validated operation → human approval → authorized server write → persisted care plan That was important to me because I wanted the “action” in agentic web to actually mean something. The agent isn't just generating text about a care plan; PawPilot can turn that approved plan into saved application state. How I built it PawPilot is a Next.js application deployed on Netlify with a browser-native WebMCP layer. The WebMCP client registers the six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(), including descriptions, JSON input schemas, read/write annotations, and executable handlers. Tool execution is routed through the application's server-side validation layer rather than trusting browser-provided parameters. The OpenAI interaction layer uses the same centralized tool catalog for its agent-facing read capabilities, while save_care_plan remains UI-controlled. This keeps the WebMCP surface and application implementation aligned instead of creating a separate set of business rules for every integration. The Safari WebMCP Bridge lives separately under safari-extension/ so it can inspect PawPilot without modifying the application's existing WebMCP registration. Its content script handles discovery, diagnostics, events, and controlled execution; the popup provides the developer-facing controls; and the background script keeps bridge event history. The care-plan persistence path uses the Netlify database and Drizzle migration already in the project. The database write remains behind the same server-side approval and validation boundary as the rest of the application. Browser testing: real WebMCP calls I tested PawPilot with WebMCP enabled in Microsoft Edge and Google Chrome. I didn't want to stop at seeing a WebMCP object on the page. The six tools were exposed through document.modelContext, discovered with getTools(), and actually invoked through executeTool() against live PawPilot implementations. The Safari extension gives me another way to inspect that capability surface and see what the browser/runtime is actually exposing. That distinction matters: PawPilot isn't just an HTTP API with “WebMCP” written on top of it. The website exposes structured capabilities through the WebMCP surface, and those capabilities connect to real application behavior and persisted state. Challenges WebMCP is an emerging standard, which meant I had to learn while building. Browser support and developer tooling are still evolving, and testing exposed differences between environments. I ended up separating several things that are easy to blur together: The website registering its capabilities The browser exposing those capabilities The agent discovering and using them The server validating and executing the underlying operation The database persisting the approved result The human deciding whether a consequential action should actually happen Building the Safari Bridge made that separation even clearer. A browser tool shouldn't quietly pretend that native support exists. It should tell you what is really happening and give you useful diagnostics when it doesn't. Safety and trust PawPilot is a demo of controlled agentic action, not autonomous pet-care decision making. Read operations can be performed through structured tools. A care-plan write requires explicit human confirmation and a server-generated approval challenge tied to the exact proposed payload. Approval tokens are short-lived and single-use within the active server instance. The demo does not claim user identity or authentication. The approval mechanism is an action-authorization boundary for this demo, not an identity system. I wanted that distinction to be clear rather than hiding it behind impressive-sounding AI language. title: REDLINE
pitch: A browser agent can propose shared changes, but only a human decides what becomes real. REDLINE makes that authority boundary visible with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A browser agent can propose shared changes, but only a human decides what becomes real. REDLINE makes that authority boundary visible with WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Shared plan — before the agent proposal Agent proposal — 5 changes, not committed Human review — 4 accepted, 1 rejected Committed result — only the accepted subset becomes shared state Architecture — page-held authority with exactly three WebMCP tools Inspiration AI agents can already read context and invoke tools. The harder question is what happens when an agent proposes a change that affects more than one person. Most interfaces collapse proposal and execution into the same moment. REDLINE explores a different boundary: an agent can prepare shared work, everyone affected can see it, but human review remains authoritative before anything becomes committed state. What it does REDLINE is a browser-local shared planning environment for two people: Alex, the reviewer, and Sam, a read-only observer. A visiting browser agent reads the live planning context through WebMCP and stages five typed changes as one proposal. Those changes immediately appear as visible, uncommitted proposal state in both browser views. Alex reviews each operation independently. In the canonical scenario, four changes are accepted and the proposed Browser QA compression is rejected. The projected outcome therefore changes from a Friday launch with compressed QA to a Monday launch with the full two-day QA window retained. Only the accepted subset becomes committed state. Sam sees the proposal, review decisions, and final result, but cannot stage, review, commit, or reset shared state. How we built it REDLINE is a deterministic TypeScript browser application built around three WebMCP tools: get_current_view reads the live browser-local planning context. propose_changes stages an atomic typed proposal against an expected plan revision. commit_proposal finalizes only the subset accepted through the page's human review state. The commit contract deliberately accepts only a proposal ID and expected proposal revision. It does not accept operation IDs or human acceptance decisions, so an agent cannot widen its own authority at commit time. The application also implements stale-revision refusals, deterministic impact calculation, idempotent commit receipts, synchronized same-origin views, and explicit observer-only enforcement. REDLINE uses native BroadcastChannel synchronization between the two open browser views. There is deliberately no server, backend, or database: the proposal exists only in the open page. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the capability boundary between the visiting browser agent and REDLINE. Instead of exposing generic page automation, REDLINE exposes exactly three typed capabilities corresponding to the lifecycle of shared work: read context, stage a proposal, and commit an already-reviewed proposal. The page retains the authority the agent must not possess. WebMCP therefore does more than provide tool access here: its contracts define what authority crosses the browser-agent boundary and, just as importantly, what authority does not. Challenges The main challenge was preserving a strict distinction between proposed state, human-reviewed state, and committed state while keeping two browser views synchronized. The commit path also had to remain safe under retries and stale state. Repeating an already-applied commit returns the same receipt without duplicating mutation, while stale plan or proposal revisions return structured refusals without changing state. A second challenge was making these boundaries visible. Proposal geometry, human decisions, observer restrictions, projected impact, and final attribution all needed to remain understandable without hiding the underlying authority model. Accomplishments that we're proud of Exactly three typed WebMCP tools with deliberately bounded authority. Atomic proposal staging without immediate mutation of committed state. Human acceptance decisions that cannot be supplied through commit_proposal . Read-only synchronized observation for Sam. Deterministic projected impact before commit. Structured stale-revision refusal. Idempotent commit behavior. 31 passing behavioral, contract, and presentation invariant tests. A fully browser-local architecture with no backend or database. What we learned Agent tooling is only one part of the problem. Once agents operate inside collaborative applications, proposal visibility, authority ownership, concurrency, retries, and attribution become first-class interface and systems concerns. The most important boundary in REDLINE is therefore not whether the agent can call a tool. It is whether calling that tool can carry authority that belongs to a human. What's next REDLINE is intentionally narrow: one shared plan, two people, one proposal lifecycle. The next step would be to explore how the same explicit proposal-before-commit model generalizes to richer collaborative workflows while preserving typed authority boundaries and deterministic review semantics. title: StocksBrew Decision Room
pitch: An agent compares the stocks. You review the trade-offs. The save tool only appears after you approve.
about_excerpt: An agent compares the stocks. You review the trade-offs. The save tool only appears after you approve. Like Comment Story Updates the problem Stock research usually ends with more tabs, more scores, and no clean decision. Agents can do the comparison faster, but a financial workflow should never hide the rules or quietly turn a suggestion into an action. what it does StocksBrew Decision Room puts the whole handoff on one page. You set the goal, time horizon, sector limit, risk limit, valuation limit, holdings, and any notes the agent should know. The agent reads those visible rules, compares two to five stocks, and renders the scores and portfolio trade-offs on the page. It can then draft one watchlist move with a rationale, evidence, and a price alert. Then it has to stop. At first the page exposes three WebMCP tools: read, compare, and draft. The fourth tool, commit_approved_plan , does not exist until the person reviews the exact plan and clicks approve. Editing the plan, rules, or comparison invalidates that approval and removes the tool. A successful save updates only this browser's local watchlist and alert, then the tool count drops from four back to three. There is no login, broker connection, trade, or money movement. why WebMCP matters here This workflow works because the browser is shared ground. The person and the agent see the same rules, evidence, proposal, approval state, and activity trail. The safety boundary is enforced by the tool lifecycle itself, not by asking the model to remember a warning buried in a prompt. The visible 3 → 4 → 3 tool transition is the product: compare and draft are always available; the final save capability is temporary, narrow, and earned by a specific human approval. how it was built Native document.modelContext.registerTool WebMCP tools Dynamic registration and teardown with AbortController Exact proposal id plus short-lived approval token for the final tool Validation at every input boundary and stale-approval rejection Visible activity trail and browser-local state Public StocksBrew comparison data with a deterministic dated snapshot fallback Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no runtime dependencies Node's built-in test runner covering validation, mandate consequences, approval invalidation, local-only commit behavior, deterministic fixture data, and tool descriptor budgets GitHub Pages deployment with no account or secret required the hard parts The hardest part was making dynamic permissions behave correctly during real browser timing. Approval can change while a tool registration is still in flight, so teardown has to cancel the old registration and restore the three-tool state without leaving a stale save capability behind. The other challenge was making the demo dependable for judges. GitHub Pages cannot run the optional proxy, so the app falls back to a bundled, dated StocksBrew snapshot. A fresh clone and the public URL still show the complete workflow without credentials or a live market dependency. what I learned WebMCP is strongest when a webpage already contains meaningful state and controls. The agent should not replace that interface. It should work through it, leave evidence behind, and gain sensitive capabilities only when the person has made the relevant choice. For high-consequence actions, a missing tool is a clearer boundary than a powerful tool plus a paragraph asking the model to be careful. what is next The next step would be reusable approval gates for other consequential browser workflows: publishing, account changes, portfolio rebalancing drafts, and team approvals. Each integration should keep the same rule: show the exact proposed change, bind approval to it, expire the capability when context changes, and leave an audit trail. title: WebMCP Operator Workspace
pitch: A shared workspace where WebMCP agents discover context-aware tools, prepare visible work, and apply sensitive actions only after human approval.
about_excerpt: A shared workspace where WebMCP agents discover context-aware tools, prepare visible work, and apply sensitive actions only after human approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration## Inspiration A website should be able to tell an AI agent what it can do, rather than making the agent infer every operation from visual controls. We built WebMCP Operator Workspace to explore a practical question: how can a human and an agent share an operational workspace while keeping capabilities contextual and sensitive decisions human-controlled? What it does The application presents a fictional hotel refrigeration incident across two pages: Case Workspace and Asset Inspector. In Case Workspace, an agent can read the incident, prepare a work plan, draft a customer update, select equipment components and prepare contextual observations. Prepared work appears in the interface for the human to review. The capability surface changes with context: Case Workspace initially exposes 11 tools. Selecting a component activates two additional tools, bringing the total to 13. Clearing the selection withdraws those tools, returning to 11. Navigating to Asset Inspector exposes six tools for that page. For sensitive proposals, the application separates preparation from approval. Applying a pending proposal is blocked. A human reviews it and clicks Approve in the page. The agent can then apply that proposal once; repeating it is rejected. There is no registered WebMCP tool to approve a proposal. On Asset Inspector, the agent can prepare an inspection note, but the final form save remains a human UI action. How we built it The project is a standalone application built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages. It registers structured capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Contextual tools are withdrawn using AbortSignal, and each document registers its relevant tool surface. A semantic capability tree describes declared pages, interface regions and capabilities. It distinguishes application contracts from runtime observations: observing an unexpected tool does not automatically add it to the application's authorized surface. Navigation uses declared page identifiers rather than arbitrary URLs. Proposal handling uses explicit states and single-use approval consumption. The reviewed candidate passed 49 automated tests covering application contracts and behaviors, including approval states, replay rejection and contextual lifecycle scenarios. GitHub Actions runs the test suite. Challenges we faced The main challenge was separating three concepts: discovering a capability, preparing work and having authority to apply a sensitive proposal. Contextual tools must disappear when their context ends. Registration failures must not leave a partially active surface. Navigation must expose the destination page's capabilities rather than preserve stale assumptions. We also needed the interface to distinguish a prepared draft from a saved note, and an approved proposal from an applied action. What we learned WebMCP is useful not only for exposing operations, but also for making the agent-facing interface reflect the current application context. Visible shared state helps the human understand what the agent prepared. Explicit approval states make the transition from proposal to application understandable and testable. Accomplishments We combined contextual tool registration, a multipage capability surface, visible agent-prepared work and a human approval workflow in one publicly accessible application. The result demonstrates a complete application-level sequence: proposal, blocked premature application, human approval, single application and replay rejection. How to try it Open the live application with a WebMCP-compatible agent client and enter the workspace. Ask the agent to read the case, select condenser_fan, prepare an observation and clear the selection. Next, request a sensitive-action proposal and observe the blocked attempt before approving it manually. Ask the agent to apply the approved proposal and then repeat the same proposal to test replay rejection. Finally, navigate to asset-inspector and prepare an inspection note without submitting the human form. The application does not require our developer tunnel, proprietary Universal MCP runtime or credentials. An ordinary browser can display the human interface, but agent invocation requires a WebMCP-compatible client. Scope and limitations All incident, customer and equipment data is fictional. State is in memory and local to the active page; reloads and navigation do not promise persistence. Drafts do not send messages. Applying a proposal records a local demo event; it does not dispatch a technician or operate real equipment. The approval boundary demonstrates application workflow enforcement, not server-side authentication or protection against arbitrary browser automation. The accompanying video is an AI-generated explanation created with NotebookLM, not a screen recording of execution. What's next We would explore further usability testing and carefully scoped operational integrations. Persistence, identity and server-enforced authorization would require additional design before production use.
