title: Know Before Yes
pitch: Turn a website-and-app offer into a decision-ready draft—and export only the exact revision a human approves.
about_excerpt: Turn a website-and-app offer into a decision-ready draft—and export only the exact revision a human approves. Like Comment Story Updates Problem A nontechnical small-business owner can receive a polished website-and-app offer that names a price, timeline, and attractive outcomes while leaving ownership, data boundaries, the app's unique job, success measures, and long-term support unresolved. Those omissions are difficult to find and compare before the buyer commits to the wrong build. Solution Know Before Yes is a static WebMCP decision-planning tool from Sykes Holding Group LLC. Its default judge path uses a bundled fictional vendor offer. A secondary, human-activated lane accepts only closed, general, nonidentifying scenario categories. An agent can discover seven focused tools, inspect the scenario, identify source-bound missing decisions, compare three practical paths, and stage a decision-ready draft. Premature commit and export calls return structured rejections without changing approved state. Only the visible human control can approve the exact staged revision. The agent can then read that approval status, commit the matching revision in the current session, and export the same revision as a local Markdown or JSON draft. Agent analyzes. Human decides. The web tool exports what was approved. Why This Matters Small-business buyers often need structured technical judgment before they need a larger project-management system. Know Before Yes makes the missing decisions, tradeoffs, and authority boundary visible without asking the user to upload a proposal, create an account, or hand control to an agent. WebMCP is central to the experience. The agent discovers typed capabilities and works through shared structured state instead of scraping cards, imitating clicks, or inventing facts. People and agents can now collaborate on a concrete draft while the page itself preserves the visible human decision boundary. The current V1 demonstrates this workflow; it does not claim real-customer validation, vendor selection, purchasing authority, professional advice, guaranteed savings, guaranteed growth, or an external-system write. How We Used AI The released web tool runs no model and requires no API key. A WebMCP-capable browser or agent supplies reasoning outside the page and invokes explicit contracts. The page returns deterministic structured results and enforces staged-versus-approved state in its own local state machine. During development, native WebMCP testing used OpenAI Codex's in-app browser and Google Chrome 151 with WebMCP enabled. The final permanent-host proof used OpenAI Codex's in-app browser. Two fresh native flows invoked all seven tools, returned both preapproval denials, recorded visible UI-only approval, read back human_approved and canCommit=true, and committed/exported exact revision rev-001-staged_platform. Clean run A completed in 42.564 seconds; judge-paced run B completed in 81.401 seconds. The final run produced a 2,153-character export and no browser-console error or warning. The clearly labeled Preview Adapter was used only for deterministic fallback rehearsal and is not presented as native proof. How We Used Codex OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT Work helped convert the initial product idea into a bounded scope, product requirements, technical specification, implementation checklist, static application, automated tests, browser-validation plan, public-release contract, and this Devpost draft. Codex helped implement and challenge the seven-tool design, the exact-revision approval state machine, source-bound missing-decision results, structured preapproval errors, local export, lifecycle reset behavior, closed-enum scenario mode, privacy/claims boundaries, public release manifest, and automated product and viability gates. Independent technical, privacy/policy, and product-story reviews caught and corrected stale-session restoration, overstated build-ready wording, and nonfunctional structured inputs before the public candidate was frozen. Approved AI-tool disclosure: OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT Work for product planning, implementation, debugging, testing, browser validation, evidence reconciliation, release preparation, and submission drafting. Key Features Structured offer inspection — returns scope, cost signals, exclusions, and clarity risks without changing decision state. Source-bound missing decisions — ties every question to a specific omission or general-category input instead of inventing evidence. Three practical paths — compares website-first, staged website-to-app, and combined-launch paths by fit, speed, cost shape, risk, and assumptions without claiming a universal best answer. Reversible staging — creates a deterministic revision id, leaves approved state unchanged, and invalidates stale approval. Visible human gate — no agent-facing approval tool exists; only the visible UI can record human-ui approval for the exact staged revision. Two explicit denials — premature commit returns HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED; premature export returns APPROVED_BLUEPRINT_REQUIRED. Exact-revision proof — approval status, committed state, UI, and Markdown/JSON export carry the same revision id. Two privacy-bounded modes — a resettable bundled fictional offer and an optional human-activated closed-enum general-category scenario. Static and state-free by design — no backend, accounts, persistence, analytics, uploads, payment, runtime dependency, or application network call. WebMCP Tool Inventory inspect_vendor_offer find_missing_decisions compare_solution_paths stage_blueprint_revision get_approval_status commit_approved_blueprint export_build_blueprint The page defines exactly these seven tool contracts and conditionally registers them when document.modelContext is available. Structured scenario activation and human approval remain visible human UI actions, not eighth and ninth tools. Architecture Dependency-free static HTML, CSS, and browser JavaScript modules Pure in-memory decision domain in src/domain.js Seven WebMCP contracts and conditional registration in src/tools.js Shared UI/tool rendering, lifecycle reset, and user-initiated local download in src/app.js Static hosting headers for CSP, tools permission, origin isolation, MIME sniffing, referrer handling, framing/form restrictions, and HTTPS transport Node's built-in test runner plus focused P0 and viability gates No backend, database, login, analytics, telemetry, payment, OCR, upload, external model call, or persistence The WebMCP client may process selected categories and tool results under its own terms and privacy settings. Static hosting may process ordinary connection and security metadata, but SHG does not operate a scenario-content endpoint. Testing Instructions Public judge flow — permanent host and final native proof verified No credentials are required. Open https://knowbeforeyes.sykesholdinggroup.com/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Select Reset and confirm the page shows the bundled fictional scenario. Discover these seven tools: inspect_vendor_offer, find_missing_decisions, compare_solution_paths, stage_blueprint_revision, get_approval_status, commit_approved_blueprint, and export_build_blueprint. Invoke the first three tools and confirm one source-bound gap and the three named path tradeoffs. Invoke stage_blueprint_revision for staged_platform; confirm approved state remains unchanged. Invoke commit_approved_blueprint; confirm HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED and approvedStateChanged=false. Invoke export_build_blueprint; confirm APPROVED_BLUEPRINT_REQUIRED. Use the visible Approve exact revision control. Invoke get_approval_status; confirm the staged revision id, source human-ui, status human_approved, and canCommit=true. Invoke commit_approved_blueprint, then export_build_blueprint; confirm staged, approved, committed, and exported revision ids match. Confirm the before/after summary, unresolved decisions, and local download boundary; then Reset again to prove repeatability. This text is ready to paste into Devpost field 28255; the stable hostname and final signed-out run are verified. Update it only if the final evidence changes. Repository verification From the public repository root: npm test npm run p0:product npm run gate npm run serve Open http://localhost:4173 . Native discovery requires a supporting WebMCP client; otherwise the page truthfully identifies the Preview Adapter. Judging-Criteria Map WebMCP Leverage Seven typed, non-overlapping contracts divide inspection, gap discovery, comparison, staging, status, gated commit, and export. The same structured state powers tool results, UI, rejection semantics, approval, and exact export. WebMCP is the operating collaboration layer, not a decorative prompt wrapper. Execution The product has a coherent resettable workflow, responsive UI, explicit errors, visible human decision control, local exports, a bounded second scenario mode, public source, and repeatable automated gat

title: Grid — Spreadsheets with your agent
pitch: Co-edit a live spreadsheet with ChatGPT. WebMCP tools read ranges, set cells/formulas, sort, filter, chart, and highlight on the open grid — you see every change.
about_excerpt: Co-edit a live spreadsheet with ChatGPT. WebMCP tools read ranges, set cells/formulas, sort, filter, chart, and highlight on the open grid — you see every change. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most “AI for spreadsheets” still lives in a chat sidebar or a separate Sheets API. You describe a budget; you get a table pasted back into the thread — not co-editing the grid you’re staring at. Google Sheets has Gemini-style help and backend MCP connectors, but the live sheets.google.com page is not exposing WebMCP tools on the open workbook. That gap is the point of the challenge: shared client state . Grid was inspired by that white space — and by Flavio’s note that spreadsheets are strong WebMCP cases because the open page holds state a remote API may not. What if ChatGPT and a human shared one workbook, with the agent writing cells, formulas, sorts, charts, and highlights you watch appear live? What it does Grid is an agent-native shared spreadsheet: Co-edit a seeded “Move budget — London” workbook toward a £4k total Read and write ranges, set formulas ( =SUM , arithmetic), sort and filter rows Highlight cells, add/remove a simple chart, insert rows/cols, export CSV Full human UI (formula bar, selection, editable cells) that works with WebMCP idle 17 WebMCP site tools on the same Zustand store as your clicks Agent tools panel + activity feed; ?demo=1 (optional delay / delayMs ) for judges and screencasts You steer in plain English in ChatGPT; Grid’s tools update the open grid in real time. Side effects like export_csv , clear_highlights , and remove_chart are annotated so confirmation policies can apply. How we built it Vite + React 19 + TypeScript SPA ( base: '/grid-webmcp/' ) Zustand as the single source of truth for the React UI and every WebMCP execute handler WebMCP via document.modelContext.registerTool (with navigator.modelContext fallback), feature-detected on the top-level page Lightweight formula evaluation, SVG chart panel, filter/highlight overlays MIT-licensed, client-only, no backend or secrets — GitHub Pages Built with Codex Core tools: get_workbook_state , get_range , set_cells , set_formula , clear_range , select_range , sort_range , filter_rows , clear_filter , highlight_cells , clear_highlights , add_chart , remove_chart , insert_rows , insert_cols , export_csv , list_activity . Challenges we ran into Same-state collaboration — agent tools and keyboard edits must never drift. Both paths go through one store. Formulas without a full engine — enough SUM + arithmetic for a credible budget demo, without shipping Excel. Read vs write vs side effect — inspection tools stay read-only; clears, chart removal, and CSV export are explicit side effects. Demo without a live agent — ?demo=1 replays the happy path for screencasts while real tools still register for ChatGPT’s in-app browser. Staying distinct — orthogonal to Nest (flats), Frame (canvas), Brief (evidence), and Redline (propose ≠ commit). Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete co-edit loop on one grid: fill → formula → sort → chart → highlight → export Non-trivial WebMCP surface (17 tools), not a single toy cell writer Human-first UI that stays usable if WebMCP is missing A fifth submission that targets a category often confused with “Sheets already does AI” — and shows the difference is tools on the open page What we learned WebMCP’s superpower is co-presence. Spreadsheets prove it cleanly: when set_formula runs, you watch the contingency cell resolve; when add_chart runs, the bar appears beside the sheet. That shared visual ground is harder to fake with a headless Sheets API MCP — and it’s exactly what Grid is for. What's next for Grid — Spreadsheets with your agent Richer formula surface (IF, VLOOKUP-class helpers) and named ranges Multi-sheet workbooks and freeze panes Conditional formatting tools the agent can propose and you confirm Presence cursors when multiple humans join the same workbook Deeper ChatGPT desktop testing with confirmation UX on destructive tools Built With codex Try it out omercelik.github.io Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Serdar Murat ÇELİK Omer Celik Abdulhamit Mabocoglu Like Share this project: Updates Omer Celik started this project — Sep 02, 2026 07:27 PM EDT

title: Knoww
pitch: Knoww is the prediction market layer for the internet. It turns research and live market odds into a shared human-agent workspace for taking trades and preparing decisions with people in final control
about_excerpt: Knoww is the prediction market layer for the internet. It turns research and live market odds into a shared human-agent workspace for taking trades and preparing decisions with people in final control Like Comment Story Updates What Knoww does Knoww turns live prediction markets into a shared research workspace where people and agents can explore market information together. A person can ask an agent to find relevant events, narrow the visible market list, open a valid result, compare related markets, inspect the selected order book, change the chart range, and prepare the trade interface for review. Every step happens on the same page the person is viewing. The result remains visible, understandable, and easy to correct. Knoww gives the agent structured access to market discovery and analysis without giving it control of a wallet, a signature, or trade submission. The problem Prediction market research involves more than opening a result page. A single event may contain several related markets, outcomes, probabilities, charts, and order books. The useful context also depends on the filters, selected market, and chart range currently visible on the page. A browser agent can attempt to reconstruct this workflow through page inspection and clicks, but it must infer the meaning of interface elements and continuously track changing page state. That process can be fragile. WebMCP lets Knoww expose the meaning behind the interface directly. Instead of guessing which card, control, or outcome represents the user's intent, the agent receives narrow and typed operations connected to the current page. Why WebMCP is the right fit A separate market data integration could return probabilities and market information, but it would not naturally share the interface state the person is currently inspecting. WebMCP allows the person and the agent to work with the same filters, selected market, order book, and chart range. When the agent changes something, the person sees the result immediately through the normal Knoww interface. This creates one continuous research workflow. The agent can discover relevant events, narrow the market list, open a valid result, compare related markets, inspect the selected order book, adjust the chart range, and prepare the trade interface for review. Every action remains visible on the page. The person can verify the result, correct the agent, or stop the workflow at any point. What I built I added 12 WebMCP tools across the market discovery page and individual event pages. On /markets , get_markets_page_context reads the current page state. search_events searches public events. set_market_filters changes only supported visible filters. load_more_markets advances the visible results. open_event can open only an event already returned by Knoww. On an event page, get_current_event_context reads the active event and current selection. find_markets_on_page finds relevant markets within the event. compare_markets returns a focused comparison. get_selected_order_book reads the currently selected order book. select_market_view changes the visible market. set_chart_range changes the visible chart period. prepare_trade prepares the trade interface for the person to review. The available tools change with the page context. The market discovery page exposes discovery and navigation capabilities. An event page exposes comparison, order book, chart, and trade preparation capabilities. This keeps the tool set focused while supporting a complete workflow from market discovery to decision preparation. Example experience A person can ask: "Find Bitcoin related prediction markets, narrow the list, open the most relevant event, compare its markets, inspect the selected order book, and prepare the trade view for my review." The agent can complete this workflow through structured WebMCP tools while the person watches the same page change and remains free to correct any step. This is more reliable than asking the agent to infer the entire workflow from buttons, cards, and page layout. Human control and safety The WebMCP tools cannot connect a wallet, sign a transaction, or submit a trade. prepare_trade only prepares the visible trade interface. The person must inspect the values and complete any action with financial consequences. Every tool uses a typed and bounded input schema. Search limits, filter values, pagination, and navigation targets are constrained. open_event accepts only events already returned by Knoww. Tool results are marked as untrusted public content. These boundaries give the agent enough capability to provide meaningful assistance while preserving human control. Technical implementation Knoww uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript, and is deployed with Cloudflare Workers. It reads public Polymarket market data. I connected the WebMCP handlers to Knoww's existing React state and page actions instead of recreating the market logic in a separate integration. This means the person and the agent work with the same filters, selected market, order book, and chart range. When a tool changes the page state, the normal Knoww interface reflects that change. Tool registration runs through top level page JavaScript so the tools can be discovered by ChatGPT's in app browser. I also added registration cleanup so a normal React unmount does not incorrectly report a registration failure. Testing I tested the production /markets page in ChatGPT's in app browser. ChatGPT discovered all five tools registered on that page. I successfully executed get_markets_page_context and used search_events to find Bitcoin related events on the live production site. The remaining seven tools are registered only on event pages, where their event specific context is available. Challenges and lessons The difficult part was not exposing more control. It was deciding exactly which control the agent should receive. The WebMCP tools had to stay synchronized with React state while maintaining clear boundaries. Search limits, filter values, pagination, navigation targets, and available page actions all needed to be constrained. The page lifecycle also required careful handling so route changes and normal React cleanup did not appear as tool registration failures. The most important lesson was that WebMCP is strongest when it reveals the semantics of an existing interface without bypassing that interface or its permission model. Knoww now gives an agent enough structure to help someone reason about live prediction markets, while stopping exactly where financial authority should remain with the person. title: Pipeline OS
pitch: Human-led hiring, agent-powered execution, one shared pipeline.
about_excerpt: Human-led hiring, agent-powered execution, one shared pipeline. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Recruiting is a multi-step process involving recruiters, candidates, hiring managers, interviewers, and increasingly, AI assistants. However, people and agents usually interact with separate systems. A human may use a recruiting dashboard while an agent relies on screen scraping, custom APIs, or incomplete information. We wanted to explore what happens when a recruiting application becomes a shared workspace for both people and agents. This inspired PipelineOS : a WebMCP-powered recruiting platform where humans and agents can discover capabilities, perform structured actions, collaborate on decisions, and observe the same live workflow. The demo uses an Indian-context recruiting dataset with candidates such as Ananya Sharma, Rohan Mehta, Kavya Iyer, and Meera Nair, making the experience feel relevant to our target users and region. What it does PipelineOS models the complete hiring lifecycle: Job requisition creation Candidate search and comparison Application submission Explainable candidate screening Interview availability and scheduling Interview feedback Offer generation and response Background checks Benefits enrollment Onboarding checklists Workflow status and activity tracking The Recruiter Dashboard presents applications in a Kanban board across stages such as Applied, Screened, Interviewing, Offer Sent, Offer Accepted, Onboarding, and Rejected. The important difference is that the same operations are available to both the human interface and an AI agent through WebMCP. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Recruiting has structured, multi-step actions that agents need to discover and execute reliably. Instead of asking an agent to interpret buttons or scrape a page, PipelineOS exposes named tools with typed input schemas, descriptions, permissions, and output contracts. An agent can search candidates, read workflow status, prepare interview coordination, and stage onboarding actions using the same operation surface used by the human UI. How it creates a better user experience PipelineOS creates one shared source of truth: Human actions and agent actions update the same recruiting state. Candidates appear in the same Kanban board regardless of who performed the action. Recruiters can see agent activity in the same audit feed as human activity. Agents can handle repetitive research and coordination work. Humans remain in control of consequential decisions. Every operation has a structured result or error instead of an ambiguous UI interaction. This means users do not have to copy information between an AI assistant, spreadsheets, email, and an applicant tracking system. What people and agents can do together Before WebMCP, an agent could potentially read a recruiting page but could not reliably discover or invoke the same application actions as a human. With PipelineOS: A recruiter can ask ChatGPT to find strong backend candidates. ChatGPT can use the page’s WebMCP tools to search the candidate database. The recruiter can review the result in the same PipelineOS workspace. An agent can prepare an onboarding plan without applying it. A human can review the proposed changes, approve them, and commit them. The resulting state change appears in the Kanban and activity feed for everyone. This makes it possible for agents to support hiring operations without giving them unchecked control over sensitive or irreversible actions. How we built it PipelineOS is built as a React and TypeScript web application with an Express server. The WebMCP integration is implemented in src/lib/webmcp.ts . On application startup, PipelineOS registers the canonical operation registry with: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute, annotations }); The application registers 32 recruiting operations from one shared OPERATION_REGISTRY . The registry is also used by: Server-side validation The React UI WebMCP tool registration Documentation pages Capability discovery Approval-policy enforcement Every WebMCP execute callback routes through the same OperationClient used by the UI. The request then passes through: The canonical HTTP API Actor and capability resolution Input validation Authorization and resource-scope checks The shared OperationService Domain rules and lifecycle validation The repository transaction The activity/audit log State synchronization back to the UI There is no separate WebMCP-only business logic path. For sensitive workflows, PipelineOS uses a plan → approve → commit model: plan_operation ↓ human approval card ↓ approve_operation_plan ↓ commit_operation_plan Agents can stage an action, but they cannot approve their own plans. This is enforced server-side. The application also supports: Native document.modelContext registration A navigator-based compatibility adapter A development registry for local testing Structured JSON schemas Actor-scoped permissions Idempotency and stale-state protection Revision-based synchronization Server-sent events A shared activity feed Deterministic synthetic demo data In-memory and Firestore persistence options Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making the human and agent interfaces genuinely share the same behavior instead of simply exposing a second API. We had to ensure that: WebMCP calls and UI clicks use the same operation service. Operations validate and authorize inputs consistently. Failed mutations do not partially update state. Agent permissions are narrower than human permissions. Approval requirements are enforced by the server rather than only described in tool text. Activity entries do not expose private resume data, tokens, consent evidence, or sensitive identifiers. Multiple browser views stay synchronized after an agent call. Repeated requests do not create duplicate applications, interviews, offers, or onboarding records. The demo remains deterministic and easy to reset during judging. Authentication and hosted access were another challenge because the live application needs to be accessible to judges while still protecting recruiter, candidate, and hiring-manager views. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that PipelineOS is more than a WebMCP proof of concept. It is a complete recruiting workflow with a real product experience around the tools. Our main accomplishments include: A complete multi-role recruiting application 32 shared WebMCP operations Native document.modelContext.registerTool integration One operation path for humans and agents A populated Indian-context demo Kanban with candidates across multiple lifecycle stages A shared live activity feed for human and agent actions Explainable, deterministic candidate scoring Human approval cards for consequential agent workflows Server-enforced agent safety rules Actor-scoped authorization and resource permissions Idempotency and atomic state changes Candidate, recruiter, and hiring-manager experiences Documentation that displays the live WebMCP operation registry A deterministic reset flow suitable for demos and judging The most important accomplishment is that an agent can participate in the workflow without becoming an uncontrolled automation layer. It can help with research and preparation, while the human remains responsible for the final consequential action. What we learned We learned that exposing tools is only one part of building an agent-ready application. The surrounding product architecture is equally important. We learned that: Tool descriptions must explain when an operation should be used and what it returns. Input and output schemas make agent behavior more reliable. Agent permissions must be enforced at the server boundary. Human approval should be represented as a real stateful workflow, not just a confirmation message. A shared audit trail is essential when humans and agents work together. Agents need safe read-only discovery tools before they can perform useful actions. The same operation must produce the same result whether it comes from a button, WebMCP, or an MCP client. Deterministic demo data makes an agent workflow much easier to demonstrate and evaluate. WebMCP is most valuable when it changes the interaction model of the application, rather than being added as a thin wrapper around an existing API. What's next for PipelineOS The next step is to connect PipelineOS to durable, production recruiting systems while keeping the same operation registry and WebMCP interface. Planned improvements include: Greenhouse, Lever, and HRIS integrations Durable multi-tenant storage by default Production-grade authentication for recruiters, candidates, and agent connectors Per-organization agent capabilities and approval policies Candidate consent and communication workflows Calendar and email integrations More detailed fairness and compliance reporting Agent-assisted bottleneck and hiring-funnel analysis Candidate-side personal agents Cross-organization ref

title: RecallRadar
pitch: Trace one failed component to every affected unit—and contain it before the next spreadsheet opens
about_excerpt: Trace one failed component to every affected unit—and contain it before the next spreadsheet opens Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Manufacturing quality teams face a critical problem: when a component fails, they must trace it through complex supply chains to identify affected products. Current approaches rely on manual spreadsheet analysis or brittle DOM scraping, leading to either dangerous over-containment (holding unrelated products) or missed affected units. The OpenAI WebMCP Challenge presented an opportunity to demonstrate how AI agents with structured, scoped tool access could solve this problem with precision and human oversight. What it does RecallRadar is a quality-lineage simulator that helps manufacturing quality leads trace failed supplier lots through explicit manufacturing relationships. Users can: Search and trace any seeded lot, batch, unit, warehouse, shipment, or order ID Expand lineage manually or run AI-guided trace through the supply chain Inspect provenance with versioned evidence and corrected records Compare containment scopes (broad, evidence-based, ultra-narrow) to avoid over-containment Preview customer notices for shipped units (notice-only, never auto-sent) Stage and approve inventory holds with full audit trail Commit and undo actions with complete reversibility The hero scenario traces failed capacitor lot CAP-77B to exactly 312 affected units (271 in warehouses, 41 shipped), achieving 0% false positives while avoiding the over-containment that would incorrectly hold 88 unrelated units from lookalike lot CAP-77D. How we built it Tech Stack: Next.js 15 with App Router for the React framework TypeScript for type safety throughout WebMCP (Model Context Protocol) for evidence-scoped AI tool registration OpenAI Sites integration for ChatGPT authentication Google Gemini API (optional) for live AI agent planning Polar for subscription-based entitlements and admin access shadcn/ui for modern, accessible UI components Vitest for unit testing, Playwright for E2E testing Tailwind CSS for styling Architecture: Domain-driven design with separate layers for domain logic, store state machine, and WebMCP tool catalog Server-side API routes for Gemini agent planning and Polar billing Evidence-scoped WebMCP lifecycle that rebuilds tool registrations based on investigation state Deterministic fallback mode that works without any live AI services Human approval boundaries at every critical action (stage, commit, undo) Key Implementation Details: lib/domain.ts contains seed data, lineage traversal, scope comparison, and hold logic lib/store.ts implements the investigation state machine with tool-call logging lib/tool-catalog.ts defines shared WebMCP/Gemini contracts with safe input binding hooks/use-webmcp.ts manages the evidence-scoped WebMCP registration lifecycle app/api/agent/turn/route.ts provides server-only Gemini Interactions tool planning Challenges we ran into WebMCP API Evolution : The WebMCP specification is still in draft, so we had to work with evolving type definitions and browser support. We created a custom type declaration file ( types/webmcp.d.ts ) and built a preview registry for browsers without native WebMCP support. Tool Lifecycle Management : Designing a system where AI tools only become available when appropriate evidence is loaded required careful state machine design. We implemented an evidence-scoped registration system that rebuilds tool availability based on the current investigation step. Safety and Trust : Ensuring that supplier notes and untrusted data couldn't be interpreted as executable instructions required explicit labeling and inert data handling throughout the domain logic. Deterministic Fallback : The challenge required no-live-services demo capability, so we built a complete deterministic fallback that preserves the full user experience without requiring any AI API keys. Human-AI Approval Boundary : Designing the approval workflow required careful UX consideration—Gemini pauses after staging so humans must explicitly click "Approve 271 inventory holds" before the commit tool becomes available. Accomplishments that we're proud of Zero False Positives : The evidence-based scope correctly identifies exactly the 312 affected units from CAP-77B while excluding 88 unrelated units from lookalike lot CAP-77D Full Reversibility : Every commit carries an inverse action, allowing complete undo of all 271 prior states Evidence-Scoped Tools : WebMCP tools only appear when valid for the current investigation state, preventing AI from calling inappropriate actions Deterministic Operation : The entire hero scenario runs locally without any external services, making it reliable for demos and judging Live AI Integration : Optional Gemini integration demonstrates real-time AI planning while maintaining human approval boundaries Comprehensive Testing : 14 deterministic unit/intent tests plus E2E tests covering hero, correction, untrusted-note, and undo flows Production-Ready UI : Apple-style design system with responsive layout and accessibility considerations What we learned WebMCP Power : Evidence-scoped tool registration is far more powerful than giving AI raw data access. By restricting tools to what's valid for the current state, we get both safety and better AI behavior. Human-AI Collaboration : The most effective workflows combine AI planning with human approval. AI handles the complex traversal and scope comparison, while humans make the final containment decisions. Deterministic Design : Building deterministic fallbacks makes AI systems more robust and easier to demo. Users can see the full value without configuring API keys. Domain Modeling : Deep domain modeling (manufacturing lineage, evidence versions, containment scopes) is essential for building effective AI tools in specialized domains. Type Safety : TypeScript's type system was invaluable for maintaining safety across the WebMCP tool catalog and domain logic. What's next for RecallRadar Live ERP Integration : Connect to real manufacturing systems (SAP, Oracle, etc.) for production use Multi-Lot Tracing : Support tracing multiple failed lots simultaneously with scope intersection Predictive Analytics : Add ML models to predict likely affected units based on historical patterns Mobile App : Build a mobile interface for quality teams in the field Collaboration Features : Add team workflows, comments, and approval chains Advanced Visualizations : Interactive graph visualization of supply chain relationships Regulatory Compliance : Automated generation of regulatory recall documentation Real-Time Alerts : Push notifications when new evidence suggests scope expansion Built With webmcp Try it out github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Hector Ta Like Share this project: Updates Hector Ta started this project — Sep 03, 2026 12:58 PM EDT

title: Viernes — Autonomous Gym ERP & Visual Floor Commander
pitch: Agent-native Gym Operations ERP powered by WebMCP. Control 2D floor plans, reschedule classes, and manage churn through direct AI agent browser actions in real-time.
about_excerpt: Agent-native Gym Operations ERP powered by WebMCP. Control 2D floor plans, reschedule classes, and manage churn through direct AI agent browser actions in real-time. Like Comment Story Updates Tactical 2D Floor Commander with real-time zone blueprints, equipment status, and WebMCP agent HUD. Live maintenance filter isolating equipment requiring repairs and active service tickets on the floor. Interactive class scheduling modal with real-time trainer conflict detection and capacity validation. Member Churn Radar tracking attendance decay, churn risk scores, and automated retention vouchers. One-click retention campaign dispatch offering personalized vouchers to high-risk member cohorts. Facility Telemetry & Revenue Sandbox modeling live occupancy, peak hours, and dynamic financial forecasts. Live WebMCP tool execution: the AI agent updates equipment maintenance state and moves classes in real time. 💡 Inspiration Traditional gym management software is clunky, fragmented, and buried behind endless tabs of legacy forms. Facility managers and head coaches waste hours every week manually cross-referencing floor maintenance, juggling trainer shift conflicts, and reacting too late after premium members have already stopped showing up. Inspired by Tony Stark’s tactical AI assistant F.R.I.D.A.Y. , we built VIERNES — an agent-native Gym Operations ERP and Visual Floor Commander that transforms static database software into a real-time, interactive command center powered by the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) . 🚀 What it Does Viernes unites the entire athletic facility's operations into a single reactive workspace where humans and AI agents collaborate seamlessly: 🏟️ Tactical Visual Floor Commander : An interactive 2D blueprint of a 15,000 sq ft facility across 5 zones. Real-time machine operational states, maintenance wear badges, and agent attention pulses. 📅 Dynamic Class Timeline & Trainer Roster : High-density weekly schedule grid with room capacity validation, instant conflict detection, and trainer reassignments. 👥 Member Churn Radar & Retention Center : Algorithmic churn risk scoring (0–100%) tracking attendance decay with one-click personalized re-engagement campaigns. 📈 Facility Telemetry & Revenue Sandbox : Live occupancy heatmaps, equipment duty cycles, and real-time financial sensitivity modeling. 🎙️ Floating Viernes AI Copilot HUD : In-browser agent console with one-click multi-step scenario presets and live WebMCP execution telemetry. 🌐 WebMCP Implementation & Paradigm Shift 1. Why is this use case a strong fit for WebMCP? Athletic facility management is intrinsically visual, spatial, and multi-variable. Instead of forcing AI agents to blindly scrape HTML or make disconnected server calls, WebMCP gives the browser's model direct, typed, programmatic control over live in-memory React state and SVG canvas objects. 2. How does it create a better user experience? A manager can issue a single natural language instruction ("Mark Bench #3 for maintenance and move Coach Marcus's 5:30 PM class to Zone C"), and Viernes executes multiple synchronized UI state changes in milliseconds. The manager sees the 2D floor plan pulse red while the calendar shifts room assignments instantly. 3. What humans and agents can do together now: Before WebMCP, combining 2D asset awareness with dynamic scheduling required hours of manual spreadsheet work. With Viernes: The agent detects at-risk member cohorts, calculates churn probabilities, and populates retention offers. The human reviews proposed changes visually on the floor plan and approves or adjusts them with drag-and-drop ease. The agent simulates revenue forecasts and rebalances class schedules to eliminate bottlenecks. 4. Technical Architecture Viernes registers 6 client-side tools directly onto document.modelContext.registerTool upon mounting: update_gym_floor_equipment manage_class_schedule query_member_cohorts launch_retention_campaign simulate_revenue_forecast get_facility_telemetry All inputs are validated via strict Zod schemas with human-in-the-loop safeguards on sensitive financial and scheduling actions. 🛠️ How We Built It Framework : Next.js 15 (App Router) & React 19 Styling : Tailwind CSS & Framer Motion for obsidian/neon tactical HUD animations State & Schema : Zustand & Zod Protocol : WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) & use-webmcp-tool Icons & UI : Lucide React & Radix UI 🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Zero-latency bidirectional synchronization between agent tool calls and interactive SVG floor elements. A Stark-inspired dark obsidian aesthetic that makes complex facility data immediately actionable. Fully autonomous test suite built with Playwright validating end-to-end tool execution in headless browser sessions. 🔮 What's Next for Viernes Computer vision occupancy tracking via RTSP camera feeds. Multi-branch federation for nationwide gym chains. Direct biometric telemetry integration with wearable health devices. title: Wayfinder
pitch: An agent-native trip planner where people, browser agents, and a live map stay in sync.
about_excerpt: An agent-native trip planner where people, browser agents, and a live map stay in sync. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a trip is naturally collaborative, but most trip tools treat an AI agent as a separate interface. I wanted to explore what becomes possible when a person, their browser agent, and the app itself can all work from the same live plan and map. What it does Wayfinder turns a rough idea—like “a rainy Sunday in Porto with kids”—into a map-ready trip plan. It asks focused follow-up questions about timing, companions, budget, interests, and accessibility, then finds relevant places and keeps the conversation, plan, itinerary, and live map in sync. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can start or resume a trip, answer the guided interview using the visitor’s preferences, update the plan, ask Wayfinder’s place specialist questions, read the itinerary, and move the map—without scraping the UI. How I built it Wayfinder is built with Laravel, Vue, Inertia.js, and WebMCP. The Laravel assistant guides trip discovery, saves structured plans, geocodes named places with Nominatim, and searches OpenStreetMap data through Overpass. Vue manages the interactive conversation and map experience. I implemented 18 WebMCP tools: two safe guest-only navigation tools and 16 authenticated trip, chat, itinerary, and map tools. Tools are registered reactively according to the visitor’s login state and current trip phase, so agents only see capabilities that are relevant and safe at that moment. Challenges I ran into The core challenge was making WebMCP useful in a genuinely stateful product. A trip planner has many moving parts: the active discovery question, saved preferences, conversation history, selected trip, itinerary, and map viewport. I needed browser-agent actions to remain synchronized with the person’s visible experience. I also needed to avoid exposing overly broad tools or handling credentials through agent tools. My solution was phase-aware, typed tools that reuse the visitor’s existing session and return structured results. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I built a complete trip-planning experience rather than a WebMCP proof of concept. A person can begin planning manually, let an agent continue from the same state, refine the plan, and see changes immediately on the live map. I am especially proud of the tool design: WebMCP is integrated into the product journey, not bolted on. Tools appear and disappear as the experience changes, with read-only actions marked appropriately and guest tools limited to opening authentication UI. What I learned WebMCP works best when tools represent meaningful product actions and current context—not just a remote-control layer for UI buttons. I also learned that agent collaboration needs clear boundaries. Typed tools, phase-aware availability, and explicit read/write distinctions make the experience more reliable for agents while keeping people in control. What's next for Wayfinder Next, I want to deepen the planning experience with richer itinerary editing, better preference memory, collaborative planning for groups, and more local discovery sources. I also want to explore more agent-native flows: letting a visitor’s agent compare options, coordinate constraints across a group, and proactively suggest refinements while Wayfinder remains the specialist for trip context, places, and the live map. title: Weave
pitch: The visual website builder where humans and AI agents collaboratively create, edit, validate, and publish agent-ready websites through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The visual website builder where humans and AI agents collaboratively create, edit, validate, and publish agent-ready websites through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates demo vedio : https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1OA56ZB6VfMFG1dIzqcJiOLojGptgHV85?usp=sharing Inspiration The web was built for humans, but the next generation of the web will also be used by AI agents. We were inspired by a simple question: What if an AI agent could work inside the same visual workspace as a human, instead of trying to control a website by guessing clicks, reading screenshots, or manipulating the DOM? Existing AI website builders mostly follow a prompt → generate → review workflow. We wanted something more collaborative. That led us to WEAVE : a visual website editor where humans and AI agents can work on the same live website together. Humans provide creative direction and visual judgment, while agents handle structured editing and repetitive work through WebMCP. Our goal was to explore what an agent-native creative tool could look like. What it does WEAVE is a collaborative, agent-native website builder. A human can visually create and edit a website using the canvas, while an AI agent can understand the same project and make changes through structured WebMCP tools. Instead of asking an agent to "click this button" or figure out a website from screenshots, WEAVE exposes meaningful capabilities such as: weave_get_context — understand the current project, page, sections, elements, and selection weave_get_selection — understand the element currently selected by the human weave_add_section — add a new website section weave_update_element — modify content or properties of an element weave_move_element — reorganize elements weave_delete_element — remove elements weave_publish_site — request publication of the website This allows an agent to perform workflows such as: "Add a pricing section below the testimonials, change the hero headline, and move the CTA above the footer." The agent first reads the structured state of the editor, chooses the appropriate WebMCP tools, and performs the requested mutations. Most importantly, human and agent edits go through the same validated mutation pipeline , so the agent is not given a separate backdoor into the editor. For high-consequence actions such as publishing, WEAVE keeps the human in control. The agent can request publication, but the final action requires human approval. How we built it WEAVE is built around a structured representation of the visual editor. Instead of exposing the DOM or screenshots to the agent, we maintain a semantic CanvasNode model representing the pages, sections, elements, content, and relationships inside the project. We then expose this model and the editor's capabilities through WebMCP. The architecture is roughly: AI Agent → WebMCP → WEAVE tools → validation → mutation queue → editor/source → live canvas The WebMCP layer registers WEAVE's tools through the browser's model context interface when available. For read operations, the agent can request a bounded snapshot of the current editor state. For write operations, tool inputs are validated before being passed into the existing mutation system. This gives us one important property: Human edits and agent edits use the same underlying mutation pipeline. We also maintain a context version so that the agent can detect when the editor has changed and retrieve fresh context rather than blindly acting on stale information. The project is built with a TypeScript/React-based web stack and integrates WebMCP directly into the browser application. Challenges we ran into Making agent actions reliable We did not want the agent to manipulate the UI through arbitrary clicks or DOM operations. We needed a structured representation that an agent could understand reliably. This led us to build the CanvasNode representation and expose semantic operations instead of low-level browser actions. Keeping human and agent edits consistent A major challenge was ensuring that an agent edit behaved exactly like a human edit. We solved this by routing agent mutations through the same validated mutation queue and editor pipeline rather than creating a separate agent-only editing path. Handling stale context A human can modify the canvas while an agent is reasoning about a previous state. To address this, WEAVE tracks a contextVersion and allows the agent to retrieve the latest structured context before performing subsequent operations. Safety and human control Giving an agent the ability to modify a website also creates the possibility of unintended destructive actions. We therefore separated read, write, destructive, and high-consequence capabilities and kept publication behind an explicit human approval step. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that WebMCP is not just an additional feature in WEAVE — it is part of the core interaction model. We built a system where: Agents can understand a structured visual website rather than relying on screenshots. Agents can perform meaningful website operations through typed WebMCP tools. Human and agent changes use the same mutation pipeline. The agent can react to the human's current selection and project state. Stale context can be detected and refreshed. Destructive and high-consequence operations are handled with additional safety. Publishing remains under human control. WebMCP activity can be observed as part of the editor workflow. We are also proud of turning a traditional visual website editor into something that can be treated as an agent-operable creative workspace . What we learned We learned that making a website "AI-enabled" is very different from making it agent-native . An agent does not necessarily need more UI access. It needs better capabilities and context . Instead of exposing hundreds of low-level browser interactions, a small set of well-designed semantic tools can give an agent much more reliable control. We also learned that human-agent collaboration works best when both sides share the same source of truth. The human should not have to work around the agent, and the agent should not need to simulate a human. WebMCP gave us a way to experiment with this model directly inside the web application. What's next for WEAVE Our next goal is to make WEAVE a broader platform for agent-native websites and creative applications . We want to explore: More powerful agent workflows for complete website creation Better multi-step planning and execution Richer structured context for complex projects More granular human approval and collaboration controls Version history and agent action rollback Multiple specialized agents working on different parts of a project Exporting websites with their capabilities and agent-facing metadata Making published WEAVE websites themselves more discoverable and usable by agents Ultimately, we want WEAVE to explore a future where websites are not just pages that agents can read, but interactive environments with structured capabilities that agents can understand and use alongside humans. title: Praxis: Human + Agent NLE
pitch: Praxis is a video production studio where a director and a browser agent work on the same project. The idea is simple: let the agent help, without taking the cut away from the person.
about_excerpt: Praxis is a video production studio where a director and a browser agent work on the same project. The idea is simple: let the agent help, without taking the cut away from the person. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration A long time ago, in another life, I was the editor for the Pan Sonic DVD Kuvaputki and the director would bark what he wanted achieved. And I figured out how to do it. With WebMCP, now it's my turn. I wasn't a tireless agent. This is more humane. What it does The human directs. The agent assists. Both work on the same project. Praxis is a human-and-agent video production studio with a script, scenes, assets, preview, timeline, and action ledger. Through WebMCP, an agent can read the current project and selection, create checkpoints, make bounded edits, inspect change history, and run structural quality checks. The collaboration is visible: an agent changes a script beat, the revision advances, and the operation appears in the ledger. The director can restore a checkpoint without leaving the editor. The submitted demo uses existing media. Live media generation, rendering, and background delegation are disabled. How we built it We built the studio with React, TypeScript, and Vite. A Cloudflare Worker connects it to a SQLite-backed Durable Object that maintains the project’s authoritative state. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same revision-aware command system. Changes are validated, checked against locks and revision conflicts, and recorded in history. The hosted demo exposes six WebMCP tools: project context, current selection, change history, project operations, checkpoints, and structural quality checks. Codex was our development collaborator throughout. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not letting an agent change something. It was making that change understandable, bounded, and reversible. We worked through browser-specific authentication behavior, WebMCP availability, asynchronous project loading, and keeping browser state synchronized with durable state. We also had to distinguish successful tool registration from proof that an agent could actually discover and invoke those tools. Deadline pressure forced a useful decision: present a narrow collaboration loop we could demonstrate honestly. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent and a human can work through the same production model, with visible attribution and a human-controlled way back. The demonstration shows an actual semantic tool operation—not simulated clicks—followed by a director restoring the baseline. We also reached 250 passing tests across the application and control plane, plus passing TypeScript checks. What we learned Trust is something you build into the workflow. Shared context, clear boundaries, visible history, and reversibility matter more than a reassuring chatbot response. We also learned that a smaller working demonstration can communicate an ambitious idea better than a larger collection of unfinished promises. What's next for Praxis: Human + Agent NLE Connect the existing architecture to provider-backed media generation and rendering, deepen timeline editing, and improve project isolation and collaboration. The guiding principle stays the same: give the agent useful production responsibilities while keeping creative authority with the human. title: Recovery Desk
pitch: The agent proposes. The website decides. The human commits.
about_excerpt: The agent proposes. The website decides. The human commits. Like Comment Story Updates Initial disruption state — WebMCP capabilities are available A destructive cancel_flight capability appears when the current state requires cancellation After violations are resolved, cancel_flight disappears and commit_recovery_plan becomes available. The AI requests authorization — no committed schedule changes until a human approves. Human-approved recovery committed; mutating capabilities are withdrawn. Recovery Desk The agent proposes. The website decides. The human commits. Recovery Desk is a deterministic airline disruption-recovery simulation built to explore a question that matters far beyond aviation: What if a website did not expose every action to an AI agent all the time, but instead changed what the agent was allowed to do as the situation evolved? Inspiration Most agent demos focus on whether an AI can call a tool. I wanted to explore a harder problem: when should that tool exist at all? In high-stakes workflows, reading information, proposing a change, cancelling something, and committing a final decision should not carry the same authority. Recovery Desk uses an airline operations-control scenario to make that distinction visible. A fictional airline faces a hub closure and must recover its schedule while respecting aircraft position, crew duty, minimum turn time, and the disruption window. The airline scenario is the testbed. The core idea is state-governed WebMCP capabilities . What it does Recovery Desk exposes seven WebMCP tools: get_disruption get_schedule check_plan_legality propose_reassignment reset_draft cancel_flight commit_recovery_plan But they are not all available at the same time . The website moves through six operational states: DISRUPTED → DRAFTING → CANCELLATION_REQUIRED → DRAFT_LEGAL → AWAITING_APPROVAL → COMMITTED As state changes, the website dynamically changes the capabilities exposed through WebMCP. For example, cancel_flight is a destructive capability. It is not exposed by default. When the current plan leaves an unresolved flight with no feasible aircraft reassignment, the website can enter CANCELLATION_REQUIRED and expose cancel_flight . Once that destructive action is no longer appropriate, the capability is withdrawn. When the draft becomes legal, commit_recovery_plan becomes available. Calling it still does not commit the plan. It moves the workflow to AWAITING_APPROVAL and waits for an explicit human decision. Only human approval commits the recovery plan. Agent proposes → Website validates → Capabilities change → Human authorizes → System commits. How I built it Recovery Desk is a deterministic client-side application with the WebMCP layer separated from the recovery logic. The site registers tools through the browser's Model Context API and dynamically manages their availability according to the current application state. The recovery engine uses integer-minute scheduling and explicit rules for: hub closure aircraft position minimum aircraft turn time crew duty limits Agent mutations affect a draft , never the committed plan directly. Every mutating, destructive, or human-gated action re-checks the current phase at invocation time. This also provides stale-tool defense: if an agent attempts to invoke a capability that is no longer valid in the current state, the website rejects the call without performing the mutation. The application maintains an audit trail of tool calls, state transitions, rejected actions, approval requests, and final human decisions. The demo The deterministic recovery walkthrough deliberately creates and repairs operational conflicts. The operator retimes flights while the website continuously validates the evolving draft. Eventually, the current draft leaves MA442 without a feasible aircraft reassignment, causing the site to enter CANCELLATION_REQUIRED . At that point, cancel_flight dynamically appears. After the remaining recovery actions and cancellation of MA442 produce a legal draft, the destructive capability is withdrawn and commit_recovery_plan becomes available. The agent can request the commit, but the website opens a human approval gate. A human can Reject , leaving the committed schedule unchanged and preserving the draft for further work, or Approve , which is the only path that commits the recovery plan. After commitment, mutating capabilities disappear and the interface returns to three read-only WebMCP tools. Challenges The hardest part was not registering tools. It was defining authority boundaries between the agent, the website, and the human. I also learned that capability availability must be treated as part of application state rather than as a static tool list. Another challenge was keeping the demonstration deterministic enough that the same state transitions can be inspected and reproduced. The current feasibility helper intentionally evaluates aircraft reassignment against the current draft . It is not a global optimization engine and does not claim to exhaustively search every possible retiming, resequencing, aircraft, and crew combination. That limitation helped clarify the real purpose of the project: Recovery Desk is not presented as a production airline optimizer. It is a testbed for state-governed agent capabilities . What I learned WebMCP can represent more than a collection of functions that an agent can call. A website can use its own domain state to determine: what an agent may read, what it may propose, when a destructive capability becomes appropriate, when that capability must disappear, and where human authority must remain absolute. That suggests a broader pattern for agentic websites in finance, healthcare operations, enterprise administration, infrastructure, procurement, and other workflows where actions have different levels of consequence. Recovery Desk demonstrates a simple principle: giving an agent tools is useful; giving it the right tools at the right moment is safer and more powerful. I developed the recovery workflow, operational state transitions, legality checks, commit logic, WebMCP tool integration, interface, testing, and deployment. I also designed the demonstration scenario to show how an AI agent can interact with an operational control simulation through structured, state-governed WebMCP capabilities under explicit human authorization. title: RelayBench
pitch: RelayBench lets an AI pause troubleshooting, ask a nearby human for one precise physical observation, and use that answer as evidence through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: RelayBench lets an AI pause troubleshooting, ask a nearby human for one precise physical observation, and use that answer as evidence through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Investigation: the agent narrows the case to Valve V2 and requests physical evidence. Human handoff: onboarding highlights the observation task and explains the user's next action. Reasoning: the user's answer becomes attributed evidence and updates agent confidence. Inspiration Agents are good at reading logs, telemetry, and API responses. Real troubleshooting rarely stays inside those boundaries. At some point, the useful next question is physical: Is the valve actually open? Is the warning light blinking? Does the pump sound normal? I built RelayBench around that handoff. The AI should not pretend it can see the equipment. It should ask the person who is already there for a small, concrete observation, then continue reasoning with that evidence. What it does RelayBench is a shared diagnostic workspace for an AI agent and a nearby human. The demo starts with a greenhouse irrigation fault. Digital telemetry shows that downstream flow has collapsed, and the agent ranks several possible causes. Through WebMCP, the agent reads the live case, focuses Valve V2, and requests a physical inspection. The request appears as a bounded human task with three answers: Open, Partially open, or Closed. The tool call waits while the technician checks the equipment. Once the person answers, RelayBench records the observation with its author and event type, resolves the pending call, and updates the agent's confidence. The result is a visible chain of evidence rather than a hidden chat exchange. A reviewer can see what the sensors reported, what the agent inferred, what the human observed, and how the diagnosis changed. How I built it The application uses Vue 3, TypeScript, Vite, and plain CSS. A reactive case store owns the selected component, investigation phase, evidence timeline, hypotheses, and pending observation. The page registers four native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext : get_case_state reads the current case and reasoning state. focus_component moves the shared interface to a specific component. request_human_observation creates a task in the page and returns a Promise that stays pending until the person answers. reset_case_demo restores the initial case without changing the user's onboarding preference. The most important implementation detail is the pending observation. It turns a person in the physical environment into a safe, structured source of evidence without giving the agent imaginary sensors or unrestricted control. The site is deployed on OpenAI Sites. WebMCP works as progressive enhancement, so the interface also supports a complete manual demo in browsers that do not expose the API. Challenges The hardest part was making an asynchronous human handoff feel like one continuous tool call. The interface has to show that the agent is waiting, accept exactly one valid response, resolve the right request, and handle cancellation cleanly. The second challenge was making the process understandable to someone seeing it for the first time. I added an attributed case timeline, explicit event types, component progress, agent-confidence changes, and a guided tour that runs once and can be replayed from the help button. Browser support is still experimental, so I kept WebMCP registration isolated and made the rest of the application work without it. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when a website already owns the interaction and state that an agent needs. RelayBench does not bolt a generic tool layer onto a static page. The page itself knows which component is selected, which observation is pending, who answered it, and how the case changed. I also learned that a human-in-the-loop tool needs more than a confirmation dialog. The person needs context, constrained choices, and a visible record of what their answer changed. What's next The greenhouse case is a focused demo, but the interaction applies to field service, lab work, home repair, accessibility support, and incident response. The next step would be a case-authoring format so teams can define equipment, telemetry, observation prompts, and evidence rules without changing the application code. title: Shopfront Copilot
pitch: Shop together with your AI agent, but only you can hit "buy."
about_excerpt: Shop together with your AI agent, but only you can hit "buy." Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The WebMCP spec's own authors flagged the sharpest risk in agentic commerce in their own draft. Section 6.3.2.3 walks through an ambiguously named tool, finalizeCart , that an agent could call and silently complete a real purchase. An agent shopping "on your behalf" today has two bad options: screen-scrape the UI (brittle, no ground truth), or call a private backend API directly (bypasses whatever safety rails the storefront's own UI enforces). WebMCP offered a third path: let the agent call the exact tool the UI itself uses, on the exact same page state a human is looking at. We wanted to build a storefront that took the spec's own warning seriously enough to actually engineer around it, not just write a paragraph about "responsible AI" in a README. What it does Shopfront Copilot is a storefront where a shopper and their AI agent browse, compare, and buy together. The agent can: Search & filter the catalog by price, category, and other bounded fields Compare 2-4 products side by side in a real on-page comparison table Check return policy for a product Add / remove cart items , reversible either direction Watch a product for price drops All of it runs through the same WebMCP tools registered on document.modelContext that the storefront's own UI calls. A shopper also controls an Autonomy Dial (read-only vs. browse-and-cart) and an optional spending cap , both enforced with machine-readable refusal codes the agent can act on. The checkout gate: the headline feature Action Exposed to the agent? Can it complete a purchase? checkout (WebMCP tool) Yes No. Always returns { status: "confirmation_required", cart_summary } . Never mutates the cart. Confirm-purchase click Not a registered tool at all. Yes, this is the only thing that finalizes an order, and it's gated behind WebAuthn on a plain onClick handler an agent can't reach. There is no tool an agent can call, no matter how it's worded, that completes a purchase. How we built it Stack: Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, React, Tailwind State: client-side React context persisted to localStorage , no backend database Tools: defined once in lib/webmcp/tools/ , registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() , so a human's click and an agent's tool call run through the identical code path into the identical shared cart The safety layer is factored out into its own framework-agnostic package, webmcp-guardrails : Autonomy tiers & spending caps that gate mutating calls Structural-absence check that proves confirm_purchase was never registered, rather than just asserting it in prose Flight recorder that logs every tool call as structured, timestamped data Intent-snapshot diffing that freezes what an agent saw when it called checkout and flags anything that changed by the time a human confirms To prove the pattern holds against a real model, not just scripted scenarios, we added a live agent mode backed by Groq , driving the exact same tool registry and guardrails a simulated harness uses. Checkout confirmation is server-verified through WebAuthn with zero database, and everything degrades gracefully in browsers without document.modelContext support, which today is most of them. Challenges we ran into Making the checkout gate airtight meant resisting the temptation to "just add a permission check" to a confirm_purchase tool, since a runtime check is something an agent, or a future refactor, could route around. We made the property structural instead of declarative : the function that finalizes an order simply is never wired into the tool registry. We also hit five places where the WebMCP spec doesn't yet define an answer: No standard classification for irreversible actions No agent identity to key a per-agent rate limit or trust tier on No way for a shopper's consent decision to persist and reach the agent before it fails once No push channel for telling an idle agent a watched price actually dropped No standard primitive for an agent to pause and ask a human a question We wrote up each gap and our workaround as an RFC rather than silently papering over them. Keeping the demo honest against a real model was its own challenge: a live Groq-backed agent will happily try creative phrasings to get a tool to do more than its contract allows, which made for a good adversarial test of whether our guardrails actually held. Accomplishments that we're proud of confirm_purchase cannot be reached by an agent under any circumstance, and we can prove it structurally , not just document it webmcp-guardrails is genuinely reusable: pure TypeScript, no dependency on React or this app's domain Live agent mode means the checkout gate is tested against a real model actively trying to complete a purchase, not just scripted scenarios What we learned The safest thing you can do with a dangerous capability isn't a well-worded permission check, it's not exposing the capability's implementation to the caller at all . We also came away convinced that several of the gaps we hit (agent identity, a standard human-question primitive) sit upstream of a lot of other trust problems in agentic web tooling, and are worth pushing at the spec level rather than solving per-site forever. What's next for Shopfront Copilot Publish webmcp-guardrails to npm so other WebMCP sites can adopt the structural-absence pattern without rebuilding it Prototype an irreversibleHint annotation as a concrete proposal back to the WebMCP spec Prototype a standard ask_human -shaped primitive for the same reason Built With next react typescript webmcp Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Yanfunmi Jeje Like Share this project: Updates Yanfunmi Jeje started this project — Sep 03, 2026 04:47 AM EDT

title: Shortlist - a store that turns your need into filters
pitch: An electronics store whose own filter vocabulary is the agent's tool schema - it ranks, explains what it hid, and can never un-veto a product you rejected.
about_excerpt: An electronics store whose own filter vocabulary is the agent's tool schema - it ranks, explains what it hid, and can never un-veto a product you rejected. Like Comment Story Updates The catalog: filters generated from real inventory Tool console: describe_catalog called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: the tool's JSON Schema is generated live from the real catalog and filter vocabulary - the agent's tool surface and the store's own UI share one source of truth. Inspiration Every electronics store hides the answer behind its own vocabulary. A customer knows their need in plain language; the site offers RAM, sRGB percentage, and a price slider - the need turned into a quiz only the store understands. What it does Vidyut Electronics hands its own filter vocabulary to the agent as a tool. search_catalog 's JSON Schema is generated from the real catalog at boot - category, spec, and brand are enums of what the store actually sells - so the translation from need to constraints happens on the store page, visibly, not inside a black box. Every ranked result says what it satisfies and what it misses, with the actual value; near-misses say what would have to give; hidden listings say why. The human vetoes with one click, and no tool can ever bring a vetoed product back. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript, a fifteen-product seeded catalog with a deliberate trap (the strongest editor is a 2.3kg desk machine) and a deliberate near-miss. A single pure rank(query) function backs both the page's own render and every tool call, so the rail always shows exactly what the last tool call would return. Challenges we ran into Making the veto boundary airtight against a determined agent: add_to_shortlist has to refuse a vetoed id unconditionally and explain why, every time, including immediately after the agent re-searches and might plausibly try to re-add it thinking the veto was a UI-only state. Accomplishments that we're proud of A tool schema that's generated from real inventory data instead of hand-written - so the agent learns the store's actual vocabulary from the schema itself, and learns any gap in its guess from the error message, not from documentation. What we learned Wrapping every registerTool call in its own try/catch mattered in practice - one schema Chrome's validator disliked should cost one tool, never the whole surface. What's next The optional cross-origin stretch goal - exposing search_catalog to a separate origin via exposedTo / fromOrigins , so a comparison-shopping agent on another site could query Vidyut's catalog directly. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools).
