title: CRM Health Doctor
pitch: A deterministic CRM reliability audit with three read-only WebMCP tools that let ChatGPT and humans co-review the same prioritized evidence on the page.
about_excerpt: A deterministic CRM reliability audit with three read-only WebMCP tools that let ChatGPT and humans co-review the same prioritized evidence on the page. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents and CRM automation are only as reliable as the data they act on. A CRM can appear operational while still containing missing ownership, stale deals, weak activity signals, or malformed fields that undermine routing, reporting, automation, and eventually agent behavior. CRM Health Doctor started as a deterministic CRM reliability diagnostic: evaluate known conditions, calculate health scores, and produce a prioritized review queue rather than asking an LLM to guess what is wrong. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore a different question: What if an AI agent and a human reviewer could inspect the same deterministic CRM evidence directly on the page, without giving the agent write access to the CRM? That became the WebMCP human-agent co-review layer. What it does CRM Health Doctor evaluates a synthetic CRM dataset using explicit deterministic rules and produces: an overall CRM health score category-level scores a prioritized issue queue record-level evidence deterministic review guidance For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended that report with three browser-native, read-only tools: get_crm_health_summary list_priority_issues explain_priority_issue Instead of asking the agent to infer findings from visible HTML, the page exposes bounded structured state through WebMCP. The most important interaction is the synchronization between agent and human. When the agent prioritizes or explains a record such as C-008 , the corresponding row is automatically focused and highlighted on the report page. This creates an observable co-review workflow where the agent and the human are reviewing the same evidence. Who this is for The immediate audience is CRM administrators, RevOps teams, and automation/AI practitioners preparing CRM systems for agent-assisted operations. These teams already depend on ownership, activity, lifecycle, and pipeline data for routing, reporting, automation, and AI workflows; unreliable CRM state makes every downstream system less trustworthy. Why WebMCP changes the interaction Without this WebMCP layer, the human can inspect the report visually while an agent must either infer state from the rendered interface or receive a separate backend integration. Here, the page itself exposes a governed structured interface to the agent and simultaneously shows the human which evidence the agent selected. The browser becomes a shared review surface rather than two disconnected experiences. How I built it The diagnostic layer is implemented in Python using deterministic normalization, rules, scoring, prioritization, and remediation mappings. The generated report is a self-contained static HTML page containing safely embedded synthetic report state. The WebMCP browser layer is implemented in JavaScript and registers three tightly scoped read-only tools. Tool inputs are validated, outputs are bounded, and CRM-derived strings are treated as untrusted evidence rather than instructions. The architecture is deliberately simple: Synthetic CRM fixture → Deterministic Python diagnostic engine → Precomputed safe report state → Static HTML report → WebMCP tools → Agent + human co-review The public challenge deployment is hosted on Render as a static site. It requires no backend, database, authentication service, or live CRM connection. CRM Health Doctor existed before the WebMCP Challenge. The pre-existing work includes the deterministic diagnostic engine, scoring logic, fixtures, and original report UI. The challenge-period contribution adds: structured WebMCP-safe report state three browser-native read-only tools strict tool input contracts bounded structured outputs deterministic remediation mappings visible synchronization between agent selection and the report UI graceful behavior when WebMCP is unavailable public WebMCP deployment and validation The repository includes explicit provenance documentation, a challenge-delta document, and a tagged pre-WebMCP baseline. Challenges I ran into Making agent behavior observable Returning correct structured data was only part of the problem. I wanted the human reviewer to see exactly what the agent was reasoning about. That required connecting tool execution to deterministic visual behavior on the page, including scrolling, row focus, highlighting, and an accessible status update. Keeping the trust boundary narrow It would have been easy to turn the demo into an autonomous remediation agent. I intentionally did not. The public challenge version has: no live customer CRM data no CRM write path no raw HubSpot record IDs no network calls from the deployed page strict tool inputs bounded outputs deterministic remediation guidance explicit human-review requirements Working with an evolving WebMCP environment WebMCP is still evolving and browser behavior remains experimental. I validated the implementation through both ChatGPT's in-app browser and a WebMCP-enabled Chrome build. During testing, I encountered a difference in how the experimental Chrome build expected tool arguments to be passed. Rather than hiding that implementation detail, I documented the exact validated invocation flow in the public repository. Accomplishments I'm proud of I am most proud that the final challenge build is small, explainable, and observable. The project successfully demonstrates: three working WebMCP tools on a public deployment deterministic CRM health evaluation bounded structured agent access visible synchronization between agent actions and the report UI explicit human review instead of autonomous writes validation in both ChatGPT and WebMCP-enabled Chrome a reproducible synthetic demo with no customer data The strongest moment in the demo is simple: the agent identifies C-008 as a priority issue, and the same record is immediately highlighted for the human reviewer. That interaction is the core idea behind the project. What I learned The biggest lesson was that agent UX is not only about giving a model more context. A stronger pattern is: deterministic evidence → bounded tool → agent reasoning → visible human review WebMCP makes the browser itself a useful coordination surface between the agent and the user. Instead of asking an agent to scrape or visually interpret a dashboard, a page can expose exactly the structured state the agent is allowed to reason over while keeping consequential decisions under human control. I also learned that deterministic systems and AI agents do not need to compete with each other. Deterministic logic can establish the evidence and operating boundaries, while the agent provides interpretation and interaction on top of that trusted layer. What's next for CRM Health Doctor CRM Health Doctor is still a narrow prototype, not a production CRM auditing platform. The next logical direction is an agent-readiness layer for CRM operations . The broader workflow is: CRM evidence → Deterministic reliability assessment → Prioritized review queue → Governed agent analysis → Human approval → Controlled remediation Future work could include: broader diagnostic coverage authenticated multi-portal assessment historical reliability trends richer evidence sources configurable policy thresholds controlled remediation workflows with explicit approval gates integration with CRM and operational MCP tools after reliability checks pass The larger opportunity is not simply to let an AI agent operate a CRM. It is to help determine when the CRM data and operating controls are reliable enough for an agent to act safely in the first place . title: First Look
pitch: Turn ChatGPT research into qualified customer conversations with WebMCP tools that expose accurate information, useful assets, site checks, and the next action on one shared page.
about_excerpt: Turn ChatGPT research into qualified customer conversations with WebMCP tools that expose accurate information, useful assets, site checks, and the next action on one shared page. Like Comment Story Updates Assets via WEBMCP Inspiration More customers now begin their research in ChatGPT. On a conventional website, the agent often has to scrape the interface, interpret incomplete context, and guess what actions are available. When the customer reaches the business, they may have to start the conversation again. WebMCP offers a better model: the website can expose accurate information, useful assets, and explicit actions directly to the agent. Commerce demos show how an agent can find a product and complete checkout. This project explores the service-business journey, where the next step often requires context, evidence, qualification, and human judgment rather than simply adding an item to a cart. What it does This page creates one shared workspace for a visitor and their browser agent. Together, they can: Understand what the page offers and what it does not claim Browse real public work without invented clients or case studies Open and explain a published brief on the same screen Run a limited analysis of a public URL Review its title, description, heading, declared tools, llms.txt , and robots.txt Fill a question using the findings Submit that question for human review The page exposes twelve WebMCP tools. Eleven are imperative JavaScript tools, and ask_rafalai is a declarative form tool with toolautosubmit . The submission is real, but nothing is automatically answered or acted upon. A person reviews every message. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the website define its capabilities instead of forcing the agent to infer them from the DOM. That produces a better customer experience because the person and the agent work with the same information, assets, actions, and visible state. The conversation can move forward instead of restarting when the customer leaves ChatGPT and reaches the business. This page is one example, not the final product. A store could expose products, inventory, recommendations, and checkout. An agency could expose services, briefs, qualification, audits, and intake. Other businesses can expose the actions that match how they actually serve customers. The commercial opportunity is straightforward: better answers, less friction, more qualified conversations, and more customers. How we built it Eleven tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool in JavaScript. The Ask form provides the twelfth tool declaratively using toolname , toolparamdescription , and toolautosubmit . The same underlying functions power both agent calls and the visible Run buttons, so the experience remains demonstrable in browsers without WebMCP enabled. The URL analysis calls GET /api/look , a Cloudflare Pages Function that fetches public HTML, /robots.txt , and /llms.txt . It rejects localhost, private networks, credentialed URLs, and unsafe redirects. It does not use paid ranking APIs. The project is hosted on Cloudflare and released in a public MIT-licensed repository. Challenges The central design challenge was creating a meaningful WebMCP experience that was not another shopping-cart demonstration. We also needed to: Keep agent actions visible to the person Separate drafting from submitting Preserve human review after submission Safely accept user-provided public URLs Avoid duplicate imperative and declarative tool registrations Demonstrate a service-business journey without inventing clients or results What we learned The difficult part of WebMCP is not registering a function. It is deciding which actions should exist, describing them clearly, and establishing the correct boundaries. WebMCP is also different from search optimization. Search helps information get discovered. WebMCP helps an agent use a website accurately once it arrives. Agent-ready websites can become a new customer-acquisition interface: a place where AI systems present reliable information, provide the right assets, and perform useful actions while people remain responsible for the work. title: Ghosted
pitch: A tracker that admits when someone's gone silent — on a job application or an unpaid invoice — and gives your agent real tools to do something about it.
about_excerpt: A tracker that admits when someone's gone silent — on a job application or an unpaid invoice — and gives your agent real tools to do something about it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We started this project somewhere else entirely — a manual leads board, then a subscription-cancellation demo — before realizing the actual differentiator was never going to be what task an app does. In 2026, almost any "paste something in, get a useful result" idea already exists as a free tool somewhere. What's structurally different about WebMCP is that your own agent — not a company's closed AI — acts live on a page you're both looking at, with real, verifiable consequences. That reframing sent us looking for a task where a live, shared, mutable record is the whole point, and where the friction is something an agent can genuinely remove rather than just reformat. Job hunting fit immediately: 53% ghosting, ~40 applications per interview, and existing trackers (Teal, Huntr) are well-built but entirely passive — you re-enter every application by hand and check staleness yourself. None of them can be handed to an agent. What it does Ghosted is a two-tab tracker — Job Applications and Freelance Invoices — exposing eighteen WebMCP tools total, because being ignored by an employer and being ignored by a client on an invoice are the same mechanic wearing a different name. Job applications (9 tools): log_application , get_application / list_applications / search_applications , update_status (applied → interviewing → offer / rejected / ghosted / withdrawn), flag_stale_applications (mark every application silent for 21+ days as ghosted in one call), get_followup_reminders , get_pipeline_summary (response rate, ghost rate, average response time), get_leverage_opportunities (cross-references live applications worth notifying once one reaches offer stage). Freelance invoices (8 tools, mirroring the same shape): log_invoice , get_invoice , list_invoices , search_invoices , update_invoice_status , flag_stale_invoices , get_invoice_followup_reminders , get_payment_summary . A human can do everything by hand too, but the point is watching an agent do the tedious parts (bulk staleness checks, cross-referencing an offer against a dozen other processes) in one call, live, on the same page: a card briefly highlights when its status just changed. The eighteenth tool, get_daily_digest , spans both trackers in one call — every stale item, every follow-up worth sending, any offer worth leveraging — rendered as a "Today" panel above the tabs. How we built it Single static HTML/CSS/JS file, no backend, no build step, localStorage for persistence, WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext . Colors follow a CVD-validated dark palette rather than hand-picked hex values, including a proper ordinal-ramp funnel chart for pipeline stage counts. Every tool was tested in a headless Node harness (mocked document.modelContext and localStorage ) before being verified live in a real browser. Challenges we ran into Three real bugs surfaced during testing: a pause action with no way back to "active" in an earlier iteration; a "leverage opportunities" tool that initially recommended notifying companies that had already gone dark for 45+ days; and, when the invoices tab was added, a "Reset demo" handler that replaced the entire saved-state object instead of just its own slice — which would have silently wiped every invoice. All three were caught by actually running the tools end-to-end, not by reasoning about the code in the abstract. Accomplishments we're proud of Getting to a concept that's differentiated by mechanism , not by chasing an ever-shrinking list of "nobody's built this exact task" ideas — after real competitive research (Rocket Money, Bobby, Monarch, MessyData, Teal, Huntr, and a direct GitHub search for other WebMCP entries), the honest answer was to lean into what the mechanism itself offers — an outside agent operating live, transparently, on shared state — and prove it generalizes by pointing it at a second real, quantified problem (freelance payment ghosting) with the same shape. What we learned That "no one else does this" is close to impossible to find for simple utility apps in 2026 — the right question is whether the mechanism (agent + human sharing live, mutable, verifiable state) does something a closed, single-shot AI feature structurally cannot. What's next Tracking interview dates directly to catch scheduling conflicts, letting a browser-extension style capture job postings or invoices straight from the page an agent is already reading, and recognizing recurring clients from a pasted bank or PayPal statement. title: Mapbox AI Trip Planner
pitch: Ask an AI to plan your trip and watch it find real places, draw a real route, and pin your itinerary live on a Mapbox map. No backend, no extension. Just WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Ask an AI to plan your trip and watch it find real places, draw a real route, and pin your itinerary live on a Mapbox map. No backend, no extension. Just WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Walking trip planned in Paris New Window to plan a trip Inspiration The WebMCP Challenge asks what the open web looks like when it's built for humans and agents at once. We'd already been building @mapbox/web-mcp-server , a library that registers Mapbox GL JS map interactions as WebMCP tools, and had written up a design thesis for it before ever building a demo: a geospatial AI agent needs two things to be genuinely useful, a data layer (geocoding, search, directions) and a live rendering surface it can actually act on. Most "AI + maps" demos fake the second half: a chat response describing a trip, maybe a static image. WebMCP is the first browser API that lets a page hand an agent direct control over a live map instead, the same way an MCP server hands it a data source. We wanted to prove that idea end-to-end, not just describe it. What it does Open the demo, paste an Anthropic API key, and ask for a trip: "Plan a half-day trip in Paris: the Eiffel Tower, a nearby cafe, and the Louvre, with walking directions between each stop." An agent geocodes the real places, drops pins, pulls a real walking route, draws it on the map, and frames the whole trip, live, while you watch. An itinerary panel and an activity log rebuild themselves from the actual tool calls as they happen, so the WebMCP mechanism is visible, not just its output. How we built it The core is a small TypeScript library ( src/ , strict mode, pure ESM) where every map capability is a factory function, createFlyToTool(map) , createAddMarkerTool(map, markers, stops) , returning a ToolDescriptor that closes over the live mapboxgl.Map instance. registerMapboxTools(map) wires all of them up against navigator.modelContext.registerTool() , plus an onToolCall hook so a host page can observe every call live. On top of that, the demo does two things most WebMCP demos skip. First, it closes the "two data layers" loop from our own design doc for real: alongside the map-control tools, the page registers a small second set, geocode_place , search_category , get_directions , that call Mapbox's public Search Box and Directions REST APIs directly via fetch() . These are demo-only and never exported from the published library, but they mean the whole trip-planning loop works from one deployed page with no server standing in as an MCP host. Second, the deployed demo is usable with zero setup: an embedded BYOK (bring-your-own-key) chat widget ( demo/chat.ts ) using the official @anthropic-ai/sdk with dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true , running a manual agentic loop against claude-opus-5 . List the registered tools, send them as the model's tools , execute whatever it calls via navigator.modelContextTesting.executeTool() , feed results back, repeat. The key never leaves the visitor's browser except to Anthropic directly. For anyone who'd rather not paste a key, the page also exposes a copyable system prompt for driving it via Claude Desktop or any other WebMCP-compatible extension instead: same tools, different agent. It's deployed as a static Vite build on Vercel, with the Mapbox token set as a public build-time config variable (Mapbox tokens are meant to be client-embedded, unlike the Anthropic key). Challenges we ran into Geocoding is pickier than it looks. Early on, a query like "Louvre Museum, Paris" returned an unrelated Airbnb listing ranked above the actual landmark; the city qualifier confused relevance ranking more than it helped. The fix was querying just the bare place name and using proximity bias to disambiguate instead, which we had to encode directly into the tool description and system prompt so the agent wouldn't do it wrong on its own. Some organizations block this pattern entirely. Mid-testing, a live call to Anthropic's API came back with authentication_error: CORS requests are not allowed for this Organization . Some orgs disable direct-from-browser API access as a security policy, which is exactly the risk dangerouslyAllowBrowser warns about, just enforced server-side. No client code can work around an org policy, so instead we made the failure mode honest: detect it and point the visitor at the Claude Desktop fallback with an accurate explanation, instead of a misleading "invalid API key." LLM tool-calling isn't perfectly deterministic. During a real end-to-end run, the agent issued an identical add_marker call twice in one turn, producing a visible duplicate row in the itinerary. We added a small guard against adjacent duplicate stops and nudged the system prompt to clear stale markers before replanning, a good reminder that a UI built on top of agent tool calls has to defend against the agent occasionally repeating itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of We shipped and verified a genuine end-to-end run, not just isolated pieces in a demo script: a real Anthropic API call driving real Mapbox geocoding and directions calls, ending in a route drawn on real streets and an itinerary that matches exactly what the agent did. The zero-backend architecture holds up under that test too: no server anywhere in the loop, yet the demo still closes the "data layer plus rendering layer" idea we set out to prove. We're also proud of how we found problems: not by guessing, but by watching the itinerary and activity log disagree with what we expected, then chasing the real cause. That's how we caught the geocoding query issue, the org CORS policy, and the duplicate tool call, each a real bug against a real API, not a hypothetical. What we learned That the "two MCPs, one agent loop" idea holds up in practice, not just on paper, and that most of the real engineering in an agent-facing feature isn't the tool-calling plumbing (which is refreshingly thin once you commit to the tool-factory pattern). It's the edge cases: query phrasing that reads fine to a human but confuses a search API, org-level policies that only surface as a runtime error, and an agent's own occasional non-determinism. Building the itinerary and activity log to render straight off live tool calls, rather than trusting the model's narration, turned out to be the single best debugging tool we had. It's also what makes the demo convincing: you're not watching a chat bot describe a trip, you're watching WebMCP actually happen. What's next for Mapbox AI Trip Planner The bigger opportunity is first-party integration. The same tool-factory pattern that controls this demo map could register Studio-specific tools, select_layer , publish_style , undo and redo , directly against Mapbox Studio's live style editor, turning "how do I write this expression" into a conversation instead of a documentation search. Closer to home, we'd like to stream the chat widget's responses instead of waiting for a full reply, and give the agent a way to search points of interest by category, price, and rating rather than just name, so trip planning can go beyond landmarks into real day-to-day recommendations. title: Novelist
pitch: AI-powered professional writer that turns any idea into a complete, personalized book in multiple languages, as an ebook, audiobook or printed copy. You bring the spark; Novelist builds the world.
about_excerpt: AI-powered professional writer that turns any idea into a complete, personalized book in multiple languages, as an ebook, audiobook or printed copy. You bring the spark; Novelist builds the world. Like Comment Story Updates Novelist helps people turn an idea into a complete novel made specifically for them. Some users want to step inside a story of their own. They can become the main character, bring in friends or family, choose the setting and decide what kind of adventure unfolds. It is a way to experience the wild, personal stories that once existed only in their imagination. Others use Novelist to create a meaningful gift. The book can be inspired by someone’s personality, memories, dreams or relationships, making it far more personal than something bought off the shelf. It can be given as a digital edition, an audiobook or a professionally printed book. The finished digital novel usually arrives by email within 45 to 60 minutes. It is ready to download and read using compatible e-reader devices and apps, as well as on a phone, tablet or computer. WebMCP support makes the process feel much simpler. A user can tell ChatGPT what kind of book they want and explore the idea through conversation. If they are unsure what to enter in the Story Builder, they can ask ChatGPT to suggest titles, genres, settings, plots, writing styles, characters, literary inspirations, tropes and endings. Users can choose their favorite suggestions, combine different ideas or ask for new alternatives. ChatGPT can then fill in the Story Builder, configure the novel and guide them through the remaining steps in Novelist. ChatGPT takes care of much of the creative setup and navigation. The user still reviews everything and remains in control of private information, generation, publishing and payment. It feels less like completing a complicated form and more like creating a book through a conversation. We integrated WebMCP by giving ChatGPT a set of structured tools that connect directly to the actions already available in Novelist. There are global tools for things like opening sections, searching the bookstore and checking the user’s library. Each relevant page also provides its own tools. For example, the Story Builder lets ChatGPT suggest and enter story details, while the audiobook and printed-copy pages (these two require signing in) provide tools for configuring and navigating those processes. These tools reuse Novelist’s existing forms, validation and navigation, so there is no separate agent-only workflow to maintain. Everything ChatGPT does is reflected immediately in the interface the user sees. Sensitive or irreversible actions remain with the user. ChatGPT cannot enter shipping addresses, make payments, publish books or start final generation. When human input is required, Novelist displays a large, clear message explaining what the user needs to do next. The integration only activates in browsers that support WebMCP, is translated into all 15 supported languages and is covered by unit, integration and end-to-end tests. title: orano
pitch: watch videos and reels with your ai and turn them into actionable tasks.
about_excerpt: watch videos and reels with your ai and turn them into actionable tasks. Like Comment Story Updates memory page video processing home page /task tracker project page projects page your saved videos What inspired this I kept losing the same thing. Someone would send me a Reel about a tool, a recipe, or a workflow. I'd save it. Two weeks later I'd want the link, the install steps, the tool name, or the recipe's ingredient list, and the video was right there in my library useless, because to answer any of those questions I had to either re-watch it or sit there transcribing it for an agent that couldn't see it. What I built For this challenge I exposed the ORANO desk web app at oranoai.com/workspace as a WebMCP surface and added nine tools that map directly to the actions a user can already take on the page: How I built it The desk is a single static workspace/index.html that loads one JS file, js/workspace.js. On load the script checks for document.modelContext and, when it's there, calls registerWebMCP() which registers the nine tools. Each tool is a plain object: a JSON Schema, an annotations block (readOnlyHint for read tools, untrustedContentHint for evidence), and an execute function that calls the same /v1 API the human UI already uses. That was the load-bearing decision: the agent doesn't get a parallel API. It shares apiRequest(), navigate(), and renderProject() with the UI, so the page state and the agent's view are literally the same state. The backend is the same FastAPI service that runs the mobile and web apps. The endpoints (/v1/projects, /v1/projects/{id}/context, /v1/profile/tasks, /v1/search, etc.) already existed to power the UI — WebMCP just gives the agent the same endpoints with structured schemas and bounded responses. The personal MCP server at /mcp/ (FastMCP) exposes the same selector through get_project_context for accounts that prefer an MCP-style integration. One concrete example of the contract. When a tool changes what's on screen (save_video, search, list_tasks), the execute function calls navigate() or renderProject() after the API call returns, so what the user sees matches what the agent was told. There's no parallel "API response" and "UI response" — there is just the workspace, and both participants read it. What I learned A few things that changed how I think about this: Agents are users, not API clients. Treating them as a separate integration channel — a separate auth flow, a separate surface, a separate data model — duplicated evidence and made the human the bottleneck. The breakthrough was giving the agent the same code path the UI uses, and the same render path so what the agent sees is what the user sees. The hard problem was boundaries, not schemas. Once the page can ask for the transcript, you have to decide how much. A bounded character budget, an allow-list of fields, and untrustedContentHint on evidence blocks were the minimum to make this safe for a real account with real saves. WebMCP made the product more human. The agent and the user doing the same work on the same data, with the same UI affordances, is the point. Writing tight tool descriptions ("List ORANO projects… use this before opening a project") forced me to write the spec for an agent that has no other context, which also helped me explain it better to humans. Challenges I faced Optimistic loading. The workbench opens with a shimmer skeleton the same shape as the real layout, so the page never looks empty while the project bundle is in flight. Cheaper to ship than a real data-fetch waterfall, and the result feels loaded within the first paint. Click-to-play embeds. Eagerly loading YouTube and Instagram iframes on every project view is slow and noisy. title: PantryOS
pitch: AI powered kitchen manager using WebMCP to recommend food to use, find recipes, track ingredients, and build smarter grocery lists.
about_excerpt: AI powered kitchen manager using WebMCP to recommend food to use, find recipes, track ingredients, and build smarter grocery lists. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Dashboard and AI activity Saved recipe Kitchen inventory Recipe matching Grocery planning Inspiration I do a ton of home cooking and managing the food in the fridge, can be a real hassle from what Ingredients I have to if they are expired or not. Inventory, recipes, and grocery lists usually live in separate places, leaving me having to compare dates, quantities, and missing ingredients manually. PantryOS explores a different model: Where I already implement AI for planning meals and recipes and managing leftover ingredients it instead homogenizes the information so an agent can access all of it at once. What it does PantryOS tracks ingredients across the fridge, freezer, and pantry, including quantities and expiry dates. It prioritizes food that should be used soon, finds suitable recipes, scales serving quantities, converts units, and can add missing ingredients to the grocery list. Instead of navigating several screens or finding recipes or copying information down and adding it to boxes of text manually the AI agent can automate this for you navigate fill out grab info from and expedite all this busy work so you can get back to your daily life. Here's an example of a use case Find a recipe for four people that uses the ingredients going bad, then add anything else I need to my shopping list. PantryOS turns that request into actual management actions keeping the interface and stored kitchen state up to date as you work or cook. Why WebMCP PantryOS is not a chatbot taped together alongside an application to manage your kitchen. Its features are exposed using structured WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect inventory, evaluate expiry dates, save and retrieve recipes, update quantities, and plan groceries without you having to feed it information about your kitchen and the recipes you have every time. What you end up with is a superior user experience, people can talk to agent in everyday language while PantryOS handles the multi-step coordination between inventory, recipes, serving sizes, and groceries. This also allows for further and more complex syncing of your information later on, the easy of use of the MCP allows for later hosted version of this demo to enable access by your AI agent wherever you are on the go. Human-agent collaboration The agent can prep and perform useful kitchen actions, but the person remains in control. Destructive actions like deleting recipes or throwing out food require confirmation to make sure the Agent doesn't run haywire and delete your grandmother long lost recipe. The activity panel records recent agent assistance, making it clear what is happening and what changed. How we built it PantryOS is a client-only React and TypeScript application deployed using Cloudflare Workers Static Assets. Zustand persists inventory, recipes, and groceries in browser localStorage . Its WebMCP tools register through document.modelContext . Every tool input is validated with Zod and described using a matching closed JSON Schema. Tool callbacks read current application state when they execute and call the same domain actions used by the interface. Automated tests cover tool contracts, persistence, malformed inputs, quantity conversion, grocery deduplication, cancellation, stale state, and confirmation races. What we learned The best agent tools don't feel like a background script or an entirely separate app. They work best when they can work with what you already have and you can see clearly their application. WebMCP made this feel like a more native interaction that just a automations or AI agent that is just added to a kitchen management app. Its quick simple to use and setup easy to for the AI to work with and access the correct information and allows me to use my already exiting workflow and models to do my tasks. What's next Future versions could add opt-in household collaboration and import integrations. I would like to have it persist across different browsers so you can access the info on the go. The submitted version intentionally remains local-first, client-only, and account-free so the WebMCP interaction is focused, private by default, and easy for judges to reproduce. But an increasing in scope and features is quite easy as there are tons of features I could have added that would be useful to me reminders, logs, side notes for recipes and so on that normal people use and interact with the kitchen everyday. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: Resume Match
pitch: Tailor your resume to the job with an agent that proposes, and a human who decides.
about_excerpt: Tailor your resume to the job with an agent that proposes, and a human who decides. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept seeing resume tools that either rewrite everything behind your back or leave you hunting for keywords at 1 a.m. Neither felt honest. If an AI is going to touch something as personal as a resume, I want to see the before and after on the actual bullet — and I want a button that says no. WebMCP clicked because the agent and I share the same page. It can read the job I pasted and the bullets already on screen, then propose a change. It cannot quietly replace my experience with something I never agreed to. What it does Upload a PDF or Word resume, paste a job posting. The agent can pull out the role and required skills, point out gaps, score ATS coverage, pull in a public GitHub or Medium profile, and suggest a rewritten bullet or a cover-letter opener. Every suggestion shows up as a diff. I accept or reject it myself. Review and Export only include what I accepted. I recorded the demo with ChatGPT desktop . It found the page tools, ran the flow, and the diffs showed up the way they should — that’s the video I’m uploading. Live demo: https://resumematch-617103164879.us-central1.run.app How I built it Python on the server (FastAPI, Jinja2, SQLite). One small JavaScript file registers the WebMCP tools and updates the page. The real work stays in Python so I can sanitize and length-cap it. Intake forms use WebMCP’s declarative form tools, without auto-submit. Analysis and rewrites use document.modelContext.registerTool() . Because the tools live on the page, ChatGPT desktop could drive them the same way Chrome’s inspector can — I didn’t have to build a custom ChatGPT plugin. Only three tools call a model: analyze the job, propose a bullet rewrite, draft a cover opener. Gap finding and ATS scoring are plain skill matching: $$\text{coverage} = \frac{|\text{JD skills} \cap \text{resume skills}|}{|\text{JD skills}|} \times 100$$ Original bullet text is never overwritten. A proposal sits as its own row until I accept it. Running on Google Cloud Run. Session secret and the server Gemini key are in Secret Manager. What I learned The agent in the desktop app and the Gemini/Vertex key on the server are not the same job. ChatGPT picks which tool to call. Our server is what actually writes a proposal. That split is why the demo could look “agentic” without letting ChatGPT silently rewrite the resume. Tools belong to the current page. Stay on Edit for matching and diffs. analyze_job_description taking {} is fine — the job text is already in the session. Challenges Session cookies once split so submit saved a job and analyze couldn’t see it. A prompt on the Upload page also looks like nothing works until you actually click Upload & Parse. I hit both while testing, including with ChatGPT desktop, and had to fix the session path and the copy on the page before the recording was worth keeping. Cloud Run with SQLite wipes sessions on a new deploy, so I recorded against a stable revision. Job descriptions are still untrusted text I treat them as data and never commit a generation without a click. title: SiteScope
pitch: Website migration intelligence for humans and AI agents, exposed directly through native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Website migration intelligence for humans and AI agents, exposed directly through native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates SiteScope SiteScope is a WebMCP-powered website audit and migration assistant for humans and AI agents. Before redesigning or migrating a website, teams need to understand what is actually live: public URLs, broken internal links, metadata that must be preserved, and migration risks that can damage SEO or user journeys. That work is usually fragmented across browser checks, crawlers, spreadsheets, and hand-written migration notes. SiteScope turns that reconnaissance workflow into a shared human-agent workspace. Why WebMCP is a strong fit A migration audit is naturally tool-oriented. The useful actions are concrete, bounded, and structured: inspect a page, discover public URLs, check broken links, and produce a migration baseline. WebMCP lets SiteScope expose those exact capabilities directly from the live website, so an agent does not need to guess through the UI or rely on a separate custom API integration. SiteScope registers five native WebMCP tools: inspect_page , scan_site , list_pages , find_broken_links , and create_migration_plan . The same capabilities are available to a person through the SiteScope interface. Better human + agent UX A person can keep SiteScope open and see what the agent is doing in real time. The live WebMCP activity panel reflects the actual native tool calls as they run, including the target URL, tool state, and concise results. That makes the agent's work inspectable instead of invisible. WebMCP implementation SiteScope uses imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) in the client application. Each tool has an explicit schema and executes the same underlying SiteScope functions used by the product. Safety and bounded execution SiteScope rejects private/local network targets, revalidates redirects, bounds response sizes and sitemap traversal, uses bounded concurrency, treats fetched content as untrusted, and never modifies the inspected website. Migration planning is deterministic rather than LLM-generated. Reproducible demo The demo target is https://sitescope-demo-target.vercel.app . It intentionally contains four sitemap pages, one 404, and several metadata/indexing issues so judges can verify the workflow deterministically. title: WebMcp.AI
pitch: Turn any website into an agent opportunity map.
about_excerpt: Turn any website into an agent opportunity map. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can understand websites, but they still interact with most of them like humans: reading pages, interpreting interfaces, finding controls, and simulating clicks. These workflows are slow, fragile, and often fail when a website’s layout changes. WebMCP offers a better approach. Websites can expose structured tools that agents discover and call directly while keeping people involved in the same visible experience. That inspired us to build WebMCP.ai: a tool that analyzes any public website and identifies the most useful opportunities for making it agent-ready with WebMCP. What it does Users provide a public website URL, and WebMCP.ai researches the website, understands its business and primary workflows, and generates an evidence-backed WebMCP opportunity report. Each report includes: An overall agent-readiness score Scores for discoverability, structured data, agent actions, automation, and MCP potential Ranked WebMCP tool opportunities Proposed tool names, descriptions, and input/output schemas User value, business value, implementation difficulty, and safety ratings Authentication, authorization, validation, confirmation, and audit safeguards Research sources and clearly identified limitations A production-ready implementation prompt for coding agents Users can filter and compare opportunities, select the tools they want to build, and export the report or implementation prompt. WebMCP.ai is itself WebMCP-enabled. It exposes three browser-native tools: analyze_website analyzes a public website and updates the visible report. get_opportunity_report returns the complete current report. select_tools_for_plan selects recommendations and creates a tailored implementation plan. This means an agent can operate WebMCP.ai directly without typing into the URL field or clicking the Analyze button. The agent and user remain in the same interface and share the same application state. How we built it We built WebMCP.ai as a full-stack Next.js application using React and TypeScript. The analysis pipeline first validates the submitted URL and rejects embedded credentials, unsupported protocols, private networks, local addresses, and unsafe redirect destinations. It then performs a bounded crawl of relevant public pages using Cheerio. The extracted content is explicitly marked as untrusted data before being sent to an OpenAI-compatible Responses API. The model researches the website’s business, workflows, public APIs, competitors, and relevant MCP precedents. Its response must match a strict Zod schema before the application accepts it. Opportunity scores are calculated deterministically rather than relying entirely on model judgment. The application then builds a structured implementation prompt containing tool schemas, safeguards, engineering requirements, testing expectations, and acceptance criteria. The WebMCP integration uses the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool API. Tools are registered once with AbortSignal cleanup and reuse the same logic and React state as the visible interface. The application is deployed on Vercel, while the source code and project documentation are hosted publicly on GitHub. Reports remain in browser memory, so no database is currently required. Challenges we ran into One major challenge was working with websites that block automated access, require authentication, or render most useful content through client-side JavaScript. We addressed this by reporting incomplete access honestly and grounding every recommendation in the evidence that was actually available. Analysis requests can also take time because they combine website extraction, research, structured generation, and validation. We introduced bounded timeouts and a fallback analysis path when enriched web research takes too long. Another challenge involved WebMCP lifecycle management inside React. Initially, tool registration could be recreated when the URL or report state changed. We stabilized the callbacks and used references to the latest report so agents retain valid tool handles while the interface updates. Security was equally important. A tool that accepts arbitrary URLs can create server-side request-forgery risks, while crawled content can contain prompt-injection attempts. We added DNS and redirect validation, private-network blocking, content-size limits, bounded crawling, strict schemas, and explicit untrusted-content boundaries. Finally, we had to ensure agents selected the WebMCP tool instead of falling back to browser interaction. Accurate read-only annotations, stable registration, and direct tool descriptions made that behavior reliable. Accomplishments that we’re proud of We are proud that WebMCP.ai does more than generate generic tool ideas. It produces ranked, evidence-backed opportunities connected to real workflows, business value, technical feasibility, and safety requirements. We are especially proud that the application demonstrates the experience it recommends. Agents can call WebMCP tools directly, update the same interface the user sees, retrieve the resulting report, and collaboratively choose an implementation plan. Other accomplishments include: Strictly validated structured model output Deterministic opportunity scoring Transparent evidence and limitations Production-oriented implementation prompts SSRF and prompt-injection defenses Stable WebMCP registration and shared UI state Automated unit, integration, lint, type, build, and end-to-end checks A responsive interface with report and prompt exports What we learned We learned that effective WebMCP tools should not simply reproduce button clicks. The best tools expose stable business capabilities with clear inputs, structured results, and well-defined safety boundaries. Tool metadata also matters more than expected. Names, descriptions, schemas, annotations, and lifecycle behavior determine whether an agent can confidently discover and use a tool. We also learned that agent readiness is not purely a technical score. Authentication, data availability, business value, user trust, implementation effort, and human confirmation all influence whether a workflow should become a tool. Most importantly, WebMCP works best as a collaboration layer. It does not need to replace the interface. It can connect agents to the application’s real capabilities while keeping the user informed and in control. What’s next for WebMCP.ai Next, we want to add: Saved and shareable reports with explicit retention controls Repeatable WebMCP evaluations that measure tool-selection accuracy Before-and-after readiness comparisons Organization workspaces and collaborative reviews Direct export to GitHub issues and engineering backlogs Automated validation of implemented WebMCP schemas Historical monitoring as websites improve their agent readiness Additional analysis of authenticated workflows through approved integrations Our long-term goal is for WebMCP.ai to become the bridge between human-first websites and agent-native experiences: helping teams decide what to expose, why it matters, how to build it safely, and whether it actually improves the experience. title: ZShop Agent Cart
pitch: A shared shopping workspace where humans set intent and WebMCP agents search, compare, and safely build the cart.
about_excerpt: A shared shopping workspace where humans set intent and WebMCP agents search, compare, and safely build the cart. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Shopping agents are often forced to infer intent from pixels, scrape inconsistent product cards, and guess whether an action is safe. ZShop Agent Cart explores a better contract: the storefront exposes precise capabilities while the shopper keeps a visible, shared workspace and remains in control of consequential choices. What it does ZShop registers five WebMCP tools directly from the live storefront: set_shopping_goal makes the shopper's brief visible to both human and agent. search_products searches the live catalog and returns compact, comparable facts. inspect_product reads current price, stock, fulfilment, description, and option requirements. view_cart reads the authenticated shopper's selected items and total. add_product_to_cart adds simple products through the existing signed-in session. The on-page companion shows the shared goal and a live activity trail, so the human can see what the agent is doing without leaving the shopping experience. Products with variants are deliberately not guessed: the tool returns a product URL and asks the shopper to select options. Checkout remains human-controlled. Why WebMCP is the right fit Commerce mixes fast-changing facts, authenticated state, and actions with different risk levels. WebMCP lets the site describe each capability with a narrow JSON schema and behavioral annotations instead of asking an agent to reverse-engineer the UI. The result is faster and more reliable than click automation, while preserving the storefront's own validation, authentication, and cart rules. Before this extension, a shopper could browse ZShop and an agent could separately offer generic advice. Now they can work in the same live catalog and session: the person states intent and handles preference-heavy decisions; the agent retrieves current facts, narrows choices, and performs bounded cart work; both share visible context. How we built it The Nuxt 4 client plugin detects document.modelContext , then registers typed tools with registerTool . Each tool has a constrained input schema, clear descriptions, and read-only, destructive, idempotent, and open-world hints. Tool handlers call the same production catalog and cart APIs as the storefront and reuse the existing auth token. A Vue composable keeps the shared goal and recent action log reactive in the companion UI. Focused Vitest coverage validates product normalization and rejects malformed search terms and numeric inputs. A CDP-based WebMCP host test injects the browser API, verifies all five registrations, executes the goal and live catalog search tools, and confirms that the human-visible companion updates. Challenges The central design challenge was choosing boundaries, not simply exposing every UI action. Product options cannot be selected safely from incomplete intent, and checkout has financial consequences, so neither is automated. Another challenge was keeping the experience useful outside a WebMCP-enabled browser; the storefront still works normally and the companion explains when agent capabilities are unavailable. Accomplishments Five working WebMCP tools backed by a live multilingual catalog. Shared human-agent context visible in the existing storefront. Authenticated cart access without a second agent-specific account system. Explicit safety boundaries for variants and checkout. Reproducible tests, public source, MIT license, and dated challenge-period commits. What we learned Agent-native UX is strongest when structured capabilities and visible human feedback are designed together. Schemas make actions reliable; the companion makes them understandable. The most important tool behavior can also be a refusal to guess. What's next Next we would add preference memory approved by the shopper, side-by-side comparison cards generated from tool results, and a confirmation protocol for reversible versus consequential actions. We would also localize tool descriptions alongside ZShop's Chinese, English, Thai, and Traditional Chinese interface. title: Actalume
pitch: The evidence ledger where agents prove work and named humans decide what becomes true.
about_excerpt: The evidence ledger where agents prove work and named humans decide what becomes true. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent systems are increasingly capable of taking actions, but the human is often left reconstructing the chain of custody afterward. What was actually requested? Which boundary applied? What changed? What proves it? Who accepted it as project truth? Actalume began with one non-negotiable idea: an agent's claim that work is complete is not the same as a human decision that the work is canonical. What it does Actalume is a human-governed system of record for agent work. A project starts with an explicit contract describing its purpose, public-data boundary, allowed actions, prohibited actions and completion rule. An agent can then propose one bounded brick, attach typed evidence receipts and request human review. Six WebMCP tools expose that workflow directly to an agent: list projects, inspect the contract, propose a brick, submit evidence, request review and inspect canonical history. There is deliberately no approval tool. Approval requires a named human and a second confirmation inside the interface. Only then is the decision sealed into immutable, evidence-linked history. All supplied demo content is fictional and public-safe. The app has no accounts, telemetry, network writes or publishing integration. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must infer controls from the interface and the human must trust an unstructured summary of what happened. With WebMCP, Actalume exposes a narrow, typed and inspectable work protocol while keeping the consequential decision outside the agent's authority. People and agents can now share one legible custody chain: the agent can inspect scope, create bounded work and submit proof; the human can review that exact evidence and decide what becomes project history. How we built it Actalume is a local-first React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vite. Browser persistence uses localStorage, with deterministic fictional fixtures and JSON import/export. The WebMCP layer registers six imperative tools using document.modelContext.registerTool, each with narrow schemas and explicit read-only or review-request semantics. The ledger reducer enforces state transitions separately from the UI. Automated tests prove that an agent cannot approve work, approved bricks cannot be mutated, evidence is required before review and all six tools register when the native browser surface is present. The challenge build was verified in Chrome 151 with WebMCP testing enabled. Chrome discovered all six tools and executed safe reads, evidence submission and a human-review request. An attempted agent approval was rejected, and canonical history stayed unchanged. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is experimental, so ordinary-browser fallback behavior had to remain honest without being mistaken for native proof. We separated the visible demo harness from native verification and only claimed WebMCP success after Chrome's getTools and executeTool APIs discovered and exercised the live registrations. The harder product challenge was making governance feel like a workflow rather than a policy page. We designed the interface around one custody line: contract, bounded brick, evidence, human decision and canonical history. Amber surfaces actions awaiting judgment; green is reserved for history already verified by a person. Accomplishments that we're proud of Six working WebMCP tools with no agent approval surface. A named-human, two-step approval gate. Immutable canonical history with evidence counts and deterministic digests. Ten automated governance, registration and deliberate-approval tests. Zero dependency vulnerabilities at submission preparation. A complete responsive product experience rather than an inert technical demo. What we learned Agent safety becomes easier to understand when it is spatial and operational. A visible boundary, a typed tool surface and a blocked transition communicate more than a long policy document. WebMCP is especially powerful when it exposes not only what an agent can do, but also what it cannot do. What's next for Actalume The next version would add pluggable receipt adapters, signed export bundles and optional team roles while preserving the same core rule: agents may propose and prove; named humans decide what becomes true. title: Amaphupho WebMCP
pitch: Culturally grounded African dream insight that AI agents can safely invoke on the open web.
about_excerpt: Culturally grounded African dream insight that AI agents can safely invoke on the open web. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP agent completing a task live: toast confirms an interpretation ran and saved to the journal, real production UI. Landing page, dark mode: crescent moon hero and the "Sangoma AI Dream Interpretation" headline. Landing page, light mode: same hero, warm parchment palette. Dream Interpreter, dark mode: "The Sangoma is listening," the core tool guests can use without signing in. Dream Interpreter, light mode: same input flow, daytime theme. Dream Symbol Glossary, dark mode: the A-Z African dream symbol reference, one of the WebMCP-exposed tools. Dream Symbol Glossary, light mode: same glossary, light theme. Sangoma Circle, dark mode: the shared dreams community feed. Sangoma Circle, light mode: same feed, light theme. Inspiration Amaphupho started from a simple problem: general purpose AI can be useful for reflection, but it should not automatically become the authority on every cultural domain. Dream interpretation is deeply contextual, and African dream traditions carry meanings that are often flattened, generalised, or completely missed by mainstream AI systems. I built Amaphupho as a culturally grounded African dream interpretation platform, drawing on Southern African traditions including Zulu, Xhosa, and Sotho perspectives. When the WebMCP Challenge launched, it introduced a new way for me to think about how a specialist website like Amaphupho could work with general purpose AI agents. The idea that shaped the project was: The agent knows the person through their conversation. Amaphupho knows the specialist cultural domain. WebMCP lets them work together. Instead of an agent scraping the site, guessing how the interface works, or reproducing Amaphupho's cultural knowledge inside another model, I can explicitly expose the capabilities I want an agent to use. What it does Amaphupho WebMCP exposes three structured tools to compatible AI agents. search_dream_symbols allows an agent to search Amaphupho's African dream symbol glossary. It is public, read only, and does not consume a user credit. interpret_dream allows a signed in user to ask their agent to interpret a dream using Amaphupho. The tool uses the same production interpretation path as the normal application, so the existing authentication, credit, rate limit, and journal persistence rules still apply. search_dream_journal allows a signed in user to search their own private dream history through an agent. It is read only and explicitly restricted to the currently authenticated Supabase user. A typical interaction could be: A user asks their agent what a snake means in Amaphupho's cultural glossary. The agent calls Amaphupho's public symbol tool. The user shares a complete dream and asks Amaphupho to interpret it. The interpretation is generated through the existing production service and saved to the user's private journal. Later, the user can ask their agent to find recurring themes in their own dream history. The website still works normally in browsers that do not support WebMCP. How I built it I implemented the WebMCP extension in TypeScript using the WebMCP imperative API. Amaphupho registers tools through: document.modelContext.registerTool() I gave each tool a clear name, description, input schema, annotations, and execution function. The main architectural decision I made was to avoid creating a separate "agent backend". The interpret_dream tool calls the existing Amaphupho production interpretation service. That means agent initiated interpretations use the same authentication checks, credit accounting, rate limiting, Gemini integration, and Supabase persistence as interpretations started through the normal user interface. The symbol search tool reads from Amaphupho's curated cultural symbol data and returns structured results. The private journal tool queries Supabase using the currently authenticated session and explicitly filters results by that user's ID. I designed the integration as progressive enhancement. If WebMCP is not available in the browser, Amaphupho continues to operate as a normal web application. I also added Playwright browser tests, conversational eval cases, tool annotations, provenance documentation, GitHub Actions verification, and automated checks for repository formatting requirements. The live application is hosted through Netlify and served from Amaphupho's own domain at https://www.amaphupho.co.za . Challenges I ran into One of the biggest challenges was deciding what not to expose. It would have been easy for me to create a broad agent endpoint that could perform many application actions, but that would also create a much larger privacy and security surface. Instead, I deliberately kept the WebMCP layer small. The public cultural search tool does not require authentication. Dream interpretation requires authentication and has a real side effect because it consumes a credit and saves an entry. Journal search requires authentication but remains strictly read only. Another challenge was making agent initiated behaviour match the existing product instead of creating a parallel implementation. Reusing the production interpretation service meant dealing carefully with sessions, credits, rate limits, failures, and journal persistence. Amaphupho also existed before the challenge, so another important challenge was making the new work independently reviewable. I therefore documented the pre WebMCP boundary and the new WebMCP extension separately in the public challenge repository. Finally, private dream journals contain personal information, so I designed the journal tool so that an agent can never provide an arbitrary user ID or search another person's data. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that the WebMCP integration is running inside a real production application rather than a standalone demonstration. I designed the three tools with different access and side effect boundaries that match what they actually do. Agent initiated dream interpretation reuses Amaphupho's existing production path instead of bypassing product rules. Private journal access is scoped to the authenticated user and remains read only. The site still works normally without WebMCP support. I also added automated browser verification and eval cases rather than relying only on manual demonstrations. Most importantly, I think the integration demonstrates a model where a general purpose agent does not need to own every specialist capability. Amaphupho remains responsible for its cultural knowledge, its user data, and its application rules, while the agent provides the conversational interface. What I learned The biggest lesson I learned was that building for agents is not mainly about exposing more functionality. It is about exposing the right functionality with clear boundaries. Tool names and descriptions matter because the agent needs to understand when a capability should be used. Input schemas matter because they make the interaction predictable. Annotations matter because read only actions should be distinguishable from actions with side effects. Authentication boundaries matter because an agent should not gain broader access simply because it is acting on behalf of a user. I also learned that WebMCP can create a useful relationship between general purpose agents and specialist websites. A general purpose agent can retain conversational context and understand what the user is trying to achieve, while a specialist service can remain authoritative for its own domain. That feels more sustainable to me than requiring every agent to replicate every specialist service internally. What's next for Amaphupho WebMCP The next step I want to explore is deeper longitudinal dream analysis with explicit user control. A user could ask Amaphupho to identify recurring themes across a selected period of their journal, compare repeated symbols, or explore how certain themes have changed over time. I also want to expand multilingual support across English, isiZulu, and Sesotho so users can interact with both the agent and Amaphupho in the language that is most meaningful to them. Future WebMCP tools could support richer cultural symbol exploration and guided reflection without exposing unrestricted access to private journal data. More broadly, I see Amaphupho as an example of how culturally specific and specialist web applications can participate in the agentic web while remaining responsible for their own knowledge, permissions, and user trust. title: Brenych Studio Agent Interface
pitch: A WebMCP-powered portfolio that lets AI agents evaluate real project evidence, focus the strongest proof, and create a local collaboration brief in the same visible interface as the human.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered portfolio that lets AI agents evaluate real project evidence, focus the strongest proof, and create a local collaboration brief in the same visible interface as the human. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most portfolios are designed for people to browse. But when an AI agent needs to understand whether a studio is a good fit for a specific project, it still has to infer capabilities from navigation, marketing copy, screenshots, and visual presentation. We wanted to explore a different model: what if a portfolio could provide structured evidence of what its work actually proves? That became Brenych Studio Agent Interface — a shared evidence workspace where people and AI agents can evaluate the same real portfolio through the same visible interface. What it does The site exposes seven structured WebMCP tools directly from the live page: get_profile get_capabilities list_projects get_project match_requirements focus_project create_collaboration_brief An agent can discover capabilities, inspect project dossiers, evaluate requirements, focus the strongest evidence, and create an editable collaboration brief. The important part is that the agent does not operate inside a separate chatbot layer. Its actions update the same interface the human is looking at. For example, when evaluating: Electron · MCP · AI automation · Supabase the deterministic evidence model returns 100% evidence coverage , ranks the strongest project evidence, and visibly recomposes the spatial evidence field. When evaluating unsupported requirements such as: Swift · Metal · native iOS the interface returns 0% coverage / NOT DEMONSTRATED instead of inventing a fit. How we built it The application is built with: React TypeScript Vite Zustand Motion WebMCP Cloudflare Pages The architecture separates the pure evidence domain from the browser integration: Pure domain → application façade → semantic state → WebMCP + visible UI Matching is deterministic rather than probabilistic. Requirements are normalized and resolved through curated relationships: exact match: 1.00 alias match: 0.90 related evidence: 0.45 missing evidence: 0.00 There are no embeddings, fuzzy matching, LLM-generated rankings, or screenshot-derived scores. The WebMCP integration uses the current document.modelContext API. Manual controls and WebMCP tools share the same application boundary, so both human and agent interactions produce the same semantic state. The production application contains seven scoring project records, four non-scoring studio showcase systems, and 18 reviewed evidence images. Challenges we ran into The most important challenge only appeared during real browser certification. All seven tools registered and enumerated correctly in Chrome, but every invocation initially failed. The development type package described an execution callback with an options argument containing a cancellation signal, while the shipping Chrome host invoked the handler with only the input object. This was invisible in our unit and type-level tests. We hardened the WebMCP adapter so the options argument is optional while preserving the same schemas, annotations, outputs, cancellation behavior, and tool semantics. We also observed a host-level limitation during ChatGPT desktop testing: the in-app browser correctly discovered all seven Site Tools, but the Work agent did not consistently route requests through them and sometimes fell back to general browsing. Since the Challenge also supports WebMCP-enabled Chrome, we completed end-to-end certification there. This exposed an important opportunity for more predictable Site Tools routing across agent hosts. Real host testing also exposed presentation issues that ordinary automated tests did not catch: scroll-position restoration, evidence metadata overlap, and motion that technically existed but was not perceptible to a human viewer. Those findings reinforced an important lesson: agent-native interfaces need both deterministic automated verification and real visual/browser certification. Accomplishments that we're proud of Seven real WebMCP tools registered on the production website End-to-end WebMCP execution verified in Chrome 152 Visible agent-driven interface recomposition Deterministic positive and negative evidence matching Exact scroll restoration for both manual and agent-driven project focus Editable page-local collaboration brief with no automatic external write Explicit public / owner-verified evidence boundaries Complete manual fallback when WebMCP is unavailable Responsive experience from mobile to large desktop Reduced-motion and keyboard-accessible interaction paths 244 automated tests across 41 test files Public Apache-2.0 repository and live Cloudflare Pages deployment What we learned WebMCP becomes much more interesting when it is not treated as a hidden automation layer. The strongest interaction we found is when the agent and the human operate on the same visible state . The agent can evaluate and focus evidence, but the human can immediately inspect why that result exists, review the actual screenshots and limitations, edit the generated brief, or ignore the agent entirely and use the interface manually. We also learned that negative evidence is as important as positive evidence. A trustworthy agent-facing site should be able to say “not demonstrated” instead of always trying to produce a confident answer. What's next for Brenych Studio Agent Interface The current project focuses on a portfolio as an evidence interface, but the same pattern could extend much further. Future directions include: richer structured evidence provenance broader agent-host interoperability reusable WebMCP evidence components client and procurement evaluation workflows deeper collaboration planning agent-native interfaces for other Brenych Studio products The larger idea is simple: A website should not only present information to an AI agent. It should expose clear, bounded operations and structured evidence that both the agent and the human can understand and verify together.
