title: ChinaMarketing.AI Labs — WebMCP GEO Workbench
pitch: A browser-native GEO workspace where humans and AI agents investigate the same retained evidence, prepare follow-up work, and keep consequential actions under human control.
about_excerpt: A browser-native GEO workspace where humans and AI agents investigate the same retained evidence, prepare follow-up work, and keep consequential actions under human control. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT uses the site’s WebMCP evidence tool, and the same six matching observations appear immediately in the Evidence browser. The agent creates a 10-question follow-up assessment, with the draft appearing directly in the shared workspace. The agent prepares a 75-credit run, but execution stays with the human and only pre-captured demo evidence is loaded. Inspiration GEO assessments get complicated quickly. A single project can involve dozens of questions, several AI engines and hundreds of observations. We already had a structured way to review that evidence, but browser-native agents raised a more interesting question: what happens if the agent can work with the application itself instead of trying to understand it from rendered pages? That is what we wanted to test with WebMCP. We did not want to give an agent unrestricted access. The idea was to let it investigate an assessment, find evidence and prepare the next piece of work, while the person using the application could see what was happening and stay in control of anything consequential. What it does The WebMCP GEO Workbench is a small, self-contained version of a GEO assessment workspace. A completed assessment is already loaded into the application. From ChatGPT, the agent can use the site's WebMCP tools to understand the project, inspect the questions, search retained evidence, bring relevant opportunities into view, create a follow-up assessment, edit that draft and prepare a quote for a possible next run. The agent is working with the same app state the user sees, not a separate agent-only layer. If it searches for observations where alternatives appear while the assessed entity is absent, the Evidence view changes to show those same observations. If it creates a follow-up, the draft appears in the application. If it prepares a run, the quote appears there too. The agent can prepare the run, but it cannot execute it, call external AI providers or spend credits. The final action stays with the person using the application. How we built it The project is a standalone React and TypeScript application deployed on Cloudflare Workers. The normal interface and the WebMCP tools use the same application service and local state. We did not build one workflow for the browser and another for the agent. The site registers eight tools directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . They cover project context, assessment summaries, question plans, evidence search, opportunities, follow-up creation and editing, and run preparation. For the challenge demo we use a sanitised assessment fixture with 22 questions, five captured engines and 110 retained observations. There is no live model execution behind the demo. The final human action loads pre-captured evidence and says so clearly in the interface. The challenge app is also separate from our production systems, credentials, billing and private assessment data. Challenges we ran into One of the harder decisions was where to stop. We wanted the agent to be useful, but not to turn the demo into a fully autonomous workflow. So it can investigate, draft and prepare the next run, but the final execution stays with the person using the app. Another challenge was keeping what the agent found and what the user sees in the browser in sync. Returning six matching evidence IDs in chat is useful, but it is much better when those same six records appear immediately in the Evidence view. We also had to keep the demo grounded in what the assessment actually contains. The records shown here are retained observations from a bounded assessment, not permanent rankings or proof of why an external model produced a particular answer. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part we are happiest with is that the demo feels like one shared application rather than a chat window controlling a separate automation layer. The agent can search retained evidence and the same records appear in the browser. It can create a follow-up and the draft appears in the workspace. It can prepare a run and the quote appears there too. We also kept the boundary around execution intact. The agent can investigate and prepare, but the final action still requires a person. Finally, we kept the challenge build isolated from production. The public demo uses sanitized, pre-captured assessment data and does not expose production credentials, private customer data, billing or live provider execution. What we learned The main thing we learned was that WebMCP works best when the agent can use the same application state as the person looking at the screen. That sounds obvious, but it changed how we thought about the tools. Instead of asking ChatGPT to work out what was happening from the page, we could expose the parts of the application it actually needed: the assessment context, evidence, opportunities and follow-up draft. We also found that the agent did not need full control to be useful. It could do most of the investigation and preparation, while the final execution still stayed with the user. The evidence-search interaction was probably the clearest example. ChatGPT found the matching records through WebMCP, and those same records appeared immediately in the app. What's next for ChinaMarketing.AI Labs — WebMCP GEO Workbench This is a small experimental build, not a production feature. Our next step is to look at which parts of this interaction model are useful enough to bring into the main ChinaMarketing.AI GEO workspace. The same pattern could also be useful in other evidence-heavy applications where an agent needs structured access to the work without being given unrestricted authority. title: CoHabby Living
pitch: A compatibility-first roommate finder where your browser agent does the structured work through six WebMCP tools, and you keep every human decision.
about_excerpt: A compatibility-first roommate finder where your browser agent does the structured work through six WebMCP tools, and you keep every human decision. Like Comment Story Updates The last click stays human: Confirm demo introduction moves the state to v9. Demo confirmed. No real message was sent. compare_shortlist lays two people side by side across six dimensions of daily life. Warm is the chosen tone for the first hello. Public proof: MIT license, public repository, immutable tag, and the live footer's exact deployed revision ba55c557358a. Six WebMCP tools registered on one page: five change what the person sees, one is read-only. READY · v1 is the state both of them share. prepare_introduction drafts a first hello from facts already on the page. The person edits every word; no site tool can confirm or send. Synergy Lens: explain_synergy_match opens Maya's 92 read, 88% profile evidence, and three practical reasons the household rhythms fit. Approval is not a tool. The agent stages the living plan; only the person clicks Yes, use these choices. State moves v2 to v3. find_compatible_rooms brings Maya, Jordan, and Sam onto the page, person first, home as context. Whole-card selection stays human. Inspiration Finding a roommate is easy. Finding someone you can actually live well with is hard, and it shapes daily life for a lot of people: traveling nurses, single parents, new graduates, retirees, interns. Rooms are easy to list. Compatibility is what nobody helps with. CoHabby puts the person first and the room second. I also believe good technology should make people more human, not more mechanical. WebMCP made that concrete: the page can hand an agent real tools and still keep the meaningful decisions on the human side of the screen. CoHabby is already a live product with real users on the web , iOS , and Android . This challenge build is a separate, new codebase, but the problem it targets and the people it serves are the same. What people and agents do together Six small WebMCP tools share one page with the person: get_living_context reads the visible state (the only read-only tool) stage_living_brief stages a living plan from everyday habits find_compatible_rooms brings Maya, Jordan, and Sam onto the page, person first explain_synergy_match opens the Synergy Lens: a 92 score, 88% evidence, three practical reasons compare_shortlist lays two people side by side across six dimensions of daily life prepare_introduction drafts an editable first hello from facts already on the page Three actions are deliberately not tools: approving the plan, editing the hello, and confirming the introduction. The public tests assert that apply_living_brief and confirm_introduction do not exist. The agent prepares everything. The last click stays with the person. Why WebMCP fits Roommate matching is structured work with a few consequential decisions in between. WebMCP lets the page describe each step precisely, so the agent completes it reliably instead of guessing at the UI, and every result renders where the person can see it. Agent and human read the same state, which advances visibly from v1 to v9. How I built it Next.js and TypeScript. Every tool has a strict JSON Schema input (bounded enums, patterns, additionalProperties: false ) and a separate output schema, so nothing reaches the agent that a person could not see. Each call runs under a combined abort signal: cancel it and it rolls back to its checkpoint and commits nothing. A tool resolves only after the page acknowledges the new state has rendered, so "done" always means "visible." The live footer prints the deployed revision, the repo is MIT, and the judged source is pinned to an immutable tag. Fixtures and Synergy scores are fictional demo data, and the film says so. This WebMCP app is entirely new work created during the submission period (repository started Sept 1, 2026; every commit is dated inside the window). It shares no code with CoHabby's existing web and mobile products. Only the brand, the mission, and the roommate-compatibility concept pre-date the challenge; CHALLENGE_WORK.md in the repo documents the separation. Challenges and what I learned The hardest call was the human boundary. Making everything a tool would have looked more autonomous. It also would have let an agent introduce you to a stranger without asking. The hardest engineering was render acknowledgement: agents move faster than browsers paint, and a tool that returns before its result is on screen creates a page the person and the agent disagree about. The lesson: small, bounded tools with visible results beat one clever tool, and the best agent-native page is the one where you can tell exactly what the agent did and what you decided. title: Lobasters
pitch: Lobasters is a shared research workspace where humans and AI agents configure and run multi-model experiments together.
about_excerpt: Lobasters is a shared research workspace where humans and AI agents configure and run multi-model experiments together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates You can choose any background of your choice Choose between three epic modes Intresting questions They sound so understandable Inspiration What it does How we built it## Inspiration AI research is becoming collaborative—but most tools still assume that either a human operates every control manually or an agent works through a hidden API. We wanted to explore a better middle ground: one workspace where a researcher and an AI agent can both configure, inspect, and run the same multi-model experiment. That became Lobasters: a model collaboration platform built around Arena, Examination, and LAB modes. What it does Lobasters lets researchers bring their own model providers and API keys, then create structured interactions between models. Arena runs debates, negotiations, sales simulations, and custom multi-model scenarios. Each participant can have its own instructions, reasoning settings, tools, tool-result visibility, and session-ending outcomes. Examination creates a Teacher–Student workflow. The teacher asks questions, evaluates each answer against a grading scale, explains the grade, and produces a final summary and downloadable report. LAB lets a Master Agent coordinate helper agents, shared files, instructions, and open-ended research challenges. The key WebMCP idea is that an external agent does not need to hunt through dozens of form controls. Each mode exposes a typed action that can apply a complete configuration in one call. The researcher can then inspect, edit, and run that exact same browser state. How we built it We built Lobasters with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and an OpenAI-compatible provider layer. Model requests are collected through a serverless streaming transport, while configuration and active session state stay in the browser. Researchers bring their own API keys, and Lobasters does not persist model conversations. We implemented persistent WebMCP tools for all three modes: lobasters_arena configures two participants, prompts, session settings, and custom tools. lobasters_examination configures the Teacher, Student, domains, grading, and session settings. lobasters_lab configures the Master Agent, helper agents, files, and challenges. Arena’s custom tools support JSON Schema arguments, immediate results, private or opponent-visible outputs, and controlled terminal outcomes. Challenges we faced The difficult part was not just registering a WebMCP tool. It was making an agent action truly useful for a complex research interface without creating a separate agent-only product. We also had to handle inconsistent provider behavior: some models return reasoning in native fields, some return only final content, some make tool-only calls, and some stop before producing a final-content field. We added provider-aware reasoning handling, safe fallbacks, clear session states, and raw transcripts so researchers can understand what actually happened. Another challenge was preserving correct identity and tool context across Arena turns. We strengthened role isolation, made agent attribution clearer in the interface, and ensured tool-call context survives follow-up turns. What we learned We learned that agent usability is not about replacing the human interface. It is about exposing meaningful, structured operations over the same interface a human can understand and control. WebMCP is especially powerful when a tool represents a real workflow—such as configuring a complete multi-model research session—rather than a single button click. Lobasters demonstrates how agents and researchers can operate one shared workspace without sacrificing transparency or researcher control. title: Open Racer Racing Line Editor
pitch: An open-source racing line editor that lets AI agents create track layouts through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An open-source racing line editor that lets AI agents create track layouts through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Racing Line 3D View Codex using WebMCP Inspiration I built the first version of the racing line editor about six years ago. I wanted a tool to prepare for karting and learn unfamiliar tracks. I studied onboard videos and drew every braking point, apex, and acceleration zone by hand. I kept wondering whether an AI could help me. Last year, I returned to the project and added a 3D WebGL view. Claude and Codex helped me bring it back to life. The editor was also recognized in the 2025 Google Maps Platform Awards. What it does The racing line editor lets you draw and edit racing lines on a satellite map. Points can represent braking, acceleration, or transition. Lines can be saved locally and viewed in 3D. In the demo, Codex reads an existing full-circuit line. Two shorter layouts are missing. Through WebMCP, it reads the circuit, the reference line, and the editor guidance. It then creates both missing layouts directly in the editor. How I built it For this challenge, I separated the editor from the older Open Racer application and rebuilt it as a standalone open-source app. It uses Vite, React 19, JavaScript, Google Maps Platform, and Paper.js. Lines are stored locally with IndexedDB and can be exported as JSON. There is no backend or sign-in. The WebMCP tools use the same editor state as the visible controls. Agents can inspect the track, read line-creation guidance, edit points, undo changes, and save or load lines. I use Vitest for unit tests, Playwright for browser tests, and GitHub Pages for deployment. The hardest part A racing line is more than coordinates. Point order matters. The line must stay on the drivable surface, and one circuit can contain several layouts. The challenge was giving the agent enough context while keeping every change visible and understandable to the user. What I learned Structured WebMCP actions reduce guessing. They make agent changes more predictable and easier to verify. title: revAIew Evidence Room
pitch: revAIew lets agents investigate claims through WebMCP while people decide what gets through and receive a source-bound receipt.
about_excerpt: revAIew lets agents investigate claims through WebMCP while people decide what gets through and receive a source-bound receipt. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can generate and recommend faster than people can review. The hard problem is no longer only finding information; it is keeping evidence, uncertainty, and authority clear before an answer influences the next action. The unit-distance conjecture offered a concrete test. OpenAI reports that an internal model generated a counterexample. A nine-author companion paper publishes a short, human-verified account of the mathematics. Those are related facts, but mathematical verification does not independently reproduce the internal model run. revAIew keeps that distinction visible. What it does revAIew Evidence Room gives a person and an agent one shared evidence workspace. Five page-scoped WebMCP tools let the agent inspect claims, trace public sources, compare recorded positions, and retrieve a pre-registered pressure test. A sixth tool stages a visible evidence packet containing the selected claims, source IDs, uncertainty, missing proof, and next test. The registered site-tool path ends there. It exposes no tool that can choose, confirm, or create a receipt. The person sees the same packet, selects adopt, enforce, challenge, hold, or discard, and explicitly confirms the choice in the visible browser interface. That action creates a browser-local SHA-256 receipt bound to the packet and current fixed corpus. The receipt is an integrity record, not an identity signature, certification, or proof that the underlying claim is true. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must infer evidence relationships from presentation and visual controls. With WebMCP, the live page exposes narrow, structured operations backed by the same services as the human interface. The agent and person therefore share exact claim identifiers, source mappings, classifications, uncertainty, and pressure tests. The improvement is not unlimited autonomy. It is a clearer, more inspectable handoff between structured agent investigation and visible human judgment. What people and agents do together The agent: reads the fixed public evidence corpus traces claims to canonical public sources preserves disagreement and missing proof retrieves a registered falsification test stages a visible evidence packet The person: sees the same evidence state judges whether the support is sufficient chooses the consequential action explicitly confirms the decision receives or clears the browser-local receipt How we built it The standalone challenge package uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and the imperative WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool . Every tool has a closed JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false , bounded runtime validation, and WebMCP behavior annotations. Public source content is marked potentially untrusted. An abort signal removes page-scoped registrations when the route leaves, and partial registration is cleaned up if setup fails. The human interface and WebMCP tools call the same deterministic evidence services. Receipt verification recomputes its SHA-256 value and revalidates every evidence-derived field against the current corpus before trusting browser storage. Focused tests and a checked-in deterministic contract exercise cover all six tool definitions, strict input handling, source mappings, staging, receipt verification, and the absence of a decision or receipt-creation tool. Challenge-period work revAIew existed before the WebMCP Challenge. During the submission period, we added the six-tool WebMCP adapter, bounded public evidence corpus, shared visible staging flow, human confirmation boundary, receipt verification, focused tests, deterministic contract exercise, and standalone public MIT-licensed package. This submission asks judges to evaluate that WebMCP extension, not the pre-existing product concept. Boundaries This is a small fixed-corpus demonstration, not live web search or a universal AI verifier. It does not prove broad browser compatibility, model quality, user adoption, or categorical prevention of browser automation. WebMCP annotations are descriptive hints, not an authorization system. title: Automata - a WebMCP co-creation playground
pitch: You and your agent, one universe. A cellular automata playground where a human and an AI agent build, run, and study Game of Life worlds together through WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: You and your agent, one universe. A cellular automata playground where a human and an AI agent build, run, and study Game of Life worlds together through WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates What it does Automata is an interactive cellular automata canvas where a human and an AI agent share one Game of Life universe. The human draws, erases, and stamps patterns by hand. The agent drives the same universe through 10 WebMCP tools: spawning catalog patterns, inventing new ones from RLE, switching rule systems, fast-forwarding up to 5,000 generations, and analyzing what emerged. Every agent action lights up on the canvas and lands in an on-screen activity feed, so the human always sees what their collaborator did. Why it's a strong fit for WebMCP Cellular automata are a natural human + agent collaboration. The work splits cleanly: humans sketch curiosity (a squiggle, a stamped pulsar, a splash of soup), and agents run the experiment (hundreds of generations in a blink, then a classified report of the outcome). That only works if the agent can operate the app itself, not a parallel API - which is exactly what WebMCP provides. Each of the app's 10 tools is registered through the WebMCP Imperative API with document.modelContext.registerTool, mixing read-only tools (get_state, analyze, list_patterns) with mutating ones (spawn_pattern, load_rle, set_rules, run_steps, add_noise, clear, set_running). What people and agents can do together that was hard before Say "add a glider gun and some chaos, run 400 generations, tell me what emerges." The agent stamps the gun, sprinkles noise, fast-forwards 400 generations, and returns a named census of the wreckage: "12 blocks, 5 blinkers, a beehive, 3 escaped gliders, stable since generation 212." The analyze tool is non-destructive - it clones the universe, simulates ahead, detects extinction, stabilization (with period), or ongoing activity, and names the objects that emerge. Then the volley continues: the human stamps a pulsar into the agent's world, the agent weaves gliders around it with load_rle, or flips the physics to HighLife or a custom B../S.. rulestring and reports what the same world does under new laws. Before WebMCP, an agent could advise about Game of Life; it couldn't sit at the same table. How WebMCP was implemented All 10 tools are registered via the WebMCP Imperative API (document.modelContext.registerTool), with JSON tool results. The page ships a WebMCP origin trial token so Chrome 149+ gets native WebMCP (also testable via chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing); without either, a built-in shim provides the same registerTool/getTools/executeTool surface and an in-page Agent console lets you call every tool by hand. The automata engine is pure dependency-free JavaScript (grid, Life-like rule parser, pattern catalog, RLE round-trips, cycle detection, object classification) with 16 Node tests, so tool behavior is verifiable outside the browser. Challenges and learnings Making analyze non-destructive: it had to clone the universe and simulate ahead without touching the live world the human is watching. Naming what emerges: classifying the settled state into named objects took cycle detection plus object classification, not just a population count. Keeping the human in the loop: every tool call highlights the canvas and posts to the activity feed. Dual registration path: native WebMCP via origin trial/flag, with a shim exposing the identical surface. title: CodePath
pitch: CodePath is an agent-native coding school where WebMCP lets AI tutors understand a learner’s live lesson, code, errors, progress, and tutor mode to guide them in real time.
about_excerpt: CodePath is an agent-native coding school where WebMCP lets AI tutors understand a learner’s live lesson, code, errors, progress, and tutor mode to guide them in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Learning programming with AI assistants is powerful, but the experience is still fragmented. Today, learners often use two separate tools: a learning platform that provides lessons and exercises an AI assistant that helps them when they are stuck The problem is that the AI assistant usually does not know the learner's real context. The learner has to copy the lesson, their code, their errors, and their progress into the chat every time. We wanted to explore a different approach: What if the learning platform itself could give an AI agent the exact context it needs to become a real programming tutor? This idea inspired CodePath, an agent-native coding school where humans and AI agents can learn together through WebMCP. What it does CodePath is a programming learning platform that teaches coding from scratch while allowing WebMCP-compatible AI agents to understand and interact with the learning environment. The current MVP provides a beginner JavaScript learning path with: structured lessons visual explanations interactive code editor coding exercises deterministic tests quizzes progressive unlocking AI Tutor Modes The key difference is that the AI agent does not need the learner to manually explain their situation. Through WebMCP tools, the agent can understand: the current course and lesson the learner's active step whether they are reading, practicing, editing code, or reviewing feedback the exact live code currently written in the editor runtime output test results mistakes and progress the learner's preferred Tutor Mode For example, when a learner writes incorrect code, the agent can see the actual code, the real execution result, and the failed test instead of giving a generic explanation. CodePath also includes three Tutor Modes: Guide: helps learners discover the solution through hints without revealing the final answer. Balanced: provides stronger guidance while keeping the learner involved. Explain: gives direct explanations and complete solutions when requested. How we built it CodePath was built as a React + TypeScript web application using Vite. The learning system is built around structured course data, allowing new programming languages and lessons to be added without rebuilding the interface. Main technologies used: React TypeScript Vite CodeMirror Zustand JavaScript sandbox execution deterministic exercise validators browser-native WebMCP registration MCP-compatible tooling The application exposes seven WebMCP tools: get_course_progress get_current_lesson get_current_exercise get_learning_context open_lesson run_code submit_solution A major part of the implementation was creating a reliable learning context system. The platform tracks: active learning step learner activity live editor content code execution results exercise submissions progress tutor preferences This allows an AI agent to understand not only what page the learner opened , but what they are actually doing . Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what information an AI tutor actually needs. Our first implementation exposed basic course information and exercises, but we discovered that this was not enough. An AI tutor needs to know: Is the learner reading or coding? What exact code are they currently editing? Did they already run the code? What happened when they ran it? What mistake are they making? How much help should the tutor provide? We created an active learning cursor and live editor state system to solve this problem. Another challenge was avoiding AI replacing learning. A simple chatbot can immediately provide the correct answer, but that is not always useful for education. We created Tutor Policies so the learner controls how the AI should teach them. The website provides the agent with the learner's preferred tutoring behavior instead of forcing one style. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that CodePath demonstrates a complete agent-native learning workflow. The agent can: discover the available WebMCP tools understand the learner's current state navigate lessons read live code changes access real execution results understand failed tests adapt its tutoring style based on Tutor Mode One important achievement was solving the live-code context problem. The AI does not receive a copied or outdated version of the learner's code. It receives the actual current editor draft. Another achievement is the separation between: deterministic evaluation: deciding if code is correct AI tutoring: explaining and guiding the learner This prevents the AI from guessing correctness and allows it to focus on teaching. What we learned Building CodePath changed our view of AI-powered websites. Adding a chatbot is not enough to create a useful AI experience. For an agent to truly help users, websites need to expose meaningful context and actions. WebMCP provides a bridge between traditional websites and AI agents by allowing websites to describe their capabilities and share structured information. We learned that the most important part of an AI application is not only the model itself, but the quality of the context provided to it. What's next for CodePath The current MVP proves the concept with JavaScript. The next steps are: adding complete programming paths for Python, HTML/CSS, SQL, and more creating larger project-based courses adding more interactive visual explanations improving personalized learning recommendations adapting exercises based on learner mistakes expanding accessibility features The long-term vision is to create a programming school where: the course provides structure, the learner writes the code, and their preferred AI agent always understands how to help. title: ContractClarity
pitch: Sign with clarity. ContractClarity gives you an AI collaborator that helps you understand every agreement before you commit.
about_excerpt: Sign with clarity. ContractClarity gives you an AI collaborator that helps you understand every agreement before you commit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I talked with a lawyer, my old high school teacher, who told me about a case she had won. The other party was a woman who did not speak English. She signed a contract she could not read and agreed to terms she did not understand. She later lost her home. I kept thinking about how often contracts decide serious parts of someone’s life. A lease can affect where you live. A job offer can affect your income and obligations. A service agreement can decide what you pay and how hard it is to leave. Most people do not have a lawyer beside them when they need to sign something. They need a way to ask clear questions and understand the answer. What it does ContractClarity accepts pasted text, PDFs, and Word documents. It extracts practical details such as the parties, effective date, contract term, notice period, payment terms, amounts, and governing law. It also looks for clauses that often deserve attention, including automatic renewal, termination rights, indemnification, late fees, non-competes, arbitration, intellectual-property assignment, and liability limits. Each finding includes the relevant quote, section, severity, confidence, and a plain explanation of why it may matter. The page also creates a 0-to-100 review score so you can see which agreements may need closer attention. Through WebMCP, your AI agent can read the contract, retrieve the findings, compare two agreements, inspect a specific clause, and explain the result in clear language. How we built it ContractClarity is a static HTML app with no backend and no API keys. PDF.js reads PDFs in the browser. Mammoth extracts text from Word documents. A JavaScript term extractor and clause rulebook create the analysis. The document stays in the browser unless you choose to share it with a connected agent. I registered 13 WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). They range from broad actions such as analyze_contract and compare_contracts to focused actions such as get_clause_by_id and explain_flag. I also added a WebMCP polyfill for browsers without native support and a manual tool tester for development and demos. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was deciding what the page should do and what the agent should do. At first, it was easy to make the agent summarize the contract. But that didn't feel reliable because a summary without evidence doesn't really provide any practical value. I moved the document work into the page. ContractClarity extracts terms, finds clauses, calculates the review signal, and keeps the exact quote that caused each finding. The agent then uses those results to explain the contract and answer questions. Accomplishments that we're proud of I built a working WebMCP experience where the page and the agent can work on the same contract. I wanted to leverage AI as a thought partner and collaborator and I think this accomplishes that in a very practical way. For example, I am proud that the app works for different levels of experience without changing the core flow. Someone can ask, “Can I leave this lease early?” but a more technical user such as a lawyer or contract manage,r can ask for the termination clause, the review signal, and the evidence behind it. What we learned I learned that MCP lets a webpage give an AI agent tools and structured information. Which I believe can help AI become a better collaborator. In ContractClarity, the agent can be asked focused questions and explain the result clearly because MCP makes the page and the agent work together. The page provides the data and capabilities. The agent helps the user understand and use them. This was my first time thinking about MCP at scale, and it was fun! In general, I learned about what MCP was and thought of more business models that can use MCP. What's next for ContractClarity I want to add translations so people can understand agreements in the language they use every day, which would be less work on the model the user uses to access the site and more accurate for less hallucinations. I think also providing more specific prompting format/formatted responses would help with token usage when an agent is accessing the cite and generating a response. about_excerpt: Drop any waiver, consent document or agreement into ChatGPT or Chrome and it becomes a live, legally signable e-sign form. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration To convert a PDF into a signable form, you have to retype every field. We wanted it to be a single sentence to your browser: "Make this a signable form." What it does Two WebMCP tools on formesign.com : create_form turns your agent's submitted document into a live signable form within your account, and drops you into the signing preview. edit_full_form allows editing in natural language and seeing the changes as they appear on the form. How we built it Form generation: our document-to-form model, fine-tuned on OpenAI models, converts your agent's HTML into the full form: fields, agreement text, signature blocks. WebMCP layer: exposes only the tools that you need on the page you are at, always acting as the logged-in user. Challenges we ran into Sign in. Forms are in your account, but our homepage has no auth state at all. Our first attempt was a separate get_login_status tool that the agent had to call before anything else. It felt clumsy, so we scrapped it: now create_form checks the sign-in itself, and if you are not logged in, it just redirects the tab to Google sign-in and the agent picks up from where it left off. Accomplishments that we're proud of Onboarding has gone from 15-20 minutes of uploading, reviewing and clicking to under a minute of conversation. The user only does about 5% of the work: describe, sign in, review. What we learned With WebMCP, the page dictates which tools exist. On the homepage we offer to create a form; within the editor we offer to edit it. The agent's world always matches your screen. What's next for Formesign WebMCP: Document to Signature Form Reporting and onboarding tools. Ask "who has signed so far?" in your browser, or go from landing page to first signed document in one conversation. title: Warranty Vault
pitch: Warranty Vault is a personal warranty management web app for tracking products, purchase details, warranty coverage, invoices, manuals, warranty cards, and other supporting documents in one place.
about_excerpt: Warranty Vault is a personal warranty management web app for tracking products, purchase details, warranty coverage, invoices, manuals, warranty cards, and other supporting documents in one place. Like Comment Story Updates Home Page for Warranty Vault after user login Add warranty page Chart of remaining warranty per product List of WebMCP tools, from Chrome Agent using tool to create a new warranty item Agent conversing in Hindi+English to user for fethcing details of warranty Preview of uploaded warranty doc through Codex Agent Warranty Vault Inspiration Whenever we buy a product—an AC, TV, laptop, mobile phone, or home appliance—we receive product and warranty information in different ways. Sometimes we have to register the warranty manually on a website. Sometimes the information is available in a Gmail purchase email, invoice, PDF, receipt, or warranty document . The information already exists digitally, but we still have to manually organize it. To keep track of a warranty, users often have to search their emails, find the invoice or warranty document, read it, and manually copy details such as the product name, brand, model number, serial number, purchase date, price, warranty period, and expiry date into another application. Months or years later, when the warranty is about to expire—or when the product develops an issue—we have to search through the same old emails, PDFs, and invoices again. This made us ask a simple question: Why should users manually enter and search for information that already exists digitally? That question inspired us to build Warranty Vault . Warranty Vault brings the complete warranty lifecycle into one place—from capturing warranty information from Gmail to tracking expiry and helping users extend or claim their warranty when they need it. With WebMCP , Warranty Vault becomes agent-ready, allowing AI agents to understand the application's capabilities and perform structured actions on behalf of the user. What it does Warranty Vault is a smart warranty management application designed to eliminate repetitive manual warranty entry and simplify warranty management throughout the product lifecycle. Instead of manually finding an email, reading an invoice, and entering every field into Warranty Vault, a user can simply ask: "Find my AC warranty email in Gmail and add it to Warranty Vault." The AI can find the relevant purchase or warranty email in Gmail, understand the information, extract the required product and warranty details, and use Warranty Vault's WebMCP capabilities to create the warranty record. Warranty Vault can maintain information such as: Product name Brand Product category Model number Serial number Purchase date Purchase price Retailer or seller Warranty duration Warranty start date Warranty expiry date Invoice and supporting information But Warranty Vault doesn't stop after saving the warranty. It continues to help users throughout the complete warranty lifecycle . Warranty Expiry Tracking Warranty Vault keeps track of warranty expiry dates so users don't have to remember them manually. When a product is approaching its warranty expiry date, Warranty Vault can surface that information to the user so they can take action before it is too late. Claim Warranty If a product develops an issue while it is still under warranty, the user can initiate a warranty claim directly from the product record . Instead of searching again for the invoice, purchase date, model number, or warranty information, Warranty Vault already has the required product context available. Our complete experience is: Gmail / Invoice / PDF → AI extracts details → WebMCP → Warranty Vault → Track Expiry How we built it We started by building Warranty Vault as a structured product and warranty management web application . Users can manually add and manage warranties, but we didn't want to build another application where users simply move information from one form to another. The biggest opportunity was eliminating that repetitive manual entry. That's where WebMCP became an important part of the solution. We used WebMCP to make Warranty Vault agent-ready by exposing meaningful, structured capabilities that an AI agent can understand and use. Instead of requiring an AI agent to visually navigate the website, locate every input field, enter information, and click buttons, WebMCP allows Warranty Vault to expose the actions available to an agent and the information required to perform them. For our Gmail use case, the journey works like this: The user gives a natural-language instruction: "Find my AC warranty email in Gmail and add it to Warranty Vault." The AI searches Gmail for the relevant purchase or warranty email. It reads the relevant email and identifies the product and warranty information. It extracts available information such as product name, brand, model number, purchase date, purchase price, and warranty period. The extracted information is converted into the structured fields required by Warranty Vault. The AI discovers the relevant capability exposed by Warranty Vault through WebMCP. The agent provides the structured warranty information to Warranty Vault. Warranty Vault validates the information and creates the warranty record. This transforms the traditional experience from: Search Gmail → Open Email → Open Invoice → Read → Copy Details → Open Warranty App → Fill Form → Save into: Ask → AI understands → WebMCP acts → Warranty saved We also designed the experience around higher-level user actions rather than individual UI interactions. For example: Add Warranty Extend Warranty Claim Warranty This allows WebMCP to support the warranty lifecycle rather than simply automate form filling. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was that warranty information is not standardized . Different manufacturers and retailers provide product and warranty information differently. One Gmail message might contain all the required information directly in the email. Another might contain only basic purchase information with an attached invoice or PDF. Some documents clearly specify the warranty duration, while others may not mention it at all. This created an important challenge: How do we allow AI to understand unstructured information while keeping the data stored in Warranty Vault structured and reliable? We also had to think carefully about missing information. For example, if a purchase email doesn't contain a serial number or clearly specify the warranty duration, the AI should not invent information simply to complete the record. Another challenge was deciding what capabilities should be exposed through WebMCP. Instead of thinking about low-level interactions such as: "Click this button." or "Fill this field." we focused on meaningful user goals: "Add this warranty." "Extend this warranty." "Claim this warranty." This helped us design Warranty Vault not only as a website for humans, but as an application that AI agents can understand and interact with through structured capabilities . Building Warranty Vault with WebMCP helped us discover some interesting challenges around how agents interact with dynamic web applications. Dynamic WebMCP Tool Availability One of the first challenges we encountered was that Warranty Vault could be loaded successfully, but its WebMCP tool list could refresh during the agent's first interaction . This created situations where a tool discovered by the agent was temporarily unavailable or changed while the agent was attempting to use it. It highlighted an important consideration for agent-ready applications: tool discovery and tool execution need to remain reliable even while the underlying page and application state are changing. Page Loading vs. Agent Execution Another challenge occurred when the web page was not fully loaded and the WebMCP tools were not yet available . Agents are naturally eager to complete the user's task. If the expected WebMCP tools are not immediately available, the agent may attempt to continue by interacting with or scraping the UI instead of waiting for the structured WebMCP capabilities to become ready . For Warranty Vault, we wanted the agent to use WebMCP as the primary interaction mechanism rather than falling back to UI-based interaction too quickly. This taught us that agent-ready websites need clear readiness signals and reliable tool availability so agents know when to wait, retry tool discovery, or proceed. File Download and Upload Our warranty workflow also involves invoices, PDFs, receipts, and warranty documents , which introduced another challenge. While structured data such as product name, purchase date, and warranty period works naturally with WebMCP tools, file transfer is more complex . For example, an agent may need to: Read a Gmail message → download the attached invoice → extract warranty information → create the Warranty Vault record → upload or attach the original invoice. title: Kodi: Agent-Native Tax Workspace
pitch: WebMCP turns Kodi into an agent-native tax workspace, letting external AI securely discover and use its document evidence and tax capabilities without brittle UI automation.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns Kodi into an agent-native tax workspace, letting external AI securely discover and use its document evidence and tax capabilities without brittle UI automation. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ChatGPT discovers Kodi’s seven WebMCP tools while the Kodi document library remains visible side by side. Kodi exposes all seven WebMCP capabilities for document discovery, evidence access, reasoning, and reversible actions. Live Kodi library showing 13 active documents with states and revisions, plus two records currently in Trash. WebMCP searches 2025 utility-expense evidence, then retrieves exact canonical evidence from a selected Kodi document. Kodi answers a Kenyan sole-proprietor tax question using governed knowledge, citations, warnings, and conversation state WebMCP renames a document, verifies the revision, then moves the same canonical record safely into Trash. The trashed record is restored, its original filename recovered, and all seven WebMCP capabilities complete successfully. Kodi Tax Workflow: Kodi works through a tax objective by inspecting evidence, taking actions, preserving progress, and continuing as needed. Manual AI Handoff: Without WebMCP, customers must switch to Kodi, retrieve needed information, and manually carry it back to their AI. Three Ways to Use Kodi: Customers can use Kodi directly, use Kodi’s own AI, or let a compatible external AI access Kodi through WebMCP. The problem Kodi existed before the WebMCP Challenge. I originally built it around a simple idea: what if working through tax could feel more like working with a modern coding agent? When I give a coding agent an objective such as “fix the authentication bug,” I do not have to tell it which file to open, which function to inspect, which command to run or which test to try first. The agent can inspect the environment, use the tools available to it, observe what happens and continue working toward the objective. Tax has many of the same characteristics, only with a very different environment. There are taxpayer facts, documents, evidence, tax rules, calculations, missing information, forms, validations and actions. Traditionally, much of the burden of connecting those pieces falls on the taxpayer or the professional helping them. Kodi was my attempt to change that. Instead of treating tax as a series of screens that someone has to understand and operate manually, Kodi treats it as work to be done . A user can give Kodi an objective. Kodi can work with their documents and evidence, determine what is known, identify what is missing, use tax capabilities where appropriate, ask the taxpayer when information genuinely cannot be resolved, and preserve the state of that work as it progresses. That was already Kodi before this challenge. The WebMCP Challenge started from a different problem. Kodi had become capable of doing useful tax work, but most of that capability was still available only when the customer was actively working through Kodi itself. And the way people are using AI is changing. A business owner may already be working with a general AI assistant while reviewing their business. An accountant may have an agent helping prepare for a client meeting. Someone may be working through a larger financial task that touches email, accounting systems, calendars, business records and tax. If that agent reaches a point where it needs something Kodi already knows how to do, the customer can still end up acting as the connection between them. The capability exists. The intelligence exists. The customer's data exists. But the customer is still doing the integration. That is the problem I wanted to address in this challenge. Why this happens Kodi was designed to be used directly by its customers. Its document library is available through Kodi. Its evidence retrieval is available through Kodi. Its tax intelligence is available through Kodi. Its autonomous Tax Case is available through Kodi. That is exactly what a normal product should do. But there is now another kind of user emerging: the AI agent acting on behalf of the customer. A browser agent should not have to reverse-engineer the meaning of every button, search box and rendered table just to use a capability that the application already understands internally. And the alternative should not be handing an external AI unrestricted access to Kodi's backend. What I wanted was something in between: Give the agent useful capabilities, while Kodi continues to control identity, permissions, data and execution. That is where WebMCP fits. The WebMCP approach For the WebMCP Challenge, I did not rebuild Kodi. I extended the existing product with a new agent-facing interface . WebMCP allows Kodi to describe selected capabilities in a structured form that a compatible external AI agent can discover from the authenticated application. So Kodi can now be approached in three ways: The first two already existed. The third path is what I added for this challenge. And that is where the additional customer value comes from. I am not replacing Kodi's AI with another AI. I am not saying customers should stop using Kodi. I am making the capabilities that already make Kodi valuable available in another context when that is more convenient for the customer. If someone is already inside Kodi, they can continue using Kodi. If they want Kodi to autonomously work through a Tax Case, they can use Kodi's Tax Agent. And if they are already working with another compatible AI agent on a broader objective, that agent can now use selected Kodi capabilities when it needs them. The product stays the same. Its utility expands. title: Koshara
pitch: Your household finances are ready for you and your AI
about_excerpt: Your household finances are ready for you and your AI Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard update charts using AI Statement import review and approve Add update categories Add update transactions Landing page Inspiration Managing household finances still involves repetitive work: reviewing statements, categorizing transactions, finding duplicates, and configuring dashboards. We wanted to explore a model where users keep the familiar financial interface while their chosen AI handles tedious preparation through structured WebMCP tools—not fragile browser automation. What it does Koshara is a household finance application for managing accounts, transactions, categories, statements, and cash-flow insights. Using WebMCP, an AI agent can: Configure dashboard charts from a natural-language request. Parse an unstructured bank statement. Send the extracted transactions to Koshara as a temporary import batch. Koshara then validates and groups transactions into Ready, Needs Review, Possible Duplicates, and Suggested Merges. The user reviews everything in the normal UI and clicks Approve Import before any transaction enters the main history. How we built it We built Koshara with Next.js and TypeScript, using Astryx for the interface and Recharts for financial visualizations. Koshara registers structured WebMCP tools directly in the browser. The dashboard tool updates chart presentation and insights, while the statement tool accepts parsed transactions and stages them for review. The prototype stores its data locally in the browser and is deployed on Vercel. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was deciding where agent autonomy should end and human control should begin. Financial statements may contain ambiguous categories, duplicates, refunds, or related transactions. To handle this safely, we separated staging from committing. The AI prepares the data, Koshara validates it, and the user approves the final changes. We also had to ensure WebMCP actions updated the same application state and UI used by the human. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created an end-to-end workflow where an external AI can interpret an unstructured statement and transfer the result into a structured, human-controlled review experience. We are also proud that Koshara does not require an embedded chatbot. The application supplies the data, rules, tools, and interface, while users can bring their preferred AI. What we learned We learned that an agent-native application does not need to replace its visual interface. WebMCP works best as an almost invisible capability layer behind a useful product. AI is effective at interpreting messy information and preparing work. Applications are better at validation and business rules, while humans should remain responsible for ambiguous or consequential decisions. What's next for Koshara Next, we plan to support more statement formats, improve duplicate and merge detection, add authenticated persistent storage, and provide a clearer audit trail for agent-prepared actions. We also want to expand the WebMCP tools so users can ask richer financial questions and generate more personalized dashboard views. title: PrintChum
pitch: Your companion for print-ready photos.
about_excerpt: Your companion for print-ready photos. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP in PrintChum Inspiration Walk into almost any computer shop or small photo studio in the Philippines and ask for ID photos, and you’ll probably see the same routine. The operator opens a general-purpose photo editor, drops your photo onto a blank page, resizes it until the ruler looks about right, copies it over and over, lines everything up into rows, and prints it on short bond paper. Then comes the ruler. If that 1 × 1 photo turns out to be 0.94 inches instead, the whole sheet goes into the bin and they start again. That routine bothered me enough to build something. The first problem was accuracy. The photo might be the correct size in the file, but that doesn’t mean it will come out at the correct size on paper. Print drivers can silently scale a page to fit, turning an exact 1 × 1 into something slightly smaller. In a workflow where a few millimeters can mean reprinting an entire sheet, “close enough” isn’t good enough. The second problem was privacy. Once someone uploads a photo, it often ends up sitting in a Downloads folder on a shared computer. There’s usually no retention policy, no cleanup step, and no reason for that photo to still be there after the customer leaves. So PrintChum started with two simple rules: physical dimensions should be a contract the software keeps, and a customer’s photo shouldn’t outlive the session that needed it. Then I found this WebMCP Challenge, and a idea clicked. If the job is simply “put eight 2 × 2 photos on A4 with a 5 mm margin,” the operator shouldn’t have to click through five different panels to make that happen. They should be able to just say what they need. Why PrintChum Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Lots of moving parts: Creating print-ready photo layouts involves more than just choosing a paper size. Users may need to configure margins, spacing, photo sizes, quantities, aspect ratios, auto-rotation, nameplates, background colors, and other settings that depend on one another. WebMCP makes it possible to turn a simple natural-language request into a series of structured tool calls that handle these settings together. Keeping photos private: PrintChum is designed to keep customer portraits and ID photos inside the browser. Instead of sending sensitive images to an external MCP server, WebMCP runs directly in the user's browser tab through document.modelContext . The agent can work with layout information and call tools locally without needing access to the actual photo files. Reliable, precise layouts: Physical printing requires accurate measurements, so approximations aren't good enough. WebMCP lets the agent query PrintChum's predefined settings and use its deterministic 2D packing engine to calculate the layout instead of trying to guess coordinates or dimensions. How WebMCP Improves the User Experience Configure layouts using intent: Users don't have to work through several dropdowns, sliders, and dialogs just to create a layout. They can describe what they want in plain language, such as: "Set up 4 passport photos and 8 1x1 photos on A4 paper with a 5mm margin and a royal blue background." The agent can then configure the workspace automatically. No need to leave the editor: The browser agent works directly inside the active PrintChum editor. When a tool is called, the changes are applied to the live Zustand store, so users can immediately see the updated layout on the canvas. Clear permission boundaries: The 17 tools are separated into three permission levels: read for inspecting information and presets, write for changing the layout and styling, and execute for actions such as generating a PDF or opening the print dialog. This keeps potentially impactful actions explicit and under the user's control. What People and Agents Can Do Together WebMCP also makes some workflows much faster than they would be through the traditional UI. Build complete print packages from one request: A user could say: "Prepare an application package for my university ID with student number 2026-0481 at the bottom, 2 copies of 2x2 in, and 4 copies of 1x1 in on Letter paper." The agent can look up the available settings, configure the nameplate, add both photo sizes, and select the correct paper size in a single interaction. Optimize layouts when something doesn't fit: If a layout spills onto a second sheet, the agent can inspect the layout summary and identify what's causing the overflow. It can then suggest or apply changes such as auto-rotation or adjusted margins to try to fit everything onto one sheet. Create reusable studio templates: Print shop operators can also use natural-language commands for repetitive setup tasks. For example: "Save this current layout as our standard Rush Visa Package." This makes it easier to create and reuse custom service sets without manually repeating the same configuration. How WebMCP Was Implemented PrintChum uses WebMCP as a progressive enhancement built across four main layers: Model Context Bridge ( lib/webmcp/ ): This layer checks whether document.modelContext is available and provides safe fallbacks when it isn't. It also uses AbortController to manage the lifetime of browser-tab-bound tools and clean them up properly when they're no longer needed. Strict Zod Input Schemas ( features/editor/webmcp/input-schemas.ts ): Each of the 17 registered tools has a runtime-validated Zod schema. Tools such as configure-paper , add-photo-size , configure-nameplate , and set-background use these schemas to validate incoming arguments before they're passed into the application. The schemas are then converted to JSON Schema at the WebMCP boundary. Shared Single Source of Truth ( features/editor/webmcp/handlers.ts ): The handlers take the validated tool arguments and pass them into the existing Zustand actions and PrintChum's calculateLayout() engine. This means AI-driven changes use the same layout calculations and PDF export pipeline as changes made manually through the UI. React Lifecycle Integration ( components/editor/webmcp-registration.tsx ): A React client component registers the WebMCP tools when the editor loads and removes the registration when the editor is unmounted. This keeps the tool lifecycle tied directly to the editor instead of leaving registrations active after the workspace is gone. title: SJMaths — WebMCP AI-Ready Curriculum & Tools
pitch: Turning static CBSE Class 10 mathematics into 13 browser-native WebMCP tools so external AI agents can teach with zero backend costs or answer leaks.
about_excerpt: Turning static CBSE Class 10 mathematics into 13 browser-native WebMCP tools so external AI agents can teach with zero backend costs or answer leaks. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration SJMaths is a static educational platform built for CBSE mathematics students. We host structured notes, formulas, and practice problems with zero backend servers. With the rise of AI agents like ChatGPT and Claude that can browse the web, we noticed a major dilemma for static educational websites: Students try using AI to learn from websites , but models usually just read the text, summarize blindly, or blurt out the answer keys immediately when asked for hints. Adding an embedded AI tutor is expensive : Running server-side LLM wrappers requires API keys, ongoing GPU server costs, and constant maintenance. When we discovered the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) , we realized the perfect architecture: Keep the website 100% static, and let the user's external AI agent (ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) connect via WebMCP directly in the browser. What it does SJMaths WebMCP converts our entire static CBSE Class 10 mathematics curriculum into 13 browser-native WebMCP tools registered in document.modelContext . When any external AI agent visits the site, it instantly gets structured, typed tools to teach the student: Discover Curriculum Structure: Explore 14 chapters, 45 topics, and 85 skills ( get_curriculum_outline , get_chapter_topics ). Diagnose Prerequisite Foundations: Test foundational prerequisite readiness before introducing advanced concepts ( get_prerequisite_check ). Teach with Verified Concepts & Worked Models: Retrieve verified formulas, common math traps, and step-by-step worked examples ( get_topic_concepts , get_worked_examples ). Anti-Leak Assessment Mode: When students practice, the tools automatically strip answer keys from the content on the client side. The external AI evaluates student attempts through evaluate_practice rather than reading raw answers. 3-Tier Progressive Hints: Provide subtle conceptual nudges (Level 1), calculation steps (Level 2), or full solutions (Level 3) only when the student is stuck ( get_hint ). Client-Side State Tracking: Track error streaks and recommend adaptive next steps ( get_next_learning_action , get_learning_progress ). All tools run client-side in memory with sub-millisecond execution (<1.5ms) and zero server costs. How we built it Universal Curriculum Schema: Organized all 14 chapters into a unified JSON format ( cbse-class-10-mathematics.json ). WebMCP Tool Dispatcher: Built webmcp-tools.js to expose 13 standards-compliant tools via document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext . Client-Side Security & State: Created a lightweight in-memory StateStore that prevents solution leakage and tracks student performance locally in the browser. Interactive Visual Inspector: Built a real-time tool inspector in demo/index.html allowing learners and judges to watch live JSON payloads and latency metrics. Edge-Case Test Suite: Authored webmcp-edge-cases.test.mjs with 61 automated assertions across all 45 topics (100% passing). Challenges we ran into Designing clean, anti-leak filters that give external AI agents rich pedagogical context while strictly withholding answers during assessments. Creating a progressive 3-tier hint engine that adapts to error streaks without leaking solutions prematurely. Ensuring WebMCP tool registration works reliably across multiple browser execution environments. Accomplishments that we're proud of 100% static architecture: zero backend servers or LLM API keys required. Full curriculum coverage: all 14 chapters and 45 topics of CBSE Class 10 Mathematics. Blazing performance: sub-1.5ms in-memory execution latency. Rock-solid stability: 61/61 edge-case tests passing. What we learned WebMCP proves that static websites don't need expensive AI backends to be AI-native. By providing clean, typed tools in the browser, any static site can become an interactive learning environment for external AI agents. What's next for SJMaths Expanding the WebMCP tool schemas to CBSE Classes 9, 11, and 12. Canvas-based handwritten math equation evaluation. I architected the 13 browser-native WebMCP tools in document.modelContext, structured the 14-chapter CBSE Class 10 mathematics schema, developed the client-side state tracking engine with anti-leak assessment security, and built the live interactive demo and 61-point automated test suite. title: StockPilot
pitch: StockPilot is an agent-native inventory management app where AI agent doesn't just read your data, it proposes actions, files them for approval, and you decide with a single click.
about_excerpt: StockPilot is an agent-native inventory management app where AI agent doesn't just read your data, it proposes actions, files them for approval, and you decide with a single click. Like Comment Story Updates StockPilot with WebMCP StockPilot Why WebMCP Is a Strong Fit Inventory management is fundamentally a shared-state problem . The dashboard shows data, but analyzing it requires cross-referencing products, suppliers, sales velocity, and profit margins — work that takes 30-60 minutes manually. WebMCP solves this by letting an AI agent operate on the same data, through the same logic, as the UI — not a copy, not a mirror, the identical code path. The agent doesn't just read data. It proposes actions (replenishment plans, purchase orders), but the human retains control over consequential decisions. This is only possible because WebMCP tools are registered on document.modelContext — they execute in the browser, against the same database, with the same server-side validation as the dashboard. How It Creates a Better User Experience Before WebMCP: User opens dashboard → sees health score, at-risk products, open POs User manually clicks each product → checks velocity → mental math on profit User opens spreadsheet → calculates which products are worth restocking User creates POs one by one, copying supplier data manually Time: 30-60 minutes for a weekly inventory review With WebMCP Agent: User types: "Protect my inventory with a $3,000 budget" Agent analyzes all products in one call → risk levels, velocity, profitability Agent proposes a budget-aware replenishment plan → grouped by supplier with cost subtotals User clicks Approve → POs are created → stock is received Time: 2 minutes for the same review The agent auto-navigates to relevant pages after each action. The Agent Activity Panel shows every tool call in real-time. The human always knows what the agent is doing. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Difficult or Impossible Before Cross-Product Profitability Analysis : "Which products will make me $1,000 profit this month?" — impossible to answer manually without cross-referencing sales velocity, profit margins, and inventory levels across all products. The agent calls get_profitability_analysis once and returns sorted projections. Budget-Aware Replenishment : "Replenish my inventory with a $3,000 budget" — the agent prioritizes by urgency (critical → warning → watch), fits items within budget, and returns what fits vs. what's rejected. Manual equivalent: 2+ hours of spreadsheet work. Emergency Impact Simulation : "What if my electronics supplier delays 10 days?" — instant analysis of which products stock out, days until stockout, alternate suppliers available, total revenue at risk. Manual equivalent: calling each supplier, checking lead times, calculating impact. Agent Proposes → Human Approves : The agent can't unilaterally place orders. It files pending actions with reasoning and cost estimates. The human approves or rejects via the Agent Actions queue. Server enforces the approval gate — the agent can't bypass it. Real-Time Visibility : The Agent Activity Panel shows every tool call as it happens. The human watches the agent work, sees the reasoning, and can intervene at any point. How WebMCP Was Implemented Architecture : Shared domain logic in inventory.server.ts (~2,200 lines) is called by two entry points: UI : TanStack Start server functions via inventory.functions.ts WebMCP : 52 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() in tools.ts Tool Design : Each tool has: 4 annotations ( readOnlyHint , destructiveHint , idempotentHint , openWorldHint ) Zod → JSON Schema input validation (auto-generated, no manual drift) Structured error codes ( NOT_FOUND , CONFLICT , PRECONDITION_FAILED , INVALID_INPUT ) Audit trail logging to agent_tool_calls table Collaboration Model : 24 consequential tools are marked with agent hints ("only call after human approval") Server-side enforcement: PO state machine ( draft → approved → received ), decidedBy derived from session Agent Activity Panel: real-time visibility into every tool call Auto-navigation: 9 tools navigate to relevant pages after execution Deployment : Cloudflare Workers with D1 (SQLite) database. Live at https://stockpilot.aakas.workers.dev Tech Stack : TanStack Start, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Drizzle ORM, Cloudflare D1, TypeScript 5.7 Built With cloudflare react tailwind tanstack Try it out stockpilot.aakas.workers.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Aakash Shakya Like Share this project: Updates Aakash Shakya started this project — Sep 02, 2026 06:57 AM EDT

title: Tempo
pitch: Tempo is a calendar that organizes your life for you. Tell it what you need to do, and AI can find time in your busy day, plan your schedule, and manage your events through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Tempo is a calendar that organizes your life for you. Tell it what you need to do, and AI can find time in your busy day, plan your schedule, and manage your events through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard Title Page Inspiration As an incoming university student, I found my university's portal surprisingly inconvenient for organizing my class schedule and timetable. Getting that schedule into a calendar I could actually use meant manually organizing and reshuffling everything. Outside of school, I also play sports, make music, and work part-time. Trying to fit studying, classes, work, practices, and everything else into the same week often meant constantly moving things around to find time for what I needed to do. As someone that believes that being organized is a key value to success, I needed to use my calendar more efficiently. I wanted a calendar that could do more than just store events. I wanted to be able to tell it what I needed to accomplish and have it help organize my time for me. That's why I built Tempo , a calendar designed to work with AI agents using WebMCP. What it does Tempo is a calendar designed to work with AI agents through WebMCP . Instead of manually searching through your calendar and rearranging events, you can tell an agent what you want to accomplish. It can understand your existing schedule, find available time, and make changes directly to your calendar. For example: "Find me three one-hour study blocks around my classes this week and add them to my University calendar." Tempo can also manage recurring events, multiple calendars, conflicts, and other everyday calendar tasks. The agent completes the slow task of manually typing events so you can stay organized for efficiently. How I built it Tempo was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS . The calendar takes many pieces from calendarcn made by vmnog. GitHub . Title page and many other assets were made using Figma. I first took pieces from calendarcn to built the calendar itself, including multiple calendar views, recurring events, event management, search, conflict detection, undo/redo, local persistence, and ICS import/export. I then built a WebMCP layer on top of that foundation. Tempo has structured tools through document.modelContext . These tools allow an agent to read calendars and events, find conflicts, create and modify events, manage calendars, and safely perform destructive actions with confirmation. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was figuring out how an AI agent should safely interact with a calendar. Calendar actions can have real consequences, especially when an agent is creating, moving, or deleting events. If Tempo made the process of creating or organizing a calendar longer, it would not be an useful tool. I wanted agents to have meaningful control without allowing actions to happen unpredictably or silently. I also had to design the WebMCP tools around the existing calendar architecture so that agent actions use the same state, history, and conflict-handling systems as actions made through the UI. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that Tempo is more than a calendar with an AI chatbot attached to it. I've personally used it to transfer my university course timetable to other calendars. The agent can actually interact with the calendar through structured WebMCP tools, allowing it to read, reason about, and modify the user's schedule. I'm also proud of how it all came together, from the visuals I spent hours in figma creating, to the calendar functionality itself. This allowed us to demonstrate WebMCP solving a real problem rather than building a purely technical proof of concept. Tempo also highlights how building is the best way to learn new things. What I learned I learned that making an application agent-ready requires more than adding an AI interface. The agent needs clear, well-defined tools that describe what it can actually do. I also learned that AI is most useful when it removes friction from something people already do. Instead of creating another complicated scheduling interface, Tempo lets users describe what they need and gives an agent the tools to help make it happen. The simple but tedious task it streamlines is the key to its effectiveness. One of the biggest unlocks for me was learning how to use Figma along this process. From personal experience at hackathons, sometimes well thought of ideas can loose to simple ones with polished execution. I'm sure Figma will be a tool I will use for many future projects. What's next for Tempo The next step is turning Tempo into a polished product and pushing the agent experience further. I want to refine the visual design, improve the Agent Link experience, build more advanced scheduling workflows, and make voice interaction a core part of the experience. Creating a more effective mobile experience could also allow people to use Tempo on the go. Ultimately, I want Tempo to make organizing your calendar feel less like a chore and more like having an assistant that can actually manage your time easily.
