title: Wilofox Deck Studio
pitch: Create and present visual lessons with an AI agent by your side—on the web, during live streams, and across multiple screens, powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Create and present visual lessons with an AI agent by your side—on the web, during live streams, and across multiple screens, powered by WebMCP. Like 10 Comment 8 Story Updates Wilofox Deck Studio: a human-and-AI workspace for creating and presenting visual lessons with WebMCP. Organize, search, create, and import presentation decks from one visual library. WebMCP connects people and AI agents through shared state and four structured presentation tools. Build structured presentations with sections, content, speaker notes, diagrams, and live previews. Control the live session with timers, speaker notes, quick navigation, and a separate audience view. Presenter control panel with slide navigation, speaker notes, timer, and blackout controls. Present lessons progressively with visual diagrams, navigation shortcuts, and annotation tools. Audience presentation mode with progressive navigation, visual diagrams, and annotation tools. Build complete lessons with structured content, live previews, diagrams, and presentation settings. Two-screen workflow: presenter controls and audience view stay synchronized in real time. Inspiration Wilofox Deck Studio began with a problem I experienced personally—and one that many educators, trainers, content creators, consultants, and live-stream presenters likely share. Existing tools allowed me to design slides, but I could not find one workspace that supported the complete reality of presenting: organizing a lesson, preparing visual content, writing speaker notes, controlling time, managing multiple screens, seeing what comes next, and annotating ideas live without interrupting the flow. I wanted the creative flexibility of a visual design tool, but shaped around how people actually teach and communicate. I needed to prepare everything in the browser, operate the presentation from a separate control screen, keep the audience view clean, and use pointers, highlights, drawings, and shapes while explaining. That personal need became Wilofox Deck Studio. When I discovered WebMCP, I saw a natural extension of the original vision: the workspace could become a shared environment where a person and an AI agent collaborate on the same presentation—not through a disconnected chatbot, but through structured actions connected to the real product. What it does Wilofox Deck Studio is a browser-based workspace for creating and delivering structured, interactive presentations. It is designed for educators, content creators, trainers, professionals, and live-stream presenters who need more than a traditional sequence of static slides. Users can: Create presentations from scratch, start from built-in examples, or import structured JSON. Organize content into sections and progressively ordered slides. Search, filter, categorize, duplicate, and manage presentations from a visual library. Combine written content with diagrams, images, videos, code, and embedded web resources. Add speaker notes and estimated presentation time. Configure formats, categories, series, production status, themes, typography, and colors. Preview content and visual resources while editing. Present using a single screen or a separate presenter-control window. See the current slide, upcoming slide, speaker notes, reference clocks, timer, and timing status. Navigate progressively or jump directly to a specific part of the presentation. Use a laser pointer, pen, highlighter, colors, arrows, rectangles, and other shapes during a live explanation. Zoom, pan, isolate the content or diagram, undo annotations, and temporarily black out the audience screen. Reserve an interface area for a camera or chat in an OBS composition. Export and reuse presentation content in formats such as JSON, HTML, PDF, and PowerPoint. The result is a workflow that connects preparation, editing, rehearsal, presentation, and live interaction within one coherent experience. How WebMCP is used WebMCP adds a structured agent layer to the existing presentation workflow. Wilofox exposes four tools: create_deck creates a complete, editable presentation from structured input. get_deck_context reads the current presentation state, including changes made manually by the user. update_slide updates one targeted slide while preserving the rest of the deck. navigate_to_slide moves the shared interface to a requested slide for review or presentation. These tools allow a compatible AI agent to understand and operate Wilofox without guessing where to click or attempting to interpret a complex editor only through pixels. The agent works with the same presentation state that the person can see and edit. There is no hidden agent-only copy. When a tool changes a slide or creates a deck, the result is validated, stored, rendered in the interface, and immediately available for human review. The user remains in control: every result can be inspected, edited manually, presented, exported, or replaced. Why WebMCP is a strong fit A presentation editor contains many controls, panels, fields, and possible actions. Asking an agent to operate that environment through visual guessing would be fragile and imprecise. WebMCP gives Wilofox a small, explicit set of meaningful capabilities with structured and bounded inputs. This makes agent behavior easier to understand, safer to execute, and more closely aligned with the user’s intention. A practical workflow can look like this: The agent creates a structured lesson. The educator reviews it and manually adjusts the content. The agent reads the latest shared state. The educator asks it to improve only one specific slide. The updated result appears inside the same editor. The person makes the final teaching and design decisions. This kind of collaboration would otherwise require copying content repeatedly between a chatbot and a presentation tool, manually reconstructing context, and risking the loss of previous edits. Human and agent collaboration Wilofox is designed around a simple principle: the agent contributes speed and structured assistance, while the person contributes judgment, subject knowledge, creativity, and final control. The shared presentation is the source of truth. Manual edits and agent actions use the same state, rendering, validation, and persistence flow. This prevents the agent experience from becoming a parallel prototype disconnected from the real application. For educators and presenters, this means less time transferring information between tools and more time reviewing, refining, and communicating ideas effectively. How I built it Wilofox Deck Studio is built with HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript using a portable single-file application architecture. It runs directly in the browser without requiring a traditional backend. Presentation data and configuration are stored locally using IndexedDB, supporting a local-first workflow. The application includes: A presentation library and filtering system. A structured slide editor. Visual diagram generators. A presentation runtime. Live annotation tools. Multi-window presenter controls. Import and export workflows. Local state and persistence management. WebMCP was implemented through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool includes: A clear name and description. An explicit JSON Schema. Bounded and validated inputs. Targeted execution behavior. Reuse of the application’s existing state and persistence functions. Visible results rendered through the normal interface. WebMCP support is implemented as a progressive enhancement. Browsers without WebMCP can still use the complete manual presentation experience. What was added during the WebMCP Challenge Wilofox Deck Studio existed before the challenge as a human-operated presentation workspace. During the challenge, I meaningfully extended it with an agent-accessible collaboration layer by: Registering four structured WebMCP tools. Defining explicit schemas and bounded tool inputs. Connecting agent actions to the application’s real state. Preserving manual changes during targeted agent updates. Reusing the existing rendering and persistence workflow. Maintaining compatibility with browsers that do not support WebMCP. Adding documentation, testing instructions, examples, and visual explanations of the human-agent workflow. The WebMCP implementation is therefore not a separate demonstration attached to the product. It extends the way the existing application can be operated. Challenges The main technical challenge was maintaining one reliable source of truth across multiple experiences: The editor. The presentation window. The presenter-control window. IndexedDB persistence. Manual user actions. WebMCP agent actions. An agent update had to preserve work already completed by the user. Improving one slide should not replace the entire presentation, remove unrelated content, or create a disconnected version. title: Pathway: Learning Plans Built with WebMCP
pitch: Pathway turns a big learning goal into a clear plan you can trust. Tell your browser agent what you know, your time, budget, and language, then search, compare, and build the path together.
about_excerpt: Pathway turns a big learning goal into a clear plan you can trust. Tell your browser agent what you know, your time, budget, and language, then search, compare, and build the path together. Like Comment Story Updates Pathway turns a big learning goal into a clear plan you can trust. Tell your browser agent what you know, your time, budget, and language, then search, compare, and build the path together. Inspiration I run workshops about developer tools, so my first idea for this challenge was a WebMCP product that could help me organize them. That product was called Backstage . An organizer could ask their browser agent to check room capacity, learner problems, staff availability, and accessibility needs, then prepare a response for the organizer to review. It sounded like a natural WebMCP use case, but testing it as a first time user changed my mind. The product made a small workshop problem feel more complicated than it needed to be. If three learners need help, walking over to them may be easier than managing rooms, staff assignments, response packets, and simulated notices. That feedback led to Pathway. I wanted to keep the idea of working with your own browser agent, but apply it to a broader problem where people really do spend hours searching, comparing, and organizing information. Learning was a natural fit. Finding one short tutorial is easy. Figuring out how to build real ability, change careers, enter a new field, or turn a hobby into paid work is much harder. Programming has many well known roadmaps and open resources. Other fields can be less clear. If I am a new photographer who wants to take professional work, where do I begin? Which lessons match what I already know? Which ones fit my budget and language? What should I learn first, and what work should I create to prove I can do it? Answering those questions can mean opening many pages and rebuilding the same plan by hand. Pathway explores a better experience. A learning platform can let a person use their browser agent to search its resources, set several filters at once, compare choices, and arrange them into a visual learning plan on the same page. The learner stays in control while the agent handles the repetitive work. What it does Pathway helps a learner go from “I want to learn this” to a clear plan they can review, change, save, and follow. The main example is someone turning a hobby into a realistic work opportunity: I manage social media for my family's café and want to start taking paid food photography work for local restaurants. Over eight weeks, I want to create a portfolio and a simple client brief. I know basic photo editing, can study five hours each week, have a budget of $100, prefer Spanish, and need resources I can use on my own time. Search first and do not build the path yet. The learner can type this information into the website or say it naturally to a WebMCP compatible browser agent. The agent fills the visible search and filters for the topic, current knowledge, language, budget, time, format, and access needs. It then runs the search in Pathway and shows the matching resources. Nothing is hidden behind an agent answer. The learner can see the words used for the search, every active filter, which resources matched, where each resource came from, and why it may be useful. They can inspect one choice or compare several choices before asking for a plan. Once the choices look right, the learner or their agent can build a draft. The plan starts with the ideas and skills the learner is missing, moves into practical exercises, and finishes with work they can show. In the photography example, the final result is a six image food photography portfolio and a simple brief for a local restaurant client. The plan uses the information from the original request. It checks the learner's Spanish preference, $100 budget, five available hours each week, current editing knowledge, preferred resource format, and eight week goal. It then places the selected resources and practical work into a weekly schedule. If one of those needs changes, the learner can ask the agent to update the filters and prepare a new version. The agent can prepare and revise a plan, but it cannot approve or save one. Those actions stay in the normal website for the learner to press. After a plan is saved, the learner or their agent can record completed steps. If life changes, the agent can create a new schedule for the work that is still left. Finished steps stay finished, and the updated plan waits for the learner to review and approve it again. Pathway currently uses a prepared catalog of 22 resources, with the visible demo focused on commercial photography and inclusive workshop facilitation. I do not have direct access to the complete catalogs of every course provider, so this demo uses a small local catalog to show how the experience would work. A production version could use permitted provider feeds, public APIs, or the catalog of a single learning platform. Why WebMCP is useful here You can ask ChatGPT for a learning plan today, but the answer usually arrives as text and links. You still have to move the useful parts into another place, remember which limits were considered, compare the options, and keep the plan up to date. Pathway lets your agent work with the learning website itself. Your agent can turn your learning request into an ordered search with the right filters, help you inspect and compare your choices, create a draft, revise it, record your progress, and rebuild the remaining schedule when your situation changes. Each action reads or updates the same page you are looking at, so you can see what happened instead of trusting an answer that disappears into a chat history. This is where WebMCP makes the experience feel different. One request can set the topic, language, budget, time, current knowledge, and format together, while the path checks prerequisites before approval. The website keeps those choices consistent while the learner can see the search, filters, sources, comparison, and plan. The agent saves time, but the learner keeps authority. It cannot approve a plan, save it, buy a course, enroll anywhere, or contact a provider. The normal interface remains fully usable without an agent. People and agents can both search, inspect, compare, build, and revise. WebMCP simply makes a long series of form changes and page actions much faster, while keeping the result visible and editable. This approach could work in a platform that brings together permitted resources from several providers, or inside one course platform with its own catalog. In both cases, the learner's agent can use the product's real tools and current information instead of guessing from page text or clicking through every filter one at a time. How I built it Pathway is a React and TypeScript application built with Vite. It uses a workspace interface where the visible request, filters, resources, comparison, and learning plan are the main experience. There is no separate chat panel because the learner should be able to understand every agent action by looking at the product. The app registers nine focused tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_learning_context reads the learner's goal, filters, current plan, and progress. prepare_learning_search turns a natural request into the visible search and filter fields. search_learning_resources searches the catalog using those fields. inspect_learning_resource opens the details and original link for one resource. compare_learning_resources compares two or three choices using the same fields. build_learning_path creates a draft from reviewed search results. revise_learning_path updates a draft when the learner changes a need. update_learning_progress records completed work after a plan has been saved. replan_remaining_path prepares a new draft for unfinished work. The tools appear only when they make sense. For example, the agent cannot build a plan before resources have been searched, and it cannot record progress before a person has approved and saved a plan. Inputs use clear schemas, results are kept short, and source content is treated as outside information rather than trusted instructions. There is no custom AI backend and the demo does not scrape live course websites. That choice is deliberate. The purpose of this submission is to show how WebMCP could make a learning platform easier to use: a learner talks to their own agent, the agent operates the platform's real search and planning features, and every result remains visible in the product. A small prepared catalog keeps that interaction fast and repeatable for the demo. Original links remain visible, and price and duration details are labeled as planning estimates that should be checked before buying or enrolling. title: AgentFlow
pitch: AgentFlow is Figma for automation , A visual canvas where humans and AI agents build real workflows together, live in the browser.
about_excerpt: AgentFlow is Figma for automation , A visual canvas where humans and AI agents build real workflows together, live in the browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration No-code tools are rigid. AI chatbots are black boxes. And agents that scrape the DOM with querySelector → click → hope break on every redesign. We asked: what if humans and agents operated the same machine — not through fragile selectors, but through typed, reliable browser tools? AgentFlow is that machine: a shared canvas where you see the workflow and the agent calls it. What it does AgentFlow is a visual instrument for Human × Agent automation — drag modules, wire pins, press RUN. Every action you take, an agent can take too, via WebMCP. 19 WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() (webmcp.ts:40, engine.ts): 8 core: add_node, connect_nodes, execute_workflow, get_available_tools, get_node_details, update_node_config, get_workflow_status, validate_workflow 11 advanced: delete_node, clone_node, get_node_connections, save_workflow, load_workflow, run_node, set_node_position, get_workflow_history, create_template, export_workflow, import_workflow Real execution, not a mock: Topological sort, branch gating on true/false wires, and fail-fast error propagation. Try the 30-second wow: ?workflow=judge-demo → Start → HackerNews API → AI summarize → Condition → Split → [download + log] — watch signals travel the wires live. True co-creation: You drag a node. The agent calls add_node. Both appear instantly in the ToolLog as YOU vs AGENT — same canvas, same truth. ## How we built it Canvas: React + React Flow + TypeScript + Vite — 15 node types with smart grid placement (utils/grid.ts), snap-to-grid, and non-disruptive wiring Engine: engine.ts — DAG-based topological execution, real fetch for API nodes, AI with graceful fallback without a key, and download / webhook / console outputs WebMCP: webmcp.ts:40 registers all 19 tools with registerTool({ signal }) for lifecycle safety, mirrored on window.__agentflow.callTool for testing without a WebMCP browser Deploy: Cloudflare Pages — https://agentflow-hackathon.pages.dev (mirror netlify.app), landing at https://agentflow-landing.pages.dev/ Auth: Zero friction — anon canvas works instantly. WorkflowManager is only gated behind user to persist to DB. No login to try. ## Challenges we overcame Discovery: WebMCP requires chrome://flags → WebMCP → Enabled + ChatGPT's in-app browser — we built the window.__agentflow mirror so judges can test without it State sync: Keeping human and agent in perfect sync without re-renders or race conditions via nodesRef/edgesRef Semantics: Nailing branch gating and split/merge/loop semantics so a workflow that looks right actually runs right ## What's next AgentFlow is the visual OS for the agentic web. Next: one-click templates, team workspaces with shared cursors, and a marketplace where any site can expose its own WebMCP tools and AgentFlow becomes the canvas that wires the open web together. Try now: open /tool?workflow=judge-demo → press RUN. title: AIMEC Alpha: From Business Opportunity to AI Implementation
pitch: AIMEC Alpha turns business automation ideas into AI implementation plans. Via WebMCP, people and agents can run ROI and readiness diagnostics, delegate to two AI specialists, and inspect the results.
about_excerpt: AIMEC Alpha turns business automation ideas into AI implementation plans. Via WebMCP, people and agents can run ROI and readiness diagnostics, delegate to two AI specialists, and inspect the results. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Businesses rarely struggle to find AI ideas. They struggle to decide which ideas are worth pursuing, whether their data and processes are ready, and what a practical implementation would require. I built AIMEC Alpha to connect those decisions in one workflow. Instead of stopping at a conversational recommendation, I wanted users to move from a business problem to measurable assumptions, an opportunity assessment, and a proposed implementation plan—with results they could inspect. WebMCP made this an opportunity to design for both people and their browser agents. A person can work through the interface, while an agent can discover and invoke the same capabilities through structured tools. What it does AIMEC Alpha evaluates a business automation opportunity using five diagnostics: AI return on investment AI operating costs Data readiness Agentic automation readiness Overall AI readiness Two complementary specialists then help interpret the findings: The AI Opportunity Analyst combines diagnostic results with the supplied business context to assess the opportunity, identify risks, and recommend whether to proceed, pilot, or hold. The AI Solution Architect receives the handoff and proposes a bounded architecture, implementation phases, and human approval points. The workflow then recalculates ROI using the estimated operating costs. Both specialists use a locally hosted Qwen model through Ollama. Financial calculations remain deterministic Python functions; the model provides interpretation and planning. The demo includes synthetic invoice-processing and customer-support scenarios. Users can change the assumptions and evaluate a different case. It proposes implementations—it does not connect to an ERP, process real invoices, or carry out business changes. Why WebMCP matters A conventional web application makes its functionality available primarily through buttons and forms. Browser agents often have to infer how those controls work. AIMEC Alpha exposes seven structured WebMCP interfaces: get_available_tools run_tool get_available_agents delegate_task get_task_status get_task_result get_execution_evidence These interfaces let a browser agent discover approved operations and their input schemas, submit a business case, and retrieve the resulting job status, output, and evidence without reconstructing the workflow from screen content. The human-facing interface remains available alongside those tools. People can review the assumptions and inspect the corresponding results in the same browser session. The value is not simply asking an LLM to calculate ROI. It is connecting discoverable capabilities, deterministic calculations, specialist interpretation, persistent task state, and inspectable results through a shared interface for people and agents. How I built it I extended existing AIMEC building blocks for capability registration, HTTP services, task persistence, and execution logging. The challenge-specific work added the WebMCP interface, browser workflow, business-agent integration, and isolated demo packaging. The application uses: Python services for diagnostics, capability execution, and specialist workflows. Qwen3:1.7b through Ollama for server-local model inference. SQLite for persistent jobs and execution events. JavaScript and document.modelContext.registerTool for native WebMCP registration. Docker Compose for the isolated runtime. Caddy for the public HTTPS endpoint. The Analyst and Architect have separate prompts and output contracts but share one model runtime. Their handoff follows an explicit, programmed workflow within the advisory service; it is not an unrestricted autonomous agent network. Results are associated with session-owned jobs. Execution evidence includes provider events and result hashes, allowing the application to check that a saved artifact matches the recorded provider output. Challenges I faced Making the model useful on a small VPS Running local inference on a CPU-only server required balancing response length, memory use, and execution time. I selected a small model, disabled its thinking mode for this workflow, bounded generation, and adjusted timeouts. A healthy model server does not necessarily mean an inference request will complete successfully, so testing the actual workflow was essential. Keeping browser sessions and results connected Early testing exposed problems restoring jobs across browser sessions. Cookie behavior and initialization order mattered: a completed backend job was not useful if the browser could no longer retrieve its result. I worked through session handling and tested status, result, and evidence retrieval together. Separating valid JSON from valid specialist output A model can return JSON that does not satisfy the application's required fields or values. I encountered an intermittent execution failure even while the underlying services remained healthy. That reinforced the importance of strict output validation and more specific failure reporting. The application does not replace failed model output with a fabricated success. Improving structured-output reliability remains an important next step. Keeping the demonstration honest I distinguished between deterministic calculations, model-generated proposals, and actions the system actually performs. I also separated native WebMCP tool checks from the broader claim that an external browser agent can independently choose and complete every workflow. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when the underlying application has clear capabilities and meaningful execution boundaries. Registering a tool is only the beginning: its inputs, permissions, task lifecycle, results, and failure behavior also need to be understandable. I learned that small local models can contribute useful interpretation when paired with deterministic tools and narrow responsibilities. They still require validation, realistic time budgets, and careful handling of failures. I also learned that execution evidence has limits. A matching result hash supports artifact integrity; it does not prove that a recommendation is financially correct or that every model-generated statement is justified. What I accomplished I deployed a public HTTPS demo with seven registered WebMCP interfaces, five business diagnostics, and two local-model specialists. Live testing demonstrated direct diagnostic execution and the Analyst-to-Architect workflow, including completed jobs, saved results, and verified result digests. The public demo export also passed ten offline tests covering business logic and packaging, with mocked model responses clearly distinguished from live inference. I published an isolated, MIT-licensed repository with the source, setup instructions, third-party notices, and a judge walkthrough. What's next My immediate priorities are stronger schema-constrained model output, clearer failure diagnostics, and repeated end-to-end reliability testing. Beyond the demonstration, I want to evaluate the assessments with real business users, improve the assumptions behind cost and readiness estimates, and add permissioned integrations that connect proposed plans to measurable pilot outcomes. The goal is to help businesses move from “I should use AI” to a specific, reviewable next step. title: Champagne - Agentic Music Mastering
pitch: Champagne is a mastering studio for AI music artists that uses a single prompt to apply advanced tonal processing to audio, making songs radio-ready in less than a minute.
about_excerpt: Champagne is a mastering studio for AI music artists that uses a single prompt to apply advanced tonal processing to audio, making songs radio-ready in less than a minute. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Champagne Landing Page Champagne Mastering Studio Inspiration I've been producing music for over 15 years. I recently jumped into making AI music, and the first thing I noticed was how thin the outputs sounded. That's where Champagne was born. As far as turning it into a ChatGPT + WebMCP integration, that magic sorta just happened! What it does Champagne masters any audio track, but it's optimized specifically for songs from Suno. Suno outputs are thin and quiet. Champagne makes them full-bodied and vibrant. Based on your prompt, ChatGPT selects one of four signature mastering styles and directs bounded refinements to Warmth, Brightness, Punch, Dynamics, Low End, Presence, Air, Width, Glue, Density, and Smoothness. Champagne’s local browser engine applies those adjustments to the audio. Champagne applies advanced tonal processing to audio, making songs radio-ready in less than a minute. How I built it I released Champagne on the Mac App Store a few days before this contest was announced. After attempting to build a different WebMCP website with no success, I had a lightbulb moment: This would be the perfect opportunity to build a web demo for my new macOS app! I ported the app from Swift into TypeScript + CSS using a blueprint roadmap method, then got to tuning the actual operation of the system. Champagne registers nine page-bound tools using document.modelContext.registerTool, allowing ChatGPT to inspect the studio, create and refine masters, compare results, apply trims and fades, and adjust track speed. Audio processing remains local in the browser. Connecting ChatGPT into the mastering engine enables specific tuning that provides artists more control over the processing adjustments than the original macOS app ever did. You can learn more about the integration specifics through the README on GitHub: https://github.com/LoganVoss/Champagne How people and agents work together ✵ Artist imports audio. ✵ Artist describes the desired result. ✵ Champagne analyzes the audio locally and exposes compact measurements through WebMCP. ✵ ChatGPT interprets those measurements and the artist’s prompt. ✵ ChatGPT chooses and calls the appropriate WebMCP tools. ✵ ChatGPT coordinates mastering, refinements, trims, fades, and speed. ✵ Artist reviews the result. Don't like it? Tell ChatGPT what to fix. ✵ Artist downloads the mastered audio file. Challenges I ran into The first major challenge I ran into was not understanding what WebMCP actually does. At first, I built a prompt box on the website that guided the mastering engine with specific presets, but that didn't feel right. There was no real AI input. The dots finally connected when I realized how you're supposed to work side by side using the ChatGPT app web browser + chat window. Once I made that connection, it all came together. The other primary challenge I faced was deciding what to show when somebody visits the site through a web browser that doesn't support WebMCP. This was a little confusing mainly because it's like building two versions of the same product, but I had experience with that from iOS development (iPhone/iPad apps), so I figured it out pretty quickly. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud of how simple it makes the mastering process for AI music artists. AI music artists can produce hundreds of songs per day, and they need an easy way to master the music they create. Champagne gives them the ability to do that rapidly, so they can share their creations even quicker. I'm also really proud of how WebMCP took Champagne to the next level through creating fine-tuned results with precision adjustments. In music, small changes make the biggest difference, and that's what makes this project really glow. What I learned I learned what WebMCP actually is, and how it can make products better through integrating AI natively. What's next for Champagne Champagne was created as a one-price replacement for pay-per-track / subscription services that perform a similar method of signal processing. With this contest, I decided to open source the code, enabling people to use the tool for free. As for building a stronger integration with ChatGPT + WebMCP, there's a universe of opportunity. Currently, the results are a little restricted with the four signature baselines. This could be removed entirely to provide an even more individualized mastering experience for each song, but it will take some work to make sure the outputs don't go completely off the rails. Another improvement I'm considering is changing the audio processing pipeline from local to server side, for further precision. title: CoWriter
pitch: A screenplay you write together with your agent- live on the same page.
about_excerpt: A screenplay you write together with your agent- live on the same page. Like Comment Story Updates CoWriter in session Inspiration Co-writing with an AI these days usually mean pasting your script into a chat window, getting a lot of text back and then copying these into your document. You loose formatting and context for every round trip. I wanted to see what happens when the agent isn't a chat window, but a real collaborator working on the same page as you are, through the same interface as you use. WebMCP made that possible: expose the app's real actions as tools, and an agent can write directly into your live document instead of describing what it would write. What it does CoWriter is a small screenwriting tool: it has a Story Bible panel (title, logline, theme, genre, tone), a real act-by-act Outline panel (paste in your own — Act 1 with its beats, Act 2 with its beats, and so on, including acts with no scenes written yet), that breaks acts and scenes into real screenplay format (sluglines, action, character cues, dialogue). It has a character bible, and a loose idea board where you can tweek ideas on the go. Every action on that script; revising the premise, importing or editing the outline, adding a scene, editing a line, revising a character, dropping an idea, reordering scenes, checking the whole thing for consistency — is exposed as a WebMCP tool ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). The agent is not clicking around a UI it has to guess at; it's calling the exact same functions the interface calls, and the result shows up on your screen instantly, on the same live document. You can keep editing by hand at any moment if you wish to. Crucially, get_script 's description tells the agent to call it first, always. It returns the human-authored, act-by-act outline and the Story Bible up front, so every scene the agent drafts, and every consistency check it runs, is explicitly grounded in the story's real throughline and theme. It does not guess at what happens next from whatever scene happens to be open. The outline (the plan) and the written scenes (what's actually on the page) are kept deliberately distinct, the way a real writer's outline and draft are. You can ask, in plain language, "write a tense scene where she finds the letter, no dialogue yet" — the agent calls add_scene and it appears, correctly formatted, right in front of you. You read it and asks for some more edit if you want it tweeked, and the agent calls edit_scene on that exact scene. The character bible updates the same way as new characters get introduced. And check_consistency hands the agent every dialogue line labeled by speaker plus the full character bible in one structured payload, so it can catch things like a character's voice contradicting itself across acts — the kind of full-document consistency pass that's genuinely tedious for a human to do by re-reading, but natural for an agent to do well. Nothing about the human side of the app changes because an agent is present — you can type directly into any line at any time, exactly like a normal document. That's the point: one shared script, two collaborators, no export/import step between them. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript — no framework, no build tooling, no backend. All 12 WebMCP tools are registered in a single readable file ( script.js ) so the integration itself is easy to inspect end to end. Data persists to the browser's local storage. Tool responses are serialized as compact JSON to keep the token footprint of every agent call low. Challenges we ran into Keeping the outline and the written scenes as two genuinely separate sources of truth, rather than letting them silently collapse into one, took deliberate design. It would have been simpler to let the agent treat whatever is on the page as the plan, but this would have let scenes drift from the story's real throughline. Instead, get_script always returns both, and the agent's own tool descriptions tell it the outline is the plan and the scenes are what is actually been written — they won't always be in sync, and that is intentional. Getting an agent to actually call a tool rather than just answer a writing request conversationally in chat also took some care in how the tool descriptions were phrased — an ambiguous prompt can be satisfied just as easily by the model generating prose in the chat window as by it calling add_scene on the page. Accomplishments that we're proud of Twelve WebMCP tools, all grounded in one shared Story Bible, with a UI that never has to know or care whether the human or the agent made the last edit. Watching a scene appear live on the page, correctly formatted and fitting the outline is genuinely satisfying to demo. What we learned That grounding matters more than raw capability. An agent that can call add_scene isn't useful on its own. It is useful because get_script forces it to read the outline and premise first, every time, so what it writes actually belongs in the story. What's next for CoWriter Multi-scene consistency diffing — let check_consistency compare against the previous run's report so an agent can flag only new contradictions instead of re-surfacing everything each time. PDF/Fountain export of the finished screenplay. Multi-document projects — more than one script per browser profile, with a lightweight project switcher. Real backend/cloud persistence, so a script isn't tied to one browser's local storage. A visible scene-level undo/history stack for agent-made edits. A richer character bible — arcs, relationships, and a "first appearance" pointer the agent can use to catch characters who show up before being introduced. A more efficient architecture for managing token consumption for each 'get_script' tool call. title: Crit Studio
pitch: Give your agent hands, not just words. Crit Studio exposes your design canvas as WebMCP tools so agents can flag, drag, and fix UI issues live not describe them in chat.
about_excerpt: Give your agent hands, not just words. Crit Studio exposes your design canvas as WebMCP tools so agents can flag, drag, and fix UI issues live not describe them in chat. Like Comment Story Updates landing page landing page landing page landing page landing page workspace view Inspiration Most AI design tools give you feedback in a chat box. “Your CTA needs more spacing.” “Your layout could be more balanced.” The problem is that design is visual. If someone tells you that something is 12 pixels too far to the left, you still have to go find it, figure out what they mean, and fix it yourself. I started wondering: what if the AI reviewing your design could actually touch the canvas? That idea became Crit Studio. Instead of having an AI describe what's wrong with a design, I wanted it to be able to point to the exact element, move it, resize it, and show you the fix directly. WebMCP made that possible in a way that felt much more natural than building another AI chat interface. What it does Crit Studio is a live design workspace where you can build a simple mockup using a Figma-style component toolbox — headings, buttons, navigation, images, and other elements — and then ask an AI reviewer to critique it. But the interesting part is what happens next. The AI doesn't just send back a list of suggestions. It can actually interact with the canvas through WebMCP tools. It can: Read the current layout with getCanvasState Flag a specific problem with flagIssue , placing a visible badge directly on the element Move an element with moveElement Resize an element with resizeElement Rebalance spacing across a group with suggestSpacing Add a comment at an exact canvas position with annotateAt So if the agent says your CTA is too small, you can actually watch it resize. And if you respond, “Make it bigger, not just more spaced out,” it can make another change on the same canvas. That back-and-forth was important to me. I didn't want Crit Studio to feel like a tool that analyzes a screenshot once and gives you a report. I wanted it to feel like you're actually working with the AI on the design. The tools are also registered through the standard navigator.modelContext API rather than being tied to my own interface. That means any WebMCP-native agent host can discover and use them independently. I also built an Export Audit feature. At the end of a session, you can export the entire critique, the elements on the canvas, issues that were raised and resolved, and the chronological tool-call history as Markdown or JSON. So the session doesn't just disappear when you're done. You have an actual artifact you can share with a team or keep for documentation. How I built it Crit Studio is built with Next.js, TypeScript, and Zustand. One decision I made early turned out to be one of the most important architectural choices: there should only be one source of truth for the canvas. The Zustand store holds the entire canvas state, and every interaction reads and writes to that same store. Whether you're dragging an element manually, the AI is calling a WebMCP tool, or the built-in review panel is making changes, everything updates the exact same state model. That kept the application consistent regardless of who's interacting with the canvas. I also decided to build the canvas using regular DOM elements with absolute positioning instead of using <canvas> or WebGL. That made styling much easier, allowed smooth CSS animations, simplified positioning annotations and badges, and made serializing the canvas state for getCanvasState much more straightforward. For the visual design, I created a small neobrutalist design system using hard borders, flat colors, and offset shadows. I wanted Crit Studio to feel like a creative design tool rather than another generic AI dashboard. The six WebMCP tools are registered client-side with navigator.modelContext.registerTool() , each with a deliberately narrow responsibility so an agent has a clear and predictable set of actions to choose from. Challenges I faced One of the biggest challenges was getting the canvas to behave exactly the way I wanted visually. I went through several different design directions before settling on the final interface, and almost every iteration revealed another layout issue. At one point, issue badges and annotation pins kept overlapping the very content they were supposed to describe. I also ran into problems with the canvas preview clipping inside its container instead of scaling properly. One particularly stubborn bug turned out not to be a React problem at all. I had a global CSS reset: * { margin: 0; padding: 0; } and it was silently overriding Tailwind utility classes because of how CSS Cascade Layers work. Since the reset was unlayered, it could override styles inside Tailwind's @layer utilities even when the utilities looked more specific. That bug took longer to find than I expected. It also changed how I approached the rest of the project. I stopped treating a clean build as proof that something worked. If I couldn't visually confirm the result in the browser, I considered the issue unresolved. I also migrated the entire project from Vite to Next.js midway through development to take advantage of built-in API routes and better font handling. That meant reworking the client and server boundaries for anything touching navigator or browser-only state, which added another layer of complexity during development. Accomplishments I'm proud of The thing I'm most proud of is the live interaction loop. There's something genuinely different about asking, “What's wrong with this layout?” and then watching an AI resize a button, move a heading, or rebalance spacing directly on the canvas. There's no screenshot round-trip, no page reload, and no copying suggestions into another editor. Everything happens in the same workspace in real time. That was the moment where the original idea really came together. I'm also proud that I kept the WebMCP tool surface intentionally small. Rather than building a huge API with dozens of overlapping actions, I focused on six tools with very clear responsibilities. I think that made the system easier to reason about and made the agent's behavior much more predictable. What I learned The biggest lesson for me was that WebMCP's real advantage isn't just speed. It's precision. A vision-based agent has to estimate positions from a screenshot, while a tool-calling agent can inspect structured layout data and interact with exact elements using deterministic coordinates. That difference completely changes the quality of interaction. I also learned the importance of being honest about what is actually AI-driven and what is deterministic logic supporting the experience. There were moments during development where it would've been easy to present deterministic behavior as if it were intelligent reasoning. I deliberately avoided that distinction becoming blurry because I think technical honesty matters, especially when building AI products. What's next for Crit Studio The next version of Crit Studio will focus on making critiques work with real-world designs instead of only manually created mockups. I'd like to add support for importing screenshots and reference images so users can critique existing interfaces directly. I'm also planning to expand accessibility checks beyond contrast ratios and introduce more typography and layout intelligence, including grid alignment, hierarchy, and spacing recommendations. The long-term goal is still the same: Don't just tell me what's wrong with my design. Show me. title: EvidenceFlow — Human-Agent Incident Investigation
pitch: EvidenceFlow uses WebMCP to let AI agents inspect structured cybersecurity evidence, propose evidence-backed findings, and route conclusions to human review.
about_excerpt: EvidenceFlow uses WebMCP to let AI agents inspect structured cybersecurity evidence, propose evidence-backed findings, and route conclusions to human review. Like Comment Story Updates 1 A natural-language investigation request leads the agent to autonomously discover and invoke EvidenceFlow’s WebMCP tools. Chrome WebMCP Tool Activity confirms the full workflow: incident discovery, evidence retrieval, and finding creation. An evidence-linked AI finding enters EvidenceFlow as pending-human-review, with confidence and human review controls visible. Human review remains meaningful: the investigator requests more evidence when the AI conclusion goes beyond what the evidence supports. Inspiration Cyber incident investigations require analysts to distinguish carefully between what the evidence actually shows and what is merely an interpretation or hypothesis. AI agents can help investigate, summarize, correlate, and organize large amounts of technical evidence. But their conclusions should remain traceable to the underlying data and subject to meaningful human review. EvidenceFlow was inspired by that problem: how can humans and AI agents investigate cybersecurity evidence together without losing the distinction between evidence, inference, and validated conclusions? What it does EvidenceFlow is a human-agent workspace for cybersecurity incident investigation. Using WebMCP, an AI agent can: discover available incidents; retrieve structured incident evidence; analyze events chronologically; propose a finding linked to specific evidence IDs; assign a confidence level; recommend a next investigative action. Every agent-generated finding enters the application as pending-human-review . A human investigator can then Approve, Reject, or request more evidence through the application interface. EvidenceFlow deliberately exposes no WebMCP tool for approving or rejecting findings. Validation remains a separate human-review step outside the WebMCP tool surface. The current demo uses a synthetic SSH authentication incident. How I built it EvidenceFlow is a static web application built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and deployed through GitHub Pages. The application exposes three browser-native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext : list_incidents get_incident_events propose_finding Together they create the agent workflow: incident → evidence → agent analysis → evidence-grounded proposal → human review The implementation also treats incident evidence as untrusted data and includes bounded inputs, evidence-reference validation, duplicate-reference rejection, text-only DOM rendering, and mandatory pending-human-review status for agent proposals. I tested the tools in Chrome with WebMCP support and the WebMCP Model Context Tool Inspector on the public GitHub Pages deployment. I also validated an agent-driven investigation workflow in which the agent autonomously selected and executed the registered WebMCP tools from a natural-language investigation request. Challenges I ran into One challenge was designing the boundary between agent capability and human authority. It would have been easy to expose a tool that allowed the agent to complete the entire workflow automatically. Instead, I chose to make proposal and validation separate operations. Another challenge was WebMCP client interoperability. Different agent environments behaved differently when discovering and invoking browser-exposed tools. Direct testing through Chrome and the WebMCP Model Context Tool Inspector helped distinguish EvidenceFlow’s WebMCP behavior from client-specific orchestration behavior. I also performed a security review of the WebMCP interaction surface and added limits and validation to prevent oversized or malformed agent inputs from unnecessarily consuming browser resources. Key accomplishments EvidenceFlow demonstrates an integrated WebMCP investigation workflow rather than simply exposing isolated tools. From a natural-language investigation request, an agent can discover an incident, retrieve structured evidence, analyze that evidence, and create a proposed finding linked to specific evidence IDs. The resulting finding is not automatically validated. It enters the application as pending-human-review , preserving a clear boundary between agent-generated analysis and human validation. The prototype makes three stages of the investigation explicit: evidence → inference → human review That separation became one of the central design principles of EvidenceFlow. What I learned I learned that exposing an application to AI agents is not only about giving the agent more capabilities. Tool boundaries, data provenance, validation, failure behavior, and human oversight all become part of the application design. WebMCP provides an interesting way to make those capabilities explicit at the browser level rather than requiring an agent to infer application behavior only from the visual interface. My background is in law and digital law rather than software engineering, and that strongly influenced this approach: traceability, evidence, authority, and review became design requirements rather than secondary considerations. What's next for EvidenceFlow The current prototype intentionally uses synthetic evidence and does not connect to live security infrastructure. A future architecture could ingest and normalize evidence from systems such as: SIEM / EDR / IDS / firewalls / authentication systems / cloud logs and expose that normalized investigation context to agents through the same WebMCP layer. Future versions could also add authenticated backends, persistent audit trails, reviewer identity and authorization, incident-ingestion pipelines, and integrations with real security platforms. The long-term idea is not to replace existing security infrastructure, but to add a controlled human-agent investigation layer on top of it. title: Exposed
pitch: Your AI agent finds your HIPAA exposure in three minutes — and can't take the one decision that matters.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent finds your HIPAA exposure in three minutes — and can't take the one decision that matters. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The sister site, lab.hipaa.technology, teaches doctors how to adopt AI safely — and its only way to raise a hand is a mailto: link in the footer. Meanwhile the practices most at risk aren't deciding whether to use AI. They already are: an ambient scribe on live patient audio, ChatGPT on a consumer tier, no BAA, no consent workflow, no risk analysis that mentions AI. They don't need another article. They need to know what they're exposed to, in the time between patients. WebMCP made it possible to let their agent do the asking. What it does Ten questions about how a practice already uses AI. A readiness score and the three sharpest exposures, free, each with the statute underneath. A personalised remediation roadmap, built from a thirty-control library, gated behind an email the human types themselves. Nine WebMCP tools: Tool Role check_ai_vendor_baa , check_state_ai_rules Hook tools — work with no assessment started start_readiness_check , answer_check_question , get_readiness_score , explain_risk The check email_remediation_roadmap , open_21_day_mission , book_compliance_review Conversion — each hands a decision back to the human How we built it React + TypeScript, imperative registration in the top-level document: document.modelContext with navigator.modelContext fallback, feature-detected, Strict-Mode safe, silent when the API is absent. Every input schema is additionalProperties: false with bounded enums. No free-text input anywhere in the assessment, so patient information cannot enter it. Every tool returns { display, spoken, next_step, disclaimer } . spoken is written to be read aloud, because in an agent flow the human may never see the page. The legal disclaimer travels inside the return value, not just the footer. The gate: email_remediation_roadmap takes no email argument and rejects one if supplied. It pauses execution and opens a real dialog on the page. The human types. The agent can't. Answers stay in the browser. The server keeps email, score, state, clinician count, specialty and three risk-category IDs — never the itemised gaps. Built entirely inside the challenge window. /webmcp on the site documents tools, schemas and the AI MAY / HUMAN MUST boundary. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext both exist in the wild; we register against whichever is present. ChatGPT's browser supports a subset — no declarative forms, no iframes. Everything is imperative, top-level. Language is a legal surface. No "audit", "certified" or "compliant" anywhere — copy, tool names, descriptions or return values. The site says what is missing ; it never says a practice is or isn't compliant. Cutting thirty controls to ten questions. Completion collapses past seven. Ten is the ceiling; the thirty stay in the codebase to power the roadmap. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent can run the whole check in one prompt, and ChatGPT's browser lists all nine tools first try. A gate the agent cannot pass on its own — designed as a feature, not a limitation. A data model chosen for the client's legal position: a written record of a named practice's admitted gaps is a discoverable document, so we never hold one. Shipped, on a real domain, with a live activity rail showing every tool call and every human decision. What we learned The best tool surface is the smallest one. Copy belongs in tool return values. And the most important tool is the one that refuses to act — the gate is the product. What's next for Exposed Roadmap email delivery, state-law overlays beyond recording consent, booking straight into a calendar, and the hand-off into the 21-day adoption mission at lab.hipaa.technology. title: Fentanyl Watch
pitch: Track fentanyl drugs throughout the United States.
about_excerpt: Track fentanyl drugs throughout the United States. Like Comment Story Updates dashboard Inspiration The fentanyl overdose crisis killed more Americans last year than car crashes, yet the public data behind it is scattered across CDC provisional files, DEA press releases, and hundreds of local news stories. We built Fentanyl Watch to pull that picture into one place — a 3D map of 56 metro hotspots, each with a sourced profile. Click on a city for the full disclosed information. But a visualization can only answer the questions its designer anticipated. WebMCP changes that: if the page exposes its data and its camera as tools, an AI agent can answer any question — and then show you the answer on the map. That felt like the right test of what human-agent collaboration on the web should look like. What it does Fentanyl Watch renders 56 overdose hotspots on an extruded, Albers-projected 3D map of the lower 48. Column height encodes annual overdose deaths; column color encodes deaths per 100,000 residents. A toggleable second layer plots 32 major fentanyl seizures from 2025–26 and the 7 southwest border corridors with their share of national seizures. Every hotspot carries a sourced profile: statistics with their exact geographic and year basis, trend, seizure activity, and dated news events with source URLs. The page registers 10 WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool. Seven are read tools — list, fetch, and compare hotspot profiles, national summary and CDC timeline, seizures, border corridors, and a get_data_caveats tool that hands the agent the dataset's honest limitations before it quotes a number. Three are control tools that move what the human sees: focus_hotspot flies the 3D camera to a city and opens its profile drawer, set_seizure_layer toggles the seizure layer, and reset_view returns to the full-country frame. Ask an agent "which metro has the worst per-capita overdose rate?" and it doesn't just answer — it flies you there. How we built it The visualization is Three.js + Vite, with d3-geo and topojson-client projecting a Census TopoJSON into an extruded landmass — no framework, no runtime dependencies beyond those. The dataset was compiled from CDC WONDER and provisional VSRR data, DEA press releases and the National Drug Threat Assessment, state and county health departments, and news reporting, then normalized through a build pipeline into one JSON file. The WebMCP layer is a single module that builds tool descriptors with JSON Schemas and async execute handlers, then registers them against document.modelContext (with a fallback to the older navigator.modelContext draft, and a graceful no-op that stages the tools on window.__webmcpTools for console testing in browsers without the API). Read tools carry readOnlyHint annotations. Control tools call the exact same functions the UI buttons call — we refactored the seizure toggle so the agent and the human drive one shared code path, and the button state can never drift from what the agent did. Challenges we ran into A moving spec. WebMCP documentation still shows several API shapes — navigator.modelContext vs. document.modelContext, provideContext vs. registerTool, string returns vs. MCP-style content arrays. We read the current W3C explainer and Chrome's implementation docs side by side and wrote a small adapter that registers correctly against whichever surface the browser exposes. Overdose figures vary in geographic basis (city vs. county) and time basis (calendar year vs. rolling 12-month provisional windows), and provisional counts get revised. Rather than flattening this into a fake-uniform dataset, every profile labels its own basis, hotspots without a published rate say so instead of getting an invented number — and we exposed all of it to agents as a first-class get_data_caveats tool. Agent-driving a WebGL scene. Most WebMCP demos manipulate DOM. Our control tools have to fly a camera through a Three.js scene, compute framing around HUD panels, and open drawers — so tool handlers had to hook into the animation system, not just flip state. Accomplishments that we're proud of A tool surface with real depth: 10 tools spanning data query, comparison, and visual control — not a single bolted-on demo tool. The human-agent loop actually closes: the agent's answer and the human's screen stay in sync, because focus_hotspot shows you what the agent is talking about. A dataset that tells agents the truth about itself. get_data_caveats means an agent quoting our numbers can also quote their limitations. Every figure in all 56 profiles traces to a named source with a URL. What we learned Designing tools for agents is a different discipline from designing UI for humans. Descriptions are prompts: the difference between an agent using compare_hotspots well or ignoring it lives entirely in one sentence of description text. Read/write separation matters — readOnlyHint annotations let an agent explore freely while being deliberate about tools that move the user's view. And the most valuable tool wasn't a data query at all: it was giving the agent the dataset's caveats, because an agent that can explain a number's basis is more trustworthy than one that just recites it. What's next for Fentanyl Watch Live data refresh — automate the CDC VSRR and DEA ingestion pipeline so the map tracks each provisional release. Richer agent tools — timeline queries per hotspot, region-level aggregation, and a find_sources tool that returns citations for any claim on screen. Declarative WebMCP — annotate the search and filter UI with the declarative API as it stabilizes. Beyond fentanyl — the architecture (sourced hotspot profiles + agent tool surface over a 3D map) generalizes to any geographic crisis dataset: xylazine spread, HIV outbreaks, disaster response. title: FrameGuard
pitch: Review AI-proposed visual edits, protect brand-critical elements, and apply only human-approved changes through a live WebMCP workspace.
about_excerpt: Review AI-proposed visual edits, protect brand-critical elements, and apply only human-approved changes through a live WebMCP workspace. Like Comment Story Updates FrameGuard is a human-in-the-loop visual change-review workspace for teams that want agent speed without surrendering brand control. Inspiration AI design tools are fast, but they can mutate protected logos, legal copy, and approved layouts without a clear audit trail. FrameGuard makes every proposed visual change explicit, reviewable, and reversible. What it does An agent inspects the visible document and creates a structured proposal. Each change appears immediately in the shared UI with its target, rationale, before/after values, status, and compatibility feedback. Protected elements are visibly blocked. A human can approve changes individually; only approved, compatible changes can be applied. Rejection leaves committed state untouched, undo restores the previous revision, and a review receipt captures the decision trail. How WebMCP is used FrameGuard registers focused page tools against one state authority: inspect_document , create_proposal / propose_adaptation , set_change_approval , apply_approved_changes , reject_change_set , undo_last_change_set , and export_review_receipt . Tool availability follows page state, inputs use bounded schemas, validation fails closed, and every successful call mutates the same React store the human sees—so agent execution and UI never diverge. Human + agent The agent proposes and explains; the human reviews and authorizes. Protected changes cannot be approved or applied. Drafting and preview never alter the committed canvas. How we built it React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Vitest, Playwright, GitHub Pages, and Chrome WebMCP. The project runs entirely in the browser and transmits no review data. Challenges and learning The hardest part was preserving atomicity across proposals, protected targets, partial approvals, undo, and dynamic tool registration. We solved this with deterministic domain functions, a single external-store authority, deep-frozen snapshots, microscopic commits, and 64 unit/component plus 4 end-to-end tests. title: Keepsake
pitch: A living family timeline written by an elder, her family, and their agent. Grandma tells a story; it becomes a card; the family asks the next question.
about_excerpt: A living family timeline written by an elder, her family, and their agent. Grandma tells a story; it becomes a card; the family asks the next question. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Rose is 84. She tells stories the way people do: out of order, with the best details buried in the middle. Keepsake listens. Her agent turns each story into a memory card on a shared timeline, links the people in it, picks a picture, and queues the question the family should ask her next time. Her granddaughter Maya reads the timeline, fixes a title by hand, asks "what was Grandpa like when they first met?", and the agent answers from Rose's own words and scrolls to the card. Live: https://keepsake-timeline.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/chinesepowered/keepsake-timeline Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP A memory book only works if the agent can write into the same book the family reads. Keepsake exposes the timeline as eleven structured tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_timeline , search_memories , add_memory , update_memory , remove_memory , add_person , link_people , add_question , mark_question_answered , focus_memory , export_book Any WebMCP-capable agent, whether ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with WebMCP enabled, or the built-in listener, edits exactly what is on screen. The tool descriptions carry the editorial rules: keep the teller's words, first person if Rose told it, never invent facts, split a story that spans two events into two cards, queue a question when a thread is left hanging. How it creates a better experience For the elder: just talk. Voice or text, no forms, no dates to look up. The agent asks at most one gentle follow-up. For the family: a timeline you can read in a minute and edit in a second (double-click a title, remove a card), with a running list of "ask Rose next time" prompts that the agent keeps topped up. Shared attention: focus_memory scrolls to and lights up the card the agent is quoting, so a question about the past ends with both of you looking at the same memory. Portable: export_book returns the timeline as a Markdown book by decade. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Before: a recording nobody transcribes, or a family member typing while Grandma waits, or a chatbot that produces a paragraph and forgets it. Now: the story goes straight into a structured, shared, editable timeline, in her words, with the loose threads turned into questions. The elder supplies the memories, the agent supplies the structure, the family supplies the judgment. Nothing is lost between visits. How WebMCP is implemented lib/webmcp.ts : tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(..., { signal }) and unregistered via AbortController on unmount. Native browser-agent calls and in-page agent calls share one execute path and one activity log. lib/tools.ts : the eleven tools with JSON Schema inputs, descriptions, and read-only / destructive annotations. lib/memories.ts : the shared store (memories, people, questions, focus). The UI's inline edits and the tools mutate the same state. components/AgentPanel.tsx + app/api/agent/route.ts : a Gemini function-calling loop that discovers the registered tools and dispatches through WebMCP, with Web Speech API for voice and a model fallback chain for free-tier limits. Tested in Chrome 153 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (DevTools → Application → WebMCP lists all eleven tools) and with the in-page Gemini agent. title: Material Notes
pitch: a shared canvas for your bookmarks, notes, and ai
about_excerpt: a shared canvas for your bookmarks, notes, and ai Like 1 Comment Story Updates Material is an app to collect the things I'm thinking about: essays, tweets, videos, screenshots, and my own notes, and arrange them on an infinite canvas to think with them. why this is a strong fit for webmcp Material is a strong fit for webmcp because it turns an infinite canvas into a shared workspace between you and an agent. normally, all the context on a canvas stays inside the canvas. if I want to work with an agent, I have to leave it, copy dozens of notes and references into a chat, explain which ones I'm looking at and how they relate, wait for a response, then bring that response back into material and reorganize it on the canvas myself. every time I do that, I lose the spatial context I was working in — and usually the flow of thought that came with it. with webmcp, the agent can work from the same context I already have in front of me. it knows what's on the canvas, what I'm currently selecting, and how things are arranged, and it can work directly in that same space. how it makes the experience better the biggest change is that interacting with the agent becomes part of interacting with the canvas. I can select a messy pile of 30 references and say "group these by theme." the agent reads them, finds the themes, writes a synthesis for each cluster, and lays everything out. or I can select three cards that caught my attention and ask "what connects these?" I don't have to name them, paste their contents, or explain what I'm pointing at. selecting something is enough. that makes the interaction much more fluid. pointing, selecting, moving, and arranging are already how I think on a canvas. now those actions can carry context to the agent too, and its response comes back as part of the canvas rather than another piece of text I have to translate into my workspace. what people and agents can do together that wasn't possible the part I find most interesting is that I don't have to hand the canvas over to the agent or stop what I'm doing to give it instructions. we can work on the same thing at the same time. I might be moving things around, reading, and selecting a few cards that feel related without knowing exactly why yet. I can ask the agent what it sees in them, and it can read much more of the surrounding material than I would at once, find a pattern, write a synthesis, or reorganize the cards around that idea. I can immediately react to what it did — move something back, rewrite a sentence, select a different group — and continue from there. the human contribution is often directional and intuitive: this feels important, these things belong together, this is the thread I want to follow. the agent can take that partial signal and work across much more of the material at once. because we're working on the same canvas, the result doesn't arrive as an answer in a separate chat. it becomes part of the thing I'm already making. how I implemented it I registered eight tools with document.modelContext.registerTool, covering canvas state, selection, card content, creation, editing, and placement. reads come directly from a ref kept in sync with the live react canvas state. writes run through the same reducers as the UI and update state immediately, so there's no server round-trip. spatial operations are batched: the agent can place an entire cluster with one call containing all of its coordinates rather than issuing individual moves. the demo is intentionally ephemeral: the initial canvas is server-rendered from a postgres space and cached for 30 minutes, but all agent and user edits stay local and a reload resets them. the same eight tools run against persistent state in the authenticated product.
