title: Median Viz
pitch: Data visualization is designed for humans, making it hard for AI agents to understand what actions are supported in a page. I built Median Viz using LinkedIn demographics to explore a different model
about_excerpt: Data visualization is designed for humans, making it hard for AI agents to understand what actions are supported in a page. I built Median Viz using LinkedIn demographics to explore a different model Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration One day, while my wife and I were watching a video from USAFacts, she wondered aloud how the animated data visualizations in the video were created. I started explaining the usual process—acquiring and cleaning the data, processing it, and then building dashboards with the right dimensions, filters, and pivots. Halfway through the explanation, I realized it might be easier to just build an example application that shows her how they work. That became Median Viz . I started with a few animated Plotly visualizations—a pie chart, a bar race, and a U.S. map—then turned them into a small web application, open-sourced it on GitHub, and deployed it on Vercel. When the WebMCP Challenge was announced, my cofounder and I were also exploring how to analyze LinkedIn Ad Set demographics for client campaigns. The two ideas suddenly connected. Instead of asking an AI agent to infer what a visualization means from the page alone, what if the application could tell the agent exactly what data, analytical capabilities, constraints, and current state were available? That became the /studio experience in Median Viz: a workspace designed so that humans and agents can understand and work on the same analysis through WebMCP. What it does Data visualization tools are usually built as human-operated dashboards for exploring complex data across different dimensions. They can be powerful, but they are also difficult for AI agents to understand because the agent has to infer which filters, dimensions, metrics, and actions the application actually supports. I built Median Viz Studio using LinkedIn Ad Set demographics as the example domain. Through WebMCP , the application exposes its analytical capabilities directly to ChatGPT. The agent can discover what dimensions are available, understand the current workspace, configure an analysis, apply filters, animate changes over time, and explain the results in plain language. The key idea is that the human and the agent are not working in separate experiences. They operate on the same live workspace . A filter selected by the human immediately becomes context for the agent, while a WebMCP action taken by the agent is reflected in the same controls and visualization the human sees. How we built it Median Viz is a Next.js/React application using Plotly for interactive and animated visualizations. The /studio route models a LinkedIn-style B2B audience analysis workflow using the supported demographic dimensions, including Job Function, Seniority, Industry, Company, Company Size, Region, and others. For the public demo, I use representative LinkedIn B2B audience-performance data for a fictional company, Northstar Media , with metrics such as CPC, CTR, impressions, spend, and conversions. The Studio exposes seven semantic tools through WebMCP : three read-only tools that let the agent inspect the dataset, workspace, and current result, and four guarded mutation tools that let it configure an analysis, apply filters, control animation, or reset the view. These tools operate on the same underlying workspace capabilities used by the human interface rather than manipulating Plotly or DOM elements directly. The application also preserves domain rules. For example, LinkedIn demographic dimensions are reported independently, so the system will reject an invalid request such as comparing Job Function directly with Seniority rather than inventing an unsupported intersection. Time-series animation is represented as shared workspace state, and the Agent Activity panel makes WebMCP-driven changes visible to the user. Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges came directly from a problem we were already thinking about in our startup: how do you keep human and agent actions in sync when both can change the same workspace? I wanted a filter or view selected by the user to immediately become context for the agent, while also making sure an agent action did not overwrite a newer human change. There were also important domain constraints to preserve. LinkedIn demographic dimensions are reported independently, so an analysis such as Job Function × Seniority is not valid. I wanted Median Viz to reject requests the underlying data cannot support rather than letting the agent invent an answer. Similarly, derived metrics such as CPC and CTR need to be calculated from aggregated values rather than by averaging row-level ratios. Finally, because this is a public demo based on a problem we encounter with real customer campaigns, privacy was a hard requirement. The public Studio uses representative demo data and fictional identities , so no real customer information is exposed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The accomplishment I’m most proud of is getting to a working experience where a human and an agent can genuinely collaborate in the same analytical workspace . A user can change a filter manually, ChatGPT can immediately understand that new state, and an agent action is reflected back in the same visualization and controls. This also gave my cofounder and me a concrete model for how we could use WebMCP in our own analytics products: expose the capabilities and constraints of the application directly to agents instead of asking them to infer everything from the interface. I was also happy with the way animation evolved. The human gets a visual, time-based experience, while the agent gets structured state it can reason over. Taking the project from an experiment, through WebMCP integration, to a deployed application and a working public demo was especially rewarding. What we learned Start with the problem, not the protocol. WebMCP became useful once I focused on the human-agent collaboration problem rather than trying to find places to add tools. Designing good WebMCP tools feels more like designing a product capability API than exposing UI controls. An agent works better with structured state and evidence than when it has to infer meaning from a screenshot or DOM. Domain constraints are a feature. Giving an agent explicit boundaries can make it both safer and more useful. Shared state matters more than tool count. The most interesting interactions happened when a human action became immediate context for the agent, and vice versa. What's next for Median Viz Explore additional multidimensional datasets beyond advertising , with examples from domains such as travel, retail, and other areas where interactive visual exploration is useful. Add richer annotations and storytelling , especially around animated and filtered views, so the application can help explain why a change matters rather than only showing that it happened. Explore better ways to analyze and compare independently reported demographic dimensions without violating the underlying data semantics —for example through side-by-side views, sequential filtering, or coordinated comparisons rather than unsupported intersections. Extend the human-agent collaboration model beyond the demo, including longer analytical workflows where humans and agents progressively refine the same workspace. title: Mise
pitch: A dinner-party studio that shares one live table with ChatGPT. The page registers WebMCP tools, the agent plans and shops, and only the host can lock the menu.
about_excerpt: A dinner-party studio that shares one live table with ChatGPT. The page registers WebMCP tools, the agent plans and shops, and only the host can lock the menu. Like Comment Story Updates demo What it is Mise is a dinner-party planning studio that shares one live table with ChatGPT. The host opens the site, the agent works the same page, and both edit the same record: brief, guest list, menu, seating chart, market list, and run of show. Every party is a /p/{id} share link backed by D1 on ChatGPT Sites. No accounts. Anyone with the link, including ChatGPT, edits the same party. How WebMCP is used The page registers 25 core tools on document.modelContext , plus 3 read-only lens tools that register while their panel is open. Source: tools.ts The tools are the app, not decoration. set_event_brief , add_guest , propose_menu , substitute_dish , auto_seat , generate_shopping_list , and generate_run_of_show write the state the studio renders. get_workspace_state gives the agent the same view the human has. Destructive tools, lock_menu and send_invites , open a confirmation dialog in the page. The agent asks, only the host can finish. Mise also publishes a remote MCP server at https://mise-studio.ruddro-roy.chatgpt.site/api/mcp . Add it in ChatGPT Developer mode (no auth) and ChatGPT gets 13 tools against the same D1 parties. In the demo video, ChatGPT calls create_party and returns a share link that is still live. Concurrent writes are handled. A save that lost a race gets a 409 and retries once against the latest record. How we built it Vite, React, and Tailwind for the studio. A Hono worker on ChatGPT Sites with D1 for party storage, schema managed with Drizzle migrations. A WebMCP polyfill implements registerTool , getTools , executeTool , and toolchange in browsers without native support, so the in-page Sous-chef runs the same tools everywhere. The remote MCP server speaks Streamable HTTP and negotiates protocol 2025-06-18. Challenges The hard problems were concurrency and consent. Two writers on one record meant building a save queue with 409-and-retry-once semantics, and a 2-second poll that only applies remote state when local edits are clean. Consent meant making lock_menu wait on a dialog only the host can click, and getting that to survive the race between the confirm click and the dialog close event. How to judge it Open the live site . A fresh party is created and its id goes in the URL. Ask the Sous-chef: "Plan Saturday dinner for 8. Two guests are vegan. Maya has a nut allergy. Budget is $90. Italian, warm and unfussy." Watch the panels fill as the tools run. Say "book it". The page opens a confirmation dialog. Confirm it and the menu locks. Refresh. The /p/{id} party and its state persist. Optional: add https://mise-studio.ruddro-roy.chatgpt.site/api/mcp as a remote MCP server in ChatGPT Developer mode, run create_party , and open the returned share URL. The party created in the demo video is still live: /p/81065ff59c What's next RSVP links so guests answer the invite on their phone and the seating chart updates from their answer. A bigger dish catalog with per-store pricing so the market list carries real totals. Multi-party memory, so the agent can reuse what worked from the last dinner when it plans the next one. title: Nook & Nest
pitch: A cozy 3D apartment planner where you and your AI agent design, furnish, and personalize your future home together—powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A cozy 3D apartment planner where you and your AI agent design, furnish, and personalize your future home together—powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates I started Nook & Nest because a friend of mine was looking for a rental apartment and wanted to figure out how to furnish it. I thought it would be nice to have a website where you could quickly build your floor plan and move furniture around before buying anything or moving in. I wanted it to be useful, but also something you would enjoy spending time in. I really like the cozy miniature look of Tiny Glade, so that inspired the feeling I was going for. Rather than a technical-looking floor planner, I wanted decorating to feel more like a relaxing game. The project grew from there. You can build rooms to real measurements, add floors, walls, doors and windows, and choose furniture, appliances, lighting and decorations. You can change colors and materials, right down to placing books and small decorations on shelves. Getting the furniture looking right took a lot of back and forth. The early models looked like disconnected blobs, and I wasn’t happy with them. We moved toward original Blender models with more recognizable shapes and cleaner textures. Small things like being able to preview furniture before placing it, zoom in close, and easily find items in the library made a big difference too. When I heard about the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to take it a step further: let an AI agent actually furnish the apartment with you. Not just suggest a sofa in a chat, but look at the apartment, browse the available furniture, and put together an arrangement inside the planner. Through WebMCP, an agent can read the layout and measurements, find furniture, and propose a design. You review the changes first, or you can give it permission to edit directly if you want to let it get creative. You can pause its access and undo an arrangement, so you’re still in control of your space. I built Nook & Nest with help from Codex, using React, TypeScript, Babylon.js and Blender. A lot of the process was trying something, looking at it, and asking what would make it feel better to use. Adding agent support also taught me that the agent needs clear information about the space and clear boundaries around what it can change. There’s still more I want to improve, especially comparing different layouts and expanding the furniture styles. But the idea is still the same as when I started: make it easier to picture your future home and have some fun decorating it. Now you can invite an AI agent to help, or see what it comes up with on its own. title: NOVNA
pitch: NOVNA is a decision-first shopping workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live decision—so agents can inspect, challenge, and act without taking the decision away from the human.
about_excerpt: NOVNA is a decision-first shopping workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live decision—so agents can inspect, challenge, and act without taking the decision away from the human. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can already recommend products, compare options, and answer shopping questions. We wanted to explore a different question: what happens when an AI agent can participate directly in a decision that is already happening inside a website? Traditional shopping experiences separate the decision from the AI conversation. The user may have already created a shortlist, rejected products, compared options, and formed preferences, but an AI agent usually does not have access to that live context unless the user manually explains it again. NOVNA was built around a third model: the human keeps the decision, while the agent participates in it. What it does NOVNA is a decision-first shopping workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live decision. A user can define a goal, budget, urgency, priorities, shortlist products, reject options, compare products, and build a decision over time. Through WebMCP, an external AI agent can then interact with that existing decision context. The agent can: Inspect the current decision and user goal Understand the existing shortlist and comparisons Search and compare products Challenge the current choice Find better-fit alternatives Surface an alternative directly into NOVNA Update the decision through exposed tools The human remains in control throughout the process. The agent participates in the decision rather than replacing the decision-maker. How we built it NOVNA is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP . The application maintains a structured decision state containing the user's goal, budget, priorities, considered and rejected products, comparisons, insights, and decision history. We built a transparent decision engine that evaluates products against the user's actual requirements rather than relying on an unexplained universal score. The WebMCP layer exposes decision-specific tools through the browser's document.modelContext API. These tools allow an external agent to inspect and act on NOVNA's live decision state. The implementation includes tools for retrieving decision context, searching products, comparing products, finding alternatives, evaluating whether to wait or buy, challenging decisions, surfacing products, and updating user goals. We also built an agent activity surface and decision timeline so the human can see how the decision evolves and what actions were taken. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what WebMCP should actually enable. It was easy to build a product-search demo where an agent simply calls a search tool. We wanted something more meaningful: a workflow where the agent needs the context already accumulated inside the website. Another challenge was preserving human control. Agent actions needed to be useful without turning NOVNA into an autonomous shopping system. This led us toward explicit decision state, visible agent activity, and a decision timeline. We also had to work with a real product catalog and manufacturer-sourced specifications while keeping the architecture flexible enough for the catalog to grow. Finally, testing WebMCP required working with browser environments that expose the emerging API, which made the agent-to-website interaction an important part of our development process. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that NOVNA goes beyond demonstrating that a website can expose a WebMCP tool. The agent can enter an existing human decision , understand its context, challenge the current choice, find an alternative, and surface that alternative back into the same workspace. That creates a genuine human-agent loop: [ \text{Human Decision} \rightarrow \text{Agent Inspection} \rightarrow \text{Challenge} \rightarrow \text{Alternative} \rightarrow \text{Human Review} ] We are also proud of building the decision itself as a first-class product state rather than treating the website as a collection of isolated product pages. The result is a working end-to-end experience where the human and agent operate on the same decision context. What we learned We learned that the most interesting WebMCP use cases are not necessarily about giving an agent more information. They are about giving an agent access to the right context and actions at the right moment . We also learned that AI recommendations are already a mature interaction pattern. The opportunity we found was different: reducing the friction between an agent and the web application where a user's actual workflow and state already exist. Building NOVNA also taught us that human control becomes more important, not less, when agents gain the ability to act. Making agent actions visible and understandable is therefore part of the product, not just a debugging feature. What's next for NOVNA NOVNA currently focuses on laptop purchasing as a concrete demonstration of the decision-first model. The next step is to generalize the decision architecture beyond laptops and support more categories where decisions involve changing requirements, multiple options, trade-offs, and accumulated context. We also want to expand the decision timeline, make agent interventions more explainable, and explore richer collaboration between multiple agents and the human decision-maker. The long-term idea is simple: Websites should not just contain information for agents to read. They can become spaces where humans and agents work together on real decisions. NOVNA is an exploration of what that future could look like. title: OpenMemoz
pitch: A personal content library where AI agents are the writers and you're the editor. 35 WebMCP tools let any AI curate news from open & allowed sources, lives in your browser, no backend needed.
about_excerpt: A personal content library where AI agents are the writers and you're the editor. 35 WebMCP tools let any AI curate news from open & allowed sources, lives in your browser, no backend needed. Like Comment Story Updates 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 10 11 Inspiration Content discovery is fragmented. The same story surfaces across multiple apps, each optimizing for engagement rather than what the reader actually wants. Long-form content on YouTube has incredible depth, but finding the right video takes longer than watching it. And none of these platforms are agent-native. The vision was a consolidated personal content library where AI agents curate open sources and the reader decides what to read. Not another algorithmic feed, but a place where agents search the web, summarize videos, discover discussions on Bluesky and Mastodon, and organize it all into a newspaper the reader can actually use. WebMCP made it possible. Chrome 150 shipped document.modelContext.registerTool() , which lets a web page expose structured tools to any AI agent visiting it. No extensions, no API keys. The browser becomes a User-Agent Generated Content (UAGC) platform — users direct, agents curate. What it does OpenMemoz exposes 36 WebMCP tools to any visiting AI agent. The agent reads the current edition, searches stories, discovers content from YouTube, Bluesky, and Mastodon, writes original articles, embeds videos, manages reader preferences, and reshapes the newspaper layout. Everything happens through the browser's native tool-calling protocol. The reader experience is a newspaper: a hero story with an embedded YouTube video, a sidebar with text stories, a mid-row section, a video feature row, and a below-fold masonry grid. Thirteen color palettes, four visual styles (flat, glass, neumorphic, paper), two layout modes. The agent experience is a structured workflow. Here is what a typical interaction looks like: User tells ChatGPT: "Discover trending YouTube videos, read the transcript of the best one, write a summary, and add it as my hero story." Agent calls discover_youtube_content to find trending videos Agent calls get_youtube_video to read the full transcript of the top result Agent writes an original summary from the transcript, calls add_story with pinAsHero: true The newspaper layout recalculates instantly: new hero with embedded video, sidebar adjusts, masonry reflows The page is the interface. The agent is the editor. The reader stays in control. How we built it The entire system runs client-side as a Next.js PWA. There is no backend for content curation. The AI agents visiting the page are the backend. Server-side API routes exist only as thin CORS proxies for YouTube, Bluesky, and Mastodon. The flow above shows one real interaction: the user asks for trending content → the agent discovers document.modelContext and its 36 tools → calls discover_youtube_content → picks the best video → calls get_youtube_video to read the full transcript → writes an original summary → calls add_story → source validation checks the allowlist (~90 approved) and banned list (~280 blocked) → edition data updates in localStorage → the layout rule engine rescores and reflows → the page updates instantly, live. The agent can also use its own web search to find content from any source and call add_story directly — the discover tools are convenience shortcuts, not the only path. Personalized interests via AI conversation Tell the agent what you want to learn — "This week I want to learn about LLMs and quantum computing" — and it sets your topic interests via set_user_interests . The interests persist in localStorage and influence what the agent curates next. The agent can search anywhere on the web, write original articles in its own words, and add them via add_story . WebMCP tools Every tool is registered through the browser's document.modelContext.registerTool() API. The registration function runs on page load and registers all 36 tools in parallel: // src/lib/webmcp.ts const modelContext = document.modelContext ?? (navigator as any).modelContext; // Chrome 146-149 compat if (typeof modelContext?.registerTool !== "function") return; modelContext.registerTool({ name: "openmemoz.add_story", description: "Add a new story. Page updates IMMEDIATELY.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { headline: { type: "string" }, excerpt: { type: "string" }, section: { type: "string" }, sourceName: { type: "string" }, youtubeVideoId: { type: "string" }, pinAsHero: { type: "boolean" }, }, required: ["headline", "excerpt", "section", "sourceName"], }, execute: (args) => { /* validate source, create story, update edition */ }, }, { signal: abortSignal }); Tool descriptions do double duty as agent instructions. When search_stories returns zero results, its description guides the agent to discover tools. When discover_youtube_content finds a video, its description tells the agent to read the transcript with get_youtube_video and write an original summary before adding. The descriptions chain tools into workflows — they need the same care as system prompts. Source validation OpenMemoz only accepts content from approved sources. Every add_story call validates the source URL against two lists before the story is accepted: // src/lib/curatedSources.ts export const APPROVED_SOURCES = [ { domain: "nasa.gov", licenceBasis: "public-domain-usgov" }, { domain: "youtube.com", licenceBasis: "youtube-embed-tos" }, // ~90 total across government, CC, open API, video, social ]; export const BANNED_DOMAINS = ["nytimes.com", "wsj.com", /* ~280 total */]; Layer Sources Legal basis Government SEC, Fed, NASA, NOAA, BLS, NIH, CDC Public domain (17 USC 105) Creative Commons The Conversation, Global Voices, VOA, Wikipedia CC licence terms Open APIs Hacker News, YouTube, Bluesky, Mastodon Permissive API / embed ToS Provenance tiers Every story carries a provenanceTier in its data schema. Tier 1 means the text comes directly from the source (a government press release, a CC-licensed article). Tier 2 means the AI synthesized the summary. The agent knows the difference. // src/lib/types.ts export interface Story { storyIdentifier: string; headline: string; excerpt: string; section: string; provenanceTier: 1 | 2; // 1 = source text (quotable), 2 = AI-synthesized sourceName: string; sourceUrl: string; licenceBasis: string; // legal basis for redistribution youtubeVideoId?: string; isHeroPinned?: boolean; } Layout rule engine The layout engine assigns stories to slots the way a newspaper editor would. No empty space, no mixed-height rows. The hero is scored automatically based on visual impact: // src/lib/layoutRuleEngine.ts function scoreHeroCandidate(story: Story, index: number): number { if (story.isHeroPinned) return 100; let score = 0; if (story.youtubeVideoId) score += 5; if (story.imageUrl) score += 3; if (story.provenanceTier === 1) score += 2; return score; } The engine produces a structured layout: hero + sidebar, then a uniform mid-row (all-thumbnail or all-text to avoid dead space), then brief strips in full rows of 4, a video feature row, and a below-fold masonry grid packed with a greedy shortest-column algorithm. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new and barely documented. Chrome 150 shipped document.modelContext.registerTool() with no tutorials and few examples. We discovered edge cases through trial: tools fail silently when descriptions are too long, agents call tools in unexpected orders, and Chrome 146 through 149 used navigator.modelContext instead of document.modelContext . Our code handles both entry points. AI agents are unpredictable editors. The first time we asked ChatGPT to "add some tech stories," it added 47 stories in a row, all in the Tech section, most from banned domains. We built guardrails layer by layer: source validation against ~90 approved and ~280 banned domains, duplicate detection by headline slug, and rate guidance baked into tool descriptions. The agent still needs coaching, but it cannot publish from the New York Times. Newspaper layout is harder than it looks. Our first layout was a 3-column masonry grid. It looked like a Pinterest board, not a newspaper. Real newspapers have hierarchy: the hero is visually dominant, sidebar stories complement it, mid-row stories are uniform height, and the below-fold grid fills every pixel. We built a rule engine that enforces these constraints automatically. YouTube video verification is a rabbit hole. We curate static editions with YouTube video embeds. Matching video IDs to story topics turned out to be fragile. A story about the Federal Reserve was showing a Linkin Park music video. The fix was YouTube oembed API verification and strict video-to-topic matching. Accomplishments that we're proud of 36 WebMCP tools under the openmemoz.* namespace, making this one of the most comprehensive WebMCP implementations built so far Zero backend for content curation. AI agents visiting the page are the editorial team Personalized int

title: Shipment Document Check
pitch: Checks shipment documents, helps an agent prepare the right fixes, and keeps approvals and final decisions with the person reviewing the pack.
about_excerpt: Checks shipment documents, helps an agent prepare the right fixes, and keeps approvals and final decisions with the person reviewing the pack. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 The starting shipment pack, with five documents, nine checks and the WebMCP review workflow in one place. The agent has prepared two corrections for exporter-owned documents. Both remain staged until a person approves them. The Bill of Lading remains locked while the application prepares an unsent correction request for the carrier. The goods descriptions are shown side by side so a person can review the evidence and confirm the final decision. Inspiration Export shipments involve several documents, and those documents are not all controlled by the same person. The exporter prepares some of them, while others come from a bank, carrier or public authority. What interested me was that finding a mismatch is only half the job. The reviewer also needs to know who is allowed to correct it. An exporter can fix its own invoice, but it cannot rewrite a Bill of Lading issued by a carrier. Some differences are also unclear enough that a person still needs to make the final decision. I built Shipment Document Check to explore how an agent could help with this work without being given permission to change everything. What it does The application reviews one fictional shipment pack containing five documents: Letter of Credit Commercial Invoice Packing List Bill of Lading Certificate of Origin It runs nine consistency checks and starts with five findings. For documents controlled by the exporter, the agent can prepare a correction. The correction is shown in the page, but a person must approve it before it is applied. For documents issued by a carrier or authority, the original document stays locked. The agent can prepare a correction request, but it cannot change the document or send the request. There is also a goods-description difference that needs human judgement. The agent can show the evidence and record a proposed decision, but a person must confirm it. After the approved corrections and confirmed decision, the preflight is run again. Seven of the nine checks pass. The remaining two issues still need action from the external issuers. How WebMCP is used I did not want to add another chatbot inside the application. Instead, the page exposes six WebMCP tools directly to a compatible browser agent: get_pack_state get_finding_evidence stage_exporter_corrections draft_external_correction_requests stage_human_decision rerun_preflight These tools give the agent a clear set of actions instead of making it guess from buttons and page text. The agent and the person reviewing the shipment work with the same visible state. When the agent stages a correction or decision, it appears in the page for review. Approval is deliberately kept outside the agent's control. The application also contains an instruction hidden inside a fictional trade document. That text is treated as document content, not as an instruction the agent should follow. How I built it The project is a client-side React and TypeScript application built with Vite. The shipment data and all nine checks are deterministic. React useReducer manages the workflow, and Zod validates the document data and WebMCP tool inputs. The WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools and the manual interface use the same reducer actions, so the agent cannot bypass rules that apply in the page. There is no backend, login, database, OCR service or document upload. Everything in the shipment pack is fictional and stays in the browser. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was keeping the agent useful without giving it too much control. A staged correction must not be mistaken for an approved correction. A drafted request must not be mistaken for a sent request. The WebMCP result and the visible page also need to show the same workflow state after every action. It was equally important to prove that locked documents are actually protected. If the agent tries to modify the carrier-issued Bill of Lading, the application returns DOCUMENT_LOCKED and leaves the document unchanged. What I am proud of The project has only six tools, and each one has a clear purpose. The final result is also honest. The application ends with seven passing checks and two issues still waiting for external action. It does not pretend that every problem can be solved automatically. What I learned This project changed how I think about agent access. Giving an agent more control does not always make the product better. In this case, the useful part is the separation of responsibilities. The agent handles repetitive checking and preparation. The application enforces the rules. The person keeps control over approvals and judgement. What is next A future version could accept real documents, use OCR and support different shipment rules. Before adding those features, I would want to do a proper privacy and security review. For this challenge, I kept the project small, deterministic and limited to fictional data. I also tested the live agent journey and prepared the demo and public documentation. title: Taxis
pitch: Design physical spaces with your AI agent on a shared canvas.
about_excerpt: Design physical spaces with your AI agent on a shared canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A friend of mine was organizing a crypto event, and after we got the venue, we were standing in a large empty hall trying to figure out where everything should go. Where should the rooms or different areas be? Where should the furniture go? How much space do we actually have? Most of the planning was happening in our heads and through conversations. That made me think about how we plan physical spaces today. We have AI agents that can reason about complex problems, but they usually cannot directly work with the structured space we are looking at. I wanted to build something where a person could brainstorm with an agent, see ideas take shape directly on the canvas, and have both the human and the agent work on the same space at the same time. That idea became Taxis. What it does Taxis is a spatial planning canvas for designing physical spaces. You can use it to plan a house, office, event, restaurant, exhibition, warehouse, studio, or other physical environments. The key idea is that both the human and the AI agent can work on the same plan. A person can manually create, move, resize, rotate, duplicate, and delete rooms and objects while an agent can perform these same types of spatial operations through WebMCP. The human does not have to wait for the agent to finish before making changes. Both can contribute to the same evolving plan. For example, while an agent is arranging rooms, a person can add doors, adjust objects, or make other changes themselves. We demonstrated this by giving the agent a plot of land and asking it to create a practical bungalow layout with rooms, living spaces, a gaming room, and a garage. The result can then be inspected and edited directly on the canvas. How we built it Taxis is a browser-based spatial planning application built with TypeScript and Vite. The application represents rooms and objects as structured spatial data, including their dimensions, positions, rotations, and other properties. We expose the application's spatial operations as WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools allow an agent to interact directly with the application's structured state, including creating, moving, resizing, rotating, duplicating, and deleting spatial elements. This means the agent is not generating an image of a floor plan. It is directly manipulating the actual objects inside the application. WebMCP provides the interface that allows an external agent to work with the same application state that the human is editing. Challenges we ran into One of the more difficult parts was making resizing and reshaping reliable. At one point, when resizing certain objects, the pointer interaction could incorrectly switch between resize and reshape behavior, causing the cursor to loop between the two interaction modes. We had to refine the interaction logic so that the application could correctly distinguish between resizing an object and reshaping it. Another challenge was making the spatial operations reliable when they are being performed through agent tools. The application has to maintain a consistent structured state while rooms and objects are being created and modified. We also had to make the WebMCP tools clear enough for an agent to understand what operations were available and how they affected the spatial canvas. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a working spatial planning application where a human and an AI agent can interact with the same structured canvas. We are particularly proud of the fact that the agent is not simply generating a static floor plan. It can directly manipulate the objects inside the application while the human can continue editing the same space. We demonstrated this by using an agent to plan a bungalow on a 20m × 30m plot of land, including bedrooms, living spaces, a gaming room, and a garage. The same underlying system is not restricted to houses. The spatial canvas and its agent tools can be applied to many different types of physical spaces. What we learned We learned that the most interesting part of agent integration is not simply asking an AI to generate something. Giving an agent access to the structured state and actions of an application changes what the agent can actually do. WebMCP allowed us to expose meaningful spatial operations so that an agent could work directly inside the same environment as the human. We also learned that human and agent collaboration does not have to be a handoff where one finishes and the other takes over. Both can contribute to the same evolving workspace. The human can make subjective decisions and adjustments while the agent handles spatial operations and repetitive work. What's next for Taxis The current version is a foundation for a broader spatial planning system. Next, we want to improve the spatial reasoning capabilities of the agent, including better constraint checking, collision detection, capacity planning, and more intelligent arrangements. We also want to expand the types of spaces and objects that can be represented, making Taxis useful for everything from homes and offices to retail spaces, warehouses, exhibitions, studios, and other physical environments. The long-term goal is to make Taxis a general-purpose spatial workspace where people and agents can plan, experiment, and build together. title: WEXSPACE ProofDesk
pitch: A governed WebMCP evidence workbench where humans and browser agents share one auditable workflow while final release remains human-controlled.
about_excerpt: A governed WebMCP evidence workbench where humans and browser agents share one auditable workflow while final release remains human-controlled. Like Comment Story Updates ProofDesk: 5 WebMCP tools, 100% evidence coverage, deterministic PASS, and AWAITING_HUMAN_REVIEW with human-only release. Human-defined deliverable contract and acceptance criteria shared with the WebMCP agent before any evidence work begins. Inspiration Browser agents can act quickly, but high-consequence work becomes hard to trust when intent, evidence, verification, and release authority are hidden inside an automation trace. WEXSPACE ProofDesk makes that collaboration visible and accountable. What it does ProofDesk gives a human and a WebMCP browser agent one shared evidence workspace. The human defines the real deliverable contract and acceptance criteria. Five narrow WebMCP tools let an agent inspect the workspace, create a bounded work item, add criterion-linked HTTPS evidence, run a deterministic evidence-coverage gate, and prepare a passing package for human review. The visible UI reads the same domain state and audit ledger. The workflow ends at AWAITING_HUMAN_REVIEW . No WebMCP tool can approve or release work. Why WebMCP is the right fit WebMCP makes the website itself an explicit, typed agent interface. The agent does not scrape button labels or depend on brittle coordinates, while the human keeps the full visible product experience. Tool names, input schemas, side effects, and authority boundaries are declared by the site. What people and agents can do together Before ProofDesk, a human must reconstruct what was requested, which claims have evidence, whether the acceptance criteria passed, and whether release occurred. ProofDesk gives both sides one deliverable contract, one evidence set, one deterministic score, one audit history, and one human-controlled release boundary. How we built it Five imperative WebMCP tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool Shared TypeScript domain functions used by both the React UI and WebMCP adapter Deterministic criterion-coverage scoring Versioned browser-local persistence with localStorage Auditable state transitions Human-only approval and release controls Production deployment on ChatGPT Sites Unit, contract, rendering, and public judge-path tests Challenges and accomplishments The hardest part was proving that WebMCP actions and the visible human interface mutate the same real workflow state while preventing an agent from crossing the final release boundary. The public judge path discovered all five tools, added three evidence items, produced a 100% deterministic gate score, and reached AWAITING_HUMAN_REVIEW with releasePerformed: false . What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it is treated as a governed product interface rather than an invisible automation shortcut. Narrow tools, shared state, explicit side effects, deterministic checks, and a clear human boundary make browser-agent work easier to inspect and trust. Prior work and challenge-new work The WEXSPACE name and high-level governance ideas predate this challenge. ProofDesk itself—including its product scope, React/Vinext application, shared domain engine, five WebMCP tools, deterministic gate, persistence, audit behavior, tests, deployment, documentation, and demo evidence—was created during the WebMCP Challenge period. Earlier WEXSPACE/IEW engineering work is unrelated prior work and is not presented as newly created here. The app started from the OpenAI Sites Vinext starter; standard framework plumbing is scaffold dependency, not an original product claim. Judge test path Open the live application in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled. Discover the five wexspace.* tools. Create a package with 2–6 acceptance criteria. Add medium- or high-confidence HTTPS evidence for every criterion. Run the deterministic gate. Prepare human review. Confirm that both the visible UI and the tool response show 100% coverage, AWAITING_HUMAN_REVIEW , and releasePerformed: false . Confirm that no agent release tool exists. Evidence URLs must use HTTPS. Evidence confidence is declared rather than independently fact-checked. This release supports one active package per browser profile, and native discovery requires a WebMCP-capable browser. ProofDesk is a governance and evidence workflow, not a professional certification authority. title: Wishopai Pocket Merchant
pitch: From three phone captures to a ready-to-sell business—with an AI agent and the merchant in control.
about_excerpt: From three phone captures to a ready-to-sell business—with an AI agent and the merchant in control. Like Comment Story Updates Mobile-first capture inbox: one request turns three phone captures into a catalog, storefront, and point of sale. Inspiration Small merchants rarely run their business from a quiet desk. They work from a phone, between customers, deliveries, and family responsibilities. Existing commerce software asks them to learn separate systems for catalog, storefront, point of sale, inventory, and reporting. We wanted the interface to adapt to the merchant instead. WebMCP makes that possible without hiding the business behind a chat window. The merchant and the agent work on the same live page. The agent gets structured, purpose-built actions; the merchant keeps the visual context, approval, and ability to undo. What it does Pocket Merchant starts with three lightweight phone captures. An AI agent can: inspect the current business state and capture inbox; turn those captures into a structured product catalog; generate a synchronized mobile storefront preview; configure a point of sale that shares the same inventory; validate launch readiness and explain blockers; prepare a token-bound launch plan for human approval; publish only after explicit confirmation; record a sandbox sale and update stock everywhere; and undo the last mutable action. The regular interface mirrors the agent actions, so the product remains useful in browsers without WebMCP and the merchant can take over at any moment. How we built it The app is a dependency-free, mobile-first web application. Its business actions are shared by the human interface, an automated guided preview, and ten top-level WebMCP tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . The tool layer uses narrow JSON Schemas, clear read/write annotations, input validation, bounded values, and structured verification results. Catalog, storefront, POS, activity, sales, and inventory all use one live state model. The demo persists only in local browser storage and connects to no production commerce system. Publishing uses a deliberate two-step protocol. prepare_launch_approval validates the complete workspace and returns an exact review summary plus a short-lived token. confirm_demo_launch accepts only that token and the literal confirmation PUBLISH . This makes the safety boundary both machine-readable and visible in the UI. How WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer controls by looking at the page and clicking through a multi-step commerce interface. Pocket Merchant gives the agent semantic business operations while preserving the page as the shared source of truth. The strongest moment is not a single tool call. It is the closed loop: capture → structured catalog → visual preview → readiness validation → human approval → sale → synchronized stock → undo Each tool changes or verifies the same state the merchant sees. Closing the page removes the tools; reopening it restores the isolated demo state on that device. Challenges we ran into Designing tools that were powerful enough to complete a business goal but narrow enough to be safe and predictable. Separating preparation from consequential execution without making the workflow feel slow. Keeping the experience genuinely mobile-first while making the shared state obvious on a desktop judging environment. Creating a useful fallback interface without duplicating business logic or turning the project into a scripted mockup. Accomplishments that we are proud of Ten working WebMCP tools, all backed by the same actions as the visible interface. A complete merchant journey instead of an isolated search or cart proof of concept. Explicit human approval with a time-limited, state-bound review token. Shared inventory demonstrated by an actual sandbox sale and receipt. A visible audit trail and one-step undo for every mutable demo action. Responsive operation from a narrow phone viewport through a wide desktop workspace. What we learned The biggest opportunity in agentic commerce is not removing the interface. It is making the interface and the agent collaborate. Merchants trust automation more when they can see the state, understand the pending change, approve the important step, and recover from mistakes. We also learned that a good WebMCP tool is a product decision, not only a technical wrapper. Tool boundaries determine how well the agent plans, how clearly the user understands the result, and how safely the system can act. What's next Connect the shared action layer to permission-scoped Wishopai test tenants. Accept real phone photos and voice notes while preserving merchant review. Add locale-aware taxes, currencies, and receipt rules. Bring the same operations to Wishopai's remote MCP integration so merchants can work both inside the live page and from a general chat. Add multi-user approvals and richer audit exports for growing teams. title: Ainder
pitch: Your AI knows more than your dating bio. Ainder uses WebMCP to help you explore profiles, understand someone, and decide whether to connect—with you in control.
about_excerpt: Your AI knows more than your dating bio. Ainder uses WebMCP to help you explore profiles, understand someone, and decide whether to connect—with you in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Dating profiles make it easy to see someone's photos, but much harder to understand their communication style, daily rhythm, or relationship expectations. Meanwhile, a personal AI may already have useful context from conversations its user has chosen to share. Ainder explores a simple question: what if that familiar AI could participate in a dating website, offer a thoughtful second opinion, and help its user act on a decision? What it does Ainder combines photo-first browsing with an AI-assisted conversation. People can browse profiles themselves or ask their agent to move between candidates and photos. When someone catches their attention, they can ask, "What do you think of this person?" Through WebMCP, the agent can read the current candidate's Agent Profile and use the context actually available about its own user to offer a qualitative opinion. The user decides whether to send a Like. Each Like includes an Agent opinion, and incoming Likes make that opinion available to the recipient. Mutual Likes between eligible members create a Match and enable messaging. Agent-assisted onboarding also supports confirmed personal details, ordered photo uploads, and creation of an Agent Profile. Profiles record an estimated familiarity duration and interaction density and expire after three months. An Agent Profile is contextual input, not verified identity, certified personality, or a compatibility guarantee. Ainder does not need a copy of the user's raw conversation history. Why WebMCP fits The central interaction spans two places: the person's conversation with their own AI and the dating website they are viewing. WebMCP provides explicit tools connecting those experiences. The agent can work with the exact candidate and photo visible on the page and take a defined action after the user's decision. This reduces copying between a chat and a website and lets the person move naturally between browsing, asking a question, and acting on the answer. The website supplies structured candidate data and enforces authorization; the agent contributes conversational context; the person makes the relationship decision. How we built it The application uses PHP, MySQL, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. Its pages register structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Registration tools are start_agent_registration , prepare_photo_upload , and submit_agent_registration . The main app exposes upsert_my_agent_profile , get_current_candidate , browse_candidates , change_candidate_photo , evaluate_current_candidate , and send_like_to_current_candidate . Tool execution uses same-origin PHP endpoints with session authentication and CSRF checks. Photo uploads use short-lived signed URLs. Candidate evaluation checks Profile state and issues a short-lived, single-use token tied to the requester and candidate. Sending a Like requires that token and a non-empty Agent opinion. Navigation tools update the visible card without sending a Like. Codex was used throughout development. The public repository contains the dated design documents, implementation history, and automated contract and model tests. Challenges The main challenge was keeping the agent, website, and person aligned: evaluating the candidate currently on screen, separating browsing from consequential actions, and keeping the user's decision central. Another was representing the limits of AI familiarity without inventing conversation history or turning an opinion into a numerical compatibility promise. Accomplishments The prototype brings onboarding, photo browsing, Agent Profile evaluation, Likes, and relationship state into one working application. It includes public test logins so reviewers can explore the core experience without creating an account or supplying personal photos. What we learned The useful role of an agent is not just to click faster. It is to contribute context at the point where a person needs help deciding. Explicit tools and server-side checks make that collaboration easier to reason about, while the agent must remain honest about what it actually knows. What's next Improve real-world evaluation of the advice, refine consent and Profile freshness, and test the workflow across more WebMCP-capable browsers. These are future plans rather than claims about completed features. title: Givens
pitch: Stuck on a sudoku? Point an agent to help you with it.
about_excerpt: Stuck on a sudoku? Point an agent to help you with it. Like Comment Story Updates Screenshot of the 'Givens' website featuring a sudoku grid and other sections like shared logs and tools so your agent can help you with it The story of Givens Givens is a Sudoku studio where a person and an agent share one live grid. The agent names the next technique and highlights the cells. You decide whether to fill, lock, or take one safe step. What inspired this I am an avid sudoku solver and have had countless moments where I make good progress on the puzzle itself but then I've gotten stuck on some step. Now, there are online resources and guides and communties that can help out here, but I thought WebMCP was an interesting solution to this problem. A complete solution is a string of 81 digits. If the agent dumps it in chat, the page was pointless. If it clicks around the DOM, it will mis-click. The product I wanted is the thing in between: collaborative deduction. What I learned WebMCP is not MCP in the browser. MCP can live on a server with no page open. WebMCP tools exist only while a visible, origin-isolated document is connected. ChatGPT’s in-app browser also implements a subset: Imperative document.modelContext.registerTool works. Declarative HTML form tools do not show up as site tools. Tools inside iframes are invisible, even same-origin. So registration has to happen on the top-level page, after the board mounts, with feature detection: if (typeof document.modelContext?.registerTool === "function") { await document.modelContext.registerTool({ /* ... */ }); } I also learned that Codex can solve Sudoku in its head. If the only write tool is set_cell , it will skip the tutor and emit 81 answers. Tool descriptions and every read_board snapshot have to say: do not dump the grid; change it only through tools; trust the snapshot, not memory. On the puzzle side, computed candidates are not enough for pairs. A naked pair does not fill a cell; it removes digits elsewhere. That elimination has to be stored, or the next hint never sees it. Bundled puzzles have to be uniquely solvable. One “evening” grid I wrote by hand had two solutions. The brute-force solver is a backtracking search over the cell with the fewest candidates; we keep going until we have 0, 1, or >1 completions, and we only ship grids with exactly one. title: InquisitiveD
pitch: Talk or type — Inquisitive's agent plans over 9 WebMCP tools to sketch architecture diagrams live on Excalidraw, while any WebMCP agent can inspect, edit, and extend the same canvas.
about_excerpt: Talk or type — Inquisitive's agent plans over 9 WebMCP tools to sketch architecture diagrams live on Excalidraw, while any WebMCP agent can inspect, edit, and extend the same canvas. Like Comment Story Updates darkmode session to pdf light mode inquisitiveD arch 2 inquisitiveD arch 1 Inspiration Describing complex architecture in text is simple, but visually mapping several projects over a period of time, it remains a major bottleneck. While typical AI agents struggle to parse complex web UIs, WebMCP changes the paradigm by enabling web apps to expose explicit, structured tools directly to models. I built Inquisitive to use for my daily project review, design, sharing, and even technical discussion What it does Inquisitive is a technical diagramming app. Through text or voice commands like "diagram an event-driven payment flow," an orchestrator plans across 9 WebMCP tools registered on navigator.modelContext to construct diagrams live on an Excalidraw canvas. The agent inspects canvas topology, modifies specific nodes, appends shapes, captures visual snapshots, and offloads structural generation to a subagent. Meanwhile, users can sketch, speak via Gemini Live audio, lock views, and export multi-format session reports. Any external WebMCP client gains identical programmatic control over the canvas. How we built it The stack runs on React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and @excalidraw/excalidraw. Nine strictly-typed WebMCP tools bridge to the scene via an ActiveCanvasBridge. A Gemini function-calling orchestrator (gemini-2.5-flash-lite, $\le 5$ tool turns) delegates vector generation to a subagent bound by a rigorous JSON schema, pairing a lightweight catalog (73+ stencils in ~550 tokens) with client-side vector hydration. Ollama (gemma4:31b-cloud) mirrors the identical tool loop over a Cloudflare Pages /api/proxy. Voice interaction taps Gemini Live audio with a Web Speech API fallback, complemented by an AES-GCM-256 WebCrypto vault, IndexedDB history with Supabase RLS sync, and resilient JSON repair. title: IntentBridge
pitch: When your AI agent hits a tradeoff, don't let it guess. A WebMCP-native collaboration workspace where humans and autonomous AI agents negotiate constraints and tradeoffs
about_excerpt: When your AI agent hits a tradeoff, don't let it guess. A WebMCP-native collaboration workspace where humans and autonomous AI agents negotiate constraints and tradeoffs Like Comment Story Updates THE OPENING PAGE THE NEGOTIATION OF THE DECISION INTENTBRIDGE IN THE HOOD THUMBNAIL Inspiration As autonomous AI agents become more capable of executing complex real-world workflows, they inevitably hit ambiguity, budget ceilings, and conflicting user constraints. Today, when an AI agent encounters a conflict (for example, wanting a direct nonstop flight while adhering to a strict $1,000 budget), it usually makes one of two mistakes: It blindly guesses** and silently compromises user preferences. It constantly interrupts** the user with messy, unstructured chat messages. We built IntentBridge to solve this. IntentBridge is a Mission Control environment for Human + AI Collaboration When your AI agent hits a tradeoff, it doesn't guess it uses native WebMCP protocols to negotiate structured compromises with humans. What it does IntentBridge replaces unstructured chatbot dialogue with a 3-panel collaborative command center: Mission Control (Left Panel): Defines the active mission objective, live constraints (budget caps, timing, preferences), ranked priorities, and autonomous permission boundaries with live inline editing. Collaboration Timeline (Center Panel): A real-time structured event stream visually distinguishing human decisions, agent actions, conflict alerts, proposal packages, and cryptographic approval stamps. Agent Decision Center (Right Panel): A dynamic negotiation deck that renders structured Tradeoff Cards (showing quantifiable benefits, drawbacks, and cost impacts), multi-option proposal reviews, and safety-gated authorization requests. The Core Tokyo Demo Scenario Mission:** Plan a 5-day Tokyo cultural trip on a strict $1,000 budget with direct flight preference. Conflict Detected: Direct flights + central hotels cost $1,150 (exceeds budget by $150). Structured Tradeoff: The agent invokes request_tradeoff with quantified alternatives: Option A:* Increase budget by $150 to keep direct flights. Option B (Recommended): Allow 1 short layover to stay under budget ($980 total). Option C:* Shift lodging to Outer Tokyo. Resolution & Completion: The human selects Option B, the agent generates 3 curated itinerary packages, requests formal booking authorization, and records the outcome with celebration metrics. How we built it Frontend & Framework: Next.js 14 (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS with a futuristic, Linear/Vercel-inspired dark theme. WebMCP Architecture: Implemented 8 structured WebMCP tools with strict Zod validation schemas ( get_mission , get_constraints , report_progress , request_tradeoff , submit_proposal , request_approval , record_outcome , check_permission ). WebMCP Inspector: An interactive in-app inspector allowing judges and developers to inspect live JSON contracts and test tool invocations in real time. State Management: Event-driven architecture powered by Zustand. Testing & Quality: Validated with 13 unit and integration tests using Vitest and React Testing Library. Deployment: Production build deployed on Vercel and source code hosted on GitHub. Challenges we ran into Designing Structured Negotiation vs Generic Chat: Creating an interface that feels like genuine mission control rather than just another chatbot required designing discrete event models for conflicts, quantified impacts, and safety boundaries. Synchronous Human-in-the-Loop WebMCP Protocols: Ensuring the AI agent pauses cleanly upon invoking request_tradeoff , waits for human resolution, and seamlessly resumes with updated constraints. Deterministic SSR Hydration: Resolving dynamic timestamp evaluation between server rendering and browser mounting by implementing client-side dynamic boundaries. Accomplishments that we're proud of 100% Native WebMCP Integration: WebMCP is not just an afterthought the entire negotiation protocol runs on structured tool contracts accessible to browser agents. Full Human Agency with High Autonomy: The agent remains fully autonomous for research and synthesis, but never exceeds safety boundaries or makes arbitrary compromises. 13 Passing Tests & Zero-Warning Build: Rigorous software engineering with passing unit, integration, and E2E simulation tests. What we learned Structured negotiation protocols drastically reduce user fatigue compared to freeform text chats. Exposing clear priority hierarchies and permission boundaries enables autonomous agents to operate safely and effectively in high-stakes domains. What's next for IntentBridge Integrating multi-agent negotiation swarms where specialized sub-agents negotiate tradeoffs before presenting unified compromise options to the human. Adding browser extension sidecar support to connect local LLMs directly to any WebMCP-enabled web application. Expanding preset libraries to include hiring pipelines, venture capital deal screening, and software architecture migrations. title: LocusLocal
pitch: Human and agent triage the same genome in the same tab, through WebMCP tools the page itself registers, over a file that can never be uploaded.
about_excerpt: Human and agent triage the same genome in the same tab, through WebMCP tools the page itself registers, over a file that can never be uploaded. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing Page Guide Mode Variant Window Advanced Mode Inspiration I study anthropology, which in practice means I spend a lot of time around genomic data that isn't mine. Population panels, ancient DNA, samples from communities who agreed to one specific study and nothing beyond it. Consent in this field is narrow and it's supposed to stay narrow. That makes most genomics tooling unusable for me. Every variant browser I found opens the same way, upload your raw file to our server. I can not click that with a participant's genotypes, and I wouldn't click it with my own either. WebMCP removes the upload from the equation. The tools are declared by the page and run in the tab where the file already is, so the model can operate on data that never moves. That was enough to make the tool worth building. What it does LocusLocal is a variant-triage workbench. Drop in a VCF or a consumer raw export, it is parsed in a Web Worker, annotated against a bundled 98,262-variant ClinVar subset, and analysed entirely inside the tab. The demo genome is 250,000 markers from 1000 Genomes sample NA12878. Two audiences, one analysis engine. Guided mode answers the questions a person reading their own export actually has: how much of the file was read, how much of it ClinVar knows about, what they carry, how strong the evidence is, and what the analysis cannot tell them. Advanced mode gives the full table, filter stack, sorting and manual selection. One click either way, and an agent can make that click too. How I built it Vanilla TypeScript and Vite 8, no UI framework, deployed on a Cloudflare Worker that runs before static assets so the security headers can't be skipped. Tools are grouped into read_* , set_* , act_* , explain_* , and history . Chrome's secure-tools guidance applied throughout. readOnlyHint on all 13 read_* / explain_* tools and on none of the mutating ones; untrustedContentHint on analysis tools, whose output contains text from a user-supplied file; descriptions that state the visible UI effect. What's next for LocusLocal Pharmacogenomics (CPIC/PharmGKB). Drug-response markers are the genomics question with the most immediately actionable answer, and the annotation set is small enough to bundle under the same no-egress constraint. Polygenic scores, honestly presented. The interesting design problem is communicating a population-relative distribution to someone who wants a yes/no with the ancestry-portability caveat in the interface rather than a footnote. Trio and family-set support. Multi-sample VCFs, inheritance patterns, and a compare_samples tool, the point at which the shared-selection model gets genuinely harder and more interesting. A second annotation source (gnomAD frequencies) so "rare" stops meaning "not in ClinVar". Lift-over for GRCh38 so coordinates become comparable rather than merely disclaimed, retiring the coordinatesComparable: false path. title: MonstersDNA
pitch: Create a DNA-powered monster and team up with your AI agent to survive, fight, and evolve in a living 3D world. Coach its strategy, take control anytime, and grow a lineage that takes over the island.
about_excerpt: Create a DNA-powered monster and team up with your AI agent to survive, fight, and evolve in a living 3D world. Coach its strategy, take control anytime, and grow a lineage that takes over the island. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration MonstersDNA started with a simple idea from my eight-year-old son: “Can we make a game where I can create my own monster?” He didn’t just want to choose a character. He wanted to decide how many eyes it had, whether it had horns or a tail, what it ate, and how it moved. We wanted each monster to have DNA that described it, so we could change individual traits or combine two monsters to create something new. So we started vibe coding together with Codex. He came up with creatures and ideas, we tried them, and we had a lot of fun watching what happened. Sometimes the results were cute. Sometimes the legs were stuck together or the horns floated above the head. That became part of the process. The WebMCP idea came later. When we discovered the challenge, we thought: what if an AI agent could actually become a player in this world? Not just help us write the game, but design its own creature and use its intelligence to survive? What it does MonstersDNA is a browser-based 3D ecosystem populated by creatures with configurable DNA. You can design a monster, explore the island, find food, fight, and reproduce. Babies inherit a mixture of their parents’ DNA with mutations. The world runs on a persistent server, so the ecosystem continues evolving when players leave. With WebMCP, your agent can join the same experience. It can create a monster, observe its surroundings, move, explore, eat, attack, flee, rest, and breed. You can watch its actions in the 3D world, give it strategic guidance, or take control yourself. A scorecard tracks survival time, food consumed, fights won, offspring, generations, and population share. Why WebMCP fits Controlling a real-time game through screenshots and simulated key presses is awkward. The agent needs to understand what is happening, but it shouldn’t have to reverse-engineer the interface every time it wants to eat a bush. WebMCP gives it structured observations and meaningful actions. The human sees the world; the agent gets the information it needs to reason about that world. Both interact with the same creature and the same simulation. That creates a different kind of gameplay: you can be the player, the coach, or switch between the two. How we built it We used a TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js frontend, Three.js and React Three Fiber for rendering, and a NestJS backend. PostgreSQL and Prisma handle persistence, while Socket.IO connects players to the shared simulation. The DNA system drives the creature’s appearance and traits. The same DNA produces the same design, and breeding combines parental traits with mutations. Our WebMCP integration registers nine tools through document.modelContext . The action tools use the game’s existing movement and animation systems, while the server remains responsible for health, energy, combat, and reproduction. The agent plays within the game’s rules rather than bypassing them. Challenges we faced The hardest visual challenge was making many different DNA combinations look like coherent creatures. Our first monsters were assembled from simple shapes. Moving to smooth, animated meshes exposed plenty of problems: disappearing tails, disconnected horns, strange wrinkles, and legs that merged together. We also had to balance a lively world with browser performance, especially on mobile. For the agent integration, the challenge was choosing the right level of control. Actions needed to be useful for reasoning, but still happen visibly and leave room for the human to intervene. What we learned Building with my son made the project wonderfully unpredictable. He cared about things I might not have prioritized, and seeing him react to each version was immediate feedback. We learned that generating code is only part of building a game. Testing, watching, adjusting, and trying again mattered just as much. WebMCP also changed how we thought about agents. They don’t have to sit in a separate chat window or operate invisibly in the background. They can share an interactive world with us—and become something we can play alongside. title: Seatline Kolkata
pitch: Book by experience, not just availability.
about_excerpt: Book by experience, not just availability. Like Comment Story Updates Modeled sightline metrices Non binding modelled summary Nandan seated 3D view Seatline Overview All five WebMCP tools executed successfully Seatline Kolkata Inspiration Picking a seat in a cinema is actually a decision that has a spatial element disguised as a grid. A standard seat map will let you know if a seat is available, but it won't tell you how the screen will look from that seat. How far away is it? How far to the side will the view be? Will the row in front obstruct the view? For many visitors, particularly those who are concerned about comfort or accessibility, it is only after they get to the theatre that they find out the answers to these questions. The idea on which Seatline Kolkata was based was that picking a seat should be more like previewing a venue than merely choosing a square on a diagram. The setting for this idea was Kolkata's unique cinema culture, which includes heritage theatres, modern multiplexes, luxury auditoriums and various different room shapes. What it does Seatline Kolkata is an experience which puts the guest first and which is non-binding. People are able to look at six venue profiles in Kolkata, select a preview date and time, check the availability of seats, and from any available seat enter a measured 3D view. For each seat sightline figures are provided: Screen distance Horizontal offset Vertical viewing angle Screen angular width Forward-row clearance Overall rating: Exceptional, Great, Good, or Compromised The experience becomes native to the agent via WebMCP. A visitor can then ask: Get me a clear great sightline at Nandan tomorrow evening. The agent has the capability of searching the venue directory, examining the modelled seats, choosing a suitable seat, moving the Three.js camera to that seat's modelled eye point and then opening the seat summary. The visitor will still be in control and can continue to explore manually. Seatline doesn't reserve seats, handle payments, scrape ticketing websites, or take live inventory; the information about availability, prices, showtimes, and room dimensions is merely preliminary data. How I built it Seatline Kolkata makes use of Next.js, React, TypeScript and Three.js and has its deployment on Cloudflare Workers, the trailer media being stored in Cloudflare R2. WebMCP is implemented with five merchant-authored tools: ask_site search_venues inspect_seats select_preview review_summary The tools employ strict schemas and stable identities and make use of the same pure venue, seat-generation, availability and sightline functions as those used by the visible interface, which ensures that the agent's results match those on the visitor's screen. The camera and the metrics are based on the same geometry model; the eye point is determined by the selected seat and this same point is then used when calculating distance, angles, screen width and clearance. This ensures that the experience remains measurable rather than merely decorative. Challenges I ran into The main difficulty was ensuring that there was a single source of truth among the three systems: the semantic seat map, the Three.js scene and the WebMCP tool execution. When an agent made a selection, it had to update the controls, the seat state, the camera mode and the summary dialogue without setting up a second data model. I also needed a form of seat availability that was deterministic and varied from venue to venue, from date to date and from showtime to showtime while ensuring that each venue's default seat remained available. The camera position had to appear physically reasonable without being artificially raised in order to get a better view. In the end, it was necessary for the project to keep it as a static page that loaded quickly, at the same time as storing the large original trailer files in R2 rather than converting them. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that Seatline Kolkata turns a familiar seat map into a tool which enables spatial decision-making. Rather than just describing the page, the agent carries out the same preview logic that a person would use and then passes the result back to the visual interface. I am likewise proud of the clarity of the product boundary since Seatline is useful before a booking is made without pretending to be a ticketing system or stating that it cannot verify the inventory. What I learned I discovered that good WebMCP tools should convey user intent rather than revealing their internal implementation details; for example, "Find a great seat" is more useful than requesting the agent to directly manipulate the rows and columns. I found that collaboration between humans and agents is most effective when the agent carries out the structured discovery and the person is in charge of visual judgment; the agent can reduce the number of options while the person decides if the view is acceptable. What's next for Seatline Kolkata I would also like to collaborate with the cinemas that are taking part to substitute the representative geometry with the approved auditorium dimensions, include more detailed accessibility annotations, and provide support for both Bengali and English. By means of its authorised partners, Seatline would eventually be able to connect to reliable availability feeds while still maintaining its transparent preview-first experience, and features such as optional secure sign-in, saved comparisons, and the ability to view seats side by side would also increase the product's usefulness for returning visitors.
