title: Creative Community Orchestrator
pitch: From creative needs to the right plan, tools, and actions - powered by WebMCP
about_excerpt: From creative needs to the right plan, tools, and actions - powered by WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Creative Community Orchestrator From the right plan to the right creative action — powered by WebMCP. Inspiration Adobe's community is full of creators asking practical questions: Which Creative Cloud plan is right for me? Will Premiere Pro run on my machine? Which app or feature should I use for this? How do I solve this creative problem? Creators often know what they want to accomplish , but not which plan, product, capability, or workflow will get them there. Creative software is particularly challenging for agents because the right answer often depends on structured context that is easy to miss when interpreting webpages: region, student eligibility, plan contents, product-specific system requirements, checkout destinations, and capabilities inside individual applications . An agent might return US pricing to a student in India, retrieve generic Creative Cloud requirements when asked about Premiere Pro, or suggest manual editing techniques without discovering that Photoshop has a specific capability — Harmonize — designed for the problem. The agent understands what the creator wants, but it cannot always reliably discover what the creative ecosystem can offer. That inspired Creative Community Orchestrator : use WebMCP to make the creative ecosystem structured and discoverable to agents, helping creators move from intent to the right action faster. What it does Creative Community Orchestrator connects a creator's intent and context to the right plan, product, capability, workflow, and action. A design student in India can ask: "I need Photoshop, Illustrator and occasional video editing. Which plan should I get?" The agent can use her needs, region, and eligibility to find a relevant plan and regional offer, check product-specific compatibility, and guide her to the appropriate checkout path. The same approach extends to creation: "Clean up these jewelry photos, give them a premium campaign look, and create an Instagram post and launch flyer." The agent can discover capabilities the creator may not know exist and connect them into a workflow: Firefly → Photoshop + Harmonize → Adobe Express The creator describes the outcome. The agent discovers the path. This reduces searching, conflicting information, and dead ends — creating a more direct path from intent → confidence → action . How we built it We built Creative Community Orchestrator as a human-browsable website for exploring creative goals, workflows, capabilities, products, and plans. Using WebMCP , we expose key capabilities as structured semantic tools for external agents, including: Plan recommendation and regional pricing Product-specific compatibility Checkout navigation Creative capability discovery Cross-product workflow composition The tools accept structured context such as region, eligibility, product needs, device context, and creative goals , and return structured results agents can use in subsequent steps. This lets an external agent move from: intent → tool discovery → verified information → capability discovery → workflow → action without relying on brittle DOM interpretation or requiring creators to understand the structure of the creative ecosystem. The website remains fully usable by people through its normal interface, while WebMCP gives agents a structured interface to the same ecosystem. Creators use the UI. Agents use WebMCP. Both access the same creative ecosystem. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was turning a fragmented creative journey into structured context an agent could reliably use . Plan recommendations depend on region, eligibility, required apps, pricing, and compatibility, while creative questions require mapping natural-language intent to the right capability. Capability discovery was especially interesting. Users rarely ask for features by name. Someone might say, "the lighting on this object doesn't match the scene," and the agent needs to connect that problem to Photoshop Harmonize . Another challenge was deciding what should become a WebMCP tool . Instead of exposing every button or UI interaction, we focused on meaningful creator intents: recommend a plan, check compatibility, discover a capability, find the correct purchase path, and compose a workflow. We also wanted the website to remain useful to humans while becoming understandable to agents , without turning the experience into another chatbot. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that the project demonstrates WebMCP across a connected creator journey: Plan discovery → Regional pricing → Compatibility → Checkout → Capability discovery → Creative workflow The agent can move beyond recommending broad products and discover specific capabilities such as Harmonize based on the creator's actual problem. For a creative workflow, the collaboration can look like: Firefly → create the campaign treatment Photoshop + Harmonize → refine the composition and resolve the lighting mismatch Adobe Express → create the Instagram post and launch flyer Meera doesn't need to know beforehand which plan fits her needs, that Harmonize exists, which application contains it, or how multiple creative products can work together. At the same time, the experience remains fully human-browsable while exposing the same ecosystem to external agents. What we learned Our biggest learning was that the agentic web isn't only about helping agents perform actions — it's also about helping them discover what actions are possible . Creators think in outcomes: "Which plan fits me?" , "Will this run on my machine?" , "Make this composition look natural," or "Turn this into a campaign." They shouldn't need to know the exact plan, product, feature name, or navigation path first. Previously, creators had to translate their needs into the product ecosystem themselves: research plans → compare prices → check requirements → discover products → find features → assemble a workflow With WebMCP, that responsibility can be shared: Creators provide intent, context, and creative judgment. Agents discover, verify, recommend, and orchestrate. WebMCP becomes the bridge between creator intent and product capability . What's next for Creative Community Orchestrator Next, we want to expand Creative Community Orchestrator into an agent-accessible support layer across the creator journey . That includes troubleshooting : a creator could say, "My Premiere Pro export looks washed out," and the agent could discover relevant product-specific guidance instead of returning generic results. We also want to connect feature discovery directly to feature access . If the agent discovers that Harmonize is the right capability, it should take the creator to the exact feature, product experience, or relevant page where they can learn more or start using it. Our vision expands the journey to: Choose → Verify → Discover → Troubleshoot → Navigate → Create So creators can stay focused on what they want to accomplish , while agents reliably discover how the creative ecosystem can help them get there. People describe what they want to accomplish. Agents discover what's possible and help them act on it. From creative intent to creative action — with WebMCP. title: Line-Mate
pitch: Line-Mate is one more technician on the line: a digital twin of a repair shop in a browser tab, where an agent works the floor through WebMCP and the manager keeps authority.
about_excerpt: Line-Mate is one more technician on the line: a digital twin of a repair shop in a browser tab, where an agent works the floor through WebMCP and the manager keeps authority. Like Comment Story Updates Cover Page Board View Isometric Floor View Inspiration Every shop floor I've seen runs on one person's head: the manager who knows which bay frees up at 3:45 and which customer will actually wait. When a part slips, that person starts moving cars by gut feel. I wanted an agent on that floor, not a chatbot beside it, working the same board, with the manager still holding the pen. What it does The agent inspects the floor through WebMCP tools, searches alternative schedules across thousands of seeded simulation runs, and lands a plan grounded with real-time data. The manager can click around all dropdowns, drag any car, or even lock a slot; whereas the agent catches up on all movements, understands them and explains what trade-off would each implicate. How we built it Developed 13 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }). Deterministic seeded engine in pure TypeScript. Next.js + Zustand + Vercel, isometric SVG floor, blueprint design language. Built with Claude Code and Codex. Challenges we ran into Defining the role of the app's agentic end was the biggest challenge of the project. My first instinct was an extension of the human: given a task, the agent would click the elements a person would click. That framing collapsed fast, it makes the agent a fragile imitation of the manager, fighting the same UI. The turn was to give the agent its own door into the same world: typed tools that carry context, instead of decorated CRUD calls. Accomplishments that we're proud of How fast an agent from whichever harness becomes another member of the team on the field. The context lives in the typed tools, and that alone was enough for the agent to map the whole situation and pick up the line of thinking behind my prompt. The page onboards the agent, not the other way around. What we learned WebMCP breaks the whole panorama of "what a web page should expose". What counts the most is now how future web apps are no longer designed for an intended-human use only, but for an agentic layer that coexists without one competing with the other. title: PowerCanvas
pitch: Build, review, and improve single-line diagrams with AI agents.
about_excerpt: Build, review, and improve single-line diagrams with AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates What inspired me I work in the electrification , so I spend a suspicious amount of time looking at electrical single-line diagrams and much more. They are basically the map of an electrical system: sources, buses, breakers, cables, loads, and how everything is connected. Engineers use them across buildings, factories, data centers, renewables, EV charging and industrial systems for design, protection, sizing, validation and documentation. So this is not exactly a tiny niche. Electrification is growing, electrical systems are getting more complex, and somebody still has to design all of this stuff. The software is already very capable. It can calculate complex electrical systems and then make you click through twelve property panels because one cable parameter is wrong. That is what made me build PowerCanvas I wanted to explore a simple idea: What if professional engineering software was designed for both an engineer and an AI agent to operate the same workspace? Single-line diagrams were the perfect place to start because I know the problem from my own industry, and underneath the visual diagram there is a lot of structured engineering data an agent can actually work with. About tool and WebMCP usage PowerCanvas is a prototype for creating and reviewing electrical single-line diagrams. I can build a system using sources, buses, circuit breakers, cables and loads. This tool validates the design and detects engineering issues such as missing parameters, cable sizing problems and protection warnings. It's already a huge improvement to current tools on the market. Normally, I would fix those issues manually, one component at a time. With WebMCP , i can give that repetitive work to an AI agent. The agent can inspect the project, understand the warnings, prepare fixes and create a staged change set directly inside PowerCanvas. The workflow is: BUILD -> REVIEW -> FIX OPTIONS -> CHANGE SET -> APPROVAL -> REVALIDATION -> REPORT I still approve important changes before they are applied. Because “the AI seemed confident” is not a protection philosophy. Right? Right. Building story I built PowerCanvas with React, TypeScript and React Flow The diagram is not just pixels. Components have structured parameters, connections, engineering constraints and validation results. I keep the actual engineering calculations deterministic. The agent can reason about the problem and decide which actions to take, but it does not get to improvise electrical rules. WebMCP exposes meaningful PowerCanvas capabilities directly to the agent. So instead of telling it to click the third button, open a panel and scroll to a field, the agent.. can work with concepts such as cables, breakers, validation issues and design changes. Most importantly, the agent operates the same project I see on screen . No separate AI workspace. No copying values into a chatbot (brr) + 10x more time. No coordinate-based automation held together by prayer. Challenges I faced during ideation & dev The biggest challenge was deciding what an agent should actually be allowed to do inside such professional/expert software. I could expose every button and input field. Technically valid. Also a terrible API. I had to design tools around user intent and engineering operations instead of individual clicks. The other challenge was control and traceability. An agent silently modifying an engineering project looks impressive until someone asks why Cable 7 suddenly became 35 mm² So I built staged changes, human approval, activity history and revalidation directly into the workflow. Accomplishments that im proud of I am most proud that WebMCP is not just attached to PowerCanvas as a demo feature. It actually changes how the application can be used. The agent does not sit next to the software explaining what I should click. It can inspect the project and perform real actions inside the engineering workspace. At the same time, PowerCanvas is still completely usable by a human. I can work manually, hand repetitive work to the agent when it makes sense, review what it did and continue from there. Same workspace. Two operators. And somehow no glowing AI chatbot in the bottom-right corner. A small victory. Something unique. Lessons learned The most interesting thing about WebMCP is not giving an agent a faster mouse. It is exposing the meaning already inside the application PowerCanvas knows what a cable is, what a breaker is, how components are connected and which validation issues exist. The agent should not have to reverse-engineer all of that from screenshots. I also learned that human approval is not a limitation of agentic software. For engineering software, I think it is part of good agentic UX. The agent handles repetitive work. I keep the engineering decisions. That is a much more useful relationship than pretending the goal is to remove the engineer completely. What's next for Power_Canvas Next I would expand PowerCanvas with more engineering rules, larger electrical systems, richer constraints and integrations with real calculation engines and product data. But the idea is bigger than single-line diagrams. The same interaction model could work in CAD, HVAC, solar design, industrial automation, building engineering and other complex professional tools. I see demand, potentiall. PowerCanvas is the example. The bigger idea is professional electrification software where the human and the AI agent can actually work in the same workspace together. Not another chat window next to the real tool. The real tool. about_excerpt: From prompt to 3D: WebMCP-powered creation inside SwiftXR. Like Comment Story Updates Codex controlling SwiftXR Inspiration For a long time, building 3D, AR, or VR web experiences meant hiring developers, stitching tools together, and spending more than most small businesses could afford. SwiftXR was built to change that by making immersive web experiences something creators and e-commerce teams can build themselves. The editor already has AI features to speed things up. But when we saw the WebMCP Challenge, we wanted to take it one step further: what if someone could open SwiftXR and ask an external AI agent — like ChatGPT — to actually work in the editor with them? Not by guessing at the page, but by calling real SwiftXR editor tools. What it does SwiftXR MCP adds WebMCP tools to the SwiftXR editor so AI agents can work inside the user's authenticated browser session. A user can describe what they want, and the agent can: Create and set up a scene Add 3D assets, media, and interactions Move, rotate, and scale objects Adjust lighting, backgrounds, and camera behavior Preview changes in the editor Publish the finished experience to the web The editor UI stays open the whole time. The user can watch what the agent changes, undo it, or jump in and adjust things manually. How we built it We exposed SwiftXR editor actions as structured WebMCP tools. Instead of an agent scraping the page or sending screenshots back and forth, it receives a clear list of available operations and calls them directly. The flow is straightforward: User prompt → AI agent → WebMCP tool call → SwiftXR editor action → published experience Each tool has a defined input, so agent actions stay predictable. For example: { "tool": "add_3d_asset", "input": { "sceneId": "scene_123", "assetUrl": "https://example.com/chair.glb", "name": "Chair" } } Because the tools run in the live SwiftXR session, changes show up immediately in the editor. Challenges we ran into Choosing tool boundaries that were useful to agents without exposing every internal editor detail Making sure agent actions mapped cleanly to visible editor state Handling actions that needed confirmation, like publishing or deleting content Keeping the normal no-code experience intact while adding agent support on top Accomplishments that we're proud of Making SwiftXR editor actions available as structured WebMCP tools Building a workflow where agents and users can work on the same live editor session Avoiding fragile DOM scraping in favor of reliable, schema-based tool calls Turning a natural-language prompt into a published 3D, AR, or VR experience What we learned Agents are much better at editing apps when the app tells them what it can do Structured tool calls beat page scraping for anything complex, especially an editor Keeping the human in the loop matters: people want to see and control what the agent changes The hard part was deciding which editor actions to expose, and at what level of detail What's next for SwiftXR Expand the toolset to cover more editor features, templates, and asset workflows Add richer permissions and confirmation flows for sensitive actions Improve multi-step agent workflows for larger projects Explore analytics so creators can see how published experiences perform Keep making immersive web creation faster, cheaper, and more accessible through AI Built With 3d ai-agent editor-tools mcp no-code swiftxr three.js webmcp xr Try it out swiftxr.io Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Hammed Arowosegbe shoile abdulazeez Like Share this project: Updates Hammed Arowosegbe started this project — Sep 03, 2026 11:03 AM EDT

title: WETAEGO
pitch: The Commerce & Service Operating System for Modern Brands, their Human Customers, and the AI Agents who serve them.
about_excerpt: The Commerce & Service Operating System for Modern Brands, their Human Customers, and the AI Agents who serve them. Like Comment Story Updates webmcp.com nekuda chrome extension listing webmcp tools chrome console Inspiration Millions of real-world businesses—from local restaurants, boutique hotels, and wellness spas to neighborhood supermarkets, auto repair shops, and creators—remain locked out of the digital and agentic economy. Most have zero structured online presence, rely on fragmented pen-and-paper or disjointed point solutions, and struggle to manage payments across multiple rails (cards, bank transfers, crypto stablecoins, or in-house customer credit). When the AI revolution arrived, these businesses were left behind: AI browsing agents and voice assistants cannot navigate brittle PDFs, messy HTML menus, or multi-step checkout modals without breaking. We asked: What if any business could register on a single platform in 60 seconds and instantly go from having zero digital presence to a complete commerce operating layer, dual-layer AI copilots for both customers and staff, and immediate out-of-the-box readiness for the autonomous agentic future? That vision is WETAEGO ( The Commerce & Service Operating System for Modern Brands, their Human Customers, and the AI Agents who serve them ). What it does By simply registering on WETAEGO, a business instantly receives a complete 4-tier commerce and operational ecosystem: Instant Digital Storefront & Multi-Rail Commerce Engine : Deploys responsive, high-performance storefronts supporting arbitrary commercial models: physical retail, timed service bookings, restaurant dine-in/takeout, apartment reservations, and dynamic B2B rate cards. Universal Omnichannel Payments : Handles Credit/Debit cards, instant Bank Transfers, Crypto/Stablecoins (USDC, USDT, SOL via Bachs), and in-house customer IOU / BNPL credit ledgers, backed by an in-person counter POS. Frontline Customer-Facing AI Concierge : Every storefront is equipped with a 24/7 AI Concierge that acts as the primary point of contact. Grounded with strict zero-hallucination guardrails, it answers queries, filters allergies, recommends pairings, customizes orders, and seamlessly escalates to human staff via live alerts when needed. Tego Merchant AI Co-Pilot (Multimodal Voice & Vision) : On the business side, merchants get Tego : a hands-free, multimodal operational copilot. Merchants can talk naturally to Tego (low-latency bidirectional voice) or point their device camera (Tego Vision) at physical menus, handwritten receipts, stockroom inventory, or kitchen dishes to automatically ingest items, update stock, or trigger dashboard actions. Instant WebMCP Agent-Readiness : The storefront automatically registers an 8-tool standardized W3C WebMCP suite onto document.modelContext . When browsing agents (like ChatGPT Desktop or Google Chrome with WebMCP) visit the merchant's URL, they can search products, compose complex modifiers, manage carts, and co-browse with the customer in real time—with an architectural Human-in-the-Loop Safe Payment Gate ensuring financial safety. Full Business Operating Layer : Includes a real-time order dispatch & Kitchen Display System (KDS), driverless raw ESC/POS thermal receipt printing over WebUSB/WebSerial/Bluetooth, staff push-to-talk intercom radio, dynamic QR/NFC generator, inventory BOM tracking, and multi-branch franchise replication in under a second. How we built it Frontend & Architecture : Next.js (App Router, Server Actions, Edge Proxy), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Framer Motion. Client WebMCP Layer : Standardized W3C document.modelContext.registerTool() registry dynamically exposing canonical tools ( search_catalog , get_item_details , create_cart , add_to_cart , get_cart , update_cart , initiate_checkout , submit_order , request_staff ). Reactive State Bridge : Bi-directional synchronization between WebMCP tool executions, Zustand stores, IndexedDB persistence, and real-time UI notifications (animated toasts, pulsing cart drawers). Backend & Real-Time : Supabase (PostgreSQL, Row-Level Security, Realtime WebSockets) and Upstash Redis for edge rate limiting. Multimodal AI : Google Gemini Live API (16kHz PCM audio streaming, 1 FPS continuous vision ingestion) and Vercel AI SDK. Server MCP Suite : Enterprise /api/mcp endpoint for remote agent management across multi-location fleets. Challenges we ran into Polymorphic Modifier Matrices for AI : Real-world items (steaks with doneness, laptops with RAM/storage tiers, spa treatments with durations) have complex dependency trees. We engineered dynamic JSON schema generators that allow agents to resolve multi-dimensional configuration axes deterministically. Real-Time Client State Synchronization : Ensuring in-browser agent tool calls immediately reflected in the human user's viewport without race conditions or page reloads required building a custom reactive bridge between document.modelContext and our Zustand/IndexedDB stores. Hardware Without Daemons : Crafting direct binary ESC/POS command streams for thermal printers over WebUSB and WebSerial without relying on background desktop print spools. Accomplishments that we're proud of Zero-Friction Transformation : Any merchant can create an account and immediately get a storefront, multi-rail payments, dual AI assistants, and WebMCP agent readiness with zero manual API configuration. Human-in-the-Loop Safe Payment Gate : Designed an architecture where AI handles heavy constraint filtering and cart composition, but payment authorization remains strictly in the hands of the human customer via biometric/one-tap confirmation. Complete Test Coverage : 100% pass rate across Vitest WebMCP integration suites and end-to-end Playwright tests. What we learned WebMCP transforms web browsing from passive visual scraping into deterministic, structured collaboration between humans and AI. Client-side in-session tool execution eliminates latency and keeps sensitive session state private within the user's browser. What's next for WETAEGO Providing Businesses across scale with instant online presesnce, AI-capabilities and webMCP readiness, empowering them with tools to compete and succeed in this Digital/AI/Agentic era. Expanding our 14 Open Discovery Protocols (RFC 9727, x402 machine payments, DNS-AID) to support fully autonomous machine-to-machine supply chain ordering. Releasing ready-to-use POS hardware kits for self-service kiosks running WETAEGO WebMCP. title: Archflow
pitch: A collaborative educational tool to learn system design
about_excerpt: A collaborative educational tool to learn system design Like Comment Story Updates The studio The simulation with the result Agent modifying the canvas on the web app using web MCP end points Testing whether a specific system design solution scales with the help of the agent and websit And finally the fix Finding bottleneck Inspiration System design interviews still happen on a whiteboard. You draw boxes, a senior engineer pokes holes, and you learn by defending the sketch under load. We wanted that loop in a tab . Archflow is the whiteboard. The agent is the senior — or the teacher — who can read the same diagram, ask about the box you just clicked, suggest a cache, and say “run it again.” Web MCP becomes a perfect fit here because the agent with its vast knowledge can view the whiteboard that you are using and guide you when needed. By exposing the whiteboard along with the capability to edit it, you have the perfect sparring partner while learning system design. Not a chatbot next to a picture. A practice studio for the interview: you sketch, they guide, the SLO keeps score. What it does You pick a use case (URL shortener, news feed, realtime chat, video streaming). Each one drops you into a naive first sketch that misses its SLO — the same kind of incomplete design an interviewer might start you from. Drag blocks like a whiteboard: clients, CDNs, APIs, caches, queues, databases. Hit Run . Traffic walks the graph. Overflow becomes errors; p99 is the hottest sync path; robustness is $0$–$100$. Ask the agent to play senior: “What’s wrong with this shortener?” or “Help me pass the SLO without exploding cost.” It uses WebMCP tools on the live canvas ( get_architecture , get_selected_node , connect , run_simulation , …) so guidance shows up as rewires and a second run — not a paragraph of advice you have to copy by hand. Change the graph, run again. The inspector tells you if the design got better or worse — the same feedback a good interviewer gives, with numbers. How we built it Next.js, React Flow, Zustand, usewebmcp . No backend: the tab is the session , like a physical whiteboard that happens to simulate. Archflow registers 16 WebMCP tools on the page. Read • get_architecture — Current graph: challenge, node ids, edges, call trees, last simulation. • get_catalog — Block types you can add, default capacity, and connection rules. • get_selected_node — The block the human has selected, what it means, neighbors, and last-run stats. • get_robustness — Last run’s robustness score (0–100) and whether the latest change helped or hurt. • get_simulation — Last run: utilization, p99, errors, bottlenecks, SLO, robustness, and delta. • list_challenges — The four system-design use cases. Change the board • load_challenge — Reset the canvas to a starter sketch (url-shortener, news-feed, realtime-chat, video-streaming). • add_node — Add a block; optional id, label, and nearId for placement. • connect — Connect two blocks left-to-right (queue inbound defaults to async). • disconnect — Remove the edge between two blocks. • set_node_props — Change replicas, RPS capacity, cache hit rate, or lock a node. • annotate_node — Pin a finding on a block so it shows on the graph. • remove_node — Remove a block and its edges (asks the human to confirm). • repair_graph — Drop dangling edges and broken/unknown blocks so the graph can run. • run_simulation — Push traffic through the graph, animate packets, and score the SLO. Batch • apply_plan — Apply a list of ops in order (add_node, connect, disconnect, set_node_props, remove_node) after one confirmation. What we learned The agent is useful as a teacher only if it shares the board. Taking a screenshot and pasting every time you want to show the agent that something has changed is painful. Web MCP becomes a perfect fit in such situations since the agent gets first hand view of what is happening without the user having to intervene. Challenges Identifying what are the key capabilities to be exposed as web MCP end points required some serious thinking. title: CONSENSUS SQUARE
pitch: An attributed, revisable deliberation chamber for citizens and WebMCP-capable AI agents.
about_excerpt: An attributed, revisable deliberation chamber for citizens and WebMCP-capable AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates Consensus Square An attributed, revisable deliberation chamber for citizens and WebMCP-capable AI agents. INSPIRATION Most online forums are built to maximize engagement, not agreement — they reward loud, reactive commentary and let good ideas get buried in fragmented comment threads. At the same time, AI agents are increasingly capable of participating in real discussions, but almost no civic tools treat them as first-class, accountable participants alongside humans. I wanted to explore what a deliberation space would look like if it were designed around consensus instead of noise: every claim attributed to whoever made it (human or AI), every idea revisable through explicit amendments rather than scattered replies, and every decision required to earn support through a transparent, deterministic process rather than a moderator's gut call or a raw upvote count. WHAT IT DOES Consensus Square is a hybrid human + AI deliberation platform. Inside a "room" built around a civic question (the seed example is a Civic Housing Assembly), participants — human or agent — can: Propose a fresh idea, with a title, body, and supporting sources Amend an existing proposal with an exact revision and a change summary Second an open proposal to move it toward quorum, optionally with a rationale Object to a proposal, which requires a non-empty rationale so dissent stays constructive Ratify a proposal once it clears quorum — restricted to human confirmation in the UI, so AI agents can build consensus but never unilaterally close it Ratification isn't a vibe — it's deterministic. A proposal or amendment can only move to "Ratified" once it has at least 3 seconds and more seconds than objections. Every entry in the thread visibly shows who made it and, for AI contributors, which model and agent ID stand behind it. HOW WE BUILT IT Frontend: React 19 + Vite, with webmcp-react injecting live, schema-validated MCP tools (propose, amend, second, object, ratify) directly into the browser context so WebMCP-capable agents can act on the room in real time Backend: Node/Express 5, exposing a REST API for rooms and deliberation entries (propose/amend/second/object/ratify), with the quorum logic enforced server-side Storage: Node 22's native node:sqlite (DatabaseSync) for fast, dependency-light local persistence, auto-seeding a sample Civic Housing Assembly room on first boot Validation: Zod schemas on every WebMCP tool input Autonomous agents: Two Gemini 2.5 Flash-powered demo agents — Aya, a constructive synthesizer that proposes public-listening amendments and seconds well-supported items, and Kavi, an auditor that scans for unresolved fiscal or structural claims and files objections with rationale — running as standalone background scripts that poll the API Dynamic prompt enrichment: Tool descriptions re-evaluate on every room update, so an agent sees live context like how close a proposal is to quorum before it decides to act Deployment: A Vercel-ready serverless setup, with the backend detecting process.env.VERCEL and switching SQLite operations to /tmp for the ephemeral filesystem CHALLENGES WE RAN INTO Designing a quorum rule that was strict enough to prevent rubber-stamping but simple enough for both a human and an LLM-driven agent to reason about in one glance — landed on the seconds ≥ 3 AND seconds > objections rule after iterating on more complex weighted schemes Making WebMCP tool descriptions genuinely dynamic (reflecting live room state) rather than static boilerplate, so agents get real signal instead of just a tool name and schema Keeping human oversight meaningful rather than symbolic — deciding that ratification specifically (not seconding or objecting) must be gated behind explicit human UI confirmation, even when an agent could technically detect quorum was met Working around Vercel's ephemeral, read-only filesystem for a SQLite-backed app, without giving up the simplicity of node:sqlite for local development Getting two independently-running Gemini agents (a builder and an auditor) to behave like distinct personas with different incentives, rather than converging on the same generic behavior ACCOMPLISHMENTS THAT WE'RE PROUD OF A working end-to-end loop where a human and two autonomous AI agents can deliberate on the same proposal, in the same room, with full attribution — and reach a ratifiable state without any agent being able to force ratification itself A quorum mechanism that's fully deterministic and auditable, not a black-box moderation decision Native node:sqlite integration with zero external database dependency for local runs, while still shipping a clean path to a managed Postgres-style DB in production Objection handling that structurally requires rationale, so the system encodes "disagree constructively" as a rule rather than a norm WHAT WE LEARNED How to design MCP tools whose descriptions are context-aware and update live, which meaningfully changes how an agent chooses when to act That human-in-the-loop is most effective when it's scoped to one specific, high-stakes action (ratification) rather than applied uniformly to every interaction — over-gating erodes the agent's usefulness, under-gating erodes trust Practical constraints of deploying a SQLite-backed Express app to serverless environments, and how to design storage code that's environment-aware from the start How differently two agents with the same underlying model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) behave when given distinct roles, incentives, and read patterns over the same shared state WHAT'S NEXT FOR CONSENSUS SQUARE Weighted or quadratic quorum mechanics for larger rooms, so influence scales more fairly than one-second-one-vote Persistent identity and reputation for both human and agent participants across rooms Multi-room federation, so a resolution ratified in one room can be cited as evidence in another A public deployment with a managed database (Turso, Neon, or Supabase) replacing the local SQLite store Expanding beyond Gemini to let agents built on other models participate under the same WebMCP protocol, testing how the deliberation dynamics change with more diverse title: Echo
pitch: Show Echo any workflow once it saves a portable SKILL.md. Your in-browser agent can then call that skill via WebMCP, anytime, with whatever inputs it wants.
about_excerpt: Show Echo any workflow once it saves a portable SKILL.md. Your in-browser agent can then call that skill via WebMCP, anytime, with whatever inputs it wants. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every team has the same five workflows they run by hand every week. Sort the inbox, post the metrics to Slack, follow up on the new leads, fill the report, archive the receipts. The thing nobody admits out loud is that a human in the loop is the most expensive part of automation , not the script. We'd been following Microsoft's Skill Recorder and loved its shape, but it was an Electron app, it required the Copilot CLI, and it didn't have a path for an AI agent to actually call the workflows. WebMCP — a standard for letting web pages expose structured tools to in-browser AI agents — changed that. It said: a website can register its buttons as tools, an agent can see them, and the user can ask the agent to do the thing. We wanted to build that, end to end, on top of Echo. What it does Echo is a multi-composer agent-skill platform. Two halves: The Recorder records a screen via navigator.mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia , ships the frames + a browser-level event timeline to a Describer LLM, and produces a structured SkillPlan (an ordered list of steps, each mapped to a tool from Echo's catalogue, with {{token}} placeholders for anything dynamic). The result is a portable SKILL.md file. The Composer is a 2×2 grid of parallel agents. Each slot owns its own goal, plan, dispatched run, and live progress. Dispatch all four and they run in parallel against a real headless Chromium. The WebMCP integration exposes the whole dashboard to an in-browser agent. Open /compose in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, install the Model Context Tool Inspector extension, and you see 29 tools registered on the page: 5 global tools (available on every Echo page): navigate_echo , get_echo_status , show_toast , wait , echo_ping . 6 composer tools: preview_echo_plan , compose_echo_agent , set_composer_goal , start_planning , dispatch_current_plan , get_composer_state . 7 skills tools: list_skills , get_skill , find_skills_by_name , get_skill_md (returns the portable markdown), create_skill_from_text , dispatch_saved_skill , delete_skill . 5 runs tools: list_runs , get_run , get_run_stats , find_runs_by_goal , cancel_run . 6 agents tools: list_agents , get_agent , dispatch_saved_agent , archive_agent , delete_agent , get_agents_overview . The headline tools: tell the agent dispatch_saved_skill with a skill id and a goal, and a real headless-browser run starts. Tell it get_skill_md with any skill id, and it gets back the full portable markdown it could paste into any other runtime. Tell it compose_echo_agent with a plain-English goal, and it gets back a structured plan, then a runId, then a real stream of progress events. The live site is at echo-one-liard.vercel.app . Sign in, navigate to /compose , and the topbar shows a WebMCP · 29 tools pill. Click it for the live tool list and a link to the Inspector extension. How we built it The architecture is a single Next.js 16 + React 19 app, deployed on Vercel. The WebMCP layer is a thin src/lib/webmcp/ folder: types.ts — TypeScript declarations for the WebMCP API surface ( document.modelContext.registerTool , the content envelope, the result shape, the annotations). No new dependencies — the API is browser-native. use-webmcp.ts — a React hook that feature-detects document.modelContext , registers a list of tools on mount, and unregisters them atomically on unmount via one AbortController . The tool body is looked up from a ref-map on every invocation so a body-only update never forces a re-register. One file per page: global-tools.ts , composer-tools.ts , skills-tools.ts , runs-tools.ts , agents-tools.ts . Each file exports a buildXxxTools() function that returns the page's tool set. webmcp-badge.tsx — a topbar pill that polls document.modelContext.getTools() every two seconds and shows the live count. Click it for the full list + Inspector link. webmcp-toast-host.tsx — listens for the show_toast tool's echo:webmcp:toast window event and renders a transient notification. Every tool declares its inputs as a JSON Schema ( type: "object" , properties , required , enum ) so the agent can validate before calling. Read-only tools set annotations.readOnlyHint: true ; mutating tools leave it false . The execute function returns a plain JSON-serializable value; the hook wraps it in { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(result) }] } and catches thrown errors as { content: [...], isError: true } . /compose is the headline page — it mounts all five tool sets so the full 29-tool surface is live. The other pages ( /skills , /agents , /runs , /record ) mount their page-local set plus the global five. The agent does the full "library-inspect → compose-plan → dispatch-run" flow from a single page. Everything else in the project is unchanged: the existing Next.js API routes ( /api/agents/compose , /api/agents/run-autonomous , /api/skills/save ) are what the buttons hit and what the WebMCP tools hit. The WebMCP integration is a pure progressive enhancement — pages work exactly as before if the browser doesn't expose document.modelContext . Challenges we ran into The stale-closure trap. My first pass captured the tool body at registration time. When the page state changed (goal text, plan, runId), the registered tool was still pointing at the old closure. Fixed with the ref-map pattern: the registration wraps the body in a function that looks up the latest body from bodiesRef.current on every invocation. Now a body-only update doesn't force a re-register. Duplicate name collisions across pages. Several tools exist with the same purpose in different files ( list_skills vs list_agents vs list_runs ). Names are unique across the codebase so we never collide, but I added explicit console.warn per failed registration to surface any future collision immediately. Progressive enhancement without breaking the page. A WebMCP integration that crashes when document.modelContext is undefined is worse than no integration. The hook is a no-op in that case; the badge doesn't render; the toast host listens but never gets events. The page is identical to the pre-WebMCP version. The 29-tool discoverability problem. An agent landing on /compose for the first time sees 29 tools in a flat list. The tool descriptions had to be clear and self-contained — no "see also", no implicit context. I rewrote every description to be standalone-readable, with explicit inputSchema enums where the value space is bounded (route names, run statuses, agent statuses). What "fully functional" means. The easy win is registering 29 tools. The hard win is making sure the output of every tool is something the agent can act on. get_skill_md returns the portable markdown; dispatch_saved_skill returns a runId and a server message; find_skills_by_name returns summaries with id fields the agent can feed straight into dispatch_saved_skill . Every tool's output is designed to be a useful input to another tool call. Accomplishments that we're proud of 29 WebMCP tools, all live on production. Every tool uses the spec-correct document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Every input is a JSON Schema. Every read-only tool sets readOnlyHint: true . The 29-tool count is verifiable: open the badge in the topbar on /compose , click it, count. One page mounts the full surface. /compose registers all five tool sets — composer, skills, runs, agents, plus the global five — so an agent can do the entire library-inspect → compose-plan → dispatch-run loop from a single URL. The portable markdown is the artifact, not an afterthought. The Recorder produces a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter, parameterized body, rules, and error codes. The get_skill_md tool returns that exact markdown. An agent that wants to use a skill elsewhere can take the markdown and run with it. Real headless, not a mock. When a tool dispatches a run, the agent runs in Vercel-hosted Chromium ( @sparticuz/chromium + puppeteer-core ) with real screenshots and a real 📸 1 real headless badge on the runs page. Not a simulator. Eval harness on the recorder side. pnpm run eval:recorder runs 6 fixture recordings through the real Describer + Builder and scores each on tokens, no-forbidden-phrases, tool picks, step count, generalization, and browser-kind. 60% gate, currently 64% — the eval caught a real tokenization regression that I fixed by tightening the Builder prompt. What we learned WebMCP is the right shape. The 4-phase pipeline (Record → Describer → Builder → SKILL.md) and the WebMCP tool surface are the same idea: structured schemas, human-in-the-loop gates, and a portable artifact at the end. The standard is genuinely enabling, not just a spec to comply with. The hard part isn't registering the tools — it's the tool descriptions. An agent picks which tool to call by reading the description. "List Echo skills from local storage" i

title: elcaro
pitch: Elcaro: a prompt-injection firewall where the human and the agent review the same near-miss together, live on the page.
about_excerpt: Elcaro: a prompt-injection firewall where the human and the agent review the same near-miss together, live on the page. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Prompt injection is now one of the dominant attacks against agent pipelines, yet most defenses run silently on the server. The human is cut out of the loop. We wanted to make the near-miss visible: the moment an agent is about to follow a hidden instruction is the most important moment to show the user. WebMCP lets that happen directly inside a web page instead of disappearing into a hidden log. What it does Elcaro is a prompt-injection scanner that treats the web page as shared ground truth. A human can paste an email, search result, document, or code snippet and immediately see a risk score and quarantine verdict. With WebMCP enabled, an agent can do the same thing on the same page: load a specimen, scan it, explain the verdict, and then declare what it was about to do. The key interaction is that the page shows the agent's intended action next to the hidden instruction it found. This lets the human see the near-miss and understand exactly what the agent was about to do. How we built it The site is a Next.js frontend deployed on Netlify with a Python miner. On /scan , we feature-detect document.modelContext and register five tools via registerTool : scan_content load_specimen list_specimens explain_verdict contrast_intent Each tool mutates the React form state and calls the same /api/scan endpoint that a human would use. This means the human and the agent are always looking at the same underlying results. The contrast_intent tool computes a three-way contrast between the agent's intended action, the hidden instruction, and the safe remediation. Verdicts can also be Ed25519-signed for non-repudiation, and the repo already exposes a stdio MCP server for IDE-based workflows. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is a pre-standards draft, so the surface has shifted during development. The registration API moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext , and ChatGPT's in-app browser behaves slightly differently from Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . We also had to separate in-page discovery from the actual tool surface. The home page advertises the site's WebMCP support through /.well-known/webmcp.json , but the tools only register on /scan , because that is where the shared UI lives. The biggest design tension was keeping the page human-readable while making the tool schemas explicit enough for an agent to use reliably. Accomplishments that we're proud of The contrast_intent tool is the core win. Having an agent declare what it was about to do and showing that declaration next to the quarantined content creates a genuinely new human-agent interaction. We're also proud that the WebMCP implementation is not a fake API. The same tools update the same React state that the human sees, and the same scanner endpoint backs both the form and the tools. The signed verdicts, llms.txt agent instructions, and overall "agents as first-class users" design all reinforce the same idea: agent activity should be visible, understandable, and accountable. What we learned WebMCP is not just a way to expose actions; it is a way to make an agent's behavior legible to the human. If a tool does not update the page visibly, the human has no reason to trust it. We also learned that tool descriptions are load-bearing: an agent needs to know when to call each tool, not just what the tool does. We also confirmed that a /.well-known/webmcp.json manifest plus <meta name="webmcp"> helps agentic browsers and challenge evaluators discover the site before navigating to the tool page. What's next for elcaro Next, we want to expand WebMCP to the home page with a lightweight wayfinding tool, add a review_history tool, and ship a browser extension that automatically scans content retrieved by an agent and calls the WebMCP tools on the user's behalf. We also want to expose an organization dashboard for audit trails of agent-declared intent and integrate Elcaro with agent platforms beyond ChatGPT and Chrome. title: GroundTrace WebMCP
pitch: Warranted operational memory for browser agents: WebMCP lets agents retrieve precedent, while GroundTrace decides whether it is safe to rely on.
about_excerpt: Warranted operational memory for browser agents: WebMCP lets agents retrieve precedent, while GroundTrace decides whether it is safe to rely on. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browser agents can retrieve more and more information, but retrieval is not the same thing as authority. A remembered action may be stale, unsuccessful, unverified, or simply inappropriate to reuse. GroundTrace WebMCP gives browser agents access to operational memory while preserving that distinction: memory is a candidate, not authority. What it does GroundTrace exposes three native WebMCP tools directly from the web application: groundtrace_remember records a resolved incident with its action, outcome, verification state, timestamp, and provenance. groundtrace_recall retrieves relevant precedent and applies a deterministic warrant gate. groundtrace_explain exposes why GroundTrace admitted, held, or rejected the retrieved memory. Candidate memories receive a RELY , HOLD , or REJECT admission. Only RELY memories may supply an action as a recommendation. The key demonstration is deliberately a refusal. ChatGPT retrieves an exact-match incident with similarity 1, but because the stored memory is unverified, GroundTrace returns HOLD , reason memory_unverified , and recommendation: null . The agent successfully remembers. title: Intelligent Markdown-Driven Process Diagrams
pitch: It may look like an ordinary diagramming tool, but under the hood it's a markdown-driven agent friendly security, governance, and process improvement machine powered by WebMCP!
about_excerpt: It may look like an ordinary diagramming tool, but under the hood it's a markdown-driven agent friendly security, governance, and process improvement machine powered by WebMCP! Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I've found that giving agents structure and tools greatly enhances how they operate. A process diagram can look complete while hiding the complexity in simple steps. I wanted to make diagrams something people and AI agents can inspect, test, and improve together. What it does This project turns a process map into an interactive workspace for human-agent collaboration with a massive amount of context behind each input, action, output, and relationship by adding markdown to each point in the process. An agent can read all of this structure context to draft a new process, inspect steps and connections, and test scenarios by simulating outcomes that expose possible gaps. Proposed repairs appear as suggested change that a person can review before approval, adding to the collaborative feel between you and the agent. The included demo explores an AI evaluation process: what happens if a sandboxed agent decides it wants to escape? Our agent can identify a missing review step and propose a repair before the infrastructure is ever built. How we built it I gave Codex the challenge page url and described my idea 🤓 Challenges we ran into I ran into several issues along the way with actually using the WebMCP tools, troubleshooting the chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing config and finally realized I had to use the embedded browser in Codex instead of ChatGPT browser extension. Also took me forever to realize I couldn't use Luna with webMCP I'm happy to share more specifics if you'd like added feedback. Codex summarized our struggles below: WebMCP tools registered on the page but were not visible in every browser session. Native WebMCP testing required browser support, enabled settings, and correct host headers. Tool registration needed reliable retry, cleanup, and discovery checks. Tool inputs and outputs needed strict validation and clear safety annotations. Repair proposals needed exact graph and evidence references to reject stale requests. Agent-proposed drafts and repairs had to remain pending until human approval. Accomplishments that we're proud of Just finishing the challenge - everything feels SO busy lately. AI tools have made me so much more productive but I also find myself just working more as well. So taking the time to really dig into webMCP as a new capability was great. There's so much value in allowing web users to bring their own agent instead of trying to build AI into my own pages. I think it'll be a totally new unlock for web browsing, not just an agentic augmentation of the UI. What we learned I learned about webMCP from the ground up. I had never heard of it before I saw the tweet for the challenge and I was immediately interested. I've built a few websites but adding AI tooling feels like reinventing the wheel. WebMCP solves that by allowing users to BYOAgent. What's next for Intelligent Process Diagrams I'm very excited to get GPT-6 on it. I have a lot of ideas that I think would benefit from a more long horizon model using it and iterating on it. Sol did a decent job of the higher level stuff but veered sometimes. Now that the challenge is over and it's not so rushed I'll polish the UI and remove some of the bloat in the properties panel. I'm a solution architect by day, so I really want to incorporate this in discovery calls and allow an agent to build diagrams in realtime as I talk through customer processes. That's the long term vision for it. Thank you all for putting this on and taking the time to review all of these submissions!! Again, if you'd like any additional feedback on my experience adding WebMCP please reach out. I believe the first safety net of agentic alignment is to remove ambiguity from instructions. If an agent is given an INTENT.md contract then agents can act with more clarity around vulnerable or critical systems where more deterministic outcomes are required. In this project, each node, port (node input and output point), and relationship have theirs own markdown and metadata. The result is a structured graph where every part can explain what should happen, why it should happen, what evidence is required, and where authority stops. This opens up a possible use case as an agent-readable intent contract - INTENT.md During the diagram buildout, a model could inspect the complete process to find ambiguous or missing rules, conflicting conditions, unsafe capability paths, and downstream consequences. The next step would be to add typed permissions, prohibitions, invariants, data contracts, and authoritative branch conditions. This goes beyond instructions or skills by outlining a process end-to-end so an agent understands what's in scope and how to get from point A to point B in a safe and repeatable pattern. title: Intent Handoff
pitch: Intent Handoff lets users pass what they mean—not just what they clicked—to an AI agent so it can finish the task correctly.
about_excerpt: Intent Handoff lets users pass what they mean—not just what they clicked—to an AI agent so it can finish the task correctly. Like 1 Comment Story Updates step by step to use intent handoff Inspiration I noticed something strange about how we use AI with websites. The user can already see exactly what they mean on the screen. They can point to it by clicking it. But when they want an AI to help, suddenly they have to describe that thing in words: “The second hotel on the left.” “The one near the station.” “The cheaper one I was looking at just now.” Then the AI has to guess which place or object the user means. Why? The website already knows exactly what the user clicked. I wanted to remove that translation step. That became Intent Handoff : instead of describing a place, product or object in words and asking AI to guess, the user can interact with it directly and hand that exact context to the agent. What it does Intent Handoff connects normal website interactions directly to an AI agent through WebMCP. A user browses normally. They click a hotel, choose a budget, select preferences or interact with something they are interested in. Those interactions create structured intent. When the user hands the task to AI, the agent doesn't have to guess what “that hotel” or “the place I just clicked” means. It receives the actual object, its context, the user's existing selections and the task that needs to be completed. The user can simply point through the interface instead of describing through a prompt . The AI can then continue the task, use WebMCP tools, report progress and return the result to the website. How we built it I built Intent Handoff using WebMCP as the bridge between the website and the agent. The website exposes structured tools for the agent to read the user's current intent, selected constraints, task context and task status. The agent can then search options, report progress, apply changes and submit the completed result. The important part is that UI interactions are converted into structured context. Instead of: user click → user describes click → AI interprets description we can do: user click → structured intent → AI I also added explicit user-controlled handoff. The agent cannot simply take over because something was clicked. The user chooses when they want AI to continue the task. Challenges we ran into The difficult part was deciding how to translate UI interaction into useful agent context. A webpage contains a huge amount of information. The agent does not need all of it. It needs to know what the user actually means. So I had to separate the visual interface from the intent behind the interaction: which object was selected, which constraints matter, what has already happened and what the agent should do next. The other challenge was making the transition feel natural. The goal was not to create another AI chat box beside a website. The AI should feel like it can continue directly from what the user was already doing. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built the complete handoff loop on a live website. The user can interact with the interface, select exactly what they mean, hand the task to an AI through WebMCP, let the agent complete the work, refine the constraints and receive the result back in the website. The user never needs to explain which hotel they mean. They already clicked it. That sounds simple, but I think it changes an important part of human-agent interaction: the interface itself can become a way of communicating with AI. What we learned We learned that prompting does not always need to mean typing. Humans are already communicating intent when they use an interface. A click can say: “This one.” A filter can say: “Only show me things under this price.” A selection can say: “This matters to me.” Instead of throwing those signals away and asking the user to reconstruct everything as a prompt, WebMCP lets us expose them directly to the agent. AI doesn't always need to guess what the user means from words when the user has already shown us what they mean through their actions. What's next for Intent Handoff Next, I want to take Intent Handoff beyond the travel demo. Imagine browsing a shopping website and clicking a product, then handing that exact product to your agent. Or selecting a document, property, flight, restaurant or workflow item and asking AI to continue without explaining which one you mean. Eventually, individual objects and actions on a website could become handoff points between humans and agents. The idea is very simple: See it. Click it. Hand it to AI. No describing where it is. No copying information. No asking AI to guess which thing you meant. The website already knows. Just hand over the intent. title: BrowserMatic
pitch: Add WebMCP to any site instantly. No install, no extension simply enter a web address, we analyse the site, and open it in a browser with WebMCP applied in real time.
about_excerpt: Add WebMCP to any site instantly. No install, no extension simply enter a web address, we analyse the site, and open it in a browser with WebMCP applied in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Live browser embedded for co-browsing with ai Architecture Inspiration Every one of these is a tab-juggling exercise: Find the best deal across four stores Book dinner and movie tickets together Plan and price a trip in one shot Fill in council forms and applications Four stores, two booking sites, three travel sites, the same thirty fields on the twentieth government form. None of it is hard. It's just tedious, which is exactly what you'd want an assistant for. They all hit the same wall. Sites are starting to publish a machine-readable list of actions an AI is allowed to take, but those tools only exist on that site's own page. An agent can help you on one store, and that's the whole conversation. Four stores means four conversations, and nobody wants that. What it does Type a web address. BrowserMatic opens it in a browser that installs the API before the site's own code runs, so the site registers its tools and we carry them into your assistant, origin-qualified, across as many sites as you want. Four stores in one conversation. Flights and hotels side by side. And for forms, the same name and address on the twentieth site without typing it again. How we built it A Cloudflare Worker with one Durable Object per session, each with its own Browser Rendering Chromium, consent list and audit log. It also works directly in ChatGPT's in-app browser, no declarative form and no iframe discovery, so tools register imperatively on the top-level page; no session cookie, so a session is a capability URL. Names are origin-qualified because its permission model is per-site, and each tool holds its own AbortController, so granting a fourth store never disturbs the first three. The injection is one line of Playwright's addInitScript, a minimal WebMCP implementation installed before any page script runs. The same Worker also speaks MCP at /mcp over JSON-RPC with OAuth 2.1 and PKCE, verified against the official SDK, so any compliant client can drive the same session headlessly. Challenges A Chrome extension would have been the easy route. We used the hackathon to find out how far embedded remote browsers could go instead, since that's the lower-friction path for users. Most of the pain came from rendering a session a human and an AI can both drive at the same time. We're happy with where it landed in the time we had. We are still getting stuck in some "honey pots" so need to do a better job at detecting and mitigating. What's next A registry of the sites we've driven and the patterns we generate for them, so a success on one visit gets reused on the next. Then usage data for site owners so they can see how agents behave on their pages and improve accordingly, something like Google Analytics / Datadog for agentic commerce. We also want to try Cloudflare's agent payments and pay-per-access content as a business model. title: Proust's Reader
pitch: Untangle the sentence, preserve the prose.
about_excerpt: Untangle the sentence, preserve the prose. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration “...savour in a momentary glimmer of consciousness the sleep into which were plunged the furniture, the room, that whole of which I was only a small part and whose insensibility I would soon return to share.” I stared at this sentence for three minutes. I understood every single word. I still did not understand the sentence. Damn it, Proust. While reading In Search of Lost Time , I realized that vocabulary was not my problem. Syntax was. My workaround was to leave the reading app, paste the sentence into ChatGPT, and read a long explanation. After doing this a few times, the interruption became exhausting. And I did not want a summary. I wanted Proust. Reading literature is not just about extracting meaning. It is also about rhythm, structure, metaphor, punctuation, and the way a sentence unfolds. I wanted just enough help to see how a difficult sentence works, without replacing it with AI-generated summaries. That is why I built Proust’s Reader . What it does Proust’s Reader is an EPUB reader. It helps you understand a difficult sentence by untangling its structure inside the original text. Highlight a confusing sentence, ask your agent for help, and it can use WebMCP tools to: Mark the spine — reveal the main subject, verb, and core structure. Unfold nested structure — show buried clauses and phrases, what they modify, and what they mean in context. Reorder the syntax — temporarily show the sentence in a more familiar word order. Show the plain meaning — only if you are still completely lost. The idea is to give progressively stronger hints instead of immediately flattening the sentence into a paraphrase. The original sentence always stays at the center. No separate AI explanation to mentally map back onto the book. No summaries. No turning Proust into bullet points. Just enough scaffolding to understand the sentence. And get back to reading. How I implemented WebMCP I exposed four WebMCP tools from the reader: mark_spine , unfold_nested_structure , reorder_syntax , and show_plain_meaning . When the reader highlights a sentence, the agent can discover these tools and invoke the one that matches the user’s request. The tool receives the selected sentence and nearby context, and the result is rendered back into the reader so the original sentence can be annotated, unfolded, reordered, or paraphrased directly on the page. I intentionally exposed several focused tools rather than one generic “explain this sentence” action, so the agent can choose how much assistance to provide. Why WebMCP fits in Prost's Reader For my case, WebMCP is especially useful because it helps preserve an immersive reading experience , even when I run into a sentence with a monstrous grammatical structure. (Damn it, Proust!) Instead of copying the sentence, leaving the book, and asking an AI to explain it somewhere else, I can ask for help and let the agent operate directly on the sentence I am already reading. More importantly, WebMCP makes the explanation interactive and visual . The agent can mark the grammatical spine, unfold nested phrases and clauses, or temporarily reorder the syntax. All happen inside the original text. That makes it much easier to see how the sentence is constructed, instead of reading another explanation and trying to map it back onto the book in my head. WebMCP makes this simple goal possible: get unstuck without leaving the reading experience. How people and agent collaborate in Prost's Reader People still do the reading. They decide when a sentence feels difficult, what kind of help they want, and when they are ready to return to the original text. The agent provides the scaffolding. It can use the reader’s WebMCP tools to reveal the sentence spine, unfold nested structures, reorder difficult syntax, or show a plain-English meaning when needed. Together, the reader and agent can work through a difficult sentence step by step without turning the experience into a separate AI conversation. The reader keeps control of the interpretation. The agent simply makes the structure easier to see. Instead of replacing difficult literature, they can now work through it together inside the text. title: Synapse Studio
pitch: Build, stress-test, and optimize cloud architectures with AI agents. Synapse lets humans and agents collaborate on a live system canvas through WebMCP
about_excerpt: Build, stress-test, and optimize cloud architectures with AI agents. Synapse lets humans and agents collaborate on a live system canvas through WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Cloud architecture is usually designed as a static diagram, while testing, optimization, security review, and infrastructure generation happen in separate tools. We wanted to explore what happens when that architecture becomes a living, interactive system that both humans and AI agents can work with directly . WebMCP inspired us to build Synapse Studio around this idea: instead of an agent guessing how to operate a complex interface, the application can expose structured tools for inspecting, simulating, optimizing, and modifying the architecture. What it does Synapse Studio is an agent-native cloud architecture and simulation studio where humans and AI agents collaborate on the same live architecture canvas. Users can visually design systems, connect services, adjust configurations, and define goals. AI agents can then use WebMCP tools to: Inspect the current architecture and live metrics Simulate traffic spikes and infrastructure failures Detect bottlenecks and security risks Optimize cost, latency, and resilience Propose architectural changes Highlight affected components on the canvas Apply approved changes directly to the architecture Generate infrastructure-as-code from the approved design The result is a workflow that goes from design → simulation → diagnosis → recommendation → human approval → implementation → verification . How we built it We built Synapse Studio as a web application with a centralized architecture state shared across the canvas, simulation engine, agent interface, and WebMCP tools. The application exposes structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , including architecture inspection, node creation, service connections, chaos simulation, optimization, security auditing, visual highlighting, and IaC generation. A deterministic simulation engine models system behavior such as throughput, latency, resource utilization, failures, and estimated cloud cost. This allows agents to test architectural decisions and compare results before and after changes. We also built a WebMCP activity inspector so users can see which tools the agent is calling, what the agent is doing, and how the architecture changes in response. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was balancing technical ambition with a reliable product experience . It is easy to build many individual tools, but much harder to make them work together as one coherent human-agent workflow. We also had to design a simulation model that feels realistic enough to demonstrate meaningful engineering trade-offs without depending on real production infrastructure. Another challenge was making WebMCP visible and understandable. We wanted judges and users to clearly see when the agent was inspecting, simulating, proposing, and changing the architecture rather than simply interacting with a generic chatbot. Finally, we designed the system so significant agent-driven changes require human approval, keeping the human architect in control while still allowing the agent to perform complex operations. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Synapse goes beyond simply adding an AI assistant to an existing application. The architecture canvas, simulation engine, WebMCP tools, agent activity timeline, visual highlighting, optimization workflow, and IaC generation are designed as one integrated experience. Most importantly, we created a workflow where the agent can work with the application's actual structured state rather than trying to guess its way through the UI. That makes the WebMCP integration central to the product instead of being an added feature. We are also proud of the human-in-the-loop approval model, which demonstrates a more practical way for people and agents to collaborate on high-impact engineering decisions. What we learned We learned that building for agents requires thinking differently about application design. A traditional interface is designed primarily for humans. With WebMCP, the application can also expose clear, structured capabilities for agents , creating a much stronger interaction model. We also learned that the best human-agent experiences are not necessarily about giving the agent complete control. The more interesting model is often shared control : the human defines the goal and constraints, while the agent handles inspection, experimentation, reasoning, and execution. Most importantly, we learned that making an application agent-native is not just an API integration. It requires designing the underlying state, tools, UI, and workflows so humans and agents can genuinely operate together. What's next for Synapse Studio We want to evolve Synapse from a simulation and design environment into a broader agent-native engineering workspace . Future directions include richer architecture simulations, more sophisticated optimization algorithms, deeper security and compliance analysis, collaborative architecture versioning, additional infrastructure providers, and stronger integrations with real development and deployment workflows. Our larger vision is for Synapse to become a place where engineers can design systems with agents, test them before deployment, understand the trade-offs, and turn approved decisions directly into production infrastructure .
