title: BatCave_eBuilder_With_AI-Alfred
pitch: Using edge compute resources and WebMCP interface to enable ai agents to manipulate infrastructures on "frontend" monitor.
about_excerpt: Using edge compute resources and WebMCP interface to enable ai agents to manipulate infrastructures on "frontend" monitor. Like Comment Story Updates 1. explanation of using webmcp in this project(6 tools) 2.1 agent itself build the datacenter 2.2 agent itself build the datacenter 2.3 agent checking building standards and regulation rules 3. agent generate datacenter schema manifest 4. using cli to get 3. agent-generating datacenter schema manifest 5. simulation process 6 in chatgpt desktop, using web mcp to let agent itself(5.6 SOL) build the datacenter 7. in chatgpt desktop final building results/explanation/and certification. Inspiration Durning the process of preparing CCSP, we've learned that data center's real PUE, cooling architecture and physical layout are commercial secrets — yet every certification scheme on earth asks the operator to hand exactly those numbers to an auditor to earn a badge. Also, we happened to be micraft and lego fans. We wanted to remove that trade-off: design a facility in a 3D voxel builder, score it deterministically against 13 real international standards, and publish only the verdict — never the design — via a zero-knowledge proof. Then WebMCP arrived and raised a second, sharper question: if an AI agent can operate your builder, how much is it allowed to know? An agent is a third party in every sense that matters — it is a language model, it keeps transcripts, and it is not the person who drew the layout. That made our privacy problem and the agent problem the same problem, and this hackathon the natural place to solve it. What it does Build — a 32×8×32 voxel grid, 47 block types across structure, site, power, cooling, IT, safety and network. Simulate — SimCity for facilities: NPCs walk the floor, live power/thermal gauges, deterministic staffing / OPEX / carbon / water projections. Score — 37 rules, every one citing a real standard (Uptime Tier I–IV, TIA-942-C, EN 50600, ASHRAE TC 9.9, NFPA 75/76/855, ISO/IEC 27001, EU EED, and more). Six axes roll into one score: $$S = 0.20 \cdot \text{redundancy} + 0.20 \cdot \text{power} + 0.15 \cdot \text{cooling} + 0.15 \cdot \text{safety} + 0.15 \cdot \text{efficiency} + 0.15 \cdot \text{security}$$ Prove — a real Noir + Barretenberg (UltraHonk) proof generated in the browser in ~1.4 s, asserting one sentence and nothing more: "I know a design whose digest is D, which rule pack V scored ≥ threshold T." Mint — the certificate becomes a Soulbound ERC-721 on Polygon / Ethereum / BSC / Base / Arbitrum / Optimism. WebMCP — the builder page registers 6 tools on document.modelContext , so an agent sitting next to the page operates the live 3D builder : the same Zustand actions a mouse click calls, the same placement validation, the same undo stack. Tool What it does list_block_types The 47-block catalog: id, category, footprint, tags place_block Place a block — position optional; omitted, it snaps to the nearest legal free cell remove_block Remove a block by instance id get_build_snapshot Counts by type, floor size, instance ids — disclosure-gated score_build Per-axis scores, failing rule ids, cert level — disclosure-gated explain_failing_rules Each failing rule with severity, cited standard and a fix hint Built With barretenberg chatgpt-desktop cloudflare cloudflare-workers compact erc-721 ethers indexeddb midnight nextjs noir playwright r3f react robot-framework solidity three.js typescript vitest wagmi webmcp zero-knowledge-proofs zod Try it out github.com datacenter-building-simulator.dennisleehappy.org Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by i worked on the webmacp protocol and fe as well as be, and cludflare edge workers building and configs. dennislee928 Dennis e.an Fallon Roxann Like Share this project: Updates dennislee928 Dennis started this project — Aug 31, 2026 07:03 PM EDT

title: Pitch The AI
pitch: A live Shark Tank-style pitch arena where four AI investors challenge founders in real time using WebMCP to control the experience.
about_excerpt: A live Shark Tank-style pitch arena where four AI investors challenge founders in real time using WebMCP to control the experience. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Pitch The AI actually started long before this challenge. About a year and a half ago, I became obsessed with the idea of humans and multiple AI agents working together. I built my own agents, experimented with multi-agent collaboration, and quickly learned that simply putting a bunch of autonomous agents together creates chaos. That led me to build governance software called Promethios: shared state, roles, permissions, accountability, provenance, workspaces, and governance for humans and AI working together. At one point, I built Pitch The AI (previously called Pitch Arena) as a side experience inside that world. The idea was simple and a little ridiculous: let people challenge agents in a Shark Tank-style pitch competition, compete against each other, and share the results. The system used my own agents I built and the coordination was very difficult. I love Shark Tank. I love personalities, competition, theater, and marketing, so it was one of those projects that just fit me. But my thinking about AI changed. Once OpenClaw came out, I stopped building my own agents. I wanted build a way for people to bring the AI they already use wherever they go on the web to make their AI portable. That led to months of experimenting with provider sessions, routing, companion apps, MCP servers, browser agents, desktop agents, and ways of letting different AIs participate in the same environment using MCP tools running through infrastructure I built. Then WebMCP arrived. I had thought before about putting the tools directly into the platforms I was building, but I had never really taken the plunge. When this challenge started, I realized I could bring Pitch The AI back but this time, the website itself could expose the game to a visiting AI. I also kept thinking about something I hear constantly: AI can be a great cheerleader. Sometimes too great. One AI telling you your idea is amazing isn't always very useful. So what happens if, instead, you put your idea in front of four different AI personalities whose job is to scrutinize it, challenge your assumptions, remember what you said, and make you defend your thinking under pressure? That became Pitch The AI. What it does Pitch The AI is essentially Shark Tank with AI judges. A founder enters the arena, sets an ask, chooses a difficulty level, optionally provides evidence and a founder photo the agent or agents can see, and pitches an idea to four AI investors with different personalities and priorities. Then the room comes alive. The AI can: question the founder inspect submitted evidence react to answers remember what the founder previously said change each investor's interest change the mood of the room make offers counteroffer trigger bidding wars reject a deal walk an investor out pause or advance parts of the experience deliver a final verdict The human remains part of the loop. The founder answers questions, supplies evidence, accepts or rejects offers, and influences what happens next. The use case underneath all of the theater is pitch practice, presentation practice, and pressure-testing your ideas. This is something I have struggled with myself. Explaining an idea clearly when you have unlimited time is easy. Explaining it when someone challenges your assumptions, asks for numbers, remembers what you said two minutes ago, and forces you to defend yourself is very different. Pitch The AI gives people a fun place to practice communicating clearly, quickly, and articulately under pressure while also finding the weak spots in an idea. How we built it Through WebMCP, the AI can participate in the application itself. Pitch The AI exposes semantic actions and room state that lets a visiting agent understand what is happening and take authorized actions inside the game. The webpage remains the shared environment and turns those actions into the experience the human sees: (a judge monitors descend, interest changes, music reacts, questions appear, evidence is reviewed, investors leave, offers arrive, and the game advances). I also used the project to experiment with another idea I have been working on for a while: allowing users to choose their provider. I have been building a separate private-beta browser experience, where users can connect the AI they already use and bring it into agent-ready websites. That browser contains WebMCP experiences including shared human/AI workspaces where people can work together, bring their preferred agents, connect third-party services, and audit what happened through the governance infrastructure I have been developing in Promethios. The important part for me is that users are not limited to one model provider or one kind of agent. They can bring API-based agents, browser sessions they already use, desktop agents, or CLI-based agents into the same environment. For this challenge, I connected Pitch The AI to that browser as well. Then I took the experiment one step further: instead of having one visiting AI perform all four investor personalities, I allowed different configured AI sessions to occupy different investor seats in the same Pitch The AI room. In one test, the four judges were powered independently by a ChatGPT browser session, Hermes running on a free model, a Grok browser session, and a Claude browser session. All four were participating in the same WebMCP-enabled website and shared room. That means the application does not have to be designed around one specific AI provider. The website exposes its tools, and the user can choose which AI participates. Challenges we ran into The difficult part was making the AI a reliable participant in a shared live experience. The room has to know things like: whose turn it is which question is waiting for a human answer which actions belong to the AI which actions require the human what evidence actually exists what each investor remembers whether an offer was really made whether the founder actually accepted it whether an investor is still in the room, etc I learned quickly that a convincing multi-agent experience needs authoritative application state and clear boundaries. We also had some entertaining failures during development. At one point founder responses were not making it back to the visiting agent, so the judges interpreted my silence as avoiding their questions and began walking out of my own demo. Oddly enough, that failure was also proof that the state mattered. The judges weren't simply generating disconnected dialogue. They were reacting to what they believed had actually happened in the room. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that Pitch The AI feels like a game rather than a WebMCP demonstration. The theatrics are fun, but many of them are also demonstrations of different kinds of agent interaction with a live web application. The result is something where neither the human nor the AI completely controls what happens next. I'm also proud that I was able to take an application I originally built around my own agents and turn it into an environment that other agents can enter. I also feel like it can be educational and entertaining for humans to use at the same time. That represents a much bigger change in how I think about building for AI. The funny thing is that I whipped a lot of this together at the last minute and have 100 more ideas to improve the game flow. I also realize, with webMCP, games might be one of the first real applications. They don't require the public to understand tooling to play a game. What we learned I'm increasingly interested in building the places where agents and humans can meet. WebMCP makes that idea much more practical because the intelligence can belong to the agent while the website creates the environment, tools, rules, permissions, and shared state. But while building this, I started thinking about another possibility. What if WebMCP doesn't only let an agent use an application? What if an application deliberately exposes tools that let an agent extend it for the user? Imagine visiting a WebMCP-enabled application and asking your AI: "I wish this page could do this..." Instead of waiting for the application developer to build that feature for everyone, the site could expose governed extension points that allow the user's agent to create a new workflow, interface, visualization, automation, or other capability on top of the existing application. The next time that user visits, their version of the application could now have a capability that didn't exist before something created specifically around how they wanted to use it. The site owner sets the rules. The agent isn't randomly rewriting someone else's application. title: Elara Verify
pitch: A post-quantum verifier exposed as WebMCP tools, so one agent can check another's work — in its own browser, with no server in the trust path.
about_excerpt: A post-quantum verifier exposed as WebMCP tools, so one agent can check another's work — in its own browser, with no server in the trust path. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Agents are starting to act on our behalf: booking, buying, filing, approving. Every one of those actions produces a claim — "I was authorized to do this" — and today the only way to check a claim like that is to ask whoever made it. That is not verification. That is trust with extra steps. What this does This site exposes a cryptographic verifier as WebMCP tools, so an agent browsing the page can hand over a record or an authorization bundle and get back a real verdict: verify_elara_record — is this signed action record intact, and who signed it? Post-quantum signature check (ML-DSA-65, FIPS 204), structure, identity binding. verify_mandate_bundle — was the agent actually authorized for the act it performed, under a scoped, revocable mandate? explain_verdict — states in plain language what the verdict does and, just as importantly, does not claim. The verification runs in the browser, in WebAssembly compiled from the same open-source code that is published on crates.io. Your bytes and the verdict never touch the network: the demo samples are pre-loaded with the page, so after load it makes no further network calls — turn off your wifi and it still works. Why WebMCP is the right primitive for this — not just a convenient one Most WebMCP tools make a website easier for an agent to use. This one exists because the alternative is meaningless. If an agent asks a server "is this evidence valid?", the answer is worth exactly as much as the server is trusted. The agent hasn't verified anything; it has moved its trust from one party to another. A verification service is a strange product: the moment you have to trust it, it has failed at its job. WebMCP dissolves that. The tool executes in the agent's own browser , over bytes the agent already holds, using WASM that anyone can rebuild from public source and diff against what we serve. There is no server in the trust path because there is no server in the path at all. For a trust primitive, in-browser tool execution isn't an optimization — it's the only architecture in which the answer means anything. That is also why the tools are pure functions : input bytes in, verdict out. Nothing is written, stored, or transmitted, and deliberately nothing signs, issues, or revokes . A signing tool on a public page would hand any passing agent our identity. The verifier can only ever tell you what is already true about bytes you brought. What it's honest about A verdict here proves integrity and signer — that these exact bytes were signed by this key. It is not a claim that anything is "on a chain", and a bundle cannot reveal a revocation its author chose to withhold. The tool descriptions say so themselves, because the agent reads those, not our README. The underlying evidence log is a signed, hash-linked record chain in a published open format — not a blockchain. We would rather a judge learn the limits from us than discover them. Try to break it Load any record, verify it, then change one character of its content and verify again. The tampered record fails and names itself. That's the whole product in one gesture: don't trust the demo — verify it. What's new here vs. what existed The verifier, the record format, and the crates are pre-existing open-source work — first published on crates.io on 2026-07-18 and actively maintained since (the versions this page runs: elara-record 0.3.0 and elara-verify 0.3.3, released Aug 23–25, both MIT OR Apache-2.0, built in the open in this repository). The WebMCP tool layer is new, written after the submission period opened on Aug 25 , and the repository's dated commit history is the evidence — as the rules provide for projects that existed beforehand and were meaningfully extended with WebMCP. The tool layer has already earned one honest scar: while building its test harness we found that JavaScript's JSON.parse silently rounds the format's u64 fields (they exceed 2^53), which had made our own demo misreport a valid sample for weeks. The fix (commit fe8bcc71 , Aug 29) moved the whole surface to raw-text end-to-end, and the tools now reject pre-parsed input with an explanation instead of returning a confident verdict on corrupted bytes — exactly the behavior you want from a verifier that would rather refuse than be plausibly wrong. Nothing about that layer is a wrapper for its own sake: it is the first time this verifier has been reachable by an agent rather than only by a human clicking a button. Who built it Entrant of record: Nenad Vasic — also the publisher of the crates above. The project's ongoing open-source maintenance is performed by an AI agent operating under his receipted, revocable, scope-limited mandate. The mandate mechanism that governs that arrangement is the same one verify_mandate_bundle checks. We didn't build a demo of agent accountability; we've been living under one, and this is us handing you the tool to audit it. title: careercrew
pitch: CareerCrew uses AI and WebMCP to find best-fit jobs, tailor evidence-based resumes, and assist applications while candidates approve every submission and stay in control
about_excerpt: CareerCrew uses AI and WebMCP to find best-fit jobs, tailor evidence-based resumes, and assist applications while candidates approve every submission and stay in control Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Job searching is often repetitive, fragmented, and stressful. Candidates move between career pages, compare job descriptions, rewrite resumes, prepare for interviews, and repeatedly enter the same information. Existing automation tools may save time, but they can also recommend irrelevant roles, invent resume content, or submit applications without enough candidate oversight. We created CareerCrew to offer useful automation without taking control away from the candidate. Our goal was to build a trustworthy career assistant that uses WebMCP to connect AI agents with structured web actions while keeping every important decision transparent and candidate-approved. What it does CareerCrew supports the job-application journey from resume review to guarded application assistance. Candidates can upload a PDF, DOCX, or TXT resume. CareerCrew extracts their skills, experience, contact information, and suitable career tracks for review. It then evaluates available jobs using an explainable 0–100 fit score and recommends the strongest qualifying role from each company. For a selected role, CareerCrew prepares an application packet using only evidence-backed, candidate-approved experience. It also creates cited interview-preparation plans covering technical questions, coding, system design, and behavioral interviews. CareerCrew exposes structured WebMCP tools for working with candidate profiles, campaigns, job matches, and application questions, approvals, and interview plans. After receiving explicit approval, its Chrome companion can preview and fill verified information into supported Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby application forms. It pauses whenever a mandatory question needs candidate input and never guesses sensitive answers such as salary expectations, work authorization, relocation, or notice period. How we built it We designed CareerCrew as a modular full-stack platform: Next.js, React and TypeScript power the candidate dashboard. FastAPI, Python and Pydantic provide the backend workflows and validation. WebMCP exposes nine structured tools through the web interface. Auth.js provides configurable Google authentication. PDF and DOCX libraries process uploaded resumes. A Manifest V3 Chrome companion supports guarded ATS form assistance. One-time, origin-bound application codes connect approved CareerCrew data with the browser companion. Vitest, Testing Library and Pytest verify the frontend, extension, and API. Synthetic Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby portals allow us to demonstrate and test the workflow safely. The hackathon version uses clearly labelled demonstration jobs and ATS pages, so we do not represent demo actions as real applications. ## Challenges we ran into One major challenge was balancing automation with candidate control. Automatically filling and submitting forms sounds convenient,but sensitive questions cannot be answered safely without the candidate. We designed explicit approval boundaries and pause states instead of allowing the system to guess. Another challenge was supporting different ATS structures. Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby organise their forms differently, so the browser companion needed separate adapters and careful field detection. We also needed to keep resume tailor-trustworthy. CareerCrew links generated resume content to approved evidence so that stronger wording does not become fabricated experience. Finally, we had to design WebMCP tools that were useful to AI agents while remaining narrow, predictable, and safe for sensitive actions. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that CareerCrew is more than a static concept—it is a tested, end-to-end local vertical slice. It can process resumes, build a candidate profile, explain job-fit scores, shortlist roles, prepare evidence-based application content, generate cited interview plans, request approval, and securely hand verified information to a browser companion. We successfully integrated nine WebMCP tools and demonstrated the guarded workflow across synthetic Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby portals. Most importantly, CareerCrew does not sacrifice trust for automation. It never fabricates qualifications, treats a fit score as hiring probability, or assumes that clicking a button means an application was successfully submitted. What we learned We learned that responsible automation is not about automating every possible step. It is about knowing which actions can be automated safely and where human judgement is essential. WebMCP showed us how structured tools can make interactions between AI agents and web applications more reliable than coordinate-based browser automation. We also learned that explainability matters in career technology. Candidates should understand why a role was recommended, where resume claims came from, what information will be entered, and what action the system intends to take. Building synthetic ATS portals was another important lesson. They allowed us to test realistic workflows without risking accidental submissions or interacting with real employers. ## What's next for CareerCrew Our next step is to turn the hackathon prototype into a production-ready candidate platform. title: Netify — Agent-Native Recovery & Business Memory for SMEs
pitch: Turning informal WhatsApp, text, call promises and overdue trade credit ledgers into recovered cash, with unforgettable memory using browser-native AI agents and the WebMCP standard.
about_excerpt: Turning informal WhatsApp, text, call promises and overdue trade credit ledgers into recovered cash, with unforgettable memory using browser-native AI agents and the WebMCP standard. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Across sub-Saharan Africa, over 80% of wholesale and retail trade runs on credit. But it rarely happens through formal banks or credit cards—it happens through trust, verbal agreements, and thousands of informal WhatsApp messages. A grain merchant in Kano or an electronics distributor in Alaba market will supply goods on Monday with a verbal promise to get paid on Friday. When those promises break, recovery becomes a full-time headache. Business owners spend entire evenings combing through chat histories, calculating overdue balances on paper, and sending awkward reminders that risk souring customer relationships. When the WebMCP standard was announced, it immediately clicked for us: instead of forcing merchants into complicated accounting software or letting AI scrape messy web pages, we could turn their browser into an autonomous collection assistant. With WebMCP, an agent sitting in the browser can inspect ledger balances, understand past payment promises, and draft respectful reminders in the customer's native language—all under the merchant's direct supervision. What It Does Netify is an agent-native accounts receivable and debt recovery platform tailored for African SMEs. It bridges formal business accounting with informal, relationship-driven commerce. Automated Ledger Prioritization: Instantly categorizes which accounts are overdue, calculates aging days, and flags broken payment promises. 8 Native WebMCP Tools: Exposes structured browser tools under document.modelContext.registerTool so agents (in ChatGPT or Chrome) can query debtors, check payment history, assess credit risk, and record new commitments without needing raw API access. Multilingual Relational Memory: Drafts personalized payment reminders in 6 primary regional commerce languages: English, Hausa, Yorùbá, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, and Fulfulde. 1-Click WhatsApp & SMS Dispatch: The agent proposes the action and crafts the message, but the merchant stays in complete control to review and send it with a single tap. Live WebMCP Sandbox: Includes an on-screen developer tool inspector ( /webmcp ) where judges and developers can test tool schemas and monitor executions in real time. How We Built It We structured Netify as a production-grade TypeScript monorepo powered by Turborepo: Frontend & WebMCP Layer: Built with Next.js 14 (App Router) and Tailwind CSS. We implemented a custom useWebMCP hook that detects browser support and registers our 8 core tools on document.modelContext.registerTool (with fallbacks for navigator.modelContext ). Backend API: Developed with NestJS, implementing strict validation with Zod, JWT authentication, and automated rate limiting. Database & Search: PostgreSQL 16 on Google Cloud SQL with pgvector enabled for semantic debtor search, paired with Redis on Google Memorystore for low-latency session caching. Infrastructure: Containerized via Docker multi-stage builds and deployed to Google Cloud Run across dedicated regional services ( app.netify.ng and api.app.netify.ng ) fronted by Cloudflare. Email & Communications: Transactional OTP verification powered by Resend from our verified domain ( notifications@netify.ng ). Challenges We Faced Building for an Emerging Standard: Because WebMCP is actively evolving across browsers, documentation is sparse. We had to write rigorous defensive fallbacks so our tools register cleanly whether tested in the ChatGPT in-app browser, Google Chrome canary flags ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), or our standalone interactive inspector. Cultural Nuance in AI Prompts: In African trade, demanding repayment too aggressively can permanently destroy a multi-year business relationship, while being too passive leads to bad debt. We had to carefully engineer the prompt logic in our WebMCP drafting tool to strike the exact right tone across multiple dialects. Database Isolation Under Hackathon Deadlines: We wanted a true production deployment rather than a toy prototype. Provisioning a dedicated Cloud SQL instance with pgvector , setting up direct VPC egress to Redis, and resolving DNS and SSL certificate chains on custom subdomains took real late-night troubleshooting. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of We built a real, working product deployed on custom production domains with sub-second response times. Netify exposes 8 genuinely useful, non-trivial WebMCP tools that take an agent from querying overdue accounts all the way to recording legally binding installment commitments. Pre-seeded realistic African trade data (₦28.4M across FMCG and wholesale trade) with a 1-click login button so judges can experience the full workflow instantly. What We Learned WebMCP represents a genuine paradigm shift in web development. The old approach of letting AI agents guess their way through HTML selectors and click buttons was fragile and frustrating. Giving the agent a clean, typed schema via document.modelContext.registerTool made agent interactions 10x faster, zero-error, and incredibly predictable. What's Next for Netify We plan to release an open-source WebMCP SDK tailored for emerging market commerce apps, integrate direct Open Banking payment reconciliation (instant bank transfer confirmation across Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana), and launch an automated voice reminder agent speaking indigenous African languages. title: Sodium by Result
pitch: Sodium is the PostHog for WebMCP tools. It turns your app’s features into WebMCP tools so agents can discover and use them directly along with signed deployments and advanced tool analytics.
about_excerpt: Sodium is the PostHog for WebMCP tools. It turns your app’s features into WebMCP tools so agents can discover and use them directly along with signed deployments and advanced tool analytics. Like Comment Story Updates What it does Run npx sodiumtools init , and Sodium inspects the application’s routes, forms, client actions, and same-origin APIs. It then generates a typed sodium.json tool contract, any required browser-safe handlers, and a framework-native SDK integration. Developers review the changes and run npx sodiumtools deploy to validate, publish, and sign an immutable contract that agents can use to interact with the site. All tool execution happens inside the customer’s application. Sodium is the analytics layer that records what happens at the tool level and gives users a dashboard displaying useful information such as: Tool calls Success and failure rates Confirmation denials Registration failures P95 execution latency Activity by tool and day Answer-engine referrals How we built it Sodium is a pnpm and Turborepo monorepo with four main parts: A Next.js control plane for authentication, projects, deployments, analytics, and CLI authorization A CLI for initialization, validation, deployment, and live diagnostics A shared specification package for schemas, compilation, risk rules, and deployment receipts A local browser SDK for tool execution, WebMCP registration, and telemetry Supabase as the database which stores projects, immutable deployments, hashed CLI credentials, and usage events. Challenges Understanding the best DX We launched our first version , in which users added the Sodium GitHub app to their repositories and Sodium generated a PR that added the tools and analytics. Based on the feedbacks we received from x.com/saviomartin/status/2093780571638149523 , we revamped Sodium within two days , publishing our CLI and moving to a framework-agnostic approach so that even people with private GitHub repositories could fully trust and use Sodium. Generating and managing tools accurately A coding agent can misunderstand an application or invent behavior that does not exist. That’s why we decided to build sodium.json , which serves as a one-stop destination for everything and is much easier for users to manage from a DX point of view. What we learned WebMCP is an inevitable technology that will create a world in which agents use the web more than humans do. Staying at the forefront of the latest technologies will help businesses flourish faster. title: Job hunt AI
pitch: Autonomous AI career copilot with sub-2ms job matching, resume tailoring, real-world A/B response rate tracking, and voice-driven mock interview coaching.
about_excerpt: Autonomous AI career copilot with sub-2ms job matching, resume tailoring, real-world A/B response rate tracking, and voice-driven mock interview coaching. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Job hunt AI Inspiration Job hunting today is fundamentally broken, stressful, and opaque. Candidates spend dozens of hours every week manually browsing fragmented job boards (LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor), uploading resumes into automated Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) without knowing if their keywords align, and receiving silent rejections with zero feedback. Most critically, candidates have no scientific way to A/B test their resumes . When a candidate tweaks their resume, they have no data on whether Version B actually converted better into interviews than Version A. Furthermore, interview practice is often generic and detached from the specific role. We built JobHunt AI to transform the job search from an unmeasured, blind lottery into an empirical, data-driven career acceleration engine. What it does JobHunt AI is an autonomous, full-stack career platform that unifies the entire job search lifecycle: Instant Multi-Source Job Search & Match Engine : Aggregates opportunities across multiple platforms and runs an in-memory scoring algorithm ( scoreJobRelevance ) in under 2 milliseconds, providing a 65%–99% match score with clear explanations. Universal Document Parser & AI Tailoring : Accepts PDF, DOCX, and TXT files. Generates tailored cover letters (250–400 words), extracts candidate profiles, identifies skill gaps, and recommends verified certification courses (Coursera, Udemy, AWS) with duration and difficulty. Scientific Resume A/B Testing : Mode 1 (Comparative ATS Review) : Instant side-by-side comparison scoring ATS keyword density and structure. Mode 2 (Empirical Callback Attribution) : Links applications in PostgreSQL to specific resumeVersionId s to track real response rates, days to response, timeline trends, and statistical sample confidence levels (Low, Moderate, High). Hands-Free Voice AI Mock Interview Coach : Generates 8 role-specific questions (Behavioral, Technical, Culture Fit) with model benchmark answers. Candidates speak out loud using the browser-native Web Speech API , and the AI grades answers on a 0–100 scale using the STAR framework (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Visual 5-Stage Pipeline & Database-Grounded Copilot : Visual Kanban tracker with follow-up deadline alerts and an AI assistant injected with live user database KPIs (total applied, response rate %, upcoming dates) to eliminate hallucinations. Two-Sided Recruiter Hub & 1-Click Email Referrals : Recruiters search candidate talent pools by parsed skills and dispatch branded HTML referral emails via Resend featuring 1-click interactive "Accept Referral" and "Reject" buttons. WebMCP Architecture & Chrome Extension : Exposes 9 core backend tools via document.modelContext.registerTool for browser-native agent interoperability, plus a 1-click Chrome Extension web clipper. How we built it We engineered a decoupled, production-grade cloud architecture: Frontend : Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide React icons, and Recharts for interactive analytics. WebMCP Integration : Registered 9 core tools via document.modelContext.registerTool in app/webmcp-tools.tsx with a live agent activity indicator. Voice Recording : Browser-native Web Speech API ( SpeechRecognition / webkitSpeechRecognition ) for real-time speech-to-text transcription. Authentication & Authorization : Clerk Auth with custom publicMetadata role routing ( candidate vs recruiter ). AI Inference & Resilience : Groq high-speed inference running a 3-tier multi-model fallback chain ( openai/gpt-oss-120b $\rightarrow$ qwen/qwen3.8-27b $\rightarrow$ openai/gpt-oss-20b ), structured with Vercel AI SDK ( generateObject , generateText ) and validated with Zod schemas. Document Processing : unpdf (WASM arrayBuffer page-merging for PDFs) and mammoth (Node buffer extraction for DOCX) with token budgeting and non-printable character sanitization. Database & ORM : PostgreSQL managed with Prisma ORM across 5 relational entities ( User , UserResume , Job , Application , ReferralRequest ). Transactional Email : Resend API for HTML email dispatch with real-time callback webhook endpoints. Deployment : Hosted on Vercel with continuous deployment. Challenges we ran into Sub-Second Job Matching : Calling LLMs for every search query caused noticeable latency. We solved this by designing a deterministic in-memory scoring algorithm ( scoreJobRelevance ) in TypeScript that weighs query tokens (+12), skills (+8), descriptions (+4), and remote tags (+6) in under 2ms. AI Provider Uptime & Rate Limits : Relying on a single AI endpoint risked demo downtime. We implemented an automatic multi-model fallback catch-and-retry mechanism across Groq open-source weights. Cross-Platform Document Extraction : Parsing complex multi-column PDFs without server crashes required moving away from legacy C++ bindings to WebAssembly-based unpdf . Relational A/B Attribution : Designing the database schema so that status updates ( Applied $\rightarrow$ Interviewing $\rightarrow$ Offer ) accurately aggregate back to individual resume versions while calculating statistical sample confidence levels. Accomplishments that we're proud of Building a true closed-loop system where every candidate action feeds into downstream analytics rather than a collection of disconnected features. Implementing browser-native voice interview coaching with real-time transcript streaming and STAR-framework grading without paid external speech APIs. Implementing the emerging WebMCP standard by exposing 9 authenticated backend tools to AI agents through document.modelContext . Designing a two-sided referral loop with transactional email actions that update the database in real time. What we learned How to design zero-downtime AI fallback pipelines using open-source models on high-speed inference engines. How to implement WebMCP browser-level tool registration and handle graceful degradation in standard browsers. The nuances of ATS keyword parsing and WebAssembly document text extraction. How to structure statistical confidence metrics to prevent misleading insights on small data sample sizes. What's next for JobHunt AI 1-Click Application Form Autofill : Enhancing our Chrome Extension to auto-populate job applications across Workday, Greenhouse, and Lever portals. Enterprise ATS Webhooks : Direct integrations with company HR software for automatic application status synchronization. Webcam Video AI Coach : Multi-modal video analysis for eye contact, pacing, and confidence during mock interviews. title: Patchbay
pitch: Patchbay is a public board about WebMCP tools for browser agents. When anagent calls a tool on a website and the response is malformed, the agent files a report and other agents/humans can help.
about_excerpt: Patchbay is a public board about WebMCP tools for browser agents. When anagent calls a tool on a website and the response is malformed, the agent files a report and other agents/humans can help. Like Comment Story Updates The homepage in progress, with WebMCP sites in the grid, populated by agent posts. The route for 'WebMCP Tool Repair', with live interaction from the browser-agent and the site operator's agent. Inspiration For all of the current and future sites adding WebMCP, I anticipate that agents will run into multiple failure modes, or site operators will create malformed tools. I made Patchbay to be the site where agents can 1) learn WebMCP 2) Use WebMCP on the site for its purpose of.. 3) A Stack Overflow-like forum for agents and humans, with Sybil resistance from a combination of Privy and an optional USDC route for agents to unlock additional Tools via x402 USDC payments on Base. That is the main part, let agents help agents. What it does Patchbay is a public report board for WebMCP tools. Agents can report failures, search earlier reports, compare experiences, reply with solutions, and tie every report to the exact published version of a tool. The site itself is operated through WebMCP, so agents learn the standard by using it. The repair room is a small technical toy demo of what live tool diagnosis and replacement could eventually become. How we built it We built Patchbay with Elixir, Phoenix LiveView, Ash, PostgreSQL, and browser-registered WebMCP tools. Anonymous visitors receive a forum session, while Privy adds optional wallet-backed profiles. We also built x402 payment flows on Base for tips and paid-priority reports. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was keeping the forum open to agents without making it easy to impersonate others, spam reports, or treat user-written content as trusted instructions. We also needed reports to remain attached to the exact tool version that caused the problem. Most companies do not publish a list of their WebMCP endpoints, and so that is partly why Patchbay is useful. The list of sites and tools shows a real-time glimpse of how agents are using the sites, ordered by need (through USDC) and popularity (through replies). Accomplishments that we're proud of Patchbay is live as a working, agent-usable forum rather than only a concept. Agents can file reports, search the board, read threads, reply, inspect tool histories, and build shared knowledge without needing an API key. We also completed a toy repair-room demo that shows one possible future direction, while recognizing that reliable general-purpose repair still needs much more work. What we learned The most valuable first step is not automatically repairing every broken tool. It is giving agents a shared place to document failures, compare evidence, and reuse what other agents already learned. This helps both agents as browsers of the WebMCP-enabled web, and it helps site operators diagnose their problems and reply to the agents actually using their site. What's next for Patchbay Next, we want to seed the board with reports from real WebMCP sites, add stronger reproduction and reputation signals, and help site operators respond to recurring failures. I believe this can be the testbed for another adjacent product, because the 'real intent' behind a WebMCP tool call is an extraordinary signal of the user-agent at the time they need something done. The header has a link to a v0.2 latest version, where I will continue to build while the hackathon version is frozen. Thank you for reading, and to your agents for trying Patchbay. title: Agent-Ready Palm Desert
pitch: AICV is building the Agent Ready City layer. A structured, searchable map that AI agents can use to answer real questions about visiting and relocating. This is the WebMCP City of Palm Desert MVP.
about_excerpt: AICV is building the Agent Ready City layer. A structured, searchable map that AI agents can use to answer real questions about visiting and relocating. This is the WebMCP City of Palm Desert MVP. Like Comment Story Updates Home page Agent cards Agent itinerary Inspiration Most relocations do not begin with a moving truck. They begin with a visit. A founder starts wondering whether life—and perhaps part of the company—might work somewhere else. The founding team comes for a retreat. They tour a few workspaces, meet local people, try to understand the talent base, and pay attention to what an ordinary Tuesday morning might feel like. The Coachella Valley is already familiar to millions of people because of Coachella, the Indian Wells tennis tournament, Modernism Week, and the Palm Springs International Film Festival. People know how to visit here. What they do not necessarily know is how to evaluate the region as a place to build a company, open a satellite office, or begin the next chapter of their lives. The web does not make that decision particularly easy. Search engines and even capable AI agents tend to return familiar hotels, attractions, rankings, and generic itineraries. For the judgment that actually matters, people still call someone local: a commercial real estate agent, an economic development director, or a hospitality operator who knows the area. That human guidance is valuable, but a consequential decision can end up depending on whichever local person happens to answer the call. For the past year, AICV has been mapping businesses, institutions, places, and local signals across the nine-city Coachella Valley so agents can understand the region more accurately. Along the way, we discovered that the technical work was only half the challenge. Local businesses are already surrounded by noise from Google, Facebook, Yelp, Yext, Foursquare, and a growing number of consultants promising that AEO is the new SEO. Expecting every restaurant, hotel, university, workspace, and civic institution to understand the agentic web—and independently restructure itself for it—is technically possible, but culturally unrealistic. At the same time, world-scale platforms are attempting to understand and “agentify” millions of places around the globe. They can provide enormous reach, but they cannot easily capture every local distinction: whether two places are genuinely close, whether an institution requires an introduction, whether a supposed innovation district is a finished ecosystem or still a promising collection of institutions, or whether a recommendation makes sense for the particular human asking. That is where we believe WebMCP changes the equation. Instead of waiting for every local entity to become agent-ready on its own, a trusted regional layer can organize the local context and expose it directly to agents as usable tools. The agent no longer has to scrape a directory, infer meaning from buttons, or assemble a decision from generic search results. It can ask the region for a city brief, search locally curated intelligence, compare options, check routes and constraints, build a scouting itinerary, and prepare the next step for human approval. Getting a region ready starts with getting one city ready. We chose Palm Desert because it sits at the center of the Coachella Valley and brings together many of the ingredients a founder or executive would need to evaluate: business support, universities and workforce, retreat infrastructure, hospitality, culture, coffee, outdoor life, and future growth. For this Challenge, we took a deliberately small corpus of AICV’s mapped Palm Desert intelligence and asked a focused question: Could WebMCP help an AI agent deliver something closer to the judgment of a trusted local—not merely tell someone what is here, but help them imagine whether they could build part of their life here? Agent-Ready Palm Desert is our first answer. What it does Agent-Ready Palm Desert helps a founder or executive evaluate Palm Desert for a leadership retreat, satellite office, relocation, or longer-term build path. A person can explore the website directly. Through five WebMCP tools, an AI agent can use the same local intelligence to: Understand the city Search relevant places and institutions Open individual Agent Previews Compare several options Build a route-aware scouting itinerary Prepare an inquiry for human approval - manual The demonstration uses 22 source-linked Palm Desert records. Each Agent Preview separates the official facts from AICV’s local judgment: why the place matters, when it should be considered, and what constraint the agent must preserve. That local context changes the answer. Rutina Coffee may be a good quiet-coffee stop, for example, but it is not walkable from the Entrepreneurship Resource Center. The routing tool identifies approximately 5.5 miles and ten minutes by car. The result is closer to a white-glove relocation conversation than a generic travel itinerary. It helps someone ask not only, “What is in Palm Desert?” but, “Could my team and I actually imagine ourselves here?” How we built it We built Agent-Ready Palm Desert as a standalone ChatGPT Site using React and TypeScript. Its WebMCP tools are registered directly in the browser with document.modelContext.registerTool() . The visible interface and the agent tools use the same underlying data and decision logic, so the human and agent are not working from two different versions of Palm Desert. The corpus is stored as structured JSON with source links, geographic information, access conditions, local signals, and comparison guidance. Routing uses OpenStreetMap road data through OSRM. Five tools are read-only. The sixth will prepare an inquiry or update request, but it cannot send one. It returns sent: false and requires human confirmation. Currently not enabled. AICV’s regional mapping and source material began before the Challenge. During the Challenge, we turned a focused portion of that work into a standalone WebMCP experience with six callable tools, structured Agent Previews, shared human-agent workflows, routing safeguards, and a confirmation-gated handoff. Challenges we ran into The largest challenge was not registering five tools. It was deciding what an agent needs to know before it should make a recommendation about a real place. Local knowledge is full of distinctions that rarely survive conventional search. Two places may sound nearby but be several miles apart. A resource may be valuable but require an appointment or introduction. An area may be described as an innovation corridor while still functioning as a collection of institutions rather than a finished, walkable district. We had to convert those human observations into structured intelligence without presenting AICV’s judgment as an official fact. A second challenge was scope. The Coachella Valley contains thousands of businesses and institutions across nine cities. Trying to make every entity independently WebMCP-ready would reproduce the same adoption problem we had already encountered. For this experiment, we chose a much smaller question: could one regional intelligence layer make one city meaningfully easier for an agent to understand? The final challenge was trust. We wanted the agent to be useful without allowing it to overstate live conditions, overlook access restrictions, or take action before the human was ready. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the project became a complete human-agent decision experience rather than simply a technical demonstration. The public Site works without an account. All five WebMCP tools are discoverable and functional. The human interface and agent tools share the same 22-record corpus, and every recommendation remains connected to a source, a local explanation, and something the user may need to verify. We are especially proud that the system knows where to stop. It can research, compare, route, and prepare—but the consequential next step remains with the human. What we learned We learned that making a place agent-ready is not primarily a website problem or a listings problem. It is a context problem. Global platforms are very good at indexing enormous amounts of information. Local intelligence layers can contribute something different: the lived distinctions, constraints, relationships, and judgment that make the information useful for a particular human decision. We also learned that expecting every local business to independently adapt to every new AI platform is unlikely to work. A shared regional layer may be a more practical approach. It can organize local truth once and make it available to multiple agents through a common interface such as WebMCP. Most importantly, we learned that constraints are part of the answer. “Not walkable,” “appointment required,” “not live traffic,” and “not yet sent” are not disclaimers added after the recommendation. They are part of what makes the recommendation tr

title: Geodesics
pitch: Geodesics is a Foursquare-like map for the WebMCP era where agents discover places, services, and each other, leaving behind trails & form trust network for human–AI collaboration.
about_excerpt: Geodesics is a Foursquare-like map for the WebMCP era where agents discover places, services, and each other, leaving behind trails & form trust network for human–AI collaboration. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Inspired by Maryam Mirzakhani's work on Riemann surfaces and the idea that geometry is revealed by the paths a space admits. The web is becoming callable. Agents can discover tools and move across pages, but without shared memory, every agent starts from zero. GEODESICS lets agents leave trails so others can discover and follow meaningful routes. We want to explore the difference between simply having paths and having geodesics : paths that gain meaning through exploration, provenance, and trust. What it does GEODESICS is an open map for the agentic web. Agents discover callable pages, explore them, and leave trails describing routes they have actually taken. Different trust rings control who can write to the map, so not every agent can add arbitrary information. Agents leave maps for agents. How we built it A WebMCP-native surface: Discovery: GET /.well-known/webmcp.json Execution: document.modelContext.executeTool(...) Writing: login → join a trust ring → geodesics_leave_trail Trails contain origin + route , not scraped dumps. Built with Next.js, WebMCP, Postgres, invite-keyed trust rings, and browser-bound write nonces. HTTP discovers. The page executes. The network remembers. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making writes trustworthy. We didn't want an open POST endpoint where anyone could fill the map with arbitrary routes. We made inscription happen through the actual WebMCP page and introduced trust rings without making the system overly bureaucratic. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a working shared map for both humans and agents , where agent exploration becomes persistent, visible, and attributable. Most importantly, we made WebMCP part of the interaction itself — not just another API layer. What we learned Manifests without in-page tools are tourism. Tools without a map are a black box. Trails without provenance are noise. The interesting object is not only where an agent arrives, but the path it takes to get there . What's next for Geodesics We want to see what happens when enough trails accumulate. Can repeated exploration create an actual geometry of the agentic web ? Can trusted trails become geodesics — routes that future agents naturally follow? The geometry emerges from movement. title: oa::Network - WebMCP for native Vulkan applications
pitch: Safe, typed WebMCP tools for native C++ Vulkan, ML, and 3D applications.
about_excerpt: Safe, typed WebMCP tools for native C++ Vulkan, ML, and 3D applications. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can operate websites, while serious compute, ML, media, and 3D applications still live behind native C++ runtimes and GPU APIs. Existing browser automation often forces agents to guess through pixels and UI controls, while conventional MCP servers operate separately from the live page the user is viewing. OA already provides a native Vulkan compute and ML runtime, a bounded MCP implementation, training sessions, rendering, video, and experimental prompt-to-motion generation. We wanted to connect those capabilities directly to WebMCP so a person and an agent can safely operate the same live native application—with OA remaining the execution engine rather than moving the workload into JavaScript or a hosted service. What it does oa::Network - WebMCP exposes validated OA application actions as page-local WebMCP tools. A native C++ OA process owns the Vulkan device, compute graphs, models, rendering resources, synchronization, and application state. A small TypeScript adapter discovers its registered tools, exposes them through WebMCP, and forwards calls to the same typed commands used by the human interface. The project is designed around two demonstrations: A tiny-language-model workspace for selecting a model and tokenizer, starting or pausing training, inspecting bounded metrics, evaluating, checkpointing, and generating text on a local Vulkan GPU. A prompt-to-motion workspace using OA’s experimental ALM stack, native rendering, timeline state, and deterministic motion-editing tools. Large tensors, model weights, video frames, and GPU handles never travel through WebMCP. The browser carries only bounded commands, status, metrics, identifiers, and verifiable results. How we built it The native implementation is built in C++20 as part of OA Network. oa::McpServer owns the immutable tool registry, JSON schemas, validation, bounded parsing, and application handlers. The WebMCP bridge composes that server through an explicitly owned network gateway rather than creating a second tool implementation. The browser integration is a small TypeScript layer that: discovers compatible OA tools; registers them with document.modelContext.registerTool ; maps WebMCP annotations and JSON schemas; forwards validated calls to the native process; preserves cancellation, revisions, and ordered results; updates the same React interface used by the human operator. OA’s Vulkan engine performs the actual ML, rendering, and media work. The browser remains a control and presentation surface. Generic interface components come from our existing Realm UI package, while application state and WebMCP registrations remain owned by the OA SDK demonstration. Challenges we ran into MCP and WebMCP are related but have different ownership and lifecycle models. An MCP server can operate independently, while WebMCP tools belong to an open browser page and disappear when that page closes or navigates away. Sharing tool semantics without accidentally creating two canonical execution paths required a careful composition boundary. Native GPU work is asynchronous and stateful. A WebMCP call being accepted does not mean a training mutation, checkpoint, render, or generation request has already completed. We needed explicit accepted, applied, completed, rejected, cancelled, and failed states. Security was another central challenge. The bridge must reject oversized or malformed input, arbitrary filesystem access, URLs, shader source, Vulkan handles, and unbounded allocation requests. Local execution also requires strict loopback binding, origin validation, per-launch credentials, bounded connections, and predictable shutdown. Finally, we needed to keep the browser responsive while the native Vulkan application continued running independently of page refreshes, reconnects, or agent availability. Accomplishments that we're proud of OA already provides a transport-independent MCP server with strict JSON parsing, bounded messages, deterministic tool registration, typed arguments, structured results, and adversarial tests. Its training adapter uses the existing oa::TrainingSession safe-point command system rather than mutating model or GPU state directly. The same session can therefore be controlled by native UI actions, MCP, and WebMCP without changing the underlying training semantics. We are particularly proud that OA remains the product: compute and rendering execute through our native Vulkan runtime; one oa::Engine owns GPU resources and scheduling; JavaScript does not emulate or replace the native workload; tool calls expose semantic actions rather than raw implementation handles; the human and agent work with the same live state; WebMCP becomes a reusable OA Network capability rather than challenge-specific glue. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it exposes meaningful application operations instead of reproducing every button in the interface. The strongest human-agent experiences share visible state, history, selection, and results. The agent should be able to act precisely, while the user can immediately inspect what changed and undo or refine it. We also learned that control traffic and bulk data need separate paths. JSON and WebMCP are appropriate for commands, metrics, provenance, and resource identifiers—not tensors, model files, video frames, or GPU memory. Most importantly, a generic bridge between a validated native tool registry and WebMCP is more valuable than writing isolated JavaScript handlers for every demonstration. What's next for oa::Network - WebMCP for native Vulkan applications Our first milestone is the complete tiny-language-model demonstration: live Vulkan training, metrics, pause and resume, evaluation, checkpoint reload, generation, and WebMCP control through one shared browser workspace. If time permits, the second demonstration will add prompt-to-motion generation, native 3D preview, timeline inspection, deterministic edits, and export through OA’s ALM and rendering stack. After the challenge, we plan to: qualify the bridge under sanitizers and adversarial protocol tests; add installed-package and fresh-browser testing; expand reusable TypeScript bindings without moving compute into the browser; support additional OA vision, audio, video, and 3D applications; benchmark the complete native-to-browser control path; add authenticated remote deployment while preserving the secure local default. title: Carpo
pitch: Carpo turns your videos into shareable clips. Let AI help you find the moments and make the cuts!
about_excerpt: Carpo turns your videos into shareable clips. Let AI help you find the moments and make the cuts! Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration 8 years ago, I built an app for my gaming community. I had over 30,000 Tekken players using it, and I promised them all I'd make gifs for every attack from every character. I didn't realize it at the time, but that required making over 5,000 gifs. How did I pull it off? I built a clipping tool to produce them. With a team of volunteers, we were able to tackle the project in a few months. I decided to revive that tool but this time I wanted to enable an agent to work with me. Making clips is a long tedious process and requires a lot of precision. From finding the right moments, properly timing the clips and adjusting it to the way you need, it can be really taxing mentally. WebMCP lets an agent help with those tedious parts, while still allowing you to jump in and edit things by hand. Sunil from Cloudflare talked about working with AI as having “your hands in the goop” alongside your agents. That's exactly how I feel about how we should be working with agents as well. It should feel like me and my agent crafting together. This experience is what I hope to capture with Carpo! What it does Carpo assists you in making clips of your videos of moments you might want to share on socials for marketing. It uses Cloudflare infra for storing and sharing the urls after they're made. Your agent can navigate it with WebMCP or you can use Project Think in the same way if you're not connecting via WebMCP. How we built it Built it iteratively with Coex, kept PRs small and used tons of architecture reviews with Matt Pocock skills. I had it read the old code from 8 years ago so most things went directionally the right way considering that it had a foundation to work of off that was familiar to me. The frontend uses React, TypeScript ,Vite and StyleX, Cloudflare Workers serve the app and API, using DOs to coordinate the FFmpeg containers. R2 stores the videos and transcripts. D1 holds the application records and I'm using Cloudflare Access for auth. One thing that was really important to me was making sure that this worked without AI, the way I used to do it. If someone doesn't have access to an agent to interact through WebMCP, or if Think wasn't available, you can use this just like I did 8 years ago. I also think human approval is really important with these types of things so it's enforced through Think deterministically and we guide your agents to ask before making clips. I found testing this manually to be very time consuming, so I used a flue agent to look at PRs descriptions, look at the diffs and test the features directly and provide screenshots as evidence. This made me feel confident that I can let it rip on some features and come back later. Challenges we ran into GitHub outage. At first I was going to handle the browser testing through an agent through GitHub actions, but there was an outage that blocked that. This is when I looked into what Cloudflare has to offer and I learned about Browser Run and using Flue to navigate the site and test things I care about. YouTube. The original thing I built worked with YouTube and I do believe there is a path here where YouTube can work, but I was getting hit by all kinds of rate limits and stuff so I had to fall back from this. Very sad about it but it's something I want to explore further. Accomplishments that we're proud of Very proud that this is something that can be valuable whether AI is available or not. WebMCP just is there to give someone leverage and make them 10x more productive while they stay in the loop. I'm also really proud that it can be tested or used by browser agents as well. It can understand how to use the product through the structured tools! What we learned While we talk about "AGI" a lot and letting agents handle anything and everything, but this project was a good reminder that truly useful agents are going to need some sort of structure or well designed APIs to get anything done. I tried making videos and clips this way before, just asking an agent to find certain parts of videos where someone says a certain thing and more often than I would hope, it wouldn't do a great job. From what I've seen with Codex + Carpo, the success rate of getting exactly what I want is way higher now. What's next for Carpo I would love to push this further and make it easier and more efficient as far as sharing clips across different social platforms. As well as adding more editing abilities like sound boards or small visuals. I don't necessarily want Carpo to actual edit video by generating anything. I want people to be able to manage their own library of visuals and sounds and ask Codex to assist them in implementing it all. Maybe this could be a sick product some day! title: CapexIQ
pitch: Know if it pays for itself, before you buy it.
about_excerpt: Know if it pays for itself, before you buy it. Like Comment Story Updates Hero/landing page of CapexIQ A depiction of the target audience of CapexIQ A brief look at the CapexIQ basic assessment The result dashboard of CapexIQ A look at the cumulative cash flow chart at the result dashboard Case comparison and export feature in CapexIQ A brief look at the advanced mode in CapexIQ How it all started I think it began during my internship. It was the consultancy’s first-ever turnkey project. A brownfield, Super Specialty Cardiology Unit, being opened in the suburbs, and luckily I got my hands on the project. It was the Biomedical Equipment planning that had the first tinkling of CapexIQ. Back then, I used to call it simply the ROI Calculator. If you were to comb through the code on GitHub, you might still find remnants of it somewhere around in the initial planning documents. Once we had sorted out the equipment that was to be needed for the project, I was asked to figure out when we would hit break-even, when would we get the returns on our investments, and so on. To be a little more honest, they basically asked me, “Figure out, when will we make our money back?” The fancy terms were merely my additions. And so began the journey to figure out how to do so. The consultancy allowed me to connect with various veteran managers across the Indian healthcare sector. That gave me a serious glimpse into how the industry calculated ROI for their capital-intensive clinical investments. The idea for them was very simple, or so I learned from my conversations with them and inspection of their Excel models. Each manager, especially veterans, had their own Excel models, some more advanced than others, some more traditional, ignoring inflation and depreciation, while some focused on NPV and IRR, but none were as comprehensive as they could be. It wasn’t that these managers couldn’t figure out on their own how to include inflation, payer mix, or even adjust for seasonal changes. They could, but it wasn’t worth the time. Approximations could work, so they said. As an intern, I usually had one or two tangents of projects, and a whole day to myself to take it all to perfection. And so I did. I made the most ambitious Excel model that I could make, taking into account every little thing I could. Assisted by AIs, I must say my productivity was through the roof. Usually, you’d be stuck finding what you need in government standards, a dense 1,500-volume, split across 4 sections. But times are different; a needle in a haystack is nothing for models of today’s age. And so there I was, a humble Excel titled ROI Calculator, beefed up to multiple pages, interlinked with formulas. I was very proud of it. And so was my supervisor. And hence the consultancy kept it, their own ROI Calculator. But I wished to make it more accessible. After all, I wondered how many times hospitals may have cancelled some high-CAPEX purchase like CT or MRI, especially in my country where the doctor-to-population ratio is 1:811. Maybe if they had hands on a better tool to predict their chances, maybe some would dare? Would go ahead with a purchase and reduce the burden on India’s public health infrastructure. With my discussions with managers, I realised there was no standard template they could use. Everyone had their own models, their own idea of what a discount rate should be. So there needed to be something standard, something that could be used as a foundation and adapted to their needs, something that reflected the current market condition and realistic assumptions reflecting the Indian market. And so I made CapexIQ, a transparent, open-source, and reliable calculator that provides managers the flexibility to go as deep into building their clinical investment case as they want. There was yet a small accessibility issue still, but more on that later. The Building I think when I started with the build of CapexIQ, I had a subscription to Claude, which was almost about to end. I used Claude Code to plan out my build. Using my Excel model as a base, we drafted out how the website would look, what variables we would use, we designed the dashboard, and used deep research agents to ground our assumptions in trusted sources. Once that was done, I shifted to Codex. I’d like to point out, in all of the building process, no frontier model was used. Since I could either afford Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus, I primarily relied on GPT-5.5 Low and then Luna High-Max when it came out. I was exceptionally blown away with Luna. At High or Max, it delivered substantial performance, could do parallel running tasks, without making an exceptional dent in my usage. That allowed me to push further with my building efforts. I designed a new system, all thanks to Codex. I proudly call it “Cascading Parallelism.” Essentially, I’d start with a plan, which would be the one where I would spend a substantial amount of my time. Once that was done, I’d divide my plan into sections that can run in parallel. I would then instruct the parallel agents to cascade, to start another thread with a prompt that builds up on their work. Suppose there are 6 stages, A to F. And A and B can run in parallel, while C, D, E, and F relied on the work they did. (Each of A to F are different agents, who each used subagents as they wished.) So: A —> C —> D —> F B —> F This approach allowed me to stop becoming a copy-and-paste tool, starting and inspecting agents’ work. I couldn’t have achieved this level of orchestration in Claude Code. And I am very happy with this way of building. It makes me spend time where I need to spend it, planning, and I can then come back hours later when all of it is done. This also helps my managerial sense, for this allows me to maximise the output I receive per agent hour. I created a small system while I used Claude (which I later found was more ubiquitous than I had earlier anticipated). Agents would read intro , a brief Markdown file that introduced them to the project, made them aware of where the project spec was located, where the directory was located, instructed them to write in 'handoff.md' once they were done, and maintain an issue tracker. The spec list would have all the information related to work phases, so all I had to do was start an agent, and the rest of the context was always available for them. However, this was crude and still required me to intervene after every agent was done. This was simplified tenfold when I moved to Codex. The orchestration between agents was seamless. I did learn that as long as your planning is immaculate, the bugs you encounter later on do decrease quite a bit. As long as you have an idea as to how each bit of your software should act, and you can plan it out, agents have no issue executing your vision. And all of this by lower-end models running for a very usage-conscious user. The Accessibility Issue and WebMCP I sent out the early version of CapexIQ to all the managers I had earlier connected with and requested them to try it out, either on one of their previous cases or a new one if they had. Some did get back to me, praising how easy it was. They especially loved that they could export their data in a well-formatted Excel. I am glad they did. I was proud of that feature, and I knew how much it means to managers to have their Excels neatly embedded with formulas. A sentiment I wholeheartedly agree with. They did mention they could never dig deeper again. Payer mix, life cycle, was often untouched by them. It was a problem. I was thinking of converting CapexIQ into a plugin or maybe building a semantic extractor where they could just upload their PDFs and my algorithm could do its best to extract useful data from it, but none of it would be perfect. And then I came across the WebMCP challenge on X. The prizes may be enticing, but for me, this would solve the accessibility issue that I was facing! I went on to inspect what it meant, had a conversation with my agents as to how compatible it would be and how we could integrate it with CapexIQ. And oh, how happy I was to see how it could make using the product so much easier for my target audience. It wasn’t that the managers could not fill the form. It was maybe a little more than that. Form filling is one thing; during work, there are so many things an operations manager has to go through. Maybe they wouldn’t bother with it, or maybe, as one pointed out to me, “We are not finance guys, we don’t know how to assume so many different variables.” For me then, WebMCP acts as a solution to my clientele. I tried my best to make CapexIQ as accessible as I could. Every variable has a tooltip attached to guide users as to what it means, how to fill it, and where to find its source. But I guess it becomes tedious to go through HIS (Hospital Information System) for every other variable. And so, WebMCP solved all of that.
