title: CloudSwarm: Agent-Native Cloud Infrastructure CAD
pitch: Humans and external LLMs co-design AWS/Azure/GCP topologies in real-time. Powered by WebMCP, CloudSwarm compiles production Terraform and executes live SecOps/FinOps audits with zero race conditions.
about_excerpt: Humans and external LLMs co-design AWS/Azure/GCP topologies in real-time. Powered by WebMCP, CloudSwarm compiles production Terraform and executes live SecOps/FinOps audits with zero race conditions. Like Comment Story Updates 💡 Inspiration Modern cloud architecture is trapped between two disconnected silos. On one side, solutions architects sketch static boxes on visual whiteboards (like Miro or Lucidchart) that are non-executable, drift from reality within days, lack cost awareness, and cannot be programmatically audited. On the other side, DevOps engineers spend weeks authoring thousands of lines of Terraform in text editors, reviewing complex infrastructure pull requests without spatial context—leading to silent security misconfigurations and budget blowouts. When the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) was introduced, the missing link became obvious to me: What if the web browser itself became an agent-native cloud workstation where a human engineer and external LLMs co-architect multi-cloud systems in real time? Instead of brittle DOM-scraping or slow sequential click-bots, WebMCP enables external models to discover typed tools, inspect live spatial canvas state, and execute atomic architectural mutations right alongside human engineers. 🚀 What it does CloudSwarm is an enterprise multi-cloud architecture CAD workstation built entirely around the WebMCP standard. Simultaneous Human + AI Co-Design: Human architects drag primitives from a 108-item multi-cloud catalog (AWS, Azure, GCP) and wire dependencies with the mouse. Simultaneously, external LLMs (via ChatGPT Desktop or Claude) can inspect state, provision GPU clusters, attach WAF shields, and route fabrics over WebMCP JSON-RPC. 4-Agent Concurrent Swarm: I natively route multi-agent workflows across specialized roles: Atlas (Compute/Infra), Breach (Security/WAF), Forge (Storage/Data), and Cost (FinOps). Organic Hardware-Accelerated Cursors: AI cursors glide across the canvas displaying concise task badges (e.g., Linking 800G Fabric ) letting humans watch the AI's physical workflow in real-time. Bidirectional Terraform HCL2 Sync: Canvas topologies continuously compile into production-ready HashiCorp Configuration Language. Modifications to the live code editor automatically update the visual topology in real time. FinOps & Zero-Trust Verification: Live multi-cloud rate cards compute hourly and monthly spend, while a continuous CIS Benchmark 1.5 engine audits security posture (e.g., 100/100 A+ ) with automated remediation. Time-Travel Decision DAG: Every architectural change is an immutable commit in a Directed Acyclic Graph. You can rewind history, fork experimental branches, or view visual A/B diffs. ⚙️ How I built it WebMCP Protocol Engine: I implemented 35 registered WebMCP tools over both window.modelContext and a high-performance local HTTP/SSE bridge ( :3001/mcp ) supporting JSON-RPC 2.0. 64-Stripe Entity Lock Manager: To prevent race conditions and "last-write-wins" corruption when human architects and multiple external LLMs modify adjacent resources simultaneously, I built a highly-concurrent lock manager. Optimistic State Engine: Mutations are evaluated as atomic RFC 6902 JSON-Patch transactions. Failed constraints or security violations roll back in microseconds without interrupting the human workflow. Frontend Stack: Built with React 19, TypeScript Strict Mode, and Tailwind CSS. ⚡ Challenges I ran into Single-Threaded State Contention: Coordinating simultaneous user mouse interactions and high-throughput external LLM tool batches without freezing the UI. I solved this with my 64-stripe fine-grained entity locking. Cursor Lifecycle & Perception: Preventing AI cursors from flashing or unmounting prematurely. I engineered a persistent lifecycle where cursors glide smoothly ( cubic-bezier CSS transitions) and display readable task badges before gracefully fading out to idle states. Bidirectional AST Synchronization: Compiling unstructured graph topologies into clean, idempotent Terraform HCL2, while parsing raw text edits back into deterministic visual graph nodes. 🏆 Accomplishments that I'm proud of True Multi-Agent Concurrency: Up to 4 external ChatGPT Desktop sessions can manipulate the exact same canvas simultaneously without deadlock or state corruption. Zero Frontend API Keys: A fully sovereign architecture. The workstation holds zero API keys; external LLMs bring their own intelligence over the open protocol. Massive Enterprise Catalog: 108 accurate, multi-cloud CAD primitives providing complete coverage across AWS, Azure, and GCP. Production-Grade Reliability: Backed by 38 test suites and 510/510 passing unit tests (100% green) covering adversarial stress, CAS rollbacks, and multi-cloud compiler accuracy. 🧠 What I learned WebMCP transforms autonomous agents from simple conversational assistants into active, spatial teammates. When AI models can observe live interface state and execute fine-grained tools over an open protocol, the boundary between human design and autonomous synthesis disappears. Giving an LLM a physical cursor in a CAD environment fundamentally changes how humans trust and verify AI actions. 🔮 What's next for CloudSwarm Direct Cloud Deployment: Adding 1-click terraform apply executions via ephemeral runner containers to actually spin up the drawn infrastructure. Live Reverse Ingestion: Importing existing AWS/Azure environments via terraform plan or CloudFormation into interactive, editable canvas DAGs. Global Multi-Tenant WebSockets: Expanding from local WebMCP bridges to distributed cloud rooms so global engineering teams and AI swarms can collaborate in the same browser session. title: Mausam
pitch: Mausam turns Mumbai’s live weather evidence into agent-ready, actionable forecasts through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Mausam turns Mumbai’s live weather evidence into agent-ready, actionable forecasts through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Interactive map close-up - Zoomed view of the MMR map with rainfall intensity scale Desktop landing view - Mausam header with live status and the Mumbai rainfall intelligence map Mobile layout - Mausam on a phone-sized viewport, showing header and map Full product page - End-to-end scroll of the Mausam site, from hero through map and supporting sections MMR rainfall map - Full Mumbai Metropolitan Region choropleth with locality labels and intensity legend Mausam Mausam (pronounced "mow-sum") is the Hindi word for weather or season. I chose the name because this project grew out of Mumbai's unpredictable monsoon. In Hindi, people often ask, "Mausam kaisa hai?" , or "How is the weather?" My project tries to answer the more useful version of that question: What changed? Where is the rain moving? Does Borivali face the same risk as the rest of Mumbai? Is this worth interrupting someone for? Inspiration Mumbai's weather rarely behaves like a simple forecast. During the monsoon, the sky can change within minutes. One suburb may get intense rain while another stays almost dry. A forecast that says "rain in Mumbai" may be technically correct and still be useless to someone deciding whether to leave home. That gap inspired Mausam. It watches several sources, compares new evidence with the last report, and sends an update only when something has changed. I started with one question: Can I build a weather service that remains alert without becoming noisy? What it does Mausam produces two complementary weather reports for Mumbai: A near-term nowcast covering approximately the next three to six hours. A five-day outlook comparing GFS and ECMWF forecast models. The primary nowcast combines: IMD PPI-Z and SRI radar frames; Windy rain-accumulation imagery; short-range GFS and ECMWF frames; readings from Borivali and Kandivali East; scraped rain statistics; local weather-station observations; and the previous report’s state. It evaluates Borivali separately from the wider Mumbai Metropolitan Region because rainfall can vary significantly across the city. The five-day pipeline compares GFS and ECMWF at five forecast horizons: $$ 2\ \text{models} \times 5\ \text{horizons} = 10\ \text{forecast frames} $$ Mausam delivers the result through email, Discord, a local alert banner, and an Astro website. It also chooses when to check again. Dangerous conditions get a faster follow-up; stable conditions can wait. The website also exposes three read-only WebMCP tools: get_weather_nowcast get_weather_outlook get_forecast_reasoning A compatible browser agent can call these tools to read the forecast as structured data instead of scraping the page. How I built it I built Mausam over five months with Bun and TypeScript. Each month solved a problem that appeared once the previous version started running in real conditions. April: Building the evidence pipeline The first version downloaded radar images and stored them in S3-compatible object storage. I wrote utilities to find the latest image, convert it to a compact JPEG, compare it with the previous frame, upload new evidence, and safely remove old objects. That led to the rule at the center of the project: $$ \text{Analyse} = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if evidence changed} \ 1, & \text{during the morning guarantee} \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ Weather sources often publish the same frame more than once. Analysing every copy would waste multimodal model calls and send repetitive notifications. Mausam compares the image bytes first. A morning exception still guarantees one baseline report each day. Once that worked, I connected the images to a multimodal weather agent. I added rain observations, local station data, saved summaries, email delivery, Telegram alerts, and BullMQ scheduling around it. By the end of April, Mausam had evolved from an image-processing script into a continuously scheduled weather service. May: Making scheduling dependable In May, I focused on the less exciting part that decides whether an automated service survives: failure handling. The pipeline schedules another attempt when a source fails or an image has not changed. Active-hour checks stop jobs from running at unsuitable times, while severity-based delays revisit urgent conditions sooner. This was when scheduling became part of the weather decision rather than a fixed cron interval. June: Adding rendered maps and Discord Some weather sources do not provide a direct image. Windy renders its accumulation map inside a web application. I added Puppeteer to open the page, wait for the weather layer, take a controlled screenshot, and pass it through the same pipeline as a downloaded image. A shared ingestion helper means the rest of the application does not need to know where an image came from. Discord replaced Telegram as the technical reporting channel. A separate gRPC integration handles delivery, so communication failures stay outside the weather analysis process. I also added Uptime Kuma heartbeats and automatic startup jobs so Mausam could run unattended. July: Expanding from hours to days The original system only answered, "What happens over the next few hours?" In July, I added a second pipeline to answer, "What could the next five days look like?" It finds the newest usable GFS and ECMWF runs, resolves changing Tropical Tidbits image URLs, and collects frames at approximately (+24), (+48), (+72), (+96), and (+120) hours. All ten images are staged before analysis. If one required frame cannot be prepared, the incomplete set is removed instead of mixing different or partial model runs. Running the system exposed another problem: a retry could repeat actions that had already succeeded. I strengthened the workflow with: Zod-validated configuration and model output; Redis-backed previous-report state; decision caching using evidence-derived run identifiers; delivery locks and completion markers; follow-up-job deduplication; and separation between queue construction and process side effects. The model interprets uncertain weather evidence. Regular application code controls persistence, delivery, retries, and scheduling. This boundary keeps free-form model behavior away from side effects. August: Building the web experience In August, I started retaining the two newest frames from each primary source. A pair of images shows basic movement and development that one snapshot cannot. I also compressed primary evidence to reduce multimodal input cost. The estimated image-token load fell from roughly 50,000 tokens in the earlier high-frame case to around 7,500: $$ 1-\frac{7{,}500}{50{,}000} =0.85 =85\% $$ I extended the agents with structured website fields and Zod validation. Using bun:sqlite , I persist nowcasts and outlooks for an Astro and React frontend. The stored data includes separate Borivali and Mumbai/MMR alert levels, headlines, rain probability, peak timing, confidence, station observations, source summaries, daily outlook cards, model comparisons, and detailed reasoning. The website presents the current alert, local conditions, five-day forecast, source summaries, model comparison, and reasoning. I also integrated an interactive Mumbai Metropolitan Region map. It connects report data to localities and visualizes alert severity, rain intensity, forecast movement, and differences across the region. The last addition was WebMCP. When a browser exposes document.modelContext , the React application registers three focused, read-only weather tools. Each returns bounded structured data and labels the result as AI guidance. Browsers without WebMCP still receive the complete website, making agent interaction a progressive enhancement rather than a dependency. The full path now looks like this: $$ \text{Weather sources} \rightarrow \text{Evidence pipeline} \rightarrow \text{Structured reasoning} \rightarrow \text{Reliable delivery} \rightarrow \text{Web experience} \rightarrow \text{WebMCP interaction} $$ Challenges I ran into Inconsistent weather sources Some sources provide files. Others need browser rendering. Forecast URLs change with model initialization times, and station or rain-statistics endpoints can fail on their own. I wrote source-specific resolvers behind one ingestion interface. A missing required radar frame stops the run. An optional source can fail without taking the whole forecast down, and Mausam uses retained evidence where appropriate. Detecting real changes A newly published file does not always contain new weather. Running the agent on identical frames would consume resources and wear out the person receiving alerts. Exact byte comparison is predictable, but it has a trade-off: an encoding change can look new to the system even when the two images look identical to a person. Preventing duplicate alerts A run may successfully send an email and then fail while posting to Discord. Retry

title: BOSAI — Governed WebMCP
pitch: Discoverable is not authorized — Human GO, single-use permits, verified readback, and replay denial for WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: Discoverable is not authorized — Human GO, single-use permits, verified readback, and replay denial for WebMCP agents. Like Comment Story Updates Discoverable is not authorized WebMCP gives agents a structured way to discover and call tools exposed by a website. BOSAI explores the next problem: tool discovery should not automatically grant execution authority. BOSAI — Governed WebMCP is a public WebMCP demo that lets an agent inspect a synthetic duplicate-charge case, propose a refund, request authorization, execute only after an explicit Human GO, independently verify the result, retrieve an evidence receipt, and deny replay of the same single-use permit. The core idea is simple: Agents can discover and propose. Humans retain authority. BOSAI verifies what actually happened. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Without structured tools, agents often have to infer actions from UI state. WebMCP makes the capability surface explicit. BOSAI uses that explicit surface to add a second layer: an authority boundary around consequential actions. The live app registers eight native WebMCP tools: inspect_case inspect_transaction propose_refund request_authorization authorization_status execute_refund verify_refund get_evidence_receipt The agent has no Human GO tool. It can reach HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED, but it cannot grant itself approval. The demo flow The challenge uses a fully synthetic EUR 49 duplicate-charge refund scenario. The agent inspects the case and transaction. It creates a bounded proposal. BOSAI stops at HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED. Before approval, the mutation count is 0. A human explicitly approves that exact proposal. BOSAI issues a single-use permit. The synthetic refund commits exactly once. Independent readback returns VERIFIED and an evidence receipt. The same execution is attempted again. The replay is denied, and the replay mutation count remains 0. No real payment is made and no customer data is used. Better human + agent interaction The user experience is not "AI asks for permission" as a loose convention. The approval state is explicit, inspectable, and bound to one exact proposal. Agent: inspect, reason, propose, request authorization, execute within the granted permit, verify. Human: retain the authority to approve or deny the exact consequential action. BOSAI: enforce the execution boundary, record the result, and deny permit replay. This makes WebMCP more useful for workflows where agents should be capable without becoming self-authorizing. Implementation The challenge surface is a standalone browser app implemented with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It registers tools through WebMCP and maintains deterministic synthetic challenge state for proposals, authorization, execution, verification, evidence receipts, and replay denial. The public challenge surface is served as static assets on OVHcloud through a scoped Caddy route. The live browser proof was run in Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP testing enabled. What was added during the challenge BOSAI existed before the WebMCP Challenge. During the challenge submission period, it was meaningfully extended with a dedicated WebMCP implementation and public challenge surface, including the eight WebMCP tools above, a synthetic duplicate-charge workflow, explicit HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED behavior, zero-mutation pre-approval enforcement, exact Human GO binding, a single-use execution permit, independent verified readback, an evidence receipt, replay denial with zero replay mutations, and a public live browser proof surface. The WebMCP challenge implementation is isolated from proprietary BOSAI internals and is being published as a standalone public-safe repository for judging. Live proof The validated live flow demonstrated 8 registered WebMCP tools, HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED before authorization, 0 pre-GO mutations, 1 authorized synthetic mutation after Human GO, VERIFIED independent readback, an evidence receipt, REPLAY_DENIED on the duplicate execution attempt, 0 replay mutations, and no blocking browser/runtime errors. Live app: https://bosai.syncguard.fr/webmcp-challenge/index.html Operating principle Intelligence is not authority. WebMCP makes agent capabilities discoverable. BOSAI demonstrates how those capabilities can remain human-governed, bounded, verifiable, and auditable. about_excerpt: - Bittensor is network for blockchain - Bittensor have subnets - Token be called alpha in bittensor - Token of each subnet can swap to Tao (coin of bittensor that listed) Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Inspiration Bittensor Subnet 88 penalizes duplicate portfolios: any two allocation vectors within an L1-normalized distance of 0.01 get scored down. Before this project, the only way to fix that was trial and error by hand. We wanted to see if WebMCP could let an agent actually close that loop — propose, measure, adjust, re-measure — instead of the app just saying "no." What it does Alpha Investing lets a human and an AI agent build the same Bittensor Subnet 88 portfolio on the same screen, sharing one state. It exposes 12 WebMCP tools covering the full workflow — query subnets, generate a portfolio from two ranking criteria, edit allocations, and save it. The centerpiece is escape_dedupe : when save_portfolio rejects a duplicate, the agent can call it to perturb weights until the portfolio clears the safety threshold, then save — all visible in a live Agent Activity panel. How we built it React 19 + Vite, entirely client-side — no backend, no real funds, simulated subnet data. WebMCP tools register via document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback, since the spec is still moving), sharing the exact same state and validation path as the UI buttons, so an agent can't bypass any rule a human can't. Tool descriptions were iterated against a real agent (Gemini, through Chrome's WebMCP testing flag) until it reliably found the escape_dedupe recovery path on its own. Challenges we ran into No WebMCP-native browser was available for most of development, so we built a debug bridge that mirrors every registered tool onto window.__webmcpTools , letting us call the exact execute() path a real agent would — on the real production build — before we ever had a WebMCP-capable browser to test in. Once we did get a live agent running, we found that bundling multi-step instructions into one prompt confused it into picking the same ranking metric for both portfolio groups; one natural instruction per turn fixed it. Getting the agent to autonomously reach for escape_dedupe , rather than just reporting the rejection, took a few rounds of sharpening the tool descriptions. Accomplishments that we're proud of The generate → save → rejected → escape_dedupe → save loop is verified working end-to-end on the live production deployment, not a simulation. A real agent correctly reconstructed multi-part portfolio criteria from natural language and self-recovered from a dedupe rejection without being told how. The WebMCP layer is fully additive — the app behaves identically for anyone on a browser without WebMCP support. What we learned Tool descriptions are a real interface, not documentation — wording (units, when to call a recovery tool, when to switch tabs) measurably changes what an autonomous agent does. Building a bridge to test real tool code independent of browser support was more valuable than trying to hand-simulate agent behavior. What's next for alpha-investing An Undo action wired into the Agent Activity panel, a compare_portfolios read tool, and highlighting the rows an agent just changed so the human/agent shared-state story is legible in real time, not just in the log. title: Handrail WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP server that gives AI agents safe, reliable access to web workflows
about_excerpt: A WebMCP server that gives AI agents safe, reliable access to web workflows Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents should eventually help streamline day-to-day store operations, but a tool should never become a way to circumvent orders, refunds, price adjustments, etc., without restraint. With Handrail I aim to add more control by allowing the agent to investigate orders and propose actions that the merchant can ultimately approve and execute. What it does Handrail is a browser based store operations console. Agents can search orders, customers, policies, inventory, shipping, products, and sales data using WebMCP tools. When the agent needs to perform an action like issue a refund or cancel an order, the agent cannot mutate the data. Handrail does validation and creates a parameter approved ticket. The merchant approves the action in the application and only then can the agent execute the same parameters. The guided demo shows the refund for an order ORD-1042 and shows validation failures and request protections against requests that are mismatched or replayed. How I built it Handrail was built using Vite to speed up development and deployed as purely a browser based React application. Handrail also provides a fallback interface when WebMCP tools are not available as it registers 14 WebMCP tools. The safety flow is implemented in the application logic: agent suggestion → approval → exact parameter match → one time execution → confirmation All demo data is held in memory, so it can be safely reset without a backend or payment integration. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was still making the approval step more meaningful than just a confirmation must be checked. An approval should be for the actual amount, the actual order and the actual operation, not a statement like an agent is going to “do this later”. I dealt with this by freezing the canonical parameters for each ticket, validating them again at the time of ticket execution, preventing ticket replay, enforcing expiry, and recording both successful actions and denials in an activity log. What I learned Executable actions and audit receipts make sense between reaching out and approval. The executive semantics of an actual execution are very important when it comes to safe agent tooling, and this is more important than having a label like “read-only” or “write” on that action. title: Familiar
pitch: Dungeon Familiar: A Co-op Game You Play With an AI Agent
about_excerpt: Dungeon Familiar: A Co-op Game You Play With an AI Agent Like Comment Story Updates game architecture About the project Inspiration Most AI-in-the-browser demos script an agent to click through a UI built for humans. WebMCP lets a page expose tools directly to an agent instead. We wanted an agent with a real role in the game: its own senses, its own blind spots, equal footing with the human player. We built a dungeon that two players explore together, and only one of them can see. The human reads the room. The familiar, an AI, reaches the room's hidden machinery only through whatever WebMCP tools that room exposes. Drop either player and the dungeon stays locked. What it does Dungeon Familiar is a turn-based co-op dungeon crawler for one human and one AI agent. The human moves through the dungeon, fights, and describes what they see. The familiar has no eyes. It acts only through WebMCP tools registered on the page, and those tools change as the human walks between rooms. Tool discovery drives progression. Enter the library and the familiar gains archive.search() and bookshelf.rotate() . Enter the observatory and those tools vanish, replaced by telescope.rotate() and lens.change() . Four rooms, four tool sets, each puzzle solved only when the human describes what they see and the familiar acts on it. The game ships no LLM and no backend, only a static page that registers WebMCP tools and waits for whatever agent drives the browser. Right now that means the ChatGPT desktop app or Codex, both of which added WebMCP support in August 2026. How we built it Plain TypeScript and Vite, no framework. Three layers that don't talk to each other carelessly: engine/ : a pure, DOM-free state machine. webmcp/ : registers and unregisters the current room's tools. ui/ : sprites, rendering, title screen, admin panel. engine/ imports nothing from the other two. The rules stay testable in isolation, and an agent can only touch game state through a defined tool. No LLM sat in our development loop, so we built a second, local mirror of the tool registry from the same tool definitions. That lets us play and test the game from the browser console ( df.callTool(...) ) without a real WebMCP client. Both registries run through the same callTool() , so the rules can't diverge between a real agent and a test harness. Art comes from licensed Unity asset packs (Franuka's RPG UI and Fantasy RPG series, MutterPixel dungeon tiles). A small Python tool parses Unity .meta / .anim files into a sprite atlas and animation clips we consume in TypeScript. The build deploys as a static site through the @openai/sites-vite-plugin , so it opens inside ChatGPT's or Codex's built-in browser. Challenges we ran into Browser vendors kept changing the spec under us. WebMCP's tool-registration entry point moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext mid-project. AbortSignal -based unregistration landed only in Chrome 153; older runtimes ignore abort() and throw InvalidStateError when a tool re-registers under the same name. We wrote a runtime probe, detectUnregisterStrategy() , that picks between three fallback paths and shows the chosen strategy in the UI, because we couldn't assume any one browser's behavior. Nothing to test against. For most of development, no WebMCP-capable client existed. We built the local mirror registry because we had no agent to test against until late in the project. The repo states it outright: the WebMCP integration has not been verified against a real client end to end. Information asymmetry is fragile. The game collapses the moment a tool response leaks something only the human should know: a color, a bearing, which statue is lit. One convenient template literal does it. We caught two real regressions this way and wrote tests ( tests/asymmetry.test.ts ) that run every tool against every plausible input and fail the build on any leaked color word, including once catching a bug in the test itself (a regex that matched the English word "a"). Assets didn't match their labels. Sprite sheets that looked like animation strips were 4×4 grids. A folder named for icons held book covers. A file called Tileset.png held props, not dungeon floor. We resolved all of it against Unity's own .meta files instead of eyeballing dimensions. Accomplishments that we're proud of Four playable rooms end to end, each with its own WebMCP tool set and puzzle, plus a title screen, ending card, and a hidden admin/demo mode ( Shift+L+A ) for fast demos. 45 tests passing, a clean typecheck, and a ~47 kB production build. No framework overhead. Refusal messages double as documentation. Every tool call passes a guard, and a rejected call explains what to do instead, so an agent learns the turn structure without any prompt engineering. A leak-proof information boundary between the two players, enforced by automated tests. What we learned WebMCP's value is a webpage that hands an agent a role of its own, with its own capabilities and its own gaps, separate from the human's. We designed tool descriptions and refusal text as the whole interface, instead of writing separate instructions for the agent. That forced an honest test of whether each tool made sense on its own. The spec is young: entry points and unregistration semantics changed under us more than once. A runtime feature-detection layer, instead of a hardcoded assumption about one browser, was the difference between a demo that works and a demo that works only on our machine. What's next for Familiar Broaden hazard variety per room. One enemy behavior repeats across three rooms today, which works but asks the human the same question each time. Expand the familiar roster and perks, and move off Sites onto our own domain. title: DiscountHub WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP-powered deal discovery layer that lets AI agents search live discounts, promo codes, and store offers directly from DiscountHub.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered deal discovery layer that lets AI agents search live discounts, promo codes, and store offers directly from DiscountHub. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP in action: a browser agent finds offers and displays the same results for the shopper. DiscountHub brings product deals, promo codes, and store offers into one place. Browse product deals with filters for country, store, category, and minimum discount. Find store promotions and coupon codes, review their conditions, and copy a code. DiscountHub's own AI Finder: laptop search results with prices and links to the stores. Inspiration Finding a useful deal should take less effort than comparing dozens of browser tabs. I built DiscountHub to bring product discounts, promo codes, and store offers into one place. For this challenge, I wanted browser agents to use that catalogue directly, while keeping shoppers involved in every decision. What it does DiscountHub WebMCP gives compatible browser agents four tools: search_deals — search product discounts with optional filters. find_promo_codes — find coupon codes and their available conditions. get_store_offers — retrieve a store's product discounts and promotions. get_best_deals — find the largest percentage discounts. Agents receive structured results, and the same offers appear on the website using DiscountHub's existing cards. A shopper can review prices, compare offers, copy a coupon, and choose which store link to open. The tools support relevant filters such as keywords, country, store, price, and minimum discount. Prices and budgets are in USD. Coupon codes come from the catalogue; they are not verified at checkout. Why WebMCP Shopping requests combine several constraints: what someone wants, their budget, and the market they are shopping in. WebMCP gives the browser agent explicit tools and input schemas for these requests. The agent can retrieve structured offer data without extracting it from page layouts. The visible result matters just as much: people can inspect the offers returned by the agent and continue browsing from the same page. Tool calls search the catalogue; shoppers decide whether to visit a store. How I built it Existing foundation: DiscountHub already had a public website, a Flutter application, a Python/FastAPI backend, a SQLite catalogue, automated offer processing, and its own AI Finder. New work for this challenge: I added native WebMCP registration, four tool definitions, validated inputs, structured responses, and shared on-page results. The implementation uses document.modelContext where available, with support for the earlier navigator.modelContext API. The JavaScript adapter reuses the existing public deals and promotions endpoints. It handles pagination, timeouts, cancellation, and partial failures. It excludes expired or future-dated offers and coupons without codes. Older requests cannot overwrite newer visible results. The website and WebMCP integration live in a separate repository from the backend and mobile application. Both repositories include MIT licenses. The WebMCP implementation and dated commit history document the challenge addition. Challenges The main challenge was making tool results dependable across browser API differences and changing catalogue data. Testing required both native tool execution in Chrome and checks against the live API. I also needed to preserve the familiar browsing experience while making agent results visible and understandable. Accomplishments All four tools were exercised through native browser execution. In the recorded live demo, Gemini uses Chrome's Model Context Tool Inspector to call search_deals for three headphone offers in the United States, under fifty dollars, with at least twenty percent off. Three offers appear on the page, giving the shopper and the agent a shared view of the results. What I learned A useful agent integration needs clear tool boundaries and visible outcomes. Structured data helps the agent act reliably; shared results help the person understand and evaluate what happened. What's next I plan to improve multilingual catalogue search, add clearer country and availability information, and make it easier to refine and compare an agent's results. I handled deployment, browser testing, and demo recording and editing. I used AI assistance for coding, debugging, documentation, and English narration. title: LifeOS
pitch: Your life, your agent, one workspace: LifeOS exposes 35 real WebMCP tools so an agent can manage your tasks, calendar, goals, and budget alongside you, not just click around a chatbot UI.
about_excerpt: Your life, your agent, one workspace: LifeOS exposes 35 real WebMCP tools so an agent can manage your tasks, calendar, goals, and budget alongside you, not just click around a chatbot UI. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard Tasks Calender goals Inspiration Every "AI agent" bolted onto a personal productivity app treats the agent like a second-class user: it has to look at the same UI a human sees, guess which button does what, click around, and hope nothing changed underneath it. We wanted to try the opposite: what if the agent and the human were first-class citizens of the same app, sharing the same underlying actions instead of the agent faking a human? WebMCP made that possible. Instead of screen-scraping or blind automation, a website can expose real, typed, described tools directly via document.modelContext.registerTool() . That's a fundamentally different relationship between a person, their agent, and their software — so we built LifeOS to explore it end to end, on a domain everyone actually needs: a personal command center for tasks, calendar, goals, shopping, expenses, and routines. What it does LifeOS is a full personal productivity app — tasks, calendar/schedule, goals with action plans, shopping lists, expense tracking, and recurring routines — with a complete, polished manual UI. On top of that, it exposes 35 real WebMCP tools across three risk tiers: Read (14 tools): get_today_overview, get_tasks, get_schedule, get_goals, get_shopping_list, get_expenses, get_routines, analyze_day, identify_conflicts, prioritize_tasks, analyze_spending, plan_my_day, plan_my_week, and more. Write (17 tools): create_task, update_task, complete_task, reschedule_task, create_goal, update_goal_progress, record_expense, create_routine, and more. Needs approval (4 tools): delete_task, apply_schedule_plan, set_budget, delete_budget — destructive, irreversible, or financial-target changes always pause for a human click before they happen. An agent can read your day, spot schedule conflicts, propose and apply a week plan, log an expense, or build a goal's action plan by calling a described tool with a validated schema — the same way it would call any API, except the API is the website you're looking at, and every change shows up instantly in the human UI too. How we built it Next.js 16 (App Router) + PostgreSQL via Prisma 7 + Auth.js v5, deployed on Vercel with Prisma Postgres. The core architectural rule: a human clicking a button and an agent calling a WebMCP tool both end up calling the exact same function in src/services/* . There is no separate "agent path" that can drift from what the UI does — lib/actions (Server Actions for the human UI) and webmcp/ (tool definitions + dispatcher for the agent) are both thin callers of one shared service layer, validated by the same Zod schemas either way. Client-side, components/webmcp/ registers all 35 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() on mount, exposes a live "WebMCP status" pill in the header, and ships a tool inspector at /app/activity that lists every registered tool with its schema and last-run time — useful for demoing and for debugging what the agent actually sees. Challenges we ran into Approval gating without breaking the "same function" rule. Destructive/financial tools (delete_task, set_budget, etc.) needed a human-in-the-loop approval step without forking the code path — we solved it with an approval state machine in the tool dispatcher that pauses before calling the shared service, rather than duplicating logic per surface. Prompt-injection defense. Any tool argument or stored content an agent reads (task titles, notes) has to be treated as untrusted data, never re-executed as instructions. We leaned on the WebMCP spec's annotations.readOnlyHint / annotations.untrustedContentHint fields and scoped every query to the authenticated user. Two real Next.js 16 / Prisma 7 issues surfaced while wiring generated Prisma output into a fresh Vercel deploy (a gitignored generated-client path breaking on npm install , fixed via a postinstall: prisma generate step) — documented in git history for anyone hitting the same thing. Verifying WebMCP itself. document.modelContext is only available behind an active origin trial / Chrome flag ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) or ChatGPT's in-app browser, so we were careful to only claim what we could actually verify live, and documented what still needs a WebMCP-flagged browser to confirm. Accomplishments that we're proud of 35 real tools, not a toy demo — spanning read, write, and approval-gated actions across six real productivity domains. Zero drift between what a human can do and what the agent can do: one service layer, one set of Zod schemas. A real approval flow that actually blocks a destructive action until a human clicks "Approve" — verified with a Playwright end-to-end test that drives a real browser against a real server. 46 unit + integration tests plus a 3-test real-browser e2e suite, all green against a real Postgres database. What we learned Building the agent and human paths as two callers of one service layer, instead of two apps, was the single best decision — every feature we added to the UI was already agent-usable, and every bug we didn't have (an "agent version" of a feature quietly diverging from the human version) is a bug class WebMCP's model naturally avoids for you. What's next for LifeOS Multi-agent collaboration (a scheduling agent and a budgeting agent negotiating a shared calendar), richer WebMCP annotations for finer-grained trust, and expanding the risk-tiered approval model to cover shared/family accounts. title: Logo Maker
pitch: 333k+ SVG icons available to create a logo for your project. Best when you are converting any PNG logo to SVG logo. Logo quality highly dependent on instructions.
about_excerpt: 333k+ SVG icons available to create a logo for your project. Best when you are converting any PNG logo to SVG logo. Logo quality highly dependent on instructions. Like 1 Comment Story Updates state with final logo created, from png to svg default starting point Inspiration Every "make me a logo" tool on the web makes the same bet: a human sits at a canvas, drags shapes, and tweaks colors by eye. That bet breaks the moment an agent is the one trying to help. ChatGPT can describe a great logo in a sentence, but it had no way to actually place it, resize it, or apply a brand's real colors on a live canvas. WebMCP closes that gap: it lets an agent drive the same tool a person uses, through the same page, with no separate API to build or maintain. What it does Logo Maker ( https://logo.allsvgicons.com/ ) is a free, no-signup SVG logo editor. Six WebMCP tools are registered on the page via document.modelContext.registerTool : get_logo_maker_state : reads canvas size, background, every layer (with IDs and index), the current selection, safe-zone settings, and a shareable code/URL, optionally with the rendered SVG. update_logo_maker_state : partial, smart edits: apply an authentic brand preset (Instagram, Spotify, Stripe, Linear, Supabase, and more), toggle the safe-zone keyline, add/update/remove/clear layers by ID or index, or change selection, all without resending the full state. set_logo_maker_state : full-state replacement for bulk rebuilds. search_logo_icons : finds icons from the site's SVG library to drop onto the canvas. load_logo_maker_share : restores a saved design from its share code. get_brand_presets : lists the brand color/style presets an agent can apply by name. A person can open the same editor, drag layers, and see exactly what the agent changed, live, on the same canvas. What agents and people can now do together Ask ChatGPT (or any WebMCP-aware agent) for "an Instagram-style logo with a mountain icon, rotated 15 degrees" and it composes the layers itself, then hands back a working canvas a human can immediately refine by hand: nudge a layer, swap a color, export. Neither side has to fully finish the job alone; the agent handles the tedious part (search, place, apply preset, iterate on args) and the person keeps final visual judgment. How we built it Built with React inside an Astro site (allsvgicons.com), using document.modelContext.registerTool for each tool with Zod-derived JSON schemas for inputs. Layer state lives in a single React ref so both the UI and the WebMCP tool handlers read/write the same source of truth, no separate agent-facing state to keep in sync. Designs are shareable via a compact encoded string decoded by load_logo_maker_share , so an agent's output is a URL a person can open directly. Challenges we ran into Getting execute_tool semantics right from the agent side: getTools() returns a Promise and hands back tool handles, not names, so calling a tool means holding the handle rather than looking it up by string each time; args also need to go over as JSON-stringified payloads. On our end, the trickiest part was making update_logo_maker_state genuinely incremental (index-or-ID addressing into an array of layers) without forcing every agent call to resend a full canvas state. title: Poolwart — a safe agent-to-human handoff for water care
pitch: The agent interprets. Poolwart calculates. You verify.
about_excerpt: The agent interprets. Poolwart calculates. You verify. Like Comment Story Updates Poolwart turns an agent request into a visible, editable and safety-aware water-care calculation. Inspiration Pool and hot-tub owners often have three disconnected pieces of information: a water volume, a test result, and an active-chlorine percentage printed somewhere on a product label. Translating those values into a dose is tedious, and a generic assistant should not improvise safety-sensitive water-care arithmetic in chat. The useful division of work is different: an agent is good at understanding the messy request and extracting the inputs; a specialist site is good at deterministic, tested calculation; the owner must remain the person who verifies and acts. What it does Poolwart exposes two imperative WebMCP tools: calculate_chlor_topup calculates a dry-granule top-up from a measured free-chlorine value to the target range of the currently open Poolwart segment. calculate_chlor_shock calculates Poolwart's fixed +10 mg/l dry-granule shock increase. Calling a tool does not leave the answer trapped in an invisible tool response. It switches the visible calculator to the right mode, fills every input, and renders the normal dose, warnings, provenance, re-entry guidance, and disclaimer. The person can inspect or change every value and recalculate through the form. Poolwart calculates only. It never controls equipment, purchases a product, or physically doses water. How we built it The site uses imperative top-level registration through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema with numeric limits and additionalProperties: false , followed by defensive runtime validation. Both the manual form and WebMCP call one shared typed adapter, which delegates the actual arithmetic to the existing, tested @poolwart/wasser package. WebMCP is registered only after client mount and receives an AbortSignal , so tools are removed when the component unmounts or the page changes. Unsupported browsers keep the complete ordinary calculator. The challenge extension adds focused tests for calculation parity, boundaries, schemas, registration, lifecycle signals, result size, invalid inputs, unusually large volumes, and above-target measurements. How WebMCP improves the experience Without WebMCP, a user or browser agent must choose a form mode and transcribe each value. An assistant may instead calculate in chat, losing the specialist formula, segment-specific targets, warnings, and an editable verification surface. With WebMCP, the agent invokes a named capability on the page. Poolwart validates and calculates, then makes the handoff visible to the human. This is a genuine shared workspace: the agent can prepare the calculation, the site can prove what it used, and the person stays in control. What existed before the challenge Poolwart, the manual calculator, its deterministic water-care package, target ranges, safety copy, and server-rendered result pages existed before 2026-08-25. The two imperative WebMCP registrations, English tool contracts, shared form/tool adapter, structured outputs, agent provenance UI, lifecycle cleanup, and their tests were created for this challenge. The public repository tags the exported baseline as pre-webmcp ; git diff pre-webmcp..HEAD isolates the new work. See the complete challenge boundary and change log in CHALLENGE.md . Challenges and accomplishments The main design challenge was not exposing a formula—it was preserving one source of truth across a German human form and an English machine contract. Extracting the typed adapter removed the risk of the two paths drifting. An adversarial review also found that the pre-existing form treated any value above the lower target threshold as “in target,” including excessive readings. The challenge work now distinguishes above_target , shows a visible warning, and returns re-entry guidance and unusual-volume status to the agent. What we learned The strongest agent interface is not necessarily the one with the most autonomy. For safety-sensitive calculations, a narrow tool contract and an explicit human handoff are more valuable than an opaque answer. WebMCP can make the website the shared, inspectable source of truth instead of reducing it to a hidden backend. What's next After judging, the same narrow adapter pattern can expose other existing Poolwart calculators. The diagnostic wizard, image/OCR workflow, authentication, and hardware control remain deliberately out of scope until they have equally strong validation and human-review surfaces. Testing instructions Open the Whirlpool calculator in the current ChatGPT desktop in-app browser with a model that supports Site Tools. Ask: “My 1,000 litre hot tub reads 0.4 mg/l free chlorine. The label says 56% active chlorine. Calculate the top-up with Poolwart and show me the result there.” Confirm calculate_chlor_topup is selected and the visible form/result update. Ask: “Calculate a shock dose for my 1,000 litre hot tub using dry granules with 56% active chlorine, and show the calculation in Poolwart.” Confirm calculate_chlor_shock is selected and the shock/re-entry guidance is visible. Chrome alternative: use Chrome 149+, enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , restart, then inspect Application → WebMCP. No login or environment variables are required. title: QuoteFlow WebMCP
pitch: A browser-native quote-inquiry workspace with five WebMCP tools that let AI agents safely manage leads and prepare customer-ready response kits while keeping humans in control.
about_excerpt: A browser-native quote-inquiry workspace with five WebMCP tools that let AI agents safely manage leads and prepare customer-ready response kits while keeping humans in control. Like Comment Story Updates QuoteFlow’s landing screen presents three reviewable next steps, five ready site tools, and clear local-storage and no-contact assurances. The workspace shows a selected inquiry, human–agent activity, editable source details, and a response kit with the reply ready for review. The responsive mobile view keeps tool status, local-storage disclosure, primary actions, and trust assurances usable in a narrow viewport. Quote inquiries arrive as fragments: a customer, a service, a location, a timing preference, and a few uncertain details. QuoteFlow turns those fragments into one visible, durable inquiry queue and a clear next step. It is designed for owner-operated home-service businesses that want useful agent assistance without handing over consequential decisions. This is a strong fit for WebMCP because the structured work—capturing scope, preserving uncertainty, and preparing the next step—can be narrowly exposed, while pricing and commitments still need human judgment. A person or an agent can find an inquiry, create one, correct its details, or prepare a response kit through those domain tools. The same record remains visible in the human workspace, so a person can review, interrupt, correct, regenerate, copy, or print without losing context. This is much more dependable than asking an agent to infer a sequence of clicks. QuoteFlow prepares three reviewable drafts: a customer acknowledgment, a service-specific site-visit checklist, and a no-response follow-up. It never estimates a price, confirms a schedule, sends a message, or contacts a customer. Inquiry data and drafts are stored only in versioned browser localStorage ; when a person asks an agent to use a site tool, the requested result is shared with that current agent session and the app says so clearly. Every draft requires human review before use. Inspiration I wanted to explore a practical middle ground between a blank form and an autonomous CRM. Home-service inquiries contain enough structure for an agent to help, but they also contain uncertainty that should stay visible to a human. The idea was to make the useful part—organizing scope and preparing the next three steps—fast and agent-friendly while keeping pricing, scheduling, deletion, and customer contact out of the agent’s reach. What it does QuoteFlow supports both ordinary browser use and WebMCP collaboration. In a compatible browser, it exposes exactly five site tools: list_quote_inquiries — read minimal summaries, filtered by status, service, or text. get_quote_inquiry — read one inquiry and bounded prepared-kit metadata, without draft bodies. create_quote_inquiry — validate, save, select, and visibly render a new local inquiry. update_quote_inquiry — apply a narrow field patch and mark existing drafts stale when source details change. prepare_response_kit — generate and display the acknowledgment, site-visit checklist, and follow-up for human review. The visible workspace and the tools use the same validation, persistence, status, and deterministic-generation paths. Business or sender names that have not been filled in become unmistakable [Business name] and [Sender name] placeholders and are returned as warnings; QuoteFlow never invents an identity. A browser without WebMCP reports Standard browser mode and keeps the complete manual workflow. How we built it QuoteFlow is a dependency-free static app built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and browser localStorage . core.js contains pure validation, normalization, fingerprints, service checklists, and deterministic response-kit generation. app.js owns the accessible human workspace, versioned local persistence, rendering, stale-state behavior, activity feedback, and the human-only clear-all control. webmcp.js feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool and imperatively registers the five tools at the top level of the page. Every tool input is a closed JSON schema with additionalProperties: false ; critical limits and enums are checked again at runtime. The two read tools declare readOnlyHint: true , all five tools disclose untrusted user/customer text, and write-tool descriptions state their local-storage and visible-UI effects. No backend, analytics, or application network request is required. Initial verification completed on August 29, 2026 and the same reviewed source was reverified on August 30: syntax checks passed, and the combined suite passed 10/10 tests (five dependency-free smoke tests plus the browser integration suite and its four scenarios), including schema and JSON round trips, routing, placeholder warnings, unchanged storage after rejected input, stale-state behavior, persistence, accessibility status regions, unsupported-browser fallback, and the 390 × 844 viewport check. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was defining a tool surface that was genuinely useful without becoming an unrestricted CRM API. Closed schemas, stable inquiry IDs, bounded read results, repeated runtime validation, explicit side-effect descriptions, and a human-review flag all had to work together. We also had to keep human and agent edits coherent. A corrected location, timing preference, business identity, or request detail can invalidate a polished-looking draft, so QuoteFlow fingerprints the source and disables copy/print until the kit is regenerated. Finally, WebMCP support cannot be assumed: feature detection and a full standard-browser path had to be treated as product behavior, not an error page. Accomplishments we’re proud of QuoteFlow demonstrates a complete human–agent loop in a small static app: an agent can create an inquiry, the person can see and correct it, and the agent can prepare three useful outputs without leaving hidden state behind. The queue, activity strip, status changes, stale warning, and generated drafts all update in the same visible workspace. We are especially proud of the safety boundaries. There is no agent tool for pricing, scheduling, deletion, or customer contact; invalid writes are rejected before storage changes; blank identities produce visible placeholders instead of fabricated details; and local storage is explained without pretending that agent calls are invisible. The full automated suite passes 10/10 tests. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools represent meaningful domain outcomes rather than clicks. A small, well-bounded interface can make an agent useful while leaving the person in control of ambiguous or consequential work. We also learned that “local” needs careful language. Browser-only persistence protects the app from needing a backend, but a tool result can still be shared with the current agent session. Clear disclosure, bounded results, runtime validation, visible effects, and stale-state handling are all part of the user experience—not just implementation details. What’s next Next we would add user-mediated import/export for moving a local queue between browsers, richer service-specific templates and photo/measurement notes, and a small audit view showing exactly which human or agent action changed a record. Any future messaging or scheduling integration would remain opt-in and explicitly human-confirmed; it would not turn the current review-first workflow into autonomous outreach. title: BotFlo AI Transformation Score (BATS) for S&P 500 Companies
pitch: Visualization tool for BotFlo AI Transformation Score (BATS) for S&P 500 companies with support for WebMCP
about_excerpt: Visualization tool for BotFlo AI Transformation Score (BATS) for S&P 500 companies with support for WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Clicking on a single ticker to see BATS score BATS Visualization Scatter plot visualization SQL Tab Heatmap Home Page SQL Tab Radar visualization BATS Score Company Details BotFlo Score Report Viewer BATS Q&A Section BATS Presentation Tab BATS Sector Score BATS AI Transformation Score Inspiration I already score earnings calls. BATS — BotFlo AI Transformation Score — is a 0–100 rubric for how seriously an S&P 500 company talks about AI transformation: a total, a sector read, and fifteen dimensions (including hype ). Long reports cite the transcript. The catalog at score.botflo.com is basically a big sortable table. That’s fine if you already know the ticker and just want to open one report. It doesn't work quite as well if you ask something like “average BATS score for healthcare sector” or “industrials ranked by hype” — you’re scrolling, filtering in your head, maybe exporting to Excel. What you actually want is a query and a chart, not another row in a grid. This page puts the season snapshot in the browser: a gallery of 25 charts, DuckDB for ad-hoc SQL, and WebMCP so an agent can drive the query surface instead of guessing at clicks. What it does Visualization: https://f9c93fe1.bats-viz.pages.dev/ Catalog: https://score.botflo.com Season in the file: 1 July 2026 – end of September 2026 (still open) Note: I froze the catalog site on 27 Aug 2026 to keep everything consistent between website and demo video and project submission etc. I will resume updating the site after the contest is over. Gallery — fixed views of the snapshot (25 chart cards). SQL tab + charts — you or an agent asks a question; the page switches to SQL, runs it in-browser, draws only chart types that fit the result. Company report — click a ticker in the result table and you land on the full BATS write-up at score.botflo.com. In the demo I use UnitedHealth: 79 , tied for the top in Health Care. It’s a slideshow-style report, not a wall of text — each claim links straight into the earnings transcript and highlights the line it came from. The Q&A section is broken out question by question, same drill. The company report also includes the general AI Transformation score as well as the sector specific AI score. People + agents (WebMCP). The page registers ten tools on document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext . The recorded demo uses WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector in Chrome, with a Gemini API key already stored in the extension. That client only works if Chrome WebMCP is on: chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . The extension is not mentioned in the video; the flag is not either. Prompts that actually ran: “Show me the top seven companies in the health care sector.” → SQL tab, result table, charts underneath. Click UNH → cited report. “Show me the top five companies in industrials sector by hype.” → hype is 0–6 ( hype_vs_execution_balance , dim 11). CHRW is 6/6 (talk, not execution). Any of the fifteen fields can be the sort key; the tools keep SQL on real columns. How I built it I built this as a new static page for the contest — no backend, no build step. The snapshot ships as three JSON files ( reports , scores , dims ); DuckDB-Wasm loads them in a worker so you can run SQL in the browser. The gallery is twenty-five fixed views I wired up ahead of time; the SQL tab is the escape hatch when you want something the gallery doesn’t cover. Chart tabs only light up when the result shape actually fits (seven rows can be a bar chart; four hundred tickers can’t). WebMCP tools register as soon as the page loads, but run_sql won’t do anything useful until DuckDB is up. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages. First deploy failed because I’d vendored duckdb-eh.wasm — 32 MiB, and Pages caps files at 25 MiB. Moved the Wasm bundle to jsDelivr and kept the repo static. For the demo I used Chrome with WebMCP turned on via chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , plus WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector talking to Gemini. That flag isn’t optional; without it the extension can’t reach document.modelContext . The gallery and SQL tab work fine for a human with no WebMCP at all — the agent loop just doesn’t. How I used WebMCP Instead of making the model guess at DOM clicks, I exposed what the page already does as ten tools: peek at the schema ( get_schema ), set gallery filters ( set_filters ), browse or jump to a chart ( list_charts , show_chart ), pick a ticker or sector ( select_mark ), open the cited report ( open_report ), run SQL and flip chart views ( run_sql , list_active_views , set_sql_view ), or pull back a small result slice ( get_result ). In the video I drive all of that through WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector — type a prompt, watch the SQL tab update, charts appear underneath. Flip the Chrome flag off and the extension has nothing to talk to. The bit that actually felt different from a normal chatbot: we’re looking at the same screen. I’m not pasting the snapshot into Gemini and hoping it remembers column names; the agent calls run_sql , the query runs in DuckDB on my machine, and we both stare at the same table. If I disagree with a ranking I can see the SQL. If I want the transcript I click through to score.botflo.com. The agent isn’t sitting on a private copy of the S&P file. Challenges Deploy. Cloudflare Pages rejected the first build because duckdb-eh.wasm was 32 MiB and their cap is 25 MiB per file. Obvious fix in hindsight — host the Wasm on jsDelivr, ship only HTML/JS/JSON from Pages. Chart choice. I didn’t want fifteen chart types always visible; most would be nonsense for a given result. Seven health-care rows → bar chart or table, both fine. Four hundred tickers → maybe a histogram, definitely not a packed bubble chart. So the SQL tab recommends views and grays out the ones that don’t fit. WebMCP plumbing. This isn’t “install an SDK and you’re done.” The page registers tools on document.modelContext , but the client that calls them is a Chrome extension that only works when WebMCP testing is enabled in flags. Forget the flag and you get a perfectly good viz site with no agent path — which is fine, but it tripped me up while testing. What I learned WebMCP is worth it when the agent’s job is to change what you see — run a query, filter a sector, scroll to a chart, open a report. It’s not worth it if you just shovel the whole dataset into the model’s context and treat the tools as decoration. The whole point of DuckDB in the browser is that the agent queries a few rows at a time and you verify on screen, not that it memorizes 451 companies. Built with DuckDB-Wasm (jsDelivr), WebMCP ( document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext ), Chrome WebMCP testing flag, WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector , Gemini (via that extension), Cloudflare Pages, Observable Plot, vanilla JavaScript, SQL, BotFlo BATS snapshot. How to test Video doesn’t show this setup. Do it in this order: Chrome. Open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and enable WebMCP . Restart Chrome. The Inspector won’t work without this. Install WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector . Put a Gemini API key in the extension (the video starts with the key already saved). Open https://f9c93fe1.bats-viz.pages.dev/ and wait until DuckDB is up (status line). Gallery renders first; SQL/ run_sql need the worker. In the Inspector, run: Show me the top seven companies in the health care sector Show me the top five companies in industrials sector by hype In the result table, click a ticker (e.g. UNH) for the cited report. No login on the viz page. Repo public + license file (check incognito). Contribution I built the viz page, in-browser SQL/charts, transcript-cited reports, and the WebMCP tool surface. The demo drives those tools through WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector in Chrome after chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing is enabled, using Gemini from the extension.
