title: Canvas Co-Pilot: WebMCP Mindmap
pitch: Human and an AI agent can draw on the same mind map at the same time — no copy-pasting, no separate windows. It's built on WebMCP, so the agent uses real page tools instead of faking clicks.
about_excerpt: Human and an AI agent can draw on the same mind map at the same time — no copy-pasting, no separate windows. It's built on WebMCP, so the agent uses real page tools instead of faking clicks. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Vertical Structure of Architecture Diagram Export (JSON, SVG, MARKDOWN, PNG, JPEG, PDF) Export as PNG Agent has completed colouring the components via script Import (JSON, SVG, Markdown) Agent has completed the import and drafted on the canvas via script Select all tool Vetical Architecture using the straight line connector Canvas Co-Pilot: WebMCP Mindmap Inspiration Every AI tool I'd used fell into one of two buckets: either the agent takes over completely and you just watch it work (and hope it doesn't do something you didn't want), or it's a chatbot bolted onto the side of an app, completely disconnected from what's actually on screen — you describe what you want in a text box, and the app has no idea an agent is even involved. Neither felt right for something as personal as a mind map. A mind map is your thinking laid out — I didn't want an agent replacing that, I wanted one that could sit down next to me and actually draw on the same page. When I found WebMCP — a way for a web page to expose its own real functions as tools an agent can call directly, in the browser, no backend required — that was the whole idea in one API. So I built the thing I actually wanted: one canvas, one undo history, a human and an agent both reaching for the same nodes. What it does Canvas Co-Pilot is a mind-mapping canvas that a person and an AI agent can edit at the same time , live, in the same browser tab. Add nodes, branch out ideas, drag things around, color-code by hand — and an agent can do all of that too, through 20 real tools registered via document.modelContext (add a branch, restyle a node, connect two ideas, reorganize the whole layout, export to SVG/PNG/Markdown/Mermaid, import any of those back in). Every change either of us makes lands in one shared undo history, so nothing an agent does is ever outside a person's ability to take back. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — no framework, on purpose, so the whole render/state pipeline stays easy to reason about. Dagre handles auto-layout, the canvas itself is hand-rolled SVG with full round-trip fidelity (export a diagram, re-import it, get back exactly what you started with, including every color and shape override). For WebMCP itself, the app checks for native document.modelContext support first and only falls back to the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill when it's not there — the header badge tells you honestly which mode you're in, native or polyfilled, rather than pretending it's always native. It's deployed on both Netlify and Vercel. Challenges we ran into Most of the real work wasn't the happy path — it was the bugs that only show up once you actually try to break the thing. A user pasted a Mermaid-style edge list ( root --> human ) into Import, and it silently created 39 broken, half-named nodes instead of failing loudly. The importer's "is this quick-outline shorthand" check was matching on any > character — which also matches an arrow. Fixed with a negative-lookbehind regex that tells an arrow apart from actual shorthand syntax, and now a bad paste tells you it didn't understand instead of quietly corrupting your canvas. "Select all connectors" would silently reset back to nothing the moment you clicked anywhere on the empty canvas — even just panning to look at something. If every connector already had its own color (which they do once you've styled a diagram), the next color change would then land on the invisible graph-wide default instead, and visibly do nothing at all . Took real reproduction work to catch, since it only shows up with an incidental click in between two actions that each look correct on their own. I tried making multiple connectors landing on the same node spread out instead of converging on one point — and it technically worked, with proper diamond/ellipse-aware geometry and everything. But it just looked wrong. "Multiple octopus hands" was the exact feedback, and it was right — I reverted the whole thing. Good reminder that a fix being technically correct doesn't mean it's the right call. Two of the 20 tools had names close enough to trip up an agent, not a human: combine_nodes and connect_nodes sound almost identical but do very different things (one creates a brand-new node, the other just links two that already exist). Caught it by checking the tool descriptions against Chrome's own published guidance for testing WebMCP tools — and fixed it with one clarifying sentence in each description. Accomplishments that we're proud of Getting a second AI vendor to prove the point without any custom integration work: I handed ChatGPT nothing but the live tool schema and a canvas snapshot, and it wrote genuinely correct document.modelContext calling code — right API shape, right pattern — with only two small gaps (a missing await , a guessed return shape) that came from never having seen a live response, not from misunderstanding the standard. That's the whole promise of WebMCP working, not just Claude working. I'm also proud of how much of this session was bug-hunting rather than feature-building. Reproducing the connector-selection bug took building the exact failure chain step by step before I even knew what was wrong — not just patching the first thing that looked broken. What we learned The most validating thing I found wasn't something I built — it was rereading WebMCP's own spec and seeing my own instincts already written into its stated goals: "enable human-in-the-loop workflows," explicitly not "fully autonomous agents operating without human oversight." I hadn't copied that language, I'd just built toward the same idea independently, which is a nice signal I was pointed the right way from the start. I also learned that small stuff in a tool's description matters far more than it looks like it should. Two similar-sounding tool names, or three tools that could all plausibly answer "make it red" — those are exactly the kind of ambiguity that trips up a model even when every individual tool works perfectly in isolation. What's next for Canvas Co-Pilot: WebMCP Mindmap Native support: Chrome 149 and Edge 150 both have live Origin Trials for real (non-polyfilled) document.modelContext — worth registering for so the badge can honestly say "Native" for more visitors, not just the polyfill. Dynamic tools: right now all 20 tools are registered once at load. The spec supports tools that appear only when relevant (e.g. a delete_node tool that only shows up once something's actually selected) — that's a more honest surface for an agent to reason about than one static list. Multiplayer: right now it's one human, one agent. Extending the same shared-state model to multiple people on the same canvas is the natural next step. Built With chatgpt core:-javascript css3 github-other:-google-fonts-ai-agents-validated-against:-claude-(anthropic) html5 mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill-libraries:-dagre.js-platforms:-netlify model-context-protocol-(mcp) openai svg-the-tech-this-project-is-actually-about:-webmcp vercel Try it out webmcp-mindmap-copilot.vercel.app webmcp-mindmap-copilot.netlify.app Created by I built the whole thing solo — the canvas, the WebMCP tool layer, the export/import round-trip, all of it. This was my first real project working with WebMCP specifically, and figuring out how an agent actually behaves against real tool descriptions (not just what looks right on paper) took a lot of live testing and bug-hunting I didn't expect going in. Debugging issues that only showed up when an agent used the tools a certain way was the most intimidating part, but also where I learned the most. sathiya prasad A Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates sathiya prasad A started this project — Sep 04, 2026 04:36 AM EDT

title: Civium Systems for Code Review
pitch: Thorough code review demands sustained attention across every changed line. Civium gives reviewers an AI-assisted first pass and brings possible issues forward for judgment.
about_excerpt: Thorough code review demands sustained attention across every changed line. Civium gives reviewers an AI-assisted first pass and brings possible issues forward for judgment. Like Comment Story Updates Civium offers two ways to try out the experience. on the demo web, the companion chatbot that does the clicks for you. on the demo web, the findings are presented inline for your approval. on the demo web, once posted, civium will remember. on GitHub with extension installed, the companion box shows on PRs page. on GitHub with extension installed, the PR details page presents a pointer to all the findings. on GitHub with extension installed, the findings are displayed inline on the changes page. Inspiration Code review is one of the highest-leverage parts of software development, but it also demands sustained attention. Reviewers have to understand context, trace impact, spot risks, and decide what actually matters. AI can reduce the mechanical work in that first pass. But replacing the reviewer with a bot creates a different problem: noisy comments, shallow conclusions, and unclear human ownership. Civium Systems for Code Review is built around a simple idea: let the agent prepare the review, and let the reviewer make the judgment. What it does Civium Systems for Code Review turns the pull-request queue into a shared workspace for a reviewer and an agent. The agent can: review one pull request or the entire open queue; surface pull requests that still need a decision; and organize the queue so reviewers can focus on the changes that deserve attention. The reviewer sees the results inside the normal review flow. Pull requests with no findings are clearly marked, so they can be skipped without opening the diff. Findings appear directly below the relevant changed lines, with the surrounding code still visible. Every finding starts as a private draft. The reviewer decides whether to dismiss it or approve it. Nothing is published simply because the agent found it. For this demo, the review engine intentionally uses one narrow, deterministic rule: it finds snake_case variable declarations on changed JavaScript and TypeScript lines. This keeps the behavior repeatable and the scope honest. The goal is not to present a complete review engine, but to demonstrate a better workflow for people and agents to review code together. WebMCP makes that workflow practical for an agent. Instead of inspecting page markup and guessing which controls to use, the agent gets a small set of meaningful actions exposed directly by the application. The same workflow still works manually when WebMCP is unavailable. How we built it The application uses: React 19 and Next.js-compatible routing via Vinext WebMCP tool registration through document.modelContext Babel's TypeScript-aware parser for deterministic AST inspection Node's built-in test runner for fixture, state, scanner, session, and comment-equivalence tests The pull-request queue exposes two WebMCP tools: review_pull_request accepts one validated pull-request number and starts its review. set_pull_request_filter accepts a constrained (demo only) mode for showing all pull requests, reviews needing action, or pull requests from a known author. Both tools update the same React state used by the visible interface, so agent actions and manual actions stay in sync. Review requests go through server routes backed by Cloudflare D1. Review projects are deduplicated by repository, pull-request number, and head SHA. The scanner parses JavaScript and TypeScript declarations, evaluates only added lines, and maps persisted findings back to the exact file and line in the diff. The on-page Civium Companion uses the same underlying operations. It maps user's semantic requests to the same actions exposed through WebMCP. Challenges we ran into The hardest design question was deciding where the agent should stop. Once an agent can inspect code and propose findings, it is tempting to let it publish those findings automatically. But that would weaken the human ownership Civium is designed to preserve. We chose a strict boundary: the agent can organize and prepare the review, but the reviewer decides what gets published. Another challenge was keeping the demo realistic without overstating what we built. We intentionally limited the review rule, constrained API inputs, and scoped GitHub publication to a small set of frozen example pull requests. We also had to make agent actions feel like part of the product rather than a separate automation layer. Using the same application state for both WebMCP actions and manual interactions helped keep the experience consistent. Accomplishments that we're proud of One natural-language request can start a structured review across the queue. The agent can narrow the queue to the pull requests that still need human attention. Findings persist across navigation and appear at the exact lines that triggered them. The scanner inspects parsed declarations rather than matching arbitrary text. Only added lines are evaluated. Repeated reviews of the same pull-request version do not create duplicate work. Agent and manual actions operate on the same application state. The workflow remains understandable and usable without WebMCP. Most importantly, the agent can take on repetitive review work without taking ownership of the final decision away from the reviewer. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when an application exposes meaningful work rather than every individual UI control. Civium gives the agent only two tools, but those tools are enough to review and organize an entire queue. The agent does not need to understand every button on the page to be useful. We also learned that agent actions need visible consequences. Reviewers should be able to see when a pull request enters review, when results arrive, and which findings still need a decision. That visibility matters because trust does not come from the agent simply saying that work was done. It comes from being able to see what it did and make the final judgment yourself. What's next for Civium Systems for Code Review The demo proves the workflow. The next step is turning it into something real engineering teams can use every day. That means supporting real repositories and organizations, production-grade authentication and permissions, and reliable handling of changing pull requests. The review engine also needs to grow beyond one fixed rule. It should understand more kinds of code issues, use repository and team context, and let teams decide what the agent should look for. As the product scales, Civium will also need stronger infrastructure around security, reliability, auditability, and background processing. The core idea stays the same: let agents do the repetitive review work, while people keep control of the decisions that matter. title: NodeCraft
pitch: A shared architecture canvas where humans and AI agents build together. WebMCP lets agents inspect live app state and create, connect, arrange, and review the same workspace humans edit.
about_excerpt: A shared architecture canvas where humans and AI agents build together. WebMCP lets agents inspect live app state and create, connect, arrange, and review the same workspace humans edit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI assistants are getting much better, but I kept noticing the same gap. Most of the time I am still talking to an AI about the application I am using instead of letting the AI actually work with me inside it. I wanted to explore a simple question: what if I and an AI agent could work on the same live application state? I chose architecture diagrams because they make this easy to see. I can move a component myself, ask the agent to continue working, and the agent should be able to understand what is on the canvas now instead of starting from a separate representation. That idea became NodeCraft. What it does NodeCraft is an architecture canvas where a human and an AI agent can work together. I can create, move, remove, and organize components directly on the canvas. At the same time, NodeCraft exposes capabilities through WebMCP that a compatible AI agent can discover and use. The agent can inspect the canvas, create components, connect or disconnect them, arrange the architecture, remove components, and flag something for design review. The key part is that there is no separate AI version of the diagram. My actions and the agent's actions update the same application state. For example, I can ask an agent to add an API service, Postgres database, Redis cache, and payment service. The agent can discover NodeCraft's WebMCP tools and create those components directly on the live canvas. I can then manually change the canvas and the agent can work from the updated state. I also added undo and redo, local persistence, editable human and agent names, an activity feed showing who did what, JSON import and export, and a simple way to start a new canvas. How I built it I built NodeCraft with React and HTML5 Canvas. The application registers seven WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_canvas_state create_canvas_node connect_nodes auto_layout_nodes remove_node disconnect_nodes flag_for_review I tried to make the tools describe useful actions rather than low level UI operations. An agent should be able to ask NodeCraft to connect two components. It should not need to know how I draw the connection on the canvas. The tools that modify the canvas update the same React state used by the normal human interface. get_canvas_state gives the agent a structured view of the nodes and connections that currently exist, and I marked it as read only. This is really the core of NodeCraft. I can make a change manually, the agent can inspect the current canvas, make its own changes through WebMCP, and I can continue working from there. I also added cleanup for registered tools, duplicate connection protection, human and agent action tracking, undo and redo, local browser persistence, and versioned JSON import and export. I experimented with WebMCP's cross origin model too. The flag_for_review tool is set up so that it can be selectively exposed to an authorized reviewer origin. WebMCP is important to the project because I did not want to build another chat box connected directly to an LLM. NodeCraft exposes what the application knows how to do, and a compatible agent can discover those capabilities and use them. The agent and the application do not have to be designed as one tightly coupled system. Challenges I ran into One of the first challenges was deciding what the agent should actually be able to do. I could have exposed low level actions that imitate how a human uses the interface, but that did not feel useful. If the user wants the API connected to Postgres, the agent should express that intent and NodeCraft should handle the visual details. Shared state was another challenge. I wanted agent actions to affect exactly the same state as my manual actions. I did not want to maintain a second representation of the architecture just for AI. There were also a lot of smaller problems that showed up while building: preventing duplicate directed connections, removing connections when a node is deleted, making sure WebMCP handlers have the latest React state, tracking whether an action came from the human or agent, safely importing project files, and cleaning up registered tools correctly. Testing was interesting too. At first I could manually execute individual WebMCP tools, which proved the tools worked, but that was not the experience I was trying to build. I then tested NodeCraft using the Chrome Model Context Tool Inspector with an actual agent. I gave it a natural language request to build part of an ecommerce architecture. The agent discovered the tools exposed by the page and created an API Service, Postgres Database, Redis Cache, and Payment Service directly on the canvas. That was the moment the idea became much more real to me. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am most proud that NodeCraft got beyond simply registering a WebMCP tool and showing that it could be called. Seeing an agent discover the tools from the page and create components on the same canvas I was editing manually was the main thing I wanted to prove with this project. I am also happy with the state reading side of it. get_canvas_state means the agent has a way to understand what currently exists instead of only having actions it can execute. I spent time on the rest of the application as well because I did not want the result to feel like only a tool calling demo. The canvas survives a refresh, actions can be undone, human and agent activity is visible, projects can be downloaded and imported again, and a new canvas can be started without manually clearing browser storage. For a hackathon project, I feel like I ended up with both a WebMCP experiment and something that feels like an actual small product. What I learned My biggest learning was that designing tools for an agent is different from adding AI to an existing interface. The agent does not need the same interface that I need as a human. I care about dragging boxes and seeing connections on a canvas. The agent needs capabilities such as create_canvas_node , connect_nodes , and get_canvas_state . I also underestimated how important reading state would be. Giving an agent actions is useful, but giving it a way to understand what the human has already done makes the collaboration much more interesting. It means the agent can continue from the current application instead of treating every request like a new task. I started the project thinking mostly about WebMCP tool calls. By the end, I was thinking about WebMCP more as an agent facing interface to the application itself. That is probably the biggest thing I will take away from this project. What's next for NodeCraft There is a lot I could take further. For NodeCraft, I would like to explore richer architecture semantics, multiple saved projects, cloud collaboration, architecture validation, and agents that can reason about architectural constraints rather than only manipulate the diagram. I also think the idea applies beyond architecture diagrams. Workflow builders, visual editors, planning tools, dashboards, and other applications already have structured state and actions that humans interact with through a UI. WebMCP creates an interesting opportunity to expose those capabilities to agents as well. NodeCraft is my first experiment with that idea, and I would like to keep exploring what applications look like when humans and AI agents can work inside the same product together. title: Triangulate
pitch: Where researchers and their AI agents triangulate real DBS research evidence together.
about_excerpt: Where researchers and their AI agents triangulate real DBS research evidence together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Deep brain stimulation programming has no standard method — patients average 6.9 clinic visits in the first year alone just to get their settings right, for a device that stays implanted for a decade or more. The research trying to fix that is real and published, but it's scattered: an image-guided algorithm out of Berlin, sweet-spot mapping out of Bern, sensor-guided approaches, a foundational protocol from Toronto that's still the baseline everyone measures against. Nobody had put it in one place a researcher could actually search. That gap, and the WebMCP Challenge's push toward tools that agents can use as first-class citizens instead of scraping a UI, was the whole starting point. What it does Triangulate is a workbench, not a chatbot. A researcher — or their AI agent, through the exact same tools — can search a curated set of 14 verified DBS programming studies, compare methods side by side, ask for a research plan built from a question and a set of studies, save that plan, and export it as a cited brief. A sixth tool reaches live into Europe PMC for anything the curated set doesn't cover, clearly marked unreviewed so it's never confused with the vetted evidence. Six document.modelContext.registerTool() calls, all wired to the same functions the on-page buttons call. That's the actual fit with WebMCP: a generic chatbot answering "find me DBS studies" gives back unstructured prose that's gone once the chat scrolls. Triangulate instead exposes real, schema-constrained tools, so results stay structured and persistent in a shared workspace instead of trapped in a transcript, and tools chain reliably — search_studies into compare_protocols into build_research_plan — because each one's output is real data, not re-parsed guesses. That's also what's newly possible: because each tool's output is exactly the input the next one expects — a study id from search_studies is exactly what compare_protocols and build_research_plan take — an agent can chain a request like 'compare the Bayesian and sweet-spot studies, then draft a plan for tremor patients' into real, structured tool calls instead of hallucinating a summary of research it never structurally engaged with. I verified every tool individually, end to end, including the exact chain of ids each one expects from the last. How I built it React, TypeScript, and Vite, in a GitHub Codespace. I started with a five-study placeholder just to prove document.modelContext.registerTool() actually worked end to end, then went and pulled real citations — Charité Berlin's StimFit trial, Bern's ARTORG sweet-spot papers, the original Toronto Western algorithms, an industry-sponsored adaptive DBS trial — and built the dataset out to 14, each with a real, checkable link. The tools were built one at a time and tested in the WebMCP Inspector before moving to the next: search first, then compare, then the plan builder, then persistence, then the brief, then live search once we confirmed Europe PMC allows direct browser requests with no backend needed. The UI went through more than one real redesign once it became clear a wall of scrolling cards wasn't going to cut it for a 3-minute demo. Challenges I ran into The biggest one: document.modelContext.registerTool() throwing InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name under React's StrictMode double-invoke in dev. Fixing it properly meant switching every registration to the current WebMCP draft's AbortSignal -based cleanup instead of trying to manually unregister — unregisterTool() was actually dropped from the spec in April 2026 in favor of that pattern. Separately, I hit a real crash: two research plans saved to localStorage before a schema change didn't have a field the newer code expected, and reading .length on undefined took the whole page down. The fix was a small normalizePlan() function that backfills missing fields on load, which is now just standard practice for anything read back out of storage. I also had a longer stretch of the research-question text not actually influencing the plan output — it was stored but not used — which I caught by testing the same three studies with two different questions and noticing the output didn't change. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Fourteen real, independently checkable citations, not filler. Six tools that all survived direct testing, not just a demo run. A working live literature search against Europe PMC with zero backend, confirmed via a real CORS test rather than assumed. And a research-plan builder that actually reads the question — mentioning "tremor" in a question the selected studies don't cover surfaces that gap by name, first, before the generic ones. What I learned The most useful distinction I learned: document.modelContext is the production registration API; navigator.modelContextTesting is a separate, narrower API that only debugging tools like the WebMCP Inspector depend on. A tool can be fully registered and working for a real agent while a specific inspector extension still shows zero — which is exactly what happened to me, and cost real time to pin down with actual console checks instead of assumptions. I also came away with a firm rule for anything touching browser storage: never trust that old saved data matches your current schema, normalize on read. What's next for Triangulate Letting a researcher promote a live, unreviewed search result into the curated tier with one click after actually reading it — a lightweight path to growing the dataset without needing accounts or moderation infrastructure. Accounts themselves, so a saved workspace follows a researcher across devices instead of living in one browser's local storage. And growing the curated set past 14 as the literature does. title: VoiceGuard
pitch: A browser agent spots risk while the human keeps the controls.
about_excerpt: A browser agent spots risk while the human keeps the controls. Like Comment Story Updates Native Chrome WebMCP inspector showing audit_guardrails structured output. Demo video contact sheet: shared cockpit, tool calls and human review. VoiceGuard hero: the agent finds the signal, the human owns the action. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for VoiceGuard Inspiration Voice AI can listen, reason and respond in real time, but consequential calls still need accountable human judgment. Conventional browser automation forces an agent to infer meaning from buttons and dashboards, while a hidden backend tool can remove the shared context that helps a person supervise safely. We wanted the agent and operator to work from the same visible page without giving the agent invisible authority. What it does VoiceGuard is a synthetic voice-operations cockpit with four WebMCP site tools. An agent can inspect the current call state, audit visible guardrails, draft short operator guidance, or stage a pause request. The first two tools are read-only. The latter two change only visible draft or request state. A trusted human click is required before guidance can be applied or the synthetic call can be paused. The public demo deliberately exposes no tool for dialing, sending guidance, speaking, listing contacts, starting campaigns, transferring or hanging up. Every call, person, transcript and metric on the page is fictional. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Supervision depends on live shared context: phase, latency, transcript, policy signals and pending actions. WebMCP lets the browser agent discover narrow, schema-defined actions directly on that same page instead of scraping the DOM or calling a detached backend. Tool calls update a visible activity trace, so the operator can see what the agent read or prepared. This makes the experience faster and less ambiguous while preserving the human-first interface. The agent finds the signal. The human owns the action. How we implemented WebMCP The static top-level page registers four imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema, bounded text inputs and explicit read-only or untrusted-content annotations. The two draft-only tools return structured proof that no call action was executed. Human review buttons require trusted click events. The optional ?inspector=1 view is a transparent native test client. It uses document.modelContext.getTools() and executeTool() to show the exact JSON returned by Chrome's WebMCP implementation. The app has no backend and makes no network request after loading. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was designing useful agent actions without quietly creating an unsafe control plane. We removed every direct call action and separated drafting from execution. We also treated transcript text as untrusted page content, bounded all inputs, made tool activity visible, and built native Chrome tests that prove the page remains live until a human confirms a pause. Accomplishments Four working top-level WebMCP tools with native Chrome discovery and execution tests. A polished responsive shared workspace rather than a hidden JSON-only demo. Visible synthetic-data and autonomy boundaries throughout the product. A clean-room public repository with no production dependency or credential. Automated static, browser, responsive, safety and public-deployment checks. What we learned The most interesting WebMCP design question is not how many actions an agent can take. It is which actions should remain deliberately unavailable. Narrow tools, shared state and visible confirmation can make an agent more useful without making it less accountable. What's next Next we would connect the same interface contract to an authenticated pilot, add role-based tool availability, retain privacy-safe audit events, and test the workflow with real operators under explicit consent and legal review. None of those future production capabilities are represented as part of this synthetic contest demo. title: Novas WebMCP Proving Ground
pitch: A live, inspectable challenge where Codex uses Nova Browser to solve real tasks through WebMCP tools - and measures the difference against the interface.
about_excerpt: A live, inspectable challenge where Codex uses Nova Browser to solve real tasks through WebMCP tools - and measures the difference against the interface. Like Comment Story Updates Nova Inspiration Most WebMCP demos prove that a tool call works. We wanted to answer the more useful question: what does WebMCP actually buy an agent? What it does WebMCP Proving Ground is a live, inspectable challenge with three tasks. Every task can be solved through the visible interface or through the page's nine WebMCP tools. Both paths use the same state and mutations, while the page measures interactions, rejected attempts, and completion. The tasks expose failures that real browser agents hit: An appointment slot that looks available until conflicts are checked An order where one item has already shipped A report where selected filters are not yet applied The WebMCP tools return the hidden state before Codex acts. Codex can therefore choose a valid appointment, cancel only eligible items, and export the intended report without guessing. The live mission monitor records every tool call and ends at 3/3 objectives complete. How we built it The project is a dependency-free static website using semantic HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It registers nine task-level tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, with navigator.modelContext and provideContext fallbacks. The interface and tool handlers share one state model, so the comparison is inspectable rather than simulated. For the recorded run, Nova Browser gives Codex control of a real browser tab through MCP. Because Nova does not yet discover native page WebMCP tools directly, the demo openly uses a main-world compatibility bridge to the exact same definitions and handlers. The page labels this boundary instead of hiding it. Why Nova Browser Nova is not just a click driver. It provides more than 800 MCP tools in 25 bundles for browser control, target ownership, safety, evidence, local memory, and unattended work. Verified website behavior can become local, evidence-bound knowledge for later agents, with drift checks to guard against stale rules. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making the comparison fair. UI clicks and tool calls had to mutate the same data, start from identical state, and be counted consistently. We also had to show why task-level tools matter without turning WebMCP into renamed UI controls. What we learned The largest benefit is not fewer clicks by itself. It is that an agent receives task-relevant state before making a consequential decision. WebMCP turns hidden interface state into an explicit contract. What's next We want to run the same patterns against larger authenticated workflows and connect native WebMCP discovery directly to Nova's browser MCP layer. title: AI-Native Contract Maker with WebMCP
pitch: A bilingual contract maker where humans and AI agents safely draft, edit, validate, review changes, and undo contract updates through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A bilingual contract maker where humans and AI agents safely draft, edit, validate, review changes, and undo contract updates through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP Tool Activity showing a real get_contract_state call. Contract Maker interface with live preview and ChatGPT integration. Inspiration I am not confident in English, so I am using translation tools to help write this submission. I am a self-employed business owner running a food truck, and I also enjoy programming as a hobby. I already had a smartphone-friendly contract maker on my own website. When I found this WebMCP Challenge, I decided to experiment with extending that existing application with WebMCP. I wanted to see whether an AI agent could work with a real web application in a more structured way, while still keeping important actions under human control. What it does AI-Native Contract Maker with WebMCP is a browser-based contract drafting application where humans and AI agents can collaboratively create and edit contracts through structured WebMCP tools. The AI agent can: Inspect the current contract state Create a contract from natural-language instructions Update only selected fields Switch between Japanese, English, and bilingual Japanese-English output Edit individual clauses Validate missing fields, dates, and bilingual consistency Review AI change history Undo the latest AI edit For example, a user can ask the AI to change only Party B's address. The WebMCP tool updates only that field and records the before-and-after values. The user can then undo the latest AI change and restore the previous state. PDF export is intentionally kept as a human-confirmed action. How we built it The application is built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, WebMCP, and Netlify. WebMCP tools are registered in the application using structured tool definitions. These tools provide operations for contract inspection, targeted field updates, language switching, clause editing, validation, change history, undo, and activity monitoring. I also added a WebMCP Tool Activity panel so users can see when a real WebMCP tool has been executed, including the latest tool call and execution status. Contract data is processed in the browser and is not intentionally stored in a server-side database. The original browser-based Contract Maker existed before the WebMCP Challenge. During the challenge period, I extended it with WebMCP support and AI-agent collaboration features. The public GitHub repository preserves the original pre-WebMCP version as its first commit so the challenge-period development can be clearly distinguished. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was determining whether the AI was actually using WebMCP or simply interacting with the normal browser interface. To solve this, I added the WebMCP Tool Activity panel directly to the application. It makes real WebMCP tool calls visible and distinguishable from ordinary browser interaction. Another challenge was making partial edits reliable. An instruction such as "change only Party B's address" should not modify unrelated contract fields. I also wanted AI actions to remain reversible and understandable, so I added before-and-after change history and undo support. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am especially proud that the application demonstrates several human-AI collaboration patterns in one working web application: Real WebMCP tool execution Natural-language contract creation Targeted field editing Japanese-English bilingual contracts Structured validation Before-and-after change history Undo support WebMCP activity monitoring Human confirmation before PDF generation The final PDF cannot be automatically generated by the AI. The user remains in control of the final action. What we learned Before this challenge, I had no practical experience building with WebMCP. Through this project, I learned how a website can expose structured capabilities directly to an AI agent instead of requiring the agent to rely only on visual browser interaction. I also learned how important transparency, reversibility, targeted editing, and human confirmation are when an AI agent can modify real application state. What's next for AI-Native Contract Maker with WebMCP I would like to continue improving: Agent-assisted contract validation Multilingual contract support More granular human approval controls Additional contract templates Safer and more transparent human-AI collaboration The broader goal is to explore how existing web applications can become interfaces designed for both humans and AI agents without sacrificing human control. This application assists with contract drafting and does not provide legal advice. Users should review all terms before using a generated contract. title: ArchFlow
pitch: ArchFlow - architecture diagrams humans and agents build together, on the same live canvas.
about_excerpt: ArchFlow - architecture diagrams humans and agents build together, on the same live canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Diagram Canvas Export as Mermaid WebMCP Invocation Logs Available Architecture Nodes Available Process Nodes Node Inspector Inspiration Architecture diagrams live in slides and whiteboards, but AI agents usually scrape the DOM or dump Mermaid in chat. When I saw the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted a canvas where agents work on structured graph semantics , not pixels, on the same page as the engineer. What it does ArchFlow is a browser-native architecture diagram editor powered by WebMCP. Describe a system in plain language; a browser agent builds it on the canvas through structured tools. You approve every structural change, see tool calls in an activity log, and co-edit the same live graph — add nodes manually, let the agent adapt, auto-layout, annotate, validate, export Mermaid. Live demo: https://archflow-two-xi.vercel.app How we built it Fully frontend — React, TypeScript, Vite, React Flow, Zustand, Ajv, Dagre. No backend, no LLM API keys. The graph is the source of truth. 13 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext expose read, mutate, layout, validate, annotate, and diff operations. Mutations go through an operation engine and a human approval modal before applying. Deployed on Vercel. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is experimental — API surface and registration timing vary by browser Agents need structured operations, not DOM scraping Balancing safety (approval modals) with speed (batch ops, auto-approve mode) Atomic multi-step changes with temp IDs and single-step undo Accomplishments that we're proud of Agent builds a full architecture from a blank canvas via natural language 13 real WebMCP tools with JSON Schema validation Human-in-the-loop approval with zero mutation on reject Fully frontend, open source (MIT), live on Vercel What we learned ArchFlow doesn't embed an LLM — the browser agent is the AI, and the website is the tool server. That kept the app fully frontend with no API keys, while still enabling real collaboration. WebMCP replaces fragile DOM scraping with structured tool calls — agents discover capabilities, invoke them with typed inputs, and get deterministic results back. Tool design matters as much as the UI: schemas, descriptions, batch semantics, and approval flows all shape how well agents actually work. Human-in-the-loop isn't a limitation — engineers want to inspect and approve changes, not have agents silently rewrite their diagrams. What's next for ArchFlow Near term: C4 and BPMN views, Mermaid/Terraform import, richer validation (PII flows, single points of failure, latency budgets). Medium term: Diagram diffs between versions, templates for common patterns (event-driven, serverless, multi-tenant SaaS), and linking nodes to real resources like repos or cloud services. Long term: Multiplayer editing with WebMCP as the agent interface, team workspaces with review workflows, and exports into design docs and ADRs. The goal stays the same: humans sketch visually, agents refactor structurally, both on one live graph. title: Cherry Agent-Native Finance
pitch: Cherry Money turns finance software into an agent-ready workspace: ChatGPT can inspect bank feeds, match invoices and stage reconciliations, while payments and final approvals stay human-controlled.
about_excerpt: Cherry Money turns finance software into an agent-ready workspace: ChatGPT can inspect bank feeds, match invoices and stage reconciliations, while payments and final approvals stay human-controlled. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Needs review from Human Human to approve reconciliation Finance Software for humans and their agents Automatic Reconciliation after review from Human approval reconciliation exception Agent prepared payment draft Inspiration Small businesses already have finance software, bank feeds and invoicing systems, but the next generation of users will increasingly include AI agents working alongside people . That creates an important question: how can an agent genuinely help with bookkeeping without giving it unrestricted control over financial actions? We started with Cherry Money , our existing accounting and open-banking product, and explored how WebMCP could make finance workflows directly understandable and actionable by browser agents. Our goal became simple: Let the agent investigate, match and prepare. Keep consequential financial decisions with the human. Instead of an AI merely clicking around a finance dashboard, Cherry exposes structured finance capabilities through WebMCP. An agent can inspect transactions, find invoice matches, identify exceptions and prepare reconciliation — while approval remains explicit and visible to the user. The WebMCP functionality in this submission was developed specifically for the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge after 25 August 2026. What it does Cherry Agent-Native Finance turns a finance workspace into an agent-accessible interface through WebMCP. The demo exposes seven structured tools: cherry_get_accounts — inspect available bank accounts cherry_get_transactions — retrieve transactions requiring reconciliation cherry_search_invoices — search invoices by customer, number, status or amount cherry_suggest_reconciliation — analyse a transaction and return the best invoice match with confidence and reasoning cherry_stage_reconciliation — prepare a proposed reconciliation for human approval cherry_get_exceptions — surface ambiguous or low-confidence cases that require attention cherry_create_payment_draft — prepare a payment draft without executing any payment A user can ask an agent: “Check the bank transactions that need review and tell me which ones can be confidently matched.” The agent can inspect the finance data, analyse the transactions and identify likely matches. For example, a transaction containing an invoice reference and matching amount can receive a high confidence score. But if two invoices have the same value and there is insufficient identifying information, Cherry deliberately returns a lower-confidence exception rather than guessing. The user can then ask: “Prepare the confident reconciliation for txn_001, but don't approve it for me.” Cherry stages the reconciliation and displays it in the human approval queue . Only the human can press Approve reconciliation . The same principle applies to payments: an agent can prepare a draft, but the WebMCP interface deliberately exposes no tool capable of executing or authorising money movement . This creates a clear safety boundary: Agent → investigate → recommend → prepare → HUMAN APPROVAL How we built it Cherry Money already contains accounting, invoicing, bank feeds and reconciliation concepts. For the challenge, we built a new public WebMCP layer around those workflows rather than creating an unrelated AI demo. The challenge application is a lightweight Vite/JavaScript finance sandbox so judges can run and inspect the complete WebMCP implementation without exposing private Cherry Money production code, credentials or customer data. The WebMCP tools are registered using: document.modelContext.registerTool() Each tool has a structured input schema, a clear description of its capabilities and explicit boundaries around side effects. The reconciliation logic follows the same principles used in Cherry Money: Compare the bank transaction amount against outstanding invoices. Analyse invoice references and customer information. Produce a confidence score. Allow high-confidence matches to be prepared. Route ambiguous transactions to an exception workflow. Require human approval before final reconciliation. We also intentionally created an ambiguous demo transaction that matches more than one unpaid invoice. This demonstrates that the system is designed to surface uncertainty rather than hide it . The application is deployed on Vercel and includes the WebMCP-compatible response headers: Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) We also added a CI pipeline that performs a clean dependency installation and production Vite build on every change. The production build is available at: https://cherry-webmcp.vercel.app Source code: https://github.com/sohamtech-uk/cherry-webmcp Challenges we ran into Designing the human-agent boundary The biggest challenge was not making the agent more powerful — it was deciding where it should stop . Finance applications contain actions with very different risk levels. Reading transactions is low risk. Suggesting an invoice match is advisory. Preparing a reconciliation changes workflow state. Approving financial records or sending money is consequential. We therefore designed separate capabilities rather than exposing one generic “do finance” tool. The WebMCP agent can analyse and prepare actions, but final approval remains a deliberate human interaction. Representing uncertainty A reconciliation system should not pretend every match is obvious. We needed the demo to show both successful automation and cases where automation should stop. The matching engine therefore returns confidence and reasoning. An intentionally ambiguous £680 transaction demonstrates how Cherry raises an exception when multiple invoices could plausibly match. Extending an existing product safely Cherry Money existed before the challenge and contains private production functionality. We wanted to demonstrate genuine product evolution without publishing credentials, customer information or proprietary production infrastructure. We therefore created a separate public challenge repository containing the complete new WebMCP implementation and representative finance data. Working with an emerging browser capability WebMCP is still an emerging browser interface. We built against the current document.modelContext.registerTool() API while maintaining graceful behaviour in browsers where WebMCP is not yet exposed. The finance dashboard therefore remains usable even when the browser does not provide WebMCP. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are particularly proud that the project demonstrates more than a chatbot sitting beside finance software. The finance application itself becomes agent-native . An agent can discover structured capabilities directly from the webpage instead of relying on fragile DOM navigation or screen scraping. During the challenge build we: created seven structured Cherry Money WebMCP tools implemented confidence-based invoice reconciliation built a genuine exception workflow for ambiguous transactions created an explicit human approval queue prevented agents from directly completing reconciliation deliberately exposed no autonomous payment-execution capability added an agent/human audit trail built a responsive finance dashboard for the demo published the complete challenge implementation under an MIT licence deployed the production application to Vercel configured the required WebMCP permissions headers added automated CI validation and achieved a successful production build Most importantly, we created a pattern we believe can extend beyond this demo: Agents should be powerful enough to remove administrative work, but constrained enough that people remain accountable for consequential financial decisions. What we learned WebMCP changes the way we think about application interfaces. Traditionally we build UI primarily for humans and then attempt to make agents understand that UI afterwards. WebMCP lets us design a second, structured interface specifically for agents while keeping both interfaces connected to the same application state. We also learned that the most useful agent tools are not necessarily the most powerful ones. A narrowly scoped tool such as cherry_suggest_reconciliation communicates intent, permissions and expected behaviour far more clearly than exposing generic application control. For financial software, confidence and explainability are also essential. Returning the proposed match together with the reason and confidence gives both the agent and the human enough context to decide what should happen next. Finally, building the human approval boundary from the beginning proved much simpler than trying to add safety controls after giving an agent broad permissions. title: Clear Dose
pitch: Transparent prescriptions. Agent-ready. Search, compare, understand, and complete simulated prescription-shopping workflows with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Transparent prescriptions. Agent-ready. Search, compare, understand, and complete simulated prescription-shopping workflows with WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Cleardose main Inspiration Prescription shopping is a good example of a workflow where ordinary browser automation quickly becomes fragile. A user may need to search for a medication, identify the correct strength and form, compare fulfillment options, understand medication information, choose delivery, manage a cart, and move through checkout. An agent trying to accomplish that by visually reading a page has to continually reconstruct the application's state from text and pixels. I wanted to explore a different model: What if the website explicitly told the agent what it can do? That is what WebMCP enables. ClearDose turns the underlying actions of a prescription-shopping experience into structured tools that an agent can discover and call directly. What I built ClearDose is a local-first prescription reference and simulated commerce application. Users can: Search medications by generic or brand name Inspect structured medication information Choose exact form, strength, and quantity configurations Compare fictional pharmacy and delivery options Compare public medication reference information Create a prescription request summary Add and remove items from a cart Compare current cart savings Select delivery options Complete a simulated checkout Inspect simulated order status The same application capabilities are also exposed to WebMCP agents. For example, a user can ask: Find available sleep medications, compare the best options, add the selected option to my cart, and prepare checkout. The agent can translate that request into a sequence of structured application operations instead of visually navigating the interface. Why WebMCP ClearDose is a strong fit for WebMCP because medication and fulfillment comparisons depend on exact structured state. A meaningful comparison can depend on: medication active ingredient dosage form strength quantity fulfillment option delivery method WebMCP lets ClearDose expose those values through explicit JSON schemas rather than asking an agent to infer them from the rendered interface. ClearDose exposes tools for medication search, medication details, exact fulfillment comparison, selecting offers, cart management, delivery changes, simulated checkout, order status, medication comparison, and Drug Explorer workflows. The result is an application contract for agents instead of a collection of buttons they have to reverse-engineer. Human + Agent Collaboration One of the most important parts of the project is that there is not a separate "AI version" of the application. The normal Vue interface and the WebMCP tools operate on the same underlying Pinia state and application services. If the agent adds an item to the cart, the user sees it. If the user changes the selection manually, the agent works with that new state. That allows control to move naturally between the human and the agent. The agent handles repetitive navigation and information gathering while the human remains responsible for decisions. ClearDose deliberately does not turn medication similarity into autonomous treatment recommendations. Public medication information is also kept separate from the fictional commerce layer used by the demo. How I Built It ClearDose is built with Vue 3, Vite, Pinia, browser-local storage, and WebMCP. I created a shared application action layer used by both normal UI components and WebMCP handlers. For example, the visible Add to Cart button and the add_to_cart WebMCP tool ultimately call the same underlying cart behavior. Medication information is normalized through a data layer that can work with sources including: RxNorm openFDA NADAC The application keeps public medication facts, cached data, fallback data, and fictional commerce information explicitly labeled. WebMCP tools use strict schemas, bounded results, runtime validation, state checks, and clear read/write behavior. I also built a WebMCP documentation and Agent Lab experience so the application's tool catalog, schemas, prompts, workflows, and recent tool calls can be inspected directly. Challenges I Faced One major challenge was handling a domain where two medications that look similar in a search result are not automatically interchangeable. That made exact state and provenance important throughout the application. Another challenge was keeping the WebMCP layer from becoming a second implementation of the product. I wanted the agent and the UI to share business logic instead of slowly diverging. Designing useful tool schemas was also more difficult than simply exposing JavaScript functions. Tool names, argument limits, outputs, recovery instructions, destructive actions, and context all affect how reliably an agent can use an application. What I Learned The biggest thing I learned is that making software "agent-ready" is much more than adding an AI chat box. Applications already contain useful domain operations. WebMCP provides a way to expose those operations explicitly. I also found that small composable tools work better than giant automation commands because an agent can inspect the result of each operation and decide what should happen next. What's Next ClearDose could be extended with additional verified public healthcare datasets and, where appropriate permissions and regulatory controls exist, real fulfillment integrations. More broadly, the same design applies to any complex commerce system where product configuration, provenance, comparisons, and human review matter. title: Cyfix
pitch: Fix web security with humans and agents together - passive-only scans an agent can run, but only a human can authorize.
about_excerpt: Fix web security with humans and agents together - passive-only scans an agent can run, but only a human can authorize. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every website has a short list of security basics that are cheap to check and cheap to fix: is HTTPS enforced, is HSTS set, does a CSP exist, are cookies flagged HttpOnly, is /.env sitting there in public. Almost nobody checks them, because the work is tedious, the output is jargon, and the tools are built for security engineers rather than for the person who actually owns the site. This is exactly the shape of work an agent should do. But "scan this domain" is not a neutral action — it touches someone else's server, and it carries legal and ethical weight. It has to stay a human decision. Most agent security tooling resolves that tension by removing the human. We wanted to keep them, visibly, in the loop. What it does Cyfix runs a passive-only security scan of a domain you're authorized to test, scores what it finds by severity, explains each issue in plain language, and gives you a copy-pasteable fix. An AI agent in the browser can drive that entire workflow itself through WebMCP — propose a domain, run the scan once you approve, triage findings, draft the CSP header, verify the fix, export the report. Every action, human or agent, lands in a shared audit log. What it will never do: exploit anything, brute force anything, scan ports, or send a single state-changing request. How we built it Next.js 15 (App Router), React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand, deployed on Vercel. Seven tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() from the root layout, so they're discoverable on every page — an agent landing anywhere on the site finds them immediately. Where a browser doesn't implement document.modelContext yet, Cyfix installs a same-shape polyfill, so the tools always exist and stay testable from the on-page Agent Console. Every tool resolves to an MCP-compatible envelope (content blocks, isError, structuredContent). The gate lives in the human's UI, not in a prompt: scan_domain reads the state of a checkbox the human can see and untick — a precondition the tool evaluates, not an instruction an agent could argue past. prepare_scan is the agent's way of asking: it proposes a domain but deliberately leaves the approval box untouched. Approval is scoped to one domain and revoked the instant the target changes. The dashboard is laid out as an application: a persistent left rail carries the sections, tracks the one you're reading, and pins the current target and score. The top bar shows a live count of the WebMCP tools currently registered on document.modelContext and whether that landed on the browser's native implementation or our polyfill. The seven tools prepare_scan — proposes a domain to the human. Cannot approve it. scan_domain — runs the passive scan. Refuses without human approval for that exact domain. list_findings — compact findings, filterable by severity or failures only. explain_finding — plain-language impact of one finding. generate_fix — copy-pasteable remediation snippet. verify_fix — re-scans the live site and confirms the fix actually landed. Human-gated like any scan. export_report — JSON or Markdown report, downloaded for the human. verify_fix is the one we'd point at. Most agent tooling stops at "here's the fix" and declares victory. Cyfix goes back to the live site and checks — and because verifying means re-scanning Cyfix scores 100/100 on itself The first thing anyone does with a security scanner is point it at the scanner. So we did — it scored 61. We fixed everything it found: a nonce-based CSP with no unsafe-inline for scripts, HSTS, nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, a referrer policy, a permissions policy, no framework banner, and a real /.well-known/security.txt. It now scores 100/100. Scan cyfix.vercel.app from the dashboard and check for yourself. Challenges we ran into Designing a gate an agent can't route around while still leaving it something useful to do. Our first version refused unauthorized scans correctly but left the agent at a dead end with no way to ask. Splitting "propose" from "approve" into two tools, and moving the target into shared state both actors read, is what made the collaboration real instead of theatrical. The second was our own CSP. The first policy we shipped used 'strict-dynamic', which silently voids the 'self' allowance — every script chunk was blocked and the dashboard rendered a blank page. The build was perfectly happy; only loading the page in a real browser caught it. A fitting lesson for a project about security headers. What's next Scheduled re-scans with diffing, a broader passive check set (TLS configuration, DNS hygiene, SPF/DMARC), and a shareable report link so the person who has to apply the fix doesn't need the dashboard open. title: GrandGrandMCP
pitch: Book a doctor's appointment just by talking — no forms, no dropdowns. WebMCP lets an AI agent do it for you, and it asks if something's unclear instead of guessing.
about_excerpt: Book a doctor's appointment just by talking — no forms, no dropdowns. WebMCP lets an AI agent do it for you, and it asks if something's unclear instead of guessing. Like Comment Story Updates GranGrandMCP Inspiration Booking a medical appointment online is a perfect example of that barrier. It's a routine task for most people, but for someone elderly, or unfamiliar with dropdowns and date pickers, a five-field form can be genuinely frustrating. We wanted to see what that experience looks like when an agent can act on someone's behalf — and, just as importantly, when it knows to ask instead of guess. What it does GrandGrandMCP is an appointment-booking calendar where a person can type or speak a plain-language request — "book me a doctor's appointment for tomorrow morning" — and an AI agent finds an open slot, books it, and drops it onto a visual calendar next to the user's existing personal events (bank errands, birthdays). If the agent doesn't have a detail it needs, like the patient's name, the app pauses mid-booking and asks — a single, friendly follow-up question instead of silently making something up. How we built it A single Cloudflare Worker serves both the frontend and the API from one origin, backed by D1 for storage — appointments and personal calendar events both persist there, so the agenda survives a page reload. The frontend registers three tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : search_available_slots , book_appointment , and check_appointment_status , each with a JSON Schema describing its inputs. book_appointment 's execute callback checks whether a patient name was provided. If not, it calls client.requestUserInteraction() — a WebMCP feature that pauses the agent's tool call and lets the page ask the person directly, right under the calendar, before completing the booking. Voice input uses the browser's native SpeechRecognition API, so a request can be typed or spoken. The calendar itself is a minimalist, pastel-themed UI built from scratch, with no framework — just HTML, CSS, and vanilla JS. Challenges we ran into executeTool() doesn't return what you'd expect. When calling our tools through Chrome's native document.modelContext.executeTool() (with the WebMCP flag enabled), the result came back wrapped in MCP-style content blocks instead of the plain object our own execute() function returns. We didn't catch this until a booking confirmation printed undefined for the date and time — which led us to write a small normalization layer that unwraps both shapes transparently. Fragile natural-language parsing. Our first attempt at pulling a patient's name out of a sentence used a regex anchored on the word "for" — which broke as soon as a message contained "for" twice (e.g. "...for John Smith for Saturday"). We replaced it with a capitalized-name heuristic, and more importantly, leaned on requestUserInteraction so the tool itself doesn't need to be clever about parsing — it can just ask. State that quietly wasn't persisting. Early on, the calendar looked complete, but personal events were only seeded in JavaScript memory, and booked appointments weren't being re-fetched from D1 on page load. Everything looked right until a refresh made it obvious. What we learned WebMCP is at its best when it replaces genuine friction — not when it's added to a flow that would work the same without it. The most valuable primitive we used wasn't tool registration itself, it was requestUserInteraction : the ability for a tool to pause and loop a human back in is what makes an agent feel collaborative instead of either fully autonomous or fully manual. What's next I want to expand this idea to other fields for someone elderly, not just medical. title: Gym & Tonic
pitch: Gym & Tonic turns “I should work out” into a week you can actually live. ChatGPT coaches, your plan stays private, and every decision remains yours.
about_excerpt: Gym & Tonic turns “I should work out” into a week you can actually live. ChatGPT coaches, your plan stays private, and every decision remains yours. Like Comment Story Updates Today: A daily dashboard with one next action, workout recovery, walking minutes, and private habit check-ins. Progress: A calm view of completed workouts, minutes, walking, habits, history, and optional weight trends. Planner 1: See your weekly status, progress, and next useful action at a glance. Planner 2: Start, resume, view, or add a short workout based on what your day needs. Coach Suggesting for schedule changes via WebMCP Coach suggesting for schedule changes via WebMCP Planner 3: Plan fourteen morning and evening sessions without overwriting your existing workouts. Planner 4: Review progress, insights, meals, templates, calendar export, and coach proposals. Workout: A focused guided workout with exercise cues, illustrations, optional timers, and explicit finish control. Meals: Searchable meal ideas with dietary filters, preparation times, ingredients, substitutions, and favourites. Settings: Personalize goals, training preferences, habits, alerts, weight tracking, analytics, and data controls. Inspiration I built Gym & Tonic because “I should probably work out” is one of the most popular fitness plans in the world, and one of the least effective. Most fitness apps give you endless exercises, complicated programs, and enough numbers. I wanted to build something that helps people turn good intentions into a realistic week they can actually follow. What it does Gym & Tonic is a local-first fitness planner for people starting or returning to exercise. It helps users plan weekly sessions, follow guided workouts, use optional timers, reflect after training, track consistency, discover practical meal ideas, and see what their next useful action is. The WebMCP integration lets ChatGPT act as a coach that understands the live training plan. It can check the week, identify gaps, suggest sessions, fill empty slots, and propose swaps. The important part is that the coach does not get to quietly rearrange someone’s life. Every change becomes a proposal that the user can approve or reject. How I built it I built Gym & Tonic with Astro, React, TypeScript, Zustand, Tailwind, and WebMCP. The application is local-first, so plans, completions, reflections, and workout progress stay in the browser. There are no accounts, no backend, and no mysterious fitness spreadsheet being sent into the cloud. I used Fraunces and Inter to give the interface an editorial feel, then added guided workout screens, progress views, accessible navigation, responsive layouts, exercise illustrations, local persistence, offline support, and privacy-conscious analytics. The agent tools are registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Read actions can inspect the plan, while write actions are staged for approval through one proposal pipeline. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was not generating a workout. The internet has generated enough workouts to keep humanity busy until the sun explodes. The real challenge was handling the small but important states: pending proposals, rejected changes, active workouts, timers after reload, completed sessions, optional reflections, local storage migrations, mobile navigation, and the difference between “planned” and “actually completed.” I also had to make sure an AI coach could be helpful without becoming an unsupervised personal trainer with admin privileges. Accomplishments that I am proud of I am proud that Gym & Tonic feels like a complete product rather than just a workout generator. A user can arrive with no plan, choose a manageable starting point, place a session, open a guided workout, complete it, reflect, and see that progress represented immediately. I am also proud of the trust model. The coach can do the planning legwork, but the user remains in control of every meaningful change. The project is open source, local-first, responsive, accessible, and designed to work for people who are building consistency rather than chasing perfection. What I learned I learned that good AI product design is often about restraint. It is easy to make an agent that can change things. It is much harder to make one that explains what it wants to do, waits for approval, and respects the user’s ownership of the result. I also learned that the most important product state is often not “success” or “failure.” Sometimes it is simply “you started, and that counts.” What's next for Gym & Tonic Next, I would like to add printable training diaries, installable PWA support, deeper exercise guidance, richer progress storytelling, and more ways for the coach to explain why it is making a suggestion. I would also like to explore a mode where the coach can defend a rejected proposal with evidence from the user’s plan, without becoming annoying enough to be muted immediately. For now, Gym & Tonic is focused on one useful promise: helping people make a plan, follow through, and come back next week. pitch: Together find and apply for the best-suited jobs with the help of AI and in-page WebMCP tools
about_excerpt: Together find and apply for the best-suited jobs with the help of AI and in-page WebMCP tools Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Job hunting isn't hard because people can't find jobs — it's hard because applying well , to dozens of listings, is repetitive: read, compare, rewrite, answer the same screening questions, repeat. WebMCP asks what's possible when a site hands an agent real capabilities instead of buttons to click. Job applications felt like the right proving ground — tedious enough to automate, risky enough that no one wants an agent auto-submitting unsupervised. Automate the drafting, never the decision became the whole design. What it does Job Application OS is a career workspace where a human and an agent (ChatGPT's browser, or Chrome with WebMCP) apply together through real tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() : search, score, rank, tailor a resume, draft screening answers, and — in one call — applyToTopMatch . Every prepared application lands in pending_review . approveApplication / rejectApplication are plain button handlers, never registered as tools — an agent has no path to approve its own work. submitApplication checks status === 'approved' and fails otherwise. How we built it Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Zustand, on Vercel — no external LLM calls, no API key; the reasoning model is whichever agent is browsing the tab. Tool execute handlers call the same store actions the UI's buttons do, so state updates render live, no polling needed. Challenges The original pitch assumed a server-side LLM key calling page functions — the spec corrected that before UI work started. A Tailwind v4 cascade-layer bug silently broke every theme color. A Zustand selector allocating new arrays per render caused an SSR hydration race and an infinite loop. The hardest problem was making the approval boundary structural — provable by grepping the tool list, not a comment asking nicely. title: Kitty
pitch: Everyone's AI agent adds their own items and allergies to one shared group order — Kitty tracks it live and splits the bill automatically, no manual collecting or spreadsheet math needed.
about_excerpt: Everyone's AI agent adds their own items and allergies to one shared group order — Kitty tracks it live and splits the bill automatically, no manual collecting or spreadsheet math needed. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group orders always end the same way: one person becomes the unpaid dispatcher, allergies get missed, and the bill math takes longer than the meal did. We wanted agents to take over the boring parts — without losing what makes ordering together social. What it does Kitty is a shared order page where everyone's own AI agent adds their items and dietary restrictions straight into one live cart via WebMCP tools — no forms, no relaying your order through one exhausted human. The host locks the order in, and Kitty splits the bill automatically. How we built it Seven document.modelContext.registerTool() calls — browse_menu , add_item , remove_item , set_dietary_restriction , get_order_summary , split_bill , finalize_order — on a Next.js app on Vercel. Every mutating call is scoped server-side to the calling participant's identity, so an agent can only ever touch its own order. State lives in a lightweight session store, synced to every viewer with plain polling — no infrastructure we didn't need. Challenges we ran into Letting several independent agents write to one shared cart safely was the real problem. WebMCP's tool boundaries had to double as both a UX contract and a security boundary — otherwise a confused or malicious agent could overwrite someone else's order or invent a priced item that doesn't exist on the menu. Accomplishments that we're proud of Real multi-agent collaboration on one mutable session — not just one agent talking to one app — with guardrails (menu allow-lists, per-participant scoping, host-only finalize) tight enough we'd trust it with an actual office lunch order. What we learned WebMCP tools aren't just an API surface — they're a trust boundary. The moment more than one agent can touch the same state, "what should this tool refuse to do" matters as much as "what should it do." What's next for Kitty Itemized (not just equal) bill splitting, real restaurant menu imports, and letting a host's agent negotiate directly with a restaurant's own WebMCP tools once more storefronts expose them.
