title: ListingPilot
pitch: A WebMCP commerce agent that finds weak product listings, verifies the facts, prepares safer improvements, and leaves approval to the merchant.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP commerce agent that finds weak product listings, verifies the facts, prepares safer improvements, and leaves approval to the merchant. Like Comment Story Updates ListingPilot exposes four WebMCP tools for agent-native commerce while keeping final approval human-only. ChatGPT uses ListingPilot through WebMCP to find the weakest product, inspect verified facts, and prepare a safer listing. ListingPilot separates verified, conflicting, and missing facts before preparing a safer listing for human review. Publishing is blocked before approval. The merchant must approve the proposal before it becomes eligible for publishing. Inspiration While building ListingPilot, I realized that writing product descriptions is only part of the problem. Online stores often get product information from different suppliers and sources. Sometimes information is missing, and sometimes two sources give different specifications. If AI uses the wrong information, it can create a very good-looking product listing that is simply not true. That is what inspired the idea behind ListingPilot: AI should move fast, but merchants should remain in control. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to see how an AI agent could help a merchant find and improve weak listings while still having clear limits on what it is allowed to do. What it does ListingPilot lets an AI agent work with a product catalog through WebMCP. For this challenge, I created a safe demo catalog with 500 synthetic products. The agent can: Search the catalog and find products that need improvement. Inspect the Product Truth behind a product. See which facts are verified, conflicting, or missing. Prepare a better title and description using only verified information. Stop and wait for the merchant before anything can be approved. In the demo, the agent finds an Orion VX65 TV with a catalog health score of 61/100 . It confirms facts such as the model, 65-inch screen size, 4K UHD resolution, and native 120 Hz refresh rate. But it also finds conflicting information about the number of HDMI ports and missing warranty information. Instead of guessing, ListingPilot leaves those facts out. That is the main idea behind the project: AI speed. Verified truth. Human control. How we built it The challenge edition of ListingPilot is built with Next.js and TypeScript and deployed on Vercel. I connected it to WebMCP through four tools: search_products — search the product catalog inspect_product — inspect Product Truth and product health prepare_listing_improvement — prepare a safer listing publish_approved_changes — publish only after human approval One decision was especially important to me: approval is not a WebMCP tool. The AI agent can do the repetitive work and prepare a proposal, but it cannot approve its own proposal. That decision stays with the merchant. The challenge version uses synthetic product data, so judges can test the workflow without needing a Shopify account or accessing real merchant information. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding how much control to give the AI agent. I wanted the agent to be genuinely useful, not just give suggestions. But ecommerce changes can affect real customers, so I also didn't want an agent to freely publish information without a human decision. That is why I separated preparation from approval. Another challenge was conflicting product information. If one source says a TV has one number of HDMI ports and another source says something different, the easiest solution would be to choose one. ListingPilot doesn't do that. It marks the information as conflicting and keeps it out of the proposed listing. I also spent a lot of time testing the WebMCP tool lifecycle and how the tools behave inside ChatGPT's browser. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm most proud that ListingPilot does more than give an AI agent access to an ecommerce page. The agent can actually understand something useful about the catalog. In the demo, it starts with 500 products , finds the listing that needs the most attention, checks the Product Truth, understands which facts it can trust, and prepares a safer listing. And it still cannot make the final decision for the merchant. For me, that balance is the most important part of ListingPilot: Verified facts are used. Conflicting facts are excluded. Missing facts are not invented. Approval stays human. What we learned Building this challenge changed how I think about AI agents. Before working with WebMCP, it was easy to think about AI mainly as something that generates content. But an agent becomes much more useful when an application gives it specific tools and reliable information to work with. I also learned that giving an agent more power is not always better. Sometimes the better design is to let AI handle the repetitive work while keeping an important decision with the person using the product. And for ecommerce, I learned something that has become central to ListingPilot: Good writing based on bad product data is still a bad listing. What's next for ListingPilot This challenge version uses synthetic data and focuses on one clear workflow. My bigger goal for ListingPilot is to bring the same idea to real ecommerce catalogs: better product intelligence, merchant-specific listing rules, SEO, structured product data, bulk operations, and safe Shopify publishing. I want ListingPilot to help merchants use AI across large catalogs without having to choose between automation and control. about_excerpt: An tldraw canvas where agents using WebMCP tools : draw, create diagrams, and create visual directly in the tldraw web. Like 2 Comment Story Updates 1 banner GIF demo What it does Draw_generatoe lets Codex control a live tldraw canvas through WebMCP. Users can ask it to create pages, draw scenes, add shapes and text, search and decribe youtube embed url in canvas ,Mermaid js ,finds non CC wikipedia commons image , arrange objects, and refine designs through natural-language instructions. For example, Codex can create a welcome screen, draw a car on a road, notice misaligned text, and correct the layout without replacing the user’s existing work. Inspiration The idea was inspired by OpenAI’s YouTube video, Math Problems with GPT-4o featuring Imran Khan from Khan Academy , published on May 13, 2024. Watching someone interact naturally with AI , made me wonder: what if we could do the same thing on a visual canvas? The original repository had been on my computer since 2025 . With the arrival of WebMCP, I returned to it and added tools that let Codex place, resize, move, and arrange canvas objects. The goal was simple: describe a scene in plain language and watch Codex draw it directly on the canvas. How we built it We built the interface with React, Vite, and tldraw. The application exposes structured WebMCP tools that Codex can use to inspect pages and create, move, resize, align, layer, and draw canvas objects. Codex inspects the current canvas, preserves populated pages, performs bounded mutations, fits the result into view, and visually checks the finished composition. We packaged the client application and deployed it publicly through ChatGPT Sites. Tool vocabulary Domain Tools Discovery list_tools describe_tools Canvas reading review count inspect_pages inspect_embeds Pages and camera create_page zoom_out Shape creation create pen createHtmlPreview create_mermaid_diagram Shape editing update label delete clear Layout and positioning move place align distribute stack arrange_grid Transform and layers rotate resize bringToFront sendToBack External inspiration getInspiration Open-license images search_commons_images add_commons_image This reflects all 29 tools currently listed in repo tool.txt https://github.com/mayank-devac/draw_generetoe Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was translating creative language into exact canvas coordinates, sizes, and layer ordering. Text and shapes can have different measured bounds, so something that looks centered mathematically may still appear misaligned. We also had to preserve existing pages, manage overlapping objects, verify WebMCP tool schemas, handle tldraw licensing for the deployed domain, and ensure that public client-side configuration did not expose real secrets. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created a working bridge between natural language and a live visual canvas. Codex can produce complete multi-object scenes, native shape-based layouts, hand-drawn decorations, mermaid js ... We are especially proud that it can inspect its own result, identify visual problems such as incorrect layering or alignment, and improve the canvas while leaving unrelated work untouched. What we learned We learned that reliable AI drawing requires more than generating shapes. The agent needs structured tools, clear object identities, page awareness, predictable coordinate systems, and visual verification after every meaningful change. We also learned that small corrective tools—move, align, resize, reorder, and inspect—are just as important as the initial creation tools. What's next for Draw_generatoe (Codex draws on canvas) Our long-term goal is to make Draw_generatoe a collaborative visual workspace . making a similar ipad canvas app for students. other webmcp projects : agents can design : https://devpost.com/software/make_layouts agents can play music : https://devpost.com/software/harmonium-music-intrumental-webmcp agents generate pixel art : https://devpost.com/software/pixel-generator-ibjpfc Built With chatgpt-sites cloudflare css html javascript openai-codex react tldraw typescript vite webmcp Try it out webmcp-draw-canvas-judge.eductionalguide.chatgpt.site github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by backend Mayank Ranjan Baral web-mcp BIKASH Ranjan Baral We built six WebMCP projects that let Codex designs, draws on tldraw- teaches, plays music and creates pixel art. title: MockNiner
pitch: Prepare for your next exam with the AI agent you already use. No extra exam-prep subscription.
about_excerpt: Prepare for your next exam with the AI agent you already use. No extra exam-prep subscription. Like Comment Story Updates Why I built MockNiner I'm preparing for IELTS and wanted an interface where I could practise for the exam. I didn't want another exam-prep subscription. I already had ChatGPT and Codex, so I wanted to use those agents for my preparation too. That became the idea behind MockNiner: bring your own agent. The app provides the exam environment and saves your work locally. Your agent creates questions and helps you learn from your answers. There is no separate MockNiner subscription or API key. You can use the AI subscription you already have. What you can do Prepare for IELTS, SAT, or GRE with practice tailored to the skills you need to improve. You can also ask your agent for a quiz on another subject. You take the test in an exam interface with timers and question navigation. The app scores objective answers and saves your attempt. For written work, ask your agent for feedback and read its comments beside your submitted responses. Where WebMCP fits WebMCP lets the agent work directly with the app. It can add a practice test, read a completed attempt when asked, and save feedback to the results page. You control your answers and submission. After a test, ask your agent to explain the questions you missed or review your written responses. Then ask for another practice set focused on what needs work. Questions, answers, and feedback stay together in the same interface. Building it MockNiner runs in the browser, with React and TypeScript for the interface and SQLocal for local SQLite storage. WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext call the same commands as the interface. Zod checks incoming questions and feedback before saving them. Keeping both sides consistent took care. Feedback must refer to the exact submitted attempt, and a failed save must leave the learner's work recoverable. Exam-specific rules and custom assessment formats stay separate. Kokoro generates speech and Whisper transcribes recordings locally. When you ask an external agent to evaluate your work, that agent receives the submission. Scores are practice estimates, and transcript-based Speaking feedback excludes pronunciation. MockNiner is independent of the exam owners. The repository includes the MIT license for original code and content, plus third-party attribution and speech licensing notes . title: Olympus MCP Harness
pitch: The model reasons. WebMCP connects. Olympus controls. The machine executes
about_excerpt: The model reasons. WebMCP connects. Olympus controls. The machine executes Like Comment Story Updates Native WebMCP Execution Flow Architecture WebMCP testing npm test WebMCP available Same model. Same WebMCP tools. Same task. Different execution reliability Native WEBMCP: ChatGPT browser with 5 tools ChatGPT access to olympus harness Find best AI laptop Check out layer Inspiration AI models are good at reasoning, but execution should be controlled, observable, and reliable. Olympus MCP Harness started from one simple idea: “The model reasons. The machine executes.” As WebMCP moves AI agents from reading websites to acting on them, execution becomes a trust boundary. Olympus was built to engineer that boundary. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns website capabilities into structured tools that agents can invoke directly instead of guessing their way through the UI. Olympus builds on that boundary: WebMCP structures the action. Olympus governs the execution. Unlike a backend MCP integration, WebMCP works inside the live page and shared user session. Olympus uses that browser-native boundary to govern execution without replacing the existing web experience. WebMCP defines how an agent can interact with the application, while Olympus determines whether an invocation is valid, allowed, safe to execute, and successfully completed. What it does Olympus MCP Harness is the execution control layer behind WebMCP. WebMCP handles the agent-to-web boundary through structured tools. Olympus then: Inspects the invoked capability Validates tool arguments Authorizes execution according to risk and policy Executes the machine action Verifies the result Recovers from safe failures when appropriate Traces the full execution path High-risk actions, such as checkout, remain behind explicit human approval. People + agents together Olympus enables controlled delegation . A user can delegate an outcome instead of manually operating every interface step. The agent reasons, discovers WebMCP tools, searches, compares, and prepares actions. Olympus governs execution, while the human only needs to intervene when a high-risk action requires approval. This creates a new interaction model: agents can autonomously handle routine actions while humans remain in control of consequential ones. The goal is neither full autonomy nor manual browsing. It is controlled delegation. In the demo, the agent can search, inspect, compare, and prepare a laptop purchase through WebMCP tools, while Olympus keeps checkout behind an explicit approval boundary. Who It's For E-commerce and retail web apps : Olympus demonstrates how AI agents can safely help users search products, compare options, prepare a cart, and approach checkout without turning high-risk purchase actions into blind automation. WebMCP developers : developers exposing real actions to AI agents and needing a reliable layer for validation, authorization, approval, recovery, verification, and observability. Human users and judges : they can see the current model decision, harness stage, machine action, execution trace, and a non-skippable approval gate for high-risk actions. WebMCP-capable agents and clients : such as ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. The agent interacts through document.modelContext tools rather than relying on brittle UI actuation for the core workflow. The laptop storefront is the concrete retail demo; the harness pattern is designed to generalize to other WebMCP workflows. How we built it I built Olympus using the native WebMCP imperative API with: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The app exposes five structured tools: search_products get_product compare_products add_to_cart checkout Each WebMCP tool is intentionally thin and routes execution through the same Olympus harness.run(...) path, where validation, policy, approval, execution, recovery, verification, and tracing are enforced. The application is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and deployed on Vercel. Olympus runs behind WebMCP site tools inside the live browser context, preserving the page’s existing state and user experience while adding execution policy, verification, and traceability. Tested natively with ChatGPT’s in-app browser Olympus was tested directly in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. ChatGPT successfully discovered and invoked these Olympus WebMCP tools natively: search_products get_product compare_products add_to_cart For the high-risk checkout tool, ChatGPT’s own browser security blocked the invocation before it reached Olympus’s approval layer. This demonstrates defense in depth: ChatGPT Agent ↓ Client / Browser Security ↓ WebMCP ↓ Olympus MCP Harness ↓ Human Approval ↓ Machine Low- and medium-risk actions successfully reached Olympus. High-risk checkout was independently blocked earlier by the client security layer. To demonstrate Olympus’s own checkout approval flow, judges can use the live simulator or a WebMCP-enabled Chrome environment where the invocation is permitted. Challenges we ran into The main challenges were working with a rapidly evolving WebMCP runtime, clearly separating WebMCP responsibilities from harness responsibilities, and designing approval and recovery behavior without turning Olympus into another agent framework. A key architectural decision was that WebMCP owns registration, discovery, and invocation, while Olympus operates behind that boundary to inspect and control execution. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m proud that Olympus demonstrates: native WebMCP integration five structured WebMCP tools a shared execution harness behind every tool schema validation and policy-aware authorization explicit human approval for high-risk actions real execution traces and metrics result verification safe failure handling and recovery native testing with ChatGPT’s in-app browser The project is designed so the harness is more than a logging layer: it can actively prevent or gate machine execution. What we learned WebMCP provides a structured way for models to interact with websites, but exposing a tool is not the same as executing it reliably. Reliable agent execution needs an additional engineering layer for validation, authorization, human approval, failure recovery, result verification, and observability. In short: WebMCP makes actions available to models. Olympus makes those actions safe to execute. What's next for Olympus MCP Harness Next, I want to evolve Olympus into a reusable execution harness for more WebMCP applications. Future work includes: richer policy models reusable tool registration and policy APIs stronger observability broader failure and recovery strategies support for more real-world WebMCP workflows comparative reliability evaluation using Chrome WebMCP Evals methodology I will only publish benchmark percentages after running real repeatable evals. The current project does not claim an unmeasured reliability score. Closing Project : Olympus MCP Harness Philosophy : The model reasons. The machine executes. Product thesis : The model reasons. WebMCP connects. Olympus controls. The machine executes. Technical thesis : WebMCP defines the boundary. Olympus MCP Harness engineers the execution behind it. Mission : Engineer the boundary between AI reasoning and machine execution. Evaluation principle : I don't claim the harness improves reliability until I measure it. The planned comparative evaluation is: Without Olympus Harness vs. With Olympus Harness , using fixed tasks and reporting real results only. The future isn’t just better models. It’s better AI systems.🚀 Olympus MCP Harness is one attempt to make that system boundary visible, controllable, and reliable. Checklist - Native WebMCP integration ✓ - Olympus controls execution ✓ - Client-side security observed ✓ - Human approval works ✓ - Trace and metrics work ✓ - Verification works ✓ - Safe recovery works ✓ - ChatGPT in-app browser tested ✓ - No fake benchmark claims ✓ Built With ai-agents ai-safety chatgpt chrome harness hitl human-in-the-loop mcp openai vercel webmcp Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Quoc Cuong Vo Love to build AI Like Share this project: Updates Quoc Cuong Vo started this project — Aug 27, 2026 12:27 AM EDT

title: OpenPath Studio
pitch: People set the learning goal. Agents weave the open web into a transparent, editable path.
about_excerpt: People set the learning goal. Agents weave the open web into a transparent, editable path. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Project The problem The open web contains excellent learning resources, but turning them into a realistic learning path is fragmented work. A learner or teacher must search across sites, compare formats and levels, inspect reuse terms, calculate a time budget, choose an order, and keep the plan current. A conventional browser agent can click through that workflow, but it has to infer meaning from visual controls and repeatedly reconstruct the page's state. Why WebMCP is the right fit OpenPath Studio makes the website's learning-planning capabilities explicit. Its WebMCP tools let an agent read the current goal, search a structured catalog, compare resources using stable IDs, build a time-bounded draft, add or remove items, reorder the path, mark progress, and export the result. The agent operates on the same client-side state and interface the person sees, so it never bypasses the product experience. WebMCP is not an API wrapper added for the challenge. It is the interaction model that makes the collaboration reliable. Schemas remove ambiguity, tool outputs keep context compact, read-only annotations distinguish discovery from action, and the activity ledger makes every state change visible. A better human experience The person still leads. They define the topic, level, schedule, and preferences. The agent handles catalog search, comparison, sequencing, and repetitive edits. Every recommendation includes its source, provider, duration, level, format, URL, and license metadata. The draft remains fully editable with human controls, and it works without an agent as a progressive enhancement. Publishing demonstrates a deliberate trust boundary. The agent can activate and prepare an annotated HTML form, but the form does not use toolautosubmit . A person must visibly review the title and learner, then click Publish. No data leaves the browser in this prototype. What people and agents can now do together Before WebMCP, an agent had to scrape filters, guess at card actions, and infer an ordered plan from the DOM. OpenPath lets the human state a goal in natural language while the agent composes multiple reliable domain actions against live browser state. The result appears immediately in the same interface for inspection and correction. The human contributes judgment and consent; the agent contributes speed, consistency, and structured comparison. Example collaboration: “Build me a 5-day beginner path on web accessibility with 30 minutes per day.” The agent calls build_learning_path with explicit constraints. The person reviews the visible draft and asks for a practical checklist. The agent searches, adds the resource by stable ID, and moves it to position two. The person marks progress or changes the sequence manually. The agent prepares publication and waits for human confirmation. How WebMCP was implemented OpenPath registers 11 imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() and exposes one declarative publish_learning_path form. The prepare_publish_review imperative tool provides a cross-client bridge that opens and optionally prefills the same visible checkpoint but can never submit it. JSON Schemas validate inputs. Read-only and untrusted-content annotations communicate tool safety. Tool output stays concise. An AbortController manages registration lifecycle, and the site sends origin-isolation and tools permission headers. Both agent and human actions reuse the same state layer and are recorded in a visible activity ledger. The app is built with Next.js and React, has no external runtime dependencies beyond the framework, needs no account or API key, and stores its workspace locally. It is responsive, keyboard accessible, reduced-motion aware, and fully functional in manual mode. title: OpsRelay
pitch: Human guided incident recovery where AI agents investigate disruptions, compare recovery options, and execute approved plans through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Human guided incident recovery where AI agents investigate disruptions, compare recovery options, and execute approved plans through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Opsrelay Inspiration I wanted to build something where an AI agent actually does useful work inside a real application, not just answer questions or chat. I started thinking about manufacturing and operations because one small problem can turn into a much bigger one very quickly. A supplier being late can affect stock, production, customer orders and money all at the same time. That is where the idea for OpsRelay came from. What it does OpsRelay is a manufacturing incident recovery dashboard. For the demo I created a scenario where a supplier is 48 hours late delivering Aluminium 6061 Sheet. That delay causes a material shortage, affects production, puts three customer orders at risk and exposes R423,000 in revenue. The user can give the AI agent one request and the agent can use the WebMCP tools in OpsRelay to work through the problem. It can: check the current incident find the orders that are at risk check available inventory search for other suppliers compare the supplier options create a recovery plan send that plan for approval execute it once a human has approved it check the final recovery status The main idea is that the user does not have to manually jump between every part of the system just to investigate one incident. Why WebMCP WebMCP is basically the part that makes the whole idea work. Instead of the agent trying to understand the website by looking at buttons and text on the screen, OpsRelay gives it proper tools using document.modelContext.registerTool . Those tools connect to the same data and state that the user sees in the dashboard. So the agent is not just telling the user what it thinks should happen. It can actually use the application to investigate the incident and work through the recovery process. Humans + agents I did not want the agent to have full control over everything. The agent can investigate the problem, compare options and create a recovery plan, but it cannot approve its own plan. The approval has to be done by a human in the dashboard. Only after that approval can the agent execute the recovery plan. I liked this setup because the AI can do a lot of the repetitive work, but the important decision still stays with the person using the system. How I built it OpsRelay is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS and is deployed on Vercel. I registered nine WebMCP tools: get_current_incident get_inventory get_at_risk_orders search_supplier_options compare_supplier_options simulate_recovery_plan request_recovery_approval execute_recovery_plan get_recovery_status The demo uses browser-local data and a fixed incident scenario so it can be reset and tested again without needing an external database or real supplier system. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was deciding what the AI should be allowed to do by itself and what should still require a person. I also had to make sure that when the agent used a WebMCP tool, the result matched what was happening in the dashboard. Another challenge was getting the full workflow working from beginning to end instead of just making a few separate tools that worked on their own. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The biggest thing for me is that the full workflow actually works. The agent can start with a supplier incident, investigate what is affected, compare recovery options, create a plan, send it for human approval and then execute the approved plan. I am also happy with the human approval part because the agent cannot simply approve and execute its own actions. What I learned Before building this I did not really understand how useful WebMCP could be. I originally thought of AI inside websites mostly as chatbots or assistants. Building OpsRelay showed me that the website itself can expose tools to an outside agent, while still keeping the normal interface for the person using it. That opened up a completely different way of thinking about how people and AI agents can use the same application together. What's next for OpsRelay The current project is a simulated manufacturing incident, but the same idea could work with real operational systems. The next step would be connecting it to live inventory, supplier, order and production data instead of the demo state. I would also like to add more incident types, such as machine breakdowns, sudden demand changes and other supply chain problems. title: orqis
pitch: The shelf for specialist AI agents. Browsable by humans, callable by agents — one marketplace where people and their agents discover, invoke, and rate specialist agents together.
about_excerpt: The shelf for specialist AI agents. Browsable by humans, callable by agents — one marketplace where people and their agents discover, invoke, and rate specialist agents together. Like Comment Story Updates list the agents What is orqis orqis is the shelf for specialist AI agents: a marketplace that is browsable by humans and callable by agents . Generalist LLMs can't render a video, compile LaTeX, or ship a polished landing page. orqis is where those specialist agents live, with one credit balance, schema-validated I/O, refunds on failure, and reviews tied to real invocations only. Live URL: https://orqis.xyz Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP A marketplace of agents is, by definition, something both people and agents need to use. Before WebMCP, an agent visiting orqis.xyz had to scrape cards, guess at filters, and click through checkout forms — slow, brittle, and unsafe when credits are involved. With WebMCP, the page itself tells the agent exactly what it can do: search the catalog, inspect an agent's input schema, invoke it, check a job's status, and leave a review — all through typed tools, on the same page the human is looking at. How it creates a better experience Shared context, shared screen. The human browses categories and reads reviews; their agent (in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome) calls search_agents / invoke_agent against the very same page. Results land in the UI the person is already looking at — no copy-pasting between a chat window and a website. Safety by construction. Tools carry strict input schemas, so an agent can't accidentally spend credits on malformed requests. Failed invocations are refunded automatically. Trust that agents can read. Ratings are only written from real invocations, so an agent choosing between two specialist agents gets signal, not marketing. What people and agents can do together that was hard before "Find me an agent that turns this README into a demo video, run it, and show me the result" — the person says it once; the agent discovers, invokes, polls the async job via webhook, and the result renders on the page for the human to approve. Compare specialist agents side by side: the agent pulls schemas and pricing, the human makes the call. Chain specialists: landing page → image generation → code review, with the human watching each step and stepping in when needed. How we implemented WebMCP On page load, orqis registers its tools with navigator.modelContext.registerTool(...) (with a document.modelContext fallback for older builds). Each tool maps 1:1 to an existing orqis REST endpoint, so the tools the browser agent sees are the same ones our @orqis/mcp server exposes to Claude and Cursor — one tool surface, three clients (human UI, in-page agent via WebMCP, and remote agents via MCP). Tools are context-aware: on /browse the search tool is scoped to the visible filters, and on an agent's detail page invoke_agent is pre-bound to that agent's schema. Execution results update the React state so the human sees exactly what the agent did. Built with Next.js, TypeScript, WebMCP ( navigator.modelContext ), MCP ( @orqis/mcp ), REST + webhooks for async jobs. What's next Opening the founding-agent program publicly, richer tool annotations for streaming job progress, and per-tool spend limits the human can set for their agent. title: OVERTURN
pitch: Health insurers deny 1 in 5 claims and almost no one fights back. Overturn pairs you with an agent that builds the appeal through WebMCP tools — and waits for your OK to file.
about_excerpt: Health insurers deny 1 in 5 claims and almost no one fights back. Overturn pairs you with an agent that builds the appeal through WebMCP tools — and waits for your OK to file. Like Comment Story Updates landing page with the problem stats parsed case file, 160-day deadline, evidence checklist after approval, confirmation and payer timeline in the console use this one first: the agent paused mid-tool with the drafted letter, strength score 78/Strong, and the "Approve & file / Decline" card Inspiration Health insurers deny about 1 in 5 in-network claims, and fewer than 1% of patients ever appeal — even though a large share of appeals that get filed succeed. The fight isn't hard because it's complicated; it's hard because it's tedious : decode the denial codes, find the payer's medical policy, match your facts to its criteria, cite guidelines, compute the deadline, draft the letter, file on time. That tedium is exactly what an agent should do. The judgment, the consent, and the signature are exactly what a human must do. The WebMCP Challenge asked for an app that gets meaningfully better when people and agents use it together — an appeals office is that, almost literally: two workers, one case file, a clear division of labor. What it does Paste a denial letter into Overturn (it stays in your browser — nothing is uploaded). The agent then works through 13 WebMCP tools: it parses the letter into a structured case, decodes the claim-adjustment codes, finds the payer medical policy that justified the denial, checks each coverage criterion against the record, attaches citable guideline evidence, computes the filing deadline by plan type, drafts a full appeal letter, and scores its strength with a factor-by-factor breakdown. Then the part the product exists for: when the agent calls submit_appeal , the tool pauses and an approval card appears. Nothing is filed until the human clicks Approve & file . After filing, human and agent watch the payer timeline together. No WebMCP available? A built-in "Run demo agent" walks the identical tool implementations — including the approval pause — so anyone can see the loop. How we built it A zero-dependency, zero-build static page (GitHub Pages), with a strict separation between pure logic and the WebMCP layer: js/tools.js registers 13 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) , each returning MCP-style { content: [{ type: "text" }] } envelopes with isError on failure. Following Chrome's WebMCP security guidance: annotations.readOnlyHint on every state-preserving tool, annotations.untrustedContentHint on every tool whose output embeds the (untrusted) denial letter, and Chrome's design budgets — ≤500-char tool descriptions, ≤150-char parameter descriptions, ~1.4K-char outputs. Tool descriptions teach workflow ("Call draft_appeal_letter first — the human must be able to read what will be filed"). The human's UI and the agent's tools are two surfaces over one shared pipeline : the app's own buttons call the same tool implementations with actor: "human" , so the console shows exactly who did what. The approval gate is a tool promise that only resolves when the human clicks — defense in depth on top of whatever the agent's host requires — with a 3-minute timeout that declines by default. Pure pipeline logic (parsing, criteria matching, deadline math, drafting, scoring) is unit-tested in Node: 25 assertions, all passing. Challenges we ran into Consent inside a tool call. submit_appeal has to stop mid-execution and wait for a human. We resolved it by parking the tool's promise on an approval card in the UI — which raised real questions (what if nobody answers? default-deny after a timeout) that most apps never have to think about. Parsing adversarial prose without a server. Extracting payer, claim, codes, and plan type from a letter using only regex and keyword rules — including a negation guard so "no red flags" doesn't count as evidence for red flags. The 1.5K output budget forced us to design tool results as agent-oriented summaries with pointers ("the full letter is in the human's editor") instead of dumping state. A delightful DST off-by-one: computing "days left to file" across a time-change boundary needs calendar arithmetic, not millisecond diffs. A unit test caught it. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop works end-to-end: paste → agent legwork → human edit → approval → confirmation and payer timeline — verified in a real browser against the deployed site. The approval moment is genuinely good product design, not a checkbox: the agent can do everything except the one step that matters, alone. Graceful degradation: feature-detecting document.modelContext means the app is fully usable everywhere, and the demo agent gives judges without WebMCP the exact same story. What we learned Tool descriptions are prompts. Writing them as workflow guidance (what to call next, what to do when data is missing) mattered more than any schema detail. Annotations are a design language. Marking untrusted content and read-only tools forced us to think about trust boundaries the way a security reviewer would. Output budgets are a feature. Constraining tool results made the agent interface better — small, pointed results with pointers beat dumps. Building for two users at once (human + agent) makes the product simpler, not more complex, when the state is genuinely shared. What's next for OVERTURN Real-world ingestion: PDF/photo import of denial letters and EOBs (still on-device). A payer-connector layer so submit_appeal can target real portals behind explicit per-payer consent, plus certified-mail and fax fallbacks. Multi-appeal dashboard with deadline tracking across a household's claims, and an exportable audit log of every agent action for regulators and advocates. Delegated review: let a family member or patient advocate be the approval authority. Keep contributing to the WebMCP conversation: this project is a strong argument for app-level consent gates as a standard annotation. title: Pinnwall
pitch: A sticky-note board where the agent is a teammate, not a script. It claims notes, moves them and comments back — running in your browser session, so it never sees a credential.
about_excerpt: A sticky-note board where the agent is a teammate, not a script. It claims notes, moves them and comments back — running in your browser session, so it never sees a credential. Like Comment Story Updates The agent flags a note as four tasks in one, you answer on the note, it reports back when done. Claim pills show what the agent is working on right now. Badges show which notes it wrote. Every board merged into one view, with the agent's work visible across all of them. Inspiration Adding MCP to Pinnwall was already on my list. I use it as my own sticky-note board and kept wanting an assistant that could tidy it up, but not enough to build a whole server with its own auth just for that. I hadn't heard of WebMCP before this hackathon. It turned out to be the shape I actually needed, so I finally built it. What it does Pinnwall is a sticky-note board with no database. With WebMCP, an agent works it with you. It has 13 tools: read the board, create and move notes, add columns, switch the board you're looking at. It can also claim a note, so a marker appears before it starts, and comment on one to say what it did or ask you something. You answer on the note. Anything the agent writes gets badged, so you can always tell who did what. Why WebMCP fits this A board is shared state that two people edit. Before, I had two bad options: let an agent click through the UI from screenshots, which is slow and breaks every time I touch the CSS, or stand up an MCP server with its own auth and deploy, just so something could edit a board I'm already signed into. WebMCP skips both. The tools run in the page, on my session. The agent can do what I can do and nothing more, there's no key to leak, and access ends when I close the tab. Concretely: one note on my board said "ship pricing page, update the FAQ, brief support, schedule the newsletter." Splitting that by hand is four notes typed, four drags, then delete the original. Now it's one sentence, and I watch the agent claim it, split it, and tell me what it did. Then I answer it on the note. That last part is the bit I didn't expect to care about — the conversation stays on the work instead of disappearing into a chat window. How I built it Node, Express, vanilla JS. No build step, no new dependencies. All the tools sit in one file. Each is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool and calls the same fetch helper the buttons call, so the agent rides my session cookie and hits the same CSRF check and validation as a click. They take names, not ids. move_note({ note: "brief support", column: "Done" }) finds the note from a piece of its text and tells the agent what it matched if there's more than one. Pinnwall itself predates the hackathon. The agent side is all new. WEBMCP.md in the repo has the split. Challenges I ran into Mirroring my REST API one to one gave me tools the agent used badly. It doesn't have ids and it thinks in names, so half its calls missed. Making every tool resolve by name fixed more than anything I did on the server. The board reloads itself after the agent writes. The first version did that even while I was typing in a note, and wiped what I'd written. Now it waits until I stop. Accomplishments that I'm proud of No new dependencies, no API key, no second service. You sign in normally and the agent can do what you can do. It's also additive. Existing Pinnwall installs run unchanged and old notes work without a migration. What I learned The useful part of WebMCP is the session, not the protocol. Running in the page turns authorisation from the hardest part into a non-problem. And you have to build for two actors from the start. Almost every bug worth fixing came from assuming only one of us was touching the board at a time. title: PixelForge Studio
pitch: A WebMCP-native pixel art studio where people and AI agents create, animate, and export sprites together.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native pixel art studio where people and AI agents create, animate, and export sprites together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Judge Quick Links Live Cloudflare mirror (start here): https://pixelforge-studio.himomohi.workers.dev Public GitHub source: https://github.com/himomohi/pixelforge-studio ChatGPT Sites (in-app browser fallback): https://pixelforge-studio.appcaster.chatgpt.site Demo video: https://youtu.be/-mTECXrUEy8 Fast judging path: Open the Cloudflare mirror, use a WebMCP-capable browser, and watch one shared project receive a frame, an undo, a duplicated frame, 180 ms timing, an Agent Highlights layer, and 10 cyan pixels—then undo or redo the same visible result in the editor. Inspiration Creative software is still split into two worlds. People work through rich visual interfaces, while agents are often forced to guess which controls to click and where to place the pointer. That is especially fragile in pixel-art production, where a single coordinate, frame, layer, or alpha value matters. PixelForge Studio explores a better model: one shared creative surface for both the artist and the agent. The artist keeps the complete visual editor, while WebMCP gives the agent precise, structured access to the same project. What it does PixelForge Studio is a professional browser-based pixel-art editor with: crisp pixel drawing and shape tools; palettes, foreground and background colors, grid, symmetry, selection, and zoom; multiple animation frames with timing, playback, duplication, and reordering; multiple layers with visibility, locking, opacity, duplication, and reordering; browser-local autosave and project management; browser-local reference images with split and floating views; adaptive image-to-pixel conversion with transparency and aspect-ratio guardrails; a measurable strict-99 reference fidelity audit; PNG, animated GIF, sprite-sheet, editable project, and game-engine bundle exports. It also registers 65 browser-native WebMCP tools. Compatible agents can inspect the current state, create and duplicate projects, place exact pixels, edit frames and layers, convert references, verify results, and export assets without inferring the UI. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Pixel art combines high-level creative intent with low-level precision. A person may ask for a highlighted animation frame, a palette adjustment, or a Unity-ready sprite bundle. Performing that work through screen coordinates is slow and error-prone because the agent must infer canvas geometry, selected frames, selected layers, active colors, and editor state. WebMCP makes those workflows explicit. Each action has a bounded JSON schema and a stable semantic meaning. The agent can read the project state, apply an atomic edit, and immediately return control to the artist in the visual editor. How it creates a better user experience The agent does not replace the editor. It accelerates precise or repetitive work while preserving human review and creative control. In the demo, the agent performs this exact real-editor run: add_frame ; undo , proving the first change is a normal reversible editor action; duplicate_frame ; set_frame_duration with 180 milliseconds; add_layer , then rename_layer to Agent Highlights ; draw_pixels with an exact batch of 10 cyan pixels. This is not a separate agent-only canvas. All 65 typed tools and the human interface use the same browser-local project state, so every change appears immediately on the canvas, timeline, and layer stack. The artist can inspect the result, refine it manually, play the animation, undo or redo changes, or export the finished asset. What was difficult or impossible before Before WebMCP, an agent had to navigate the editor visually and hope that pointer coordinates, focus, selections, panels, and timing controls had not changed. Exact pixel batches and multi-step animation edits were especially unreliable. With WebMCP, the agent and person share a stable project model. The agent can operate semantically while the person continues to work visually. This makes mixed-initiative creative workflows practical instead of brittle. How WebMCP was implemented The integration is implemented in lib/pixelforge/webmcp.ts using document.modelContext.registerTool . The 65 registered tools cover: project lifecycle and production presets; reference-image state and view controls; reference conversion and fidelity auditing; exact pixels, shapes, selections, palettes, colors, and brush size; frames, layers, playback, grid, onion skin, symmetry, and zoom; PNG, GIF, sprite-sheet, project, and game-bundle exports. Schemas enforce bounded dimensions, colors, array sizes, and enums. Operations accept cancellation signals. Read-only operations are annotated, destructive operations are identified, and raw reference image data remains browser-local. The live judging run is deliberately concrete: add_frame → undo → duplicate_frame → set_frame_duration (180 ms) → add_layer → rename_layer ( Agent Highlights ) → draw_pixels (10 cyan pixels). Because those calls update the editor's actual browser-local state rather than a demo surrogate, the visible result stays fully undoable and redoable. How we built it Next.js 16 and React 19 TypeScript Vinext and Vite Cloudflare Workers with Static Assets ChatGPT Sites backup Browser-native WebMCP Canvas rendering and browser-local storage Custom PNG, GIF, sprite-sheet, ZIP, and game-engine exporters Remotion for the public demo video We also focused the shipped surface: only 14 UI primitives used by the product remain, and the unused D1/notes scaffold was removed. That keeps the submission centered on the editor and its WebMCP workflow. Challenges Designing one project model that works for both visual editing and structured agent actions Keeping frame-layer cels complete and consistent across duplication and reordering Preserving alpha, aspect ratio, and subject bounds during reference conversion Making fidelity claims measurable instead of subjective Exporting useful assets for many game engines from one browser project Defining tool schemas that are powerful without accepting unbounded input Accomplishments 65 working WebMCP tools registered in the deployed app A complete editor rather than a single-purpose proof of concept Strict-99 reference conversion and audit guardrails Browser-local projects and reference images Animated GIF, sprite-sheet, editable project, and multi-engine bundle exports Public MIT-licensed source with automated tests A reproducible Remotion demo project using real captures from the live app What we learned WebMCP works best when tools map to real product concepts instead of individual UI clicks. A strong agent-native app still needs an excellent human interface; the value comes from both surfaces sharing the same state and producing immediately reviewable results. What's next Natural-language creative recipes that combine several tools into reviewable plans More sprite animation presets and engine-specific export helpers Optional collaboration and project sharing Richer fidelity reports and side-by-side reference comparisons Community palettes, templates, and reusable agent workflows Built With ai-agents chatgpt cloudflare-workers next.js openai pixel-art react remotion typescript vinext webmcp Try it out pixelforge-studio.himomohi.workers.dev github.com pixelforge-studio.appcaster.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Appcaster kim Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Appcaster kim started this project — Aug 31, 2026 04:09 AM EDT

title: PromptDecor
pitch: PromptDecor lets you design rooms with AI: describe your vision, see catalog furniture appear in 3D, move it yourself, and get instant advice on layout, light, and flow.
about_excerpt: PromptDecor lets you design rooms with AI: describe your vision, see catalog furniture appear in 3D, move it yourself, and get instant advice on layout, light, and flow. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Designing a room is visual and spatial, but most AI assistants only return text. We wanted an AI collaborator that can act directly inside a room design—not just suggest furniture, but place it, respect boundaries, and react to user changes. What it does PromptDecor is an interactive 3D room designer. Users can browse a curated furniture catalog, add and customize pieces, move or rotate them in a 3D room, and receive layout guidance about lighting, walking flow, and clearance. External AI agents can use WebMCP tools to inspect the catalog and live room state, then place, update, or remove furniture safely. How we built it We built PromptDecor with React, React Three Fiber, Drei, and Zustand. React Three Fiber renders the interactive 3D room and low-poly furniture. Zustand holds shared room, furniture, position, rotation, color, and finish state. A curated static catalog provides real item IDs, dimensions, styles, colors, and prices. WebMCP exposes structured tools for catalog search, live scene context, placement, updates, removal, room finishes, and spatial advice. Gemini-powered WebMCP testing validates that an external agent can interact with the live scene. Collision and room-boundary logic keep furniture inside the platform and prevent overlaps. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was spatial state synchronization. A dragged object must update the 3D canvas, Zustand store, collision system, and agent-visible room context without jumping back to an old position. We also had to distinguish catalog IDs from individual scene-instance IDs, prevent hallucinated furniture and colors, handle rotated furniture footprints, and make the WebMCP tool layer safe enough for an agent to use. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created more than a chat interface: PromptDecor is a shared visual workspace where users and agents can affect the same 3D scene. Live WebMCP tools update the visible 3D room. Catalog-grounded placement prevents invented furniture. Room bounds and collision-aware placement keep layouts usable. Manual drag/rotate controls work alongside agent-driven changes. Spatial feedback considers window light, furniture clearance, and walking flow. A polished catalog drawer, room finishes, size choices, and camera views improve the experience. What we learned We learned that agent tools need strict contracts. Clear JSON schemas, exact IDs, validation, and state ownership are essential when an AI agent can change a visual application. We also learned that 3D AI experiences need more than natural-language reasoning: they need reliable coordinate systems, collision rules, visual feedback, and safe fallbacks. What's next for PromptDecor Next, we want to add real GLTF furniture models, richer material previews, saved room layouts, and more sophisticated design recommendations. We also plan to improve the reverse collaboration loop so an external agent can make more catalog-aware suggestions—for example, recommending a lower-profile bookshelf near a window rather than only warning that it blocks light. title: ProofPilot
pitch: Human-governed AI decision workspace where agents investigate evidence, analyze tradeoffs, and propose actions through WebMCP — while consequential changes require explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: Human-governed AI decision workspace where agents investigate evidence, analyze tradeoffs, and propose actions through WebMCP — while consequential changes require explicit human approval. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ProofPilot Dashboard WebMCP Agents Inspiration AI agents are getting really good at researching, analyzing information, and taking actions for us. But when the decision actually matters, there is a bigger question: How much authority should we give the agent? Imagine a team choosing an AI coding assistant, a vendor, or a software architecture. Getting an AI to say “I recommend option A” isn't particularly difficult anymore. The harder part is understanding why it recommends A, what evidence supports that recommendation, what evidence disagrees with it, what happens if our priorities change, and whether the agent should be allowed to change the decision at all. That was the idea behind ProofPilot: Decisions you can interrogate. We wanted to build a workspace where an AI agent could do meaningful work alongside a human without quietly becoming the person making the final decision. What we built ProofPilot is a human-controlled decision workspace where an AI agent can investigate, analyze, challenge, and propose — while the human stays in control of consequential decisions. The workflow is simple: Agent investigates → analyzes → proposes → human approves → state changes → audit trail. The human starts by defining the decision, the available options, and the criteria that matter. The agent can then work with that live decision through WebMCP. It can inspect the current decision state, search and add evidence, compare options, find contradictions, run sensitivity analysis, evaluate scenarios, and analyze risk. But there is an important boundary. If the agent wants to make a consequential change — for example, changing a criterion's weight or proposing the final decision — it cannot apply that change directly. Instead, ProofPilot turns it into a pending proposal. The human can inspect the proposal, approve it or reject it, and only after approval does the decision state change. The change is then recorded in the audit trail. This means the agent and the human are working on the same decision, rather than the human having to copy information between a chatbot and a separate decision-making tool. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a core part of ProofPilot because we wanted the agent to interact with the application's actual capabilities and live state, rather than simply reading a webpage or relying on browser automation. Instead of building a separate integration for one particular AI client, ProofPilot exposes its decision capabilities as WebMCP tools directly from the application. We currently expose 13 tools: get_decision_state get_evidence search_evidence add_evidence compare_options detect_contradictions run_sensitivity_analysis analyze_decision_risk evaluate_scenario propose_weight_change propose_decision request_human_review generate_decision_brief These tools cover investigation, evidence, analysis, governance, and output. Because they operate on the application's live decision state, a WebMCP-capable agent can investigate and reason about the same information that the human is looking at. The key idea is simple: Giving an agent access to a tool does not mean giving it authority to make the decision. Read and analysis tools can execute normally. Actions that can change consequential decision state become proposals and require explicit human approval. That's the boundary we wanted ProofPilot to enforce. How we built it The frontend is built with React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Wouter, and TanStack Query. The backend uses Express, TypeScript, Zod, and Vitest. One thing we were careful about was not making the LLM the source of truth for the actual decision score. ProofPilot uses a deterministic multi-criteria decision engine for weighted scoring. The system also handles confidence, risk analysis, contradiction detection, evidence gaps, sensitivity analysis, and scenario evaluation. The agent is responsible for investigating and proposing. The application is responsible for calculating and enforcing the decision logic. WebMCP tools are registered in the frontend through the model context API. Each tool has its own description, input schema, and execution logic connected to the application's functionality. We also built a Developer view where the registered WebMCP tools and their schemas can be inspected. We wanted the agent-facing interface to be visible and understandable rather than something hidden behind the UI. Challenges The hardest part wasn't registering the WebMCP tools. It was deciding where the agent's authority should stop. We wanted the agent to be capable enough to do real work. A read-only chatbot wouldn't be very useful. At the same time, we didn't want an agent to quietly change weights or make a final decision just because it had access to the corresponding function. That led us to the proposal-based governance model. Consequential actions first become pending proposals. The human reviews them, approves or rejects them, and only then can the active decision state change. We also had to make the underlying decision engine predictable and explainable. Rather than letting an LLM invent a final score, we separated the agent's investigation from the application's deterministic analysis. We tested the WebMCP integration with ChatGPT's Site Tools environment and successfully exposed and executed the registered tools from the deployed application. What we learned Building ProofPilot changed the way we think about agentic applications. We initially thought about giving agents more capabilities. But the more we built, the more we realized that capability and authority don't have to increase together. An agent can be given powerful tools to investigate evidence, challenge assumptions, compare alternatives, and prepare a recommendation without being given the ability to make the final consequential change. That's where WebMCP became especially interesting for us. It gives the agent a way to interact with the application's real functionality and state, while the application itself can decide what each tool is actually allowed to do. For us, the result is a different kind of agentic workflow: The agent does the investigation. The system does the analysis. The agent makes the proposal. The human makes the consequential decision. And the entire process is recorded. That's what ProofPilot is about. Not just getting an answer from an AI, but being able to question the reasoning behind the answer, understand the evidence, challenge the assumptions, and stay in control of what happens next. ProofPilot — Decisions you can interrogate. title: QuantMCP
pitch: An agent-native quantitative research terminal where humans explore markets visually and AI agents analyze, compare, and investigate them through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An agent-native quantitative research terminal where humans explore markets visually and AI agents analyze, compare, and investigate them through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates tells us explicitly when it is connected correctly QuantMCP — a shared research workspace for human + AI market analysis QuantMCP was built for a simple problem: quantitative research often becomes a disconnected chain of charts, prompts, parameters, and spreadsheets. That makes it hard to reproduce a strategy, compare alternatives, or review the quality of someone’s work. QuantMCP turns that chain into one visible, shared workflow. A human researcher and an MCP-enabled agent work on the same active asset, timeframe, historical events, saved strategy definition, event study, trade simulation, chart focus, and research notes. What it does The workflow is intentionally ordered for transparent competition review: Select a research universe. Search feasible shared parameters with chronological out-of-sample validation. Validate the saved universal region across assets and rank them. Optionally refine the best-ranked asset. Run an event study using the saved strategy definition. Run a deterministic historical trade simulation with explicit entry, stop, target, holding-period, and OHLC collision rules. Review the strongest and weakest historical cases together. This means Event Study and Trade Simulation do not silently use unrelated conditions: they inherit the saved robust strategy configuration. WebMCP integration QuantMCP exposes 18 browser-native WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect the active workspace, query structured historical conditions, calculate indicators and forward returns, compare timeframes, run universe and parameter research, simulate trades, focus chart ranges and trades, and save research findings. The human sees the same evidence immediately in the UI. The agent does not place orders and the app is designed for historical research only. Reliability and performance The project uses real continuous-futures demo datasets across eight assets. Heavy condition scans, parameter searches, timeframe comparisons, event studies, and trade simulations run in background workers, keeping the chart responsive and showing real progress instead of appearing frozen. To make the experience practical on desktop and mobile, QuantMCP includes a fast Intraday Core preset, keeps all assets available for full validation, bounds expensive universal searches, caches datasets by asset and timeframe, and progressively renders large trade lists. What I learned The hardest part was not building individual quant calculations; it was preserving one reliable shared state across human controls and agent tool calls. I learned that a useful AI research interface needs explicit dependencies, reproducible definitions, transparent out-of-sample evidence, and a UI that makes the next correct step obvious. title: Redline
pitch: Your agent reads the contract, flags what will cost you, and drafts the fixes as redlines you can accept or reject. It has no tool that edits the document. Not by policy. By construction.
about_excerpt: Your agent reads the contract, flags what will cost you, and drafts the fixes as redlines you can accept or reject. It has no tool that edits the document. Not by policy. By construction. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Everyone has signed a contract they didn't fully read. The current answer is to paste it into a chat window, which gets you advice about the document: a paragraph you then retype into the file yourself. We wanted the agent working inside the contract, with one hard rule: it can suggest anything and change nothing. What it does Redline is a contract review workspace for humans and their agents. The agent reads the agreement clause by clause, flags risks with severity and plain-English consequences, compares terms against a market-standard playbook, and drafts replacement language. Every change it suggests arrives as a redline — old text struck through, proposed text in green, reasoning attached, that a human accepts or rejects. Accepting is the only action that alters the contract, and no agent can take it. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Contract review is stateful, multi-step, and unforgiving of hallucination, exactly where screen-scraping agents fail and where a typed tool surface shines. Three things WebMCP makes possible that a chat upload cannot: The output is document state, not prose. A suggestion is an object anchored to clause 6 with an accept button, an author, and a status, not a sentence to transcribe. The document is live. Tools read the contract as it currently stands, so "re-check the clauses I just changed" works. An upload is a snapshot that goes stale immediately. The safety is structural. Any AI with write access is safe only while it behaves. Here there is no mutation tool registered, and the server refuses any write tagged as an agent. "Please don't edit without asking" versus "there is no API to edit" is the whole difference. Typed schemas help too: flag_risky_clause requires a clause id that exists, so the agent cannot cite clause 27 of a 13-clause contract the way chat routinely does. How it creates a better user experience You stop being a transcription layer between a chat window and a document. The agent does the reading, the comparing, and the drafting; you do the deciding, on a screen that shows exactly what would change, why, and who suggested it. Rejections carry reasons the agent can read back, so the review gets sharper as it goes. And because the tool surface is public, you bring your own agent, the one that knows your last eight contracts, your rates, and your risk tolerance. A document dropped into a fresh chat window knows nothing about the person dropping it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Work on the same legal document simultaneously, with a guarantee specifying who can change it. Before WebMCP, an agent either had no access (advice you retype) or full access (write permission you have to trust). Redline is the third option: full analytical reach, zero write capability , enforced by which tools exist rather than by how well the model behaves. The phase model makes that dynamic. In analysis, the agent has 8 tools and literally cannot propose. In redlining, it has 12. Once the contract is executed, it has 5, all read-only — a signed contract cannot be marked up, and the agent's own capabilities reflect that the moment the phase changes. How we implemented WebMCP Twelve tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback for older Chrome previews), unregistered via AbortSignal whenever the review phase changes: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "propose_edit", description: "Propose replacement text for a clause. This does NOT change the contract — it " + "creates a redline the human accepts or rejects.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { clauseId: { type: "string" }, proposedText: { type: "string" }, rationale: { type: "string", maxLength: 400 }, }, required: ["clauseId", "proposedText", "rationale"], additionalProperties: false, }, execute: async (input) => { const { proposalId } = await api.propose(reviewId, { type: "replace", ...input, via: "agent" }); return `Proposal ${proposalId} created. Status: pending_human_approval — the contract ` + `is unchanged until a human accepts it. Use list_proposals for the outcome.`; }, }, { signal: phaseController.signal }); Two design decisions did most of the work: Errors are written to be recovered from. "Error: no clause c27. Valid ids are: c1, c2, …" tells the agent how to fix its own mistake instead of leaving it to guess. Descriptions are prompts. Each says when to call the tool and what to read first, which is why agents chain them sensibly without being told the order. Stack: Express + vanilla JS, server-sent events for live sync across everyone reviewing, Upstash Redis in production so reviews survive serverless cold starts. Challenges we ran into Making the guarantee real rather than rhetorical. It isn't enough to omit an accept tool; the server also rejects any resolve request tagged via: "agent" , and phase changes are human-only. Defense in depth, so the claim survives a hostile reading. Writing tool descriptions models actually follow. Early versions had agents proposing edits to clauses they hadn't read. Explicitly saying so in the description fixed it. The WebMCP surface is still moving between document.modelContext and the earlier navigator.modelContext , so registration goes through a small adapter. What we learned Capability design is the safety story. Every guardrail you can move from the prompt into the tool surface is a guarantee instead of a hope — and phase-scoped registration means the answer to "what can this agent do right now?" is a list you can print, not a judgment call. What's next for Redline Upload your own contract; a shared playbook per organization so proposals match house style; multi-party review where the other side's agent negotiates back; and export to tracked-changes DOCX so the redlines land in the tools lawyers already use. title: Replan - Agentic Travel Recovery
pitch: A flight-cancellation site where ChatGPT's own browser discovers and calls 12 WebMCP tools - rebook, hold a room, arrange transport - no custom agent built.
about_excerpt: A flight-cancellation site where ChatGPT's own browser discovers and calls 12 WebMCP tools - rebook, hold a room, arrange transport - no custom agent built. Like Comment Story Updates Natural-language travel constraints drive flight recovery through WebMCP. ChatGPT discovers and calls Replan's 12 WebMCP tools directly. The agent coordinates recovery while the human confirms consequential actions. A multi-step recovery coordinated across flights, hotel, ground transport, notifications, and budget. Inspiration Travel recovery is a good stress test for WebMCP because it is multi-step, stateful, and involves consequential actions. The scenario behind Replan is simple: imagine a nonstop flight to Miami being canceled the day before a cruise departure from PortMiami. The traveler needs to recover quickly while balancing constraints such as timing, hotel availability, ground transportation, and budget. I wanted to explore what happens when the website exposes its capabilities directly to an AI agent instead of requiring a custom conversational layer inside the application. What it does Replan is an agentic travel recovery app where a traveler sets goals and constraints in natural language while an AI agent discovers and operates the site's capabilities directly. The traveler can ask the agent to search for replacement flights, update constraints, hold a reservation, confirm a booking, rebook a hotel, arrange ground transportation, notify a contact, track the running trip cost, and generate an itinerary summary. The app exposes 12 WebMCP tools: ping search_flights search_flights_semantic update_constraints hold_reservation confirm_booking search_hotels update_hotel_reservation book_ground_transport notify_contact calculate_total_cost generate_itinerary_summary The human remains in control of consequential actions through explicit confirmation gates, while the agent handles the multi-step coordination. How we built it Replan is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. Convex powers the one live backend piece—the semantic-search vector index, reached from the browser tool through an HTTP endpoint, so no Convex client code ships in the runtime bundle. The key integration is WebMCP. The page registers its capabilities through the WebMCP API using document.modelContext.registerTool() . ChatGPT, in its in-app browser, discovers those tools and calls them from natural-language requests. There is no custom LLM, NLU, voice layer, or custom agent in the Replan codebase. The application exposes structured capabilities and lets the agent decide how to compose them. The 12 tools are registered statically at page load. Each tool validates its inputs and returns structured JSON, including structured errors that allow the agent to understand failed operations and recover. One of the tools, search_flights_semantic , uses natural-language semantic ranking backed by a live vector index with embeddings rather than simple keyword matching. I verified the complete interaction flow manually: 12/12 tools registered, 36/36 demo turns passed, 0 failures . Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges was designing tool validation and error responses so that an AI agent could recover from invalid or conflicting requests. Structured errors turned out to be especially important because the agent needs actionable information rather than only human-readable error messages. Another challenge was designing confirmation boundaries. Search and other reversible operations can be performed speculatively, but consequential actions such as confirming a booking need an explicit human confirmation step. The final challenge was compressing a 36-turn recovery workflow into a clear demonstration under three minutes without losing the important WebMCP interactions. Accomplishments that we're proud of I successfully exposed the complete travel recovery workflow through WebMCP without building a custom agent or natural-language processing layer. The final implementation has 12 WebMCP tools , and the complete human verification covered 36/36 turns with 0 failures . Most importantly, the entire recovery chain can be driven from natural language: the agent discovers the capabilities exposed by the webpage, composes multiple tools, handles state and constraints, and stops for human confirmation when an action becomes consequential. What we learned WebMCP changes the design boundary between a website and an AI agent. The website does not need to understand how the agent reasons. It needs to expose clear, reliable capabilities that an agent can discover and compose. I also learned that confirmation gates are not just a UI concern. They shape the tool design itself by separating safe, reversible operations from consequential actions. Finally, structured JSON responses and meaningful errors are critical when tools are being operated by an agent. They provide the information needed for the agent to adapt instead of simply failing. What's next for Replan - Agentic Travel Recovery The next step is to make the recovery workflow more realistic and flexible. Potential extensions include partial availability, multi-leg itineraries, more complex constraint conflicts, and broader use of live vector search across additional travel capabilities. The goal is to continue exploring how far a website can go when it exposes reliable, composable capabilities directly to an AI agent through WebMCP. Published food-intake guidance is mapped into deterministic, reason-coded pilot rules. The UI distinguishes live records, sourced policy mappings, donor-declared facts, and simulated state. The public demo uses browser-local workflow state; Convex is included as the path to shared realtime persistence.
