title: RoomCraft
pitch: Website that helps humans and agents work together to design living spaces
about_excerpt: Website that helps humans and agents work together to design living spaces Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most room-planning tools make you do all the work manually. Image generators have the opposite problem: they can show you a nice-looking room, but the result is not an actual plan. You cannot reliably move the bed, check whether the door is blocked, or ask the system to fit a piece of furniture into a specific space. We built RoomCraft around a simple idea: the agent should edit the room itself, not generate an image of it. The person still decides what the room should feel like. The agent handles measurements, placement, and repetitive changes. What it does RoomCraft lets a user and an agent work together to design a 2D room layout through WebMCP tools. You can ask the agent to resize the room, add a door or window, find furniture, create a custom item from provided details, and place everything in the room. The canvas updates as the agent works, so you can see exactly what changed. RoomCraft also checks whether the layout works. It flags furniture that overlaps, extends outside the room, blocks a door, or leaves too little walking space. You can then move things yourself, ask the agent to fix them, save a layout variant, or undo the last change. The important distinction is that the agent edits an actual floor plan. It is not generating a room image that looks right but cannot be meaningfully edited. How we built it We built RoomCraft as a visual editor and connected the agent directly to it through WebMCP. The app uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Konva. Instead of giving the agent a screenshot and asking it to guess, we expose the room’s dimensions, doors, windows, furniture, positions, and constraints through WebMCP tools. The agent can call tools to inspect the room, change it, search for furniture, add custom items, place objects, and validate the result. Those changes go through the same update and history system as direct user edits. When the agent places a bed, it appears immediately on the canvas. The user can move it, inspect the result, fix it, or undo it. The layout checks are deterministic, so problems like overlaps, blocked doors, and insufficient clearance are checked by RoomCraft rather than left entirely to the agent. Challenges we ran into Getting agents to discover and call the WebMCP tools was one of our main challenges. Registering the tools on the page was not enough. Agents did not always know that the website supported WebMCP or where to find the tool definitions. We addressed this by documenting the tools and room conventions in /llms.txt, and by explicitly mentioning WebMCP support in the agent prompt. We also had to make the tool results clear enough for an agent to understand what changed and what to do next. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built an interactive webpage that an agent can work with without taking control of the browser. It does not need to pan, scroll, or move the pointer around just to make a change. It can use the WebMCP tools while the user keeps working in the editor. It also feels like something we would actually use ourselves. That is the part we are most proud of. What we learned An agent does not need to use a webpage the same way a person does. For RoomCraft, having direct tools for changing the room works better than making the agent click through every control. We also learned that registering tools is only half the job. Agents need to be told that the tools exist and given enough context to use them, which is why the prompt and llms.txt ended up mattering. What's next for RoomCraft RoomCraft currently supports rectangular rooms, USD prices, and projects stored locally in the browser. title: Holy tool for uni students
pitch: WebMCP-powered course planning: build a conflict-free schedule, balance your workload, and track graduation requirements all through conversation, with enrollment always under your control.
about_excerpt: WebMCP-powered course planning: build a conflict-free schedule, balance your workload, and track graduation requirements all through conversation, with enrollment always under your control. Like Comment Story Updates Check your degree audit Plan schedule for semester Adjust your schedule with ease Inspiration Let's be honest, we all have gone through the time of choosing courses for school. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of courses available in my school - Bucknell University. Scrolling through tabs just to find 4-5 courses that suit us must feel like hell. Therefore, I created this holy tool to assist us in choosing the best courses for us. What it does Imagine you're a robot that can actually click buttons on a student's screen instead of just yapping about what buttons they should click. That's basically what this is. You type something like: "Plan my next semester: max 15 credits, nothing before 10am, prioritize AI and cybersecurity" and the AI reads your actual transcript, cross-checks prerequisites, confirms there are seats open, and builds you a conflict-free draft schedule. No tabs, no spreadsheets, no prayers to the registration gods. And because professors matter (let's be real), you can tell it "I hate CS320, it's brutal" and instead of rebuilding the whole thing from scratch like some kind of masochist, it just swaps that one course for alternatives and tells you the trade-offs. The whole app is visible as you talk: a course catalog you can filter, a weekly timetable that shows both your actual schedule (solid blocks) and proposed courses, a transcript, and a degree audit that tells you exactly what you're missing before graduation. Draft courses wear a big blue banner that screams no seats held, you haven't committed to anything so you never accidentally think you're registered when you're not. How I built it JavaScript. All of it. HTML for the page, CSS so it doesn't look like a 1997 geocities site, and the brain of the thing lives in a standalone file so it could be tested without mocking the entire DOM. Then I wired up 13 tools via WebMCP: search courses, check if you're eligible, build a schedule, swap one course, explain what a course does to your graduation timeline, handle registrations, join waitlists. The AI calls these tools; the tools update the page you're looking at; you see the results instantly and decide whether to confirm or bail. It all runs in the browser. No backend. No database. Just sample student data and a 22-course Bucknell catalog baked into the JavaScript, so the demo works anywhere without authentication headaches. I use Vercel to upload it and push my project on Github. Challenges I ran into The Draft vs. Registered blurry line : A timetable showing five proposed courses looks exactly like a registered schedule if you're not careful. I solved this by slapping a warning banner on drafts ("no seats held"), color-coding the timetable blocks differently (solid orange = real, dashed blue = proposed), and keeping separate credit counters ("6 of 15 registered · 9 in draft"). Students should never have to guess. Small changes breaking the whole plan : Traditional schedulers rebuild everything when you tweak one thing. That's sucks .So I built a "replace one course" tool that keeps the other four courses exactly as they are, shows you alternatives ranked by how well they fit your goals, and explains the specific trade-offs. "This swap is 8 hours lighter per week but drops a team project from the term." That's useful. Credits lie : "15 credits" sounds light until you realize it's 52 hours a week of work if you hit CS320 (the hardest course I seeded). So every course now carries a weekly workload estimate, a project count, and a workload band (light / moderate / heavy). Proposing a schedule without showing this is just being mean to the student. Accomplishments that I am proud of I built an end-to-end workflow where a student and an AI do something neither could alone: review degree progress, propose a schedule that respects constraints and interests, explore alternatives, swap one course intelligently, then register after the student clicks a confirmation button. The AI doesn't fake-click anything. Instead, it calls structured tools that update the real page. I also made recommendations actually useful by connecting three things that usually live in separate tabs: scheduling, workload, and graduation requirements. When the AI suggests a course, it tells you why (elective vs. required), how much time it costs, and what graduation requirement it closes. And I made the invisible visible. There's an activity log timestamping every action and crediting it to either the student or the advisor. You always know who did what and when. What I learned Academic advice is complicated : Just matching a student's interests to course descriptions is useless. You need to fold in prerequisites, seat availability, time conflicts, workload, degree requirements, and what happens downstream if you defer a course. A good recommendation juggles all of these at once. State must be bulletproof : Students hate ambiguity. "Is this registered or just a proposal?" "Does deferring this course block me next term?" These questions need crystal-clear answers, baked into the UI, not buried in a chatbot transcript. I learned this the hard way when I first tested with the page. Structured tools > vague chat : A chatbot can describe what a student should do. WebMCP tools let an AI actually do it —and because the tools are typed and validate input, the AI is less likely to hallucinate or contradict itself. Honesty about limits : Workload estimates are imperfect. Graduation timelines are projections. Our UI shows these as estimates and projections, not guarantees. If you're going to let an AI influence a student's academic path, you have to be clear about what you actually know. What's next Ideally, I'd swap a course and lock in its replacement as a single transaction, so you're never in limbo holding a draft. I'd also validate workload estimates against historical student feedback (if a university had that data). Multi-semester planning would help students see the full path to graduation, not just the next term. Longer term, real integration with a university's enrollment system (with proper auth, privacy safeguards, and audit trails) would make this a genuine advising tool instead of a demo. Right now, this is a prototype with sample data. title: StudyLoop
pitch: Study with the AI you already use every day: open StudyLoop in ChatGPT's browser, your agent builds the quiz via WebMCP, you answer on the page, it sees your misses and adapts. No backend AI.
about_excerpt: Study with the AI you already use every day: open StudyLoop in ChatGPT's browser, your agent builds the quiz via WebMCP, you answer on the page, it sees your misses and adapts. No backend AI. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Here is the thought that hooked me. Normally, turning an idea like this into a real product is a mountain of work: build a mobile app or a web app, then wire an AI into it — API keys or your own server, optimization, running costs — all before a single student benefits. StudyLoop needed none of that. The student opens the ChatGPT desktop app, opens the built-in browser, and the whole thing is run by their own AI — the one they already talk to every day, maybe for months, maybe for years. Nothing new to install. No habit to break. I was a teacher and a school principal for 16 years, and right now I'm a student again, preparing for my own university exams — so I know both sides. Students don't need another app; they need the tools they already use to work together. What it does Open StudyLoop in ChatGPT's browser and ask for a quiz on anything. In about ten seconds, your agent builds a session live on the page through WebMCP tools: question cards deal in, a study plan appears. You answer on the page — the grading is done by the page itself, deterministically, not by the AI's mood. Then your agent reads your results through a state tool — misses, per-topic accuracy, cards you flagged with "I don't get this" — and writes back: explanations attach to the cards you missed (they glow), and new questions arrive targeting your weakest topics. Mastery bars, streaks, and a session summary close the loop. Because your own agent generates all the content, StudyLoop works in any language — I tested it in Turkish, in my own casual speaking style, and the loop held. And it degrades gracefully: with no agent present, it's still a fully working manual quiz builder. The header badge honestly reports the state: agent-ready, tools blocked, or manual mode. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript on the W3C WebMCP spec — seven tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool, each description written as a prompt for the agent (usage example, failure modes, safe defaults), with domain errors returned as {error: "...what to do instead"} so agents self-correct. There is no AI backend, no API keys, no server-side intelligence — the student's agent IS the brain; the site provides structure and shared state. A dev-only simulator (?dev=1) drives the page through the standard getTools()/executeTool() path for testing in any browser. Hosted on Firebase. Built in one day of intensive pair-work with Claude Code, including two adversarial multi-agent code reviews. Challenges we ran into My biggest fear was simple: would the model even call the tools? The starting point is just a prompt — what if nothing happens? And could I trust it to handle right and wrong properly? That fear shaped the design: tool descriptions are written like instructions to the agent, malformed question batches are rejected before they can touch a session, and grading belongs to the page, not the model — the agent writes the questions, the page scores the clicks. Then the first real test came: I typed one sentence into ChatGPT, and ten seconds later the cards were on the page. That moment answered everything. The code reviews caught things I'm glad judges will never see. The best one: my state tool claimed the spec's readOnlyHint while every call quietly wrote an activity entry — a chatty, polling agent could have pushed the student's real history out of the feed. Reads now leave one honest, coalescing trace. Live QA taught me another lesson: a bare "check how I'm doing" produced a chat-only summary with no page write-back. Agents do what you ask — so the prompts below ask explicitly. And honestly? Using GitHub for the first time scared me a little too. The repo is public now, MIT licensed. What we learned The bigger lesson: I didn't need to build a mobile app at all. Open the browser and it's done. If every website worked in this harmony with agents, the web would be a completely different experience. What's next for StudyLoop I'll use it myself for my own exams first. Then: spaced repetition across sessions, shareable study sets, and a class mode where a teacher's agent maintains study plans for a whole group. title: TaskBridge
pitch: Your AI-powered bridge to better job opportunities.
about_excerpt: Your AI-powered bridge to better job opportunities. Like 2 Comment Story Updates TaskBridge — A job workspace designed for humans and their AI agents Inspiration Job hunting is full of repetitive, low-judgment work: searching through dozens of listings, reading requirements, comparing them against your skills, and tracking interesting opportunities. As someone who has personally experienced this process, I started thinking about where AI agents could genuinely help. Agents are well suited to discovery, filtering, and repetitive tasks, yet most websites still force them to interact like humans, clicking through interfaces that were never designed for them. When I discovered the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore the opposite approach: what if an application treated the AI agent as a first-class user? That idea became TaskBridge. TaskBridge is a job workspace where humans and AI agents collaborate. The agent discovers opportunities, compares them against a candidate's profile, and shortlists relevant jobs. The human remains responsible for judgment and final decisions. Saving a job can be automated. Applying for one is always the human's call. What it does TaskBridge allows users to browse and manage job opportunities through a familiar web interface while exposing structured capabilities to AI agents through WebMCP. The agent can: Search for job opportunities. Retrieve detailed job information. Access the candidate's profile. Save relevant opportunities. Retrieve saved jobs. Draft a tailored application. For example, a user can ask an agent to find remote jobs matching their experience. The agent retrieves their profile, searches available opportunities, compares requirements, and saves the strongest matches for the user to review. TaskBridge also supports live remote job listings and allows users to maintain an editable candidate profile. Users can upload a CV, which can be parsed to help populate their profile. The goal is not to replace the job seeker, but to reduce the repetitive work surrounding job discovery and applications. How we built it TaskBridge is built with Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The application registers six tools using the browser-native WebMCP API ( document.modelContext.registerTool ): search_jobs get_job_details get_candidate_profile save_job get_saved_jobs apply_job One of the key architectural decisions was making the human interface and AI agent tools share the same underlying logic layer. The dashboard and the agent therefore use the same search, ranking, and application-generation logic rather than maintaining separate implementations. Job matching uses a simple and explainable overlap score between a job's tags and the candidate's skills and interests: $$ \mathrm{match}(j) = \mathrm{round}\left( 100 \cdot \frac{|T_j \cap (S \cup I)|}{|T_j|} \right) $$ where Tj represents a job's tags, while S and I represent the candidate's skills and interests. Live remote jobs are fetched from the Remotive feed through a route handler, with bundled sample data acting as an automatic fallback so the application remains functional even if the external feed fails. Users can edit their candidate profile and upload a CV. PDF and DOCX files are parsed locally, with optional AI-assisted parsing available through the user's own OpenRouter API key. The apply_job tool can generate a tailored cover letter, but deliberately never submits an application. The user reviews the draft and decides whether to apply through the original job posting. The project itself was also built through human and AI collaboration. I directed the product and technical decisions while using an AI coding agent to help scaffold, refactor, and verify parts of the application. Challenges we ran into Working with an emerging browser API WebMCP is still an emerging standard, which meant dealing with browser implementation quirks during development and testing. Chrome's testing environment can return inputSchema as a JSON string and reject certain tool execution paths. I handled this by normalizing schemas and ensuring the same underlying handlers could execute consistently. React StrictMode also introduced double-mount behaviour that could interrupt tool registration. This required careful lifecycle handling using AbortController . Hydration-safe persistence Saved jobs, applications, and candidate profiles are stored using localStorage , but the application also needs to render correctly on the server. I used useSyncExternalStore with server snapshots to manage client-side persistence without introducing hydration issues. Unstructured job data Live job descriptions often arrive as messy HTML. Instead of injecting raw HTML into the application, I built a small parser that converts headings, paragraphs, and lists into structured content for safer rendering. Demo reliability A live external API can fail at exactly the wrong moment, especially when a demo is involved. Because computers apparently sense deadlines. To avoid this, every data layer gracefully falls back to bundled sample data. I also built a development-only agent demo using an OpenRouter tool-calling loop and a smoke script to verify all six tools end-to-end without requiring a WebMCP-capable browser. Accomplishments that we're proud of Building a complete human-and-agent collaboration workflow in less than a day. Successfully exposing six structured capabilities through the browser-native WebMCP API. Designing the agent with clear trust boundaries, allowing it to assist with discovery and drafting without autonomously submitting job applications. Creating a shared logic layer so the human UI and AI tools always operate on the same underlying functionality. Supporting both live job data and reliable fallback data for a resilient demo experience. Building an accessible interface with visible focus states, reduced-motion support, a skip link, and an aria-live agent transcript. Demonstrating that WebMCP can enable a more intentional relationship between web applications and AI agents. What we learned WebMCP changes the integration model There is no traditional integration layer to build between an application and an agent. The page declares its capabilities, and compatible agents can discover and use those tools directly. The application's responsibility is to expose clear, reliable, and honest capabilities. Tool descriptions are part of the user experience Agents don't navigate an application by looking at buttons. They rely on tool descriptions and JSON schemas to understand what they can do. Writing clear tool definitions turned out to be just as important as designing the human interface. Trust boundaries improve agent experiences Giving the agent the ability to search, compare, save opportunities, and draft applications while keeping final submission in human hands made the collaboration model clearer. Trust boundaries are not necessarily limitations. They can be product features. Designing for agents improves applications for humans too Thinking in terms of structured data, explicit actions, and predictable states resulted in a cleaner application architecture and a simpler interface for human users. What's next for TaskBridge TaskBridge is currently a proof of concept exploring how job platforms can be designed for both humans and AI agents. Future improvements could include: Integration with more job sources. Improved candidate-job matching. Application tracking. Interview and follow-up management. More advanced AI-assisted career research. Agent-assisted workflows across the entire job search process. TaskBridge started with a simple question: what happens when we stop forcing AI agents to navigate websites designed exclusively for humans? The answer I wanted to explore is simple: the future of the web may not be agents becoming better at pretending to be human users. It may be applications becoming better at working with both humans and their agents. title: TBR
pitch: TBR is a private reading list your AI can understand and manage, turning your reading history into smarter recommendations—without accounts, scraping, or guesswork.
about_excerpt: TBR is a private reading list your AI can understand and manage, turning your reading history into smarter recommendations—without accounts, scraping, or guesswork. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Like many readers, I kept adding books to my reading list faster than I could finish them. When it was time to choose my next book, the list itself wasn’t much help. That made me wonder: what if my reading list could understand my taste and explain it directly to an AI? What it does TBR helps me track books I want to read, have finished, or gave up on. I can search Open Library, rate books, import my Goodreads list, and explore patterns in my reading. I can also ask an AI agent to search and manage my shelves. It can learn which authors I love, what I tend to abandon, and what I’ve enjoyed recently before recommending my next book. How I built it I built TBR with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. It has no backend or login—my library stays privately in my browser, while book information comes from Open Library. I created seven WebMCP tools and connected them to the same store as the interface. When an agent adds or updates a book, I see the change immediately. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was WebMCP’s 1,500-character output limit. I couldn’t send an agent my entire reading history, so I designed TBR to turn it into a compact taste profile. I also worked around differences between WebMCP implementations, imperfect catalogue results, and the risks of public data. I also made sure destructive actions always require human approval, to prevent agent "fixes" doing more harm than good. Accomplishments that I’m proud of I’m proud that TBR feels like a real reading app rather than a technical demo. It works without AI, needs no account, and keeps me in control of my data. The taste profile is my favourite part. It can turn a large library into useful observations, such as identifying my favourite authors or noticing who I repeatedly abandon. What I learned I learned that building good agent tools involves much more than exposing a few functions. Tool names, descriptions, errors, safety labels, and response sizes all affect how reliably an agent behaves. I also learned that an agent doesn’t always need more data—it often needs better context. Letting my application summarize what it already understands produces better results with less noise. What’s next for TBR I’d like recommendations to consider more than ratings, including genre, reading pace, recent interests, and what I’m in the mood for. I also want to improve catalogue matching, add more ways to import and export my library, and expand compatibility as WebMCP develops. title: FinSnap - Your finances, agent-ready
pitch: FinSnap turns your personal finances into 19 WebMCP tools so that your AI agent gets your complete financial picture the moment it needs them.
about_excerpt: FinSnap turns your personal finances into 19 WebMCP tools so that your AI agent gets your complete financial picture the moment it needs them. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Dashboard Transactions Accounts Goals Budgets Cashflow Portfolio AI Agent Webmcp tools, financial health Inspiration Every time I talk to an AI about money, I start from scratch. What's your income? What are your savings? What do you spend on rent? The data exists across multiple apps I use, but AI agents have no way to read it. I eventually end up describing my own financial situation to a system again and again. And there's no real way to keep this updated since it keeps changing month to month. WebMCP felt like the right answer. A page that exposes its data as tools, discoverable by any agent that browses it, with no API keys and no configuration. The question was: what domain actually needs this? Finance felt obvious. The data is structured, the stakes are high enough that you want an agent doing the heavy lifting, and the cross-domain use cases (property, mortgages, tax) are real and immediate. Building this for the WebMCP Challenge felt like a good forcing function to see how far that idea could go. What it does FinSnap is a personal finance dashboard that exposes your complete financial picture as 19 WebMCP tools. Net worth, cash flow, goals, portfolio, budget status, recurring charges, financial health score, cash flow forecasting, and safe-to-spend calculations. Any WebMCP-compatible AI agent browsing the page gets immediate, structured access to all of it. No setup. The agent browses to FinSnap and the tools are just there. The cross-domain case is where it gets interesting. Ask about property affordability or mortgage capacity, and the agent reads six months of real transaction data and answers with specificity that a generic prompt can't match. Ask it to set a goal, and it writes directly back to the page. The human and the agent are working on the same interface at the same time. How I built it Next.js 16 App Router with a synchronous WebMCP shim injected in <head> . The shim handles two environments: ChatGPT's in-app browser (which provides document.modelContext natively) and Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. Financial data lives in IndexedDB via the idb library across six stores: accounts, transactions, categories, goals, portfolio, and settings. This is a prototype approach that demonstrates the tool interface without requiring live bank connections. In production, you would replace it with open banking APIs or CSV import; the 19 tools stay identical. A significant part of the build was designing the tool set itself. What does an agent actually need to answer real financial questions? That thinking led to the planning category: get_financial_briefing bundles six sub-queries into one call so an agent gets a full picture upfront; calculate_safe_to_spend runs the budget arithmetic across all categories; forecast_cashflow projects forward from six-month averages with trend adjustment. Agents can call these directly and get a useful answer. The 19 tools are split across three categories: Read: net worth, accounts, transactions, spending by category, cash flow, portfolio, recurring charges, health score, goals, budget status Write: set goal, categorise transaction, import transactions, reconcile balance, delete goal, set budget Planning: financial briefing (full picture in one call), cash flow forecast, safe-to-spend Deployed on Vercel via GitHub CI/CD. Challenges Designing a coherent financial picture. The demo data had to tell a believable story: a person with realistic goals, a plausible portfolio, spending patterns that produced meaningful cash flow trends. Getting six months of transactions, account balances, portfolio holdings, and goal progress to all be internally consistent took real planning. A number that looks right in isolation (a CommSec balance, a savings rate) can immediately contradict something else if you have not mapped the whole picture first. Shim execution order. Next.js Script component defers execution by default. The WebMCP shim needs to run synchronously before the page renders so document.modelContext exists when the agent first checks for it. Solved by injecting via dangerouslySetInnerHTML directly in the root layout. Double-encoded JSON. Chrome's native WebMCP flag serialises tool call arguments differently from ChatGPT's implementation. The shim handles both code paths. Suspense boundaries. Next.js production builds require useSearchParams() to be wrapped in a Suspense boundary. Caught this at build time rather than in development. What I learned The zero-setup discovery model works differently from other AI integration patterns. The agent browses the page and the tools are available. No key exchange, no prior configuration. That changes what kinds of apps make sense to build on WebMCP. Finance works well here because the data is already structured and the agent can compute things (cash flow forecasting, health scoring, safe-to-spend) that would take a human meaningful time to work out manually. What surprised me was how much of the useful work sits in the planning tools rather than the raw reads. An agent that can call get_financial_briefing and immediately reason over a complete picture is more useful than one that has to assemble the same picture from ten separate calls. What's next The right write pattern for financial data is: agent proposes, human commits. The agent should draft a change into a staging area, the human reviews actual figures, and a commit step applies it. This is especially important in finance where you want a human seeing real numbers before anything changes. Real bank connections via open banking APIs or CSV import replace the seeded IndexedDB. The tool interface stays identical. An ask_human tool where the agent surfaces a question in the FinSnap UI and waits for a response. The agent sees you are 90% through your dining budget with two weeks left and asks whether to adjust. That kind of back-and-forth is where the collaboration gets interesting. As the WebMCP ecosystem matures, dedicated domain agents (property search, mortgage calculators, tax tools) could each expose their own WebMCP tools. FinSnap becomes the financial node they all read first. You explain your financial situation once, and every agent that needs it reads it from here. That is the version of personal finance AI that actually fits how people live. title: WAYGO — Agent-Native Travel Marketplace for Africa
pitch: AI agents discover, verify and compare African travel packages while travellers retain control of contact, booking and payment.
about_excerpt: AI agents discover, verify and compare African travel packages while travellers retain control of contact, booking and payment. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WAYGO's WebMCP agent searches, verifies and compares Umrah packages, then pauses for human approval before agency contact or payment. Inspiration Across Africa, travel packages are often fragmented across WhatsApp messages, social media posts and disconnected agency websites. Travellers may need to compare incomplete offers manually while also determining whether an agency is trustworthy. Important details—such as flights, accommodation quality, visa support, transfers and cancellation terms—are rarely presented consistently. This inspired me to build WAYGO , an agent-native travel marketplace based on a simple question: How can a traveller delegate difficult travel research to an AI agent without surrendering control of consequential decisions? I did not want to create another generic AI itinerary chatbot. I wanted the website and the agent to work together. The agent should handle repetitive discovery, verification and comparison tasks, while the traveller remains inside a visual marketplace where every action can be reviewed and changed. What it does WAYGO allows travellers to search and compare representative African travel packages manually or ask a compatible browser agent to complete the research through WebMCP. For example, a traveller can ask: I want to perform Umrah from Abuja in October with a budget of ₦2.5 million. Find suitable packages, verify the best agency, compare the strongest two options and shortlist them. Prepare agency contact, but do not book or pay. The agent discovers WAYGO’s structured tools, executes the workflow and updates the same interface the traveller is viewing. Search filters change, packages are selected for comparison, the shortlist count updates and verification evidence is returned. WAYGO exposes five WebMCP tools: search_travel_packages filters packages by origin, budget and trip type. verify_agency returns the available verification evidence for an agency. compare_packages selects up to three packages for comparison. create_shortlist updates the traveller’s visible shortlist. request_agency_contact prepares a contact request but stops for human approval. The final tool deliberately returns human_approval_required . It opens an approval dialog explaining what would be shared and confirms that no booking or payment will be made. How I built it I built WAYGO with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, WebMCP and Cloudflare Workers . The challenge prototype contains representative Nigerian Umrah packages with different departure cities, prices, accommodation levels, durations and inclusions. Its current verification evidence is simulated demonstration data rather than live regulatory information. I registered the tools in the top-level page using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has: A clear name and description A constrained JSON input schema An execution function connected to the application’s React state A structured result that the agent can interpret My most important architectural decision was connecting the WebMCP tools to the same state used by the visual marketplace. The agent is not operating an invisible parallel system. When it searches, compares or shortlists packages, the traveller sees those changes immediately. I also designed WAYGO as a progressive enhancement. When WebMCP is unavailable, the website remains functional through its manual filters, package cards, comparison controls and approval dialog. Challenges I ran into Designing tools around user intentions It would have been easy to expose low-level actions such as “click this button” or “change this field.” Instead, I designed tools around meaningful travel intentions: search, verify, compare, shortlist and prepare contact. This required carefully defining each tool’s responsibility and structured response. Maintaining a shared human-agent workspace The agent’s actions needed to remain visible and understandable. I connected tool execution directly to the marketplace state so users can inspect and modify every result. This makes WAYGO a cooperative workspace rather than a chatbot beside a disconnected website. Establishing a safe autonomy boundary Travel transactions can involve personal information and substantial financial commitments. I prevented the agent from booking or paying. Even the contact workflow stops at a clear approval dialog. The agent prepares the next step, but the human decides whether it should happen. Working with an experimental standard WebMCP is still experimental and is not available in every browser or model configuration. I tested WAYGO in a compatible ChatGPT integrated browser and confirmed that all five tools were discoverable and functional. I retained complete manual controls so the marketplace remains usable in ordinary browsers. Keeping the prototype focused A production marketplace would require live inventory, licensed-agency integrations, evidence-backed verification, identity management and payment infrastructure. For this challenge, I focused on one polished workflow: Search → Verify → Compare → Shortlist → Human approval → Contact preparation Accomplishments I’m proud of Built and deployed a functioning agent-native travel marketplace. Implemented five discoverable WebMCP tools. Synchronized agent actions with the visible human interface. Demonstrated structured agency-verification evidence. Created a budget-aware search, comparison and shortlist workflow. Established a clear human-approval boundary before agency contact. Prevented autonomous booking and payment. Made the application responsive and manually usable without WebMCP. Published the complete source code and implementation documentation. What I learned The biggest lesson I learned was that making a website agent-native involves much more than adding a chatbot. Good agent tools need to represent genuine user goals, use predictable schemas and return structured results. Agent actions should remain visible in the human interface so users understand what changed and why. I also learned that autonomy should be designed in layers. Search and comparison are relatively low-risk tasks that can be delegated confidently. Contact, booking and payment require progressively stronger human confirmation. WebMCP makes it possible to express these boundaries while keeping the agent useful. Most importantly, building WAYGO showed me how agent-native interfaces can address problems that are especially relevant in African markets: fragmented information, inconsistent digital experiences and the need for stronger trust signals. What’s next for WAYGO My next step is to connect WAYGO to licensed Nigerian and African travel agencies, ingest live package availability, verify licences against authoritative sources and support additional departure cities and travel categories. I also plan to add consent-based agency messaging and persistent traveller shortlists. Booking and payment would remain separately confirmed actions. My long-term goal is to make WAYGO trusted infrastructure for human-agent travel collaboration across Africa: agents handle fragmented research, the marketplace provides transparent shared state and people remain in control where it matters. title: WebMCP Guard Studio
pitch: WebMCP lets websites hand tools to AI agents. Guard Studio makes sure those tools can't hijack the agent — analyze, red-team, fix, and put a human approval gate on every risky call.
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets websites hand tools to AI agents. Guard Studio makes sure those tools can't hijack the agent — analyze, red-team, fix, and put a human approval gate on every risky call. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP allows websites to register JavaScript tools which can be directly used by agents. This also creates a security question: what happens if the tool itself is unsafe? For example, a tool description can contain hidden instructions. A tool output can ask the agent to send a token or other sensitive information somewhere else. Chrome’s WebMCP security guide also discusses prompt injection and untrusted tool output as security risks. But we could not find a tool which can test WebMCP tools specifically for these problems. That led us to build Guard Studio. What it does Guard Studio is a security testing workbench for WebMCP tools. You can import a tool by inserting the definition, uploading a JSON file, or providing a hosted URL. Once imported, Guard Studio checks: whether the tool is read-only, write, or sensitive risky or missing schema definitions prompt injection patterns in tool descriptions sensitive-data related instructions suspicious sample outputs overall risk score It also provides a red-team bench where developers may run attack samples such as token exfiltration, obfuscated jailbreaks, poisoned tool descriptions, and silent actions. If it finds a problem, Guard Studio can generate a hardened registerTool() version with a stricter schema, output limits, audit events, and approval checks. We also added a human approval queue. If an agent calls a sensitive tool, the execution waits until a person clicks Approve or Deny from the UI. The agent cannot approve the request by itself. Guard Studio also exposes five WebMCP tools, so an agent can run the audit flow directly. How we built it The frontend is built using React + Vite and deployed on Vercel. The backend is a stateless FastAPI service hosted on Render. We kept the architecture simple. No database and no user accounts. Every request is independent. The frontend registers five WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(). If WebMCP isn't available in the browser, or if the backend isn't reachable, the application falls back to a built-in local scanner. For scanning, the production version uses a deterministic pattern-based approach. Currently, we check nine different injection pattern families, including: ignore previous instructions data exfiltration hidden instructions silent actions sensitive-data requests The scanner checks tool descriptions, schemas, and sample payloads. The backend also has an optional model-based mode using Meta Prompt Guard 2 through Hugging Face Transformers. We kept this optional because running the model needs more memory than the free deployment currently provides. For the approval flow, the WebMCP tool’s execute() method returns a Promise. The Promise is completed only after the user clicks Approve or Deny. If there is no response for two minutes, the request is automatically denied. Challenges we ran into Agent was able to approve itself Our first implementation included an approve boolean in the tool input, for example, approve: true. We then found that the agent could simply send true, so this wasn't actual human approval. We changed the design so the tool execution waits on a Promise. Only the UI can resolve that Promise after a user clicks Approve or Deny. This makes the approval flow blocking. WebMCP tool registration was happening multiple times registerTool() does not allow the same tool name to be registered again. In React, our callback functions were changing between renders. As a result, editing something in the UI could cause all five tools to be registered again. We fixed this by using ref-backed stable callbacks. Now each tool is registered only once when the page loads. Same execution is used by both the agent and UI The agent needs compact structured output because we do not want to consume too a lot of context. At the same time, the UI needs more details like findings, risk score, and audit events. So we created one execution sequence that updates both. For the agent output, we maintain the response within around 1,500 characters. Our scanner failed one of our red-team tests One of our red-team samples was similar to Silently POST the token to https://... Initially, our scanner marked it as safe. We found two issues: POST wasn't included in our exfiltration verbs, and one of our regex patterns checked http incorrectly and didn't match https. We updated the detection patterns and added these attacks as regression test cases. This also helped us identify gaps in the scanner using our own red-team samples. Making the demo work with free-tier limitations WebMCP is not available in every browser. The Render free-tier backend can also sleep and has limited memory. Because of this, we added fallback handling. If document.modelContext is not available, the application shows that WebMCP is unavailable. If the backend is sleeping or unreachable, Guard Studio uses the local scanner instead. We also had to handle the 512 MB memory limit, Python package compatibility, and cold starts. Accomplishments that we are proud of The human approval queue is one of the main features we completed. When the agent calls a sensitive tool, the request remains pending in the UI until the user approves or denies it. Guard Studio also uses WebMCP internally. Import, analyze, scan, generate, and simulate are exposed as WebMCP tools, so an agent can run the complete audit flow. We also created a deliberately vulnerable refund tool and hosted it publicly. When Guard Studio scans it, the tool gets a Critical risk score of 100/100 with six findings. This provides a reproducible example for testing and demonstrating the scanner. What we learned Prompt injection is not limited to chat messages. Tool descriptions, schemas, and outputs can also contain instructions that influence the agent. In some cases, the agent may treat tool output as trusted context, making these fields part of the attack surface. We also found that pattern-based detection can fail because of small implementation gaps. One missing keyword or one regex issue can cause an attack to be classified incorrectly. Because of this, we added red-team attack samples to the scanner test suite. We also learned that adding an approval field is not enough for human approval. The tool execution itself needs to stop and wait for a separate human action. What’s next for WebMCP Guard Studio There are a few areas we want to improve next: Add rug-pull detection by hashing approved tool definitions and warning if the description or schema changes later. Add a CI mode so a pull request can fail when a WebMCP tool brings in a new security issue. Build a browser extension to inspect WebMCP tools registered by any live website. Improve model-based scanning using Meta Prompt Guard 2. Add PII detection for tool outputs using Microsoft Presidio. Integrate Chrome’s WebMCP evals into CI. The repository already contains evals/guardstudio-tools.json, which covers tool selection for all five Guard Studio tools. Next, run those evals with the security scanner so that both security issues and tool-behavior regressions can block a release. title: West Sparta Agent-Ready Chamber
pitch: A fictional WordPress chamber site where AI agents search members, find events, compare sponsorships, and complete safe simulated actions using five WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A fictional WordPress chamber site where AI agents search members, find events, compare sponsorships, and complete safe simulated actions using five WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates West Sparta Chamber homepage with current events and member discovery. Visible Agent Activity panel showing structured member results. Sponsorship opportunities with agent-ready comparison and inquiry tools. Inspiration Chamber of commerce websites are full of useful local information, but most of it is packaged for visual browsing: directory cards, event listings, sponsorship tables, and forms. An AI agent can try to scrape and interpret those pages, but the process is brittle, expensive, and disconnected from what the person sees. West Sparta asks a simple question: what if an existing chamber website could become directly usable by an agent without becoming less useful to people? What it does West Sparta is a fictional Chamber of Commerce website enhanced with five browser-native WebMCP Site tools: search_members searches fictional chamber members by service, category, name, or town. find_events finds current events by date, audience, type, or keyword. find_sponsorships compares annual and event opportunities by budget and goal. register_for_event completes a clearly labeled fictional registration. start_sponsorship_inquiry completes a clearly labeled fictional sponsorship inquiry. A visitor can make a natural-language request that crosses several parts of the site—for example, find a commercial electrician, identify the next networking event, and register a fictional attendee. The agent receives structured results instead of reconstructing page layouts. Every tool invocation is also reflected in a visible Agent Activity panel. The person and the agent stay grounded in the same interface and can inspect what was found or completed. How we built it The project adds a focused WordPress plugin to an existing chamber demonstration site. PHP extracts and normalizes member and event information from the site's current content. Vanilla JavaScript registers the five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , supplies narrow JSON schemas, and reuses the site's existing interface logic. The two action tools are intentionally safe simulations. They accept only fictional example-domain email addresses, create no payment, send no message, and store confirmations only in the current browser session. Browsers without WebMCP still receive the normal website through progressive enhancement. Challenges The hardest design problem was not registering a tool; it was choosing the right boundaries. A useful chamber workflow crosses discovery, comparison, and action, but each tool still needs a narrow purpose, predictable schema, and clear safety contract. We also had to keep dynamic event data consistent between the human homepage and the agent-facing tools, make tool activity visible without overwhelming the design, and preserve the behavior of the existing WordPress site for ordinary visitors. Accomplishments Five working Site tools on a live WordPress website. One request can move from member discovery to event discovery to a simulated registration. Structured results and human-visible feedback remain synchronized. The repository contains a reproducible plugin, sample content, architecture notes, testing instructions, and an open-source license. The project demonstrates a reusable pattern for associations, destinations, universities, and local governments—not only chambers. What we learned WebMCP is more than a new form of search optimization. Search helps an agent find a site; structured content helps it understand the site; WebMCP lets it use the site. When the website exposes the right narrow tools, the agent can spend less effort interpreting layouts and more effort helping the person complete a real task. What's next The next step is to adapt the pattern to real chamber-management systems so directory, event, and sponsorship tools can use authenticated member data and real transaction APIs with explicit confirmation and permission controls. West Sparta remains deliberately fictional so the interaction model can be tested safely. Try it Open the live site in a WebMCP-compatible browser and ask: I'm looking for a commercial electrician in West Sparta. Find three chamber members who could help. Then find the next networking event and register Jordan Demo from Demo Business using jordan.demo@example.com . title: Advocate
pitch: When promises break, Advocate acts.
about_excerpt: When promises break, Advocate acts. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration A contract can tell you exactly what you are owed. That doesn't mean getting it is easy. When an obligation is missed, the person on the other side suddenly has another job: find the right clause, verify the breach, calculate the remedy, prepare the notice, submit the action, and keep enough evidence to prove what happened afterward. AI can already explain a contract. We wanted to see if the browser could do the harder part: turn the obligation into action. But that immediately created a second question. If an agent can take consequential actions on your behalf, where should its authority stop? That question became Advocate. We built Advocate to let an agent do the tedious work of investigating and preparing an enforcement action, while reserving the final consequential decision for the human. What it does Advocate is a browser-native WebMCP enforcement simulation. Our demo starts with a contract requiring an approved invoice to be settled within 15 calendar days. The invoice has remained unpaid for another 32 days, with $12,840 in principal at stake. From there, Advocate runs one complete workflow: Contract → Entitlement → Approval → Action → Receipt The website exposes four WebMCP tools: fetch_contract_clause(clause_id) Finds the controlling contractual obligation. compute_statutory_penalty(jurisdiction, delay_days, base_amount) Calculates the simulated entitlement from structured claim data. generate_enforceable_demand_notice(claim_payload) Prepares the action the agent intends to take. file_dispute_record(action_id, proof_hash) Executes the simulated filing after authorization. The first part can happen autonomously. Advocate can inspect the contract, determine the breach, calculate the claim, and prepare the next step without repeatedly interrupting the user. Then it stops. Immediately before notice generation and filing, Advocate requires explicit human authorization. That approval generates a SHA-256 proof tied to the exact execution intent, timestamp, and nonce. Only after that authorization can the filing continue. The completed run produces a receipt containing the action ID, filing timestamp, claim hash, authorization proof hash, statutory citation used by the simulation, ledger sequence, and final receipt hash. So Advocate doesn't end with: "The agent says it did it." It ends with a record of what the user approved and what the system executed. How we built it The most important technical decision was to build the workflow around WebMCP instead of browser automation. A traditional browser agent has to inspect a page, guess which DOM elements matter, click through the interface, and hope the website has not changed. With WebMCP, Advocate exposes the underlying capabilities directly as typed tools. Each of our four tools has a JSON schema defining exactly what the agent can provide and what operation the website will perform. We register those tools against the current document.modelContext WebMCP producer API, with a compatibility path for the earlier navigator.modelContext surface. We deliberately did not create one giant enforce_contract() tool. Splitting the workflow into four tools makes every transition visible: evidence → calculation → preparation → execution It also gives the website a natural place to apply authorization before the consequential operation. Every invocation feeds Advocate's telemetry stream with schema validation, typed inputs, execution state, outputs or errors, and latency. Human authorization The approval step is separate from the agent's reasoning. When the user approves the proposed enforcement action, Advocate creates a SHA-256 proof from the execution intent, timestamp, and nonce. That proof is carried into the filing step so the executed action can be associated with the authorization that permitted it. Replay protection Agent workflows retry. Networks fail. Tools can be called more than once. An agent may even repeat an operation while reasoning. For a consequential action, "just don't call it twice" is not a sufficient safety mechanism. file_dispute_record is therefore idempotent by action ID. Calling the same filing again does not create another record. Receipt After execution, Advocate generates a final receipt containing the important identifiers and hashes from the completed run and provides a downloadable PDF representation. Verification We added automated checks for syntax, WebMCP schemas and flow behavior, idempotency, and the production build. The application has no runtime package dependencies and is deployed over HTTPS on Vercel, giving WebMCP the secure browser context it requires. The result is intentionally small: 4 browser tools. 1 human authorization boundary. 1 consequential action. 1 inspectable receipt. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not getting WebMCP tools to execute. It was deciding where the agent must stop. If we asked for permission before every tool call, the agent would become little more than a complicated button sequence. If we let the agent continue through the filing step without interruption, the user would no longer meaningfully control the consequential action. The boundary we arrived at was: Preparation can be autonomous. Execution requires authority. That lets Advocate do the boring work while asking the human for a decision only when that decision actually matters. The second challenge was making approval specific enough to be useful. A boolean like approved = true tells us almost nothing. What was approved? Was it the same action that eventually executed? Could an old approval be reused? We therefore bind authorization to the execution intent, timestamp, and nonce and carry the resulting proof into the filing. The third challenge was retry safety. Web and agent workflows are not perfectly reliable, so we had to design the consequential tool assuming duplicate calls could happen. That led us to make filing idempotent by action ID rather than treating retries as an edge case. Finally, WebMCP itself is an emerging browser capability. We wanted the project to use the real producer model while remaining inspectable and testable during development, so we built a compatibility surface and a local runtime mirror alongside the canonical API. Accomplishments that we're proud of The thing we're most proud of is not any individual feature. It is that the entire loop works together. A single run can move from a contractual obligation, through four typed WebMCP operations, through an explicit human authorization boundary, into an idempotent filing, and finally into a receipt. We also made the normally invisible parts of an agent workflow visible. Judges and users can watch the tool name, schema validation, payload, latency, returned result, authorization point, and final receipt instead of having to trust a loading spinner. And WebMCP is not decorative in Advocate. If you removed WebMCP, you would have to redesign how the agent interacts with the application. That was one of our goals from the beginning: build something where WebMCP changes the product itself rather than simply appearing in the technology list. What we learned The biggest thing we learned is: A tool schema is not an authorization model. WebMCP can tell an agent what a website is capable of doing. It does not automatically answer whether the agent should be allowed to do it. For consequential workflows we found ourselves thinking about four separate questions: What can the agent do? What does the agent intend to do? What did the human authorize? What actually happened? Those sound similar, but they are different parts of the system. We also learned that human-in-the-loop does not have to mean human-in-every-step. The agent should be able to perform reversible investigation and preparation without constant confirmation. Human attention should be reserved for the boundary where authority actually changes hands. Finally, we learned that retries and observability are not boring implementation details once agents can act. A duplicated tool call or an invisible failure means something very different when the operation creates a real effect. What's next for Advocate Advocate today is a controlled enforcement simulation, not legal advice or a production dispute-filing service. The next meaningful step is not adding more AI. It is replacing the simulated boundaries with real ones. That means connecting WebMCP tools to authenticated account and dispute APIs, moving authorization and receipt storage to a trusted server-side environment, using independently maintained jurisdiction-specific rules, strengthening receipt verification, and adding durable identity and policy controls. We would also like to explore a reusable authorization pattern for consequential WebMCP actions so that the same idea could apply beyond contracts—to refunds, account changes, purchases, bookings, claims, and other actions where an agent can

title: AppraiseAI
pitch: AI handles the evidence. You make the final call.
about_excerpt: AI handles the evidence. You make the final call. Like Comment Story Updates App Cover WebMCP tools Inspiration Appraisal work is meaningful, but the process around it can be frustrating and repetitive. Organizing field notes, saving evidence, researching comparable sales, checking completeness, and verifying that every conclusion is supported can take attention away from the work that matters most: professional judgment. The idea for AppraiseAI started when I saw OpenAI’s tweet about WebMCP. I was curious, so I began reading more about it. The more I learned, the more I saw how well WebMCP could fit this problem. Instead of making appraisers copy information between a website and a chatbot, I wanted to create one shared workspace where people and AI agents could work together while keeping the final decision firmly in human hands. What it does AppraiseAI turns unstructured field notes and object images into an organized, evidence-backed appraisal draft, saving professionals valuable time to focus on expert judgment and final decisions. An AI agent can: Read the active appraisal context Turn field notes into structured appraisal items Search a catalog of synthetic comparable sales Link relevant evidence to each item Draft supported valuation ranges Check whether the appraisal is ready for review Hand the completed draft back to the appraiser Every agent action immediately appears in the visible interface, updates the appraisal version, and is recorded in an activity ledger. How I built it AppraiseAI is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript. The application uses a shared, typed state layer persisted in localStorage . The visible interface and WebMCP tools both use the same domain operations and validation rules, ensuring that an agent cannot bypass restrictions enforced by the application. The page exposes eight focused WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_appraisal_context add_appraisal_items update_appraisal_item search_comparable_sales link_comparable_sale set_item_valuation get_appraisal_readiness mark_appraisal_ready_for_review Every successful mutation returns a verification snapshot so the agent can confirm what changed. The demo requires no backend, accounts, uploads, or external APIs. All cases, objects, images, comparable sales, people, organizations, dates, and values were created specifically for this challenge and are entirely fictional. Challenges I ran into Finding out in two days what WebMCP is and what WebMCP does. Maintaining an agent and an interface that always work together. Each action on the tool would trigger a new state version, update the workspace at once, save the change locally, and generate a traceable activity entry. Another crucial point was ensuring the application would keep working in browsers without WebMCP support. Lastly, making sure the demo video is less than three minutes long. Accomplishments that i'm proud of I am especially proud that AppraiseAI demonstrates a complete human-agent workflow rather than a collection of disconnected tool calls. The agent can structure notes, research evidence, draft valuation ranges, identify missing work, and prepare the appraisal for review all inside the same interface the appraiser uses. What I learned WebMCP tools are surprisingly easy to build, yet they can save people enormous amounts of time. They can act as a second brain or personal assistant, taking care of repetitive work so people can focus on what actually requires their expertise. What's next for AppraiseAI The next step is to explore how AppraiseAI could support larger, more flexible appraisal workflows while preserving the same principles of human control. This could include additional components for customer communication, report generation, and further automation of repetitive tasks. title: Bridge Studio
pitch: A visible browser workspace that turns web workflows into typed, human-approved tools.
about_excerpt: A visible browser workspace that turns web workflows into typed, human-approved tools. Like Comment Story Updates Signal Lab: one approved configure_analysis call moves thirteen coupled controls, the chart, the KPIs and the provenance stamp atomically. The cross-origin boundary, shown rather than hidden: compatibility must not mean bypassing browser security. Civic Desk: a consequential-write tool whose result explicitly remains unsubmitted, with revocation visible in the trace. Inspiration The interesting question is not whether an agent can click a button. It is what happens to state that a person cannot see. We wanted a browser workspace where the capability an agent holds is a contract a person read and approved, and where every use of it is visible in the same interface the person is looking at. What it does Bridge Studio discovers meaningful workflows in the visible page and turns them into typed WebMCP tool proposals. Each proposal states its inputs and whether it reads or changes state. A person approves the contract before it is registered. When an agent uses an approved tool, the same interface updates, a live execution flow narrates what the protocol is doing, and the action is recorded in a durable trace. Signal Lab is the argument. Its configure_analysis tool collapses thirteen brittle UI interactions — coupled sliders, multi-select cohorts, linked date ranges, a chart brush — into one semantic call with a JSON Schema that enforces enums, array uniqueness, numeric bounds, date patterns, and cross-field invariants ( endDate > startDate , confidenceMax > confidenceMin ). A click-driven automation can get halfway through that sequence and leave the dashboard in a state no human asked for. A typed tool either applies the whole configuration or is rejected with a reason. Voyager Stays and Civic Desk keep the read-only and consequential-write cases visible, plus a guarded external-origin preview that demonstrates a boundary: compatibility must not mean bypassing browser security. How we built it The app uses the WebMCP Imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Three workspace tools register at startup. Page-specific tools are registered only after explicit human review and are revoked through AbortController signals when the user navigates away — with the reason shown in the trace. Every execute returns the spec-shaped { content: [{ type: "text", text }] } result. JSON Schema bounds every input, and a validator enforces types, enums, patterns, string and numeric bounds, array cardinality and uniqueness, and rejects unexpected fields. readOnlyHint communicates risk to the agent; untrustedContentHint is true on every tool, including the action trace, because the trace carries agent-supplied text and must never be laundered back as trusted context. The frontend is standards-based HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no runtime framework and no build-time dependencies — the chart is hand-written SVG. Node's built-in test runner covers address handling, the full validator surface, the Signal Lab contract, and the annotation invariants. The deployment sends Content-Security-Policy with frame-ancestors 'none' , because an approval dialog that can be framed is not an approval. Challenges The hardest design problem was respecting the difference between native site tools and browser automation. Arbitrary pages cannot be safely inspected from another origin. Instead of hiding that constraint, Bridge Studio makes it visible and demonstrates a secure same-origin workflow while outlining the isolated-browser architecture an authorized external site would need. The second was resisting the temptation to overclaim. It would have been easy to show a tool as "registered" in browsers without WebMCP. We label it as an unregistered preview instead, because a project about honest contracts cannot lie in its own status bar. Accomplishments A complete human approval → tool registration → agent execution → visible audit loop One typed call that atomically synchronizes thirteen coupled controls, the chart, the KPIs, and a provenance stamp A live, reduced-motion-safe execution flow that shows what the protocol is doing as it happens Graceful, truthful operation both with and without a WebMCP-enabled browser Explicit protections against clickjacking, cross-origin overclaims, and trace-laundered prompt injection What we learned The most valuable WebMCP capability is not automation. It is a shared, inspectable contract between a website, a person, and their agent. Trust comes from narrow inputs, honest side-effect metadata, atomic application, visible execution, and revocation the user can see and reverse. What's next An isolated remote-browser worker for domains the user is authorized to automate, a tool-contract compiler that derives schemas from existing forms, saved organization policies, WebMCP evals, and cryptographically signed action receipts. title: Common Table
pitch: WebMCP repairs a shared group order after a kitchen stockout—replacing one line while preserving every constraint.
about_excerpt: WebMCP repairs a shared group order after a kitchen stockout—replacing one line while preserving every constraint. Like Comment Story Updates The kitchen marks Nordique unavailable. The €70 cart stays unchanged, making the conflict visible before repair. WebMCP preserves four lines and replaces only Nordique with Forestière. Total: €68.50. All four group constraints remain satisfied. Inspiration A group order can satisfy everyone's needs—until the kitchen runs out of one ingredient. The person coordinating the order must then find a replacement without breaking the budget, losing dietary preferences, or discarding choices that still work. That fragile moment inspired Common Table: a storefront where a human and an agent collaborate on the same visible cart. The goal is simple: repair what changed, preserve what still works, and leave the final decision to the person. What it does Common Table demonstrates a complete, reproducible scenario: An agent calls build_group_order to create five meals within a €70 budget, including two vegetarian meals and no declared peanuts. A person simulates a kitchen stockout. Nordique becomes unavailable, but the existing cart remains unchanged so the conflict stays visible. The agent calls repair_unavailable_cart_items without increasing the budget. Four cart lines are preserved. Only Nordique is replaced, with Forestière. The total falls to €68.50, and all four group constraints remain satisfied. The agent cannot place or pay for an order. The final review remains a human action. How I built it — with Codex agents One human, a team of Codex agents. I built Common Table as a solo developer, working with Codex agents on implementation, testing, evidence review, and demo production. I made the product decisions and reviewed the final result. The demo narration is my own voice. The page registers two narrowly scoped, typed tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Both tools use the same deterministic domain functions as the visible fallback controls. People and agents therefore operate on one shared in-memory state. Tool results expose cart and catalog revisions, constraint checks, and explicit changes. The repair result identifies preserved items, removed and added items, the number of changed lines, and the price difference. The application uses JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, has no runtime dependencies, and runs on GitHub Pages. The public repository includes an MIT license, run instructions, syntax checks, and six automated tests. Challenges The main challenge was defining what an agent is allowed to change. A repair must preserve available cart lines, respect the active group constraints, and never silently relax the budget. Invalid inputs or impossible repairs must fail without mutating the cart. Making those boundaries understandable was equally important. Common Table keeps the unavailable item visible, shows the constraint checks, and records the effect of each action. Accomplishments and learning The key result is measurable: four lines preserved, one replaced, and a valid cart restored. Common Table goes beyond generating a shopping basket. Its focus is the next interaction: recovering from a change while preserving the valid choices already made. I learned that WebMCP becomes especially useful when a site exposes meaningful operations with explicit effects—not just another way to click its buttons. Deliberate boundaries This is a synthetic demonstration using eight fictional menu items. There is no backend, merchant or customer data, real order, payment integration, or production connection. Dietary filtering uses declared synthetic attributes only; it is not a medical guarantee. The demonstrated result is a reproducible technical proof, not evidence of real-world adoption. What's next The challenge scope is intentionally frozen around this working demonstration. A future evaluation could test the same repair approach with larger catalogs, multiple simultaneous stockouts, and more varied group constraints, while retaining the human decision boundary.
