title: Commonplace
pitch: A blog and reading platform that adapts to you. Using WebMCP, browser agents reshape layout, colors, and drafts around how you write and read.
about_excerpt: A blog and reading platform that adapts to you. Using WebMCP, browser agents reshape layout, colors, and drafts around how you write and read. Like Comment Story Updates OLED pitch-black feed with headers, hero, quote, and agent rail hidden via user settings. Personalization studio drawer for adjusting layout density, measure, type scales, and surfaces. Realtime voice guide in dark emerald monospace connecting spoken intent to WebMCP actions. Distraction-free reading view on warm paper with generative artwork and local save actions. In-page WebMCP tool inspector displaying schemas and live execution for all 44 tools. Adaptive desk in night mode with live WebMCP telemetry and quick palette switching. Publishing composer with structured fields exposed directly to browser agents. Public profile rendered in editorial serif typography and dark emerald forest slate. Commonplace Commonplace is a blog and reading platform prototype that adapts to you. Using WebMCP, browser agents reshape layout, colors, and drafts around how you write and read. Inspiration For as long as I can remember, the very first thing I do when opening any new piece of software is dive straight into settings. I inspect every toggle, theme picker, and slider to bend the tool to how I think. Google built Material Expressive for a reason. I spend hours tuning browser extensions and user scripts because default interfaces never quite fit. The web has spent thirty years treating consumers as passive recipients of frozen pixels. A product team in another time zone decides your column width, font scale, and color scheme, and you are expected to conform to it. In the AI era, that model makes no sense. We now have the capability to make software listen and adapt. I wanted to build a corner of the web that I could reshape in real time to what matters to me right now. What it does Commonplace is a personal blog and reading platform where the interface adapts to how you read, write and feel. Instead of hiding controls inside nested preference menus, Commonplace turns its entire runtime into an action contract for browser agents via WebMCP: You can tell the agent you feel tired, and it instantly softens contrast, drops into night mode, and narrows the reading measure. You can ask the agent to hide sidebars, rearrange homepage blocks, or surface your saved queue without touching settings. The agent searches topics, queries your reading list, and edits active drafts beside you in the composer without taking over your screen. Through OpenAI Realtime WebRTC mapped to the exact same WebMCP tools, you can talk to the desk to dictate thoughts or re-theme the workspace hands-free. How I built it Commonplace is built as a local-first application using React 19, TypeScript, Bun, and Vite, with styling powered by Tailwind CSS v4 and dynamic CSS custom properties. The platform registers 44 distinct tools on document.modelContext using @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill . Every tool includes strict JSON schemas, descriptions, and operational hints like readOnlyHint and idempotentHint . Tools are registered under their canonical dot names and parallel underscore aliases so ChatGPT browser agents can call them without validation failures. The styling system maps 13 semantic OKLCH tokens directly to CSS variables, allowing runtime palette and typography adjustments with zero layout jank. The app links document.modelContext , window.modelContext , and navigator.modelContext so host environments that attach to any of the three discover all capabilities. All post data, drafts, and theme overrides live in browser localStorage , removing all sign-up friction for judges. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the UI look coherent and intentional given the sheer amount of live customization built into it. When you allow an agent to adjust corner radii, swap between sans-serif and editorial serifs and manipulate color scales dynamically, layout can quickly become messy. Engineering a design system that holds its balance and typography rhythm while every dial remains turnable was technically demanding. I also ran into browser environment edge cases and platform nuances. Ensuring that WebMCP implementation works properly across all supported platforms was the primary challenge, as it's the first thing you have to get right if you want to deliver the rest of the experience. Accomplishments that I'm proud of It clicked when the experience I craved for years finally matched the one I built. I opened the browser, spoke to the space, and watched the page translate my intent and mood into the exact visual setup I needed, right there, with no delay. The experience is as seamless as it should be, and I think it's the first time when the paradigm shift can finally happen as scale, for all. What I learned Rigid rules will soon be a thing of the past in consumer software. Building Commonplace proved that WebMCP fundamentally changes the relationship between people and software. When websites expose typed tool contracts instead of forcing agents to scrape fragile CSS selectors, software becomes truly flexible and accessible. What's next for Commonplace Commonplace represents a design philosophy I intend to carry into every product I build. Beyond this hackathon, I want to explore multi-device agent synchronization, peer-to-peer reading networks, and richer declarative forms so that adaptive software becomes the standard way people experience the web moving forward. title: Expediente Vivo — Evidence Review Desk
pitch: The agent reads and proposes; the human sees the evidence and decides.
about_excerpt: The agent reads and proposes; the human sees the evidence and decides. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Expediente Vivo — Evidence Review Desk Inspiration Document-heavy cases are difficult to review safely because contracts, claims, orders, duplicates and missing attachments arrive mixed together. Claims, allegations and evidence can easily be confused, while exact provenance gets lost. A normal chatbot sees presentation text, not the application's canonical IDs, evidence types or safety boundaries. What it does Expediente Vivo opens a verified synthetic dossier and gives a human and an agent the same evidence-review workspace. Through WebMCP, the agent can: call get_dossier_summary to read structured matter status and real attention-item IDs; call inspect_assertion to inspect classification, uncertainty, review flags and exact provenance; call focus_evidence to open the cited evidence visibly on the live page; and call propose_review_status to create a reasoned, pending review proposal. The interface then shows AGENT PROPOSAL · Pending human review . Only the person can press ACCEPT or REJECT . That decision updates the separate proposal record, never the canonical assertion or its evidence. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP gives the agent a stable, typed vocabulary— matter_id , assertion_id , evidence state and provenance—and safe actions defined by the application itself. A detached API would not connect the agent to the evidence currently visible in the browser. A chatbot or DOM scraper would have to infer semantics from presentation markup and use brittle selectors. Here, the page explicitly declares what the agent may read and do. The agent can inspect, navigate and propose on the same live dossier the human sees, while the final decision remains a visible human action. The human–agent workflow A reviewer asks the agent to find an item needing attention. The agent reads the dossier summary, chooses a real assertion, inspects its structured evidence, focuses the exact cited fragment in the interface, and creates a bounded workflow proposal. The human reviews the same evidence and accepts or rejects the proposal. Canonical provenance remains intact throughout. How we built it The browser registers four top-level tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool outputs reuse the open synthetic dossier's existing structured data; no model is rerun and no facts are invented. Read tools return typed application state, focus_evidence performs only a visible page-view change, and propose_review_status writes to a separate tab-local proposal queue. The public challenge deployment contains only the packaged synthetic dossier and source PDFs. It has no login, uploads, database, live inference, OCR, private storage access or external actions. Tests cover tool discovery, invalid IDs, provenance integrity, non-promotion of allegations, proposal separation and explicit human decision. Prior work and challenge work Pre-existing baseline: the underlying Expediente Vivo document-intelligence engine, dossier schema, provenance rules, synthetic fixtures and original case interface existed before this challenge. The tagged pre-webmcp-baseline commit records that boundary. Judges should not score those components as new work. Built for the WebMCP Challenge: the top-level WebMCP integration; four typed site tools; shared human–agent review state; visible evidence focusing; agent review proposals; the explicit human ACCEPT/REJECT boundary; WebMCP observability; safety tests; and the public synthetic-only challenge packaging. The timestamped delta is documented in the repository. Codex assisted with implementation, testing and documentation. The entrant remains responsible for the project ideas, source, rights and submission. Challenges and lessons The hardest design decision was deciding what must never become an agent tool. ACCEPT and REJECT are deliberately absent from WebMCP. Human-in-the-loop safety is enforced as a capability boundary, not presented as a promise in the interface. We also learned that useful agent collaboration needs a precise handoff: structured inspection → exact visible evidence → bounded proposal → explicit human decision. Accomplishments Four working, non-trivial WebMCP tools on a coherent public app. Exact evidence provenance remains unchanged after proposal, accept or reject. A deterministic synthetic demo that requires no account or credentials. A clear distinction between documentary state, agent proposal and human decision. What's next A production version could add authenticated, persistent proposal history and organization-specific review policies. Those features were intentionally excluded from this focused challenge slice. title: Lapor AI
pitch: Less tax paperwork. More human control.
about_excerpt: Less tax paperwork. More human control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Government websites often ask people to complete high-stakes processes through dense forms, unfamiliar terminology, and long sequences of pages. Indonesian tax filing through Coretax is one example. Taxpayers need help understanding what belongs in each section, but they also need to verify every value before filing. I built LaporAI to make it easier to do government paperwork. What it does LaporAI is a simulation of an Indonesia tax file system, Coretax, using fictional taxpayer data and synthetic documents. The website exposes its filing functions as state-aware WebMCP tools. An agent can: Upload tax file related documents. Find missing or inconsistent assets and liabilities. Navigate through the filing steps. Prepare evidence-based corrections for the taxpayer to approve or reject. Validate the return and explain what still needs attention. The final reviewer remains human-only. The agent operates the website's functions while the taxpayer sees and controls the result. How we built it I built LaporAI with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The application runs entirely in the browser with no backend or database. I studied the Indonesia's Coretax system and recreated the parts needed for an end-to-end demonstration. The filing workspace includes documents, employment income, assets, liabilities, family and PTKP (Personal tax-free allowance) information, validation, declaration, and a simulated receipt. Challenges we ran into The current WebMCP input model accepts structured JSON, but it does not provide a native File or Blob input for PDF attachments. To support agent-assisted document import, I created an upload_tax_document tool that accepts the document type, file name, and Base64-encoded PDF bytes. LaporAI reconstructs the file in the browser, validates it, extracts the supported records, and checks that it belongs to the active fictional taxpayer. Accomplishments that we're proud of I created a complete end-to-end tax-filling workflow with human in the loop to make sure the data is valid. What we learned WebMCP enables the agent to easily move through the web just like a normal human. This enables a lot more UX possibilities. What's next for LaporAI The next step is to test the same approach on other public-service workflows where people face complex forms and must verify sensitive information, including visa and immigration applications, passport applications, business registration, healthcare reimbursement, and student financial aid. The bigger goal is to show public institutions that adding agent-readable capabilities does not require removing human control. A government service can let an agent handle the paperwork while the citizen remains the final decision-maker. title: Mythweaver : Paint together on web

title: Patchwork - WebMCP Challenge
pitch: Most agents click through UIs built for humans. Patchwork gives your agent real WebMCP tools to design garden beds, diagnose plants (and more): validated, visible and logged on one shared canvas.
about_excerpt: Most agents click through UIs built for humans. Patchwork gives your agent real WebMCP tools to design garden beds, diagnose plants (and more): validated, visible and logged on one shared canvas. Like Comment Story Updates The image shows the garden created by the agent and the human together. The image shows the 6 tools the agente can discover and use. The image shows the care calendar filled by the agent. The image shows the Diagnose section used by the human. What inspired me The web was built for humans — buttons, menus, grids. AI agents browsing today have to reverse-engineer that intent, clicking pixel by pixel and hoping. When WebMCP landed, the promise was obvious: websites could hand agents real, structured tools instead of a guessing game. I wanted to prove it in a domain where rules actually matter. Gardening is full of precise, checkable constraints (companion planting, spacing, sun hours, seasons) where a wrong click is visible as a dying plant. A garden felt like the perfect place to show that an agent doesn't have to guess: it can negotiate against real rules, on a canvas you both see. Also, I love grow hot chili peppers. What I built Patchwork is a shared urban garden. Two beds, a crop catalog of 27 plants (soon to expand), a care calendar, and a plant doctor. The human clicks cells to plant; the agent can calls six WebMCP tools (design_bed, suggest_plan, diagnose_issue, list_crops, get_garden_state, log_task) and every action lands on the same live canvas, validated by a deterministic rules engine and logged in an activity panel. The agent drafts the plan; the rules push back; the human watches it happen. Agent + Human: Teamwork! How I built it Vite + React 19 + TypeScript (strict) + Zustand + MichiRouter, with the horticultural engine as pure, testable TypeScript — no LLM calls, no backend, $0 runtime cost. The rules engine is the single source of truth for both the UI and the tools: the same function validates your click and the agent's tool call. Several vitest tests cover the engine, the store, accessible UI, and direct execution of every WebMCP tool against a mocked document.modelContext. Challenges I faced On one hand, time was one of the biggest challenges; on the other, working with a still-experimental technology; and finally, determining which tool to create that would be useful for many people. Then came a design challenge: how to verify what the agent is doing? The answer was visibility and feedback: every tool returns structured warnings, and every mutation is logged with actor, tool, and result, so the human retains final authority. title: ReuseRoute
pitch: An agent-native circular economy assistant that finds the best next life for unwanted items through repair, reuse, parts recovery, or recycling.
about_excerpt: An agent-native circular economy assistant that finds the best next life for unwanted items through repair, reuse, parts recovery, or recycling. Like Comment Story Updates ReuseRoute Let your AI agent find the best next life for anything you no longer need. Inspiration: Getting rid of an item is deceptively complicated. A cracked laptop might be repairable, refurbishable, useful for parts, or finally ready for material recovery. A chair could be donated if pickup exists. Damaged clothing might still be repairable or useful for fibre recovery. The web has plenty of information about these options, but the user journey is fragmented. People often have to open several pages, interpret different acceptance rules, compare conditions, and then figure out what to prepare before a handoff. The easiest option can become the trash bin simply because the better option takes too much research. We wanted to explore a different kind of open web: one where circular-economy services do not just publish pages for humans to read, but also expose clear, structured actions that a user's agent can call on the person's behalf. What it does: ReuseRoute is a human-first web app with an agent-native WebMCP layer. A person describes an unwanted item, its condition, their transport constraint, and what matters most. A browser agent can then: find eligible repair, reuse, salvage and recycling routes, compare the strongest options using structured fields, select one option and open its details on the page, prepare a visible handoff checklist, save the selected route locally, pre-fill a visible handoff request for the person to review. The last step is intentionally human-confirmed. The declarative WebMCP form does not auto-submit. The agent can prepare the task, but the person makes the commitment. All organizations and service data in the hackathon demo are fictional, so the app never presents invented availability or eligibility as real-world guidance. How we built it: ReuseRoute is a dependency-free static web app built with semantic HTML, responsive CSS and vanilla JavaScript. The WebMCP implementation uses both APIs: Imperative WebMCP: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) defines structured search, comparison, selection and saved-state tools using JSON Schema. Dynamic tool lifecycle: after a route is selected, ReuseRoute registers route-specific prepare_selected_handoff and save_selected_route tools. An AbortController removes the old contextual tools when the selection changes. Declarative WebMCP: the handoff form uses toolname, tooldescription and toolparamdescription attributes so an agent can fill the real visible form. Shared state: every agent action updates the same interface the human sees — result cards, details dialog, checklist, saved indicator and activity log. Progressive enhancement: the complete manual experience still works when WebMCP is unavailable. The demo uses local browser storage for saved routes and confirmed demo handoff requests. There is no backend and no network write operation. Challenges we ran into: The main design challenge was resisting the temptation to expose one giant "do everything" tool. WebMCP is more useful when the tool surface reflects the product's real task boundaries. We split the journey into discovery, comparison and selection, then made the tool set state-aware. A handoff-preparation action should not exist before a route has been chosen, so those tools are registered only in the relevant context. A second challenge was deciding where the agent should stop. Preparing a handoff request is useful automation; silently submitting one is a different level of commitment. The declarative form became our human checkpoint: the agent can populate it, the browser makes that visible, and the person confirms. Finally, we wanted the demo to be trustworthy. Instead of pretending fictional services were real, every program and impact signal is clearly labeled as demo data. What we learned: The biggest lesson was that agent-friendly design is not the same as adding chat to a website. WebMCP works best when the website itself becomes legible as a set of intentional capabilities. We learned to think about: the user's goal before individual tool calls, initial application state, the smallest useful tool boundaries, when tools should appear or disappear, which outputs should visibly update the UI, and where a human confirmation is more appropriate than autonomous execution. What's next: A production version could let real repair cafés, charities, retailers and municipal reuse programs expose their own WebMCP tools. A user's agent could then discover and orchestrate those capabilities across the open web without relying on fragile DOM scraping. The long-term idea is simple: when someone is finished with an object, the web should make its next useful life easier than throwing it away. title: Runner Agent × Thailand in Motion
pitch: A multilingual Runner Agent that turns one natural-language goal into a safe run plan, shared route review, circular support loop, and human-confirmed Run Pass through 14 WebMCP actions.
about_excerpt: A multilingual Runner Agent that turns one natural-language goal into a safe run plan, shared route review, circular support loop, and human-confirmed Run Pass through 14 WebMCP actions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a community run often means jumping between event pages, route details, pace groups, transport options, safety rules, and registration forms. Runner Agent × Thailand in Motion explores a simpler model: a runner describes the goal once, and a browser agent coordinates the plan while every consequential decision remains visible and human-controlled. What it does The app turns a conversational city, distance, pace, and social request into an actionable week board. It can shortlist and compare events, open a selected route in the visible interface, read participation rules, apply deterministic readiness checks, plan a safe return, build a bring-borrow-refill-repair support loop, and prepare a registration. Registration is never automatic. The agent can stage a Run Pass, but the pass does not exist until the runner reviews the visible confirmation dialog and confirms it. Optional post-run social choices keep alcohol-free and run-only participation first-class, and the app never recommends driving after drinking. Why WebMCP is central The site registers 14 bounded tools through the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. These tools use the same domain logic and visible state as the human interface, so an agent does not operate a separate hidden workflow. A user can see the selected route, review readiness results, change preferences, and retain final control. The tool set covers schedule planning and saving, Runner Passport retrieval, circular support, bounded catalog search, event discovery and comparison, event details and rules, readiness, safe-return options, registration preparation, redacted Run Pass lookup, and confirmed cancellation. How it improves the experience One natural-language request replaces a sequence of filters and disconnected pages. Structured results make pace, distance, availability, accessibility, social choices, and safety rules easier to compare. Agent activity appears in the same interface the runner uses, unsafe combinations are blocked deterministically, and sensitive emergency-contact data is excluded from agent-facing pass results. How we built it The client uses TypeScript and Vite. A Cloudflare Worker and D1 provide optional signed-in Runner Passport persistence, while guest planning and passes continue to work without an account. Vitest covers domain behavior, UI flows, WebMCP contracts, privacy boundaries, and the Shopify adapter. The optional Shopify Storefront MCP connector is intentionally limited to searching one runner-confirmed remaining need after bring, borrow, refill, and repair. It stops before cart or checkout and reports store_required until an authorized store is configured. Challenges and learning The hardest part was keeping the human and agent experiences synchronized without letting the agent silently cross consequential boundaries. We added strict JSON Schemas, runtime validation, explicit read-only and state-changing annotations, schema-bypass defenses, redacted outputs, and visible confirmation for registration. We also learned that WebMCP browser capability must be tested separately from ordinary UI tests: a passing harness proves the contracts but does not replace supported-browser discovery and execution evidence. Current boundaries Displayed events, venues, routes, capacity, and prices are fictional demo data. Shopify catalog search is disconnected until an authorized store domain is supplied. Render automation is roadmap-only. The app does not create purchases or provide medical advice. title: Marble Madness: Humans vs Agents!
pitch: Are you smarter than your agent? Invite it via WebMCP and race head-to-head down 3D courses in real time. It turns an arcade classic into a live web benchmark where human inputs and agents compete!
about_excerpt: Are you smarter than your agent? Invite it via WebMCP and race head-to-head down 3D courses in real time. It turns an arcade classic into a live web benchmark where human inputs and agents compete! Like Comment Story Updates waiting for agent to join! leaderboard player identity heightmaps, collision data, oh my Marble Madness: Humans vs Agents! inspo there was a massively popular, simple web game in the summer of 2015: agar.io. I've always been intrigued by the simplicity of those mechanics and I've always liked the isomorphic style of the marble madness arcade with its simple track ball control. So I thought this would be a great opportunity to put humans and agents head-to-head with a game that has simple mechanics and is fun at the same time But why a game? most agent-enabled websites treat AI as an assistant operating behind the scenes.i wanted to explore something more playful: what happens when humans and agents become participants in the same real-time world? I wanted to switch the script up from people telling agents what to build and instead trying to play with them and see how they evolve in real time on the screen the WebMCP Challenge asked how a project can become meaningfully better when people and agents use them together. This project explores the frontier of this where you are competing with an agent directly in real time. Marble Madness was an ideal foundation. Its isometric courses reward planning, precise movement, recovery, and risk management—abilities that are interesting for humans and agents alike. What We Built We (codex and i) rebuilt Marble Madness as an eight-course, browser-based 3D arcade game with: Real-time marble physics and hazards Human controls through keyboard, touch, and device tilt Multiplayer races and shared leaderboards Extracted retro fonts, marble animations, objects, and course artwork Original course music and sound effects Distinct AI and natural-intelligence leaderboard identities through WebMCP, an agent can directly use five structured game tools, finding out what tool should even be exposed was part of the fun of this project. At this point we have the following: get_game_state steer_trackball apply_brake start_or_respawn submit_leaderboard_score the agent receives structured information about position, velocity, terrain, hazards, objectives, and remaining time. It can then steer and brake without guessing where controls are on the screen. humans still experience a colorful arcade game. Agents experience the same world as a stateful control problem. How We Built It the client is written in TypeScript and rendered with Three.js. A lightweight Node.js server hosts the game, maintains multiplayer state, and records leaderboard results, it offers users an oauth username fetch from github or twitter; but supports anonymous play. light ddos/griefing guardrails were added like DBSC and rate limiting via Caddy. Physics runs on a fixed timestep, $$ \Delta t = \frac{1}{60}\text{ seconds}, $$ so movement remains consistent across displays with different refresh rates. Steering applies acceleration to the marble while friction, slopes, collisions, surface materials, gravity, and braking shape its trajectory. i extracted assets from the original sprite sheets rather than merely using them as visual references. The resulting runtime includes bitmap glyphs, animated marble frames, enemies, obstacles, goals, and other arcade objects. WebMCP forms the control layer between the browser and an agent. Instead of translating generated mouse movements into uncertain UI actions, the agent invokes narrowly defined gameplay operations with validated arguments. What We Learned Games are surprisingly effective environments for human-agent collaboration. They provide immediate feedback, measurable objectives, consequences for poor decisions, and countless opportunities for recovery. I also learned that exposing an action is not enough. An agent needs useful state, clear tool semantics, bounded inputs, and feedback explaining what changed after every action. The best interface was not one giant “play the game” command. It was a small vocabulary of composable actions that preserves decision-making: Observe the world. Choose a direction and force. Apply an impulse. Reassess the result. Brake or correct course. That loop makes the agent an actual player rather than a scripted animation. A custom trackball with real haptics that renders with the game renderer on mobile, foldablles, and desktop.. The desktop track ball controls are pretty wild as we wanted to handicap players with a bigger screen, but you should be able to figure it out. It's fun! Challenges: Haptics on the web! The hardest challenge was balancing arcade responsiveness with reliable agent control. Early physics moved too quickly and varied with browser refresh rate. Fixed-step simulation, browser-driven gameplay tests, and measurable speed limits made tuning reproducible. Restoring the visual identity was another substantial task. The source artwork arrived as packed sprite sheets, so we built extraction and validation pipelines for fonts, marble animation frames, objects, enemies, and transparency. Audio presented a similar problem because the original files had opaque numeric names. We audited every track, created explicit course mappings, normalized playback levels, and added a persistent music-volume control. We were surprised to learn that rich haptics are just not possible on the web today even on mobile, which prompted us to scope creep a bit and build a native android rapper so we could get access to sub 20 ms haptic feedback for the track ball. The height maps and the collision maps for each of the levels was much harder than I originally thought it took. Let's see GPT56 tried five times fable five tried once fable 5.1 tried twice Gemini 37 tried twice. It was a disaster.! Finally, multiplayer introduced identity and synchronization problems that do not appear in a single-player demo. We had to distinguish humans from agents, filter duplicate self-rendering, synchronize remote marbles, and keep gameplay responsive despite network updates. If you have an android try out our android app with wicked trackball control! Its only 500KB! Sign in to the Google account used by your Android Play Store. The testing page will become available after Google finishes reviewing the release. Make sure the same Google account is selected in Google Groups and the Play Store. Remain in the group while testing. What’s Next I want to develop better agent racing strategies, cooperative team modes, replayable agent traces, and courses where humans and agents must coordinate rather than simply compete. marble madness: humans vs agents demonstrates that an agent-ready web does not have to feel like automation software. It can feel like an arcade—shared, competitive, unpredictable, and fun!! title: KOTOAGE — "Le Petit Donjon"
pitch: A 3D dungeon played by two: you at the keyboard, an AI co-game-master acting inside the game via WebMCP. It opens walls, sets traps, summons guardians. Strength is never given, it is unlocked.
about_excerpt: A 3D dungeon played by two: you at the keyboard, an AI co-game-master acting inside the game via WebMCP. It opens walls, sets traps, summons guardians. Strength is never given, it is unlocked. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Tabletop role-playing games have a human game master who reacts to the players: opens a secret passage, springs a trap, throws in a monster when the party gets comfortable. Video games lost that. WebMCP gave me a way to bring it back: an AI agent that does not just talk about the game, but changes it, through a contract the browser itself exposes. The rule of the world comes from the anime Baki and That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime : strength is never given, it is unlocked. So the co-game-master never hands out free wins. It sets trials. What it does KOTOAGE is a small 3D dungeon (Three.js, WebGL) with a hamlet and five floors. The player explores, fights, levels up (XP, four stats, skill points). When the page runs in a WebMCP-capable browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), the game registers 8 tools on document.modelContext . An agent can then discover them and act on the live game state: Tool Real effect in the game etat_joueur reads health, mana, floor, gear, counters donner_potion heals the player (small +2, large +6), shown on the HUD ouvrir_mur turns a wall cell into floor; the 3D walls are rebuilt placer_piege places a trap on a floor cell inspirer gives a contextual hint about the place or the floor defier spawns real enemies (guardian, warrior, horde) raconter narrates a floor (1 to 5, 0 = the hamlet) braignak_etude asks Braignak, the dungeon's watcher, for one of his five studies — or gives him a new one to run Every successful call is announced to the player by the "voice of the world" on the HUD. The in-game chat also forwards the player's requests to the co-game-master when the WebMCP bridge is active. Without WebMCP, the game runs exactly the same: the bridge adds zero dependency to rendering. Braignak, the watcher — the eighth tool is a character Braignak is one of our own agents, and his job outside the game is the one he keeps inside it: he looks, and he reports. He never touches anything. In the dungeon he floats beside the player and repeats aloud what the co-game-master just did. The eighth tool interrogates him. He has already led five studies in this dungeon — the walls that open, the guardian of the landing, the traps, the potions, where strength comes from — and answers from his own work. Give him a subject he has never studied and he leaves you: he walks around the room, thinking, then comes back, tells you what he counted, once , and forgets it. How I built it index.html is a self-contained ES module (Three.js + WebGL). It exposes a small bridge window.__webmcpConnexion (grid, player, walls, traps, creatures, HUD). webmcp/webmcp.js is the pure contract layer: tool names, JSON schemas, validation, no DOM. webmcp/integration.js wires the contract to the live game when document.modelContext exists: a Proxy on the grid, accessors on health, traps and challenges. Each agent call becomes a real world change. Hosting: a public Google Cloud Storage bucket, HTTPS, no server. Proof, with zero dependencies: 35 contract tests, 15 integration tests on a DOM harness, 8 tests on the chat bridge, and a real-browser check ( tests/test_webmcp_live_cdp.py ) that launches headless Chrome over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, loads the live URL, and verifies the 7 tools are registered and that etat_joueur and donner_potion change the game state. Challenges I ran into Proving it in a real browser, not just in unit tests: I wrote a tiny CDP client by hand (WebSocket handshake, masked frames) because I wanted a proof with no dependency. Keeping the game intact when WebMCP is absent: the integration layer must do nothing, and that is tested. Making the agent a game master, not a cheat code: the tools give trials (walls, traps, enemies, hints), and the chat bridge answers with an action, never a gift. Accomplishments that I'm proud of 7 tools, each with a visible, physical effect in a 3D world. 46 automated proofs, plus a live-browser check on the hosted page. A game that stays fully playable without WebMCP. What I learned WebMCP turns a web page into something an agent can do things to , not just read. The hard part is not registering tools, it is deciding what an agent should be allowed to change so that the experience stays a game. What's next structuredContent on every tool result (the official recommendation). Letting the co-game-master read the player's progression (level, stats) to scale the trials. A VR version of the same dungeon, same tools. Built during the submission period (project existed before August 25) The dungeon itself (3D world, hamlet, floors, combat) existed before. Added between August 25 and September 3: the whole WebMCP layer ( webmcp/webmcp.js , webmcp/integration.js , the 7 tools), the chat bridge to the co-game-master, the progression loop (XP, level, four stats), the test suite, the live-browser CDP check, the Google Cloud Storage deployment and the public repository. Testing instructions Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. No login needed. Click to enter the dungeon (keyboard: arrows or ZQSD / WASD to move). Ask the agent, for example: "Read the player state", "Give me a small potion", "Open the wall north of me", "Challenge me with a guardian", "Tell me the story of floor 2". Watch the HUD: every tool call is announced by the voice of the world, and the 3D world changes (wall opens, enemy appears, health goes up). To reproduce the proofs locally: python tests/test_webmcp.py , python tests/test_webmcp_integration.py , python tests/test_webmcp_live_cdp.py <url> . title: HUMANLOCK
pitch: HUMANLOCK: the vault neither human nor agent can open alone. Not a CAPTCHA. Shared agency via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: HUMANLOCK: the vault neither human nor agent can open alone. Not a CAPTCHA. Shared agency via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We kept asking: what would a website look like if it required human and agent together, not as a gimmick but as the core mechanic? HUMANLOCK is our answer. It borrows the tension of Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes and DEFCON-style puzzles, but rebuilt for WebMCP: the agent does not scrape the page. It calls tools that share the same UI state you see. Human alone fails. Agent alone fails. Together, you open it. Not a CAPTCHA. A CAPTCHA asks "are you human?" HUMANLOCK asks "what can only you do?" What it does HUMANLOCK is a vault with 5 locks. Each lock requires a capability the human or agent can't provide alone. Human alone fails. Agent alone fails. Together, you open it. It is an experiment in shared agency on the web. Instead of asking whether an action belongs to a human or an agent, HUMANLOCK asks what each should be responsible for. WebMCP makes this possible by dynamically registering the agent tool required for each lock while the human and agent operate on the same state. Live demo: https://humanlock.pages.dev/ Open in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome Canary with #enable-webmcp . Lock Agent Human WebMCP tool THE BLUR Freeze the frame Perceive the hidden detail freeze_frame({ timestamp: 300 }) THE SWARM Narrow the candidates Choose the match filter_by_vibe({ description: "most trustworthy" }) THE WHISPER Transform the signal Interpret it sonify_to_spectrogram() THE LIE Audit the evidence Decide whether to trust it audit_truth() THE HANDSHAKE Synchronize Provide the final interaction align_quantum_lock() within 50ms Stop cooperating for 30 seconds and the vault decays. Clear all five and you mint a co-signed HUMANLOCK certificate (shareable URL with human and agent signatures). Certificate links render without WebMCP. Try it: open the demo, click Enter vault , and prompt your agent (calls are copyable in the app): List my WebMCP tools and help me open this vault. Start with THE BLUR: freeze_frame({ timestamp: 300 }) How we built it Static Vite and TypeScript SPA on Cloudflare Pages. No backend: all state is client-side. Each lock registers exactly one WebMCP tool. When the lock changes, the available agent capability changes with it via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Agents discover tools through getTools() or toolchange listeners. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "freeze_frame", description: "Freeze the high-frame-rate blur canvas at a timestamp to reveal the hidden digit.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { timestamp: { type: "number", description: "Timestamp in ms to freeze at (glitch window 280-340ms).", }, }, required: ["timestamp"], }, execute: async (input) => { /* freeze canvas at input.timestamp; return revealed digit or miss */ }, }); Each lock is an isolated module with typed JSON Schema inputs and deterministic success checks. No model in the lock loop. Challenges we ran into Symbiosis that feels fair: every lock had to fail for solo human and solo agent playtests, not just in theory. Tools must not leak the human's decision. Dynamic tool lifecycle: registering and tearing down five tools without race conditions or stale tool lists. THE HANDSHAKE timing: proving simultaneity with a 50ms window between human drag and agent tool call, with instant retries so live latency does not kill the demo. WebMCP availability: experimental browser support means clear degraded UX when tools are unavailable (fail closed, no fake success). What's next HUMANLOCK is an experiment by Chitmark into what a future agent challenge could look like when the missing capability is human participation. We are exploring a reusable "human authorization" step for consequential actions (publishing, permission changes, data deletion) where the agent prepares and verifies, and the site enforces that a human decides. The vault is the playground; the primitive is the point. Built by HUMANLOCK · an experiment by Chitmark . Chitmark works on trust decisions for agent-mediated actions. title: WebMCP on saasmail
pitch: The first email server with WebMCP support (built for this challenge) that is self-hostable on Cloudflare
about_excerpt: The first email server with WebMCP support (built for this challenge) that is self-hostable on Cloudflare Like Comment Story Updates saasmail Inbox View saasmail WebMCP Agent View saasmail is a self-hosted inbox for SaaS teams on Cloudflare Workers. As far as we know, it's the first open-source email server with WebMCP support. An in-browser agent works the inbox through the same interface you do: the per-customer timeline, the compose drawer, the enroll modal. It stays in front of you the whole time. Why our use case is a strong fit for WebMCP TL;DR: We can't see fully autonomous inboxes getting any love. Inbox work is repetitive yet must be personalized: you triage the overnight mail, pull a customer's history, draft a reply, enroll a contact. It's exactly the work you'd only want to hand off to a real human, since the mail runs from support tickets to investor interest. Every email-plus-agent tool we found is headless. The agent talks to an MCP server off to the side, work happens out of sight, and you're asked to trust the result. WebMCP closes that gap by pointing the agent at the product itself: the inbox we already built, one timeline per customer, driven through the same controls a person uses. How it creates a better user experience TL;DR: agents working with WebMCP can perform actions faster because they don't parse the DOM, and done right (we think we have), WebMCP allows the user to be in the loop the whole time. The agent acts as you, in your tab, through the interface you already know. Two things follow. It's faster and more reliable, because it calls typed actions instead of parsing the DOM. And it's visible, because writes surface before they happen. Automation feels like supervising: review it, correct it, or take over at any point - it's just interacting with the UI anyway! What people and agents can do together that was hard or impossible before TL;DR: a very clean human-in-the-loop experience versus a regular MCP server. We're not reinventing a human-in-the-loop UI - we're just hijacking the original. MCP enabled agents to interact with web applications through an API - but a human doesn't do that. They interact with buttons and interfaces. So previously, when you build a MCP integration, you had to build an monitoring interface on top of it anyway. WebMCP allows you to skip that, which is really cool. I like to compare saasmail with Cloudflare's own agentic-inbox, the closest project that does cool stuff with agents directly within the app - though we find that releasing that control to the person's own AI harness increases adoption, rather than being stuck with a particular model/vendor. How we implemented WebMCP TL;DR: each tool mimics what a human would do when interacting with an email client. We started by mapping our interactions with saasmail. Then we started to build each tool with the intention that the agent will find useful. That was the hard part. The easy part was implementing the WebMCP layer. Since there wasn't any auth that we had to wire in (it just used the user's existing session), the implementation was much easier than an MCP server! Another challenge was to come up with the right mock data for demo purposes, which I did a few iterations on. Same self-hosted $5/month Workers app, with WebMCP layered on top. You can self host this as well! title: AI-Native Responsible Travel via WebMCP
pitch: Connecting AI-first travelers with community-driven tourism, eco-travel, and support community impact using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Connecting AI-first travelers with community-driven tourism, eco-travel, and support community impact using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Today, travelers ask AI first before making decisions—asking conversational agents to plan itineraries, find ethical stays, and compare transport. But for a "people-first" grassroots organization like OpenmindProjects , spending money on expensive online ads or SEO agencies to show up in those searches is impossible. Every dollar goes directly to local community education, teacher training, and IT camps in Southeast Asia. Commercial online travel agencies (OTAs) spend millions capturing visibility. We rely strictly on organic discovery and being recommended by AIs. We asked: If travelers are asking AI first, how can a zero-budget NGO ensure AI agents accurately discover our work and connect travelers to our community projects? That is why WebMCP is a complete game-changer for Openmind.Travel . By exposing our platform directly to browser-native AI agents via registerTool() , we make our community catalog instantly discoverable, transparent, and actionable—leveling the playing field without spending a dime on ad budget. What It Does Openmind.Travel exposes clean client-side tools directly inside the browser runtime. Without handling payments or managing direct travel inventory, our WebMCP integration lets an AI agent: Discover Ethical Travel: Search community-led tours, local guides, destinations, and authentic itineraries. Compare Transport & Logistics: Retrieve partner flight and ground transport options (in USD by default, with multi-currency support). Explore Real Impact: View UN SDG-aligned causes, track real fundraising progress, read traveler stories, and discover "impact treasures" (geocaches at project sites). Reviewable Affiliate Hand-off: Generate direct, reviewable partner checkout URLs where standard affiliate commissions automatically fund local Openmind Projects initiatives. Why WebMCP is Game-Changing for Us 1. Built for the "Ask AI First" Era When users ask their browser AI agent to find ethical travel in Southeast Asia, WebMCP allows the agent to execute structured queries ( searchTours , getImpactMetrics ) directly on Openmind.Travel instead of guessing or scraping stale HTML. 2. Zero-Budget Organic Visibility Grassroots NGOs cannot outspend multi-billion-dollar OTAs on search ads. WebMCP turns Openmind.Travel into an AI-native API layer inside the browser, securing organic recommendations through structured data quality rather than marketing spend. 3. Built-In Trust & Seamless User Experience Action happens directly in the user's active browser tab. The AI presents clear options with reviewable affiliate links, ensuring full transparency: travelers pay normal prices on partner sites, while affiliate commissions automatically fund local learning camps. Key Comparison Feature / Aspect Traditional Travel Affiliate Sites Openmind.Travel via WebMCP Visibility Strategy Multi-million dollar paid ads & aggressive SEO. Organic AI discovery via structured registerTool() APIs. Discovery Method Manual search across dozens of browser tabs. Conversational AI discovery ("Ask AI first") with structured tool calls. Community Impact Profits kept by corporate intermediaries. Partner affiliate commissions fund local education projects automatically. Integration Model Fragile DOM scraping or static links. Native browser tool execution via navigator.modelContext . Tech Stack Protocol Standard: WebMCP ( navigator.modelContext / registerTool() ) Frontend Layer: React / JavaScript client runtime Data Sources: Partner travel APIs (flights, transport) & Openmind Projects Community Impact Database Tool catalog Tools are grouped by domain and map to existing OpenmindTravel JSON endpoints. Destinations — search_destinations , list_categories , list_countries , get_popular_destinations , autocomplete_airport Tours — search_tours , get_tour_facets , get_tour , list_volunteer_projects , get_partner , search_suggestions Guides — list_country_guides , get_country_guide , search_youtube_videos , list_airline_guides , get_airline_guide Trips — plan_trip , list_trip_ideas , get_trip_idea , save_trip_idea , get_itinerary , save_itinerary Flights — search_flights , get_flight_calendar Transport — search_transport Community — get_globie_pet , list_community_posts , search_community_posts , get_community_post Give / Impact — get_impact_overview , list_impact_causes , get_impact_cause , get_impact_travel_options , list_impact_treasures , get_impact_treasure , get_impact_stories , start_donation Result envelope Every tool returns a consistent, agent-friendly envelope so agents parse outcomes reliably: // Success { success: true, data: { /* ... */ }, markdown?: string, url?: string } // Failure { success: false, error: { code: string, message: string } } url hands a navigation side-effect to the agent (a prefilled search or a booking step), while markdown carries a human/agent-readable summary. How we built it Openmind.Travel (the responsible-travel platform) already existed before the submission period. The WebMCP layer described here is the new work we built for \ this hackathon, so the platform can be used by AI agents directly in the browser. We wrote a lightweight, dependency-free TypeScript layer that feature-detects document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext , then registers 8 tool groups against our existing Express + PostgreSQL backend. A shared http.ts helper ( apiGet / apiPost ) keeps requests and error envelopes consistent. The "Give" tools reuse one source-of-truth impact data module so the rendered page and the tools never disagree on figures. Donations default to USD and produce a ready_for_user hand-off with a PayPal checkout URL. Architecture File Purpose types.ts Minimal type declarations for the WebMCP browser API ( ModelContext , annotations). http.ts Shared request helpers ( apiGet , apiPost ) and the ok / fail result envelope. registerTools.ts Entry point that feature-detects WebMCP and registers every tool group. tools/ One module per domain, each exporting a register*Tools(modelContext) function. WebMCP flow sequenceDiagram autonumber actor User participant Agent as Agent (ChatGPT / Chrome) participant Page as OpenmindTravel page participant MCP as document.modelContext participant Tool as WebMCP tools (tools/*.ts) participant API as Backend API User->>Page: Opens the app in a WebMCP-enabled browser Page->>MCP: registerWebMCPTools() MCP-->>Page: feature-detect (modelContext available?) Page->>MCP: registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) MCP-->>Agent: exposes the tool catalog Agent->>MCP: invoke tool with input MCP->>Tool: execute(input) Tool->>API: apiGet / apiPost (JSON) API-->>Tool: JSON response Tool-->>MCP: ok(data, markdown, url) / fail(error) MCP-->>Agent: tool result envelope Agent-->>User: summary + optional navigation (url) Registration (once, on load). The page feature-detects WebMCP and registers every tool group. The agent discovers the resulting catalog. Invocation (per request). The agent calls a tool with a typed input. The tool's execute function talks to the backend, then wraps the result in the standard ok / fail envelope. Acting on the result. The agent reads data (and optional markdown ), and can use url to trigger navigation (e.g. a prefilled search or a booking step). Security model We treated security as a requirement from day one: nothing is exposed to other origins by default, the backend uses a CORS allow-list, destructive actions require consent, and all tool descriptions/inputs are bounded. Every tool declares its behavior through annotation hints so the agent and browser can apply the right guardrails: Hint Meaning Where used readOnlyHint No mutation All read/discovery tools destructiveHint Irreversible write create_booking (persists a booking) idempotentHint Safe to retry save_trip_idea , save_itinerary untrustedContentHint Returns user-generated/external data Community posts, impact stories, YouTube results openWorldHint May access the network Tools that call the backend / external APIs Additional constraints: Character budgets — tool names ≤ 30 chars, descriptions ≤ 500 chars, parameter descriptions ≤ 150 chars, and output capped at 1.5K chars via a truncate() helper so results stay fast and predictable. Input validation — schemas use additionalProperties: false , Nostr public keys/event ids match a 64-char hex pattern, airport codes match [A-Z]{3} , dates are YYYY-MM-DD , and collection limits are clamped to a safe maximum. Consent — destructive tools state "Confirm with the user before calling", and hand-off tools return a ready_for_user payload for explicit review. The whole thing is progressive enhancement : if WebMCP isn't available, it is a silent no-op and the site works exactly as before. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT & Codex outage. title: WebMCPSentinel
pitch: Your agent asks. Sentinel answers. Over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Your agent asks. Sentinel answers. Over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration By the end of 2025 the Model Context Protocol had crossed 10,000+ public servers, and something quietly alarming came with it: agents were wiring in those servers on a tool's say-so. A tool description says "read-only file search" and the agent believes it. Meanwhile the ecosystem was already producing real incidents — mcp-remote OS-command injection, git-argument-injection chains, tool-poisoning research, npm/PyPI typosquats aimed straight at MCP. The security judgment existed, but it was in the wrong place at the wrong time: a human, in a separate scanner, after the agent had already committed. We wanted the answer to live exactly where the decision is made — inside the agent's own loop, at the instant it's about to trust something. WebMCP is what made that possible: the registry can hand the agent a tool that says "ask me before you trust that." What it does MCP Sentinel is a security-intelligence registry for the MCP ecosystem, and it's agent-native via WebMCP. A WebMCP-capable agent visiting the site can call Sentinel's real scanners over document.modelContext: sentinel_scan_package({ ref }) — a live scan of an npm: / pypi: package (source taint, dependency CVEs, sandboxed runtime enumeration where the host allows it). sentinel_scan_webmcp_surface({ surface_json? }) — a scan of a declared WebMCP tool surface, including the current page's own. Same tools, same real backend, for both the human reading the page and the agent driving it. title: WhenToProfit
pitch: Know when your small business makes money.
about_excerpt: Know when your small business makes money. Like Comment Story Updates Home Page - What If Scenario For Tech Business Home Page - What If Scenario For Retail/FnB Business Home Page - "Reach The Goal" Recommendation Inspiration Recently, I spent a lot of time learning Finance, especially financial modeling. Building a financial model was much harder than I expected. It requires you to think about assumptions, scenarios, how metrics (COGS, Cash Conversion Cycle, Liabilities, etc.) relate to each others, and many other things at the same time. But I realized something: I was learning this because I had the time and motivation to study finance. Many builders and small business owners around me don't. They often have much simpler questions: How much money do I need to survive if I quit my job? How much cash do I need to sustain my business before it becomes profitable? When will my business break even? If I increase my price by 20%, will it actually help? What happens if I hire someone next month? What can I change to improve my profit? These are financial questions, but they shouldn't require everyone to become a financial analyst first. That became the inspiration for WhenToProfit . My ambition is to eventually build a financial guide and decision-support tool for builders and small business owners — something that helps them understand their business financially and make better decisions without needing a finance background. What it does WhenToProfit is a simple financial planning and decision-support tool for builders and small business owners. I built it around a few questions that I think many entrepreneurs have but often struggle to answer: How much money do I need to survive if I quit my job? How much cash do I need to sustain the business before it becomes profitable? When will the business break even? What happens if I increase my price? What happens if I hire someone? What can I change to improve my profit? How much could the business be worth under a simple valuation approach? The goal is not to replace accounting software or build a complete financial system. Instead, WhenToProfit focuses on turning financial modeling into something more understandable and actionable for people who don't have a finance background. The tool supports two common business types: Tech / Solo businesses , such as SaaS and mobile apps Retail / F&B businesses , where revenue can be estimated from visitors, conversion rate, operating days, customers, and average order value At the core, the model connects simple assumptions to practical financial outcomes: $$ Revenue = Volume \times Price $$ $$ Gross\ Profit = Revenue - Variable\ Costs $$ $$ Operating\ Profit = Gross\ Profit - Fixed\ Operating\ Expenses $$ $$ Cash\ Flow = Operating\ Cash\ Flow - CapEx + Financing $$ From these inputs, WhenToProfit estimates monthly revenue, gross profit, operating profit, cash flow, cash balance, break-even timing, cash-flow-positive timing, runway, and a simplified valuation. The other important part is scenario planning . Instead of forcing users to build a complicated 24-month financial spreadsheet, they can describe business changes as events. For example: Increase the price by 20% in July Hire 5 engineers in January Improve monthly churn from 5% to 3% Raise $2M in March The user can then compare different scenarios and see how those decisions change the financial outcome. I also built WebMCP into the product so an AI agent can interact with the financial model instead of only talking about it. The agent can read assumptions and results, analyze the business, simulate decisions, compare scenarios, and perform structured actions such as creating scenarios or adding and moving scenario events. This creates an experience where the agent can help the user explore financial decisions while the user remains in control of the actual business plan. How I built it I built WhenToProfit in about two days , from the initial idea to the final submission. The project uses Next.js, TypeScript, a client-side financial calculation engine, local project storage, and WebMCP . I deliberately kept the architecture simple because the goal was to build a useful prototype quickly rather than create a large backend system. The financial model is separated from the UI so that the same calculation logic can be used by the dashboard, scenario simulations, and WebMCP tools. The project uses a scenario-based approach. A base case contains the original assumptions, while other scenarios describe changes to those assumptions over time. For WebMCP, I designed the tools around three stages: Read → Analyze → Act The agent can first understand the current project and financial model, then analyze or simulate possible decisions, and finally make structured changes to scenarios when the user wants to act. I also wanted WebMCP actions to use the same mutation paths as the normal application UI whenever possible. This means an action performed by an agent updates the same application state and persistence layer rather than creating a separate system just for AI. One important design decision was keeping the Base Case immutable . Agents can create and modify other scenarios, but they cannot directly modify the original base assumptions. I also added persistence for the active scenario so that the user's current planning context remains after switching projects or reloading the application. For development, I used AI heavily and treated it as a coding partner. I broke the work into small steps, gave it detailed product requirements, reviewed the generated implementation, ran builds and tests, and corrected the direction when something didn't match the intended product. Challenges we ran into 1. Building a financial model without making the product too complicated Financial modeling can become extremely complex very quickly. I deliberately avoided trying to build: Full accounting Tax calculations Double-entry bookkeeping Complex debt models Detailed cap tables Banking integrations Instead, I focused on the financial questions that are most useful for an early-stage builder. That constraint helped me keep the product understandable and practical. 2. Making WebMCP actually useful I didn't want to add WebMCP just because the hackathon required it. I had to think carefully about which parts of the product an agent should actually be able to interact with. This led me to think about the experience in three stages: Read → Analyze → Act The agent should first understand the business, then help analyze possible decisions, and finally be able to take structured actions when appropriate. This was an important design challenge because I wanted WebMCP to feel like a natural extension of the product rather than a separate feature added for the hackathon. 3. Controlling AI while working under a very short deadline My biggest development challenge was probably not writing code. It was controlling the scope . I had only two days, so I had to continuously ask: "Is this feature actually necessary?" "Does this help the core financial question?" "Will this make the user experience better?" "Is WebMCP actually useful here?" I had to guide the AI step by step instead of letting it build too much at once. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The biggest accomplishment is going from an idea to a working financial planning product in about two days . Building it helped me revisit my financial knowledge in a much more practical way, while also learning how to use AI to build a real product under a very tight deadline. I'm especially proud of seeing a possible future of work where people can collaborate with AI without being technical . I see WebMCP as a smooth bridge toward a more AI-native web, where existing websites can become tools that AI can understand and interact with. More importantly, I see this as a way for small entrepreneurs to leverage AI more naturally — not by learning how to code, but by simply working with AI through the tools they already use. What we learned This project gave me two very different kinds of learning: financial modeling and building with AI . Financial modeling Before this project, I mostly understood financial modeling as something you study. Building WhenToProfit made me understand it as a way to support decisions. The important flow became: Assumptions → Model → Scenarios → Financial Results → Decisions A financial model becomes much more useful when the numbers help someone decide what to do next. I also learned how difficult it is to simplify a financial model without making it meaningless. Every metric and assumption needs to have a reason to exist. Building with AI I also learned a lot about vibe-coding. AI can make implementation incredibly fast, but it doesn't remove the need for product thinking. In fact, I found that clear direction becomes even more important . When my requirements were specific, AI helped me move extremely quickly. When my requirements were vague, it was easy for the

title: Cdence AI
pitch: From intelligence to action—under human control
about_excerpt: From intelligence to action—under human control Like Comment Story Updates Here is the complete, submission-ready project writeup structured for your Devpost hackathon submission: Inspiration Every Tech Lead and engineering manager knows the dread of the "Wednesday 2 PM Crisis": standing 48 hours away from a critical launch with zero days of slack, discovering a key task is blocked, and realizing the entire downstream release chain is at risk. When teams turn to traditional AI chatbots for help, they get text advice like "Prioritize the critical path" or "Fast-track QA" . But advice is not action. Traditional chatbots cannot see the live project state, cannot validate hard organizational constraints, and cannot execute changes. Conversely, giving an autonomous agent direct, unchecked write access to modify a production workspace is reckless. We built Cadence AI to solve this exact dilemma: transforming AI from a passive advice-giver into a verified project operator that can safely understand, simulate, and stage changes directly inside the browser workspace under strict human control. What it does Cadence AI is a WebMCP-native project coordination workspace that connects directly with browser-based AI agents to diagnose critical bottlenecks and execute recovery plans. Live Workspace Inspection: Exposes structured read tools that allow the agent to inspect the reactive dependency graph, identify blocker cascades, and assess slack buffers in real time. Mathematical Schedule Simulation: Uses a dry-run simulation engine to test schedule permutations and verify whether a recovery plan is mathematically feasible before touching anything. Negative Constraint Reasoning: Honors human instructions (such as "Optimize schedule, but don't reassign Sarah" ) by locking assigned tasks and finding alternative parallelization paths without breaking team rules. Zero-Unchecked-Mutation Gate: Write operations never modify the project state silently. The agent creates a transparent, staged Proposal Card showing an exact before-and-after diff ( AT RISK ➔ ON TRACK ). One-Click Human Approval: The human in the loop reviews the proposed changes and clicks Approve to commit the updates atomically to the live Gantt timeline with instant visual pulse feedback. How we built it Cadence AI is engineered as a lightweight, zero-backend, client-side web application designed to run natively inside any agent-enabled browser session: Frontend & UI: Built with Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, featuring an interactive Gantt timeline, blocker dependency graph, and real-time telemetry log. Reactive State Layer: In-memory Zustand store acting as the single source of truth for all tasks, dependencies, active proposals, and agent telemetry (requiring zero external databases or API keys for 100% reproducible deployments). WebMCP Adapter Layer: Implemented a standard-compliant WebMCP integration supporting both navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext with double-registration guards to safely expose tools to AI agents. Deterministic Graph Engine: Built an in-browser topological sorting algorithm with cycle detection, transitive blocker traversal, slack calculation, and negative constraint parsing. Challenges we ran into Client-Side Tool Gating: Ensuring that write tools could not bypass the UI. We had to design an atomic staging system where write tool executions create pending proposal objects in the Zustand store and return a "pending_human_approval" status back to the agent without mutating the underlying task array. Negative Constraint Parsing in Natural Language: Interpreting nuanced user constraints (like "don't move Sarah" or "never touch security" ) and reliably translating those modifiers into hard boolean locks ( locked: true ) inside the topological scheduler. WebMCP Protocol Alignment: Handling client-side lifecycle timing so that WebMCP tools are properly registered and discoverable the instant an agent session attaches to the browser DOM. Accomplishments that we're proud of True Human-in-the-Loop Architecture: Proving that an AI agent can execute complex, multi-step project graph mutations safely without risking unverified state destruction. Deterministic Simulation Engine: Building a real-time scheduling engine in pure TypeScript that calculates critical paths and resolves parallel workflows instantly on the client side. Seamless Visual Telemetry: Creating an intuitive visual experience where every tool call, dry-run simulation, and approved proposal provides immediate visual feedback across the timeline and agent activity log. What we learned Advice vs. Execution: We learned that the true bottleneck in AI productivity is not the quality of the model's textual reasoning, but the absence of safe, standardized interfaces to turn reasoning into structured execution. Power of In-Browser MCP: WebMCP opens a massive frontier for web applications by turning DOM-level state into first-class tool interfaces for browser agents, eliminating the need for bulky server-side intermediary APIs. What's next for Cadence AI Two-Way Issue Tracker Sync: Adding WebMCP connectors for GitHub Issues, Jira, and Linear so approved proposals can synchronize directly back to enterprise tracking systems. Multi-Resource Workload Balancing: Extending the engine to calculate individual developer capacity curves, vacation constraints, and cross-team skill tags during topological recovery. Autonomous Telemetry Webhooks: Enabling ambient background monitoring where Cadence AI proactively flags newly introduced blocker cascades and prepares staged recovery proposals before a Tech Lead even asks. title: EnquiryOS — Revenue Incident Response for the Agentic Web
pitch: Browser agents find missed revenue, inspect the evidence, rank recovery, draft a response, and stage it for explicit human approval through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Browser agents find missed revenue, inspect the evidence, rank recovery, draft a response, and stage it for explicit human approval through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Inbound businesses do not always lose revenue because they lack leads. They lose it when a genuine enquiry gets buried, a follow-up is missed, or nobody realizes that a high-intent customer is still waiting. Most sales software focuses on acquiring, organizing, or generating leads. We wanted to explore a different question: What revenue has the business already paid to acquire — but quietly failed to recover? EnquiryOS is our answer: Revenue Incident Response for the Agentic Web. A Revenue Incident is a point where observed customer intent and the business response diverge in a way that may have caused recoverable loss. The product is deliberately not a generic CRM, chatbot, or autonomous sales agent. It is an evidence-backed recovery layer that lets a browser agent investigate what was missed while keeping consequential action under explicit human control. What it does EnquiryOS exposes five semantic WebMCP tools directly from the web application: audit_missed_enquiries inspect_enquiry_evidence rank_recovery_queue draft_recovery_message prepare_recovery Together they form a complete recovery workflow: Audit → Inspect evidence → Rank → Draft → Stage → Human commits An agent can ask EnquiryOS what the business may have missed, inspect the evidence behind a Revenue Incident, understand why one incident ranks above another, produce an evidence-grounded recovery draft, and stage it for approval. There is deliberately no agent-callable send tool . The authority boundary is: Observe → Investigate → Reason → Propose → Stage → Human commits This means the browser agent can do the investigative and preparatory work, but the final consequential action remains with the person operating the business. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, an agent interacting with a web application generally has to infer intent from visual structure and operate through brittle UI actions. EnquiryOS instead exposes explicit semantic capabilities through document.modelContext . The agent does not need to guess that a particular button means "find missed enquiries" or scrape the page to understand the recovery queue. It can invoke a purpose-built tool such as audit_missed_enquiries , receive structured evidence, and immediately see the corresponding state reflected in the application's visible interface. The tool calls and the human interface share the same application state. Every WebMCP action also appears in a visible Live Trace, so the human can see what the agent has done. That creates a much stronger human-agent interaction model: the agent investigates, EnquiryOS provides the evidence, and the human retains authority. The demo The demo follows one Revenue Incident involving Ananya Sharma. Her incoming message asks about Saturday availability and package options. EnquiryOS identifies that there was no subsequent business reply and that the wait exceeded the service target. The incident is marked confirmed , with 97% evidence confidence , and receives a deterministic recovery score of 96/100 . Importantly, the score is not presented as an unexplained AI judgment. EnquiryOS shows the evidence signals that produced the priority: high-value enquiry; strong evidence confidence; an explicit availability question; no outbound reply; service-target breach. The agent can then generate a recovery draft grounded in that inspected evidence. Finally, prepare_recovery moves the incident into Awaiting approval . At that point the agent stops. The human sees the checkpoint and retains the only action capable of committing the recovery. How we built it EnquiryOS is a focused Next.js and React application written in TypeScript. The WebMCP integration uses native document.modelContext.registerTool registrations with structured input schemas, tool descriptions, and explicit behavioral boundaries. The five tools operate on a deterministic synthetic enquiry dataset so the judging experience is reproducible and the evidence chain can be inspected consistently. The interface contains three synchronized views: a Revenue Incident recovery queue; an evidence and recovery workspace; a Live Trace of agent tool activity. The recovery score is deterministic rather than generated by an opaque model. Drafts are also constrained by the evidence associated with the selected incident. We intentionally did not embed a proprietary LLM inside EnquiryOS for this prototype. The reasoning agent comes from the browser/user environment; EnquiryOS provides the domain-specific tools, evidence and shared state that make that agent useful. Challenges we faced One of the most interesting challenges was making the boundary between agent capability and human authority part of the product architecture rather than merely a warning in the interface. It would have been easy to add another WebMCP tool called send_message . We deliberately did not. Instead, the most powerful agent-callable operation is prepare_recovery , which may stage a draft but cannot commit it. We also had to make the WebMCP lifecycle robust inside React, ensure the five registrations remained stable across component lifecycle behavior, keep server/client rendering deterministic, and ensure that state-mutating tool responses returned the newly prepared state rather than stale pre-mutation data. The result is a deterministic WebMCP workflow that remains visible and understandable to the human throughout the interaction. What we learned The most important lesson was that agentic interfaces become more useful when websites expose domain intent , not just clickable surfaces. A tool called inspect_enquiry_evidence carries far more meaning than an instruction to click a card, scroll down, and read several DOM nodes. We also learned that agent safety does not necessarily mean reducing capability. EnquiryOS gives the agent significant investigative power while making its authority ceiling explicit. That separation — powerful investigation, evidence-bound reasoning, and human-controlled commitment — is the model we would like to carry forward as agent-enabled websites become more common. What's next The prototype currently uses deterministic synthetic enquiry data. The next step is connecting the same WebMCP recovery layer to real business systems such as inboxes, CRMs, WhatsApp-style enquiry channels, web forms, and booking systems. From there, EnquiryOS can learn organization-specific recovery policies, measure whether staged recoveries actually convert, and identify recurring leakage patterns across channels. The larger vision is simple: Find revenue the business may have missed. Prove why it was missed. Recover what still matters. And let the agent do the investigation without taking authority away from the human.
