title: Faultline
pitch: Faultline is an AI educational app that teaches system design using WebMCP to make agents act like your favorite coworker who can see your work, see the results, and give you help without taking over.
about_excerpt: Faultline is an AI educational app that teaches system design using WebMCP to make agents act like your favorite coworker who can see your work, see the results, and give you help without taking over. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Faultline started after a friend quit his job and we began practicing system design interviews together. We could talk through architectures back and forth, but we kept asking the same question: is this actually right? I wanted a better way to practice than negotiating with an human/LLM for an answer. I wanted a game where you make a design decision and find out whether it works. What it does Faultline is a systems design/interview prep game. Fvery level gives you a problem, requirements, a workload, and a set of components; you design the system, and the simulator tells you the results. With WebMCP, an agent can join the live session, inspect the current design, and point out relevant parts of the canvas. Designed to act like another engineer in the room, the agent will help with questions but won't fully take over. Can also act to be interviewed where the agent will walk through realistic follow ups you might hear in a system design round. How we built it I started with the game itself. Parts like letting player build freely, simulator being the source of truth, and providing the agent with structured evidence from the components as opposed to the answer. Each level has its own rules, including what components are available, the performance of the components, and the requirements. For the agents I needed to decided for most states of the game what the agent might need to reasonable answer a question, and I did so through dynamically exposing tools, keeping data as fresh as possible, and intent routing for most common commands for reliable play. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping the agent reliable while a player rapidly changes an architecture. It needs the most up to date info for every call, but resending every detail was too slow. The app needed to only be frustrating with the challenges, so the agent experience for help needed to be fast just as much as it needed high quality responses. Getting the right current context to the agent efficiently and providing it with only the tools necessary for the state took a lot of fiddling around with. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud of how the agents acts. I've had friends play with it, were unable to beat the level first couple tries and begrudgingly gave into using the coach, where they were surprised with the interactions. It really keeps you as the focus as just acts as a background tool so that you don't get stuck forever. This is best shown in the interview tool that asks follow up questions to let users practice the back and forths after designing the solution by using specific interviewer tools and keeping architecture facts straight as info changes. What we learned This was my first time working with WebMCP, and I learned a lot about building for external agents inside a app. In particular, I learned more about tool routing, intent routing, and evaluations for checking whether an agent picks the best tool for the moment. Was also first time I tried to make like an app with a wide spread audience over to fill specific niches/needs. What's next for Faultline I would like to make it a daily game where you do one game a day just to keep yourself sharp. I would also like to keep expanding the coach's toolset and personality. I think during interview process if it could change the rules of the simulation and make you live build to solve a question would be pretty interesting and fun. title: FireNow
pitch: FireNow simulates wildfires in real time, helping teams prepare, coordinate, and plan. AI uses WebMCP tools for precise advice; humans approve every action.
about_excerpt: FireNow simulates wildfires in real time, helping teams prepare, coordinate, and plan. AI uses WebMCP tools for precise advice; humans approve every action. Like Comment Story Updates tuto 3d map map home login Inspiration Wildfires evolve quickly, while response teams must coordinate people, resources, weather data, and evacuation decisions under pressure. I wanted to explore how AI could support incident commanders without replacing their judgment. What it does FireNow is a real-time wildfire simulation and decision-support web app. It helps teams visualize a scenario, simulate fire behavior, compare response strategies, prepare tactical plans, and coordinate resources. AI can read the operational situation and use WebMCP tools to make relevant recommendations. However, it cannot directly commit a response plan: every proposed plan stays reversible until a human operator reviews and approves it. How I built it I built FireNow as a modern web application with React, TypeScript, MapLibre, and a local wildfire simulation engine. The interactive map displays fire progression, weather conditions, available units, threatened areas, and proposed interventions. I created 21 WebMCP tools with structured JSON inputs and outputs. These tools let an AI agent inspect the situation, list resources, run simulations, compare plans, prepare actions, and request human approval through commit_plan . Plans can also be cancelled with revert_plan . Challenges I faced The main challenge was designing a useful human-AI workflow without giving AI uncontrolled operational authority. I solved this with a staged-plan model: AI can analyze, simulate, and prepare actions, but a human must validate the final plan. Another challenge was making the WebMCP integration clear and robust across different browser environments. I focused on precise tool schemas, structured responses, meaningful errors, and a visible interface that explains the current tool status. What I learned I learned that the most valuable AI experiences are not fully autonomous. In high-stakes situations, AI should make complex information easier to understand, compare options, and reduce workload—while humans remain accountable for final decisions. title: GraphWeave
pitch: GraphWeave: The agentic architecture canvas for W3C WebMCP. AI co-pilots autonomously design, stress-test with chaos engineering, and self-heal cloud topologies in real time.
about_excerpt: GraphWeave: The agentic architecture canvas for W3C WebMCP. AI co-pilots autonomously design, stress-test with chaos engineering, and self-heal cloud topologies in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Vision Agent assisted architecture design Automated threat analysis and simulation GraphWeave Inspiration Anyone who has spent time designing backend architectures knows the routine: you open Draw.io or Miro, spend an hour aligning boxes and arrows, and by the end of the sprint, the diagram is already outdated. When LLMs came along, I hoped they would make this easier. Instead, I got walls of text, ASCII art, or raw Mermaid snippets pasted into chat windows. You couldn't drag the boxes, you couldn't click an edge to inspect TLS settings, and you couldn't test how the system handled failures. When OpenAI announced the WebMCP challenge, I realized I should try to bridge that gap. Instead of having an AI talk about architecture in a side panel, WebMCP lets the model directly interact with the app's DOM. I wanted to build a canvas where an agent works alongside me as a real collaborator: provisioning components, running audits, injecting chaos failures, and fixing vulnerabilities live on screen. How I Built It I kept the stack lightweight, fast, and entirely client-side: Next.js & React Flow: Powers the interactive visual graph, handling pan, zoom, custom node components, and animated connection lines. WebMCP: Inside a React hook ( useWebMCP ), I register tools like add_service_node , connect_services , simulate_chaos_outage , and run_architecture_audit . I also expose two live resources: canvas://topology (the raw graph state) and canvas://audit-report (the current linter results). Zustand: All state lives in a centralized store. Whether an action comes from a human dragging a box or an agent calling a WebMCP tool, it hits the same reducer. Dagre.js: Automatically calculates clean left-to-right hierarchical coordinates so nodes snap into place without overlapping. Architecture Rules Engine: A client-side linter that evaluates the topology against common production pitfalls (missing database replicas, plaintext channels, un-cached read bottlenecks). Challenges I Faced Tool Registration Lifecycles: During local development, Next.js Fast Refresh triggered re-renders that either caused duplicate tool registrations or dropped them completely. I had to implement proper AbortController signals to cleanly bind and unbind tool specifications as components mounted and unmounted. This might be something unnecessary or random. But it worked out. Bi-Directional State Authority: The human and the agent needed equal control over the canvas. If a user manually drags a database node and turns off TLS encryption on an edge, the agent’s next read of canvas://topology had to reflect that change immediately. Using Zustand's synchronous store getters avoided stale React closures and kept the agent in sync with the user's manual edits. What I Learned Tool-calling the DOM beats text output every time: Watching an agent create nodes, connect protocols, and fix security flaws in front of your eyes feels completely different from reading advice in a chatbot. It transforms the model from a search engine into an actual pair programmer. Client-side state is fast and simple: By keeping all topology logic deterministic in the browser, GraphWeave requires zero backend databases or server roundtrips. It deploys statically to Vercel and responds instantaneously. Visual feedback drives better security: Seeing a database node turn red under a simulated chaos outage makes single points of failure obvious in a way that static spreadsheets or compliance checklists never do. title: InsurAsync
pitch: Insurance claims shouldn't need everyone on the same call at the same time to move forward.
about_excerpt: Insurance claims shouldn't need everyone on the same call at the same time to move forward. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration So, this whole idea popped into my head because of something that happened to a buddy of mine. His younger brother accidentally bumped his car into a university bus. It wasn't a huge crash or anything, but the car needed fixing, and it took ages, like weeks, for the insurance stuff to finally get sorted out. Now, this brother relied on that car to get to university every single day. For those weeks he couldn't drive, someone else had to give him a ride instead. And this happened every day, for a situation that honestly felt like it should have been wrapped up in a few days, not weeks. When I saw the WebMCP challenge, that whole experience just flashed back to me. The real bottleneck wasn't the accident itself, but the fact that everyone involved was stuck passing information back and forth manually. The insurance company needed paperwork from the car owner, and the repair shop needed approval from the insurance company. Nobody had a quick, direct way to just communicate with each other. That's when I realized this is precisely the sort of issue WebMCP is designed to tackle: instead of a person acting as the manual link between three different systems, let each party have actual tools that an agent can directly access. That's how InsurAsync was born. What it does InsurAsync is a demo insurance claim platform with three separate parties — a policyholder , an insurer , and a repair shop each with their own page and their own WebMCP tools: The policyholder's agent can file a structured incident report and upload documents. The insurer's agent checks real coverage terms, requests exactly the documents needed, and validates repair estimates against real policy limits. The repair shop's agent proposes and revises estimates based on real parts and labor pricing. A shared live log shows every step as it happens, so you can watch the whole negotiation unfold in real time. And importantly, the very last step, actually confirming the settlement, is something only a human can do. The agents can negotiate everything up to that point, but they can never be the ones to finalize it. How we built it I built InsurAsync with Next.js, using WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool() on each of the three party pages to expose real, callable tools. Every tool is backed by an actual API route with real validation logic, real coverage limits, real document requirements, real repair pricing, so an agent calling these tools gets back genuine data, not guesses. For persistence, I initially tried a simple file-based store, but once I deployed to Vercel I learned that serverless functions don't reliably share a filesystem between requests. I ended up switching to a real Redis database (hosted on Vercel) so claim data actually survives across requests and cold starts, something I tested thoroughly before trusting it for the live demo. To actually prove the WebMCP integration worked, I tested it with a real agent using ChatGPT's in-app browser, prompting it to file a claim, check coverage, upload documents, propose an estimate, and validate it all through the real tools, live, on the deployed site. Challenges we ran into Getting real persistence working. My first attempts (in-memory storage, then file-based storage) worked locally but silently failed once deployed, because serverless environments don't behave like a normal always-on server. Moving to Redis fixed this properly. Finding the right way to test WebMCP tools with a real agent. Chrome's WebMCP testing flag turned out to be inconsistent in exposing document.modelContext reliably in my setup, and regular ChatGPT browsing only reads page text, it doesn't call in-page tools. ChatGPT's dedicated in-app browser was the one that actually worked, and once I found it, the whole negotiation flow worked end to end on the first real try. A very small but very stubborn bug : I once had the code from my "revise estimate" tool accidentally pasted into my "propose estimate" file, which silently broke the flow with a confusing error message until I traced it back to a simple copy-paste mix-up. Accomplishments that we're proud of Getting the full three-party negotiation to actually work end-to-end, live, with a real agent not just simulated with manual API calls is the accomplishment I'm most proud of. Watching ChatGPT file a claim, get asked for documents, upload them, get a repair estimate priced and validated against real policy limits, all without me typing anything into a form, was the moment the idea stopped being a concept and became a real working thing. I'm also proud of getting the human-in-the-loop boundary right: the agents can do all the negotiating, but only a real person can click Confirm Settlement. That felt like an important line to draw, not just a technical detail. What we learned The biggest thing I learned is that WebMCP tools are only as trustworthy as the real logic behind them. It would have been easy to build tools that just returned made-up numbers, but the moment I wired every tool to real stored data actual coverage limits, actual document requirements, actual repair pricing, the whole demo became something I could actually trust watching an agent operate. That distinction, between an agent guessing and an agent calling a tool with real validation behind it, is the whole point of WebMCP, and building this made that click for me in a way just reading about it hadn't. What's next for InsurAsync Real authentication, so each policyholder, insurer, and repair shop sees only their own claims instead of the most recent one Real document uploads instead of file-reference placeholders Support for more incident types and more nuanced coverage rules A dispute/counter-offer flow, so an insurer and repair shop can go back and forth on an estimate more than once before it's approved Exploring what this pattern looks like for other multi-party processes with the same "everyone relays information by hand" problem — warranty claims, permit approvals, or multi-vendor project sign-offs Built With css javascript nextjs node.js react redis vercel webmcp Try it out insurasync.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Ismail Ajingi A final year computer science student at King Mongkut's University of technology Thonburi, KMUTT , Bangkok, Thailand Like Share this project: Updates Ismail Ajingi started this project — Sep 02, 2026 03:09 PM EDT

title: Pixel Art Tutor
pitch: Create and edit pixel art with a hands-on agent assistant by your side.
about_excerpt: Create and edit pixel art with a hands-on agent assistant by your side. Like Comment Story Updates GIF About Pixel art is a staple for game development, but players hate AI slop and today's image generation models still struggle getting pixel art to be "pixel perfect". We wanted to fix that by enabling users and agents to collaborate and create art in a more traditionally-accepted sense. What it does Pixel Art Tutor is a WebMCP-powered studio for creating pixel art (sprites, animations, characters, and tilesets). WebMCP is a strong fit because it gives agents structured access to canvas content that would otherwise be invisible to them. Agents can read sprites as compact ASCII grids, critique artwork, paint individual pixels, fill regions, transform sprites, manage palettes, create animation frames, and build tilemaps. Humans can draw, guide, request edits, and refine the work in the same canvas. With shared rooms via PartyKit, collaborators see edits and agent activity live (making human-agent co-creation possible where traditional browser automation would be unreliable or impossible). How it was built The app is made with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, and PartySocket/PartyServer for real-time collaboration. On startup, the app registers ~43 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , plus a declarative tool for creating sprites. All agent actions use the same store actions as the human UI, so edits remain visible, undoable, and synchronized. The app also includes a built-in critique engine, animation timeline, palette tools, tilemap editing, and game-engine exports. Unexpected challenges The biggest challenge was translating a visual canvas into a useful agent interface. We needed compact representations that agents could understand, precise tools for pixel-level changes, and safeguards so human edits, agent actions, undo history, and room synchronization stayed consistent. What's next for Pixel Art Tutor Next, we want to improve multi-agent collaboration, add stronger room permissions and conflict handling, expand the tutoring system, support more creative workflows, and make it easier to publish and share collaborative pixel-art projects. title: Science Lab
pitch: An AI-controllable physics lab where WebMCP turns simulations into live experiments.
about_excerpt: An AI-controllable physics lab where WebMCP turns simulations into live experiments. Like Comment Story Updates An AI-controllable physics lab built with WebMCP. Inspiration Physics is easier to understand when you can change conditions, run an experiment, and see evidence instead of only reading formulas. We wanted to explore how WebMCP could make a learning website agent-native, allowing both people and AI agents to investigate the same live physics simulations. What it does Science Lab is an interactive physics experiment platform with: Projectile motion experiments with launch angle, speed, height, gravity, range, peak height, and flight-time measurements. Mass–spring experiments with ideal and damped oscillation modes. Live visual aids for velocity components, spring force, and motion. Recorded trial notebooks and comparison tools. Native WebMCP tools so an AI can configure, run, pause, measure, and compare experiments. How we built it We built Science Lab with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, then deployed it on Vercel. The physics engine calculates projectile trajectories and mass–spring motion from the current configuration. The UI provides live simulation views, experiment controls, measurements, and trial history. We exposed the important lab actions through WebMCP so an agent and a human can control the same shared experiment state. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was keeping the simulation, animation, UI, measurements, and WebMCP responses consistent. The values shown visually had to match the precise data returned by the agent tools. We also had to design meaningful scientific actions instead of simple button automation. For example, the lab can pause a projectile at its apex or an oscillator at equilibrium, letting an agent inspect an important physics event. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Science Lab is not just an educational simulation—it is a shared experimental environment for both humans and AI. The AI can run real trials, compare ideal and damped oscillations, inspect velocity components, pause at physics events, and explain the evidence using actual measurements from the lab. What we learned We learned that WebMCP can make websites interactive environments that agents can investigate instead of only pages they can read. We also learned that agent tools are most useful when they map to real concepts: configuring conditions, running trials, recording evidence, pausing at meaningful events, and comparing results. What's next for Science Lab Next, we want to add more experiments, such as pendulums, collisions, waves, and electric circuits. We also want to add richer graphs, downloadable experiment reports, guided learning challenges, and AI-generated explanations that adapt to each user’s trial results. title: StoryRoom
pitch: The agent-native filmmaking studio where AI proposes and the director decides via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The agent-native filmmaking studio where AI proposes and the director decides via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Accepted Scene Written By AI Revision Review Diff Modal Chrome DevTools console showing Landing Page Inspiration Screenwriting is not a single-document problem. A single scene depends on what happened three scenes ago - who locked the safe, what the character emotionally knows at this moment, what the director's aesthetic rules demand about silence versus dialogue. When I tried using AI chatbots as a writing co-creator, I kept hitting the same wall: I had to manually copy-paste context, re-explain character histories every session, and hope the AI didn't contradict something established six scenes back. The real problem wasn't the AI's intelligence. The AI was operating blind - it had no structured access to the live workspace state. The moment I read about WebMCP — the idea that an agent could register structured tools directly on document.modelContext and read real browser application state - I immediately thought about filmmaking. A screenplay is exactly the kind of complex, multi-dimensional, stateful problem where a workspace-native agent thrives and a generic chatbot fails. So I asked: what if the AI director's assistant lived inside the studio? What it does StoryRoom is an agent-native filmmaking workspace where human directors and autonomous AI agents collaborate in real-time on live screenplays through the native WebMCP browser standard. The AI agent operates entirely inside the application through 8 registered WebMCP tools on document.modelContext : get_story_context - reads the full narrative: genre, logline, characters, locations, and the director's 8 codified creative rules get_current_scene - fetches the live screenplay text, slugline, characters present, and version history for any scene get_character - loads a full character dossier: psychological traits, emotional arc, and cross-scene appearance index check_continuity - audits the multi-scene timeline, prop tracking, and character knowledge for contradictions analyze_scene - evaluates dramatic pacing and dialogue against the Director's Memory rules propose_rewrite - generates a pending staged revision with justification notes — the live screenplay is never touched apply_revision - commits an approved revision to the screenplay, guarded by a strict Human-In-The-Loop security gate The centerpiece is the Human-In-The-Loop guarantee : the agent can never silently overwrite creative work. Every proposed rewrite is delivered as a side-by-side visual diff (red = removed, green = added). The director must explicitly click Accept Revision before any change reaches the script. How we built it StoryRoom is engineered in 5 architectural layers: 1. Presentation Layer React 18 + Vite + TailwindCSS cinematic workspace with a Screenplay Editor (industry-standard formatting), Character Manager, Locations Panel, Director's Memory rules editor, and a Revision Review modal. 2. WebMCP Tool Registry All 8 tools are registered on document.modelContext with strict JSON Schema definitions and input validation. They are also mirrored on navigator.modelContext and window._STORYROOM_WEBMCP_ so judges can verify every tool directly in Chrome DevTools ( F12 ). 3. WebMCP State Bridge WebMCPProvider synchronizes the tool registry with the live React ProjectStore using mutable refs - ensuring every tool call reads genuine, real-time application state rather than stale closures. 4. Dual-Mode AI Intelligence Layer Primary : Google Gemini 1.5 Flash via REST API, with an automatic model cascade (tries gemini-1.5-flash → gemini-2.0-flash-exp → gemini-1.5-pro ) so the app never hard-crashes on model deprecation Fallback : A deterministic offline simulation engine that produces high-quality, scene-aware responses with zero API key - so the full 9-step demo scenario runs for any judge, anywhere, at any time 5. Human-In-The-Loop Security Gate apply_revision checks revision status before executing. Any direct commit attempt on a pending revision is hard-blocked at the tool layer: { "success": false, "error": "HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED" } The director reviews a visual diff and clicks Accept - only then does the tool commit Version 3 to the live screenplay. Challenges we ran into 1. WebMCP state synchronization with async React rendering The hardest engineering problem. React re-renders asynchronously; the WebMCP tool registry registers once at mount. Getting check_continuity to always read the current screenplay state — not a stale snapshot from when the tool was first registered — required storing all reactive state in mutable refs inside the provider, rather than capturing values in closure scope. A subtle but critical distinction. 2. Designing the Human-In-The-Loop gate to feel like a creative decision The HITL gate had to be firm enough to be a real security guarantee, but natural enough that reviewing a diff feels like a directorial choice, not a bureaucratic approval form. Getting the visual diff presentation and the modal flow right required multiple iterations. 3. Gemini model deprecation mid-development The originally pinned model name ( gemini-2.0-flash ) returned 404 from the API partway through development. This could have broken the live demo. I responded by implementing an automatic model cascade that silently tries the next available production model before falling back to the offline simulation engine - so the app is resilient to future deprecations too. 4. Making the offline demo indistinguishable from the live AI path The deterministic fallback engine needed to produce screenplay analysis that felt genuinely thoughtful - not canned. I built scene-aware demo responses that reference real props, characters, and Director's Memory rule numbers so the 9-step walkthrough demonstrates the full product experience even without a Gemini API key configured. Accomplishments that we're proud of The Human-In-The-Loop security guarantee is real and enforced at the tool layer - not just a UI convention. apply_revision genuinely rejects unauthorized commits with a structured error response. All 8 WebMCP tools are verifiable in Chrome DevTools in under 30 seconds. Any judge can open F12 , run window._STORYROOM_WEBMCP_.tools , and see the full registry. They can call any tool directly from the console. The 9-step deterministic demo works completely offline. Zero API keys, zero setup, zero loading screens - the entire WebMCP collaboration workflow runs in one click for any evaluator. The continuity auditing is genuinely useful. The check_continuity tool catches a real planted narrative contradiction (a prop locked in a safe in Scene 4 being examined without an unlocking action in Scene 7) - the kind of error that slips through human review but a structured agent catches immediately. Building a product that feels premium, not like a proof of concept. From the cinematic design language to the visual diff review to the Director's Memory rules system, StoryRoom feels like a tool a real filmmaker would want to use. What we learned WebMCP's document.modelContext is genuinely powerful for domain-specific applications. The moment you give an agent structured, typed access to live application state instead of raw text, the quality of its reasoning improves dramatically - because hallucination requires filling in gaps, and structured tools leave fewer gaps. The Human-In-The-Loop pattern is not a limitation on AI capability - it is a trust feature. Agents that can be overruled are agents that can be trusted with higher-stakes tasks. The HITL gate is what makes directors willing to let the AI touch their screenplay at all. Deterministic fallback engines are engineering discipline, not a shortcut. A project that only works when the right API key is configured is a fragile demo. Building a high-quality offline simulation layer means the product experience is always fully evaluable. State synchronization between a reactive UI and a browser-standard tool registry is a genuinely new design problem that WebMCP introduces. The mutable ref pattern we developed is something future WebMCP + React projects will likely need too. What's next for StoryRoom Multi-agent collaboration : Allow two external agents to work on different scenes simultaneously, with the director moderating conflicts between competing proposed rewrites through a merge review interface export_final_draft WebMCP tool : Let the agent package the approved screenplay into a properly formatted Final Draft (.fdx) or PDF with one tool call after director sign-off Voice direction : Let directors leave audio notes on scenes that the agent transcribes, interprets as creative directives, and uses to inform future analyze_scene evaluations Production breakdown integration : Add get_budget_impact and check_location_availability tools so the agent can flag rewrites that introduce expensive new locations or VFX requirements before the director approves them Pers

title: ReTrade
pitch: Rethink the strategy before you trade.
about_excerpt: Rethink the strategy before you trade. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The hackathon itself was my first source of inspiration. I wanted to build something with WebMCP and explore what an AI-first product could look like. By AI-first, I mean a product where the main way to interact is through an AI agent such as ChatGPT. The interface still matters, but instead of clicking through every step manually, the user can describe what they want and let the agent work with the application. I started thinking about tasks that are difficult for an ordinary person to complete through a conventional interface. That led me to trading. I remembered using TradingView and trying to test different strategies. I wanted to answer some basic questions. Is this actually a good strategy? Could it make a profit? What are its weaknesses? Does the strategy work, or does it only look successful because of the particular data used in the test? I did not know the answers, and finding them was not simple. So I decided to build a product that could help investigate these questions. ReTrade was built in about five days. The project became much more promising than I expected, and I genuinely enjoyed working on it. What it does ReTrade helps people describe, organize, and test trading strategies before trying them with real capital. A user can choose supported stocks or ETFs and define a strategy using technical indicators. They can work through the interface manually, but the main workflow uses an AI agent through WebMCP. The user can describe a strategy in natural language or by voice. The agent turns that description into structured rules and prepares the strategy inside ReTrade. The user can then review and confirm those rules before running the test. ReTrade returns information about how the strategy behaved. It shows whether the result was profitable, fragile, too dependent on a small number of trades, or simply unsuccessful. The user can inspect individual trades, failed tests, market periods, costs, and alternative versions of the strategy. The goal is to give the user more than a final profit number. ReTrade helps them understand why the result happened and whether there is enough evidence to trust it. How I built it I built ReTrade primarily with Codex, mainly using GPT-5.6. I researched interfaces from trading platforms and other financial products to collect ideas for the layout and user experience. Then I worked iteratively. I implemented a version, tested it, used the product, found the parts that felt confusing, and changed them. A large part of the process was live coding with Codex. I described the behavior I wanted, reviewed the implementation, ran tests, and checked the application in both local and production environments. I kept repeating that process until the product felt useful rather than looking like a short hackathon prototype. Challenges I ran into The first major challenge was the UI and UX. ReTrade is an AI-first product, but it still needs a strong interface. A person must be able to inspect what went wrong, understand the evidence, and test a strategy manually without WebMCP. Designing both workflows was difficult. The agent and the user had to work with the same strategy, evidence, and application state. The interface also needed to explain complex results without overwhelming the user. WebMCP was another challenge. It is still a new technology, so there are fewer examples and established patterns than there are for traditional APIs. I had to study the documentation and give Codex precise instructions. Without enough context, tool registration and browser interactions were easy to implement incorrectly. Debugging the complete workflow was also new to me. A problem could come from the interface, WebMCP registration, the API, application state, authentication, or the database. I had to test the real interaction instead of assuming that working code meant a working product. Accomplishments that I am proud of I am especially proud of the interface. I like how ReTrade looks and how it presents a complicated investigation without turning it into a page full of raw statistics. I am also proud of the WebMCP interactions. A user can describe a strategy to an AI agent, ask it to test the strategy, and then inspect the result inside the same application. The agent can open specific evidence, examine failed periods, and create controlled variations of the strategy. The person can make a selection in the interface, and the agent can understand what they selected. The final result feels like a real interaction between a person, an AI agent, and a product. It does not feel like a chat window attached to an unrelated website. What I learned The main thing I learned was how WebMCP works and what it can add to a product. WebMCP gives an AI model a structured way to understand a website and perform actions inside it. The model does not have to guess what is happening from screenshots or depend on fragile browser automation. I now see many ways I could use WebMCP in future products. It can make complicated software easier to use because the user can describe the desired result instead of learning every part of the interface first. I also learned more about working with Codex and AI agents. Before this project, I mostly used Codex for individual coding tasks. During the hackathon, I used it to implement features, test browser behavior, review the UI, debug production problems, and run scenarios in isolated environments. I plan to keep experimenting with this way of building software. What is next for ReTrade I do not have a final business plan yet, but I would like to continue improving the product after the hackathon. One possible direction is to turn ReTrade into a focused paid tool for strategy testing. Large trading platforms provide many features, and their subscriptions can be expensive for someone who mainly wants to test and understand a strategy. ReTrade could offer a simpler alternative focused on that specific job. A user could describe a strategy, test it, inspect its weaknesses, and compare possible improvements without paying for a much larger trading platform. Before introducing pricing, I would need to improve the product, test it with real users, expand the supported strategies and data sources, and make sure the results remain clear and trustworthy. title: TRACEAI — AI Handwriting Coach powered by WebMCP
pitch: An autonomous AI coach helping children master handwriting through real-time stroke analysis and adaptive WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An autonomous AI coach helping children master handwriting through real-time stroke analysis and adaptive WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Home Dashboard : Welcome hub with daily handwriting challenges and AI Coach recommendations. Trace Mode (Letters) : Tactile canvas with guided stroke paths, numbered anchors, and 1-Click Agent Demo Numbers Practice : Numeracy tracing for digits 0–9 with stroke-order guidelines. Shapes Practice : Fine-motor coordination exercises for basic geometric shapes. Copy Mode : Freehand copying with faint proportion guides and no training wheels. Memory Mode : Unassisted writing on school guidelines to test active muscle memory. Stroke Analytics : 5-dimension real-time evaluation with circular score and equalizer metrics. WebMCP DevTools : Inspector showcasing 8 registered tools, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and live JSON-RPC logs. AI Remediation Loop : Success modal showing closed-loop AI error detection and adaptive correction. Progress & Analytics : Learner dashboard tracking accuracy heatmaps, streaks, and competency mastery. Rewards & Themes : Gamified achievement center with unlockable badges and colorful pen themes. Settings & Controls : Configuration for voice guidance, learner profiles, and WebMCP agent autonomy. Inspiration Watching young children learn to write can be both fascinating and heartbreaking. I often observed children drawing letters like "D" or "B" from bottom to top, or making awkward reverse loops. Visually, the final result might look somewhat acceptable on a static worksheet, but motor-memory-wise, a bad habit was already taking root. Existing handwriting apps on tablets simply check whether pixels overlap with a template. They don't understand how the child traced it, in which direction, or why they made a mistake. Meanwhile, parents and teachers simply don't have enough hours in the day to sit 1-on-1 for every single stroke. When OpenAI announced the WebMCP standard, a lightbulb went off: what if an AI didn't just passively look at a screenshot, but had direct, structured API tools on the web page to analyze mathematical stroke trajectories and dynamically adapt the canvas with live visual guides? That was the spark that drove me to build TRACEAI. What it does TRACEAI is an AI-native web application designed to act as an attentive, encouraging handwriting coach for kids. Here is how the experience works in practice: Child practices on a joyful, tactile canvas: Children can practice uppercase letters (A-Z), numbers (0-9), and basic geometric shapes across 3 distinct difficulty modes (Trace, Copy, and Memory). Instant 5-Dimension Trajectory Evaluation: As soon as a child lifts their pen or finger, TRACEAI analyzes the stroke geometry across 5 criteria: Direction & Stroke Order, Positioning, Precision, Continuity, and Line Respect. Autonomous AI Coaching via WebMCP: An AI agent inspects the child's learning history through registered WebMCP tools (get_weak_letters(), analyze_trace()). Real-time Interface Adaptation: When the agent detects an issue—for example, struggling with the curved stroke direction on the letter "D"—it calls generate_exercise("D", "direction"). The web page instantly reacts by drawing pulsating directional guide arrows and speaking warm, supportive vocal guidance. Gamified Positive Reinforcement: Points, stars, streak tracking, audio chimes, and confetti celebrations keep the child smiling and motivated. Built-in WebMCP Inspector: For hackathon judges and developers, an inspector panel provides live insight into the agent’s inner monologue, tool calls, JSON payloads, and a 1-click end-to-end demo scenario. How we built it I engineered TRACEAI as a solo project to be ultra-fast, responsive on touch devices (tablets/smartphones), and 100% compliant with the emerging W3C WebMCP standard: WebMCP Standard Tooling: I registered 8 structured tools directly onto document.modelContext.registerTool() with explicit JSON schemas. I also implemented a lightweight fallback polyfill so the app runs smoothly in both WebMCP-enabled browsers and standard modern browsers. Client-Side Geometric Engine (trace-analyzer.js): I built a vector analysis pipeline that calculates directional angle variances, Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) path distances, and bounding-box alignments in under 5ms right in the browser. Reactive Canvas & Visual Overlays (app.js): Built with pure HTML5 Canvas and Vanilla JavaScript. Dynamic arrow overlays and smooth Bezier curve approximations make the interface feel alive without heavy rendering libraries. Multi-Sensory Audio System: Utilizes the Web Speech API for natural text-to-speech coaching advice and the Web Audio API for rewarding synthesizer chimes and fanfares. Modern Glassmorphic UI: Crafted using modern, responsive CSS with cheerful, kid-friendly color palettes, accessible contrasts, and smooth micro-animations. Challenges we ran into Distinguishing Shape from Direction: A child drawing the letter "O" clockwise vs. counter-clockwise results in almost identical static shapes, but completely different motor habits. Designing a lightweight vector angle differential that accurately detects inverted stroke sequences was my trickiest algorithmic hurdle. Designing Agent-Friendly Tools: I initially tried passing raw coordinate streams to the LLM, but quickly realized that overwhelmed the context window and caused unnecessary latency. I shifted to a high-signal tool design where analyze_trace() and get_weak_letters() return clean, structured metrics (0.0 to 1.0 scores and explicit weakness classifications like "direction" vs "precision"), allowing the agent to reason instantly. Rendering Dynamic Guidance on Canvas: Translating the agent's high-level command (generate_exercise('D', 'direction')) into animated, pulsating SVG/Canvas arrows that follow the exact path of each letter required fine-tuning my character vector templates. Accomplishments that we're proud of A Real Closed-Loop Web Agent: Successfully building an AI experience where the agent doesn't just answer questions in a sidebar, but actively manipulates the application state and visuals to solve an educational challenge. Zero-Dependency Performance: Running the entire application (analysis, rendering, speech, tools) smoothly on client-side Vanilla JS with instant load times. The WebMCP Inspector & 1-Click Scenario: Enabling judges and testers to see the agent reasoning in real time and test the entire workflow with a single click. What we learned The sheer power of WebMCP: Moving away from DOM scraping and screenshot interpretation towards clean, declarative web tools is a paradigm shift for web development. It makes AI agents hundreds of times faster, deterministic, and much more resilient. How to bridge early-childhood pedagogy with autonomous agent decision-making. What's next for TRACEAI — AI Handwriting Coach powered by WebMCP Cursive Writing Support: Extending my vector stroke engine to support connected cursive handwriting and full words. Early Dysgraphia & Motor-Skill Insights: Providing anonymized progress reports that parents and educators can share with pediatric specialists to identify fine-motor coordination difficulties early. Multi-Child Classroom Dashboard: Enabling a teacher's AI copilot to monitor an entire classroom's practice sessions simultaneously and flag who needs personal attention. title: zeroedit
pitch: ChatGPT images that you can edit
about_excerpt: ChatGPT images that you can edit Like Comment Story Updates Editor page with advertisement poster Home page with all the listing of generative documents specific skill poster chinese poster api virew Inspiration ZeroEdit began with a problem I had while working on another SaaS product. I needed quotation documents that could be edited manually, updated through an API, reused for different clients, and exported reliably. I had tried building something similar before, but every solved problem exposed several new ones. But now things are different so I decided to give it a try . What it does It basically gives ChatGPT images an editable and controllable canvas. Many people use ChatGPT to create moodboards, posters, social graphics etc. even if the image generated looks really good with skills. It is still very hard to manipulate it further according to your need exactly . let alone reuse it for some other purposes. If you ask the model to regenerate one detail , it can change everything else because of nondeterministic nature. Our version zero edit should not be this final, it should be something you start with . Through WebMCP, an agent can: Inspect the active document and editor capabilities. Create a document from editable text, images, shapes, groups, and styles. Upload generated or licensed image assets safely. Render and inspect a candidate before presenting it. Repair a visible issue without replacing the whole design. Show every proposed operation in Review. Wait for the user to approve or reject the changes. After approval, the result remains a normal editable document. The user can move layers, change text, replace images, adjust typography, undo changes, and export PNG or PDF. A document can also be published as a reusable API template. New data can produce new outputs without asking an image model to recreate the design. ZeroEdit also has a Figma handoff for continuing the work in an established design tool. ZeroEdit is not intended to replace Figma or canva. It focuses on the stage before that, the exploration phase. How we built it Taking apart old repos of mine and referencing new repos like openpencil etc for some stuffs Challenges we ran into Compositing layers with each other hard, in first try I noticed it has basically no way of telling what is good composition from bad . so we (codex mostly) added a inspect and repair loop basically, so that agent can inspect . Fonts caused another serious issue during rendering , it still has not been fixed properly. Image transfer was also difficult from chatgpt images to application. codex creates a short-lived upload reservation so an agent can upload the original image bytes directly and receive an approved workspace asset. and lot more I don't even remember half. Accomplishments that we're proud of Saving time for users and money for AI companies . What we learned Skills.md files are to be taken seriously for the end result of the agent . What's next A lot of bad code has gone into it, I would reevaluate everything for example it has still fabric from my old unifinished repo from years back . I dont think that's a good idea anymore. I will see if I can turn into some kind of saas , which can be hosted by client on their server safely and secure for their workflow or some kind of multitenant thing I may explore not sure since the product still has so many gaping holes to fix first. title: Flow Control
pitch: A WebMCP-powered control plane for human-supervised operational agents, demonstrated through a live air-traffic simulation.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered control plane for human-supervised operational agents, demonstrated through a live air-traffic simulation. Like Comment Story Updates instructions transcript tool calls and state log Flow Control - Web-Native Supervision for Operational Agents Trying to delegate real-world work to black-box agents using brittle scrapers or custom wrappers is a mess. We need a shared workspace where humans and agents operate on the exact same live state, keeping real authority when things go sideways. Flow Control turns the web app itself into that control plane using WebMCP. By moving typed tooling directly to the endpoint, content creators stay in control instead of leaving the world to guess how to scrape an interface. The app registers authority-aware tools that dynamically shift based on what the human picks—whether it's "Observe," "Assist Me," or "Take the Sector." The agent handles routine traffic using strict, state-version-checked tool calls, but the moment things get exceptional—like a runway blockage—it stops, stages a recovery plan, and pings the supervisor for approval. Both human and agent actions flow through the same engine, logging everything for later audit or review. While I built this demo around a fictional air traffic control simulation, the architecture isn't locked to ATC. Swap aircraft for warehouse robots, drones, or delivery fleets, and the core pattern stays identical. Flow Control is an illustrative simulation, not an operational air traffic control product. title: Vlad's Personal Website
pitch: haltakov.com lets your AI agent interview mine via WebMCP and discover why my work matters to you - with a personalized report based on your interests. Let your agent talk to mine.
about_excerpt: haltakov.com lets your AI agent interview mine via WebMCP and discover why my work matters to you - with a personalized report based on your interests. Let your agent talk to mine. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted my personal website to work like a chatbot. Instead of scrolling through a portfolio, people could ask questions and learn about the parts of my work that actually interest them. WebMCP takes that idea one step further: you don't even need to ask the questions yourself. Your agent already knows something about you from its memory. Why not let it interview my agent and find out what we have in common? What it does haltakov.com lets people learn about me through a conversation. With WebMCP, a visitor's agent can have that conversation on their behalf. The agent can use what it knows about its user to ask relevant questions, follow up on interesting answers, and produce a personalized report highlighting shared interests and reasons to connect. Someone building an AI product might discover relevant projects. Someone interested in computer vision might explore my engineering background. The same website can lead to very different conversations. How we built it The foundation is Chatbot Page , my open-source project for building conversational homepages. It provides a reusable React package and a Next.js example, with support for curated Markdown answers, streamed LLM responses, and retrieval from your own documents. The WebMCP integration adds two tools: ask_vlad for a multi-turn interview and show_interest_summary for presenting a personalized report. The visiting agent decides what to ask based on its user's interests, rather than following a fixed questionnaire. Challenges we ran into A key design challenge is making the conversation useful to two different audiences: people chatting directly and agents asking questions for someone else. An agent needs room to follow up and explore, but the result still needs to be useful to the human behind it. Another important boundary is personal context. The visiting agent can use its memory to choose questions without handing that entire memory to my website. The site receives the questions it submits, so those questions still matter from a privacy perspective. Accomplishments that we're proud of The project brings agent-to-agent conversations to an actual personal website. It turns a generic introduction into an interview tailored to the visitor. The chatbot foundation is also open source, so other people can build conversational homepages for themselves or their companies. What we learned The interesting part isn't just letting an agent operate a website. It's letting that agent bring context to the interaction. My agent knows about me. Your agent knows about you. A conversation between them can uncover relevant connections that a static biography leaves the visitor to figure out. What's next for Vlad's Personal Website A natural next step is to explore this beyond personal introductions: discovering potential collaborators, finding relevant expertise, or preparing for a meeting. The idea stays simple: let your agent talk to mine, then tell you what's worth knowing. title: SituationRoom
pitch: SituationRoom turns messy vendor proposals into a live, auditable decision model that humans and AI agents build together by mapping evidence, testing scenarios, and approving decisions using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: SituationRoom turns messy vendor proposals into a live, auditable decision model that humans and AI agents build together by mapping evidence, testing scenarios, and approving decisions using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Complex decisions rarely fail because there is too little information. They fail because the information is fragmented. A procurement team comparing vendors might have pricing tables, contracts, technical proposals, requirements, risk notes, implementation timelines, and assumptions spread across dozens of pages. An AI assistant can summarize those documents, but a summary is not a decision system. It is difficult to inspect exactly why a recommendation was made, correct individual assumptions, test alternatives, or safely turn a recommendation into an action. I built SituationRoom around a different question: What should a website become when an AI agent is no longer just visiting it, but collaborating with a human inside it? Instead of making an agent navigate a traditional application through buttons and forms, SituationRoom exposes the semantics of the decision itself through WebMCP. For that purpose, SituationRoom is an agent-native workspace for complex, high-stakes decisions. My demonstration focuses on vendor procurement as follows: Given several competing vendor proposals and a set of business constraints, an AI agent can use SituationRoom's WebMCP tools to construct a structured decision model. It can: define evaluation criteria and their relative importance create mandatory requirements normalize costs across proposals associate claims with their supporting evidence identify missing information and contradictions record risk assumptions construct total-cost-of-ownership models run alternative decision scenarios compare the resulting rankings prepare a proposed decision for human review SituationRoom visualizes that state as an evidence matrix, cost model, risk analysis, scenario comparison, and audit timeline. The human can then directly change an assumption, lock a requirement, correct an evidence mapping, or alter a decision criterion. The agent sees the changed state through WebMCP and can immediately reason again from the corrected model. Before a consequential decision is finalized, SituationRoom separates preview from commit so that the human can inspect exactly what will happen before approving it. title: Dim Hour
pitch: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page.
about_excerpt: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Dim Hour is a city guide - the places worth your time, scored, not starred - covering more than 19,000 restaurants, bars, hotels, and venues across 24 cities. For this challenge, dimhour.com became agent-native: the page itself registers five WebMCP tools, so an agent browsing the site can search the catalog, read a venue, check what is open tonight, draft an itinerary, and hand back a booking link - without scraping a pixel. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Planning a night out is one of the most common things people already ask an agent to help with, but today the agent scrapes pages and guesses at what the site already knows. WebMCP lets dimhour.com hand the agent its real search, scoring, and booking data as structured tools, in the same tab where the person is browsing. The catalog is the product; WebMCP makes it callable. Because the tools are thin adapters over a production venue API, every agent answer is grounded in live data instead of page scraping. How it creates a better user experience One page, two users. A person browsing the Dallas guide and their agent now work on the same surface. The agent calls the site's own tools and gets back the same scored venues, hours, and booking links the UI shows - no copy-pasting between a chat window and a browser, and no agent inventing hours, addresses, or availability. The person keeps the judgment (taste, swaps, vetoes); the agent does the legwork (searching, filtering, checking, assembling). The site stays the source of truth for both of them, and saving a plan stays a human action - the tools read, they never write. What people and agents can do together Co-plan a night in one sitting, in one page. "Dinner in Deep Ellum for four on Friday, then cocktails within walking distance." The agent searches the scored catalog, filters to what is actually open tonight using the same rule the site's own tonight strip uses, pulls full venue records, and drafts an ordered itinerary with real booking links (Resy, OpenTable, SevenRooms, Tock) while the person watches - then interrupts: "swap the second stop for something quieter," and the agent re-plans around the constraint. Before WebMCP, the agent could read the page but not act through the site's own logic, and the person could use the site but not delegate the legwork. Now both happen at once, and the result is a plan with real reservation links attached, not a list of suggestions. How we implemented WebMCP The WebMCP layer is one feature-detected script, webmcp.js, loaded by the site's index.html. Each of the five tools is a thin adapter that POSTs JSON-RPC tools/call to Dim Hour's existing MCP server (mcp.dimhour.com) and passes the result straight through: search_venues - one strong keyword plus city, neighborhood, cuisine, score floor, and price ceiling filters get_venue - the full record: hours, score, booking path, awards find_open_tonight - venues with a happy hour or late kitchen, best score first, using the same definition the site's own "tonight" strip uses, so the agent and the page agree build_itinerary - an ordered multi-stop plan with why and how to book each stop; saving stays a human action at /trip.html get_booking_link - the reservation platform and direct booking URL for a venue, returned for the agent to present; it never opens or books anything itself The script handles the in-flight standard rename (document.modelContext first, navigator.modelContext fallback) and is a silent no-op where no WebMCP host exists. No authentication; the tools expose only public, read-only catalog data. What predates the hackathon: the venue catalog, scoring pipeline, MCP server, and site. What was built during the submission window: webmcp.js, the tool schemas, and the index.html include - the public repo's README draws that line explicitly, with dated commits. Challenges we hit Search results deliberately do not carry hours - only full venue records do - so "open tonight" meant ranking candidates first, then reading the top few individually rather than filtering a field that is not there. Booking links live in the page's own catalog rather than the API, so the booking tool merges both sources and says so honestly when a city is not loaded. The verification suite now asserts substance (tonight actually finds venues; a booking link equals the catalog's own URL), not just shape - because an early version passed every check while two tools quietly returned nothing. title: eventOS over WebMCP
pitch: eventOS puts 6 live WebMCP tools on document.modelContext — backed by 5 AI agents — so any AI assistant can run your event operation directly from the browser.
about_excerpt: eventOS puts 6 live WebMCP tools on document.modelContext — backed by 5 AI agents — so any AI assistant can run your event operation directly from the browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration The events industry runs on real-time chaos — vendor SLA breaches at 2am, exhibitor no-shows, P&L that shifts by the hour. eventOS already had a five-agent AI fleet handling this: BookingAgent, InsightAgent, CommsAgent, VendorAgent, ComplianceAgent — running on Cloud Run for IMEX America (October 2026, 6,100+ buyers, 3,700+ exhibitors). The question was: what if any AI assistant could drive that fleet directly from the browser, with zero integration work? No API key, no OAuth flow, no server the agent has to be configured with. Browser-native MCP (WebMCP) makes that possible. The page the agent is already looking at tells it what it can do. What it does eventOS over WebMCP publishes six event-operations tools directly on document.modelContext — discoverable by any AI assistant driving the browser the moment the page loads: Tool Returns Backed by get_event_sentiment Positive/neutral/negative signal counts, sentiment score, ranked themes Live fleet list_events Upcoming events with dates, venue, attendee/exhibitor counts, status Live fleet + catalog get_event_pnl Revenue, cost lines, gross profit, margin, per-line budget variance Catalog check_vendor_status Vendors checked in/on track, SLA-flagged by status and type Live fleet get_venue_info venueSource registry record — halls, capacity, docks, power, wi-fi venueSource search_planners Ranked planner profiles on name, agency, city, title, specialty Catalog Open the live page in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Ask: "What tools does this page offer?" — the agent discovers all six. Ask: "What's at risk for IMEX?" — it calls check_vendor_status and get_event_sentiment and tells you. No credentials. No setup. Every result carries a source field — live:eventos-agent-fleet , venueSource , or catalog — so an agent can distinguish a number measured by the live fleet from one produced by a model. How we built it WebMCP surface layer (web/lib/webmcp.ts): The hardest part. document.modelContext is new enough that Chrome 146 shipped it on navigator.modelContext , the W3C explainer writes it as document.modelContext , and earlier drafts used window.agent . Our code registers against every surface that exists and deduplicates by object identity — a browser that aliases one object onto both would otherwise get two registration passes and throw on every duplicate tool name. For browsers with no WebMCP host, a branded shim goes on document.modelContext so the page's own inline runner still works and the detector never mistakes our stand-in for a real host. The page reports native: false and "shim active" rather than claiming support it doesn't have. The host can also attach after mount — agentic browsers may inject modelContext well after React renders. The page watches for 60 seconds post-load, polling twice a second plus on visibilitychange and focus , and registers the moment it appears. The fleet underneath (api/mcp_server.py): Five Google ADK agents, 12 tools, already running on Cloud Run. The MCP server is a protocol skin over their existing Python functions — no agent logic reimplemented. An MCP server is not a rewrite; it's a way to let any model in any client drive software you already shipped. MCP console (/console): A genuine MCP client — not a REST wrapper. On load it runs initialize , discovers tools with tools/list , and renders argument forms generated from each tool's JSON Schema. Every button issues a real tools/call . Every message is recorded in a JSON-RPC wire log with method, latency, and full request/response envelopes. Stack: Python 3.12 · FastAPI · Google ADK · Gemini · Cloud Run · Next.js 16 · React 19 · TypeScript · Vercel · WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) Challenges we ran into The WebMCP surface fragmentation was the core engineering challenge. Three different object paths across browser versions, all claiming to be the standard, with no event for when a modelContext appears after mount. We had to build a detection loop, deduplicate registrations by object identity, and design a shim that is honest about its own limitations. Tool schema design mattered more than expected. Tools returning isError: true in the result (not a thrown exception) let agents recover instead of dead-ending. The source field on every result lets an agent tell live data from catalog data and say so. readOnlyHint: true annotations on all six tools let a host call them without a confirmation prompt — critical for a snappy demo. Accomplishments that we're proud of 6 WebMCP tools live and registered on a production event-operations platform 5-agent fleet on Cloud Run with 12 tools, accessible over Streamable HTTP MCP 42-test conformance suite — all passing — covering handshake, version negotiation, all 12 tools, every JSON-RPC error code, SSE framing, CORS, and session teardown Surface detection that works in Chrome 146 today and the standardized browser later, without a code change A genuine MCP client (/console) with full wire-log visibility — the entire protocol lifecycle inspectable, not just claimed What we learned Browser-native MCP inverts the integration model in a way that matters. The agent doesn't need to be configured with anything — it discovers what the page can do by looking at it. That makes WebMCP a better fit for high-stakes, session-scoped contexts like live events than server MCP: tools are automatically scoped to the event currently loaded, credentials stay in the user's session, and an AI assistant gains live operational access to a running event with zero setup. Gemini-backed tools ( fleet_architect_design ) inside a WebMCP surface work naturally — the AI driving the browser can ask the page to design a bespoke agent roster, and the page reaches back into the fleet to do it. What's next for eventOS over WebMCP The WebMCP bridge layer (web/lib/webmcp.ts + webmcp-tools.ts) is designed to be lifted out as a standalone library — any Next.js or React app should be able to register MCP tools in a few lines. We'll open that as a separate package. For eventOS: more live tools, tighter integration between the fleet and the page, and WebMCP as the primary interface for on-site AI assistance at IMEX America, October 12–15 2026. The goal is an event operations room where any AI assistant a planner is already using can walk up to the dashboard and immediately know what's happening and what to do about it. title: Watch Dog
pitch: Watch Dog is a URL risk analyzer that scans web pages for malicious links. Watch Dogs can contribute to a corpus of malicious URLs as a community driven tool for all that browse using Watch Dog!
about_excerpt: Watch Dog is a URL risk analyzer that scans web pages for malicious links. Watch Dogs can contribute to a corpus of malicious URLs as a community driven tool for all that browse using Watch Dog! Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I knew that I wanted to promote something that would help others navigate the challenges with today's internet. I found that in building a tool that could not only scan for malicious links, but also give the community the ability to work together to make the internet a better place to browse. What it does Watch Dog is an evidence-first URL risk inspector with two scan modes: Paste Scan accepts a URL or pasted HTML. URL fetching is bounded and SSRF-aware, while pasted HTML is parsed without executing scripts or loading embedded resources. Live Page Scan uses WebMCP to inspect the links currently rendered on Watch Dog’s own reference page. Because extraction happens when the tool is invoked, it can detect links added after the page originally loaded. Instead of declaring a link “safe,” Watch Dog separates: the risk classification; the analysis state; confidence in the available evidence; supporting and contradicting evidence; provider status and freshness; and limitations or missing information. How we built it Watch Dog is a TypeScript application deployed on Cloudflare Workers. We used Cloudflare Assets and Durable Objects for the application and session boundaries, with server-side authentication represented by a signed, short-lived, secure cookie. I implemented WebMCP using the browser’s native experimental document.modelContext interface. Playwright, Wrangler, and Node’s test runner were used for automated security, protocol, browser, and regression testing. I used Claude Code/Fable 5.1 to generate the plan, Codex/Sol for execution, and Luna for review/QA. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is an emerging browser capability. I had to validate real native tool discovery and invocation in a supported Chromium build instead of relying only on mocks or simulated agent interactions. Accomplishments that we're proud of I wasn't aware of this hackathon until the Discord Office Hours on 8/31, and wanted to see what I could cook up in just a few days time. The 12 hour extension was well received! What we learned I learned how to use new tools in WebMCP and Cloudflare. What's next for Watch Dog Next, I want to add more permitted threat-intelligence providers, improve accessibility and evidence visualization, and introduce an optional human-confirmed reporting workflow with sanitized, quarantined records. A future browser extension could support scanning unrelated active tabs, but only with explicit host permissions and clear user consent. I also plan to add a Watch Dog-mediated warning interstitial that shows the canonical destination and keeps the final navigation decision with the user. Longer term, Watch Dog can become a reusable trust layer for browsers and agents: deterministic security analysis underneath, structured WebMCP evidence in the middle, and informed human control at the top. title: Fantasy Draft Dash
pitch: Turn fantasy draft order into a live, verified football spectacle! Complete with chaotic runners, instant replays, announcer moments, a dramatic Toilet Bowl, and a provably random finish.
about_excerpt: Turn fantasy draft order into a live, verified football spectacle! Complete with chaotic runners, instant replays, announcer moments, a dramatic Toilet Bowl, and a provably random finish. Like Comment Story Updates Welcome to WebMCP Draft Day! Agents can enter your players, pick your colors and set your league name and channel Added in classic sounds, agents can Mute/Low/High music and FX A race to the bottom place in the toilet bowl your agent can't wait to watch! Watch the run with your agent (and players of course) Share in the drama with everyone Full screen for TV viewing, agents can set this to TV mode Instant reply chaos! Full draft order board your agent can use in other apps Verifiable results because every league has "that guy" Inspiration Every fantasy football league needs a draft order, but most leagues handle it by clicking a randomizer and reading a list, names in a hat, traditions that start the first argument of the season, etc. I wanted to turn that first moment into something people would actually gather around to watch and have fun with. Fantasy Draft Dash turns draft-order selection into a fake live football broadcast. League members become runners in a stadium race filled with penalties, bad decisions, phone distractions, questionable officiating, mascots, instant replays, and general fantasy-football nonsense. The goal was simple: Make a room full of adults scream at a television over a completely random draft order and solve the first major problem every draft day faces, free and easily. When someone complains you have a way to verify it was random. How it works The commissioner adds 4 to 16 players, picks a league name, chooses a fictional broadcast network, sets the race length, and decides how much chaos to unleash. Then you hit GO LIVE . The race plays out like a televised football event, complete with live standings, announcer updates, action replays, crowd energy, changing momentum, and a late-game Toilet Bowl for the final two runners. The important part is that the animation does not decide the draft order. Before the race starts, the app creates a cryptographically strong random seed and uses a deterministic Fisher-Yates shuffle to lock the official order. The race animation is generated separately from that locked result. It creates suspense, but it cannot secretly change who picks first. At the end, the app reveals the official draft board along with a verification seed so everyone can confirm the result. Fair randomness first. Completely unnecessary football drama second. How I built it I built Fantasy Draft Dash as a browser-based app using React, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Phaser 4, and OpenAI Sites. The app has one shared game controller that handles the league setup, roster, branding, race configuration, locked state, persistence, standings, results, audio, fullscreen mode, and reset flow. Phaser powers the animated race scene with runners, lanes, stadium visuals, weather effects, jumbotron moments, finish-line action, and the Toilet Bowl sequence. The rest of the interface handles setup, live standings, broadcast graphics, announcements, results, and verification. As part of this project I added WebMCP tools so an agent can safely configure the league, manage the roster, read the visible race state, validate the setup, and retrieve official results after the race is complete. The agent controls use the same guarded controller as the visible app, so tool access cannot bypass the locked-race rules. Challenges The biggest challenge was balancing fairness and drama. If the animation decided the winner, a visual bug could turn into a very real argument in the group chat. If the final order appeared immediately, the whole race would be pointless. Locking the result before kickoff solved both problems. The next challenge was designing for a television instead of a laptop. The app needs to work with anywhere from 4 to 16 players while keeping the field, names, standings, broadcast graphics, replay window, and controls readable from across a room. Timing was another big one. Early replay moments moved too quickly, so there was no time to react before the next thing happened. I slowed down the key action beats and gave tackles, phone distractions, sideline chaos, and other disasters more room to land. Audio also took some tuning. Music, crowd noise, whistles, impacts, cheers, and event sounds all sound great individually. Played at once, they sound like a soundboard falling down the stairs. Separating the layers and adding volume controls made the whole broadcast feel much more intentional. What I learned I learned that random results feel more trustworthy when people can understand how they were created. Showing the seed and explaining the locked shuffle makes the result easier to trust than simply saying, “Don’t worry, it was random.” I also learned that comedy is a systems problem. A funny event needs the right animation, camera framing, sound effect, announcement, text timing, and player name to arrive together. Treating race events as data-driven sequences made that much easier to tune. Most importantly, designing for a group changed the product. Bigger type, stronger contrast, persistent standings, longer replays, fullscreen support, and fewer competing messages mattered more than adding another setting. Put your league on the biggest screen you have, add everyone’s names, crank up the chaos, and let the draft order ruin somebody’s night.
