title: E-nvoice
pitch: e-nvoice — Free client-side Factur-X / EN 16931 e-invoicing for the 2026 French mandate.
about_excerpt: e-nvoice — Free client-side Factur-X / EN 16931 e-invoicing for the 2026 French mandate. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration In September 2026, French businesses must start emitting electronic invoices (freelancers and small companies join in September 2027). As my wife is a freelancer, I wanted to first understand the rules and requirements. Then I looked what was available for freelancers to generate invoices. I found that most of the available tools were either too complex or too expensive. So I decided to build a free, client-side tool that could generate Factur-X / EN 16931 invoices. Apart from creating a compliant invoice, the main part of the tool would be to connect it to a platform like Chorus Pro, but I didn't work on that, I only built the invoice generator and added a WebMCP API for it. So anyone can call my invoice generator through the WebMCP API and generate an invoice in a compliant way. What it does e-nvoice is a free, 100% client-side app that generates Factur-X / EN 16931 invoices: a PDF/A-3 with embedded UN/CEFACT XML, ready for Chorus Pro. No server, no API key, no data leaving the machine. It covers B2B/B2C, four currencies, and French legal mentions — and exposes everything as four WebMCP tools agents can discover, validate with, compute, and generate with end to end. How we built it I started from scratch with a prompt trying to understand the new legislation and what the steps are to create a compliant invoice. Then I started to build the application using React 19 + TypeScript + Vite. I delegated the PDF and XML development to the AI, then I started looking into WebMCP and how to use it. I also added SEO, llm.txt and openapi.json to make it discoverable by AI agents. Challenges I ran into WebMCP is brand new: document.modelContext only exists in flag-enabled, origin-isolated Chrome. I just started the implementation thinking that it would be handled eventually. At first I deployed the website on github pages, but then entering this context, I realized that it was not the right move, so I moved it to cloudflare pages. Then I let the AI analyze what I needed to do to make it work. I verified it end to end in a flag-enabled Chrome; shipping without a fallback still feels risky. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A complete, validated Factur-X generator that runs 100% offline in a browser tab, with nothing leaving the machine. That was my main goal. The WebMCP tools were a bonus to provide a different way to interact with the application and to make it discoverable by AI agents. The full loop works — validate against EN 16931 + CIUS-FR, compute HT → VAT → TTC, download the PDF/A-3 — and it's fully open source. What I learned I first learned about this new legislation, what are the requirements to create a compliant invoice, how to validate an invoice, and how to generate the PDF/A-3. Then, I started looking into WebMCP and how to use it. I also added SEO, llm.txt and openapi.json to make it discoverable by AI agents. In a compliance product, the regulation is the real work. And WebMCP is young — keep a fallback always on. What's next for E-nvoice Right now no idea. I might find a way to integrate with Chorus Pro or other platforms. I am also interested in the WebMCP project and how to use it to create more tools and applications. Built With pdf-lib react typescript vite Try it out e-nvoice.pages.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I started e-nvoice as a tiny side-project and kept going because nothing for freelancers was both free and compliant. I went with the WebMCP layer so agents could generate invoices right in the browser — and built the engine, deployment, and end-to-end verifications myself, with AI help on the code. title: Matchday: Accessible Football with WebMCP
pitch: Inspired by my blind uncle, Matchday uses WebMCP to let football fans ask for scores and fixtures and control what’s on screen—without navigating endless links. Less navigation. More football.
about_excerpt: Inspired by my blind uncle, Matchday uses WebMCP to let football fans ask for scores and fixtures and control what’s on screen—without navigating endless links. Less navigation. More football. Like Comment Story Updates Matchday: Accessible Football Fixtures with WebMCP Matchday: MCP in action Inspiration My uncle is 80 years old and has loved football since he was a boy. He follows teams at every level, from the Premier League down to local amateur leagues. He has also been blind for most of his life. He has embraced talking mobile phones, voice assistants and AI to help him keep up with his hobby. But getting a simple answer can still take a surprising amount of effort. The problem Football scores and fixtures pages, such as those on BBC Sport, contain a huge amount of information. For my uncle, navigating these dense pages with a screen reader can mean working through many links and headings before reaching the fixtures, then listening through long lists of matches. That is a lot of navigation when the question is simply: “When does my team play next?” Voice assistants can help, but in his experience their coverage of smaller clubs is limited and their answers can be inflexible. They might return a few upcoming fixtures without offering an easy way to ask for a different date range or a longer list. What Matchday does Matchday is a football scores and fixtures website with a familiar, information-rich layout inspired by conventional sports sites. You can browse competitions, search for clubs, filter matches and follow your favourite teams and leagues. With WebMCP , there is another way to interact: ask an agent connected to the site for the information or view you want. For example: “When does Liverpool play next?” “Show me AFC Telford United’s fixtures in October.” “Show Scottish competitions on 30 August.” “Show matches involving teams I follow.” The aim is not to replace an accessible interface. It is to complement it with a more direct route to the information , including for supporters of lower-league clubs. How I implemented WebMCP Matchday registers five page-level tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : search_football_teams — find clubs by name, partial name or alias. get_team_fixtures — retrieve a team’s results and fixtures within a date range. show_team_fixtures — display a selected team’s fixtures on the page. get_match_filter_options — discover the available countries and competitions. set_match_filters — update the visible date, status, country, competition and Following-only filters. Each tool has a description and input schema, with validation for its arguments. The tools use the same football data and page state as the interface , so an agent can both answer a question and change what the user sees. Rather than relying only on interpreting the page and navigating its links, the agent has explicit operations for the task. How I built it The site uses TanStack Start, TanStack Router, React and TypeScript , and is deployed on Cloudflare Workers . Football data is imported from the Sportmonks API. The demonstration uses a locally stored snapshot covering 32 competitions, including lower-league football. It is not a live scores feed , and answers are limited to the imported coverage and dates. Followed teams, competitions and preferences are saved on the user’s device. Challenges and lessons The work went beyond retrieving fixtures. Team names and aliases need to resolve consistently, date ranges need validation, and agent actions need to stay in sync with the visible filters. The interface also needed attention: keyboard-accessible search, labelled controls, dropdown behaviour, modal focus and background scrolling all matter. WebMCP is an additional way to use a website, not a substitute for that work. The most useful distinction is between getting an answer and controlling the page . Matchday demonstrates both. What’s next I would like to test the experience with my uncle and other screen-reader users, improve data freshness and coverage, and use their feedback to guide the next changes. The goal remains simple: less time navigating, more time enjoying football. title: Noa
pitch: Noa gives AI agents direct, structured access to a patient's clinical memory, so a doctor's assistant can pull a full history, draft a SOAP note, or flag a red symptom without anyone touching a form.
about_excerpt: Noa gives AI agents direct, structured access to a patient's clinical memory, so a doctor's assistant can pull a full history, draft a SOAP note, or flag a red symptom without anyone touching a form. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Healthcare conversations contain some of the most valuable information about a patient's condition, but much of that knowledge is lost after every consultation. A patient may explain their symptoms, previous experiences, concerns, and medical journey to one doctor, only to repeat the same story when they visit another provider. Doctors often spend valuable consultation time collecting information and documenting notes instead of focusing on care. We were inspired by a simple question: what if healthcare could remember every conversation? Noa was created to build a continuous memory layer for healthcare, preserving patient stories and transforming them into actionable clinical context. When the WebMCP Challenge launched, we saw an obvious next step. Noa already had structured clinical memory. What it didn't have was a way for agents to reach that memory directly. What it does Noa is a voice-first medical intelligence platform with two core experiences. Before a consultation, patients open a simple web interface and speak naturally about their symptoms, having an AI-guided conversation instead of filling out forms, while Noa asks adaptive follow-up questions and captures their medical story. During consultations, doctors record their conversation with the patient, and Noa converts it into structured clinical documentation, including SOAP notes, patient summaries, triage scores, red flag indicators, and doctor briefings. With WebMCP added, that same clinical intelligence is now reachable by agents directly. A doctor working inside an agent-enabled browser can ask for a patient's history and get a real answer pulled from Noa's records instead of switching tabs and searching manually. An agent can draft a follow-up care plan from an existing SOAP note and hand it to the doctor for review. Voice intake data a patient recorded before their visit can be summarized and surfaced the moment a doctor needs it, cutting the time spent re-explaining a story that was already told. How we built it Noa's core platform runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock Nova 2 Sonic handles real-time voice conversations and contextual interaction, Amazon Bedrock Nova 2 Lite handles clinical reasoning and structured summaries, Amazon DynamoDB stores patient profiles, consultation sessions, transcripts, and medical memory records, Amazon Cognito manages authentication, and Amazon S3 stores session recordings and generated files. The application is built with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and WebSocket-based real-time communication. For the WebMCP integration, we built a full agent-facing tool layer on top of that platform. On the server, a spec-compliant JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint at /api/mcp handles tools/list, tools/call, resources/list, resources/read, prompts/list, and prompts/get, with support for both single-turn requests and SSE streaming for external agents. On the browser side, we implemented the native WebMCP standard directly on document.modelContext, with aliases on window.webmcp and navigator.modelContext, so any page in Noa auto-registers its tools on load and agents in a WebMCP-aware browser can discover and call them without a server round trip. Noa's clinical AI functions, patient and session data, and clinical templates are exposed as MCP tools, resources, and prompts respectively. We used synthetic patient data throughout development and demo to keep the focus on the integration itself. What we built during the challenge A JSON-RPC 2.0 MCP server at /api/mcp, supporting standard MCP methods and SSE streaming for external agents and MCP clients A browser-native WebMCP runtime on document.modelContext (aliased to window.webmcp and navigator.modelContext), letting agents in a WebMCP-enabled browser list and call Noa's tools directly on the page A registry exposing Noa's clinical AI functions as callable tools, including SOAP note generation, clinical insight generation, triage priority scoring, and patient-friendly summary generation Structured clinical resources addressable by URI, covering patient records, consultation sessions, transcripts, and SOAP notes A set of clinical prompt templates exposed through MCP, covering SOAP note generation, triage assessment, and follow-up care planning A React provider that safely attaches the WebMCP runtime across the app and bridges it to Noa's live session state, so an agent can query things like the active consultation or current transcript in real time None of this tooling layer existed before the hackathon. Noa's voice-to-SOAP pipeline and dashboard were already live; the agent-facing protocol, tool registry, and browser runtime were built during the challenge window. Challenges we ran into Designing a system that handles natural human conversation while producing structured clinical information was already hard before WebMCP, since patients describe symptoms differently, give incomplete information, and explain problems in their own words. Adding an agent-facing layer on top raised the stakes on that structure, since a tool an agent calls needs a predictable schema every time, not just an output that reads well to a person. We also had to think carefully about exposing patient data through MCP resources: we used synthetic data throughout and kept access scoped to what a specific tool call needs, rather than exposing broad record dumps. What we learned Building Noa showed us that the future of healthcare AI is not only about generating answers, it's about preserving context. Adding WebMCP showed us the next layer of that: context is only useful if something can act on it. By exposing Noa's structured clinical memory through a standard agent protocol, we saw firsthand how an agent and a doctor can split the work of a consultation, with the agent handling retrieval and drafting while the human keeps clinical judgment. What's next for Noa We want to expand the WebMCP tool surface to cover longitudinal care planning across multiple visits, add scoped permission tiers so different agents can be granted different levels of access to a patient's record, and pursue formal HIPAA compliance review now that clinical data is reachable through an external protocol. title: Sardrobe
pitch: Use Sardrobe to create your own digital capsule wardrobe and plan trips, all with the power of WebMCP and by treating ChatGPT as your own personal stylist.
about_excerpt: Use Sardrobe to create your own digital capsule wardrobe and plan trips, all with the power of WebMCP and by treating ChatGPT as your own personal stylist. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Capsule wardrobes are ideal for decluttering and making the most out of your clothes. The digital capsule wardrobe apps my wife tried embodied the opposite of the concept; they all felt like shopping apps, with ads and upsells. What it does To address these issues, we created Sardrobe. You can snap pictures of your clothes, automatically remove the background in the browser, visually assemble outfits from them, and create packing lists for trips. There’s no social feed, ads, subscription model, or pressure to buy more clothes. The app also includes WebMCP tools so that you can offload any step to whichever capable agent you have a subscription for, like Claude or Codex. You can even have the agent act as your own personal stylist. How we built it We used a full-stack architecture for this: Astro and React Hono and Cloudflare Workers Cloudflare D1 and R2 Better Auth and Google OAuth Drizzle ORM Base UI ONNX Runtime Web Transformers.js Vercel AI SDK WebMCP Challenges we ran into The main challenges were feeding images to ChatGPT via WebMCP, building a full-stack app with Astro, and getting ChatGPT to work consistently and well with UI/UX design. Accomplishments and lessons learned Divide and conquer helps a great deal with large applications like these. I'm also proud of the fact that I've built something my wife and I can use daily with our existing AI subscriptions. Per-user software like this feels very personal and rewarding. What's next for Sardrobe Avatar outfit previews, on-device planning AI for drafts, and see if I can reduce the number of WebMCP tools while still achieving the same objectives. title: CYBERGUARD:Agent-Native Cybersecurity Investigation Platform
pitch: An AI security analyst that investigates threats, detects anomalies, and protects your website through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An AI security analyst that investigates threats, detects anomalies, and protects your website through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP tools let the AI agent search logs, investigate users, analyze IPs, score risk, and generate incident reports. AI-driven security investigation turns raw events into evidence-backed findings, threat classification, risk scores, and recommendations. CyberGuard: Agent-native cybersecurity powered by AI, WebMCP, ML, and real-time threat intelligence. AI-driven security investigation turns raw events into evidence-backed findings, threat classification, risk scores, and recommendations. CyberGuard: an agent-native SOC console CyberGuard hands a security console's telemetry and its ML models to an AI agent as real, callable tools through WebMCP. Point an agent at the dashboard and it works a login-abuse case start to finish: find the worst account, pull its history, score it, name the technique in MITRE ATT&CK terms, and write the incident report. Built for the WebMCP Hackathon. FastAPI, scikit-learn 1.6.1, a FastMCP stdio server, and a plain-JS dashboard with no build step. Why we bothered A Tier-2 analyst starts a shift with tens of thousands of auth events spread over three or four consoles. Reading any single log is easy. The slow part is the pivoting: rank the accounts, open the ugliest one, line its telemetry up against a model score, work out whether the one success buried in forty failures is the breach, then map it and write it up. Same moves every time. The other half of the problem is how an agent even touches a web app. Scripting clicks is fragile and scraping the DOM is worse. WebMCP lets the page say what it can do as typed tools, so the agent calls investigate_user with a user_id instead of hunting for a button. Old dashboard CyberGuard Getting data to an agent it scrapes the DOM or you script clicks it calls a named tool with a JSON schema What's exposed whatever the UI renders six tools on navigator.modelContext , mirrored on REST and stdio Time to a verdict manual pivoting across consoles one POST, five tool calls When it breaks half-loaded panels, console errors a JSON error object with a correlation id What the agent may do anything a logged-in analyst can, kill switches included look, score, attribute, recommend. nothing that changes state How it fits together [ Browser client / agent ] | v navigator.modelContext, or REST if that is missing [ WebMCP bridge frontend/webmcp_bridge.js ] isWebMCPSupported() ? native registerTool(6) : CyberGuardFallbackClient 15s abort timeout, retry with backoff on reads only | v JSON-RPC 2.0 or plain HTTP, X-API-Key [ FastAPI gateway + PII redaction cyberguard_api/ ] api key, slowapi rate limit, CSP / HSTS / nosniff, 1 MB body cap, /readyz | +----+----------------------------+ v v [ agent_controller.py ] [ ML core model_loader.load_verified() ] five-step loop isolation forest + two random forests masked trace, md report 32 -> 1037 ft / 13 ft / 65 ft, 15 classes | | +----------------+----------------+ v [ telemetry store services/telemetry.py ] one source of truth, project_user() masks every record mock store of 10 profiles, or an HTTPS backend in prod Native WebMCP is the headline, but a normal browser tab has no navigator.modelContext yet, so the fallback client is what actually runs most of the time. Same tool schemas, same JSON, just over REST. The stdio MCP server ( cyberguard_mcp_server.py , wired up in .mcp.json ) is a third door into the same helper functions. The six tools Tool Takes Gives back get_security_summary nothing monitored / flagged / high-severity counts and a status band get_suspicious_users limit , 1 to 100, default 5 masked accounts ranked by anomaly score investigate_user user_id that account's auth telemetry, email and IPs masked, 404 if unknown get_user_risk_score user_id a 0-100 score, a band, and factors that each trace to a real field detect_attack_pattern user_id , plus an optional login_event or network_flow vector pattern, confidence, MITRE id, and which inference path ran generate_incident_report user_id , threat_type , severity , recommendations an INC-2026-XXXXXXXX record. it writes the record and does nothing else Every execute checks its args against the tool's JSON Schema before it touches the network, then wraps the result in the MCP content[] + structuredContent shape. The investigation loop DISCOVER --> INSPECT --> CORRELATE --> ATTRIBUTE --> REPORT Step Tools What changes DISCOVER get_security_summary , get_suspicious_users(limit=3) grab posture and the top candidates, pick the highest anomaly score. skipped if you named a user INSPECT investigate_user the raw record goes through project_user() and comes out masked CORRELATE get_user_risk_score the anomaly score becomes a 0-100 index plus grounded factors ATTRIBUTE detect_attack_pattern counters run through classify_pattern() . out comes a pattern, a MITRE id, a confidence, and an evidence{} block, and the step logs which function ran REPORT generate_incident_report severity gets set (a real attack never drops below HIGH), recommendations get built, and an incident id plus a markdown report come out with the full audit_trace If POST /api/v1/agent/investigate cannot be reached, the bridge runs the same five calls itself and returns the same shape, with _source set to client_fallback instead of server_agent . The models Isolation Forest, for finding anomalies. Input is a 13-feature behavioural vector: login counts and failure rate, distinct IPs, countries, devices and ASNs, hour-gap stats, device changes, account age, logins per day. The forest isolates a point with random splits, and an anomaly falls out in fewer splits, so a shorter path means a higher score: $$s(x, n) = 2^{-\frac{E(h(x))}{c(n)}}$$ $h(x)$ is the path length to isolate $x$ in one tree, and $E(h(x))$ is that averaged over the forest. $c(n)$ normalises it, the average path length of a failed search in a binary search tree of $n$ nodes: $$c(n) = 2H(n-1) - \frac{2(n-1)}{n}, \qquad H(i) \approx \ln(i) + 0.5772$$ At serve time the score is $-\,\text{decision_function}(x)$ rounded to 4 dp, and a scikit-learn label of $-1$ means outlier. That maps onto the operator index: $$\text{risk} = \text{round}(100 \cdot s), \qquad \text{band}(s) = \begin{cases} \text{CRITICAL} & 100 s \ge 80 \[2pt] \text{HIGH} & 60 \le 100 s < 80 \[2pt] \text{MEDIUM} & 100 s < 60 \end{cases}$$ Anything at $s \ge 0.80$ is CRITICAL and goes straight to deep inspection. The pool is flagged at $0.60$ and counted high-severity at $0.85$. Random forests, for naming the threat. The login model takes 32 engineered features, a fitted pipeline blows them up to 1037 encoded columns, and 300 trees vote: $$P(\text{attack} \mid x) = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} p_t(x), \qquad T = 300, \qquad \text{alert if } P \ge \tau$$ $\tau$ sits at $0.70$. It started at $0.55$ and we moved it up, because precision down there was about $0.30$. Held-out ROC-AUC is around $0.88$, and the response always carries the raw probability and $\tau$ so a caller can pick its own line. The network model is separate: 65 flow features, 15 CICIDS2017 classes, and a second "is this a bot" forest that overrides a Bot call when its own probability is under $0.90$. The agent path never runs the login forest, since all it has is a user_id and no feature vector. It uses classify_pattern() instead, and the confidence there is a closed form. For $f$ failed logins and $k$ distinct IPs: brute force: $\min(0.97,\ 0.50 + f/100)$ credential stuffing: $\min(0.95,\ 0.40 + 0.10\,k)$ account takeover, or anything still suspicious: $s$ itself normal: $1 - s$ The security side MITRE ATT&CK, deterministically. classify_pattern() reads a telemetry signature and returns a technique. No model in the loop, the same input always gives the same id, and every id is a real one you can look up. Classification Signature Technique Account Takeover a success, geo_velocity_violation set, and failed ≥ 10 or device_changes ≥ 3 T1078.004 , Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts Brute Force failed ≥ 20, no successes, ≤ 2 source IPs T1110.001 , Password Guessing Credential Stuffing ≥ 3 distinct source IPs, failed ≥ 10 T1110.004 , Credential Stuffing Suspicious Authentication anomaly is up, nothing matches cleanly T1078 , Valid Accounts Normal failed ≤ 3, anomaly under 0.40 none Network detections have their own map: T1046 for a port scan, T1498 and T1499 for the DoS families, T1071 for bot C2, T1190 for Heartbleed and SQLi, T1059.007 for XSS. The audit trail. Every tool call lands in audit_trace as { step, tool, input, output, ts } . The attribution step also records the exact function it ran and the inference mode. Each verdict carries an evidence{} block with the counts it used. The correlation_id on the report matches the X-Request-ID on the HTTP response, so a finding walks straight back to its log line. title: S.O.L.V.E.R.
pitch: Introducing a 3D On-Chain Forensics Platform for Solana, DuckDB-Wasm locally gives sub-millisecond, zero-latency queries over hundreds of on-chain transactions with zero backend overhead.
about_excerpt: Introducing a 3D On-Chain Forensics Platform for Solana, DuckDB-Wasm locally gives sub-millisecond, zero-latency queries over hundreds of on-chain transactions with zero backend overhead. Like Comment Story Updates Banner Inspiration Tracing on-chain transactions during a fast-moving exploit or de-peg is brutal on 2D block explorers with dozens of open tabs. We created S.O.L.V.E.R. (Solana On-Chain Live Visualization & Exploration Engine) to give developers and security analysts a 3D, interactive flight deck that turns complex block history into clear, spatial intelligence. What it does S.O.L.V.E.R. connects directly to Solana mainnet to stream live transaction history for any wallet address into an interactive 3D spatial graph. The application parses raw blockchain data into a client-side DuckDB database, allowing users to run instant SQL queries to filter and analyze transaction flows right in their browser. Crucially, S.O.L.V.E.R. integrates the new W3C WebMCP standard, enabling AI agents to autonomously control the 3D camera, execute data filters, and highlight suspicious wallet activity alongside human analysts. How we built it We built the application using React 18, TypeScript, and Vite, leveraging Three.js and React Three Fiber to render the glowing 3D node graph. To process on-chain data entirely in the browser, we integrated DuckDB-Wasm alongside @solana/web3.js for live RPC communication. We used the @mcp-b/webmcp-types library to register WebMCP tools via document.modelContext, creating a seamless bridge between AI agents and our UI. For production, we crafted a multi-stage Dockerfile that packages a Caddy web server, which is deployed and running live on PaaS. Challenges we ran into Our biggest hurdle was getting DuckDB-Wasm to bundle cleanly inside Vite's production environment, which required handling WebAssembly binaries and Web Worker imports with specific URL directives. We also had to build a robust multi-endpoint RPC fallback system to handle public Solana rate-limits smoothly. Finally, implementing the experimental WebMCP standard meant designing a resilient polyfill fallback so the app works flawlessly on both standard and AI-enabled browsers. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are thrilled to have built a fully functional 3D forensics tool that runs 100% client-side with zero backend server dependencies for data processing. Achieving sub-millisecond SQL query execution over live blockchain data in WebAssembly was a massive win for us. Furthermore, being among the first applications to natively implement W3C WebMCP for AI-driven 3D canvas control showcases how AI agents can operate inside modern web apps. What we learned Building S.O.L.V.E.R. taught us how to effectively combine 3D graphics state with browser-level AI agent protocols. We learned how to manage camera lerping and smooth animations without interfering with user controls, as well as how to harness in-browser WebAssembly to offload heavy data parsing from servers directly to the client. What's next for S.O.L.V.E.R. Moving forward, we plan to implement real-time WebSocket streams so new blocks automatically pop into the 3D graph the second they are mined on-chain. We are also expanding the 3D engine to support multi-wallet cluster analysis, allowing analysts to map complex token-siphoning networks across hundreds of addresses simultaneously. Eventually, we want our AI agents to act as fully autonomous 24/7 sentinels that flag exploit patterns as they happen. title: Archipelago
pitch: Map your Notion workspace as a shared visual interface for humans and AI agents, powered by WebMCP and running entirely in the browser.
about_excerpt: Map your Notion workspace as a shared visual interface for humans and AI agents, powered by WebMCP and running entirely in the browser. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Ask your AI to map your Notion. That single sentence is all it takes: Archipelago draws the chart on the right. Each database is an island sized by its rows; used relations become routes. The lighthouse marks the hub, a black flag an isolated base. The four WebMCP tools: draw a map, read it as structured data, highlight a computed set, annotate islands. Human and agent share one screen. One call to archipelago_draw_map: database names, row counts and relation metadata in, a live chart out. Rendered locally in the browser. Why I built it I'm a certified Notion consultant. A lot of my work is helping companies turn collections of databases, documents and workflows into actual operational systems. The problem is that systems are hard to explain. Most people are not technical, and looking at a workspace page by page makes it difficult to understand the whole thing. Is everything connected? Where does the structure actually live? Which databases are sitting alone? So I wanted a very simple visual language. In Archipelago, databases become islands, relations become routes, and linked data becomes convoys on those routes. You can look at the map for a few seconds and start asking better questions. That was the original idea: make a complex workspace easier to see and discuss. What it does Drop a Notion .zip export into Archipelago and it builds the map directly in your browser. Nothing is uploaded and Archipelago never connects to your Notion account. The result is deliberately playful rather than overly analytical. No score, no grade. The map gives you the structure and a one-line reading of it; what it means stays your call. It also makes a useful teaching tool when discussing a workspace with people who would never want to look at a database schema. Then came WebMCP The WebMCP part felt obvious to me quite quickly. If a human can use the map to understand a system, an AI agent should be able to use the same map rather than living in a separate chat window. So during the Challenge I added four WebMCP tools that let an agent: build a map from structured workspace data; read the map currently on screen; highlight databases; add its interpretation directly to the map. A user can now ask something like: "Show me everything connected to Clients." and the answer appears on the map they are already looking at. The actual challenge I'm not a developer by background, so part of the challenge was simply understanding a very new standard well enough to implement it properly. But the harder problem is still the one I'm working on: How do you make an agent visiting a website immediately understand that it can act there? I don't want the user to have to explain: "This site supports WebMCP. Go read the documentation, find the tools, then use them." The ideal experience is that the agent arrives, understands the capabilities exposed by the page, chooses the right tool and acts. Because WebMCP is still experimental, getting that discovery and tool-routing behavior to feel reliable across agents and browsers has been the most interesting part of the project. I have tried to follow the emerging best practices closely: explicit tool names, precise descriptions, structured schemas, state-aware error responses , and additional agent-oriented documentation. There is still a lot to learn. How I built it Archipelago is intentionally small: vanilla JavaScript, static files, no application backend and no build step. I built it with extensive AI assistance: ChatGPT as a strategic and tactical sparring partner, and Claude Code as the primary implementation agent. That workflow is also part of what made this project interesting to me. I don't come from a traditional software engineering background, but I could still spend most of my time on the parts I care about: the concept, the interaction model, the visual language and what the tool should actually do. What's next Notion is the first use case because it is the environment I know best, and because it already has a large community of people building increasingly complex systems with it. But I think the underlying idea can go further than mapping. Once a human and an agent can share the same visual representation of a system, the next step is to design and evolve that system together . The map could become a working surface for proposing a new structure, comparing it with the current one, highlighting dependencies, testing changes and progressively co-constructing an operational system. Archipelago starts with visibility. What interests me next is what happens when that shared visual interface becomes a place where humans and agents can actually build together. title: Hold the Bill
pitch: A WebMCP bill review desk where people and agents check the same hospital statement before payment.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP bill review desk where people and agents check the same hospital statement before payment. Like Comment Story Updates The default demo statement: an itemized hospital bill before anyone has reviewed a line. After Run review: five findings, five lines marked — duplicates, misc, wrong-patient test, post-discharge. Hold locked: flagged lines are frozen and the call script is ready so you do not pay them yet. PDF / paste import: load a text-layer PDF, paste lines, or hit Load bill for the test statement. Inspiration Hospital bills are one of those documents people know they should review, but almost nobody actually checks line by line. The statements are dense, the codes are confusing, and most people either pay the full amount or paste the bill into a chatbot and get back a paragraph they still cannot act on. I wanted to build something more practical: a shared review surface where a person and an AI agent can look at the same live bill together before any payment is made. That became Hold the Bill . What it does Hold the Bill is a WebMCP app for reviewing itemized hospital bills before payment. The app loads a statement, lets each line be marked as Unseen , OK , Question , or Dispute , and blocks the final hold step until every line has been reviewed. It also runs deterministic billing-shape checks for: duplicate charges charges after discharge miscellaneous unexplained items wrong-patient tests facility + physician informational pairing Once every line has been checked, the user can Lock hold . That freezes the review, calculates how much should not be paid yet, and generates a ready-to-use call script for the billing office. Why WebMCP This use case is a strong fit for WebMCP because the problem is not just “give me advice.” The real problem is tying that advice to the exact line items on the page the user is about to pay . Without WebMCP, an agent would return a paragraph in chat and the user would still have to map that advice back to the bill manually. With WebMCP, the website exposes structured tools directly from the page. The agent can: read the current statement review the bill explain specific lines mark lines lock or unlock the hold import pasted bill text That means the human and the agent operate on the same live state , not in separate places. How we built it I built Hold the Bill as a client-side React + TypeScript app with Vite. The app uses a shared local store for both the UI and the WebMCP tools, so actions taken by a person or an agent update the same statement immediately. WebMCP is implemented with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) on the top-level page. Each tool calls the same internal store logic as the visible buttons in the interface. I included: the default City Ridge sample statement for judge demos a PDF / paste import path for text-based statements browser-only PDF text extraction using pdfjs-dist a hold pack generator and call script activity logging for human and agent actions There is no backend and no OCR pipeline in this version. For the hackathon, I intentionally kept the upload path focused on digital PDFs and pasted text instead of trying to support low-quality phone photos. Challenges we ran into The biggest product challenge was keeping the app useful without pretending to be a hospital billing system or a medical truth engine. I narrowed the scope to billing-shape checks instead of broad medical correctness. That made the behavior explainable and demo-friendly. Another challenge was the import flow. Full OCR for arbitrary bill photos would have added complexity, model downloads, and unreliable results, so I avoided that and built a safer import path for text-layer PDFs and pasted statement text. On the WebMCP side, the main challenge was making the tools feel like a natural extension of the UI, not a second product. The solution was to keep the human path and the agent path backed by the exact same store and review logic. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is most powerful when the agent is not replacing the interface, but joining the user inside it . This project made that very concrete: the value is not an AI summary by itself, but the combination of: agent speed shared page state visible line-by-line decisions a final human-controlled lock step That pattern feels useful well beyond this project. What's next Next, I would improve parsing, support more statement formats, and make the hold pack easier to export or send. I would also explore stronger rules and a safer path for authenticated patient portals. But for the hackathon, the core idea is already here: do not pay a confusing hospital bill until every line has been seen. title: Nonprofit Pass
pitch: Nonprofit Pass helps youth-led organizations outlive graduation by enabling founders, successors, and AI agents to discover opportunities, prepare applications, and complete handoffs together.
about_excerpt: Nonprofit Pass helps youth-led organizations outlive graduation by enabling founders, successors, and AI agents to discover opportunities, prepare applications, and complete handoffs together. Like Comment Story Updates Home Page Throughout high school, I led a nonprofit that impacted more than 20,000 people. Building the organization was one of the most meaningful experiences of my life, but when I moved to college, I could no longer give it the time and attention it deserved. I began trying to transition the organization to a new leader, only to discover how difficult nonprofit succession can be. The organization’s knowledge, relationships, documents, and responsibilities were spread across different places, and there was no simple way to prepare another student to take over. In college, I was selected to attend one of America’s premier youth service summits. At the conference, I met other young nonprofit founders who were experiencing the same problem. They had created organizations that were making a real difference, but graduation, college, and new responsibilities made it difficult for them to continue leading. Their nonprofits were not ending because their missions were no longer important. They were at risk because they did not have an effective way to find, prepare, and support their next leaders. That experience inspired me to build Nonprofit Pass, a WebMCP-powered platform that helps student-led nonprofits survive leadership transitions. The platform gives founders, potential successors, and AI agents a shared space in which they can plan and complete a responsible handoff. A student interested in becoming a successor can use Nonprofit Pass to discover leadership opportunities, search and filter organizations, save nonprofits to a shortlist, compare opportunities, and prepare an application. A founder can evaluate whether an organization is ready for succession, identify missing documents or institutional knowledge, create a structured 30-day transition plan, and leave important notes for the next leader. Both people can see the same transition progress, creating continuity between the person who built the organization and the person who will lead it next. I built the project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with browser-based storage to preserve user progress. I integrated WebMCP through the document.modelContext API, allowing AI agents to understand and interact with the application through structured tools. The project includes 11 WebMCP tools that can search for nonprofits, retrieve organization details, maintain a shortlist, compare opportunities, prepare and review applications, assess handoff readiness, update transition tasks, add shared notes, and summarize transition progress. My goal was not simply to let an agent click buttons. I wanted the agent to become a useful collaborator. An AI agent can organize information, identify gaps, prepare drafts, and recommend next steps, while people remain responsible for consequential decisions. Submitting an application and approving a final leadership handoff are intentionally human-only actions. This makes the agent helpful without allowing it to make irreversible decisions on someone’s behalf. One of the greatest challenges was determining how much authority an agent should have. Leadership succession affects real organizations and the communities they serve, so completely automating the process would be irresponsible. I addressed this challenge by separating assistance from approval. Agents can help people understand their options and prepare their work, but final decisions stay with the founder and successor. Another challenge was designing the application for two users with very different needs. Successors need a simple way to discover and evaluate opportunities, while founders need tools for documentation, readiness assessment, and transition planning. I created role-specific experiences for each person while connecting them through a shared transition workspace. I also added visible activity tracking so users can understand which actions were completed by a human and which were assisted by an agent. Building Nonprofit Pass taught me that an agent-native application requires much more than exposing existing interface controls to AI. It requires carefully deciding what context agents receive, which actions they may perform, how their contributions are communicated, and where human judgment must remain mandatory. I also learned that succession is not a single moment when one leader replaces another. It is an ongoing process involving trust, documentation, training, shared memory, and accountability. In the future, I hope to connect Nonprofit Pass with real nonprofit opportunities and verified organizational accounts. The platform could eventually include document integrations, mentor verification, founder-successor introductions, transition health monitoring, and long-term impact tracking. My goal is to ensure that a student’s graduation does not have to mean the end of an organization. Young founders create projects that address meaningful needs, and those projects deserve the opportunity to continue. By helping founders, successors, and AI agents work together, Nonprofit Pass creates a path for a nonprofit’s mission and impact to outlive its original founder. pitch: SNIPR uses WebMCP to let AI agents safely query renovation assignments, inspect spatial room context, and propose actions while keeping SNIPR the source of truth.
about_excerpt: SNIPR uses WebMCP to let AI agents safely query renovation assignments, inspect spatial room context, and propose actions while keeping SNIPR the source of truth. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Renovation platforms contain a lot of operational knowledge, but that knowledge is often locked inside dashboards, planning tools, room editors, documents, and product choices. We wanted to show what happens when an AI agent can use WebMCP to access that context safely and directly. What it does SNIPR WebMCP lets an AI assistant answer real questions about a renovation assignment. In the demo, a contractor asks which shower mixer belongs to a specific bathroom. WebMCP reads the selected SNIPR assignment, address, room data, and resident choices, then returns the exact product information. The demo also shows the answer visually: the user opens the execution map, selects the address, opens the 3D building view, moves to top view, selects the bathroom, and clicks the shower element to see the attached specifications. Finally, the project demonstrates safe actions. WebMCP can propose an operational action, such as finding an inspection slot, but SNIPR requires explicit human approval before anything is written back. How we built it We integrated WebMCP endpoints into SNIPR so agents can access structured assignment context, address data, room information, planning data, communication state, documents, catalog information, and controlled actions. The frontend demo combines the normal SNIPR dashboard, WebMCP chat, an execution map, and a 3D building/room view. The video script uses Playwright and FFmpeg to record a reproducible demo with synchronized scene-based voice-over. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making the demo coherent. Browser loading, 3D interactions, voice-over timing, and human approval flows all needed to line up. We also had to make sure WebMCP felt like part of the real operational workflow, not just a chatbot bolted onto the side. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the demo shows three important things together: structured context, visual proof, and controlled writes. The agent can answer useful questions, the user can verify the answer spatially, and the system still protects operational changes with human approval. What we learned WebMCP becomes most valuable when it connects AI to the existing source of truth, instead of replacing it. The best experience is not just “AI answers a question”, but “AI helps the user navigate, verify, and act inside the real system.” What's next Next steps are deeper WebMCP coverage, more robust permission scopes, richer 3D evidence, and production-grade audit trails for every agent-assisted action. title: AquaEye
pitch: Agentic water safety system that connects live industrial sensors, PLC control, and WebMCP tools for intelligent monitoring and safe pump decisions.
about_excerpt: Agentic water safety system that connects live industrial sensors, PLC control, and WebMCP tools for intelligent monitoring and safe pump decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP tools Siemens_TIA_Portal_PLC_Program AquaEye dashboard Sensors + PLC + Raspberry Pi Inspiration## Inspiration Water safety systems often generate large amounts of sensor data, but operators still need to interpret those signals and interact with industrial control systems manually. We wanted to explore how an AI agent could work with a real physical system while keeping industrial safety logic in control. This led to AquaEye — an intelligent water safety system combining real-time water sensing, Siemens PLC control, Raspberry Pi edge computing, and WebMCP-based AI-agent interaction. What AquaEye Does AquaEye monitors water conditions using pH, turbidity, and flow sensors connected to a Siemens PLC. The system architecture consists of: Industrial sensors for real-time water monitoring Siemens PLC for industrial control and safety logic Raspberry Pi as the edge-computing layer Python backend communicating with the PLC using Snap7 Web dashboard for human monitoring WebMCP tools that allow AI agents to interact with AquaEye through the browser The backend converts the physical sensor signals into structured information and evaluates the water condition against configured safety limits. WebMCP Integration WebMCP is the key interface between AquaEye and AI agents. AquaEye exposes five tools: get_water_status — retrieves the current water measurements and system condition. analyze_water_safety — analyzes the current water parameters and returns a safety decision. get_system_status — provides the overall system state. start_pump — provides controlled pump-start interaction. stop_pump — provides controlled pump-stop interaction. This allows an AI agent to discover AquaEye's capabilities and interact with live system information through the browser instead of relying only on a traditional dashboard. Human + Agent Collaboration The dashboard is designed for the human operator, while WebMCP provides an interface for AI-agent interaction. The human can visually monitor the physical system and dashboard, while an AI agent can request structured system information and analyze the current water-safety condition. Importantly, the AI interaction does not replace the industrial safety layer. The PLC and programmed safety logic remain responsible for the physical control system. How It Was Built The physical sensors are connected to the Siemens PLC. The Raspberry Pi communicates with the PLC using Snap7 and runs the AquaEye backend. The Flask backend exposes the system data through APIs. The web frontend presents the live information to the operator. WebMCP is implemented directly in the frontend using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each registered tool connects an agent request to the corresponding AquaEye backend capability. Challenges One of the main challenges was connecting the browser-based WebMCP layer to a real industrial PLC system. We had to integrate PLC communication, Raspberry Pi networking, the Python backend, the web dashboard, and WebMCP while maintaining a clear separation between AI interaction and physical safety control. Another challenge was making the system work with live industrial data rather than a simulated software-only environment. What I Learned This project demonstrated how WebMCP can become an interface between AI agents and real-world systems. I learned how to combine industrial automation, PLC communication, edge computing, web technologies, and agent-facing tools into one architecture. The project also showed that AI-agent interaction can be added on top of an existing industrial control architecture without removing the deterministic safety logic that protects the physical system. What's Next The next stage for AquaEye is to expand the system with additional water-quality parameters, richer historical analysis, predictive monitoring, and more intelligent agent workflows. The long-term goal is to develop AquaEye into a platform where AI agents can assist operators in monitoring, diagnosing, and managing industrial water systems while maintaining appropriate industrial safety boundaries. title: Sivan AI
pitch: Autonomous multi-chain settlement and Service Agreement layer for browser AI agents, enabling milestone payments on Solana, Base, Stellar, Celo, and bank payouts.
about_excerpt: Autonomous multi-chain settlement and Service Agreement layer for browser AI agents, enabling milestone payments on Solana, Base, Stellar, Celo, and bank payouts. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents inside web browsers (ChatGPT, Google Gemini in Chrome, Claude) are rapidly advancing from passive text generators to active digital workers capable of negotiating deals, booking services, and coordinating freelance work. However, when browser agents attempt commercial transactions, they hit a major bottleneck: UI Fragility: Scraping DOM elements or simulating blind clicks often fails when layouts shift. Direct Transfer Risk: Upfront payments carry severe counterparty risk with zero delivery guarantees. Disconnected Financial Rails: Agents lack unified multi-chain settlement capabilities and cannot bridge crypto assets into local fiat banking. Sivan AI was built to solve this by providing the first autonomous, multi-chain settlement and Service Agreement layer for browser AI agents using the open W3C WebMCP standard. What it does Sivan AI enables AI agents in browsers to negotiate, draft, fund, and complete commercial Service Agreements with milestone protection. By registering typed financial tools on document.modelContext, web pages allow browser agents to interact with Sivan AI natively: Create Milestone Agreements: The agent drafts clear deliverables and milestone terms. Query Spendable Balances: The agent checks available USDC balances across Solana, Base, Stellar, Celo, and BSC. Human-in-the-Loop Safety: Every funding action and milestone payout requires on-screen human approval via interactive review cards before any blockchain transaction moves. Instant Local Fiat Settlement: Settled USDC can be off-ramped directly into local bank accounts (e.g. Nigerian Naira via instant NGN bank rails). How we built it WebMCP Client Layer: Implemented in TypeScript using official webmcp-types declarations, registering document.modelContext tools on https://staging.sivantech.online . Multi-Chain Core: Node.js and Fastify microservices orchestrating Privy embedded wallets, Stellar Horizon RPC, Solana web3.js, and EVM adapters. Edge Gateway: Cloudflare Workers (sivan-gateway) managing edge routing, CORS, and Model Context Protocol streaming. Cloud Backend: High-availability microservices deployed on Render with PostgreSQL persistence on Neon. Challenges we overcame Multi-Chain Fan-Out Latency: Grouped multi-chain RPC reads into deduplicated queries, preventing public RPC rate limits and timeouts from blocking balance rendering. Agent Security Boundaries: Designed a strict human-in-the-loop authorization modal so autonomous agents can never drain or move funds without explicit user confirmation. Cross-Chain Key Unification: Unified distinct cryptographic wallet families (ed25519 Solana, secp256k1 EVM, Stellar StrKey) under a single cohesive WebMCP tool schema. Accomplishments that we are proud of Delivering a fully functional, live multi-chain settlement platform on staging ( https://staging.sivantech.online ) and Telegram AI (@SivanStaging_Bot). Achieving sub-second Solana and Base transaction broadcasts with verifiable block explorer receipts. Creating an open-source, standards-compliant WebMCP tool provider available on GitHub ( https://github.com/Sivan-Technologies/Sivan ). What we learned WebMCP fundamentally transforms web applications from human-only interfaces into dual-purpose environments where humans and AI agents collaborate seamlessly without breaking authentication or state boundaries. What is next for Sivan AI Extending WebMCP tools to background service workers for asynchronous milestone monitoring. Enabling automated recurring service agreements and escrow-free micro-payouts. Onboarding global freelance marketplaces to Sivan AI agentic settlement rails. title: Verdiqt
pitch: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict.
about_excerpt: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI made building software cheap. It did not make building the right software cheap. People now ship a SaaS product in a weekend, and find out at launch that nobody wanted it. Verdiqt moves that painful discovery to before you write the first line of code. You put your idea on trial, and a court decides whether it deserves to live. What it does You file a case: your SaaS idea in a sentence, or a link to a public GitHub repo you already built. Then the courtroom goes to work, and you watch every step happen live: The case file. The court reads your idea and writes it up: who it's for, what problem it solves, what to search for. The investigation. Real research across five real communities : Hacker News, Reddit, GitHub, Stack Overflow, and Product Hunt. Every finding appears on screen with a link to its source, and every source reports honestly: gathered, failed, or empty. If the first search comes back thin, the court automatically widens its search. The deliberation. Six AI judges each take one question: "Is the pain real? Is anyone actively looking for this? Who already exists? Who would pay? Can you reach these people? Can you build it fast enough?" Each judge delivers their score the moment they finish, you literally watch the bench board fill in, one verdict at a time. The ruling. A presiding judge reads the entire case file and rules: BUILD, PIVOT, or KILL —> with a score out of 100, the reasoning behind every number, and exactly one recommended next step (a real, cheap test you can run this week). A full trial takes about a minute. And if you refine your idea and try again, the court remembers: the evidence you marked as important and the previous ruling follow your case, so every iteration builds on the last. How we built it Zero cash out of pocket. The whole product runs on free tiers and hackathon credits: one small server runs the website and the research pipeline, the AI judges run on free model APIs, and when one provider's daily quota runs dry, the court automatically switches to a backup provider mid-trial and keeps ruling. Constraints became design: the court paces itself under rate limits, shows its deliberation while it works, and never wastes a token. The model argues; the code rules. Anti-hallucination isn't a prompt, it's enforced in code. Judges may only cite evidence the court actually gathered: invented citations are stripped automatically, and a high score that loses its citations gets capped. When public evidence is thin, the judge is allowed to use domain judgment but the ruling must say so, out loud, in the rationale. Uncertainty is never dressed up as certainty. Privacy without accounts. No sign-up. Your browser gets an unguessable key; only its fingerprint is stored. Your cases are yours, anyone else asking for them gets an identical "not found.", don't worry. Challenges we ran into Running a multi-stage AI pipeline on free tiers meant treating every token and every request as scarce... the wait-and-retry pacing, the provider failover, and the one-at-a-time trial queue all exist because of it. And WebMCP is new enough that the tool contract itself was a design problem: we learned that the workflow belongs inside the tool descriptions, so agents teach themselves the journey. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, evidence-cited validation trial in about a minute. A deliberation you can actually watch. A surface that serves two audiences at once... humans get a courtroom, agents get a toolbox, and each can see the other working. What we learned Never think you have enough time to build something. What's next for Verdiqt GitHub sign-in to put your whole repo graveyard on trial at once, re-trials over time to watch a verdict change as markets move, and Reddit's expanded API access for even deeper community evidence. title: Navwebmcp
pitch: You already write your way for other to use your platform, don't hide it in your browser, expose it using Navwebmcp cuts agent tool, tokens and latency measured, not estimated without browser.
about_excerpt: You already write your way for other to use your platform, don't hide it in your browser, expose it using Navwebmcp cuts agent tool, tokens and latency measured, not estimated without browser. Like Comment Story Updates GIF GIF GIF GIF NavWebMcp — Devpost Submission This is a young repo that takes the MCP and WEBMCP approach and tries to build a new approach that takes the benefits of both and give answers to their weaknesses. Inspiration Every existing way an agent touches a web app pays the same tax: either the agent orchestrates a sequence of raw API calls itself — search, then create, then verify — reasoning about your domain on every single round-trip, or it drives the page like a human would, reading an accessibility tree and clicking through a UI built for eyes and fingers, not for a model. Both cost tokens and latency that have nothing to do with the actual task, and both grow worse as the surface area of the app grows and it is not deterministic. WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) is a promising browser-native answer to half of that problem — a page can register callable tools for an agent the same way it registers event listeners for a user. But the draft standard stops at "here's how a tool gets registered." It doesn't say how an agent should discover fifty tools without paying for fifty tools' worth of schema on every connection, how to layer permissions on top, or how to collapse a five-call workflow into one. That gap — protocol on top of primitive — is what NavWebMcp exists to fill. This repo is also a deliberate proof point for the AOD/ADD methodology (AI-Oriented Development / AI-Driven Development): intent specs framed up front, implementation delegated to agents, and every claim independently verified before being accepted — including, especially, the benchmark numbers below. What it does AgentBridge is a reference implementation of NavWebMcp , a protocol layered on top of WebMCP that adds progressive tool disclosure, RBAC, and composite operations. Instead of an agent stitching together searchAvailability → createReservation → getReservation , it calls one tool — book({ date, time, partySize, name }) — and gets back a validated result. The multi-step orchestration (precondition checks, the write, post-condition validation, and a compensating rollback on failure) runs invisibly behind that single call. On connect, an agent sees only 8 lightweight navigation/meta tools (~180 tokens total) — explore , search , describe_tool , invoke , load_tools , unload_tools , getContext , getCapabilities . The other 48 business operations across reservations, CRM, front-office, tasks, housekeeping, and finance are discovered on demand and either invoked directly or promoted to native tools — so registry size never inflates the cost of connecting. getContext and getCapabilities , called in parallel right after connecting, tell the agent who the user is and exactly what their role permits before it explores anything, so it can ask the user one consolidated question instead of a drip-feed of prompts. Every operation carries a role list ( customer , support , admin ) checked at every call boundary, and destructive operations carry an enforced confirmation gate. The same 48 operations are exposed identically over two surfaces from one registry: in-page WebMCP (session-cookie auth, for browser-native agents) and MCP Streamable HTTP (bearer-token auth, for external agents connecting with no browser at all ). That second point matters more than it sounds: hostVipGuest , a 7-step chain spanning CRM and front-desk, has no UI in this app whatsoever — there is nothing a click-driven tool could even target — yet it's fully callable over MCP HTTP because the tool was never built to depend on a rendered page. It's designed to work identically whether the connecting client is Claude Code, Claude Desktop, MCP Inspector, ChatGPT, or OpenAI's Codex — the orchestration runs in-process against the same handler code no matter who's calling. We proved it against a working demo: a hospitality platform with 56 operations, three composite tools, three role-scoped demo users, and a live audit log streamed over SSE. How we built it Next.js 15 (App Router, React 19) and TypeScript, with Zod as the single source of truth for both runtime validation and JSON Schema generation on both surfaces. @modelcontextprotocol/sdk plus mcp-handler provide the MCP Streamable HTTP transport; zod-to-json-schema converts the same Zod shapes for in-page WebMCP tool registration. Playwright and Vitest back the test and benchmark harnesses. The core design decision was keeping orchestration surface-agnostic: lib/core/book.ts , seatGuest.ts , and hostVipGuest.ts take a call function as a dependency and know nothing about HTTP, cookies, or bearer tokens. The browser wrapper injects serverCall ( fetch("/api/call") , cookie auth); the MCP operation injects makeDispatch(ctx) (in-process, bearer auth). Same business logic, same validation, same RBAC — the only thing that changes is what's plugged into one function parameter. Adding a new operation means writing one file in lib/operations/ and registering it in one index — it then appears on both surfaces automatically with disclosure, RBAC, and audit logging already wired. Following AOD/ADD, the process itself was: write the intent (what the protocol needed to guarantee) before writing code, delegate implementation to agents against that spec, and independently verify — most concretely, by insisting every number in the README's benchmark tables come from an actual measured run ( scripts/bench.mjs , scripts/speedbase.mjs , n=5, real MCP transport, real headless browser) rather than an estimate. Challenges we ran into Getting progressive disclosure right without breaking usability was the hardest design problem — too little detail at connect time and the agent flails; too much and the token savings evaporate. The explore / search / describe_tool split (navigate by path, discover by pattern, fetch schema only when needed) came out of iterating on that trade-off. Keeping the two surfaces genuinely equivalent — not just superficially similar — meant RBAC, confirmation gates, and audit logging all had to live at the operation-registry level rather than in either surface's adapter, or they'd have silently drifted apart the first time someone touched only one of the two files. Benchmarking honestly was its own challenge: it's easy to produce numbers that flatter the architecture. We insisted on comparing against a real Playwright browser-automation lane, not a hypothetical one, which is also what surfaced the finding that mattered most — hostVipGuest has no Playwright row at all, because there's no UI for it to drive. That's not a benchmark gap, it's a demonstration of the actual capability boundary of UI automation versus tool calls. Versioning also took more thought than expected: a single version number couldn't distinguish "the protocol contract changed" from "this role's tool set changed," so getCapabilities() deliberately returns two separate fields — a hand-bumped protocolVersion and an automatically computed, role-scoped capabilityHash — so agents can tell which kind of change happened and react accordingly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The benchmark numbers are real, not estimated, and they're strong: composite calls cut tokens by 72–87% and latency by 67–88% versus raw multi-call orchestration, on both the MCP HTTP and in-browser WebMCP surfaces, with 5/5 reliability across every lane. The saving compounds with orchestration complexity — a 7-op CRM+front-desk chain collapses to a single call with an 87% latency reduction — and testing the operation layer directly is up to 1,300× faster than driving the same flow through a browser. We're equally proud of the fact that the protocol holds up structurally: one operation registry drives two authentication models, two transports, and two calling conventions with zero duplicated business logic, and RBAC/audit/disclosure behavior is provably identical on both because they're enforced in one shared place, not two. And we shipped the consumer half of the protocol too — skills/navwebmcp-agent/ , a portable agent skill for connecting efficiently, discovering operations, and preferring composite calls — versioned independently of the server implementation, so it isn't tied to this one demo app. What we learned The biggest lesson: token and latency cost in agent tooling is mostly a protocol design problem, not a model problem. The same LLM calling the same underlying operations pays wildly different costs depending on whether it has to orchestrate three calls itself or one — that's architecture, not intelligence. We also learned that "the agent needs a browser" is frequently just false. Once business logic is expressed as composable server-side operations, the browser becomes one optional caller among several rather than a load-bearing dependency — which is what let hostVipGuest exist at

title: Rally by Agent9
pitch: Create role-based AI specialists with real company addresses. Each teammate uses only the data and systems you approve, coordinates the right workers behind the scenes, and replies with deliverables.
about_excerpt: Create role-based AI specialists with real company addresses. Each teammate uses only the data and systems you approve, coordinates the right workers behind the scenes, and replies with deliverables. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every company can buy excellent AI. The broken part is the work between them. At Agent9, we felt that problem firsthand. We could give one task to Gemini, another to Claude, and another to Codex—but a person still had to act as the message bus between them. These capable systems behaved like brilliant employees who had never met. People still carry context between tabs, decide which model should do what, restart work when an API balance or subscription usage window runs out, reconcile conflicting answers, and police confident results. Small-business owners and operators feel that management tax most sharply: they can afford excellent AI, but not a dedicated AI operations team. The All Things Agentic brief challenged us to move beyond a standard chat loop and build an agent that could keep working asynchronously, take real action, and prove what it accomplished. We built Rally by Agent9 for that challenge—and for the unlikely hero who needs enterprise-grade execution without an AI operations department. The idea was simple: give a company an email-first, accountable AI team, equip it with only the systems that company approves, and govern the work through a secure Google-backed control plane. A person should be able to send one familiar message and receive finished, independently verified work—not supervise another chain of prompts. What it does Rally is our Fortified Enterprise Fleet entry: it turns the AIs and company systems a team already trusts into one accountable AI workforce . A user can commission work from either a private dashboard or an ordinary email to rally@updates.agent9.dev . Both doors enter the same replay-safe queue and the same governed runtime. The user can leave; Rally keeps working in the background. Rally preserves the business goal, decomposes it into independently checkable work, routes that work across configured model families, and returns the result where the request began. Stage What the user experiences What Rally enforces Commission Send an email or create a dashboard job Stable identity, idempotent intake, preserved intent Govern Describe the goal, choose bounded recovery, and approve systems Frozen model order, connector scope, retry, turn, and send ceilings Execute Gemini, Claude, and Codex work under configured roles and independent review Durable state, isolated workers, asynchronous progress Prove Receive a finished deliverable, evidence, and residual risk owner != verified_by for every completed checklist item Rally's completion rule is a persisted invariant, not a suggestion inside a prompt: $$ \operatorname{Complete}(c) \Rightarrow \operatorname{owner}(c) \ne \operatorname{verified_by}(c) $$ Rally's key product capabilities are: Email-first commissioning. Work begins in a universal interface employees already understand, while the authenticated dashboard provides setup, progress, evidence, and control. Role-shaped onboarding. The dashboard translates the workforce concept into familiar roles while Rally keeps configured model routing out of the user interface. Approved company systems only. Connector authority is per user and fail-closed. A configured adapter is never presented as connected until live discovery proves exactly what it can do. Second Wind recovery. When one worker hits a usage limit, tool failure, or evidence blocker, Rally preserves accepted state and hands recoverable work to the next eligible model without transferring approval authority. Independent verification. No model can sign off on its own work. Unsupported claims are rejected, repaired, and checked again. Real deliverables. Rally can return polished email, images, audio, and downloadable artifacts—not merely chat text. Our live proof includes a Lyria 3 Pro Preview song and Nano Banana 2 image with prompts, hashes, and provider receipts. Open agent boundaries. Rally implements an A2A v1 admission boundary for governed agent tasks and exposes bounded WebMCP actions for inspecting evidence and preparing human-approved jobs. 🎧 Proof of action: Play the 73-second All Things Agentic hip-hop song Rally generated with Lyria 3 Pro Preview on Vertex AI . The repository also preserves the original MP3 , exact prompt , model ID, hash, and provider receipt. Rally's completed-run delivery path supports bounded audio attachments and inline image previews; we keep the media generation receipt separate from the email-run receipt. The live product is at rally.agent9.dev , and the full evidence-first repository is on GitHub . How we built it We deliberately separated coordination authority from model execution . Email or Dashboard | Replay-safe edge inbox + workspace identity | Google control plane: Cloud Run + Gemini + ADK + Firestore | Controlled licensed-worker host: Gemini / Claude / Codex CLIs | Independent verifier + evidence receipts | Executive email + authenticated dashboard + deliverables Google is load-bearing in Rally: Gemini 3.7 Flash through Vertex AI interprets the commission and coordinates governed handoffs. Google ADK defines the coordinator and its strictly scoped tools. Cloud Run provides the IAM-protected coordination and customer control-plane services. Firestore atomically claims coordination work, fences retries, and persists cross-session coordination state. Cloud Trace records content-free execution metadata so operations remain observable without storing prompt content. Cloud KMS protects connector credentials with envelope encryption; models receive bounded tools, never raw tokens. Vertex AI media models provide real creative output through Lyria 3 Pro Preview and Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (Nano Banana 2). Cloudflare complements that Google core. Pages serves the product UI, a Worker verifies Resend/Svix webhooks and protects the browser boundary, D1 holds the replay-safe inbox and tenant-scoped projections, and R2 stores verified artifacts privately. Resend gives each workflow a professional HTML email with a text fallback, thread-safe replies, inline image previews, and attachments. The execution loop runs on a controlled licensed-worker host so each provider remains isolated behind its own supported CLI boundary. Its local state.json is authoritative for checklist completion, while Firestore coordinates authenticated handoffs and retry fencing. The runtime itself is a deterministic state machine: prompts may propose work, but they cannot change model families, ownership, verification rules, send authority, retry ceilings, or connector scope. Every accepted transition is saved before the next worker is dispatched. Artifact delivery is also two-phase: Rally stages metadata, uploads bounded bytes, verifies the checksum, and only then exposes the file as ready. The architecture, security boundaries, deployment receipts, and reproducible setup are documented in our architecture guide , security guide , and judge packet . Challenges we ran into Making a workflow instead of another chatbot. The hardest design decision was refusing to make the chat box the center of the product. Email had to become a real asynchronous command surface, and the dashboard had to show durable state rather than animated sample data. Recovering without weakening governance. It is easy to retry a model call. It is much harder to preserve accepted work, reject stale attempts, select a new worker, and guarantee that recovery does not silently transfer approval authority. Second Wind came directly from solving that problem. Keeping credentials out of model context. A frictionless connector can easily become a security liability. We separated human identity, provider OAuth, storage encryption, runtime tool authority, and model context. The connector catalog intentionally says “coming soon” or “setup required” when a provider application has not completed live discovery. Making email genuinely professional. Real mail includes signatures, quoted threads, malformed HTML, retries, and client-specific rendering. We built multipart templates with clean executive summaries, text fallbacks, stable threading, attachment support, and signature-aware request extraction. Proving execution honestly. A polished fake run would have been faster. Instead, Rally displays an explicit failure when live state is unavailable and commits sanitized receipts for real runs, live ADK evaluations, provider-generated media, deployment versions, and known limitations. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real 13-turn executive research run coordinated three model families, rejected unsupported claims, repaired the brief, and closed 6/6 independently verified checks with zero self-approvals .
