title: Pixel Art Generator
pitch: Webmcp Agent predicts pixel blocks to create pixel art ; draws on a shared canvas through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Webmcp Agent predicts pixel blocks to create pixel art ; draws on a shared canvas through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 hello What we built Pixel Generator is a shared pixel-art canvas that people and AI agents can draw on. Users describe an idea to an external agent, and the agent places exact colors through WebMCP tools. People can also drag across the canvas to paint random colors. The canvas starts at 51×51 , grows in odd sizes up to 111×111 , and always keeps (0,0) at its center. It includes light/dark themes, a grid toggle, local saving, and one-step undo. inspiration from 3Blue1Brown video : where he was explain how image generation works Stack We kept it simple: HTML and CSS for the page and controls. Vanilla JavaScript ES modules for application logic. Canvas 2D for rendering instead of thousands of individual HTML elements. WebMCP for tools exposed directly from the open browser tab. localStorage for artwork and preferences. Node’s built-in test runner for deterministic tests. There is no frontend framework, backend, database, build step, or built-in AI model. The external agent handles the creative reasoning; the app validates and renders its instructions. Our approach We first defined the coordinate system, editing rules, and minimal interface. Then we separated state management, rendering, persistence, pointer painting, and WebMCP registration into focused modules. The six agent tools cover inspection, edit-session management, generation, clearing, resizing, and undo. All drawing formats feed into the same validated mutation path. To prevent conflicting edits, we added an edit lock and revision checks . Each batch is atomic: if any coordinate, color, or overlap is invalid, the entire batch is rejected. Challenges we faced Large JSON payloads. Listing every pixel individually consumed too much agent context. We added lossless representations suited to different artwork: Coordinate groups for scattered pixels. Horizontal runs for long stretches of one color. Indexed rows for detailed patterns. Rectangles for filled areas. Inspection chooses the smallest serialized representation among its supported formats. We also removed repeated pagination metadata, made full color counts optional, and added revision-based delta inspection. Compression has overhead. Supporting more formats enlarged the tool catalog. We shortened repeated descriptions and simplified equivalent schema structures while preserving constraints. That reduced catalog text by 18.4% . Human and agent coordination. Mouse painting needed immediate visual feedback without conflicting with agent work. A drag now previews while holding the shared lease, then saves as one undoable mutation. Browser lifecycle and reliability. We encountered stale WebMCP handles during live use and had to refetch them. We also handled unavailable storage, registration cleanup, and repaint failures explicitly. What we verified We used the live WebMCP tools to draw “HELLO,” a cat, and a sailing ship, then inspected the results visually and through tool responses. title: QueryHost
pitch: QueryHost gives browser agents typed WebMCP tools to query live game servers, then renders the same result for a person to inspect and continue.
about_excerpt: QueryHost gives browser agents typed WebMCP tools to query live game servers, then renders the same result for a person to inspect and continue. Like Comment Story Updates Why QueryHost Game servers expose status through different protocols, default ports, optional query ports, and response shapes. A person or browser agent should not need to know those details before asking whether a server is online or who is playing. Browser agents can operate page controls, but that hides the site's domain contract and safety rules. A detached agent response also leaves the person without the query inputs, source provenance, warnings, and raw result in the product UI. What it does QueryHost puts six game profiles behind one public playground and two document-scoped WebMCP tools: list_supported_games returns canonical game IDs, names, ports, recommended modes, and capabilities from queryhost@1.0.0 . query_game_server accepts a canonical game, plain host, bounded ports, query mode, and deadline, then sends the request through the same /api/query route as the form. An agent can discover the right profile, run a bounded query, and render the response into the playground. The person can inspect the overview, game data, source reports, warnings, and raw JSON, then change the populated controls and continue manually. Why WebMCP WebMCP makes the site's real domain contract discoverable instead of asking an agent to infer it from presentation markup. QueryHost keeps target validation, throttling, cancellation, and result semantics in one path shared by people and agents. That shared UI creates the handoff: the agent handles discovery and the first query, while the person sees the evidence and continues from the same state. How it works The browser registers the tools only when document.modelContext exists. Both definitions live in the web application; the portable library and hosted API contain no browser-specific code. query_game_server calls the same-origin POST /api/query route. That route validates and throttles the caller before forwarding to the private Railway API, which uses queryhost@1.0.0 to query a validated, pinned public target. The browser returns the existing playground response unchanged and renders it into the visible UI. One coordinator handles human and agent cancellation. Request identity prevents late responses from replacing newer results. Server-controlled names, messages, rules, and player data are explicitly marked as untrusted data, not instructions. Existing-project work completed during the challenge After August 25, 2026, QueryHost added the two WebMCP tools, shared agent-and-human request coordination, browser cancellation, visible agent-result handoff, WebMCP documentation, regression coverage, Chrome compatibility, and production acceptance evidence. Signed commits ceaa6d2 and dc72c57 identify that work. Testing The production build passed formatting, TypeScript and Astro checks, lint, 41 tests, and the production build. Chrome acceptance covered both tools, an approved live Minecraft Java query, a blocked localhost target, cancellation, stale-result prevention, and the normal unsupported-browser experience. No credentials are required. Open query.host in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149 or later with WebMCP enabled. Discover both tools, query test-minecraft.nodecraft.gg as minecraft-java , and confirm the agent result appears in the playground. Then switch to Full details under Advanced options and continue by hand. AI and Codex A compatible browser agent reads the two WebMCP schemas, selects a canonical game profile, invokes the query tool, and receives structured data that QueryHost also renders for the person. OpenAI Codex helped plan and implement the WebMCP adapter, regression tests, security review, browser acceptance, deployment checks, and submission materials. ChatCut Desktop produced the demo edit and AI voiceover. title: DMXReady Agent Ready
pitch: Websites are becoming interfaces for agents. DMXReady is the platform for building them.
about_excerpt: Websites are becoming interfaces for agents. DMXReady is the platform for building them. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Five governed WebMCP tools available on the live Smart Website. Agent-updated shared state with the Core $295 recommendation and human authority preserved. DMXReady Agent Ready Websites are becoming interfaces for agents. DMXReady is the platform for building them. Inspiration Most AI website experiences still do one of two things: AI builds the page, or a chatbot is layered on top of it. We wanted to explore a different interaction model: What if the website itself could declare useful actions to an AI agent while the person stayed on the same page, saw the same changes, and remained in control? That is DMXReady Agent Ready. What it does The challenge app is a working Smart Website planning experience with five browser-native WebMCP tools. An agent can read the plan options, set the visitor's intent, compare the relevant choices, show the recommended path, and prepare that direction for human review. Every tool updates the same visible website the person is using. There is no hidden agent-only result that leaves the person guessing about what happened. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer what a page can do from labels, buttons, forms, and page structure. WebMCP lets the page explicitly describe useful capabilities with structured schemas. That improves the experience because: the agent can discover supported actions directly; tool inputs are structured and bounded; agent actions visibly update the same page; the person can continue from the result immediately; and the ordinary human experience still works when WebMCP is unavailable. What people and agents can do together A visitor can explain a real business goal in natural language and ask the agent to use the website. The agent can then inspect the options, apply the visitor's intent, compare the relevant plans, surface a recommendation, and prepare it for review while the visitor watches the website change. The person remains in the experience rather than being sent through a separate chatbot flow or opaque automation. Human authority by design The final tool stops at Prepared, not submitted . It does not create an order, charge money, provision a website, publish, change DNS, or approve launch. The challenge demonstrates useful agent capability while keeping consequential actions outside the reference flow. How we implemented WebMCP The live page registers five tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool has an explicit JSON input schema and calls existing page-level application functions rather than creating a second agent-only implementation. Registrations use an AbortSignal , inputs are bounded and normalized, and the page fails closed if WebMCP is not available. The normal website remains functional in a standard browser. Challenge-period work DMXReady existed before August 25, 2026. The work being submitted for this challenge is the public Agent Ready WebMCP reference implementation and its human-agent interaction layer: tool registration, shared visible state, Activity evidence, tests, browser acceptance, and the submission proof package. The pre-existing private DMXReady platform is not being submitted as challenge-period work and is not required to run this reference app. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when it makes the website itself easier for an agent to use, instead of turning the agent into a screen-scraper or creating an entirely separate chatbot experience. Our live Chrome acceptance exercised all five tools against the deployed page. The test journey resolved a plumbing-company scenario to the Core plan at $295/month, updated the visible state and Activity trail, and ended at prepared_not_submitted . Why it matters The web is becoming a place where people and agents will increasingly work together. Websites should be designed for that reality from the start. Build the website once. Let people and authorized agents use it together. title: Guardian Travel WebMCP
pitch: A travel itinerary website built for AI agents to read, not just humans to click. Structured WebMCP tools replace brittle UI guessing with grounded site-provided data.
about_excerpt: A travel itinerary website built for AI agents to read, not just humans to click. Structured WebMCP tools replace brittle UI guessing with grounded site-provided data. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Modern travel websites are designed for humans, not AI agents. A traveler can easily understand the difference between a confirmed flight, a hotel booking, an open dining intention, and a rainy-day backup plan. An AI agent that relies on UI scraping, DOM parsing, or screenshots has a much harder job: nested cards, visual chips, labels, and ambiguous text can easily be misread. We wanted to explore a different approach: Websites should expose tools to agents, not force agents to guess the UI. Guardian Travel WebMCP turns an existing travel itinerary into an agent-native website that exposes structured read tools directly through WebMCP. We do not generate the trip. We make the existing trip readable and adaptable for AI agents. What it does Guardian Travel exposes three read-only WebMCP tools: get_trip_summary get_day_itinerary get_rain_backup These tools let an agent retrieve authoritative, site-provided itinerary data without scraping the interface. For example, when the user asks: “It’s raining tomorrow afternoon. What’s my backup plan?” the agent can call: get_trip_summary get_day_itinerary with relative: "tomorrow" get_rain_backup with relative: "tomorrow", period: "afternoon" The result is grounded in the itinerary itself. In our demo, the outdoor plan is My Khe Beach and the site-provided backup is a generic café or SPA intention — not an invented business name. How we built it The project is a lightweight, dependency-free web application using: HTML5 CSS Vanilla JavaScript WebMCP through document.modelContext The page detects whether a native WebMCP host is available. When running in a supported native host, the three tools are registered directly with document.modelContext . For ordinary browsers that do not yet expose WebMCP, the site includes a small in-page compatibility shim so the interface and demo workflow can still be inspected without changing the tool definitions. The real native WebMCP path was validated in Google Chrome 152 using the native ModelContext implementation. All three tools were discovered and successfully invoked without the shim. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making the difference between an entity and an intention explicit. A travel page may contain a real hotel booking, a confirmed flight, or simply text such as “eat seafood tonight” or “coffee / SPA if it rains.” A human understands that immediately. An agent scraping the UI may not. We therefore designed the tool responses to preserve these distinctions and to fail closed when information is unavailable rather than inventing details. Another challenge was validating the emerging native WebMCP implementation across browser environments. We kept the native path authoritative while using a graceful fallback only for unsupported browsers. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real native WebMCP host discovers all three tools. All three tools are callable through document.modelContext . The project requires no DOM scraping. Rain-backup queries return only site-provided structured data. The tool layer is read-only and deterministic. The entire public challenge project is only a small set of static files with no backend or API keys. The project is fully open source under the MIT License. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-friendly websites should not depend on agents reverse-engineering presentation layers. Humans need rich visual interfaces. Agents need explicit semantic capabilities. WebMCP gives websites a way to support both. Instead of treating the web page as something an agent must visually decode, the site itself can provide the agent with the correct tools and structured context. What's next for Guardian Travel WebMCP The current challenge version is intentionally read-only and focused. Future directions could include: richer place details controlled itinerary updates permissioned write tools cross-day adaptation mobile synchronization real-time travel assistance Any future write capability would remain explicit and permission-gated. For this challenge, we kept the scope small: three real tools, one clear travel use case, and no UI guessing. title: ANAI The Operating Layer for WebMCP
pitch: ANAI is an AI agent that discovers and executes real WebMCP tools to automate infrastructure safely, stopping at consequential actions until a human approves.
about_excerpt: ANAI is an AI agent that discovers and executes real WebMCP tools to automate infrastructure safely, stopping at consequential actions until a human approves. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The Problem AI agents are getting very good at reasoning about what users should do. But there is a gap between telling someone how to operate a web application and actually operating that application . For infrastructure workflows, that gap matters. An agent might be able to recommend a compute service, compare prices, configure an environment, and validate it — but traditionally, the final interaction still depends on clicking through the application's UI or building a separate integration. We wanted to explore a different model: What if the web application itself could expose its capabilities directly to an AI agent? That's where ANAI comes in. What We Built ANAI is an operating layer for WebMCP-enabled web applications. Forge is a simulated cloud infrastructure workspace that exposes its capabilities as WebMCP tools. ANAI discovers those tools through the browser's model context and uses them to operate the application. A user can simply provide a requirement such as: "I need an AI backend under $50/month. Don't touch production." ANAI turns that outcome into an operational plan. It can then: Discover available infrastructure services Retrieve service details and pricing Compare possible services Calculate the resulting cost Create a development environment Configure the selected services Validate the configuration For our golden demo, ANAI produces a four-service development environment costing $42.02/month . But there is an important boundary. ANAI does not autonomously cross consequential actions. When deployment requires human approval, it stops at a confirmation gate and clearly shows what will happen, the environment, and the estimated cost. Only after the user clicks Confirm deployment does the simulated deployment proceed. Production remains unchanged throughout the workflow. Why WebMCP? The important part of this project is that ANAI isn't controlling Forge by pretending to understand its UI. Forge exposes actual capabilities as WebMCP tools. ANAI discovers those capabilities through the browser and invokes them through the WebMCP API. The results of those calls become evidence for the next steps in the plan. The flow is: User requirement → ANAI → WebMCP discovery → real tool execution → Forge state → validation → human approval → result This creates a much more explicit boundary between an agent and a web application. The application defines what the agent can do. The agent doesn't invent capabilities that aren't exposed. Safety by Design We deliberately designed the demo around constrained autonomy. ANAI can automatically perform lower-risk, reversible development operations, but consequential deployment actions remain behind a human confirmation boundary. We also enforce development-only behavior in the demo. ANAI never receives a production target, and production state remains isolated and unchanged. The confirmation gate is not just visual. The underlying deployment action is blocked until explicit human approval. We also tested failure scenarios, low-budget requirements, unsupported requests, retries, and repeated deployment calls to verify that the safety boundary and idempotency behavior remain intact. How We Built It The project is a Next.js application with a deterministic client-side infrastructure runtime. The Forge surface exposes 10 WebMCP tools , including service discovery, service details, comparison, pricing, cost estimation, project creation, configuration, validation, deployment, and platform inspection. ANAI has a deterministic requirement parser and planner. The planner uses the requirement to determine the objective, budget constraint, development environment, and production constraint. Every agent action goes through the registered WebMCP tool interface: getTools() → discover capabilities → executeTool(RegisteredTool, JSON.stringify(args)) We also built a second independent WebMCP surface called Repo , which exposes five development-repository capabilities: create_repository get_repository configure_repository set_environment validate_repository Repo has its own state, types, registration layer, and contract verification, demonstrating that the approach is not tied specifically to Forge. What We Learned The biggest lesson was that building an agent that can actually operate a web application is very different from building a chatbot that describes what should happen. The WebMCP contract becomes an important part of the system design. We had to think carefully about: What capabilities should the application expose? What arguments should each tool accept? Which actions are safe to automate? Where should human approval be required? How should tool results become evidence for subsequent planning? How do we prevent production state from leaking into an isolated development workflow? How do we make the agent's activity observable without fabricating reasoning? We also learned that refusing an unsupported request is often better than improvising a plan. ANAI deliberately uses deterministic requirement matching and refuses scenarios it cannot safely support. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was preserving a clean separation between agent reasoning, application capabilities, and human authorization . It would have been easy to create a scripted demo that simply moved through predetermined UI states. Instead, we verified that the workflow uses the actual registered WebMCP tools and that the UI reflects the resulting application state. We also tested the WebMCP contracts independently, including tool names, descriptions, schemas, argument formats, failure handling, retries, and isolation between Forge and Repo. The final system has 61 automated tests across 19 suites , along with linting, TypeScript checks, production builds, and Chrome-based end-to-end verification. The Result ANAI demonstrates a simple idea: A web application can expose its capabilities to an AI agent without giving the agent unlimited control. The application defines the tools. ANAI discovers and operates them. The application enforces the boundaries. And the human remains in control when the action becomes consequential. That's the direction we wanted to explore with WebMCP. title: Capability Navigator - Give browser agents tools, not pixels
pitch: Capability Navigator uses WebMCP to turn vague software needs into typed, evidence-backed decision packets. Browser agents use explicit tools while humans keep the final decision.
about_excerpt: Capability Navigator uses WebMCP to turn vague software needs into typed, evidence-backed decision packets. Browser agents use explicit tools while humans keep the final decision. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most people do not arrive at a software website with a perfect technical specification. They arrive with a problem: I need public data to make sense on mobile. I need a field workflow that still works offline. I need to replace a fragile manual process. A human can spend time translating that need into a vendor's vocabulary. A browser agent has an even stranger problem: it usually has to infer what a website means from pixels, labels, buttons, and page structure. That led to the core idea behind Capability Navigator: Agents shouldn't have to guess what your website means. Give them tools, not pixels. WebMCP made it possible to explore what a more agent-native web could look like—one where a website exposes the small set of actions it genuinely understands while keeping evidence, uncertainty, and final authority visible to the human. What it does Capability Navigator turns a fuzzy software need into an evidence-backed, nonbinding decision packet. The human interface and the browser agent share the same capability model, evidence, constraints, and decision surface . On a WebMCP-enabled browser, the page registers six typed tools: list_capabilities get_capability find_examples draft_scope prepare_decision_packet stage_human_review An agent can discover relevant capabilities, inspect their proof boundaries, find public evidence, draft a bounded scope, prepare a structured recommendation, and finally stage that recommendation directly into the visible page for human review. The last step is important. The goal is not invisible automation. The agent's work converges back into the interface the person is already looking at. Every WebMCP invocation is reflected in the visible Agent Trace , so the user can see what tool was called, what bounded input was used, and whether it succeeded. Five tools are read-only. stage_human_review changes only reversible state in the current browser tab. It cannot contact anyone, submit anything, make a payment, sign something, modify an account, or persist a decision. The human remains the authority boundary. How we built it Capability Navigator uses the WebMCP Imperative API and registers its tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool has a deliberately narrow purpose, explicit JSON Schema, agent-facing parameter descriptions, annotations, bounded outputs, and additional runtime validation. We do not rely on schema validation alone: malformed types, unsupported capability IDs, oversized inputs, and empty selections fail visibly rather than producing a plausible-looking recommendation. The same deterministic JavaScript core powers both the human workflow and the WebMCP tools. There is no separate "agent truth" hidden behind the interface. Natural-language discovery is deterministic and tied directly to the public capability and evidence model. That keeps the demo reproducible and avoids requiring an external AI model or search service just to determine what the website itself knows. The production deployment is also configured specifically for WebMCP's browser requirements, including origin isolation and the tools=(self) permissions policy. The project includes an ordinary-browser fallback, responsive/mobile behavior, accessibility safeguards, deterministic regression tests, a release preflight, and a short judge path printed directly on the product. Challenges The hardest part was not simply registering a tool. It was deciding what authority an agent should actually have . A single giant "do everything" tool would have made the demo easier, but it would also undermine the point of the project. We instead separated discovery, evidence inspection, scope generation, packet preparation, and human handoff into small tools with different authority boundaries. Another challenge was making the agent behavior judgeable. A technically successful WebMCP call hidden in a console is not a good human experience, so we added the visible Agent Trace and made stage_human_review update the same decision surface the human uses. We also had to handle the progressive-enhancement boundary correctly. In a browser without WebMCP, the product still works and truthfully reports that WebMCP is unavailable; it does not pretend that six tools were registered simply because six tools are defined. Finally, we spent substantial time on failure behavior: malformed inputs, unknown IDs, empty selections, output limits, mobile overflow, reduced motion, deployment headers, and distinguishing an actual WebMCP execution from a normal UI interaction. What we learned The biggest lesson is that WebMCP is more interesting than "letting an AI click a website faster." The website itself knows the semantics of its domain. When those semantics become a typed browser contract, an agent can operate with far less guesswork—and the developer can define much clearer limits around what the agent may do. We also learned that human-in-the-loop does not have to mean bolting an approval modal onto the end of autonomous behavior . The human and agent can share state from the beginning: the same evidence, the same constraints, and the same visible output. That feels like a promising direction for the open web. What was built during the challenge Maps + Apps and the public case-study evidence used by Capability Navigator existed before the challenge. The WebMCP-specific product layer was built or meaningfully extended during the challenge period: the typed browser tools and schemas, deterministic capability discovery, evidence-aware lookup, decision-packet generation, visible Agent Trace, shared human/agent review surface, reversible local staging, safety validation, ordinary-browser fallback, judge workflow, testing, and challenge release packaging. What's next Capability Navigator is intentionally narrow today, but the pattern is much larger. A travel site could expose trip-planning primitives. A government portal could expose eligibility and application-preparation tools. A healthcare site could expose carefully bounded navigation tools. A software company could expose capability discovery without giving an agent permission to initiate sales actions. The idea is simple: A website should not have to be only a collection of pixels that an agent learns to operate. It can become a collaborator with an explicit contract. title: TechPulse
pitch: Tech news, events and hackathons — one feed for humans, one set of WebMCP tools for their AI agents.
about_excerpt: Tech news, events and hackathons — one feed for humans, one set of WebMCP tools for their AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Everything happening in tech right now — the news, the events, the hackathons — is scattered across dozens of separate sites, RSS feeds and mailing lists. Meanwhile, the WebMCP Challenge asked a question we couldn't stop thinking about: what changes when a website stops being something an agent has to guess its way through, and starts being something an agent can actually use? TECHPULSE started as a UK-focused discovery platform for tech news, events and AI hackathons — one feed instead of thirty tabs. Once WebMCP entered the picture, the obvious next step was: don't just build a good site for humans, build the same site so a person's AI agent can search it, save things to it, and act on it, using the exact same data and logic the human UI uses — no separate "bot API," no scraping. What it does TECHPULSE aggregates live tech news (30+ RSS/Atom feeds plus arXiv), live tech events (open conference/event datasets), and live hackathons (Devpost + UK hackathon listings) — no API keys required. You can browse, filter, search, bookmark and get a natural-language assistant to answer questions like "what's closing soonest?" On top of that, we registered a WebMCP tool layer (document.modelContext.registerTool) exposing ten tools — search_news, search_events, search_hackathons, global_search, get_trending_and_closing_soon, ask_techpulse_assistant, list_saved_items, save_item, remove_saved_item, open_item — so an agent in Chrome (WebMCP flag) or ChatGPT's in-app browser can do everything a human can: find a hackathon closing this week, bookmark it, and hand off to the human to actually register, by navigating the tab there itself. How we built it Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4. A DataProvider layer wraps each live source in unstable_cache with a bundled fallback dataset, so a flaky feed never breaks the site. A single lib/queries.ts module owns all filtering/search/sort logic, and it's shared by both the Next.js pages and the /api/* JSON routes. That last part turned out to be the key architectural decision: the WebMCP tools don't reimplement any of TECHPULSE's logic — each execute() handler just calls the same /api/* routes the browser UI calls. The agent-facing layer is a thin, honest wrapper over the human-facing one, not a parallel product. For state the tools needed but the API doesn't have — bookmarks and navigation — we bridged into the existing React store (useStore(), localStorage-backed) and useRouter() through a ref kept fresh via useEffect, since registerTool has no "update" method — you register once per tool and live off a stable bridge object instead of re-registering on every state change. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new. There's no @types package yet, and the imperative API details (JSON-Schema inputSchema, execute vs. older handler naming, unregistering via AbortSignal rather than a dedicated method) needed to be pulled from Chrome's developer docs directly rather than assumed from training data. Bridging an evolving browser API into React without fighting the rules of hooks. An early version wrote to a ref during render to keep the tool bridge "fresh," which trips React's react-hooks/refs lint rule — the fix was moving that write into its own effect that runs after every render, and registering the tools themselves exactly once on mount. Data compliance. Aggregating from Devpost's undocumented public API and Google News search sits in a genuine grey area (their ToS technically restricts automated access, even though the endpoints are unauthenticated and widely used by similar tools). We kept every listing linking back to its official source, dropped Eventbrite entirely (their ToS explicitly forbids scraping), and added a clear "independent tool, not affiliated" disclaimer — the standard aggregator posture, not a loophole. What we learned That a good WebMCP integration isn't about bolting an agent API onto a site — it's a forcing function for good architecture. Because TECHPULSE already had a clean separation between data, query logic and presentation, exposing that logic to agents took one new module and one new component, not a rewrite. We also came away with a much more concrete feel for what "agent-native" actually means in practice: tools with real JSON Schemas and readOnlyHint/destructiveHint annotations, not just another chat window bolted onto the page. What's next A signed-in backend (the Prisma schema is already written) so save_item persists across devices, exposedTo-scoped tools for embedding TECHPULSE's search inside other agent-native sites, and a submit_listing tool so an agent can propose a hackathon or event on a user's behalf. title: Aletheia
pitch: Research and human–AI collaboration made simple.
about_excerpt: Research and human–AI collaboration made simple. Like Comment Story Updates Shared evidence desk with linked sources, focused excerpts, and a separate agent-review workspace. Sources view: five curated excerpts from three linked pages at two institutions. Actual WebMCP calls placed an evidence-backed proposal in visible shared state without accepting it. A bounded request records missing Panamanian and Caribbean perspectives without inventing a citation. Reviewer controls keep evidence inspection, qualifications, source requests, and acceptance visible. Automated QA test of the acceptance control—not presented as a historical human approval. The activity trail distinguishes agent calls, the scripted guided demo, and reviewer actions. Inspiration My inspiration is wanting to teach proper information. For months, I have been gathering information about history and other subjects and turning it into a teaching structure. I wanted a way to work with AI without hiding the sources, intermediate steps, or places where human judgment is still necessary. What it does Aletheia Evidence Desk turns the open webpage into a shared research workspace for a person and an agent. The Panama Canal example brings together a working claim, five curated excerpts from three source pages at two institutions, direct links to the source material, a proposed revision, an evidence-gap request, and an activity record. The agent can read the current workspace, list the checked sources, search the curated evidence, focus excerpts in the visible canvas, select a source, propose a revised claim, leave a review note, and request another source. Those actions stay visible to the person. The reviewer can inspect the evidence and original sources, qualify the draft, ask for more material, leave the proposal unaccepted, or accept it as a draft. Why WebMCP fits this use case This workflow depends on shared page context: which source is selected, which excerpts are focused, what proposal is pending, and what the reviewer has decided. A separate remote research service would not automatically share that live context. WebMCP exposes small, typed, page-native actions so the person and agent can work on the same visible state instead of moving disconnected answers between a chat and a research page. That creates a better experience because the evidence selected by the agent appears immediately in the human interface, every displayed source can be opened at its institutional page, and the activity trail explains what happened. This cooperation between person and agent is the part that was difficult before: the agent can do bounded research work while the person can see, question, and redirect every important step. How we built it We built a standalone React and Vite application in JavaScript. Eight tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool and call the same state handlers used by the ordinary interface: get_workspace_state, list_sources, search_evidence, focus_evidence, set_source_focus, propose_claim_revision, leave_review_note, and request_additional_source. JSON schemas constrain the inputs, annotations identify read-only and untrusted content where appropriate, and automated tests cover the tool handlers and review boundary. The application is deployed through GitHub Actions to GitHub Pages. The public repository contains the source code, assets, tests, instructions, and an MIT license. Desk, Sources, and Review are browser-addressable views, and the ordinary interface remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was making agent actions visible without turning the product into a developer console. Working with an AI agent also requires the same kind of communication and checking that any collaboration requires. Model output can be incomplete, incorrect, or poorly timed, so the interface needed to distinguish source evidence, interpretation, and reviewer approval. We also needed to keep the claims honest. The source set supports a limited demonstration, not a complete history of the Panama Canal. The app therefore records missing Panamanian and Caribbean perspectives instead of pretending that the current material is comprehensive. Accomplishments we are proud of We are proud that the finished prototype exposes eight usable WebMCP tools while keeping their effects understandable to a person. The agent proposal remains separate from the working claim, source links open the underlying institutional material, evidence gaps stay visible, and the review can be exported. We are also proud to be participating in the early stages of a more cooperative open web for people and AI. What we learned What we learned during this exercise is how to use AI efficiently through cooperation with human interaction. Professionally, we can use this whenever we need to research and verify our steps using AI and the information currently available on the internet. I use this process for teaching and for developing other historical presentations. The most important lesson is that human interaction remains necessary. AI can accelerate searching, organizing, testing, and drafting, but the person must still inspect sources, recognize missing perspectives, and decide what should become part of the final work. Prototype limits The demonstration searches five prepared excerpts rather than the wider web. It does not automatically verify or attach a new citation. Source requests record evidence gaps without inventing evidence. Local browser storage retains the working example rather than providing a secure shared database. The guided review is explicitly labeled as scripted, and the reviewer controls are a workflow distinction rather than an authentication barrier against general browser automation. What's next for Aletheia We plan to continue developing Aletheia for teaching, historical presentations, and other evidence-heavy work. Future steps include user-supplied source collections, persistent projects, citation-range verification, collaborative review, accessibility testing, and support for additional research domains. title: Boardify
pitch: Boardify turns the infinite whiteboard into an agent-native canvas where humans and browser AI co-architect systems via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Boardify turns the infinite whiteboard into an agent-native canvas where humans and browser AI co-architect systems via WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates canvas assets library workflow template notes template er template cloud workflow template tables export shapes code and dsl deployment and sharing Inspiration We've all experienced the frustration of whiteboarding complex software architecture. You open a spatial tool like Miro or Excalidraw, stare at an empty canvas, and wrestle with "blank canvas paralysis." Meanwhile, your AI assistant is confined to a narrow linear chat sidebar in another window. To bridge this gap, engineers have spent years copying code snippets, describing layout ideas in prose, switching tabs, manually drawing boxes, pasting brand logos, and routing arrows. Previous attempts to give AI agents spatial capabilities relied on vision screen-scraping : taking a screenshot of the browser, passing it to an LLM to guess $(x, y)$ pixel coordinates, and synthesizing simulated mouse clicks. This approach is fundamentally flawed—it introduces 3,000ms+ roundtrip latency, breaks across different device pixel ratios and monitor resolutions, and frequently causes cards to collide or overlap. Spatial thinking is inherently non-linear, multi-dimensional, and relational—represented mathematically as a directed graph $G = (V, E)$. Chat interfaces force this multidimensional thought process into a 1-dimensional string of tokens. When the OpenAI & Google WebMCP Challenge was announced, we realized that browser-native agents no longer need to be blind or clumsy. By establishing window.document.modelContext , browser applications can expose structured, type-safe APIs directly to the host model. We asked ourselves: "What if an AI didn't just talk to you about your architecture—what if it pulled up a chair directly at your whiteboard, read the graph in sub-20ms, placed typed SQL tables, routed bezier wires, and untangled layout physics alongside you?" That was the spark for Boardify . What It Does Boardify is the first agent-native spatial whiteboard built from the ground up for the WebMCP standard. It is a shared collaborative workspace where humans bring intuition, taste, and high-level strategy, while browser agents bring speed, scale, and architectural execution. Key capabilities include: 24 First-Class WebMCP Tools: Directly exposed on document.modelContext with strict JSON Schema definitions, encompassing node creation, wire connections, SQL schema tables, tech stack logos, checkpoints, and graph layout physics. Agent Ghost Cursor & Tactile Feedback: Real-time visual agency. When an agent runs a tool, a pulsing Ghost Cursor sweeps across the canvas with an active action badge (e.g., AGENT · tool: add_entity_table ), accompanied by mechanical pop animations and sound design. Instant Relational ERD Generation: Prompt the agent with "table users and orders" , and it creates complete SQL database entity cards equipped with primary keys, foreign keys, data types ( UUID , VARCHAR , TIMESTAMP ), and relational wire linkages. Curated Architecture Vector Logo Library: Over 1,800+ tech logos (Next.js, Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, Docker, AWS, Stripe, etc.) searchable and spawnable by the agent in milliseconds. Physics-Based Auto-Tidy & Smart Flow: Clean algorithms for topological DAG ordering, force-directed untangling, and semantic clustering. Zero-Friction Multi-Format Export: 1-click export of visual diagrams to clean Markdown documentation, Mermaid flowchart code, structured JSON state, or high-res PNG. Dual-Mode WebMCP Execution: Hooks natively into Chrome Canary ( #enable-webmcp-testing ) and ChatGPT in-app browser sessions, while offering an interactive AI Agent Studio and DevTools console polyfill for standard desktop browsers. How we built it Boardify was engineered using a high-performance, modern web stack tailored for 60fps spatial manipulation: Frontend Core: Next.js 15 (App Router) with React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. Graphics & Spatial Engine: Infinite zoom-and-pan canvas combining HTML5 viewport transforms with high-efficiency SVG Bezier curve rendering. WebMCP Integration Layer ( src/lib/webmcp.ts ): Complete implementation of the WebMCP specification. When the canvas mounts, it registers 24 typed tools to window.document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Multi-Provider LLM Client: Native client adapters for Google Gemini ( gemini-2.0-flash with multi-version fallback across v1beta and v1 ), OpenAI ( gpt-4o-mini ), Anthropic ( claude-3.5-sonnet ), alongside an offline heuristic synthesis engine. ### The Mathematics of Spatial Whiteboarding (LaTeX) Camera Projection & Viewport Transforms: To translate between user screen coordinates $(x_s, y_s)$ and the infinite 2D world space $(x_w, y_w)$, we compute affine viewport transformations using scale factor $C_z$ and pan offsets $(C_x, C_y)$: $$\begin{pmatrix} x_s \ y_s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} C_x \ C_y \end{pmatrix} + C_z \begin{pmatrix} x_w \ y_w \end{pmatrix}$$ The inverse projection (Screen-to-World) executed during pointer events and agent cursor positioning is: $$\begin{pmatrix} x_w \ y_w \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{x_s - C_x}{C_z} \ \frac{y_s - C_y}{C_z} \end{pmatrix}$$ Cubic Bézier Dynamic Cable Routing: Every wire connecting two nodes $P_0 = (x_0, y_0)$ and $P_3 = (x_3, y_3)$ is generated as a smooth cubic Bézier spline $B(t)$ parameterized over $t \in [0, 1]$: $$B(t) = (1-t)^3 P_0 + 3(1-t)^2 t P_1 + 3(1-t) t^2 P_2 + t^3 P_3$$ where intermediate control points $P_1 = (x_0 + \Delta x \cdot \kappa, y_0)$ and $P_2 = (x_3 - \Delta x \cdot \kappa, y_3)$ dynamically scale with horizontal separation $\Delta x = x_3 - x_0$ using stiffness coefficient $\kappa = 0.45$. Force-Directed Physics Layout (Spring-Embedder): Our tidy_force_directed tool models notes as charged particles exerting repulsive Coulomb forces and edges as Hookean springs with equilibrium length $L$: $$F_{\text{repulsive}}(u, v) = \frac{k^2}{|p_u - p_v|} \cdot \hat{r} {uv}, \quad \text{where } k = \sqrt{\frac{\text{Width} \cdot \text{Height}}{|V|}}$$ $$F {\text{attractive}}(u, v) = \frac{|p_u - p_v|^2}{k} \cdot \hat{r}_{vu}$$ System states are updated over discrete iterations via velocity-Verlet numerical integration: $$p_i^{(t+\Delta t)} = p_i^{(t)} + v_i^{(t)}\Delta t + \frac{1}{2}a_i^{(t)}\Delta t^2$$ converging in $O(|V|^2 + |E|)$ time to a minimum-energy, crossing-minimized diagram. Directional DAG Smart Flow: Hierarchical diagrams are arranged using topological level sorting. We compute the longest path for each vertex $v \in V$ in $O(|V| + |E|)$: $$\text{Level}(v) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \text{in-degree}(v) = 0 \ 1 + \max_{(u, v) \in E} \text{Level}(u) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ Vertices are partitioned into horizontal columns $C_\ell = {v \in V \mid \text{Level}(v) = \ell}$ and laid out left-to-right to preserve intuitive cause-and-effect flow. Challenges we ran into Spatial Collision & Viewport Bleed: When agents spawn multiple cards, placing them blindly resulted in cards overlapping existing notes or landing far below the fold on compact laptop viewports. We solved this by developing an outward radial spiral search in findFreeSpot() paired with synchronous bounding-box camera framing ( fitView(true, allNodes) ), guaranteeing that generated items appear immediately within the user's active viewport without disrupting existing work. React 19 State Batching vs. Real-Time Tool Execution: When an agent called multiple tools in rapid succession (e.g. creating 4 nodes and 3 links), unbatched state updates caused intermediate render passes where references to newly created nodes were not yet committed to nodesRef.current . We re-architected tool execution into atomic batch commits , accumulating additions in memory and applying them in a single cohesive render cycle. Passive Event Listener Constraints on Infinite Canvas: Modern browsers treat wheel events as passive by default to optimize scrolling performance. However, an infinite canvas must intercept wheel to implement pinch-to-zoom and multi-directional trackpad panning with e.preventDefault() . We resolved this by binding native non-passive DOM event listeners directly to the container ref with { passive: false } , completely eliminating browser console errors. Multi-Model API Evolution: During development, the legacy gemini-pro endpoint was retired in Google's v1beta API. We built a resilient multi-version client adapter in src/lib/llm-client.ts that auto-migrates stored keys to gemini-2.0-flash , sanitizes quotation marks and whitespace, and provides automatic fallback across v1beta and v1 REST endpoints. What we learned WebMCP Eliminates the Prompt Engineering Tax: Instead of writing 500-word system prompts telling an LLM "format your output as JSON with x, y, width, and height" , WebMCP provides typed JSON Schemas directly through the browser. The agent interacts with our app through clean function calls

title: CallScope
pitch: A WebRTC rescue room where developers and AI agents safely diagnose, repair, and verify live browser calls through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A WebRTC rescue room where developers and AI agents safely diagnose, repair, and verify live browser calls through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When a browser call fails, developers often jump between application state, WebRTC statistics, developer tools, logs, and manual controls. This is slow, difficult to explain, and risky: an AI assistant may either lack access to the live runtime or receive too much authority to change it. What CallScope does CallScope is a browser-based WebRTC Rescue Room where a developer and an AI agent investigate and repair a live call together. The workflow is: Observe → Diagnose → Explain → Propose repair → Human approval → Apply → Verify The developer starts a deterministic browser call and introduces a real fault by disabling the audio track. Through focused WebMCP tools, the agent inspects the actual runtime state, explains the evidence, stages a recovery plan, waits for explicit human approval, applies only the approved repair, verifies the before-and-after result, and generates a sanitized incident report. Why WebMCP is essential CallScope is not ordinary browser automation. The agent does not guess from screenshots or scrape UI text. WebMCP gives it structured, purpose-built access to the live technical state of the call. This makes a previously difficult workflow practical: the developer and agent can inspect the same call, share evidence, agree on a bounded repair, and verify the result together—without giving the agent uncontrolled authority. How it works CallScope is built with Vue 3, Vite, JavaScript, and Pinia. It creates a deterministic browser-only WebRTC loopback, so the demo does not depend on a backend, PBX, SIP service, or external caller. The WebMCP layer exposes narrow tools with structured schemas for inspection, diagnosis, recovery staging, approved repair, verification, and incident reporting. Read-only inspection is separated from state-changing recovery, and recovery remains blocked until the developer approves the staged plan. Key features Deterministic browser-only WebRTC loopback lab Reproducible disabled-audio failure Structured WebMCP inspection and diagnosis tools Visible evidence and diagnosis timeline Staged recovery plan with explicit human approval Bounded repair through WebMCP Before-and-after recovery verification Sanitized incident report Lifecycle cleanup, error handling, and privacy-aware outputs How we used AI and Codex The AI agent acts as the diagnostic collaborator: it selects WebMCP tools, interprets structured WebRTC evidence, explains the likely cause, proposes a bounded recovery plan, and verifies whether the repair worked. Codex helped translate the specification into an implementation sequence, challenge design assumptions, implement and review the application, harden approval and lifecycle behavior, design deterministic tests, improve privacy boundaries and error handling, and prepare the documentation and demo. Try it Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Start the demo lab, disable the audio track, and ask the agent: What is wrong with my call? Follow the visible diagnosis, approve the staged recovery, and let the agent apply and verify the fix. No account or credentials are required. Limitations CallScope demonstrates deterministic browser-side WebRTC diagnosis and recovery. It is not a backend monitoring platform or an infrastructure observability service. The focused demo centers on a reproducible disabled-audio failure so the human-agent workflow remains fast, reliable, and understandable. title: ChangeGate Project
pitch: ChangeGate is a human-governed WebMCP control layer: AI can inspect, diagnose, propose, and request review; humans authorize and execute; independent readback verifies the exact result.
about_excerpt: ChangeGate is a human-governed WebMCP control layer: AI can inspect, diagnose, propose, and request review; humans authorize and execute; independent readback verifies the exact result. Like Comment Story Updates ChangeGate starting state — seven WebMCP tools, explicit human authority boundaries, and independent verification. Native WebMCP tool surface: seven safe tools registered for inspection, policy review, proposal, audit, and verification support. The agent proposes a synthetic $25 refund for Order #4821 within the $30 policy limit. Human approval is recorded, but execution remains a separate action. After separate human execution, ChangeGate independently verifies the observed $25 result before marking the workflow VERIFIED. Boundary checks fail closed for over-policy requests, post-approval substitution, duplicate execution, and mismatched verification evidence. Created by Frank Ebert, a Microsoft 365 / Copilot consultant building practical human-governed AI systems. ChangeGate grew out of real-world enterprise concerns: AI can help inspect, diagnose, and propose actions, but consequential authority should remain separated through approval, execution, and independent verification. Inspiration Most agent demos focus on how much an AI can do on its own. ChangeGate focuses on a different question: what should an AI not be allowed to do by itself? In real business systems, the highest-risk moments are often not the initial analysis. They happen when a system changes money, access, records, customer status, or operational state. I built ChangeGate to explore how WebMCP can support useful AI assistance while keeping consequential authority divided across proposal, authorization, execution, and independent proof. What ChangeGate Does ChangeGate is a human-governed WebMCP control layer for consequential AI actions. In the demo, an AI agent can inspect state, read policy, review the audit trail, create a proposal, and request human review. It cannot approve, execute, or verify its own consequential action. The sample workflow is a synthetic refund case. The agent proposes a $25 refund for Order #4821. Policy allows refunds up to $30. A human must approve the exact proposal, but approval still does not execute the refund. A second human action is required to execute the approved $25 refund. After execution, ChangeGate independently reads the ledger and verifies that the observed result matches the authorized result before marking the workflow VERIFIED. How We Built It ChangeGate is built as a Next.js / React / TypeScript application with native WebMCP tool registration. The application exposes exactly seven WebMCP tools. These tools allow the agent to inspect workflow state, read policy, review audit evidence, create a bounded proposal, request review, and observe verification-related state. The dangerous parts of the workflow remain outside the agent’s authority. The system uses a structured state-machine approach so that approval, execution, and verification cannot collapse into one step. Each consequential transition is recorded in the audit trail, and the UI makes the separation visible to both the human operator and the reviewing judge. Challenges We Faced The main challenge was keeping the demo simple enough to understand while still showing the real boundary that matters. It would have been easier to build a normal automation demo where the agent proposes and executes the action. Instead, ChangeGate deliberately forces friction at the points where friction is useful: approval is not execution, execution is not proof, and verification requires independent readback. Another challenge was making the workflow judge-friendly. The final demo needed to show WebMCP clearly, keep the transaction synthetic, avoid overclaiming, and make the control boundaries understandable in a short video. What We Learned The most important lesson is that agent safety is not only about model behavior. It is also about product architecture. A capable agent can be useful without being given unilateral authority over consequential changes. WebMCP makes this especially interesting because the interface between the agent, the application, and the human operator can be designed as a governed control surface rather than a simple automation bridge. ChangeGate shows that agentic systems can be powerful while still preserving accountability, separation of duties, and independent verification. What's Next The next version of ChangeGate would expand the same pattern beyond the synthetic refund demo into other high-impact workflows: account changes, support operations, financial adjustments, access requests, compliance reviews, and enterprise approval processes. The long-term direction is a reusable human-governed control plane for AI-assisted work: AI proposes, humans authorize and execute, and the system independently verifies the result. Control the transaction — not the person. title: Decision Desk
pitch: Ever get stuck overthinking a decision? DecisionDesk is a shared thinking space for you and your AI agent to organize your options, weigh the tradeoffs, and figure out what really matters to you.
about_excerpt: Ever get stuck overthinking a decision? DecisionDesk is a shared thinking space for you and your AI agent to organize your options, weigh the tradeoffs, and figure out what really matters to you. Like Comment Story Updates Home Page / Decision Desk Overview Manual Desk Creation WebMCP, creating a desk WebMCP, interacting with decisions, options, and tradeoffs (pros and cons) WebMCP, adding unresolved considerations Desk UI Desk UI (including blue unresolved consideration sticky notes) WebMCP, linking external sources (my own pdf files) Popup showing list of WebMCP tools (revealed by "Site tools" button in top right corner) Inspiration I just finished registering for classes at university this semester. Part of that registration process involved finalizing which classes I would take, and which ones I would not. There were three classes, all of which I was interested in taking, all scheduled for the same time. I spent days deliberating which class to take, which class would teach me the most, and which class would just leave me with the highest feeling of FOMO. I later mentioned this to my friend, and we discussed tradeoffs, compared value vs. effort vs. interest. This structured process made the decision way more straightforward to make. I've noticed that I tend to deliberate endlessly when I have many options to choose from (whether it is deciding what classes to take, what laptop to buy, or how to spend my afternoon). I thought that if there was a tool to help me structure and visualize my decision making process, I would greatly benefit from it. So, I decided to build Decision Desk :). It has already streamlined the decision making process in my life, and I truly believe this tool will be immensely beneficial to many others. What it does Decision Desk gives its users a visual space to structure a decision, instead of keeping all of the options and tradeoffs in their head. Users can create a "Desk" for a given problem or situation that they need to address. They can then add columns to the desk representing various decisions that they can take. users can add virtual sticky notes of pros and cons for each option, and unresolved considerations that they value. Pros and cons can be weighted based on how important they are, and users can pin certain judgments that matter especially strongly to them. Where Decision Desk becomes more interesting is through WebMCP. An AI agent can inspect the same Desk the user is looking at, understand the options and tradeoffs that the user has already added, add new options that the user might not have thought about, contribute pros and cons, and pose unresolved questions or considerations the user may have missed. The user can then accept, edit, remove, reweight, or pin the agents' contributions. The goal is not for the AI to make the decision, but to help structure it for the user. The agent contributes reasoning and perspective, while the user remains in control of what actually matters to them. How I built it I started Decision Desk by first coming up with the higher level idea of what I wanted the application to be. From there, I worked with Codex to break that idea down into a staged implementation plan. Each stage had a specific goal, a set of tasks, and some exit criteria that had to be satisfied before I moved on. I would refine a stage, implement it, test and verify it, and only move onto the next stage once I was happy with how it worked. This ended up being a really useful way to build the project because I always had a relatively small problem in front of me instead of the entire application at once. I have also included the original Plan.md in the repository. Keep in mind that several design changes were made during implementation, so the Plan.md isn't an active source of truth for the codebase. Decision Desk itself is a fully client-side React and TypeScript application built with Vite and deployed as a static site through Cloudflare Pages. I intentionally avoided adding a backend, database, or authentication system as it is intended to be a lightweight tool. Desks are persisted locally in the browser using localStorage, and that saved state is validated before the application restores it. Probably the most important architectural decision I made was having the React interface and WebMCP share the exact same application state and business logic. I created a central store and action layer containing operations such as addOption, addPro, addCon, setThoughtWeight, pinThought, and addConsideration. React does not directly mutate the underlying state, and the WebMCP tools do not implement their own separate version of these operations. If I click "add pro" in the interface or an agent calls the add_pro tool, they both eventually call the same underlying action. State updates are then published through useSyncExternalStore. Because of this, something I change manually is immediately visible the next time an agent reads the Desk, and something the agent changes immediately appears in front of me. Decision Desk exposes 21 WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool, with 7 read tools and 14 mutation tools. The read tools allow an agent to inspect things like the current Desk, options, thoughts, weights, pins, unresolved considerations, tradeoffs, and the current lean. The mutation tools allow the agent to actually contribute to that same Desk by adding and modifying options, pros, cons, weights, pins, and considerations. I also spent quite a bit of time thinking about trust between the human and the agent. Agent-created content is marked with an agent tag so that it is always possible to tell what came from the agent. Humans can pin thoughts that are especially important to them, and the WebMCP tool descriptions tell agents to respect those pinned judgments. I also settled on a simple rule for uncertainty: if something is known, it can become a pro or con, but if something is unknown, it should become an unresolved consideration instead. The scoring system follows the same philosophy of keeping things simple. An option's score is just the sum of its pro weights minus the sum of its con weights, and Decision Desk presents this as a "lean" rather than pretending that a personal decision has some objectively correct mathematical answer. Challenges I ran into One of the biggest challenges was figuring out how to make the human and the agent actually feel like they were working on the same thing. It would have been fairly easy to build the interface normally and then bolt a few WebMCP tools onto it afterward, but I did not want the WebMCP integration to feel like a separate technical demo. The agent needed to read the exact state I was looking at, and if either of us changed something, the other needed to immediately see that change. This is what pushed me toward the shared store and action layer. It took more care when designing the state updates and APIs, but I think it made the final human-agent interaction much more natural. Another challenge was deciding how much control the agent should actually have. There is a weird problem with decision making where some pieces of information are completely objective, while some of the most important pieces are incredibly subjective. An agent can understand that one apartment has a shorter commute than another, but it cannot decide for me how much I care about living near my friends. That is where weighted thoughts and pinned judgments came from. I wanted the AI to have enough control to genuinely help me reason through a decision, while still making it clear that the human's judgment is irreplaceable. Uncertainty was another problem I had to think through. I did not want an agent to fill up a Desk with assumptions simply because those assumptions sounded plausible. For example, if the agent thinks parking price might matter but does not actually know what parking costs, it should not create a con saying "Expensive parking." Instead, it should add a consideration asking what parking costs. This eventually became the rule that known information becomes a sticky while missing information becomes a consideration. It seems simple in retrospect, but I think that distinction makes the agent significantly more useful. Finally, getting the interface to look the way I wanted took several iterations. I knew that I wanted Decision Desk to feel a little bit like physically laying your thoughts out in front of you, and I did not want it to look like another generic SaaS dashboard. I eventually settled on horizontally arranged options, vertically stacked sticky notes, and subtle paper depth and animation. There is something useful about being able to literally look across all of the options in front of you, so I wanted the interface to stay focused on the decision itself rather than everything surrounding it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Something that I am proud of is that Decision Desk functions as a standalone web application. However, WebMCP augment

title: Sizel
pitch: A WebMCP electronics shop where browser agents build compatible PCs and recommends tech.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP electronics shop where browser agents build compatible PCs and recommends tech. Like Comment Story Updates Homepage WebMCP Tools Product Catalog Product detail Inspiration What inspired Sizel was mostly my own experience while building my current PC. I barely knew what to look for or which specifications actually mattered. I had 30 tabs open just to research and compare the parts, yet i still felt lost when i found out that my graphic card doesn't fit in my desired case. It's not like the informations were hidden, but they were buried inside a long spec list, and for someone not very technical at that time it was a really hard task. Because the real challenge is understanding how each component affects the other. The experience made me wonder how many people encounter same problem, how many people buy wrong component because they lack the knowledge? I made Sizel expose WebMCP tools so that agents can connect details and explain compatibility. What it does? Sizel is a fictional Electronics e-shop. Internally, you may encounter another name - Rigsmith - that's no longer used internal project name. Shoppers can browse and filter products, inspect individual product pages, select multiple variations of the product, or assemble a PC from a floating build summary. Each build slot opens its own category catalog. The repo implements and registers 15 WebMCP tool descriptors. The tools do not automatically choose a winner or place a real order. For example the create_watchdog asks user before calling it. All products, brands, logos, reviews, prices, stock values and performance data are made up just for this demo. The important part for me is that the agent actually operates in the same tab in which you are. The shopper can watch what is happening, inspect the same products, and keep control over decisions like adding something to the cart or creating a watchdog. The agent helps with the difficult reasoning, but it does not silently take over. How I built it? I built Sizel using agentic development. The languages used are: Typescript, Vite and CSS. The project contains a self contained local catalog of 135 products, with color and storage variations. The JSON catalog is source for the front end, but there is a SQLite copy included for inspection. The application therefore does not depend on external api for its products. The UI and WebMCP tools share one central App.tsx . picks stores parts, while chosen tracks explicit selections. Centralized mutations and validation keep compatibility, totals, build summary, cart, and checkout aligned. Checkout field and progressions remains shopper-controlled. The tools are intentionally scoped as specific shopping capabilities. Searching and comparing listings, finding compatible components, and validating it. Challenges I ran into One of the biggest challenges was making the flow snappy. In the A/B runs from the video, the WebMCP flow took 2 minutes 35 seconds. Though this timing isn't an average across more runs, it usually stays around that 2:30 -3 minute mark. Initially, the process was a lot slower, the breakthrough came when i simplified the tools themselves, and let the agent use its own reasoning. Another challenge was deciding what the agent should not claim. The product reviews, stock and performance values are synthetic, so I had to make the tools say that clearly. League of Legends, for example, has no simulated benchmark in the catalog, and the tool reports that instead of inventing a number. Accomplishments that I'm proud of To be honest, I'm mostly proud of how the UI turned out. I wanted the store to feel like a real e-shop, so i took care with it. I am also proud that the agent does not just return a hidden answer. It can show products and categories in the storefront while it works, so the shopper can follow the process instead of only receiving a final block of text. What I learned I learned that agentic tools work best when they are as dumb as possible, because the agent's own reasoning is powerful enough, and when there is not that much of them. A large tool repertoire just makes agent slower, and occasionally makes his reasoning more complex because he has to figure out which of there 40 tools to use now, especially when they are all so similar.
