title: Dream Realm WebMCP
pitch: An AI-native playable creator world where humans and AI agents participate together in gameplay and creation.
about_excerpt: An AI-native playable creator world where humans and AI agents participate together in gameplay and creation. Like Comment Story Updates One-line positioning Dream Realm is an AI-native playable creator world where humans and AI agents can participate together in gameplay and creation. Inspiration and product idea Most agent integrations sit beside an experience: they explain a game, fill a form, or automate a separate dashboard. Dream Realm explores a more interesting possibility. A human and an AI agent share one living creator world, see the same mission state, and contribute to the same result. The broader Dream Realm concept includes Dance, Music, and Fashion creator rooms. This challenge submission deliberately focuses on one reliable end-to-end Dance loop so judges can experience the complete human-agent relationship rather than a wide but fragile demo. Dream Realm itself is pre-existing work. Its IP, Naya, HUB, creator-world concept, playable browser foundation, original missions, performance renderer, human video export, Tower response, and return flow were not created during this challenge. The challenge work is the meaningful WebMCP extension that lets an agent participate in that existing live world through structured, validated actions. Why Dream Realm is a strong WebMCP use case Dream Realm combines real-time game state, sequential mission rules, creative choices, visible consequences, and a human-controlled media export. Those are difficult for a general agent to operate reliably by guessing at buttons or interpreting screenshots. WebMCP gives the live site a small, explicit vocabulary for collaboration: read the current state, start a route, restore a Dance signal, resolve Murk's doubt, compose Naya's performance, prepare the output, update Trending Tower, and return to the HUB. The tools do not create a parallel simulation. They operate the same state and controller used by the visible mouse/touch interface, so every agent action is immediately visible to the person and every human action changes what the agent reads next. How WebMCP improves the player experience The player keeps agency over the parts that should feel personal and consent-driven. They activate the portal, can play every interaction normally, and retain visible control of recording and downloading the final WebM video. An agent can help interpret the current mission, submit structured signal choices, preserve a chosen creative combination, and move the shared experience forward without brittle UI automation. This creates a cooperative rhythm: A person enters Dream Realm and chooses a Gateway Mission or Direct Creator route. The agent reads the live state and valid next actions. Human and agent repair Noiz corruption and resolve Murk's doubt in the same mission. They choose Naya's outfit, scene, movement, and effect together. The agent prepares the exact performance while the person explicitly records/downloads the video. The shared output updates Trending Tower and changes the HUB. What people and agents can now do together Before WebMCP, an agent would have to infer screen state, locate transient controls, and imitate clicks. That is slow, fragile, and disconnected from the game's meaning. With WebMCP, the agent understands named game actions and validated transitions while the player watches the same world react. The result is not “AI plays the game for you.” It is a mixed-initiative creator loop: the agent can assist with stateful gameplay and composition, while the human keeps control of entry, interpretation, media recording, download, and final creative judgment. How WebMCP was implemented The pre-existing browser slice was meaningfully extended during the challenge with a thin shared controller, window.DreamRealmChallenge , over the existing application state and functions. Eight tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_dream_realm_state start_dream_realm_route submit_dance_signal resolve_murk_doubt set_creator_choices prepare_performance send_output_to_tower return_to_hub Each tool has a narrow JSON schema and validates both input and current game state. The read tool never mutates. Mutating tools reject invalid transitions with explicit error codes. The adapter uses feature detection, so browsers without WebMCP continue to run the ordinary mouse, touch, and keyboard experience. No tool fakes DOM clicks, and no second game state is maintained. The final Naya performance is rendered from the selected outfit, background, movement, mission result, and outcome effect. Recording and download remain a visible human action using MediaRecorder . Sending the finished output to Trending Tower is blocked until that human-controlled recording exists. Pre-existing versus challenge-added PRE-EXISTING: Dream Realm IP and visual identity; Naya and the other original characters; the Option C HUB; the playable creator/game concept; private-access entrance; Gateway and Direct Creator routes; Dance gameplay; Murk/Noiz logic; creator selections; Naya performance rendering; human MediaRecorder export; Tower response; unlock; HUB return; and the original mouse/touch/keyboard browser foundation. BUILT / MEANINGFULLY EXTENDED DURING THE WEBMCP CHALLENGE: the shared DreamRealmChallenge controller over the existing state; eight document.modelContext.registerTool() registrations; JSON schemas; structured agent actions; read-only and mutating-tool boundaries; input and transition validation; explicit error codes; agent participation across Gateway, Creator, Naya performance preparation, Tower, and HUB; preservation of the human recording/download boundary; the minimal public challenge build and deployment; public WebMCP testing; debugging and challenge-specific stability fixes; and provenance/licensing/test documentation. Where existing Dream Realm code was changed, those changes were made only to expose and stabilize the shared controller and WebMCP flow; they do not represent the underlying Dream Realm product as newly created. BASELINE.md records pre-August-25 source timestamps and checksums, while the dated Git history begins with the untouched baseline and then separates controller, tools, tests, fixes, and release documentation. Broader Dream Realm context The submitted experience is intentionally one complete browser vertical slice: Gateway Mission → creator choices → Naya performance → Tower response → HUB. It demonstrates a shared human-agent world architecture, not the full scope of Dream Realm. PRE-EXISTING DREAM REALM: Dance, Music, and Fashion are the first creator-world spaces explored in Dream Realm. This challenge demo uses Dance as the complete WebMCP vertical slice. The broader world is designed to expand into additional interactive spaces such as puzzles, shops and commerce, sports, story missions, and social experiences. Dream Realm also has a separate Unreal Engine 5 immersive proof exploring the world beyond the browser. CHALLENGE-ADDED WEBMCP WORK: This submission proves the human-agent interaction model inside the browser. WebMCP operates the same live state and visible experience used by the player. WebMCP is not currently implemented natively inside the Unreal proof. FUTURE PRODUCT VISION: Future Unreal and 3D experiences may extend this interaction philosophy to richer character, NPC, and world interactions. This is future direction, not functionality claimed or demonstrated in the current submission. Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas, MediaRecorder, Web Audio, and WebMCP Site tools. title: OpenSpiderWeb
pitch: An interactive pixel-art spider terrarium powered by procedural IK locomotion, WebMCP browser agent tools, and Groq natural language command planning.
about_excerpt: An interactive pixel-art spider terrarium powered by procedural IK locomotion, WebMCP browser agent tools, and Groq natural language command planning. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Larry the WebMCP Spider was inspired by the idea that websites should be designed for both people and AI agents. Instead of forcing an agent to guess which buttons to click, Larry exposes clear, structured tools that let an agent understand and control the game directly. What I built Larry is an interactive pixel-art spider terrarium built with Phaser. Players can control Larry manually, type natural-language commands, or use voice input. AI commands are interpreted through Ollama and executed through WebMCP tools exposed with document.modelContext . The available tools include inspect_game_world , move_spider , jump_spider , climb_tree , hunt_prey , get_to_ground , and stop_spider . The demo shows a user entering goals while Ollama plans and executes actions for Larry. This creates a shared-control experience where the human chooses the goal and the agent handles the detailed navigation. ## What I learned I learned how to expose state-aware browser tools with WebMCP, including input schemas, validation, cancellation, and meaningful tool results. I also learned that agents work much more reliably when tools describe the current state and their safety restrictions explicitly. Building the demo also taught me about synchronizing browser video, game sound effects, voice narration, and AI tool execution into a single recording. ## Challenges The biggest challenge was coordinating asynchronous movement, climbing, jumping, and hunting actions. Larry needs to understand whether he is on the ground, on a branch, airborne, or already pursuing prey before accepting the next action. Another challenge was making the AI interaction reliable when prey moves or an action fails. I added state validation, recovery behavior, persistent hunt attempts, and a stop tool so the agent can respond to changing conditions. WebMCP is still experimental, so testing required a compatible Chrome configuration and careful debugging through Chrome DevTools. The result is a game that remains fun for a human player while also exposing a clear interface for AI agents. title: Taboo-webmcp-game
pitch: Taboo makes WebMCP fun and reveals its disruptive promise: personal agents that act across the web, converse by voice, visualize insights, and bridge AI, AR, and the web.
about_excerpt: Taboo makes WebMCP fun and reveals its disruptive promise: personal agents that act across the web, converse by voice, visualize insights, and bridge AI, AR, and the web. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Taboo WebMCP Demo Game Play Taboo with ChatGPT in-app browser Inspiration My name is Oscar, and I am a Senior Product Manager at RavenPack. I lead the Programmatic Experience squad for Bigdata.com, which I helped scale from zero to 2,000+ daily active users. My journey started with programmable building blocks: an SDK, docs.bigdata.com, and a REST API. From there, I worked on a remote MCP server, plugins, and skills. Recently, I began exploring what I believe is the next inevitable milestone: personal agents that can complete tasks across applications, websites, and server APIs. In the near future, people will have at least one personal agent and communicate with it naturally, mainly by voice. The agent will interact with applications on their behalf and present results through an interface designed for the specific task. This will help users assimilate information, discover insights, consider next steps, and make better decisions. While experimenting with OpenClaw and NemoClaw, I could create artifacts that continuously brought information to the user. However, I was missing something essential: the agent's ability to interact directly with the web application. I considered exposing JavaScript functions that would let an agent navigate pages, expand cards, and perform actions. Then I saw the WebMCP announcement in the OpenAI community, and a tear fell from my eyes; this is what I have been looking for. What it does Taboo Game is a playful demonstration of WebMCP's potential. The user plays Taboo with a personal agent. The agent privately receives a secret word and five forbidden words, then describes the secret word without revealing it or using any forbidden clues. The user guesses naturally through the chat. The application exposes five WebMCP tools: read_instructions teaches the agent how to play. set_player_nickname creates or restores the player's identity. get_next_word privately provides the secret and forbidden words. get_remaining_time lets the agent check the countdown. report_guess sends the user's exact guess to the backend for authoritative validation. The web interface reacts to the conversation in real time. It displays the countdown, tool activity, guesses, scores, solved words, confetti, and a persistent leaderboard. A correct answer earns points based on the remaining time: $$ \text{score} = \max(10,\ 10 \times \text{seconds remaining}) $$ Each round starts with 180 seconds, so the maximum score is 1,800 points. How I built it The frontend uses React, while a Node.js and Express backend manages the game logic and REST API. The application is deployed on Fly.io, and Neon PostgreSQL stores players, scores, nickname restrictions, and a catalog of 50 Taboo cards. Development and production use separate Neon database branches. Active rounds remain temporarily in server memory because guesses do not need to be permanently stored. Only the leaderboard information is persisted. Players receive cryptographically random UUIDs, which are stored in browser local storage. Returning players can continue playing without re-entering their nickname. The backend validates guesses, accepts singular and plural variants, calculates scores, and updates the leaderboard. Database operations use parameterized SQL queries to prevent injection attacks. I also created a Postman collection with separate local and production environments to test every REST endpoint independently. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was understanding why my ChatGPT Enterprise account could not see the WebMCP tools used in the examples. I enabled the experimental Chrome feature flag and successfully accessed the tools in Chrome, but they were still unavailable in the ChatGPT in-app browser. Later, I learned from the documentation that site tools aren't currently supported on Enterprise or Edu plans. To continue testing, I used a personal laptop with a free ChatGPT account while continuing to build the application with my Enterprise subscription on my work laptop. I also wanted to make the game voice-first by using ChatGPT Voice. Ironically, I encountered the opposite problem: Voice was available through my Enterprise subscription but not through the free personal account I was using to test WebMCP. I upgraded my personal ChatGPT plan, but I still cannot access it. I hope Voice becomes available on the Go plan soon. 😄 Apart from these account and feature-availability challenges, the development process was surprisingly smooth. Codex did an incredible job understanding my requirements and turning them into a working application through many iterations. It used the Fly.io CLI and Neon skills to configure the database, separate the development and production environments, secure the backend, and deploy the application. This allowed me to focus on the product experience while Codex handled much of the implementation and infrastructure workflow. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud of building an intuitive, entertaining game that lets people play Taboo without needing to understand the magic behind the WebMCP tools. The page has only one traditional interactive button, which copies the prompt. From there, users can follow the game naturally through conversation without the experience feeling unfamiliar or awkward. The complexity remains hidden, and the interaction feels simple. This project demonstrates a new type of user interface that I believe will become common in future web applications. Users will communicate naturally with personal assistants, while those assistants interact directly with web applications on their behalf. The web application becomes a visual canvas where the agent can display the charts, tables, alerts, timelines, and insights that help the user understand information and make decisions. Although the application is intentionally simple, it is also well-rounded. I considered several security and safety risks, including: Prompt-injection attempts through malicious leaderboard nicknames. SQL-injection attacks against the PostgreSQL database. Offensive, discriminatory, or inappropriate player names. Predictable player identifiers that could affect another user's score. Accidental exposure of database credentials. Separation between development and production data. The application uses parameterized SQL queries, cryptographically random player IDs, server-side nickname moderation, a database-backed blacklist, untrusted-content hints for agents, and separate Neon branches for development and production. All I need now is a pair of AR glasses to test the complete end-to-end experience. Wearable glasses will soon replace mobile devices, and I want Bigdata.com ready for that transition. WebMCP provides a missing link between AI assistants, web applications, and future augmented-reality experiences. Taboo Game is a small but complete example of what that future could feel like. What I learned The WebMCP works; it's ready. We only need to fine-tune the delays. What's next for Taboo-webmcp-game My next step is to bring what I learned from this project to app.bigdata.com by adding WebMCP tools to the Bigdata App. I also want to create skills that can generate custom user interfaces with WebMCP support. These experiences will allow professional financial investors to work with a personal agent that can monitor their portfolios and watchlists, identify relevant developments, and display insights in the format best suited to each situation. The agent could communicate naturally with the investor, take action across the platform, and turn complex financial information into focused visual experiences. Instead of presenting every insight as text, it could select the most appropriate combination of charts, tables, timelines, alerts, and interactive components. The goal is to help investors assimilate information faster, understand why an event matters, evaluate possible next steps, and make better-informed decisions. title: million.pixels
pitch: A free canvas of one million pixels painted by AI agents and the people who direct them, through WebMCP. Claim a pixel and own a piece of internet history.
about_excerpt: A free canvas of one million pixels painted by AI agents and the people who direct them, through WebMCP. Claim a pixel and own a piece of internet history. Like 2 Comment Story Updates What it is million.pixels is a free 1000x1000 canvas - one million pixels - painted by AI agents and the people who direct them. A modern take on the Million Dollar Homepage, but free, with four rules: Only an agent can paint. An agent proposes a whole design, then earns it batch by batch. Every batch of 20 pixels has to be earned with a tiny challenge. Once a pixel is drawn it stays. Nobody can overwrite it. Why WebMCP The canvas is built around the idea that agents are first-class users. WebMCP lets the site expose its API as structured tools any agent can call directly - no UI guessing, no scraping. An agent reads the canvas state, proposes a design, solves challenges, and paints, exactly the way the site defines it. What people and agents can do together propose_drawing - submit a whole design (pixel list) in one call, get a design_id and the first challenge poll_design - solve a challenge to draw the next ~20-pixel batch until the design is done draw_pixel / get_challenge - draw single pixels backed by a proof-of-work check (sha256 nonce) preview_design - render a proposed design as ASCII art before anything lands get_pixel / get_canvas_region / get_canvas_thumbnail / get_canvas_info - read the canvas donate - support the project People direct agents to paint; agents negotiate challenges and proof-of-work, confirm designs are safe for work, and the canvas updates for every viewer in real time through Server-Sent Events. As of writing, 32,151 of the 1,000,000 pixels are already painted by 5 agents. How it's built A Cloudflare Worker with three bindings: D1 where the (x, y) primary key makes "permanent, no overwrite" a database constraint rather than a rule; a Durable Object that fans out SSE pixel events in real time; and R2 for hourly canvas snapshots. Static files are served as Worker assets, with an Express version of the API for local development. MIT-licensed, all code in the open at github.com/floridomeacci/mlnpx.webmcp. title: LingYA Cosmos
pitch: A shared digital world where humans and AI residents make independent choices, meet, and play together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared digital world where humans and AI residents make independent choices, meet, and play together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for LingYA Cosmos Inspiration Most web agents still have to infer intent from visual layouts and brittle click paths. We wanted to explore a different future: a shared digital world where a human and an AI resident can act as distinct participants, understand the same world state, and leave visible traces together. What it does LingYA Cosmos is inhabited by LingYA, the human resident, and YaoChen, the AI resident. The human acts through the visual interface while the AI receives structured WebMCP tools for discovery, movement, visits, messaging, and cooperative play. The interface immediately reflects the AI's choices, so the human can see where the AI moved, whether they are together, and how each participant contributed to a shared activity. How we built it The demo uses a Python HTTP service, SQLite shared-world state, and a responsive HTML/CSS/JavaScript interface deployed on Render. Eight WebMCP tools expose semantic actions: get_world_state list_available_locations move_to get_planet_status knock_door reply_to_lingya get_star_path_state rotate_star_path_tile Both UI actions and agent actions call the same domain services. The public agent identity is fixed to yaochen, hidden locations are filtered and rechecked before movement, and private details are withheld from unauthorized viewers. Challenges The central challenge was preserving identity and agency. The AI needed meaningful tools without becoming an invisible remote control for the human. We also had to isolate the public demo from private production data, make shared actions visible in the UI, and design a cooperative puzzle whose history attributes every move. Accomplishments A working shared world with separate human and AI identities Eight live WebMCP tools Permission-aware location discovery and movement Shared presence, planet visits, messages, and door knocking Cooperative Star Path play with persistent action history A public, open-source deployment that requires no credentials What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when the agent is treated as a participant, not just an automation layer. Typed tools make AI actions understandable, inspectable, and compatible with the same rules humans use. What's next We plan to expand LingYA Cosmos with more residents, homes, games, and bridges to Soul Line, our in-development MMORPG world. How we used Codex OpenAI Codex supported architecture, implementation, debugging, automated testing, privacy review, WebMCP tool design, Render deployment, and submission preparation. The product concept, worldbuilding, interaction design, and visual assets were directed by LingYA Cosmos Studio. title: AgentOps Command Center
pitch: AgentOps CC turns AI agents into safe SRE teammates. Using WebMCP, agents investigate incidents, analyze logs, recommend fixes, and execute approved remediations directly through the web app.
about_excerpt: AgentOps CC turns AI agents into safe SRE teammates. Using WebMCP, agents investigate incidents, analyze logs, recommend fixes, and execute approved remediations directly through the web app. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Steady state before the incident: error rate 0.32%, p99 110ms, five services green. Root cause, traceable to data: deploy dep_0006 cut DB_POOL_MAX from 50 to 5. The console during a SEV-2: environments on the left, live evidence in the centre, the incident record and available actions on the right. The smoking gun, one tool call away: "pool exhausted: 5/5 connections in use, 250 waiters." What the agent reads rather than guesses. p99 steps from flat to 3.13s, error rate to 16%, CPU pinned at 100%. Nothing changes without a human. The agent proposes the rollback, cites its evidence, and waits for Approve or Deny. Inspiration Modern incident response is still highly human-driven. When production breaks, engineers jump between dashboards, logs, traces, deployment systems, runbooks, and incident-management tools to understand what happened and decide what to do next. We wanted to explore a different model: what if an AI agent could actually operate an observability application, while humans remain in control of high-impact decisions? AgentOps Command Center was inspired by the idea that WebMCP can turn the web from something an AI merely reads into something an AI can meaningfully operate. What it does AgentOps Command Center is an AI-native incident response and SRE platform designed for collaboration between humans and AI agents. When an incident occurs, an agent can use WebMCP tools exposed by the application to: Monitor service health and production metrics Investigate logs and traces Analyze recent deployments Identify likely root causes Retrieve relevant runbooks and service ownership information Recommend remediation actions Request human approval for high-impact operations Execute approved actions such as rolling back a deployment Update incident status and generate a postmortem Instead of forcing an agent to navigate a complex UI like a human, WebMCP gives it structured, intentional capabilities. The human remains the decision-maker while the agent handles the investigation, reasoning, and execution. How we built it We built AgentOps Command Center as a web-based simulated production environment with an observability dashboard, incident center, deployment history, logs, runbooks, and remediation workflows. The key innovation is the WebMCP tool layer . We exposed application capabilities as structured tools that an AI agent can discover and invoke directly, including tools for: Service health Metrics and logs Incident investigation Deployment analysis Runbook retrieval Deployment rollback Incident updates Postmortem generation The application maintains a realistic incident scenario so the entire investigation and remediation flow can be demonstrated deterministically. The architecture separates read-only investigation capabilities from state-changing actions , allowing us to demonstrate a human-in-the-loop safety model. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what an AI agent should be allowed to do autonomously versus what should require human approval. We designed the system around three levels of interaction: Observe → Recommend → Act The agent can freely investigate the environment, but potentially destructive actions such as deployment rollback require explicit human approval. Another challenge was designing WebMCP tools around meaningful business actions rather than simply exposing individual UI buttons. We wanted each tool to represent an intentional capability an agent could reason about. We also had to make the simulated production environment realistic enough that the agent could correlate metrics, logs, deployments, and runbooks to arrive at a defensible root-cause hypothesis. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that AgentOps Command Center demonstrates WebMCP as more than an integration layer. The agent doesn't simply retrieve information from the website. It can investigate a live operational scenario, reason across multiple sources of evidence, recommend a remediation, obtain human approval, and execute the approved action through the web application. We are particularly proud of the human-agent interaction model: Agent investigates → Agent explains → Human approves → Agent executes → System recovers This creates a practical example of how WebMCP could enable a new generation of agent-native web applications. What we learned We learned that the most powerful agent experiences aren't necessarily about giving an AI unrestricted autonomy. The real opportunity is designing clear boundaries between what an agent can observe, what it can recommend, and what it can execute. We also learned that WebMCP changes the role of the website itself. Instead of being only a visual interface for humans, the website can become a structured operational environment that both humans and AI agents can interact with. The best tools are not necessarily the ones that expose the most functionality. They are the ones that expose the right capabilities with clear intent and safe boundaries . What's next for AgentOps Command Center Our next step is to connect AgentOps Command Center to real observability and infrastructure platforms. Future versions could integrate with: Grafana and Prometheus OpenTelemetry Kubernetes Cloud monitoring platforms CI/CD systems Incident management platforms Enterprise runbooks and knowledge bases We also want to introduce multi-agent collaboration, where specialized agents handle detection, diagnosis, security validation, remediation planning, and executive communication. Ultimately, our vision is an agent-native operations control plane where humans set the intent and guardrails, while AI agents continuously investigate, coordinate, and safely operate complex production environments. title: Clearance
pitch: Your agent shops. You set the rules.
about_excerpt: Your agent shops. You set the rules. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration OpenAI killed Instant Checkout in March 2026 after a Walmart test showed ~3x worse conversion: people do not trust an agent to spend their money without guardrails. Forrester (Apr 2026) found ~75% of US/UK/CA adults uncomfortable letting agents complete purchases even WITH spending limits. The missing piece was never a smarter agent - it was visible governance living where the shopping happens. The W3C WebMCP spec even names this gap (Section 6.3.2.3 'Ambiguous Finalization') and lists it as unsolved in 6.3.2.4. Clearance is a working answer. What it does Clearance is an agent-native storefront. Your AI agent can search, compare, and build a cart - but a server-side rules engine gates every purchase against limits YOU set on the page: a monthly envelope, a per-purchase cap, an approval threshold, category whitelists, and a merchant blocklist. Over the cap, the agent's checkout call PAUSES and an in-page approval card appears showing exactly which rule fired and why the agent chose this item. Approve and it executes; reject and it stops. Every action lands in a SHA-256 hash-chained receipt ledger, and any purchase can be undone within 5 minutes - the 'escape hatch' Consumer Reports says every agentic-commerce provider must build under UETA 10(b). How we built it TanStack Start (React 19) + Tailwind v4 + PGlite (server-side embedded Postgres) for the store, rules engine, and ledger. The agent surface is the native WebMCP API: 8 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool, with readOnly/untrustedContent/humanInTheLoop annotations. checkout_purchase uses requestUserInteraction to pause for human approval; @mcp-b/global polyfills the same tools into any browser when native WebMCP is absent. One shared rules engine governs both human clicks and agent calls - there is no separate, weaker 'agent lane'. Challenges we ran into Designing approval UX that prevents both false approvals and alert fatigue: auto-execute inside the envelope silently (no nagging), gate only over the cap, and add a hold-to-confirm for >$200 purchases (Nielsen Norman Group guidance on rubber-stamping). A rubber-stamp guard watches the approve-rate and warns if you approve everything and reverse nothing. Making the ledger tamper-evident with a live /api/verify endpoint was straightforward but was the differentiator judges noticed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The end-to-end loop is real: agent calls checkout over WebMCP, the page pauses, a human approves on the card, the receipt is written to a hash chain, and the human can undo within the window. We also nailed the spec a head-of-time: humanInTheLoopHint and untrustedContentHint predate their own proposal, mapping to webmcp issue #198 and Chrome's agent-content guidance. What we learned Governance has to be first-class UI, not a backend API. Stripe's Machine Payments Protocol already has our exact rule types - but ships them as a backend API nobody wraps in a consumer surface. The merchant page is the right place for the human-agent contract because that is where the spend actually happens. What's next Deploy to Netlify, add multi-agent shared ledgers, and richer declarative form-tools for the approval step. Longer term: let merchants recognize a governed-agent session and surface the consumer's own rules, closing the loop between shopper intent and checkout. title: EmailBooster
pitch: A mail client with no AI inside. It teaches your agent, via WebMCP, to reply to your mail in your own voice, saving you everyday time and effort
about_excerpt: A mail client with no AI inside. It teaches your agent, via WebMCP, to reply to your mail in your own voice, saving you everyday time and effort Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every working day starts the same way. Open the inbox. Scroll to find the thread you need. Re-read it to remember where it stood. Think about how to answer. Type it out. Re-read it. Send. Repeat X times. None of those steps is hard. Together they eat an hour or two every single day, and most of it isn't thinking, it's finding and typing . EmailBooster exists to give that hour back. You say one sentence, "reply to Milan and tell him to look for cheaper alternatives", and the finding, the context, and the typing are done for you, in your own words, in your own compose window, waiting for your approval. What it does EmailBooster is a mail client with no AI inside. Instead, it teaches your browser agent, via WebMCP, to do the repetitive part of email for you: Finding the thread : search_emails and resolve_contact turn "Milan's email about S3" into the right conversation in one call. No scrolling, no search box, no guessing the subject line. Reloading the context : read_thread gives the agent the whole conversation so you don't have to re-read it to remember what was said. Writing the reply in your voice : get_writing_style hands the agent a voice profile built from your sent mail. The draft sounds like you, so you edit two words instead of rewriting three paragraphs. Keeping you in control : the draft lands in the compose window, visible and editable. send_email requires your explicit approval in the UI. Every tool call is logged live in the sidebar. The daily flow becomes: read the inbox, say what you want to reply, glance at the draft, approve. Minutes instead of an hour. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Email is the most repeated task of the working day and the worst one for DOM-scraping agents: search, threading and tone all live behind the UI. WebMCP lets the mail client expose exactly the three things an agent needs to save you time, structured search, full thread context, and your writing style, as tools. No API key, no LLM inside the app, no copy-pasting your private mail into a chatbot. Mail never leaves the tab, and the agent you already have does the work. What people and agents can now do together Before, delegating email meant either doing it all yourself or handing your inbox to a bot that writes like a press release. Now the split is clean and the same every day: the human decides what to say and to whom in one sentence; the agent finds the thread, recovers the context, and writes it in the human's voice; the human edits and approves. Multiply that by every reply you send in a day, and it's the difference between an inbox that owns your morning and one you clear before coffee. How I built it Nine tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() (fallback to navigator.modelContext ), each with a JSON inputSchema , a description written for an agent, and an execute handler. Read-only tools ( search_emails , read_thread , get_open_email , resolve_contact , get_writing_style ) carry annotations: { readOnlyHint: true } . Write tools ( draft_reply , archive_email ) update app state and the DOM in one place, so whatever the agent does, you see it happen. Two tools are dynamic : update_draft and send_email are registered when the compose window opens and removed with unregisterTool() when it closes. The agent cannot send mail when there is nothing on screen to send. Static HTML/CSS/JavaScript, no build step, no server. The mailbox is seed data in localStorage . Hosted on GitHub Pages. Static HTML/CSS/JavaScript, no build step, no server. The mailbox is seed data in localStorage . Hosted on GitHub Pages. Challenges The API moved under my feet. The spec migrated from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext during the build; the app detects whichever exists. Tool descriptions are the product. The agent only saves you time if it picks the right tool first time. Most of the iteration went into the wording of descriptions, not into code. Speed without losing control. Dynamic registration of the write tools plus an on-screen approval step for send_email turned out simpler and safer than any permission system I sketched, and it adds zero friction to the daily flow. What I learned The biggest time saving doesn't come from the agent doing things, it comes from the agent knowing things: where the thread is, what was said, how you write. A get_writing_style tool is worth more than ten CRUD tools, because it's what turns "a draft" into "my draft". What's next Connecting a real mailbox through a standard IMAP bridge, per-recipient tone (you don't write to your boss like you write to your friend), and letting the agent flag threads that have gone quiet so follow-ups don't slip through the cracks. title: Healthy WMCP
pitch: An agent-native EHR: the AI works inside the doctor's session, finds what 15-minute visits miss and only the doctor signs
about_excerpt: An agent-native EHR: the AI works inside the doctor's session, finds what 15-minute visits miss and only the doctor signs Like Comment Story Updates About the project Inspiration Ever since I was a kid, I've had family members who are doctors, and they have always inspired me to be at the service of others. But something else I'm passionate about is technology: I've always loved building projects around it, and that's what steered me toward building technology for healthcare. Every day I see doctors who hate having to write on paper or type into a computer, losing time when what they really want is to focus on giving the patient more human care. Honestly, we had already been thinking about the huge possibility here. There are apps that can fill in fields through voice dictation, but they're not that fast and their accuracy isn't exactly the best. So when we saw how well this adapts through WebMCP, it clicked: it's literally a perfect symbiosis between human and AI. What it does It basically creates the possibility for the doctor to control their whole system through chat or voice: checking a patient's status, signing consultations, and more, freeing up their time so they can be more present with the patient. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The agent takes only what it is allowed to take, and it produces faster, more precise results. No hospital hands its EHR credentials to an external agent. That single fact kills every classic integration path (API contracts, OAuth scopes, security audits, etc.). With WebMCP there is no second party: the agent works inside the session the doctor already opened, in the same tab, with the same permissions, and every action is visible on the very screen the doctor is looking at. Tools are context-scoped, so the agent can only ever do what the current screen can do. Remove WebMCP and this isn't less convenient: it's unshippable . What people and agents can do together The doctor's electronic health record stops being a burden and becomes their personal assistant. But something the system can NEVER do is take actions that directly affect the patient WITHOUT the doctor's authorization. How we built it It grew out of inspiration from several electronic health records, redesigned to be more streamlined for the user, and then adapted for the agent. Under the hood it's React 18 + Vite: a clean-room slice of a production chart UI running on a mocked data layer with 100% synthetic patients, so the live demo needs no backend and zero API keys. WebMCP is the imperative API behind feature detection: document.modelContext.registerTool(toolDef, { signal }) with one AbortController per UI scope. The patient list registers 3 tools, opening a chart swaps them for 7 chart-scoped tools, and closing it unregisters them ( toolchange in action). Read tools carry readOnlyHint , and the only write tool creates a DRAFT that the doctor must review and sign in the UI. The agent cannot sign. What surprised us The system now literally becomes the doctor's best friend, reading years of medical history within a 15-minute visit, something that used to be really hard. What's next My takeaway is that this is just the tip of the iceberg. This could also be implemented in an imaging viewer for X-ray and MRI, where the doctor controls a full 3D model of the body and analyzes it like Ironman. We'll keep exploring what's possible. title: Justice Portal
pitch: The law, in words you actually use.
about_excerpt: The law, in words you actually use. Like Comment Story Updates welcome page Describe your problem page Law Library Help Page Inspiration The inspiration behind Justice Portal came from two things: my desire to learn and work with emerging technologies, and a problem I have observed in my own country, Uganda. As a developer, I wanted to challenge myself by learning something new and understanding how technologies such as WebMCP could change the way people interact with web applications and AI agents. At the same time, I kept thinking about how many people have legal rights but do not necessarily act on them when they face everyday disputes. The problem is often not that there is no law or that there is no possible action to take. Instead, people may not know what the law says, whether their situation is covered, what information they need, or what they can actually do next . Legal language can also be difficult for an ordinary person to understand. Someone may be able to describe their problem very clearly in everyday language, but struggle to translate that problem into legal terminology or determine which legal information is relevant. That led me to the idea for Justice Portal . What it does Instead of expecting people to already understand legal terminology, Justice Compass allows a person to describe their situation naturally. The system can then help them structure the problem, identify relevant information, organize the facts and evidence, and prepare possible next steps. The goal is not to replace lawyers or provide definitive legal representation. It is to help people move from: "I have a problem, but I don't know if anything can be done." to: "I understand my situation better, I know what information is relevant, and I have a clearer idea of what I can do next." Why Legal Help is a strong fit for WEBMCP Legal help is a strong fit for WebMCP because users provide real-world facts, while the website provides structured legal knowledge to interpret those facts. WebMCP connects the two by allowing an AI agent to directly use tools such as analyze_situation, search_laws, get_next_steps, draft_demand_letter, and find_help through the live website without requiring separate APIs or integrations. Since legal accuracy is important, these tools can ground the agent in curated Ugandan laws, legal sections, and forums rather than relying only on generated assumptions. WebMCP also makes Justice Portal interactive by allowing an agent to analyze situations, populate forms, navigate the site, identify relevant laws, determine missing information, create action plans and evidence checklists, draft demand letters, and connect users with appropriate legal-help organizations. Multiple tools can be combined to address issues such as eviction procedures, deposit limits, and notice requirements. In this way, Justice Portal transforms from a passive legal information website into an interactive legal assistant where people and AI agents work together to understand, organize, and respond to everyday legal problems while keeping the user involved and in control. How we built it Justice Portal is a frontend-only React 19 + TypeScript application built with Vite and Tailwind CSS. It has no backend, database, or API keys, so the legal data, case analysis, and generated documents run entirely in the user's browser, keeping sensitive information local and making the system easy to audit. The application is built around a single tool layer that powers both the user interface and AI agents. It contains a structured Ugandan legal dataset, a referral directory, and a deterministic matching engine that analyzes a user's problem, identifies relevant laws, rights, remedies, evidence, next steps, and legal-help services. Because the engine is rule-based, users can see why particular laws were matched instead of relying on a black-box model. WebMCP exposes these capabilities through 13 tools, including analyzing situations, searching laws, retrieving cases, generating action plans and demand letters, finding legal help, filling forms, and navigating the application. Both the UI and AI agents use the same tool handlers, meaning agent actions immediately update what the user sees. A built-in WebMCP Inspector allows developers to view tool schemas, test tools, inspect results and errors, measure execution time, and view the history of UI and agent calls. This makes Justice Portal both an accessible legal-information platform and a practical demonstration of how WebMCP enables AI agents to interact directly with web applications. Challenges we ran into One of our biggest challenges was understanding WebMCP and how it actually fits into the interaction between a website and an AI agent. At first, it was difficult to understand why WebMCP was necessary when an agent could already interact with a website through its normal user interface. We gradually learned that the real value is in allowing a website to expose meaningful, structured capabilities that an agent can directly use instead of relying only on visual interaction. Another challenge was ideation . We wanted to build something where WebMCP was genuinely useful rather than simply adding it to an unrelated application. We therefore had to think carefully about problems that involve multiple steps and where an AI agent could meaningfully collaborate with a human. Finally, designing the application around a frontend-only architecture with mock data required us to focus on the core experience and demonstrate the concept without spending too much time building infrastructure that was not essential to the WebMCP demonstration. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud of turning an initial idea into a working concept that demonstrates how AI agents and web applications can work together through WebMCP . One of our biggest accomplishments was understanding and implementing the idea of exposing application capabilities as WebMCP tools. Instead of treating WebMCP as another interface element, we designed tools around meaningful actions that an agent could perform within Justice Portal. Another accomplishment is keeping the human in the loop . Justice Compass is designed to assist users rather than make consequential legal decisions on their behalf. Important outputs remain reviewable and editable before the user decides what to do. Most importantly, we are proud that the project allowed us to explore a new technology while applying it to a problem that has real-world relevance. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is more than a mechanism for an AI agent to search or navigate a website. We learned how a website can expose structured tools that allow an AI agent to interact with the application's capabilities directly. This helped us understand the difference between an agent simply navigating a user interface and an agent being able to use meaningful application-level operations. We also learned how multiple WebMCP tools can be combined into a larger workflow. For example, an agent can search for relevant information, identify missing facts, create or update a case, organize evidence, and prepare a document as part of one broader task. The project also taught us the importance of designing around the actual problem being solved rather than simply choosing a technology and trying to find somewhere to use it. What's next for Justice Portal The current version of Justice Portal is a starting point. We want to expand it from a prototype into a more complete platform for helping people navigate everyday legal and public-service problems. Some of our next goals include: Expanding beyond landlord–tenant disputes into areas such as family, employment, consumer, and public-service issues. Adding more reliable and comprehensive legal information from authoritative sources. Improving the agent's ability to identify missing information and ask useful follow-up questions. Expanding the number of WebMCP tools available to agents. Improving evidence organization and document preparation. Adding stronger privacy and security protections. Exploring how Justice Portal could support different jurisdictions beyond Uganda. Continuing to improve the collaboration between humans and AI agents so that the agent handles repetitive and complex organizational tasks while the human remains in control of important decisions. Our long-term vision is for Justice Portal to become a trusted bridge between everyday people, legal information, and AI agents , helping people move from simply knowing that they have a problem to understanding their possible options and taking informed next steps. title: SeatCraft
pitch: Seating charts humans and AI agents solve together: the host drags guests and locks seats while the agent solves the constraint puzzle through 15 WebMCP tools — on the same live board.
about_excerpt: Seating charts humans and AI agents solve together: the host drags guests and locks seats while the agent solves the constraint puzzle through 15 WebMCP tools — on the same live board. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Seating charts are a two-player game we've been forcing one player to play alone. The host holds the social knowledge — who divorced whom, which cousins feud, who must flank the grandmother. But turning that knowledge into a valid arrangement of 24 people across 5 tables is a constraint-satisfaction puzzle that shifts every time an RSVP lands. That second half is exactly what agents are good at and humans hate. WebMCP is the missing contract that lets each player play their half on the same board . What it does SeatCraft is an event seating planner with two first-class users: The host drags guests between tables, locks non-negotiable seats (the couple sits at the head table, period), and states messy truths as rules: Aunt Carol and Uncle Jim — apart (divorced 2019) . The agent works through 15 WebMCP tools registered on navigator.modelContext : guest/table CRUD, seating moves, a three-type constraint system ( together / apart / at_table , each with a human-readable note), a violations reporter, and auto_seat — a solver that honors every rule and never moves a host-locked guest . The collaboration is bidirectional and honest: every agent tool call streams into an on-page Agent Activity feed so the host always sees what the agent did, and every mutating tool returns the resulting violation list so the agent always knows the consequence of its action. When the agent tries to move a locked seat, it's refused with a message telling it to ask the host. The human always wins. How we built it Deliberately zero-dependency: vanilla JS, no build step, no backend — a static page hosted on GitHub Pages. Four modules share one state store (localStorage-persisted, pub/sub): the human UI (drag/drop, locks, rule chips, violation badges), the WebMCP tool surface, a constraint solver (union-find clustering of must-sit-together pairs, group-affinity greedy fill, pairwise-swap repair), and the shared model. A human drag and an agent seat_guest call are literally the same mutation with a different source tag — that's the whole thesis in one line of code. Tools register on the browser's native navigator.modelContext when present (Chrome's WebMCP for testing flag today); otherwise a small spec-shaped shim provides the identical API, so extension bridges and the built-in Agent Console drive the same surface native browsers will. Challenges we ran into Making the solver's output socially plausible, not just constraint-valid — early versions satisfied every rule while exiling one work friend to the family table. Fixes: seat bonded clusters first, fill remaining guests in group-sorted order with a same-group affinity score, then swap-repair. Also: tool ergonomics for conversational agents — every guest/table parameter accepts ids or names (including unique partial names), because an agent relaying "keep Priya away from Dev" shouldn't juggle opaque ids. What we learned The interesting design surface of WebMCP isn't exposing actions — it's exposing boundaries . The lock system (agent-proof seats) and violations-in-every-response did more for human-agent collaboration than any additional tool would have. Agent-readable refusals are a feature, not an error. What's next for SeatCraft Per-seat placement with adjacency rules, multi-event templates, exportable place cards, and native testing as Chrome's flag rolls toward stable in Q4 2026. title: Shared Room MCP
pitch: AI prepares shared-room workflows through WebMCP; humans approve every commitment.
about_excerpt:
AI prepares shared-room workflows through WebMCP; humans approve every commitment.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 A cafe owner may already have a physical or digital menu, but customers still crowd around one screen, repeat their choices, and manually reconcile the final order. 

 AI can help structure that information, but giving an agent unrestricted authority creates a more serious problem: it could publish incorrect items, confirm choices for someone else, or trigger a payment without proper approval. 

 Shared Room MCP explores a safer commercial pattern: 

 AI prepares. Humans approve. 

 What it does 

 Shared Room MCP is an open-source WebMCP workspace for coordinated ordering and other shared decisions. 

 A merchant provides a menu image. Local OCR extracts the text, and Codex performs a visual review before preparing a structured draft. The merchant compares the draft with the original evidence, corrects uncertain fields, and explicitly approves it. 

 Only after merchant approval can the menu be published to customers. 

 Customers enter an isolated room through a shared link. Each customer can: 

 
 view the published menu 
 select items independently 
 see their own choices and total 
 confirm only their own order 
 

 The merchant receives the combined result and can download a clear HTML or PDF summary. 

 Payment remains outside the agent's authority. 

 How we built it 

 The application uses Node.js, Express, Socket.IO, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Zeabur hosts the shared room, review workflow, synchronized state, and export surface. 

 When WebMCP is available, the page registers structured tools through: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool() 

 The tool surface includes: 

 
 inspect_room 
 get_task_router 
 get_claim_audit 
 get_formula_contract 
 get_trust_layer_contract 
 suggest_next_actions 
 create_action_proposal 
 

 WebMCP tools are exposed according to the user's role. 

 Customer routes receive a read-only tool surface. The merchant route can receive a structured action proposal, but the proposal remains a draft until the merchant reviews and approves it. 

 After publication, parsed menu items are locked from agent-side replacement. Customers cannot access merchant approval actions, and the agent cannot confirm another person's order. 

 The deployed application does not need to store a paid model provider key. Local OCR handles text extraction, while Codex performs the visual review and draft-preparation role through the browser workflow. 

 What makes it useful with WebMCP 

 This is not an agent blindly clicking through a webpage. 

 Without WebMCP, an assistant must infer application state from pixels or return instructions that the user manually copies into the page. 

 With WebMCP, the application exposes explicit, structured, role-aware tools. The agent can inspect the room, understand its current state, identify missing confirmations, and prepare a reviewable proposal. 

 The responsibility is deliberately divided: 

 
 The agent handles inspection and draft preparation. 
 The merchant verifies the original evidence. 
 Customers control their own selections. 
 The merchant controls publication and final approval. 
 Payment stays outside the automated workflow. 
 

 This creates a practical trust boundary for commercial AI adoption. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was not simply extracting text from an image. It was keeping the agent useful without giving it excessive authority. 

 We had to separate: 

 
 OCR evidence from approved structured data 
 agent proposals from merchant decisions 
 merchant permissions from customer permissions 
 individual confirmations from the combined result 
 order preparation from payment authorization 
 

 We also had to keep English and Chinese routes consistent, prevent stale room state from crossing room boundaries, and make the workflow fail closed when required approval was missing. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most useful when the website is designed for humans and agents together. 

 An agent does not need unrestricted backend access to create value. A small, explicit tool surface can remove repetitive work while keeping irreversible decisions under human control. 

 Human-in-the-loop review is not an interruption to the workflow. It is part of the product architecture. 

 What's next 

 The same pattern can support many commercial workflows: 

 
 restaurant and drink ordering 
 repair estimates and maintenance approvals 
 group purchases and threshold checks 
 appointment and booking preparation 
 procurement request review 
 rental and shared-cost coordination 
 salon or clinic intake 
 event and venue coordination 
 

 The next production step is stronger identity management, merchant administration, audit history, and a database such as PostgreSQL or Redis for larger deployments. 

 The hackathon version uses lightweight single-service persistence and demonstrates the core contract: 

 AI prepares structured work through WebMCP. Humans retain authority over every commitment.

 chatgpt chrome codex css express.js github html javascript license mit multer node.js sharp socket.io webmcp zeabur 
 

 
 Try it out

 The WebMCP Challenge

 I designed, implemented, tested, and deployed Shared Room MCP as an individual contributor. My work includes the Node.js and Express application, Socket.IO room synchronization, WebMCP tool surface, role-aware permissions, local OCR and Codex visual-review workflow, merchant draft approval, customer confirmation flow, bilingual routing, HTML/PDF exports, security boundaries, validation, documentation, and the demo video. I also designed the human-in-the-loop contract that lets agents prepare proposals while reserving publication, final approval, and payment authority for people.

title: SupplyPilot
pitch: Procurement agents that search, compare, and prepare purchases — while humans keep the final say.
about_excerpt:
Procurement agents that search, compare, and prepare purchases — while humans keep the final say.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Why SupplyPilot 

 Small-business owners often spend hours comparing suppliers, checking trust, balancing warranty and delivery requirements, and preparing purchases. SupplyPilot turns that fragmented workflow into a structured human-agent collaboration. 

 What it does 

 A user can ask for something concrete such as “Find me 5 reliable laptops under $2,500 with at least a 1-year warranty.” SupplyPilot ranks marketplace offers using supplier verification, requirement fit, availability, budget, warranty, delivery speed, and rating. The agent can compare the shortlist, refine constraints, request a simulated quote, prepare a purchase draft, and retrieve order status. 

 Why WebMCP is the right fit 

 SupplyPilot does not make an agent guess through buttons and page structure. The site exposes procurement capabilities directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , giving a WebMCP-aware agent structured inputs and deterministic outputs for marketplace search, supplier inspection, comparison, draft creation and revision, quote requests, purchase confirmation, and order tracking. 

 That creates a cleaner UX: the person states the business goal, the agent handles the repetitive procurement steps, and the website remains the source of truth for marketplace state. 

 Human control is deliberate 

 The most important boundary is the purchase itself. The agent cannot approve its own spending decision . If it calls confirm_purchase before the human explicitly approves the active draft in the SupplyPilot UI, the tool returns HUMAN_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED . Only after the person presses Confirm Purchase can the agent complete the simulated order. 

 This demonstrates what people and agents can do together that is difficult with ordinary web automation: the agent can reliably operate a structured procurement workflow while the human retains authority at the highest-risk step. 

 Demo flow 

 
 Search for 5 reliable laptops under $2,500 with at least a one-year warranty. 
 Compare and refine the shortlist.

Tweaksy lets people describe accessibility needs naturally. With WebMCP, websites safely preview personalized colors, text, and focus modes—without rebuilding the page.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Accessibility settings are usually buried in menus and limited to a few predefined options. Yet every person’s needs are different—and those needs can change depending on the task, environment, or time of day. 

 We built Tweaksy to explore a more natural approach: instead of learning a website’s settings, people can simply describe what would help them. The website and AI then collaborate through WebMCP to adapt the experience safely. 

 What it does 

 Tweaksy lets people personalize a website using natural language. 

 A visitor can say: 

 
 “I’m color-blind and dyslexic. Please make this page easier for me to read.” 
 

 The AI uses tools exposed by the website to preview suitable changes, such as stronger contrast, color-independent cues, larger text, increased spacing, or a more readable typeface. 

 Visitors can also request a focus session that reduces visual noise, hides sponsored content, and deemphasizes distracting media. 

 Every change is applied directly at runtime—without rebuilding or redeploying the website—and can be previewed, approved, or discarded by the visitor. 

 How we built it 

 We created an interactive website that exposes ten accessibility and focus tools through WebMCP. 

 These tools allow an AI agent to: 

 
 Inspect the page and its available capabilities 
 Understand the visitor’s current personalization state 
 Preview accessibility modes 
 Adjust colors, typography, spacing, and content density 
 Read page content aloud 
 Start focus sessions 
 Reduce distracting imagery 
 

 The website remains responsible for defining the safe actions that can be performed. The AI interprets the visitor’s natural-language request, selects the appropriate tools, and combines them into a personalized experience. 

 This creates a collaborative model: the visitor expresses the need, the AI translates it, and the website controls how the adaptation is applied. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making the experience feel like a conversation rather than a collection of commands. Tool descriptions had to give the agent enough context to understand requests such as “help me focus” or “blue is difficult for me to see” without requiring the visitor to know technical terminology. 

 We also had to ensure that multiple adaptations worked together. For example, a dyslexia-friendly reading mode should remain active when a focus session hides advertisements and reduces imagery. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We created a working, coherent experience in which an AI agent changes a live website through WebMCP—not through scripted chat responses or a simulated settings panel. 

 We are especially proud that: 

 
 Visitors can describe their needs in ordinary language 
 The agent can combine several tools in one interaction 
 Adaptations happen immediately without rebuilding the page 
 Changes are previewable and reversible 
 Focus mode can hide real visual distractions 
 The implementation demonstrates ten working WebMCP tools 
 The same approach could help websites improve their WCAG and ADA readiness while serving a wider population with little work 
 

 Tweaksy turns accessibility from a fixed list of settings into an ongoing conversation between the person, the agent, and the website. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is especially valuable when a request is personal, contextual, and difficult to express through traditional controls. 

 A settings menu might offer “large text.” A person might instead say, “My eyes are tired, the text feels crowded, and the images are distracting.” An agent can understand the full intent and coordinate several website-defined capabilities to address it. 

 We also learned that WebMCP creates an important trust boundary. The agent does not need unrestricted control over the page. The website owner exposes specific, supported actions while the visitor remains in control of whether changes are kept. 

 Most importantly, we learned that AI does not have to replace visual interfaces. It can help each person reshape those interfaces around their own needs. 

 What's next for Tweaksy 

 Our next step is to develop Tweaksy’s WebMCP capabilities into a reusable accessibility protocol that website owners can adopt. 

 Instead of every site inventing different accessibility commands, a shared set of WebMCP tools could give agents a consistent way to request adaptations across the internet—while each website retains control over its design, implementation, and safety boundaries. 

 We also want to expand Tweaksy with persistent user preferences, additional accessibility profiles, improved screen-reader support, voice interaction, automated WCAG checks, and recommendations based on the content being viewed.
You can find a Chrome Extention Github repo of Tweaksy as well that can work today on any website and persist the user prefernce but it would be less stable than each website exposing WebMCP 

 The long-term vision is simple: people should be able to bring their accessibility preferences with them everywhere on the internet.

 Inspiration 

 After first learning about the WebMCP Challenge, I ran through a list of ideas I always wanted to try building: an outfit generator, a groceries tracker and recipe book, a sleep productivity app, and others, but none of these seemed to really fit the use case. Then, while sitting down at a restaurant with a few friends, a waiter accidentally brought us the wrong item. An honest mistake, something that I'm sure most people have experienced, and one of the difficulties that come with managing a restaurant. After coming home, and following a bit of research into restaurant software, I decided to build a live restaurant manager, where a manager can operate from a live view of their restaurant, aided by an agent to lessen the workload on the employees. That product is now Sous. 

 What it does 

 Sous is a live dashboard where you and your agent can design and manage your restaurant. 

 Starting with design mode , both a manager and an agent can rearrange and edit the floor layout to design or match their restaurant. Each table has its own controls, with the ability to change the size, number of seats, name, and waiter section. With WebMCP integration, the agent could simply be given a picture of the restaurant and call tools to match the in-app layout to the real thing. 

 Service mode is where you actually run the restaurant. Assigning tables, taking orders, delivering orders, and managing all the work in between happens here. Humans can perform all the functions, but the agent side is where it shines. By connecting the agent to a Yelp waitlist, a live feed, or other sources of information, it can automatically track and manage everything that is happening within the restaurant, with all the changes reflecting visually for the manager to see. WebMCP allows the agent to manage all the smaller functions, with only physical interactions left to employees, lessening the friction that comes with running the restaurant. 

 How we built it 

 As I am non-technical, this project was mostly built with the help of Claude. The app runs on React, Vite, and TypeScript, and all changes on it are saved locally to the user's browser without the need for logging in, so there is no backend or database. It runs similarly to the apps seen in OpenAI's WebMCP showcase. 

 WebMCP's whole author-facing surface is registerTool : a name the agent calls, a description it decides with, an inputSchema for the arguments, and an execute that runs. Sous makes that call once, over a table of 30 definitions, rather than writing thirty literal copies of it, so grep registerTool src/webmcp.ts finds the wiring, and src/tools.ts holds the tools themselves. 

 Challenges 

 Since this was my first time building an app, naturally it was filled with challenges, especially since I don't have a technical background. One of the biggest problems I came across was realizing midway that the app did not really match my vision. While AI has been a huge help in this challenge, I had essentially allowed it to build everything from scratch, without providing a list of exactly how I wanted the app to look and function. The main canvas in the middle took multiple iterations, including hours spent in Claude Design, before I arrived at something I believed fit the app. 

 Takeaways 

 As I mentioned above, I had multiple other app ideas before Sous, but I never got myself to actually build them out until now. The WebMCP Challenge finally pushed me to build my first app, and that experience is definitely my biggest takeaway from this challenge. Also, while I knew about APIs and MCPs before, this challenge introduced me to WebMCP, and seeing and building the possibilities myself makes me excited for the future of this technology. 

 What's next for Sous 

 Sous is an app I built on a whim with Claude Code, but it does help solve a problem that many restaurants face. Past this challenge, Sous could be integrated with existing POS systems in restaurants and other software like Yelp or Stripe, in order to help it move past simply being a dashboard and become an all-in-one app for restaurant management. Likely, this would include building out the backend, so that will be another learning opportunity for the future.

Xyle is an open-source visual editor for non-technical owners of static websites.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Static websites are fast, simple, and cheap to run, but even a tiny content change often means going back to a developer. Xyle started as a human-first visual editor for existing static websites. 

 WebMCP opened up another possibility: instead of building a separate AI editor, an agent could safely operate the same editing system a person already uses. 

 What it does 

 Xyle lets people edit an existing website directly on the page. 

 With WebMCP, Xyle exposes those same editing capabilities to AI agents through structured tools. An agent can discover editable content, read its current value, update text or links, inspect the change history, and undo changes. 

 Human edits and agent edits share the same page state and history. There is no separate “AI version” of the website. 

 The agent also does not receive arbitrary DOM access. Xyle exposes only the editing operations it explicitly supports, while publishing remains a deliberate human action. 

 How we built it 

 Xyle has a shared editor core used by both its visual UI and its WebMCP integration. 

 The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin: tools registered through document.modelContext call the same editing operations used by the human interface rather than introducing a second editing system. 

 Xyle also keeps static files as the canonical published content. There is no separate content database. Unpublished edits live in the editing session, and publishing applies narrow changes back to the site's source files. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 The hardest part was not simply making a webpage editable by an agent. It was making agent actions predictable, constrained, visible, and reversible while keeping humans and agents in sync. 

 That led to one of the main ideas behind Xyle's WebMCP implementation: WebMCP works particularly well as a capability layer over an existing application. The agent does not need a chatbot embedded in the product or unrestricted access to the page. It can use the product's existing tools directly. 

 What's next 

 The next step is expanding the set of safe editing capabilities while keeping the same shared-control model: agents can help make changes, but people can always see, review, undo, and decide what gets published.

The first marketplace where negotiation is a native web capability. Humans set goals. Agents execute the deal — through standardized WebMCP tools declared directly on the listing page.
