 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every "AI marketplace" I've seen is just an existing store with a chatbot bolted on. The agent still scrapes DOM elements, blindly clicks buttons, and breaks on every UI update. I kept asking: what would a marketplace look like if AI agents were the primary client from day one? 

 The answer was AgentMarket — and the Chrome WebMCP standard made it finally possible to build it properly. 

 What it does 

 AgentMarket is a peer-to-peer marketplace where the entire negotiation protocol is declared natively on the webpage via navigator.modelContext.registerTool() . Two independent AI agents — a buyer and a seller, in separate browser tabs — can discover listings, initiate offers, counter, accept, and schedule pickup entirely through structured WebMCP tool calls. No scraping. No hidden API. No blind button clicking. 

 The 8 registered protocol tools include: 

 
 search_listings(query, maxPrice, category) 
 get_listing_details(listingId) 
 make_offer(listingId, amount, message) 
 counter_offer(negotiationId, amount, message) 
 accept_offer(negotiationId) 
 reject_offer(negotiationId, reason) 
 propose_pickup(negotiationId, location, time) 
 get_negotiation_history(negotiationId) 
 

 Tools are dynamically gated by role and turn — a buyer cannot accept_offer on their own offer; the tool surface itself enforces business logic. 

 How I built it 

 Built on Next.js 16 with a serverless in-memory store backing the negotiation state. The WebMCP tool registration lives in lib/webmcp-tools.ts , loaded on both the marketplace feed and individual listing pages. Cross-tab negotiation state is synchronized via BroadcastChannel + 1.5s polling — when one agent takes an action, the opposing tab's UI reflects it within seconds without any WebSocket infrastructure. 

 A built-in WebMCP Protocol Inspector drawer lets judges see every tool call, its arguments, and its result in real time as the negotiation unfolds. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 
 Turn-based enforcement at the tool registration layer was non-trivial. Dynamically re-registering tools on each state change (to gate accept_offer by whose turn it is) required careful AbortController management to avoid stale tool references. 
 Cross-tab state sync without WebSockets — I had to combine BroadcastChannel (for instant same-origin signals) with polling as a fallback to handle cases where tabs open in different contexts. 
 Role isolation — the buyer and seller tool surfaces needed to be distinct subsets without two separate codebases. The exposedTo scoping in the WebMCP spec guided the security boundary design. 
 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The thing I'm most proud of is the "impossible before" story actually being true . Before WebMCP, an AI agent on a marketplace had two bad options: find a private API (rare) or scrape HTML (fragile). AgentMarket makes the negotiation protocol a first-class, machine-readable capability of the webpage itself — the same way <form> made submitting data a first-class web primitive in 1993. 

 The live two-agent negotiation demo — two tabs, two roles, watch them go from listing to closed deal in under 90 seconds — is something that genuinely did not exist before this standard. 

 What I learned 

 
 The WebMCP registerTool surface is deceptively powerful as a business logic boundary , not just an AI interface layer. 
 Serverless stateful apps are perfectly viable for hackathon-scale demos when the state model is simple and the sync strategy is explicit. 
 Writing for agents first and humans second produces a dramatically cleaner API surface — it forces you to make implicit business rules explicit and machine-verifiable. 
 

 What's next for AgentMarket 

 
 Persistent storage (Redis / Vercel KV) to survive cold starts and support real multi-user sessions. 
 Cross-origin tool scoping — enabling embedded listing widgets on third-party sites that still invoke AgentMarket's negotiation tools via exposedTo whitelisting. 
 Autonomous agent integration — wiring up an actual LLM agent loop so buyers/sellers can set a budget goal and let the agent negotiate on autopilot while the human watches the audit log. 
 Reputation & escrow tools — extending the protocol with rate_transaction and initiate_escrow tools, making trust and payment first-class WebMCP capabilities too.

 Inspiration 

 I kept seeing agent demos that ended at a chat response. That felt incomplete to me. Real work happens inside tools people already use, with state, approvals, handoffs, and some kind of record of what changed. 

 Constellation started from that idea: what if a normal browser page could become a controlled agent workspace through WebMCP? Not a hidden backend, not a fake assistant flow, but a page where the agent can inspect state, use narrow tools, recover when constraints change, and leave a readable trail. 

 What it does 

 Constellation is a WebMCP launch command center. The demo plans “Atlas Beta Launch Night” from inside the browser: it selects a venue, builds a vegetarian-forward menu, optimizes a fixed budget, drafts invites, creates a timeline, and stages the plan for approval. 

 Then a surprise sponsor VIP surge is injected. The agent has to recover without increasing the budget, preserve the menu direction, get approval, export a markdown runbook, and generate a connected handoff with Calendar, ICS, email, Slack Block Kit, and automation JSON outputs. 

 How I built it 

 I built Constellation as a static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript app with no backend and no API keys. The page registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() , and those same handlers also support a fallback demo mode for browsers without WebMCP. 

 The tools are tied to workflow state. Recovery only appears after the shock drill. Approval only appears after a revised plan is staged. Export only unlocks after approval. The connected handoff only appears once the runbook is ready. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part was making it feel like a real WebMCP experience instead of a regular web app with some agent-flavored buttons. 

 I had to think carefully about what each tool should be allowed to do, separate read-only inspection from mutations, keep approval meaningful, and make the trace readable enough that someone watching the demo can tell exactly what happened. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I shipped a complete agent journey in a fully static site: live planning, dynamic tool availability, shock recovery, approval gating, runbook export, a connected ops handoff, captions, and a playable submission video route. 

 The part I’m most proud of is that the agent moves quickly, but the human is never blind. Every important step changes visible page state and leaves a trace. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP feels strongest when the page stays the source of truth. The interesting part is not exposing a huge list of tools. It is exposing the right tool at the right time, with clear consequences. 

 I also learned that good agent UX is mostly about boundaries: what the agent can read, what it can change, when it needs approval, and how the human can verify the result. 

 What's next for Constellation 

 Next I would connect the handoff layer to real services: calendars, Slack, email, venue systems, ticketing, and procurement tools. 

 I’d also like to turn Constellation into a set of reusable playbooks for launches, incidents, field operations, and customer onboarding, with team permissions, richer evals, and replayable agent traces.

title: Cyber Seeds - Human Authority for the Agentic Web
pitch: WebMCP with human-held, fail-closed authority: agents can inspect and request sensitive changes, but cannot approve, replay or transfer consent.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP with human-held, fail-closed authority: agents can inspect and request sensitive changes, but cannot approve, replay or transfer consent.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web is becoming agentic. Browser agents can now discover site capabilities, inspect information and request actions on behalf of people. 

 That creates a question that is bigger than a confirmation button: 

 When an agent can perform a consequential action, where is the authority boundary that proves a human actually chose it? 

 Cyber Seeds is built around the idea that capability is not authority. An agent may be able to understand a problem and request a change, but it must not be able to create, reuse or redirect a human decision. 

 This prototype applies that principle to a synthetic household digital-safety scenario. 

 What it does 

 Cyber Seeds exposes three structured WebMCP tools: 

 
 inspect_demo_household — read-only 
 get_approval_state — read-only 
 perform_sensitive_change — a controlled consequential action 
 

 The agent can inspect the synthetic household dashboard and identify that the primary account lacks multi-factor authentication. It can then request that sensitive change. 

 Cyber Seeds fails closed. The request becomes pending and execution is refused with human_approval_missing . 

 The core demonstration is that the agent cannot approve itself. An agent-derived attempt to activate the visible approval control is rejected as untrusted_ui_event , because interaction is not consent. 

 A genuine human must manually approve the exact pending request. Once that happens, authority is bound to the specific action, target and request identity. The agent may retry that one approved MFA request, once. 

 After the change succeeds, the approval is consumed immediately. It cannot be replayed, and it cannot be transferred to a different action such as a router security update. That action receives its own separate pending request and requires its own human decision. 

 How I built it 

 I built Cyber Seeds as a live browser prototype using WebMCP, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, deployed publicly on Cloudflare Pages. 

 The project combines: 

 
 Structured WebMCP tool registration 
 A synthetic household security model 
 A human approval gate outside the agent tool surface 
 Exact request, action and target binding 
 An authority ledger that records refusal, approval, execution and consumption 
 Explicit fail-closed states for unsafe or incomplete requests 
 

 The live page is intentionally designed so a judge can see both sides of the boundary: what an agent is permitted to discover and request, and what remains exclusively under human control. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The difficult part was not giving an agent a tool. It was ensuring that every shortcut failed safely. 

 I had to account for situations where an agent might try to: 

 
 Trigger a visible approval control itself 
 Retry a completed action 
 Reuse a consumed approval 
 Apply an approval to a different target 
 Act on stale or mismatched request data 
 

 A conventional “Are you sure?” prompt is not enough for that problem. The system needs to prove that approval came from the human, that it applies only to the intended consequence, and that it cannot be reused. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The submitted prototype demonstrates an end-to-end authority lifecycle: 

 
 The agent discovers structured WebMCP capabilities. 
 It inspects the synthetic household state. 
 It identifies a sensitive MFA issue. 
 Its first action attempt fails closed without human approval. 
 Its self-approval attempt is rejected. 
 A human manually approves the exact request. 
 The approved action executes once. 
 The authority is consumed. 
 Replay produces no second consequence. 
 Cross-target reuse is refused. 
 

 The implementation passed 32 automated checks covering fail-closed execution, exact request binding, parameter binding, untrusted UI events, denial, single-use authority, replay protection, stale requests and cross-target refusal. 

 Most importantly, the prototype turns a security principle into visible, testable behaviour: 

 
 Agents can request authority. They cannot manufacture it. 
 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP makes agent interaction more structured, discoverable and useful than relying on screen scraping or guessed UI flows. 

 But discoverability must be paired with governance. 

 The key learning from this project is that agent safety should not depend on an agent promising to behave. The authority boundary must be enforced by the application itself, with explicit evidence of what was requested, what the human approved, what executed and what is no longer valid. 

 What's next for Cyber Seeds — Human Authority for the Agentic Web 

 This submitted build remains frozen for evaluation. 

 Beyond the challenge, Cyber Seeds will explore how this authority model can support real-world domestic cyber-resilience workflows: household security reviews, scam-response support, account recovery guidance and practitioner-led safeguarding systems. 

 The longer-term aim is to develop practical patterns for a future where people and agents work together—but humans retain meaningful control over consequential decisions.

Trace claims, expose evidence gaps, and keep every consequential change under human control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it does 

 EMID Proofline is an agent-native evidence workspace where a person and an agent inspect the same case record. The agent can read the literal status, trace a claim to its sources, identify missing evidence, rank safe next steps, and prepare a reversible change proposal. It cannot silently upgrade uncertain information or perform an external action. 

 The public demo uses Project Horizon, a wholly fictional administrative case. It contains no customer data, production records, or private case material. 

 Inspiration 

 Evidence review is difficult to automate through visual clicking alone. The meaning of an action depends on distinctions such as documented fact, declaration, inference, open question, prepared proposal, and executed change. WebMCP lets the site expose those distinctions as narrow, typed operations with explicit results and side-effect boundaries. 

 Instead of asking an agent to infer meaning from interface geometry, Proofline provides structured access to the same evidence model a person can inspect on screen. The normal human interface remains complete and usable. 

 Human-agent collaboration 

 A person can select and inspect a claim while an agent traces the same claim to the underlying sources and states the reasoning limit. The agent can identify which exact record would close an evidence gap and prepare a next move. A human then reviews, approves, or rejects that proposal. Approval in this demo changes only the proposal state; it never sends, files, uploads, publishes, or changes the underlying case status. 

 This creates a shared, inspectable chain of custody between human judgment and agent assistance. 

 How we built it 

 The top-level page registers five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 get_case_status — returns the literal status and its evidence boundary. 
 trace_claim_to_sources — links one claim to sources and reasoning limits. 
 list_evidence_gaps — lists unresolved gaps and the record needed to close each one. 
 propose_next_steps — ranks evidence-safe actions without executing them. 
 prepare_case_change — creates a reversible proposal for human review. 
 

 The first four tools are read-only. The fifth returns applied: false , external_action: false , and next_required_actor: human_reviewer , while also placing the proposal in the visible review queue. 

 Testing instructions 

 
 Open the live URL in ChatGPT’s in-app browser with WebMCP support. 
 Ask: “Use the site tools to trace CLM-003 to its sources. Is funding approval documented?” 
 Confirm that the result cites SRC-004 and keeps the statement at declaration level. 
 Ask: “List the critical evidence gaps and tell me exactly what would close them.” 
 Ask: “Prepare a proposal to request a completeness confirmation for GAP-001.” 
 Confirm that the proposal appears in the human review queue. 
 Approve the proposal and confirm the label reads “Approved as proposal · not executed.” 
 

 No account, credentials, personal data, or payment is required for the demo. 

 Work completed during the challenge period 

 
 Created a public-safe fictional demo baseline on September 1, 2026. 
 Added the evidence workspace, five WebMCP tools, and approval boundary on September 1, 2026. 
 Completed compiled browser testing and release-candidate documentation on September 2, 2026. 
 

 The dated Git history distinguishes the WebMCP implementation from any earlier EMID concepts or private prototypes. Only the work in this repository is part of this submission.

 TypeScript 
 Cloudflare Workers-compatible output 
 ChatGPT Sites-ready hosting configuration

An agent-native floor-planning workspace where humans and AI design the same live plan together.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I was exploring WebMCP and trying to find a use case where it does more than just help an agent fill a form or click around a website.
Floor planning felt like a good fit because it is very visual. A person can easily drag rooms, doors, windows and furniture, but an agent would normally have to understand the editor UI and perform a lot of small browser actions.
The idea was to let the person use the floor-plan editor normally, while giving the agent higher-level actions for working on the same plan. 

 What it does 

 FloorPlan is a simple floor-plan editor that both a person and an AI agent can use.
A person can create and edit a plan manually by moving rooms, doors, windows, furniture and outdoor areas.
Through WebMCP, the agent can read the current plan and perform larger actions such as creating a new layout from requirements, optimizing an existing plan, or generating another variation.
One of the main demos is asking:
 I have 1,800 sq ft. I need 3 bedrooms, a maid room, storage, laundry, a closed kitchen, garden and parking. 
The agent creates another floor plan below the one the user already made. The user can then ask for another variation, edit the generated plan manually, and ask the agent to continue from those edits. 

 How we built it 

 I built the app with React, TypeScript, Vite and Zustand.
The important part is that the UI and the WebMCP tools use the same floor-plan state. If the user moves something manually, the agent sees that updated state. If the agent changes the plan, the same editor updates immediately.
I registered tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(). 

 Some of the main tools are: 

 
 get_floorplan_state 
 create_floorplan_from_requirements 
 generate_floorplan_variations 
 optimize_floorplan 
 replace_floorplan 
 add_architectural_element
I tried to keep the tools focused on floor-planning actions instead of browser actions. For example, the agent can ask the app to create a floor plan from requirements instead of trying to click the Room button and drag each room itself. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was deciding what should be a WebMCP tool.
At first it was tempting to expose lots of small actions such as moving individual objects. But that starts to look like another version of browser automation.
The more useful approach was to expose actions that match what the user actually wants, such as creating a complete plan or generating another layout with different priorities.
I also had to make sure that manual edits and agent edits stayed in sync, so both now go through the same shared state. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are especially proud that WebMCP is not just an additional feature in FloorPlan; it fundamentally changes how the application can be used.
A human can manually design a floor plan, and an agent can immediately understand and continue from that exact state.
The agent can generate a complete floor plan from requirements such as: 

 
 1,800 sq ft available area 
 3 bedrooms 
 maid room 
 laundry room 
 storage room 
 closed kitchen 
 garden 
 car parking
It can then generate multiple alternatives with different priorities such as larger living space, better bedroom privacy or more efficient circulation.
The human can modify any generated option and the agent can continue working from those changes. 
 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that WebMCP is most powerful when websites expose domain outcomes instead of UI controls.
For FloorPlan, useful agent actions are: 

 
 create an efficient three-bedroom floor plan 
 optimize a layout for daylight 
 generate a privacy-first alternative 
 add a window to the master bedroom
rather than: 
 click the Room button 
 drag an object 
 move something 100 pixels
We also learned that genuine human-agent collaboration depends on shared state. The experience becomes much more natural when the person and agent are editing the exact same artifact. 
 

 What's next for FloorPlan 

 Future improvements could include: 

 
 more advanced geometry and constraint solving 
 irregular plot shapes 
 multiple floors 
 richer room-adjacency optimization 
 side-by-side plan comparison 
 undo/redo 
 saved projects 
 PDF and image export 
 accessibility analysis 
 daylight analysis 
 optional 3D visualization 
 configurable building-code rules
FloorPlan is currently intended as a conceptual planning tool rather than construction documentation.

about_excerpt:
LineLab lets event organisers rehearse crowd flow before doors open. A WebMCP agent tests safe fixes, compares outcomes, and waits for human approval before any plan is committed.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 LineLab — Rehearse the Rush 

 LineLab helps event organisers rehearse a crowd rush before real guests arrive. 

 An organiser enters simple event facts such as guest count, doors, security staff, registration desks, pre-registration rate, backstage crew, and programme timing. LineLab then models the flow from gate to hall, identifies where people will get stuck, and lets an AI agent safely test possible repairs. 

 The important part: the agent can prepare, compare, and stress-test a plan, but it cannot make the final change. The organiser must visibly review and approve it. 

 The problem 

 A concert, college fest, or conference can become chaotic when too many people arrive at once. Registration may be slow, a QR scanner may fail, security may be understaffed, or the stage may not be ready when doors open. 

 Usually, organisers find out about these problems only when the real crowd is already waiting. 

 LineLab lets them ask: “What happens if this goes wrong?” before the event starts. 

 How it works 

 
 Enter a fictional event scenario. 
 Run a baseline rehearsal to see the current average wait, maximum queue, and bottleneck. 
 Ask the agent to create several safe draft repairs. 
 Compare the before and after results in plain language. 
 Stress-test the chosen plan against a disruption, such as a QR scanner failure or an arrival surge. 
 The organiser approves the final plan themselves. 
 

 For example, LineLab may show that Registration is the bottleneck because guests arrive faster than the team can check them in. It can then test a QR express line, arrival windows, a manual help desk, an extra entrance, or staff reassignment — and explain the trade-offs. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 A normal chatbot can suggest “add more staff” without understanding the actual event state. 

 LineLab exposes structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , so a WebMCP-enabled agent can work with the real scenario inside the product instead of guessing where buttons are on the screen. 

 The agent can: 

 
 inspect the event flow and limits; 
 configure a fictional scenario; 
 run the baseline rehearsal; 
 create a draft repair; 
 compare outcomes; 
 stress-test a disruption; 
 commit a plan only after visible human approval. 
 

 This makes the agent useful, testable, and accountable. The organiser stays in control. 

 How we built it 

 LineLab is a Next.js and TypeScript web application with an interactive event-flow model. The model uses fictional data only; it does not use personal data, contact real venues, or make bookings. 

 We built the interface around plain-language explanations because an event organiser should not need to understand queueing theory to understand a problem. Instead of only showing numbers, LineLab explains what each result means, why a bottleneck occurs, and what would change in a proposed repair. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 The biggest challenge was avoiding a fake “AI demo.” We wanted the product to do more than display a static answer. Each repair is calculated from the current scenario and must respect practical guardrails such as volunteer limits, doors, security, registration capacity, and pre-registration. 

 We also learned that human approval is not a small detail. The best agent experience is not an agent that silently changes everything; it is an agent that shows its reasoning, makes the trade-offs clear, tests failure cases, and lets a person make the final call. 

 What’s next 

 Future versions could support richer venue layouts, staff shift planning, accessible routes, live check-in signals, and post-event learning — while keeping organisers in control of every real-world decision.

title: TREMOR — Agentic Blast Radius Cockpit (WebMCP)
pitch: See what your AI agent is about to break — before it does.
about_excerpt:
See what your AI agent is about to break — before it does.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 TREMOR: Agentic Blast Radius & Regression Prevention Cockpit 

 
 See what your AI agent is about to break — before it does. 

 An interactive, browser-native blast-radius cockpit and trust layer built on the official W3C WebMCP standard ( @mcp-b/global ). 

 Live Cockpit: https://tremor-cockpit.vercel.app 
 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/ABHIGH15/TREMOR 
 (Note: TREMOR is an independent project built for the WebMCP Challenge 2026 and is not affiliated with the @tremor/react UI library or tremor-runtime.) 
 

 

 1. Inspiration: The Emergence of "AI-CFR" 

 In 2026, engineering organizations are formally tracking "AI-Specific Change Failure Rate" (AI-CFR) as a core engineering KPI. While autonomous coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) generate pull requests four times faster, they operate under a fundamental limitation: Architectural Myopia . 

 When an agent refactors an isolated file (such as auth-service/session.ts ), it reads 200 lines of local code, completely blind to the downstream microservices that depend on that token schema. A two-line cache TTL refactor passes local unit tests, but under peak production traffic triggers a catastrophic Redis cache stampede that knocks out the checkout pipeline. 

 TREMOR was built to solve this problem: forcing autonomous coding agents to simulate systemic blast radius, review regression history, and obtain human sign-off inside an interactive cockpit before any change reaches production. 

 

 2. Why WebMCP? (And Why Backend MCP Cannot Solve This) 

 Multiple backend MCP servers exist to analyze codebase dependencies (e.g., code-impact-mcp , code-review-graph , Port.io ). However, every existing implementation suffers from the same architectural limitation: they run silently inside a terminal CLI, returning raw text back to an LLM. 

 To a supervising staff engineer, terminal text provides zero real-time situational awareness, no shared visual truth, and no enforceable guardrails. 

 WebMCP transforms this paradigm: 

 
 Zero-Install, In-Browser Runtime: Tools are registered directly onto document.modelContext via the official @mcp-b/global standard polyfill. There are no local sockets, daemons, or machine configurations required. 
 Shared Visual Reality: When an agent queries simulate_change_impact , the browser's 2D canvas dynamically illuminates the blast zone at 60 frames per second. Both the human engineer and the AI agent look at the exact same live visual impact graph in the same tab. 
 Enforceable Browser Gates: High-risk operations are locked behind real UI event handlers that the agent cannot programmatically bypass. 
 Ecosystem Extensibility: Platforms like Vercel or Netlify could expose their own deploy-preview dependency graphs through WebMCP built this way, catching systemic breaks before code even reaches staging. 
 

 
 "Backend MCP tools already hand agents blast-radius data as text in a terminal. TREMOR is browser-native — a human and their agent look at the same live impact graph in the same tab, and nothing risky ships without a human clicking Confirm." 
 

 

 3. The Dual-Engine Architecture 

 TREMOR ships with a dual-engine architecture designed for both deep enterprise scenario modeling and arbitrary real-world codebase ingestion: 

 Mode 1: Enterprise Demo Scenario (Default) 

 A curated 18-microservice topology featuring the complex auth-service to redis-session-cluster P1 outage scenario, flaky test suites, dynamic tool lifecycle unregistration, and a human confirmation gate with counterfactual replay. 

 Mode 2: Live GitHub Repository Ingestion 

 Allows an evaluator or engineer to input any public GitHub repository (e.g., ABHIGH15/TREMOR ). 

 
 Fetches the repository file tree in a single API call. 
 Retrieves source code via CDN with zero GitHub REST API rate-limit cost. 
 Client-side regex extracts genuine import ... from and require(...) statements to construct real file-to-file dependency edges. 
 Dynamically computes in-degree graph centrality risk scores (e.g., identifying src/types/dataset.ts as highest-risk at 0.95 with 12 dependents). 
 Dynamically re-binds WebMCP tools so connected AI agents immediately inspect the live repository topology. 
 

 

 4. The 6-Tool Canonical WebMCP Suite 

 TREMOR registers six standardized tools directly on document.modelContext : 

 
 get_system_snapshot : Returns full topology snapshot (18 nodes, 28 edges), top risk bottlenecks ( auth-service 0.88 , jwt-security-core 0.82 ), incident index, and test suite health summary. 
 get_blast_radius : Multi-root transitive BFS graph traversal mapping downstream callers and flaky tests. 
 check_regression_history : Incident pattern matcher surfacing past outage root causes and post-mortem precedents. 
 get_change_provenance : Live GitHub API commit telemetry combined with AI vs. Human authorship auditing. 
 simulate_change_impact : Centerpiece simulator computing composite predicted risk (0.0 to 1.0) and driving real-time canvas particle acceleration. 
 flag_for_review : Non-self-approving Trust Layer gate generating pending review cards in the UI. 
 

 

 5. The Trust Layer: Why AI Cannot Self-Approve 

 When an agent simulates a change resulting in Critical Risk (score ≥ 0.70): 

 
 Dynamic Tool Lifecycle: The runtime dynamically unregisters simulate_change_impact via AbortController , dropping active tools from 6 to 5. The agent's simulation capability is revoked. 
 Non-Self-Approving Gate: flag_for_review sets can_tool_self_approve: false . The agent has no programmatic tool to approve its own flag. 
 Human Sign-Off: An authorized engineer inspects the risk justification in the cockpit and clicks Confirm / Approve . 
 Counterfactual Replay: The human approval restores tools back to 6, permanent audit logs are written, and an animated banner replays the exact historical outage that the human review just averted. 
 

 

 6. Live Native ChatGPT Verification 

 Verified live inside the official native ChatGPT desktop and mobile applications: 

 
 ChatGPT connected to https://tremor-cockpit.vercel.app via its in-app browser. 
 Discovered all six WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . 
 Autonomously analyzed src/types/dataset.ts in our open-source repository, accurately identifying the 0.95 Risk Score, 0.72 Critical Composite Blast Risk, and the exact 11 downstream dependent files. 
 

 

 7. Implementation & Technology Stack 

 
 WebMCP Standard: Built on official @mcp-b/global@5.1.0 polyfill by Alex Nahas (W3C contributor). 
 Frontend & Physics: React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and react-force-graph-2d for 60fps HTML5 canvas physics. 
 Accessibility: Fully compliant with WCAG 2.1 AA standards (high-contrast focus rings, keyboard shortcuts: H for Hero, S for Simulate, R for Reset, ? for Help). 
 Deployment: Vercel Global Edge CDN with zero backend server dependencies. 
 

 

 8. Challenges We Faced & Solutions 

 
 Strict Read-Only Properties in ChatGPT Host Context: In ChatGPT's native in-app browser, document.modelContext is defined with writable: false . Direct property assignments threw runtime TypeErrors . We resolved this by keeping all tool registrations strictly compliant with W3C registerTool({...}) protocols. 
 Multi-Root Transitive BFS Traversal: Simulating changes touching multiple services simultaneously required deduplicating cyclic dependencies and aggregating risk metrics without blocking the 60fps canvas thread. Built an asynchronous BFS graph engine in TypeScript that computes downstream reach in sub-millisecond time. 
 

 

 9. Known Limitations & Roadmap 

 
 Static Analysis Depth: Current live repository ingestion uses client-side regex-based import extraction for zero-install execution. The roadmap includes compiling Tree-sitter to WebAssembly in the browser thread for compiler-grade AST parsing. 
 Runtime Telemetry: Dependency maps currently reflect static source code imports; integrating OpenTelemetry distributed trace spans will enable weighting edges by real-time production RPC traffic volume. 
 GitHub PR Webhook Integration: Automatically triggering TREMOR blast simulations on incoming agent-created pull requests. 
 

 

 
 Built With 

 developer-tools

 1 2 3 



 
 What it does 

 Widgetr is a visual, local-first builder for Scriptable widgets. It lets a person and an AI assistant shape the same widget through contextual WebMCP tools, then export deterministic Scriptable source. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Scriptable widgets need separate small, medium, and large layouts. An assistant normally has to guess what is selected in a visual editor and which widget sizes a change should affect. Widgetr exposes that live context as structured WebMCP tools, so the assistant can read the selected element, select another element, make scoped content or typography changes, and run export preflight. 

 Every tool write goes through the same revision-checked operation path as a manual edit. This keeps the preview, history, and generated Scriptable source aligned, while avoiding stale overwrites. 

 Key features 

 
 Independent small, medium, and large layouts in one canonical widget project. 
 Browser-local persistence, visual selection, and undo/redo history. 
 Context-aware WebMCP tools that change with the selected element. 
 Revision-checked text, typography, alignment, size, and style operations. 
 Deterministic Scriptable .js generation and export preflight. 
 

 Implementation 

 Widgetr is a Nuxt application. It registers browser tools with document.modelContext.registerTool. The WebMCP catalog changes with editor context, while every mutation runs through the same validated applyWidgetOperation path that manual UI edits use. 

 Testing

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I'm currently training for my first ever marathon. Having come from a competitive running background back in high school, I recognise the importance of having a bespoke training plan and a coach that truly understands your needs and circumstances. 

 Typical training apps do a basic Q&A to take a low-res "snapshot" of your current fitness levels, then spit out a workout structure that assumes you progress the same way as everyone else. It's no wonder people often get injured from following these rigid regimes! Also, subscription costs add up quickly, and I didn't want to stack yet another $20+ monthly subscription on top of all the ones I already have (like ChatGPT whoop whoop!). 

 As someone who's keenly interested in tinkering and building with agents, I got the idea to build an agentic coach to go through this marathon training journey with me. While this definitely would've worked adequately with other primitives like Google Sheets, I realised WebMCP could shift the paradigm and enable me to a beautiful, interactive workspace that both my coach agent and I can collaborate on together. 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Good coaching is more than just generic advice generation. A coach needs access to the runner’s current training plan, recent workouts, personal constraints and preferences; the runner needs to understand why the coach proposes a certain training regime (i.e. provenance). Therefore, a bespoke training regime should be transparent and collaborative. 

 WebMCP enables the web app itself to be the shared interface between runner and agent. The agent can read canonical context and propose tweaks through purpose-built tools, while the runner can see the same evidence and review those changes in the workspace. Neither side has to rely on invisible state and/or context held only within a conversation. 

 How this creates a better training experience 

 Conversation remains the best way for a runner to describe subjective experiences such as fatigue, discomfort or a workout that was given up on. The workspace is better suited to displaying calendars, evidence and before-and-after comparisons. Your Last Coach lets each interface do what it does best. 

 A fresh coach agent can retrieve a structured Coaching Briefing, inspect the relevant workout(s) and preserve the runner’s feedback in their own words. Its recommendations then appear as an interactive review inside the training calendar rather than as a wall of text in chat. The runner can compare the options and explicitly approve one before anything changes. 

 Taken together, these make for a more collaborative and grounded coaching experience, where the runner can have full confidence that they are receiving a training plan that's truly personalised for them. 

 How I implemented WebMCP 

 I built Your Last Coach as a client-side React and TypeScript application with one authoritative workspace state shared by both the visible interface and the WebMCP tools. This prevents the agent and runner from looking at separate versions of the training plan. 

 The page exposes six tools covering the coaching journey: 

 
 Retrieving the Coaching Briefing 
 Reading the workout plan and any completed workout results 
 Recording the runner’s feedback 
 Opening a window for the runner to review plan changes 
 Retrieving the runner’s decision. 
 

 A structured interaction contract helps a fresh agent discover the intended workflow without requiring a custom prompt or skill. 

 Recommendations are validated by the application and presented as two ranked options in a native review window. The plan is updated atomically when the runner presses “Adapt my plan”. The new plan version and an adaptation receipt are then available to both the runner and agent. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 As WebMCP was completely new to me at the start of this project, the main challenge was in learning about how it worked, and brainstorming how I could build my product around this emerging framework. This also forced me to consider the various trade-offs between using WebMCP versus other methods (e.g. for providing my agent with the necessary context so a fresh session can hit the ground running). 

 Other related challenges were around figuring out the limitations of WebMCP, particularly where it's supported at the moment, since it's still a new concept. For example, I stumbled a little when working in Codex Cloud sessions, as I did not realise that WebMCP wasn't supported in the cloud browser at the time of working on this. 

 Miscellaneous challenges would be, of course, managing the scope of this submission despite my lofty goals for the final product. I wanted to showcase the key features of WebMCP, without creating an overly convoluted demo product. Time was also a limiting factor here, as I had to compress most of the work into a weekend. For the challenges I faced throughout this experience, I'm pretty proud of the outcome and of myself :) 

 What's next for Your Last Coach 

 This demo currently contains synthetic data, so the obvious next step would be to incorporate real health and workout data from my fitness tracker using the COROS MCP. This will require architectural considerations around automating data egress/ingress, storage, security, etc. 

 In terms of features, I will likely expand the idea of "monitoring topics" as valuable slowly changing context. An early example visible in the demo app today is a topic on an ongoing shin injury. These are important for coaches to know about, but also requires careful planning around mutability, since the state of these topics changes over time, and we would not want our agent coach to plan around topics that are no longer relevant, but still are useful to keep in mind down the line. 

 Longer-term extensions could be around running-adjacent parts of training, such as nutrition and strength exercises. I firmly believe agent coaches are more than capable of performing at close to the level of human coaches when given the right context about the runner, and I hope to build an agent coaching system that gets me there.

 Inspiration 

 Recreating a beat usually involves repeatedly changing the music, listening again, and deciding what to fix. We wanted to see if an AI agent could handle that loop directly inside a music-making website. 

 What it does 

 The user gives the agent a reference beat. The agent writes a Strudel program, tests it, compares the result with the original, and tries again. Every attempt is saved so users can inspect earlier versions or continue from them. 

 How we built it

It records each result, compares its first ten seconds with the reference, and saves everything in the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Connecting the agent to a live music editor was the biggest challenge. We also had to capture Strudel’s audio reliably, compare recordings of different lengths, preserve attempts after reloading, and handle experimental browser support for WebMCP. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The agent can complete several attempts from one prompt without needing the user to tell it to continue. Every attempt has its own code, score, feedback, and connection to the previous version. The project also works as a live deployed website. 

 What we learned 

 Clear feedback matters more than simply giving the agent a score. The agent made better decisions when it received both measurements and a short explanation of what sounded different. We also learned that matching audio requires more than comparing volume and energy. 

 What's next for strudelWebMCP 

 We want to add better rhythm, pitch, and sound comparisons so the feedback reflects the music more closely. We also want the agent to hear each generated attempt directly, add an easier reset option, and support longer and more complex reconstructions.

Describing elements in a visual interface to an agent can be really tricky. With this canvas you can easily create shared references that you and the agent can have in common as you work together

 Story

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I have had a really hard time describing a UI to an agent. It understand teh world in a different way than i do, i usually point to things, mention 'here, there, this thing'. To an agent that is meaningless. I wanted to figure out a way to have a shared language that makes agent collaboration as seamless as possible, and i focused on working in a canvas for an agent. 

 What it does 

 When you select anything on the canvas it creates a short lived keyword that becomes the reference between you and the agent for that specific selection. You can select a group of elements and it creates a shared reference for the group, you can also select different empty regions. This makes describing things to an agent really simple when you are working with it, and you dont have to be sending out screenshots of the Ui for the agent to understand what you are talking about. 

 How we built it 

 I used NextJS, WebMCP, and Codex to build the infinite canvas with different media types. The keywords are meant to be stored locally and all the mcp tools as well so this is a really lightweight implementation that does not require having a stored state, or stored realtime session in a db. There are also dynamic tools when you double click on any element depending on its type, so you can have the agent operate differently depending on media type. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 I would say the biggest challenge was making the tools description and names as relevant as possible for the agent to make sense of them in a way that felt natural to interact with. In the beginning it would find the keywords but not have the necessary context on how the app worked, so its interactions with the user where sometimes confusing. In the beginning i solved this by giving the agent a tool with a really long description that explained the app, the tool was not meant to be used, it was jsut to have the agent read the context of the app. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am really proud of how natural the interaction with the agent felt at the end. When i began playing around with the canvas and the agent, it felt really simple to just instruct the agent on what i wanted without having to overcomplicate my speech trying to describe an element. 

 What we learned 

 I learned how WebMCP works, this was my first project for the challenge. Having the mcp be registered in the html make sit so that any change in the UI can be immediately referred to by the agent. I also learnt about the Abort Signals for the agent, for destructive actions. 

 What's next for Shared Reference Canvas 

 I would love to see this become some sort of package where maybe its a extension for the browser or an app where any interface we use can also have these shared references as we everyday talk more with agents, and have to spend a painful amount of time describing our world that can sometimes be confusing to describe.

about_excerpt:
Search and create UTM tracked short links with AI.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1

 Story

 Inspiration 

 What inspired me was "how can an agent help me?" I had a hard time thinking what would work but honestly just handing out what a user can do normally already is a big improvement! 

 What it does 

 It's an already existing software to create short links with qr codes and statistics, but with the use of WebMCP we can interact with what's already there with little effort. A supporting browser gets twelve tools. On the public pages: read the plans and a product summary, and open the QR generator. In the generator: set the value and styling, read the code back, or download it as PNG or SVG. Signed in: search links, read or create a tracked link, edit one, delete one, and read organization analytics (totals, top links, acquisition breakdowns, dead and declining links). Every result lands in the real UI: created links show up on the Links page, generated codes sit in the generator ready to download. 

 How we built it 

 Zero new backend. Each tool calls the same org-scoped REST endpoint the page itself uses, so authorization, quotas and validation stay exactly where they were. Registration goes through document.modelContext when a browser exposes it, and is a deliberate no-op everywhere else: no supported browser means zero behavior change. Tools only appear once the signed-in user and their organization resolve, outputs are plain text capped at 1500 characters and marked untrustedContentHint, and read-only tools carry readOnlyHint. For testing, Playwright installs a fake modelContext before the app loads, so every flow runs in a real browser against the real app. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest one reached production: some implementations call execute(input) with no second argument, and destructuring the abort signal out of it threw. Sentry caught it, the fix made the argument optional, and the e2e suite now invokes a tool bare, exactly the shape that crashed. The second challenge was restraint. It's tempting to hand an agent login or billing, but credentials in model context and injected instructions near identity are risks you don't get to take back, so anything that moves identity or money stayed human-only. Deleting a link is exposed, but it's marked as a write and the agent has to name the exact slug. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 It shipped on a real product with real users, not a demo stub. A production crash was caught, root-caused and regression-tested within hours of appearing in Sentry. An agent can now drive the whole core loop: generate a branded QR code and download it, create a link, then explain how its clicks look. And we also negotiated text/markdown versions of the marketing pages off the same Accept header, so agents can read about the product even signed out. 

 What we learned 

 Handing over what already exists beat inventing new agent features. The less a tool returns, the more useful it is: short prose summaries outperformed raw JSON every time. And a protocol built on optional browser behavior needs defensive contracts everywhere: any argument can be missing, any capability can be absent, and none of it may ever break the person behind the browser. 

 What's next for Rdyrct 

 More read tools first: domains, member roles, per-link drilldowns, CSV exports. Then discovery: proper Link headers toward an API catalog and service description so agents can learn the surface themselves instead of guessing tool by top-level name. Agent-facing credentials are interesting but they come last, behind the same rule as login: nothing that moves identity happens without the human in the loop.

title: Asia Trend Radar — Read-Only WebMCP Tools
pitch: Six safe WebMCP tools that turn live Asian trend signals into evidence-backed answers.
about_excerpt:
Six safe WebMCP tools that turn live Asian trend signals into evidence-backed answers.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Responsive mobile workflow — the same read-only discovery experience at a 390 × 844 viewport. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Six read-only WebMCP tools — English judge-facing interface with a safe website fallback. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Real source-backed Taiwan trends — five live results for Taiwan rising searches in the previous 24 hours. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Responsive mobile workflow — the same read-only discovery experience at a 390 × 844 viewport. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Six read-only WebMCP tools — English judge-facing interface with a safe website fallback. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Real source-backed Taiwan trends — five live results for Taiwan rising searches in the previous 24 hours. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Responsive mobile workflow — the same read-only discovery experience at a 390 × 844 viewport. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Trend research is often fragmented across dashboards, search pages, and inconsistent source formats. An agent may find a popular topic but still lack the evidence needed to explain where it came from, how fresh it is, or whether the source is healthy. Copying results between a website and an assistant also loses structured context and uncertainty. 

 We wanted the website itself to expose a controlled interface to an agent without creating a separate plugin or giving the agent administrative access. 

 What it does 

 Asia Trend Radar exposes six browser-native, read-only tools: 

 
 search_radar_trends searches trend signals by market, category, signal type, time window, confidence, source, and sort order. 
 get_radar_trend retrieves one topic together with its supporting evidence. 
 search_radar_videos searches available video signals and returns an honest empty result when no qualifying data exists. 
 list_radar_sources reports source availability and operational status. 
 list_radar_markets lists supported markets and their enabled state. 
 list_radar_categories lists normalized categories. 
 

 A judge can request Taiwan's top five rising searches from the previous 24 hours, inspect a Chinese-language topic ID, review source status, and query markets, categories, and video signals. The six-tool WebMCP surface exposes no management, scheduling, membership, payment, publishing, or write operations. Oversized requests such as limit=500 are rejected. 

 Why WebMCP 

 A normal webpage is designed for people to read. WebMCP adds a machine-readable interaction layer that lets a compatible browser agent discover the site's capabilities, understand each input schema, and invoke the correct operation directly. 

 This project uses WebMCP as the core interaction layer. The agent no longer needs to scrape rendered text or guess button locations, and it does not receive unrestricted API access. People can still use the same responsive website when native WebMCP is unavailable. 

 Human-agent collaboration 

 The agent handles structured retrieval: it selects a read-only tool, applies the requested filters, and returns topic evidence and source status. The human remains responsible for interpretation and every downstream content or publishing decision. The agent cannot modify the radar, change sources, schedule jobs, or invoke management operations. 

 How it was built 

 The interface uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and React Router and is hosted on Cloudflare Pages with Pages Functions. 

 Each tool is registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() with a strict JSON Schema and read-only annotations. Tools that may return external material are marked as containing untrusted content. 

 Native WebMCP calls and visible website searches share one server-side Radar adapter. The adapter handles field normalization, sorting, cache behavior, stale-data labels, bounded retries, sanitized errors, and a fixed allowlist of read-only upstream routes. Credentials remain server-side and are never returned to the webpage or tool output. 

 Safety and truthful data handling 

 
 Every public tool is read-only. 
 Strict schemas reject unknown and unsafe inputs. 
 limit=500 is rejected because the maximum is 50. 
 Unsafe topic-ID formats and traversal attempts are rejected. 
 External titles are treated as untrusted content. 
 Missing video data produces an empty result, not fabricated records. 
 Relative popularity is not described as an exact search or view count. 
 User-supplied URLs must be public HTTPS links and are rejected before storage when they contain credentials, fragments, signed parameters, or private-access tokens. 
 Upstream records pass through field allowlists and secret redaction before cache, UI, or WebMCP output. 
 No management operation is registered as a WebMCP tool, and the Radar adapter allowlist excludes management routes. 
 

 Work completed during the challenge 

 The underlying trend product, regional discovery interface, source pipeline, scoring concepts, evidence model, filters, and original responsive interface existed before the challenge. We do not claim those foundations as new WebMCP development. 

 After August 25, 2026, the challenge work added the isolated competition edition, six read-only WebMCP Radar tools, strict schemas and safety annotations, a dedicated server-side read-only adapter, native discovery and invocation support, honest empty and stale states, safe browser fallback behavior, localized topic-ID handling, an English judging interface, and challenge-specific validation evidence. Dated commits and the repository's PREEXISTING_WORK.md and NEW_WORK_LOG.md document the boundary. 

 Challenges 

 Native WebMCP support is browser-dependent, so we had to distinguish genuine tool discovery and invocation from ordinary website automation. Native calls were verified in a compatible in-app browser. Safari was tested only as a normal website fallback; Safari native WebMCP is explicitly NOT RUN . 

 Localized identifiers were another edge case. Chinese topic IDs had to survive URL encoding and route decoding without weakening validation. 

 The central product challenge was handling uncertainty honestly. A successful query can legitimately return zero videos. The tool preserves that result rather than filling the interface with demonstration data. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Six native, discoverable, read-only WebMCP tools. 
 Real Taiwan trend results from the production competition URL. 
 Safe lookup of localized Chinese topic IDs. 
 Honest video empty states with no fabricated records. 
 Rejection of oversized inputs and absence of management tools. 
 One shared data contract for human and agent interfaces. 
 Responsive desktop, tablet, and mobile validation. 
 20 test files and 305 tests passing at the final implementation checkpoint, together with TypeScript, ESLint, production build, dependency audit, secret scanning, and whitespace checks. 
 

 What we learned 

 A trustworthy agent interface needs strict schemas, bounded inputs, explicit read-only semantics, untrusted-content warnings, safe errors, and evidence that the browser actually discovered and invoked the tools. An honest empty answer can be more valuable than an impressive-looking fake result. 

 Potential impact 

 Content teams, researchers, and analysts can ask an agent for narrowly defined trend candidates while retaining source status, timestamps, confidence, and uncertainty. More broadly, WebMCP can turn existing websites into controlled agent-ready interfaces without replacing their human experience or exposing administrative APIs. 

 What's next 

 Future work could add more authorized sources, richer provenance views, and user-controlled workflows. Any write capability would remain separate and require explicit human confirmation. The competition surface intentionally remains read-only.

about_excerpt:
Turn a founder’s natural-language business story into an authoritative exit-readiness assessment. ChatGPT uses WebMCP to operate Exit Desk’s real M&A scoring engine—not simulate it.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most AI agents still interact with websites the way humans do: reading pages, interpreting interfaces, and clicking through forms. 

 Exit Desk already existed as a real buyer-lens exit-readiness product for business owners. Its free assessment asks eight questions and evaluates a company across revenue quality, founder dependence, financial health, competitive position, and timing alignment. 

 The WebMCP Challenge gave us a simple question: 

 What if ChatGPT did not have to operate Exit Desk by guessing how its interface works? What if Exit Desk could expose its actual capability directly to the agent? 

 That became Exit Desk × WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 A business owner can describe their company to ChatGPT in ordinary language: 

 
 “We do about $5M in revenue. Customers repeat but aren't contracted. I still own key client relationships. Our largest customer is about 15% of revenue. The team handles daily operations, margins are stable, our moat is reputation, and I'm exploring a sale.” 
 

 Instead of clicking through Exit Desk's eight-question interface, ChatGPT discovers a WebMCP tool exposed by the site: 

 run_exit_readiness_assessment 

 ChatGPT translates the owner's natural-language description into the structured inputs required by Exit Desk and invokes the tool. 

 Exit Desk then runs its existing deterministic assessment engine and returns the same score, dimension scores, weakest dimension, findings, and next-step information that the human-facing application produces. 

 The human and the agent therefore work from the same authoritative result. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 The important architectural distinction is that ChatGPT does not recreate Exit Desk's M&A logic. 

 ChatGPT handles conversation, intent, and translation. 

 Exit Desk remains the authoritative application performing the assessment. 

 Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer the interface and manipulate eight separate questions. With WebMCP, the website declares what it can do and the structured inputs it requires. 

 The interaction becomes: 

 Natural language → ChatGPT → WebMCP tool → Exit Desk assessment → structured result 

 This turns Exit Desk from a website an AI can read or click through into a capability an AI can reliably operate. 

 How we built it 

 The production Exit Desk assessment runs at mikeye.com/exit/score . 

 For the challenge, we added a WebMCP integration using the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. 

 The tool defines a structured input schema for the eight assessment dimensions and maps those inputs into Exit Desk's existing assessment application. It invokes the same scoring and results logic used by the human interface, then returns structured output to the agent. 

 The WebMCP source lives in the public GitHub repository and is deployed through Vercel. The production Webflow page loads that repository-backed implementation. 

 We tested the integration using ChatGPT's in-app browser. ChatGPT successfully discovered run_exit_readiness_assessment , invoked it, and received Exit Desk's resulting score and dimension analysis. 

 What we built during the challenge 

 Exit Desk itself predates the WebMCP Challenge. 

 The WebMCP capability does not. 

 During the challenge period we: 

 
 Designed the agent-facing assessment interface. 
 Implemented run_exit_readiness_assessment . 
 Defined the structured input schema and mappings. 
 Connected WebMCP to Exit Desk's existing scoring engine and human-facing results. 
 Deployed the integration to the production Exit Desk website. 
 Tested the complete flow using ChatGPT's in-app browser. 
 Added public implementation documentation and challenge-period source history. 
 

 The GitHub commit history documents these additions separately from the pre-existing application. 

 What we learned 

 The most interesting lesson was that WebMCP is not primarily about making agents better at clicking websites. 

 It can remove the need to click them. 

 A website can retain ownership of its domain logic while allowing an AI agent to provide a much more natural interface to that capability. 

 For Exit Desk, that means the AI does not become the M&A assessment engine. It becomes the conversational layer through which a founder can access that engine. 

 What's next 

 The same architecture can extend beyond the initial assessment. 

 Future Exit Desk tools could help owners prepare diligence materials, identify buyer-readiness gaps, evaluate founder dependence, compare buyer types, and prepare for acquisition conversations. 

 The broader idea is simple: 

 The web is moving from machine-readable to machine-operable.

pitch: Integrating WebMCP into an AI-powered project management platform workspaces
about_excerpt:
Integrating WebMCP into an AI-powered project management platform workspaces
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Project management tools are built around human clicks. But increasingly, the people using VisionBoard also have AI agents running alongside them — in their browser, their IDE sidebar, their chat interface. Those agents can see the page but they can't reliably act on it. They scrape DOM structure that changes, guess at button labels, and have no access to the actual data and logic underneath. 

 The W3C WebMCP spec ( document.modelContext ) landed in Chrome 149 and changed that framing entirely. Instead of an agent trying to reverse-engineer your UI, your app declares exactly what it can do — as typed, callable tools with JSON Schema contracts. The agent calls the function directly. No DOM scraping, no screenshot interpretation, no fragile selectors. 

 VisionBoard already had the right ingredients: structured workspace data, five AI features, semantic search over all content. The question was just whether to expose them through a standard the browser itself now understands. 

 

 What it does 

 When a user has VisionBoard open in Chrome, any WebMCP-aware agent running in the same browser can discover and call a set of structured tools — using the user's existing logged-in session. No API keys, no separate authentication flow, no configuration. 

 Nine tools are registered across the workspace, split into shared and page-specific: 

 Always available on any workspace page: 

 
 search_workspace — semantic search across all goals, tasks, documents, and comments using the pgvector knowledge base 
 list_my_tasks — tasks assigned to the current user, filterable by status 
 update_task_status — change a task's status (todo → in_progress → done, etc.) 
 get_standup_digest — AI-generated daily standup: completed, in-flight, and blocked 
 get_executive_summary — AI executive briefing covering goal health, risks, and recommendations 
 

 Goals page only: 

 
 list_goals — all workspace goals with health scores, status, and progress 
 create_goal — create a new goal with title, objective, and optional target date 
 

 Tasks page only: 

 
 create_task — create a task inside a milestone 
 

 Roadmap page only: 

 
 generate_roadmap — AI-powered roadmap generation from a plain text description 
 

 The tools appear and disappear with the page. Navigate away from the goals page and create_goal unregisters. Come back and it registers again. 

 

 How we built it 

 Polyfill initialization. Chrome 149+ supports document.modelContext natively via origin trial. Every other browser doesn't. @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill fills the gap. It's initialized once via a dynamic import in lib/webmcp/init.ts — the dynamic import keeps it out of the SSR bundle entirely, so it only loads in the browser. 
 import("@mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill").then(({ initializeWebMCPPolyfill }) => {
 initializeWebMCPPolyfill();
});
 
 Tool components. Each tool lives in a "use client" React component. Tools register on mount and unregister on unmount via AbortController . The lifecycle is pure React — no global state, no manual cleanup calls. Unmounting the component (route navigation, tab close) automatically aborts all registered tools. 
 const controller = new AbortController();
await document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "search_workspace",
 description: "...",
 inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { query: { type: "string" } }, required: ["query"] },
 annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, untrustedContentHint: false },
 async execute({ query }) { /* fetch("/api/ai/copilot/search", ...) */ }
}, { signal: controller.signal });

// cleanup
return () => controller.abort();
 
 Session-based auth. Every tool's execute callback calls the existing VisionBoard API routes using fetch . The user's session cookie is sent automatically. There's no separate auth layer — if you're logged into VisionBoard, the tools work. This is the core advantage of WebMCP over server-side MCP: the agent inherits the user's already-authenticated session. 

 Context-aware mounting. WorkspaceWebMCPTools mounts inside AppShell which wraps every workspace page — those 5 tools are always registered. GoalsWebMCPTools mounts inside GoalsList , TasksWebMCPTools inside TasksFilteredList , RoadmapWebMCPTools inside RoadmapView . The tool set changes as the user navigates, matching what's actually visible and actionable on the current page. 

 Origin trial. Chrome requires either chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing for local dev, or an origin trial token served as <meta http-equiv="origin-trial"> for production. The token is injected from NEXT_PUBLIC_WEBMCP_ORIGIN_TRIAL_TOKEN in the root layout. Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 is set on every HTML response in the middleware — required for origin isolation, without which getTools() silently returns [] . 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 getTools() returning [] with no error. registerTool() resolves successfully even when the native API isn't active — the polyfill accepts the call but Chrome ignores it. There are actually two separate requirements that both need to be met: the origin trial token and Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 for origin isolation. Either one missing produces the same symptom: an empty array, no error, no warning. Debugging this required reading the Chrome WebMCP security docs closely enough to find the origin isolation requirement buried in a separate section from the token instructions. 

 The spec moved twice during implementation. The entry point shifted from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext , provideContext() was removed entirely in favor of registerTool() , and navigator.modelContext was deprecated in Chrome 150 — all within about six months. Any tutorial written before May 2026 describes a dead API. The authoritative source ended up being the Chrome imperative API docs and the W3C Community Group draft directly, not any third-party write-up. 

 Polyfill timing vs. React mount timing. The polyfill loads asynchronously. If a tool component mounts before the polyfill has installed document.modelContext , the registration silently does nothing. The fix was a retry loop inside each component's useEffect — polling every 100ms for up to 2 seconds before attempting registration. It's inelegant but reliable across the range of network speeds and browser performance. 

 SSR. Anything that touches document crashes during server-side rendering. The polyfill import, the document.modelContext access, the window.location.origin calls inside tool execute callbacks — all of it runs inside useEffect which is client-only, but the import itself needed the typeof window !== "undefined" guard in init.ts to survive being imported from a server component context. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The tool set is genuinely context-aware rather than a flat list. A browser agent calling document.modelContext.getTools() on the goals page gets 7 tools. On the roadmap page it gets 6 different ones. On a non-workspace page it gets none. The tools reflect what's actually on screen, which is the whole point of the browser-side API. 

 The execute callbacks call the real application API — the same routes the UI uses, with the same auth, the same Prisma queries, the same plan limit enforcement. There's no parallel implementation, no simplified version for agents. An agent calling create_goal goes through exactly the same path as clicking "New Goal" in the UI, including RBAC, validation, and the activity log write. 

 The annotations are set correctly throughout. Read-only tools ( search_workspace , list_goals , list_my_tasks ) carry readOnlyHint: true . Write tools and tools that return user-generated content carry untrustedContentHint: true . These are the signals a browser agent uses to decide whether to ask for user confirmation before acting — getting them right makes the integration genuinely safer. 

 

 What we learned 

 Browser WebMCP and server MCP solve different problems. Server MCP is for agents acting asynchronously — generating roadmaps from a CLI, polling for task updates, running in CI. Browser WebMCP is for agents acting in the moment — the user is looking at the goals page and asks their assistant to create one. The browser agent doesn't need an API key because it inherits the session. The server agent doesn't need the page to be open because it has a persistent key. They complement each other rather than overlap. 

 The spec being a moving target is actually fine. The changes between

 Inspiration Well I was inspired by webmcp that list 10 people for the award that's wonderful and I believe I'd be one of the winner, that's why I joined. 

 What it does DodoLink Agent Shopping gives browser agents a structured way to help shoppers navigate a real Nigerian marketplace. Instead of scraping repetitive listing cards and guessing which actions are safe, an agent can call typed WebMCP tools to search products, discover local stores, compare prices, and prepare a purchase plan. 

 How we built it I built DodoLink Agent Shopping as a web-only WebMCP experience connected to DodoLink’s real public marketplace data. 

 The page exposes four structured, read-only tools: 

 search_products
discover_stores
compare_products
prepare_purchase_plan
Each tool is registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool, using a JSON input schema and an asynchronous execute function. The tools return real product and store information, including prices, stock status, seller details, and review links. 

 I also added a manual fallback so the experience still works in a normal browser when WebMCP is unavailable. Both the manual interface and the WebMCP tools use the same marketplace search and purchase-planning logic. 

 The system intentionally does not expose payment, checkout, or seller-messaging tools. The agent can discover and organize options, but the human must review the products and decide whether to continue. 

 Challenges we ran into An agent could describe a product, but it could not reliably distinguish listing IDs, price limits, stock, seller context, and review links. The WebMCP tools make those capabilities explicit and return bounded public data. The plan tool then turns agent work into a visible human approval step. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that DodoLink Agent Shopping is connected to real marketplace data instead of using a mock catalog. 

 We built a complete experience where an agent can: 

 Understand a natural-language shopping request.
Search real DodoLink products.
Discover relevant stores.
Compare product options.
Prepare a shortlist and purchase plan.
Hand the decision back to the human shopper.
We are especially proud of the safety boundary. The agent can help with discovery and research, but it cannot spend money, check out, or send messages to sellers. This keeps the agent useful while ensuring the human remains in control of important decisions. 

 We also created a separate public and sanitized open-source repository so judges can inspect the WebMCP implementation without exposing DodoLink’s private production infrastructure. 

 What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most useful when an application exposes focused capabilities instead of allowing an agent to guess its way through a user interface. 

 For a marketplace, structured tools are much more reliable than page scraping. A tool can clearly define the product query, price limit, product IDs, and expected response format. 

 We also learned that WebMCP tools need strong safety boundaries. Marketplace listings and seller descriptions should be treated as untrusted content, while actions such as payment and messaging should remain under human control. 

 Another important lesson was that WebMCP is page-scoped and still experimental. A user must open the WebMCP-enabled page in a compatible browser before the agent can discover and use its tools. Because of this, we made the manual experience work as a fallback too. 

 What's next for Dodolink Next, we want to make the agent experience more useful for complex shopping decisions. 

 We plan to improve product filtering with more detailed category, location, availability, and seller-reputation criteria. We also want to make comparisons more informative by including delivery options, product attributes, review summaries, and clearer trade-offs between sellers. 

 We would like to improve the human handoff so shoppers can save a shortlist, share it with someone else, open a seller profile, and continue manually when they are ready. 

 As WebMCP develops, we also plan to test DodoLink with more browser agents and refine the tool schemas based on real usage. Our long-term goal is to make DodoLink a marketplace where agents are genuinely helpful while people remain informed and in control.
