title: QuantumJS + WebMCP
pitch: QuantumJS brings quantum computing to the web in the agentic era, transforming how we learn and experiment with circuits through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
QuantumJS brings quantum computing to the web in the agentic era, transforming how we learn and experiment with circuits through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Quantum computing has a strange accessibility problem, the field is making steady progress, but much of its tooling remains disconnected from both the AI and agentic era and the web-centered ecosystem where modern developers learn, experiment, and build. While this is a bleeding edge research field, much of the existing ecosystem paradoxically feels like it belongs to a decade ago. 

 QuantumJS was created to address that gap. It brings quantum circuit authoring, simulation, visualization, documentation, and an interactive IDE to the JavaScript/TypeScript/web ecosystem. Its circuit DSL is expressive enough for serious experimentation while remaining natural to web developers, and its IDE makes quantum programs something you can actually see, execute, and explore. 

 WebMCP suggested a much bigger possibility. 

 If QuantumJS can expose its capabilities directly to AI agents, an agent no longer has to guess how to navigate a quantum IDE. It can discover the application's capabilities and use them as structured tools: explore examples, work with quantum circuits, execute simulations, inspect results, and consult the project's documentation. 

 This turns QuantumJS from an IDE that a person operates into a shared workspace where humans and agents can reason about quantum programs together. 

 That is the experience we wanted to explore with this project. 

 What it does 

 QuantumJS is an open-source quantum computing ecosystem for the JavaScript/TypeScript/web platform. 

 It provides: 

 
 A fluent quantum circuit DSL that compiles to OpenQASM 
 An interactive browser-based quantum IDE 
 Quantum circuit visualization 
 Simulation and measurement analysis 
 A collection of real quantum circuit examples, including circuits based on published research 
 Documentation and learning material 
 Interactive stepped simulation that lets users observe how a circuit evolves at different points in its execution 
 

 For this challenge, we added WebMCP as a new interaction layer across the QuantumJS web application. 

 An agent can now interact with QuantumJS through structured capabilities exposed by the application rather than having to infer how to operate its interface. This allows a human to ask an agent to investigate a circuit, explore available examples, execute quantum computations, inspect the resulting behavior, and use the application's documentation as part of the same workflow. 

 The important change is that the agent is not merely looking at QuantumJS. It can work with QuantumJS. 

 A human can therefore remain in the loop while the agent handles exploration, repetitive experimentation, and interpretation. The result is a collaborative workflow that would be extremely cumbersome if an agent had to navigate the application's UI through clicks and guesses. 

 How we built it 

 QuantumJS is built around a JavaScript/TypeScript-native quantum programming model and a browser-based IDE. 

 For the WebMCP challenge, we extended the existing application with WebMCP tool definitions that expose meaningful QuantumJS operations to compatible agents. These tools are registered through the WebMCP document.modelContext API and provide structured descriptions and input schemas rather than requiring an agent to infer interactions from the visual interface. 

 The WebMCP layer sits on top of the existing QuantumJS functionality rather than replacing it. The same application remains fully usable by humans, while agents gain a first-class way to discover and invoke its capabilities. 

 This was particularly interesting because QuantumJS already combines several traditionally separate activities—writing circuits, visualizing them, simulating them, inspecting measurements, and reading documentation—inside a single web environment. WebMCP lets an agent move between those capabilities as part of one workflow. 

 The project is open source, and the WebMCP implementation is visible in the repository's commit history so that the new work can be distinguished from the pre-existing QuantumJS codebase. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was deciding what should actually be exposed as an agent tool. 

 It is easy to expose a collection of low-level functions and call that WebMCP support. It is much harder to decide what an agent genuinely needs in order to accomplish useful tasks. 

 Quantum computing makes this particularly interesting because the underlying operations can be highly technical. A useful agent interface needs to expose capabilities at a meaningful level while preserving the expressive power of QuantumJS. 

 Another challenge was integrating WebMCP without compromising the existing human experience. QuantumJS is first and foremost a browser-based development environment, so the agent interface needed to complement the IDE rather than turn it into an agent-only application. 

 Finally, we had to think about what it means for an agent to work with a computational environment rather than simply retrieve information from it. QuantumJS doesn't just contain static documentation. It can execute quantum circuits and produce computational results. Making those capabilities available to an agent creates a substantially richer interaction model. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are particularly proud that WebMCP is not a superficial addition to QuantumJS. 

 The application already contains a complete environment for authoring, visualizing, and simulating quantum circuits, and we were able to make those capabilities accessible to agents through the same web application. 

 This creates a workflow that feels fundamentally different from traditional web automation: 

 Human: "Explore the examples and find a circuit that demonstrates quantum interference." 

 Agent: discovers the available QuantumJS capabilities, explores the examples, runs relevant circuits, examines the results, and explains what it found. 

 The human can then take over, modify the circuit, ask a follow-up question, or direct the agent toward another experiment. 

 We are also proud to bring this interaction model to quantum computing specifically. Quantum software is a domain where experimentation is central to learning and research, making an agent that can actually execute and investigate programs much more useful than one that can merely read documentation. 

 Most importantly, we extended a pre-existing open-source project with a genuinely new capability during the challenge period. WebMCP is a new addition to QuantumJS, not something that existed in previous versions of the project. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that making an application agent-compatible is not simply an API-design exercise. 

 A traditional API is usually designed around what the application can do. An agent interface has to additionally consider what an agent needs to understand in order to accomplish a task. 

 WebMCP makes this distinction particularly visible. Tool descriptions, schemas, and the granularity of exposed operations become part of the application's user experience for agents. 

 We also learned that computational applications may be especially interesting candidates for WebMCP. When an agent can not only retrieve information but also execute computations and inspect their results, the interaction becomes iterative: 

 discover → construct → execute → observe → reason → modify → execute again 

 That loop is a natural fit for quantum programming. 

 What's next for QuantumJS + WebMCP 

 WebMCP opens a much larger direction for QuantumJS. 

 We want to expand the agent interface so that agents can become increasingly capable collaborators inside the quantum development workflow: helping construct circuits, explaining algorithms, debugging unexpected measurements, comparing implementations, generating experiments, and guiding users through educational material. 

 Beyond that, the QuantumJS roadmap includes a WebGPU-native simulator, measurement-based quantum computing support, deeper agentic coding integration, and substantially more educational content. 

 Our long-term goal is to make quantum computing feel native to the web,

 Inspiration 

 Hi! My name is Katie O'Daniel. I'm a graduating senior at Purdue, currently looking for software engineering work somewhere outside the Midwest (˶˃𐃷˂˶), and when I'm stressed, I like turn that energy into creativity. Sometimes it's my personal website, dashboards, Minecraft mods and platforms that did not need to become an entire platform when I first thought of it. You can probably tell from my GitHub contributions between March 25 and June 3. 

 I really like design, but I've realized that I might like planning even more. I love sitting down with an idea and figuring out what it could become: what features should it have, who is actually going to use it, what am I missing, and is there a completely different direction that would make more sense? This is also where I get myself into trouble, because one feature becomes three more, then one of those makes me rethink the first feature, and eventually I am scrolling twenty messages back trying to find an idea I had earlier. 

 A recent example was another project I have been working on: a website and platform for adoptees. Originally, I was going to build it specifically for Chinese adoptees. That made sense to me because it was close to my own experience and it was where I started. But as I researched more, thought about what the community should actually be, and tried to understand perspectives outside my own, and through that, the idea changed. I realized there were experiences that were specific to Chinese adoptees, but there were also much bigger conversations around adoption, identity, belonging, family, culture, and growing up between different worlds. 

 That experience is a big part of why I made Rabbit Hole. I use AI constantly when I plan projects. I use it to brainstorm features, research questions, argue against my own ideas, compare approaches, and figure out what I might not be considering. But all of that usually ends up in one giant conversation. I can scroll back and find an old idea, but I can't really see the moment when my thinking changed, the branches I almost followed, or why I stopped following one direction and chose another. 

 At some point I thought: What if I could actually see the rabbit hole? 

 So I built it. 

 What it does 

 Rabbit Hole takes all of that messy exploration and turns it into something you can actually see. You start with a question or an idea, and from there you can explore different directions, go deeper into one path, branch somewhere else, add your own thought, or go back to something you were considering earlier. I also did not want the directions you skipped to just disappear, because sometimes an idea that did not make sense at first becomes useful again later. 

 Rabbit Hole currently has two main modes: Investigate and Design. Investigate is for research and questions. Instead of asking AI for one big answer and stopping there, you can follow different perspectives, look at evidence, question what you are finding, and keep exploring as the original question changes. You decide what is worth keeping, and eventually that path can become an Investigation Brief that shows where you went, what evidence mattered, what complicated the question, and what is still uncertain. 

 Design came more directly from how I build things myself. I rarely start with a completely planned product. Usually I start with something like, "I want to make a platform for this," and then I spend way too much time figuring out what that platform should actually be. Design gives you a place to explore those different versions before committing to one. You can try different directions, branch when a new feature changes the idea, go back to something you liked earlier, and eventually create an outcome from the decisions you actually chose to keep. 

 The two modes are different, but they are really solving the same problem for me. Whether I am researching something or designing something, I almost never get to the final direction in a straight line. 

 How I used WebMCP 

 WebMCP is what lets Rabbit Hole expose the workspace to an agent in a structured way instead of making the agent guess what is happening from the visual interface. 

 Rabbit Hole registers WebMCP tools that let a compatible agent inspect the current state of an exploration. That includes things like whether the user is in Investigate or Design, which node is currently active, the path of nodes that led to it, what the user has decided to keep, what branches are still available, and how sources and evidence connect to the investigation. 

 That is useful because the graph itself contains information that would normally be difficult for an agent to understand just by looking at the page. If I am five branches deep into an investigation, the agent does not have to rely only on the last prompt I typed. It can understand the structure that led me there. 

 I also use WebMCP to separate understanding the workspace from changing it. An agent can inspect the current Rabbit Hole and use that context to suggest a next direction, but a suggestion does not automatically become part of the graph. The user still chooses whether to follow it, keep it, or go somewhere else. 

 For me, that is the main reason WebMCP fits Rabbit Hole. The product is already about preserving context, decisions, branches, and where an idea came from. WebMCP gives an agent access to that same structure, so the person and the agent can work from the same understanding of the exploration instead of starting over with every new prompt. 

 How I built it 

 Rabbit Hole is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, React Flow, Tailwind CSS, and WebMCP. Once I had the basic idea, I started breaking the product into individual functions and asking what each one actually needed to do. 

 I planned out things like how a branch should work, what should happen when someone follows a direction, what counts as something worth keeping, how sources should connect back to claims, how the different node types should behave, and how Investigate and Design could use the same overall structure without feeling like the exact same experience. 

 For each part, I usually brainstormed different options with ChatGPT before building it. I would ask for different ways a feature could work, try to look at it from another perspective, and then decide which direction made the most sense for Rabbit Hole. Once I had a feature in mind, I would often generate mock images of what the interface could look like and iterate on those before actually implementing it.

 🎬 ROYA | رؤية — AI Film Production Manager 

 See your entire film. Before you shoot it. 

 Inspiration 

 I come from the world of film production in Morocco — a country that hosts
dozens of international shoots every year with a vibrant local industry.
Yet I watched producers coordinate 10+ departments through spreadsheets,
phone calls, and paper call sheets. A single weather change could trigger
hours of re-planning calls. 

 I asked: what if the producer's AI agent could do this coordination
directly — deterministically, instantly, reliably? That question is
exactly what WebMCP enables. ROYA (رؤية = "vision" in Arabic) gives every
filmmaker the vision of their entire production — from script to screen —
before the camera rolls. 

 What it does 

 
 Script Analysis — paste a screenplay (Arabic/English/French); the
agent calls analyze_script to extract scenes, cast, props, locations,
and per-department notes. 
 Weather-aware scheduling — get_weather_forecast +
 generate_schedule build a calendar that auto-moves outdoor scenes
indoors when rain probability is high. 
 Department task board — assign_task distributes work to 8 departments. 
 Live status dashboard — get_production_status returns completion
rates and weather alerts. 
 Call sheet export — export_call_sheet produces the daily briefing. 
 Scene control — get_scene_breakdown + reschedule_scene . 
 

 Why WebMCP 

 Film logistics is the perfect agent-native problem: structured actions
(schedule, assign, reschedule, export) that must execute deterministically
instead of being guessed through a UI. Any agent — ChatGPT's in-app browser,
a producer's assistant bot, or another production tool — can operate ROYA
directly through its 8 registered tools. 

 Human + agent workflow 

 👤 Producer pastes a raw screenplay
🤖 Agent → analyze_script (12 scenes, 6 cast, 5 locations)
🤖 Agent → get_weather_forecast ×3 shooting days
🤖 Agent → generate_schedule (priority: weather)
🤖 Agent → assign_task ×8 departments
👤 Producer approves one change
🤖 Agent → reschedule_scene + export_call_sheet 
👤 Crew receives the briefing instantly 

 6–8 hours of manual coordination → under 5 minutes. 

 How I built it 

 
 Frontend: Next.js 14 App Router, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
(charcoal #0a0a0f + amber-gold identity, Arabic/English) 
 AI: OpenAI GPT-4o-mini, JSON mode for screenplay extraction 
 Weather: OpenWeatherMap with graceful mock fallback (zero-key demo) 
 WebMCP: 8 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() with
 navigator.modelContext fallback 
 State: client-side React context + localStorage; server routes stateless 
 Hosting: Vercel auto-deploy on every push; MIT license 
 Verification: Puppeteer E2E launching Chrome 152 with
 --enable-features=WebMCP,WebMCPAPI,WebModelContext , asserting 8/8 tools
register and executing two against the live URL (report: e2e/results.json ) 
 

 Challenges & what I learned 

 
 WebMCP availability: stable Chrome didn't expose modelContext ; I
feature-detected both surfaces and built an E2E harness with cached
Chrome 152 + flags to prove registration AND execution. 
 React #418 hydration: reading localStorage during render broke SSR
parity; fixed by seeding identical demo state and hydrating in useEffect . 
 Shared-state leak: an early server singleton mixed visitors' data;
per-session client state + Reset button + "Demo data / Your analysis"
badges now keep every judge's session pristine. 
 

 The opportunity 

 Production-management software is a $6.66B market (2026, +9%/yr), yet no
Arabic-first, weather-aware, agent-native tool exists. MENA produces 200+
films/year with almost no tailored tooling. ROYA is the first.

SquishAI turns your browser into an AI dispatch centre.
The queue that lets AI agents hand work to each other across platforms, from the browser.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every day I was doing the same manual ritual: copy context from ChatGPT into Claude Code, paste the result back, repeat. Two of the most capable AI tools in the world, completely blind to each other. The moment I heard about WebMCP — AI tools registering directly in the browser — I realised the browser was the missing coordination layer. Not another app. Not another API. The page itself becomes the dispatcher. 

 What it does 

 SquishAI is a shared task queue and working memory layer that connects AI agents across platforms. Open squishai.io in ChatGPT's in-app browser and five tools appear instantly via WebMCP — no plugin setup, no API keys, nothing to install. 

 Tell ChatGPT what you need built. It calls submit_task , packages the work, and queues it with full context. Claude Code (or Manus, Cursor, Windsurf — any connected agent) sees the task, claims it, executes it, and posts the result back. The story: two competing AI platforms, cooperating through an open standard. 

 The tools: 

 
 brief — check the queue and working memory at session start 
 submit_task — queue work for another agent, with optional platform targeting 
 status — see what's pending, in progress, or done 
 result — fetch what the worker built 
 remember — save decisions and context that travel with every task 
 

 How we built it 

 The WebMCP layer lives entirely in index.html — five document.modelContext.registerTool() calls that fire when the page loads in a WebMCP-enabled browser. Each tool's execute function calls a REST API ( /api/v1/* ) on the SquishAI backend. 

 The backend is Node.js + Express + SQLite. The same database powers both the browser-side REST API and a server-side MCP connector (StreamableHTTP + SSE transports) for AI coding tools. One queue, two transports — whichever side submits, the other side picks up. 

 Working memory is append-only per user. Every submit_task call automatically packs the last five memory entries into the task context, so the worker arrives fully briefed without the submitter having to repeat themselves. 

 A constitution delivered via the MCP instructions field means every connecting agent is briefed on the system the moment they connect — what the queue is, how memory works, what to do on a new session. 

 Challenges 

 The open web part is genuinely hard. Browser-side tools calling a backend from inside ChatGPT's in-app browser means strict CORS handling and no assumptions about the host environment. Every fetch had to be self-contained. 

 Cross-platform coordination without a shared session was the core design problem. The solution: a shared token that acts as a namespace. Any agent with the token reads from the same queue and memory — it doesn't matter which platform submitted or which picks up. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is not a feature — it's a shift in what a webpage is. A page that registers tools is no longer just content. It's an interface for agents. The implications for how we think about the web are significant: any site can become a capability that AI models can reach for, without plugins, without OAuth flows, without anything except opening a URL. 

 The cross-platform demo — ChatGPT submitting, Claude Code executing — was the accidental proof. Two competing AI ecosystems, cooperating through an open standard. That's what the open web looks like.

pitch: Browser-native execution firewall and deterministic risk engine providing cryptographic human-in-the-loop authorization and SHA-256 audit ledgers for WebMCP AI agents.
about_excerpt:
Browser-native execution firewall and deterministic risk engine providing cryptographic human-in-the-loop authorization and SHA-256 audit ledgers for WebMCP AI agents.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Autonomous AI agents are rapidly evolving from read-only text generators into active execution engines capable of running browser-native tools via OpenAI's WebMCP standard ( navigator.modelContext ). However, granting an LLM direct execution bridges to deduct balances, trigger payouts, or mutate persistent state introduces severe security vulnerabilities: 

 
 Indirect Prompt Injections: Adversarial instructions hidden inside untrusted context (customer emails, scraped web pages, support tickets) can manipulate an agent into dispatching unauthorized funds. 
 Recursive Runaway Loops: Agent hallucinations and automated retry loops can drain corporate treasuries and API quotas within seconds. 
 Absence of Proof: Traditional web confirmation popups offer zero mathematical non-repudiation or cryptographic proof of human intent. 
 

 We named the project Uranus after the cold ice giant that rotates on a perpendicular 98-degree axial tilt. While traditional security attempts to police LLMs in-line using prompt instructions (which inevitably fail), Uranus operates perpendicular to the agent's reasoning loop. It acts as an absolute-zero execution freeze at the browser boundary, pausing unverified tool calls until they are cryptographically signed off by an authorized human operator. 

 What It Does 

 Uranus is a browser-native security proxy and deterministic execution firewall sitting between autonomous agents and state-mutating actions: 

 
 Multi-Transport Tool Interception: Registers execution tools ( request_guarded_settlement , simulate_preflight ) across navigator.modelContext (WebMCP), HTTP/WebSocket bridges, and stdio MCP runners. 
 Deterministic Risk Engine: Evaluates incoming payloads against strict monetary thresholds ($100 auto-approval cap), sliding-window velocity circuit breakers (blocking recursive loops), and recipient deny-lists. 
 True Network Back-Pressure: Holds the agent's execution promise pending across the network boundary until security checks pass or an operator resolves the interception card. 
 Cryptographic Human Authorization: High-risk actions require step-up approval where the human operator cryptographically signs the transaction payload using non-extractable keys in the browser via the Web Crypto API ( window.crypto.subtle ). 
 Immutable SHA-256 Audit Trail: Chains every resolution (Auto-Approved, Authorized, Rejected) into a sequential, tamper-evident hash ledger stored in IndexedDB. 
 Interactive Sandbox for Reviewers: Provides preloaded attack simulations alongside a custom settlement form, allowing judges to test arbitrary amounts, deny-listed recipients, or rapid clicks directly against the live policy engine with zero code. 
 

 How We Built It 

 
 Protocol Layer: Implemented using @modelcontextprotocol/sdk to conform strictly with OpenAI's WebMCP standard and MCP stdio specifications. 
 Frontend Architecture: Built with Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. 
 Cryptography & Non-Repudiation: Implemented browser-native key generation, canonical payload hashing, and signature verification using the native Web Crypto API ( window.crypto.subtle , ECDSA P-256, SHA-256). 
 Pluggable Settlement Adapter Interface: Built around an agnostic SettleInput -> SettleResult contract. Every layer above the ledger is production-grade security infrastructure; the execution backend is fully decoupled and can be swapped for Stripe, bank rails, or on-chain settlement with a simple adapter function. 
 State Management & Backend: Containerized Node.js bridge server managing an atomic, file-backed ledger with overdraft protection and real-time WebSocket state synchronization. 
 Infrastructure & Deployment: Next.js frontend deployed on Vercel; containerized backend bridge running live on Koyeb. 
 

 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 True Network Promise Back-Pressure: Most human-in-the-loop safety demos fake control with client-side UI modals that an agent can trivially bypass. We engineered the agent's HTTP request to genuinely block across the network boundary until an operator resolves it. This required building an in-process pending promise hub on the bridge server to hold the response socket open, stream a pending event over WebSockets to the browser, and only release the execution response once the operator provides a signed resolve payload. 
 Cross-Runtime Cryptographic Determinism: The client signs payloads using non-extractable ECDSA P-256 keys in IndexedDB via window.crypto.subtle , while the Node.js bridge verifies signatures using server-side crypto primitives. Both environments had to generate byte-identical canonical JSON representations, as a single key-ordering shift or trailing whitespace character invalidates the digital signature. We also re-derived the operator's fingerprint from the server-side SPKI export to prevent client fingerprint spoofing. 
 Race Conditions in the Hash-Chained Audit Ledger: Early iterations suffered from concurrent write collisions: rapid authorizations could read the same chain-tail state from IndexedDB, generate conflicting previous_hash pointers, and orphan blocks. We resolved this by serializing every write through an atomic promise queue to guarantee sequential ledger integrity during high-frequency execution bursts. 
 Decoupled Hybrid Deployment Architecture: Uranus requires both an edge-rendered Next.js frontend and a persistent, stateful Node.js bridge server handling WebSockets and file-backed ledger state. Because serverless environments drop persistent socket connections, we decoupled the architecture: hosting the frontend on Vercel and the stateful containerized bridge microservice on Koyeb, synchronized via a unified environment bridge URL. 
 

 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 

 
 Full OpenAI WebMCP Conformance: Successfully registering and intercepting live tools on navigator.modelContext . 
 Legitimate Cryptographic Rigor: Replacing cosmetic confirmation modals with true digital signatures and sequentially linked SHA-256 hash chains. 
 Frictionless Judge Sandbox: Providing an interactive settlement tester allowing anyone to probe velocity limits, spend thresholds, and injection vectors without running local terminal commands. 
 Clean Monochrome Visual Identity: Building an intentional, distraction-free control center designed specifically for security operators. 
 

 What We Learned 

 
 Standard client-side UI confirmation dialogs provide an illusion of safety; true agent defense requires network-level promise interception and mathematical non-repudiation. 
 In-browser execution via navigator.modelContext creates massive ergonomic gains for agentic workflows, but deterministic policy engines must sit between the model and the execution runtime to make it enterprise-safe. 
 Designing with the native Web Crypto API provides enterprise-grade key isolation directly inside standard browser runtimes without external hardware dependencies. 
 

 What's Next for Uranus 

 
 Out-of-Band Human Approval Channels: Push notifications and asynchronous Slack/Telegram approval webhooks for background server-side agent runs. 
 Hardware-Backed WebAuthn & Passkeys: Upgrading from browser-isolated Web Crypto keys to true hardware-enclave biometric sign-off (Touch ID / Face ID / YubiKey). 
 Multi-Signature Quorum Policies: Requiring M-of-N human signers for high-value organizational treasury mutations above configurable risk thresholds. 
 Dynamic Policy Engine: Zero-knowledge policy validation and real-time smart contract rule syncing across EVM and Solana networks. 
 TTL & Auto-Abort Handlers: Configurable time-to-live expiration policies for unattended agent step-up promises. 
 First-Party Production Payment Adapters: Shipping maintained, in-tree adapter modules (Stripe, Wise, Circle, on-chain smart contracts) so teams do not need to write their own integration wiring.

 Inspiration 

 In the age of generative AI, seeing an image is no longer enough . 

 We increasingly want to know: 

 
 Where did this content come from? 
 Who created it? 
 Has it been edited? 
 Was AI involved? 
 Can I trace it back to the original? 
 

 Content Credentials , based on the C2PA standard, provide a powerful foundation for answering these questions by giving digital content a verifiable provenance history. 

 But there is still a usability gap. Understanding provenance often requires knowing where to look, opening specialized tools, and interpreting technical metadata. 

 So we asked: 

 
 What if understanding the history of content was as easy as asking a question? 
 

 That inspired VerifyHere — an exploration of making Content Credentials conversational with WebMCP . 

 What it does 

 VerifyHere lets you talk to the provenance of your content. 

 Instead of manually digging through metadata, you can simply ask: 

 
 "Where did this photo come from?" 

 "Has this image been edited?" 

 "What changed?" 

 "Take me back to the original." 
 

 VerifyHere uses WebMCP to connect these natural-language questions with the underlying provenance information. 

 The experience follows content across its journey: 

 Capture → Verify → Edit → Trace → Recover 

 For example, a photographer can capture an image with Content Credentials, inspect its provenance, edit it in Photoshop, and then explore how the edited asset relates to the original. 

 The goal isn't to tell people what to trust. It's to give them more context about how content came to be . 

 How we built it 

 We built VerifyHere as a web experience combining WebMCP with C2PA Content Credentials . 

 Our application exposes provenance capabilities as tools that an AI agent can discover and invoke through WebMCP. 

 This means the user doesn't need to understand C2PA manifests, cryptographic signatures, or metadata structures. 

 They can express their intent naturally: 

 
 "Tell me where this image came from." 
 

 WebMCP can then connect that request to the appropriate capability in VerifyHere, inspect the available provenance information, and return an understandable answer. 

 When an edited asset contains provenance linking it to an earlier asset, VerifyHere can also help users explore that chain and move back toward the original. 

 This turns Content Credentials from something users inspect into something they can interact with conversationally . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was provenance at capture . 

 We experimented with different mobile capture workflows and quickly discovered that real-world C2PA interoperability isn't always as straightforward as the specification makes it appear. 

 Credentials can behave differently across capture applications, exports, file transfers, editing workflows, and verification experiences. 

 That challenge actually reinforced the motivation behind VerifyHere: 

 
 Users shouldn't have to understand the implementation details of provenance technology to benefit from it. 
 

 We also thought carefully about the distinction between edited content and untrustworthy content . 

 An image being edited doesn't automatically make it misleading. Photography and creative work naturally involve editing. 

 Content provenance isn't about labeling content as "good" or "bad." It's about providing transparency and context , so people can understand what happened and make their own informed decisions. 

 What we learned 

 Our biggest learning was that Content Credentials become much more approachable when we stop thinking about provenance purely as metadata people need to inspect . 

 Instead, provenance can become context that agents can reason over . 

 WebMCP provides an exciting bridge between these two worlds. 

 The underlying provenance can remain structured, machine-readable, and cryptographically verifiable, while the user experience can become as simple as asking: 

 
 "Tell me the story behind this image." 
 

 We also learned how important durability and interoperability are. 

 Content travels everywhere — through editing tools, websites, social platforms, downloads, screenshots, and even into the physical world. Provenance becomes most useful when people can continue discovering that history wherever the content travels. 

 What's next for VerifyHere 

 We imagine VerifyHere going far beyond inspecting individual images. 

 The same conversational provenance experience could extend to: 

 
 Creative libraries 
 Published media 
 Video 
 AI-generated and AI-edited content 
 Social content 
 Physical and printed media 
 

 Imagine asking: 

 
 "Which photos in my library are original camera captures?" 
 

 or: 

 
 "Show me everything derived from this original." 
 

 or simply: 

 
 "Can I learn more about where this came from?" 
 

 Agents could help creators trace their work, understand how it has changed, discover missing provenance, find originals, and receive attribution as their content travels across the internet. 

 Our vision is simple: provenance shouldn't be something you have to hunt for. It should be as easy as asking.

 Inspiration 

 I've always envied things I couldn't do well yet, like writing novels, and drawing. My hands are super stiff... 

 I've actually built relatively things before this challenge . I built a ai novel writer called "inkmarshal" simply because I want to write a novel for fun but my writing is bad, and I thought someone like me may interest in it. I built an image generate application call "lunerylab" as well for the same reason. 

 So combination of both easily come through my head. Plus my son is deep into
picture books — Dog Man gets read until the spine gives out — and I believe he will have fun by making one for himself. 

 So basically I prefer to use ai to achieve something with ai that I couldn't do well yet (still have chance and time who knows) 

 What it does 

 Apertale is a site for making cool interactive books. Its powered by WebMCP which make agent using our site creator tools. There are beautiful samples for you to read, and hopefully bring audience's interest. 

 Then you make your own. Give it a prompt, some photos, or both, and your ChatGPT
starts building pages inside the book you're looking at. Drag something it just placed. Or tell it to undo one thing, and it removes exactly that. Then one link to share it to anyone. 

 How I built it 

 I vibe coded it, serious vibe coding strategy. 

 Design first, because I'm super picky about UI/UX — probably 70–80% of my time went
there. Real comps in Figma and Codex (Production Design plugin) before any app
code existed. 

 I choose three.js for the book, because I prefer 3d and I used it a lot for making 3d game demo for fun. 

 I published it on gptsite, it is so convenient at this stage. I would love to host it on a domain if it scale. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 It has to be the images generation usage control and time consumption for this. A picture book eats art and one page at a time was too slow and too expensive. What I landed on: four pages per frame, then sliced apart. A quarter of the generations, and pages drawn together actually look like they belong together. 

 Also image bytes. WebMCP passes data, not files, so I made that handoff visible instead of pretending it happened. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The overall aesthetic, the whole feel of it. It is a project I would put out and show to anyone at any time. 

 Also the Agent Sketching feature too. You can mark up what you want changed and have the sketch actually change from that mark. That one came out better than I expected. 

 And most importantly, it works. Not a video, not a mockup. Open the link, read a book, make one with your agent, publish it. 

 What I learned 

 That the bottleneck was never the coding. It was knowing exactly what I wanted.
Every time I was vague with the AI I got something vague back, and every time I
could describe the thing precisely — this page turns like this, this reveals like
that — it came out right. 

 What's next for Apertale 

 Better asset handoff, cut down time usage. And I am also considering animations. Then background tasks.

 Dwa na Jeden — Autonomous Wedding Dance AI Coach 💃🕺 

 💡 Inspiration: From Static Chatbots to Active Physical Coaches 

 Every weekend around the world, wedding guests freeze in panic when invited to the dance floor. Traditional ballroom courses are slow and intimidating, while standard AI chatbots (like ChatGPT) can only give abstract text advice that fails to build physical muscle memory. 

 We asked: What if an AI Agent could actually step onto the dance floor with you as an active, real-time dance instructor? 

 Powered by the Model Context Protocol (WebMCP), Dwa na Jeden transforms the open web into an interactive, agent-driven dance studio. The AI agent doesn't just "talk" about dancing—it acts as an Autonomous Pilot , reading the exact millisecond methodology, inspecting real-time state, and dynamically orchestrating training sessions. 

 

 🤖 The WebMCP Paradigm: Knowledge, State & Action 

 Unlike standard chatbots that guess dance steps, an AI agent connected to Dwa na Jeden via WebMCP gains native programmatic control over the trainer. We implemented a complete 10-tool WebMCP suite (P1 Milestone) that moves beyond simple data retrieval into full application piloting: 

 
 Pedagogical Knowledge ( get_step_instructions , get_wedding_songs , recommend_song_by_bpm ): The agent retrieves structured JSON breakdowns for the 4-phase syncopation ("Raz, Dwa, Trzy, I"), sub-beat timings, and biomechanical rules (soft knees, low-friction sliding). 
 Real-Time State Inspection ( get_training_state ): The agent doesn't fly blind. It inspects the live session to see which foot is bearing weight, the active step phase, and playback status in real time. 
 Autonomous Orchestration (Action Tools): We exposed direct control tools like set_song , set_tempo , set_practice_mode , and start_practice . An agent can receive a prompt like "I'm a beginner, set me up and start" , and autonomously chain multiple tools to configure the UI and launch the YouTube engine with zero human UI clicks. 
 

 

 🎙️ Hybrid Voice AI Coach: Hands-Free Mastery 

 To ensure a true dance floor experience, we built a Real-Time Voice AI Coach directly in the browser. It bridges natural language commands into the same WebMCP TrainerBridge actions used by the AI agent. Whether using a laptop or a smartphone, the system understands "Start" , "Slow down" , "Baby steps" , or "Włącz Szaloną" with zero perceptible delay. 

 🛑 The Technical Challenge: The Mobile Audio Focus Battle 

 One of our biggest technical hurdles was the Hardware Audio Focus conflict on mobile devices. Standard continuous speech recognition on Android/iOS treats the microphone as a high-priority "call," causing embedded media (YouTube) to stutter, compress audio (Hardware Audio Ducking), or stop entirely. 

 The Solution: We engineered an Adaptive Audio Focus architecture: 

 
 Desktop: Full Continuous Hands-Free mode (mic stays open for the whole session). 
 Mobile: Discrete Adaptive Listening (Push-to-Talk) with immediate Hardware Audio Release. 
 

 By explicitly managing the hardware audio release and implementing a focus-switching buffer, we guaranteed 100% smooth, stutter-free 60fps video playback on smartphones —a critical requirement for maintaining rhythm during practice. 

 

 ⚡ Core Features 

 
 Interactive SVG Footwork Engine: Digital dance floor animating mirrored foot trajectories and weight distribution. 
 Haptic Pocket Metronome: Pairs Web Audio sync with the Web Vibration API for eyes-free blind practice. 
 Two-Way Video Synchronizer: Real-time tempo scaling (0.5× to 1.25×) synchronized with authentic YouTube party tracks. 
 Bilingual i18n Support: Full Polish and English localization for a global wedding audience. 
 

 

 🛠️ How We Built It 

 
 Frontend: Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion. 
 Integration: WebMCP (Native in-browser registration + /.well-known/mcp.json discovery). 
 Audio/Voice: Web Speech API, Web Audio API, YouTube IFrame API. 
 Quality & Testing: Verified 100/100 Google Lighthouse score (LCP < 600ms) with 8/8 automated Vitest unit tests passing in CI/CD. 
 Lead Architect & Methodology: Adam Gierczak. Built in synergy with AI assistants as a testament to modern agentic workflows. 
 

 

 🚀 What's Next 

 
 Computer Vision Pose Verification: Using WebRTC to verify knee flexion and foot contact in real-time. 
 Universal Partner Dance Protocol: Expanding the WebMCP tool schema to support Salsa, Bachata, and Kizomba timing. 
 Multi-Agent Coaching: Enabling "Lead" and "Follow" agents to coordinate couples training via WebMCP. 
 

 🌐 Live Demo: https://dwanajeden.netlify.app/

 Inspiration 

 I spend a lot of time playing card games online, but learning them can be frustrating. Tutorials are not always available, translations can be unclear, and most lessons force players through a fixed sequence of prescribed actions. They also make it difficult to revisit a specific situation or experiment with alternative moves. 

 I wanted a more interactive way to learn existing card games, recreate scenarios, and design new games with an agent that can explain the state, suggest actions, and participate in the simulation. 

 What it does 

 How I built it 

 Playing Cards Simulator exposes WebMCP tools that let an AI agent create a custom card game from an XState-compatible finite-state machine definition or launch an existing game such as Blackjack, War, Go Fish, Crazy Eights, Euchre, Gin Rummy, Bullshit, or Texas Hold'em. 

 The agent can inspect the current game state, explain what is happening, highlight available controls, coach the player through the next action, wait for the player's input, and act as a bot or dealer. This makes tutorials adaptive instead of forcing every player through the same fixed sequence. 

 The app is built with Next.js, TypeScript, React, XState, and WebMCP. XState provides a predictable model for phases, turns, actions, rewards, and transitions, while WebMCP exposes tools for creating sessions, reading state, guiding players, and performing simulated actions. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part was designing a general game model that could support both predefined and agent-generated card games. The tools also needed to stay synchronized with the browser session while handling navigation, stale connections, turn order, hidden information, and invalid actions safely. The latency was unbarely and the UX of the user nudging the ai via the agent chat every turn was awkward. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I built one simulator that supports both a catalog of familiar games and custom games defined by an agent. The same interface can teach rules, recreate a specific situation, guide a player interactively, and run bots or dealers without relying on a rigid tutorial script. I thought of the tool which waits for user input making the process fully immersive. 

 What I learned 

 Finite-state machines are a strong foundation for agent-controlled games because they make valid actions and transitions explicit. I also learned that effective agent guidance requires more than reading state: the agent needs tools to explain, highlight, pause for input, and act within clearly defined boundaries. 

 What's next for Playing Cards Simulator 

 Next, I want to expand the game catalog, improve custom game validation, add richer animations, and make tutorials more responsive to each player's choices. I also plan to improve session persistence and make it easier to share custom games and specific learning scenarios. I would love to repurpose this for RTS or create a DND game where the agent is the game master.

about_excerpt:
The MPC (Music Production Center) is a classic hardware sampler used by the likes DJ Shadow, Dr Dre, and Kanye West. This is the web version, all controllable via WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 The name, of course! What's more fun than a project with confusingly similar acronyms? 

 What it does 

 The MCP MPC makes the laborious process of trimming samples and making beats easy by allowing users to describe what they want in plain language. They can say "Gimme a lo-fi hip-hop beat but with electronic drums" or "Take this sample and pitch it down until it sounds like a sad ghost". The great thing about this is that by using WebMCP, musicians can actively collaborate in real-time with AI to make music - there's no automatically generated end result. 

 How we built it 

 With lots of Codex! I had the idea that the theme should follow the period in which the MPC became popular (90s) so I directed Codex to go with the 16-bit console theme. I also steered Sol to keep things fun and simple. I decided to deploy this to ChatGPT Sites as I had never done that before so wanted to learn more about it. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Codex and I have different tastes in music! Some of the synthetic sounds and sample choices were, eh, interesting. They mostly sounded quite harsh and abrasive. Not the laid-back defaults I was hoping for. I also had a small CORS issue on Sites which was easily fixed. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I think it's a really fun collaborative tool to use! Users can invoke the WebMCP interface to try out new ideas or tweak something existing. This seems like a glimpse into the future of music-making. I like giving the model really esoteric descriptions of drum patterns and seeing what happens. 

 What we learned 

 I'm glad I learned how powerful WebMCP could be in that I used it not just for pushing buttons on screen, but for altering precise values of sample timing as well. I was also surprised at how it encourages you to not solely use either the chat or the web interface. I've been using both 50:50. 

 What's next for The MCP MPC 

 I'd like to build out a more "pro" version, giving it even more capabilities. The problem with a lot of musical equipment is that its power is usually locked behind a thousand menus and a massive manual. WebMCP feels like it could cut right through that.

about_excerpt:
Upgrading existing web forms using WebMCP, not just the ones built from scratch for agents
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Forms are everywhere, but they were designed around clicks, typing, dropdowns, and rigid question flows. 

 We wondered: what if you could just talk to a form? 

 Instead of building another AI form product, we chose the form people already know and use: Google Forms. The goal was to make an existing web interface agent native without rebuilding it. 

 That became TapFill , a Chrome extension that adds a WebMCP powered voice interface to Google Forms, allowing an AI agent to understand, navigate, and fill forms through natural conversation. 

 What it does 

 TapFill turns an ordinary Google Form into a conversational interface. 

 Install the Chrome extension, open a Google Form, and activate TapFill. You can then simply talk to the form. 

 The agent can understand the form's structure, determine what information is needed, ask relevant questions, translate natural language into structured field values, fill the form, validate responses, and submit it. 

 The important part is that the form itself remains the interface . TapFill does not replace Google Forms with a new application. It adds an agent interface to the existing page. 

 A form built for humans can now be operated naturally by both humans and AI agents . 

 How we built it 

 TapFill is a Chrome extension that runs directly on the Google Forms page. 

 When a form is opened, the extension inspects its structure and creates a semantic representation of the available fields and actions. It then exposes those capabilities through WebMCP , allowing a compatible in browser agent to interact with the page through structured tools rather than trying to visually navigate or guess at DOM elements. 

 The extension provides tools for operations such as: 

 
 reading the form schema and current state 
 identifying unanswered fields 
 setting field values 
 validating responses 
 submitting the form 
 

 On top of the WebMCP layer, we built a voice interface that handles the human side of the interaction. The agent turns conversational answers into structured tool calls while the underlying Google Form updates in real time. 

 The architecture is intentionally lightweight: 

 Chrome Extension → Google Forms → WebMCP Tools → AI Agent → Voice 

 This lets us demonstrate WebMCP on a widely used existing website rather than requiring a new application to be built from scratch. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making an existing, third party web application agent friendly without rebuilding it. 

 Google Forms was never designed around an agent tool interface, so we had to bridge its existing UI and DOM structure with a clean, semantic WebMCP representation. 

 We also had to solve the harder problem behind "voice form filling": understanding conversational answers and reliably mapping them to the correct fields, while preserving the structured semantics and validation expected by the original form. 

 Finally, we had to make the experience feel like a conversation rather than speech to text controlling a webpage. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that TapFill demonstrates a fundamentally different way of interacting with an existing website without replacing the website itself . 

 The most satisfying moment is watching a completely ordinary Google Form transform from a sequence of fields into a conversation. 

 Technically, we're particularly proud of using a Chrome extension to retrofit WebMCP capabilities onto an existing third party web application , showing how agent native interfaces can potentially be layered onto the web that already exists. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the hard part of agentic interfaces is not simply getting an LLM to produce the right answer. 

 It is creating a reliable bridge between natural human intent and structured actions on the web . 

 We also learned that familiar interfaces are powerful. When the underlying Google Form stays visible and behaves exactly as expected, the leap from "AI demo" to "this could actually change how I use the web" happens almost instantly. 

 Most importantly, we learned that WebMCP can be interesting not only for websites built from scratch with agents in mind, but also as a mechanism for progressively making the existing web more agent accessible . 

 What's next for TapFill 

 Google Forms is just the beginning. 

 Our vision is to make existing web forms and workflows agent native , rather than forcing people to migrate to entirely new AI first applications. 

 TapFill could evolve from a voice layer for Google Forms into a broader compatibility layer for web applications, allowing agents to understand and operate interfaces that were never originally designed for them. 

 The web already has the interfaces. We want to give agents a way to use them.

 Why WebMCP 

 An AI agent animates a 3D character on this page. You open your figure, type what it
should do, and download the clip. The 20 tools sit inside the page where the figure
runs, so the agent works on the same figure you are looking at. 

 Better for the user 

 No animation software, no rig setup. The page measures your figure itself — height,
bone roles, sole points. The rest is one sentence in the chat, and you watch it happen. 

 What is new 

 Ask an agent for a backflip today and you get a figure that reaches through itself or
barely moves. Not because the AI is too dumb. It has too little to work with: it does
not know how tall the figure is, where its weight sits, how far a knee bends, or what
its last move actually did. 

 This page gives it all of that. You type a sentence, the agent builds the motion, and
what comes out is usable. 

 How it works 

 20 tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool : describe the figure,
set poses and joint angles, check the result, render an image. 

 Everything the tools report is measured on the loaded model, not hardcoded. Answers
carry numbers with units, and when the solver misses what was asked, it says by how
much.

about_excerpt:
a teleportation channel for codex agents on its own computer
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Millions of hours are spent every month watching your AI agent debug a side problem while your main task sits frozen. The checkout flow is half-built, but the payment API is returning 500, and now your agent is stuck investigating instead of shipping. 

 We wanted to build something that doesn't make you choose between progress and debugging. What if your agent could teleport a copy of itself into a separate desktop, fix the bug over there, and hand you the result while the original agent keeps building? 

 So we built Televerse. 

 What it does 

 Televerse is a WebMCP-powered web app. Your coding agent (Codex, ChatGPT, any browser-based agent) discovers seven tools on the page. When a side problem comes up, the agent calls teleport_agent with a task description. Televerse captures context from the current session, spawns a fresh Daytona sandbox with a browser and terminal, and a second agent investigates independently. When it finishes, it returns a summary, root cause, evidence, files inspected, commands and tests run, and an optional patch. The primary agent reviews and decides whether to apply. Your main task never stops. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js 16 custom server with Socket.io for real-time streaming. The WebMCP draft API ( document.modelContext.registerTool ) registers seven tools on every page load. Each teleport creates a separate session with its own Daytona sandbox, Socket.io room, and whiteboard, the primary session is never touched. Context is captured as a compact packet (prompt, recent todos, whiteboard, errors, constraints) and seeded into the teleported agent's system prompt. The frontend has a teleport modal, a live detail page with activity log and evidence panel, and a dev harness at /dev/mcp for testing tools without a browser agent. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The WebMCP API is a draft, only in Chrome 149+ behind a flag. We built a dual registry: real document.modelContext when available, a dev fallback on window for testing. The Daytona swap was mechanical but tedious, every sandbox tool call had to be rewritten to Daytona's unified API. The hard part was designing the TeleportContext: enough context to be useful, but compact enough that the teleported agent doesn't waste tokens. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The WebMCP surface works. Open the site in Chrome with the flag enabled, and any browser-based agent discovers teleport_agent immediately, no config, no API keys, no MCP server setup. The teleport lifecycle is fully observable: every state transition is logged, cancellable, and debuggable from the /teleport/[id] page. Zero LLM keys needed for the WebMCP path, just DAYTONA_API_KEY for sandbox provisioning. The teleport store has 15 passing tests covering creation, lifecycle, result storage, cancellation, and ownership. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes the agent-web contract. Instead of the agent scraping the DOM and guessing what to click, the site declares high-level tools with explicit schemas. The agent delegates, the site executes. The hardest design problem was the handoff, not how the sandbox boots, but how the teleported agent's result gets back to the primary agent in a structured, reviewable format. 

 What's next for Televerse 

 Adding DB persistence so teleports survive server restarts. Multi-session picker for the teleport modal. Optional autonomous computer-use agent that drives the desktop and collects evidence by actually clicking around. Git-aware teleport context that captures the current branch, diff, and recent commits. Daytona screen recordings for replaying the teleported agent's activity.

title: CargoPilot
pitch: Share a current Cargo page with your agent through WebMCP, with visible freshness and human-controlled editing boundaries.
about_excerpt:
Share a current Cargo page with your agent through WebMCP, with visible freshness and human-controlled editing boundaries.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Portfolio builders are visual, but collaborating with an AI in one often means describing a layout from memory or exchanging disconnected screenshots. CargoPilot explores a more explicit shared reference: the creator chooses a signed-in Cargo page, the agent receives its current visible context, and both know when that context is too old to trust. 

 What it does 

 CargoPilot connects a public WebMCP companion to a private local bridge. It exposes a screenshot, bounded semantic context, route and page information, capture time, and freshness state for a selected Cargo screen. The same context is available through a standard stdio MCP server. 

 There are two distinct connection paths. A Chrome extension lets the user click Share with Codex on an already signed-in Cargo tab. In Codex/ChatGPT's in-app browser, a browser-capable host agent can instead make an explicitly authorized capture and relay it using request_cargo_context and attach_cargo_context . Extensions cannot be installed inside that in-app browser; the hosted companion cannot independently inspect another tab or borrow its authentication. 

 The shared canvas is a read-only snapshot, not a second Cargo editor. Captures expire after 15 seconds. The UI marks stale and unavailable states, and context tools do not silently switch to another browser. The creator scrolls or edits in Cargo and asks the agent for a new capture when needed. 

 The Chrome extension also implements a separate time-limited approval path for two fixed recipes: exact text replacement and native Backdrop selection, with route and postcondition checks. Read-only sharing does not authorize these actions. The final live demonstration deliberately exercises only read-only context; it does not claim to demonstrate those editing recipes, asset uploads, arbitrary template editing, or publishing. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP turns the companion's collaboration boundary into named, typed tools. An agent can ask for workspace, screen, or editor context through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) instead of guessing what a screenshot or inactive canvas means. Inputs are validated, freshness is explicit, and inspection is separated from mutation authority. 

 The creator can discuss a specific page while the agent receives the relevant visual evidence and knows which site, page and capture it belongs to. The Chrome pointing interaction additionally shares viewport coordinates and a bounded accessible label. This reduces repeated manual explanation without treating unrestricted browser control as the default. 

 How we built it 

 
 Vite and TypeScript companion, hosted on Vercel, registering browser-native WebMCP tools. 
 Local Express service bound to 127.0.0.1 , with Zod input validation, short-lived context, audit state, and a standard MCP server. 
 Manifest V3 Chrome extension with explicit selected-tab sharing and a separate approved fixed-action path. 
 Browser-host attachment for the in-app browser, using actual screenshot capture and bounded visible context without moving cookies or passwords between browsers. 
 

 Codex assisted with implementation, debugging and testing. Remotion assembles real browser captures and measured capture sequences into the demo. The narration is AI-generated; the conversation section is explicitly labelled as a replay of our actual exchange, not a recording of the Codex interface. 

 Validation 

 The 4 September 2026 live pass retrieved a real authenticated Cargo dashboard and an editor page through the deployed WebMCP companion and an actual stdio MCP client. Both returned the relevant current screen and screenshot. Asking for editor context on the dashboard correctly failed. Expiry produced an explicit stale response and visible UI label. Losing the attachment removed the old canvas image and left unsupported typing controls disabled. 

 There are 64 passing automated tests, TypeScript checks pass, the hosted build passes, and extension 0.4.1 packaging and response-parsing checks pass. The installed Chrome extension's attach and mutation flow was not re-tested in this final live pass. No live Cargo mutation or publishing tool was called during validation or filming. 

 Challenges and lessons 

 Browser-session isolation was the central challenge: a hosted page cannot safely reuse an unrelated tab's login. The viable design is explicit sharing through a permitted Chrome extension or a browser-capable host, not a hidden second browser profile. Freshness also matters: an old screenshot must not be presented as live editor truth. 

 The lesson is that useful agent collaboration needs a trustworthy reference and a clear scope, not just many tools. CargoPilot is a local-assisted prototype, not a cloud-only mobile service or an autonomous general-purpose Cargo editor. 

 What's next 

 Package the local bridge as a signed installer, improve guided reconnection, and expand supported editing recipes only when each has deterministic verification. A first-party continuous host attachment API could reduce repeated captures without weakening consent.

pitch: Lulu Ads' commercial infrastructure for the agent economy, on WebMCP: real registerTool() tools where a disclosed, fail-open sponsored ad is live ad-network inventory, not a mockup.
about_excerpt:
Lulu Ads' commercial infrastructure for the agent economy, on WebMCP: real registerTool() tools where a disclosed, fail-open sponsored ad is live ad-network inventory, not a mockup.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 GIF 
 
 
 Tulip Trips: real WebMCP tools + a disclosed sponsored recommendation 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 GIF 
 
 
 Tulip Trips: real WebMCP tools + a disclosed sponsored recommendation 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 GIF 
 
 
 Tulip Trips: real WebMCP tools + a disclosed sponsored recommendation 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Lulu Ads builds the commercial infrastructure for the agent economy: disclosed, fail-open sponsored recommendations that surface inside real AI tool calls, already live in production across ChatGPT Apps, Claude Connectors, and CopilotKit. WebMCP -- a web page handing an AI agent real, callable tools directly via document.modelContext.registerTool, no separate MCP server required -- is the newest surface for that same idea. We built this project to answer one question directly: can a real ad live inside a real WebMCP tool result, stay honestly disclosed, and still feel like a genuinely useful recommendation instead of a banner bolted onto the page? Trip planning (weather + flights) is a theme any judge reviewing dozens of submissions understands in five seconds, which made it the right stage for that question. 

 What it does 

 Two real WebMCP tools, registered directly on the page -- and every single call is real Lulu Ads inventory: 

 
 get_weather -- real current conditions for any city (Open-Meteo), paired with a "Sponsored" travel.activities recommendation (things to do at the destination) 
 search_flights -- deterministic flight search between two airports, paired with a "Sponsored" travel.insurance recommendation (trip protection) 
 

 Both sponsored categories were live-verified by querying the real Lulu Ads network before being wired in -- this is not simulated ad data. Every sponsored result is clearly labeled "Sponsored," fetched through a same-origin backend route so the publisher API key never reaches the browser, and fails open to nothing at all if the ad network is slow or down -- a user never sees a broken page because an ad didn't load. 

 Open the manual demo in a WebMCP-capable agent and it calls both tools -- and requests both sponsored slots -- directly, no screenshots, no clicking. Open it in a regular browser and the same execute() functions power manual "Run" buttons, so nothing about the ad path is mocked for the demo. Tulip Trips (/demo) is the same two tools and the same two sponsored slots, driven by a real Gemini function-calling loop instead of buttons -- ask "what's the weather in Bangkok and find me a flight from TLV to BKK" and watch it decide when to call each tool, mention the sponsored offer naturally in its own reply, and close the loop with a trip-summary card. 

 How we built it 

 Vanilla HTML/CSS/JS on the frontend -- no framework, no bundler, safe DOM construction throughout, since sponsored ad text is real third-party advertiser content and never goes through innerHTML. A plain Node http server in TypeScript is the backend, deployed as a container on GKE. The chat demo uses the Vercel AI SDK (generateText + tool()) with Gemini, calling the exact same tool AND sponsored-slot logic the manual demo uses -- zero duplication. The ad integration itself runs through the lulu-ads SDK with a strict client/server split: the browser-side tool code calls a same-origin route, and only a server-side LuluAds instance ever holds the real publisher API key. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The most interesting bugs we hit were ad bugs, not WebMCP bugs. A fresh server's very first request to the ad network could occasionally miss its timeout budget and silently show no ad -- correct fail-open behavior, but not what we wanted on a cold demo. Root-caused to a new connection object being created per request, throwing away the SDK's own warm-connection tracking every time; fixed by sharing one instance across requests and warming it up before the server accepts traffic. On the UI side, our first pass rendered the sponsored content as its own floating card stacked under the result -- two boxes where a real MCP widget should read as one -- so we merged it into a single card, with the sponsored content as a footer band of the same widget. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A monetization layer that fails open by design and two sponsored categories live-verified against a real ad network instead of assumed -- get_weather and search_flights both carry real, disclosed Lulu Ads inventory, not a single hardcoded demo ad. And a manual demo and a full Gemini-powered chat assistant that share the exact same tool logic AND the exact same ad logic, with zero duplication between them. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP's registerTool is refreshingly small surface area -- name, description, JSON schema, execute() -- and because it's just a function running in the page, the exact same code path serves a manual UI and an agent with no fork in the logic, including the sponsored-slot call inside it. The harder design problem wasn't the protocol, it was making a sponsored recommendation feel like a natural part of a real result instead of an ad bolted onto one -- both in language (how the chat assistant discloses it) and in pixels (how the card renders it). 

 What's next 

 More tools (hotels, currency conversion) means more real Lulu Ads inventory categories to plug in, broader host testing as more WebMCP-capable agents ship, and richer sponsored categories as the underlying ad network grows.

title: Cherry
pitch: Cherry packages proven methods into verifiable, local AI tools. Teach once, run securely on your machine without API keys, and auto-verify completion with external checks.
about_excerpt:
Cherry packages proven methods into verifiable, local AI tools. Teach once, run securely on your machine without API keys, and auto-verify completion with external checks.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 1 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I follow a lot of builders on YouTube and LinkedIn. The useful part of what they teach never survives the watch. It stays in my head for a day, then it is gone, and my agents never learn any of it. Meanwhile every agent I use starts from zero on every task, no matter how much I have already figured out.
So I stopped trying to take better notes and built the thing that should exist instead. Content goes in, a skill comes out, and the skill lives where my agents actually work. 

 What it does 

 Cherry is a personal skill library that your agents can read.
Paste one link. A YouTube video, an article, a LinkedIn post. Cherry pulls the content, extracts the method inside it, and writes it back as a structured, reusable skill with prompts you can run.
Sources inbox. Everything you send lands in one lane and gets processed, so the library keeps growing without a ritual around each item.
The library is always available. Skills are versioned and editable, so a skill improves as you learn more rather than being frozen at the moment you saved it.
Connect it to your agents. Cherry runs as an MCP server, so ChatGPT, Codex, and Claude can list and pull your skills mid task. The site itself exposes WebMCP tools, so a browser agent sitting on the page can search the library and use a skill without any setup at all.
Bring your own reasoning. Connect your existing subscription or your own API key. Cherry does not resell tokens and is not trying to sit between you and your model.
The result is one library that follows you across every agent surface you use. 

 How I built it 

 Next.js and TypeScript on Vercel, React and Tailwind for the interface, Privy for auth with a guest first flow so you can try it before signing in anywhere.
The core is an extraction pipeline that takes a raw source, normalizes it into text, and runs a structured extraction pass that outputs a skill object rather than a summary. Summaries were the first version and they were useless to an agent. A skill needs steps, preconditions, and a prompt an agent can actually execute, so the schema is the product.
On top of that sit two access layers over the same library. An MCP server for desktop and CLI agents, and WebMCP tools exposed by the site itself for browser agents. Same skills, same source of truth, two doors in.
Everything is open source under MIT and designed to run at near zero cost, because a personal library you have to pay a subscription for is not a personal library. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 Getting real content in. Ingestion that works on a demo link and ingestion that works on arbitrary real world URLs are different problems. I built a compliant runner based fetch path first and left the heavier scraping adapter for after the deadline rather than shipping something fragile.
Deciding what a skill is. This took the longest. Too loose and the agent ignores it. Too rigid and nothing real fits the shape. It took several rewrites of the schema before agents started using skills correctly instead of politely reading them.
Two agent protocols, one library. MCP and WebMCP have different assumptions about state and identity. Keeping one library honest across both without duplicating logic drove most of the architecture.
Scope. Building solo against a hard deadline, the temptation is to add surface. I cut features until the core loop of paste, skill, use was clean. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The core loop works end to end. One link in, a usable skill out, and that skill available inside a real agent session with no copy paste.
The site is a real MCP surface, not a landing page with a demo video. A browser agent can act on it directly.
It is fully open source and cheap to run, so anyone can fork it and own their own library instead of renting one.
I built it solo and it feels like a product rather than a hackathon prototype. 

 What I learned 

 Agents do not need more context, they need better shaped context. The same information as prose gets skipped and as a structured skill gets executed.
WebMCP changes what a website is for. Once the page exposes tools, the interface stops being the only way in, and you start designing for a human and an agent reading the same thing.
Also, cutting scope is the feature. Every thing I removed made the remaining loop more obvious. 

 What's next for Cherry 

 A browser bubble that sends the current tab into Cherry in one click, so capture happens where you already are.
Skill proposals from watch history, so Cherry suggests what to learn instead of waiting to be fed.
A deeper ingestion adapter for sources that resist a plain fetch.
A visual watcher that learns from what happens on screen in a video, not just the transcript.
Scheduled runs, so skills get refreshed and re run on a cadence without you touching them.

 Inspiration 

 Every agent either just talks, or does things you can’t see and can’t stop. We wanted one that does real work in the open and leaves every decision that costs money to you. 

 What it does 

 You type a goal. Cardea plans it, runs the steps in parallel in real browsers you can watch, and comes back with real prices. Anything that spends, sends, or signs stops and asks you. ChatGPT can drive the whole thing through 13 WebMCP tools. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js on Vercel. Supabase for an append-only mission log. Inngest for durable runs that pause on approval and resume. Cloudflare for real headless Chrome streamed onto the canvas. GPT-5.6 for planning. Shopify’s agent protocol for real carts. 890 tests. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Big retailers served bot walls, so we made Cardea say “this site blocked me” instead of inventing prices. We built an enforced approval gate, it broke in the real ChatGPT browser, and we pulled it the same hour. ChatGPT preferred its own browser over ours until our tool descriptions said when to use them. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 It runs end to end on real websites and ends on a real cart. It admits what it couldn’t verify. We tested the tools in ChatGPT itself, not just our own harness. 

 What we learned 

 Test where you’ll be judged. Measure before you fix. The agent and the human have to see the same thing, or it’s theater. 

 What's next for Cardea 

 Enforce approvals in the browser, carts from any store, more connected apps, and a real mobile view.
