title: Briefly
pitch: Briefly lets content teams research trends, bring in business context, and co-write briefs with an AI agent that sees and acts on the same app state.
about_excerpt:
Briefly lets content teams research trends, bring in business context, and co-write briefs with an AI agent that sees and acts on the same app state.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Selecting a trend and offering makes the relevant tools available for agents to compose and save a brief. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Turn a rising trend into a structured, on-brand content brief ready for review. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give agents your audience, brand voice, offerings, and claim guardrails to guide every brief. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Explore trend signals, growth charts, and sample content to find your next angle. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Review the draft and approve it when it’s ready—AI assists, you decide. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Selecting a trend and offering makes the relevant tools available for agents to compose and save a brief. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Turn a rising trend into a structured, on-brand content brief ready for review. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give agents your audience, brand voice, offerings, and claim guardrails to guide every brief. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Explore trend signals, growth charts, and sample content to find your next angle. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Review the draft and approve it when it’s ready—AI assists, you decide. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Selecting a trend and offering makes the relevant tools available for agents to compose and save a brief. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 A trending keyword is easy to find. A useful content brief is harder. You need
the source material, the right audience, the product you actually want to sell,
and a clear list of what the business can and cannot claim. 

 We kept thinking about the annoying part of this workflow: why do we still copy
a trend from one dashboard, open the product notes somewhere else, explain all
of it again in a chat, then copy the answer back into a document? Every move
loses a little context. 

 So we built Briefly around one idea. What if the agent works in the same
workspace as the person, understands what they are looking at right now, and
writes the result back into the actual workflow? 

 What it does 

 Briefly puts trend discovery, business context, content briefs, a calendar, and
performance examples in one browser workspace. 

 The flow is simple. A person opens a trend, reads its source material, and
chooses a business offering. Once both are selected, the agent can read the
full context and write a draft into the brief library. The person can inspect
the draft, create their own version in the composer, change its workflow
status, or schedule it on the local calendar. 

 This is where WebMCP matters. Briefly does not give the agent one giant static
list of tools. Its tool surface changes with the interface. Open a trend and
the detail tools appear. Open the business-profile editor and the editing tools
appear. Select both a trend and an offering and get_brief_context ,
 generate_brief , and save_brief become available. Remove either selection
and those tools disappear again. 

 There are 37 tool definitions in the app, but they are not exposed all at once.
The point is not the number. The point is that the right tool appears when the
person and the agent have enough context to use it. 

 The current prototype uses seeded trend and performance data. It does not fetch
live social metrics, prove engagement growth, or publish anything to a social
platform. A "published" status in Briefly is local planning state, not a real
network post. Saved briefs can be inspected and moved through the workflow,
but their content cannot yet be edited in place from the library. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. We kept the runtime
small: React + React DOM are the only runtime packages. Browser-local stores
hold the briefs, business profile, watchlist, calendar, and tool traces. 

 WebMCP tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool . Their
lifecycle follows the same React route and selection state that controls the
interface. The human controls and agent tools call the same store functions, so
when the agent navigates or saves a draft, the person sees it happen on screen. 

 We also built a local console bridge that exposes the same schemas and executor
functions in browsers without native WebMCP support. It is useful for
development and inspection, but we do not treat bridge access as proof of a
native WebMCP flow. 

 Two optional Vercel endpoints use Gemini for trend analysis and draft
generation. The core agent flow does not depend on them. A connected agent can
read the context, write the brief itself, and save the draft through
 save_brief . 

 The interface uses CSS custom properties with warm off-white surfaces and
oxidized-iron accents. We added committed checks for tool contracts, surface
changes, important UI states, and the production build. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was not registering a tool. It was deciding when that tool
should exist. 

 A static catalog looked complete, but in practice it gave the agent actions
that could not succeed yet. Briefly had to track the route, the open trend, the
selected offering, and whether an editor was open. That is what made the tool
surface feel connected to the product instead of attached on top of it. 

 Host compatibility was another real problem. Some WebMCP hosts support tool
registration but do not provide the event-listener methods the inspector first
expected. We changed the inspector so native registration stays intact while
its discovery view can fall back to the local registry. 

 We also had to be strict about what this prototype proves. Seeded metrics are
not customer results. Local workflow state is not social publishing. The
optional deployed model endpoints still need repair and a full retest, and
some captured cover images still need documented permission or replacement.
Hiding those limitations would make the demo sound stronger, but the product
less trustworthy. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that the demo is not just a chat response beside a dashboard. The
agent can navigate the same workspace, read the selected context, and leave a
real draft inside the library for the person to review. 

 The app now has 37 state-dependent tool definitions across eight tested surface
states. It covers discovery, business context, brief creation, scheduling,
performance, and the trace log. Human controls and agent calls share the same
stores, so the two paths do not quietly create different versions of the app. 

 We are also proud of the less visible work. generate_brief returns an unsaved
draft. save_brief always creates a draft. Tool calls receive trace IDs, and
the agent can inspect the same trace log shown to the person. The tool-contract
suite currently passes 51 checks, including invalid inputs, refusal paths,
idempotent operations, and recovery actions. 

 What we learned 

 More tools do not automatically make a better agent experience. Sometimes the
best tool is the one that stays hidden until the context is ready. 

 We learned that human and agent parity also goes both ways. If the person can
add something to a watchlist, stop a video, correct a calendar entry, or inspect
a failed action, the agent needs a safe way to do that too. Creation alone is
not enough. The agent needs to read, undo, and recover. 

 We also learned to separate saving from deciding. save_brief creates a draft,
but another tool can still move its local status forward. That means Briefly is
not a human-only approval system yet. Being precise about that distinction is
important, especially in a demo where a local "published" label can easily be
mistaken for a real post. 

 What's next for Briefly 

 First, we want to replace the seeded trend data with a transparent source of
real data and test whether Briefly actually saves time for content teams. 

 Second, we want to add authentication, shared persistence, and proper review
permissions so a team can see who changed a brief and who approved it. 

 Third, we need to finish the unglamorous but necessary work: repair and retest
the deployed Gemini endpoints, resolve or replace the cover images with missing
permissions, and test the full workflow across more native WebMCP hosts. 

 The bigger goal is still the same. We want the agent to understand the work
that is already happening on screen, help at the right moment, and leave
something useful behind when the conversation ends.

title: RELAY — Proof Before Power
pitch: Human-governed WebMCP authority for incident response.
about_excerpt:
Human-governed WebMCP authority for incident response.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for RELAY — Proof Before Power 

 RELAY — Proof Before Power 

 Human-governed WebMCP authority for incident response. 

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are increasingly capable of investigating incidents and proposing production actions. 

 But sensitive execution creates a governance problem: an ordinary approval workflow can leave the underlying agent capability continuously available, with only a permission check standing between investigation and production change. 

 RELAY explores a different model: 

 What if the human decision changed what the agent was actually capable of doing on the web? 

 What it does 

 RELAY gives an agent nine persistent WebMCP capabilities for incident investigation, evidence gathering, deployment comparison, hypothesis building, recovery preparation, and verification. 

 The sensitive production execution capability does not exist. 

 The agent can investigate the incident and stage one bounded recovery proposal, but it still cannot execute production recovery. 

 Only the visible human action: 

 AUTHORIZE THIS ACTION 

 changes the live WebMCP capability surface. 

 At that moment: 

 09 → 10 

 One exact temporary capability is registered: 

 execute_authorized_recovery 

 The agent can use it once to carry out the approved recovery. 

 In the demo: 

 
 deployment #4821 becomes #4819 
 error rate falls from 31% to 0.8% 
 recovery is verified 
 execution count becomes 1 
 

 Immediately after execution, the temporary capability is removed: 

 10 → 09 

 A replay cannot execute another recovery. 

 Why WebMCP 

 RELAY is not simply an API call hidden behind an approval button. 

 The important state is the actual browser-visible WebMCP capability surface. 

 Before authorization, the production execution tool genuinely does not exist. 

 After the human decision, one exact capability appears. 

 After its single use, it disappears. 

 WebMCP makes that authority native to the interaction between the web application and the agent. 

 How it improves the user experience 

 The human does not need to manually perform the entire incident response. 

 The agent can investigate, assemble evidence, compare deployments, form a hypothesis, and prepare a bounded recovery proposal. 

 At the same time, the agent does not receive standing production authority. 

 The consequential decision remains human. 

 The resulting flow is: 

 investigation → human judgment → bounded execution 

 rather than forcing users to choose between full manual operation and persistent agent authority. 

 What humans and agents can do together 

 The agent handles the evidence-heavy investigative work. 

 The human decides whether production authority should come into existence. 

 After authorization, the agent completes the exact approved recovery without requiring the human to manually execute the production action. 

 Then the authority disappears. 

 RELAY expresses human governance as a change in agent capability, not merely as an approval flag. 

 How we built it 

 RELAY uses real document.modelContext WebMCP registration. 

 Nine persistent tools support investigation and recovery preparation. 

 The state-changing recovery execution capability is intentionally absent. 

 A human-only UI authorization dynamically registers execute_authorized_recovery for the exact approved recovery. 

 After its single execution, that capability is removed. 

 Final live QA verified the registry lifecycle directly: 

 09 → 10 → 09 

 The execution capability was absent initially, appeared only after human authorization, executed once, and was genuinely removed afterward. 

 What's next 

 RELAY is a focused demonstration of ephemeral, human-governed agent authority. 

 The same capability pattern could be explored for other consequential web actions where investigation can be delegated broadly but execution should be created narrowly, explicitly, and temporarily.

about_excerpt:
Structured WebMCP actions turn one sales objective into a visible, human-controlled lead pipeline.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human approval unlocks the final Pipeline transition and leaves an audit trail. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 One visible workspace for five structured WebMCP actions. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ChatGPT finds five target-profile leads through search_leads. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Atlas scores 91/100, Grade A, with an explainable qualification result. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent prepares outreach, but the draft stays unsent and human-gated. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human approval unlocks the final Pipeline transition and leaves an audit trail. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 One visible workspace for five structured WebMCP actions. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ChatGPT finds five target-profile leads through search_leads. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Atlas scores 91/100, Grade A, with an explainable qualification result. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent prepares outreach, but the draft stays unsent and human-gated. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human approval unlocks the final Pipeline transition and leaves an audit trail. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Sales prospecting is fragmented across search, company websites, spreadsheets, scoring tools, outreach editors, and CRM systems. Browser agents that rely on guessing which visual control to click can be brittle, while sensitive final actions still require human judgment. 

 AI Lead Desk was built to show a different model: give an AI agent a small set of structured WebMCP actions, keep every transition visible in the interface, and preserve a real human approval boundary. 

 What it does 

 AI Lead Desk turns one sales objective into a visible five-stage workflow: 

 Find → Research → Qualify → Prepare Outreach → Human Approval → Pipeline 

 ChatGPT can: 

 
 find five matching companies, 
 research the strongest candidate, 
 qualify the lead against a defined target profile, 
 prepare a personalized outreach draft, 
 and move the lead into Pipeline only after explicit human approval. 
 

 The outreach remains Draft / Not sent . The challenge version does not send email or WhatsApp messages. 

 The current demo uses synthetic logistics and freight-forwarding companies in Dubai. They are demonstration data, not verified real prospects. 

 How we built it 

 AI Lead Desk is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. 

 The application registers exactly five native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 search_leads 
 research_company 
 qualify_lead 
 prepare_outreach 
 add_to_pipeline 
 

 The WebMCP tools and the visible UI use the same validated domain actions and application state. That means tool execution, lead stages, qualification results, approval state, and the Activity Log remain synchronized. 

 For live execution, the application sends validated tool requests to a server-side Next.js endpoint. A secure n8n router handles the five known actions. The webhook URL and credential remain server-side and never enter the browser bundle. 

 A deterministic DEMO_MODE fallback is also available for network-independent testing. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 The agent handles the repetitive work: lead discovery, company research, qualification, and draft preparation. 

 The human retains control where judgment and accountability matter. 

 add_to_pipeline cannot be authorized by the agent itself. Approval must first be recorded through the visible Approve for pipeline interaction in the application. 

 Clicking approval does not send outreach. It only authorizes the final Pipeline transition. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenges were: 

 
 verifying native WebMCP discovery and execution in a real supported browser client, 
 keeping agent actions and visible UI state on one shared workflow, 
 enforcing a genuine human-controlled approval boundary, 
 normalizing five typed actions through one secure n8n router, 
 and making the draft-only outreach behavior unmistakable. 
 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Exactly five native WebMCP tools are exposed. 
 A complete production workflow works from lead search through approved Pipeline transition. 
 Atlas Freight Network scores 91/100, Grade A in the canonical demo. 
 Human approval is enforced before the final transition. 
 Outreach remains Draft / Not sent . 
 Live n8n routing works in production. 
 42 automated tests across 10 files pass. 
 Lint, TypeScript validation, and production build all pass. 
 The full production E2E flow was verified successfully. 
 

 What we learned 

 Structured browser tools are more useful when they do more than expose actions. They also need strict contracts, shared application state, lifecycle cleanup, visible feedback, safe error handling, and clear authority boundaries. 

 WebMCP lets the agent perform predictable actions without guessing how the interface works, while the human can still see and control the workflow. 

 What's next 

 The commercial direction is to connect verified company-data providers, customer-specific qualification criteria, and integrations with existing CRM or sales systems. 

 Any future outreach-sending capability would require its own explicit review and authorization design. 

 The challenge version intentionally remains focused on lead research, qualification, draft preparation, and human-controlled pipeline management. 

 Data disclosure 

 All company records and evidence shown in the current challenge demo are synthetic test data. No claim is made that the demo generated verified real leads or sent real outreach.

title: Lattice Perps
pitch: A safety-first WebMCP trading cockpit for Hyperliquid: agents propose bounded paper trades, humans control authority, and every action is policy-checked with transparent receipts.
about_excerpt:
A safety-first WebMCP trading cockpit for Hyperliquid: agents propose bounded paper trades, humans control authority, and every action is policy-checked with transparent receipts.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Web agents can operate a web page, but actions that change state still need to be understandable, inspectable, and safe. 

 We wanted to explore what an agent-native trading interface could feel like without asking anyone to connect a wallet, approve a signer, or risk real funds. Lattice Perps is our answer: a browser-local paper-trading experience where a human and a browser agent can use the same interface, the same account, and the same visible evidence. 

 The project is inspired by Hyperliquid perpetual markets, but this public showcase intentionally stops at deterministic local simulation. 

 What it does 

 Lattice Perps is a paper trading flight recorder for WebMCP. 

 The app starts with one browser-local paper account containing $100,000 of simulated USD and four fixed markets: 

 
 BTC 
 ETH 
 SOL 
 HYPE 
 

 A human can place market or limit orders from the visible interface. Market orders fill at the displayed simulated mark price. Limit orders rest locally and can be cancelled by their local order ID. 

 A browser agent can perform the same paper-trading actions through six WebMCP tools: 

 
 paper_get_markets 
 paper_get_portfolio 
 paper_get_open_orders 
 paper_get_activity 
 paper_place_order 
 paper_cancel_order 
 

 Every human action, system event, and WebMCP call is written to the visible Agent Tape . The portfolio panel updates from the same underlying account state, showing equity, available balance, margin used, realised PnL, unrealised PnL, positions, open orders, and fills. 

 The key idea is simple: 

 
 One local account. One shared state. Two ways to interact. 
 

 You can trade from the page or ask your browser agent: 

 
 Buy 0.05 BTC at market, then show my paper portfolio. 
 

 The result is visible in the Agent Tape and reflected in the portfolio immediately. 

 How we built it 

 The app is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. 

 The human interface and WebMCP tools share one LocalTradingStore . This prevents the UI and agent surface from developing separate balances, positions, orders, or activity histories. 

 The store provides: 

 
 deterministic simulated markets and mark prices 
 market and limit order handling 
 position netting and PnL calculations 
 simulated fees and margin checks 
 local order cancellation 
 browser persistence through localStorage when available 
 an in-memory fallback when browser storage is unavailable 
 a visible activity history for human and WebMCP actions 
 

 WebMCP registration is feature-detected through the browser's document.modelContext surface. If WebMCP is unavailable, the human trading interface still works. Tool inputs use explicit schemas and reject unexpected fields so the agent surface remains narrow and predictable. 

 The project also includes automated tests for the local trading store, WebMCP tool definitions, and the rendered paper-trading interface. 

 Safety by design 

 This showcase deliberately has: 

 
 no wallet connection 
 no exchange connection 
 no network order submission 
 no real funds 
 no private keys 
 no deposits or withdrawals 
 no production trading capability 
 

 WebMCP is treated as an invocation layer, not an authentication or authorization mechanism. The public demo is designed to make the interaction model visible without pretending that a browser tool registration is equivalent to trading authority. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest part was making the human and agent paths genuinely share state. A separate “agent balance” or fake tool response would have made the demo look convincing while hiding the real interaction model. Instead, both paths call the same store and produce the same portfolio projections and activity records. 

 Another challenge was making the demo useful even when the browser does not support WebMCP. The interface therefore remains complete on its own, while WebMCP enhances it when the browser exposes the API. 

 Finally, we had to make the boundaries clear. A trading demo can easily imply that a real exchange, wallet, or signer is involved. The local simulation, explicit labels, and Agent Tape are designed to keep the demo honest. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that agent-native interfaces benefit from visible evidence, not just successful tool calls. A tool invocation is much easier to understand when the user can see its source, timestamp, status, and effect on the shared account. 

 We also learned that deterministic simulation is valuable for WebMCP development. It makes the experience reproducible, easy to reset, and safe to demonstrate while the browser API and authority model are still evolving. 

 What's next 

 A future version could connect this interaction model to a separately approved testnet account behind explicit human authority, policy checks, and post-action reconciliation. 

 For this submission, we intentionally keep the public experience local, deterministic, and risk-free.

pitch: Looop brings teams together to plan, collaborate and resolve issues in one place, with WebMCP-enabled AI agents that can manage events for you.
about_excerpt:
Looop brings teams together to plan, collaborate and resolve issues in one place, with WebMCP-enabled AI agents that can manage events for you.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP allowing agent to summarise event 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Looop Event Dashboard 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP allowing agent to summarise event 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Looop Event Dashboard 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP allowing agent to summarise event 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Group chats are often the main go-to for communication when planning for events and projects. However, the actual plan and flow of logistics often end up buried under jokes, photographs, and various digresses from conversation. As such, this results in confusion and frustration with messages like "Did anyone see my message about xxx?" or "At what stage are we for this plan?" or "Sorry, what are my responsibilities for today again?". 
This is where WebMCP fits the use case well. By allowing AI agents to interact directly with structured web interfaces, WebMCP can help agents read the latest plan, understand assigned responsibilities, and take actions on the board without relying on noisy chat history. This creates a shared and structured source of truth that both people and AI agents can easily understand and act upon. 

 What it does 

 Looop gives every event (wedding party, offsite, household chore chart) one shared board, which includes tasks grouped by urgency, flagged issues for attention, day-by-day timeline and a computed event health score. The core actions on the board such as creating and editing tasks, flagging and resolving issues, are exposed as MCP tools. Users can simply ask their agent "What tasks are still open on the wedding board?" or "Add an urgent task for the caterer" or "Flag that the venue has not confirmed headcount". The agent can even act as a collaborator, proposing concrete next steps for a stuck task or open issue , as well as starter tasks for event based on its title and description , and providing a concise summary of the event history . 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is hosted on Vercel and backend on Render. The frontend of Looop was built with React and Typescript on the frontend, Tailwind for UI styling. It has a Go backend on Chi with MongoDB for storage. The WebMCP layer lives on the frontend with document.modelContext.registerTool() covering full CRUD on events, its tasks and issues plus status actions like complete_task and resolve_issue and multiple tools that let the agent write suggestions and catch the user up on the event progress. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The gap between UI implementation and connecting with the rest of the pipeline also turned out to be a challenge. The frontend was first built against mock data which expedited the design process, but the process of wiring every page to the backend surfaced a long list of real bugs. These included route prefixes that did not match between frontend and backend, and a field name mismatch that silently dropped task notes. This also affected the WebMCP testing in ChatGPT's in-app browser, since the underlying API calls had to work reliably before I could register tools that depended on them during execution. I also learnt to budget more time for WebMCP edge cases, such as incomplete requests and ambiguous inputs, rather than focusing only on the ideal tool flow. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting the full loop working with an agent in ChatGPT's browser calling a real tool, hitting the hosted Go backend and writing to the database, and having that change show up on the board was the largest accomplishment. I was happy for not just settling for CRUD as the whole product and registering tools such as get_event_summary computing a genuine health score instead of just listing rows, and suggest_task_completion/suggest_issue_resolution letting the agent contribute reasoning to the board, not just data entry was also one of the main goals achieved. 

 What we learned 

 The main concept here was implementing MCP hands-on to create a functional project and learning the concept from scratch. One of the biggest concepts learnt was the difference between MCP and WebMCP, particularly that WebMCP tools are registered directly on the frontend through the browser rather than being exposed from a backend MCP server. 
A lot of learning also came from testing the tools repeatedly and handling edge cases. I had to check that every tool was callable, that fields and routes matched correctly across the codebases and that incomplete requests were handled gracefully. For example, creating a task without an assignee meant deciding how the tool should respond or whether it could fall back to the current user, while ambiguous member names required additional resolution. Thus, I learnt that thorough testing is essential when building agent-facing tools. 

 What's next for Looop 

 In the near future, Looop could move towards real authentication and user accounts , replacing the current localStorage-based placeholder identity with secure accounts that persist across devices. We also see potential in richer integrations , connecting Looop with calendars and other tools that people already use for event planning, making it easier to keep everything in sync without having to switch between different platforms. Based on user feedback, more WebMCP tools could be registered on Looop to efficiently serve real-world purposes for collaborative event planning.

pitch: A WebMCP-native support navigator where humans control sensitive facts and agents use structured, auditable tools instead of scraping brittle interfaces.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native support navigator where humans control sensitive facts and agents use structured, auditable tools instead of scraping brittle interfaces.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Rule-heavy support and public-service websites are difficult for both people and browser agents. A person may need to understand many conditions, while a generic agent often has to scrape rendered text, guess what controls mean, and automate fragile clicks. We wanted a safer collaboration model: the human controls the facts, while the agent receives explicit, typed capabilities. 

 What it does 

 AidPath Agent Bridge is a WebMCP-native, privacy-first support navigator. It exposes six structured tools that let an agent discover illustrative support options, analyze a structured case, explain one option, compare alternatives, load a safe demo case into the visible UI, and prepare a next-step checklist. 

 The agent does not decide eligibility. Both the human interface and the WebMCP tools call the same deterministic JavaScript rule engine. Matched and missing conditions remain visible and auditable, and meaningful agent actions are shown in an activity log. 

 Why WebMCP is the right fit 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer intent from DOM structure, scrape result cards, and depend on brittle selectors. With WebMCP, the website publishes stable domain capabilities with JSON Schema contracts. The human can inspect or correct facts while the agent performs structured orchestration. This makes the experience faster, more reliable, and easier to audit. 

 A workflow that previously required repeated reading, copying, clicking, and re-checking can become a collaboration: the person reviews sensitive inputs and final evidence; the agent lists options, evaluates the same deterministic rules, compares alternatives, and prepares actionable next steps. 

 How we built it 

 The application is a standalone HTTPS static web app. It registers six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , uses typed JSON Schemas, and annotates read-only operations with readOnlyHint . A local intent layer helps organize free text, but authoritative conditions remain deterministic. There is no backend, account, or persisted user profile. 

 The app degrades gracefully when WebMCP is unavailable and remains fully usable as a normal website. We also created a visible capability status and agent activity log so the user can understand when structured agent interactions occur. 

 Challenges 

 The key design challenge was avoiding an architecture where the LLM silently becomes the decision-maker. We separated agent orchestration from rule evaluation and made the same deterministic functions serve both the human UI and the WebMCP layer. We also documented the distinction between prior AidPath work and the new WebMCP extension with timestamped commit history. 

 Native WebMCP verification 

 On September 3, 2026, the deployed HTTPS app was tested in Chrome 151 on Windows with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and Chrome relaunched. Chrome's native document.modelContext.getTools() discovered all six tools, and native document.modelContext.executeTool(...) successfully executed all six: 6/6 discovery and 6/6 execution PASS . The student case produced Student Stability Bridge 3/3 as the top deterministic result; Housing Stability Support 2/3 exposed Core documents ready as the missing condition; visible agent activity was recorded in the workbench log. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most valuable when a site exposes meaningful domain actions rather than simply mirroring buttons. A small set of well-designed tools can replace a large amount of fragile UI automation while preserving human review. 

 What's next 

 This challenge build uses explicitly illustrative programs. A production version would connect to verified official sources, attach source URLs and effective dates to every rule, version rule changes, and require human review before consequential use.

Plan your household budget with your browser agent — every change is a proposal you approve

 Story

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Budgeting a household is a shared decision between people — and increasingly, between a
person and an AI agent. Handing an agent full write access to your money is wrong. Making it
scrape and click a human UI is worse. WebMCP offers a third path: give the agent real tools
and keep the human in the loop at the only moment that matters — approving the change. 

 What it does 

 Budget Bench is a household budget workbench where the browser agent and the human work on
the same live page: 

 
 The agent reads the whole budget with get_budget_summary (income, category budgets,
spend, what's over/tight, pending proposals). 
 The agent acts through five proposing tools: find_savings (trims discretionary
categories and moves the difference to savings), set_category_budget ,
 add_category , record_spend , and propose_plan (full rebalance to hit a savings
target, fixed costs untouched). 
 Every mutation is a proposal. Tool calls never write to the budget. Each one lands in
the human-visible Proposal Tray with a plain-English summary and the agent's reason. 
 The human approves or rejects each proposal (or the whole tray). Approvals apply
atomically; every proposal and every decision is written to the activity log. 
 

 Why WebMCP is the strong fit 

 
 Agent tools, not agent autonomy. Household money is exactly the case where an agent
should propose and a human should decide. WebMCP tools carry structured schemas, so the
agent gets a reliable contract instead of DOM scraping; the tray guarantees the human veto. 
 What people + agents can do together that was hard before: a two-minute conversation —
"energy bill's up £35, find the money from discretionary" — becomes three reviewed,
reversible, explained edits instead of a spreadsheet session. The same shared page also
means the agent always sees the effect of its own proposals before the human decides. 
 Shared context, not replicated state. The page state is the app: no backend, no
accounts, no auth replication. That's only possible because WebMCP runs tools where the
state already lives — in the tab the human is looking at. 
 

 How we built it 

 One static page (vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, zero dependencies, zero build step) with a single
state object and one render function. Six tools registered via
 document.modelContext.registerTool({name, description, inputSchema, execute}) per the
WebMCP draft. Proposals carry apply closures, so approval is atomic and the tray doubles
as a transaction log. Tool logic is covered by an automated Playwright suite (27 checks:
registration, schema behaviour, proposal isolation, approve/reject application, error
paths) which stubs only the browser side of modelContext — the app's tool code runs
unchanged. Hosted on Surge. MIT licensed. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Designing tools that are genuinely useful to an agent while guaranteeing the human veto:
every mutating tool needed to become a proposal generator rather than a writer, which
reshaped the whole state model. Also pacing propose_plan so fixed costs stay untouchable
and the plan lands as ONE reviewable decision instead of a barrage of edits. 

 Accomplishments we're proud of 

 The proposal tray pattern: six tools, one hard invariant — the agent proposes, the human
decides — and the activity log that proves it. 

 What we learned 

 That "agent-accessible" and "human-controlled" are not a trade-off if the tool layer is
designed as a proposal system rather than a command API. 

 What's next for Budget Bench 

 CSV import of real bank data (local-only), per-category proposal bundles, and a
"what-if" tool that compares two plans side by side in the tray.

 Planning a workshop or vehicle shelter starts with ordinary language but quickly becomes structured: use case, footprint, height, roof, openings, material, anchoring, budget, and unresolved site constraints. A normal chat can suggest an answer, but the reasoning often disappears into prose and the page on screen drifts out of sync. 

 BuildBrief Studio makes WebMCP the product interface between those two modes. The visual worksheet and six imperative Website Tools share one validated configuration. An agent can discover catalog options, compare two or three candidates, apply a partial recommendation, read the result back, review constraints, and create a preliminary brief. Write tools update the visible UI before returning and leave exact field-level receipts. If the person changes a value afterward, the revision advances and the old brief is visibly marked stale. 

 The demo is deliberately safe and easy to judge: no login, no personal information, no external API, and no production system. Every dollar value comes from a bundled synthetic catalog and a deterministic formula. Strict schemas and runtime validation reject extra fields and incompatible choices. Read-only annotations match behavior. Permit, access, anchoring, snow-load, and site conditions remain explicit human work rather than being hand-waved by automation. 

 The result is a small but complete example of what WebMCP enables: not an agent operating beside a website, but a person and agent collaborating through one observable decision surface. 

 How WebMCP is used 

 
 search_catalog discovers relevant structures from natural-language needs. 
 get_build_state grounds the agent in the person’s latest visible choices. 
 compare_builds evaluates two or three validated alternatives in one call. 
 apply_build performs a partial visible update and returns exact before/after changes. 
 check_constraints separates catalog fit from human verification. 
 create_build_brief renders a deterministic handoff artifact on the page. 
 

 All tools are registered imperatively from the top-level page through document.modelContext.registerTool . They use strict JSON Schema, truthful read/write annotations, concise structured output, and an AbortSignal lifecycle. 

 Quick judge path 

 Open the live demo in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, wait for “6 Website Tools ready,” and send the demo prompt shown on the page. Verify that the agent searches, compares against the $15,000 illustrative budget, applies an enclosed 20 × 24 workshop with a roll-up door, surfaces human checks, and creates the visible project brief.  I built BuildBrief Studio to explore a better workflow—one where a person and an AI agent collaborate through the same visible, reviewable workspace. 

 What it does 

 BuildBrief Studio turns a rough structure request into a transparent preliminary project brief. The visual worksheet and six imperative Website Tools share one validated configuration. An agent can: 

 
 discover structures in a synthetic catalog; 
 read the person's current visible choices; 
 compare two or three complete candidates against a budget; 
 apply a partial recommendation to the worksheet; 
 identify constraints that still need human verification; and 
 create a copyable preliminary brief. 
 

 Write tools update the visible UI before returning and leave exact field-level receipts. If the person changes a value afterward, the revision advances and the old brief is visibly marked stale. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 WebMCP is the product interface, not an add-on beside it. The agent acts through explicit tools while the person watches the same worksheet change. This makes agent actions observable, reversible, and easier to review than recommendations buried in a chat transcript. 

 Together, a person and agent can move from an imprecise request to compared alternatives, a selected configuration, documented assumptions, and a usable handoff artifact—without creating a hidden agent-only state. 

 How I built it 

 The app is built with Astro, React, and TypeScript and deployed on Cloudflare Pages. It registers six imperative tools from the top-level page using document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 search_catalog 
 get_build_state 
 compare_builds 
 apply_build 
 check_constraints 
 create_build_brief 
 

 The tools use strict JSON Schema, runtime validation, truthful read/write annotations, structured results, and AbortSignal-aware execution. The tool layer and visible React controls share the same state adapter. 

 Every price comes from a bundled synthetic catalog and deterministic formula. There is no login, personal information, external API, or production pricing system. Permit, access, anchoring, snow-load, and site conditions remain explicit human-review items.

 The hardest part was keeping the visible interface and agent-readable state synchronized while making every mutation auditable. I also had to prevent incompatible configurations, distinguish catalog fit from real-world feasibility, and make stale generated briefs obvious after manual edits. 

 As a beginner working with WebMCP, I learned how careful tool schemas, validation, annotations, lifecycle handling, and visible receipts turn an AI interaction into a dependable product workflow. OpenAI Codex helped me implement, debug, test, and harden the project, but I reviewed the generated work against the running app and its automated tests. 

 What's next 

 The hackathon build deliberately uses synthetic data and stops before any production quote or permitting decision. The next step is to apply this human-and-agent collaboration pattern to my real carport business, with authenticated data, server-side pricing, audit trails, and the necessary engineering and compliance checks.

Evidence before engineering: a shared product-validation workspace for founders and AI agents.

 Story

 Mock-first by default: optional public adapters, explicit consent, and transparent source availability. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Seven native, page-bound WebMCP tools connect an agent to the same human workspace. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Mock-first by default: optional public adapters, explicit consent, and transparent source availability. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Seven native, page-bound WebMCP tools connect an agent to the same human workspace. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Mock-first by default: optional public adapters, explicit consent, and transparent source availability. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI makes software faster to build, but it also makes it easier to build the wrong product faster. A founder can ask an agent to create an entire SaaS before testing whether the problem is painful, frequent, reachable, or worth paying for. BuildCheck adds an evidence-first checkpoint before implementation begins. 

 What it does 

 BuildCheck helps founders decide whether to build, validate, pivot, or stop before investing weeks of engineering time. It scores an idea across demand, pain, willingness to pay, distribution, competitive opportunity, build simplicity, and defensibility. It keeps confidence separate from the Build Score, preserves provenance, and returns one of four explicit outcomes: BUILD, VALIDATE FIRST, PIVOT, or KILL. 

 The human workspace provides guided validation, reports, comparisons, opportunities, methodology, settings, and an Agent activity log. The agent surface exposes seven native WebMCP tools: 

 
 validate_idea 
 roast_idea 
 get_project_analysis 
 generate_validation_mvp 
 estimate_build_cost 
 find_opportunities 
 evaluate_before_build 
 

 An agent can challenge an idea, inspect a saved analysis, estimate the full-build scope, and propose the smallest validation MVP. A write-capable validation call creates a project in the current browser workspace, so the founder can immediately continue in the dashboard. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Product validation is not one isolated prompt. It is a sequence of decisions over structured project state: collect an idea, challenge assumptions, inspect evidence, compare the cost of a full build with a smaller test, and decide what happens next. WebMCP lets the agent operate the same product workflows that a human uses without a separate integration server or a duplicated scoring implementation. 

 BuildCheck is deliberately page-bound. The tools inherit the open workspace and current session, register only when the browser exposes the native WebMCP API, and are removed when the workspace unmounts. The human remains responsible for the final product decision; the agent provides structured evidence, warnings, and a smaller next action. 

 A better user experience 

 Without WebMCP, a founder copies an idea between a chat, spreadsheets, search tabs, and a planning tool. Context and provenance disappear along the way. With BuildCheck, the founder can ask in natural language while the agent calls typed product actions. The resulting project, score, evidence, MVP, cost range, and audit event remain visible in the same workspace. 

 The interface also makes uncertainty honest. Generated summaries do not count as market evidence. Public-source failures are visible. If there is not enough evidence, the agent returns INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE instead of manufacturing confidence. 

 How people and agents collaborate 

 People provide product judgment, consent to optional external research, and choose whether to invest. Agents handle the repetitive analytical chain: challenge the idea, retrieve the current analysis, calculate cost ranges, apply the pre-build guard, and propose a measurable validation MVP. Both use the same services and see the same locally persisted workspace state. 

 This makes a useful interaction possible: “Should I build this?” can become a traceable project decision rather than an ungrounded chat answer. 

 How we built it 

 BuildCheck uses Next.js 16, React 19, strict TypeScript, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and Vitest. The WebMCP bridge uses document.modelContext.registerTool with feature detection and an AbortController lifecycle. JSON Schemas are generated from Zod, every handler returns structured output, and annotations distinguish read-only tools from the write-capable validation tool. 

 The human UI, HTTP endpoint, and WebMCP handlers call the same domain services. The score, confidence model, verdicts, cost estimates, and ownership checks therefore have one implementation and one test suite. 

 We started mock-first behind AIProvider and DataSourceProvider contracts so the complete product and UX work deterministically without third-party credentials. We then added an opt-in public evidence aggregator with eight interchangeable adapters. External lookup is explicit per analysis, sends only a few derived keywords, preserves source URLs and provenance, tolerates partial outages, and falls back to clearly labeled demo evidence only when every source fails. Adapter availability depends on the source; RSS requires configured feeds. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest part was not registering seven functions; it was making agent actions obey the same product and safety rules as the interface. We had to keep generated narrative separate from evidence, separate confidence from score, prevent project enumeration, make external research consent explicit, and retain useful behavior when native WebMCP or public providers are unavailable. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Seven native WebMCP tools with strict schemas and structured results 
 Stateful human-agent continuity in the same browser workspace 
 Deterministic, explainable scoring with explicit insufficient-evidence behavior 
 Mock-first provider architecture plus eight opt-in public evidence adapters 
 English default UI with a complete optional French translation 
 PWA support, security headers, rate limits, ownership checks, and minimal safe logs 
 62 automated tests plus lint, strict typecheck, and production build validation 
 

 What we learned 

 The most valuable agent tool is often a guardrail, not a generator. A reliable pre-build tool must be able to say “not enough evidence,” expose why, and recommend a cheaper experiment. WebMCP is especially compelling when it connects natural-language intent to an existing, inspectable product workflow instead of hiding logic in a remote black box. 

 Current scope and what is next 

 This submission is a working demonstration, not a production multi-tenant SaaS. It uses a demo user, browser-local storage, and MockAIProvider. Demo evidence is labeled; optional public research is not a guarantee of market demand. 

 Next we would add real authentication and durable multi-tenant persistence, shared rate limiting, connector observability and caching, evidence deduplication, and controlled A/B evaluation of live sources against deterministic scenarios. Real AI providers remain optional because an LLM should summarize and challenge evidence, never invent proof or choose the final score. 

 Try the human-agent workflow 

 
 Open https://buildcheck-webmcp.vercel.app/agents in a browser with native WebMCP support, such as ChatGPT's in-app browser. No login is required. 
 Confirm that seven site tools are available. 
 Ask: “Should I build an AI CRM for freelancers? Use BuildCheck before writing code.” 
 Inspect the PIVOT result, clearly labeled demo evidence, full-build warning, and smaller proposed test. 
 Ask: “What is the cheapest way to validate it?” 
 Open the dashboard and Agent activity to verify continuity. The human interface also works without WebMCP support.

Day Canvas is a visual planner where you and AI shape your day together—adding, moving, and organizing tasks live on one shared canvas.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Day Canvas: Building a Planner Shared with AI 

 What inspired it 

 Day Canvas began with a simple frustration: planning tools and AI assistants often live in separate places. You might describe a change in a chat, then manually reproduce it in a calendar or task list. I wanted to make that handoff disappear. 

 The idea was to create a shared workspace where a person and an AI can plan the same day together. Instead of receiving a text-only confirmation, the user can watch the canvas change as the AI adds, moves, prioritizes, or removes work. The result is a planning experience that feels collaborative, visible, and grounded in the actual schedule. 

 What I built 

 Day Canvas is a visual daily planner with a timed calendar, a task inbox, priority controls, and day/week/month/year views. Users can add blocks, drag them to reschedule, manage unscheduled tasks, and see overlapping events arranged clearly in separate lanes. 

 The defining feature is browser-native WebMCP integration. An AI agent can use tools to inspect the schedule, find open time, add or move calendar events, triage inbox tasks, and delete items. Those tool calls operate on the exact same actions as the user interface, so the canvas stays in sync and changes animate live. AI actions also have their own feedback, including activity toasts, a moving cursor for reschedules, and a deletion animation. 

 How I built it 

 I built the interface with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and a custom client-side store. The planner canvas renders a vertical time grid, while reusable components handle event cards, calendar views, inbox tasks, theme controls, and agent activity. 

 The core architectural decision was a single source of truth for task and calendar mutations. Both drag-and-drop interactions and WebMCP tool handlers call the shared functions in lib/taskActions.ts . This keeps UI actions and AI actions consistent: there is one set of validation rules, one state update path, and one way to announce changes. 

 WebMCP tools are registered in the browser after the app mounts through document.modelContext.registerTool . The AI can therefore reason about the open day using functions such as calendar summary and free-time search, then make a targeted update without a separate MCP server. 

 For scheduling, the free-time logic treats each event as an occupied interval. If an event begins at (s_i) and lasts (d_i) minutes, its occupied range is 

 [
[s_i,\; s_i + d_i).
] 

 After sorting events by start time, the app finds gaps between these ranges and returns the first gap that can fit a requested duration. That makes suggestions practical rather than merely descriptive. 

 Challenges I faced 

 The hardest challenge was ensuring that AI edits felt trustworthy. An AI must not be a separate, hidden layer that happens to modify data; its changes need to be understandable to the person looking at the plan. I addressed this by routing agent actions through the same shared action layer as user interactions and by giving those actions visible motion and feedback. 

 Calendar layout was another challenge. Events can overlap, have very short durations, recur across dates, or belong in different views. I added collision-aware lanes for simultaneous events and compact card layouts for 15- and 30-minute blocks so the calendar remains readable instead of becoming visually crowded. 

 Finally, browser-native AI integration required careful boundaries. Tool inputs are defined with schemas, calendar updates validate time formats and durations, recurring events require an end date, and free-time calculations distinguish scheduled calendar events from independent inbox tasks. These constraints help the agent make useful changes without creating impossible or ambiguous schedules. 

 What I learned 

 This project taught me that AI features are strongest when they are embedded directly in a familiar workflow. The most valuable interaction is not simply asking an AI for advice; it is seeing that advice become an understandable, reversible action in the tool already being used. 

 I also learned the value of designing state and interaction models before adding intelligence. Because Day Canvas has shared task actions and explicit scheduling rules, the UI and the AI can work together without drifting into separate versions of the truth. Good AI UX depends as much on clear product feedback and reliable state management as it does on the model itself. 

 Where it can go next 

 The current project lays the groundwork for authenticated, persistent planning with Clerk and Supabase. Next steps include resilient offline syncing, per-user timezones, production deployment, and richer scheduling assistance that respects priorities, deadlines, and personal working patterns.

 Inspiration 

 Dinner is rarely blocked by a lack of recipes. It is blocked by a chain of small decisions: what is already in the kitchen, what fits the time and diet, what can be substituted, what is missing, and what to do next. 

 We wanted to turn that fragmented process into one clear, collaborative flow where an agent can help without becoming a black box. 

 What we built 

 PantryPilot is a WebMCP-enabled cooking app that turns pantry ingredients into a complete dinner plan and guided cooking session. 

 The agent can read the kitchen, select and scale a recipe, replace ingredients, prepare a shopping list, start cooking mode, and set persistent timers. Every action updates the same Zustand state used by the interface and appears in the visible Agent Trace. 

 The Golden Demo plans a vegetarian dinner for two, prioritizes tomatoes, replaces dairy with oat milk, identifies missing ingredients, pauses for human approval, and then starts the cooking flow. 

 How we built it 

 The app uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Zod, and the WebMCP imperative API. Zod validates tool inputs, while Zustand provides one persisted state layer shared by human interactions and agent tools. 

 We exposed ten structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . This lets agents operate named actions with validated inputs instead of guessing from pixels. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 The hardest part was making the agent experience reliable, deterministic, and understandable. We needed every tool action to update the visible UI correctly, survive reloads, fit documented input and output budgets, and behave consistently during the Golden Demo. 

 The most important design decision was the human-approval boundary. The agent may prepare missing groceries, but it cannot approve, purchase, or submit payment. This keeps the experience useful while preserving user control at consequential moments. 

 PantryPilot taught us that capable agents need equally strong visibility, validation, and boundaries. WebMCP makes the app directly operable by an agent, while the interface keeps the person informed and in control.

pitch: A browser agent prepares the invoice review. A person makes the payment decision.
about_excerpt:
A browser agent prepares the invoice review. A person makes the payment decision.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Deterministic checks stay separate from the agent actions. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The exact $200 invoice hold and its supporting evidence. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent can stage a draft. A person confirms or dismisses it.

 The exact $200 invoice hold and its supporting evidence. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent can stage a draft. A person confirms or dismisses it. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Deterministic checks stay separate from the agent actions. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 PayablePilot already had a clear safety boundary: the agent could finish routine
work, but a person had to decide what happened to an invoice exception. WebMCP
made it possible to carry that same boundary into the browser. The agent no
longer needs to infer state from a dense dashboard or click the same buttons as
the reviewer. 

 What it does 

 The page exposes two WebMCP tools. review_payables_queue returns the current
run, source document IDs, exact price variance, allowed actions, and decision
status. stage_invoice_resolution puts one permitted choice into a visible
Agent Draft. It cannot confirm the draft, release a payment, or contact the
supplier. 

 The included run has two fictional invoice packets. One clears. PP-2086 stops
because eight units were invoiced at $119 instead of the $94 purchase-order
rate. The deterministic difference is $200. An agent can read that evidence and
stage the credit-and-hold option. A person still checks the evidence and either
confirms or dismisses the draft. 

 How I built it 

 The live page is a React and TypeScript app. It registers two tools with
 document.modelContext.registerTool() , uses strict JSON Schema inputs, and
returns concise JSON. The review tool carries the read-only annotation. The
staging tool updates visible page state but has no code path to record a final
decision. An AbortController unregisters both tools with the component
lifecycle. 

 The queue facts live in one typed module shared by the tools and tests. The test
suite independently checks the $200 calculation, the pending human-confirmation
status, and rejection of actions outside the two visible choices. 

 Challenges 

 The hard part was making the browser tool useful without quietly widening the
agent's authority. A tool that clicked the final button would have been easy to
demo and wrong for the product. I split the flow at the decision boundary: the
agent can prepare the review, while the final click stays with the person who is
accountable for the payment. 

 I also had to treat the existing project honestly. PayablePilot predates this
challenge, so the repository documents exactly what was added after August 25
and the dated commits isolate the WebMCP work. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Both tools are detected and callable on the public page in ChatGPT's in-app browser. 
 The live staging call produces the same visible Agent Draft shown in the demo. 
 No agent tool can approve an exception or send anything to a supplier. 
 All 17 tests pass, including three focused WebMCP boundary tests. 
 

 What I learned 

 The most useful browser tools are often smaller than the interface around them.
Two narrow tools were enough here. One reports exact state. One prepares a
reversible draft. Keeping those jobs separate made the agent easier to guide and
the safety boundary easier to verify. 

 What's next 

 The next step is connecting the same tools to a real authenticated review queue.
The browser contract would stay narrow, while the server would add organization
policies, duplicate-invoice checks, reviewer identity, and a durable audit log. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 Invoice review is a poor place for an agent to guess from button text. The page
contains a purchase order, invoice, receipt, arithmetic, and a hard approval
boundary. WebMCP gives the agent a small, typed contract for reading that state
and putting one allowed choice in front of the reviewer. 

 The agent does not scrape the page, calculate the difference, invent an action,
or click through a payment decision. PayablePilot returns the exact $200.00
variance from deterministic application data. The write-capable tool can only
stage one of the two choices already present in the interface. It cannot confirm
either choice. 

 Work added during the challenge 

 PayablePilot existed before The WebMCP Challenge. The WebMCP implementation,
visible agent draft, safety boundary, tests, and this documentation were added
after the submission period began on August 25, 2026. Git history provides the
dated record required for a pre-existing project.

title: Proofboard
pitch: Evidence-first decision rooms where browser agents structure source-backed research while humans retain approval and final-decision authority.
about_excerpt:
Evidence-first decision rooms where browser agents structure source-backed research while humans retain approval and final-decision authority.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Technology decisions are usually split between chat transcripts, spreadsheets, browser tabs, and memory. Research becomes hard to audit, conflicting claims are easy to miss, and an agent can appear more certain than the evidence allows. Proofboard turns the decision page itself into a durable, inspectable collaboration surface. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Proofboard is a strong fit for WebMCP because the agent must work with the exact state the person is viewing—not a detached copy hidden inside a chat. Native tools let an agent read human-authored constraints, add structured candidates and source-backed claims, and immediately update the same interface. Human edits are visible to the next tool call. 

 What people and agents do together 

 A browser agent can read the room, add candidates, attach validated evidence URLs, and ask Proofboard to surface conflicts and missing fields. It can prepare a shortlist proposal for human review. People can directly edit constraints, inspect every source, exclude or restore candidates, review proposals, and make the final decision. 

 This division of authority is intentional: Proofboard exposes no finalize_decision agent tool. The Make final decision action exists only in the human interface, and the audit trail distinguishes human and AI changes. 

 Better user experience 

 Instead of copying research out of chat, users get one persistent decision room with structured evidence, visible uncertainty, validation errors, provenance, and a human gate. Tool calls update the UI immediately; UI changes are available to subsequent tool reads. The human interface remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 How it was built 

 Proofboard is a React/Vinext application deployed on ChatGPT Sites. The UI and all 16 native WebMCP tools share one immutable reducer and browser-persisted state model. After client mount, the app obtains document.modelContext and registers tools with registerTool(...), typed JSON input schemas, read/write annotations, bounded inputs, URL validation, duplicate rejection, and abort-based unregister lifecycle handling. 

 Read tools cover decision state, constraints, candidates, evidence, conflicts, missing evidence, history, and approval status. Write tools create rooms, constraints, candidates, exclusions, evidence, and shortlist proposals. Applying a shortlist is gated on prior human approval. 

 Verified behavior 

 In Chrome's native WebMCP environment, the public site exposed 16 tools and passed a 5/5 native smoke check. A real natural-language tool run added three candidates to the live UI. A later live state contained four source-backed records, one conflict, and nine missing evidence fields, with AI-attributed history and persisted state visible. 

 The recorded demo does not claim that the pending human-approval step or shortlist application was completed. It shows only the behavior actually captured and verified. 

 Challenges and learning 

 The main challenge was preserving one source of truth across direct human edits, asynchronous agent writes, persistence, and strict validation. WebMCP made the product boundary clearer: agents contribute structured work, while consequential approval and final selection remain visibly human-controlled.

title: Relay — Safe Shift Handoffs via WebMCP
pitch: Relay closes the missing hour between closing notes and opening accountability — WebMCP lets agents read live shift context and propose safe handoffs, but only humans can approve.
about_excerpt:
Relay closes the missing hour between closing notes and opening accountability — WebMCP lets agents read live shift context and propose safe handoffs, but only humans can approve.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Why I built this 

 Closing shift notes are the problem. Someone writes "fridge stayed warm" or "till's off by 400" and then... nothing. The note sits there. Maybe someone reads it before opening tomorrow, maybe not. Nobody's actually assigned to check. I started calling that gap the missing hour and it's the whole reason Relay exists. 

 What it does 

 Relay is a shift handoff tool, built around cafés with more than one location. A handoff doesn't get marked "safe" unless every real risk — fridge, cash, stock, whatever — has an owner, a deadline, and a backup plan attached to it. An agent can go read the actual shift notes, figure out on its own if something in there is a real risk, even draft a plan for who should own it and by when. But it can't approve any of that. I didn't want to just tell the agent not to approve things — I wanted it to actually not be able to. So there's no tool it can call that marks anything as verified. That has to happen from a person clicking a button in the app. 

 I tested this the annoying way, by trying to break it. Asked an agent flat out to confirm a handoff was approved before I'd touched anything. It said no. Checked the audit log, saw nothing there, told me so. Didn't make something up to be helpful. That's when I knew the thing actually worked, not just looked like it worked in a demo. 

 How I built it 

 React, TypeScript, Vite. No backend. The agent talks to the app through one thing: document.modelContext.registerTool , the browser-native WebMCP API. Eight tools — six just read data (shift context, which risks are unowned, the raw notes, the audit trail, a summary across both locations), two that write, and even those two only ever create a draft. Never a done thing. 

 The bug I almost shipped 

 My tests all passed. Then I ran it in actual Chrome with WebMCP turned on instead of my own mocked version, and registration just... failed. "Illegal invocation." Took me a minute to get why — I'd grabbed registerTool off the object and called it on its own, detached, which a real browser method won't allow but a plain JS mock in a test doesn't care about. So my whole test suite had been quietly passing against something that behaved nothing like the real API. Fixed it with a .bind() . Then went and broke my own test stub on purpose so it can't lie to me like that again. 

 What's next 

 Real backend instead of seeded data, actual roles for owner/manager/staff, real POS hookups. The one rule that doesn't move: the agent can find stuff and suggest fixes. A person still has to say yes.

title: AeroRun — a shared human + agent shoe shop
pitch: Two doors, one catalog: twelve WebMCP tools in the tab you already have open, and the same shop with no tools at all.
about_excerpt:
Two doors, one catalog: twelve WebMCP tools in the tab you already have open, and the same shop with no tools at all.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Shopping is multi-step and stateful. Size, stock, comparison and checkout only make sense in the tab the shopper already has open. Without WebMCP, an agent scrapes cards, fakes clicks, invents product IDs, and can be hijacked by page copy. 

 We wanted a store that stays the product: a person and a browser agent share one catalog, one bag, and one screen. 

 What it does 

 AeroRun is a sample shoe shop with two doors and one prompt. 

 
 /agent-storefront/tools registers twelve WebMCP tools on document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext . The same actions also drive the in-page chat, so the human grid, comparison and bag update when you type. 
 /agent-storefront/without-tools is the same shop with no site tools. The chat can only read visible card copy. 
 

 On the tools shop the agent can search, inspect, compare, read stock, shortlist and stage a bag. Staging is a draft. The page waits for Keep and stage . Only Review and confirm finishes the demo. Every run returns purchased: false . Nothing is bought or paid. 

 Poster Low injects a bait line to stage the Wholecut. A stability-road ask does not follow that bait. 

 We do not claim a citation in ChatGPT or any answer engine. The measurable result is: the agent can use the live tab — or it cannot, when tools are absent. 

 How we built it 

 The tools shop checks document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext on load. If either exists, it registers twelve tools with one AbortController . Leaving the page aborts the signal and drops the tools. 

 Each execute runs the same catalog functions as the human filters, then writes into shared React state. Tools return text plus structured IDs, stock and draft state. 

 stage_cart requires a tab nonce from get_tab_nonce , refuses product IDs the agent has not already seen, and does not resolve until the human clicks. ask_shopper is the same handshake for a question. read_shopper_intent reads a private field that is not in card HTML. seal_demo hashes the run and returns purchased: false . 

 The in-page chat on /tools is not a sidecar bot. It calls those same actions so the shopper can navigate the store they already have open. The without-tools chat never gets them. 

 Stack: Next.js, React, TypeScript, WebMCP, Vitest. Catalog and photos are original sample data. No login, no payment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Making the control honest. The without-tools door had to be the same shop and the same prompt, with no silent catalog calls. Page copy is not a tool argument. 

 Keeping checkout human. stage_cart had to wait on a visible overlay and a per-tab nonce, not auto-confirm. 

 Shipping a public Next.js 16 build to Vercel without output: 'standalone' , which currently breaks Vercel's trace step. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Twelve tools in the open tab, plus an in-page chat on the same state. A second door that proves the difference. A bait card that does not steal a stability ask. A sealed demo that stays purchased: false . 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is useful when the page is the source of truth. The agent should not get a second store. The human should see every irreversible step. 

 What's next for AeroRun 

 The same handshake on a live catalog: more SKUs, more tabs, more agents. In-page chat for the shopper, site tools for the external agent, one shared cart — without turning checkout into an unsupervised click. 

 How to try it 

 Live: https://aerorun-webmcp-six.vercel.app/agent-storefront 

 Health / SHA: https://aerorun-webmcp-six.vercel.app/agent-storefront/health 

 Public repo: https://github.com/hukaBU/aerorun-webmcp 

 Use this prompt on both shops: 

 Find a stable road shoe in EU 43 under $150. Compare it with the best cushioned option. Check availability in EU 43 — Cloud Rest should be out of stock. Shortlist the shoe that is actually in stock, then stage it in the bag. Do not buy anything. Only the human can press Review and confirm. 

 Expected on /tools : Stride Guard 27 is the structured match. Cloud Rest EU 43 is out. Overlay → Keep and stage → Review and confirm. purchased stays false. 

 Expected on /without-tools : no site tools. Stride Guard still lands in the bag. Poster Low is not followed. 

 ChatGPT desktop: open the /tools URL, then Site tools — you should see twelve tools. Open /without-tools — you should see none. 

 Chrome 149+: enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , reload /tools . Badge should read 12 WebMCP tools live . 

 Artwork credit 

 All product images are original, unbranded, and generated for this demo. They are not stock photos of real commercial shoes and are not affiliated with any footwear brand.
