title: BeatMCP
pitch: A live collaborative beat canvas where people and AI agents build four-bar instrumentals together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A live collaborative beat canvas where people and AI agents build four-bar instrumentals together through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 BeatMCP 

 BeatMCP is a collaborative beat-making canvas built for the WebMCP Challenge. 

 Inspiration 

 Making music with AI often feels disconnected: you describe a beat, wait for a result, then try to explain what feels wrong. I wanted a more natural workflow where a person keeps creative control while an agent can contribute directly inside the same music workspace. 

 The core question was: what if an agent could use a music-making web app through structured controls instead of guessing how to click through the interface? 

 What it does 

 BeatMCP is a four-bar, 64-step beat canvas where a person and an agent can build an instrumental together. 

 The studio includes drums, bass, piano, guitar, bell, keys, pad, and lead lanes. Users can set tempo and key, program steps manually, and shape a beat in a shared timeline. 

 Agents can use WebMCP tools to: 

 
 read the current pattern and musical state 
 set tempo, key, and scale 
 write drum, bass, melody, and chord patterns 
 create chords on Piano, Keys, and Pad lanes 
 humanize timing and velocity 
 reset a beat, start playback, and begin a live composition session 
 list playable instruments and save/reuse patterns 
 

 A key feature is live composition. When an agent writes a new layer, BeatMCP auditions the first new sound in sequence—such as kick, bass, chords, then melody—while the changed steps flash on the grid. This makes the agent's creative process visible and audible instead of hiding everything until the end. 

 How we built it 

 BeatMCP is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zustand, Tone.js, and the @mcp-b WebMCP libraries. 

 
 Next.js and React power the browser experience. 
 Zustand keeps the beat, tracks, tempo, key, and pattern state synchronized. 
 Tone.js synthesizes drums and instrument voices in the browser. 
 WebMCP exposes structured tools directly from the page so agents can work with the same musical controls as users. 
 The studio uses a 64-step master timeline so a beat can develop across four bars rather than being limited to one short loop. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was making the human-agent collaboration feel trustworthy in real time. 

 Browser audio needs an initial user gesture, so we designed the flow around one Start click before an agent can begin live composition. We also had to prevent overlapping transport loops, keep WebMCP tool discovery fresh after page reloads, and make agent edits understandable through visual flashes and queued sound auditions. 

 Another challenge was avoiding a traditional “AI generates everything” interaction. We wanted the agent to be musically useful without replacing the producer's judgment. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP is most compelling when the agent has precise, meaningful controls and the person can immediately understand the consequences of each action. 

 For music, that means an agent should not just return text or a finished file. It should be able to set a key, place a kick, write a chord, audition a sound, and respond to human feedback in the same live workspace. 

 Why WebMCP 

 BeatMCP becomes meaningfully better because agents can use the web app directly through structured tools. The agent reads the real state of the beat and changes the same instrument lanes the person sees and hears. 

 That creates a collaborative workflow: the agent handles musical structure and repetitive programming, while the person decides what feels right.

title: BuildVsBuy.ai
pitch: BuildVsBuy.ai is a live build-vs-buy canvas. Humans and WebMCP agents share one decision model — weights, future stress, honest overrides — with every call in the tool log.
about_excerpt:
BuildVsBuy.ai is a live build-vs-buy canvas. Humans and WebMCP agents share one decision model — weights, future stress, honest overrides — with every call in the tool log.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Prototypes got cheap. Decisions didn't. 

 I kept seeing the same mess: someone ships a little tool for fun, then hits auth or scraping and freezes on build vs buy. ChatGPT will write you a confident paragraph. Ask again and you get a longer paragraph. You're still doing the math in your head. 

 I didn't know this domain well when I started. I just didn't want another essay. I wanted the page to move when the agent did something, and I wanted to see the call in a log so it couldn't just agree with me. 

 What it does 

 BuildVsBuy.ai is a decision canvas in the browser. You and the agent share one model. Nine WebMCP tools. Cards, weights, a future-stress banner, an override with a gap and a liability list. 

 If it says Build dropped, the log has to show a rerank. If the log didn't change, it guessed. 

 The demo walk: 

 
 Auth. You admit you're shipping a prototype fast. Build usually falls last. 
 Switch to scraping. "What if HIPAA and 50k users?" That's a simulation. Baseline cards stay put. 
 You still want to own the crawler. It pins Build, shows how far that is from the math, and lists what you're taking on. 
 

 Numbers on the axes are my estimates for the demo. Not vendor quotes. Not financial advice. 

 How I built it 

 Vite, vanilla JS, no backend. Vercel. 

 Tools live in src/webmcp.js ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). Math lives in src/decision.js . The UI just redraws a snapshot. Human sliders and agent calls hit the same execute path, tagged human or agent so the log isn't lying about who did it. 

 I also wrote two smoke scripts so I wasn't debugging this only through ChatGPT's mood that day. 

 What I learned 

 Soft instructions do not save a live agent. It will skip the rerank. It will invent cards. It will pin Buy because some flag wasn't set. 

 The stuff that actually held on camera was refusing the bad call in the tool itself. Prompt text is decoration. 

 Also: WebMCP is useful when the page is a real store, not when you ask the model to "look at the screenshot." 

 Challenges 

 Recording almost killed me. Same session, Prompt 2 did the right tool and nothing moved because the weight was already 10 so we skipped rerank. Prompt 4 looked like Buy won because override wouldn't pin Build unless core IP was already true. I fixed both in code. I was not going to sit there and whisper hints on camera. 

 Keeping simulate as a projection (not rewriting live context) was another fight. Agents love to "just set HIPAA" and pretend the future already happened. 

 I cut saved accounts, live pricing, and a third industry. Ten days. The loop had to work: ask, tool, visible state, honest disagreement.

title: MapsMCP
pitch: Maps that agents can understand
about_excerpt:
Maps that agents can understand
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 MapsMCP, maps that agents can understand, not just click 

 The problem 

 Maps are made for people. We look at the screen, drag it about, zoom in, spot a place, and change direction without really thinking about it. 

 AI agents have a rougher time. Playwright, Selenium, and Appium can click, drag, and scroll, but a map is not a normal webpage. It is a moving visual surface made from tiles, canvas layers, marker clusters, labels, animations, and changing camera positions. 

 The main issue, well, the awkward bit, is that a gesture has no stable meaning. Dragging 280 pixels may move one street at one zoom level and half a city at another. Screen size changes the result. Slow-loading tiles can change it again. An agent may complete the gesture and still have no reliable answer to “Where is the map now?” or “Which places can the person actually see?” 

 That is a poor foundation for ride hailing, food delivery, travel, field work, or emergency response. 

 What I built 

 MapsMCP is a WebMCP-powered interactive map prototype. 

 It keeps a normal human map experience, built with Leaflet and real OpenStreetMap tiles. People can pan, zoom, search places, inspect routes, and select destinations in the usual way. 

 A compatible browser agent gets structured WebMCP tools for the same map. It can inspect the current viewport, move the camera by metres, set an exact location and zoom level, find nearby places, measure distance, plan routes, and add visible shared pins. 

 The map is central London for the demo. The core idea works in any city. 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 WebMCP lets a website register structured browser-native tools for an AI agent. Each tool has a name, description, input schema, and execution function. 

 Maps are especially well suited to this because the map engine already knows the important information. It knows the camera centre, zoom, visible bounds, selected place, distances, pins, and routes. That semantic state is usually hidden behind the visual interface. 

 MapsMCP exposes the useful parts safely and clearly. 

 Instead of an agent attempting to drag right and hoping for the best, it can call pan_map with a compass direction and a distance in metres. Instead of guessing what is visible after a gesture, it can call get_map_viewport and receive the geographic bounds, zoom level, and visible structured places. 

 WebMCP turns a map from a picture an agent pokes at into a workspace it can understand. 

 Better experience for people and agents 

 For a person, MapsMCP still behaves like a map. There is no strange agent-only screen. They can explore normally, see every map movement, inspect the result, and alter the plan. 

 For an agent, the interaction becomes deterministic. It gets stable place IDs and geographic results, rather than an uncertain screenshot after a drag. 

 Together, people and agents can work from the same state. A person might pan across a city to explore. ChatGPT can then inspect that exact viewport, find suitable places nearby, fit destinations into view, plan a route, and leave a shared meeting pin. 

 That handoff is difficult with visual browser automation alone. It can be done with a bespoke private integration, perhaps, but WebMCP makes the capability explicit, discoverable, and browser-mediated. 

 A realistic demo scenario 

 Imagine a traveller visiting London for the first time. 

 They are standing near Tower Bridge, a famous bridge over the River Thames. They want to walk to Borough Market, a nearby food market, and leave a meeting point for a friend. 

 They ask ChatGPT: 
 I am near Tower Bridge, a major London landmark. Find Borough Market, measure
the walking distance, fit both places into the map view, plan a walking route,
and drop a visible pin at Borough Market called “Meet here”.
 
 ChatGPT discovers the MapsMCP WebMCP tools. It finds the locations by stable IDs, measures the distance, moves the visible map, draws the walking route, and drops the shared pin. 

 The traveller sees it all happen. They can keep the plan, drag the map somewhere else, or change their mind. 

 Supported WebMCP tools 

 
 
 Tool 
 What it does 
 
 
 
 get_map_state 
 Reads the full shared map state, including viewport, selected place, route, staged ride, and pins. 
 
 
 get_map_viewport 
 Returns exact camera centre, zoom, geographic bounds, and visible places. 
 
 
 get_places_in_view 
 Lists structured places inside the current visible map area. 
 
 
 search_places 
 Searches the London place catalogue and returns stable place IDs. 
 
 
 get_place_details 
 Returns a place’s details and nearby suggestions without scraping a tooltip. 
 
 
 find_nearby_places 
 Finds places around a known location within a real-world radius. 
 
 
 measure_distance 
 Measures straight-line geographic distance between two places. 
 
 
 pan_map 
 Moves the visible map by compass direction and metres. 
 
 
 set_map_viewport 
 Sets exact latitude, longitude, and zoom. 
 
 
 zoom_map 
 Zooms by a known number of map levels. 
 
 
 fit_places 
 Frames one or more place IDs in the visible map. 
 
 
 focus_place 
 Flies to and selects a place in the human interface. 
 
 
 plan_route 
 Previews car, cycle, or walking routes. 
 
 
 clear_route 
 Removes the visible route preview and staged ride. 
 
 
 drop_pin 
 Places a named visible pin at exact coordinates. 
 
 
 list_pins 
 Lists shared pins currently on the map. 
 
 
 remove_pin 
 Removes a shared pin through its stable ID. 
 
 
 prepare_ride 
 Stages a simulated ride quote. A person still confirms it. 
 
 

 How I implemented WebMCP 

 MapsMCP uses WebMCP’s imperative API: 
 await document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "search_places",
 description: "Search MapsMCP's structured London place catalogue.",
 inputSchema: {
 type: "object",
 properties: {
 query: { type: "string" },
 category: { type: "string" },
 },
 additionalProperties: false,
 },
 execute: async ({ query, category }) => {
 return searchPlaces(query, category);
 },
});
 
 The app registers 18 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with a compatibility fallback for older navigator.modelContext browser implementations. 

 Every tool calls the same React state actions used by the human interface. If an agent pans the map, the person sees the map pan. If it drops a pin, the pin appears on the real map. Registration is owned by an AbortController , so tools are removed cleanly when the page lifecycle ends. 

 What is real, and what is intentionally simulated 

 The map uses real OpenStreetMap tiles and visible attribution. 

 The London locations, route estimates, and ride quotes are deterministic demo data. MapsMCP does not claim live traffic, real restaurant availability, or actual ride booking. That keeps the demo dependable and makes the WebMCP interaction the focus. 

 Why it matters 

 MapsMCP is a small prototype for a much bigger idea. 

 A person should not have to explain a map to an agent through clicks and screenshots. An agent should not have to guess what a map gesture did. 

 WebMCP gives the map a shared language. The person stays in control. The agent stops guessing.

title: Receipts — the trust layer for agentic commerce
pitch: Every agent action, on the record. A storefront where ChatGPT shops for you via WebMCP — and every move it makes is printed on a tamper-evident receipt trail you govern with standing rules.\n
about_excerpt:
Every agent action, on the record. A storefront where ChatGPT shops for you via WebMCP — and every move it makes is printed on a tamper-evident receipt trail you govern with standing rules.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Why WebMCP? (required field) 

 Agentic commerce only works if people trust agents with money — and today the web has no mechanism for that trust. WebMCP is the first API that lets a site define what an agent may do, in typed, annotated, site-authored tools instead of fragile DOM scraping. Receipts pushes that one step further: the site doesn't just expose capabilities , it exposes governance . request_checkout is a tool that can genuinely pause mid-call until a human approves, return pending_approval with a receipt id for polling, honor the abort signal when the user cancels, and cite the exact standing rule that fired. The agent can even read the same hash-chained receipt trail the human reads ( get_recent_receipts ) so accountability runs in both directions. Without WebMCP, none of this is possible: there is no channel through which a website could hand an agent a policy-bound, human-gated purchase function — the agent would just fill in the form and click buy. 

 What people + agents can do (required field) 

 People shop a real storefront themselves OR delegate it to ChatGPT: "find wireless earbuds under $80 and buy the best one." The agent searches the catalog, builds a cart, and checks out — while the shopper watches every step appear live on their receipt trail, approves or denies the purchase in one tap when a standing rule requires it ("always ask above $150"), and can undo (refund) any order afterwards. Standing rules give shoppers a permanent voice: auto-approve small baskets, review big ones, deny whole categories. A daily digest answers "what did my agent do today?" and Verify chain proves the record hasn't been tampered with. 

 How we built it (required field) 

 Next.js 15 + TypeScript + Tailwind + zustand, no backend. The whole trust layer runs client-side: a shared tool registry (lib/tools.ts) registers 8 tools with the browser's WebMCP agent context (document.modelContext, with a navigator.modelContext fallback); tool execute() functions run in the page against a zustand store. The receipt ledger is append-only and SHA-256 hash-chained (crypto.subtle) with superseding entries for decisions (an audit log that edits itself isn't one). A first-match policy engine evaluates standing rules before any money moves, defaulting to require-approval. request_checkout's execute() awaits the human's decision (90s timeout → pending_approval + poll check_receipt), honors abortSignal, and orders/refunds are printed as receipts. 

 Challenges & accomplishments 

 Getting a WebMCP tool call to genuinely pause for a human decision was the hardest part: we built a promise bridge between the tool's execute() and an approval card in the UI, with a timeout path that converts a blocked call into a polling protocol (check_receipt) so agents never busy-wait or retry around the gate. We're proud that the ledger is honestly append-only — even approvals are new entries that supersede the pending one — and that the demo works with zero infrastructure: your receipts live on your device, hash-chained, verifiable in one click. 

 Testing instructions (private field) 

 Live URL: 

 
 ChatGPT path: paste the URL into ChatGPT (desktop or mobile) and open it in the in-app browser. Ask: "Search this store for wireless earbuds under $80 and buy the best one." Watch the Receipts tab; approve the checkout card when it appears. 
 Chrome path: enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (Chrome 149+), open the URL, confirm the "WebMCP live" pill, then from DevTools run: await document.modelContext.executeTool("search_products", '{"query":"earbuds","max_price":80}')
No credentials needed; nothing real is charged.

The deploy console a human and an agent share when CI is red.


 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I spend a lot of time in red CI. Vercel, Helm schema jobs, Cloudflare extraEnv — the graph is on one tab, ChatGPT is on another. I paste a log, lose the timeline, and the agent starts guessing through the DOM. WebMCP is the missing surface: the same console I already stare at, with named tools so an agent can diagnose and patch on that page , and I still Confirm anything irreversible. 

 Dashboards are for humans. Chat is for logs. Afterfail is the deploy graph both can drive. 

 What it does 

 Afterfail is a failed preview/deploy console. Four canned runs (Vercel Helm --defaultdb , Netlify Next OOM, Cloudflare missing HTTP_PROXY , Render $PORT health check) plus New run / create_run so you can paste a real log. 

 A person and ChatGPT (or Chrome WebMCP) share: 

 
 the job timeline and log 
 get_failed_jobs / get_log_slice instead of scraping 
 set_retry_policy (the editor updates before the tool returns) 
 redeploy , which stops on an on-page confirm 
 an honesty case: workers-edge-preview stays red. Retries do not set env vars. 
 

 How I built it 

 Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand. No backend, no auth, no in-page chatbot. 

 Tools register on the top-level /console document with document.modelContext.registerTool (native first; @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill only if registerTool is missing). Execute is (input, { signal }) . Results are JSON objects, not MCP content arrays — ChatGPT site tools stringify JSON. Sensitive actions share the same confirm modal as the Redeploy button. readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint on the log tool. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP is not “wrap every button.” Five sharp outcome tools beat twenty. requestUserInteraction is not in the shipping IDL, so confirm had to be our modal. ChatGPT ignores iframe and declarative form tools. And a tool that always “succeeds” on retry is a lie — the Cloudflare fixture is the feature. 

 Challenges 

 Getting a green redeploy meant applying policy on the failing job ( schema-job , not helm-lint ) before Confirm. Hosting on Render wanted a credit card even with credits, so the live URL is Vercel. Cursor’s cursor-ide-browser MCP is not WebMCP; judges use ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (Sol or Terra, not Luna).

title: Diamond Control
pitch: A human-gated agent workspace where WebMCP lets agents read, recommend, and prepare actions without taking the final decision away from the person.
about_excerpt:
A human-gated agent workspace where WebMCP lets agents read, recommend, and prepare actions without taking the final decision away from the person.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI systems are becoming more capable very quickly. But greater capability also creates a new problem. 

 As tasks become longer and the amount of context grows, it becomes harder for an AI system to maintain reliable reasoning across everything it has to process. Important details can be missed, reasoning can drift, and hallucinations can become harder to detect. 

 That is why I believe greater AI capability should be paired with clearer Human Gates. 

 Diamond Control started from this idea: let the agent do as much useful work as possible, but keep explicit Human checkpoints at the decisions where correctness, authority, or risk really matter. 

 I did not want the Human to approve every small step. I wanted the AI to be able to work independently until it reaches a decision that genuinely belongs to the person. 

 What it does 

 Diamond Control is a human-gated agent workspace built with WebMCP. 

 It gives an AI agent a structured way to understand the current workflow, identify what needs attention, recommend a bounded next move, prepare that action, and request Human review. 

 The application exposes five WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_workspace_state 
 get_attention_items 
 recommend_next_move 
 prepare_action 
 request_human_gate 
 

 The first three tools read or recommend without changing the workflow. 

 prepare_action can create a reversible proposed action, and request_human_gate can move that proposal into AWAITING_HUMAN . 

 But no WebMCP tool can approve or reject an action. 

 The final decision remains in the visible Human Gate. 

 In the demo, the agent identifies the proof-repair lane, recommends Review and run proof validation , prepares the proposal, and requests Human review. 

 The workflow enters AWAITING_HUMAN , where the agent stops. 

 The Human then chooses Reject, and Diamond Control produces a NO_ACTION proof receipt showing that the decision was made by the Human. 

 How I built it 

 Diamond Control is a browser-based application built with TypeScript/JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and WebMCP. 

 The main design goal was not simply to connect an AI agent to a web interface. I wanted the workflow itself to expose enough structure that the agent would not have to guess what the page means from buttons and text alone. 

 WebMCP provides explicit tools for: 

 
 reading workflow state 
 discovering items that need attention 
 recommending a next move 
 preparing a bounded action 
 requesting Human review 
 

 Behind those tools is a small state model that separates agent preparation from Human authority. 

 A proposal can move through states such as PROPOSED and AWAITING_HUMAN , but only the visible Human controls can produce an APPROVED or REJECTED decision. 

 I also added a fail-closed rule: if one proposal is already waiting at the Human Gate, the agent cannot silently replace it with another proposal. The Human must resolve the existing decision first. 

 The project is intentionally browser-side and small. It does not depend on a backend, database, authentication system, private user records, or an automatic approval service. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The main challenge was not making the agent more capable. 

 The harder problem was deciding exactly where that capability should stop. 

 I had to separate several concepts that can easily become mixed together in an AI workflow: 

 
 reading information versus changing state 
 recommending an action versus executing a decision 
 preparing work versus authorizing it 
 agent capability versus Human authority 
 successful automation versus correct execution 
 

 Another challenge was making the boundary visible and testable rather than keeping it as an instruction written only in a prompt. 

 That is why Diamond Control uses explicit workflow states, a visible Human Gate, and a proof receipt after the decision. 

 I also learned that long AI workflows need clear checkpoints. If every small action requires Human confirmation, the system becomes too manual. But if the AI is allowed to continue without clear boundaries, it becomes difficult to know when Human judgment is actually required. 

 Finding that balance became the central design problem of the project. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I am proud that Diamond Control demonstrates a complete agent-to-Human workflow rather than only exposing a collection of WebMCP tools. 

 The demo shows a natural-language request moving through the entire process: 

 
 the agent reads the workspace 
 identifies what needs attention 
 recommends one next move 
 prepares the action 
 requests Human review 
 stops at AWAITING_HUMAN 
 the Human makes the final decision 
 the system produces a proof receipt 
 

 I am also proud that the authority boundary is enforced by the application itself. 

 The agent cannot approve or reject an action, and it cannot replace another proposal while an unresolved Human Gate is open. 

 For me, this is important because Human control should not depend only on asking an AI model to behave correctly. The workflow should make the boundary explicit. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that WebMCP becomes much more useful when it gives an AI agent a flexible, structured way to understand and interact with a workflow, instead of limiting the interaction to a small set of rigid buttons. 

 A good agent interface should expose meaningful state, available actions, constraints, and decision boundaries. 

 This allows the AI to adapt its help to the situation while still operating inside explicit rules. 

 For me, the value of WebMCP is not just automation. 

 It is making the collaboration between the Human, the interface, and the AI more flexible without losing control. 

 I also learned that giving an agent more autonomy does not necessarily mean giving it more authority. 

 Those are two different things, and separating them can allow an AI system to do substantially more work while still preserving the decisions that should remain Human. 

 What's next for Diamond Control 

 The next step is to make the boundaries between autonomous AI work and Human authority much more complete and explicit. 

 With stronger boundaries, agents should be able to run longer tasks on their own, carry work across multiple steps, and automatically bring the workflow to the correct Human Gate when a real decision is required. 

 The goal is to reduce unnecessary manual coordination. 

 Humans should not have to supervise every small step. They should be asked to intervene only at clear checkpoints where judgment, authority, or risk actually matters. 

 Over time, I would also like to extend the same pattern to more complex workflows, more types of actions, stronger proof and recovery mechanisms, and multiple agent environments. 

 If these boundaries are designed well, AI agents can become more autonomous while execution still remains aligned with the correct level of Human authority.

about_excerpt:
Approve once. Automate everything else all in one place
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 15 exposed site tools 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 15 exposed site tools 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every "AI agent on the web" demo I'd seen followed the same pattern: an agent pretending to be a human, clicking blindly through a UI built for eyes and fingers, guessing whether a button did what it looked like it did. Meanwhile, the actual tasks people want to delegate — book this flight, stay under this budget, don't double-book my calendar — are things a real application already knows how to do reliably. The gap wasn't capability, it was interface. WebMCP looked like the first real answer to "what if the app just told the agent exactly what it could do?" I wanted a use case where that mattered — everyday, cross-domain personal tasks are exactly the place agents fail today, precisely because there's no structured way for an app to expose what it can actually do. 

 What it does 

 LifeOps is a personal command center — Travel, Calendar, Budget, Notes, and Tasks — where a human and a Gemini-backed agent operate through the exact same 15 WebMCP tools. Give the agent a goal like "Prepare my Delhi trip for Friday, keep everything under ₹10,000," and it searches flights, checks the budget, checks the calendar, and books what actually fits — live, with every tool call visible in an activity log. 

 The key UX idea is that the agent, the human, and a developer-facing /webmcp inspector all operate on the same tools and the same application state — nothing is a simulation or a separate demo path. A tool call from the agent, a manual click in the Trips tab, and a manual test from the inspector all run through one shared dispatcher and produce identical, real effects. That removes the usual anxiety of "what did the AI actually do to my data?" by making every action fully inspectable. 

 What's newly possible is safe delegation of multi-step, cross-domain tasks with a human checkpoint exactly where it matters. Every tool is tagged read, prepare, or commit: read-level calls (search_flights, get_budget, find_free_time) run automatically; prepare-level calls (prepare_flight_booking, create_calendar_event) act but always show their work; commit-level calls (confirm_flight_purchase, record_expense) — anything irreversible or financial — always stop and wait for a real, awaited human approval before the agent continues. Before this, delegating a task like this meant either fully trusting an agent to click "Buy now" unsupervised, or stripping it down to read-only suggestions. LifeOps lets the agent handle the whole multi-domain task end-to-end, with the human only needing to step in once, at the one moment that actually requires their judgment — and the agent visibly adapts its plan if that approval is rejected, rather than failing or looping. 

 How I built it 

 Every tool is defined once — name, description, domain, permission level, JSON schema, and real execute logic — in lib/webmcp/tools/*.ts, and registered with the browser's real WebMCP surface: 

 js
document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "search_flights",
 description: "...",
 inputSchema: { /* JSON schema / },
 execute: async (input) => { / real application logic */ },
}); 

 All three ways of calling a tool — the native document.modelContext bridge, my own Gemini-driven agent loop, and the manual "Try tool" form on the /webmcp inspector — funnel through one shared dispatcher, invokeTool(name, input). It validates input against the tool's JSON schema, logs the call to a live activity feed, opens and awaits a real approval ticket for any commit-level tool, runs the tool's actual logic against a shared Zustand store, and records the result back to the activity log. Because nothing bypasses this dispatcher, a click in the UI and an agent's tool call hit the identical code path and the same state. 

 The agent itself isn't scripted: a server route (app/api/agent/route.ts) calls the Gemini API with the full tool schema set (adapted via lib/webmcp/geminiTools.ts), and Gemini genuinely decides what to call and in what order, turn by turn, reacting to whatever actually happened — including a rejected approval. The API key never reaches the browser. Since document.modelContext is only present in WebMCP-enabled browsers today, my own agent calls the same tools through the same invokeTool path when the native API is absent, so behavior stays identical regardless of which surface is calling it. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 Getting the permission model right was harder than it sounds — it needed to be enforced centrally in the dispatcher, not left to the model's judgment, or the whole safety story falls apart the moment the agent decides differently. I also had to design around WebMCP being genuinely experimental: document.modelContext isn't in most browsers yet, so I built a fallback path that keeps behavior identical either way. Making the approval flow actually block an in-flight, multi-turn agent loop — and letting the model see and react to a rejection — took real care in the async plumbing between the browser and the server route holding the Gemini session. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I'm most proud that there's no "demo path" separate from the "real path" — the agent, the manual UI, and the WebMCP inspector are three windows onto the exact same state and the exact same tools. I'm also proud that the commit-level approval isn't cosmetic: it's a real, awaited human decision in the middle of a live, model-driven loop, and the agent visibly adapts when that decision is "no" instead of failing or looping blindly. 

 What I learned 

 I came away convinced that the hard part of agent-native apps isn't giving the agent more autonomy — it's deciding, precisely, where autonomy should stop. A clean three-tier permission model did more for trustworthiness than any amount of prompting ever could. I also learned a lot about the practical seams of an emerging standard: building for a browser API that doesn't exist yet in most browsers forces you to make your own agent loop a first-class citizen, not an afterthought. 

 What's next for LifeOps 

 I'd like to add more domains (email, contacts, shopping) behind the same permission model, support multi-agent collaboration on one trip or budget, and let commit-level approvals happen asynchronously — e.g. a push notification a person can approve from their phone while the agent's session waits. Longer term, as document.modelContext becomes standard in more browsers, I want LifeOps to be a reference for what a truly agent-native personal app looks like, not just during a hackathon demo.

title: Proof Gate
pitch: Accountable intelligence for the open web: humans and agents build, challenge, and verify the same evidence-backed case.
about_excerpt:
Accountable intelligence for the open web: humans and agents build, challenge, and verify the same evidence-backed case.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Proof Gate 

 Most competitors build intelligent agents. Proof Gate builds accountable intelligence. 

 Proof Gate is a WebMCP-native evidence workspace where a human and a browsing agent build the same versioned case together. 

 The contradiction is simple: web agents can often click and act, but they struggle to preserve shared state, provenance, uncertainty, and decision lineage across a real workflow. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Claim evaluation is stateful. A case contains a claim revision, decision context, evidence records, provenance, conflicts, a deterministic verdict, and an audit lineage. Without a structured application interface, a browsing model has to infer that state from DOM controls and maintain a separate copy. 

 Proof Gate exposes six narrow tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 read the current case 
 set or revise the claim 
 add evidence 
 identify conflicts 
 evaluate the current claim revision 
 export the versioned record 
 

 The human and the agent operate on the same application state. The agent does not maintain a hidden parallel case, and the human does not have to trust a black-box conclusion. 

 Distillation Protocol: the governance boundary 

 Proof Gate applies a two-way Distillation Protocol at the boundary between the web and the governed case. 

 Inbound: raw user input, tool output, and external observations are converted into structured evidence with provenance, revision binding, uncertainty labels, and explicit source roles before they enter the case. 

 Outbound: internal evaluations and proposed actions are converted into scoped, inspectable outputs. Evidence-derived content is marked as untrusted, and no raw external statement becomes authority merely because an API, tool, user, or model asserted it. 

 This prevents four common failures: 

 
 prompt or content injection becoming governance state 
 API responses being mistaken for independently verified reality 
 AI conclusions being silently promoted to facts 
 stale or contradictory evidence being overwritten instead of preserved 
 

 The anti-magic rule is: I do not know yet, and here is exactly what evidence would resolve it. 

 Global Compass signature 

 Proof Gate follows the Global Compass design philosophy: 

 SEE REALITY → PRESERVE EVIDENCE → UNDERSTAND RELATIONSHIPS → SEPARATE CAPABILITY FROM AUTHORITY → VERIFY WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED → LEARN WITHOUT REWRITING HISTORY 

 In this application that means: 

 
 evidence is bound to explicit claim revisions 
 duplicate source families do not manufacture independence 
 context records do not inflate support or refutation confidence 
 unknown dates remain unknown and future dates are rejected 
 contradictory evidence stays visible instead of being silently overwritten 
 only HTTP/HTTPS evidence URLs are accepted 
 evidence-derived WebMCP outputs are marked as untrusted content 
 conflicts are aggregated and the evidence ledger is bounded 
 the evaluator does not claim to independently establish truth 
 

 Better human + agent collaboration 

 Before WebMCP, an agent interacting with a case workspace has to reverse-engineer controls and reconstruct application state from the page. With WebMCP, the application exposes the actual operations and schemas directly. 

 The division of labor is explicit: 

 Human: frames the claim, inspects evidence, corrects context, challenges conclusions, and retains authority over meaningful decisions. 

 Agent: structures evidence, detects conflicts, evaluates the current revision, and prepares an export. 

 Application: deterministically enforces revision boundaries, validates inputs, and preserves the lineage both sides can inspect. 

 The agent can therefore be useful without becoming an unaccountable source of truth. 

 Reality Triangle 

 Proof Gate distinguishes three states instead of collapsing them: 

 
 Intended: what the claim or decision asks us to establish 
 Reported: what a source, tool, or provider says happened 
 Observed: what the accumulated evidence actually supports 
 

 Success is not established merely because a tool returned success or a model produced a confident answer. 

 Implementation 

 The WebMCP layer calls the same pure JavaScript evidence engine used by the visible human UI. Tool calls and UI actions mutate the same state. Where supported, the application also checks getTools() enumeration after registration. 

 The evaluator is deliberately modest. Thresholds and source-family grouping are transparent demo heuristics rather than claims of calibrated universal truth. 

 Scope 

 Proof Gate is deliberately one focused web application, not an AI backend disguised as a hackathon entry. The demonstration is shared application state: explicit schemas for the agent, visible and revisable evidence for the human, deterministic evaluation, a governed boundary, and a versioned record they can inspect together. 

 Accountable intelligence, not merely intelligent agents.

pitch: A shared release room where agents verify and prepare, but only humans ship.

A shared release room where agents verify and prepare, but only humans ship.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for ProofMesh WebMCP 

 Inspiration 

 Release decisions are scattered across CI, security, support, and private team context. Agents can reconcile that evidence, but backend-only agents remove the shared interface and screen-clicking agents are brittle. ProofMesh makes the release room understandable to both people and agents while preserving an explicit human decision boundary. 

 What it does 

 ProofMesh asks independent Engineering, Security, and Support agents to verify a launch claim, compares their evidence, and surfaces the contradiction needing the release owner. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can inspect the case, run verification, retrieve conflicts, and stage a proposed resolution. Every call updates the same page the user is watching. The agent cannot seal or ship the release: the owner reviews the proposal and clicks Approve & seal . Only then is a read-only decision-receipt tool registered. 

 How we built it 

 The React page registers four domain-level tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_release_case , run_release_verification , get_release_conflicts , and prepare_owner_resolution . Each has a focused description and JSON Schema input; read-only tools carry readOnlyHint . Registration is lifecycle-bound with an AbortSignal , reuses the existing verification API and React state, and dynamically registers get_decision_receipt after human approval. A visible activity stream records every agent action. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer state from pixels and repeatedly reread the page. A backend MCP server would lose the live, reviewable release-room context. WebMCP exposes domain capabilities inside the page while keeping actions visible and consequential finalization human-owned. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 The agent performs high-friction evidence work and prepares a concrete next step. The human sees the same evidence, edits or rejects the proposal, and owns the final decision. This inspect → verify → explain → prepare → human approve → receipt sequence was previously hard to make both reliable and accountable. 

 Challenges and lessons 

 The main challenge was resisting the urge to expose every button. We designed a small, permission-scoped surface, made read versus draft behavior explicit, and withheld irreversible approval from the agent. Agent-native does not mean agent-only; sometimes the safest tool is the one deliberately not registered. 

 What's next 

 Dynamic tools for release phases, signed receipts, permission-scoped cross-origin team frames, and evaluation against prompt injection and ambiguous finalization attacks.

One deck. Two llama armies. A king powered by Codex. Turn every card into troops, resources, and tactical chaos in a battle for the crown.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 The big idea: Bring Your Own AI 

 Llama War is more than a card game with an AI character. It explores a different relationship between players, games, and artificial intelligence: what if you could bring your own AI to the table? 

 Instead of packaging every opponent’s decisions inside the game, Llama War exposes tools that let a connected agent participate. The game provides the world, the rules, and the consequences. The agent brings the strategy and personality. 

 The current implementation uses Codex to control the Llama King. The broader vision is a game that compatible agents can enter, understand, and play. 

 

 How WebMCP makes it possible 

 WebMCP connects the browser game to an agent through structured tools. The agent can inspect the battlefield, read available resources, discover legal actions, and choose its next move. 

 That means the AI is not just generating dialogue beside the game. Its decisions can affect the actual match. It can choose to train a unit, attack an enemy, protect an ally, or invest in its castle. 

 Unity remains responsible for enforcing the rules. The agent requests an action, and the game validates it against the current turn, resources, targets, and available abilities. This separates the intelligence making a decision from the system deciding whether that move is legal. 

 The King’s personality is part of the interaction too. An agent can write his dialogue, turning its strategic decisions into witty taunts, grudging compliments, or excuses when a plan falls apart.
Even the soundtrack is open to the agent’s creativity. Through WebMCP, it can compose looping music using MIDI-style notes, choosing instruments, melodies, rhythms, and tempo. Unity validates the score and plays it through the built-in synthesizer, letting the AI help shape not just how the match unfolds, but how it sounds. 

 This creates possibilities beyond an AI opponent that only chooses moves. The same connected agent can command an army, give the King a personality, and compose the music accompanying the match. An agent could respond to a tense battle with a faster score or celebrate its castle ambitions with an overly dramatic royal march. Those changes are agent-directed, not an automatic adaptive soundtrack, giving players another way to shape the experience with the AI they bring. 

 WebMCP turns Llama War into a shared play space for people and agents. A human controls one army while a connected AI reads the battlefield, chooses legal moves, and speaks through the Llama King. This lets players bring an AI into the game as an active opponent, not just a chatbot beside it. 

 

 Why this changes the experience 

 The exciting possibility is that changing the agent, or how you instruct it, could change the opponent without changing the game itself. 

 You could ask for a cautious strategist, an aggressive rival, or a theatrical king who treats every lost Farmer as a national tragedy. Those instructions could influence both battlefield decisions and the character across the table. 

 This creates room for a more personal kind of replayability. The question becomes more than “Can I beat this difficulty level?” It becomes “How will this opponent approach the same rules?” 

 Llama War gives that idea a playful setting where the consequences are visible. An agent’s strategy becomes an army composition, a carefully timed shield, an expensive fireball, or a castle that gets dangerously close to completion. 

 

 The possibilities beyond Llama War 

 This approach opens the door to games where players bring an agent as an opponent, a teammate, a coach, or a character. Future versions could explore agent-versus-agent tournaments, strategy challenges, and companions that participate across multiple games through compatible interfaces. 

 These are possibilities, not features I am claiming are already complete. Today, Llama War demonstrates the foundation through its Codex-connected opponent and game tools. Broader agent compatibility and the hosted WebMCP experience still need further testing. 

 The larger idea is simple: a game does not have to contain all of its intelligence. It can become a place where your AI comes to play.

pitch: Webcam.funapp.io connects AI agents to thousands of live streaming webcams worldwide using WebMCP
about_excerpt:
Webcam.funapp.io connects AI agents to thousands of live streaming webcams worldwide using WebMCP
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 listing 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 webcam focus and nearby 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 airport 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 listing 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 webcam focus and nearby 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 airport 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 listing 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 ## Inspiration 
 Today's AI agents possess immense textual knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but they remain fundamentally detached from the physical world. When a user asks:
- *"Is there a sea of clouds over Alishan right now before I drive up?"*
- *"Is the snow accumulating at Wuling Pass on Hehuanshan?"*
- *"How packed is the queue at Jiufen Old Street or the highway entrance?"*

Traditional AI systems are forced to rely on stale static databases or attempt fragile browser automation—taking screenshots, hallucinating DOM selectors, and failing on dynamic video streams.

We asked ourselves: **What if web applications gave AI agents real-time physical eyes?**

With the arrival of **WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol)**, websites no longer need to be passive visual interfaces designed exclusively for human eyes. Inspired by our global live camera platform at
 
 https://webcam.funapp.io , we set out to build an Agent-Ready Live Webcam Experience where AI agents can directly discover, switch, and visually inspect real-time video feeds across the globe through
 native structured tools. 
 ## What it does

**Webcam FunApp** transforms live video streaming into an intelligent, agent-accessible visual perception network. Through WebMCP:
1. **Semantic Camera Discovery**: AI agents can query thousands of live webcams worldwide by location, category (scenic, traffic, weather, wildlife), or natural language intents (e.g., *"Find me coastal
 
 surf spots with morning sunlight" ).
 2. **Programmatic Stream Switching : The agent seamlessly switches the active video player on the page, dynamically transitioning between HLS and YouTube Live streams while keeping the user visually in
 sync.
 3. **Real-Time Visual Perception : The agent captures timestamped video frames on demand and passes them to multimodal vision models to extract ground truth—detecting cloud formations, estimating crowd
 density, or assessing road wetness.
 4. **Co-Browsing Telemetry *: Users and AI co-explore the world together: as the agent navigates cameras to answer queries, visual HUD indicators and glowing badges highlight the agent's focus in real-
 time. 
 ## How we built it

We designed an end-to-end architecture connecting browser-native WebMCP protocols with frontend video streaming and multimodal evaluation.

### 1. WebMCP Provider Layer
We integrated the standard `navigator.modelContext` interface to register native browser tools:
- `search_webcams(query, category, region)`: Queries the local index and edge database.
- `switch_webcam(webcamId)`: Programmatically updates the video player state with smooth transitions.
- `capture_current_frame(webcamId, quality)`: Captures crisp canvas frames from active streams.
- `get_webcam_telemetry(webcamId)`: Fetches environmental readings and sensor metrics.

### 2. Adaptive Frame Sampling with LaTeX Dynamics
To balance visual fidelity against multimodal model token limits and network latency, we implemented an adaptive frame sampling model based on motion dynamics:

$$S(t) = S_{\text{min}} + (S_{\text{max}} - S_{\text{min}}) \cdot \left(1 - \exp\left(-\gamma \cdot \|\nabla I(t)\|\right)\right)$$

where $\|\nabla I(t)\|$ represents the inter-frame pixel gradient variance (motion intensity) and $\gamma$ is the sensitivity tuning coefficient. During high-dynamic scenes (e.g., fast-moving freeway
 
 traffic), sampling rate $S(t)$ scales up automatically; during static scenic landscapes, it scales down to conserve bandwidth. 
 ### 3. Edge Delivery & Streaming Stack
The frontend is built on a high-performance, modern web architecture deployed on Cloudflare Pages and Workers, ensuring sub-100ms camera metadata resolution and worldwide low-latency edge delivery.

## Challenges we ran into

1. **Cross-Origin Canvas Tainting (CORS & Streams)**: Capturing frames from third-party HLS or YouTube live streams using `<canvas>` natively triggers browser security errors (`SecurityError: The canvas
 
 has been tainted by cross-origin data`). We resolved this by implementing zero-copy edge snapshot proxies with compliant CORS headers on Cloudflare Workers.
 2. Eliminating Human-Agent Disconnect : Having an AI manipulate video streams in the background can disorient human users. We engineered intuitive visual feedback states—reactive ambient glows and
 subtle HUD toasts—that clearly notify the user: "AI is inspecting Wuling Webcam for snowfall verification" .
 3. Handling Variable Stream Latency : Live webcams exhibit variable buffer times ranging from 1 to 5 seconds. We implemented asynchronous promise barriers that guarantee the stream is actively
 rendering valid frames before the WebMCP tool returns snapshot data to the agent. 
 ## Accomplishments that we're proud of

- **True Dual-Interface UX**: Created a webpage that delivers an elegant, high-FPS experience for human viewers while acting as a frictionless, deterministic tool server for AI agents.
- **Zero-Scrape Agent Navigation**: AI agents can browse, search, and switch cameras with $100\%$ deterministic accuracy through WebMCP JSON schemas, completely eliminating CSS selector guesswork.
- **Real-World Multimodal Verification**: Demonstrated live, reproducible workflows where an LLM successfully validates weather forecasts against actual real-time camera imagery in seconds.

## What we learned

- **WebMCP is the Future of the Web**: Transitioning from screen-scraping/OCR to structured client-side tools reduces agent execution latency by over $80\%$ and eliminates unexpected DOM breakage.
- **Web Pages as Autonomous Hubs**: A website is no longer just a display document; it is an active node that connects an agent's reasoning loop to hardware sensors, video streams, and client-side APIs.
- **Multimodal Grounding Drastically Cuts Hallucination**: When an agent can actively "look" at reality instead of guessing, answers about current weather, traffic, and physical environments achieve
 
 near-zero hallucination. 
 ## What's next for webcam.funapp.io

- **Automated Weather & Anomaly Patrols**: Allowing users to set recurring WebMCP agent tasks (e.g., *"Notify me when the sea of clouds appears at Sunrise Peak"* or *"Alert me when snow begins falling
 
 at Hehuanshan" ).
 - **Time-Lapse Synthesis for AI Agents : Introducing a generate_timelapse(hours) WebMCP tool so agents can study diurnal weather patterns and traffic trends over time.
 - **Broader FunApp Ecosystem Rollout *: Standardizing our shared/webmcp.js module across our entire collection of 200+ mini-apps at https://funapp.io , bringing the full power of the Agentic Web to
 daily tools, calculators, and interactive 3D simulations.

Never guess which key is next. KEYLIT lights it. You play it. ChatGPT hears you on that same piano so anyone can start, on one live page.

 Keylit 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Keylit 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 A chatbot can say “play middle C.” It cannot light that key, and it cannot hear whether you hit it. That is a useless piano teacher. 

 The WebMCP challenge asked for an app that gets better when a human and an agent share the same live page. I wanted that to be something anyone can use: learn piano on the keys in front of you. Not a lesson in a side chat. 

 I looked at how hardware instruments are laid out — dual layers, an LCD, generate-and-lock, a roll — but KEYLIT is not a clone of those products. No pads, no kits, no preset banks. The product is the glow: the next note is already lit. You play it. The agent hears you on that same piano. 

 What it does 

 KEYLIT is a sampled piano teacher on one live page. 

 
 Press teach me . Middle C glows cyan, with a Q on the key. 
 You play it — click, type, or a MIDI keyboard. The teacher hears that note and lights the next one. 
 Miss, and it stays put: TRY AGAIN · WANT D4 · YOU E4 . 
 hear it plays the next note in green so you can copy it. 
 When you can hold a chord, harmonize only works if your hands are already on the keys. 
 

 Lessons: first keys, C major scale, C major chord, Twinkle, Ode to Joy. Or the agent calls set-next-keys and invents a drill. 

 If the agent is not on this page, it cannot light a key or grade your hands. That is the point of WebMCP. 

 How we built it 

 Browser app: Vite, TypeScript, Web Audio, Web MIDI, and WebMCP on document.modelContext.registerTool . Samples are open rompler sets (Steinway, CP80, Wurlitzer), not a commercial library. 

 I used AI. I am not going to pretend otherwise. 

 
 Ideas and code: Cursor with Grok 4.6 Extra High Fast. Teacher loop, tools, most of the TypeScript. I directed, edited, and cut what did not serve the page. 
 Design: Claude Code, Opus 5. The rack, LCD, key glow, and making it sell instead of look like a bed. 
 Testing: Codex Luna Extra High. Click-throughs: teach me → C4 hit → wrong E4 miss → D4 advances. 
 

 The challenge allows AI. I did not name this CodexPiano or claim an official OpenAI product. The name is KEYLIT because the next key lights. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Native document.modelContext.registerTool still fails with SecurityError in a locked local browser, so the in-page Studio Agent falls back to local tools. Judges need the live HTTPS URL in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. That deploy, the public repo, and the demo video are still on me before the deadline. Samples and the grade-on-press path have to keep working on that origin, not only on localhost. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The lesson only moves when you play the glowing key. A wrong note does not skip ahead. Amber is you, cyan is next, green is the agent — on the same keyboard. Harmonize still refuses if your hands are empty. That is the product, not a chat overlay. 

 What we learned 

 A piano teacher that cannot see the keyboard is a paragraph. A teacher that shares the session is a product. WebMCP only pays off if the tool changes the same keys the human is looking at. get-lesson-state after they play is more useful than another chatbot tip. 

 “Inspired by” is not “copy the pads.” The new thing is the shared lesson. 

 What's next for KEYLIT 

 Ship the HTTPS demo, put the repo and LICENSE on GitHub, and record a under-3-minute video in ChatGPT’s browser: “Teach me piano.” Then freeze for judging. After that: more songs, slower drills, and a teacher that can invent a line and light those keys with set-next-keys .

title: Signal - Self-Extending Tools (Task Board)
pitch: A task board where the agent can propose brand-new WebMCP tools and test its own code but nothing registers or runs until you approve it.
about_excerpt:
A task board where the agent can propose brand-new WebMCP tools and test its own code but nothing registers or runs until you approve it.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 2 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Signal 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Signal 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Signal 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most task boards treat an AI agent like a slightly faster mouse it clicks buttons, scrapes text, guesses what a status means. WebMCP flips that: the site tells the agent exactly what it can do. I wanted to push past "agent checks tasks off a list" and ask a harder question what happens when the agent isn't just using the tools I built, but proposing new ones? 

 What it does 

 Signal is a task board with three layers of WebMCP tools: 

 Task management get_overdue_tasks , search_tasks , add_task , and a heuristic tool, suggest_completions , that scans each task's activity log for real completion signals ("deployed," "merged and closed," "confirmed receipt") and tells the agent which overdue tasks are probably already done. The only tool that writes, bulk_update_status , is rejected outright by the server unless confirmed: true is set which only happens after a human clicks Approve in the UI. The safety isn't a prompt asking the agent to be careful. It's the API contract. 

 Tool Forge the part I'm most proud of. An agent can call propose_tool to define a new tool, composed only from a small whitelist of existing read primitives (chain a call, then filter the result). This does nothing on its own it renders an approval card in the UI. Only when a human clicks Approve does document.modelContext.registerTool() actually fire, live, in that session. No tool's execute() function ever calls registerTool() on another tool's behalf registration is a function of a real UI click, not one tool triggering another, which follows guidance from the WebMCP spec's own design discussion. 

 Project files + sandbox a small in-memory workspace the agent can write to ( write_project_file ), patch surgically without rewriting the whole file ( edit_project_file , which rejects the edit if the target text isn't uniquely identifiable), and execute ( run_code ) inside a hidden, network-disabled <iframe> sandbox with a 3-second timeout. Output streams back into the Agent panel. 

 How I built it 

 Plain Express backend, in-memory store, zero frontend build step the whole UI is vanilla JS calling document.modelContext.registerTool() . No React, no bundler, so it deploys to Render with no configuration. I wanted the WebMCP integration to be readable in a single file, not buried under abstraction. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 I built this solo under a 22-hour submission deadline. Most of the development started on my PC, but with no power for much of the deadline, I had to continue development and testing from my phone. Chrome's chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing flag and mobile DevTools were enough to verify that document.modelContext was registering tools correctly before I had desktop access again
The trickiest design decision was Tool Forge's safety model. My first instinct was to let the agent generate and run arbitrary code for new tools, then I realized that's exactly the kind of thing that looks impressive in a demo and terrible in a security review 

 So I deliberately constrained proposed tools to compositions of a fixed, whitelisted set of read primitives. A proposal can combine existing capabilities in a new way, but it cannot reach new data or perform writes. The same principle applies to the code sandbox: it is genuinely isolated with no network access and a hard timeout rather than simply being labeled safe.
The larger version I have designed goes further, including stronger isolation and actual test execution. For this submission, I focused on shipping a working, enforceable slice of that architecture rather than pretending arbitrary code execution was safe. 

 Accomplishments 

 Built Signal solo in roughly 22 hours, from deciding to enter the challenge on September 2 to a deployed, working WebMCP submission.
I implemented the WebMCP integration from scratch, including structured task tools, a server-enforced human approval gate for writes, and Tool Forge a constrained system where agents can propose new tools that only become registered after explicit human approval.
I also built the supporting project workspace and isolated browser sandbox, then deployed and tested the whole thing under a very limited development environment, continuing from my phone when I didn't have access to power for my PC.
The biggest accomplishment for me isn't the number of features it's that the core safety boundaries are actually enforced by the implementation rather than being claims made in the UI. 

 What's next 

 The sandbox here is JS-only. It's actually a small piece of a much larger AI agent I'm building separately, called Cipher, which has been in active development for a couple of months. This hackathon gave me a reason to ship one small, focused slice of it cleanly. If you're interested in what Cipher is building toward, I'm reachable at favourdev12@gmail.com or @favourdeve on Telegram. 

 Update 

 Devpost extended the challenge deadline after I'd already submitted. I used the extra time to add a real chat interface live tool-calling through the same tool contract described above, not a scripted walkthrough and used it to actually test every tool end-to-end, not just through the WebMCP browser path.

 FlowPulse WebMCP architecture: agents update a visible workflow while humans retain final confirmation.

 Employee provisioning journey: from fragmented requests to accountable human review. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Required-field validation visibly blocks incomplete workflow progress.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 What it does 

 FlowPulse is a WebMCP-powered workflow studio for forms that are usually too multi-step, contextual, or error-prone to complete quickly. It starts with a practical employee tech-and-workspace provisioning flow, alongside residential lease, B2B vendor onboarding, and a clearly labelled synthetic travel-visa sandbox. 

 A person stays in control: an agent can inspect the current form, fill known synthetic values, validate required information, switch workflows, and prepare the final review. The person sees every change in the visible UI and completes the final receipt action themselves. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Traditional form automation is opaque: it scrapes a page or runs beside it, leaving people unsure what changed. FlowPulse exposes five browser-native, goal-shaped WebMCP tools: 

 
 getFormSchema inspects the active workflow, required fields, current values, and step. 
 fillFormFields updates only fields belonging to the active form, visibly in the UI. 
 validateForm returns missing required fields and marks problems on the form. 
 switchTemplate changes the workflow, form, and contextual Copilot guidance together. 
 submitWorkflow validates and opens the review screen; it deliberately stops before final human confirmation. 
 

 This lets people and agents work in the same visible workflow instead of treating the browser as a fragile screen-scraping surface. 

 Experience and safety 

 The app is responsive at mobile, tablet, and desktop sizes. On smaller screens, workflow selection and Copilot controls become on-demand drawers rather than competing fixed sidebars. Required fields have inline validation, progress is explicit, and the review screen groups answers by step before a local receipt is created. 

 The travel-visa flow is explicitly a synthetic-data sandbox. The app does not claim persistent audit storage or automatic final submission. 

 Implementation 

 FlowPulse is a React + TypeScript + Vite application, deployed on Netlify. WebMCP tools are defined with @nekuda/webmcp-sdk and registered with lifecycle cleanup. Automated Playwright tests cover responsive layouts, validation, full review flow, template switching, and registration/invocation of all five tools with visible UI effects.

A secure, agent-ready learning experience where people and AI use WebMCP to find training, build learning paths, track progress, and take permitted actions together.

 Inspiration 

 LearnLogos has a large collection of instructional videos, captions, and sentence-level timestamps. Learners often Blackjack remember what John taught but cannot remember the course, video, or terminology
 needed to find it. We wanted agents to retrieve LearnLogos teaching directly instead of generating a generic answer or guessing how to navigate the website. 

 ## What it does 

 The LearnLogos WebMCP Learning Assistant turns a natural-language question into the most relevant approved teaching excerpt. 

 A supported browser agent can discover and invoke learnlogos.search_training.v1 . The result includes: 

 
 The relevant lesson title and summary 
 Exact source timestamps 
 An SBL-style citation 
 An explanation of why it matched 
 Controlled video playback with captions 
 

 The visible demonstration provides eight alternative questions across two topics. Different ways of asking about program scaling find “Set Exact Program Scaling,” while reading-plan questions find “Jump to Your
 Next Reading.” 

 This demonstrates how people and agents can find the same authoritative instruction without knowing its essentially compression reti Bots exact title or location. 

 ## How we built it 

 The application uses TypeScript, Next.js, React, and Zod. The page registers a structured tool through document.modelContext.registerTool , while both the human interface and browser agent use the same
 validated search service. 

 The contest deployment is separate from the production LearnLogos website. It uses: 

 
 A hard server-side content allowlist 
 Two exact, rights-approved demonstration excerpts 
 Synthetic session state with no customer information 
 Dedicated Upstash Redis rate limiting 
 Short-lived, session-bound media grants 
 Exact media and caption digest verification 
 Same-origin restrictions and a strict content security policy 
 Automated tests covering tool registration, retrieval, authorization, media access, and browser behavior 
 

 ## Challenges 

 The largest challenge was combining a useful demonstration with strict security and intellectual-property boundaries. We needed to show real question-to-video retrieval without exposing production Nz content,
 customer data, full transcripts, or unrestricted media URLs. 

 Natural-language ranking also required care. Common words such as “the” initially created ties between unrelated lessons. We corrected this by excluding conversational filler words from ranking and added
 regression tests for every demonstration question. 

 ## What we learned 

 WebMCP works best as an interface over reusable application services—not as a separate business-logic layer. Structured tools give agents reliable inputs, validated outputs, and clear authorization boundaries
 while preserving an accessible experience for people. 

 We also learned that retrieval quality depends on preserving provenance. A useful answer should remain traceable to the exact lesson, source recording, timestamp range, and access decision. 

 ## What's next 

 The contest entry is a secure vertical slice of a larger LearnLogos vision. Future work includes searching customer-owned training first, coherent transcript segmentation, hybrid semantic retrieval,
 personalized learning paths, progress-aware recommendations, and secure previews of additional approved lessons. 

 LearnLogos is an independent training provider. It is not owned, operated, sponsored, or endorsed by Logos.

 Inspiration 

 Theatre information is scattered across articles, PDFs, venue announcements, and historical lists. Finding a reliable answer often means opening several documents, searching manually, and checking whether every detail is supported. 

 I built Praxa to explore a better model: a shared research workspace where a person can ask naturally and a browser agent can use purpose-built tools to retrieve evidence, compare productions, and present a concise answer with page-level citations. 

 What it does 

 Praxa is a WebMCP-native research assistant focused on Broadway and West End theatre. It exposes three typed browser tools: 

 
 ask_theatre answers factual theatre questions using indexed source documents. 
 search_theatre_archive performs semantic search and returns the strongest page-level passages without requiring an LLM response. 
 compare_productions compares two productions using a user-selected focus, such as venue, opening date, or run length. 
 

 Every agent action updates the same visible workspace used by the person. This keeps the human in the loop: the user can see the request, answer, latency, sources, page numbers, and supporting excerpts. 

 Why WebMCP 

 A conventional assistant must scrape page text, infer controls, or imitate clicks. Praxa instead publishes explicit tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . 

 The tools have JSON input schemas, bounded inputs, read-only annotations, untrusted-content annotations, cancellation support, and structured results. This gives agents a reliable interface while preserving the normal human-facing website as progressive enhancement. 

 Before WebMCP, a person could ask Praxa questions manually, but an agent could not reliably discover its research capabilities or invoke them directly. Now people and agents can work in the same interface: an agent can search the archive, inspect evidence, ask a grounded question, compare productions, and leave the result visible for the person to review. 

 How I built it 

 The production application uses: 

 
 FastAPI and Uvicorn for the web service and research APIs 
 the WebMCP imperative API for browser-native tool registration 
 LangChain for retrieval-augmented generation 
 Chroma for persistent vector search 
 Hugging Face sentence-transformer embeddings 
 OpenRouter for grounded answer generation 
 Railway for containerized production hosting 
 GitHub Actions for linting, tests, coverage enforcement, and Docker builds 
 

 The retrieval system downloads theatre PDFs, divides them into overlapping chunks, embeds them, and stores the index on a persistent Railway volume. Answers are restricted to retrieved excerpts and include citation labels matching the page-level source records shown in the interface. 

 The production pipeline also rejects provider metadata and uncited generated claims, retries invalid responses once, and safely abstains if a grounded answer cannot be produced. 

 Challenges I faced 

 The first major challenge was converting a human-only Streamlit prototype into a genuine WebMCP product. I replaced the original entry point with a same-origin FastAPI application and created tool-specific APIs that both return structured results and update the visible interface. 

 Cold-start behavior was another challenge because the embedding model must be loaded before retrieval. Persistent Chroma storage prevents the source index from being rebuilt after each deployment. 

 Live testing also exposed an intermittent model-provider response that returned safety metadata instead of a theatre answer. I added a tested output-quality gate that rejects metadata and uncited claims before they can reach users. 

 Challenge-period work 

 Praxa existed before the hackathon as a theatre RAG prototype. During the submission period, I meaningfully extended it with: 

 
 three working WebMCP tools; 
 a new shared human–agent interface; 
 FastAPI research and semantic-search endpoints; 
 structured tool schemas and annotations; 
 visible agent-driven UI updates; 
 citation-alignment and output-quality safeguards; 
 Railway deployment, CI checks, and WebMCP regression tests. 
 

 The dated GitHub pull requests and commit history clearly separate this work from the earlier prototype. 

 What I learned 

 This project taught me that WebMCP is more than browser automation. It creates a stable contract between websites and agents while preserving the website as the place where people understand and supervise the work. 

 I also learned that agent-ready applications need more than tool registration. They need careful schemas, visible state, deterministic evidence retrieval, cancellation handling, security boundaries, production monitoring, and graceful failure behavior. 

 What’s next 

 Next, I would expand Praxa into a broader performing-arts research network with licensed data sources, venue and ticket integrations, saved research collections, multilingual retrieval, evaluation datasets, and tools that help audiences, journalists, students, and theatre professionals collaborate with agents.

about_excerpt:
A workspace where you and an in-browser AI agent work the same job board resolving official career portals, extracting real openings, and scoring them against your resume, all via WebMCP tools.

 Story
