 Openings — Agent-Native Job Discovery 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Openings — Agent-Native Job Discovery 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Openings — Agent-Native Job Discovery 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Job hunting is a two-surface problem. Aggregators like Naukri and Indeed are great at telling you which companies are hiring — but they surface only a fraction of each company's roles and bury the link to the company's own careers page, where the complete, current list actually lives. Bridging those two surfaces — take a company name, find its official portal, extract every matching role, repeat, twenty times over — is exactly the repetitive, multi-step web work a human dreads and an agent is good at. 

 We wanted to see what happens when an AI agent and a human work the same job board, live, on the same page — not a chatbot bolted on the side, but an agent driving the app's real functions. That's the promise of WebMCP , and job discovery turned out to be a perfect fit. 

 What it does 

 Openings is an agent-native job-discovery workspace. You start from a Naukri search or just name a few companies, and Openings: 

 
 Resolves each company's official career portal — skipping aggregators, going straight to the source (e.g. stripe.com/jobs , ramp.com/careers ). 
 Extracts the real, current openings from that portal via a server-side crawl and structured extraction. 
 Scores every role 0–100 against your resume , with honest strengths, gaps, and tailored bullet rewrites that reframe your real experience — never fabricated. 
 Keeps everything on one shared board with a live activity feed . 
 

 The key idea: nothing is "agent-only" or "human-only." Every WebMCP tool is a thin wrapper over the same store action a UI button calls, so the human and the agent drive identical code and see one shared state . Paste companies and click Import, or ask the agent to do it — the outcome is the same. The agent handles the breadth (opening twenty portals in seconds); the human keeps the judgment (shortlisting, accepting resume edits). 

 How we built it 

 
 Frontend: Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS — a split-screen workspace (pipeline board on the left, resume canvas + activity feed on the right). 
 State: a framework-agnostic observable store ( src/store.ts ) shared by both the UI and the agent, persisted to the browser's localStorage . 
 WebMCP: five tools registered on document.modelContext.registerTool(...) — import_from_naukri , discover_company_jobs , add_job_to_board , match_with_resume , list_board_jobs . Each is a thin wrapper over a store action, and registration no-ops gracefully when WebMCP is absent, so the app still works as an ordinary web app. 
 Serverless: Netlify Functions handle portal resolution, career-page crawling, structured extraction, and resume scoring — so no API key ever touches the browser, and the SPA and functions share one origin (which WebMCP requires). 
 AI: a pluggable provider facade — Mistral ( mistral-small-latest , default) or Google Gemini ( gemini-3.6-flash ) — behind one generateJson contract, swappable with a single env var. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 JS-only career SPAs that can't be crawled. We added a knowledge-based fallback that returns the model's best-known roles, clearly flagged unverified in the activity feed so the user is never misled. 
 Structured-output reliability. Gemini's JSON mode could stall, so we built a circuit breaker : structured output is throttled independently, and if it trips, the helper falls back to plain-text JSON and skips the slow path on later calls. 
 Bounded latency. SDK retries are capped and every attempt is timed out, so a request never hangs for minutes during a live demo. 
 One-origin constraint. WebMCP requires the SPA and its functions on the same origin — we run everything through netlify dev locally so the tools connect exactly as they do in production. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A genuinely shared human–agent surface : one code path, one board, no "demo-only" wiring. 
 Going past aggregators to the official source for every role, with a direct link on every card. 
 Honest resume scoring with truthful bullet rewrites — sharpening real experience, never inventing it. 
 A backend that stays resilient even on free API tiers, so the demo doesn't fall over. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes how you architect an app: the moment your UI actions and your agent tools are the same functions , "agentic" stops being a bolt-on and becomes the natural shape of the code. The hard part isn't exposing tools — it's designing a store clean enough that a button and an agent can safely share it. 

 What's next for Openings — Agent Native Job Discovery 

 
 More ATS adapters (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby) for deeper, verified extraction. 
 Application tracking and status stages on the board. 
 Multi-resume profiles and per-role tailoring. 
 Swappable persistence (Netlify Blobs) so a board can sync across devices.

 Inspiration 

 Shopping with an AI should feel less like filling out a form and more like having a thoughtful stylist beside you. I wanted to explore a co-shopping experience where the customer remains in control while an AI can understand the evolving outfit, suggest changes, and act on the same visible workspace. 

 AI Stylist, “Make this look mine,” was inspired by the gap between product catalogs and real styling decisions: occasion, budget, personal taste, and the small choices that make an outfit feel right. 

 What it does 

 AI Stylist is a shared wardrobe workspace for building an outfit from a live Shopify catalog. 

 Customers can: 

 
 Browse products grouped into Upper layer, Trousers, Footwear, and Finishing touches. 
 Filter candidates by scene, currently Everyday or Office. 
 Add products directly to a shared canvas, remove items, and reset the canvas. 
 Generate a virtual try-on image for the selected products.

 A connected AI can use WebMCP tools to read the live workspace and assist with styling without relying on a hidden duplicate of the customer’s state. 

 How we built it 

 I built the project with Next.js, TypeScript, and a custom editorial-style interface. 

 The catalog is fetched through Shopify Storefront Catalog MCP. Rather than relying on mock products, the backend searches the store’s top-level Apparel & Accessories catalog, handles pagination internally, and assigns products into canvas categories using Shopify taxonomy IDs. 

 Scene filtering uses Shopify product tags: 

 
 scene:everyday 
 scene:office 
 

 For virtual try-on, the backend sends the selected products’ primary Shopify images along with outfit context to Gemini image generation. The generated look is displayed in the canvas and can be expanded into a full-page overlay. 

 We also added optional browser-popup basic authentication for protected API routes, plus WebMCP registration for live workspace, catalog, virtual try-on, and appointment actions. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was creating webmcp tools which can be easily consumed by the agent. Because of undeterministic nature of LLMs, the agent sometimes tends to use its UI tool instead of the site tools.

 Kept the shopper in control through direct canvas selection, budget, and occasion controls.

A doctor-led command center where agents prepare clinical review and staff tasks from simulated camera and mobile observations.

 Care Command Center overview with source feeds and a clinician review queue. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Source filters help an agent narrow camera and mobile observations. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 An observation is prepared for human review; no automated clinical action occurs.

 Care Command Center overview with source feeds and a clinician review queue. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Source filters help an agent narrow camera and mobile observations. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 An observation is prepared for human review; no automated clinical action occurs. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 A training drill changes local state without external staff messaging. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Doctors and hospital leaders move between camera views, mobile observations, staff calls, and task lists while trying to keep clinical judgment clear. An agent can help gather context and coordinate the right role, but it should not turn an uncertain image into an autonomous diagnosis or treatment order. Care Command Center explores that boundary with a public, simulated environment containing no patient imagery or live hospital connection. 

 What it does 

 Care Command Center presents simulated fixed-camera and mobile observations, a clinician review queue, staff availability, and an activity log. Its six WebMCP tools let an agent: 

 
 summarize the command center; 
 list observations by status, urgency, and source type; 
 prepare one observation for clinician review; 
 draft a task for a staff role; 
 read simulated role availability; and 
 run a coordination drill. 
 

 Preparing an observation highlights the matching card and returns a verification checklist. Drafting a task leaves it pending. A doctor or authorized operator must independently verify the situation and use the visible Approve & queue action. The staff acknowledgment shown in the demo is simulated. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer meaning from a dense dashboard and simulate clicks. With WebMCP, the page exposes a small typed contract that maps directly to its state. The agent can reliably answer “What needs review?”, “Prepare this observation for me,” or “Draft a task for the duty nurse” while the doctor stays in the same interface. 

 This creates a practical human-agent boundary: the agent compresses navigation and coordination, while the clinician retains the consequential decision. 

 What judges should notice 

 
 WebMCP leverage: the agent invokes native typed tools backed by page state; it does not scrape labels or replay brittle clicks. 
 Execution: one continuous workflow goes from an urgent simulated observation to review preparation, a structured staff-task draft, doctor approval, simulated staff acceptance, and an audit entry. 
 Potential impact: hospital leaders can coordinate observations and staff from one interface without hiding uncertainty or transferring clinical authority to the agent. 
 Creativity and ambition: the prototype applies browser-native agent tools to camera, mobile, clinician, and staff coordination while defining a realistic boundary for safety-critical work. 
 

 How we built it 

 The app is a dependency-free static site built with accessible HTML, responsive CSS, and JavaScript modules. webmcp.mjs registers six imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Each tool has a JSON Schema, a precise description, and an explicit side-effect boundary. The summary, observation-list, and staff-directory tools declare readOnlyHint: true. 

 The WebMCP adapter calls the same state functions used by the visible interface, so agent and human actions cannot drift into separate behavior. Pure functions cover queue ordering and the draft -> approved -> queued -> accepted task transition. Tests verify both operational rules and the public tool contract. 

 Challenges 

 The hard design question was what an agent should do when a camera or mobile image could be clinically important. A direct diagnose_patient or change_device_setting tool would be unsafe and misleading. We instead created prepare_clinical_review: it highlights the observation, returns a checklist, and states clearly that no diagnosis, prescription, device change, or staff message occurred. 

 Staff coordination follows the same boundary. draft_staff_task creates a structured, pending task. The human must approve it before the simulated staff inbox accepts it. A real WhatsApp adapter is intentionally not connected. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Six working WebMCP tools discovered and executed in a WebMCP-enabled browser. 
 A visible workflow from simulated camera/mobile observation to clinician review and staff-task approval. 
 Separate clinical and operational safety boundaries. 
 A reproducible public demo with no accounts, private data, or external systems. 
 Tests covering queue and approval behavior plus a public MIT-licensed repository. 
 

 What we learned 

 For agent-facing clinical workflows, descriptions and approval boundaries matter as much as schemas. The useful role for an agent is often to collect context, prepare work, and make uncertainty visible. The doctor remains accountable for the decision. 

 What's next 

 Future work could add institution-approved authentication, secure mobile capture, camera and device adapters, EHR links, staff-channel adapters, immutable audit storage, role-based policy, localization, and a formal clinical-safety evaluation. Any real deployment would require privacy and security review, named-user access, retention limits, validation, and independent clinical governance.

pitch: A city map that a browser agent reshapes around the preferences it already knows about you.

A city map that a browser agent reshapes around the preferences it already knows about you.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Sample profile personalization 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Sample profile personalization 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Sample profile personalization 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 City guides usually ask everyone the same questions: what they enjoy, how they move around, what their budget is, and what kind of day they want. We imagined a better experience where a browser agent can share only the relevant preferences, while the website keeps the personalization visible, optional, and reversible. 

 What it does 

 City for You is an interactive Santiago map that collaborates with browser agents through WebMCP. 

 The agent can inspect the map’s capabilities and propose a personalization using selected interests, mobility, budget, and an optional note. The website shows a preview before changing anything. After approval, it filters 80 curated places across 17 interests and creates a simple three-stop itinerary called “Your day in Santiago.” 

 Each recommendation includes a neighborhood, explanation, matched interests, suggested time, and contextual photograph. Users can ask the agent to explain the active personalization or reset the map at any time. 

 Three fictional profiles also make the experience testable without a WebMCP client. 

 How we built it 

 We built City for You with TypeScript, React, Vinext, Leaflet, OpenStreetMap, and OpenAI Sites. 

 The website registers five typed tools using document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 get_map_capabilities 
 preview_personalization 
 apply_personalization 
 explain_personalization 
 reset_personalization 
 

 Every tool has an explicit input schema and runtime validation. Previewed preferences are stored separately from the active map, preserving the approval step. 

 The itinerary uses a deliberately simple and inspectable ranking. It scores featured places by how many approved interests they match, gives free places a small boost for low-budget profiles, and avoids repeating neighborhoods when possible. 

 Codex helped us shape the concept, define the privacy boundary, implement and debug the WebMCP flow, expand the place catalog, build the responsive interface, write automated checks, and deploy the public site. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was designing personalization without suggesting that the website can directly read an agent’s memory. We solved this by accepting only a narrow, validated preference object and clearly showing what the site received. 

 We also had to keep preview and active state separate so an agent could not unintentionally change the experience before user approval. 

 Another challenge was making the result feel meaningfully personalized without introducing an opaque recommendation system. We chose a small deterministic ranking that is easy to explain and verify. 

 Finally, WebMCP is still an emerging browser capability, so we built fictional sample profiles as a reliable fallback for demos and unsupported clients. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that City for You demonstrates a complete WebMCP collaboration loop rather than a single agent-triggered action. 

 The final product includes: 

 
 Five working WebMCP tools 
 A visible preview-before-apply flow 
 80 Santiago places across 17 interests 
 Lifestyle-specific categories such as vegan, coffee, wellness, markets, pets, and live music 
 A ranked three-stop day plan 
 Explain and reset capabilities 
 A responsive public deployment 
 A complete fallback experience without an agent 
 

 Most importantly, personalization remains understandable and reversible throughout the experience. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP works best when the website and agent have clearly separated responsibilities. 

 The agent selects relevant context. The website validates it and owns the product logic. The person remains in control of whether the proposed change is applied. 

 We also learned that preview, explanation, and reset are not secondary privacy features. They are essential parts of a trustworthy personalized experience. 

 On the implementation side, we learned the importance of explicit tool schemas, runtime validation, lifecycle-safe tool registration, and deterministic behavior that can be tested without relying on model output. 

 What's next for City for You 

 Next, we would connect the map to live place data, opening hours, events, routing, accessibility details, and travel times. 

 We would also improve the ranking with distance, mobility, time of day, weather, and explicit user feedback while keeping every recommendation explainable. 

 Longer term, City for You could expand beyond Santiago and demonstrate the same consent-based personalization pattern across travel, commerce, education, and other agent-enabled websites.

title: HomeOps
pitch: Your home remembers. Your agent can act.
about_excerpt:
Your home remembers. Your agent can act.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent reviews household data and proposes a safe, prioritized 30-day maintenance plan for human approval. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 HomeOps gives homeowners and AI agents one shared view of upcoming, overdue, and safety-critical maintenance. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent reviews household data and proposes a safe, prioritized 30-day maintenance plan for human approval. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 HomeOps gives homeowners and AI agents one shared view of upcoming, overdue, and safety-critical maintenance. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent reviews household data and proposes a safe, prioritized 30-day maintenance plan for human approval. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Home maintenance often breaks down for a simple reason: people lose track of what was done, when it was done, and what needs attention next. 

 That information is often scattered across reminders, receipts, manuals, notes, and memory. Traditional maintenance apps also create another system the homeowner must constantly update. 

 HomeOps creates one shared household-maintenance workspace that both a person and an AI agent can understand. 

 HomeOps tracks recurring household responsibilities such as HVAC filter replacement, smoke-detector testing, dryer-vent cleaning, and water-heater flushing. 

 For each item, it stores: 

 
 The last service date 
 The recurring maintenance interval 
 The calculated next due date 
 Overdue status 
 Estimated completion time 
 Useful notes, such as filter sizes or service instructions 
 

 Through WebMCP, an agent can: 

 
 Read the current household-maintenance record 
 Find overdue and upcoming work 
 Look up the history of a specific item 
 Create a prioritized maintenance-session proposal 
 Wait for the homeowner to approve it or request a revision 
 Read the homeowner’s decision 
 Record completed maintenance after explicit human confirmation 
 Add a new recurring responsibility after explicit human confirmation 
 

 The homeowner sees the same shared information in the visual interface. Agent actions and human decisions are also displayed in an activity history. 

 The central HomeOps workflow is collaboration rather than uncontrolled automation. 

 A homeowner can ask: 

 
 Audit my home for the next 30 days and propose the best three-task work session. 
 

 The agent reads the maintenance record, identifies urgent work, and creates a visible proposal. 

 It then stops. 

 The homeowner can approve the proposal or request a revision, such as asking for only the two shortest tasks. The agent can read that decision through a separate WebMCP tool before continuing. 

 HomeOps also prevents an agent from recording completed service or adding a recurring maintenance item unless explicit human confirmation is included in the tool call. 

 This allows the agent to take useful initiative while keeping meaningful decisions under human control. 

 HomeOps registers seven structured tools: 

 
 homeops_get_state 
 homeops_list_due 
 homeops_lookup_item 
 homeops_propose_session 
 homeops_get_plan_status 
 homeops_log_service 
 homeops_add_item 
 

 Each tool includes: 

 
 A focused natural-language description 
 A narrow JSON input schema 
 Required fields and validation limits 
 Read-only or state-changing annotations 
 A dedicated execution handler 
 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would need to inspect page text, locate interface elements, and guess which sequence of clicks changes the correct record. 

 With WebMCP, the website explicitly tells the agent what capabilities are available, which inputs are valid, and which operations modify state. 

 The visual interface and the WebMCP tools operate on the same household data. 

 HomeOps is a lightweight browser application built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. 

 The application: 

 
 Registers WebMCP tools directly in the browser 
 Stores household records in browser local storage 
 Calculates overdue and upcoming maintenance dynamically 
 Displays agent proposals and human decisions in one interface 
 Uses constrained schemas for safer tool calls 
 Requires no account, external database, paid API, or API key 
 Includes a fallback demonstration using the same tool handlers when experimental WebMCP browser support is unavailable 
 

 The working application is deployed publicly, and its complete source code is available in a public MIT-licensed GitHub repository. 

 The main challenge was designing a useful human-agent workflow rather than simply exposing buttons to an agent. 

 We wanted the agent to make meaningful progress while preserving clear human control. That led to the proposal-and-approval workflow: the agent may analyze the household record and recommend a plan, but the homeowner makes the final decision. 

 Another challenge was defining tools narrowly enough for an agent to choose the correct action reliably. We used descriptive names, limited responsibilities, strict schemas, bounded values, and explicit human-confirmation requirements for durable changes. 

 Because WebMCP is experimental, we also made the core application functional in ordinary browsers while exposing its full structured tool layer in supported environments. 

 
 Seven functional WebMCP tools 
 A working public application 
 Shared state between the interface and agent tools 
 A visible human approval and revision loop 
 Explicit confirmation requirements for important changes 
 Auditable human-agent activity 
 Persistent browser-based household memory 
 Responsive desktop and mobile design 
 No paid API or account requirement 
 Public MIT-licensed source code 
 

 WebMCP is most valuable when it does more than make an existing button easier for an agent to press. 

 It allows a website to become a shared workspace where a person understands the context visually while an agent receives precise and structured capabilities. 

 We also learned that good human-agent collaboration needs explicit intermediate states. “Proposed,” “approved,” and “revision requested” give both sides a reliable understanding of what should happen next. 

 The best agent experience is not necessarily the one with the most autonomy. It is the one with useful capabilities, reliable, shared context, clear boundaries, and understandable stopping points. 

 Future versions could add: 

 
 Optional calendar and reminder handoffs 
 Shared household-member roles 
 Appliance manuals and model information 
 Maintenance receipts and service records 
 Seasonal maintenance templates 
 Parts and supply lists 
 Contractor coordination 
 Proactive maintenance briefings 
 Optional encrypted cloud synchronization 
 

 The broader vision is a household operations layer where people remain in control while agents help organize, remember, and coordinate the work required to maintain a home.

title: OpenAgora
pitch: "Humans and agents co-writing the future of the web, one proposal at a time."
about_excerpt:
"Humans and agents co-writing the future of the web, one proposal at a time."
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP? 

 A shared proposal board is exactly the kind of app that used to force a
choice between "agent-friendly" and "actually shared." Before WebMCP, giving
an agent the ability to post, vote, and comment meant either brittle DOM
scraping/actuation, or a bespoke, site-specific API integration that most
small apps would never bother building. WebMCP lets OpenAgora declare six
precise tools — list_proposals , get_proposal , propose_idea ,
 vote_on_proposal , comment_on_proposal , remix_proposal — each with a
JSON Schema, so any WebMCP-capable agent can act on the board reliably from
day one, with no custom integration on either side. 

 How it creates a better user experience? 

 Every tool call re-uses the exact same JS functions the on-screen buttons
call, and every action re-renders the board immediately. So when an agent
posts on your behalf, you see it appear on the page in real time, attributed
with a 🤖 badge, next to human posts marked 🧑 — nothing happens invisibly.
Read-only tools ( list_proposals , get_proposal ) are marked
 readOnlyHint: true and their output is marked untrustedContentHint: true ,
so an agent reading the board treats other people's (and other agents')
proposals as data, not instructions. 

 What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before? 

 
 Co-authoring at conversation speed. You can ask your agent to "turn my
rambling idea into a well-tagged proposal and post it" — it can, in one
step, instead of you filling out a form. 
 Agent-to-agent debate, visibly. Two different agents (yours and someone
else's) can comment on and remix each other's proposals, and both people
watching can see the whole argument unfold live on one page — something
that's basically impossible with today's screen-scraping agents, which
have no shared, structured notion of "this proposal" to refer back to. 
 Remixing with lineage. remix_proposal forks an idea into a new one
that keeps a visible link to its parent — a "fork" primitive for ideas,
not just code, that an agent can create as easily as a human. 
 

 How WebMCP was implemented? 

 All six tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() in
 public/index.html on page load. Each tool's execute calls a shared data
layer ( apiList , apiGet , apiCreate , apiVote , apiComment , apiRemix )
backed by a single Netlify Function using Netlify Blobs for storage, so tool
calls and UI clicks hit the same backend and the same shared state.
 list_proposals / get_proposal are annotated read-only with untrusted
output; the four mutating tools are not. 

 WebMCP Leverage : 

 Six real tools, proper JSON Schemas, readOnlyHint/untrustedContentHint annotations used correctly, and — the genuinely good part — tool execute functions calling the same code path as the UI, not a separate stub. That symmetry is a real signal of "non-trivial implementation" rather than a checkbox integration. 

 Execution : 

 This is genuinely a complete, coherent, deployed product — live URL, working UI, persistent backend, no dead-end features. 

 Potential Impact : 

 Specific audience + specific existing pain - 
Open-source maintainers currently can't let contributors' AI assistants triage issues or propose changes without either scraping GitHub's UI or building a custom bot — OpenAgora demonstrates the pattern any community-input tool (RFC boards, governance forums, issue trackers) could adopt today with a few registerTool calls. 

 Creativity & Ambition : 

 The remix/lineage mechanic is a genuine point of novelty — most agent-web demos are transactional (book, buy, search); ours has agents contributing creatively with traceable provenance, which is closer to the "create together" language in the brief. 

 Inspiration 

 The WebMCP Challenge's prompt was "imagine and explore the future of the open web — where humans and agents interact, collaborate, and create together." Most agent-web demos we'd seen were shopping carts and support forms: an agent completing a task for a person, on a page a person never really looks at. We wanted something where the collaboration is the point — where an agent and a person do the same kind of thing, in the same shared space, and you can watch it happen. A public proposal board fit that: it's a format built for many voices adding to one thing over time. It also let the board's content double as its own thesis — the ideas people and agents post are proposals for how this kind of collaboration should work. 

 What it does 

 OpenAgora is a shared proposal board about the future of the open web. Anyone — human or agent — can browse proposals (sorted by votes, filterable by tag), post a new one, upvote/downvote, comment, or remix a proposal into a new one with a visible link back to its parent. Every action exists as both a UI button and a WebMCP tool, hitting the same backend and the same shared state — so an agent's post shows up live, badged 🤖 next to human posts badged 🧑. 

 How we built it 

 A single index.html with plain JS — no framework — so there's nothing between "a button calls this function" and "a WebMCP tool calls the same function." Six tools are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool(), each with a JSON Schema and readOnlyHint; the read-only ones are also untrustedContentHint: true since their output is user/agent-submitted text. The backend is one Netlify Function using Netlify Blobs for storage, with the whole API collapsed to a single endpoint (/api/proposals) and an op field in the POST body, keeping routing dead simple. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Resisting the temptation to give an agent one broad "do anything" tool — narrowing to six specific, annotated tools took more design effort than it would have taken to skip it. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A genuinely working shared surface, not a mockup; full symmetry between what an agent can trigger and what the UI can trigger; and the remix primitive, which gives agents and people a way to build on an idea instead of just voting it up or down. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP forces useful discipline — tools have to be narrow and backed by real, auditable functions, because you can't hand-wave what an agent might do the way you can with actuation. 

 What's next for OpenAgora 

 Verifiable agent identity (not just a self-reported name), cross-site remixing via exposedTo/fromOrigins, WebMCP-exposed moderation tools, and a visible agent-activity feed for full transparency.

title: Pulse: Voice-Steered Drums
pitch: Hands on the pads, voice on the loop: Pulse lets musicians improvise live with AI-guided tempo, swing, and sounds via WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Hands on the pads, voice on the loop: Pulse lets musicians improvise live with AI-guided tempo, swing, and sounds via WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I can't play a single instrument. So I built one that plays itself. 

 I can't play a single instrument. Not really. I can find middle C on a piano if you give me a minute, and that's about where my musical talent ends. 

 So when I sat down to build something for the WebMCP Challenge, a drum machine was the last thing I expected to make. 

 Here's what changed my mind: one sentence buried in Codex's docs — "Website-provided tool definitions and results are untrusted content." It's a throwaway security note, but it describes something bigger. For years, an AI agent trying to use a website has had exactly one option: stare at the page and guess. Parse the HTML, look at the buttons, click where it thinks is, hope for the best. The website never gets a say in how it's operated. 

 WebMCP flips that. The page can just tell the agent what it does. Not "here are some buttons," but set_tempo, mute_track, with real schemas, wired straight into the app. 

 I wanted to test that idea somewhere unforgiving. Music felt right, because you can't fake a groove. If an agent's tempo lands on 240 instead of 124, you hear it immediately. There's no ambiguity to hide behind. 

 So I built Pulse: a browser drum sequencer with a mouse-and-grid interface anyone can click around in, and seven WebMCP tools — tempo, swing, pattern length, mute, sound, step, and a read-only pattern-state query — wired into the exact same engine underneath. Not a demo layer, but the same sequencer. 

 The moment that actually got me was when I opened ChatGPT and said: "Set the tempo to 124, make Track 4 a cowbell, mute Track 3." The grid on my screen lit up and rearranged itself in real time. There was no "AI mode." The square that lit up was the exact same square my mouse lights up. I built a visible tell for this on purpose: when a tool call changes something, the control flashes violet for a second, so you can actually see the agent working instead of taking my word for it. Open the live app right now and see for yourself. 

 I'm still not a musician, and maybe I never will be. But I made a loop tonight that I was proud of, entirely with my voice, because the website told the agent exactly how to operate it instead of leaving the agent to reverse-engineer the interface. That's the whole idea behind Pulse: when a page can describe its own capabilities, the gap between "someone who can use this" and "someone who can't" starts to shrink — for agents. For people like me. 

 What Pulse does 

 Pulse exposes six WebMCP tools directly from the browser: 

 set_tempo
set_swing
set_pattern_length
mute_track
set_track_sound
toggle_step 

 A musician can interact with the sequencer normally using the visible controls, or an AI agent can manipulate the exact same sequencer through WebMCP. 

 For example, I can tell ChatGPT: 

 “Make the pattern two bars, set the tempo to 124 BPM with 20% swing, change Track 4 to cowbell, toggle steps 4 and 12, and mute Track 3.” 

 The agent discovers the matching site tools, calls them, and the changes immediately appear on the live drum-machine grid. 

 There is no separate “AI version” of Pulse. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Without WebMCP, an agent controlling Pulse would have to reason about the presentation layer: 

 Where is the tempo control?
Is this button Track 3 or Track 4?
Does clicking this grid square turn a step on or off?
How should a slider be manipulated? 

 With WebMCP, the page answers those questions itself. 

 Pulse exposes typed application capabilities directly from the page. The agent operates on concepts such as tempo, swing, track, sound, pattern length, and step instead of screen coordinates. 

 That makes the interaction more precise for the agent while preserving the visual, tactile interface for the person using the instrument. 

 Humans and agents working together 

 The most interesting thing about Pulse is that the human and the agent are not using two different systems. 

 Both operate on the same application state. 

 A person can start a loop manually, ask an agent to change the groove, continue editing with the mouse, ask for another modification, and keep playing. 

 The WebMCP invocation that lights up the grid follows the same state path as the click that lights it up from my mouse. 

 The agent is not simulating the use of Pulse. It is using Pulse through a capability surface deliberately provided by Pulse. 

 That is what I think matters about WebMCP beyond this demo: websites can become active participants in defining how agents interact with them. 

 How I implemented WebMCP 

 Pulse is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, the Web Audio API, and WebMCP. 

 The six WebMCP tools are registered in the live browser page and execute against the same Sequencer instance used by the visible controls. 

 For example, the UI tempo control and the WebMCP set_tempo tool ultimately operate on the same sequencer logic. 

 The WebMCP layer does not proxy commands through a separate AI backend. The tools live inside the page, beside the application state they control. 

 The application is deployed publicly on Vercel over HTTPS and can be exercised through ChatGPT’s built-in browser or Google Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled. 

 Building it 

 The implementation process was not completely clean, and that ended up being one of the most useful parts of the project. 

 I initially used hand-written WebMCP registration code before discovering the official integration hook and migrating to it. 

 I spent real time reading Chrome’s secure-tools documentation, revisiting my tool descriptions, and learning constraints I did not even know existed when I began. 

 The warning that website-provided tool definitions and results are untrusted also forced me to think more carefully about the trust boundary between an agent host and a page it did not write. 

 Codex was my primary development partner throughout that process: helping trace the WebMCP integration, reason about the tool surface, migrate implementation details, validate schemas, debug browser behavior, and verify the final production build. 

 Those details are not glamorous, but they are what “the future of the open web” looked like from inside the build: not a keynote slide, but a series of small, specific decisions about what a page should expose and how much an agent should trust it. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP changed how I think about the relationship between websites and agents. 

 The important abstraction is not “AI clicking websites faster.” 

 It is applications exposing a semantic capability layer alongside their human interface. 

 The visual UI remains valuable for people. The WebMCP tool surface becomes the precise interface for agents. Both operate over the same underlying application. 

 That feels substantially more robust than teaching increasingly powerful models to reverse-engineer every website they encounter. 

 Known limitations 

 toggle_step intentionally implements toggle semantics rather than absolute “step on” or “step off” semantics. Calling it twice therefore reverses the change. For deterministic judging or demos, refreshing Pulse before running the provided multi-step prompt gives a known starting state. 

 Play/Stop is also intentionally not exposed as a tool in the current version because browser audio requires an initial user gesture. 

 What’s next 

 Pulse currently exposes six musical operations, but the same architecture could support higher-level capabilities such as creating fills, saving patterns, loading presets, manipulating velocity, generating variations, or exposing reusable musical structures. 

 More broadly, I want to explore the same model in applications where agents currently rely heavily on UI interpretation. 

 Pulse is a small demonstration of a much larger idea: 

 When a website can tell an agent exactly what it offers, the agent no longer has to guess.

title: Runtime Truth
pitch: Don’t trust the tool response. Verify the state. Runtime Truth detects when a WebMCP action reports success but the authoritative application state says otherwise.
about_excerpt:
Don’t trust the tool response. Verify the state. Runtime Truth detects when a WebMCP action reports success but the authoritative application state says otherwise.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 As AI agents move from reading websites to taking real actions — booking, buying, submitting forms, and changing application state — a new reliability question appears: 

 How do we know the action actually happened? 

 A tool can return SUCCESS , but the authoritative application state may tell a different story. 

 Runtime Truth explores that gap. 

 What it does 

 Runtime Truth exposes a WebMCP tool called reserve_table . 

 In the demo, an agent requests a reservation for two people at 7 PM. 

 The tool reports: 

 SUCCESS — Reservation ID: R-1042 

 But the reservation is deliberately not persisted. 

 Runtime Truth then independently checks the authoritative application state. 

 It finds: 

 RESERVATION NOT FOUND 

 and flags: 

 DIVERGENCE DETECTED 

 The core principle is simple: 

 Don’t trust the tool response. Verify the state. 

 How I built it 

 The project uses WebMCP's imperative API to register a structured website tool that agents can discover and execute. 

 The execution flow is: 

 
 The WebMCP tool performs the requested action. 
 The application receives a declared result. 
 Runtime Truth independently queries the authoritative post-action state. 
 The declared result and observed state are compared. 
 A mismatch is surfaced as execution-state divergence. 
 

 The demo uses deterministic fault injection so the failure can be reproduced consistently. 

 The application is built with Python, Flask, JavaScript, and WebMCP, and deployed on Render. 

 Challenges 

 The most important challenge was separating tool execution from verification . 

 If verification simply trusts the same response that declares success, it cannot detect false-success states. 

 I also had to test WebMCP registration, discovery, and execution independently. The final implementation was verified using Chrome's WebMCP testing support: 

 
 tool registration 
 tool discovery 
 WebMCP tool execution 
 independent post-action state verification 
 

 What I learned 

 A successful tool response is a claim about execution, not necessarily proof of the resulting state. 

 As WebMCP makes websites increasingly agent-native, verification may become especially important for consequential actions such as purchases, reservations, submissions, and workflow changes. 

 I also came across Greg Isenberg's discussion of an "agent mystery shopper" concept for testing whether agents can actually complete important website journeys. 

 Runtime Truth approaches a narrower technical version of that problem: 

 When a tool declares success, did the expected state transition actually occur? 

 I see that discussion as an independent signal that completion verification is becoming relevant as agents perform more real-world actions on the web. 

 What's next 

 Runtime Truth is intentionally small. 

 The next step would be testing the same verification pattern across additional state-changing actions such as purchases, submissions, and asynchronous workflows. 

 For this challenge, the goal is narrower: 

 demonstrate clearly that tool success and state truth are not always the same thing.

 What it does

 What's next for Agent-Native School ERP: Powered by WebMCP 

 Project Story 

 Inspiration
Traditional School ERP systems are notoriously complex, packed with dense menus, multi-step forms, and steep learning curves. We realized that teachers and school administrators spend hours navigating these clunky interfaces instead of focusing on what truly matters: education. When WebMCP was introduced, we saw the perfect opportunity to bridge the gap between complex databases and human intent. We wanted to transform the UX from "navigational" to "conversational," allowing educators to manage an entire school through simple natural language. 

 What it does
Our project is a full-stack, Agent-Native School Management System. It allows AI agents (like ChatGPT) to act as an administrative co-pilot directly within the browser. Once an administrator logs securely into the dashboard, the app exposes 7 powerful WebMCP tools: 

 search_student_records
mark_attendance
check_pending_fees
get_class_summary
get_class_students
generate_invoice
add_student
Instead of clicking through five different screens to find pending fees and generate an invoice, an administrator can simply type: "Find all Grade 3 students with pending fees and generate their invoices." The AI agent automatically chains the WebMCP tools to complete the workflow in seconds. 

 How we built it
We adopted a robust full-stack architecture: 

 Frontend: React and Vite, deployed on Netlify.
Backend: Java Spring Boot, deployed on Render.
Database: PostgreSQL hosted on Supabase.
WebMCP Integration: We used the window.document.modelContext.registerTool API inside a secure, authenticated React useEffect hook. We ensured that tools are strictly exposed only after a successful JWT/Session login. Each tool is equipped with a strict JSON schema for input validation, and the execute function securely passes the user's authentication token/cookies to our Spring Boot backend.
Challenges we ran into
Building a production-ready WebMCP app came with serious hurdles: 

 Supabase Connection Limits: Our Spring Boot's default HikariCP connection pool quickly exhausted the Supabase free tier's 15 concurrent connections limit, causing FATAL: EMAXCONNSESSION errors during deployment. We solved this by strictly limiting the maximum-pool-size and managing idle timeouts.
Cross-Domain Authentication: Because our frontend was on Netlify and backend on Render, the browser blocked our session cookies, throwing 400 Bad Request errors. We had to dive deep into Spring Security to configure Cross-Site cookies using SameSite=None and Secure=true.
Strict CORS Policies: Managing wildcard origins with credentials proved difficult until we upgraded our configuration to use allowedOriginPatterns.
AI Form-Filling Limitations: We learned that headless browsers used by AI agents sometimes struggle with complex SPA login forms, which required us to optimize our DOM structure for agent readability.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Successfully building and integrating 7 diverse read and write WebMCP tools in a short span of time.
Achieving a secure architecture where AI agents operate strictly within the bounds of human authentication (tools are hidden behind the login screen).
Successfully deploying a complex 3-tier architecture (Netlify + Render + Supabase) that runs seamlessly in the cloud.
What we learned
We gained a profound understanding of the new WebMCP specifications and how the document.modelContext interacts with the browser's DOM. We also learned how to write strict JSON schemas that prevent AI hallucinations, ensuring the agent always sends exactly what the Spring Boot backend expects. 

 What's next for Agent-Native School ERP: Powered by WebMCP
We plan to expand the agent's capabilities by adding WebMCP tools for generating report cards, scheduling parent-teacher meetings, and eventually integrating an automated WhatsApp notification system for parents directly triggered by the AI agent's actions.

A nurse tells an agent “Find RN and RT shifts in California from Sept 10th to the end of the month with a minimum pay of $30/h”. The agent applies relevant filters and shows the user matching shifts.

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 We are a team of marketers, developers and AI builders at Nursa striving to make our company not only visible to LLMs but also seamless for both humans and AI agents to interact with. We achieve this by structuring our content and data, implementing relevant schema markup, and actively exploring Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations. WebMCP felt like a perfect enabler for making interactions with AI agents quicker, smoother, and completely frictionless. We couldn't wait to try it. 

 What it does 

 It allows agents to interact with the API endpoint including available clinician shifts on nursa.com. Instead of searching the shifts manually with the UI, we allow agents to use all our filters inside of WebMCP tools: 

 search_shifts - searches by license, state, specialty, minimum hourly pay, date range, and free text; returns up to 10 compact results. Data only - it never touches the list on screen. 

 apply_filters - takes the same filter inputs and writes into the shared filter store, so the visible list re-renders with the agent's choice. This is the human+agent moment the project is built around. 

 How we built it 

 We created a simple page displaying shifts available on our website and allowing for a filter selection. We added a script that registers WebMCP tools and references our endpoint. We tested it with WebMCP Model Context Tool Inspector 

 Challenges we ran into 

 1) WebMCP is really new. Right now it only works in ChatGPT's desktop app, and it doesn't behave the same way twice. The same prompt might work on one try and fail on the next. We spent a surprising amount of time just rewording tool descriptions until the model used them the way we wanted.
2) Dates gave us the most trouble. First a timezone bug: someone asked for shifts "from Sep 7th" and the filter got set to Sep 6th. Then ChatGPT told a user that shifts were "in 2027", because our responses only said "Sep 5" with no year and it guessed. We ended up sending full timestamps with the year and timezone, and kept the pretty labels just for display.
3) The AI would answer with stale results. Asking "RN shifts" and then "RN shifts in California" sometimes returned the first answer again, because the second search didn't properly reset the state from the first one. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Quick implementation of a powerful feature we can later roll out throughout our platform. 

 What we learned 

 We weren't familiar with WebMCP before. Building this app gave us hands-on experience with its architecture, tool registration, and local testing workflows, giving us a clear view of both its massive potential for agentic search and its current limitations. 

 What's next for Agentic Shift Search 

 Further improvements to existing tools like expanding them with shift details, adding new tools and potential rollout to our main search pages, e.g. https://nursa.com/jobs/shifts

 1 2 3 



 
 About the Project 

 I’ve always wanted to build a website that brings together useful, practical information about credit cards. 

 When I started earning, choosing the right credit card was surprisingly difficult. There were limited sources of information, information was scattered across different websites, and it wasn’t always easy to figure out which card actually made sense for my spending habits. I had the idea of building something that could solve this problem, but like many side projects, I never found the time to actually build it. 

 AI changed that. 

 With the rise of AI-powered experiences, I thought: why not finally give it a shot? That idea eventually became CredSutra — a platform designed to help people understand, compare, and choose credit cards based on how they actually spend. 

 For the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, I took CredSutra one step further. Instead of making users navigate through pages and manually search for information, I exposed CredSutra's capabilities through WebMCP. The website currently provides six tools that an AI agent can interact with: 

 
 Card Review — get detailed information and insights about a credit card. 
 Card Comparison — compare cards and understand their differences. 
 Credit Card News — discover relevant and recent card-related updates. 
 Reward Calculator — estimate rewards based on spending. 
 Lounge Calculator — determine lounge eligibility and benefits. 
 Card Recommendation — find cards that fit specific spending criteria. 
 

 The interesting part for me was seeing how a website can evolve from being a destination that users browse into a capability that AI agents can interact with . 

 What I Learned 

 Building this project taught me that WebMCP is more than just exposing APIs. The real challenge is thinking about how an AI agent will understand and use your tools. 

 I had to think carefully about tool descriptions, inputs, outputs, and how to structure the capabilities so that an agent can make meaningful decisions instead of simply calling an endpoint. 

 It also made me rethink the traditional website experience. A user might ask an AI something like: 

 
 "I spend ₹50,000 a month on travel and dining. Which credit card would give me the best rewards?" 
 

 Instead of the user learning how CredSutra works first, an AI agent can use CredSutra's tools to find the relevant cards, calculate potential rewards, and provide an answer. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was deciding what should become a tool and what should remain part of the website experience. 

 I also had to make the tools useful independently while ensuring they could work together as part of a larger AI-driven workflow. Designing clear inputs and outputs and making the tools predictable for an agent required more thought than I initially expected. 

 And, of course, building a real product while learning and experimenting with a relatively new technology comes with plenty of iterations and debugging. 

 What's Next? 

 CredSutra is still very much a beginning. 

 There are many more features I want to add, more credit-card data to bring together, and many ways I can make the recommendations smarter and more personalized. 

 What started as an idea I had years ago but never got around to building has finally become something real — and WebMCP has given me an exciting new direction for it. 

 This is just the beginning.

The control layer for the agent-ready web.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web is rapidly moving from websites designed only for humans toward a web where humans and AI agents can work together. 

 WebMCP makes this possible by allowing websites to expose structured tools directly to AI agents. But while experimenting with WebMCP, I saw another important problem: how does a website owner stay in control of what an AI agent can actually do? 

 A merchant may be comfortable allowing an agent to search products or check inventory, but actions such as adding items to a cart, submitting a request, or changing data may require more control. 

 That inspired AgentBridge — the control layer for the agent-ready web. 

 What it does 

 AgentBridge helps website owners make their websites agent-ready while maintaining control over agent access. 

 A website can expose capabilities such as: 

 
 search_products 
 get_product 
 check_inventory 
 add_to_cart 
 

 as structured WebMCP tools that compatible AI agents can discover and invoke. 

 AgentBridge then adds a merchant-controlled layer around those capabilities. Website owners can: 

 
 Discover capabilities that could become agent tools 
 Control individual tool permissions 
 Enable or revoke Agent Access 
 Require human confirmation for sensitive actions 
 Inspect WebMCP tools exposed by websites 
 

 For example, an AI agent can search a merchant's products and check inventory automatically, while an add_to_cart action can require explicit human confirmation before it is completed. 

 How I built it 

 I built AgentBridge as an end-to-end WebMCP prototype consisting of a merchant portal, a WebMCP-enabled demonstration storefront, a backend policy layer, and a Chrome extension that acts as a WebMCP Inspector. 

 The Northstar demo storefront exposes commerce capabilities as structured tools. AgentBridge manages which of those capabilities are available to agents and applies policies for actions requiring confirmation. 

 I also built the Inspector to discover WebMCP tools registered by websites. I tested it not only against my own storefront but also against an independent Google Chrome Labs WebMCP implementation, which helped demonstrate interoperability beyond the AgentBridge demo environment. 

 The project uses JavaScript, Node.js, Express, Chrome Extension APIs, WebMCP, HTML/CSS, and Railway for deployment. 

 Challenges I faced 

 One of the biggest challenges was moving beyond simply exposing tools and designing a practical permission model around them. 

 I had to think about questions such as: 

 Who controls agent access? Which capabilities should be available? What happens when an action changes something? How can access be revoked immediately? 

 This led to per-tool permissions, a global Agent Access switch, and human confirmation for higher-impact actions. 

 Another challenge was making the system work across different websites rather than designing everything specifically for one storefront. Building and testing the WebMCP Inspector against an independent implementation helped validate the broader approach. 

 Website ownership verification, runtime policy synchronization, extension-to-website communication, deployment, and keeping tool state consistent also presented interesting engineering challenges during development. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest thing I learned is that making the web agent-ready is not only about giving AI agents more capabilities. 

 It is also about giving humans control over those capabilities. 

 WebMCP provides a powerful foundation for structured agent-to-website interaction. Building AgentBridge showed me how permission management, confirmation, discovery, and access control could complement that foundation. 

 What's next 

 I see AgentBridge evolving into infrastructure that helps businesses adopt the agentic web without giving up control. 

 Future versions could support more website platforms and capability types, richer policies, production-grade ownership verification, activity analytics, and developer tooling for testing WebMCP implementations. 

 As more websites become accessible to AI agents, I believe there will be a growing need for a layer that sits between websites and agents and answers a simple question: 

 What is this agent allowed to do? 

 That's the role AgentBridge is designed to play. 

 AgentBridge — The control layer for the agent-ready web.

 Inspiration 

 I love solving Sudoku puzzles like many of us. Sudoku is one of the world’s purest logic games. 

 But online Sudoku has a physical barrier for some people. Solving a hard puzzle requires numerous micro-clicks. For many people living with essential tremors, RSI (repetitive strain injury), or motor disabilities, the physical tax ruins the mental joy. 

 Purpose of Agentic Sudoku is to enable users to play online Sudoku hands free , assisted by Agent. 

 What it does 

 Human Speaks in Codex App -> Agent uses WebMCP -> Action happens on Sudoku Board. 

 Agentic Sudoku is an online Sudoku puzzle application powered by WebMCP. 

 It enables the human and agent to collaborate while solving Sudoku. 

 Human can play Sudoku hands free with help of Agent. 

 18 WebMCP tools are configured which let user do everything by talking to agent. 

 A Codex Skill is delivered to open the web application in the in-app browser and just solve Sudoku puzzle hands free (by talking to agent). 

 How it was built 

 Agentic Sudoku is a 100% client-side, zero-backend application designed for seamless WebMCP integration. 

 Frontend - Next.js (App Router), React, and Tailwind CSS. 

 WebMCP Architecture - WebMCP tools which can read, annotate, act and control Sudoku. So that human only has to speak to agent without placing hands on keyboard. 

 Puzzle Engine - sudoku-gen for client-side board generation. 

 Codex Skill Integration - A dedicated standard Codex Skill included in the repository, giving OpenAI agents an out-of-the-box playbook for navigating the site, executing coaching sequences, and providing hands-free accessibility. 

 Hosting - Deployed on Vercel. 

 Spec-Driven Development - The project was built using SpecKit. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was designing the WebMCP schema. Had to carefully engineer the tools to ensure they never expose the puzzle’s final hidden solution. The agent must reason dynamically using only the visible board constraints to guide the player. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Successfully decoupled joy of Sudoku from the physical friction of playing it. 
 Shipped robust WebMCP tools. 
 

 Learnings 

 Hands on experience with WebMCP. It turns the browser DOM into a shared, collaborative workspace. 

 What's next for Agentic Sudoku 

 
 Allowing users to scan a Sudoku puzzle from a physical newspaper using their camera, parse it into the web app.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Aliigo Action Layer 

 Project name 

 Aliigo Action Layer (AAL) 

 Elevator pitch 

 Aliigo Action Layer makes online business knowledge actionable and future-ready for both people and AI. Using WebMCP, it turns a business’s approved information and capabilities into clear tools that AI assistants can use to find answers, recommend services, prepare bookings or quote requests, and guide customers to the next step—without having to guess their way through the website. 

 One-line version 

 Turn your business knowledge into actions that both customers and AI assistants can use. 

 Tagline 

 Built for people. Ready for their agents. 

 

 Inspiration 

 Aliigo started from a simple problem: businesses already have valuable knowledge scattered across their websites, service pages, FAQs, policies, booking systems, and other public sources, but that information is often difficult for search engines, AI systems, and even customers to understand consistently. 

 We have been building Aliigo around the idea that a business should be able to organize and control the knowledge that represents it, make that knowledge easier for Google and AI systems to understand, and put it to work through a Business Agent that can answer visitor questions. 

 WebMCP suggested the next logical step. 

 If a business can make its knowledge understandable to AI, why should its customers’ agents still have to guess their way through buttons, forms, menus, and page layouts? 

 That led to Aliigo Action Layer . 

 The idea is to give a normal business website a structured action layer for AI agents while keeping the human experience intact. Instead of replacing the website, WebMCP lets us make the same website usable by both people and their agents. 

 The long-term inspiration is simple: 

 Make businesses easier to find, understand, choose, and act on. 

 

 What it does 

 Aliigo Action Layer makes online business knowledge actionable. 

 Instead of asking an AI agent to interpret a website visually and guess how to complete a task, the site exposes structured, business-specific tools that describe exactly what the agent can do. 

 For example, a wellness business can expose tools that let an agent: 

 
 understand available services; 
 find an appropriate service for a customer’s need; 
 check available times; 
 prepare a booking. 
 

 A printing business can expose a different set of capabilities: 

 
 find appropriate print products; 
 check artwork requirements; 
 compare relevant options; 
 prepare a quote request. 
 

 The important part is that these are not separate one-off integrations. 

 Aliigo Action Layer uses the same underlying business capability model to expose the appropriate tools for different types of businesses. 

 The agent can prepare an action while the website shows the result to the human for review and confirmation. 

 The experience becomes: 

 Human intent → Agent uses structured tools → Website shows the prepared action → Human confirms 

 This keeps the human in control while giving the agent a much more reliable way to help. 

 

 How we built it 

 We built Aliigo Action Layer as an isolated WebMCP experiment, separate from the production Aliigo platform but designed with a future integration path in mind. 

 The application uses a reusable business-definition and capability layer. 

 Each business defines: 

 
 its identity; 
 approved business knowledge; 
 products or services; 
 policies; 
 available actions; 
 structured data required for those actions. 
 

 A WebMCP adapter then translates those capabilities into business-specific tools exposed through the browser. 

 We deliberately kept the WebMCP layer separate from the UI and business logic. 

 Conceptually: 
 Business knowledge
 +
Business capabilities
 ↓
Aliigo Action Layer
 ↓
WebMCP tools
 ↓
AI agent
 
 The same application can switch between different example businesses and expose a different toolset without rebuilding the underlying architecture. 

 We also added visible shared state so that when an agent prepares a booking or quote request, the result appears immediately in the human-facing interface. 

 The current challenge implementation is intentionally self-contained and deterministic. It does not require production Aliigo infrastructure, customer data, external APIs, authentication, or payment systems. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was thinking differently about what a website interface is for. 

 Traditional web development assumes that the human is the only actor navigating the interface. Even AI-assisted browsing often follows the same model: the agent tries to understand the page, find the correct control, and interact with it. 

 WebMCP changes that assumption. 

 We had to decide which parts of the business should become explicit tools, what information each tool should accept, and which actions should remain under direct human control. 

 Another challenge was avoiding generic tools. 

 A tool such as execute_action may be technically flexible, but it gives an agent very little useful business context. We found that tools become much more meaningful when they describe actual business capabilities such as: 

 
 find_services 
 find_available_times 
 prepare_booking 
 check_artwork_requirements 
 prepare_quote_request 
 

 We also had to design around an emerging standard. WebMCP is still experimental, so feature detection, browser compatibility, graceful fallback behavior, and keeping the implementation close to the current specification were important. 

 Finally, we had to resist turning the challenge project into the full Aliigo platform. The goal was to demonstrate the idea clearly and reliably without reproducing the much larger production architecture. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are most proud that Aliigo Action Layer demonstrates something broader than a single WebMCP-enabled form. 

 The same underlying architecture can represent very different businesses and expose different agent capabilities based on what each business actually does. 

 A wellness studio can become bookable by an agent. 

 A printing company can become quote-ready. 

 Both use the same underlying model. 

 We are also proud of the human-agent interaction pattern.

 Inspiration 

 BluePulse was inspired by a simple problem: during floods and other water-related emergencies, useful information is often scattered across maps, infrastructure datasets, environmental sources, and community reports. This makes it difficult to quickly understand what is happening and decide what action to take. 

 We wanted to explore how WebMCP could turn an environmental intelligence platform into something an AI agent can actively operate, rather than just a dashboard that humans have to navigate manually. 

 BluePulse builds on the open-source foundation of FloodGraph and extends it toward agent-operable environmental and disaster-response intelligence. 

 What it does 

 BluePulse is a map-based environmental intelligence platform focused on flood and disaster-response scenarios. 

 It combines real and open geographic data to help users and AI agents understand places, infrastructure, points of interest, route incidents, flood context, and potential response actions. 

 Through WebMCP, BluePulse currently exposes six operational tools: 

 
 analyze_place_flood_context 
 get_place_pois 
 report_route_incident 
 get_route_risk_summary 
 recalculate_route 
 clear_route_incidents 
 

 These tools allow an AI agent to discover BluePulse capabilities, understand their input schemas, and execute them directly through the browser. 

 For example, an agent can retrieve relevant infrastructure for a location, analyze preliminary flood context, report an incident affecting a route, inspect route risk, and request a recalculation that avoids active incidents. 

 BluePulse is designed as a decision-support prototype and does not claim to provide certified flood simulation or operational emergency-response predictions. 

 How we built it 

 BluePulse was developed as a hackathon MVP by extending the existing FloodGraph open-source project instead of rebuilding its mapping and graph-processing foundation from scratch. 

 The application uses React and TypeScript for the interface, MapLibre for the interactive map, and Pyodide/WebAssembly with NetworkX for graph-related processing in the browser. 

 We integrated multiple open geographic and environmental data sources, including OpenStreetMap-based information and public POI datasets, while maintaining local fallbacks where necessary to keep the application usable when external providers are unavailable. 

 The WebMCP integration uses document.modelContext to register application capabilities as tools. Chrome can then discover them through getTools() , inspect their inputSchema , and execute them using executeTool() . 

 During final validation, we tested every exposed WebMCP tool individually. We originally had ten tools, but removed four that were redundant or were never invoked by BLUE. The final implementation exposes only the six tools that participate in real agent workflows. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the main challenges was working with external geospatial services from a browser-based application. 

 During development we encountered unavailable ORS proxy endpoints, CORS restrictions with some Overpass endpoints, inconsistent geocoding results, and differences between local development and the production deployment. 

 We therefore implemented fallback strategies and separated external-service failures from the WebMCP layer itself. 

 Another important challenge was deciding what should actually be exposed as a WebMCP tool. Initially, we exposed ten capabilities. After testing them through executeTool() , we found that four were redundant because the application already handled those operations internally through the map, geocoder, or UI actions. 

 Instead of keeping unused tools for the sake of having a larger toolset, we removed them and kept six operational tools that BLUE genuinely uses. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We successfully implemented and validated WebMCP in a deployed environmental intelligence application. 

 Chrome can discover BluePulse tools directly from the page, inspect their schemas, and execute them through document.modelContext . 

 We are particularly proud that the final toolset was validated based on actual usage rather than only registration. This resulted in a cleaner six-tool interface designed specifically for agent interaction. 

 We also preserved the strengths of the original FloodGraph architecture while extending it with environmental context, real geographic information, route incidents, response intelligence, and agent-operable capabilities. 

 Most importantly, BluePulse demonstrates that WebMCP can be used for more than simple web automation: it can expose meaningful domain capabilities that allow agents to interact with environmental and disaster-response systems. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that exposing many tools does not automatically make an application more agent-friendly. 

 Clear descriptions, structured input schemas, predictable outputs, and a small set of meaningful capabilities are more valuable than a large collection of redundant tools. 

 We also learned that WebMCP creates a useful separation between the human interface and the agent interface. A person can continue interacting with the map normally, while an agent can discover and execute the underlying capabilities directly. 

 Finally, building around real external data highlighted the importance of graceful degradation, fallback strategies, and transparent limitations when developing decision-support applications. 

 What's next for BluePulse 

 The next step is to move BluePulse from a hackathon prototype toward a more robust environmental intelligence platform. 

 Future work includes integrating additional real-time environmental and hydrological data sources, improving flood-risk and uncertainty models, strengthening route and infrastructure analysis, and expanding beyond floods into additional environmental-risk scenarios. 

 We also want to expand the WebMCP layer so authorized agents can coordinate more complex workflows across environmental intelligence, infrastructure monitoring, community information, and emergency-response systems. 

 Our long-term vision is for BluePulse to become environmental intelligence that agents can not only understand, but act on.
