title: Packedup
pitch: Plan together, travel better. \nDrop a code, vote as a group, get an itinerary everyone actually wants.
about_excerpt:
Plan together, travel better. 
Drop a code, vote as a group, get an itinerary everyone actually wants.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every time I travel with friends, the same thing happens: someone drops
five hotel options and a dozen restaurant links into WhatsApp, everyone
votes with thumbs-up reactions scattered across different messages, and a
day later nobody can remember what actually won. The votes get buried
under new messages, there's no single place to look back at what was
decided, and by the time we land, half the group doesn't even have a
day-by-day plan — just a chat log full of half-finished decisions. 

 I wanted a place built specifically for that moment: drop in the options,
let everyone vote, lock in a winner, and have it turn into an itinerary
automatically — instead of relying on a chat app never designed for
decision-making in the first place 

 What it does 

 PackedUp is group trip planning built around three boards — Stay, Eat, and Visit. Anyone with a 7-character invite code joins as a guest and drops in a suggestion — a hotel, a restaurant, a hike — for the group to vote on, up or down, in real time. The trip's creator finalizes a winner on each board, and those winners flow straight into a day-by-day itinerary — no re-typing, no digging through chat history to remember what won. 

 No sign-up is required to participate. A guest is identified by a session token stored locally, so joining a trip takes a name and a code, not a password — the whole reason WhatsApp felt easier than "download an app" in the first place, minus the part where votes get lost. 

 The newest layer is agent support: PackedUp exposes create_trip, get_trip_board_info, and add_recommended_suggestion as WebMCP tools — an emerging browser standard (document.modelContext) that lets an AI agent fill in the trip form or drop a recommended restaurant onto a board on a user's behalf, the same way a person would from the UI. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js 14 (App Router) for both the UI and the API — Route Handlers sit between the client and Supabase. 

 
 Supabase (Postgres) for data, with row-level security enabled on every table. Guest writes go through a service-role client scoped strictly to server-side route handlers, since a guest has no auth.uid() for RLS to key off of. 
 Zustand, persisted to localStorage, holds the guest session (member_id, trip_id, session_token) across visits. 
 TanStack Query manages server state — trip details, suggestions, members — with short polling intervals standing in for full realtime where it wasn't worth the complexity yet. 
 Framer Motion for the transitions between states (voting, finalizing, empty boards). 
 WebMCP, via the use-webmcp-tool React hook, registers tools directly on the page components where the corresponding UI action lives — create_trip on the landing and create pages, the suggestion tools on the board page — so a tool only exists while its page is actually mounted. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting from "WhatsApp thread full of forgotten votes" to an actual finalized itinerary in three clicks — join with a code, vote, finalize — without ever asking a single friend to make an account. Getting real-time-feeling voting working with plain polling instead of reaching for a heavier realtime setup before it was needed. And shipping WebMCP support early enough to be one of the first trip-planning tools an AI agent can actually operate, not just read. 

 What we learned 

 That an emerging standard is still an emerging standard — WebMCP is real, shipping behind flags and origin trials, but building against it means designing for graceful absence: useWebMCP reports supported: false in any browser without the API, and the app has to be just as usable without an agent in the loop as with one. We also learned, the hard way, that the fastest debugging step for a "healthy app, broken deploy" is checking whether the database itself is still awake. 

 What's next for Packedup 

 Real Supabase Realtime subscriptions in place of polling, an actual MCP server (not just WebMCP) so agents like Codex or Claude Desktop can drive trip creation without a browser tab open, and per-day budget estimates rolled into the itinerary so the group knows the damage before they land.

 Inspiration 

 I set up OpenClaw to help with marketing and watched it fail at the last step: actually posting. Cloud browsers get blocked. Official APIs are expensive, limited, and missing things like Facebook member groups. So I built Claw Post at clawpost.net: the agent writes, your already-logged-in desktop Chrome publishes. 

 What it does 

 Claw Post is posting infrastructure for AI agents. A paired Chrome extension publishes from the browser session where you are already logged into X, LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and Reddit. No social passwords in the agent. No headless VPS.
Claw Post is not a spray tool. There is a strict built-in delay between actions. The agent asks, the human’s already-logged-in Chrome publishes, then we wait. That is the product. 

 This submission is a thin public page that exposes those actions as WebMCP tools (clawpost_create_post, clawpost_reddit_comment, clawpost_status, clawpost_job_status) so ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled can call them on the page. 

 How we built it 

 The product is a Chrome extension plus a REST/MCP API. I built it with Cursor and Codex.
For this challenge we added a public static demo (MIT) that registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool. The tools call the public Claw Post API with a key the human pastes in the page (localStorage only). If the extension is not paired, judges still see the tools work and get an honest EXTENSION_NOT_PAIRED. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Media was painful. We upload to short-lived storage, then the extension attaches the file in the real composer. 

 WebMCP only exists in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with the testing flag. The demo has to explain that or it looks broken. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A working loop: agent to API to desktop Chrome to a live postUrl. Community interest, a few paying users, and so far no account bans from posting this way. 

 What we learned 

 Build the thing you actually need. Other people probably need it too.
We are in a weird spot: people are handing more work to agents, and social platforms still treat that as malicious. Official APIs are limited. Cloud browsers get blocked. The remaining path is a real desktop session. 

 What's next for Claw Post WebMCP (clawpost.net) 

 Put WebMCP on the real clawpost.net dashboard, not just this demo. Reddit-style comments for more platforms. Keep the product private. Keep this wrapper public.

A reproducible WebMCP benchmark for agents making economic decisions under pressure.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration\n\nBrowser agents can complete a task and still leave reviewers unable to answer basic questions: What actions did the agent take? Did the policy really improve the outcome? Can the result be reproduced? MarketBench makes those questions measurable.\n\n## What it does\n\nMarketBench is an interactive evaluation lab for browser-agent market policies. A visitor selects a scenario and seed, runs a 12-week simulation, and gets:\n\n- a clear business outcome and plain-language insight\n- the full WebMCP tool-call and state history\n- integrity hashes for trace and final state\n- a deterministic baseline comparison\n- three-seed aggregates with mean, standard deviation, and worst-seed results\n- downloadable evidence for audit and replay\n\n## How we built it\n\nThe app is a React and TypeScript web application deployed on Vercel. WebMCP exposes typed browser tools for configuring and running experiments. The evaluation engine uses versioned deterministic fixtures for three scenarios and three seeds, so baseline and signal-aware policy runs can be reproduced exactly. Each step records its input, tool call, output, state transition, and hash.\n\nThe comparison view aggregates the same fixed seed set rather than presenting a single lucky run. It visualizes distributions and reports mean, standard deviation, and worst seed. The repository includes tests for determinism, trace completeness, hashes, aggregate math, and export structure.\n\n## Challenges\n\nThe main challenge was making rigor understandable. A raw trace is useful to an engineer but intimidating to a first-time visitor. We rebuilt the experience around a three-step flow, visible progress, a human-readable takeaway, compact trace summaries, and expandable evidence. We also made the distinction between deterministic policy fixtures and model output explicit.\n\n## Accomplishments\n\n- Full trace, state, and history export with integrity hashes\n- Transparent baseline vs signal-aware comparisons\n- Three-seed aggregate metrics and charts\n- A first-run experience that explains the value before exposing technical detail\n- A live, reproducible demo with tested fixtures\n\n## What we learned\n\nAgent evaluation needs both observability and a decision-relevant metric. Traces explain how an outcome happened; controlled repeated runs show whether the policy actually helped. Neither alone is enough.\n\n## What is next\n\nNext, MarketBench can add imported real-world task traces, more scenario packs, signed evaluation bundles, and CI checks that compare agent-policy revisions before deployment.

about_excerpt:
Teach students with your agents on Chalkboard: a collaborative infinite canvas where 23 WebMCP tools let your AI co-teacher draw, write, highlight and react live as you teach together.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 A real classroom isn't a lecture; a board everyone can point at. 

 Online, that feeling disappears. A teacher talks, students watch. The board is gone. 

 We built Chalkboard to bring it back: a shared infinite canvas where a teacher and students draw, write and react together, live. 

 Then we wondered, what if a third participant could join? Not a chatbot on the side, but a classmate who can use the board. 

 Teach students with your agents. 

 What It Does 

 Create a room, share the link, and everyone sees the same chalkboard. When someone draws a line, it appears for everyone. When someone sends a ❤️, it floats across the screen. 

 Now invite your agent. 

 Say: “Teach the Pythagorean theorem.” 

 Your agent doesn't just reply in text. It opens the same room as you, picks up the chalk, writes $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, draws the triangle, labels the sides, and highlights the proof stroke by stroke, while students watch. 

 It’s not controlling a copy of the classroom. It’s in the classroom. 

 Why WebMCP 

 We could have built a separate API for every agent action one for drawing, one for writing, one for reacting. Instead we let the website speak for itself. 

 With WebMCP , Chalkboard simply says: here are the things I can do: draw, write, highlight, react, raise a hand, manage the room. 

 The browser exposes those capabilities at navigator.modelContext . The agent discovers them and calls them like any other tool. No custom wiring, no shadow app. 
 Your Agent → WebMCP → Chalkboard → Everyone's Board
 
 The agent doesn't need to know how our canvas works. It just knows what the classroom allows. 

 How We Built It 

 Chalkboard is a web app: a canvas for drawing, Socket.IO for real-time sync, and LiveKit for voice. 

 We wrapped every classroom action — drawing a stroke, writing text, sending a reaction as a simple tool. The browser gathers those tools and offers them through WebMCP, the new web standard for agents. 

 When an agent joins a room, it joins like any student over a websocket. It listens to the room, remembers what's on the board, and when asked to teach, it chooses tools and emits the same events your browser does. A reaction tool even opens the emoji picker and picks one, so you see the interaction, not just the result. 

 If a viewer asks the agent to do something only an editor can do, the agent politely refuses it borrows your permissions, not its own. 

 What We Learned 

 The moment an agent can act instead of just answer , everything changes. A lesson feels real when you watch it being made. 

 We also learned that the web doesn't need a separate world for AI. If a site can tell an agent what it can do, the site itself becomes the interface. 

 Challenges 

 Making a remote agent feel present was hard. It had to join the same room, see the same board, and act through the same browser tools, without lag, without breaking the live sync, and without giving it more power than the student who invited it. 

 Getting browsers, real-time sync and WebMCP to agree was the puzzle. Solving it meant the agent is no longer outside the classroom looking in. It's sitting at the desk next to you. 

 What's Next 

 We started with drawing. Next is understanding an agent that watches the board, notices a mistake, circles it, and offers a hint. A classroom that is collaborative and agent-accessible by default. 

 Chalkboard is our small experiment in that future: where you don't build a separate app for your agent — you just bring it to class.

LuxeSalon & Spa turns a normal booking site into one an AI agent can search treatments, check live stylist availability, and book an appointment.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I'd already spent a few hackathons this year building agent-driven tools for local businesses — a WhatsApp front-desk agent for salons and clinics being one of them. The recurring problem was always the same: to let an agent act on a business's behalf, you had to build a whole separate backend integration for it, replicating auth and state that already existed in the web app. 

 WebMCP flips that. Instead of standing up a server-side API just so an agent can act, you expose the tools directly in the browser, in the same JavaScript that already runs your app. When the WebMCP Challenge came up, a salon booking flow felt like the perfect fit — it's a pattern (search → check availability → book) that's instantly understandable in a 90-second demo, and mirrors exactly the kind of local-business use case I'd been building toward already. 

 What it does 

 LuxeSalon & Spa is a booking storefront that an AI agent can operate directly, not just describe. It registers four tools on document.modelContext : 

 
 salon.search_services — find treatments by keyword, category, or budget 
 salon.get_available_slots — check live stylist openings for a service and date 
 salon.book_appointment — propose a reservation, gated behind a human confirmation step 
 salon.get_booking_status — look up an existing booking by reference or phone number 
 

 Every tool call reacts live in the UI — the catalog filters as the agent searches, the schedule panel highlights the chosen slot, the appointments drawer opens when a booking is checked. A built-in Agent Inspector panel also lets anyone watch tool calls happen in real time, without needing dev tools open. 

 How we built it 

 I forked the WebMCP pattern from vercel/shop 's reference PR (#498) into a fresh Next.js app, then built out the salon's own domain model — services, stylists, time slots, and bookings — backed by a React context. 

 Each tool's inputSchema was written as strict JSON Schema aimed at an LLM reader rather than a human one: field descriptions spell out exactly what format and values are expected, since that's what the agent actually reasons over when deciding how to call a tool. 

 The part I spent the most care on was book_appointment . Chrome's WebMCP security guidance is explicit that state-changing tools shouldn't commit silently, so instead of booking immediately, the tool suspends on a Promise and surfaces a confirmation modal — the appointment only becomes real once a human clicks "Approve & Confirm." Read-only tools are marked with readOnlyHint: true ; the booking tool isn't. 

 Testing went through three layers: a custom in-app inspector for quick iteration, Google's official Model Context Tool Inspector Chrome extension to verify the tools were actually reachable via the real browser API, and finally a Gemini-backed agent inside that extension calling the tools from plain-language prompts — not scripted JSON. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 WebMCP is Chrome-only right now. I do most of my daily browsing in Safari, so development and testing ended up split across two browsers — build and iterate anywhere, but every real verification had to happen in Chrome behind chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . 
 The flag needs a real relaunch, not just quitting the browser. I lost real time thinking my tool registration code was broken, when it was actually a stale flag state — document.modelContext simply wasn't injected yet. 
 Vercel's preview URLs are login-walled by default. Right before wrapping up, I nearly submitted a preview deployment link that silently sits behind Vercel's SSO protection — invisible to anyone without account access. Caught it just in time and switched to the public production alias. 
 Building a genuine human-in-the-loop pause , not a fake one — the booking tool's execute() had to actually suspend on a real Promise tied to a user click, so an agent calling it truly waits on a person, rather than the UI just cosmetically showing a modal after the fact. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Verified spec compliance the hard way: not just "the code looks right," but confirmed via Google's own inspector extension and a live Gemini agent successfully discovering and calling the tools from natural language. 
 A confirmation flow that's a real safety mechanism, directly reflecting the WebMCP security guide's read-only-vs-action distinction, rather than a decorative modal. 
 Going from a forked reference PR to a fully deployed, agent-tested, submission-ready storefront solo, inside the hackathon window. 
 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP's actual value isn't just "another API" — it's giving an agent access to a page's real client-side state and logic, instead of screen-scraping a UI built for humans. 
 Tool descriptions are a UX surface too, just for a different reader. An agent decides whether and how to call your tool based entirely on how well you've described it. 
 Agentic tools need the same "don't trust the caller blindly" instincts as any other security-sensitive code — read-only actions can run freely, but anything that spends money or commits a resource needs a checkpoint a human controls. 
 

 What's next for LuxeSalon & Spa — WebMCP Autonomous Storefront 

 
 Extend from a single salon to a small directory of local Bengaluru businesses, closer to the original WhatsApp front-desk concept this grew out of. 
 Add cancel_appointment and reschedule_appointment tools, plus stylist-specific search. 
 Look into a WebMCP polyfill so agents in non-Chrome browsers can still discover and call the same tools. 
 Apply for the Chrome Origin Trial so the experience works for real users without requiring the testing flag.

pitch: A WebMCP-powered remote job board where AI agents can search, compare, open, save, and manage jobs through structured site tools . while humans keep a familiar job-board experience.

A WebMCP-powered remote job board where AI agents can search, compare, open, save, and manage jobs through structured site tools . while humans keep a familiar job-board experience.

 WebMcp 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Imagine searching for a remote job. You look up React Native roles, open a few listings, and find three worth considering.
Then come the simple questions: Which pays the most? Which am I actually eligible for from India? Which needs the least experience? How do their tech stacks differ? Which company has better benefits? What was that seventh listing again, and how does it compare to the first?
None of this is hard. It's just tedious. Multiple tabs, scattered details, manual comparison, and it only gets worse as the number of listings grows into the hundreds or thousands. 

 The Problem 

 There's a mismatch between how much useful information exists and how much a person can realistically explore. Comparing job listings by hand, salary, eligibility, experience, tech stack, benefits, is annoying even with three jobs and basically impossible at scale. 

 Why AI Agents Alone Don't Fix It 

 Agents seem like the obvious answer. You should be able to just say "compare the top three" or "which pays more but needs less experience?" and get an answer.
But most websites are built for humans, not agents. That means an agent has to reverse-engineer meaning from a visual interface, cards, buttons, clicks, rather than working with clean, structured data. 

 The Fix: WebMCP 

 Instead of forcing agents to scrape and interpret the interface, WebMCP lets a website expose its data and actions directly as structured tools: search_jobs, get_job_details, compare_jobs, save_job, unsave_job, get_saved_jobs, and get_filter_options.
The agent can just ask the site directly. No guessing required. 

 What We Built: TrueRemoteJobs 

 TrueRemoteJobs is a job board prototype with 200 fictional listings. It works normally for humans browsing the site, and it exposes WebMCP tools for agents working alongside them.
A typical flow looks like this: "Find React Native jobs open to India, paying $60K+" returns nine results. Then: "show me the first," "compare the first and seventh," "save the first and third." 

 Interfaces Can't Anticipate Every Question
You simply can't build a button for every possible query, like comparing jobs one, seven, and twelve on compensation, location, React Native experience, and benefits alone.
With structured data, the agent can combine and filter information however the user actually wants, without anyone needing to pre-design every possible screen. 

 A Real Bug That Proved the Point 

 During testing, the agent misidentified "the first result" because it was inferring meaning from whatever happened to be on screen rather than from real structure.
The fix was straightforward: every result now carries a stable jobId and an explicit resultNumber, so references like "the seventh one" are unambiguous.
The lesson stuck with us: giving an agent access to a webpage is not the same as giving it access to the actual information. 

 Humans and Agents Coexist 

 This isn't about replacing the website. It's the same underlying data and the same actions, just two ways of reaching them.
Browse visually when you want to. Delegate deep comparison and research to an agent when you don't. And the two stay in sync, if the agent saves a job, it's saved in the real app too. 

 Takeaway 

 Websites already hold rich information, and agents already have the reasoning ability to make sense of it. WebMCP is the structured bridge between the two, letting anyone, human or agent, dig as deep into a site's data as they want, rather than only as deep as the UI happened to be designed for.

A rooftop action game where people play with keyboard or touch while AI agents inspect and control the same live world through WebMCP.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Platform games are easy for a person to understand by sight, but they are difficult for an agent to control. The agent must track gaps, moving enemies, collectibles, momentum, and a camera that keeps changing. I wanted one open web page that gives each player the interface they need without maintaining a second game server or an agent-only copy of the world. 

 What it does 

 Mike's Moonlight Run is a three-stage rooftop action game. A person runs and jumps with a keyboard, touch controls, or on-screen buttons. The goal is to cross each skyline, avoid gaps and hazards, collect fish, and reach the red postbox. 

 The game renders the world as real-time 3D geometry with Three.js. It resembles a 2D platformer from the side, then the camera orbits through 360 degrees and reveals the depth of the scene while the game continues. 

 An AI agent controls the same cat through two WebMCP tools: 

 
 moonlight_run.get_state returns Mike's position and velocity, ground segments, gaps, obstacles, moving enemies, collectibles, the goal, and the camera angle. 
 moonlight_run.play_actions runs a short sequence of timed actions such as run_right , jump_right , or wait , then returns the resulting state. 
 

 The person and agent share one authoritative game state. A person can start a run, hand it to an agent, and take control again. Manual input cancels the active agent sequence, so the handoff happens inside the live game. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 Screenshot interpretation and coordinate-based clicking give an agent a fragile view of a platform game. A rotating camera makes that approach harder, and moving enemies can invalidate a plan before the next click. 

 WebMCP lets the page expose stable world coordinates and game semantics while preserving the visual experience for the person. The agent can observe, act, inspect the result, and adjust through short action sequences. The person keeps the direct controls and can take over at any point. Both players use the same public URL and the same running world. 

 How I built it 

 Codex wrote all of the project's code. I focused on the output: how the game felt, how Mike looked from each camera angle, whether the handoff between a person and an agent made sense, and whether the published build matched my intent. I reviewed the live game and screenshots, gave Codex concrete correction instructions, and accepted each change after checking the visual and functional result. 

 For the technical implementation, Codex used React, TypeScript, Three.js, Vite, and vinext. The shared GameState and physics live in lib/moonlight-game.ts . Keyboard input, touch input, rendering, collisions, and WebMCP calls all read or update that state. 

 The page registers both tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) in app/page.tsx . moonlight_run.get_state reads the live world. moonlight_run.play_actions accepts one to thirty timed actions, supports cancellation through AbortSignal , and stops when the person resumes manual control. 

 Codex also ran the checks, prepared the public repository, and deployed the game to ChatGPT Sites. I reviewed the output at each stage. The complete source is available under the MIT license, and the project does not require an account, API key, database, or private testing credential. 

 Challenges 

 Directing Codex through the visual corrections took more work than the initial build. I evaluated screenshots and the live site, then turned each mismatch into a specific instruction. I asked Codex to align Mike with the README artwork, keep the scarf wrapped around his neck, move the mouth to the front of the face, and replace separate front and side eyes with one coherent 3D eye layout. 

 The rotating camera exposed mistakes that a side-view screenshot hid. One revision made Mike's tongue and white muzzle look like thick lips from the side. I asked Codex to remove the tongue, shorten the muzzle and nose, refine the mouth, reduce the eye size, and add small glints. I required screenshots from the side and front angles before publication so I could judge Mike as one 3D character. 

 I also corrected product details after using the build. I asked Codex to keep the English and Japanese READMEs aligned, repair the Japanese artwork text, show per-stage fish counts in the HUD, include the total fish count in the result, restore the paw favicon, and simplify sharing to an X link plus clipboard copy. The hard part was giving precise feedback, checking each new output, and noticing when a fix introduced a new problem from another angle. 

 What I learned 

 An agent interface works best when it exposes intent, state, and constraints instead of mirroring every visual control. Short tool calls also produce better results in a changing world because the agent can inspect each outcome before continuing. 

 WebMCP made the handoff between a person and an agent part of the product rather than a separate automation demo. The same pattern could support editors, simulations, accessibility tools, and other interactive web apps.

A job-search workspace where people and AI agents work the same page — agents search, score, and draft applications via WebMCP, humans keep control with one-click approvals.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 ApplyFlow: a job-search workspace for people + agents 

 I built ApplyFlow for The WebMCP Challenge because I kept hitting the same wall: applying to jobs is half product, half chore, and no tool today lets an AI assistant genuinely help without fighting the UI. Chat agents can write a cover letter in a chat box, but they can't see your board, work your pipeline, or edit the same document you're editing. Raw MCP servers operate on data, not on the page you're looking at. WebMCP is the missing bridge — agents finally run inside the app you use. 

 The idea. ApplyFlow is one workspace where a person and an AI agent work the same live page in the same session. The human browses roles, filters, and writes like always. The agent calls the exact same app: it searches and scores jobs against a résumé, drafts tailored cover letters, advances applications through a pipeline, and pins notes. The critical rule: every state-changing action the agent takes is staged as a pending action and must be approved by the human in a shared activity feed. The agent does the tedious work; the human keeps ownership. That's the collaboration model WebMCP is designed for, and it shows up in every one of my tool choices. 

 How I built it. Next.js 16 + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind, no backend — the whole product is a static SPA whose state lives in localStorage, so it deploys anywhere and works fully offline. WebMCP was brand new, so the WebMCP layer was built from the Chrome/W3C specs and iterated on: 

 Imperative tools — 9 registered via document.modelContext.registerTool: list_jobs, get_job_details, score_cv_match, get_application_overview (read-only, readOnlyHint: true); create_application, update_application_status, draft_cover_letter, tailor_cv_highlights, add_note (write tools that stage a pending action the human approves or dismisses).
Declarative API — the application form uses toolname, tooldescription, and toolparamdescription attributes so the agent can pre-fill it, and deliberately omits toolautosubmit so only the human submits.
Security hints the WebMCP spec cares about: readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint on the tools that deserve them.
Shared documents — the cover letter and CV-highlights playground live in one editor both parties mutate, so a draft from the agent is immediately visible to the person.
Challenges. WebMCP is simultaneously public and moving fast. The spec changed between the docs I first read and the API surface, which taught me to build a thin adapter and keep tool behavior decoupled from registration. Speech-to-text and event APIs like toolactivated aren't in the standard WindowEventMap, so I had to extend types carefully. My React+TS setup needed module augmentation to expose the declarative attributes (toolname, toolparamdescription, …) as typed JSX props. And there was the usual 10-day crunch: decide the demo, cut scope, ship a build that passes, then make the human-in-the-loop experience the star rather than an afterthought. 

 What I learned. The biggest lesson is that the human-agent boundary is a product decision, not an API detail. Every Write tool in ApplyFlow returns "staged for approval" — the agent never mutates state unilaterally — and that one design constraint is what makes the experience feel safe and fun instead of scary. I also learned that a great WebMCP app doesn't need to be more than a static page; the agent is a full environment away. The judge's ChatGPT browser is the demo machine. 

 I hope ApplyFlow shows what "agent-native" means in practice: software a person can use alone, an agent can use alone, and — for the first time — both can use together.

A WebMCP storefront where shoppers and AI agents collaborate in the exact same session, featuring live UI grounding and secure human-in-the-loop checkout validations.

 Inspiration 

 We realized that real agentic checkout,the kind large merchants will actually ship to production,needs a human sign-off gate for the same reason two-factor authentication exists. An agent should be able to do the tedious 90% (searching the catalog, comparing specs, filling the cart, applying discount codes) autonomously, but the final "place an order with real money" step requires a deliberate, visible human decision. CoShop was born out of the necessity to build a secure, collaborative, and beautiful environment where humans and agents can shop together without liability risks. 

 What it does 

 CoShop is a high-performance, stateless e-commerce storefront that exposes its entire architecture to AI agents via WebMCP. 

 
 Live UI Grounding: When the AI agent interacts with the store (e.g., searching or adding an item to the cart), the human shopper's screen visually reacts. The cart slides open, the product card pulses, and an accessible activity log narrates the action. The AI doesn't work in a black box; the human watches exactly what it is doing. 
 Human-in-the-Loop Checkout: When an agent attempts to check out, it is securely gated. The agent can only stage the checkout, which summons a live confirmation banner on the human's screen. The transaction is completely halted until the human physically clicks "Confirm Order." 
 

 How we built it 

 We built CoShop using Next.js 16 (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS v4, styling it with a premium "Midnight Violet" glassmorphism aesthetic and 8K photorealistic product assets. 

 The core of our WebMCP integration relies on the use-webmcp-tool React hook. We registered 11 distinct tools to document.modelContext . 

 The architectural magic happens in our state management. We used Zustand as a single source of truth. When an AI agent executes a WebMCP tool (like add_to_cart ), the callback fires a Zustand state mutation. Because the React UI is listening to that exact same store, the UI instantly animates via Framer Motion to reflect the agent's action to the human user. Furthermore, the cart state is persisted into secure, HTTP-only cookies, ensuring the app remains entirely stateless and scalable on Vercel's Edge network without requiring an external database. 

 

 The WebMCP Fit & User Experience 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP: 
Most agentic-commerce demos rely on brittle DOM-scraping or disjointed chat widgets that act on a storefront rather than with it. CoShop leverages the Model Context Protocol for Web (WebMCP) to expose 11 schema-defined tools directly to the agent's context window. This eliminates hallucination-the agent doesn't guess how to buy a shoe; it natively calls add_to_cart(productId, size, qty) with 100% deterministic accuracy. 

 What humans and agents can do together now: 
Before CoShop, you either shopped yourself, or you handed a task to an autonomous agent and hoped it didn't accidentally drain your credit card. CoShop introduces the Shared Session . A human can manually add a shirt to their cart, and concurrently ask their AI agent to find a matching pair of waterproof boots and add them to the same cart. They are no longer isolated; they are collaborating in real-time. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was bridging the gap between the agent's headless execution and the human's visual experience. Initially, when the agent added an item to the cart, the human wouldn't know it happened unless they manually checked. We had to heavily engineer our state synchronization so that WebMCP execution callbacks directly triggered UI animations, sidebars, and focus states, ensuring absolute transparency. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are incredibly proud of achieving true Live Agent Grounding . Being able to give an agent a complex prompt-
 "find me a waterproof running shoe under $120, add a size 10 to my cart, and stage a checkout" 
and then literally sitting back and watching the website's UI animate and scroll on its own as the agent executes the tasks is a magical experience. We are also proud of building this with zero external database dependencies, making it blazing fast and infinitely scalable. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the future of agentic web isn't just about giving AI access to APIs; it's about building secure hand-offs. The Model Context Protocol for Web proves that we don't have to choose between full autonomy (which is dangerous) and manual labor. We can have collaborative autonomy, where the AI does the heavy lifting and the human provides the final, secure consensus. 

 What's next for CoShop: The Agent-Native Storefront 

 We plan to expand the WebMCP toolset to include dynamic sizing recommendations (where the agent reads the user's past purchase history to determine the best shoe size) and real-time inventory negotiations. Ultimately, we want to open-source the "Human-in-the-Loop Checkout" component as a standalone NPM package so any e-commerce store can securely integrate agentic checkout.

RelayPay uses WebMCP to let an AI agent investigate refund exceptions and prepare recovery actions, while a human approval gate controls consequential execution and verification.

 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Refunds are simple when everything works. But when a return is verified and the money never arrives, resolving the exception can require checking multiple systems, interpreting evidence, deciding what action is safe, and manually coordinating the recovery. 

 We wanted to explore a different model: what if an AI agent could investigate the exception and prepare the recovery, while the human remained firmly in control of the consequential action? 

 That became RelayPay. 

 What it does 

 RelayPay is a WebMCP-powered refund recovery system where an AI agent can investigate refund exceptions through structured browser tools. 

 The agent can discover and call tools to find an order, inspect return status, check refund status, prepare an escalation, and verify the resulting case. 

 The critical boundary is human approval: the agent can investigate and prepare a proposed recovery, but cannot authorize its own consequential action. The human reviews the exact proposal and explicitly approves it before recovery submission. 

 This makes WebMCP more than a way to expose buttons to an agent—it becomes the interface through which an agent collaborates with a human inside a real application workflow. 

 How we built it 

 RelayPay was built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js/React Three Fiber, and browser-native WebMCP. 

 We registered six structured WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(): 

 find_order
get_return_status
get_refund_status
prepare_escalation
submit_escalation
verify_case 

 The workflow separates investigation, preparation, consequential execution, and verification. 

 We also built an application-enforced human approval boundary. Approval is tied to the exact proposed action, is single-use, and is consumed when the recovery is successfully submitted. 

 The result is a deterministic demo environment that lets an agent repeatedly reproduce the same recovery scenarios without relying on external merchant or payment APIs. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making WebMCP the actual product interface for the agent, rather than adding WebMCP as a thin integration on top of an existing UI. 

 We had to think carefully about tool boundaries, structured inputs, read-only versus consequential operations, and what an agent should be allowed to do autonomously. 

 The hardest design problem was the approval boundary. We wanted the agent to be genuinely useful without allowing it to silently turn its own recommendation into an irreversible action. 

 We also had to make the experience work across WebMCP-capable environments while honestly handling browsers where WebMCP is unavailable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that RelayPay demonstrates a complete agent → tools → reasoning → human approval → action → verification loop rather than just a chatbot calling an API. 

 The agent can investigate a real-looking refund exception through multiple WebMCP tools, build a recovery proposal, and reach a clear human decision point. 

 We're especially proud of the separation between preparation and execution. The agent can do the investigative work, but the application—not the agent—enforces the final approval boundary. 

 We also built an execution trace so the interaction is observable rather than hidden behind a black box. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building an agent-native application requires designing around capabilities and boundaries, not just adding AI to an existing interface. 

 WebMCP made us think of the browser itself as an agent-accessible application surface. Tool descriptions, schemas, permissions, state transitions, and failure cases all become part of the product design. 

 Most importantly, we learned that human-agent collaboration works best when the agent handles the tedious investigation and preparation while the human retains authority over consequential decisions. 

 What's next for RelayPay 

 The next step is connecting RelayPay to real commerce and payment infrastructure so the same workflow can operate on live refund data. 

 We want to add richer evidence collection, policy-aware recovery recommendations, merchant-side integrations, audit trails, and stronger verification. 

 Longer term, RelayPay could evolve from a refund exception tool into an agent-native operations layer for commerce, where humans set the boundaries and agents handle the repetitive work inside them.

title: Approval Desk
pitch: The agent does the work. The human holds the pen.
about_excerpt:
The agent does the work. The human holds the pen.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 What it is 

 Approval Desk is a WebMCP powered approval surface for agentic work that should not be allowed to complete itself. 

 The core idea is simple: an agent can do useful work, propose revisions, draft engagement letters, estimate scope, check availability, and prepare decisions. But when the work reaches a trust boundary, such as approval, booking, pricing, or publication, the human has to act. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 This is a strong fit for WebMCP because the tool surface changes with the work. The page registers 12 baseline tools through document.modelContext. When a human approval gate is pending, a 13th tool appears. When that gate closes, the extra tool disappears. 

 The tools are not just a fixed manifest. They reflect the live state of the work. 

 Better experience 

 For the human, the page reduces decision fatigue. Instead of hunting through drafts, calendars, pricing notes, and approval threads, the person sees what is waiting, what changed, why the agent proposed it, and the exact decision needed. 

 For the agent, the page removes guesswork. It can call structured tools for pending approvals, deliverable review, revision proposals, variant queues, scope, quotes, availability, and staged engagement letters without scraping the layout or pretending that a click equals judgment. 

 The human and agent boundary 

 The demo's Judge mode shows the central proof: a scripted approval click is refused. The gate only closes on a trusted human gesture. 

 That is the memorable point of the project. WebMCP is not only about making websites easier for agents to use. It can also make websites safer by giving agents useful tools while preserving human authority. 

 Implementation 

 Approval Desk is a fully static app hosted on Cloudflare Pages. It registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, uses typed input schemas and tool annotations, listens for toolchange, and reads back the active tool registry with document.modelContext.getTools. 

 The approval flow uses an abortable human gate. The agent can ask for approval and can withdraw its own pending request. It cannot approve, publish, book, or send on a person's behalf. 

 All engagements shown in the demo are invented sample data. No real client work appears in the project.

pitch: An Online Go Game Where Humans Play by Click and AI Plays Through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
An Online Go Game Where Humans Play by Click and AI Plays Through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Human vs. AI Go, Powered by WebMCP 

 Inspiration 

 Go has extremely simple rules, yet every move can change the direction of the entire game. That contrast made it an ideal environment for exploring a larger question: 

 
 What happens when an AI does not merely generate an answer, but directly participates in an interactive application? 
 

 Most AI board-game demos hide the interaction behind a traditional backend API. The AI receives a board state, returns a coordinate, and the application handles everything else. I wanted to make the interaction more explicit. The human player should place stones naturally by clicking the board, while the AI should observe the game and make its own moves through WebMCP tools. 

 The project became an experiment in building a shared digital environment where a human and an AI interact with the same game state through different interfaces. 

 What the Project Does 

 The project is an online Go game in which: 

 
 The human player places stones by clicking intersections on the board. 
 The game engine validates moves, captures stones, and updates the position. 
 The AI reads the current game state through WebMCP. 
 The AI chooses a move and calls a structured WebMCP tool to place its stone. 
 Both players see the updated board immediately. 
 

 The AI does not directly manipulate the page or bypass the game rules. It must submit a move through the same controlled game interface used by the rest of the application. 

 Conceptually, the game follows a state transition model: 

 S t + 1 = T ( S t , a t ) 

 where: 

 
 (S_t) is the current board state, 
 (a_t) is the move selected by the human or AI, 
 (T) is the rule engine that validates and applies the move. 
 

 A move is accepted only when: 

 a t ∈ A ( S t ) 

 where (A(S_t)) represents all legal actions available in the current position. 

 How I Built It 

 I separated the project into three main layers: the interface, the game engine, and the AI interaction layer. 

 Interactive Go Board 

 The frontend renders the Go board and converts mouse clicks into board coordinates. When the human clicks an intersection, the interface sends the selected coordinate to the rule engine. 

 The board component is responsible for displaying: 

 
 Empty intersections 
 Black and white stones 
 The latest move 
 Captured stones 
 The current player 
 Invalid-move feedback 
 

 Keeping the visual board separate from the underlying game state made the interface easier to update and debug. 

 Go Rule Engine 

 The rule engine is the source of truth for the match. It determines whether a move is legal before modifying the board. 

 Its responsibilities include: 

 
 Enforcing turn order 
 Detecting occupied intersections 
 Calculating connected stone groups 
 Counting liberties 
 Removing captured stones 
 Preventing illegal self-capture 
 Handling repetition rules 
 Supporting pass actions 
 

 Neither the human interface nor the AI can directly modify the board. Every attempted move must pass through this engine. 

 WebMCP Integration 

 I exposed a small set of structured tools that allow the AI to interact with the game. The core tools provide functionality similar to: 
 get_board_state()
play_move(x, y)
pass_turn()
get_game_status()
 
 The AI first retrieves the current position, reasons about possible moves, and then calls play_move with a board coordinate. 

 The tool layer validates the request before forwarding it to the rule engine. This prevents the AI from playing outside the board, moving twice, placing a stone on an occupied point, or acting on an outdated game state. 

 The complete interaction loop is: 
 Human clicks the board
 ↓
Rule engine validates the move
 ↓
Board state is updated
 ↓
AI reads the state through WebMCP
 ↓
AI selects and submits a move
 ↓
Rule engine validates the AI move
 ↓
The interface renders the new position
 
 Challenges I Faced 

 Keeping the AI and Interface Synchronized 

 The most difficult problem was maintaining one authoritative game state. 

 The human interface, rule engine, and AI operate asynchronously. Without careful coordination, the AI could read an older position and attempt a move after the board had already changed. 

 I addressed this by treating every move as a transaction. Each action is checked against the latest board state and current turn before it is accepted. 

 Implementing Go Rules Correctly 

 Go looks simple until captures, liberties, suicide rules, and repeated positions are introduced. A single move can affect several neighboring groups, so validating a move requires more than checking whether an intersection is empty. 

 I learned to model the board as a graph. Each stone is a node connected to adjacent stones, and group traversal can be used to calculate liberties and determine whether a group should be captured. 

 Designing Tools for an AI 

 Giving an AI unrestricted access to application state would have been easy, but unreliable. The harder and more useful approach was designing a small tool interface with clear inputs, outputs, and validation rules. 

 For example, the AI should not need to understand the internal structure of the frontend. It only needs a stable representation of the board and a safe way to submit an action. 

 This taught me that effective AI tools should be narrow, predictable, and difficult to misuse. 

 Coordinate Conversion 

 Go coordinates can be represented in several ways: array indexes, screen positions, human-readable coordinates, or protocol-specific notation. Mixing these formats caused incorrect moves during early development. 

 I solved this by defining one internal coordinate system and performing conversions only at the boundaries of the application. 

 Handling Failed AI Actions 

 An AI can occasionally submit malformed parameters, select an illegal move, or act on stale information. The application needed to recover without freezing the game. 

 Instead of silently ignoring errors, the WebMCP layer returns structured feedback explaining why the move failed. The AI can then request the latest board state and try again. 

 What I Learned 

 This project changed how I think about AI integration. 

 I learned that an AI becomes much more useful when it can interact with a structured environment instead of only exchanging text. WebMCP allowed the browser application to expose meaningful capabilities while keeping the game engine in control. 

 I also learned that tool design matters as much as model intelligence. A powerful model connected to vague or unsafe tools can still behave poorly. A smaller set of well-defined tools often produces more reliable results. 

 From the game-engine side, I gained a deeper understanding of state machines, graph traversal, asynchronous synchronization, and defensive validation. 

 Most importantly, I learned to treat AI actions as untrusted external input. Every AI move must be checked exactly as carefully as a human-generated request. 

 What I Am Proud Of 

 I am proud that the project creates a direct and understandable interaction between a human, an AI, and a live application. 

 The human simply clicks the board. The AI observes the same match, reasons about the position, and responds through WebMCP. Both participants operate inside the same rule-controlled environment. 

 The result is more than a Go game. It is a small demonstration of how AI agents can safely participate in interactive web applications. 

 What Is Next 

 Future improvements could include: 

 
 Adjustable AI difficulty 
 Multiple board sizes 
 Move history and SGF export 
 Game replay 
 Position analysis 
 Suggested moves for beginners 
 Timed matches 
 Spectator mode 
 Support for different AI models 
 Human-versus-human and AI-versus-AI modes 
 

 I would also like to expose richer analysis tools, allowing the AI to explain candidate moves, identify weak groups, and teach Go while playing. 

 The long-term goal is to turn the project into both a playable online game and a practical example of human–AI interaction through WebMCP.

 Inspiration 

 The meme "I want AI to do my laundry and dishes so that I can do my art and my writing..." and not the other way around. What does it look like to start employing robots to do work in our everyday lives so that we can be freed to do the parts that we enjoy more? 

 What it does 

 A simple cozy farm simulator game (think Harvest Moon or Stardew Valley)
Also: A detailed WebMCP inspector built into the game to give a transparent view to tool-calling under the hood. 

 How we built it 

 GPT 5.6 in Github Copilot, deployed on Github Pages, using 98.css for a retro feel that gives lots of popup explorable dialogs to have deeper insights into the WebMCP protocol and understand it on a more fundamental level. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting good artwork was a challenge. Eventually found the public domain Kenney set of artworks (TinyFarm, TinyTown, TinyDungeon) and was able to use that to cobble together enough assets for a complete-ish game. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Really happy with the debug view into WebMCP and being able to inspect and see what the LLM sees, and how it looks at the world.
Also happy that the human player and robot player controls go through the same basic interface. The only thing that matters is their source (keyboard or tool-call) -- but otherwise they're on an equal playing field. 

 What we learned 

 That there is a LOT that goes into a full / fun game. It's just a basic shell of a game, and there is not yet enough fun stuff to do. 

 Also learned that balancing the right number of tool calls for WebMCP is a tricky thing, and there is a LOT of tinkering that one can do with making a sensible interface for agents and humans alike. 

 What's next for VibeFarmer 

 Expand the simulator, add more things to do -- especially more time-consuming but fun activities (exploration, decoration, etc) and give a rich environment for collaborating on things that make sense to delegate to the agentic AI, and things that make sense to do yourself.

A collaborative doc editor where AI agents read and write your real document state not screenshots through WebMCP.

 Story

 1 2 3 4 



 
 About the Project 

 The idea 

 We wanted to explore a simple question: 

 What if an AI agent could work inside a document with you, instead of just looking at the document from the outside? 

 Today, when an AI agent interacts with a web application, it often has to rely on screenshots, DOM inspection, or simulated clicks. For a document editor, that means the agent has to figure out what the user is looking at, where content belongs, and what actions are available. 

 We wanted to try a different approach using WebMCP : let the website expose its actual application state and capabilities as structured tools that an AI agent can call directly. 

 That became Co/Draft — a document where humans and agents edit together. 

 The core interaction is deliberately simple. A human writes and selects content normally, while an agent can use tools such as get_document_state , get_selection , add_comment , and insert_block . The agent therefore works with the same structured document state that the human sees, rather than trying to reconstruct it from the UI. 

 How we built it 

 Co/Draft is a lightweight React + TypeScript application using Zustand for document state. 

 The document is represented as structured blocks rather than one large piece of HTML. Each block has an ID, text, creation source, and author information. Comments are also attached to specific block IDs, which gives the agent an unambiguous way to refer to a section of the document. 

 On top of this state, we registered five WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_document_state — lets the agent read the current document, pending suggestions, and comments. 
 get_selection — tells the agent which block the human is currently working on. 
 insert_block — lets the agent propose a new section. 
 add_comment — lets the agent leave feedback on a specific block. 
 resolve_comment — lets the agent mark feedback as resolved. 
 

 These tools are registered through document.modelContext , using a React hook so that the tools operate against the same live state as the UI. 

 We also added a small human-in-the-loop trust boundary . An agent doesn't directly insert arbitrary content into the document. Instead, insert_block creates a visible pending suggestion. The human can then accept or reject it. 

 That gives us a workflow like: 

 Human writes → Agent reads → Agent reviews → Agent proposes → Human approves → Document changes 

 The agent can participate meaningfully without silently taking control of the document. 

 For collaboration, the prototype uses the browser's BroadcastChannel API. This allows multiple tabs in the same browser to exchange document mutations and presence information without requiring a backend. The project is intentionally a prototype rather than a production collaborative editor. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest thing we learned was that giving an agent structured tools changes the interaction completely . 

 Instead of asking an agent to “look at the page and figure out what to do,” we can give it explicit capabilities: 
 get_document_state()
get_selection()
add_comment(blockId, text)
insert_block(text, afterBlockId)
resolve_comment(commentId)
 
 This makes the boundary between the application and the agent much clearer. 

 We also learned that the interesting part isn't simply allowing an agent to edit. The more important question is how much control the agent should have . 

 For example, comments are relatively low-risk, so an agent can add one directly. Inserting actual document content is more consequential, so we introduced an approval step. 

 That led us to think about agents less like automated scripts and more like collaborators with explicitly defined permissions . 

 We also learned about the practical distinction between exposing application functionality to an agent and actually building a collaborative application. WebMCP solves the first problem very nicely, but synchronization, persistence, identity, and conflict resolution are separate engineering problems. 

 The challenges 

 One of our biggest challenges was synchronization. 

 Our first implementation used BroadcastChannel to send mutations such as: 
 editBlock
addComment
resolveComment
proposeBlock
acceptSuggestion
deleteBlock
 
 between tabs. 

 However, simply broadcasting mutations isn't enough to create a reliable shared document. Each tab initially creates its own in-memory state, so two tabs can start with different randomly generated block IDs. A mutation referring to a block that only exists in the sender's state cannot be correctly applied by another tab. 

 This forced us to think about an important distinction: 

 sharing events is not the same thing as sharing state. 

 A reliable prototype needs both a consistent initial document and a way for a newly opened tab to obtain the current state before applying future mutations. 

 We therefore treated the synchronization layer as a separate problem from WebMCP itself. The eventual direction is a lightweight state handshake for new tabs, while keeping the mutation-based synchronization simple enough for a hackathon demo. 

 Another challenge was deciding what not to build. 

 It would be possible to turn Co/Draft into a much larger system with a backend, WebSockets, persistent documents, authentication, CRDTs, conflict-free editing, and cross-device collaboration. But that would move attention away from the actual experiment we wanted to demonstrate: 

 
 Can a web application expose meaningful, structured capabilities to an AI agent so that the agent can genuinely collaborate with a human? 
 

 For this project, we chose to keep that question at the center. 

 Why this matters 

 Co/Draft is intentionally small, but the idea can extend much further. 

 A document editor is just one example. The same pattern could apply to design tools, spreadsheets, project-management applications, whiteboards, educational software, or any interactive application where an AI agent needs to understand and manipulate structured state. 

 Instead of building agents that merely see interfaces, we can build applications that explicitly tell agents: 

 “Here is what I am. Here is what you can understand. Here is what you are allowed to do.” 

 That is the direction we wanted to explore with Co/Draft.

 Story

 home page

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Initially, I wanted to create a head-to-head competitive game for two players. However, after experimenting with Codex to control a webpage via WebMCP, I abandoned that idea due to excessive latency and slow response times. 

 This led to the creation of SplitSight—an escape room game consisting of three stages. The human player can see real-time visual cues that are not captured in the system's output, while the AI ​​agent can check the game state and operate mechanisms that the human cannot control. Neither party can escape alone; success requires cooperation. 

 Feature Overview 

 SplitSight guides the human and the AI ​​agent through three interconnected rooms: 

 
 Mirror Chamber: The human identifies and shares a flashing symbol; the agent reads this information and adjusts the angle of the mirrors. 
 Portrait Gallery: The human focuses on a flashing portrait; the agent uses the shared information to open the corresponding hidden compartment. 
 Twin-Door Hall: The agent analyzes structural information regarding two exits, while the human observes real-time "guardian markers" and selects the corresponding door; the agent can only open the door if its proposal aligns with the human's decision. 
 

 Every action—reading, selecting, blocked attempts, mechanism changes, and successful outcomes—is recorded in a shared causal log, with the source (human, agent, or room) clearly marked. The interface also indicates whose turn it is and what needs to be done next. 

 Technical Implementation 

 Implemented using Codex and "vibecoding"; the specific technology stack was also selected by Codex. 

 Challenges Faced 

 The biggest challenge was choosing the concept; I actually discarded three other ideas before settling on this one. 

 Achievement I'm Proud Of 

 Implementing the entire project using the "vibecoding" workflow.

 Make frequent use of AI and Codex.

AgentInbox is a Gmail manager that exposes WebMCP tools so any AI agent can read, organize, and reply to your email — inside your own authenticated browser session, with no API keys shared.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Today, giving an AI agent access to your inbox usually means one of two things: handing over a personal API key to a third-party service, or trusting a closed chatbot with full access to your private data. Both approaches break the trust boundary that should stay with the user. WebMCP offered a different model — register tools directly on the page, inside the user's own authenticated session, and let any compliant agent discover and call them. AgentInbox is our exploration of what that looks like for one of the most personal apps people use every day: email. 

 What it does 

 AgentInbox is WebMCP powered Gmail manager. You can sign in with Google , view your inbox , read messages, mark them as read and reply. Built as normal website with FastAPI for backend, PostgreSQL for DB, and html/css/js for frontend 

 What makes it different is that every core action is also registered as a WebMCP tool with document.modelContext.registerTool(): 

 list_emails — retrieve the user's messages, optionally filtered to unread only
get_message_detail — fetch the full content of one message (subject, sender, date, body, read status)
mark_as_read — mark a message as read
reply_to_email — send a reply within the correct Gmail thread (using proper In-Reply-To/References headers) 

 Any WebMCP-compatible AI agent running in the user's browser can discover these tools with getTools() and call them with executeTool() — no separate integration, no API key handed to a third party, and no action taken outside the user's own real, authenticated Gmail session. 

 How we built it
Backend: FastAPI (Python), with a layered architecture — routers → services → repositories → models
Database: PostgreSQL via SQLAlchemy 2.0
Auth: Google OAuth2, JWT stored in an HttpOnly cookie
Email: Gmail API (list, get, mark-read, reply — with correct thread headers)
Frontend: plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript, no framework — served directly by FastAPI from the same origin as the API
WebMCP: four tools registered with the imperative API (document.modelContext.registerTool()), verified end-to-end via getTools()/executeTool() — including real Gmail reads and a real reply sent inside the correct thread
Deployment: live on Render (single service, backend + frontend together)
Challenges we ran into
WebMCP is a very new, fast-moving spec — the tooling ecosystem around it (browser extensions, inspectors) is still immature, and some third-party inspector extensions didn't reliably detect our imperative-API tools. We worked around this by verifying everything directly through the browser console (getTools() / executeTool()), which is exactly what an agent does internally.
Google's sensitive Gmail scopes mean full app verification wasn't realistic within the hackathon timeline, so the app runs with a whitelisted Test Users list and demo credentials for judging (see Testing instructions).
Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A complete, working product — not just a proof of concept — with real OAuth, a real database, and four WebMCP tools that actually call a real Gmail account and produce real results, deployed live. 

 What we learned 

 How the WebMCP imperative API actually behaves end-to-end in a real Chrome build: tool registration, discovery via getTools(), and execution via executeTool(), including the JSON string in/out data flow. 

 What's next for AgentInbox
Improving WebMCP tools. Making UI more better and user-friendy. Adding real AI agent.

A live funding-search agent, now callable by agents directly via a real WebMCP tool.

 Story

 Grant Scout is a live, search-grounded funding research agent for solo, non-incorporated founders — every answer comes from a real SerpApi/grants.gov search, reasoned by Gemini, with real cited sources, never invented. 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Grant Scout already solves a real problem for a real audience (solo founders finding funding they can actually apply for). WebMCP lets us extend that from "a page a human visits" to "a real capability an agent can call directly" — without building a second, parallel, disconnected demo. 

 What's new for this challenge 

 The app's existing live search — the exact same pipeline a human visitor triggers by typing a question and pressing Send — is now registered as a real WebMCP tool via document.modelContext.registerTool() : 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "search_funding_programs" , 
 description : "Search for real, currently-open funding programs ..." , 
 inputSchema : { type : "object" , properties : { query : { type : "string" } } , required : [ "query" ] } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 const data = await runQuery ( input . query ) ; // the SAME function the UI form calls
 return { answer : data . answer , sources : data . sources } ; 
 } , 
 } ) ; 
 
 An agent-native browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) can now call search_funding_programs directly and get back a real, live, cited answer — the identical pipeline a human sees, not a mock or a shadow path. The tool call drives the same visible UI state (pipeline ticket, rendered answer, sources) that a human's own search would, so the page stays truthful about what just happened. 

 Feature-detected: on any browser without WebMCP support, this code no-ops entirely — zero effect on the default experience. 

 What people and agents can now do together that was hard before 

 Before: a founder had to remember to visit Grant Scout, type their situation, and read the results themselves. After: an agent working on a founder's behalf — inside a WebMCP-aware browser — can call the real search directly as part of a larger task (e.g., "find me funding I don't need a company for, then draft an application checklist"), grounded in the same live, cited, non-fabricated results a human would get. 

 How it works (full stack) 

 Agent: Google's Agent Development Kit (google-adk), a single Agent with two live-grounding tools — SerpApi's Google Search API and grants.gov's public Search API, chosen deterministically based on whether the question signals US federal funding.
Reasoning: gemini-flash-lite-latest reviews only the real returned results and cites every claim to a real source URL.
Backend: Vercel Python serverless function (frontend/api/chat.py).
Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4.
WebMCP: frontend/components/gs/TryIt.tsx registers the tool in a useEffect , sharing its query-execution logic with the human-facing form via a single runQuery function — one pipeline, two callers. 

 Try it live 

 https://grant-scout-jayblast.vercel.app — the human UI. The WebMCP tool registers automatically in any WebMCP-capable browser visiting the same page. 

 Repo: https://github.com/jayblast-spec/grant-scout (see frontend/components/gs/TryIt.tsx for the tool registration)

A simple meal planner that provides access to all its functionality via the WebMCP protocol. This integration allows an AI agent to plan your meals all throughout the week; and locate promotions.

 Story

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 First and foremost, I have been experimenting with AI. One of my main goals was to see how much work I could realistically get done with AI assistance. I pitched the idea, tested the website, reviewed changes, and repeatedly stripped away unnecessary bloat. 

 I decided to build a meal planner because eating well and staying consistent can be difficult, whether you are trying to gain weight, lose weight, or simply eat better. Automating parts of meal planning can make that process much easier to maintain. 

 What it does 

 Meal Planner allows users to plan breakfast, lunch, and dinner in advance. Meals are linked to recipes, while recipes can also be stored independently for later use. 

 Users can keep track of pantry inventory, calculate what ingredients they still need, and generate a shopping list based on their planned meals. 

 All of these core functions are also exposed to an AI agent through WebMCP. An agent can read recipes, inspect pantry inventory, plan multiple meals, update stock, calculate shopping requirements, and help research prices or promotions based on a location the user explicitly provides. 

 The application also supports importing and exporting meal data between devices. 

 How we built it 

 The application was largely vibe-coded. I pitched the meal-planning concept and used ChatGPT to help implement it. 

 My role was defining the product, testing the implementation, making architectural decisions, reviewing changes, and removing features that made the application more complicated without making it more useful. 

 The final application is deliberately simple: HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, browser localStorage, and WebMCP. It runs as a static site with no required backend or database. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our original project idea was significantly more ambitious. Because of time constraints and implementation complexity, we abandoned it and focused on building something smaller that worked well. 

 Another challenge was designing the application so that the same functionality could be used by both humans and AI agents without building two separate systems. 

 The final application runs entirely as a static site. User data is stored locally in the browser, and no third-party API is required for the core functionality. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The entire application was built in one day. 

 Despite the short development time, it includes recipe storage, meal planning, pantry management, shopping-list generation, import/export, and 20 WebMCP tools that expose the application to AI agents. 

 What we learned 

 Vibe-coding works, but only if you understand what you are trying to build. 

 AI can produce a large amount of implementation very quickly, but a human still needs to define the goal, make architectural decisions, test the result, identify unnecessary complexity, and decide what should actually ship. 

 For this project, having a human in the loop was indispensable. 

 What's next for Meal Planner 

 With more time and resources, I would expand the agent integration, improve local price and promotion discovery, add better cross-device synchronization, and continue improving the meal-planning workflow. 

 The core idea would remain the same: let the website manage structured meal data while an AI agent handles the repetitive planning and orchestration.

 The hard part was choosing a useful boundary without exposing account, customer, checkout, payment, or order workflows to an agent. about_excerpt:
Betatrace, a diabetes log you and your AI agent can use together, right within the browser.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 2 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates

 Live Dashboard 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP Graph Use Case 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Seven-Day Graph with Meal Markers 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Three Registered Tools 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Landing Hero Page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Meal Log Showing Agent Provenance

 Seven-Day Graph with Meal Markers

 Landing Hero Page
