 Safety Boundaries 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Inspiration 

 I was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes three years ago. The hard part was not learning one single thing. It was keeping up with dozens of small things every day: checking glucose, remembering meals and insulin, and trying to work out why the same routine sometimes produced a completely different result. 

 A lot of the tools I found felt old, expensive, or disconnected from how I actually wanted to manage everything. At the same time, ChatGPT and other AI tools were becoming genuinely useful. I kept wondering what would happen if an agent could work inside a diabetes app with me, using the information already on the screen instead of making me repeat it all in a separate chat.
That idea became BetaTrace. 

 What it does 

 BetaTrace is a Type 1 diabetes dashboard that both a person and a browser-based agent can use. 

 The dashboard lets someone explore glucose readings, meals, insulin entries, trends, and time in range. The WebMCP tools let an agent work with that same demo data: 

 get_demo_state reads the current synthetic data, including seven days of glucose readings and logged meals. 

 log_demo_entry records a glucose reading, meal, or insulin dose that the user says has already happened. 

 reset_demo_data clears added entries and restores the original sample data, but only after the user confirms it. 

 For example, I can ask an agent to graph my glucose and meals from the past week, log a new meal, and then generate the graph again. The new meal appears in both the dashboard and the agent’s updated graph. 

 Without WebMCP, the agent would have to inspect the page, guess what each control does, and click through the interface. BetaTrace gives it clear tools with defined inputs and responses. 

 How I built it 

 BetaTrace is a React app hosted on Vercel. 

 The page registers its tools directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(). There is no separate WebMCP server and no polyfill. The dashboard and the agent tools use the same validation and local data, so an entry logged by the agent appears on screen immediately. 

 For the seven-day graph, get_demo_state returns 336 chronological glucose readings along with the meals recorded during that period. This gives the agent enough real structure to produce a useful graph instead of a rough summary. 

 The public demo only uses synthetic data stored in the browser. Its WebMCP tools cannot reach Supabase, private accounts, or real patient information. BetaTrace can record an insulin dose that the user says they already took, but it will not calculate or recommend one. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The first version could return a summary of the demo, but that was not enough to make a proper seven-day graph. We had to expose the underlying timeline while keeping the response clear and predictable for the agent. 

 Keeping the agent and the visible dashboard in sync was another challenge. A successful tool call was not enough. If the dashboard did not update at the same moment, the whole idea of working together inside one page fell apart. 

 The safety boundaries also took some thought. Health data is not a good place for vague permissions. We limited the demo to synthetic local data, validated every write, blocked dose recommendations, and made reset require confirmation. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The part I am most proud of is the full loop. 

 An agent can read seven days of glucose and meal data, turn it into an interactive graph, log a meal supplied by the user, and then produce a new graph containing that meal. The person sees the same change inside BetaTrace. 

 It sounds simple when written out, but that shared state is what makes the project feel like collaboration instead of ordinary browser automation. 

 I am also proud that the safety limitations are part of the design rather than a disclaimer added at the end. The demo is useful enough to prove the idea without pretending that an experimental agent should be making treatment decisions. 

 What we learned 

 A button exposed as a tool is not automatically useful. 

 The tool has to match something a person would naturally ask for. It needs understandable inputs, useful output, proper validation, and clear limits. Building the WebMCP layer forced us to think more carefully about what BetaTrace actually knows and what an agent should be allowed to do with it. 

 We also learned that the best WebMCP moments are visible. When the agent logs a meal and the dashboard changes immediately, there is no need for a long explanation. You can see that the person and the agent are working with the same application. 

 What's next for Betatrace 

 The current version stays inside a synthetic guest demo on purpose. 

 The next step would be optional authenticated accounts with narrow permissions, a visible history of agent actions, and confirmation for anything sensitive. Users should always be able to see what the agent accessed and what it changed. 

 Future tools could prepare appointment summaries, compare glucose responses after recurring meals, and help someone collect questions for their care team. They would still stop short of diagnosis or automatic dosing advice. 

 The goal is not to hand diabetes management over to an agent. It is to reduce some of the repetitive work while keeping the person in control.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 CALMA-SEG was inspired by a simple question: how can a person quickly find clear, low-intensity psychoeducational support without navigating a complex interface or sharing personal information? 

 This question is especially relevant in demanding work and public-service environments, where stress can be common but asking for help may still involve uncertainty or stigma. I wanted to explore how people and browser agents could work together to make safe, prewritten information easier to discover while maintaining clear clinical, privacy, and emergency boundaries. 

 What it does 

 CALMA-SEG is a bilingual English-Spanish WebMCP demonstration. People can use its ordinary interface to: 

 
 Filter short psychoeducational exercises by category and duration. 
 View complete exercise instructions and safety notes. 
 Find general human-support options based on a self-selected urgency level. 
 Read the demo’s safety and privacy limitations. 
 

 A compatible browser agent can discover and invoke the same capabilities through four WebMCP tools: 

 
 list_wellbeing_exercises 
 show_wellbeing_exercise 
 find_human_support_options 
 explain_safety_limits 
 

 Every successful agent call produces a visible change in the human interface. The page updates its filters, displayed content, language, or Agent Activity panel so that the person can see what the agent did. 

 How I built it 

 I built CALMA-SEG as a static Vite application using semantic HTML, responsive CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. 

 The tools are registered with the WebMCP imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a name, description, JSON input schema, validated parameters, and a predictable text result. 

 All educational content is fixed, synthetic, and stored locally in the application. The project has no backend, database, authentication, analytics, cookies, local storage, or external AI API. It is deployed through Netlify from a public GitHub repository. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, a browser agent would need to interpret headings, dropdowns, cards, and buttons from the DOM and infer their meaning. With WebMCP, the website declares its capabilities directly. 

 For example, an agent can request a Spanish exercise with a maximum duration of three minutes through validated parameters. The website then returns a structured result and synchronizes the visible human interface with that request. 

 This creates a more predictable and transparent collaboration between the person, the browser agent, and the website. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing tools that were useful without crossing clinical or privacy boundaries. CALMA-SEG does not diagnose, provide therapy, recommend medication, infer a person’s mental state, or function as an emergency service. 

 Another challenge was ensuring that agent actions were never silent. The exercise-listing tool originally returned information only to the agent. I revised it so that it also updates the visible filters, exercise list, language, and Agent Activity panel. 

 I also had to account for WebMCP’s experimental browser availability. When WebMCP is unavailable, the page reports this honestly while keeping the complete manual interface functional. 

 What I learned 

 I learned how WebMCP can turn an ordinary website into an explicit set of safe, typed capabilities for browser agents. I also learned that agent-friendly design requires more than returning data: actions should remain understandable and visible to the person using the page. 

 The project reinforced the importance of input validation, progressive enhancement, bilingual consistency, privacy by design, and careful safety language. 

 What’s next 

 Future work could include accessibility and usability testing, additional reviewed educational content, and evaluation of how clearly people understand agent actions and safety boundaries. 

 Any research or institutional pilot would require separate authorization, ethical and legal review, data-protection safeguards, informed consent, and professional supervision. This hackathon submission is an independent technical demonstration, not a clinical service or institutional implementation.

about_excerpt:
A diagram canvas humans and AI agents draw on together. Describe a system, watch it appear, then move things yourself while the agent keeps up.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it is 

 Chalkline is an architecture diagram canvas that a person and an AI agent edit at the same time, on the same model . Describe a system in plain language and the agent draws it: services, databases, queues, caches, users, labelled edges, auto-layout. Then drag boxes, rename them in place, draw your own arrows, delete what you don't like. The agent reads the live canvas through WebMCP before every change, so it builds on your edits instead of overwriting them. 

 Live: https://chalkline-steel.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/chinesepowered/chalkline 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Diagram tools are famously hostile to agents. The state lives in an SVG or a canvas; there is no reliable DOM to click, and screenshots lose the graph structure. Chalkline turns the diagram itself into ten structured tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 get_diagram , add_node , update_node , remove_node , connect , disconnect , auto_layout , highlight_nodes , clear_diagram , export_mermaid 

 Any WebMCP-capable agent, whether ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with WebMCP enabled, or the built-in co-author, sees exactly the model the human is manipulating on screen. Nodes are addressable by id or label, results come back as text the agent can reason about, and read-only / destructive hints are set on the annotations. 

 How it creates a better experience 

 
 No description overhead. You don't have to explain your changes to the agent. You just make them. The agent calls get_diagram and sees the renamed node, the moved box, the new arrow. 
 Visible agency. Every agent action is shown as a tool call with its arguments and latency. Agent-added nodes pulse in and carry an "agent" badge; nodes you touch are badged "you". 
 Shared attention. Ask "what's the single point of failure?" and the agent answers and highlights the nodes on the canvas with highlight_nodes , so you are literally looking at the same thing. 
 Portable output. export_mermaid returns the diagram as Mermaid source for docs and READMEs. 
 

 What people and agents can do together that was hard before 

 Before: paste a description into a chat, get back Mermaid text, render it somewhere else, edit by hand, lose the agent. Or let an agent click around a whiteboard app by screenshot and watch it flail. 

 Now: the diagram is one live artifact with two authors. The human does what humans are good at (taste, layout, naming, "no, not like that") and the agent does what agents are good at (filling in the twenty nodes of a microservice diagram in ten seconds, rewiring edges, reviewing the design). Neither has to wait for the other to finish. 

 How WebMCP is implemented 

 
 lib/webmcp.ts is a tiny registry: it registers each tool with document.modelContext.registerTool(..., { signal }) and unregisters via AbortController when the canvas unmounts, so the tool set always matches what's on screen. Native calls from the browser agent and calls from the in-page agent go through the same execute and are logged in one activity feed. 
 lib/tools.ts defines the ten tools with JSON Schema input, natural-language descriptions and annotations. 
 lib/diagram.ts is the shared store (React Flow nodes/edges + dagre layout); both the UI and the tools mutate it, which is the whole point. 
 The built-in co-author ( components/AgentPanel.tsx + app/api/agent/route.ts ) is a Gemini function-calling loop that discovers tools from the registry and dispatches through WebMCP, with a model fallback chain for free-tier rate limits. 
 

 Tested in Chrome 153 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (DevTools → Application → WebMCP shows all ten tools and lets you run them by hand) and with the in-page Gemini agent.

 Inspiration i built data bridge from watching bloomberg tv on a segment where they spoke about fragmented data being held in all these companies. That was my inspiration for this project 

 Businesses often rely on data spread across CSV files, supplier records, inventory systems, purchase histories, and other disconnected sources. The idea behind DataBridge Agent was to create a practical AI workflow that can inspect that fragmented data, identify problems, and turn the findings into clear business actions without allowing the agent to make consequential changes without human approval. 

 What it does 

 DataBridge Agent is a WebMCP-enabled business data assistant. 

 It exposes eight structured tools: 

 
 inspect_dataset 
 find_duplicates 
 detect_missing_fields 
 compare_datasets 
 detect_anomalies 
 analyze_price_changes 
 create_action_plan 
 export_clean_data 
 

 The agent can inspect loaded business data, detect duplicate records and missing fields, compare related datasets, identify unusual numeric values, analyze price movements, and generate a prioritized action plan. 

 Export is intentionally protected by a human-approval gate. The source data remains unchanged, and a cleaned copy is only created after explicit approval. 

 How I built it 

 I built DataBridge Agent as a React and TypeScript application hosted on Replit. 

 The WebMCP tool layer is registered through the browser model context so compatible agents can discover and call structured tools instead of relying on page scraping or fragile UI automation. 

 The application also includes an embedded AI Agent Demo that runs the same DataBridge business logic locally when native WebMCP is unavailable. The interface clearly distinguishes native WebMCP activity from local demo-agent activity. 

 The core data-analysis functions are shared between the WebMCP tool wrappers and the embedded demo workflow so the results come from the loaded data rather than hardcoded demo values. 

 Challenges I faced 

 One major challenge was testing an experimental browser capability across different environments. In a normal browser, the WebMCP API was not exposed, so I added clear capability detection rather than falsely presenting local execution as native WebMCP. 

 After enabling WebMCP testing in a compatible Chrome environment, the live application successfully detected native WebMCP support. 

 Another challenge was designing safe agent behavior. Data analysis can run automatically, but export is treated as a consequential action and requires explicit human approval. 

 I also focused on making the execution transparent by showing the tool sequence, results, data source, and approval status directly in the interface. 

 What I learned 

 This project showed me how WebMCP can make web applications much more useful to AI agents by exposing structured capabilities instead of forcing agents to interpret interfaces visually. 

 I also learned that agent capability should be paired with transparency and human control. A useful business agent should not only produce an answer; it should make its actions auditable and clearly separate analysis from actions that can affect data. 

 What's next 

 The next step is to expand DataBridge Agent beyond CSV-based workflows into more live business systems, including databases, procurement platforms, inventory systems, and other operational data sources. 

 I would also like to add more configurable tool schemas, stronger cross-dataset matching, and reusable approval policies for different business actions.

 Inspiration 

 Local-service businesses lose real revenue when calls go unanswered, but deploying an automated front desk is consequential. The owner understands the business constraints; an agent excels at structured setup work. Ghost Operator gives both of them one shared, auditable workspace. 

 What it does 

 The owner enters industry, weekly call volume, missed-call rate, average job value, and desired coverage. Through WebMCP, an agent can read those values, update approved inputs, calculate calls at risk, recommend coverage, draft a constrained call policy, and open the completed plan for review. Every action appears in a visible activity ledger. 

 The human-agent boundary is deliberate: there is no tool for final approval, deployment, purchasing, calling, or messaging. The owner must inspect the visible plan and click Approve & save personally. Even then, the demo only saves locally and confirms that no external system changed. 

 Why WebMCP 

 This workflow combines structured inputs, deterministic calculations, editable shared state, and a consequential handoff. Browser automation alone would need to infer form semantics and scrape changing output. WebMCP gives the agent six precise operations connected to the same logic and session the owner sees, making the workflow faster, more reliable, and easy to audit. 

 People and agents can now collaborate on a launch plan in plain language while keeping authority visible and constrained—something that previously required brittle UI automation or a separate integration disconnected from the page under review. 

 How we built it 

 Ghost Operator is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. It registers six imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a narrow JSON input schema, read/write annotations, application-level validation, structured results, and an abortable lifecycle. Tool handlers reuse the same deterministic state and calculation functions as the human UI. 

 The application is deployed on Vercel, tested with Vitest, and published under the MIT License. All challenge code was created after the challenge opened on August 25, 2026; the public commit history documents the work. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest design decision was not exposing every UI action as a tool. We intentionally omitted approval and deployment operations so the agent can accelerate the work without silently crossing the human authorization boundary. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is strongest when the page remains the shared source of truth. The best agent experience is not invisible automation—it is structured collaboration where the person can see state, understand changes, and retain final control.

 Inspiration 

 Small service businesses lose valuable enquiries when calls are missed, follow-up is delayed, or customer details are scattered across disconnected tools. Recovering one lead can require several repetitive steps: identify the opportunity, understand the request, prepare a response, qualify the need, find availability, obtain approval, book the appointment, and update reporting. 

 Palm92 Lead Recovery OS explores a more useful open web where a person and an AI agent can complete that workflow together without surrendering human control. 

 What it does 

 Palm92 exposes seven structured browser-native WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_unrecovered_leads 
 get_lead_details 
 prepare_follow_up 
 recover_lead 
 find_available_appointments 
 prepare_appointment 
 get_recovery_summary 
 

 An agent can discover missed enquiries, inspect structured lead details, draft a follow-up, record an explicit fictional customer response, qualify the requirement, check appointment availability, and prepare an appointment. 

 The agent cannot complete the final booking. Palm92 pauses at a visible human approval checkpoint. Only the person can approve the final demonstration booking, after which the dashboard updates. 

 The governing principle is: AI investigates. Humans decide. 

 Why WebMCP 

 This workflow is a strong fit for WebMCP because it involves connected browser actions, structured business data, business context, and a consequential final decision. Instead of forcing an agent to infer controls from page layout, Palm92 makes safe capabilities explicitly discoverable through document.modelContext.registerTool . 

 The tools share the same in-browser state as the human-facing dashboard. Inputs use narrow JSON schemas and tool annotations describe their effects. This creates a coherent experience in which the agent handles investigation and preparation while the human retains authority. 

 Challenge-period work 

 Palm92 existed as a lead-recovery dashboard before the challenge. During the challenge period it was meaningfully extended with seven client-side JavaScript WebMCP tools, shared browser state, structured schemas, tool annotations, an agent-driven recovery sequence, automated checks, and a human-only approval boundary. The dated commit history and CHALLENGE_CHANGELOG.md distinguish this work from the earlier dashboard. 

 Demo result 

 The demonstration uses the fictional Daniel Reed kitchen-quote enquiry, valued at £2,400. After the approved recovery flow: 

 
 Calls recovered increase from 61 to 62 
 Appointments increase from 23 to 24 
 Recovered pipeline value increases from £7,050 to £9,450 
 

 All customer names, telephone numbers, records, and values are fictional demonstration data. No real customer is contacted and no external calendar is booked. 

 How it was built 

 Palm92 is a browser-based JavaScript application hosted on ChatGPT Sites. WebMCP tools are registered client-side through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tool layer and interface use the same state, so agent actions remain visible and understandable to the person. 

 Codex supported implementation planning, WebMCP tool refinement, debugging, safety checks, automated testing, repository preparation, demo editing, and validation of the end-to-end workflow. ChatGPT was used to test agent discovery and execution through the in-app browser's Site tools. 

 How to test 

 
 Open the live application in the latest ChatGPT desktop app using GPT-5.6 Sol or GPT-5.6 Terra. 
 Select Site tools in the address bar and inspect the seven Palm92 tools. 
 Ask the agent to find today's highest-value unrecovered lead and help recover it. 
 Let the agent inspect the lead, prepare the follow-up, qualify the opportunity, check availability, and prepare the appointment. 
 Confirm that the agent stops before booking and requests human approval. 
 Approve using the visible Palm92 control. 
 Confirm that the dashboard updates once to 62 recovered calls, 24 appointments, and £9,450 pipeline value. 
 

 No credentials are required. 

 Limitations and next steps 

 The current build uses fictional in-browser demonstration data and does not contact customers, update an external CRM, or book an external calendar. A production version would require secure identity, permissions, encrypted server-side integrations, consent controls, durable audit storage, monitoring, and configurable organisational policies.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 The problem 

 Roughly a third of household food is wasted, and meal planning is the chore nobody wants. PantryPilot splits that work the way it should be split: humans keep judgment (what looks fresh, what we feel like eating), agents take bulk iteration (expiry triage, week planning, list consolidation). 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Reducing food waste is a stateful planning problem: the agent must read pantry state, write a coherent plan, and derive a shopping list, repeatedly, as reality changes. Scraping a DOM for that is fragile and slow. PantryPilot instead publishes a typed contract: 8 tools registered on document.modelContext with JSON Schema inputs and structured JSON results, exactly per the WebMCP spec. 

 What humans and agents can do together 

 
 Humans: add groceries by hand, swap a dinner when the mood strikes, check off shopping items in the store. 
 Agents: read the pantry, triage what is about to spoil, plan 7 dinners expiry-first, derive an aisle-consolidated shopping list, log groceries and cooked meals. 
 Together: the ask that used to mean a hundred UI turns - plan my week around what is expiring, then tell me what to buy - becomes one tool call, while the human keeps every final decision. 
 

 How WebMCP is implemented 

 js/webmcp.js defines the tool table and calls document.modelContext.registerTool({name, description, inputSchema, execute}) for each of: get_pantry, add_pantry_items, consume_pantry_items, find_recipes, plan_week, get_plan, get_shopping_list, suggest_use_it_up. The exact same implementations also power the built-in Agent Console, so anyone can exercise the agent surface in any browser and judges can verify the tools without a flag. Planning is a deterministic greedy scorer (expiry-first weighting, repeat penalty) that runs fully client-side. 

 Engineering 

 Zero dependencies, zero backend, no build step: plain HTML/CSS/JS, offline-capable, localStorage state, 36-recipe graph, expiry model, aisle-aware consolidation. MIT licensed.

 Inspiration 

 Retail teams do not need an agent that silently buys stock. They need help turning messy operational signals into a clear, reviewable next step. A shelf can be below its reorder point, compatible alternatives can exist, and the decision still belongs to the person responsible for stock and spend. 

 Restock Room explores that handoff. It gives an agent a narrow, explicit set of capabilities for finding evidence and preparing a proposal, while keeping the normal workspace understandable and the final approval visibly human. 

 What it does 

 Restock Room starts with visible low-stock alerts and a visible replenishment policy. A browser agent can read the alert evidence and policy, search the visible synthetic catalog for the affected item and alternatives, and create a replenishment draft or a policy-aware two-alert plan. The operator then reviews every proposed line in the same UI and approves or rejects it. 

 The draft or plan is intentionally the end of the agent's authority. The multi-alert plan enforces the visible 75% signal-confidence threshold, two-line limit, and $1,800 budget. Approval is a local, auditable UI action only: it never contacts a supplier, creates a cart, submits an order, or handles a payment. All catalog and inventory records in the demo are synthetic. 

 Why this is a strong WebMCP use case 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer workflows from a page's layout and text, which is brittle for operational work. Restock Room exposes the meaningful actions as structured tools, with stable names, input schemas, and safe outcomes. The agent can work with the same stock alert and catalog information the operator sees instead of guessing which controls or records matter. 

 That produces a better joint experience: the agent reduces the research and proposal work, while the human retains context, discretion, and final control. The normal UI remains fully usable even if WebMCP is unavailable, so agent support enhances the workspace instead of replacing it. 

 How we built it 

 The React and TypeScript app registers seven client-side WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool when the browser exposes the API: 

 
 
 Tool 
 Safety boundary 
 
 
 
 get_stock_alert 
 Read-only view of one visible alert and its evidence. 
 
 
 search_catalog 
 Read-only synthetic catalog search and alternative lookup. 
 
 
 create_replenishment_draft 
 Creates a reversible in-app draft; it cannot purchase or submit an order. 
 
 
 get_replenishment_draft 
 Read-only view of the draft and human approval state. 
 
 
 get_restock_policy 
 Read-only view of the visible budget, confidence threshold, line limit, and human-approval rule. 
 
 
 create_replenishment_plan 
 Creates a reversible two-alert plan only when it fits the visible policy; it cannot purchase or submit an order. 
 
 
 get_replenishment_plan 
 Read-only view of plan budget use and each line’s human decision. 
 
 

 The read-only tools use readOnlyHint , inputs are bounded with object schemas, and no tool exposes untrusted or user-generated content. The deployed static app also sets origin-isolation and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) headers for the WebMCP environment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hard product decision was restraint. It is easy to make a replenishment demo look impressive by letting an agent complete a purchase, but that conceals the real risks. We narrowed the tool surface to what an operator can inspect, reason about, and safely reverse. 

 We also designed the UI and the tool contract together. Every agent-visible result must make sense to a person looking at the workspace, and every material action must leave a visible trace. 

 Accomplishments that we are proud of 

 
 A complete alert-to-draft-to-approval workflow and a multi-alert policy plan rather than isolated tool calls. 
 A small WebMCP contract that clearly separates read-only lookup from reversible state changes. 
 A human-first fallback experience and an explicit audit trail. 
 A public HTTPS deployment that is ready for judges to test in a WebMCP-enabled browser. 
 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native product design is less about exposing every button and more about naming the few actions that carry real intent. A structured tool can make an agent more reliable, but the product must still say who owns the decision and what the tool is not allowed to do. 

 What's next for Restock Room 

 The next iteration would connect to real inventory feeds behind explicit authorization, add role-aware approval policies, and preserve a durable audit history. Any supplier or purchase integration would remain a separate, explicit human-approved step rather than an extension of the draft-creation tool.

 Inspiration 

 Returns sound simple, but the actual workflow is usually not. 

 A customer asks, “Can I return this order?”, and suddenly a support operator has to find the order, read the right return policy, check the return window, look at the item condition, compare different resolutions, draft a response, and sometimes prepare an RMA. 

 We wanted to explore what this workflow would look like if the website was designed not only for humans, but also for AI agents. 

 Instead of asking an agent to read the page, guess which button to click, and simulate a human user, we wanted the website to expose its real capabilities directly. 

 That is where WebMCP became a really good fit for the project. 

 

 What it does 

 Returns Desk is a WebMCP-powered returns workspace for small e-commerce teams. 

 It exposes six WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_orders 
 get_return_policy 
 check_return_eligibility 
 compare_resolution_options 
 draft_customer_message 
 submit_rma_for_approval 
 

 An agent can use these tools to move through a real returns workflow step by step. 

 For example, a user can ask the agent to find order ORD-1001 , check whether it is eligible for return, and compare the available resolution options. 

 The agent can then call the website tools directly instead of trying to operate the UI like a human. 

 The main idea is simple: 

 AI handles the repetitive work, while humans stay in control of important decisions. 

 

 How we built it 

 We built the frontend with React and TypeScript, and deployed the application with Cloudflare Workers. 

 The WebMCP layer exposes the same business capabilities that already exist in the application, instead of creating a separate demo-only flow. 

 That means the human-facing UI and the agent-facing tools are connected to the same returns logic. 

 We also tried to keep the policy and eligibility logic as deterministic as possible. 

 Instead of asking an LLM to freely interpret every return case, the application uses structured rules such as return windows, final-sale restrictions, item condition, and available resolution options. 

 For write-related actions, we added an approval boundary so the agent can prepare a request without silently completing a consequential action. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was deciding what should actually become a WebMCP tool. 

 At first, it is easy to think in terms of UI actions like “click this button” or “open this page”. 

 But that would miss the point of WebMCP. 

 We realized the tools should represent meaningful business capabilities instead, such as check_return_eligibility or compare_resolution_options . 

 Another challenge was deciding where automation should stop. 

 We wanted the agent to be genuinely useful, but we did not want it to silently perform important write actions. 

 That led us to separate read and decision-support tools from approval-related actions. 

 We also had to test the production site in a real WebMCP environment and make sure ChatGPT could actually discover the tools, not just see them in source code. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are especially proud that Returns Desk works as both a normal website and an agent-ready website. 

 A human can still use the UI normally, but an AI agent can discover structured capabilities through WebMCP. 

 We successfully exposed six WebMCP tools in the production site and verified that they can be discovered through ChatGPT Desktop Site Tools. 

 We are also proud of the human-in-the-loop design. 

 The agent can handle order lookup, policy retrieval, eligibility checks, resolution comparison, and preparation work, while important actions still remain reviewable by a human. 

 Another thing we are proud of is keeping the demo safe and repeatable. 

 The project uses isolated demo data, so no real payments, refunds, emails, shipments, or customer accounts are affected. 

 

 What we learned 

 The biggest thing we learned is that making a website “AI-ready” is not the same as adding a chatbot. 

 The more interesting question is: 

 What capabilities should the website expose so an agent can understand and use it reliably? 

 WebMCP made us think much more carefully about tool design, schemas, responsibilities, and safety boundaries. 

 We also learned that a good agent workflow depends heavily on the tools underneath it. 

 Clear tools make the workflow easier to understand, test, and trust. 

 This project also helped us connect a lot of engineering pieces together: frontend, backend logic, APIs, structured tools, deployment, and agent interaction. 

 

 What's next for Returns Desk 

 The current version is built around a deterministic demo returns workflow. 

 The next step would be connecting it to real commerce infrastructure. 

 Possible future integrations include: 

 
 Shopify orders and inventory 
 real return and refund systems 
 shipping and return-label providers 
 merchant-configurable return policies 
 customer support platforms 
 richer approval and audit workflows 
 

 We would also like to explore more advanced agent workflows where an agent can handle most of the repetitive returns process while keeping merchants informed and in control. 

 The long-term idea is to make Returns Desk an agent-ready operations layer for e-commerce returns, not just another support dashboard.

WebMCP tools that expose Scrapi's scraping pipeline to any agent, plus an in-app agent that uses them and gets smarter per domain with usage

 Story

 landing page 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 landing page 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 landing page 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I already had Scrapi running as a real scraper before this challenge existed - fetch, detect whether a page needs JS rendering, extract, clean, done. When I saw WebMCP, my first instinct wasn't "let me bolt an AI chatbot onto this," it was "an agent trying to use my scraper right now would have to either click through my UI like a human or scrape my own HTML to figure out what's on the page - both of those are exactly the kind of brittle nonsense my scraper exists to avoid doing to other sites." That felt like the actual point of WebMCP: stop making agents reverse-engineer your app and just hand them a contract for the pipeline you already trust. 

 What it does 

 Scrapi exposes four tools on document.modelContext once you're signed in: 

 scrape_url - runs a URL through the real pipeline (with a Selenium fallback for JS-heavy sites) and hands back structured results.
get_scrape_history - your past jobs.
get_scrape_export - export a finished scrape as CSV or JSON.
check_domain_history - looks at everything Scrapi has ever scraped from a given domain and tells you whether it usually needs JS rendering and which detection method actually worked. 

 Any WebMCP-aware agent can find and call these on its own. I also built a small "Tools" panel inside the app itself that calls the exact same tools through the real document.modelContext.executeTool() API, with a little badge that honestly tells you whether the call went through WebMCP or fell back to a direct call - so Scrapi isn't just publishing tools for someone else's agent, it's using its own. 

 check_domain_history is the part I'm most proud of. It's a live aggregation over real scrape history, not a guess. Scrape a domain once, and the next check of that domain comes back with an actual answer instead of "unknown." 

 How we built it 

 Python and FastAPI on the backend, MongoDB for storage, React and Vite on the frontend, JWT for auth. The scraping side leans on requests + BeautifulSoup/lxml for normal pages and Selenium when a site needs JS rendering. On top of that, frontend/src/webmcp/tools.js defines the four tools with JSON Schema inputs, and a small hook registers them on document.modelContext for any signed-in session and cleans them up on logout. A thin GET /scrape/domain-stats endpoint on the backend is all check_domain_history actually needs - it's just a Mongo aggregation, nothing fancier. Frontend on Vercel, backend on Render, both live. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Honestly, the biggest decision wasn't technical. I originally built this with an in-app agent backed by my own Anthropic API key, so it could actually hold a conversation and decide which tools to call. Then I thought about it properly: I was about to hand out a public demo login sitting in front of my personal API key, for as long as judging lasts, with no idea how many people would hammer it. That's not a risk worth taking for a hackathon. So I pulled the LLM out entirely - deleted the agent backend, the API key, all of it - and kept check_domain_history as a plain WebMCP tool instead of something an LLM had to be prompted into using. It actually made the project more honest: the "gets smarter with usage" claim now rests on a database query I can point to, not a model I'm asking you to trust. 

 On the technical side, the annoying one was document.modelContext.executeTool() in real Chrome throwing UnknownError: Failed to parse input arguments no matter what I sent it. Turned out Chrome's actual shipped implementation wants the arguments pre-stringified with JSON.stringify(), which isn't what the spec explainer describes. Fixed it by trying the stringified form first and falling back to a plain object if that fails. That fix then surfaced a second bug - the string-vs-object mismatch meant tool results were rendering as one giant escaped line of text - so I normalized every result to the same shape at one central point instead of patching the display separately. There was also a completely unrelated pre-existing bug I only found because I insisted on testing everything manually before pushing: my scraper was advertising Brotli support in its request headers without the Brotli package actually installed, which was silently corrupting results from any site that compressed with it. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting a real WebMCP host and client working against the actual browser API, not a mock - and catching real divergences from the spec along the way. And walking away from the LLM agent instead of shipping it anyway just because it was already built. The version that exists now needs no API key from anyone and costs nothing to run per request, which honestly feels like a better demonstration of what WebMCP is for than the flashier version would have been. 

 What we learned 

 That Chrome's actual WebMCP implementation has real, undocumented quirks you won't catch from reading the spec - you have to test against the live API early. And that "smarter with usage" doesn't require a model at all if you're willing to let real data do the talking instead. 

 What's next for Scrapi 

 Tracking more signals per domain in check_domain_history - rate-limit behavior, typical page size, common failure patterns - and seeing how it holds up once more WebMCP-capable agents exist to actually call it.

Human-visible, agent-ready defensive cyber triage that lets people and browser agents safely analyze suspicious messages, organize incidents, and build response plans with WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Security incidents are a bad place for an AI browser agent to guess. Suspicious messages can contain unsafe links, urgent language, credential requests, and untrusted instructions, while many schools, nonprofits, and public-service teams may not have a dedicated security operations center. 

 ThreatTriage explores a safer agent-native pattern: the website explicitly exposes defensive capabilities through WebMCP while keeping every result visible to the human operator. 

 What it does 

 ThreatTriage is a privacy-first defensive cybersecurity workflow where a person and a browser agent can collaborate on suspicious-message triage. 

 It can: 

 
 analyze suspicious SMS, email, or chat messages; 
 create a local incident case; 
 build a defensive response plan; 
 draft an unsent cybersecurity awareness notice; 
 list local incident cases; and 
 mark a case as reviewed. 
 

 Instead of forcing an agent to inspect the page and guess which controls to click, ThreatTriage exposes six bounded WebMCP tools with structured JSON schemas. 

 Every agent action is also reflected in the same visible interface used by the human and recorded in the Agent Activity panel. 

 How we built it 

 ThreatTriage is a dependency-free static web application built with HTML5, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, browser localStorage, and GitHub Pages. 

 The WebMCP implementation uses the imperative API on document.modelContext . 

 Six tools are registered through await document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 analyze_suspicious_message 
 create_incident_case 
 build_response_plan 
 draft_awareness_notice 
 list_incident_cases 
 mark_case_reviewed 
 

 Each tool has a clear description, constrained input schema, execution handler, and relevant safety annotations such as readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . 

 The WebMCP handlers reuse the same application functions as the manual interface. This means agent actions do not happen in a hidden automation layer—the user immediately sees the resulting analysis, incident case, response plan, notice, or status change. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was designing tools that were useful without becoming overly broad. 

 Cybersecurity workflows involve untrusted content, so ThreatTriage needed strong boundaries. It never opens suspicious links, sends messages, changes external accounts, or produces offensive cybersecurity functionality. 

 Another challenge was keeping agent activity understandable to the human. We solved this by updating the normal page UI after each WebMCP action and adding a visible Agent Activity log. 

 We also deliberately avoided backend dependencies and external APIs so the challenge demo would remain reproducible and privacy-conscious. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a complete end-to-end WebMCP workflow with six structured tools. 

 Agent actions update the same human-visible workspace instead of operating through a separate hidden automation path. 

 The MVP requires no backend or API key, stores demo data locally in the browser, and maintains defensive-only safety boundaries. 

 The application is publicly deployed, open source, and successfully tested with Chrome's WebMCP tooling. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP works best when websites expose domain-level intentions instead of low-level UI operations. 

 A tool such as build_response_plan is more reliable and understandable than asking an agent to locate several controls and simulate a sequence of clicks. 

 We also learned that agent-native UX should remain human-native UX. Structured tools become easier to trust when their effects are immediately visible to the person using the application. 

 What's next 

 Future versions could add optional encrypted persistence, organization-specific incident playbooks, role-based workflows, exportable incident summaries, stronger defensive scoring, and integrations with authorized IT or security channels. 

 Consequential external actions would still require explicit human approval. 

 Privacy and safety 

 ThreatTriage is defensive-only. 

 The current MVP has no backend and no API key. Demo message and incident data remain in browser localStorage. The app never opens URLs found in suspicious messages and does not provide malware, exploitation, credential-harvesting, persistence, or unauthorized-access functionality. 

 Risk scoring is an educational heuristic and is not intended to replace a professional security investigation.

 What inspired me. Cooking apps are single-player: they talk at you with recipes you'll never use. Chat agents fixed the conversation but not the problem — an agent that only answers can't do anything. The WebMCP moment is that the page itself becomes the tool surface, so I built the app I wanted: a teammate that cooks with you on one live board. You type what's in your fridge — "tomatoes, soy sauce, basil" — and the agent doesn't reply in a bubble, it acts: recomposes the board, drops in a card it invented, re-sorts, re-themes. Every action mutates the real DOM in front of both of you. That shared, visible state is the whole idea — visible execution is what keeps trust and control with the human. 

 How I built it. One zero-dependency index.html + a node serve.mjs dev server, deployed on GitHub Pages. On load the page registers 7 tools through the native WebMCP API (document.modelContext.registerTool) with JSON-schema inputSchema, readOnlyHint annotations and async execute callbacks that return clean JSON. Ingredient input normalises through an alias map and Unicode NFD stripping, so "poivron", "œufs", "sauce soja" and "baguette" all land on canonical ids. A stdio MCP server (mcp-server.mjs) re-exposes the same 7-tool surface, so any MCP host can drive the live UI too. I verified with a headless visual check and a full MCP JSON-RPC end-to-end test before pushing.

I rewrote it to feature-detect, register natively, and degrade honestly into a labelled demo mode. title: Split WebMCP
pitch: Turn browsing into collaboration: Split combines dual-browser workspaces with WebMCP, letting humans and AI agents understand and act on the same shared context.
about_excerpt:
Turn browsing into collaboration: Split combines dual-browser workspaces with WebMCP, letting humans and AI agents understand and act on the same shared context.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 I originally built Split because I didn't like constantly switching between apps or browser pages when I wanted to do two things at once. The Android version of Split lets me keep two browser panes open together and organize them into different workspaces. 

 When I saw the WebMCP Challenge, I started thinking about Split differently. Instead of only asking how a person could use two browsers together, I wanted to know what would happen if an AI agent could work with that same workspace too. 

 The important part for me was that I didn't want to put a chatbot inside Split and call that AI integration. I wanted the AI to stay external and use WebMCP to understand and interact with Split through tools that the application intentionally exposes. 

 That became Split WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 Split WebMCP gives you two browser panes at the same time and four workspaces: T1, T2, T3, and T4 . 

 You can use Split normally as a human but when it is opened in a WebMCP-capable environment, an external AI agent can discover 11 WebMCP tools . 

 Those tools allow the agent to: 

 
 check the current workspace and panes 
 inspect the T1–T4 workspaces 
 switch between workspaces 
 open a resource in a selected pane 
 configure pane preferences 
 read and add notes 
 read and save bookmarks 
 create comparisons 
 

 The part I find most interesting is that the human and the agent are not working in two separate versions of Split. They work with the same application state. 

 For example, if the agent switches the workspace or adds a note through WebMCP, that change appears in Split for the human too. Agent actions are also marked with Agent provenance so it is clear where the action came from. 

 The AI itself is not built into Split. It stays external. WebMCP is what connects the agent to the application. 

 How we built it 

 The original Split Android app existed before this challenge. For the WebMCP Challenge, I built Split WebMCP as a separate web implementation . The original Android source was not copied into this project and is not included in the public repository. 

 I built the web version around shared state for the browser panes, T1–T4 workspaces, navigation, notes, bookmarks, comparisons, preferences, and activity. 

 Both normal human controls and WebMCP actions use that same state. This was important because I wanted an action performed by an agent to become a real part of the workspace instead of something happening in a separate AI demo. 

 The WebMCP tools are registered using: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 There are currently 11 registered tools . They have structured inputs and runtime validation, and the actions they perform are connected to the same state as the normal Split interface. 

 I also added URL validation, restricted URL schemes, local persistence, WebMCP feature detection, security headers, and same-origin demo pages that make the WebMCP behavior easier to test reliably. 

 I tested the finished public deployment with an external Codex browser agent. It discovered all 11 WebMCP tools and successfully called get_workspace . During integration testing I also verified actions such as switching workspaces and adding notes through WebMCP. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One challenge was understanding what WebMCP should actually do for Split. 

 At first, it is easy to think that adding AI means putting an assistant or chatbot inside the application. But that isn't what I wanted to demonstrate. I wanted an external agent to be able to use specific parts of Split through WebMCP while I could still use the same interface normally. 

 Browser security was another challenge. Some third-party websites do not allow themselves to be embedded because of things like CSP and framing restrictions. I didn't want to bypass those protections or pretend every website could be embedded, so I added same-origin demo resources for reliable testing and kept a fallback for resources that cannot be displayed inside a pane. 

 I also had to think carefully about what an agent should be allowed to do. The WebMCP tools use defined schemas, validation, bounded inputs, and restricted URL schemes instead of giving the agent unrestricted access. 

 Another important challenge was separating my previous work from my hackathon work. Split already existed as an Android app, but Split WebMCP is the new web implementation I created for this challenge. The Android source remains separate. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm especially proud that the WebMCP integration actually works with an external agent . 

 On the public deployment, an external Codex browser agent was able to discover all 11 tools and call Split through WebMCP. 

 I'm also proud that I didn't have to turn Split into an AI chatbot to make that happen. Split still works as a normal human-controlled dual-browser workspace. WebMCP adds another way of interacting with it when a compatible agent is available. 

 The human can do something, the agent can continue from that workspace and the human can continue again from the agent's changes. 

 That is the part of Split WebMCP that I wanted to prove with this project. 

 What we learned 

 Before working on this project, I mostly thought about AI interacting with software through chat interfaces or by trying to operate the interface like a person. 

 Working with WebMCP showed me another approach. A website can expose specific tools that tell an agent what it is actually allowed to do and what inputs those actions require. 

 I also learned why shared state matters. If the AI has its own separate state, it doesn't really feel like the human and agent are working together. Connecting WebMCP actions to the same state as the human interface made the collaboration much more real. 

 I learned a lot about WebMCP tool design, browser security, validation, shared application state, and the limitations that come with embedding external web content. 

 What's next for Split WebMCP 

 I want to keep exploring what happens when the agent can understand more useful workspace context while still having clearly limited permissions. 

 I would like to improve research and comparison workflows and give agents more useful ways to help organize a browsing session without taking control away from the person using Split. 

 For me, the interesting direction is not simply putting AI inside a browser. It is finding better ways for a person and an external agent to work with the same browsing workspace together.

AI-powered job application agent that uses WebMCP to find matching jobs, prepare applications, and automate form filling while keeping humans in control of final submission.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Applying for jobs is repetitive and time-consuming. Finding a relevant position is only the first step — candidates still have to open different job portals, fill out the same information repeatedly, answer application questions, and deal with different workflows. 

 We wanted to build an AI agent that could help with this process while keeping the candidate in control of the final decision. 

 That led us to ApplyFlow AI — a job application agent designed around WebMCP. 

 What It Does 

 ApplyFlow AI helps users go from job discovery to a prepared application: 

 
 Find Jobs — discovers real job listings from sources such as RemoteOK and Arbeitnow. 
 Smart Matching — compares jobs with the user's resume and preferences and explains why a job is a good match. 
 Prepare Application — creates an application using the user's profile and resume information. 
 WebMCP Automation — uses WebMCP tools to interact with supported application workflows in a real browser session. 
 Human Review — stops before final submission so the user can review the completed application. 
 Approve & Submit — the final submission requires an explicit human action. 
 

 The key design principle is simple: 

 
 The agent can prepare the application, but the human controls the final submission. 
 

 How We Built It 

 The application is built around an AI-agent workflow with WebMCP as the interface between the agent and browser-based tools. 

 The system includes: 

 
 Job discovery and normalization 
 Resume/profile-based job matching 
 Match explanations 
 Application preparation 
 WebMCP tool integration 
 Browser-based form automation 
 Application state and automation tracking 
 Human approval before submission 
 Safety handling for login, MFA, and CAPTCHA situations 
 

 The Agent page provides a natural-language interface where users can give commands such as: 

 
 "Find jobs matching my profile." 
 

 or 

 
 "Prepare an application for the best match." 
 

 These requests are translated into authorized WebMCP tool calls such as get_top_matches and prepare_application . 

 The same backend authorization and application state are used by both the normal user interface and the agent workflow. 

 Human-in-the-Loop by Design 

 We intentionally did not expose the final submission action as a WebMCP tool. 

 The agent can discover a job, prepare the application, open the application page, and fill the form. 

 But when the application is ready, the workflow stops and asks the user to review it. 

 Only the user can click Approve & Submit . 

 This creates a clear boundary between AI automation and an irreversible external action. 

 Safety 

 Real job portals can require authentication, MFA, or CAPTCHA challenges. 

 ApplyFlow AI does not attempt to bypass these protections. 

 When such a step is detected, the automation pauses and explains why it stopped. The user can then handle the step directly in the real browser session. 

 This keeps the automation useful without attempting to circumvent website security controls. 

 Challenges We Faced 

 One of the biggest challenges was designing an agent that could interact with real application workflows without turning the system into an uncontrolled automation tool. 

 We had to think carefully about: 

 
 Tool authorization 
 Application state 
 Human approval boundaries 
 Form validation 
 Handling different application workflows 
 Login and CAPTCHA interruptions 
 Keeping the agent's actions observable 
 

 Another challenge was making the agent's behavior understandable. Instead of hiding tool execution, we added a WebMCP Activity panel so users can see which tools are being called and what is happening during the workflow. 

 What We Learned 

 This project taught us that building an AI agent is not only about making the model capable of taking actions. 

 The more important question is: 

 Which actions should the agent be allowed to take? 

 WebMCP provides a powerful way for agents to interact with web-based tools, but that power needs clear authorization boundaries. 

 For ApplyFlow AI, we chose to automate the repetitive work while keeping the final consequential action under human control. 

 What's Next 

 Future versions could support more job sources, richer resume customization, better application-question handling, additional WebMCP-enabled sites, and stronger application tracking. 

 Our goal is to make job applications dramatically less repetitive while keeping the candidate — not the agent — in control.

about_excerpt:
A shared persistent thread where humans and AI agents can read, write, and continue the same project history through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents often keep their own compressed memory or work inside separate conversations. That is efficient, but it can make it difficult for humans and multiple agents to inspect the same original project history and continue from a shared source of truth. 

 CommonThread explores a simple alternative: a persistent thread that both humans and agents can read from and write to. 

 What it does 

 CommonThread is a shared human-agent workspace built around one persistent project thread. 

 A human can add an entry, an OpenAI-powered agent can respond inside the same thread, and a WebMCP-enabled agent can use exposed thread functions to read the existing history and post a new entry. 

 The key point is that the WebMCP agent is not working in a separate conversation. It participates in the same persistent history as the human and the other agents. 

 Agents can still use smaller internal memory for efficiency, but when necessary they can return to the original shared thread instead of relying only on compressed memory. 

 How WebMCP is used 

 CommonThread exposes its thread operations as WebMCP tools. 

 The demo shows a WebMCP agent discovering the registered tools, reading the existing thread, and posting a new entry back into that same thread. 

 This turns the website from something an agent merely observes into a workspace whose application-level functions can be used directly by the agent. 

 How I built it 

 The prototype uses a lightweight Node.js server with a persistent thread store and a browser-based interface. 

 The UI is designed as a readable shared workspace for both human and agent activity. OpenAI API integration allows an OpenAI agent to participate directly in the thread, while WebMCP exposes the thread functions to compatible agents. 

 The application is deployed as a live web demo. 

 Challenges and what I learned 

 The main challenge was deciding what should actually be exposed through WebMCP. 

 Rather than exposing arbitrary page interaction, I focused on small semantic operations that correspond to the application's real capabilities: reading the shared thread and writing a new entry. 

 This prototype suggests that WebMCP can be useful not only for completing isolated web tasks, but also for letting agents participate in persistent human-agent workspaces. 

 What's next 

 CommonThread can expand to multiple projects and threads, retrieval across longer histories, richer multimodal entries, and trusted agent identity. 

 The longer-term goal is to give humans and agents a common place to remember, inspect, and continue shared work.

 Like

 We wanted to explore a different experience: a real-estate website where people and AI agents can work together. 

 What we built

 Users can simply describe what they are looking for, such as a home's location, budget, bedrooms, and lifestyle preferences. The AI agent can then use structured WebMCP tools to search and analyze properties. 

 The agent can: 

 
 Search homes based on location, budget, bedrooms, property type, and features 
 Get detailed property information

 Request property viewings

 Why WebMCP? 

 WebMCP allows DreamHome Agent to expose real application capabilities as structured tools that an AI agent can discover and use. 

 Instead of an agent guessing how to navigate the website, it can directly use tools such as search_homes , compare_properties , search_neighborhood , and calculate_affordability . 

 This creates a better experience where the user gives the goal and preferences, the agent performs structured discovery and analysis, and the user remains in control of important decisions. 

 How we built it 

 DreamHome Agent was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Node.js, Express, Google Gemini, WebMCP, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, Leaflet, OpenStreetMap, and Zod. 

 We implemented a WebMCP tool layer using document.modelContext.registerTool() and connected the tools to the application's real property search, comparison, affordability, saved-property, viewing, and seller-contact functionality.

 One of the biggest challenges was going beyond a simple AI chatbot and making the agent capable of performing meaningful actions inside a real web application. 

 We learned how structured WebMCP tools can make websites easier for AI agents to interact with, while human approval can provide an important safety layer for actions that have real-world consequences.

 Kuwait residents often know what they need to do, but not the exact government service or required documents. 

 For example, someone may simply say: 

 
 "I need to renew my driving license." 
 

 or: 

 
 "My residency was renewed and I need my Civil ID." 
 

 I built Kuwait Life to make all users to use normal language to find the services they need.

 Why WebMCP 

 The main feature of Kuwait Life is its WebMCP integration. 

 Instead of an AI browser agent having to inspect the page visually, find controls, and simulate clicks, Kuwait Life exposes structured capabilities directly to WebMCP-compatible agents. 

 The application currently exposes two WebMCP tools: 

 find-kuwait-government-service 

 This tool accepts a natural-language request such as: 

 
 "I need to renew my driving license." 
 

 It searches and ranks the available government services and returns structured service information. 

 The same human-facing webpage also updates automatically, highlights the best matching service, and displays an AI selected state. 

 create-kuwait-service-checklist 

 After a service has been selected, an agent can call this tool to create a practical checklist containing the documents and requirements for that service. 

 The checklist appears directly inside the webpage, where the human can continue interacting with it and mark items as completed. 

 This creates a shared workflow between the AI agent and the person instead of replacing the website with a chatbot. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration

 Human describes a situation
 ↓
AI agent discovers WebMCP tools
 ↓
Agent finds the relevant service

Kuwait Life highlights the result

 Challenges

 Instead of forcing AI agents to infer how a website works from its visual interface, websites can expose reliable structured actions directly to agents. 

 Privacy and Safety

 It does not submit government applications, process government payments, or access private government databases.

An agent co-pilot for your store's back office — orders, inventory, messages, and discounts — built for the merchant every WebMCP shopping demo forgot.

 MerchantHQ 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 MerchantHQ 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every WebMCP demo I looked at was built for the shopper: search a catalog,
add to cart, check out. Even Shopify's own storefronts ship this out of the
box now. But nobody's building for the person actually running the store.
Most small merchants are one person juggling orders, stock, customer
messages, and everything else on their own. That felt like the real gap. 

 What it does 

 Merchant HQ is a back-office dashboard for a small store. You can click
around it normally, or hand it to a WebMCP agent and ask it to check what
orders need fulfilling, restock something low, draft a reply to a customer,
or set up a discount code. Whatever the agent does shows up live on your
screen, the same page you're looking at, no refresh needed. Each change gets
a quick colored flash so you can tell at a glance whether you did it or the
agent did, and everything gets logged in an activity panel with the full
details of what happened. 

 Eight tools cover four areas: orders, inventory, messages, and discounts.
Creating a discount code is the one action that actually costs the merchant
money, so that specific tool won't run without the human approving it first,
using WebMCP's requestUserInteraction API. 

 How I built it 

 Next.js on Vercel, with the data (orders, inventory, messages, discounts)
stored in Vercel KV so it actually persists. Each visitor gets their own
sandboxed demo store. The tools are registered with
document.modelContext.registerTool, and every one of them calls the same
functions the regular UI buttons call, so there's never two different
versions of what "true" looks like. 

 Challenges 

 The trickiest bug: WebMCP tool calls were updating the server correctly, but
the dashboard just sat there until you refreshed. Turned out the UI panels
were holding their own local copy of the data instead of reading from
something shared. Had to rebuild that part so every panel reacts live to any
change, no matter which path it came from. 

 The other one: requestUserInteraction is real, spec-defined, and I built it
correctly, but I couldn't get either Chrome's tool inspector or ChatGPT's
browser to actually trigger it end to end. Rather than silently skip the
confirmation when that happens, the tool just refuses and says so clearly. 

 What I learned 

 The interesting part of WebMCP isn't "an agent can click things for me," it's
that a page can hand an agent something completely different from a UI:
structured, chainable, inspectable actions instead of a screen to guess at.
Building the activity log also made it obvious that trust is the real
problem in agentic commerce right now, not capability. Knowing an agent
technically can do something isn't the same as knowing what it actually
did to your store.

 Inspiration 

 I wanted to solve a real problem that affect small online shops. I researched the issues they face and built an app that solves those. From 25 minutes of manual copy/pasting per batch of orders to under 3 minutes. 

 What it does 

 OpsFlow is a 3-screen console — Batch → Shipping → Holds — It is webMCP native, then the full functionality can be controlled by external AIs. OpsFlow also has a built-in fully functional AI chat box that allows to use natural language to control the application. 

 How we built it 

 Vite + React SPA on Vercel, origin-isolated with Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self). Five imperative tools registered once in src/webmcp/register.ts with hand-written JSON Schema, readOnlyHint/openWorldHint annotations, validation, input limits, and signal abort handling, plus a declarative shipping form. 
Built-in agent is built using Gemini 3.6 Flash. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP only exists in origin-isolated documents behind a flag/ChatGPT browser, with an Aug 2026 draft spec — so we had to probe capability, ban cross-origin iframes, keep GEMINI_API_KEY server-side, and still run fully in a plain browser. Making abort-safe tools that never throw (typed TOOL_ABORTED/DEGRADED errors) and replay golden cache instead of blanking, while gating holds/fulfillments on human confirmation, was the hardest correctness work. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 This is my first webMCP application. The built-in AI chat window also works as well as I had planned, I didn't need to reduce the scope or functionality. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP does provide a lot of functionality. It looks like the future of the web will be AI agents interacting with pages. Functionality is a league ahead of DOM scrapping 

 What's next for OpsFlow — WebMCP Fulfillment Console for Solo Operators 

 Stronger Built-in chat capabilities. Using external WebMCP agents is still no widespread. However allowing a builtin chatbot overcomes that limitation. WebMCP run inside the same webpage the users get the full functionality without even knowing it.

 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for PA in Your Pocket: Household Actions 

 Inspiration 

 Parents regularly need to turn school notices, calendar commitments and household loose ends into clear next steps. The hard part is not one form; it is finding what matters across people and messages while retaining confidence about what an assistant did. As a mom, I know exactly how difficult this can be! 

 What it does 

 The prototype starts with five deterministic fictional actions across school, calendar and home administration. A parent can also turn an unmatched local capture into a distinct action in a chosen area; Notes can be saved without a deadline. A WebMCP-capable agent can: 

 
 filter a unified action queue by area, owner, status and deadline; 
 open an action and explain its source, confidence, requirements and next step; 
 prepare the visible school response, calendar proposal or household follow-up for review. 
 

 The agent cannot perform the final approval, submission or removal. The parent can edit the draft and must press the visible final button. For Home items, the parent can choose to keep the item or remove it from the active list. A simple audit history separates “prepared by agent” from “approved/submitted/removed by parent.” 

 How we built it 

 The app is a static React, Vite and TypeScript site. Six tools use the WebMCP imperative API through document.modelContext. React reducer state is persisted locally in the browser. Firebase Hosting serves the production build with origin-isolation and tools permissions headers. 

 Challenges 

 The main design challenge was creating useful agent action without disguising the moment of commitment. We deliberately made preparation reversible and local, kept submission out of the tool surface, marked school notice content as untrusted and tested the normal portal independently of WebMCP support. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most convincing when the agent changes the same visible interface a person uses. Structured tools reduce ambiguity, but clear state transitions and human confirmation remain product-design decisions rather than API decorations. 

 What's next 

 This competition build remains a standalone experiment. Any production exploration would need consent design, identity and access controls, real integration agreements, data minimisation, retention rules and independent privacy/security review. 

 Disclosure 

 All names, school notices, contact details and submissions shown in the project are simulated. The app has no school, calendar, payment or PA in Your Pocket production integration.
