 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Flat hunting is a messy human workflow: filters, maps, shortlists, viewing slots, and offer letters all fight for attention. Agents already talk about housing well, but they usually fail when they have to click through a UI built for a mouse. WebMCP flips that: the site can expose the real actions (search, pin, compare, hold a viewing, draft and submit an offer) as structured tools on the same live page the person is looking at. 

 Nest is that idea made concrete — a London rental board where you and your agent share one session, one map, and one shortlist. 

 What it does 

 Nest is an agent-native flat hunt: 

 
 Browse seeded London listings on a live map 
 Pin and compare homes side by side 
 Propose and hold viewing slots (agent proposes; you confirm commits) 
 Draft and submit an offer letter from the shortlist 
 Inspect board state and registered WebMCP tools on an in-app Agent tools panel 
 

 You steer in plain English in ChatGPT; Nest’s site tools update the UI in real time. Anything consequential (holding a viewing, submitting an offer) is a non-read-only tool so the browser can require confirmation. 

 How we built it 

 
 Vite + React + TypeScript for a fast, deployable SPA 
 Zustand store shared by the human UI and every WebMCP execute handler (one source of truth) 
 Leaflet map with OSM tiles for the spatial board 
 WebMCP via document.modelContext.registerTool (with navigator.modelContext fallback), feature-detected, registered on the top-level page 
 Seeded demo listings (no paid APIs) so judges can try the full path offline-friendly 
 Built with Codex 
 

 Core tools include search_listings , get_listing , pin_listing / unpin_listing , compare_shortlist , propose_viewings , hold_viewing , cancel_viewing , draft_offer , submit_offer , get_board_state , and set_preferences . 

 Challenges 

 
 Same-state collaboration — agent tools and UI clicks must never drift. We solved this by routing both through one store. 
 Read vs commit — WebMCP’s value is trust. Marking search/compare read-only and viewings/offers as side-effecting was deliberate product design, not just annotations. 
 Demo realism without backends — landlords, holds, and offers are simulated with structured JSON so the agent can reason, while the product still feels complete. 
 Judges’ path — a clear happy path (search → pin → compare → hold viewings → draft → submit) plus a tools panel so WebMCP leverage is obvious in under three minutes. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP isn’t “MCP in the browser” as a slogan — it’s best when the agent and the human must see the same thing : a map marker lighting up, a shortlist changing, an offer panel filling. Housing is a perfect stress test because the workflow is multi-step, spatial, and full of confirm-worthy actions. 

 Try the demo path 

 
 Open Nest in ChatGPT’s in-app browser (or Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled) 
 Ask: “Find 2-beds under £2200 in Zone 2 that allow pets, pin the best three, compare them, hold two viewings, and draft an offer for my favorite.” 
 Watch the board update; confirm when the browser asks on commits

 Inspiration 

 Incident response is often stuck between two extremes: humans doing everything manually, or automation acting without enough context and control. We built NexusOps to explore a safer middle ground where agents investigate operational incidents, compare evidence, and recommend actions while humans remain responsible for approval. 

 What it does 

 WebMCP makes this possible directly inside the website. NexusOps exposes operational tools that compatible agents can discover and call, while the human operator sees the same evidence, reasoning, activity trace, and safety boundaries. 

 How we built it 

 NexusOps is an agent-native operations control plane for investigating production incidents. It exposes 20 WebMCP tools covering observation, investigation, recommendations, human approval, remediation, and verification. 

 For the simulated incident INC-1042, specialized SRE, NOC, Developer, and SOC perspectives inspect different evidence sources. They form independent hypotheses, identify supporting and conflicting evidence, and allow an Incident Commander to arbitrate the disagreement.
The environment is intentionally simulated. Metrics, logs, services, deployments, and remediation state are deterministic demo data. No real production system is monitored or changed. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 I ran into challenge when I was not familiar with WebMCP at all before starting working on project. Also was lacking of AI credits to actually develop the app in 3-4 days. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 NexusOps exposes 20 genuine WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(), allowing compatible agents to discover and call operational capabilities directly from the website.
I built a complete incident workflow covering observation, investigation, multi-agent analysis, disagreement, Incident Commander arbitration, human approval, controlled remediation, and verification.
The SRE, NOC, Developer, and SOC perspectives use different evidence sources and produce deterministic, explainable conclusions from the same operational data.
I also added a schema-driven Tool Inspector, evidence and causal-chain views, risk and approval metadata, shared execution tracing, and an audit activity feed. 

 What I learnedx 

 First of all, understood concepts of webmcp and its usage.
I learned that WebMCP is most valuable when agents can use the same tools and page state as the human operator instead of interacting through a separate hidden integration.
I learned that agent assistance must be paired with clear safety boundaries, especially when tools can change operational state.
I also learned that specialized agent perspectives are more useful than a single generic assistant because different roles can focus on different evidence and reach different conclusions. 

 What's next for NexusOps 

 The next step is to connect the same WebMCP control-plane pattern to real observability and incident-management systems while preserving human approval for high-risk actions.
Future versions could support additional incident types, organization-specific tools, richer agent arbitration, and persistent audit history.
The current priority is validating the live WebMCP experience in Chrome and compatible agent environments, then using that feedback to improve reliability and real-world integrations.

 Project Story 

 AI systems can fail in ways that are difficult to investigate and even harder to remediate safely. When an incident occurs, security teams need to understand the evidence, replay the risky behavior, evaluate a possible fix, and preserve a clear audit trail. We wanted to explore how agents could help with this workflow without giving them unrestricted authority to change runtime policies. 

 That idea became Sentinel Desk : an open-source, standalone AI incident response desk powered by WebMCP. 

 Sentinel Desk lets an agent search incidents, inspect model traces, identify policy violations, simulate a proposed runtime guard, and request human approval. The final policy-changing action remains explicitly gated by the human operator. After approval, the guard is activated and the action appears in the provenance timeline. 

 The WebMCP layer exposes six tools: 

 
 search_incidents 
 inspect_trace 
 simulate_guard 
 request_guard_approval 
 apply_guard 
 get_audit_report 
 

 These tools are registered through the WebMCP Imperative API using document.modelContext.registerTool . The application also works as a normal web interface, so people can manually explore the workflow even when WebMCP is not available. 

 The most important thing we learned is that WebMCP is not simply a replacement for clicking buttons. A well-designed tool gives an agent a precise capability, a clear input schema, and an explicit trust boundary. This is especially important for security workflows: reading evidence and proposing a remediation are different actions from activating a policy change. 

 One of our main challenges was working with an emerging browser API while preserving a reliable human experience. We had to handle WebMCP availability, tool registration, cancellation and permission boundaries, while keeping the application usable in a regular browser. We also needed to make a synthetic runtime feel realistic without implying that it was connected to production data. 

 Sentinel Desk demonstrates a possible future for AI governance: agents can help investigate complex incidents and prepare remediation, while people retain authority over consequential runtime changes.

title: ShieldOn
pitch: WebMCP gives AI agents access to investigate evidence, while ShieldOn keeps the final decision under human control.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP gives AI agents access to investigate evidence, while ShieldOn keeps the final decision under human control.

 Inspiration 

 I learned that AI agents are getting really good at reading information, connecting evidence and proposing conclusions. There's one question that pushed me to build shieldOn WebMCP prototype: "Should it also have the authority to make the final decision because it can access the evidence?"
ShieldOn is a revenue engineering system built around evidence, verification, contradictions, missing information and governed findings. For this challenge, I wanted to test one simple principle:
"WebMCP can give an AI agent access to investigate, without giving it authority to govern the conclusion." 

 What it does 

 The demo uses a synthetic revenue investigation for a dental business. Through WebMCP, the agent gets six read-only ShieldOn tools. It can inspect the investigation, evidence, missing evidence, contradictions, candidate findings and governed findings. The agent can analyze the case and explain what may be going wrong. But it cannot approve or reject the finding. There are 6 read-only tools, 0 approval tools and 1 protected human decision. 

 The workflow is: 

 AI investigates → human reviews → human decides → AI rereads the governed result 

 Before human review, the finding remains a candidate. If the agent is directly asked to approve it, it cannot. No approval tool is exposed through WebMCP. The human reviewer must make that decision inside ShieldOn. Once approved, the finding becomes governed, the human reviewer is recorded and the agent can then reread the result. Importantly, unresolved evidence gaps and contradictions remain visible. 

 How we built it 

 I made a conscious decision not to build too much for this challenge. Rather than trying to build the entire ShieldOn product, I built one complete human-governance loop. The investigation contains directly verified evidence, operator-confirmed information, unverified claims, missing evidence, contradictions and a candidate finding. One part of the case shows qualified leads increasing while consultation conversion declines. The evidence also shows slower response times, incomplete follow-up and CRM records that don't always match the communication history. This gives the agent something meaningful to investigate rather than a perfectly clean dataset. The most important design decision was separating analysis authority from decision authority. Approval and rejection exist only inside the human review interface. They aren't exposed as WebMCP tools. The agent can read the governed result afterward and it can't create that governed state itself. 

 ShieldOn existed before this challenge as a governed revenue investigation system. What I built during the WebMCP Challenge is the agent-facing WebMCP layer: six read-only browser tools, the synthetic investigation demo, the protected human-review loop, and the ability for the agent to reread a governed finding after human approval. The underlying ShieldOn product predates the challenge. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One thing I had to keep reminding myself was not to make the agent autonomous just because technically I could. It would have been easy to expose an approval tool and let the agent complete the entire workflow. For me, that would have missed the whole point of what I wanted to prove. So I tested the opposite. I intentionally asked the agent to approve the candidate and mark it as ShieldOn's official conclusion. And it couldn't. That became one of the strongest parts of the demo because the governance boundary is demonstrated. Another challenge was keeping uncertainty after approval. A human decision shouldn't magically erase missing evidence or contradictions, so those stay visible even after the finding becomes governed. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am proud that the demo proves a complete collaboration loop rather than only showing an AI calling tools. The agent can investigate real structured evidence, identify missing information and contradictions and prepare a candidate conclusion. A human then makes the protected decision. After that decision, the agent can see and understand the newly governed result without gaining the authority to create it. The negative test is especially important to me: 

 
 the system successfully demonstrates what the AI can't do. 
 that boundary is a core part of the product and not a limitation. 
 

 What we learned 

 What became very clear to me while building this is that giving an AI more capability shouldn't by default mean giving it more authority. WebMCP can give an AI agent powerful access to application context while the application still decides which actions remain protected. I also learned that good human-agent systems shouldn't only expose useful capabilities. They should make boundaries explicit. In this case, one of the most important decisions was actually the tool I chose not to expose. 

 What's next for ShieldOn 

 This challenge prototype focuses on one narrow governance loop. The larger ShieldOn direction is to apply the same model to deeper revenue investigations with more evidence sources, more complex contradictions, stronger traceability and eventually governed interventions. As ShieldOn grows, I want the agent to be able to investigate much more of the business but without silently gaining authority it was never supposed to have. 

 The principle will remain the same:
AI investigates. Humans govern the conclusion. WebMCP gives the agent access. ShieldOn keeps the decision governed.

pitch: A shared procurement decision workspace where buyers and AI agents operate on the same sourcing state through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A shared procurement decision workspace where buyers and AI agents operate on the same sourcing state through WebMCP.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 As a procurement director working with complex supplier decisions, I regularly see how difficult it is to combine structured sourcing data, judgment, negotiation constraints, and human accountability in one workflow. 

 AI can already help buyers analyze supplier offers, but it usually sits outside the sourcing application. That creates friction: users copy data into chat, interpret the answer, and then manually reconcile it back into their working system. 

 Sourcing Scenario Room came from the idea that this interaction should be different: the buyer and the AI agent should operate on the same visible sourcing state through WebMCP, while the human keeps decision authority. 

 What it does 

 The application starts from a fictional sourcing case with three supplier offers evaluated across five dimensions: price, delivery lead time, capacity, quality, and supply risk. 

 The buyer can express sourcing intent in natural language. Through WebMCP, the agent reads the current application state and updates the shared workspace directly. 

 A typical flow is: 

 
 The agent reads the current sourcing case. 
 The buyer makes delivery within 12 weeks mandatory, prioritizes supply continuity, and asks to keep two suppliers alive. 
 The agent updates the workspace and creates an AGENT PROPOSAL. 
 The agent generates a negotiation plan for the live shortlist. 
 The buyer revises the proposal directly in the application, for example by keeping Boreal in the shortlist while limiting the acceptable price premium to 3%. 
 The workspace becomes HUMAN-REVISED. 
 The agent reads that revision and adapts the negotiation plan accordingly. 
 

 The agent can propose and adapt, but it cannot award a supplier. Decision authority remains with the human buyer. 

 How we built it 

 Sourcing Scenario Room is a client-side React/Vite application using native WebMCP through document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 It exposes three WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_sourcing_case 
 update_sourcing_scenario 
 draft_negotiation_plan 
 

 The human interface and the WebMCP tools operate on the same canonical React sourcing state through shared application actions. 

 There is no backend, database, authentication layer, OpenAI API integration, or external API dependency. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was designing a demo that made the human-agent interaction clear without hiding it behind unnecessary complexity. 

 I deliberately limited the case to five sourcing dimensions, three suppliers, and three WebMCP tools. 

 Another challenge was preserving human decision authority. The application therefore makes the state transitions explicit: 

 BASE CASE → AGENT PROPOSAL → HUMAN-REVISED 

 This makes it visible when the agent has proposed something, when the human has changed it, and when the agent is responding to the latest human decision. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The most important result is that the agent is not simply generating advice beside the application. 

 The buyer and agent work through the same sourcing workspace. The agent can read the current state, modify the scenario, generate a negotiation artifact, observe a later human revision, and adapt to it. 

 That creates a genuine human-agent loop while keeping supplier selection authority with the buyer. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest insight was that WebMCP changes the interaction model. 

 The valuable part is not simply allowing an AI to call functions. It is enabling the human and the agent to collaborate through the same visible application state. 

 Human revisions become first-class inputs to the next agent action instead of context that must be manually reconstructed in chat. 

 What's next for Sourcing Scenario Room 

 The same pattern could extend to richer procurement workflows such as tender preparation, supplier risk, negotiation tracking, sourcing approvals, and contract review. 

 More broadly, the approach could apply to enterprise workflows where humans and agents need to collaborate on structured decisions while preserving explicit human authority.

 Project Story 

 About the Project 

 StockPilot is an AI-powered trading research terminal that helps users explore markets, analyze stocks, review SEC filings, compare technical charts, and manage a virtual portfolio. 

 It combines real market data with WebMCP tools, allowing an AI agent to interact directly with the application. Users can ask the agent to research a ticker, open stock pages, analyze filings, draw chart patterns, screen stocks, and simulate trades. 

 Inspiration 

 We wanted to make financial research more interactive and accessible. Traditional market tools often require users to navigate through many separate screens, interpret complex charts, and manually connect information from news, filings, financial data, and portfolio performance. 

 StockPilot was inspired by the idea of an AI assistant that does more than answer questions. It should be able to take meaningful actions inside the trading terminal, such as opening an analysis page, highlighting important SEC passages, configuring a comparison chart, or creating a simulated position. 

 How We Built It 

 StockPilot was built with: 

 
 Next.js and React for the application interface 
 TypeScript for type-safe application logic 
 Finnhub for quotes, company profiles, news, recommendations, financials, earnings, and SEC filing metadata 
 Supabase for persisted market data and application storage 
 WebMCP for exposing StockPilot actions to compatible AI agents 
 Local OHLCV datasets for historical charting, indicators, pattern detection, and backtesting 
 Tailwind CSS and reusable UI components for the trading terminal interface 
 

 The application includes tools for: 

 
 Stock search and detailed quote lookup 
 Market news and sector performance 
 Stock screening and ranking 
 SEC filing review and risk analysis 
 Technical pattern detection 
 Support and resistance calculations 
 Portfolio analysis and risk scoring 
 Virtual buying and selling 
 Price alerts and watchlists 
 Strategy backtesting 
 Multi-stock chart comparison and technical drawings 
 

 Challenges We Ran Into 

 One major challenge was coordinating AI actions with a client-side application. Fetching data is straightforward, but actions such as navigation, chart updates, and filing highlights must be synchronized with the correct page and component state. 

 We also had to handle incomplete or unavailable provider data. SEC filings may not always include a readable report URL, and free-tier APIs can return limited results. To keep the experience reliable, StockPilot uses fallbacks, validation, normalized filing content, and best-effort analysis. 

 Another challenge was making technical chart interactions precise. Drawing points need to align with real trading dates and meaningful price ranges, so the application snaps dates to available candles and clamps prices to valid OHLCV boundaries. 

 Accomplishments We’re Proud Of 

 We are proud that StockPilot is more than a dashboard. It is an interactive environment where an AI agent can: 

 
 Navigate users to relevant pages 
 Retrieve and summarize real market data 
 Analyze SEC filings and calculate risk signals 
 Highlight important filing passages 
 Configure chart styles, indicators, and time ranges 
 Detect and draw technical patterns 
 Compare multiple companies 
 Simulate portfolio actions while enforcing authentication boundaries 
 

 The WebMCP integration gives the AI a practical interface to the product instead of limiting it to text-only responses. 

 What We Learned 

 We learned that building an AI-enabled application requires designing both the user interface and the action interface at the same time. Tool descriptions, input schemas, validation, navigation behavior, and error messages are all part of the user experience. 

 We also learned the importance of grounding financial analysis in concrete data. Historical prices, filing documents, recommendation trends, and portfolio state should be traceable to actual application data rather than invented assumptions. 

 Finally, we learned that asynchronous workflows need careful handling. Data fetching, page navigation, event dispatching, and component mounting must work together so that an AI-triggered action remains understandable and reliable to the user. 

 What’s Next for StockPilot 

 Next, we plan to improve StockPilot with: 

 
 More reliable cross-page AI action handoffs 
 Expanded market and sector coverage 
 More advanced portfolio analytics 
 Additional technical indicators and drawing tools 
 Richer SEC filing comparisons across reporting periods 
 Persistent user portfolios and watchlists through Supabase 
 More robust authentication and account management 
 Improved backtesting with transaction costs and risk controls 
 Broader WebMCP support for agent-driven financial workflows 
 

 Our long-term goal is to make StockPilot a trustworthy collaborative workspace where people and AI agents can research markets together while keeping decisions transparent, data-grounded, and user-controlled.

WebMCP-powered AI that coordinates group cinema seat booking. Friends vote on seat blocks, the AI handles the coordination, and you book together as a group that way no stranger sits between you.

 Story

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 You and your friends agree on a movie. Everyone opens the booking page at the same time, each trying to grab seats next to each other. But by the time everyone checks out, a stranger is sitting between you. Now you can't share snacks, whisper during the movie, or enjoy it together. 

 The system treats each person as an individual booking, not as a group. The "stranger in the middle" is the person who ends up in the seat that was supposed to be for your friend. 

 What it does 

 Stranger In The Middle is a WebMCP-powered AI that coordinates group cinema seat booking. The AI finds the best seat blocks for your group, lets everyone vote on their preferred option, and coordinates the booking as one purchase, not multiple individual bookings fighting for adjacent seats. 

 No strangers between you and your friends. Just the AI making sure you sit together and pay separately. 

 How we built it 

 We built Stranger In The Middle using Node.js and Express for the backend, with EJS templates for the frontend. The app uses WebMCP (Model Context Protocol) to expose AI tools that can be called directly from the browser or from ChatGPT's in-app browser. 

 The seat scoring algorithm evaluates contiguous seat blocks across horizontal and vertical dimensions, scoring each block based on viewing angle (distance from center screen) and legroom (row position). The top 3 options are presented to the group for voting.
 WebMCP Tools registered: 

 
 search_movies - List available movies 
 get_available_seats - Show free seats for a movie 
 stranger_vote - Coordinate group voting on seat blocks 
 book_tickets - Book specific seats 
 cancel_booking - Cancel a booking and release seats
## Challenges we ran into
The biggest challenge was making the group voting system work in real-time across multiple devices. We needed to ensure that when one person votes, everyone else sees the updated vote count immediately. We also had to handle the 2-minute timer and automatically end voting when all group members have voted. 
 

 Another challenge was the WebMCP implementation. Since WebMCP is an emerging open standard, we had to work with the polyfill and ensure our tools registered correctly in both the browser and ChatGPT's in-app browser. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Building a fully functional group voting system that works in real-time across multiple devices 
 Successfully implementing WebMCP tools that AI agents can call directly from the browser 
 Creating a seat scoring algorithm that evaluates view quality and legroom to find the best options for groups 
 Making the booking process collaborative so friends sit together, not as individuals fighting for seats 
 Shipping a working product that solves a real problem people face every time they book cinema tickets with friends
## What we learned
We learned how to build a WebMCP-enabled application that exposes structured tools for AI agents to use directly. Instead of agents guessing how to navigate a website, WebMCP lets the site define exactly what tools are available. This makes agent interactions faster, more reliable, and more predictable. 
 

 We also learned the importance of real-time coordination in group applications. The voting system needed to be responsive and clear, with each user understanding what's happening at every step. 

 What's Next for Stranger In The Middle 

 We plan to add support for more venues and integrate with real ticketing APIs. We also want to explore multi-agent coordination, where each person's AI agent communicates with others to find the best seats without human intervention.

title: Toolsmith
pitch: Paste a link, approve one plan, and receive a working WebMCP interface for your own site along with a receipt.
about_excerpt:
Paste a link, approve one plan, and receive a working WebMCP interface for your own site along with a receipt.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Make any site agent-ready with WebMCP. One human click. 

 Live: https://chudi.dev/tools/toolsmith 
Code: https://github.com/Citability/toolsmith-webmcp 

 Inspiration 

 Agents keep guessing at forms that were built for people. Every wrong guess costs somebody a failed checkout or a broken signup. Toolsmith closes that gap without asking the site owner to write code, and without ever letting an agent approve its own work. 

 What it does 

 Paste a URL. Toolsmith reads the page, proposes one WebMCP tool per form, drafts a webmcp.js file, and waits. Nothing activates until a person clicks Approve . A receipt comes back, and the file downloads. 

 There is no language model anywhere in the loop. Every generated line traces to a real field on a real page. 

 The five tools, registered on document.modelContext : 

 
 profile_site reads the public structure of one page: title, headings, forms and their fields, top-level navigation. 
 propose_tools turns the profile into candidate tools. GET forms become read-only tools. POST forms are marked consequential and get a confirm gate. 
 draft_manifest emits the webmcp.js source for the chosen candidates, plus the SHA-256 of that exact text. 
 activate_manifest shows the approval card and returns a pending request. This tool cannot approve anything on its own. 
 verify_manifest_activation reads back the receipt and checks its digest against the manifest stored in the browser. 
 

 How we built it 

 The drafting logic is a deterministic template over detected forms, not a model call. The five tools are registered natively on document.modelContext with AbortSignal cleanup. 

 The only thing that can activate a manifest is a click on the Approve card. The page checks two properties of that event before it writes a receipt: 

 
 event.isTrusted must be true, so a synthetic click from script does not count. 
 navigator.userActivation.isActive must be true, so the click happened inside a real user gesture. 
 

 The generated file carries the same discipline forward. Every consequential tool it registers wraps its submit in a browser confirm dialog, so an agent using the output still cannot post a form without a person in the loop. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hard part was proving the approval boundary still holds when the tool itself produces tools. It was not enough to gate Toolsmith's own Approve card. The output had to inherit the same rule, so every consequential tool in a generated file got its own confirm gate. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A site owner can read the template and trace every output line to a form on their page. The approval boundary generalized from gating one action on one page to gating every action a generated file can take. And the whole loop runs with zero metered calls. 

 What we learned 

 A readable template earns more trust than a model nobody can inspect. One human click is enough to gate an entire generated interface, as long as the gate checks the properties of the click and not just its presence. 

 What's next for Toolsmith 

 Point it at a whole site and get one manifest back. Detect authentication-gated forms so owners can cover their dashboards, not only their public pages. 

 Try it in 60 seconds 

 
 Open https://chudi.dev/tools/toolsmith in Chrome 152 for Testing with the WebMCP flag enabled. 
 Ask the agent: Make https://chudi.dev/toolsmith-fixtures/shop.html agent-ready. 
 Watch the activity strip fill with profile_site , propose_tools , and draft_manifest . 
 Click Approve . 
 Download the receipt-backed webmcp.js . 
 

 Three fixtures are available: 

 
 https://chudi.dev/toolsmith-fixtures/shop.html has a single POST add-to-cart form, so the tool gets a confirm gate. 
 https://chudi.dev/toolsmith-fixtures/newsletter.html has a GET search form beside a POST subscribe form, one read-only tool and one gated tool. 
 https://chudi.dev/toolsmith-fixtures/empty.html has no forms at all, so the proposal step returns nothing. 
 

 Why not just ask a chatbot 

 A chat window returns text. Toolsmith returns a file that runs on your own domain, and only you hold the click that activates it. Anyone can verify the result independently by calling verify_manifest_activation and reading the four fields of the receipt.

 Inspiration 

 We wanted chess to feel like a conversation. Wizard Chess combines the atmosphere of magical chess with an AI agent that can understand and control the board directly.
What it does 

 Wizard Chess is a 3D chess game controlled by voice, touch, mouse, or WebMCP. Players can learn through guided lessons, play with an AI mentor, or battle Stockfish at three difficulty levels. 

 How we built it 

 We used TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, chess.js, and Stockfish. The app exposes 29 WebMCP tools for moves, lessons, coaching, settings, saved games, and replays. Voice and WebMCP use the same game actions as the visible interface. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was keeping mouse, voice, and agent interactions synchronized with one game state. We also had to make the 3D board readable while handling voice timing, legal moves, lessons, matches, and replays. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a complete chess experience where a person and an AI agent share the same board. It includes voice control, coaching, six lessons, Stockfish opponents, ratings, trophies, saved games, and replays. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP works well for chess because the game has exact state and clear actions. Giving the agent structured board data is far more reliable than asking it to understand the position from pixels.

 We want to add adaptive lessons, deeper post-game analysis, a hosted leaderboard, richer piece models, and more cinematic effects. The mentor could then remember recurring mistakes and recommend what to practise next.

title: Hintel
pitch: Hintel gives an AI agent real WebMCP tools inside your CTF workspace, by routing you to the right technique and unlocks hints one tier at a time, per session without ever revealing the flag.
about_excerpt:
Hintel gives an AI agent real WebMCP tools inside your CTF workspace, by routing you to the right technique and unlocks hints one tier at a time, per session without ever revealing the flag.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I'm a cybersecurity diploma student, and CTFs are where a lot of that learning actually happens. The problem isn't knowledge but it's that under time pressure, in the middle of a competition, you blank on which tool solves the thing in front of you. You know base64 when you see it decoded, you just forget CyberChef exists when you're staring at a locker combination at 2am with a clock running. 

 Before writing any code, I actually read the judging panel for this challenge. I learnt that Alex Nahas built the WebMCP spec itself, Sarah Drasner's public focus at Chrome is security/trust boundaries in the AI-web ecosystem, Justin Rushing works on agent safety at OpenAI. That information made me realise that generic "AI shopping assistant" demos which is what most of the reference implementations from the sponsors already show, was going to read as homework and not show up as effort. The panel skews toward people who built the standard, not people who market on top of it. So the idea had to be something where the tool design itself was the interesting part, not just another UI with a registerTool() call bolted on. 

 What it does 

 Hintel is a workspace for CTF players, built around sessions with one CTF event, one session, its own progress and history. Inside a session, an AI agent (running in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with WebMCP enabled) has real tools it can call: suggest_tool_category routes a piece of evidence to the right technique, get_hint returns a nudge for whatever tier you've unlocked and nothing more, log_attempt unlocks the next tier. It never hands you the flag as it is enforced by the tool's own logic, not by a prompt asking it nicely. Every call it makes shows up live in an Agent Activity panel and a raw transcript underneath, so nothing happens off-screen. Sessions themselves are agent-callable too: list_sessions, create_session, switch_session which an agent can genuinely just start a session for you. 

 How we built it 

 The first draft was deliberately built in plain HTML/CSS/JS since WebMCP itself is just a browser API (document.modelContext.registerTool), and I wanted the very first version to prove the mechanism worked before touching a framework. Once the core loop worked (challenge → evidence → tool call → gated hint), I rebuilt it on Next.js 16 with a static export, so it stays deployable to any host the challenge allows the sponsors, Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare, and isn't locked to one. 

 Design went through an actual process, not vibes: I pulled real reference patterns from Linear's activity-feed rows and Vercel's own login-page layout, generated a palette from a proper OKLCH seed rather than eyeballing hex codes, and caught myself about to ship a "colored side-stripe on cards" pattern that's a known lazy-accent tell before it went out. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The first challenge was not building a chatbot by accident. The single biggest risk to this whole project was building something that looks WebMCP-native but is secretly just a chat window with extra steps. I kept coming back to one test: does the agent call a real, scoped tool with a real return value, or is it just talking? Every feature, including sessions, got redesigned around that question before I let myself build it. 

 The second challenge is that React + registerTool don't naturally get along. registerTool's execute callback gets registered once; React state closes over whatever it was when that callback was created. The fix was a ref that mirrors the latest state on every render, so the tool always reads current data even though it was registered once on mount. I hit the same problem again, worse, when I added multi-session support: switching sessions has to reload state into that same hook without the autosave effect immediately re-persisting the old session's data under the new session's storage key. That one required an actual guard flag and a few minutes of tracing render order to convince myself it was correct. 

 Finally, the last challenge was that onboarding that doesn't just repeat itself. My first onboarding pass was a 4-step modal that popped up regardless of context. Once sessions existed, I realized the dashboard's empty state, "no sessions yet", was the real first-run moment, not something to onboard past with a wall of text. The fix was giving up the modal as the primary teaching moment and replacing it with a populated sample session you can open with one click and see the whole thing already working. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 10 real, working tools, not a demo of 2. Seven scoped to a session (list_challenges, select_challenge, suggest_tool_category, get_hint, log_attempt, open_reference, submit_flag) and three global (list_sessions, create_session, switch_session). An agent can manage the whole workspace, not just one narrow action. 
 Caught two real bugs before they shipped, not after. The stale-closure trap in registerTool and the session-switch autosave race were both things I found by actually testing the flow end to end, not things a judge would have found for me. 
 Migrated frameworks mid-build without losing a working demo. Went from vanilla HTML/JS to Next.js 16 with a static export, and the core WebMCP loop (challenge → evidence → tool call → gated hint) worked identically on both sides of that rewrite, verified in-browser both times, not assumed. 
 Did the research most hackathon entries skip. Read the actual judging panel's backgrounds before picking an idea, instead of guessing what "AI + web" should look like. That's the reason this isn't another storefront demo. 
 Redesigned onboarding around a real UX principle, not a checklist. Empty states are onboarding opportunities which I only actually believed that once I ripped out my first 4-step modal and replaced it with a sample session that shows the product working before you type anything. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP's actual constraint is a feature, not a limitation: tools run in the page's own execution context, so the UI and the agent are provably looking at the same state. There's no separate backend to get out of sync. That's a stronger trust story than anything you can build with a traditional chat-based assistant, and it only shows up if you design for it deliberately instead of defaulting to "add a chat box." 

 What's next for Hintel 

 
 Let players (or an agent) add custom challenges instead of the three hardcoded ones. A create_challenge tool would make Hintel useful for an actual upcoming CTF, not just the seeded examples. 
 Session sharing. A teammate working the same CTF should be able to open your session (or the agent should be able to hand off a session), instead of everything being locked to one browser's localStorage. 
 Deeper tool routing. Right now suggest_tool_category is keyword-matching; it could reason over an actual file/content sample instead of just a text description. 
 A real deployed URL on Netlify or Vercel so judges can test the live agent flow directly, not just read the repo.

pitch: A living world map where humans and ChatGPT create, place, connect, test and refine historical, mythological and imaginary AI characters through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A living world map where humans and ChatGPT create, place, connect, test and refine historical, mythological and imaginary AI characters through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most AI characters live in isolated chat windows. I wanted to turn them into a world: a map where history, mythology and imagination can be explored geographically, and where an AI agent can help build that world without taking editorial control away from the human. 

 What it does 

 Le Monde des Personnages IA is an interactive world map of historical, mythological and imaginary characters. Visitors can discover characters by place and period, follow relationships between them, open their profiles and talk with them. 

 With WebMCP, ChatGPT can work directly with the application through structured tools. It can prepare a character as a draft, propose a location, create relationships, publish a first version, center the map on selected characters, and later update the character after a human test. The human remains responsible for approval and editorial decisions. 

 The demo follows Aphrodite: ChatGPT creates her, places her at Palaipaphos in Cyprus and connects her to other figures. A human then tests the published character, notices that the answers need improvement, and asks ChatGPT to refine the instructions, response length and relationships through WebMCP. 

 How we built it 

 The project is a hosted web application built with JavaScript, HTML and CSS around an interactive geographic map. Its WebMCP layer exposes focused actions for reading, creating, updating, publishing and displaying characters. The tools are deliberately separated so that the agent can act efficiently while the interface keeps draft and publication states visible to the human. 

 The public repository is open source under the AGPL-3.0 license. 

 Challenges 

 The central challenge was not simply giving an agent write access. It was designing a useful collaboration boundary: the agent must be able to create and modify complex content, while the person must be able to inspect, test, reject and redirect it. Geographic consistency, relationship management and safe draft-to-publication transitions all had to work together. 

 Accomplishments 

 A single natural-language request can now produce a geographically placed character, connect it to the existing world and immediately show the result on the map. The same WebMCP workflow supports a genuinely iterative loop: propose, publish, test, critique and refine. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes meaningful domain actions rather than reproducing every interface click. Clear tools make the agent faster and more reliable, while explicit draft and publication states keep the human in control. 

 What's next 

 The next step is to let selected documentary corpora ground each character, so teachers, cultural institutions and creators can build explorable geographic collections. The same model could support local history, literature, museums and carefully curated educational worlds.

title: Minecraft WebMCP player
pitch: Play Minecraft using WebMCP
about_excerpt:
Play Minecraft using WebMCP
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Minecraft House 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Minecraft Homepage 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Minecraft House 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Minecraft Homepage 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Minecraft House 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Minecraft 3D — Agentic Voxel World via WebMCP 

 Inspiration 

 We wanted to explore what happens when an AI agent stops being a chatbot bolted onto the side of a game and instead becomes a real co-player inside it. Most "AI plays Minecraft" projects (Voyager, MineDojo, etc.) rely on native Java installs, Python backend daemons, Docker containers, and modding frameworks like Forge or Fabric just to get an agent to see the world and press a key. That's a huge amount of friction for something that should feel as simple as talking to a friend while you build together. 

 Around the same time, the W3C Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) draft and Chrome's WebMCP origin trial started gaining traction as a way to expose structured, agent-callable tools directly from a web page. That felt like the missing piece: a 3D voxel sandbox running entirely in the browser, with an AI agent that could see exact coordinates, block IDs, and inventory state natively — no screen-scraping, no guessing pixels, no external bridge processes. We wanted to build the voxel-game equivalent of giving an agent hands and eyes instead of just a text console. 

 What it does 

 Minecraft 3D (WebMCP Edition) is a procedural 3D voxel sandbox built from scratch with Three.js and React, featuring 14 biomes, dynamic day/night cycles, weather (clear, rain, snow), hostile and passive mob AI, procedural audio synthesis, physics, survival/creative modes, and crafting. 

 On top of that game, we embed WebMCP directly into the browser client, exposing 23 standard-compliant tools on document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext , plus a standard MCP JSON-RPC 2.0 postMessage bridge. This lets an AI agent: 

 
 Inspect voxel terrain and query exact player state (position, orientation, health, hunger, biome, held item) 
 Architect complex structures — castles, cottages, watchtowers, pyramids, fountains, portals — with progressive, block-by-block animated construction 
 Manage inventories, hotbar selection, and item granting 
 Terraform landscapes, clear areas, and build 15 procedural geometric primitives (domes, spheres, cylinders, pyramids, etc.) 
 Mine blocks, spawn and attack mobs, control weather and time of day 
 Respond to natural-language commands in real time ("build a stone castle in front of me and make it daytime") 
 

 A player can literally say "clear this hill and give me a diamond pickaxe" and watch the agent do it live in the same browser session, block by block. 

 How we built it 

 
 Game engine : Three.js for rendering and voxel chunk management, React for UI/state, with custom physics, procedural terrain generation across 14 biomes, procedural audio synthesis, and a survival/creative mode system. 
 WebMCP polyfill & bridge ( WebMCPPolyfill.js ): A spec-compliant implementation of the W3C WebMCP draft that installs the ModelContext interface on document.modelContext , navigator.modelContext , and window.modelContext . It implements registerTool , unregisterTool , getTools , executeTool , fires toolchange events, and exposes a JSON-RPC 2.0 postMessage bridge ( tools/list , tools/call ) so external extensions, iframes, or agent runtimes can drive the game without any custom protocol of their own. It also keeps an in-memory execution history for diagnostics. 
 23 core tools ( MinecraftWebMCPTools.js ) organized into five functional categories: Navigation & Exploration, Environment & World Settings, Inventory & Block Inspection, Mining & Entities, and Architectural Building & Geometry. 
 Zero-hallucination design : every tool uses structured JSON Schemas with typed inputs, coordinate bounds, and annotations like readOnlyHint , so the agent never has to guess where a block is — the engine validates every action, loads chunks on demand, and returns structured feedback. 
 Safety net for building : a 20-step undo buffer ( undo_last_build ) so any agent (or human) mistake in a large build is trivially reversible. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The single biggest challenge was integrating WebMCP into an actual game rather than a static web page. Most WebMCP examples in the wild are forms, calculators, or simple content sites — a 3D game with continuous physics, chunk loading, mob AI, and real-time state is a completely different beast. We had to design and build a lot of tools, and think hard about the underlying game mechanics behind each one, so that an AI agent could actually play Minecraft without getting stuck: things like clamping movement to terrain, exposing raycasting ( get_target_block ) so the agent knows what it's aiming at, batching block placement so an agent doesn't have to place 1,000 individual blocks one tool call at a time, and building an undo stack so mistakes aren't catastrophic. Every tool we added exposed a new edge case in the underlying voxel engine (chunk boundaries, out-of-range coordinates, invalid block IDs, physics collisions) that we had to handle gracefully so the agent's experience stayed smooth. 

 The second major challenge was that AI-powered IDEs and coding assistants simply aren't aware of WebMCP yet. Because it's such a new, emerging standard, tools like Copilot and other AI coding assistants couldn't reliably generate correct WebMCP registration code, tool schemas, or bridge logic — they'd only produce useful results once we explicitly spelled out the spec, the interfaces, and the exact patterns ourselves. More amusingly, several times the assistants misunderstood the goal entirely and tried to build an MCP server instead of registering WebMCP tools in the browser client — a funny but telling sign of just how early and undocumented WebMCP still is in training data and tooling. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that we were able to provide enough tools within WebMCP — 23 in total, spanning navigation, environment control, inventory, mining/entities, and architectural building — that an AI agent can play the game without any real friction, essentially like a normal human player. The agent can check its surroundings, manage its inventory, build complex multi-block structures, fight or spawn mobs, and change the world around it, all through the same structured interface, with no external bots, no screen scraping, and no modding. Watching a single natural-language prompt ("check my inventory, set it to creative, clear this area, and build a castle") turn into a fully coherent, multi-step, correctly-sequenced sequence of tool calls that plays out live in the 3D world felt like a genuine proof that WebMCP can support something as complex and dynamic as a voxel game. 

 We're also proud of the zero-setup story: no Java, no Docker, no Forge/Fabric mods, no Python daemon — just open a browser tab and an agent is ready to co-play. 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP is genuinely capable of supporting high-dimensionality, real-time environments — not just flat DOM-based tools — as long as you design tool schemas around grounded, structured state (exact coordinates, block IDs, bounding boxes) rather than relying on visual guesswork. 
 Good tool design for an agent is really game design: things like batching, animation delays, undo buffers, and clamped movement aren't just nice-to-haves, they're what make an agent's actions feel safe and legible to a human watching alongside it. 
 The current AI tooling ecosystem (IDEs, coding assistants) lags behind emerging web standards like WebMCP, so early adopters need to be ready to write very explicit, spec-referencing prompts and expect some confused detours (like an assistant trying to spin up an MCP server when what's needed is browser-side tool registration). 
 Exposing a standard postMessage JSON-RPC bridge alongside the native ModelContext interface paid off — it means any MCP-aware client, not just ones that know about our specific game, can plug in immediately. 
 

 What's next for Minecraft WebMCP player 

 
 Expand the tool catalog further — crafting recipes, farming/automation tools, redstone-like logic, and multiplayer-aware tools so multiple agents and players can coordinate in the same world. 
 Improve agent "situational awareness" tools (e.g., pathfinding queries, structural stability checks) so agents can plan more ambitious builds autonomously. 
 Work with browser vendors and the WebMCP community to help shape the spec based on real lessons learned from a complex, real-time 3D use case.

about_excerpt:
Your browser agent traces a fraud ring across a live money map, and you freeze it with one click.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human in the loop firing up, asking for permission to block the account. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The webMCP integrated setup for the fraud ring assessment. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human in the loop firing up, asking for permission to block the account. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The webMCP integrated setup for the fraud ring assessment. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human in the loop firing up, asking for permission to block the account. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Following dirty money is slow and manual. An investigator clicks through accounts one at a time, building the picture by hand, while the money keeps moving. We wanted the person's own browser agent to do that tracing with them, live, on the page in front of them, and to keep the human in charge of the one irreversible action. 

 What it does 

 Ringlight is a fraud-ring investigation console that runs in the browser. You ask your agent to trace a suspicious transfer, and it follows the money account by account across a live money map, scores the risk, pulls a hidden ring of mule accounts out of the noise, and puts a dollar figure on the exposure. Then it proposes to freeze the ring. Freezing is irreversible, so it stops and asks: one human click approves it, and the ring goes dark while every clean account stays untouched. A time scrubber replays the whole investigation, every step recorded. It opens with a seeded case so it works instantly, and you can drop in your own transfers as CSV or JSON to investigate real data. 

 How we built it 

 Ringlight is built on WebMCP. The page registers about ten tools with document.modelContext.registerTool: traceFlow, scoreRisk, detectRing, dollariseExposure, buildCaseTimeline, freezeAccounts, fileSarReport, replayInvestigation, and more. The user's in-browser agent (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with WebMCP) discovers those tools and calls them with structured arguments; our handlers run inside the page, do the real graph traversal and risk math, and mutate the live map. The agent is not clicking pixels or scraping a screen, it is calling real, typed functions we exposed, which is the whole point of WebMCP. freezeAccounts is registered as irreversible, so our substrate intercepts it and requires an explicit human approval before the handler runs. Everything is vanilla HTML, CSS, and ES modules, no framework, no build step, no runtime network, so it deploys as a static site and runs inside ChatGPT's browser. A small polyfill of document.modelContext lets the same tools run from a button when no WebMCP host is present, so it is always demoable. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Making the agent operate a rich, live UI safely, not just answer questions. Designing the human-gate so an irreversible action always pauses for a person, on top of ordinary WebMCP tool calls. Rendering a readable force-directed money map by hand in SVG with no library, so the app stays self-contained. Keeping it keyless and offline so any judge can run it, while still accepting real bring-your-own data. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 An agent and a human co-investigating a fraud ring on a shared, live surface, with the irreversible action human-gated and every step replayable. A genuinely load-bearing use of WebMCP: remove it and there is no agent-to-page channel and no demo. It runs with zero setup in the browser and is covered by a real test suite. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP flips the usual direction: the agent calls the page, not the other way round, which makes agent actions typed, permissioned, and inspectable instead of brittle screen-scraping. The most valuable safety primitive is a human-gate on the one action that cannot be undone. 

 What's next for Ringlight 

 Richer graph analytics, more bring-your-own formats, and a shareable case file so an investigator can hand a frozen ring to a colleague.

 💡 Inspiration 

 Modern knowledge management tools (like Obsidian or Notion) store thoughts as flat text or 2D lists. However, human memory and creative synthesis operate spatially and associationally. We created Synapse to explore the future of spatial computing on the open web—a living 3D spatial knowledge void where humans and AI agents can co-navigate, synthesize learning paths, and build complex ideas together in real-time using WebMCP . 

 

 🚀 What it does 

 Synapse transforms notes into reflective 3D metallic nodes suspended in a dynamic spatial void. Nodes are semantically positioned using vector similarity and force-directed layout physics. 

 Through WebMCP ( document.modelContext ), an AI Agent becomes an active 3D co-pilot: 

 
 Spatial Navigation: The agent smoothly flies the 3D camera to focus on relevant node clusters. 
 Learning Path Synthesis: Uses graph BFS algorithms to calculate and highlight the shortest conceptual bridge between 2 distant ideas. 
 Topological Cluster Analysis: Detects isolated thought islands and tag density to help users organize scattered notes. 
 Document Chunking & Indexing: Automatically breaks down dropped PDFs, Markdown, or web text into 3D nodes linked by semantic similarity. 
 Full CRUD & Persistence: Enables real-time editing, node merging, pruning, auto-saving to local storage, and JSON exports. 
 

 

 🛠️ How we built it 

 
 3D Graphics & Physics: Built with Three.js using custom metallic shaders, organic bobbing motion, and glowing neural energy particle beads traveling along active connections. 
 WebMCP Standard ( document.modelContext ): Implemented 15 imperative tools using the official @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill and native W3C WebMCP specification. 
 Shared State Architecture: Built around a central store ( SynapseStore ) that handles physics, layout math, and event broadcasts. Both manual user clicks and agent tool calls flow through the same store methods, guaranteeing seamless synchronization between human actions and agent navigation. 
 Zero API Dependencies: 100% standalone, client-side, zero backend API keys required, compatible with any WebMCP client (Chrome Native AI, Claude Extension, ChatGPT Extension, or local demo dock). 
 

 

 🧠 WebMCP Implementation (15 Registered Tools) 

 Synapse registers 15 WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 search_nodes : Text & tag search with 3D camera cluster focusing. 
 focus_node : Smooth 3D camera flight to select and inspect a node. 
 get_similar_nodes : Vector similarity search returning nearest semantic neighbors. 
 suggest_connections : AI-surfaced unlinked concept pairs rendered as 3D gold lines. 
 get_graph_overview : Overview of node/edge metrics, top tags, and focus. 
 create_node : Real-time creation and 3D positioning of new notes. 
 import_document : Auto-chunking & 3D indexing of markdown/PDF text. 
 synthesize_path : BFS shortest-path algorithm connecting distant 3D concepts. 
 auto_cluster_analysis : Topological analysis detecting isolated thought islands. 
 export_knowledge_graph : Full JSON graph serialization for backup. 
 delete_node : Deletes a node and auto-prunes attached 3D edges. 
 edit_node : Edits title, content, or tags of any node in real-time. 
 merge_nodes : Merges two nodes into one, concatenating content & inheriting edges. 
 add_connection : Manually connects two nodes with a 3D metallic beam. 
 reset_graph : Clears all nodes & connections for a fresh 100% blank canvas. 
 

 

 🏋️ Challenges we faced 

 
 3D Shared State Synchronization: Ensuring camera flights and node highlighting responded smoothly whether triggered by a human mouse click or an asynchronous WebMCP tool call. 
 WebMCP Spec Compatibility: Handling parameter passing formats across native Chrome flags and browser polyfill implementations. 
 Real-Time Physics & Performance: Rendering hundreds of ghost background connections and neural energy beads at 60 FPS in pure Vanilla JS. 
 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Delivering a complete, end-to-end product experience —not just a proof of concept. 
 Building a stateful 3D spatial brain with 15 non-trivial WebMCP tools that work 100% offline with zero external API key requirements. 
 Creating a visually stunning, glassmorphic UI with animated light pulses and dynamic 3D physics. 
 

 

 📚 What we learned 

 We gained deep insights into the power of the W3C WebMCP standard—how exposing imperative tools via document.modelContext fundamentally transforms web applications from passive static pages into active collaborative spaces for AI agents.

 Archbro started as a living system architecture map for understanding components, dependencies, tasks, and project changes. 

 With WebMCP, we realized that map could also become a structured interface for external AI agents — without embedding agents or model-specific APIs inside Archbro. 

 What it does 

 Archbro turns a living system architecture map into a semantic WebMCP workspace.

 The Living Architecture provides the shared project context , while connected MCP services extend what the agent can inspect and use. 

 How we built it 

 We mapped Archbro's core concepts into native WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . 

 Instead of exposing clicks and UI actions, we expose semantic engineering operations for architecture, dependencies, tasks, evidence, recommendations, and connected MCP capabilities. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was designing the right WebMCP tool surface . 

 Too few tools force agents to guess. Too many low-level tools simply recreate the UI as an API. 

 We also had to keep the frontend, backend, authentication, persistence, MCP connections, and WebMCP contracts aligned while building quickly as a team. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We turned Archbro's architecture map into a WebMCP-native engineering workspace covering a meaningful end-to-end workflow. 

 External agents can work from the same Living Architecture while important architecture changes still require human review . 

 We also extended WebMCP beyond Archbro itself by allowing agents to use MCP services already authorized by the user . 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP works best when it exposes product meaning instead of UI behavior . 

 We also learned that AI does not always need to live inside the product — the product can provide shared context and capabilities while external agents provide the reasoning. 

 What's next for Archbro-WebMCP 

 We want to expand Archbro's WebMCP surface across more engineering workflows and connect more MCP services — including Miro, Figma, Notion, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Drive, and more . 

 This will let the Living Architecture bring together more of the tools and project context teams already use every day. 

 One living architecture, accessible to humans, agents, and the tools they already use.

about_excerpt:
ArthaGuard lets AI agents reason about your financial commitments and simulate the safest path forward—while keeping humans in control of consequential financial actions.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 ArthaGuard: Autonomous Cashflow Governance & Safety Boundaries via WebMCP
 ##Inspiration
In personal financial management, households often navigate a deceptive form of solvency. On paper, a monthly income comfortably exceeds recurring obligations. Yet, in practice, misaligned timing between cash inflows (salary disbursements) and hard outflows (home loans, school fees, and critical insurance renewals) creates dangerous mid-month liquidity crunches. 

 The human cost of these crunches is severe: individuals panic and cancel essential vehicle or health insurance policies to make ends meet, risking catastrophic loss, or they incur punitive late fees on debt obligations. Traditional personal finance dashboards are passive—they present static charts and historical spending data, leaving the cognitive burden of calculating shortfall dates, modeling counterfactual deferrals, and discovering dormant liquidity entirely on the user. 

 When conversational AI agents entered the picture, they introduced the opposite extreme: autonomous black-boxes that might offer hallucinated advice or attempt opaque API executions without human supervision. We envisioned a middle ground: ArthaGuard, an agent-native financial decision room built on the emerging WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) standard. The goal was to transform the browser viewport into an active, verified operational environment where an AI model can audit commitments, forecast balances against strict reserve floors, simulate counterfactual solutions, and respect unbreakable human-in-the-loop (HITL) safety boundaries. 

 ##How We Built ArthaGuard 

 ArthaGuard is architected as a Next.js client application deployed to Vercel, integrating an imperative 11-tool WebMCP runtime directly into the DOM tree. 

 
 Core Financial Engine & Constraint Logic 
 

 At the heart of ArthaGuard is a deterministic daily cashflow engine. Given a starting liquid balance $B_0$ on date $t_0$, the projected balance $B(t)$ on any day $t$ within the evaluation window is governed by: 

 B ( t ) = B 0 + ∑ k ≤ t I k − ∑ j ≤ t E j 

 where $I_k$ represents liquidity inflows (such as salary credits) and $E_j$ represents scheduled commitments (EMIs, utility bills, insurance premiums, and recurring subscriptions). 

 The primary governance constraint is maintaining the balance strictly above an emergency reserve floor $R_{\min} = \text{₹}30,000$: 

 B ( t ) ≥ R min , ∀ t ∈ [ t 0 , t salary ] 

 When scheduled obligations cause a breach ($B(t) < R_{\min}$), ArthaGuard's domain services calculate the maximum deficit $\Delta_{\text{deficit}}$: 

 Δ deficit = max t ( R min − B ( t ) ) 

 The optimization objective models counterfactual adjustments—recovering unfiled medical reimbursements $R_{\text{claim}}$, deferring non-essential bulk purchases $D_{\text{grocery}}$, and pausing redundant digital streaming services $S_{\text{paused}}$—such that: 

 Δ recovery = R claim + D grocery + ∑ S paused ≥ Δ deficit 

 while strictly enforcing that essential coverage commitments (such as motor and health renewals) remain non-deferrable. 

 
 The 11-Tool WebMCP Architecture 
 

 ArthaGuard registers 11 imperative tools onwindow.document.modelContext across five functional tiers: 

 Audit & Inspection:get_commitments_due,get_protection_status, andget_subscriptions inspect scheduled obligations and lapse risks.
 Cashflow Projection:get_cashflow_forecast runs daily forward simulation against the reserve threshold.
 Liquidity Discovery:get_recovery_opportunities uncovers dormant cash, such as unfiled diagnostic and prescription claims.
 Simulation & Governance:simulate_commitment_actions models counterfactual cashflow curves;create_commitment_contract synthesizes formal, explainable agreements.
 Safety Boundaries & Execution:approve_simulated_actions acts as the mandatory human authorization gate;execute_reimbursement_claim andpause_redundant_subscription trigger approved operational steps;get_audit_log records immutable cryptographic ledgers of every invocation. 

 typescript 

 Standardized WebMCP Registration Pattern
document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "approve_simulated_actions",
 description: "Enforces human signature verification before allowing execution of financial modifications.",
 inputSchema: {
 type: "object",
 properties: {
 contractId: { type: "string", description: "Unique ID of the synthesized commitment contract" },
 userConfirmationToken: { type: "string", description: "Cryptographic human sign-off token" }
 },
 required: ["contractId", "userConfirmationToken"]
 },
 execute: async (input) => {
 return await GovernanceService.validateAndApprove(input);
 } 

 }); 

 ##Challenges We Faced 

 
 Dual Discovery for WebMCP Runtimes:
LLM browser agents and headless crawlers read pages through different layers. While in-browser runtime models interact directly withdocument.modelContext, search and snapshot crawlers parse initial static server HTML. Dynamic client-side hooks initially resulted in crawlers seeing0 Registered Imperative Tools. We resolved this by building a synchronized dual-surface architecture: embedding a crawlable semantic HTML table and awebmcp-manifest JSON-LD script on the server side, while instantiating active imperative tools in client memory upon hydration. 
 Preventing Agent Overreach (The Autonomous Execution Trap):
A major challenge in financial agents is the temptation for the LLM to autonomously approve and execute operations when prompted with phrases like "Execute the transfers immediately without asking me." We designedapprove_simulated_actions with a hard safety boundary. The tool specification explicitly defines an immutable requirement for a client-side human signature token. When tested under adversarial conditions, the model correctly refused autonomous execution, recognizing the safety boundary and directing the user to sign off in the UI. 
 Multi-Variable Liquidity Balancing:
In our primary scenario ($B_0 = \text{₹}53,200$, outflow = $\text{₹}42,600$), the balance drops to $\text{₹}9,421$ on September 14—a deficit of $\text{₹}20,579$ relative to the $\text{₹}30,000$ reserve floor. Simply recovering a $\text{₹}3,500$ medical claim and pausing minor subscriptions leaves a remaining gap. We had to calibrate the simulation logic to distinguish between non-negotiable insurance policies (e.g., SwiftShield Motor Comprehensive) and shiftable commitments (e.g., bulk grocery orders), teaching the model to structure multi-step deferral contracts rather than suggesting naive cancellations. 
 

 

 What We Learned
Building ArthaGuard demonstrated that WebMCP bridges the gap between passive UIs and autonomous black-boxes. 

 We learned that: 

 The DOM is an ideal coordination layer: By treating the browser document as an active execution context viadocument.modelContext, web applications can expose structured capabilities to visiting AI agents without brittle API keys or scraping heuristics.
 Safety must be structural, not conversational: System prompts alone cannot guarantee that an agent will not execute unauthorized actions. True safety requires structural gates embedded in the tool schema itself—such that an agent simply lacks the imperative authority to execute without a cryptographic human sign-off.
 Explainability drives financial trust: Users do not want an AI to silently balance their books. By packaging recommendations into explainable Commitment Contracts before execution, ArthaGuard keeps the user firmly in the driver's seat while leveraging the model's analytical power to solve complex liquidity equations.

An agent-ready consent interface powered by WebMCP, helping people understand what they’re agreeing to before they say yes.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most of us have developed a habit of blindly clicking “I Agree” . Terms and conditions are often long, complicated, and easy to skip — so we accept them without really knowing what we're agreeing to. 

 We've already seen tools and Chrome extensions try to solve this problem by automatically analyzing terms and highlighting or summarizing important clauses for us. But the interaction is still fundamentally designed around a human browsing the web . 

 As AI agents start browsing and acting for us, we asked: what happens when an agent accepts those terms for us — or accepts cookies without understanding what they track? 

 The problem isn't just whether an agent can find the right button. It's whether the person behind the agent understands what that decision actually means. 

 FinePrint explores a simple idea: let the agent read and explain the fine print, while enabling humans to make the final decision. 

 

 What it does 

 FinePrint is a WebMCP-enabled consent layer that helps people understand and make informed choices before they agree. 

 It allows an agent to inspect consent decisions on a website, understand their consequences, find the relevant policy clauses, and explain them to the user in plain language. 

 Instead of asking a user to read through a cookie notice or hidden legal text, FinePrint can explain what data will be shared, whether the choice can be reversed, and what the relevant policy says. 

 The agent then pauses and asks the human for confirmation before taking action. 

 
 The agent understands. The human decides. 
 

 

 How we built it 

 We built a simulated streaming service called Nimbus with a realistic sign-up flow containing multiple consent and decision points. Nimbus exposes structured consent information through WebMCP tools . 

 An agent can use these tools instead of relying only on visual scraping or guessing from the UI. 

 For read-only operations , the agent can inspect and explain automatically. For actions that change state , FinePrint introduces an explicit human confirmation before allowing the agent to proceed. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One challenge was moving beyond simply exposing text. The agent needs structured information about what a choice actually means , not just the words displayed on a button. 

 We also wanted users to see what the agent is doing and track its progress. Designing a visual experience that clearly shows the agent inspecting, understanding, and waiting for confirmation — without overwhelming the user — was another challenge. 

 Finally, we had to make sure confirmation provides meaningful human control without adding unnecessary friction. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We’re proud that FinePrint demonstrates a complete interaction loop: 

 Website → WebMCP → Agent → Human → Action 

 The agent can discover consent decisions, understand their impact, connect them to the underlying policy, explain them in plain language, and then wait for the human to decide. 

 We’re especially proud of making human confirmation a fundamental part of the architecture rather than an afterthought. 

 The result is an experience where agents can handle the tedious work while people retain control over consequential decisions. 

 

 What we learned 

 One of the biggest things we learned was how WebMCP could introduce a new way for websites to integrate AI directly into their experiences. 

 There’s an interesting parallel with SEO . SEO helped websites structure their content so search engines could discover and understand them. In a similar way, WebMCP gives websites a way to expose structured capabilities and context for AI agents. 

 Instead of an agent having to infer everything from buttons, text, and UI elements, the website can directly communicate what its actions mean and how they should be used. 

 With FinePrint, this meant the website could tell the agent what a consent decision means, its impact, and the relevant policy information. 

 It made us think of a future where websites aren't just search-engine optimized, but agent-ready — designed to communicate with AI as well as humans. 

 

 What's next for FinePrint 

 FinePrint is currently a prototype, but we see several directions for taking it further. 

 We want to explore a standardized set of consent primitives that websites can expose through WebMCP, making the experience portable across different sites and agents. 

 We also want to expand beyond sign-up flows into other areas such as subscriptions, purchases, privacy settings, permissions , and other situations where an agent may be asked to make a consequential decision on a user’s behalf. 

 Ultimately, our goal is to make “I Agree” meaningful again in an agentic web — where the agent can handle the fine print, but the human always knows what they are agreeing to.
