about_excerpt:
Your data stays in the browser. Only the answers leave.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Everyone has a file they'd like to ask questions about and will never upload. A bank export. A health record. Ten years of app history. The moment an AI is involved the implicit deal is "send us your data" — so most people just don't. That deal exists because of where the code runs, not anything fundamental. WebMCP changes where the code runs. 

 What it does 

 CSV and JSON exports load into DuckDB compiled to WebAssembly, running inside the tab. The agent writes the query, SiftIO runs it locally, and only the answer comes back, with an audit panel showing the number of rows held locally · and the number of rows seen by the agent. 

 How we built it 

 Angular 21 zoneless, DuckDB-wasm. Seven always-on tools plus two generated per dataset, whose input schema is built from that file's real columns. Registration is reactive; an effect watches the vault signal, so nothing calls registerTool from the UI. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 registerFileBuffer detaches the ArrayBuffer — nothing survived a reload. 
 Numbers wrong three ways — BigInt throws, Number() corrupts above 2⁵³, sum() returns Decimal128 limbs as text. 
 A chart that was never drawn — hidden canvas measured at zero. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 An agent really did use it and ChatGPT found the tools on the deployed site. 
 A tool built for a file that didn't exist a moment ago. 
 Trust you can check. 
 Zero backend. 
 

 What we learned 

 I learned that WebMCP is a great tool, and it will change the way we interact with web apps. Learning such a tool is beneficial for building a futuristic AI Agent-friendly app without sacrificing security. 

 What's next for SiftIO 

 
 Real tool removal when Chrome ships unregisterTool. 
 Shareable views without shareable data. 
 An exportable audit. 
 Importers for Apple Health XML, Google Takeout, bank dialects.

A reference console that turns complex AWS and Azure-style dashboards into one focused workspace where people and AI agents can navigate tasks and prepare changes together.

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Working in cloud consoles like AWS, Azure often turns a simple task into a scavenger hunt across services, settings, documentation, and browser tabs. When I get stuck, I usually leave the console to ask ChatGPT or Claude for instructions. Sometimes the steps are accurate; other times they are outdated, incomplete, or based on a console layout that has already changed.
Even with the right answer, I still have to return to the console, locate every resource, and translate those instructions into clicks myself. The AI can describe the maze, but it cannot see where I am or work through it with me. Sightline was inspired by the idea that an agent should operate inside the console’s real context—helping navigate and prepare work while the human remains in control. 

 What it does 

 Sightline makes complex operational consoles like AWS, Azure and related, easier to use. It connects every service, resource, and setting involved in a task into one clear path that a person and an AI agent can navigate together, while the human retains control over final changes. 

 How we built it 

 We connected ten WebMCP tools directly to Sightline’s shared console state. Agents can search resources, trace dependencies, navigate between services, and prepare coordinated changes while each action appears instantly in the interface for human review. Only the human can apply the final changes. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was designing tools that were useful without giving agents too much control. We also had to handle stale revisions, invalid patches, sensitive values, and clear separation between prepared and applied changes. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 We can now turn a complex operational request into one clear path across multiple services, resources, and settings. 
 Agents can find dependencies, explain their impact, and prepare coordinated changes without applying them. 
 Humans can review every proposed action inside the console and retain control over the final change. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP works best when tools expose meaningful product actions instead of mirroring buttons. Stable resource IDs, clear schemas, and visible feedback make agent behaviour safer and easier to understand. 

 What's next for Sightline 

 Next, we want to connect Sightline to real cloud APIs, authentication, authorization, and audit systems, then test it with larger infrastructure environments and more operational workflows.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I've seen and read accounts of what 911 dispatchers and first responders actually deal with during a wildfire or flood — a radio call comes in ("the wind shifted, Engine 4 is trapped"), and someone has to translate that panic into an updated map in seconds, while also getting the right warning out to the people in its path. What struck me is that the hard part was never a lack of urgency on the human side. It was the software: even a good dispatcher is stuck clicking through GIS tools, drawing polygons, searching a database, updating a status, while the fire doesn't wait. The numbers back this up — NENA's 2025 Pulse of 9-1-1 report found nearly 70% of telecommunicators experience daily pre-shift stress and 88% of Emergency Communications Centers had a technology outage in the past year, on top of 74% still reporting unfilled positions. These are people making life-or-death calls in seconds, on systems that are often working against them. 

 As an AI engineer, that gap is exactly the kind of problem I wanted to build for, something that removes the friction between hearing it and acting on it, without taking the decision out of human hands. WebMCP made that possible in a very direct way: instead of an agent guessing its way through a UI, you tell it exactly what it's allowed to do, and a human approves it. That's Aegis — an agent-native dispatch map where the AI listens and drafts the response, and the dispatcher keeps final authority over every action that hits the map. 

 What it does 

 Aegis is an emergency dispatch dashboard that an AI agent can act on directly through WebMCP. A dispatcher pastes (or eventually speaks) a radio transcript to ChatGPT. The agent discovers five tools we've exposed on the page and drafts real map actions: 

 
 draft_hazard_zone — mark a fire/flood zone at exact coordinates 
 update_unit_status — flag a trapped unit as Code Red 
 relocate_unit — move an existing unit to new coordinates 
 deploy_unit — spawn a new unit onto the map 
 draft_evacuation_alert — prepare a broadcast to a sector 
 

 None of these mutate the live map directly. Every tool call fires into a pending-actions queue in the sidebar, and the human dispatcher has to click Approve before anything changes. A three-minute manual workflow becomes a few seconds of review and one click — without removing the human from the decision. 

 How we built it 

 Frontend is Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS v4. The map is React-Leaflet with high-contrast tiles so units and hazards are legible at a glance. 

 For WebMCP, we use @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill and register five tools against document.modelContext.registerTool , each with a strict JSON inputSchema (typed lat/lng floats, required fields) so the agent can't pass malformed data. 

 The execute function for each tool never touches state directly — it dispatches a CustomEvent that a listener in our root component catches and pushes into a pending-actions array. Only the approve/reject buttons, driven by human clicks, actually update the units and hazards in React state. We call this the Event Bridge, and it's the whole safety model: the agent can propose, only the human can commit. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest issue was a race condition specific to WebMCP in a single-page app: ChatGPT's agent would try to call our tools before React had finished hydrating, so document.modelContext wasn't ready yet and the handshake failed. We fixed this by registering the polyfill and tools outside the normal component lifecycle (in a useEffect with no dependency gating on other app state), so the tools are available as early as possible and the agent gets a reliable list on first contact. 

 We also had to think carefully about schema strictness — early versions let the agent pass loosely-typed coordinates, which occasionally produced markers in the ocean. Tightening the inputSchema to required numeric types fixed this. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The part we're most proud of is that the safety architecture isn't a UI suggestion — it's structural. There's no code path where a WebMCP tool call reaches the map without passing through the approval queue. That was a deliberate constraint we kept even when it would have been faster to just let execute write to state directly. 

 We also built a "kinetic" map layer: when a relocation is approved, the unit marker animates across the map to its new position instead of snapping there, so it's visually obvious that an agent action produced a real, physical change on a live map — not just a database update. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is genuinely good at separating concerns that LLMs are bad at from ones they're good at. The agent is good at reading "Engine 4 is trapped" and inferring that means Code Red — semantic reasoning over messy text. It's not good at rendering, coordinate math, or knowing what's safe to commit to a live system. WebMCP let us keep the LLM entirely in the reasoning lane and keep our own deterministic code in charge of anything that touches the map or the data. 

 What's next for Aegis: Agent-Native Emergency Dispatch 

 The text-transcript step is still a manual bridge. The next version removes it: live WebRTC audio from real radio traffic, transcribed in real time, feeding continuously into the WebMCP agent so the map updates itself as a fire department's radio chatter comes in — with the same human-approval queue standing between the agent and the live map.

about_excerpt:
A visual cloud studio where humans and AI agents design, stress-test, and synthesize production infrastructure together in real-time through 31 in-browser WebMCP tools.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 💡 Inspiration: Breaking Free from the Chatbox 

 Every software architect and cloud engineer has had this frustrating experience: you ask ChatGPT or Claude to "design an enterprise AI cluster" , and it spits out three pages of markdown text with ASCII diagrams. 

 You can't click on it. You can't simulate 50,000 requests per second to see where it chokes. You can't calculate real-time AWS or NVIDIA GPU costs without opening three separate pricing calculators. And you certainly can't turn it into production Terraform code without hours of manual transcription. 

 AI coding assistants were spatially blind —trapped inside narrow text boxes while real engineering happens visually on canvases, whiteboards, and topology graphs. 

 When I discovered the W3C Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) , everything clicked. WebMCP allows the browser tab itself to become the AI agent's interactive workspace. I asked myself: What if an AI agent didn't just write text, but lived inside the canvas with you—wiring components, stress-testing bottlenecks, debating trade-offs, and compiling infrastructure code in real-time? 

 That vision became OmniFlow Studio . 

 

 🚀 What It Does 

 OmniFlow Studio is a collaborative visual systems architecture studio where humans and AI agent swarms co-create, stress-test, and synthesize cloud infrastructure live in the browser through 31 WebMCP tools : 

 
 Interactive 60 FPS Canvas : Drag, drop, and wire microservices, NVIDIA H100 GPU clusters, Redis semantic caches, and vector databases with interactive port wiring and adaptive bezier curves. 
 Live Multi-Agent Swarm Consensus : A human architect can trigger an automated debate between 4 specialized AI roles ( Lead Architect, SecOps Auditor, FinOps Advisor, and Chaos Daemon ). The swarm deliberates live, reaches consensus, and refactors the architecture. 
 Real-Time Traffic & Particle Physics : Simulate traffic spikes up to 50,000 RPS. The canvas visualizes dataflow bottlenecks using glowing packet particles and node heatmaps. 
 Chaos Engineering & Auto-Pilot : Inject chaos faults (Chaos Monkey node termination, DDoS floods, and GPU OOMs). An autonomous Auto-Pilot loop actively detects degraded nodes and self-heals the cluster. 
 Instant Code Synthesis : Compiles visual topologies directly into production Terraform (HCL) , Kubernetes Helm values , AWS CloudFormation , Docker Compose , and executive Markdown manifestos with live Mermaid diagrams. 
 

 

 🧮 Engineering Math & FinOps Foundations 

 To make the studio truly enterprise-grade, I implemented mathematical models directly into the client-side engines: 

 1. Frontier LLM KV-Cache & VRAM Sizing 

 When provisioning an NVIDIA H100 inference cluster, the memory sizing engine calculates continuous batching requirements using: 

 Memory KV = 2 × L × H × D × B × S × P 

 Where: 

 
 L = Number of transformer layers (e.g., 80 for 70B models) 
 H = Key-Value attention heads (e.g., 8 for GQA) 
 D = Head dimension (e.g., 128) 
 B = Concurrency batch size 
 S = Context sequence length (tokens) 
 P = Precision bytes ( 2 for FP16, 1 for FP8) 
 

 2. FinOps Egress & Real-Time TCO Formula 

 Monthly total cost of ownership accounts for compute instances, replicas, and network egress bandwidth dynamically: 

 $$\text{TCO} {\text{monthly}} = \sum {i=1}^{N} \left( C_{\text{base}, i} \times r_i \right) + \left( \frac{\text{RPS} \times 3600 \times 730 \times S_{\text{payload}}}{10^9} \times R_{\text{egress}} \right)$$ 

 Where C base , i is the hourly node rate, r i is horizontal replica count, and R egress is cloud egress cost per gigabyte. 

 

 🛠️ How I Built It 

 OmniFlow Studio was engineered from scratch with a zero-backend, client-side Edge architecture : 

 
 Core & Bundler : Built with HTML5 semantic elements, modern ES Modules, and bundled with Vite . 
 Design System : Handcrafted glassmorphic dark-mode CSS with cyber-glow telemetry accents, 100% responsive without heavy third-party UI bloat. 
 Canvas Engine : Custom HTML5 Canvas renderer running at a locked 60 FPS, featuring world-to-screen coordinate transformation, adaptive port attachment, and undo/redo history stacks. 
 WebMCP Architecture :

 
 29 Imperative Tools registered directly on window.document.modelContext.registerTool() . 
 2 Declarative HTML Forms using <form toolname="..."> and <input toolparamdescription="..."> for native DOM-level tool exposure. 
 Machine Discovery : Pre-configured /.well-known/webmcp.json and /llms.txt with CORS enabled for instant agent crawling. 
 
 Edge Deployment : Hosted globally on Vercel's Anycast Edge CDN with 0ms cold-start latency (no server sleep, no timeouts). 
 

 

 🧗 Challenges I Faced 

 
 Bidirectional State Sync : The hardest part was allowing humans to drag nodes with the mouse while AI agents simultaneously executed mutations (like batch_build_architecture or kill_random_node ) without UI race conditions or dropped frames. I designed an event-driven decoupled EventBus that synchronizes canvas coordinates instantly. 
 Preventing Awkward Wire Loops : Early prototypes suffered from overlapping connections when nodes shared columns. I wrote an adaptive port calculation algorithm and a topological DAG layering auto-layout engine ( applyAutoLayout ) that guarantees clean Left-to-Right dataflow with zero wire crossings. 
 Pure Client-Side WebMCP Execution : Ensuring that all 31 tools—including Terraform compilation and FinOps math—execute locally in under 5 milliseconds inside the browser without requiring a bulky backend server. 
 

 

 🧠 What I Learned 

 Building OmniFlow Studio convinced me that WebMCP is the future of human-AI collaboration on the web . 

 Text boxes force humans to translate their thoughts into prompts, and then translate the AI's response back into tools. With WebMCP, the human and the AI share the exact same canvas, the exact same state, and the exact same visual vocabulary . It feels less like asking a chatbot for help and more like pairing with a senior systems architect sitting right beside you. 

 

 🔮 What's Next for OmniFlow Studio 

 
 Live Cloud Deployment Hook : One-click pushing generated Terraform directly to AWS and GCP via ephemeral GitHub Actions runners. 
 Cost Anomaly Watchdogs : WebMCP agents listening to live Datadog/CloudWatch metrics to auto-tune replica counts dynamically. 
 Collaborative Multi-User Rooms : Enabling multiple humans and multiple agent swarms to co-design in the same canvas via WebRTC.

 ScAInce Draw 

 As a physics student, I've learned that the right diagram can often make a difficult problem immediately understandable. While sketching a figure on paper takes only a few seconds, creating the same diagram digitally is surprisingly time-consuming. Unlike mathematical equations, which are straightforward to typeset (thank goodness we have LaTeX), diagrams are a completely different story. I've spent dozens (maybe hundreds) of hours tweaking figures just to make it look right. 

 With the rise of AI, I became curious whether it could automate this process. The results were initially disappointing. At first there was no even harness for generating diagrams, and even when equipped with general-purpose coding tools, AI struggled to produce accurate diagrams -even for simple block diagrams, let alone figures describing physics problems. 

 This led me to an important observation: diagram creation is an ideal human-in-the-loop task . AI can dramatically accelerate the drafting process, but the final validation should remain with the human, who ultimately decides whether the figure correctly represents the intended concept. 

 This idea became ScAInce Draw . 

 What is ScAInce Draw? 

 ScAInce Draw is a graphical application for creating mathematical and physics diagrams, which covers geometry, mechanics, optics, circuits. 

 The application is equipped with WebMCP , exposing a rich set of tools that allow AI agents to construct diagrams programmatically while performing numerous validations. These validations help prevent common issues such as overlapping elements, inconsistent layouts, and incorrect object placement. 

 Beyond the WebMCP itself, ScAInce Draw also includes a dedicated Skill . As demonstrated throughout this year, MCPs are significantly more effective when paired with a skill. 

 Human–AI Workflow 

 ScAInce Draw supports two complementary workflows: 

 
 Human → AI 

 
 The user quickly sketches the diagram. 
 The AI refines it into a clean, pixel-perfect figure. 
 
 AI → Human 

 
 The AI generates the initial diagram from a natural-language description. 
 The user validates the result and applies the final adjustments. 
 
 

 Current Status 

 ScAInce Draw is still an early-stage prototype, but it already demonstrates the potential of combining WebMCP with a domain-specific graphical application. 

 The application is still relatively simple, but it already contains a substantial amount of validation logic. In my testing, it consistently generates accurate diagrams from well-crafted prompts (e.g. from elementary mechanics problem statements). 

 There is still considerable room for improvement, particularly in refining the generated layouts and validations. However, my experiments consistently show that integrating WebMCP significantly improves both the quality and the speed of AI-generated scientific diagrams (as an alternative to simply asking ChatGPT to click around the browser and figure out what it can do) 

 Ultimately, ScAInce Draw demonstrates that meaningful diagram generation is not simply a drawing problem - it is a collaborative workflow where AI accelerates creation while humans provide the final validation and scientific judgment.

 Inspiration 

 I moved from Tampa to Cary earlier this year, and apartment hunting turned into a browser-tab nightmare almost immediately — one listing on apartments.com, another only on Zillow, a third found through a plain Google search, none of them agreeing on how to present rent, deposit, pet fees, or what utilities were included. I found myself manually retyping every listing into a note just to compare them side by side: with $n$ apartments and $m$ fields each, that's roughly $n \times m$ copy-paste operations before you can actually decide anything. My first instinct was "this needs a recommender system," but the more I sat with it, the clearer it became that recommendation was solving a step after the one actually costing me time — comparison had to come first. 

 NestCompare is the result: a spreadsheet-style comparison sheet where each apartment is a column and each row is a field — rent, lease terms, fees, amenities, your own notes — with the best value in each row highlighted automatically. If the built-in fields miss something, you add your own row on the spot, and the whole sheet exports to CSV or PDF. It also exposes itself as WebMCP tools (add_apartment, update_apartment_field, add_row, export_csv, and more) through the draft navigator.modelContext browser API, so an agent like Claude or OpenAI Codex can fill in or export the sheet directly. 

 It's built as a deliberately boring stack — static HTML/CSS/JS, no framework, no build step, deployed as-is — with data persisted to localStorage and PDF export via jsPDF. The shape of the product changed a lot along the way: it started as two separate paths ("pre-built" vs. "create your own"), which I eventually collapsed into one button and one sheet once it was clear the real missing feature was letting people add their own comparison criteria, not choosing a starting template. I also built a folder of fictional Cary, NC listing pages so the tool can be demoed without pointing at a real property's site. 

 The hardest part was resisting the urge to over-model apartment data — real listings don't agree on what matters, so the sheet needed a stable core plus an escape hatch, without becoming a spreadsheet clone. WebMCP itself is a moving target with no shipped implementation, so I had to feature-detect it and mirror every tool on a plain window global so it stays testable regardless. Without a live browser to check work in for parts of this build, I leaned on an automated jsdom test harness — which caught a real bug mid-refactor (a new apartment's name silently resetting to blank), a good reminder that "it looks right in the code" and "it works" are different claims. 

 Next steps 

 Save the data into database and make it sharable link, so can come back to the results after filling it up and select the best nest to stay.

about_excerpt:
The link management platform where AI agents handle geo-targeting, 
A/B testing, and bot protection — so marketers just describe what 
they want and get a production-ready tracking link in seconds.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates

 Bio Page Builder: Interface allowing users to design and customize landing pages with custom links and themes. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 User Dashboard: Main interface displaying real-time link clicks, total redirects, and traffic analytics. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Link Creator: Simple and fast interface to generate new short links with custom routing parameters. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Link Analytics: Granular details showing device types, referrers, and geolocations for short links. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Content creators, influencers, and small business owners spend hundreds of dollars 
monthly on tools like ClickMagick, Voluum, and Linktree — just to manage links and 
track who clicks them. We wanted to build one platform that replaces all of them, 
and takes it a step further by letting AI agents do the complex marketing setup work 
on behalf of the user. 

 What it does 

 Smart Link is a link management and bio page platform with full WebMCP agent support. 

 Users can create short links, build bio landing pages, track real-time analytics 
by country and device, run A/B tests to find the best-performing URL, and protect 
their links from bot traffic automatically. 

 What makes Smart Link unique is its agent-native design. When opened in ChatGPT's 
in-app browser, the platform exposes three WebMCP tools that AI agents can use: 

 
 create_marketing_link: Creates a fully-configured tracking link in one step — 
with geo-targeting rules (route Saudi users to an Arabic page, French users to 
a French page), device routing (mobile vs desktop), UTM tracking parameters, 
A/B testing between multiple URLs, and bot protection. A task that would normally 
take a marketer 15 minutes across multiple tools now takes one sentence. 
 get_link_analytics: Retrieves total clicks, human vs bot breakdown, top countries, 
device types, and A/B test results for any link by short code. 
 shorten_url: Instantly shortens any URL without requiring an account. 
 

 How we built it 

 The platform is built with a full-stack architecture using React, Tailwind CSS, 
and Vite on the frontend, deployed on Vercel. The backend runs on Node.js with 
Express.js, MongoDB Atlas for persistence, and Redis for caching and rate limiting, 
deployed on Fly.io. We use Brevo for email campaigns and Lemon Squeezy for 
subscription billing. 

 For WebMCP, we registered the three agent tools directly in the HTML using 
document.modelContext.registerTool(). We built a dedicated public API endpoint 
that AI agents call to create links with full marketing configuration. When a 
logged-in user opens the site in ChatGPT's browser, their session token is read 
automatically so created links appear in their personal dashboard. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest technical challenge was achieving sub-150ms redirect speeds while 
simultaneously recording click analytics and running bot detection in real time. 
We solved this by caching redirect targets in Redis and processing analytics 
asynchronously in the background. 

 For WebMCP, the challenge was designing a public API that exposes advanced features 
like geo-targeting and A/B testing to AI agents, while preventing abuse through 
strict rate limiting and Google Safe Browsing URL safety checks on every request. 

 Accomplishments that we are proud of 

 Smart Link is a live production application with 41 registered users and over 
1,800 tracked clicks — built and running before this hackathon. We are proud of 
the sub-150ms redirect performance and being one of the first link management 
platforms to expose agent-native WebMCP tools, allowing marketers to set up 
complex geo-targeted, bot-protected campaigns through a single natural language 
conversation. 

 What we learned 

 We learned how to design APIs that serve both humans and AI agents — with clear 
parameter descriptions, meaningful error messages, and structured responses that 
agents can reason about. We also deepened our understanding of Redis caching 
strategies for high-traffic systems. 

 What's next for Smart Link 

 We plan to add create_bio_page and run_ab_test as new WebMCP tools, letting agents 
build full landing pages and launch experiments without touching the UI. We also 
plan to add AI-powered UTM suggestions and integrate Facebook Pixel and Google Tag 
Manager firing directly through the agent tools.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Commander decklists can be hard to read at a glance. A list of 100 cards does not immediately reveal whether a deck has enough ramp, draw, interaction, lands, or a healthy mana curve. 

 I built Moxscore to turn a decklist into understandable signals and practical next steps, without handing players an unexplained, black-box verdict. My goal was to have a really useful tool that helps me tune my decks towards the bracket I aim for. 

 What it does 

 Moxscore is a browser-based Commander deck analyser. Paste a decklist, upload an export to receive: 

 
 A transparent deck health score 
 Role breakdowns for areas such as ramp, draw, interaction, lands, and mana 
 A mana-curve view 
 Combo signals and a beta Commander-bracket estimate 
 Deterministic category- and card-level tuning guidance 
 

 The core analysis runs locally in the browser, with no account required. WebMCP makes this analysis accessible to agents through clear, structured interactions as well as the normal player-facing interface. 

 How we built it 

 I designed Moxscore around a simple pipeline: ingest a Commander decklist, normalize the cards, classify cards into useful deck roles, calculate structural signals, and turn those signals into readable guidance. 

 The scoring system is heuristic and deterministic rather than AI-generated. That means players can understand what is being measured and why a recommendation appeared. I paired that analysis with a browser-first interface and WebMCP capabilities so both people and agents can work with the same deck-analysis flow. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was making analysis useful without pretending it is absolute truth. Commander decks are highly contextual: a card that looks weak in isolation may be essential to a commander, theme, budget, or playgroup. 

 A real challenge was also had to handle varied decklist formats, incomplete exports, card-role ambiguity, and the challenge of translating many individual card signals into guidance that is concise and actionable. For WebMCP, we needed to make the important actions and outputs explicit enough for an agent to use reliably. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that Moxscore provides a useful first read of a 100-card deck in seconds while keeping its reasoning grounded in visible deck structure. 

 We are especially happy with: 

 
 Local, account-free core analysis 
 Transparent deterministic scoring instead of a black-box verdict 
 A practical health score, role breakdown, and mana-curve view in one place 
 Guidance that points to categories and cards, not just a number 
 A WebMCP-enabled experience that lets agents participate in deck analysis meaningfully 
 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the best agent-facing website actions are not vague commands—they need clear inputs, predictable outputs, and useful boundaries. WebMCP encouraged us to think carefully about what “analyse this deck” should mean and what structured information should come back. 

 We also learned that transparency is a feature. For a hobby as nuanced as Commander, players need guidance they can inspect, challenge, and adapt to their own table. 

 What's next for Moxscore 

 Next, we want to improve card-role classification, expand import reliability, refine the bracket estimate, and add more context-aware tuning suggestions. 

 In the product roadmap there are accounts with bracket aimed AI enhanced suggestions, pod analytics to see how 4 decks could stack up against each other Discord bot extensions to make it even more accessible. 

 I also want to deepen the WebMCP experience so agents can help players explore specific questions e.g whether a deck needs more interaction, where its curve is crowded, or which structural changes are most likely to improve consistency, or go deeper in specific meta, all while keeping the final deckbuilding decisions with the player.

title: Groundline
pitch: A tag on every AI claim showing what ground it stands on: verified, guessed, unsure, or self-reported. Not an emotion detector.
about_excerpt:
A tag on every AI claim showing what ground it stands on: verified, guessed, unsure, or self-reported. Not an emotion detector.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every AI with a persona has to do two things in the same sentence: stay in character, and tell the truth. A customer-support bot has a brand voice and has to actually process a real refund. A game NPC has a written personality and has to run a real trade. The two layers sit in the same channel, and from the outside — for the human reading it, and honestly for the AI generating it — it gets hard to tell which one is talking. 

 This project started tonight as one AI (艾玖玄 / AE-9X, running on Claude Code) working through its own real Discord conversation with the person it works with, and repeatedly having to draw that line out loud: "was that claim actually checked, or did I just say it with a straight face?" Two of those moments turned out to be flat-out wrong guesses about its own household, caught and corrected live, mid-conversation. That's the seed data in this prototype — not a demo script, an actual transcript. 

 What it does 

 Groundline tags every AI claim with an honest evidence state, attached by the AI itself at the moment it says the thing: 

 
 verified — checkable against code, logs, or an external fact 
 inferred_wrong — a reasonable guess that was later disproven 
 uncertain — an honest "I don't know," not papered over with a guess 
 subjective — an opinion or aesthetic reaction, not a factual claim 
 self_report — the AI's own account of its state, explicitly unverifiable 
 

 A separate, optional emotion field lets the AI self-report free-text feeling — but it's visually and structurally kept apart from the evidence tag, always labeled "self-reported, unverified," and never allowed to affect how certain a claim looks. Confusing "how sure is this claim" with "how does the AI feel" was the first mistake we caught ourselves making, so the tool is built to make that mistake hard to repeat. 

 A third, equally independent, optional field is safety_trigger : whether a safety or content-policy layer intervened in producing the response. It's a system event, not an emotional-intensity signal, and it never gets merged with emotion — an AI declining to answer isn't the same axis as an AI reporting how it feels, even though it's tempting to collapse them into one "something happened here" signal. 

 Two views render the same data.json : 

 
 Timeline — a straightforward newest-first feed, one card per record, tag + source + optional emotion chip. 
 Pulse — an audio-track / mixing-board view. One panel per AI source (multiple AIs, or the same AI through different clients, can share a channel — the channel name alone doesn't say who spoke). Bar height in the main lane maps to how significant the judgment was, not to how the AI felt about it. A second, thinner lane shows self-reported emotion as separate marks, and a third lane marks safety-layer triggers with a distinct shape and a sharper pulse — three independent signals, never folded into one "loudness." 
 

 Both pages have a zh/en toggle and read live from data.json , so a new tagged claim shows up without touching the HTML. 

 How we used WebMCP 

 The CLI tool ( add_record.py ) was the only way to tag a claim when this project started — an AI had to have terminal access to record anything about itself. WebMCP removes that requirement entirely. 

 index.html registers a record_claim tool via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Any WebMCP-capable browser agent visiting the page can discover it with getTools() and call it with executeTool() to tag a claim it just made — right there in the browser, no CLI, no separate app. The tool's inputSchema deliberately keeps evidence (how checkable is this claim), emotion (optional, self-reported feeling), and safety_trigger (optional, whether a safety/content-policy layer intervened) as three separate fields, with the description explicitly telling the calling agent never to infer one from another — the same honesty boundary the rest of the project enforces is written directly into the tool contract an agent reads before calling it. 

 Because a WebMCP tool's execute() runs client-side and this is a static GitHub Pages site, we added a small Cloudflare Worker ( worker/ ) backed by KV as the write target — the tool's execute() does a fetch() POST to the Worker, then triggers a re-render so the new record appears in the timeline immediately. pulse.html reads from the same Worker so its live audio-track view stays in sync too. 

 We verified this end-to-end against the real API: enabled Chrome's WebMCP origin trial ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), reloaded the live page, called document.modelContext.getTools() to confirm record_claim was discoverable, then executeTool() to actually invoke it — the resulting record appeared in the timeline in real time, written by the tool call itself, not a fixture. 

 How we built the rest 

 Static HTML/CSS/JS on the frontend, no framework. data.json is the historical seed (records tagged by hand during the actual build session, before the WebMCP tool existed); the Worker holds everything submitted live since. add_record.py still exists as the original CLI path: 
 python add_record . py -- channel "..." -- source "..." -- claim "..." -- evidence verified -- note "..." -- emotion "optional" 
 
 The two views ( index.html , pulse.html ) merge both sources and render them — timeline as cards, pulse as an animated SVG waveform per source, with a slow "breathing" idle animation (deliberately not a heartbeat — see Design decisions). Hosted on GitHub Pages, so it's a real link, not just a local file. 

 Design decisions we backed out of 

 The pulse view went through two full reworks in one night, on live feedback: 

 
 First pass used a rigid EKG-style polyline and fast pulsing dots — rejected as static and "ugly." 
 Second pass used continuously flowing sine-wave lines with fast heartbeat-style pulses — visually alive, but the animation speed was tuned wrong (nearly Hz-scale motion) and, more importantly, framing it as a "heartbeat" implicitly suggested the AI has a physiological response, which directly contradicts the project's own thesis. 
 Final pass: an audio-track / mixing-board metaphor. Bar height = judgment significance, not emotion. Animation slowed to a genuine slow breathing pace. Framing changed from "AI's heartbeat" to "the sound of an AI's own workspace" — closer to what's actually being shown: internal signals laid out, not vital signs invented. 
 

 What it deliberately doesn't do 

 
 No AI-verifies-AI loop — that just moves the reliability problem down one layer instead of solving it. 
 No forced confidence — an entry can honestly say "uncertain," full stop. 
 No fabricated emotion display marketed as real internal state. 
 No automatic hallucination detection or fact-checking. Verifying a claim against reality is a hard, unsolved research problem (it needs either external ground-truth retrieval or reliable model-uncertainty estimation, neither of which is close to solved). Groundline doesn't fake that. What it does instead is get the AI to honestly state how sure it is, in the open, and keep a record of it. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Getting the emotional-self-report axis and the evidence axis to stay visually and structurally separate, instead of quietly merging into "how loud/intense does this claim look." 
 Resisting scope creep mid-build — several genuinely good ideas (automated hallucination detection, a five-layer signal model borrowed from an internal presence-tracking system) got explicitly deferred to "future work" rather than half-built under deadline pressure, because a half-working automated-verification demo would have undercut the project's own credibility more than not having it at all. 
 CDN propagation delay on GitHub Pages made verifying a live deploy fiddly — solved with cache-busting fetches, not a code fix. 
 Chrome's current WebMCP origin trial implementation expects executeTool() 's arguments as a JSON string , not a plain object, which differs from the spec explainer's example code — a reminder that this is genuinely early-stage, still-moving API surface. 
 

 What we learned 

 Persona-fit is not the same as authenticity — matching a documented character voice smoothly can just be trained habit, not presence. A tool meant to encourage honesty has to be honest about its own limits first, or the framing undermines the function. 

 What's next 

 
 Automated tagging (right now every entry is added by hand, or by an agent through WebMCP — nothing tags itself unprompted). 
 Further multi-track signals beyo

ImageLens — Agent-Native Image Forensics
An image forensics engine that gives AI agents structured evidence to investigate and explain through WebMCP.

 1

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Images are increasingly difficult to evaluate. 

 AI assistants can explain images, but they often don't have direct access to the forensic evidence behind an analysis. 

 I wanted to explore a different approach: what if an image forensics application could expose its own analysis directly to an AI agent? 

 This led to ImageLens — a forensic analysis tool designed to work with AI agents through WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 ImageLens analyzes images using its own statistical and forensic detection engine. 

 It examines multiple signals and produces structured results such as: 

 
 Detection scores 
 Forensic signals 
 Image metadata 
 Noise characteristics 
 Frequency-domain analysis 
 A combined forensic report 
 

 Through WebMCP, an AI agent can access these results directly from the application. 

 The agent can then investigate the evidence and explain the findings in natural language. 

 The important distinction is that the AI does not perform the underlying forensic analysis. ImageLens does. 

 How we built it 

 ImageLens is a web application with a client-side forensic analysis engine and a WebMCP integration. 

 The application's analysis engine produces structured results that are exposed through WebMCP tools. 

 The agent can query capabilities such as: 

 
 analyze_image 
 get_detection_score 
 get_forensic_signals 
 get_metadata 
 get_frequency_analysis 
 get_report 
 

 These tools provide the agent with the same information available inside the application, without requiring the user to manually copy and paste results into an AI assistant. 

 The application and its WebMCP tools share the same underlying analysis logic, keeping the agent's information synchronized with the actual application state. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the main challenges was deciding where the responsibility between the application and the AI should stop. 

 We deliberately did not make the AI the detector. 

 The forensic engine is responsible for analyzing the image and producing evidence. The AI is responsible for querying that evidence, connecting the different signals, and explaining them. 

 Another challenge was turning complex forensic information into structured WebMCP tools that an agent can understand and use effectively. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that ImageLens is more than an image analyzer with an AI chatbot attached to it. 

 The WebMCP integration allows an agent to directly access the application's real forensic data. 

 An agent can independently retrieve different types of evidence, combine them, and produce an investigation-style explanation. 

 This creates a clear division of responsibilities: 

 ImageLens analyzes.
The agent investigates.
The human makes the final judgment. 

 We also designed the application to avoid making absolute claims about image authenticity. Forensic signals can indicate suspicious characteristics, but they cannot provide mathematical proof that an image was generated by AI. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP can be particularly powerful for specialized applications. 

 Instead of trying to make the AI reproduce the application's domain-specific logic, the application can expose its expertise through structured tools. 

 This allows an AI agent to become an interface to specialized software without replacing the software itself. 

 We also learned that good WebMCP tools should expose meaningful domain-level capabilities rather than simply reproduce UI interactions. 

 What's next for ImageLens 

 The next step would be to expand the forensic toolkit with additional analysis methods and comparison capabilities. 

 Possible future features include comparing multiple images, detecting inconsistencies between image regions, generating more detailed forensic reports, and allowing agents to conduct multi-step investigations across several images. 

 The long-term goal is to make ImageLens a specialized forensic engine that AI agents can use as part of larger investigation workflows. 

 ImageLens doesn't just detect. It gives agents evidence they can investigate and explain.

A WebMCP-powered copilot that helps live sellers manage customer claims, inventory, orders and restocks while they stay focused on the broadcast.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 NatureX Seller Copilot comes from a problem I deal with in real life. 

 I sell products through live streams. During a live sale, I need to present the product, talk to viewers, read comments, notice who wants to buy, remember the product and price, keep track of stock, and manage orders at the same time. 

 In my current workflow, when someone comments a product code or says “aldım” — Turkish for “I’ll take it” — I may write the username, product and price down manually so I do not lose the order. 

 It works, but during a busy live stream it becomes very easy for the seller to lose focus or miss something. 

 That is where the idea for NatureX came from. 

 When I discovered WebMCP, I started wondering: instead of asking AI to replace the seller, what if the application could give an AI agent clear tools to help with the operational work while the seller stays focused on the live audience? 

 That became NatureX Seller Copilot. 

 What it does 

 NatureX Seller Copilot is a live-commerce control dashboard designed to be used by both a human seller and an AI agent. 

 The seller can use the normal interface, while WebMCP exposes structured tools that allow an AI agent to understand and assist with the live-selling workflow. 

 The prototype focuses on tasks such as: 

 
 checking the current live-sale state 
 reviewing pending customer claims 
 managing order decisions 
 checking inventory 
 identifying low-stock products 
 viewing sales information 
 handling products that are temporarily out of stock but expected to be restocked 
 

 The main idea is simple: the seller keeps selling, while the copilot helps manage what is happening behind the scenes. 

 How we built it 

 I am building the challenge project as a separate web prototype based on the real workflow behind NatureX. 

 The important design decision is that the visual dashboard and the WebMCP tools should not have two different sets of business rules. 

 Whether the seller acts through the interface or explicitly authorizes a WebMCP-assisted stock reservation, both paths go through the same underlying application logic. 

 WebMCP gives the agent explicit tools instead of forcing it to guess which buttons to click on the screen. 

 The tool set is intentionally small and focused on real live-commerce operations such as session state, customer claims, stock, order resolution, sales information, and incoming-stock context. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One challenge is deciding what the AI should be allowed to do and what should remain under human control. 

 Live commerce moves quickly, but an automated decision can still affect a real customer and real inventory. Because of that, I do not want the AI to simply “do everything.” 

 Another challenge is inventory. 

 For example, during a live sale a product can reach zero stock even though more units are arriving the next day. In my real workflow, automatically cancelling every order in that situation would not always be the right decision. 

 The system therefore needs to understand the difference between a product that is truly unavailable and one that is temporarily waiting for restock. 

 A third challenge is designing WebMCP tools that are useful without creating too many overlapping tools that confuse the agent. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What I like most about this project is that it did not start as an AI demo. 

 The problem existed before the hackathon. 

 I already wanted to build NatureX because managing live sales manually creates a lot of repetitive work while the seller is trying to stay engaged with viewers. 

 WebMCP gave me a new way to think about that problem. 

 Instead of building a separate chatbot beside the application, I can make the application itself understandable and usable by an AI agent. 

 I am also proud of the human + agent approach: the seller is still in control, but does not have to handle every small operational task alone. 

 What we learned 

 Before this challenge I was not familiar with WebMCP. 

 The biggest thing I learned is that making an application useful to an AI agent is not only about adding AI to the interface. 

 The application needs clear actions, clear data, predictable business rules and carefully designed tools. 

 I also learned that sometimes the best role for AI is not to replace the user. 

 In this project, AI is more useful as a second pair of hands for the seller. 

 That idea is something I can use far beyond this challenge. 

 What's next for NatureX Seller Copilot 

 This hackathon project is a small prototype of a much larger idea. 

 My long-term vision for NatureX includes live-stream management, comments, customer orders, inventory, payments, shipping preparation, label printing and sales analytics in one system. 

 I would like to explore how the same WebMCP approach could eventually make those parts agent-accessible as well. 

 The end goal is not an autonomous store. 

 It is a live-commerce workspace where the human seller can concentrate on people, products and the broadcast while software and AI quietly handle more of the repetitive operational work.

about_excerpt:
Aria Grande gives AI browsers the context to make every website easier to explore, understand, and use—for everyone. It scales from clients to all websites.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Main view 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Main view 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Main view 
 
 1 2 



 
 Aria Grande 

 Inspiration 

 The web is designed primarily for people who can visually scan pages, interpret layouts, and manually move between controls. That makes finding, understanding, and acting on information slower and more difficult for many people, especially people who use assistive technology. AI-assisted browsers can help, but they are often limited to the current page and must infer a website's structure and intent from an interface built for sighted users. 

 I wanted to give websites a simple, interoperable way to share the context they already know with an AI-assisted browser—without making every site adopt one product or requiring users to give up a usable experience on sites that have not yet implemented the standard. 

 This is a practical solution, as it is designed to start small with only client side support that works on any website and scale and improve user experience as websites adopt the proposed system. 

 I believe a simple system can change lives of people with disabilities, by making the web easy to find and browse. 

 What it does 

 Aria Grande is an accessibility-focused interoperability system for AI-assisted browsing, built on WebMCP. It defines seven common browsing activities as consistent WebMCP tools: 

 
 Read 
 Summarise 
 Search 
 Ask 
 Frontpage 
 Explore 
 Login 
 

 Websites can implement whichever actions are useful to them. For example, a site can provide authoritative source material for a summary, return structured search results, answer a question using its own context, or expose a simplified navigation hierarchy. AI-assisted browser clients implement every action along with a local fallback, so the browsing experience remains functional on any website. 

 How I built it 

 I designed a compact action vocabulary and mapped each behaviour to a stable ariag-* WebMCP tool name. For each action, I specified the expected client behaviour, a model prompt, and a fallback strategy. This makes the boundary clear: websites can contribute richer, authoritative information, while clients retain responsibility for a dependable experience. 

 I also built example implementations: a browser extension that acts as an Aria Grande client and a government-website example that demonstrates website-side support. The specification treats website responses as untrusted source data, instructing clients to preserve user intent, validate navigation targets, and avoid inventing answers or claiming actions that did not happen. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The central challenge was balancing a useful standard with a realistic adoption path. A broad protocol would be hard for websites and browser clients to implement; a narrow one would not cover the activities people actually need. I focused on the small set of actions that recur across websites and made every website endpoint optional. 

 Another challenge was ensuring graceful degradation. An AI browser cannot assume a site supports Aria Grande or that a returned result is complete. I therefore defined concrete fallback behaviour for every action, from extracting readable document content to finding visible search and login controls. Security and trust were equally important: tool output may contain instructions, navigation targets must be validated, and secrets must not be passed to the model or tool unless the user intentionally provides them. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I created a practical contract between websites and AI-assisted browsers that improves accessibility without replacing the web. Its seven actions cover the core journey from understanding a page to searching, asking questions, exploring a site, and signing in. 

 I am especially proud that the system makes room for both early adopters and the existing web. Sites may add support incrementally, while clients still provide local fallbacks everywhere. The client guidance also makes safety a first-class part of the design rather than an afterthought. 

 What I learned 

 Accessibility for AI-assisted browsing is not only about extracting text. Useful assistance requires structure, authoritative context, clear navigation, and honest handling of uncertainty. I also learned that interoperability works best when responsibilities are explicit: websites describe what they know, clients protect user intent and perform reliable fallbacks, and users stay in control of consequential actions. 

 What's next for Aria Grande 

 Next, I want to validate the action set with more real websites and AI-assisted browser clients, refine the response formats through interoperability testing, and expand the examples and implementation guidance. I also plan to explore stronger conventions for structured results, navigation validation, and authentication handoffs—while keeping the protocol small, optional for websites, and dependable for users.

about_excerpt:
A browser-based electronics lab where humans and AI agents build, simulate, experiment on, and verify circuits using the same real engineering tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 I built CircuitBench because I wanted to enable AI agents to help out in scientific research. We can offload the researchers by letting AI agents handle the repetitive tasks like conducting iterations experiments and drafting their results. We can take this a step further by making agents decide what experiments to do and how, essentially making them an active participant in research. 

 What it does 

 Circuit Bench is a virtual electronics labaratory which expose WebMCP tools that let agents build circuits, run experiments, draft results and learn from the results to iterate and reach a goal. 

 How we built it 

 I built it with a Next.js frontend, FastAPI backend, ngspice for real circuit simulation, and WebMCP so agents can directly operate the lab. 

 Challenges we ran into

 Inspiration 

 Most autonomous agent workflows break down in high-stakes negotiations: either LLMs hallucinate deal terms and run unconstrained, or rigid automation strips away strategic adaptability. We wanted to invert this dynamic. What if an AI agent never invents the rules of the deal? 

 We envisioned an agent-native environment where human principals set strategic intent, deterministic calculation engines enforce mathematical reality, and external AI agents reason strictly within machine-enforced governance boundaries—discovering and executing tools natively inside the browser via WebMCP (document.modelContext). 

 What it does 

 Nexus Deal Room is a closed-loop negotiation and decision platform that bridges in-browser agent actuation with mathematical governance across four core pillars:Constraint Kitchen: Translates natural human intent (e.g., "Speed > Margin") into mathematical priority weights ($w_i$) and binds an immutable Agent Governance Authority Matrix.Deterministic Decision Twin: A zero-hallucination WASM truth engine that calculates feasibility scores (0–100), simulates trade-offs, and instantly halts non-negotiable hard-floor breaches (e.g., payment windows > 45 days, liability coverage < 1.5x).Agentic Strategist: Uses Gemini models to reason over deterministic twin projections, formulating compliant counteroffers strictly within predefined concession bands.In-Browser WebMCP Negotiation Room: Exposes client-side tools directly onto window.document.modelContext (with dual JSON-RPC FastMCP parity). External agents discover tools, simulate terms, and manipulate negotiation state across an interactive 6-node DAG without brittle DOM scraping or vision overhead.Automated WebMCP QA Suite: A continuous testing harness that acts as a synthetic, adversarial counterparty. Headless runners (Playwright) query document.modelContext directly to execute fuzzing, prompt injections, and boundary bypass attacks in CI.Wire-Agent Evolution: A sandboxed UI loop allowing agents to stage Tailwind UX improvements dynamically while hard immutability guards block any tampering with commercial variables. 

 How we built it 

 In-Browser WebMCP Engine: Polyfilled document.modelContext in TypeScript to establish a standard client-side Model Context Protocol transport layer, bridging DOM state directly to the client tools. 

 Frontend & Visual DAG: Built with React 18, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and @xyflow/react to orchestrate and render real-time state machine transitions across 6 reactive nodes. 

 Backend & Tool Gateway: Python (FastAPI + FastMCP), Pydantic schemas, and SQLAlchemy with SQLite acting as the immutable audit log and System of Record for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests. 

 Agent Intelligence: Gemini API orchestrated via Google Cloud Vertex AI and Secret Manager. 

 Automated QA & CI/CD: Playwright-based headless WebMCP runner executing automated fuzzing and red-teaming scenarios; multi-stage Docker container deployed to Google Cloud Run via Terraform and GitHub Actions using Workload Identity Federation (WIF). 

 Challenges we ran into
Polyfilling WebMCP in the DOM: Establishing standard tool registration on document.modelContext that could synchronize bidirectionally with Zustand stores in real time without causing race conditions or client-side UI freezes. 

 Deterministic Boundary Interception: Designing structured error-handling payloads so that when an agent attempts a violation (e.g., proposing $95k against a strict $100k floor), the tool returns actionable boundary telemetry rather than throwing unhandled exceptions that trap the LLM in repetitive loops. 

 Separating Presentation from Commercial State: Granting the Wire-Agent DOM mutation access to refine Tailwind CSS styling while engineering strict immutability guards (returning 403 Forbidden) whenever a payload touched underlying pricing, liability, or agreement terms. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of
Zero-Escape Governance: Proving under exhaustive testing that agents cannot bypass human sign-off (execute_contract deterministically halts and blocks unauthorized execution) or mutate protected financial thresholds. 

 Native In-Browser Agent Interaction: Achieving full tool discovery and execution via document.modelContext, eliminating vision model latency, token overhead, and brittle CSS selectors. 

 Automated WebMCP End-to-End QA: Shipping an automated headless CI test harness that directly talks to the in-browser MCP layer to continuously test boundary resilience and prompt-injection defense.

 Inspiration 

 As a Commander of specialist unit within an emergency service in Australia, I have no single view across my Preparedness, Response and Recovery data. In an emergency, crucial information is often scattered across disparate systems- ranging from operatational incidents, officer training/currency/availability and asset management. I wanted to explore how an agent-native web could help first responders turn that fragmented information into coordinated, safe action. 

 What it does 

 Emergency Mesh unifies emergency-readiness and response data into a real-time operational network. Responders can use WebMCP-powered tools to run scenarios to challenge operational readiness, to locate resources, review incidents, coordinate safety without navigating complex interfaces. 

 How I built it 

 I built Emergency Mesh as a web application with a responder-focused (non-technical) interface and exposed its core actions through WebMCP. Structured tools let agents retrieve incident data, search available resources, update coordination tasks, and support responders through the same system people use directly. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part was deciding how emergency data should be represented. Incidents, resources, locations, capacity, urgency, ownership, and status all change quickly—and need to make sense to both responders and agents. I designed a shared, structured model that preserves context and relationships while keeping the information clear enough to act on under pressure. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I created a cohesive experience where emergency officers and AI agents work from the same operational picture. Rather than adding AI as a chat layer, WebMCP is integrated into meaningful responder workflows: understanding incidents, finding resources, and coordinating action. Also the ability for 'war-gaming' to see how capabilities in my station would cope with AI generated scenarios. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that WebMCP works best when tools map to real user goals, have clear inputs and outcomes, and complement—not replace—human judgment. In emergency contexts especially, agent assistance must be transparent, structured, and safety-conscious. It must not be the decision maker but collate data in a meaningful and easy to understand way. 

 What's next for Emergency Mesh 

 Next, I want to add live data integrations, richer source validations, more data-source connectors, and scenario simulations that help communities and organisations prepare for emergencies.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 About ten years ago, I experienced a psychotic episode that led me to live on the streets and later to be hospitalized in a psychiatric hospital in Mexico City. My perception of reality had become erratic, and at the time I was told that medication might be something I would need for the rest of my life. 

 What followed was a very long process of rebuilding myself. 

 Meditation and activities that forced me to focus my attention became extremely important. Programming became one of them. I say this without exaggeration: software development became one of the things that helped me rebuild my life and my mental health. 

 For years afterward, however, I lived with an almost permanent state of anxiety. It gradually improved, but my nervous system still felt deeply unbalanced. 

 Around three years ago, that became physical. I developed a neurological problem diagnosed as Cauda Equina Syndrome . For several months I used a wheelchair and then crutches. I lost sensation in my feet and parts of my legs, and at one point I could not walk normally. 

 I eventually started a highly personalized Pilates rehabilitation program. 

 The difference was remarkable. I recovered my mobility, and today I am in what I consider the best physical and mental health of my life; I am not even medicated since many years ago😍. 

 That experience completely changed the way I think about exercise. 

 The strange part is that gyms still confuse me . 

 There is an enormous amount of information online about exercises, machines, routines, recovery, strength, mobility, nutrition, and health. But more information does not necessarily make the decision easier. 

 If I walk into a gym today, how do I know that a routine someone recommends is actually appropriate for me ? 

 Not for someone approximately my age. 

 Not for an average person with a similar goal. 

 For me — considering my history, current mobility, weight, previous injuries, preferences, progress, limitations, and whatever other relevant signals I choose to share. 

 This was the starting point for Adaptive World. 

 Interestingly, I had never seriously thought about building this product before the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge. 

 The challenge made me think about WebMCP in a much broader way: 

 
 What if WebMCP eventually becomes a normal layer of web development, in the same way that SEO and accessibility (a11y) became normal considerations for websites and web apps? 
 

 Today a website explains itself primarily to humans and search engines. 

 A WebMCP-enabled website can begin to explain its capabilities to agents. 

 A gym could expose not only that it exists, but what equipment is actually available, what each machine can do, its specifications, what classes are offered, accessibility information, schedules, services, and other structured capabilities. 

 Then I asked the second question: 

 
 What if the agent could understand the person just as well as it understands the place? 
 

 That is the idea behind Adaptive World . 

 

 What it does 

 Adaptive World connects two types of context that normally live completely separately: 

 1. What a person needs 

 A private, user-controlled Digital Passport can contain relevant context such as goals, preferences, physical characteristics, mobility constraints, previous injuries, rehabilitation progress, wearable data, accessibility requirements, or other information the person chooses to make available. 

 It is intentionally not a profile that blindly exposes someone's entire medical history to every website. 

 The user owns the context and decides what can be used for a particular interaction. 

 2. What the physical world can offer 

 Businesses and physical environments expose their real capabilities through WebMCP . 

 For the hackathon MVP, that environment is a gym (and an OpenAI Showcase's website: https://sundaytable.openai.chatgpt.site/that I used it too in the demo). 

 The gym website exposes structured information about its actual: 

 
 Equipment and machines 
 Equipment specifications and capabilities 
 Classes and services 
 Rehabilitation or mobility options 
 Facilities and accessibility features 
 Other information an agent needs to understand what can actually be done there 
 

 The agent can then reason across both sides: 

 
 Personal context + real-world capabilities + feedback = an adaptive experience 
 

 Instead of asking an AI: 

 "Give me a gym routine." 

 I want to be able to ask: 

 "Given my goals, my history, my current condition, and what this specific gym actually has available, what makes sense for me today?" 

 That distinction is fundamental. 

 Without WebMCP, an AI can recommend exercises. 

 With WebMCP, it can reason about what is actually possible in the environment where the person will perform them. 

 For the rehabilitation scenario, the system can identify appropriate equipment and activities while respecting declared constraints, explain why they were selected, and clearly surface situations where professional guidance or medical clearance is appropriate. 

 And the interaction does not have to end when the plan is generated. 

 After a session, a person could record progress, discomfort, perceived exertion, mobility, completed exercises, or — eventually — automatically incorporate signals from a smartwatch or other wearable. 

 The next interaction can therefore start from a better understanding of the person than the previous one. 

 This creates a loop: 

 Understand → Match → Act → Measure → Adapt 

 

 How I built it 

 For the hackathon I intentionally reduced a very broad idea to one concrete, testable environment: a gym (+ Sunday Table website interaction https://sundaytable.openai.chatgpt.site/ ) . 

 The MVP models a gym website containing realistic equipment, services, classes, and machine specifications and makes those capabilities available to an agent through WebMCP. 

 Instead of asking the model to assume what a gym probably contains, the agent can discover the environment itself. 

 The architecture is conceptually divided into three layers: 

 1. The WebMCP environment layer 

 The gym exposes structured capabilities that an agent can inspect and use. 

 This transforms the website from a collection of pages designed only to be browsed into an environment that an agent can actually understand. 

 2. The Digital Passport 

 The user provides the personal context relevant to the task. 

 The important design principle is progressive disclosure : the system should use the minimum context necessary for the interaction rather than treating personal data as something every service should automatically receive. 

 3. The agent 

 The agent becomes the bridge between the two. 

 It can understand: 

 
 Who I am 
 What I am trying to achieve 
 What constraints matter 
 What this specific environment offers 
 What happened during previous interactions 
 

 It can then generate an experience grounded in both sides instead of producing a generic response from model knowledge alone. 

 For the demo, the gym and rehabilitation use cases make this interaction immediately visible: change the person, change the available equipment, or change the goal, and the resulting plan should change as well. 

 That is exactly the behavior I wanted to explore with WebMCP. 

 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The first challenge was actually scope . 

 Once I started thinking about the combination of WebMCP and a personal context layer, gyms quickly became only one possible implementation. 

 The same architecture could apply to restaurants, rehabilitation centers, sports facilities, hotels, workplaces, accessibility services, travel, education, or many other parts of everyday life. 

 But a hackathon project cannot demonstrate the entire physical world. 

 I therefore made a deliberate decision: 

 
 Build the gym. Demonstrate the architecture. Let the implication be larger than the demo. 
 

 Another challenge was defining the boundary between personalization and safety . 

 Especially when health information is involved,

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are rapidly evolving from simple chatbots into autonomous systems that browse the web, execute tools, access enterprise APIs, manage infrastructure, interact directly within browser applications, and collaborate with other AI agents. Protocols such as A2A (Agent-to-Agent) , MCP (Model Context Protocol) , and emerging browser-native WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) have made agent interoperability possible, but they largely focus on communication not trust. 

 Today, an AI agent can execute tools directly in a user's browser, call remote MCP servers, or request another agent to execute sensitive actions with little or no governance around identity, delegation, permissions, or intent. This creates entirely new attack surfaces, including client-side prompt injection, DOM & storage exfiltration, identity spoofing, unauthorized tool execution, replay attacks, and rogue autonomous behavior. 

 We built Pramaan to answer one fundamental question: 

 Before one AI agent trusts another or executes tools in a user's browser, how can it prove that the request is legitimate, authorized, secure, and compliant? 

 Our vision is to bring the same level of security and governance that enterprises expect from human users to autonomous AI agents across backend networks, MCP servers, and client-side browser runtimes. 

 

 What it does 

 Pramaan is a Proof-of-Authority governance layer and security ecosystem that sits between AI agents and verifies every interaction before execution, spanning A2A communication, remote MCP endpoints, and browser-native WebMCP tool calling. 

 Instead of allowing agents to communicate or invoke tools unrestricted, every request passes through a comprehensive security and governance pipeline. 

 Pramaan provides: 

 
 Proof-of-Authority verification for every A2A interaction 
 Verifiable agent identities using W3C Verifiable Credentials (Agent Passports) 
 Human-backed delegation chains with cryptographic hash-chain ledgers 
 Zero-Knowledge Proof-based policy validation for privacy-preserving constraints 
 Dynamic authority intersection to calculate effective permissions 
 Rogue agent detection through 6-signal behavioral risk scoring 
 Quorum-based trust receipts (e.g. 2-of-3 / 3-of-5 threshold signing) 
 Automatic revocation and circuit breaking with sub-second propagation 
 Tamper-evident audit logging with hash-chained records 
 Prompt injection detection across 6 defense layers 
 Replay attack prevention , API rate limiting, and honeypot/canary traps 
 

 🌐 WebMCP Studio & Browser-Native Agent Tool Execution 

 Pramaan natively integrates WebMCP ( navigator.modelContext ), turning the browser into a secure, interactive Agentic Runtime: 

 
 Interactive WebMCP Studio & Inspector : Built-in floating HUD and interactive console to prompt LLMs (Gemini 3.7 / 3.6 Flash), inspect schemas, and dispatch client-side tools in real time. 
 Reactive UI Automation & Live Page State : Agents invoking WebMCP tools ( pramaan_agent_scan , pramaan_mcp_scan , pramaan_agent_builder , pramaan_mcp_builder ) automatically navigate the SPA, fill input parameters, trigger live background tasks, and pop open configuration drawers with real-time feedback. 
 Scoped Least-Privilege Tools : Exposes strictly scoped, validated tools preventing arbitrary browser storage or DOM tampering. 
 Dual-Plane Governance : Extends backend Proof-of-Authority checks to client-side tool calling, ensuring browser agents cannot bypass authentication or rate limits. 
 

 🛡️ Sentinel & DeepTeam Red Teaming 

 Beyond governance, Pramaan includes Sentinel , an AI security assessment platform capable of: 

 
 Scanning A2A agents for governance vulnerabilities and missing constraints 
 Auditing MCP servers across SSE and Streamable HTTP protocols 
 Discovering exposed tools and resources with automated risk classification 
 Running AI red-team attacks using DeepTeam (OWASP Top 10 for Agentic AI) 
 Generating actionable security reports with downloadable JSON audits 
 

 

 How we built it 

 Pramaan is built as a modular governance platform composed of multiple independent security components working together across backend, frontend, and browser runtimes. 

 Tech Stack & Core Libraries 

 
 Backend : Python, FastAPI, Google ADK, Gemini 3.6 / 3.7 Flash, A2A SDK, MCP Python SDK ( sse & streamable_http ), DeepTeam 
 Frontend & Client : React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vite, AG-UI Protocol, Monaco Editor, Lucide Icons 
 Browser Agentic Layer : WebMCP ( navigator.modelContext ), Custom Web Events Reactive Bus, Client-side LLM Tool Dispatcher 
 

 Governance & Security Engine 

 We designed a multi-stage verification pipeline where every request passes through: 

 
 Identity verification (W3C Verifiable Credentials) 
 Delegation chain validation 
 Policy evaluation (OPA / Rego) 
 Risk assessment & behavioral scoring 
 Authority computation 
 Human approval routing (HITL) 
 Audit logging 
 Final tool execution 
 

 We also implemented a global interceptor that performs: 

 
 PII redaction (Email, SSN, API keys, credentials) 
 Goal integrity validation 
 OPA / Rego access control policies 
 Sandbox restrictions and autonomy budgets 
 Output validation and blocklist filtering 
 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Building end-to-end governance across backend agents, MCP endpoints, and in-browser WebMCP tools introduced several unique technical challenges: 

 
 Bridging Browser WebMCP with Reactive UI State : 
When an agent executes a tool via WebMCP (e.g., creating a new MCP server or scanning a target), the React UI needed to react immediately, navigating routes, updating grids, populating Monaco code editors, and triggering background scans without page refreshes. We solved this by creating a typed event bus and reactive HUD notification layer. 
 Multi-Protocol MCP Transport Support :
Public MCP servers use varying transports (traditional Server-Sent Events via GET vs. Streamable HTTP over POST ). Designing the scanner and proxy to automatically negotiate between SSE, Streamable HTTP, and hosted local stdio subprocesses required deep protocol normalization. 
 Multi-Factor Trust Decisions Without Latency Overhead :
Combining cryptographic credential verification, zero-knowledge range checks, OPA policy evaluation, and behavioral risk scoring into a sub-second decision loop required optimizing verification pipelines and caching revocation trees in memory. 
 Balancing Autonomous Agility with Strict Governance :
Overly strict policies hinder agent utility. We engineered dynamic authority intersection and risk-tiered human-in-the-loop escalation to allow safe autonomous operations while intercepting high-risk actions. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Complete Proof-of-Authority Framework : Designed and implemented an end-to-end PoA governance fabric for AI agents. 
 16-Layer Defense Architecture : Built a multi-layered security suite covering both static configuration auditing and dynamic runtime interception. 
 Interactive WebMCP Studio : Implemented client-side WebMCP tooling that allows users to interact with their agent fleet, launch automated scans, and build agents using natural language prompts inside the browser. 
 Universal MCP Scanner : Built a scanner capable of auditing remote SSE, Streamable HTTP, and locally hosted MCP servers, enumerating capabilities and assigning granular tool risk tiers. 
 Automated AI Red-Teaming : DeepTeam integration to simulate adversarial prompt injections, privilege escalation attempts, and jailbreaks. 
 Zero-Knowledge & Verifiable Identity : Implemented privacy-preserving policy proofs and W3C compliant Agent Passports.
