 💡 Inspiration 

 Recently, I was filling out a questionnaire that asked me to name my favorite artist. I honestly didn't know what to answer, and spent a couple of hours figuring out which paintings I actually liked and which I didn't — watching videos about the lives of the artists and watching films about them. 

 When the email from Devpost about The WebMCP Challenge arrived, there were only a couple of days left before the deadline. The new technology intrigued me, and I registered right away. I spent the first day studying the resources tab to learn what WebMCP was, and then I needed to choose an idea. I chose one that would solve my own recent problem. I also believe the target audience of this application is not limited to everyday users — it is capable of being used in real-world art galleries to assist tour guides and docents. 

 Naming it was an adventure in itself — I chose Mostra d'Arte (Italian for "Art Exhibition"). 

 ✨ What it does 

 To be honest, when I saw the demo projects with WebMCP, I was amazed. I really liked this technology, I realized that this was impossible before, and I wanted to make my own contribution. Mostra d'Arte is an agent-native web application built so that people and their agents can use it together to explore art. 

 The idea of the application is to provide structured tools agents can use directly. When a person wants to study a painting, it becomes meaningfully better if you and your agent can interact, collaborate, and explore together. 

 In the app, you talk to your browser agent naturally: 
 "Exhibit the Mona Lisa, turn on the focused spotlight for dramatic atmosphere, and zoom in on her hands." 
The agent then immediately switches the artwork on the wall, dims the room with a focused spotlight, and smoothly zooms in on the hands. 

 🛠️ How I built it 

 With very little time on the clock, I used Google AI Studio to rapidly prototype the visual aesthetics and curatorial concepts, and engineered the application in Antigravity IDE, and deployed it on Vercel . Along the way, I replaced traditional server-side function calling with direct client-side WebMCP tool actuation in the browser. 

 (A fun milestone: when I kicked off the project, my assistant was Gemini 3.7; by the time I finished, Gemini 3.8 had just been released!). 

 Thanks to the clear documentation (Resources tab), I implemented the WebMCP specification using document.modelContext.registerTool() , creating 12 client-side tools across 4 functional areas. All tools include strict JSON Schema definitions, Google character budgets, readOnlyHint security declarations, and AbortSignal cleanup tied to component lifecycles. 

 1. Spatial Navigation 

 
 zoom_painting : Takes { x, y, zoom, detail_name } and animates the camera to specific percentage coordinates on the canvas. 
 reset_view : Resets the camera back to 1.0x view and restores normal gallery lighting. 
 switch_masterpiece : Switches the displayed painting between 7 available artworks. 
 

 2. Lighting & Audio 

 
 toggle_spotlight : Turns on a spotlight on the canvas and dims the surrounding room. 
 toggle_ambient_acoustics : Starts or mutes ambient background sound generated via the Web Audio API. 
 toggle_composition_grid : Shows or hides a Golden Ratio and Rule of Thirds composition grid overlay. 
 

 3. Information & Guided Tours 

 
 get_artwork_details : Returns artwork description, pigment information, and focal point coordinates. 
 toggle_curatorial_dossier : Opens or closes the side drawer with historical background and pigment data. 
 start_guided_tour : Starts an automated multi-stop tour with text-to-speech audio narration. 
 docent_speak : Outputs agent commentary into the on-screen Virtual Docent dialogue and reads it aloud. 
 open_salon_browser : Opens a full-screen gallery view displaying all 7 paintings. 
 

 4. Ticketing 

 
 reserve_gallery_pass : Generates a modal with a VIP admission ticket and QR code for the visitor. 
 

 🧪 How to test 

 The application is deployed on Vercel at https://mostra-darte.vercel.app and can be tested via: 

 
 Google Chrome with the testing flag enabled:

 
 Open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and set to Enabled (relaunch Chrome). 
 Inspect tools via Chrome DevTools ( Application > WebMCP ) or the official Model Context Tool Inspector extension. 
 
 

 Sample prompts to test with the agent: 

 
 Multi-Tool Chaining & Spotlight: 
 "Exhibit the Mona Lisa, zoom in on her hands, and turn on the focused spotlight for dramatic atmosphere." 
 Camera Zoom & Details: 
 "Show me the details of the moon in this painting." 
 Reset View: 
 "Show me the edge of the cliff with flowers, then reset the view." 
 Switch Artwork: 
 "Show me Michelangelo painting." 
 Guided Audio Tour: 
 "Start a guided tour of The Starry Night." 
 Historical Dossier & Pigments: 
 "Show me pearl. What pigments and colors did Vermeer use for this masterpiece? Show me the palette." 
 (To close: "Close the dossier and return to full canvas.") 
 Composition Grid: 
 "Switch to Botticelli. Analyze the geometric balance of this painting and show the composition grid." 
 (To hide: "Hide the composition grid.") 
 Ambient Acoustics: 
 "Turn on the gallery ambient music to set a contemplative mood." (To mute: "Mute the gallery ambient sound.") 
 Salon Wall Collection: 
 "Show me the entire gallery collection on the salon wall." 
 VIP Ticketing: 
 "Book 2 VIP passes for Jude on tomorrow's evening session." 
 

 🏆 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I am proud that I studied the documentation for the new WebMCP technology and built a working MVP in just a few days. I managed to implement 12 tools that let the agent control the camera, museum lighting, audio, and guided tours. 

 The project is fully open source under the MIT license, so other developers can explore how WebMCP works in practice.

 Here are the submission section details for THE LAST TERMINAL : 

 

 Inspiration 

 Traditional browser AI agents interact with web applications through brute force: taking high-resolution screenshots, parsing complex DOM trees, predicting CSS selectors, and firing simulated mouse clicks. This approach is fragile, slow, and burns tens of thousands of tokens per action. 

 When WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) emerged as a proposed browser standard ( navigator.modelContext.registerTool ), we realized web applications no longer had to be passive visual interfaces. Websites could directly expose machine-readable capabilities to AI agents. 

 We wanted to showcase this paradigm shift in a way that was instantly understandable and fun. An escape room was the ultimate sandbox—demanding puzzle reasoning, state prerequisites, data extraction, and tool sequence execution! 

 

 What it does 

 THE LAST TERMINAL is an interactive, browser-based cyberpunk escape room where human players and AI agents collaborate to escape an abandoned digital research facility before the emergency countdown reaches zero. 

 
 5 Interconnected Subsystems : Surveillance Matrix, Security Terminal, Auxiliary Power Control, Archive Database, and Emergency Exit Override. 
 10 WebMCP Capabilities : Exposes structured capabilities ranging from inspect_surveillance("CAM-07") and read_log("LOG-2049") to restore_power(["C","A","D","B"]) and unlock_exit("7319") . 
 Dual Execution Engine : Human UI interactions and AI WebMCP tool calls invoke the exact same underlying JavaScript game engine logic. 
 Real-Time Agent Feed & Trace : A live terminal logs tool calls in real time, accompanied by a full JSON execution trace inspector for hackathon judges. 
 Demo Agent Simulator : Includes a 90-second automated execution mode so anyone can watch an AI agent solve the room step-by-step without needing external API keys. 
 

 

 How we built it 

 
 Core Tech Stack : Next.js 14 (App Router), React 18, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. 
 WebMCP Integration ( src/lib/webmcp/ ) : Registered 10 structured tools with strict JSON Schemas using navigator.modelContext.registerTool imperative API, wrapped in a hydration guard to prevent re-registration during React re-renders. 
 Unified Game Engine ( src/lib/game/ ) : Built a central state machine ( gameEngine.ts ) powering both human clicks and agent tool calls. 
 Web Audio API Synthesizer ( src/lib/audio/sound.ts ) : Built a zero-external-asset audio generator for terminal typing clicks, success chimes, failure buzzers, and power-up sweeps. 
 Developer Debug Bar ( ?debug=true ) : Added a secret query parameter mode for instant puzzle completion and state inspection during testing. 
 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Enforcing Prerequisites Without Crashing : Ensuring that tools like open_archive() correctly check state prerequisites ( power === 'online' ) and return structured error payloads ( PREREQUISITE_NOT_MET ) rather than throwing unhandled exceptions. 
 Graceful Fallback & Polyfilling : WebMCP is an emerging browser feature. We needed to support native navigator.modelContext while building an in-memory tool polyfill and automated simulator for standard browsers. 
 Zero-Dependency Architecture : Ensuring the entire application ran client-side with zero backend infrastructure, zero paid APIs, and zero external databases while keeping the build Vercel-ready. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 >90% Token Reduction : Demonstrated how structured WebMCP tool calls eliminate the heavy token overhead of DOM parsing and visual screenshot analysis. 
 Zero Paid Dependencies : Built the entire experience to run 100% locally in the browser with zero external infrastructure. 
 100% Test & Build Validation : Achieved a clean Next.js static build and 100% pass rate on our standalone engine test suite ( npm run test:engine ). 
 

 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP transforms web applications from passive UIs into agentic APIs . 
 Human + Agent co-op design patterns—where humans supply visual intuition and agents perform rapid tool inspection—create a powerful collaboration model. 
 

 

 What's next for The Last Terminal 

 
 Multi-Agent Co-Op : Expanding to multi-agent escape rooms where specialized WebMCP agents (e.g. Security Agent, Power Agent) solve puzzles in parallel with human teams. 
 useWebMCPTool React Hook : Packaging our WebMCP registration layer into an open-source React hook library for Next.js developers. 
 Community Puzzle Creator : Allowing developers to construct their own WebMCP escape rooms using custom JSON schemas!

title: Plasma-trace
pitch: One physics model, two operators. A human drags sliders; an AI agent calls WebMCP tools. Both hit the same functions and the same chart -a shared instrument for sub-centimetre orbital debris detection
about_excerpt:
One physics model, two operators. A human drags sliders; an AI agent calls WebMCP tools. Both hit the same functions and the same chart -a shared instrument for sub-centimetre orbital debris detection
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Sub-centimetre orbital debris is a genuinely unsolved problem. Objects
this small are difficult to track with radar or optical systems, yet at
orbital velocities they carry enough energy to damage spacecraft. 

 NASA-funded research has been exploring an indirect approach: a charged
fragment moving through ionospheric plasma can excite nonlinear waves —
solitons — that might be detectable even when the object itself is not.
The physics comes from Sen et al. (2015) on forced-KdV soliton excitation
by charged orbital debris, developed further in Christine Hartzell's NASA
NIAC work at the University of Maryland. 

 I did not invent that science, and this project does not claim to. What
interested me was a different question: exploring a model like this means
sweeping parameters — size, velocity, altitude, day/night ionosphere —
and that is exactly the kind of tedious, click-heavy loop where a human
and an agent should be able to work on the same instrument instead of in
separate tools. 

 What it does: 

 Plasma-trace is a browser-based forward model for debris detectability.
Set a fragment's size, relative speed, and altitude, pick a daytime or
night-time ionosphere, and it returns a detectability score plus a
breakdown across eight altitude bins. 

 The point is that there are two ways to drive it, and they are the same
instrument: 

 
 A person drags sliders and watches the chart redraw. 
 An AI agent calls WebMCP tools registered on the page — and the
sliders and chart move exactly as if a person had dragged them. 
 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit: 

 Scientific parameter exploration is a bad fit for the usual ways agents
interact with web pages. Screen-scraping a slider is fragile and
lossy: an agent reading "38/100" off the DOM has a rendered string, not
a result it can reason over. 

 WebMCP changes the contract. The page exposes typed tools with schemas,
so the agent calls a function and gets structured data back, while the
human sees the same state update visually. Neither operator is
second-class. That is what makes this feel like a shared instrument
rather than an agent puppeting a UI built for someone else. 

 What people and agents can do together that was difficult before: 

 The clearest example is sweep_altitude . A person exploring where a
5 mm fragment is most detectable has to drag the altitude slider through
eight positions and read the chart each time. An agent runs the whole
sweep in one call and returns the best altitude with the full profile —
while the human watches the same chart update. 

 Before WebMCP, that meant either building a separate API (and now the
human and agent are using different systems that can drift apart) or
having the agent scrape the UI (fragile, and it gets strings instead of
data). Here there is exactly one code path. 

 explain_regime is the inverse case: the agent asks the instrument to
explain why detectability peaks where it does, so the reasoning comes
from the page's own model rather than the language model's guess. 

 How I built it: 

 One self-contained index.html — no backend, no database, no build
step. Chart.js from a CDN is the only dependency. 

 
 runForwardModel() computes detectability from an altitude-dependent
plasma density term, a size factor, and a speed factor. 
 The sliders call that function directly. 
 Four tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() :
 set_debris_params , run_forward_model , sweep_altitude , and
 explain_regime . Each one calls the same functions the sliders call
and updates the same chart. There is no parallel agent code path —
that constraint is the whole design. 
 The page feature-detects document.modelContext and degrades
gracefully: in a non-WebMCP browser it shows a banner explaining how
to enable it, and every slider still works. 
 

 Challenges: 

 The WebMCP API is new enough that several third-party guides describe it
incorrectly — a number of them say navigator.modelContext when the
spec defines document.modelContext . Writing that line from memory or
from a blog post would have produced a page that looks completely normal
and silently registers nothing. I sourced the signature from the W3C
explainer and cross-checked it against the spec IDL. 

 A second one: executeTool takes its arguments as a JSON string, not an
object. Passing an object returns "Failed to parse input arguments" with
no further detail. Worth knowing if you are testing via
 navigator.modelContextTesting in the console. 

 What's real, and what isn't 

 I would rather be precise about this than oversell it. 

 Real: the forward model runs in-page, the WebMCP registration is
functional, the deploy is live, and agent tool calls demonstrably move
the same sliders and chart a person uses. 

 Simplified: the ionosphere data is hardcoded. The model uses
closed-form terms, not a plasma solver. Nothing here is validated
against observations. 

 Not claimed: this does not detect debris. It is not an early-warning
system — solitons propagate near the ion-acoustic speed while debris
moves far faster, so this is a mapping and survey concept, not a
collision alarm. The science is attributed to published research. 

 The contribution I am putting forward is the interaction pattern: a
scientific instrument that a human and an agent operate through one
shared set of functions. 

 What's next 

 Real ionosphere data (IRI or GNSS TEC) instead of hardcoded values, a
trained ML model for the inverse problem — recovering fragment
properties from an observed signature, which is not analytically
solvable and is exactly what the NIAC team is working on — and
multi-sensor localisation.

 Inspiration

 What it does 

 Agent Rescue is an AI Reliability & Recovery Control Room built around a shared human-agent workflow. 

 In the demo, Research Brief #247 reaches 73% completion when Provider Alpha fails with an HTTP 429 rate limit. Agent Rescue preserves the checkpoint, diagnoses the failure, discovers available providers, evaluates recovery options, and recommends a recovery path. 

 Before changing providers, the system stops at HUMAN APPROVAL REQUIRED. 

 After approval, Agent Rescue switches providers, resumes from the preserved 73% checkpoint instead of restarting, and verifies the job at 100% RECOVERED. 

 How we used WebMCP 

 WebMCP gives the agent structured capabilities instead of forcing it to guess its way through the visual interface. 

 Agent Rescue exposes seven tools:

 inspect_failure 
 list_available_providers 
 recommend_recovery 
 switch_provider 
 resume_job 
 verify_completion 
 

 The human interface and WebMCP tools operate on the same application state. The agent can observe, diagnose, compare options, recommend recovery, resume work, and verify results while the human retains control over the consequential provider-switch decision. 

 How we built it 

 The challenge prototype is a deterministic single-file web application with an explicit recovery state machine, structured tool contracts, an audit trail, provider comparison, checkpoint preservation, and a mandatory human-approval interlock. 

 The deterministic scenario makes the complete recovery sequence reproducible for judging without requiring accounts, API keys, or external AI-provider credentials. 

 What's next 

 The same architecture can extend from the deterministic challenge prototype to real multi-provider AI infrastructure, helping individuals and organizations preserve work, control failover, reduce wasted resources, and improve AI reliability.

A workspace built for two users: humans and AI agents. Humans set intent; agents use WebMCP to plan, create, modify, and organize real workspace data under human control.

 Inspiration 

 Most AI web experiences stop at conversation: the agent tells you what to do, while you still have to operate the application yourself. We wanted to explore a different model—what if a website could expose its real capabilities directly to an agent? 

 That idea became Forge , a workspace designed from the beginning for both humans and AI agents. 

 What it does 

 Forge lets a person describe a goal in natural language, such as creating a realistic two-week product launch plan. 

 The agent can inspect the workspace, create and organize tasks, build milestones, modify existing work, and propose changes through WebMCP tools . 

 Humans stay in control: they can review agent-proposed changes, approve or reject them, and undo important actions. 

 Instead of an AI that only generates suggestions, Forge lets the agent actually work with the application's structured state. 

 How we built it 

 We built Forge as a web application with a visual project workspace, an integrated agent panel, structured project data, an activity log, and a human approval workflow. 

 The core of the project is WebMCP. Forge exposes real application capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , including project, task, planning, workspace, approval, and undo operations. 

 The UI and agent use the same underlying application state, so an agent action immediately becomes a visible change in the workspace. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was making WebMCP more than a technical demo. The tools had to perform real application operations and work together as a coherent workflow. 

 We also had to design a clear boundary between agent autonomy and human control, especially for changes that modify or remove existing work. 

 Accomplishments we're proud of 

 We built a complete human-agent workflow instead of a chatbot wrapper. 

 A user can give Forge a goal, the agent can use multiple WebMCP tools to work on the project, the application can show exactly what the agent did, and the human can review, approve, reject, or undo changes. 

 We are especially proud that WebMCP is part of the product's interaction model rather than an add-on feature. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that making a web application agent-friendly requires more than adding AI. The application's capabilities need clear structured interfaces, predictable inputs and outputs, good state management, and strong human feedback loops. 

 WebMCP gave us a way to think about the website itself as something an agent can understand and operate. 

 What's next for Forge AI 

 We want Forge to evolve from a project workspace into a broader agent-native environment where humans and agents can collaboratively create, organize, and execute complex work across different types of web applications.

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but collaboration across sessions, tools, and people is still fragile. When a conversation ends, the next person or agent often has to reconstruct what happened, what decisions were made, and what work should happen next. 

 Handoff explores a different model: a shared web workspace where humans and AI agents operate on the same project state. 

 What it does 

 Handoff gives a project a persistent shared state built around: 

 
 goals 
 open work 
 evidence 
 decisions 
 activity 
 the next handoff 
 

 Humans interact with that state through the web interface. AI agents interact with the same underlying capabilities through WebMCP tools. 

 An agent can inspect the current project, understand unfinished work, search existing evidence, contribute findings, propose results, record agreed decisions, complete work, and determine the next handoff. 

 The key idea is simple: 

 The conversation can end. The work doesn't. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer how to use the interface by reading the page and manipulating UI elements. 

 With WebMCP, Handoff exposes the application's meaningful actions directly as structured tools. 

 The human UI and the agent tools operate on the same domain actions and shared state. WebMCP is therefore not an add-on to Handoff; it is what allows the application to become a genuine human-agent workspace. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 A human can define a goal, add context, review evidence, and make important decisions. 

 An agent can then pick up the project, determine what remains unfinished, inspect existing evidence, contribute work, and leave the project in a clean state for whoever comes next. 

 The next worker can be the same person, another person, or another AI agent. 

 Built for the WebMCP Challenge 

 Handoff was created for the 2026 WebMCP Challenge as an experiment in agent-native web applications. 

 The goal is to demonstrate that websites do not only need to be readable by agents — they can explicitly expose the actions and state that agents need to collaborate safely and effectively with humans.

 Why I Built INTENT 

 I kept coming back to a simple problem: when we use AI, we usually start with a prompt and immediately ask it to do something. But sometimes the hardest part is figuring out what we actually want to do in the first place. 

 That became the idea behind INTENT — a workspace where the human and the AI can work on the intent itself before jumping into execution. 

 How I Built It 

 I built INTENT as a Next.js web app with a structured workspace for an evolving intent. Instead of keeping everything inside a chat, the application keeps track of things like intent nodes, decisions, actions, and open questions. 

 The interesting part for this challenge was connecting that workspace to AI agents through WebMCP. 

 I exposed six tools that let an agent work with the actual application state: 

 
 "inspect_intent" 
 "add_intent_node" 
 "focus_attention" 
 "surface_contradiction" 
 "propose_intent_evolution"

 These aren't just functions that return text. They are connected to the workspace, so when an agent uses them, the changes can be reflected in the UI. 

 What I Learned 

 The biggest thing I learned was that agent interaction feels different when the agent can actually interact with the application instead of only generating a response. 

 Designing the tools also made me think carefully about what an agent should be allowed to do. I wanted the human to remain in control while still giving the agent enough access to be genuinely useful. 

 I also learned a lot about the practical side of WebMCP — especially tool registration, connecting tools to application state, and testing the experience in the browser. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was getting the WebMCP integration working with the current API. My initial implementation used an older registration pattern, which caused the tools to fail during registration. 

 I had to update the implementation to the current "ModelContext" API and make sure the tools were registered correctly without causing repeated registrations during React development and refreshes. 

 Another challenge was making the tools useful enough to represent real actions in the workspace rather than just creating a collection of demo functions. 

 What's Next 

 INTENT is still an early version, but the direction I find interesting is giving agents more meaningful ways to participate in applications while keeping the human in control.

 Inspiration 

 Agents are useful when they can act directly on Git problems, but they become fragile when they have to guess through a UI or pretend every conflict is machine-solvable. GitWand started from a boundary-first idea: resolve what is objectively deterministic, surface what is ambiguous, and keep the human in control of the decision. 

 What it does 

 GitWand Agent turns a Git conflict into a shared Merge Room for humans and agents. The page exposes three WebMCP tools: resolve_conflict , parse_git_error , and list_cases . Deterministic hunks are settled automatically; genuinely ambiguous ones are filed for the human to choose; and the agent can read the room back to resume work once a decision is made. 

 How we built it 

 We registered the tools directly on the page and wired the UI around live case state. The same browser tab that the agent sees also shows the Merge Room, so the result is visible in real time. The implementation keeps the resolution logic narrow and explicit: no guessing, no hidden side effects, and no tool that can silently pick a side for you. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was resisting the temptation to make the agent do too much. Git conflicts often mix deterministic edits with real intent decisions, so the product had to make that boundary obvious. Another challenge was designing list_cases so the agent can return after a human decision and continue without losing context. 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native software works best when it is precise about what the machine can and cannot decide. WebMCP is a good fit because it lets a website define exactly how an agent should interact with it, instead of forcing the agent to infer the UI. 

 What's next 

 More conflict patterns, richer case history, and tighter integration with real repository workflows.

 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for sms-florin eSIM - WebMCP checkout on a live product 

 Inspiration 

 Most "AI agent buys something on a website" demos are toy stores built for the demo. We wanted to answer a harder question: can WebMCP be dropped onto a real product that already takes real money without rebuilding the checkout, and without opening a security hole? sms-florin sells eSIM data plans with live Stripe billing, so it was the honest test case. 

 What it does 

 The live page flo-voice1.com/esim exposes two WebMCP tools to any WebMCP-aware browser (e.g. ChatGPT Desktop): 

 
 list_esim_plans — returns the live plan catalog: country, data amount, duration, price. 
 buy_esim_plan — takes a plan slug and creates a real Stripe Checkout session, handing the agent the checkout URL. No money moves until a human enters card details on Stripe's own page — the tool starts a real purchase, it doesn't complete a charge on its own. 
 

 An agent can go from "find me a 7-day UK data plan" to a fully-formed Stripe checkout for that exact plan in two tool calls, without ever parsing the page's HTML or clicking a button it had to locate visually. 

 How we built it 

 
 Tool registration : a ~40-line client component calls document.modelContext.registerTool() for the two tools on page mount. It's feature-detected — document.modelContext only exists in a WebMCP-aware browser, so the component is a silent no-op everywhere else and ships to production safely. 
 Backing endpoints : two public, unauthenticated routes — GET /api/v1/esim-catalog (returns the same data the page renders) and POST /api/v1/esim-checkout (creates the Stripe session, returns its URL). 
 Shared checkout path : the Stripe session creation was refactored into one function used by both the human checkout form and the WebMCP endpoint, so the agent and the human get identical pricing, identical metadata, identical guarantees. There is no separate "agent checkout" to drift out of sync. 
 Stack : Next.js (App Router) on the existing production deployment, Stripe Checkout, WebMCP via the browser's document.modelContext API. Deployed as-is on the live site — this is not a separate demo environment. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Doing this on a commercial product. The full sms-florin app has live billing and stays closed-source, so we carved out just the WebMCP integration layer (tool component + two routes + the shared checkout lib) into a public MIT repo that still reflects exactly what's deployed. 
 A tool's execute() returns a value; a form action redirects. The human flow does a server-side redirect to Stripe. An agent tool needs a value back, so the endpoint returns the checkout URL as JSON and the tool hands it to the agent instead of navigating server-side. 
 Not opening an abuse surface. The new endpoints are unauthenticated (same guest-checkout model the human form already uses) but IP rate-limited, and buy_esim_plan cannot move money — worst case is a created-but-unpaid Stripe session, which expires on its own. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 WebMCP added to a product that already has paying customers, in hours not days, with one shared code path for humans and agents and no new security hole. The integration is live in production right now, not staged for judging. 

 What we learned

 Inspiration 

 The Mind Archetype was inspired by a simple question: what if a psychology website could be designed not only for people, but also for the AI agents helping them? 

 In mental health, the journey often starts long before someone books an appointment. People may first want to understand what they are experiencing, explore possible areas of support, learn how therapy works, or simply figure out where to start. 

 Traditional websites provide this information through pages, menus, and buttons designed for human navigation. But as AI agents increasingly become an interface for discovering and interacting with services, I saw an opportunity to make that experience more direct. 

 As a psychologist and the founder of The Mind Archetype, I wanted to explore how WebMCP could bring agent-native interaction into a real psychology service while keeping professional care and human decision-making at the center. 

 What it does 

 The Mind Archetype is an agent-native psychology website that allows compatible AI agents to discover and interact with structured capabilities exposed directly by the website. 

 The application currently provides 12 WebMCP tools covering: 

 
 Mental health information 
 Care-area discovery 
 Service information 
 Consultation guidance 
 Resource discovery 
 Organization information 
 Contact options 
 Consultation preparation 
 Appointment booking 
 

 For example, get_mind_archetype_profile allows an agent to discover structured information about the organization, while book_appointment provides a dedicated capability for starting the appointment process. 

 This means an agent does not have to rely exclusively on interpreting the visual interface and guessing where to click. 

 At the same time, the human remains in control. The system is designed to help people navigate information and access professional support, not to replace a psychologist or make clinical diagnoses. 

 How we built it 

 The project was built as a real, deployed web experience using: 

 
 HTML 
 CSS 
 JavaScript 
 WebMCP 
 Netlify 
 Google Calendar for appointment scheduling 
 

 Rather than creating a separate prototype, I extended the existing The Mind Archetype website with a WebMCP layer. 

 The WebMCP implementation exposes tools through document.modelContext , allowing compatible agents to discover the capabilities available on the page. 

 I tested the deployed implementation directly in Chrome with WebMCP enabled and verified that all 12 tools could be discovered through: 
 ( await document . modelContext . getTools ( ) ) . map ( t = > t . name ) 
 
 The appointment capability is connected to a real Google Calendar scheduling experience, so the agent-assisted flow can ultimately lead to an actual human-selected appointment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was working with a new and evolving web capability while keeping the existing website stable. 

 I had to understand how WebMCP exposes tools through the browser, how those tools are discovered, and how to define capabilities that are meaningful from an agent's perspective. 

 Another challenge was balancing the agent experience with the existing human experience. I did not want to rebuild the website around AI or remove the visual interface people already understand. 

 Instead, I treated WebMCP as an additional interaction layer. 

 Testing was also an important part of the process. I had to verify the implementation directly in the browser, troubleshoot differences between the WebMCP tool representation and traditional JavaScript APIs, and make sure the appointment flow connected to a real scheduling experience. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The biggest accomplishment is that this is not just a concept or mockup. The Mind Archetype is a live psychology website with a working WebMCP implementation. 

 I am particularly proud of: 

 
 Successfully exposing 12 distinct WebMCP tools. 
 Integrating WebMCP into an existing production-style website without replacing its human interface. 
 Connecting the appointment capability to a real Google Calendar scheduling flow. 
 Creating tools around meaningful psychological-service tasks rather than adding AI functionality for its own sake. 
 Keeping human control at the center of the experience. 
 Making the complete project publicly available with its source code and documentation. 
 

 For me, the most important achievement is demonstrating that WebMCP can be applied to a real-world professional service where trust, clarity, and human oversight matter. 

 What we learned 

 This project changed how I think about websites. 

 Previously, I primarily thought of a website as an interface between a person and a service. Building with WebMCP made me think of it as an interface between people, services, and agents . 

 I learned that making a website agent-friendly is not simply about adding AI. It is about identifying meaningful actions and exposing them as clear, structured capabilities. 

 I also learned that giving an agent more capabilities does not necessarily mean giving it more control. 

 In a sensitive field like psychology, the better approach can be to let an agent help someone understand options, find information, prepare an action, or begin a process, while leaving important decisions to the human. 

 What's next for The Mind Archetype 

 The current implementation is a foundation for a larger agent-native psychology platform. 

 Next, I want to expand the capabilities around psychological education, resource discovery, consultation preparation, corporate mental health services, and access to professional support. 

 I also want to explore richer agent-assisted experiences where a person can describe what they need conversationally and the agent can help them navigate the appropriate information and services exposed by The Mind Archetype. 

 The long-term vision is not to automate the psychologist. 

 It is to make the path from a person's first question to appropriate human support simpler, more accessible, and more intelligent. 

 The Mind Archetype is an exploration of what psychology on an agent-native web could look like.

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming a new way for people to interact with the web, but most small-business websites were built for humans and search engines — not for agents. 

 A business may have products, services, prices, booking options or contact flows publicly available, yet an AI agent can still struggle to reliably understand what the business offers or how to take action. 

 AgentReady started from a simple question: how can a small business know whether its website is actually ready for AI agents? 

 What it does 

 AgentReady audits a real website and evaluates its AI commerce readiness across three dimensions: 

 Visibility → Understanding → Buyability 

 It analyzes observable commercial information, evaluates what an AI agent can reliably understand, and produces evidence-based scores and prioritized recommendations. 

 The goal is not simply to make websites more machine-readable. The goal is to help businesses move from being visible to AI agents to becoming genuinely understandable and actionable by them. 

 AgentReady also exposes its audit capability directly to AI agents through WebMCP. 

 The native WebMCP tool agentready.run_audit allows an agent to launch the same website audit available to a human through the AgentReady interface and receive structured results including readiness scores, observed evidence, recommended actions, rendering provenance and monitoring eligibility. 

 This creates one capability for two users: 

 Humans get a clear visual audit. AI agents get a structured, callable tool. 

 How we built it 

 AgentReady uses an evidence-first audit architecture designed to avoid inventing commercial facts. 

 The challenge demo combines a browser interface with a bounded server-side audit function. For JavaScript-heavy websites where the initial HTML does not expose enough reliable evidence, AgentReady can use a controlled browser-rendering fallback and clearly reports that provenance. 

 The WebMCP integration registers agentready.run_audit through: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 The tool calls the same AgentReady audit capability used by the human interface and returns structured content that an AI agent can consume directly. 

 This means WebMCP is not a separate demonstration layer: humans and agents access the same underlying capability. 

 AgentReady also includes monitoring of comparable audits over time, allowing businesses to identify improvements or degradation in their AI readiness while avoiding false comparisons when an acquisition is incomplete. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest problem has been factual reliability across very different types of websites. 

 Real-world sites contain navigation elements, product cards, booking flows, duplicated prices, dynamic JavaScript content and commercial information distributed across different structures. 

 AgentReady therefore follows a simple principle: 

 Observed, not assumed. 

 If reliable evidence cannot be observed, the system should report uncertainty rather than manufacture a confident answer. 

 Another challenge was making dynamic website audits reproducible. The browser-rendering fallback and monitoring eligibility rules were designed to prevent incomplete page acquisition from creating misleading readiness changes. 

 What's next 

 The next step is expanding AgentReady from one callable audit capability into a broader AI commerce readiness layer where detected gaps can map to additional WebMCP actions. 

 The longer-term loop is: 

 Audit → Detect capability gap → Expose capability → Agent takes action 

 The vision is to make AI commerce readiness accessible to small businesses that do not have dedicated technical teams — so they can participate in an increasingly agent-driven web without having to understand the underlying technology.

A human + agent weather experience for Indonesia

Ask the app what you want to know in natural language, and let a WebMCP-capable agent turn that intent into live weather actions on the page.

 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Indonesia is a country of thousands of islands, diverse climates, and rapidly changing weather conditions. Yet checking the weather often still means opening multiple apps, searching for a city, interpreting forecast charts, and deciding what the information actually means for a trip or daily activity. 

 We wanted to explore a different experience: what if people could simply tell a weather agent what they need, and the agent could understand their intent, find the relevant weather information, and take action for them? 

 That idea became Nusantara Weather - WebMCP Agent Weather . 

 The project was inspired by the emerging WebMCP vision of a web where humans and AI agents can interact through real, useful tools. Instead of building another static weather dashboard, we wanted to create a weather interface that acts as a bridge between human intent and structured weather actions . 

 A user should not need to know which forecast API to call or which data points matter. They should be able to say: 

 
 “Find the safest dry window to travel in Bandung this afternoon.” 
 

 And the application should understand the request, gather the relevant weather data, analyze it, and present a useful answer. 

 What it does 

 Nusantara Weather combines a beautiful weather dashboard with an agent-ready WebMCP interface . 

 Users can explore weather across Indonesia by selecting a city or searching for a city through the Find a city interface. The main dashboard highlights five major cities for a clean and focused experience, while typing into the search bar reveals additional Indonesian cities as suggestions. 

 The application can also understand natural-language weather requests through WebMCP tools. 

 For example: 

 
 “Find the next dry window in Jakarta.” 

 “Compare Bandung and Surabaya for rain today.” 

 “What is the safest time to travel in Bali this afternoon?” 
 

 The agent can use registered WebMCP tools to retrieve weather information, compare locations, identify upcoming rain windows, and follow the user's intent. 

 The project includes tools such as: 

 
 get_indonesia_weather — retrieves current and forecast weather for a selected Indonesian city. 
 compare_indonesia_weather — compares weather conditions between cities. 
 find_next_rain_window — identifies upcoming periods with higher or lower rain probability. 
 follow_weather_prompt — interprets a natural-language request and drives the application according to the user's intent. 
 

 The key idea is that the user describes the goal, while the agent handles the interaction with the web application . 

 How we built it 

 We built Nusantara Weather as a lightweight web application with a strong focus on progressive enhancement and agent interoperability. 

 The frontend provides: 

 
 A modern weather dashboard 
 Indonesia-focused city search 
 Top-city recommendations 
 Forecast and rain information 
 Natural-language prompt interaction 
 Agent activity and decision feedback 
 Responsive UI for different screen sizes 
 

 For weather data, the application uses live forecast information from Open-Meteo. 

 For the agent layer, we implemented the WebMCP Imperative API using the required tool registration pattern: 
 await document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "get_indonesia_weather" , 
 description : "Get weather conditions and forecast for an Indonesian city." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 city : { 
 type : "string" , 
 description : "Indonesian city name" 
 } 
 } , 
 required : [ "city" ] 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 // Fetch weather data
 // Update application state
 // Return structured weather information
 } 
 } ) ; 
 
 This means the application is not only designed for humans clicking buttons. It exposes structured capabilities that an AI agent can discover and execute. 

 The architecture follows a simple flow: 

 Human prompt → Agent intent → WebMCP tool → Weather data → Decision → UI update 

 We also designed the application with progressive enhancement in mind. The weather website remains usable as a normal website, while WebMCP-enabled environments can interact with the same application through agent-accessible tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was designing an interface that works well for both humans and agents. 

 Traditional web interfaces are usually built around clicks, buttons, forms, and navigation. Agents need something more structured: clearly defined tools, predictable inputs, meaningful descriptions, and structured outputs. 

 Another challenge was handling natural-language intent. 

 A request such as: 

 
 “When should I leave for Bandung if I want to avoid rain?” 
 

 doesn't directly map to a single API call. The system has to translate the user's goal into a sequence of actions: 

 
 Identify the destination. 
 Understand the requested time period. 
 Retrieve forecast data. 
 Evaluate rain conditions. 
 Determine the most suitable window. 
 Present the result in a human-friendly way. 
 

 We also wanted the interface to stay visually simple even though the application supports a large number of Indonesian cities. Instead of showing every city immediately, the frontend focuses on five major cities and reveals additional cities dynamically through search suggestions. 

 Finally, WebMCP is an evolving part of the web platform, so we had to think carefully about compatibility and progressive enhancement rather than assuming every browser has the same capabilities. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that Nusantara Weather is more than a weather visualization. 

 It demonstrates how a web application can become agent-interactable without sacrificing the human experience . 

 Some highlights we are especially proud of: 

 
 We implemented real WebMCP tool registration with document.modelContext.registerTool() . 
 We created multiple purpose-built weather tools instead of exposing one generic API endpoint. 
 We added a natural-language follow_weather_prompt workflow that connects user intent to application behavior. 
 We created an Indonesia-focused city dataset with coverage across major regions and islands. 
 We designed the city search so the interface stays clean while still supporting many locations. 
 We built the product around decisions and actions rather than simply showing raw forecast numbers. 
 We created a polished visual identity for the project, including a custom Indonesia weather favicon. 
 

 Most importantly, we believe the project demonstrates a compelling direction for the open web: 

 websites that are understandable not only to humans, but also to intelligent agents. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building an agent-friendly web application requires a different way of thinking about product design. 

 It is not enough to expose data. The application needs to expose capabilities . 

 A useful agent tool should answer questions like: 

 
 What does this tool do? 
 What input does it expect? 
 What result will it return? 
 Can the action change application state? 
 Is the result meaningful enough for an agent to reason about? 
 

 We also learned that natural-language interfaces work best when the underlying system is structured and predictable. 

 The prompt may be unstructured, but the execution should not be. 

 That led us to a design principle we will continue using: 

 Unstructured human intent in, structured actions out. 

 Finally, we learned that great agent experiences should not replace good human interfaces. The strongest experience is one where humans can interact directly while agents can use the exact same web capabilities programmatically. 

 What's next for Nusantara Weather - WebMCP Agent Weather 

 Nusantara Weather is only the beginning. 

 Our next step is to make the agent significantly more capable of understanding real-world context. 

 We want users to eventually be able to ask things like: 

 
 “I have a flight from Jakarta to Bali tomorrow. When is the safest time to leave for the airport?” 
 

 or: 

 
 “I'm planning an outdoor event in Bandung this weekend. Find the best day and explain why.” 
 

 From there, Nusantara Weather could combine weather with additional web capabilities such as: 

 
 Traffic and travel conditions 
 Flight and transportation information 
 Local ev

title: Shredly
pitch: Shredly is MCP as a Service. Create and manage MCP servers for your products, no code to deploy, no infrastructure to manage. Now Shredly offers WebMCP to dynamically update your site tools
about_excerpt:
Shredly is MCP as a Service. Create and manage MCP servers for your products, no code to deploy, no infrastructure to manage. Now Shredly offers WebMCP to dynamically update your site tools Like Comment Story Updates 1 2 3 Inspiration Shredly lets developers host MCP servers without managing infrastructure. You define your tools in a dashboard and Shredly handles the rest. But those tools lived entirely server-side. WebMCP changes that, the new browser-native standard lets a webpage register tools directly for AI agents to discover and call. The gap was obvious to us, if we could bridge Shredly's hosted tool definitions into site tools, a site owner could add a new tool in their Shredly dashboard and have it appear as a live site tool for ChatGPT — no redeploy, no code change. What it does shredly-webmcp is a tiny CDN library that bridges Shredly's hosted MCP servers to the browser's WebMCP API. Drop one tag into your page, point it at your Shredly MCP slug, and AI agents browsing your site immediately see your tools in their Site tools panel. Add a new tool in the Shredly dashboard — it appears on your site automatically, with no redeployment. For tools that require user context, a getToken callback resolves the user's Bearer token fresh on every invocation, so per-user auth works even when the user logs in after the page loads.

How we built it

The library is a plain ES module, no build step, no bundler, no dependencies. It calls tools/list on Shredly's JSON-RPC API at page load to fetch tool definitions, then registers each one via document.modelContext.registerTool(). An execute handler proxies tools/call back to Shredly, injecting the user's token at invocation time. A 30-second polling loop picks up any tools added or changed in the dashboard without a page reload. We also built a demo site showing the full flow: connect to any Shredly MCP slug, watch the tools render live, and invoke them directly from the UI. The library ships on a CDN at cdn.shredly.io

Challenges we ran into

document.modelContext did not seem to exist until the ChatGPT desktop app companion browser injects it — and that injection can happen asynchronously after the page scripts have already run. The library had to queue pending tool registrations and flush them the moment the API became available, using a polling loop rather than a one-shot check. We also had to rethink authentication: tools/list (tool discovery) must be unauthenticated so tools register at page load without requiring a token, while tools/call injects the user's token only at invocation time. Getting that split right in the MCP handler required restructuring the auth check to happen after body parsing, not before. CDN cache headers were another gotcha — immutable cache during active development meant stale builds were served long after deploys.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The zero-redeploy update loop works. You can add a tool in the Shredly dashboard, wait 30 seconds, and watch it appear in the ChatGPT Site tools panel on a live deployed site — without touching any code. The library is also small: a single ES module file with no dependencies that any developer can drop into an existing site in two lines. The getToken pattern for per-user auth is clean — it decouples tool registration (which happens at page load) from authorization (which happens at call time), making it work naturally with any auth flow.

What we learned

WebMCP is strict about timing: tools must be registered during the initial page load, not behind a user interaction or async gate. That constraint shaped the entire architecture — the library has to start fetching and registering immediately, before the user has done anything.

What's next for Shredly

Publishing shredly-webmcp to npm so React, Vue, and Svelte apps can bundle it properly without CDN workarounds. Deeper dashboard integration — showing site owners which of their pages have the library installed and surfacing per-tool invocation analytics. OAuth support for getToken flows where the user needs to authorize access before tools can be called. And as WebMCP adoption grows beyond ChatGPT, making sure the bridge works across every agent that implements document.modelContext.

Threadwise turns body measurements into brand-specific apparel size recommendations, helping shoppers avoid poor fits with explainable, privacy-first WebMCP tools.

 Story

 Threadwise 

 Threadwise helps online shoppers find the right apparel size when every brand uses a different size chart. 

 The Problem 

 A shopper may wear a medium in one brand and a large in another. 

 Traditional size labels are too generic, and product pages often make it difficult to compare chest, waist, shoulder, and sleeve measurements. 

 This leads to uncertainty, poor fit, and unnecessary returns. 

 Our Solution 

 Threadwise lets shoppers enter their measurements and preferred fit, then compares them against each garment’s own size chart. 

 It returns: 

 
 A recommended size 
 A confidence score 
 Area-by-area fit details 
 Possible warnings 
 An alternative size 
 

 Threadwise also supports real product links. 

 A shopper can paste a product URL and the size-chart rows from that page, then receive a real-time recommendation without requiring marketplace scraping or retailer credentials. 

 Why WebMCP? 

 WebMCP allows Threadwise to expose structured tools that AI agents can discover and use. 

 The available tools include: 
 list_garments
get_size_chart
recommend_garment_size
compare_product_fits
analyze_product_link
 
 Instead of guessing from labels such as “medium” or “large,” an agent can call the appropriate tool, provide structured measurements, and receive an explainable result. 

 The shopper remains in control of their measurements and decisions. 

 Privacy First 

 Measurements stay in the browser by default. 

 Threadwise does not require an account and does not send body measurements to retailers. 

 The app does not use body photographs, infer sensitive personal attributes, or claim guaranteed fit. 

 Recommendations are presented as transparent estimates, not certainty. 

 Built For 

 Threadwise is designed for online apparel shoppers who want more confidence before ordering. 

 The same approach can later help independent apparel stores reduce size-related returns and improve product size charts. 

 What We Built 

 The prototype includes: 

 
 A responsive apparel catalog 
 Store-specific body and garment size charts 
 Unit conversion between centimeters and inches 
 Slim, regular, and relaxed fit preferences 
 Explainable scoring and confidence levels 
 Real product-link analysis using user-supplied chart data 
 WebMCP tool registration 
 Browser-only measurement handling 
 Accessible and responsive UI 
 

 Future Improvements 

 Future versions could support authorized merchant feeds, official retailer APIs, better garment-category models, and feedback loops based on anonymized fit outcomes.

Spotigo lets you describe a civic problem out loud — a pothole, a downed power line — and an agent turns that into a filed report, but it can never hit submit without your explicit yes.

 Comment

 Gemini : POW of WebMCP integration 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 architecture diagram 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 website 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Gemini : POW of WebMCP integration 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Spotigo — Project Story 

 A WebMCP-powered civic agent that turns human intent into safe, executable web actions. 

 
 Describe the problem. Let the agent handle the workflow. Keep the human in control of the part that matters. 
 

 Inspiration 

 The web already has the services people need. The friction is almost never "does this exist" — it's "can I get from what I want to say to the specific form this particular website expects." A citizen who sees a pothole thinks someone should report this , not let me figure out which municipal category this falls under, whether it's already been reported, and how to phrase it correctly. The problem exists. The digital service to fix it probably exists too. The gap is entirely in connecting human intent to that workflow — and that gap is exactly what WebMCP is positioned to close. 

 My first idea wasn't civic reporting at all — it was an accessible, voice-first grocery storefront. Before building much of it, I checked what was already in the WebMCP showcase and found Verdant Market already occupying that lane: "browse groceries and build a shared cart with an agent." Rather than build a variation on an existing reference app, I kept the one pattern worth keeping — the agent prepares, the human confirms — and moved it to a domain where getting that confirmation wrong actually matters: civic reporting, where the output is a public record, not a grocery order. 

 What it does 

 A citizen describes a civic issue by voice or text — "there's a huge pothole near my office" — and an agent turns that into a real, trackable report, gated by explicit human confirmation at the one step that counts. 

 Spotigo registers 10 WebMCP tools in the browser through document.modelContext , deliberately shaped as a workflow rather than a flat list: 

 
 
 Stage 
 Tools 
 
 
 
 Understand 
 describe_issue_accessibly , report_civic_issue 
 
 
 Validate 
 check_duplicate_reports , list_nearby_reports 
 
 
 Explain 
 read_report_summary 
 
 
 Authorize 
 confirm_submission , acknowledge_safety_guidance 
 
 
 Act 
 submit_report 
 
 
 Recover / Track 
 undo_last_action , get_report_status 
 
 

 A real pass through it: the agent structures "huge pothole near my office" into a draft — category pothole , description, resolved location — checks it against nearby reports and comes back with a graded confidence assessment (not a flat yes/no), then reads the draft back in plain language: "I'm about to report a large pothole at this location with this description. Submit it?" Only after an explicit confirm: true does submit_report become callable, returning a real tracking ID the citizen can check later with get_report_status . 

 How we built it 

 Zero build step, zero runtime dependencies, static files only — deliberate, so the WebMCP layer itself stays the thing under inspection, not something buried under framework abstraction. 

 One execution path, not two. The human-facing UI and the agent-facing WebMCP tools call the same tool.execute() closures — there's no separate "demo path" for the agent. If a judge opens the on-page Tool Tester and fires submit_report before confirming, they get the identical rejection an agent would get, because it's literally the same code running either way. 

 Ten tools, not one do_everything() . It would have been simpler to expose a single submit_report(details) function and let a system prompt handle the reasoning. That would hide exactly the part worth demonstrating — the validation, the safety boundaries, the point where understanding what someone wants stops being enough to act on it. Decomposing the workflow into explicit stages made the tool surface mirror the actual application logic instead of papering over it. 

 Intent is not authorization. The agent can understand the issue, check for duplicates, and explain what it's about to do — none of that authorizes submit_report . That gate is enforced in code: confirm: "yes" is truthy in JavaScript but explicitly rejected, because a loose check could let an ambiguous model output pass as authorization. Only strict confirm: true opens the gate. 

 The gate adapts to risk. Routine issues get one confirmation. Safety-critical ones — a downed power line, a suspected gas leak — route through a distinct acknowledge_safety_guidance step first, and lose the normal undo safety net once submitted. A pothole and a live wire aren't the same category of decision, and treating them identically would have been the easier, lazier design. 

 A second, separate experiment. server.js and server/ implement a persistent, authenticated MCP service for agents connecting outside the browser — real action storage, ownership isolation, rate limiting, a fail-closed authority resolver. It is explicitly not part of the deployed judged demo. I kept that line hard rather than implying a backend was live when it wasn't. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Choosing what not to build. The competitive check that killed the grocery idea happened before most of the code existed, which made it cheap. That ordering — research first, fall in love with the implementation second — was the single highest-leverage decision in the project. 

 Making confirmation a real boundary, not a suggestion. Getting the strict-boolean check right ( confirm: true vs. anything merely truthy) sounds trivial until you consider that an LLM producing "yes" or 1 instead of true is a completely plausible failure mode, and a loose check would have let it silently authorize a submission. 

 A Windows path bug invisible in my own dev loop. Automated smoke tests passed cleanly in my Linux sandbox and failed immediately on the actual Windows machine, with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_ESM_URL_SCHEME — Node's dynamic import() requires a proper file:// URL on Windows; a raw path like D:\...\app.js doesn't qualify, even though the POSIX equivalent works fine elsewhere. One-line fix ( pathToFileURL() ), but a reminder that "tests pass" and "tests pass in the environment a judge will actually use" are different claims. 

 Git history discipline under time pressure. A substantial chunk of work — the entire server/MCP layer — sat uncommitted for longer than it should have while heads-down building it. A last-minute dump commit would have technically satisfied "real commit history" while missing its point. Going back and committing it in logical pieces was extra effort late in the process, but it was the honest version of the requirement. 

 Resisting the urge to claim more than was deployed. Once the server prototype worked locally, the tempting move was to fold it into the headline pitch. The harder, better call was a README section that draws a hard line between what's live and judged versus what's a local Phase 2 prototype — because a panel this technical will check claims against what's actually running, and a claim that doesn't reproduce live costs more than the claim was worth. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A confirmation gate that's a real, tested execution boundary — including catching and rejecting confirm: "yes" , the exact kind of loose value a model might plausibly produce. 
 A risk-tiered version of that gate, where safety-critical issues require a distinct second acknowledgement and lose the undo safety net, because not every civic issue carries the same stakes. 
 One execution path for humans and agents — no shadow demo logic, verifiable by anyone who opens the Tool Tester. 
 22 passing tests, including one that runs the full judge-facing scenario — draft → duplicate check → review → both negative confirmation cases → submission → tracking ID → status lookup — against the real tool closures. 
 One honestly-scoped, fully-working vertical, with a second experimental server layer clearly labeled as not part of the judged demo, instead of five thinly-demonstrated domains. 
 

 What we learned 

 The real opportunity here isn't "AI plus websites" — it's AI agents plus websites that expose capabilities an agent can reliably us

title: Rx WebMCP Pharmacy
pitch: Built with WebMCP: a pharmacy site where AI agents call real tools for refills, interaction checks, prescription reads , while a human still approves anything sensitive.

Built with WebMCP: a pharmacy site where AI agents call real tools for refills, interaction checks, prescription reads , while a human still approves anything sensitive.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 A live record of every decision made, whether by a caregiver clicking Approve or an agent calling a tool 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The pharmacy page — medications, refill status, and a smart prescription upload box, all exposed to agents via WebMCP tools. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 An uploaded prescription photo, read automatically by AI vision and held for caregiver review before anything is added 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Every sensitive action — a controlled-substance refill or an AI-read prescription — waits here for a real person's approval 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 A live record of every decision made, whether by a caregiver clicking Approve or an agent calling a tool 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The pharmacy page — medications, refill status, and a smart prescription upload box, all exposed to agents via WebMCP tools. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 An uploaded prescription photo, read automatically by AI vision and held for caregiver review before anything is added 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Every sensitive action — a controlled-substance refill or an AI-read prescription — waits here for a real person's approval 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 A live record of every decision made, whether by a caregiver clicking Approve or an agent calling a tool 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Now there is somewhere an adult child who holds onto the phone at a pharmacy trying to refill their mother’s prescription for blood pressure medicine before the weekend. Elsewhere a caregiver tries to figure out whether the two medications his parent is taking can be taken together, but the only person who would know about that is a pharmacist at work behind a desk. 

 This project came into existence when the question popped up in our mind: what if an AI could really help with that? Not impersonating a customer clicking through the website but rather being trusted in doing something which is a responsibility of a regular person. 

 The reality is, most of existing AI agents are not trustworthy when comes to such kind of jobs. They browse the websites like a tourist browsing the menu without knowing the language — guessing, clicking wrong links, and sometimes making serious mistakes. For the healthcare sector, "occasionally wrong" means something different than just a rounding error. It's the wrong medication! 

 This is what WebMCP was designed to overcome. 

 What it does 

 WebMCP Pharmacy is a demonstration site designed to showcase the capabilities of WebMCP in a practical and high-pressure situation — a simulated pharmacy rather than a real one, based on the needs of managing prescription medication for an elderly parent (Meera Sharma) for her family members. 

 This is a simulated scenario on purpose, as it is relatively simple to simulate an agent clicking a button, and quite hard to simulate an agent taking action that matters. This demo, therefore, showcases twelve WebMCP tools over three pages – from searching for medications, checking for refills, identifying possible drug interactions, to even reading a photo of a prescription using artificial vision – demonstrating an agent taking precise action like a human would do. 

 However, there was also much more to show than mere capacity. In order to make precision with no control mechanisms a real thing, we created a proof of concept for a human in the loop system. Each critical operation – restocking the controlled substance, confirming the prescription from an AI-driven source – requires approval from a real person via an operational interface based on real architecture. Agent suggests. Human approves. Every approval is logged. This is not a mere illustration of how oversight could be implemented – this is a real-life implementation. 

 Finally, we created something that the competition didn’t ask for at all: a side-by-side comparison mode (?webmcp=on / ?webmcp=off) that would enable anyone to confirm empirically rather than take our word for it the difference between an agent guessing what to do in an interface and an agent using a functional tool – on the exact same website, with the exact same amount of friction, but different tool access. 

 How we built it 

 Plain HTML, plain JavaScript, and document.modelContext.registerTool() . Plain because the narrative we wanted to tell wasn’t about how sophisticated the framework could be, but rather about what happens when an application decided to speak in an agent’s language instead of having agents mimic humans. 

 The reality of the underlying infrastructure, though: Upstash Redis for the caregiver-approval queue so two different browser tabs — the agent’s tab and the human’s tab — can communicate in real time. Google’s Gemini Vision model for interpreting prescriptions. And Vercel serverless functions to bring it all together. No mockups here, just live infrastructure being called out by each and every tool in this demo. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The most difficult issue was not a technical one, but rather a philosophical one: how could we show that the tool was better , and not just faster? In the beginning, we fell into the trap of measuring "who clicks through the UI quicker" — and soon understood that this was the wrong question, as chat interfaces incur costs regardless of what lies under the hood. What made the difference was that we found a question, the answer to which could not possibly be guessed: Does this pharmacy's database indicate that there is a problem with those two drugs together? With access to tools, an agent could get the perfect response instantly, drawing from actual data. Without it, they could not know this — since such data was never supposed to be scraped and only requested properly. 

 We also had to confront an uncomfortable design issue: if an agent is capable of approving a prescription on behalf of a caregiver, who is really in charge? Our solution was to make the capability clear, rather than ambiguous — all caregiver-facing tools are described as features which, when used in production, will only ever be accessible to an authenticated caregiver's session. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Everything you see in the demo is genuine, not a simulation. Caregiver consent form is no mere illustration, it is built on live Redis backend that truly enables the coordination between two browser windows in real time, exactly as in real-life applications. Prescription image upload functionality truly invokes the vision model and pulls out structured data from the actual photograph. Finally, the ?webmcp=on/?webmcp=off contrast is no mere demonstration, it is exactly the same website, exactly the same level of friction, only with access to tools as the only variable, so you don't need to trust us, you can check it yourself. 

 We are especially proud of the fact that there are 12 tools spread across three pages, not just one, showing that WebMCP is good to go even for multi-page apps. 

 Actually, what we feel the most pride in is the amount of knowledge we acquired during this work, there were no pre-existing answers for us in this project. There were some non-typical issues we had to face: dealing with a depreciated version of Gemini we were using in the project while debugging the 404 to the actual answer of the API; the caregiver dashboard that failed to display the requests in progress because of mismatching the Redis key which required tracing the issue from the server side, and not the browser one; understanding that our "on vs off" comparison didn't make any sense since there was nothing in common between two modes until we rebuilt the friction and made it the same in both of them. 

 In addition, there was another thing we have learned. The implementation of the mechanism of building the trust to the agentic system is not a separate thing, which you just implement after you've finished your product. The determination of which actions the agent can perform independently and which need a human's interference affected the development process from the very beginning. 

 What we learned 

 The future of the agentic web is not in agents becoming increasingly adept at impersonating humans. Rather, it's in websites improving their ability to tell agents the truth about their capabilities — and, perhaps more importantly, what they must never be able to do on their own. 

 What's next for WebMCP Pharmacy 

 A backend that is real, meaning that a verified prescription will update the actual medical record, not some dummy entry for a demonstration log. Authenti
