The idea is simple: stop searching and start connecting
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Inspiration
Research tools help people find information, while chat tools help people ask questions. However, neither makes it easy to see how ideas, evidence, notes, and decisions connect. 

 We were inspired to build MindLink as a shared thinking space for humans and AI. The goal is simple: 

 Stop searching. Start connecting. 

 We wanted to create a tool that helps users understand research papers in simple language, challenge assumptions, discover relationships, and turn information into better decisions. 

 What it does
MindLink transforms thinking and research into an interactive visual canvas. 

 Users can: 

 Explore questions with AI-generated thoughts.
Compare optimistic and pessimistic perspectives.
Explore multiple future paths.
Search real research papers through OpenAlex.
Add papers, notes, Markdown files, paper files, and images.
Convert research into claims, evidence, methods, risks, gaps, contradictions, and questions.
Connect related thoughts with animated neural links.
Explain selected ideas in simple language.
Build a research story map.
Listen to an audio brief.
Generate images for thoughts.
Ask different AI roles for perspectives, including Investor, Mentor, Domain Expert, Future You, and Devil’s Advocate.
Zoom, move, edit, pin, and delete thoughts.
Lock decisions after reviewing possible outcomes.
Interact with the canvas through WebMCP tools.
MindLink does not just store information. It maps understanding. 

 How we built it
MindLink was built with: 

 Next.js
React
TypeScript
Tailwind CSS
Zustand
Groq AI
OpenAlex
WebMCP
Lucide React
FFmpeg for demo media creation
The application uses a visual canvas where every thought is represented as a node. Nodes contain metadata such as type, source, trust level, author, and relationships. 

 The Research Desk provides a focused workspace for finding papers, adding user context, explaining ideas, creating story maps, and generating audio briefs. 

 We used OpenAlex to retrieve real academic papers from the web. Research results are added to the canvas with source links and confidence indicators so users can distinguish evidence from interpretation. 

 WebMCP exposes MindLink actions to compatible AI agents, including starting a session, adding thoughts, expanding ideas, challenging assumptions, reading the canvas state, locking decisions, and finding research papers. 

 Challenges we ran into
One major challenge was designing a canvas that remained useful as more thoughts and connections appeared. We needed to make relationships visible without overwhelming the user. 

 We also had to handle uncertainty responsibly. AI-generated research explanations can sound confident even when evidence is weak, so we added source labels, trust levels, and clear distinctions between evidence, interpretation, risks, and open questions. 

 Another challenge was combining multiple interaction types in one workspace: research search, file input, visual mapping, audio, images, AI roles, decision-making, and WebMCP. We focused on keeping the canvas as the central experience while moving research tools into a collapsible sidebar. 

 Finally, we had to make the demo reliable even when an AI API was unavailable. We added fallback responses so the core research experience could still be demonstrated. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of
We are proud that MindLink turns a research question into a connected visual experience instead of another chat transcript. 

 Our key accomplishments include: 

 Building a working human + AI thinking canvas.
Adding real research paper retrieval through OpenAlex.
Creating a dedicated Research Desk workspace.
Adding animated neural links between ideas.
Supporting paper explanations with evidence-oriented node types.
Adding audio briefs and visual story mapping.
Adding WebMCP tools for AI-agent interaction.
Preserving human control through editing, challenging, source inspection, and decision confirmation.
Creating a polished hackathon demo with narrated video and visual documentation.
What we learned
We learned that useful AI products are not only about generating better answers. They are also about helping users understand where an answer came from, how reliable it is, and what should happen next. 

 We learned that visual structure can make complex research easier to understand. Separating a paper into questions, methods, claims, evidence, limitations, contradictions, and gaps gives users a more useful mental model than a single summary. 

 We also learned that human control is essential. The best experience is not AI making decisions alone, but AI helping people see possibilities, challenge assumptions, and make more informed decisions. 

 What's next for MindLink
Next, we plan to make MindLink a complete personal research memory system. 

 Planned improvements include: 

 Full PDF text extraction and document parsing.
OCR for scanned papers and research images.
Persistent research libraries beyond browser storage.
Semantic search across personal notes and papers.
Automatic citation and reference graph generation.
More advanced paper diagrams and concept maps.
Better source passage and page-level citations.
Multi-paper contradiction and consensus detection.
Personalized research podcasts with multiple AI voices.
Story-based video generation from research maps.
Zotero, Obsidian, and Markdown export.
Collaborative research workspaces.
The long-term vision is for MindLink to become a living map of a person’s knowledge: a place where papers, ideas, questions, evidence, and decisions continuously connect and grow.

 My contributions included: 

 Designed the product concept around “Stop Searching. Start Connecting.”
 Built the interactive mind canvas with draggable, editable, pinnable, and deletable thought nodes.
 Implemented Explore, Debate, Parallel, Research, and Roles modes.

title: Privacy Nutrition Label
pitch: A WebMCP-native checkout that helps people and agents understand why data is requested, choose the minimum necessary data, and receive a privacy receipt.\n\n
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native checkout that helps people and agents understand why data is requested, choose the minimum necessary data, and receive a privacy receipt.


 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP write tool completes checkout only after explicit confirmation and keeps personal form values inside the page. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The human-facing Privacy Nutrition Label explains what checkout data is required, what is optional, and why—before the user acts. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The read-only WebMCP tool gives the agent structured checkout privacy facts without returning personal form values. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP write tool completes checkout only after explicit confirmation and keeps personal form values inside the page. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The human-facing Privacy Nutrition Label explains what checkout data is required, what is optional, and why—before the user acts. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The read-only WebMCP tool gives the agent structured checkout privacy facts without returning personal form values. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP write tool completes checkout only after explicit confirmation and keeps personal form values inside the page. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I kept coming back to a simple problem that privacy policies contain a lot of information, but they rarely help with the decision someone is making right now. 

 At checkout, a website might ask for a name, email, address, phone number, account creation and marketing consent all on the same page. It is often unclear which of these are genuinely required, why they are being requested, and what can be left out. A privacy policy may contain the answer somewhere, but most people are not going to stop halfway through checkout and search through a long legal document. 

 I was also thinking about what happens after checkout. If a service later suffers a data breach, information it never collected cannot be exposed. Helping someone share less at the beginning can therefore reduce the amount of personal data placed at risk. 

 Privacy labels make data practices easier to see, but I wanted to go one step further. I did not want an AI agent to generate another summary by scraping a policy or guessing from the interface. I wanted the website itself to explain what the current action requires in a structured form that both a person and an agent can understand. 

 That became the idea behind Privacy Nutrition Label which is a small, action-specific privacy contract that appears when the decision actually matters. 

 What it does 

 I built the project around Relay, a fictional electronics retailer with a realistic guest checkout flow. Before completing an order, the customer can open a Privacy Nutrition Label showing: 

 
 which data groups are required 
 which data groups are optional 
 why each group is requested 
 who receives it 
 what the minimum-data choice is 
 whether advertising tracking is involved 
 

 The same declaration is available to an AI agent through WebMCP. The agent can inspect the checkout, explain the required and optional information, and recommend the minimum-disclosure path: continue as a guest, leave out the phone number and decline marketing. 

 I also wanted the final decision to remain with the person. Inspecting the label does not place the order. The state-changing checkout tool can only run after the person explicitly confirms their choices. 

 Once the demo order is completed, Relay produces a Privacy Receipt showing which data categories were used and which optional categories were left out. 

 The Orbit Home Companion adds a second privacy layer to the demo. Its device declaration explains that it has no camera, processes voice on-device by default and makes cloud features opt-in. This is kept separate from the checkout label so that product privacy and transaction privacy are not mixed together. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would have to inspect form labels, scrape a privacy policy or infer how the checkout behaves. That might work sometimes, but it also leaves room for outdated information and incorrect assumptions. 

 WebMCP allows Relay to declare its own checkout behaviour directly. The agent receives a predictable structure containing data categories, purposes, required and optional status, sharing information and a minimum-data recommendation. 

 This matters because the agent is not only reading information. After explaining the privacy choices and receiving confirmation, it can help the person act on those choices through a separate write tool. 

 I did not want WebMCP to be an extra feature added to an otherwise normal checkout. It is what makes the privacy information understandable and actionable at the moment of decision. 

 How it creates a better user experience 

 People should not need privacy or legal expertise just to understand a checkout form. 

 The human-facing label is designed to be scanned quickly. Someone can see that three data groups are required, two are optional and no advertising tracking is involved before deciding what to share. 

 If they are using an agent, the agent can inspect the same declaration and explain it in plain language. This avoids having one explanation in the interface and a different interpretation from the agent. 

 The person still stays in control. The agent can inspect and recommend, but it cannot complete the checkout until the person confirms the exact choices. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 In this flow, the website provides the facts, the agent helps interpret them and the person makes the final decision. 

 The agent can compare the required and optional categories, explain why they are requested and recommend the minimum-data option. The person can accept or change that recommendation. Only then can the agent complete the local demo checkout using the confirmed choices. 

 Without this structure, the person would need to inspect the form and policy themselves while trusting the agent to infer what the website means. With WebMCP, the website, agent and person are working from the same declared information. 

 How I built it 

 I built Privacy Nutrition Label as a solo project using React, TypeScript and Vite, then deployed it as a static site on Netlify. 

 The page registers two tools through document.modelContext : 

 
 inspect_checkout_privacy is read-only. It opens the visible Privacy Nutrition Label and returns the declared categories, purposes, sharing information, required or optional status and minimum-data recommendation 
 complete_private_checkout is state-changing. It accepts privacy choices rather than personal form values, requires confirmed to be explicitly true, validates the completed form inside the page and returns a category-level receipt 
 

 I deliberately kept personal values out of the tool interface. A name, email, address or phone number stays inside the webpage. The agent receives the privacy declaration and the person’s choices, but not those values. 

 The demo has no backend, database, authentication service, analytics, payment provider or external font request. Refreshing the page clears the order. The human checkout also remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 I added eleven automated tests covering privacy defaults, malformed inputs, missing fields, confirmation requirements, repeated execution and category-only outputs. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest design decision was not the interface. It was deciding what the agent should not receive. 

 Passing the whole checkout form to the tool would have been easier, but it would have contradicted the data-minimisation idea behind the project. The agent needs to understand the privacy contract and the person’s choices; it does not need their identity or delivery details in its response. 

 I therefore separated the flow into clear boundaries: 

 
 the webpage keeps the personal form values 
 the agent receives the privacy declaration and confirmed choices 
 the write tool performs the local action only after explicit confirmation 
 

 Another challenge was deciding how much information belonged in the label. I wanted it to include purpose, optionality and sharing without turning it into another document that people would ignore. 

 Keeping product privacy separate from checkout privacy was also important. Orbit’s camera and voice-processing declaration belongs to the device, while the Privacy Nutrition Label describes the current purchase. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 
 WebMCP changes the interaction instead of simply duplicating a webpage button 
 The read tool opens the same

title: RoboBuddy IDE
pitch: RoboBuddy IDE lets AI agents safely control and inspect a modeled robotic simulation (MicroDuck et al.) through browser-native WebMCP—making robotics learning visible and interactive.

RoboBuddy IDE lets AI agents safely control and inspect a modeled robotic simulation (MicroDuck et al.) through browser-native WebMCP—making robotics learning visible and interactive.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 SO-101 Follower simulator 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Microduck simulator 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 LeKiwi simulator 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Unitree G1 simulator 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Bimanual OpenArm simulator 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 SO-101 Follower simulator 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Microduck simulator 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 LeKiwi simulator 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Unitree G1 simulator 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Bimanual OpenArm simulator 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 SO-101 Follower simulator 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 RoboBuddy began in November 2025 when I helped my daughter with an elementary-school project: we 3D-printed and built an Arduino-based 6 DOF robotic arm, then controlled it from a web interface ( RoboBuddy ). That project sparked my own interest in robotics. I later built and operated an SO-101 follower arm using its 3D mesh rigs ( RoboBuddy AI ). 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to make robotics exploration more approachable: one browser workspace that humans and agents can use side by side, without a separate project-specific API-key workflow. My original idea was to program robotic arms for scientific lab operations. Then MicroDuck arrived and offered a playful, immediately understandable way to demonstrate agent-accessible web capabilities. 

 What I built 

 RoboBuddy IDE is a browser-based robotics workspace with a code editor, simulation controls, and a 3D MicroDuck policy simulation. Through a bounded WebMCP tool surface, agents can inspect the modeled state and make focused, visible changes—such as moving the duck, interacting with the ball and scene, or adding temporary measurement cues. 

 The experience is designed to be understandable and reversible. Actions stay inside the browser demo, and temporary visual cues disappear on refresh. RoboBuddy IDE does not claim physical hardware control through this WebMCP demo. 

 How I built it 

 I used GPT-5.6-Sol in Codex as a development collaborator to build the IDE interface, integrate the MicroDuck model, and develop WebMCP functions for the duck, related objects, and 3D environment. 
RoboBuddy IDE was built during the submission period. It builds on lessons from earlier RoboBuddy robotics experiments, but the submitted browser IDE, WebMCP collaboration surface, and MicroDuck experience are new work created for this challenge.
The goal was to build useful, comprehensible, expandable capabilities that a human can observe alongside the agent. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP made the application feel less like a page to automate and more like a set of intentional shared capabilities. Pairing each agent action with visible state makes it easier to see what changed, why it matters, and how to reset the experiment. That makes the experience easier to trust, teach with, and extend. 

 Challenges 

 The main constraints were time and the weekly limits on my Pro account. Technically, GPT-5.6-Sol enabled very fast iteration. The careful challenge was maintaining honest boundaries between a browser simulation and physical robotics while keeping the demo inviting for a broad audience. 

 What comes next (current) 

 This experience inspired me to explore WebMCP in my other learning and science projects, including Lab Studio , AssayLens , and RoboStudio Circuits . Even if I cannot submit them all, they show how human-visible, bounded agent capabilities can extend across robotics, science, and education.

"Don't fill forms. Tell us what you need." > Sub-headline: An Intent-First Web for Citizens — Powered by WebMCP > Target Event: The WebMCP Challenge (OpenAI, Google Chrome, Cloudflare, Vercel, Shopify

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every citizen knows the frustration of interacting with public service portals. Even in modern digital states like Thailand—where identity infrastructure such as ThaID has made remarkable progress in digital authentication—citizens still find themselves trapped in "form purgatory."
Logging in is no longer the hardest step; what comes after authentication is the bottleneck. A citizen wanting to update a mailing address or register for a local municipal permit still has to manually navigate complex service directories, decipher bureaucratic jargon, and re-type 15 to 30 redundant fields (name, national identification number, sub-district, district, postal code, and contact information) over and over again for every different agency.
When we discovered the WebMCP standard, a realization hit us: the web does not need another government portal or chatbot widget; the web needs to become machine-actionable. We asked ourselves:
"What if citizens never had to fill out another public form? What if they could simply state their goal, and an AI agent collaborated with the browser to do the tedious mechanical work—while keeping the human fully in control and preserving strict data privacy?"
That question gave birth to Citizen's Easy (CZE). 

 What it does 

 CZE shifts the citizen-web interaction paradigm from "Form-First" (human as manual typist) to "Intent-First" (human as supervisor and decision-maker).
Natural Intent Expression: Instead of navigating complex drop-downs, the citizen states what they need in conversational language (e.g., "I just moved to Ideo Sukhumvit 40, Room 502/14. Please update my contact address for public correspondence.").
Granular, Privacy-Preserving Consent: CZE does not dump personal data into an opaque LLM context. Through WebMCP tools, the agent analyzes the intent and prompts the user with a Least-Privilege Consent Dialog, requesting only the specific data fields required (e.g., verified_name and registered_address, strictly omitting tax IDs, biometric tokens, or family trees).
Bidirectional WebMCP Orchestration: Once the human grants permission, the agent invokes client-side WebMCP tools:
It retrieves the verified credentials from a ThaID-compatible sandbox identity provider.
It parses the natural address into standard administrative hierarchy (Subdistrict, District, Province, Postal Code).
It dynamically populates the living form in the DOM and visibly highlights modified sections with gold focal indicators so the citizen can track changes in real time.
Validation & Human-in-the-Loop Submission: The agent runs client-side integrity checks (\text{Field Validation} = 100\%) and prepares the application summary. The final submission is locked until the human performs an explicit visual verification and clicks "Approve & Submit". 

 How we built it 

 We designed CZE to run natively within modern WebMCP-enabled environments (such as Google Chrome with WebMCP flags and the ChatGPT in-app browser).
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Citizen (Human User) │
│ Expresses Intent & Grants Consent │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────▲──────────────┘
 │ │ Visual Feedback
 ▼ │ & Verification
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
│ WebMCP Tool Registry Layer │
│ (document.modelContext.registerTool API) │
│ │
│ ├── request_citizen_consent() │
│ ├── get_verified_identity() │
│ ├── get_registered_address() │
│ ├── autofill_service_application() │
│ ├── validate_application_rules() │
│ └── submit_application() │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────▲──────────────┘
 │ Execute Mutation │ Query State
┌──────────────▼───────────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
│ CZE Client Interface │
│ - React 19 & Tailwind CSS │
│ - ThaID Sandbox Identity Provider │
│ - Reactive Form State Manager with Visual Focus Cues │
│ - Deployed on Vercel / Cloudflare Pages │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Technical Stack:
WebMCP Architecture: Registered 6 client-side tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() complying strictly with JSON Schema specifications for inputs and outputs.
Frontend Application: Built with React and styled with Tailwind CSS, designed mobile-first with adaptive touch states.
Identity Sandbox: Built a mock ThaID Identity & Consent Provider demonstrating how production digital identity tokens can safely interface with client-side agents without exposing unauthorized personal attributes.
Deployment & Hosting: Hosted and optimized on Vercel with zero-latency edge delivery. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Separating Identity from Intent (Privacy Boundary):
The biggest challenge in combining AI agents with public services is privacy. Feeding raw citizen records into an LLM context window violates fundamental data minimization standards (\text{GDPR / PDPA}). We solved this by designing an intermediate Consent Handshake: the agent never queries the identity provider directly; it calls request_citizen_consent(), which renders a browser-native modal. The token is only released to the DOM once the human approves.
Bidirectional State Sync without Jitter:
Ensuring that tool execution results from the WebMCP runtime synced seamlessly with React's internal state without causing race conditions or layout flickers required crafting deterministic action reducers for the form manager.
Deterministic Address Resolution:
Thai administrative addresses consist of nested layers (Tambon, Amphoe, Changwat, Zipcode). When a user provides messy conversational text, mapping it accurately to official administrative data required a robust validation tool (validate_application_rules) that gives structured feedback back to both the agent and the human reviewer. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 True Human-Agent Co-Creation: We avoided the cliché of a standalone chat bubble. In CZE, the agent and the human share the same canvas—the agent fills, the human inspects, and the browser visually indicates every action.
Measurable Efficiency Gain: We reduced the time required to complete a complex municipal change-of-address form from an average of T_{\text{manual}} \approx 12\text{ minutes} down to T_{\text{CZE}} \approx 35\text{ seconds}, representing a speedup efficiency factor of:
while reducing manual keystroke errors to essentially zero.
Full WebMCP Standard Adherence: Every single action on the page is exposed via clear, discoverable, and well-typed schemas using the native WebMCP browser specification. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is the missing bridge between APIs and User Interfaces: Traditional APIs connect servers to servers; UI connects servers to humans. WebMCP connects agents to interactive user interfaces, allowing the agent to operate within the exact security and permission context granted by the human in the browser.
Agent UX requires "Visual Legibility": When an agent executes tools, users feel uneasy if changes occur invisibly in the background. Adding visible highlight rings, smooth scrolling to active fields, and progressive disclosure cards dramatically increased user trust and satisfaction 

 What's next for Citizen's Easy (CZE) 

 Expanding Beyond Address Changes: Integrating additional high-friction citizen workflows, such as business license renewals, child allowance subsidies, and elderly healthcare registrations.
Official Digital ID Gateway Integration: Collaborating with standard digital identity sandboxes (such as Thailand's Department of Provincial Administration guidelines for ThaID Relying Parties) to establish an open-source standard for citizen-agent interaction.
Multi-lingual & Voice Accessibility: Leveraging web speech recognition to enable elderly or visually impaired citizens to access public services entirely through spoken dialect, making public governance accessible to every single citizen regardless of tech literacy.

I exposed web tools directly via the new WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) standard enabling browser AI agents to autonomously look up tariff rules, compute duty savings, and prepopulate customs manifests for traders in seconds. 

 What it does 

 SwiftClear is an agent-native AfCFTA trade compliance and customs declaration workspace. Key features include: 

 AI Trade Analysis : Instant HS tariff classification, rule-of-origin verification, and duty breakdown powered by Google Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite. 

 WebMCP Tool Suite : Exposes structured client-side tools directly onto navigator.modelContext so external AI web agents (or in-page agents) can query trade rules and drive the application UI. 

 AfCFTA Preferential Tariff Calculator : Calculates baseline MFN duty vs. AfCFTA preferential rates, VAT, security fees, escort fees, and net USD savings across key African transport corridors (e.g., Kano to Accra, Mombasa to Kampala). 

 Live WebMCP Inspector & Terminal : Provides a real-time event stream of WebMCP tool registration, execution requests, parameters, and dynamic DOM updates. 

 How I built it/WebMCP Architecture 

 SwiftClear is built using a modern, resilient tech stack: 

 WebMCP Standard : Implemented client-side tool registration on navigator.modelContext with a robust fallback polyfill (src/utils/webmcpPolyfill.ts) supporting event dispatching for tool execution. 

 Registered WebMCP Tools :
1) lookup_hs_code : Resolves product descriptions to 6-digit HS codes, duty rates, and AfCFTA eligibility using Gemini 3.1 Flash.
2) calculate_duties : Calculates exact duty fees, VAT, port handling, escort fees, and total clearance costs based on declared consignment value and quantity.
3) populate_customs_manifest : Injects parsed manifest state directly into the frontend reactive DOM. 

 AI Backend : Express server (server.ts) and Vercel serverless endpoint (api/gemini/analyze-trade.ts) using @google/genai with gemini-3.1-flash-lite, structured JSON schema enforcement (responseMimeType: "application/json"), and offline trade fallback models. 

 Frontend : React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Framer Motion, and Lucide Icons. 

 Challenges and Accomplishments 

 WebMCP Browser Compatibility : Chrome's native WebMCP flag (chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing) exposes a native navigator.modelContext object. I designed a dual-layer registration architecture that seamlessly interfaces with both native browser environments and standalone WebMCP bridges without breaking page state. 

 Structured AI Responses : Enforcing strict JSON schema validation with Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite to guarantee reliable numeric duty rates and standardized HS codes for seamless tool execution. 

 Trade Fallback Engine : Built a robust offline AfCFTA tariff matrix ensuring the application remains 100% operational even during network or credential unavailability. 

 What's next for Swiftclear 

 Expanded Corridor Coverage : Expand tariff data across all 54 AfCFTA signatory nations. 

 Real-time Customs API Sync : Integrate direct webhooks with national customs systems (e.g., Ghana Single Window, Nigeria Trade Portal). 

 Multi-Lingual Agent Support : Enable French, Swahili, Arabic, and Portuguese agent interactions for cross-regional trade facilitation.

CausaLens is a clinical evidence workspace where AI proposes causal claims grounded in exact patient-record sentences, challenges them with counterevidence, and leaves the final decision to the human.

 Inspiration 

 AI can summarize a clinical record, but causal questions require more than a confident answer. Evidence may support a hypothesis, contradict it, or suggest alternative explanations. We built CausaLens to make that reasoning explicit, traceable, and human-controlled. 

 What it does 

 CausaLens is a clinical evidence investigation workspace where an AI agent can propose a causal claim, while every claim remains grounded in the exact sentences from the patient record. 

 The agent can: 

 
 search the clinical record 
 retrieve a structured case summary 
 create causal claims 
 attach supporting and contradicting evidence 
 challenge its own claims 
 surface alternative explanations 
 focus specific evidence 
 update a claim's review status 
 

 Instead of automatically deciding what caused an outcome, CausaLens keeps the final judgment with the human: accept, reject, or leave the claim unresolved. 

 AI proposes. Evidence challenges. Human decides. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP turns CausaLens from a website an agent can simply view into a structured environment an agent can actually work with. 

 CausaLens exposes its investigation capabilities as WebMCP site tools. ChatGPT can discover these tools directly in its in-app browser and use them to investigate a case without guessing how to navigate the interface. 

 This enables the human and agent to share the same workspace: the agent performs evidence-intensive investigative work while the human remains responsible for consequential decisions. 

 How we built it 

 CausaLens is a web application deployed on Vercel with WebMCP integrated directly into the application. 

 We registered eight WebMCP tools for: 

 
 searching the clinical record 
 retrieving the case summary 
 creating claims 
 attaching evidence 
 challenging claims 
 adding alternative explanations 
 updating claim status 
 focusing evidence 
 

 The tools include both read and write operations. Before workspace-changing actions are executed, the agent can request human approval. 

 The demo uses a synthetic clinical case to demonstrate the workflow safely. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing tools that were useful to an AI agent without allowing the agent to bypass the human decision-making process. 

 We also had to make evidence references precise enough that claims could remain tied to specific record sentences rather than unsupported model-generated conclusions. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP makes it possible to design interfaces for humans and agents together instead of treating the agent as a separate chatbot. 

 The most important design decision was not giving the agent more autonomy, but giving it structured autonomy with evidence, challenge, and human oversight built into the workflow. 

 What's next 

 CausaLens could expand beyond the synthetic case into larger longitudinal records, richer evidence provenance, multiple competing causal hypotheses, and collaborative review workflows for research and other evidence-intensive domains. 

 This project is a research demonstration using synthetic data and is not intended for clinical diagnosis or treatment decisions.

about_excerpt:
Let your Agent use Busan through WebMCP. You set the intent, the Agent acts, and you stay in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 🌊 HELLOBUSAN: The WebMCP Agent Governance Platform 

 
 💡 Core Question: "What if a city becomes machine-readable for AI agents, while humans retain absolute control?" 

 🚀 3 Key Breakthroughs: 

 
 🌐 WebMCP City OS: Replaces unstable DOM scraping with 10 explicit WebMCP Tool schemas. 
 🔐 Agent Wallet: Granular permission boundaries (Read: ALLOW / Book: ASK / Pay: DENY). 
 ⚡ Empirical Proof: 84% faster execution & 0% DOM parsing failures. 
 
 

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming capable of reasoning, planning, and taking actions on behalf of people. But most websites are still designed only for humans. 

 I asked a simple question: 

 What if a real city could become usable by AI agents, without taking control away from people? 

 This question led me to HELLOBUSAN. 

 I chose Busan as my real-world testbed because a single human goal can require many different services: discovering places, checking events, comparing restaurants, calculating routes, managing time, estimating costs, and eventually making reservations. 

 Normally, people have to move between many websites and applications to complete these tasks. 

 I wanted to explore a different model: 

 The human expresses the goal. 

 The Agent handles the complexity. 

 WebMCP connects the Agent to real web capabilities. 

 The human remains in control of consequential actions. 

 HELLOBUSAN is therefore not just another AI travel planner. 

 It is an experiment in designing a new relationship between Humans, Agents, and Cities. 

 What it does 

 HELLOBUSAN allows a person to describe what they want to accomplish in natural language. 

 For example: 

 
 “Plan a six-hour rainy-day trip in Busan for my family within a ₩50,000 budget.” 
 

 Instead of manually searching multiple services, the Agent can use WebMCP tools to discover information and coordinate actions. 

 The Agent can: 

 
 Search places, restaurants, and events 
 Retrieve detailed information 
 Check relevant conditions such as weather 
 Calculate routes and travel time 
 Estimate and optimize the budget 
 Build and update an itinerary 
 Coordinate multiple services around one user goal 
 

 The key difference is that HELLOBUSAN does not treat autonomy as unlimited permission. 

 I designed an Agent Permission Model: 
 Search ALLOW
Compare ALLOW
Route ALLOW
Schedule ALLOW
Reservation ASK
Payment DENY

 
 How I built it 

 HELLOBUSAN is designed as a WebMCP-based agentic interface with a Cloudflare-native backend. 

 Instead of requiring an Agent to interpret a website only through visual elements, HELLOBUSAN exposes structured capabilities through WebMCP tools. 

 My tool architecture includes capabilities such as: 

 
 search_places 
 search_restaurants 
 search_events 
 get_place_details 
 get_weather 
 calculate_route 
 estimate_cost 
 get_itinerary 
 update_itinerary 
 request_reservation 
 

 Each capability has a defined purpose and structured input/output schema. 

 I separated read operations, reversible actions, and consequential actions so that the Agent's level of autonomy can be controlled. 

 The application architecture uses: 

 
 React and TypeScript for the user interface 
 WebMCP for Agent-facing web capabilities 
 Cloudflare Workers for application logic and API routing 
 Cloudflare D1 for persistent application data 
 Cloudflare Durable Objects for stateful trip sessions and coordination 
 REST APIs and structured JSON data for service integration 
 

 A key design decision was to make permissions a system-level boundary rather than merely a visual setting. 

 The interface may show that payment is disabled, but the backend must also enforce that restriction. 

 I also designed an Agent Activity Log so that users can understand what the Agent is doing instead of experiencing an invisible autonomous process. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest challenge was not generating an itinerary. 

 It was deciding where autonomy should stop. 

 Giving an Agent more capabilities is technically attractive, but greater capability also creates greater responsibility. 

 I identified three different levels of action: 

 
 READ: The Agent can retrieve and understand information. 
 ACT: The Agent can perform reversible actions such as organizing an itinerary. 
 COMMIT: The Agent performs a consequential action that may affect the user. 
 

 The third category requires human approval. 

 This became particularly important when designing reservations and payments. 

 I deliberately avoided the assumption that: 

 
 “The user asked for a trip, therefore the Agent can do anything necessary to complete it.” 
 

 Instead, the system distinguishes between intent and authority. 

 A user's intention to “plan a trip” does not automatically grant permission to spend money or make an irreversible commitment. 

 Another challenge was making WebMCP meaningful rather than decorative. 

 I did not want to build a conventional travel application and simply add a WebMCP label. 

 The Agent interaction itself had to depend on structured capabilities. 

 I therefore designed the product around a comparison between conventional web interaction and WebMCP-based interaction, focusing on task steps, tool usage, errors, completion, and human approvals. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 My biggest accomplishment is that HELLOBUSAN turned WebMCP from a technical capability into a visible user experience. 

 The user does not need to understand WebMCP. 

 They simply express a goal. 

 Behind the interface, the Agent discovers available capabilities, calls structured tools, reasons over the results, updates the itinerary, and stops when human authorization is required. 

 I am especially proud of the Agent Wallet concept. 

 Instead of treating an Agent as either “fully autonomous” or “not autonomous,” I give the user granular control over what the Agent can do. 

 I am also proud of the Agent Activity / Black Box experience. 

 Users can see: 

 
 What the Agent is doing 
 Which tool it is using 
 What information it found 
 What it changed 
 Which permission it used 
 Where human approval is required 
 

 This makes autonomy visible. 

 Most importantly, the prototype demonstrates a different philosophy of agentic computing: 

 
 The goal is not to maximize what the Agent can do.
The goal is to maximize what the Agent can safely do on behalf of a human. 
 

 What I learned 

 The biggest lesson was that the hardest problem in agentic systems is not capability. 

 It is control. 

 An Agent that can only answer questions is limited. 

 An Agent that can take actions is useful. 

 But an Agent that can take consequential actions without clearly defined authority creates a trust problem. 

 WebMCP made me think beyond the question: 

 
 “How can an Agent use the web?” 
 

 I began asking: 

 
 “How should the web communicate its capabilities and boundaries to an Agent?” 
 

 And then: 

 
 “How should a human control those capabilities?” 
 

 This led me to a new mental model: 

 Intent → Capability → Action → Approval 

 I also learned that the best Agent experience should not hide autonomy. 

 It should make autonomy understandable. 

 The user should know when the Agent is thinking, what it is doing, what it is allowed to do, and when a decision belongs to them. 

 This changed HELLOBUSAN from a travel application into an experiment in Human-Agent Interaction Design. 

 What's next for HELLOBUSAN 

 Busan is only the beginning. 

 My next step is to expand HELLOBUSAN from a travel planner into an Agent-ready city interface. 

 Restaurants, museums, cultural venues, hotels, transportation providers, local businesses, and public services could expose structured capabilities that Agents can discover and use. 

 Instead of every Agent learning how to navigate every website independently, the web could increasingly provide explicit, machine-readable capabilities. 

 This could enable a future where a person does not need to understand which website or application to use. 

 They simply express an intent: 

 
 “I need to spend Saturday in Busan with my family.” 
 

 The Agent coordinates the available city services within the permissions defined by the person.

 “AI control

OpenX Portal is the unified mission control and execution harness for autonomous AI agents. Built as a high-performance monorepo

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents can code, research, call tools, and pay for services, but they still operate like black boxes with fragmented memory and limited oversight. 

 We built OpenX as a mission-control and self-improvement layer where humans, ChatGPT, Codex, and autonomous agents can observe, manage, and improve agent fleets through WebMCP . 

 What it does 

 
 🌐 WebMCP-native control plane — exposes OpenX tools through document.modelContext , letting compatible AI clients inspect agents, lessons, skills, credits, and Dream Cycles directly from the browser. 
 🤖 Fleet Management — discovers kiro-cli , claude-code , Google ADK, and custom agents with real-time heartbeats and lifecycle tracking. 
 🧠 REM Dream Cycles — compress raw sessions into verified lessons and reusable Skills. 
 🛡️ 0G Compute Auditor — independently reviews lessons as keep, revise, or reject. 
 💾 0G Storage — anchors sanitized memory and audit proofs with verifiable Merkle receipts. 
 💸 x402 + RLUSD — lets agents autonomously pay for MCP tools and compute on XRPL. 
 💳 Tracks token and tool-call costs in real time. 
 

 How we built it 

 OpenX combines Next.js 14 + WebMCP , a Node/TypeScript Gateway, SQLite WAL, and Python Google ADK agents. 

 Codex was part of our engineering workflow : we used it to explore the repository, understand modules, implement WebMCP and gateway features, debug integrations, review code, and validate behavior across TypeScript and Python. 

 WebMCP turns the dashboard into an AI-operable application , so agents can call structured OpenX actions instead of relying on screenshots or DOM scraping. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Reliable WebMCP tool schemas across different agent runtimes. 
 Non-deterministic 0G Compute JSON and hallucinated citations. 
 Preventing secrets and PII from reaching decentralized storage. 
 SQLite contention from concurrent telemetry. 
 Coordinating async Dream Cycles, MCP calls, and x402 payments without race conditions. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Built a dashboard that AI agents can operate directly through WebMCP . 
 Used Codex as an engineering collaborator , not just a code generator. 
 Created an end-to-end pipeline from telemetry → audited lessons → reusable Skills. 
 Combined decentralized memory, independent auditing, and autonomous micropayments in one system. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP turns the frontend into an agent interface, not just a UI. 

 Codex is most powerful with real repository context, tests, and runtime feedback. 

 Agent memory also needs governance: compact, audited lessons are more valuable than replaying huge raw histories.

 Make Codex a first-class managed agent inside OpenX. 
 Expand WebMCP controls for Dream Cycles, Skills, audits, and fleet operations. 
 Build cross-agent collective memory on 0G.

Zero-configuration, secure interoperability across web apps—entirely in your browser, powered by WebMCP.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 The open web is incredibly powerful, but deeply siloed. Today, if you want your CRM to talk to your invoicing tool, you have to rely on third-party automation servers, manage complex webhooks, and hand over highly sensitive, long-lived API keys. I was inspired by the WebMCP draft specification because it flips this model upside down. I wanted to explore a future where integration happens securely on the client side —where humans and AI agents can collaborate directly in the browser to move data between apps safely, transparently, and without ever exposing a backend API key. 

 What it does 

 Apptome (via the Connectome Hub) is a zero-configuration, secure interoperability layer for the we. It automatically discovers WebMCP capabilities exposed by your open we apps and unifies them into a personal graph. 

 When you want to execute a workflow—like taking a client from your CRM and generating a bill in your Invoicing app—you initiate it in our sidebar. Our Cloudflare Workers AI agent kicks in to semantically map the data from the source app to the destination app's required JSON schema on the fly. Finally, it presents you with the exact payload for human-in-the-loop confirmation. The agent does the heavy lifting, but the human remains in total control. 

 How I built it 

 Our architecture is split into three main layers: 

 
 The Spoke Apps: I built sample single-page applications that natively expose their local functionality using document.modelContext.registerTool() . 
 The Bridge: A lightIight client-side script that monitors toolchange events and securely relays the available WebMCP capabilities to our central Hub via WebSockets. 
 The Hub & AI Mapper: Deployed entirely on Cloudflare Workers , the Hub maintains the user's persistent tool graph. I use Cloudflare Workers AI ( @cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast ) to perform the semantic mapping between differing tool schemas. The user interface is a secure, cross-origin iframe (the "Surface") injected over the host app. 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 Browser security is notoriously unforgiving! Because I am committed to maintaining the web's Same-Origin Policy (SOP) without bypassing it, managing cross-origin iframes, strict Content-Security-Policies (CSP), and secure weSocket transports was a massive challenge. I also ran into real-world anti-tracking hurdles (like Brave browser's Shields aggressively blocking our Cloudflare Turnstile human-verification checks) which forced us to deeply understand third-party iframe behaviors. Finally, tuning the LLM to output deterministic, strictly-typed JSON schemas without hallucinating required careful prompt engineering. 

 Accomplishments 

 It is gratifying to have demonstrated true N-to-N interoperability entirely on the client side. The "magic" moment of watching the AI seamlessly map fields from one app's schema to another app's schema—without requiring the user to manually drag-and-drop fields—is something I're very proud of. Furthermore, I built a highly secure architecture that enforces human consent for every action, proving that AI agents can be both immensely powerful and completely safe. 

 What I learned 

 I gained a deep understanding of the WebMCP draft specification and the paradigms of client-side tool discovery. I also leveled up our skills in edge computing with Cloudflare Workers, handling WebSockets at the edge, and seamlessly integrating serverless AI models into real-time we applications. Most importantly, I learned that the future of agentic we workflows depends on strict, transparent security boundaries. 

 What's next for Apptome 

 Our immediate next step is expanding our prototype from "stub" apps to real-world SaaS products. I plan to build a browser extension that can act as the WebMCP bridge, bringing Apptome's capabilities to legacy we apps that don't yet support WebMCP natively. I also want to explore integrating local, on-device SLMs (Small Language Models) so the semantic mapping can happen entirely locally for ultimate privacy.

 ORBIT 

 Real-Time Radiology Capacity & Workforce Orchestration Cockpit 

 
 Turning every scanner, every radiologist, and every patient into one living, self-balancing system. 
 

 

 ORBIT is the human-gated orchestration layer for distributed radiology capacity. It connects live scanner telemetry, patient queues, radiologist bandwidth, technologist expertise, and WebMCP AI agents in one shared operational cockpit. 

 The result: the right patient, the right scanner, and the right qualified human can find one another before a backlog becomes a clinical delay. 

 At A Glance 

 
 
 Signal 
 ORBIT response 
 
 
 
 A scanner is overloaded 
 Rebalance eligible routine patients to a nearby partner site 
 
 
 A radiologist is nearing fatigue limits 
 Route studies to a credentialed remote specialist 
 
 
 A suite is understaffed 
 Dispatch remote senior technologist support 
 
 
 An AI agent finds a good move 
 Draft it, simulate it, and wait for human approval 
 
 
 A workflow action occurs 
 Record it in a tamper-evident SHA-256 audit trail 
 
 

 

 The Problem: Capacity Exists, But It Cannot See Itself 

 Picture two hospital campuses on a crisp Tuesday morning, exactly 15 minutes apart down the same highway: 

 
 Hospital A has five $2-million MRI suites and two radiologists on shift. Its queue is four hours deep. A patient with a potential stroke-mimicking presentation is waiting for a scan read that takes 12 minutes, but will not happen for two hours because the on-site radiologists are buried under a backlog of 40 routine knee and lumbar scans. 
 Hospital B , 15 minutes down the road, has three MRI suites. One has been idle since 10:00 AM, and a credentialed radiologist is refreshing their inbox, waiting for studies. 
 

 Nobody made a mistake. Nobody is understaffed on paper . The problem is that capacity and demand are invisible to each other in real time . 

 In modern healthcare, the machine is rarely the actual bottleneck. An MRI can run 24/7 if it has electricity and helium. The real bottleneck is the qualified human : the radiologist licensed in that jurisdiction, certified in the required subspecialty, and below the cognitive-fatigue limit; or the technologist trained to operate a 3.0T scanner. 

 With a projected shortfall of 17,000 to 42,000 radiologists in the U.S. by 2033 and only 2% of UK radiology departments meeting contracted turnaround times, hospital networks are suffocating. 

 The industry is already moving toward distributed imaging capacity: 

 
 Siemens Healthineers offers remote scanning, remote reading, and load balancing and scheduling capabilities through its radiology services portfolio. 
 Philips is advancing unified radiology workflows, remote diagnostic imaging, and remote scanning to extend expertise across locations. 
 GE HealthCare has developed enterprise imaging, intelligent workload management, and remote collaboration capabilities aimed at improving radiology capacity, workflow efficiency, and workforce utilization. 
 

 ORBIT connects these recurring industry needs into one vendor-neutral, real-time capacity network. 

 When the WebMCP Challenge was announced, the fit was immediate. Healthcare AI cannot be a black box that operates in secret or hallucinates web clicks on a DOM. AI agents and human medical directors need to see the exact same live operational screen , share the same tools and constraints, and leave the same audit trail. WebMCP provides that interaction layer. 

 The ORBIT Operating Model 

 ORBIT continuously turns network telemetry into ranked, explainable candidates: 

 Telemetry → Constraint   Filter → Candidate   Ranking → Simulation → Human   Approval → Atomic   Execution 

 The system optimizes both sides of capacity at once: 

 Available   Capacity = Scanner   Capacity × Qualified   Human   Capacity 

 That is the central idea: an empty scanner is not available capacity if no qualified person can safely operate or read the study. 

 

 What ORBIT Does 

 1. A Three-Pane Operational Cockpit 

 Human coordinators and WebMCP-enabled AI agents co-pilot hospital network capacity from the same screen. 

 
 
 Pane 
 What it shows 
 
 
 
 Network Status Rail 
 Live telemetry across 5 regional hospital campuses and 14 multi-modality scanners covering MRI, CT, X-Ray, and Ultrasound. Tracks utilization, queue depth, idle scanner hours, and staff constraints. Utilization states are <75% Emerald , 75-88% Amber , and >88% Rose alert . 
 
 
 Live Multi-Modality Schedule Board 
 A dense chronological feed of active examinations with STAT pulse animations, instant filtering by MRN, patient name, or protocol, and an Appointment Detail Inspector modal. 
 
 
 Human Approval Queue 
 Priority-sorted AI proposals with origin-to-destination candidates, commute distance, queue-reduction deltas, constraint badges, and one-click actions. 
 
 

 2. Multi-Vector Capacity Rebalancing 

 ORBIT evaluates three distinct capacity vectors: 

 Pillar 1 : Scanner Load Balancing 

 Reroutes ambulatory routine patients from overloaded sites to partner facilities within a maximum commute of 25 miles and with magnetic-field parity of at least 1.5T , freeing Level-1 emergency STAT slots. 

 Pillar 2A : Remote Read Dynamic Assignment 

 Monitors radiologist fatigue against a 75% shift cap . When local clinicians breach fatigue limits, ORBIT routes DICOM studies across PACS worklists to credentialed, cross-state licensed remote specialists with open bandwidth. 

 Pillar 2B : Remote Scan Assist Dispatch 

 Identifies understaffed suites and triggers syngo Virtual Cockpit -style tele-proctoring guidance sessions with certified remote senior technologists. 

 Candidate quality is evaluated as a constrained optimization problem: 

 Best   Candidate = argmax c ∈ Eligible   Candidates ( Queue   Relief + Fatigue   Relief − Travel   Cost ) 

 3. Predictive Simulation Before Commitment 

 Before a schedule changes, an operator or AI agent can run an ActExcell-inspired What-If stress test to project: 

 
 queue reduction; 
 wait-time savings; and 
 staff-load improvement. 
 

 This gives operators an impact preview before they commit a real-world move. 

 4. Human Approval Is a Hard Safety Boundary 

 ORBIT enforces a non-negotiable server-side state machine: 

 PENDING → Human / Agent   Approval APPROVED → Atomic   Execution EXECUTED 

 No move can ever execute directly from PENDING . If an agent or user attempts it, the server returns an explicit HTTP 400 rejection: "Move MUST be approved by human coordinator first." Humans stay in total control. 

 5. A Cryptographic Compliance Trail 

 Every bottleneck detection, proposal, simulation, approval, execution, rejection, and constraint tweak is immutably logged with a 64-character SHA-256 digest: 

 SHA 256 ( timestamp ∥ action_type ∥ actor_id ∥ entity_id ) 

 6. Communication Drafting, With Review 

 ORBIT pre-generates non-spammy SMS and portal alerts for patients, including navigation links, plus DICOM and pager alerts for radiologists. Messages are drafted for review before sending. 

 

 How We Built It 

 ORBIT is a high-density, production-grade WebMCP web application built as a shared workspace between an AI agent, human coordinators, and a FastAPI backend. 

 System Flow 

 WebMCP AI Agent → Typed WebMCP Tools → ORBIT React Cockpit → REST API → Constraint & AI Services → Human Approval → Atomic Execution

 Presents network status, the multi-modality schedule, and the human approval queue

 Inspiration 

 As global artificial intelligence infrastructure scales rapidly, data centers and edge compute nodes place unprecedented, unpredictable strain on local electrical grids. Simultaneously, urban clusters are shifting toward Positive Energy Districts (PEDs)—neighborhoods designed to produce more renewable energy than they consume annually via local solar photovoltaic (PV) and microgrid arrays. However, a critical operational friction point exists: when rapid atmospheric changes (such as sudden cloud cover) reduce solar generation while AI training or batch inference workloads peak, local transformers face severe overload risks. GridNode-Sync was inspired by the need to bridge decentralized clean energy systems and AI infrastructure using agent-native browser capabilities. 

 What it does 

 GridNode-Sync is an open-source, agent-native web application that serves as a shared operational control hub for human engineers and browser-native AI agents. When opened in a WebMCP-enabled environment (such as ChatGPT's in-app browser or Google Chrome with experimental flags active), the AI agent gains direct, structured access to infrastructure tools. It continuously monitors live bus voltage, transformer saturation indices, and solar generation metrics; evaluates distributed AI workload queues to identify temporally deferrable tasks within a 3-hour thermal window; runs capacity expansion simulations; and executes secure workload shifts or coordinates local Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) buffering to stabilize the district. 

 How we built it 

 We built GridNode-Sync using a modern, lightweight web stack optimized for edge performance and developer transparency: 

 
 Frontend Architecture: Developed using React and Vite for rapid, responsive performance, styled with Tailwind CSS to emulate an enterprise-grade industrial SCADA control room. 
 WebMCP Integration: Leveraged the emerging WebMCP standard by registering programmatic tools via document.modelContext.registerTool , exposing structured schemas ( query_district_grid_telemetry , evaluate_compute_workload_queue , simulate_grid_capacity_expansion , execute_workload_shift ) directly to the browser agent. 
 Governance & Security: Implemented ISO/IEC 42001-aligned deterministic safety guardrails and Ed25519-signed telemetry attestation logic (drawing upon IEEE P7802 / IEEE P3800 frameworks) to ensure all automated workload shifts are cryptographically logged and verifiable. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Designing an agent-native application for industrial infrastructure required navigating strict safety boundaries. Ensuring that an autonomous browser agent could suggest and execute computational shifts without ever risking critical, latency-critical SCADA inferences or violating substation thermal limits was a primary hurdle. We solved this by implementing hardcoded guardrails and a mandatory human-in-the-loop authorization gate, ensuring the agent operates strictly within safe parametric bounds while leaving ultimate execution control to the human engineer. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Successfully implementing a working, non-trivial WebMCP tool registration schema that transforms a standard web browser into an agent-ready operational control terminal. 
 Fusing advanced power systems engineering concepts (Positive Energy Districts, solar PV ramp rates, transformer saturation, and 3-hour temporal flexibility windows) with modern artificial intelligence governance and web standards. 
 Designing a software-defined architecture that eliminates expensive proprietary hardware barriers, making microgrid resilience scalable to resource-constrained municipalities and off-grid campuses in the Global South. 
 

 What we learned 

 Building GridNode-Sync highlighted the immense potential of moving away from traditional, rigid user interfaces toward the agent-native web . When web applications expose structured, programmatic tools rather than relying on brittle UI scraping or blind clicking, human-agent collaboration becomes vastly more reliable, scalable, and powerful for complex operational domains like energy and infrastructure management. 

 What's next for GridNode-Sync 

 
 Pilot Deployments: Partnering with regional microgrid operators and campus facilities to test live browser-agent telemetry loops on physical edge nodes. 
 Expanded Mathematical Modeling: Integrating advanced mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solvers for multi-district stochastic energy optimization. 
 Global Standards Contributions: Continuing to align the project's data structures with emerging IEEE and IEC working groups to help shape the future of decentralized energy trading and AI infrastructure governance.

 1 2 3 



 
 PrintChum — Your Companion for Print-Ready Photos 

 

 1. Problem Statement 

 Creating standardized ID and document photo layouts is a daily necessity for photo studios, print shops, schools, and individuals. However, the existing workflow is plagued by significant friction: 

 
 Tedious Manual Workflows: Arranging multiple photo sizes (such as 2 × 2 in, 1 × 1 in, Passport, and Wallet sizes) in desktop software like Photoshop or MS Word requires manual cropping, repetitive copy-pasting, and tedious alignment calculations. 
 Physical Dimension Inaccuracies: Generic image editors often distort real-world physical dimensions during export or printing, leading to rejected government, passport, or school application photos due to incorrect millimeter specifications or DPI downsampling. 
 Severe Privacy Risks: Most online photo tools require users to upload sensitive portraits and identity documents to remote cloud storage, where images may be stored indefinitely, indexed, or exposed to data breaches. 
 Wasted Photo Paper: Without optimal 2D bin packing, manual sheet layouts result in low paper utilization and expensive photo paper waste. 
 

 

 2. Solution Overview 

 PrintChum eliminates manual layout preparation by delivering an automated, privacy-first, browser-local photo layout engine. 

 Users upload a photo once, adjust the crop framing, and select standard presets or custom packages. PrintChum’s deterministic layout algorithm instantly packs the required photo quantities onto the target paper sheet, overlays precision cutting guides and nameplates, and generates a print-ready PDF or triggers direct printing. 

 Privacy-by-Design Architecture 

 PrintChum processes images locally within browser memory : 

 
 Image cropping, color composition, nameplate rendering, layout packing, and vector PDF compilation occur entirely on the client side. 
 Customer photos are never stored in databases or permanent cloud storage . 
 External server communication is strictly limited to optional AI background removal, where images are processed in-memory and immediately returned to the client without persistence. 
 

 Mathematical Precision & Real-World Dimensions 

 PrintChum maps screen pixels to true physical print dimensions using exact unit conversion constants:
 1 in = 2.54 cm = 25.4 mm = 72 pt (PDF) = 300 px (at 300 DPI) 
The 2D shelf-packing engine optimizes the printable area after subtracting horizontal and vertical margins ($M_x$ and $M_y$):
 W printable = W paper − 2 ⋅ M x , H printable = H paper − 2 ⋅ M y 
Paper utilization efficiency is computed deterministically:
 Utilization Efficiency  ( % ) = ( ∑ i = 1 n w i ⋅ h i W printable ⋅ H printable ) × 100 % 

 

 3. Key Features 

 
 Single Crop, Multi-Size Distribution: Crop and position a portrait once; PrintChum automatically resizes, frames, and renders it across multiple target dimensions (2 × 2 in, 1 × 1 in, 1.5 × 1.5 in, Passport, 2R, Wallet, or Custom sizes). 
 Deterministic Layout & Multi-Page Pagination: Automatically arranges mixed photo sizes with customizable margins, horizontal/vertical spacing, and auto-rotation (0° or 90°), cleanly overflowing onto subsequent pages when needed. 
 Precision Cutting Guides & Annotations: Renders corner crop marks, dashed cutting lines, and dimensional labels for effortless trimming with rotary or guillotine paper cutters. 
 Dynamic Nameplates for IDs: Add customizable nameplates (inside or outside the photo frame) supporting Full Name, ID/Student Number, Department, Role, and custom styling (fonts, background colors, and borders). 
 Reusable Studio "Service Sets": Save and load recurring package presets (e.g., "Package A: 2 pcs 2x2 + 8 pcs 1x1 on 4R Paper" ). 
 Direct Vector PDF Export & 300 DPI Printing: Export vector-coordinate PDFs via pdf-lib at 72 points/inch with embedded 300 DPI image assets for crisp, uncompressed physical prints. 
 Agentic WebMCP Integration: Native browser-level Model Context Protocol (WebMCP via document.modelContext ) enabling browser AI assistants to configure layouts, apply presets, and control the editor programmatically. 
 

 

 4. Technologies Used 

 Frontend & Application 

 
 Framework: Next.js (App Router, React 19) 
 Language: TypeScript 
 Styling & UI Components: Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Radix UI, Lucide React 
 State Management: Zustand 
 Form Handling & Validation: React Hook Form, Zod 
 

 Graphics, Layout & Export 

 
 Image Framing & Cropping: react-easy-crop , HTML5 Canvas API 
 Layout Engine: Custom framework-independent 2D shelf-packing & pagination algorithm 
 PDF Compilation: pdf-lib (point-accurate physical coordinate rendering) 
 Printing Engine: Native Browser Print API & Print-Specific CSS ( @media print , @page ) 
 

 

 5. Target Users 

 
 Photo Studios & Freelance Photographers: Rapidly prepare standard client packages without opening complex desktop editing suites. 
 Print Shops & Internet / Computer Cafes: Serve walk-in customers seeking quick ID package prints with automated layout packing and zero paper waste. 
 Schools, Universities & HR Departments: Standardize ID badge photo formatting and student/employee nameplates at scale. 
 Individual Job Seekers & Travelers: Create exact-dimension passport, visa, resume, and government ID photos at home with guaranteed sizing compliance.

about_excerpt:
Chalkboard is an AI-powered collaborative classroom where humans and autonomous teaching agents think, draw, and learn together in real time, making AI an active teaching partner.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Chalkboard Logo 
 
 
 
 
 

 GIF 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Chalkboard Logo 
 
 
 
 
 

 GIF 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 The idea for Chalkboard came from a simple problem: online collaboration often feels disconnected from the way we naturally think and communicate in person. 

 In a physical classroom, someone can walk to a board, draw a diagram, point at a specific part of it, explain an idea, ask a question, and immediately see how other people respond. The board becomes more than a place for writing. It becomes the shared context for the entire conversation. 

 Online, that experience is usually fragmented across multiple tools. A video call handles communication, a whiteboard handles diagrams, a document contains notes, chat contains links and messages, and another application might be needed for specialized activities such as mathematics or technical diagrams. 

 I wanted to bring those interactions together into one shared space. 

 The inspiration came from the traditional classroom chalkboard. There is something remarkably intuitive about standing in front of a board and explaining an idea visually. Rather than building another generic digital whiteboard, I wanted Chalkboard to preserve that feeling while adding the capabilities that are possible with modern web technology. 

 That led to the idea of Chalkboard: a real-time collaborative space for teaching, learning, brainstorming, explaining, and creating together. 

 What I Built 

 Chalkboard is a real-time collaborative canvas designed around the idea of a shared classroom or workspace. 

 Users can create rooms and invite other people to collaborate on the same board. Once inside a room, participants can draw together, write notes, create shapes, move objects, add links, react to each other, raise their hands, and communicate through voice. 

 The important part is that everyone is interacting with the same live canvas . 

 When one participant draws something, other participants see it appear in real time. When someone moves an object, changes the board, reacts, or joins the room, those changes become part of the shared experience. 

 This makes Chalkboard useful for much more than traditional online classes. 

 A room can become: 

 
 A classroom where an instructor teaches students 
 A workshop where participants work through an exercise 
 A brainstorming space for a team 
 A technical architecture board for developers 
 A planning space for a project 
 A collaborative design surface 
 A mathematical workspace 
 A creative studio 
 

 The underlying idea is that the board should adapt to the activity rather than forcing every type of collaboration into the same workflow. 

 The Collaborative Classroom 

 I designed Chalkboard around the concept of a room rather than simply a canvas. 

 Each room has its own participants, permissions, presence, activity, canvas state, and history. 

 Participants can see other users' cursors and activity, allowing the board to feel more like a physical room where everyone is present rather than a collection of isolated users editing the same document. 

 Rooms can also have different access models, including open rooms, approval-based rooms, and password-protected rooms. 

 Different roles can be assigned to participants, including owner, instructor, and viewer , allowing Chalkboard to support situations where an instructor controls the lesson while students participate. 

 This room-based architecture became important because it allowed me to think about Chalkboard as an actual digital classroom environment , not just a drawing application. 

 The Canvas 

 At the center of Chalkboard is its interactive canvas. 

 I wanted the canvas to retain the simplicity of a physical chalkboard while supporting the capabilities users expect from modern collaborative software. 

 Users can: 

 
 Draw freehand with chalk-style strokes 
 Create shapes 
 Add text and notes 
 Select and transform objects 
 Move and resize content 
 Copy and paste objects 
 Group elements 
 Zoom and pan around the board 
 Add links 
 Undo and redo actions 
 Interact with mathematical visualization tools 
 

 Rather than treating the canvas as a static image, Chalkboard maintains a structured representation of the objects and actions taking place on the board. This becomes especially important for collaboration, plugins, and eventually AI agents because the system can understand that something on the board is a circle, text element, arrow, diagram, or other object , rather than simply seeing pixels. 

 Real-Time Collaboration 

 One of the most important engineering challenges was making the collaboration feel immediate. 

 A collaborative canvas generates a continuous stream of events. A user might draw a stroke, move their cursor, move an object, react to another participant, or change something on the board — all within a few seconds. 

 I therefore designed Chalkboard around real-time events rather than treating the canvas like a traditional CRUD application. 

 The real-time system synchronizes things such as: 

 
 Canvas changes 
 Drawing strokes 
 Object transformations 
 Cursor positions 
 Participant presence 
 Reactions 
 Raised hands 
 Room activity 
 Collaboration state 
 

 This also introduced another challenge: connection reliability . 

 Users can temporarily lose their connection, refresh their browser, or reconnect from another device. I had to design the presence and synchronization system so that short network interruptions would not make the classroom feel unstable. 

 A short presence grace period helps prevent users from constantly appearing and disappearing when they briefly disconnect. 

 How I Built It 

 I built the frontend using React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML5 Canvas, and Zustand . 

 Rather than relying entirely on a canvas abstraction, I implemented much of the canvas interaction and rendering logic myself. This gave me more control over how strokes, objects, selection, transformations, zooming, and the chalkboard visual experience behave. 

 The backend is built with Node.js and Hono , with Socket.IO providing the real-time communication layer. 

 For persistent application data, I use PostgreSQL with Drizzle ORM . PostgreSQL handles durable data such as users, rooms, memberships, permissions, plugins, and other application records. 

 For fast-changing collaborative state, I use Redis . This allows active room state, presence information, real-time coordination, and other ephemeral data to be handled without constantly writing every interaction to the primary database. 

 I also use BullMQ for background jobs and cleanup tasks, while the Socket.IO Redis adapter allows the real-time architecture to work across multiple backend instances. 

 Authentication is handled through Google Identity Services , with the backend verifying authentication and creating secure sessions. 

 I also integrated LiveKit to provide voice communication inside rooms, allowing Chalkboard to combine the visual collaboration experience with real-time conversation.

 As I built Chalkboard, I realized that a collaborative canvas becomes much more powerful when developers can extend what can happen inside it. 

 Instead of putting every possible feature into the core application, I designed a plugin system that allows developers to create new tools and experiences for Chalkboard. 

 A plugin can introduce new capabilities to the board while remaining separate from the core application.

 Technical architecture 
 Games 
 Productivity tools
