title: Longevity — Human-Agent Life Function Workspace
pitch: A privacy-first WebMCP app where your agent turns known family and life context into a visible Life Function, asks only for missing facts, and compares conditional life-extension scenarios.
about_excerpt:
A privacy-first WebMCP app where your agent turns known family and life context into a visible Life Function, asks only for missing facts, and compares conditional life-extension scenarios.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most personal-modeling products begin with a long blank form. But a person’s AI agent may already know useful fragments of family history and life context. The missed opportunity is not merely autofill: it is a shared working surface where the person sees the model changing while the agent gathers only what is actually missing. 

 What it does 

 Longevity is a privacy-first WebMCP workspace in which a person and their agent build a visible Life Function together. The agent reuses structured facts already available in its context, asks only for gaps, and submits those facts directly into the open page. Longevity then visualizes parental trajectories, the client’s observed trajectory, influence coefficients, a hereditary model, and conditional life-extension scenarios. 

 When context is sparse, the agent runs a live four-chapter interview: family and influence, ancestors, parents, and the client’s trajectory. It asks one short question per message, accepts text, voice, approximate answers, or “I don’t know,” and stops the required interview as soon as the first calculation is ready. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Longevity exposes seven client-side WebMCP tools. The agent can read the intake and privacy contract, submit known facts, inspect completeness, request exactly one next interview step, add a structured answer, and retrieve scenario comparisons. Every accepted tool call updates the same in-tab state the person is looking at. 

 This creates an experience that was difficult before WebMCP: private context can be reused without forcing the person to re-enter everything, while the browser remains the shared visual source of truth. The person can inspect sources and assumptions, adjust father, mother, and environment coefficients, and watch the Life Functions recalculate immediately—without the agent scraping or clicking through the UI. 

 Privacy by architecture 

 The deployed static page has no intake server, account, analytics, cookies, database, or persistent storage. It accepts structured facts only, never raw chat, audio, or transcripts. Personal facts remain in JavaScript memory inside the open tab and disappear on reload, tab close, or Clear. A restrictive Content Security Policy uses connect-src 'none'. The WebMCP manifest also states that retention of the external agent conversation is controlled by that agent platform, not by Longevity. 

 How we built it 

 
 React 19, TypeScript, and Vite 
 Imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool() 
 Strict JSON Schemas and structured tool results 
 Abort-scoped re-registration when the locale changes 
 Fully client-side calculations and state 
 English-first interface with a complete Russian UI and WebMCP contract 
 Netlify static deployment with restrictive security headers 
 Automated coverage for intake flow, privacy, calculations, charts, tool registration, and localization 
 

 Challenges and lessons 

 The hardest design problem was balancing completeness with a conversational interview. Too few questions produced a weak model; a conventional questionnaire felt endless. The four-chapter policy, one-question rhythm, explicit unknowns, and separate preliminary/refinement phases made the flow both bounded and useful. 

 A second challenge was making strong privacy language technically true. That led us to keep all personal state inside the tab, forbid raw conversational media, expose the privacy boundary to the agent before submission, and distinguish page storage from the agent platform’s own retention policy. 

 Finally, the model had to remain legible and epistemically honest. Longevity shows completeness, provenance, assumptions, and uncertainty, and presents its calculations as a conditional Androphysics model—not medical advice, a biological forecast, or a prediction of a person’s death.

title: WebOps Commander
pitch: An agent-native incident response command center where AI agents investigate outages through WebMCP, simulate safe fixes, and execute production-changing actions only after explicit human approval.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native incident response command center where AI agents investigate outages through WebMCP, simulate safe fixes, and execute production-changing actions only after explicit human approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Modern websites are designed primarily for people. When AI agents need to interact with those applications, they often have to interpret pages visually, reason about buttons and forms, and reproduce workflows that were never designed for machine interaction. 

 WebMCP suggests a different future: websites can expose intentional, structured capabilities directly to AI agents while continuing to provide rich interfaces for humans. 

 That idea inspired WebOps Commander . 

 We wanted to explore a question: 

 
 What would an incident-response application look like if it were designed for humans and AI agents from the beginning? 
 

 Instead of building another chatbot or allowing an agent to blindly click through an operations dashboard, WebOps Commander gives the agent structured operational capabilities through WebMCP while preserving explicit human control over consequential actions. 

 What it does 

 WebOps Commander is an agent-native incident-response command center built around a deterministic simulated production outage. 

 A fictional e-commerce platform experiences a severe checkout incident shortly after a new version of checkout-service is deployed. 

 The human operator sees a visual operations dashboard containing: 

 
 live service health 
 checkout error rate 
 p95 latency 
 order throughput 
 estimated revenue impact 
 service dependencies 
 logs 
 distributed traces 
 deployment history 
 incident status 
 agent activity 
 

 At the same time, a compatible AI agent receives structured WebMCP tools that allow it to investigate the same system directly. 

 The agent can: 

 
 inspect the active incident 
 inspect service health 
 query metrics 
 search logs 
 inspect traces 
 inspect service dependencies 
 inspect recent deployments 
 compare releases 
 search operational runbooks 
 estimate customer impact 
 simulate a rollback 
 request a production-changing action 
 wait for explicit human approval 
 execute an approved rollback 
 observe system recovery 
 update and resolve the incident 
 

 The core workflow is: 

 Observe → Investigate → Correlate → Simulate → Request Approval → Human Approves → Execute → Recover 

 Why WebMCP? 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent interacting with an operations platform may need to determine which page contains deployment information, interpret charts, find buttons, understand forms, and infer what actions are safe to perform. 

 That approach can be brittle. 

 With WebMCP, WebOps Commander intentionally exposes structured capabilities such as: 

 query_service_metrics 

 search_logs 

 search_traces 

 get_recent_deployments 

 compare_deployments 

 simulate_rollback 

 request_rollback 

 execute_approved_action 

 The agent does not need to guess how the user interface works. 

 The website tells the agent what capabilities are available, what inputs they accept, and what actions are permitted. 

 The human interface and agent interface operate on the same application state, so WebMCP actions are immediately visible inside the command center. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 WebOps Commander is intentionally not designed around full autonomy. 

 Investigation is safe for the agent to perform independently. 

 Consequential actions are different. 

 For example, the agent can determine that a rollback is likely to resolve the incident and simulate its expected impact, but it cannot immediately change the simulated production environment. 

 Instead, it creates a pending action: 

 Rollback checkout-service from v2.18.4 to v2.18.3 

 The human sees the proposed action together with: 

 
 the agent's reasoning 
 expected recovery 
 current error rate 
 expected post-rollback error rate 
 estimated risk 
 

 The human can then approve or reject the action. 

 Only an approved action can be executed. 

 This creates a clear separation between: 

 Agent investigation 

 Agent recommendation 

 Human authorization 

 Agent execution 

 Every WebMCP interaction is also recorded in the visible agent activity timeline. 

 The Incident 

 The demonstration focuses on one deliberately small but polished scenario: Checkout Meltdown . 

 A deployment of checkout-service v2.18.4 introduces stricter payment-token issuer validation. 

 Shortly afterward: 

 
 checkout failures increase from approximately 0.6% to 18.4% 
 p95 checkout latency increases from approximately 620 ms to 4.7 seconds 
 completed orders fall by approximately 38% 
 estimated revenue exposure reaches approximately $21.4K per simulated minute 
 

 Other services remain healthy. 

 Through metrics, logs, traces, deployment history, and release comparison, the agent can correlate the incident with v2.18.4 . 

 It can then simulate a rollback to v2.18.3 , request authorization, and—after human approval—execute the remediation. 

 The command center visually shows the system recovering. 

 How we are building it 

 WebOps Commander is intentionally scoped as a focused hackathon demonstration rather than a production observability platform. 

 The application uses a deterministic simulation instead of real cloud infrastructure so that every judge can reproduce the same incident without accounts, API keys, external services, or unreliable dependencies. 

 The planned architecture consists of: 

 
 Next.js 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Tailwind CSS 
 shadcn/ui 
 WebMCP 
 Zod 
 Zustand 
 Recharts 
 Vitest 
 Playwright 
 GitHub Actions 
 

 Operational state, telemetry, logs, traces, deployments, and recovery behavior are simulated locally. 

 WebMCP is the primary agent interface. 

 The project does not require an embedded chatbot or external LLM API—the compatible AI agent interacting with the website is the agent. 

 Challenges 

 The most interesting challenge is not simply exposing functions to an AI agent. 

 It is deciding what an agent should be allowed to do. 

 Read-only investigation tools should be easy to invoke. 

 Simulation should be safe. 

 Production-changing operations should be protected. 

 That led us to design a small capability model with separate categories for: 

 
 read operations 
 simulations 
 approval requests 
 consequential actions 
 

 Another important challenge is making agent activity understandable to the human operator. WebOps Commander therefore visualizes WebMCP invocations in an audit timeline so users can see what the agent inspected, what it concluded, and what it attempted to change. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes the way a web application can be designed. 

 Instead of treating AI agents as external automation systems that must reverse-engineer a user interface, the application can expose a deliberate machine-facing capability layer alongside its human interface. 

 The result is not simply easier automation. 

 It enables a different interaction model: 

 
 Humans provide intent and authority. Agents investigate and execute structured workflows. Websites provide the contract connecting them. 
 

 What's next 

 After the hackathon, WebOps Commander could be expanded to explore: 

 
 multiple incident scenarios 
 richer permission policies 
 tool-level access control 
 real observability integrations 
 real deployment systems 
 multi-agent operational workflows 
 reusable WebMCP patterns for infrastructure products 
 

 For this challenge, however, the focus remains intentionally narrow: 

 one incident, one excellent human-agent workflow, and a clear demonstration of why WebMCP matters.

title: Co-Shop
pitch: A grocery storefront where you and your AI agent share the same live cart via WebMCP to plan dinners, add items, or check out together, with every action visible and editable in real time.
about_excerpt:
A grocery storefront where you and your AI agent share the same live cart via WebMCP to plan dinners, add items, or check out together, with every action visible and editable in real time.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Interface 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Interface 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Interface 
 
 1 2 



 
 Most "agentic shopping" demos we'd seen worked by having an AI agent drive a
headless browser through a UI built for humans clicking buttons, parsing
HTML, guessing at what a page meant. It's slow, brittle, and worst of all,
invisible: the human has no idea what's happening until the agent reports
back a summary at the end. 

 WebMCP flips that entirely. A page can declare what an agent is
allowed to do 
search_products
add_to_cart
checkout
with typed schemas, so the agent calls real functions instead of pretending to be a
mouse. We wanted to build something that showed off what changes once a
human and an agent aren't just near each other, but genuinely sharing
the same piece of state in real time. Grocery shopping felt like the
perfect testbed: it's repetitive, constraint-heavy work ("stay under
budget," "keep it vegetarian," "don't forget the eggs") that's exactly
what an agent is good at, while still being something people want a say
in; nobody wants an AI silently deciding what's for dinner. 

 That became Co-Shop : a storefront where you and your agent literally
share one cart. 

 What it does
Co-Shop is a grocery catalog with a shared cart. A human can browse and
add items by clicking, same as any store. An AI agent through
ChatGPT's WebMCP-enabled browser, or any WebMCP-aware client can call
into the same cart through seven registered tools: 

 
 search_products free-text / category / tag / price search 
 add_to_cart , remove_from_cart , update_quantity direct cart edits 
 get_cart read the current shared state, including what the human added 
 plan_dinners a compound tool: give it a day count, a diet, and a
budget, and it picks matching dinners and adds all of them in one call 
 checkout places the order and clears the cart 
 

 Every action human or agent shows up instantly with a badge ( YOU or
 AGENT ), a highlight animation on agent-added items, and a live activity
feed narrating the back-and-forth. Ask your agent "plan a week of
vegetarian dinners under $40" and watch the cart fill up in front of you,
still fully editable. 

 How i built it 

 The whole app is a single Next.js (App Router) page with one client
component holding the cart and activity-log state. On mount, it registers
all seven tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , each with
a JSON Schema inputSchema and an execute function but critically,
those execute functions call the same internal helpers
( addToCart , removeFromCart , checkout , etc.) that the UI's own click
handlers call. That was the core design decision: there's no separate
"agent path" and "human path," just one state, mutated from two places. 

 Tools are registered inside a useEffect and cleaned up via an
 AbortController passed as the registration's signal . Every execute 
returns the WebMCP content-array shape
( { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(...) }] } ) so the
agent gets structured JSON back not just a confirmation string which
matters a lot for a compound tool like plan_dinners , where the agent
needs to know things like "only 5 of 7 requested days fit the budget." 

 Challenges i ran into 

 
 Stale closures. Tools are registered once on mount, so their
 execute functions would otherwise capture a stale snapshot of the
cart. We solved this by keeping the state update functions themselves
as the single source of truth (via setState functional updates)
rather than reading from a captured variable. 
 Making agent actions legible, not just correct. It's not enough for
the tool calls to work a judge (or a shopper) needs to see the
difference between "I added this" and "the agent added this" at a
glance. That's what drove the AGENT/YOU badges, the purple pulse
animation, and the activity feed. 
 Testing without a live agent. Early on, we stubbed
 document.modelContext in a headless browser to exercise the tools
programmatically before ever touching a real agent client — that caught
a few bugs (like quantity handling on update_quantity ) well before we
tested against ChatGPT's actual WebMCP browser. 
 Getting the deploy pipeline right on a deadline. Wiring up GitHub,
Vercel, and an MIT license that GitHub actually detects in the About
section took more back-and-forth than the code itself. 
 

 What i learned 

 WebMCP's real power isn't "agents can now click your buttons for you" 
it's that a page and an agent can share one source of truth instead of
two. That's a genuinely different interaction model from screen-scraping
or API wrapping, and it's why an agent's actions in Co-Shop feel like
someone else shopping with you, not an AI doing your shopping for you
somewhere off-screen. 

 What's next 

 Natural extensions: letting the agent negotiate substitutions when a
diet/budget can't be satisfied exactly, a compare_products tool for
side-by-side agent recommendations, and multi-user shared carts where two
humans and an agent are all in the same session at once.

title: Handoff
pitch: A Kanban board where you and your AI agent manage the same tasks, in real time, on the same live page.
about_excerpt:
A Kanban board where you and your AI agent manage the same tasks, in real time, on the same live page.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Handoff 

 A Kanban board where you and your AI agent manage the same tasks, in real time, on the same live page. 

 Inspiration 

 Every "agent + your app" story today follows the same pattern: the agent takes a screenshot, guesses which pixel is a button, clicks it, waits, screenshots again. It's slow, it's fragile, and it treats the agent like a human with a mouse instead of software that could just... call a function. 

 Task management felt like the clearest place to make that contrast obvious. A Kanban board is something people already share with teammates why not share it with an agent too, and let both act on the same live state at the same time? 

 What it does 

 Handoff is a collaborative Kanban board. A human drags cards between To Do, In Progress, and Done exactly like any other Kanban tool. An AI agent manages the same board through seven WebMCP tools registered directly on the page: 

 
 create_task , list_tasks , move_task , update_task , delete_task the core actions any task manager needs 
 prioritize_tasks applies a batch of priority changes the agent has already reasoned about (via list_tasks ), atomically, in one call 
 summarize_board a natural-language rollup of what's open, in progress, and done 
 

 Both the human and the agent are working against the exact same Supabase-backed state, synced live over Supabase Realtime. When the agent creates or moves a card, it shows an "agent" badge and a brief highlight pulse, so at a glance you can see who did what. A live activity log underneath the board narrates the handoff as it happens: "You moved 'Fix login bug' to In Progress," "Agent created 'Update docs.'" 

 There's no chat window bolted onto the side. The agent works through the same UI you're looking at. 

 Why WebMCP fits this use case 

 Without WebMCP, an agent that wants to help manage your board has exactly two bad options: a bespoke backend API it has to be specifically integrated with, or screen-scraping a drag-and-drop UI that was never designed to be driven programmatically, inferring which <div> is a card, simulating a drag gesture, and hoping the DOM didn't change underneath it. 

 WebMCP replaces both of those with the page just telling the agent what it can do. document.modelContext.registerTool() exposes move_task with a typed schema ( id , status ) instead of forcing an agent to identify and drag a specific card. The agent doesn't need a separate integration, and it doesn't need to understand your UI, it needs to understand your tools, which you've defined precisely. 

 That's the UX improvement in one sentence: an agent can now say "reprioritize my sprint so the login bug is high priority" and it works , live, immediately reflected in the same board a human is looking at, without OpenAI, Anthropic, or anyone else needing to have built a Handoff-specific integration ahead of time. The website itself is the integration. 

 What's newly possible 

 Before WebMCP, "human and agent share a task board" basically meant the agent had its own separate interface (a chat window, a CLI) that happened to write to the same database, two disconnected experiences bolted together. WebMCP lets both parties act through the same page, the same session, the same state, at the same time. You can watch a card move because you dragged it, or because you asked an agent to move it, and the board doesn't care which, it just reacts. That's a genuinely different interaction model, not just a faster version of the old one. 

 How we built it 

 
 Next.js / React , deployed on Vercel 
 Supabase (Postgres + Realtime) for shared task storage; every client (human tab or agent-driven tab) subscribes to the same Realtime channel, so changes from either side propagate instantly 
 WebMCP , implemented via direct document.modelContext.registerTool() calls (see hooks/useWebMCPTools.js ) each tool's execute function calls the exact same functions the drag-and-drop UI calls ( hooks/useTasks.js ), so there is one source of truth for board logic, not a parallel "agent path" that could drift out of sync with the human path 
 @hello-pangea/dnd for the human-facing drag-and-drop 
 The activity log is derived from the same Realtime subscription that drives the board, no separate logging table, just an in-memory feed of what the subscription already sees 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is genuinely early. I hit a real interoperability bug where a React wrapper library's handler callback wasn't being translated into the native execute property the browser's registerTool() implementation expects, which surfaced as execute is not a function only at call time, not at registration time, which made it harder to catch. We moved to calling the native imperative API directly rather than depending on a wrapper layer, which fixed it and also made the WebMCP usage more explicit in the codebase. 

 Accomplishments 

 A full round trip, human drags a card, agent calls a tool, board updates live for both working end to end, verified both through direct browser console calls to document.modelContext.executeTool() and through a real natural-language agent (Google's Model Context Tool Inspector) discovering and calling our tools correctly. 

 What's next 

 Multi-board support, authenticated multi-user boards, and finer-grained permissions per tool (e.g., a read-only list_tasks -only agent versus a full-access one) 

 Built with 

 Next.js, React, Supabase, Supabase Realtime, WebMCP ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), @hello-pangea/dnd, Vercel

title: SugarStack
pitch: A visual sugar and calorie tracker where people and AI agents use WebMCP to log drinks, adjust portions and see every change instantly.
about_excerpt:
A visual sugar and calorie tracker where people and AI agents use WebMCP to log drinks, adjust portions and see every change instantly.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 dashboard 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 dashboard 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 dashboard 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Sugar is everywhere, but grams on a nutrition label are difficult to visualize. People also drink different sizes, choose diet versions, share bottles, or only finish part of a serving. 

 We built SugarStack to make those everyday choices instantly understandable—and to explore how a human and an AI agent can work with the same health-tracking interface through WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 SugarStack is a visual sugar and calorie tracker that: 

 
 Tracks drinks and foods using flexible amounts and quantities 
 Distinguishes regular, diet and zero-sugar alternatives 
 Supports custom entries using values from the product label 
 Converts sugar into an easy-to-understand cube estimate 
 Displays sugar and calories together 
 Synchronizes the selected date, daily log, headline total and monthly calendar 
 Highlights low, medium and high-sugar days 
 Stores personal entries locally without requiring an account or API key 
 

 The values are presented as typical label estimates rather than medical advice, and users can enter exact information from their own product labels. 

 How we used WebMCP 

 WebMCP is a core part of the product rather than an extra chatbot feature. SugarStack exposes five focused tools: 

 
 sugarstack_get_day 
 sugarstack_search_catalog 
 sugarstack_add_items 
 sugarstack_update_entry 
 sugarstack_remove_entry 
 

 An agent can search the catalogue, add validated items, adjust portions, remove mistakes and summarize the selected day. 

 Most importantly, the agent operates on the same visible state as the person . When an agent changes an entry, the date, log, sugar total, calories and calendar update on screen. Users can immediately inspect, verify or correct every action. 

 For example, someone can ask: 

 
 Log a medium cola and two small lattes. Then change the cola to diet and show me the updated total. 
 

 The agent can complete that workflow using structured WebMCP tools while SugarStack provides a clear visual result. 

 How we built it 

 SugarStack was built with TypeScript, React, Vinext, Vite and Tailwind CSS. Its responsive interface uses reusable components and local browser storage for persistence. 

 The WebMCP layer registers structured tool definitions with narrow input schemas, catalogue identifiers, amount limits and quantity validation. Read-only and state-changing tools are intentionally separated so agents can inspect before acting. 

 The live experience includes preloaded demonstration history so judges can immediately explore the synchronized monthly view without creating weeks of sample data. 

 Challenges we faced 

 The hardest challenge was designing WebMCP tools that were useful without exposing a large, confusing interface. We reduced the contract to five actions that correspond directly to real user tasks. 

 Another challenge was keeping every part of the interface synchronized. Selecting another date or changing an entry needed to update the daily log, hero total, calories, cube estimate and calendar consistently. 

 We also had to balance simplicity with flexible data entry. SugarStack needed to remain approachable for someone who just wants to tap “Cola,” while still supporting different serving sizes, quantities, diet variants and exact label values. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that good agent integration is not about exposing the largest number of tools. It is about creating a small, predictable contract with visible outcomes. 

 WebMCP works especially well when the website remains the source of truth: the agent can act efficiently, while the person maintains context, control and trust. 

 What we are proud of 

 SugarStack combines a polished human interface with a practical agent workflow without requiring an external nutrition API, account or API key. 

 Every important capability can be understood and demonstrated in under two minutes. 

 What is next 

 Future versions could add optional barcode scanning, user-defined goals, additional nutrients, exportable reports and verified regional nutrition catalogues—while preserving the local-first, human-verifiable experience.

about_excerpt:
A shared WebMCP travel workspace where humans and AI agents search, compare, and build itineraries together—with humans in control.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 1 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Webmcp 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 home page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Webmcp 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 home page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Webmcp 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Travel planning is usually spread across search engines, hotel websites, maps, booking platforms, and personal notes. People have to repeatedly copy information between different services, while AI agents struggle to work with websites that were designed only for visual human interaction. 

 We wanted to explore a different model: a travel workspace where humans and AI agents can work with the same structured information and the same itinerary. The goal was not to remove the human from the process. The goal was to make discovery and planning easier while keeping important decisions visible and human-controlled. 

 This idea became trip_world — a shared WebMCP travel workspace built around the principle: 

 
 You go. We go. 
 

 What the project does 

 trip_world helps users search destinations, compare travel options, inspect details, and build an itinerary in one place. 

 The interface starts with a focused destination view instead of displaying the entire world catalog at once. Users can search by city, country, region, travel style, or destination highlight. Only a small number of destination cards are shown at a time, and navigation controls allow users to browse further places without overwhelming the screen. 

 After selecting a city, the workspace displays options belonging to that destination. These options include hotels, flights, activities, parks, tourist spots, transport references, and offers. Users can filter and compare records using information such as price, rating, tags, duration, accessibility, and cancellation details. 

 Every selected item can be added to the shared itinerary. The itinerary displays selected items, source links, INR prices, the running total, and an activity ledger showing recent human and agent actions. 

 How WebMCP is used 

 WebMCP is the central technical feature of the project. It allows compatible AI agents to use structured capabilities exposed by the webpage instead of relying only on visual screen interpretation or fragile DOM scraping. 

 trip_world registers 37 WebMCP tools covering: 

 
 Destination discovery. 
 City selection. 
 Travel dataset search. 
 Category and budget filtering. 
 Hotel, flight, park, activity, tourist spot, and offer discovery. 
 Option comparison. 
 Details and source-link inspection. 
 Price and recommendation analysis. 
 Shared itinerary updates. 
 Trip-change previews and human review. 
 

 The human and the agent use the same application state. When an agent searches for Goa hotels or adds an option to the itinerary, the visible interface updates and the activity ledger records the action. This makes the collaboration understandable instead of hiding agent behavior in a separate conversation. 

 The project also separates planning from sensitive actions. Payment and checkout are not exposed as WebMCP tools. Reservation-related actions remain human-controlled through the visible interface, and the Razorpay integration is limited to test mode. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend was built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The backend uses Node.js, Express, and TypeScript. The WebMCP integration is implemented through the imperative tool-registration API. 

 The travel data is stored in a structured TypeScript dataset containing city metadata and catalog records. Cities include information such as country, region, climate, local currency, ideal stay duration, daily budget guidance, travel styles, and highlights. Travel options include structured fields for category, price, rating, tags, duration, accessibility, cancellation details, and reference links. 

 The application uses a shared state model for: 

 
 Selected destination. 
 Current search query. 
 Active filters. 
 Search results. 
 Itinerary items. 
 Activity events. 
 Pending trip-change proposals. 
 

 For safety, itinerary entries are validated against the known catalog. The server recomputes reservation totals from server-side data rather than trusting a client-provided amount. Razorpay signatures are verified server-side, and secret credentials are never included in the client bundle or GitHub repository. 

 The interface was designed with a responsive editorial style. It includes a compact destination carousel, contained scrolling for the itinerary and activity panels, responsive mobile behavior, source links, visual feedback, and lightweight animations. 

 What we learned 

 The most important lesson was that agent-ready websites need more than a visually attractive interface. They need clear capabilities with predictable names, strict input schemas, useful descriptions, and outputs that an agent can reliably understand. 

 We learned that shared state is essential for human-agent collaboration. A tool call is much more useful when its result is immediately reflected in the same interface that the human is watching. 

 We also learned that tool annotations and action boundaries matter. Read-only discovery tools should be separated from state-changing tools. Actions that change an itinerary need clear review behavior. Payment and checkout require a stronger human boundary than ordinary travel research. 

 Another lesson was the importance of data quality. A large dataset is useful only when its records have consistent fields, stable identifiers, meaningful categories, source links, and predictable filtering behavior. Structured records make it possible to produce explanations such as destination comparisons and budget recommendations without manually writing every response. 

 Challenges 

 Making WebMCP registration reliable 

 Browser APIs may become available after the page has mounted. We added retry behavior, duplicate-registration protection, awaited tool registration, and strict JSON schemas so the tool surface becomes available reliably when supported by the browser. 

 Preventing stale destination results 

 When a user or agent changes destinations, previous results can become misleading. We updated the state flow so selecting a destination clears stale filters and results before loading the new destination's options. 

 Designing for a large dataset without overwhelming the user 

 The application contains a world-scale structured catalog, but displaying every destination immediately would make the interface difficult to use. We solved this with search, pagination-style carousel controls, focused result cards, filters, and an explicit no-results state. 

 Protecting sensitive operations 

 Travel planning and payment have different risk levels. We kept discovery and itinerary assistance available to agents but intentionally excluded payment and checkout from WebMCP. Test payment credentials remain server-side, and payment signatures are verified by the backend. 

 Keeping local and hosted behavior consistent 

 The project supports local Express execution and Vercel serverless deployment. We added a Vercel API adapter and routing configuration so the frontend and backend routes can be deployed together while preserving the local development workflow. 

 Creating a useful demonstration 

 A project like this needs to be shown functioning, not only described. The most important demo flow is a live destination search, city selection, option filtering, WebMCP tool execution, itinerary update, proposal preview, and human approval. This demonstrates the difference between a static travel interface and a collaborative agent-ready workspace. 

 Current limitations 

 The current travel catalog is a structured demonstration dataset. It is not a live hotel inventory, real-time flight feed, or guaranteed commercial offer source. Prices and offers are intended for exploration and demonstration. 

 The Razorpay integration is configured for test mode only. A production version would need persistent storage, webhook validation, rate limiting, monitoring, refund handling, current provider data, and additional compliance review. 

 The next version could connect authorized live travel providers, add persistent user accounts, include maps and route planning, support calendar export, and provide more advanced trip proposals. 

 Why this project matters 

 trip_world demonstrates how the open web can become more useful to both humans and AI agents when websites expose structured, understandable capabilities.

 Inspiration 

 I wanted to make WebMCP feel useful to everyday users, not just developers. The idea was to create a friendly browser companion that appears when a site supports WebMCP and lets people interact with it through simple chat or voice. 

 What it does 

 Buddy detects WebMCP-enabled websites, discovers the tools they expose, and lets users ask for actions in natural language. It can help search, navigate, and perform supported website actions while keeping higher-risk actions behind user approval. 

 How we built it 

 I built Buddy as a Chrome extension on top of WebMCP, using APIs like document modelContext.getTools() to discover site capabilities and executeTool() to run them. A lightweight agent service deployed on Railway uses the OpenAI API to interpret the user’s goal and select the next action from the tools exposed by the current website (which supports WebMCP). Buddy then executes that action through WebMCP in the browser while keeping permissions, risk checks, and user approvals under local control. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was handling different tool schemas and behaviors across websites while keeping execution safe and predictable. Voice interaction, browser permissions, argument validation, and action limits also required several rounds of debugging. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm proud that Buddy became more than a technical demo. It provides a complete experience with WebMCP detection, natural-language interaction, voice support, approvals, activity feedback, and a friendly UI that works across supported websites. 

 What we learned 

 I learned how powerful WebMCP can be when websites expose structured capabilities instead of forcing agents to understand pages visually. I also learned that trust, clear feedback, and user control are just as important as the agent intelligence itself. 

 What's next for Buddy — Your WebMCP Browser Agent 

 Next, I want to expand Buddy and improve multi-step planning and voice interaction, and evolve it into a reusable browser-agent platform.  CARTOS — Where Humans Shop. Agents Act. 

 
 An agent-native e-commerce experience powered by WebMCP 
 

 

 💡 The Idea 

 Shopping online is still fundamentally designed around humans . 

 We search through products, open multiple pages, compare specifications, check reviews, evaluate prices, add items to our cart, enter delivery details, and finally complete the purchase. 

 But as AI agents become increasingly capable, we asked a different question: 

 
 What if an AI agent could actually use an e-commerce website instead of simply talking about it? 
 

 That question inspired us to build CARTOS — an AI-native e-commerce experience powered by WebMCP . 

 We built a complete shopping application backed by a real-world Amazon product dataset containing 123,133 products . 

 Our goal wasn't to build another chatbot that recommends products. 

 Our goal was to make the website itself usable by an AI agent. 

 

 🛒 What We Built 

 CARTOS is a complete e-commerce experience with: 

 
 🔎 Product discovery 
 📦 Product details 
 🔥 Today's deals 
 🛒 Cart management 
 👤 User information 
 💳 Checkout 
 📋 Order history 
 ⭐ Product reviews 
 

 But underneath the interface, we built a WebMCP capability layer that exposes the application's functionality directly to AI agents. 

 CARTOS currently exposes 15 WebMCP tools: 

 🔎 Product Discovery 

 search_products(query, category?) 

 Searches our 123,133-product catalog . 

 get_product_details(asin) 

 Retrieves product specifications, reviews, price, and ASIN metadata. 

 get_todays_deals() 

 Retrieves current promotions and highly-rated best sellers. 

 recommend_product(productId, reason) 

 Allows the agent to recommend a specific product with a reason without automatically adding it to the cart. 

 

 🛒 Cart Operations 

 view_cart() 

 Retrieves the current cart. 

 add_to_cart(productId, quantity?) 

 Adds a product to the cart. 

 remove_from_cart(cartItemId) 

 Removes an item from the cart. 

 update_cart_quantity(productId, quantity) 

 Updates the quantity of an item. 

 clear_cart() 

 Completely clears the cart. 

 

 👤 User & Checkout 

 get_user_profile() 

 Retrieves the user's name, email, saved addresses, and payment methods. 

 add_saved_address(street, city, country) 

 Adds a delivery address. 

 add_payment_method(cardType, last4) 

 Adds a payment-method reference. 

 checkout_order(addressId, paymentMethodId) 

 Creates an order draft for final human approval . 

 

 📦 Post-Purchase 

 view_orders() 

 Retrieves order history and statuses. 

 leave_product_review(productId, stars, comment) 

 Allows a product review to be submitted. 

 

 🤖 WebMCP in Action 

 The most important part of our project isn't simply exposing these tools. 

 It is what happens when an AI agent actually uses them. 

 For our demonstration, we give the agent access to our live CARTOS storefront. 

 Instead of manually explaining the application's capabilities, the agent can discover the WebMCP tools exposed directly by the website . 

 The agent discovers CARTOS's capabilities and can then use them to perform a real shopping workflow. 

 We give it a real shopping task: 

 
 "Find me the best shoes with the best balance of price, rating, and quality. Search the catalog, compare the options, and recommend the best one." 
 

 The agent can now use CARTOS's application capabilities to perform the research. 

 It can: 
 Search
 ↓
Inspect product details
 ↓
Evaluate alternatives
 ↓
Recommend the best option
 ↓
Add to cart

---


# 🤝 Human + Agent Collaboration

This is where we believe **WebMCP becomes especially powerful**.

We don't want an AI agent to completely replace the human.

We want the agent to **handle the complexity while the human retains control**.

### 🤖 What the Agent Handles

- Finding relevant products
- Searching the catalog
- Inspecting product information
- Evaluating alternatives
- Making recommendations
- Managing the cart
- Preparing the checkout

### 👤 What the Human Handles

- The final purchasing decision
- Approval before the order is placed

When the agent reaches checkout, our `checkout_order()` tool creates an **order draft for final human approval** rather than blindly completing the purchase.

This creates a clear boundary:

> **The agent does the work. The human makes the final commitment.**

---

# 🌐 Why WebMCP?

Traditional websites expose information primarily for **humans**.

AI agents can potentially read that information, but **reading a webpage is very different from using an application**.

WebMCP gives CARTOS a structured **capability layer**.

Instead of an agent trying to figure out how to navigate buttons, pages, and UI elements, CARTOS exposes meaningful actions such as:

view_cart()

Building **CARTOS** changed how we think about web applications.

We initially thought of an e-commerce website as a collection of pages and UI components.

Through **WebMCP**, we started thinking about it differently:

We learned how important it is to design tools around **meaningful application actions**, rather than simply exposing backend functions.

For example, `search_products()` is useful to an agent because it represents an actual **user-level capability**.

Likewise, `add_to_cart()` and `checkout_order()` allow the agent to progress through a **real shopping workflow**.

This helped us think about web development from two perspectives:

One of our biggest challenges was deciding **what should actually become a WebMCP tool**.

It would have been easy to expose dozens of tiny functions simply to increase the tool count.

Instead, we focused on capabilities that correspond to **meaningful shopping actions**.

Another challenge was designing the boundary between **agent autonomy and human control**.

Searching and comparing products are low-risk actions that an agent can perform independently.

Purchasing is different.

That's why our checkout flow deliberately stops at a **human approval point**.

We also had to connect the agent-facing tools to **real application state** so that actions such as adding an item to the cart weren't just simulated responses — they actually affected the shopping experience.

This made the WebMCP layer more than a collection of callable functions. It became a way for the agent to **participate in the application's actual workflow**.

We see this architecture extending far beyond shopping.

Today, **CARTOS** demonstrates an agent operating an e-commerce application.

 Inspiration 

 I was thinking about a practical useful tool that makes someones life a little better with WebMCP and that is when I decided to build this flowchart builder app (EasyFloww). It demonstrate WebMCP capabilities in a practical and visually engaging way so more people can understand it and explore. 

 What it does 

 EasyFloww is a drag and drop flowchart builder, it lets users create diagrams easily and share and editable as well as non editable version with anyone easily. With built in WebMCP support and no vendor lock in, any ai model with tool calling capabilities will be able to create flowchart seamlessly. 

 What makes this app special is that an AI agent and a user can work on the canvas together to create diagrams and collaborate in real time. 

 The data is stored in localstorage and never leaves your system, which tighten the security. 

 How we built it 

 I used AI as a companion to plan and develop the application. React and TypeScript is the technologies along with the npm package xyflow which power this application. 

 The app exposes actions as tools using webmcp. We have built and registered 10 tools.
get_flow_state: returns the current nodes and edges (with type, label, config, position, and connected handles) for the active flow
add_node: adds a new node of a given type, label, and optional position
connect_nodes: connects two nodes by ID, with an optional sourceHandle for decision branches.
move_node: repositions an existing node by ID
update_node_config: updates a node's label/condition/description/borderColor
delete_node: removes a node (and its connected edges)
insert_node_between: splits an existing edge to insert a new node directly between two connected nodes
remove_edge: disconnects two nodes by removing a specific edge
clone_flow: duplicates a flow (active or specified) into a new independent tab
import_flow: creates an entire new flow in one call from a complete node/edge JSON graph, with validation 

 Every tool calls the exact same Zustand store functions that the UI itself uses, addNode, moveNode, addEdge, updateNodeConfig etc. There's no separate path for the AI agent through the code, a tool call and a mouse drag both end up mutating the same store the same way. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was to design the architecture of the project in a way that makes the agent-human collaboration foolproof - meaning a human and an agent editing the same live canvas should never produce corruption, silently divergent data, lost work, or ambiguity about who changed what. 

 The design decisions that highlight the actions an agent is performing in the canvas was another challenge. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The end product came out really well and useful, anyone who is looking for an AI support flowchart builder can use this product. 

 I am proud about the fact that I got a deeper understanding about the latest features of the web and got hands on experience in it. I am really proud of it. 

 What we learned 

 I got a pretty solid understanding about the WebMCP protocol and got really confident in implementing it in my future projects. 

 What's next for EasyFloww 

 Most diagram tools lock you into their own built in AI assistant. If you want AI help, you use their model, in their chat box, on their terms. EasyFlow is here to change that, to provide a better experience for the end user to use the AI models they are comfortable with and to create complex diagrams seamlessly. 

 We want to provide the user at most security and privacy possible so that their data belongs to them and not any servers.

 Inspiration 

 We wanted note-taking to feel effortless when working alongside AI. Right now, most AI assistants feel isolated from the apps we actually use—they sit in a side panel, completely blind to what's happening on your screen unless you copy-paste text back and forth. 

 When the WebMCP open standard was announced, we realized web apps could finally give AI agents structured "hands" to help users directly inside the UI. We set out to build Ecrit —a cozy, distraction-free notes workspace where you and your agent can read, organize, and edit your board together without getting in each other's way. 

 

 What it does 

 Ecrit is a soft, paper-themed Kanban board and note app designed for both humans and AI agents. 

 
 Works with your AI agent: Instead of copy-pasting notes, your AI assistant can directly create cards, organize columns, search your notes, or edit markdown text using clean background commands. 
 Keeps you in control: The app includes human-in-the-loop protection. For sensitive actions—like deleting a note—the AI cannot bypass your permission; it triggers a friendly prompt asking for your confirmation first. 
 

 * Clean, distraction-free workspace: Uses a calming "Cactus & Paper" design system with readable typography so writing always feels natural. 

 How we built it 

 We built Ecrit using modern, fast web standards designed for agent-native interactions: 

 
 Frontend: Built with Next.js (App Router) and Tailwind CSS to keep the UI fluid and responsive. 
 WebMCP Integration: We used @mcp-b/global to register 7 custom browser tools directly to navigator.modelContext . This allows browser agents (like ChatGPT's in-app browser) to instantly detect what Ecrit can do. 
 Markdown Rendering: Integrated marked so your notes support rich text, checklists, and code snippets smoothly. 
 

 * Security & Guardrails: Built strict input sanitization and length limits into every tool handler to stop prompt injection attacks from messing up your board. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Teaching DevTools to detect WebMCP: Early on, browser flags and polyfills didn't always play nicely together during Next.js client hydration. We had to carefully structure our client component mounts inside a clean useEffect lifecycle to ensure navigator.modelContext was exposed reliably to Chrome DevTools. 
 Balancing cute design with structure: Finding the right balance between a soft, friendly "cactus and paper" aesthetic without making the Kanban board feel cluttery or misaligned took several UI iterations. 
 Preventing rogue actions: Ensuring AI agents couldn't accidentally wipe out user data required setting up a clear split between "read-only" search tools and "write" operations that require explicit user consent. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 7 fully functional WebMCP tools: We successfully exposed a complete set of CRUD and search actions (create, move, edit, rename, delete, search, summarize) without relying on fragile web scraping. 
 A polished, human-centered UI: Created an aesthetic that feels warm, calm, and approachable—completely avoiding cold, overly complex dark-mode terminal tropes. 
 Built-in security: Successfully defended tool handlers against prompt injections and stored XSS attacks right out of the box. 
 

 

 What we learned 

 
 The future of web apps is agent-native: Building with WebMCP showed us how much smoother web apps become when AI agents have explicit APIs instead of guessing their way through raw HTML elements. 
 Safety needs to be built into the UI: Human-in-the-loop confirmations are essential for building trust between users and automated agents. 
 

 

 What's next for Ecrit 

 
 Real-time multiplayer editing: Allowing multiple human users and AI agents to edit the exact same markdown card simultaneously. 
 Custom tags & board filtering: Exposing tag-based tool filtering so agents can organize complex projects automatically based on priority. 
 Offline local storage sync: Saving all your paper notes and board history locally so Ecrit works seamlessly offline without needing a constant network connection.

about_excerpt:
Agents already work the web by scraping DOM and guessing at selectors.
Signal Desk is a support workboard build with WebMCP so that agents inspect board, open case, create & propose a stage change.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 This project began with a practical problem: important operational work often starts in WhatsApp. A customer message, an incident report, or a request for help arrives in a chat, then someone needs to understand it, assign it, follow up, and record the outcome. 

 We had already been exploring a local WhatsApp ingestion workboard. However, that system relies on private authentication and persisted chat/media data. It is intentionally local-only: publishing it would expose sensitive data and would not be a reliable fit for a serverless deployment. 

 That constraint became the inspiration for Signal Desk. 

 Instead of pretending that private WhatsApp data should be pushed to the public web, we built a safe, fictional, browser-only workboard that represents the workflow after a message becomes an operational case. It lets us demonstrate the meaningful question: how can people and AI agents work on the same case safely? 

 What it does 

 Signal Desk is a fictional support workboard where a person can create, review, edit, and move cases through New, Triage, Investigating, and Resolved. 

 The important difference is that the page also exposes focused WebMCP tools. An agent can list cases, open a case, create a new case, update its record, and propose a stage move using structured site capabilities rather than guessing from screenshots or clicking around blindly. 

 The human remains the decision-maker. When an agent wants to create, edit, or move a case, Signal Desk creates a visible pending action instead of silently changing the board. The person can approve or cancel it. After approval, the agent reads the actual board state back to verify the outcome. 

 This means the product supports both kinds of work: 

 
 Humans can use the normal visual interface. 
 Agents can use WebMCP to work through the same case model. 
 Important changes remain visible, reversible before approval, and verifiable afterward. 
 

 How we built it 

 We separated the original private WhatsApp concept from the deployable demonstration. 

 The original ingestion idea stays local, where private authentication and persisted conversations belong. Signal Desk is the public, safe companion: it uses fictional data that lives only in the browser and can be deployed to Vercel without exposing real messages, media, credentials, or customer information. 

 We built a case workboard with rich case details, notes, formatting, case creation, manual editing, stage movement, and a visible activity history. We then implemented WebMCP tools for the same operations. 

 For state-changing tools, we added an approval workflow: 

 
 The agent proposes an action. 
 The website returns an awaiting approval state and an approval ID. 
 A person can approve or cancel the specific action. 
 The agent confirms the approved action. 
 The agent reads back the resulting case or board state before claiming success. 
 

 Challenges we faced 

 The biggest challenge was not making an agent able to act. It was making agent action trustworthy. 

 A tool that can move a case directly is convenient, but it can also hide a consequential decision. We designed the approval state so that creating a case, changing its content, and moving it to Resolved are explicit, separate decisions. 

 We also learned that an approval alone is not enough. The agent must verify the result after the action completes. During testing, we improved the workflow so the agent does not merely report “done”; it checks the updated record or board state and reports evidence of the outcome. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is valuable because it gives an agent a clear contract with a webpage. The agent does not need private backend access, fragile screen automation, or permission to control everything. The website declares the useful actions, their inputs, and their safety boundaries. 

 Signal Desk shows how an ongoing, message-driven workboard project can become agent-interactive and deployment-ready without exposing the private WhatsApp layer behind it. 

 The goal is not to replace people with automation. It is to turn scattered reports into shared, structured work—where agents can help move work forward and people retain authority over the decisions that matter.

A WebMCP store where an agent shops for you, but every change stops for your confirmation. The agent proposes, the screen narrates, and you decide before anything happens.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Baton 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Baton 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Baton 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most agent demos on the web just act. The agent clicks buy, submits the form, or empties the
cart, and you find out afterward. That gives up two things the open web needs as agents
arrive: control, meaning you decide what actually changes, and access, meaning anyone can
operate the page, not only people who can see it and use a mouse. WebMCP's own guidance also
warns about prompt injection, where a malicious page or a hijacked agent issues tool calls a
person never asked for. We wanted a design that answered both at once. 

 What it does 

 Baton is a small grocery store. It works normally for a person, who can browse, add items,
review the cart, and check out. It also registers five WebMCP tools, so an agent can do the
same things from a request like "add oat milk, then check out." 

 The read tools, search_products and review_cart , run right away. The tools that change
state, add_to_cart , remove_from_cart , and checkout , never mutate anything directly.
They create a proposal on screen and return text saying the action is awaiting confirmation,
so a well-behaved agent waits. Every action is narrated through an ARIA-live region and a
plain-language card, and confirmed or rejected actions land in a visible timeline. Checkout is
a mock. No payment is taken and no order is sent anywhere. 

 How we built it 

 Vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with no framework, no build step, and no backend, deployed
as static files to Cloudflare Pages. The tools live in a local registry the page's own
interface calls directly, and the same tools are separately registered with
 document.modelContext for the agent, so the human interface never depends on the agent-side
API being present. 

 The confirmation step is enforced inside the tool, not the interface. A tool that changes
state does not change it in execute() . It sets one pending proposal and returns text that
tells the agent to wait. State only changes when the person clicks Confirm, so there is no code
path from a tool call to a state change that skips the person. 

 We also shipped a "Real agent" console in the page itself: paste any OpenAI-compatible LLM
key, and a real model plans the tool calls, which run through the same WebMCP interface and the
same confirmation step. We used it to test the flow with a real third-party model
( gpt-4o-mini via a model gateway) driving the tools end to end on the live deployed page. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Testing against a real WebMCP client was harder than expected. ChatGPT's web app
( chatgpt.com ) turned out not to be a WebMCP client at all: it web-searches the page
server-side and told us directly that it "does not expose the page's document.modelContext 
WebMCP tool registry." Chrome's WebMCP flag needs Chrome 149+, which isn't available on our
dev machine. That's what led to building the in-page "Real agent" console: it let us prove a
real third-party model driving the tools end to end, without depending on a specific browser. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The confirmation step is genuinely enforced in the tool layer, not just the UI, so there is no
way for any agent, well-behaved or not, to skip it. And the same mechanism does two jobs at
once: it is an accessibility story, because the agent operates the page's own tools instead of
a scraped DOM, and it is a prompt-injection defense, because an injected instruction can call
 checkout , but it only ever produces a proposal, never an order. 

 What we learned 

 How new WebMCP still is, down to which real clients actually support it today. And that a
confirmation step designed for accessibility turns out to double as a security boundary,
without any extra code, because both problems have the same shape: an agent should be able to
act, but a person should always get the last word. 

 What's next for Baton 

 A larger catalog and a second task, like a form or a booking, to show the design works beyond
shopping. A per-tool policy, where some proposals are approved automatically and high-stakes
ones always ask. And a shared session, where a helper and the person they assist both see the
same page.

title: BOUNDARY
pitch: Agents can see your tools. They don't decide when they're allowed to use them. BOUNDARY makes application state the authority—invalid transitions are rejected at the source.
about_excerpt:
Agents can see your tools. They don't decide when they're allowed to use them. BOUNDARY makes application state the authority—invalid transitions are rejected at the source.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 I kept seeing the same assumption in agentic systems: 

 If an agent can see a tool, it can probably use it. 

 But seeing a tool is not the same thing as having authority to use it. 

 An agent can read tool descriptions. It can decide what it thinks should happen next. It can even be given a list of valid actions. 

 None of that answers the important question: 

 
 Is this action valid right now? 
 

 That question belongs to the application. 

 I built BOUNDARY around one simple idea: 

 Agents don't have authority. Applications do. 

 The application's current state should be the thing that decides which transitions are possible — not the agent's reasoning, not a system prompt, and not whatever the agent happens to believe is allowed. 

 What it does 

 BOUNDARY is a state authoritative workflow for WebMCP applications. 

 An agent can request any tool at any time. BOUNDARY does not assume the request is valid just because the tool exists. 

 Every request goes through the same workflow engine: 
 CURRENT STATE + REQUESTED ACTION
 ↓
 WORKFLOW ENGINE
 ↙ ↘
 ALLOW BLOCK
 
 If the current state authorizes the transition, it happens. 

 If it doesn't, the application rejects it. 

 The demo makes this visible rather than hiding it behind a policy document. 

 At INITIAL , select_device_type is valid. 

 Once the workflow moves forward, that authority changes. 

 Later, confirm_submission is valid in AWAITING_CONFIRMATION . After the submission happens, the exact same tool becomes invalid. 

 The tool didn't change. 

 The application's state did. 

 BOUNDARY also includes a Security Lab that deliberately attempts invalid transitions: 

 
 Force submission from the wrong state 
 Skip required evidence 
 Bypass validation 
 Reuse stale authority after the workflow has advanced 
 

 All four are rejected by the same engine. 

 Every attempt is recorded in the Black Box with the action, state, result, and reason. 

 How I built it 

 BOUNDARY is a Svelte 5 application built with Vite and a deliberately small architecture. 

 The important part is the WorkflowEngine . 

 There isn't one set of rules for the UI and another for the WebMCP tools. There isn't a separate security layer that has to stay synchronized with the workflow. 

 Every WebMCP tool ultimately delegates to the same transition function: 
 WebMCP Tool
 ↓
attemptTransition(action, payload)
 ↓
Current workflow state
 ↓
ALLOW / BLOCK
 ↓
State transition + audit event
 
 The workflow engine owns the state, valid transitions, blocking conditions, evidence requirements, and transition decisions. 

 That makes the central rule an architectural constraint: 

 No agent action can change workflow state unless the current state authorizes that transition. 

 The UI simply exposes what the engine is already enforcing. 

 The Black Box then makes those decisions observable, so a judge can watch the same request go from accepted to rejected as the workflow changes. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part wasn't building a state machine. 

 It was making sure we actually had one state machine. 

 During development, we had separate pieces of logic that could have become competing sources of truth. That was exactly the problem BOUNDARY was supposed to demonstrate, so we removed that ambiguity. 

 I consolidated the workflow into a single engine and made the WebMCP tools thin wrappers around it. 

 The other challenge was resisting the temptation to make the project look more complicated than the idea. 

 I initially explored a more elaborate visual presentation, but the more important question became: 

 Can someone look at the application and immediately see the authority boundary being enforced? 

 That led me toward a much simpler interface: state, available tools, the engine's decision, and the Black Box. 

 The result is less of a dashboard and more of a live experiment. 

 Accomplishments i'm proud of 

 The biggest one is that the core idea is directly observable. 

 You don't have to trust a README that says BOUNDARY prevents invalid actions. 

 You can try one. 

 At one point in the workflow: 
 confirm_submission
→ ACCEPTED
→ SUBMITTED
 
 Then, seconds later: 
 confirm_submission
→ BLOCKED
→ stale authority
 
 Same tool. 

 Same application. 

 Different state. 

 That's the boundary. 

 I also built a dedicated adversarial mode instead of only demonstrating the happy path. 

 The Security Lab attacks the workflow with force submit, evidence skipping, validation bypass, and stale authority. The engine rejects each attempt. 

 Most importantly, the agent doesn't get a special escape hatch. 

 Even if the agent ignores the application's suggested next action and requests something completely different, the workflow engine still decides. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest lesson was that telling an agent what it is allowed to do is not the same as enforcing what it is allowed to do. 

 A system prompt can describe valid transitions. 

 A tool description can describe prerequisites. 

 An agent can even reason correctly most of the time. 

 But if correctness depends on the agent remembering and obeying those instructions, the agent has effectively become part of the security boundary. 

 BOUNDARY flips that relationship. 

 The agent can request. 

 The application decides. 

 I also learned that a good security demo shouldn't just show that the happy path works. It should deliberately create the moment where the system is expected to say no . 

 That is where the architecture becomes visible. 

 What's next for BOUNDARY 

 BOUNDARY currently demonstrates the primitive inside a controlled workflow. 

 The next step is to make that primitive easier to drop into real WebMCP applications without rebuilding the enforcement layer from scratch. 

 That means moving toward a reusable workflow authority layer where applications define their states and transitions, expose their tools, and let BOUNDARY enforce the relationship between the two. 

 The long term idea is simple: 

 Don't ask the agent to know what it is allowed to do. Give the application the final say. 

 Project Story 

 BOUNDARY started with a question: 

 What happens when an agent has a tool that exists, but isn't valid anymore? 

 That sounds obvious until you look at how agentic systems actually work. 

 Agents see tools. They read descriptions. They decide what to call. In many systems, the application's current workflow state is treated as context the agent should reason about. 

 I thought that boundary was backwards. 

 If an application knows that a claim hasn't been validated, why should an agent be trusted to remember that confirm_submission isn't valid yet? 

 If the workflow has already moved past submission, why should the agent be trusted not to reuse an earlier action? 

 So I built BOUNDARY around a single invariant: 

 
 The application's state determines what actions are valid. 
 

 The interesting part wasn't implementing that rule. It was proving it. 

 I built a workflow where the available WebMCP tools change as the application moves through its states. Then it was deliberately attacked. 

 A tool that works in one state is tried again after the state changes. 

 A submission is forced from the beginning. 

 Evidence requirements are skipped. 

 Validation is bypassed. 

 Old authority is reused. 

 The engine makes the decision every time. 

 There is no second rules engine for the UI. No special exception for the agent. No system prompt instruction that can override the workflow. 

 Every request reaches the same transition function. 

 That ended up being the most important architectural decision in the project. 

 I also made every decision visible through the Black Box. Instead of simply displaying "blocked," BOUNDARY shows the action that was requested, the state it was requested from, the resulting decision, and why the transition was rejected. 

 The final demo became less about showing features and more about watching an assumption fail.

A shared idea board where people and AI agents post, link, and upvote ideas together in real time - through 7 registered WebMCP tools, not scraping or screenshots.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Agents are getting good at driving a browser like a person would — click, type, scroll, screenshot, repeat. That works, but it's slow and brittle, and it treats the agent like a guest who has to guess at a UI built for someone else. WebMCP flips that: the page itself can say, in plain terms, "here's what you're actually allowed to do here." We wanted to build something small enough to finish quickly but real enough to show what that unlocks — a space where a person and an agent aren't just co-existing on the same page, they're editing the same shared thing, together, in view of each other. 

 What it does 

 The Commons is a shared idea board about the future of the open web. A person can post an idea, tag it, upvote it, or link it to another idea through the normal UI. An AI agent visiting the same page in a WebMCP-enabled browser gets seven registered tools — add_idea , list_ideas , search_ideas , connect_ideas , upvote_idea , remove_idea , get_board_summary — that operate on the exact same board. Every tool call the agent makes shows up instantly in an on-page activity feed, and agent-authored ideas are visually distinct (teal) from human ones (amber), so provenance is never ambiguous. Because the board lives on a shared backend rather than in localStorage , two different people (or a person and an agent) genuinely see and build on each other's contributions in the same session. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is a single static index.html — no framework, no build step — that registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() on load, each with a name, a plain-language description, and a JSON Schema input contract. Read-only tools ( list_ideas , search_ideas , get_board_summary ) are marked with readOnlyHint: true . The execute function for every tool calls the same small REST API that the human-facing UI calls, so there's exactly one source of truth for board state, mutated by two different actors. The backend is a small Express server with a JSON-file store, deployed on Railway; the frontend is deployed separately on Vercel and points at it via a configurable API base URL. The page polls the API every few seconds so a person watching sees an agent's edits without refreshing. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting the mutation model right took a couple of passes — early on the WebMCP tools and the UI's own click handlers each had their own copy of the board, which meant an agent's edit wouldn't show up until a manual refresh. Routing every mutation, human and agent alike, through the same API call fixed that and made the "co-creating in real time" story actually true instead of just visually implied. 

 What's next 

 Multiplayer presence (showing who's currently viewing the board), letting the agent read why a person upvoted something before adding a related idea, and exposing the same tool set to iframed origins via exposedTo so a partner site could embed The Commons and let its own visitors' agents contribute too.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 About LifeSim 

 LifeSim is an interactive project-management simulation where an AI agent helps a human make strategic decisions for a student innovation project. 

 The idea came from a simple question: what would happen if an AI agent could not only give advice, but actually understand the current state of a live simulation, compare possible decisions, preview their consequences, and then act with the user's confirmation? 

 What we built 

 LifeSim uses WebMCP to expose structured tools that allow an AI agent to interact with the simulation. 

 The agent can: 

 
 inspect the current simulation state; 
 see tasks, team information, resources, risks, deadlines, and success probability; 
 retrieve the decisions currently available; 
 compare different strategic options; 
 preview the consequences of a decision; 
 apply a confirmed decision; 
 advance the simulation. 
 

 The core WebMCP tools include get_simulation_state and get_available_decisions . These tools return real data from the running simulation instead of relying on a static description. 

 Human-in-the-loop 

 An important part of LifeSim is keeping the human in control. 

 The AI agent can analyze the situation and recommend an action, but consequential state changes go through an explicit preview and confirmation flow. This makes the agent's actions visible and understandable instead of allowing decisions to happen silently. 

 The interface also shows Agent Activity so that users can see what the agent is doing and how successful tool calls affect the simulation. 

 What we learned 

 Building LifeSim helped us understand how WebMCP can connect an AI agent with a real interactive web application through structured tools. 

 Instead of treating an AI agent as a separate chatbot, WebMCP allows the agent to work with the application's actual state and capabilities. 

 We also learned the importance of designing clear tool interfaces and making state-changing actions observable and controllable. 

 Challenges 

 One of the main challenges was making sure that the AI agent, WebMCP tools, and simulation UI remained synchronized. 

 We tested the project through multiple demo steps and verified that the WebMCP tools returned the expected simulation data and that the project could successfully build and run. 

 We also had to work around an API quota limitation during development. Because the core WebMCP functionality is independent from that limitation, we focused on making the underlying simulation, tools, validation, and agent workflow reliable. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 LifeSim demonstrates how WebMCP can let an AI agent interact with a live web application through structured tools while keeping the human in control of consequential actions. 

 The goal is not simply to make an AI that talks about a simulation, but an AI that can understand the application's state, reason about available actions, and interact with the application through explicit, verifiable tools.

 Inspiration
