Discovering WebMCP gave me an opportunity to explore those ideas in a practical environment rather than building only a theoretical demonstration. 

 What it does 

 This project adds a WebMCP-powered interaction layer to the real GodreryTone Jewellery Shopify storefront. 

 It allows an AI agent to work with structured shopping capabilities such as: 

 
 Customer intent 
 Occasion 
 Style 
 Recipient 
 Regional context 
 Budget and currency 
 Product discovery 
 Pricing 
 Shipping eligibility 
 Customer decisions 
 Final product routing 
 

 The goal is to help customers move from naturally describing what they want to finding relevant products in the actual Shopify store. 

 How we built it 

 We built the project by integrating WebMCP into the existing GodreryTone Jewellery Shopify storefront and exposing specialized tools for different parts of the shopping journey. 

 The implementation connects the customer's natural-language request with the store's existing commerce data and logic. 

 It also incorporates: 

 
 Market-aware product availability 
 Budget and currency handling 
 Pricing considerations 
 Shipping eligibility 
 Direct routing to Shopify product pages 
 

 The project was developed around the principle that: 

 
 Shopify remains the commerce platform while WebMCP provides an additional AI-agent interaction layer. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the main challenges was working with the realities of a developing Shopify store rather than a simplified demonstration environment. 

 Product availability can depend on the customer's country and supplier capabilities. Different markets can have different product availability, while the current Shopify subscription also creates limitations around currency handling. 

 Another challenge was ensuring that the AI experience does not make assumptions on behalf of the customer, particularly when regional alternatives, availability, pricing, or shipping need to be considered. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that the project moved beyond a theoretical WebMCP implementation and was applied to a real Shopify jewellery storefront with real products and real commerce considerations . 

 We created a set of specialized WebMCP tools that work together as part of a broader customer journey rather than functioning as isolated features. 

 We are also proud of demonstrating how a customer can express a complex shopping request naturally and how that request can be connected to structured store capabilities and ultimately to the real Shopify shopping experience. 

 What we learned 

 This project taught us that building an AI-powered shopping experience is not simply about adding an AI interface. 

 We learned the importance of understanding the underlying: 

 
 Business rules 
 Product availability 
 Regional differences 
 Currency 
 Pricing 
 Shipping 
 Customer control 
 

 before an agent can provide a genuinely useful recommendation. 

 Most importantly, I learned how WebMCP can turn existing web functionality into structured capabilities that an AI agent can use to help customers interact with a real business. 

 What's next for WebMCP-Project-GodreryToneShopify-Storefront-Testing-Project 

 The next step is to continue developing GodreryTone Jewellery into a fully functional online store while expanding the WebMCP experience alongside it.

 Deeper market-aware shopping

 Richer personalization

 what they want, who it is for, where they are, and what they can spend 
 

 and have the store intelligently help them discover what they can actually buy .

 Inspiration 

 Presentation tools are designed primarily for humans, while AI agents often interact with applications indirectly through prompts, APIs, or simulated UI actions. We wanted to explore a different model: what if an AI agent could become a first-class user of a web application? 

 That idea led to AG-Slide, a presentation editor built around WebMCP. The goal is not simply to generate slides with AI but to let a human and an AI agent collaboratively work on the same live presentation. 

 What it does 

 AG-Slide provides a real-time presentation canvas where users can create, edit, and organize slides while an agent can directly operate the application through structured tools. 

 The application exposes four core tools: 

 
 ``— create a new presentation slide 
 ``— modify slide content 
 ``— change the presentation theme 
 ``— add data-driven metric cards 
 

 Instead of an agent trying to understand buttons, DOM elements, or screen coordinates, it can use structured capabilities exposed by the application. 

 For example, a user can ask: 

 
 "Create a slide about market opportunity with three metrics." 
 

 The agent translates that intent into structured tool calls, executes them, and the presentation updates immediately on the same canvas. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 The most important part of AG-Slide is the shared application state. 

 Humans can edit slides manually while the agent can modify the same presentation through tools. Every agent action is visible in the Agent Inspector, including the tool name, arguments, execution status, and result. 

 This makes the interaction transparent instead of treating AI as a black box. 

 How we built it 

 Ag-Slide is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and Lucide React . 

 The core architecture follows: 

 User / Agent → Tool Call → Validation → Tool Executor → Zustand → Live Canvas 

 We also built an agent simulator with a deterministic fallback so the core experience works without requiring an external AI API. This allowed us to focus on demonstrating the WebMCP interaction model reliably. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was designing the boundary between the agent and the application state. We wanted agent actions to be real application operations rather than simulated UI interactions. 

 We also had to make tool execution observable and reliable while keeping the interface simple enough for a human to understand what the agent was doing in real time. 

 What we learned 

 Building Ag-Slide changed our perspective on agentic applications. The interesting question is not only "How can AI generate content?" but also "How can applications expose meaningful capabilities that agents can use?"
WebMCP provides a compelling direction for this: instead of building AI around a UI, applications can make their functionality directly understandable and usable by agents. 

 AG-Slide is our exploration of what that future could look like for creative software.

 Tariffiq: instant import tariff analysis, now callable by AI agents via WebMCP 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 My inspiration stems from the fact that small business owners importing goods often don't find out the real cost of a shipment: tariffs, duties, and margin impact: until after they've already committed to an order. Tariffiq exists to answer that instantly, before the purchase order goes out. 

 What it does 

 Tariffiq calculates the full landed cost of an import: base price, tariff rate, total duty owed, and the resulting hit to profit margins. It also surfaces cheaper sourcing alternatives, comparing the same product from other origin countries and showing the potential savings. 

 How we built it 

 Tariffiq is a React + Vite app. We used document.modelContext.registerTool to expose two tools: 

 
 analyze_tariff : runs a full tariff analysis for a product, origin country, quantity, and unit price 
 switch_origin_country : re-runs the last analysis with a different origin country, so an agent can compare sourcing options without re-entering the rest of the shipment details
Both tools call the app's existing analysis functions directly, so when an agent invokes a tool, the result renders live on the same page a human is looking at not in a separate chat window. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our biggest challenge wasn't writing the tools, it was proving they actually worked. ChatGPT wasn't reliably discovering our registered tools on our account, which initially made us think our WebMCP implementation was broken. After re-reading the submission rules closely, we realized judges can test via either ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, so we shifted to verifying everything through Chrome's own WebMCP DevTools panel instead. 

 That came with its own hurdles: getting the manual "Run Tool" test interface to actually render (it turned out to be a cramped panel/viewport issue, not a missing flag), and separately, fixing a bug where React's StrictMode was double-registering each tool in development. Working through both taught us to verify assumptions directly against official tooling rather than relying on any single client's behavior. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that Tariffiq's WebMCP tools aren't just registered they're genuinely functional. When an agent calls analyze_tariff , it's not returning a canned response; it's running the same real calculation logic a human would trigger through the UI, and the result appears live on the same page. We verified this end-to-end using Chrome's own official WebMCP DevTools panel, invoking the tool directly, with no manual form-filling, and watching the live production site update in real time. 

 We're also proud of not overclaiming: rather than assuming our implementation was broken because of one client's inconsistent tool discovery, we diagnosed the actual cause, confirmed our tools work correctly against the official spec, and built our submission around what we could concretely prove. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP support isn't uniform across clients yet, a tool can be correctly implemented per spec and still behave inconsistently depending on which agent or browser is testing it. That pushed us to test against the official Chrome WebMCP DevTools panel directly rather than trusting any single client's behavior as the ground truth. 

 We also learned the value of reading requirements literally rather than assuming the strictest interpretation. The rules stated judges could test via ChatGPT or Chrome, once we confirmed that, we stopped chasing an issue that wasn't actually blocking our submission, and redirected that time toward strengthening what we could already prove worked. 

 On the technical side, we got a much clearer picture of how document.modelContext.registerTool interacts with React's lifecycle, specifically how StrictMode's double-invocation in development can silently duplicate tool registrations if you don't guard for it. 

 What's next for Tariffiq 

 We want to expand the tariff engine beyond a single-shipment lookup into ongoing monitoring, letting an agent check in periodically as tariff rates change and proactively flag when a cheaper sourcing country becomes available for a product a user has already analyzed. 

 We'd also like to add more WebMCP tools: one for bulk-comparing an entire supplier list at once, and one that lets an agent draft a sourcing recommendation report a user can hand directly to a supplier or customs broker. 

 Longer term, we're interested in exposing historical tariff trends as a tool too, so an agent could tell a user not just today's cost, but whether tariffs on a product have been rising or falling useful context for timing a purchase.

 Atelier is a generative-art studio with zero buttons, menus or forms. Every capability it has — perceiving the canvas, changing palettes, composing scenes, adding textures, critiquing, proposing variations, exporting the artwork — is declared as a structured WebMCP tool via document.modelContext.registerTool(), with JSON schemas and natural-language descriptions. The browser agent (ChatGPT in-app browser, or any WebMCP client) is not an assistant bolted onto the app: it IS the interface. 

 The human keeps the most natural human interface — direct manipulation (drag, resize, click, scroll) — and delegates everything linguistic or generative to the agent: "make it warmer", "give me three alternatives", "export". Both actors share one canvas and one history, so a human adjustment and an agent transformation compose naturally, including undo. 

 Ten tools are registered: get_canvas_state, set_palette, add_shape, remove_shape, move_shape, apply_composition, add_texture, semantic_query, suggest_variations, export_artwork. Each tool mutates one serializable scene object (seeded, deterministic procedural generation) and redraws a 2D canvas. An in-page fallback registry (clearly labeled in the UI) mirrors the same tool surface for browsers without the WebMCP flag, so the studio stays fully agent-drivable anywhere.

 Inspiration 

 Creators already have the content. The hard part is everything between recording and publishing. 

 A creator might have a video, an idea, or a piece of writing, but turning it into something ready for different platforms often means jumping between editors, research tools, formatting tools, and publishing workflows. 

 We wanted to explore a simpler idea: 

 What if a creator could tell an agent what they want to do, and the agent could actually operate the creator workspace instead of just giving instructions? 

 That became CreatorFlow. 

 CreatorFlow is not an AI creator that replaces human creativity. It is an agent-native creator workflow where the creator provides the idea, content, and judgment while the agent helps with repetitive production work. 

 What it does 

 CreatorFlow gives creators one simple workspace to: 

 Research → Edit → Prepare → Publish 

 For example, a creator can ask: 

 
 "Find the strongest 30 seconds and make it ready as a vertical short." 
 

 Instead of manually navigating through the editor, the agent can use CreatorFlow's WebMCP tools to understand the project, find a useful moment, create an edit plan, apply the edit, change the aspect ratio, and add captions. 

 The creator can then review the result, modify it, or undo the changes. 

 CreatorFlow can also prepare content for different publishing formats such as: 

 
 YouTube 
 Instagram 
 LinkedIn 
 X 
 Medium 
 

 The goal is not to replace professional editing software. It is to make the repetitive workflow around publishing faster and easier. 

 Why WebMCP fits CreatorFlow 

 Content creation is full of small, repetitive actions —finding a moment, trimming a clip, changing the format, adding captions, and preparing content for a platform. 

 WebMCP fits because it lets CreatorFlow expose these real application capabilities as tools an agent can directly use , instead of making the agent click through the interface like a human. 

 What people + agents can do together 

 The creator provides intent and creative judgment : 

 
 “Find the best part of this video and prepare it as a short.” 
 

 The agent handles the workflow : 

 Understand content → Find moment → Edit → Reframe → Caption → Prepare for platform 

 The creator can then review, change, approve, or undo the result. 

 So the key difference is: 

 Without WebMCP: 
Agent → tries to navigate the UI → clicks buttons → hopes it works. 

 With WebMCP: 
Agent → discovers CreatorFlow's tools → performs structured actions → UI updates → creator reviews. 

 That's why WebMCP is the core of CreatorFlow : it doesn't just put an AI assistant beside the editor; it makes the creator workspace operable by an agent while keeping the human in control. 

 How we built it 

 CreatorFlow is built as a web application using: 

 
 Next.js 
 TypeScript 
 React 
 Zustand 
 HTML5 Video 
 WebMCP 
 

 The most important part is the WebMCP layer. 

 Instead of creating a separate AI system that controls the UI through clicks, we exposed meaningful CreatorFlow capabilities as WebMCP tools. 

 Examples include: 

 
 get_project_state 
 get_transcript 
 find_best_moment 
 create_edit_plan 
 apply_edit_plan 
 change_aspect_ratio 
 add_captions 
 prepare_for_platform 
 undo_last_action 
 

 These tools operate on the same project state used by the CreatorFlow interface. 

 This means the agent and the human are working with the same workspace rather than maintaining two separate systems. 

 We also added a WebMCP activity panel so users can see which tools are being called and what the agent is doing. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was understanding how to make WebMCP meaningful instead of simply adding tools for the sake of the hackathon. 

 We initially thought about building a much larger AI video editor, but that quickly became too complicated. 

 We narrowed the product down to the workflow that matters: 

 Understand the content → make an edit → prepare it for publishing. 

 Another challenge was keeping the creator in control. 

 Some operations change the project, so we designed the workflow around proposals, approval, and undo rather than allowing an agent to silently change everything. 

 We also had to make sure that WebMCP tools were connected to real application state instead of being disconnected demo functions. 

 Accomplishments we're proud of 

 We are proud that CreatorFlow demonstrates a different way of thinking about web applications. 

 The important part isn't simply that an agent can chat with the application. 

 The important part is that the application's actual capabilities are exposed as tools that an agent can understand and operate. 

 A creator can express an outcome such as: 

 
 "Make this into a vertical short." 
 

 The agent can translate that intent into a sequence of structured operations while the creator watches the workspace change. 

 We are also proud of the shared state architecture, where human interactions and WebMCP tool calls use the same underlying operations. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building for agents changes how we think about UI design. 

 Traditional interfaces are designed around: 

 buttons → menus → clicks → navigation 

 An agent-native interface can instead expose: 

 intent → tools → actions → result 

 WebMCP makes this possible directly inside the web application. 

 We also learned that agents should not necessarily replace the user. In creative workflows, the better experience can be human + agent collaboration , where the agent handles repetitive work and the human remains responsible for taste and final decisions. 

 What's next for CreatorFlow 

 This hackathon version focuses on demonstrating the core idea. 

 Next, we would make the workflow production-ready by adding: 

 
 Real video processing and rendering 
 Real transcription 
 More intelligent editing suggestions 
 Direct publishing integrations 
 Platform-specific content optimization 
 More WebMCP tools for research and content preparation 
 Better agent approval and safety controls 
 

 The long-term vision is simple: 

 CreatorFlow becomes a place where people bring their content and intent, while agents handle the repetitive work required to turn that content into something ready to publish.

A WebMCP-powered Next.js command center that transforms an LLM into an active operational partner to orchestrate cloud escalations, map blast radiuses, and stage human-approved remediation patches.

 Task-liaison 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Task-liaison 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Drawing from my background as a certified Google Cloud Professional Cloud Architect, I've seen firsthand how chaotic infrastructure incident management can be. When a GKE node pool fails or a Cloud SQL database spikes, the resolution process is usually a messy combination of frantic Slack messages, manual Jira routing, and repetitive UI clicks. I wanted to see if the new WebMCP standard could transform an LLM from a passive conversational chatbot into an active, operational partner that orchestrates incident workflows directly on the canvas. 

 What it does 

 Task-Liaison is an AI-orchestrated command center for infrastructure escalations. Instead of clicking through menus, engineers talk to the board. The application uses a three-column Kanban layout: 

 
 The Command Center: Unassigned, critical incidents. 
 The Priority Reward Exchange: An incentivized bounty market where the AI can dynamically price and route tasks. 
 Active Engineering Workloads: Real-time on-call assignments. 
 

 By exposing strict JSON-schema React state mutations to the LLM's runtime environment, the AI can map cascading blast radiuses, re-route workloads between engineers to prevent burnout, and stage mock Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform/Bash) patches. Crucially, the system enforces Human-in-the-Loop execution: the AI stages the complex configurations, but human engineers retain physical click-approval authority to apply the patches. 

 How we built it 

 Task-Liaison is a frontend-only React application built on the Next.js framework and styled with Tailwind CSS. The core innovation lies in leveraging the document.modelContext API. I registered custom JavaScript tools ( post_bounty_to_market , propose_ticket_swap , analyze_blast_radius , stage_remediation_script ) with rigid input schemas. When the user types a natural language command, the LLM extracts the parameters, maps them to the schema, and triggers instantaneous React state mutations without any backend database. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Maintaining the state synchronization between a non-deterministic AI and a deterministic frontend UI was the biggest hurdle. During development, local hot-reloading would frequently wipe the WebMCP tool registrations from the AI's memory, causing the LLM to fall back into "chatbot mode" where it would hallucinate actions instead of firing the API tools. I had to implement strict lifecycle management using React useRef and useEffect hooks to ensure the JSON contracts remained tethered to the agent's context window. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am exceptionally proud of the closed-loop execution flow. When a user tells the AI to "stage a mock Terraform script for INC-102," the AI perfectly formats the code block, injects it into the specific React component, and generates an actionable "Approve & Execute" button. SEO for the agentic web to help website owners understand, measure, and improve how effectively AI agents can discover, understand, and operate their websites.

 Story

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I am a technical SEO, so I spend a lot of time thinking about how machines understand websites: search crawlers, rich result parsers, AI assistants, and now agentic browsers. Technical SEO has always been about making the web more readable to non-human users. 

 That made WebMCP immediately exciting to me. Instead of an agent guessing how to use an SEO interface from buttons, screenshots, and page text, the site itself can expose structured SEO tools directly. Agent Search Console came from that idea: what would an SEO tool look like if it was built for both humans and agents from the start? 

 What it does 

 Agent Search Console is a WebMCP-powered technical SEO toolkit. 

 A human can paste a public URL and generate a technical SEO report. The app checks indexability, schema, robots.txt, sitemaps, redirects, HTTP headers, headings, meta tags, broken links, and SERP snippet signals. It then turns those checks into a readable report with scores, findings, raw evidence, and a prioritized action plan. 

 An agent can call the same functionality through WebMCP. Instead of scraping the UI, the agent can call tools like generate_seo_report , check_indexability , check_schema , or check_robots_txt and receive structured results it can use for follow-up work. 

 How we built it 

 The app is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. 

 The SEO checks run on server-side API routes that safely fetch public URLs, parse crawler-visible HTML and headers, and return structured JSON. The full report generator runs the core checks together and creates an executive summary, section scores, detailed findings, raw checker output, and an agentActionPlan . 

 For WebMCP, the app registers browser tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . The WebMCP surface is intentionally capped at ten tools: one full report generator plus focused technical SEO checkers. The app also exposes static discovery JSON at /webmcp.json and /.well-known/webmcp.json . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was the steep learning curve around WebMCP itself. The standard is new, and it changes how you think about a web app. I had to stop treating the UI as the only product surface and start thinking about the agent interface as a first-class experience. 

 Another challenge was output quality. SEO tools often dump raw data, but agents need structured, specific, actionable evidence. A lot of the work went into making the outputs useful: clear statuses, scores, findings, metrics, raw results, and prioritized next steps. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am proud that this became a genuinely passionate project, not just a wrapper around a demo API. 

 Agent Search Console has a real product direction: technical SEO tools at the core, a human-readable report experience, and an agent-readable WebMCP interface. It shows how SEO workflows can become more collaborative when humans review strategy and agents handle structured diagnosis, evidence gathering, and follow-up tasks. 

 I am also proud of keeping the tool surface focused. Instead of exposing too many generic tools, the app centers on a small set of practical technical SEO checks that map to real SEO work. 

 What we learned 

 I learned what WebMCP really is: not just another integration format, but a way for websites to describe what agents can actually do. 

 The most important shift is that agents should not have to guess. A good WebMCP app gives agents clear tool names, clear input schemas, safe execution boundaries, and useful structured outputs. That makes the web feel less like a visual maze for agents and more like a set of intentional capabilities. 

 I also learned that agent-facing output design matters as much as human UI design. If the result is vague, too raw, or poorly structured, the agent cannot do much with it. 

 What's next for Agent Search Console 

 Next, I want to scale Agent Search Console into a production-grade, comprehensive technical SEO product. 

 That means deeper crawling, richer schema validation, rendered-page analysis, historical reports, project tracking, issue monitoring, exports, and integrations with real SEO workflows. I also want to expand the WebMCP side so agents can not only diagnose issues, but help create implementation briefs, compare reports over time, and coordinate SEO fixes with developers and content teams.

A WebMCP-powered healthcare price transparency agent that lets AI search claims, compare procedure prices, and summarize provider data.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ClearHealth AI dashboard showing healthcare price transparency data and the three WebMCP capabilities available to AI agents. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 ClearHealth AI dashboard showing healthcare price transparency data and the three WebMCP capabilities available to AI agents.

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Healthcare price-transparency data can be difficult to search, compare, and understand through a traditional web interface. I wanted to explore how WebMCP could make an existing healthcare application more useful to AI agents without removing the human experience. 

 The project originally started as a healthcare claims and Machine-Readable File (MRF) coding challenge. I extended it for the WebMCP Challenge so that both humans and AI agents can interact with the same underlying healthcare claims data. 

 Why WebMCP is a Strong Fit 

 Healthcare price transparency is a strong fit for WebMCP because users often need to search, compare, and summarize structured pricing information rather than simply browse a webpage. Traditional web interfaces are designed primarily for humans, requiring an AI agent to understand the interface and determine how to perform these tasks. 

 This project exposes three meaningful healthcare capabilities through WebMCP: searching claims, comparing procedure prices, and summarizing provider claims. These operations have clearly defined inputs and structured outputs, making them natural capabilities for an AI agent to invoke. 

 For example, instead of an agent navigating the application to compare prices for a procedure, it can call compare_healthcare_prices with a procedure code and receive the relevant billed, allowed, and paid statistics. Similarly, an agent can search claims or obtain a provider summary without relying on UI navigation or screen scraping. 

 This creates a human-and-agent experience in which people can continue using the visual healthcare application, while agents can directly access its core capabilities. WebMCP therefore transforms the website from a human-only interface into one that can be used by both humans and AI agents. 

 What it does 

 ClearHealth AI is a healthcare price-transparency application enhanced with WebMCP. 

 A human can use the web application to explore healthcare claims and pricing information. An AI agent can access the same data through three read-only WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_healthcare_claims — searches claims using structured filters such as provider name, procedure code, and place of service. 
 compare_healthcare_prices — calculates billed, allowed, and paid price statistics for a procedure, including averages, minimums, maximums, totals, and amount differences. 
 summarize_provider_claims — provides an aggregate summary of a provider's claims, including claim count, billed, allowed, and paid amounts, average allowed amount, and associated procedures. 
 

 For example, an agent can search for claims associated with Michael Poole, compare prices for procedure s5301 , and then summarize Michael Poole's claims without having to navigate the application's user interface. 

 How I built it 

 The application is built with React and TypeScript and uses a healthcare claims data layer to provide structured data to the WebMCP tools. 

 The WebMCP implementation is located in: 

 frontend/src/webmcp/tools.ts 

 I check whether WebMCP is available and register the tools through: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 Each tool provides a unique name, human-readable title, description, structured input schema, read-only annotation, and asynchronous execution function. 

 The tools are read-only and reuse the application's healthcare claims data without modifying the underlying dataset. 

 I also use Mantine for UI components, Tailwind CSS for styling, PapaParse for CSV parsing, AG Grid for data presentation, Zod for schema validation, MobX for state management, and React Router for navigation. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The main challenge was deciding which application capabilities would provide real value to AI agents. 

 Instead of exposing simple UI actions, I focused on meaningful healthcare operations with clearly defined inputs and structured outputs. I also needed to make the WebMCP layer work alongside the existing human-facing application rather than replacing it. 

 Another challenge was designing the tool outputs so that an agent receives useful structured information that can be directly interpreted and communicated to a user. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I successfully extended an existing healthcare claims application with an agent-facing WebMCP layer. 

 The application now provides three distinct healthcare capabilities that an AI agent can discover and invoke: 

 
 Search healthcare claims 
 Compare healthcare prices 
 Summarize provider claims 
 

 I'm especially proud that the same underlying healthcare data can support both a traditional human interface and direct agent interaction. 

 I also kept the WebMCP tools read-only so that agent interactions do not modify the underlying claims data. 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand how WebMCP can provide a structured interface between a web application and AI agents. 

 I learned that an effective agent-facing interface is not simply about exposing more functionality. The capabilities need to represent meaningful user tasks, have clear inputs and outputs, and be easy for an agent to invoke. 

 I also learned that WebMCP can complement a human-first interface: people can continue using the application visually while agents can directly access the application's capabilities. 

 What's next for ClearHealth AI: Healthcare Price Transparency Agent | WebMCP 

 My next step is to expand the agent capabilities while maintaining clear, read-only boundaries around healthcare data. 

 Future improvements could include additional healthcare analytics tools, richer natural-language interactions, stronger validation and error handling, and additional ways for humans and AI agents to collaborate when exploring healthcare price-transparency information. 

 My goal is to continue evolving ClearHealth AI into an application where healthcare data is accessible through both intuitive human experiences and well-defined agent capabilities.

Turn confusing government forms into a guided conversation — the agent fills fields, a human approves before submission.

 Story

 Inspiration## Inspiration 

 Government-style forms — like a PAN application — are dense, jargon-heavy, and intimidating, especially for first-time applicants unfamiliar with formal English. I've filled out this exact kind of form for my own PAN card update, and for my brother's, from a remote village in Assam where digital form-filling isn't second nature for most people. I wanted to see whether an AI agent could handle the confusing parts directly, through the website's own tools, instead of a person having to decode every field alone. 

 What it does 

 PaperBridge lets a person describe their PAN application details once, in plain language, to an AI agent. The agent then calls the site's own WebMCP tools to fill out the form field by field — full name, father's name, date of birth, address — live, on screen. Once everything is filled, the site checks completeness and asks the human for a single Yes/No approval before anything is "submitted." Nothing happens without that explicit confirmation. The site also keeps a searchable history of past applications, useful if one device is used to help multiple people — like a shared community device. 

 How we built it 

 Built entirely on an Android phone using Termux, GitHub's web editor, and Vercel for deployment — no laptop involved. The frontend is vanilla HTML/CSS/JavaScript with no framework and no backend; state is held in-memory and mirrored to localStorage. Three tools are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() : start_form , fill_field , and validate_form , chained together through a form_id returned by the first call. The agent performs all the reasoning — deciding field values from natural language — while the website only exposes structured capabilities, validates input, and renders the result. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was verification. WebMCP's live agent support in ChatGPT is currently limited to the desktop app, and I had no desktop access at any point while building this. To verify the tool logic was correct despite this, I wrote an automated test harness (Node.js + jsdom) that simulates the exact sequence of tool calls an agent would make — registration, chaining via form_id , field updates, and validation — and confirmed all three tools execute correctly and update the UI as expected. I also added a "Simulate Agent Call" button directly in the app, which manually triggers the same tool functions with sample data, so the flow can be demonstrated visually even without a live agent connection. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting a fully working, correctly-chained three-tool WebMCP flow built and verified entirely from a phone, with no desktop access at any point — including independently proving the tool logic works through automated testing rather than just assuming it does. 

 What we learned 

 That verification doesn't have to mean live end-to-end testing in the exact target environment — when that environment isn't accessible, testing the underlying logic directly and being transparent about what wasn't (and couldn't be) verified is an honest, credible alternative. 

 What's next for PaperBridge 

 Testing live agent execution once desktop access is available, extending support to the minor-to-major PAN correction flow (the same three tools, a different application_type ), and exploring what other government-style forms could benefit from the same conversational approach.

pitch: Browser-native, verifiable fintech tools and OpenChainGraph workflows that AI agents can call through MCP. Private and serverless by default.
about_excerpt:
Browser-native, verifiable fintech tools and OpenChainGraph workflows that AI agents can call through MCP. Private and serverless by default.

 Story

 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are increasingly asked to help with consequential financial and compliance work, but a fluent answer is not enough. A user, reviewer, or auditor needs to be able to inspect the inputs, reproduce the calculation, and verify the result independently. 

 AINumbers brings that standard to browser-native fintech tooling. It makes deterministic tools usable by people in a web page and by agents through the same underlying computation. 

 What it does 

 AINumbers is an open-source suite of browser-native fintech tools and OpenChainGraph workflows. The tools cover payments, AML/KYC, risk, regulatory compliance, tokenization, and more. 

 Each OpenChainGraph workflow produces a reproducible SHA-256 execution hash over canonical inputs and outputs. That gives an agent's result a verifiable receipt rather than asking users to trust a black box. 

 For this WebMCP submission, AINumbers exposes browser tools to agents through WebMCP while preserving the ordinary human-facing form. The same computation powers both paths, so a person and an agent receive the same structured result and the same receipt. 

 How we built it 

 The site is built as self-contained HTML and JavaScript tools with no account requirement and no data transmission after page load. Calculations run locally in the browser using deterministic logic and WebCrypto hashing. 

 We added WebMCP registration using the current document.modelContext API, with a fallback to the earlier navigator.modelContext surface. Browsers without WebMCP retain the same normal web experience. 

 The project also offers an MCP server for agent integrations and publishes its source code, manifests, schemas, and OpenChainGraph specification publicly. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is a draft browser API, and its surface moved during implementation. A registration pattern that had previously worked through navigator.modelContext no longer registered tools in current Chrome. 

 We diagnosed the issue with a small probe tool, updated registration to prefer document.modelContext , preserved a compatibility fallback, and documented the complete debugging session so others can reproduce it. 

 What we learned 

 Agent tooling is more trustworthy when it is not a separate, opaque path. A shared human-and-agent computation path, structured output, and independently verifiable receipt make it easier to test, inspect, and rely on agent-assisted work. 

 What's next 

 We will continue expanding WebMCP coverage across AINumbers tools, keep compatibility checks current as the draft API evolves, and make verifiable browser-native tools easier for agents and humans to use together.

Get help. Hire a Tasker. Or let an agent book the same site.

 1

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Websites are still built as if only humans will use them: click, search, filter, compare, book. Agents can already drive that UI, but they do it by guessing at buttons. WebMCP flips that. A page can expose the same capabilities as tools — document.modelContext.registerTool , getTools , executeTool — so an agent uses the site the way a developer would use an API, while a person still uses the normal interface. 

 TaskRabbit is the perfect test of that idea. A move-in is never one listing. It is furniture assembly, cleaning, and TV mounting, coordinated under a budget, with a human still in the loop before anything is booked. We wanted a marketplace that looks like a real service site and behaves like an MCP server in the browser. 

 What it does 

 TaskFlow is a dual-use TaskRabbit-style marketplace. 

 For people: browse services, compare Taskers, and book from a profile — search, listings, hourly rates, availability, confirm. 

 For agents: the same pages register WebMCP tools ( searchServices , findTaskers , getTaskerAvailability , getTaskerPricing , createTaskRequest , scheduleTask , …). An in-page agent dock takes an outcome like “I just moved in. Make my home ready tonight. I have a $250 budget.” It discovers those tools, builds a plan (Marcus $85, Sarah $95, David $60 = $240), and waits for approval before it schedules. 

 Both paths write to the same booking store. My Tasks shows You booked next to Booked by agent . One website, two clients, one set of capabilities. 

 How we built it 

 
 Next.js App Router , TypeScript, Tailwind, and shadcn/ui — no backend, no real payments, no live TaskRabbit API. 
 A shared marketplace layer ( search , findTaskers , pricing, create/schedule). Human buttons call those functions. WebMCP execute callbacks wrap the same functions. 
 A spec-faithful document.modelContext polyfill so the demo runs in current browsers, using the official WebMCP shape if the native API exists. 
 A deterministic planner (no LLM) so the killer demo is reliable, with staged delays so the tool activity is visible. 
 A TaskRabbit-like light marketplace plus a dark agent dock that keeps Show WebMCP on screen for judges. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is still a draft. Most browsers do not ship document.modelContext , so we had to match the spec closely without pretending the API is everywhere. 

 The harder product problem was not building another chatbot. The original instinct was an AI-only command center. That hid the point. WebMCP only lands if the human site is real and the agent uses that site’s tools — not a parallel fake API. 

 Shared state was picky too: a full navigation wiped in-memory bookings until we persisted them and tagged each row by source ( human | agent ). Tool registration also had to survive hot reload without double-registering names. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A 2–3 minute demo where you book Marcus as a person, then let the agent plan a $240 move-in, and both appear on My Tasks . 
 Judges can see WebMCP: live getTools / executeTool calls, not a hidden prompt. 
 Human-in-the-loop: the agent never books until Approve & Schedule . 
 One implementation for both audiences — not two products glued together. 
 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native websites are not “add a chat sidebar.” They are capability design : the same operations must be safe, named, and schema’d for a model and obvious in a UI for a person. 

 We also learned why the spec cares about annotations ( readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint ) and approval. Tool descriptions are easy to trust too much. Keeping consequential actions behind a human confirm is the product, not a footer. 

 What's next for TaskFlow 

 
 Native WebMCP in a supporting browser, dropping the polyfill on that path. 
 Declarative tools from real forms, as the spec’s declarative section lands. 
 A real LLM planner behind the same tools, with the deterministic demo kept as a fixture. 
 Richer trust UX: show which origin registered a tool, and treat tool output as untrusted when the hint says so. 
 

 TaskFlow’s bet is simple: the next marketplace is designed for both hands and agents.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 🌐 Nexus Weave — Zero-Egress WebMCP Dependency Graph Engine 

 
 Autonomous Tarjan Cycle Isolation • Human-in-the-Loop Safety Gate • Zero-Egress In-Browser Execution 
 Built for the OpenAI & Chrome WebMCP Challenge 2026 — Agent-Native Open Web Track 
 

 

 

 🌟 The 4 Core WebMCP Challenge Pillars 

 1. 🎯 Why This Use Case is a Strong Fit for WebMCP 

 Enterprise dependency graphs (microservices meshes, cloud infrastructure topologies, CI/CD pipelines) represent proprietary, security-sensitive architecture. Uploading raw architectural graphs and telemetry traces to remote third-party LLM cloud servers violates corporate data residency standards and creates catastrophic network egress liability. 

 WebMCP makes the browser an agent-executable execution runtime. Instead of exfiltrating sensitive graph data to remote backends, WebMCP enables external AI agents (in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome Canary) to inspect, diagnose, and untangle complex dependency topologies directly inside the client browser’s volatile memory — executing deterministic graph algorithms with 0 KB of network egress . 

 2. ⚡ How It Creates a Better User Experience 

 Traditional APM visualizers force DevOps engineers into manual log correlation, multi-dashboard context switching, and speculative guesswork. Nexus Weave transforms passive observability into a reactive, agent-native workspace: 

 
 Instant Mathematical Diagnosis: Sub-3 millisecond graph algorithms (Tarjan's SCC for circular deadlocks, DAG topological sort for critical paths) replace LLM text hallucinations with mathematical certainty. 
 Visual-First Affordances: Rather than dumping conversational text walls, the AI agent drives reactive 60 FPS SVG spring transitions , pulses highlighted cyclic corridors (crimson dashed loops), and projects coordinate ghost-node previews directly onto the engineer’s canvas. 
 

 3. 🤝 Human-Agent Co-Creation (What People and Agents Can Do Together) 

 Nexus Weave establishes mechanically enforced, bidirectional safety boundaries between human operators and autonomous agents: 

 
 Pinned Infrastructure Boundaries: Engineers can click the pushpin icon on any foundational service node (e.g., API Gateway / api-gateway ). This commits the node ID into an in-memory bitmask. WebMCP mutating tools structurally guarantee pinned nodes are immutable and strictly rejected from any agent-driven layout displacement. 
 Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Safety Gate: Whenever an autonomous agent proposes a layout reorganization exceeding a 30% blast radius (or targeting the full topology), execution halts deterministically. The engine renders a live Ghost-Node coordinate preview overlay , requiring explicit human review and sign-off ( confirm_pending: true ) before layout mutation commits. 
 

 4. ⚙️ How We Implemented WebMCP 

 
 Universal Dual-Detection & Multi-Surface Discovery: getAvailableModelContexts(): ModelContext[] resolves both document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext simultaneously, registering tools across all active browser surfaces while defensively suppressing duplicate-registration errors. 
 Defensive Argument Normalization: The normalizeToolArguments(rawArgs: unknown) runtime layer (in src/tools/dispatch.ts and src/webmcp/register.ts ) guarantees resilience against stringified JSON arguments, null/undefined payloads, and malformed inputs from autonomous LLM callers. 
 Dispatch Proxy Architecture: The src/webmcp/dispatch.ts re-export proxy module cleanly decouples WebMCP registration and host binding from internal graph dispatch logic. 
 Compiled Ajv JSON Schemas: All 5 tool definitions strictly enforce runtime schema validation using compiled Ajv v8 JSON Schema Draft-07 definitions via the canonical inputSchema property. 
 Deterministic 6-Step Dispatch Lifecycle: Validate ➔ Trust & Scope Check ➔ Branch Decision ➔ Compute-Then-Atomic-Apply ➔ Pure Reducer Commit ➔ In-Page EventBus Emission. 
 Canonical Imperative Registration: Registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() : 
 
 // Canonical WebMCP Imperative Registration (W3C / WebMCP Challenge Compliant)
document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "detect_cycles_and_bottlenecks",
 description: "Deterministic detection of circular dependency deadlocks (using Tarjan's SCC) and bottleneck nodes in the microservice topology. Call this whenever the user asks about deadlocks, cycles, loops, or bottlenecks.",
 inputSchema: detectCyclesAndBottlenecksInputSchema,
 execute: async (input) => {
 return dispatchToolCall("detect_cycles_and_bottlenecks", input, stateAccessor);
 }
});
 
 

 💡 Inspiration 

 Enterprise incident rooms are chaotic: when a cascading microservice outage strikes, teams spend hours deciphering tangled dependency spaghetti across siloed cloud dashboards. We asked ourselves: What if an autonomous AI agent could sit directly alongside the engineer inside the browser tab, running graph-theoretic algorithms on the live topology without sending a single byte of proprietary architectural data over the wire? WebMCP made this vision possible. 

 🔍 What It Does 

 Nexus Weave is an agent-native, zero-backend dependency graph engine pre-loaded with a realistic 16-node, 23-edge microservices topology: 

 
 Autonomous Deadlock Isolation: Runs Tarjan’s Strongly Connected Components (SCC) algorithm in $O(V + E)$ time ($< 3\text{ms}$ execution) to highlight the 3-node cyclic deadlock between Order Service, Payment Gateway, and Notification Service. 
 Deterministic Critical Path Analysis: Computes the longest latency path across acyclic DAG subgraphs using dynamic programming while enforcing a strict Silence-Over-Guessing policy on cyclic graphs. 
 Planar Crossing Minimizer with HITL Gate: Reduces edge crossings (from 2 crossings to 0) using bounded barycenter relaxation with a 450ms cubic-bezier transition, gated by ghost-node human pre-flight approval. 
 Mechanical Pinning Guardrails: Locks critical infrastructure nodes against agent movement via immutable state bitmasks. 
 Proactive Chaos Cascade Simulator: Simulates live downstream service failures (e.g., Payment Gateway outage) with in-memory OpenTelemetry GenAI span emissions. 
 

 

 🖥️ Visual Grounding & Live Engine Showcase 

 1. Autonomous Deadlock Detection via Tarjan's SCC (<3ms) 

 

 Real-time isolation of the 3-node cyclic deadlock between Order Service, Payment Gateway, and Notification Service. 

 

 2. Enterprise Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Safety Gate & Ghost Node Overlay 

 

 Autonomous layout reorganization intercepting mutations >30% blast radius with live coordinate ghost previews. 

 

 3. Proactive Resilience: Zero-Dependency Chaos Engineering Cascade 

 

 Simulating Payment Gateway outage cascading downstream in real time with local OpenTelemetry span emissions.

 ✈️ FlightClaims — Instant Statutory Flight Compensation 

 💡 Inspiration 

 When a flight is delayed, cancelled, or overbooked, most passengers don't know what to do. 

 They may not know: 

 
 Whether they can get a refund 
 Whether they can receive compensation 
 Whether the airline should provide meals or accommodation 
 How to contact the airline 
 How to write a proper complaint or claim 
 

 Passenger rights are often written in complicated regulations and spread across different websites. 

 FlightClaims makes this process simpler. 

 A passenger enters their flight details, tells us what happened, and FlightClaims helps them understand their possible options and prepare a professional request to the airline. 

 

 🛠️ What It Does 

 FlightClaims helps passengers in three simple steps : 

 1️⃣ Enter Your Flight Details 

 Enter your: 

 
 Airline 
 Flight number 
 Origin and destination 
 Flight date 
 What happened 
 

 The user can select: 

 
 ✈️ Flight delayed 
 ❌ Flight cancelled 
 🚫 Denied boarding 
 

 The app can also support uploading a boarding pass or ticket to extract flight details automatically. 

 

 2️⃣ Understand Your Possible Rights 

 FlightClaims: 

 
 Identifies the flight route 
 Calculates the route distance 
 Detects the relevant passenger-rights framework 
 Analyzes the disruption details 
 Shows possible passenger options 
 Estimates potential compensation when enough information is available 
 

 The app supports passenger-rights frameworks such as: 

 
 🇮🇳 India — DGCA 
 🇪🇺 Europe — EU261 
 🇬🇧 United Kingdom — UK261 
 

 
 Note: Results are presented as guidance or estimates and are not guaranteed compensation. 
 

 

 3️⃣ Prepare Your Airline Request 

 FlightClaims generates a professional request based on the passenger's case. 

 The passenger can: 

 
 Review the request 
 Edit the request 
 Approve the request 
 

 Then they can copy and send it through the appropriate airline channel. 

 

 🤖 How WebMCP Is Used 

 FlightClaims demonstrates how WebMCP allows AI agents to interact with a live web application . 

 Normally, an AI assistant may need to guess what information is currently available on a website. 

 With WebMCP, FlightClaims exposes structured tools that allow an AI agent to safely interact with the real application. 

 Example Tools 

 query_disruption_rights 

 Allows an AI agent to analyze the current flight case and its possible passenger options. 

 prepare_passenger_request 

 Allows an AI agent to prepare a passenger request using the flight details currently available in the application. 

 The important part: The AI works with the application's actual live state , not fake or hardcoded data.

 FlightClaims uses airport coordinates to calculate the approximate distance between airports using the Haversine formula . 

 This helps the application analyze routes where distance is relevant to the passenger-rights framework.

pitch: Turn receipts into intelligent assets with WebMCP-powered warranty tracking and claims, while keeping every important action under human control.

Turn receipts into intelligent assets with WebMCP-powered warranty tracking and claims, while keeping every important action under human control.

 LifeReceipt — Your Purchases, Remembered 

 The Idea 

 We’ve all been there — you buy something expensive, keep the receipt somewhere “safe,” and then completely forget about it until you actually need it. 

 A warranty expires, a receipt is difficult to find, or you realize too late that you could have made a claim. 

 That made us think: what if our receipts could actually remember things for us? 

 That’s where LifeReceipt came from. 

 What We Built 

 LifeReceipt is a purchase vault that turns ordinary receipts into useful, intelligent assets. 

 Instead of simply storing receipts, it keeps track of purchases, warranty deadlines, receipt details, and potential claims. More importantly, we made these capabilities accessible to AI agents through WebMCP . 

 An agent can search for a purchase, check its warranty, find the receipt, and prepare a claim without the user having to manually navigate through everything. 

 For example, a user can ask: 

 
 “Find my Sony headphones, check if they’re still under warranty, retrieve the receipt, and prepare a claim if eligible.” 
 

 LifeReceipt can handle the investigation and preparation — but it stops before submitting the claim . 

 The user has to explicitly approve the action. 

 That human approval step was an important part of our design because we don't want an agent making consequential decisions completely on its own. 

 How We Built It 

 We built LifeReceipt as a React + Vite web application and created a WebMCP layer that exposes the application's capabilities as agent tools. 

 We implemented 9 tools covering purchase search, warranty checking, receipt retrieval, claim preparation, approval, submission, and claim status. 

 The UI was designed to make the whole process visible. Users can explore their purchases through the Purchase Vault, see upcoming warranty expirations through Warranty Radar, and follow the agent's actions through the Agent Activity Log. 

 What We Learned 

 The biggest thing we learned was that building for agents is different from building a normal website. 

 We had to think about what an agent should be allowed to do , what information it needs, and where a human should take over. 

 WebMCP made us think of the website as more than just pages and buttons. Each useful capability can become something an agent can discover and use. 

 Challenges 

 Getting the WebMCP integration and the normal website experience to work together reliably was one of our biggest challenges. 

 We also faced deployment issues with Netlify, including SPA routing and JavaScript MIME types. Fixing those issues taught us that a project isn't finished when it works locally — it also needs to work reliably in the real environment where people and agents will use it. 

 Why LifeReceipt? 

 We don't want LifeReceipt to be another place where receipts go to be forgotten. 

 We want it to be a place where your purchases stay useful long after you buy them — with an agent handling the boring work and a human staying in control of the important decisions.

 \section*{Inspiration} 

 I got the though for the first time when I arrived at the "Mediterranean Village" in Oran, which to my surprise didn't have a proper map that indicates the places of the buildings. I ended up spending about 30 walking around searching for the building where my room is located. 

 After watching a certain video on Youtube explaining how google maps calculates the different routes and its relation with dijkstra's algorithm, I figured out a way to solve a problem, which is by building my own google maps, but rather than mapping the entire earth, a single organization is mapped, and the map is created by the organization itself to provide to the users a way to walk around. 

 \section*{What it does} 

 MapForge is a platform where organizations can build structured indoor maps for their facilities so that users can use them for navigation, I believe everyone has had at least one experience of getting lost inside a building, whether it was the first time to go to university, the first time to visit a certain amusement park or maybe even staying in a big hotel. MapForge is a tool that ensures doesn't happen, an editor can import a blue print to create the map he wants, trace the different building of the organization, add floors to them and create rooms, entrances and other different types of instances inside the buildings. A normal user on the other hand inspects the maps created by the editors and uses them for navigation 

 \section*{How we built it} 

 The tech stack i relied on consists of symfony-php for the backend and a create-react-app setup for the frontend. 

 The backend is responsible for the application logic, persistence, map structure, validation, and routing, while the React frontend provides the visual map editor and navigation interface. The platform uses a graph-based representation of maps, with nodes representing locations such as rooms, entrances, and stairs, and edges representing the connections between them. 

 For the hackathon, I also integrated WebMCP into the frontend, exposing MapForge's core capabilities as tools that AI agents can use to inspect and modify the actual map state. Routing is handled by a deterministic Dijkstra-based shortest-path system, allowing both users and agents to find routes through the map. 

 \section*{Challenges we ran into} 

 Given that I have participated as a solo developer, the main challenge that I ran into was time, I had to brainstorm ideas for the project, determine the core functionalities, what to implement and what to sacrifice, come up with the business logic and of course implement everything by coding the backend, the frontend, the webMCP integration, testing, fixing the different errors and bugs and finally deploying the application. So if anything, I believe that my greatest adversary throughout this challenge was time. 

 \section*{Accomplishments that we're proud of} 

 There is nothing that I am particularly proud of, because I am proud of everything, this challenge was by far the greatest experience that I had in my entire life, it helped me learn a lot of new things and concepts including webMCP itself as i wasn't aware of its existence before. 

 \section*{What we learned} 

 I learned a lot of things throughout the course of this challenge, but I must admit that the greatest concept was webMCP itself, the main idea of this challenge considering the fact the i didn't know it even existed before this experience. 

 \section*{What's next for MapForge} 

 The current version of MapForge can be considered as a draft or a proof of concept if I may say, the perfect version of the project that is in my head would go much further. It would integrate indoor localization, similar in principle to GPS, so that the user could be located inside a building and receive directions from their actual position. Navigation would become much more sophisticated, with support for accessibility-aware routes, multiple route options, complex floor and building transitions, and potentially real-time navigation. The platform would also have a much more robust authentication and authorization system, where organizations control their own maps, administrators only access the maps they are responsible for, and different users can have different permissions. QR codes could also be placed at entrances, rooms, or specific locations, allowing visitors to instantly open the corresponding location in MapForge and start navigating. Other future improvements could include better floor-plan importing and tracing, more detailed building geometry, richer location information, mobile support, and more advanced tools for organizations to maintain and update their maps over time. The WebMCP integration could also become much more powerful, allowing agents to perform more complex maintenance, validation, and navigation tasks while still keeping humans in control.

 Inspiration 

 When I reviewed the hackathon details, I started thinking about what I would really want to do with an AI agent. Usually, doing a task purely on your own is faster than delegating it, or having the agent do it completely autonomously is faster than doing it yourself. I wanted to focus on the type of task where a human and an agent work together efficiently. 

 Looking at the sponsors, I saw Shopify. Having done some research into dropshipping and e-commerce, I know how much work goes into managing a store. Fully autonomous agents run into permission and safety issues, since an agent cannot just be allowed to do everything without supervision. In physical retail stores, owners have managers and assistants to help run day-to-day operations. For an online store, an agent can play that exact role. That is where the name Merchant Assistant comes from: an assistant to the merchant who owns the store. 

 What Merchant Assistant Does: 

 
 Product Research and Proposals:
The task that takes merchants the longest is research. When prompted by the merchant, the agent researches top-performing products in specific categories using ShopifyQL under the hood, exposed via WebMCP. Instead of just pulling data, the agent creates actionable proposals for items the merchant can procure and add to the store. 
 Interactive Control via ChatGPT:
Through WebMCP, merchants can interact with the agent directly in the ChatGPT app or on the web. Once the agent creates a proposal, the merchant reviews and accepts it. The changes can then be applied immediately with a single click, or the merchant can instruct the agent to apply multiple approved proposals. 
 Product Audits and Optimization:
The agent audits existing listings, checking descriptions and top-performing products based on sales data. It highlights areas for improvement and suggests updated descriptions aligned with current market trends. 
 

 The merchant remains in control: they trigger the agent, review its findings, and approve every change. 

 How I Built It: 

 I built the project using WebMCP, ShopifyQL, and Shopify MCP to give the agent the tools needed to query store analytics and execute store actions. 

 Challenges I Ran Into: 

 
 Shopify Permissions: Securing Level 2 permissions to read merchant reports and sales data, which are necessary for the agent to audit the store and propose optimizations. 
 Judge Access and Testing: Shopify's standard security makes it difficult to grant external test access simply via email. I implemented a workaround so judges can test the integration live.

SuggestAPI helps people find what matters faster. We’ve added MCP and WebMCP to our Search and Discovery Layer, so AI assistants can use our search engine in their workflows, or while helping visitors

 SuggestAPI Architecture 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP for Search Demo 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 SuggestAPI Architecture 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP for Search Demo 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 SuggestAPI Architecture 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are increasingly capable of helping people research products, compare options, and make purchasing decisions, but most ecommerce websites were designed exclusively for humans. 

 An agent visiting a storefront often has to scrape the website to get context. Interpret buttons and forms, scrape product information, or rely on a separate API that may not represent the experience available to the shopper. 

 We built SuggestAPI around a simple idea: merchants shouldn't have to rebuild their search and product discovery infrastructure for every new AI interface. We bring Agentic Commerce to any ecommerce platform without replatforming. 

 WebMCP gave us an opportunity to bring that idea directly into the browser. 

 Instead of making an agent guess how a storefront works, the website can explicitly expose the actions it supports as structured tools. Humans continue using the normal storefront while agents get a reliable interface to the same underlying product catalog. 

 What it does 

 SuggestAPI adds an agent-ready product discovery layer to existing e-commerce search infrastructure. 

 For our WebMCP implementation, a participating storefront exposes structured browser tools that an AI agent can discover and invoke while visiting the website. 

 Our demo provides four core commerce capabilities: 

 
 catalog_search — search a merchant's catalog using natural-language shopping intent 
 product_lookup — retrieve structured information about a specific product 
 compare_products — compare multiple products and their attributes 
 recommend_products — find products matching a shopper's requirements 
 

 This enables interactions such as: 

 
 "Find me waterproof trail running shoes under $150." 
 

 Instead of scraping the storefront or figuring out how to operate its search UI, the agent can call the catalog search tool directly. 

 The shopper can then ask: 

 
 "Compare the first two." 
 

 or: 

 
 "Which one would you recommend for wet trails?" 
 

 The agent can continue using the structured tools exposed by the page while the human remains in the same shopping experience. 

 The important part is that SuggestAPI doesn't require the merchant to replace their existing search engine, storefront, cart, or checkout.

Brow is an experimental Chrome side-panel AI browser agent for builders who want WebMCP, LangGraph.js, MCP, , and semantic browser automation inside a real Chrome session.

 1 2 3 



 
 Brow 

 Inspiration 

 Brow started because I wanted to experiment with WebMCP inside a real Chrome session. 

 While building it, I became convinced that WebMCP represents something much bigger than browser automation. 

 The Web is currently designed mainly for humans. Websites expose their capabilities through HTML, buttons, forms, menus, and visual interfaces. Agents do not fundamentally need that presentation layer. They need structured access to what an application can actually do. 

 A website already knows that it can send a message, create a document, search for a flight, add something to a cart, or execute a query. Agents should not always have to rediscover those capabilities by interpreting pixels or reverse-engineering the DOM. 

 I believe the future Web should expose two interfaces: one for humans through HTML and UI, and one for agents through structured tools. 

 I am confident that agents will represent an increasingly large share of Web interactions, potentially more than direct human interactions in the long term. That is why I hope WebMCP becomes part of the standard Web platform and eventually reaches broad W3C adoption. 

 Web applications across every domain should be able to expose native interfaces for agents. 

 How I built it 

 That initial experiment became Brow, an open-source agentic stack running directly inside Chrome. 

 Brow operates in the user's real browser session instead of launching a separate automation browser. 

 It combines WebMCP page tools, remote MCP servers, semantic browser automation, reusable Skills, memory, and workflow demonstrations. 

 For websites that support WebMCP, the agent can use structured capabilities directly. For the rest of the Web, Brow falls back to semantic browser automation. 

 I also wanted Brow to remain model-independent, with support for OpenAI-compatible models, Claude, local models, and future providers. 

 The agent runtime is built with LangGraph.js and runs alongside a Chrome side-panel interface. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest thing I learned is that browser automation and browser understanding are very different problems. 

 Clicking an element is easy. Understanding what it means, whether it is still valid, what changed after an action, and what the application is capable of doing is much harder. 

 I also learned that raw HTML is not a great interface for agents. Modern pages contain huge amounts of implementation detail that models do not need. 

 This is why Brow uses semantic browser snapshots and structured information rather than simply sending the full DOM to the model. 

 Another important realization was that interoperability matters more than any individual model. Models and agent frameworks will change, but an open interface between applications and agents could remain. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was dealing with constantly changing browser state. Modern applications update dynamically, elements become stale, forms change, and single-page applications can completely change state without a page reload. 

 Another challenge was combining multiple tool systems — browser actions, WebMCP tools, MCP servers, Skills, and memory — into one coherent environment for the agent. 

 Chrome extensions also have strong security and execution boundaries, which makes coordination between the side panel, background worker, content scripts, page context, and agent runtime more complex. 

 What's next 

 The Chrome extension is only the beginning. 

 I eventually want Brow to give the agent its own secure development environment: a sandbox, container, or VM where it can create files, write code, install packages, execute commands, start servers, build applications, test them in the browser, and iterate autonomously. 

 This is difficult to do cleanly within the limitations of a standard Chrome extension. 

 One longer-term direction is therefore to move Brow toward a Chromium-based browser where agent capabilities can become first-class features rather than being layered on top through an extension. 

 The goal would be to combine the browser, WebMCP, MCP, Skills, memory, and an isolated computing environment into one agent-native platform. 

 Brow started as an experiment to test WebMCP. 

 It became an experiment around a bigger question: 

 What should the Web look like when many of its users are agents acting on behalf of humans? 

 I believe agents should not always have to pretend to be humans to use the Web. 

 HTML gave humans a universal interface to the Web. WebMCP could help give agents one.

about_excerpt:
An AI agent completing real-world multi-step errands across three independently-owned websites with zero backend integration, zero API keys, and pure WebMCP discovery.

 Completed Itinerary — Verified cross-merchant receipts with zero backend API keys 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Merchant 1: Artisan Roast Café — Exposing check_menu & order_coffee tools

 Merchant 3: Paper & Ink Bookstore — untrustedContentHint protection against prompt injection

 Completed Itinerary — Verified cross-merchant receipts with zero backend API keys 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Merchant 1: Artisan Roast Café — Exposing check_menu & order_coffee tools 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Merchant 2: Luxe Grooming Studio — Calendar slot discovery & appointment booking 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Merchant 3: Paper & Ink Bookstore — untrustedContentHint protection against prompt injection 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Today's agentic web demos fall into one of two traps: 

 
 Brittle Screen Scraping : Agents using vision or accessibility trees to click coordinates and type blindly into DOM elements, which break the moment a CSS class, layout, or modal changes. 
 Walled-Garden Aggregators : Agents restricted to closed ecosystem APIs where independent neighborhood businesses must surrender 30% take rates and hand over customer relationships to centralized platforms. 
 

 When the W3C and Chrome WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext ) emerged, we saw the foundation for a third, better future: the open web itself as the native agent runtime . 

 We asked ourselves: Could an AI agent coordinate a real-world multi-stop morning errand across three completely independent, standalone neighborhood businesses—a specialty coffee shop, a boutique grooming studio, and an indie bookstore—with zero backend integration, zero proprietary API keys, and pure on-page tool discovery? 

 That question led to Open Web Concierge . 

 

 What It Does 

 Open Web Concierge is an autonomous multi-vendor assistant that plans, negotiates, and executes unified errands across the open web while keeping the human firmly in control. 

 
 Dynamic Instruction-Driven Scoping : The user speaks naturally (e.g., "I want an iced cold brew with oat milk" , "Book a haircut with Marcus at 11:15" , or a multi-stop Saturday routine). The agent dynamically parses intent and activates only the merchant services requested, gracefully omitting non-relevant stops with zero wasted spend. 
 User Identity Profile & Live Form Reflection : The Concierge maintains the user's default credentials (Name, Email, Mobile No., Gender). As the agent navigates each merchant website, it emits live synchronization events over a shared errand bus—allowing the user to watch the merchant's counter form or booking calendar populate live on screen with an active sync indicator. 
 Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Security Gates : The agent never silently commits funds. Before finalizing any transaction, a modal confirmation gate halts execution, presenting itemized pricing, timing, and merchant verification for explicit user approval. 
 Live Cross-Side Checkout Reflection : Once authorized, dual-layer real-time synchronization ( BroadcastChannel and reactive storage) immediately posts the confirmed order to the merchant's Active Barista Queue , Client Appointment Log , and Front Register Holds across independent windows and tabs. 
 Auditable Receipts : Upon completion, the Concierge compiles an itemized trip log with verifiable order IDs and costs, exportable as Markdown or JSON. 
 

 

 How We Built It 

 We built the application as a production-grade multi-page web ecosystem using React 19 , Vite 6 , and Tailwind CSS , adhering strictly to the Chrome & W3C WebMCP specification: 

 
 Merchant Tool Registration on document.modelContext :

 
 Artisan Roast Café ( /cafe/ ) : Exposes check_menu ( readOnlyHint: true ) and order_coffee (with strict parameter schemas and customer contact info). 
 Luxe Grooming Studio ( /salon/ ) : Exposes check_availability ( readOnlyHint: true ) and book_slot for stylist and calendar scheduling. 
 Paper & Ink Bookstore ( /bookstore/ ) : Exposes search_catalog ( untrustedContentHint: true ) and reserve_book for front-desk holds. 
 Concierge Orchestration Hub ( / ) : Exposes get_errand_briefing and log_completed_step . 
 
 Prompt Injection Defense via Chrome Hints :

 
 Following WebMCP security guidelines, search_catalog marks query results with untrustedContentHint: true . This informs the consuming LLM that merchant book blurbs and user reviews are untrusted third-party content, neutralizing indirect prompt injection vectors. 
 
 Idempotency Protection :

 
 Implemented client request tokens ( clientRequestId ) cached in a 15-second sliding window to prevent accidental double-billing or duplicate holds from rapid agent loops. 
 
 Bi-Directional Errand Bus :

 
 Combined the HTML5 BroadcastChannel API ( webmcp_errand_bus ) with reactive window storage listeners to ensure sub-millisecond, cross-tab synchronization between the Concierge hub and open merchant tabs without requiring an intermediary WebSocket server. 
 
 Built-in WebMCP Inspector :

 
 Included an interactive on-page drawer allowing judges and developers to inspect live registered schemas, test parameter validation, and trigger manual tool executions. 
 
 

 

 Challenges We Faced 

 
 Contextual Linguistic Disambiguation : Natural language is messy. In a prompt like "Book a haircut with Marcus" , the word "book" is a scheduling verb, not a request for literature. We engineered a contextual parser that accurately distinguishes verbal actions ( "book an appointment" ) from literary nouns ( "read a book" , "buy a novel" ) to prevent erroneous merchant activations. 
 Zero-Flicker Live Form Population : Connecting cross-tab React state to live agent actions without causing form resets or race conditions required decoupling tool discovery from UI input bindings, synchronizing through a predictable broadcast event contract. 
 Eliminating "AI Slop" Aesthetics : We committed to an authentic, human-crafted design language. We eliminated all emojis, avoided generic gradient pills, and designed a neutral, high-contrast dark palette ( #0C0C0C , #121110 , #141414 ) inspired by Swiss editorial typography and physical ledger boards. 
 Cross-Window Consistency : Ensuring that checkouts made in the Concierge immediately reflect in the merchant's Barista Queue or Appointment Log across separate browser tabs and embedded multi-views required implementing dual-channel sync ( BroadcastChannel with storage event fallbacks). 
 

 

 What We Learned & The Future of the Open Web 

 WebMCP represents a paradigm shift for web development. For the last 15 years, the web has been pressured into walled gardens and mobile app silos because machines couldn't reliably interact with standard HTML. 

 By standardizing document.modelContext , the open web becomes the agentic web . A local family-owned bakery or indie bookstore can become fully AI-operable in an afternoon simply by exposing standard tools on their existing website. No platform monopolies, no 30% tolls, and no closed ecosystems—just humans, agents, and merchants collaborating over the open protocols of the web.
