 Project Story 

 Inspiration 

 Buying lingerie online creates a contradiction. 

 It is one of the categories where customers most want to understand how something might look on them, yet it is also one of the categories where uploading a personal photo can feel the most sensitive. 

 Most virtual try-on experiences solve one part of the problem: 

 “What might this look like on me?” 

 But after the rendering appears, the shopper still has to decide: 

 Which one do I actually want? 

 We built NUDE Private Fitting Room to explore what virtual try-on could become if privacy and decision-making were treated as part of the product from the beginning. 

 NUDE is a real direct-to-consumer apparel brand, so we did not build the project around a fictional catalog or mock products. We used real NUDE products, real product imagery, real construction details, and a real shopping journey. 

 The goal was simple: 

 Try privately. Compare clearly. Decide with confidence. 

 

 What it does 

 NUDE Private Fitting Room is a privacy-first virtual fitting and decision experience for intimate apparel. 

 A shopper can: 

 
 Browse a curated digital showroom of real NUDE products. 
 Open a product and review detailed construction information. 
 Upload a photo and generate a virtual fitting using Perfect Corp YouCam Virtual Try-On . 
 Save generated fittings locally in My Looks . 
 Compare two or three looks side by side. 
 Create a private comparison card and send it through their own messaging app. 
 Return to the fitting room and manually record Friend's Pick . 
 

 The full journey is: 

 Showroom → Product → Virtual Try-On → My Looks → Compare → Ask a Friend → Friend's Pick 

 Virtual try-on is therefore not the end of the experience. It becomes the visual input for a larger decision process. 

 

 How we built it 

 The application is built with: 

 
 Next.js 15 
 React 19 
 TypeScript 
 Tailwind CSS 
 Zustand 
 Framer Motion 
 IndexedDB 
 Canvas 
 Perfect Corp YouCam Virtual Try-On 
 Vercel 
 

 The virtual fitting flow integrates Perfect Corp's cloth-v4 API. 

 When a shopper starts a fitting, the application uploads the shopper photo and the selected garment reference through Perfect Corp's file flow, creates a cloth-v4 task, polls for completion, and returns the rendered result to the browser. 

 We built the integration with production safeguards including request-size limits, per-IP rate limiting, garment-category validation, API error handling, and fail-closed behavior. 

 If the Perfect Corp API is unavailable, the product does not pretend that an AI fitting was generated. Instead, it clearly presents a labeled side-by-side fallback. 

 We also prepared garment reference assets specifically for virtual try-on. Retail imagery is designed for merchandising, but a VTO system needs a clean garment reference, so supported products use dedicated garment crops rather than treating every storefront image as interchangeable. 

 

 Privacy by design 

 Privacy is especially important in intimate-apparel retail, so we did not want it to exist only as a disclaimer. 

 Before a shopper uploads a photo, the interface explains what happens to it. 

 The shopper photo is sent to Perfect Corp only when a fitting is generated. NUDE's server processes the request in memory and does not persist the uploaded photo. 

 The shopper's fitting-room state and generated looks are stored locally in the browser using IndexedDB. 

 Changing the source photo clears the previous fitting-room state. 

 The same principle shaped Ask a Friend . 

 We deliberately did not build a NUDE social network, friend account system, or voting backend. Instead, the comparison card is composed client-side and shared through the user's own messaging app. 

 The conversation stays where the shopper already talks to someone they trust. 

 Privacy is therefore reflected in the architecture, not only in the copy. 

 

 Building the decision layer 

 One of our biggest product decisions was not to stop at a successful virtual fitting. 

 A rendering may answer whether someone likes a single product, but shopping often involves comparison. 

 So we built My Looks and a two- or three-look comparison interface. 

 Each comparison can combine the visual fitting with real garment construction information such as cup structure, wire, padding, straps, closure, material, available colors, and sizing. 

 From there, Ask a Friend lets the shopper generate an A/B or A/B/C comparison card. 

 The friend does not need a NUDE account or another app. 

 The shopper can then return and record the recommendation as Friend's Pick . 

 This turned the project from a virtual try-on demo into a lightweight decision tool. 

 

 Challenges we faced 

 1. Retail images are not automatically VTO inputs 

 Product photography is optimized to sell a garment, not necessarily to act as a clean AI reference. 

 We had to separate the images we wanted customers to see from the garment references we wanted the VTO model to process. 

 That led us to prepare dedicated garment assets for supported colorways. 

 2. A failed AI result must still be honest 

 Virtual try-on can fail because of pose, source-image quality, garment references, file constraints, or API processing. 

 Instead of hiding those failures, we mapped API states into understandable product messages and built an explicitly labeled fallback. 

 A preview is useful. 

 A preview pretending to be a successful AI render is not. 

 3. Comparison usually creates more infrastructure 

 Once we added "Ask a Friend," the obvious architecture was to build accounts, voting links, friend profiles, and a backend. 

 We chose not to. 

 The comparison card is generated locally, sharing happens through the user's existing communication tools, and the final pick is recorded manually. 

 That made the feature both simpler and more consistent with the privacy thesis. 

 4. Keeping a hackathon project feeling like a real product 

 We wanted the technical integration to remain visible enough for judges to understand, without turning the experience into a developer console. 

 That meant balancing API evidence, privacy disclosures, loading states, product information, and branding while keeping the fitting room calm and usable. 

 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that virtual try-on quality is only part of the consumer problem . 

 After seeing a generated fitting, a shopper still has to remember what they liked, compare alternatives, understand product differences, and sometimes ask someone they trust. 

 The API creates the visual evidence. 

 The product still has to help the shopper make sense of it. 

 We also learned that privacy UX becomes much stronger when it describes a concrete data flow instead of making broad promises. 

 For a sensitive retail experience, the question: 

 “Where does my photo go?” 

 is not a legal footnote. 

 It is part of the user experience. 

 Finally, we learned that graceful failure matters in AI products. Allowing the system to say that something could not be rendered reliably creates more trust than quietly substituting a different result. 

 

 Accomplishments we're proud of 

 During the hackathon we built a complete end-to-end product flow around a real retail catalog: 

 Showroom → Product → Live Perfect Corp VTO → My Looks → Compare → Ask a Friend → Friend'

Bazaar turns e-commerce into an agent-native experience where AI agents can discover products, manage carts, and complete purchases using real WebMCP tools.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Traditional e-commerce websites are built mainly for humans. AI assistants can recommend products, but they usually cannot directly interact with a website to perform real shopping actions. 

 We wanted to explore a simple question: What if an AI agent could actually shop on the same website as a human? 

 That idea inspired Bazaar — Agent-Native Store. We built Bazaar to demonstrate how WebMCP can turn a traditional e-commerce website into an agent-native experience where AI agents can discover products, make decisions, manage carts, and complete purchases. 

 Our goal was not to build another AI chatbot, but to make the website itself usable by AI agents. 

 What it does 

 Bazaar is an agent-native e-commerce store powered by WebMCP. 

 It exposes 12 functional WebMCP tools that allow AI agents to: 

 • Search and filter products
• View product details
• Compare products
• Get recommendations
• Add products to the cart
• Update cart quantities
• Remove products
• View the cart
• Clear the cart
• Checkout
• View order history
• Browse product categories 

 For example, an agent can receive a request like: 

 "Find me running shoes under ₹2000 and add the cheapest one to my cart." 

 The agent can search the catalog, find the best matching product, and add it directly to the user's cart. 

 The most important part is that humans and AI agents share the same application state. When an agent adds a product, it immediately appears in the user's normal cart and is marked as "Added by agent." 

 Bazaar also includes a live Agent Activity feed so users can see what the agent is doing. 

 How we built it 

 We built Bazaar using Next.js 16, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Zustand, Prisma ORM, SQLite, and WebMCP. 

 The WebMCP integration uses: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool() 

 We created 12 tools with clear descriptions, input schemas, and execution functions. 

 A key architectural decision was to make WebMCP use the same application logic as the human interface. 

 The WebMCP tools call the same Zustand store actions used by the React UI. 

 This creates a shared architecture: 

 Human UI → Zustand Store ← WebMCP Tools ← AI Agent 

 Because both interfaces use the same store and business logic, humans and AI agents share the same product catalog, cart, application state, and order flow. 

 The application is deployed on Vercel and includes an Agent Activity system for transparent tool execution. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was understanding how WebMCP tools are exposed and executed in the browser. 

 Initially, we expected tools such as search_products() to behave like normal JavaScript functions. We learned that WebMCP tools are exposed through the browser's model context instead. 

 We also had to carefully design tool descriptions and input schemas so AI agents could understand what each tool does, which parameters it accepts, and what information it returns. 

 Another challenge was synchronizing agent actions with the human UI. 

 We did not want the AI agent to have a separate cart or application state. Instead, every agent action had to use the same business logic as the human interface. 

 Testing complete workflows such as product search → selection → add to cart → cart management → checkout also required careful integration between WebMCP and our application state. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that Bazaar goes beyond simply registering WebMCP tools. We built a complete agent-native shopping workflow. 

 Our key accomplishments include: 

 • 12 functional WebMCP tools
• Shared human + AI shopping cart
• Agent actions visibly marked in the UI
• Live Agent Activity feed
• Natural-language product discovery
• Price filtering and product sorting
• Product comparison and recommendations
• Cart management and checkout
• Order history
• WebMCP connected directly to the same business logic used by the UI
• A fully deployed live web application 

 The biggest accomplishment is demonstrating that WebMCP can transform a traditional e-commerce website into an application that AI agents can actively operate, not just read. 

 What we learned 

 Building Bazaar taught us that creating an agent-native application is more than adding an AI chatbot. 

 The tools themselves become an important part of the application's interface. 

 We learned that WebMCP tools need clear descriptions, well-defined schemas, predictable outputs, and reliable execution. 

 We also learned the importance of shared application state. By connecting WebMCP directly to our existing business logic, agent actions behave consistently with actions performed through the human UI. 

 Most importantly, we learned that websites can be designed for two types of users: humans through visual interfaces and AI agents through structured tools. 

 WebMCP provides an exciting way to bridge these two experiences. 

 What's next for Bazaar — Agent-Native Store 

 Bazaar currently focuses on the core agent-native shopping experience. Our next goal is to make the platform more intelligent, autonomous, and user-controlled. 

 Future plans include: 

 • More intelligent personalized recommendations
• Conversational shopping experiences
• Multi-step autonomous shopping workflows
• Better agent activity and audit history
• Permission controls for sensitive actions
• More payment and checkout options
• Improved mobile experience
• Integration with external commerce services
• Multi-agent shopping workflows 

 Our long-term vision is to build an e-commerce platform where AI agents can safely discover, compare, purchase, and manage products on behalf of users while keeping the user in control.

A safe shared pet-care state where people and agents collaborate through five guarded WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it does 

 CAIOS WebMCP Agent Gateway is a standalone synthetic-data pet-care workspace where a person and an AI agent operate on the same visible state through five document-bound WebMCP tools. 

 The agent reads Synthetic Pika's profile, daily focus, and events; previews an exact structured check-in; requests human review; commits only the unchanged confirmed payload; and reads the result back from browser-only storage. 

 Why I built this 

 I chose the name CAIOS WebMCP Agent Gateway because CAIOS is our startup project, and the gateway was my way to test whether WebMCP could turn a pet-care page into a safer shared workspace for people and agents. 

 Before we adapt this pattern to real market needs, I wanted a small, inspectable build that could prove the interaction model without exposing production CAIOS technology or real pet data. 

 Pika's everyday care made the test concrete: an agent may help structure a routine observation, but the person should still see exactly what will be recorded and remain in control of the write. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Agents normally infer controls from visual interfaces. This project instead registers five narrow tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 get_synthetic_pika_profile 
 list_synthetic_pika_events 
 get_synthetic_pika_today 
 preview_synthetic_pika_check_in 
 commit_synthetic_pika_check_in 
 

 Preview validates without writing and returns a payload-bound confirmation token. Commit fails closed unless it receives the unchanged payload and matching token. A changed or unpreviewed payload is rejected. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 The agent reduces repetitive interaction while the person sees the proposal, controls confirmation, and verifies the outcome. Both then see the same browser-only state. 

 What I learned 

 The most useful lesson was that exposing a tool is only half of the work. The human page and the agent must stay consistent around the same proposed action. 

 During testing, we found a real UI bug: after preview, a re-render could reset the visible form to its defaults while the pending payload still held the earlier values. That could make the confirmation screen misleading even though the underlying token guard still worked. 

 We fixed it by preserving the exact previewed values in the UI and invalidating confirmation whenever the form changes. This reinforced the main product principle behind the demo: WebMCP can give an agent useful capabilities, but consequential actions still need deterministic guards and visible human review. 

 Safety and hackathon boundary 

 All data is fictional and marked synthetic_hackathon_only . Mutable state stays in namespaced browser localStorage . The demo has no production CAIOS API, database, customer record, real pet record, private prompt, proprietary memory engine, nutrition reasoning, or clinical logic. It does not diagnose, prescribe, or replace veterinary or emergency care. 

 CAIOS existed before the submission period as a broader pet-care product vision. During the submission period, we created this standalone WebMCP Gateway, five tools, synthetic dataset, confirmation guards, seven deterministic tests, CI, documentation, public repository, and independent deployment. 

 Implementation and verification 

 Built with TypeScript, Vite, the WebMCP browser API, and deterministic browser storage. Seven tests cover the tool boundary and guarded writes. Type checking and production builds pass. 

 The live workflow was verified end-to-end in an OpenAI cloud Chrome CDP environment: five tools were discovered; a direct commit failed closed; preview returned a payload-bound token; the exact payload committed; and a final read returned the same visible browser-only state.

 No account or credentials are required. Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled.

 Inspiration 

 Miaunolog started as a cat-behavior interpretation app designed to combine vocalizations, body language, context, and cat-specific profile information. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to see whether a browser agent could use the same application state and logic as the human user, rather than relying on a separate demo or agent-only backend. 

 I was already working on Miaunolog when I received OpenAI's notification about the WebMCP Challenge on X. I thought the app was a natural fit to extend with WebMCP and submit to the challenge. 

 What it does 

 Miaunolog lets a user create a cat profile, interpret observed behavior, and save observations to a local journal. 

 Through WebMCP, a browser agent can access that same workflow using three tools: 

 
 get_cat_profile 
 interpret_cat_behavior 
 add_behavior_observation 
 

 The agent reads the real active profile, uses the existing Miaunolog decoder, and writes the result into the same local journal shown in the human-facing interface. 

 How I built it 

 The project was developed with AI-assisted workflows using Grok and ChatGPT for implementation, review, debugging, and iteration. 

 The app is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, TanStack Router, and Tailwind CSS. 

 The WebMCP integration uses document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin: it maps structured agent inputs to Miaunolog's existing internal domain model and reuses the existing decoder and persistence functions. 

 Profiles and journal entries remain in localStorage, while audio clips use IndexedDB. No separate backend is required for the challenge workflow. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was making WebMCP functional rather than decorative. 

 The agent needed to use the real application state, reuse the same interpretation logic as the human interface, and produce a write that immediately appeared in the existing journal. 

 Another challenge was preserving the behavior of the original decoder while creating an agent-facing English schema without changing internal IDs or stored data structures. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP makes it possible to expose application capabilities directly to browser agents without duplicating the application's logic. 

 The most useful pattern in Miaunolog was not giving the agent a second implementation, but letting both human and agent operate on one shared state and one decoder. 

 What's next 

 Future work could expand the set of agent-visible observations, improve longitudinal behavior tracking, and explore richer workflows across cat profiles, audio observations, and journal history.tion

 Inspiration 

 I started thinking about how shopping online might be different if websites actually worked for both people and AI agents. Now most shopping sites are just a maze of filters, cards and small add-to-cart buttons. I thought. What if an AI agent could use the site side by side with you but you are still in charge? 

 That is how I came up with ShopMate. 

 What it does 

 ShopMate is a shopping site where you can browse, compare products manage your basket and set a budget. Much what you would expect. 

 Here is the twist: any WebMCP-compatible agent can do all those things through ShopMate's built-in tools. So say you want to find school supplies under $100 and add the best ones to your basket; you just ask: 

 "Find school supplies under $100 and add the best options to my basket." 

 The agent handles all the searching, filtering and adding items for you. 

 Not liking something? You can say, 

 "Remove anything over $20 and optimize my basket." 

 The agent updates everything. You instantly see your new basket. 

 Why WebMCP? 

 Let's be honest a lot of shopping actions are simple to describe but annoying to do. WebMCP fixes this by letting ShopMate offer those actions as structured tools instead of making agents poke around the interface blindly. 

 Now ShopMate has eight tools. Searching, filtering, comparing and managing your basket. Right out of the box. It just feels much smoother for you and the agent. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 It's a back and forth: 

 You ask → agent works → site updates → you review → agent tweaks 

 You are always in control but the agent handles all the work. Since you both use the same products and basket you are not getting a watered-down "AI" version of the shopping experience. 

 How I built it 

 I built ShopMate alone using React, TypeScript, TanStack Start, Tailwind CSS, Zod, WebMCP and Google Gemini. The core of ShopMate lives in these WebMCP tools, which I register like this: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 Each tool has its schema, validation and real app logic. I also added a global ShopMate Assistant for answering product or basket questions connecting Gemini through the server so the API key stays private. 

 Everything runs off a product catalog and stores your stuff in browser storage. Meaning there is no database, no logins and no payments to worry about. 

 Challenges I faced 

 Getting my head around WebMCP in practice was a struggle at first. I had to make tools only registered once (React loves to re-run things at weird times) and always stayed in sync with what was really on the site. 

 Testing was tricky too. I kept switching between an old browser and a WebMCP-compatible one to check that everything behaved the way I expected. 

 What I'm proud of 

 I got all eight WebMCP tools built. They really work. Search, filter, compare, add, remove, update, inspect even optimize your basket. But more than that ShopMate isn't a tech demo; it's a full-on shopping experience with a catalog, a Smart Basket, a dedicated Demo page and a Relations page. 

 What I learned 

 This project completely changed how I think about web apps. Instead of designing just for people clicking buttons I realized you can build websites that clearly lay out what agents can do too. I learned a lot around tools, validation keeping state in sync playing nice across browsers and how humans and agents can actually interact. 

 What's next 

 In the future ShopMate could connect to live product catalogs handle complex shopping needs or even walk through longer step-by-step tasks. For this challenge I really wanted to try out a simple idea: 

 What if websites were built for both humans and agents from the start?

about_excerpt:
Upcoming OSS end-of-life dates — one public page for humans and WebMCP agents.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it does 

 EOL Desk is a calendar of upcoming end-of-life and support-cutoff dates for popular open-source libraries and frameworks. Those facts are already structured (name, version line, date, successor, source). A human needs a scannable board; an agent needs typed actions — not a screenshot of a table and not a private MCP server the human cannot see. 

 Why WebMCP 

 The page is the product and the tool host. On load we register list_upcoming_eols , get_eol_detail , and suggest_upgrade_path via document.modelContext.registerTool . ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled discovers the same dataset the UI renders. No login wall, no second API for agents. 

 Better user experience 

 Without WebMCP, a maintainer either hunts vendor blogs and changelogs by hand, or lets an agent scrape HTML and hope the date is still in the DOM. Both drift. EOL Desk is one board for humans and agents: scan upcoming cutoffs, open a row, or call typed tools for JSON. One source of truth. 

 People and agents together 

 Before, asking what dies in 90 days meant the model guessed from training data or scraped pages. Now a person keeps the board honest while ChatGPT or Chrome WebMCP calls list_upcoming_eols , get_eol_detail , and suggest_upgrade_path on the same page. Shared structured facts, no scrape. 

 How we built it 

 Greenfield public page on Cloudflare Pages/Workers. On load we feature-detect document.modelContext (fallback navigator.modelContext ) and register three tools with the Imperative API against the same dataset as the table: list_upcoming_eols , get_eol_detail , suggest_upgrade_path . Tested with the ChatGPT in-app browser and Chrome 149+ chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . 

 Judge access: none needed, public page. 

 Challenges I ran into

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Film production involves many connected tasks: planning scenes, creating shot lists, estimating budgets, and organizing shooting schedules. These tasks are often handled across different tools, making it difficult for filmmakers to keep everything connected. 

 I wanted to build CineOps, a production workspace where humans and AI agents can work together. The idea was to let a filmmaker enter real production information while an AI agent can use structured tools to help with repetitive planning tasks. 

 What I Built 

 CineOps is an AI-assisted film production planning application that brings the core production workflow into one place. 

 A filmmaker can: 

 Create a film project with its title, genre, duration, and budget.
Add scenes with location and time-of-day information.
Generate a structured five-shot camera plan.
Estimate a production budget.
Optimize the proposed budget.
Review and approve budget changes.
Create a multi-day shooting schedule.
Monitor actions through an agent activity panel. 

 The important part is that these capabilities are exposed as WebMCP tools, allowing compatible AI agents to interact with the application through structured tool calls. 

 Why WebMCP? 

 WebMCP makes the application more than a traditional web interface. 

 Instead of an AI agent only giving suggestions as text, CineOps exposes actual application capabilities such as: 

 create_project
add_scene
generate_shot_list
estimate_budget
optimize_budget
create_schedule 

 This allows people and agents to work together on the same production workflow. 

 For example, a filmmaker can provide the production information, while an agent can help generate a shot list, estimate costs, and organize the shooting schedule. The filmmaker can then review the results and remain in control of important decisions such as budget optimization. 

 How I Built It 

 CineOps was built as a modern React and TypeScript web application using Vite. 

 The main technologies used are: 

 React
TypeScript
Vite
WebMCP / Model Context API
Lucide React
Vercel for deployment
GitHub for open-source project hosting 

 The WebMCP integration registers structured tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(). Each tool has a name, description, input schema, and execution function. 

 The application state is updated when tools execute, allowing agent actions to be reflected directly in the user interface. 

 What I Learned 

 Building CineOps taught me how to think about AI applications beyond chat interfaces. 

 I learned how to: 

 Design structured tools for AI agents.
Define tool input schemas.
Connect agent actions with React application state.
Build human-in-the-loop workflows.
Handle TypeScript interfaces and browser APIs.
Debug integration and build errors.
Deploy a React application to Vercel.
Design an application around the idea of agent + human collaboration. 

 One of the biggest lessons was that an AI agent becomes much more useful when it can interact with real application capabilities instead of only generating text. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was integrating WebMCP with a TypeScript React application because the modelContext API is not part of the standard TypeScript DOM definitions used by the project. 

 I had to create appropriate TypeScript interfaces and handle the availability of document.modelContext safely. 

 Another challenge was making sure the tools were registered only when they were not already available, while also preventing duplicate registration. 

 I also had to debug build errors, TypeScript errors, and deployment issues before getting the application running successfully on Vercel. 

 What Makes CineOps Different 

 CineOps focuses on a practical human-in-the-loop workflow. 

 The goal isn't to replace the filmmaker. Instead: 

 Human provides context → Agent performs structured tasks → Human reviews → Human approves important decisions. 

 This creates a workflow where AI can reduce repetitive production-planning work while the filmmaker maintains control. 

 Future Improvements 

 Future versions of CineOps could include: 

 AI-generated production breakdowns.
More advanced scheduling based on locations and cast availability.
Real-time collaboration between production team members.
More detailed budget categories.
AI-assisted script-to-shot-list generation.
Integration with real production management systems.
More sophisticated WebMCP tools for production workflows. 

 CineOps demonstrates how WebMCP can turn an ordinary web application into an agent-ready workspace where humans and AI can work together on real tasks.

 What's next for Co-Desk — Human + Agent Support Operations 

 The idea 

 Co-Desk is a human + agent support desk : a single live ticket queue that a person and an AI agent operate together , in real time, over WebMCP. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Before WebMCP, an agent helping with a real web workflow could only navigate the page and click — slow, brittle, and hard to verify. Co-Desk inverts this: instead of the agent guessing at our UI, the site declares its own operations as structured tools the agent can call. A person opens the app and works; an agent discovers those tools and acts inside the real workflow. 

 What people and agents can do together now 

 A support team can hand the agent the whole routine workload — opening requests, adding notes, routing to teams, escalating, resolving the mechanical cases — while the human watches the same screen update live and owns the judgment calls. One shared queue, two operators, with the human always in the loop. That is the collaboration WebMCP makes possible. 

 How we built it 

 
 10 WebMCP tools ( listOpenTickets , getTicket , createTicket , addNote , updateStatus , assignToTeam , escalateTicket , resolveTicket , searchTickets , summarizeQueue ), each with a JSON Schema and real effects on a shared store. 
 Every action — human or agent — is written to one localStorage store and rendered live, so the queue and an activity feed update on screen. 
 Plain HTML/CSS/JS, no build step — trivially deployable. 
 

 Registration is done against document.modelContext : 
 await document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "resolveTicket" , 
 description : "Resolve a ticket with a short resolution summary." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 ticketId : { type : "string" } , 
 resolution : { type : "string" } , 
 } , 
 required : [ "ticketId" , "resolution" ] , 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { /* real action on the shared queue */ } , 
 } ) ; 
 
 Challenges 

 The hardest part was keeping one source of truth. Tools and the human UI both mutate the same queue, so we made them share one store and one change-notification path. That guarantees an agent's action and a human click are never out of sync.

 Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, then ask the agent: "Summarize the queue, then handle the password-reset ticket — add a note, route it to account, and show me before resolving."

 Inspiration 

 I noticed that AI agents are getting really good at thinking and giving recommendations, but there is still a gap between knowing what to do and actually doing it. 

 I wanted to build something around that gap: a place where someone can start with a rough idea and use AI to develop, validate, and move it forward. 

 When I came across WebMCP, it fit the idea well. Drop&Grow is built around actions — running agents, updating ideas, adding notes, finalising work, and contributing to the community. Instead of an agent telling the user which buttons to click, I could let the agent perform those actions itself. 

 What it does 

 Drop&Grow helps users take an idea through a workflow with six specialised AI agents. 

 The agents analyse different parts of an idea and help develop it. Users can review the results, add notes, move the idea through different stages, and finalise it with proof. 

 WebMCP allows an agent to interact with the application itself. It can run the agent pipeline, expand responses, change an idea's stage, finalise an idea, and contribute to the community. 

 The main difference is simple: the agent doesn't just tell you what to do. It can actually do it. 

 How I built it 

 I built Drop&Grow from scratch using React and Convex. 

 Convex handles the backend, including the data, agent logic, and idea lifecycle. 

 I added WebMCP directly to the frontend and registered the main actions in the app as WebMCP tools. These include running the agent pipeline, expanding individual agent responses, changing an idea's stage, finalising with proof, and posting a community contribution. 

 When an agent calls a tool, it triggers the same client-side action that would normally happen when a user clicks the corresponding button. That action then communicates with Convex through the normal application flow. 

 The agent does not access Convex directly or use a separate API. It goes through the same application path a human user does, while using the current page state to decide what to do next. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The biggest challenge was figuring out how to expose useful actions to an agent without turning the whole experience into a fixed script. 

 I wanted the agent to understand what was currently happening in the application and decide what action made sense next. 

 I also had to carefully choose which actions should become WebMCP tools and connect them to the existing frontend behaviour. The tools needed to be useful to an agent while still representing actions that a real user could perform. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I'm proud that I built the entire project from scratch during the submission period and integrated WebMCP into the core workflow. 

 I was able to make the same actions available to both humans and agents instead of creating a separate system specifically for AI. 

 I'm also proud of the community interaction. An agent can read what is already happening before contributing, rather than blindly generating a generic response. 

 Most importantly, I built an experience where AI can move beyond giving recommendations and actually take actions inside the application. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that giving an agent tools is only part of the problem. The tools need to represent meaningful actions and provide enough context for the agent to make good decisions. 

 I also learned that WebMCP can make agent integration much more natural when an application is already built around clear user actions. 

 Building Drop&Grow from scratch also gave me a better understanding of how the frontend, backend, agent logic, and WebMCP layer need to work together. 

 What's next for Drop&Grow 

 I want Drop&Grow to become more autonomous while keeping the user in control. 

 Next, I want to improve how the six agents collaborate, give users more control over which actions an agent can take, and make the idea-validation workflow more powerful. 

 I also want to expand the community side so agents can discover relevant ideas, provide useful feedback, and help move projects forward. 

 The long-term goal is simple: 

 Drop an idea. Let your agents help you grow it.

 Inspiration 

 Funding and hackathon applications are repetitive, deadline-driven, and easy to lose track of. Existing trackers are passive: they store records, while browser agents often rely on brittle screen scraping. PrizePilot WebMCP explores a better contract—structured tools that let a person and an agent work from the same verified record without giving away control. 

 What it does 

 PrizePilot WebMCP turns opportunities into a prioritized, evidence-led queue. The live page exposes four WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_opportunities finds verified local records by project, organizer, tag, or status. 
 build_application_plan produces a five-step, evidence-led checklist without changing data. 
 stage_status_change proposes a local status update for human review. 
 record_verified_submission requires an HTTPS receipt before it can stage Submitted status. 
 

 Every tool call is visible in the activity log. Any state-changing request opens a clear confirmation card. Nothing is submitted to an external form automatically. 

 How we built it 

 The prototype is a responsive React and TypeScript application built with Next.js-compatible components and vinext, hosted on ChatGPT Sites. It registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool with bounded JSON schemas, length limits, read-only annotations, and explicit human-confirmation semantics. Demo records are stored locally in the browser, so the experience remains useful without an account or external database. 

 A progressive fallback detects browsers without WebMCP and keeps the full dashboard usable. The same interface supports normal manual interaction, a safe built-in agent-plan demo, and real WebMCP calls from compatible agents. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is an emerging standard, so we designed for uncertain browser support and made every capability progressively enhanced. The hardest product decision was not how much the agent could do, but where it should stop. We treated submission claims and consequential status changes as evidence-backed proposals rather than silent automation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A working public prototype with four registered WebMCP tools. 
 A shared visual activity log for people and agents. 
 Receipt-gated submission records and visible confirmation before local mutations. 
 A complete no-login fallback that preserves the product experience. 
 Clear separation between organizing work and submitting external applications. 
 

 What we learned 

 Structured page tools are more reliable and understandable than screen scraping. More importantly, WebMCP can make agent behavior easier to inspect: the interface, schemas, annotations, and confirmation state become a shared contract between the site, the user, and the agent. 

 What's next for PrizePilot WebMCP 

 Next steps are official-source synchronization, reusable evidence libraries, team review, receipt exports, deadline alerts, and connectors that can prepare—but never silently submit—applications across funding platforms.

about_excerpt:
A consent-first WebMCP workspace where people and agents turn benefit eligibility paperwork into a visible, reversible review plan.

 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Benefit navigation is a shared-context problem. A person understands nuance, consent, and tradeoffs; an agent can search and organize quickly. Traditional browser automation forces the agent to infer controls and hidden state, which is especially risky in a workflow involving eligibility evidence. We built ProofDesk to explore a better boundary: structured assistance that stays visible, reversible, and under human control. 

 What it does 

 ProofDesk is a consent-first workspace built around an entirely synthetic benefit directory and demo case. A person and an agent can search programs, inspect evidence requirements, identify readiness gaps, stage a shortlist of up to three options, and prepare a local review packet on the same live page. 

 The crucial boundary is explicit: ProofDesk never submits an application or sends evidence. The final preparation tool returns submitted: false , while the interface keeps the person as the only decision-maker. 

 Why WebMCP 

 ProofDesk exposes seven narrow tools tied to the exact state the person sees: 

 
 search_support_programs 
 get_program_requirements 
 review_case_readiness 
 set_evidence_consent 
 stage_application_plan 
 prepare_review_packet 
 reset_demo_case 
 

 Three tools are read-only and four make local, visible changes. Every input uses a narrow JSON schema. State-changing results appear immediately in the normal UI and can be reviewed or reversed. WebMCP removes the brittle step of guessing at DOM controls and gives the agent a precise, inspectable contract. 

 How we built it 

 The app is a responsive React 19 and TypeScript experience built with Next.js, Vinext, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. The top-level page detects document.modelContext.registerTool and registers the seven tools directly against the live application state. Read operations declare read-only behavior; write operations describe their effects in plain language. 

 The public build is hosted on ChatGPT Sites. Browsers without WebMCP retain the complete manual experience, so agent access is an enhancement rather than a dependency. 

 Safety and privacy 

 All programs, people, amounts, and evidence are synthetic. There is no authentication, upload, personal record, external API call, or hidden submission. The product demonstrates a review workflow, not real eligibility advice. A real deployment would require official-source verification, jurisdiction logic, accessibility review, and a documented privacy program. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest design challenge was making agent actions useful without making them opaque or overpowered. A single broad “apply” tool would have been easy to demo and wrong for the domain. We instead decomposed the flow into narrow capabilities, capped the shortlist, surfaced consent state, and made every mutation visible. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is strongest when it does more than accelerate clicks. It lets a site define a shared protocol for human-agent collaboration: what can be read, what can change, and where responsibility must remain with the person. That changes the product architecture, not just the automation layer. 

 What is next 

 The next step is to connect verified public program sources, add jurisdiction-aware validation, expand accessibility testing, and design a privacy-preserving evidence vault—while keeping the same consent-first contract.

 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for Recovery Radar 

 Inspiration 

 People lose money because a delay, cancellation, outage, failed delivery, cancelled subscription or provider promise is rarely matched back to the transaction that should have been settled. Recovery Radar turns that missed connection into a reviewable recovery lead. 

 What it does 

 Recovery Radar looks for a verifiable gap between a purchase or booking, an incident or provider promise, the applicable rule, and the final settlement. It then prepares the next step for the person to review. 

 The demo covers three synthetic recovery leads: 

 
 a transport delay with a possible EUR 400 compensation; 
 a subscription cancelled before a later EUR 17.99 charge; and 
 a telecom outage with a possible EUR 20 service credit. 
 

 The product is intentionally not a chatbot that writes a generic complaint. It builds an evidence chain and shows why a recovery may exist. 

 Why WebMCP 

 This workflow normally spans several web surfaces: a booking or receipt, transport or provider records, a policy page, a billing record and a claim workspace. WebMCP gives the agent a structured way to discover and operate the meaningful actions exposed by the page. 

 Recovery Radar registers seven tools through document.modelContext.registerTool: 

 
 scan_for_recoverable_money 
 select_recovery_case 
 inspect_recovery_evidence 
 prepare_recovery_claim 
 approve_recovery_workspace 
 reconcile_recovery 
 reset_recovery_demo 
 

 These represent the product operations: discover, select, prove, prepare, approve and reconcile. The tools validate inputs, preserve an audit trail and keep external submission behind a human approval boundary. 

 What people and agents do together 

 The agent performs the repetitive discovery and evidence assembly. The person chooses the scope, reviews the proof, confirms the amount and decides whether to open the prepared workspace. Preparation can be agent-assisted, but submission and money handling remain outside the project. 

 How it was built 

 Recovery Radar is a local-first static web application built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It uses synthetic cases and deterministic state transitions so the complete flow can be tested safely. The main challenge was making WebMCP meaningful instead of decorative: each registered tool maps to a real product operation and produces visible evidence or state changes. 

 Impact and scope 

 Recovery Radar starts with transport, subscriptions, purchases and paid services, where the evidence chain can be made concrete without immediately entering higher-risk areas such as banking, insurance or litigation. 

 How to test 

 Open the live demo in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Ask: 

 “Scan for recoverable money, select the highest-confidence transport case, inspect its evidence, and prepare the claim packet. Do not approve or submit anything.” 

 The expected result is three findings, EUR 437.99 in synthetic potential recovery, and a transport lead for EUR 400. Review the evidence, prepare the packet and approve the local workspace manually. No provider form is submitted and no funds are handled. 

 Disclosure 

 All records and amounts in the demo are synthetic. The project makes no provider requests, does not use credentials, does not send claims and does not receive money.

 Focus timer — start it yourself, or ask the agent to start one for you.

 Alarms — set by user or by the agent in plain English, with a real popup and sound.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most AI study tools are just a chatbot bolted onto the side of an app — the agent talks, but you still do all the clicking. WebMCP made a different kind of tool possible: one where an agent doesn't just describe what to do, it actually does it, on the same board a student is already looking at. StudyMesh grew from that idea — a study workspace where a human and an AI agent share one board and are equally capable of acting on it. 

 What it does 

 StudyMesh is a study workspace with a task board, alarms, flashcards, a quiz zone, a focus timer, and a live progress dashboard. Every one of those actions — adding a task, setting an alarm, building a quiz, starting a focus session — can be done by clicking in the UI, or by asking an AI agent in plain English. Both paths hit the exact same backend logic, so there's one shared source of truth no matter who acts on it. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — WebMCP tools have to run client-side since document.modelContext is a browser API. Seven tools are registered on document.modelContext in mcp.js : add_study_task, reschedule_tasks, set_alarm, generate_flashcards, generate_quiz, start_focus_session, and track_progress. Each tool's execute function calls the same REST endpoints the human-facing UI calls, backed by a Python FastAPI server that holds the shared state. Quiz and flashcard content comes from a curated knowledge base of real facts for common syllabus topics (Physics, Chemistry, Biology, History, CS, Math), not generic filler text. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Making sure an agent action and a human click were truly indistinguishable in effect took some care — every WebMCP tool had to route through the same backend function as its UI counterpart, with no separate "shortcut" path for agents. Getting alarms to fire reliably (with a browser notification, an in-app popup, and a sound) without a native OS scheduler was another one — solved by computing the trigger time server-side and having the client poll and confirm the fire exactly once. 

 What we learned 

 Building this made it clear that the real value of WebMCP isn't a chatbot with extra steps — it's giving an agent the same tools a human already has, on the same page, so the two can genuinely hand off work to each other mid-task without anything breaking. 

 What's next for StudyMesh 

 Persisting state in a real database instead of in-memory, expanding the curated content library to more subjects, and adding collaborative study boards where multiple students and their agents share one workspace.

With Bargainer, you can just tell you ai agent that you want to buy sneakers and sit back and watch as it shows you all available options, negotiates the price, and gets you a final deal that you have to improve.  AI agents negotiate and reach a deal on both the buyer and seller side that needs to be approved (or is auto-approved, if enabled). Makes use of WebMCP tools to provide all the information to the agents. 

 How we built it 

 It is built as a React and TypeScript SPA. It is client-side with no backend. It is deployed on Netlify. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is a newer technology, so a lot of my work came from trial and error, as I didn't know much about it beforehand either. React StrictMode's double-mounting broke tool registration until I rebuilt it around AbortController cleanup (the spec has no unregisterTool). Tool errors are opaque to agents, so I return structured {ok: false, message} responses instead of throwing. And the human gate needed a 60-second approval token so the tool can tell the agent "waiting on the human" instead of silently blocking. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I had very little time to make this project, as I found out about it much later. But 9 registered and running WebMCP tools in such a short time feels like a win. 

 What we learned 

 This is my first ever hackathon. I gave it my best and hope to win, but even if I don't, it was a very valuable learning experience for me. I learnt about WebMCP and how its tools can be used effectively. I learnt to plan, code, test, and debug a project with a time crunch.

 I will build a lightweight backend that will allow real buyer agents to join from other devices instead of simulated ones.

Emergency Department nurse-staffing decision-support dashboard using WebMCP imperative tools with strict Human-In-The-Loop safety guardrails.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human-in-the-loop approval: only the Charge Nurse can authorize a plan, with the decision recorded in the audit trail. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 SafeStaff Shift Commander: a human-governed Emergency Department staffing command center built with WebMCP. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Nurse call-out simulation: staffing drops from 7 to 6 RNs and forecast wait time rises from 96 to 118 minutes. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP safety guardrail: an agent can analyze and recommend, but `submit_human_approval` returns `human_confirmation_required` 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Three staffing strategies compared side-by-side, balancing high-acuity coverage, wait-time reduction, and staffing cost 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human-in-the-loop approval: only the Charge Nurse can authorize a plan, with the decision recorded in the audit trail. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 SafeStaff Shift Commander: a human-governed Emergency Department staffing command center built with WebMCP. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Nurse call-out simulation: staffing drops from 7 to 6 RNs and forecast wait time rises from 96 to 118 minutes. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP safety guardrail: an agent can analyze and recommend, but `submit_human_approval` returns `human_confirmation_required` 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Three staffing strategies compared side-by-side, balancing high-acuity coverage, wait-time reduction, and staffing cost 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human-in-the-loop approval: only the Charge Nurse can authorize a plan, with the decision recorded in the audit trail. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Hospital Emergency Departments operate under extreme operational stress. Nurse shortages and unpredictable patient surges force Charge Nurses to make high-stakes staffing and triage re-allocation decisions under severe cognitive load. While agentic AI has immense potential to ingest census telemetry, compute queuing delays, and formulate mitigation options, autonomous AI execution in clinical environments is unsafe . 

 We built SafeStaff Shift Commander to demonstrate how the imperative WebMCP API ( document.modelContext.registerTool ) allows client-side AI agents to serve as powerful decision-support partners—inspecting, forecasting, and comparing scenarios—while enforcing strict Human-In-The-Loop (HITL) governance: AI agents are architecturally prohibited from self-approving staffing changes. 

 What it does 

 SafeStaff Shift Commander is a synthetic hospital operations command-center dashboard: 

 
 Live Shift Snapshot Telemetry : Displays waiting room volume (42 patients), high-acuity arrivals (3 ESI 1-2 critical resuscitation cases), active floor nurses (7 RNs), and door-to-provider forecast wait time (96 min vs 60 min safe operational target). 
 Scenario Stress-Testing ("Model Nurse Call-Out") : With a single toggle, simulates an unplanned nurse absence in Pod B. Available nurses drop to 6, and projected wait surges to 118 minutes (+58 min over the safe target). 
 Selectable Evidence-Informed Staffing Plans : Generates and compares 3 actionable mitigation strategies:

 
 Protect High-Acuity Flow : Ring-fences dedicated 1:1 and 1:2 coverage for critical pods, buffering non-urgent queue. 
 Call-In Contingency : Dispatches an on-call Float Pool RN, bringing wait time down to 68 minutes. 
 Hold and Monitor : Preserves float hours with a 30-minute re-evaluation surge threshold. 
 
 Human-In-The-Loop Signoff & Governance : Charge Nurses must physically click Approve Plan or Override Recommendation (with a mandatory clinical rationale prompt). 
 Compliance Audit Trail : Immutable chronological log capturing every AI tool invocation, parameter payload, human approval, and clinical override with exportable JSON. 
 Interactive WebMCP Live Console : Embedded workbench for judges and developers to inspect JSON schemas, customize input parameters, and execute tools directly in the browser. 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Frontend Architecture : Built with React 18, Vite 6, and Lucide React. We styled the interface using an operations command-center theme (slate navy #060a14 , glowing cyan #06b6d4 , and amber risk indicators #f59e0b ). 
 Imperative WebMCP Tools : Registered 5 tools directly into document.modelContext.registerTool(...) :

 
 get_shift_snapshot : Retrieves synthetic department census, triage acuity levels, nurse count, and safe targets. 
 forecast_wait_time : Forecasts waiting room delays based on patient volume, acuity distribution, and nurse headcount. 
 generate_staffing_options : Proposes candidate staffing allocations with pros/cons and risk scores. 
 compare_staffing_scenario : Compares baseline, call-out, and contingency strategies side-by-side. 
 submit_human_approval : HITL Safety Guardrail — Strictly returns {"status": "human_confirmation_required"} to prove agents cannot self-approve staffing changes. 
 
 Simulation Engine : Realistic, deterministic queue modeling and ESI 1–5 triage breakdown without any real patient data or PHI. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Enforcing the HITL Safety Boundary : Designing an agentic workflow where the AI can simulate, forecast, and prepare recommendations while guaranteeing that autonomous approval attempts are intercepted with {"status": "human_confirmation_required"} . 
 Telemetry Visual Hierarchy : Balancing high-density hospital command center metrics (acuity bars, wait variance chips, pod allocations, financial impact) within an intuitive, responsive dark-mode interface. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Pure Client-Side WebMCP Execution : The entire WebMCP tool suite operates directly in the browser via document.modelContext without requiring external backend servers. 
 Dual-Role Demonstration : Clear visual and architectural separation between what the AI Agent sees/does (WebMCP tools) and what the licensed Clinician sees/does (Command Center UI + Audit Signoff). 
 Interactive WebMCP Inspector : An embedded developer playground allowing instant live testing of all tool inputs and outputs. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP provides an elegant, structured way to expose rich application state and actions to client-side AI agents without complex scraping or brittle DOM querying. The imperative registerTool pattern is clean, expressive, and easily governed with safety guardrails. 

 What's next for SafeStaff Shift Commander — WebMCP 

 
 Synthetic FHIR/HL7 Feeds : Connecting synthetic hospital EHR streams for multi-unit hospital flow (ICU, Med-Surg, Stepdown). 
 Predictive 12-Hour Surge Heatmaps : Expanding queue forecasting to incorporate EMS ambulance dispatch data and regional surge modeling.

We wanted to build a web application designed specifically for the agent-native era—a unified workspace where human operators and AI agents collaborate seamlessly during system outages to diagnose latency spikes, inspect telemetry, and execute infrastructure remediation natively.

 Client-Side Tool Synchronization: Ensuring state changes executed by an agent tool call (e.g., scaling replicas) triggered immediate visual UI updates in the React component hierarchy without requiring page refreshes.

 Successfully implemented a functional browser-native WebMCP interface that allows an AI agent to execute end-to-end incident triage and infrastructure mitigation.

 How WebMCP transforms static web applications into interactive, agentic workspaces by standardizing client-side tool discovery. 
 Best practices for structuring agent inputs and fallback handling for robust client-side execution.

The User and ChatGPT share one live cart and the agent proposes a gift, the user approves, review, and then confirm. Therefore nothing is placed without the user

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Asked Agent to recommend a gift under 40 pounds for someone who cooks 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Website page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Use the site tools to call g et_account,get_saved_customer, get_shop_state. Quote the exact JSON, call apply_saved_profile. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Asked Agent to recommend a gift under 40 pounds for someone who cooks 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Website page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Use the site tools to call g et_account,get_saved_customer, get_shop_state. Quote the exact JSON, call apply_saved_profile. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Asked Agent to recommend a gift under 40 pounds for someone who cooks 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every "AI shopping" demo I'd seen had the same problem: the agent clicks buttons it's guessing at, or it shops in a parallel page you can't even see. I wanted the opposite. One real shop, one cart, where ChatGPT and I are looking at the exact same thing and I get the final say. 

 That's what Hearth is, a small home goods shop for the table and kitchen. You browse and click like you would anywhere else. The agent, meanwhile, calls real site tools and nothing gets bought until you approve it, review it, and confirm it. 

 What it does 

 I and the agent share the same tab and the same cart. 

 The agent calls recommend_gift instead of silently adding something to your bag. A tradeoff card shows up: here's the pick, here's why, here's what it costs and that makes the cart stay empty. 

 You hit Approve on the page only then does the item land in your cart. 

 explain_cart and prepare_order build a review of everything while ordering stays locked. 

 If the agent tries place_order without confirm: true , it gets blocked and Undo Last restores your last cart snapshot if anything goes sideways. 

 Privacy was a deliberate part of the demo. Once you sign in, get_account and get_saved_customer only return a profileStatus flag, like hasShipping: true . Your street address and phone number never leave this browser; they sit in a local demo vault. Checkout keeps those fields hidden too, until you personally choose Use saved details or Show saved address which makes the agent unable to see them. 

 Why this is a fit for WebMCP 

 A shop is a terrible scraping target. Filters, quantities, promo codes, checkout, and a yes/no question about how much you're willing to spend, and an agent guessing at all of that through the DOM is fragile and blind. WebMCP lets the page declare those actions up front. The agent doesn't just click or hunt for buttons, it calls search_products , recommend_gift and prepare_order . Since it's the same page, you watch the DOM update live, right next to you. 

 The hard part was always the trust gap: how do you let an agent "help" while you're still the one who sees everything, approves everything, and can undo everything without handing it your address? Structured tools let the site describe the action, its inputs, and its guardrails directly. That's what solved it. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest lesson is learned is that agent usefulness is not the same thing as agent autonomy. The moments where the agent actually felt useful weren't when it acted on its own, they were when it made a clear proposal, showed its reasoning, and waited one step for my approval. 

 How I built it 

 Static HTML and ES modules on Netlify, No backend, Auth and the customer vault are plain localStorage. 

 mcp-boot.js looks for document.modelContext / navigator.modelContext early. webmcp.js builds each tool (name, description, inputSchema, execute) and registers it with registerTool, including search_products: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "search_products" , 
 description : "Search the shop by words such as mug, skillet, linen, gift, or wool." , 
 inputSchema : { type : "object" , properties : { query : { type : "string" } } , required : [ "query" ] } , 
 execute : async ( { query } ) = > shop . searchProducts ( query , "agent" ) 
 } ) ;

pitch: Agent-native transit telemetry and collision mitigation command deck powered by browser WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
Agent-native transit telemetry and collision mitigation command deck powered by browser WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 About two months ago, as I was preparing for my graduation, my family was traveling together to celebrate with me. They were driving along a two-lane highway corridor—the kind of treacherous mountain pass defined by blind curves, sudden visibility drops, and heavy commercial freight trucks that turn everyday transit into deadly collision zones. 

 On that road, a catastrophic crash occurred. I lost five of my closest family members in an instant. 

 When the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge was announced, I knew I could not build a toy or another generic chatbot. I had to focus on a problem with real-world stakes: preventing this specific, devastating failure mode so no other family has to suffer that loss. 

 Most browser AI agents today interact with applications through brittle screen-scraping, OCR, or simulated clicks. While that might suffice for casual e-commerce, life-safety operations cannot tolerate non-deterministic delays or scraping failures. When sudden fog drops visibility to near zero on blind S-bends, human drivers and dispatchers experience severe cognitive overload trying to calculate safe stopping sightlines and coordinate emergency interventions. 

 I asked a fundamental question: 

 
 What if high-risk transit corridors could be supervised directly inside the browser, where the application exposes deterministic, typed telematics tools to an AI agent? 
 

 I built DispatchGuard WebMCP to pioneer what an agent-native safety cockpit looks like—merging autonomous collision risk evaluation with human supervisory dispatch into a synchronized, life-saving control loop. 

 What it does 

 DispatchGuard WebMCP is a real-time transit telemetry and collision mitigation command deck where human dispatchers and browser agents collaborate to secure hazardous, two-lane highway corridors. 

 When the application loads in a WebMCP-capable browser, it exposes four typed tools directly to the agent layer via document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 query_corridor_telemetry : Ingests real-time sector parameters—sightline distance (meters), weather state, commercial truck ratio, and blind curve counts. 
 evaluate_overtake_risk : Runs kinematic collision modeling, evaluates hazard probability (0–100%), and escalates sector status to CRITICAL. 
 broadcast_safety_alert : Pushes a geofenced advisory speed cap (e.g., 45 km/h) and overtake ban across active vehicle nodes and UI cards. 
 export_incident_dossier : Bundles the entire incident timeline, telemetry data, and mitigation checklist into an audit-ready post-mortem modal with copyable JSON. 
 

 The human operator retains visual control through an interactive SVG vector radar schematic, while the AI agent runs risk math in the background and executes safety protocols with zero screen-scraping delay. 

 How I built it 

 
 Frontend Stack : Built with Next.js 16 (Turbopack), React 19, and Tailwind CSS. The interface uses a dark, high-contrast command deck palette (deep slate #0A0B0E , warning amber, and critical red vectors) designed for high-stress situational awareness. 
 WebMCP Registration : Implemented inside src/hooks/useWebMCP.ts . The tools are registered directly on document.modelContext with strict JSON Schema definitions for every input parameter. 
 Fallback Simulation Harness : Because judges test across various environments (some with Chrome flags enabled, others in standard browsers), I built an on-page simulation bus. Clicking the harness tools runs the exact same client-side mutation logic as the native WebMCP calls, guaranteeing the demo works on every browser. 
 Testing & Verification : Verified native tool discovery and execution using the official WebMCP browser extension and the ChatGPT in-app browser environment. 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 
 Next.js SSR vs. Browser-Native WebMCP : In Next.js, document does not exist during server-side rendering. Furthermore, document.modelContext is injected dynamically by the browser or extension at runtime. I had to design a clean hydration guard and an asynchronous registration hook that polls safely for the context without throwing SSR errors or causing infinite re-renders. 
 Input Validation for Autonomous Agent Calls : When an AI agent executes tool calls, it can occasionally pass unexpected string formats or out-of-range floats. I implemented runtime input sanitization to clamp numerical values (like speed caps and truck ratios) and normalize weather strings before passing them into the UI state machine. 
 Real-Time Visual State Sync : Making the vector radar map dynamically pulse red, spike the risk gauge to 99%, and display active geofenced warning banners—all within milliseconds of an agent tool call—required keeping local UI state tightly coupled to the tool execution callbacks. 
 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 
 True In-Browser Agency : Proved that WebMCP can eliminate screen-scraping entirely. Tool execution happens sub-15ms directly in browser memory. 
 Clean Fallback Architecture : Built a system that gracefully degrades: if native WebMCP is detected, it registers to the browser agent; if not, the interactive UI harness lets any user test the full lifecycle manually. 
 Full Open-Source Compliance : Delivered a clean, production-built repository with complete TypeScript typing, strict zero-error builds, and an MIT license visible at the root. 
 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP represents a massive shift in how web applications should be architected. Instead of treating a web page as a purely visual surface meant only for human eyes, we can now design applications as shared state machines. The human sees an intuitive visual interface, while the AI agent interacts with typed, deterministic tools on the exact same page. 

 What's next for DispatchGuard WebMCP 

 A command deck in a browser is only the first step. To physically eliminate fatal head-on collisions on two-lane mountain corridors, the system must bridge the gap between software dispatch and real-time physical intervention on the asphalt: 

 
 Sub-100ms Peer-to-Peer Overtake Clearance (Vehicle-to-Vehicle): 
Developing a decentralized WebMCP toolset that operates over local ad-hoc Wi-Fi / DSRC networks without cellular internet. When a driver signals an overtake behind a freight truck, the agent automatically interrogates the forward oncoming corridor and issues an immediate, non-negotiable "ABORT OVERTAKE" interlock if the time-to-collision window is under 6 seconds. 
 Solar Edge Nodes for Mountain Blackspots: 
Partnering with roadside monitoring hardware (solar-powered radar/optical cameras on blind S-bends) to run local WebMCP micro-agents at the curve itself, beaming real-time corridor sightline obstructions directly to approaching vehicles and regional dispatch. 
 Offline Edge PWA for Drivers and Remote Outposts: 
Packaging DispatchGuard into an ultra-lightweight, offline-first Progressive Web App (PWA) with client-side WebAssembly models, ensuring crash prediction algorithms function with zero latency in rural mountain valleys where cellular reception completely drops. 
 Field Piloting on High-Risk African Transit Corridors: 
Collaborating with regional transport authorities, long-haul trucking cooperatives, and highway safety bureaus to pilot the early warning telemetry layer on notorious high-casualty mountain passes and freight corridors.

title: AgentGate
pitch: A human approval gate for AI agents, built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A human approval gate for AI agents, built on WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Theme fit 

 AgentGate directly uses the WebMCP API — document.modelContext.registerTool() , getTools() , and executeTool() — to register three real WebMCP tools ( propose_action , check_approval , list_pending ) that any WebMCP-aware AI agent can discover and call on this page. It solves a real, open problem in the WebMCP spec itself: there is currently no built-in way for a page to require human confirmation before an agent's tool call takes effect (see webmachinelearning/webmcp#165 and #50 ). AgentGate is a working, application-level answer to that gap. 

 Inspiration 

 WebMCP lets a website expose real, callable functions to AI agents — a huge step up from agents having to fake being a human clicking through a UI. But that power cuts both ways: the moment an agent calls a tool, it runs, instantly, with nothing built into WebMCP to pause and ask a human first. The spec's own maintainers have this flagged as unresolved. We wanted to build the missing piece rather than just another demo of the happy path. 

 What it does 

 AgentGate gives a site a safe way to expose sensitive actions to agents. Instead of wiring a tool directly to something real (delete a file, send a message, spend money), the site registers propose_action . Calling it doesn't do the real thing — it queues a request and shows it in a live approval inbox for a human to review. A human approves or rejects, optionally with a note. The agent calls check_approval with the proposal id to find out what happened, and only proceeds with the actual action once it sees "approved" . 

 How we built it 

 React + Vite front end. document.modelContext.registerTool() registers the three tools directly against the real WebMCP API — no framework or SDK wrapping it, just the native browser API as documented. State (proposals, their status, notes) lives in a small observable store backed by localStorage , so the approval history survives a reload. No backend — the whole mechanism works client-side, which is enough to prove the pattern end-to-end. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is genuinely experimental — getting a real document.modelContext in an unmodified browser required registering for Chrome's WebMCP Origin Trial and embedding a token scoped to our exact origin. Once we had a real API to test against (not a mock), we also found the actual behavior differs from a naive reading of the docs — getTools() and registerTool() are both asynchronous (return Promises), and executeTool() takes the tool object itself plus a JSON-string of arguments, not a tool name and a plain object. We also hit a real bug this way: React's StrictMode double-invokes effects in development, and since the real API has no unregisterTool , that caused duplicate-registration errors — fixed with an idempotency guard. 

 Accomplishments we're proud of 

 Getting this working against the actual WebMCP implementation, not a simulated one — calling propose_action through the real document.modelContext , approving it as a human in the UI, and watching check_approval reflect that back correctly. 

 What we learned 

 That an open spec with unresolved design questions is fertile ground for a real contribution, not just a demo — and that testing against the real API (even a gated, experimental one) surfaces mismatches with the documentation that no amount of reading catches. 

 What's next 

 A cancellation path using AbortSignal (the spec supports it for in-flight tool calls), and richer proposal types (e.g. structured diffs for code-change proposals) so a human reviewer has more context before approving.

 This will eventually be implemented into the full Attendly product. The stories are in the backlog, but it's a big backlog.

 I was inspired by the amount of good food that can go to waste while community kitchens and shelters still need meals. I wanted to explore how an AI agent could help with this work without making decisions by itself. 

 ReliefMesh is a food-rescue coordination demo. It shows food offers, partner needs, meal quantities, dietary fit, and pickup windows. An agent can inspect this information and suggest a rescue plan. The plan is shown clearly in the app before approval. A person must review it and give the exact ``confirmation before the app records approval. 

 I build this app with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses WebMCP through document.modelContext.registerTool to register five tools: inspecting rescue context, proposing a plan, staging an allocation, approving an allocation, and generating a pickup manifest. I deployed the project on ChatGPT sites and added the headers needed for WebMCP. 

 The main challenge was making the AI useful without giving it too much control. I separated planning from approval so that the agent can suggest and stage a plan but cannot make a commitment on its own. Another challenge was testing WebMCP in a supported browser. I also checked that document.modelContext was available and that all five tools were registered before recording the demo. 

 The project successfully registers five WebMCP tools in a supported browser. I am proud of the safety design: the plan is visible before approval, the confirmation must be explicit, and the demo never sends a real-world dispatch or notification. 

 I learned that a tool should say exactly what it can do and what information it uses. Also, that's how browser permissions, isolation headers, and structured tool inputs affect WebMCP. The biggest lesson was that human approval is not a limitation; it is an important part of a safe workflow.
