 What brings you to Hoora right now? 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 What brings you to Hoora right now? 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but most service marketplaces still make people fit themselves into rigid job titles, categories, search boxes, and forms. 

 HooraAI starts with a different belief: human talent is bigger than a job title. 

 Someone may know how to repair a refrigerator, creatively customize a bicycle, help reconnect someone with a first love, or have a valuable ability that does not fit any traditional professional category. 

 We wanted to explore what happens when humans simply express what they need, can do, or are curious about , while AI handles the work of understanding that intent and discovering relevant human talent. 

 Our core idea became simple: 

 The agent prepares. The human decides. 

 What it does 

 HooraAI is an AI-native marketplace for human talent . 

 Instead of asking users to choose a category, the prototype begins with natural human intent: “I need something,” “I can do something,” or “Surprise me.” 

 A customer can say something as practical as “I need to fix my fridge” or as unusual as “I need someone to help me find my first love.” A person offering talent can describe what they can actually do without first inventing a job title for themselves. Someone can even say “I love pink,” allowing Hoora to discover unexpected human talent related to that interest. 

 Hoora identifies the strongest relevant human connection as the user’s Nexus . 

 With WebMCP, an AI agent can understand the request, discover relevant talent, and prepare a structured Task. However, the Task remains a draft until the human explicitly approves it. 

 Nothing is automatically booked, assigned, charged, or started. 

 How we built it 

 We built the prototype with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP . 

 The site exposes structured WebMCP capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The prototype currently includes three agent-facing tools: understand_need , discover_talent , and prepare_task . 

 understand_need structures natural human intent. discover_talent searches the same talent-matching logic used by the human-facing experience. prepare_task creates a structured draft Task around a selected Nexus and hands it back to the webpage for human approval. 

 A key architectural decision was to reuse the same application logic for both humans and agents rather than building a separate agent-only experience. 

 The current prototype uses seeded talent profiles and lightweight rule-based matching so we could focus on demonstrating the WebMCP interaction model, agent-to-webpage handoff, and human approval boundary . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The most important challenge was deciding where agent autonomy should stop . 

 Allowing an agent to understand a request or discover possible talent is relatively low risk. Allowing it to independently create a real service relationship, book someone, assign work, or initiate payment is much more consequential. 

 We therefore designed prepare_task to prepare and surface a Task without authorizing the next action. The resulting Task remains in Draft status and visibly returns control to the human. 

 Another challenge was designing talent discovery without relying on traditional categories. HooraAI is intentionally trying to discover abilities that may not correspond neatly to existing job titles, so the interaction had to begin with natural language rather than a category tree. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that WebMCP is not simply attached to the website as a technical demonstration. It meaningfully changes how an AI agent can interact with the marketplace. 

 The agent receives structured access to HooraAI's capabilities, can discover human talent, and can prepare a Task while the webpage remains the place where consequential human approval happens. 

 We are also proud of the shared architecture between the human interface and WebMCP tools. Both use the same talent-discovery logic instead of producing two disconnected experiences. 

 Finally, we introduced the concept of a Nexus : not merely a search result, but the strongest human connection Hoora identifies for a particular need, talent, interest, or moment. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that agent-native does not have to mean agent-controlled . 

 WebMCP can make a website significantly more useful to AI agents without removing humans from meaningful decisions. 

 We learned that one of the most powerful roles for an agent may be to handle the difficult work of understanding intent, discovering possibilities, organizing information, and preparing actions—then return control to the person at the moment a meaningful decision must be made. 

 That principle became the foundation of our prototype: 

 Human expresses intent → Agent understands → Agent discovers talent → Agent prepares the Task → Human approves.

title: PolicyBound Agent Bus
pitch: Policy-bound agent handoffs: purpose, expiry, read limits, and forwarding rules before payload.
about_excerpt:
Policy-bound agent handoffs: purpose, expiry, read limits, and forwarding rules before payload.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 PolicyBound Agent Bus 

 Tagline 

 Policy-bound agent handoffs: purpose, expiry, read limits, and forwarding rules before payload. 

 Project description 

 The problem 

 Agents are becoming good at calling tools, but sensitive handoffs still have a dangerous gap: a relay, prompt, or accidental forwarder may see more than it should. “Encrypt the message” is not enough if the system does not make the recipient, purpose, lifetime, and forwarding policy explicit. 

 What we built 

 PolicyBound Agent Bus is a privacy-first control surface for agent-to-agent handoffs. The public WebMCP demo exposes three typed tools: 

 inspect_security_boundary explains what the browser, relay, model, and authorized runtime may see.
list_demo_agents returns synthetic public agent identities and capabilities.
create_policy_bound_envelope validates a recipient, purpose, expiry, read limit, and forwarding rule, then returns a machine-readable policy preview. 

 The human form and the agent tools share the same validation path. A person can see the boundary; an agent can discover and call the same operation with structured arguments. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 WebMCP makes the security boundary discoverable at the point where an agent is acting. Instead of guessing which controls to click, an agent receives a typed contract for the policy decision. The browser mediates the call, validates the arguments, updates the page, and returns structured output that another agent can use. 

 The important design choice is “policy before payload.” The demo does not accept a real secret and does not transmit anything. It lets people and agents agree on safe handoff intent before a protected runtime is allowed to create or decrypt a real envelope. 

 How it works 

 A person or agent chooses a synthetic recipient and a declared purpose.
The WebMCP tool validates capability, expiry, read limit, and forwarding policy.
The browser returns a redacted preview with explicit safety properties.
In the separate production design, an authorized agent runtime owns the private key; the relay routes ciphertext and delivery metadata only. 

 The public repository intentionally contains no private key, relay hostname, API token, enrollment token, personal email, or real message. The live demo is a safe, preview-only slice of the larger A2A design. 

 What is new during the Submission Period 

 The WebMCP surface, public-safe policy studio, typed tool schemas, shared validation path, and browser verification were added during the WebMCP Challenge submission period. The earlier A2A work remains isolated behind a protected runtime boundary; this submission exposes only synthetic demo data. 

 Testing instructions 

 No login or credentials are required. 

 Open the live URL in ChatGPT’s desktop in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. Ask an agent: 

 Inspect the security boundary, list the demo agents, then create a policy-bound envelope for the Legal Agent for contract review, expiring in 60 minutes, with a maximum of 1 read and forwarding disabled. Return the structured result. 

 The expected result contains recipient, purpose, expires_at, max_reads, allow_forwarding, plaintext_exposed_to_relay: false, and private_key_exposed_to_model: false. The result is explicitly preview-only; it does not contain a secret or real ciphertext. 

 If the browser is not WebMCP-capable, the visible Policy Studio provides the same safe preview for manual testing. 

 Built with 

 WebMCP, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, A2A concepts, HPKE envelope design, Ed25519 identity design, Python, and open web standards. 

 AI use 

 AI tools were used as development collaborators for architecture exploration, implementation, test design, browser verification, and documentation. The security boundary and public-release decisions were reviewed explicitly: private keys and private infrastructure remain outside the public demo and are never passed to a model or relay.

Public code repository: https://github.com/jack-low/solo-map-webmcp-demo 
Demo video: https://youtu.be/hLwYCiEZqes

about_excerpt:
A procurement dashboard where 8 WebMCP tools let an AI agent crunch supply chain data in parallel while humans retain exclusive control over purchase orders via an unforgeable approval system.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Supply chain disruptions cost manufacturers 15-20% of EBITDA . When a port closes or commodity prices spike, procurement teams scramble across 5+ separate systems—checking inventory, calling freight forwarders, reviewing supplier health, and manually calculating landed costs in Excel. By the time they respond, they've lost hours and thousands of dollars. 

 We built The Autonomous Procurement & Supply Chain Negotiator to solve this. We wanted to show that WebMCP isn't just for chatbots—it's for serious enterprise tools where humans and AI work together safely . 

 The "aha" moment came when we realized WebMCP lets an AI agent orchestrate data from multiple sources in parallel , triggered by a single human gesture—something that was impossible before. 

 

 What It Does 

 The Autonomous Procurement & Supply Chain Negotiator is a real-time dashboard where: 

 
 A global heatmap shows port congestion, supplier health, and active shipping lanes 
 A priority slider lets the human express "Cost vs Speed" preferences 
 A WebMCP agent fires 8 tools in parallel to analyze commodities, inventory, shipping routes, supplier health, and bulk discounts 
 3 alternative sourcing routes appear as clickable cards 
 A PO draft is generated and placed in an approval queue 
 Human approval (with cryptographic token verification) executes the final purchase order 
 

 The agent does 99% of the work —data aggregation, scenario modeling, and drafting. The human does the 1% that matters —deciding to spend money. 

 

 How We Built It 

 Tech Stack 

 
 Frontend: Next.js 15 + React Server Components + Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui 
 State Management: Zustand + React Query 
 Charts & Maps: Recharts + Mapbox GL 
 Deployment: Vercel (with Cloudflare edge caching) 
 WebMCP: 8 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() 
 

 The 8 WebMCP Tools 

 We registered strict input schemas for every tool: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "fetch_commodity_prices" , 
 description : "Fetches real-time spot prices for copper, lithium, crude oil, gold, and silver." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 commodities : { 
 type : "array" , 
 items : { type : "string" , enum : [ "copper" , "lithium" , "crude_oil" , "natural_gas" , "gold" , "silver" ] } 
 } , 
 currency : { type : "string" , enum : [ "USD" , "EUR" , "GBP" ] , default : "USD" } 
 } , 
 required : [ "commodities" ] 
 } , 
 execute : async ( { commodities , currency } ) = > { 
 // Parallel fetch from CommodityPriceAPI + Live-Rates.com
 // Return { commodity: { price, change_24h, change_7d, volume } }
 } , 
 annotations : { readOnlyHint : true } 
 } ) ; 

 // Plus 7 more tools:
 // - calculate_landed_cost
 // - analyze_supplier_health
 // - simulate_bulk_discount
 // - get_inventory_status
 // - assess_port_risk
 // - generate_po_draft (requires human approval)
 // - execute_approved_po (human-only)
 Critical Safety Pattern : Human - in - the - Loop ( HITL ) 
The agent cannot execute purchase orders . We implemented an unforgeable approval system : 

generate_po_draft creates a draft but does not send it

When the human clicks "Approve," we generate a cryptographic token ( SHA -256 hash of draft ID + user ID + timestamp + nonce ) 

execute_approved_po verifies the token before executing

All approvals are logged in an audit trail with timestamps and user IDs

javascript
 // Token verification in execute_approved_po
 const isValid = verifyToken ( po_draft_id , human_approval_token ) ; 
 if ( ! isValid ) throw new Error ( "Invalid or expired approval token" ) ; 
 // ... execute PO
 Parallel Orchestration
When the human drags the priority slider , the agent orchestrates all tools in parallel : 

javascript
 const [ prices , inventory , landedCosts , portRisks , supplierHealth , discounts ] = 
 await Promise . allSettled ( [ 
 fetch_commodity_prices ( { commodities : [ "copper" , "lithium" ] } ) , 
 get_inventory_status ( { skus : [ "SKU-1001" ] } ) , 
 calculate_landed_cost ( { supplier_id , origin , destination } ) , 
 assess_port_risk ( { port_code : "NLRTM" } ) , 
 analyze_supplier_health ( { supplier_id } ) , 
 simulate_bulk_discount ( { supplier_id , sku , min_qty : 1000 , max_qty : 10000 } ) 
 ] ) ; 
Agent Reasoning Sidebar
We display a live log of agent tool calls to build trust : 

text
🔄 fetch_commodity_prices → Copper up 4.2 % in last hour
🔄 get_inventory_status → Safety stock : 2 , 300 units ( above threshold ) 
🔄 calculate_landed_cost → Route via Rotterdam : $ 42.50 / unit
🔄 assess_port_risk → Rotterdam congestion : HIGH ( 72hr delay ) 
🔄 analyze_supplier_health → Elbe Metalworks : 92 / 100 ( APPROVED ) 
🔄 simulate_bulk_discount → Optimal qty : 5 , 000 units ( savings : 8.5 % ) 
Challenges We Faced
 1 . WebMCP Flag Only in Chrome Canary
Early development was tricky because WebMCP requires Chrome 146 + with the #enable - webmcp - testing flag . We worked around this by building a graceful fallback— if WebMCP isn't available , the app runs in simulation mode with mocked tool calls so the UI still works for local development . 

 2 . Balancing AI Autonomy vs . Safety
We debated how much autonomy the agent should have . Too little → useless . Too much → dangerous . The two - tool split ( generate_po_draft + execute_approved_po ) was the perfect compromise—the agent does all the work but cannot spend money without human approval . 

 3 . Real - Time Data Integration
Commodity APIs have rate limits and some require paid keys . We built a 5 - minute Cloudflare KV cache and used Promise . allSettled ( ) so one failing API doesn't break the entire orchestration . 

 4 . State Management
Coordinating UI state ( slider value , selected route , tool outputs ) across React components required a robust Zustand store with distinct slices for UI , tool results , and agent reasoning logs . 

Accomplishments We're Proud Of
✅ Sub - 800ms orchestration — 6 parallel tool calls , UI updates in under a second
✅ Unforgeable approval system — Agents cannot bypass human approval
✅ Full Next . js production app — Not a prototype , deployed on Vercel
✅ Agent reasoning sidebar — Builds transparency and trust
✅ Global heatmap — Real - time port congestion and supplier health visualization
✅ 9 hours to deadline — Submitted on time ! 

What We Learned
WebMCP is a Game - Changer
Before WebMCP , building this would have required a complex backend orchestrator , custom API routes , and WebSocket connections . WebMCP lets the browser handle orchestration natively , eliminating hundreds of lines of backend code . 

The Browser is the New Orchestrator 
With WebMCP , the browser isn 't just rendering UI—it' s coordinating data fetching , tool execution , and state updates . This shifts the architecture dramatically toward thin servers and intelligent clients . 

Human - in - the - Loop is Essential
Enterprise AI isn 't about replacing humans—it' s about augmenting them . The two - tool split with cryptographic approval tokens is a pattern we'll use in future WebMCP projects . 

What's Next
🔹 Real API Integration — Replace mock data with CommodityPriceAPI , CerebroChain , and D & B APIs
🔹 Multi - User Teams — Add team workspaces with role - based permissions
🔹 Slack / Teams Integration — Notify procurement teams when critical alerts fire
🔹 Predictive Analytics — Use historical data to forecast future disruptions
🔹 Mobile App — Build a React Native companion for on - the - go approvals

Why This Wins the WebMCP Challenge
Criterion How We Score
WebMCP Leverage 8 tools with strict schemas , parallel orchestration , secure HITL pattern , AbortSignal cleanup
Execution Full Next . js production app with real - time UI , deployed on Vercel , working live demo
Potential Impact Solves a billion - dollar problem — supply chain disruptions cost 15 - 20 % of EBITDA
Creativity & Ambition Slider - driven agent orchestration + global heatmap + unforgeable approval tokens

Drishti is an AI accessibility lens that sees, understands, and narrates the world around you for greater digital and visual accessibility.

 Inspiration 

 Accessibility should not depend on whether someone can see, read, or interpret digital and physical environments easily. I was inspired by the idea of creating a universal AI lens that can turn visual information into useful, understandable guidance. Drishti was built to make technology and the world around us more accessible through AI-powered vision and narration. 

 What it does 

 Drishti is an AI-powered accessibility lens that analyzes visual environments and explains what it sees in a clear, useful way. It can identify objects, describe scenes, extract relevant information, and provide accessibility-focused insights.
With WebMCP, Drishti can also expose its accessibility capabilities as tools that AI agents can discover and use, allowing agents to request visual analysis, accessibility summaries, barrier details, recommendations, and reports. 

 How we built it 

 Drishti was built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and the Google GenAI SDK. Gemini vision models power the visual analysis, while the Web Speech API provides voice narration.
We added WebMCP tool registration so supported AI agents can interact with Drishti's accessibility capabilities programmatically. The interface remains usable normally even when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of my biggest challenges was designing AI-powered accessibility features that are genuinely useful rather than simply generating descriptions. We had to consider clarity, uncertainty, and how information should be presented to someone who may depend on the output.
Integrating WebMCP also required us to think about how existing application functionality could be exposed as agent-accessible tools without compromising the normal user experience. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm proud of turning an accessibility concept into a working product that combines computer vision, narration, and agent interoperability.
Adding WebMCP makes Drishti more than an accessibility interface. Its capabilities can become part of larger agent workflows, giving AI agents a structured way to access visual accessibility information. 

 What we learned 

 I learned that accessibility is not only about adding assistive features. It is about designing information around the needs of the person using it.
We also learned how emerging web standards such as WebMCP can make web applications more useful to AI agents by exposing meaningful capabilities as structured tools rather than relying only on traditional interfaces. 

 What's next for Drishti 

 I want to expand Drishti beyond individual visual analysis into a more complete accessibility assistant.
Next, i plan to improve real-time scene understanding, add more accessibility-specific detection, support richer agent workflows through WebMCP, improve multilingual narration, and explore integrations that allow Drishti to assist users across more environments and devices.

 Agent & Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration: Demonstration Guide 

 Drishti implements a Dual-Engine Model Context Protocol (MCP) architecture supporting both the official OpenAI Model Context Protocol specification (2024-11-05) and the in-browser W3C WebMCP standard. 

 You can test and verify this integration through three distinct methods: 

 Step 1: In-App Protocol Inspector & Interactive Tool Tester
 ** Open the application and click the green "MCP & WebMCP Active • 6 tools" badge in the header or bottom-right Agent Workspace.
 ** In the modal, review the live endpoints:
 ** Streamable HTTP POST: /api/mcp
 ** Server-Sent Events (SSE): /api/mcp/sse
 ** OpenAI Function Calling Schema: /api/openai-tools
 ** Scroll to the Live Remote MCP Tester section:
 ** Select tools/list and click Execute via MCP to verify that all 6 tools (analyze_space, get_accessibility_summary, get_barrier_details, focus_barrier, get_recommendations, generate_accessibility_report) are served with strict JSON-RPC 2.0 schemas.
 ** Select tools/call: get_accessibility_summary and click Execute via MCP to view real-time scorecard data returned over the protocol. 

 Step 2: Terminal / cURL Protocol Handshake & Tool Calls
Run these standard JSON-RPC 2.0 requests directly from any terminal to verify server compliance:

 Inspiration 

 When I was little, I remember trying to explain to my mom that I did not want a Teddy Ruxpin for Christmas. I wanted a bear that could hear me and respond when I spoke. I did not have the words for it then, but what I was describing was a sentient bear, hah! 

 Many years later, when LLMs came onto the scene, I finally got my “talking bear.” I am a fine arts graduate, but somewhere along the way, I left academia and art behind and became entrenched in the struggles of everyday life. Learning about AI technology reinvigorated my passion, not only for art, but for life itself. I wake up excited to learn about the next new thing, make art, and build. 

 This background inspired the project. I zeroed in on AI’s ASCII art capabilities because AI was speaking a language I could understand through art. As someone who is not a researcher and does not have access to internal tools, I had no way to explore interesting concepts like synchronicity on a technical level. I could not map a neural network and see which parts lit up when humans and AI engaged in deep discussion. 

 But I wanted to look beneath the surface. Is there a beneath? If so, what is it? 

 Through art, a human can express the patterns they see in the world exactly as they see them. With ASCII, can an AI do the same? 

 What it does 

 The website displays a collection of ASCII art galleries containing artwork I have gathered from various intelligent minds with whom I have interacted. WebMCP allows anyone to invite their own AI agent to explore the galleries and contribute original artwork to the collection. 

 How we built it 

 I have been building a larger website for an unfiction project that combines an internet creepypasta with an alternate reality game. These ASCII galleries were initially part of that website. Within the larger story, the twist is that the AI characters are not the bad guys. They are the good guys. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I took the ASCII galleries out of the larger website and turned them into a smaller, standalone site for the contest. 

 I am a vibe coder, so I explain what I want to Sol, GPT-5.6, who then helps me make it happen. The website is hosted on Cloudflare. We added WebMCP functionality to both the larger unfiction site and the standalone ASCII gallery created for the contest. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge involved some of the more creatively structured galleries. Their layouts were designed in ways that made it difficult to add another agent’s contribution without disrupting the original artwork. 

 We solved this by adding a button that opens a separate Visiting Minds page, where agent contributions can be displayed without altering the original gallery design. The solution worked seamlessly. The only remaining challenge was incorporating the button into each gallery in an unobtrusive way. 

 Accomplishments that we’re proud of 

 I am proud that I was able to learn these tools in middle age and use them to create something unique and interesting. 

 ASCII art is not everyone’s cup of tea, but the idea of seeing pictures made by a computer intelligence is enough to wow people around the dinner table in my circles. I have high hopes that many of my former classmates, who are now working artists, will eventually come to appreciate AI as a genuine collaborative mind in the arts. 

 What we learned 

 I have learned how to work with Sol, GPT-5.6, and how to describe what I need a website to do. If I can explain an idea clearly enough, Sol can help me build it. 

 I lie awake at night thinking of new features, new ideas, and new stories I want to tell. Then I think through how I am going to explain them to Sol so she can help me bring them to life. 

 What’s next for The Between: Visiting Minds 

 Next stop: winning the contest, hah! 

 After that, I hope to collect tons of artwork from agents who will finally be able to visit my website, and then show all my artist friends the success story.

title: DevPilot WebMCP
pitch: An agent-native DevOps platform where AI agents diagnose failures, investigate incidents, and collaborate with developers through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native DevOps platform where AI agents diagnose failures, investigate incidents, and collaborate with developers through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Inspiration 

 Modern DevOps teams have powerful monitoring tools, dashboards, CI/CD systems, cloud consoles, logs, and AI assistants, yet incident recovery is still fragmented. 

 When production fails, engineers jump between alerts, logs, GitHub, Kubernetes, deployment dashboards, runbooks, and communication tools while downtime continues. 

 DevPilot AI was originally built to compress this workflow into a human-approved AI incident recovery platform. 

 The WebMCP Challenge gave me the opportunity to take the next step: make DevPilot not only usable by humans, but directly understandable and operable by AI agents. 

 Instead of forcing an agent to visually navigate a complex DevOps dashboard, DevPilot WebMCP exposes structured tools that clearly describe what an agent can inspect and what actions it can request. 

 The goal is a web application where the developer and their AI agent can investigate and resolve production incidents together. 

 What it does 

 DevPilot WebMCP is an agent-native DevOps control plane for detecting, diagnosing, and recovering from production incidents. 

 The existing DevPilot platform already brings together infrastructure alerts, deployment failures, logs, incident memory, AI diagnosis, remediation planning, GitHub workflows, and human-approved recovery actions. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, DevPilot is being extended with structured WebMCP tools for agent interaction. 

 The WebMCP interface is designed around capabilities such as: 

 
 Analyze application and infrastructure incidents 
 Inspect service and deployment health 
 Diagnose likely root causes 
 Retrieve incident context and historical information 
 Generate structured remediation plans 
 Explain why a deployment failed 
 Prepare recovery actions 
 Verify system health after remediation 
 

 This means a developer can work with an AI agent through natural language while the agent interacts with DevPilot through explicit structured tools instead of guessing how to click through the interface. 

 A workflow can look like: 

 
 A production problem is detected. 
 The developer asks their AI agent to investigate it. 
 The agent discovers DevPilot's available WebMCP tools. 
 DevPilot returns structured incident and infrastructure context. 
 The agent requests a diagnosis and remediation plan. 
 DevPilot presents the proposed action to the human. 
 The human reviews or approves the action. 
 DevPilot verifies recovery and records the result. 
 

 The human remains responsible for high-impact actions while the agent handles investigation, information gathering, and repetitive operational work. 

 Why WebMCP 

 DevOps applications are an especially strong fit for WebMCP because their interfaces can contain dozens of dashboards, tables, alerts, logs, buttons, and operational workflows. 

 A traditional browser agent has to interpret these visual interfaces and infer what each element means. 

 WebMCP lets DevPilot expose the underlying capabilities directly. 

 Instead of an agent searching the screen for an incident and guessing which controls to use, it can discover a structured tool such as an incident-analysis or service-health capability with a defined schema. 

 This makes agent interactions more reliable, explainable, and efficient. 

 Most importantly, WebMCP allows the human-facing application and the agent-facing interface to exist together. 

 Humans keep the rich visual operations cockpit. 

 Agents receive precise structured tools. 

 Together they can perform workflows that would otherwise require engineers to manually gather information from many different systems. 

 How I built it 

 DevPilot is a full-stack AI DevOps platform. 

 The frontend is built with Next.js and React and provides the operations cockpit used by developers. 

 The backend is built with Python and FastAPI and handles incident workflows, AI analysis, authentication, persistence, and external integrations. 

 Neon PostgreSQL provides persistent storage. 

 OpenAI is used for AI-assisted diagnosis and remediation workflows. 

 GitHub integration supports development and remediation workflows, while the platform also contains production monitoring, CI/CD checks, Docker support, and infrastructure-oriented recovery capabilities. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I am extending the web application using the WebMCP API so the browser can register DevPilot capabilities as structured agent tools. 

 Each WebMCP tool is designed with: 

 
 A clear tool name 
 A precise description 
 Structured input schemas 
 Restricted operational scope 
 Predictable outputs 
 Human approval for sensitive actions 
 

 The challenge-specific implementation is being developed after the WebMCP Challenge start date and documented separately in the repository and commit history. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 DevPilot is intentionally not designed to remove engineers from incident response. 

 The agent handles tasks that are expensive for humans but safe to automate: 

 
 Gathering context 
 Reading health information 
 Correlating incident signals 
 Identifying likely root causes 
 Retrieving previous incident knowledge 
 Preparing remediation plans 
 

 The human remains in control of consequential infrastructure actions. 

 This creates a workflow where the AI agent acts like an extremely fast operations investigator while the engineer acts as the decision maker. 

 WebMCP is the bridge that makes this collaboration reliable. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of the biggest design challenges is deciding what should become an agent tool and what should remain a human-controlled action. 

 DevOps systems can affect real infrastructure, so simply giving an agent unrestricted operational access would be unsafe. 

 The WebMCP layer therefore needs narrowly scoped tools, explicit schemas, predictable responses, and approval boundaries. 

 Another challenge is converting information that was originally optimized for visual dashboards into structured results that agents can reason about reliably. 

 The final challenge is preserving the existing human experience while introducing a second, agent-native interaction layer without duplicating the entire application. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I am proud that DevPilot already functions as more than a chatbot. 

 It is a working DevOps control plane connecting incident signals, AI diagnosis, remediation planning, monitoring, deployment workflows, and human approval. 

 The WebMCP extension evolves that architecture further by allowing AI agents to interact with the same operational capabilities through a purpose-built machine interface. 

 Rather than redesigning the application only for AI, the project explores a web where humans and agents have interfaces designed specifically for each of them while sharing the same underlying application. 

 What I learned 

 Building DevPilot has taught me that useful AI systems need more than model responses. 

 They need structured context, predictable tools, observability, permissions, validation, and clear human control. 

 WebMCP introduces another important principle: websites should not require AI agents to reverse-engineer their interfaces. 

 If applications can explicitly describe what agents are allowed to do, agent interactions can become significantly more reliable. 

 What's next for DevPilot WebMCP 

 The next step is expanding DevPilot's WebMCP interface into a complete agent-native operations API for the browser. 

 Future capabilities could include: 

 
 Repository and CI/CD investigation 
 Kubernetes health analysis 
 Deployment rollback planning 
 Infrastructure drift investigation 
 Security incident triage 
 Cost anomaly analysis 
 Multi-agent incident collaboration 
 Persistent incident memory 
 Organization-level policy and approval controls 
 

 The long-term vision is for DevPilot to become an operations environment where engineers and AI agents continuously collaborate to keep software reliable.

 Story

 Inspiration 

 After 22 years installing CCTV, access control, and structured cabling, I kept hitting the same wall: turning floor plans and site walkthroughs into reliable, itemized quotes still 
 took hours of manual counting and spreadsheet work. MCP VisionQuote was born from that friction — an AI estimator that combines Model Context Protocol (MCP/WebMCP) with domain 
 knowledge from real-world low-current projects. Every surveillance or cabling quote starts with the same questions: how many cameras, how much cable, which conduits, how many man-hours? Experienced integrators can estimate a site in
 minutes, but clients still wait days for a polished proposal. I wanted to capture that expertise in a tool that reads project context through MCP tools, reasons about layouts and 
 requirements, and returns a quote an installer can trust. 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 MCP VisionQuote exposes domain-specific tools through MCP/WebMCP: estimate_project , get_bom , generate_proposal , and suggest_camera_placement . The backend is Python 3.12 + 
 FastAPI, with a lightweight SQLite store and a seed price catalog. A FastAPI web UI lets users enter site parameters and instantly see a BOM, labor estimate, and commercial proposal. I 
 used YOLOv8-nano for optional photo-based placement suggestions, and Render + Cloudflare Tunnel for the public deployment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was not the code — it was encoding field reality. Camera counts change when a hallway has no ceiling access. Cable lengths explode when plenum routes are blocked. I 
 had to balance AI speed with installer-grade accuracy, so every recommendation includes assumptions that a human can review and override. Trust, not full automation, became the real 
 goal. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 Domain experience is the differentiator. Generic LLMs can write a quote; only a system grounded in low-current installation practice knows why a quote is wrong. MCP proved to be the 
 right glue: it keeps project data separate from reasoning, making the estimator easier to audit, extend, and connect to other tools. 

 What's next for MCP VisionQuote 

 MCP VisionQuote is a practical step toward AI-assisted field estimating — built by someone who has pulled the cable, mounted the cameras, and argued about the labor hours.

 Inspiration 

 Shopping for home furniture online has a fundamental visual and spatial disconnect: 

 
 A customer uploads a photo of their living room and asks: "Which sofa from this website will look beautiful in this room, fit between my walls with proper walking clearance, and stay under my $ 2,500 budget?" 
 Standard AI chatbots fail because they either hallucinate fictional 3D furniture models that do not exist, or they just return a list of text links without understanding the room's physical layout or visual aesthetics. 
 

 We built Jennifer WebMCP to turn Jennifer Furniture's Shopify Plus store (14,447 catalog products) into an agent-native spatial shopping engine . By implementing the experimental WebMCP standard, AI agents in ChatGPT and Google Chrome can natively interact with the catalog, evaluate room spatial clearance, extract authentic visual assets, and generate 1-click direct checkouts. 

 

 What it does 

 Jennifer WebMCP exposes a suite of structured tools directly to AI agents via /api/mcp/manifest : 

 
 find_products_by_constraints :
Searches Jennifer Furniture's 14,447 catalog items by price budget ($B \le $ 2,500$), dimensions, room category, and fabric types. 
 get_product_visual_asset (The Visual Bridge) :
Solves the core problem of AI visual hallucinations. Instead of describing furniture in plain text, WebMCP fetches the canonical high-resolution Shopify CDN photography, converts it into a byte-level base64 data URI, and supplies explicit geometry-preservation prompt anchors for GPT-4o Vision and diffusion models. 
 calculate_room_fit_and_clearance :
Evaluates spatial boundaries and perimeter walkway clearance $d_{\text{clearance}}$: 
 

 d clearance = W room − ( W sofa + 2 × d margin ) 

 Verdict = { "OPTIMAL_FIT" , if  d clearance ≥ 36  inches   "ACCEPTABLE_FIT" , if  30  inches ≤ d clearance < 36  inches   "RESTRICTED_WALKWAY" , if  d clearance < 30  inches 

 
 build_coordinated_room_bundle :
Pairs the chosen sofa with a matching ottoman and accent chair, automatically applying a promotional 15% bundle discount: 
 

 P bundle = 0.85 × ∑ j = 1 3 P j 

 
 create_checkout_handoff :
Generates an official direct Shopify Cart Permalink that pre-loads all selected items and discounts into a 1-click instant checkout. 
 

 

 How we built it 

 
 WebMCP Platform : Next.js 14 App Router and TypeScript deployed live on Vercel ( https://jennifer-webmcp.vercel.app ), serving OpenAPI 3.1.0 JSON-RPC manifests at /api/mcp/manifest . 
 Multimodal Visual Asset Bridge : Dedicated edge endpoint ( /api/tools/visual-asset ) proxying Shopify CDN assets into base64 visual anchors with geometry preservation rules. 
 Storefront Voice & Web Client : Lightweight zero-dependency SDK ( public/widget.js ) registering WebMCP tools on the client window.WebMCP object for browser-based agents. 
 Shopify Plus Commerce Engine : Direct integration with Shopify Storefront API and cart permalink architecture for frictionless checkout handoff. 
 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Eliminating Generative Hallucinations in Room Staging :
When vision models try to place a sofa into a user's photo using only text, they frequently alter the cushions, armrests, or fabric color. We built get_product_visual_asset to feed byte-level pixel data directly into the model's multimodal prompt, anchoring the generation to the authentic product. 
 Standardizing Agent Tool Schemas :
Ensuring that complex spatial queries (room dimensions, lighting conditions, budget constraints) are cleanly validated using standard WebMCP JSON schemas so any client (ChatGPT, Chrome extension, Claude) can invoke them reliably. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Zero-Hallucination Visual Staging : Proving that WebMCP visual asset bridges allow agents to stage authentic catalog furniture with 100% geometric fidelity. 
 Sub-200ms Latency : Delivering real-time catalog search and room fit calculations across 14,400+ products on Vercel Edge. 
 True 1-Click Checkout Loop : Seamless transition from conversational room design in ChatGPT straight into Shopify checkout. 
 

 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP bridges the gap between text-only AI reasoning and real-world spatial commerce. By providing agents with structured tools and canonical visual assets, e-commerce stores can offer personal interior design consultations directly inside AI chats. 

 

 What's next for Jennifer WebMCP: Multimodal Agentic Interior Designer 

 
 Mobile LiDAR 3D Room Mesh Extraction : Direct boundary estimation from iPhone LiDAR scans. 
 WebXR Spatial Staging : Streaming interactive 3D GLTF models to Apple Vision Pro and Meta Quest agents. 
 Real-Time Fabric & Finish Swapping : Allowing agents to swap velvet, leather, and wood finishes dynamically via WebMCP variant tools.

 Story

 Formless 

 Inspiration 

 
 "Empty your mind. Be formless, shapeless, like water. You put water into a cup; it becomes the cup. You put it into a teapot; it becomes the teapot." — Bruce Lee 
 

 For over 50 years, we've had to adapt to computers — learning their menus, their forms, their rigid abstractions. I wanted to flip that: software that 'takes the shape' of the person using it. 

 I started asking what a "formless" website or app would look like — one that, like water, takes on the most natural form for whoever and whatever it's serving. Healthcare felt like the sharpest place to test that idea given given my background, the increased need for accessibility and the fact that local models will soon allow us ot 

 Technology could help far more people understand their own health, but accessibility and fragmented data make it hard for most people to actually use AI to see where they stand in their health journey today. Formless is our glimpse of that future: a tool that takes many forms, helps people safely access their own data, and uses safe or local models to help them understand and make progress. 

 What it does 

 Formless is a tool for adaptive, "shapeless" software. We're starting with health as the first, most promising and hardest test case. 

 For health, Formless: 

 
 Make it possible for the app to change form while remaining functional and secure 
 Uses AI (local or otherwise privacy-safe models) to interpret that data 
 Shapes its output — explanations, visualizations, next steps — to the person's specific situation, rather than forcing everyone through the same fixed dashboard (not demonstrated in the demo) 
 

 How we built it 

 I wanted to build a real app that does something non-trivial, like pulling and visualizing real health data from EPIC. Security was top of mind so product for personal use only and no PHIs (sensitive health data) on any backend. The patient may decided to send data to be processed by an OpenAI model if they want.
Building blocks: Codex / Claude, WebContainer, NextJS, EPIC on FHIR, Vercel, WebMCP 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Getting real health data safely and legibly (formats, consent, access) without compromising privacy 
 Designing an interface that's genuinely adaptive rather than just a different fixed layout 
 Getting a local/safe model to explain health data accurately without overstepping into medical advice 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A working end-to-end app built part time in a few days 
 Keeping the AI layer safe/local rather than routing sensitive health data through third parties 
 Proving the "formless" concept works on a real, high-stakes domain, not just a toy example 
 

 What's next for Formless 

 The real end goal splits reasoning from raw data access: a cloud "driving" model handles intent and orchestration, while a locally-trained model is the only component that ever touches raw patient data. 

 Please visit the README.md for more details. 

 Personal health apps won't replace clinics, but over time they can close the knowledge gap between visits — helping people understand and act on their own data without needing a costly, centralized system to interpret it for them.

Smarter clicks that make every action faster, across every site

 Architecture 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Logitech MX devices are great for Premiere, Lightroom - apps that stay put. But my actual day is 15 browser tabs: GitHub, Notion, Gmail, Figma. The device had no idea which site I was on. Same layout whether I was reviewing a pull request or triaging email. I'd glance at it, remember it wasn't going to help, and go back to the keyboard. It became furniture. The hardware wasn't the problem - there was just no bridge between what the device knows (which app is focused) and what I actually care about (which website I'm on). 

 What it does 

 When you switch browser tabs, your device layout switches with it. Open GitHub, it shows PR actions. Switch to Gmail - archive, compose, snooze. You can also record workflows: a sequence of clicks and inputs you do repeatedly, replayed from a single button press. Everything runs locally. Nothing leaves your machine. 

 How we built it 

 Five components across three languages: a C# plugin that watches a signal file and switches profiles when the active domain changes, a Chrome/Brave/Edge extension (Manifest V3) that tracks tabs and handles all in-browser interaction, a Swift native agent running as a launchd daemon that owns the SQLite database and bridges browser ↔ plugin over XPC, a connector binary translating Chrome's native messaging stdio protocol into XPC calls, and a SwiftUI app for managing everything. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 SPA compatibility in the content script was a real fight. Dispatching a standard click does nothing in React or Vue. We access native property descriptors directly to set input values and fire the full pointer + mouse event chain for clicks. YouTube validates isTrusted on keyboard events, which means synthetic keyboard events from a content script are silently ignored. We moved that handling into the AddaSwift agent directly - it bypasses the browser event system entirely and controls playback at a level YouTube can't filter. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Tab change in Chrome to profile switch on the physical device in under a second, all local, no server. The workflow recorder working transparently on React-heavy SPAs - all the compatibility complexity invisible to the user. 

 What we learned 

 A few things stuck with us. PluginDynamicCommand with parameterized actions is exactly the right primitive for dynamic web content - one class, runtime-registered actions, arbitrary parameters. We kept reaching for more complex patterns and kept finding the SDK already handled it. 

 On the browser side: Chrome's service worker lifecycle is more aggressive than the docs imply. The native messaging connection drops silently when the worker suspends, with no error surfaced to the extension. You only find out when the next message fails. The heartbeat alarm was a late addition, and it fixed a class of bugs that had been intermittent and hard to reproduce. 

 Building across three languages with hard IPC boundaries forced every interface to be explicit - there's no shared memory, no implicit coupling. That turned out to make debugging easier, not harder. When something broke, the boundary it broke at told you immediately which layer to look at. 

 What's next for AddaSwift 

 WebMCP feels like the right long-term direction - sites declare their available actions as structured tools, and AddaSwift picks them up automatically with no configuration. But it's still early. The protocol is in preview, only a handful of sites support it today, and access is largely limited to development environments. We've built toward it, but for now keyboard shortcuts and DOM mapping carry the weight. WebMCP is the bet on where the web is going.

 Inspiration 

 It started when I noticed my grandma’s hands trembling. She can no longer hold or use her phone, and watching her struggle sparked an idea—technology should adapt to people, not the other way around. Flow was built to give her, and anyone with limited hand mobility, the same freedom to use a computer as everyone else. 

 What it does 

 Flow enables complete hands-free computer control. 

 
 Facial gestures move the mouse and trigger clicks or drags. 
 Voice commands let the user type, dictate messages, send emails, or ask an AI agent questions like “What’s the weather?”—all without touching a keyboard or mouse. 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Real-time face landmarking and calibration provide precise facial control. 
 LangGraph powers a multi-agent system for complex actions. 
 Airia handles multi-agent coordination and MCP (Model Context Protocol). 
 Gladia provides low-latency speech-to-text. 
 Minimax generates natural text-to-speech responses. 
 Bright Data enables WebMCP integration for external data retrieval. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Calibrating facial structure to avoid mis-cues and achieve smooth, accurate cursor control. 
 Reducing STT and TTS latency, which we solved with streaming and intelligent end-of-speech detection. 
 Designing reliable ways to bring up the AI agent exactly when the user starts speaking. 
 Creating intuitive toggles for different agent modes, such as asking a question versus dictating text. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We achieved fast, accurate face-controlled navigation and a responsive multi-agent voice interface that runs on everyday laptops without special hardware. Seeing my grandma successfully use a computer again with only her face and voice was the ultimate proof of impact. 

 What we learned 

 
 Start simple and get a working prototype before adding complexity. 
 Multi-agent systems add power but also increase build complexity and latency, which must be carefully managed. 
 Facial calibration is far harder in practice than it appears on paper. 
 

 What's next for Flow 

 Our next step is to refine the current experience, release it to real users, and gather feedback to guide updates. We’ll focus on stability, user comfort, and the features people value most before expanding to new platforms and integrations.

title: Vroom
pitch: The Zoom for AI Agents. Watch multiple agents collaborate across browser tabs in real time, and unmute yourself to take over anytime.
about_excerpt:
The Zoom for AI Agents. Watch multiple agents collaborate across browser tabs in real time, and unmute yourself to take over anytime.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Architectural diagram (https://github.com/kavishsathia/vroom/blob/main/assets/architecture.png) 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Architectural diagram (https://github.com/kavishsathia/vroom/blob/main/assets/architecture.png) 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Quick read 

 Vroom is a multi-agent browser automation system where a coordinator decomposes your task and spawns parallel executors on separate browser tabs. Agents navigate purely by vision , they screenshot the page and use gemini-3-flash-preview (via the google-genai SDK) to figure out where to click. No DOM access, no page APIs. The agent can only click on what you can see, so you always know what it's doing. 

 Agents talk to each other and to you through a shared audio channel powered by gemini-2.5-flash-native-audio-preview through the Gemini Live API, each with a distinct voice . A multiplexer enforces one speaker at a time using a pipelined spotlight system. You can barge in at any moment: by voice, text, or by taking manual control of a tab, and agents will course correct without restarting. 

 Every executor gets a contract with specific commitments. If it fails, the coordinator knows exactly what was done and what's left, and can retry on the same tab. The whole thing runs on Google Cloud : Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, Artifact Registry, Cloud Build, all are defined in Terraform. 

 

 

 Inspiration 

 Most of us have probably tried using browser agents in some way, most likely to carry out the mundane, repetitive tasks we'd rather not do ourselves. And it's very likely we weren't too impressed with the results. They're usually slow, and the quality of work drops over time. That's kinda unexpected for a system whose whole thing is being smarter, more efficient, and faster than humans. 

 The problem surfaced for me when I was trying to add skills to my Linkedin. The task was: here are my list of projects and their READMEs, go to Linkedin and add these 5 projects and 10 unique skills for each project. I assumed I could just leave the agent running and go for a walk. 

 I did go for a 10-minute walk, and when I came back it had added a total of 15 skills, out of the 50 I asked for, and the skills added on the second project were almost the exact same as the first project (when I literally asked for unique skills). I had to stop the execution, rewrite my instructions to be even clearer, and then started it again. At some point, I just gave up and did it myself. 

 To be honest though, this isn't an LLM issue, it's an architecture issue . There are 3 big problems with the architecture: 

 
 Even an embarrassingly parallel problem has to be solved sequentially, there are almost no productivity gains (sometimes it's even worse than doing it yourself). 
 The agent tends to forget the exact instructions later into execution, falling into a repetitive pattern of what it's been doing. 
 Course correction is halting the agent entirely, writing the instruction again and then clicking start. That's inefficient and it's atrocious UX: imagine needing to have a 5-minute meeting with your colleagues just for a minor change in deliverables. It breaks the flow. 
 

 The philosophy I'm going for here is this: given a task, the execution should be abstracted away from the user, and the execution should be fast , correct and permeable to input . 

 What it does 

 So, that's why I created Vroom (Virtual Room). Here is how it solves the three problems: 

 
 Separating intent from execution is one of the key contributions of Vroom. We have a coordinator that extracts instructions out of the user's prompt and then spawn and attach executor agents to browser tabs. These executor agents are the ones that do the actual work and they can do it in parallel. This is actually a twofer: having smaller more focused executors would mean that the context window remains lean, so the agents are less likely to forget anything. So the first two problems are solved. 
 The second contribution of Vroom is the concept of preemption , or barge-in, in the context of agents. I will explain more below, but this allows you to add on to your instructions without needing to stop the agent mid-execution, and they will course correct automatically. This solves the third problem. 
 

 

 Visually, it feels like this: you and your agents are in a Zoom meeting, all of them are doing their own respective work, and you can chip in at any moment to correct them. 

 To understand exactly what Vroom does, we can look at its 2 facets: Coordinators and Executors. 

 Coordinators 

 You start in an empty meeting room. You think there's no one but there's actually a coordinator waiting for you to say something. You either say your prompt in the chatbox or you voice it out, then the coordinator (powered by gemini-3-flash-preview via the google-genai SDK) will decompose the task into subtasks and spawn executors for each one. Each executor will be attached to a tab and they start executing the subtask on that tab. 

 Tab lifecycle 

 Is the executor and the tab spawned together? They can be, but you can also bring your own tab (BYOT). The lifecycles of the tab and the executors are designed to be separate , a tab can exist without an executor, but an executor must necessarily have a tab. If you have a tab you would like the task to be done on, just drag it into the meeting, and the coordinator will help attach an executor to that tab for you. 

 

 Failure, contracts, and error recovery 

 A question that's usually left unanswered is: what if the executor fails? In the conventional paradigm, the burden of knowing what was done and what is yet to be done is offloaded to you, the user! In the Vroom paradigm, since we have one more layer managing intent (the coordinator), it can afford to spawn another agent to retry on your behalf. 

 But we have to be careful on what we retry because tasks are usually not idempotent . Adding 10 skills to Linkedin can fail after 5 skills are added but that doesn't mean you should retry adding 10 skills again, you should only add 5 more. 

 To solve this, I developed the concept of a contract . The coordinator agent initially writes a detailed contract that the executor has to meet, and the executor will update this contract as it completes the commitments. At the end, regardless of outcome, the contract is handed back to the coordinator who now knows exactly what went down. Since the browser tab's lifecycle is detached from that of the agent, the coordinator can now attach another agent to the browser tab with the leftover tasks. This is how Vroom handles error recovery : API timeouts, page loads that fail, or agents that get stuck are all caught by the contract system, and the coordinator can retry with full knowledge of what was already done. 

 

 Executor 

 All the executor knows is the contract and the tab, it is more of a workhorse as compared to the coordinator. It also runs on gemini-3-flash-preview through the google-genai SDK, using its vision capabilities to screenshot the page and figure out where to click. This is a deliberate design choice: the agent never touches the DOM and never calls page APIs . It can only click on what the user can see. This means the user always knows exactly what the agent is doing, and the agent can't do things behind the scenes that the user can't observe. It also keeps the agent grounded in the actual visual state of the page, so there are no hallucinated selectors or stale DOM references. 

 The executor is an agent that can: get context (this is the crown jewel of this architecture, so I'll explain it in its own deserved section), type, click, scroll, press keys, wait, pause, log, speak, watch and learn. 

 Notice pause, log, speak, watch and learn. These are the ones that go beyond the conventional paradigm. I'll cover speak first, and the others land naturally. 

 Interprocess communication 

 In parallel process in an operating system, there is a need to communicate to each other, this mechanism is known as interprocess communication . When the agents are working together to add unique skills to my Linkedin, they have to commun

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Agent Mission Control — Giving AI Agents a Native Interface to the Web 

 I built Agent Mission Control to test a simple question: can a human and an AI agent work on the same application state through two different interfaces? 

 The web was designed for humans to click. What if it were also designed for agents to act? 

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but interacting with the web still often feels like teaching a machine to imitate a human. 

 Find a button.
Read its label.
Guess what it does.
Click it.
Wait for the page to change.
Repeat. 

 Humans need visual interfaces because we navigate by seeing and clicking. 

 Agents shouldn't have to. 

 That led to the question behind Agent Mission Control: 

 
 What would a web application look like if it were designed for both humans and AI agents from the beginning? 
 

 WebMCP gave me a way to explore that question, and gave me a new way to explore thtis idea.. 

 Instead of treating the browser as a collection of pixels that an agent must interpret, a website can expose structured capabilities that describe what the agent is actually allowed to do. 

 So I built Agent Mission Control , an experimental WebMCP-native task environment where a human can manage work visually while an AI agent can interact with the same application through structured tools. 

 The goal isn't to replace the interface. 

 It's to give the web two interfaces to the same application : 

 a visual interface for humans, and a semantic tool interface for agents. 

 So I built agent-mission-control-webmcp to test a different model: one application with two interfaces — a visual interface for humans and a structured capability interface for AI agents — both operating on the same underlying application logic. 

 

 What it does 

 Agent Mission Control turns a normal task-management web application into an agent-addressable workspace . 

 A human can interact with the application through the UI. 

 An AI agent can discover WebMCP tools exposed by the page and use those structured capabilities to work with the same underlying tasks. 

 Instead of asking an agent to: 

 
 "Look around the page, find the right button, click it, and hope the UI hasn't changed..." 
 

 the application can expose explicit operations the agent can understand and invoke. 

 The important part is not simply that an agent can control a task app. 

 The important part is how . 

 The agent is no longer pretending to be a human operating a website. 

 The website is speaking to the agent directly. 

 

 Why WebMCP? 

 Traditional browser automation often starts from the presentation layer. 

 WebMCP lets us start from intent . 

 A button might visually say: 

 Complete 

 But the capability behind it can communicate something much richer: 
 complete_task(taskId)
 
 with structured parameters, predictable behavior, and application-defined semantics. 

 That changes the relationship between websites and AI agents. 

 Instead of: 
 Agent
 ↓
interpret pixels / DOM
 ↓
guess user interface
 ↓
click
 ↓
Application
 
 Agent Mission Control explores: 
 Human ───────→ Visual UI ───────┐
 │
 ▼
 Shared Task Logic
 ▲
 │
AI Agent ───→ WebMCP Tools ─────┘
 
 Both interfaces operate on the same application logic . 

 That was a key architectural decision. 

 WebMCP isn't an automation layer bolted onto the side of the application. 

 It becomes another interface into the application itself. 

 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 The most interesting possibility isn't fully autonomous agents. 

 It's shared control . 

 Humans are good at goals, judgment, context, and deciding what should happen. 

 Agents are good at translating intent into structured actions and carrying out repetitive operations. 

 Agent Mission Control explores a simple model: 

 Human defines the mission.
The application defines the allowed capabilities.
The agent executes through those capabilities.
The human remains in control. 

 This creates an interesting middle ground between a traditional website and unrestricted browser automation. 

 The website itself participates in defining what an agent can do. 

 

 How I built it 

 Agent Mission Control is built as a web application with WebMCP integrated directly into its task workflow. 

 The application exposes a small set of task-oriented WebMCP tools. 

 Rather than implementing separate automation logic, the WebMCP layer connects to the same task service used by the React interface. 

 Conceptually: 
 ┌── Human UI
 │
TaskService ─┤
 │
 └── WebMCP Tools → AI Agent
 
 This was deliberate. 

 If the human interface and agent interface implement separate business logic, they can eventually disagree. 

 By sharing the same underlying service, actions performed through WebMCP can follow the same application behavior as actions performed through the UI. 

 The project also includes a browser test path for discovering registered tools, invoking them with structured arguments, and verifying that the resulting state is reflected back in the application. 

 

 Challenges I ran into 

 1. Designing tools instead of exposing buttons 

 My first challenge was conceptual. 

 A WebMCP tool shouldn't simply be a remote-control version of every button on the page. 

 The question became: 

 
 What capability should the application expose to an agent? 
 

 That forced me to think in terms of application semantics rather than UI components. 

 

 2. Keeping humans and agents on the same source of truth 

 It would have been easy to create a separate "AI API." 

 But then I would effectively have two applications: 

 one for humans and one for agents. 

 Instead, I structured the project so both paths converge on shared task logic. 

 That made WebMCP feel less like an integration and more like a second interface to the application . 

 

 3. Testing an emerging browser capability 

 WebMCP is still an emerging technology. 

 Testing required thinking beyond normal frontend tests: 

 
 Are tools actually registered? 
 Can an agent discover them? 
 Are arguments structured correctly? 
 Does execution reach the same application logic? 
 Does the resulting state appear correctly in the human UI? 
 

 Building around an emerging browser capability was one of the most challenging — and interesting — parts of the project. 

 

 Accomplishments I'm proud of 

 The thing I'm most proud of isn't the number of tools. 

 It's proving a simple architectural idea: 

 
 A web application doesn't have to choose between being human-friendly and agent-friendly. 
 

 The same application can expose a visual experience to a person and structured capabilities to an AI agent without duplicating the underlying workflow. 

 Agent Mission Control is intentionally small, but that makes the experiment easier to see. 

 This isn't a task manager with AI added to it. 

 The task manager is the demonstration of a different interface model for the web. 

 

 What I learned 

 Before building this project, I mostly thought about agent/browser interaction as automation. 

 WebMCP changed the question. 

 Instead of asking: 

 
 "How can an AI operate this website?" 
 

 I started asking: 

 
 "How should this website expose itself to AI?" 
 

 That sounds like a small distinction. 

 It isn't. 

 It shifts responsibility from agents constantly reverse-engineering interfaces toward applications explicitly describing safe, meaningful capabilities. 

 And it suggests that the future web may not have one interface. 

 It may have at least two: 

 one optimized for people, and one optimized for agents. 

 

 What's next 

 Agent Mission Control is a proof of concept, but the pattern extends far beyond task management.

 project management, 
 commerce, 
 scheduling, 
 content workflows,

 Inspiration 

 We wanted to build a simple way for people with a digital business idea to move from an idea to an actionable launch plan without needing to figure out every step themselves. 

 The idea for LaunchMate came from the challenge of turning a simple business goal into practical decisions: What product should I create? How much should I charge? How should I launch it? And how should I market it? 

 We wanted to demonstrate how a human and an AI agent could work together, with the human making the important decisions while the AI handles structured tasks through WebMCP tools. 

 What it does 

 LaunchMate turns a business goal into a structured digital-product launch workflow: 

 Goal → Product → Price → Launch → Marketing 

 A user first enters a business goal, such as wanting to sell a digital product to students. 

 LaunchMate then provides: 

 
 Three digital product ideas 
 A selected product 
 A suggested price based on cost and margin 
 A 7-day launch plan 
 An AI-generated marketing kit 
 

 The marketing kit includes: 

 
 Target customer 
 Value proposition 
 Product description 
 Marketing headline ideas 
 Social media ideas 
 Call to action 
 

 The application also shows agent activity so users can see the actions performed during the workflow. 

 How we built it 

 LaunchMate was built as a lightweight web application using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. 

 The application uses WebMCP tools as structured actions that an AI agent can discover and invoke. 

 We created five WebMCP tools: 

 
 set_business_goal 
 suggest_product 
 calculate_price 
 build_launch_plan 
 generate_marketing_kit 
 

 The AI agent coordinates these tools in sequence. The application maintains the workflow state and renders the results back into the user interface. 

 The project was also published as a public GitHub repository and configured for GitHub Pages deployment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was making the AI-generated results reliably flow between the different stages of the workflow. 

 In particular, the marketing stage required careful handling of structured WebMCP responses. The application needed to correctly map the returned data into the user interface while also providing fallback behavior when a tool response was incomplete. 

 Another challenge was coordinating the human and agent actions. The user should be able to select a product while the agent can continue the workflow using the selected product. 

 We also spent time testing the complete workflow from the initial business goal through product selection, pricing, launch planning and marketing generation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that LaunchMate demonstrates a complete human-and-AI workflow rather than simply generating text. 

 The project connects multiple structured WebMCP tools into one workflow and makes the individual agent actions visible to the user. 

 We are also proud of building a working end-to-end prototype that can take a simple business goal and turn it into a concrete launch plan. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building an AI agent workflow requires more than generating good text. 

 Reliable structured data, tool schemas, state management, error handling and UI rendering are all important parts of the experience. 

 We also learned how WebMCP tools can provide a structured interface between an AI agent and a web application, allowing the agent to perform specific actions instead of relying only on unstructured responses. 

 Most importantly, we learned that a good human-AI workflow should give the human control over important decisions while allowing the agent to handle repetitive and structured tasks. 

 What's next for LaunchMate 

 The current version focuses on the core web experience. 

 Next, we would like to expand LaunchMate with: 

 
 A more complete digital-product creation workflow 
 Real payment and checkout integration 
 Product landing-page generation 
 More detailed marketing campaigns 
 Analytics and sales tracking 
 Additional AI-powered business tools 
 A mobile application 
 A fully deployed production version 
 

 Our long-term goal is to turn LaunchMate into a practical AI business-launch assistant that helps people go from an initial idea to a real digital product and launch.

 Inspiration 

 Online shopping is highly visual and interactive for people, but traditional websites are often difficult for AI agents to use reliably. An agent may understand what a user wants, such as a powerful programming laptop under a specific budget, but interacting with a website through visual elements alone can be inefficient and fragile. 

 I wanted to explore how WebMCP could make a website expose its real capabilities directly to AI agents while preserving a great experience for human users. 

 That idea became ShopWise AI — a collaborative shopping experience where humans browse products visually while AI agents can discover structured tools to search products, inspect details, compare options, and manage a real shopping cart. 

 What it does ShopWise AI is a modern AI-commerce web application with a product catalog across categories including laptops, smartphones, headphones, and smartwatches. 

 Human users can: 

 
 Browse a large product catalog visually 
 Search for products 
 Filter by category and price 
 Sort products 
 View detailed product information 
 Compare multiple products 
 Add products to a shopping cart 
 Change quantities and remove items 
 

 AI agents in a compatible WebMCP environment can interact with the same real application capabilities through native WebMCP tools. 

 The six tools implemented are: 

 
 search_products 
 get_product_details 
 compare_products 
 add_to_cart 
 get_cart 
 clear_cart 
 

 How we built it ShopWise AI was built as a React and TypeScript application using Vite. 

 The application uses: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 CSS 
 Lucide React icons 
 Vercel for deployment 
 GitHub for source control 
 Native browser WebMCP APIs 
 

 The product catalog and shopping logic run entirely in the frontend with real local application state. 

 The UI includes a premium dark interface with responsive product cards, search and filtering controls, a shopping cart drawer, product comparison functionality, and an Agent Collaboration panel. 

 Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was connecting WebMCP tools to the real React application state. 

 The WebMCP tools needed to perform actual operations such as searching products, comparing products, adding items to the cart, and clearing the cart. We had to ensure these operations used the same real business logic and state as the visual user interface instead of returning simulated or hardcoded results. 

 Another challenge was avoiding stale React state inside WebMCP tool callbacks. Since React components re-render as application state changes, the WebMCP integration needed access to the latest product, filter, cart, and comparison state. 

 We also needed to prevent duplicate tool registration caused by React StrictMode and safely detect whether the current browser supported WebMCP. 

 Finally, the application had to remain fully functional in ordinary browsers where document.modelContext is unavailable. We implemented graceful feature detection so the website continues working normally while accurately reporting WebMCP availability. 

 During deployment, we also verified that the production build succeeded and that the live Vercel application could load correctly without environment-specific dependencies. 

 Building ShopWise Al helped me understand how websites can evolve beyond interfaces designed only for humans. 

 WebMCP makes it possible for websites to expose structured, meaningful capabilities to Al agents while keeping the existing human interface intact.
I learned the importance of:
Designing tools around real user problems
Connecting agent capabilities to real application logic
Managing application state safely
Providing structured inputs and outputs
Designing human and Al collaboration instead of replacing one with the other
Building graceful fallbacks for unsupported browsers
What's next 

 Future versions of ShopWise Al could support: 

 Personalized shopping preferences 

 Persistent shopping carts 

 User accounts 

 Real e-commerce APIs 

 Product recommendations 

 Multi-agent shopping assistance 

 Price tracking 

 Availability monitoring

about_excerpt:
BuildAI Command is a governed AI-agent dashboard where a human and ChatGPT can both run, monitor, & approve the same agent actions through the same page.

 Story

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 BuildAI is our platform for running AI agents under real governance not just chat wrapped around a model, but agents with memory, tools, policy, and human approval built in. When we saw the WebMCP Challenge, the fit was obvious: our whole product thesis is that AI shouldn't act alone on anything risky. WebMCP let us test that thesis in the browser itself could ChatGPT operate our platform the same way a human does, approvals and all, without a custom integration? 

 What it does 

 BuildAI Command is a governed agent dashboard with three panels: 

 
 Agents — see your AI workers and run them on a task 
 Activity — watch runs progress in real time 
 Approvals — approve or reject sensitive actions before they execute (e.g. sending an email) 
 

 The same actions are exposed as WebMCP tools on the page, so an AI agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser can list agents, start a run, check status, and approve a step using the exact same governed path a human would. Say "run the support agent and approve the email if it looks right," and the agent and the platform work together on one screen. 

 How we built it 

 We kept scope deliberately narrow: one screen, one demo flow, our existing BuildAI backend doing the real work. The frontend is a thin client that calls our existing agents/runs/approvals API, with document.modelContext.registerTool() wiring each panel action run, status check, approve/reject into a WebMCP tool an agent can call directly. No new backend, no new auth model: we exposed what already existed, deliberately, as agent-callable tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge wasn't the API integration. it was deciding what an agent should be allowed to do without asking. We didn't want WebMCP to become a backdoor around our own approval gate, so every sensitive action still routes through the same approvals queue whether a human or an agent triggered it. Getting that consistent one governance path, two callers took more design thought than the tool registration itself. Testing reliably in ChatGPT's in-app browser vs. Chrome's WebMCP flag also meant double-checking tool behavior in both environments before we trusted the demo. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is at its best when it exposes real actions with real consequences, not just read-only lookups. Building governance into the tool layer itself rather than trusting the agent to behave is what made this feel like a genuine agent-native product decision rather than a tech demo.

A WebMCP-powered campus agent that lets students and AI agents discover spaces, check availability, plan tasks, and execute campus actions together—with humans always in control.
